title: My Chemical Romance: The Black Parade 20th Anniversary Edition – One of the few albums from 2006 that may live forever
description: The band’s operatic rock is made for our era of reduced attention spans, pivoting from punk to prog and back with such feral joy that you can’t not pay attention
content:
When My Chemical Romance performed their landmark album The Black Parade in full over three nights at Wembley Stadium, in London, this summer it was striking just how many in the audience were too young to have first-hand memories of its release, in 2006.
But for those ancient enough to recall My Chemical Romance’s original incarnation as pasty-faced kids filtering suburban angst through an onslaught of flamboyant punk-pop, it was astonishing to witness how enthusiastically later generations have embraced them and The Black Parade.
In London that week you were constantly coming across people wearing MCR merch. A band widely dismissed in the early 2000s as a comfort blanket for weirdos had been reborn as superstars, despite having split in 2013 and released almost no new material since 2010.
There are many possible reasons why MCR speak to young people today, and why a 20th-anniversary edition of The Black Parade will be embraced as a red-letter release by devotees old and new. The most obvious one is that their operatic rock is made for our era of reduced attention spans. They pivot from punk to prog and all the way back with such feral joy that you can’t not pay attention.
They’re also a natural fit for a world teetering over the void. Gerard Way formed the group after witnessing the 9/11 attacks while commuting from New Jersey to his internship at Cartoon Network in Manhattan.
The anxiety pervading his lyrics feels entirely of a piece with the apocalyptic 2020s, when the spectre of global war and the rise of artificial intelligence have given us our pick of dystopias. My Chemical Romance were always the perfect soundtrack for the end of civilisation. Is it any surprise that kids today would embrace their songs about death and oblivion?
The story threaded through the album is of a man dying from cancer, seeing his life flash before him in hospital. Introduced with the sound of a failing heart monitor on The End, it hits its stride with Dead!, a bleakly humorous punk-pop avalanche heavily indebted to the ELO song Mr Blue Sky.
As with much of the LP it’s defined by Way’s dark wit, as the narrator rhymes “hospital bed” with “dead” and implies he is looking forward to shuffling off into the great beyond and leaving this forsaken world behind.
That engaging excursion into punk pomposity is followed by the more aggressive This Is How I Disappear. The tune is a short, sharp shock inspired by the pact Harry Houdini made with his wife, Bess. If either died the other would try to make contact from beyond the grave, using a secret code, so that they would know if a medium was a fake.
This is all by way of building up to the title track, a pocket symphony in part inspired by Way’s childhood memory of being brought to see a marching band by his father and where the ever-present sense of doom calls attention to itself like a bug on a birthday cake.
My Chemical Romance brought the album’s concepts bang up to date on their anniversary tour, where the big conceit was that the band had been resurrected to perform for a dictator who watched from his throne as they blazed their way through the record.
The implication was that ours is an age when entertainment and politics are one and the same. This was made chillingly explicit in a nightly sequence in which a masked figure was dragged before a firing squad and the audience was asked to vote, using “Yea” and “Nay” signs, on whether they should be spared. More often than not, Way revealed, the crowd voted for death. It was a close-to-the-bone critique of our willingness to tolerate any outrage so long as it’s entertaining.
That democracy might be subverted to an existential degree by bread-and-circuses populism would have seemed absurd in 2006. Yet the sense of unease we live with today was already part of the MCR sound, as you can hear on an LP that blends splenetically heavy guitars with carnivalesque numbers such as the polka-inspired Mama and the vaudeville-style “secret track” Blood, both of which feel like something from a haunted amusement park.
The anniversary edition leans into the overblown dynamics of the original with a raft of bonus material. In addition to the basic 13 tracks are three B-sides plus live recordings from a 2007 show at Maxwell’s in Hoboken, the 200-capacity club where My Chemical Romance played some of their first gigs.
The pick of the bunch is Someone Out There Loves You, an almost mythic entry in the MCR canon that fans have long referred to as Stay and where the narrator hauntingly tries to talk a friend out of suicide.
As a prog-rock-coded exploration of sickness and mortality, The Black Parade is constantly at risk of tipping into the overblown and portentous. Yet it is rescued again and again by Way’s theatricality. (He sings Mama as if auditioning for a part in a Tim Burton movie.)
And how fitting that this reissue is coming out at Halloween: there was always something of the PG-horror movie about My Chemical Romance. What’s most striking today, however, is the album’s grandiosity and fearlessness. A record about death has been revealed to be one of the few albums from 2006 that may well live forever.

title: Fright sites: eight eerie Irish locations to chill the bones
description: Take a walk on the witchy side this Halloween with these spooky places to visit around Ireland
content:
A n old truism holds that if people want to believe something, they will, and in every age, there have been those with an unshakeable certainty that something lies beyond the material world. Stories of hauntings and the macabre have been passed on from one generation to the next.
If you’re searching for something spooky to do over the Halloween break, these eight sites and walking trails are guaranteed to send a chill down your spine.
Exposed and isolated, Tory Island has been the scene of many shipwrecks. One such ship was Wasp, a royal navy gunboat that sank beneath Tory lighthouse in 1884. On a mission to evict tenant farmers on Inishtrahull Island during the Irish Land Wars, the gunboat sank after hitting rocks on a clear, calm night. Of the 60 crew members, only six survived, with the bodies of those who died washed ashore and buried in Reilig Ghallda, the island cemetery where those lost at sea were interred.
Tradition holds that the disaster was caused by the then king of Tory. He used an ancient cursing stone to bring about the Wasp’s inexplicable destruction because he believed the gunboat was coming to evict tenants living on Tory. Later the island priest was said to have thrown the cursing stone into the ocean to ensure it could never be used again to bring about destruction.
Tory Island makes an interesting place to visit at any time of year, since its compact size makes it perfect to discover on foot. You can explore the west of the island on a pleasant 4km walk, taking in the lighthouse, Reilig Ghallda and the remote studio where renowned artist Derek Hill worked. Information on ferry times to Tory at toryferry.com
Tragic love is among the most enduring themes for stories of the supernatural, with the White Lady of Charles Fort in Kinsale being no exception. The daughter of the fort’s commander married an army officer at the fort. On their wedding night, the groom fell asleep on the walls of the fort. The commander discovered the sleeping figure, mistook him for an intruder and shot him dead, before realising it was his son-in-law. When the new bride discovered this, she threw herself from the battlements in her wedding gown. As a result, the ghost of the young bride wanders the battlements of Charles Fort at dusk, dressed in her flowing white gown.
The full story of the White Lady is recounted on a guided tour of Charles Fort, which is open from 10am to 5pm throughout the winter months. Admission: adults, €5; concessions, €4;
Even in high summer, you are unlikely to see swimmers in Bay Lough, Co Waterford . A local tradition warns that this haunted lake is the last resting place of local witch Petticoat Loose. If you have brought along the kids, you can recall the story of how this alleged sorceress was banished into the lake by a local priest. As revenge, her ghostly arm will rise from the depths to ensnare anyone foolhardy enough to enter her watery abode.
You can, however, have a good time visiting Bay Lough without daring to enter the waters. The good news is that a newly resurfaced 1km path makes this haunting corrie lake accessible to all, including buggies and wheelchairs. It starts from the high point of the Vee Gap in the Knockmealdown Mountains on the Tipperary-Waterford border.
Even without the macabre echoes, this makes a nice family walk. Follow the blue arrows for the 4km Bianconi Loop from the Christ the King trailhead at Aherlow , Co Tipperary . Continue along a path through natural forest to reach an old road once used by the long cars of the 19th-century transport innovator Charles Bianconi. Downhill at a pretty little bridge, you will encounter a forlorn-looking sessile oak that is nearing the end of its long life. Known as the Hanging Tree, this is where people were executed in the 18th century for inconsequential crimes and their bodies left hanging as a warning to passersby not to tangle with authority. Afterwards, complete the Bianconi Loop by following the arrows back to the trailhead, while perhaps breaking for a cuppa in the atmospheric Aherlow House Hotel, just off the trail.
Atop a rocky outcrop, Dunluce Castle is an eerie place that seems the perfect abode for a restless spirit returning after a tragedy. And indeed, tales of hauntings abound. One such concerns Lord McQuillan of Dunluce Castle, Co Antrim , who betrothed his daughter Maeve to a family ally despite her passion for Reginald O’Cahan from a rival clan. To cool her ardour, Maeve was locked in the northeast tower at Dunluce to await her assigned fate in marriage.
Undeterred, Reginald entered the castle on a stormy night and led Maeve away. The lovers followed a steep path downhill and escaped through the Mermaid’s Cave lying beneath the castle. Launching a boat into the turbulent Atlantic, their tiny craft was thrown against the rocks, with both perishing in the freezing waters. Since then, visitors have reported hearing anguished cries from the northeast tower during storms.
You can follow in the footsteps of the tragic lovers starting from a gate outside the main castle area at Dunluce. Descend, with care, the 115 steps to the Mermaid’s Cave, which, ghost or not, makes for a dramatic spectacle. Please note, the route may be closed in stormy weather.
A Catholic priest in Co Tipperary during the 18th century, Fr Nicholas Sheehy became a powerful symbol of resistance to Penal Laws. Having angered the local gentry with his opposition to tithes paid to the Anglican Church and his sympathy for the Whiteboys, who defended tenant farmers, he was charged with the murder of an informer named John Bridge. Despite the prosecution being unable to prove Bridge was even dead, Sheehy was convicted and hanged in Clonmel. The jury, drawn from the local Protestant elite, had been carefully selected with a view to obtaining a conviction. Local folklore holds none of this jury died naturally: all were consumed by maladies and accidents such as drowning, choking and leprosy, while another died by his own hand. The tomb of Fr Nicholas Sheehy lies in Shanrahan Cemetery, on the Clogheen Loop Walk. This scenic but easy 8km woodland walk starts and finishes in Clogheen village.
In medieval Europe there was widespread paranoia around the supposed evil caused by witches. Viewed as enemies of society and Christianity, they were seen as creating misfortunes such as famine or disease outbreaks and were routinely burned as a public spectacle. In 1324 Dame Alice Kyteler, a wealthy Kilkenny woman, and her servant Petronilla became the first Irish people condemned for witchcraft. Kyteler immediately fled the country, but Petronilla confessed under torture to the crime of heresy. She was flogged and burnt at a stake on High Street, Kilkenny, in 1324. Historians now believe that Kyteler was the victim of her stepchildren, who coveted the wealth she had received from her four dead husbands. Her Kilkenny home has now been converted into Kyteler’s Inn, a historic pub and landmark in the city centre. On the Kilkenny Ghost Tour you will hear the full story of Kyteler and another spectre who haunts Kilkenny Castle and is believed to be Margaret Butler, grandmother of Anne Boleyn. Information and bookings at kilkennyghosttours.com .
A tour of Crumlin Road Gaol, Belfast , is an eerie experience, with its spooky underground tunnel linking the gaol and the old Crumlin Road Courthouse along with the condemned cell and execution room. Here, the hangman’s rope is guaranteed to send a shiver down your spine. At this time of year, the experience is intensified as the prison goes all out for Halloween, offering “an intense journey where terrifying encounters, unexpected scares and sinister surprises await around every corner”. Seventeen men were executed here, and some of their ghosts are reputed to move restlessly through the building, with the tour searching for evidence of their presence.
Jail of Horror runs each evening until October 31st, starting at 7pm, but may not be suitable for those of a nervous disposition. Tickets cost £20 and must be booked in advance at crumlinroadgaol.com .
John G O’Dwyer’s latest book, Stories Beneath our Feet, will be published in November

title: ‘The focus is finding people from Ireland’: The EU’s big ask for new English translators
description: It will be an uphill battle, with Ireland having the lowest proportion of secondary school students who study two or more foreign languages
content:
T he list of unintended consequences caused by Brexit runs quite long – and reads somewhat smug when compiled on this side of the Irish Sea – but it can be briefly summarised as political upheaval, economic uncertainty and social division.
Aside from the macro-woes, Britain’s formal departure from the European Union in 2020 has also proved a headache for the diplomats and administrators tasked with running EU institutions for more than 450 million citizens.
“We’re constantly getting requests,” says Linda Forde, the head of the European Parliament’s English-language translation unit, as she takes a short break from her duties during a work trip to Dublin.
Draft after draft of legal documents and policy papers arrive in her inbox daily to be distributed among her team of translators and proofreaders – often with same request: “Can you do this for tomorrow? The day after tomorrow?” she says, quoting colleagues based mostly in Brussels, a three-hour train ride away from her office in Luxembourg.
English, while officially of equal status alongside the EU’s 23 other languages, carries more weight than most because of its status as a “pivot language”.
The term is not easily defined, so Forde provides an example: “Legislation comes in Romanian, we translate it into English and then, for example, the Irish unit will translate it from English because they will not be able to translate it from Romanian.”
The parliament’s translation service employs more than 1,100 people. A standard translation unit is made up of about 30 staff members, but the English unit is among the smallest. This is partly because many texts are originally drafted in English and do not require translation, but the unit’s small size is also a product of its time.
Recruiting translators from Britain has been “problematic” since Brexit, Forde says, due to the EU’s policy of employing strictly its own citizens. The only Britons who can bypass this rule are those with dual citizenship from an EU member state.
“With Ireland being the biggest English-speaking country [in the EU], definitely the focus is finding people from Ireland, because they’re native speakers and that’s what we’re looking for,” says Forde, who is from Co Antrim.
[ Ireland faces ‘significant’ loss of influence in EU institutions due to retirements Opens in new window ]
The career translator was in Dublin in early October to speak at an outreach event at the European Parliament’s Liaison Office close to Grafton Street, organised as part of the State’s six-month presidency of the Council of the EU.
Between panel discussions and Q&A sessions, the European Parliament’s director general for translation, Valter Mavric, spoke to The Irish Times about the need for Irish-citizen, English-language translators in the institution.
Irish people “are the only ones that actually can apply. Not formally, not officially, but practically”, the Slovenian man, who is also fluent in Italian, says.
“Theoretically, a Slovenian who has excellent English and has maybe studied in an English-speaking country, might be able to apply. But what’s more important with English, for example, is that you translate the laws or communications for citizens of Ireland primarily.
“So you have to know the Irish version of English,” Mavric says. “That’s why it’s very important to have English native speakers from Ireland.”
[ ‘If you want to get a job immediately in Brussels, speak Irish and do a law degree’ Opens in new window ]
They may well be important to have, but are they difficult to get?
“I think there might be many reasons, before I reply to you, whether it’s difficult or not,” he says in the Robert Schuman breakout room, named after the French elder statesman credited for his role in rebuilding postwar Europe.
Irish citizens “don’t want to leave their country”, he notes, “maybe because it’s so beautiful to live here”. High salaries on offer at home don’t help either, he says.
“Still, we do not have many problems with attracting Irish citizens – we have not had, let’s say it like that, so far,” Mavric adds.
However, “the English team is not complete ... because there are still some colleagues from the UK that work there [since] before Brexit and so they have stayed. But of course, someday these colleagues will retire or will leave and we have to think of succession planning already.”
This is what brought him to Dublin: “We are here this week to promote both English and Irish as the two official languages – for me, it is very important to get that message across.”
Both languages face similar challenges in attracting qualified candidates from Ireland to the highly competitive application process called “translator competitions”, which require applicants to prove fluency in three European languages.
[ Why foreign governments are paying lobbyists to make their case in Brussels Opens in new window ]
“Deficiency in knowledge of foreign languages” is the main concern, Mavric says.
Data from the European Commission shows the proportion of Irish secondary school students learning two or more foreign languages was the lowest in the EU, at just 5.2 per cent. In 10 countries, such as Finland and Italy, the proportion was more than 90 per cent.
It appears to be an uphill battle for Ireland to reach the heights of trilingualism, but Mavric is optimistic.
“For me, language is always linked to an identity, to a culture, and that’s why it’s so important to include language as the conditions for the European Union, for the European project. Languages, as part of our lives in Europe, are here to stay.”

title: Blockers by Michael Lewis: A page-turner about civil servants, and Trump’s war on them
description: Although brilliant at showing the consequences of Trump administration actions, the book is limited in explaining the reasons behind them
content:
Michael Lewis didn’t set out to become a famous journalist with an easily imitable style. In fact, he began his career on Wall Street. But he discovered he excelled at long-form writing. Talking to people and telling their stories came naturally to him. He owed his success – several of his books have been best-sellers and three have been turned into movies – to his ability to use those stories to dramatise some new development in finance, sport or politics.
Lewis had written about the US federal government before, so when he saw how Donald Trump and Elon Musk were wrecking the civil service, he knew he had the subject for his next book.
Lewis has a style that’s easy to parody, and it can grate at times. But it is also what allows him to perform the miraculous feat of turning a book about civil servants into a page-turner. Blockers chronicles the impact of Trump’s reckless war on the US federal government. Convinced that his first presidency was undermined by a “deep state” and with no consideration for legality, Trump returned to office determined to bend the civil service to his will. Aided in his early months by Musk and his Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), Trump has laid off or forced into retirement about a tenth of the federal workforce (about 300,000 people). Entire agencies have been eliminated or shrunk beyond recognition.
Blockers explores this story from the standpoint of individual civil servants who were affected: the chief security officer at the US Institute for Peace; a fixer in the Office of Personnel Management; a senior administrator in the Internal Revenue Service (IRS); a fire researcher at the National Institute for Standards and Technology; and a medical researcher at the National Institutes of Health.
Lewis makes you understand their selfless devotion to public service and see the important social contributions they made – most of them in parts of the government that few even know existed. The US federal government, Lewis claims, is “arguably the most complex machine ever designed by man”, and he has a clear admiration for it and for its workers.
Because you come to care about these individuals and to understand their significance, the cavalier way they were dismissed is infuriating. They typical DOGE agent was a “twenty-five-year-old tech guy dying to breathe the same air as Elon Musk and only just now grokking the fact that the United States government had three branches”.
Wilfully ignorant DOGE agents didn’t try to understand what government departments and their employees did; they just wrecked them. In other cases, people were forced out for refusing to carry out illegal orders. IRS chief privacy officer Kathleen Waters, for example, resigned rather than share the tax returns of undocumented immigrants. That request was not only illegal, it was a betrayal of trust because the IRS had promised never to share that data. Acquiring these addresses allowed the Trump administration to raid and deport thousands of undocumented immigrants.
Blockers is brilliant at showing you the consequences of Trump administration actions but limited in explaining the reasons behind them. From the perspective of many of those affected, the assault seems irrational if not insane. The one explanation that Lewis gives of DOGE’s motivations – that Musk simply wanted to secure his own business interests – makes little sense because Musk could easily have done this without DOGE.
Lewis shows how the powerful right-wing functionary Russell Vought – architect of the infamous Project 2025 – was probably responsible for firing the medical researcher who had found the cure to his daughter’s cystic fibrosis. But Lewis has little to say about where Vought’s ideas came from. To really understand why this happened, you need to grasp that Republicans have been attacking the federal civil service for half a century. Ronald Reagan took office in 1981 declaring “government is not the solution to our problems; government is the problem”.
While much of Blockers is riveting and illuminating, Lewis at times gets sidetracked. Over the course of an hour, I read an entire chapter portion that was only about the mechanics of fire suppression and never touched on Trump’s assault on the civil service. Towards the end of the book, the writing even gets a bit loopy. One chapter is framed as a murder mystery: a “whacking” with one person rendered as speaking in Mafia dialect. The book concludes with a bizarre analogy likening the US federal government to a broken water fountain.
Yet reading Blockers makes abundantly clear the gravity of Trump’s damage to the US civil service. It will be extremely difficult to repair and unlikely that those responsible are ever held accountable. Most of those civil servants forced out won’t ever be coming back and with them the US has lost their knowledge, experience and passion. Lewis might be the only writer out there who could truly capture this tragedy.
Daniel Geary is Mark Pigott professor in US history at Trinity College Dublin

title: Lula wins fourth term as Brazil’s president over Flávio Bolsonaro
description: Claiming historic fourth term in power, 80-year-old leftist received 51.75% of the vote
content:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , the Brazilian president, has staged a dramatic election fightback, defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, to claim a historic fourth term in power.
With nearly 99 per cent of votes counted the 80-year-old leftist received 51.75 per cent of the vote to his 45-year-old rival’s 48.25 per cent.
Lula narrowly lost the first round of the election to Bolsonaro in early October, casting his political future into doubt and plunging progressive Brazilians into three weeks of despair. Never, since the return of democracy in the 1980s, has the first round runner-up won the second vote.
But Lula did precisely that on Sunday, prompting joyous scenes on the streets of São Paulo, where he had been following the count, and at the hotel where he was watching the count.
As the result was confirmed, Reginaldo Lopes, a key Lula ally, said: “I feel incredible ... This is Brazil telling the world that the extreme right is fascist, that the extreme right is against black people, is against the poor, against the state, against gay people ... We are going to reorganise the democratic forces [in this country.”
The incumbent, who had lost by 2.2 million votes three weeks ago, has now won by 4.3 million.
The 81-year-old leftist appears to have made up much of the difference through what his allies had identified as his main opportunity: persuading his voters to turn out. After a record abstention rate of 21.08 per cent in the first round, which disproportionately affected Lula voters because they tend to live farther from polling stations, the rate fell to 19.21 per cent.
For Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, the victory represents a sensational final chapter in a storied political career that began when he emerged as a union leader in São Paulo’s industrial suburbs in the late 1970s.
After entering politics, the former factory worker who was born in rural poverty made three unsuccessful presidential bids, in 1989, 1994 and 1998, before finally becoming Brazil’s first elected working-class president in 2002.
Lula stepped down after the maximum two consecutive terms allowed by the constitution but returned to power after winning the 2022 election against Bolsonaro’s father, then the incumbent president Jair Bolsonaro, who was subsequently jailed for plotting a coup.
Lula’s win is bad news for Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year sentence for that botched power grab and was hoping to be freed and given a role in government had his son prevailed.
It is also a blow for Donald Trump, the Bolsonaro clan’s most important international ally. The US president had been hoping Bolsonaro would become the latest in a series of pro-Trump leaders to take power in Latin America, including Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia, Daniel Noboa in Ecuador, José Antonio Kast in Chile and Javier Milei in Argentina.
Confirmation of Lula’s victory was greeted with anger and bewilderment in Brasília, where Bolsonaro is living under house arrest and where his son watched the count.
Lula’s victory came after his supporters staged two massive shows of support on Saturday, with more than a million people flocking to Rio’s Copacabana beach and an even larger number marching on Paulista Avenue at the heart of São Paulo.
Speaking at the Rio rally, truck driver Josias Silva said he said he was confident of a Lula comeback, after weeks of student-led anti-Bolsonaro protests.
“The people have woken up ... There’s never been a demonstration like this one. This is the biggest protest in the history of Brazil. And we are going to win tomorrow with more than 60 per cent of the votes,” Silva claimed.
Hundreds of Lula supporters returned to Paulista Avenue on Sunday evening to watch the vote count, waving red flags stamped with the face of the president.
Related: ‘We can’t let the far right take power again’: Lula voters in final push before Brazil runoff
“I feel so very happy being here, and being here fighting for Lula,” said Camilo Buarque, 35, as he watched Lula take an early lead. “My confidence comes from the energy and the happiness and the love of these people [around me]. This is democracy.”
“My heart is beating a thousand beats a second but I’m confident,” said Ester Almeida, 28, another Lula supporter who was at the rally.
Many people on the streets of São Paulo were angry at an apparent attempt by pro-Bolsonaro politicians to derail the election by sabotaging public transport in Lula-leaning voting areas across the country.
“I think it’s another coup attempt that the extreme right is trying in Brazil. But we need to really fight so we can win,” said Lucas Lopes, a 32-year-old from São Paulo who works with public relations.
But that alleged attempt to scupper a Lula victory failed.
“I’ll be sincere: in the first round the left failed. But in the second round they woke up,” said Caio Marques, a 40-year-old photographer from Franca, a city in the interior of São Paulo state. “And there is no coup that will take this away from us.” – The Guardian

title: AI apocalypse? ‘The end of the world is nigh’ is one of humanity’s oldest catch cries
description: In a Word: Doomsday. Dire predictions have accompanied every so-called dangerous advance
content:
H alloween beckons so let’s have a horror story. “The end of the world is nigh” - and to think you worry about the pension contributions!
By now everyone is familiar with the prevalent predictions that the wondrous AI technology is about to “do a Frankenstein” on us, probably going further than Mary Shelly’s [1818] creation.
Last month Evan Hubinger, a researcher with AI company Anthropic, said he believed there was a greater than 10 per cent chance that future AI systems could “kill all humans” within the next decade.
He did add that current risks remained low. His concern was that AI could soon develop a superintelligence that might lead, quickly, to the extinction of humanity.
Now, I have no desire to lessen your enjoyment of all this horror, particularly in this season of Halloween, but you should be reminded that “the end of the world is nigh” is one of the oldest catch cries of humanity.
Concepts such as Doomsday or the Apocalypse are not new and have featured greatly in the traditions of those three Abrahamic religions – Judaism, Christianity and Islam, for thousands of years. Today you might say the only difference is that this too has become secularised.
[ For 10 years, I’ve listened to people say AI will kill us all. Here’s what I think Opens in new window ]
In the world of science dire predictions have accompanied every so-called dangerous advance. It followed the discovery of electricity – that innocuous plug in your wall has the power [literally] to kill you.
Such, it is said, was Alfred Nobel’s crisis of conscience over his invention of dynamite [in 1867] – with its power to kill large numbers - he set up the annual Nobel Prizes to celebrate humanity’s positive achievements.
Similarly with Robert Oppenheimer, credited with leading research which created the first atomic bomb. Witnessing the first atomic explosion at New Mexico in 1945, he remembered a line from the Hindu Bhagavad Gita; “Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.”
He was revolted by the bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and went to Washington on a fruitless mission to have nuclear weapons banned.
Dynamite, electricity, nuclear energy have tremendously destructive power where humanity is concerned, yet we are still here.
Humanity is proven to have a deeply ingrained resistance to collective suicide.

title: Death of soldier Seán Rooney among issues on agenda as Helen McEntee heads to Lebanon
description: Minister to reiterate Ireland’s ‘commitment to ensuring accountability and justice’ over killing of peacekeeper in country almost four years ago
content:
Minister for Foreign Affairs and Defence Helen McEntee is travelling to Lebanon this week for discussions, including on matters related to the death of Irish soldier Pte Seán Rooney almost four years ago.
The 24-year-old, from Co Donegal, was killed in an attack on a convoy of Irish peacekeepers serving on a United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (Unifil) deployment on December 14th, 2022. His inquest is due to begin next month.
McEntee will travel to the area for meetings with Irish Defence Forces personnel serving with Unifil, Lebanese government representatives, United Nations officials, international partners and humanitarian organisations.
“The Minister will also discuss matters relating to the death of Private Seán Rooney, reiterating Ireland’s commitment to ensuring accountability and justice,” said the Department of Defence in a Sunday statement.
“She will reaffirm the importance Ireland attaches to the ongoing judicial process and continued co-operation between the Irish and Lebanese authorities.”
The Fine Gael TD will meet Lebanon’s president, Joseph Aoun, minister for foreign affairs Youssef Rajji, minister for justice Adel Nassar and members of the 128th Infantry Battalion, who are serving at Camp Shamrock in the south of the country.
Speaking in advance of her visit, McEntee said the State’s peacekeepers had made “an extraordinary contribution to peace and stability in Lebanon over almost five decades”.
Discussions will also focus on the State’s relationship with Lebanon, regional developments, support for peace and stability, and international engagement in assisting the country.
“While Ireland’s military contribution to Unifil is entering its final phase, our commitment to Lebanon and its people will remain strong,” added McEntee. “Ireland will continue to work closely with our partners in the United Nations, the European Union and the wider international community to support peace, stability, and security in Lebanon.”
Ireland has maintained a continuous peacekeeping presence in Lebanon since 1978 and remains one of Unifil’s longest-serving troop-contributing countries.

title: Half of consumers use Revolut app, with 6% indicating option as main banking account
description: One in five of all shoppers continue to pay for goods with cash, according to banking survey for 2026
content:
Almost half of consumers in the Republic now hold an account with online bank Revolut , the latest annual survey of banking practice and sentiment has found.
Revolut continues to grow strongly in the market here. Moreover, there is evidence that a growing number of consumers now see it as something more than a money transfer app.
The Consumer Sentiment Banking Survey for 2026 found that 48 per cent of consumers hold an account with Revolut, up from 43 per cent in 2025. While most still use it to transfer money, 6 per cent identified it as their main account, up from 3 per cent the previous year.
[ Revolut’s outage was a warning to us all Opens in new window ]
Tánaiste Simon Harris said the survey exposed a “striking gap” between savings and investment.
It found that 77 per cent of Irish consumers hold savings accounts, but only 3 per cent have an investment account.
“We are a nation of savers, but far too few people see investing as an option for them.”
Harris has plans to introduce a new investment account next year that will encourage consumers to switch from saving to investing. The scheme will have no minimum contribution and a tax-free threshold of €50,000.
One in five of all shoppers still pay for goods in cash, a figure that has stayed constant, the survey said.
However, the use of contactless smartphone as a payment method has risen sharply. Its use has increased from 27 per cent in 2025 to 35 per cent in 2025. The use of cards for contactless payments is falling.
There has been consistency in the habits of consumers with other financial products. Nearly all consumers hold a current account, while 77 per cent have a savings account and 25 per cent hold a mortgage account.
There has been a slight drop in the number of people who have credit cards, down from 37 per cent in 2025 to 35 per cent in 2026.
Credit unions also remain popular, with a third of all consumers holding an account. However, only 3 per cent of people said that their main banking account is with a credit union.
In new findings, one in five reported that they have used artificial intelligence (AI) to obtain information or advice on financial services. There are striking generational differences in attitudes, with younger consumers the primary users of AI.

title: Serbia’s strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic concedes defeat to student-led movement
description: Seismic political shift as youth movement topples right-wing party
content:
The long-serving strongman leader of Serbia , Aleksandar Vucic, conceded defeat on Sunday in an election that pitted him and his right-wing party against a diverse student-led opposition movement that spent two years protesting his government.
It was a seismic political shift in the Balkan country where Vucic, who had been endorsed by Russian president Vladimir Putin and who denounced the student movement as a foreign-led attempt to unseat him, led with virtually absolute power for 14 years.
High turnout and gathering tensions marked the highly contested parliamentary election that was a showdown between Vucic and his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party and university students who, accusing the government of corruption and dismantling democracy, had built a popular following across the country.
Serbia’s 6.4 million voters were electing legislators to the 250-member Parliament.
In conceding the election, Vucic said his party projects that his opponents, the youth-backed Student List, will take between 135 and 140 seats while his SNS party will have around 105.
“The Student List has won,” Vicic told supporters at his party’s election night event, though he blamed Serbia’s independent media as well as alleged interference by unnamed European countries and an “American deep state” for the loss.
Vucic said his SNS party won around 1.7 million votes compared to the Student List, which he said took around 2.2 million.
Supporters of the Student List immediately flooded on to the streets of Belgrade and other cities, honking horns, shouting and chanting “Aleksandar is gone”, referring to Vucic.
The outcome, which Vucic announced only around an hour-and-a-half after polls closed, came after tensions had built as voting progressed during the day.
Police in anti-riot gear cordoned off an area in central Belgrade around the election commission headquarters.
[ Marine Le Pen begins ‘great battle for France’ with presidential campaign launch Opens in new window ]
Special police vehicles could be seen near a Belgrade park where Vucic’s loyalists have been camping for more than a year, and large groups of black-clad men had congregated at various points throughout the city.
Vucic was seeking to become Serbia’s prime minister after serving two near-full terms as president.
He resigned the presidency last month to lead the campaign.
Support for the populist had eroded since 16 people were killed in 2024 when a concrete canopy collapsed at a train station in Novi Sad.
That set off a wave of youth protests that blamed the collapse on high-level corruption, cronyism and rampant graft during renovation work at the station.
Despite the protests, Vucic retained considerable support among many of Serbia’s voters.
Admirers viewed him as a capable leader who can steer the nation through global uncertainties – an image that was carefully crafted by the mainstream media.
While the increasingly authoritarian Vucic has routinely outplayed Serbia’s fractured opposition in the past, the leaderless youth movement proved to be a tough opponent that rattled his firm grip on power in Serbia like no one else in the 14 years since his party took office.
The newly formed Student List movement was shaped by university students but none actually appeared on the election list. Instead, its candidates are little-known experts, athletes, farmers and artists.
This approach was meant to counter Vucic’s one-man rule and restore a sense of community and solidarity.
The students’ message during the campaign focused on a non-partisan effort to rebuild Serbia’s economy and restore its democracy.
The students have used youthful energy to attract voters who are disillusioned with local politicians.
[ Israeli army launches big West Bank operation in advance of election Opens in new window ]
Vilified by pro-government media, they cycled and walked through the country to reach voters in rural areas – Vucic’s traditional strongholds.
The student victory echoed the recent electoral defeat of a Vucic ally in Hungary, where youth participation helped oust the autocratic Viktor Orbán after 16 years and bring in a new pro-European government.
It was likely to resonate beyond Serbia as countries across Europe have faced angry youth and student protests.
Monitors predicted that total turnout in the election could reach around 70 per cent, unseen in Serbia since 2000.
During the day, long queues formed at polling stations in Serbia and in cities around the country.
Some in the Serbian diaspora were made to vote in the middle of the night after authorities tied voting hours to local Serbian time.
[ Andy Burnham’s call for debate on free movement with EU draws mixed Labour response Opens in new window ]
Recent Serbian elections had been marred by irregularities and the EU was closely watching the conduct of Sunday’s vote in a candidate nation for the bloc’s membership.
Independent election monitors reported dozens of cases of irregularities on Sunday, such as photographing of ballots that suggested pressure on voters and attempted vote buying.
Both international and local election monitors had expressed concern about the safety and fairness of an election campaign marked by detentions, near-total government control over the media and reports of surveillance and cyberattacks against activists.
Local elections earlier this year in 10 municipalities in Serbia saw violent attacks on journalists and activists.
The previous parliamentary vote in 2023 was followed by opposition protests alleging fraud.

title: Séamus Power set for Monday sudden-death playoff with Austin Smotherman in Bermuda
description: Waterford golfer is looking to win the tournament for the seconds time in four years
content:
Ireland’s Séamus Power will face American Austin Smotherman in a Monday playoff for the Butterfield Bermuda Championship after play was scrapped on Sunday due to inclement weather and the ​PGA Tour shortened regulation play to 54 holes.
Power, who won the second of his two PGA Tour titles in Bermuda in 2022, will take on Smotherman in a sudden-death playoff that is scheduled to start at 9am local time on Monday morning (noon in Ireland). Smotherman secured his first PGA Tour win at the Bank of Utah Championships at the start of October.
Golfers waited for word from the tour after it was decided ​early on Sunday that the entire fourth round would be ⁠postponed due to heavy rain and high winds that topped 40mph on Sunday morning. The ‌next ​update came at 5.17pm local time at Port Royal Golf ⁠Course in Southampton.
“Due ​to the unfavorable weather ​forecast for Monday at the Butterfield Bermuda Championship ‌and the uncertainty surrounding the ​completion of the entire final round on Monday, ⁠the tournament results ⁠will ​be considered final through 54 holes in accordance with PGA Tour regulations,” the tour said in a statement.
Power and Smotherman ​were tied at ​16-under-par 197 after three rounds.

title: Marine Le Pen begins ‘great battle for France’ with presidential campaign launch
description: Right-wing populist has seen poll boost following unrest
content:
Marine Le Pen vowed to restore order to France and ensure the supremacy of French interests and law over international courts as she launched her campaign for the presidency as the favourite.
Polls show support for the right-wing populist has solidified since the recent unrest in France. She is the first choice of about a third of the electorate, according to Ipsos, making her the clear front-runner in advance of an election in April.
Le Pen told a crowd that recent scenes of arson and looting in France had vindicated the positions of her National Rally party, which has blamed the violence on immigration and the left wing.
“Everyone in France now agrees with us,” she said.
There was an intense security presence around the party conference in the city of Orléans, where over 10,000 people held a protest against the far right as the conference began.
The city was chosen for its connection to Joan of Arc, who helped lift an English siege there in 1429. Le Pen has adopted her as a campaign symbol, selling mugs and posters depicting France’s warrioress patron saint.
“Here in Orléans our national heroine, symbol of a refusal to give up, began her great battle for France,” Le Pen told supporters.
She promised to restore the rule of law, push back against “punitive” green measures and introduce the automatic and “definitive” deportation of any foreigners convicted of a crime.
[ Israeli army launches big West Bank operation in advance of election Opens in new window ]
In response to the unrest on the sidelines of protests, her party has proposed reducing the age of criminal responsibility to 16, charging rioters the cost of repair, and introducing “collective responsibility” for violence so that any participant in a protest that turns violent can face charges.
Le Pen raised a huge cheer from the crowd when she promised French citizens would enjoy “national priority”, meaning they would have priority over foreigners for services such as public housing.
[ France dodges rerun of looting and riots after security boost Opens in new window ]
International courts should not be able to overrule decisions such as deportation orders, Le Pen said.
“The president of the republic is first and foremost the guardian of French interests,” she said, not to “distribute French money to the entire world” or to favour “supranational entities”.
“No text, no authority, and especially no foreign one, even European, will supersede the constitution,” she said.
The Ipsos polls showed Le Pen had the support of 33.5 per cent of respondents, with her nearest rival the hard-left Jean-Luc Mélenchon on 17 per cent, indicating the two may face each other in a second-round run-off vote in May.
“The old major parties are burning with their last embers,” Le Pen said as she concluded her speech.
“We are not living through the end of the world, but the end of a world: their world. It is up to us to reinvent the one to come.”

title: Cork SFC final: Nemo Rangers weather late Finbarr’s storm to end three years of heartbreak
description: ‘I was struggling to speak lifting that cup’, said captain Stephen Cronin after emotional title victory
content:
In the end, relief. No matter how much Nemo Rangers have won over the last 50 years, the gap between this title and their last will have felt like a hellish eternity. They had lost each of the last three county finals and no club in Cork had lost four in a row since the 1930s. Nemo didn’t make their reputation on that kind of history.
“It’s been a long four years,” said their captain Stephen Cronin in the opening line of his victory speech, and he repeated the same words in the closing line, as if they were stuck in his throat and he needed to spit them out.
He said afterwards that they had addressed the defeats of the last three years at the beginning of the season and then moved beyond them. But there was no way of knowing if that process had worked until the fracture was tested at breaking point.
Deep in the second half, that moment came. Nemo had led by six points at the break, and by eight points 12 minutes into the second half, but the Barrs reduced the deficit to a point with four minutes of stoppage time left. If there were hidden doubts waiting in ambush, now was the time. Instead, Nemo kicked the last three scores.
“There is huge relief,” said Cronin. “There was huge emotion. You could see it on the pitch. Jesus, I was struggling to speak lifting that cup. There is emotion to have lost the last three [finals], without even realising it, just that pent-up emotion. It’s great to be able to break that and enjoy it.”
While tens of thousands of pleasure seekers circulated the city trying to avoid anything that resembled jazz, 7,054 die-hards descended on Páirc Uí Chaoimh and were treated to a terrific final. Under the new rules, convulsive scoreboards have been the greatest gift to the game, and even though Nemo led by seven points in the first half and eight points later on, the game was never dead.
That was partly due to the wind that blew fiercely towards the City End in the first half but eased perceptibly as dusk fell. Nemo had first use of the wind and made it tell.
Against the elements, St Finbarr’s suffered on their own kick-out. They went long with 11 kicks in the first half and lost eight of them, three of which went over the sideline. From that platform, Nemo squeezed the Barrs.
After 15 minutes, Nemo were 0-7 to 0-0 ahead and were not flattered by their lead. St Finbarr’s corner back Sam Ryan deflected a ball off the line when a cross from Ross Corkery was only waiting for a Nemo touch, and they had valid claims for a penalty turned down after corner forward Bryan Hayes was floored inside the large parallelogram.
The Barrs, though, steadied themselves in the second quarter. William Buckley, one of four Barrs players who had lost the hurling final a week ago, stormed into the game. They had cut the deficit to three points when Nemo struck for a goal in first-half stoppage time.
Mark Cronin’s two-point attempt dropped short, but his brother Stephen recovered the ball near the small parallelogram and played a cute pass to Luke Horgan, who palmed the ball to the net.
Nemo must have been braced for a Barrs surge after the break but instead Nemo kicked on. When Briain Murphy kicked their second two-pointer, 12 minutes into the second half, they held a commanding lead, 1-13 to 0-8.
The Barrs comeback was ignited by Brian Hayes. The Cork hurler was switched from centre field to the edge of the square and he scored his team’s first goal after Mark Hill was stripped of the ball in a goalmouth scramble. Two minutes later, substitute Cillian Myers-Murray kicked a two-pointer and after that, nothing was certain.
Hayes was instrumental in the build-up to the Barrs’ second goal 11 minutes later, coolly finished by Jonathan Wigginton Barrett. When Myers-Murray scored a point in the next Barrs attack, there was just a point between the teams, 1-15 to 2-11, with three minutes of normal time remaining.
Everything that happened next was a test of Nemo’s nerve. Neither team had dominated centre field in the second half, but in the closing minutes Nemo won critical kick-out duels, on both sides of the ball. That was the final twist.
“You have to look back at what happened last year and the year before,” said Robbie O’Dwyer, the Nemo manager. “You just think, ‘are we going to get over the line at all?’. If we didn’t get over the line today, maybe there’d be more doubts creeping in. But that’s finished with now.”

title: The Irish Times view on food security: time is short to avert a crisis
description: Disruptions to the supply of grain, fertiliser and energy threaten to take a heavy toll
content:
Much of the wealthy world is facing a testing winter with adverse conditions lingering throughout 2027 as food inflation, high energy costs and rising general inflation hit home. This is a mild version of what threatens developing countries, notably many in Africa; a food security crisis with the inevitability that many people will starve without a coordinated international intervention.
This has been a looming risk for months due to conflict in Ukraine and the Middle East, which is disrupting the production and distribution of grain, fertiliser and energy. This is predicted to curb production of wheat, maize and rice next year. Climate-related extreme weather events are heightening food insecurity. These circumstances are exacerbated by withdrawal of overseas aid by some rich countries and an El Niño, a natural warming period predicted to be the worst in 1,000 years. Meanwhile, there is a dearth of political leadership as geopolitics has undermined the role of the United Nations.
Anticipating the El Niño, the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation and World Food Programme launched an appeal for $202 million targeting 22 high-risk countries. It has secured a mere $40 million. Already, nearly 300 million people suffer from severe food insecurity.
Food security specialists Cary Fowler and Tom Arnold, writing in The Irish Times, have warned that “despite these steadily increasing risks there has been an alarming lack of political action and resultant preparedness”. They still believe hunger can be substantially eliminated by 2050, by applying the lessons of the Green Revolution and the deployment of new technologies including genomics in generating resilient plant species. Sustainable progress requires, however, an end to damaging conflicts, moves to ensure supports reach the most vulnerable and the scaling-up of agriculture research.
That will challenge political leaders in developing states, but the international community must play a partner role, backed by the provision of adequate climate finance. This sits comfortably with Ireland, which has credibility in providing aid which has a lasting social and economic impact in least developed countries.
It is in a position to help move food and nutrition security up international agendas. Taoiseach Micheál Martin should underline to the incoming UN secretary general that this must be an immediate global priority. Under its EU presidency remit, Ireland can help conclude negotiations for Europe’s next multi-annual budget, advocating to protect and increase EU official development assistance and humanitarian aid allocations for fragile and conflict-affected states. This collective action could help avoid the spectre of millions of people facing acute hunger or famine-level conditions in the months to come and beyond.

title: Ross Banville leads Shelmaliers to first Wexford hurling title since 2020
description: Round-up: Naas beat Maynooth to wrap up their eighth Kildare SHC title in a row
content:
Kilkenny great Richie Power tasted managerial success as he led Shelmaliers to the Wexford SHC title with a two-point victory over Rathnure St Anne’s on Sunday.
Ross Banville scored 0-12 (nine frees) as the Castlebridge club upset the favourites by 1-18 to 2-13 to claim their third RJ Bowe Cup, and first since 2020.
Rathnure have now lost back-to-back finals since returning from the intermediate ranks in 2024.
The record winners struck the first major blow when Shane Lawler swooped upon a defensive error for a tap-in goal.
Backed by the wind, Banville manoeuvred Shels into a 0-11 to 1-4 lead by half-time.
They gained momentum by hitting the net within 14 seconds of the second-half throw-in. Captain Conor Hearne surged forward to skim a low shot under the goalkeeper.
Shels retained that seven-point advantage until the 53rd minute when Rory Higgins’s solo run turned defence into attack, playing in Jack Redmond to hammer home, which brought his tally to 1-4.
Shels survived another goalmouth scramble as their lead was trimmed to two points. Banville’s 12th point gave them some insurance as it came down to the last play. Man-of-the-match Simon Donohoe came up with the all-important moment to deflect Eamon Wickham’s equalising attempt over the bar.
They will visit Westmeath winners Lough Lene Gaels for the Leinster quarter-final on November 8th.
Meanwhile, Naas wrapped up their eighth Kildare SHC title in a row with a 3-13 to 0-11 victory over Maynooth .
Having seen their footballers shocked by the university town last weekend, Naas clinched their 14th hurling crown with second-half goals from Cathal Dowling, Brian Byrne, and Fionn Maher.
They had to come from behind as Tom Power steered the wind-assisted outsiders into a five-point head start before Charlie Sheridan got Naas on the board.
Maynooth, appearing in their fourth successive final, couldn’t hammer home their advantage as they led 0-7 to 0-5 at half-time.
Dowling gave Naas their first lead in the 38th minute, robbing the goalkeeper before firing the sliotar to the far corner.
They laboured to put Maynooth to bed with four points separating the sides as late as the 59th minute until Byrne dashed in for the clinching goal.
Maher was introduced to the field and less than 60 seconds later, he whipped home their third green flag.
Naas will host Offaly kingpins Kilcormac-Killoughey in their Leinster quarter-final in a fortnight.
Wexford SHC final: Shelmaliers 1-18 Rathnure St Anne’s 2-13
Kildare SHC final: Naas 3-13 Maynooth 0-11

title: Silent, tense and barricaded, Orléans reveals a deeply divided France
description: Le Pen launches presidential campaign amid security lockdown and protest
content:
For 366 years, the George V Bridge has connected the historic city of Orléans to its south bank across the Loire. This weekend, it became a symbol of France’s deep political divisions.
The crossing was sealed off by police barricades to keep left-wing protesters separate from the party conference of the far-right National Rally and the launch of Marine Le Pen’s presidential campaign.
The barriers were reinforced with metal buttresses attached to a special police vehicle, as though they expected to be rammed. No vehicle traffic was allowed to pass; pedestrians had to account for themselves to be allowed through.
Orléans, normally vibrant on Saturday nights, was damp and silent. Car traffic had been banned from the city centre and tram services suspended. Police officers patrolled trains to the city and screened incoming passengers.
Members of the National Rally were instructed that, if travelling by train, they should disembark a stop early, where they would be bussed to the conference venue, avoiding the centre.
Shops were boarded over in case of unrest; almost all bars and restaurants were shut.
I stayed in a hotel emptied out by cancellations; just two other guests remained. It was almost invisible to the street behind the metal security doors, which the owner had drawn shut. “It’s a bit sad tonight,” she welcomed me apologetically. “Normally Orléans is much more lively.”
Polls show that the scenes of arson, looting and unrest that accompanied last week’s protests have further polarised a deeply divided electorate.
The hard-left Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who marches with protesters and accuses the police of provoking the violence, is polling at his highest level yet with 17 per cent support, according to the latest Ipsos poll.
He is the closest runner-up to Marine Le Pen, who is on 33.5 per cent, and appears more likely than ever to be elected French president next spring.
Right-wing voters overwhelmingly see Mélenchon’s France Unbowed as responsible for the violence, while his supporters reject that.
The Ipsos polling found that the scenes of October 17th evoke a feeling of hope for about a third of Mélenchon’s supporters; and for a 10th, satisfaction. For Le Pen’s supporters, their feelings are overwhelmingly anger and shame.
There are violent extremists on both sides. French media documented the appearance of groups of extreme-right militants who attacked protesters in several cities.
A man went on a shooting spree apparently targeting Muslims and black people in an outer Paris suburb on Friday, killing one man and seriously wounding a 12-year-old girl.
On Saturday, a crowd of at least 110,000, according to the Government – organisers estimated many times more than that – filled Paris’s interior ring road, a sea of humanity representing the left of every stripe. They were overwhelmingly peaceful, but disinclined to disown last week’s riots, saying it was understandable in the circumstances.
Some placards targeted President Emmanuel Macron: “Here’s your ‘republic on the march’, as**hole,” read one, a pun on the name of the political movement Macron founded a decade ago with the aim of superseding France’s political divisions.
Others targeted the National Rally, or the “fascists”, to use the term they favour. “Acab, Acab,” they chanted, an English acronym that stands for “all cops are bastards”.
In Orléans, National Rally members applauded and thanked passing police officers walking by on patrol. From a passing car, people screamed something inaudible. Police stopped an approaching young man with dark skin, putting his hands against a metal fence to pat him down.
Jean Francois Niel, a resident of the greater Paris region, said he had joined the party last year in response to what he saw as “despicable” attempts by the left-wing to prevent Le Pen from running through the courts. (She has been convicted of the misuse of public funds; an appeal is ongoing).
“This party has no racism, no anti-Semitism whatsoever; those are shameless lies,” he said. “The evil is on the left and the far-left.”
Inside the venue, unmarked security officers moved with tense urgency through the crowds, their faces partly covered by black masks.
“In our country, thousands of police officers and gendarmes must be deployed to allow a political party to meet,” the party’s proposed prime minister Jordan Bardella began his speech.
Minutes later, a disturbance broke out in the crowd to his right. Bardella urged supporters to remain calm. “Don’t give any publicity to this far-left that hates democracy,” he said. He led the crowd in a fierce rendition of La Marseillaise as security officers hustled the interlopers out.

title: The Irish Times view on AI investment: market concerns need to be watched
description: Meta’s plans were greeted nervously and this is an important signal
content:
The boom in investment in artificial intelligence is facing serious questions, judging by the market reaction to Meta’s latest set of results. The company behind Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram, shed over $100 billion in its value as investors took fright at the level of investment in AI it plans for the next few years.
Meta’s performance was strong. Revenue for the three months from July to September of this year was $64.6 billion, up 26 per cent from a year earlier, while profit was $9.8 billion, up from $2.7 billion for the same period in 2025.
However, even though the company is generating record levels of revenue, it is running out of cash because of the extent of its investment in AI. It has raised its capital expenditure target for 2026 to at least $135 billion, most of which is earmarked for data centres and building out its AI infrastructure.
It plans to raise hundreds of billions of dollars in new share sales and borrowings over the next few years to maintain robust levels of investment in AI. In other words, one of the most valuable companies in the world is effectively becoming a one-way bet on the AI boom.
Yet, instead of urging caution, US president Donald Trump and his administration have fanned the AI boom. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, told investors after the negative market reaction to Meta’s results that he did not see a “systemic problem” with the AI investment cycle.
Increasing investment in AI comes at a time when there are growing calls, even from prominent figures within the industry, for greater regulation amid warnings about the threats it poses. But with US economic growth reliant on AI investment, the Trump administration will not be inclined to agree to a global rules-based system, or anything that could hinder its growth.
There is no doubt that the AI frenzy has many of the characteristics of a bubble, including heady market valutions. But if it bursts the fallout will not be confined to the stock market .

title: Last-gasp Tomo Culhane goal hands Galway SFC title to Salthill-Knocknacarra
description: Substitute turns the tide to land fourth title and first since 2012
content:
Substitute Tomo Culhane was the hero for Salthill-Knocknacarra as he slotted home a match-winning goal 10 seconds from the end of injury-time in a gripping finish to the Galway SFC final.
It seemed that champions Maigh Cuilinn, who came from six points adrift with 12 minutes left, had retained their crown when Peter Cooke pushed them in front in the second and final minute of stoppage time.
But Galway captain John Maher won the kickout and he set up the impressive Matthew Thompson, who presented the opportunity for Culhane to slot the ball low into the bottom right corner to secure their fourth title and first since 2012.
Salthill-Knocknacarra looked dead and buried when Culhane, working his way back from injury, was drafted after 21 minutes when they trailed by 0-4 to 0-0 after shooting half a dozen wides when failing to make use of the wind.
But his introduction led to a Salthill-Knocknacarra revival and after Mark Mannion finally got them off the mark on 25 minutes, Culhane landed five points, including a couple of two-pointers, to lead 0-6 to 0-4 at the break.
[ Mayo SFC final: County stars make difference as Castlebar Mitchels win 32nd title Opens in new window ]
Earlier Dessie Conneely had put Maigh Cuilinn in a strong position with four points against the wind.
Salthill-Knocknacarra introduced injured captain Daniel O’Flaherty at the break and with Michael Kitt and Maher dominating midfield and Matthew Thompson taking the game to the champions, they pulled 1-12 to 0-9 in front after 48 minutes. Colm Finnerty got the goal after a delivery from brother Rob, who was surprisingly held scoreless.
Former Antrim and Galway player Owen Gallagher and Niall Walsh did most to revive Maigh Cuilinn, with a two-pointer from Conneely narrowing the gap.
Paul Kelly got an equalising goal after Gallagher hit the crossbar but just when it seemed Cooke had won it for the champions, Culhane produced his dramatic winner at the death.

title: Mayo SFC final: County stars make difference as Castlebar Mitchels win 32nd title
description: Garrymore fought gallantly but were second best throughout
content:
In the year when Mayo ended a 75-year wait to lift Sam Maguire , Castlebar Mitchels ended a drought of their own. When you’ve won 31 county senior championships, waiting nine years for your next can feel like a lifetime.
The seriousness with which Mitchels approached Sunday’s final was exemplified by their five All-Ireland winners declining the Mayo team’s recent USA tour. That commitment paid off handsomely as midfielder Bob Tuohy kicked six points on his way to the man-of-the-match award while Paddy Durcan contributed superbly to nullifying the threat of county colleague Enda Hession.
Garrymore got more out of their other Mayo star, Eoin McGreal, who supplied three second-half points. Together with four by Darren Quinn, it helped reduce the deficit to four by the 58th minute. In truth, Castlebar had played all the football up to that point. Garrymore, appearing in their first final since 1982, had no more to give.
A foul by corner back Justin Commins on John MacMonagle denied the Castlebar captain a goal-scoring opportunity. Commins was black-carded and Cian Walsh dispatched the penalty. A 60th-minute point by substitute Eoghan Hughes left eight between them at full-time. It was a fair reflection of a game bossed by Mitchels from the opening stages. They had led by seven as early as the 17th minute.
Tuohy opened the scoring with a two pointer and added a pair of singles. There were also scores from Walsh and Joe Forry as Kevin Filan’s side made light work of the stiff breeze against them. The picture could have been bleaker for Garrymore had Colin Commins not blocked a fourth-minute goal effort by Durcan.
The chasers were to score just twice in the first-half, both times from outside the arc by Aaron Hughes and Trevor Nally. The latter had also forced an early save from Mitchels goalkeeper Rory Byrne but it was a rare lapse by the Mitchels defence. By half-time, with Seán Morahan and Anthony O’Boyle registering late points, the town outfit held a 0-9 to 0-4 lead.
Strangely, like Mitchels in the early stages, playing against the elements seemed to suit Garrymore better. They looked a much improved outfit in the third quarter, cutting the gap back to three points. McGreal traded a two-pointer with Durcan, while Trevor Nally had goal on his mind when flashing over Byrne’s crossbar in the 39th minute. But the same was true of Tuohy at the other end in the 47th minute, when he scored his sixth point, after some attacking brilliance by Durcan.
A glorious two-point free curled over by Mitchels full-forward Forry pushed the gap back out to five. MacMonagle foiled Garrymore’s best chance of a route back into contention when throwing himself in front of Caolan Crowe’s swing for goal in the 52nd minute.
Quinn did, though, boot over a two-pointer as his team gallantly refused to give up belief, but Castlebar’s game management – and late penalty award – secured title 32.
Also crowned champions in Mayo’s previous All-Ireland winning years of 1950 and 51, Mitchels will travel to London in three weeks’ time to play Fulham Irish in the Connacht semi-final.

title: Limerick SHC final: Kilmallock dethrone county kingpins Na Piarsaigh
description: Goals from Shane O’Brien, Oisín O’Reilly and Graeme Mulcahy prove to be the difference
content:
Kilmallock have dethroned Limerick kingpins and outgoing champions Na Piarsaigh as “The Balbec” tasted Limerick SHC title success at the TUS Gaelic Grounds to raise the John Daly Cup for a 13th time on Sunday evening.
Goals from Limerick star Shane O’Brien, Oisín O’Reilly and Graeme Mulcahy proved to be the difference as Kilmallock now face All-Ireland champions Ballygunner in the Munster Club semi-final in three weeks’ time.
After a slow start, James Hickey’s charges turned the game on its head, leading for the first time just before the half-time break, until William O’Donoghue’s goal seven minutes from time, before restoring their lead just 40 seconds later as Oisín O’Reilly found the net.
A repeat of the 2022 final, Na Piarsaigh were in search of their seventh Limerick senior title in 10 years, while Kilmallock hoped to lift the John Daly Cup for the first time since 2021.
It was all Na Piarsaigh in the opening 10 minutes as Conor Boylan (two), Keith Dempsey (free), Ronan Lynch (free) and Peter Casey had the Caherdavin men 0-5 to 0-0 ahead inside 10 minutes.
The margin could have been higher, however, had Keith Dempsey found the net after just six minutes, but Kilmallock goalkeeper Conor Hanley Clarke was equal to the former Limerick senior hurler.
Kilmallock started to get on top from midway through the opening half, and after Mike Foley pointed for Na Piarsaigh in the 11th minute, the winners scored seven of the next nine scores to draw level through a long-range Hanley Clarke free, seven minutes shy of half-time.
Kilmallock led for the first time just shy of the break after Pierce Connery scored his fourth free of the evening to push them into a 0-10 to 0-9 lead.
Further scores from Connery and Hanley Clarke, both frees, gave Kilmallock a three-point lead: 0-12 to 0-09.
The half-time whistle was met with a scuffle between players and management after Michael Houlihan caught James Finn with a late shoulder into the chest.
Kilmallock extended their lead just a minute after the restart, O’Brien superbly catching his own side’s puck out before bursting through the Na Piarsaigh defence, blasting into the far corner to raise the game’s first green flag.
Eleven minutes from time, Conor Boylan, set up superbly by Will O’Donoghue, should have found the net but again Hanley Clarke was on hand to deny the city side.
By the time Mike Foley pointed in the 51st minute, Na Piarsaigh had brought it back to a one-point game, before O’Donoghue turned supplier to goalscorer to give Shane O’Neill’s side the lead for the first time in over 20 minutes.
Kilmallock had other ideas, however, and less than a minute later, Oisín Reilly superbly found the net to give Kilmallock the lead once again.
Both sides exchanged points before a looped, high ball into the box was misread by the Na Piarsaigh defence as Kilmallock captain Graeme Mulcahy fittingly secured the hard-fought victory for the Balbec.
