title: Two Irish boxers into finals at World Boxing Under-19 Championships in Montenegro
description: Team Ireland have the opportunity to add two golds to their six-medal haul on Tuesday
content:
Kalib Walshe and John Donoghue have guaranteed silver medals with wins in semi-final bouts at the World Boxing Under-19 Championships in Budva, Montenegro.
The Irish team have collected six medals so far, with four bronzes coming on Sunday and a possible two golds to come on Tuesday.
Walshe of Wexford CBS qualified for the men’s 60kg final with a win over Greece’s Nearchas Konstantinoudis.
Walshe fell behind after a close first round was scored to the Greek fighter, but adjusted well in the second, keeping the fight at longer range and scoring with some well-timed right hands.
Walshe received what seemed a harsh standing count in the third round and picked up the pace in the final minute to try to make up the deficit.
When the scores were read out, four of the judges felt that Walshe had done just that, and he won the bout on a 4-1 split decision, despite protests from Konstantinoudis’s coaches.
Mullingar’s Donoghue produced a fine display to defeat Armenia’s Artyom Stepanyan via split decision, guaranteeing at least a silver medal at 70kg.
The reigning European champion forced a standing count in the first round, and then controlled the action with his lead left hand in the second, setting him up well for the final round.
A point deduction for Donoghue and a better round from Stepanyan looked to have put the result in jeopardy, but the Irish fighter was on the right side of the 3-2 decision.
His brother Jason was on the wrong end of a 3-2 split decision in the 65kg semi-finals against Spain’s Pablo Souto Macias.
Olympic BC Mullingar collected a third medal, as Louise Byrne lost by unanimous decision in her semi-final to Elissandra Santos of Brazil, taking home a bronze medal at 48kg.
Kaysie Joyce from Clonmel BC won a bronze medal after being stopped in the second round of her 70kg semi-final against America’s Marley McNealy.
Dublin Docklands BC’s Jason Whelan also took bronze after a loss to Uzbekistan’s Suhrob Rakhmatullaev, where Whelan was deducted two points by the referee.

title: Magherafelt end Newbridge’s hat-trick ambitions to take Derry SFC title
description: Round-up: Ultan Kelm stars as Erne Gaels secure a third straight Fermanagh title; Rathgormack make it four-in-a-row in Waterford
content:
There are new football kings in Derry as, having lost three finals since 2020, Magherafelt got their hands on the John McLaughlin Cup with a 3-17 to 0-20 victory over hat-trick-chasing Newbridge , producing a devastating scoring burst either side of half-time.
The holders started brightly, Oisín Doherty prominent as they established a 0-7 to 0-4 lead, but Magherafelt took control through the outstanding Conall Higgins.
Higgins landed three two-pointers and a 45 as Magherafelt surged into a 0-13 to 0-7 interval advantage.
The winners made a blistering start to the second half, Johnny McErlain finding the net and Eoin McEvoy and Shane Heavron stretching their lead to 1-16 to 0-7.
Newbridge battled back impressively, with Doherty leading the charge, but an Aidan McCluskey goal on 56 minutes dealt their hopes another blow.
The challengers continued to fight, reducing the deficit to three points in injury-time, before Eoin McEvoy steadied Magherafelt with a crucial point.
Cormac Murphy then struck a third goal with the final action to seal an emphatic victory.
There was one three-in-a-row secured in Ulster, however, as Erne Gaels claimed a commanding 1-21 to 1-12 victory over Derrygonnelly Harps in the Fermanagh SFC final at Brewster Park.
Ultan Kelm was the star of the show, contributing 1-7 in an outstanding individual performance as Barry O’Hagan’s side retained their crown.
The Belleek men dominated the opening half, with Kelm finding the net and adding a two-pointer as they raced into a 1-9 to 0-0 lead.
Derrygonnelly rallied impressively before the interval, captain Gary McKenna leading the fightback as they reduced the deficit to six points.
However, Erne Gaels regained control after the restart, with Jack McCann, Dan McCann and Tommy McCaffrey prominent. An own goal briefly offered Derrygonnelly hope but the champions finished strongly, Kelm continuing to torment the Harps defence, while Dan McCann added 0-4.
The Belleek men now advance to face Donegal champions St Eunan’s in the Ulster Club SFC at Brewster Park in a fortnight.
There was a familiar winner in Waterford , too, as Rathgormack claimed a fourth successive SFC title for the first time in their history with an impressive 2-13 to 0-10 victory over The Nire at Fraher Field.
Kenny Hassett’s side produced a clinical counterattacking display; their nine-point winning margin was the widest of all four finals they have won on this run.
The Nire started brightly but Rathgormack soon seized control, Jason Curry landing an early two-pointer before his brother Stephen finished a flowing move to the net.
Further scores from Francis Roche and Adam Murray helped the champions establish a commanding 1-9 to 0-5 interval lead.
The Nire battled back after the restart and Conor Gleeson struck the crossbar with a gilt-edged goal opportunity but Rathgormack remained composed. Reece O’Mahony added the gloss with an injury-time goal as the champions retained the Conway Cup.
Rathgormack now face Clare winner Éire Óg in the Munster championship on November 8th.
Meanwhile, Ballinamore Sean Ó Heslin’s claimed their 22nd Leitrim SFC title with an impressive eight-point victory over Fenagh St Caillin’s in the final replay at Páirc Seán Mac Diarmada.
Fenagh, under the management of former Cavan forward Martin Dunne, started brightly with early points from Fergal McLoughlin and Ruairí O’Rourke but Ballinamore soon took control, Paul Moran levelling with a two-pointer before Tom Prior struck a superb goal.
Paul Honeyman converted a penalty and added a two-pointer as Ballinamore established a commanding 2-10 to 0-7 half-time lead.
Fenagh battled gamely after the restart, with Riordan O’Rourke and Oisín McLoughlin among their scorers, but the defending champions maintained their grip on proceedings.
Paul Moran effectively settled the contest when he fired home Ballinamore’s third goal with seven minutes remaining. Honeyman finished with 1-6 as Ballinamore completed a convincing victory.

title: Foul play ruled out in death of man (35) near Crookstown, Co Cork
description: Body of Dunmanway native was found in house at Farran early on Sunday morning
content:
Gardaí have ruled out foul play in the death of a 35-year-old man whose body was found in a house in mid- Cork after they received the results of a postmortem examination.
The body of the man, a native of Dunmanway in west Cork, was found by the emergency services when they responded to a 999 call from a rented house at Currahaly, Farran, on the main N22 Cork to Macroom Road at around 3.30am on Sunday morning.
The man, who had suffered head injuries, was pronounced dead at the scene. Gardaí immediately cordoned off the scene and requested the services of the State Pathologist’s Office. and Assistant State Pathologist Dr Margaret Bolster.
Assistant State Pathologist Dr Margaret Bolster confirmed following her postmortem on the deceased at Cork University Hospital that the head injuries were the result of a fall where the man hit his head, and were not caused by a blow. Foul play was not involved in his death.
Gardai will now prepare a file on the man’s death, including witness statements for the Cork County Coroner, who will hold an inquest into the man’s death at a later date.

title: Former Ireland and Munster prop Phil O’Callaghan dies, aged 83
description: Former Ireland captain Terry Kingston leads tributes to his former Dolphin clubmate
content:
Tributes have been paid to former Ireland and Munster prop Phil O’Callaghan, who has died in Dublin at the age of 83 after a short illness.
Former Ireland captain and fellow Dolphin player Terry Kingston led the tributes to O’Callaghan, who played for Dolphin for over 20 years in a career that saw him capped 21 times for Ireland and 34 times for Munster.
“Philo was an absolute legend here at Dolphin for both his personality and his rugby exploits with club, province and country. He was a huge influence on me in my early career as I joined Dolphin in 1982 after school and he was the Under-20 coach at the time.
“In many ways you could say he took me under his wing as he became my coach, my mentor and my friend. He taught me about tenacity, team work, continuous improvement and ambition, he coached me to senior level and his influence stayed with me throughout my career.”
O’Callaghan’s nephew, Mark O’Leary, told The Irish Times that his family were extremely proud of their uncle’s achievements with Dolphin, Munster and Ireland as well as playing with and against some of the greats of the game in the 1960s and 1970s.
“He played with some tremendous players when he was capped by the Barbarians – people like Barry John, Gareth Edwards, Phil Bennett, JPR Williams and Gerald Davies from Wales and David Duckham from England, whom he became great friends with,” said O’Leary.
“And he played with some of the greats of Irish rugby – Willie John McBride, Mick Doyle, Barry McGann, Mike Gibson, Syd Millar but he always maintained the three greatest players he had played with were Tony O’Reilly with Dolphin and Tom Kiernan and Noel Murphy with Ireland.”
O’Callaghan, who grew up in Ballyphehane and later moved to Lehanaghmore in Cork, lived in Ashtown in Dublin in recent years. He is survived by his wife Anne, his brother Paddy and sisters, Marie and Eileen. Funeral arrangements have yet to be announced.

title: Kilkenny SHC final: Merciless Shamrocks Ballyhale leave sentiment at the door against Tullaroan
description: TJ Reid reminded Kilkenny boss Henry Shefflin of his age-defying qualities with a commanding display
content:
When the Shamrocks players gathered on Friday evening for their last meeting before the Kilkenny Senior Hurling Championship final, there was a picture waiting for them in the room.
It was of them standing on the Croke Park pitch last December, heads down and shoulders low as St Martin’s lifted the cup after winning the Leinster club final by a point.
The message was pretty clear: that’s how last year ended, don’t be the ones looking at the other team lifting the cup again this Sunday.
The Shamrocks players took it on board. Just a few minutes after demolishing Tullaroan by 22 points – their largest ever winning margin in a county final – TJ Reid referenced the St Martin’s defeat.
“That was a big loss for us to take,” he said. “That hurt was there from last year.”
Reid contributed five points to Shamrocks’ latest local success, the club’s 22nd and his 13th.
The 38-year-old’s clubmate, and former county colleague, Henry Shefflin , was among the 7,149 spectators. Shefflin is the new Kilkenny manager and he will surely be contacting Reid shortly to ask about his 2027 plans.
And, it turns out, he is likely to receive a favourable response from the veteran attacker.
“At the moment, I’m still a Kilkenny player,” said Reid. “So that’s still there. We’ll see. Ballyhale Shamrocks is first and foremost. Obviously you want to play forever. I’ll try my best to do that.
“As I said, we’ll regroup first. If there’s a panel picked and I’m called for it, I’ll be there. And if not, so be it.”
Shefflin will be an interested observer again on November 8th when Shamrocks begin their latest Leinster club campaign, against Laois champions The Harps in Portlaoise.
“We’re going to drive on,” said Reid. “We want to drive on because that was a big statement [defeat] up in Croke Park last year. We’ll train hard and we’ll get back to action on Wednesday.”
It’s the end of the line for Tullaroan and they will have nightmares about how this final – their first since 1994 – unfolded.
Pre-match discussion had featured some romantic elements. It was the first ever competition winners, Tullaroan, taking on the last, Shamrocks. And if Tullaroan could deliver a surprise win, they’d balance the record books by joining Shamrocks on 21 titles.
If it wasn’t already clear, however, the likes of Reid, captain Joey Holden and Adrian Mullen aren’t much into sentiment. The embers had been stoked on Friday evening and by Sunday, Shamrocks were well and truly fired up.
The game was only 23 seconds old when Mullen pounced on a blocked shot and whipped the ball to the net. Shamrocks added six more points before Tullaroan finally scored.
John Walton’s point in the 25th minute was Tullaroan’s first score from play. By that stage, Shamrocks had already hit 1-11.
Tullaroan might revisit their decision to play into the wind in the first half. Shamrocks built up a 1-15 to 0-2 half-time lead, thanks in part to three booming points from defender Evan Shefflin. It felt like the game was already over.
That suspicion was confirmed when Shamrocks restarted with another 1-3, the goal coming from teenager Jake Mullen in the 40th minute. A Leinster Under-20 finalist last summer, he is Adrian Mullen’s younger brother.
“Four 18-year-olds played today, two started and two came on,” said Shamrocks manager Mark Aylward, ominously. “Jake started and Killian Ryan was the other, he was tremendous.”
Shane Walsh scored a couple of points for Tullaroan but four wides signalled his difficulties with the wind. Pádraig Walsh struggled with an injury and came off. Goalkeeper Niall Holland was Tullaroan’s best player, scoring a second-half point and pulling off four exceptional second-half saves, two from Adrian Mullen and two from Eoin Cody.
At the other end, the goals Tullaroan required to make a game of it never materialised, with just four points from play overall and more wides – a dozen – than points.
Shamrocks, meanwhile, continued to pick off the singles late on with substitutes Dylan Aylward and Michael Barron among 13 different scorers.

title: The first Irish-language book to top the bestseller list
description: Published 50 years ago this week, Breandán Ó hEithir loosely based Lig Sinn I gCathú on his own college experiences
content:
D espite the conservative nature of the teacher training college experience in the late 1980s and a less-than-adequate disposable income, I still managed to enjoy a satisfactory social life in the public houses around Drumcondra.
Recent coverage of damage caused to a house in Limerick that was linked to a student party caused me to consider what a relatively benign existence my own college days had been.
Not that we didn’t have any parties, and some wild ones at that, but mercifully things never escalated to the level of criminal damage. Among my close circle of friends at the time were two nephews of the well-known journalist Breandán Ó hEithir and we spent many afternoons in conspiratorial conversation over pints of porter in Fagan’s pub on the banks of the river Tolka.
Far from house demolition, my college life seems to have had more in common with Máirtín Ó Méalóid, the main protagonist of Ó hEithir’s novel Lig Sinn I gCathú (Lead Us Into Temptation), which was published 50 years ago this year in 1976.
The novel is set in Easter week 1949 at the time when Ireland exited the Commonwealth and the Irish Republic came into being. Ó Méalóid is a university student in Baile an Chaisil, a fictional representation of Galway, and finds himself in the midst of something of an existential crisis. His father is dying and his mother is pressurising him to return home to look after the family business.
Meanwhile his academic studies are suffering because of his failure to attend lectures, and his lack of attendance is in turn causing the payment of his scholarship to be withheld. The main cause of him missing lectures is a busy social life, including a fondness for alcohol and the pursuit of the fairer sex.
His girlfriend is also on his case, not just for the aforementioned vices, but also for the lowly company he keeps and his poor attitude to religion.
Breandán Ó hEithir, one of Ireland’s foremost writers, journalists and broadcasters, was born in Inis Mór in the Aran Islands in 1930 into a family with a rich literary tradition. Two of his mother’s brothers were the writers Tomás and Liam O’Flaherty.
Liam, who was a political activist and one of Ireland’s most famous writers, led an extraordinary life, including time spent fighting on the western front in the first World War and as a Hollywood screenwriter working with the director John Ford.
[ The bestselling Irish-language author who captivated young readers Opens in new window ]
He wrote many novels, several of which were banned by the Irish Censorship Board. Ó hEithir, who was an avid reader from a young age, was undoubtedly familiar with his uncle’s books, which were kept locked away at the family home in Inis Mór.
Those banned novels and O’Flaherty’s disdain for the Catholic church brought the Ó hEithir family into conflict with the local clergy. In the Dictionary of Irish Biography, Ó hEithir’s biographer, Liam Mac Con Iomaire, describes the efforts of successive parish priests on the island to get Ó hEithir’s parents to leave Inis Mór to take up teaching posts on the mainland in Galway.
The reason for this was the belief that if Ó hEithir’s mother left, her brother Liam would stop visiting the island. This appeared to have the opposite effect on Ó hEithir, however, and if anything, it reinforced his conviction to follow in his uncles’ footsteps as a writer.
Ó hEithir considered himself to belong to two places – the boy who belonged to the island and the young man who belonged to the mainland. So, leaving Inis Mór, he finished his second-level education in Coláiste Éinde in Galway and went on to study English, history and philosophy in University College Galway, where he finished the course but left without completing his final exams.
Ó hEithir, who died on October 26th, 1990, loosely based Lig Sinn I gCathú on his own college experiences. The receipt of a grant of £2,000 from the Irish-American Cultural Institute in 1975 allowed him to devote more time to his writing.
Early extracts from the book won Ó hEithir the Gradam an Oireachtas for Irish publications in 1975 and the book was published by Sáirséal and Dill in March 1976. It was a ground-breaking publication and went on to be the first Irish-language book to top Ireland’s hardback bestseller list. Ó hEithir translated the novel into English himself in 1978.
[ The best Irish-language books of 2025 Opens in new window ]
Ó hEithir had previously worked as the Irish-language editor for the Irish Press and later wrote a regular Irish-language column, among other contributions, for this newspaper. Other journalistic work included a stint working for RTÉ on the Irish-language current affairs programme Féach. With his wife Catherine he lived at various times in Germany and later Paris but he retained a love for the island. For the documentary series My Own Place, Ó hEithir returned to Inis Mór where he reminisced about his childhood and time spent fishing with his uncle Liam on the island.

“Nemo Rangers have beaten St Finbarr’s by 1-19 to 2-12 to win their 24th county title after a terrific second half in Páirc Uí Chaoimh. Nemo led by eight points early in the second half but St Finbarr’s reduced the deficit to a point with just four minutes left and playing with a dying wind the odds had shifted in their favour.
“Nemo - who had lost the last three finals - managed the closing minutes though with great calmness and kicked the last three scores to win by four.”
Galway: GOAL FOR MOYCULLEN! Madcap finish in the Galway final, as Paul Kelly buries a chance for Moycullen after the initial shot came back off the crossbar. That makes it all square in Pearse Stadium as the clock ticks past 58 minutes. Moycullen 1-12 Salthill-Knocknacarra 1-12
Cork: GOAL FOR ST FINBARR’S! Game on now, as John Wiggington Barrett taps gome from close range to bring the Barrs to within two of Nemo with five minutes to go. Nemo Rangers 1-16 St Finbarr’s 2-11
Limerick: GOAL FOR KILMALLOCK! That’s that. A freak goal, with Graeme Mulcahy launching a long ball in from out the field and everyone missing it as it dropped into the net behind Shane Dowling in the Na Piarsigh goal. Kilmallock are champions for the 13th time. Kilmallock 3-19 Na Piarsigh 1-22
Cúl eile!! Cad é mar críoch ansin i bPáirc na nGael!!!😱 Graeme Mulcahy's long ball goes all the way into the Na Piarsaigh net! 63 nóim @KilmallockGAA 3-19 @NapGAA 1-21 @GAA_BEO #GAABeo pic.twitter.com/pDI8KP5HkE
Limerick: GOAL FOR NA PIARSIGH! AND THEN GOAL FOR KILMALLO0CK!
A wild 90 seconds in the Gaelic Grounds. First Will O’Donoghue steamed through for Na Piarsigh to put them into the lead for the first time in the game. But no sooner had they gone ahead than they were behind again, as Kilmallock went up the other end of the pitch qand struck back immediately with a goal of their own. Level game, 15 minutes to go. Brilliant stuff. Kilmallock 2-17 Na Piarsigh 1-20
Cúl! Neadaithe go sneasta ag Will O'Donoghue!🔥 Will O'Donoghue steps up and fires home an unstoppable shot! 52 nóim @KilmallockGAA 1-17 @NapGAA 1-19 @GAA_BEO #GAABeo pic.twitter.com/oFSuxr6hwr
Cork: GOAL FOR ST FINBARR’S! Brian Hayes gives the Barrs a lifeline with a goal in the 47th minute. It had been plain enough sailing for Nemo up to that but it’s all in the balance now. Nemo Rangers 1-13 St Finbarr’s 1-10
BRIAN HAYES THE MAN OF THE HOUR!?🤯 A goal in back to back finals from the Barrs and Cork star, what a goal💪 #ClubberTV 📺 pic.twitter.com/cI1mjmXzGr
Mayo: And that is surely that in MacHale Park, where Castlebar have found the goal they needed to wriggle clear of Garrymore. It came from a penalty, slotted home by Cian Walsh. The underdogs stuck in there for the longest time but Mitchells will see this out now. Castlebar Mitchells 1-16 Garrymore 0-12
Wexford: All over in wexford Park, where Shelmaliers are county champions for the third time. It got hairy enough for them near the end as Rathnure chased a goal but they hung on for a well-deserved win. Shelmaliers 1-18 Rathnure 2-13
Limerick: Kilmallock’s tails are up here. A few bad wides from Na Piarsigh and there are four points in it now. But Ronan Lynch pulls oner back and there’s only a goal in it. If Na Piarsigh fix their shooting, they’ll fancy closing the gap. Kilmallock 1-16 Na Piarsigh 0-16
Wexford: Rathnure are coming. Jack Redmond banged home their second goal on 52 minutes after a fine run by Rory Higgins. Shels had been coasting, with a seven-point lead, but scores from AJ Redmond and Eoin O’Neill have hauled Rathnure back into it. Shels are three up with 57 minutes on the clock. Can they hang on? Shelmaliers 1-17 Rathnure 2-11
Cork: Half-time dispatch from Denis Walsh in Páirc Uí Chaoimh...
“Nemo lead by St Finbarr’s 1-8 to 0-5 after a lively first half. Nemo led by seven points to nil after 15 minutes but the Barr’s had dragged themselves back into the game before Nemo struck for a goal in first half stoppage time.
“Mark Cronin’s two-point attempt fell short but his brother Stephen rescued the ball and played a pass across the square for Luke Horgan to apply the finish.
“The Barr’s had threatened a goal on at least three occasions, forcing one really good save from Mícheál Aodh Martin, but the champions have a mountain to climb in the second half, even with the wind at their backs.”
Limerick: A couple of yellow cards on the resumption in Limerick and that’s that. Let’s Dance plays out over the PA system and off they go for the second half. And straight away Shane O’Brien chips in with a huge score, pinging the game’s opening goal for Kilmallock! Kilmallock 1-12 Na Piarsigh 0-11
Cúl inspioráideach faighte ag Shane O'Brien!🤩 'The Bull' O'Brien fires past Shane Dowling!! 31 nóim @KilmallockGAA 1-12 @NapGAA 0-10 @GAA_BEO #GAABeo pic.twitter.com/payC8wzA5V
Wexford: Shelmaliers have sprinted from the blocks in the second half, slapping 1-4 past Rathnure to push on into a commanding lead. Rathnure had the best of the opening period but Shels have really taken hold of this now, with a goal from Conor Hearne and excellent shooting from Ross Banville. Big job for Rathnure over the closing 15 minutes here. Shelmaliers 1-15 Rathnure 1-6
Limerick: It wouldn’t be county final Sunday without at least one all-in scrap and the Limerick hurling final has provided it. Things were getting to bit saucy just before the break and as soon as the whistle went to call half-time, both sides started bumping off each other and it was one-in-all-in. Let’s see if the referee takes any action when the teams come out for the second half.
Limerick: It’s been a cracking battle in the Gaelic Grounds. Na Piarsigh skated into an early lead but Kilmallock have dug in to haul themselves back into it and have inched themselves a couple of points ahead coming up to the break. For all of Kilmallock’s pluck in coming back into it, Na Piarsigh will have the wind in the second half so you’d imagine they’ll be happy enough with the scoreline. Kilmallock 0-12 Na Piarsigh 0-9
Mayo: Castlebar were the ones to hit the ground running in MacHale Park, totting up a seven-point lead in the early exchanges against Garrymore. Bob Tuohy, their Mayo midfielder, got things underway with a classy two-pointer and Garrymore struggled to make any impression for long passages of the opening half but to their credit, they dug out a couple of two-pointers in the closing five minutes of the half. Castlebar Mitchells 0-9 Garrymore 0-4
Wexford: Shelmaliers look like they are going to eke out a slim half-time lead in Wexford Park but with the wind behind them in that opening half, they would surely have expected to be further ahead. Rathnure have been the better side and Shels have had to rely on Ross Bannon frees to keep their noses ahead. Big job for them in the second half. Shelmaliers 0-10 Rathnure 1-4
Kildare: Naas have turned it around in Newbridge, as expected. A goal from Cathal Dowling kicks them into a two-point lead with the wind behind them. Big job for Maynooth now. Naas 1-7 Maynooth 0-8
Cork: Denis Walsh has a dispatch for us from Páirc Uí Chaoimh, where the Cork football final is throwing in at 4pm.
“While tens of thousands of pleasure seekers circulate the city centre trying to avoid anything that resembles jazz, a sparse crowd has descended on Pairc Ui Chaoimh for the meeting of St Finbarr’s and Nemo Rangers in the Cork football final. The rain that lashed the city for the last three days has moved on but there is a bitter wind blowing towards the City End.
“The Barrs lost the hurling final last weekend and four players who started that game line out again: Brian Hayes, William Buckley, Ciarán Doolan and Jonathan Wigginton Barrett.
“Nemo last won the title in 2022, but have lost three finals since. No team has lost four finals in a row since the 1930s.”
Limerick: Underway in the Galeic Grounds between Na Piarsigh and Kilmallock. No end of Limerick All-Ireland stars on show here as Na Piarsigh go for their eighth title in 12 years.
Wexford: Early goal for Shelmaliers in Wexford Park after a bad mix-up at the back left a handy chance for Shane Lawler to tap home to an empty net. Sloppy from Rathnure who had otherwise made a decent start. Shelmaliers 1-1 Rathnure 0-2
Rathnure St. Anne’s raise the first green flag of the game! 💪 Shane Lawler punishes the Shelmaliers defence and pulls the ball into the back of the net 🔥 @RathnureGAA | @OfficialWexGAA | #ClubberTV pic.twitter.com/dI3QlOpeUt
The first wave of games are either over or entering the final stretch. So we’ve had wins for old firm teams in the shape of Ballyhale and Dr Crokes already with finals in Fermanagh, Leitrim and Waterford still up for grabs. The next wave of throw-ins are imminent, with Wexford (hurling) and Mayo (football) just underway.
Kerry: All over in Killarney and Crokes see it out to take their 15th Kerry title. It was a right ding-dong of a game but that spell of four two-pointers in the space of five minutes midway through the second half settled it for the Killarney side. Dr Crokes 1-24 Kenmare Shamrocks 2-14
Kildare: Fast start for the underdogs in Newbridge, where Maynooth have taken a four-point lead against heavy favourites Naas with five minutes left until the break. They’ve used the wind to build their lead, albeit you’d imagine Naas won’t be too perturbed with the best of the conditions to come. Maynooth 0-7 Naas 0-4
Waterford: Back underway in Dungarvan and The Nire have tacked on two quick points upon the restart to cut the gap to five points. Rathgormack 1-9 The Nire 0-7
Kerry: The tide feels like its turning in Dr Crokes’ favour now. Back-to-back two-pointers from Tony Brosnan and David Shaw push them into a two-point lead. Kenmare have fought bravely so far but with the wind against them, it’s going to take something special for them to hang in here. But Brosnan bangs over another one! That’s four orange flags in the space of a few minutes to completely turn this one on its head. Dr Crokes 1-22 Kenmare 2-13
Kerry: It’s turning into a thriller in Killarney, as Kenmare dig in to try and fend off this Dr Crokes comeback. The Crokes managed to get back level through Brian Looney and Cian McMahon but that man Seánie O’Shea is carrying his side like a man possessed and his two-point free into the wind eased Kenmare clear again with a quarter of an hour to go. Kenmare 2-12 Dr Crokes 1-13
Sean O'Shea listen to the roar🤩 Seanie is a walking highlight reel today, what a performance👏 #ClubberTV 📺 pic.twitter.com/lTOLTRiU6t
Kilkenny: All over in Nowlan Park and Ballyhale go two clear at the top of the roll of honour. It was over early, as Tullaroan simply didn’t turn up. Ballyhale Shamrocks 2-24 Tullaroan 0-8
Fermanagh: A one-sided contest in Enniskillen, where Ultan Kelm has been outstanding for Éire Óg Beleek. The wind has clearly played its part but 1-3 from Kelm put Beleek in a commanding position. Derrygonnelly went almost the whole half without scoring but a brief flurry just before the break has given them a chance. Éire Óg Beleek 1-9 Derrygonnelly Harps 0-5
Kerry: Big start to the second half with a goal for either side. Kerry midfielder Mark O’Shea finished off soccer-style for Dr Crokes within two minutes of the restart to bring the margin back to just a point. But less than 60 seconds later, Kenmare hit back with a goal of their own after a goalmouth scramble. They still lead by four. Kenmare 2-8 Dr Crokes 1-7
Waterford: Goal for Rathgormack, as full-forward Stephen Curry makes his first meaningful contribution, getting through the cover quite easily. The Nire had been hanging in there pretty well against the wind but that’s a big score for the defending champions. Rathgormack 1-7 The Nire 0-4
Leitrim: Ballinamore have made decent use of the wind in Carrick-on-Shannon so far, with a couple of two-pointers from Tom Prior and Paul Moran earning them an early lead halfway through the first of the replay. Ballinamore 0-6 Fenagh 0-2
Kilkenny: It’s a dead duck in Nowlan Park at this stage. Ballyhale have come out just as able to do what they please in the second half as in the first. They’ve added 1-3 against the wind in the first 10 minutes, Tullaroan haven’t been able to raise a gallop at all. With 20 minutes to go, both sides are just playing out the string now. Ballyhale 2-18 Tullaroan 0-2
Kerry: Half-time in Fitzgerald Stadium, Kenmare lead by 4. Seánie O’Shea has scored six points of their 1-8 total, including a two-point free and another two-pointer from play. On a day when weather is going to have its say everywhere, four points feels like a slim enough lead. We’ll see. Kenmare Shamrocks 1-8 Dr Crokes 0-7
Throw-in time imminent in the Fermanagh, Leitrim and Waterford football finals. Hold onto your hats.
Kerry: Dr Crokes have settled a bit in Killarney, with Tony Brosnan, Charlie Heating and Cillian Fitzgerald chipping in. Kenmare know they have to build a score with this wind though and Seanie O’Shea is keeping them ticking over. They lead by five with five minutes to go until the break. Kenmare 1-7 Dr Crokes 0-5
Kilkenny: Ballyhale are comfortable in Nowlan Park. It took Tullaroan 24 minutes to find a score from play but with Cody, Mullen and Reid dominating matters, the Shamrocks have barely put a foot wrong. They lead by 16 at half-time, despite a few slightly careless wides just before the break. The wind is strong but it ain’t 16 points strong. Ballyhale Shamrocks 1-15 Tullaroan 0-2
Cúilín uimhir a trí scóráilte ag Evan Shefflin!👊 Ballyhale at their ease as half-time approaches. 27 nóim @BallyhaleGAA 1-12 @TullaroanHurlin 0-02 @GAA_BEO #GAABeo pic.twitter.com/YeTXkBjJxh
Kerry: Kenmare are making full use of the wind so far. Seánie O’Shea swings over a two-pointer from play to kick them into a seven-point lead inside the opening 10 minutes. Kenmare 1-5 Dr Crokes 0-1
Kerry: Underway in Killarney, where Dr Crokes are chasing their 15th county title. Facing them are Kenmare Shamrocks, chasing their first. A few of these Kenmare players have been in a final before as part of the Kenmare District team back in 2016 but this is their first time in the decider as a standalone club. And it’s the newcomers who have made the better start, with a goal from David Ciuciu pushing them into an early lead at Fitzgerald Stadium. Kenmare 1-3 Dr Crokes 0-0
Kilkenny: Ominously for Tullaroan, TJ Reid has got in on the act now. It took him 12 minutes to even get the ball into his hand but he’s just iced a free and that’s an eight-point lead for the champions. Brian Cody follows up with another from play. This could be over already. Ballyhale 1-6 Tullaroan 0-0
Brian Cody, thar an trasnán!🫡 The Shamrocks are already building up a healthy lead. 13 nóim @BallyhaleGAA 1-06 @TullaroanHurlin 0-00 @GAA_BEO #GAABeo pic.twitter.com/dqa5zaWhtl
Kilkenny: Ballyhale have settled much the better in Nowlan Park. Cody (2) and Mullen have tacked on points to push them six ahead inside the first seven minutes. They do have the wind but Tullaroan need to find a way to settle here. Ballyhale 1-4 Tullaroan 0-0
Kilkenny: GOAL FOR BALLYHALE! The Kilkenny final starts with a bang, as Adrian Mullen scrambles home a goal after 21 seconds. Eoin Cody streaked through but his shot was saved. Mullen was quickest to tidy up the rebound. Ballyhale 1-0 Tullaroan 0-0
"Cúl! A leiithéid de thús ag na Seamróga agus Adrian Mullen!🦾 Ballyhale hit the net in their first attack! 1 nóim @BallyhaleGAA 1-00 @TullaroanHurlin 0-00 @GAA_BEO #GAABeo pic.twitter.com/fEnjBj9Hfq
Like the runners in the Dublin marathon this morning, the game are staggered in terms of start times this afternoon. For the first while, we’ll be mostly keeping an eye on matters in Kilkenny in hurling and Kerry in football.
The Kilkenny final is fascinating, with Ballyhale and Tullaroan facing off not just for this year’s bragging right but also for top spot in the Kilkenny roll of honour. Up until last year, Tullaroan had never not been top of the list in terms of county championships, either jointly or, for the vast majority of the competition’s history, on their own. Ballyhale’s win in 2025 was their 21st title, pushing the one past Tullaroan for the first time ever. And so this is Tullaroan’s chance to grab that back, despite not having been to a final since 1994.
We’ve already had a couple of champions crowned this weekend, of course. Following on from Edendork’s historic first Tyrone title on Friday night, Kilmacud Crokes became Dublin hurling champions for the eighth time last night in Parnell Park. It was ultimately a bloodless enough affair against Cuala, with Crokes using the wind to build up a big half-time lead and Cuala making no real impression after the break. Gordon Manning was there for us and you can read his report here .
[ Kilmacud Crokes ease to Dublin SHC win that crushes Cuala’s double dream Opens in new window ]
It’s late October, the wind is howling and there’s a massive Sunday of county finals ahead. We’ll keep you updated throughout the afternoon as a dozen titles are down for decision right around the country. The Kilkenny and Limerick finals are on TG4, with finals in Cork, Kerry, Limerick and Kildare available on Clubber. Fun day ahead.

title: Israeli army launches big West Bank operation in advance of election
description: More than 400 different locations affected over weekend and 40 Palestinians arrested, says military
content:
The Israeli army carried out a massive operation in the occupied West Bank over the weekend, displacing hundreds of Palestinians and placing big restrictions on movement, in response to a gun attack that killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded three others in Hebron on Friday.
The operation comes as Israel enters the final days before a tense election, which is largely seen as a referendum on prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu’s leadership and security policies during the past three years of war.
Most Palestinian workers with permits will not be allowed to enter Israeli communities for work in the occupied West Bank on Sunday and Monday, and crossings into Israel will remain closed until after elections on Tuesday, the Israeli military said.
The military said it operated in more than 400 different locations over the weekend and arrested 40 Palestinians it claimed were affiliated with Hamas or Palestinian Islamic Jihad.
The operation displaced hundreds of families, forcing some to navigate crossings on foot after the roads were closed to traffic.
At some military gates, people passed sacks of flour and gas canisters through the gates, while an elderly man pushed his wife in a wheelchair through an opening beside one of them. Another family attempted to navigate the gate to access medical appointments.
After Friday’s attack, Israel’s military said it found weapons in the gunmen’s car and that they were likely planning to attack Israeli civilians before being stopped at the checkpoint.
The military said that troops were “conducting precise, targeted and thorough searches” in the area where the gunmen operated, and warned residents to evacuate Deir Bahha, the suspected gunmen’s neighbourhood.
Hebron municipal officials said between 200 and 300 families had been displaced from Deir Bahha and four surrounding neighbourhoods overnight, most going to other parts of the city.
Six Israelis have been killed this year in attacks in the West Bank, which is experiencing a surge of violence.
During the same period, 112 Palestinians have been killed, including the suspected gunmen, according to the Ramallah-based Palestinian health ministry.
The attack sparked outrage in Israel, with Netanyahu and three members of his right-wing government giving statements from the site of the attack on Friday afternoon, vowing to respond forcefully.
Netanyahu is under pressure to demonstrate a strong show of force against Palestinian attackers to bolster his image for Israelis concerned with security.
Approximately three million Palestinians and 540,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank, which Israel occupied in the 1967 Middle East war.
Hebron is one of its most tense cities and the only place where Jewish settlers live in the heart of a densely populated Palestinian area under Israeli military protection.
Meanwhile, billionaire American investor Bill Ackman on Sunday said ‌that Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich should not serve in Israel’s next government, saying the two far-right politicians had caused enormous damage to the country’s reputation.
The ​public intervention by the prominent hedge fund manager, who is Jewish, comes just two days before Israel’s general election, in which polls show a tight race between Netanyahu’s coalition and the opposition.
Ackman wrote on X that from the perspective of someone who had an understanding of how ​Israel was perceived in the United States, “Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have caused Israel enormous reputational damage with their statements and actions.”
The founder of ⁠Pershing Square Capital Management, who praised Netanyahu last week, said a government without the two ministers would send a ‌message ‌that ​Israel was “turning a new page”.
“This will allow Israel to rebuild lost credibility, increase the opportunity for an expansion of the Abraham Accords, and enjoy a better relationship with Democrats and Republicans and Americans ⁠at large,” he said. – Guardian/Reuters

title: Manchester United board hold crisis talks over Michael Carrick’s future
description: Carrick defiant despite humbling 3-0 defeat to Bournemouth and insisted he was not expecting to be removed from his post
content:
Manchester United’s hierarchy are in crisis talks over whether or not to sack Michael Carrick as head coach after he oversaw another torrid defeat, against Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday, that appeared to leave his job in the balance.
Carrick was defiant after the 3-0 humbling, insisting he was not expecting to be removed from his post. “I totally understand the situation [regarding his job],” Carrick said.
“I’m not expecting anything in particular, to be honest. [I’m] carrying on as normal, and I love this place.”
But the United executive are actively considering his dismissal. Eddie Howe remains the preferred candidate of Jason Wilcox, United’s director of football, should there be a change in the dugout, with the former Newcastle manager’s extensive Premier League experience placing him ahead of other potential targets.
Howe would be less expensive to bring in than Unai Emery, another admired candidate, given that Aston Villa would demand about £20 million in compensation for the Spaniard.
Julian Nagelsmann, the former Germany and Bayern Munich head coach, is highly regarded by Christopher Vivell, United’s head of recruitment, but Wilcox’s view may hold more sway with Jim Ratcliffe, who controls football policy at United. Antonio Conte is another who may be in the frame.
Carrick, who left Bruno Fernandes out of his starting line-up – insisting before kick-off that he did so for football reasons and not because of the captain’s criticism of his tactics following the midweek Champions League defeat at Como, said: “I’ll always do what I feel is going to be the best for the football club, whatever decision is made on anything really. So that’s kind of it. I’m not expecting anything either way.
“It’s a tough situation, there’s no hiding from it. What it looks like and what’s next I really don’t know. I will always do my best for the football club and I won’t change that now. I love what I do and I feel the responsibility – we’ll have to wait and see.”
United endured a sixth defeat in 12 games in all competitions after Rayan, Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson scored for Marco Rose’s side. They have won only once in the league this season and sit in 16th. Their last win was on September 10th against Sabah in the Champions League.
Carrick made a point of applauding the home supporters at the end of the match, pumping his hand to his chest as he walked past a supportive Stretford End. As soon as he disappeared down the tunnel, boos met Fernandes, who was following in the manager’s footsteps, alongside other United players.
“It wasn’t a farewell from me,” Carrick said. “I’m feeling it for my players, they’re going through a tough spell. Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment. Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way.
“To have that connection with the supporters it’s mixed emotions, it’ll take a bit of time to digest but I certainly appreciate their support. The situation is where we are and we haven’t had results or performances that have been good enough.”
Speaking after the defeat about his decision to leave out Fernandes, who was an unused substitute, Carrick said: “There’s always times when you’re trying to make decisions that are to change the course of play and made a difference, but those are the decisions we made today.”
Harry Maguire, United’s captain in Fernandes’s absence, insisted that the squad were “fully behind” Carrick. He said: “Coming into the team last season he turned things around and got Champions League football this season.
“As individuals, we’re not playing well enough. We have to look at ourselves and find something within ourselves to bring more to the team. That’s every player that I’m talking about. When things aren’t going your way you have to do the basics well.” – Guardian

title: Irish player tracker: David Moyes leaves Jake O’Brien in no doubt about pecking-order fall
description: Troy Parrott squanders late chance for Betis, Owen Elding scores against Celtic and Jimmy Dunne nets QPR brace
content:
Trust the sting of a backhanded compliment to not only sharpen the mind but drain the joy from a step in the right direction.
Jake O’Brien went from being a regular starter at Everton last season to scrapping for recognition this season. And having stayed at the club amid summer transfer speculation, he only made his first Premier League start of the campaign on Saturday.
The Republic of Ireland defender got a rare opportunity to play in his preferred position of centre back for the trip to champions Arsenal . That was facilitated by Jarrad Branthwaite’s unavailability as he follows concussion protocols. Manager David Moyes opted for O’Brien ahead of Michael Keane, a player previously favoured in that position by Moyes.
The towering Cork man lost sight of Gabriel at the back post in the 68th minute, allowing the Arsenal defender to head in the Gunners’ second goal all too easily. In that moment, O’Brien looked every inch an out-of-favour player with just 29 minutes of Premier League action under his belt going into the game.
It’s no wonder Moyes’s post-match assessment was delivered with a sting in the tail that will serve as a sobering warning to O’Brien.
“Jake did well, he did a lot of good things,” said Moyes. “He’s got pretty big competition as Jarrad Branthwaite is an excellent player and Tarky [James Tarkowski] is a bit of a leader for us and trains every day like a beast and gets himself ready for all the games and prepares himself.
“There’s competition there. He didn’t do himself any harm today in some of it, [but] he’s got lots of things he has to improve on for him to step up.”
While O’Brien fights for every minute he can get, Nathan Collins is hoping it’s only a matter of time before he is back playing regularly. Injured since early September – and ruled out of all four of Ireland’s recent Nations League games – he warmed the Brentford bench for the second game running in Sunday’s 1-1 draw away to John Egan’s Hull City.
Over in Spain, Troy Parrott was also a substitute for Real Betis, who drew 0-0 away to Celta Vigo. It’s been a tough week for Parrott following a break-in at his Seville home the previous weekend. He squandered a fine injury-time chance to win it, but it might irk him more that Betis started without a recognised striker.
With Cucho Hernández out injured, Parrott may have expected to get more than 30 minutes, even if it was off the back of a 79-minute Champions League outing in midweek. Instead, Betis started with midfielder Nelson Deossa – who has never scored for the club – as a false nine before his withdrawal on the hour.
Owen Elding will hope to one day create some Parrott-like memories of his own in an Ireland shirt. The 20-year-old did his reputation no harm by scoring his fourth goal of the season for Hibernian in a 2-1 loss to Celtic at Easter Road on Sunday. Elding capitalised on a quick free kick in the third minute to finish low and hard into the corner. Jamie McGrath and Liam Scales also started the game for Hibs and Celtic respectively.
Ireland defender Jimmy Dunne scored twice in QPR’s 5-0 rout of Swansea City, heading home a cross by his international colleague Harvey Vale to score the fourth goal, before adding the fifth from another set piece.
The win saw QPR climb to eighth in the Championship, just three points behind second-placed Swansea – who had Adam Idah in their starting lineup – and five off leaders Middlesbrough.
Jack Moylan played in a deeper midfield role than of late in Cardiff’s 1-0 win over Birmingham. There was no room in the Bluebirds squad once again for Callum Robinson, who fell foul of manager Brian Barry-Murphy before Cardiff’s previous game against Middlesbrough.
“We have certain standards that all the players have to adhere to before they’re considered for selection,” said Barry-Murphy of Robinson, who is the forgotten man of the Republic of Ireland squad having last featured two years ago.
“Callum missed out on some of those before [Middlesbrough], so he wasn’t available. The standards we expect in the dressingroom are internal. We’re always judged in public and that’s fine, but the dressingroom and how we work day by day are private.”
While Robinson is out in the cold, fit-again Bosun Lawal has been putting his best foot forward for Stoke City. He started his second game in succession as the Potters were held scoreless at home by Jason Knight’s Bristol City.
Josh Cullen has missed all of Ireland’s games this year due to the ACL injury he sustained last December, but the midfielder was finally back in action last Friday night with a 45-minute run-out for Burnley’s under-21s in a defeat at West Ham.
“In the early days after the operation you’re kind of wondering how you’re going to walk again, never mind playing a game of football again. To be back playing football after 300 days was an amazing feeling,” he said.
Once Cullen is up to speed, he will have a new first-team manager to win over as the Clarets sacked Nicky Hayen on Saturday having blown a 1-0 lead in a 4-1 defeat to Lincoln City. The Belgian was in charge for just 14 games but Burnley are third-from-bottom in the Championship and felt compelled to act.

title: Woman (80s) dies from suspected smoke inhalation following fire at her home in east Cork
description: Woman pronounced dead at scene following fire believed to involve fabric items
content:
An elderly woman has died after being injured in a fire incident at her home in Co Cork late on Saturday night.
It is understood that the woman, who was in her mid-80s and lived alone, suffered from smoke inhalation when some items of clothing or fabric caught fire at her semidetached cottage at Monagoul near Ballymacoda in east Cork shortly before 11pm on Saturday.
The woman managed to raise the alarm using her panic button and gardaí from Youghal and local emergency services responded and attended to the woman.
It is understood the woman had suffered from severe smoke inhalation and, despite attempts to resuscitate her, she was pronounced dead at the scene. Her body was removed to Cork University Hospital where a postmortem examination will take place in the coming days.
Garda technical experts have begun an examination of the scene to try to establish how the clothing or fabric caught fire but foul play is not suspected. Gardaí will include the technical findings in a file for an inquest at the Cork county coroner’s court.
Local Fine Gael member of Cork County Council Michael Hegarty said everyone in the community was shocked at the news of the tragedy, and people’s thoughts and prayers were with the family of the dead woman.
It is the second fatal fire incident in Cork in the space of a week, following the deaths of husband and wife Willie and Geraldine Hawkes. The couple were in their 70s and died after fire broke out at their home at Raheen near Crossbarry in west Cork on the morning of October 20th.
Willie Hawkes was well known in farming circles, having worked until recent years in milk recording with Munster Bovine, while Geraldine Hawkes, who was known as Tina, had trained and worked as a midwife at the Bon Secours Hospital in Cork.
The couple will be buried on Monday following requiem mass at St Patrick’s Church, Knockavilla.

title: ‘I’m in total disbelief’ - storming finish secures Irish marathon title for Judith Storm
description: City of Derry Spartans AC runner passes long-time Irish women’s leader Sorcha Nic Dhómhnaill inside the last 400m
content:
Trouble can come at you from all directions in the marathon, particularly on a blustery day, which also means nothing ever is decided for certain until the finish line.
Judith Storm provided ample reminder of that, the only real hint of which was already in her name, after she whipped up a brilliant sprint finish to cross the line as the top Irish woman in the Irish Life Dublin Marathon .
Storm eventually got past long-time Irish women’s leader Sorcha Nic Dhómhnaill inside the last 400m, just before the Pepper Canister Church, then raced 12 seconds clear to reach the finish line on Mount Street Upper in 2:35:46.
That also earned Storm the national marathon title which goes to the first Irish finishers in Dublin, her first podium finish in any event. At age 39, Storm only took up competitive running after the pandemic, and the mother of four – including seven-year-old triplets – was visibly thrilled with her effort.
“I’m in total disbelief, it’s all a bit of a blur, but I just managed to sprint at the end to catch her,” said Storm, a Scottish native who moved to Northern Ireland 16 years ago, and now runs with City of Derry Spartans AC.
“I remember at mile 23, 24, I just started thinking, ‘well, this is my time, if I’m moving, I need to move now’. The wind in parts, even at the end there, was brutal. So I just about closed the gap somehow.”
With perhaps a wink and smile from the marathon running gods, the properly stormy winds of the previous 48 hours had certainly eased by the 8.45am starting time, with bright sunshine also holding up throughout the race.
Still, there was no running away from that strong wind in parts, which was at the backs of the runners heading towards the infamous “wall” around the 21-mile mark, before it turned into their faces again for the closing miles.
Despite her relative lack of marathon running experience, Storm has little fear of the distance. After running 2:47:07 on her Dublin debut last year, she lowered her best to 2:39:09 in Belfast, then won the Belfast Half Marathon last month in 1:14:14, another hint of her potential.
A medical doctor by profession, Storm also uses her running as a way of balancing her busy lifestyle, with clear potential to run significantly faster in better conditions.
“I was a medical doctor in hospitals, right up until I had the triplets, and we now have an aesthetic business in Belfast, and I have my own online skin care business as well. So it’s busy, three different businesses, and kids and running, that’s my life.
“But I never did any exercise growing up. I bought a bike, during Covid, just to get out of the house. Then when we moved to Derry from Belfast, four years ago, I took up running, met my coach Emmett McGinty, who’s guided me through the whole thing, just built it up over the course of three to four years.
“It just shows you, if something’s important to you, you’ll make it happen. I have four children, my eldest daughter is eight, the triplets seven. Running obviously comes secondary to the kids, but I make it work, and it’s something that I give back to me. So any mums out there, if I can do it, you can too. I’m not talented in any way, I’m just determined, and stubborn.”
She also credits her husband Chris, a Derry native, and the support of her club: “I just love my City of Derry Spartans family, they really are the most supportive people I’ve ever met.”
For Nic Dhómhnaill, running for her club West Limerick, the Irish women’s title looked certain to be heading her way, with the 41-year-old over 90 seconds clear of Storm at the halfway mark.
“I did think I had it, I felt good, but the wind was horrific,” said Nic Dhómhnaill, also coached by Feidhlim Kelly in Dublin. “So time is obviously out the window. I was still feeling good with 10km to go, but she just passed me at the wrong time, my legs just turned to jelly.
“I might feel happier in a few days time, but I felt like that was my race to lose, and I lost it.”
Indeed at the front of the race, Enock Kipkemboi from Kenya also looked to be cruising towards the outright victory and the $15,000 top prize, before he suddenly keeled over when passing the RDS, with just under two miles left to run.
That left Ethiopia’s Abay Alemu Lesa and Sweden’s Ebba Chala locked in battle for outright victory, which was also decided on the last turn at the Pepper Canister Church, with the 22-year-old Lesa winning in 2:10:28, eight seconds ahead of the Ethiopian-born Chala.
Kipkemboi did recover to finish fourth, in 2:12:17, before immediately falling to the ground again, a clear indication the wind had taken a heavy toll on him.
“It was a very hard race, but I didn’t really see what happened behind,” said Lesa. “But I pushed to the last and I was happy with my performance, and very happy to win.”
After Sahlesilassie Nigussie, also from Ethiopia, rounded out the men’s podium, running 2:11:25 in third, a trio of Ethiopian women took the top podium places. Zenebu Fikadu narrowly missed out on the women’s course record with her time of 2:24:26, highly impressive given the testing conditions. Tenebeb Nega Aynalem was runner-up in 2:25:50, and Sechele Dalasa Adunga third in 2:27:22.
Despite the windy conditions, 19,190 of the 22,500 entries started the race, the highest number of starters in the history of the Dublin event, which has been running since 1980.

title: Further weather warnings issued as thousands remain without power after Storm Boelo
description: National Directorate for Fire and Emergency Management urges the public to remain cautious
content:
A fresh set of weather warnings has been issued by Met Éireann for Monday, with the last of those related to Storm Boelo having expired on Sunday afternoon.
The storm brought strong southwest winds and severe gusts over the weekend and left tens of thousands of homes and businesses without electricity. The northwest and west regions were hardest hit.
The last Met Éireann weather warning related to Storm Boelo – a Status Yellow wind alert for Co Donegal – expired at 3pm on Sunday. A UK Met Office alert covering Northern Ireland has also passed.
The State planning body for severe weather, the National Directorate for Fire and Emergency Management, met on Sunday and urged the public to remain cautious.
“Although the storm has passed, I would urge people along coastal areas to continue to take note of prevailing conditions,” said Keith Leonard, head of the directorate.
“We will continue to see strong onshore winds, high tides, surge and large waves, which may continue to cause overtopping and coastal flooding along all coasts on Monday into Tuesday.”
ESB Networks said around 41,000 homes, farms and businesses, mostly in the northwest, were without electricity at 7.45am on Sunday as a result of the storm.
The number of affected properties had fallen to 18,000 by 12pm and the expectation was that “the vast majority of impacted customers” would have their supply restored by Sunday evening.
“ESB Networks crews have been deployed since first light in all impacted areas to continue to carry out the necessary restoration work where safe to do so,” the company said.
[ Dogs not welcome if we want to to enjoy the spectacle of returning overwintering birds Opens in new window ]
Leonard said conditions were challenging for those working to restore power supplies and that “some households may remain without power overnight”.
“Very close attention is being paid to the welfare of vulnerable people in affected areas,” he said.
In Northern Ireland, NIE Networks said it hopes to restore power to all customers by Sunday night.
Approximately 1,000 customers in the North remained without electricity as of 5pm on Sunday.
The high winds caused by Storm Boelo on Saturday night and Sunday damaged parts of the electricity network across Northern Ireland, with approximately 12,500 customers affected in total.
Andrew Cupples, head of system operations at NIE Networks, said that “thanks to the efforts of our engineers, contracting partners and support staff, we have now been able to restore power to around 11,500 customers”.
Up to 350 storm-related incidents, including fallen trees and flooding, were reported to the Department of Infrastructure, and a number of roads were closed for a time on Sunday.
The Foyle Bridge in Derry, which closed on Saturday due to high winds, reopened on Sunday afternoon.
More rain and strong winds are expected on Monday, with Status Yellow warnings issued for the west, south and southeast.
A rain warning for counties Cork and Kerry, which runs from 1am to 9am on Monday, advises of the potential for difficult travelling conditions and localised flooding.
[ ‘Having Manchán Magan as part of the Hometree journey was pretty deep and meaningful’ Opens in new window ]
A separate Status Yellow rain warning covering Cork, Kerry, Galway and Mayo will come into effect at 4pm on Monday and runs until 10pm.
“Soils are also saturated and more rainfall may cause some localised flooding, particularly in the southwest and west. River levels are also expected to remain elevated in the southwest and west on Monday and into Tuesday,” the directorate said.
A Status Yellow wind warning for counties Carlow, Clare, Cork, Donegal, Galway, Kerry, Kilkenny, Mayo, Waterford, Wexford and Wicklow covers the period from 5pm on Monday to midnight.
The stormy weather caused some transport disruption, with a number of flights cancelled at Dublin Airport on Saturday and several ferry crossings not departing between Dublin and Holyhead.
A number of weekend events were cancelled as a result, including the Lú Festival of Light in Drogheda and Trick or Treat in the City in Limerick.

title: Dr Crokes land 15th Kerry SFC title after scoring surge against Kenmare Shamrocks
description: Mark O’Shea finds the net as nine-point blitz turns contest on its head
content:
Dr Crokes are champions of Kerry again, with a late devastating burst delivering a 15th title against a Kenmare Shamrocks team who had a ringside seat to the awesome scoring power of the new champions when they get in their groove.
Having trailed for three-quarters of the game – and finding themselves seven points down in just the 10th minute – Dr Crokes did what they so often do, and nine unanswered points in a four-minute period late in the second half flipped the contest on its head.
A gallant Kenmare Shamrocks team, appearing in their first ever county final, simply had no answer to the power of Dr Crokes, with even the superb Sean O’Shea – who posted nine points – powerless to stop the Killarney club’s surge.
The victory moves Dr Crokes two clear at the top of the roll of honour, sees them regain the title they held two years ago and delivers a remarkable ninth county championship medal for Brian Looney and Fionn Fitzgerald.
For Kenmare Shamrocks – only a senior club for the last decade – this will be a tough defeat to swallow having led by two points with 10 minutes to go before being blown away.
Tony Brosnan, twice, David Shaw and Tom Doyle raised orange flags in rapid succession between the 52nd and 55th minutes and when Cian McMahon raised a white flag the Killarney club went from two points behind to seven in front.
There was a late exchange of pointed frees between Sean O’Shea and Brosnan, but Dr Crokes were celebrating another county championship success by then.
It has all started so well for Kenmare who ran up a 1-3 to no score lead after just seven minutes; the goal coming from David Ciuciu’s fist in the sixth minute as the underdogs played with a stiff wind advantage under a winter sun.
Dr Crokes finally got a score from Alex Hennigan, and they picked away at the scoreboard through the second quarter with Brosnan, Cillian Fitzgerald, Charlie Keating and Shaw among the scorers as they trailed 1-8 to 0-7 at the interval.
[ Hugh Armstrong inspired by Mayo GAA stars as he lands Irish men’s marathon title Opens in new window ]
The Crokes started the second half with a 32nd-minute goal from Mark O’Shea, but Kenmare struck back within 30 seconds with Kevin O’Sullivan getting the final touch to restore his team’s four-point lead.
By the 42nd minute Dr Crokes had pulled level, 1-12 to 2-9, and while the Shamrocks momentarily pushed the lead back out to three thanks to Sean O’Shea (two-point free) and Donal O’Sullivan, the Kenmare men – who had Jack O’Sullivan sent off late for a second yellow card – had no answer to Dr Crokes’ late, great scoring blitz.

title: Gardaí release details of unidentified man found dead at Dublin recycling depot
description: Body found at Dublin facility in the early hours of Saturday
content:
A man found dead at a recycling facility in Dublin lay at the premises for several days before being found. Efforts were continuing this weekend to identify him.
Gardaí have released a description of the man, with a photograph of a tracksuit top he was wearing, in the hope somebody will recognise him and come forward.
“He is described as being aged between 20-50 years, slim build, white complexion, brown/blonde hair and has no tattoos,” a Garda statement said.
“The clothing on the deceased was a white Adidas t-shirt with three light blue stripes on each shoulder, a blue Nike sweatshirt/jumper, a grey Nike tracksuit bottoms and a navy/white Adidas tracksuit top.”
The discovery of his body is the latest incident in which human remains have been found in recycling or refuse mounds at processing depots.
Some of those cases involved accidental deaths, but in others the victim was murdered and their remains dumped in refuse bins.
Gardaí are investigating all circumstances surrounding Saturday morning’s discovery and have yet to determine the deceased man’s identity. A postmortem examination has been concluded, though gardaí have not released the details.
Workers at the waste recycling facility in Clondalkin found the body just before 1am, with work stopping immediately and An Garda Síochána alerted.
The scene was sealed off pending the arrival of a pathologist to examine the remains in situ before they were removed by ambulance to undergo a postmortem. The resources of a homicide inquiry have been committed to the case.
“A senior investigating officer has been appointed to lead the investigation. An incident room has been established at Ronanstown Garda station,” said the force, as it appealed to anyone with information to come forward.
Local Sinn Féin Cllr William Carey said: “I just feel for the family. My thoughts would go out for any family of any person who is found in those circumstances.”
[ Gardaí treating discovery of man’s body at Clondalkin waste-recycling plant as suspicious Opens in new window ]
The depot where the remains were found is the same facility where the body of Co Meath man Andrew Haire was discovered in July . The 35-year-old, from Foxtown, Summerhill, had used homeless services in Dublin and Cork.
A postmortem on his remains was inconclusive as to the cause of his death, and the investigation into how he died and how his remains were brought in a bin to the Dublin facility is ongoing.
Rough sleepers at times seek protection from the elements by climbing into industrial bins, which are collected by refuse trucks and the contents crushed by the vehicles.
In Haire’s case, it is unclear if he climbed into a bin or if his body was placed there by unknown parties after his death.
In 2014, the dismembered remains of Mark Burke (36) , originally from Sandyford, Dublin, were found at a recycling centre in Ballyfermot. The last confirmed sighting of the father of seven had been in Dún Laoghaire.
He had to be identified using DNA testing and searches located only about 60 per cent of his remains. An inquest in 2016 heard that tools were used to dismember his body. His murder remains unsolved.

title: Dublin marathon: Family rivalry, lengthy friendships and a group of lads ready to go ‘wild’
description: Thousands line the streets to cheer on record number of runners
content:
On a cold and windy Sunday morning, thousands of people, many waving flags, holding posters and ringing bells, lined the streets to watch their loved ones take part in the Irish Life Dublin Marathon .
A record of 19,190 participants took part in this year’s event, with Ethiopia’s Abay Alemu Lesa winning the men’s race with a time of 2:10:28. Zenebu Fikdau Jebesa, also from Ethiopia, took the women’s title with a time of 2:24:26.
The trip around the 42.2km route took more than three hours for most, with many entrants hugging friends and family, posing for photographs and changing into warmer clothes after crossing the finish line at Mount Street Upper.
One of the participants was Chris Connolly, better known by his social media handle Get Better With Chris. He overcame addiction and started documenting his recovery and running journey online.
As he stood speaking to The Irish Times, passersby called out “well done Chris” and “well done, man” to him.
“For most of my life, people used to run away from me and to be here where I’m from, Dublin, run the Dublin marathon, hearing my name, other people’s names and hear people’s stories, it’s incredible,” he said.
Connolly said his goal was to encourage others “to get themselves out of the darkness”.
Only two weeks ago he ran the length of Spain, a distance of around 1,400km.
“I was running double marathons a day so to only have to do one marathon, it’s a treat,” he said. “I’m so grateful for running, I’m so grateful for a second chance and I’m so grateful for each and every single person who supports me.”
Connolly said he could feel blisters forming but was “oozing gratitude” having finished his run in three hours and 10 minutes.
[ Hugh Armstrong inspired by Mayo GAA stars as he lands Irish men’s marathon title Opens in new window ]
“You get to hear people’s stories and you get to connect with people in the most vulnerable and the most amazing way.”
Jean Coleman, from Galway, completed her 20th marathon alongside her son, Seán Ryan.
She found it “really, really tough” this year but achieved a personal best time despite the elements.
The 61-year-old, who received a silver medal in her age category, said she loves the “freedom” running gives her and “knowing I’m living the best version of myself”.
“I’m better at everything else in my life because I get out to have a run and I feel great about it,” said Coleman, who said she felt “privileged” to get to the start line “injury free”.
It was Coleman’s second year entering the race with her son and it was clear there was a competitive streak in the family. She noted that she had beaten him by seven minutes last year but this year he took bragging rights by nine minutes.
“It’s very, very special,” she said, adding that her husband and another son had turned out to support them at Ballsbridge.
To celebrate, she planned on warming up, eating pizza and enjoying a glass of wine.
Dubliners Jenny Keegan and Nicola Brennan, friends for more than 20 years, completed their second marathon together.
The pair are both in their early 40s and Brennan said it was “way tougher than I thought it was going to be”.
Keegan said Brennan was “dragging me through it” as “she was the one with the strength this year ... I couldn’t even talk”.
The friends said seeing their children at around the 27km mark provided “a big pick-me-up”. Brennan said they were “doing it for the mammies”.
[ Abay Alemu Lesa wins men’s Dublin Marathon Opens in new window ]
Friends Eamonn Yeates, Luke O’Halloran, James Kealy and Cillian Kelly were waiting on their friend Ben Cranley to complete the marathon, wearing white T-shirts featuring his face and holding signs.
The friends, aged 20 and 21, said Cranley was running the marathon for Breakthrough Cancer Research in memory of his father, JP, who died last year. He has raised €13,000 to date.
“JP was a great man and we’re all up here supporting him today,” Yeates said.
The friends from Co Meath said Cranley was “always a big runner” but said the death of his father “really drove him on to do something in his memory”.
They supported him at different points around the course, including at the 15km mark near Chapelizod, at which point Cranley was “absolutely flying it”.
They were planning to surprise him later, with an overnight hotel stay and dinner before going “wild” for the night to celebrate his achievement.
