title: Michael Carrick on the brink after Manchester United are humiliated by Bournemouth
description: Manager dropped Bruno Fernandes but players failed to respond as Bournemouth run out easy winners at Old Trafford
content:
After Bruno Fernandes was dropped for “pure football” reasons – according to Michael Carrick – could Manchester United actually win a game of football?
The answer, again, was a resounding, humiliating no, and if the manager’s job remains in real peril, you have to wonder, too, if this beleaguered team should steel themselves for a relegation dogfight. They lack imagination, cohesion, fight, confidence, and anything resembling joy, and so now hovering a point above the drop zone, survival cannot be taken for granted.
Goals from Rayan, Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson downed United, yet what has killed Carrick and his side in the past fortnight is the insubordination of Fernandes and Lisandro Martínez plus the deeper malaise of a club that is riven by factions.
The Jim Ratcliffe-led football department may issue Carrick the bullet but the next man – Eddie Howe is favoured and is open to the job – will surely not break the boom-bust cycle that is each new manager’s fate. Before this latest debacle, you had to flick the calendar back 45 days to September 10th (eight games ago), for the last time United chalked up a “W” and gave their fans reason to cheer.
Once more Carrick’s men failed to do so. Equally as disappointing is how, in the days since Fernandes’s public takedown of Carrick, no apology has been forthcoming from the captain.
Where Martínez did say sorry for criticising Jason Wilcox (though, not to the director of football), the United captain’s silence speaks volumes. If Carrick made an error in not dropping Martínez for his outburst, discarding Fernandes was the correct call and so Harry Maguire’s redemption arc was complete, being handed the armband, after it was taken off him and given to the Portuguese in July 2023.
Now, Carrick surely fears being removed after a buoyant Bournemouth made it four successive wins versus an opponent offering scant resistance, as the boos ringing out at the end signified.
As is the case for this Carrick iteration, midfield control was an issue throughout. Youri Tielemans lost the ball, Bournemouth’s passing went tap-tap-tap, and United were turned.
Even when Leny Yoro fashioned a one-two with Tielemans and swept the ball left to Diogo Dalot, the move foundered, and moments later the young right back was clearing from beneath his bar as a Rayan cross went close to teeing Evanilson up. All of this, yet again, pointed to a team that seem unable to execute whatever Carrick’s plan is.
Senne Lammens would hoof upfield aimlessly, Maguire heads possession back to a white shirt instead of chesting down, and as the half-hour passed a wild Dalot shot was their sole one registered.
So, when Bournemouth scored it was due to United shooting themselves in both feet. First came Ayden Heaven’s wild scissor challenge that had Evanilson leaping out of danger and was adjudged a yellow-card offence.
The second self-inflicted moment came when Justin Kluivert’s free-kick, on a diagonal from Bournemouth’s right, was allowed to drop on Rayan’s boot freely with the Brazilian entirely unmarked.
“Sacked in the morning” came the derisory chants from the travelling faithful and when their men doubled then lead on 42 minutes you wondered if Carrick might not last until then.
Again, this should have been avoided. This time Yoro was to blame as he contrived to slip near United’s area, allowing Adrien Truffert to collect, the left back squared to Tavernier, who slid into the net.
Cue the unfurling of a Stretford End tifo that said: “STANDARDS” above the faces of Eric Cantona, Bryan Robson and Roy Keane, the Cherries congregation this time offering, “going down with the City”, on repeat.
Carrick’s move for a second half that might decide his fate was to take off Tielemans for Matheus Cunha, Mason Mount (anonymous again), taking the No 10 position. If the manager had, indeed, dropped Fernandes for his form, then the opening period was a fair argument to reinstate him. Yet if Rayan had not fluffed a simple chance to make it 3-0 even the mutineer would not be able to save United.
Next, though, it was game – and, possibly Carrick’s tenure – over. Lammens charged out to clear a through ball, Evanilson beat him to it, rounded the flailing goalkeeper, and from around 40 yards out on the right sliced a curving finish into the waiting net.
Carrick’s visage was a picture of hurt. On the bench, Fernandes zipped his top right up, while in his posh seat, Wilcox sank lower into his winter coat. This would not stop him hearing, towards the end, the chants of “Jason Wilcox is a w****r”. Cruel but there is true pain being felt in these parts. – Guardian

title: Citing official set to trigger disciplinary case after Gavin Coombes allegations
description: Munster backrow forward alleges his testicles were grabbed by a Leinster player during Saturday’s game
content:
The citing commissioner for the Leinster - Munster game in the Aviva Stadium on Saturday, Scotland’s Peter Ferguson, is expected to initiate a disciplinary case following the allegation by Munster number 8 Gavin Coombes that his testicles were grabbed by an opposing player.
Ferguson has a 48-hour window from the full-time whistle to decide whether the incident should warrant a citing, and the likelihood is that at some juncture on Monday the URC will announce details of a formal disciplinary process.
Coombes made the allegation to the match referee Andrew Brace in the 39th minute of Leinster’s 24-18 win in front of a 37,000 attendance. Brace referred the allegation to his TMO Colin Stanley, but they could find no evidence to substantiate the claim.
However, it is understood that as part of the coverage there is another camera angle – which was not made available to Stanley – that Munster back-room staff, among others, have seen and that does increase the grounds for a citing.
Ferguson spoke to several players immediately after the game, as is standard practice, and Munster head coach Clayton McMillan said: “It’s one of those things that we leave in the hands of the powers that be. All I know is that I back our players 100 per cent that if they make an allegation like that, they wouldn’t do it lightly, and that’s not the sort of person Gavin is, so we’ll see where that goes.”
His counterpart Leo Cullen said he had not seen the incident and intimated that Coombes had backed down on his allegation to some degree.
“It looked like he [Coombes] had changed his mind halfway through that accusation as well. So I don’t know.”
In clarifying, Cullen added: “Well, that’s the way it sounded, once the scrum was packing down. But I don’t know. Obviously, once that accusation is made, it becomes a serious matter for the citing commissioner. So my comment is not going to help in any way here. But from what I’ve seen, I can’t see anything.”
However, it is understood that Coombes fully stands by his allegation and, given the claim was made against one of his own Leinster players, Cullen admitted: “It’s not ideal. Yeah, it’s not ideal. So, you’d want to be very clear if something’s happened.”
Ironically, it is almost a year to the day since the Bulls’ hooker Jan-Hendrik Wessels was handed a nine-week suspension for grabbing the testicles of Connacht’s Josh Murphy during a URC game in October last year at the Dexcom Stadium.
Murphy’s red card for punching Wessels following the alleged grab before the Springboks’ hooker was cited and suspended for nine weeks on the balance of probabilities rather than video evidence, much to the annoyance of the Bulls, South African supporters and Rassie Erasmus. Wessels’s ban was reduced by only one week following his appeal, and he was ruled out of their end-of-year tour.
The match-citing commissioner that day in Galway was also Ferguson.
Cullen had not had any discussion with any of the officials about the incident and he laughed off his exchange with the Munster defence coach Denis Leamy, who was previously an assistant to Cullen at Leinster.
“Yeah, but we were former coaching mates, so we were just having a very passionate discussion about the game,” said Cullen. “We’re still very good mates, yeah.”
Regarding Leinster’s comeback from 13-0 down with four tries to earn a bonus-point win, Cullen hailed his team’s composure.
“They’re always unbelievably fiercely contested derby games. Munster, I thought, were good in the contact area, probably a little bit better than us in the first half, both sides of the ball, and obviously they went into a 13-0 lead.
“I was like, ‘Oh, is this going to be a bit like it was last year in Croke Park?’” added the Leinster coach in reference to Munster’s win there a year ago.
“But I thought the players showed good composure to come back and get a try, and we started getting a little bit of an ascendancy, but then we would give away a turnover.
“You had to carry into that breeze. Obviously, it’s tricky enough conditions, the way it looked, certainly from the wind point of view. So you’re going to have to carry; you’re going to have to roll your sleeves up in the first half.

“There was a couple of times we were just a little bit off, gave away turnovers, and that gives Munster life. But the message really at half-time was ‘just stick to it’ and make sure they enjoy themselves. And keep pounding away.
Although Munster rallied to earn a losing bonus point with Ben O’Connor’s try from the last play of the game, McMillan’s overriding emotion was one of disappointment.
“We didn’t come here to lose and we don’t take any satisfaction out of being gallant losers. To walk away with a bonus point is nice because you look at the table and it’s pretty congested, but it was genuine disappointment in the changing shed because we felt like we had enough opportunities and we didn’t nail them all.”

title: Hugh Armstrong inspired by Mayo GAA stars as he lands Irish men’s marathon title
description: Ballina man driven on by All-Ireland glory as Judith Storm claims women’s title
content:
With no fear of any exaggeration, Hugh Armstrong traces his decisive moment in Sunday’s Irish Life Dublin Marathon straight back to Mayo winning the All-Ireland football title in Croke Park last July.
On a day when fast times and perhaps some higher finishing positions were blown off course, Armstrong delivered on the promise he made to himself when his native county ended their 75-year wait for the All-Ireland, as he won the Irish national marathon title which goes to the top men’s and women’s finishers in Dublin.
The 32-year-old from Ballina made his marathon debut in Dublin seven years ago, finishing third best Irishman. Thoroughly reinspired this time, he judged his effort to perfection to finish in 2:14:51, eighth best overall, just one place ahead of Killian Mooney, who had matched him stride-for-stride for long stages, before finishing in 2:15:44.
“I was at the match when Mayo won, and honest to God, I thought to myself that day, I’ll try go out now and win my cup as well,” said Armstrong, who had played some underage football with Knockmore before winning his first senior running title as national half-marathon champion two years ago.
“Obviously that was a great day for Mayo, and we were all out celebrating and everything, but that was the day I decided I’m going to win my national title as well.”
He also attended secondary school in Crossmolina with the likes of current Mayo footballer Conor Loftus, the same school Kobe McDonald attended some years later.
Mooney was nonetheless satisfied with finishing second best Irishman, the 31-year-old from Dundrum South Dublin making the national podium for the first time. Stephen McAuley from Letterkenny AC was also content with his hard-fought bronze medal, finishing in 2:16:37, good enough for 10 th best overall.
With Ethiopian runners ultimately dominating the elite international races – Abay Alemu Lesa and Zenebu Fikadu taking the top men’s and women’s prizes of €15,000 – the race for the first Irish women’s finisher was only decided inside the last 400m, when Judith Storm finally reeled in long-time leader Sorcha Nic Dhómhnaill.
In contrast to Armstrong, Storm only took up competitive running four years ago, the 39-year-old mother of four joining City of Derry Spartans AC, having originally moved to Belfast from her native Scotland 16 years ago.
After a conservative first half, passed in 1:18:08, at that point over 90 seconds behind Nic Dhómhnaill, Storm finished in 2:35:46, 10th best woman overall and just 12 seconds clear of Nic Dhómhnaill. Meghan Ryan from Dundrum South Dublin, who’d finished fourth best Irishwoman last year, was well satisfied with her performance to claim bronze in 2:40:47.
[ Abay Alemu Lesa wins men’s Dublin Marathon Opens in new window ]
Armstrong considers himself more a lifelong runner, going back to his schoolboy days in Mayo, and later while on a running scholarship in Providence College in Rhode Island – following in the strides of David McGlynn, another Providence graduate who was the first Irish finisher last year.
Living in Portarlington and an accountant with An Post, Armstrong also became a father to son Conor for the first time last November, along with his Kenyan-born wife Shiru.
He also credits his coach Feidhlim Kelly of the Dublin Track Club for keeping him on course in recent years: “Feidhlim puts an awful lot of his life into this sport, he deserves a lot of praise. I think this is one of the titles he hadn’t won yet, as a coach. So I can’t wait to give him a hug and celebrate with him,” he said.
[ Podcaster Ger Gilroy on moving to RTÉ, his upstart attitude and starting over: ‘Your job is to win, right?’ Opens in new window ]
“I was also watching the interview with Jerry Kiernan, after he won Dublin in 1982. It was the year Kerry lost the All-Ireland to Offaly, when they were going for the five in a row, and he was saying this was good compensation for Kerry, that he went and won the marathon title. For me it’s both titles for Mayo, so no need for compensation.
“Maybe if we had better weather today, I might have run a bit faster, but I won’t worry about that. I’m glad just to take the Irish title. It probably is the pinnacle for me. I’d say the marathon title is probably one of the toughest ones to win and one of the most high-profile ones.”
Patrick Monahan from Le Chéile AC in Kildare won his ninth title in the wheelchair race in 1:46:03, and will take on the New York Marathon next Sunday.

title: Alexander Isak applies finishing touch as Liverpool bring Brighton’s winning run to an end
description: The expensive trio of Isak, Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola look increasingly at home under Andoni Iraola
content:
Brighton’s emphatic run was blown off course at Anfield as Liverpool moved up to fourth with an appetite and urgency at both ends of the pitch that showed Andoni Iraola’s methods taking root. It is Liverpool, convincing winners on home soil for the first time this season in the Premier League, who looked upwardly mobile.
Florian Wirtz was instrumental in an opening goal officially credited to Brighton’s Pascal Gross and Alexander Isak converted his sixth league goal of the campaign to shatter the visitors’ sequence of four successive Premier League wins.
Brighton’s winning streak had included 15 goals and none against but there was neither attacking verve nor defensive resilience on show from Fabian Hürzeler’s side. Liverpool had a monopoly on both, and the sight of Bradley Barcola racing back to defend and Ronald Araújo thundering into challenges will have satisfied Iraola just as much as the incisiveness up front.
Storm Boelo raged outside the stadium but inside it was relatively calm, vindicating the decision to proceed with the game. But not for Brighton. The run of wins and clean sheets that had swept Hurzeler’s team into third place before kick-off was devastated by Liverpool’s attacking force. The home side’s superior first-half performance was another demonstration of the expensive trio of Wirtz, Isak and Barcola feeling increasingly at home under Iraola.
Liverpool were aggressive and sharp from the start, in contrast to their opening against Villarreal in the Champions League on Tuesday, and opened the scoring just as Brighton were beginning to exert their first serious spell of pressure.
There was an element of good fortune about the breakthrough but it also encapsulated the differing intensity between the teams when Wirtz held off Lewis Dunk and Araújo beat both the Brighton captain and Oliver Boscagli to the loose ball. His low cross pinballed off two Brighton players before rebounding to Wirtz, whose first-time shot deceived Bart Verbruggen via another deflection off Gross. Wirtz’s low-key celebration hinted at what was to come. It was not his first league goal of the campaign and second goal in successive games after all. The breakthrough was officially credited as an own goal from the Brighton midfielder.
It should also have been a Liverpool equaliser rather than the opener as Yasin Ayari had a glorious chance to give Brighton the lead moments earlier. Diego Gómez and Gross combined to pierce Liverpool’s left flank and present Ayari with a free sight of goal with Alisson dragged across to his left. The Brighton forward blazed high into the Kop and would soon have added reason to rue the miscue.
Liverpool quickly doubled their lead when capitalising on more casual Brighton defending. Boscagli was again found wanting when attempting to deal with Alisson’s clearance deep into the visitors’ half. The left back struck a clearance straight at Barcola and was then left floundering as the France international, deployed on the right, brushed aside his efforts to recover possession.
Isak steered Barcola’s delivery inside the far corner with a deft, sidefoot finish to score in three consecutive league games for the first time since January 2025. It was Liverpool’s first goal in the first half of a Premier League game at Anfield this season. There was no surprise whatsoever when Boscagli was withdrawn at half-time.
Brighton attacked with greater conviction than they defended but with Araújo, Jérémy Jacquet and Virgil van Dijk all making telling interventions, and receiving impressive support from all quarters, Alisson was not seriously tested. The visitors’ best hope of a recovery stemmed from the Liverpool goalkeeper’s own risky pass to Alexis Mac Allister, which gifted possession back to Brighton and resulted in Ayari striking a post from 20 yards out.
Jack Hinshelwood, Boscagli’s replacement, and fellow substitute Malick Yalcouyé injected more energy and bite into Brighton’s second-half display but an end product from the visitors remained lacking. Too many overhit crosses and poor final balls enabled Liverpool to protect their lead in comfort. – Guardian

title: O’Brien secures more ‘classic’ success with Queenstown to top triple-Group One weekend
description: Irish trainer now on 25 Group One victories for 2026 and closing on 2017 world-record tally of 28
content:
Aidan O’Brien emerged from the weekend in familiar territory, having uncovered two more prime classic prospects for 2027 and collected a final “classic” for 2026 with the six-year-old gelding Queenstown at Saint-Cloud on Sunday.
The Prix Royal Oak is still widely referred to as France’s version of the St Leger, although it was opened to older horses in 1979, preceding the Curragh Leger’s same move by four years.
It means that, strictly speaking, it isn’t a classic contest any more, and O’Brien had won it just once before with Yeats in 2008.
However, Queenstown, a horse whose day job often involves leading younger stable companions at Ballydoyle and was runner-up in the 2025 Royal Oak, finally stepped up to Group One glory of his own with success in the near-two-mile test.
On the back of being placed in last weekend’s Long-Distance Cup, and the Prix Du Cadran a fortnight before that, it was an admirably gritty performance by a son of the legendary sire Galileo who was having his 21 st career start.
There was no fluke about it either, as Queenstown was there to be shot at after making most of the running, and a proven Group One winner in Consent couldn’t haul him in, ultimately going down by three-parts-of-a-length.
Earlier on the card, the much younger Drumbeat graduated to Group One success too with a smooth performance when giving O’Brien a seventh success in the Criterium de Saint-Cloud.
All of it came 24 hours after Giant Sequoia was perhaps most impressive of all, notching a three-length Futurity success at Doncaster that all but assures O’Brien of a ninth British trainers’ title.
On the back of an unusually quiet period during August and some of September when the Ballydoyle team battled a viral infection, it has been a much more productive October for O’Brien that ensures he once again goes into the winter loaded with classic shots for next year.
Darkness Falls, successful in the Dewhurst, tops betting lists for the Guineas and Derby, and Giant Sequoia could have similar targets after landing Britain’s other top juvenile contest.
The apparent third string of a Ballydoyle trio, the Frankel colt was a first Group One winner for Ballydoyle for Dylan Browne McMonagle.
Ryan Moore had to settle for third on Noble Exhibit in the Futurity but was very much on the right one in Paris as Drumbeat proved much too good for his stable companion Shakespeare. Joseph O’Brien’s Jesus Green was third.
Having previously won the Zetland Stakes over a similar 10-furlong trip at Newmarket, O’Brien was keen to dismiss the idea that Drumbeat might automatically be a staying type in 2027. The colt is a 12-1 shot for the Epsom Derby.
“I think he’s come forward since Newmarket. It was a classy performance today. He came up through the middle of them, and you’d have to be happy.
“He’ll be trained for the classics. He’s not a slow horse, and I’d say he’d have no problem starting in a Guineas, whether it’s an Irish, a French, or an English. And then he’ll be very comfortable going up to a mile-and-a-quarter, and maybe even further.
“He’s by Wootton Bassett, and usually they’re pacy enough; they’re not slow. And he had to be pacy today. He’s not just a stayer; he quickened through the middle,” he said.
Earlier, the O’Brien pair, Capability Brown and Aix La Chapelle, filled the frame in the Group One Criterium International behind local winner Master Man.
The Irish man’s Group One tally for the year is now 25 – just three shy of his 2017 world record – and it delivered a confidence boost in advance of this week’s Breeders’ Cup action in Keeneland.
O’Brien holds a record 21 Breeders’ Cup victories, a feat matched only by US trainer Bob Baffert. They include eight wins in the Juvenile Turf for colts, and Great Barrier Reef is favourite to add to that when the meeting opens on Friday.

However, it is the triple-Group One winner Sun Goddess who is a general odds-on favourite to score in the Juvenile Turf Fillies on the same card.
Elsewhere, the jumps campaign continues to crank into a higher gear, and a pair of Grade One winning mares are set to return to action at Wexford on Bank Holiday Monday.
Colm Murphy’s Zanoosh, winner of the top-class novice Mares event at Fairyhouse last Easter, makes her debut over fences in a Beginners Chase where testing ground conditions will help her on a return to the minimum trip.
However, the going is just what The Big Westerner needs when she has just a third start over fences in the Listed chase. Henry de Bromhead’s runner beat Jade De Grugy in Limerick’s Grade One novice chase last Christmas and hasn’t been seen since.

title: Andy Burnham’s call for debate on free movement with EU draws mixed Labour response
description: Senior cabinet ministers are keen for the UK to form closer relationship with the EU
content:
Andy Burnham ’s call for the UK to consider a return to free movement with Europe has been backed by senior cabinet ministers including Angela Rayner, but risks causing concern among fellow red wall MPs.
The British prime minister made his plea for an “honest discussion” about free movement in an interview with the Sunday Times, making it clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU .
“Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” Burnham said.
“Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”
His remarks were supported by Rayner, the housing secretary, who told Sky News that it was “just pragmatism”.
“It’s about what is the best deal for Britain and that’s what we are asking the public to look at. The prime minister is clear that you can’t take anything off the table when you’re having a conversation,” she said.
Stella Creasy, a Labour MP and the chair of the Labour Movement for Europe, said Burnham was right that the UK was “long overdue for a grown-up conversation about what EU freedom of movement actually means to our supply chains and for jobs for British citizens”.
A number of senior cabinet ministers are keen for the UK to form a much closer relationship with the EU to help boost growth, potentially involving a return to the single market and accepting free movement as a result.
[ Andy Burnham is removing a Victorian-era law that singled out Catholics and Jews. Why now? Opens in new window ]
However, a number of Labour MPs with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the so-called red wall in the north and midlands are wary about reopening the arguments for free movement or rejoining the EU.
Burnham’s comments drew an immediate response from the right of politics, with the Conservatives and Reform UK criticising the idea of reopening the debate. Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said the idea of reopening free movement was “another example of Burnham’s foot-in-mouth syndrome”. – Guardian

title: AIL round-up: Terenure take D6W Derby after arm wrestle against St Mary’s
description: Old Belvedere go top of the table after a first win over Clontarf in a decade
content:
Back in 2017, PBC Cork beat Glenstal Abbey 11-3 in the Munster Schools Cup final at a sodden, wind-battered Thomond Park to draw level with their rivals CBC on 29 titles.
The Pres team featured Peter Sylvester and Seán French, scorer of all 11 points, as well as prop Brian O’Connor, while Aran Egan and Caolan Dooley were in the Glenstal squad.
All five were in the Terenure team which went to local rivals St Mary’s in similar conditions on Saturday and came away with a 17-12 victory in the D6W Derby. Paul Barr, their coach that day and on Saturday, had a simple prematch message. “I said to them that ‘this is Pres-Christians, all right?’.”
Critically, Terenure led 14-12 after facing the elements. Mary’s prop Michael McCormack finished from close range following Ruairí Shields’s 50-22 before tries by O’Connor and the outstanding Sylvester – Adam La Grue’s grubber and Harrison Brower’s jackal earning the attacking lineouts.
Myles Carey regathered Conor Dean’s restart to set up Aaron O’Sullivan but as conditions worsened Egan’s scrum penalty was the second-half’s only score.
An arm wrestle of key moments, each one celebrated more loudly than the last, was bookended by Will Hickey somehow holding up Shields over the line and Seán Rigney preventing Carey from grounding the ball.
“You come here and you take on a champion side and because they played like a champion side I am very satisfied with the performance and result,” said Barr.
“It’s disappointing to lose the derby at home,” admitted St Mary’s head coach Mark McHugh. “But it’s a long season, a lot of derbies to be played and we know that if we continue to show some of the dog in the fight that we showed today, then we’ll be competitive more often than not.”
With eight points covering the top nine, Old Belvedere are the new leaders above ‘Nure on points difference after a gutsy 11-7 win at home to Clontarf , their first over their rivals in a decade.
Sam Wisniewski kicked two penalties but Dylan Donnellan’s sixth try of the campaign earned ‘Tarf a 7-6 interval lead. Replacement George Hadden’s 61st-minute try proved decisive in another tough, physical game.
UCD showed character aplenty following their 61-15 loss to ‘Tarf with an 18-13 win at home to Cork Constitution . Their young pack went to war, with Dylan McNeice and Dan Barron outstanding, and they were well directed by halfbacks James Sherwin and Paddy Clancy. Charlie Molony and Maxim Aschenbrenner scored tries, while Billy Scannell and Bobby O’Callaghan replied for Con.
A couple of breakaway tries by Matias Jensen and Páidí Farrell earned Old Wesley a 14-7 interval lead at Energia Park before Young Munster’s set-piece buckled and they conceded four yellow cards. Welsey capitalised, Rian Handley and Liam Grover tries sealing Division 1A’s only attacking bonus point.
In their very own microclimate at Ballymacarn Park, Ballynahinch secured their first win of the season by holding off Lansdowne 21-17. In an old-school performance, a 65th-minute try by captain Claytan Milligan increased their lead to 21-5 into a gale before late tries by Daniel Hurley and Juan Beukes earned Lansdowne a bonus point.

title: Celtic come from behind to beat Hibernian after Owen Elding’s early goal
description: Camilo Durán was Celtic’s match-winner as they bounced back from their latest European disappointment
content:
Camilo Durán moved into double figures for the season as Celtic reasserted themselves at the top of the Scottish Premiership by coming from behind to defeat beleaguered Hibernian 2-1 at windy Easter Road.
After another Europa League setback at home to Celta Vigo on Thursday, the champions bounced back with a victory that restored their four-point cushion over Rangers at the top.
Bottom side Hibs took an early lead through Ireland international striker Owen Elding but it was swiftly cancelled out by a Jason Kerr own goal before Durán’s 10th of the season edged the Hoops ahead just before the break.
It proved enough to secure a ninth win in 10 league games this term and ensure recently appointed Hibs boss Marink Reedijk suffered a third straight defeat since succeeding David Gray.
There were a couple of blemishes for Celtic, however, as substitute Alistair Johnston’s return from injury lasted barely 20 minutes before he had to go off, while £11 million forward Kasper Hogh – restored to the starting line-up after notching in just one of his 13 previous matches for the Hoops – again drew a blank before being replaced in the 64th minute.
Hibs made two changes, with Irish international midfielder Jamie McGrath and Joe Newell in for Azeem Abdulai and Martin Boyle, who withdrew late on due to illness.
Hogh’s introduction in place of Haissem Hassan was Celtic’s only tweak to Thursday’s line-up, while key duo Johnston and Cameron Carter-Vickers were on the bench after their recent layoffs.
Easter Road was significantly below capacity, owing to Hibs’ poor form, a ban for the hosts’ Block Seven ultras group, Celtic again being allocated only half of the South Stand even though the rest of it was all but empty, and probably due to some being put off leaving the house amid the ongoing gusts of Storm Boelo.
But the home support were swiftly warmed as Hibs grabbed the lead in the third minute. Newell slipped a quick free-kick in behind the unprepared Celtic defence and Elding got himself clear on the left of the box before the former Sligo Rovers frontman drove a low angled shot from seven yards out beyond Sam Johnstone and in at the far post.
Captain Callum McGregor helped Celtic summon a fifth-minute equaliser as he drove forward and saw a deflected shot from edge of the box tipped wide by Raphael Sallinger. After the first corner was scrambled behind by the hosts, the second – an inswinger from Benjamin Nygren – was inadvertently headed into his own net by Kerr from a couple of yards out.
Hogh then had three sights of goal from close range that could have brought an end to his barren run, with the third of those the best as he was denied by a brilliant save from Sallinger.
Moments after Thibault Klidje threatened for the hosts with a lob that drifted just over, the Hoops went ahead in the 43rd minute.
Hibs defender Marko Ivezic intercepted Nygren’s pass just outside the box, but the loose ball broke to the alert Durán, who drove forward and rasped an emphatic strike beyond Sallinger from 17 yards out.
The only notable events of the second half were Johnston’s return being cut short and Hibs sending on centre back Grant Hanley to play up front in the 82nd minute, which – after initial bemusement from the home support – helped make them a slightly more dangerous proposition in the closing stages.

title: Haunted Dancehall 2026 at NCH: Kelela brings superstar aura to risk-taking festival’s first night
description: Review: The avant-garde R&B singer embodies the genre-blurring ethos of a line-up that also features Nashpaints, Shampain, Voice Actor and Proc Fiskal
content:
Halloween has arrived a week early at the National Concert Hall , where a crowd fancy-dressed as the coolest people in Dublin – if you don’t have an ironic mullet you’ll feel out of place – has gathered on Saturday for the first day of Haunted Dancehall .
The charmingly esoteric festival grew out of an ambition to open up the 19th-century NCH building to an audience that might not typically don a dicky bow to attend a sit-down recital. Where else would you see people dressed as random members of Fontaines DC lining up to shuffle into a classical-music chamber?
The tension between the left-field attendees and the formal setting gives the event a distinctive ambience, and nobody better embodies its genre-blurring ethos than Kelela, the opening-night headliner.
The avant-garde R&B singer from Washington, DC, exists in a pop netherworld entirely of her own imagining. Think Janet Jackson singing over a grime remix of My Bloody Valentine. Then add the presence of a singer who brings a superstar aura to the comparatively small auditorium.
Kelela attracts a huge crowd to the main stage, where, framed by dry ice and backlighting, she shape-shifts from the bruised power balladry of Goin Down to the weightless space rock of Idea 1. She dances like a sad robot, while her voice, whether processed through a Charli XCX-style filter or gloriously unadorned, adds human vulnerability to her songs.
Her star power contrasts with an intimate early-evening set in the Kevin Barry Room by the Dublin musician Finn Carraher McDonald, aka Nashpaints, who delivers a suite of gauzy postrock. There’s the bonus of an early jump scare when someone turns the lights up and the audience can see the whites of each other’s eyes.
The same space later hosts the Galway DJ, broadcaster and barber Cóilí Collins, aka Shampain. He weaves through a selection of electronica, crouching studiously over his decks like a one-man west-of-Ireland Kraftwerk.
But perhaps the most atmospheric component of opening night is the Studio room, which has the feel of an illegal rave in a cave in the early 1990s. A highlight is the woozy turn by Voice Actor, the stage name of the Sheffield producer Noa Kurzweil, whose processed vocals unfurl like mysterious diary entries.
She is followed by Edinburgh’s Proc Fiskal, whose blend of electronic music, grime and Scottish trad attracts a decent crowd despite drawing the short straw of going on opposite Kelela.
Haunted Dancehall takes a real risk by unleashing hordes of hipsters on the genteel National Concert Hall. Out of this brew emerges a microfestival that is big on thrills and has more highs than a fistful of Halloween Haribo.

title: Listowel assault investigation expected to be upgraded to murder inquiry after man’s death
description: Glen Keane (21) was left in a critical condition after being attacked during last month’s racing festival
content:
A young man who was seriously injured in an assault in Co Kerry last month has died in hospital.
Glen Keane (21), from Slí na Spéire, Listowel, had been in a critical condition at Cork University Hospital ( CUH ) for the past month but died late on Saturday night.
He had been transferred to CUH after initially being brought to University Hospital Kerry following an assault in Listowel town centre on September 24th, during the Listowel Racing Festival.
Glen Keane suffered significant head injuries in the attack, which happened outside a pub in the Square at around 8.40pm.
Three men, one in his 30s and two in their 20s, were later arrested by gardaí and taken to Garda stations in Tralee and Listowel for questioning about the incident.
They were detained under Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act, which allows suspects to be held for up to 24 hours. They were all released without charge late on September 25th.
Gardaí have requested the services of the State Pathologist’s Office following Glen Keane’s death, and a postmortem is expected to be carried out on his body in the coming days.
The force will await the findings of the postmortem, but it is expected they will upgrade their investigation from one of assault to murder when they receive the results.

title: Kilmacud Crokes ease to Dublin SHC win that crushes Cuala’s double dream
description: It is Kilmacud’s first Dublin SHC triumph since 2022, achieved with an 11-point victory at Parnell Park
content:
On a weekend of storms, Kilmacud Crokes whipped up their best performance of the season at Parnell Park on Saturday night to win an eighth Dublin senior hurling title and rip through Cuala’s dreams of claiming a maiden county double.
Crokes led from the opening minute until the final whistle to win a first Dublin hurling championship since 2022 in a game shaped by the squally conditions but nonetheless dominated by the Stillorgan outfit.
With the storm at their back in the opening half, Crokes led 1-11 to 0-6 at the turnaround – Ronan Hayes netting an early goal. Given the conditions, it would have been natural if some of the chatter among supporters during the interval was to wonder if an eight-point lead was a wide enough gap. It was, and then some.
When Oisín O’Rorke scored a second Crokes goal eight minutes after the resumption to put them 2-11 to 0-8 in the ascendency, there was only going to be one winner.
Cuala, whose senior footballers had triumphed in the big-ball final last weekend, just never got going here. They were flat from the get-go. The Dalkey side managed to score just six points in each half and only 0-4 of their total was from play. You don’t win county finals with those numbers.
Crokes now move joint fourth in the roll of honour alongside Cuala, O’Tooles and UCD.
“Coming into this game, we probably weren’t playing that well. We’d had seven games in the Dublin championship and in none of them did we really put in a proper performance,” said Paddy Linehan, the joint manager of Crokes alongside John Dillon.
“Today they just went out and expressed themselves and they worked hard. This was a day for heart, spirit, determination and fight. I don’t think anyone could argue that we won nearly every battle out there. In fairness to Cuala they came back at us, but when it counted we stood up.”
Crokes attacked the game from the throw-in and the impressive Brian Hayes had a point on the board after only 30 seconds. They immediately set about using the power of the wind to their advantage – smacking over three points in the opening two minutes.
Cuala possibly felt they had stemmed the early Kilmacud pressure when Donal O’Shea tapped over a free in the third minute. But from the resulting puckout, a booming clearance by Eddie Gibbons was carried by the wind downfield and caused panic in the Cuala defence. When the ball broke out from within a ruck of bodies, Ronan Hayes was on hand to strike the loose ball first-time with a groundstroke that sent it beyond Seán Brennan, 1-3 to 0-1.
Cuala struggled to get their inside line on the ball and their sole score from play in the entire first half only arrived from Jamie Conroy one minute before the interval. They had already taken on plenty of water by that stage and trailed by 10 – as scores by Ronan Hayes, Finnian Donohoe, Dara Purcell and Fergal Whitely put Crokes in a strong position.
Cuala needed to start the second half strongly and they did register the first two scores after the break, from O’Shea and Liam Murphy. But there was to be no heroic comeback.
Brian Hayes picked out O’Rorke with a wonderfully arrowed pass in the 38th minute and the team captain made no mistake with his finish to put them nine ahead. Cuala were done. There would be no double.
“The wind was obviously a big factor, in fairness they probably managed playing into it in the second half better than we did in the first half,” said Cuala manager Donal Murphy. “At half-time maybe we thought that the score was appropriate to the wind, if you like, but it was clear in the second half they were just hurling that a little bit better than us. On the day I think they adapted better and their hurling was that bit sharper than us.
“On balance, I’m sure when we look back at it we’ll realise that the better team won on the day. We’d just be disappointed that we didn’t bring our best performance to the biggest day of the year. And we can’t use the weather as an excuse because they were playing in the same weather as we were.”
Crokes will meet Mount Leinster Rangers in a Leinster club quarter-final on November 8th. Kilmacud have never won a provincial hurling crown – they lost the 2022 Leinster final to Ballyhale Shamrocks.
“We’ll enjoy the next couple of days. Then we’re going to be looking at the Carlow champions. We’ll have to analyse them. We’ll get down to the training ground, we’ll start working on certain things. We’ll be taking Leinster really seriously,” added Linehan. “Cuala have won two All-Irelands, Na Fianna won an All-Ireland, we’ve been in one Leinster final. You have to deliver on the (big) days. We’ll enjoy this and then fingers crossed we can drive on in Leinster.”
Out in Stillorgan, a purple and gold tempest might be about to gather some momentum.

title: Thomas Markle snr may be ‘sex offender of grossest kind’, says Philippine minister
description: Metropolitan police gave letter to Meghan Markle in 2019 concerning ‘alleged offending’ involving her father
content:
All signs point to Thomas Markle snr being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind” although a full forensic investigation will give a “definitive picture”, the Philippine interior minister has said.
Authorities in the southeast Asian country are analysing digital images allegedly belonging to the estranged father of the duchess of Sussex that were said to have been found at his former home in Cebu. Meghan Markle ’s half-brother, Thomas Markle jnr, reported to authorities last week that he had apparently discovered a stash of child sexual abuse images.
“In these cases where family disputes are mixed up, we have to consider all the angles,” said Jonvic Remulla, the interior minister. “Right now all signs point to a possible sex offender of the grossest kind. We want to be sure before we release the findings. The forensics data will be complete in a week.”
Remulla said a statement would be released once the data had been analysed, without giving a specific date. “Please give us a week to determine the contents and to come up with a definitive picture,” he said. “We will release a statement then.”
Markle snr has denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail the accusations were “sick lies”.
Philippine police are also investigating a laptop found at the home in Cebu where Markle snr had been living until he returned to the US earlier this year.
In a statement given to Agence France-Presse, Remulla said the Philippine national police inspected Markle’s former home and found a “trove of child pornography materials as well as a laptop”.
“The PNP will co-ordinate with their counterparts to locate and take appropriate legal actions against Mr Markle if found that there is sufficient evidence to charge him,” he said.
Markle told the Mail the computers had not been in his possession since he left Mexico with his son in 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”.
He said: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.
“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”
Meghan Markle has said she is “ deeply distressed ” over the allegations, which were first reported in the Sun. She said she had broken off contact with her father to protect her children, prince Archie, seven, and princess Lilibet, five. He has never met them.
On Saturday, the Metropolitan police confirmed they gave a letter to Meghan in 2019 concerning “alleged offending” involving her father, but said they did not pass it on to other law enforcement agencies. Scotland Yard is considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to review its actions.
In a statement, a Met spokesperson said: “Following a thorough review of Met police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019 we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. It was sent to the MPS (Metropolitan Police Service) Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the duchess of Sussex.
“The letter was reviewed, and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the duke and duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.
“The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach.”
[ Meghan Markle ‘deeply distressed’ over allegation her father had child abuse images Opens in new window ]
In a statement on Friday issued through her spokesperson, the duchess said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.
“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father, and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.
“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.
“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”
She later said she had misremembered the year the Met had contacted her, and confirmed it had been 2019, not 2018 as she said on Friday.
A spokesperson for the duchess said: “In recalling events from more than seven years ago, without the benefit of a diary entry or contemporaneous record, it is understandable that she may have been mistaken by a few months.
“If the MPS holds a time-stamped record confirming that the letter was reviewed in 2019, that should be treated as the accurate reference point for when it was received and shared with the duchess.”
Sources said that although Meghan Markle was made aware of the allegations in 2019, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her.
The Sun reported that Markle jnr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu. Markle jnr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported. – The Guardian

title: Impossible to look away from Elizabeth Holmes in latest documentary on the Theranos fraudster
description: Her unblinking gaze, like the disembodied blue eyes on the billboard in The Great Gatsby, represents moral decay
content:
Y ou’d think we’d be weary of flimflam artists, tech vampires and alternative realities by now. But no.
It’s like Gertrude’s lust for Claudius in Hamlet: “As if increase of appetite had grown / By what it fed on.”
In a time of deceit, political, algorithmic and every other kind, a meditation on deceit has taken culture by storm.
Meditation is not the right word, actually. It’s more like a film noir thriller with a manipulative femme fatale, a destructive romance, a man meant to play the fall guy and an atmospheric cottage by the sea.
The three-hour documentary about Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, You Can See Everything, is paradoxically titled, because you can’t see much of anything. (Except her naked narcissistic fiance preening in the shower.) Holmes is busy obscuring the truth and building an illusory world where her dangerous fraud about comprehensive medical testing with a pinprick of blood was just an innocent hiccup.
“I know I didn’t commit any crime,” she assures filmmaker Nathan Fielder, training her big, blue Furby eyes on him. She doesn’t think she has ever lied in her life, she says. It was all just a misunderstanding. Never mind the threatening lawyers like David Boies she sicced on anyone who questioned her phantom technology.
Holmes abandoned her Steve Jobs black turtleneck for soccer mom sweaters. But she remains the perfect avatar for our age: She promised tech that would help humanity, then unleashed a deception that could have hurt humanity.
Holmes and her partner, who had two children before her 11-year sentence for fraud began in Texas in 2023, wanted a sympathetic documentary charting her last weeks with her family before she got locked up. They stumbled upon Fielder, who directed the movie along with Lance Oppenheim, and ended up starring in it.
Fielder originally did not intend to appear on-screen, but Holmes irresistibly drew him into her web, and the resulting game of cat-and-mouse between the two magicians is astonishing.
[ What is the reason for the enduring public fascination with Elizabeth Holmes? Opens in new window ]
The deadpan Fielder is a Canadian-born satirist who worked with Sacha Baron Cohen on the 2018 mockumentary Who Is America? and on his own shows, Nathan for You on Comedy Central and The Rehearsal on HBO, where he has built elaborate ruses. He is a master at spinning his own absurd reality, and so is Holmes.
The sparring of these two raises the question: Is there any point in searching for the truth, or is it better to settle into our own fractured, subjective realities?
At 30, Holmes became the first self-made female billionaire after she dropped out of Stanford at 20 and started Theranos. But she’s no role model for women. When she got in trouble, she embraced victimhood, turning from a confident Silicon Valley founder who dominated every room into a damsel in distress. In court, she blamed her lover/partner, Sunny Balwani, who got an almost 13-year sentence for helping Holmes defraud investors of more than $700 million. She said he abused her psychologically and sexually and controlled everything from her clothes to her diet. The jury was unconvinced.
Holmes tries to turn Fielder into a film-noir sap, someone who will believe her lies about her lies, be emotionally drawn to her and come to her rescue. And the documentary projects, then calls into question, a scenario where her current lover/partner, Billy Evans, is manipulating her, asking for a cut of the documentary’s profits supposedly behind her back, taking over her X account and putting up foul-mouthed posts pretending to be her, releasing a hologram of Holmes that he nonchalantly acknowledges might be used by some men online for porn.
The woman famous for her guile – suckering George Shultz, Jim Mattis, Henry Kissinger, Sam Nunn, Larry Ellison, Rupert Murdoch and other brainy older men – plays guileless, acting as if she can’t even scramble eggs without her controlling fiance’s help, or understand the simplistic joke in the classic Abbott and Costello Who’s on first? comedy routine. Fielder jokes that if Holmes had “just said that Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free”. The couple talk about building “monuments of love” to each other, but it’s more like monuments of manipulation.
Shultz’s grandson, Tyler Shultz, who was an intern and researcher at Theranos and then left and blew the whistle on Holmes, said on CBS Mornings that Holmes took in Fielder enough to allow doubt to creep in about her guilt.
“She knows that she was lying,” Shultz said, “because she created this whole web of lies that you would not have needed to create if you actually believed the lies.”
[ Spoiler alert: Slow Horses, Strictly Come Dancing and an Irish actor’s strange beach limbo Opens in new window ]
Shultz said that the harm to patients was horrible and that Fielder never laid out the dimensions of her crimes.
“We told people that they had HIV when they did not,” he said. “We told people that they had cancer when they did not. We told expecting mothers that they had lost their unborn child when they had not.”
Amanda Seyfried, who won an Emmy for playing Holmes in Hulu’s The Dropout, also wonders if Fielder is too “protective of her”. The actor reprises her role in some scenes in the documentary and visits Holmes’ family after she goes to prison, getting chided by Evans for her Hulu portrayal.
Evans is a handsome, buff man, the scion of a wealthy hotel family now determined to work with Liz, as she is known now, to straighten out the problems with her blood-testing method. But as the film goes on, there’s a Dorian Gray effect, where his face grows scarier, twisted into a mask of rage and subterfuge. Is Evans, not Fielder, the sap? As in film noir, the boyfriend carries a rod and is vowing vengeance.
Whether or not you think Fielder isn’t tough enough on Holmes, it is impossible to look away from her. Her unblinking gaze is like the disembodied blue eyes on the haunting billboard in The Great Gatsby, and both represent the same thing: moral decay.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

title: AIG executive accused of posting anti-Semitic comments no longer working for company
description: John Gillick claimed his X account, which accused Jewish people of being ‘filthy dogs’ and ‘human scum’, was hacked
content:
A senior executive at insurer AIG who allegedly posted anti-Semitic comments on his X account is no longer working with the company.
John Gillick was head of consumer marketing and sponsorship at AIG Ireland for more than 20 years and was involved with Dublin GAA , the Golfing Union of Ireland and Hockey Ireland in many of their sponsorship campaigns.
He posts on X under the handle @JohnnyGpops. Posts on his account described Israel and Jews as “human scum” and Jewish people as “filthy dogs”.
Another post stated: “Jews in Ireland need to be thrown out. They are traitors and land thieves. Our children need to be educated more about how evil Israel and Jews are”. It also stated that “no one should associate with murdering jew war criminals”.
After Newstalk FM aired an interview with a member of the Jewish community who was concerned about how the community was perceived after October 7th, the account posted: “I’m pulling all advert­ising from this.”
Members of the Jewish community in Ireland screenshotted the posts, which are no longer visible on the account.
On September 2nd, the account posted: “I want to let people know that my account has been compromised by unauthorised person(s) and that recent posts containing anti-Semitic content were not written, published or endorsed by me.
“The fraudulent posts have been removed, and the matter has been reported to the appropriate law enforcement authorities and the platform provider.
“I unequivocally condemn the views expressed in those posts. They do not reflect my beliefs or values. I strongly oppose discrimination and hate in all forms”.
[ Anti-Semitism is serious enough without conflating it with legitimate criticism Opens in new window ]
When the matter was brought to the attention of AIG, the company opened an internal investigation and issued a statement saying Gillick was fully complying with it and had reported the alleged hacking to An Garda Síochána .
AIG stated that the social media posts in question were “fraudulently published following the unauthorised compromise of an employee’s personal social media account”.
However, in an email sent this week to the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland (JRCI), AIG’s president and chief executive Eric Andersen stated that Gillick is no longer working for the company.
He said AIG is continuing to co-operate fully with An Garda Síochána and “we continue to stand ready to support that investigation in whatever manner we can”.
Andersen thanked the council for bringing his attention to the matter, adding: “As I have said before, AIG stands with you and the JRCI in an unequivocal condemnation of discrimination and hate of any kind and hate speech, including anti-Semitism.”
JRCI chair Orli Degani said she did not know the circumstances surrounding Gillick’s departure, but welcomed AIG’s investigation.
[ Zionism is not racism, any more than Irish nationalism is sectarianism Opens in new window ]
“This case became important to the Jewish community far beyond the actions of one individual,” she said.
“When Jewish people are described as evil and human scum, and when there are calls for Jews to be thrown out of Ireland, people need to know that this is given due weight.
“The Jewish community in Ireland is relieved and grateful to see that AIG treated the complaint seriously and acted following its own review.
“We appreciate AIG’s engagement throughout this process, its unequivocal condemnation of anti-Semitism, and the personal attention given to the matter by its president and CEO, Eric Andersen.
“This is also an important reminder that reporting anti-Semitism matters.”
Gillick, who still lists himself as an employee of AIG on his LinkedIn profile, was contacted for comment.

title: France dodges rerun of looting and riots after security boost
description: French government deployed some 70,000 security officials, including elite anti-terror forces
content:
France avoided a repeat of large-scale violence and looting that marred nationwide protests a week ago, suggesting the government’s decision to boost police numbers and contain marches paid off.
About 110,000 people took part in a mostly peaceful demonstration confined to the edge of Paris on Saturday, and another 300,000 turned out across the country, according to the interior ministry. The CGT union put the figure at 800,000.
Some scuffles broke out, especially on the margins and at the end of processions, with hundreds of masked individuals dressed in black taking on security personnel, who used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds.
While the level of violence toward the police was again high, interior minister Laurent Nuñez said authorities were able to prevent the looting of shops and damage to buildings seen on October 17th. He blamed the clashes on the ultra-left, which he said was seeking to “start and finish the uprising”.
“All the warning signs were there so that we put in a place a significant presence,” he said late on Saturday. “We will of course remain fully focused in the days and weeks ahead to face up to this threat, because it is a threat.”
The government deployed some 70,000 security officials, including elite anti-terror forces, after being caught flat-footed a week ago, when nationwide demonstrations drew more than half a million people and descended into violence and looting .
Rioters attacked public buildings and broke into stores across the country, including in the capital, as well as fighting with police and setting fire to cars. French president Emmanuel Macron , the target of much of the anger, on Thursday acknowledged “planning failings and elements of surprise”.
For the latest protests, soldiers were brought in to guard sensitive buildings, and helicopters and armoured vehicles known as centaurs were made available on Saturday. Some cities banned protests and extended curfews.
Museums, including Paris’s Louvre, were closed, while many shops were boarded up. A football match between Paris Saint-Germain and Olympique Lyonnais in Paris was postponed.
[ France is falling to the extremes of left and right. Ireland cannot be complacent Opens in new window ]
The protest movement began last month with high schoolers blockading establishments, calling for more teachers, repairs to buildings and an end to Parcoursup, a computerised college admissions system.
Nathanaël Combary, of the Renouveau Lycéen high school union, which is due to meet prime minister Sébastien Lecornu on Monday, said students were ready to continue demonstrating in the absence of concrete measures.
“The period of dialogue has lasted long enough,” he told Sunday newspaper La Tribune Dimanche. “We now expect action.”
Labour unions are calling for a major day of strikes and protests on November 5th, and the CGT pledged to expand the movement until its demands are met.
“The anger is immense, and our determination is even greater,” the CGT said in a statement. “The government and employers must urgently respond to our social demands.”
Backed by a disparate group of social media figures, students, unions and left-wing parties, Saturday’s demonstrations were framed as an “Acte II”, or second round, of the movement, which still has majority support in polls.
An Ipsos-BVA-Cési École d’ingénieurs survey for Le Parisien published on Saturday showed that while far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is still firmly in the lead in advance of next April’s presidential election, the far-left France Unbowed leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has also received a boost from the unrest and stands in second place, ahead of various centrist competitors. The poll of 1,500 adults was taken online on October 21st and October 22nd.
[ France is likely heading towards ECB support and a Marine Le Pen presidency Opens in new window ]
Mélenchon has been blamed by political rivals for stoking tensions, while he has accused the police of violence and called on Macron to give in to the movement’s demands or risk having to do so in much more hazardous conditions.
The unrest has come amid concerns about France’s public finances that have pushed a closely-watched gauge of bond risk to levels last seen during the euro-area debt crisis.
The bloc’s second-biggest economy dodged a downgrade at Moody’s Ratings late on Friday, but the company warned that the widespread protests “could constrain fiscal consolidation efforts”.
Preliminary gross domestic product data for the quarter through September 30th is due on Friday. Analysts expect expansion of just 0.1 per cent after zero growth in the previous quarter, adding to the fiscal challenge faced by the government.
Elsewhere in Europe, about 100 people were arrested in Barcelona while thousands marched in cities across Italy amid a heavy police presence, with scattered clashes reported. Albania ’s capital, Tirana, continued to be rocked by demonstrations against its prime minister.
Protesters burned containers, vandalised shops and threw stones at police in the area around Catalunya Square in central Barcelona. About a quarter of those detained were minors, Nuria Parlon, the Catalan head of security, and Jaime Collboni, mayor of Spain’s second largest city, said at a joint press conference. – Bloomberg

title: What limits apply to the new personal investment accounts?
description: Investment will be limited to Irish residents over a certain age in whatever products are offered by providers
content:
T he Finance Bill published last week puts further detail on and provides legislative underpinning for the new personal investment accounts. So we are taking the chance this week to run through in a quick-fire style a series of recent readers’ questions on various aspects of the personal investment account scheme as providers start working on the shape of products that they will offer under the scheme.
As a non-resident Irish citizen but with a PPSN, can I invest in the proposed investment scheme?
No, you cannot open an account unless you are over 18, resident in the State and hold a PPS number. The fact that you are an Irish citizen is irrelevant. And if someone opens an account and subsequently moves outside the State, they can no longer contribute to the account during any period when they are non-resident.
Money you would put in the investment scheme would be money you had likely already paid tax on (maybe at 52 per cent or 55 per cent if you are self employed). Why should this money be taxed again? It makes more sense to tax gain, not original contributions. It isn’t like you are getting a tax credit or deduction with your contributions. This investment scheme doesn’t make sense to me. You could actually lose money and yet still pay the 1 per cent tax.
Taxing money you have already paid tax on is nothing new in Ireland or other jurisdictions – think VAT, excise on petrol and even customs duty on online shopping outside the EU. Or deposit interest retention tax (Dirt), capital gains tax and exit tax on savings and investments.
You are certainly correct that you could be taxed at 1 per cent on part of your fund even if it makes a loss in a given year, as long as its balance exceeds €50,000. That is the outcome of the Government decision to follow the Swedish model for such investments rather than the UK individual savings account model. I can only assume that was done (a) for simplicity and (b) to allow the Government set the tax rate at as low an advertised figure as possible.
Can I invest overseas in the new scheme?
You can as long as it is through an investment account provider registered with Revenue for the purposes of providing these accounts. A register will be available as the scheme gets up and running. What investments they offer and in which markets remains to be seen.
My wife and I will have approx €60k to deposit in the investment scheme next July. Are we limited to a total of €12,000 deposited annually or could we both take out a separate plan to let us deposit €24,000 during the year?
You are each limited to contributions of up to €12,000 in any tax year. You cannot hold a joint account but you can each hold an account, allowing you to invest €24,000 between you.
[ First-time buyers account for almost two-thirds of Irish mortgage transactions Opens in new window ]
Can I transfer my existing vanguard ETF to this investment account (new one) without any tax if it’s less than €12k threshold? Or should I sell this and transfer?
This has cropped up a few times. The purpose of the new personal investment account is to encourage new investment by people of savings largely held in deposit accounts.
There is nothing to stop you moving money from an existing investment – such as your Vanguard ETF – to one of these new accounts as long as you stay within the contribution limits but each will be treated on a stand-alone basis so you will have to settle any tax due on the Vanguard investment before lodging the money to one of the new accounts.
In sum, no, you will not be able to avoid existing tax liabilities on an investment simply by transferring it to one of the personal investment accounts.
Am I reading the rules wrong, or could investors do the following: build up gains under the €50k limit and when nearing it, withdrawing some funds (free of CGT). Rinse and repeat, like making bread from a sourdough starter?
As long as the balance of the account stays below €50,000, no tax is due. The account provider will be obliged to keep tabs on the account balance each day over the course of the year and if the balance exceeds it on any day, the account starts being liable for tax.
But as long as the particular investment is liquid enough, there is nothing to stop you withdrawing funds from the accounts on occasion as you approach the limit to avoid tax, although you obviously are limiting your potential investment gains.
[ Tech sell-off deepens, dents rate hike bets Opens in new window ]
Will dividend income within the personal investment account be tax free (up to €50k value), can you move existing investments to the new account without triggering a taxable event and finally will you be able to fully choose your own investments or will a fund manager do it for you?
Dividend income on investments within the new personal investment account will be tax free subject, as you say, to the €50,000 tax free balance. Transfers from other investments will trigger any tax provisions attaching to those investments as stated above. You will be able to choose from the investment options offered by one or other fund provider. We don’t yet know how much flexibility that will offer though we do know that you will not be able to get interest in any uninvested cash held in your account.
Is there any age limit to the investment scheme? Myself and my wife plan to set up an account in each of my two kids’ names (ages 16 and 12). We want to fund this by the two of us giving them €3,000 each (€6,000 per child) as this is the limit of the small gift exemption. Is there anything preventing us from doing this and what, if any, tax liabilities apply?
There is an age limit and neither of your children will be eligible for at least a couple of years. No one under the age of 18 can hold one of these new accounts. You, as an adult, cannot open one in the name of your child and you cannot hold more than one account. However, you and your wife can each open an account in each individual’s name.

title: Message from the Editor: France on edge
description: IT Sunday: Protests and political paralysis have cast a shadow over the twilight of Emmanuel Macron’s presidency
content:
The French word “polycrise” was coined in the 1990s by the philosopher Edgar Morin and his co-author Anne Brigitte Kern to describe a set of overlapping crises, each of which makes the others worse. Translated into English as polycrisis, it became popular among analysts of the successive economic, political and environmental challenges that have buffeted Europe over the past decade.
It seems particularly apt now in the country where it was coined. The violent scenes on the streets of French cities have been matched by a fiscal squeeze, with a budget deficit of 5.4 per cent of GDP, rising national debt and nervous bond markets. Meanwhile the country’s politics are paralysed. President Emmanuel Macron cannot muster a majority in the Assemblée nationale, budget negotiations are stalled and public services face a prolonged period of austerity and cuts. In response to the unrest, Macron has turned to executive actions, restricting demonstrations and accusing far-left groups of sedition, while his prime minister has imposed curfews in Paris and Lyon.
Protest organisers accuse him of authoritarianism, while Marine Le Pen charges the government with losing control. The centre ground Macron has occupied during his two terms in the Élysée Palace looks fractured and demoralised. It currently trails both Le Pen’s far-right National Rally and Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s far-left France Unbowed.
Our Europe Correspondent Naomi O’Leary has been on the streets of Paris all week, talking to people caught up in the violence and examining the tensions beneath it. She explains how a student movement campaigning over underfunded schools converged with a revived Yellow Vest movement whose grievances stretch from fuel prices to farming, and why it remains unclear whether the looting that followed, which damaged at least 3,000 businesses, had any political motive.
She also sets out the electoral arithmetic behind efforts by mainstream politicians to pin the blame on Mélenchon , whose place in a second-round run-off is widely expected to hand victory to Le Pen.
In her latest analysis, Naomi turns to what the past week reveals about Macron himself as his decade in power draws to a close. Elected in 2017 on a promise to transcend France’s old divisions and revive growth, he now leaves a country even more polarised than before, with long-term borrowing costs above 5 per cent for the first time since 2002. His televised address after the riots was widely judged to have said very little, and his decision to leave almost immediately for the Gulf drew criticism even from one of his own advisers. He returned with deals to secure gas and diesel supplies for the winter, only to find that the questions awaiting him were about order on the streets rather than energy.
“France may calm the violence in the short term, but the country is infused with long-term dread,” writes Lara Marlowe in her analysis . She writes that France Inter radio hosted a debate between philosophers asking if France is heading towards civil war.
Our editorial sets out the stark choices facing French voters as they approach next spring’s election . Few across the political spectrum dispute that the country’s problems must be tackled. The disagreement lies in how, with the right favouring deep spending cuts, the left arguing for debt cancellation and higher taxes on the wealthy and the centre struggling to reconcile pensions, welfare and rising defence costs with heavier taxation. Whatever the outcome, the consequences will be felt well beyond France, across a European Union in which it plays a pivotal role.
The economies of many Irish towns are built on tourism, but how do they cope when the visitors leave? In the opening instalment in a new series, Dara Bradley looks at Clifden, Co Galway , where the only thing keeping some businesses open is loyalty to staff.
In Opinion, Liz Carolan wonders why people continue to be fascinated by the disgraced tech entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes ; Daniel Geary warns us not to mistake protest votes for support for the Democrats in the US midterms; and in a week that saw a big fall in share prices of the big AI players, Cliff Taylor reflects on Ireland’s position as “an intensely interested bystander in what is shaping up as a big financial drama.”
Finally, we lost one of the most influential figures in Irish music on Friday with the death of Dónal Lunny – a founding member of Planxty, The Bothy Band and Moving Hearts. As our obituary puts it, “traditional music owes much of its propulsive force, its appetite for innovation and its wide-lens perspective to a singular musician who has played a key role in propelling it to heights previously unimagined.”
We like to hear from you. Feel free to send comments, feedback or suggestions for topics you would like to see covered to feedback@irishtimes.com .

title: Musk won his battle with Swedish union but it is still business as usual
description: Sweden has one of the most pro-technology labour movements anywhere in the world
content:
One of my bugbears about journalists – myself included – is that we tend to pile into stories when they first develop, explain why they matter, then forget about them and move on to the next new thing. But there is value in paying attention to how stories end.
Take, for example, the battle that broke out three years ago between Elon Musk and Sweden’s trade union movement. In 2023, a group of Tesla mechanics in Sweden went on strike over their employer’s refusal to sign a collective agreement with their union, IF Metall.
Other unions joined in. They halted postal deliveries, waste collection and the unloading of cars at ports.
The stakes were high. Musk did not want to set a precedent that he would recognise unions anywhere. And Sweden’s trade unions did not want to allow Tesla to undermine the country’s labour market model, in which government regulation takes a back seat and employers and unions negotiate the rules between themselves.
Journalists flocked to cover it. Musk called it “insane”. But how did it end?
Musk won. This summer, IF Metall announced that it was calling off the strike after more than 1,000 days because Tesla had bought out all the striking members.
“Without workers on strike, there is no strike,” said Veli-Pekka Säikkälä, the collective bargaining secretary at LO, the Swedish trade union confederation, in a statement at the time.
What does it mean that Musk was victorious? For the global labour movement – and indeed anyone with ambitions to curb the power of the tech titans of our age – it is hardly encouraging that even one of the strongest trade union movements in the world could not force Tesla to the table.
After all, the Swedish unions have high membership levels, deep pockets and a supportive institutional set-up, all things that elude unions in many other countries.
In the US, for example, trade unions thought they had secured a historic victory in 2022 when workers in an Amazon warehouse in Staten Island voted to form a union. But more than four years later, Amazon has still not even negotiated a contract.
But while the “Swedish model” could not break Musk, it does not seem as if Musk has broken the Swedish model either. Although trade union officials did worry that Tesla could be the thin end of the wedge, those I spoke to on a recent visit to Stockholm took some solace from the fact that they have continued to sign collective agreements with other companies, including with tech firms that will help to shape the future of the economy.
After a year of negotiations, for example, including a strike threat, video games company King (maker of Candy Crush) signed a collective agreement with Swedish unions last month.
“The Tesla strike is important because it’s an emblematic company in the green transition – at least it was,” German Bender of the think tank Arena Idé, who wrote a book on the conflict, tells me. “But the strike ended, the union lost, and the Swedish model hasn’t crumbled.”
What if the strike had gone the other way and Musk had been the one to lose? Entering into the Swedish way of doing things could have given him an insight into a very different type of trade unionism from the American style he knows and dislikes.
Although they have become known in recent years for their fight with Tesla, in fact, Sweden has the most pro-technology trade unionists I have come across.
Susan Schurman, professor of labour studies and employment relations at Rutgers University, says that Nordic unions in general understand that it is vital for employers to remain competitive in export-led economies.
“They don’t focus on restraining technology; they focus on: ‘How do we incorporate this in a way that will help our companies remain competitive and make sure our members get their fair share of the profits?’” she tells me. “American unions have not historically thought this way.”
Indeed, the Nordic region’s powerful unions have hardly held companies back on implementing the latest tech. Sweden has been called the Silicon Valley of Europe because of its high number of start-ups.
