Meanwhile, the percentage of businesses that have adopted artificial intelligence is higher in Denmark, Finland and Sweden than any other country in the OECD’s database – and well in excess of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development average.
As one Swedish trade unionist put it to me: “We don’t fear new technology. We fear old technology.” A sentiment with which Musk – were he willing to listen – would probably agree. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: TV guide: the best new shows to watch, starting tonight
description: October 25th-30th highlights: including Dr Marie Cassidy Investigates Ireland’s Last Witch Trial, the Celebrity Traitors finale, and The Handel Scandal
content:
Among a heap of spooky TV shows this week is this historical one with former State pathologist Dr Marie Cassidy at the helm. She looks back at Ireland’s last witch trial, which took place on the peninsula of Islandmagee, north of Belfast. In 1711 rumours swirled that an 18-year-old woman named Mary Dunbar was demonically possessed, but Mary accused eight local women of practising witchcraft on her. The women were put on trial and found guilty before being brutally punished. Dr Cassidy travels to Dublin, Edinburgh, Belfast and Islandmagee to meet experts including Dr Gillian Kenny, who compares the beliefs around witchcraft in Gaelic Ireland to those held by Dunbar’s Scots Presbyterian community. She also meets an expert in the case, Dr Andrew Sneddon, heads to the Ulster Folk Museum to find out about life for Ulster-Scots Presbyterian women at that time, and then goes onwards to Edinburgh to hear from Witches of Scotland podcasters and campaigners Claire Mitchell KC and Zoe Venditozzi about how women were targeted with witchcraft accusations. The programme concludes on Islandmagee itself, where Dr Cassidy visits a memorial to the accused women.
More spookiness for youngsters. The Unreal is back for a third series, with two episodes under the title Curse of the Morrigan. This is a comedy-horror that’s centred on the Kelly family: parents Mary and Tom and their kids Katie and Kevin. In the first episode of the new season, Kevin receives a mysterious postcard that contains a threat to reveal his secret: that he’s a fictional character who has escaped into the real world. The entire family head to a spooky island to investigate what’s going on, but find that the locals living there have plenty of secrets of their own. One for young people who like supernatural mysteries.
About 7,500 people in Ireland are admitted to hospital because of strokes every year. But it’s not just people in their later decades who are impacted by strokes. As this programme shows, in the UK alone 10,000-20,000 people under the age of 50 suffer from strokes annually. The documentary, which was filmed over seven months, focuses on the stories of three young people. One is Saskia, who nine months after a stroke is living at home and trying to overcome her debilitating OCD in order to regain her independence. Then there’s the former dancer Dan, who is using a wheelchair and relearning how to speak. Dec is in a coma after suffering a stroke, and his girlfriend and family are at his bedside hoping he will survive. The programme makers describe it as “an ambitious and important series that challenges perceptions and gives a voice to young people whose lives have been transformed by stroke”.
Ireland is very proud of its link to George Frideric Handel’s Messiah. The iconic oratorio premiered on Fishamble Street in Dublin in 1742 to a sell-out crowd, after an invite to Handel from the lord lieutenant, Lord Devonshire. The young English actor and singer Susannah Cibber performed on the night, and it was her first time singing in front of an audience since a sordid adultery scandal had attracted a lot of attention. This documentary programme is directed by Lisa Fairbank and presented by soprano Danielle de Niese , and looks at the controversial genesis of Handel’s Messiah and its connection to the disgraced Cibber.
It’s the final episode in the current – and seventh – series of Cheap Irish Homes, where Maggie Molloy and architect Tadhg Casey have been travelling across the country to find affordable homes for buyers. So far this season they’ve found everything from forgotten cottages to town-centre treasures. In this final episode, Maggie and Tadhg help 56-year-old Yvonne Rooney find a new abode. She’s living in Gorey, Co Wexford, but wants to move to a quiet, rural location. She has a budget of €200,000, and is seeking a home that offers both privacy and a good size garden – and she doesn’t mind if it needs some renovation. Let’s see what the experts find for her.
It’s been a busy year for British mathematician, author and broadcaster Hannah Fry . She’s been on the Celebrity Traitors (whose finale is also this week – see below), and also presents Radio 4’s Curious Cases with Dara Ó Briain and cohosts The Rest Is Science podcast. She’s back this week for the second series of this show where she uses her knowledge to help explore the world’s technological future, and explain what that might mean for us all. It might be no surprise to hear that the subject of this first episode is AI . Thankfully, you’d trust Fry to be the one to explain both the drawbacks and benefits of AI, across all its many applications.
In 2005, Robert McCartney – a 33-year-old father of two – was killed by members of the IRA outside Magennis’s Bar in Belfast city centre. After his death, his sisters Catherine, Paula, Gemma, Donna and Claire, as well as his fiancee, Bridgeen Hagans, fought for justice in the face of innumerable barriers and intimidation of potential eyewitnesses. They travelled the world and met political leaders, and this programme details their fight as well as the impact of McCartney’s tragic death on the family.
This series of the Celebrity Traitors has certainly been an entertaining and juicy watch. It started off with a bang when in the very first episode actor Richard E Grant told the Faithfuls that he was a Traitor, one of the most iconic moments in the show’s history. The aftermath of this meant the rest of the contestants had plenty to chew on over the next few days. But Grant didn’t last long, and soon both comedian James Acaster and broadcaster Hannah Fry were recruited as Traitors – despite being quite reluctant to be on that side of the competition. Now everything will come to a head in the final episode, presented as always by Claudia Winkleman . Let’s hope it’s as explosive and bonkers as the rest of the series has been. It’s followed by an episode of The Celebrity Traitors: Uncloaked, which looks behind the scenes.
Liev Schreiber and Stephen Graham are the heavyweight names on opposite sides of the law in this dark crime series based on the bestselling Scandi-noir novels. For this series the action has been moved to the United States, where Schreiber is the former soldier Jonah Lynn, a homicide detective in Philadelphia who has decided to get away from the pressure cooker of big-city policing and move with his family to a small town in Pennsylvania. But if he thinks he’s in for a relaxing time, he’s in for a shock when the town is terrorised by a serial killer, Jurek Walter (Graham), who likes to bury his victims alive so he can taunt their loved ones. No prizes for guessing that Lynn’s own family is targeted by Walter, and he’s forced to make some agonising choices to save those he loves the most.

title: Ireland’s left has failed to penalise government for decades of inaction but the right has
description: Political failure around protests is a result of the left being unable to take Irish economic dysfunction and turn it into a larger project of reform
content:
A cross France, town halls are being petrol bombed while half a million people are drawn to the streets to revolt. I do not need to belabour the extent to which the French, rather famously, tend to go all-in on their protests
Curiously though, in the same week, Ireland staged its largest strike since 2009 – with about 300,000 teachers, nurses and civil servants downing their tools for a single day. The strikers were looking for a pay rise, which can be thought of as a short-term solution to the structural quagmire the country finds itself in, at best.
While the majority of people I meet seem to lament endlessly their dissatisfaction and even anger with the state of Ireland’s economy, at some stage the inevitable question arises: why does anger about our fast-deteriorating living conditions never amount to pressure for structural reform?
The answer, I suspect, lies in how that frustration is organised. While the proclivity for protest runs through French culture deeply, Ireland has a pressure-release mechanism that ensures our anger rarely spills into the streets: we negotiate politely, we distribute out money and subsidies, and eventually, should that fail to satisfy us, we emigrate.
This creates what we see today; a dystopian equilibrium in which people’s disillusionment is matched equally by their desire to maintain the status quo – in a system that never quite reaches the boiling point of being challenged. And as long as there is enough cash to be handed out and enough one-way flights to Sydney available to escape the problems, this will continue.
So if Irish people just leave before we get too angry, why did the fuel protests in April manage to create so much disruption over fuel prices, while the wider anger with housing, public services and the cost of living rarely gets airtime outside of WhatsApp group chats? Is it because the right are able to mobilise, while the left are not?
[ Europe is changing, but Ireland has yet to notice Opens in new window ]
Perhaps the lens to understand this question is not political, but economic. Because while political ideology was a useful sorting mechanism for most of the postwar period, our differences in class conflict fragment today between two groups: those who are protected by the current economic system and those who are locked out of it.
And mobilising action within these groups is then decided, very simply, by whether the lack of delivery of the political class has become sufficiently intolerable – and whether the Government can respond to the resulting disquiet.
The people benefiting from the status quo aren’t necessarily those who are wealthy, nor are they all on the left or right. This is somewhat due to Ireland not quite developing a clear left-right divide seen in other European countries
A public sector worker who is asking for a pay rise is very different from a young student in rental accommodation who is asking for a functioning housing market . For starters, one has an organised constituency with a recognised negotiating mechanism within the Government and a specific, numerical demand – and the other doesn’t.
The interests of renters are widespread and vary enormously – including across left and right political ideologies – and what they need is much harder to deliver than a pay cheque. They need the Government to change the system entirely, including removing policies which protect existing housing prices, that a large voting base relies on.
[ It seems we will tolerate any wrong so long as it is small Opens in new window ]
This creates an intriguing complexity in Irish class conflict. The people benefiting from the status quo aren’t necessarily those who are wealthy, nor are they all on the left or right. This is somewhat due to Ireland not quite developing a clear left-right divide seen in other European countries. After all, for the last century, we’ve had the same two parties – Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael – alternating and more recently coalescing – in government, with the economic model staying the same.
This means that people who are losing out from the current system are not brought together under a single political project that is capable of challenging the Government. Our frustration finds ways to leak away.
But this is not always the case, as we saw in April in the fuel protests . Disruption can happen – and especially when people can identify a collective demand; a demand which is directly connected to their lives, and that can reasonably force a Government response.
The fuel protests have often been described as a worrying demonstration of power by far-right political operators that were acting outside of the established system; that the right were willing to disrupt the daily life of the hard-working people that the left purportedly represents. But again, this political lens isn’t as useful as an economic lens.
[ Europe does not need Patrick Collison to ‘fix’ it Opens in new window ]
The protests were organised around real and material problems, and it just so happened that in the political vacuum in which these problems are barely acknowledged by Ireland’s political class, right-wing operators were the only available conduits to translate the hauliers’ grievances into political pressure.
To show just how little the left-right axis had to do with the protests, a poll at the time showed that 56 per cent of Irish people supported these protests. It is hard to reconcile this with the narrative that it was a fringe operation outside of the political mainstream. However, the left-right framing gives the political class a very convenient way to dismiss their protests.
Isn’t it easier, after all, to condemn the dangerous politics of those who want recognition of their problems, rather than to explain to the same voters why that problem has become so big in the first place? Or why the politicians have, decade after decade, proven themselves entirely incapable of doing anything about it?
The vacuum that gave air to the right was created by the left’s habitual inability to organise people around specific demands, despite it being able to explain structural inequality so precisely. This gap between “talking about” and “doing” is often driven by the breadth of the left’s constituents: small businesses, the youth, renters, public sector workers, the educated elite – people that don’t necessarily have identical immediate needs that can be used to create immediate pressure.
The political failure around protests can therefore be explained by the left being unable to take Irish economic dysfunction and turn it into a larger project of reform. Said another way, the left has failed to impose any cost on the government for its decades-long inaction, whereas the right has.
The right makes it clear that the State can be forced to act – but only if disruption becomes more expensive than inaction. And unless the left learns to impose that same cost, the Irish structural failures will continue to be managed and negotiated away by one-day strikes rather than creating the urgently-needed reform.

title: Babies may be conscious at birth ‘to help them really hit the ground running’
description: What is consciousness and how can we tell if another being possesses it?
content:
I magine that a scientist sits you in a device that can detect changes in the activity of your brain, and then plays a cycle of sounds. Over and over you hear three low tones, followed by a high one. Then you hear something different: four low tones in a row.
The scientist doesn’t have to ask you if you were aware of the change. That’s because our brains typically respond to an oddball sound with a brief, distinctive blip.
That blip turns out to be a surprisingly reliable marker of consciousness – that complex, mysterious state of being aware of one’s own thoughts and one’s existence in the world, which may also be present to some degree in other animals. People in a coma don’t produce this blip when they hear oddball sounds. Nor do people who are asleep.
Now imagine that the parents of a newborn bring their baby into the same lab for the same test.
Is that squirming, gurgling infant conscious?
As humans, they are potentially conscious; we know that much. But in the moment, with their semi-developed brains and cognitive limitations – they can’t yet speak, focus their eyes, respond to instructions – they don’t seem to be conscious, at least not in the way adults are.
Indeed, there’s an active scientific debate over whether newborns possess consciousness. Resolving it could help solve one of science’s most stubborn mysteries: what is consciousness, how does it emerge and how can we know if another being possesses it?
[ Babies can categorise objects better at two months than previously known, study finds Opens in new window ]
Ask any researcher who studies consciousness, and they probably have a rough but useful definition. “Consciousness is a process of being receptive to the outside world and mixing that with our own internal world, to create the feeling of who we are and where we are,” said Dr Topun Austin, a neonatologist at the University of Cambridge .
But Austin is well aware that this definition doesn’t speak to how that process plays out, where in the brain consciousness arises from the activity of neurons or how their symphony of signals creates that feeling of being ourselves in the world.
Scientists have developed many detailed theories to address those questions. But there’s little accord on which is right, with no resolution in sight. “There’s not a consensus that we all agree on,” said Joel Frohlich, a cognitive neuroscientist at the University of Tübingen in Germany .
The stakes have only grown in recent years. Researchers have implanted millions of functional human brain cells in mice, for instance, prompting speculation that the work might someday endow mice with consciousness. Philosophers and theologians are musing about whether artificial intelligence will become conscious, and how we can know for sure.
Amid all the uncertainty, there’s one fact that everyone can agree on.
In each of our lives, there was a time when our brains were still too rudimentary to support consciousness, and there was a time when that changed. Even if we can’t say when babies gain consciousness, Austin said, “one thing we can be certain of is that they will become conscious.”
In recent years, Austin and other researchers have zeroed in on that transition. They are using new kinds of brain-scanning technology to study the brains of babies as never before, giving infants not only the blip tests, but even investigating what babies experience before birth. By determining when consciousness fully blooms, perhaps they can advance our understanding of how it works, and what it does, in all of us. “I really see it as a frontier area in consciousness science,” Frohlich said.
Other studies have found signs that babies are capable of surprisingly complex forms of thought long before they can speak. They can recognise that a face is more than the sum of its parts; they can carry out simple forms of math in their heads. Findings like these made scientists think that perhaps consciousness emerges earlier than previously believed.
To explore that possibility, researchers have borrowed some of the methods used to gauge consciousness in adults, like playing those oddball sounds. In an experiment in Germany, scientists placed newborns in a special crib lined with sensors that could detect tiny magnetic fluctuations, then outfitted the babies with earphones. When the researchers played combinations of low and high tones, the brains of the babies produced distinct blips in response.
“It shows that the newborn brain is already performing very close to what we find in an adult brain,” said Claudia Passos-Ferreira, a philosopher at New York University .
But Passos-Ferreira and other researchers don’t consider that one finding conclusive. Some experiments have failed to find certain other markers of consciousness in babies, so researchers are running many different tests. “If we see a lot of markers appearing at the same time, that’s highly suggestive that this is when consciousness begins,” Frohlich said.
Some of the most promising recent results have come from a major effort in London called the Developing Connectome Project. To carry it out, scientists had to modify a functional magnetic resonance imaging device. Normally, adult subjects lie on a table that slides into a large cylinder. Instead, engineers built a small cradle with a plastic head-cap at one end, to detect activity in a baby’s brain.
[ Will science be able to explain consciousness? Opens in new window ]
The project team ran brain scans on hundreds of babies, including newborns. They drew maps of the infant brains and recorded electrical activity that arose spontaneously during the 15-minute-long scans.
Lorina Naci, a neuroscientist at Trinity College Dublin , and her colleagues have been busy analysing those recordings. One hallmark of consciousness in adults is the way different parts of the brain become active in a co-ordinated fashion. Those connections can evaporate when adults are asleep or are under anaesthesia.
In recent studies, Naci’s team has discovered that regions of baby brains become active together in networks that are similar to those of waking adults, offering another early marker of consciousness.
As more markers of consciousness turn up in newborns, scientists have begun wondering what’s happening in the foetal brain before birth.
Naci and her colleagues have found that some babies born prematurely also display networks of active brain regions that hint at conscious experiences. Frohlich and his colleague are studying foetuses that are still in utero, by having pregnant volunteers lean their bellies on a device that can detect the faint magnetic fields produced by foetal brains.
For now, consciousness before birth is an even bigger mystery than consciousness in newborns. Scientists generally agree that consciousness cannot emerge before the foetal brain has matured enough to receive signals from the senses, and then integrate them into a unified experience. Before about 26 weeks of gestation, those neural connections don’t exist.
How soon afterward these connections develop, scientists can only guess at.
As they map the birth of consciousness, scientists hope to gain a better understanding of how it evolved in humans in the first place. For children and adults, consciousness is vital for communicating through language, and for carrying out complex forms of thought. But if babies turn out to be conscious at birth, and long before they can talk or make plans for the future, then it must serve some additional purposes.
Perhaps, Naci said, consciousness allows babies to start making sense of the world as soon as they enter it, “to help them really hit the ground running in terms of learning and development as soon they are born”.
But, she added, understanding consciousness in babies may demand a change in how we typically think of consciousness in general. By counting all the ways that the regions of a baby’s brain interact with each other from second to second, Naci and her colleagues have found that the baby brain actually exhibits more complexity than a waking adult’s.
We tend to think of consciousness along a single line, on a gradient from unconscious to fully conscious. It’s the road we travel each day as we wake, and sleep. But what if consciousness has more dimensions, more ways of being?
Naci speculates that babies may be conscious at birth, but in a way that is perhaps more open to the world.
“The idea is that they have this capacity to perceive more of the environment in much richer and more diverse ways,” she said. “They could have a very different experience than we have as grown adults.” – This article originally appeared in the New York Times

title: Ulster University to make almost 500 redundancies as provost warns education quality under threat
description: University having to make almost 500 redundancies as third-level institutions across North face reduced funding
content:
Ulster University , which is having to make nearly 500 redundancies, is near the limit of its ability to absorb cutbacks without threatening top-class education, the university’s provost has said.
In a direct message to Stormont, Cathy Gormley-Heenan said the Northern Ireland Executive must set long-term priorities, “not lurch from crisis to crisis”, and provide key institutions in Northern Ireland with “the certainty that we need to plan”.
If Stormont cannot sustain the institutions “that educate its workforce, drive innovation, support public services and underpin economic growth”, then difficult questions arise about delivering the changes needed across Northern Ireland.
“If higher education continues to be weakened through underinvestment and short-term decision-making, Northern Ireland loses much more than university capacity,” said Gormley-Heenan.
Speaking on Friday at a conference in the university on the need to “reboot” public services in the North, the Ulster University (UU) provost said Northern Ireland’s third-level institutions are now faced with another “significant reduction” in teaching grants.
The financial challenges facing the North’s universities are not just “a university problem” because universities create value far beyond the university campuses and the university walls. “This is what’s at stake in the choices that Northern Ireland now faces,” she said.
Because Northern Ireland deliberately keeps undergraduate tuition fees lower than they are in England, Stormont tops up university finances, but this sum has come under increasing pressure year on year.
More than 750 university staff have applied for the 450 places on the redundancy programme, though it is not yet clear how this will impact on the courses offered to students.
“The consequences of continued uncertainty are not abstract or years away. They are affecting decisions now about student places, staffing, research capacity and long-term investment,” she said, warning there are limits to what can be absorbed.
[ The Irish Times view on Ulster University cuts: an insoluble problem Opens in new window ]
“Once capacity is lost, it is really hard to build it back up again. The people who will ultimately pay the price are not universities. It’s the students seeking opportunities, the employers looking for talent who are saying we have a skills deficit.
“It’s the public services out there that need our skilled professionals that we are producing for the health service and others,” Gormley-Heenan told the conference run by UU and the University of Notre Dame-backed ARINS project.
Defending the university’s performance, she said UU has been named the Times Higher Educational Supplement UK and Ireland University of the Year, while nine out of ten graduates go directly into jobs or further study.
“We’re among the leading UK universities on research impact across the board. In the top 10 in many areas. Our own students have ranked us first in the UK for teaching quality. What they say is the quality of the education they get here is extraordinary.
“We’re one of the engines to make a lot of those other things happen. It’s about Northern Ireland’s ability to transform itself. Universities sit at the heart of all of that,” she went on.
[ Potential 450 job cuts at Ulster University will have ‘far-reaching, detrimental’ impact Opens in new window ]
So far, 735 staff – nearly a quarter – have applied for the 450 redundancies on offer, though it is not yet clear if management can avoid compulsory redundancies as it seeks to cut costs but maintain courses and research.
UU’s underlying deficit now stands at over £20 million (€23.8 million), up by £15 million in just a year. Income increased by about 4 per cent, but spending excluding pension adjustments rose by about 9 per cent. Equally, tuition fees have not kept pace with inflation.

title: Restaurant criticised for using Dutch chicken brings ‘luxury’ award home for Ireland
description: Plus: Plenty in a name for Maurice Regan’s ‘Luck Penny’; Vincent Browne recalls Charles Haughey’s guile and greed; and Garda to clamp down on souped up e-bikes
content:
S ole Seafood & Grill had something to celebrate this week after being at the centre of a storm over the long distance some of its produce travels to diners’ plates.
The Dublin 2 eatery was selected as “Global Winner in the Luxury Seafood Restaurant category” for a third straight year at the World Luxury Restaurant Awards in Romania.
Sole, part of a group owned by Padraic O’Kane and Bord Bia chairman Larry Murrin , recently attracted the ire of farmers after a review by the late Irish Times food critic Corinna Hardgrave . She was shocked to see a restaurant with a food philosophy “honouring seafood sustainability and local Irish producers” charging €35 for a chicken supreme involving non-free-range Dutch meat. She also noted the presence of Polish chicken and farmed seafood originating in Spain, Turkey, Greece, Scotland and Bangladesh on the menu.
Members of the Irish Farmers’ Association , which has previous with Murrin over his Dawn Farms food group importing Brazilian beef, subsequently held a protest outside the Drury Street restaurant, arguing its use of imported chicken was “making a mockery of Bord Bia ”.
Sole, in its defence, said it sourced as much of its chicken from Ireland as possible, but it had not been possible to find a consistent supply.
O’Kane described winning the award, based on an online public vote, as “a wonderful achievement” and expressed gratitude to “our guests from Ireland and around the world”.
“We are proud of the Irish and international producers we work with, and the quality ingredients they bring to our menu,” he said, noting Sole’s “commitment to quality, provenance and transparency”.
Luck Penny, a horse owned by construction magnate Maurice Regan’s Newtown Anner Stud, claimed a first victory at Belmont Park in New York last Sunday. The two-year-old filly went off at 8-1 and finished strongly under jockey Flavien Prat in the 6½-furlong Maiden Special Weight event.
What a 𝗟𝗨𝗖𝗞(y) 𝗣𝗘𝗡𝗡𝗬! ✨🪙 Jockey Flavien Prat pilots the 2y/o filly through rivals and finds space to get up for the win in R6 at Belmont Park! The daughter of MCKINZIE is trained by George Weaver. pic.twitter.com/oAm8s1dRfq
In William Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet, the female protagonist reflects on forbidden love and the meaningless nature of family rivalry as she ponders “what’s in a name?”. In Luck Penny’s case, there appears to be plenty.
The notion of a “luck penny” came up during last year’s High Court litigation over billionaire Coolmore owner John Magnier’s failed purchase of the Barne Estate in Co Tipperary. Magnier believed he had a €15 million deal but was gazumped by a €22.25 million bid by Regan, who was not a party to the court case but loomed large throughout.
The court heard that Richard Thomson-Moore, then an heir to the 751-acre estate, was “shocked” by an “untoward” offer of “two envelopes stuffed” with €50,000 in total from the Magnier camp.
This was meant as a “luck penny”, the court heard, a sum normally given by a seller to a buyer to bring good fortune. In this case, the Magnier side said the money, later returned by the Thomson-Moores, was a token of “appreciation” for letting them on to the land before the purported deal was finalised.
Judge Max Barrett ultimately found no binding €15 million deal had ever existed and dismissed Magnier’s claims.
Luck Penny, who the cynical might speculate was named by Regan’s camp with intent, won a little more than the aforementioned “luck penny”, securing $63,000 (€56,084) for her first-place finish.
There was standing room only in Dublin’s Royal Irish Academy (RIA) on Wednesday for the launch of Vincent Browne’s new book – Charles Haughey: Glory, Greed and Guns.
The book had a significant gestation period, with the journalist first mooting it in 1980, just after Haughey took power. He didn’t start work on it until 2017, after his departure from TV3 (now Virgin Media).
Browne recalled a fraught meeting at the Berkeley Court Hotel in Dublin in 1979, during which Haughey held his head in his hands.
“I said to him: ‘There are people over there looking at the two of us and they are probably thinking we’re having a homosexual tiff,’” he said.
The pair’s love-hate relationship spanned decades and Browne’s speech highlighted Haughey’s greed and bad faith acts, but also his achievements in office. These included free travel for pensioners, which – Browne joked – “most of you here tonight have availed of”.
[ Vincent Browne: Haughey loved Terry Keane. She made his life miserable Opens in new window ]
Former tánaiste and Labour Party leader Dick Spring, who once compared Haughey to a “cancer eating away at our body politic”, launched the book and recalled a confrontation he had with the former Fianna Fáil leader and taoiseach.
“How did you get away?” Spring asked him.
“Get away with what?” Haughey responded, innocently.
“I live in a modest house in Tralee. If I change my car in Kerry, they are talking about me for a week. You live in a Gandon mansion, you have a yacht and you own an island in my county. How do you get away with it?” Spring explained.
The Garda recently reported that officers in Co Wexford had seized a “significantly adapted” e-bike being ridden by a 13-year-old, with a 16-year-old passenger on board.
The souped-up machine was “capable of speeds of up to 79.9km/h”, the force said in a social media post highlighting “the serious risks” of modified e-bikes, which the Road Safety Authority notes are expected to obey a 25km/h limit.
Pressure has been mounting to halt injuries and deaths related to e-scooters and e-bikes, with age restrictions and requirements around helmets and high-visibility clothing introduced recently.
Legislation that would put the machines in the same category as motorcycles and cars, requiring users to hold licences and insurance, has been promised.
Another tool will be coming soon, and the Garda wants this one to fit in a car boot. The force this week sought tenders, worth up to €4.5 million over several years, for roadside test rigs to identify illegal modification of the machines. The “portable dynamometer systems” must be able to measure their speed, power output and “unladen weight”.
[ ‘Incredibly dangerous’ but ‘the only way I can get to work’: what readers think of e-scooters Opens in new window ]
The initial contract, for 60 portable rigs and associated servicing, is valued at €900,000 excluding VAT. These must be “transportable in the luggage compartment of a standard Garda patrol vehicle” and ready for testing “within five minutes of removal from its transport case”.
The successful bidder will have to agree to provide expert testimony in court during prosecutions, where necessary, should the integrity of evidence need defending.
“No charge shall apply for witness attendance at the Criminal Courts of Justice [in Dublin],” the tender documents note, but for those travelling “more than 7km” to the courts, “applicable Civil Service rates shall apply”.

title: Mark O'Connell: Every year, as I get ready to file a tax return, I experience a strange sort of reckoning
description: The tedium and banality of the experience gives way, at a certain point, to a sense that I am reading my own autobiography
content:
Every year around this time, as a self-employed freelance writer, I spend several days going through the previous year’s income and expenditure in preparation for filing a tax return . And during this personal harvest ritual – with its stocktaking of the year’s yields and losses, its offerings of tribute and appeasement to the Revenue gods – I find that two big personal phenomena are to be observed.
The first is that, through those long and tedious evenings of fiscal self-reckoning, I find myself drifting inexorably rightward from my ordinary political position. For about eleven months of the year, I am basically a democratic socialist; once October comes around, though, just as surely as the leaves will start to turn gold and fall from the trees, I will find myself grumbling about the parasitic accumulation of capital by the State at the expense of free individuals and small-business owners like myself. I will find myself having become, in other words, an October libertarian.
This is a cyclical phenomenon, as reliably transient as the seasons themselves. By the time you read this column, I’ll with any luck be done with the whole process, and returned to my entrenchment on the leftward flank of Irish Times columnists.
The second phenomenon is, I think, less shallow, and more worthy of contemplation. Every October, as I work my way through the previous year’s bank and credit card statements, marking off items as taxable income and deductible expenses, the tedium and banality of the experience gives way, at a certain point, to a sense that I am reading my own autobiography. It is an autobiography of a peculiar sort, certainly: one that was produced in loose collaboration between me, a cluster of financial institutions – Visa , Stripe , PayPal , my bank – and countless retail businesses. It is focused solely on my identity as an economic actor, as a buyer (and sometimes seller) of services and goods.
There is a strange, productive tension between the austere formal radicalism of the text and the immediacy of its effect on the reader – which is to say, me. It can only really have one reader – and not merely for GDPR reasons, but because only I, its unwitting co-author and subject, can have any hope of understanding the thing, any chance of interpreting its gnomic entries, its dates and places and numbers.
For instance, as I write these words, I am sitting in a cafe tapping away at my laptop between sips of my second cup of coffee. This is a fairly unremarkable set of circumstances for me, and I’m likely to think no more of it as soon as I walk out the door. But this time next year, I will be going through my expenditures for October 2026, and I will come across a row containing today’s date and the current time, and the name of the coffee shop, and the sum of €62 (or whatever it is two flat whites in Dublin costs these days).
And I will think for a moment, and suddenly remember that it was a weekday morning, and that I was writing this very column. And then I’ll likely remember other things about the day. I might also think: can I write off the coffees as a business expense? If the coffees were bought to legitimise my presence in a cafe while I work, are they not roughly equivalent to the renting of office space? And then I will imagine my accountant narrowing his eyes, heavy with scepticism and filing-deadline exhaustion, and I will abandon the idea.
There are larger and more high-level realisations, of course, that emerge from perusing these data points. That I spend far too much money on takeaway coffees. That I have a helpless and financially crippling addiction to buying books at a rate that far outstrips my capacity to read them. And that the Apple corporation has over the years cleverly manoeuvred itself, and manipulated me, in such a way that a constant supply of direct debits and incidental transactions is being slow-dripped from my bank account into its coffers.
But it’s the smaller realisations that are the more remarkable; it’s the expenditures whose itemisation amounts to a kind of narrative of my movements through space and time (legible as autobiography in the way that a snail’s glistening trail is legible as autobiography). Why did you spend €50 on a taxi on the first week of February last year? Oh yes, you were on the way to the airport. And why were you on the way to the airport?
You read on, then, and see that the next item is a Stansted Express ticket to Liverpool Street, that the one following is a sum in British pounds for what seems to be a restaurant – and all of a sudden you remember that you were in London for book research, and that you had lunch with your friend in Spitalfields, and though you might not remember everything you talked about, you’ll remember that she was getting work done on her house, and that you ordered some kind of terrine, and that there wasn’t nearly enough bread to spread it on and that you had to ask for more.
And then other things about the trip will come back to you. The place you had dinner, the Waterstones in which you bought yet another book you still haven’t read. The fact that you were at a loose end that evening and bought a ticket on your phone for a cinema around the corner, and that you never saw the film because you’d failed to notice that it wasn’t actually on release yet, that you’d somehow booked a ticket not for that night, but for the Thursday of the following week when you’d no longer be in town.
And so all sorts of things – your minor administrative idiocies, your profligate consumption of coffee and books, your friendships, the pleasurable melancholy of an evening alone in central London – will come to you as you work your way through the double-entry bookkeeping of your days. And in this way, from these most numbing of absolutes – consumption, surveillance, good old-fashioned death and taxes – the particular details of your particular life can be reclaimed, and considered anew.

title: When will reality of energy prices bite markets?
description: All signs point to higher-for-longer oil prices, with long-term consequences for economic growth
content:
B ack in the mists of time (July), Cantillon suggested that a rout in chip stocks and the wider tech sector had administered a small but much-needed dose of reality to markets. Something similar may be happening at the moment.
July’s downturn in tech and semiconductor stocks, specifically, turned out to be fairly short-lived. It manifested as what Cantillon described as a relatively brief but “disorderly scramble to exit positions in US chipmakers such as Micron and Nvidia, which had helped power Wall Street indices to new records earlier in the year”.
No single factor caused the decline. There was, however, a sense that investors were asking more difficult questions about the assumptions behind bets on artificial intelligence (AI) that had powered the recent stock market boom.
All of that predated a rout in global sovereign bonds, which began in August and sent government borrowing costs to multi-decade highs in recent weeks.
Yet, while equities recovered from their midsummer malaise, tech stocks came under significant renewed selling pressure in a volatile session on Friday. Cycling out of tech stocks, investors sought refuge in safe-haven assets such as bonds, helping to arrest some of the jump in bond yields, particularly in the US.
[ International investors give Ireland the thumbs up, ignoring corporate tax warnings Opens in new window ]
Once again, there is no one reason for the sell-off, which may yet prove to be short-lived. Factors also vary by region. In Europe, for example, France’s ongoing political uncertainty is heaping pressure on the country’s stocks.
At a higher level, the surge in global crude oil prices on Friday to their highest level since April is also causing significant anxiety. With the Trump administration threatening to ramp up strikes on Iran after next month’s midterm elections and Saudi Arabia being rattled by Houthi military activity in Yemen, there is a growing sense that energy prices could remain higher for longer, with long-term consequences for economic growth.
[ AI bubble? Nvidia is now bigger than Japan Opens in new window ]
Simply put, as Cantillon said previously, markets have been in fantasy land this year, largely shrugging off the quite obvious question marks hanging over the debt-fuelled AI boom on the one hand, and the Trump administration’s disastrous war in the Gulf and its impact on energy prices on the other. Whether it happens sooner or later, reality will have to bite at some point – and it’s probably going to hurt.

title: Brazilian democracy in the balance as voters consider giving the Bolsonaros another chance
description: Lula has spent weeks highlighting corruption allegations surrounding Flávio Bolsonaro, but signs are that many voters may be willing to look past them
content:
B razilian striker Richarlison may be a forgotten man at Tottenham Hotspur, cut from the Premier League club’s squad and forced to train with the Under-21s. But back in Brazil he has emerged as a surprise player in the country’s acrimonious presidential election campaign.
This culminates on Sunday when incumbent leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva faces far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro in a run-off that polls show heading for a photo finish. The race has been dominated by accusations and counteraccusations of corruption, which this week has included Richarlison’s dispute over a mansion on an island facing a glamorous stretch of Rio de Janeiro’s coast.
His antagonist is the lawyer Willer Tomaz, a close and very wealthy friend of Flávio. The footballer claims Tomaz used undue influence with Rio’s courts to seize the property. He says this followed his refusal of an offer from Flávio to buy the occupation rights to the property, which sits on federal land. “I didn’t want to sell him the island,” Richarlison said in a video posted on social media. “Since I didn’t, these guys just snatched it through the courts.” Flávio and Tomaz deny any wrongdoing, the latter saying he acquired the rights legitimately.
The player’s cause has now been taken up by Lula’s supporters. “Give back Richarlison’s island” has trended on social media, with the president himself posting a video in support. The island dispute helps highlight a key element of Lula’s strategy during the campaign’s final weeks as he seeks to overturn the 2.22 million vote deficit from his loss in the first round on October 4th. Since then Lula has sought to focus the minds of undecided voters on Flávio’s plans to make swingeing cuts to public spending, while simultaneously emphasising the multiple allegations of corruption the senator faces.
Sharper scrutiny of the activities of Tomaz is central to this effort. A lawyer based in the capital Brasília, he is no stranger to controversy. His most recent brush with the law started with an investigation into his alleged involvement in a scheme to defraud Brazil’s social security system. This led police to probe his online gambling activity that in 2025 saw him deposit 258 million reais (€45.5 million) with an online betting site. Police are now investigating indications Tomaz controlled the site and used it to launder money.
[ Brazil turns right: Bolsonaro in pole position as election goes to run-off Opens in new window ]
Tomaz says he has a gambling addiction and that the funds “originate from lawful sources” and are compatible with his income. Flávio has defended Tomaz, saying they have a “legitimate friendship”, though he denies that the two are business partners. But as part of their investigations, federal police have found evidence they say indicates Flávio was the “master user” of a bank account belonging to a company owned by the lawyer. Flávio denies the accusation and Tomaz says the account was opened in error.
In 1989, during Brazil’s first presidential election following its 21-year military dictatorship, Paulo César Farias was the unknown treasurer-cum-bagman of Fernando Collor, the right-wing candidate who defeated Lula in the first of his seven presidential runs.
During the contest only a small circle in Brazil’s elite knew the pair were operating a huge kickback scheme that netted them tens of millions of dollars, typically in cash. The revelations about their activities led to Collor’s impeachment, Farias’s eventual murder – still unsolved to this day – and the bitter realisation for many Brazilians that democracy would not necessarily lead to the cleaning-up of public life.
Now, 37 years later, Flávio goes into Sunday neck and neck with Lula despite the almost daily airing of serious allegations into his affairs, the voluminous reporting often based on police investigations.
To deepen the irony for many Brazilians, the Bolsonaros first rose to national prominence on the back of anger at revelations of systematic corruption by the traditional political elite, which after more than a decade in power included Lula’s Workers’ Party.
When Flávio’s father, Jair Bolsonaro , won the presidency in 2018, he promised to end corruption. But once installed, his government was plagued by scandals and cover-ups. A survey this week by the news publication Folha de S Paulo revealed 18 former cabinet members and aides of Jair Bolsonaro were serving sentences, facing trial in court or being investigated by the police for various crimes.
In contrast just six similarly ranked members of Lula’s administration are under investigation. When he lost his re-election bid in 2022 to Lula, Jair Bolsonaro attempted a coup, for which he is serving a 27-year sentence.
[ Deforestation in Brazil’s Amazon falls to all-time low ahead of pivotal election vote Opens in new window ]
Flávio has vowed to free his father if elected. To this day the Bolsonaros hammer away at allegations against Lula’s family, especially those against Lula’s eldest son over his relationship with a lobbyist under investigation who had extensive access to his father’s administration. All the while Flávio denies any wrongdoing by his own family despite the evidence against them.
If Flávio wins on Sunday, he will be an embattled president-elect. As well as the investigation into his relationship with Tomaz, there is another involving money laundering connected to Daniel Vorcaro, the jailed owner of Banco Master, accused of Brazil’s biggest ever financial fraud. In a bad-tempered TV debate last Sunday Lula referred to his opponent as “a Rio scoundrel, who pretends he isn’t pretending and lies shamelessly” and challenged him to open up their bank and phone records and those of their families to public scrutiny.
At first, Flávio demurred, trying to impose conditions but with a final TV debate between the two men due 48 hours before polling, he indicated he would. But so close to the polls opening it is unclear whether the president’s tactic will do anything to change votes even in the unlikely event something is found lurking in the records.
Instead, Lula’s best chance of being the first-ever candidate to come from behind to win a run-off lies in mobilising enough of the 49 million voters who did not vote for either man in the first round to rally behind his candidacy at the last minute. Sunday is too close to call according to polls that have narrowed to within the margin of error. The widely watched poll by Datafolha released on Thursday last shows Lula having caught up with Flávio, each candidate now on 50 per cent once undecideds and spoiled votes are excluded.
But since 2018, opinion polls have tended to underestimate the Bolsonaro vote. As the campaign closes Lula’s disapproval rating has fallen slightly but remains dangerously high for an incumbent running for re-election. His campaign has offered little of the optimistic vision for the future like when he first won power back in 2002.
Instead he has relentlessly targeted his opponent’s policies and character. Yet tens of millions of Brazilians look ready to take another chance on the Bolsonaros. This is despite their promise in 2018 to end graft being followed by a scandal-plagued four years in power that culminated in an effort to overthrow an election result after voters rejected Jair Bolsonaro for Lula in 2022.
Whether Lula has done enough to convince a majority not to return to power a family whose patriarch is serving 27 years for his coup attempt is about to be decided, and, possibly with it the future of Brazilian democracy.

title: Dublin tenant who told RTB of ceiling piece falling on ‘son’s cot’ awarded damages
description: Tenant Stephen Russell initially awarded €20,000, but deductions made over failure to pay rent and refusal of access
content:
A Dublin tenant who told a Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) tribunal of “seagulls” living in his water tank and a piece of a ceiling falling on his son’s cot has been awarded more than €1,000 in damages.
Damages against landlord Ian Kingsnorth were initially set at €20,000 over his failure to remedy issues reported by his tenant Stephen Russell, with the tribunal describing a council inspection report on the condition of the property as “damning”.
The sum was offset against more than €14,100 in rent arrears. A further €4,800 was deducted over Russell’s failure to allow Kingsnorth access last year.
The tenant had told the tribunal the home on Little Strand Street was in a “poor condition” from the start of his tenancy in 2020.
Describing the structure as “dangerous”, he said the condition of the home deteriorated over time, noting there were cracks in the walls and ceilings. At one point, a piece of the ceiling fell on to his son’s cot, he said.
Ceiling plaster also collapsed in the sitting room, he said, which he reported to his landlord in July 2024.
Months later in December, what he thought was a section of the roof “blew off” and landed in the garden of the local Garda station, he said. Russell later discovered it was the cover of the water tank.
The water quality subsequently became “very poor” after it became exposed to the elements, he told the tribunal, describing the water as “brown”, while seagulls had begun “living” in the uncovered tank.
His family had been drinking and bathing in the water, he said, adding his two infant children, one of whom was a newborn, were “constantly sick” and had to attend the hospital.
The tenant’s partner ultimately left the property with their children and moved in with her sister in Balbriggan, while he began showering in the gym. He ultimately left in December last year.
In January last year, he reported to Kingsnorth that water had started to come through the bathroom ceiling and hot press, with the landlord replying that he would have the roof replaced in the “next few weeks”.
However, Russell said no repairs were “ever carried out”.
Russell said he had “had enough” and decided to stop paying the monthly rent of €1,600 in February, with his landlord responding that he would “not engage anyone” for repairs until the rent was paid.
Kingsnorth told the tribunal it was a “stalemate”.
An inspection of the property organised by Fingal County Council in April last year identified “major” noncompliance, Russell said, including relating to the walls, ceilings and water leaks.
Around the same time, Kingsnorth said his tenant would not allow him access to the property for an inspection.
Russell told the tribunal he was “frustrated” and his relationship with his landlord had “completely broken down”. Kingsnorth accepted he had been made aware of the issues in July 2024 and did not attend to them.
He said a roofer attended the cottage and wanted to replace the entire roof immediately, though Kingsnorth said he was “not happy” with the quote received. He accepted the roof repairs were never carried out.
The tribunal described Russell’s “very detailed” evidence, which included photographs of all defects, as “very compelling”, while the report of the independent contractor was “damning”. It said Kingsnorth failed to carry out the necessary repairs within a reasonable time frame, causing inconvenience and “detriment” to Russell.
It noted the landlord was unable to carry out required works due to Russell’s refusal to allow access in spring last year.
Having made the deductions from the €20,000 in damages, it ordered the landlord to pay €1,032.40 within 28 days.

title: Who are the Burke children trying to impress? Could it be their mother?
description: Rite and Reason: Who are the controversial children trying to impress? Could it be their mother?
content:
T he Burke family from Castlebar have been in our news for some time now. In fact, for so long, many of us may have difficulty remembering a time when one or more of them were not making either a local, or national media splash.
Whether it was Jemima Burke berating former chief medical officer Dr Tony Holohan during Covid-19; Ammi Burke (with her mother Martina) creating mayhem at a Workplace Relations Commission hearing and, more recently, appearing at the Labour Court; Simeon Burke demanding equal rights for Cambridge educated lawyers at the Irish Bar; or any number of the family getting dragged out of various courts, their ability to attract media attention has had few rivals.
The star attraction for those who adore this family circus, has, however, been Enoch Burke who, when not commuting to Co Westmeath from Castlebar every day to walk around a school and go home again, has been walking in and out of Mountjoy Prison, with one detour to Castlerea Prison along the way, and now back again to prison.
Frankly it’s all a bit exhausting and surely no one can be feeling more tired than the Burke family themselves.
True, there are some recent subtle indications that the air may be slowly releasing from their ultimo evangelical tyres. Although Northern Ireland’s Free Presbyterians in particular have continued to feel the ire of the Burkes, the family’s attention has recently turned to more mundane, somewhat bizarre concerns; not least the proliferation of nail bars in their home town.
[ Martina and Ammi Burke lose appeals over two-week jailing for criminal contempt Opens in new window ]
Regardless, the Burke family behaviours are as old as man himself. After all, we all have axes to grind – this family just seem to bury theirs deeper into their targets.
They do appear remarkably disinhibited. The family’s ability to be wholly unembarrassed at the possibility, or indeed the certainty of being publicly called out and ridiculed, is worthy of inquisition and yet the answer may be much more mundane than we think.
The Burkes are not trying to impress or convert the general public, or any of the people they may meet in the criminal justice system. Indeed, they are not trying to be heard by anyone – anyone, that is of course, outside the family unit.
If there is a person who the Burke children, for example, wish to hear them, it is surely the matriarch of the family, Martina Burke. It is reasonable to assume they are essentially preaching to an audience of one – who also happens to be their former teacher.
All families are of course complex units at the best of times. Children can seem on the outside to have everything – good parents, income, education and advantage, and yet the reality can be something different.
The hardest lesson for children later in life is realising that their childhood was really about living the unlived lives of their parents. Yet children want for only one thing and that is to rest – not to have to earn parental approval based on the success or otherwise of a CAO application, or having an uncanny ability with an obscure musical instrument.
Nor can the issue of the Burke parents’ “born-again” version of their faith, from Roman Catholic to turbocharged Christian Evangelical, be ignored. Black and white thinking has become the new normal. Nuance is for the little people and certainty is craved in an uncertain world, a world that the Burkes inhabit just as much as the rest of us.
The Burkes want the same as we all do – to be relevant, to have personal significance and to have, as the psychologists advise, “cognitive closure”. The military wing of “born-again” Christianity can often appear to facilitate these concerns by hitching a lift on any number of contemporary social issues, not least matters concerning non-traditional sexuality. “Gay/transgender = bad, straight/heterosexual = good, and if you don’t believe us, it’s in the Bible.”
So the Burke family performances have never truly been about pronoun use or misuse, the LGBTQIA+ discussion, or indeed the inexplicable expansion of nail bars in Co Mayo. These were and are just the window dressing and capricious news pegs for something far deeper and something that we can all relate to – the problem of being a fearful human.
[ Jemima Burke’s public order conviction quashed after she wins High Court review Opens in new window ]
The Burke family were not and never will be “the problem”. The problem is the rest of us and how we feel zero inhibition about “othering”, eviscerating and parking those who don’t conform to our model or behaviours or beliefs – to make us appear better than them.
Sorry to disappoint – there is no evidence that Christ gave us any such instructions in Scripture.
In truth, what the Burke family really deserve is our authentic compassion and our kindness. Not because we may necessarily agree with any issue they may espouse, or any illegal or uncivilised behaviour they may indulge in – but for the very reason that we don’t.
No one ever said this Christian thing was easy.
Rev John Deane-O’Keeffe is a minister in the Reformed Episcopal Church and a departmental tutor in forensic criminology and theology at the University of Oxford.

title: Barolo, Amarone, St Émilion: Should I buy supermarket versions of higher-end wines?
description: How to Drink Better: There are a few rules to follow if you want to get this right
content:
A reader has a question about supermarket wines .
“The multiples stock budget-friendly (€15-25) versions of the easily recognised ‘marquee’ wines – Barolo, Amarone, St Émilion, and even Brunello. Could you help the average pleb like me to work out whether or not these represent good value compared to more expensive labels from off-licences?”
The big names in wine rarely offer value for money. Famous around the world, the good producers in a well-known region can almost always charge premium prices for their wines. If you do find an inexpensive one, you have to ask why a producer is selling the famous name so cheaply. There are exceptions: the Aldi Monsigny Champagne (€22.99), the Château Lacombe Cadiot Bordeaux (€12 on promotion in SuperValu), and the Château Les Trois Manoirs Médoc (Aldi, €11.99) all offer fantastic value for money. But as a general rule, I would avoid cheaper versions of wines from the best regions.
Instead, I would look to cheaper wines from the same top producers. A Bourgogne pinot noir from a top Gevrey-Chambertin producer will have a little of the magic at a much lower price. So too will a Rosso di Montalcino instead of a Brunello di Montalcino or a Côtes du Rhône instead of a Châteauneuf-du-Pape. I always look out for a Langhe Nebbiolo from top Barolo or Barbaresco estates, or Crozes-Hermitage from a great Hermitage producer.
It is also worth looking out for neighbouring less famous regions; Marsannay is not far from Gevrey-Chambertin, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano from Montalcino, and Vacqueyras is a short drive from Châteauneuf-du-Pape (SuperValu Vacqueyras, sometimes on offer at €10, is great value). In Spain, Navarra is right beside Rioja and produces some great wines. All of these names can offer real value for money.
As for the good, expensive, famous names, most of them have increased dramatically in recent years, and few are worth the money.
Sadly, as the big names are an easier sell, most of the multiples offer inexpensive versions and ignore alternatives. You may have to go to your local independent to find the less familiar wines above.
In recent months, I have done large comprehensive tastings of multiples’ budget Marlborough sauvignon , albariño and malbec (24 th October). Perhaps I should have included some of the more expensive wines from the independents too. I will do so in the future. The problem is I can only taste so many wines.

title: The Irish Times view on O’Connell Street: the seeds of a revival
description: Planning moves show a desire to create welcome change, though much remains to be done
content:
A fter years of neglect, there are some signs of change on Dublin’s O’Connell Street. For years councillors have complained about the proliferation of takeaways. Now a new restaurant has been granted planning permission, but on the basis that there is no takeaway added on. Meanwhile, there have been more than a dozen planning enforcement cases taken by Dublin City Council over unauthorised shopfronts and advertising on the street.
This may seem like a limited response, given the depressing degradation of the street over the years. But what is important is to get some momentum behind the drive to revive its fortunes. Enforcing planning rules and starting to address the pile of takeaway wrappers strewn around the street is a start. Big investment plans will take time to bear fruit, but small things can make a difference and help to win public support.
Numerous plans over the years have failed to amount to much. Now senior public servant Robert Watt is heading a new Dublin City Development Company, following on from the work of a taskforce. His office needs to become a champion for O’Connell St – otherwise improvements will continue to fall between the stools of a council without sufficient powers and a central government with other things on its mind. The recent planning actions taken by the council followed complaints from Watt’s company.
New investment is on the way, with the company to take a key role in developing the site previously owned by UK developer Hammerson, in co-ordination with Transport Infrastructure Ireland’s MetroLink project. The Office of Public Works is to redevelop the adjacent GPO, where great care is needed to adequately reflect the history and potential of this building. And Dublin City Council has this week started work on a new library on the north side of Parnell Square.
All this must be brought together into a coherent plan. A street that has seen such key moments in Irish history deserves a revival that respects and enlarges local communities and attract Dubliners and tourists alike.

title: El Clásico: The real José Mourinho hasn’t gone away, you know
description: Real Madrid travel to Barça on Sunday, so get ready for the Special One’s fireworks, haranguing and computer printouts
content:
September was a difficult month for José Mourinho . His troubles began when Troy Parrott was sprung from the bench to score a late, historic winner in La Liga for Real Betis against Mourinho’s Real Madrid at La Cartuja.
Two weeks later, Real Madrid went down 2-1 to Atletico in the Madrid derby , which left them trailing a rampant Barça by six points in the league, a sizeable gap before leaves began falling from the trees.
Backed into a corner, the Real Madrid manager came out swinging. We saw the old Mourinho. Has he ever gone away?
During summer, when Mourinho (63) was unveiled as head coach – the fourth in a little over a year to sit in the electric chair at Real – there was talk about how he had mellowed in old age.
Yet only last year he got a fine and a three-match ban in Turkey for pinching rival coach Okan Buruk’s nose after an Istanbul derby. Buruk, theatrically, fell to the ground, holding his face as though his nose had been hacked off. A leopard cannot change its spots. Mourinho said as much during an unguarded moment in August, admitting: “I can’t be what I am not.”
In the post-match press conference after defeat to Diego Simeone’s Atletico, Mourinho paused for what seemed an eternity before answering the first question. His arms were folded. He sat directly behind a small LG monitor. Its brand slogan caught the eye. The South Korean electronics company’s exhortation, “Life’s Good”, was completely at odds with Mourinho’s mood. Mourinho was sullen. He seemed tired. He spoke slowly and deliberately.
“We can skip the press conference because the story of the game is here,” he said, raising up a coloured printout of two over-the-top tackles on his players during the game, one by Cuti Romero on Jude Bellingham, the other by Kang-in Lee on Fede Valverde. These were fouls that warranted “clear” red cards in Mourinho’s opinion.
Instead, it was Real who were reduced to 10 men in the game’s decisive moment. A gormless challenge by centre back Dean Huijsen on Atletico’s Giuliano Simeone, early in the second half, led to a penalty and Atletico’s opening goal.
Mourinho sensed there were unseen forces acting against him. “It is all very strange,” he said, inviting us into the haunted house of his mind, adding mysteriously: “A week before, it was already known who the referee was.”
The fault lay not with the referee, though, he said. The referee was not personally to blame. Mourinho felt sorry for him: “A 41-year-old referee who isn’t even an international. The poor guy came here, and he couldn’t handle the pressure.”
Mourinho then had a dig at the video assistant referee , “Mr Trujillo”. He was extremely knowledgeable on his track record, listing several matches in which Daniel Jesús Trujillo Suárez ruled against Real Madrid in VAR decisions, including a Copa del Rey tie against Real Sociedad and matches against Osasuna and Girona.
Not to mention, Mourinho said, VAR decisions that went in favour of Atletico and Barça in other games, citing specific examples. He had his homework done. The joke doing the rounds, especially given the dramatic flourish with the printout, was that Mourinho prepared better for the press conference, excuses at hand, than he did for the match.
Mourinho was helped by Real’s communications department, which cranked a mobile printer into action at Atletico’s stadium minutes after the final whistle – using images taken from the sports newspaper Marca’s Instagram account – so Mourinho could be armed before facing the world’s media. The following day Catalan newspaper Sport carried a front-page photo of Mourinho with the headline “Unhinged”.
Mourinho had left Real in 2013 after three scorched-earth years in charge. It was the height of the Lionel Messi-Cristiano Ronaldo rivalry, both players achieving feats unseen in living memory. In the dugouts, Mourinho’s anti-Barça tactics were so abrasive that it left his rival, Pep Guardiola, burnt out and forced into a year’s sabbatical in New York. Now Mourinho has returned to Spain .
Before finishing his speech, Mourinho said he had been naive: “I thought I’d find a league different from the one I left. They told me, ‘No,’ and they explained why it wasn’t different from the league I left years ago.”
No one is better at relaying Real’s party line than Mourinho. It’s a big part of the reason he was summoned from the wilderness, more than a decade after he’d won his last league title (at Chelsea in 2015), by Real’s embattled president Florentino Pérez, a man also prone to bouts of paranoia. It’s why Mourinho is the only Real Madrid coach to have his name serenaded at the Santiago Bernabéu Stadium during matches.
Mourinho lacks some of the sparkle since last he managed Madrid. He has been sleeping at Valdebebas, the club’s training ground. He looks increasingly dishevelled. Gone is the €26,000 grey Giorgio Armani overcoat. Now he wears mostly crumpled polo shirts or a training top. His smouldering good looks have departed him. Often, he is unshaven or sporting a grey beard.
He has, however, lost none of his deviousness. During the recent, three-week international break he carried on his “victimismo” communications strategy, stoking the fires about an anti-Real Madrid refereeing conspiracy in La Liga, airing, for the first time in public since his Second Coming, the explosive name “Negreira”, a reference to former senior Spanish refereeing official Jose Maria Enriquez Negreira.
The Negreira case dates to 2023 when the radio station Cadena Ser broke the story about an investigation by the Spanish tax authority into filings by Negreira companies, including payments from Barça, over the period 2001 to 2018, totalling €8.4 million.
What was expected in return for these generous payments to a vice-president of Spain’s referring association? According to leaked testimony given by Negreira to the Spanish Tax Authority, they were “to make sure no refereeing decisions were made against them, which is to say, for everything to be neutral”.
Barça claim innocence, maintaining the club had hired Negreira to provide reports “related to professional refereeing”. Former coaches Luis Enrique (2014-2017) and Ernesto Valverde (2017-2020) have both testified they were unaware such refereeing reports existed. The investigation is continuing.
Mourinho has his own thoughts about the saga. While giving an interview to Corriere dello Sport, the Italian sports newspaper, earlier in the month, he hinted he always suspected the success of Guardiola’s immortal Barça team was helped by an invisible hand: “I arrived at Real Madrid during prime Negreira years. I remember no one knew about it, but we felt and lived it.”
Mourinho’s tactics – causing distraction and playing the victim – are working to a point. After a recent, edgy 1-0 victory over Villarreal in La Liga – in which Real’s Vinícius Júnior was sent off – Mourinho and his coaching staff spent the game haranguing the ref and the fourth official. Afterwards, he picked up a fine for refusing to do the game’s post-match press conference.
Kylian Mbappé and Vini jnr have been in the crosshairs with Real’s fans. At the Bernabéu during the Villarreal game, though, fans took to whistling the referee instead of their two privileged, lacklustre stars. There is less talk in Spain about Mourinho’s underperforming team than about referees and alleged conspiracies.
Javier Tebas, La Liga’s president, has weighed into the arguments with both feet. In a salty social media post, Tebas compared Real’s communications tactics to those of Joseph Goebbels, the Nazi propaganda minister. Real Madrid called on him to resign. Tebas has refused, claiming he won’t bow to Real and their “lapdogs” in the media.
Mourinho has a tricky hand to play. The pressure is huge. At his disposal, he has the most talented squad in world football, including Mbappé, a resurgent Bellingham, the gifted Arda Güler and teenage sensation Yan Diomande, reportedly the most expensive player in Real’s history.
But the pieces of the jigsaw aren’t fitting together – yet. Since the departure of Toni Kroos and Luka Modric, Real lack control in midfield. This has been made more glaringly apparent since the club bungled the signing of Spain’s midfield general Rodri during the summer.
Rodri has joined ancient rivals Barça instead. Barça are averaging more than four goals a game. All eyes will be on Mourinho as his men take on Barça at the Camp Nou on Sunday. If Barça were to administer a heavy defeat and open an insurmountable nine-point gap in the title race then Mourinho’s bench would begin to tremble.
Two years ago, Trent Alexander-Arnold told Sky Sports in an interview how he wanted to win the Ballon d’Or award. At the time, it seemed an audacious thing to say. Now it feels even more ridiculous.
After nine, trophy-laden seasons at Liverpool, his boyhood club, where he was a captain-in-waiting, Alexander-Arnold decided to hit out for Spain. It’s been a disastrous move. His career is dead ending. He has just turned 28. During the summer, he missed out on the World Cup finals, failing to make Thomas Tuchel’s England squad.
The previous summer, his long signposted move to Real was fast-tracked – the club paying a reported fee of €10 million, when they could have got him for free by holding out for a couple of weeks – so he could join their squad for the inaugural Fifa Club World Cup in the United States.
At his Real Madrid unveiling, he won over Madridistas by speaking in Spanish. He held his own in the Club World Cup, starting five of six games, before Real were knocked out in the semi-finals. But last season in La Liga was a disappointment as he struggled with two injuries. This season has been worse.
Mourinho has been favouring new signing Denzel Dumfries as a right back. Mourinho has even started to play Fede Valverde in that berth, which leaves Alexander-Arnold as third choice. At this rate, he may well return to England next summer humbled, dreams of the Ballon d’Or having turned to dust.

title: Podcaster Ger Gilroy on moving to RTÉ, his upstart attitude and starting over: ‘Your job is to win, right?’
description: After 24 years at the helm of Off the Ball on Newstalk, Gilroy has jumped to RTÉ to present a new daily sports podcast, Howler
content:
The long ponytail he sported across his final few months as presenter of Off the Ball Breakfast is gone, chopped now to a standard-issue back and sides. Is this RTÉ propriety in action?
“No,” says Gilroy with a smile. “My wife made me cut my hair.”
After 24½ years at the helm of Off the Ball on Newstalk , Gilroy has jumped to RTÉ to present a new daily sports podcast, Howler. Gilroy built a sports broadcasting juggernaut at Newstalk virtually from scratch and remained its sole consistent voice from its founding, so his move made waves within Irish media circles and ripples of disquiet within RTÉ itself. He insists he has not exchanged the insurgent, bustling energy of commercial media for the staid etiquette of the national broadcaster.
“It’s the energy of being a start-up again,” says Gilroy when I ask what most excites him about his move. “Newstalk was a start-up in 2002, and then in 2017 we built the [Off the Ball] studio as it is now, and that was a start-up. There’s something magic about it.”
The start-up’s scene is the RTÉ administration building, a drab office block that stands beside the canteen and around halfway between the radio centre and the television studios. RTÉ has inaugurated a new podcast department and housed it within this building, on a floor recently vacated by the finance department.
The clerical greys and deep-blues of the office decor are interrupted by a trio of pop-up podcast studios that are scattered across the floor. Howler’s is the largest, with leather chairs arranged around a large desk in front of a brick-effect wall on which the podcast title is graffitied.
Despite this time of retrenchment, RTÉ is investing in a podcast department because it believes it will help capture a younger audience. This is why Gilroy has been hired: RTÉ believes its best avenue to the attention of young men is through sport. Gilroy has signed up a series of recurring pundits, including Diarmuid Connolly (Gaelic football), Austin Gleeson (hurling), Noel McNamara (rugby) and Kevin Kilbane (soccer). The show launched on Monday with an hour-long studio interview with recently-retired Mayo Gaelic football great, Cillian O’Connor.
[ Too much Overlap? Gary Neville’s podcast empire knows no bounds Opens in new window ]
“We want to create this podcast network to get to the under-45s,” says Gilroy, adding that his podcast is targeting a male audience and that a “female-targeted product” will be launched in the new year.
He wants to make the impression on younger generations that shows like Nighthawks, No Disco and Scratch Saturday had on him. In an obvious nod to Nighthawks, adjacent to Howler’s main set is a high table with a couple of bar stools, intended to resemble a pub smoking area.
It’s an ambitious vision, but how can Gilroy’s show stand out in the highly saturated sports podcast market?
“One of the things that we’re going to do is that we are going to work with independent producers to produce documentaries, and tell those big Irish stories,” he says. The show also doesn’t intend to stick solely to sport, with plans in place to cover social and political issues. “Sports fans are people too,” says Gilroy. “They’re genuinely interested in politics and culture and travel, so why should we not reflect that?”
Gilroy founded Off the Ball in 2002, modelling it on Eamon Dunphy’s “anarchic and wild” hour of sport on The Last Word on Today FM.
