He also took lessons from American sports radio and didn’t want to copy RTÉ in operating a call-in show. Presenters were therefore loosened to give strong, irreverent opinions. Gilroy says the show had a “current affairs sensibility” without losing sight of the fact that sport is “supposed to be a diversion from all of the shit in the rest of our lives”.
Implicit within much of Off the Ball’s editorial direction was that it would do what RTÉ would not do and Gilroy rarely shied away from criticising the State broadcaster.
Shortly after RTÉ announced Gilroy’s move in June, a Sunday newspaper reported on subsequent unease within RTÉ, quoting an anonymous source saying: “Ger Gilroy slagged off RTÉ for years on Off the Ball, and then all of a sudden RTÉ are giving him a job, and he says he is looking forward to working with the team? How does that work?”
“If people are in any way upset, I understand,” says Gilroy. “My gig before I got here was to do the very best for the people who worked on the team and sometimes that meant having an upstart attitude to things, and it generally worked. Off the Ball was ultimately really successful. My welcome here has been great, like honestly. You see we’re in a separate building from everybody else and we’ve been in our bubble here for the last couple of weeks. No one has said anything and I don’t really expect them to either. Those comments are unattributed but if anybody wants to have a chat, I’m more than open to it.”
So was all of his criticism on Off the Ball, as Dunphy would say it, just showbusiness, baby?
“No. Everything I said would have been authentic to the time and the place. Like, your job is to win, right? And now I’ve switched teams. I don’t think it’s that unusual. People change jobs.”
Gilroy is a staff member at RTÉ and declines to share his salary. He says he has taken a “significant pay cut” from his previous job as managing director of Off the Ball, and says he won’t be appearing on RTÉ’s list of top earners. RTÉ also declined to disclose Gilroy’s salary, saying it only publishes the remuneration of its highest earners.
Howler has launched less than a year after RTÉ Radio 1 launched a new evening sports show, Inside Sport, segments of which are podcasted. Does RTÉ really need more sport content?
‘I fundamentally believe that our democracy is under threat from the tech oligarchs’
“Look at the media landscape in any other of the countries in the civilised world, there’s a full 24-hour sports radio station in almost every single one of them. We need more sports content, not less sports content,” says Gilroy. He says the two offerings are different: the radio show has a faster metabolism, reacting to the day’s news, while the podcast can take a longer-form look at sports issues. The podcast does plan to publish additional episodes reacting to breaking news stories. Howler pundits are not precluded from appearing on the radio show and the two shows will share running orders with each other to avoid a scenario in which they are effectively competing for guests.
[ How the LA Clippers bent the financial rules to become the Manchester City of the NBA Opens in new window ]
Gilroy says joining RTÉ has already changed his perception: stumbling across the Fair City set and passing The Late Late Show studio has taught him how “this stuff matters to people”.
“We could have bad days,” he says of Off the Ball, “and people would be mean to you in the YouTube comments, or they would go on Reddit and destroy you, and it’s like, ‘oof’. But here, people are under much more scrutiny – you could end up in an Oireachtas Committee really easily.”
Gilroy rose to become Off the Ball’s managing director, one of the loftiest roles in Irish sports media. Why leave?
“I was kind of edging back from presenting,” he says, recounting a conversation with a former colleague in 2023 who told him: “Anybody can be a media executive, but not everybody can be a presenter. Don’t do it.”
He went to the 2024 Olympics as a reporter for Off the Ball, which he says went “relatively well” but would have gone much better if he was not simultaneously dealing with the various commercial, marketing and HR issues thrown up by his executive role. But given he was the boss at Off the Ball, why not change his own role rather than leave altogether?
“Potentially I could,” he says, “but I kind of felt like I’d done everything that I wanted to do at Off the Ball. We’d been through that cycle of building different teams and were entering into a brand refresh, and I was not sure I had the appetite to go again on this.”
The first team of Ken Early, Eoin McDevitt, Ciarán Murphy, Mark Horgan and Simon Hick abruptly left in 2013 after a dispute with station bosses over scheduling, founding their own podcast, Second Captains . Their exit was initially so contentious that some regular Off the Ball contributors refused to join Gilroy on air as he was frantically pulling together a show for that evening. Gilroy says that whenever he meets any of the quintet now, relations are “incredibly cordial and warm”.
[ There’s a clear reason the world’s best players are staying away from the Premier League Opens in new window ]
“They’re obviously geniuses,” he says. “This [interview] is coming out in the aftermath of the George Gibney sentencing. That’s very special work that Mark and Ciarán Cassidy [co-producers of the podcast series Where is George Gibney?] have done. Ken’s obviously a genius, and the rest of the lads have been unbelievably successful in all of their chosen fields across television, print and their audio empire.”
Gilroy rebuilt the presenting team, many of whom have now left, including Joe Molloy – poached by the Irish Independent – and Nathan Murphy, who became the managing editor of Today FM.
Gilroy’s own career thoughts were relegated to the trivial at Christmas 2024, when his wife Aifric found a lump. She underwent five surgeries across the following year and has now been given the all-clear. Once he had that peace of mind, Gilroy thought once again about his career. He got a call earlier this year from a former Newstalk colleague, Hugh Ormond, now RTÉ’s head of podcasts, who pitched a daily sports podcast to him.
Gilroy and Ormond first crossed paths as students at Trinity College, where Ormond was a year ahead. Both worked in the college’s publication office, Gilroy with Trinity News and Ormond with the satirical newspaper, Piranha. Gilroy says they got to know each other at Newstalk: Ormond produced the breakfast show presented by Eamon Dunphy, on which Gilroy was a regular stand-in presenter.
Today, Gilroy says he has a “total preoccupation about the internet and AI”. He talks at length about Cambridge Analytica, online surveillance, AI slop and social media disinformation. All of these disparate anxieties crystallised in 2024 when he and his wife gave their daughter her first smartphone as she started secondary school.
[ Hurling advisory group hope new rules experiment will be broadcast Opens in new window ]
The result is that he has come to believe more strongly than ever in the importance of a strong and regulated media.
“I fundamentally believe that our democracy is under threat from the tech oligarchs who don’t give a f**k about us,” he says. “They don’t care about anything. Like they certainly don’t care about the little worker drones here in Ireland, they care about our tax laws. By creating a big audience of people who will listen to our sport and other content, hopefully they’ll migrate on to the RTÉ platform and listen to the incredible current affairs and analysis that’s happening here.
“This is real. The stuff we’re doing is real. There are really high editorial standards. I’m not saying that wasn’t the case at [Newstalk owners] Bauer, but I had two jobs at Bauer, and I have one job here.”
This doesn’t mean that Gilroy regrets Off the Ball’s prolific use of social media in recent years and he says Howler will publish to social media, too.
“The audience is there,” he says. “I think that a blanket withdrawal from these algorithms also isn’t the right way to go. Helping to put good content in front of people, and showing that all the content doesn’t have to be AI-generated is the Faustian pact that we’ve entered into with these people.”
Gilroy says he has no interest in being a future head of sport at RTÉ. “I have no interest in that,” he says. “You’re giving me all the rumours, now. I want to present. I want to tell stories. There’s never been a more important time to tell stories.”
Gilroy says there are specific audience targets for Howler. He declines to share them, but adds one more metric for success. “Causing a bit of trouble and doing some journalism, which you’re allowed. Just asking good questions is causing trouble.”

title: Dogs not welcome if we want to to enjoy the spectacle of returning overwintering birds
description: Pets should be kept away or kept on leash as bay welcomes these beautiful visitors
content:
A fter a summer catching the high tide for a swim in Dublin Bay – accompanied by swifts screaming overhead – I’m now waiting for the low tide to walk the undulating sands in search of returning overwintering birds.
From as early as August, they arrive in dribs and drabs – some still with vestiges of breeding plumage – and soon more than 20,000 of them will make North Bull Island their home, while the rest of the bay will be populated by light-bellied Brent geese who’ve flown from Arctic Canada, bar-tailed godwits from northern Europe to western Siberia, and a plethora of other beauties including sanderling, golden plover, redshank, curlew, turnstone, knot and dunlin.
Their return each winter is one of Dublin’s great free spectacles. One thing we could all do while sharing the bay with them is to keep our dogs away, or at the very least, in control on a lead.
In 1897, the naturalist Charles Patten stood before the Dublin Naturalists’ Field Club and read out a list of the birds of Dublin Bay. While doing so, he gave a top tip for anyone heading out to the shore: “Never bring a dog with you.” He bluntly stated what anyone walking the bay today knows: a dog drives the birds away.
Ten years later, the naturalist Alexander Williams described what happened when people ignored Patten’s advice. On the Shelly Banks in Irishtown, little terns and ringed plovers nested among the shells and in summer, Williams wrote, tern chicks ran across the sand “like mice”. But every weekend, cyclists and walkers, “often accompanied by dogs”, visited the bay and raided their nests.
One person who did a lot to protect the bay was Jesuit priest Fr Patrick Kennedy. In 1930, as the Wild Birds Protection Act was being drafted, he persuaded a senator to add a clause allowing bird sanctuaries to be created, and he convinced a hesitant Dublin Corporation to use it. By 1931, North Bull Island became Ireland’s first bird sanctuary, a move, according to Kennedy, that nature lovers might imagine would make the place “sacred and inviolable for evermore”.
They were wrong. In 1949, he wrote an essay, titled Violation of Sanctuary, for the Jesuit journal Studies. There were plans for a cinema, dance halls and a bus road on the island, and shooting had returned to the lagoon. The birds, which had become almost tame under protection, had once again become “shy and wary”. “Birds know the difference between a man with a gun and a man with a pair of field glasses,” Kennedy wrote.
Over the last century, the Bull has lost a lot. Patten recorded little terns, ringed plovers and wheatears breeding; none breed there now. In the 1950s, UCD botanists surveyed the salt marsh and found hares in such abundance that they had worn tracks across it. The last known sighting of hares on the island was in 2016 and dog disturbance is believed to be the main pressure.
[ What Paris can teach Ireland about clean water Opens in new window ]
Bull Island is among the country’s most protected places: part of an Unsesco biosphere, a national nature reserve, a Ramsar wetland of international importance, and protected under two EU directives. Bylaws from 1994 require dogs to be kept on leads, but the Irish Wildlife Trust say these laws were not enforced. In 2023, Dublin City Council asked dog owners to keep their pets on short leads in the dunes and to keep them out of the salt marshes and the island’s northern tip altogether. But these are voluntary codes, leaving the conservation rangers hired last year in a weak position: they can only ask, not enforce.
As winter approaches, this matters most. When the tide goes out, birds like curlews and geese must feed constantly to survive. Every time a dog appears, a flock will either take to the air for safety or move away with vigilance, both burning energy it likely cannot spare. To a flock of curlew or oystercatcher, a dog off its lead and a man with a gun look the same: the birds flee.
[ ‘Grand Canyon-esque’: Atlas of the unseen brings Ireland’s deep sea wonders into the light Opens in new window ]
Dublin Bay has a long list of protections: it’s an Unesco biosphere and much of it is protected under EU law for its birds and habitats. But if our dogs are allowed to run rampant, what’s the point?
Germany’s Wadden Sea has been a Unesco biosphere since 1990 and it attracts 10 million holiday visitors and 16 million day-trippers every year. Dogs must be kept on a lead at all times. The dunes are closed to them altogether and owners have designated dog beaches. Breaches of the law carry fines of up to €10,000. The rules are clear and are enforced.
For dog owners like me, the rules need to be consistent across the whole bay, clearly marked and enforced. If we know what to expect and the difference it makes to the birds, I believe most of us will comply. For the few who don’t, a steep fine is a fast lesson.
The wintering birds are back and we’re lucky to have them. The pressures they face are immense. Geese that have flown 5,000km to be here shouldn’t be pestered and chased all day by our pet dogs. The authorities should act fast and make one clear rule: dogs on leads.

title: Ireland has the worst public access to countryside in Europe. How did this happen?
description: How has our country ended up with perhaps  the worst public access to the countryside in Europe? There’s none of the ‘right to roam’ you find elsewhere
content:
I need to get away from my desk. For the past three years I have been obsessively researching the complex history of Ireland’s vanished footpaths, trying to work out how this country has ended up with probably the worst public access to the countryside in Europe: none of the “right to roam” in the woods and mountains that you’d find in Scotland and Scandinavia; no network of rights of way along the field edges of the sort that you’d encounter in France or England.
That research involved a 678km walk from the tip of the Dingle Peninsula to Burr Point in Co Down to find out how much – or how little – of Ireland remains accessible to an off-road walker in the 21st century. But the blisters have long since healed, and for months I’ve been stuck indoors, grappling with the meaning of “trespass” in the Brehon Laws, searching 19th-century Irish novels for mentions of footpaths, wrangling with the finer details of the 1995 Occupiers’ Liability Act, and poring over digital copies of old Ordnance Survey maps. This morning I need a break. I need to get out into the fresh air and go pathfinding.
I drop my daughter at preschool, and then, instead of heading straight back to my desk, I drive up to the far end of the small east Galway town where I live. I park near the GAA pitch, dash across the busy main road, and walk north on a meandering lane.
I’ve never been this way before, and the sudden elevation is unexpected. This is esker country, rumpled by the vanished glaciers. An ascent of just a few metres can throw an astonishing distance into view. It’s a grey morning, with a fine gauze of mizzle in the air. But I can see the dark crenellations of the Maamturks and the Twelve Bens, 90km away in Connemara . It’s like looking into another continent.
A big ringfort comes into view beside the road, a double rampart with a deep fosse between. I stop here, and look out uneasily across the land to the east. One of the lines I want to follow runs that way. But there are two men digging foundations for a new house in the road frontage right next to the ringfort. So I stay going, stick to the road, turn right and then right again.
Two white dogs rush out from an enormous roadside newbuild to proclaim my passing. A green lane strikes off southward here. It’s blocked by a rusty gate, but there’s no sign forbidding trespass, so I squeeze past. The green lane ends at the head of a big field. There’s another big ringfort 700m away across country with a small block of forestry behind it. But all the roadside bungalows look onto the land here. I’d be in view the whole way.
I suck my teeth, frustrated by my own lack of boldness. But this is the point: I don’t want to trespass, don’t want to stride out with haughty entitlement, convinced that I should have the right to “roam” across all of this. I just want a way through – a way that countless others have walked before me. I go back towards the road and flinch at the sight of a figure watching me from a huge floor-to-ceiling window in the house with the dogs.
[ Ireland’s ancient pilgrim paths: 14 trails to walk across the country Opens in new window ]
The lane brings me back around to the main road, a kilometre and a half from where I started. Morning traffic streaks along it at 100km an hour. But there’s a wide shoulder on either side and it’s safe enough to walk here; people stride this way in their hi-vis vests every evening. I’m almost back at the car now, and it looks like the morning will be a disappointment. But there’s one last chance – a lane striking back inland from the main road, hemmed with blackthorns. Where it ends, a new farm track cuts away to the right.
I steel myself, climb the gate and hurry along it to a ruined cottage nestled in a little hollow. I follow a wall north from the ruin, cross a low ridge – and there it is, right where it should be : a simple step-across stile; a long slab of limestone set crossways through the wall to allow a walker to pass easily into the next field. I give a little whoop of triumph, stamp down the nettles and step onto the stile myself – the first person to do so in how many decades?
I have never been here before. But I knew I would find this smallest and simplest piece of infrastructure right here – because I am following a footpath marked on a six-inch map published in 1920.
The problematic colonial context of the 19th-century mapping of Ireland – the context famously explored in Brian Friel’s 1980 play, Translations, and more recently in Maggie O’Farrell’s novel, Land – is well known. But a map is a many-layered thing, and as it moves from current document to archival matter – which happens inevitably even before it is complete – it quickly escapes the intentions of its makers. It carries secrets and subversions for future generations.
[ Leitrim’s ‘stairway to heaven’ gets upgrade in bid to lure tourists Opens in new window ]
When discussing the vexed issue of countryside access, people sometimes insist to me that Ireland never had footpaths across the landscape, that for some reason they “weren’t needed here”, that they are a uniquely “English thing”. But the second large-scale Ordnance Survey map of the 1880s plainly records a huge network of Irish footpaths, a network confirmed in later updates, well into the 20th century: a record of persistent human movement across the landscape, regardless of the iniquities of its ownership. Once you know to look, you can find this archival record confirmed in the field-scape all over Ireland.
If people know of these old Irish paths at all, they usually refer to them as “mass paths”. But these were not exclusively routes connecting outlying settlements with places of worship. Some run across fields to the former site of a shop or pub or post office. Others are simply general-purpose lines of least resistance for those travelling across country on foot.
What happened to these paths is no great mystery. They were there in the 1880s and they were there into the 1940s, and there are still fading memories of their use in some rural communities today. But as emigration emptied the countryside in the mid-20th century, and as those who remained got bicycles and cars, the ways through the fields fell out of use, and the “no trespassing” signs went up in the gateways.
The stile I found this morning lay on a path that led towards a former schoolhouse. It was surely heavily used each morning and afternoon by local children. But once that school closed in the mid-20th century, fewer and fewer people walked it. In the same period, the exact same thing was happening to the old customary footpaths in Wales and England. But the 1949 National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act ensured that the surviving British path network was recorded and protected for future generations before the atrophy was complete. In Ireland that never happened.
[ Ireland’s lost roads: pathways to our past Opens in new window ]
This is a peculiarity – a perversity, even – in the long story of Irish land reform. In its radical redistributions, the Land Commission at times allowed the old landlord class to retain their rights of access to hunt and shoot and fish on land that had been handed over to their former tenants. But it had no interest in formalising and protecting a far more important and democratic right: the right of all people to move along the time-honoured ways through the countryside – whether they led to a Mass rock or a holy well or simply to the local pub.
But the presence of these lost paths is still fossilised in their simple stiles. The little rectangle of road-bounded East Galway countryside I circuited this morning covers just 2.5 square kilometres. But when I measure up all the footpaths recorded on the old map – the cross-country route running towards the school, a shortcut from the main road at the eastern edge of the rectangle, two dead-end doglegs leading to springs in the boggy centre and a short line in the northwest corner giving access to a cillín – they add up to 5km. Five kilometres of forgotten footpaths, just in this one tiny postage stamp of land.
Now zoom out – zoom out to parish level, county level, zoom out to take in the whole island of Ireland. Imagine the tens of thousands of kilometres of paths, clearly recorded on the old maps and still just about tangible in the landscape.
Tim Hannigan teaches writing and literature at Atlantic Technological University Sligo. His book, The Pathless Land: Finding A Way Across Ireland, is published by Bloomsbury Apollo.

title: I love Vinted. I just wish it loved me back when I was scammed
description: ‘No! You don’t understand!’ I typed, feeling like K in Kafka’s The Trial, if K had simply been trying to return an ugly blouse
content:
I t’s with some shame that I write yet again about online shopping, especially given that I was recently scammed.
I purchased an “Anine Bing” shirt on Vinted for a suspiciously low price and wasn’t at home to inspect the package when it arrived. Vinted gives buyers 48 hours post-delivery to raise the alarm, which can be tricky if “delivered” means left in your neighbour’s or the green bin. When I examined it, I soon saw that my stripy shirt was more Shein hate-crime than Scandinavian chic. The bold seller explained that they had name-checked the brand in the listing but “not selected it from the drop-down menu”.
I contacted Vinted. “I’ve checked the transaction details,” the reply read, but the two-day deadline had passed. I asked what happened when an item was found to be counterfeit after two days. Days later, a new reply appeared: “I do apologise. Please disregard that last message …” I was asked to send detailed photos of the counterfeit item and receipts if I had them. I was pleasantly surprised, if confused, by the receipts request.
An hour after sending the photos, I was brushing my teeth when my phone lit up with a notification preview. “I’ve checked the transaction details …” it read and my heart sank. The two-day deadline had passed.
“No! You don’t understand!” I typed, shooing my son into bed, feeling like K in Kafka’s The Trial, if K had simply been trying to return an ugly blouse. “Your …” I paused. “... colleague requested these. See above thread??” I hit send, groaning into my phone and scaring the dog.
[ The pleasures of Vinted have often little to do with money, although the cash is nice Opens in new window ]
“I’ve checked the transaction details …”
“Conversation ended. Thank you for contacting Vinted support.”
I’m an OG second-hand shopper, with an eBay account older than some university graduates. When I was a student I learned that items beyond my budget could be found used online. I also love the goodwill of peer-to-peer shopping. In Summer 2025, when tariffs threw US post into chaos, I shipped a skirt to a Depop buyer in New York. It came back twice, costing more in postage than I earned. “It came!!!” she messaged in November, with a flourish of hearts, and I let out a little whoop on the bus.
Tariff skirts and counterfeit shirts are the outliers. Most resale transactions go off without a hitch. And for the handful that don’t there’s customer support. When Vinted closed the chat and left me holding the shirt, I felt strangely adrift with no “contact us” button in sight, not even a well-hidden one at the end of an obstacle course of help topics.
After losing money when a buyer claimed her parcel arrived empty, Catherine Warrilow started a website called Sad Vinted Faces for disgruntled users. It launched in June 2026 and has so far collected 7,000 submissions. There are sellers who say bots wrongly identified their items as counterfeit and banned them. One was flagged for art fraud on listing a “Monet” necklace, another for uploading cocktail spoons that were marked “dangerous weapons”.
[ ‘Vinted is a wolf in sheep’s clothing’: Ireland’s vintage stores on facing down online challenges Opens in new window ]
Like Warrilow, many report no recourse when a buyer falsely reports an item is damaged or missing. Buyers also feel unsupported, being asked to pay for faulty returns or engage in lengthy appeals. “AI bots”, “automated responses”, and “no human” appear in many stories. My own experience feels tame next to the user who claims their appeal denial was signed off with pawprint emojis.
Instead of charging sellers a commission, Vinted charges buyers a fee. In Ireland this is approximately 5 per cent of the item price plus 70c. Until recently this was the “buyer protection fee” and ostensibly covered customer support. It was criticised by consumer advocacy groups that felt “protection” promised more than it delivered.
In October 2025, the European Consumer Centre in the Netherlands announced it would cease handling complaints against Vinted because it could not compel the platform to reconsider decisions. Vinted’s buyer protection scheme, it pointed out, is a contractual service, not statutory consumer protection. The company sets the terms for resolving disputes.
Since October 5th, that charge is now called the “Vinted fee”. It’s a big source of revenue for the marketplace, alongside paid seller promotions such as item bumps and highlights and, potentially, interest on customer balances as it brings payments in-house through Vinted Pay.
Vinted told the Guardian that appeals are reviewed by humans. When I contacted it about buyer protection and its approach to counterfeit items, a spokesperson said Vinted remained “committed to tackling them using a combination of detection tools and human review”.
We are familiar with the platform model. On top are human exchanges that feel better than shopping from Zara, like social media once felt better than simply browsing the web. Buyers and sellers produce value. They take on risk. The platform controls the rails and takes a cut of each exchange. What might be new here is not only the risk that consumers are being exposed to, but the automation of accountability when things go wrong.
This is not just a Vinted problem. This week the European Commission opened an investigation into Booking.com , alleging the platform may have failed to prevent fraudulent listings and phishing scams aimed at consumers. It asks how much responsibility platforms have to protect users.
[ Visitors arrive ‘almost daily’ at my house expecting to stay in tourist accommodation Opens in new window ]
Users may believe there is an adequate taskforce of humans at hand whose job it is to help and keep them safe, until they’re locked out of their account and locked into a nonsense debate at 2am. They may assume that the platform is accountable to basic consumer protection, only to find it is accountable to itself.
I love Vinted. I just wish it loved me back.

title: Was that a stock market wobble, or the start of something more serious?
description: Markets becoming nervous about the scale of borrowing by ‘hyperscalers’
content:
I t’s shaping up to be a spooky Halloween on the markets. Nerves over AI , fears about France and soaring oil prices are more than enough to keep any investor awake at night. They also underline the threats to economic confidence and growth over the winter.
So far the world economy – and Ireland – has shown a remarkable resilience, particularly to uncertainty and rising energy costs . More challenges, however, lie ahead over this winter. The era of uncertainty just keeps rolling on.
Oil prices are rising again and so are wholesale gas prices, threatening higher household and business bills . Global bond markets are nervous at the level of debt in the world economy, with France in particular in the spotlight. Ireland’s cost of borrowing is on the rise, though it remains close to the lowest in the EU.
But the big news on markets this week was an AI scare leading to a fall in share prices of the big AI players on Thursday. As the European home of some of the big AI companies and an economy among the most reliant on the US, Ireland has skin in the game here. How this pans out matters.
The trigger for this week’s nerves was results from Meta . They underlined the rising scale of investment by big companies in AI and, crucially, how much of it was now reliant on borrowing.
Meta increased expected AI investment this year to around €140 billion (that’s about €30 billion more than Ireland will collect in tax this year.) This renewed the focus on the telephone numbers which the so-called hyperscalers – the big tech firms trying to get ahead in the race – are investing, added to by a whole phalanx of smaller companies trying to position themselves for the AI future.
Big companies like Meta are highly profitable and generate lots of cash. But such are the demands of AI investment that all the money they generate is still not enough to fund the building out of data centres and other AI infrastructure. This means an increased reliance on borrowed money to fund ever higher investment.
S&P Global, the ratings agency, reckons total annual investment by the big six hyperscalers – Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle and SpaceX – will reach $1.3 trillion (€1.16 trillion) by next year and total $7 trillion up to 2030.
[ AI being examined for use in State’s breast cancer screening amid missed targets Opens in new window ]
So far, some $450 billion has been borrowed this year alone by the hyperscalers and the poor reaction to the Meta results reflects nervousness among big institutional lenders, who typically operate under rules limiting the amount they extend to any one sector. Meanwhile, a whole range of complex financial arrangements means the full extent of debts are not visible.
In the benign scenario, the large investments start to pay off over the next few years and the companies can scale back borrowings as profits rise. Meanwhile, economies well positioned to take advantage of AI see big rises in productivity.
[ Tech sell-off deepens, dents rate hike bets Opens in new window ]
The malign scenario is obvious – the expected profits disappoint and the whole thing starts to unravel. Or some companies “win” in the AI race and the losers suffer. The pushback against data centres and AI in general is also part of the mix. History shows how the road to introducing transformative new technologies can be bumpy.
The amount of money now being borrowed – some of it deliberately off balance sheet – is key when it comes to spreading risk across the wider economy. It spreads the risk beyond the company’s shareholders and employees to a whole range of financiers and lenders, with implications for the financial system. Remember that while equity holders in banks were wiped out during the 2008 crash, the real damage came from the infection of the wider banking and financial system. And the complex financial structures being dreamt up to fund AI have uncomfortable echoes of what went on in the early 2000s, as debt was sliced up and sold on with little focus on the associated risk.
For Ireland, all this is important. Our economic reliance on the US and a few of its biggest multinationals for exports and tax revenue is well known.
But AI is also driving investment here – with large amounts going into new data centres and associated projects. The Central Bank estimates that AI-related investment in Ireland was up 24 per cent in the second quarter of this year, compared to the same period last year and is the key driver in higher multinational investment at the moment.
The vast bulk of the goods involved were imported – some €7.7 billion in AI-related imports were recorded in the second quarter, the bank calculated – though some of these appear to be re-exported by Irish multinational hubs. Ibec’s recent economic outlook pointed out that Ireland is both the 9th largest exporter (€22 billion in 2025) and importer (€24 billion) of AI-enabling products in the EU.
[ Germany offers a stark vision of Ireland’s possible future Opens in new window ]
But the investment that is taking place in Ireland is a boost to Ireland’s economic activity. And like corporate tax revenue, it depends on a few big players. As a key home for US investment in the EU, Ireland thus has a big interest in the wider AI economy and the bets that are being made by the big players who are the State’s biggest private sector investors and also, of course, big taxpayers.
AI is a key driver of the US economy – along with resilient consumer spending. And Ireland is the economy in Europe most reliant on the US. The boom could roll on. But the high valuations on the US stock market and the increased debt levels associated with the investment drive increase the risks of some disruption.
This is why we need to watch the US stock market and ask whether what we saw this week was a temporary wobble, or the start of something more serious. The AI soap opera features big figures like Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk, but the economic stakes are huge.
No one doubts the power of AI or its future economic importance. But, equally, no one knows how this will all pan out and where the economic winners and losers will be. As the large bets are placed by the hyperscalers, Ireland is an intensely interested bystander in what is shaping up as a big financial drama.

title: ‘We are sleeping in separate rooms. How do I know when I have given the relationship a fair chance to change?’
description: Ask Roe: ’I am not prepared to move back into the same bedroom unless we address these issues properly through couples therapy’
content:
My partner and I have been together for 10 years. We have a comfortable life together and enjoy many aspects of our life. But we have become increasingly distant over the past few years because of issues in our relationship that we have never managed to resolve. We have very different temperaments. He is often loudly reactive to even relatively minor things that bother him, often ranting at me for long periods rather than discussing and resolving the issue. I have gone through the full gamut of responses: tears and upset, loud reciprocal retaliation, empathy and efforts to work through things with him, and eventually complete withdrawal and disengagement. We have been sleeping in separate rooms for several months, for the second time in our relationship, because I cannot tolerate this dynamic and the lack of resolution around these outbursts and their impact. We have both had individual therapy (he eventually went at my insistence, following my lead) and things have temporarily improved, but the same pattern eventually returns.
The difficulty is that when he tries to repair the rift afterwards, I find myself becoming warier and less reassured, as the core issue of how we communicate and repair problems is never addressed. He generally tries to gloss over the issue by being exceptionally nice and tiptoeing around me, then things improve and eventually the same cycle happens again. He thinks I take these episodes too seriously and should simply move on because there is a lot that is good about him and our relationship and that this is just his nature. But for me, the cumulative effect is that the relationship feels unstable. Separating would involve significant financial and practical upheaval. I have said I am not prepared to move back into the same bedroom unless we address these issues properly through couples therapy, because I foresee us otherwise falling back into the same cycle of conflict, repair and distance. If I am not prepared to accept the status quo, how do I know when I have given the relationship a fair chance to change?
You and your partner are caught in a cycle of bad communication, and you have wildly different ideas of repair. Your partner believes that an apology is enough to end the argument of the present moment and go back to “normal”. You believe that repair is about repairing the overall pattern, and so needs to involve a commitment to changing the pattern and genuine efforts to do so, which involves disrupting what has now become normal.
Real repair would require him to acknowledge not only that an outburst occurred, but what it was like for you to experience it, why it was unacceptable and what he intends to do differently the next time he becomes frustrated. It would also require him to tolerate the discomfort of knowing that his behaviour has affected your trust, and committing to building that trust back up over time.
[ ‘I love my husband but I’m also so angry at him all the time’ Opens in new window ]
This differing idea of what repair entails is now resulting in you having wildly different experiences of your relationship, and is leading you to have existential doubts about whether you want to continue this relationship like this, or at all.
Because your idea of repair hasn’t been enforced in the relationship, and your partner’s outbursts and his idea of repair have been normalised, it’s not fully surprising that his behaviour has not changed. To him, you always get over these incidents and move on, so it’s not a big deal.
But to you, this repeating cycle of outbursts and apologies is weakening your sense of safety in the relationship and your confidence in its future. And because this pattern has been affecting you for so long, any outburst from him is now not being experienced in isolation, but is adding to a pile of distrust and resentment that has been building for a while.
With that in the background, I understand how even his periods of kindness and effort following a rupture may feel empty, or even painful, as they hint of the relationship you could have – but are constantly interrupted by these unchanging outbursts, so that you don’t trust them.
I also understand how his suggestion that you take these incidents too seriously may be infuriating. He is entitled to feel that your relationship has enough good in it to outweigh the more challenging moments, and he is entitled to accept apologies as he wishes to. But he doesn’t get to decide that you need to constantly absorb hurtful behaviour, he doesn’t get to decide what matters to you and he doesn’t get to decide that because he recovers from arguments quickly, you should match his speed – especially if he’s the one instigating the arguments. Of course the person expressing anger might recover more quickly than the person on the receiving end. A relationship cannot be considered repaired simply because the person who caused the hurt is ready to feel close again.
[ ‘My boyfriend has temper tantrums and verbally attacks me over chores’ Opens in new window ]
At this point I need to point out that there’s a difference between someone being reactive and someone being abusive. If his outbursts feel aggressive, if he puts you down, if you ever feel threatened, intimidated or unsafe, then you need to leave this relationship.
If this is genuinely just a person who expresses frustration in a heightened way, there is absolutely hope for turning this relationship dynamic around. It is entirely possible for people to learn healthier ways of managing conflict, even after many years of entrenched habits. The good news is, couples therapy is designed for this – to allow you both to express your different experiences, to highlight the urgency of this issue for you, and give you both concrete tools and new ways of communicating so that you can argue better and repair more fully.
The even better news is that your partner was open to the suggestion of individual therapy and seems to have made progress there, and so there’s real hope that couples counselling will make a huge difference.
You ask what would count as having given the relationship a fair chance, and I think engaging with couples therapy will definitely be part of this process. You could then commit to a period of mutual work, say six to nine months (your therapist can advise you on this), to enact everything you both learn in therapy. This time isn’t an audition or a test, but a way of seeing if the dynamic of your relationship is genuinely changing.
Does he actively engage in therapy? Does he learn more self-regulation tools, and does he become able to recognise an escalation and interrupt it? Can he genuinely take your experience of arguments seriously, and accommodate your emotional needs? Are you able to express your boundaries clearly in the moment, and when you do, are they respected? If he does upset you, can he reflect on his behaviour and express awareness for how it happened? When something goes wrong, do you both leave the conversation with a greater sense of understanding, rather than simply relief that it is over? And most importantly, do you start to feel more respected, connected and trusting because he is offering you repeated experiences of the dynamic being more stable and respectful over time?
If after attending therapy, expressing your needs and honestly trying to create a new dynamic with your partner, his behaviour doesn’t meaningfully change, you will have learned something vital and can decide what to do from there. But you do deserve better than this.

title: ‘Your best friend on the Cayman Islands is someone who owns a boat’
description: Wexford-born lawyer Pádraig Brosnan moved to Cayman around 15 years ago and is raising his family there
content:
The Cayman Islands hold many attractions for young Irish professionals, especially those with legal or financial backgrounds. Apart from being a big centre for financial services , its sunny climate, world class beaches and tax-free status have seen a surge in Irish people spending time working there in recent decades.
Many move on after a few years, making some tidy money along the way, but for an increasing number of people, Cayman is becoming a more permanent home.
When the opportunity to work in Grand Cayman came for Pádraig Brosnan around 15 years ago, the young Wexford-born lawyer jumped at the chance. Like many, the newly-married Brosnan and his wife Anita, also a lawyer, saw Cayman as an opportunity to build a nest-egg while furthering their careers in a very different part of the world.
What was to have been a transitory experience has proved anything but as the couple are now raising their young family in Cayman and enjoying everything it has to offer.
“It was everything it was cracked up to be,” he says, recalling being picked up at the airport in a limo when the couple arrived. They were soon settled in accommodation at the edge of the famous Seven Mile Beach and felt that they had arrived in paradise.
“The picture you would have of the beaches, the boats and being out on the water –if you want that life, it’s there for you. I still remember that day we first arrived. There were three couples and a single woman on that flight coming to work here. All of us are still on the island, which I think says a lot.”
What brought them there was Maples Group, a Cayman-island founded law and professional services firm with offices in Dublin, among other global locations. Brosnan followed his boss to their newly-established Dublin office in 2006 having started his career at A&L Goodbody .
When the opportunity to set up an Irish funds desk in Cayman came up, the couple felt the timing was right to try something different, with Anita also securing a position at the firm.
[ Sun and sand of the Cayman Islands proved too powerful a lure for an accountant in cold and wet Cork Opens in new window ]
Brosnan is now a partner specialising in financial services law and leads the Maples Group’s Irish team in the Cayman Islands, which is the world’s largest investment funds hub. Working with big international asset managers and financial institutions, he advises on the launch, regulation, and ongoing operation of investment structures across multiple jurisdictions.
His practice also extends to advising fund administrators, depositaries, prime brokers, investment advisers, and boards on Irish regulatory and governance matters.
While Cayman is home, Brosnan’s role involves a lot of travel, especially to North America. “On one of my last trips, I was on the 92 nd floor of a building overlooking the Hudson River in New York. It still astonishes me that I’m there helping these massive-named managers and global law firms helping them structure massive deals. I still get a massive thrill from that.”
On Cayman, the family has a busy life. “We have four kids under 12, two boys and two girls, so life is pretty full on at the moment. Thankfully, I’m only a four-minute drive from work which is very convenient. While the island is very small, I need to be out the door by 7am otherwise the traffic can get very heavy. I work until 6pm or later but I get home at lunchtime when I’m here.”
“The sun comes up around 6am and goes down early evening all year round. There are no seasons like we would be used to at home so that makes the time fly by. It gets very warm in the summer, and a lot of people go back to where they are from. Christmas time, the weather is at its best and a lot of people visit,” he explains.
While the climate is good, Cayman is still prone to hurricanes and tropical storms. “It was before our time here, but people still talk about Hurricane Ivan which hurt the island badly in 2004, causing huge damage,” he says.
Brosnan says that while the Cayman Islands was always prosperous relative to its neighbours, it is currently going through a Celtic Tiger boom with many new high-end hotels and private residences being built in recent years.
There is a well-established group of expat Irish on the island now, supporting a GAA club which fields multiple teams. Brosnan is active in the club, still playing Gaelic football, as well as soccer, and coaches junior teams. The family also enjoy life on the water. “Your best friend in Cayman is someone who owns a boat,” he says.
The family are well-settled now, and Brosnan says he cannot foresee a move back to Ireland anytime soon though he does not rule it out in the longer term. They make visits to Ireland twice a year typically.
“We’ve been away a long time at this stage, and you do miss friends and family, so we try to catch up with as many people as possible on these trips. WhatsApp is great but it’s not the same as sitting down and having a pint with someone.”

title: Have Berkshire Hathaway investors really moved on from Warren Buffett?
description: The recent rally suggests a flight to safety amid growing nerves over AI
content:
Berkshire Hathaway shares have hit record highs, prompting a Bloomberg headline that investors have “moved on” from Warren Buffett (disclosure: I own shares in Berkshire).
Shares have certainly had a good run, hitting their first all-time high since May 2nd, 2025, the day before Buffett announced he was stepping down.
The rise has been rapid, with Berkshire going on a 10-day winning streak, its first since 2018. The gains came as nerves over the AI trade rattled semiconductor stocks, with Berkshire outperforming the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index by 22 percentage points in little over a fortnight.
That’s an impressive level of outperformance, but it doesn’t change the bigger picture. Since Buffett announced his impending departure 17 months ago, Berkshire shares have been essentially flat, whereas the S&P 500 advanced some 35 per cent.
The valuation story is similarly revealing. Immediately before Buffett’s announcement, Berkshire traded at about 1.8 times book value, well above its historical norm of roughly 1.4-1.5 times.
That looked generous even with Buffett still in charge. The subsequent sell-off wrung out that excess, with Berkshire trading at 1.55 times book value at the end of 2025. By March 2026 it had slipped further, to about 1.45, and it remains around that level today.
The recent rally, then, doesn’t so much suggest new-found confidence in Buffett’s successor, Greg Abel, as it does a flight to safety amid growing nerves over AI.
In fairness to Abel, nor do the figures amount to a vote of no confidence. However, if investors once paid a premium for Buffett himself, that premium is difficult to discern today.

title: Andy Irvine on Dónal Lunny: ‘He glued Planxty together and made the structure work’
description: The friends made music together through decades when Ireland became a lot more liberal. But it could still be more egalitarian, like the society Irvine’s hero Woody Guthrie campaigned for
content:
I n the basement of the International Bar in Dublin, Andy Irvine , of Sweeney’s Men, Planxty , Mozaik, LAPD and Usher’s Island, is playing me the songs of Woody Guthrie while wearing an Industrial Workers of the World T-shirt.
“This is all good practice for tonight, because I’m playing in Tower Records and I’m not quite ready,” he says, and his wife, Kumiko, laughs.
They met in 2000, when she was roped in to help organise a tour for Irvine and the late Dónal Lunny in Japan . Irvine is 84 years old and about to go on tour once more. He is holding his guitar-shaped bouzouki and has a harmonica upside down in the harness in the same style as Guthrie. He recently released Devoted, a record made up of Guthrie songs and one of his own that’s a tribute to the American singer.
“I discovered Woody Guthrie when I was about 16,” Irvine says. “First of all, I was fascinated by the music he played, and I took that on board. And then gradually, as I got to know more and more about Woody, I took his politics on board as well. I took everything on board in the end.”
Guthrie’s music speaks remarkably well to the current age, with songs warning against fascism, decrying injustice, lamenting the plight of refugees and urging the people to unite against the tycoons who exploit them.
“Woody wanted to see a more equal world,” Irvine says. “In the 1940s, when he was travelling around in the south [of the United States], there was segregation. Woody used to play with Sonny Terry and Brownie McGhee, two black men, and he insisted that they all go into white places.”
Irvine was obsessed with Guthrie as a teenager. “I met Pete Seeger in London” – Irvine’s family lived there – “and I asked him where Woody was, because there was no way of finding out these things in those days,” he says. “There was no internet or even an encyclopedia to tell you.
“So I found out that he was in hospital in New Jersey with Huntington’s disease, which he had inherited from his mother, and he was no longer able to sing and play.
“He couldn’t write, but a lovely woman called Sid Gleason, who lived in East Orange, New Jersey, with her husband used to take him out at weekends.
“Sid was great with me. We became really close friends. She was the one who called me Andy first. She said, ‘Oh, Andrew sounds so formal. Do you mind if I call you Andy…?’
“The letters to Woody Guthrie were all discovered about 10 or 15 years ago, when they knocked down Greystone Park” – a psychiatric hospital in New Jersey – “and they’re all now in the Woody Guthrie archive…
“I was 16 or 17, and the things I said … I shiver with embarrassment.”
One evening at Peggy Seeger and Ewan MacColl’s club in London, Guthrie’s friend Ramblin’ Jack Elliott played.
[ Peggy Seeger: ‘I met Bob Dylan before he was Bob Dylan. He came for my autograph’ Opens in new window ]
“People rushed towards Jack, all these extrovert people, and I thought, well, there’s no point in me joining them, because I’m not one of them. So I stalked him all the way back to his house and noted the address. I went home and wrote him a letter with my phone number, and he rang me up the next day and said, ‘Come on over,’ and I couldn’t believe my luck.
“I rode over on the bicycle. I was 17. They didn’t know what they were letting themselves in for. I’d go over every morning. I’d get there about 9.30 or 10am and I’d bang on the door. And June, Jack’s wife, would get up and she’d come to the door and go, ‘Oh, it’s you! Come in…’
“Jack was hanging out of Woody when he was about my age or a little bit older, so I don’t know if that’s the reason he accepted my friendship, but we became really good friends.”
He plays Ramblin’ Round , a song Guthrie wrote about dust bowl refugees in the 1930s. He plays a bit of another Guthrie song, The 1913 Massacre , about a real attack on miners and their families by a mine owner’s goons.
“It’s a great last line,” he says. “‘See what your greed for money has done…’ Everything wrong with the human race is in that line.”
Next Irvine plays Wallace Taylor Train/Bet on Wallace, a hybrid of two campaign songs Guthrie wrote for Henry Wallace, Franklin D Roosevelt’s vice-president before he was ditched in favour of Harry Truman.
This meant Truman was the man in office when Roosevelt died. So Wallace ran independently for president as an out-and-out socialist candidate. He lost.
“That was the end of any chance of progressive politics [in the United States]. The reason [Wallace] didn’t get the vice-presidency of 1944 was because a lot of the Democratic senators and House representatives from the south disagreed with his policy of ending segregation.
“It would have been interesting to see how he would have managed if he had been president of the USA.”
Irvine also plays Mister Charlie Lindbergh, an attack on the fascism-curious American aviator. It contains the line, “They say America First, but they mean America Next.” “That song was not released on record until the 1960s,” Irvine says. “I imagine it might have been something to do with libel possibilities.”
In his own Guthrie tribute song, Never Tire of the Road, he also quotes the singer’s refrain “All you fascists bound to lose”. “I sang that at the end of [an American] show, and everybody joined in with gusto.” Irvine laughs. “There probably wasn’t one Republican in the audience.”
What is he thinking as he plays this music?
“At this moment I’m probably thinking, ‘What’s the next verse and where am I on the fingerboard?’” He laughs. “They become more dramatic and emotional as time goes on.”
Guthrie’s egalitarianism is what attracted Irvine, he says. “When I was quite young I used to get up early and travel around the block of flats that we lived in with the porter. He’d be emptying the bins, and I’d be fascinated by what [would] be in the bins. I collected things…
“I really liked Jack very much, but my parents were saying you shouldn’t really be hanging around with this working-class man, and I didn’t understand that. So I think I had it in me anyway. But, yeah, Woody shaped it.”
His mother was the musical comedy performer Felice Lascelles, and Irvine became a child actor. “My mother was very showy. A couple of drinks and she’d sing at the drop of a hat. And everybody loved her except her miserable 10-year-old son, who was embarrassed by almost everything she did.”
[ Phil Coulter: ‘The song Congratulations has fed, clothed and educated my children’ Opens in new window ]
Irvine doesn’t seem particularly showbiz. “No, I absolutely hate showbiz.”
Is his more earthy and introverted musical career a response to that?
“It could be … I’m not an extrovert at all, and in fact I get very nervous on stage, which is why I’m having a drink now. If I’m playing well I love it. I love myself … I think I want to be loved, you know? And if the audience loves me and loves my music, I’m brought back up to self-confidence zero.”
“I don’t know. I’m a nervous man. It’s no hardship. Ronnie Drew [of The Dubliners] was also really nervous. He’d get sick before going on the stage.”
Irvine met Drew when he came back to Dublin at the age of 20 and found a new ballad scene around O’Donoghue’s Bar.
“At that time almost no pubs allowed music. Even in O’Donoghue’s, a year or two before I arrived, Johnny Moynihan [who became his bandmate in Sweeney’s Men] would play the tin whistle under his coat and Maureen O’Donoghue would be going, ‘Who’s playing music there?’ I think by the time I arrived O’Donoghue’s allowed music, and that was the big attraction of it.”
He loved The Dubliners. “They were very kind to me, and welcoming, and when they were away on tour O’Donoghue’s wasn’t quite the same,” Irvine says. “Ronnie giving out yards to people…
“In the early 1960s Dublin was a very conservative place. And people were very much ruled by the Catholic hierarchy. Sometimes if you went out in the street with your jeans and a beard, people would look at you and go tsk-tsk.
“O’Donoghue’s was a planet where you were among your own people.”
The toilet there even made a musical drone that Irvine liked to sing to, he says.
“I was very disappointed when I went in last year and the drone wasn’t there any more.”
“I hadn’t enjoyed it since I was about 14 or 15, when the dreaded puberty hit me and I suddenly became a lot more self-conscious… When I played music with Johnny and other people it was a lifestyle. I didn’t have any ambitions. We very rarely played for money. Johnny had a set of rules by which he lived, and I kind of agreed with him.”
Moynihan brought the bouzouki to Irish music.
“One weekend he came over with a bouzouki, and that was the beginning of it. We didn’t like it at all. It was a Greek bouzouki, and I can’t remember what we didn’t like about it. But he then was told of a flat-back instrument of the same type available from a maker in London, and he flew over there and he bought it, and that was the beginning of the Irish bouzouki.”
It became Moynihan, Irvine and, later, Lunny’s go-to instrument.
“The trouble with the guitar, if you played a G chord, it had too many thirds in it. And thirds were not good if you were accompanying reels and jigs.”
When did Irvine realise he was a “professional musician”?
“Sweeney’s Men was formed in 1966. The summer of 1966 was magnificent. We travelled around Ireland… I keep diaries quite often but never when things are going really wonderfully.
“It’s a great shame I can’t remember too much about it. We came back to Dublin at the end of the summer of 1966, and we shared a house in the North Strand, and we got almost no work and we were really rat poor.
“I think that’s when I decided I was a professional musician, in the attic with nothing to eat.”
They were managed by Des Kelly, the leader of the Capitol Showband, who got them gigs. They often played at the interval during showband gigs with terrible sound set-ups.
“I remember singing our hit song The Old Maid in the Garret… I set off in a key hoping it was the right one. At the end of the first verse I discovered it wasn’t.”
“Along with the rest of European youth, I got this buzz to get out on the road, hitchhiked to Bulgaria and Romania, and the rest is history,” he says.
“A ‘sunburnt thumb’ was what Woody used to call it. As Galway Joe Dolan [another Sweeney’s Men founder] wrote, ‘Why we’re travelling, I don’t know, just pack up your bag and get up and go.’
“The realisation that one could go to all these places and see them without having a load of money, young people all over Europe in 1967, 1968 all discovered that at the same time.”
Irvine has always been an internationalist, happy to play Irish music, American music, Scottish music and Balkan music on this Irish-Greek instrument .
He’s surprised it wasn’t more controversial among the purists.
“In 1970 I worked up this song, which I’d learned most of from Eddie Butcher, The Plains of Kildare… Part of [the arrangement] is in seven-eight [time] … I remember playing a gig in the Neptune rowing club, and I thought ‘God knows what they’ll think. People like [the accordion player] Tony MacMahon might come up and hit me.’”
He laughs. I tell Irvine that I find those time signatures difficult to play and that I’m more comfortable in four-four or three-four time. He laughs. “Good for you. I’m not that good in four-four.”
Planxty first came together to accompany Christy Moore on his album Prosperous; then Moore had the idea that they should form a permanent ensemble. There was a magic to it.
“I think Christy and Liam [O’Flynn] and myself just did what we did when we played solo, but Dónal [Lunny] glued it all together and made the structure work … We were just chemically the right four people.”
Irvine and Lunny subsequently worked together on many other projects. Lunny “just gets into everybody’s brain”, he says. “Whoever he’s playing with, he plays exactly what they would like to hear.”
Lunny, who is unwell when Irvine and I talk – it was announced on Friday afternoon that he had died , at the age of 79, after a long illness – was the subject of a moving documentary, In Time, by Nuala O’Connor . Irvine saw Lunny recently. “He was in great form ... The number of bands on hold because of Dónal [being ill] is in the millions.”
[ Siobhán Long: Dónal Lunny’s legacy will be his openness to new ways of interpreting old music Opens in new window ]
Irvine is heartened by the way younger people keep finding his music. In 2005, when Planxty re-formed, they benefited from a No Disco documentary and book about the band from the writer and promoter Leagues O’Toole.
“I remember playing in the National Concert Hall and the first two rows were all people under 25 who wouldn’t have been born the first time we played.”
Some of Irvine’s oldest material still gets the best response.
“The West Coast of Clare, the first song I ever wrote, continues to be the audience’s favourite of my songs, which is a little bit annoying.” He laughs. “I sang it with John Doyle in North Carolina quite recently, and the audience actually gave it a standing ovation.”
Does he consider the rearrangements he does of songs from the traditional canon to be a form of writing?
“I might change the odd word. I might even change the odd tune… I’m not averse to meddling.”
When Irvine is working on a song, he says, he goes “to a different dimension.”
Of the current wave of young Irish trad acts, he particularly likes Daoirí Farrell and Ye Vagabonds . He still plays with the Swedish group Quilty; they’re about to tour Ireland together.
“My latest excitement became Swedish polskas and fiddle music. It’s very odd. A polska seems to go on about four bars longer than it should.”
Does he have any thoughts on the music industry? “I’m not a fan of the music industry. One hopes for success. But it’s not the most important thing.”
“Doing it and loving it.” He laughs. “And getting loved for it.”
Why do this album now, almost 70 years after first discovering Guthrie?
“I was always a little bit aggrieved that the powers that be recognised so many people as being Woody Guthrie fans and not me. So that might have been one of the reasons. I thought, ‘Right, f**k this. I’m weighing in.’”
Andy Irvine and Quilty begin their tour of Ireland at Belfast International Arts Festival on Wednesday, November 4th, followed by dates in Dún Laoghaire and Naul, Co Dublin; Newbridge, Co Kildare; Kilmacow, Co Kilkenny; Galway; Limerick; Cork City; and Clonakilty, Co Cork. Andy Irvine also plays with Oisín Leech in Navan, Co Meath, on Saturday, November 21st. More details on andyirvine.com . His album Devoted: Songs of Woody Guthrie is released by the Last Music Company

title: Artist Patrick Graham: ‘I can sit with an empty canvas for months. I can sit there and almost weep’
description: The inaugural winner of the Francis Bacon Award for lifetime achievement in Irish visual art on his creative process
content:
A visit to a painter’s studio can go in one of two ways: the artist might have lined up works for you to view as if at an exhibition, or they might have turned canvases to face the wall, like shy kids at a party.
Patrick Graham , winner of the lifetime-achievement prize in Dublin Gallery Weekend ’s inaugural Francis Bacon Awards for Irish visual art, is in the latter category. The 83-year-old artist, who prefers to go by Paddy, is also unmoved by honours, shrugging when I ask what the €25,000 accolade might mean to him.
Instead he’s preoccupied with solving the puzzles of making art that satisfies him. “Every painting I do, I love it for about a week,” he says. And while some artists work on a number of pieces at once, Graham concentrates on a single canvas, from start to finish. “They all have their own life. They all take their own time. They’re like children. And some of them are very bad children.” He smiles.
There’s something mischievous about Graham, a leavening to his seriousness as an artist. He is also rather charming.
We are meeting at his studio at the Fire Station building, on Buckingham Street in north inner-city Dublin. He’s been here since 1993, when he moved from Temple Bar Gallery and Studios, which had closed for renovations.
[ Subscriber Only Art The life-changing work of Alice Maher, an artist to her bones Opens in new window ]
The Arts Council invited Graham to rent a space at the Fire Station to help raise the profile of the new, community-oriented centre; its studios are residential, meaning artists don’t have to find accommodation in the city. “I hadn’t enough money to buy a chicken run then,” he says.
In the studio today, only one canvas faces out, its layered, textured greys relieved by a line of marks, each of them one of the seven colours of the rainbow. It is a strange painting, simple from a distance but with more of a sense of barely controlled chaos close up, the colours either hopefully emerging or about to be consumed.
Graham’s benches, table and shelves are highly ordered, their pastels, paints and inks lined up. His knife-sharpened pencils are different lengths, but their bases are aligned as straight as a ruler. There is a neat pile of pages from a sketchbook, some torn-out shapes of drawings, annotated with letters. A pencilled arrow, marked “deep red”, points to a spot in a drawing.
“The process is the same, over and over again,” Graham says. “And every time I say: ‘When you think you’ve learned something, you know you’re an idiot.’ But it’s a pattern I have to go through to resolve each painting. It’s about ego and surrender.”
“Paddy struggles to finish each one,” says John Daly, Graham’s Dublin gallerist at Hillsboro Fine Art. (The artist is represented in the United States by Jack Rutberg, who is based in California.) “I might come in and a painting looks finished. Then the next day he’s wiped it all off again.”
Graham’s paintings have been compared to those of Anselm Kiefer and Cy Twombly ; the influential US critic Donald Kuspit called his paintings masterpieces “on a grand physical, emotional and intellectual scale”, declaring them “among the most complicated salient reflections on modern existence that have ever been made”.
Even allowing for hyperbole, that’s quite the statement. But Graham’s talent is of a phenomenal order.
When the artist was growing up, in Mullingar, Co Westmeath, his father left the family to work in England.
“He was a complete wanker. I hate saying that, but in a way it’s true. He was considered a rogue and a rascal. That kind of thing. He was an engineer, and he wound up with a brilliant job in England. Later, I found little notebooks of his with beautiful drawings.”
After his mother contracted tuberculosis, Graham and his siblings were sent to live with different relatives. He wound up with his grandparents, a period that gave him a love of nature. But he loved drawing more.
At school, his art teacher, Diarmuid Larkin, recognised his talent and invited him to work on stage sets at the local drama group. Larkin also entered him in art competitions, with the result that Graham was awarded a scholarship to the National College of Art and Design when he was 13 – too young to go. He took up his place three years later.
Francis Bacon , who the new awards are named after, was a hero “for about, I’d say, 10 years. Then I got tired of them. Something went amiss. I don’t want to talk like I’m the kind of person who can judge someone like Bacon, but I think he got caught up in being Francis Bacon.”
Instead, Graham’s art heroes are “Goya, della Francesca and Rembrandt. Not many outside those”.
He talks about trying to get beyond his skill, which he describes as “a nice pair of hands”. They were much-lauded hands, too, as his tutors lined up to praise his work. But he describes art college as all about skill and style. “You can make and do a painting that is startlingly beautiful, but there it stops, he says. “This is about the struggle to make art that resonates with your very being.”
Graham’s breakthrough came in 1963, when he chanced on an exhibition by Emil Nolde , the German expressionist painter. He experienced the idea that art can act like a punch to the stomach, and to the soul.
After that he didn’t paint again for years.
“I couldn’t bear what I was producing. It was just coming off my hand, and there was a whole lot of something else churning around myself. The way I found to explain it to myself was to nearly drink myself to death,” Graham says.
“At certain points, what I got from booze was an absolute exquisite kind of silence, and the depth of it seemed a potential for something, but that something was never available.”
A long period of recovery followed, and with it the realisation that he had to relearn how he made art.
“My hands interfered all the time – they couldn’t help looking for style – so I had to be prepared to be taught by what I was doing. I tried some awful stuff,” he says.
“I can sit with a canvas, an empty canvas, for months, I can sit there and almost weep. There’s this fight with myself and my ego. I want people to understand that I’m brilliant, and I’m afraid to let that go. But one day I’ll make a mark and it has a voice, and I hear it, and it carries the painting through. And I find it still beautiful, still amazing.”
A breakthrough of a different kind came when the Hollywood horror actor Vincent Price came to see his exhibition at the now-closed Lincoln Gallery in Dublin. Price had heard about Graham’s work from a friend and was waiting outside when the gallery opened. He not only bought paintings but also encouraged Graham to show at an art fair in Los Angeles.
“He was a very nice man. He spoke like he did in the movies, and he had an extraordinary collection,” Graham says. “He’d bought his first print, a Rembrandt, when he was 14.”
The art fair was a success: Graham’s booth won the award for best in show. Gallery representation in the US followed. Cameron Diaz bought his work, as did big public collections, although Graham refuses to name-drop.
A significant survey exhibition of his work, Transfiguration, was held at the Hugh Lane Gallery , in Dublin, in 2022. Did he ever get to a point where he thought: “That’s me, made”?
“No, you learn to love the insecurity of it,” Graham says. “Because you then imagine today as eternity. ‘This is my hour. That’s all I have. F**k it.’”
While Patrick Graham is the winner of Francis Bacon Award for lifetime achievement in Irish visual art, Cathy Wilkes has picked up the €15,000 mid-career award.
The Belfast-born artist, who now lives and works in Glasgow, where she went to art college, was nominated for the Turner Prize in 2008; she represented Scotland at the Venice Biennale of 2005 and then represented Britain in 2019.
Wilkes makes elusive, often introspective collages, installations and sculptures; her art tends to take ideas and memories of domestic scenes but make them troubling and strange.
The awards, which are part of the ever-expanding Dublin Gallery Weekend, are supported by Château La Coste, the hotelier and businessman Paddy McKillen ’s wine estate, hotel and sculpture park in southern France.
[ Paddy McKillen’s French idyll: A place of great architecture and stunning art Opens in new window ]
The winners will each have a solo exhibition at the Provence chateau, where the permanent collection includes work by such artists and architects as Tadao Ando, Louise Bourgeois, Alexander Calder, Sophie Calle, Tracey Emin, Sean Scully and Ai Weiwei.
The very generous prize fund will help raise the profile of the Francis Bacon Awards – although that perhaps also only emphasises the financial insecurity that dogs artists, even those with long and successful careers.
Aosdána , of which Graham is a member, offers support to a few. Sadly, however, the Basic Income for the Arts scheme, lauded during its post-lockdown pilot phase as an innovative way to recognise how artists work and to provide meaningful long-term support, has not been extended beyond 36 months per recipient or expanded to all artists in its newly permanent version.
Instead, of the 10,000 artists who applied, it will provide 2,000 – the same number as in the pilot scheme – with payments of €325 a month for three years, very much in the model of Mexico’s long-running art-creators programme.
[ Basic income for the arts is now permanent. But for artists who apply, the money is not Opens in new window ]
What the Francis Bacon Awards and events such as Dublin Gallery Weekend best achieve is the shining of a spotlight on Ireland’s phenomenal art talent.
It sometimes takes big chunks of money, whether in the form of a high sales price or that of a big prize pot, to focus the mind on a different type of value, and on artists who uncompromisingly put up with the financial insecurity, precarious studio tenures and fickle nature of public opinion as they keep on making their remarkable work.
Dublin Gallery Weekend runs from Thursday, November 5th, until Sunday, November 8th. Patrick Graham joins the gallerist Robert Diament for a free but ticketed Talk Art podcast recording at the National Gallery of Ireland on Saturday, November 7th. Cathy Wilkes has work in Technologies of Peace, at the Irish Museum of Modern Art in Dublin, until May 9th, 2027, and a solo show at the Model , in Sligo, until January 17th, 2027.

title: I’m tired of watering my polytunnel. Should I install an irrigation system?
description: Drip irrigation systems water the ground rather than the plants, ensuring that their root systems receive sufficient water
content:
After spending what felt like way too many valuable hours watering my polytunnel this summer, I’m thinking of installing some sort of irrigation system to make life easier. What would you recommend? D Byrne, Kildare
My sincere sympathies. I can’t think of a chore I dislike more than watering a polytunnel in the middle of a summer heatwave. It’s tedious, time-consuming and uncomfortable to boot, plus you never really feel that you’ve fully succeeded in giving plants the kind of proper drenching to their roots that’s required.
My advice would be to invest in a drip irrigation system, which uses a series of interlocking perforated water pipes laid in a grid formation across the ground, connected to a water supply. This has a number of advantages over sprinkler systems. The most significant is that it waters the ground rather than the plants, ensuring – importantly – that their root systems receive sufficient water rather than simply drenching their leaves.
Another is that it maximises plant health by minimising the risk of fungal and bacterial plant diseases such as blight and powdery mildew caused by high humidity as a result of overhead irrigation overly wetting foliage, flowers and fruit.
Drip irrigation also helps to minimise water wastage, as well as the run-off of valuable plant nutrients that can sometimes be a problem with overhead watering systems. Another bonus is that it can be paired with smart features such as timers, moisture sensors and zoning controllers that allow you to fine-tune the amount of water based on the requirements of the particular crop.
[ Plant, mulch, move: essential garden jobs as autumn closes in Opens in new window ]
Unlike sprinklers, you can also use it in cases where you’re relying on a low-gravity water feed rather than a pressurised feed, meaning it can be hooked up to a rainwater harvesting system. Just make sure the water tank is suitably elevated, ideally 1.5 metres above ground level to guarantee sufficient pressure. Install a filter to prevent any debris such as rotting leaves clogging up the pipes and get advice from your supplier on using the correct type of drippers.
On the downside, it’s not the cheapest system, can be complicated and time-consuming to install correctly and works best on level ground and on neat lines or rows of crops. On uneven ground, the watering can be patchy and uneven. The pipes can also sometimes get clogged by debris, while it’s also not the most aesthetically pleasing to look at. But all these considered, it would be my first choice over other options and is the irrigation system most commonly used by professional growers.
[ Your gardening questions answered: Is a polytunnel too much work? Opens in new window ]
Recommended Irish suppliers of drip irrigation systems include Quickcrop ( quickcrop.ie ) and Fruithill Farm ( fruithilfarm.com ), both of which will also provide valuable advice on site-specific design and installation. Both also supply high-quality drip irrigation systems that are resistant to frost damage. Finally, irrigation systems aside, bear in mind that you can also help the soil in your polytunnel to retain moisture and be more drought-resilient by adding organic matter in the shape of home-made compost, well-rotted manure, seaweed, grass clippings or commercial mulches.

title: From breezy floorboards to a cosy A rating: A Lucan refurb more than worth the wait
description: This family went with a one-stop shop when planning the renovation and retrofit of their Lucan home
content:
Y ou know your home needs a deep energy retrofit when you can feel a breeze rising from the floorboards.
