Phil Tomlinson and Sarah Duke felt breezes coming from all directions when they bought their home in Lucan , Co Dublin, in 2020. “We were spending a fortune on heat,” she recalls. “You’d have to have the heat on all the time in the winter. And as soon as it was turned off, the house was cold again.”
They bought the 1960s three-bedroom dormer bungalow with an immediate plan to renovate it to suit the needs of their household – a family of five with two dogs.
“We loved the location. We love the very private, big south-facing back garden,” Tomlinson says. “But the head space in the upstairs bedrooms was very restricted because of the sloped roof. And we wanted to modernise the house, both in terms of the flow and the use, and energy performance wise.”
They commissioned an architect and got planning permission for an extensive renovation project. “It included a double-storey extension with a master bedroom upstairs overlooking the garden, but when we priced it, it was 20 or 30 per cent more than we paid for the house. Construction prices went crazy during Covid,” he recalls.
Duke remembers one builder who gave her a quote that matched their budget, but when they examined it, the price did not include floors, kitchen or bathrooms. “It was just for the shell of the building and you can’t live in that.”
They decided to press pause on their plans and this gave them the breathing space to figure out what they really needed. “Everybody says this, but it’s so true – wait until you’ve lived in the house for a good two or three years before even getting the architect in,” she says. “I was so impatient. I had all these ideas and it was all very exciting but it didn’t make sense, because I wasn’t 100 per cent sure what I wanted.”
Tomlinson says the extra time helped them realise what they needed to change. “I love to cook, and the way the kitchen flowed really got under my skin. To get to the back garden, the children and dogs would come running through the kitchen, sometimes running between me and the hob when I was cooking. The fridge was down in the utility. It just wasn’t working.”
They were watching the deep retrofit of a house on RTÉ’s Room to Improve one night and liked the work done by the builder, Larkrock Homes. While some builders specialise in extensions, and others in retrofitting, this firm does both. It is one of a number of firms approved by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) to offer the One Stop Shop service. This service helps people to avail of grants for energy upgrades by managing the entire project, including the grant application. The building firms deduct the value of grants upfront, making the project more affordable for homeowners.
“It was exactly what we wanted. We just needed a crew to come in and take it over from start to finish. And it’s one bill as well at the end, rather than us having to source windows, floors and tiles and pay all those different places,” Duke says.
Larkrock recommended an architect – and when they received his plans, they finally had what they wanted at a price they could afford. “He came in with a fresh set of eyes on it. The previous plans were very elaborate, transforming the whole house, but he was like, no, just use the space a little differently. It ended up being a lot cheaper and made sense for us because we didn’t have to add a ton of square metres,” she says.
Larkrock co-owner Damien Tracey says homeowners sometimes believe they need a big extension, but by reconfiguring the space they have, they will greatly reduce building costs.
“Just try to keep it as simple as you can. What do you actually want? It might come down to someone wanting an en suite so they’re not queuing to get into the bathroom. It’s the simple things that make people happy, like living in a warm house with a stable temperature. Do you really need this extension when underfloor heating might be better?”
This couple settled on a 28sq m (301sq ft) extension at the back of the house. They raised the dormer roof on the bedrooms and put their money into windows, underfloor heating and other energy conservation measures.
“We put in Aluclad windows – triple glazed, new doors, external and internal insulation, underfloor heating throughout, new radiators, a heat pump, 18 solar panels, and we did the attic insulation.”
Their home went from D1 to A0 – a new Ber category for the most energy‑efficient homes that do not use fossil fuels. The solar panels were recently installed, so it’s too soon to see the difference they are making, but they have two electric cars, so they expect to see a significant reduction in their home and motoring bills over time.
The couple started the project last November and moved into their revamped home in July. The first thing they noticed was the silence in the house. It is close to the N4, but the new windows and insulation have blocked out the traffic sounds. “The kids could have all their pals in the sittingroom or bedrooms and you don’t hear a thing. The constant access to hot water is really nice too,” Duke says.
“We’re actually looking forward to the winter for the first time, because we know the house is going to be warm and cosy and not too expensive to heat.”
Larkrock’s calculations show that the home’s energy consumption was 239.04 kWh/m²/yr, but it has now become a net-energy producer thanks to solar panels, heat pump and insulation. “The combination of energy upgrades, thoughtful renovation and the new extension creates a home ready for the future,” Tracey says.
Tomlinson says his favourite thing is the kitchen. “It’s the dream kitchen that we’ve wanted since we’ve first known each other,” he says.
The soft-closing cabinet doors are still a delight, and they appreciate the pull-out larders and clever storage solutions. They sourced the pendants over their island and the dining table light from Copperfish Lighting Company, a family business in Co Wicklow. “The wood is 400 year-old French oak from a church in France, and he [Eoin Shanley] takes it and blackens it up by hand and makes all the lights for it.”
The Dekton worktop from Granite and Marble Crafts complements the light fittings, and the cabinetry [from Good Brother Kitchens] feels luxurious. “It’s such a nice space to be in and to cook in.”
The Neff induction hob has a built-in extractor system so there’s no need for an overhead fan. “You could be cooking steaks at a high heat and you can’t smell it at all. And we’ve got the double Neff ovens as well with the slide-and-hide doors.”
The couple were comfortable making all the interior design choices “but what we found difficult were the practical things, like where sockets and light fixtures should go, things like that”.
Tomlinson advises people to have a clear plan for lighting before embarking on a similar renovation. “You need certain types of lighting for working and for ambience. Where are you going to put them? Do you need LEDs and where do you want them? We hadn’t thought that through so we were kind of rushed at the end trying to figure it all out.”
Since this project, Larkrock has begun offering its own interior design service to help customers with this part of the renovation.
If they hadn’t added a few extras, the project would have come in on budget. “It was very transparent,” they say. “For example, we hadn’t factored in putting in new stairs. But the old stairs were kind of creaky, and we thought, ‘Why would we have these lovely new floors, and these old stairs?’ So halfway through the job, we decided to put it in a new stair and that added €5,000 to the cost.”
They estimate that the SEAI grants covered up to 15 per cent of the total cost of the renovation. “It could be better, but it’s better than nothing,” Duke says. “Hopefully the Government will continue to give grants for people to be able to tap into systems like this because it is still out of reach for a lot of people.”
Tracey also encourages homeowners to consider the Home Energy Upgrade Loan Scheme . This Government-backed initiative offers low-interest loans from €5,000 to €75,000, with repayment terms of up to 10 years (rates start from about 3 per cent). “We are hopeful that this might be extended above the €75,000 limit to closer to €150,000, to allow homeowners do a deeper retrofit and avail of the hassle-free low-cost loans.”
[ A Galway kitchen ‘refresh’ ended up gutting half the house, but the owners couldn’t be happier Opens in new window ]
These homeowners estimate that the money spent on their renovation has increased the value of their home by the same amount. But whatever their home is now worth, they have no plans to sell it. “We’re not going anywhere,” Tomlinson says. “This is the house we’ve been wanting for our family for ever. We love where we live.”

title: Sarah Moss: Is it possible for me, an immigrant writer, to produce ‘Irish fiction’?
description: Sarah Moss: Is it possible for me, an immigrant writer, to produce ‘Irish fiction’?
content:
Whenever I give a straightforward answer to the question “where are you from?”, I feel as if I’m lying.
In Ireland, I say “northern England” – it’s important to insist, not London , not the south – though I’ve now spent far more of my life in other places and neither of my parents is from the city where they raised me. They themselves moved away years ago. When I’m actually there, I don’t claim to be from Manchester . I say “I grew up here”, and people look doubtful because I don’t sound that way.
Elsewhere in Europe, I say “I live in Dublin”, which is true and has been for six years. But you’re not from the place where you moved in your 40s.
My delight at being awarded a prize for Scottish writers last year was partly because recognition is heart-warming, and also because I’d rarely dared to call myself Scottish. Accepting the prize, painfully conscious of my English accent, I told the story of my great-grandparents finding a place of safety in Glasgow after fleeing Russia and Latvia 100 years ago, though what qualified me officially was that my American father and English mother were living in Scotland when I was born.
I like being Scottish. I have beloved Scottish friends and relatives. I’ve spent time in and set novels there. Often I’d also like to be in some hyphenated or qualified way Irish. But I’m patently neither, though my British passport names Glasgow as my place of birth and as I write I’m awaiting my certificate of Irish naturalisation.
Writers’ national identity sometimes seems to matter as much as sports players’ , and for similar reasons. Whose team are you on, which country are you playing for, which prizes can you win? Like many writers and artists, I have never been a team player. I dislike clubs and competitions, distrust cliques and gangs. Writers are, often, to generalise, outsiders, observers, given to the long view, odd if not downright awkward. We see patterns uninteresting to other people and question what seems self-evident. How do these propensities relate to the construction of literature as an international sport?
The definition of an Irish, English or Scottish writer is not obvious to me. (I’m sure Welshness is at least as complex, with a distinctive language politics, but I have no claim at all there.) Following a long and honourable tradition, many “Irish” writers don’t live in Ireland, and some of those regarded as Irish here have more fluid identities elsewhere; sometimes this fluidity is at least as much the product of transnational lives and careers as of the international tendency to confuse Ireland and Britain. Some writers, artists and musicians who live and work in Ireland are not habitually included among “Irish artists”. I do not know if it is possible for an immigrant writer to produce “Irish fiction”; there are, after all, no official rules, and probably customs vary. (I wonder as I write, is this another example of the loud-mouthed immigrant saying what should not be said? Or is it my immigrant writer’s job to do just that?)
The first novel I published after moving here was written feverishly in the locked-down autumn of 2020, and set on the Derbyshire moors for which I longed as I worked, like many others that year, on a makeshift desk in the corner of a small bedroom. I wrote myself back into a place I missed, among people whose voices I knew from childhood. I was still getting to know my allotted 5km and none of us was fully present.
[ Sarah Moss: One phrase has always annoyed me: ‘Remember there’s always someone worse off than you’ Opens in new window ]
After that, I set a novel between Italy and north Clare, partly because I had fallen in love with the Burren and also because I wanted to explore the idea of belonging to a place through love and knowledge rather than birthright. My central character had lived in Ireland much longer than I have and married into an Irish family, but she was English. By then I’d been here long enough and made enough friends that she could have an Irish best friend in whose speech patterns and ways of thinking I had reasonable confidence, but I asked my own Irish friends to read drafts. I constructed the novel so there was no scene without an outsider to Ireland; as Austen is reported to have said of conversations between men, I don’t know what they sound like when I’m not there.
By this point, three years in, I found myself interestingly constrained as a novelist. I had been away from Britain too long to set a contemporary novel there. I return several times a year for work and to see friends, but I’m not breathing that air or hearing those conversations. I still vote in England, but when I hear myself describing life there to friends here I’m increasingly aware that I’m describing a different time as well as a different place. I live here. I work here and socialise here, vote and pay tax and have opinions and generally, I hope, participate. Ireland is where I listen to people on buses and in cafes and where I chat to friends and strangers and where I teach and go to meetings and bike in traffic and run in weather, and also where I read and where I write.
Hiberno-English trickles through my prose and speech. My accent hasn’t changed much, but my syntax and vocabulary have. Increasingly I find myself editing Irish dialogue out of English characters as I write.
So in some ways it’s natural, inevitable, that I would find or invent my stories here, except that I’m still an outsider and I expect the observer effect still shapes my experience. However hard I work on integration, I am and will always be English in Ireland and that does and will always mean that some elements of Irish life are understandably and probably rightly closed to me. Which means I can’t set a novel among Irish people in Ireland, and also, now, I can’t quite set a novel among British people in contemporary Britain.
It’s fine. I’ve been writing about the English abroad in the postwar decades, a rich seam that could perfectly well see a novelist through a respectable career and invites me to think about emigration and exile and war and belonging. Creativity thrives on constraint, and – being trained as an academic – I’ve always enjoyed the research required for historical fiction. But I do also like to write to the moment, have sometimes been accused of making news into art faster than is tasteful. It would be good to be able to keep doing that too.
Earlier this year my editor asked me if I’d consider writing a little Christmas book. I’d just finished a first draft of an English-abroad novel and was trying to leave it in peace for a while but restless without a project under way. I am not fond of Christmas, disliking organised fun, crowds, parties, over-heated rooms and disrupted routines. As sometime readers of my column will know, I don’t forget that domestic violence, suicide and divorce initiation peak at Christmas, because trapping families behind closed doors with too much drink, too much expenditure and hysterically high expectations is destructive. But from the novelist’s point of view, that trap is interesting. I like a closed-room story, and Christmas can be as much of a closed room as a bank heist or hijack or hostage-taking.
[ Sarah Moss: Christmas - and the perfect family life it represents - is an oppressive fantasy Opens in new window ]
I thought of outsiders, people closed out of the traditional family gathering. I thought of the allure of a hotel at Christmas, the dream of someone else doing the hard work in exchange for money rather than the queasy blend of love, obligation and resentment current in domestic settings. I thought how much fun it might be, to write about candlelight and flowers and discreet, all-seeing service, and I thought about how Christmas can focus yearning and regret more or less repressed by work and routine all year. Everyone wants to go home at Christmas, even or especially if “home” is in the past as well as far away, and the Irish tradition of the emigrant’s return was irresistible to the immigrant novelist.
So I set my Christmas book in Ireland, in a hotel I greatly enjoyed inventing on a clifftop in the west, it doesn’t matter exactly where. I started with an English woman, older than me and with a different life experience, and an Irish man, a little younger than me and with a past that has no overlap with my own. It’s a novelist’s job to inhabit other lives and I do it with commitment and appetite, but in the first draft I shied from the Irish man’s point of view. How dare I, English or maybe Scottish immigrant, imagine that I could see through Irish eyes? In the second draft, it seemed to me that I could, that much of my work of integration is to see Britishness through Irish eyes.
I had caught myself, at a dinner in a mixed group of English and Irish people, half-thinking that often the English, however pleasant and kind as individuals, simply don’t know how to behave, say what should not be said and fail to hear what others are not saying. It’s not that hard, I thought irritably, if they’d just listen. They? We. I. How often had I been that oblivious person? I could recall a few times. How often am I still that person? (See above?) It’s a life’s work, immigration.
[ Paul Gillespie: Monocultural Ireland was always a fantasy Opens in new window ]
I found, as I revised and rewrote The Winter Guest, that I was developing confidence in the Irish characters, that all the work I do in daily life observing and learning and listening, paying attention the way immigrants do, was useful to me as a writer. There are elements of the novella that will be invisible to many English readers, though whether that makes it an Irish book is for you to say.
The Winter Guest is published by Picador

title: YA fiction: Filthy is a terrific book, though perhaps a tad awkward as a class read
description: Plus Winterveil by Ava Reid; Firstborn by MJ Hastings; and don’t read E Lockhart’s The Pools on public transport, whatever you do
content:
When we first meet college student Theodore Brown, he is relieved to “only have another 365 days” of the “insufferable purgatory” that is the teenage years left. Viewing the world through this ticking-clock lens dates back to his father’s sudden death, and the number zero Theo could see in his eyes that final day. Since then, he’s tried to avoid eye contact, to ensure he doesn’t know how much time he has left with anyone – after all, “in the end / time screws us all”.
This appealing premise is brought to us by debut writer Daniel Devenney, originally hailing from Donegal and now based in New Zealand . Counting Down with Theodore Brown (Allen & Unwin, £8.99) relates the anxious narrator’s attempts to step outside his comfort zone, as prompted by both his English professor and his therapist, and to navigate his first romantic relationship. The magical-realist element here is low-key; the question, really, is how any of us dare to love when we understand that loss is inevitable.
Devenney uses a journal-style approach to Theo’s summer quest, allowing for both immediacy and reflection. At times the musings can become a little too preachy – for example, although Theo is utterly correct in saying that “I reckon we won’t be able to treat [mental] illness until we eradicate the stigma around it … We’ve got to do better. We’ve got to get comfortable with uncomfortable conversations. Nothing will improve until we do,” it feels like a moment where the author, rather than the character, is up on a soapbox. Nevertheless, it is a thoughtful read, with a quirky, relatable protagonist.
Lucy Cuthew’s second verse novel for teens, Filthy (Fox & Ink Books, £9.99), initially seems a prime candidate for sternly lecturing the youth of today – it is a story about what happens when teenagers learn about sex from the often-problematic (understatement) world of online pornography. Cuthew is worried, but also conscious, as she writes in an author’s note (and has explored in more depth in a full-length paper), of not wanting to “add to the moral panic” or to focus solely on “the worst, most shocking stories”.
And so we have Joss, looking at “the closest thing / I have to a nature documentary / about my own species” to try to figure out what she’s supposed to do with Griff, the cute boy who finds her fascination with animals endearing rather than dorky, but who is just as useless at clear communication about sex as she is. Her friends – “all in couples / and me trailing” – are not much help, and her mother still thinks of her as a child; of course she turns to the internet to gain understanding of the “flash of glitter” that hits whenever Griff touches her, “like a firework fuse lighting / inside me.”
Cuthew ultimately suggests, rather delightfully, that the real sexiness is to be found in film adaptations of novels once banned for obscenity; it’s a nice nod to how often there is still controversy over sexual content in teen novels, particularly if characters are not punished dramatically for it. She has an eye, too, on the “tightrope” girls are expected to walk between “prude / or / slut”, and is sympathetic to their urge to perform, rather than experience, pleasure.
There’s also plenty of humour here, including some hilariously embarrassing moments for Joss, recalling the late, great Louise Rennison in its attention to everyday disasters. A terrific book, though perhaps a tad awkward as a class read.
Warning: do not read the latest E Lockhart novel, The Pools (Hot Key Books, £9.99), on public transport. You will ugly-cry like a toddler who has lost their teddy bear, utterly forlorn and heartsick, and it will be mortifying. You must instead save this experience for somewhere with a pillow to howl into, as you step into the town of Covington, where stories are told about the hot springs, where once upon a time those who swam there were turned into birds.
And then it happens again: “It is kind of like a fairy tale, but it really happened.” The five “new birds”, as they come to be known, include Lexie’s younger sister, who becomes a chickadee, and her boyfriend, who is transformed into a swan. “It’s not the swan she knew. She knew the boy. / Same thing. The swan is the boy. / Not if you ask me. The boy is gone. The swan is what’s here in his place.”
Lexie consults librarians, the internet, folklore to try to figure out if there is a way of saving the boy she loves, or if he, like the other birds, needs to be set free. Readers continue weeping into their pillows as their hearts clench and unclench in time with the line breaks. Smart, stylish, emotionally devastating – a must-read.
[ Hope amid the dangers of tech, magic, and bad breakups: this month’s YA recommendations Opens in new window ]
In the late 2030s, in a world where the cold war continues (“Gorbachev’s assassination was always emphasized as a major historical moment”), there is a school for “precocious teenage offenders” nestled away in the “stygian haze of the Blue Ridge Mountains”. Here brilliant young criminals might redeem themselves by training in “the finer points of military strategy, statecraft, tradecraft, and even a bit of tactical combat if you’re feeling adventurous”, ready to serve their country “dutifully until your dying days, in anonymity, winning yourself no personal glory or esteem”. Enter four complicated protagonists with knotty, troubled backstories, and you have the latest thriller from Ava Reid, Winterveil (Electric Monkey, £16.99).
The smart worldbuilding is the most intriguing element of this page-turner, and there’s a lot in here for game theory nerds; the cast is a little too busy, though, and the pacing uneven in parts. It is too clearly a first book in a series – not unusual in the fantasy or dystopian realm but still frustrating at times. See also MJ Hastings’s Firstborn (Stonefruit Studio, £8.99), the first in a trilogy, which ends with a three-word shock reveal, though in this instance there is some sense of narrative resolution, albeit temporary.
Hastings’s title refers to the segregation of a fantastical society by birth order – the eldest, like protagonist Bryn, become warriors, “makers of a new world, one without war, without the threat of our oppressors”. The middleborn, like her brother, become scholars; it is said his “current research will usher in the bloodiest era of war yet”. The youngest are sacrificed, though the precise details are unclear; her sister is about to be “taken” in this manner.
As Bryn sets out on a rescue mission, accompanied by a sexy rebel (essential in such works), she uncovers some of the secrets of this fractured world: “Don’t you think it’s strange that every time we get close to integration, there’s another uprising in the Oval?” While readers may be suspicious of what she’s been told long before Bryn starts to question the ideology, it is still satisfying to watch her coming-of-age journey. Part of the appeal of the fantasy bildungsroman is how the acquisition of adult knowledge in such worlds is a more intense, more coherent version of reality’s messier path; part of their joy is that reminder of our own agency. (Perhaps we can forgive the cliffhangers – somewhat.)

title: Author Emma Heatherington: ‘Losing a parent as a child shapes your life right into adulthood’
description: The writer on new novel Together for Christmas, the Omagh bombing, and writing Country Girl: The Musical
content:
Cara Mallon, who is licking her wounds after a break-up, organises a festive press trip to Ashford Castle, where she meets travel blogger Dermot Walsh. It’s a love story that is both festive and multilayered with a cast of endearing, relatable characters.
Christmas can be wonderful one year and incredibly tough the next, so I can always find a story around that time of year.
I have no idea how we coped but we had no choice. Losing a parent as a child shapes your life in many ways, right into adulthood. I still miss her every day.
It was a surprise, but my daughter’s birth brought so much joy and a welcome distraction from our grief at that time.
My writing saved me emotionally while my body fought the physical side of my illness. It kept my head busy when I could easily have gone to a very dark place. The support I’ve received from my online community has been life-changing. I don’t take it for granted.
I went to Nashville with my fiance, Jim, my cousin Leone and her hubby, Laurence. We had the best time ever. Months on I still smile at the memories we made there, It was everything I’d dreamed of and more.
I’m a huge country music fan, so combining my love of songwriting and storytelling equals joy. Country Girl is like my books, with themes of grief, love and family, only it’s live on stage with an amazing soundtrack. Rosie has inherited an Irish pub from her late grandmother but plans to sell it and return to Australia. When Luke Adams, a rising country star, walks into the bar one night, a spark of chemistry changes both their plans. I’m immensely proud of Country Girl and can’t wait to bring it to theatres across Ireland in early 2027. My favourite lyric is “I thank God for letting me love you”. It’s from the song Rosie’s Lullaby, which I wrote on my mother’s anniversary a few months after my cancer diagnosis.
[ Having babies young: how does it work out? Opens in new window ]
Shopping for Jordyn’s wedding dress was incredibly special. It’s going to be a very proud, emotional day for us all. Jade moved to Perth on St Patrick’s Day. I’m more settled now she’s settled. We talk on Facetime almost every day.
I’m working on my 2027 novel as well as producing Country Girl, so my head is very busy!
I like to write by the sea in Downings, Co Donegal. My sister and I have a mobile home there so I retreat with my laptop when I can.
Without a deadline, an idea will always be an idea.
I’d rewrite a whole lot of Irish history.
I’m not up to speed with films, but books, I recommend Broken Country by Clare Leslie Hall, and podcasts, On the Couch with Rachel and The Digg Podcast.
The Omagh bombing was a dark day for my home county and all the families affected.
Geneva was breathtakingly beautiful, but Nashville has my heart.
My mummy’s wedding band, which I keep in a jewellery box she got me for Christmas just before she died.
A copy of Jane Austen’s Emma I was given when in hospital.
Seamus Heaney, Rebecca Yarros and Samuel Beckett. We all share the same birthday.
Donaghmore is bursting with creativity. I’d love to be closer to the sea.
Together for Christmas was published on October 22nd

title: Elon Musk says SpaceX behind Starlink restriction that disrupted Ukraine’s defences
description: Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelenskiy says country’s access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been fully restored
author_name: Susie Blann and Elise Morton, Associated Press
content:
Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine , disrupting operations that the country relies on to defend itself against Russia.
Musk’s admission on social media came after Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy said that Ukraine’s access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted frontline operations for more than a week.
Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Musk-made satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow’s attacks.
“The speeds are now where they need to be,” Zelensky wrote on X, adding that restoration began on Friday night and were sufficient by Saturday morning, improving frontline logistics and defence against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
After Ukraine said the services had been restored, Musk spoke out on the speed restrictions that began last week. In a post on Saturday on X, Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink satellite internet service.
“Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” Musk wrote.
“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.”
But he maintained that the US government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink that is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication.
He also defended the role of SpaceX in bolstering Ukraine’s defences since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the country’s military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.
The restoration follows a new US diplomatic push to end the war.
Russia agreed on Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month.
On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localised ceasefire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region.
[ Russia and Ukraine agree to local ceasefire in Oleshky amid deepening humanitarian crisis Opens in new window ]
The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by president Donald Trump’s reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.
Ukraine’s defence minister Yevhenii Khmara credited “direct dialogue” and Zelenskiy’s diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most “for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications”.
Trump has maintained that he did not make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed.
Vice president JD Vance has hinted at White House co-ordination with Musk, while US secretary of state Marco Rubio and defence secretary Pete Hegseth have denied any administration involvement.
Meanwhile, a man was killed and two others wounded in a missile attack on the city of Lozova in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region, local officials said on Saturday.
Moscow-installed authorities in cities across Russian-occupied Crimea reported power blackouts on Saturday following overnight Ukrainian attacks.
Ukraine’s General Staff said on Saturday that its forces hit a chemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, which produces materials used in rocket fuel.
Tolyatti mayor Ilya Sukhikh said the overnight attack damaged industrial facilities in the city.
Ukrainian forces also hit an electronics plant in the city of Oryol, Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed on Saturday.
Local officials in Oryol said on Saturday that three people were killed in Friday’s attack.
The General Staff said the plant makes components for the cruise and ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities.
Ukrainian drones also reached Russia’s Omsk region in western Siberia, more than 2,000km from the border with Ukraine.
Omsk regional governor Vitaly Khotsenko said drones “reached a northern industrial hub”.
Online retailer Ozon said on Saturday that its logistics centre in Omsk has been attacked by a drone, but there were no casualties.

title: Gavin Coombes’ allegation his testicles were grabbed against Leinster to be investigated
description: Munster head coach Clayton McMillan says he ’100 per cent’ backs his player, with the report to be sent to the citing commissioner
content:
Gavin Coombes ’ allegation that his testicles were grabbed nearing the end of the first half of Leinster ’s 24-18 win over Munster at the Aviva Stadium could not be substantiated during the match on review, but the matter is sure to be investigated further.
Although the referee Andrew Brace and his TMO Colin Stanley could find not find any evidence to support the claim by Coombes, which was made in the 39th minute, as it will be in Brace’s report the citing commissioner, Peter Ferguson of Scotland, is thus duty bound to investigate the matter.
He has a window of 50 hours from the full-time whistle to do so.
“It’s one of those things that we leave in the hands of the powers that be,” said the Munster head coach Clayton McMillan.
“All I know is that I back our players 100 per cent that if they make an allegation like that, they wouldn’t do it lightly, and that’s not the sort of person Gavin is, so we’ll see where that goes.”
Asked about the allegation, McMillan’s counterpart Leo Cullen said: “I can’t see anything there, from what I can see. So, yeah.
“And obviously, that is the accusation, but I’m not seeing anything on first view. So, I don’t know. It looked like he [Coombes] had changed his mind halfway through that accusation as well. So I don’t know.
Clarifying that he was suggesting Coombes had altered his allegation, Cullen said: “Well, that’s the way it sounded, once the scrum was packing down. But I don’t know. Obviously, once that accusation is made, it becomes a serious matter for the citing commissioner. So my comment is not going to help in any way here. But from what I’ve seen, I can’t see anything.”
But given the claim was made against one of his own Leinster players, Cullen admitted: “It’s not ideal. Yeah, it’s not ideal. So, you’d want to be very clear if something’s happened.”
Cullen had not had any discussion with any of the officials about the incident and he laughed off his exchange with the Munster defence coach Denis Leamy, who was previously an assistant to Cullen at Leinster.
“Yeah, but we were former coaching mates, so we were just having a very passionate discussion about the game,” said Cullen, adding: “We’re still very good mates, yeah.”
Regarding Leinster’s comeback from 13-0 down with four tries to earn a bonus-point win, Cullen hailed his team’s composure.
“They’re always unbelievably fiercely contested derby games. I thought Munster were good in the contact area, probably a little bit better than us in the first half, both sides of the ball and obviously they went into a 13-0 lead.
“I was like, ‘Oh, is this going to be a bit like it was last year in Croke Park?’” added the Leinster coach in reference to Munster’s win there a year ago. “But I thought the players showed good composure to come back and get a try, and we started getting a little bit of an ascendancy, but then we would give away a turnover.
“You had to carry into that breeze. Obviously, it’s tricky enough conditions, the way it looked, certainly from the wind point of view. So you’re going to have to carry, you’re going to have to roll your sleeves up in the first half.
“There was a couple of times we were just a little bit off, gave away turnovers, and that gives Munster life. But the message really at halftime was ‘just stick to it’ and make sure they enjoy themselves. And keep pounding away.
“I think we’ve dominated territory and possession. Play the game in the right areas of the field. The scrum gets dominant, which is good as well.
“And Munster, I thought they’re hanging in, they’re giving away penalties, a lot of penalties. Eventually someone goes to the bin.
“So, the composure is good, the players stick to it, which is big.
“This time last year, we were poor when we got ourselves in that position. We made life more difficult for ourselves, we weren’t clinical, but [we were] so much more clinical in the second half [today].
“But Munster brought a huge amount to the contest, didn’t they? We had to find a way out there today in difficult conditions. So, yeah, pleased to get a win, bonus point. And we move on.”
Although Munster rallied to earn a losing bonus point with Ben O’Connor’s try from the last play of the game, McMillan’s over-riding emotion was one of disappointment.
“We didn’t come here to lose and we don’t take any satisfaction out of being gallant losers. To walk away with a bonus point is nice because you look at the table and it’s pretty congested, but it was genuine disappointment in the changing shed because we felt like we had enough opportunities and we didn’t nail them all.”
The Munster captain Tadhg Beirne conceded: “You’ve got to give credit to Leinster.”
He added: “The wind was strong, we had the advantage in the first half, and they capitalised on that [in the second], but I think the discipline is probably something we need to work on, particularly the second half of games at the moment.”
Munster conceded the first eight penalties of the second half in losing that count 17-12.
“We’re kind of falling off a little bit and letting teams back into it through our ill-discipline, and it’s just giving teams a little bit of momentum or even a little bit of belief against us and making it more difficult for ourselves.”
“Ultimately, I thought the first half we were really good, but second half we just compounded errors on our end, whether it was a penalty or just an individual skill error like myself, the ball going straight through my hands in the lineout and they score not long after that.
“So yeah, I think if we can clean those up, we’ll be in a much better place, but they did well to get the momentum and keep the foot on the peddle today.”

title: Andy Burnham calls for ‘honest discussion’ on freedom of movement between UK and EU
description: British PM says he wants to consider options including return to full EU membership or joining single market
author_name: David Hughes, Press Association Political Editor
content:
Andy Burnham said he wants an “honest discussion” about the possibility of a return to free movement between the UK and European Union as part of his plans for a new relationship with the bloc.
Britain’s prime minister wants to consider various options for a new relationship with Brussels, potentially including a return to full EU membership or joining the single market – which would require free movement.
He told the Sunday Times: “I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this.”
Burnham has previously committed to the red lines in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto – which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union – suggesting any fundamental change in the relationship would have to wait until after a general election.
The issue of migration was one of the dominant factors during the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign.
But the prime minister suggested the type of migration experienced during the years of EU membership was different from the challenges faced now.
“It was generally younger people, not always, but spending a few years, then going back,” he said.
“And obviously the ease of that worked for British people as well.”
Burnham will meet the European Union’s chiefs at a summit on November 20th in Brussels. He has said he will take the opportunity around the summit to lay out to the British public different options for the future relationship with the bloc.
[ Why Andy Burnham says ‘Brexit has done more harm than good’ Opens in new window ]
The prime minister acknowledged freedom of movement “had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament”.
“But at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now].
“Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different.
“The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”
But Burnham said he could not imagine recommending the UK joins the Schengen borderless area or ditches the pound to adopt the euro.
“I can’t see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen,” he said.
[ Downing Street trying to play down Andy Burnham comments on Russia’s role in Brexit Opens in new window ]
Nigel Farage said the comments were a betrayal of voters who backed Brexit, including in Burnham’s Makerfield constituency.
The Reform UK leader said: “This is a total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch.
“He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty.”
Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: “Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe.
“The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it.”

title: Four more Irish fighters win medals at World Boxing Under-19 Championships
description: The Irish team will take home six medals and have the chance to upgrade each in the final days of the tournament
content:
Four more Irish boxers secured medals on Saturday at the World Boxing Under-19 Championships in Budva, Montenegro, bringing the team’s medal haul to six.
John Donoghue, Kalib Walshe, Louise Joyce and Jason Whelan won their quarter-final bouts to guarantee at least bronze medals, joining the already qualified Kaysie Joyce and Jason Donoghue in the semi-finals.
Reigning 70kg European champion John Donoghue joined his brother Jason in the semi-finals with a unanimous decision win over Hungary’s Levente Turos.
The fight ended up being a routine victory for the Olympic BC Mullingar man, as he won every round on the scorecards to earn his third international medal.
Kalib Walshe secured at least a bronze in the 60kg class with a dominant win over Algerian fighter Smail Sahraoui.
The Wexford fighter also won all three rounds on each of the judges’ scorecards, enjoying success both on the back foot and as the aggressor in a superb performance.
In the evening session, Louise Joyce added a fifth medal for Ireland with a split decision win over Ciana Nonphala of the US at 48kg.
The former European medallist from Olympic BC Mullingar fell behind after the first round, but boxed her way back into the contest on the backfoot in the second and third to win 3-2 on the scorecards in a close and entertaining fight.
Co-captain of the Irish team, Jason Whelan of the Dublin Docklands club guaranteed his medal with a decision win at 75kg.
The Dublin fighter won well on the scorecards in his quarter-final contest against Nikolay Sabev of Bulgaria, winning 5-0.
Whelan’s fellow co-captain, Grace Bailey of Castelbar BC was defeated by unanimous decision by Harsika Harsika of India in the 65kg quarter-finals in a physical encounter.
At 55kg, Lee Largey Snoddon of Immaculata BC in Belfast exited the tournament on a 3-2 split decision in a quarter-final bout against Nihat Gasimov of Azerbaijan, where both fighters received standing counts.
Gorey ABC’s Kayleigh Byrne also lost out on a 3-2 split decision to Nazokat Mardonova of Uzbekistan at 51kg.
Byrne fought her way back into the contest after falling behind early on, but despite forcing a standing count in the final round, she lost that round on one scorecard, costing her the victory and a world medal.
Ireland’s semi-finalists will be back in action on Sunday, with all six boxers having the chance to upgrade their medals.

title: Séamus Power going for first PGA Tour win in four years as he ties lead in Bermuda
description: Irishman has chance to win on Sunday and secure his card for another two years with victory
content:
Séamus Power stayed in the hunt in Bermuda in search of his first PGA Tour victory in four years after a third round of 67 left him tied for the lead with Austin Smotherman.
After previous rounds of 66 and 64, a four-under-par 67 was Power’s highest score of the week on paper but may be his most impressive as high winds made for tricky conditions at Port Royal Golf Course.
The Irishman made a fast start to his round with birdies at the first and third holes after approaches to 11 feet and seven feet. All pars followed in until the 10th with another superb wedge to three feet for birdie.
A bogey followed at the 13th when he hit his approach over the green and failed to get up and down, but he bounced back immediately with a birdie at the 14th with a remarkable holeout from the fairway after finding trouble off the tee.
Perfection from Power 💪 Seamus drops it in for birdie despite the tough conditions @Bermuda_Champ pic.twitter.com/s0OdHEPdUZ
Power then birdied the par 5 17th after hitting a solid wood into the heart of the green and two-putting, before just leaving his birdie putt short on 18 to take the outright lead.
Power and Smotherman are on 16 under, with Taylor Moore, Corey Conners and Ben Silverman on 14 under, while five players are on 13 under.
“It was tough. I think the toughest part was the contrast from the first two days, which were as easy as I’ve ever seen the course playing,” said Power.
“All of a sudden there were shots out there that were unrecognisable. So it was just trying to reset the goals and hitting simpler shots.”
On the holeout on 14 he said: “That was obviously a huge bonus. It’s a part of my game I’ve worked on in the couple of weeks leading up to this, so it was nice to see it pay off there. Hearing the cheer was great and such a bonus to get momentum back on my side.”
The 39-year-old expects conditions to be tough tomorrow.
“With the wind up again, it’s just going to be more of the same. Don’t try to take on too much and just hang in there,” he said.
Power won the event in 2022, his previous victory on the PGA Tour, and has been showing form recently with a tied seventh placing at Biltmore Championship Asheville and a tied 21st finish at the Bank of Utah Championship.
A good week for Power in Bermuda could be crucial in keeping his PGA Tour card for next year. Currently 103rd in the FedEx Cup standings, the top 100 players at the end of FedEx Cup Fall keep a fully exempt card. Players finishing 101 to 150 earn conditional status, giving them limited start opportunities. A high finish could ensure he finishes in the top 100, while winning the event would come with an added bonus of a two-year exemption.

title: Leinster come from behind to beat Munster in URC clash - as it happened
description: Leo Cullen’s side get bonus point after being behind at half-time
content:
[ Leinster huff and puff to eventually subdue Munster in tetchy contest Opens in new window ]
Jamison Gibson-Park speaking on Premier Sports:
“I’m very happy to be back. It was awesome. We didn’t start well, but we were able to turn it around second half. We have to hand credit to Munster, they were good defensively. We felt a momentum shift with the yellow card and we took advantage.”
“It was a bit nerve-wracking at the start playing number eight, but I enjoyed every minute of it. You’re more involved. I was fairly cramping at the end there. That’s a huge bonus point, it’s a massive win for us, happy with the performance.”
80 mins: Try for Munster! O’Connor gets a losing bonus point, good play by McCarthy with a great carry and offload, Nankivell to O’Connor to finish on the wing. Conversion is missed.
Leinster showed their power and depth in the second half, Jamison Gibson-Park was back to his best.
77 mins: Munster spray the ball about well from side to side but Max Clein on as a replacement misjudges the ball and ends that attack.
72 mins: Slightly shaky kick by Carbery which was almost kept from touch, then Gus McCarthy overthrows, but O’Donoghue is immediately turned back over. McCarthy gets another go at the lineout, successful this time and they’re inside five metres.
Try for Leinster! Osborne scores on the wing, same as earlier, an inch-perfect pass, put on a plate for him to score. Bonus-point try for Leinster. Carbery converts well.
70 mins: Daly gets a bang to the head in a collision with Carbery in the tackle, doesn’t look good unfortunately, there will be a stoppage.
64 mins: Considerable pressure by Leinster. Gus McCarthy nearly gets over but held up just short. Penalty advantage for Leinster, last-gasp defending by Munster.
Try for Leinster! Gibson-Park finds a quick pass to Charlie Tector, who came on at half-time, who finds a gap and touches it down. Bad miss by Carbery from the conversion.
62 mins: From midfield, Carbery breaks free but Munster are over it again, Beirne with more world-class breakdown play. Clarkson and Gus McCarthy are off the bench and into the game.
58 mins: Edogbo and Gleeson on for Munster to refresh their pack.
56 mins: Try for Leinster! It was a long time coming but it seemed inevitable. Ryan Baird scores the try, his carry was too strong. Converted by Carbery.
Yellow card for Munster. Nankivell in the sin bin.
54 mins: Leinster get another penalty from the scrum, the pressure is relentless. Another advantage, but then Carbery is rattled by Shay McCarthy. Munster warned the next one will put them in the bin. This whole attacking passage has taken more than five minutes, lots of stoppages.
51 mins: Clean lineout and then a maul that retreats, they go wide but Keenan drops the ball. Back for another penalty though. Tap and go for Leinster, Leinster held up a few times at the line, TMO check.
No try given, inconclusive, back for a scrum for Leinster. Beirne says it should have been a knock on, but not given.
49 mins: Leinster ease up the pitch and have advantage, before a wild kick by Carbery but it’s back for the penalty. Now a five-metre lineout.
47 mins: Coombes has turned over plenty of ball today but infringes this time and concedes a penalty, which causes a bit of pushing between the teams, but the penalty is turned over after a TMO check for a late tackle by Munster.
40 mins: Leinster probe, trying to find a gap in the wall of the 22, but nothing is given by Munster and they get a deserved turnover.
Big second half by Leinster needed to turn this around, Munster have been excellent and deserve to lead at half-time.
Here is the Munster try, well worth a watch:
It's a wonderful @Munsterrugby try 🔴 Shane Daly with a superb finish for the first try of the game 💥 pic.twitter.com/yl0VTfWFX5
There is an accusation that Coombes was grabbed in the groin area in a ruck but there is no video evidence so nothing is given by the TMO. Munster win a penalty after the scrum.
38 mins: Leinster are coming into the game now, making plenty of metres with their carries and sharper passes. Joe McCarthy though makes the error and takes his eye off the ball, although may not have expected the pass from Gibson-Park. Knock on and chance gone.
Try for Leinster! Magnificent pass by Jamison Gibson-Park from the scrum, gets the ball quickly and flings a wonderful long pass straight into Tommy O’Brien for an easy try. Carbery misses the conversion.
34 mins: An unusual moment as the referee Andrew Brace gets stuck inbetween Leinster and Munster players and gets a big hit and is on the ground. Leinster had been threatening in attack and carried to within five metres.
31 mins: Penalty scored by Munster! Yet another turnover for Munster and O’Shea lands a kick from inside his own half. Fantastic kick even if it was with the wind behind.
27 mins: Try for Munster! Just a brilliant try, Daly scores it after some wonderful back play. O’Shea with the good gamebreaking pass at first then Casey with the clever assist to Daly. O’Shea converts.
26 mins: Ben O’Connor is put under pressure with the ball in behind and is forced into touch. From the lineout, Leinster only get a few phases before Coombes turns it over, can’t get through Munster at all so far.
21 mins: From the scrum, sharp play by Leinster and Tommy O’Brien is almost through but the ball comes loose and Casey clears but can’t get to touch. But Munster manage to turn the ball over.
18 mins: Big hits going in, Wycherley on Jimmy O’Brien in particular. Leinster win a scrum in Munster’s half after a knock on from Gibson-Park’s box-kick.
16 mins: Good defensive effort by Leinster to turn over Munster and Carbery kicks into Munster’s half for the first time really.
13 mins: Leinster haven’t really got going yet, summed up by Gibson-Park hitting it out in the full, a few moments after they were penalised in the scrum.
A minute’s applause for the Anthony Foley in the eighth minute, who died 10 years ago.
8 mins: Penalty scored by Munster! O’Shea scores as they opt for the posts, with Casey holding the ball still for him.
6 mins: Munster go nowhere from the lineout and lose the ball, but then win a penalty off Kelleher. Better play from the lineout by Munster, some nice play by the backs and they win another penalty to get to the 22. But then Shay McCarthy carries to close the five-metre line. O’Shea tries a crossfield kick, doesn’t work but back for the penalty.
3 mins: Both teams testing the other with high balls in the blustery conditions, O’Shea kicks in behind and Keenan doesn’t have the best kick so Munster have a lineout from the 22.
Kickoff is in a few minutes, should be an entertaining one.
It’s going to be wet and wild at the Aviva tonight, difficult conditions for flowing rugby, it could be a case of who makes the fewest mistakes. Dan Sheehan will have a new experience at number eight, while Joey Carbery is at outhalf against his former team. Gerry Thornley writes about Sheehan and the Springboks and French penchant for hybrid players, if this could be the start of something new for Leinster and Ireland:
[ Dan Sheehan’s versatility could be an asset ahead of World Cup Opens in new window ]
From Nathan Johns : Watching Leinster’s victory over Clermont last weekend, a text was sent to a former analyst at a professional team.
“Light the beacons, Leinster have scored on transition.”
The exchange was in reference Sam Prendergast’s length of the field score, an audacious decision to counterattack from deep. Not playing with freedom while padding a lead, but running from their own 22 while trailing by a point away in France.
Something to watch out for tonight, you can read more here:

In the earlier URC match today, Ulster were beaten by Bulls in South Africa but put in a second-half performance they could be proud of.

Hello and welcome to live coverage of the URC match between Leinster and Munster at the Aviva Stadium. Kick-off is at 6pm. The old rivals go up against each other once more after fine wins in the Champions Cup. Leinster will be big favourites but Munster always give it their best shot against them.

title: Leinster huff and puff to eventually subdue Munster in tetchy contest
description: It always felt that Leinster’s greater depth would tell once they upped their intensity in the second half
content:
Munster may have been rank underdogs more than is usually the case despite last year’s win in Croke Park, but they rose to the occasion and even took the game to Leinster by roaring into a 13-0 lead. Leinster’s heavier power game and quality prevailed with a dominant second period, but on a blowy night in Ballsbridge they had to huff and puff to eventually subdue their auld rivals.
There were a couple of unsavoury incidents as the Munster number eight Gavin Coombes claimed he had his testicles grabbed in the 38th minute, and though nothing was proved on immediate video review, that is sure to be investigated. Leo Cullen and the Munster defence coach, who formerly worked under the Leinster head coach, had an altercation at the full-time whistle.
Munster were full value for both their 13-0 lead in a high quality if tetchy first half – the red hordes making their voices heard in a crowd of 37,193, and the bonus point which Ben O’Connor’s try with the last play earned them. For all their disappointment, given Munster injury toll this was further evidence of their progress this season.
In a tetchy game, it always felt that Leinster’s greater depth would tell once they upped their intensity and camped in Munster’s half, albeit they had to dig deep. Ultimately, they were heavily indebted to the enduring brilliance of Jamison Gibson-Park, who hardly showed a trace of rust in his man of the match seasonal return which was garnished with three high-quality try assists.
In his first game for Leinster since the 2018 Pro14 final win here over the Scarlets, Joey Carbery glided over the turf and provided a running threat. Although he had a few missed kicks, he struck the ball smoothly. Their big forward guns went well and although Dan Sheehan experiment at eight was not without its positive moments, with Cullen hailing his performance as “excellent” and he was the game’s leading carrier with 17 carries.
Their 62 per cent and 63 per cent share of the territory and possession was also reflected in the toll it took on Munster’s defence, as they made 243 tackles to Leinster’s 115, as did a costly 17-12 penalty count against the visitors. But, all in all, the watching Andy Farrell could feel encouraged with where many of his frontliners are at.
A good start always seemed more imperative for Munster and so it came to pass. The slick passing which has been a feature of their recent games was quickly in evidence as sharp passing by Alex Nankivell and O’Shea created space for Shay McCarthy off his wing to make inroads twice, as well as reclaiming a Craig Casey box kick in another impressive outing by the winger.
A combined high tackle by Rónan Kelleher and James Ryan on Kieran Brookes enabled O’Shea to have an early settler to open the scoring before a minutes’ applause in the eighth minute to honour Anthony Foley in a classy touch by Leinster.
Another dominant feature of the first half was the regularity with which Munster players chop-tackled and their team-mates were quickly over the ball to win penalties in the jackal, be it Alex Kendellen, Josh Wycherley or Coombes.
Soon after the latter’s effort, Munster struck deservedly and stealthily, launching off a lineout and striking three phases later which was again testimony to the work done under Jared Payne and Mossy Lawlor.
Alex Nankivell’s disguised pullback, when it looked for all the world like he was going to truck it up, was clearly called by Charlie O’Shea who saw Andrew Osborne shooting up. His flat pass put Sean O’Brien through a gap. He linked with Casey on his inside, the scrumhalf then working a switch with Shane Daly for a superb try which O’Shea converted.
The 20-year-old outhalf made it 13-0 with a somewhat questionable penalty from halfway before Leinster went up a gear. Tommy O’Brien was launched up the middle in trademark style off a lineout and, but for Andrew Brace being sandwich by Kelleher’s carry and Josh Wycherley’s tackle, looked set to score.
From the resultant scrum, there was plenty of animation as Jimmy O’Brien went blind, and Henshaw shaped to truck it up before Gibson-Park went to the open side and floated a long pass over Ben O’Connor, who was a tad too narrow, for Tommy O’Brien to score untouched. Gibson-Park’s skill off his left hand was admirable, it was not so much a bridge pass as a meteor from outer space.
Before the break there was a claim from Coombes that his testicles had been grabbed in a ruck and Andrew Brace went to his TMO Colin Stanley but they agreed that there was “nothing clear” to substantiate the charge there and then.
The second half was largely one-way traffic although it pivoted on one key reversed penalty when, on review, Kieran Brookes was pinged for an off-the-ball shoulder hit on Kelleher, and after the latter had been warned for using foul language at Brace by the referee.
Despite one good defensive maul by Munster a procession of penalties and stubborn last-line defence from a power play, two scrum penalties against Brookes eventually led to Joe McCarthy’s close-range finish and, critically, a penalty against Nankivell and “repeated infringements”.
Another penalty in the jackal, by Tadhg Beirne, lifted another siege before the increasingly influential Carbery found a 50-metre penalty to the corner. Gus McCarthy atoned for an overthrow by winning a turnover penalty. Cue another power play and another assist for Gibson-Park, as he picked out Charlie Tector, an interval replacement for Jimmy O’Brien.
Ryan Baird’s one-handed take led to another power play and a third try assist for Gibson-Park as he floated a bridge pass to the touchline-hugging Jamie Osborne.
To their credit Munster had the final say after McCarthy won a penalty to the corner. Nankivell’s pickup and Sean Edogbo’s carry led to the former giving O’Connor a good finish by the corner flag. Munster were worthy of their bonus point.
Scoring sequence: 7 mins: O’Shea pen 0-3; 28: Daly try, O’Shea con 0-10; 30: O’Shea pen 0-13; 34: T O’Brien try, 5-13; HT: 5-13; 55: McCarthy try, Carbery con 12-13; 63: Tector try 17-13; 73: Osborne try, Carbery con 24-13; 82: O’Connor try 24-18.

Replacements: Charlie Tector for J O’Brien (HT), Gus McCarthy for Kelleher, Thomas Clarkson for Furlong (both 62 mins), Scott Penny for van der Flier (68), Conor O’Tighearnaigh for Ryan, Fintan Gunne for T O’Brien (both 69), Alex Usanov for Porter, Caspar Gabriel for Carbery (both 75).
Munster: Ben O’Connor, Shay McCarthy, Seán O’Brien, Alex Nankivell, Shane Daly, Charlie O’Shea, Craig Casey; Josh Wycherley, Marnus van der Merwe, Kieran Brookes, Fineen Wycherley, Tadhg Beirne (capt), Jack O’Donoghue, Alex Kendellen, Gavin Coombes. Replacements: Gordon Wood for O’Brien (39 mins), Mark Donnelly for J Wycherley (56), Seán Edogbo for Kendellen, Brian Gleeson for Coombes (both 58), Michael Ala’alatoa for Brookes (60), Ben O’Donovan for Casey, JJ Hanrahan for O’Shea (both 65), O’Shea for Daly (71), Max Clein for van der Merwe (75).

title: Mike Penders’ misjudged punch helps Tottenham to long-awaited win at Chelsea
description: Premier League wrap: Arsenal wipe out gap to leaders Manchester City as defensive duo score to down Everton
content:
Mike Penders’ own-goal and a sensational solo effort by Mathys Tel helped Tottenham end their Stamford Bridge hoodoo with only a second win at Chelsea in the Premier League era.
Roberto De Zerbi’s team arrived in west London with a torrid record at rivals Chelsea after only one triumph from their last 41 visits to SW6, but turned history on its head with a dominant display in a 2-0 win against Xabi Alonso’s 10 men.
Spurs, who only got off the mark in the league on Monday at home to Coventry, broke the deadlock when Penders punched the ball into his own net after 77 minutes from Mateus Fernandes’ corner before red mist descended over Cole Palmer.
Palmer had already received a yellow card for barging into Fernandes when he received his marching orders by referee Chris Kavanagh for catching Conor Gallagher late with 10 minutes left.
Tottenham were minutes away when Tel collected the ball inside his half, raced past Maxence Lacroix and rifled it into the bottom corner to send De Zerbi off in celebration down the touchline as the north London club claimed the points at Chelsea for the first time since 2018.
Centre-back partners Ezri Konsa and Gabriel celebrated personal milestones as Arsenal beat Everton 2-0 to move level on points with Premier League leaders Manchester City.
England defender Konsa scrambled home from a corner in the seventh minute at the Emirates Stadium to claim his first goal for the club since arriving from Aston Villa in the summer.
Gabriel sealed victory with a second-half header on his 200th Premier League appearance, ensuring the Gunners took full advantage of City’s 2-1 defeat at Aston Villa in Saturday’s early kick-off.
Victory for Mikel Arteta’s reigning champions was a seventh from eight top-flight fixtures this season and an 11th from 13 games in all competitions.
Everton had opportunities to spring a surprise, with Thierno Barry and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall wasting their best openings before they slipped to a second-successive defeat.
Oscar Bobb’s first Premier League goal for Fulham earned a 1-0 win over Coventry that lifted the Cottagers clear of the relegation zone.
Bobb produced a fine bit of individual skill to strike in the 80th minute as he twisted his way into the box and bent a shot into the far corner, only his second goal for the club in any competition since his £27million move from Manchester City back in January.
That was enough to give Fulham their first away win in nine attempts, a run that dated back to February, only a week after they ended their winless start to the league campaign by edging out Hull 1-0 as the pressure continues to ease on Alvaro Arbeloa.
Josh King had earlier hit the post for the visitors, who edged Coventry in just about every department to leave Frank Lampard’s side second-bottom of the table.
The hosts had only brief spells of sustained possession in Fulham’s half, but did little to trouble Bernd Leno on a frustrating afternoon which bought the CBS Arena back down to earth after their 4-1 win over Newcastle in their last home outing.
Quality was in short supply between two sides who started the day in the bottom three.

title: Ulster beaten by Bulls despite brave second-half fightback
description: Hard-fought win for the South African side in 31-degree heat in Pretoria
content:
A lot of teams come to South Africa and simply roll over. Ulster did not do that, which is something that coach Richie Murphy is most pleased with following his side’s narrow 26-34 defeat against the Bulls in Pretoria.
“You’ve got to stick in the fight here,” Murphy says. “I’m really proud about the way the lads stuck to the task.
“We had a way that we wanted to try and play. We probably moved away from that early in the game, but we got more towards what we wanted to do towards the back end of the half and into the second half.
“We struggled at the start of the game to get a foothold into it, and turned over possession too easily. That puts you under pressure, especially if you’re playing against a team like the Bulls.
“They got access into our 22 and coming up to halftime they had almost 65 per cent territory and possession. It’s hard to stop them.
“I thought our guys did a really good job in relation to sticking to the plan. And to put ourselves within two or three plays from actually winning the game. We’re disappointed in the end. Disappointed not to get the last try, and disappointed not to get another bonus point at the end of the game.”
The game at Loftus Versfeld was played in pretty alien conditions for the men from Belfast. The temperature in Pretoria was 31 degrees, with water breaks and umbrellas to boot, introduced midway through each half and the halftime break extended to 20 minutes.
Significantly, whereas the altitude, with Loftus Versfeld being 4,429 feet above sea level, was expected to start taking its toll on Ulster in the second half, Murphy’s side emerged strongest after the break. In fact, Ulster “won” the second stanza 19-13, outscoring the 2025/26 finalists by three tries to one. The eventual try tally was four apiece, with the Irishmen enjoying 51 per cent possession and territory.
“It was really hot, and we’re at altitude,” Murphy says. “All those factors come into the game.
“It’s a combination of the Bulls being a really good team and being at Loftus, but I think over the course of the game we became more used to where we were and, again, we weren’t too far off at the end. We were still competing.
“We did a lot of work preseason in relation to our fitness. And, as far as the culture of this team is concerned, we’re not a team who likes to roll over.
“The lads worked really hard, and they’re very proud to play for Ulster. We always knew that this would be a tough period in relation to the season, but the lessons learned here will drive us forward.
“Although we have drawn two and now lost two, the opposition that we played were all tough teams. In the long term, looking at the rest of the season, we should really benefit from these games.
“We were in tight battles, and at one stage it looked like it might end up in a draw again. We’ve got to keep putting ourselves in that situation. The lads have learned some lessons, and the lessons are around our discipline. Our discipline wasn’t good in the first half, we gave them access to penalties.
“Also our ability to hold on to our ball in multiphase. When we played some really nice rugby, we turned the ball over probably too much.”
The visitors from Ireland suffered a horror start when Bulls captain and former Ulster backrow Marcell Coetzee powered across from an attacking lineout with the first two minutes.
Thereafter, Ulster composed themselves reasonably well to restrict the Bulls from scoring for the next 15 minutes. Tom Stewart and his warriors certainly defended bravely during this period, even holding Springbok hooker Johan Grobbelaar up across the line in the 11th minute, while halfback Nathan Doak relieved pressure effectively with his kicks from the base of the ruck.
Stewart even turned possession over, burst into Bulls territory and forced a penalty in the 12th minute, but Ulster were unable to benefit from the resultant 22 entry.
Bok number eight Elrigh Louw finally crossed for the Bulls’ second try midway through the half, and Coetzee smashed through for a brace of tries after half an hour. That opened up a commanding 21-0 lead, with the home side enjoying 62 per cent possession and 64 per cent territory.
With no time left in the opening half, however, winger Chay Mullins raced in for an important try, after number eight Juarno Augustus, who stood his ground against the Bulls in the physical exchanges, had powered across the gainline and Stewart drew the defence brilliantly to create the overlap. Jack Murphy converted from up against the touchline to reduce the half-time deficit to 7-21.
Ulster carried on where they left off in the first half, to manoeuvre flanker David McCann for their second try five minutes after the break.
In addition, Coetzee was yellow carded for head contact, yet Ulster were unable to capitalise during the 10 minutes the Bulls were reduced to 14 men.
However, midway through the second half, Augustus ripped the ball from Handré Pollard’s hands and charged into Bulls territory to set up a great attacking penalty. Mullins dotted down in the corner for his second try following sustained pressure from the subsequent lineout, but the Bulls struck back almost immediately through Grobbelaar to stretch their lead to 31-19.
Still, Ulster refused to toss in the towel and kept the pressure up for Stuart McCloskey to cross for their bonus-point try. With 10 minutes left and the Bulls clinging to a 31-26 lead, it was still anyone’s game.
Ulster just could not get over the line in the end, and instead Bulls’ replacement Curwin Bosch nailed a long-distance penalty in the 82nd minute to seal a hard-fought win for the home side.
Apart from Stewart, who led from the front, and Augustus, Michael Lowry was all energy on the left wing, while loosehead Tom O’Toole was a major steadying influence in the Ulster pack, which refused until the very end to succumb to their Bulls counterparts at scrum time.
