title: Gardaí recover gun they believe was used in ‘execution style’ killing in Co Cork
description: Body of Paul ‘Bosco’ O’Connor (56) found beside river Blackwater near Mallow on October 15th
content:
Gardaí have recovered a gun that they believe was used to murder a man found dead beside the river Blackwater in north Co Cork earlier this month.
The weapon has been sent for ballistic examination in an attempt to determine if it can be forensically linked to the killing of Paul “Bosco” O’Connor.
Detectives investigating the murder of the 56-year-old, from Connolly Road, Ballyphehane, Cork City, recovered the shotgun with the assistance of a sniffer dog. It had been dismantled and concealed in a secret compartment, accessed using a lever, in a car that was parked in Mallow.
It is understood that the compartment also contained a quantity of cocaine which gardaí believe can be linked to O’Connor’s murder.
Gardaí were on Saturday continuing to question a woman (40s), arrested in Mallow on Thursday night and detained at Cobh Garda station under Section 50 of the Criminal Justice Act 2007, about the murder.
They were also questioning a man in his 30s from eastern Europe who was arrested at an address in Mallow on October 19th. He is being detained at Mallow Garda station under Section 50 of the Criminal Justice Act 2007, which allows suspects to be detained for up to seven days.
O’Connor was found dead on the banks of the Blackwater near Ballyellis, some 2km east of Mallow, on October 15th. A man out walking his dog made the discovery and alerted gardaí, who cordoned off the area and declared it a crime scene.
Gardaí did not release the results of the postmortem, carried out by Assistant State Pathologist Dr Margot Bolster at Cork University Hospital, for operational reasons. However, The Irish Times has learned that O’Connor was shot in the back of the head and in the face with a shotgun.
Gardaí established from CCTV footage that O’Connor travelled by train from Kent railway station in Cork City to Mallow at 7.20pm on the previous night, October 14th, and were able to trace him via CCTV footage calling to a house near where his body was found.
They believe O’Connor went to Mallow to retrieve a consignment of cocaine that had been stolen from an Irish criminal organisation but he was instead shot in what one Garda source described as “an execution-style killing”.
O’Connor, who had convictions for armed robbery and assault in the 1990s, is survived by his brother Terry and sisters Mary and Valerie.

title: Police use tear gas and water cannons as more than 400,000 protest across France
description: Authorities had confined march away from centre of Paris to prevent repeat of last weekend’s violence and looting
author_name: Thomas Adamson and Tom Nouvian, Associated Press
content:
More than 100,000 people have marched in Paris over school funding and soaring living costs, challenging president Emmanuel Macron ’s government as police fired tear gas and water cannons near the end of the protest.
Paris police estimated the turnout at 110,000, with demonstrators mobilising despite restrictions that confined the march to the city’s southeastern edge, away from the centre.
Police used tear gas in several cities, including Lyons, Clermont-Ferrand and Strasbourg, and water cannons in Nice and Nantes, French media reported.
In Marseilles, officers fired tear gas during clashes with several dozen people near the march’s endpoint. The Paris prosecutor’s office said 64 people had been arrested in connection with Saturday’s demonstration and 40 placed in police custody.
Most arrests concerned suspected weapons offences or participation in a group preparing violence or property damage, the office said.
The unrest is testing Macron’s authority in the final months of his presidency before voters choose his successor in May. The stakes are high: the far-right National Rally has accused his government of failing to protect the public and urged people to channel their anger into votes for them.
[ Can Emmanuel Macron pull France back from the brink? Opens in new window ]
Interior minister Laurent Nuñez had announced a nationwide deployment of up to 70,000 officers, backed by helicopters, armoured vehicles and water cannons. Authorities had confined the Paris march to the city’s southeastern edge, away from the centre.
An Associated Press journalist saw tens of thousands of people marching from Porte d’Italie early in the afternoon. Trade unions led the procession, followed by protesters in raincoats carrying flags and handmade placards.
After reaching the authorised endpoint at Porte de Vincennes, some demonstrators tried to continue towards Place de la Nation, but police blocked their path, French media reported.
Camille Chesnier, 27, said she had been unable to find work despite having an engineering degree and a master’s degree.
“There are enormous numbers of people in the same situation as me but who aren’t privileged and who find themselves living on the streets and in squats and, frankly, it’s very tough,” she said.
Organisers from the “yellow vest” movement called for another day of protests on Saturday October 31st to defend the right to demonstrate.
Police changed the Paris route on Friday.
At Bastille, the original starting point, police used a megaphone to tell people to leave or face a €135 fine.
Soumaya Abed, a 58-year-old nurse wearing a red CGT union vest, said she had been joining protests for more than 30 years but had never seen a march start at Porte d’Italie.
“They are using what happened last week as an excuse to quiet protesters,” she said.
“But it won’t stop the movement. It won’t stop students from demanding better conditions in schools.”
In Marseilles, police put attendance at 17,000, while the CGT union estimated 100,000. In the southwestern city of Toulouse, 26,500 people joined the protests, according to authorities.
Authorities had banned rallies in cities including Lyons, Nice and Montpellier. Trade unions have criticised the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.
Thousands also marched on Saturday in Orleans, south of Paris, in a separate peaceful protest against the far right as Marine Le Pen ’s National Rally held a two-day congress in the city.
[ The Irish Times view on protests in France: uncertainty and discontent Opens in new window ]
Macron, a centrist, has entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures restricting protests are needed to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings.
Nuñez acknowledged on Monday that police had lost control in some cities during last weekend’s unrest. He offered to resign, but Macron refused the offer.
More than half a million people took to the streets last Saturday, October 17th. Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted over that weekend amid street violence not seen in years.
Gendarmes stood guard beneath the Arc de Triomphe on Saturday as shopkeepers boarded up storefronts across Paris.
The city’s main museums, including the Louvre, Musée d’Orsay, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais – where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display – were shut on Saturday.
Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public on Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organisers to cancel the weekend programme.
Paris protester Louis Ledoux-Xatard voiced frustration over inequality.
“Looking at countries like the United States, we don’t want to end up like them, where part of the population has everything and the others have nothing,” he said.
“I never imagined that I’d be taking to the streets so much before my 30s.”
While protests in France have claimed most international attention, large demonstrations also rocked many European cities on Saturday from Milan to Madrid, Lisbon and Tirana.
Thousands of young people marched through the streets of Milan, where large numbers of soldiers were deployed and luxury boutiques were boarded up in case of a repeat of last weekend’s chaotic looting and clashes.
Prime minister Giorgia Meloni announced a raft of measures, including sending an additional 500 soldiers to Milan and tougher penalties for minors, who police said made up a large part of the violent protesters last week.
In Albania’s capital Tirana, riot police used water cannons on large groups of protesters, some of whom set government buildings on fire and threw projectiles at police.
Authorities said 2,500 officers patrolled the streets on Saturday.
High school and university students are demanding lower tuition fees, greater state investment in education and protesting against corruption in the education system.
Some have joined a broader anti-government movement calling for the resignation of socialist prime minister Edi Rama.

title: Storm Boelo: Status orange wind warnings in place for five counties
description: Met Éireann Status Yellow warnings in place or coming into effect for more than a dozen counties on Saturday evening into Sunday
content:
A status orange wind warning will be in place for counties Galway , Donegal , Mayo , Leitrim and Sligo until 9am on Sunday as Ireland feels the effects of Storm Boelo .
The storm is forecast to bring gusts of up to 130km/h when it peaks, with counties in the west and northwest expected to be hardest hit.
The high winds have caused some travel disruption and prompted the cancellation of a number of Halloween themed events around the country.
A Status Red Marine warning from Rossan Point to Bloody Foreland to Fair Head came into place at 7pm Saturday and remains in effect until 6am Sunday.
“Westerly winds will reach violent storm force 11 at times,” it cautions.
A number of Status Yellow warnings have also been issued by Met Éireann and the UK Met Office has put an Amber Alert in place for counties Antrim and Derry.
The Amber Alert comes into effect at 9pm and runs until 10am Sunday, with a yellow wind warning in place for all of Northern Ireland until noon on Sunday.
The PSNI on Saturday evening advised motorists that a fallen tree was blocking a lane of the M1 on-slip at Blacks Road. He said delays should be expected in the area until the tree has been removed.
The Status Orange wind warning for Galway, Donegal, Mayo, Leitrim and Sligo came into effect at 2pm and Met Éireann said possible impacts include power outages, difficult travel conditions and disruption to public transport, fallen trees and coastal flooding.
A Status Yellow wind warning for Connacht, Clare, Kerry and Limerick came into effect at 1pm and runs until midnight. A similar warning is in place for Donegal until 3pm Sunday.
A Status Yellow wind warning covering counties Cavan, Dublin, Longford, Louth, Meath, Monaghan and Westmeath came into effect from 6pm on Saturday and remains in place until midday on Sunday, with very strong winds and severe gusts forecast.
The timing means that around 22,000 people will run the Dublin City Marathon with a wind warning in place. Organisers said preparations “are progressing as planned’.
“As part of our routine planning for all events, Dublin Marathon Group monitors weather conditions, with established adverse weather arrangements included in our overall Event Management Plan,” a spokesman said. “We encourage runners to bring suitable layers to keep warm before the start and have warm, dry clothing available after finishing.”
The National Directorate for Fire and Emergency Management (NDFEM) said meetings of the National Severe Weather and Flood Coordination Group were being convened as Storm Boelo was bringing disruptive weather to much of the country.
The Lú Festival of Light in Drogheda has been cancelled on Saturday because of the weather. “While this will be disappointing, the safety of attendees, staff and performers remains our priority,” Louth County Council said.
Halloween events in Limerick city have also fallen victim to the storm, with the ‘Trick or Treat in the City’ in Arthur’s Quay Park cancelled.
Speaking on RTÉ’s Brendan O’Connor Show, Met Éireann meteorologist Niall Donlan said there had been no reports of flooding as of lunchtime, but there was still a risk, especially in west Cork and Kerry where the “ground is already very saturated and waterlogged”.
“It is recommended, if you’re going to the coast or living in and around the coast, to be careful and if you can, stay away,” he said.
Donlan said gusts of wind could reach up to 130km/h in the west and northwest.
“Where we have that Status Yellow (warning) out, the winds will reach between 50 and 65km/h with gusts between 90 and 110km/h,” he said.
“Then where you have that Status Orange (warning) ... the mean wind speed can reach up to 80km/h and the wind gusts can reach 130 km/h.”
A number of roads in Co Kerry have been impacted by the storm, with flooding reported on the R553 Listowel to Lisselton. The civic amenity site and recycling centre in Cahersiveen closed on Saturday in response to the conditions.
The stormy weather has had some impact on the transport network. Some Stena Line sailings from Dublin to Holyhead were cancelled on Saturday, including the 10.15am, 4.30pm and 10.30pm crossings from Dublin to Holyhead. The 4pm and 10.15pm crossings from Holyhead to Dublin were also cancelled.
Irish Ferries cancelled its 7.45pm crossing from Dublin to Holyhead on Saturday, with a 7.30pm crossing from Holyhead to Dublin listed as being “in doubt”.
Dublin Airport said nine outbound and 10 inbound flights had been cancelled by airlines on Saturday due to weather issues.
“Winds are forecast to remain strong for the rest of the day, which may lead to further disruption.”
Bus Éireann has also warned that some routes will be disrupted or cancelled as a result of the storm. It encouraged would-be passengers to check its website for service updates.

title: Ireland grind out hard-earned victory over South Africa in Cape Town
description: Captain Erin King was outstanding despite being in sinbin, while Ireland’s improved control after the interval proving decisive
content:
Ireland ground out a hard-earned victory in their first women’s Test on South African soil, overcoming a spirited Springbok Women side to take a valuable win in the opening match of the WXV Global Series double-header at Athlone Stadium.
Scott Bemand’s side, ranked fifth in the world, eventually pulled clear of their 10th-ranked opponents after a pulsating first half in which both defences struggled to contain the opposition.
Ireland scored six tries overall, with Dannah O’Brien converting five, but South Africa’s five touchdowns ensured the contest remained competitive until the closing stages.
Captain Erin King was outstanding despite spending 10 minutes in the sinbin during the first half, while Ireland’s improved control after the interval proved decisive ahead of next Saturday’s rematch at the same venue, although Bemand and his players will take a close look at their defensive frailties over the coming days.
King made an immediate impact, stealing a lineout and winning two breakdown penalties. Ireland capitalised on the second in the eighth minute, with Robyn O’Connor carrying strongly before Aoife Dalton held off two defenders to score and O’Brien converted.
The tourists threatened again, but King was unable to find Beibhinn Parsons with the killer pass and South Africa took advantage of the reprieve, number eight Aseze Hele exploiting a big gap in the defence to score in the 20th minute.
Ireland’s task became more difficult when King was sinbinned four minutes later after making shoulder to head contact on Unam Tose, who had stooped low to collect the ball.
South Africa immediately exploited their numerical advantage, with props Sanelisiwe Charlie and Xoliswa Khuzwayo helping create the opening for lock Vainah Ubisi to score. Jakkie Cilliers converted to put the hosts 12-7 ahead.
Yet Ireland responded impressively. Following another high tackle, this time on Parsons, Anna McGann carried before Linda Djougang powered through traffic to score beneath the posts.
O’Brien’s conversion restored Ireland’s lead just as King returned. The Springboks struck back after Ireland conceded two penalties inside their own 22. Byrhandre Dolf was just short of the try line, but quick recycling allowed Maria Tshiremba to score out wide.
However, Ireland regained the advantage before half-time through a determined Jane Clohessy’s first Test try, and O’Brien added the extras for a 21-17 lead. And they flew out of the blocks to start the second half, Parsons racing over after Neve Jones reacted quickly at the ruck to offload – it was the scrumhalf’s final act of her 50th Test appearance, with Aoibheann Reilly replacing her.
Reilly helped maintain Ireland’s momentum, and after the newcomer almost scored, King did so next after taking an offload from replacement Niamh O’Dowd and O’Brien extended the lead further. Reilly subsequently thought she had scored after a break by Brittany Hogan, but the effort was ruled out for a knock-on by the backrow.
King then produced crucial defensive work close to her own line as South Africa threatened, but the hosts crossed again in the 68th minute, shortly after Ireland centre Eve Higgins received a yellow card.
Nevertheless Djougang settled matters six minutes from time, grounding the ball after sustained pressure on the South African line, and O’Brien’s conversion brought Ireland to 40 points and secured a deserved victory before the hosts celebrated a late consolation.

title: Man accused of recording intimate image without consent at Dublin Airport remanded in custody
description: None of 16 defendants who appeared during Saturday’s main daytime sitting at Dublin District Court legally represented due to dispute
content:
A man accused of recording an intimate image of another man without his consent in Dublin Airport has been remanded in custody.
The accused (25), a foreign national who cannot be named for legal reasons, appeared before Judge Máire Conneely at Dublin District Court on Saturday.
With most criminal law solicitors in the capital having withdrawn their services over July’s criminal legal aid payment reforms, the man was unrepresented as he faced Garda objections to being granted bail.
He faces a single charge under Section 3 of the Harassment, Harmful Communications and Related Offences Act 2020.
The allegation is that he recorded an intimate image without consent, causing alarm, distress or harm at pier 2 in the airport on Friday.
The man, whose address on the charge was listed as “unknown”, has not entered a plea.
Garda Maitiú Fitzpatrick said the man “made no reply” when charged. Evidence about the alleged incident was not heard.
The judge advised the accused that he could proceed with his bail application himself without legal representation or wait for an adjourned date when a solicitor might be available.
The man, whose nationality was not stated, requested an adjournment and deferred his bail application. He consented to being remanded in custody to appear again next week.
It was an emergency court sitting on Saturday and none of the 16 defendants in the main daytime sitting, which deals with urgent cases, had legal representation due to the ongoing industrial action. Three were held in custody and the remainder were granted bail, mainly unopposed.
One man facing accusations of breaching bail terms acted for himself. He successfully resisted a Garda attempt to hold him in prison pending trial after explaining that he could not hear gardaí calling at his door because extra soundproofing had been installed at his mother’s home.

title: ‘Very heartbreaking’: The Cedar Tree, Ireland’s first Lebanese restaurant, set to close
description: Manager of St Andrew’s Street eatery, which opened in 1986, says ‘it was fun while it lasted but every good thing must come to an end’
content:
Rising rent and the cost of living crisis have claimed another victim, with the oldest Lebanese restaurant in Ireland set to close after the bank holiday weekend.
The Cedar Tree, which opened on St Andrew’s Street in Dublin in June 1986, will take its final orders on Monday evening and has invited regulars to come for its “last hurrah”.
In a social media post, the owners of the family-run restaurant described the decision to call time on the operation after 40 years as “very heartbreaking”.
“It’s been a pleasure bringing you a taste of Lebanon since 1986 and an honour to be Ireland’s first and oldest Lebanese restaurant,” they said.
“We are so thankful to all our customers, community and staff who have been with us over the years. It has been wonderful to be part of one big family with you all.”
Restaurant manager Sereen Sarhan told The Irish Times the writing had been on the wall for some time as a result of rent increases, but the family fought to keep the doors open.
“We were hoping to have one last Christmas with our regulars because we love them so much and wanted to give them something special to say goodbye but unfortunately that won’t happen,” she said.
“Between Covid and higher rents and other things, everything just stacked up. We did our best, we really did.”
She said the closure was really sad for her family and the staff. “I grew up here and our staff have been here for at least 10 years and some have been here for 35 years. Everyone is broken-hearted but our hand has been forced and it wasn’t really our choice.”
Sarhan said her parents were really upset by the closure and her uncle, who established the restaurant with her father, now lives in Australia and was saddened to hear the news.
She added: “It was fun while it lasted but every good thing must come to an end.”
Regular customers were shocked by the news, with many expressing sadness in response to The Cedar Tree’s Instagram post announcing the upcoming closure.
“This breaks my heart,” one person posted. “Truly my favourite place in the world. Every time we visit Dublin, we make a point of having dinner with you!”
Another described The Cedar Tree as their “home away from home” and expressed gratitude for “everything you’ve shared with us over the years”.
“I can’t believe you will be closing your doors,” they said.
A third person said the restaurant was staffed by the “loveliest people” and that they had “such warm personal memories in this place”.
Writing in The Irish Times in 2019 , restaurant critic Catherine Cleary described The Cedar Tree as “the kind of restaurant that’s becoming as rare as hen’s teeth in this food quarter of the south city centre”.
She suggested it was “the kind of place that can probably rise above the mania of the market thanks to its old lady status”.
“These walls hold a long tradition of providing reasonably priced Middle Eastern cooking without a single pomegranate being bothered in the process. It feels as old as the hills depicted in its mosaics where little has changed over the years. And these days that feels like no bad thing.”

title: Man found on Cork golf course died from hypothermia, postmortem finds
description: Foul play ruled out in death of Jack O’Donovan (28), whose partially clothed body was discovered on Macroom golf course on Friday morning
content:
A postmortem has ruled out foul play in the death of a man who was found partially clothed on a golf course in Co Cork .
Assistant State Pathologist Dr Margot Bolster confirmed to gardaí on Saturday that 28-year-old Jack O’Donovan, who was from Macroom, had died as a result of hypothermia.
His body was found on Macroom golf course at 9.30am on Friday by a staff member of Macroom Golf Club.
The staff member contacted the emergency services and the man was pronounced dead at the scene a short time later.
Officers from Macroom Garda station cordoned off the scene and erected a tent to protect the body from the elements.
Some of Jack O’Donovan’s clothing, a shirt and top, were found a few hundred metres away, which led some gardaí to suspect he may taken them off when suffering from hypothermia.
People suffering from hypothermia can believe their body is overheating, a Garda source said, so they counter-intuitively take off clothing in what is known as paradoxical undressing. This is believed to have happened in Jack O’Donovan’s case.
Gardaí are still trying to piece together his last known movements and are trying to confirm reports using CCTV footage that he was last seen alive with two or three other men in Macroom town centre at around 10pm on Thursday.
[ Gardaí investigate after body of man found on golf course in Macroom, Co Cork Opens in new window ]
An Garda Síochána said in a statement that a full file on Jack O’Donovan’s death, including the postmortem results, would be compiled to assist an inquest, which is to be held at a future date at the Cork county coroner’s court.

title: Aston Villa and Jackson end Manchester City’s perfect run with stunning win
description: Erling Haaland was on target but City lose for the first time Premier League this season at Villa Park
content:
Manchester City have added a loss in the Premier League to the one to the Premier League, as their perfect on-pitch record vanished at Aston Villa . The two most in-form strikers in England did battle and it was Nicolas Jackson’s double that meant his side come out on top against Erling Haaland.
City are certainly fallible, losing for the fourth time in a row here, and it was a reminder that life will not always be as simple as their first seven games. Mistakes cost them as Marc Guéhi and Gianluigi Donnarumma played their part in Jackson’s goals, which will give him greater pleasure as they ended Enzo Maresca’s perfect start.
Aston Villa started at lightning pace while City cowered. City were so ponderous in the opening stages they gave away a corner after being penalised for taking too long over a goal-kick. After two mistakes last weekend against Ipswich gave away goals, Guéhi would have hoped for a more reassured performance, but he was once again punished for the opener, miscontrolling a Rúben Dias pass to allow Jackson in, with the striker rifling home in the sixth minute.
City did not look like a side who had won every Premier League game thus far. The hosts, on the other hand, had forgotten their mid-table tag and were more reflective of the team sitting second in the Champions League standings with three wins out of three.
The inflatable fruit enthusiasts got to witness an improving situation on the pitch as City enjoyed plenty of possession in and around the Villa area, but Iliman Ndiaye, who had a penalty claim waved away, and Rayan Cherki, were thwarted by Zion Suzuki’s reactions. Villa defended with commitment and discipline to limit the space available with great success.
While City constantly threatened and Ndiaye struck the post, there was always a nagging doubt that Villa could cause problems on the counterattack.
Jackson against the unfortunate Guéhi was starting to look like a mismatch, as the defender was unable to cope with the speed and physicality of the striker. Guéhi was booked for pulling down Jackson on the edge of the area to leave him in a precarious position on every level, forcing him to be replaced at the break.
The entertainment and exhilaration of the first half was always going to be difficult to sustain, but there was no backing down from either side. City’s endeavour was rewarded in the 53rd minute when Ndiaye got the better of Ian Maatsen and found Haaland finally able to connect with a cross, heading home from close distance for his 13th of the season. It is hard to keep that man quiet.
There was a sense City could take control of the match and went close through Josko Gvardiol and Doku, but once again lapsed. Villa did not need an invitation to burst into life and were unable to contain them as the ball moved quickly from back to front, with Jackson sending the ball out to Ibrahim Mbaye before getting on the end of the cross for his second. Donnarumma should have done better, letting the shot slip under him.
The academy trio Phil Foden, Rico Lewis and Ryan McAidoo were sent on to change things for the visitors and they provided energy, but when chasing the game there was a loss of focus. Passes and crosses were misdirected and needless bookings were collected. If City could point to perfection before this, the label was rapidly fading as the seconds ticked by.
Jackson went off with eight minutes left to a standing ovation. Haaland had a very late chance to level, but Maatsen cleared off the line, to ensure Jackson and Villa claimed the glory. - Guardian

title: Thousands march in Paris as France deploys extra police and museums shut
description: French police have made more than 135 arrests so far, the interior minister said
content:
Thousands of protesters have marched in Paris, with French police making more than 135 arrests so far, the interior minister said.
The thousands gathered in the French capital to walk along the designated 1.5km route from Porte d’Italie to Porte de Vincennes.
The march has been organised by a coalition of unions and supporting student federations, but there are also protesters of all stripes – many young people, but also families, office workers and retirees.
France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, earlier said that there was a turnout of about 35,000 people in marches across the country, compared with 60,000 last Saturday.
He said authorities had counted 136 public street actions, down from 264 the previous weekend.
Nuñez said police have seized a variety of items from protesters, including metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana and airsoft weapons.
Major museums in Paris closed and authorities deployed a sizeable police force for a round of new protests on Saturday across France , hoping to prevent a repeat of last week’s violent unrest that shocked the country.
Scenes of looting, burnt-out cars and attacks on public buildings left the impression that the government had lost control, as groups of masked vandals targeted businesses in Paris and other city centres.
Nuñez said as many as 70,000 officers will be deployed nationwide, along with helicopters, armoured vehicles and water cannons.
Major museums including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais – where a major Cezanne exhibit is on display – are closed on Saturday.
Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public on Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organisers to cancel the weekend programme.
Shopkeepers in Paris have been barricading their stores all week. Near Place de la République, one of last weekend’s hot spots, a bank branch and other businesses were boarded up with wooden panels to deter potential looters.
Following the unrest, Paris police prefect Patrice Faure urged shopkeepers to hire security guards. He later clarified that protecting business owners and their establishments is the responsibility of the government.
Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted last weekend.
Protest marches were scheduled in Paris and Marseilles, but some other rallies, including in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier, have been banned by local authorities.
Cities outside Paris were hit hard by the unrest. In Limoges, a suspected arson nearly destroyed the 19th-century city hall.
Trade unions have criticised the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.
President Emmanuel Macron entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term, with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures are needed to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings.
Saturday’s demonstration in the city of Orleans, about 110km (70 miles) south of Paris, will also be closely watched.
About 50 organisations have called for a protest against the far right on the sidelines of the two-day congress of Marine Le Pen’s nationalist, anti-immigration party ahead of next spring’s presidential election. Organisers include labour unions, left-wing parties, student and antiracism groups.
The demonstrations first erupted last month in a high school southeast of Paris over a lack of staff.
From there, class boycotts and demonstrations spread to other Paris suburbs and nationwide, including smaller towns.
High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods. Some also called for a reform of the university admissions system, seen by many as unfair.
With the government seemingly unable to respond to students’ demands, the movement has morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, just months before the vote to choose Macron’s successor.

title: Gardaí treating discovery of man’s body at Clondalkin waste-recycling plant as suspicious
description: Gardaí believe unidentified male may have been murdered, says source
content:
Gardaí believe a man whose body was discovered at a waste-recycling facility in west Dublin on Saturday died in suspicious circumstances.
The man, whose identity is not yet known, was found dead at the plant in Clondalkin at about 1am.
The investigation is at an early stage and the findings of a postmortem will determine its course.
However, a Garda source said the case was being treated as suspicious and investigating officers believe the man may have been murdered.
In a statement, the force said a senior investigating officer had been appointed to lead the inquiry, with an incident room established at Ronanstown Garda station.
The Garda said it was investigating “all the circumstances” surrounding the discovery and that the Office of the State Pathologist had been notified.
The man’s body remained at the scene on Saturday morning with the Garda Technical Bureau due to carry out a technical examination.
Local Sinn Féin councillor William Carey said: “I just feel for the family. My thoughts would go out for any family of any person who is found in those circumstances.”

title: Christy Moore pays tribute to ‘best man and dear friend’ Dónal Lunny
description: Childhood friends had a transformational impact on Irish folk music and supported various political and social causes
content:
Musician Christy Moore has paid tribute to his “dear friend” Dónal Lunny (79) who died on Friday after a long illness.
Moore and Lunny were childhood friends while growing up in Newbridge, Co Kildare , and began a career-long collaboration that transformed Irish traditional music.
The lifetime achievement award was presented to Lunny by Moore at last year’s RTÉ Radio 1 Folk Awards.
The pair first met at Newbridge College in 1959 when Moore noticed that Lunny had little interest in homework and was more content to tickle trout or climb trees to gaze at wild birds’ nests.
[ Obituary: Lunny leaves indelible mark on Irish traditional music Opens in new window ]
They formed The Rakes of Kildare, their first band together, as teenagers along with Lunny’s brother Frank. They were later members of Planxty and Moving Hearts, two of the most influential Irish trad bands, and collaborated when Moore embarked upon a solo career.
In a statement to The Irish Times, Moore said: “From 1962 to 2026 Donal was a constant presence in my working life, a dear friend, a sensitive and creative collaborator, a huge influence on later generations, many of whom may not yet realise what he has given.”
The pair recorded seven albums together as part of a band or collaborating on Moore’s solo projects.
Moore and Lunny were politically active throughout their respective careers and shared the same republican politics.
Together they wrote and recorded Ninety Miles to Dublin and then The Time has Come, both songs about the hunger strikes.
Other songs with a political tint that they recorded together were On the Bridge, about the women in Armagh Prison, and The Wicklow Boy, a song for Nicky Kelly who was wrongfully convicted over the 1976 Sallins train robbery.
They were also involved in the Carnsore movement in the late 1970s when the government was considering locating a nuclear power plant at Carnsore Point in Co Wexford.
[ Dónal Lunny central to the vibrant spirit of Irish music Opens in new window ]
Moore stated: “We stood together on many campaigns, H Blocks, hunger strikes, Carnsore, Stardust, Section 31, prisoner rights and Traveller rights.
“He was an artist, musician, activist, friend and best man.”
Many tributes have been paid to Lunny with President Catherine Connolly describing him as “one of Ireland’s greatest musical figures, a wonderfully talented musician and producer who was central to so many of the most influential moments of the last 60 years of Irish music”.
Lunny is survived by his three children Oisín, Cora Venus and Sora. He also had a son with the late singer Sinéad O’Connor. Shane O’Connor died in 2022.
He is survived by his current partner of many years, Úna O’Boyle.

title: Israel imposes closures across West Bank city after two soldiers die in attacks
description: Israeli troops reportedly forced dozens of residents from their homes in parts of Hebron
content:
Israel imposed widespread closures and displaced people across the West Bank city of Hebron on Saturday following attacks by Palestinian gunmen on Friday that Israel said killed two of its soldiers.
Taxis piled up behind gates controlled by Israel’s military outside Hebron waiting for Palestinians forced to cross on foot. All gates leading in and out of the city were impassable by car, according to Basma Radio, a crowdsourced Telegram channel Palestinians use to monitor checkpoints and road closures.
Palestinian news outlet WAFA said on Saturday that Israeli troops forced dozens of residents out of their their homes in some neighbourhoods of Hebron and closed all entrances and roads leading into the city.
Israel’s army did not respond to questions about Saturday’s evacuations.
On Friday, it said that in response to the killing of two soldiers and wounding of others, its forces had begun “conducting precise, targeted and thorough searches” in the area of Hebron from which the two gunmen had operated.
Such closures in the West Bank have grown increasingly common, particularly around Hebron. They have disrupted Palestinians’ ability to travel to work, attend school and move between villages. – AP

title: Dónal Lunny obituary: Innovative musician who leaves indelible mark on Irish folk and traditional music
description: Lunny never tired of seeking out new collaborations, novel sounds and fresh perspectives on the music that defined him
content:
T raditional music owes much of its propulsive force, its appetite for innovation and its wide-lens perspective to a singular musician who has played a key role in propelling it to heights previously unimagined. Dónal Lunny has been at the heart of some of the most seminal musical collaborations over the past six decades: playing, producing, composing and arranging tunes and songs with such boundless imagination and creativity that they resonated with audiences who might never have cocked an ear to traditional music had he not inspired such explosive creativity in the heart of tunes both familiar and newly composed.
His central role as a founder member of Planxty , The Bothy Band and Moving Hearts would be calling card enough for a lesser musician, but Lunny never tired of seeking out new collaborations, novel sounds and fresh perspectives on the music that defined him as a person.
Speaking to The Irish Times in 2009, Lunny underscored his belief in the importance of change and development in traditional music.
“I think the movement and evolution of Irish music is a very good thing, and should be fostered and encouraged, because that’s the thing that keeps it alive. It’s the paradox of change: some people want to keep things the way they were, and others want to change them, and there’s a tension there – and that’s how it should be.”
Born on March 10th, 1947, in Tullamore , he was one of nine children: four boys and five girls. His father Frank was from Enniskillen and his mother, Mary (née Rogers) was from Ranafast in Donegal. The family moved to Newbridge when Dónal was five years old. He attended Newbridge College and later, the Patrician Brothers School.
His early musical explorations were modest. Early piano lessons left him cold and almost a decade elapsed before he found his way to the guitar and drums.
As a young teenager Lunny forged a close relationship with Christy Moore , and for many years the pair were more like brothers than friends. During their teens, along with Dónal’s older brother, Frank, they formed their first band, The Rakes of Kildare.
[ Dónal Lunny’s legacy will be his openness to new ways of interpreting old music Opens in new window ]
In 1965 he went to the National College of Art and Design and became a skilled gold and silversmith, but music was at the heart of who he was and so he devoted his time to becoming a full-time musician.
It was during this period that he first encountered the bouzouki, thanks to Andy Irvine . This Greek instrument offered Lunny an uncharted route into the percussive forces of the Irish tradition, which he mined with an exhilarating mix of authority and an unfettered spirit of adventure.
It is thanks to Lunny that the bouzouki is now a central feature in Irish traditional music. He was also highly influential in his mandolin playing, taking both instruments to the heart of the tradition, while also being a masterful guitarist and drummer. In the early 2000s he invented an acoustic drum kit to meet what he saw as the bass and percussive requirements of traditional music.
During the mid-late 1960s he formed The Parnell Folk with Mick Moloney , Seán Corcoran , Johnny Morrissey and Dan Maher. That was followed by Emmet Folk and ultimately, Emmet Spiceland, a folk sensation formed by Dónal and the late Moloney, which had a number one hit with Mary from Dungloe in 1966 when Dónal was just 19 years old and still in college.
Their early success saw them experiencing scenes reminiscent of Beatlemania, a source of acute embarrassment to Lunny at the time.
In 1970, Dónal partnered with Irvine to found The Mug’s Gig, a regular club night downstairs in Slattery’s pub on Capel Street. It was here it became abundantly clear that the pair were not just interpreting Irish folk and traditional music, but were making it their own, with their shared love of complex, hip-swivelling rhythms and innovative melodic arrangements.
For decades, Dónal Lunny could be seen cycling all over Dublin, a low-key figure with a ready smile and a diary bursting with commitments
In 1971 Dónal produced Moore’s debut solo album, Prosperous, which also featured Irvine, the trio whetting their appetites for what was to follow with the formation of Planxty in 1972. This was the band where the whole was unquestionably greater than the sum of the parts, and one that revolutionised traditional music with what Moore called the “spontaneous combustibility” of Dónal Lunny, a musician who was, he said, “without doubt the funniest man I know”.
Dónal cofounded Mulligan Records with Seamus O’Neill in 1971, which became one of the most important independent Irish record labels. As well as releasing traditional and contemporary folk music, the label released several new wave singles.
Dónal Lunny met his first wife, Judy, who was American, when he was 20, and together they had a son, Oisín. He had a daughter, Cora Venus Lunny, with German photographer Julia Buthe. Cora is now a successful musician in her own right.
He later married Japanese musician Hideko Itami and they have a daughter, Sora Chan. They separated and she now lives in Japan. He had a son, Shane, with Sinéad O’Connor ; Shane tragically died in 2022.
He was also romantically involved with Sharon Shannon and collaborated extensively with her from the time of the recording of her landmark solo debut in 1991.
For decades, Dónal Lunny could be seen cycling all over Dublin, a low-key figure with a ready smile and a diary bursting with commitments. His energy didn’t wane, nor did his enthusiasm for collaborating with all manner of musicians from Frank Harte (with whom he released the landmark Napoleonic ballads albums) and Mark Knopfler to Elvis Costello , Kate Bush , Baaba Maal and Van Morrison .
[ Tributes paid to musician Dónal Lunny after his death aged 79 Opens in new window ]
Throughout his long and picaresque career, Dónal Lunny thrived on collaboration. In 1974 he produced the debut album for Celtic Folkweave, a duo consisting of Mick Hanly and Micheál Ó Domhnaill. Many of his collaborations evolved into some of the most seminal band formations from Planxty to The Bothy Band and later, Coolfin, Mozaik, LAPD and Usher’s Island.
More recently, he forged new paths in the company of fiddle player Zoë Conway and box player Máirtin O’Connor . He made generous contributions to many TV documentaries, from Bringing It All Back Home to A River of Sound, Sult and Lorg Lunny.
His many compositions for theatre, film and TV led to his induction into Aosdána in 2007. In 2008 Dónal received an honorary doctorate in music from Trinity College. In 2009 he was appointed artist in residence at the University of Limerick, where he frequently taught. The late Micheál Ó Suilleabháin described Dónal Lunny as “a very gentlemanly, quiet person”, while the late Liam O’Flynn, his co-conspirator in Planxty, loved how Dónal “never held a tune back”.
The Bothy Band reunited magisterially in 2024, on foot of a TG4 documentary on the band. Their planned live performance was cut short by Dónal’s unexpected health issues, but a magical concert in The Complex in Smithfield underscored yet again the central role that Lunny played in arranging and anchoring the band’s extraordinary sound, one that is as groundbreaking today as it was when they were in their heyday in the mid 1970s.
His self-effacing manner belied a powerful musical intellect that was as much at home in a quiet session in The Rosses of Donegal as it was in the heady environs of the National Concert Hall and the Royal Albert Hall. He was a leviathan who has left an indelible mark across and beyond Irish folk and traditional music.
Dónal Lunny is survived by his children, Oisín, Cora Venus and Sora Chan, and by his former wives Judy and Hideko.

title: Three people released after questioning over fatal arson attack in Waterford city
description: Philip and Kim English, and their children Callum (12) and Jayden (9), were killed in fire at their home in Birchwood area on October 13th
content:
Three people arrested in connection with a fatal arson attack on the home of the English family in Waterford city earlier this month have been released without charge.
Philip and Kim English, and their children Callum (12) and Jayden (9), died in the fire.
Two other children – a girl (14) and a boy (6) – were rescued from the house and taken to hospital in a critical condition.
In a statement on Saturday, An Garda Síochána said it continues to “investigate the multiple murder” that occurred in the Birchwood area of Waterford City shortly after 5am on October 13 th .
It said a man in his 50s and two women in their 30s, who were arrested on Tuesday, had been released without charge. The force said a file would be prepared for the Director of Public Prosecutions.
They had been detained under Section 50 of the Criminal Justice Act 2007, which allows gardaí to hold suspects for up to seven days before they must be released or charged.
“A fourth person, a male in his 20s arrested on Thursday, remains in Garda custody,” the statement added.
Two others have been charged and have appeared before the courts in connection with the arson attack. Jessica Dalton (31), with an address in Waterford city, and Cian Stacey (21), of no fixed abode, are in custody after being charged with causing criminal damage to the English family’s home at Birchwood Avenue on October 13 th .
A Waterford drugs gang is suspected to have ordered the attack. The family’s car was attacked outside their home as far back as August 2023 and a petrol bomb was thrown at the house just last month, though nobody was injured.
Threats had also been made against members of the family on social media.
Gardaí suspect Philip English was being pressured to pay a €20,000 drug debt owed by a man he knew.
Detectives believe the attacks and threats against him and his family represented a campaign of drug-related intimidation to extort that money from Philip English, even though he had no involvement with drugs.

title: Ukraine says restrictions on Starlink speed now lifted
description: Restrictions undermined Ukraine’s ability to intercept ‌Russian attack drones and disrupted frontline ​communications
content:
The Starlink satellite communications system and ‌its military version Starshield are operating again at speeds over 400km/h, ‌Kyiv’s defence minister said on Saturday.
“The Ministry of Defence’s monitoring systems are recording a return to normal speed for Starlink/Starshield. We are recording a speed of over ​400km/h. The connection is stable,” Evhenii Khmara told reporters.
His comments come after more than a week of service restrictions that slowed ​connections and disrupted military operations .
The Ukrainian military does not ⁠disclose the systems’ maximum operating speeds, and the defence ministry ‌did ‌not ​say whether service had been fully restored.
“Monitoring systems had previously recorded disruptions to the Starlink/Starshield service. The ⁠speed metrics have ​now returned to normal,” the ministry said.
The ​restrictions, first reported on October 14th, undermined Ukraine’s ability to intercept ‌Russian attack drones and disrupted frontline ​communications, Ukrainian officials said. Sources said connection speeds had been ⁠reduced to about 160km/h or ⁠less.
Ukraine’s ​problems with SpaceX-owned Starlink came after US president Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow while pressing Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries.
Neither SpaceX boss Elon Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. ‌Both have said ⁠publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.
Reuters has reported that the order ‌to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House.
Trump said on Friday that ​if problems with access to Starlink communications systems ​in Ukraine persisted, he would “get it straightened out”.
Speaking to Bloomberg News last weekend, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy accused Trump of trying to pressure Kyiv into surrendering to Moscow.
He also said the US was delaying deliveries of crucial Patriot air defence interceptors used to defend Ukraine’s cities. The US also failed to share early warning alerts about Russian ballistic missiles attacking Ukraine several times, he said. – Reuters, Bloomberg

title: Taipei Story by Rebecca F Kuang: A compulsively paced and humorous coming of age tale
description: Teenage ache captured beautifully in author’s most assured work
content:
In an interview with this newspaper last year, Rebecca F Kuang said: “I think any good party should involve a whiteboard and magic markers.” Kuang’s seventh novel, Taipei Story, is equally, delightfully nerdy.
Having just finished her first year at Yale University, Lily Chen is spending the summer in Taiwan on a 10-week Chinese language course. Her family moved from China to the US when she was young and Lily goes to Taipei determined to get to grips with a language and culture which might offer some sort of self-definition (despite, as she notes, her parents never having stepped foot in Taiwan).
Lily is constantly clawing at a cultural identity which feels out of reach, always aware of what might mark her as an outsider: mosquito bites on the backs of her legs, or her panic when a restaurant she found online isn’t where the map says it is. “Our parents had survived Communism . Couldn’t we be so resilient?”
Kuang’s protagonist is self-aware and academically brilliant, but also as silly and sometimes selfish as any other late teen or 20-year-old. Kuang imbues both the specificities of Taiwanese culture and the commonalities of coming of age with wry humour. When Lily tells her tutor she feels like an idiot, Teacher Sun says: “You have always sounded like an idiot. It is considerable progress that you can now hear it.”
The moments when Lily feels she is failing at the Chinese language tend to coincide with periods of instability in her friendships, complicated romantic encounters or confusing grief.
[ Partita by Barbara Kingsolver: What keeps people from their birthright in beauty? Opens in new window ]
Taipei Story is seemingly a simpler tale than Kuang’s previous novels, which range from fantasy set in 1830s Oxford to identity theft in modern-day publishing. But it is also more assured and compulsively paced so that explorations of linguistic idiosyncrasies or complicated history are elegantly woven within Lily’s day-to-day life.
Taipei Story is also a portrayal of how lonely it can feel to be in a place you don’t know when you also don’t entirely know who you are. Lily’s desire to close the gap between what she wants to communicate and what she is able to say mirrors the teenage ache of trying to bridge who you are and who you would like to be. We are lucky to have Kuang to articulate this for us.
Phoebe Pascoe is a journalist at The Times.

title: Don’t mistake protest votes for Democrat support in US midterms
description: Voters in Carroll County, New Hampshire like to ‘keep their political options open’, prioritising a government that puts schools, healthcare, and housing first
content:
B ased on widespread public revulsion, Trump and Republicans should receive what Obama called a “shellacking” in the 2010 midterms when Democrats lost scores of seats. However, the question this time is whether the staggering $1.3 billion being spent by Republicans on Senate attack ads on Democrats, plus Elon Musk’s $366 million, will reduce the number of Democratic wins.
Carroll County in the rural state of New Hampshire offers some clues as to the likely outcome on November 3. Named for Charles Carroll, the only Irish Catholic signatory of the US Declaration of Independence, it is a swing county of 50,000 people in a swing state. This time of year, the peak Fall colours are fading, but it is still staggeringly beautiful with its lakes, mountains and forests.
However, the soaring price of gas, heating oil and healthcare is souring the mood for local folks. Those living in rural areas have to drive at least 20 miles round trip to a grocery shop or even to fill the gas tank. The housing stock is older and often poorly insulated, which adds to heating costs during the long winter for those least able to afford them.
Many retirees are attracted to New Hampshire because it has no income or sales tax, but properties are heavily taxed to pay for schools, road maintenance and police. Many services have to be supplemented by volunteers. The state motto of Live Free or Die appeals to their sense of self-reliance
Traditionally, residents of the Granite State have been able to agree on the expenditures at New England-style town meetings where locals gather to vote on property taxes and expenditures. But that tradition is under assault by a combination of Maga extremism and the Free State movement, which 20 years ago targeted New Hampshire as the location of its campaign to destroy state government, including public education and social services.
[ This year won’t see the end of Trumpism. But it might see the beginning of the end Opens in new window ]
Many Carroll County citizens like to keep their political options open, reflecting the 36 per cent of eligible New Hampshire voters who register as “undeclared”, a larger percentage than for either political party. Local folks prefer to focus on what we can all do together; when your car goes off the road in a winter storm, neighbours rush to the rescue without concern for your politics. The most popular political sign on the roads here is: “We all do well when we all do well.”
In interviews with nearly 1,000 of these key “undeclared” voters in Carroll County, local Democratic volunteers are finding that for many, the flood of Republican attack ads seem irrelevant and hackneyed. This has been a year when costs are soaring, billionaires are getting richer and the important Canadian tourism fell by 30 per cent because of Trump’s attack on Canada and his punitive tariffs .
People are stressed by the loss of control in their lives. Many are struggling – or care about their neighbours who are – and just want their government to put schools, healthcare, and housing first.
These household interviews also reveal that many will vote for Democrats as a protest against Trump, not necessarily because they love the Democratic Party. Unlike in Ireland with its third-party alternatives, the way to express voter anger is to vote for Democrats or not to vote at all.
Some locals feel that over recent decades the Democratic Party became too woke, focusing on identity issues rather than helping them to get good jobs. As a result, local Democrats frequently emphasise their record of “getting shit done” rather than being in the Democratic Party.
One of those interviewed was a young woman who is just now able to live independently, but her healthcare is not affordable. “Republicans keep telling us to have more children than you can afford and then they eliminate services,” she complained. “There is very limited access for women, health clinics are too far away.”
Another is an 89-year-old woman who has lived in her home for many decades and is very community minded. She is distressed at the lack of civility that is causing a heated division in her town. She believes that “the underfunding of schools and the decline in affordable healthcare are limiting the future for young people.”
These responses have given rise to a “Down Ballot” election strategy by Democrats whereby they publicise the familiar local candidate that the voter knows to motivate him or her to get to the polls. Once there, they hopefully vote up the ticket for Democratic Congressional candidates, a reverse coattails approach.
We will know on the night of 3 rd of November whether Big Money or the people have prevailed in the United States. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a progressive Rhode Island Democrat who would be chair of the powerful Judiciary Committee if Democrats win the Senate, was asked recently if we will see a powerful “blue wave” similar to the one that swept him and other Democrats into office in 2006. “The difference this time,” the Senator responded, “is back then we didn’t have creepy billionaires spending over a billion dollars to smear Democrats.”
[ US midterms: how likely is a blue wave? Opens in new window ]
Based on the findings in Carroll County, this election may not so much be a blue wave as a protest wave against the corruption and incompetence of Trump and his supine Republican Party.
If the election does result in Democrats controlling Congress and key States, the Democratic Party has only two years before the next presidential election to demonstrate to angry Americans that it is once again the party of the working people fighting for their interests against the billionaires.
Ted Smyth is president of the advisory board Glucksman Ireland House, NYU.

title: Denis Halliday obituary: Irish diplomat who left UN over what he described as genocide in Iraq
description: The senior UN diplomat and pacifist became disillusioned with the organisation and lived his life to Quaker ideals
content:
Denis Halliday, who has died aged 85, was an Irish diplomat with the United Nations and an anti-war activist.
After over three decades with the world body, he grew disenchanted with its structure and operating procedures, which he saw as giving veto power over solutions to the very countries that were responsible for many of the world’s most pressing problems.
He resigned in 1998 in protest at sanctions against Iraq, which he argued were hurting ordinary people there, especially children. He devoted the rest of his life to campaigning, in which he was highly critical of the world order and its great powers, of Israel’s treatment of Palestinians and of the Irish government’s decision to allow United States forces use Shannon Airport for stopover and refuelling purposes.
He was heavily influenced by his father, a pacifist, and was raised a Quaker, the faith movement known formally as the Religious Society of Friends. Its philosophy and values informed Halliday throughout his life.
“I was brought up to accept a basic Quaker belief, namely that in every man and woman there is goodness, or there is God, as perhaps most Friends would say,” he said in 2003 when accepting the Gandhi Foundation International Peace Award.
[ Former Irish diplomat Denis Halliday dies aged 85 Opens in new window ]
“Therefore, I believe there are no evil people. No one is inherently evil. There are evil actions, evil consequences and frightening decisions in great chambers made by men in pinstriped suits that have evil impact on innocent people.”
Denis Halliday was born in Dublin in 1941 and grew up on the south side of the city with his parents and an elder brother, Leo. Home was a happy place, made richer by the presence of pets and through enthusiastic participation in sport, especially badminton, at which he excelled, and tennis at Brookfield Lawn Tennis Club in Rathmines.
But home was also a place where Leo and Denis learned about the travails of the world beyond Ireland. His parents, Stanley McClure Halliday and Kathleen Halliday, provided a home for refugees from conflicts abroad, including, during the war years, two young girls from Germany.
This, coupled with the family’s Quaker faith and the example of his campaigning father, shaped Halliday’s own values and outlook on life.
Paying tribute to his father many years later, Denis said: “My father was head of the Irish Pacifist movement for over 20 years and devoted most of his life to nonviolent approaches and solutions. He was active in the successful movement to keep Ireland neutral.”
As for the young Halliday, he attended Rathgar Junior School, which adhered to Quaker principles and had been established by his aunt, Isabel Douglas, who was a teacher. Thereafter he went to The High School (then on Harcourt Street) and eventually to Trinity College, where he was awarded a master’s in economics, geography and public administration.
While still a teenager, it was apparent that he would follow in his father’s footsteps. Aged 17, he spent a week at a UN school in Geneva – a sojourn that appears to have helped fashion his career trajectory.
As a Trinity student, in 1960 he participated in the Irish contribution to the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament’s annual anti-nuclear march from London’s Trafalgar Square to the UK’s Atomic Weapons Research Establishment at Aldermaston in Berkshire.
After college, in 1962, he signed up as a Quaker volunteer in Kenya and two years later was employed by the UN itself – the start of a career that lasted 34 years.
He worked initially in Iran in the UN’s Technical Assistance Board and Special Fund and was based in Tehran.
Rapid promotion followed. From 1966 to 1972, he was at the Asia Bureau of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and was headquartered in New York before being transferred to Malaysia in 1972.
From there he worked on programmes locally as well as in Singapore and Brunei, eventually becoming deputy regional representative and, in 1979, was appointed UNDP resident representative in Samoa, covering that country, the Cook Islands, the Tokelau Islands and Niue in the south Pacific.
In 1981 he returned to New York to serve in the Asia and Pacific Bureau, where he was involved in setting up the first round-table meetings of UNDP for Asia. In 1985 he took up the post of deputy director in the division of personnel before becoming chef de cabinet in 1987.
From 1989 to 1994 he was director of personnel at the UNDP before being appointed assistant secretary-general for human resources management of the UN, based at its New York headquarters. In this role and on behalf of the secretary general, he introduced to the general assembly a development and performance management strategy for some 15,000 United Nations staff worldwide.
In 1997 the then secretary general, Kofi Annan, promoted him to his highest rank within the organisation, that of assistant secretary-general, and put him in charge of the UN humanitarian aid programme in Iraq, then under UN sanctions following Saddam Hussein’s invasion of Kuwait in 1990.
But Halliday soon came to view the UN’s so called oil-for-food programme was wholly unjust for a country of 20 million people. He branded the sanctions a “totally bankrupt concept” that punished civilians rather than targeting the regime, and resigned in 1998.
In September the following year, he told students at Swarthmore College in Philadelphia, where he was visiting Lang professor, that between one million and 1.5 million Iraqis had died from malnutrition or inadequate healthcare resulting from economic sanctions, and that the UN’s treatment of the country was a “genocide”.
In an interview published by the Tehran Times in August 2014, he said: “Many children and aged Iraqis suffered and died from various forms of malnutrition, all suffered from inadequate calorie intake as there was no provision for animal or adequate vegetable protein and other basic nutritional and human needs, such as adequate healthcare, education, electric power production, water and sewage systems, agriculture, animal health, employment, manufacturing etc.”
In the same interview, he attacked the UN for its failure to resolve the Israel-Palestine conflict, a failure he argued “stems from the corruption which lies within the UN Security Council itself”.
This, he maintained, stemmed from the creation of the UN Security Council in 1945 with five permanent members – the US, Russia, China, France and the UK – each of whom had “veto power in complete contradiction to genuine global representation and without any provision for member state equality”.
“This decision,” he told the Tehran Times, “was made by three men many consider to be war criminals, namely Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt.”
In retirement he moved to his parents’ former seaside holiday home at Errislanan near Clifden, Co Galway, with his pet cats, but he remained very active.
[ Halliday in protest over honorary degree for Enda Kenny Opens in new window ]
He campaigned against Shell’s gas extraction project in north Mayo and the use of Shannon Airport by the US military, defending those who, in 2003, attacked and damaged a US naval service aircraft there.
The attack was “a form of violence I would support”, he said.
He also argued trenchantly in support of neutrality .
In the same year he was awarded the Gandhi International Peace Prize. In 2010 he took part in the flotilla of small boats that tried to beak the long-standing Israeli blockade of Gaza.
His funeral this week, in the Friends Meeting House in Churchtown, Dublin, was attended by more than 100 family members and friends, including Roger Cole of Pana (the Peace and Neutrality Alliance); Des Geraghty, the former Democratic Left MEP and Siptu trade unionist; and many lifelong friends from school days, from campaigns, and from the Quaker community.
Following the Quaker tradition, several attendees spoke. His niece Orla praised him for what he gave to young people: “He made them feel alive; he gave them hope,” she said. A nephew, Paul, read a poem.
A friend, Jude Lal Fernando, associate professor and director of the Irish School of Ecumenics at Trinity, said that even while dying and in pain, Halliday had “turned hopelessness ... into an unceasing defiance reminding us all that if we do not resist, we surrender our humanity. If we do not identify with the powerless, our humanity is at risk.”
Other speakers remembered his kindness and his stylish attire, including colourful socks and love of flowers. A recurring theme was that he had “lived what it means to be a Quaker”, as one speaker put it.
The funeral was presided over by Heather Bewley, whom Halliday has asked to be his Friend responsible for the occasion. It ended with flute player Cormac Breatnach giving a rendition of Turlough O’Carolan’s Princess Royal.
Denis Halliday was predeceased by his parents and brother. He is survived by his partner, Lena; their daughter, Fransisca; and his grandson, Keaton; his sister-in-law Eileen, and by Orla and Paul.

title: Fresh books: Catalpa by Michael B Barry; Vigilante by Meera Syal; White Lines by Ryan Caldwell
description: Reviews by NJ McGarrigle, Céire Sadlier and John Walshe
content:
Barry brings to light a ripping story from 19th-century Irish history that takes in remote Western Australia, Tammany Hall-tied New York and (inevitably) the British Empire and Ireland’s republican movement battling its misrule. Dozens of Fenians were sent to the infamous, British-controlled Fremantle Prison during the second half of the century for rebel activity. A smuggled prison letter to Irish republican John Devoy in the US saw him and others organise a whaling ship, Catalpa, to sail to Australia and set up a prison break that would end with six Fenians on board returning to the US in 1876. “It was the product of precision and daring ... they defied the British and won,” writes Barry, who tells this remarkable story with forensic detail and a flowing narrative. – NJ McGarrigle
Vigilauntie is a detailed account of Meera Syal’s renegade acting ambitions to overcome racism, rejection and harassment, bringing South Asian perspectives to mainstream UK culture. The granular chronicle of her career should fascinate fans and entertainment professionals. Of wider appeal is her upbringing in a mainly white town, the expectations of Indian “aunties” and vignettes of domestic abuse, arranged marriages, sex-selective abortion and sexual assault. She recounts with humour her defiance of and pride in her community, touching on love and motherhood. My 15-year-old daughter saw the book and said, “She’s a legend”. Vigilauntie adds another string to the bow of this accomplished writer – her book Anita and Me is on the English GCSE curriculum – proving her multigenerational and multicultural appeal on stage and page. – Céire Sadlier
Ulster rugby lock Ryan Caldwell had the world at his feet, until injury cut short his sporting career and chronic pain sent him spiralling into depression and addiction . This unflinching account captures the highs of professional rugby – the breathless account of Caldwell’s Ulster debut at Ravenhill is particularly superb – and its absolute opposite: the chilling night in a Maghaberry prison cell when, but for one guard’s decision to walk down a corridor he usually avoided, Caldwell would have succeeded in taking his own life. Whether discussing the toxic masculinity of dressingroom culture, the gradual erosion of his moral compass after he stopped playing, or how his long road to redemption involved an ayahuasca ritual in the Colombian jungle, the two-time Irish international proves a superb and insightful narrator. – John Walshe

title: Suspect arrested over fire at Adolf Hitler’s former ‘Eagle’s Nest’ retreat in Germany
description: Building, set in spectacular Alpine surroundings, owned by state of Bavaria and classified as a historical ​monument recalling Nazi period
content:
Police in Germany have detained a suspect ‌after fire broke out at a historic mountain guest ​house known as the “Eagle’s Nest”, used as a retreat by Nazi officials, including dictator Adolf ​Hitler .
Around 200 firefighters and emergency personnel in ⁠the area around Berchtesgaden in the southern ‌region ‌of ​Bavaria were battling the flames after the building, known as the Kehlsteinhaus, ⁠caught ​fire on Friday, police ​said.
Police said they were investigating whether the suspect, ‌who was detained close to ​the scene, was connected to the ⁠fire.
There was no immediate word about a possible motive.
Built in 1938 as a guest house for Nazi officials and their guests, the building, sits at an altitude of 6,000ft in a spectacular Alpine ‌setting, is separate ⁠from Hitler’s nearby summer residence, known as the Berghof.
Now owned by the ‌state of Bavaria, the Kehlsteinhaus was classified after the ​war as a historical ​monument recalling the Nazi period. – Reuters

title: ‘There were ones I didn’t save:’ Father who killed Oregon school shooter describes anguish
description: Kaylub Giamanco (36) shot a former student who killed a teacher and three children at Bend school
content:
The Oregon father hailed as a hero for stopping a school shooting last week spoke for the first time about the incident, describing his experience and how he told a 911 operator: “I have to go in. People are going to die.”
Kaylub Giamanco (36), a carpenter, has received national attention and praise for stopping the bloodshed at Silver Rail elementary in Bend, Oregon, where his children attend school.
He fatally shot Griffin J John II, a 16-year-old former student at the school, who broke in and shot six people, killing Megan Lambert (25), a teacher, and three children, including five-year-old Rhoam Summer.
In an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB), his first since the October 15th shooting, he recounted that day. He told reporters that he was only in the area because he had decided to return home and eat lunch with his wife rather than the meal he brought to work that day.
For a moment, Giamanco, who lives near the school, thought it was a prank when he saw a man in black armed with a gun headed toward Silver Rail, he said. Then he saw the man fire the gun and climb over a school fence. Giamanco pulled out a .40 calibre handgun from his centre console and headed into the school parking lot, calling 911, before himself hopping over a fence to pursue the shooter.
He quietly followed Griffin without the teenager seeing him, at one point crawling on his hands and knees when he heard “children pleading for their lives”.
“I just started army crawling faster and faster and I told myself this is probably the last thing that I’m ever going to do,” he told OPB.
Giamanco crawled through a broken window and toward the special education class Griffin had entered, where a teacher was fighting with the shooter. He came into the classroom and fired his gun. Griffin fell and was reaching for his weapon before Giamanco, who said he “was afraid of him shooting anybody else”, shot him two more times.
He told OPB that he lies awake at night thinking of what he saw that day and the teenage perpetrator, and wonders if he could have done more.
“I want to apologise for not saving their babies,” Giamanco told the outlet. “The gratitude for saving people’s children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn’t save.”
Giamanco said he wants to see safer schools with school resource officers at every site, and that he would like to raise funding to support school safety efforts. – Guardian

title: Storm Boelo: Flood warnings issued for nine coastal counties and riverside areas
description: Emergency co-ordinators say wet ground and high rivers after Storm Austen increase risk of inland flooding
content:
Flood warnings have been issued for nine coastal counties and numerous riverside communities as Storm Boelo makes its way across Ireland this weekend.
Met Éireann has placed Galway, Mayo, Sligo, Donegal and Leitrim under an orange alert for very strong winds, and under a yellow warning for rain until Saturday afternoon.
Kerry and Galway are under an orange alert for intense rain over the same period.
Kerry is also under a yellow warning for wind, with Clare and Limerick. Connacht had also been put under a yellow wind warning yesterday.
A yellow rain warning is in effect for counties Clare, Cork, and Limerick. It extends until 3pm on Saturday.
Donegal is also subject to a yellow status wind warning until 3pm on Saturday, while Cavan and Monaghan will be under the same wind-level warning from Saturday 6pm until midnight.
In all affected coastal counties, the forecaster is warning that the conditions, combined with high tides, means flooding is likely to occur.
There is also an increased risk inland as river levels are high in some areas and the ground is saturated after heavy rain on Thursday night as Storm Austen swept across the country.
With Boelo due to bring further heavy rain, Met Éireann said: “This will lead to rapid runoff, rising river levels, and an increased risk of both surface water and river flooding, particularly across the west and southwest.”
The latest #MeteorologistsCommentary on provides more details on the incoming #StormBoelo (Boo-loh), how it is developing, the associated warnings and expected impacts. 🔗 https://t.co/rcCVOl1CKf #BeEmergencyReady #StaySafe pic.twitter.com/GQfyZLiVY5
The forecaster added: “Smaller rivers are at the greatest risk of responding rapidly to rainfall, while larger rivers will respond more slowly and may continue to rise even after rainfall has eased.
“Fallen debris may block or impede rivers and drainage channels.”
Another potential hazard is storm surges blocking the escape of water at river mouths which adds to the flood risk upstream, particularly in the west and northwest.
A meeting of the National Severe Weather and Flood Coordination Group heard on Friday afternoon that frontline staff in local authorities were monitoring conditions closely and remain on call throughout the weekend.
It comes after crews spent much of Friday clearing fallen trees and branches and inspecting for damage after Austen blew through.
“Unfortunately, with Storm Boelo on the way, there will be no respite,” said Keith Leonard, head of the National Directorate for Fire and Emergency Management which convened the meeting.
“Local severe weather assessment teams are working all day today and through the weekend to mitigate and manage the impacts to come.
“Of particular concern is the challenge expected from extremely strong winds in the northwest.
“I would advise everyone to avoid coastal areas during the period of the weather warnings and heed all coastguard advice.
“We will also be closely monitoring tidal and river levels throughout the country for flooding dangers and are prepared to act promptly and effectively.”
Met Éireann is also advising people to hold off on putting up outdoor Halloween decorations until the windy spell passes.
While having two storms so close together is not a regular occurrence, it is not exceptional either.
The 2015/2016 storm season began with Storm Abigail in mid-November and was followed four days later by Barney.
Storms Clodagh and Desmond were also four days apart that season and Gertrude and Henry were just two days apart.
During the 2016/17, 2018/19, 2021/22 and 2023/24 seasons, there were storms with only a day’s break in between.

title: What the British budget tells us about Irish politics
description: The traditional dividing lines have returned to Westminster. In Ireland, things look rather different
content:
I t’s midterm break on Kildare Street, but across the water the government of prime minister Andy Burnham faces a big test with its first budget on Wednesday.
