Nothing tells you as much about an administration as its budget does, but how it plays out tells you a lot about the broader politics as well. That’s as true in the UK as it is in Ireland. But the British budget also tells us a few things about Irish politics.
As Wednesday is likely to make clear, the primary opposition voice to Burnham’s Labour government is once again the Conservative Party . That doesn’t mean that the UK is reverting to a two-party landscape; it remains (like here) a multiparty system, though (unlike here) with an electoral system wholly unsuited to that reality. However, the heyday of arch-disrupter Nigel Farage has passed, and the central arguments about politics are once again dominated by Labour and the Tories. These are the eternal questions of the size of the state – how much it should do, how much it should tax to finance that, and the management of the economy that produces that taxation.
It’s not true to say nothing else matters in politics – culture does, and so do culture-adjacent issues like immigration – but usually these distributional and economic issues matter more than everything else. As British politics calms down following a period of unprecedented volatility and change, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch seems to have intuited that her party’s route to relevance is through its traditional strengths on the economy. So she has promised big cuts to welfare spending in order to finance tax cuts, a smaller state and less regulation on business. This also suits Burnham, promising the opposite, and clarifying the dividing lines of British politics. In the absence of excitement (well, you know) in Leinster House next week, watch it play out in Westminster.
Over here, of course, it’s quite different. Everyone is in favour of expanding the size of the state – the only arguments are about how much, and how quickly.
We have recently seen the Government express its priorities and values through a budget that promised to expand public spending (20 per cent of the package was made up by tax reductions) by €8.5 billion, or 6 per cent, in Europe’s fastest growing economy.
[ Andy Burnham is removing a Victorian-era law that singled out Catholics and Jews. Why now? Opens in new window ]
Despite the almost universal warnings of economists that public spending is increasing too rapidly and that potentially temporary tax revenues are being used to establish permanent new spending commitments, the predominant political criticism of the budget was that it did not spend enough money. Spend more. Quicker. Everywhere.
Actually, the boom in corporation tax revenues in the last decade has already facilitated a rapid expansion in the size and expense of the State. Look at the numbers. Total expenditure (including everything the Government spends on) has more than doubled in the last decade, from €68 billion in 2016 to more than €140 billion this year. Numbers employed by the public sector have gone from more than 300,000 to more than 440,000, with the pay bill almost doubling from €17 billion to €34 billion, though it’s important to note the population has increased by nearly 800,000, or one sixth, in that period.
[ Ireland’s corporate tax advantage is over. So what’s the plan? Opens in new window ]
This expansion of the State has been paid for by economic growth generally, but especially by corporation tax receipts, which have increased from about €7.5 billion in 2016 to probably €35-36 billion this year.
The bust-boom-bust-boom recent history has meant that Ireland hasn’t really had any sustained experience of the sort of political and economic trade-offs that are usual for governments, and which you’ll see in action next week in the UK. The Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael-led semi-permanent recession of the 1970s and 1980s gave way to the Bertie Boom. That, alas, was followed by the Bertie Bust. And now we have the second boom.
The usual trade-offs – less tax equals less spending; more spending requires more tax – haven’t applied in the past, and still don’t. Instead, in the booms we have lower taxes and higher spending, and in the busts we had higher taxes and lower spending. So booms got boomier and busts got bustier.
[ David McWilliams: There’s a reason the State gets away with wasting so much of our money Opens in new window ]
You know what I’m going to say next: sooner or later the normal gravitational forces of political economy will assert themselves. It would be very, very, very unusual for our current good fortune of constantly, spectacularly increasing corporation tax revenues to continue indefinitely. Yes, people have been warning about this for years and it hasn’t happened yet: this is not a good reason to ignore the warnings now. At the end of the story of the boy who cried wolf, the bloody wolf turns up. And when normality reasserts itself, our politics will have to accommodate itself to that.
How that looks is hard to predict; it depends on how it is managed by the government of the day. That in turn depends on how prepared it is.
One thing that would help is a standing review of public expenditure that would systematically look at areas of government spending and ask: what is the justification for this? Do we need to do it? It should question the premise that every budget in the public sector can only go up – that this year’s budget is comprised of last year’s budget plus whatever increase we can wheedle out of the system.
[ The most interesting assessment of the budget is the one you haven’t yet heard Opens in new window ]
Jack Chambers , the Minister for Public Expenditure, announced something along these lines in his recent budget. The last spending review was in 2011. His department says terms of reference are being drawn up. Let’s see if it has the resources and teeth it needs to be effective. One suggestion for it: maybe it should examine the power of state-funded NGOs to spend taxpayers’ money on mad advertising campaigns .

title: How does abandoning the triple lock make the people of Ireland safer?
description: Removing requirement for UN mandate weakens a safeguard against participation in conflicts whose consequences we cannot control
content:
Sir, – Ireland ’s reputation as a safe place to live is a national asset. For many people who build their lives here, or choose to remain here, the prospect of raising a family in a peaceful country matters enormously. That deserves greater weight in the debate about abolishing the triple lock .
Removing the requirement for a United Nations mandate for overseas troop deployments may not formally end military neutrality, but it weakens a safeguard against participation in conflicts whose consequences we cannot control.
The Government argues that UN vetoes obstruct peacekeeping. That is a legitimate concern. It does not follow that removing the international mandate requirement is the wisest response.
There is an economic dimension too. Ireland depends heavily on international confidence, investment and trade. Any erosion of our reputation for stability could introduce uncertainty for businesses and households alike. A recession cannot be predicted from this change alone, but neither should the economic risks of deeper military entanglement be dismissed.
Neutrality does not require indifference to suffering. We can defend international law, support humanitarian relief and contribute to peacekeeping while retaining firm limits on military deployment.
Before dismantling those limits, the Government should answer a straightforward question: how does this make the people of Ireland safer?
Peace is part of our prosperity. It should not be treated as expendable. – Yours, etc,

title: Inspections likely to see if Sunday’s bank holiday racing can go ahead
description: Champion jockey Jack Kennedy off the mark on first day of the season at Cheltenham aboard Bowensonfire
content:
With the clocks going back, news of postponements and cancellations, as well as likely inspections, there’s no doubt about the shifting of the racing seasons, with the domestic focus on National Hunt action this bank holiday weekend.
Storm Boelo has already resulted in a blank Saturday due to Orange-rated wind warnings, and now officials at Galway and Wexford are keeping everything crossed that they can go ahead on Sunday and Monday.
Both tracks are expected to get heavy rainfall on Saturday, with the result that Sunday morning inspections are likely.
“Shane Ryder [clerk of the course at Galway] and Niall Madden [Wexford clerk] will look at the tracks tomorrow afternoon. Depending on that, and the forecast, they will assess the situation. But if the forecast is any way correct, it’s likely they will call inspections for the morning,” an Irish Horseracing Regulatory Board spokesman said on Friday.
“There is a status yellow rain warning at Galway which could see the track get up to 30mm of rain. Wexford isn’t involved in any warning. But it got 27mm last night. The track took it very well and the going is soft. However, it could get a further 25mm throughout tomorrow,” he added.
Throw in Cheltenham’s start to the new campaign and the jumping tone is increasingly apparent.
There’s a smattering of Irish-trained runners at Cheltenham on Saturday, including Butch Cassidy, who must concede weight in a novice chase. Henry de Bromhead’s runner impressed with a pair of victories over fences at Killarney during the summer. Ground conditions will be different this time.
They will certainly be very different in Ireland should the weather fates play ball.
Champion jockey Jack Kennedy has four scheduled rides at Wexford, including on the Gigginstown Stud pair Soul Asylum and Huntin Boots, who line up over hurdles.
Huntin Boots has some form on soft ground and faces an interesting newcomer to jumping in Square Neckar. He ran off 97 on his last start in the Ebor, and the AMO-owned horse now has a first start for Emmet Mullins. Local trainer Paul Nolan has a handful of runners in this race, including four fillies making their debuts.
Soul Asylum ran a decent race in a Punchestown festival bumper and brings jumping experience to another maiden hurdle. That could prove decisive against his likely rival Lirakali.
On Friday, Kennedy got off the mark at Cheltenham’s first fixture of the season with the quirky Bowensonfire landing a novice chase there. Trainer Gordon Elliott is already eyeing a long-range return to Prestbury Park for the Grand Annual in March.
“On ratings, he was entitled to do it, but Jack gave him a beautiful ride. He said he slipped going into the first, and that he lost his confidence a bit, but he got into it nicely and got the job done.
“I was a bit worried whether he would go by him as he was jumping a bit right, and he didn’t jump great today, but Jack being Jack is different class, and he did a great job,” Elliott said.
“The horse does have his own ideas, and sometimes they are not the best ones. He is a very talented horse, and he has won a lot of prize money. I think big fields he loves, and passing horses, so he is a horse that could suit a Grand Annual,” he added.
Even this weekend’s flat action on the Continent has a distinctly National Hunt flavour with plenty of attention likely to be on Milan and another flat start for the former Champion Hurdle winner Constitution Hill.
Nicky Henderson has opted for the Group Two Gran Premio del Jockey Club at the San Siro track for his enigmatic superstar, one of the best hurdlers of the modern era, who wound up not being able to jump.
Some bookmakers rate him a 9-2 shot to land the historic Group contest on what will be his fourth start on the flat. Irish man Rossa Ryan rides Constitution Hill for the first time.
However, the partnership faces a task against likely favourite Dubai Honour. Once a proper globetrotting Group One performer, William Haggas’s stalwart may not be quite what he once was, but still represents a formidable challenge for his compatriot.
Soft ground conditions are likely at the San Siro.

title: Age no barrier to current blossoming of Irish women’s marathon runners
description: The absence of defending Irish women’s title holder Ava Crean clears the way for a new champion in Sunday’s Dublin Marathon
content:
W hen Ava Crean crossed the finish line as the first Irish woman in last year’s Dublin Marathon , with her time of 2:34:12 good enough for sixth-best woman overall and some nine minutes faster than she’d run before, she straight away became a sort of outlier of her generation.
Because at age 19, Crean was by some distance the youngest woman to win the national marathon title, which is awarded to the top Irish finisher in Dublin. The previous youngest before Crean was Carey May, who at age 21 won the women’s race outright in the first running of the Dublin Marathon back in 1980.
Irish women’s marathon running was in a very different place in 1980, and May had to endure all sorts of obstacles – before, during and after the race. Starting with the notion that no woman of any age should even consider running 26.2 miles.
With her performance last year, Crean also broke the clear and present trend of Irish women’s marathon runners reaching their prime when well into their 30s or 40s. And in many cases after childbirth. Ann-Marie McGlynn, the mother of two who’d won the previous back-to-back Irish women’s marathon titles, was 45 when she finished runner-up to Crean last year.
Nichola Sheridan, who was the third-best Irish woman in Dublin last year, turns 30 next Thursday, and last Sunday week she finished third overall in the women’s race at the Melbourne Marathon. Her time there of 2:29:13 was the fastest by an Irish woman this year, moving her to sixth on the Irish all-time list.
Based in Sydney for the last year, Sheridan returned to the family home in Meath on Wednesday and is still tinkering with the idea of running again in Dublin on Sunday. She’s leaving that final decision as late as possible before Sunday morning’s start, although either way, her marathon running career is only getting started.
“I definitely know there’s a lot more to come,” says Sheridan, whose time in Melbourne improved her previous marathon best by just over four minutes. “Since I started training with this group in Australia, there are so many areas I know I can improve on. Already my coach there, Gary Howard, is sending me videos of my running gait, and what needs to be improved.
“And when you’re in that training environment, it does just bring you on so much. Because just in normal conversations, people are talking about the World Championships, and the Olympics, and it does feel a lot more within reach.”
Sheridan’s trip home was already planned months ago, in part to celebrate her 30th birthday next Thursday along with her twin sister, Gillian. Sheridan also points to the influence of Mayo-born Sinead Diver, now running for Australia, and who at age 49 finished one place ahead of her in Melbourne last Sunday week. In 2022, Diver, a mother of two, ran 2:21:34 at the Valencia Marathon, although the official Irish women’s marathon record still belongs to Catherina McKiernan, who ran 2:22:23 in Amsterdam, 28 years ago this month.
[ The long history of runners taking shortcuts in the marathon Opens in new window ]
At age 42, Fionnuala McCormack has been Ireland’s leading women’s marathon runner for over decade now, and this time last year finished 10th in the New York City Marathon, just seven weeks after finishing in ninth at the World Championships. The mother of three is the only Irish woman to compete in five Olympics, but with LA less than two years away, she’s still eminently capable of making it Olympics number six.
Also lining up in the Dublin Marathon on Sunday is Judith Storm, who has been enjoying her most successful marathon running season to date. The City of Derry Spartans AC runner has also been improving again this year at age 39. After running 2:47:07 on her Dublin debut last year, she lowered her best to 2:39:09 in Belfast in May, and then won the Belfast Half Marathon in September in 1:14:14.
A mother of four, including triplets, Storm only took up running after moving to Derry in 2022. “It would be an absolute dream of mine to go a step further and be crowned national champion of Ireland,” says Storm. “I want to show women, especially mums, that they don’t have to put themselves last, and that it’s never too late to start something new.”
Sorcha Nic Dhómhnaill, who turns 42 in December, is also among the contenders to land her first senior title on Sunday. After the birth of her daughter Siún in April last year, she returns to the marathon distance with a best time of 2:38:19, set in Berlin in 2022.
Nic Dhómhnaill also won the Dublin City Half Marathon in May, in a course record of 71:25, after which she spoke about her return to competitive running after several years away: “You’re still busy with a baby, but it’s a different kind of busy. I’ve missed a good few years, so hopefully I can just continue going like this for a while more.”
Also catching up fast on all the above is Meghan Ryan, a 32-year-old from Dundrum South Dublin AC, who finished as the fourth-best Irish woman in the Dublin Marathon last year. Although she’s been running with her home club since the age of 12, Ryan also believes her marathon running career is only getting started.
“Last year in Dublin was only my second marathon,” says Ryan, “and because my first marathon didn’t go very well, it took a while for me to feel ready, and to convince my coach Donal Hennigan to give it another shot.
[ Former drug addict to run Dublin Marathon on ‘the streets where friends died over the years’ Opens in new window ]
“Last year, I was also juggling a lot going into the marathon. I’d just gotten married, we’d sold our apartment, and were buying a house. So, there was a lot going on, life-wise, outside of running.
“We haven’t changed much, but going into this year, I think the consistency helps. It’s also been a bit more settled. I still work full-time [as a business analyst with Aviva], but I’ve been lucky, sometimes getting through a marathon block healthy and fit is a challenge in itself.”
Ryan did achieve some success on the track and cross-country, before ultimately turning all her attention to the marathon: “I had a few years where I didn’t really progress at all, then in my mid- to late 20s, I ended up winning a medal in the national senior 3,000m, indoors, in 2018, and then in the national senior outdoor 5,000m in 2021.
“I always knew I wanted to do the marathon, but I wanted those individual medals on the track before I moved up. Not to say you can’t do those, but I definitely wanted to get that out of my system.
“Donal Hennigan has coached me for the last 20 years, in DSD, and he would also take the view of a longer-term development. In the marathon, it’s still quite early days. I don’t do massively high mileage, and I feel like there’s room to grow in the event. I am 32, but I always say to Donal, you’re not allowed to retire until I’m at least 45, and ready to retire.”
[ It’s going to be a windy Dublin Marathon. What should I do? Opens in new window ]
Crean, meanwhile, isn’t among the starters in Sunday’s race due to a long-term hip injury, which has slowed her progress. As for her own marathon future, she said during the summer: “Missing Dublin is disappointing, but at the same time, I’m 20 now, there’s going to be another, I don’t know how many, probably another 15 more.”
Which going on the current trend of success among Irish women’s marathon runners would certainly appear to be the case.

title: Leinster comfortable favourites for Saturday evening clash with Munster
description: Joey Carberry makes his first start in blue for eight years against a side he represented 68 times
content:
Nothing beats a vibrant domestic derby, and this provincial rivalry has underpinned the Irish team for much of the professional era. The more competitive and edgier, the better as well.
By extension, nothing has weakened the rivalry like Leinster’s dominance of Munster in recent times – witness 15 wins in the last 18 meetings. Hence, Munster’s semi-final win at the Aviva three seasons ago en route to the URC title, and storming of Croke Park last October when beating Leinster 31-14, was a boost.
Not that you’d necessarily think so judging by a couple of factors this week, notably Leinster again heavily outnumbering Munster with 17 players in the Irish squad compared to just Tadhg Beirne and Craig Casey for their opponents.
Granted, that has been a trend for a while and, allowing for the absence of several injured players in Munster’s physio room, if the truth be told, of them only Jack Crowley would have been a guaranteed inclusion. Caelan Doris , Jack Conan , Paddy McCarthy and Jack Boyle among others.
Clayton McMillan had expressed the hope that his young number eight Brian Gleeson would at least be in the conversation before admitting: “We’re desperate to get a few bodies in there and the only way we’re going to do that is by putting in performances that actually draw the attention of selectors.”
“It’s a quality team,” added McMillan of Ireland. “And it’s not easy to get into it, and it shouldn’t be easy to get into it. All we can do is control how we prepare and perform.”
This fixture is a key building block in that process. As Munster frequently demonstrated in their heyday, a rising tide lifts all boats and only on the back of strong collective performances will that bear fruit for individuals, notably when playing against their chief rivals and standard bearers.
Munster arrive on the back of some encouraging performances and a three-game unbeaten run, with an improved scrum after some smart work in the transfer market and some notably crisp handling as well as clever starter plays under the Jared Payne/Mossy Lawlor attack.
[ Conor Murray: Snubbed Munster players can make statement against Leinster Opens in new window ]
In addition to bringing in good players, nothing generates excitement within a team and the supporter base more than the emergence of home-grown talent. Twenty-year-old Charlie O’Shea’s confidence and maturity, as well as his skills and irreverent approach, have made him a breath of fresh air. It will be intriguing to see how he goes in just his third start.
Alas, their resources have been further stretched by the loss of Tom Ahern, John Hodnett, Dan Kelly, Jeremy Loughman and Jack Aungier after picking up injuries in last week’s win over Racing 92, thereby joining Lee Barron, Edwin Edogbo and Will Harrison on the sidelines.
Further freshening the backrow by promoting Jack O’Donoghue and Gavin Coombes, as well as Alex Kendellen, looks a smart move. They and the rest of this team will be hugely motivated, but their depth still appears a little thin, and last week’s emotional rollercoaster with the 10th anniversary of Anthony Foley’s death falling in a big European week might have been somewhat draining.
Not so Leinster, albeit handing Dan Sheehan the number eight jersey as well as the captaincy is undoubtedly a punt. But he is still part of a pack of Lions, save for Ryan Baird, who is gifted enough to have been one by now.
Then there’s also the seasonal return of their world-class conductor in chief Jamison Gibson-Park and, outside him, an intriguing first start in Leinster blue for Joey Carbery since the Pro14 final win over the Scarlets in this stadium back in May 2018.
Following last week’s cameo in Clermont, fate decrees that Carbery’s first start after eight seasons away is against Munster, for whom he played 68 times in six seasons after his high-profile move down the M7 in that summer of 2018. Carbery has since earned a couple of Champions Cup medals from his time in Bordeaux. Still only 30, this classy, versatile rugby player should still have plenty to offer.
The scary aspect of Leinster’s seven tries to two, 48-23 win in Clermont last weekend was that it took them half the game to hit their straps. There is actually plenty more in them.
So it is that the bookies make Leinster whopping 17-point favourites on the handicap, or 1/14 to win with Munster 8/1 shots. So much for last year’s storming of Croke Park.
Maybe this partially explains the apparent drop in interest compared to a year ago. That game, it’s worth reminding ourselves, drew an 81,700 sell-out. By contrast, seemingly less than half that total is set to be in attendance for this renewal of hostilities given ticket sales were at 38,000 on Friday.
As with the difficulty in generating sell-out crowds for last week in Páirc Uí Chaoimh and the upcoming November Tests against Argentina and Fiji, one ventures that Irish rugby is simply over-pricing its matches, especially considering the increasing cost of living and exorbitant diesel and petrol prices, although grim weather warnings may have been a significant factor too.
Leinster-Munster is worthy of a capacity crowd. These matches are rarely dull, save for a few Christmas arm wrestles in Limerick when exposed to the brunt of an Irish midwinter. All in all, this feels like more of a litmus test for Munster. By any yardstick, Leinster look significantly stronger. Whatever happens, for the sake of the rivalry, one hopes not too much so.

title: Health staff face sweeping promotion restrictions under spending controls
description: Staffing rules introduced by HSE to tackle potential €1bn overrun as doctors, nurses warn of significant patient risk
content:
About 100,000 staff across large parts of the health service face restrictions on promotions as part of incoming controls on filling new posts and vacancies.
The move has been described by doctors as a “de facto recruitment freeze which presents clear and significant risks to patients”. Nurses said staff and patient safety have been “thrown out the window”.
A new four-stage recruitment authorisation process has been introduced which culminates in each individual position now having to be approved by the Department of Health – even in cases where posts had previously been authorised within the Health Service Executive .
[ Health budget no longer based on evidence, consultants’ conference told Opens in new window ]
“The above sanction requirement applies to all recruitment, replacement, promotion and conversion posts without exception, including graduate appointments, agency conversions and any other category of appointment or internal progression that would impact the overall pay bill,” a directive to top-level HSE management, which came into effect in recent days, states.
The new measures, which have no specified end date, come as the latest HSE forecasts to Government maintain it will face a €1 billion cash deficit by the end of the year. The projections suggest the health service will overspend its official pay budget by €142 million.
HSE regions which overspent on staffing this year are now expected to have to make cuts to recruitment in 2027.
The new enhanced control measures will apply to four HSE regions which have gone 2 per cent or more above their official pay bill. These are HSE South West, HSE Dublin South East, HSE Dublin and Midlands and HSE West and North West.
While the new controls stipulate that the department will make the decisions on sanctioning recruitment and promotions, they also indicate “the HSE remains responsible for managing the identified clinical and service risk at all times, including while an application is prepared or considered”.
“Submission does not transfer risk to the Minister [for Health] or department and does not relieve the HSE of its obligation to implement safe interim arrangements,” notes the Government document on the revised recruitment/promotion financial sanction process – which is quoted in the memo to senior management.
The president of the Irish Medical Organisation, Dr Matthew Sadlier, on Friday warned that “with this measure, the reality is there will be no new services or expansion of capacity while those currently in place could be under threat. It is obvious that the Government’s aim is to reduce the number of people delivering care, not increase them.
“Where will accountability lie for the introduction of this measure when it inevitably has a negative effect on doctor numbers, waiting lists and patient outcomes?”
The Irish Hospital Consultants Association (IHCA) said the move to cede authority over HSE recruitment to the department represented a “watershed moment” which set a dangerous precedent.
Its president, Prof Gabrielle Colleran, said the authority of the HSE chief executive had “not only been undermined but usurped”.
“I cannot see how this move can possibly align with patient safety, the required drive to cut hospital waiting lists, or the idea of a fit-for-purpose HSE,” she said.
[ Senior hospital doctors criticise Minister for Health’s ‘closed-door’ approach to engagement Opens in new window ]
General secretary of the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation Phil Ní Sheaghdha said: “The Department of Health is essentially telling hospital and community care managers that they need to find ways to not fill posts. The department will not use patient safety and risk as a reason to fill a clinical post. This is unheard of in a country that has never been wealthier with a growing and ageing population.”
She said the Government had essentially torn up every staffing agreement aimed at protecting the physical and mental health of staff and of the nation as a whole.
“It is baffling that the HSE board have seemingly gone along with these new measures. The HSE board must now outline exactly if it has sanctioned the decision to throw patient and staff safety out the window.”
The new rules state that regions seeking to fill posts “must demonstrate consideration of all reasonable alternatives, including service redesign, redeployment, alternative grades or professions, roster changes, shared services and wider regional resources before seeking additional staffing”.

title: Public service retention crisis
description: Columnists are clinging to a romanticised fiction of inflated pay, golden pensions and cushy working conditions
content:
Sir, – Dr Travis Lines ( Letters , October 19th) succinctly captured why so many of his colleagues have emigrated when he observed that “the best Irish doctors are looking after mums and dads in Sydney rather than Sligo because the Irish Government refuses to pay or treat them properly”.
His observation exposes the root cause of the recruitment and retention crisis across our public services. It is astonishing, then, that so many of your columnists remain detached from this reality, clinging instead to a romanticised fiction.
Pat Leahy (“ Are public sector workers all as badly off as strikes might suggest? ”, Opinion, October 17th) cites “guaranteed pensions”, “job security” and “automatic increments”. Cliff Taylor (“ A public pay deal will be done – and here’s what it will look like ”, Opinion, October 17th) argues that pensions and increments give public servants “a significant boost compared to the private sector”.
Meanwhile, Stephen Collins (“ Unsustainable pay increases for public sector workers will put Ireland’s stability at risk ”, Opinion, October 16th) not only blames public servant pay for the last economic crash but claims that “Even after the crash ... salaries for Irish public servants remained significantly higher than in most other developed countries”.
If this narrative of inflated pay, golden pensions and cushy working conditions were true, one question remains: why are Irish teachers, nurses and doctors choosing to care for children, patients and communities in Sydney and Dubai rather than Sligo and Dublin?
Columnists can benchmark theoretical benefits all they like, but young professionals judge their real-world quality of life. Until the Government and its defenders acknowledge this reality, our public services will continue to haemorrhage talent to countries that actually value it. – Yours, etc,

title: Women need to be supported from a young age to express their right to bodily autonomy
description: Ireland has a shameful history of child abuse and abuse of women perpetrated by family members and people in positions of power
content:
The Government ’s intervention in an advert by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre that depicts a teenage girl declining physical contact with her grandparents places the Government at risk of not representing the views of the people who voted them into office.
How can our Government stand over a statement that implies that a grandparent’s feelings supersede those of a child? Our country has a shameful history of child abuse and abuse of women perpetrated by family members and people in positions of power.
We also have ongoing issues of sexual assault against women. Women need to be supported from a young age to express their right to bodily autonomy in all areas and understand that they, and only they, get to decide who touches them in any manner.
A disappointing statement by the Minister for Justice, Jim O’Callaghan , who needs to be educated on the reality of life for women and girls in Ireland. I hope he will reflect on this, retract his statement and support the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre in their work. – Yours etc,
Sir, – The demeaning depiction of grandparents in the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre advertisement about hugging individuals without their consent would appear to be yet another cack-handed attempt to deal with this contentious subject.
[ Advert showing grandparents hugging grandchildren is taken down amid criticism Opens in new window ]
Consent encompasses a myriad of situations and such advertisements are at best clumsy, at worst patronising. Irritating the grandparents of Ireland is an unfortunate consequence particularly for those who provide invaluable care to those same grandchildren. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Surely those, including the Minister for Justice, complaining about the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre’s consent video featuring grandparents, are missing the point. The point, clearly, is about listening. And specifically listening to children.
If a child expresses discomfort about specific physical contact, whether it be from a grandparent or anybody else, their discomfort needs to be listened to and respected.
Have we learned nothing from where not listening to children led us in this country’s bitter experience of the abuse of generations of children? – Yours, etc,

title: A rational solution to ballooning healthcare budgets has been talked about for 10 years
description: A transition to a money-follows-the patient system of funding is long overdue
content:
Sir, – In disputes pitting the leaders in our Government and healthcare system at odds with each other, two things seem clear. One is that everyone would rather see the problems solved, and the other is that real data can be cited to support either viewpoint.
This leads to an argumentative stalemate. If no one is shown to be “wrong”, no one will change their mind. A new approach is needed, and oddly it is one that has been proposed and anticipated for more than a decade.
A transition to a money-follows-the patient system of funding is surely long overdue. At present the incentives of taxpayers and healthcare providers are completely misaligned.
The State effectively grants a (very large, apparently) sum of money to a hospital as an annual budget. Arguably, then, the less work that gets done over that year, the better the hospital’s ultimate financial position will be.
A shift to a culture whereby each case or admission is reimbursed at a defined rate provides the opposite motivation. As a year ends, rather then slowing down as funds deplete, healthcarers would ramp up work to maximise that year’s revenue. This seems indisputably rational.
The big difficulty is in defining rates for each case. However, the private fees of the large insurers provide a platform to start that process. Artificial intelligence could help greatly.
In practical terms, a plan to allocate, say, 10 per cent of each hospital’s budget on this basis in 2028 could be followed by an increase of a further 10 per cent annually for five to six years.
My instinct is that, as many costs are fixed and incurred early – insurance, for example – a full transition would be unwise. But perhaps the present stand-off between those at the very top of the €30 billion system tells us that the time has come to try something different on this scale.
It would at least be impossible to have a situation where funding was consumed with no evident improvement in performance. – Yours, etc,

title: As Donald Trump weighs up options, could inflation be about to get worse?
description: Reports of US escalation plan in Iran send oil prices up again
content:
Reports that the US is planning further strikes on Iran – potentially after the US midterm elections next month – have triggered another surge in oil prices. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose to a five-month high of $114 (€102) a barrel on Friday.
US president Donald Trump is apparently being briefed on two possible options for ending the current deadlock. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is said to be arguing that Iran is on the brink of economic collapse and that the US’s continuing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz combined with sanctions will soon force Tehran to cut a deal, one that is favourable to Washington.
At the same time, Israeli leader Binyamin Netanyahu is said to be trying to convince Trump that another round of even more devastating air strikes could topple the regime.
According to reports from inside the White House, Trump is said to be considering combining the two approaches: betting that an economically weak regime in Tehran could be pushed over the edge by more air strikes.
The political calculus in Washington aside, oil is now up nearly 60 per cent since the start of the war and around 90 per cent in the year so far.
Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities combined with Ukraine attacks on Russian diesel refineries are further adding to supply concerns.
The deteriorating geopolitical situation is fanning fears that inflation could be about to get a lot worse.
The European Central Bank (ECB) is expected to leave interest rates unchanged at 2.5 per cent when it meets next week.
[ US and Israel draw up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after midterm elections Opens in new window ]
“With little evidence of second-round inflation effects, the Governing Council is unlikely to feel compelled to deliver consecutive rate hikes,” says Tom Pugh, chief economist with consulting firm RSM UK and Ireland.
“However, we expect the ECB to raise rates again in December, pushing policy modestly into restrictive territory.
[ Can 2,000 people in a hangar in Sioux City influence the US midterms? Trump is banking on it Opens in new window ]
“Beyond that, the outlook will depend heavily on energy markets. If tensions ease and prices normalise, policymakers may pause.”
At the moment, tensions don’t seem to be easing and prices are spiralling up rather than normalising. All of which creates a very uncertain outlook.

title: ‘We’re always prepared for a physical battle’: Ireland ready for South Africa challenge
description: Dorothy Wall relishing opportunity to face passionate Cape Town crowd
content:
Opponents singing in the tunnel before kick-off and playing in front of a passionate Cape Town crowd are among the things that make international rugby special for Dorothy Wall, as Ireland prepare for their first women’s Test on South African soil at Athlone Stadium on Saturday.
A safari has been among the highlights of her first visit to the Rainbow Nation, but the bottom line is taking home two victories over the Springbok Women to complete this opening WXV Global Series window.
Ireland’s players have found a few favourite coffee spots near their hotel, where curious locals have been asking about their presence.
“Obviously, we come as a group, so people inquire while we’re there, and we tell them about the rugby,” said Wall. “Everyone we talk to says, ‘oh, yeah, we’ll watch that game’ or ‘we’ll go to that game’ but they always finish off with, ‘we won’t be supporting you’.
“They’re obviously a very proud nation. You definitely won’t be swaying them over a flat white in the morning. It’s an amazing country, with a very rich historical background. You have to pay respect to what’s happened here and the culture of the people.”
Ireland’s only previous meeting with South Africa ended in a 37-0 victory at the 2006 World Cup. While video analysis will help Scott Bemand ’s side prepare, there is an undeniable excitement about facing an unfamiliar opponent.
One of two changes to the starting line-up following the victory over Japan in Cork three weeks ago, Wall is relishing the occasion.
“Those are the moments that particularly get me up for Tests, like facing the Haka two years ago in WXV1 in Canada against New Zealand, or running out against France last year in the Six Nations with the bands and fireworks, and the way the French crowds turn up,” reflected the 26-year-old.
“The South Africans love to sing, and that’s part of their culture in the tunnel. Those moments make you realise how lucky you are to do what you do, but also how exciting it is to face these women, who are equally impressive and play a different brand [of rugby].
“You still really want to beat them, but you have to soak up those moments, because how many people get to do that?”
[ Erin King hoping to cap memorable week with victory in inaugural away Test against South Africa Opens in new window ]
Ireland want to build on successive wins over Japan and Wall expects a formidable physical examination, but she believes her side has the attacking weapons to prevail.
The maul has been a major focus after the USA overturned a 19-point deficit in Tallaght just over a month ago. Discipline will also be crucial, with penalties potentially handing South Africa easy access to Ireland’s 22.
“Their set piece, especially their scrum, is incredibly dominant,” said the Exeter Chiefs secondrow. “They have size, as comes with every South African team. I believe our set piece and lineout are better.
[ Hiko Tonosa returns to Dublin Marathon looking to regain national title Opens in new window ]
“Our kicking game, especially with Dannah [O’Brien], is very influential on how we play, and we’re a very fit team. We’re always prepared for a physical battle. If you can’t get yourself up aggressively, with intent and physicality, you probably shouldn’t be a rugby player.
“It’s about how much you engage in a kicking battle to run them around before bringing them to the set piece. Chop tackles and all the obvious things against a heavier side are what we’re going to do.”

title: James McClean’s stance on opening up may work for him but we are not all elite sportspeople
description: We must look inside ourselves from time to time – and talking this through with another person can be a crucial part of this
content:
J ames McClean, the former Republic of Ireland soccer international, raised a storm last week when he told Paul Kimmage in the Irish Independent : “I see it as a weakness that I’d have to speak to someone about my feelings, my emotions.” And he viewed players who talked to a team psychologist as weak too – “As a man, I see that as a weakness. I don’t need to open up.”
I recognise this macho stance about emotions from growing up in Glasgow. Only in his cups was it acceptable – just - for a red-blooded male to indulge his emotions – anger being an exception, of course. The cultural taboo went further than mistrust – it verged on a phobia about delving too much inside – what might he find?
Thankfully, the world has changed and that phobia has faded for most men and women, even if James McClean is not one of them. Even the Football Association of Ireland finally conscripted a psychologist into its ranks after the first Israel game.
For the pressures of elite sport are considerable. Young men and women sacrifice enormous chunks of their early lives to training, travelling, playing and recovering. Relationships can suffer, careers may stall and the constant threat of failure or career-ending injury haunts them.
Physical fitness, self-discipline, team camaraderie and a sense of purpose, on the other hand, may help elite athletes bolster their mental resources and help shield them from some of the anxieties and vulnerabilities that afflict their non-sports peers in increasing numbers.
That being said, elite athletes are more susceptible to mild eating disorders and a survey of elite GAA players found that gambling is widespread, with around 6 per cent of them – mainly men – having a gambling problem.
Irish rugby international Hannah Tyrrell continued to play elite sport right through the torment of a bulimic eating disorder and bouts of self-harm. Like James McClean, she shied away from revealing what was going on inside her head for a long time. But sport offered a distraction and a relief from these torments until she could finally speak up.
And this chimes with research showing lower levels of anxiety and depression in teenagers who take part in sport, compared to those who do not. Freeing children from solitary bedroom screens, fostering social interaction and friendship, building a sense of belonging and boosting self-esteem are all potential outcome of taking part in sport. Importantly, these have also been shown to be important antidotes to anxiety and low mood.
[ ‘She’s a special person’: Stephen Bradley hails impact of psychologist Opens in new window ]
The benefits of team sports are even greater in adolescents who have had adverse experiences in childhood such as neglect, abuse, parental substance abuse and single parenthood. Followed-up over 13 years into young adulthood, team sport participations was linked to a very significant reduction in depression or severe anxiety.
This fact is very relevant for the super-elite athlete who, research shows, is more likely to be driven by early negative experiences in childhood compared to merely elite athletes. Take the golfer Tiger Woods, for example. He was bullied and mocked as a child for his crippling stutter. The enduring psychological imprint of early tough experiences can trigger a hunger for success and the relentless drive and self-sacrifice that are crucial for elite success.
Woods’s yawing fortunes with police and drugs since the peak of his career show elite athletes’ troubles don’t necessarily end when they retire. Stepping out of the cocoon of an elite team and its supports and demands is a shock for many retiring sports men and women.
Former Republic of Ireland and Liverpool footballer Jason McAteer describes how retiring from elite soccer left him in a void of identity, meaning, structure and purpose. US swimmer Michael Phelps and basketball player Michael Jordan also found the transition to mere mortals very difficult.
But all of us face life transitions that can unsettle us and create problems that we can either adjust to and address or retreat from and avoid. On average, retired elite athletes are no more or less anxious or depressed than the rest of us .
Which begs the question – are we all feeling more mentally unsettled? The answer to that is definitely yes for Gen Z (born 1997-2012), to some extent for millennials (1981-1996) but no for baby boomers (1946-1964) like me. Why is this?
[ It’s no wonder people my age are miserable. Everyone keeps telling them they’re totally screwed Opens in new window ]
Ask any boomer and they will likely tell you how they were let out the door to play on the street and beyond with scarce oversight from their parents – that was certainly my experience. Having this sort of personal control – as opposed to being constantly ferried from one organised activity to another - builds confidence in children and confidence is the greatest antidote to anxiety.
Yes, smartphones and social media play a part in this generational shift in behaviour: there was nothing to do in a boomer’s bedroom so you had to go out or else you would die of boredom.
Another generational difference lies in expectations . Comparison is the thief of joy, a saying attributed to Theodore Roosevelt, tallies with research: happiness is the what we expect minus what we perceive; if the result is a positive number, then we feel happy, if negative, we feel unhappy. What we expect in the way of personal achievement, looks, goods or other attributes has risen. But so also has the accessibility of people in comparison to whom we feel we are lacking or failing.
Adolescents have lost the reference group of contentedly miserable peers who could hang about on the street corner mutually commiserating about their fate in consoling solidarity.
The author of The Anxious Generation , Jonathon Haidt, wrote another book called The Coddling of the American Mind, in which he argues that by trying to protect young people from psychological discomfort, we have by mistake made them more fragile, anxious and less capable of dealing with tough times.
Key to this has been the trend to medicalising normal emotions - “I have anxiety” – as if this was a medical condition rather than an understandable emotional response to what you are thinking and doing. Once you start seeing your emotions as medical diagnoses that arise uncontrollably, it sabotages your ability to deal with them.
[ Extreme sports – where self-absorbed masochism gets dressed up as sport Opens in new window ]
We must look inside ourselves from time to time – and talking this through with another person can be a crucial part of this, whatever James McClean says. But it is equally important to realise that how we behave moulds how we feel just as much as vice versa: we can learn, sometimes with help, to become masters of our emotions and not their slaves.
Elite sportspeople have to do this – and so does every GAA, soccer or hockey child stepping out on to the turf on a damp Saturday morning.
Ian Robertson is e meritus p rofessor of p sychology at Trinity College Dublin

title: Zionism and supporting Palestine
description: The repetition of history Fintan O’Toole fears has already occurred
content:
Sir, – Fintan O’Toole’s column ( “ Zionism is not racism, any more than Irish nationalism is sectarianism , ” October 20th ) reinforces the trope that elements discriminate against Jews because of their faith.
It is a misrepresentation spuriously based on the horror of the Holocaust. He says “not to be aware of that history is to be at risk, through ignorance and thoughtlessness, of repeating it”. I was well aware of it from a very young age and it’s a critical element in my advocacy for Palestine .
The “repetition” O’Toole fears has already occurred; unless what worried him was the welfare of Jewish people alone. The genocide, sponsored by the West, now in its fourth year, was recognised as such in 2024 by Amos Goldberg, professor of Holocaust studies at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
Far from being concerned that readers’ “ignorance or thoughtlessness”’ could lead to any repeat of such barbarity, it’s seeing Israel ’s conduct and being aware of precedent that moves people to act.
Zionism is a political ideology, one that is inherently expansionist, as Israel displays in real time; not satisfied with Palestine, its designs on parts of Lebanon and Syria are manifest in the Zionist wish that Greater Israel reach from the Nile to the Euphrates. I know this prospect is every bit as threatening to Palestinians and Lebanese as crowds chanting “from the river to the sea” is to some Israelis.
Zionism is also racist; its settler-colonial ambition demands the dehumanisation of the indigenous people. Some believe Israel is a democracy because it has regular parliamentary elections (as it will next week). It is not; it is an ethnocracy whose political structures protect only one group’s interests. Israel is not governed to serve the interests of all its citizens. It is an apartheid state.
We need to take on Ireland’s Zionist lobby for what it is: a pro-Israel group within our Jewish community. Its supporters will fight its case. That is their right, as it is ours, to call out Israel as a genocidal, apartheid, settler-colonial state that is inherently expansionist.
Those who support Palestine and express outrage at Israel’s have taken the time to inform themselves, not, as O’Toole suggests, because they form judgments through “ignorance and thoughtlessness”. That charge is better levelled elsewhere.
Our institutional ignorance and thoughtlessness have allowed a genocide to occur; the task now is to bring it to an end and to ensure those responsible face justice. I’m happy to have Jewish friends who believe that just as intensely. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Fintan O’Toole’s article (October 20th) is a welcome and thoughtful contribution to a difficult debate.
His comparison of Zionism with Irish nationalism is particularly apt. Neither should be judged solely by its more extreme expressions. It is entirely possible to condemn the actions of the Israeli government and support the rights of Palestinians while recognising the historical legitimacy of Jewish national aspirations.
Equally, criticism of Israel must never become an excuse for anti-Semitism or collective blame.
Ireland’s own history should encourage us to appreciate the complexities of national identity, persecution and displacement rather than reduce them to simplistic arguments.
O’Toole reminds us that sympathy for the Palestinians and an understanding of Jewish history are not mutually exclusive. – Yours, etc,
Sir,- Fintan O’Toole’s opinion piece on anti-Semitism in The Irish Times is greatly to be welcomed. Such a sensitive and balanced analysis on a complex and difficult subject for us all has been needed for a long time. – Yours, etc,

title: Terenure and St Mary’s renew rivalry in AIL derby clash
description: Old Belvedere host Division 1A leaders Clontarf in another Dublin derby
content:
Three games into Division 1A of the Energia All-Ireland League and no team remains unbeaten, while only Ballynahinch are winless, with six points separating the leaders Clontarf from Old Wesley in ninth.
But no matter the state of the table, any clash between local rivals St Mary’s and Terenure is never less than crucial in Dublin 6W. St Mary’s suffered a late loss to Cork Constitution in Temple Hill two weeks ago and the champions will be eager to return to winning ways.
Mark McHugh promotes Stephen McLoughlin, their ex-Young Munster hooker/flanker, to the backrow with new Australian Michael Icely part of a 5-1 split on the bench. The props switch, with Oisin Michel and Ronan McCormack starting, and Thomas O’Reilly and Andrew Sparrow on the bench.
Terenure are unchanged from the side that staved off an Old Wesley fightback to claim a bonus-point win last time out. All five meetings since St Mary’s returned to 1A have been won by the home side, including last season’s semi-final sell-out.
The grim weather forecast and Leinster-Munster will reduce the crowd but it still should be the day’s biggest. Terenure haven’t won in Templeville Road since 2017.
Old Belvedere, whose early season form was rocked by Lansdowne two weeks ago, welcome Clontarf to Ollie Campbell Park in another Dublin derby with an intense rivalry. As the prolific Rob Russell is training with Munster, James Dillon switches to 15 with Andre Ryan on the wing. Peter O’Beirn is at scrumhalf, in what is believed to be the first instance of a son of a reigning IRFU president, Tony, starting an AIL game during his father’s tenure.
Clontarf are missing a couple of try scorers from their 61-15 win over UCD a fortnight ago in Leinster lock Brian Deeny and centre Daniel Hawkshaw, as well as tight-head Niall Smyth and Alex Soroka. Charlie Ward, Jim Peters and ex-Connacht flanker Oisin McCormack come into the pack, as does Alex O’Grady in midfield.
Old Wesley make two changes, Luke O’Connor at eight and Lachlan Stewart at 10, for Young Munster’s visit to Donnybrook in what was quite a rivalry back in the day. Veteran prop Paul Allen returns for the Cookies, as does Munster lock Evan O’Connell and Canadian scrumhalf Brock Gallagher, with Kelvin Langan shifting to outhalf and Orin Burke on the wing.
UCD host Cork Constitution in the Bowl and start two of last season’s stand-out schools players in the Mary’s Cup – winning hooker Joe Christle and centre Bernard White, while Oisin Spain is in the backrow. Con are strengthened by the return of Munster lock Michael Foy in an otherwise unchanged team which dug deep for that win over Mary’s.
Ballynahinch are boosted by the return of ex-Sevens and Ulster winger Aaron Sexton for the visit of Lansdowne, who bring in prop George Morris, backrowers Matt Healy and Hardus Van Eeden, winger Hubert Gilvarry, and Hugo McLoughlin, who replaces Todd Lawlor as he is rested by Leinster.
[ Conor Murray: Snubbed Munster players can make statement against Leinster Opens in new window ]
The 1B leaders Naas travel to Shaw’s Bridge to face Instonians, seeking a first AIL victory at the venue after their 54-14 win over Blackrock, while Instonians edged Nenagh Ormond 23-22.
Second-placed Highfield visit MU Barnhall at Parsonstown, Trinity welcome Nenagh Ormond to College Park, Blackrock College host City of Armagh at Stradbrook and UCC seek their first win against Garryowen at the Mardyke.
Energia All-Ireland League (2.30pm unless stated) Men’s Division 1A: Ballynahinch v Lansdowne, Ballymacarn Park; Old Belvedere v Clontarf, Ollie Campbell Park; Old Wesley v Young Munster, Energia Park, St Mary’s College v Terenure College, Templeville Road; UCD v Cork Constitution, UCD Bowl.
Men’s 1B: Instonians v Naas, Shaw’s Bridge (2.00pm); Blackrock College v City of Armagh, Stradbrook; Dublin Uni. v Nenagh Ormond, College Park; MU Barnhall v Highfield RFC, Parsonstown; UCC v Garryowen, The Mardyke.
Men’s 2A: Dungannon v Shannon RFC, Stevenson Park; Galwegians v Ballymena, Crowley Park; Queen’s Uni. v Greystones, The Dub; UL Bohemian v Corinthians, UL 4G; Wanderers v Cashel RFC, Merrion Road.
Men’s 2B North: Banbridge v Enniskillen RFC, Rifle Park; Malahide v Sligo, Estuary Road; Navan v Ballyclare RFC, Balreask Old Rainey RFC v Malone, Hatrick Park; Skerries v Clogher Valley, Holmpatrick.
Men’s 2B South: Bruff v Dolphin, Kilballyowen Park; Buccaneers v Bective Rangers, Dubarry Park; Clonmel v Thomond RFC, Ard Gaoithe; Midleton v Monkstown, Towns Park; Old Crescent v Enniscorthy, Takumi Park.
All-Ireland men’s Junior Cup, first round: Ballina v Clonakilty RFC, Heffernan Park; Boyne RFC v Ballinasloe, Shamrock Lodge; Dromore v Creggs, Barban Hill; Dunmore v Omagh Academy, Fairgreen Pitches; Kilfeacle & Dist v Suttonians, Morrissey Park; Mallow RFC v Wicklow, Mallow RFC; Portadown v Bandon RFC, Chambers Park; Tullamore v Lurgan, Spollanstown.

title: Bumper Group One weekend for Aidan O’Brien could rejuvenate world record hopes
description: Irishman aiming for 13th Futurity victory at Doncaster that could also seal ninth British trainers’ title
content:
Talk of Aidan O’Brien breaking his own world record for Group One wins in a year subsided recently, although it could be rejuvenated this weekend with the Irish trainer competing in four top-flight contests.
A 13 th William Hill Futurity success at Doncaster on Saturday may secure O’Brien a ninth British trainers’ title before the two-year-old focus switches to Paris on Sunday.
Puerto Rico and Pierre Bonnard delivered for O’Brien a year ago in the two Group One juvenile contests up for grabs at Saint-Cloud, and he has a handful of runners spread around the Criterium International and the Criterium de Saint-Cloud this time.
He also runs Queenstown and Amelia Earhart in the €350,000 Prix Royal Oak due off at 2.50pm Irish time. Queenstown found only Arrow Eagle too good for him a year ago in the race widely described as France’s St Leger.
Ross O’Sullivan will also have a shot at Royal Oak glory through his stalwart Chally Chute, winner of the Curragh Cesarewitch on his last start.
Joseph O’Brien has Jesus Green in the Criterium de Saint-Cloud, a race that he and Dylan Browne McMonagle won with Tennessee Stud two years ago. O’Brien has four other starters in Group Three contests on the Saint-Cloud card. The trainer runs his Royal Ascot winner Kizlyar in a Group Two contest in Flemington early on Saturday morning.
Both the Futurity and Saint-Cloud’s top-class juvenile contests have delivered rich pickings for Ballydoyle over the years.
O’Brien reached 22 Group One successes this season when Minnie Hauk scored at Ascot last week. His 2017 world record tally is 28. A dominant weekend could mean that target comes back into sight in advance of next week’s Breeders’ Cup action. There may be further targets, particularly in the Far East, towards the end of the year.
Camelot and Auguste Rodin are among some O’Brien A-listers that have won the Futurity. The wide-margin Beresford winner Noble Exhibit tops a Ballydoyle trio this time in a field that also contains Gran Dia, a sole representative for O’Brien’s championship rival Andrew Balding.
The English man looks to be fighting a losing battle to secure a first title. The championship runs to the end of the year, but Britain’s final Group One of the season is potentially decisive in terms of significant prize money.
Gran Dia won his sole start to date at Salisbury and a spokesman for his owner Tony Bloom conceded: “He’s a horse who has won a maiden going straight into a Group One and we’re under no illusions how difficult that will be. But we want to give him a second run before the end of the year.
“We’re going to be taking on battle-hardened two-year-olds who have runs under their belt and our fellow has only had one, so it will be very much a learning curve for him. But we hope he goes there and shows enough to think we can be dreaming with him over the winter.”
It’s no surprise Ryan Moore has opted for Noble Exhibit. The Frankel colt broke his maiden to the tune of seven lengths at Punchestown before dominating the Beresford 11 days later. The Curragh contest is traditionally a signpost to Futurity success.
Sergei Diaghilev found only the highly rated Rock Montreal too good at Newmarket recently, which was a much better effort than Giant Sequoia’s in last month’s National Stakes. The Futurity winner never figured behind Folsom Blues and may not relish testing conditions.
The main domestic hope appears to be Karl Burke’s Burning Up, but he proved no match for another O’Brien colt, Haffner, at Newmarket in the Royal Lodge, which should leave the Irish camp knowing where they stand with him.
In contrast, the two Saint-Cloud races have traditionally had a second-division vibe for O’Brien, although Irish Derby winners Fame And Glory and Los Angeles feature among six victories in the race. O’Brien has won the Criterium International seven times.
There is plenty of evidence of how O’Brien can get his horses to back up quickly for this Saint-Cloud programme, having scored the weekend previously at Leopardstown.
Capability Brown made light of a drop in trip to land the Killavullan Stakes at Leopardstown last Saturday and will bid to step up to Group One status in the International. He is joined by stable companion Aix La Chapelle in a seven-runner contest.
There are also seven for the 10-furlong Group One, although just one of them is local. Moore is on board the impressive Zetland Stakes winner Drumbeat while Christophe Soumillon is on Shakespeare. Victory Speech is Wayne Lordan’s mount.
Charlie Appleby’s Godolphin team have supplemented both Al Jabbar and Royal Acclamation. William Buick has opted for the former, leaving new British champion jockey Billy Loughnane in for a good spare.
Jesus Green also takes his chance and enjoyed a confidence boost when easily scoring in a Navan maiden last time. He’d previously chased home Darkness Falls in the Golden Fleece.
It’s 18 years since O’Brien landed his sole Royal Oak success with the outstanding Yeats.
Queenstown’s status in the Ballydoyle pecking order is much more prosaic, but the gelding is a smart stayer in his own right. Only Mount Atlas was too good for him at Ascot last weekend, and before that he was third in the Cadran. He’s certainly being kept busy, although he still looks the best shot at an Irish success.
Lordan will do 8st 8lbs on the quirky filly Amelia Earhart while Donagh O’Connor has a shot at Group One glory aboard Chally Chute.

title: ‘I’ll probably cry a lot’: Six people tell us why they’re running the Dublin Marathon
description: Six people share their reasons for signing up, and what has kept them going through the hundreds of kilometres they have run in preparation
content:
I t is one of the toughest challenges in sport , a 42km test of the human body’s capacity for endurance, yet its difficulty is what makes the marathon distance attractive to so many people.
A record 47,000 people entered the ballot for this year’s Dublin Marathon , more than double the race’s capacity. Alongside those running, thousands more will line the streets to cheer on friends and strangers. Recognised as one of the most emotional and joyful days in the city’s calendar, it is also a mass fundraising event with €9 million projected to be raised for hundreds of charities.
At the front, there will be a few elite runners competing for prize money and prestige, but just behind them are thousands of first-timers, veterans and marathon addicts, people who love running, and some who loathe it.
We spoke to six people taking on the challenge this year to find out what led them to sign up for the race, and what has kept them going through the hundreds of kilometres they have run in preparation.
This is a big year for me. I am turning 40. It’s a milestone. I didn’t know where I would be when I was 40. I didn’t think I’d be in Ireland. I didn’t think I’d be alive. The marathon is a celebration of my life, to say that I am here now. I am safe. There’s a lot to live for. Each mile is going to be dedicated to something, and I’ll probably cry a lot.
When I came to Ireland in 2023, I didn’t know anyone. I was staying in Direct Provision , and I saw a poster on the notice board that said: “Come for a run, a jog, come for a cup of tea.” Where I was coming from, you couldn’t just go outside for a walk as a woman on your own. You could never go for a run. It was like a sign of disrespect. I contacted Sanctuary Runners, and a lady called Deirdre came and picked me up on a Saturday morning, and we went to the parkrun at Poolbeg. It was so nice to be able to get out of my room and go outside. The Irish people I had been speaking to were all connected to the asylum process. It was so nice just to have a coffee with someone and talk about things, to be an individual, to be Patience.
I looked forward to every weekend from then on. Then one of the ladies from Sanctuary said: “You don’t need to wait for Saturday; you can go outside anytime for a run, for a walk.”
[ It’s not just the Berlin Marathon. Cheating runners everywhere are now being closely watched Opens in new window ]
I fell in love with it. I started running and running. I didn’t have gear, so the Sanctuary Runners gave me runners and a watch I could connect to my phone. I started tracking my runs. For me, it was an escape to be able to get out of the room. I was sharing with other people, and it sometimes became too much. So I would just run and run and run, and then I would look for a bus that said city centre, and I knew how to get home from there.
I did the Dublin Marathon in 2024, my first one. I had no idea what I was doing. This time I have an idea, and I know what is expected. I have a feel for it. I know the stages.
I think about my son a lot when I’m running. We aren’t together, and I miss him a lot. He’s 10, and I left him when he was eight. He gets me through. He tells me funny things when we talk, and I think about that when I run. I’m hoping he will be proud of his ma.
The discovery of running is that there is always someone who has run further and always someone who has run faster than you. This will be my 14th Dublin Marathon, my 30th marathon ever, and I am celebrating 20 years of running. It’s a big year.
I always liked the idea of running in my childhood, but I never got the opportunity to. In Italy , there wasn’t a culture of amateur running, so when I got to Ireland, it was a bit weird for me. I started with triathlon, but I realised I prefer the freedom of running. You just put your shoes on, and you go. At the beginning, it was unbelievable to me that I could build up the distances. When I started telling people I was running the marathon, they were shocked, thinking I was crazy. After my first one, I immediately wanted to run again. I started to run Dublin and Cork every year.
I love the sensation of freedom, of being with myself. I feel my breath, my heartbeat; I check with myself how I am. People ask whether it’s boring to run without music. In a sense, maybe, but I never get bored. I always find something to think about.
When you get older, you challenge the distance, not the time. In 2017, I chased my second dream of running 100km. I was 48, I had recently lost 10kg, and it felt like I was moving on air. The race started at 3pm in Florence under the hot sun; it goes up to the mountains and then finishes in Faenza. I remember I was feeling lightheaded on the descent, and I met this guy who was running in flip-flops, and he gave me a big sugary date. I know that the date fixed me.
That same year I ran the marathon in Milan. My dad was in a nursing home at the 30km point of the marathon. I knew exactly what time I would get there. So he got the nurse to get him out. I was very fit, and I was running well, and I knew I was going to lose time, but I stopped to give my dad a hug. I remember another runner said: “That hug will last forever.” It is true. You’re so focused on the nitty-gritty, but if I got a personal best in Milan, what would have changed? Nothing. What remains is the hug I gave to my dad.
For me, it all started back in April. I woke up early, and I just wanted to go back to sleep. So I got dressed and went on a 5km run, hoping I’d get tired and could go back to bed. But then I was awake for the day. Two days later, I went on another 5km run. At that point, I was stringing each kilometre together. My relationship had just ended, and my friends were encouraging me to do something new, to get a new hobby, just to move my body. They started joking with me, saying: “Get your ass marathon ready.”
I started looking through the charities connected with the Dublin Marathon. I saw LA519 on RealBuzz, and that is when I applied. I went through a mental health dark spot last year, and I saw similarities in what they’re doing, trying to connect people who are looking for services and not knowing where to go. I was shocked when I found out in May that I was running it. I thought, if I’m going to do this, I might as well do a 10km and then a half marathon. It just snowballed from there.
[ Sing for joy: ‘One of the best things you can do for your mental health is join a choir’ Opens in new window ]
I used this app called Rally for my half marathon. Every kilometre you can hear a voice note from family and friends. You don’t hear the recordings people have left until the day. I ran the half on the August bank holiday. I had a knee injury, and after the first mile I wanted to give up, but then I heard my nieces and nephews talking to me. I just had to keep going. I ran six miles in pain before I got ibuprofen from my family. I was catching up to people after that, and the last stretch was just pure emotion.
I think about my kids when I run. I live in Leitrim , and they live with their mum near The Halfway House in Dublin, which is about 23km into the Dublin route. Whenever I get to 21km on my runs, I think, “Oh, they’re going to be here soon.” I get emotional around those distances.
I’m proud of myself for how dedicated I am now. A few Saturdays ago, I got up at 6.30am to drive to Dublin and bring my kids to the zoo for the day. I dropped them off at 7pm, and then I went on a 34km run. I was at 30km when my legs started to go. I just went at a slower pace, and for the last kilometre I ran and walked. It wasn’t until the next day, at sunset, that I really thought: “That was it.”
All these runs I’m doing are the actual marathon; October 25th will be a victory lap.
I would never describe myself as a runner. I’m a jogger. I’m a plodder. My natural inclination is sitting on the couch reading a book. By doing the marathon, I’m basically tricking myself into aerobic exercise.
This will be the third year in a row I’ve run the Dublin Marathon. I decided I wanted to do it in 2018 when some friends were running. I’d never been a spectator before, and I hadn’t appreciated how big the event was, how incredible the support on the streets was. The minute I was there watching the runners go by, it was inspirational. We were in Milltown, which is around 30km in, and is generally accepted as the point where the sheer misery begins. The crowds were massive, and people were really pushing the runners on. It was people like me, not elite athletes. They were so impressive. The thing about a marathon is that almost no one can spoof it. There are lots of people who could probably run a 10k if they had to, but for a marathon, you have to do lots and lots of training.
I am not suited to long-distance running. I don’t enjoy it, and that’s the appeal, knowing it is a big mental and physical challenge. Part of what keeps me going is that I publicly committed to doing it for Special Olympics Ireland . So you’re letting people down if you don’t do it. It’s a way of making sure you push through. Last year my sister wished me luck, saying: “You’ll do it because you’re so unbelievably stubborn.”
Going into it, I always said I’m not living a Spartan life; I could live like a monk, and it wouldn’t make much of a difference, but the one thing I try to do is get a long run in on a Sunday and do as much as I can during the week. I listen to podcasts in training and music during the race. Classic rock, 1980s – that’s my vintage. To me, it’s less about the songs and more about the rhythm. A cheesy 1980s rock anthem can be just what you want to hear. You can’t think about how far you have to go. You have to think about everything other than the pain in your legs. It can become a spiral, and you don’t want to go down that path.
It’s always brilliant to hear your name shouted out on the course by friends and family. Every year the support gets bigger. Certain villages are just amazing. Castleknock is exceptional, and so are Chapelizod, Terenure, Walkinstown, Drimnagh and Crumlin; all the locals come out, and it definitely helps.
Once you’re over the finish line, there is definite relief that you have done it. And if this year is like either of the other years, I will instantly want to do it again.
I was at the Dublin Marathon finish line two years ago waiting for my boyfriend and sister, and it was lashing rain, and I thought: “Why not me? Why can’t I do that? I want to be like them.” We went for pizza afterwards, and we were all sitting round chatting, and I just said, “I’m going to apply.” When I got the entry in the ballot, I decided I wanted to run for the Irish Road Victims Association. They helped us after my dad passed away seven years ago. He was crossing the Malahide Road as a pedestrian. It was so sudden and so quick. I don’t think I fully felt the impact of the grief for two years.
I found being outside and just walking really helped during that time. Sometimes people were running by me, and I’d think I’d love to be able to run like them. I started with 5km, then 10km, and I’ve done a few half-marathons now. Each new distance was so rewarding. I never thought training for a marathon would be this hard. Sometimes when you’re passing other runners, they say hi or give you a thumbs up, and that really keeps you going. I train three days a week: Monday is an easy run, Wednesday is intervals and the weekend is a long run. I like to run down the coast road. We have a plaque on the Wooden Bridge at Dollymount for my dad. He used to love going for swims down there with his friends. So I run and touch the plaque and keep going. He had all those memories there, and I’m creating new memories there now.
A few times on my long runs I’ve been in the pits, and I’ve called my boyfriend Johnny. He’s so gentle and supportive, saying, “You can do this. It’s you versus you.” Everyone keeps asking, “Are you going for a time?” but I’m just going for fun and want to roll with the emotions. The longest run I’ve done is 32km, so the last 10km will be a mental challenge. I’ve been there cheering people on at the last stretch, and I know everyone is really rooting for everyone. I know it will be full of love. When I picture myself crossing the finish line, I hope I see my mum, and I’ll probably cry. I can’t wait to get there, but I also love the build-up.
Before this marathon, life was pretty simple. I was playing lots of padel with my mates, keeping active and enjoying family life. Then we got the heartbreaking news that our good friend Tim had died at just 42. It changed everything. Our friend James suggested that, instead of just sitting with our grief, we should try to turn it into something positive. Our group of schoolfriends, nine deaf men and one CODA (child of deaf adults), came together under the name Help Each Other in Tim’s memory and in memory of other deaf people whose lives have ended too soon. We wanted to raise awareness of the unique barriers deaf people face when trying to access mental health support and help push for deaf-led mental health services in Irish Sign Language. This fight isn’t just about a marathon; it’s about saving lives.
Having run the Dublin Marathon two years ago, I knew it wouldn’t be easy running another one. Even though I’m fit and athletic, it’s a massive challenge trying to fit marathon training around a full-time job, two young kids and everything else. I’ve stuck to a routine that suits me best, running three to four times a week in a compressed 12-week block before race day.
For some of the boys who haven’t exercised much, it must be so difficult, yet they are all showing up. I’ve never once thought of giving up.
The long runs give you time to think. It is scary to think that there are no mental health services to address the specific needs of our deaf community. There are only two psychologists in the country who are fluent in Irish Sign Language. People are left relying on interpreters, family and friends for deeply personal conversations. The last three weeks dealing with my friend Tim were some of the most difficult I have ever experienced. After what I witnessed, the issue became impossible to ignore.
Tim and I first met at Beechpark Deaf School when we were just four years old, and we grew up in the same class right through post-primary school. Knowing him well for 38 years, sharing holidays, weddings, parties and so much of life, it’s still so hard to accept that he’s not around any more. It feels strange not being able to text him.
Running for a long time can be brutal, and sometimes my body just tells me to stop. But the thought of doing this for the deaf community keeps me strong. I am actually looking forward to race day, and crossing that finish line means I finally won’t have to train hard any more.

title: Wariness grows in legal aid row after week of bitter recriminations
