description: Solicitors and Minister for Justice face criticism as positions become entrenched ahead of Law Society meeting with Jim O’Callaghan
content:
H opes of peace breaking out between Jim O’Callaghan and criminal defence solicitors over the new legal aid payment model for the District Courts appear remote after a week of increased disruption across the criminal courts.
As solicitors escalated their withdrawal of services last Monday, and O’Callaghan, the Minister for Justice, slammed them for their disruption while refusing to budge over his changes, both sides faced sharp criticism over their actions.
Solicitors extended their four-month withdrawal of services to include cases involving people in custody, drawing the ire of some judges, including Central Criminal Court judge Paul McDermott and Dublin Circuit Criminal Court judge Martin Nolan.
[ Judge ‘coerced’ into adjourning six rape and sexual offences trials as solicitors withdraw Opens in new window ]
[ ‘It is the most basic duty of a solicitor to represent a client in custody’, says judge Opens in new window ]
Both judges pointed out that solicitors were required under law to secure court permission to come off record for clients, with Nolan describing a unilateral decision by some solicitors not to represent clients in custody as “astounding”.
The legal aid row centres on a new €520 flat-fee payment model introduced by the Department of Justice , based on an average of five appearances, replacing the previous model of €240 for the first appearance and €60 for each subsequent appearance.
“If solicitors think their dispute with the department is more important than representing their clients in custody ... I find it hard that solicitors would adopt this position,” Nolan said.
Solicitors attended hearings of five of 16 defendants up for sentence, with the remainder all adjourned to next month.
In the Children’s Court in Dublin, District Court president Paul Kelly had 16 cases on Tuesday, with solicitors appearing in just three.
Solicitors attend when a client who is about to turn 18 is facing sentence because any delay in sentence would mean the defendant is sentenced as an adult, not a minor.
O’Callaghan came under fire from politicians, the Law Society and others, particularly over his claim the solicitors’ action “deliberately” affected new rape trials listed last Monday.
Six rape trials at the Central Criminal Court did not proceed that day because the accused – all on bail – were not represented.
Solicitors were incensed at the Minister’s claim that they targeted such cases, pointing out their withdrawal has from July 1st affected all types of cases in all criminal court divisions, including rape and other sexual offences, assault, theft, burglary, drug offences and arson.
They strongly disputed the Minister’s suggestion the extension of their action to affect cases of people in custody and “protocol” cases – sexual offence cases involving young people as accused or complainants – meant rape cases were “deliberately affected”.
O’Callaghan repeated his “targeting” claim when he appeared before the Oireachtas justice committee on Tuesday, drawing criticism from several members, including Fine Gael TD Barry Ward, a barrister, who described it as “grossly unfair” and asked him to withdraw the claim.
Labour TD Alan Kelly said he agreed about the need for criminal legal aid reform but told the Minister his claim about targeting rape cases was “beneath your role” and a “tactic” that was both “unjustifiable and wrong”.
The committee chairman, Sinn Féin TD Matt Carthy, reflected the views of many court users, including judges, barristers, solicitors, court staff, defendants and victims of crime, when he urged the Minister to lower the temperature and “engage constructively” with the Law Society.
There is now a “real prospect” of significant parts of the criminal courts system “grinding to a halt”, Carthy warned.
O’Callaghan maintains the courts are functioning and has pointed to the fact there are 177 solicitors across the State engaging with the new scheme. He accepted this week that some, “particularly in Dublin”, have withdrawn their services.
[ The criminal courts are operating, but not ‘effectively’, as Jim O’Callaghan claims Opens in new window ]
Sources across the Courts Service, judiciary and legal professions agree the criminal courts are operating but are very concerned that the large and increasing numbers of case adjournments means further hearing delays compounding existing backlogs.
The impact of such delays on accused people and complainants has been highlighted by organisations including the Irish Council for Civil Liberties.
The council referred to one of almost 90 High Court applications taken since July by unrepresented people alleging unlawful detention. It noted that the High Court had ruled that a lone parent with no previous convictions who was charged with robbery – and who had told the District Court she did not know how to represent herself – had been deprived of a fair hearing.
In another case, the High Court found an illiterate man who had visible injuries during the District Court hearing was subject to “a fundamental denial of justice”.
O’Callaghan has consistently mounted a strong defence of his new payment model.
He says it is the “most significant reform and modernisation” of District Court criminal legal aid in years and argues it is necessary in the interests of an efficient and cost-effective system and will not be revoked. He says he has made “tweaks”, including increasing the proposed flat fee from €455 to €520 and signalled a willingness to discuss further tweaks in cases involving children.
The new scheme is aimed at stamping out “abuses” of the old system, he says, particularly concerning the numbers of multiple legal aid certificates (invoices) granted in a context where spending on criminal legal aid rose from €19 million in 2015 to more than €41 million in 2025.
Solicitors argue their concern is to ensure they are paid for the work they carry out. They want two key changes.
First, where cases exceed five appearances due to prosecution or judicial applications or interventions, they argue that an additional certificate should be granted to cover their additional work.
Second, where an accused person is subject to separate and distinct prosecutions, they should receive a certificate for each distinct prosecution. Under the new scheme, just one certificate would be issued, irrespective of the number of distinct prosecutions.
O’Callaghan wrote this week to Law Society president Rosemarie Loftus, saying he is happy “to continue my engagement” with the solicitors’ representative body in advance of the delivery, on November 3rd, of the High Court’s judgment on a challenge by solicitor John Quinn to the lawfulness of his scheme.
[ Jim O’Callaghan accused of treating solicitors’ pay dispute ‘like it’s a game’ Opens in new window ]
He told Loftus he had asked his officials to organise a meeting before that judgment “to hear your viewpoint and specific concerns”.
That meeting is expected to be held on Wednesday.
In her response, Loftus asked the Minister to attend the meeting “in person”.
It “should take place without further delay”, she said, and the society trusted it would “address the substance of this dispute and support a meaningful resolution”.
Loftus referred to the “real and significant” impact of the impasse on the administration of justice. She said that behind each adjourned case was “a defendant without representation, a victim whose wait for justice goes on, and many others who are directly affected”.
[ Law Society seeks to meet O’Callaghan ‘in person’ to solve legal aid payments impasse Opens in new window ]
The society, she said, had been calling for criminal justice reform for years. Its concern is that any new model is “practical, evidence-based and capable of protecting the constitutional rights of accused people while remaining sustainable for those who provide publicly funded legal representation”.
The society had previously set out to the Minister the two core issues it believed would resolve the key concerns of criminal defence solicitors, she said.
In advance of the meeting between the sides, solicitors remain wary.
Tony Collier, a partner in Dublin firm Ferrys Solicitors LLP, said the Minister’s comments about solicitors targeting rape trials had caused “extensive dismay” among solicitors who lack trust in whether the offer of a meeting is “a response to political pressure or a sincere effort to resolve matters”.
Some have suggested an independent third party could facilitate a meeting between the sides, “given the breakdown in relations”, said Collier.
For now, after one of the most bitter weeks in the months-long dispute, the two sides seem very far apart.

title: ‘Economically it probably would make sense to close’: Clifden businesses prepare for barren winter
description: As the summer tourist throngs thin out, then disappear, the only thing keeping some businesses in the Co Galway town open is loyalty to staff
content:
I t’s mid-afternoon, midweek, mid-October and Clifden , Co Galway , is quiet.
A temporary mural, titled Welcome, by award-winning artist James Kirwan, commissioned for Clifden Arts Festival, is still visible on the Town Hall on Sky Road.
That wall painting, and colourful bunting that flaps in the autumn wind blowing through Market Square, are the only visual reminders of the festival that attracted thousands of tourists to the town over 10 days taking in the two final weekends of September.
Since then, the capital of Connemara, like seasonal tourist towns right across Ireland, has been hurtling towards hibernation.
A large “Dúnta/Closed” sign hangs in the window of the Clifden Tourist Information Centre on Galway Road. It won’t reopen until June 2027.
A number of seafood restaurants have shut for the season, too.
“Once arts week ends in Clifden it gets very quiet, very fast. There’s a big bang on the Saturday night of arts week and then by Monday the town is just dead,” says Lisa King, manager of King’s Paper and Gift Shop.
Almost proving her wrong, a family of six French speakers searching for sweets, squeeze into the shop owned by her mother, Joan.
“Surprising,” says King, adding there are “a few [tourists] around today” but “yesterday was dead. It was painful.”
Outside on Main Street, the visitors – or “strangers”, as Clifden locals affectionately call them – that throng the streets in summer are outnumbered by residents going about their business.
On Bridge Street, an elderly German-speaking couple have no problem finding parking for their electric hire car.
They look on curiously at two burly, bearded Connemara men across the road erecting a red-and-white flag on an electricity pole ahead of the local GAA club’s appearance in a county minor final – a healthy sign there are enough youngsters around to sustain a Gaelic football team at a high level.
Farther along, on Market Street, an American, or possibly Canadian, customer’s voice can be heard chatting inside Love Vintage, a quirky clothes store run by mother-and-daughter duo, owner Carol Anne Joyce and manager Emma O’Sullivan.
“We are all absolutely exhausted after the summer. There are about six weeks when it’s mad in July and August,” says Joyce, who exudes positive energy.
O’Sullivan agrees with King’s analysis that the arts festival marks the “last hurrah” for many Clifden businesses until December, but her mother says she’s “not sure the season ends any more”.
They close their clothing and jewellery shop when schools return early in the new year, but according to Joyce, “even in January, you could open, particularly at weekends”.
They used to shut for at least six weeks until St Valentine’s Day but a new bank holiday in early February to celebrate St Brigid means their off-season is truncated.
“Bloody Bridget! I mean I love Bridget, but feck her, she’s put the kibosh on the holiday,” says Joyce, laughing.
Joyce is a Clifden native. Her mother was from Inishbofin; her father, from Clifden, ran a local grocer’s and supermarket.
[ ‘It is so important to support smaller shops’: west coast villages count on loyal locals at Christmas Opens in new window ]
She opened Love Vintage 17 years ago after becoming “fed up” of the drudgery of working in “high fashion, forward ordering” in France and Copenhagen.
It’s her 13th shop and it has its origins in good luck.
“I won €35,000 on Spin the Wheel,” she says, referring to an appearance on the National Lottery’s former TV gameshow Winning Streak thanks to a scratch card.
She invested the winnings into Love Vintage, which started as a pop-up during Connemara Pony Show in August 2009.
O’Sullivan says Americans are big spenders.
Joyce says Irish visitors give repeat business.
She senses visitors to west Connemara have an “appreciation of wildlife, a quieter and more authentic way”. This, she says, attracted well-known people such as actor Peter O’Toole, Sting, U2 and Bill Whelan of Riverdance to the area.
“There are very unusual shops in Clifden, like my own, that buy out of the ordinary and don’t present the same as the cities or mass produced.
“We’ve always been a bit mad in Clifden,” she adds. “It’s a funky town; a lot of that is because we are so far out. The thing about a small town like this is you don’t pass through it. We are the end. The sea is next. New York is over there.”
Clifden is a coastal market town about 80km west of Galway city. Founded more than 200 years ago by John D’Arcy – of one of the famous merchant families or 14 tribes of Galway – it has a rich history that attracts cultural visitors.
Clifden “townie” Eileen Mannion, a county councillor, describes her hometown as “vibrant, resilient and welcoming”.
She says the town has upped its game in trying to attract tourists in off-season.
Christmas in Clifden, launched one year by Ryan Tubridy – who has a soft spot for and familial connection to the town – provides a boost over three winter weekends.
The county council’s planned public realm enhancement project is also geared towards improving amenities that can be enjoyed year-round.
A planned redesign of the town centre and Market Square, which proved controversial due to a planned reduction in parking spaces, has been put off in favour of focusing on securing national funding for improvements at Beach Road Quay and Harbour Park.
The Fine Gael councillor hopes work can start in 2028 to deliver an amphitheatre performance space, climbing wall, picnic area and other sports facilities.
“It will enhance the area for locals and tourists and provide an amenity park, which we don’t have at present,” she says.
Clifden is well known for the Connemara pony; Alcock and Brown, pilots who made the first nonstop transatlantic flight, from North America to Europe, in 1919; the Marconi radio transmission site that sent the first transatlantic wireless message 12 years earlier; and Richard Martin or “Humanity Dick”, a 19th-century MP and animal rights activist.
“Clifden has a great story to tell, and every night before dinner, we tell that story with pride, vim and vigour,” says Brian Hughes, manager of the family-run Abbeyglen Castle Hotel.
The genial, piano-playing host recites Clifden’s story in his hotel bar, where he vies for customers’ attention with Froda, a resident parrot, who lives in a cage in the lobby next to an open turf fire.
The seven-year-old bird, who speaks intermittently – “see you later”, “goodbye” – recently started imitating meowing cats to bemused guests in the foyer.
“It’s about character, atmosphere and charm – and the application of common sense,” says Hughes as he explains the attraction of the hotel.
Renowned for its warm hospitality and entertainment, it’s not unusual for the likes of Irish singer Eleanor Shanley to give impromptu renditions of Hard Times or Maggie before or after dinner.
[ Family shops in Mayo on their challenges: ‘At one point council rates were almost €20,000 a year’ Opens in new window ]
“Our leisure centre is the piano in the bar, and the atmosphere in the diningroom. We create an atmosphere and product you won’t find anywhere else in Ireland or the world – it is unique,” says Hughes.
Fáilte Ireland, the national tourism agency, published a Business of Tourism Report in July, which highlighted that overseas tourists spent €5.7 billion in Ireland in 2025.
It showed that overseas tourism was seasonal, with more than two-fifths of visitors arriving between June and September. Domestic demand – worth €3.6 billion – “was more evenly spread”, with 69 per cent of short trips taking place outside the summer peak.
Those figures are broadly reflected in the bottom line of hotels such as Abbeyglen.
In peak season, “we make our living by selling beds primarily to Americans who stay one night, and one night only, and they never come back again”, says Hughes.
Off peak they focus on the home market, luring customers mostly from Galway city and Dublin with special offers, including dinner, B&B and golf at Connemara Golf Club.
They don’t make profit from off-season visitors, but it means they can remain open for most of the year and employ about 75 staff.
“A good hotel is always about a culture. To maintain that culture, you have to keep the team with you the whole year,” he says. “You can’t expect people to come in, work very hard for nine weeks in July and August, and then let them go. We keep people here all the time and we look after them.”
This theme is touched on by another Clifden businessman, Declan Mannion, who closes in January allowing international staff to return home.
Opening the doors of Mannion’s Seafood Bar and Restaurant on Market Street on rainy Monday nights in November “erodes the bottom line” but “you have to be loyal to the staff”, he says.
“Economically, it probably would make sense to close. But staff are loyal to you in the busy times, and you have to be loyal to them in the quiet times,” says Mannion.
The Abbeyglen closes for a period in January, too. When their regular staff take leave, an army of about 40 tradespeople replace them and focus on renovations.
“We plan that work and book our tradesmen in September,” says Hughes.
Americans travelled later than usual this year, he says, but they were replaced in summer by so-called “coolcation” European visitors.
“In July and August, we had a lot of very well-heeled Europeans who left France, Germany, Holland and Italy to avoid very hot weather on mainland Europe.”
Mannion’s restaurant is a family business, which opened in 1930. Like many old-school Irish retailers, it was previously a butcher’s and grocer’s that happened to have a bar.
Nowadays it makes its money from selling quality meats and fish, such as lamb cutlets, T-bone steaks and scallops, to hungry – but not necessarily thirsty – tourists.
“Turnover is 80 per cent food. Drink sales are decreasing as a percentage of overall turnover every year,” says Mannion. “Turnover is going up but the drink element of turnover is going down.”
It is popular with Irish visitors but he says they would “be goosed” without North Americans, who account for about 25 per cent of custom.
“[Americans’] pain threshold is higher,” he says. “Continental Europeans don’t think we are good value. They don’t think we are bad value, but they wouldn’t classify us as cheap. The Americans think we are still good value.”
[ ‘We can’t afford to live here’: Westport housing crisis leaves no room for locals as homeowners turn to Airbnb Opens in new window ]
Small retailers such as King’s Paper and Gift Shop rely on locals, although “tourists do help, and having a few busy months in summer helps us get through the winter”, says Lisa King, who first started working in the shop 26 years ago, aged 14.
She appreciates the locals who sustain the family business she operates with her mother, and brother Declan, during lean winter months.
To entice them into their treasure trove of toys, gifts, stationery and sweets, during off-peak days in October, they’ve already opened a “Christmas shop” to the rear of the building.
It’s subtle, for now. But once Halloween is over, “the Christmas shop explodes into the rest of the shop, and it will be everywhere”, she says.
“We’ve been so busy in there,” she adds. “We have great bargains. Some local people are very big into Christmas and the bargains in there are helping during this quiet month to get money in for new stock.
“Our suppliers tell us that our type of small family-run shop is a dying breed in towns around the country. So, our locals are the only reason we are still here.”
Clifden is not a backpack or stag-party destination, and its visitors are “more well-heeled, more discerning”, due to the presence of unique, quality hotels in Connemara such as Ashford Castle and Ballynahinch Caste, Mannion says.
As well as rising business costs, he fears succession is threatening seasonal tourist towns such as Clifden, where many businesses are family owned and independent.
“That’s coming under pressure because we are all around the same age, and there’s going to be a challenge as to whether the next generation are willing to do this,” he says. “I’m not sure they will. It’s a lot easier to make money sitting at a desk than it is in hospitality.”
After the Sun, a series about how tourist places cope when the holiday season ends, continues next week with Andrew Hamilton in Inis Mór; Sorcha Crowley in Bundoran, Co Donegal; and Noel Baker in Glengarriff, west Cork

title: New disclosure rules expose big gap between Analog Devices’ Irish tax charge and sum paid
description: Chipmaker’s Irish accounts suggested effective tax rate of 11%, but new filings show it paid 2.7% on $2.5bn Irish profits
content:
New European Union transparency rules for large companies have revealed that chipmaker Analog Devices paid an effective tax rate of less than 3 per cent on $2.5 billion (€2.23 billion) of Irish profits last year, well below a previously implied rate of 11 per cent.
The US semiconductor maker’s latest annual report published in March said most of its pretax earnings are booked in Ireland at a tax rate of 12.5 per cent.
In August, the firm’s main Irish subsidiary, Analog Devices International Unlimited Company, reported it made $1.8 billion of pretax profits in the year ended November 1st, 2025.
It recorded a total tax charge of $198 million for the year, with $105 million related to corporation tax, which meant the company’s effective tax rate for the year was 11 per cent.
A new filing by Analog Devices, published by the firm to comply with new EU financial transparency rules for large companies, has consolidated earnings at all seven of its Irish entities and indicated its Irish effective tax rate was a fraction of a previously implied rate.
The filing showed Analog Devices’ seven Irish firms made total revenues of $10.05 billion and combined pretax profits of $2.56 billion in the latest financial year. It said Irish cash-tax payments totalled $69.9 million in the financial period, which equates to an effective tax rate in Ireland of 2.7 per cent.
It showed the company made cash tax payments totalling $562.2 million globally during the year, with $34.9 million paid in Germany and $450.1 million to non-European tax jurisdictions.
Analog Devices’ latest annual report said its effective tax rate rose from 8 per cent to 16.4 per cent in the latest fiscal year.
The company said its effective tax rates for the two most recent fiscal years were lower than the US statutory rate of 21 per cent due to lower statutory tax rates applicable abroad.
[ CRH set for earnings boost from early closing of $8.5bn Arcosa deal Opens in new window ]
In addition to shedding more light on the company’s cash tax payments, the figures in Analog Devices’ EU transparency filing have shown for the first time that 94 per cent of the company’s pretax profits were booked in Ireland, where 1,765 of its 24,500 global workforce are based.
Analog Devices, valued at more than $188 billion, has offices in Limerick, Dublin and Cork. Its largest operation in Ireland is a 65,775sq m fabrication plant in Limerick.
The Irish Times asked the company if it could explain why the EU filing produces an effective tax rate of 2.7 per cent while the subsidiary’s Irish accounts and the group’s annual report suggest higher rates.
A spokesperson for the company said it “remains committed to complying with applicable tax laws and reporting requirements in the jurisdictions where we operate”.
The company is one of a number of Irish-based multinationals expected to comply with the European Union’s new country-by-country reporting directive, which has mandated firms with global revenues of more than €750 million to disclose specific financial data, including how much tax was paid in EU states and their pretax profits.
[ Pretax profits at Irish arm of Deliveroo up 37% to €2.9m Opens in new window ]
The State’s reliance on a select number of multinationals for tens of billions of euro of corporation tax receipts, which totalled €32.9 billion last year, has been exposed under these financial transparency rules.
Separate filings by tech firms Apple and Microsoft have shown they paid $17.1 billion and $5.6 billion in Irish taxes respectively last year.
Analysis by The Irish Times showed there was a significant drop-off to the next biggest contributors to Irish corporation tax, with consultancy firm Accenture paying $303.4 million , Bank of America Corporation paying $90.6 million and Analog Devices paying $69.9 million.
None of the pharma firms with large operations in the Republic, which are understood to also be significant contributors to corporation tax receipts, have filed their EU financial transparency reports yet.

title: Dear southerners, Ireland does not stop just outside Derry or Dundalk
description: Ronan McGreevy suggests nationalists ask what the South could have done differently but that would be futile
content:
Sir, – Ronan McGreevy suggests that reconciliation between northern and southern nationalists should begin by asking what the South could have done differently. I suggest that few exercises would be more futile than sterile arguments about alternative histories (“ Leo Varadkar thinks we should apologise to northern nationalists for partition. Why? ,” Opinion, October 20th).
Instead, southerners could look forward and make a decent start to reconciliation by ending the exclusionary fiction that the 26-county state is “ Ireland ”, as captured in the now ubiquitous official phrase “Ireland and Northern Ireland ”.
Semantically, that phrase includes the North twice, since my native Antrim and five other counties are manifestly both in Ireland and in Northern Ireland. Politically, it suggests that Ireland stops just after Dundalk and just before Derry.
Breaking news from Ireland (North): Ireland doesn’t stop just outside Derry or Dundalk. A State that prides itself on its efforts at equality, diversity and inclusion should know better. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Éamon de Valera gets off too easy in Ronan McGreevy’s account of partition (Opinion, Oct 20th).
Contemporaneous evidence shows that de Valera was obsessed, during the negotiation of the 1921 Treaty, with minutiae such as the form of words comprising the oath to the king.
Even in his alternative to the Treaty – the so-called Document No 2 – de Valera accepted partition as a fait accompli. While it is true that the British parliament had legislated for partition the year before, it is also true that parliaments constantly change laws to bring them into conformity with new treaty obligations.
When Churchill held out the offer, why didn’t de Valera have the gumption to demand a new treaty as the price of Ireland entering the war? Unkind critics might say he didn’t try hard enough. – Yours etc,

title: Denis Walsh: Can GAA sides buy a title, like Manchester City?
description: Dublin, Donegal and Tipperary are among six sides to spend upwards of €2m a year on the likes of mileage, meals and training camps. Does it give them an edge?
content:
A t a media event, a couple of weeks before Donegal upended Dublin in the 2014 All-Ireland semi-final, Jim McGuinness inveigled Roman Abramovich into a conversation about Dublin’s resources. The language he used was fuzzy, but the point was clear.
“Dublin have just, you know, it was like Abramovich going into the Premier League,” he said. “It’s a different ball game.”
From that jumbled sentence the only word that travelled on the information superhighway was the name of the Russian oligarch who had invested billions in Chelsea. The implication was that, in Dublin, money had made a game-changing difference. Dublin’s supporters were incensed.
Then it emerged that in the build-up to the All-Ireland semi-final the Donegal squad had been taken on a five-day training camp to Johnstown House in Meath. Maybe no expense had been spared. Whether or which, Donegal were 7/1 outsiders and won.
In the empire-building years that followed, accusations of “financial doping” against Dublin grew louder and more explicit. In 2019, when Dublin became the first team to win five All-Irelands in a row, their commercial income was €2,258,695, which was four times more than Kerry, the team they had beaten in the final. No other county had reached even €700,000 in commercial revenue.
But just because Dublin were so far in front didn’t mean that others had given up the chase. By the end of 2025, just six years later, 13 counties had generated more than €700,000 in commercial revenue according to figures excavated by journalist Colm Keys, and eight of them had broken seven figures. Dublin’s income from this source was still more than €2 million but their lead at the top of the table had been cut in half.
They had stopped winning All-Irelands, though. The group that had won seven titles in nine years had reached a staggered end and, remarkably, their replacements couldn’t be bought.
Dublin’s retreat into the pack of also-rans prompted their chief executive Finbar O’Mahony to issue a retrospective rebuke in his 2024 report to annual convention.
“It is not too long ago that the commentary in certain quarters spoke of juggernauts and 10-in-a-row,” O’Mahony wrote. “[Commentators] talked pejoratively about financial doping and other such nonsense. That talk all seems a bit silly now.”
So, which is it? Does money matter? If so, how much does it matter? And if not, why is every county desperate to have it? Is it possible to buy titles in the GAA, as Manchester City have done in the Premier League?
When the Limerick hurlers started bingeing on All-Irelands, as the Dublin footballers had done, the same accusations of “financial doping” materialised. But the billionaire JP McManus had been their main sponsor since 2004, and yet, in the first 14 years of his patronage, all the Limerick seniors won was a single Munster title. If money was so important, why did it not make a difference in those years?
“Once we got successful, it just felt like you weren’t fighting for things any more,” says Barry Hennessy, the former Limerick player. “I was the GPA rep with Seamus Hickey for a while and it just felt like you were fighting for things towards the end of TJ [Ryan’s] time as manager and the start of John [Kiely’s] time.
“Then, all of a sudden, after 2018 [when Limerick won the All-Ireland for the first time in 35 years] it was just a case that that we were very well looked after. Now, don’t get me wrong, we were always very well looked after, but there might be a delay. You would eventually get it, but it was a case that you were constantly looking for it. When we started to win, a lot more people came out of the woodwork and wanted to support us.”
The costs associated with training intercounty teams have been characterised as a “runaway train” for many years. Every year brings a new peak. The figures for 2026 are not available yet, but last year the total cost was in excess of €45 million, an exponential jump of nearly €13 million in just three years. Six counties spent more than €2 million each.
In an attempt to impose some order on the chaos, a licensing system was passed at GAA Congress in February. Among other provisions under this system, management teams will be restricted to four people, paid service providers will be capped at 10, and intercounty panels will be no bigger than 36 players. There will also be an overall spending cap.
It was expected that the system would be in place for 2027, but according to Croke Park, it has been delayed for a year and will be rolled out on a phased basis.
How the money is spent, though, is interesting. For obvious reasons, payments to managers are made off the books and never declared in the end of season accounts. But there is a money trail for the day-to-day outlay. In that context, the two biggest items are mileage payments and food.
[ Denis Walsh: GAA must take a leap on paying managers and deal with the consequences Opens in new window ]
“What I would say about food is that match days are crazy,” says one former manager of a tier-one county. “You’re going to a hotel for a prematch meal, three hours beforehand, and then you have a meal afterwards. Some hotels will even charge you separately for the rent of the room.
“The catering in hotels is off the f**king wall. For the pre-match meal you could be charged 25 quid a head because you’re giving the players choices and you could be charged 30 quid a head for the meal after the match. You have no idea the amount of food the players will consume – it’s off the charts – but they have to have it. Our biggest problem was keeping weight on fellahs – getting them to eat enough calories.”
This experience is not peculiar to elite teams. According to the manager of a third-tier hurling county food on their road trips routinely cost in excess of €3,000. The players are given a hot meal after training, in accordance with the GPA player’s charter, and they are also given a meal to take away for the following day.
Between mileage, food and payments to professional service providers such as physios, masseurs, medics and strength and conditioning coaches, the average cost of a training session for that third-tier hurling county is about €3,500. In that case, the supports provided are nothing out of the ordinary: it is what the players expect.
[ Former GAA president Nickey Brennan fears bloated payroll could damage volunteerism Opens in new window ]
Last year, Andy Moran made a concerted effort to encourage Mayo players to find a job closer to home, not to save on mileage expenses but to aid their performance. Historically, though, Mayo’s mileage bill has been huge. In 2019, for example, it ran to €927,444, which accounted to more than half of their total spend on the team.
The only county who spent more than Mayo on their intercounty teams in 2019 were Tipperary, who won the senior All-Ireland and the under-20 title. Their spending increased by €623,693 to more than €1.77 million, a figure that didn’t include whatever funds had been raised by the Commercial Board – a new entity at the time populated by Declan Kelly, the former head of Teneo, Niall Quinn, Alan Quinlan and others.
The money underwrote a clinic in best practice. Cairbre Ó Cairealláin was headhunted to lead their strength and conditioning programme; he committed solely to Tipp for the season and was housed in the Ragg, near Thurles, so that he would be available to the players at all times. To complement his work they hired Gary Sweeney, a nutritionist with Leinster Rugby at the time.
Supervised gym sessions were held at four different centres around the county; on the day after games, collective recovery sessions were held in the pool at the Horse and Jockey Hotel and other venues convenient to the players.
Wives, girlfriends and parents were encouraged to join the team for post-match meals. When Tipperary had a free weekend in their Munster championship campaign the players were invited to take their wives or partners for dinner and Tipp would pick up the tab. The value of those interventions is abstract but, instinctively, nobody says they were worthless.
They had a training camp in Portugal and training weekends in Carton House; they made a trip to Cork where they stayed in the Castlemartyr Resort and trained at Fota Island. Everything was five-star. And they looked a million dollars: on the weekend of the All-Ireland final all the Tipperary players and support staff were provided with formal wear for the banquet and casual wear for the homecoming. A party of 105 went on the team holiday and everybody was kitted out for that trip too.
They retained 40 players on their panel for the entire season and Liam Sheedy’s back room stretched to 25 people. No corner was cut.
The biggest spike in Tipp’s spending, though, was in food and supplements. A year earlier, when Limerick had won the All-Ireland, the biggest area of increased spending between John Kiely’s first year and his second was in food and supplements too. It was no coincidence that Tipp followed suit.
How much of all that stuff made the difference between winning and losing? It is impossible to say. For the players, though, that management set-up had painted a picture of winning that took their eyes out. In the years that followed, none of them would have wanted to settle for less.
Six years later, when Tipperary won the senior and under-20 All-Irelands again, Tipp’s spending on their intercounty teams had climbed to €2,483,600 – a jump of three quarters of a million euro since 2019. Staggering.
In the coming weeks this year’s spending figures will emerge at county conventions all over the country. When the numbers are collated, Galway will expect to be close to the top of the national list.
“I am sick to the back teeth of the lazy articles that will come out again at the end of the year,” says Paul Bellew, the Galway chair. “Galway will be top [of the spending list] again because we’re the only county that’s been in Division One in both codes for the last five years, and we’ve also contested three [senior] finals in the last five years.
“We spend about 70 per cent of our budget on requirements mandated by the GPA player’s charter – food, gear, mileage, medical support. I’m fully in support of those rights for the players. I just think it needs to be understood that that’s where the vast, vast, vast majority of the money goes.”
Word circulates too about the latest edge and who has it. Nobody wants to be left behind. All of that fuels escalation. Keeping up is expensive. “You can call it peer pressure,” says Bellew, “or you can call it people learning from each other. There’s no doubt there’s a copycat element on some things.
[ Not even Jim McGuinness could persuade Finnbarr Roarty to stay – that’s a bad omen Opens in new window ]
“I do think there is a cult of manager’s back-room teams. From interactions with other chairpersons, I know there’s a competition for talent around the professional services and the cost of that. I’ve been very lucky to work with very practical managers.”
So, the wheel keeps turning. In 2025 Donegal spent €2,094,330 on preparing their intercounty teams, €126,000 more than Dublin. And not a Russian oligarch in sight.

title: David McWilliams: France is likely heading towards ECB support and a Marine Le Pen presidency
description: The country is being pushed closer to the once-unthinkable possibility of bankruptcy
content:
F rance is in flames. Is this a precursor of things to come all over Europe or a display of French exceptionalism? France is facing a polycrisis, a once-in-a-generation moment where various separate crises - political, demographic, economic and cultural - converge at the same time. Any one of these would be difficult to solve on their own, coming together they threaten to overwhelm the Macron government. Looking on, Marine Le Pen eyes up the Élysée.
France is a peculiar case. For many, it is a paradise: Europe’s earliest retirement age, generous pensions, reasonably cheap housing for the majority, brilliant transport infrastructure and a health service that works for the most part. It also has beautiful landscapes and historical towns, evidenced by the fact that France is the world’s most visited country. Despite this, enough French people have convinced themselvesthey live in a hellhole and the only solution is to tear it down.
Protesting is in the French DNA. These people gave the world the French Revolution- not the French Negotiation or the French Re-evaluation – which was the most consequential political upheaval of the past 300 years and it started in Paris. France is also a country on its fifth republic, the previous four having been swept away by events. What price a sixth republic under a President Le Pen?
For the past two decades, French economic growth has been stagnant, yet persistent inflation has driven up the cost of living , leaving many citizens just getting by and highly sensitive to price changes. A few years back, the widespread “Gilets Jaunes” (Yellow Vests) national protest movement was triggered by the threat of a small carbon tax on motor fuel. Such is the economic precariousness of the people, particularly outside Paris, which is a city blessed with an impressive public transport system, that the prospects of a small increase in petrol prices prompted revolt. These protesters occupied roundabouts, signalling that these country people drive everywhere and are not protected by the urban Metro. The Gilets Jaunes look tame, almost quaint, when contrasted with this week’s urban rioters.
On top of rising inflation in recent weeks, the financial markets have begun to question whether France can pay back its national debt, which stands at 120 per cent of GDP. Interest rates of French debt have recently risen from 3.1 to 4.8 per cent. This might not seem like much but it is about a 50 per cent increase in the cost of paying back debt. As the interest on French government debt rises, this drags up the interest rates that French borrowers must pay on their car loans, mortgages and overdrafts. Youth unemployment is above 20 per cent, which is twice the overall rate.
Since the second World War, France has been governed either by the centre left in the guise of the French Socialist party or the right, normally the Gaullist party – the Republicans. Over time, both interventionist left and expansionist right came to a truce in the centre, so much so that E mmanuel Macron , a minister in an ostensibly left-leaning cabinet, saw his chance and set up his own centrist party called En Marche! (Forward!). He has dominated French politics for the past decade. Without a local political power base, Macron has governed from on high, leading to criticism that he is removed from the masses, and is seen as the creation of big business rather than the people. Some even refer to his style as Jupiterian, sitting on top of his Olympus, directing the lesser mortals below.
Now the people are revolting, but against what is hard to pin down. Behind all the sloganeering is the essential fact that France is experiencing a generational conflict pitting the late middle-aged and the retirees against the young.
France’s last major street rebellion took place in 1968, when radical students took against Charles de Gaulle. These idealistic kids, born in the boom years after the end of the war, promised to change France, making it more dynamic, democratic and modern. In truth, this one-time revolutionary generation, the soixante-huitards or the 68ers, would end up pilfering the place, lining their pockets with well-endowed pensions, higher property prices and a bourgeois lifestyle, unmatched elsewhere in western Europe.
In the process, they gave the bill to the generations coming behind them and, as France’s fertility rates plummeted in the 1980s and 1990s, the country finds itself in the position that there are not enough young people to pay for all these well-heeled retirees. The centre’s solution to too few French young people is not to reduce their own expectations of their retirement entitlement, but to call for more immigrants to pay the bill. Thus, an economic or commercial problem has morphed into a cultural and racial one, playing directly into Le Pen’s hands.
[ ‘A bombshell’: French teachers spot something on payslips that reveals scale of funding crisis Opens in new window ]
The promise of the centre has been betrayed and this feeling of abandonment is exacerbated by the sight of rich French people getting richer over the past two decades while the average worker treads water. Since the advent of the euro, French interest rates have dropped below where they had been for many years, driving up asset prices. But the wages of workers were anchored to the floor by competition from China. Workers’ incomes barely budged, while the wealth of asset owners – property, companies, shareholders – rose, leaving millions feeling on the outside, without a stake. But they have a vote and they are seeking revenge in the presidential election of 2027.
[ ‘I have never felt anything so painful in my life’: Irish caught in French riots Opens in new window ]
Supposed to bring prosperity and security, the Macron centre has failed. The electorate is ready for a real alternative. This internal pressure is being made more acute by capital flight as investors who have lent money to the French government are selling French bonds, implying that the political/demographic crisis is driving the financial crisis, pushing France closer towards the once-unthinkable possibility of bankruptcy.
The most likely way this pans out is that over the next few months the European Central Bank steps in and buys French bonds on the basis that France is too big to fail, Le Pen wins in April and, within her first term, a new, sixth French republic is declared. And they’ll still win the Six Nations.

title: Tighter oversight of health service spending likely to stoke simmering tensions
description: Nine months into a new funding system, most health regions have autonomy on day-to-day spending revoked
content:
Just over two weeks ago, Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill was firm in her assertion that she did not accept estimates of a €1 billion deficit in the health service by the end of this year.
Steps were being taken to reduce the overruns, she said, but now it appears that optimism has all but disappeared.
A recent expenditure forecast shows the Health Service Executive predicts a deficit of €1 billion for 2026, including a pay deficit of €142 million.
The Department of Health “based on present trends and the lack of operational control broadly concur with the HSE assessment for the likely out-turn for 2026”, the memo said.
It added that any pay deficit this year would “need to be addressed by the HSE in 2027 and will be applied to the regions where the overrun occurred”.
Tensions between regional management, central HSE management and the department have ratcheted up in recent months.
[ No link between healthcare staff recruitment and hospital performance, says Minister Opens in new window ]
But as the Minister tightens her control on the health service’s purse strings, and introduces further rules on recruitment and promotions, the prospect of souring relations has become a real possibility.
This year marked the first time funding was devolved to the six regions. Nine months into the new system and two-thirds of those areas had their autonomy over day-to-day spending revoked.
Carroll MacNeill has been clear about who is to blame for this situation, describing it as a “test for management of the different regions”.
A directive to top-level HSE management, which came into effect in recent days, states that for those regions that have exceeded their budgets by more than 2 per cent, “there is no approval for the addition of any employees to payroll without prior formal Department of Health Sanction”.
The new recruitment and promotion rules set out a 20-day time frame for applications to be processed by the HSE and the department. However, there is provision for a “fast track pathway” in exceptional cases, and the memo says patient safety is “paramount”.
But unions have argued the restrictions were being imposed at a time when the State was already short of medical and nursing staff.
Irish Medical Organisation (IMO) president Matthew Sadlier said doctors who had applied, interviewed for, then accepted a role, “would now have no guarantee it would be funded”, adding that the union was “representing members who have been impacted in this way”.
[ Senior hospital doctors criticise Minister for Health’s ‘closed-door’ approach to engagement Opens in new window ]
The Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation said an estimated 2,228 nursing and midwifery posts were vacant.
The IMO said the State needed 6,050 consultants to meet population needs. “We currently have 4,945 whole-time equivalents and, of those, 20 per cent are not filled on a permanent basis, with over 325 posts unfilled.”
It is not only unions who have taken issue with recruitment rules. Cork University Hospital chief executive Jennifer Kearney has also repeatedly raised patient safety concerns due to staff shortages.
As the annual rise in winter illnesses begins to surface in the weeks ahead, and demand on the health system inevitably increases, it will not be long before the impact of the new measures is seen.

title: Ruth Kelly Walsh obituary: Fashion writer who lived life to the full
description: She was famously gregarious, hosting lunches and dinners in her various homes and in hotels around Dublin
content:
Ruth Kelly Walsh was the sort of woman who, if a character in fiction, would have hurtled through her life, social and professional, like a seasonal firework display, startling but simultaneously entertaining all around her.
Sometime after the death of her husband, she was asked if she fancied another relationship.
“Not really,” she told the writer Emily Hourican. “I couldn’t be bothered, and the really nice ones, the ones that you could really share a life with, are gay. But I’ve loads of friends. Life is full of things to do, people to see.”
And though well into her 80s at the time of that interview, she adapted Yeats to pronounce: “Old and grey and not full of sleep!”
Ferociously intelligent and at times acerbic, while she was known mainly as a fashion writer, she was also hugely interested in politics and current events. She had a knowledge of and love for plants and animals, was quietly kind and a lot of fun to be with.
She died in her 98th year and, while missed by those who loved her, “you couldn’t mourn her because of the person she was”, according to her friend and fellow journalist, Micheline McCormack.
Francesca Ruth Kelly was born in Dublin in September 1927. She was the daughter of Frank Kelly and his wife Anna (née Fitzsimons). A second, adopted daughter, Nancy, was seven years younger than Kelly Walsh.
[ Niamh Flatley: Riverdance star who played leading role in troupe’s global success Opens in new window ]
Kelly Walsh’s lineage was somewhat exotic and filled with seeming contradictions, a heady mix that translated into her own life.
Her early years were spent in Oldcourt House in Bray, Co Wicklow , where her father was something of a dilettante chicken farmer as well as an accomplished amateur painter. Born in England but of Irish extraction, Frank Kelly met Michael Collins while both were working in the post office in London.
Recruited into the Gaelic League and possibly also the Irish Republican Brotherhood, the main organisation behind the Easter Rising , Frank Kelly moved to Dublin in 1916. As a member of the Kimmage garrison, he took part in the Rising, was in the GPO and was later interned.
Afterwards, and as a confidant to Collins, he worked in the Sinn Féin headquarters at No 6 Harcourt Street. He helped Collins effect the escape of Éamon de Valera from Lincoln Gaol in February 1919, as well as his onward flight to the United States , where he drummed up support for Irish independence.
Meanwhile, Anna Fitzsimons came from a well-to-do rural background but was tired of the social swirl associated with countryside living. As her daughter Ruth Kelly Walsh later put it, she could not “take another hunt ball”, and ran off to Dublin where she too met Collins.
From 1917 on, she was secretary to Sinn Féin general secretary Patrick O’Keeffe, as well as to Collins. Known to all as Fitzie or Miss Fitz, her role thrust her into contact with Frank Kelly and, in July 1921, they married.
Frank Kelly’s chicken farming days were shortened by a fire at Oldcourt House, and the family moved, variously, to Blackrock and Rathgar, settling on Rathgar Avenue in the former home of George Russell, the writer and artist who used the pseudonym AE.
[ Eva Marie Saint, Oscar-winning actor who lived to 102 Opens in new window ]
Ruth Kelly Walsh’s secondary education was at Alexandra College, then in Earlsfort Terrace in central Dublin, from where she went to Trinity College. There, however, she failed to pass what was known colloquially as the “Little Go” exam, a test at the end of second year to determine whether a student had learned enough to progress.
Kelly Walsh’s mother, Fitzie, was by now a senior figure in the Irish Press, the newspaper founded by de Valera in 1931 to reflect the Fianna Fáil worldview. Although women’s editor, Fitzie also reported from de Valera’s speeches to the League of Nations in New York and once interviewed Adolf Hitler.
Initially, Kelly Walsh had little love of journalism. She said later that she was thrown into it “because my fed up mother didn’t know what to do with me”. She added, however: “I had great fun.”
In those early days, Kelly Walsh reported on everything from the Children’s Court to agriculture shows. Like her mother before her, she too wrote for the women’s page, the contents of which were of their time – advice for homemaker matters, such as knitting and cooking.
It was while at the Irish Press that she met her husband, Dick Walsh, later political editor of this newspaper, who was 10 years her junior. After their marriage, she became known as Ruth Kelly Walsh, and the couple initially lived in the Kelly house in Rathgar, Kelly Walsh’s mother by now being deceased and her father living alone.
Soon, however, they moved to London where their twin daughters, Francesca and Suzie, were born. There, Kelly Walsh worked for the Farmers’ Union and the Manchester Evening News while Dick Walsh worked variously for London local newspapers, including the Kilburn Times and the Wimbledon Borough News.
They returned to Ireland when the girls were two. Dick Walsh initially worked for Arrow Advertising, the Connacht Tribune and eventually, The Irish Times. At the same time, Kelly Walsh cut a swathe through the Dublin media world: she helped found, and was the first editor of, Women’s Way; she hosted RTÉ Radio sponsored programmes, That’s Life and Help Yourself; she succeeded her mother as women’s editor at the Irish Press and, for 27 years, was fashion editor at the RTÉ Guide.
She was famously gregarious, hosting lunches and dinners in her various homes and in hotels around Dublin. One such was a regular Friday gathering in the art deco Camden Delux Hotel of what she called her “press gang”. Regular attendees included, but were not confined to, McCormack, fashion photographer Eve Holmes and Mairead Dunne, public relations officer for the Goods Council.
Others in her circle included Charles Haughey’s mistress, the socialite and journalist Terry Keane.
“She was fashion mad,” McCormack said of Kelly Walsh.
A regular feature of the lunches involved Kelly disappearing to trawl the swop shops of the Camden Street area, returning with castoffs from others that looked a million dollars on her. She always wore a hat.
[ Carmel Heaney obituary: Diplomat who took on dissident Irish republicans and sympathisers in US Opens in new window ]
There was more than a touch of Absolutely Fabulous about her life and personality, according to Francesca – Keane notionally being Joanna Lumley’s hilariously over-the-top Patsy while Kelly Walsh was cast notionally as Edina.
“She was difficult,” recalled another friend. “No. She wasn’t difficult. She was impossible! Nothing was ever enough, nothing was ever good enough.”
Behind the AbFab persona, however, there was a sharp intelligence.
When Soviet president Mikhail Gorbachev visited Ireland, the press corps greeted him and concentrated on him alone. Kelly Walsh, on the other hand, also welcomed his wife, Raisa Gorbacheva, shaking her hand and asking her questions as well.
In the mid-1970s, her marriage to Walsh broke down. “She rose,” said Francesca, “and kept the show on the road. She really was a woman out of her time.”
After 10 years, Walsh returned – “he just gradually moved back”, said Francesca. By now, Walsh’s condition (he suffered from ankylosing spondylitis) was gradually buckling his back and crushing his chest organs.
They lived initially in Shankill and then in Bellevue, a 19th century home on Bray’s Killarney Road with a rambling garden. There, the couple indulged their love of plants and animals.
Their seven cats and four dogs included Hoover, a pointer Kelly Walsh acquired at a car boot sale and who had a penchant for bringing sticks into Dick Walsh’s bed, where they both – man and dog – slept. There was a lone chicken named Hen, who had the run of the house and liked to sit on Dick Walsh’s lap, eyeballing anyone who came near.
[ Corinna Hardgrave obituary: A widely respected food writer and restaurant critic Opens in new window ]
Shortly after moving again (this time to a grand house: Kilmurray in Thomastown, Kilkenny), Dick Walsh died in 2003, and Kelly Walsh eventually returned to Bray. She spent her latter years enjoying the company of friends, reading, watching documentaries and travelling (Egypt was a favourite).
“She was stylish, loving and kind,” said Francesca. “She had a wonderful life. She had guts – no one ever told her ‘no’.”
Ruth Kelly Walsh is survived by her twin daughters, Francesca and Suzie; her son-in-law, Jonathan; and grandchildren, Millie and Sara.

title: Lara Marlowe: France may calm violence in the short term but it is infused with dread
description: The scale of the violence, high stakes of the upcoming presidential election and international reach of the protests distinguish them past riots
content:
T he police and rioters who fought running street battles in France last weekend were de facto proxies for populist leaders Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Le Pen’s National Rally (RN) and Mélenchon’s France Unbowed (LFI) are the public faces of more radical groups – referred to as ultra-right and ultra-left – on the fringes of their parties.
A majority of French security forces support Le Pen. Mélenchon participated in a peaceful protest march in Paris on October 17th but stands accused by the centrist government and the French right of having instigated the violence. The investigative website Médiapart reported that interior minister Laurent Nuñez asked the domestic intelligence service to falsely accuse LFI of responsibility.
Mélenchon’s supporters claim that French president Emmanuel Macron ’s contempt for the underprivileged and police brutality provoked the unrest.
Six protesters have been maimed in recent weeks, including two last Saturday. A 17-year-old girl lost an eye in Mulhouse and a maths student, also aged 17, lost his right hand in Saint-Étienne. Tear gas, anti-encirclement and stun grenades used by the CRS riot police destroyed dozens of eyes and hands during the 2018/9 yellow vests revolt.
Prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said it was “a miracle” that no one was killed, but two corpses found on the margins of the riots remain unexplained. Videos showing riot police beating unconscious a 26-year-old volunteer street medic called Antoine circulated widely online.
The latest violence gave rise to comparisons with the storming of the Bastille, the Paris Commune and the May 1968 revolution. Before October 17th, polls showed that a majority of French people supported the student demonstrations which began on September 21st in protest at poor conditions in French secondary schools.
Foreign media focused on violence, including students whose hands were blown off, and arson attacks. French radio and television tended to portray initial protests as a rite of passage, until the extreme violence of last weekend quelled romanticism about the beauty of revolt.
More than half a million protesters marched peacefully last Saturday, but their exercise in democracy was stained by the vandals and looters who laid waste to large parts of French cities. Security forces were concentrated along the main route for the Paris march, but were thinly spread across the rest of the city. Using social media to organise, small groups of hooded and masked youths appeared suddenly to attack shops and hurl metal barriers at police.
Nuñez made the alarming admission that the government “lost control in certain big cities.” Justice minister Gérald Darmanin said French domestic intelligence had been so focused on Islamists, organised crime and foreign interference that it failed to conjure with the ultra-left.
Le Pen told France Info radio: “The state is collapsing. The government has lost control of everything.” She promises to restore law and order.
[ ‘I have never felt anything so painful in my life’: Irish caught in French riots Opens in new window ]
In the aftermath of the riots, tourists wandered through streets littered with broken glass and spent spray paint cans. Nearly a third of the more than 2,500 people detained were minors. Anti-capitalist demonstrators who looted some 3,000 shops sold plunder on the internet. The government vowed to punish looters by withholding social welfare payments. Le Pen warned darkly that “next time they’ll break into apartments”.
Video footage led to the arrest of a 34-year-old left-wing extremist charged with burning down Limoges’ graceful, 1883 town hall. The owner of a ransacked optician’s shop said looters returned the following evening to take security cameras. Police used suspects’ mobile phones to track their whereabouts at the time of attacks.
The sheer scale of the violence, the high stakes of next year’s presidential election and the international reach of the protests distinguished them from dozens of riots in recent decades. Absurdly, friends in Kyiv, who endure near-constant Russian drone and missile attacks, sent messages asking if I was okay.
The root causes of the riots are global: high cost of living, particularly fuel, housing shortages, disillusionment with politics. Similar protests occurred in Albania, Belgium, Greece, Italy, Portugal and Spain. The latter three will, like France, hold general strikes next month. Corriere della Sera reported that many of the rioters arrested in Italy were aged 11-14. Le Monde found a looter under age 10 in Paris.
Financial markets “are treating France as the economic sick man of the western world”, Nobel laureate Paul Krugman warned. The government can no longer buy social peace. France’s debt of nearly €3.6 trillion is a colossal 119 per cent of GDP.
French youth feel they have no future in a world plagued by war and climate change, where AI threatens employment opportunities. They have flocked to LFI in part because it is the only party that supports Gaza. Palestinian flags are a feature of the protests, as emphasised by Israeli media.
Macron’s detractors from what he calls the “reactionary international”, including Donald Trump, JD Vance, Putin’s confidant Kirill Dmitriev, Nigel Farage and Alice Weidel, portrayed the French riots as being the result of Muslim immigration. Fake AI-generated images and videos originating in Iran, Israel, Russia and the US spread lies about the riots, as reported by journalist Barry Lando on Substack.
Macron’s televised address sounded like an abdication speech. With only six months left in office, he is inaudible and ineffectual.
The resuscitated yellow vests have called for Act II of the protests today and Act III on October 31st. The Paris prefect advised businesses to “strengthen security”. Some shopkeepers are buying weapons. Patchy curfews are imposed in many towns and cities. France Inter radio hosted a debate between philosophers asking if France is heading towards civil war.
[ France is falling to the extremes of left and right. Ireland cannot be complacent Opens in new window ]
Lecornu promises a “massive” security presence for demonstrations while conservative politicians call for a state of emergency. France may calm the violence in the short term, but the country is infused with long term dread. If the presidential election were held now, polls indicate Le Pen would defeat all rivals. If she is elected next May 2nd, ultra-right and ultra-left are likely to fight in the streets. Last week’s riots could be the harbinger of worse to come.

title: Defence Forces to seek more than 550 armoured vehicles from France
description: Vehicles will transform Army from mostly peacekeeping force to military capable of limited conventional war fighting
content:
Irish military planners are to recommend the purchase of more than 550 armoured vehicles for the Defence Forces , enough to transform the Army from a primarily peacekeeping force into one capable of limited conventional war fighting.
Experts have warned, however, that the Defence Forces is ill equipped to undertake such a transformation and that the cost of such an acquisition could easily exceed €14 billion.
The measure is part of a move to transform the Irish military into a force capable of the home defence of the country along with taking part in EU expeditionary operations such as the EU Rapid Deployment Capability, also known as the EU Battlegroup.
It is also designed to provide soldiers with the protection needed to embark on peacekeeping missions in highly unstable areas, such as the Sahel region in Africa.
As previously announced , the armoured vehicles will be purchased from France under a government-to-government scheme as part of the “Scorpion Programme”
Vehicles to be acquired under the proposed deal will include the Griffon, a six-wheel APC; the Serval, which is a smaller four-wheeled armoured car; and the Jaguar, a tank-like “armoured fighting vehicle” equipped with a large turreted gun.
These will complement the Defence Forces’ existing fleet of Mowag APCs, which recently completed a midlife refit at a cost of €95 million.
The new armour programme will transform the Irish Army from a light infantry force, with limited armoured elements, to one with enough armoured vehicles to equip an entire brigade of 4,000 troops.
The recommendation for more than 550 vehicles is significantly higher than previous estimates of 300 to 400 vehicles.
[ Minister wants role for Irish Navy in EU mission targeting Russia shadow fleet Opens in new window ]
The programme will require significant assistance from France in maintenance of the vehicles. According to military sources, it is likely some of the initial training on the vehicles will take place in France.
The Government has yet to detail the cost of the programme, much of which will depend on how much funding the Department of Public Expenditure is willing to grant.
Alan Kearney, a retired Defence Forces weapons specialist, said the procurement cost would be “a drop in the ocean” compared with the total lifetime cost.
In 2018, Belgium signed a deal to purchase 442 Scorpion vehicles from France with an announced cost of €1.6 billion.
Last year Belgium’s spending watchdog, the Court of Auditors, stated that the total lifetime cost of the purchased vehicles would be more than €14 billion. This includes €60 million a year on maintenance.
Kearney, who has prepared a report on the planned armoured vehicle purchases for the Oireachtas Public Accounts and Defence and National Security Committees, also questioned the ability of the Defence Forces to take on such a large project, given previous procurement failures.
[ Most Defence Forces personnel fear mental health disclosure could harm careers, study finds Opens in new window ]
“Where are they going to go? Who is going to maintain them? Who is going to fix the guns?” said Kearney, pointing to the fact that the Army is short of enlisted personnel specialising in vehicle maintenance.
Numbers are slowly growing but it takes years to build up the experience necessary for the upkeep of a large, armoured fleet. “It’s a recipe for disaster,” Kearney said.
Previous procurement issues include problems with maintenance and spare parts for the Mowag fleet, including an incident which led to two machine guns breaking during a firefight with Islamic forces in Syria in 2013.
Earlier this month, the State’s spending watchdog, the Comptroller and Auditor General, found the purchase of 27 light armoured vehicles in 2008 wasted millions in taxpayer funds. The Department of Defence said it had “learned lessons from this procurement”.
In the Air Corps , all four of the PC-12 aircraft in 2020 for close to €50 million are out of service due to maintenance issues.
Asked about the programme to upgrade the armoured fleet, the Department of Defence said: “A whole-of-capability approach is being adopted, integrating vehicle procurement with doctrine, training, infrastructure, personnel and interoperability requirements.
“As the programme remains in the assessment phase, specifications, role, fleet size, timelines, costs, training arrangements and support requirements remain subject to ongoing negotiations and the necessary approval processes.”

title: Yoto Mini 4th Gen review: Screen-free entertainment device for kids gets an upgrade
description: Audio player adds extras to justify raising price to almost €100
content:
In a world where screens constantly clamour for our children’s attention, the Yoto is a breath of fresh air. Aimed at kids aged three and over, the audio players offer a mix of stories, podcasts, and music. And most importantly, aside from the initial set-up of the system, they aren’t dependent on a smartphone.
If you aren’t familiar with the Yoto system, it has two options: the full-sized player and the portable Yoto Mini. Both work with physical cards – NFC (near field communication) enabled – that you insert into the player, or with digital ones through the Yoto app.
Kids have access to more than 1,000 titles, from well-known audiobooks such as Matilda and Diary of a Wimpy Kid to cards with information and quizzes on the flags of the world and ancient Rome. You can even record your own stories to play back. Any cards you insert into the player are downloaded to the device over wifi, where they are stored safely for easy playback.
The Yoto Mini is now in its fourth generation. It keeps all the best things about the previous versions of the Yoto Mini, and adds a few new extras to justify raising the price to almost €100.
[ ‘We banned television and screens after a sad epiphany during an episode of Bluey’ Opens in new window ]
The design is still very child-friendly. It has all rounded edges and easy-to-use controls, with two dials on the front for controlling volume and changing tracks. It has a power button and a small screen that displays the time, helps you select content, and shows you the battery level. If you want your children to keep the audio to themselves, there is a headphone jack; you can also use Bluetooth headphones with the player.
So what is new about the Yoto Mini? It comes with a new processor and downloads content faster than its predecessor. Another new addition is the green side button, which takes over playing and pausing tracks, and also gives quick access to a playlist of up to 20 of your child’s favourite cards.
You create these playlists through the Yoto app, which is installed on a parent’s phone, mixing cards with podcasts or your own recordings.
That’s not all the app does. Aside from the initial set-up of the player – connecting it to wifi – and managing the library of stories, the app also gives you control over settings on the player. You can set limitations on how loud the player will go, with different settings for daytime listening and night, along with battery management options and alarms.
[ Brick review: This simple device helped me halve my screen time Opens in new window ]
The player will store cards too, but when the memory is finally full it will make room for new content by getting rid of the oldest, least played options so you never lose a favourite story.
You might baulk at the idea of paying close to €100 for an audio player when you could get the same functionality from your phone or a smart speaker. Yet, from personal experience, even in a house of children who have been reading independently for a few years, the Yoto Mini is fought over. At night it is used for sleep stories or sounds; during the day, the choices range from Harry Potter to the Unicorn Academy and Roald Dahl. Ladybird’s Everything Under the Sun taught them – and me – a few things, with a question for every day of the year.
And the whole point of the Yoto is to keep children away from screens and intrusive technology, while still giving them independent access to entertainment.
The only downside is remembering to charge it, although you can check on the battery level through the app too. Plus, the battery life runs to about 16 hours of use, which is a lot of entertainment, even for the most demanding of audiences.
Small and light enough to carry around, the Yoto Mini is also durable. And it needs to be . Given the target market, it is bound to take some bumps, drops and knocks. It is water and dust-resistant too, which means if it accidentally winds up in the sink, it isn’t the end of the world.
All the buttons are appropriately sized for smaller hands, and if you are new to Yoto, the controls are intuitive.
The ability to store around 1,000 hours of content on the device means you don’t need an internet connection all the time, just the first time you load the new card into the player.
For those familiar with the Yoto Mini player, the addition of the green button might introduce a bit of confusion. It takes over some of the functions of the orange dials, so it takes a bit of getting used to.
The player needs wifi and access to a smartphone for the initial set-up; after that, you can use the wifi connection to download the card content so it can be played when you are on the move.
The cards you scan into the app’s library will also be available to play directly in the app, without having the physical card every time
If you want extra protection for the player, you can buy a silicone jacket. They come in an assortment of colours and give you an extra layer of protection against scratches.
The Yoto Mini Gen 4 is a handy device that could help you keep control of your child’s screen time for a little longer.

title: ‘Nail in the coffin of Irish neutrality’ or global reality check? The triple lock war rages on
description: War of words breaks out over legal measure that requires Government, Dáil and UN approval to deploy troops abroad
content:
The Opposition was similarly agitated but not entirely aligned during a fractious debate on legislation to abolish the triple lock in the Dáil on Wednesday.
The triple lock is a legal provision that effectively requires three hurdles to be cleared before Irish troops can be deployed abroad: a decision of the Government, a majority in the Dáil and the authorisation of the United Nations .
Social Democrats TD Sinéad Gibney spoke for many on the left when she declared: “This is an absolute nail in the coffin of Irish neutrality.”
Labour ’s Duncan Smith took a more nuanced view: “I do not believe the triple lock is the full manifestation or expression of Irish neutrality. I believe it is part of it and an important part of it at that,” he said.
Other contributions to the debate were less reserved than both.
For People Before Profit TD Richard Boyd Barrett , the Bill is “a historic betrayal of this country’s tradition of neutrality, instigated by people like Wolfe Tone and later by James Connolly, Patrick Pearse and Constance Markievicz”.
These are familiar refrains. Defenders of neutrality have been warning that neutrality was being destroyed by each EU treaty (including the original accession treaty in 1972, which both Sinn Féin and Michael D Higgins warned would be the end of Irish neutrality) through to the Nice and Lisbon treaties, by successive EU defence co-operation projects such as Pesco , by membership of Nato’s partnership for peace alliance and by the use of Shannon Airport by the US military.
If they were right, then how could there be anything left of Irish neutrality at this stage?
But at least the defenders of neutrality are consistent.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin – as he was reminded many times by speakers – previously said the triple lock was “central to our neutrality”. Now he says getting rid of the triple lock will leave Irish neutrality unaffected.
His explanation – that the world has changed since then – might be true but it sounds glib. There is unease on the Fianna Fáil benches, with John McGuinness and Willie O’Dea absent from Wednesday’s first Dáil vote on the issue – with permission, the chief whip’s office confirmed – but not enough for a full-scale rebellion – not at this stage anyway.
This week’s vote on legislation that would end the need for UN approval before Irish troops can be sent abroad was won by the Government by 79 votes to 71 following the fractious debate.
The Government argues that because the UN Security Council – the body that has previously authorised missions – is mired in a stalemate and has not given the go-ahead for any new missions since 2014, it should remove the effective veto the permanent members of the council have on Irish deployments.
Opponents say there are other possible avenues of UN approval, such as through the General Assembly, though diplomats say this is far-fetched.
But opponents also say the Government is getting rid of the requirement for UN approval because it wants to join western “imperialist wars” – effectively, that it wants to abandon neutrality and join the side of the West, led by the US.
“It is a clear Government declaration of a rejection of Ireland’s positive active neutrality that has supported Ireland’s long-serving United Nations peacekeeping contributions and a sign of the Government’s determination to foment a military industrial complex at the EU level and to send the Irish Defence Forces abroad – without UN authorisation – to takes sides in conflicts and war,” says Dublin City University academic Karen Devine, an assistant professor in politics.
Ben Tonra , professor of European foreign, security and defence policy at UCD, disagrees.
“Ireland will be as neutral after the triple lock as it was before,” he says. “This step is a simple recognition of the geopolitical realities we face.”
John O’Brennan, professor of European politics at Maynooth University, has little time for doom-filled warnings about the end of neutrality.
“A lot of what passes for argument among those who defend the triple lock is straight out of Alice in Wonderland. These people are completely detached from reality,” he says.
Moderation has never been a staple of this debate. Since the 1970s, people have been warning that the cream of Ireland’s youth will be sent off to fight in foreign wars. It hasn’t happened (yet) but that hasn’t stopped its reliable repetition.
