In a public meeting earlier this year, Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald said: “I’ve one son. Over my dead body will my son be deployed to fight an imperialist war of aggression on any people.” Sinn Féin made this a theme of a series of public meetings on the issue.
Concerns about and attachment to neutrality are real and enduring. Polls show a continuing strong attachment to the idea of neutrality, even if there might be a range of definitions of what that actually means. On the specific question of the triple lock, polls show that a majority of those who express an opinion favour its retention, though it is hardly overwhelming.
Last month, when The Irish Times asked the question , 44 per cent said they favoured retention of the triple lock, 34 per cent its removal and 22 per cent said they didn’t know, according to the opinion poll conducted by Ipsos B&A.
O’Brennan has little time for the way the triple lock constrains the elected parliament and the government answerable to it.
“Why on earth do proponents of the triple lock deny to Ireland’s elected representatives the right to take decisions on behalf of the Irish people? Why would we insist on attaining the agreement of the leader of Burundi or 100 other states on deployment decisions, rather than the men and women we elect to take decisions on our behalf?” he asks.
“Ireland is a parliamentary democracy and only Irish people should have input into these critical decisions on deployment. Why subcontract those decisions to a multitude of other states in the General Assembly or even worse the UN Security Council?
“I don’t vote for leaders in Brazil, India or Australia, so why should our decisions depend in part on how those countries vote? Other countries think we are completely mad in operating the way we have been.”
[ Minister wants role for Irish Navy in EU mission targeting Russia shadow fleet Opens in new window ]
Sources familiar with thinking on the issue in Government say the signal it would send to Ireland’s EU allies that the country was getting serious about defence would be an important one. They point out there is decreasing patience with Ireland’s approach to security, an issue with which EU members are increasingly preoccupied.
“We are regarded as complete freeloaders,” says one source.
[ ‘A bunch of freeloaders’: Increasing UK pressure on Ireland to invest in defence Opens in new window ]
Military types also fret the retention of the triple lock would mean the end of peacekeeping missions abroad and that would inevitably mean a decline in skills and capacities in the Defence Forces.
Cathal Berry, a former Army Ranger and Independent TD, says the “vast majority” of the military and defence community in Ireland want to see the end of the triple lock.
A further concern for soldiers is that overseas deployments – with no cost of living and special allowances payable – are a chance to save money for a house deposit, or other big purchase. It would become harder to retain military personnel without peacekeeping missions, Berry says.
Having passed its first vote during the week, the Bill now moves to its committee stage.
“We’ll delay it there as much as we can,” says one Opposition TD frankly.
But the Government has the numbers. It should be possible to get it passed through the Oireachtas by Christmas.
[ Nato chief calls for ‘conversation’ on usefulness of Irish neutrality in changing world Opens in new window ]
However, Sara O’Rourke of the Irish Neutrality Alliance says there are “constitutional considerations” that could yet come into play.
Some pro-neutrality campaigners expect that President Catherine Connolly – a fierce advocate for the triple lock when she was a TD – may refer the Bill to the Supreme Court to test its constitutionality. Others – on both sides of the argument – think a private legal challenge is more likely.
Paul Murphy , People Before Profit-Solidarity TD, says the “fight to defend the triple lock and Irish neutrality is far from over”.
The Government will face weeks of intense debate in the committee rooms, in the Dáil and in the Seanad. At the same time, the Irish Neutrality League has a campaign to mobilise large numbers of people on the streets and add pressure on Government TDs and Senators to defend the triple lock, or at the very least to allow the people to decide on it in a referendum.
“There were only eight TDs in the difference on Wednesday night. I expect this number to keep coming down as TDs go back to their constituencies and realise public opinion is against the Government on this one,” says Murphy.

title: Parents fear of dying before their disabled children: ‘Our family will be thrown into a crisis’
description: Some such parents have transformed their lifestyles in the hope of outliving offspring who cannot live independent lives
content:
A fter the birth of Christopher with Down syndrome 16 years ago, Joseph Birchall realised this boy would be relying on him, not just to 18 but way beyond. Joseph immediately gave up smoking and, based on longevity research, switched to a plant-based diet. He runs, goes to the gym and manages stress and sleep as well as he can.
“It is about health span as opposed to lifespan,” says Joseph, a business owner and author. “It’s about remaining healthy.”
Joseph, who is 56, believes that if he and his 49-year-old wife, Eileen, a psychotherapist, had not, through “sheer bloody-mindedness and love for our son”, poured time and money into him, he would not have developed into the “unique, funny, beautiful personality” he is today.
When Christopher was diagnosed with autism around age five, they paid a child behavioural therapist to come to their home in Tallaght, Dublin, every week. She helped them manage their son better.
“Christopher is an amazing kid,” he says. “He’s extremely verbal and he has a great vocabulary. A lot of that comes from talking to ChatGPT. His communication skills are incredible.”
An unspoken implication of Joseph’s dedication to longevity is the prospect that a parent might outlive a child. He and Eileen cannot envisage the State providing the care and understanding their son would need without his parents. They say the current lack of support and services makes the future appear “bleak”. But as to any thoughts that the generational order of death might be reversed, Joseph says, “it’s too early to even go there”.
For older parents of adults with a disability that leaves them unable to live independently, the future wellbeing of their sons or daughters is an urgent concern. Gerry and Geraldine Conroy have cared for their eldest son, Donal, who has Down syndrome, for 40 years and say “we will continue to do so for as long as we are able”. But they are both in their 70s and know the time will come when, due to failing health or death, they will not be able to manage his onerous, full-time care.
“It is then that our family will be thrown into a crisis situation. What we are looking for now is a very clear plan for Donal, as to what would happen.” He is one of an estimated 2,300 adults with an intellectual disability being cared for at home in Ireland by parents aged over 70. Donal needs help with all his personal care, including toileting, and is nonverbal. But, worse than that, says Gerry, “he doesn’t understand anything we’re saying to him. He can’t watch a programme on television. He can’t look forward to something that’s happening tomorrow. He’s living absolutely and totally in the present.”
[ ‘Community care’ is exposed as an empty concept when a carer dies Opens in new window ]
Donal attends day services during the week, leaving home in rural Co Meath just before 9am and returning at 3.30pm. He has a younger brother and sister, Brendan and Áine, and Gerry believes the siblings are often forgotten about in these situations.
“Over the years they have been absolutely selfless in regards to Donal and have been a tremendous help to him and to us. Now we are very worried about the pressure they may come under when the crisis occurs in relation to the lack of housing – and even a plan to have housing.”
Gerry is alarmed to hear other parents say they hope their disabled adult child will die before them. “This is because of the very genuine fear they have as to what would happen when they are gone.”
It is a fear shared by the Conroys, who have asked services about that eventuality. Donal would be seen as an emergency case, put into respite care and “advertised out to private providers”, says Gerry. “Seemingly, then, family would have no say in where he goes or what kind of people he’s with or what situation he’s in.”
Donal is familiar with his locality, although he cannot go out alone. The couple hate to think of him being taken to another part of the country for residential care. Their ideal for Donal would be step-up accommodation nearby right now, for two nights a week. It would help to prepare him for living elsewhere, as well as giving the couple much-needed rest.
“The amount of sleep we get is very much determined by how he sleeps. There are times he sleeps through the full night, there are times he’ll sleep for a couple of hours and there are times he won’t close an eye.
“We could retire from our own jobs,” adds Gerry, a former national schoolteacher, “but we can’t retire from this job.”
‘My daughter will end up as a commodity being exploited by the profit sector’
Another set of parents of an adult with Down syndrome, Paul and his ex-wife, Hazel, are already struggling with unexpected, serious illness in their late 60s. Foremost in their minds is what will happen to their daughter Susan, who is in her late 20s. (All names in this family have been changed at their request.) Soon after Hazel was diagnosed with stage-four cancer, Paul, who is Susan’s primary carer, was told he had stage-four chronic kidney disease and would require dialysis within one or two years.
[ Ageing parents of adults with disabilities say: ‘I hope they go before me’ Opens in new window ]
The theoretical question of their daughter’s care after they die, which he had raised with his ex-wife a few years ago, is now an all-too-real issue. Paul has always maintained, “I don’t want Susan to become a multigenerational burden”. He would ask her siblings to be “the best advocates for her” but not take over her care.
While Paul uses the term “burden”, he quickly stresses, “I love her to death”, glancing at the large black-and-white photograph of Susan that he has placed on the table we are sitting at in their Dublin home. “Having a child with a disability changes your whole perspective on life.”
Paul chokes back emotion as he talks about how he is beginning to prepare his daughter for a possible deterioration in his and his ex-wife’s health. All she has been told is that her mother has a “sore back”, which is why she has seen very little of her over the past year.
He poses, and proceeds to answer, the question: if he and his ex-wife die, what happens to Susan?
“She’s classified as an emergency by the HSE. That means they put her care package out to the private, for-profit sector, which is exactly what it says on the tin.
“In one fell swoop, Susan loses her dad, her carer, her home, her community. She loses her choice because she’s placed in there. She loses her buddies, which is the big thing for her, and she loses her voice because I’m no longer there to represent her.”
He sees parallels between the plight of adults with intellectual disabilities and women who were placed in Magdalene laundries where they were exploited for profit. “Institutions look at cost. My daughter will end up as a commodity being exploited by the profit sector.”
Paul is associated with Before We Die (BWD), a parents’ group lobbying the Government to fund and deliver residential places for adults with intellectual disability. It says the Budget 2027 provision of funding for 212 residential places for people with disabilities is a continuing “crisis-first policy”, as 112 of those places are ring-fenced for emergency cases.
“Ageing parents need residential homes arranged while they are still alive to support their sons and daughters through the transition – not emergency beds sourced in the days following a parent’s funeral,” a statement from BWD adds.
Ireland signed up to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of People with Disabilities in 2018. “That gives voice to every person’s right to live in their local community,” says Derval McDonagh, chief executive of Inclusion Ireland, the national association for people with an intellectual disability.
“Unfortunately, a lot of the narrative around people with intellectual disabilities is not about people’s rights. It’s about grouping people together or putting people into large settings.” Inclusion Ireland argues that there needs to be a three-choice test for every individual: do I have choice about where I live, who I live with and how I spend my time?
“If we’re answering no to any of those, then unfortunately we’re perpetuating institutional-type models.” Almost 200 people have been accommodated more than 100km away from their family and community, says BWD. For people with intellectual disabilities, “the consequences of that are utterly devastating”, says McDonagh. “Things can’t be fixed overnight but at least there should be a plan.”
In response to queries from The Irish Times, the Department of Children, Disability and Equality says a key focus of the Government and the HSE is increased emphasis on longer-term planning for residential placements. As of last August, 142 new residential placements had been created and provided to people with disabilities out of 152 funded in Budget 2026, bringing the total number of residential places to over 9,000.
Budget 2027 brings the entire disability services budget to over €4 billion for the first time, it points out and, contrary to the BWD assertion, “it is not the case that just 100 places are available for individuals to transition out of their family home”, because funding “will also support a number of new placements into existing vacant places with necessary enhancements”. Government departments are, it adds, working with local authorities to set targets for housing people with disabilities for the first time.
Meanwhile Joseph, whose latest book is a crime thriller, Reported Missing (Poolbeg), will step back within two years from an online business he runs with his brother. He wants and will need to spend more time with Christopher, who currently attends St Michael’s Grosvenor School in Leopardstown but that will stop at age 18.
“There are adult services but nothing is guaranteed,” says Joseph, who has an older daughter from a previous relationship. He and his wife have always regarded Christopher as their responsibility and never want their younger son, Jamie (13), to have to take that on. They hope Christopher will have the chance of further education, a part-time job, and, ideally, could move into residential care nearby, returning home at weekends.
“Christopher has surprised us his whole life and, if anything, we’ve learned not to put limitations on him,” says Joseph, who has no doubt his own retirement will be enhanced by his eldest son.
“I like being who I am when I’m with him. He brings an energy and a youth to me – and a purpose.”

title: Lara Gillespie: ‘I had an eventful childhood ... sport was my outlet from life stress’
description: Ireland’s double world champion only took up cycling at 16, but she will be a medal hope at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028
content:
Enniskerry on a windy morning. The leaves are dancing around the lopsided village, whipping past your ankles and plastering the sides of the roadworks bollards. They’ve had rain here overnight and there’s plenty more in the post. Pop your umbrella with care, or you risk being Mary Poppinsed off to the top of the Sugar Loaf.
Lara Gillespie arrives, bundled up and gleaming. This is her home, swaddled by the Wicklow Mountains, somehow a place of both transience and permanence. She never gets to stay here for long. She makes sure to never quite leave it either.
“It grounds me, definitely,” she says. “If ever I’m overwhelmed or if everything is just a lot, all I want is to go to Wicklow, to go to the mountains. I just love being out in nature and just not even doing anything. Just being there, walking there with the dog and with family.
“It can feel like it’s calling me. Whenever I was sick in Germany, where I have a base, all I was thinking was that I know I would get healthier if I was in Wicklow right now. Also, with my mum’s food, we grow our own food. It’s a very calm place to be.
“You don’t need much here. You don’t need to be going to the shops. You don’t need to be driving. It’s very self-sustained, everything is in the one place. And it’s just a complete contrast to the other life of airports and moving and hotel rooms, blah, blah, blah. So I think I definitely crave that downtime.”
Her life doesn’t grant her a lot of it. Gillespie became a track cycling world champion for the second time in Shanghai last Sunday. She’s gone again next week, out to Abu Dhabi to start preparation for the 2027 road season. So when she’s here, it’s not just about resting and lolling. It’s a more purposeful thing than that.
“My family, my friendships, relationships – they’re all very, very important to me and I don’t have much time to invest in them or in their lives,” she says. “So when I’m home I’m very intentional about making time.
“When I’m away, my life is very regimented. When I’m here, I say no to a lot of things so I can make that effort with the people I need to. And in turn, it does make me feel better and stronger and healthier on the bike if I have that balance.”
Still only 25, Gillespie is comfortably the most successful female cyclist Ireland has ever produced, regardless of the surface under her wheels. Winning the points race in China last weekend made her the first Irish cyclist, male or female, to become a double world champion, having won the elimination race in Chile the previous year. We’ve had world champions before. We’ve never had one person with two rainbow jerseys.
[ The long history of runners taking shortcuts in the marathon Opens in new window ]
On the road, she was national champion for the third time this year and added the time trial title for good measure. Back in March, she had the biggest road win of her career, taking the prestigious Le Samyn one-day race in Belgium . She finished fourth in the points classification at the Giro d’Italia in June . Earlier this month, she was second in the Tour of Chongming Island, the final event of the season in the Women’s World Tour.
She keeps finding new levels in a world that was alien to her starting off. Gillespie wasn’t one of those sportspeople who are born into their event – she didn’t take up cycling until her late teens. Instead, she was the sort of kid who played every sport that was going. Saturdays were a trolley dash, shuttling in the car from this football match to that Irish dancing feis, taking the plaits out of her hair and cleaning the muck off her knees with baby wipes as they went.
“I did everything. It was always go, go, go. There was always a bag to be packed. My mum always made us put a list on the side of our sports bag with everything that we needed. So it was always just like that. My sister Bobbi is three years younger than me and she was always kind of dragged everywhere as the plus one.
“Not that she didn’t enjoy it, but if you ask her now does she cycle, she’ll be like, ‘I have an e-bike ...’ She’s not competitive, except maybe with board games. She did the same sports but she was able to lose without thinking about it for the rest of the day. Which, apparently, I wasn’t. I always said I wasn’t competitive and Bobbi would be like: ‘You are, Lara.’”
[ How Manchester United became a club too big not to fail Opens in new window ]
Growing up, life was never still. Never felt that way, at any rate. Her parents weren’t together so she and Bobbi were, as she puts it, “always living in a suitcase, always ready to go different places”. Her mother, Suzanne Clarke, herself an Irish international in orienteering, did a degree in sports science and passed down an interest in psychology, sometimes using the simplest form of it on her.
“I used to get so nervous for cross-country running,” Lara says. “I don’t know what it was. I just felt like when you’re in the field and everyone’s watching you run around like that, they’re watching you the whole time. I found something about that really nerve-racking.
“And she just said: ‘Oh, just don’t do it then. You don’t need to race.’ And then I’d be like: ‘Well I’m definitely doing it now. How dare you say that? I want to win.’ That’s always been her way, she’d never be pushing me. She’d never be like: ‘Go there and do that.’ So I think I’ve been drip-fed psychology my whole life. But in a very natural way.”
As the elder sister in a single-mum family, life accelerated under her feet from pretty early on. In that scenario, you have to sprint to stay upright sometimes, whether you’re ready for it or not.
“I had an eventful childhood, let’s say. I definitely grew up very fast and I was very much in some ways responsible for my sister, even at the age of five. So it was very much growing up fast, not really having, like, a child’s life. Sport was my outlet from life stress.
“And that’s why I just did every sport. I think it was my happy place. Because there, you don’t have to worry about your family, you don’t have to worry about where you’re sleeping that night. You’re just having fun with your friends and expressing yourself. So I think that’s also why I don’t take… obviously, I take sport seriously, but I know it’s sport as well.”
Maybe it’s no big surprise then that the road she took to the top of her sport wasn’t exactly linear. She thought she was going to be a runner and as a teenager she trained in a group with future European champion Sarah Healy. But she was doing triathlons as well and it was through them that she ended up in cycling.
She went to the European Youth Olympics in Hungary in 2017 and won silver in the time trial on the road. She was 16 years old and had only been cycling competitively for a few months, but it was the first time she thought that maybe this should be the sport she focused on. But it took a few more years for her to properly get it.
“I went to the World Championships as a junior in 2019 and I was getting my Leaving Cert results literally on the day of the worlds. And my coach was like: ‘Why do you even care? Why are you even looking at your results? This could be your job. Cycling could be your job.’
“And I was like: ‘No it can’t.’ I did not believe that that was a thing. I didn’t even know about road cycling. I didn’t know that it could be a professional job at that point. But I won a medal at that Worlds and then I qualified for Sport Ireland carding. And I was like: ‘Oh, maybe there is a future here.’”
[ Hiko Tonosa returns to Dublin Marathon looking to regain national title Opens in new window ]
Her talent carried her, as did the fact that she played so many sports growing up. Even the couple of years she missed out on through illness in her early 20s have possibly stood to her in some respects. Gillespie was born with a rare gynaecological condition that started causing her issues when she was 15 and which she will probably have to deal with throughout her life.
She had surgery in 2021 but had a difficult recovery from it and ended up with glandular fever. All in all, she lost the thick end of two years to it. Hard as it was at the time, she’s able to look back now and see a blessing in disguise.
“Definitely. It taught me to not compare myself with anyone. Because I remember at that time I was so jealous of the girls that I knew I was as good as. They were on world tour contracts and stuff and they were getting all these opportunities and I was like: ‘Oh, that could have been me.’
“And I’m getting much more opportunity than some of those riders just simply because they went into the professional world very early and got worked and worked and worked. I was out of it so I wasn’t burning myself out. It also gave me the opportunity to finish college, which I don’t think I would have been able to do at the time if I was competing.
“My grandad was dying around that time too and I wouldn’t have been able to spend as much time with him. So I’m really grateful to actually have been sick at that time. It meant I was able to be home and help care for him. We lived with my grandparents from the age of five. Caring for them and being with them really gave me another angle on life.”
So here she is. Ireland’s top cyclist, a medal hope when it comes to LA in 2028. Her first Olympics experience in Paris was a bit of a write-off – the focus was more on the team pursuit but when it came to the day, Ireland didn’t get through the qualifying round.
She gave the Omnium everything she had and was within three points of a medal at one stage. But ultimately, it washed out as a 10th-place finish. Not terrible for a first attempt. But not what she was after either.
She was the last Irish competitor of the Games as well, which sucked some of the joy out of the whole experience. Her race took place an hour outside Paris on the last morning of the Olympics, meaning that by the time she got back to the rest of the Irish team, they were all demob happy. Make-up on, hangovers percolating, ready to go again for the closing ceremony. And all she wanted to do was eat something.
“They had all been partying for days at that stage. I missed all that, in my own little bubble. I think the next time I’d like to be a bit more relaxed and actually enjoy it. Even though maybe at the next one I’ll have more pressure, more expectation. But I think for me, I need the balance of fun as well. I don’t like it to be all just serious. I think it takes away the joy of it.”

title: Take it from a proud 2CV owner, it’s the little things ...
description: I am delighted to read Citroen plans to start rebuilding its iconic car
content:
Sir, – I am the proud owner of a 1988 Ferrari-red 2CV. I am delighted to read in the Irish Times that Citroën is planning to start rebuilding this iconic French car for delivery in 2028 (“ Citroën’s relaunch of a classic could be just what the electric car market needs ,” Technology, October 15th).
The original car was last produced in 1990 with a 602cc capacity engine and I have always felt that it was the last 2cc that got me up the hill. – Yours, etc,

title: Ireland’s military is moving into the 21st century – some fear it is not ready
description: Purchasing gaffes, malfunctioning machine guns and planes too big for hangars show the Defence Forces has a lot to learn
content:
In late November 2013, two months after their arrival in Syria as part of a United Nations observation force, Irish Defence Forces troops had their first contact with hostile forces.
The patrol comprising 36 troops travelling in five Mowag armoured personnel carriers (APCs) were ambushed by an armed Islamic group about 25km from their camp in the Golan Heights, the rocky plateau in southwestern Syria overseen by UN peacekeepers supervising a ceasefire between Israel and Syria since 1974.
The soldiers went to return fire using the heavy mounted machine guns on the vehicles’ roofs. However, when the gunners on two of the APCs cocked the weapons, they heard a snap. The internal cables broke, making the weapons useless.
Fortunately for the patrol, the guns on the other three Mowags still worked and were enough to drive off the attackers. One APC lost a wheel when it hit a landmine as they withdrew but there were no Irish injuries. Replacement parts for the guns were urgently dispatched from Ireland, stowed in the personal baggage of a soldier.
It was the type of incident that still keeps Alan Kearney, a former Defence Forces weapons specialist, up at night 13 years later.
For Kearney, who retired from the Army at the rank of commandant last year, the incident spoke to the often slapdash approach by the Defence Forces to equipment procurement and maintenance.
The cocking cables were a known point of failure in the weapons, but this was ignored. And the weapons systems were sent to a war zone without adequate spare parts.
The incident was a “direct and foreseeable consequence” of procuring a custom weapons system without the ability to support it, he says.
Now, with the Defence Forces about to acquire billions of euro in new equipment under chief of staff Lieut Gen Rossa Mulcahy as part of a modernisation programme, Kearney worries the same mistakes will be repeated.
[ Minister wants role for Irish Navy in EU mission targeting Russia shadow fleet Opens in new window ]
These mistakes include purchasing equipment without the necessary personnel to maintain it or a clear plan of how it will be used. The result is sometimes expensive military systems that sit in storage for years.
Kearney has detailed many of these concerns in a damning report he is to submit to the Oireachtas Committee on Defence and National Security and the Public Accounts Committee.
“I’m all for ambition. But this is a complete and utter transformation. It’s not just buying a few vehicles. It is enormous,” says Kearney.
For the army, one of the biggest aspects of this modernisation is the Scorpion programme involving the acquisition of hundreds of cutting-edge armoured vehicles from France as part of a government-to-government deal.
A final decision has yet to be made on the number of armoured vehicles to be purchased. This will depend on the results of a project overseen by a board of military officers and civilian servants who will devise the requirements. Even more important will be how much funding the Department of Public Expenditure is willing to allocate to the project.
Sources familiar with the purchasing plans say a figure of more than 550 vehicles is being recommended by military planners, far higher than the previously reported figure of between 300 and 400.
[ Defence Forces officers earning as little as €4 an hour for working overtime Opens in new window ]
Vehicles to be acquired under the proposed deal will include the Griffon, a six-wheel APC; the Serval, which is a smaller four-wheeled armoured car; and the Jaguar, a tank-like “armoured fighting vehicle” equipped with a large turreted gun.
The new armour programme will transform the Irish Army from a light infantry force with limited armoured elements, to a partially mechanised force equipped with modern armour and heavier weaponry.
“Where are they going to go? Who is going to maintain them? Who is going to fix the guns?” says Kearney.
He points to the fact that the Army is desperately short of enlisted personnel specialising in vehicle maintenance. Numbers are slowly growing but it takes years to build up the experience necessary for the upkeep of a large, armoured fleet, he says.
Then there is the ancillary equipment and infrastructure needed for such a fleet.
[ France is falling to the extremes of left and right. Ireland cannot be complacent Opens in new window ]
“When the Mowag armoured fleet was introduced, infrastructure and sustainment capacity lagged behind the vehicles themselves, creating logistical challenges that required years to resolve,” says Kearney.
Workshops in the Curragh in Co Kildare, the primary military base of the Defence Forces, were initially too small for the APCs, while there were persistent issues with obtaining spare parts. This meant many of the vehicles’ optical systems were unusable for years.
“It took years to stabilise and that fleet was far simpler than Scorpion,” says Kearney.
These problems were seen on a more serious scale in the fleet of light armoured tactical vehicles purchased for the Defence Forces in 2008.
The 27 vehicles broke down frequently and were extremely difficult to maintain. On one occasion in 2011, a light tactical armoured vehicle (LTAV) went on fire while it was being driven on the motorway. As a result, they were used sparingly, with some vehicles going years without being driven.
Earlier this month, the Office of the Comptroller and Auditor General, the State’s spending watchdog, found millions of euro in public funds was wasted in the purchase of the LTAVs. The Department of Defence, which is led by Minister Helen McEntee, said it had “learned lessons from this procurement”.
[ Triple lock Bill passes Dáil vote amid Opposition anger Opens in new window ]
Procurement failings are not just confined to the Army. Senior naval officers have expressed frustration with the purchase of two second-hand patrol vessels from New Zealand that have been plagued by problems since their arrival two years ago, including serious issues with the hulls.
In the Air Corps , all four of the PC-12 aircraft purchased in 2020 for close to €50 million are currently out of service due to maintenance issues.
Perhaps the clearest example of military shortsightedness was the Gulfstream aircraft purchased in the 1990s for transporting government ministers.
For years the Air Corps lacked a hangar big enough to store the aircraft. The solution was to cut a hole in an existing hangar, leaving the plane’s tail exposed outside leading to corrosion in the airframe of the aircraft.
That problem involved just one aircraft and one hangar but took years to resolve, Kearney points out.
“The proposed Scorpion programme involves hundreds of platforms across multiple sites,” he says.
Many other examples can be found across the military, such as shotguns purchased for military police officers and night vision scopes for machine guns which sat in stores for years without being used because no one was sure what purpose they were intended to serve.
However, history does not have to repeat itself and it is possible lessons have been learned from these mistakes.
Nicholas Moran, an Irish-American armoured vehicle expert and US National Guard officer, says there will be a significant delay in the delivery of any Scorpion vehicles to Ireland and that “there should be ample time to create a support structure”.
“Where that support structure will be, though, is an issue,” he says. “Can you fit 80 large [armoured fighting vehicles] in Renmore or Cathal Brugha [Barracks]?” he says, referring to the Defence Forces locations in Galway and Dublin.
It is not clear how much the Scorpion programme will cost. Estimates have ranged from €400 million to €1 billion. If at least 550 vehicles are to be purchased, the cost will likely be much more, particularly when maintenance and parts are factored in.
In 2018, Belgium entered a deal to purchase 442 Scorpion programme vehicles from France with an announced cost of €1.6 billion.
Last year, Belgium’s spending watchdog excoriated the deal and found the total lifetime cost of the vehicles will be more than €14 billion. This includes €60 million a year on maintenance.
[ Were bad landlords partly to blame for race riots in Northern Ireland? Opens in new window ]
Whatever purchase price is announced by the Irish Government for the vehicles will be “a drop in the ocean” compared to the lifetime cost, Kearney says.
The acquisition of some 550 vehicles would allow the Army to transform one of its two brigades into a fully armoured fighting force supported by advanced artillery system.
Another question about the purchases is: why?
Ireland is a militarily neutral country. For decades, the focus of its military has been on peacekeeping operations and, until 1998, responding to paramilitary activity.
What need does it have for hundreds of sophisticated combat vehicles?
The official doctrine for the Defence Forces says Ireland must be able to deter or resist any attack on the State until the international community steps in.
Its latest published version of the doctrine states that deterrence requires “the maintenance of a credible military capability to convince potential aggressors that the consequences of hostile activity targeted against Irish sovereignty and territorial integrity would outweigh any potential gains”.
The statement is undoubtedly ambitious. As the document notes, the Defence Forces is equipped for “constabulary and overseas tasks, rather than for a conventional territorial defence”.
But the development of a highly mobile brigade equipped with the most modern equipment money can buy would move the Defence Forces more into the realm of a conventional war fighting force.
Another consideration for military planners is Ireland’s contribution to European defence initiatives, specifically the EU’s Rapid Deployment Capacity, commonly known as the EU Battlegroups.
These are units of about 1,500 combat troops designed to deploy to trouble spots within 10 days. The objective of the groups is to respond to humanitarian crises and act in emergency peace support roles, although critics argue they are a precursor to the EU military command.
A modern Irish armoured fleet, built by an EU member and designed from the ground up to integrate with Nato forces, would be warmly welcomed by Battlegroup commanders.
Moran, the US tank expert, believes the vehicles could serve a wide variety of roles.
He says the purpose of an armoured personnel carrier is “the safe transportation of troops in a hostile area” and that could include “a nation intent on an incursion on to Ireland’s territory, unfriendly forces on a peacekeeping mission, or to move troops to an eastern European battlefield as part of a multinational force”.
“The bottom line is that the fewer troops you have not under armoured protection as they move, the safer it is for them,” he says.
Asked about the programme to upgrade the armoured fleet, the Department of Defence said: “A whole-of-capability approach is being adopted, integrating vehicle procurement with doctrine, training, infrastructure, personnel and interoperability requirements.
“As the programme remains in the assessment phase, specifications, role, fleet size, timelines, costs, training arrangements and support requirements remain subject to ongoing negotiations and the necessary approval processes.”
Regardless of how they will be used, the military needs vehicles capable of standing up to modern threats, says Mark Mellett, the Defence Forces former chief of staff.
“The Mowags have level three armour protection. Most armoured fleets are up around level five. We have to move into that space,” the retired admiral says.

title: Kerry Group rediscovers its mojo – with a little help from RFK jnr and Ozempic
description: Nutrition giant has seen a 17% jump in sales to US snacks sector in an otherwise flat, highly competitive market
content:
Robert F Kennedy jnr , the divisive US health secretary, is discovering that taking on Big Food is easier said than done.
His Make America Healthy Again (Maha) pledge to publish a first-ever US government definition of ultra-processed foods by April came and went. A second attempt, scheduled for August, was shelved at the last minute as food-industry lobbyists turned up the heat on the Trump administration.
Then, on Thursday, a key RFK jnr adviser, Calley Means, quit in frustration at the lack of progress on flagship policies, denouncing “a corrupt DC bureaucracy that is doing everything possible to protect the status quo”.
Still, their crusade against salt, sugar and artificial food dyes has tapped into widespread consumer anxiety.
A survey released this month by the American Heart Association said that more than 70 per cent of adults in the US say they are now trying to avoid ultra-processed foods.
Edmond Scanlon, chief executive of Kerry Group , one of the world’s largest taste and nutrition ingredients groups, seems to have been ahead of the game.
[ Weight-loss drug revolution proves ‘accelerator’ for Kerry Group Opens in new window ]
He told analysts at an investor day earlier this month that when his team began talking about the opportunity in “food renovation” – industry-speak for reformulating existing products to improve their nutritional profile without sacrificing taste or texture – “everybody was wondering, ‘What’s Kerry talking about?’” The jargon, perhaps, wasn’t doing them any favours.
“This was actually prior to RFK, prior to Maha, etc,” he said. “I suppose, back then, we thought it was going to be maybe regulatory that was going to kind of push it. It’s actually been more the consumer pull that has been playing out.”
Kerry has seen a 17 per cent jump in its sales to the US snacks sector – spanning crisps to cereal bars – in an otherwise flat, though highly competitive, overall market. This has been driven by Kerry coming up with solutions to reduce salt while maintaining taste. Even after this, 80 per cent of snack products in the US still contain sodium levels above World Health Organisation guidelines, according to Kerry.
Scanlon said that Kerry – with an army of 1,200 food scientists working on enzymes, fermentation, natural food extracts, bio-preservation and “modulation” technologies to cut salt, sugar and fat content – is the “go-to in the industry” for renovation. He sees this driving expected growth in the addressable “value-added speciality ingredients” space from €87 billion to more than €100 billion in the next five to 10 years.
The chief executive has said his “biggest hope and expectation” is that Kerry will be able to replicate the recent snacks success in the meals sector, where the market opportunity is much greater.
The explosion of weight-loss GLP-1 medications like Ozempic and Mounjaro is also playing into Kerry’s hands, contrary to predictions, Scanlon told my colleague Eoin Burke-Kennedy on Thursday as the group reported better-than-expected third-quarter results.
“Three years into the mainstreaming of GLP-1s, I think we can now point to the fact that it has been and will be more of an accelerator to our business,” Scanlon said. “The prevalence of these drugs, whether you’re taking them or not taking them ... is driving a narrative around health and wellness that is better for our business.”
With GLP-1s fuelling the world’s protein craze, Kerry’s technology to mask its bitter and chalky taste is making the boom more palatable.
Shares in Kerry have soared about 55 per cent since late March – coming within 20 cent of €100 on Friday in Dublin – as Kerry’s brand of renovation and innovation is winning over investors even as Scanlon is factoring in a flat performance by its end markets in retail and food service over the coming years.
It follows a 50 per cent slump from an all-time high reached five years ago. Kerry missed a goal of growing sales volumes by 4-6 per cent annually in each of the past three years amid particularly weak end markets.
Still, it managed to increase its earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation margin from 14.5 per cent to 17.9 per cent over the period – helped by the sale in late 2024 of a majority stake in its legacy, low-margin dairy processing business to Kerry Co-op.
Kerry’s new volume target, unveiled in July as part of a number of goals stretching to 2030, is for it to grow 3-5 per cent a year. It’s altogether more reasonable than the last objective. It also wants to lift margins to 20-21 per cent, with a helping hand from Accelerate 2.0, a programme to squeeze more efficiency out of its factories, supply chain and technology.
The group reported on Thursday that its volume growth in the third quarter rose to 4.1 per cent from 3.6 per cent for the first half of the year – and that it is on track to maintain the higher level for the final months of the year. The growth is being led by North America as Europe – a much more fragmented market – remains relatively weak. Kerry shares have advanced as much as 5.7 per cent since the release.
“Kerry’s Q3 update and subsequent [analysts’] call reinforce our confidence that the recent step-up in volume growth is sustainable, supported by renovation rather than any material improvement in underlying end markets,” said Barclays analyst Alex Sloane in a report on Friday.
Not bad for a company viewed by some long-time observers just a year ago as having lost its mojo.

title: Colm O’Regan: ‘I’m tipping away at sorting my parents’ stuff into artefacts and rubbish’
description: The comedian’s new book, Tipping Away, is his second on Hiberno-English expressions. Sure, what else would he be doing?
content:
C olm O’Regan is sorry he doesn’t have a garden shed for “tipping away” at stuff. The comedian and author grew up on a small farm in Dripsey in west Cork , where his father was often “out, like, tinkering” – building fences, picking stones, mending things. He would see a job that needed doing, then tip away at it in the grand stretch of a summer’s evening. Tipping away has an “elastic” meaning, he says, in that it can mean working steadily at something, often to just avoid being idle, but it can also be an Irish euphemism for being absolutely “up the walls”.
He likes the phrase so much it’s the name of his new book on Hiberno-English, his second in two years. It’s also what he’s been doing recently with the belongings of his late parents. “In a kind of full circle, I’m gently tipping away at sorting their letters and old bills and receipts and stuff into artefacts that are interesting and pure rubbish.”
His mother, who died in late 2024, was a teacher, and last year he was delighted to be able to return a 60-year-old copybook he found among her things to one of her former pupils, whom he tracked down through social media. In an age of ephemeral digital communication, he often pleads with people to hold on to their children’s copybooks.
One of the things O’Regan has taken from writing Tipping Away and its 2025 predecessor, Gallivanting with Words , is that it is never too soon to start preserving language. Even the fact that fewer Irish people grow up on a small farm now than in the 1980s – he was born in 1978 – has lent a greater impetus to his desire to record the kinds of words that were ingrained in him when he was five years old, but that he hasn’t used with other people since leaving home.
He adopts a narrator’s voice. “With tears in his eyes, Colm said, ‘I have no one to talk with about beastings.’”
By beastings – “not a good word” – he means the agricultural slang for colostrum, or the first milk from a cow, though Google AI prioritises the British military definition (harsh punishment or extreme training exercises), while Apple’s AI transcription of our interview hears it as “bee stings” and “beef things”. With AI yet to grasp Hiberno-English, maybe we will end up keeping our language away from its automated small-talk prompts, the way we used to keep it away from the English, he suggests.
Tipping Away, or what he jokingly calls “the second book in the Gallivanting Cinematic Universe”, includes a chapter on farms, bogs and “mart lingo”, another on what the decline in religiosity means for language, and another devoted to “fighting words” such as ructions, kerns (Gaelic warriors) and galloglass, which he loves. It comes from gall óglaigh, meaning foreign warriors, which he thinks sounds like a health and beauty product or an up-and-coming software company, not a word for mercenaries from the western highlands of Scotland.
His father, who died in 2015, kept an “inner circle” of books that included English As We Speak It in Ireland by Patrick Weston Joyce, which recorded expressions in circulation in 1910. “People seemed to delight in two things in Hiberno-English then: criticising women and people being perceived as eejits. So there was ‘she’d coort a haggard of sparrows’, as in she’d go with anyone.”
It’s not necessary to understand the exact context of phrases like these, he notes, to pick up on the general tone of sexist disapproval. “It’s like, f**k’s sake.”
I confess my fondness for the Dublin term “gurrier” (used, often lightheartedly, to describe young troublemakers) and wonder if it’s dying out. “ The band Gurriers will keep it alive, just like there’s a band called The Latchikos that keeps my favourite word my father used alive,” he says. (Latchiko is a catch-all term for an untrustworthy person.)
Dose, meanwhile, is one useful Hiberno-insult I’ve adopted in conversation more recently, usually as a label for a vaguely annoying and massively over-exposed celebrity. “And it was a venereal disease in [James] Joyce’s writing, you know? It’s great. I love that. The other thing is that words will survive if they sound good. Like why has f**k survived for however long it is? It just sounds like frustration. You can mourn the decline of some words, but others were simply never going to make it. The ones that did well were good product.”
I ask about the Cork use of “septic” to identify someone suffering from high self-esteem. “Yeah, septic as a noun – he’s a septic. It just means that you love yourself.”
He’s not sure if the traditional mortal fear of being accused of being “up your own hole” is as strong in Ireland as it used to be, but he did see some graffiti near Smithfield that implied it definitely still lingers. “Somebody had written, ‘You need to love yourself.’ It was this really lovely sentiment. Then about two days later somebody had added, ‘You need to shove it up your hole.’ It was like we just couldn’t bear the idea of self-care.”
O’Regan also explores the meaning of county names in Tipping Away and his favourite, “in fairness”, is Dublin, which has two: Dubh Linn (black pool) and the adjacent settlement of Baile Átha Cliath (town of the ford of the hurdles), the hurdles being the wooden rails that were placed where the river was low enough to cross or, alternatively, the mythological bones of a slain monster.
He can’t remember being struck by any unfamiliar slices of Dublinese when he moved to the capital in 2000 – after graduating from University College Cork with a degree in civil engineering – but he does associate that era with suddenly hearing a wider variety of accents on television and radio and the start of what he loosely terms the “culchie revival”.
He mentions the Irish propensity for filler words such as “ara” and “yerra” to mean “ah, sure” or perhaps nothing much at all. When he started doing comedy pieces for BBC Radio , he became “acutely conscious” of the way he would pepper his speech with ums and ahs rather than slide into a second of silence.
Hiberno-English, as a subject, is “sort of grist to a general mill” he has. “In comedy, you see the difference that swapping one word in for another makes to a joke,” he says. The order of words is also crucial in both stand-up and written humour. “Some comedy is the gap between what the person is expecting to hear and what they actually hear, and then that surprise hopefully makes them laugh.”
[ Throwing shapes: Frank McNally on the mysteries of the Hiberno-English ‘gimp’ Opens in new window ]
This is his ninth book, and for his 10th he would like to write something in the same vein about maths. He used to have a “labour of love” maths and numbers podcast called The Function Room. “I would love to write a funny, interesting book that you could give to a transition-year student and go, ‘This is not going to come up in the exam, this has no use to you, but here’s why you learn some of the stuff you do,’” he says.
“We shut off difficult, complicated topics from people, because we don’t think they’ll get it. They will, if you put it the right way.”
He would also like to start a podcast on language. “I’m going to start tentatively doing videos. I have to get over myself and get the stuff out,” he says. He sees his 11-year-old daughter Ruby making videos with her friends – it might be a lip-sync video with cutaways and interesting angles – in half an hour, but it takes him that long to figure out how to introduce himself.
O’Regan (48) lives in Inchicore in Dublin 8 with his wife, Marie Dunne, a librarian, and their two daughters: Ruby and nine-year-old Lily. Parenting gives him a window into how words can abruptly fall in and out of favour, he says.
“When my children are looking for something on the internet, they don’t say Google, they say ‘search it up’. And it seems like a very mundane difference, but that represents the fact that Google no longer means anything to them and they’re searching within an app. It’s a tiny little tweak of language, but hidden behind it is the entire philosophy of how the internet has gone in the last 20 years.”
His also loves hearing his daughters use Korean words when they sing along to the girl group Katseye, who incorporate the language into their lyrics. The first song he remembers singing along to himself was Karma Chameleon by Culture Club. “And I didn’t hear it properly, so I was singing, like, Come a Comedian. Come, come, come, come, come a comedian.”
O’Regan runs the Inn Jokes comedy club at The Patriots Inn in Kilmainham, where in 2024 he also started hosting Innfant Jokes, or relaxed morning comedy events for people with babies. The “baby gigs” have since expanded beyond their original venue, prompting him to discard the Innfant pun and rename them as Little Laughs.
“It’s a different type of gig, because you can’t be roaring ‘hey, everybody’ into the microphone and get huge applause. People can’t applaud if they’re holding a child. I tell any comedian who does it that if their joke works at this, it’s a really good joke, and if people don’t get it, don’t worry. They’re distracted, they’ve had four hours’ sleep.”
His main advice to the comedians who sign up for Little Laughs is not to stand on a baby on their way to the microphone. He did one event in Clonsilla earlier this month where the babies climbed on to the stage. “It was a bit like Father Ted – the Bishop Brennan episode with the rabbits. There were all these babies crawling around me.”
We talk a little about his weekly column for the Irish Examiner (now on Saturdays), his love of how language sometimes evolves from mistakes and misheard words, and his defence of the Irish language’s “mysterious spelling changes” (thanks to the tuiseal ginideach, or genitive case), then I switch off my recording, wish him luck with Tipping Away and self-consciously deploy a classic slice of Hiberno-English to say goodbye.
Tipping Away by Colm O’Regan will be published by Gill Books on October 29th

title: Fresh attacking ideas make Leinster v Munster an enticing prospect
description: Both teams arrive on Saturday for URC clash offering something different from what we have seen before
content:
Watching Leinster’s victory over Clermont last weekend, a text was sent to a former analyst at a professional team.
“Light the beacons, Leinster have scored on transition.”
The exchange was in reference Sam Prendergast’s length of the field score, an audacious decision to counterattack from deep. Not playing with freedom while padding a lead, but running from their own 22 while trailing by a point away in France.
Started and finished by Sam Prendergast 🔥 @leinsterrugby go from back to front to take the lead 🔵 #InvestecChampionsCup pic.twitter.com/iwn5DesQH7
“And an offload,” came the response from our analyst friend, pointing to Jimmy O’Brien’s final pass that sent his outhalf under the sticks.
The incredulity was due to the try’s origin. Transition. Counterattack. Offloading. Unpredictability. These are all words used to describe the damage done by French teams to Leinster and Ireland in recent years. In the Irish context, they have largely been used to describe what they’d like to do, rather than what is actually happening.
Ahead of this weekend’s interpro with Munster, Leinster are now more consistently turning words into action.
For their part, Clayton McMillan’s side have also undergone a shift. Their set-piece strikes have been the best in the country so far this season. Ditto their scrum. All of which leaves the fascinating scenario of the two largest Irish provinces looking altogether different from the sides that featured in Munster’s Croke Park heist 12 months ago.
[ Why perfecting the counterattack is central to Ireland’s World Cup evolution Opens in new window ]
This time last year, the Ireland coaches came out with a clear goal to improve on transition and counterattack. In recent weeks, Leinster have been making similar noises. At the start of the season, attack coach Tyler Bleyendaal used rugby’s magic E-word – evolve.
Was he talking about transition, the area of the game prioritised by the Bordeaux side that filleted Leinster in May? The evidence of the early season, young fullback Todd Lawlor running back kicks in South Africa (he is fifth in the URC this season for metres carried despite only playing twice) would seem to suggest so.
“Exactly,” confirmed Leo Cullen. “There are certain players, Caspar [Gabriel] has the ability to take the line on, Todd, he’s an instinctive player. It’s bringing more unpredictability to their games.
“They’ve worked hard during the course of preseason. We started with a young group and ... [we’re] adding senior players into the group all the time. I’m curious to see how guys run out.
“We’ve tried to always stay ahead of the curve. There’s lots of little things we’re doing. The group are buying into it as well, which is the important thing.”
When the senior players came back, they took on the counterattacking mantle. See Jack Conan’s try against Cardiff, Joe McCarthy and Tadhg Furlong pouncing on a spilled ball to feed Prendergast running up from the backfield à la Mathieu Jalibert. One last-ditch tackle prevented Leinster from scoring a coveted “zero-ruck try”, with Conan crashing over a phase later.
Tús spleodrach ag Leinster anocht agus aimsíonn Jack Conan an tríú úd dóibh. A blistering start for Leinster as Jack Conan scores their 3rd try of the night. 19 nóim ⏳️ @leinsterrugby - 15 @cardiff_rugby - 0 @RSAIreland @IrishRugby #URC pic.twitter.com/ASBxuFO6gd
Add to that list the Prendergast score in Clermont, arguably the most aesthetically-pleasing try scored by the province in years. The shift in attitude is leading to results, albeit in October and not yet in a May final.
For many reasons, it’s a shame that Prendergast misses Saturday’s Munster clash. One is the inevitable billing of young outhalf taking on young outhalf, the public deprived of the current holder of the Ireland 10 shirt facing Charlie O’Shea, a man who may well challenge him in the not-too-distant future.
In the shorter term, though, Prendergast is the single best individual illustration of Leinster’s desire to be more unpredictable. He has spoken of his wish to become more of a running threat. Hence he took on two frontrow forwards in his own 22 in Clermont. It was certainly a better decision that his previous one to take on a wing, almost coughing up possession close to his own line.
Last season, in more than 1,000 minutes of action, Prendergast made 588 carry metres and 13 line breaks. This year, in just 183 minutes, he is has already made four breaks and 124 metres. In other words, Prendergast is already 30 per cent along the way to match last year’s total line breaks and 20 per cent for yardage. All in circa 15 per cent of equivalent game time.
Alas, he will not bring that newfound game to Lansdowne Road this weekend. Albeit with Joey Carbery at the helm, a man fresh off the boat from – checks notes – Bordeaux, counters cannot be ruled out.
O’Shea is a natural where Prendergast has laboured to improve. Watch him break the line against Racing last weekend. Or finding gaps in chaotic situations when scoring a hat-trick for Ireland Under-20s in the summer. He is a counterattacking dream.
While that new youthful exuberance to Munster’s play will dominate attention, arguably their most significant change this season has come up front. The very front. The frontrow.
Marnus van der Merwe was signed as hooker, while tighthead props Kieran Brookes and Jack Aungier also came in the door. After a litany of frontrow injuries in recent years, general manager Ian Costello was good value when explaining the recruitment process for these players at the start of the season.
“We’ve targeted frontrow and set-piece as one of the key gaps in the squad,” he said. “Marnus [van der Merwe] has lots of other qualities but set-piece hooker is definitely one of his points of difference. He offers something different from the other hookers we have.
“Tighthead is probably the most obvious [area for improvement]. We were very unfortunate with Roman [Salanoa] and Oli [Jager] and the injuries that they have sustained. That placed a massive load on Michael Ala’alatoa and our young props. We addressed that by recruiting quality but also players that have evidence of being robust.
“Brookesy [Kieran Brookes] has over 300 first-class games, he’s played across multiple leagues and has so much experience, but he’s played 20 games a year plus for the last six years. Jack Aungier is the same, relatively young but has over 100 first-class games and plays 20 games a year.
“Them as people, the quality of them from a set-piece and rugby point of view, but also the robustness. It’s pretty clear what our intention around recruitment there was.”
Acknowledging the small sample caveat, the benefits of this recruitment are clear to see. In three of their four games so far, Munster have won all of their own scrums. The exception, curiously, was the Ulster game, that contest bringing a return of 83 per cent despite the Munster pushing Ulster off their own ball at times.
That opposition point is also worth raising, with Munster winning the ball back off opponent put-in this year. Only Racing had a clean scrummaging day at the office against the province so far this year, as Glasgow (80 per cent success rate), the Bulls (80 per cent) and Ulster (88 per cent) all faced a stern contest. Last season, Munster won the bull on just three per cent of opposition scrums.
The benefit of a good set-piece, for one, is avoiding penalty concessions that have you marching back towards the 22. Especially in this day and age of dominant rolling mauls.
On the other side of the ball, being able to attack off a solid basis is equally valuable, as Munster are showing under the tutelage of Jared Payne. The former Ulster and Ireland centre is responsible for the first three phases of Munster’s attack. At times, their first phase strike plays have been excellent.
Against Glasgow – who were down to 14 at the time – a lineout play put the ball in the hands of scrumhalf Ben O’Donovan, forcing the defence to deal with another playmaker in a dangerous position.
In later games versus the Bulls and Racing, Munster’s centres played crucial, decision-making roles in try-scoring strikes, adding width early in the phase and opening up space for running threats. Even when O’Shea dropped Alex Nankivell’s pullback against Racing, the ball landed perfectly to Shay McCarthy mid stride.
"There was something zebo-esque about that finish" 🗣️ Shay McCarthy turns on the burners to grab @munsterugby 's second of the game 🔥 #InvestecChampionsCup pic.twitter.com/BOod8HQthE
With Leinster’s transition looking more threatening and Munster shoring up their set-piece, all while adding some strike-play creativity, both teams will arrive on Saturday offering something different from what we have seen before. Not that Leinster have a weak set-piece or Munster a poor counterattack. O’Shea alone ensures the latter is not true.
Yet both sides come to this latest showdown resembling better teams that have made genuine progress at improving the areas that have let them down in recent times. Saturday is flirting with being one of the more watchable derby days in recent memory.

title: How can the public sector pay deal get over the line?
description: Pay remains at the top of the agenda, while the Government will have to clarify its demands for ‘productivity improvements’ in the public sector
content:
A unique aspect of the public sector pay talks that began on Monday, following the one-day strike on October 14th , is that there will be beneficiaries from any deal on both sides of the negotiating table.
Senior civil servants will directly benefit from whatever increases they concede to with the union negotiators by seeing their own wages increase as a consequence of any deal that is agreed.
On the other side, two of the four trade unions with people at the heart of the negotiation process, Fórsa and the Irish National Teachers’ Organisation , base their own salary scales on grades in the public service.
Other unions are onlookers in the talks but rely on them and will likely be influenced by them.
Pay was moved to the top of the agenda for the talks after an initial standoff. Unions insisted that agreeing a pay deal first amounted to a precondition.
[ ‘It’s not going to be smooth’: Government and unions start on long road to pay deal Opens in new window ]
The headline figures over the negotiations playing out behind closed doors at the Workplace Relations Commission are out there.
The unions want the Government to go beyond the €1.2 billion set aside in this month’s budget for a public sector pay deal. It has been suggested that the Coalition could stretch to €1.6 billion.
But the unions point to inflation that is now running at just over 4 per cent and have suggested inflation-proofing the wages of their members is essential. They have seized on the €2 billion figure that they say was floated by the Government side in advance of the talks.
In a briefing to his union’s members on issued on Friday, Kevin Callinan, general secretary of Fórsa, the biggest union in the public and civil service sector, described the talks so far as “slow and arduous” but suggested they would like conclude next week even if it was with no deal being agreed.
Productivity has been highlighted as a key issue by the Taoiseach and Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform and, as part of that discussion, artificial intelligence and its impact on work, hybrid working and mobility are all likely to be the subject of talks.
The umbrella term “productivity” raises some hackles on the union side.
“You should bring them down to the Mater emergency department on a Saturday night if they want to see how hard people work,” says one union official who dismisses the suggestion that adoption of technology is a major issue.
Alan Eustace, assistant professor at the School of Law in Trinity College Dublin , suggests productivity is tricky to measure.
“What does it mean?” he asks. “If it means more teaching hours, that’s one thing,” he adds, offering a view of how it works in academia.
“If it means more students taught, that’s a very different thing. The term gets thrown about a lot, but many of the conventional metrics for productivity don’t really work. And to achieve others might require additional spending when funding of third level is already a huge issue.”
Previous deals were rooted in broad terms around co-operation with change in the workplace. The Government will have to show sceptics in negotiations something tangible around what this means to strengthen its hand in the many engagements to come.
That, suggests Colm McLaughlin, professor of employment relations at UCD’s School of Business, is the more likely goal on the Government’s side.
“The Government has explicitly stated it wants productivity improvements as part of any new agreement,” he says.
“I suspect what it may actually be looking for is greater union co-operation with its modernisation agenda, particularly around technological change and new working practices.”
Advances in AI technology since 2024 means it will have to form more than a vague paragraph in any agreement about the importance of Ireland adapting and the public sector playing a leading role.
“In terms of productivity, the appropriate adoption of things like AI would be a great benefit,” says Danny McCoy, chief executive of business representative group Ibec .
He sees benefits too in the “ability to reallocate people across the public service and to things we are valuing much more highly, which would include things like defence and security”.
“I think there should be an openness to move in that direction,” he says.
He adds that the “need for ongoing change is always a factor”.
“We’re in a world of change and so it’s important there is the willingness to change but I think that’s probably there,” he says.
Kevin Callinan made it clear in the run-up to the talks that hybrid working was an important issue for his members, which include many white-collar workers.
It remains to be seen if the Government seeks to make significant changes to an employment landscape as varied as the private sector that would affect very senior staff.
The unions will likely want evidence justifying any requirements for increased in-person working.
There has already been resistance to a move by the Department of Social Protection to the number of days some staff were required to attend in-office.
Employers have repeatedly held that they have the final say on the issue, but, in the context of the negotiations, it may prove difficult for the Government to shift the dial.
A repeat of the last deal’s clauses on outsourcing is likely to be sought and with management in the Health Service Executive (HSE) trying to reduce its heavy reliance on outside agency staff due to the added costs, the unions will have a case to make for holding what they have in key areas.
What could prove to be a major stumbling block in the negotiations is the issue raised by the union side of restoring trust in the public sector’s industrial relations processes.
They make no secret of the fact they think the Department of Public Expenditure has too much power and exercises it as though the country is still in the grips of the recession that led to its establishment in 2011 in the wake of the economic crash.
Union officials will face challenges persuading senior officials from that department that changes are required.
The announcement by Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers in the budget of his intention to establish a new agency to evaluate spending and ensure value for money suggests movement in the opposite direction.
The Government side is bound, in any case, to insist that there be no further strikes and no clauses involving cost-increasing claims. A handful of currently unresolved disputes will normally be excluded so that separate processes can be completed. Nine were excluded in the last pay deal.
Overall, the negotiation process is far from perfect and both sides are aware of its limitations.
Much of the final language will likely be vague with dispute resolution mechanisms laid out and possibly a review process.
In the end, says TCD law professor Eustace, “the process works until it doesn’t but it has previously resulted in deals. They have contributed to prolonged periods of industrial peace.”
There are good reasons for both sides, he suggests, to want to agree another pay deal. However, the October 14th strike – and the significant recruitment to the unions around it – is a reminder why it is good, from the perspective of the unions, to be seen to pick a fight from time to time.
“Getting public sector pay index-linked now might be viewed as a major achievement,” says Eustace, of a potential measure that ties pay rises to inflation.
“But then people would take that for granted; the unions wouldn’t be seen to have a role in it.
“It’s like the State pension – a lot of politicians go around telling constituents: ‘I got you that tenner.’ The unions need to be able to point to what they got for their members.”
The unions have pushed for some mechanism to be established to ensure members are not caught out again by any spike in the rate of inflation.
McCoy of Ibec believes indexation should be a red line for the Government.
“It’s a reasonable expectation for any workers to be getting cost-of-living increases. It’s also a reasonable expectation for the Government, as the employer, to ensure they get productivity to justify any future price or wage increases,” he says.
“In that conundrum, it is never a good idea for a society to have a public sector that has index-linked wages to inflation.
“Once inflation is 15 per cent but your wages grow by 15 per cent you don’t care. But the public sector is only a subset of society and them saying: ‘I’m all right, Jack’ is not a good look for those on the outside.”
McCoy argues that the reasonable expectation is for a pay increase at or close to inflation but he believes linking inflation to wages would be “a kernel mistake”.
“Despite the strike, which was about the unions demonstrating the power they have, though, I don’t think any of this should all be dramatised too much,” he says.
“It’s a regular enough pay round in my view. And we have a functioning public service, which a lot of societies don’t have right now because of issues with their public finances.
“Ours could be better, of course, but ensuring a continuation of what we have, ensuring it doesn’t slide backwards, is an important starting point for this process.”

title: Irish fashion influencer Verona Farrell: ‘My final exit from the Gaeltacht was a teary car ride’
description: The Kildare woman, who divides her time between Stockholm and Dublin, on why her friends sometimes call her The Dictator
content:
I love people. I’m generous and open-minded and I am great craic at a party. I am also easily irritated. I’m trying to find a way to answer this that doesn’t make the idea of doing business with me unattractive, but when I am under pressure, particularly with work, I can become impatient. My friends refer to that version of myself as The Dictator. She gets things done but can be a bit of a cow in the process.
I regret going to Paris fashion week alone on my 26th birthday. I regret taking myself out for lunch at that crap restaurant and ordering that crap steak for €35. I learned to never, ever spend a birthday alone. There is no city romantic or fantastic enough to spend that day alone with your thoughts.
I am the youngest of five. I think it is the reason why I am a thick-skinned total chancer. I also think it is the reason my mam made me a fry every morning before school and why I didn’t know how to clean a toilet until I was 23.
My middle name is Rose, and I think that Verona Rose has a nice ring to it. I’ve always felt that I should do something with such a special name. If I wasn’t an influencer, I think it would be a great name for a stripper.
I get angry when people don’t use headphones in public spaces. This week in a restaurant I was subjected to the mind-numbing clatter of a children’s TV show from an iPad at the table next to me. I considered asking the little girl’s parents to turn it off, but it felt like a cartoonishly cruel thing for a childless person to do. I wish I had, because on reflection, it ruined my lunch.
[ Catherine Corless: ‘I was always a bit determined. I was teased a lot growing up’ Opens in new window ]
When I was about seven, I was in Dunnes Stores with my mam and I was allowed to pick out a packet of crisps. I came up with the idea that I would remember that exact moment for the rest of my life. It was a packet of prawn cocktail Skips and I can recall the entire scene in vivid detail. When I catch myself making an excuse for forgetting someone’s name, or a friend’s birthday, I always think about the determination I felt that day and I am reminded of the simple fact that if you really want to remember something, you will.
I am my happiest when surrounded by a large group of people who are doing the same thing as I am, every day. For that reason school in general really did it for me. In particular, sixth year stands out. I was unburdened by self-consciousness, the excitement of adulthood was just around the corner and I met and fell in love with someone totally fantastic and I spent most of my days in fits of laughter.
You either turn to dust, or into someone else, or meet Himself at the big pearly gates. I haven’t decided which to go with yet.
[ Comedian Justine Stafford: ‘I thought if I lost weight, it would help, but it spiralled’ Opens in new window ]
I get told that I look like Cate Blanchett, Sarah Jessica Parker or Celine Dion. Maybe someone that could sing like Celine, dress like Sarah Jessica and act like Cate.
The kitchen at home in Kildare when the seven of us are all home, slung over couches and chairs around the dinner table, discussing a topic in detail until three in the morning. It is simply the most loveliest place in the world to me.
Outside of that kitchen, the west of Ireland stands out to me. I went to the Gaeltacht every summer throughout secondary school, mostly in Connemara and once on Inis Mór. I always chose the coláistí with a reputation of being laid back to maximise potential “divilment”. I remember hopping over the dry-stone walls every morning as I ran for the bus to class and sneaking out to drink cans on the beach with the bean an tí’s son, and all of us jumping into the ditch when a car passed. My final exit from the Gaeltacht was a teary car ride back to Kildare with one of the cinnirí, having been kicked out two days before the last disco.

title: Simon Harris silent on Patrick O’Donovan phone call that preceded hospitalisation
description: Events in build up to Minister falling ill remain subject of much speculation in Fine Gael
author_name: Jack Horgan-Jones, Pat Leahy, Cormac McQuinn
content:
Tánaiste Simon Harris has declined to say if he spoke to Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan before he became ill at an EU event in Limerick last week.
O’Donovan, who has epilepsy, is recovering in hospital while speculation continues about events preceding the episode after which he was taken to hospital on Tuesday of last week. The Fine Gael Minister was treated in the intensive care ward for several days.
Colleagues, including Harris, have wished him a speedy recovery and return to Cabinet. Meanwhile, his department is being overseen by his secretary general, Feargal Ó Coigligh.
However, the events of last week continue to fuel speculation around Leinster House. In comments to journalists that morning, O’Donovan had criticised what he said were briefings against him, reported to be from a Fine Gael Cabinet Minister, that questioned whether his health would allow him to remain in Cabinet after next year’s expected reshuffle. The story ran on news bulletins and online for the morning.
A few hours later, O’Donovan stepped out of the EU meeting to take a call, according to reports, from a senior Government figure. Some time later, journalists were told that the afternoon press conference had been cancelled. The Minister was taken to hospital in an ambulance.
There has been considerable speculation about who O’Donovan spoke to during that phone call and what was discussed. Asked repeatedly this week if the Tánaiste had spoken to him, a spokesman for Harris declined to say yes or no. Instead, he said: “The Tánaiste speaks to his Ministers on a regular basis and has been in close contact with Patrick and his family in recent days. The Tánaiste spoke to Patrick as recently as [Wednesday].
“Patrick is stable and continues to be treated at University Hospital Limerick. The Tánaiste looks forward to welcoming him back.
“As you are aware, the Tánaiste has been on paternity leave and issued a detailed statement last Friday in consultation with Patrick’s family. The statement reflects the Tánaiste’s views. All the focus now is on the Minister’s recovery.”
Fine Gael deputy leader Helen McEntee said this week that she did not speak to O’Donovan.
