While he is recuperating, some TDs and Senators want to draw a line under recent weeks and move on. But others say there has been much discussion of recent events within the Fine Gael parliamentary party.
[ Minister rails against anonymous briefings Opens in new window ]
That includes the issuing of dual statements last Friday – first by the O’Donovan family, and shortly afterwards by Harris, both of which emphasised his ongoing participation as a Cabinet Minister.
Fine Gael TDs have privately shared “surprise” at the tone of the statements, particularly that issued by Harris, who said O’Donovan “serves with distinction in a key Government department and naturally will continue to do so”, adding that he had worked “diligently and competently in every role he has been entrusted with”, which Harris believed would “continue long into the future”.
It also admonished those who briefed against O’Donovan anonymously, saying such steps had “no place in the Fine Gael party and will not be tolerated”.
There is a view among some in the parliamentary party that Harris, as party leader, would be better served not issuing statements about anonymous briefings to newspapers – and puzzlement at the strength with which the Tánaiste endorsed O’Donovan’s continuation at Cabinet.
“Obviously on a personal level, we all hope he gets better, but you cannot say he’ll definitely be back and always be back,” said one TD.
Another Fine Gael member said: “We’re all paying attention to it because it’s a little bizarre.”
Earlier this week the deputy Government spokesman said O’Donovan’s department continued to operate as normal and further decisions would be made by the Minister in due course.
It was confirmed that Ó Coigligh would discharge the department’s administrative functions during the Minister’s absence.
The Irish Times asked O’Donovan’s department what kind of decisions must be made by the Minister himself and which can be made in his absence by Ó Coigligh.
The department said Ó Coigligh was continuing to discharge administrative functions and was ensuring continuity in the management of the department’s business in line with “the long established legal principle” known as the Carltona Principle. The department added: “This would not extend to significant policy or financial decisions.”
Under the Carltona Principle – named after a company involved in a legal case in the UK in the 1940s – the acts of departmental officials are synonymous with the actions of the Minister with responsibility for that government department.
The department did not offer details of any pending decisions that cannot be made until O’Donovan returns.
[ A flat tyre that’s also about to blow out from over-inflation – welcome to Budget 2027 Opens in new window ]
Following Budget 2027 , O’Donovan was embroiled in a row over funding for RTÉ after it was allocated €240 million for 2027, €20 million less than the broadcaster had been expecting under a deal reached with the last Government.
After a meeting between O’Donovan and RTÉ, his department said it would continue to “engage constructively” with the broadcaster over the coming weeks on issues that had been discussed, including RTÉ’s funding concerns and the delivery of reforms at the broadcaster.
The Irish Times asked his department if talks with RTÉ over its strategy for reforms, and ultimately any decision on its funding, would be delayed as a result of O’Donovan’s absence.
The department said it was envisaged that engagement between it and RTÉ “would be at official level in the first instance and that remains the case”.
In a statement, Fine Gael said its national executive had considered recent events. A spokesman said: “At the Fine Gael Executive Council meeting, members expressed their view that the anonymous briefing about the health of a Fine Gael colleague was not in keeping with the party’s values.
“The Executive Council supported the statement of the Tánaiste and Party Leader that such commentary is hurtful and has no place in the Fine Gael party.”

title: Dating in your 50s: Sharon Horgan is wrong. It’s not all freaks and weirdos
description: I admire Sharon Horgan but I strongly disagree with her depiction of dating in your 50s as scary
content:
I’d handed her over my phone so she could have a final read of the dating profile I had been tinkering with for the previous few weeks. Quiet evenings, lolling on the sofa, the app had asked me: “What three qualities do you like in a man?” I’d perused the adjectives offered, and decided on kindness, curiosity, confidence.
I’d answered more questions. “Age?” Fifty five. “Do you drink?” Eh, sometimes. “Exercise?” Yes. “Politics/children/star sign?” I left these blank – those were for conversations to have in real life (except star sign).
It asked for photos. Should I put up one of me in graduation gown from my master’s last winter, and the one in a swimsuit under a dazzling blue November sky? “Definitely,” my daughters said. The eldest swapped a picture where I was wearing a black jumper (“boring”) to one she had of me on a hike, back turned, surveying Djouce mountain.
Both daughters approved of the bio I’d written. The app also liked it. It gave me a thumbs up and said, “Great answer! This has the spark that gets people talking.” I was flattered.
“What are you looking for?” it asked me. “A long-term relationship? Or are you open to see where things go?” What a thing to have to decide there and then. There wasn’t really a description for what I wanted – which was to sit in the sun, have a glass of wine and a chat with a man that wasn’t my brother, an old buddy, or the husband half of one of my many lovely couple friends. I missed – to paraphrase Mark Zuckerberg – male energy. The good kind.
After four years I was ready to date again.
My beloved boyfriend died in spring of 2022 after a shock cancer diagnosis. His rapid decline from good health and wellbeing in just 14 months tilted the world off its familiar axis and broke my heart. My grief was very physical. I got sick a lot – throat of broken glass, painful rashes, a swollen ear cartilage. I lay in bed with Covid for a month, feeling like there was a tiny clawed creature sitting on my chest. Until, in the dark, rainy January of this year, I felt a change, and on the fifth spring, my dating profile complete, my eldest pressed upload.
The profiles of men came in. Divorcees, dads, the never-marrieds. Men who liked reading, and movies, and travelling. I went on dates. I talked. They talked. About their daughters in London, their sons in America. Respectful (mostly) mentions of their former wives and partners. Their gym routines, their fathers, the upcoming Leaving Cert. Their business plans, camper vans, football games. Their dogs, their mothers, their bosses. The books they’d read and gigs they had tickets for. I realised men wanted something similar to me; to sit in the sun sometimes, and enjoy a woman’s company.
I like Sharon Horgan . She is my age, so I take note of her. After she got divorced, she was snapped in the tabloids having a great, big, dirty snog on the side of a busy London road with Tim Burgess from The Charlatans. It made me laugh out loud and I thought, fair play to you Sharon. My admiration increased further when I read that she was in a relationship with Barry Ward , a very handsome Irish actor 10 years her junior. She was an inspiration to me.
When I saw the headline on her recent interview ahead of her new series Youth in The Irish Times – “ Sharon Horgan on suddenly being single in your 50s: ‘Will I just attract weirdos and freaks? ” – oh dear, was my first thought, have Sharon and Barry broken up? I opened the article and began reading.
“If you are in your mid-50s and you haven’t found your person to get old with, then you’re kind of f**ked.”
I was, ironically enough, away at a 60th birthday, and was having breakfast in the hotel with a group of 50-somethings – some married, some single, many dating. “Would you think of going on Bumble?” I’d asked a woman I’d met at the party the night before whose marriage had broken up. “Fumble, more like,” she said, but yeah, sometime, she would. We drank our coffee, a bit hungover, and I read some more of the article out loud.
“To suddenly find yourself single and thinking, well, what now? … At a certain age, who will be left? Will it just be the weirdos and freaks?”
Horgan asked: “How do you put yourself out there as a sexual person when you’re a pensioner nearly?”
In the final paragraph of the interview, it was revealed that Horgan was still with the lovely Ward.
It all reminds me of a new iteration of the cliched myth I’d hated for years (long before I turned 50 myself) that women become invisible in mid-life. It simply isn’t true, in my experience.
[ Youth: This might be the best art-imitates-life show Sharon Horgan has attempted Opens in new window ]
I believe people want someone to go out for dinner with, or see a movie, go dancing, grab a pizza and a beer, or share a bottle of wine with. To take a sauna and a sea swim, a hike, a bike ride, a gig, or a walk after coffee and cake, to grab a break from the routines of adult life – filling out health insurance forms, shopping lists, filing taxes, caring for elderly parents, completing work reports, giving lifts to grown-up kids. To cultivate a bit of adventure and magic with. Most people are well meaning, I’ve found.
So why am I not seeing this represented more in the media? Why does Sharon, cool Sharon Horgan, who kisses gorgeous men in public, who probably has oodles of her own money, who has shiny, bouncy hair, who wears vampy see-through black dresses to awards events, has toned arms and a fabulously high arse, who had the balls to leave her “proper” job at the age of 31 to write freelance comedy sketches and went on to become a hugely successful actor, director, writer – why does the noise around her new TV series tell me that dating in your 50s is scary?
One of the very best things for me about being in my 50s – besides the thrilling company of my two brilliant, beautiful grown up daughters – is that I do not want to get married, and I will not be having more babies. I have wonderful friends. I like to spend lots of time with them, and my sister and brothers, and my parents. I travel, go to gigs, parties, festivals. I write, read, garden, lift weights, box, swim, cycle. I like my own company. I know the difference between solitude and loneliness.
In your 50s, when it comes to romance, there is far less pressure than before, and none of the intimidating milestones of 25, 35, even 45, the obligations, the tedious routines. Dating in your mid-50s is about the craic, desire, distraction, friendship, amusement, admiration, affection, attention.
“One of the great things,” I said to the lovely man I’m seeing, “is that I never have to go shopping in Tesco with you.”
[ In your 50s it feels like time is rapidly running out. Time for what though? Opens in new window ]
It’s sort of like being a teenager again. The best parts. With the hard-earned knowledge that, at the end of the day, your life deep down is about what you want – not what society or culture tells you to want. Or any man. Or your mother. Or a journalist. Or a famous actor.
Life. It can overwhelm and sadden, but it also has a mysterious, regenerative quality, and this year, I have been reminded of this, of our creative capacity to begin again, and for new understandings. At any age. Youth or no youth.
Ann-Marie Power worked in media for 25 years. She recently completed an MFA in fiction at UCD. She lives in Dublin.

title: Now is the perfect time to plant roses. Which varieties should make the cut?
description: Desirable qualities include vigour, disease resistance, scent and a long flowering period
content:
I ’ve spent the last week thinking about roses. Climbing and rambling roses in particular, which I hope to use to partially screen one of my garden’s dilapidated but still beautiful stone outbuildings. The problem, much like Goldilocks in her pursuit of the perfect bowl of porridge, is the surfeit of choice. Almost inevitably, my shortlist of varieties has turned into a long one, with the emphasis on a host of desirable qualities including vigour, disease resistance, scent and a long flowering period as well, of course, as an abundance of beautiful flowers.
Determined to avoid choosing anything too chocolate-box in style, I’ve ruled out the perennially popular variety known as Rose ‘Constance Spry’, despite its famously beautiful, large, deep pink, scented blooms. It’s a similar story for Rose ‘Gertrude Jekyll’. Shocking, I know.
Rose ‘Pierre de Ronsard’, also known as ‘Eden’, is also off my list for the same reason, despite its long-flowering ways, excellent disease resistance and general vigour. My sincere apologies to all its many fans. But to paraphrase Goldilocks, it’s just not quite right for what I have in mind.
Wary of its vulnerability to blackspot and powdery mildew, the famous heirloom variety Rose ‘Zephirine Drouhin’ also hasn’t made it on to my long list, though I’ve plenty of gardening friends who love it for its almost thornless branches, shade tolerance and clouds of scented, deep-pink flowers. It’s a similar story for both Rose ‘Alfred Carriére’ and Rose ‘Albértine’, two varieties I’m forever prejudiced against, having grown them in the past and watched them succumb to black spot so often and so severely that by late summer the plants were almost leafless.
And while I’m still dabbling with the thought of ‘Rambling Rector’, this rampageous rose’s reputation for growing into a huge – albeit spectacular – beast almost impossible to keep in shape makes me very chary, the same reason why I’ve also ruled out Rosa ‘Kiftsgate’; Rose ‘Bobby James’; Rosa banksia ‘Lutea’; Rose ‘Paul’s Himalayan Musk’; and Rose mulliganii. All are unruly beauties only suitable for huge gardens where there’s scope for them to grow relatively unchecked.
If the rambling Rose ‘Frances E Lester’ flowered more than once in a growing season, it would be top of my list for its floriferous ways, dense clusters of pale, scented, elegant blooms, decorative hips and graceful growth habit. So too would the white-flowering and very beautiful Rose ‘Adélaïde d’Orléans’. But both are what is known as once-flowering, meaning they have one spectacular display each year in June-July rather than a succession of blooms over many months.
Likewise, I love the sound of Rose bracteata, a species-type, semi-evergreen, vigorous climbing rose whose clouds of golden-eyed, single white flowers appear from midsummer until the first harsh frosts. The only problem is that it’s not fully hardy, requiring a warm, sheltered spot with protection from cold winds, which is equally true of the delightful white-flowering climber known as Rose ‘Cooperi’. This makes both varieties unsuitable for my Midlands garden with its colder-than-average winters. A shame.
On the other hand, I reckon the climbing variety known as Rose ‘Crépuscule’, which was introduced into cultivation in 1864 by the famous French breeder Dubreuil, is “just right”, as Goldilocks would say. A historic noisette-type rose prized for its vigorous growth habit, long flowering period, tolerance of heat extremes, almost thornless branches and semi-double to double, scented, apricot flowers, it needs a high, sunny wall and a fertile, moisture-retentive but free-draining soil, both of which I can give it. Also “just right” for my purposes is Rose ‘Blush Noisette’ or ‘Noisette Carnéé’, a more compact, repeat-flowering climbing rose with large clusters of pale pink, deeply-scented flowers produced throughout the months of summer and early autumn. Introduced into cultivation in 1817, it remains a classic.
[ How to reimagine your garden with fresh eyes Opens in new window ]
If space allows, Rose ‘The Generous Gardener’ is also nudging towards the top of my list. From the stable of the late rosarian and breeder David Austin, it’s rated highly for its long flowering season, disease resistance, vigour, shade tolerance and the beauty of its scented, pale pink flowers. One of its few failings is that those same flowers are short-lived and vulnerable to damage by heavy rain. Another is its stiff, thorny stems, which make it more difficult to prune and train.
Others jostling for prime position include the semi-double, repeat-flowering compact climber Rose ‘Meg’, whose luminous, scented, pale peach flowers appear through summer and autumn; the white-blooming, repeat-flowering, modern climbing rose ‘Guirlande d’Amour’; and Rose ‘Desprez à Fleur Jaune’, a heritage variety from the early 1800s with creamy-yellow to apricot, deeply-scented flowers produced generously throughout the summer and early autumn months.
[ ‘I love the evening primrose in my garden. But will it become invasive?’ Opens in new window ]
Which will make the final cut? I’ve yet to decide. But I’ll need to do so soon, because late October-November is the best time of the year to plant all roses as bare root specimens, allowing the plants time to stretch their root systems deep into the ground before leafy growth begins again in spring.
Where to get them? Recommended stockists include altamontplants.com in Carlow; futureforests.com in Cork; riverlane.ie in Meath; Dublin-based mrmiddleton.com ; and online suppliers including pharmarosa.ie ; promessedefleurs.ie ; roses-andre-eve.com (André Eve, the famous French nursery specialising in heirloom rose varieties); and osen.de/en/ (Kordes, the famous German rose nursery).

title: Róisín Ingle: I used to hate hospitals, but becoming ill made me fall in love with them
description: Under-appreciated staff deserve better pay for the essential, vocational work they do
content:
N obody likes hospitals. This sounds like a statement of fact, but I’ll go out on a limb here and suggest that it might actually be an example of fake news.
For a start, it excludes a lot of people. The main people in the excluded category are those of us who had our lives saved or prolonged in a hospital. The so-called fact that “nobody likes hospitals” also fails to consider most of the people who work in hospitals, some of whom are in their dream jobs, helping the most vulnerable people in society.
I used to be in the “nobody likes hospitals” brigade. “I don’t like hospitals,” I’d say as a child if anyone suggested going near one. This aversion can probably be traced back to the time I got my tonsils and adenoids out, which was a scary time. But my aversion remained well into adulthood when I really should have known better.
Years ago, a close relative was in hospital for a prolonged period. While others in my family visited every day, I was, to my shame, mostly absent. When I did visit somebody in hospital, I usually kept the encounter as brief as possible. The hospital smell scared me. I felt lost in the endless corridors with crucifixes on the walls. I just didn’t like the places.
Then I was diagnosed with an illness. It has meant that, for the past three years, I’ve been in and out of the Mater public hospital in Dublin . I’ve spent time in the A&E, in surgical wards, in phlebotomy, in oncology clinics, in coffee shops, in hospital beds, in physio and on trolleys. I go to the cancer day ward every three weeks to get an injection of immunotherapy treatment from some of the finest people I’ve ever met, including many people making new lives in this country. I can honestly say I now love hospitals, especially that particular hospital.
I don’t wrinkle my nose up when I go into the Mater anymore. The fragrance of chemical cleaning products, with a hint of boiled carrots, smells like compassion to me now. When a friend was in the Mater for heart surgery, my love for the place meant I could show him around and visit him for hours, chatting to nurses and doctors and porters like they were old friends. The Mater is where I’ve had some of the most challenging moments of my life, but it’s also where I feel safe and cared for in a profound way.
I was in the Mater again the other day to get my big toenail removed. The worst part turned out to be the five or six injections around the toe to deliver the local anaesthetic. As usual, everyone I encountered was kind and caring and did their best to make me comfortable. I lay on the surgical trolley and I found myself sobbing in front of Sylvia, one of the medical staff. While her colleague tugged away at my toenail, I cried. I was not weeping for my ingrown toenail. Believe me, I was happy to have it gone. I was crying because I’ve come to know this place so well.
Nobody likes hospitals. And of course, I would prefer if I was never in here. But I am a regular now and I will be for as long as I live. Coming to know this place so intimately has been a gift. I don’t know what other adventures await me in the Mater, but it will always feel like a safe space to me. A place where I can weep out loud in comfort.
Nobody Likes Hospitals. A German indie-rock band called Giant Rooks has a song of that name. I discovered them while writing this column. It’s a song about visiting a person in hospital, thunderclouds hovering over the building, rain falling like tears on the concrete walls. “Every time I visit you, you talk about just how much you hate this place. And I answer every time that nobody likes hospitals.”
Nobody likes hospitals? Not true. There is a lot of love for them. Or there should be anyway. Love for the people who work on hospital wards across this country. I especially love the ones who are not paid enough and who are not recognised adequately for the incredible work they do. There are too many of them, unfortunately.
Some of these workers who love hospitals and love what they do have recently had to stand outside with signs protesting their current rates of pay . They are standing up for their rights at a time when their pay has fallen way behind the cost of living and diminishing resources are making their jobs even harder.
This is not an original thought, but whether it’s nurses or teachers, most public service workers are not paid enough for the important, essential, vocational work they do.
Nobody likes hospitals. But everybody should love hospitals. Give them more money. Show them more love. For crying out loud.

title: Tesco’s Irish profits rise 9% as it pays €120m dividend to British parent
description: Retailer’s Irish arm increased its turnover last year by 4.6% to €3.75bn
content:
Tesco ’s Irish operations increased its pretax profits last year by 8.6 per cent to €211.6 million, latest accounts show.
This allowed the company to pay a €120 million dividend to its British parent, the same amount it paid out in 2024.
Its corporation tax bill amounted to just under €32 million last year, up from €28.9 million a year earlier. At the end of February, the Irish company’s accumulated profits had tipped over the €1 billion mark for the first time.
Accounts for the 53 weeks to February 28th, 2026 for Tesco Ireland Ltd show its turnover rose to €3.75 billion from €3.45 billion. There was an extra week of trading in last year’s figures.
The directors’ report states that like-for-like sales growth was 4.6 per cent. Its pretax profit margin ticked up last year, coming in at 5.7 per cent versus 5.4 per cent in 2024.
According to the directors’ report, Tesco’s online shopping business covers 92 per cent of the population of Ireland. Online sales achieved double-digit growth while nine new shops were opened in the period. It also launched its Whoosh rapid delivery service here, connected to 31 stores.
Food sales grew by 5.1 per cent on a like-for-like basis while its Finest range of products achieved growth of 11.8 per cent.
The directors said the company’s strategic priority was a focus on removing price as a reason for customers to shop elsewhere. Last year it ran an Aldi price match scheme and partnered with Aer Lingus on the airline’s Avios rewards programme.
Tesco employed 13,676 staff (up 206 on the previous year) in 2025, with its total payroll costs amounting to €503 million.
The company said it spent €18 million in increased pay and benefits for staff, increasing the average hourly rate to a market-leading €18.13.
Directors’ remuneration last year reduced to €2.6 million from €3.4 million in 2024. The number of directors who served during the year reduced from five to four.
Tesco has 194 outlets in the Republic at present, with another four due to open by the end of 2026. This means it is set to open its 200th Irish store early in the new year.
The accounts show that Tesco acquired McEvoy’s Eurospar retail supermarket in Virginia, Co Cavan last year for €3.24 million.
In August, it was announced that Andrew Yaxley would return as chief executive of Tesco Ireland, a role he first held 11 years ago, as he effectively traded positions with Geoff Byrne, who took over from Yaxley as chief executive of Booker Group.
Yaxley has worked in various roles across the group for nearly 25 years in Ireland, Britain and Czechia. He served as the head of the Irish arm of the retailer from 2015 to 2018, before moving to the UK parent as its chief commercial officer.
He subsequently served as chief executive of Booker, a wholesale group owned by Tesco since 2020.
The Tesco group is led by Irishman Ken Murphy. Latest results from the Tesco group showed sales at its Irish business rose in the first half of the year, driven by growth in its fresh and packaged food offering.
Tesco, which claims a 24.1 per cent share of the Irish grocery market, said strong like-for-like sales growth of 4.1 per cent was driven by volume increases. Total sales growth of 6.7 per cent was driven by a contribution from new space.

title: Tesla and SpaceX merger: can Musk defy the conglomerate discount?
description: Investors are usually wary of sprawling enterprises, whose market value tends to fall below the combined value of its constituent businesses
content:
Investors are usually wary of companies that try to do everything. Elon Musk has made a career out of persuading them to make an exception, so perhaps it wasn’t surprising when investors cheered the idea of a combining SpaceX and Tesla , with both stocks rising in price.
Bulls point to the obvious links between the companies. Tesla sells cars, batteries and power infrastructure to SpaceX, and is collaborating with it on Terafab, a chipmaking venture.
A merger could also cut through the bureaucratic complications of Musk’s sprawling empire, making it easier to shift capital and resources between businesses without having to secure separate board and shareholder approvals.
However, a merger would also create a potential valuation headache, and raise the question as to what exactly investors would be buying.
SpaceX has already expanded beyond rockets and satellites into artificial intelligence and social media. Add Tesla’s electric cars, energy business, self-driving technology and robotics ambitions, and the result would be a company spanning a huge range of industries.
Normally, investors are wary of such sprawling enterprises, resulting in a conglomerate discount – the tendency for a company’s market value to fall below the combined value of its constituent businesses.
Complexity makes performance harder to assess, while profitable divisions risk subsidising loss-making ventures. Investors keen to cash in on SpaceX’s lucrative satellite business, for instance, might be less keen on funding a robot army, doubting Musk’s boast that Tesla’s Optimus robot will be “10 times bigger than the next biggest product ever made”.
[ Elon Musk sets lower sales target for Tesla as it explores SpaceX merger Opens in new window ]
Then again, should this $3.5 trillion merger eventually come to pass, perhaps the conglomerate discount will not apply. After all, financial fundamentals have never been successful at explaining the head-scratching valuations underpinning Musk’s companies. Why should a merger be any different?

title: What is the reason for the enduring public fascination with Elizabeth Holmes?
description: You Can See Everything, a new documentary about the disgraced tech entrepreneur, is breaking box office records
content:
T he Lighthouse cinema in Dublin has already sold out multiple screenings of You Can See Everything, a full month before the film ’s Irish release. UK cinemas are reporting “bonkers” demand for the movie, which debuted in the US last week to sold-out theatres, grossing the highest opening weekend for a documentary in 22 years. Reviews for the film have been glowing, but it is still unusual for any documentary to achieve this kind of reception, especially one that is three hours long. The world, it seems, just cannot get enough of Elizabeth Holmes , the film’s subject. But why has her story proven so compelling?
If you do not know Holmes’s story, it is not for a lack of popular cultural artefacts telling it. John Carreyrou’s book Bad Blood propelled the scandal to global attention in 2018, spending 100 weeks on the New York Times bestseller list. Then there was also a star-studded TV series spawned by an equally popular podcast, both called The Dropout, and a HBO documentary too.
Each of these tells the story of how Holmes dropped out of college to build a Silicon Valley empire backed by the likes of Henry Kissinger and George Shultz . Her company marketed and deployed a blood testing invention that, it turned out, wasn’t doing what she said it would. Once a darling of 2010s tech optimism, gracing magazine covers and with a paper net worth of $4.5 billion, Holmes is now an inmate at a minimum security women’s prison in Bryan, Texas, having been given an 11-year sentence for multiple counts of fraud for deceiving investors (the sentence was subsequently reduced).
So what is it about her that people find so compelling? It could simply be the morbid fascination we experience watching someone fall from such a high pedestal. Or perhaps there is something satisfying in seeing a chancer face their comeuppance. It can often feel as if justice, whether of the criminal or poetic variety, has limited reach in Silicon Valley. Holmes is from the same generation – is the same age, in fact – as that other college dropout, Mark Zuckerberg, who has managed to come through a decade of scandals and congressional hearings, only to end up even richer, more powerful and owning more castles than ever .
Holmes’s pedestal was higher than the rest of her generation. Her promise was loftier, that a single drop of blood was enough to diagnose disease. Her personal branding was not the hoodie and the MacBook of the tech bro with an idea; it was the ascetic minimalism and turtleneck of the genius with a vision. She was Steve Jobs, but young. And photogenic.
[ What Elizabeth Holmes and the Salt Path controversy tell us about stories Opens in new window ]
And her particular pedestal was gendered. She was the bossiest girlboss of the girlboss era, which was, in retrospect, higher in expectations for women than it was in actual opportunities.
I worked around a lot of start-ups in that period, and the people who got ahead were not usually the ones with the best ideas, but rather the ones who had the kind of unwavering self-belief that could convince investors they were worthwhile recipients of funding. They were the ones who could treat being told that they were wrong or misguided as proof that they were on the right track, that they were “disrupting” something that was clinging to old ways.
They were the ones with the laptop stickers emblazoned with “the people who are crazy enough to think they can change the world are the ones who do”. And for whatever reason, they were mostly men (they still are; even today 84 per cent of venture capital money goes to all-male teams).
Elizabeth Holmes seems to have had a kind of blind, almost preternatural self-confidence. Bad Blood is full of tales from people who knew her and who recall her imperviousness to facts or advice that would contradict her vision.
Perhaps this kind of extreme self-belief is what let her emerge unscathed from the gauntlet of criticism, belittling and doubt that would have made a more self-aware person falter, and whose blades seem sharper for women.
[ Kathy Sheridan: Tech bros welcome masculine energy back to workplace. It’s news to me it ever went away Opens in new window ]
This blind self-belief is also, probably, what led to her downfall. It is one thing to ignore the doubters, but quite another to ignore the experts who tell you that your idea is a scientific impossibility, or that wire fraud is illegal.
Here, I believe, also lies the thing that makes her – or at least her persona – so compelling. Even after everything was revealed, she maintained that same posture of defiance, telling The New York Times in 2023 that she was still working on healthcare inventions, and naming her baby, born during the legal proceedings, Invicta, meaning invincible.
Even this Shakespearean tragic flaw and the resulting downfall appear to have led to no epiphany. Instead the trailer for the new film depicts her, just weeks before reporting to prison, smiling serenely as if suspended in amber, impervious to our judgment, to facts, to reality, but still imploring us to trust her.
Nevertheless, as we would have said at her peak, she persisted.

title: Spoiler alert: Slow Horses, Strictly Come Dancing and an Irish actor’s strange beach limbo
description: As the BBC and Apple shows illustrate, the art of not revealing too much too soon has been complicated by on-demand viewing and the popularity of reality TV
content:
This column contains spoilers. Boring, isn’t it? But necessary. They’re for the finale of the sixth season of Slow Horses , which landed on Apple TV on Wednesday. That’s aeons ago in media time, and the season was based on novels published in 2019 and 2021, but it seems sensible to start with a warning in case the statute of limitations on spoiler crimes hasn’t expired as quickly as I thought.
I would like to talk about the death of Emma Flyte. She was the ex-copper turned “head Dog”, or MI5 head of security, and she had a good shot. Jackson Lamb, leader of the MI5 fringe office known as Slough House, described her as a “cracker” in Mick Herron ’s books, but her boss, Diana Taverner (played by Kristin Scott Thomas ), was less enamoured, pushing her into the chaotic orbit of Lamb ( Gary Oldman ) and his crew, where this week she came a cropper on a sandy Suffolk beach.
Shortly after being hailed a legend by another admirer, the openly salivating Roddy Ho (Christopher Chung), Flyte went for her tea, heroically taking out one redshirt mercenary but running out of bullets before she could dispatch Frank Harkness ( Hugo Weaving ), a recurring baddy, who fired a second, fatal gunshot.
I bring this up because when I interviewed Ruth Bradley , the Irish actor who played Flyte for three seasons, soon after watching a preview of the upcoming episodes in August, I asked if there was a day when she knew it would be her last day on the show. She gave a lovely answer.
“I had three, maybe four, days of lying on the beach when she’s already dead,” she said. Around her, the crew and her castmates were still filming. “Adam [Randall], the director, would come back and I’d be bawling, just, like, in tears. I was, like, ‘It feels like such a strange thing. I’m in this kind of suspended world where this character has died, but you’re all still doing your stuff.’ It was like limbo.”
When they finally wrapped, she went straight to the make-up bus, got the nod from producers and cut off her – or, rather, Flyte’s – long hair. “Usually when you finish a job, you go home and you kind of grieve the character in privacy, but having those days of just lying there was really cathartic,” she said.
It’s a strange game, acting, to borrow the lyric from Mick Jagger’s Slow Horses theme tune. I thought Bradley’s answer beautifully encapsulated the way in which actors maintain a parallel existence to the people they play until the day they don’t. I also knew it was unusable in the piece I was writing, as it was a spoiler. Even readers of the books, if they were expecting Flyte to die a quieter death in snowy Welsh woodland, as she does in Herron’s 2019 novel Joe Country , might have been miffed by the reveal.
As a viewer, avoiding spoilers can be hard work. Right now it’s a full-time job trying to swerve smugly enigmatic hints about You Can See Everything, the “mind-bending” documentary about Elizabeth Holmes , the Theranos fraudster, which has sold out some Dublin cinema screenings a whole month before it‘s released in Ireland.
As a journalist, meanwhile, the business of avoiding responsibility for spoilers has been complicated by two things: on-demand viewing, which muddies how long certain twists and plot points should ideally be kept on the down low, and the popularity of reality TV, which has done its bit to dismantle the old reporting principle of scooping your rivals at any cost.
There’s a reason, for example, that British media outlets don’t race to report the outcome of the BBC’s Strictly Come Dancing on Saturday nights, when the weekly eliminations are filmed and the results are discoverable, but wait instead for the Sunday show to air. Nobody wants to be hated for ruining everybody’s fun.
[ Mick Herron: the joyous juxtaposition of disgraced spies and cranky office politics Opens in new window ]
Darren Smith, managing director of Kite Entertainment, spoke about this on a set visit to Slane Castle last year while Kite was filming the first series of The Traitors Ireland months before its broadcast date. “In the early days of reality shows, people were happy to run spoilers. Now you guys don’t, because your readers don’t want them.”
It really is that simple. Indeed, the media has grown steadily coyer about the outcomes of television programmes even after they have aired, with the lucky coincidence being that nameless headlines encourage clicks anyway.
As for the high-jeopardy world of Slow Horses, the much-battered River Cartwright ( Jack Lowden ) seems to be having a spot of Russian nerve-agent trouble at the end of this season and makes no appearance in the trailer for the next one. Is he dead or is that classic misdirection? At the risk of contradicting myself, I think the answer is obvious, but I also wouldn’t dare state it here.
[ The Experiment on Channel 4: An unflinching and provocative horror show dressed as satire Opens in new window ]

title: ‘The stupidest way to make a movie’: Travis Knight on Wildwood
description: For the Masters of the Universe film-maker, bringing his latest stop-motion animation movie to the big screen has been a lengthy labour of love
content:
Travis Knight had recently scored a hit as the lead animator on Coraline, the Oscar-nominated film from 2009, when he read the still unpublished manuscript for Wildwood, a dark fantasy novel that follows a teenage girl who stumbles into an enchanted forest just outside Knight’s home city of Portland, Oregon.
A decade and a half later, Knight − who’s also the head of the Laika animation studio, and since Coraline was made has directed Kubo and the Two Strings and Bumblebee − has finally brought the story to the big screen.
It has been a busy year. Following his improbably hilarious Masters of the Universe , Wildwood is Knight’s second feature of 2026. Only weeks before its release, he’s still beavering away on post-production in London.
“I’ve been working on Wildwood for most of my career,” he says. “It’s just a crazy whim of the universe that things happen. It was not easy to do both these things at the same time, but I’m proud of both films. By the way, it’s not something I recommend to anyone.”
Brought to the big screen? Perhaps more accurately, Knight has brought Wildwood to life. Since 2005, Laika, an independent operation that specialises in stop-motion, has reinvigorated a cinematic technique that dates back to 1898. For Missing Link , its lovable Victorian misadventure from 2019, Laika’s five 3D printers produced more than 100,000 interchangeable facial pieces, often running around the clock. For Wildwood, the studio had to wait for the technology to catch up.
“The things we use to tell our stories don’t know they’re alive,” Knight says of the 136 sets and 231 practical puppets used in the making of his new film. “Metal, wood, fabric, silicone: left to their own devices, these things would happily sit on a tabletop, quietly doing nothing.
“An artist has to persuade them otherwise. You’re looking at something that’s inert, and with an adjustment of the eyes, a sagging of the shoulders or the reaching of a hand, you suddenly stop seeing what’s in front of you as an object and start seeing it as a person.
“To me that’s magic. Somebody takes a bit of their own life and puts it into something that has never lived. Someone thousands of miles away watches it in the dark and recognises the humanity there. That’s why I’m such a huge champion of this medium.”
In common with Laika itself, Wildwood is a proud product of Portland, the perfect quirky hometown for the film’s McKeel family, overprotective hippie parents who live with their preteen daughter, Prue, and her baby brother, Mac.
With a nod to Labyrinth, a babysitting stint goes horribly wrong when a murder of crows snatches Mac from a playground and brings the toddler deep into the nearby forest.
Joined by her awkward classmate Curtis, Prue ventures into that forbidden Wildwood only to find a fantastical netherworld of talking animals, powerful sorceresses, warring factions and grief, where a ruthless dowager governess, Alexandra (voiced by Carey Mulligan , leading an A-list voice cast that includes Mahershala Ali , Awkwafina, Angela Bassett and Tom Waits ), commands her army of mangy coyotes to annex kingdom after kingdom.
“I fell in love with this story immediately,” Knight says. “It felt like it breathed the same air as the kind of fantasies and fairy tales I loved growing up, things like Tolkien , Baum and CS Lewis . But it had its own unique flavour.
The original book was written by Colin Meloy, of the US indie band The Decemberists, and illustrated by Carson Ellis.
“Colin is an extraordinary artist. He set it in Portland, which is where I’m from, of course. Underneath that, it felt like an opportunity to tell a big, sweeping, fantastic story, but it also had an emotional core, a very primal drive at the centre, which I thought was pretty profound.”
The ambition of Christopher Nolan ’s Dunkirk and Peter Jackson ’s Lord of the Rings trilogy noted, few films since Hollywood’s golden age of biblical blockbusters and swords and sandals have attempted to stage battle scenes as ambitious as the denouement of Wildwood.
Caleb Deschanel, the veteran cinematographer behind Being There and The Passion of the Christ, swoops his camera through rushing troops as opposing tribes and magical animals clash violently. The breathtaking composition and movement would be almost impossible to recreate in live action.
“I deeply love animation,” Knight says. “One of the things we set out to do with this movie is to show that animation can be used to tell incredible, big, epic and emotional stories in ways that people don’t typically think of in this medium. It’s not easy to do that, particularly in stop-motion. It’s challenging. It’s also really rewarding when it works.”
It’s not just the technical requirements. In Kubo and the Two Strings, his directorial debut, the film-maker – who is the son of Phil Knight , one of the founders of Nike, and his wife, Penny – explored animation with an emotional depth that has more in common with the indie stylings of Don Hertzfeldt or Nina Paley than with conventional studio animation.
The emotionally impactful Kubo was shaped by the death of Knight’s older brother, Matthew, in a scuba-diving accident in El Salvador in 2004, when he was 33.
Wildwood revisits the grief of its predecessor.
“There’s more of my own life in this film than anything I’ve ever done,” Knight says. “Making this movie, you end up sharing so much of your life with someone else, revealing so much about yourself.
“Some people I’ve worked with on this movie know things about me that hardly anyone else knows. That stuff makes its way into the movie.
“It can be fatiguing to live in that space for a long period. But I am at the end of this 16-year-long journey. We did a soundcheck just the other day in Dolby Atmos. I’ve seen the movie a million times. I know every single frame, every line of dialogue. Yet I sit there and watch it with fresh eyes, and it moves me.”
[ Tycoon towers: Irish castles and houses owned by the global super rich Opens in new window ]
The film’s soulfulness manifests in its bemused and playful version of Portland, featuring such Portlandia-friendly establishments as Dripsters coffee emporium, and populated by oddballs likely to dress up as Darth Vader for a spin of their gyroscope.
Wildwood’s characters are equally drawn from life. Prue, the film’s heroine, looks rather like Maryse Knight, Travis’s Irish wife. (She was born in Portlaoise.)
“That’s funny,” he says. “Other people have said that Alexandra reminds them of Maryse. My Irish nephew is definitely the spitting image of Curtis. I love that these things find their way into your work, maybe without you even being aware of it.”
The daringness of Wildwood seems at odds with the rest of the industry. The homogenisation of contemporary animation is reflected in the box office. All four of the highest-grossing animated films worldwide – Ne Zha 2, Zootopia 2, Inside Out 2 and Frozen 2 – are sequels, highlighting studios’ increasing reliance on established franchises over original stories.
Laika (which is owned by Knight’s father) has never made a sequel. It’s not working to algorithms, the film-maker says.
[ ‘We said to Natalie Portman, we need you to protect the movie. And she did’ Opens in new window ]
“We live in an era that’s designed to be frictionless, where the world is increasingly designed to remove the effort and care that actually go into making something meaningful,” he says.
“Take artificial intelligence . You can create an entire world with nothing but a prompt. What we do at Laika really requires time, effort and care. The making of this film is a quiet act of rebellion, because it feels like a celebration and a triumph of artistry.
“There’s a human, an artist, behind every choice. It’s definitely not the easiest way to make a movie. In fact it’s the stupidest, hardest way, and the most painful way. But I think it gives the final film a soul.”
On that note, does Knight the chief executive ever clash with Knight the animator and director?
“I’d like to think that CEO Travis always lives somewhere in the brain of Director Travis. He’s saying: ‘Okay, look, we have to be responsible about some of the things we’re doing.’ I always make sure the work is approached in a really methodical and thoughtful way. We’re not playing jazz with the movie. We storyboarded this thing within an inch of its life over the years. All the money’s on the screen.”
“But I only feel like I’m on the right track if it scares me.”
Wildwood is in cinemas from Friday, October 23rd

title: Paul Henry painting fetches world-record price for the Irish artist
description: The Potato Harvest has sold for more than €1 million at auction in London
content:
Paul Henry’s The Potato Harvest, depicting Mayo people digging for potatoes, set a world record price at auction for the Irish artist last week, selling for more than €1 million at Sotheby’s in London.
Henry, described as a “visual poet” of the west of Ireland by Sotheby’s, is known for his landscapes and seascapes of Achill Island, where he lived between 1910 and 1919.
The Potato Harvest, an oil on canvas, which had an estimate of £250,000-£350,000, gained the top price in the Sotheby’s auction in London on October 14th, selling for £883,200 (€1,048,535), including the buyer’s premium.
André Zlattinger, head of UK and modern art in Europe for Sotheby’s, says the painting was bought by an international collector with Irish roots, who already has Paul Henry paintings and other Irish works.
“Paintings by Roderic O’Conor, William Orpen and Paul Henry are sought after by Irish collectors, expat Irish collectors, American, English and international collectors,” he says.
Irish art, he says, is comparable to Scottish and modern British art in terms of price and demand, adding that beautiful figurative paintings such as The Potato Harvest and Turf Gatherers by Paul Henry rarely come up for auction.
“There is a number of them in public collections, but there has only been a handful of them in auctions over the last 20 years,” he says.
Arabella Bishop, an art adviser in Dublin, says the world-record price achieved by Paul Henry “demonstrates the appetite that exists for Irish art internationally and highlights the value of exposing our artists to a wider pool of collectors”.
Bishop believes such international exposure strengthens its international reputation, and proves there is a wider market appeal for Irish art. The previous highest price achieved for a Paul Henry painting was £622,500 at a Christies auction in July 2021 for the painting, Mountains and Lake, Connemara.
Other Irish artists also made an impact at the auction of modern British and Irish art. William Orpen’s painting Little Spanish Dancer – which was auctioned for the first time – sold for £358,400, almost double its lower estimate of £180,000 at Sotheby’s.
Gerard Dillon’s Boy Catching Crabs in Connemara sold for £281,600 to an international collector – more than double its upper estimate of £120,000. And Roderic O’Conor’s painting, Red Rocks and Foam, sold for £243,200, above its estimate of £150,000-£200,000.
Not all Irish paintings sold – two Jack Butler Yeats paintings and a Paul Henry failed to sell. It shows that even works by these famous artists are sensitive to asking prices.
Also in London, Christie’s held an auction of British and Irish art on Wednesday, where another Paul Henry painting, The Fairy Thorn (£100,000-£150,000), held in the same collection since 1929 went under the hammer. It sold for well in excess of its estimate, achieving £256,000. It was first exhibited in New York as part of Contemporary Irish Art: First American Exhibition and bought by John Jakob Raskob, a prominent businessman who built the Empire State Building in New York. Jack Butler Yeats’s The Crown of Ocean, painted in 1945, had an estimate of £100,000-£150,000 and sold for £128,000.
There were also high expectations for the Gerard Dillon painting The Cottage Window (£70,000-£100,000), which had been in the collection of the late Zoltan Lewinter-Frankl since 1950, the year it was painted. Hungarian-born, Belfast-based Lewinter-Frankl was a significant patron of fine art in Northern Ireland, collecting works by artists including Dillon, Colin Middleton, Daniel O’Neill, Basil Blackshaw and others. It sold for £200,000.
Meanwhile, new collectors of art looking to buy more affordable paintings by living Irish artists may be drawn to works in the current online auction of prints, paintings, photographs and posters by Lot 100, which ends on November 3rd.
Some of the standout pieces in the current auction include Cora Cummins’s etching Hedge Verge (€300-€400), Gillian Hennessy’s oil on canvas, Coastal Lines (€500-€700). The watercolour on paper of Lake Constance by Sophia Rosamund Praeger (1867-1954) also has a keen estimate of €300-€500. The Co Down born artists and sculptor also wrote and illustrated children’s books as well as providing botanical illustrations from the books of her brother, the naturalist, Robert Lloyd Praeger.
Finally, antique dealers throughout Ireland mourned the death of Robin O’Donnell this week. O’Donnell, who ran Hibernian Antique Fairs in venues throughout Ireland for over 30 years, was an enthusiastic and charismatic promoter of antiques and fine arts. A friend to small dealers and antique shop owners in towns across Ireland, he described himself in an Irish Times interview with Michael Parsons in 2016 for this column as “a complete antiques nut who loved everything old”. O’Donnell grew up in Limerick and ran an antiques shop in that city from 1984 to 2000. He lived with his wife Lorraine in their home near Ballina, Co Tipperary. O’Donnell died on Sunday, October 18th, following a short illness.

title: Two punchy, perfect salad recipes for shorter days
description: We have an abundance of great salad leaves in Ireland at the moment and these two sides will allow them to shine
content:
T his week we are moving towards winter salads – dishes perfect for when darkness has arrived but we’re not quite ready to leave behind the feeling of heat and light on our skin. Salads still have a massive part to play in our cooking over the next few months; they just have a different ethos.
The trick at this time of year comes in moving to more robust ingredients, namely cabbages and kale, root vegetables and bitter leaves. Luckily, we have loads of winter produce thanks to the polytunnels and controlled environments modern farming now offers. This week’s recipes focus on bitter leaves and kale, both packed with flavour and nutrition. They show that fancy food can also be healthy.
First up it’s the bitter leaves, in what we call a “Green Goddess” dressing. It’s essentially like a salsa verde with some dairy added to let it out a bit. This coats a mixture of mustard leaf, baby gem and deep red radicchio. The contrast of herbs, acid and capers with the bitter leaves is beautiful alongside a range of dishes. I’ve topped this with some toasted pine nuts and grated Parmesan to give it a nutty, creamy finish. This can be served as a standalone dish but is also beautiful alongside a steak, some roasted chicken or dare I say ... at the Christmas table.
The second salad involves stunning Irish kale, which will be in abundance over the next few weeks. It’s both robust and tough to eat in its raw form so it gets a little blanch and refresh in iced water before we start cooking it. After that, it’s dried off and the classic Caesar dressing is applied. This involves blending a collection of ingredients that pack a punch: mustards, anchovy, Worcestershire sauce, pepper, Parmesan and sea salt make up the foundation before being mixed with some vegetable oil to a salad cream texture. The kale gets a liberal lathering before it’s crowned with crispy fried breadcrumbs and some more Parmesan. Like its predecessor, this is beautiful on its own or you can power it up with some poached fish or a crispy skinned chicken breast for a midweek meal that delivers on flavours while also providing autumnal fuel.
Tip of the week: Kale can be tough when raw, so give it little blanch and ice bath before cooking.

title: I tasted 21 affordable malbecs and the results were surprising
description: John Wilson: I just don’t think this grape was meant to be turned into lower-alcohol wine
content:
Having looked at some premium malbec a few weeks ago, today I turn my attention to the less expensive wines. I tasted 21 malbecs in total, mostly from Argentina but also some French, Chilean, and Australian wines. My test selection included wines from all of the major multiples, and all cost €12 or less.
Malbec is originally from southwest France , where it was one of the blending grapes in red Bordeaux and the primary variety in the wines of Cahors. Today, Argentina is comfortably the world’s largest malbec producer and has been very successful around the world, including in Ireland.
I was looking forward to this tasting; malbec from Argentina is typically perfumed, rich in dark fruits with velvety smooth tannins and good balancing acidity, and the inexpensive versions can be very good. But it didn’t work out as I expected.
At one stage, most malbec from Argentina came in at a warming 14-14.5 per cent alcohol, but more recently producers have been pulling back a little, possibly to appeal to consumers seeking lighter wines, and also to fit in with UK excise duties. Whatever the reason, the vast majority of wines in this tasting were 11-13 per cent. And it didn’t always make for pleasant tasting.
I don’t think malbec is designed to be a low-alcohol wine. Instead of all that lovely ripe fruit, some had high acidity and seemed a little too light and scrawny. With others, including the wines below, it worked better. Malbec is the usual suggestion to match with steak, but with these lighter wines you could think about most red and white meats.
Lovely floral aromas, fresh juicy dark plums with good acidity and plenty of rich fruit. A great budget-friendly wine to enjoy on cold autumn nights.
Rich, ripe, sweet dark fruits with a rounded finish and decent length. A stand-out at the tasting.
Light to medium bodied with concentrated plum fruits, subtle vanilla and toasted oak, and good acidity.
Medium bodied with good, sweet, ripe dark plum fruits and a soft easy finish.

title: In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak: Wonder and intrigue on every page
description: A work with two crowning glories: the inventive narrative architecture and the luxurious prose
content:
Writing has been described as an act of daring. For a writer to present a 600-page novel takes some neck. My pyjamaed eight-year-old hauled Elif Shafak’s In One Brief Moment All Eternity into her lap and read excitedly: “When he wakes up this morning, only two thoughts cross his mind: that he is going to kill the woman he loves, and that he is going to do it today.”
The opening line is dazzling. Wonder and intrigue continue on every page of Shafak’s semifictional chronicle of French author Gustave Flaubert’s life and writings. The work has two crowning glories – the inventive narrative architecture and the luxurious prose.
Flaubert’s dark imagination and his fascination with those most marginalised are dissected through the fictionalised perspectives of people, characters, places and objects that shaped his life and his stories. Each new point of view, including The Corpse, The Acrobat, The Green Ribbon and Syphilis allows anticipation to canter throughout. The prose is lush with sensory detail, a tense air described as “thick as dough”.
Flaubert is an odd little boy, born in Rouen in 1821. His family lives on the grounds of the hospital of which his father is chief surgeon, providing a wonderful hunting ground for the child’s story-hungry mind. Sent to study law in Paris and secretly exploring his talents as a writer, Flaubert enters a colourful and hedonistic period of his life, adventuring through the backstreets of cities as far as Istanbul.
Like the horse in Flaubert’s most famous carriage scene in Madame Bovary , Shafak’s writing begins to gallop as middle age takes hold of Flaubert and the Franco-Prussian War takes hold of France. An indelible portrait of the people of Paris is captured in a staggering account of desperation that assuages all fears for the reader of a saggy middle in this epic.
For readers of Flaubert’s works or biographies, the novel may be even more indulgent. Regardless of familiarity with the man or his writings, Shafak’s reimagining of the author’s creative inspirations is fascinating. In One Brief Moment All Eternity is a kaleidoscope of observations of a great artistic intellect, of a tumultuous 19th-century France, and of the torturous life that every lover of literature knows all too well.
Céire Sadlier is a writer and a freelance reviewer

title: Letters from Irish in the US, 1818-1972: Writing back with bitterness, fondness and more
description: A new collection of 62 letters shows the enormous emotional range of Irish emigrants’ experiences in the US – and complicates narratives of national loss and American opportunity
content:
“I suppose ye thought I had forgotten ye altogether,” wrote Mary Anne Rowe from Massachusetts to a friend in Co Kilkenny in 1888, “but my dear friend, it is not through any lack of friendship that I stayed so long without writing to ye. I do feel so bad when I go to write to home … that I scarcely know what to do.”
For generations of Irish people, letters across the Atlantic were the only thread connecting their new world to an Ireland lost and left behind. Their correspondence recorded not just their experiences in America, but also their memories and feelings about the place they almost always called “home”.
Nobody has done more for the preservation of these letters than historian Kerby Miller, whose landmark 1985 book Emigrants and Exiles used them to argue that many saw emigration not just as seeking a new life across the ocean, but as a collective tragedy of deoraíocht (exile) .
More than 7,000 letters collected and transcribed by Miller form the Imirce Collection at the University of Galway , and this new selection of 62 letters shows the enormous emotional range of emigrant experience. Coming from all corners of Ireland, all confessional and class backgrounds, they complicate narratives of both national loss and American opportunity. Letters home were not just communication and news, but personal and collective narratives often trying to explain, encourage, self-justify or lament.
Emigration was a defining feature of Irish life, and the “successive waves of departures from Ireland constitute”, Breandán Mac Suibhne writes in an excellent introduction, “one of the largest population movements in the modern era”, one with important echoes in Ireland today. That mass movement was “at once coincident with and commanded by” the emergence of global capitalism and imperialism. For the Irish in the United States, whose numbers are hard to fathom, that movement was only ever one-way: of those in the early 1900s, just 10 per cent ever went home, compared with more than half of Italians.
Sooner than I would work for a farmer in Ireland, I would cut off my good right hand … Homesickness is something that’s natural. I often get a relapse of it, but somehow there seems to be no cure only to stand it
Many looked back with bitterness even when missing home. Neal Campbell wrote from Ohio to Tyrone in 1819 lamenting “the systematic tyranny, distress and oppression” at home. “I am proud to be away,” Margaret McCarthy wrote to her family on the Cork-Kerry border in 1850, from a country where a landlord or tax collector “would have the satisfaction of once impounding my cow”. Though she fondly remembered the “innocent amusement” of home, she saw Ireland now as “the gulf of misery, oppression, degradation and ruin of every description”.
The greatest contrast between America and Ireland was the promise of “independence”. “After the Famine,” Miller writes, “most Irish emigrants were the sons and daughters of landless agricultural labourers, who often had been more exploited by their farmer-employers than were the latter by their landlords”. “Sooner than I would work for a farmer in Ireland,” wrote John F Costello to his family in Croagh in 1883, “I would cut off my good right hand.”
America was, Costello wrote, “as good a country as there is in the world today for a poor man. The majority of what men is in the country have risen from their own industry. Any man here that will work and save his earnings, and make use of his brains can grow rich.” “You can be,” Bartholomew Colgan wrote in 1854, “your own master.”
Miller’s introductions to each letter show not just his vast knowledge of the sources but also vital contextual information. He notes, for example, the Presbyterian and United Irishman family of William Hill, who wrote home to Antrim from South Carolina that he had enslaved “property” worth $6000. “Isn’t this horrid? say you,” he added, anticipating the condemnation of his republican religious relatives, one of many examples of values and politics diverging across the Atlantic, even if a commitment to Irish independence was near universal.
[ Love charms, frog bread, letters and wakes: How the Irish and Italians handled emigration to the US Opens in new window ]
Letters were often clear-eyed about the inequalities and exploitation that coloured the American dream. “The name of America at home sounds extra,” explained James Chamberlain in 1889, “but when people get there, they find it a different world. Any person who can make a fair living at home are better stay there,” rather than compete with the endless supply of immigrant labour “from all nations”. Yet even when they lament their challenges and misfortune, emigrants show a striking confidence in opportunity. “I would not advise any one to come here that can live comfortable at home,” wrote Ellen Rountree back to Dublin in 1851, “yet there is work for every person.”
[ Letters from America: ‘I would not advise anyone to come here that can live comfortable at home’ Opens in new window ]
People would bear a lot in America given what they were leaving behind, the horrors of which were difficult to describe during the Famine. An illiterate Irish-speaking Mrs Nolan from near Kilkenny dictated a letter to her son in Rhode Island in 1850, saying “on my two bended knees fresh and fasting, I pray to God that you nor one of you may never know nor suffer what we are suffering at the present”. “We will all die of famine,” wrote John Nowlan from Bunclody in 1847; “the people the young and old are dying as fast as they can bury them.”
Such letters show how distance rarely severed family ties and obligations. Nowlan and many others begged for money or tickets across the ocean. Mary Rush from Sligo pleaded with her father in Quebec that “if you knew what hunger we and our fellow-countrymen are suffering, if you were ever so much distressed, you would take us out of this poverty isle … for God’s sake take us out of poverty and don’t let us die with the hunger”.
Remittances often did come, in their millions, vital lifelines for families to be “able to pay our debts and raise our heads”, as Miller notes a grateful Donegal man saying. “I hope you do not think it is degrading you I am by offering you money,” wrote Colgan to his brother. Miller recounts one Roscommon man commenting that his relatives need not send pictures of themselves (“for we know well what they look like”), as the “pictures that I would like to see are a few of Abraham Lincoln’s” from $5 bills.
News was often as eagerly sought as money. “Write to me about all the folks, what has become of them, etc”, wrote Rose McCormick Williams back to Westmeath in 1879; “inform me all about Ireland, as I have but little recollection of it”. Many feared forgetting, and never escaped the longing. “Homesickness is something that’s natural. I often get a relapse of it,” wrote Costello, “but somehow there seems to be no cure only to stand it.”
On both sides of the Atlantic people yearned for letters, often with endless gossip about people from home and questions about those still there. Mac Suibhne notes how the 19th-century Donegal diarist Hugh Dorian wrote that an American letter was always “anxiously awaited and as joyously received”. “You would often write,” James Nowan wrote to his brother in Nova Scotia of their father, “if you witnessed the poor old man striving to open and read your letters when he receives them. He would almost be beside himself from ecstasy of joy.”
Perhaps what comes across most from Miller’s selection is what Mac Suibhne calls the “deep ambivalence” many show to both Ireland and the United States. “Things are the same as in Ireland,” wrote James McFadden from Iowa to Donegal in 1897, “every year something new comes up to make the rich man richer and the poor man poorer.”
“When you have money, it is all right,” wrote Alexander Wilson from Brooklyn to Ballymena in 1899, “but when you have none, you are not wanted.” Thomas McIntyre wrote from Boston to his sister in Tyrone in August 1855 saying that “as I sit here alone” they all back home would be at the local fair: “but as Robert said one time there are no Donemana fairs here. There is nothing here but work hard today and go to bed at night and rise and work harder tomorrow. Nothing but work, work away.”
For millions the journey was into the future, one they often struggled to explain to the isle they left behind. “You see, in this country,” Margaret McNally Keefe wrote home to Armagh in 1933, “the working class of people have everything in their homes … electric lights, bathtubs, gas stoves, and about every family has an automobile.” Agnes Kelly wrote home to Roscommon in 1967 that by contrast “Ireland is a sort of fairy tale. We have never told [our children] of the realities of life or living over there and would not encourage any of them to visit there. When we left there, we left the old world behind; we are all American citizens and proud of it.”
No amount of correspondence could stop the Atlantic widening, but millions of Irish-Americans have of course come to visit their ancestral homeland, at times with views and expectations that seem foreign to Ireland today. Hundreds of thousands of emigrants and exiles have also come to our shores seeking opportunity and prosperity in an Ireland our ancestors could only dream of abroad. This rich collection reminds us of the diversity and complexity of the migrant experience, and of our shared history as a migration nation.
Christopher Kissane is a historian and the host of Ireland’s Edge.
[ Ireland is experiencing a surge in immigration. This raises questions for our tax and welfare system Opens in new window ]
