Emigrants and Exiles: Ireland and the Irish Exodus to North America (Oxford, 1985) by Kerby A Miller
Miller’s book remains seminal for exploring the Irish emigrant experience in America.
Plentiful Country: The Great Potato Famine and the Making of Irish New York (Eriu, 2024) by Tyler Anbinder
By analysing emigrant savings, Anbinder shows how Famine emigrants fared surprisingly well.
The End of Outrage: Post-Famine Adjustment in Rural Ireland (Oxford, 2017) by Breandán Mac Suibhne
Through the story of one small Donegal village, Mac Suibhne reveals the revolutionary social upheaval of post-Famine Ireland.

title: The Real Nigel Farage by John Sweeney: Author offers a trial of the protagonist
description: A hearing from which defence counsel is largely absent and where the voters must be the ultimate judge
content:
Nigel Farage, MP for Clacton in Essex, is the leader of Reform UK, formerly the Brexit Party, and before that, the United Kingdom Independence Party (Ukip). He was one of the main forces behind the campaign to take Britain out of the European Union and has been in politics all his adult life, having joined the Conservative Party as a teenager but left soon after the deposition of Margaret Thatcher.
He was most recently in the news when, facing charges that he had failed to declare a £5 million gift from Thai tax exile and crypto-multibillionaire Christopher Harborne, aka Chakrit Sakunkrit, he resigned his Clacton seat and refought it in a by-election. “Let the people decide” seemed to be the message. The people did not let him down. Labour, the Conservatives, the Lib Dems and the Greens declining to play along, he was comfortably re-elected, polling twice the vote of his only serious opponent, a man in a dustbin.
John Sweeney’s book surveys the career from its beginnings, when, as a schoolboy at the elite private school Dulwich College, Farage was, according to the recollections of many contemporaries, noted for his racist language and “jokes” about the Holocaust.
Despite the no-doubt excellent teaching on offer, he seems to have left school with few, if any, academic qualifications but quickly found work in the City of London as a commodities trader, embracing the work-hard-play-hard culture of the “red braces” era. He is remembered as a moderately successful trader and a heroic boozer.
Sweeney offers “a trial” of Farage, but it is one from which defence counsel is largely absent and where the voters must be the ultimate judge. His case for the prosecution is robust, relentless and sometimes knockabout in style: the supremely dodgy friends and donors in business, the casual racism and cruelty, lack of interest in policy and reliance on easy bonhomie, but chiefly his responsibility for Brexit, which has massively damaged the British economy.
One can by no means be sure that the significant resentful vote that Farage has built up and nurtures will quickly disappear. All the more reason for those possessed of a little common sense or common decency to make sure they act, and vote, against it.

title: Yiyun Li on her sons’ deaths by suicide: ‘You can carry on being an alcoholic or you can carry on writing’
description: The Chinese-born writer on her new novel centred on Irish composer John Field, how she goes about writing exclusively in her second language, and coping with suicide
content:
Y iyun Li appears on my computer screen from her home in Princeton, New Jersey. There is a beautiful old fireplace behind her, artwork above, and in the far background, what looks like an exercise ball.
“I’m very happy,” she says. “Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize.”
It’s 8am where Li is, 1pm in Ireland. The Nobel winner was announced the morning we speak. I suggest Li might have been in the running, but she shrugs it off.
The 53-year-old “baby writer” is nevertheless a much-admired figure by readers and her writer peers. Among her celebrated works are the short story collections A Thousand Years of Good Prayers; Gold Boy, Emerald Girl; and Wednesday’s Child; and the novels Kinder Than Solitude; Where Reasons End ; and The Book of Goose . Her latest novel, Music Against the Night, is the first in a trilogy centred on the life of Irish Romantic composer John Field , and French pianist Adelaide Percheron, with whom he had an unhappy marriage in Moscow.
A familiar figure to many Irish people (at least those who have frequented the National Concert Hall, where there is a room named after him), the man who invented the nocturne is less well known internationally – he is remembered as a footnote in Chopin’s biography, if he is remembered at all. Li first came across him through Tolstoy.
“I always say I met John Field in Tolstoy’s autobiography,” she says. “He had a passage about listening to his mother playing, on the pianoforte, John Field’s composition. He went on to say Field was Mama’s master ... I started to do research, and I found him fascinating – the trajectory of his life and also that he no longer remains a well-known figure, even though he was influential.”
A slim biography from the 1970s gave some insight into Field’s life, though it was relatively scant in detail. Adelaide appeared only in a few short paragraphs, as an orphan who started life in Pondicherry, India, and wanted to be a pianist.
“It was just: by the way, he had this wife, he didn’t love her. They separated.”
I am curious about prodigyhood. Because prodigy is always a myth. The myth is made by people
Even Field’s life was loosely sketched, with more of a focus on music and scores. But Li says novelists “always get attached to things that are mysteries to us”.
“It’s always good when there are things unknown to us. I think I liked to make sense of these two characters, how they travelled so far, and how they carved a life in Moscow.”
She read work by contemporaries of John and Adelaide – a French female actor’s memoir about travelling from France to Russia, for example, and a French man’s memoir about living through the 1812 fire of Moscow. For the sections set in Ireland, she approached author and Irish Times columnist Fintan O’Toole, who was teaching in Princeton at the time. He gave her a reading list to familiarise her with Dublin of the late 1700s.
Naturally enough for the first in a trilogy, Music Against the Night focuses on the early lives of John and Adelaide. The structure is a kind of musical counterpoint – two separate lives speaking to one another across time and space.
The figure of the prodigy is important. Field, the son of a violinist and grandson of an organist, is musically talented but, like Mozart before him, his success is also calculated and cultivated.
“I am curious about prodigyhood,” says Li. “Because prodigy is always a myth. The myth is made by people.”
[ Partita by Barbara Kingsolver: What keeps people from their birthright in beauty? Opens in new window ]
There is also a neat counterpoint in the book between music as a utilitarian, profit-making endeavour and music as a higher force. At one point we encounter the composer Czerny writing and publishing compositions he has never played or heard.
“I’m not driven by anything – profit, of course, but not anything ineffable,” he says, to the astonished Field. “You seem to equate music with life itself.”
“No, no, no!” retorts Field. “I don’t equate them. I place music above life.”
I wonder does Li feel the same way about her own art.
“Ah, that’s a good question. Do I place my writing above life? No, I actually don’t think that’s the case. I am interested in life. I’m curious about a lot of things. I don’t usually make my art so glorious or mythical ... In the novel, [the composer] Clementi says even God cannot make perfect music. And I think art is the same way. It’s limited. Art falls short.”
Li, who was born in Beijing in 1972, was raised a maths prodigy. It was not until she moved to the United States in her twenties that writing entered the fold, and even then it was only by chance. In 1996 she arrived at the University of Iowa to study Immunology, only to discover the place was a writing mecca (among the graduates of its famed Iowa Writers’ Workshop are Flannery O’Connor, John Irving and Ann Patchett). She couldn’t help but catch the bug, taking up writing first in a bid to improve her English, but by 2005, she had a master of fine arts degree in creative nonfiction and fiction, and had already begun placing stories in The Paris Review, The New Yorker and elsewhere.
Thirty years on from that first move, Li still lives in the United States, and has always written in her second language of English. (Her relationship with China is complicated, she says. Until recently, she did not allow her works to be translated into Chinese.)
If you carry on, you can carry on being an alcoholic, or lying in bed screaming all day, or you can carry on gardening and playing music and writing
“Writing in a second language is an important part of my work because I always say a word has to be [used] only after I have thought about it thoroughly,” she says. “There’s that intimacy between a native speaker and the language, but I don’t have that intimacy with English. English is entirely acquired. So, I use dictionaries often, and look up the etymologies of words, so that I can have a better understanding of every single word I use.”
Li’s literary sensibilities were shaped by Russian writers – during her upbringing, Russian translations were among the few works of foreign literature not banned in China. But later, when she began to study creative writing, she found herself equally influenced by Irish writers.
“I always say I learned writing by reading William Trevor ,” she says. (The Cork-born author would later become an important friend to Li.) “But also, other Irish writers – John McGahern , for instance. I’ve probably read every single word by him.” (Li writes the foreword to a recent Faber reissue of McGahern’s Memoir.) “And Elizabeth Bowen , Molly Keane , this older generation. And of course, Colm Tóibín , Anne Enright and the younger generation. I suppose there is something in my nature that feels attracted to Irish literature.”
Li has been to Ireland many times and will pay a brief visit later this month for an event with Anne Enright. She hopes to see the Field Room in the National Concert Hall, but can’t stay long, as she has to dash back to the United States for the Pulitzer Prize presentation. She was announced a winner earlier this year, for her 2025 book, Things in Nature Merely Grow, a memoir for her son James, who died by suicide in 2024. Her son Vincent also died by suicide in 2017. Li describes herself as living in “an abyss”. She has no desire or capacity to escape this abyss, only to endure it.
[ Guilty Pleasure by Patricia Nilsson: Exposing how online porn has shaped our lives Opens in new window ]
“I saw someone this weekend – an acquaintance – I haven’t seen her since James’s death, and she said, ‘How are you doing?’ Then she said, ‘That’s such a bad question.’ ‘Well, yes,’ I said. ‘That’s the only question you can ask. How are you doing?’ I said, ‘Now listen, I have only two options. One is to drop dead, the other is to carry on.’ ... I seem to have chosen to carry on. I then think, if you carry on, you can carry on being an alcoholic, or lying in bed screaming all day, or you can carry on gardening and playing music and writing.”
Li was halfway through writing Music Against the Night when James died. After, she carried on.
“I think this novel, or, at least, working on it, sustained me and has sustained me since then.”
The work of Anne Carson, most notably her translation of four plays by Euripides, Grief Lessons, is also something Li cites as an important force in her life and experience of loss. She does not know Carson personally, but “love[s] her words from afar”.
And then there is music. When embarking on the project of Music Against the Night, Li took up piano lessons. (She jokes that she approached her teacher, a professional pianist who doesn’t take on hobbyist adult students, with a “book proposal”). Two days after James’s death, she arrived, as usual, for her lesson.
“People always ask that question: how could you do this? Even my piano teacher said: how could you do this? Or sometimes people would say: I would not be able to do it if I were you. Which is a very funny comment, because they are not me, right? They were not in my shoes. They would never know what I feel at that moment.”
“I could certainly just cancel the piano lesson, say I’m not up to it, which is understandable, but then I still have an hour that I have to face, in what I call this abyss. [So] I might as well just go to the piano lesson. My piano teacher and I were so sad we couldn’t talk to each other. She just sat there and said: ‘I don’t know what to say, let’s just do the drills.’ I learned a lesson that when we cannot say anything, we might as well just move our body ... To move the body and to use your brain are good ways to endure something tremendous.”
Music Against the Night is published by 4 th Estate. Yiyun Li will be in conversation with Anne Enright on Wednesday, October 28 th in Dublin’s Unitarian Church, hosted by Dubray Books. Tickets available on Eventbrite

title: Tries aplenty as Connacht secure bonus-point win over Zebre
description: Irish province showed lots of attacking flair, but defensive vulnerabilities will be a concern
content:
After the excitement and optimism generated by last week’s Champions Cup win over Saracens, this was more of a mixed bag for Connacht but still a much-needed bonus-point win against the URC’s basement club.
For Stuart Lancaster, there was satisfaction in seeing summer recruits Jerry Cahir and, coming off the bench, Will Connors make their debuts, along with the eight tries his side accumulated.
At the same time, he will be less impressed that his defence coughed up five tries and that the second half was equal on the scoreboard until Dave Heffernan’s last-minute try. Despite the glut of five-pointers in Galway, the province has scored 24 and conceded 23 tries so far this season.
Some satisfaction, too, for Andy Farrell, who named five Connacht players in his Nations Championship squad in midweek. In particular, he would have enjoyed the effective combination play of Ciarán Frawley and Mack Hansen.
The latter looked really sharp in his fourth game back from a lengthy injury absence while, notably, the former took over the kicking duties on the night from Sam Gilbert, and successfully made four of six conversions.
With Sam Prendergast nursing a wrist injury, Frawley is in position to start at outhalf for Ireland against Argentina on Friday week, so it was important for the Skerries man to get those opportunities off the tee.
The home side started where they left off in Europe six days earlier with a slick attacking move in the opening moments, but it was first blood to Zebre through Giacomo Ferrari after Connacht botched a lineout and Allesandro Fusco sniped to within touching distance, with Giacomi Ferrari punishing sluggish defence on the hosts’ own line.
Connacht responded through Finlay Bealham, who found a gap at close range off an effective lineout move, before Frawley converted. Hansen’s midfield break then created the opening for Harry West, with Sean Jansen powering over for the second try.
Cathal Forde finished another slick backline move before Gilbert crossed from a lineout attack, Frawley converting both to establish a commanding 26-5 lead.
Zebre hit back through Jacopo Botturi after a fortunate grubber, but Connacht responded as skipper Cian Prendergast finished a lovely move involving Forde, Hansen and Frawley.
However, the visitors then exposed Connacht out wide, Simone Gesi fending off Finn Treacy to set up Mirko Belloni to score in the corner. Subsequent sloppy handling and kicking from the hosts let Zebre off the hook before half-time.
Not surprisingly, Connacht played with greater focus from the restart, but Paul Boyle was held up over the line before Hansen raced back to prevent another score for the visitors.
Replacement hooker Heffernan eventually crossed in the 55th minute, and Frawley’s missed conversion was his last act before coming off. West added Connacht’s seventh try with 13 minutes remaining.
The hosts then switched off, allowing Zebre to cross twice in the final 10 minutes, before Heffernan’s last-gasp second try ended the scoring.
But Lancaster will demand a defensive improvement after a performance that mixed attacking promise with alarming vulnerability with Leinster next up.

title: Irish man (62) detained in West Bank
description: Ian Hutcheson travelled from Dublin to support Palestinian farmers with the olive harvest
content:
A 62-year-old Irish man is among a group of activists who have been detained by Israeli authorities in the West Bank.
People Before Profit Councillor Conor Reddy told The Irish Times that his constituent Ian Hutcheson was detained while supporting Palestinian farmers.
He said that the activists were in the West Bank to support farmers with the olive harvest amid attacks by Israeli settlers.
Hutcheson and 10 other solidarity activists from Italy, Germany, the United States, Britain and Australia were arrested on Thursday morning while visiting a Palestinian family.
International observers have said this year’s olive harvest has been one of the most violent in years, with numerous attacks on Palestinian farmers.
The Dublin North West councillor Reddy said that Ian Hutcheson travelled from Dublin to the West Bank two weeks ago as an act of international solidarity with the people of Palestine as they try to harvest their crops under constant threat of attack by Israeli settlers and police.
“Ian and 10 other solidarity activists were arrested yesterday in the village of Al Buweib while they were visiting a local family. They were not engaged in harvesting or other field action at the time of their arrest and Al Buweib is not in a closed military zone.
“It is outrageous that Ian went to the West Bank to offer support and protection to Palestinians as they harvested their crops, and for this he was arrested and detained and appears set to be deported.”
The Department of Foreign Affairs is aware of this case and is providing consular assistance, a spokesperson said.
“As with all consular cases, the Department does not comment on the details of individual cases.”

title: Bohemians fall to Shelbourne defeat to hand title to Shamrock Rovers
description: Odubeko’s sucker-punch goal silences home fans at Dalymount Park as Hoops secure league
content:
Shamrock Rovers are the League of Ireland champions for 2026 after Bohemians lost to Shelbourne in the same way St Patrick’s Athletic were caught by John Russell’s side last Friday at Richmond Park.
The sound of stunned silence was punctured by the 800 Shelbourne fans among a 4,425 attendance at Dalymount Park when Mipo Odubeko scored the game’s only goal in the 85th minute.
It was a classic sucker-punch as an increasingly desperate Bohs piled forward in search of a winner that would take the title race to the final Friday.
Odubeko put aside his injury-disrupted few months with a fourth goal of the season. But it is one that will be remembered as it allowed the visiting supporters celebrate like they were bringing silverware home to Tolka Park.
THAT COULD DECIDE THE TITLE! 85' - Mipo Odubeko may have just handed the title to Shamrock Rovers. It looks like a fatal blow to Bohemians in the title race. 0-1 #VMSport #LOI pic.twitter.com/1dJktIWcc8
Back-to-back victories in Dublin derbies away from home is not a bad way to end a disappointing campaign.
Across town at Tallaght Stadium, the party could finally begin as Dylan Watts made it 4-0 to Shamrock Rovers against Sligo Rovers.
Before kick-off, the Shelbourne ultras in the Mono stand unfurled a banner that stated in block capitals: “F**k Dalymount.” The neighbours from Drumcondra felt this was an appropriate way to mark the last match at the old ground before the floodlights are removed ahead of a €64 million revamp.
Bohs will remain at Dalymount until next summer, playing games on Saturday afternoons before moving between Richmond Park, the RDS and the Aviva Stadium until construction of their 8,000 capacity venue is complete.
The current estimate has them returning to Friday nights at Dalymount in 2029.
Eight days before Halloween, kick-off was delayed by seven minutes as both sets of supporters launched rockets and lit flares that left the pitch shrouded in smoke.
“If any more objects are thrown on the pitch the referee has said that the players will leave the pitch,” said the stadium announcer. “This game is going out live on Irish television so can we have some behaviour from the Mono stand please.”
The opening 45 minutes lacked the intensity of recent Dublin derbies, particularly Rovers 2-1 defeat of Bohemians on October 12th and Shels 2-1 defeat of St Pat’s last Friday.
Bohs captain Dawson Devoy was suspended for the rest of the season, after being found guilty of violent conduct against Rovers, so Sadou Diallo was tasked with running midfield alongside Jordan Flores.
Alan Reynolds’ was forced into another significant change five minutes before half-time when Zane Myers replaced the injured Ross Tierney.
Myers brought energy down the right wing, even hitting the post before Shelbourne’s Sean Moore almost scored down the other end. Moore’s shot just cleared Paul Walters crossbar.
The usually ebullient Jodi Stand went quite before the second-half began as news filtered through from Tallaght that Adam Brennan had scored twice to give Shamrock Rovers a 2-0 lead.
Inevitably, the game turned into a ragged, end-to-end affair as Shels repeated the trick that ended St Pat’s title challenge by soaking up Bohs aimless attacks and hitting them on the break; Daniel Kelly almost got on the end John Martin’s low cross before Kerr McInroy shot straight at Walters.
Reynolds telegraphed an agricultural end game by replacing Diallo with Patrick Hickey. The big American slotted into defence but it seemed only a matter of time before he was sent into the Shelbourne box as a target man.
But the long ball approach never happened. Shels manager John Russell, perhaps sensing the ploy, withdrew a midfielder in Jonathan Lunney and added another striker in Odubeko.
Bohemians missed Devoy. There is nobody like him in the League of Ireland. Capped last summer by Heimir Hallgrímsson against Canada, the 24-year-old makes his team tick.
An exchange of views near the Bohs dugout prompted referee Robert Harvey show Shels fitness coach Mauro Martins a red card.
Reynolds kept pushing for a goal to take the title race to the last Friday, when Bohs face St Pat’s at Richmond Park and Rovers play Dundalk at Oriel Park. On came Senan Mullen, Collie Whelan and Latvian international Markuss Strods.
Seconds later Aaron Greene made it 3-0 to Rovers in Tallaght. Watts added the fourth to give Stephen Bradley’s men their sixth Premier Division title in the 2020s.
Meanwhile, down the other end of the table, Waterford beat Drogheda United 3-1 at the RSC to allay concerns about a relegation playoff ahead of their FAI Cup final against Derry City on November 8th.

title: Racially motivated attack suspected after one killed in France shooting spree
description: In Paris suburb incident, man appeared to be firing at ​random and seemed intent on ‘carrying out ‌a massacre’, local mayor says
content:
A gunman firing from a vehicle in a Paris suburb on Friday killed one person and wounded several others, including a 12-year-old girl, in what French authorities suspect may have been a racially motivated attack.
France ’s national antiterrorism prosecutor’s office took charge of the case and interior minister Laurent Nunez spoke of a “terrorist crime”.
A suspect was arrested and taken into police custody, police said.
President Emmanuel Macron said it was “a racist terror attack” and the suspect’s statements suggested it was premeditated.
“These people were targeted because of their skin colour or perceived religion, and for no other reason,” Macron said.
Nunez said the shootings happened at three separate locations in the towns of Trappes and La Verriere, near Paris, and that they took less than 15 minutes in total.
“A deadly rampage took place this morning,” he told reporters in Trappes.
According to Nunez, the attacker fatally shot one person and wounded five others, three of them very seriously, with their lives in danger.
Nunez said the attack was considered a “terrorist crime” by prosecutors, with a possible racist motive.
He praised the five officers from the anti-crime brigade who stopped the suspect. “I commend them for their swift response,” he said.
Aurore Berge, the minister for gender equality and fight against discriminations, said the 12-year-old girl was very seriously injured.
“If a racist motive is established, I hope that the whole nation will stand alongside the residents of Trappes, La Verrière, and the victims.
“We cannot tolerate even the slightest racist remark in the French republic,” she said.
Asked about reports that the suspect’s home had been booby-trapped with gas cylinders, Nunez said: “We have heard those reports. The investigation will establish the facts.”
Nunez said the suspect fired “what appears to have been a military-grade weapon, or at least an automatic weapon”.
Trappes mayor Ali Rabeh said the gunman appeared to have fired relatively randomly, targeting passersby at several locations including a playground.
“This is probably one of the first attempted mass killings motivated by Islamophobia and racism,” he told reporters.
“This was a terrorist attack with racist, likely Islamophobic, overtones.”
Rabeh previously said the person killed was of African origin, while one of those critically wounded was of North African origin.
France’s national antiterrorism prosecutor’s office said it opened a criminal investigation into several offences, including “murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise with the aggravating circumstance that the act was committed on account of the victim’s actual or perceived membership of a particular race, ethnic group, nationality or religion”.
The shooting happened as France braces for another day of protests against the high cost of living on Saturday, with major museums closing their doors and the government deploying a significantly larger security presence to prevent a repeat of last week’s violent unrest, which shocked the country.

title: Shamrock Rovers retain their crown as rivals fail to seize opportunity
description: St Pat’s and Bohs faltered late on while Shels and Derry never managed to enter League of Ireland title race
content:
The gap between Shamrock Rovers and the rest has narrowed, but not enough to deny Stephen Bradley an eighth major trophy over his 11 years at the Tallaght club.
This could prove to be Bradley’s final season as the Rovers manager. Offered the Hibernian job last month, the 41-year-old decided to stay until a sixth title in seven seasons was secured.
“When it came down to it, I genuinely don’t think I could look at the players, the fans, the club and walk out the door with five games left,” he revealed.
The comment suggests that Bradley would be tempted by an opportunity in Scotland, England or further afield, instead of returning for a 12th season.
And anyway, the law of diminishing marginal returns is beginning to take hold. Rovers will finish their Premier Division campaign on 71 points if they beat Dundalk at Oriel Park next Friday.
The 78 points winning total in 2021 and 79 points in 2022 fell to 72 points in 2023 as Derry City, St Patrick’s Athletic and Shelbourne strengthened their squads.
Rovers topped the table last year on 66 points after finishing runners-up in 2024 with 61 points, when Damien Duff’s Shelbourne claimed the title on the last night.
The story of how Rovers won the league in 2026 is as much about their rivals faltering at crucial moments than it was about the defending champions.
Pico Lopes’s World Cup adventure with Cape Verde left them without a natural on-field leader for a chunk of the summer. With Dan Cleary injured for 18 games, veteran defenders such as Lee Grace and Enda Stevens made plenty of timely interventions.
Victor Ozhianvuna showed glimpses of his potential with Bradley playing the 17-year-old as a deep-lying midfielder who can pass and beat opponents at will. An injury in July effectively ended Ozhianvuna’s League of Ireland career as both Rovers and Arsenal were overly cautious ahead of the teenager’s move to London in January.
By September, the title race was wide open. Poor away results in European qualifiers denied Rovers a third consecutive year in the Conference League group stage before St Pat’s knocked them out of the FAI Cup.
Expected challenges from Derry City and Shelbourne never materialised. Shels parted company with Joey O’Brien in June, while Tiernan Lynch left Derry in early August.
An injury crisis ensured that Shels fell well short of their own expectations, despite a partnership with Jamestown Analytics, the recruitment specialists associated with Brighton and Hearts. It prompted a reset at Tolka Park as John Russell is now tasked with rebuilding the squad for 2027.
Derry’s operations also came under scrutiny after Sean Barrett stepped down as chief executive in December and chairman Philip O’Doherty took a more hands-on role.
In his autobiography, The Walls, James McClean revealed that Barrett had been talking to him “for years” about coming home to finish his career.
“He’d also teach me the ropes for a role beyond football,” McClean wrote.
Amid the club’s increasingly bitter and public dispute with McClean, interim manager Mark Connolly somehow managed to steady the ship after Lynch left.
Connolly revived Derry’s expensively assembled squad to finish mid-table with an FAI Cup final against Waterford at the Aviva Stadium to follow on November 8th. But the expected rivalry with Rovers throughout the 2020s has yet to materialise.
Instead, the Hoops’ wobbles through August presented an opportunity for St Pat’s, under Stephen Kenny, and Alan Reynolds’s Bohemians.
A three-way title race developed until mid-October when St Pat’s self-destructed, losing at home to Shelbourne last Friday and away to Derry on Monday. Kenny subsequently waved the white flag.
“There was a league title there to be won this year with Rovers in transition,” former Dundalk manager Vinnie Perth said on Virgin Media this week. “Pats let them off the hook. It was up for grabs. Pats left a title behind them.”
The quality at Kenny’s disposal was reflected in the PFAI Premier Division team of the year as four St Pat’s players – Joey Anang, Joe Redmond, Luke Turner and Kian Leavy – were selected by their peers.
Rovers only had three representatives: Pico Lopes, Tunmise Sobowale and Graham Burke.
Burke was outstanding as a roaming number 10, John McGovern filled Rory Gaffney’s big boots up front and Will Fitzgerald immediately excelled after his midseason arrival from Sligo.
Bohemians’ challenge ultimately faltered in a tempestuous Dublin derby on October 12th. The enduring health of the league was evident on that Monday night as a crowd of 10,208 crammed into Tallaght Stadium to see Dylan Watts score Rovers’ 76th-minute winner. Losing to Shelbourne at home in the penultimate game handed Rovers the title.
At the final whistle, a brawl erupted and when the dust settled, Bohs captain Dawson Devoy received a three-game ban for violent conduct. Devoy’s absence proved far more damaging to his club than Rovers losing Noonan, Matt Healy, Naj Razi and Danny Grant to suspension.
Bradley wasted no time twisting the knife.
“We are playing to win a league, they are not,” he said, knowing full well that Reynolds could not respond as Bohs had imposed a media blackout to protest the FAI’s fixture schedule.
Rovers suffered one final setback, losing away to Galway United last Friday. But, once again, they did just enough to win the league after a comfortable victory over Sligo Rovers.

title: Father of murder accused reported ‘serious concerns’ for family’s safety to social worker
description: Trial hears Robert O’Connor was considered appropriate for detention by mental health services in 2014 after he threatened to kill his parents
content:
The father of Robert O’Connor, who is accused of murdering his parents and younger brother, who had special needs, reported to a social worker a decade ago that he had “serious concerns” for his family’s safety and thought they “could be killed in the future”, a psychiatrist has told the Central Criminal Court .
The trial also heard that the accused was considered appropriate for detention by mental health services in 2014 after he threatened to kill his parents.
Consultant forensic psychiatrist Dr Fiona Toal, called to give evidence by the defence, also told the trial that the accused was experiencing a relapse of schizophrenia when he fatally stabbed the three members of his family and did not know what he was doing was wrong.
The expert witness found that the accused meets the criteria for a special verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity under the Criminal Law (Insanity) Act 2006.
From her engagements with O’Connor, the witness found the accused had very clear psychiatric symptoms, had bizarre beliefs regarding his parents and thought they were impostors who controlled his thoughts. The accused also told her he thought his brother Evan was controlling him on an iPad on the night of the fatal attack.
Robert O’Connor, of Drumgowna, Louth Village, Dundalk, Co Louth, has pleaded not guilty of murder by reason of insanity, or guilty of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility to the triple murder of his mother, Louise (56), his father, Mark (54), and his younger brother Evan (27) at their home between September 28th and 29th, 2025, both dates inclusive.
The Central Criminal Court jury has been told that the accused accepts he caused the deaths of the three victims, who had sustained a combined 139 stab wounds.
In her evidence, Toal told barrister Michael Bowman, defending, that her and the State’s psychiatrist’s conclusions are “incredibly aligned”, with both parties agreeing that diminished responsibility is made out for the three deaths.
Toal said both psychiatrists agree that the accused suffered a relapse of schizophrenia in September 2025. She said the symptoms were probably present for many years before this.
The witness said the accused started smoking cannabis at 13 years old and this later progressed to cocaine, which caused significant arguments at home. He spent time in a drug rehabilitation facility at 17 years old and intermittently engaged with drugs and alcohol services.
O’Connor was assessed by a psychiatrist at 19 years old, where he reported feeling increasingly paranoid and anxious. The accused’s symptoms were attributed to drug psychosis and social anxiety, for which he was prescribed antipsychotic medication.
In 2014, the witness said O’Connor went to a psychiatrist after reporting feelings he wanted to hurt and hit out at people at certain times. She said the accused was considered appropriate for being detained by mental health services in March 2014 after he threatened to kill his parents. He applied to be admitted as an involuntary patient but, as he had taken LSD the week before, there was an impression of drug-induced psychosis.
Toal said notes indicated that the accused’s parents were very concerned for their own safety. O’Connor continued to describe paranoid delusions about his parents and was put on quite a high dose of antipsychotics. In another review, on March 31st, 2014, the accused denied having continuing paranoid thoughts, accepted his symptoms were drug-related and was discharged.
Toal said a discharge note written by a social worker communicating with Mark O’Connor had documented “very, very significant family concerns”. Mark O’Connor reported that his son had been depressed for two years and was hearing voices for the previous 18 months. He expressed “serious concerns” for his family’s safety and “there was an indication that they could be killed in the future.”
Toal said the accused’s mother reported her son’s extreme moods, aggression and talking to himself in 2018.
Robert O’Connor was formally diagnosed with schizophrenia at the end of 2018 and was started on stronger antipsychotic medication.
She said O’Connor was last reviewed by a psychiatrist in August 2025 and denied any psychotic symptoms. The impression was his illness was stable, he was put on a newer drug and scheduled for an outpatient review.
The witness said at the time of the killing O’Connor was under the care of a mental health team. She said the accused reported that he stopped taking his medication in August 2025 and, in the 24 hours before the killing, the accused reported taking cocaine mixed with mephedrone.
She said the accused is on a waiting list for the Central Mental Hospital .
In conclusion, the witness said the accused’s psychotic symptoms presented early in life and were initially attributed to drug use. She said substance abuse disorder is extremely common in schizophrenic patients. She said the real point of difference between her opinion and that of Dr Ronan Mullaney, for the prosecution, was in what way they found the mental disorder affected the accused’s thinking and behaviour at the time of the offence.
Toal found the accused did know the nature and quality of the act. However, she said the accused’s thinking was extremely disordered in the context of experiencing a resurgence of delusions he had held for 15 years.
She also found that Robert O’Connor was not in control of his functioning and his understanding of reality was “warped”.
The trial continues on Monday before Judge Mícheál P O’Higgins and a jury of six men and six women.

title: Séamus Power one off the lead in Bermuda after second-round 64
description: Irish golfer is 12 under after two rounds as he looks to keep PGA Tour card for next season
content:
Séamus Power is one off the lead at the Butterfield Bermuda Championship on the PGA Tour after a superb seven-under-par 64 in his second round.
The Irish golfer is 12 under after two rounds after he followed up an opening 66 with a bogey-free 64 that included seven birdies at Port Royal Golf Course.
Power had reached seven under after 14 holes in his round yesterday and struggled with bogeys at 15 and 16 to finish, but there would be no mistakes this time. His putting stood out in the second round, holing five birdie putts between 10 and 20 feet.
The 39-year-old Waterford man held the early clubhouse upon finishing, before Kensei Hirata and Chandler Blanchet went one shot ahead on 13 under.
A good week for Power in Bermuda could be crucial in keeping his PGA Tour card for next year. Currently 103rd in the FedEx Cup standings, the top 100 players at the end of FedEx Cup Fall keep a fully exempt card. Players finishing 101 to 150 earn conditional status, giving them limited start opportunities, while those who finish outside the top 150 lose status and must qualify through Q-School.
Power won the event in 2022, his previous victory on the PGA Tour, and has been showing form recently with a tied seventh placing at Biltmore Championship Asheville and a tied 21st finish at the Bank of Utah Championship.

title: The Irish Times view on the triple lock debate: more heat than light
description: The amendment will pass but a calmer debate would be  welcome
content:
The heated exchanges in the Dáil this week over changes to the triple lock reflected the fact that this is an issue on which clear blue water exists between Government and Opposition. The sometimes bitter accusations and counter-accusations, particularly between Taoiseach Micheál Martin and Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald , revealed once more how each side believes the other to be acting in bad faith.
Opponents of the change have some justification for their belief that it is being rushed, with debate guillotined at under four hours. The triple lock, which requires that any overseas deployment of more than 12 Defence Forces members be approved by the Dáil, the Government and the UN Security Council, codified a long-standing policy and became a key reassurance to voters whose concerns had contributed to the initial defeat of two EU treaty referendums. The Government’s argument that geopolitical change has made the Security Council veto an unacceptable constraint on Irish sovereignty has considerable merit, but it is easy to portray the amendment as reneging on promises made to those voters, or as a first step towards Nato membership. The Opposition parties also know they have popular opinion on their side. A recent Irish Times poll found 44 per cent of voters wanted the triple lock retained, against 34 per cent who favoured its removal.
There is a certain absurdity in the fact that people who argued a quarter of a century ago that the triple lock was a guarantee of Irish neutrality now say it is no such thing, while those who argued then that it was no safeguard at all now say it is essential. If nothing else, that goes some way to supporting the Government’s assertion that we now live in a different era. And public opinion is less settled on this issue, with more than a fifth of voters undecided, than on the core question of preserving neutrality, which more than two-thirds support.
There is also something incongruous about a country which has conspicuously failed to invest in the minimum requirements for its own defence engaging in disputation over notional military adventures overseas.
The Government is correct, however, that it is no longer sustainable for the final say over Irish participation in peacekeeping missions to rest with Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump or Xi Jinping.
In a multipolar world where threats emerge without warning, decisions on security and defence belong with the Dáil and the government of the day. Public attachment to neutrality remains steadfast, but how it is expressed in policy is a matter for parliament. The amendment will pass, despite some unease on Government backbenches. If a calmer debate on those policies followed, that would be very welcome.

title: Well-known Co Limerick private school Glenstal Abbey set to close
description: Internal assessment finds ‘the kind of school we have here at Glenstal is not sustainable into the future’
content:
One of Ireland’s best known private schools, Glenstal Abbey in Co Limerick, is set to close after almost 100 years in operation.
Parents, students and staff were informed on Friday of the decision to wind down operations by August 2028.
The school said it has spent years wrestling with uncertainty around its future amid a declining demand for boarding education and the rising cost of operating.
Current first, third, fourth and sixth year students will finish in June 2027, while second years will complete their Junior Cycle in 2028 alongside fifth years who will complete their Leaving Certificate in 2028.
The Benedictine school for boys takes day students and boarders and is seen as one of the most successful second level schools in the country.
The main building of the school is set on over 500 acres outside the village of Moroe in northeast Limerick and was built in the 1830s for the Barrington family. It was later sold to a local priest, who invited the monks of Maredsous Abbey in Belgium to settle there in 1927.
A secondary school for boys opened there in September 1932. A monastry of Benedictine monks remains on the grounds and will remain there.
The school has a student population of just over 200 boys and its current fees are €14,950 for day pupils, €21,500 for five-day boarders and €24,000 for full boarding.
International student fees are €25,950 for Europeans and €29,150 for the rest of the world.
Past pupils include businessman John Magnier and Web Summit founder Paddy Cosgrave.
“This decision has not been made suddenly, nor has it been made lightly. The Abbey has wrestled with the future of the school for many years. During that time, we have sought to support it financially, to strengthen enrolment and to consider whether changes to the school’s model could secure a sustainable future,” the Trustees of Glenstal Abbey said in a statement.
“However, the environment in which Glenstal Abbey School operates has changed significantly. Demand for boarding education has declined over time, while the cost of operating a small boarding school and providing the quality of education, care and facilities expected of Glenstal has continued to rise. A detailed external assessment of the school has confirmed that the kind of school we have here at Glenstal is not sustainable into the future.”
The trustees also said the school was not alone in facing these challenges, and that “boarding schools across Ireland and elsewhere are experiencing similar pressures”.
There just over 20 boarding schools across the country, compared to almost 40 fee-paying schools for day students only.
While it was a “very difficult decision for the Monastic Community” to make, the Abbey must also “meet its responsibilities to the monastic community and steward its resources responsibly”.
“We have concluded, with immense regret, that we cannot continue to guarantee the school’s longer-term future,” the trustees said.
A letter from Columba McCann, abbot of Glenstal, to past pupils known as ‘Old Boys of Glenstal’, said the school would “need support” to complete the exam cycles for 2027/28 and it was “determined to do everything possible to complete these”.
“However, this will depend on student numbers, staffing availability, Department of Education processes and other practical considerations,” McCann said.

title: Musician Dónal Lunny dies aged 79
description: Multi-instrumentalist founder of Planxty and Bothy Band produced albums for Elvis Costello, Sinéad O’Connor and others
content:
Tributes have been paid to musician Dónal Lunny , who has died aged 79. He died on Friday morning in St James’s Hospital of cancer.
Friends and collaborators described Lunny as a “genius” and saluted his “immense” contribution to Irish music. He was one of the central figures in folk and traditional music for the past 60 years.
He joined his first band with his older brother Frank and neighbour Christy Moore when they formed the Rakes of Kildare as teenagers.
Moore, who was two years ahead of him in school, maintained a friendship and a professional collaboration with Lunny for decades afterwards.
Last year Lunny received the lifetime achievement award at the RTÉ Radio 1 Folk Awards. “I’ve known Dónal Lunny for 66 years,” Moore said when presenting Lunny with the award.
“I met him first in 1959 in school, and what I remember most from those years were his lack of homework, that he was more interested in being out on the Liffey trying to tickle trout, or climbing trees to gaze into the wild birds’ nests.”
Born in Tullamore, Co Offaly, but brought up in Newbridge, Co Kildare, from the age of five, Lunny was the middle child of nine children.
He was a multi-instrumentalist from the beginning, learning the harmonica at the age of six. He could drum and play the bodhrán, and was capable of playing the guitar, bass, mandolin and keyboard, but it was the bouzouki for which he was most famous. He picked it up from sometime bandmate Andy Irvine and made it his own.
Lunny designed his own bouzouki, an instrument associated with Greek music, to fit in with his style. It was an instrument, he believed, much more suited to the Irish traditional genre than the guitar. “The chords were less dense. It was far easier to play chords. The bouzouki gave a much more open accompaniment to Irish music.”
He enrolled in the National College of Art & Design in 1965 and studied basic design and graphic design for three years, but he was always destined to be a full-time musician.
His first success came with the teenage folk band Emmet Spiceland, which had an Irish number one with Mary from Dungloe.
In 1970, Lunny formed a musical partnership with Andy Irvine that would prove to be a catalyst for many important folk acts that would dominate the scene for decades afterwards.
They created their own club night downstairs at Slattery’s pub in Capel Street, Dublin, which they called The Mug’s Gig. Two years later Lunny and Irvine joined up with Liam O’Flynn and Moore to form Planxty.
Two years later he left Planxty to join The Bothy Band, playing guitar and bouzouki. The Bothy Band quickly became one of the prominent bands performing Irish traditional music.
The third Irish traditional “supergroup” that Lunny was involved in was Moving Hearts where he again joined Moore and added the piper Davy Spillane. Moving Hearts combined rock beats with Irish traditional music and had a significant impact in the early 1980s.
After Moving Hearts split up in 1985, Lunny became a successful producer on his own record label, Mulligan Records. He was the producer and music director of the soundtrack of the five-part 1990 BBC documentary Bringing It All Back Home charting the influence of Irish music throughout the world.
He produced albums for Paul Brady, Elvis Costello, Indigo Girls, Sinéad O’Connor among others. He also played with Kate Bush and Mark Knopfler.
Lunny’s first marriage was to Judy Slott, with whom he had a son, Oisín, who is a musician. Cora Venus Lunny, also a musician, is his daughter with German photographer Julie Buthe.
He later married Japanese musician Itami Hideko and they had a daughter, Sora. He also had a son with the late singer Sinéad O’Connor. Shane O’Connor died in 2022.
President Catherine Connolly said: “Dónal was one of Ireland’s greatest musical figures, a wonderfully talented musician and producer who was central to so many of the most influential moments of the last 60 years of Irish music.
“Dónal will be particularly remembered for his long partnerships with fellow musicians such as Christy Moore and Andy Irvine and for the innovative music he has left behind both as a musician in groups including Planxty, The Bothy Band and Moving Hearts and also as a renowned producer.”
Arts Council director Shona McCarthy said Lunny’s “championing of Irish traditional music was instrumental in bringing the art form to the fore. Donal was a trailblazer, inspiring generations of musicians and expertly balancing tradition and reinvention.”
Lunny’s good friend, the broadcaster Philip King, described Lunny’s contribution to Irish music as “immense” not just as a musician, but also as a producer. “There’s nobody compared to him from the beginning. His musical world was very wide. You look across the list of Irish musicians he has produced, his influence his huge. You hear it today in Amble and Kingfishr and many others. We would sonically and rhythmically not be in this place with Irish music without him.”
He was the “Quincy Jones of Irish producers”, King added.
King’s wife Nuala O’Connor was the maker of the RTÉ documentary entitled In Time: Dónal Lunny which was released last year. She also made Bringing It All Back Home.
Filming for the documentary began in 2024 and Lunny suffered his first bout of serious illness during the making of it. “We got there in the nick of time,” she said.
She described him as a “genius” and a “totally naturally gifted musician” who had no ego and lived for playing music.
In January Lunny, during an appearance on the Late Late Show, he became the first inductee into the Trad Music Hall of Fame.
The Irish Traditional Music Archive paid tribute to Lunny in an extensive statement listing some of his contributions to the genre.
“His musical life was founded on creativity, friendship and collaboration,” it read.
“His work with the likes of Christy Moore, Andy Irvine, Liam O’Flynn, Paddy Glackin, Matt Molloy, Maighréad and Tríona Ní Dhomhnaill, Frank Harte and so many others places him at the heart of some of the most important developments in Irish music of the modern era.
“His election to Aosdána reflected the wider significance of that contribution to Irish artistic life.”
Taoiseach Micheál Martin described Lunny as a “colossus of Irish music, as a performer, songwriter and producer”.
“Uniquely gifted, Dónal carried traditional and folk music to new audiences through Planxty and his many other endeavours,” he said.
Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald posted on X: “Dónal helped shape the sound of Irish music for generations, bringing our rich musical heritage to audiences at home and around the world. His contribution to Irish music and culture will never be forgotten.”
The Waterboys singer Mike Scott described Lunny as the “greatest of all time. What a wonderful musician and person”.

title: The Irish Times view on winter time: stop the clocks
description: Debate continues but political inertia likely to stymie change
content:
Tonight Irish households gain an extra hour’s sleep as the clocks go back and winter time begins. The lie-in is welcome, but the shift in sunrise and sunset has grown controversial.
The European Parliament voted to scrap the twice-yearly change in 2019, but member states could not agree on a replacement. Spain revived the issue last year. Brussels has commissioned a study due by December, and 44 MEPs have urged ministers to break the deadlock. The US House voted in July for permanent summer time, but the bill has stalled in the Senate. Canada has moved faster, with British Columbia, Alberta and Manitoba among provinces abandoning the change this year, creating a patchwork of time differences.
Popular opinion and much health advice favour ending the ritual. The division is over which time to keep. Sleep experts say permanent winter time better suits the body’s circadian rhythms, while business lobbies want brighter evenings. Among them is Donald Trump, who complained in Ohio this month that golfers were being forced off the course after 14 holes.
Trump was echoing those who run his favourite sport. The PGA Tour’s boss had recently written seeking more afternoon light. Setting clocks to suit one sport would be curious. Against that, permanent summer time would mean sunrise in Donegal close to 10am in late December.
No arrangement pleases everyone. The change brings little benefit in the far north and none near the equator. Longitude matters as much as latitude. Spain uses Central European Time, thanks to Franco’s alignment with Berlin, though most of it lies west of Greenwich, and Madrid has signalled it would probably keep winter time.
Ireland, on its time zone’s western fringe, has it harder still. Bizarrely, MEP Seán Kelly has suggested moving to Central European Time. Dublin’s priority will be avoiding two time zones on the island if Britain does not follow the EU. Most likely, the Earth will keep orbiting the sun and political inertia will ensure nothing changes, as sure as night follows day.

title: Gardaí investigate after body of man found on golf course in Macroom, Co Cork
description: Man, who has not been formally identified,  was found dead at about 9.30am
content:
Gardaí have begun an investigation following the discovery of a man’s body at Macroom Golf Club in Co Cork .
The man, understood to have been in his late 20s and from the town, was found on the golf course at 9.30am by a staff member. The body was between the first green and the second tee box at the 18-hole golf course, which is behind the grounds of Macroom GAA club.
The staff member contacted the emergency services, and the man was pronounced dead at the scene. Officers from nearby Macroom Garda station cordoned off the area.
Gardaí said it was too early to know whether the man was the victim of foul play but said they would be guided by the findings of a postmortem.
Assistant State Pathologist Dr Margot Bolster is due to carry out the postmortem on the deceased at Cork University Hospital on Saturday. The pathologist carried out a preliminary examination of the man’s body before he was removed to Cork University Hospital and technical experts from Garda HQ began a forensic examination of the scene.
Gardaí would not be drawn on initial reports that the man had suffered injuries that appeared to indicate he may have been assaulted.
Some of the man’s clothing was found a few hundred metres away.
“It seems he was out on Thursday night so he may have got hypothermia, and sometimes when people are suffering from hypothermia they can remove their clothing in a phenomenon known as ‘paradoxical undressing’,” said one source.
It is understood the man is from the Dan Corkery Estate in the town and gardaí have established that he left his family home early on Thursday morning.
Gardaí have begun checking CCTV footage from around the town centre and have started inquiries to try to establish when the dead man was last seen alive. They are seeking to confirm a report that he was seen with two or three other men around the Castle Gates in Macroom at around 10pm on Thursday.
A senior officer has been appointed to lead the investigation and a family liaison officer has also been named.
Gardaí have appealed for anyone with any information to contact them and for any motorists with dashcam footage of the area from around the time of the discovery of the man’s body to make it available.
They say they want anyone who noticed anything unusual around Macroom Golf Club, Macroom GAA Club or the town centre between 6pm on Thursday and 9.30am on Friday to contact them at Macroom Garda station on 026-20590.

title: Accountant’s office searched as gardaí investigate alleged money laundering at charity
description: Arrests expected after luxury goods and two BMW X5s seized in bid to learn what happened to funds held by Liberty Recycling
content:
An accountant’s office has been searched by gardaí investigating allegations of money laundering at the Dublin-headquartered charity Liberty Recycling.
The search came after two BMW X5 luxury SUVs, valued at €250,000, and designer goods worth €40,000 were seized by gardaí .
The Irish Times understands the criminal investigation into the alleged misappropriation of funds held by the charity is expected to involve arrests during its next phase.
Detectives from the Garda National Economic Crime Bureau are reviewing records of funds raised by Liberty Recycling, and outgoing money, in a bid to determine if funds were diverted away from the charity for personal use. Sources said a very small number of people were under suspicion.
Gardaí went to the accountant’s office to secure financial records in a bid to get a picture of sections of the charity’s activities the money is alleged to have been misappropriated from. The charity is chaired by Sinn Féin TD Aengus Ó Snodaigh, though there is no suggestion he is under investigation. He is not linked in any way to the assets seized.
The two BMW X5 SUVs, along with Louis Vuitton bags, Rolex watches and jewellery with a total estimated value of €40,000, were seized during searches in Dublin, the east and southeast on Tuesday and Wednesday.
The assets were confiscated on suspicion their purchase was funded, or part-funded, with money that should have been spent on the charity’s core activities.
If money was taken in that way, and converted into assets that were privately owned, that may be classified as money laundering. The economic crime bureau’s money laundering investigation unit is carrying out the investigation, which also involves the Charities Regulator.
Liberty Recycling has declined to respond to questions put to it by The Irish Times, including whether any of its personnel have been suspended pending the outcome of the investigation.
It was established more than 20 years ago as a spin-off from the Merchants Quay Ireland drug treatment organisation, initially as a community employment scheme. Merchants Quay Ireland said it has no governance, operational or financial relationship with Liberty Recycling and has no involvement in its management or activities.
The operation has since grown considerably and employs 60 people full-time, collecting textiles at a vast network of clothes banks nationwide. It sorts approximately eight 40ft containers of clothing every week at its depot in Bluebell, Dublin 12, offering training to people recovering from drug addiction.
Its expenditure grew to €4 million in 2024, up from €2.5 million in 2022. It has received almost €2 million from the State , to fund its community employment scheme, since 2020.
Most of the textiles, and items such as shoes and handbags, donated to Liberty Recycling are sold to traders in Africa and Asia while some is sold via its network of nine shops across the country. Its operations are continuing, despite the Garda and Charities Regulator investigation.
The regulator, which appears to have taken its concerns to the Garda, prompting the investigation, has confirmed its involvement but stopped short of issuing comment.
However, the Garda confirmed the investigation was centred on “a Dublin-based charitable organisation”. It also confirmed the seizure of the vehicles and luxury goods and that the money laundering unit was carrying out the inquiry.
While no reference was made to an accountant’s office being searched during the operation on Tuesday and Wednesday, sources have confirmed this.
The offices of accountants and lawyers can be searched, and records and other items taken away from examination, during criminal investigations. However, this is done as part of the investigation into suspects’ financial background rather than the financial or legal professionals being under investigation.
Sinn Féin confirmed it was aware of the investigation and “fully supports” it. “Deputy Ó Snodaigh has engaged with the office of the Charities Regulator. He has not been contacted by gardaí, but if required, he will make himself available to assist with their inquiries,” it added in a statement.

title: Minister for Justice’s intervention in hugging consent video is ‘unsettling’, ICCL says
description: Jim O’Callaghan’s comments interfered with work of non-profit organisation, Irish Council for Civil Liberties says
content:
The Irish Council for Civil Liberties (ICCL) has said Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan ’s comments over a controversial hugging video were “unsettling”.
The Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) has removed the consent video, which featured grandparents hugging their grandchildren, after widespread public criticism.
In the video, meant to highlight consent, a girl was visibly uncomfortable over receiving a hug from her grandparents.
A voiceover said: “Not everyone wants a hug. Even from the people who love them. Awkward? Maybe. Important? Absolutely.”
O’Callaghan issued a statement after the video generated controversy online.
He said the video “does not represent the views of the Government ”.
“It was both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents and has been removed by DRCC following my officials’ engagement with them.
“While it is vital to ensure that people understand the concept of consent when it comes to sexual relationships, this video did not advance that aim and in many ways was counterproductive.”
[ Advert showing grandparents hugging grandchildren is taken down amid criticism Opens in new window ]
In a statement, the ICCL said: “No doubt most people in Ireland will have a conversation with friends and families about their understanding of consent this week on foot of the We-Consent video shared by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre and its subsequent removal, five weeks after it was first posted. That is a valuable conversation, whether or not people agree or disagree with the execution of the video in question.
“What is unsettling though is a Minister for Justice interfering with the work of a non-profit organisation, partly funded by the Department of Justice , and pressuring it to pull and delete a video that seeks to educate people about consent.”
It cited a report two years ago which found that State funding can create pressure on civil society organisations to limit their advocacy and campaigning.
“Episodes like this risk creating a pervasive chilling effect and self-censorship within civil society, a risk we outlined in our report. They also raise serious questions about Government or ministerial interference in the work of civil society,” the statement concluded.

title: Dr Muiris Houston: Why it’s time the clocks stopped going back an hour
description: Although the clock change twice a year is a shock to the system, and should probably be ditched, the healthiest alternative also has drawbacks
content:
A re you looking forward to an extra hour of sleep this weekend?
Or are you dreading the reduction in evening light that comes with the seasonal clock change?
Wouldn’t it be easier if there was no biannual challenge to our circadian rhythms?
In 2019 the European Parliament voted to end our seasonal clock change. But the initiative remains deadlocked in the Council of the European Union. Member states cannot agree on whether to stay on permanent standard time or to settle on year round daylight savings time. Lithuania, which takes over the EU presidency in January, has signalled it will try to resolve the issue next year.
Elsewhere, there has been a concerted move towards permanent daylight saving time. In Canada, British Columbia, Alberta and the Northwest Territories adopted the policy this year. And in the US, the House of Representatives passed a Bill in July to establish permanent daylight saving time nationwide, although the measure remains before the Senate.
[ Clocks will move back on October 25th for winter time Opens in new window ]
However, research just published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal (CMAJ) points to permanent standard time as the healthier option, because it keeps the clock more closely aligned with human circadian rhythm. The authors note that permanent daylight saving time would push sunrise an hour later. The extra hour of morning darkness could leave people travelling to work or school before sunrise during the winter, with consequences for sleep, mood, learning and productivity, they say.
“Our biological clocks need morning light to stay synchronised with the 24-hour day,” said Simon Fraser University’s Prof Ralph Mistlberger, co-author of the study. “Permanent daylight saving time moves that light an hour later just when winter mornings are already darkest.”
Our biological clocks follow a circadian rhythm, around (circa) which the day (dies) revolves. The circadian rhythm is an internal clock that makes the brain cycle between intervals of alertness and sleepiness. Circadian rhythms comprise various elements that influence these intervals, including eating habits, body temperature and duration of sleep, as well as external factors such as darkness and lightness.
Our circadian rhythms actually run on a longer schedule than a full day – for 24.2 hours. For that reason we rely on natural sunlight to keep us synchronised with the world around us. Morning light is some of the most important, the authors note, because it jump-starts that rhythm, wakes us up and gets us moving. Evening light, on the other hand, delays the circadian rhythm, interfering with our sense of “social time” and making it tougher to get to sleep and wake up rested in the morning.
Moving to daylight savings time in the spring is especially detrimental to our health. In a 2020 report in the journal PLoS Computational Biology, researchers identified a significant increase in fatal traffic accidents (up to 30 per cent on the day of commencing daylight savings time), a short-term rise in workplace injuries (up 5.7 per cent after the spring clock change as employees sleep 40 minutes less on average) and elevated rates of acute heart attacks (up by about 4 per cent).
[ A good night’s sleep is a class issue Opens in new window ]
The Canadian researchers acknowledge that adopting permanent standard time also has drawbacks. Earlier summer sunrises could cause problems for people prone to waking early, while earlier winter sunsets could limit evening outdoor and commercial activity. They recommend relatively modest measures such as blackout curtains and public education on sleep health to address those effects.
Permanent daylight saving time, in contrast, would require a much broader set of measures to reduce the effects of darker winter mornings.
These include better street lighting and pathways, improved traffic safety, reflective equipment for children, later school start times, flexible work schedules and increased morning lighting in schools and workplaces.
There is broad agreement on the need to end our biannual clock changes. However, the health arguments for permanent standard time stand in stark contrast to an apparent societal preference for permanent daylight savings time.

title: Builder Clearwater Construction owes creditors €2.4m
description: Sports organisations, many of them in southeast, due significant sums for work that has yet to be completed
content:
A building company that folded leaving sports clubs with bills for unfinished work owes creditors more than €2 million.
Grangecon, Wicklow -based Clearwater Construction & Landscaping Ltd, known to most customers as CWC, ceased trading earlier this month.
Creditors heard on Friday that the business has a deficit, the difference between liabilities and assets, of €2.37 million.
The firm, run by director PJ Norton, owes €2.06 million to unsecured creditors, mostly suppliers with unpaid bills or customers with unfinished work.
They voted to appoint KPMG as joint liquidator with another firm instead of the company’s nominees, Eoin Massey and Anthony Glennon of Friel Stafford.
Clearwater owes Revenue €230,176, including €87,412 in PAYE and PRSI along with €64,239 in unpaid VAT and more than €33,000 in corporation tax.
An estimation of the realisable value of Clearwater’s assets comes €5,011, according to a statement of affairs given to shareholders on Friday that was seen by The Irish Times.
Sports organisations, many of them in the southeast, are owed significant sums for work that has yet to be completed.
[ Building company ceases trading, leaving sports clubs with bills for unfinished work Opens in new window ]
Leaving the meeting, which ran for 90 minutes in a hotel in Stillorgan, Dublin , creditors said they did not expect to receive the sums they are due from Clearwater.
A spokesman for Kilmacthomas GAA Club in Co Waterford , said the organisation paid Clearwater a €50,000 deposit to secure an astroturf pitch in July after the company sought the payment.
“We had concerns about a making a payment at that level but we did our due diligence, we had our contracts in place and had our solicitor review them, but then the purchase was never made by Clearwater,” he said.
The spokesman pointed out that many of the organisations now left with unfinished work had paid Clearwater with money received through the Government’s Sports Capital Grants scheme, one the main funding sources for community groups across the Republic.
All of them also rely heavily on voluntary raising efforts by members and their committees, he added.
Jamie Farrell, chairman of Bunclody Association Football Club in Co Wexford confirmed that the meeting heard that Clearwater began to experience difficulties in March and these had become more serious by July.
His organisation paid Clearwater €313,000 for work left incomplete as a result of the company’s failure.
He said he hoped that the liquidators “act on behalf of creditors and that they look into the company in great detail”.
The well-known Athboy Celtic Association Football Club in Co Meath is owed €135,800 according to a list of creditors.
Following news that the company ceased trading the week before last, several of the organisations hit complained that Clearwater had not been communicating with them.
Norton refused to comment following Friday’s meeting.

title: Irish researchers discover how cancers evade chemotherapy by entering ‘zombie-like state’
description: Findings by scientists at Trinity College Dublin offer hope for improved treatment options in future
content:
Irish researchers have discovered how cancers evade chemotherapy by entering a “zombie-like state”, offering hope for improved treatment options.
Scientists at Trinity College Dublin examined how cancerous tumours can escape the cell-killing effects of commonly used chemotherapy drugs by entering what is called premature senescence, which attracts the wound-healing properties of the immune system.
A person’s immune system plays a critical role in co-ordinating repair and replacement of damaged tissue, which is a process called wound healing.
[ Woman (28) with stage 4 cancer awarded large sum after radiologist misread scan Opens in new window ]
However, the researchers said cancers can exploit these wound healing capabilities for their own ends.
The cancers can masquerade as damaged tissue and trick the immune system into helping malignant cells to divide and acquire extra oxygen and nutrients rather than killing them.
They are often referred to as “zombie-like cells” because they have stopped dividing after treatment but do not die and continue to linger in the body and negatively affect the health of surrounding tissues.
For this reason, cancers have been described as “wounds that do not heal”.
However, how cancers switch on the wound healing capabilities of the immune system is still poorly understood.
The Trinity team found that molecules called Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins (IAPs) functioned in this setting by neutralising the cell-killing effects of molecules called “death receptors” that were switched on in response to DNA damage caused by chemotherapy.
Improved treatment options that neutralise more of these tumours promise to improve quality of life and survival rates, but to deliver these treatments, scientists need to understand how tumours function and where their weaknesses may lie.
[ Davina McCall reveals new health battle against cardiovascular disease Opens in new window ]
The research isolated a new mechanism that explains how some tumours evade death and use the body’s immune system to aid their recovery, as well as pinpointing promising new drug treatments, such as IAP antagonists, that kill them.
The research was led by Prof Seamus Martin, Smurfit professor of medical genetics, and Dr Gokhan Gunay, postdoctoral research fellow. Supported by the European Research Council and Research Ireland, it was published in the leading journal Science Advances.
“Discovering how tumours can evade the cell-killing effects of chemotherapy and enter senescence is an important and challenging problem,” said Martin.
“These new findings suggest ways in which we may be able to lower the defences of tumours by neutralising IAPs after the delivery of chemotherapeutic drugs, which should block their entry to senescence and kill more cells of the tumour.”

title: Dead Sails in the Sunset: Frank McNally on the cultural evolution of a Dublin windmill
description: Liberties tower is getting a second wind with new event space
content:
I f the buildings around St Patrick’s Tower in Dublin are now the Digital Hub, as they are, then I suppose the tower’s green dome must be the Digital Hubcap.
But the upper reaches of what used to be a windmill are still off-limits to the public. And the focus of an event on Wednesday night was 40 metres below the copper cupola: the opening of the ground floor as a new cultural space.
The inaugural concert did not put wind in the old mill’s sails, because it no longer has sails, Not since 1820, when steam rendered them redundant.
Even so, aptly, there were some wind instruments – a set of uilleann pipes and a flute – involved in a show that marked the building’s transition from industrial past to cultural future.
The ground-floor venue will help belatedly put the tower on the map of Dublin. For although its silhouette is an unmistakable landmark on the south inner-city skyline, the name is not well known beyond the neighbourhood.
That may be in part because it was a historic afterthought. The original smock windmill, so called for its resemblance in shape to the garment, was a purely functional facility, built in 1757 and long the tallest of its kind in Europe.
Milling grain for whiskey, it became the centrepiece of Roe’s Distillery, which over the next 150 years grew to be world’s biggest, covering 17 acres from Thomas Street to the Liffey, with a mile of conveyor belts turning 1,500 barrels of barley a day into an annual two million gallons of alcohol.
That was a glory era for Irish whiskey generally, and the Liberties version in particular. The “Golden Triangle” of local distilleries then also included those of the two Johns, Jameson and Power.
But thanks to steam, the working windmill was soon superfluous. And it was only when the sails were long gone, in the late 19th century, that the tower acquired an onion-shaped dome along with a weathervane that gave it its modern name.
[ Free Show: Frank McNally on the liberating power of prison art Opens in new window ]
You may strain to see it from the ground, but that’s a four-foot-high St Patrick on the top.
In a development Father Mathew would have approved of, the national saint’s likeness went on to overlook a precipitous decline in the fortunes not just of Roe’s but of Irish whiskey generally, which spent the next century becoming a poor relation to Scotch.
Mind you, in the meantime, the behemoth that is Guinness rose to take over the 17 acres vacated by the distillers.
It’s a curious footnote to history, of which Father Mathew would surely not approve, that the two great cathedrals of Dublin 8 are both, in a sense, monuments to drink.
St Patrick’s was rescued from near ruin in the 1860s by the benevolence of Benjamin Guinness. Then Henry Roe underwrote a similarly expensive refurbishment of Christ Church, which helped usher his company towards ruin instead.
[ Mr Nobody and a broken vase: Frank McNally on a British Museum accident with historic resonance Opens in new window ]
Amid all this rise and fall of business empires, by the way, someone planted a pear tree beside the old windmill in 1850. A century-and-three-quarters later, it’s still there and producing fruit.
Wednesday night’s celebration of the new cultural space, hosted by Digital Hub CEO Fiach Mac Conghail, included the world premiere of a poem specially commissioned for the occasion.
“The Angels’ Share” by Annemarie Ní Churreáin takes its title from the portion of a spirit that evaporates during oak-barrel maturation, although in the poet’s telling the evaporation in this case animated the surrounding community:
“And the angels’ share is the woodsweet heart of Dublin/trembling, like a secret cabinet of bees, in a garden of thyme/a colony of wings, in this city within a city/that is eternally flickering.”
The night also featured music from Na Píobairí Uilleann and a young folk band, Heron Red, recent graduates of the local BIMM musical school that also produced Fontaines DC.
Towards the other end of the oak-barrel maturation spectrum, meanwhile, there was an unofficial competition between poet/Irish Times man Gerard Smyth and the veteran trade unionist/singer Des Geraghty as to which was the most aboriginal citizen of the Liberties present.
[ Irish Book Awards: Maggie O’Farrell, Vincent Browne, Sally Hayden and Louise Kennedy on shortlist Opens in new window ]
Smyth grew up in Francis Street and read poems inspired by such memories as Mushatt’s Pharmacy (operated by two Lithuanian brothers who attracted queues outside the shop on Sunday mornings, supposedly for their trademark hangover cure).
