Geraghty was born in Cornmarket, before it was destroyed to make way for a dual carriageway, and went to St Audoen’s National School, “on the city walls”. Like all true Libertarians, as he told me afterwards, he also grew up hearing stories of an urban banshee variant who haunts the “Forty Steps” in particular.
I don’t know whether historic sightings of her were influenced by the amount of angels’ share whiskey in the surrounding air. But hearing about her reminded me of an old nickname for absinthe. And just in case she needed immortalisation, Des did the job a few years ago by writing a fine song about her called “The Green Lady”.

title: Oil price surge and AI nerves weigh on shares
description: Irish market quiet in advance of bank holiday as Kingspan and Ryanair retreat
content:
A surge in oil and continued jitters over the resources needed for AI development kept shares depressed on Friday.
Brent crude hit $115 (€103) a barrel early in the day, its highest for five months, as fears grew that the US would renew strikes on Iran.
The Irish market was relatively quiet, closing slightly down at 13,938.20, in advance of the October bank holiday weekend, dealers said.
Insulation and building materials group Kingspan shed 2 per cent to €89.35.
Dealers said the stock, which has gained ground on the back of the global rush to build data centres, suffered as investors turned against AI-linked stocks this week.
Airline Ryanair retreated 1.87 per cent to €22.53 on the back of oil price gains.
Traders noted that most European carriers suffered on Friday, some losing between 3 per cent and 3.5 per cent.
Housebuilder Glenveagh climbed 1.89 per cent to €2.425 while rival Cairn Homes was flat at €2.71.
AIB added 1.65 per cent to €10.81 but its peer Bank of Ireland edged 0.64 per cent down to €17.92.
Oil price gains boosted BP, which rose 4.35 per cent, and Shell, which gained 3.72 per cent. Both report third-quarter results next week.
Medical equipment maker Smith & Nephew firmed 1.7 per cent after the Financial Times reported it came close to combining with Johnson & Johnson’s DePuy Synthes orthopaedics unit, but discussions fell apart over a leadership disagreement.
Aircraft engine maker Rolls-Royce led the blue-chip fallers, down 7.6 per cent, weighed by the current geopolitical uncertainty, the high jet fuel price environment and an underwhelming response to earnings from French peer Safran, which fell 10 per cent.
Fellow aerospace firm Melrose Industries was off 4.7 per cent.
Aer Lingus owner International Consolidated Airlines Group slipped 3.52 per cent as air travel shares tumbled across Europe following the hike in oil prices. “They move in lock-step,” said one dealer.
Europe’s Stoxx 600, which tracks 18 markets, was poised for a weekly fall on Friday following a rout of tech stocks earlier in the week.
Luxury goods group Kering plunged 16.6 per cent to €178.12 after ​third-quarter sales at its flagship Gucci brand fell as the Middle East and a Chinese wealth tax crackdown hit home.
Shares in luxury goods businesses have been among Europe’s worst hit this year.
Among other stocks, Holcim gained 5.5 per cent to €66.80 after the Swiss ‌cement maker raised its full-year earnings forecast.
French caterer Sodexo rose 6.3 per cent to €59.95 after reporting stronger-than-expected full-year revenue.
Volvo Cars slumped more than 20 per cent to 10.7 Swedish kroner after reporting a bigger-than-expected third-quarter operating loss and said it would cut ​a further 2,500 jobs.
L’Oreal climbed 4 per cent after the French cosmetics group beat third-quarter sales forecasts.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq edged higher on Friday, helped by signs of stabilisation in some tech stocks, while telecom shares tumbled on concerns that SpaceX’s entry in the sector could ​heighten competition and threaten their market share.
For the week, the benchmark S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were on track for losses, while the blue-chip Dow remained slightly higher, supported by gains in defensive stocks.
AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile fell between 1.3 per cent and 5.6 per cent after a report said Elon Musk’s SpaceX was in talks with cellular ‌infrastructure companies about launching a nationwide wireless carrier programme. SpaceX ​shares gained 2.2 per cent.
US cell tower operators gained from the news, with Crown Castle up 11.11 per cent and American Tower up 4.8 per cent. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg, PA, Reuters

title: Jason Donoghue and Kaysie Joyce guarantee at least bronze at World Boxing Under-19 Championships
description: Seven more Irish boxers could earn medals in quarter-final bouts on Saturday in Montenegro
content:
Two Irish boxers have secured medals at the World Boxing Under-19 Championships, with seven more fighting for podium places on Saturday in Budva, Montenegro.
Jason Donoghue (65kg) and Kaysie Joyce (70kg) each guaranteed at least a bronze medal with decision wins on Friday evening, and will box to upgrade their medal later this week.
Donoghue won by the narrowest margin, earning a closely contested 3-2 split decision over Kazakhstan’s Akzhurek Kalabay in the 65kg division.
The Olympic BC Mullingar man enjoyed a really strong start to the fight, outlanding his opponent with straight right hands in the first.
The fight became rough, as both boxers were docked points, but the Irish fighter was well ahead on three cards by the end of the second.
Despite a spirited attack from Kalabay, Donoghue boxed clever in the final round, avoiding any further deductions to claim a 3-2 victory and a world medal.
Clonmel BC’s Kaysie Joyce overcame England’s Shannon Warren in a gruelling fight to earn a medal in the women’s 70kg class.
In the first round, Warren used her physical strength to push Joyce to the ropes, but the Irish fighter scored the better shots, landing often with the left hook, and taking the first round on the judges’ scorecards.
The second proved tougher for Joyce, as Warren pushed a higher pace, and the Irish fighter also had a point taken off for dipping her head below the beltline.
That deduction left Joyce facing a major deficit, but an outstanding final round performance allowed her to complete the comeback and claim a world medal with a 4-1 split decision.
Earlier on Friday, Louise Joyce of Olympic BC Mullingar won a split decision to reach the quarter finals of the 48kg class.
She joins Kayleigh Byrne (51kg), Grace Bailey (65kg), Lee Largey Snodden (55kg), Kalib Walshe (60kg), Jason Whelan (75kg) and reigning European champion John Donoghue (70kg) who could all guarantee medals with quarter-final wins on Saturday.

title: Sex tourism concerns led Dublin-based Airbnb to suspend account
description: Columbian property letting company  brought proceedings in High Court, which were successfully opposed
content:
Airbnb , which has its European, Middle East and Africa headquarters in Dublin, has successfully opposed High Court proceedings requiring it to reinstate the account of a Colombian property letting company which was terminated due to concerns about a breach of its ban on listings for sex tourism.
Medellín-based Turisvivienda SAS operates a portfolio of short-term rentals in the Colombian city which are close to the nightlife area and described as akin to Dublin’s Temple Bar.
Turisvivienda brought injunction proceedings in the High Court against Airbnb Ireland Unlimited Company, as under the terms of service between the parties, the Irish courts have exclusive jurisdiction to determine disputes between them.
Judge Marguerite Bolger refused the injunction application, saying she was not satisfied that Turisvivienda had established a strong case that it would succeed at trial that Airbnb’s conclusions before it disabled the account were unreasonable, groundless and/or unlawful.
The judge said that under its terms of service relating to its sex tourism policy, Airbnb does not permit paid sexual services at a listing, even in locations where these activities are legal.
She said there are long-standing issues in Colombia, and in particular in Medellín, in relation to sex tourism and sex trafficking. Sex work is not illegal in Colombia for sex workers aged 18 years or over.
Since September 2024, Airbnb has actively engaged with the authorities in Medellín on this issue and has recently removed over 150 Medellín-based hosts from its platform under its policies on sex work.
Turisvivienda said it has also proactively put steps in place to prevent sex work in its properties, which include 24-hour security, the display of an anti-sex tourism statement in its listing descriptions and around the properties and requiring all guests and visitors to sign a contract prohibiting sex work and providing personal ID.
On June 21st last year, Turisvivienda filed a safety report with Airbnb about a guest’s behaviour and was unhappy with the response to its complaint. Two days later, it was advised that, following an investigation, its account was being terminated for violating the defendant’s sex work policies.
Turisvivienda appealed and provided documentary evidence on its policy to prevent sex tourism.
Airbnb later responded, saying it had identified “direct on-platform communications with booking guests that violate our Terms of Service, specifically our policies prohibiting sex tourism”.
It listed extracts from online conversations between Turisvivienda and its guests, including references to the phrase “guest friendly”, which it described to Airbnb as “a common coded phrase used by sex tourists travelling to Colombia to connect with hosts that permit sex work in their listings”.
Airbnb also said that although this term is not solely an indicator of complicity in sex tourism, it is “a strong signal when observed in combination with other indicators”.
Turisvivinda’s founder and 90 per cent shareholder, David Emch, sought to have the dispute dealt with by arbitration at the International Centre for Dispute Resolution (ICDR) but an arbitrator found the ICDR lacked jurisdiction to decide the claim.
Last May Turisvivienda brought an application here for an injunction to have its account restored.
It claimed Airbnb was in breach of contract for reasons including that it failed to follow its own terms of service and by disabling its account for a reason not provided for in the contract.
As part of its case, an affidavit was sworn by one of its employees who responded to posts on the Airbnb system. The employee said she understood the use in some guest queries of the words “girls” and “chicks” not to refer to sex workers, but simply to be alternative terms to describe women.
She described her understanding of a message from a guest, “get me a bride”, as meaning “the fact that the guest was hoping to find someone to marry while visiting Medellin, and I did not think it appropriate or necessary for me to respond”.
Airbnb opposed the injunction application.
Bolger said it was not for the court to determine whether the communications did or did not indicate sex work but rather to decide whether Airbnb’s conclusion that they did was reasonable and lawful.
She was not satisfied Turisvivienda had established a strong case that it would succeed at trial.
She also said that in the absence of a statable claim that Turisvivienda’s financial viability is seriously at risk, its losses to date are entirely financial, for which it can be adequately compensated in damages.

title: Josie Ray murder accused allegedly headbutted her daughter night before, court hears
description: Deceased’s daughter previously threatened to stab her mother
content:
A man accused of murdering a pensioner in her home allegedly headbutted the deceased’s daughter the night before the alleged killing, his trial heard Friday.
Evidence was also heard on Friday that a daughter of the deceased pensioner previously threatened to stab her with a knife.
The deceased, Josephine Ray (89), known as Josie, of St Joseph’s Park, Nenagh, Co Tipperary , was found allegedly strangled and smothered in her bed, on August 4th, 2024.
Hasan Ali Gori (52), originally from Chad, Africa, and with an address at St Joseph’s Park, Nenagh, has pleaded not guilty at the Central Criminal Court , sitting in Limerick , to a single charge of murdering Ray.
At the time, Ali Gori was living in Josie Ray’s home, while in a relationship with her daughter, Mary Ray, who has a learning disability.
The court has heard from several witnesses that said Josie Ray, Mary Ray and Ali Gori were constantly arguing with one another and their quarrelling was often “volatile” and foul-mouthed.
Josie Ray did not approve of Mary Ray’s relationship with Ali Gori, and Mary Ray suspected Ali Gori of being unfaithful to her, the court heard.
[ Josie Ray murder accused told her daughter one of them would have to leave, court hears Opens in new window ]
On Friday, Charlotte Moran, a girlfriend of a grandson of the deceased, gave evidence she saw the accused, Ali Gori, “headbutting” Mary Ray outside Josie Ray’s house on the night before the alleged killing.
Moran said Ali Gori “looked very cross” and he “gave a headbutt to her face”.
Moran said she also heard Ali Gori shouting four times: “No one will murder me.”
“He was very cross, he was just shouting, he leaned in his head into Mary’s forehead,” said Moran.
The witness said she also saw Ali Gori shoving Mary.
Josie Ray did not approve of Mary having relationships with men and her bringing the men back to her house. She also “did not like” Ali Gori, members of her family said.
[ Josie Ray’s grandchildren had told gardaí of safety concerns before her death, court hears Opens in new window ]
Two of the deceased’s grandchildren told the court that, prior to her death, they had each contacted gardaí, social workers and their local authority, to voice concerns for their grandmother’s welfare in her home, while she was living with the accused and her daughter Mary.
Louise Walsh told the court that Josie was very protective of Mary because of her intellectual disability and that she would often chaperone Mary when her daughter would travel by bus from their home in Tipperary to meet men in Limerick.
Walsh said Josie Ray would sometimes sleep rough on benches in Limerick waiting for Mary, if she spent the night in the city.
Walsh agreed with the accused’s barrister, Aidan Doyle, that it upset Josie that Mary had a penchant for African men specifically.
“Yeah, it used to really agitate [Josie] a lot,” said Walsh.
The prosecution’s case is that Ali Gori murdered Josie Ray by strangulation and smothering her.

title: Woman arrested over Cork murder of man shot while ‘trying to retrieve stolen drugs’
description: Paul ‘Bosco’ O’Connor found dead by banks of Blackwater river at Ballyellis by a man walking his dog
content:
Gardaí investigating the murder of a man who was found dead from gunshot wounds in north Cork have arrested a woman (40s).
Paul “Bosco” O’Connor (56), from Connolly Road in Ballyphehane, Cork city, was found by the banks of the Blackwater river at Ballyellis, just downstream of Mallow , at 1.30pm on October 15th.
Gardaí believe he had gone to retrieve stolen drugs when he was shot.
O’Connor’s body was discovered by a man walking his dog. The man immediately alerted the emergency services and gardaí sealed off the scene for a technical examination.
A postmortem by Assistant State Pathologist Dr Margot Bolster at Cork University Hospital later confirmed that O’Connor had died from gunshot wounds.
Gardaí did not release the results of the postmortem for operational reasons, but The Irish Times has learned that O’Connor was shot both in the back of the head and face at close range.
Gardaí established from CCTV footage that O’Connor travelled by train from Kent Station in Cork city to Mallow at 7.20pm on the previous night, Wednesday, October 14th.
They believe that O’Connor went to Mallow to retrieve a kilo of cocaine that had been stolen from an Irish criminal organisation and had been hidden in a ditch in the field in Ballyellis.
However, O’Connor was instead shot dead in what one Garda source said was “an execution-style killing” and the drugs removed by his killer who left the scene.
The garda investigation focused on O’Connor’s phone activity and who he may been in contact with before journeying to Mallow and if he met anyone on arrival in the north Cork town.
The woman arrested on Thursday at an address in Mallow is being held at a Garda station in the Southern Region under the provisions of Section 50 of the Criminal Justice Act, 2007, which allows gardaí to hold suspects for up to seven days.
On Monday, detectives arrested an eastern European man in his 30s at his home in the Mallow area for questioning about the murder of O’Connor.
The man was taken to Mallow Garda station where he was detained under Section 50 of the Criminal Justice Act 2007.
The man had his initial period of 24 hours extended by a chief superintendent in keeping with the legislation and he continues to be questioned by gardaí.
Gardaí carried out a search of a property near the scene of the shooting but to date have not recovered the shotgun that they believed was used in the murder.
The Garda Water Unit carried out a search of the Blackwater in case the gun had been thrown in the river but searches have so far failed to locate the weapon.
O’Connor, who had convictions for armed robbery and assault in the 1990s, is survived by his brother, Terry, and sisters, Mary and Valerie. His private funeral service is due to be held this weekend.

title: Gardaí arrest two men and seize explosives, with assistance from army bomb squad
description: Both individuals detained at Garda stations in northeast of country after Co Louth search operation
content:
Gardaí arrested two men and seized explosives in Co Louth in an operation assisted by the army bomb squad on Friday.
Component parts and suspected explosive material were seized in the search, assisted by the Defence Forces Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) team.
Two men, one in his 50s and another in his 20s, have been arrested as part of the investigation.
Both are currently being detained at Garda stations in the northeast of the country under the Offences Against the State Act, 1939.
Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said: “This is a particularly significant find. This search and arrest operation by our counter-terrorism unit, the Special Detective Unit (SDU), demonstrates the important work carried out by Garda national security personnel every day to protect people on this island.
“It also shows that we must continue to degrade and dismantle the threat from those who are intent on destroying peace by harming others.”
He added: “I have been in contact with the PSNI Chief Constable Jon Boutcher this morning and our close co-operation in relation to countering dissident groups continues. I would also like to thank the Defence Forces for its assistance in today’s search operation.”

title: Face paints containing lead found by health watchdog
description: HPRA advises parents and guardians to buy from reputable retailers
content:
Parents and guardians have been warned about the danger of buying face paints or Halloween cosmetics from outside the European Union , after some items were found to contain elevated levels of lead.
The Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) said that over the past two years, seven out of 40 products sampled by the safety watchdog were found to be non-compliant with EU cosmetic requirements and were removed from the Irish market.
The surveillance activities found cosmetics containing restricted or undesirable substances, including elevated levels of heavy metals such as lead.
Exposure to lead should be minimised, particularly among children, whose skin is still developing and may be more sensitive to certain substances, the HPRA said, warning that the use of products that do not meet EU safety requirements may “increase the risk of adverse health effects”.
“While cosmetic products sold in the European Union must meet strict safety requirements, products purchased from unknown or unverified sources, including some online marketplaces, may not comply with EU legislation and could pose risks to consumer health,” the HPRA said.
The HPRA contributes to the monitoring of all cosmetic products placed on the market, including cosmetic ingredients and emerging safety issues.
In the lead-up to Halloween, the HPRA undertakes targeted market surveillance activities focusing on face paints and other children’s cosmetic products that experience a seasonal increase in demand.
Although most cosmetic products available through reputable retailers comply with regulatory requirements, the HPRA is advising parents to remain vigilant of the dangers posed by substandard face paints, to check product labels carefully, and ensure that face paints and other cosmetics are purchased from reputable sources.
Lisa Byrne, cosmetic product manager at the HPRA, advised parents to buy these products from “reputable retailers and trusted online suppliers”.
[ Halloween festivals, spooky parades and ghoulish galas to consider this midterm Opens in new window ]
“While the vast majority of products available through established retailers comply with EU safety and regulatory requirements, caution is advised when purchasing from unfamiliar online sellers or sources outside the European Union,” she said.
“Choosing products from trusted suppliers helps ensure that appropriate safety assessments have been carried out, reducing the risk of exposure to non-compliant products and helping children enjoy Halloween safely.”
There are a number of indicators that could suggest a product is non-compliant or counterfeit, the HPRA said, including missing or poor-quality labelling, spelling errors, or products being sold at unusually low prices.
It said a face paint patch test should be carried out before the product is applied to larger areas of skin, and that it should not be applied to broken, irritated or sensitive skin.

title: Vincent Kompany taken to hospital after collapsing during Bayern Munich training
description: The Belgian had been nursing a virus in recent days and had missed some of his team’s training sessions
content:
Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany was rushed to hospital ‌on Friday after collapsing during a training session, the German champions ​said.
The Belgian had been nursing a virus in recent days and had missed some of his team’s training sessions.
“On ​Friday, Vincent Kompany required medical attention after collapsing during a ⁠training session for Bayern’s reserve team,” the club ‌said. “The ‌head ​coach of the professional squad had been observing the second team’s session.”
“Kompany is ⁠currently undergoing ​a thorough examination in the ​hospital and will remain under medical care. For ‌the time being, his ​coaching staff will manage all training and match-related ⁠operations.”
The Bundesliga leaders, who ⁠drew ​2-2 at home against Arsenal in the Champions League earlier this week, are due to travel to Freiburg on Sunday.
“Vincent Kompany’s health is our top priority,” said Max Eberl, Bayern’s Board Member for Sport. “At Bayern, we ‌will do everything ⁠we can to ensure he makes a speedy recovery.”
“Vinnie is receiving all the necessary medical ‌care and support, and he will be given as ​much time as he needs. Everyone ​at FC Bayern wishes Vinnie a quick recovery.”

title: Can Emmanuel Macron pull France back from the brink?
description: Protests and paralysis have cast a shadow over the twilight of a presidency once defined by ambition and confidence
content:
E mmanuel Macron had a spring in his step. Passing the reporters who were accompanying him on his four-day trip to the Gulf this week, he gave them a wink.
It was a turnaround in the French president’s mood. He had left Paris for Kuwait on Sunday October 18th under a cloud.
The remains of Limoges town hall were still smouldering. While the worst of the unrest had abated, bands of youths still roamed the Marais district of Paris looking for shop windows to smash. The president’s grave address to the nation on Sunday evening had fallen flat.
But now Macron had a win to announce: he had secured shipments of liquefied natural gas from Qatar to furnish France through the winter, and extra sales of diesel from the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain .
The deal would have a “direct impact on French citizens”, Macron told reporters, and “avoid the shortages that suppliers have been anticipating”.
Yet the press did not allow him to dwell for long on his success.
“Mr President, 24 hours after your much-criticised address to the French people, there’s a call for fresh protests this Saturday, October 24th,” a reporter began.
“Violence, vandalism, looting, the town hall of Limoges in ashes ... Are you concerned about a return to violence? Are you concerned about losing control?”
As he approaches the end of his final term as president, Macron faces a bleak conclusion to 10 years in power.
His aims were ambitious when, at age 39, he was elected in 2017 at the head of a newly-created political movement uniting France’s centre ground, promising to rise above France’s traditional divisions and bring competent people from outside of politics into a government that would revive economic growth.
A decade on, France is more divided than ever. Polls show an electorate polarised between hard-core left and right candidates, with the centre ground fragmented.
This week, the cost France must pay to borrow exceeded 5 per cent for long-term bonds for the first time since 2002 as spooked investors noted the political division, scenes of unrest, and one of the highest budget deficits in the euro zone.
Public debt has ballooned, as government spending careered out of control during the Covid-19 pandemic and struggled to come back down afterwards.
[ Europe’s angry autumn: what’s driving the wave of protests? Opens in new window ]
It was whispered that France, perhaps even more than a possible artificial intelligence bubble, could be the trigger for a new global economic crisis.
At the heart of the sense of crisis is France’s hung parliament, which limits the government’s ability to act. It’s the consequence of a disastrous decision by Macron to call a snap election in the summer of 2024, which lost his centrist coalition its parliamentary majority.
While cutting an impressive figure on the international stage, Macron’s achievements at home have long been seen as more mixed.
Renaud Foucart, an economist at the University of Lancaster, believes a failure to reform France’s pension system, which hobbles public finances, will be Macron’s “main domestic legacy as president”.
“A man elected with a huge majority to reform, who failed to do so, leaving a divided country of angry people who don’t seem to understand the cause of their problems,” Foucart summarised.
There was a note of gravity to the announcement from the Élysée Palace last Sunday afternoon that the head of state would address the French people that evening.
Live television channels switched to show the president as the clocks struck 8pm.
“I speak to you this evening at an extremely grave moment,” he began from his desk within the gilded Élysée Palace, the flags of France and the European Union stationed behind him.
The government was “doing the maximum” to address high fuel prices, he said, and working on solutions for problems raised by students. “We’ll go on taking action.”
Local authorities would consider whether to allow further demonstrations, he said, and might refuse some – something they do already. “We need unity, calm and respect.”
When a radio producer called this reporter shortly afterwards to ask what Macron had said, it was difficult to pinpoint anything in particular.
Baffled commentary broke out among politicians, officials, journalists and the general public, asking why the president had announced an address to the nation only to have little to say.
“I would have preferred decisions,” Édouard Philippe, a centre-right politician who served as prime minister under Macron, wrote in a public message addressed to the president. “Our country needs to be governed.”
Others were harsher. “Emmanuel Macron’s address is deeply worrying,” wrote the conservative presidential candidate Bruno Retailleau. “The president of the Republic appears completely overwhelmed.”
Protesters and their sympathisers said Macron should have announced actions to meet their demands; others called for the declaration of a state of emergency to restore order.
Macron left the country almost immediately afterwards to begin his Gulf tour.
[ ‘There’s nothing left’: French businesses count the cost of a weekend of unrest Opens in new window ]
“A few of us tried to dissuade him from leaving, but he was determined,” an adviser to Macron, François Heisbourg of the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London, told French newspaper Le Monde.
The trip is “out of touch with reality, showing that the president has not grasped what is happening in the country”, Heisbourg said.
The far-right National Rally, whose support has risen in polls since the unrest, promised its supporters it would restore the authority of the state if Marine Le Pen is elected president in six months’ time.
“Faced with scenes of insurrection and civil war that engulfed the country, the government abdicated,” the party told supporters.
Macron brushed off the criticism, telling reporters that it was important not to show “nervousness” and “stick with the original plan”.
“The hand must not tremble at the head of the state,” he said.
On his return to France, Macron convened a series of meetings, summoning the intelligence services to the Élysée on Thursday morning and resuming talks with the main political parties.
Macron seemed all business as he made public remarks afterwards. It quickly became clear there would be no declaration of emergency.
“The general recommendation is that there be no demonstrations in the coming days,” he announced . Only protests by trade unions would be permitted, and they would be directed away from city centres “to ensure calm, to protect businesses, and to protect public buildings”.
A student protest amassed in Paris’s 13th arrondissement as the news trickled down, having secured a court ruling overturning an initial police ban.
An unauthorised protest formed in Lyons, where demonstrators had sacked and burned the tourism office days before.
“We will not be silenced,” a student union member told French television in Lyons, calling for better conditions in schools, more funding for research and more university places. “Anger won’t be assuaged by a repressive response from the state ... What we want is to be heard, for our demands to be met.”
Members of the yellow vest movement were refused permission to march on Saturday from Place de la Bastille to Place de l’Opéra in Paris, a route that would have taken them in the direction of France’s seats of power.
However, the CGT union, one of the largest and oldest trade unions in France, received permission to march from Place de la Bastille to Place de la Nation – a march in the opposite direction, still in central Paris, but moving towards the outskirts.
The yellow vests – who have declined to distance themselves from the violence and have called for an “act two” – immediately announced they would join.
The French government promised a large security presence to ensure order, including the deployment of members of the army.
The city of Paris, however, was unconvinced. The Louvre and Musée d’Orsay announced they would shut their doors. Up and down the main shopping streets, shops could be seen covering their glass with chipboard.
[ Macron tightens curbs on protests and accuses far left of ‘seditious acts’ Opens in new window ]

title: Man (44) who threw beer bottles at police during Ballymena riot jailed for one year
description: ‘This is the worst thing I have ever done’, Gary McCrystal told probation officer after his arrest
content:
A father-of-five who threw two beer bottles at police during a racially-motivated riot in Ballymena was jailed for a year on Friday.
When he is released from prison, Gary McCrystal will spend an additional two years on supervised licence.
He admitted a charge of rioting on June 10th last year and was handed the three-year sentence by Judge Laura Ievers.
Belfast Crown Court heard that there was a spike in public disorder aggravated by hospitality towards ethnic groups for three consecutive nights in June 2025.
While there was no loss of life, eight families were displaced.
During the disorder, police officers were attacked with petrol bombs, fireworks and masonry resulting in over 50 officers in Ballymena being injured.
On June 10th, 2025, hundreds of people gathered in the Clonavon area of the Co Down town.
McCrystal (44) was identified on police footage as being present.
At around 8pm he made his way to the front of the crowd towards police lines.
A group of masked men took items from the rear of a residential property and created a barricade in front of PSNI vehicles.
This masked group then started pelting police with bricks and other items while McCrystal stood and observed from around 3m away.
As officers moved the crowd back, McCrystal remained at the front talking to masked men around him.
McCrystal then joined a large crowd who were throwing missiles at police and it’s at this point that a masked rioter removed a beer bottle from a bag held by McCrystal and threw it at police lines.
Following this, McCrystal started distributing bottles from his bag to other rioters before removing two from the bag and launching them at officers.
He then set the bag down and walked into the crowd.
Footage of the rioting was viewed and police released a series of images of those involved in the riot.
During interview he made some admissions.
After he pleaded guilty to the charge of rioting, McCrystal spoke to a probation officer.
He said he’d been at the scene when the disorder broke out, that he intended to meet a friend on the North Road and that a masked individual took a bottle from his bag and threw it at police.
McCrystal also told the officer he threw two bottles himself and remained in the area for around an hour before going home.
In addition, he expressed shame and embarrassment about his behaviour and told the probation officer “this is the worst thing I have ever done”.
During Friday’s sentencing, Ievers said she had considered defence submissions made on McCrystal’s behalf by his barrister Neil Moore.
These set out the extensive caring responsibilities he has for both his mother and his son who has special needs.
Ievers also noted McCrystal’s “vintage” but “relevant” criminal record for criminal damage and disorderly behaviour dating back to 2001.
As she imposed the sentence, evers addressed McCrystal and told him:
“People should be able to feel safe in their own homes. They should not have to live in terror.”

title: WRC upholds mandatory retirement of Eircom technician after 44 years on job
description: Employee worked for contractor after termination of his role
content:
A tribunal has upheld the imposition of a mandatory retirement age on an Eircom worker who said he was “fully capable” to keep working past 65.
The ruling comes despite the fact the worker was called back to do “identical” work for Eircom via a third-party contractor when severe weather hit after the termination of his job in September 2024.
Dermot Hayes, a telecoms technician of more than 40 years’ service, had pursued a complaint alleging ageist discrimination under the Employment Equality Act against Eircom Ltd.
It was rejected by the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) in a decision published on Friday.
Eircom cited “intergenerational fairness, succession planning, and health and safety” in a letter in August 2024 declining a request he had made to keep working past his 65th birthday the following month, the tribunal heard.
Representing himself before the WRC earlier this month, Hayes said he started his career as a trainee at the Department of Posts and Telegraphs in October 1980, prior to Eircom being founded with the privatisation of the telecoms system.
His evidence was that he attended a medical appointment with an occupational health assessor in June 2024 and was deemed “fit for work”.
Hayes added that after his retirement on September 24th, 2024, he was brought on by a third-party contractor to do work for Eircom which was “identical” to what he was doing before.
He said that the health and safety concerns Eircom was relying on to justify his mandatory retirement at 65 did not actually prevent him doing the work.
He told the WRC he was “fully capable” of doing the job for longer, and set out a claim for financial loss calculated on the basis of working to the age of 70.
Úna Stafford, managing director of Open Eir Networks, said retiring at 65 was the long-standing practice at the firm as part of a workforce planning strategy which involved taking on apprentices.
Cross-examining Stafford, Hayes pointed to “staffing shortages and overtime demands” which he argued showed there was an “ongoing need for experienced technicians”.
He questioned the reliance of the firm on contractors. Stafford said contractors were being used “only in limited or exceptional circumstances” and that the retirement was “necessary” for workforce planning.
Stafford also said in her evidence that Hayes had an “unblemished career” with the utility and his service was “hugely appreciated”.
Adjudicator Úna Glazier-Farmer wrote it was of “some significance” that Hayes was let do “substantially identical work” for Eircom Ltd through a third-party contractor.
It undermined Eircom’s stance on health and safety as a justification for mandatory retirement, she wrote.
“This tends to weaken the respondent’s reliance on health and safety as a justification for requiring the complainant to retire at age 65, particularly where he had also been certified fit for work,” Glazier-Farmer wrote.
However, she noted that Hayes’s post-retirement work was “a once-off six-week contract” to respond to “a rare occurrence of an extratropical cyclone, and not enough to make the retirement policy disproportionate.
Glazier-Farmer concluded that Eircom was pursuing “legitimate aims” by imposing a retirement age of 65, which was an “appropriate and proportionate” way to pursue workforce planning, intergenerational fairness and health and safety.
She dismissed Hayes’s complaint on that basis, ruling he “was not discriminated against”.
The respondent was represented by Peter Ward, who appeared with Morgane Conaty, instructed by Arthur Cox .

title: Campaigners call for Roger Casement’s remains to be returned to Co Antrim as he wished
description: Revolutionary is buried in Glasnevin, where he was returned in 1965, decades after his execution
content:
The repatriation of the remains of Roger Casement was so secret that the first the public knew about it was when they arrived in Dublin on February 23rd, 1965.
Casement was hanged for treason in Pentonville Prison in August 1916 and the repatriation of his remains to Ireland was a campaign that went on for decades.
It was only in 1965, with the advent of better relations between Ireland and Great Britain, and, in particular, between taoiseach Seán Lemass and British prime minister Harold Wilson, that agreement was reached to bring his body back to Ireland.
Many English and unionist commentators still regarded him as a traitor because of his involvement in the Easter Rising and his attempts to recruit Irish-born British soldiers to fight with the German army during the first World War.
Casement was given a State funeral and huge crowds lined the route. He was buried in Glasnevin Cemetery with an oration from 1916 veteran and then president Éamon de Valera .
There had been “long years of waiting”, de Valera said. “We are glad to have him back among us. We are glad that the British government have been wise enough that this request should be met.
“It required great courage to do what Casement did, and his name would be honoured, not merely here, but by oppressed peoples everywhere, even if he had done nothing for the freedom of our own country.”
[ Roger Casement told own defence team ‘black diaries’ were a forgery Opens in new window ]
He anticipated that Casement’s grave would become a place of pilgrimage for those “wishing to make this land worthy of the sacrifices of the past”.
Casement’s is one of the best-known graves in Glasnevin Cemetery, but his interment in Dublin was not in accordance with his dying wishes as articulated to his cousin Elizabeth Bannister just after he lost his appeal against his death sentence.
“Don’t let my body lie here – get me back to the green hill by Murlough – by the McGarry’s [sic] house looking down on the Moyle – that’s where I’d like to be now and that’s where I’d like to lie,” he wrote from Pentonville Prison in July 1916.
A group of volunteers are now seeking for his dying wishes to be honoured. The Roger Casement Commemoration and Reinterment Association has applied for an exhumation licence to remove his body from Glasnevin Cemetery and rebury it on a spot overlooking Murlough Bay in Co Antrim .
Association chairman Alan Daly acknowledged that the final decision, if granted, would be made at Government level given Casement’s historical significance.
“If I thought this wasn’t going to happen I wouldn’t put so much time and effort into this,” he said.
“In my opinion this will happen and it will be for the right reasons. We want to honour a dead man’s wish. He knew what he wanted and it wasn’t granted.”
[ ‘I left Ireland and became foreign correspondent for The Guardian, only to encounter echoes of Roger Casement’ Opens in new window ]
In 1965 Casement’s remains were not brought back to Northern Ireland because of the volatile political situation at that time. Things have changed, said Daly, and attitudes in the North are unlikely to be an obstacle for the reparation of his remains.
A site has already been chosen should his remains be reinterred. It is consecrated ground in an old churchyard overlooking Murlough Bay.
Dublin City Council , Glasnevin Trust and the Government have been contacted for comment.

title: Russia and Ukraine agree to local ceasefire in Oleshky amid deepening humanitarian crisis
description: People in Russian-occupied city facing severe food and water shortages, with some reportedly surviving on weeds
content:
The White House has said that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive.
In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from October 29th to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians.
Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations.
Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire.
The White House statement said the ceasefire was brokered by Melania Trump , and her representative worked directly with ​Russian and Ukrainian ‌leadership to define the ​terms. “Residents who wish to evacuate will receive co-ordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” the first lady said.
Despite the claim the ceasefire had been brokered by Melania Trump, there had already been protracted efforts to organise a humanitarian ceasefire, with claims by Ukrainian officials that it had been Russia that had rejected previous calls.
Calls for a ceasefire had been issued by Pope Leo XIV – who discussed the issue with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskiy – the United Nations, EU officials and the Council of Europe. As recently as October 18th, Ukraine’s Ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, had also said he thought agreement was close without any mention of the first lady’s involvement.
Ukraine has for weeks been pushing for a civilian evacuation from Oleshky and nearby settlements, at times using drones to airdrop emergency food and medical supplies into town.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces continue to report widespread disruptions to the Starlink satellite network, despite Donald Trump’s claim that Elon Musk had lifted restrictions on the service.
The slowdown, which has affected the communications system used by Ukrainian troops, began last week after Trump and Elon Musk, the founder of Starlink, publicly criticised Zelenskiy over continued strikes on Russian oil refineries.
The restrictions have raised questions and confusion about who ordered the slowdown and why, with Trump and Musk denying responsibility. Asked about the Starlink slowdowns on Friday, Trump said he would speak to Musk if the restrictions remained in place.
“I’ve heard it was fixed, but if it’s not, I’ll speak to him,” he told reporters.
Ukrainian officials said throughout the day on Friday that speeds remained capped at about 160km/hr, with no indication that the restrictions had been lifted.
“At present, we have not observed any lifting of the restrictions on Starlink,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Zelenskiy.
“There have been isolated cases in which Starlink has operated at speeds slightly above the imposed limits, but this is likely due to SpaceX’s algorithms or specific conditions of use, rather than any lifting of the restrictions,” Beskrestnov added.
The speed restrictions have prevented Ukrainian military equipment, including drones, from maintaining a connection to the satellite network when travelling at high speeds, hampering offensive drone operations and efforts to intercept incoming Russian attacks.
The slowing down of Starlink, coupled with Zelenskiy’s complaints that Washington had temporarily suspended intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, has plunged relations between Ukraine and the US to a new low in recent days.
Tensions first flared after Washington’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel, as Trump sought to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections. Maritime tracking data showed that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel was en route to New York on Thursday. – Guardian

title: ‘Jumping the queue’: Several people allegedly trespassing at Peter McVerry Trust flats
description: Homelessness organisation says occupation preventing it from using apartments to shelter those ‘genuinely in need’
content:
Several people are allegedly illegally occupying a number of Peter McVerry Trust flats in Dublin ’s north inner city, the High Court has heard.
The housing and homelessness charity is seeking court orders requiring several individuals to vacate the four flats at Dorset Lane, Lower Dorset Street, Dublin 1.
Lawyers for the trust were last week granted permission to serve legal proceedings on “persons unknown” in occupation of the flats.
On Friday, two individuals who said they were living at the properties in question appeared before Judge Siobhán Stack.
Cornel Alexandru Eme and Eve Moses sought time to file written evidence in response to the trust’s case against them.
The judge gave Alexandru Eme, Moses and three other named individuals – also with addresses at Dorset Lane – two weeks to file their responding affidavits.
Barry Mansfield, barrister for the trust, said he had no objection to the directions.
In written evidence before the court, David Fee, Peter McVerry Trust director, said the individuals’ occupation of the flats is preventing the trust from using the property to provide housing to homeless people. Fee said he became aware the flats were being occupied in mid-September.
Ktech, a security firm engaged by the trust, attended the property and reported the alleged trespassing to the gardaí , he said.
An officer advised Ktech personnel he “did not wish to assist”, and advised that the trust seek a court order, Fee said.
Solicitors for the trust subsequently received an email from individuals who Fee believes are in occupation of the flats.
In the email, the occupants acknowledged the trust’s role in housing homeless people and outlined a settlement agreement to avoid litigation, according to Fee’s written evidence.
Per their settlement agreement, the occupants, noting their own need for housing, said they would retain possession of the property for 18 months before vacating.
Fee said the offer was “entirely unacceptable”, particularly because it had already agreed to make the property available to Dublin City Council .
Outlining the trust’s reasons for seeking orders against the occupants, Fee said they were “jumping the queue” by preventing the trust from using the apartments to shelter those “who are genuinely in need”.
Fee said he also had concerns about the health and welfare of the occupants.

title: Galway gift card to help people shop local this Christmas
description: Businesses are being encouraged to sign up to the love Galway/Grá do Ghaillimh gift card
content:
A gift card specifically for Galway is to be rolled out in the run-up to Christmas to encourage locals to spend their money in the city and wider county.
The Love Galway/Grá do Ghaillimh gift card is a collaboration between Galway Chamber, Galway City Council and Galway County Council, and is hoping to tap into a desire among many to shop locally
All types and sizes of customer-facing businesses, including retail, hospitality, leisure, accommodation, health and beauty, and services, are being encouraged to sign up to the scheme, which uses technology supported by Mastercard, so no additional equipment is required.
Once launched, the Love Galway card will be commission-free for registered businesses and come in both a physical and virtual format.
The initiative is part of the Town & City Gift Card set-up, which is running countrywide, with more than €17 million worth of cards sold last year and about 3,000 businesses aligned to such initiatives in the Republic.
“The popularity of gift cards is growing, as is the desire to shop local,” said Galway Chamber chief executive Karen Ronan. “We’ve seen the power of local gift cards across Ireland to tap into these trends ... We’re building on brand Galway with our own gift card so we can direct spend to Galway businesses.”
Mayor of Galway City Helen Ogbu said the card was one of several initiatives developed to encourage people to spend money in their local community.
“Having our own gift card will be a huge opportunity for businesses ... to drive business through their door, ring-fencing gift card spend into our local economy,” she said.
Galway County Council cathaoirleach Andrew Reddington echoed that and suggested the wider county, including Connemara and the islands in Galway Bay, were “among the most recognisable parts of Ireland, and we are lucky to have such a great range of towns and villages, with excellent local shops, restaurants, boutiques and businesses”.
He said that as Christmas approached, he would encourage “all customer-facing businesses across the county to register to accept the Love Galway/Grá do Ghaillimh gift card”.

title: By accident or design, Mark Allen and James McClean made it a good week for men’s mental health
description: For two high-profile Irish sportsmen to show entirely different attitudes to struggles in public is a sign of progress
content:
Ultimately, this was probably a good week for men’s mental health. It didn’t feel like that at times but that’s all part of it too. Very little about mental health is ever straightforward and neat.
For now, a couple of high-profile Irish sportsmen talked in public about their mental health and, intentionally or not, conveyed something about broader issues and attitudes towards it. That’s good. That’s progress.
James McClean and Mark Allen are in two different places, living two different lives, facing two different scenarios. McClean is selling a book, his terrific autobiography The Walls, skilfully rendered by Daniel McDonnell. Allen is stepping away from snooker, maybe for a while or maybe for good, in an attempt to get himself back on an even keel.
So it’s not necessarily easy to draw a line between the two of them. They don’t, on the face of it, have a lot in common. But that’s sort of the point.
When we talk about a subject as wide and varied and amorphous as men’s mental health, we are usually dealing in generalities. That’s why it helps for individuals to present themselves as case studies, whether that’s what they mean to do or not. McClean and Allen are real people but serve as pretty useful archetypes too.
Plenty of friend groups have had experience of the James McClean approach to mental health. The guy who buries all the shit deep down under layers of bravado and bluff and bench-pressing. The chap who is a bit out there, no-filter, erratic. Someone you find yourself telling outsiders is actually a grand lad underneath it all.
By the same token, plenty of us have seen friends gradually drift into Mark Allen’s position too. Haunted and withdrawn. Self-esteem on the floor. Quiet and apologetic and second-guessing themselves. Retreating into solitude, unable really to articulate what it is that’s causing them to feel this way.
So much research into mental health pinpoints acceptance as being a key component in any progress you hope to make. The more people who see traces of themselves in McClean or Allen, or any other public figure when it comes to this stuff, the better. Mental health struggles are a lonely station. It’s never bad to see you’re not the only one who feels like this.
Even if, in McClean’s case, what he said didn’t seem to be particularly helpful. He threw around some loose language in an interview with Paul Kimmage, talking about therapy as a sign of weakness. It brought condemnation from all quarters in the early part of the week, including from his wife Erin, who was moved to put out her own statement in response. “I do not agree with James’s opinion on the subject of therapy and mental health,” she wrote on social media. “I’m working on getting him to a place where he recognises that speaking about this is not a sign of weakness.”
There is no greater hero in The Walls than Erin McClean, a formidable Derry woman whose husband, to his credit, genuinely acknowledges how lucky he is to have her. By the end of the week, McClean was on UTV, clarifying and maybe even softening. Maybe.
“Any man that goes to therapy, any man that seeks help, I couldn’t commend them any bigger for doing that,” he told a reporter at his book launch. “But I was talking about me and my own situation. And probably using that word ‘weakness’ or having that view that it’s a weakness for me, maybe that’s my weakness.”
The contrast with Mark Allen couldn’t be more stark. The Antrim snooker player played in Belfast on Tuesday, his first match since April. He played it out of duty, basically – he was drawn against his friend Jordan Brown and the tournament was in The Waterfront. He had spent 10 weeks in a mental health clinic before willing himself to go and play in it. Then he gave an interview to TNT’s Rachel Casey and talked about how he was in a bad place and “just trying to survive”.
This is heartbreaking to watch 🥺💔 Mark Allen admits he may never play snooker again. We’re all rooting for you, Mark 🙏❤️ pic.twitter.com/9v6wvWMflE
Allen’s interview was so bracing that it couldn’t but bubble up out of the usual swamp of content around the internet. It broke through for a couple of reasons. One, though Allen is curiously under-celebrated here, he is one of the best snooker players in the world. For someone in the elite tier of his sport to be so frank and vulnerable took enormous strength. No weakness on show there.
The other reason it caught a viral wave was Casey’s sensitive handling of the other side of the microphone. She didn’t push Allen to say more than he wanted to. She didn’t overload him with questions. She didn’t hurry things along to fit the TV schedule. Her affection for a struggling fellow citizen in snooker’s small world was obvious. When she reached in for a hug, it didn’t feel unprofessional. It felt as if he mattered.
People matter. People with high profiles and people with none. If you have any sort of sporty bent to your media consumption, you heard about either James McClean or Mark Allen, or both, this week. That mattered.
Maybe it made you think about a friend and you checked in for the first time in a while. Maybe it made you think about yourself. Maybe it had no effect whatsoever on the vast majority of people. Maybe it had some small effect on someone who needed it. One way or another, people were talking about men’s mental health.

title: Dónal Lunny’s legacy will be his openness to new ways of interpreting old music
description: The musician, who died on Friday, has been central to the vibrant, innovative spirit of Irish music for more than six decades
content:
There is one figure who has been central to the vibrant, innovative spirit that suffuses Irish traditional music and that is Dónal Lunny , who died on Friday after a lengthy illness. He was at the beating heart of The Bothy Band, Planxty and Moving Hearts, three of the most seminal bands to ever play a traditional tune. His quiet, unassuming presence (and wry wit) have been woven through the fabric of our music for more than six decades, and his passing leaves an immense void that will be felt not just in Ireland but internationally.
Dónal Lunny was one of nine children. He was born in Tullamore, Co Offaly but the family moved to Newbridge, Co Kildare when he was five. He took up guitar and drums as a young teenager and his early friendship with Christy Moore proved to be a catalyst for an extraordinary musical partnership that found its first footing in The Rakes of Kildare, a band formed along with Dónal’s older brother Frank.
Lunny’s appetite for exploration was evident from his earliest forays with Emmet Spiceland, a band he formed with the late Mick Moloney in the mid-1960s. He undertook a degree in the National College of Art and Design and became a gold and silversmith, but an unquenchable thirst for music drew him back to sessions and to the stage, where he forged many successful ensembles, including Coolfin, Mozaik, Usher’s Island and the pithily titled LAPD (Liam O’Flynn, Andy Irvine, Paddy Glackin and Dónal Lunny).
Andy Irvine introduced the Greek bouzouki to Lunny and it proved to be a turning point for him. He loved the instrument’s percussive qualities and its richly-textured acoustic range, and he became inextricably linked with the instrument, skilfully embedding it at the heart of Irish traditional music, and in the process revealing countless new colours in tunes handed down through the generations.
He was instrumental in the founding of Mulligan Records, ensuring Irish artists had the backing of a label which understood the need for musical diversity at a time when there were scant sympathetic recording houses for traditional and folk music.
He collaborated with Sharon Shannon on her peerless debut album in 1991, which is still Ireland’s best-selling traditional music album. They were also involved romantically for a time, and continued to collaborate musically on various projects down through the years, including another Lunny brainchild, the band Coolfin.
Dónal Lunny’s insatiable appetite for exploration saw him travel extensively, and for a time he lived in Japan where he found a natural kinship with traditional Japanese kodo drummers, and ultimately toured with them.
His ability to bring disparate sounds and instruments together was epitomised by the complex and intricate arrangements he wrote for not just the expected instruments that featured in The Bothy Band and Planxty (guitar, keyboards, pipes, fiddle, flute) but also for the saxophone, bass and drums of Moving Hearts. This expansive sound palette allowed the band to build exponentially on what had come before them, reaching a wider audience enthralled by their driving rhythms and visceral engagement with song choices such as Jackson Browne’s Before the Deluge and the Jim Page song Landlord that were politically charged and utterly in tune with their time.
His later collaborations with Máirtín O’Connor and Zoë Conway underscored his love of charting new territory, stripping back the soundscape to mine even further into the tradition, and in the process training a lens on further riches embedded not only in old tunes, but in vibrant, newly composed tunes too.
Never a man to rest on his laurels, Lunny collaborated with countless musicians nationally and internationally, from Sinéad O’Connor to Kate Bush, Elvis Costello, Jane Siberry, Baaba Maal and Mark Knopfler.
[ Atlantic Arc: Dónal Lunny steers a new Celtic musical course Opens in new window ]
Perhaps Dónal Lunny’s greatest legacy was his unapologetic openness to new ways of interpreting old music. He sought out novel ways of engaging with our music, informed by a deep understanding of its roots and its branches. His collaboration with the song collector and singer Frank Harte epitomised this curiosity of spirit, resulting in the release of the album My Name Is Napoleon Bonaparte, a celebration of the immense body of Napoleonic ballads that had nestled quietly (and unnoticed by many) in the tradition for so long.
Two of Dónal Lunny’s own children also became musicians. His son Oisín Lunny pursued a career as a DJ and producer while his daughter Cora Venus Lunny is a classical violinist. He had a son with Sinéad O’Connor, Shane, who died in 2022. He also has a daughter, Sora Chan, with Japanese musician Hideko Itami.
Lunny was inducted into Aosdána in 2007 and was appointed musician-in-residence at the Irish World Academy of Music and Dance at the University of Limerick in 2009. He was recognised by TG4 with a Gradam Saoil in 2017 and he received a lifetime achievement award at the RTÉ Folk Awards in 2025.
The depth and breadth of Dónal Lunny’s influence in Irish traditional and folk music, and his openness to deep cultural exchange, set him apart as a musician, composer, arranger and producer. It is a rich legacy that will fuel current and future generations, ensuring that Irish traditional music continues to train its sights both outward and inward.

title: Manchester United boss Michael Carrick delivers defiant five-minute monologue at press conference
description: Carrick hasn’t ruled out dropping Bruno Fernandes or stripping him of the captaincy when Bournemouth visit on Sunday
content:
Michael Carrick began his Friday media conference with an extraordinary five minute and 27 second monologue that cited Manchester United’s values of “humility”, “resilience” and “earning the right to win” in what could be read as a public address to his players after the season’s dismal start.
The head coach, whose job is under threat, later stated “100 per cent” he could turn United’s form around and sought to underline his selfless attitude by saying he would hold an umbrella for “everyone else to stay dry” while he got wet.
The downpour on Carrick intensified on Wednesday when Bruno Fernandes questioned his tactics after a 4-1 Champions League loss at Como and the 45-year-old did not rule out dropping the midfielder or stripping him of the captaincy when Bournemouth visit on Sunday.
“I’ll always do what’s best for the football club,” he said. “The most important thing for me is the team, first and foremost – the squad, the dynamics in the squad.”
Carrick decided to make his speech, delivered without being asked a question, after events in Como and Lisandro Martínez’s criticism of Jason Wilcox a week earlier for the director of football’s recruitment. United have won only two of 11 games and are 13th in the Premier League.
Carrick said: “We need to respect what it takes to be here, respect what it takes to win, what you have to do to win. I’m not entitled to be here. Entitlement cannot be at this football club. We’re not entitled to win. We’ve won in the past, we’ve got an incredible history, but that doesn’t mean that you’re entitled to just win.”
Carrick, a highly decorated United player for 12 years until 2018, cited two of his former team-mates.
“Ryan Giggs, arguably one of the greatest to play for this club, it was never about Ryan Giggs, it was about Manchester United. Wayne Rooney was top goalscorer of this football club. His biggest thing was playing for the team, sacrificing for the team, and what was good for Manchester United.
“Sir Alex Ferguson, the best manager of all time, the greatest for me ... his main priority was Manchester United. Going back to Sir Matt [Busby], Sir Bobby [Charlton], the resilience was beyond belief of what they showed and the way they rebuilt this football club [after the Munich disaster of 1958].”
Carrick insisted he could embody these values and transform United’s campaign. “One hundred per cent, yeah,” he said, before confirming he had spoken to the hierarchy and players about the crisis.
“There’s always conversations going on. It’s pretty obvious how we’re all feeling. The responsibility for me to be in this position is to lead.”
Warming to his theme, he said: “I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and for everyone else to stay dry. That’s the position I’m in, and it’s a privileged position.”
Carrick believes all of his squad share his determination.
“If you don’t, this is not the place for you,” he said before insisting there were no factions. “It’s not divided. We just need to get back to doing what we do best, and we will.” – Guardian

title: No solicitor for man charged over fatal Dún Laoghaire shooting amid legal aid dispute
description: Mark Cullen shot in the leg at Patrician Park, Kill Avenue, on July 5th and died at the scene
content:
A man charged last weekend over a fatal shooting in Dún Laoghaire during the summer still has no solicitor assigned to represent him amid the ongoing legal aid dispute.
Mark Cullen was fatally injured in a gun attack at Patrician Park on Kill Avenue on Sunday July 5th last.
The father of three, from Shanganagh Cliffs, Shankill in south Dublin, was shot in the leg and died at the scene.
Gardaí arrested Edward Andrews (32) of Radharc na Farraige, Wicklow town, Co Wicklow, and charged him with Cullen’s murder.
He was remanded in custody after appearing before Judge John Hughes at Dublin District Court on Saturday.
Many solicitors have withdrawn their services in response to legal aid payment reforms introduced in July, causing widespread disruption to the criminal justice system.
As a result, the solicitor who normally acted for him was unable to take an active role in the proceedings, meaning Andrews was unrepresented in court.
The judge had commented that it is a “most unique position” for a person to appear before the court charged with murder, having the presumption of innocence and a solicitor not formally representing the accused or taking an active role in the proceedings.
The case resumed at Cloverhill District Court on Friday when Judge Alan Mitchell adjourned it pending the preparation of a book of evidence.
Andrews greeted the judge with: “How are you?”
The judge noted he was aware the accused had no solicitor representing him in the District Court due to ongoing industrial action, but reminded him he could still apply for High Court bail.
“That won’t be happening,” Andrews replied.
Asked if he would consent to a two or four-week adjournment, Andrews answered “four”.
Mitchell remarked that in his experience, the book of evidence would not be ready by then.
He remanded the accused in continuing custody.
He also warned Andrews that should he secure High Court bail, he would be expected to appear in person for his next District Court hearing on November 19th. Otherwise, if he remains in custody, the appearance will be conducted via video-link.
Earlier, Det Sgt Grace O’Boyle of Dún Laoghaire station gave evidence that Andrews said, “no comment” when charged.
The District Court does not have jurisdiction to consider bail in a murder charge, which requires an application to the High Court, and he was automatically remanded in custody.
The accused is eligible for legal aid and was granted it at his first hearing on Saturday, because he was unemployed and receiving social welfare. However, he has no solicitor assigned.

title: Dan Sheehan’s versatility could be an asset ahead of World Cup
description: South Africa and France have experimented with hybrid players to give their teams an extra dimension
content:
Rarely can a selection in Irish rugby have been quite so leftfield or caused quite such a double take. And rarely can one choice have led the debate on Leinster chat groups to such an extent. Dan Sheehan at number eight? There seemed more than a whiff of Rassie Erasmus about it.
The ex-Munster and back-to-back World Cup winning head coach of the Springboks has been ahead of the posse in thinking outside the box, notably 6-2 or 7-1 splits on the bench and the creation of hybrid players such as Deon Fourie or latterly André Esterhuizen.
Fourie is a flanker who Erasmus picked also as a third hooker at the 2023 World Cup, and when Malcolm Marx was forced out of the tournament after their first match with a knee injury, he was replaced by Handrè Pollard. The gamble could be said to have worked when Bongi Mbonambi was injured in the opening five minutes of the final and Fourie played the last 76 minutes at hooker, although the Boks’ lineout struggled, and but for a couple of refereeing decisions history may well have decreed that Erasmus was ultimately too clever for his own good.
But whereas that was more akin to what Leinster are doing with Sheehan against Munster this weekend, Esterhuizen has become a bona fide hybrid player who can be employed in both his customary position of centre but also as a flanker, thus permitting the Boks to employ both a 6-2 and 7-1 split in a given match.
Indeed, in their win over France last year, after their lock Lood de Jager was red carded, Esterhuizen alternated between the backrow and midfield as the Boks won 32-17.
Intrigued by most things Erasmus does, apparently, Fabien Galthié emulated this selection ploy against Ireland in the Aviva Stadium last March when naming the La Rochelle flanker Oscar Jégou as a hybrid in what was ostensibly a 7-1 bench split.
Having lost Antoine Dupont early on, an injury to centre Pierre-Louis Barassi meant Jégou played the last 33 minutes in midfield, but it was no bother to him as France won 42-27. Indeed, Jégou looked a natural.
Sheehan’s selection at number eight does not fall into that category. It appears the primary purpose of making Sheehan a sometime backrower is to have the option of keeping a world-class player on the pitch for 80 minutes, as was the case when Leinster beat Sale in the Champions Cup quarter-final last April.
It is also a handy, in-game contingency plan and one can’t help but wonder if Jacques Nienaber had a hand in this leftfield thinking or, with the World Cup now less than a year away, whether Andy Farrell and/or David Humphreys had a word in Leo Cullen’s ear. Maybe none of that is true and this is entirely Cullen’s idea. Maybe we’ll be told one day. But most likely not.
Unlike against Sale, when Sheehan looked a tad surprised that he and Rónan Kelleher were in the same huddle after the latter had replaced James Ryan, he will have prepared and trained at number eight this week. It is in his remit and in the blood. His brother Bobby, also a hooker with a roving role who is devastating in the wide channels, has started at least 10 AIL games for UCD in the backrow and finished there in many more matches.
To some degree, it is a case of needs must too, given Jack Conan has joined Caelan Doris and James Culhane on the sidelines. But one glaring caveat is that Sheehan’s selection at number eight is not a ringing endorsement of either Alex Soroka, who was also not brought to South Africa, or Josh Ericson, who played both games there in the position.
Ultimately though, Ireland are still no nearer to unearthing a true forward/back hybrid in the manner of Esterhuizen or Jégou, which would be a very handy trick card at the World Cup. Bundee Aki has been employed in the backrow of scrums when his side are a man down and loves to join in an attacking maul. One wouldn’t rule out Ireland’s Swiss Knife, Josh van der Flier, from effectively fulfilling such a role or perhaps Nick Timoney could do so.
But if there is one forward who has the skill, pace, strength and intelligence to double up as a midfielder/winger in an emergency, once again Dan is probably the man.

title: World marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir provisionally banned over EPO finding
description: Former Olympic champion returned positive test in an out-of-competition sample taken in Kenya
content:
Kenya’s world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended after testing ‌positive for the banned blood booster EPO in a sample taken before ​her Sydney Marathon victory, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said on Friday.
The AIU added that the out-of-competition sample collected in Kenya returned an adverse ​analytical finding for EPO (erythropoietin), which boosts the production of red blood cells.
“I ⁠can only say that I feel terrible about what ‌happened ‌and ​I think it’s only right that an athlete who uses the performance enhancing drugs ⁠should be disqualified,” her ​agent Gianni Demadonna said in ​an emailed statement.
The 33-year-old is a former Olympic champion ‌and half-marathon world record holder ​as well as a four-times World Marathon Majors winner.
She won ⁠gold at the Tokyo ⁠Games ​in 2021 and has also claimed major marathon victories in New York (2021), Boston (2022), London (2024) and Sydney (2026).
Jepchirchir dominated the women’s race in Sydney in August, pulling clear of the field to finish in 2:18:31, more than three minutes ahead of second-placed compatriot Irine Cheptai.
Last ‌year, Kenya’s women’s ⁠marathon world record holder Ruth Chepngetich was banned for three years after admitting anti-doping rule violations ‌involving hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ), a prohibited diuretic, though her world record of 2:09:56 remained ​on the books because it was set ​before her positive test.
