title: CRH set for earnings boost from early closing of $8.5bn Arcosa deal
description: Some analysts had been expecting CRH to struggle to meet its earnings forecast
content:
CRH ’s full-year earnings will benefit from an earnings boost from the earlier-than-expected closing of an $8.5 billion (€7.6 billion) deal to acquire US peer Arcosa.
The Dublin-based building materials and solutions giant had said, when it was unveiled in July, that it expected its largest-ever deal to close in the first quarter of 2027.
The early completion may prompt earnings upgrades from some analysts that had otherwise estimated CRH would struggle to meet its full-year earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) forecast of $8.1 billion$8.5 billion.
Truist Securities analyst Keith Hughes recently downgraded his Ebitda estimate for CRH to $7.87 billion.
“The cut at CRH is particularly notable given a long history of hitting numbers, but we now see the possibility of an estimate range reduction,” Hughes said.
Shane Carberry of Goodbody, one of the group’s corporate brokers, recently reduced his projection to $7.99 billion.
CRH said it would provide updated full-year 2026 guidance reflecting the completion of the Arcosa acquisition with its third-quarter results on October 29th.
“Arcosa is an excellent strategic fit for CRH and fully aligns with our growth ambitions. With high-quality aggregates assets and attractive positions in the growing US energy transmission market, the acquisition strengthens our connected portfolio and reinforces our position as the number-one infrastructure player in North America,” CRH chief executive Jim Mintern said.
The transaction is the largest of more than 1,200 deals that CRH, which was formed in 1970 through the merger of Cement Limited and Roadstone Limited, has carried out in its history.
It eclipsed CRH’s €6.5 billion deal to buy cement and construction assets that European rivals Holcim and Lafarge had to sell to appease competition authorities before their own merger in 2015.
North America accounted for 71 per cent of CRH’s $7.7 billion adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation last year and three-quarters of its net profit. The Arcosa deal would increase CRH’s reliance on that market.
Mintern set out a strategy last September for CRH to spend $40 billion on investment and cash returns to shareholders over the next five years as it continues to grow revenues and earnings apace. Some $28 billion was earmarked for investment. The Arcosa deal equated to about 30 per cent of the investment pot.
CRH’s focus is on four key areas: aggregates, cement and sustainable alternatives, roads and water. It sees these benefiting from three infrastructure mega-trends: continuing investment in the transport system, from roads to airports; a need to develop water management; and the reindustrialisation of the US.
Mintern said the Arcosa transaction fed into these megatrends and increased CRH’s exposure to the utilities sector.
Arcosa produces 35 million tonnes of high-quality, natural and recycled aggregates and serves 13 of the 50 largest US metropolitan regions, across Texas, New Jersey, Arizona, Florida and Tennessee. It will bring CRH’s total annual production to more than 265 million tonnes.

title: Storm Boelo: Ireland braces for second storm and ‘intense rain’ as cleanup continues after Austen
description: Orange and yellow weather warnings as more strong winds and heavy rain follow Storm Austen
content:
Fresh orange and yellow weather warnings have been issued by Met Éireann as Storm Boelo is due to cross parts of the country over the bank holiday weekend.
The forecaster has warned of an increased flooding risk as the ground is already saturated from Storm Austen. It said “very heavy and intense rain” is expected in the south of the country.
A status-orange rain warning will come into effect for Kerry from 7am on Saturday until 2pm.
An orange wind warning for Donegal, Leitrim, Mayo and Sligo will be in place from 2pm on Saturday until 9am on Sunday.
A yellow rain warning has been issued for Clare, Cork, Donegal, Galway, Kerry, Leitrim, Limerick, Mayo and Sligo for between 4am and 3pm on Saturday. A yellow wind warning is in place for Connacht, Clare, Kerry and Limerick from 1pm on Saturday until noon on Sunday.
A yellow wind warning is also in place for Donegal from 1pm on Saturday until 3pm on Sunday.
Met Éireann said that further rainfall on Saturday will lead to “rapid runoff, rising river levels, and an increased risk of both surface water and river flooding”, particularly across the West and Southwest.
“Smaller rivers across the country have the biggest risk of flooding quickly as they will take the shortest time to overflow, whereas largest rivers may take longer to rise,” it added.
The “strong onshore winds” likely to come with the storm, alongside high tides, may result in wave overtopping, and thus coastal flooding along the west coast.
The Galway Races rescheduled Saturday’s “National Hunt” races due to Storm Boelo, while events have been cancelled in Kerry.
Cleanup operations continued on Saturday afternoon following the arrival of Storm Austen, with council crews clearing falling trees in many counties. Met Éireann’s figures would suggest that Dublin got the heaviest of the rain with more than 20mm falling overnight at Dublin Airport, but the rain has now tailed off considerably.
The ESB reported 3,000 properties are without power after Storm Austen, while Bus Éireann has cancelled a number of services
The UK Met Office has issued a yellow warning for Northern Ireland from 6pm on Saturday until 3pm on Sunday. The forecaster warned of 80km/h to 90km/h gusts, with winds up to 120km/h in exposed areas.
England was particularly affected by Storm Austen, where part of Brighton’s West Pier collapsed during the storm and almost 7,000 homes were left without power.
In northern France, a gust of 148 km/h was recorded at Seine-Maritime as the storm made landfall there.
Saturday morning is expected to be wet and windy with widespread rain and fresh to strong and gusty southerly winds, reaching near gale force or gale force near coasts.
[ Storm Austen: Thousands without power, Bus Éireann services cancelled as storm brings disruption Opens in new window ]
The rain is likely to be heavy at times, especially in the west and southwest with spot flooding possible, said Met Éireann.
A clearance to blustery showers will follow through the afternoon, with isolated thunderstorms possible in the northwest. Highest temperatures are likely to be between 12 and to 15 degrees.
Sunday morning will be breezy with fsunny spells and scattered showers in the morning and longer spells of rain possible in the northwest.
A combination of wind and rain warnings will come into effect for southern, western and northwestern counties this weekend, due to #StormBoelo If you are on or near the coast during this time, Stay Back, Stay High and Stay Dry. Full details at https://t.co/jBP7uaJ0Pc pic.twitter.com/BjlGY2Do6p
Rain will extend northeastward through Monday morning with moderate to fresh south-easterly winds. Some drier intervals are expected and temperatures will probably be mild and humid, with highs of 14-17 degrees.
The storm on Saturday is taken from a three-country list of names.
Boelo is a Dutch name, whereas Austen was a contribution from the Met Éireann.
Since 2015, the Irish forecaster has been working with the UK Met Office on a naming convention to keep public messaging “consistent” and “authoritative” and they were joined by the Netherlands’ KNMI in 2019.
Four of Met Éireann’s names were historical contributions from the service; Austen, Evelyn, Kilian, Miriam, with three more from public suggestions; Heather, Laoise and Phelim.
The full 2026/27 list is Austen, Boelo, Chloe, Dano, Evelyn, Finn, Gwendolyn, Heather, Ivy, Jake, Kilian, Laoise, Miriam, Nicola, Olaf, Phelim, Ruban, Shaun, Theo, Vesna, and Wende.

title: Owner of €2.5m ‘uninhabitable’ house in Dalkey seeks its demolition
description: ‘Extremely high’ and ‘dangerous’ levels of radon gas cited
content:
A homeowner who paid €2.5 million last year for a coastal home in Dalkey , south Dublin , wants to demolish the “uninhabitable” home due to the presence of “extremely high” and “dangerous” levels of radon gas.
In February 2025, Peter Woods paid €2.5 million for Nirvana on Coliemore Road, Dalkey.
Woods has lodged plans with Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council to demolish Nirvana and construct three new houses on the site.
The houses would comprise a 349sq m three-storey, four-bedroom dwelling with a sauna; and two two-storey, three-bedroom dwellings of 124sq m each.
The larger home is to be located at the rear of the steep sloping site with the two smaller homes closer to Coliemore Road.
A report by planning consultant Kiaran O’Malley, concerning the Woods application, said that, initially, Woods had intended to renovate Nirvana “but following a number of radon surveys and remediation measures, the radon levels could not be brought down to safe levels so it was recommended to demolish the house”.
O’Malley said the radon levels detected at the home were “dangerous”.
Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive gas and is classified as a group-one carcinogen and is the second-biggest cause of lung cancer in Ireland.
Radon is colourless, odourless and tasteless and can be measured only using specialised equipment.
Tests carried out at Nirvana by Cora Consulting Engineers between May and July 2025 detected radon levels more than five times the maximum limit for a domestic house and 13 times the average level in Ireland.
[ Tech multimillionaire wins planning battle over demolition of €7.5m Dalkey home Opens in new window ]
In his report lodged with the application, John Casey of Cora Consulting Engineers said the only feasible option was “to demolish and replace the house with a new structure with continuous radon membranes from inside to outside”.
Woods has retained award-winning ODAA Architects to design the proposed scheme.
In a report, ODAA Architects said Nirvana, which was built in 1958, had been vacant for a number of years and was generally in very poor condition.
On the need to demolish Nirvana due to the high radon levels, ODAA Architects said “according to the Environmental Protection Agency approximately 300 people die per year in Ireland due to radon, so it is a necessity to achieve compliant radon levels at the dwelling”.
Woods provided the radon findings to the Revenue Commissioners and Revenue confirmed in writing that the existing structure was classified as uninhabitable and therefore exempt from local property tax.
A decision is due on the application in December.

title: Thalidomide survivors a ‘glaring omission’ from list of recent recipients of State apologies
description: Fiona Cassidy of Irish Thalidomide Association: ‘We’ve repeatedly asked for State apology and fear some of our survivors and families won’t be around to hear it’
content:
Renewed calls have been made for the Government to urgently issue a State apology to the remaining thalidomide survivors following the Taoiseach’s formal apology to the family of the late prison officer Brian Stack .
Former Ceann Comhairle Seán Ó Fearghaíl said the State had recently issued a number of “long sought and richly deserved apologies”.
That includes apologies to the victims of paedophile Bill Kennelly , the family of Shane O’Farell who was killed in a hit-and-run incident, the survivors of institutional abuse, the families of the Stardust victims and for the CervicalCheck scandal .
But Ó Fearghaíl said the “glaring omission” from the list is “the survivors of thalidomide, the 40 or so people still living who were abjectly failed by the State over 60 years ago”.
He asked when they “and maybe even more significantly the tiny number of remaining mothers who are at very advanced age” would receive the apology “to which they are most definitely entitled and the supports they need to live out the rest of their lives in dignity”.
Thalidomide was a drug developed in the 1950s to treat morning sickness during pregnancy.
It was withdrawn from most markets in 1961 following widespread evidence it was linked to birth defects but continued to be sold in Ireland until 1964.
Many children were born without limbs or with shortened limbs, with hearing and vision impairment and internal organ injuries.
When Ó Fearghaíl raised it in the Dáil, Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill said there is a “strong desire” to address “very real concerns”. She expects they “may be resolved and that any remaining barriers on any side would be set aside for that to be completed for the benefit of the survivors of thalidomide”.
[ ‘Say sorry and put an end to it’: Why are Thalidomide survivors still waiting for a State apology? Opens in new window ]
The Irish Thalidomide Association (ITA) has campaigned for the last 15 years and their efforts included a 2024 letter from thalidomide mother Mary Clarken, who is 96, to then Taoiseach Simon Harris seeking an apology.
The association also wants recognition of the “unacknowledged” survivors whose mothers took the drug after it had been officially withdrawn, statutory supports and a fair compensation scheme.
Finola Cassidy of the ITA said: “While the Government has indicated a State apology will follow eventually we fear that some of our survivors and families won’t be around to hear it and we’ve repeatedly asked for it to happen in good faith as soon as possible.”
The association last met the Taoiseach, Tánaiste, the Attorney General and senior officials in June with a further meeting scheduled for the autumn.
“Micheál and Simon have said they have taken personal and political responsibility,” Cassidy said.
She has been contacted by Government and “I am assured that an early date will be found to recommence the discussion”.
This meeting is very important because “some of the issues still being negotiated remain challenging,” including finding the right compensation scheme and the promised legislation to give statutory effect to the healthcare supports for remaining survivors.
“Since 2017 they have repeatedly said they are working on the heads of a Bill on a Thalidomide and we’ve repeatedly asked to see these heads of the Bill and continue to seek that.”
November marks the 65th anniversary of the international withdrawal of the thalidomide drug and the failure of the State to act on that notification.
Cassidy celebrates her own 65th birthday on Monday when she will attend in the Netherlands flying the biggest gathering in a decade of worldwide thalidomide survivors, some 350 people.
She is reflecting on “who will be the last thalidomider (STET) standing in the world” and asks “how could we have had to do this for so long. Our health is failing and there are very few remaining mothers,” of those affected by thalidomide.

title: Conor Murray: Snubbed Munster players can make statement against Leinster
description: There is no harm in Munster carrying a little bitterness up to Dublin over only two players being called up by Andy Farrell
content:
There is no better way to kick start a World Cup season than Leinster versus Munster at the Aviva Stadium.
I wonder if Leo Cullen’s selection is the same 15 players we’ll see for Ireland against Argentina in a fortnight.
Certainly, the Leinster pack has eight established internationals. Joey Carbery at outhalf, instead of the injured Sam Prendergast, is the only starter not included in Andy Farrell’s squad for the Nations Championship .
If Joey hits the ground running at the Aviva, he immediately comes into the frame. That’s the power of this fixture.
Clayton McMillan has enough on his plate to be overly concerned by just two Munster players – Tadhg Beirne and Craig Casey – being named on the 36-man Ireland panel.
Still, McMillan should mention it in passing this week. In between Jared Payne’s three-phase attack patterns or Jimmy Duffy’s lineout sessions, he could slip in the fact that Craig and Tadhg made the cut while everyone else missed out.
I am not suggesting a bias on Andy’s part towards the other provinces. He only selects on form and the potential to develop a player.
But it cannot be glossed over. As everyone in Munster attempts to turn the page on what has been a rough few years, there is no harm carrying a little bitterness up to Dublin.
Really though, it is not the Leinster players taking national contracts off Munster fellas. It is a gang of young Connacht forwards and Ulster backs who have climbed up the pecking order.
Farrell invests in people. He encourages all sorts of personalities to be themselves in camp. He wants the introverts and extroverts to show their true character.
Because it is character that will drag a team through a World Cup campaign and out the other side. That’s the secret to Ireland finally making it past the quarter-final in 2027. A dollop of luck on the injury front and some X-factor is also needed.
It should not come as a surprise to hear the Irish starting XV for Argentina, Fiji and the seemingly invincible Springboks under Rassie Erasmus, will be picked from an established list of 23 or 24 names.
But the Ireland team will have to change, ever so slightly, to challenge South Africa. One or two players need to break through in the next month.
At the very least Leinster and Ireland are thinking outside the box and presumably communicating with each other about Dan Sheehan’s move to number eight.
What’s not to like about this very Erasmus-like move?
Anyone paying attention will know this has not come out of the blue. Cullen moved Dan to the backrow against Sale in the Champions Cup quarter-final last season when Rónan Kelleher arrived at hooker for the last 14 minutes. It worked.
Really, Dan is a backrower disguised as a hooker. Always has been and with Jack Conan joining Caelan Doris on the sidelines, the Ireland captain should be on the pitch for 80 minutes. It makes a lot of sense. Get your best players on the grass for as long as possible.
That said, a Leinster hooker at number eight should be a red rag to Gavin Coombes and Brian Gleeson.
Both men have time to earn a recall, but as it stands Munster players are missing out on an important November camp. The World Cup in Australia next year has four knockout rounds, so the finals weekend at Twickenham next month will be used as a dry run to the final.
This is nothing new. We used to imagine the November series as a quarter-final, semi-final and final.
Leinster are the old enemy and Munster can charge straight into them on Saturday night but, really, it is Stuart Lancaster’s rising tide out west that has caught Farrell’s attention.
It is evident in every position up front: Andrew Porter and Tadhg Furlong remain the premier props in the country, while Tom O’Toole and Tom Clarkson are the established backups, but it is the Connacht boys Billy Bohan and Sam Illo who have usurped the Munster props.
Bohan and Illo will get a chance to impress at training, or when somebody inevitably goes down injured. Ireland pitch sessions find out what a player is all about.
It’s the same story at secondrow. Beirne will feature beside Joe McCarthy or at blindside. James Ryan and the returning Ryan Baird are two locks Farrell knows he can rely on.
It’s an area of strength but if Ireland’s lineout is to take a giant leap between now and the World Cup, to compete with South Africa and New Zealand, maybe Darragh Murray is the man who can make this happen.
Murray only featured as a second-half sub against Scotland during last season’s Six Nations but he looked like an international lock. He even powered over for a try.
The Roscommon man is named ahead of Evan O’Connell, who already looks like he is benefiting from being coached by his uncle Paul, while Edwin Edogbo and Tom Ahern also missed out.
That’s a serious statement by Farrell. O’Connell has earned a call-up and Edogbo, when fully fit, is as destructive as any forward in the world. But Murray gets the nod on form.
Same story in the backrow. James McNabney, Cian Prendergast and Sean Jansen are picked ahead of Gleeson, Coombes and Seán Edogbo.
McNabney is someone to watch closely to see if he can bring the power surge that big Ulster forwards like Jeremy Davidson and Stephen Ferris added to Ireland down the years.
I can only hope that Munster, with a new CEO coming in, and McMillan a year in the role, will change the narrative around the province.
It’s all well and good saying this. Plenty of Munster sides have come up to Dublin in the past 15 years expecting to damage the Leinster machine. There’s been some flag-planting wins, like last year at Croke Park, that were quickly forgotten due to a lack of consistency.
The narrative will be dictated by the result. Munster players haven’t earned the right to populate the Ireland squad. That doesn’t mean they have to accept it as the way it will go this season.
I can’t wait for the Aviva under lights to see how Charlie O’Shea goes against Joey Carbery in the battle of the number 10s. Didn’t think I’d be writing that sentence about Munster versus Leinster in 2026. Selection can change in an instant.

title: It’s going to be a windy Dublin Marathon. What should I do?
description: Seasons turn, years pass, but there’s no deterring the hardiest of marathon runners
content:
W e were sitting outside the Glendalough Green cafe last Sunday afternoon and the October sun was brilliantly illuminating the edges of the ancient valley just below. A day sent straight from distance running heaven, we philosophised, and just about perfect for the Dublin Marathon .
If only there was some way of guaranteeing such calm and blissfully clear conditions come the actual race day itself. Maybe then a lot more runners would be confident about making it to the start line in the first place. Of course it doesn’t work that way, and so a week on, and in the aftermath of Storms Austen and Boelo, much of the talk around this Sunday’s event concerns the weather forecast.
The “ah sure there’s always next year” mindset may already be some comfort to anyone having second thoughts about starting or finishing on Sunday, but who knows what the future might bring? The Glendalough Green, by way of a transient reminder, is set to close after this bank holiday weekend, a sad loss to Laragh village and passing bikers of all kinds – motor, electric, and old-fashioned push.
Such unpredictable weather conditions, incidentally, have nothing to do with the fact my first and almost certainly last Dublin Marathon was 25 years ago this weekend. Despite the many promises to someday make it back to the start line, life just keeps on getting in the way.
For the 22,500 runners who have signed up this year, the one certainty is that whatever the weather in Dublin come Sunday morning, it will be the same for everyone. According to the latest weather charts, it looks like being partly sunny and fair, though likely on the cool and windy side.
Nothing an extra layer of clothing while waiting on the start line shouldn’t address. Because once up and running, there’s no reason why anyone’s predicted finishing time should be significantly blown off course. Or as Noel Carroll, the co-founder of the event once mused, “there is no such thing as bad weather, only weak runners”.
The sort of figure-of-eight nature of the Dublin Marathon route also means the wind will keep changing direction, depending on which way the runners are headed. Still, no matter what way that wind is blowing, the most testing part of the course comes between miles 20 and 22, around Clonskeagh and Roebuck Roads, although from there it’s a straight downhill along Fosters Avenue, and then a more-or-less flat run to the finish.
Not that the hardiest of Dublin Marathon runners would ever let something as uncontrollable as the weather drag them down. I got a timely reminder of that earlier this week talking to Martin Kelly, who is one of the last of the eight Dublin Marathon “originals”, having started and finished all 44 marathons to date, beginning in 1980 – no matter what the weather conditions come actual race day.
All going to plan, Kelly will line up for the 45th time on Sunday morning, having joined the 2,100 runners who started the first Dublin Marathon on the October bank holiday Monday in 1980, and almost a third of which failed to finish. Kelly had just turned 18 at the time, and although confronted with various running obstacles in all the years since, none compared to the challenge he was presented with before this Sunday’s race.
Following a routine blood test at the end of last year, it was discovered Kelly would require surgery for a cancerous growth on his prostate, which he underwent on June 29th. That then meant 10 weeks of no running at all, although after easing himself back into training at the start of September, Kelly is headed with the starting line this year with a renewed sense of gratitude.
“We’ll see what Sunday brings,” he says, the weather being the last of his concerns, and rightly so. “Everybody was saying to me ‘what were the symptoms?’ but I had absolutely none. I did have a very on-the-ball GP, who happens to be running the marathon himself, and he referred me to a urologist, who’s also a pretty avid runner, And he just said, ‘look, we need to get this sorted’.
“I had it done by keyhole robotic surgery, and recovery was reasonably fast. You don’t want to push yourself too much, maybe have a bit of a relapse. But at no stage was I told medically that it wouldn’t be a good idea to run another marathon. So once those words aren’t uttered, you’re happy enough to stick with it. I also took comfort from the fact that it was discovered. because the last thing you want is to feel unwell in a few years’ time.
“I was also told it’s important to give yourself something else to focus on, and that there wasn’t any reason not to go to the start line, and see how you are feeling after a few miles.”
Kelly, who turned 64 last Tuesday, also ran and finished both “virtual marathon events” during the pandemic years of 2020 and 2021, which, like takeaway pints and Zoom parties, no one wants to speak about ever again.
“I say it every year, when I’m asked why I’m still doing it, and I just say, ‘because we can’. Plenty of people would love to be able to do, but I suppose it does take on an extra significance this year. I know I can do 17, 18 miles, then I’ll just take it from there.”
And his advice to runners starting their first Dublin Marathon on Sunday?
“Just take it handy in the early miles. There’s plenty of time to catch up. And to hydrate a little, and hydrate often. People do tend to get carried away, especially if it’s your first marathon, and the first two or three miles may be behind your time. But don’t panic, when you get into the Phoenix Park, there’s plenty of time to start getting yourself back on track.”
The seven other Dublin Marathon originals set to line up again on Sunday are Peadar Nugent (Galway), Donal Ward (Donegal), Séamus Cawley (Limerick), Séamus Dunne (Meath), Patrick Gowen (Dublin), Dominic Gallagher (Dublin), and Mick Carolan (Dublin).
Long may they run – in all weather conditions.

title: Storm Boelo latest: Ireland braces for ‘damaging’ second storm as Met Éireann issues new orange warnings
description: Storm Austen leaves thousands without power
content:
⚠️ STORM AUSTEN - 22 & 23 October 2026 Status Orange and Yellow warnings are in place nationwide for rain and wind for 22 and 23 October. If you are on or near the coast during this time, Stay Back, Stay High and Stay Dry. For full details see: https://t.co/94v6dGeWcJ pic.twitter.com/rihC74FhTQ
The storm set to hit Ireland’s west coast tomorrow is taken from a three-country list of names.
Boelo is a Dutch name, whereas Austen was a contribution from the Met Éireann.
Since 2015, the Irish forecaster has been working with the UK Met Office on a naming convention to keep public messaging “consistent” and “authoritative”.
They were joined by the Netherlands’ KNMI in 2019, and publish a list of storm names during “storm season”, which starts on September 1st and lasts for a year.
The current list of names is made up of seven from each of the three forecasters.
Four of Met Éireann’s names were historical contributions from the service; Austen, Evelyn, Kilian, Miriam, with three more from public suggestions; Heather, Laoise and Phelim.
The full 2026/27 list is Austen, Boelo, Chloe, Dano, Evelyn, Finn, Gwendolyn, Heather, Ivy, Jake, Kilian, Laoise, Miriam, Nicola, Olaf, Phelim, Ruban, Shaun, Theo, Vesna, and Wende.
All is calm in Donegal today but the county is now bracing itself after Met Éireann issued an orange weather warning, reports Stephen Maguire.
The forecaster warned that Storm Boelo will bring gale force westerly winds, with severe gusts hitting Donegal, Leitrim, Mayo, Sligo.
The wind warning will be in effect from 2pm on Saturday until 9am on Sunday.
The public has been warned there could be damage to already weakened structures, damage to power lines and power outages.
There will also be disruption and delays to public transport likely, with fallen trees, large coastal waves and falling debris forecast.
There may also be coastal flooding where winds are onshore and very difficult travelling conditions, dangerous conditions at sea.
Earlier, Met Éireann issued a yellow wind warning for Donegal today. The wind alert will be valid from 1pm today until 3pm tomorrow.
The rainfall during Storm Austen has led to “saturated ground and increased river levels”, Met Éireann has warned.
“Further heavy rainfall associated with Storm Boelo is forecast over the weekend, falling on already saturated ground,” Met Éireann said.
“This will lead to rapid runoff, rising river levels and an increased risk of both surface water and river flooding, particularly across the west and southwest.”
Smaller rivers across the country have the biggest risk of flooding quickly as they will take the shortest time to overflow, whereas largest rivers may take longer to rise.
The “strong onshore winds” likely to come with the storm, alongside high tides, may result in wave overtopping, and thus coastal flooding along the west coast.
The organisers of the Galway Races have rescheduled races set to take place at the racecourse citing health and safety concerns due to Storm Boelo.
Michael Moloney, Galway Racecourse chief executive said: “We’re obviously disappointed that racing cannot go ahead on Saturday.
“Given the current ground conditions and the forecast arrival of Storm Boelo on Saturday morning, we believe rescheduling our fixtures is the most responsible course of action.
Storm Austen seems to have got stronger since it left Ireland.
In England, part of Brighton’s West Pier collapsed during the storm.
Almost 7,000 homes were left without power in Cornwall.
In northern France, a gust of 148 km/h was recorded at Seine-Maritime as the storm made landfall there.
Some 290,000 homes in 23 departments in France are without power currently.
Storm Austen is due to be followed presently by Storm Boelo.
Met Éireann’s figures would suggest that Dublin got the heaviest of the rain, with more than 20mm falling overnight at Dublin Airport, but the rain has now tailed off considerably.
There has been no repeat of the flooding which affected the river Dodder area the last time there was a major rainfall event.
All roads and rail services are working as normal, as is Dublin Airport.
Waterford Council ground crews have so far tended to over thirty incidents of fallen trees blocking roads and footpaths, while Waterford Fire Service have attended four sites with fallen trees, reports Darragh Murphy .
Gabriel Hynes, director of services with Waterford City and County Council, said: “The worst of Storm Austen has passed, and thankfully the impact was not as serious as it could have been.
“Our outdoor crews and Fire Service were on the ground since before light attending to fallen trees, blocked roads and paths and dealing with flooding issues.”
Maria Goff, senior executive engineer with Waterford Council, said at a meeting with elected members this morning that the Council will continue to assist locals where possible.
There is now an orange alert for rain Saturday morning - even as the cleanup from Storm Austen is underway in road clearing, Anne Lucey reports.
Storm Boleo will see a number of outdoor events cancelled; possible closure of parks and very difficult driving conditions between 7am and 2pm.
Rivers are already swollen from Austen and the expectation is there will be a further accumulation of water. Winds are also expected to be high and coasts will be dangerous.
Met Éireann has forecast the rain in the east of the country will clear through the morning, while sunshine and scattery, blustery showers will feature for the rest of the country with temperatures of 8 to 12 degrees throughout.
Tonight will be mostly dry, with some isolated showers on the west coast.
Cloud will build from the west with rain following, becoming widespread by morning and turning heavy at times in the west and southwest, Met Éireann said. Temperatures will drop to between 2 and 8 degrees as the country is set to welcome Storm Boelo.
Saturday morning will start out being “rather wet and windy” widespread rain and fresh to strong and gusty southerly winds, reaching near gale force or gale force near coasts.
Isolated thunderstorms are possible in the northwest with very strong winds as Boelo moves north.
The State is now clear of Met Éireann weather warnings as the yellow rain warnings in Leinster and Munster have expired with the worst of the storm now passed.
The attention now turns to the forthcoming Storm Boelo, the first warnings for which begin at 4am on Saturday morning.
Maritime warnings remain in place off the Irish coast from Fair Head to Carnsore Point to Slyne Head, on the Irish Sea until 7pm today, Friday. The Storm Austen marine gale warning is forecasting cyclonic variable winds, which could reach up to gale force 8 or strong gale force 9 at times.
The Cork County Council local area office in Carrigaline will be closed to the public today due to a tree which has fallen on its grounds.
“We apologise for any inconvenience this may cause and appreciate your patience while the area is made safe,” the council said.
Due to a fallen tree within the grounds of the Carrigaline Area Office, the public counter will be closed today for health and safety reasons. We apologise for any inconvenience this may cause and appreciate your patience while the area is made safe. For any queries or… pic.twitter.com/c9Qepro9H2
Drivers have been warned to slow down and expect longer braking distances today due to surface water on Irish motorways, Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) has warned drivers.
With heavy rain across parts of the country today; Expect surface water on some roads! Slow down to avoid the risk of aquaplaning! Increase your braking distance! Think safety at all times! Be the driver you'd want beside you!🤗 #TII #RoadSafety #Bethedriver #Slowdown #Buckleup @GardaTraffic
More Bus Éireann routes have been cancelled, while Dublin Bus and Luas services are running normally.
The Bus Éireann 9am Dublin to Drogheda bus was cancelled, both 131 bus services at 9.30 and at 11.30, serving the Wicklow to Bray route have been cancelled.
The 7.45am Parkway Station to Drogheda bus is operating 30 minutes behind schedule, while the 9.15am Parkway Station to Emerald bus has been cancelled.
A status-orange rain warning has been issued for Co Kerry on Saturday from 7am until 2pm as Met Éireann has warned that Storm Boelo will bring “spells of very heavy and intense rain”.
Flooding, and damage to homes and businesses is “expected”, the national forecaster said, with likely disruption and delays to public transport and “very difficult travelling conditions”.
A status orange wind warning will be in place for Donegal, Leitrim, Mayo, Sligo from 2pm on Saturday until 9am on Sunday.
Gale force winds are likely, alongside damage to “already weakened structures”, power lines and power outages.
Met Éireann has warned residents to prepare for fallen trees, large coastal waves and the possibility of loose objects being displaced.
Coastal flooding is possibly where winds blow onshore, and the conditions at sea were described as “dangerous”.
Met Éireann has issued a status yellow rain warning for much of the south-west and west coastal counties from 4am on Saturday morning until 3pm in the afternoon.
The warning is being issued as Storm Boelo is due to land in Ireland and is expected to bring “spells of heavy rain”.
The national forecaster said the storm could cause difficult travelling conditions, localised flooding possible and impact outdoor events in Clare, Cork, Donegal, Galway, Kerry, Leitrim, Limerick, Mayo, and Sligo.
An orange marine storm warning is in place on Irish waters from Erris Head to Bloody Foreland to Belfast Lough from 6pm on Saturday to 10am on Sunday.
West to northwesterly winds could reach storm force 10 at times, Met Éireann said.

Council crews have been clearing debris and tending to floods in Waterford, reports Darragh Murphy .
On the Outer Ring Road, Waterford city, a tree was obstructing part of the road this morning.
Lots of debris is being cleared from the N25 near McGrath’s Cross. On the N25 in Dungarvan town, traffic has been reduced to single lane due to flooding. In Dunmore East, a tree has fallen onto a streetlight.
A Council spokesperson said that flooding and fallen trees have been reported across the city and county. The public have been advised to “exercise caution on the roads this morning”.
ESB Networks are reporting that over 1,500 homes in Cork city and county have been left without power, Barry Roche reports. Falling trees brought down powerlines with Ballydehob in West Cork the worst affected with almost 1,200 homes and businesses left without power.
Elsewhere, some homes in Glengarriff, Bantry, Enniskeane and Kinsale were affected as were some homes in Kanturk and Fermoy in North Cork and Ladysbridge and Cloyne in East Cork while a small number of homes in Fairhill in Cork city have also lost power.

The road is closed, Cork County Council said, with ESB and council teams at the scene attempting repairs.
“Motorists are advised to avoid the area and use alternative routes where possible,” the council has warned.
The council is also reporting that the regional road, R612 which links Carrigaline with both Myrtleville and Crosshaven in South Cork is impassable due to flooding at Frenchfurze and Hoddersfield just outside Carrigaline.

Trees are down on the L3919 at Crough Wood, on the L3025 outside the Woodhouse estate at Stradbally, and the Outer Ring Road in Waterford City.

Both towns have been hit badly by flooding in recent years with Storm Babet causing up to 200 million euros worth of damage in Midleton in 2023 and Bantry being hit by seven floods between 2020 and 2025.
But gardaí in both towns told The Irish Times this morning that they had received no reports of flooding from anyone in either town or surrounding areas despite the heavy rain.
High tide in Bantry passed off without incident at 2.30am and in Midleton at 3.56am, similarly without incident.
Gardaí did report some trees down on secondary roads around Mogeely and Cloyne in east Cork.

Council crews are working to clear affected areas “as quickly and safely as possible”, the council has said.
As much as 60mm of rainfall has been recorded in parts of Co Cork overnight, but no river flooding has been reported.
“However, localised ponding and surface water remain a concern and may create hazardous driving conditions during the morning commute,” the council said.
Commuters living in Cork were urged to “take extra care if travelling this morning”.
