title: Disquiet on political front amid legal aid row, triple lock debate and ‘demeaning’ advert
description: Inside Politics: Jim O’Callaghan objects to ‘inappropriate and demeaning’ video by Dublin Rape Crisis Centre
content:
As Ireland is battered by not one but two storms – named Austen and Boelo – the political weather has also been far from settled this week.
The row over changes to the criminal legal aid system blew up on Tuesday after protesting solicitors expanded their withdrawal of service and Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan accused them of deliberately targeting rape cases in the Central Criminal Court, a claim solicitors denied. There is likely to be talks between O’Callaghan and the Law Society next week.
Meanwhile, as Marie O’Halloran reports , Hurricane Triple Lock blasted its way through the Dáil on Wednesday with the Government facing Opposition criticism over plans to overhaul the rules for deploying soldiers overseas.
There were signs of some calm being restored on one front after the public sector strike last week, with talks on a new pay deal beginning on Monday.
However, perhaps the most unexpected political storm (the strained weather metaphors will end here) came after the emergence of a social media advertisement from the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) about consent featuring grandparents hugging their grandchildren.
As Sarah Burns, Vivienne Clarke and Marie O’Halloran report , the advert depicts a young girl being uncomfortable receiving a hug from her grandparents.
O’Callaghan said the advertisement was “inappropriate and demeaning” to grandparents and has been removed by the DRCC following engagement with officials from the Department of Justice. He said the video “does not represent the views of the Government”.
In the Dáil, Aontú TD Paul Lawless claimed the video was Government-funded and conflated “issues of sexual violence on the one hand and affection exchanged by a grandmother to a grandchild on the other”.
DRCC said its We-Consent campaign was part of its prevention work to increase the awareness and practice of consent in the Republic.
The organisation said it created a video series for its social media channels based on feedback from more than 20 consent workshops with younger and older people.
DRCC said the series was made on a low budget and promoted online via its social media channels.
“The video was launched exclusively on social media in mid-September, but we have removed it from our social media channels due to the negative attention it has attracted in the last 24 hours,” it added.
It is seven months since The Irish Times, in co-operation with the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, first turned a spotlight on Aughinish Alumina’s exports to Russia.
This week our Europe Correspondent Jack Power reported that sanctions prohibiting the Co Limerick plant from continuing to export material to Russia were not included in a draft of the European Commission ’s next package of measures targeting the Russian wartime economy.
Today, Power, Conor Gallagher and Jack Horgan-Jones report that the EU’s envoy on sanctions, David O’Sullivan, has said alumina produced at Aughinish Alumina “undoubtedly” ended up supplying, at least in part, the Russian military-industrial complex. O’Sullivan also said any action taken on Aughinish Alumina had to be mindful of Europe’s complex supply chains.
Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee was asked about the issue in advance of a meeting of European trade ministers in Dublin on Friday. She said the State would support whatever the European Commission proposed when it came to the next sanction package against Russia . McEntee also said she was not aware of any lobbying by the Government to keep alumina out of the package and that the only thing it had done was to send its own report on Aughinish Alumina to the commission.
Gardaí have conducted several searches and seized assets, including luxury vehicles and designer goods, as part of an investigation into allegations of money laundering at registered charity Liberty Recycling. Conor Lally and Hugh Dooley report that the group has also proven adept at attracting well-known figures in politics and the charity sector to become involved in its activities, so boosting its profile and reputation.
Sinn Féin TD Aengus Ó Snodaigh is listed as the chairman. There is no suggestion whatsoever that he is under investigation. Liberty Recycling did not reply to queries from The Irish Times. Sinn Féin said it had become aware of the investigation by An Garda Síochána and the Charities Regulator. “Sinn Féin fully supports any investigation,” it added. “Deputy Ó Snodaigh has engaged with the office of the Charities Regulator. He has not been contacted by gardaí, but if required, he will make himself available to assist with their inquiries.”
Our Washington Correspondent Keith Duggan is out on the Midterm Elections campaign trail , this time following President Donald Trump to Iowa. Duggan asks whether 2,000 people in a hangar in Sioux City can influence the US midterms and says Trump is counting on them doing so.

title: Man arrested for deportation after Citywest sexual assault case is dropped
description: Man (27) was charged with two counts of sexually assaulting girl (10) last October
content:
Allegations that a failed asylum seeker sexually assaulted a 10-year-old girl in Dublin last year, which sparked three nights of violence, have been withdrawn. But the formerly accused man was rearrested for deportation almost immediately after he was told by a court he was free to go.
In the wake of the charges being dropped, calls began circulating on social media for a protest outside the Citywest IPAS centre, Saggart, Dublin. Some of those promoting that protest are known far-right agitators.
The Irish Times understands gardaí are monitoring the activity online and reviewing the scale and nature of the security operation required for the planned event on Saturday evening.
Last year, in the days after the man was accused of sexually assaulting the child, a large protest at the Citywest IPAS centre turned violent. Lines of gardaí were attacked by rioters using bricks, bottles and fireworks for well over an hour before order was restored.
At one point horses were charged at Garda lines and some of those present, shouting racist and xenophobic slogans, broke down walls in a nearly housing estate so the bricks could be thrown at gardaí. There was sporadic violence in the area over the following two nights.
The Director of Public Prosecutions has not explained why the two charges of sexual assault against the now 27-year-old man, who is from an African nation, have been dropped.
However, The Irish Times understands the decision to discontinue the prosecution was made by the DPP in advance of the latest, and now final, court hearing in Dublin on Friday. It was a not a decision by gardaí and did not involve Judge Martin Nolan , who was presiding at Friday’s court hearing.
The accused man, who cannot be named under court rules relating to sexual crime cases, appeared before Dublin Circuit Criminal Court by video-link, from the Midlands Prison, Portlaoise, Co Laois, where he was in remand.
A senior counsel representing the State told Nolan that nolle prosequis were being entered in relation to both charges, meaning they were being withdrawn.
The judge said the man should be released from custody and the man then replied: “Thank you.” Sources said he was then prepared for release from the Midlands Prison.
However, immediately after he was freed, he was arrested by members of the Garda National Immigration Bureau on foot of a deportation order. The man is now expected to remain in custody until he is deported.
His deportation was ordered in the spring of last year, months before he was accused of the sexual attack, but the order was never executed and the man remained in the Republic.
After he was accused of the sexual assault, on October 20th last year near an IPAS centre, the man was immediately arrested and charged with one count of sexual assault. At a court hearing last December a second charge of sexual assault was introduced. When that second charge was put to the man by gardaí, the court heard he made a reply.
“I spoke to my solicitor and told him she sat beside me,” he told gardaí. “You can check the CCTV. She started talking to me and I asked her her age, she told me she was 18. I just kissed her.”
The case was a very controversial one for several reasons, aside from the now-dropped sexual assault allegations and rioting, as the child and family agency Tusla was forced to apologise for a statement it issued at the time.
It said the girl had been voluntarily placed into its care earlier in 2025 “due to significant behavioural issues”. It added she had “absconded” while on a recreational trip with staff in the city centre in the hours before the incident that later led to the sexual assault charges.
The Dáil was told at the time the Tusla statement “verged on victim blaming”. Tusla chief executive Kate Duggan later apologised for “the way it was released, and the impact of it, and the wording around it”.

title: The 18-year legal battle over a news report that a jury took just 48 minutes to dismiss
description: Engineer sought total of €6m ‘index linked’ from Irish Times and other newspapers following reporting of his trial for assault
content:
A jury this week found against a man seeking damages from The Irish Times and three other newspapers arising from reports published 22 years ago that, he claimed, defamed him.
Kevin Tracey lodged his High Court claims in December 2008 over reports published in September 2004 in The Irish Times, the Irish Independent, the Evening Herald and the Irish Daily Star.
The case, in which Tracey was a lay litigant – meaning he did not use a lawyer but instead represented himself – took almost 18 years to be heard for various reasons including hearings before the Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court appeal, where Tracey successfully challenged a decision of the High Court in favour of the newspapers to strike out his claim, took eight years before a decision was reached.
On a separate matter, the Court of Appeal decided in favour of the newspapers on whether the four claims should be dealt with in the High Court at the same hearing and separately ruled that a legal issue the newspapers wanted decided on as a preliminary issue should be determined at the High Court trial.
At the centre of the case were reports about a Dublin District Court hearing where Tracey, an engineer living at Park Lane in Chapelizod, west Dublin, was charged with assault arising from a confrontation with a neighbour, Gabby Skinner, whose children were among a number of children playing ball outside Tracey’s home.
During the confrontation Skinner was pushed by Tracey, who denied touching her.
The judge in the case, Michael Connellan, said that as far as he was concerned “there was an assault on Mrs Skinner, but it was of a very technical nature”.
The report in The Irish Times stated Tracey had been convicted of assault. The report stated that the judge had granted leave to appeal, “saying that even though there was no penalty, the Probation Act was still a criminal conviction”.
The reports published in the other newspapers were broadly similar. All the reports were written by court reporter Tim Healy, who wrote his reports using shorthand notes he took on the day in court.
Tracey wrote to the newspapers in the wake of the reports, claiming he had been defamed, as the application of the Probation Act meant he had not been convicted.
He sought a statement on the front page of each newspaper that he had been defamed and a payment of €1.5 million from each title. He was offered a clarification, though not an apology, by the Irish Independent, in August 2008, but did not accept that.
The defamation case was heard before Judge Tony O’Connor over five days and the jury gave its decision on Wednesday after just 48 minutes of deliberation.
All the newspapers were represented by the same barrister, Eoin McCullough, though separate barristers and solicitors acted for The Irish Times and the other publishers.
McCullough argued that reports of court hearings had “absolute privilege” under defamation law and that as long as they were fair and accurate reports of what had happened in court, they were protected from defamation claims.
“So in a case of absolute privilege all we have to show is that this was a fair and accurate account of what Judge Connellan said on 16th September, 2004,” he told the jury.
“You are not concerned with anything else except that.”
The judge made the same point in his charge to the jury before they went out to consider their decision.
Newspapers, O’Connor said, report what was said. “They don’t get involved in interrogating whether [what was said] was rightly said or not.”
The only witnesses in the case were Tracey and Healy. Tracey, in his address to the jury, said Connellan had dismissed the charge against him using the Probation of Offenders Act 1907.
“I was clearly not convicted. These false publications defame me and were unfair and inaccurate,” he said.
“I am not asking you to disregard the finding, made by the District Court, that the facts were proved,” he said.
“I am asking you to distinguish between findings of fact proved and a formal criminal conviction. The newspapers reported a conviction.”
The jury was given “issue papers” containing the two questions about each newspaper.
The first was whether the report published by the newspaper was a fair and accurate report of what was stated by Connellan in the 2004 District Court sitting.
The second, concerning the amount of damages Tracey should be awarded, was only to be answered if the jury’s answer was no to the first question.
In the end, the jury decided after its very brief deliberations that the answer was yes to the first question for each of the newspapers.
As a consequence, the second question of damages did not arise.
A key item of evidence in the case was Healy’s notes, in a spiral backed notebook, that recorded the words attributed to the judge in the September 2004 case. The same notebook contained notes from other court cases before and subsequent to the date of the Tracey case.
When Healy was being questioned by Tracey, the reporter was asked if he knew there was a machine that could remove a spiral binding, allow a person to slip new pages into a notebook and then replace the binding.
“I didn’t know it was possible and I didn’t know there was a machine so that’s certainly of interest,” Healy replied.
Asked to explain the sentence in his notes that recorded Connellan saying, “the Probation of Offenders Act is a conviction but it does not carry any penalty,” Healy said: “The judge said it. You would have to ask him.”
In the reports written by Healy it was stated that Tracey had in 2003 taken a case against his next-door neighbour, Circuit Court judge Michael White, complaining of noise nuisance arising from White’s children playing musical instruments.
The complaint was withdrawn before it came to hearing but Tracey was ordered to pay €1,500 in legal costs because he failed to turn up in court to say he was withdrawing his complaint, Healy reported.
When it was his time in the witness box, Tracey was questioned about conspiracy proceedings he had initiated in 2008 against 23 people, including Connellan.
In the proceedings Tracey claimed the Skinner assault charge had been “orchestrated” against him by his neighbour, White, and that the defendants, who included the then minister for justice, Garda commissioner, Director of Public Prosecutions, and others, including Skinner, had all either committed perjury or conspired against him.
In 2010 Judge Peter Charleton in the High Court found in favour of the defendants where they had argued that the conspiracy claim was frivolous and vexatious and should be dismissed.
The judge said the claim was motivated by Tracey’s desire to overcome the “finding of fact” in the 2004 District Court assault case.
In the defamation hearing McCullough asked Tracey about the conspiracy case.
“Did you maintain the proposition that all this was a conspiracy against you?” he said, meaning the assault charge.
Asked if he still did, Tracey said: “I still do. Yeah.”
After the jury delivered its verdict, O’Connor directed that Tracey pay the legal costs incurred by the newspapers. Tracey said he wanted to reserve his right to appeal.

title: Gardaí believe foul play very unlikely to be a factor in deaths of Bray couple
description: Inquest rather than criminal process likely to follow in cases of Jamie McGinn (38) and Bridget ‘Biddy’ O’Brien (45)
content:
Gardaí believe foul play of any kind is very unlikely in the deaths of Bridget “Biddy” O’Brien (45) and Jamie McGinn (38) at the home they shared in Bray , Co Wicklow.
However, the precise cause of O’Brien’s death has not been fully determined and gardaí believe the results of toxicology tests will be required before they can be certain how she died.
Sources told The Irish Times no evidence has been found to suggest anyone else was present when O’Brien or McGinn died and that nothing suggested third-party involvement or foul play.
McGinn, whose remains were discovered in the garden of the property in the Cois Cairn estate on Old Connaught Avenue, suffered wounds that gardaí believe were self-inflicted.
O’Brien was found inside the house and there were no signs of violence on her body or in the bedroom.
Gardaí believe O’Brien may have been dead for a period before McGinn found her and then took his own life. However, sources stressed it may be several weeks before the full set of toxicology results was available. At this stage, gardaí are treating the deaths as a tragedy.
The investigation team would likely only compile a case file for a coroner’s inquest, sources said. A criminal file would not be prepared for the Director of Public Prosecutions unless something unusual emerged from the toxicology tests, sources said, as the circumstances of their deaths suggest no criminal charges should arise.
If that remains the case, details of how the couple died will emerge during an inquest, the purpose of which is to determine a cause of death only.
The couple lost their two children, Jordan (4) and Holly (3), in a fire in Clondlakin, Dublin almost 10 years ago. A number of locals in Bray, and others who knew them, said the couple had struggled in the years since and turned to drugs due to their trauma.
The house where the couple died has remained sealed off since their remains were found at about 8am on Wednesday, with the Garda Technical Bureau carrying out a full examination.
O’Brien suffered extensive and life-changing burns in the 2017 fire in which Jordan and Holly died. The blaze broke out at a facility for women moving on from domestic violence, which they had been visiting. O’Brien’s relative Anne-Marie O’Brien (27), her daughter Hannah-Paris (2) and her unborn son AJ also died in the Clondalkin fire.
O’Brien was the only survivor of the fire and missed the funerals of her two children due to her injuries. She only learned Holly and Jordan had died about six weeks after the incident. During her long stay in hospital, McGinn maintained a vigil at her bedside.

title: Man (30s) dies in early-morning car crash in Carrigaline
description: Two cars crashed at about 6.35am, with one driver pronounced dead at the scene
content:
A man in his 30s has died after a crash early on Friday morning in Carrigaline, Co Cork .
Gardaí are appealing for witnesses after the fatal crash that took place at about 6.35am on Friday.
The incident involved two cars, with the driver of one of the vehicles pronounced dead at the scene.
His body was removed to the mortuary at Cork University Hospital for a postmortem, and the coroner has been notified.
The driver of the other car, a man in his 50s, was taken to the same hospital for treatment. His injuries are not believed to be life-threatening.
The R612 road between Carrigaline and Crosshaven was closed on Friday afternoon, with local diversions in place.
Gardaí appealed for witnesses to contact them, and for anyone with relevant video, including dashcam footage, to make it available.
The death is the 11th on Irish roads in October and the 153rd of the year, according to statistics updated by An Garda Síochána daily.
The man killed in the crash was the 57th driver to be killed in a collision in 2026.
Fatalities in 2026 are tracking significantly ahead of the 2025 figure, which was at 139 at the same date last year.
Gardaí warned motorists on Thursday to be vigilant as days become darker, with a greater risk on the roads as a result.

title: Pretax profits at Irish arm of Deliveroo up 37% to €2.9m
description: Revenue increases to €64m at takeaway food delivery service
content:
Pretax profits at the Irish arm of takeaway food delivery service Deliveroo last year increased by 37 per cent to €2.89 million as revenues further increased.
Accounts show that revenues also increased by 10 per cent from €58.08 million to €64.09 million.
In a note with the accounts, the directors said that the revenue increase in 2025 was “as a result of increased demand, the change in ordering behaviour and sales mix”.
The accounts said gross profit increased from €28.09 million to €30.15 million, representing a 7 per cent increase “which is reflective of both increased demand and the scalable unit economics of the business model”.
The company’s operating profits increased by 10 per cent from €1.5m to €1.66m and profits were further increased by finance income of €1.2m.
On the company’s future developments, the directors said: “The development and growth of existing activities and improving key customer value proposition pillars will continue to be the focus of attention in the coming year, with an increased focus on supporting sustainable profitability and cash generation, through driving efficiency.”
Numbers directly employed by the company here last year decreased further from 27 to 23 as staff costs dropped from €2.06 million to €1.89 million. It included a share-based payment charge of €37,730.
The company’s non-cash depreciation costs last year totalled €151,063. The company’s cost of sales came to €33.94 million and other operating expenses amounted to €24.54 million, while administrative expenses came to €3.94 million.
The firm recorded post-tax profits of €2.23 million after incurring a corporation tax charge of €666,087.
At the end of December last, the firm’s accumulated profits totalled €10.9 million while the company’s cash funds decreased from €52.09 million to €47.43m.
[ Lidl has moved into Irish mobile phone market. Can it save you money? Opens in new window ]
In October 2025, the San Francisco-headquartered firm DoorDash finalised its $3.9 billion (€3.48 billion) in cash acquisition of Deliveroo’s global business.
In 2025, DoorDash generated nearly $75 billion (€67 billion) in sales for local merchants across over 40 countries and over $20 billion in earnings for its independent contractors, known as “Dashers”.
This year, Deliveroo Ireland’s parent, the UK-based Deliveroo Ltd, approved and paid interim dividends totalling £275 million (€328 million) to the company’s sole shareholder, DoorDash.
The £275 million comprised dividends of £100 million approved on February 12th, 2026; £100 million on March 25th, 2026; and £75 million on May 27th, 2026.

title: Ballinahown in Co Westmeath is named Tidy Towns overall winner for 2026
description: More than 600 volunteers from across the country at Croke Park awards ceremony
content:
Ballinahown in Co Westmeath has been named the overall winner of the 2026 SuperValu TidyTowns Competition.
The tidiest large town award went to Buncrana, Co Donegal with the small town award going to Abbeyleix, Co Laois. The award for tidiest village was also won by Ballinahown.
Tralee in Co Kerry won the tidiest large urban centre award while the Gaeltacht Award went to Carraig Airt,Co. Donegal. The Young Persons in TidyTowns award was won by Dromiskin, Co. Louth.
The award ceremony took place in Croke Park on Friday and was hosted by RTÉ Sports presenter Marty Morrissey , with Minister for Rural and Community Development Dara Calleary handing out awards to winners across several categories.
All told 936 towns were competing, the highest number of entries ever received in the competition’s history which stretches back to the late 1950s.
“I offer my heartiest congratulations to Balliahown and its TidyTowns volunteers for becoming Ireland’s Tidiest Town for 2026,” Calleary said. “This is a wonderful achievement and a special moment of immense pride for Ballinahown and indeed the wider county of Westmeath.”
He noted how the town had consistently entered the competition over the last 40 years and won Ireland’s Tidiest Village in 2024, - a title it also won this year.
“Ballinahown have finally achieved their goal of winning the competition outright. This achievement today continues to showcase all that is good about resilience, innovation, sustainability, community spirit and volunteerism.”
The minister said the win was “even more impressive given the fantastic results the village has achieved over the last three years with a population of just 160 people. This dedication is at the core of what the competition is all about.”
Calleary hailed the vital role of volunteers across the country “who are working so hard all year round to ensure our communities are vibrant, sustainable places to live, work and visit. The passion and dedication of these volunteers is the embodiment of everything that is good in our communities.”
SuperValu has sponsored the competition for 35 years and the chief marketing officer at the chain’s owner Musgraves, Margaret Barron, said the winning town was “a shining example of what can be achieved when communities come together with a shared sense of pride and a commitment to making a lasting, positive difference to their local area”
There were more than 600 volunteers from across the country present at the ceremony.
About 30,000 volunteers took part in hundreds of Tidy Towns projects through the year so far, representing close to €40 million in economic value.
More than 220 prizes were awarded, with about €270,000 in main awards and €70,000 in special prizes given out.
The national TidyTowns initiative was launched in 1958 by Bord Fáilte, which has since been renamed Fáilte Ireland.
It was born out of a national “spring clean campaign” that ran between 1953 and 1957.

title: It’s ‘all hands on deck’ as Big Dunc faces mammoth task at Glentoran
description: Duncan Ferguson looking for Damien Duff effect in bid to light up ancient terraces at The Oval
content:
T he pigeon fancier was smiling and laughing. Sometimes these are the best hours as a football manager – introduction day – before a ball has been kicked. Certainly it looked that way for Duncan Ferguson as he walked into Glentoran on Monday morning.
This is “the” Duncan Ferguson, by the way. Everton Ferguson, Scottish Ferguson, “Big Dunc”. And, yes, he has just succeeded Declan Devine as head coach of Glentoran. Ferguson becomes the Glens’ 12th manager of the 21st century, not the most reassuring statistic.
It is an appointment with an echo of Shelbourne ’s announcement of Damien Duff five years ago. That wrong-footed a few.
Duff talked the talk, then walked the walk. His talent and determination brought a step change at Shels; his charisma brought attention to the League of Ireland. Duff gave everyone involved, colleagues and opponents, a competitive spark.
Duncan Ferguson’s status in Irish football is hardly Duff’s, but there are similarities in Premier League profile and in the context of Glens and Shels, not least The Oval and Tolka Park, two grounds that could double as museum pieces. Shels had not won the League of Ireland since 2006 when Duff jinked in; Glentoran have not won the Irish League since 2009.
So far, and it is barely a week, there have been comparable reactions to Ferguson in Belfast with Duff in Dublin. Reputation alone does not mean success, but it does ensure people stop and stare, and Irish football can never get enough eyeballs. Duff pushed Shelbourne to the Cup final in his first season, then won the title in his third. Every week he seemed to send volts through the League.
Were Ferguson to emulate that, they will be happy at The Oval, not least because it would mean he has seen out the third year of a three-year contract.
Last season was an improvement, but the joke was Glentoran finished third in a two-horse race. The suggestion is there is something “Spursy” about Glentoran. Ferguson, one imagines, won’t like that.
[ How Manchester United became a club too big not to fail Opens in new window ]
But Day One is no time for such reflection, it’s about the future, optimism, and so Ferguson was in fine form. Noting the Glens’ nickname is the “Cock ‘n’ Hens”, he said: “I still keep my pigeons.” Informed that the blue of Everton and Rangers, while it may have been part of him forever, will not be welcome due to its Linfield connotations, he said Glentoran’s “shirt is lovely”. He had already taken his first training session and laughed that only one player had been sick.
He will live in Belfast – “I’ll be fully committed, all hands on deck.” He is 54 and has not coached for two years, since Inverness Caledonian Thistle fell into administration. That was not his fault, but after a short stint at Forest Green Rovers did not go well, Ferguson needs this to. There is some motivational jeopardy for both parties, because Glentoran cannot keep trundling along.
The club is run by Ali Pour, part of a 2019 consortium takeover. Money has been pumped into the team, but the sum which could transform The Oval sits in a fund at Stormont awaiting disposal. Just as the League of Ireland is held back by infrastructure, so is the Irish League. A functioning local government focused on delivering local services rather than exacerbating local division would be of use.
So when Ferguson sends out his first selection on Saturday to face Ballymena United, it is into an arena Danny Blanchflower would recognise – and he left Glentoran in 1949. More worrying, Peter Doherty might recognise it and he left in 1933. The 2019 film about Manchester City’s German goalkeeper Bert Trautmann used The Oval for scenes of 1950s Maine Road.
Some of us are almost as old as Trautmann. My first Glentoran match was this month in 1977. It just happened to be against Juventus in the second round of the European Cup. What a team the Glens had then, and Juve weren’t bad – Dino Zoff in goal, Claudio Gentile in front of him, Marco Tardelli, who scored that goal in the 1982 World Cup final, Roberto Bettega and Roberto Boninsegna – the man who scored Italy’s goal in the greatest World Cup final of them all, 1970’s against Brazil. He must have been thrilled to be at The Oval.
In a young boy’s memory, though, none of them compared to Franco Causio, one of those wingers who sent the crowd the wrong way. Some ended up in the shipyard that night.
[ Manchester City’s inflatable bananas are back. Business is booming for Imre Varadi Opens in new window ]
Causio scored the only goal, but Johnny Jamison hit the bar and Warren Feeney missed a penalty – or had it saved by Zoff. Feeney, Jamison, Victor Moreland, Billy Caskey, these were serious players and Jimmy Cleary was yet to arrive at The Oval.
Giovanni Trapattoni was Juve manager and thought his part-time hosts were “too eager”. Juve won the second leg 5-0 on the way to the semi-final.
Trap and Tardelli would return to Ireland many years later, of course, though not to watch Shelbourne v Glentoran because there is no all-island league in Ireland despite the first Irish League season being 1890-91. Glentoran were in it and Shels joined them in it in 1904.
More World Cup figures came to east Belfast in 1992 in the new Champions League. Marseilles had Didier Deschamps, Basile Boli and, up front, Rudi Völler. They won 5-0 as Voller was subjected to insulting and, frankly, the most improbable abuse. There’s no way he had family on the New Lodge Road.
Returning three weeks ago for Glentoran-Carrick Rangers, the old ground looked the same as in 1992 and 1977. Because, essentially, it is. There were “Groundhoppers” over from the Netherlands – The Oval has become a place to tick off. They stood outside the club shop in new merchandise and beamed, then moved across to ancient terraces to take in the vista as planes from George Best Airport came and went. The attendance was around 2,000-3,000 including lots of youngsters. The potential is obvious; it so needs redevelopment.
It was the first match after Devine and the “Glentoran Gazette” – published by “the oldest supporters’ club in Ireland” – said a touching farewell to the Derryman, a popular former Glens’ player. Out on the pitch Greg Sloggett was part of a comfortable home win.
There have been two more since and Big Dunc’s new team sit third, but 11 points behind leaders Coleraine, where there has been investment.
Duff changed Shelbourne, and outsiders’ idea of the club, through energy and effort. Equal it, and Ferguson can have a comparable impact at Glentoran. Already his mere presence has provoked a new conversation about the Irish League.

title: F1 crown in reach for Kimi Antonelli at bumpy Austin circuit drivers insist is ‘unacceptable’
description: Max Verstappen says bumpy Texas track makes drivers ‘suffer’
content:
The Formula One world championship is within reach for Kimi Antonelli at the US Grand Prix in Austin this weekend. But while the young Italian approaches the race intending simply to have fun, there is disquiet among other drivers about the potential long-term health dangers posed by the state of the Texas circuit.
The 20-year-old Antonelli will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he claims the title at the Circuit of the Americas on Sunday, eclipsing Sebastian Vettel’s record from 2010, when the German driver was 23 and Antonelli was four.
It is an outside chance as the Italian has acknowledged. He must win while needing his rivals to endure a poor day. His Mercedes team-mate, George Russell, would have to finish outside the top eight and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton outside the top four.
Nonetheless, while Antonelli knows the title race is effectively over, he is keeping the cool head that has brought him to this point with such alacrity. The Mercedes ship, helmed by his race engineer Pete Bonnington, who was alongside Hamilton for his six titles with the team, is steady as she goes.
“We had a meeting with Bono [Bonnington] this morning and we said: ‘Just have fun’,” Antonelli said. “It’s the same mindset I’ve had all year. One race at a time. Just try to do the best I can every race weekend, and then we’ll see.”
After a tricky rookie season last year, Antonelli has adapted remarkably quickly to competing at the front of the grid. But as he looks to close it out, he feels able to draw on previous experience.
“Formula One is different because the pressure is a lot bigger than in anything else,” he added. “The competition is a little bit higher as well because you’re racing with 21 of the best drivers in the world. But when you fight for championships in karting and junior series, the mindset is very similar in the way you approach races and the way you think.”
Going into the weekend, however, the circuit has drawn unusually severe criticism from drivers. The race was first held in Austin in 2012 and has a contract until 2034. It has become hugely popular, with sold-out crowds, but the track has come under intense scrutiny.
Built on marshland, the bumps caused by the ground beneath the tarmac have been condemned in Austin as potentially harmful, with the uneven surface forcing impacts into the base of the drivers’ spines.
“The bumps are unacceptable. Over time they’ve been grinding a little bit here and there but it’s just putting a plaster on the big problem,” said Max Verstappen of Red Bull. “You need to really fully open up the track. That costs a lot of money and time but that’s the only way to get rid of it because these bumps are not natural and they are out of control.
“From the checks that I’ve done from my spine, the bottom end doesn’t look that great. I know that’s part of racing. I know that can be part of sport but it’s also further damage from the cars that we had the last few years. If we continue with finding this acceptable to drive on, then you are going to suffer with that much more.”
Verstappen’s opinion was echoed by the defending world champion, Lando Norris, who is frustrated that drivers’ concerns are not being listened to.
“It’s pretty bad. There’s a lot of places I need to take headache tablets before I go out simply because it’s so bumpy and you’re hitting your head pretty hard against the headrest because of the bumps. So it’s certainly not a nice thing,” Norris said.
“There’s not much we can do. I mean, we complain about it, it’s stuff we’ve brought up many, many times but there’s only so much we can complain about things.” – Guardian

title: Non-jury trial for civil servant accused of leaking sensitive information to hostile power
description: Yevgen McKeeffe (46), originally from Ukraine but with Irish citizenship, accused of twice breaching the Official Secrets Act
content:
A civil servant accused of leaking sensitive State information to a hostile foreign power has been sent forward for trial to the non-jury Special Criminal Court .
Yevgen McKeeffe (46), an Irish citizen originally from Ukraine, is accused of two breaches of the Official Secrets Act, breaching the Data Protection Act, and disclosing confidential information from a government department between July 11th, 2025 and May 28th last.
McKeeffe, who denies the four allegations, was arrested at Dublin Airport on May 28th last while attempting to leave the State. He was carrying €5,650 and had a one-way ticket.
Reporting restrictions prohibit the reporting of the accused’s Dublin address, the department in which he works, the other country involved and the information allegedly disclosed.
The case resumed on Friday at Cloverhill District Court when McKeeffe was served with a book of evidence. Judge Alan Mitchell noted the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) had authorised that McKeeffe be returned for trial to the Special Criminal Court, which usually hears terrorism or organised crime cases.
State solicitor Mark Donnelly said the DPP had issued a certificate stating that the ordinary courts were not suitable for the administration of justice in this case.
A date for McKeeffe’s appearance before the three-judge, non-jury court has not yet been set. Legal aid, covering a solicitor and three counsel due to the complexity of the case, was granted.
McKeeffe has lived in Ireland for 24 years and changed his name by deed poll. The IT worker, who was refused bail at a previous stage, was remanded in continuing custody.
During a bail hearing in June, Det Sgt Shay Palmer told the court McKeeffe had been in his latest job since 2022, having worked in another department for six years beforehand. He is suspended from work pending the outcome of the case.
Palmer said the Special Detective Unit opened an intelligence-led investigation that led to McKeeffe’s arrest as he was about to fly to Turkey. It was alleged he would then proceed “on to his final destination where he would meet his contact and share confidential information which had the potential of creating risk to the Irish State”.
Palmer maintained that McKeeffe received payments in a foreign currency equivalent to €250–€260 for his efforts, which were lodged into his mother’s account. Given the nature of the other country involved, he said it was not possible to determine whether the accused received further sums there.
Palmer raised concerns about a potential flight risk, with the court hearing the accused, who said he came to Ireland because he faced discrimination for being homosexual, had used four other variations of names. McKeeffe held an Irish passport and two other non-Irish travel documents and had been in Ireland lawfully since 2002.
Defence counsel said the accused had changed his name to a more Irish one and had ties to the State through his job, friends and a mortgage on his home.

title: Euro zone growth slows to four-month low amid rising costs and French strife
description: EUROZONE-ECONOMY/PMI (UPDATE 1, PIX):UPDATE 1-Euro zone growth slows to 4-month low amid rising costs and French strife, survey shows
content:
Growth across the euro zone’s private sector slowed to its weakest pace in ‌four months in October, hurt by an energy-driven rise in costs and a renewed contraction in France amid political and financial instability, a survey showed.
The S&P Global Flash Eurozone Composite PMI Output ​Index fell to 51.9 in October from September’s 53.1, its lowest reading since June and lower than all forecasts in a Reuters poll which had predicted a modest dip to 52.7.
A PMI (purchasing managers index) reading above 50.0 indicates growth.
“Following a spring and summer where the euro zone economy defied expectations, the flash October PMIs pour a little bit of cold water on just ​how much further sentiment could improve,” said Rory Fennessy at Oxford Economics.
“The volatile situation in France weighed heavily on the euro zone picture, with government borrowing costs spiking further as the fiscal ⁠situation worsens.”
French business activity unexpectedly contracted this month, reflecting a sharp decline in demand for goods and services which businesses surveyed tied to ‌heightened ‌political uncertainty ​and economic pressures.
Government borrowing costs in France have jumped in recent weeks on investor concerns about the country’s ability to repair its finances, while waves of street protests have raised the political temperature ahead of a presidential election ⁠in the spring.
Meanwhile in Germany, Europe’s largest economy, private sector growth ​also softened.
Britain’s PMI showed resilience with firms having their strongest month for ​activity since February.
But British consumers reined in shopping last month as higher fuel prices ate into household budgets, official data showed earlier on Friday, and GfK ‌said consumer confidence suffered its sharpest month-on-month fall since early ​in the Covid-19 pandemic in October.
Input costs in the currency union accelerated for the second consecutive month linked to higher energy, fuel and ⁠transport costs in part due to the Middle East war. Despite ⁠this, firms raised their selling prices ​at a slower pace than in September, suggesting some margin compression.
“While manufacturers are continuing to feel the squeeze of higher energy prices, there is still little evidence of second-round effects, which will be reassuring for the ECB,” said Harry Chambers at Capital Economics.
The European Central Bank will hold its deposit rate at 2.5 per cent next week but raise it by 25 basis points in December as inflation runs nearly double its 2 per cent target, a Reuters poll found earlier this month.
Business confidence in the euro zone fell to a five-month low, the survey showed, with optimism dropping most sharply in manufacturing.
France, beset by financial pressures and political turbulence, stood out for its pessimism. Its PMI pointed to economic ‌contraction with business confidence hitting its ⁠lowest since 2012 outside the pandemic period.
New orders in the euro zone – a key gauge of demand – grew at their slowest rate in the current four-month expansion sequence, with both manufacturing and services posting only modest gains. New export ‌orders rose for a third consecutive month, however, an encouraging sign after nearly 4-1/2 years of continuous monthly declines.
The preliminary services PMI fell to a two-month low while a manufacturing output ​index – which feeds into the composite reading – dropped to a four-month low.
Hiring in the single currency ​area came close to a standstill, the survey showed, with employment barely rising after slight gains in the prior two months. Services sector job creation eased to a five-month low and manufacturing payrolls edged down after two months of improvement. – Reuters

title: French seek removal of champagne levies after Trump’s Irish whiskey move
description: Removal of US tariffs on Irish whiskey was promised by Donald Trump in September, though it is yet to come into effect
content:
US trade tariffs should be removed from cognac and champagne in the same way they are being lifted on Irish whiskey , according to France’s trade minister.
Nicolas Forissier made the remarks in advance of an informal meeting of European trade ministers on Friday, which is being held in Dublin as part of Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the European Union .
During his visit to Ireland last month, US president Donald Trump made the surprise announcement that he would remove tariffs from Irish whiskey.
A spokesman for Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee said that “intensive engagement” with the US on technical implementation of the planned removal of the tariff is ongoing and aims to get it over the line “as soon as possible”.
Trade relations with the US are on the agenda for talks at Friday’s meeting of EU ministers in Dublin.
Speaking to reporters in advance of the talks, Forissier brought up how the EU made a deal with the US on tariffs, the Turnberry Agreement, saying this fixed the tariff limits and was “positive”.
However, he added that “exemptions for certain sectors are necessary”, citing wine and spirits.
He added: “Each time I meet an American leader… I’m asking for it on behalf of France.”
He said he made the same request with US trade representative Jamieson Greer recently.
“I noticed that the Irish whiskeys had been a concern and have no duties now” Forissier added.
“It should be the same for French cognac [and], I think, champagne.”
Taoiseach Micheál Martin raised the tariff issue with Dublin during his meeting with Trump in Dublin last month.
The US tariff on Irish whiskey was as high as 15 per cent last year, but that was subsequently reduced to 10 per cent.
The US president announced he would remove the tariff during the prize-giving ceremony at the end of the Irish Open tournament at his golf resort at Doonbeg which was won by Irish golfer Shane Lowry .
As he wrapped up his address to the crowd Trump said: “I want to mention one thing [the] Taoiseach and I talked about it, and Shane [Lowry] talked about it.
“Everybody’s been bugging me. They’re saying, ‘Will you do me a favour, it’s so unfair what’s going on. Could you possibly take the tariffs off of Irish whiskey?’
“And I said, on behalf of the United States of America, I am going to take the tariffs off.”

title: Eddie Howe is Jason Wilcox’s choice if Manchester United replace Michael Carrick
description: Head of recruitment Christopher Vivell is understood to prefer the option of Julian Nagelsmann
content:
Eddie Howe is the current preferred candidate of Jason Wilcox to replace Michael Carrick should Manchester United decide to change manager, with the director of football believing Howe’s extensive Premier League experience places him ahead of other potential targets.
Howe left Newcastle in late July to take a break from the game but would seriously consider a return for the United role, it is understood, should this be offered.
Howe would be less expensive to bring in than Unai Emery, another admired candidate, because Aston Villa would demand about £20m in compensation for their manager.
In five years managing Newcastle Howe impressed, leading the team to the 2025 Carabao Cup, ending a 70-year wait for a domestic trophy. After taking over from Steve Bruce in November 2021, Howe led Newcastle to 11th, winning 12 of the last 18 games. The team had gone 14 games without a victory at the start of the season.
Howe also took Newcastle back into the Champions League after 20 years in 2023 and qualified again two seasons later. He managed Bournemouth for five seasons in the Premier League from 2015.
Julian Nagelsmann, the former Germany and Bayern Munich coach, is highly regarded by Christopher Vivell, United’s head of recruitment, but Wilcox’s view may hold more sway with Jim Ratcliffe, who controls football policy.
Carrick is under serious pressure after the club’s poorest start since 1986. The 45-year-old is expected to remain in place for Sunday’s visit of Bournemouth – he is due to hold his pre-game media conference on Friday – but the 45-year-old’s job is in the balance after two wins from 11 games this season.
United are inviting fans to offer their views on the design of the proposed new 100,000-seat stadium. A survey will be sent to season-ticket holders, cup season-ticket holders, executive club members, official members, supporters who have purchased hospitality at Old Trafford within the past three years and season-ticket waiting list members. — Guardian

title: Ireland to back ‘whatever’ sanctions European Commission proposes for Russia, McEntee says
description: Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade not aware of any lobbying by Government to exclude alumina from latest set of measures
content:
Ireland will support whatever the European Commission proposes when it comes to the next sanction package against Russia , the Minister for Foreign Affairs has said.
Helen McEntee also said she was not aware of any lobbying by the Government to keep alumina out of the package and that the only thing it had done was to send its own report on Aughinish Alumina to the commission.
The Co Limerick plant is owned by Russian metals giant Rusal and ships vast quantities of alumina to smelters in Russia, where the raw material is turned into aluminium, a key ingredient in the industrial supply chain.
The plant, which employs hundreds in the Foynes area, previously warned it could be forced to shut if its exports to Russia were barred by EU sanctions.
A draft of the commission’s 22nd package of sanctions does not propose measures prohibiting alumina exports , according to one senior source briefed on the details. However, sources in Brussels noted that changes were often made following confidential talks.
Aughinish’s exports of alumina to Russia have been in the spotlight after reporting by The Irish Times tracing the shipments to smelters in Russia, where it is made into aluminium that is sold to a company known to supply the alloy to Russian arms and missile manufacturers.
David O’Sullivan, the EU envoy on sanctions, said on Thursday that alumina produced by Aughinish “undoubtedly” ended up supplying, at least in part, the Russian military-industrial complex. He said any action taken against the company had to be mindful of Europe’s complex supply chains.
“We just have to find the best way of doing it, which doesn’t have unhelpful collateral consequences,” he told an Institute of International and European Affairs event in Dublin.
McEntee spoke to reporters in advance of an informal meeting of trade ministers being held on Friday as part of Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the European Union.
She was asked whether Ireland could stand over a situation that saw alumina from the plant having a part in supplying Russian war efforts. She said a Department of Enterprise report on Aughinish Alumina had been given to the commission.
“We engaged directly with our colleagues in Ukraine on that, and we’ve been very clear that whatever the commission proposes in terms of the next package of sanctions, we will support that.”
The department’s report could not find proof that alumina from Aughinish was ultimately being used by Russian arms and missile manufacturers. However, officials qualified their conclusions by admitting their inquiry had “no means” to trace the supply chain once the product entered Russia and that they had limited access to reliable trade data.
McEntee said the next sanctions package was being worked on and that sanctions “have had an impact on Russia’s ability to wage this war and so we’ll work with the commission, whatever is proposed”.
She added: “We’ve been very clear ... we do not want to be contributing to this war. We do not want a situation where any product could be contributing to this war coming from Ireland.”
She said Ireland had not rejected or pushed back against any sanctions package that had been proposed.
The Estonian minister of economy and industry, Liina Vahtras, was on Friday asked about her country’s push for sanctions restricting alumina exports to Russia. It was put to her that this did not appear to have support from many EU members.
Vahtras said: “We are strong on the message and we remain very strong ... that the sanctions must be there to end the conflict in Ukraine.”
After Russia, France is Aughinish Alumina’s next biggest market. It supplies significant quantities of material to an aluminium smelter in Dunkirk.
On his country’s stance on the inclusion of alumina in sanctions against Russia, French trade minister Nicolas Forissier said: “France doesn’t take any position on this, in this field alone, so we will discuss it. I can’t give you an answer on this question today.”
He added: “We have always been very clear on the necessity of having sanctions towards Russia.”
The trade ministers are due to discuss EU trade with China and the US at Dublin Castle, as well as how trade with other countries can be strengthened as the EU seeks to diversify its markets.

title: Carla Lockhart’s decision highlights the internal tensions within the DUP
description: MP’s resignation as a party officer not ideal for leader Gavin Robinson, but a defection, and with it the loss of an MP, would be a serious blow
content:
Throughout much of the Drumcree dispute, the loyalist activist and legal adviser to the Portadown Orange Order , Jamie Bryson , and the DUP MP for Upper Bann, Carla Lockhart, were side by side.
During the stand-off over the controversial parade, and indeed since, Lockhart – on the ground with the local Orange Lodge at Drumcree – has struck a more strident note than her party colleagues at Stormont , not least her party leader, Gavin Robinson .
Lockhart’s repeated call was that it could not be “business as usual” at Stormont.
“People are angry that we have a self-proclaimed ‘First Minister for all’ in office who is currently under investigation for lawbreaking,” she told the BBC this week. “That lawbreaking has to have criminal sanctions, but also political consequences.”
The First Minister, Sinn Féin vice-president Michelle O’Neill , and party president Mary Lou McDonald were interviewed at a Belfast police station this week about their involvement in allegedly unlawful protests on the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road. These blocked the Orange Order – which had been granted permission by the Parades Commission – from marching from Drumcree church on September 27th. Other Sinn Féin politicians are due to attend police interviews today.
The political consequence Lockhart wanted was the withdrawal of her party colleague Emma Little-Pengelly as Deputy First Minister, which, under the powersharing rules governing Stormont, would also see O’Neill lose her position as First Minister.
This has not happened and, as things stand, is not going to. Stormont looked to be on shaky ground at the outset of the Drumcree crisis, and there has been no shortage of acrimonious exchanges in the chamber since. But it is clear there is no appetite in the DUP for collapsing Stormont, not least because, with an Assembly election fast approaching, the party does not want to take the blame on the doorsteps.
On this, Lockhart was at odds with the DUP’s leadership team, hence her decision, revealed by the Belfast Telegraph on Thursday night, to quit as a party officer.
Rumours have long swirled about Lockhart’s possible defection to the Traditional Unionist Voice . Though she remains a DUP member and MP, this could be the first step towards such a move – or towards sitting as an independent unionist.
That would be more dangerous for Robinson, though his position is secure as it stands, with the DUP’s senior leadership team clearly backing him over Lockhart.
The loss of an MP would represent a serious blow to the party, taking it down to four Westminster seats, compared with Sinn Féin’s seven, and would inevitably raise questions about Robinson’s leadership.
But Lockhart’s departure as a party officer has also illuminated the internal tensions always at work within the DUP: between grassroots opinion and the elected representatives at Stormont or Westminster; between the moderates and the harder right of the party; all against the backdrop of constant fear within the party of the TUV snapping at its heels.
That fear is never more profound than at election time. An Assembly election is due by May and it is clear there will be political consequences – to borrow Lockhart’s phrase – for unionism and nationalism.
Unionism is already grappling with the fragmentation of the unionist vote, which this latest development has only served to underline. By contrast, Sinn Féin has been strengthened by what has been perceived within the nationalist community as taking a principled stand on a question of – to borrow from O’Neill this time – a matter of right and wrong.
There is still much to happen between now and the election; what is clear is that it will all play out in the shadow of Drumcree.

title: ‘Whatever Trump and Putin agree, we’ll fight the invaders’: Inside the dugouts powering Ukraine’s drone war
description: Vast network of underground dugouts, simultaneously spartan and high-tech, underpin the nation’s drone defence
content:
I n his dugout near the front line, a Ukrainian soldier with the call sign Seal sits surrounded by the essentials of a drone pilot’s life.
Energy drinks, coffee and protein bars are in easy reach, as are small tools, rolls of tape and two drone batteries clad in blue plastic.
In front of him glow the screens through which he views the battlefield, the drone controller rests easily in his hands and a tortoiseshell cat named Murka is napping on his lap.
Everything else he needs – his bunk bed and sleeping bag, store of food and water, camping stove and automatic rifle – are just a few steps away.
It is a scene repeated, underground and painstakingly camouflaged, across a vast swathe of eastern Ukraine, where the front line snakes for some 1,200km from Sumy region on the Russian border to the coast of the Black Sea.
These bunkers vary in size and technical sophistication, and in their proximity to Russian positions, but the men and women who inhabit them and the air and land drones they operate – whether for surveillance or attack, delivering supplies or evacuating casualties – underpin Ukraine’s success in holding back a vastly larger enemy.
Dugouts combine the cutting edge and the spartan. They access satellite internet service and Ukraine’s innovative Delta system of live battlefield management. But they are still holes in the earth where soldiers must meet challenges that are timeless: endure privations, control fear, savour victories and small pleasures, survive.
As autumn turns to winter, the day now begins at 6am for Seal (39) and the other soldier in the dugout, who uses the call sign KVN. It is from the Club of the Funny and Smart, a long-running television comedy competition in which one Volodymyr Zelenskiy , now Ukraine’s president, first came to public attention.
They brush their teeth and make coffee, and prepare drones for the first flight.
“Daytime is getting shorter and we don’t have night-vision cameras at the moment, so we don’t work at night,” says Seal, who is a member of the Ronins drone unit of 65th Separate Mechanised Brigade.
“So we’re probably working from 7am until 6pm. Now we get maybe seven hours’ sleep. In summertime we were only getting three or four, because daylight lasted longer and flying conditions were better. That meant more Russian flights incoming, and so more flights for us. It was pretty tough. But now we’re getting enough sleep.”
Seal and KVN (24) use first-person-view (FPV) drones to intercept larger Russian attack drones that target Ukrainian troops and armour around the front line in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region. Their most common target is the Molniya (Lightning), a drone resembling a small plane that can carry a 10kg antitank mine.
Their screens in the dugout show a video feed from their FPV drone and, ideally, an intercepted feed from the drone they are attacking. When the FPV is alongside its target, they press a button on the hand-held controller and detonate their drone.
The FPVs have a relatively short range and battery life, so must be flown from correspondingly close to the front line. Seal says Russians are positioned only 7-8km from his bunker, and send out small teams from there to probe for gaps in Ukrainian defences.
“They’re pretty near, and sometimes their infiltration groups come closer – maybe only 4km or 5km away. You can’t relax in that situation.
“The scariest moments are when some good Samaritan calls and says: ‘Put on your armoured vest and helmet and get your gun close.’ ‘There is some information,’ he says. ‘I can’t tell you everything but be prepared’ – and that’s it. Be prepared for what? You don’t know … That’s the worst,” Seal says.
“Or when KABs [air-launched bombs weighing up to 3 tonnes] or huge-calibre artillery is incoming, and landing closer and closer, and you realise it’s just logs and soil above your head and it would be impossible to dig your way out.”
The dugout consists of a main room that is about 2m high and 2m by 4m wide, with a small hallway and storage space for drones, supplies and other gear. The floors and doors are made of wood, logs form the walls and ceiling, and metal foil and plastic sheets provide insulation. Seal describes it as “pretty comfortable” – warm and dry, with a diesel heater for winter.
“We bring about 15kg of food to the position – soda, energy drinks, ramen noodles, instant mashed potatoes. Mostly dried food. Sausages. Candy. Coffee and condensed milk to put in it,” he says.
They also order supplies from base – basics such as bread, pasta, eggs, vegetables, cheese and tinned food – and can buy extras with their own money.
But getting food, water, fuel and ammunition to forward positions is difficult, when FPV drones roam a 30km-deep “kill zone” that straddles the front line.
Deliveries are moved forward first by car, then ground drone and then attached to a heavy-lift aerial drone that can fly a 20kg payload to the bunker
They use bottled water and wet wipes to wash, and a hole dug in a nearby trench as their toilet.
“If you want to go at night, you take your gun, because you never know who could crawl into the trench,” Seal says. “You’ve got to be ready to defend your poop station.”
[ Lara Marlowe: Robots have brought a ‘horrifying intimacy’ to warfare Opens in new window ]
Murka (“Purrer”) defends the dugout’s food stores from mice and makes life more pleasant for each two-soldier team that spends a fortnight or so there before returning to base to rest.
She helps them relax at night, when they also go online and check the news.
Seal says their Starlink connection was stable this week, while Ukrainian units using its military-grade Starshield version suffered problems amid a new push from US president Donald Trump for Kyiv to make concessions to Russian leader Vladmir Putin.
“Of course we follow the news,” says Seal. “But we have a routine and stability here. We don’t get more scared or worried, and we know we will stay here and destroy the invaders and their forces, whatever Trump and Putin agree on.”
[ A drone-maker in Lviv: Stopping Russians from killing Ukrainians is ‘an act of love’ Opens in new window ]
Seal had no romantic ideas about army life, and previously told The Irish Times about how he was mobilised , then fled his assigned unit and crossed Ukraine to join his preferred brigade in Zaporizhzhia, where he describes conditions and morale as good.
“The main satisfaction from this work is saving lives. The Molniyas are basically flying bombs, so by destroying them we help protect our soldiers,” he says.
[ Russia’s new jet-powered drones are fuelling anxiety in Ukraine Opens in new window ]
“Money also makes our mood better. When you go to a forward position you receive 100,000 hryvnia (€1,980) for the month, and you get substantial bonuses for hitting targets … That’s compared to basic pay of about 30,000 hryvnia.”
He describes the world outside the bunker as both “beautiful and devastated”.
“It is burned-down fields and treelines between them, abandoned and destroyed homes and villages, roads covered with destroyed cars … But there are also very beautiful moments, when you fly in the morning above the water,” he says. “Lots of animals live in this nightmare too … Peacocks and many other birds, foxes, rabbits. A falcon was living in a high tree next to our position.”
Now he and KVN are nearing the end of another stint in the dugout, and preparing for the nerve-racking journey out through the kill zone, which begins with a 20km trek and then a car ride under threat of attack by Russian FPVs.
“Everything must go smoothly so you get back,” he says. “You are planning to rest, but to get there, to get your rest, you have to take this final leap of faith.”

title: New York ban on horse-drawn carriages ends 160-year-old industry for Irish emigrants
description: Sligo carriage driver says operators are being unfairly blamed for wider public safety concerns after a tourist died in a carriage crash in June
content:
A ban on horse-drawn carriages in New York City’s Central Park by 2028 will end an industry that has provided a livelihood to hundreds of Irish emigrants for more than 160 years.
The legislation, passed on Thursday afternoon in a vote by the city’s council, is known as Romanch’s Law, after 18-year-old Indian tourist Romanch Mahajan, who died last June following a carriage-related crash in Central Park while visiting New York with his family.
Among those gathered outside City Hall in lower Manhattan in advance of Thursday’s vote was political activist Curtis Sliwa, a two-time Republican nominee for New York City mayor.
“My wife Nancy and I have supported banning these horses being tortured since 2020. It was part of my 2021 mayoral campaign against [former mayor] Eric Adams. He made fun of me, but it’s good to see everybody get on board with this campaign,” Sliwa told The Irish Times.
“Today is history in the making. It should have happened a long, long time ago. Imagine, there are other cities who have stopped this barbaric behaviour, even in third-world countries. We’re one of the holdouts.”
Carriage operators and their families argue that proposals to help those affected by the ban find other jobs do not go far enough, while the Transport Workers Union is expected to challenge the decision.
Among those opposing the ban are Irish-born operators who fear losing not only their livelihoods but businesses into which they have invested decades of work and savings.
Conor McHugh, 62, from Co Leitrim, arrived in New York in May 1986 and began driving a horse-drawn carriage several months later. He has since become a part-owner of Clinton Park Stables.
[ ‘It’s a dying trade’: Dublin’s horse-drawn carriage drivers stage protest Opens in new window ]
“I’ve invested not only my life’s savings, but my life, into this business. I own two horse-drawn carriages, and part of the stable, and I also manage the stable where we keep the horses,” he said.
“This is what I’ve put my time and effort into, and I’ve worked hard for it. If you’d told me on the day I arrived in the US that one day everything I own would be taken off me on trumped-up charges, I’d have told you that could never happen, yet here we are.
“They’re not only taking away what I own, but what everybody in the business owns.”
His friend Thomas Quinn, a native of Co Sligo who has worked with horses in New York City for 31 years, said operators were being unfairly blamed for wider public safety concerns.
“We’re being thrown under the bus, really. It was incredibly unfortunate that a child was injured and killed, it really was, and we are so sorry for the family,” he said.
He argued that the horse and carriage operators were being used “as a scapegoat”.
Quinn pointed to recent fatalities involving scooters and bicycles, arguing that the carriage industry was being singled out for accidents that could occur in other forms of transport.
“If this does all go through now, what does the future hold? I’m 58 years old. I mean, what do you do at 58 when your livelihood is gone?” he said.
The bill now goes to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani , who has 30 days to act, but is expected to support it into law.

title: Hurling’s new rules were trialled last night. How did it go?
description: A clampdown on fouled handpasses was the biggest feature of the MTU-UCC game in treacherous conditions on Thursday night
content:
Rain comes in a variety of bright colours now, but the type that lashed the hurlers of MTU and UCC on Thursday evening was old-fashioned black. Their match in Division One of the Higher Education League was the latest vessel for hurling ’s new rules and, in the circumstances, it was remarkably free of incidents or accidents.
It is much too soon to make firm judgments, but opinion never pauses for breath. There was groaning in the stand as referee Simon Stokes repeatedly and correctly penalised fouled handpasses. But if reform of the handpass is going to be achieved, there is bound to be a spate of on-the-spot fines. Hurlers have been parking on double yellow lines with impunity for far too long.
MTU were penalised eight times in the first half for making a handpass without a clear striking action, but their best player, the Cork senior Barry Walsh, made a visible effort to abide by the new directive: every time he handpassed the ball, there was murky daylight between his hand and the sliotar.
Only one free was awarded for consecutive hand passes, which was a remarkably quick adjustment by the players. But in any other era of the game, nobody would have even considered short passing in these conditions. One of the UCC mentors eventually implored one of his half backs to “get rid of it”, but modern players are not wired that way. One short pass usually starts a sequence.
There was one incident near the sideline in the first half where the consecutive-hand -pass rule had an unintended consequence. The UCC corner forward Darragh Verling controlled a poor hand pass with a sublime piece of skill that was instantly acknowledged by the crowd.
But he was near the sideline and closely marked. Another UCC player made a support run that was crying out for a quick hand pass but in abiding by the rules Verling tried to make a stick pass instead. With not enough room to make an unimpeded swing, he was hooked and the ball went to ground. If hard cases make bad law, here was your example.
It has been suggested the experimental rules will lead to fewer rucks, partly on the grounds that six steps will give players more latitude to get away from contact. There is also a hope that the new rules will lead to more long striking, which would in turn stretch the play. The jury is out on both of those assertions. The MTU-UCC game was full of rucks, which is what you would have expected in the conditions: balls were being miscontrolled and mishandled and spilling loose. On a couple of occasions players struck the ball and the hurley flew out of their hands, like a javelin.
Under the trial rules, every puckout must pass the 45m line, with three forwards and three defenders standing between the 20m line and the 45. What it meant here was that every puckout was driven into the other half of the field and was contested beyond the other 65m line.
At this time of the year, third-level teams spend very little time training together and it is unlikely any of the college teams will come up with a funky way of winning a puckout inside their own half. But if this rule comes into force, the elite teams and the finest coaching brains are bound to devise ways of managing their own puckouts without driving the ball 100m into an uncertain future.
The 15 Higher Education League games being monitored and tagged by the Hurling Expert Advisory Group (HEAG) over the next couple of weeks are unlikely to provide satisfactory feedback on this rule.
The HEAG clearly wants the ball to go long from restarts to create more contests for possession, but the elite teams, at club and intercounty level, will baulk at that. It is easy to imagine more puckouts driven towards a moving target, 50m or 60m away – which clearly carries more risk but might not result in a contest.
Under the experimental rules 65s are to be taken from the farthest 65: only one was awarded and it was missed. But the first two-point sideline cut was recorded – given that none was scored in Belfield on Tuesday night and the other games on Thursday evening had later throw-ins.
Mikey Finn played an extraordinary shot to score from outside the 45m line, in front of the stand. For a right-hand hurler it would have been easier to score from the other wing, but it was such a pure strike that the ball hardly deviated in the air.
It came at a time in the game, midway through the second half, when MTU were six points down and struggling to stay in the hunt. But the two-pointer gave them an injection of energy, just as it routinely does in Gaelic football now. This experimental rule might have a life.

title: The crumbling Galway school that typifies Ireland’s underspending on education
description: Irish education results are remarkable against a backdrop of low State investment by international standards
content:
“I ’m shaving and shaving all the time, and that’s not right. I’m not in this job to be a barber, yet that’s what I’m doing every single day.”
Claire Mac Loughlin is principal of Coláiste Muire Máthair in Galway city, a secondary school of more than 800 students on St Mary’s Road.
The main building, which stands on an elevated site overlooking Galway Bay, was designed by architect William Alphonsus Scott and opened in 1912.
Since then, it has been through many iterations, its most recent being an amalgamation between Our Lady’s College and St Mary’s College.
That amalgamation means it only receives part- Deis status, despite a rising level of disadvantage among its student population.
The school has therefore had to take a loaves-and-fishes approach to keep the doors open and ensure all students are treated the same regardless of their socioeconomic background.
“We have students here whose parents are very well off, and then we have people who are living on the absolute bare minimum,” Mac Loughlin says.
The school uses any money it has to level the playing field for its students. They only get the hot school meals scheme for 250 children, but rather than treat some differently, they reduce the price of food for everyone.
Under the new senior cycle curriculum, students require laptops for some subjects to complete their additional assessment components (AACs). Rather than put families under pressure to buy their own, the school has bought a number of laptops to be shared among everyone. As a consequence, staff do not get a work laptop.
However, as their 100-year-old building begins to crumble around them and the boundary of their financial ingenuity is pushed too far, it begs the question: are we investing enough in our education system?
Coláiste Muire Máthair is a prime example of how so many educational institutions across the country have had to work with relatively little funding while still producing world-class outcomes for the children who attend.
Ireland spends the least on its education system across all OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) countries, yet it continually ranks among the top in the world for educational outcomes.
The latest report of the Pisa (Programme for International Student Assessment) rankings, run by the OECD, found Irish students are first for reading, third for science and fourth for maths out of 27 EU countries.
Such results are even more remarkable given they come against a backdrop of very low State investment by international standards.
[ Leaving Cert students: What you need to focus on at college open days Opens in new window ]
From primary to tertiary education, Ireland spends the least on education as a percentage of its gross domestic product (GDP) compared with all other OECD countries.
Nowhere is this more apparent than at Coláiste Muire Mhaithair, where the roof is literally caving in.
The entire top floor of the building is closed off to students and is being held up with scaffolding.
There are several “crash decks” installed around high-traffic areas on lower floors, and windows are cordoned off in some rooms because the water ingress is so bad it can lead to falling debris.
“That fell down from the ceiling just the other week,” Mac Loughlin says, holding up a tray of concrete shards, some bigger than an A5 notepad, and pieces of steel rebar which would have been used to keep the ceiling together.
[ ‘My son is in sixth year and has no idea what he wants to study’ Opens in new window ]
Squeezing past the scaffolding occupying the staircase leading to the top floor, it is hard to imagine students still using this space until last year.
“Children’s dignity has to be at the core of how we operate. We can’t have the kids in dirty, mouldy spaces,” Mac Loughlin says.
The windows have to stay open to address the dampness in the walls, which means the plaster falls off in chunks.
The school has applied to the Department of Education to have remedial works carried out and is waiting for approval.
A department spokesperson said on Thursday it was actively engaging with the school. It said scaffolding works had been completed, with further remedial works “expected to commence in the coming weeks”.
Separately, the department said, a major building project for the school was progressing and department officials would be in contact with the project manager and the school to schedule a stakeholders meeting.
In the meantime, the principal relies on caretaker Frank Nee, who she says “keeps the wolf from the door”, but also her deputy principal and all of the teaching and administrative staff, as well as the board of management.
“I have a team here that keeps us going through their skills, through their determination. They keep the doors open, and they keep the ceilings up, literally.”
The sharing of laptops between classes also creates its own difficulties, logistically and technically.
[ Inside Ireland’s only boarding school offering the Leaving Cert and International Baccalaureate Opens in new window ]
There are 24 laptops on a trolley, which must be booked by teachers and rolled between classes.
Students must sign in to each machine every time they use them, find somewhere to charge them and, sometimes, share with a classmate when there are not enough to go around.
While this might be fine for lower classes, it can create real disadvantages for senior cycle students who only get a set amount of time in the year to complete their AACs and are competing with others across the country with far better access to tech.
“People are losing time because they don’t have a laptop, or they’ve had to go across the school trying to find laptops,” sixth-year student Alvin Ngani says of the time drain the sharing creates.
