Blanka Klanowska, also a sixth-year student at the school, agrees the practical implications of sharing laptops have real-life consequences.
“If you’re using the laptops two or three times a day in different classes, you have to log in each time, which can take up to 10 minutes each class. That adds up to maybe half an hour overall, which is time wasted and can cause you to fall behind,” Klanowska says.
On a broader point, students believe the increased time looking at screens is a further difficulty of the curriculum reform.
“I feel like we’re going to get overwhelmed by looking at the screen so much. We work on the laptops in school, we might have to work on them at home and then, of course, we’ll also want to have time on our phones as well,” Klanowska says.
“I feel like it’s going to be too much for our eyes, and it might bring us down a good bit, and I feel like we’ll lose a lot of motivation.”
While the sharing arrangements are not ideal, and the efficacy of the new AACs remains up for debate, one thing that is certain is the teachers and leaders of this school are doing all they can to level the playing field.
[ Open days: Key details for NCI, NCAD, technological universities and other institutions Opens in new window ]
Standing at the window of the abandoned top-floor room, with dead birds at her feet and plaster in piles on the ground, Mac Loughlin is clear on her vision and that of the school.
“This school is a jewel in the crown of Galway, and we must do everything we can to look after children as far as the eye can see out there,” she says.
“Yet here we are standing in a space that’s not safe. It’s not right. It’s not respectful of our children; it’s not respectful of our community.
“It’s not true to what our mission is, and the mission is the work to care for the children.”

title: ‘When they get going, they’re hard to stop’: Ulster chase opening URC win against Bulls
description: Richie Murphy’s side need to find heroic effort to weather power surge in Pretoria
content:
Though it has been a decent week for Ulster after banking a first win of the season, against Zebre in Europe, and then having nine players included in the Ireland squad, the province will need to channel all that feelgood factor and more for what comes now.
The Bulls at Loftus Versfeld would hardly be the place many would choose when still seeking an opening URC victory following a defeat and back-to-back draws, but this is what Ulster now have in front of them, with the Stormers to follow in Cape Town next weekend.
With the Bulls, Richie Murphy ’s side must also contend with Pretoria’s altitude and heat; the early afternoon temperature is expected to be in the region of 30 degrees come kick-off.
Although Cormac Izuchukwu has missed out on being part of Andy Farrell’s plans for next month, he is part of a strong looking Ulster selection which has eight of the province’s Ireland call-ups in the match-day squad.
“I think as a forward, you really can’t afford to get it wrong over there,” said Izuchukwu, who has been selected at lock.
Continuing the theme of having to face a power surge up front from their hosts, he added: “Just with how they play the game and how they approach it.
“Especially on the set piece, they’re going to be looking to use that as a weapon to break us.
“Whenever you have the ball or you’re on top, you have to keep the foot down because whenever they get going, they’re really hard to stop.”
Ulster know that the Bulls, with former Ulster player Marcell Coetzee back as skipper as part of a rotated pack, will come at them with their heavy artillery up front; the plan being to eviscerate the visitors’ hardly rugged scrum and shred them defensively.
Surviving and putting up a robust resistance at the scrum, lineout and breakdown will be essential if Ulster are to avoid being put through the mincer.
[ ‘There could be carnage in Dublin’: Ian Madigan and Alan Quinlan on Leinster v Munster Opens in new window ]
All bar Robert Baloucoune of their Ireland contingent get to lock horns against the Bulls, with Jamie Benson at centre alongside Stuart McCloskey and other notable national squad call-up James McNabney awaiting introduction from the bench.
While Ulster will want to move the Bulls around, they require heroic work in the trenches for this to happen and another standout effort from Juarno Augustus, who was a pivotal figure against Zebre, will be central to their hopes.
Nick Timoney, Tom O’Toole and the ever-consistent David McCann need to also set the tone and Ulster’s bench has some presence about in McNabney, Eli Snyman, James McKillop and Scott Wilson. The Bulls, though, clearly trump any of this, having Marco van Staden, Cobus Wiese and Cameron Hanekom included as their impact players.
[ New London Irish owners aim to return club to English rugby’s second tier Opens in new window ]
Should things turn out badly, Ulster have a week to regroup, though seemingly without their Ireland contingent, before another troublesome looking mission awaits them at the Stormers.
BULLS: L Giliomee; S de Klerk, S Xamlashe, H Vorster, C Jooste; H Pollard, P de Wet; G Steenekamp, J Grobbelaar, F Klopper; R Vermaak, R Ludwig; M Coetzee (capt), H Liebenberg, E Louw.
Replacements: M van Staden, A Tshakweni, K Mchunu, C Wiese, C Hanekom, Z Burger, C Bosch, D Maart.
ULSTER: J Stockdale; C Mullins, J Benson, S McCloskey, M Lowry; J Murphy, N Doak; T O’Toole, T Stewart (capt), K Knox; B Donnell, C Izuchukwu; D McCann, N Timoney, J Augustus.
Replacements: H Walker, E O’Sullivan, S Wilson, E Snyman, J McNabney, M Devine, J Flannery, J McKillop.

title: New London Irish owners aim to return club to English rugby’s second tier
description: Consortium involving Kyle Jordan sell club after goal of entering club in URC were knocked back
content:
A consortium involving Kyle Jordan, son of the late Formula One team owner Eddie Jordan, has sold London Irish.
The club has not played professional rugby since entering administration in 2023.
The Jordan consortium had explored bringing Irish into the United Rugby Championship, with a hope to appeal to Irish and South African expats living in London, but found that path blocked by a number of national unions.
It is understood that the new owners, Steve and Sarah Daniels of Gamechanger Investments Limited, are hoping to return Irish to the Champ, English rugby’s second tier, next season. They are also assessing the viability of entering a team into Premiership Women’s Rugby (PWR).
The move ends the formal involvement of the Jordan family in London Irish. Daniel McKeown, the Dublin-born chair of the club, is also moving on. Jamie Balls, the current chair of the London Irish amateur club, will become chief executive of the pro outfit.
“We explored every credible route back, including beyond the English game, and concluded that London Irish is better served playing and building now than waiting on a path that is not viable at this time,” said McKeown.
“Steve, Sarah and Jamie have the ambition and commitment to do exactly that and we are proud to hand this great club on to them.”
“Our focus is on creating a resilient, self-sustaining rugby organisation that can stand on its own feet from day one, with the foundations in place to deliver long-term stability, growth and future opportunities,” said Balls, the new CEO.
“The immediate priority is to establish the infrastructure needed for the relaunch, including a dedicated communications and media operation and full access to the club’s digital assets. Details of the proposed home ground, competition pathway and wider plans will follow.”
London Irish last played in professional rugby in 2023, their final game bringing a win over Exeter Chiefs at the end of that year’s Premiership campaign. At that stage, they played their games at the home of Premier League football outfit Brentford.
They became the third English team to fold in quick succession after Worcester and Wasps had collapsed earlier that season. The club was suspended by the Premiership after missing a deadline to pay players and staff amid financial difficulties and an attempted takeover by a US-based consortium.
Worcester have since rejoined the English rugby pyramid, finishing fourth on the Champ table last season. They went on to beat Ealing in the playoff final.
Founded in 1898, London Irish was formed after the likes of London Scottish and London Welsh gave expats the chance to play rugby with fellow Irish people in the English capital.
A number of prominent Irish players have been involved in the club, including internationals David Humphreys, Conor O’Shea and Bob Casey. Declan Kidney, the former Ireland head coach, was the club’s director of rugby when ownership’s financial difficulties forced its suspension.

title: Meghan Markle ‘deeply distressed’ over allegation her father had child abuse images
description: Meghan’s brother alleges he found a stash of images belonging to her father
content:
Meghan Markle has said she is “deeply distressed” by accusations her father had a hoard of child sex abuse images.
Meghan’s brother, Thomas Markle jnr, alleged that he had found a stash of images belonging to her father, Thomas Markle snr, at his former home in the Philippines, The Sun reported.
In an interview with the Daily Mail, Thomas snr denied possessing child sex abuse images, calling the accusations “sick lies”.
Meghan said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.
“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me.
“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.
“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them.
“I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.
“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.” – PA

title: Asian backing boosts Gianni Infantino’s hopes of fourth term as Fifa president
description: After criticising Infantino during the summer, the confederation is now supporting his election bid
content:
Gianni Infantino’s prospects of securing a fourth term as Fifa president have been given a significant boost after the Asian Football Confederation officially offered its backing on Friday.
Infantino has been under pressure since it emerged on July 28th that he had sidelined the Fifa Council and national associations over a plan to sell stakes in a company to run the World Cup and other tournaments to private investors.
On August 10th, AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa co-signed a letter along with his counterparts at two other continental confederations – Europe and Concacaf, made up of North and Central American nations plus the Caribbean – which was heavily critical of the plan.
At that time Sheikh Salman is believed to have supported the idea of Infantino resigning and leaving with dignity.
However, Infantino has since consolidated his base, winning unanimous support in Africa and having already secured backing from key Asian nations including Qatar and Saudi Arabia. He also counts on significant support in South America and Oceania.
Now Sheikh Salman has confirmed Infantino has the backing of the confederation at its Congress in Bangkok.
“Our greatest strength lies in our unity, and we have all seen the historic heights Asian football can achieve when we stand together,” Sheikh Salman told the Congress in quotes reported on the AFC website.
“The Asian game’s remarkable journey and historic achievements are deeply rooted in the strong partnership, trust, and shared vision that we share as one united family.
“As we look toward a brighter and more competitive future, our solidarity remains our greatest strength. We are ready to move forward, united in support of Fifa president Gianni Infantino.”
Opposition to Infantino is now largely centred in Europe. Uefa said in August it had lost confidence in Infantino over the private investor plan and has pledged to identify a credible alternative candidate to stand against him in the election in Morocco next March.
The deadline for candidates to be submitted is November 18th.
Earlier this week, Uefa wrote to Fifa seeking answers to a series of questions linked to Infantino’s leadership, including the private investor plan but also his handling of the Folarin Balogun case, the World Cup final half-time show and hydration breaks at those finals.

title: PTSB says Axis bid interest ‘highly speculative’ as it sticks to Bawag deal timeline
description: Axis Capital is a corporate advisory firm cofounded by former banker Mark Duffy
content:
PTSB said the 11th-hour bid interest from Axis Capital was “highly speculative and conditional”, as the bank confirmed on Friday that a High Court sanctioning hearing on its planned €1.62 billion takeover by Austria’s Bawag would proceed on Tuesday morning as planned.
The 57.5 per cent State-owned bank noted that four shareholders, known to include long-term dissenting investor Scotchstone Capital, led by Piotr Skoczylas, had indicated they planned to object to the sanctioning of the deal, being carried out as a so-called scheme of arrangement that requires court approval.
“These shareholders have, over a prolonged period, pursued a number of unsuccessful legal proceedings” since the State effectively nationalised the bank in 2011, PTSB said in a statement.
“The court hearing is expected to take place over a number of days. The timing of the judgment, following the satisfaction of scheme conditions and the conclusion of the application for sanction of the scheme, will be a matter for the High Court,” it said.
The statement comes a day after Axis Capital, a corporate advisory firm cofounded by former banker Mark Duffy, said it would ask the High Court next week to delay ratifying PTSB’s takeover by Bawag by up to six weeks as it sought to put together a potential offer for the bank.
[ Mark Duffy’s Axis to ask court to delay ratifying Bawag’s PTSB takeover Opens in new window ]
The company said investment bank Keefe, Bruyette & Woods (KBW) had introduced it to a “large global investment manager”, which was weighing acting as lead investor in the financing of a potential bid.
“The possible funder is evaluating acting as lead anchor investor in the financing of a possible offer, with the balance of the capital to be syndicated to its limited partners and other co-investors,” Axis said.
KBW has not been engaged by either side. Axis is advised by Berlin-based Quirin Privatbank. Duffy was the chief executive of the now-defunct Bank of Scotland (Ireland) , which was closed after the 2008 crash.
“The possible funder has indicated that completing its confirmatory due diligence is essential before it can syndicate the balance of the capital to its partners and provide a formal letter of support,” Axis added.
PTSB confirmed in its statement on Friday that no offer had been made by Axis. The bank “is firmly of the view that this latest announcement remains highly speculative and conditional and that no new information has been provided by Axis or its advisers that has changed that position”, it said.
The bank’s board “remains focused on delivering value and certainty to the company’s shareholders and, in accordance with its legal obligations, is continuing to work with Bawag” on completing the planned deal.
Scotchstone also signalled on October 9th that it was considering making an offer for PTSB, but has yet to say whether it has lined up necessary funding.
The chief executive of Bawag said earlier this week the Austrian banking group was “rising above the noise” as it awaited High Court approval of its takeover of PTSB later this month.

title: Three arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after man stabbed near Belfast
description: Incident happed in Doagh just after 11pm on Thursday
content:
Three men have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after a man suffered multiple stab wounds near Belfast .
Emergency services were called to the Templepatrick Road area of Doagh, Co Antrim, just after 11pm on Thursday amid reports of an assault.
The Police Service of Northern Ireland said officers arrested three men, two aged in their 30s and one in his 40s, who remain in custody.
Paramedics attended the scene and the man was taken to hospital for treatment.
Police have appealed to anyone who witnessed the incident or has information to come forward.

title: Lidl has moved into the Irish mobile phone market. Can it save you money?
description: Lidl Connect is much cheaper than what Irish mobile phone users on long-term contracts are paying
content:
Earlier this month Lidl created quite a stir when it announced it had started selling something somewhat unexpected – and not just the jack hammers, blow torches and inflatable swimming pools that we have grown accustomed to finding in the middle aisles.
The new unexpected thing that Lidl started selling was mobile phones – or at least access to the Irish mobile phone network.
The first 100,000 people who signed up to Lidl Connect were promised a monthly charge of €8.99 for life. They were given the option of picking up a physical SIM in any Lidl store for an additional €0.99 or selecting an eSIM and completing their registration via the Lidl Plus app at no extra cost.
The monthly rolling plans require no long-term commitment and include unlimited 5G data; unlimited calls and texts to any Irish and UK network; 50GB of EU and UK roaming data and 100 international minutes per month to more than 38 countries.
People who decided to migrate to Lidl Connect were told they could keep their existing mobile numbers or choose a new one if they were so inclined.
But bells and whistles and portability aside, it was the price tag that got Lidl the most attention, although we should point out that its offering is not all that much cheaper than Tesco’s SIM-only deal, which costs a tenner a month.
Lidl Connect is, however, much cheaper than what many Irish mobile phone users who are on long-term contracts are accustomed to paying.
A typical bill pay customer might be paying €50 a month – a price that might include a free handset every couple of years. Or might not.
Leaving aside the handset for a moment, a 20-year-old who chooses the €8.99 a month deal at Lidl and lives for the next 70 years and never leaves the German discounter will end up paying a total of €7,551.60 over the course of their – hopefully – long and happy life.
Were this notional 20-year-old to instead sign up to a monthly bill pay deal with one of the State’s leading operators and live for the same 70 years without ever switching, the total cost of their mobile phone will come in at €42,000 in today’s money.
Now we know we are making a lot of assumptions here, not least that we will still be using money, mobile phones or indeed Lidl 70 years from now.
But you get the idea. SIM-only, pay-as-you-go deals are much cheaper than the alternative.
But despite the savings to be made, a great many people ignore them. Sometimes, they don’t even know the savings are on the table.
The way the system works sometimes actively works against us. Mobile phone contracts often include a new phone as part of the initial deal and they last for two years. A significant chunk of the monthly tariff over those two years is used to pay for the “free” handset that was given out at the outset.
But under the terms and conditions of almost all bill pay contracts, once the two years is up, you own the handset outright so obviously the monthly cost should fall.
After the first two years are up, a mobile provider can offer you a new phone in return for a new contract.
But if you’re happy with your current handset or don’t get the offer or contact your provider to arrange a better deal – the company will keep charging the original monthly fee.
Actually, they might even charge more because, over the two years, as a bill pay customer you will most likely have been hit with two automatically-imposed price hikes. Virgin Mobile is an exception to this rule.
So, if you sign up to a two-year contract with a monthly payment of €50 and continue to pay in full after the contract ends, you’re giving the company at least €40 a month for absolutely nothing. That is €480 a year.
According to admittedly self-interested research published by Sky Mobile to coincide with its arrival in the Irish mobile market a couple of years ago, about 300,000 people in Ireland are overpaying each year.
If they all overpay by €40 a month, then Ireland is collectively wasting close to €150 million every single year.
Under ComReg rules, the mobile phone providers “must make you aware that your contract is coming to an end and that you may cancel your current plan”.
“Your provider should also send you ‘best tariff advice’ highlighting the best tariff, price plan or bundle from your current service provider that suits your needs.”
No doubt that is done but if it is to make any difference you have to actually read the correspondence you are sent and we all know that is a big ask.
In a moderately ideal world, the price of your phone contract would automatically drop after two years to reflect what you are actually paying for, rather than what you were paying for at the start.
But our world is a long way from ideal, which is why you need to look after yourself.
If you own a phone outright the cheapest thing to do is to hang on to it and request your current provider to unlock the device, allowing you to switch to a SIM-only plan with another provider, or with the likes of Lidl.
The switching process is not overly complicated, although it is not always free of complications, and you obviously get to hang on to your existing number.
As well as Lidl and Tesco Mobile there is also the likes of Sky Mobile, Clear Mobile and GoMo, all of which piggyback on the main providers’ networks, so the level of coverage should be comparable.
A lot of higher-priced contracts are sold with the promise of huge amounts of data. But most users rarely exceed the standard amounts on the table, particularly if they are good at connecting to free wifi when out and about.
Another easy money-saving measure is a good haggle. Before your contract is due to end work out what the alternatives are and then demand better value. If you are getting nowhere with the person you are speaking to, ask to talk to someone in their retention unit; they might be more receptive to your threats to leave.
No matter who you are with or how much you are paying, do pay attention to roaming charges. Thankfully – because of our friends in Brussels – roaming charges are not the same money-grabbing gouging curse they once were (at least when you are using your phone across the EU) but if you are outside of the EU – or taking a ferry from Ireland to France, for instance – you could still be hit with a savagely high bill if you roam like you’re at home.
And do consider insurance. It can cost over €10 a month but if you are prone to breaking or losing your phone, it can be money well spent. Before you sign up, check if the contents insurance you have for your home covers personal possessions, as that might give you a safety net of sorts. If you do have specific mobile phone insurance and do change your handset, don’t assume the old policy will cover the new phone. It might not and that could see you paying for insurance on a phone you no longer have.
And if you are going SIM-only, consider buying second hand. There are a lot of platforms offering refurbished handsets for a whole lot less than they cost new, and even Apple sells refurbished phones. Just make sure you check the terms and conditions and make sure you have a degree of protection should things go wrong.
You can contact us at OnTheMoney@irishtimes.com with personal finance questions you would like to see us address. If you missed last week’s newsletter, you can read it here .

title: Eason celebrates 140th anniversary
description: Books newsletter: a preview of tomorrow’s pages and wrap of the latest news
content:
Eason, Ireland’s leading book retailer, is marking 140 years in business as a constant presence at the heart of Irish culture and education.
To mark the milestone, Eason has launched Our Story in Books, a curated collection spotlighting the literary, social, and cultural movements that have shaped modern Ireland throughout the company’s 140-year history. The collection spans iconic works from W.B. Yeats, Oscar Wilde, and James Joyce through to contemporary voices including Roddy Doyle, Sally Rooney, and Maeve Binchy. The curated collection is available to view online here .
Readers can explore the defining chapters of Eason’s own history here.
Founded in 1886 and still Irish-owned, Eason has been part of Irish life and society across generations. It briefly employed a young Seán O’Casey, who was sacked after refusing to remove his cap to collect his wages. Eason traded through the 1913 Dublin Lockout, was destroyed by fire during the 1916 Easter Rising and rebuilt to serve readers through the struggle for independence and the birth of the new State.
As Ireland modernised, Eason championed generations of Irish writers, and saw queues down the street for midnight launches such as Harry Potter. The flagship O’Connell Street store has only locked its doors for three high-security signings: Bill Clinton, Tony Blair and U2.
“Reaching 140 years in business is an incredible milestone, reflecting the special, lasting connection Eason shares with communities across Ireland,” Lisa O’Brien, group head of ecommerce and marketing, said. “While the ways people browse, read, and shop have transformed since our founding in 1886, our core purpose of fostering a lifelong love of reading and championing Irish voices remains unchanged.”
“This anniversary is an opportunity to express our gratitude to our dedicated teams, the brilliant Irish writers and publishers who inspire us, and the generations of loyal customers who have made Eason a beloved part of their lives. We are proud to honour our heritage while looking forward to the next chapter.”
In The Irish Times tomorrow, Sarah Moss writes about setting her first book entirely in Ireland, her adopted homeland, and what it means to be an immigrant writer. Yiyun Li talks to Niamh Donnelly about her new novel, Music Against the Night, reimagining the life of Dublin composer John Field, and coping with the loss of two sons to suicide. Tim Hannigan, author of The Pathless Land: Finding A Way Across Ireland, discusses the lack of public access for walkers. And there is a Q&A with Emma Heatherington, author of Together for Christmas and a new country & Irish musical.
Reviews are Christopher Kissane on A Letter Home by Kerby A Miller and Breandán Mac Suibhnel Donald Clarke on The Queerest of Folk by Russell T Davies and Out Now by Scott Bryan; Eamon Sweeney on Edged in Blue: A Rock & Roll Odyssey with Rory Gallagher by Dónal Gallagher; Claire Hennessy on the best new YA fiction; Kevin Gildea on Gift Grub & Me by Mario Rosenstock; Henrietta McKervey on Music Against the Night by Yiyun Li; Phoebe Pascoe on Taipei Story by Rebecca F Kuang; John Quin on Dodge City by Patrick deWitt; Enda O’Doherty on The Real Nigel Farage: A Would-Be Prime Minister On Trial by John Sweeney; Céire Sadlier on In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak; Roe McDermott on Guilty Pleasure: The Pornification of the Internet, the Economy, and Everything Else by Patricia Nilsson; and Daniel Geary on Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State by Michael Lewis.
Leaves Festival of Writing and Music returns to Laois from November 5th to 7th, bringing three full days of talks, workshops and performances to venues throughout the county, including bestselling Aisling series authors Emer McLysaght and Sarah Breen in conversation.
Laois’s One County One Book is The Boy from the Sea and author Garrett Carr will take part in a number of events, including a conversation with debut novelist Neil Tully, author of The Visit .
Other events include Dermot Bolger in conversation with Carlo Gébler and a special evening marking Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the European Union will be celebrated in the company of Nina George alongside Hugo Hamilton.
Musical artist and singer Méav comes to Leaves with her blend of traditional Irish, classical, and folk songs. For rock music fans, Dónal Gallagher will discuss his new biography of his brother Rory with Ann Marie Kelly.
As always, home-grown Laois talent is showcased with Portlaoise-born novelist Helen Cullen and renowned harpist Tríona Marshall.
The Nine Dot Prize, a global problem-solving competition, has just launched its new question for its 10 th anniversary. Every two years it sets a question of worldwide importance, awarding $100,000 and a book deal for the best and most original response.
For its 2026/27 edition, the prize jury asks: “Who gains from saving nature?” The prize is looking for responses of true originality, regardless of the individuals previous experience and writing. Submissions must be 3,000 words and should be accompanied by an outline detailing how the entrant would expand their argument into a short book of between 25,000–40,000 words, supported by independent research.
The winner will receive $100,000 and a book contract and editorial support from Cambridge University Press, as well as the opportunity to spend a term at the Centre for Research in the Arts, Social Sciences and Humanities at Cambridge University.
The Nero Book Awards have announced the shortlist for this year’s Nero New Writers Prize in association with Brunel University of London. Stories by five authors, two with a strong Irish connection, were chosen by a panel chaired by Paul Murray, 2023 Nero Gold Prize winner for The Bee Sting, Booker Prize winner and Professor of Creative Writing at Brunel, Bernardine Evaristo, and Irish writer Helen Cullen, Reader in Creative Writing at Brunel.
Launched last year to run alongside the prestigious and highly successful Nero Book Awards, the Nero New Writers Prize in association with Brunel University of London seeks to discover the writing stars of the future and support their development.
Donagh O’Malley was shortlisted for Holding On. A successful artist living in New York visits his parents in Ireland for what may be the last time, following an HIV diagnosis. Without a cure in sight, will his parents rise to care for their ailing son, or yield to stigma?
The judges said: “This is a sensitive and soulful story that exhibits great restraint and control of its form. It offers a poignant lens through which to consider the impact of the HIV crisis.”
O’Malley is a Dublin-based writer with a background in music licensing. After living in New York and London, he returned to Ireland, where he is raising his young son.
Harriet Bradley was shortlisted for Conamar, in which a nurse in England returns to the west of Ireland with her siblings to bury their mother. Old tensions resurface as ghosts from the past – real and imagined – linger. The judges described Bradley’s story as ‘emotionally impactive’ and ‘suspenseful’. Bradley, whose grandmother is from Limerick, is working on a novel-in-stories following three generations of an Anglo-Irish family across continents.
Also shortlisted were Saadiya Chaudary Alam, Eleanor James and Tom Milner.
Each author will receive £1,000 and go on to compete to win the Nero New Writers Prize, which will be announced at a ceremony at Brunel on November 18th. The winner will receive £3,000, a scholarship to study for an MA in Creative Writing at Brunel and an introductory meeting with a literary agent.
The 2027 Women’s Prize for Fiction, the largest celebration of women’s creativity in the world, will be chaired by Merve Emre, scholar, critic, editor and professor, joined by Eimear McBride, novelist and writer; Charlotte Collins, Editor-in-Chief of SheerLuxe, broadcaster and podcast host; Esther Freud, novelist and playwright; Theresa Lola, poet, writer and artist.
The 2027 Women’s Prize for Non-Fiction will be chaired by Susie Dent, lexicographer, writer and broadcaster, joined by Shrabani Basu, historian, biographer, and journalist; Reeta Chakrabarti, journalist, broadcaster and novelist; Sophie Morgan, writer, broadcaster, artist and disability advocate, and Emma Reed Turrell; psychotherapist, author, podcaster and speaker.
Dublin City Council’s Ballymun Library has marked its 50th anniversary with a community celebration hosted by the Lord Mayor of Dublin, Daryl Barron. Officially opened by then lord mayor, Jim Mitchell, on October 13th, 1976, the library was at the time the largest and best-equipped library in the city, with an opening stock of 35,000 books.
It was the third branch library built by Dublin Corporation in the 1970s, after Dolphin’s Barn and Raheny, and today serves Ballymun, Glasnevin, Santry, Whitehall and the surrounding areas. Built by Kenneally and O’Keeffe contractors at a cost of £150,000, the distinctive cruciform building was designed by Dublin Corporation Architects in the Civic Amenities Department.
The library has its own place in Dublin’s cultural history. Its visitors have included President Patrick Hillery and Roddy Doyle, and the writers Patricia Scanlan and Pádraig Kenny both worked there.
Brendan Teeling, Acting City Librarian, said, “Ballymun Library opened in 1976 with a clear idea of what a modern public library could offer its community, and it has never stood still. People still come here for books, and they also come to study, get online, borrow a laptop, play games or take part in one of the hundreds of events held here every year. The library has changed with Ballymun, and Dublin City Council will keep investing in it so that it continues to meet the needs of the people it serves.”

title: Global crude oil prices surge to highest level since May amid Middle East attacks
description: US escalation with Iran threatens higher-for-longer energy prices
content:
Global crude oil prices are set for a third weekly gain on Friday as intensifying attacks on Saudi Arabia raise the risk of wider Middle East supply disruptions.
Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, traded around $114 (€100.72) a barrel, up almost 4 per cent this week, while West Texas Intermediate, the US benchmark, was above $100. Iran-backed Houthi militants claimed recent attacks on the Saudi Red Sea port of Yanbu, as well as deadly strikes on an oilfield and airport in the kingdom.
The flare-up threatens to widen hostilities around the Strait of Hormuz, where crude exports have recovered to near pre-war levels. Brent is up more than 85 per cent this year because of the US-Iran war, now approaching its ninth month, while refined-product prices have risen even faster, most notably diesel.
Higher oil prices dragged on European shares on Friday. The pan-European Stoxx 600 index was ⁠down 0.13 per cent in early trading, ‌after ‌logging ​its biggest one-day drop in three weeks on Thursday and putting ⁠the index on ​course for a weekly decline.
At the White House on Thursday, US president Donald Trump told reporters that the US has “knocked” out Iran and threatened to go “a little bit further”, without elaborating. The New York Times reported this week that the US and Israel have developed plans for renewed strikes against the Islamic Republic after the American midterm elections early next month.
“The latest geopolitical escalations are pointing to a more intensified strike on Iran, which is pushing crude higher throughout the price curve,” said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president for trading at BOK Financial Securities. Most traders expect oil prices to be higher for longer, he said.
The Yemen-based Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi Arabia in recent months. State-owned Aramco evacuated its Dhahran headquarters on Thursday and asked staff to work from home after an alarm, according to people familiar with the matter. The reason for the alarm was not immediately known.
While crude flows from the Gulf have recovered, oil-product shipments from the region remain constrained. That squeeze, along with intensifying Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, has prompted governments to tap stockpiles. Trump is also pushing measures to lower prices in advance of the midterm elections, including a diesel deal with Moscow.
Russia, meanwhile, is seeing some relief in its domestic fuel market, with gasoline and diesel production rising, Interfax reported, citing the government. Fuel inventories are also being replenished, it said. – Bloomberg, Reuters

title: Ireland squad selection sets scene nicely for Leinster v Munster
description: Gavin Cummiskey talks to Shamrock Rovers captain Pico Lopes; Gavin Cooney imagines the future for Manchester United
content:
When Andy Farrell named his squad earlier in the week for the Nations Championship, it was hardly a surprise that Leinster had, by a country mile, the highest representation. But 17 players to Munster’s two ? Former Irish international Alan Quinlan reckons that will have come as a shock to Clayton McMillan’s crew, so, he tells Michael Scully, “if they roll up their sleeves” when they meet Leinster tomorrow at the Aviva Stadium, “there could be carnage”.
Judging by the length of their injury list, Leinster have experienced a bit of carnage already, Sam Prendergast and Garry Ringrose joining it this week with wrist and hamstring issues. Leo Cullen has, then, had to do some tweaking, which includes starting captain Dan Sheehan at number eight . Daire Walsh hears from the head coach.
Connacht’s chief ambition when they host Zebre this evening will be to maintain the standards they set against Saracens in the Champions Cup last weekend. “And there’s no harm in setting a high bar,” writes John O’Sullivan in his preview of the game.
Ireland’s women, meanwhile, are fine-tuning their preparations for the first of two tests against South Africa in Cape Town, captain Erin King hoping to cap a memorable week that saw her turn 23.
In football, Gavin Cummiskey hears from Shamrock Rovers captain Pico Lopes ahead of a night that could see them seal their sixth title in seven seasons. Rovers manager Stephen Bradley is, though, still smarting from three of his players picking up bans. The league’s disciplinary system? It’s “ not fit for purpose ,” he says. Bradley also took time to praise the impact of the club’s psychologist Mary Larkin in the aftermath of James McClean suggesting that speaking to a therapist is a sign of “weakness”.
Speaking of weakness - Manchester United. After another calamitous week, during which Bruno Fernandes turned a touch “toxic” , Gavin Cooney is now imagining them replacing Michael Carrick with Antonio Conte , before bringing in a beloved former player as an interim and then replacing him with Eddie Howe, before bringing José Mourinho out of retirement to return to the sinking ship. He could be right, you know.
It’s 16 years since Dave Mulcahy scored for a League of Ireland selection against United at the redeveloped Lansdowne Road. He’d probably fancy scoring against them this weather, but, Gordon Manning tells us, his focus is on managing his Tullaroan side to success against reigning champions Ballyhale Shamrocks in Sunday’s Kilkenny hurling club final.
Gordon also talks to Cork man Seamus Harnedy who announced his retirement from intercounty hurling recently. He thought his playing days at Páirc Uí Chaoimh were over, but he’ll be in action there again tomorrow in the hurling-shinty international against Scotland .
In racing, Brian O’Connor doffs his cap to Billy Lee who, at the age of 40, is about to be crowned champion jockey . And in athletics, Ian O’Riordan previews Sunday’s Dublin Marathon as well as telling us of some of the quirkier examples of marathon cheating down the years . Like when a member of the Garda anti-corruption unit (allegedly) travelled the latter portion of the Dublin course on, well, the Luas. Like you do.
TV Watch: Séamus Power had a solid start at the Bermuda Championship yesterday, his round of 66 leaving him just three shots off the lead - you can see the second round from 6pm on Sky Sports Golf this evening. At 7.45pm, Bohemians will attempt to keep their League of Ireland title hopes alive when they play Shelbourne (Virgin Media Two), and at the same time Connacht host Zebre in the URC (TG4 and Premier Sports 1).

title: AI being examined for use in State’s breast cancer screening amid missed targets
description: Health Service Executive says it is ‘exploring’ using new technology due to increased demand and shortage of radiographers
content:
The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is being examined in the State’s breast cancer screening service as increased demand and a shortage of radiographers has led to the programme missing targets .
The Health Service Executive (HSE) said it was “exploring” using AI in BreastCheck, Ireland’s free national breast screening programme for women and anyone aged between 50 and 69 with breasts or female breast tissue.
This includes some transgender, non-binary and intersex people, according to the HSE.
A record number of people were screened last year, but the programme missed its target for the third consecutive year due to increasing demand on the service.
The HSE posted a market consultation on the eTender website, consulting with AI companies to discuss potential use of this technology in BreastCheck.
[ I had my first breast check in my mid-thirties – here’s how it went Opens in new window ]
“All modern breast screening programmes face increasing operational pressures including rising patient volumes, radiologist workforce shortages, and growing demands for faster turnaround times while maintaining diagnostic accuracy,” the eTender notice says.
“The complexity of mammographic interpretation, combined with the need for consistent performance across large screening populations, creates challenges in delivering timely, high-quality care.
“Reader fatigue and workload pressures can impact diagnostic consistency, particularly during extended screening sessions.”
The notice added that additionally, there is “mounting pressure to improve early detection rates while minimising false positives and unnecessary recalls”.
“To address these challenges and enhance our screening programme’s effectiveness, we are exploring AI solutions that can augment radiologist capabilities, improve workflow efficiency, and maintain consistent diagnostic performance across our national screening network,” the notice said.
“As part of our due diligence process for implementing AI technology in BreastCheck, the NSS (National Screening Service) are conducting a comprehensive premarket consultation with potential AI solution providers.
“This consultation aims to evaluate available technologies against our specific clinical, technical, and regulatory requirements before making procurement decisions.”
Speaking at a conference organised by the Royal College of Physicians in Ireland (RCPI) on Thursday, Damian McCallion, chief technology officer at the HSE, said Ireland was a laggard in the European context on digital health.
[ ‘Potential to be transformative’: Hiqa to look at including breast density in screening Opens in new window ]
However, he said significant work is under way to increase digitisation, adding that he believes the use of AI in screening services is a particular opportunity.
McCallion referred to the lack of public trust in the CervicalCheck programme, following the 2018 revelations that hundreds of women were not informed that their previous cervical smear test results had been audited and changed
“The key thing there is patient confidence. It will not be perfect. But it will improve accuracy. If we bring patients along with that, that will make a huge difference. That will bring confidence in play,” he said.
The HSE has said BreastCheck will be the first programme to explore the use of AI because it has “the most mature evidence base for immediate implementation”.
International research from Sweden found AI-supported breast screening detected 20 per cent more breast cancers while potentially halving radiologist workload.

title: One third of HSE areas have curtailed public health nursing to priority cases
description: Routine development checks for babies are being triaged in seven health areas, raising concerns that children are ‘being left behind’
content:
One third of HSE areas have curtailed public health nursing to priority cases, new figures show, raising concerns that children are “being left behind”.
Public health nurses (PHNs) are qualified general nurses and midwives employed by the HSE to deliver free community-based healthcare.
They provide important development checks for children from birth to five years of age. Appointments are typically conducted in the family home or at a local health centre.
Data from the HSE shows that seven of the 20 integrated health areas have caseload prioritisation in place to some extent.
These are: the Cavan/Monaghan IHA, Dublin South City and West, and some areas within Dublin South and Wicklow, Dublin North City and West, Dublin North County, South Cork and Dublin South West.
Under prioritisation, rather than delivering universal, routine check-ups to every household, services are triaged so that infants, children, or adults with proven medical risks, disabilities or immediate clinical vulnerabilities are seen first.
Consequently, routine and non-priority developmental assessments may be delayed, limited or suspended for many babies.
The HSE data also shows there has been a small reduction in PHN staff since December 2020, falling from 1,557 whole-time equivalents to 1,535 at the end of last year. Four of the six HSE regions saw a decrease in staff.
[ Minister wants HSE to cap hospital parking fee at €10 a day Opens in new window ]
The figures were obtained by Labour’s health spokeswoman Marie Sherlock, who described them as “deeply alarming”.
“PHNs are the first line of defence when it comes to identifying developmental, child welfare and maternal wellbeing issues and the least expensive part of the health system,” she said.
“It is simply unacceptable that we now have less public health nurses across the whole country than five years ago and it flies in the face of the commitments to increasing care in the community.”
Sherlock said parents have reported cases of the four-year check being replaced with a phone call in which they are asked if they have any concerns, and that the file is closed if they do not.
She added that nurses have told her they feel “overworked and under-resourced”.
“We need a specialised workforce plan particularly targeting deployment of new staff to areas of social deprivation and ensure that new pathways are opened up for paediatric nurses to become PHNs,” she said.
The HSE’s performance committee in May discussed the regional variation of PHN assessments, with concerns being raised about the “low rates” of child health and development checks in some areas.
[ No link between healthcare staff recruitment and hospital performance, says Minister Opens in new window ]
The HSE has previously acknowledged the challenges with the recruitment and retention of PHNs, particularly in the Greater Dublin Area.
The HSE said it introduced short-term measures to tackle the issue, including service integration, workload reorganisation and staff redeployment.
“Where staff shortages occur, the HSE prioritises and supports children and families with the greatest need in the community.”

title: Israeli government orders army to prepare for full closure of West Bank
description: Order comes after Israel’s army said it had killed two gunmen and thwarted a ‘terror attack’ that injured several people
content:
Israel ’s government has ordered the country’s army to prepare for a full closure of the West Bank , following a deadly shooting earlier in the day in the occupied territory.
Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu ’s office said it had instructed security forces to immediately cordon off the city of Hebron and prepare to fully close all of the West Bank, starting on Friday.
The orders came after Israel’s army said it had killed two gunmen and thwarted a “terror attack” that injured several people.
Earlier, the army said it had prevented a “terror attack against Israeli civilians” and that the gunmen carried an M16 rifle and a handgun. It did not elaborate on the target of the alleged attack. There was also no word on the identities of the two dead and those injured.
The military subsequently set up roadblocks and closures in Palestinian towns in the area.
Emergency responders said five people were injured, some critically, and were being evacuated to hospitals in Israel.
A statement from the responders said gunfire was continuing as they arrived at the scene of the attack near the Yehuda Junction on Friday morning.
Two men in their 20s had gunshot wounds to their lower limbs, with one unconscious and seriously injured, the responders said.
“We arrived at a difficult scene while shooting was still taking place in the area,” said Tzuriel Edri with the response team.
An investigation is under way, authorities said.
The deadly shooting comes as Israeli voters decide next Tuesday whether to grant Netanyahu yet another term as prime minister – or usher in a new era of Israeli politics. The election comes three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that triggered the war in Gaza.
Israel’s government has warned of potential attacks by the country’s “enemies” in the lead-up to the election.
Following the shooting, Netanyahu held an emergency meeting of his security cabinet and officials from top military and security agencies.
He blamed Hamas, saying the militant group was “planning a major attack aimed at murdering innocent civilians”.
“Our brave soldiers thwarted this attack with courage and determination,” he said, without elaborating on what the planned attack entailed.
“I commend them for their actions and wish our wounded a speedy recovery,” he added but did not say whether the wounded were soldiers or civilians.
Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for extremist views, said the Hebron attack showed that Israel needed to restrict the Palestinians’ freedom of movement in the West Bank.
“The lives of the residents of Judea and Samaria, of the settlers, the lives of the soldiers, the lives of the police officers, the lives of our fighters are a million times more important than freedom of movement,” he said, using an Israeli reference to the West Bank.
[ Palestine supporters such as Sally Rooney are demonised like apartheid opponents, says Mary Robinson Opens in new window ]
In advance of the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack of October 7th, 2023, that triggered the war, Netanyahu said the Palestinian militant group could attack Israel in a bid to influence the outcome of the elections. He did not provide evidence to back up the claim. – AP

title: The Irish Times Business Person of the Month: Donal Murphy, CEO DCC Energy
description: Murphy secured shareholder approval for DCC’s sale to two US private equity firms
content:
DCC Energy chief executive Donal Murphy has been chosen as The Irish Times Business Person of the Month for September, an award run in association with Bank of Ireland.
During the month, Murphy, who has led the group since 2017, succeeded in securing shareholder approval for the Irish company’s sale to two US private equity firms in a deal worth up to £5.73 billion (€6.69 billion). This was in spite of opposition from some major shareholders, including the company’s founder Jim Flavin.
The deal, structured as a so-called scheme of arrangement, now requires High Court approval and is expected to complete in the first quarter of 2027.
“We’ve had a really strong turnout, and we’re very happy with the result,” Murphy said after the vote.
DCC revealed in late April that it had received a €58-a-share offer from KKR and Energy Capital partners.
While the initial proposal was rejected, DCC agreed in late July to sell itself to the consortium for a £65.25-a-share upfront payment and the prospect of an additional payment related to the sale of its tech division.
The takeover deal valued the upfront cash offer at a 21.3 per cent premium to DCC’s closing share price in London on April 28th.
Once a conglomerate spanning various sectors, the Dublin-based but London-listed company is now focused on the energy sector.
Following the shareholder vote, Murphy signalled that he would like to remain on board to see out DCC’s goal to double the operating profit of the remaining energy division to £830 million between 2022 and 2030.

title: New cars you’ll see for the first time at Nevo EV show 2026
description: One of the big attractions of the show has always been the chance to see new models long before they become a familiar sight on Irish roads
content:
The countdown is on for the Nevo EV Show 2026, and for many attendees one of the biggest attractions is the opportunity to see the latest cars in the metal, often long before they become a familiar sight on Irish roads.
This year will be no different, with Irish launches to cover all motoring needs and budgets, from affordable new electric city cars to family SUVs, luxury models, performance EVs and even an electric pickup among the first confirmed newcomers.
With the countdown under way, here’s a selection of the new cars making their Irish debuts at the Nevo Show, with even more debuts expected to be confirmed before the doors open at the RDS.
The Dacia Spring is back, but this time it is essentially an entirely new car. The second-generation Spring represents an important step in Dacia’s growing electric ambitions and retains the straightforward, affordable approach that made the original interesting, while addressing many of the first generation’s shortcomings.
The new Spring is now produced in Europe and sits on a new platform, with Dacia again concentrating on keeping weight, complexity and cost under control. The latest model uses a 27.5kWh battery, offers around 250km of WLTP range and retains the compact dimensions that make it ideally suited to urban driving. For Irish buyers interested in getting into a new EV at the more affordable end of the market, this could be one of the most interesting cars at the show.
BYD has become one of the fastest-growing automotive names in Ireland, and its latest Dolphin G takes the brand into another important part of the market. Unlike the familiar all-electric Dolphin, the new Dolphin G uses BYD’s DM-i plug-in hybrid technology. That means meaningful electric-only driving for everyday journeys combined with the flexibility of a petrol engine for longer trips.
BYD says the compact hatchback can offer a combined driving range of more than 1,000km, while retaining the practicality and accessible positioning that have become key ingredients in the Dolphin family. It will also demonstrate that the transition to electrified motoring doesn’t necessarily mean one solution for everyone.
There is considerable interest surrounding the Volvo EX60, and for good reason. Positioned in one of the most important areas of the premium SUV market, the fully electric EX60 arrives with new technology and some seriously impressive numbers. Volvo Ireland lists three power-train options, with ranges stretching from 611km in the rear-wheel-drive P6 to as much as 810km in the P12 AWD.
An 800-volt electrical system also brings extremely rapid charging, while the familiar Volvo emphasis on safety, comfort and understated Scandinavian design remains. With pricing starting from €66,695 in Ireland, the EX60 could become one of Volvo’s most significant electric cars yet.
Another model that should attract plenty of attention is the new Lexus TZ. This is a large, fully electric premium SUV with three rows and seating for six, moving Lexus into a part of the electric market it hasn’t previously occupied. The interior is particularly interesting, with Lexus describing its new approach as a “Driving Lounge”. The idea is to use the inherent quietness and smoothness of an EV to create a genuinely relaxing environment for everyone on-board, including adults sitting in the third row. Combine that with the refinement, build quality and distinctive design traditionally associated with Lexus and the TZ promises to be a fascinating addition to the show.
French luxury will also be represented by the new DS No7, the replacement for the familiar DS 7 and an important new model for DS Automobiles. Available with both electric and hybrid power trains, the No7 mixes the bold styling and highly detailed interiors we have come to expect from DS with the latest driver assistance and infotainment technology. The fully electric No7 E-Tense Long Range is capable of up to 740km on the WLTP cycle, giving it genuine long-distance credentials to go with its premium positioning.
If you have a large family and have been waiting for more choice among seven-seat electric SUVs, the Skoda Peaq deserves a close look. At 4.87m long, it is the largest SUV Skoda has produced and effectively brings the space and practicality associated with the Kodiaq into the electric era. Irish pricing starts from €54,995, while different battery and power-train options allow buyers to prioritise affordability or range. The Peaq 90, for example, uses a 91kWh battery and offers up to 637km of range. As ever with Skoda, practicality is likely to be one of its biggest attractions.
Nissan is returning to the smallest end of the European car market with the new Pixo, and this little EV could be one of the surprise stars of the show. The Pixo is a compact A-segment electric city car offering up to 259km of WLTP range and 50kW DC rapid charging. More importantly, it represents Nissan re-entering a market for small, accessible cars at a time when affordable electric motoring is becoming increasingly important. Visitors will be among the first in Ireland to get a proper close-up look.
We have been hearing about the Cupra Raval for some time, but the production car is finally here. At just over 4m long, it brings Cupra’s sporting personality into the increasingly competitive compact EV sector. Different versions will offer different combinations of performance and range, with the longer-range models capable of around 440km, while the range-topping 226hp Raval VZ adds a more serious performance flavour. It’s compact, distinctive and aimed at buyers who want their small EV to have a little personality.
BMW will bring two particularly important newcomers to Dublin. The new i3 is no longer the quirky carbon-bodied hatchback many will remember. Instead, the name now belongs to the first fully electric BMW 3 Series and the second production model developed around BMW’s Neue Klasse technology. For Ireland, the i3 will initially be available as the i3 40 xDrive and i3 50 xDrive, with BMW quoting up to 912km WLTP range for the latter and charging at up to 400kW. It brings the Neue Klasse technology first introduced with the iX3 right into the heart of BMW’s range.
Alongside it will be the larger new BMW iX5. This takes BMW’s electric SUV range further upmarket, with the iX5 60 xDrive offering preliminary WLTP range figures of between 645km and 845km. Seeing these two cars together should provide a fascinating look at where the next generation of BMW electric models is heading.
Mazda’s electric range continues to expand rapidly. Following the Mazda6e, the new CX-6e takes the same broader collaborative approach into the SUV market. Developed with Changan Automobile, the CX-6e combines Mazda’s own design philosophy and European-focused driving dynamics with a new generation of electric and intelligent technology. Voice and gesture recognition, advanced assistance systems and available digital side mirrors highlight just how different this new generation of Mazda EVs will be.
Few names demonstrate how far electric cars have progressed quite like Porsche, and the arrival of an electric Cayenne is another significant milestone. The Cayenne Electric sits alongside combustion and hybrid Cayenne models rather than immediately replacing them but introduces an entirely new level of electric performance to Porsche’s large SUV. Three electric derivatives are offered − Cayenne Electric, Cayenne S Electric and Cayenne Turbo Electric − all with electric all-wheel drive. Even the regular Cayenne Electric can accelerate from 0–100km/h in just 4.8 seconds.
Hyundai will have two very different electric newcomers to explore. The Ioniq 3 could ultimately prove more significant in sales terms, bringing Hyundai’s dedicated Ioniq thinking into a compact hatchback designed specifically with European customers in mind. Two battery choices are offered, with the long-range version targeting up to 496km WLTP. Despite its compact dimensions, Hyundai is promising genuine five-seat accommodation and a 441-litre luggage capacity, while DC charging from 10 to 80 per cent takes around 29 minutes.
At almost the opposite end of the spectrum sits the Staria Electric. Hyundai’s futuristic MPV gains an 84kWh battery and 160kW electric motor while retaining the huge interior space that makes the Staria so distinctive. For large families, shuttle operators or anyone who simply needs serious passenger space, it demonstrates just how broadly the EV market is now expanding.
Leapmotor will once again have a big presence at Nevo, and the B03X gives visitors another opportunity to see just how quickly the brand’s range is developing. Described as a smart urban crossover, the B03X has been developed from the outset as a global model and is designed to bring much of Leapmotor’s technology into a smaller, more accessible package. With European orders already opening during the summer, it is another model that could significantly broaden the company’s appeal.
There are few small cars with the character of the original Renault Twingo, and Renault has very deliberately tapped into that heritage with the new Twingo E-Tech Electric. Bright, compact and full of familiar design references, the new Twingo is designed to make electric motoring affordable and genuinely useful in the city. It also offers technology normally associated with larger cars, including Google-based infotainment, one-pedal driving and, depending on specification, bidirectional charging capability. This should be one of the most instantly recognisable newcomers at the show.
Finally, something completely different. The KGM Musso EV brings full electric power to the pickup market and demonstrates that battery power is no longer confined to hatchbacks and SUVs. The Musso EV uses an 80.6kWh LFP battery and is offered in both two-wheel-drive and dual-motor all-wheel-drive forms. The 2WD model offers up to 419km of range, while practical features include a 500kg payload, vehicle-to-load capability and a 1.5-tonne towing limit. For visitors who need a vehicle for work as well as everyday driving, it will be well worth investigating.
These cars are only the beginning. With the Nevo EV Show still several weeks away, more new-model announcements and first appearances are expected as the final line-up takes shape. Alongside these newcomers, each participating manufacturer will showcase a wider selection of its current electric and electrified range, making the show an opportunity to compare cars from across the market under one roof.
Visitors will also be able to see selected models in action in the ESB Live Demo Area, where Derek Reilly will once again take a closer look at the technology, design, practicality and performance behind some of the most interesting new vehicles at the show. The Live Demo programme provides a different experience to the static manufacturer stands, allowing visitors to see and learn more about selected cars in action across both days.
The Nevo EV Show takes place at RDS Simmonscourt, Dublin, on Saturday and Sunday, November 7th and 8th.
Whether you are already driving electric, considering making the switch or simply want to see what the next generation of cars looks like, this year’s show is shaping up to offer one of the broadest selections of new electric and electrified vehicles yet.
Sign up at Nevo.ie and follow Nevo across its social media channels to keep up to date with the latest show news, vehicle reveals and further launches as they are announced in the run-up to November. With plenty more still to be confirmed, this is only the first look at what’s coming.

title: US country singer John Anderson dies aged 71
description: Anderson’s extensive body of work included five number ones on the country charts
content:
John Anderson, the traditionalist US country singer whose extensive body of work included five number one hits on the country charts, has died aged 71.
The news was announced on social media by his family, who said: “To the world, he was a gifted country music singer whose voice and songs touched countless lives. To us, he was so much more. He was the heart of our family, the one who made us laugh, loved us fiercely and made every ordinary moment feel special.”
So woven into the culture of country music that he once worked as a roofer on the genre’s focal point, Nashville’s Grand Ole Opry, Anderson’s career spanned nearly 50 years and resulted in him being inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2024.
Among those paying tribute to Anderson was country singer and friend Blake Shelton: “I am a very lucky man. I got the opportunity to find out that my hero wasn’t just the guy I hoped he’d be.” Shelton’s wife Gwen Stefani wrote: “We loved him. His music is part of our family’s hearts for ever.”
Born and raised in Florida in a music-loving family whose tastes spanned big band jazz to the Rolling Stones, Anderson headed to Nashville after graduating high school to try to make it in the city’s country music scene by playing live sets at night while doing manual labour during the day. “I’d fill up the truck with gravel and take the truck to wherever the order was and drop it off. A lot of odd jobs, but never lost sight of the fact that I really wanted to play,” he said in 2024.
Writing his own material as well as performing that of others, he released his debut single in 1975, but broke through two years later with I’ve Got a Feelin’ (Somebody’s Been Stealin’), and inched his way up the country charts with each subsequent release. He had his first country top-five single in 1981, I’m Just an Old Chunk of Coal (But I’m Gonna Be a Diamond Someday), which earned him his only Grammy nomination, for best male vocal country performance – and was a typical showcase of his wry, earnest and pure vocal tone.
It ushered in a number of years of commercial success, with the songs Wild and Blue, Black Sheep and Swingin’ all becoming country chart-toppers – the slick, hard-driving sound of the latter gave it crossover appeal and it became Anderson’s only hit on the US pop chart.
The latter half of the decade was a frustrating time for Anderson as he was dropped by his label Warner Bros and shuttled between others, before finding his groove again with 1992 album Seminole Wind, containing three top-three hits; the title track, an ode to his birth state of Florida, and Straight Tequila Night have endured as country radio staples and streaming successes. Follow-up Solid Ground was also a hit, containing the chart-topping Money in the Bank.
Anderson ended up recording 22 studio albums, most recently 2020’s Years, recorded with Dan Auerbach of blues-rockers the Black Keys. That was a proud and hard-fought return for Anderson, who faced illness with a non-cancerous tumour in 2017 that left him hospitalised. “I had been very, very ill,” he told Billboard in 2020. “I had almost 100 per cent hearing loss … that really almost put an end to me. I just started praying and praying harder than I’ve ever prayed in my life and you know what? My hearing started coming back.”
Anderson continued to perform live thereafter, saying in 2024 that since his recovery, “I’ve really been enjoying every day. I live out in the woods and take a lot of lessons from my little wildlife friends. They pretty much live day to day, minute to minute. Enjoying that minute, enjoying this time. I’m very thankful to be able to go out and play any music at all.” – Guardian

title: Shouty phone calls on buses, cyclists on footpaths ... Civilisation is falling apart
description: The more we tolerate mé féinism the less likely we are to treat each other as human beings, and the more society tears itself apart
content:
A ndy Burnham is being pelted with online invective after announcing his crackdown on train passengers playing audio aloud on their phones.
“Twat,” declares one of Instagram ’s teeming amateur anthropologists.
“Prick,” agrees someone aptly named andy.craven12.
“Traitourous (sic) c**t,” chimes dukewinston11.
Others suggest the British prime minister should get off the effing train and stop the effing migrant boats, rising prices, the riots in France, wars, pestilence, famine and Man City scoring goals. (OK, that last one might be poetic licence.)
The vitriol shows Burnham has hit a nerve with his “enough is enough” campaign. Let’s hope the Taoiseach takes note and copies it, pronto.
Slapping £100 (€119) fines on selfish passengers who force their horrible, tinny music and video babble on everyone else in the carriage is a simple measure. But it just might stop civilisation from collapsing.
If engagement with social media is making the world more turbulent, involuntary engagement with it is leaving many of us seething. TikTok is noxious enough without it being forced upon innocent bystanders. Incessant eruptions of canned laughter has a way of fomenting murderous thoughts in a normally peaceable mind.
[ Sally Rooney could have made things a great deal easier for herself. She chose not to Opens in new window ]
When all you want to do is sit quietly or read or gaze out the window and daydream, it’s a triggering start to the morning having Clint Eastwood growling “make my day, punk” on the phone beside you. Because you’re too polite or too shy or too intimidated to ask your neighbour to wear headphones or switch if off, you alight in a state of fuming resentment. Maybe you’ll snap at a shop assistant, let a door swing in a stranger’s face, arrive in the office fulminating and despairing.
We wonder where all the anger is coming from these days. It’s coming from:
[ Andy Burnham making TikToks about parking tickets seems to be missing the point Opens in new window ]
The more ways modern life is dehumanised, the more our quality of life is impaired and the angrier we humans get. This is how social cohesion begins to unravel.
It starts small. Avoiding eye-contact; acting impervious to each other. Eschewing headphones because other people don’t matter. Bullying others out of your way, on the footpath or in traffic. Barging through a door held open by others without a word of thanks or a smile of acknowledgment. Belittling shop assistants. Gratuitously ugly language with a ring of menace. Vaping sickly-sweet fumes on the bus. Dropping litter in the street and expecting someone else to pick it up.
When society tolerates the small things, the small things get bigger. Speed limits are flouted, verbal abuse is normalised, tailgating too. Fireworks are thrown at a neighbour’s shed and passersby are accosted for daring to even be in the country. Some days, it feels like there is somebody spoiling for a fight around every corner.
And on it goes, getting bigger, getting worse, poisoning the atmosphere. Fuel protesters think it’s justifiable to use their trucks and tractors to impede others from going about their normal lives, regardless that pregnant women are trying to get to hospital or that airline passengers must drag their suitcases behind them as they trudge alongside the M50 to the airport. The more we tolerate mé féinism the less likely we are to treat each other as human beings and the more society tears itself apart.
[ Fr Dougal Maguire hit on an under-recognised truth about faith and religion Opens in new window ]
Mutual respect is an old-fashioned value that needs to be reclaimed because, without it, civilisation is going to hell in a handcart. Its absence is what provides the oxygen for all those noisy phones and slammed doors, the road rage and aggressive abuse.
It’s no coincidence that Burnham is also planning to clamp down on impossible-to-contact customer service departments. The attitude du jour is self-service or no service, from the bank to the supermarket to the airport check-in desk. It’s an ethos predicated on the disposability of humans and it’s adding to the general anxiety of modern life.
Shutting down everyday opportunities for social engagement has to be affecting the way we communicate with one another. Social media’s proclivity for scatological discourse (see above) and the isolation caused by technology are rightly blamed, but the shrinking interludes of routine human engagement cannot be overlooked as a contributing factor in the simplism of public conversation.
Calling someone “a twat” – or worse – is unlikely to be entertained as serious debate, unlike the specious either-or argument that is offered with alarming frequency in the guise of intellectual rigour. You know the this-or-that routine that goes “Burnham should be fixing the train tracks instead of fining passengers” or “why build a Dublin metro when we can’t fix the ghost buses?” Believe it or not but governments can, actually, manage to do two things at once.
The banal choice-argument licenses yet more anger. It inculcates a sense of powerlessness. It leaves those who think their wishes are being deprioritised for the benefit of others feeling aggrieved and it pillories all politicians – some of whom, clearly, need no help in this regard – as galumphing incompetents. Next thing they know, Government ministers are receiving death threats and their families are being evacuated from their homes because they are no longer regarded as human beings.
So, let’s deal with the everyday intrusions that are making the world angrier. Ban the sneaky charges and the automatically renewed subscriptions. Ban the cacophonous phones on public transport. At the same time, make the trains big enough so that passengers are not squeezed into them like sardines and, Dublin Bus, please restore the exit door beside the driver to let passengers say thanks when disembarking.
Otherwise, we might as well invite the robots to take control. After all, they ape us in every way, except for our humanity.

title: The Chinese car revolution is moving faster than Europe expected
description: Leapmotor’s Irish boss says customers no longer ask whether Chinese cars are good enough. Instead, they’re deciding which Chinese brand to buy
content:
Five years ago, few mainstream Chinese brands had a meaningful presence in Ireland. Today, showrooms are crowded with names such as BYD, MG, Xpeng and Leapmotor. Several more are on the way.
Leapmotor Ireland brand manager Stephen McGrath reckons what has caught European rivals off guard is the sheer pace of innovation and development at the Chinese car companies.
He sees the key differences between Chinese and European carmakers “are ultimately the speed of getting the technology and the product to market. It’s unrivalled.
“Leapmotor is a brand that produced in 2019 about 1,400 units. This year they will produce over a million units,” he says, pointing out there are now more than 1,000 Leapmotor retail outlets across Europe.
Much of that growth is built on manufacturing systems that European executives are increasingly travelling to China to study. In May, McGrath visited Leapmotor’s operations in Shanghai.
“I am 20 years in the industry. I’ve never seen factories, production and automation like it.”
He says it’s this level of production innovation that delivers the competitive pricing that is a big lure for many buyers and delivers on the Leapmotor tagline of “value without compromise”.
McGrath says control of the supply line for its models is also key to Chinese brands success. Leapmotor builds many of its own batteries, motors and related components from scratch, giving it greater control over costs and development cycles.
As for the quality of the facilities, McGrath says that if he had arrived in the motor factory blindfolded, he “would have said [it was] a pharmaceutical factory”.
A visit to a quality check line also revealed the startling pace of change. He was told that currently 30 people work per shift completing a set of specific checks. However, by the middle of next year they will no longer be needed for these shifts “because the cars will self-drive and self-check. They’ll either go back if there are any quality issues, or they drive themselves out to the car park to be picked up by a transporter.
“That’s the kind of level of savings they can make through having the latest technology to manage the factories and being just so up to date on the forefront of it all.
“It’s amazing what they can achieve and have achieved in such a short space of time.”
McGrath, who spent decades in his career working with European mainstream brands, says “European brands refresh products every few years. Chinese brands are launching entirely new vehicles at a pace that legacy manufacturers struggle to match.”
A case in point: Leapmotor plans to add six additional model ranges in the next 18 months, expanding into almost every major market segment.
“To be launching six model ranges and multiple power trains and batteries within the space of 18 months is completely unheard of,” says McGrath.
“We’ve recently launched the B05 hatchback and that’s our fourth model range so far. We’re launching another one in the coming months. And then come February we’ll have B03 after the B03X. So within 18 months, we’ll have about 90 per cent coverage of the leading segments in the market.”
Are Irish buyers still nervous about Chinese brands?
“Consumers are happy now to go Chinese because they really trust the brands in a way they wouldn’t have five years ago. But these days our phones, our fridges, our laptops come from China. We know the quality is good. I think, for Leapmotor, they’ve gone above and beyond that.”
He argues that Irish buyers have moved beyond concerns about Chinese manufacturing quality and are increasingly judging Chinese brands against each other rather than against European counterparts.
It also helps that Leapmotor has strong links to an established European giant, Stellantis.
With brands such as Opel, Citroen, Peugeot, Fiat and Alfa Romeo, to name but a few, Stellantis has a 51 per cent stake in Leapmotor International, which holds exclusive rights to sell and manufacture Leapmotor products outside China.
At an Irish level, the brand is operated by Gowan Group, which already holds the Irish distribution rights for Stellantis brands, along with others including Honda.
So, are customers considering their purchase as a car from China, a car from the Stellantis Group or a car from the Irish Gowan Auto Group?
