“I think it’s a combination of all three. As you know, people are very well researched.” But the Gowan link also helps. “You know we’re pushing 60 years now, and people buy cars from people as well. So, there’s definitely a strength in that.
As for the Stellantis connection, he says that helps because you’re in the same brand houses as tried and trusted brands.
“But I think ultimately what has helped as well is we went for a six-year unlimited mileage warranty. Chatting to our dealers, that seems to be something that really gives the customer peace of mind.
“We knew the cars were good and the quality was absolutely excellent, but for something unknown, you want to let people know that they have that security there.”
“I think the levels of tech and spec that are on our vehicles is second to none. Our top-selling trim level is Design. There’s only about a €1,500 price walk on a retail level there after EV grants. But ultimately, the customer is getting about €4,000 worth of spec on a B10 or C10. So, it’s back to our tagline ‘value without compromise’ but it’s really secured by our underlying warranty.”
McGrath predicts Leapmotor will finish its first full year of Irish sales with more than 600 new cars on the road. In 2027 they expect that figure to reach 1,300 sales. He says it’s going better than even the initial ambitious plans.
What is luring customers to the brand? “I think what’s working extremely well for us is the price point. And the quality is phenomenal.”
Since its introduction to the market last autumn with two models, Leapmotor has secured a network of 12 dealers, with ambitions to double that for nationwide coverage.
McGrath says demand has already outstripped supply this year, with dealers selling out of some models before replacement stock has arrived. “We sold completely out of C10 and B10 EVs by July 1st and we have customers waiting on the C10s which landed last week and the B10s are now landing this week. It’s about keeping the momentum going for us.”
Part of that momentum is having a strong presence at events such as the Nevo EV show. “For us, we’re ultimately the newest kids on the block. We get to raise our profile and awareness as a brand.
“Ultimately, as the brand sponsor, it was very important for us to make a very, very big statement. We’ll obviously be sharing the models we have currently, which is T03, C10, and B10, and then our newly launched B05.
“Then we’ll be revealing the B03X also.” This new model is a small compact crossover, aiming to win sales from rivals like the Volkswagen T Roc and Kia EV3.
McGrath says the show gives him and his team a chance to engage with the public “and chat to them, especially around the savings offered by EVs over regular combustion-powered cars. He says that after three years of driving an EV “there’s potentially €4,000 worth of savings”.
“I think everybody would want €4,000 in their back pocket.”

title: Eyes wide open: Swapping pistons for electric motors doesn’t mean things will not go wrong
description: Regular maintenance is, even in the electric age, the true secret to keeping any electric car reliable in the long term
content:
What are the common issues with EVs and what are the repair bills like compared to similar problems encountered by ICE engines?
It’s a question with some potentially serious implications, as many electric cars on our roads are now past the point of their original warranties, while many have also outrun their original eight-year, 160,000km battery warranty.
Does buying a used electric car, or keeping one in the longer term, open you to a world of financial pain? No, not quite. It’s more of a case of all cars can be potentially unreliable, so the trick is to buy carefully (especially second-hand) and keep up with maintenance.
Regular maintenance is, even in the electric age, the true secret to keeping any electric car reliable in the long term and making sure that any repair bills that do crop up at (hopefully) the more affordable end of things.
Many electric car makers have stretched out servicing intervals for their battery-powered cars, reckoning that the fact that these cars have fewer moving mechanical parts means that they need less regular attention.
This, though, isn’t a good idea – even if the recommended service interval is every two years for a new EV, we’d suggest you should still book your car in for an annual check-up, as it means you’ll catch problems when they’re still small.
Initially, the biggest number of issues seen with electric cars, according to data taken from reliability experts at JD Power, was nothing to do with big-ticket items such as batteries or motors, but with infotainment systems.
These problems can be generally categorised as minor, but they can still be a major pain in the backside, not least because glitching or “bricked” screens are expensive to put right out of warranty, and can mean you don’t have access to all of the car’s functions.
The best advice here is to make sure you’re uploading all of the software updates that are released for the car – that should help to keep you one step ahead of any issues.
If you need a full replacement screen, such as the one used by a VW ID.4, that can be as much as €2,000 just for the part, let alone the labour cost, but this is certainly not an EV-only issue. Equally, you can get used and reconditioned parts such as a screen for considerably less than that.
Of course, the big worry is the battery, and what if something goes wrong with that? In general, batteries aren’t cheap in any sense to replace or repair, but that’s not just down to the physical item. The cost of a full replacement battery will vary wildly depending on the electric car you’re talking about. For a smaller car such as a Hyundai Inster, it could be around €7,000. For a larger car, such as a Volvo EX90, you could be looking at €20,000 and even more.
Those are big, scary figures and at the top end there’s little else in the motoring world, short of a total chassis swap, that compares.
At the lower end, back down among the Insters and the old Nissan Leafs, the cost comparison is more in line with those for combustion cars.
With a smaller battery, the unit replacement cost may be in and around the same for a diesel car’s main engine control unit (ECU).
There’s plenty of chatter in insurance circles about EVs being written off because of minor damage to the battery, but such is also true of relatively recent combustion-engined cars that suffer ECU damage either through a collision or just through water getting into delicate electrics. It’s important to keep these things in perspective.
Equally, it’s very, very rare that a whole battery will need to be replaced. US-based electric car experts Redcurrent carried out a major large-fleet EV survey last year and found that only 2.5 per cent of all electric cars on the road had ever needed a complete battery replacement.
So yes, the “My EV battery died and cost me €20,000” headlines can be true, but are also rare. If only 2.5 per cent of EVs needed new batteries, then that means 97.5 per cent didn’t. Those are good odds.
Carmakers are also starting to design more repairability into their vehicles. Jean Louis Martins is a battery expert with Dacia, which is just launching its second-generation Spring, and he told us that the battery in that car has been specifically designed to be simple to repair when needed: “We’ve really thought about repairability, and you can see if you look at the battery pack that the cells and the electronic control systems are quite separate, so it’s easy to remove a module for repair, or even an individual cell.
“It was thought to be to be repairable from the start. It’s not the case in some other brands where you know that when you’ve got a problem with the battery, you’ve got to replace the whole pack.”
That repair and replacement of modules rather than whole batteries is the answer to keeping longer-term EV running costs down to acceptable levels. A full, new battery for the hugely popular Tesla Model Y can cost as much as €18,000 but a battery module – and it’s usually only one damaged module that’s causing a problem at any one time – can be as little as €1,100 if you buy a used one that’s been reconditioned.
Of course, part of the cost puzzle is labour prices, and these are being driven up both by a need to give expert training in handling high-voltage batteries to servicing technicians and also to simply find, train and bring into employment enough technicians – although the staff shortages of 2022 and 2023 have eased a little, it’s still an issue for many.
Encouraging more independent garages to train and equip for electric car repairs would doubtless help, but at that level there are still issues. We spoke to independent technician David Corbally, who runs the Service Stop garage in north Co Dublin.
“There’s an attitude problem in the industry, where the carmakers are focused on PCP deals that last for three years, and for the most part warranties that last for three years, and once those are up the car is traded in, out the door, and not their problem any more,” said Corbally.
“My whole thing with EVs is that the reward system is wrong – you should be rewarded for producing a quality product with longevity, not for producing substandard vehicles that you then sell lots of.”
Corbally’s reasoning is that if carmakers were made, through legislation, to stand over a product that lasts, repair costs and reliability issues would become a thing of the past. “I’m not a conspiracy theorist, but it’s very obvious to me that the carmakers’ systems are designed to maximise car sales, but it’s because they’re not accountable. If they were accountable, it’d be a very different playground.”

title: Palestine supporters such as Sally Rooney are demonised like apartheid opponents, says Mary Robinson
description: Former president visited West Bank with Elders group and was shocked by ‘Israeli flags asserting a kind of supremacy’
content:
Attempts to stop people including writer Sally Rooney from expressing support for Palestinians facing genocide have been likened by Mary Robinson to the demonisation of opponents of South African apartheid.
Speaking before an event on international law held at the Museum of Literature on Dublin’s St Stephen’s Green, the former president said that over her long career “this is the most difficult time [and] the challenges are more serious than they’ve ever been”.
She said the decision by British publisher Faber not to sell Rooney’s books in the UK over concerns the author’s support for Palestine Action could expose her to legal jeopardy was “a very worrying constraint and repression”.
Robinson, a former UN commissioner for human rights, said the current conflict had been “so complicated by the need to address and combat anti-Semitism, and that is important, but it’s also now constraining genuinely legitimate protest on the Palestinian side”.
Before the event examining the pressures on international law and global accountability, she said “you have to allow people to protest when they see that a genocide is unfolding, that horrible things are happening in the West Bank ”.
On a recent fact-finding mission there, with other members of the Elders, a global group of leaders that she chaired until two years ago, Robinson said she had been shocked by “Israeli flags asserting a kind of Jewish supremacy”.
“It is now official policy,” she told The Irish Times. “There’s no doubt that [Binyamin] Netanyahu has completely bought into the far right. And hopefully that is what will be displaced if there is a change of government.”
She said it was “‘hard to foretell” the result of the upcoming Israeli general election, but said it was “clear that Israel as a whole has moved to the right, perhaps understandably, after the terrible attacks of October 7th”.
She said a new government, “if it isn’t led by [Netanyahu], probably won’t shift too dramatically, but [it] can change an overall approach and that’s, I think, the best we could hope for”.
The Dublin event, titled What’s Law Got to Do With It? Power, Accountability and the Future of the International Rule of Law, was organised by Irish Rule of Law International with the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.
Robinson said the rule of international law had to be defended “because it’s under attack. It’s under threat, but it’s also very resilient. And just because key leaders, who should know better, haven’t upheld the rule of law doesn’t undermine [it].”
She highlighted the undermining of previous norms by social media, which “divides people into extremes and the loudest voices can be persuasive. And the loudest voices are telling us it’s elitist somehow to uphold all the rules, that we need to have freedom, whatever that is.”
“And it’s appallingly stupid, but it seems to try to influence people and people are anxious at the moment because of the confusing messages and that is deliberate,” Robinson said.
In her address to about 200 delegates including a visiting delegation of Ukrainian judges and justice officials, she said “authoritarian political forces are working hard to undermine” international law.
“We live in an age where populism is in the ascendancy, driven by a combination of economic insecurity, falling trust in politics and institutions, a wave of disinformation and hate speech on social media and a pervasive feeling that leaders do not listen to ordinary citizens,” Robinson said.
“In such a climate, it is all too easy for loud and powerful voices to peddle superficially attractive notions of ‘taking back control’, whether on immigration, trade or labour and social rights, and to dismiss legal safeguards and counter-arguments as elitist, technocratic and at odds with the will of the people.”
She suggested that international law had “a communications problem” and said it was “critical to articulate the fact that international law isn’t an abstract set of treaties debated by lawyers and diplomats. It is the architecture behind many aspects of our daily life.”
She cited the phones and other digital communications devices used daily, and the fact that “a plane can fly over borders safely, or that food and goods are traded freely and young people are able to work between countries” as well as “vaccines approved and shared internationally, and the co-ordinated response to global health emergencies” and said they were all the “result of decades of international legal agreements”.
She noted that “when international law is ignored, we also feel it directly” through “higher energy and food prices because conflicts disrupt supplies, from Ukraine to the Strait of Hormuz”.
She said that although the consequences of “deliberate attempts to weaken the international rule of law are felt by all of us”, they are felt most strongly by the most vulnerable including “the widows and orphans of Khan Younis, the victims of air raids and drone strikes in Kyiv and the survivors of the most horrendous forms of sexual violence in Khartoum”.
She pointed out that if “we are to rebuild and re-energise support for the international rule of law at a national level, we need to also consider how well we are doing to secure equality and protection closer to home”.
She said Northern Ireland was facing rising challenges to progress on women’s rights, with “more than 31,500 domestic abuse incidents recorded by police in the year to March 2026, while Women’s Aid reported that 30 women had been murdered since 2020.
“At a time when far-right, anti-migrant agitators here and across Europe are trying to frame their thuggery and intimidation as ‘protecting our women’, it is even more important that people, governments, legal bodies, police services and the judiciary step up their efforts against gender-based violence and not leave any vacuum that can be exploited. Human rights and gender equality cannot continue to be weaponised. Leaders must support the protection of civic space and human dignity.”

title: Tech sell-off deepens, dents rate hike bets
description: Instead of abandoning the stock market entirely, investors rotated into defensive dividend-paying staples and utilities
content:
Asian stocks extended losses, tracking declines on Wall Street as investors rotated out of technology giants following a blistering rally earlier this year and sought safety in US Treasuries and currencies such as the yen.
MSCI’s regional equities benchmark slipped 0.3 per cent, declining for a second day, leaving the gauge hovering around levels last seen in July.
Taiwan’s stock exchange will be shut Friday due to a typhoon. Sentiment stayed weak as contracts for the Nasdaq 100 Index fell 0.3 per cent in early Asian trading.
Earlier, the Nasdaq 100 tumbled 2.9 per cent and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sank 6.7 per cent, their biggest declines since late June. Tesla and Meta Platforms were among the megacaps that came under pressure following their earnings. Instead of abandoning the stock market entirely, investors rotated into defensive dividend-paying staples and utilities.
Tech remained in focus as South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix scrapped an initial public offering for its US subsidiary Solidigm after facing shareholder opposition.
The rout in the artificial intelligence trade drove investors toward the safety of bonds, with Treasuries staging their biggest rally in more than two years. The benchmark 10-year yield declined 17 basis points to 4.95 per cent, while the yen outperformed all its major counterparts. Australian sovereign debt tracked the gains in Treasuries in early Asian trading.
Brent crude broadly held its gains to trade at around $113.10 per barrel. Oil rallied Thursday as deadly attacks in Saudi Arabia heightened concerns over supplies.
Technology megacaps that powered a four-year bull run in US equities bore the brunt of the selling as earnings from megacap companies added to concerns their rebound since late March had gone too far, too quickly. The group faces fresh tests next week with results from Microsoft, Amazon.com. and Alphabet landing alongside the Federal Reserve’s policy decision.
“Sentiment seems to be shakier these days as investors reconsider AI-related assets,” said Eugene Leow, senior rates strategist at DBS Bank Ltd. “With US yields still elevated by recent standards, investors may want to hedge off some of these risks by seeking safety in Treasuries.”
Treasuries surged across the curve Thursday as the deepening rout in AI-related shares, turmoil in French markets and renewed Middle East tensions fueled haven buying. The rally pushed the 10-year yield below 5% for the first time in a month, with buying in Treasury futures accelerating as traders unwound bearish positions.
In other corners of the market, the yen extended its gains to 156.60 per dollar. The US currency was a touch weaker against most of its Group-of-10 peers.
Gold held its losses from Thursday’s session, when it slumped 2.8 per cent to trade just under $4,205 an ounce.
Concerns about the sustainability of artificial intelligence investment and its eventual payoff have knocked technology shares from recent highs and are beginning to weigh on the broader economic outlook. Traders also pared expectations for another Fed interest-rate increase this year.
Crude oil was another market that traders were paying attention to.
A drone strike on Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah field killed two people without disrupting operations, while an attack on King Fahd International Airport caused casualties. Houthi rebels also claimed strikes on the Saudi port of Yanbu.
Investors are concerned that “post-election, the Iran war may escalate and potentially continue for a longer time than anticipated,” said Joseph Saluzzi, partner and co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading LLC. “The bond rally also confirms the risk-off approach.”
In Asia, Chinese stocks will be in focus after a $2.4 trillion slide from their May peak pushed them into a bear market. Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. suffered its steepest drop in two months Thursday, dragging the Hang Seng Tech Index down 5%, its biggest decline since April 2025.
“Investor sentiment remains very poor for China’s onshore and offshore markets, and without new policy or tech catalysts, this kind of volatile, directionless environment may persist into early 2027,” said Homin Lee, senior macro strategist at Lombard Odier in Singapore. - Bloomberg

title: Callum Turner among James Bond finalists set to screen-test for role this week
description: Group of actors, reportedly including Callum Turner and Slow Horses’ Jack Lowden, to audition to be new 007
content:
The search for the next James Bond may finally be nearing its end: according to reports, a very select group of actors will screen-test to become the next 007 this weekend.
According to the Hollywood Reporter and Variety, citing several sources, a group of actors, reportedly including Callum Turner and Slow Horses’ Jack Lowden, will appear in front of cameras as the secret agent this weekend in London.
The tests supposedly include three elements: stunts, camera presence and dialogue. Reports vary that between three and five actors are finalists for the role, which was vacated by Daniel Craig after 2021’s No Time to Die.
Despite speculation to the contrary, Sinners’ Jack O’Connell and Wuthering Heights star Jacob Elordi are not testing, according to the Hollywood Reporter.
Dune film-maker Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next instalment of the Bond franchise for Amazon MGM studios, which bought the series rights as part of an $8.45bn (€7.553bn) deal in 2022. The Peaky Blinders writer Steven Knight will pen the script.
The company, which paid more than $1bn last year to wrest “creative control” from the Broccoli family, has neither confirmed nor denied the reports, and referred the Hollywood Reporter to its earlier statement: “The search for the next James Bond is under way. While we don’t plan to comment on specific details during the casting process, we’re excited to share more news with 007 fans as soon as the time is right.”
In April of this year, Amazon film executives urged fans to exercise patience in waiting for the casting announcement, citing an abundance of caution in making the closely watched decision.
“I know you’re all wondering when we’re going to announce who’s playing James Bond,” said Courtenay Valenti, the company’s head of film. “Don’t get too excited. Please know that we’re taking the time to do this with care and deep respect. It is the dream of a lifetime for all of us to bring audiences this next chapter, and it’s a responsibility we don’t take lightly.”
Villeneuve, a “diehard Bond fan”, has said the opportunity to add to the franchise is what drew him away from the Dune franchise that has consumed the better part of a decade of his life.
“I said, ‘Maybe it’s a good idea to go back to this project, not out of nostalgia, not because I miss it, but the opposite – I’m tired of it,’” he told Empire of Dune: Messiah, which will premiere this December.
“I want to make sure that I will be severe with the material. That I will not be complacent,” he said. “I thought, ‘When it’s done, I need a very powerful rocket to pull me away from Arrakis.’ When I was asked to do the next Bond, I said: ‘OK, this is what I need.’”
It’s been more than 20 years since the last full screen test for Bond; future Superman Henry Cavill was reported to be a finalist, but the role eventually went to Craig, who first appeared in 2006’s Casino Royale.
Speculation over the new Bond has intensified in the months since Villeneuve was revealed as director in 2025. The film is still reportedly positioned for a 2028 release. – Guardian

title: Can 2,000 people in a hangar in Sioux City influence the US midterms? Trump is banking on it
description: In another turbulent week for the Republican Party, including controversy over a ‘deeply troubling’ ad in Ohio, Donald Trump went to a pocket of Iowa and felt the love
content:
I f you are to come to Sioux City on a Thursday evening in late October, then there can be few more spectacular ways to arrive than this: that iconographic plane swooping low over the golden fields where, at an airport hangar below, waiting supporters are pointing their phones skywards, while Belinda Carlisle’s Heaven is a Place on Earth blasts out of the speakers and a harvest moon’s already visible even though its warm enough to wear T-shirts long after dusk. And the excited shout: “Here he comes!”
“This feels like God’s country,” Tim Scott, the South Carolina senator who was among the list of warm-up acts here to entertain the crowd over the hot afternoon, had thundered earlier in the day.
The crowd cheered. And it was true. If these midterm elections are to mark the first tolling of the bells on Donald Trump’s fierce grip on US politics, then nobody told them in this western pocket of Iowa. It’s an unpretentious city, tucked between the prairie grasslands of South Dakota and Nebraska, and although Lewis and Clarke passed through here on their immortal expedition in the early 19th century, in 2026 most visitors have a specific reason to come here. President Trump’s reason was that few states have shown him as much love as Iowa.
“I love our farmers – I know you’re not all farmers, but I love Iowa,” Trump told them after taking the stage to rapturous applause sometime after 7pm. The most loyal had turned up in the morning to wait in line.
“I shouldn’t brag but ... I won [in Iowa] all three times by more than any candidate in political history.”
[ What are the US midterms? A visual guide Opens in new window ]
A furious midterm election cycle, defined by reckless and bitter exchanges by the candidates in the key states, has reached the phase of inevitable repetition. Everyone has said everything a thousand times, the president included. If anything, Trump is doubling down on his promise to hold daily rallies to bolster the chances of Republican candidates – whereas the commentariat and strategists argue those chances would be improved if he spent the month holed up in the movie room of the White House, watching Citizen Kane and other favourites. But Trump works to his own instinct and has made this election cycle a personal popularity contest.
So, what is to be extrapolated from this vivid scene of Trump devotion in a regional airport hangar? Everything and nothing. On the surface, these events are a reminder that once he cedes the stage, Trump-rally theatre will be remembered, in his strongholds, as a kind of folkloric mirage. Americans won’t see anything like this again. Any Trump rally is a strange confection of pageantry and patriotism, speeches filled with nostalgia and dark premonition, of many hours of waiting. The mood at these events is one of wilful escapism from the mundanity of ordinary life. To be up close and personal with Trump is, for his supporters, to commune with the fantastical.
[ Trump is about to discover the political cost of inflation Opens in new window ]
The Iowa GOP had their homework done, selecting this small airport hangar and festooning it with the familiar backdrop so that the place was packed by midafternoon. Does the attendance of a couple of thousand people in a corrugated box on the edge of Sioux City have any real significance on the overall senate vote in a state of 3.2 million people? Trump, in defiance of the polling numbers, is banking that it does.
All day, a small, voluble group of protesters stood at the entrance to the parking fields. Joining them was Helen Doidge, who pulled a “Putin Is Not Our Friend” placard from the boot of her car.
“The numbers are very close. Which is unbelievable. After everything that has happened. And now this,” she says pointing to her placard. We talk for a while about being an Independent voter in a deeply Republican patch of the land.
“After a while, you can’t change anyone’s mind. We lost friends because of it. Relatives, we had our words and made up. But we don’t discuss politics any more.”
Nearby, Chris Klein was headed to the rally with his friends. The 19-year-old grew up in Sioux City but has just joined the US marines and leaves for San Diego, for boot camp, on Sunday. I ask him what it was like growing up here, and whether he will miss it.
“I love Sioux City. But I definitely saw with the open borders a lot happening. I went to Sioux City North. My freshman year we were a white-majority school. By the time I transferred the majority became Hispanic and Latinas and other migrants . I saw that in my small town in the middle of Iowa. I can’t imagine everything else that is going on in other places.”
Klein is courteous and quick-speaking, and says he was fascinated by politics from an early age. He agrees his decision to join the marines has concerned his mother.
“For sure. Being worried about her young son going into the military – especially with the job I want to do. I’m going to be in the infantry. It’s definitely a risk and a risky job but I know I have a great God who is going to be protect me through all of that. How could I not serve such an amazing country that has provided so much for me?”
In the hangar, the series of speeches reinforce the overall threat represented by the insurgent Democratic candidates. Josh Turek, the Iowa state representative who is narrowly leading Ashley Hinson in the polls, is linked and aligned with Texas’s James Talarico and Michigan’s Abdul El Sayed by repeated anecdote.
[ Branded ‘lazy’ by Trump, Democrat Josh Turek is mounting an unexpected challenge in a Republican stronghold Opens in new window ]
“The 42 per cent of the time he actually showed up for work, he was voting like Bernie Sanders,” Hinson tells them.
“Josh Turek voted to allow illegal immigrants have welfare benefits here in Iowa. He also voted to make it harder for law enforcement to deport dangerous illegal criminals out of our communities. He voted to allow taxpayer dollars to go fund sex changes. Have their kids be able to change their gender pronouns and not tell their parents. He is too liberal for Iowa.”
That’s the central contention of the Republican message. Although Trump’s speech follows a familiar litany of accomplishments, his overarching theme in recent weeks has been to warn his supporters of a resumption of rampant border crossings, and crime, should the Republicans lose control of Congress. Turek, he told them, “even wrote a memo giving illegal aliens instructions on how to evade capture – murderers, drug dealers ... how to evade capture. Why can’t I have somebody like that to run against? Actually, I did.”
He launched a fresh attack on Ilhan Omar, the Minnesota congresswoman whose Washington home was recently raided by the FBI , citing a fraud probe. He announced that a federal court filing had identified the Somalian native by a different name, Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, and called on her to resign as she had been sworn in under another name. He waited as the crowd broke into a chant of “Lock Her Up”, temporarily drowning out the background hum of the power generators. It was a return to the messaging of 2024: the threat of outsiders, of otherness, of danger threatening the pastoral – which he can ward off.
“I think Trump and his whole administration have a lot of common sense compared to the other side,” Lonnie, who preferred not to give a surname, said as we waited in line to buy water.
“I love that he closed the border immediately. I feel safer with him. The gas prices are higher, I know, right now. I think they will come down but they were also super high under Biden.”
Trump’s arrival in Sioux City coincided with another turbulent week. The surface depiction of the Republican midterm prospects is of a campaign putting out fires everywhere. His Wednesday-night rally in South Carolina was subject to some 30 protesters interrupting his presidential riff. They were, as usual, quickly booed and removed by security to loud chants of “USA USA”. But the protests, becoming more numerous and brazen, would have been unimaginable two years ago.
Then, in Ohio, came outrage over an advert broadcast on behalf of the Republican gubernatorial candidate, Vivek Ramaswamy. It features Donna Arthur, the estranged mother of Democratic candidate Amy Acton, in which she urges people not to vote for her daughter, and calls her a “liar”. Acton had suffered physical and sexual abuse by her stepfather as a young child, and she and her brother were removed by social services following a court hearing. Arthur remained with the stepfather. Several Republicans have condemned the advert, including Mike DeWine, Ohio’s governor, who described is as “deeply, deeply troubling”.
“It was wrong to run this ad. I would just urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take it down,” he said.
Vice-president JD Vance – a native Ohioan – was among those who doubled down in a stumps speech that will almost certainly be quoted back at him, ad nauseam, if he runs for president, scolding party members because Ramaswamy’s campaign “had the audacity to run a TV commercial that calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar”.
Trump himself castigated DeWine as a “Rino [Republican in name only] governor” who was “disloyal to the Republican Party” on Thursday afternoon.
By Thursday, reports began to emerge of heightened Republican concerns – and an influx of money into the normally safe senate seats in Mississippi and South Carolina. As if all of this wasn’t enough to contend with, along came the farcical news that the staff of embattled war secretary Pete Hegseth had, in responding to the secretary’s impatience to add to his office furnishings the unique globe reputedly used by Dwight Eisenhower in the planning of the D-Day landings, dropped it while transporting it, and partially broke it.
[ Is controversy-plagued Pete Hegseth eyeing up a 2028 presidential bid? Opens in new window ]
None of these events were likely to enhance Trump’s mood on this latest leg of his relentless national tour of the republic. But in a field in Iowa, as evening fell, he felt the love.
Both parties in Iowa agree this race is likely to come down to a narrow number of votes either way. Although Turek has mounted a compelling case against the Trump administration, persuading Iowa’s farmer class to abandon Trumpism will be key.
“I think there’s a lot of tribalism,” Turek had told me on Tuesday evening when asked why, if Iowans are hurting as much as he claims, the race is so close.
“And that’s hard to overcome. Ultimately, I don’t think about why it’s so close, I think about it in the reverse. This is a state that Trump ended up winning by nearly 13 points and in one calendar year we have taken this from solidly Red to toss-up to leading in the polls. I look at it as: what amazing work to go to all 99 counties in 400 days and, more and more, I think a lot of moderate Republicans are seeing a difference between myself and Ashley Hinson. I am hearing people say: ‘Look, I voted for Trump two times, three times, but you got my vote. Because this is about the person and not the party.’ And that’s something I’m excited about – I am genuinely bipartisan and I don’t think any party has a monopoly on good ideas.”
Out at the airport hangar, parents with children began to file out of the rally after the first hour. It was dark and many had already been here for five hours. It may also be true that the Trump era has reached the stage where for some supporters, the thrill now is in seeing him, in their town, maybe for the final time, and to feel the energy of all that dark drama that surrounds him, and to have the photographs for posterity.
There was something unforgettable about the scene for those of us trooping out to the rows of cars in darkened fields; the secret service and police leaning on metal railings, the Trump merch hawkers packing away their wares and that voice that has dominated the country for a decade drifting from the hangar into a dream of a Midwestern evening. Sooner rather than later, these events, this night, will form part of the mad tapestry of American history.
Shortly before he headed into his last pre-military weekend in Sioux City, Klein had offered a final thought in the bright sunshine before going to wait for his president. He was talking about the book of revelations in the Bible, and a reference to the world being under one leadership.
“So, I believe there will come a time when America will fall,” he said.
“Whether that’s in the next 100 years, 150 years, I don’t know. But I’m not gonna just stand by and just wait for it to happen. I’m going to go fight for my country. It’s an amazing country. I can join the military because I want to do it. I’m not forced. There is so much freedom that people take for granted. I take pride in our country. I honestly think the last presidency was not pro our country. They want people to come out here with signs, and they want people to go against each other. We have an amazing country. The American way is great. People want to come to our country and live the American dream – but it’s not the same any more because people are so divided.”

title: Top 10 EV myths that need to die
description: And one that’s absolutely true …
content:
We’ve all heard them from the pseudo engineer neighbour or the barstool expert, but why do these EV myths still linger? And what can we do to dispel them?
This one dates back to the initial arrival of the earliest modern-day electric cars, back in 2010, and chiefly to the original Nissan Leaf. Back then, Nissan was playing things very safe and said that there was a chance that the battery pack might be exhausted within seven years (or that it would fall below 70 per cent of its original charging capacity).
EV critics leapt on that and continue to do so, but it’s simply not the case. Nissan was merely being – understandably – conservative in its estimates. Not only do batteries last way, way longer than that, but we recently had a spin in a decade-old Leaf, and it would still do 90km of its original 160km on a not-quite-full charge (and bear in mind that the original range estimate was done under the more lenient old NEDC test). Beyond that, batteries can be replaced – such as by Range Therapy in Kildare – and can even be replaced by more energy-dense, longer-range batteries while the old packs can often be reused as home energy storage, or they can be sent to be recycled into brand new batteries (try doing that with a litre of petrol).
Absolutely not the case, in either sense. It’s 233km to drive from the centre of Dublin to Donegal town, and you could do that in a Hyundai Inster – the smallest and currently most affordable EV on the market – with range to spare. Once you’re in Donegal town and the surrounding area, there are more than a dozen charging locations, including ESB fast chargers with up to 200kW of DC charging power and slower kerbside chargers if you want to top up overnight. A 30-minute stop at a DC fast charger in most electric cars will give you plenty enough charge to get back to Dublin without stopping.
Wrong, wrong, wrong. With lots of home charging, The Irish Times has calculated that an average family-hatchback-sized EV can be powered up for 16,000km annually for around €800, and that includes a little bit of public fast charging for longer journeys. By comparison, an equivalent petrol-powered hatchback, averaging 6.0 litres per 100km, will set you back more than €1,800 in petrol costs at current pump prices.
That was true at one time. Carmakers front-loaded their electric tech (which, in fairness, is expensive to develop) into larger, more luxurious, and therefore more profitable models. Now, though, as batteries and their associated technology become much cheaper, in terms of wholesale costs, and the initial research and development cost starts to get soaked up, we’re seeing a positive glut of very affordable electric cars.
The Hyundai Inster – which is way more capable all-round than you’d think for such a small car – starts at €19,595. A Renault 5 E-Tech, with a 410km range, can be bought for €29,295. The new Volkswagen ID.Polo will be priced from around €20,000. A Peugeot E-3008 costs pretty much the same as the hybrid-engined version. Electric cars haven’t just become more affordable; they’ve actually become cheaper than their petrol-powered counterparts in many cases, and that’s before you factor in cheaper running costs.
Don’t be silly. Batteries and motors are weather-sealed, so they’re actually less likely to be damaged by water than an air-breathing petrol or diesel engine. Electric cars are also better in flood conditions, up to a point, than their combustion counterparts, as there are no worries about sloshing water down the air intake (although you do need to be careful that grit and contaminants from dirty floodwater don’t damage the electric motor or get into high-voltage wires).
A car wash is absolutely fine. And a lightning storm? Quite apart from the fact that the batteries are fully sealed and the high-voltage components equally so, what lightning is trying to do is to find its way quickly to the ground, and cars – of any sort – don’t offer it an easy path. It’s not the rubber tyres; it’s actually the steel and aluminium structure, which acts as a Faraday cage, diverting electric current around the edges of the bodywork. You’re in far greater danger walking through a lightning storm than driving an EV.
We will grade this as partially true. It’s certainly the case that public charging, both rapid and slow, still has a lot of work to do in building out the network, but according to estimates, Ireland is just about installing enough charging coverage to keep pace with the growth of EV sales. More would be nice, of course, and will definitely be needed in the near future as more and more of us switch to electric power. It’s a bit of a case of some done, lots to do.
Nope. It’s true that nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) batteries can, when damaged or when they overheat, enter a state called “thermal runaway”, which causes a catastrophic fire that is very hard to extinguish, as the burning battery chemicals actually make their own oxygen. Lithium-iron-phosphate batteries, though, are much less likely to suffer this, and they’re becoming much more common, and the switch to solid-state batteries, which will take place over the next decade, will eradicate the issue entirely.
In the meantime, EVs actually have a lower pro-rata rate of fire incidents than petrol or diesel cars – you are carrying around a 60 litre tank of highly flammable fluid, after all.
“I served in the fire service for 14 years, so I’m well aware of vehicle fires; I’ve first-hand experience,” says Nevo’s Derek Reilly. “The data globally shows that petrol and diesel fires are far more likely to happen. Yes, when an EV catches fire, there is a chance of thermal runaway, but fire services are adapting to this with new techniques and equipment. Manufacturers are also aware of this and developing less volatile battery chemistry make-ups, along with working with emergency services to allow easy access to flood the battery compartment.
Again, partially true. There’s a complex dance to be carried out when you plug in, between the battery of your car and what sort of state it’s in, the charging system fitted to your car and the type of charger and the amount of power actually reaching it. It’s always an imperfect science, but when it works right, it’s brilliant.
We’ve done plenty of 10-80 per cent charges in fast-charging models such as the Kia EV6 and Audi e-Tron GT and were back on the road in little more than 20 minutes. Newer cars, such as the Mercedes CLA, can potentially add as much as 330km of extra range in just 10 minutes, and BYD is working on new ultra-fast chargers that can deliver a 97 per cent charge in just five minutes. In the meantime, it’s not really an issue for most EV drivers, who mostly charge – cheaply – at home overnight.
It’s true that if every driver in Ireland owned an electric car and all plugged in to charge at the exact same moment, there wouldn’t be enough power to go around. But that’s not how these things work. In fact, having lots of EVs connected to the grid can help the way engineers balance the demand load of the entire island. Already, Ohme chargers and the ESB are conducting experiments to see exactly how far they can push this, and equally, people are using their cars as power banks (or installing home storage batteries) to power their homes during power cuts or when there’s high demand on the system.
Electric cars charging up at night are also a fantastic way to make good use of wind energy generated at times when there’s not a lot of grid demand, so that energy won’t go to waste as it largely does now. If anything, having lots of EVs on the road is going to drastically improve Ireland’s power grid.
Derek Reilly has come across this myth a lot at Nevo’s various shows. “EirGrid have constantly confirmed that our network has plenty of capacity, especially for electric vehicles. It suits a grid perfectly because most of the charging happens overnight when we have excess energy with low demand and usually high renewable wind energy with nowhere else to go. In other markets we see the benefits of dynamic tariffs, but that’s for a different article.”
EVs are like any other type of car in this respect. Some are deeply dull to drive. Most are fine, but perhaps unexciting. A few are absolutely brilliant. The brilliant ones? The Renault 5 – Nissan Micra – Alpine A290 trio. The Audi e-Tron GT, Porsche Taycan and new Cayenne Turbo. The Porsche Macan. The Volkswagen ID.7 GTX. The BMW iX3. The Mercedes CLA and GLC. The Kia EV4, the Hyundai Ioniq 5 and the Ioniq 6 (and no, not just the N versions). The Kia EV6. The Polestar 2, 3, 4, and 5.
Electricity is just a power source. What matters when it comes to driving fun is sharp steering, good body control, and well-tuned suspension. Plenty of EVs have all three, and many more are on the way.
Yup, this is an absolute, at least for the moment. With home charging, you unlock way more convenience (your car is full every time you walk out the door in the morning) and enormous cost savings. Equally, it means that you only need to use the – too often too expensive – public charging network, which can exceed €40 for a top-up depending on the car, and dependency on which can make an EV simply too expensive to run.
Does that mean that EV ownership will always be effectively restricted to those with a driveway? Not necessarily – some solutions for home charging have been introduced for those with apartments, and there are calls to equalise the VAT costs between home charging and public charging, which would bring down the cost of public charging quite a bit. There is also talk of discounted local community public charging being rolled out. Other solutions will be needed, but for now, yes, you’re better off with a home charger than without.

title: What do experienced EV drivers think of their electric motoring lives?
description: We spoke to Irish drivers who’ve had their electric cars for at least three years — sometimes longer — to see if their experience has changed over time
content:
Electric motoring is evolving fast. Since the original Nissan Leaf was launched, we’ve gone from EVs having a range of around 160km to cars that can quadruple that figure, or even more. We’ve gone from 50kW being considered a fast charge to seven times that power and further. We’ve gone from a charging network that didn’t exist to one that, mostly, does.
So what do Irish EV drivers actually think? How has their experience changed over time? And are they happy to stick with electric cars?
Mona and Mike Wheatley, from Monaghan, have been at this for a while. Mona got her first Nissan Leaf back in 2016, and she’s had two more since then before switching to a larger, longer-ranged Nissan Ariya a year ago.
“The range was fine back then, but you know the charging network across the country at that time wasn’t very good,” said Mona. “It’s not much better at the moment … Well, it is better at the moment, but unfortunately there are more electric cars queuing to make use of them. That’s the problem.”
“We’ve mostly been able to charge at home,” she continued. “That was a big plus. Across all the years of owning an EV, I’ve never found a major drop-off in performance nor range as the cars aged, other than you’d notice a drop in range in the winter. I would normally have turned the car over every two to three years, though.”
Mona and Mike’s driving takes them regularly from their home to see family in Dublin, and also to Westport and to their holiday home in Ennis. Do they find those longer journeys difficult? Certainly not with the Ariya they don’t.
“I left Monaghan the other day with a 95 per cent battery and a displayed range of 535km” said Mike. “I pulled in to Ennsicrone with 63 per cent and 354km showing, although in fairness I did give it a very quick top-up, an extra 28km worth, in Ballina.”
The secret to keeping electric motoring costs down, reckons Mike, is to be on the ball with your home energy provider. “People who are seriously into electric cars, they need to get streetwise from a point of view of a yearly basis, looking at their provider. I’m with Bord Gáis. I moved there about six months ago, and I have a 25 per cent discount there. So we can charge, you know, from 12 o’clock to eight in the morning, and that’s at 20 cent per kWh.”
Bryan McCoy is from Kildare and is currently on his second car from all-electric Sino-Swedish brand Polestar. “I had a Polestar 2 since 2023 and have just recently changed to a Polestar 4. Overall, my experience of owning an EV has been very positive. Most of my normal driving is relatively local, commuting and shorter journeys, mainly Maynooth to Tallaght for work, but I do plenty of longer trips around the country as well.
For everyday driving, I find an EV incredibly easy to live with. I charge at home, generally overnight, and we recently had solar panels installed, so most mornings the car is ready to go and public charging isn’t something I need to think about very often.”
As well as having his second Polestar, Byran has also managed to convince his partner, Sandy, to switch to electric too, and she now drives a Cupra Born VZ. “Public charging is probably a bit of a mixed bag,” said Bryan.
“There are definitely more chargers and much better high-speed charging options than there were a few years ago, which makes longer journeys easier. At the same time there are a lot more EVs on the road, so busy charging locations can still occasionally be frustrating. For me, though, because the vast majority of charging is done at home, it hasn’t really been a big issue.
“I think one of the biggest misconceptions is that you spend your time worrying about charging. Once you have home charging, you very quickly stop thinking about it. It just becomes part of the routine. I actually find it more convenient than having to stop at a petrol station.”
It certainly doesn’t seem as if Bryan will be dropping electric motoring any time soon. “Moving from the Polestar 2 to the Polestar 4 has also been a fairly big step forward,” he said. “The extra range, space and technology make it feel like EVs are maturing quite quickly. I certainly couldn’t see myself going back to petrol or diesel at this stage.”
Frank Gleeson lives in the midlands, and he’s on his second Volkswagen ID.4. Having started with a small-battery ID.4 52kWh, he’s recently upgraded to the bigger battery version, with 77kWh, for longer journeys such as holidays and trips to see family.
“I generally do a round trip of 70km twice a week to play golf. I drive to local towns a few times a week, round trips of 20km and 40km. I visit family in Dublin, Sligo, Westport and Mullingar on occasions. These journeys range from 240km to 300km round trips. My wife and I travel to the southeast for a number of breaks during the year, a round trip of 400km.
“I did not notice any significant battery degradation in the first ID.4, which I owned for three years. I only have the current car for eight months. I have had no issues with either car. I have observed major improvements in the availability of fast charging on all routes that I use and at all destinations that I travel to. I do not normally need to use these facilities, but the improvement is obvious.”
Frank is another who’s managed to convince a family member to change their car to electric – his wife, Una, now drives a Ford Puma Gen-E.
Moira Hallissey, from Cork, converted herself from a diesel Audi A3 to an electric Nissan Leaf four years ago, largely because, as an accountant, she just couldn’t ignore the benefit-in-kind advantages. “I suppose that was initially my main reason for moving to the EV [even though] that benefit eroded over the years.
“But at this stage I’m converted and there’s no going back. I started with the Leaf four years ago, and now I’ve upgraded to a Nissan Ariya.
“I generally use the ESB’s app when I’m charging away from home, and that has been very positive, as you can see in advance where there are available chargers or how long you’re likely to be waiting. I’ve no issues with that – it’s part of the game, isn’t it? I don’t have the figures to hand, but I would think, along with the solar panels I have on the house, that I’m only paying around 25 per cent for charging compared to what I used to pay in diesel costs.”

title: EV battery jargon buster
description: Do you know your solid-state from your LFP? If not, then you need to read this
content:
If your new car is going to be powered by batteries, instead of petrol or diesel, you’d better get to know the different types of battery that are available.
No, actually what we mean is that there are two distinct and different types of electric car battery available, which use different battery chemistry.
No, we’ll keep this as simple as we can. Both types of battery use lithium for energy storage, because lithium is great at separating out the electrons from its atoms, thereby creating an ion – hence the name lithium-ion battery. Those electrons flow through the battery from a cathode to an anode, creating a flow of electricity, before joining up with their original atoms again and keeping the battery in balance.
The basic principles are the same, but the two variations of the chemistry – lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) work in subtly different ways.
Not specifically, no. They’re good (and bad) at different things. Let’s start with NMC batteries, as those are currently the most common, and they’re the ones we’re more used to. With lithium as the storage material, the nickel, manganese and cobalt refer to the materials used for the battery’s cathode and anode, its negative and positive terminals.
NMC batteries can be designed around seriously high power outputs and can generally store more energy for a given size and weight than an LFP battery. So far, they’ve also had generally faster charging speeds (although that’s starting to change).
The downsides? NMC batteries are more expensive, generally, and use more rare earth metals, which can be environmentally (and socially) damaging. They are also much more likely to suffer “thermal runaway” and fires if damaged.
In some ways, yes. LFP batteries use simple iron in the cathode (hence the name – the F in LFP comes from ferro, the Latin for iron) and don’t need any cobalt, so they’re much less harmful in terms of mining, etc. They’re also much more tolerant of regular fast charging and don’t mind being charged up fully to 100 per cent, unlike NMC batteries, which are happier being charged between 20 and 80 per cent most of the time.
LFP batteries are also much more robust when damaged and much less likely to start a fire. And they’re cheaper to make in the first place. So why doesn’t everyone use LFP batteries? Because, mostly, they’re less energy dense than an NMC battery, which affects range, and so far they’ve usually not been able to charge up as fast as a high-performance NMC battery.
Yes, some LFP batteries are now starting to match their NMC equivalents. The likes of BYD (which designs and makes all its own batteries and only uses LFP chemistry) and Xpeng are now making LFP batteries that are a closer match for energy storage to NMC batteries and that can charge at frankly ludicrous speeds. Xpeng already has a battery in its G6 SUV that can charge at up to 541kW on a DC connection (that’s way more powerful than any current Irish charging point), while BYD is currently rolling out in China batteries that can charge at up to 1,500kW (!) potentially allowing for a 95 per cent charge in just five minutes.
Possibly so, but that’s without considering solid-state batteries …
Yes, this is technology that’s been bandied about for almost a decade as the game-changer for electric car batteries, but that has also seemed just out of reach in production terms.
Batteries need an electrolyte – a pathway for the stored energy to travel from the negative to the positive terminals – and in both LFP and NMC designs this is a liquid electrolyte, which usually contains a chemical called lithium hexafluorophosphate, often dissolved in an alcohol-based solution.
It’s this electrolyte that’s the limiting factor in current battery design, and it’s why batteries need complex cooling and heating systems. Keep that electrolyte in its happy temperature zone – usually around 21 degrees – and all is well. Let it get too cold, and performance drops. Let it get too hot, such as when fast charging, and you can damage the battery. Let it get really too hot, and you’ve got a battery fire.
A solid state battery does away with all that, using an electrolyte that suspends the lithium hexafluorophosphate, or other chemical, in a ceramic material.
Well, it almost entirely eliminates the possibility of a battery fire, for a start, but better still is the effect on how much energy a battery can store and therefore how big a battery needs to be. It’s been estimated that a solid state version of a current 50kWh NMC battery, for example, could weigh as little as 100kg, instead of 500kg with current tech. Solid state batteries are also supposedly going to be way, way faster to charge, and harder to damage with repeated charging, improving battery life.
Probably the Chinese. Geely has said that its solid-state batteries should be on sale from next year, and the good news is that, as well as Geely models, European-friendly Polestar and Volvo models are due to get these new batteries too. Geely is already talking about 1,000km ranges from these new batteries.
Stellantis Group (the likes of Peugeot, Fiat, Opel, Citroen, Jeep etc) and Mercedes are reckoned to be hot on Geely’s heels with solid-state tech, but there’s an interesting wrinkle – Ford is working on a new battery chemistry called Lithium Manganese Rich (LMR), and it reckons that this new design could be as safe and reliable as an LFP battery but much more energy-dense, which means more range for a given size of battery.
Most likely, it’ll be a multi-battery solution. Solid-state tech is, for now, expensive, so it will probably be mostly fitted to more expensive cars at first, while more affordable models will increasingly switch to LFP and, maybe, Ford’s new LMR design.

title: Henry VIII was reason for Annals of Inisfallen finding their way to Britain
description: We must not forget that valuable British manuscripts have found their way here, too
content:
Sir, – It is unfair of Chris Doyle to imply that the Bodleian Library’s possession of the Annals of Inisfallen was due to British imperial expansion and colonisation (“ The Annals of Inisfallen are part of Irish history. They don’t belong in a British library ”, Opinion, October 21st).
The main reason for the movement of this and many other medieval manuscripts away from their place of origin in Britain and Ireland was Henry VIII’s dissolution of the monasteries, not British imperialism.
We should be grateful to Finghín MacCarthy Rea, James Ware, Richard Rawlinson and the Bodleian Library for preserving (legally) this wonderful text for posterity rather than complaining that people Chris Doyle talked to in Munster feel it should be in Ireland.
Similarly, I hope the British people are grateful that one of the finest British medieval manuscripts, Matthew Paris’s Life of St Alban, in danger of disappearing from the world when the Abbey of St Alban’s was closed by Henry VIII, was acquired by the Elizabethan scholar John Dee, then by James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh , and finally made its way, with the rest of Ussher’s collection, into the library of Trinity College Dublin , where it has been carefully looked after since 1661.
Should Trinity College be returning this and Ussher’s other British medieval manuscripts to their place of origin? I don’t believe so. The dissolution of the monasteries dispersed many important ancient texts to various destinations.
The acquisitions of British imperialism are another matter altogether. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Chris Doyle thinks the Annals of Inisfallen should be permanently returned to Ireland from the Bodleian Library, Oxford. Maybe we could do a swap.
Many experts believe the Book of Kells was produced on Iona. Iona is, for good or ill, still part of the United Kingdom . You give us Inisfallen, we’ll give you Kells? – Yours, etc,
Professor Emeritus of Medieval Irish History,

title: Smaller cars a simple solution to congestion issues
description: No need for large SUVs and crossovers in our cities
content:
Sir, – “ Car size isn’t everything ” (Letters, October 21st) makes a good point. Cities and towns are seeing a huge increase in larger cars , even though there is less space available due to bus and cycle lanes.
People not using public transport should be encouraged more to purchase the smaller electric cars that are now available. Sponsored celebrities and sports stars driving these cars would make it “more acceptable” for city dwellers to drive smaller vehicles.
Most cars, even electric, on our streets are too big and do nothing to alleviate traffic congestion. People living in urban areas driving large SUVs and crossovers should be curtailed, especially as most have only one person on board for most journeys.
Smart cars, which are so popular and fashionable in other European cities, are a much better alternative and more environmentally friendly. – Yours, etc,

title: Connacht aim to maintain high standards for Zebre clash
description: After brilliant Champions Cup victory over Saracens, Connacht must follow up with victory over Italian side in URC
content:
Connacht can choose to label a brilliant Champions Cup victory over Saracens in whatever fashion they care but a legacy is that it will be a benchmark of sorts against which subsequent performances will be measured. And there’s no harm in setting a high bar.
Not everything was perfect in victory but boy there was plenty to admire, particularly the way Connacht ripped holes in the Saracens defence. For the most part they did the groundwork to tie in the defenders before transitioning to the space in the wider channels. Occasionally, as in Ciarán Frawley’s try straight from a long lineout throw, they discovered an unmanned gap.
It was a great occasion on and off the pitch, raucous and colourful. Those noise levels won’t be replicated on Friday night but therein lies the challenge, Connacht must get up for the game, play with purpose and accuracy. That’s the respect they’ll pay a Zebre team who lost heavily at home last weekend to an Ulster side missing a host of frontline players.
Connacht head coach Stuart Lancaster acknowledged the need for continuity in personnel and performance. “Last Saturday was special for a few reasons, but now we’ve fully shifted our focus back to the URC, particularly with the six-day turnaround.
“There are still a few areas for us to work on, and having coached against Zebre many times we know how challenging this game will be. It’s great to have eight players selected for Ireland duty, so we’re hoping they’ll make another positive impact before they head to camp next week.”
He has rested just two, Bundee Aki and Billy Bohan, of the players selected in Andy Farrell’s Ireland squad for the Nations Championship. Aki’s absence sees Harry West come into the team at outside centre for his first game of the season, Cathal Forde switches to the 12 jersey, while Mack Hansen returns after missing the victory over Saracens.
Lancaster freshens up the pack, with Jerry Cahir making his competitive debut for the province after his summer move from Leinster, Eoin de Buitléar swaps the bench for a starting role, with Finlay Bealham completing the frontrow.
Brothers Niall and Darragh Murray link up in the secondrow, while Paul Boyle is promoted to the backrow where he joins Ireland internationals, captain Cian Prendergast and Sean Jansen.
Hooker Dave Heffernan has recovered from injury and is named among the replacements, a group that also includes Will Connors, who will make his Connacht debut having joined from Leinster. Daniel Ryan is a young prospect who has made great strides and will add quality off the bench. The same could be said of Sean Naughton and West.
Increasing the depth of quality in the Connacht squad has promoted greater competition for places and this aspect along with injured and rested players returning should galvanise the home side to produce the type of display that can build on the Saracens win.
Frawley’s game management, allied to the work of his halfback partner Colm Reilly, and the running threat in the three-quarter line should thrive based on the likely platform provided by the pack.

Replacements: D Heffernan, J Duggan, S Illo, D O’Connor, W Connors, C Blade, S Naughton, D Ryan.
