title: Running the rule over new changes to Gaelic football rules
description: Perhaps we could keep the old ways to reduce the confusion
content:
Sir, – There are more rule changes proposed for Gaelic football . On top of that, the old new rules may be revised. Soon we will have new old new rules and new new new rules.
The speed of change is too much. It is as though someone gave backchat to the rules committee and the ball was moved up 50 metres.
For what it’s worth, I believe that the old new rules rule okay and I suggest that the new rules be ruled out. It’s a hard decision. Who would be a ruler? – Yours, etc,

title: Paddy McKillen’s Clarendon refinances London retail properties with private lender
description: Bank of Ireland debt has been refinanced under a new €17m facility with Hilco Real Estate Finance
content:
Paddy McKillen and Tony Leonard’s Clarendon Properties has refinanced debt on a number of prominent retail properties in west London through a new £14.6 million (€17.43 million) facility from private credit lender Hilco Real Estate Finance.
The property group owns 20,000sq ft (1,858 sq m) of retail property across seven properties on Kensington High Street in London through two Irish subsidiaries called Ringston Investments Limited and Jackson Investments Limited.
The latest accounts for the companies, which reported bank borrowings of £16.6 million at the end of June 2025, showed they owned a combined £22.9 million of property on the popular retail street.
New filings by each company with the Companies Registration Office show they have refinanced existing Bank of Ireland borrowings with Hilco Real Estate Finance under a new £14.595 million facility.
The documents said the financing deal was linked to its west London properties 146 and 148 Kensington High Street and 150–158 on the same street, some of which are occupied by sports store Decathlon and homeware shop Robert Dyas.
Ringston Investments Limited and Jackson Investments Limited have both granted Hilco security over the properties under an agreement in recent days.
Further documents showed additional security has been provided by Clarendon Properties Limited, Clarendon Properties (Holdings) Unlimited Company, Puzzle Investments and Signature Concepts, which each pledged debt owed to them as part of the financing agreement.
No interest rate or maturity date for the debt with Hilco Real Estate Finance was provided in the filings.
[ New Premier Inn hotel at Clerys Quarter seeking more than €66m Opens in new window ]
Clarendon Properties, founded by McKillen and Leonard in 1996, also owns a number of prominent properties in Dublin , including Powerscourt Town Centre on South William Street and several Victorian-era buildings on College Green in the city centre.
Its portfolio is held across a network of more than a dozen companies. Earlier this year, financial filings for 11 of its subsidiaries showed its Irish-based properties were valued at a combined €147.3 million at the end of June 2025, a 3 per cent increase year on year.

title: Racing has feel-good story with Billy Lee a deserving champion jockey
description: Oldest first-time champion in almost 50 years is professional’s professional
content:
Deserve is a luxury concept in racing. Plenty of shady individuals have got a lot more than they should reasonably be entitled to. Almost as rare in professional sport is a general sense of goodwill towards individual good fortune. But racing has just such a feelgood story with Billy Lee about to be crowned champion jockey.
The title is in the bag. Lee is uncatchable with a 19-winner lead over his nearest rival Colin Keane, 98 to 79. The campaign ends next weekend. It’s an outcome that has seemed fated, another wishy-washy concept usually useful only to those scrambling for a narrative structure but in this case apt.
Another ‘Billy’ was crowned champion jockey in Britain last weekend. At 20, Billy Loughnane is the youngest British champion in over a century. Already earning comparisons to Lester Piggott and Frankie Dettori, Loughnane enjoys a rapidly growing popular profile and promises to be the face of the sport for years to come.
In contrast, Billy Lee is 40, and almost an epitome of understatement. He has never won a classic race. His Group One tally is four. Loughnane already has one more than that. Lee will be the oldest new champion jockey in Ireland in almost half a century. Tommy Murphy was 42 when successful in 1978.
But while the youngster deservedly revels in his new status, there are no offers about which of the titles will be more professionally satisfying. Loughnane could be champion for years to come. Lee has succeeded through years of persistence, professionalism and repeatedly putting himself in a position to avail of opportunity.
Runner-up three times previously, including when beaten by just three winners by Keane in 2022, Lee’s chance looked to have gone. Without one of the major jobs to call on, the fact he regularly got close to championship success was a remarkable feat of improvisation, reflective of a willingness to ride for most anyone and everyone.
When Keane landed the Juddmonte job last year, it opened a chink of light only for Lee’s chances to be scuppered by a broken collarbone at the height of the summer. It wasn’t injury but suspension that had previously compromised his chances. They are the twin threats to any championship challenge as this season has underlined once again.
Dylan Browne McMonagle was eventually crowned champion in 2025 and started very short odds to repeat this year. With the unparalleled numerical strength in depth of Joseph O’Brien’s yard behind him, as well as momentum from big-race successes such as Ethical Diamond in the Breeders’ Cup, it wasn’t hard to see the bookies’ reasoning.
But injury meant he missed the opening weeks of the campaign. Lee and Keane cut out an impressive tempo at the top of the table, although when Browne McMonagle returned it only looked a matter of time before they were reeled in. Sure enough, the latter remorselessly closed only to pick up a significant injury towards the end of August.
Combined with Keane’s Juddmonte commitments repeatedly taking him to ride abroad, it was finally Lee’s turn to put his stamp on the championship. Paddy Twomey and Willie McCreery have supplied the backbone of his winners, but he has ridden for more than 50 trainers in all. He is also the only rider in the country to have had more than 600 mounts. There have been just two short suspensions.
The title will reflect consistency, application and professionalism, virtues that mightn’t smack of glamour but underpin a singularly demanding job. Lee is the professional’s professional. He hasn’t been appointed to one of racing’s top jobs but there can hardly be anyone who doesn’t believe he wouldn’t measure up to such a position. This title reflects a lifetime’s hard work.
Just how hard will really resonate with those who have also had to battle the scales themselves. Physically Lee is no featherweight, but the job demands he weighs in daily as one. As a younger man, it looked like he would lose the fight when he started riding over hurdles. He says his weight eventually settled, a bland phrase that hardly reflects the effort of will behind it.
Such are the tiny margins that the 3lb increase in minimum weights on the flat introduced by the Irish Horseracing Regulatory Board in 2021 has proved transformative. The life of a jockey means light is always right. But there are degrees and the IHRB move reflected the reality of general societal trends.
“What helped me was the weights going up. That allowed me a bit more comfortable, 100 per cent,” he commented. “There weren’t many taller than me in the weigh-room when I started. But now, they’re all towering over me.”
Lee goes to Dundalk this evening for five rides with four different trainers. He’s got a first “century” of winners in his sights. There’s a trip next week to the Breeders’ Cup to look forward to. He will continue riding on the all-weather during the winter, doing what he’s always done, but this time as champion jockey.
“The hunger to do it was always there and for it to be finally happening is special. It’ll be lovely to have on the CV, and it’ll be there forever, thank God,” he says.
An unsettled weather outlook for the Bank Holiday weekend means it could pay to check tonight’s Dundalk action where Henry De Bromhead’s Premier View (6.45) can make a successful debut on the artificial surface. He is on a hat-trick after a pair of wins at Down Royal last month and can exploit a low draw.
Billy Lee will at Doncaster tomorrow for a Listed contest on the Goffs Million runner-up Hi Corbett Court. He faces a task though against Begal Tiger (2.05) who won by 12 lengths on soft ground at Naas 12 days ago and should be right at home in testing conditions.

title: ‘She’s a special person’: Stephen Bradley hails impact of psychologist
description: Shamrock Rovers manager praises Mary Larkin’s work in wake of James McClean comments
content:
Shamrock Rovers manager Stephen Bradley has highlighted the impact of psychologist Mary Larkin as the club looks to secure a sixth League of Ireland title in seven seasons over the coming week.
Having worked with the Rovers first team for three years, Larkin expanded her role in 2026 to include academy players.
“The club has brought her in to work with the kids,” said Bradley. “I love her, she’s a special person and she’s so good at what she does. She helps so many of us around the [Roadstone] building.
“It’s great that it’s filtering down to our young boys and girls at the club and their parents and their coaches. It’s brilliant to break that stigma with the kids, and that it’s okay to talk. I feel good when I do.
“It’s important what we are doing with Mary, so when the players become young men and women, they are comfortable in that environment and comfortable expressing who they are. She’s incredible.”
Bradley also noted Caroline Currid’s work with the Limerick hurlers, having spent time in John Kiely’s camp the week of an All-Ireland final.
The conversation with Bradley centred around James McClean’s interview in The Sunday Independent when the former Republic of Ireland international described speaking to a therapist “as a weakness”.
Bradley, who considers McClean a friend, said: “My view is that young men, especially in this country, understand that speaking to anyone, a close friend, a stranger, a professional, will help you.
[ Shamrock Rovers boss Stephen Bradley claims FAI disciplinary system ‘not fit for purpose’ Opens in new window ]
“When you speak, it sharpens you. It makes you more focused, more hungry, because you are so much clearer in your head and that’s what I’ve found over the years with Mary.
“I’ve done it for a number of years and have done it since I lost my mam and before that when I got stabbed; I learnt how powerful speaking to someone was, how much it can help you grow as a man, as a person, as it gives you perspective.”
[ How Manchester United became a club too big not to fail Opens in new window ]
When Bradley was an 18-year-old in the Arsenal academy, he was stabbed three times in his London home by an intruder.
“Arsene Wenger said it maybe 15 years ago: you’re not getting a better athlete than Ronaldo, you’re not getting a more skilled player than Messi, but we haven’t tapped into the mind.
“Wenger was always ahead of the game. There is no doubt that it’s the next frontier.”
McClean’s wife Erin McClean released a statement this week after his club Derry City posted on social media that the player’s comment did “not reflect our core values or beliefs”.
“James is struggling at the moment and has been for some time,” she said. “I’m working on getting him to a place where he recognises that speaking about this is not a sign of weakness. When James is suffering from stress or anxiety about a situation his instinct is to lash out.”
Bradley added: “Erin’s [statement] is powerful and shows a picture of what’s going on. She is the one who loves him more than anyone, sees him more than anyone and understands him more than anyone.”

title: Séamus Harnedy back at Páirc Uí Chaoimh as he lines out for hurling-shinty international
description: Double header in Cork on Saturday as Irish camogie and hurling teams take on Scotland
content:
Cork ’s Séamus Harnedy believed his days playing at Páirc Uí Chaoimh were over after announcing his intercounty retirement, but a phone call from Eamon O’Shea will now see the St Ita’s forward line out for Ireland against Scotland at the Leeside venue on Saturday.
Harnedy only brought the curtain down on his 15-year Cork senior career earlier this month but he will be swapping red for green this weekend as one of the players selected by Ireland manager O’Shea to face Scotland in the 2026 hurling-shinty international.
“Finishing up my intercounty career, I probably didn’t envisage being asked to do this, but it’s a great opportunity and I’m delighted to be involved,” says Harnedy.
“Talking to lads who had played it before, it was a no-brainer. They told me about the physicality of the game and how the Scots bring a lot of it to the contest. They’re very passionate about it.
“I thought my days of getting back to the Páirc might be over, so it’ll be incredibly nice to be there.
“Having looked at the rules and watched previous games over the last few days, it’s alien to a GAA player that you can’t catch the ball.
“Even if the ball hits the ground in a ruck, you can’t kick it out of there. It’s going to pose a huge challenge for us, but it’s very exciting and a great opportunity to play in Cork and meet lads from other counties.”
Harnedy (36) is at peace with his decision to step away from the Cork squad, but in paying a glowing tribute to Pat Ryan, he says the former Cork manager actually convinced him not to retire ahead of the 2023 season.
“I was going to step away after 2022, and the county board’s decision to appoint Pat as manager was a major factor in my decision to continue,” admits Harnedy.
“There were two pivotal moments in my career – 2017 and 2023. We won Munster in 2017 and Pat’s coaching, working alongside Kieran Kingston, was hugely important. He’s a wonderful mentor and a wonderful person.
“Patrick Horgan has spoken about how Pat put Cork before himself during a difficult year a couple of years ago. Some of the leaders in the group thought we were going to lose him, but he stayed with us.
“I can’t speak highly enough of Pat Ryan. He’s a brilliant coach who sees the game differently to most people. He’s also an incredibly nice, genuine man who was very important to me throughout my career.”
Harnedy admits a lack of game time this year was a contributing factor in his decision to retire now.
“Did I sometimes think I deserved a little bit more [game time this season]? Yes, I did. But that’s the nature of sport. I’d received the benefit of the doubt so many times throughout my career, and perhaps my run was coming to an end. I’m still incredibly grateful that I went back in last year.”
– The 2026 hurling/camogie-shinty internationals will take place as a double header at Páirc Uí Chaoimh on Saturday. The Ireland v Scotland camogie-shinty game will start at 4pm, followed by the hurling-shinty fixture at 6pm.

title: Trump is about to discover the political cost of inflation
description: US president’s approval rating has crashed in tandem with the squeeze on households
content:
T he great slayer of political careers – inflation – has come for Donald Trump .
The irony is that it won’t be the racist rhetoric, his role in the Capitol riots , or the self-sabotaging tariffs that remove the Teflon, but something entirely more mundane: gas prices.
They have averaged over $4 a gallon for a record 169 days, a timeline that runs concurrent with the Iran war . The average cost of gas in California, the most expensive state, has been over $6 since late September.
Car ownership is a necessity in many parts of the US, with motorists spending on average two-thirds more on fuel than their European counterparts. That’s why fuel costs are such a flashpoint.
The country’s 196,000 gas stations and their price billboards serve as a daily reminder of Trump’s failed war aims, a political burden he now carries into the midterm elections. Polls suggest he will lose big.
[ US and Israel draw up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after midterm elections Opens in new window ]
The latest Reuters/Ipsos survey indicates Trump’s approval rating has fallen to a record low of 31 per cent. It was 44 per cent at the same point in his first term.
More worrying for Trump’s avowedly pro-business administration is that more than two-thirds (68 per cent) of voters disapprove of his handling of the economy, including 37 per cent of republicans.
Asked which party they would vote ⁠for if the elections were held today, some ​47 per cent of registered voters chose Democrats, while 35 per cent chose republicans.
The 12-point advantage in favour of Democrats ​is the widest in the current election cycle and could, if translated into actual votes, see the Democrats seize control of both houses, the House of Representatives and the Senate.
[ What are the US midterms? A visual guide Opens in new window ]
This would hobble Trump’s presidency as Democrats would be in a position to block cabinet and judicial appointments while having subpoena powers to investigate the administration.
The top Democrat on the House oversight committee, Robert Garcia of California, says he will prioritise the examination of Trump’s family businesses, the Epstein files, immigration enforcement, corporate profiteering, and how US health secretary Robert Kennedy jnr has handled vaccines.
US inflation accelerated to 3.7 per cent (in annual terms) in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This was faster than the annual growth in wages (3 per cent), meaning real wages are falling.
Trump’s big mistake has been to dismiss this marker or at least be insensitive to it, repeatedly telling voters that the economy is great and that they’ve never had it so good.
“We have the hottest country anywhere in the world,” he repeatedly says at rallies.
To be fair, the US economy is faring better than many had predicted in the wake of his sweeping “Liberation Day” tariffs in 2025. Unemployment has been at or below 4.5 per cent for 60 consecutive months, a postwar record. Consumer spending remains solid while business investment is being fuelled by the AI boom.
But Trump is falling into the same trap as his predecessor, Joe Biden, in talking up the macroeconomy when consumers and households are being screwed by the micro one: prices.
Jame Carville’s’s famous maxim, “It’s the economy, stupid”, might need to be refined to “It’s the price economy, stupid”, to highlight what matters most to voters in the 2020s.
The Irish Government has learned not to make political capital out of its turbocharged GDP numbers or its windfall taxes, as it only antagonises households in the grip of a price squeeze.
US inflation peaked at 9 per cent in June 2022 as the reopening of the economy after the pandemic led to a burst in price growth. A year later it had fallen to 3.1 per cent and by Trump’s election win in November 2024, it was down to 2.6 per cent. It had been expected to fall to the Federal Reserve’s target rate of 2 per cent by the end of 2025, paving the way for growth-affirming interest rate cuts.
But Trump destroyed that trajectory by imposing tariffs on imported goods. Inflation stopped falling and started to rise again, hitting 3 per cent in September 2025.
Even with the tariffs, US inflation would probably have slowed again this year if the US leader hadn’t gone to war with Iran, triggering a spike in global oil prices.
This has not just driven up petrol prices but also the cost of diesel, the fuel needed to transport everything.
The full ramifications of Trump’s war can be seen through the prism of producer prices, which surged by 6.3 per cent in September. This will translate into further consumer price inflation in the coming months.
High inflation is also resulting in upward pressure on interest rates, further anchoring household spending and Trump’s poll ratings.
Trump’s political shtick has always been to proclaim everything he touches gold. It won’t wash this time.

title: Zenith crowned agency of the year as Digital Media Awards celebrate 2026 winners
description: More than 550 leaders gathered in Dublin for the landmark event, featuring the inaugural digital media hall of fame award
content:
The Dublin Royal Convention Centre played host to the 2026 Digital Media Awards on Friday, October 9th, bringing together upwards of 600 innovators, creators and agency leaders to acknowledge top-tier performance across Ireland’s digital landscape. title: Hiko Tonosa returns to Dublin Marathon looking to regain national title
description: In the absence of the injured Ava Crean, the women’s Irish title race appears wide open
content:
The absence of last year’s two top Irish finishers has opened fresh possibilities for podium places at Sunday’s Dublin Marathon , with Hiko Tonosa hoping for a return to the form that saw him finish third best overall in 2024.
Dublin has doubled as the national championship marathon since 2003, and with last year’s first-time women’s champion Ava Crean ruled out through injury, that crown appears there for the taking.
Tonosa was with the elite leaders until the 30km mark in last year’s race, before running into some difficulty and then dropping out. The 31-year-old from Dundrum South Dublin AC has shown some signs of returning to his best, winning the Antrim Half Marathon in August, clocking 62:07. He won the Irish title in 2024 when clocking a then national record of 2:09:42.
Last year’s top Irish man, David McGlynn, is also absent, still recovering from injury after dropping out of the European Championships marathon in Birmingham in August. Seán Tobin, who won the Dublin Half Marathon in May, is also targeting his first marathon title, along with Clonmel AC club mate William Maunsell, who finished third best Irish man in 2024.
Among the other contenders for the Irish men’s title are Hugh Armstrong from Ballina AC, who ran 2:13:55 to finish fifth in Düsseldorf in April, and Stephen McAuley of Letterkenny AC, a latecomer to marathon running, who finished fourth best Irish man last year.
Crean made national headlines last October when, still only 19, she finished sixth best woman overall. Her time of 2:34:12 was nine minutes faster than she’d run before. With that the Limerick runner also became the youngest Irish athlete to win a national marathon title.
Crean, however, has been sidelined from competitive running since sustaining a hip injury in February. With two-time previous champion Ann-Marie McGlynn also absent on Sunday, having won the Irish women’s title in 2023 and 2024, Sorcha Nic Dhómhnaill is among the favourites to land her first senior title.
Nic Dhómhnaill returns to the marathon distance with a best time of 2:38:19, set in Berlin in 2022, the 41-year-old winning the Dublin City Half Marathon in May in a course record of 71:25, having run a 10km personal best of 32:20 in Valencia in January. After the birth of her daughter Siún in April last year, Nic Dhómhnaill has also impressed with victories in the Dunshaughlin and Dunboyne 10km, also finishing second at the Women’s Mini Marathon in May.
Although her head and heart are telling her yes, Nichola Sheridan is still undecided on whether to line up on Sunday. The event comes just two weeks after Sheridan produced another breakthrough run to finish third overall in the women’s race at the Melbourne Marathon, her time of 2:29:13 the fastest by an Irish woman this year, moving her to sixth on the Irish all-time list.
Sunday also presents Sheridan with the possibility of a first senior title, having finished third best Irish woman last year behind Crean and McGlynn, but the 29-year-old is said to be keeping her options open as close to Sunday’s start as possible.
Based in Sydney for the last year, Sheridan had already planned a return trip to her home in Meath this week, in part to celebrate her 30th birthday next Thursday, along with her twin sister Gillian.
Meghan Ryan, also of Dundrum South Dublin, is back and eager to improve on her fourth-place finish in the Irish women’s race last year. The 32-year-old has been running into excellent form, winning the half-marathon race series in Phoenix Park last month in 1:16.46, adding to her national five- and 10-mile titles in recent years.
Judith Storm of City of Derry Spartans AC has also been improving again this year at age 39. After running 2:47:07 on her Dublin debut last year, she lowered her best to 2:39:09 in Belfast, and won the Belfast Half Marathon last month in 1:14:14. A mother of four, including triplets, Storm only took up running after moving to Derry in 2022.
With a total prize pot of €120,000, including time bonuses, the expected windy and possibly wet conditions mean Sunday morning may not be conducive to fast times. However, the elite international entries include Ethiopia’s Abay Alemu, whose personal best of 2:06:50, set in 2024, is two seconds inside Dublin Marathon course record of 2:06:52, set by his fellow countryman Kemal Husen in 2023.
Ethiopia’s Askale Alemayehu leads the elite women’s field, her best of 2:22:56, clocked in Dubai earlier this year, more than a minute inside Asmarech Nega’s Dublin course record of 2:24:13, set in 2024. Kenya’s Risper Chebet is another starter with a career best inside the course record, having run 2:23:45 in 2021.
Patrick Monahan is back in search of a ninth Dublin Marathon title in the wheelchair race, the two-time Paralympian from Kildare first off the line on Sunday morning, when that races begins at 8.40am, before the first mass wave starts at 8.45am.
Live coverage begins on TG4 from 8am, with global viewing also available through TG4 Player.

title: Shamrock Rovers’ Pico Lopes credits ‘enthusiastic’ new signings as title is within grasp
description: Rovers lead Bohemians by three points with two games remaining in the League of Ireland Premier Division, as they face Sligo Rovers on Friday night
content:
Not exactly down to the wire, but close enough, Shamrock Rovers ’ 2-0 loss to Galway United last Friday at Eamonn Deacy Park kept St Patrick’s Athletic and Bohemians in the League of Ireland title race .
Rovers were caught cold by two goals from long throws.
“Our set-up was slow and sloppy,” admitted Pico Lopes , the Hoops skipper. “Credit to Galway after that, they defended really well.”
Stephen Bradley’s men will be crowned Premier Division champions for a sixth time in seven seasons if they overcome Sligo Rovers in Tallaght on Friday night, and Bohs fail to take three points off Shelbourne at Dalymount Park.
Shelbourne silenced Richmond Park last Friday with two breakaway goals to undo St Pat’s, so John Russell’s side will relish the chance to do the same to Bohs in the north Dublin derby.
In year three of the Stephen Kenny project, St Pat’s lost control of their destiny by losing away to Derry City on Monday. Six points behind Rovers, Kenny admitted that their title race is run.
Bohs seemed out of contention after losing 2-1 to Rovers in Tallaght on October 12th. The fight on the pitch in the immediate aftermath led to the suspension of four players, including Bohs talisman Dawson Devoy.
The League’s disciplinary process came into sharp focus this week as five suspensions were handed down on Wednesday, 12 days after the fracas was broadcast live on Virgin Media.
Devoy is an incalculable loss, but Bohs’ defeat of Waterford last Friday cut Rovers’ lead to three points.
Despite being without the suspended Matt Healy, Danny Grant, Michael Noonan and Naj Razi, while Jack Byrne is injured, the Rovers squad remains strong enough to make light work of relegated Sligo.
But stranger things have happened. Considering the former Sligo Rovers captain Will Fitzgerald was signed by Shamrock Rovers in July, the visitors have a ready-made well of motivation.
The secret to Rovers’ success under Bradley has been their ability to keep a squad of strong characters intact while adding pieces every year like Fitzgerald and former Down Gaelic footballer John McGovern.
“They’ve given us a real injection of enthusiasm,” said Lopes. “We’re trying to guide them and show them the way we’ve done it, but they’re eager and hungry to get their hands on a league medal.
“You can see it. John [McGovern] has been amazing when he’s been fit. He’s chipped in with some really important goals and his all-round play has been improving every time he plays.
“Will’s performances over the last few years have always caught the eye, but to see it in the flesh and what he brings to you is amazing for our team.
“You’re relying on all these players to come in, grab the baton and drive on with it. They’ve done that.”
Lopes rediscovered his groove recently. There was an inevitable post-World Cup dip, after the high of Cape Verde taking Argentina to extra-time in the round of 32, as some uncharacteristic errors coincided with Rovers being knocked out of Europe and the FAI Cup in August.
“Obviously there was a lot of noise when I came back, which was probably to be expected. How much there was blew my mind a little bit.
“But I’ve had some really good people around me to keep me grounded. The best thing I had was the football schedule to try to focus on. Getting back into that was great, because that was normal, that’s what I do, and everything else is a distraction.
“Getting a handle on that for the run-in has been really important.”
If Rovers and Bohs both win tonight, the final Friday night of the season will see the defending champions travel to Oriel Park, where Ciarán Kilduff’s Dundalk could spoil the party, as Bohemians trip across town to face St Pat’s.
Down in the relegation/promotion playoff spot, Drogheda United and Waterford are locked on 37 points ahead of their meeting at the RSC.

title: First-time buyers account for almost two-thirds of Irish mortgage transactions
description: BPFI report indicates there were 8,164 first-time buyer mortgages drawn down in third quarter
content:
First-time buyers continue to dominate the State’s mortgage market , accounting for almost two thirds of transactions.
The latest figures from Banking and Payments Federation Ireland (BPFI) indicate there were 8,164 first-time buyer mortgages drawn down in the third quarter.
This was “the highest Q3 volume since 2008”, the banking group noted.
Three Government-backed programmes – the Help to Buy scheme, First Home scheme and the Local Authority Home Loan scheme – are helping fuel demand for first-time buyer mortgages.
A total of 14,217 mortgages with a value of €4.6 billion were drawn down by all borrowers between July and September this year.
This represented a 13 per cent increase in volume terms and a 15.7 per cent increase in value compared with the same period last year.
First-time buyers remained the single largest segment by volume (57.4 per cent) and by value (58.3 per cent).
Re-mortgaging and switching volumes and values increased by 41.7 per cent and 50.9 per cent year on year respectively, the banking group said.
[ What you need to know about financing a new-build home Opens in new window ]
BPFI chief executive Brian Hayes said: “Our latest figures show continued momentum across the mortgage market, with growth in drawdowns across every customer segment during the third quarter of 2026.”
He noted there were 35,449 mortgage drawdowns valued at almost €11.4 billion in the first nine months of 2026, with volumes up by 8.2 per cent and values up by 12 per cent year on year.
“First-time buyers continue to drive the mortgage market, accounting for almost six in every 10 drawdowns,” Hayes said.
The BPFI said that 3,244 of first-time buyer mortgages drawn down in the third were for new properties, up 7.5 per cent year on year “and the highest Q3 level since 2007”.
The increase in new properties was driven by mortgages on new-build property purchases rather than self-builds, where first-time buyer volumes fell by 5.8 per cent year on year to 666.
The figure indicated that approvals activity also grew in September, up 13.3 per cent in volume and 17 per cent in value year on year, with growth recorded across both first-time buyer and mover purchase segments.
[ Opinion: Subsidies like Help to Buy are no longer needed as homebuyer demand weakens Opens in new window ]
Despite the increased activity, a recent report by the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland found that a first-time buyer couple with two incomes availing of the Government’s Help to Buy scheme still faced a considerable affordability gap when trying to buy a home in Dublin or surrounding counties.
It found that buying couples on a combined income of €113,000 with a 10 per cent deposit (and with the Central Bank’s mortgage rules) would face a shortfall of almost €25,000 in Kildare, €20,500 in Wicklow and €11,500 in Meath.

title: Leinster's Leo Cullen believes Munster clash is the perfect time for experimentation
description: Time is right for Dan Sheehan experiment as Blues prepare to welcome Munster at Aviva
content:
Leo Cullen believes it is an ideal time in the season for experimentation after naming Dan Sheehan at number eight in his Leinster team to face arch rivals Munster in Saturday’s United Rugby Championship game at the Aviva Stadium (kick-off 6pm).
Ordinarily in competition with Rónan Kelleher for the starting hooker spot in the Leinster and Ireland sides, both players will instead be part of the same scrum this weekend.
The Leinster head coach’s decision to select Sheehan alongside Ryan Baird and Josh van der Flier in the backrow is partly brought about because of an injury sustained by Jack Conan in last Saturday’s Champions Cup win at Clermont Auvergne and the continued absence of club captain Caelan Doris.
While Max Deegan and James Culhane have also donned the number eight jersey for Leinster on numerous occasions, Cullen has named Sheehan at the base of the scrum, with Gus McCarthy providing frontrow cover for Kelleher among the replacements. Sheehan had previously featured in the backrow during the latter stages of at least one game and Cullen is confident he can fill the position from the word go on Saturday.
“We’ve tried it a little bit last season. Jack obviously dislocated his shoulder at the weekend, so he’s going to have an op on that. That’s the first bit. We’re blessed with Rónan and Dan, and even with Gus McCarthy and Stevie Smyth there as well coming through. It’s very early in the season still, so it’s worthwhile us trying some things,” Cullen said.
“Rónan starts [at hooker]. He’s played for the Lions, played for Ireland multiple times and then Dan on the team as well. We’ve been discussing it for quite some time at the back of last season and there was an opportunity to try it this weekend.
“He’ll find himself in a similar situation defensively where he would normally be, because the twos and the eights can be quite similar in terms of where they defend. So that role is not going to change drastically for them.”
Although it was known at the beginning of the week that Conan was going to be ruled out of contention for Munster’s visit to the Aviva, there have been some fresh worries for Cullen coming into this weekend’s tussle.
After picking up hamstring and wrist injuries respectively, both Garry Ringrose and Sam Prendergast will be marked absent, with Jamie Osborne and Joey Carbery taking over from them at outside centre and outhalf respectively.
It remains to be seen if this will cast doubt over their availability for Ireland’s Nations Championship Northern Hemisphere Series opener against Argentina on November 6th – Cullen was uncertain of how long either player might be sidelined for – but Leinster will have to persevere without their services for the time being.
A win on Saturday over Clayton McMillan’s side will help Leinster to climb up the URC rankings as the province find themselves occupying 10th spot in the championship table at present.
Yet when you consider Leinster were without the majority of their international contingent, a haul of three points from away encounters with the Lions and the Sharks in South Africa was commendable, and they followed up these games by claiming a bonus-point victory over Cardiff in the revamped Laya Arena.
Last weekend also saw them securing an impressive 48-23 pool stage triumph over Clermont. And Cullen feels the main objective coming into Saturday’s fixture is to keep enhancing the level of their performance.
“It’s just as long as we keep that trajectory of trying to keep improving as a group,” he said.
“We’re sitting down in 10th in the league, so we know we’ve got a hell of a lot of work to do now and to get ourselves up the table. We need to be ready. We’ve tried to prepare well this week.
“It’s a great rivalry, great occasion, and I believe there will be a huge crowd there as well. Which is fantastic and what we all want. We’ve tried to build on the first game in the Laya Arena and we just need to try and keep improving the performances.”
LEINSTER: Hugo Keenan; Tommy O’Brien, Jamie Osborne, Robbie Henshaw, Jimmy O’Brien; Joey Carbery, Jamison Gibson-Park; Andrew Porter, Ronan Kelleher, Tadhg Furlong; Joe McCarthy, James Ryan; Ryan Baird, Josh van der Flier, Dan Sheehan (captain).
Replacements: Gus McCarthy, Alex Usanov, Thomas Clarkson, Conor O’Tighearnaigh, Scott Penny, Fintan Gunne, Caspar Gabriel, Charlie Tector.
MUNSTER: Ben O’Connor; Shay McCarthy, Seán O’Brien, Alex Nankivell, Shane Daly; Charlie O’Shea, Craig Casey; Josh Wycherley, Marnus van der Merwe, Kieran Brookes; Fineen Wycherley, Tadhg Beirne (captain); Jack O’Donoghue, Alex Kendellen, Gavin Coombes.
Replacements: Max Clein, Mark Donnelly, Michael Ala’alatoa, Seán Edogbo, Brian Gleeson, Ben O’Donovan, JJ Hanrahan, Gordon Wood.

title: Australia welcomed tens of thousands of young Irish in recent years. That’s about to change
description: Adjustments to backpacker visas could make staying on less attractive
content:
T he coastal walk between the beaches of Coogee and Bondi is a must-do for visitors to Sydney. The seafront hike, with its spectacular views out to the Tasman Sea, attracts thousands every day.
Last weekend the crowds were particularly large, lured by sunny spring weather and the quirky attractions of the annual Sculpture by the Sea exhibition.
As I trekked north from Coogee, past Bronte and Tamarama and on to Bondi, I was struck by something else. Irish accents were almost as conspicuous as Aussie twangs, a reminder of how Australia has become almost a rite of passage for Irish twentysomethings.
While some young Irish are drawn to Melbourne, Perth and Brisbane, the eastern suburbs of Sydney have long held a siren call. In the 1990s and early 2000s, “County Bondi” was the epicentre of the Irish enclave. Now it’s “County Coogee” (pronounced cudgy), the slightly more affordable beach suburb just south of Bronte.
During the pandemic , many younger Irish headed home. The vulnerability of being a temporary resident with no access to the public health system (apart from emergencies) or welfare became all too real for many. But post-pandemic, the Irish returned in enormous numbers, eclipsing the scale of earlier influxes.
Since Australia’s borders reopened in February 2021, approximately 90,000 young Irish nationals have been granted a Working Holiday (417) visa. This figure does not include those who arrived on permanent residence, skilled sponsorship, spouse or student visas.
Just 3,697 of these visas were granted to Irish nationals in 2020-21. In 2021-22 the number increased to 10,491 before doubling to 21,525 in 2022-23. It rose again to 21,997 the following year and then, in 2024-25, 24,165 Irish citizens – equivalent to the total population of Mullingar – were granted their first Working Holiday visas.
But changes to the visa rules and pressure on the government to cut arrival numbers have created a new sense of uncertainty, which may mean the mass influx is coming to an end.
Irish and other backpackers can apply for a second one-year visa if they complete 88 days of specified regional work. This can include work in agriculture, mining, construction, tourism and hospitality, as well as bushfire and natural disaster recovery. (British citizens are not compelled to undertake regional work to get subsequent visas, a consequence of Australia’s free trade agreement with the UK. Some eligible Irish nationals have taken up British citizenship to avoid the obligation.)
[ Broke in Australia, I took a street sales job - but sidelined my better instincts Opens in new window ]
Those on a second Working Holiday visa who complete six months of regional work during their stay become eligible to apply for a third. Both are particularly popular with Irish applicants.
According to the Department of Home Affairs, Irish applications for second Working Holiday visas increased from 7,482 in 2023/24 to 9,585 in 2024/25, a 28 per cent hike. Applications for third visas rose even more sharply, from 1,000 to 3,692, an increase of 269 per cent. Irish passport holders account for 15.2 per cent of total applications, second only to UK citizens.
[ A Dublin woman in Ottawa: ‘Canadians take time to adapt to our humour and way of doing business’ Opens in new window ]
But the Australian government is about to change the rules in a way that will directly affect Irish passport holders.
Merely completing your regional work obligation will no longer guarantee you a second or third visa. Under changes being rolled out over the next 12 months, backpackers who want to stay on will have to enter a ballot, with second-year visa places capped at 45,000, down from 57,000 issued in this financial year. Third-year places will be capped at just 5,000, down from 31,000.
According to Sydney-based registered migration agent Fred Molloy, some young Irish have decided it’s all getting too difficult.
“The main issue with the new ballot system is the uncertainty it creates,” the Dubliner tells me. “We’re already seeing Working Holiday visa holders deciding to go home. We are coming into harvest seasons and many Irish Working Holiday visa holders will quite reasonably ask: ‘Why bother doing the regional work if there is no guarantee of getting a second or third Working Holiday visa?’ The whole attraction of doing the regional work was that there was a clear benefit at the end of it.”
[ A Belfast designer on making it big in New York: ‘There are still days when I have to pinch myself’ Opens in new window ]
Another Irish migration agent, Donegal native Andrew McDonagh, predicts the changes “will address the supply but not the demand – people are still going to want to come to Australia”.
“[But] what it will do is reduce the numbers of people staying, especially for the third year, and probably push more people towards earlier applications for longer-term visas,” he says.
Immigration is a hot-button topic in Australian politics. The Labor government is under pressure from the far-right One Nation party and the conservative Liberal-National Coalition to cut net overseas migration. But the business community has pushed back on cuts to skilled immigration, so the government has focused on students, temporary residents and working holidaymakers.
However, the refocused immigration programme may open up more opportunities for Irish nationals to get a permanent visa, according to McDonagh.
“The focus on priority sectors – among them construction, healthcare and teaching – plays very much to the core of the Irish diaspora. Opportunities for people with the right skills to stay here and eventually gain permanent residency remain very good.”
Billy Cantwell is an Irish journalist based in Sydney.
