title: Who owns Galway’s main thoroughfares? From Shop Street to the Spanish Arch Car Park
description: An examination of property records from Quay Street to Williamsgate Street shows much of the area remains in local hands
content:
F or five years, artist Patrick Loewen has used the vacant facade of 47 William Street in Galway as a shop window to sell his small paintings.
“I paint them on the street,” Loewen says. “This is my mercenary work to finance my exhibition coming up in Dawson Street [Dublin] at the end of October.
“I’ve sold to 50 US states from this wall. I’ve got art in Iran, Bahrain, Kuwait as well. None from internet sales, all from the street, and I let everyone pay whatever they can afford so no one’s out of budget.”
The artist from Vancouver , whose studio, People Loves Diamond, is nearby on Dominick Street, has also sold his art on the streets of many cities in North America. He says Galway’s main thoroughfare “is the healthiest street I’ve ever been on”.
“It feels healthier than Dublin, Limerick or Cork too. It’s very friendly. I always say, ‘if you’ve got problems with Galway, you’re looking for them’.”
Nearby on the corner of High Street and Cross Street, stone carver Daithi O’Gorman sells Celtic-designed slates. O’Gorman, who has also done large commissions for local businesses such as Thomas Dillon’s Claddagh Gold, etches many of the slates he sells to tourists on the street.
“Depending on the weather, I could be here three to five days a week.
“I share the street with the buskers, so when I’m finished, the buskers usually come along and ask me, ‘Has anybody asked you for the spot?’ I say no and they take the spot when I finish. So it’s rotation.”
[ Who owns Galway’s Eyre Square? The billionaires, hoteliers and publicans running the central plaza Opens in new window ]
Loewen and O’Gorman share Galway’s thoroughfare with more than 100 shops, restaurants and bars trading from the 120 buildings that line Quay Street, High Street, William Street and Williamsgate Street.
Based on a review of planning, company and Tailte Éireann (formerly the Land Registry) records, The Irish Times has established who owns half of the buildings and the results show a large portion of the properties remain in local hands.
At the southernmost point of Galway’s thoroughfare is the Leonardo Hotel Galway, known as the Jurys Inn until 2023. The 130-bedroom property, operated by Israeli group Fattal Hotels, has been owned by Swedish hospitality group Pandox since 2017 when it acquired the wider Jurys Inn chain.
Built into the facade of the Leonardo Hotel is the entrance to the Spanish Arch Car Park, which is linked to agri supply and property investor Thomas McDonogh & Sons Limited Group, led by Tom McDonogh, Patrick Neville and Matthew Jennings. The company’s latest financial accounts for the car park valued the property at €6 million.
Clothing brand Aran Sweater Market owns the building it trades from at number 25. The business controlled by Colm MacCarthy also runs Weavers of Ireland, which trades from number 24. This premises, which was put on the market in 2023 for €1.15 million, is also owned by MacCarthy.
Shiqi Chen and Jun Yan, who own Xi’an Street Food, also own number 9 from which their Asian restaurant trades. The company also owns numbers 6 and 8 directly across the street, which houses the restaurant Ithe. The properties are ultimately owned by their company, Galway Chocolates Limited, which has more than €7 million of real estate.
The Halls, an office space at number 15, is owned by Peter and Mary Coyne. The pair also own the premises at ground level that houses Freddy’s restaurant.
A company called Snoozles Quay Street Limited, owned by Michael and Diane Burke, controls The Snug Townhouse at number 10, a 35-room boutique hotel opened in 2022. The pair are also behind housing developer Burkeway Group.
Barbara and Nanke Ulrichs, who set up toyshop Wooden Heart after moving to Galway from Berlin in 1979, first opened in Loughrea before moving the business to number 3 in the 1980s. Their son Daniel now helps with the business and, in 2015, opened the cafe and design shop Coffeewerk + Press at number 4, across the street. Daniel initially leased the Coffeewerk premises, but new Land Registry records show his company, Oberon Design Limited, became the registered owner of the building in March 2025.
Land registry records show number 12, occupied by Sergio Magnetti’s Italian restaurant Magnetti’s, is owned by Barnacles Accommodation Limited, which lists Galway businessman John Lally and members of his family as directors. Lally, alongside business partners Paul Higgins and US billionaire John Malone, control the MHL Hotel Collection, which owns The Galmont, Glenlo Abbey and Harbour Hotel in Galway.
Louis Fitzgerald’s pub group owns some of Dublin’s most popular pubs, including Kehoes and the Stag’s Head. In 2020, it bought the property housing storied Galway pub Tigh Neachtain. At the time, Fitzgerald confirmed that tenant Jimmy McGuire would remain in place as the operator of the pub, which faces on to Quay Street but has an official address of 17 Cross Street Upper. Fitzgerald already owned The Quays pub on the other side of the street.
Outdoor clothing brand Portwest, based in number 20, has been a feature of High Street since opening in 2009. The business, set up more than 120 years ago by Charles Hughes, has remained in the family. Land Registry records show that Charles Hughes Limited, a company linked to the Hughes family, owns number 20.
Publican John Mannion has a significant foothold in Galway. The businessman is behind city centre venues including The Dáil Bar and Blakes Corner Bar. His premises The Front Door, which is based in number 3, is a large interconnected pub complex containing five bars, including Sonny Molloy’s whiskey bar. The property is owned by Mannion’s firm Peakhill Limited, which valued its property at €14.3 million at the end of 2024. It is owned by his Highcross group, which made €3 million profit from €20.5 million of revenue in 2024 and recorded €37.7 million of property interests.
[ ‘If it’s lost it will be lost forever’: What future for Galway Airport? Opens in new window ]
Marian O’Gorman’s giftware group has traded from number 6 for more than 20 years. Ownership documents show its parent company, Clydaville Investments Limited, is the registered owner of numbers 6 and 7, the latter of which is a Ladbrokes betting shop.
Mangan and Checkley, who cofounded the perfume and candle brand Cloon Keen Atelier, trading from number 21A, have owned their small archway-shaped store since 2015.
Following his deal to acquire Tigh Neachtain’s property in 2020, Fitzgerald’s group added Murphy’s Bar at number 9 to its portfolio in 2022. The premises, purchased from the Murphy family, was refurbished and reopened in 2023.
The Freeney family has operated Freeney’s bar at number 19 since 1938. Records show the property is equally owned by Anthony Freeney and Marie Freeney-Loughnane. Last year, the pair secured permission to expand their premises into another building to the rear that faces on to Middle Street.
For 35 years, Paul and Mary Grealish were the proprietors of The King’s Head at number 15, Galway’s oldest pub. Last year, they sold the venue to the Linnane family’s Runtur Hospitality. Conor Linnane, Claire Magee and Emmet Linnane are now directors of Galway Taverns Limited, the company behind the pub, which has traded for 800 years.
Galway’s oldest department store Anthony Ryans has been a stalwart of Shop Street since 1909. The business, run out of three addresses split by Buttermilk Lane that links Shop Street to Middle Street, is owned by Anthony Ryan Limited.
Business partners Graham Quinn and Sean Dooley are linked to Jessed Limited, the registered owner of the vacant number 21. The low-profile pair are also linked to a larger student accommodation group called Hazelwood Walk Holdings Limited, which owned €69 million of property at the end of 2025.
Shoe shop Brennans is one of the oldest retailers in the area. Martin Brennan’s firm Blackbrook Limited still trades from number 11, which has been in family ownership since it was set up in 1881. It also owns number 10, according to recent planning records.
Several Shop Street properties are linked to the Sherry family, who have controlled hospitality group Lydon House Catering since John Sherry led a management buyout in 1987. The company, which runs Donnelly’s of Barna, Franklin’s restaurant in Galway Shopping Centre and hospitality services for the Galway Races, has ties to the area going back decades to when Lydon’s restaurant traded from numbers 5 and 6. This premises is now owned by the family’s Minterburn Property Company. Land Registry and company records indicate that Minterburn also owns number 9 and has interests in parts of numbers 3-4 and 7-8. Its latest accounts record assets of €4 million.
McCambridges has been a staple of Shop Street for more than 100 years, and was kept in the family for three generations. In 2022, the supermarket at numbers 38 and 39 was sold to Musgrave Group for an undisclosed fee. Musgrave owns the property through subsidiary Cedarglade Limited.
The family of the late Tim Naughton, who ran a hardware and furniture store from number 35, own the property now occupied by Boots. The property is held by Timon Securities Unlimited Company, which is owned by his wife Margaret Naughton and other family members. Naughton, who died in 2014, was a prominent Galway businessman, serving as chairman of The Connacht Tribune, Galway Bay FM and the Galway Race Committee.
[ Galway’s Taaffes shop, empty for 30 years, has a new owner Opens in new window ]
The late Galway businessman Tom O’Connor ran O’Connors Audio Visual from Shop Street from 1970 to 1996 until it moved out of the city centre. The O’Connor family’s entity Hemoko Limited still owns its old premises at numbers 14 and 15, which are now occupied by River Island. The company, which lists his son Ronan as its sole director, valued its investment property at €6.5 million most recently. Land Registry records filed in 2022 showed another company led by O’Connor’s son Shane, called Roshin Limited, owns number 37, which houses shoe store Ecco. The property was valued at €1.7 million in its 2025 accounts.
Asset manager MNK Partners has owned Eason’s store at number 33 since 2019, when it completed a €8.1 million sale-and-leaseback deal with the books retailer. The French firm, controlled by Mansour Khalife and Miranda Khabiri, has bought a number of Irish-based commercial property assets since it was formed in 2017. Eason’s store was recently put on the market by real estate agents Colliers for €7.5 million.
The Divilly family’s connection to Shop Street began in the 1960s when Martin Divilly opened his butcher’s at number 34, but the store closed after being ravaged by a fire in 1979. Brian Divilly, who took over his father’s business in 1972, still owns the property that is vacant at ground level, but the upper floors are occupied by late bar Coyotes. The property is controlled by the businessman through Thornwood Property Holdings Limited, which valued its assets at €3.9 million at the end of 2025.
Number 1 is owned by the Lannon family, who control Mayo-based chicken producer Western Brand Group. They hold the property through Lannon Investments Limited, which is owned by Andrew, Clodagh, Seán and Eugene Lannon. The firm most recently valued its property at €2.6 million.
Lynch’s Castle at number 40, built around the 1500s, is now used by AIB as its main Galway city branch. Recent planning records show the property is still owned by AIB.
Garavan’s bar has traded from William Street for almost 90 years, and its current proprietor Paul Garavan has retained a significant foothold in the area. Garavan owns numbers 42, 44, 46 and 48, from which jewellers Ór, Espresso 44, Rituals and his own pub trades. Filings show the properties are linked to Garavan’s firm MRCS Limited, which owned €17 million of investment property at the end of 2024.
The building, which has been vacant for the past 30 years, was recently acquired by Tafko Limited, an entity linked to US-based investors Laura and Michael Higgins. The pair, both in their 60s, are behind several companies that own Galway properties, including Árd Rí House on Abbeygate Street Lower and the Bridge Mills building on Dominick Street Lower.
Outdoor clothing store Mountain Warehouse relocated to numbers 31/33 in May from Mainguard Street. The store is owned by Patrick and Anne Jordan who are behind Atlantic Aviation Group and telecoms firm Secto Services, which reported combined turnover of €148 million and after-tax profits of €6.1 million in 2024.
Numbers 3 and 5, occupied by Holland & Barrett, are owned by Hill and Son (Galway) Unlimited Company, a firm led by directors Seamus and Michelle Hill. A recent planning application by Krispy Kreme relating to its William Street store stated Seamus Hill was also the owner of number 27.
[ A guide to who owns St Stephen’s Green, from wealthy Irish families to private clubs Opens in new window ]
Carrolls Irish Gifts and Galway Camera Shop stores
A number of companies linked to Mayo-based beef and lamb processor Martin Jennings Wholesale Limited have owned number 1 William Street and 10 and 12 Williamsgate Street since 2017. Three years ago, Land Registry filings named Killara Investments Unlimited Company as the buildings’ owner. It is controlled by businessman John Vaughan, who has been a shareholder in the aforementioned meat processing business for many years.
In 2025, an update to Land Registry filings stated ET Burke Construction Limited was the owner of number 35, which is occupied by Fields the Jeweller. In April, owners of the firm Eamon and Marie Burke started a voluntary liquidation process.
Department store Brown Thomas, called Moon’s until the late 1990s, has an official address of 1-2 Eglinton Street, but fronts on to part of William Street. Brown Thomas Arnotts Limited, controlled by UK-based Selfridges Group, owns the property.
The Colonial Buildings straddle the border of William Street and Williamsgate Street, but have an Eglinton Street address. Land Registry records show the property, built in 1866 and housing Beef and Lobster restaurant and Tomodachi sushi bar, is owned by Martin and Roisin Proulx’s Fides Playhouse Limited. The pair operate The Cellar Bar in the Colonial Buildings, Seven Bar and Restaurant nearby on Bridge Street and An File bar in Westport, Co Mayo. Their firm’s latest accounts showed it owned €11.5 million worth of property assets.
The family-run GBC Restaurant has been operated from number 7 since 1936. The eatery, known for its traditional Irish breakfasts and carvery lunches, is run by Jeremiah and Brid McSweeney, who own the unit through GBC (Restaurant) Limited.
Men’s clothing store Hanley & Co, which was established in Galway in the 1960s by Joe Hanley, has traded in the city for more than 50 years. The business owns its store at number 8.
Jeweller Stephen Faller opened his store on Williamsgate Street in 1899 and his family has traded from the Galway city centre location ever since. The family business, now run by managing director Paul Faller, owns its premises at number 10 and 12 through Stephen Faller (1879) Limited.
Located between numbers 9 and 10 Williamsgate Street is an entrance to Eyre Square Centre. The property, with 72 tenants, is owned by International Investment ICAV, which bought the centre in 2022. The ICAV is not required to disclose its underlying investors, so the beneficial investors are unknown. The centre is managed by David Goddard’s firm Lanthorn, which acquired Davy’s real estate business in 2024.

title: Dave Mulcahy: From scoring against Manchester United to taking on Ballyhale Shamrocks
description: Former League of Ireland stalwart Dave Mulcahy is managing Tullaroan as they look to win the Kilkenny SHC final
content:
Dave Mulcahy once outscored Wayne Rooney at the Aviva Stadium and on Sunday he will be hoping to outfox TJ Reid at Nowlan Park.
In a county where hurling is the established church of the masses, one of the most capped players in the history of the League of Ireland has managed Tullaroan to the 2026 Kilkenny SHC final against reigning champions Ballyhale Shamrocks.
Mulcahy, who made 373 appearances in the Premier Division, was appointed Tullaroan manager at the start of the year and has guided the club to a first senior county final appearance since 1994.
“He came out to meet us and after about three minutes it was his job. His level of preparedness, his research and the detail he brought was just incredible,” recalls Tullaroan chairman Peter Holland.
Tullaroan are one of the most decorated clubs in Kilkenny, sitting second in the roll of honour with 20 senior titles behind Ballyhale on 21. But their golden period is from another era – Tullaroan’s last triumph was 1994, before that it was 1958.
From the outside, appointing Mulcahy might have seemed like a questionable roll of the dice.
“We were so blown away by him at the interview we didn’t think it was a risk at all,” adds Holland. “Then when we announced it, the slagging started and you’d be hearing that we were going to be playing with a 4-4-2 or a 4-3-3 this year.”
And while Mulcahy spent his playing days carving out a long and notable soccer career, he is of hurling stock. Both his grandfathers – Jack Mulcahy and Paddy Grace – won All-Ireland senior hurling titles with Kilkenny. And he is related to the famed Walsh family of Tullaroan – counting Tommy Walsh as a cousin.
A member of the James Stephens club in Kilkenny city, he has coached underage teams in the Village in recent years. And an electrician by trade, with his company David Mulcahy Electrical he has put in a significant effort helping the club with upgrade works in their facilities.
Mulcahy played football until his early 40s, putting down a career that spanned eight League of Ireland clubs – starting off with the now defunct Kilkenny City in 2000 before stints with Waterford United, St Pats, Cork City, Bray Wanderers, Bohemians, Drogheda United and Shelbourne (2018).
He also made history in the summer of 2010 during the first football game at the redeveloped Lansdowne Road when a League of Ireland selection played Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United.
Played in front of almost 50,000, Mulcahy’s 78th-minute goal ensured he will forever remain the answer of a table-quiz question on who was the first player from the Republic of Ireland to score at the new stadium. (He also scored in the last soccer game at the old Lansdowne Road – the 2006 FAI Cup final.)
The Manchester United team at the Aviva in 2010 included Rooney, Michael Owen, Nemanja Vidić, Michael Carrick, Antonio Valencia, Javier Hernandez and was captained by John O’Shea. United won 7-1, but Mulcahy’s strike received the grandest ovation.
Owen Heary, one of the most respected footballers in the history of the league, played both with and against Mulcahy.
“Around the time we were playing together Kilkenny were one of the best hurling teams in the country and he used to be talking about his cousin, Tommy. Hurling would be a topic that would come up regularly with him, he always had that in his blood,” remembers Heary.
“Now, sometimes after he’d try make a pass to me, I’d say to him that maybe he’d be better off playing hurling!”
Mulcahy played mostly as a central midfielder but was also often deployed as a centre-back. He featured alongside Heary with Bohs in 2012 and 2013 when Heary was team captain.
But when the Dalymount board parted company with manager Aaron Callaghan midseason in the summer of 2013, Heary stepped up as interim manager. He immediately asked Mulcahy to take up the captaincy.
“In terms of leadership, he led by example on and off the pitch. He was one of those players you could trust,” says Heary.
In one of his first games as captain, Mulcahy put in a roof-lifting early tackle in a crunch fixture against Shamrock Rovers and scored the only goal in a 1-0 victory for Bohs.
“That’s the kind of leadership he showed on the pitch, the tackle was right over in front of the Bohs fans, it was a great tackle, the fans were jumping around the place. He set the tone for everyone else and then went and scored the winner.”
And Tullaroan are not the only ones to have noticed his leadership qualities – Henry Shefflin has brought Mulcahy in as part of his management team with the Kilkenny senior hurlers for next season.
“I remember going down for the opening of a pitch in Kilkenny and you could see the respect people there had for him,” adds Heary.
“The fact he is going in with the Kilkenny hurlers is testament to what he’s done. For a footballer to be asked into that sort of environment is pretty major.”
But none of it has come as a surprise in Tullaroan, as they have watched him shape their senior hurlers this season.
“When you’re talking to him or you’re in his surroundings, there’s never a doubt in your mind,” says Holland. “It’s the calmness and the professionalism, he’s so organised, everything is done when and how it should be done.”
And it’s not like he was ever really a stranger around the parish.
“We knew he scored in the last game at Lansdowne Road and he was the first Irish person to score in the Aviva, but really to us he was Tommy Walsh’s cousin inside in town there, he plays with Bohs or whoever it was at the time. That’s who he was then.”
But these days Dave Mulcahy and Tullaroan are co-writing a new chapter to an unparalleled Kilkenny sports story.

title: Abolishing ‘ridiculous’ triple lock is right step forward for our country
description: It gives world powers a veto over Irish military deployments
content:
Sir, – Following Wednesday’s vote to abolish the triple lock , it is important to state the facts.
The triple lock’s affording to Russia , China and the United States a veto over Irish military deployments is the antithesis of the “neutrality” and “sovereignty” it supposedly protects.
Similarly farcical are calls that this vote should be put to a referendum. Nowhere in the Constitution does the triple lock appear, thus a referendum is not required.
Facts matter more than feelings especially when it comes to national defence and foreign policy. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Finally, an adult decision on Irish foreign policy. I am very happy to see the Government’s vote win on abolishing this ridiculous requirement. It was long overdue.
The spurious opposition claims were laughable to anyone with a basic grasp on Irish foreign policy and how international missions function are deployed.
Neither neutrality nor the triple lock is an element of the Constitution; there is no need for a referendum.
While we may have a pitifully small defence budget, we have at least taken a step towards deciding what to do with our own troops to assist international peace support operations, and not wait for permission from a dysfunctional United Nations Security Council. – Yours, etc,

title: If you think legal aid is expensive, wait until you hear how costly the alternative is
description: Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan needs to reach agreement with solicitors to end industrial action
content:
Sir, – In the past year, my wife and I have had occasion to engage, separately, the services of a locksmith and a washing-machine technician.
Each attended our home for about 20 minutes and provided expert service and they charged about €400 and €300 respectively for the call-out and a nominal amount for the parts.
To the best of my information and belief each only needed a website, a van and a bag of tools to practise their trade.
Solicitors on the other hand, to practise their profession, need to finance an office, car/travel expenses, clerical/secretarial staff wages, annual practising certificate, independent auditor, professional indemnity insurance, mandatory continuing professional education seminars, phones, office equipment, computer services and staff and personal pension contributions.
The cost of all of the foregoing is a necessary expense before the practitioner turns the key in the office on January 2nd and earns a cent.
May I respectfully suggest that Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan descend from the cosseted Ivory Tower of the Law Library and chauffeur-driven ministerial comfort and get real.
The provision of publicly funded legal aid in criminal matters to those without the means to afford it is properly regarded as a human right.
The Minister might do well to consider what it would cost the State to engage, accommodate and service hundreds of solicitors and barristers as permanent and pensionable employees/public servants, which is the only alternative to agreeing reasonable contractual terms with those highly qualified professional independent contractors.
I retired as a solicitor at the end of 2019 and was never on the criminal legal aid register. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – The extraordinary allegation by Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan that solicitors have deliberately targeted rape cases in order to press their grievances on the legal aid reforms is a grotesque smear of the profession and is a stain on O’Callaghan’s office.
If O’Callaghan’s calculated and scurrilous claim is not publicly withdrawn, the Law Society of Ireland should respond by bringing the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme to an end for once and for all.
Then let the Minister introduce a US-style “public defenders” system, which the last Government explored but quietly abandoned in 2023 on cost grounds, and then explain to taxpayers why he has brought about a system that costs radically more than the existing scheme. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – The dispute between the Minister for Justice and solicitors over the adjournment of rape trials illustrates a familiar problem in industrial relations: both sides attribute responsibility for the same harm to the decisions of the other.
The Minister points to the solicitors’ withdrawal of services. The solicitors point to the Minister’s decision to change the criminal legal aid fee structure. Each treats its own conduct as a response to the other’s.
The law and economics scholar Ronald Coase described such problems as reciprocal, arguing that the attribution of blame risked distracting from the real question: how to avoid more serious harm?
The consequences for complainants are profoundly serious. The history of industrial relations would suggest that dialogue, not accusation, is the path forward. – Yours, etc,

title: ‘There could be carnage in Dublin’: Ian Madigan and Alan Quinlan on Leinster v Munster
description: Former Ireland pair also hail ‘outstanding’ Dan Sheehan, named as Leo Cullen’s number eight for Saturday
content:
So it’s front to back for Dan Sheehan in terms of his position in the pack on Saturday for Leinster against Munster . It’s a headline move from Leo Cullen .
And it stirs memories of the start of the 2005/06 Celtic League season for Alan Quinlan. Declan Kidney wanted all his Munster forward Galácticos on the pitch, so he played some of them as backs.
In the province’s opening game, openside David Wallace was selected on the wing. Munster beat Border Reivers 9-7.
Wallace returned to his usual backrow berth against Ospreys, but Kidney also wanted Denis Leamy to start as he needed game time. The flanker was named at outside centre, where he also started a fortnight later against Scarlets. Munster won again, but the experiment was abandoned.
“Kidney wanted to have Alan Quinlan, Anthony Foley, Jim Williams, David Wallace and Denis Leamy on the field at one time,” Quinlan said.
“It didn’t last too long. Wally wasn’t too comfortable on the wing. Leamy actually did quite well, but probably didn’t have the gas for some of the defensive work you have to do in that outside channel.”
His recollection follows the selection of Leinster hooker Dan Sheehan’s at number eight against Munster. The 28-year-old has played in that role before, but never from the start of a game.
With Caelan Doris and Jack Conan sidelined through injury, Cullen decided to move his stand-in skipper from the front to the back of the pack, with Rónan Kelleher named at hooker for Saturday’s United Rugby Championship encounter (6pm).
It is an intriguing pick, particularly with Ireland’s Nations Championship fixtures approaching, beginning with Argentina’s visit on November 6th.
The loss of Doris and Conan leaves Ireland short of Test experience at the back of the scrum. While Quinlan initially described Sheehan’s selection there as a “mad one”, he believes there is method in it.
“I genuinely wouldn’t be surprised if Dan Sheehan was an option in the backrow for Ireland. He [Ireland head coach Andy Farrell ] could start with Kelleher and have Tom Stewart on the bench,” the former Munster and Ireland flanker said.
“It could happen, particularly with two world-class number eights gone for Ireland. I’m sure the other loose forwards would be disappointed if Dan Sheehan was starting ahead of them, but who knows.”
Quinlan referenced how Springboks maestro Rassie Erasmus has successfully experimented with positional switches, including the deployment of flanker Deon Fourie at hooker during the 2023 World Cup final. Erasmus subsequently moved André Esterhuizen from centre into the backrow.
“It’s not something I’d be against,” he said. “Sheehan is such an athletic player and an outstanding athlete that it wouldn’t surprise me if we saw him in the back line; he could play in the centre as well.
“His ability to carry and do damage in the loose would probably make him enjoy the role. It’s a little bit of a left-field selection, but he’s well capable of doing it.”
Ian Madigan believes Leinster’s game plan, which revolves heavily around the fit-again Jamison Gibson-Park , should help Sheehan settle into his new role.
“Everyone will be helping Sheehan and saying, ‘On this set-up, we want you in this position, just hold your feet, be patient, the play will come to you’,” former Leinster and Ireland outhalf Madigan said.
“He is so physically gifted that if his timing is slightly off, he misses the jump or goes too early, it doesn’t really matter. It’s about getting the ball into his hands, and then he can physically impose himself on the opposition. He’s that good.”
With outhalf Sam Prendergast absent through injury, Joey Carbery will make his first start since returning to Leinster against the province he left eight years ago.
Madigan has no concerns about Carbery’s lack of game time after he came on late in Clermont to complete his comeback from an anterior cruciate ligament injury, but expects an emotional occasion for the 30-year-old.
“He’ll want to make a mark. I know how ambitious Joey is and how he’ll want to become Leinster’s first-choice outhalf and get himself back into the Ireland set-up. There’s no better way to do that than playing really well in an interprovincial game,” Madigan said.
“This is very much going to kick-start his season and his return to Leinster. He’s a quality player and I’d expect him to step up and get up to speed very quickly.”
As far as Munster are concerned, Quinlan believes having only two players selected for Ireland will come as a “shock” to the dressingroom and motivate Clayton McMillan’s side on Saturday.
“If Munster rolls up their sleeves here, it could ignite. There could be carnage in Dublin,” he said. “But I don’t think it’s nasty or narky, a lot of them get on with each other.
“I’m not saying our day was any better, but I just don’t think it captures the same imagination.”
Madigan, meanwhile, expects Leinster to use last season’s defeat to their rivals at Croke Park as motivation. “This is a fixture Leo Cullen loves. He absolutely savours every interprovincial, but particularly Leinster v Munster,” he said.
“Last year’s defeat would have left a deep scar, and you can be guaranteed that he and Jacques Nienaber are lighting a fire under Leinster this week. I’d expect them to get on top, but it’s going to be a hell of a battle.”
Alan Quinlan and Ian Madigan were speaking on a media call for the BKT United Rugby Championship. Ian Madigan will be part of the Premier Sports team showing live coverage of Leinster v Munster on Saturday from the Aviva Stadium at 5.15pm on Premier Sports 1. To join in visit www.premiersports.com @PremSportsTV

title: Sweet and sour: Frank McNally on how Russian brutality brought the Mary cake to Ireland
description: Henry Spelter, one of the Hungarians who fled his native land 70 years ago, found work at Bewley’s
content:
S eventy years ago this Friday, October 23rd, 1956, thousands of protesters gathered at a square in Budapest to demand the end of communist rule.
It was the start of the Hungarian uprising, which lasted for 15 days until brutally crushed by Soviet tanks and troops under the direction of Moscow.
The events have many resonances today, and not just because this was a Russian invasion of a European neighbour. It also resulted in an international refugee crisis, including the first mass influx of asylum seekers to independent Ireland.
Of the more than 200,000 who fled Hungary , 548 were given emergency accommodation at an Army camp in Knocknalisheen, Co Clare.
And even in an impoverished Ireland, where enforced emigration was a reality for many, the Catholic Hungarians were broadly welcomed.
The feeling was reciprocated too. An RTÉ archive report from the period includes grateful children at the camp singing a hymn in Irish: “Céad míle fáilte romhat, a Íosa.”
But it was not an entirely happy experience. As Bryan Fanning wrote in this newspaper some years ago, Ireland had just ratified a UN convention that gave such refugees a right to work. Even so, “considerable efforts were made to prevent the Hungarians seeking employment”.
[ Last Post and Chorus: Frank McNally on memories of a long-lost Dublin restaurant Opens in new window ]
There also soon developed a struggle for control of the camp between the Hungarians, who elected a representative committee, and the Red Cross administrators, who sought to suppress it.
The latter complained to Government about “agitators” among the refugees, including a man who had survived a Siberian prison camp.
Allegations included the supposed invitation to his hut one night of “an undesirable woman”. In fact, as Sheehan wrote, she was a respectable lady from Limerick “attempting to recruit refugee musicians to play in a band”.
Conditions at Knocknalisheen were so far from luxury it was likened to “internment”. And the Hungarians’ protests culminated in that great Irish tradition – a hunger strike – until their demands to meet senior civil servants were met.
For most, in any case, Ireland was just a staging post. After a two-year stay, the great majority moved on to Canada. But some remained, including a few who found work the Quaker-owned Bewley’s Cafés in Dublin, a subject to which we’ll return.
As the current Hungarian ambassador to Ireland, Gergely Bánhegyi, reminded guests at a commemoration earlier this week, fellow feeling between his country and this one goes back several centuries.
In 1649, fleeing Cromwellian persecution, the Catholic bishop of Clonfert, Walter Lynch, made a new home in the Hungarian city of Gyor.
He brought with him a painting of the Madonna and Child. And when he died, his remains and the picture both took up permanent residence in the local cathedral.
There, some years later, the painting became the focus of apparently miraculous events. On St Patrick’s Day in 1697, a year in which all priests were banished from Ireland, the Madonna was seen to weep tears of blood, over several hours.
Reports of the phenomenon are said to have been signed by hundreds of eyewitnesses, including local “Calvinist and Lutheran ministers, and a Jewish rabbi”.
Ever since, the “Irish Madonna of Gyor” has attracted pilgrims, while a copy of the original painting now hangs in St Brenda’s Cathedral in Loughrea, Co Galway.
But getting back to Bewley’s, as the ambassador also mentioned, the Hungarians who found work there in the late 1950s included a man named Henry Spelter.
And among Henry’s contributions was a local version of a dessert popular in his home country as the “Marika Cake”.
A drum-shaped chocolate, sponge, and marzipan confection, it became known in Ireland as the “Mary cake” and was for many years a staple of the Bewley’s menu.
It was never perhaps as famous as the sticky bun or almond roll, with which the cafes were synonymous.
But I see, for example, that during coverage of the threatened closure of Bewley’s Grafton Street in 2004, nostalgic former customers quoted in a newspaper feature include the writer Liz Ryan lamenting: “It had everything – real fires, warm decor, good coffee, those lovely Mary cakes.”
Alas, during one of the cafe’s refurbishments, the recipe was lost. And since Henry Spelter was long gone by now – he had re-emigrated at some point – it looked like it would stay lost.
Then, two decades later, Bewley’s food detective Hazel Carmichael got on the case. She tracked Spelter to the US, only to find he had just died there, aged 95.
But via the obituaries, she found one of his grandchildren. And with some assistance from old Bewley’s ledger books – they were together able to bring the storied dessert back to life last year.
The cake was a star feature at the embassy’s commemoration on Monday, where guests included current Bishop of Clonfert Michael Duignan and historian Vera Sheridan, whose 2023 book Suitable Strangers tells the story of the 1956 refugees.
Another notable feature of the event were the miniature Hungarian Tricolours, each with a hole cut in the middle. This replicated the action of protesters 70 years ago when they edited the flag of its postwar communist insignia.

title: Children are entitled to their own boundaries, which deserve respect
description: Adults must get real about children’s rights, particularly those adults responsible for child protection
content:
Sir, – The criticism of the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre ’s recent consent advertisement misses the point entirely (“ Advert on consent showing grandparents hugging is taken down amid criticism of ‘demeaning’ message ,” October 22nd).
The criticism appears to rest on a misunderstanding of the advert’s message. It was not an attack on grandparents, nor did it suggest that affection between grandparents and grandchildren is somehow inappropriate.
It simply illustrated that children should be allowed to decide whether they are comfortable with physical affection, even when that affection comes from people who love them.
Many parents already teach this lesson. Children may be shy, overwhelmed, feeling unwell or simply not want a hug at a particular moment.
Respecting that choice does not undermine family relationships. It teaches respect for personal boundaries and allows affection to be given freely rather than out of obligation.
The suggestion that lessons about consent should be confined to discussions of adult sexual relationships misses the broader point. Consent begins with understanding that every person has autonomy over their own body and that “no” should be respected, even in entirely innocent situations.
The advert’s message was neither demeaning nor controversial. It reflects the simple idea that children, just like adults, are entitled to their own boundaries and those boundaries deserve respect.
If some adults are offended by being told that children are not obliged to hug them, that reaction only demonstrates why these conversations remain important. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – The Department for Justice described as “inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents” the video by Dublin Rape Crisis Centre about consent, in which a young girl declines a grandparent’s hug. The department demanded the video be withdrawn.
This was not a campaign against grandparents. Many families could not manage without their support, most importantly, for disabled and neurodivergent grandchildren. But loving grandparents and a child’s right to say no, do not conflict.
The department’s statement said that consent matters “when it comes to sexual relationships”. However, children learn consent long before then, every time their “no” is heard. The Stay Safe programme in our primary schools teaches children to “say no, get away and tell”. That message only works if a child has learned that their no counts, including with the adults they love and trust.
For many neurodivergent children, unwanted touch can be overwhelming at a nervous system level. Many of these children say no without spoken words: by pulling away, by freezing, or through their communication devices.
When adults learn to read and respect those signals, children are safer. When the message from Government is that a child’s discomfort should be set aside to spare an adult’s feelings, the children with the least power to say no are the most exposed.
Ireland has committed, under the UN conventions on the rights of the child and of people with disabilities, to hear children’s views and to respect their physical integrity. Those commitments do not stop when grandparents are at the front door.
A hug only means something when a child wants it. Teaching a child that their body belongs to them demeans no one, but is how we keep children safe.
Adults in this country must get real about children’s rights, particularly those adults who are responsible for child protection. – Yours, etc,

title: Charity in money-laundering investigation received €2m in State funding since 2020
description: Liberties Recycling has nine charity shops and operates 180 recycling banks around Ireland
content:
A charity at the centre of a Garda money-laundering investigation has received more than €2 million in State funding since the start of the decade, records show.
Liberties Recycling Training and Development company received the money from the Department of Social Protection under the community employment (CE) scheme. The idea behind the scheme is that the department pays employers such as Liberties Recycling, which has 95 staff, to provide community jobs to unemployed or disadvantaged people to help them back to work.
Financial statements show the Liberties organisation – also known as Liberty Recycling – received €487,213 from the department in 2024, €416,201 in 2023, €377,154 in 2022, €405,106 in 2021 and €517,772 in 2020.
The Garda inquiry and seizure of luxury goods has drawn a new degree of scrutiny to Liberties Recycling, which operates under the supervision of the Charities Regulator .
“We can confirm that we are engaging with the charity’s trustees,” said the regulator in reply to questions. “As there is an active Garda investigation, the Charities Regulator cannot comment further at present.”
[ BMWs, Louis Vuitton bags, Rolex watches seized amid charity money-laundering allegations Opens in new window ]
Based at Bluebell Industrial Estate in west Dublin, Liberties Recycling has nine charity shops in Dublin, Limerick, Waterford, Wexford, Ennis, Bray, Mullingar, Drogheda and Cork. It operates 180 recycling banks around the State, collecting used clothes, shoes and textiles, which it then sorts, grades and packs for reuse in clothes markets in developing countries and for sale in its own shops.
The organisation aims to help people recovering from drug addiction to progress “through their rehabilitation and into employment”. Workers can receive certified training in forklift driving, computer applications and also in maths, first aid and payroll.
The chairman is Aengus Ó Snodaigh , long-time Sinn Féin TD for Dublin South-Central, and the chief executive is Philip Moloney. There is no suggestion whatever that either man is under investigation.
Liberties Recycling has its origins in the closure of the Iveagh Market in Dublin, where Moloney’s family historically traded used clothes. When the market closed in 1995, a group led by Moloney came together with the idea of involving the community in a clothes recycling initiative to provide jobs and training to local people affected by drugs.
The latest available accounts for the charity show a financial deficit of €347,632 in 2024, an increase from the €255,447 deficit in 2023.
[ Fighting Blindness charity paid for Mediterranean cruise and Majorca stay for businessman Opens in new window ]
The charity reported income of €3.63 million in 2024 and expenditure of €3.98 million. Republic of Ireland income was €1.76 million and “rest of the world” income was €1.34 million.
In a statement, the Department of Social Protection said it had “recently become aware of the investigation”.
“The department funds a drug rehabilitation community employment programme in this company. The programme operates as a drug rehab CE programme, working with recovering addicts.
“Referrals to the programme are made by HSE and addiction counsellors. Departmental staff audit the CE company annually, ensuring that all funds provided by the department are used appropriately on the CE programme.
“The department will continue to work with the sponsor board and scheme supervisors to ensure the participants can continue to benefit from this rehabilitation programme.”

title: Some alumina from Aughinish ‘undoubtedly’ supplies Russian military, EU envoy says
description: Possible quotas for Aughinish exports to Russia considered by Brussels officials
author_name: Jack Power, Conor Gallagher, Jack Horgan-Jones
content:
The EU’s envoy on sanctions has said alumina produced by Aughinish Alumina in Limerick “undoubtedly” ended up supplying, at least in part, the Russian military-industrial complex.
David O’Sullivan, who was previously the European Commission’s top civil servant, said any action taken on Aughinish Alumina had to be mindful of Europe’s complex supply chains.
“We just have to find the best way of doing it, which doesn’t have unhelpful collateral consequences,” he told an Institute of International and European Affairs event in Dublin, during which he said there was “no doubt the investigative journalists got it right” on the plant’s supply relationship with Russia.
It is understood European Commission officials had privately considered proposing a quota system that would limit Aughinish Alumina’s exports to Russia, giving the Co Limerick plant time to find alternative markets for its material, before Brussels parked the idea.
Measures prohibiting the Irish refinery from selling alumina to Russia are not included in a draft of the commission’s next package of sanctions, according to senior EU sources briefed on the closely guarded details.
The commission, which is the union’s powerful executive body in Brussels, has put together a draft of what will be the EU’s 22nd package of sanctions, aimed at making it harder for Russia to sustain its war in Ukraine.
Confidential discussions will take place over the coming weeks between commission officials and senior diplomats from all 27 EU states to sound out support for the sanctions package, and make changes, before governments start negotiating between themselves.
Aughinish Alumina is owned by Russian metals giant Rusal and ships vast quantities of product to smelters in Russia, where the raw material is turned into aluminium and sold to a Moscow trading company known to supply the alloy to Russian arms and missile manufacturers.
Aughinish Alumina’s exports to Russia have significantly increased since the invasion of Ukraine and account for about half of Aughinish’s business.
The plant, which employs several hundred people in the Foynes area, previously warned it could be forced to shut if these shipments were barred by EU-level sanctions.
It is understood the commission had internally debated proposing some type of quota system to limit Aughinish’s exports to Russia, rather than a full export ban. The restrictions would in theory reduce sales to Russia gradually over time, to give the Irish refinery a chance to find other markets for its material.
Concerns about disrupting wider European supply chains that rely on alumina and aluminium alloys led the commission to refrain from targeting Aughinish in the coming 22nd round of sanctions.
The commission has not taken sanctions on alumina off the table entirely, meaning it is possible an export ban or quota proposal features in later packages.
Several EU sources cautioned that changes were often made to draft sanctions packages, following confidential talks involving national diplomats, which have yet to begin.
[ ‘A ticking environmental time bomb’: What lies beneath Aughinish Alumina in Co Limerick Opens in new window ]
Estonia has said it plans to push for sanctions on alumina in the coming set of measures. “We can confirm that yes, Estonia has made such a proposal at the EU level,” said a spokesman for the Estonian foreign ministry.
New sanctions must be unanimously agreed by all 27 EU states.
Aughinish Alumina’s exports to Russia have been in the spotlight on the back of reporting by The Irish Times , in co-operation with the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project.
The Irish Government would back “any measures that are being proposed or put forward” by the commission on Aughinish, Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee said when asked yesterday. “We’ve been very clear in saying, if measures need to be taken, that we will work closely with them,” she said.

title: ‘Having Manchán Magan as part of the Hometree journey was pretty deep and meaningful’
description: Matt Smith was drawn to Ireland to surf. Now he runs Hometree, the nature restoration charity in Co Clare, planting and conserving native woodland
content:
I can’t remember where I was exactly, maybe the Pacific or Indonesia, when my friend sent me a message saying, “I’ve just found the best wave in the world; you’re not going to believe it.”
This was in 2007, and I came to the Cliffs of Moher for Aileen. It was waves like we’d never seen, and it had just been sitting there, forever unsurfed.
I’m Cornish, and Ireland, especially the west coast, felt really like what I remember Cornwall to be.
I travelled over with two other boys, and we had a really sweet time just surfing here. We spent like 100 days sleeping together in a double bed and tents, just trying to save money, surfing and making friends.
The three of us had a trip planned to the Canary Islands, when one of our friends changed his plans and flew to London a day early. He got killed by a bus that night.
When that happened, it really shook our little surf community.
After the funeral, everyone went a bit psychotic on the waves. We had people with broken legs and arms and backs, and near-drownings. We were 19 years old and thinking, if we can get hit by a bus, then why are we holding back?
In that small group of friends, it had a really big impact. Everyone has gone on to have an interesting life.
Even though I left Ireland to go sailing around the world, hitchhiking, moving boats, exploring, I would always come back here two or three months a year. I just felt so much more at home here than in Cornwall.
On one of the trips back to Clare , two of my friends, Fergal Smith and Mitch Corbett, had started growing vegetables and I got involved. We started a farm called Moy Hill Community Farm, and we ran it as community-supported agriculture. People bought a share of the harvest rather than individual products.
It was working really well, and then in 2014, Manchán Magan and I set up Hometree to restore woodlands within the landscape and connect people with nature .
At the beginning it was just a community garden project, a weekend thing where we’d do tree-planting. Initially we used surfing connections to get the first few donations. The likes of Finisterre gave us €1,000, and we would buy a bag of trees and plant them at the farm.
Manchán was a really big part of Hometree for many years. He wasn’t operational, but he was one of the founders and sat on the board. For me, as an expat, having him as part of that journey was pretty deep and meaningful.
I used to ask him once or twice a year: “Do we need to remake the website so that it’s in Irish?” And he always said, “No, you just need to get on and do the nature thing.” I really miss him.
After a few years, we saw that Hometree had tons of potential and it needed to go out and have a bigger impact in the wider landscape, so in 2020 we hired staff and gave it our full attention. We let it do whatever it could, and the phone kept ringing, and we worked hard. We got our first staff member in October 2021, and now there are 40 of us.
[ ‘Grand Canyon-esque’: Atlas of the unseen brings Ireland’s deep sea wonders into the light Opens in new window ]
Over the next 10 years, we are trying to add nearly 60,000 acres of land into restoration through land partnerships and site acquisition. We are working with communities to ensure they are part of the restoration process both financially and practically.
We’ve heard the stats over and over again that our landscape is in the worst condition it’s ever been in, and while Hometree might now be the biggest nature restoration NGO in the country, we probably don’t make any more than a fancy Dublin coffee shop.
It is a hard thing for anybody to hear, but when we look back in 20 years, and we think, “I knew this, and yet I invested my money in that coffee shop every single day because it was slightly more convenient, or it took away the pain of existing a tiny bit more, rather than doing everything I could ... ” I wonder does that feel okay for people?
It can be hard to consider these things, so I always say to turn it into an anecdote, a real one.
Ask yourself whether the land that’s in your family, or the land that you know, has gotten better or worse in your lifetime. Be truthful to yourself.
The next question is: what is a realistic response to the ecological situation that we’re in? Is a realistic response that you decide to join a nature charity and give them 25 bucks a month? Does that really change things? Or does it need to be more radical than that? I believe yes.
Radical responses often turn people off. But I always think that with these big points of view, you need to ask yourself: in 20 or 30 years, will I regret not doing something about nature, or will I regret planting trees in my garden?
I’m pretty sure you’re going to wish you’d done something.

title: ‘I wish your mummy was still alive,’ my daughter says, before the conversation swiftly changes
description: Speaking to my children about my mother’s death, with all their bluntness, candour, even indifference, has been bracing, but also strangely joyous
content:
M y four-year-old daughter takes my hand, adopts a meaningful expression and gently squeezes my fingers. “I wish your mummy was still alive,” she says.
This sets me on my heels a little, since it has come entirely out of left field. We are walking my son to football training and, up to this point, conversation had been circling the prospect of us all getting ice cream once it finished.
“I know, pet,” I say, buffering slightly, “I do too; she would have loved you very much.” Warming to the theme, my son chimes in. “You can’t really have a complete family without two nanas,” he says. “Well, no,” I reply, “that’s not true – you can have all kinds of families with loads of different combinations of parents or grandparents or siblings.”
He holds my gaze for what seems like an eternity, long enough that I reckon I can see the little cogs behind his eyes processing my wisdom in real time, before tilting his head and asking, with the sincerity of a Trappist monk: “Who’s the best striker in the Bundesliga?”
My daughter is no longer present to see my face set back into its standard factory setting of polite bafflement, since she has ambled ahead of us, my mother’s tragic absence entirely forgotten.
This has been my general experience of speaking to my children about life, death and specifically my own bereavement; brief and abrupt moments of crystalline poignancy scattered at high speed, and punctured by an immediate reversion to cheery indifference. My son’s meditations on grief began when he was roughly his sister’s age, since the philosopher within us seems to take shape at four or five years old. He had, presumably, started doing the sort of mental arithmetic that revealed he was down one nana compared with some of his friends, and would pepper me with questions about this shortfall.
Eventually, conversations like these would teach me the gloriously insensitive patterns of children’s thoughts and reveal that real life rarely adheres to the rhythms of a Very Special Episode of a heartwarming family drama. But I’ll admit the first few times it happened, I steeled myself for the scene I imagined was soon to come: me doling out tender epiphanies to my wise and inquisitive son, scored with soft, swelling music and the sound of his gentle, sniffled tears. And each time, I’d be mildly deflated when my stirring response would be interrupted, about five words in, by him changing the subject to something more interesting like, say, trains or farts.
A lover of maths, he was briefly preoccupied with the idea that all human beings live to be 100 years old. One afternoon, he deployed this grisly calculus to predict the year that he and we, his parents, would die. “Well,” I said, sidestepping his breezy prediction of his own death date, “some people do live that long, but most people die a little before that.”
“Oh yeah! Like your mum!” he said, with a cheeriness fitting the occasion, before turning back to his Play-Doh.
Aside from being extremely funny, I’ve grown to find these exchanges soothing. Last week marked the 35th anniversary of my mother’s passing, and I’ve spent most of my life treating the subject with the tact and poise that society – rightly and thankfully – insists on. The tactful hesitance in speaking about it too much myself, the tiptoe tightrope of apologies and silences it tends to engender in others. Speaking to my children about it, with all their bluntness, candour, even indifference, has been bracing, but also strangely joyous.
[ I routinely have intrusive thoughts about horrible things that could happen to my children Opens in new window ]
Of course, somewhere within the innocence of their responses lurks a sharp little ice-pick of sadness; the knowledge that I myself was that same insouciant, carefree child, at precisely the moment my mother died. I’ve tried, over the years, to recall the things people said to me that made sense of any of it, things that could explain an existentially unexplainable thing. Some perfect words to get across that someone, that any of us, could be here one day, and not the next, and that seven-eighths of a life later their loss will still be mourned, but life will still go on.
My daughter returns to hold my hand, my son bringing up the rear. We are quiet now, the three of us. He pats my arm. She squeezes my palm. “Probably Harry Kane,” I tell my son, breaking the silence with the only response that seems appropriate in this moment, “although Patrick Schick at Leverkusen is having a great start to the season.”

title: What will €285,000 buy in France, Canada, Thailand, Spain and Co Galway?
description: One price, home and away: A thatched cottage in Lisdonagh, a villa in Chiang Mai and more
content:
Bluebell Cottage is a picture-perfect thatched property in Lisdonagh, Co Galway , that was built in 1840. It has been restored and well maintained by its owners and comes with an E energy rating. It has a kitchen/dining/livingroom, a utility, two ground-floor bathrooms and three bedrooms. It is surrounded by beautiful gardens and comes with a detached garden room and a collection of stone outbuildings.
At 133sq m (1,427sq ft), this stone house just outside the spa town of Salies-de-Béarn has everything you need for a holiday home. It has a kitchen, a livingroom, two bedrooms and a bathroom on the ground floor. Upstairs is another bedroom, a livingroom and a bathroom. The interior is traditional and well kept, and the gardens are lush and vast. It is located an hour from Biarritz and 90 minutes from ski resorts in the Pyrenees.
This villa in Chiang Mai was built in 2024 and has a generous floor area of 300sq m (3,229sq ft). It is in turnkey condition and comes with a private pool, large garden, a rooftop terrace, covered parking and outdoor showers. It comprises a kitchen, diningroom, livingroom, five bedrooms and four bathrooms. It is in the San Phisuea area close to San Sai golf club and comes fully furnished.
Built in 1968, this renovated farmhouse is surrounded by mature trees with the back garden sloping down to a river. It has an open-plan living space with a cathedral ceiling, three bedrooms and a bathroom. It is located is Saint-Liguori, which is in the Lanaudière region of Quebec . It is in turnkey condition, with new floors, kitchen and bathroom fittings.
On the southern Costa Blanca in the residential area of Los Altos, this two-bedroom apartment is set out over 75sq m (807sq ft). Located on the second floor, the accommodation includes a kitchen/dining/living area that leads out to a covered terrace, the two bedrooms and two bathrooms. Residents have access to a communal pool, play area and sports facilities. It has air conditioning, an alarm and underground parking.

title: Purges and political uncertainty deepen unease inside China’s ruling elite
description: As Beijing hosts a pivotal leadership meeting, attention is focused on who has fallen from favour and who could emerge as the next generation of China’s rulers.
content:
T he weather turned in Beijing this week with temperatures dropping suddenly by about 10 degrees, although the days are still sunny, the parks are filled with people and the autumn gloom has yet to set in. But there is a familiar tension in the air, with more frequent identity card checks and more pairs of guards from the People’s Armed Police standing at acute angles to one another at subway stations.
This kind of security tightening is often a prelude to a major Communist Party meeting in Beijing and next week sees one of the biggest events in the party’s calendar. This is the fifth plenum of the central committee, possibly the most important meeting of the broader leadership before next year’s party congress.
The party congress takes place every five years, usually in October, and it sees the election of the central committee, about 300 people who form the party leadership. The central committee elects the 24 members of the politburo, who in turn choose the seven-member standing committee, the top leadership led by the party’s general secretary Xi Jinping .
The politburo meets once a month but the central committee comes together in plenary session only about once a year, with each plenum having a specific agenda. The fifth plenum traditionally focuses on party governance and next week’s meeting is likely to see a deepening of Xi’s campaign to improve internal discipline, the most prominent element of which is his anti-corruption drive.
More than a decade into the campaign, it remains intense and relentless, with more than one million party members disciplined last year and a raft of serious, high-profile cases in the last two weeks alone. They include the indictment of a former mayor of Chengdu, the arrest of a former mayor of Chongqing (and his son), the jailing of a former mayor of Wuhan, the prosecution of the former police chief of Heilongjiang and the indictment of a former university president.
In all of these high-profile cases, the charges are connected to bribery and the abuse of public office for personal gain, sometimes involving huge sums. Former Wuhan mayor Zhou Xianwang was sentenced to 14 years in prison for taking more than 60.5 million renminbi (€8 million) in bribes over two decades.
One point of interest at next week’s meeting will be to see who is missing or has been purged from the central committee after the investigation or expulsion of dozens of its members since 2022. This includes three members of the politburo – two generals in the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) and a former party secretary in Xinjiang.
The purge of the PLA leadership has been so extensive that of the six generals appointed to the party’s Central Military Commission, which oversees the armed forces, only one remains. The fifth plenum could see some figures named to fill the vacant places.
[ Chinese Communist Party may be set for a dramatic transformation but Xi’s grip on power as strong as ever Opens in new window ]
Next week’s meeting comes as the party leadership is vetting prospective candidates for the central committee that will be formed at next year’s party congress. Xi has frequently complained about the quality of some party cadres, criticising officials who publicly appear loyal but quietly avoid implementing directives as they build their own cliques.
Xi’s control over the system is such that nobody believes he can be denied a fourth term as general secretary next year if he wants to remain party leader. And there is no sign that he is preparing to leave office, nor is anyone from the broader leadership being obviously groomed as a successor.
But other members of the politburo will retire next year and despite Xi’s dominant position, the party retains the architecture of a collective leadership. Changes within the leadership are likely to be reflected in policy, and generational change could have a more profound impact in China than elsewhere.
The formative experience for Xi’s generation was the Cultural Revolution and the chaos, violence and cruelty it visited on so many, including Xi’s own family. But the rising generation of party cadres now in their fifties grew up under Deng Xiaoping’s reform and opening up and saw life in China improve dramatically in each decade.
Last August, Xi paid tribute to the late Chinese leader Jiang Zemin on the 100th anniversary of his birth, an event that led the front pages of much of the state media. Xi portrayed the party’s current leadership as a continuation of Jiang’s political project, which promoted private business and wealth creation.
[ China’s quiet reform could reshape life for hundreds of millions of migrant workers Opens in new window ]
As they watch the formation of the next party leadership, China’s rich recall the years of lightly regulated wealth creation under Jiang with fondness. And they hope that Xi’s tribute to his predecessor signalled the possible return of some of that spirit.

title: I’ve changed my mind about extensions. They can be great for women with thinning hair
description: Experts advise on the hair types best suited to extensions and those who should avoid taking the plunge
content:
F or years, my view of hair extensions was rather archaic. Rapunzel-like locks with obvious bonds or tapes came to mind, mostly on younger women who wanted to change their style or have very long hair. I had briefly tried them myself about a decade ago, but could not manage the maintenance, and they were whipped out shortly afterwards.
Recently, my hairstylist suggested I try them again. I was growing my hair and wanted a little more volume, especially at the sides. She felt my hair could support them and assured me that the quality, fitting methods and maintenance required had moved on considerably since my first (failed) attempt.
So, I took the plunge. And I love them. They’re all but undetectable, adding fullness exactly where I wanted, while still looking like my own hair.
Conversations with friends, colleagues and industry experts have since revealed what I’d been missing. Hair extensions are more advanced than ever, and being used by women dealing with thinning hair, including during perimenopause and menopause, and sometimes alongside treatments aimed at improving hair growth and scalp health.
If you’re considering hair extensions, a consultation with an experienced specialist is the best place to start. There are many options available now, including wefts, tapes, individual bonds, clip-in pieces, halo extensions, mesh integration systems and hair pieces, using natural and synthetic hair. Prices vary considerably, from several hundred euro for a volume boost up to €2,000 and above for a bespoke mesh system, depending on the method, the amount and quality of hair, whether it can be reused, and the maintenance involved.
To find out more, I spoke to Dr Emma Fanning, an aesthetic doctor and founder of Le Formulaire clinic in Dublin 2, who has a particular interest in treatments to support hair growth, and hair extension specialist Nancy Costello, founder of The Belle Brush and Belle Hair Salon in Galway .
The first thing Fanning aims to establish is what someone means when they describe their hair as thin. Is it shedding more than usual? Are fewer or finer hairs growing from the scalp? Or, is it breaking along the length? These are different problems requiring different approaches. A widening parting alone is worth having medically assessed, she says, “because it is the classic early sign of female pattern hair loss, and treatment works best when started early. Styling can disguise it, but it won’t change its course”.
Fanning says treatment starts with getting that diagnosis right. That might mean correcting a deficiency, looking into a trigger that causes shedding, or prescribing medical treatment. Her three favourite approaches at her clinic are LaseMD Ultra, polynucleotides and platelet-rich plasma (PRP).
According to Fanning, the latter “has the strongest evidence of any in-clinic hair treatment, with studies showing improved density and reduced shedding, particularly while the follicles are still active”. PRP works using your own blood. A small sample is spun to concentrate the platelets and plasma, which are rich in growth factors. These are then injected or lasered into the scalp at the follicle level.
She’s keen to stress, however, that no treatment produces an overnight result. Results take time. Can extensions help someone feel better about their hair while they wait? Fanning says yes, but the diagnosis matters here too. “Extensions attach to existing hair, so the real question is whether the hair and scalp can bear the load.”
[ I have alopecia – I always have at least one small patch of hair loss on the go Opens in new window ]
She says that mild pattern thinning is very different from an active shed, alopecia areata (a condition where the immune system attacks hair follicles, causing hair to fall out) or a scarring condition. The strength and density of the hair and the health of the scalp also need to be taken into consideration, along with the weight, extension method and how long they will be worn. The main risk factor she highlights is traction alopecia – hair loss caused by repeated pulling on the follicles.
Costello agrees and says that sometimes, the most professional thing a hair-extension specialist can do is turn the client away. For others, she might recommend less hair, or a different method. “The health of the client’s own hair should always dictate the extension plan, rather than the other way around.”
For those seeking fullness rather than length, Costello says people are often surprised by how little extension hair is actually needed to make a noticeable difference. A “volume boost” is one of the most popular services at her salon, with small amounts of hair placed strategically, close to the client’s existing length.
With fine hair, Costello says there is no single extension method considered universally best: “What matters is weight distribution, placement and the ratio of extension hair to the natural hair supporting it. The cut is also important. Too much length or bulk through the ends can make extensions harder to blend and manage.”
Her approach takes account of lifestyle as well as hair: how much maintenance someone wants, how often they can return to the salon, and whether something worn occasionally like a hair piece would suit them better. If someone swims in the sea every day, for example, she would be cautious about recommending extensions.
Once the extensions are fitted and you’ve skipped out of the salon feeling fabulous, Costello says not to forget about maintenance. “Extensions should never be something that are fitted and then forgotten about. Monitoring the health of the natural hair is just as important as the initial application.”
For first-time wearers, she recommends a check-in at the four-week mark to make sure everything is comfortable and that your scalp and hair are happy. After this, follow-up appointments will depend on the type of extension you opted for and the condition of your own hair.
Fanning points out things to watch for post-application, including persistent pain or pulling, itching, redness, bumps around the attachments, or broken hairs and thinning at the bond sites. “If any of these happen, go back to your stylist and have them loosened or removed professionally – don’t pull them out yourself, as that can cause more damage.” She recommends medical assessment if symptoms persist or the thinning doesn’t improve.
Fanning also emphasises the emotional impact of hair loss, which she describes as quietly devastating for confidence. With treatment taking time to produce results, how someone feels about their hair in the meantime matters. For suitable candidates, she sees extensions as a “cosmetic bridge” – a way to restore fullness and confidence while treatment for the underlying hair loss has time to work.
“Used thoughtfully, they work together,” she says. “Used without a diagnosis, extensions can mask – or even worsen – a problem that would have been far easier to treat early.”

title: Late Irish Times restaurant critic Corinna Hardgrave wins top Irish Food Writing award
description: Hardgrave honoured for a knowledge of food and wine ‘as extensive as her passion for small producers and farmers’
content:
Irish Times restaurant critic Corinna Hardgrave , who died earlier this month , was awarded the top honour at this year’s Irish Food Writing Awards, held in Dublin on Thursday evening. Paying tribute to Hardgrave, awards founder Suzanne Campbell said she was “a rigorous restaurant critic and writer, whose knowledge of international food and wine was as extensive as her passion for small producers and farmers”.
Noting that Hardgrave had won restaurant critic of the year at the awards three times in the past five years, Campbell said her reviews had been a highlight of Irish Times food coverage. Hardgrave was, she said, also “kind, encouraging, enthusiastic and wonderful company”.
The Food Writing award, accepted by Hardgrave’s husband Steve Hardgrave, was given for a Saturday Magazine cover story on Ireland’s bakery boom , which judge Hannah Twiggs, food and drink editor of The Independent (UK), said contained “extensive” reporting and “excellent” detail.
“She clearly knew the industry inside out,” Twiggs said. She also praised Hardgrave’s foodie guide to Co Clare from late last year, saying it told a story about “farming, food and place”, leaving the reader feeling as if they were exploring with her, “smelling and tasting everything along the way”.
Irish Times features journalist Sylvia Thompson was also a winner at the event, taking an award for her writing on Irish food producers. She entered articles on women in farming and food producers working to strengthen local food systems .
Drinks writer Shamim de Brún took the drinks writing award for an article on building an exclusively Irish drinks cabinet published in The Irish Times and other work published in Image.
Other Irish Times nominees included John Wilson for wine writing, Niamh Browne in the emerging writer category and Úna McCaffrey for editing food magazine pages. In the food writing category, Aideen O’Flaherty was nominated, as was Ali Dunworth, whose work in Guzzle was also recognised. Dunworth was nominated in the critic category too.
[ Never flippant or headline-grabbing, our restaurant critic Corinna Hardgrave always kept the reader in mind Opens in new window ]
Hardgrave was also nominated in the restaurant critic category, which was won this year by Conor Stevens for work in the Sunday Times.
The outstanding achievement award was taken by food writing veteran Máirín Uí Chomáin.

title: Automatic annual pay increments for the public sector are a myth
description: If not for public sector pay agreements, may workers would suffer serious erosion of their standard of living
content:
Sir, – Pat Leahy perpetuates the myth of automatic annual increments for public sector workers in his article “ Are public sector workers all as badly off as strikes might suggest? This is what the data says ” (Opinion, October 18th).
To be clear, there is no system of annual increments in the public sector. What there is a collection of (publicly available) salary scales for all grades and professions in the public sector. Employees’ salaries progress up these scales until they reach the top point.
I worked for 40 years in the public sector. I was fortunate to be promoted three times during my career, moving to a higher salary scale each time. Despite this, for almost 20 of those 40 years, I received no increase.
For colleagues that did not secure as many, or indeed any, promotions, the situation is worse. Having reached the top point of the relevant salary scale, they did not receive any further increase.
There is no system of salary review within the public sector. Because there is no system of annual increments, these colleagues were on the same salary point for years and in some cases decades.
Were it not for the public sector pay agreements in place over those years, their standard of living would have been hugely eroded.
There are advantages to working in the private sector and there are advantages to working in the public sector. Annual increments, however, is not one of the advantages for public sector workers. – Yours, etc,

title: Increasing number of girls lack confidence in Stem abilities, survey finds
description: Six in 10 identify lack of confidence in their Stem subject ability as barrier to pursuing career in the sector, survey finds
content:
The number of girls lacking confidence in their science, technology, engineering and mathematics (Stem) abilities is rising and causing a barrier to women pursuing a career in the area.
That is according to this year’s I Wish Survey of Female Students’ Attitudes to Stem, published on Friday.
The survey involved 1,660 secondary students and 662 primary students, with data collected on the I Wish app and analysed by Jen O’Shea and Ella Doran, both psychology researchers at University College Cork .
I Wish is a programme aimed at encouraging teenage girls to pursue careers in Stem.
Some 60 per cent of those surveyed identified a lack of confidence in their Stem subject ability as a barrier to pursuing a career in the sector, up from 55 per cent in 2025 and 50 per cent in 2024.
Some 66 per cent of girls surveyed said gender inequality in Stem was the most significant barrier to pursuing a career in the sector, while 66 per cent also reported a lack of information about Stem careers as a barrier.
“Disparities in subject availability, particularly for hands-on Stem subjects in single-sex schools, remain a persistent concern,” the report stated.
It found just 27 per cent of girls in single-sex schools have access to computer science at Leaving Certificate level, and only 23 per cent had access to technology. That compares with more than 60 per cent in mixed-gender schools.
