Similarly, hands-on Stem classes such as construction studies, engineering and design and communication graphics are much less available in single-sex schools compared with mixed-gender schools.
Despite this, the number of women entering Stem undergraduate programmes at third level has been steadily increasing, starting at 31 per cent in 2018 and now standing at 36 per cent in 2025.
In a speech launching the survey, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said the Government has projected a strong growth in demand for digital specialist jobs over the next four years in Ireland – yet women make up only one fifth of this workforce.
“Addressing that imbalance is essential to building the talent our economy needs,” Martin said.

title: History shows there’s no room for ambiguity when it comes to drinking and driving
description: Minister Seán Canney was right to stand down an RSA plan to install breathalysers
content:
T his newspaper noted in October 1969 that there was “surprisingly little public debate concerning the imminent introduction into this country of the use of an estimation of the level of alcohol in a drivers’ blood as a means of assessing his ability to drive a car ”. The new initiative centred on the breathalyser and the blood and urine tests that would accompany it if necessary. If there was to be debate, it was also suggested, it would centre very much not “on matters of principle, but of technology” and the questions of accuracy and loopholes.
From the vantage point of today, the 1969 rules seem astonishingly lax. Even at the time, it was noted that the permitted limit of “125 mg per 100ml of blood” was “a generously liberal one – perhaps equivalent to six small whiskies or four pints of beer taken by an eleven stone man over a period of two hours”. I’m not sure about the strict accuracy of that, but today we would call that binge drinking. And today the legal limits are 50mg of alcohol per 100ml of blood for fully licensed drivers and 20mg of alcohol per 100ml of blood for professional, learner and novice drivers.
The new dawn in 1969 certainly did not inaugurate an era of vigilance; the then minister for health, Fianna Fáil’s Erskine Childers , remarked on the Irish determination to shove problem drinking “under the carpet”. In February 1972, Bobby Molloy , the minister for local government, whose department had responsibility for roads, wrote an unusually emotional letter to taoiseach Jack Lynch about road deaths. Molloy was alarmed that the “figures issued by the Gardaí for January show another shocking increase to 62 deaths – 22 more than in January 1971. It looks as if we must expect 700 road deaths this year and at least 25,000 people injured unless we can take some drastic action to prevent it ... Above all, there is frightening (though confidential) evidence of the level of alcohol in the bodies of accident victims, while drivers under the influence are a common sight after closing hours ... drunk driving and excessive speed should be eliminated or reduced to a tolerable level.” He finished by writing of the “despair which I feel. I even thought of asking for a day of national mourning for the 600 dead last year and making it an annual event.”
The mourning days came in time, under a global umbrella, in the form of World Day for Remembrance of Road Traffic Victims, which – starting in 2005 – the United Nations asked governments to hold on the third Sunday of November each year. To mark that day in November 2015, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) noted that since the first recording of Irish road traffic victims in 1959, “23,752 people have been killed on roads in the Republic of Ireland. Records began in 1931 in Northern Ireland and since then, 14,767 people have been killed on the roads. This means that 38,519 people have died on Irish roads since the record system was first put in place.” The following year, the RSA revealed alcohol had been a factor in 38 per cent of all road deaths between 2008 and 2012.
The progress made over the decades has been remarkable, though understandable concern remains about recent increases; there were 182 people killed in road crashes in the Republic in 2025, according to the RSA, up from 171 in 2024. Road safety awareness is a relatively recent development; the RSA was established in 2006, taking over from the National Safety Council. The previous year there were 399 deaths on Irish roads. Fifty years after Molloy’s plaintive letter, in 2022, 155 people died in road crashes.
Many factors contributed to the improvement, including the quality of roads and cars, but much effort was also expended on education and high-profile campaigns warning about the dangers of drink driving. This makes it all the more puzzling that the RSA even considered it was a good idea to install breathalysers in pubs and hotels; as reported this week, it has been ordered by the Minister of State for Road Safety Seán Canney to abandon this plan, as it was “ offering ambiguity ”.
[ Drug-driving surging due to ‘really concerning’ rates of cocaine use Opens in new window ]
He is surely right. As far back as 1969, as the breathalysers were introduced, this newspaper wondered whether it would be possible in time “that the only way in which the testing of a driver for the exact amount of alcohol in his blood can be applied ... will be to assert that a driver with any alcohol at all in his bloodstream should not drive? It would, in effect, bring us back to the old thesis on drinking and driving; if you drink, don’t drive. And who could say that our accident statistics would be any the worse for that?”
If it was an old thesis in 1969, it surely should be more than well established by now.
[ All cars should have inbuilt breathalysers to combat drink-driving, Oireachtas committee told Opens in new window ]

title: Three-bed Terenure penthouse with views over Bushy Park
description: Spacious apartment surrounded by parkland in the heart of Dublin 6W
content:
The views of the surrounding parklands are good from any apartment at Bushy Park House, but the treetop setting of the penthouses is the prime spot at the Terenure development. These top-floor homes were in high demand when first released on to a Celtic Tiger market in 2003, with the larger types coming with a €1 million price tag.
Number 60 is a penthouse at the O’Mahony Pike-designed development that is now for sale with Lisney Sotheby’s International Realty, seeking €895,000. While not the biggest penthouse in the scheme, it is spacious, with three bedrooms, and is set out over 98sq m, with a wraparound balcony adding another 25sq m.
There are a total of 254 apartments and 18 houses at Bushy Park House, which was built in the early 2000s. It was developed on the grounds of an 18th-century property that was later owned by the Religious Sisters of Christian Education, who established Our Lady’s School there in 1953 and went on to sell it in 1998.
The scheme is beside the 51-acre expanse of Bushy Park, and number 60 is on the corner of the block, looking directly over its playing fields. It has stood up well over the years and shows no sign of ageing. It’s surrounded by greenery, with mature landscaping and the park’s trees around the boundary.
The building is entered through a spotless shared lobby with a lift up to the top floor. Inside number 60 are two storage cupboards off the hall, two bedrooms straight ahead and the third bedroom and living areas to the right.
A set of doors allow the kitchen to be closed off from the open-plan living/dining space whenever necessary. The kitchen is a decent size and comes with plenty of wall and floor units, as well as a double oven, a dishwasher, a washing machine and a Siemens hob.
The living/dining space is bright and uncluttered, with floor-to-ceiling glazing wrapping around the corner site and doors out to the balcony. It comfortably fits a large sofa in front of a gas fire with a limestone hearth, and a dining table.
The south/southwest-facing terrace is large enough for outdoor dining, with one side looking over the development and the other out to the park.
The three bedrooms are doubles. The main bedroom is en suite, and there is a second bathroom that can be accessed from the hallway and one of the other bedrooms.
Number 60 comes with three secure underground car park spaces as well as a separate large storage unit of about 13sq m.
The location is pretty good too, with the park on your doorstep, and Terenure, Templeogue and Rathfarnham all within easy reach.
The penthouse has a B energy rating and the annual service charge is about €2,996.

title: Extended Rathfarnham six-bed with multiple living spaces
description: Works have added an extra livingroom and two en suite bedrooms to well-maintained home
content:
Open-plan kitchen/dining/livingrooms are commonplace these days, but they don’t work for every household. The owners of 10 Orlagh Close, a six-bedroom detached house on a quiet cul-de-sac off Scholarstown Road in Rathfarnham , knew they wanted to incorporate some separate living spaces for their growing family when they redesigned this home in 2003.
“The open-plan layout can be irritating in terms of noise, if someone is on the phone or boiling a kettle, for example. There’s also no privacy if you have visitors, and if you’re cooking, you can smell it throughout the room,” says one of the owners, who bought the house in 1992 with her husband.
They opted to turn the garage at the side of the house into a separate livingroom, and went with an open-plan layout for the kitchen/diningroom. There was already a separate lounge and a diningroom, but they wanted more space for their three children.
Glass doors leading out to the back garden were installed off the dining space, and remote-controlled Velux windows. In addition, underfloor heating and marble flooring was installed.
Upstairs, two bedrooms, both en suite, were added, and the attic was converted. Battery-operated blinds were installed in most of the rooms and the entire home was redecorated.
Now extending to 265sq m (2,852sq ft) with a C Ber, 10 Orlagh Close is for sale through DNG Rathfarnham with an asking price of €1.25 million.
The home has been well looked after over the years. Three years ago, the owners added new kitchen units by Jonathan Williams and engaged Dell Interiors to redesign the kitchen/diningroom, which now has an island with wood panelling on the sides and four high seats. A three-tier rectangular pendant light by Eichholtz from Wilde Interiors illuminates the dining table.
The back of the house faces east and, despite the extension, there remains a good-sized garden with a patio and a lawn. In the front, there’s parking space for three cars.
[ Look inside: Large and luxurious six-bed home with verdant views in Rathfarnham Opens in new window ]
Although they planned to make 10 Orlagh Close their “forever home”, the couple, whose children are now grown up, have decided to sell up and move to an older house, which they’re renovating.
“We’ve mixed emotions about letting it go as we’ve had many happy years here,” says the owner. “We’ll miss the house and the area. You’re so close to amenities and the Dublin Mountains here, and you can be on the M50 motorway within minutes.”

title: Beoga on quitting Ed Sheeran’s tour: ‘You have to hold your friends accountable’
description: The Irish trad band say the star should have cancelled tour dates rather than allow Macklemore to be dropped from the bill over his support for Palestine
content:
T wenty-five years is a long time to be together in a band. You couldn’t stay the course, according to Niamh Dunne, unless you genuinely enjoyed being in a room together and making music. That’s something celebrity plays no role in.
“We have always been low-key,” Beoga ’s singer and violinist says as she sips a black coffee with Eamon Murray, the band’s bodhrán player. “We’re not pushing ourselves for the exposure or the limelight.”
Dunne and Murray are friendly, unassuming and good company. Beoga are not a band who sought to make a splash, as their manager knows well, Dunne says, with a wry laugh. What they are is a band who have to follow their principles, as became clear last month.
Beoga, whose other members are Liam Bradley, Seán Óg Graham (who is married to Dunne) and Damian McKee, spent the summer on tour in North America as Ed Sheeran ’s house band. It was a big gig for them, a “life-changing” role with opportunities that could have gone on for years.
In early September, the American rapper Macklemore performed at two shows in New Jersey as Sheeran’s opening act. He urged support for a free Palestine and sang his pro-Palestinian song Hind’s Hall. In response, the Israeli-American Council launched a petition calling for him to be dropped from the tour.
Venue owners, led by Robert Kraft of the Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, who is a donor to Israeli causes, said they did not want Macklemore on their stages. On September 14th Macklemore was removed as the opening act from the remainder of Sheeran’s tour.
When Sheeran released a statement that said the decision was the promoter’s and not his, Beoga and their fellow tour acts Aaron Rowe, the Irish singer-songwriter; the Danish band Lukas Graham; and Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and producer, left the tour in solidarity with Macklemore.
With their manager Sarah Casey (“who is amazing,” Dunne says), Beoga released a statement on Instagram: “To play in venues that silence anyone advocating for a Free Palestine is not an option for us.”
The band refused all interviews bar a short one with RTÉ Radio, to speak about the Garvaghy Road protests in Portadown. “I didn’t see any point,” Dunne says.
Now they’re ready to talk about what happened in North America, albeit still looking slightly shell-shocked. Dunne has driven to Dublin from her home in Antrim. Murray has taken a flight from his home in Co Kerry. It’s the day of the public-sector strikes, and cars are honking as I drive to meet them, which feels cosmically appropriate.
The band were in Ireland when the statement from Sheeran came through on September 15th. They had flown from New York as Dunne’s father, the uilleann piper Mickey Dunne, was receiving a lifetime-achievement award, and Murray’s wife, Pauline Scanlon, had won singer of the year at the TG4 Gradam Ceoil. “We were celebrating,” Dunne says.
They were planning to fly back to the US the next day, for a stadium show in Philadelphia, when Sheeran delivered his statement distancing himself from responsibility for Macklemore’s firing.
“It was a red line,” Murray says. “Statements were flying. We made it clear we would not be going back out on the road.”
“The decision to stand up for free speech and the right to speak about Palestine was a very easy decision for us as a band to make,” Dunne says. “The professional and financial stakes are very real. But the decision was easy. We jumped on Zoom and it was, like, ding-ding-ding, done.”
What happened next was hard for a band who don’t seek the limelight. “Our phones were exploding,” Murray says. “The world’s looking at you and wanting to talk – every news outlet.”
John Reynolds, Sinéad O’Connor ’s producer, called them to offer support.
“John is a good friend. He said, ‘Watching the news cycle post Saturday Night Live and what Sinéad did’” – in 1992 the late singer ripped up a photograph of Pope John Paul II on the television show, to protest against child sexual abuse and its cover-up in the Catholic Church – “‘I remember feeling like the world is going to eat me up.’ He was talking about the overwhelmingness of it. He said, ‘Sinéad was right, and [Sheeran] is wrong and you are right.’”
What did they think about Sheeran’s performance in Philadelphia, when, performing solo, with no tour support, he cried as he spoke, saying that he was not an “activist musician”, had made mistakes, was “deeply worried” about the idea that venues should preapprove the content of a performance, and felt abandoned by friends and family?
“My position has been to Ed and anybody, you can say whatever you want; if you don’t take action, it doesn’t matter,” Murray says. “You can make 100 statements. But if you don’t cancel the shows, it doesn’t matter what you say if you don’t do anything.”
So Sheeran needed to cancel the shows? “In our opinion, yes,” Dunne says. “We should all be able to freely and openly stand up and say ‘Free Palestine’. We support a free Palestine.”
[ You don’t boycott an Ed Sheeran tour just to look cool with a peace sign. Boycotts hurt Opens in new window ]
“We haven’t fallen out with Ed,” Dunne says.
“No, we haven’t,” Murray says. “But you have to hold your friends accountable here and there.”
“Whether it’s Ed Sheeran or your mad neighbour,” Dunne says.
Murray says he believes that the singer had “counsel coming from 100 places” and that the stance Sheeran has taken will haunt him.
“People will remember that’s the position we took and they’ll remember that Ed took that position. That will follow him around. He will have to wrestle with that.
“A friend of mine said, when we knew we were going to be put in an awkward position, ‘Courage can’t see around a corner.’”
S ince Beoga came home they’ve been touched by the way people in their home communities in Kerry and Antrim have approached them.
“You’d meet in the street and they’d say, ‘We’re very proud of you for taking that position,’ people who you didn’t think would be paying attention to what you’re doing or global affairs or the news,” Murray says. “It’s been life-affirming at times.”
Murray and Scanlon have a nine-year-old daughter, Kitty, so now, instead of playing stadiums with Sheeran, the bodhrán player is listening to her beloved hip-hop with her. He’s grateful to have the time together – “My wee girl is delighted that I’m home. That’s the hardest bit of being away” – but the pendulum swing from touring life to domestic life has been disorientating.
There are days, he says, when it’s hard to grapple with.
“In terms of the material cost to us all, nobody thought about that at the time. It’s since then that you think about it and go, ‘Okay, right.’ But you’d torture yourself if you thought about all the things that were going to come.”
Some of the “jubilant responses” to Beoga’s decision to walk away from the Sheeran tour irked him. “The decision was obvious for our own moral compasses, but I don’t think anybody would be celebrating if their friends had lost a big job – you know, they’ve got a really good job and suddenly they had to exit and know they wouldn’t be able to be hired again for a year or two, because of lack of venues or whatever.”
Formed in 2002 at the All-Ireland Fleadh, Beoga (whose name translates from Irish as Lively) have won considerable accolades over their years together, but the path of the musician is rarely straightforward. They have released acclaimed albums – their third record, The Incident, was shortlisted for a Grammy nomination in 2010 – but it was their alliance with Sheeran that brought them a measure of financial stability.
The singer invited them to collaborate with him more than a decade ago; they wrote the songs Galway Girl and Nancy Mulligan together, and they performed on stage with him when he headlined Glastonbury in 2017. Over sessions and live shows, Beoga developed a strong working shorthand with Sheeran.
“He doesn’t like to rehearse that much, but over the years we have done so much together that it was second nature,” Murray says. “We were, I suppose, an asset, in that he could say the name of a song and then 20 minutes later we’d have it nailed down between the five of us. So that’s what he was getting. He could say whatever he wanted to play and we would have it.”
[ ‘A maelstrom of his own making’: how Ed Sheeran’s tour turned into a moment of reckoning Opens in new window ]
For Sheeran’s Loop tour they were the only musicians on stage with him, playing to audiences of 50,000 for up to 45 minutes each night as part of his 2½-hour set.
“It was the first time that we all felt we had job security in 25 years and that we could see that job security through for three or four or five years,” Dunne says. “I wasn’t worried about money for the first time in my life.”
“Any Irish artist would have done the same thing,” she says. “If you’re thinking of Fontaines, if you’re thinking of Lankum, of CMAT, we’re all in the same boat.”
“We’d make the same decision any day. We were flung into it. But anybody that knows us, or knows Irish people, knows we can’t do it any other way. Irish artists are very unified and united. We’ve just never had to say it out loud.”
Beoga’s social conscience runs as a thread through everything they do. Close to a decade ago Dunne founded FairPlé , an organisation for gender balance and equal opportunity in traditional music, with Scanlon, Karan Casey, Muireann Nic Amhlaoibh and others.
More recently Beoga cofounded Irish Artists for Palestine , to help raise funds and bring musicians here, as they did with the Daughters of Jerusalem choir in 2025 for concerts in Dublin and Belfast.
“They came to Ireland, where people can actually bring a small Palestine flag to the gig and wave it. They can’t fly a flag in their own country. Every night we were in floods of tears. You can hear how much grief is in the music,” Murray says.
“Like an awful lot of people, we’ve been going to the protests and pounding the pavement and writing to TDs,” Dunne says. Everyone has the power to withhold labour and to boycott, she says, not just artists. “Please don’t let it be all down to the artists.”
[ The Ed Sheeran controversy made Irish artists the biggest in the world Opens in new window ]
“This needs the workers,” Murray says about the stadiums on Sheeran’s tour. “If all the workers in those places, or all the crew on these tours, decided that they weren’t going to work, then what happens? There’s a blueprint of how it can work.”
“If you withdraw labour it can make a difference,” says Dunne. “The power of the little guy can be so great.”
Murray believes Irish people are more likely to support Palestine because of their shared history of colonisation. “Lots of people were saying recently, ‘You didn’t take the soup.’ Even for that to be still in the vernacular, albeit as Béarla, any politically astute person knows what that means,” he says.
Sheeran recently pledged $2 million in humanitarian aid to the region, although, unlike Macklemore, who donated his $1 million fee from the tour to six organisations for Palestine, Sheeran did not specify that the money should go to Palestinian groups.
Is there a way back for Sheeran and Beoga down the road?
“I’d say it’ll be a work in progress,” Murray says. “I haven’t fallen out with anybody. He would say the same. There’s no fiery spat back and forwards. With activism you want to be changing people’s minds and reaching them rather than alienating them.”
But he reiterates that their principles of free speech are what’s at issue.
“We would really need to see some actual action.”
Beoga performed at a singsong on Garvaghy Road to protest the decision to permit an Orange Order march there. “Myself and Damian and Seán Óg went down, and it’s probably the happiest I’ve been in the last few weeks,” Dunne says with a laugh.
“The community and the people power, the idea that we can come together, that is powerful. They were all standing out in terrible weather for days on end, doing shifts.
“They shouldn’t have had to be put in that position, but they did it because it’s a matter of standing up for the peace and dignity of your community.”
The community Beoga have found in music has been important to them. Kneecap ’s manager, Daniel Lambert , was hugely helpful, Murray says.
“He was very good counsel. He was a great sounding board, because obviously they have been in the trenches as well.”
Industry stalwarts and other “decent skins” have done their best to give Beoga a leg-up.
“Mick Dolan of Dolans” – the Limerick music venue – “was straight on the phone and said, ‘I have a date in October. It’s yours. I’ll hold it for you,’” Murray says. “ Christy Moore is putting on a show in solidarity with us in Vicar Street on December 7th. People see the very real opportunity we walked away from.”
There were other boosts, such as their Instagram following growing from about 30,000 people to almost 350,000, as well as 1.2 million people favouriting their Instagram statement to show support for the band’s decision to pull out of the Loop tour.
And Beoga’s song Exploding Bow recently made it on to school exams.
“You get an email to say that, out of 10,000 tracks, you’re now on the Leaving Cert curriculum for the next five years,” Murray says. “Which doesn’t mean anything [financially], but it’s support. It’s somebody somewhere in an office.”
In December they’re due to share stages in Belfast and Dublin with Duke Special, Rua Rí and MayKay. Before that, in November, they’ll perform at the RTÉ Radio 1 Folk Awards, where they are nominated for best folk group.
“Having things like that to look forward to is great,” Murray says.
Macklemore is staging a Free Palestine benefit show at 3Arena in Dublin next week, the proceeds from which will go to organisations that support the Palestinian movement. It would be no surprise if Beoga became part of it.
“We have found ourselves with lots more free time, and it’s, ‘How can we best serve the people of Palestine?’” Murray says. “It’s not us jumping from one train to another.”
“We all saw the hot takes and the TikToks,” Dunne says. “We’re not interested in any of that.” They have a record of political engagement, she adds. “It’s who we are.”
The day after we meet, the newspapers are full of headlines about another Irish artist. Faber & Faber is withdrawing Sally Rooney’s books from sale in the UK because the writer ’s support for the Palestine Action group means that, under British antiterrorism law, the publisher cannot pass on earnings to her from her book sales there.
“Sally’s very dignified and very bright,” he says. “She has handled it very well. Whatever the UK government are trying to achieve, I think it’s going to spectacularly backfire. Nobody, particularly any institutions in England, should be lecturing Irish people on what constitutes terrorism.”
Beoga will soon begin work on a new album. There’s a palpable excitement as they suggest who they might work with. (The didgeridoo player William Barton is mentioned.)
“We’re going to keep going,” Murray says. “We often say the easiest part of this is us playing music together. We were fine before, and we will be fine again.”
Dunne nods at her bandmate. “Let’s go do that.”
Beoga play at Dolans , Limerick, on Saturday October 24th, and the RTÉ Radio 1 Folk Awards , at Vicar Street in Dublin, on Tuesday November 10th. They’re at the Empire Music Hall , in Belfast, on Wednesday, December 2nd, with Huartan; Friday, December 4th, with Pauline Scanlon and Barry Kerr; and Sunday, December 6th, with Brian Finnegan and Duke Special. They then play dates in Dublin: Whelan’s , on Saturday, December 12th, with Aldoc; the Workmans Club , on Sunday, December 13th, with Rua Rí; and the Grand Social , on Monday, December 14th, with MayKay

title: EY chief Frank O’Keeffe: ‘We are well on our way to becoming a billion-euro business’
description: Frank O’Keeffe talks about EY’s new strategy, its plan to hit €1.3bn in revenues and the impact of AI on the firm
content:
“T his view is great but upstairs will knock your socks off,” says EY managing partner Frank O’Keeffe as he takes in the views of Dublin on a mild and sunny morning from the rooftop of its new headquarters at Wilton Park , alongside the Grand Canal.
He’s not wrong, though my socks survive the blast.
The nearby Aviva Stadium looms large on one side, Liberty Hall can be seen on another and there are wonderful views in the distance of the Dublin mountains and the bay.
The rooftop has a few levels, with a small amphitheatre for outdoor gatherings, some neatly clipped lawns and a forest of colourful shrubs and trees.
It’s a statement investment by EY. So much so that O’Keeffe won’t disclose how many millions were spent on fit-out costs, only that it was delivered “on budget and on time”.
Two of the floors are an acre each in size, and the new HQ can accommodate 3,500 “colleagues and about 600 external guests” at any one time, O’Keeffe says.
On the ground floor, it has three meeting rooms that are available for use by the near 670 alumni of its successful and high profile EY Entrepreneur of the Year programme.
Totalling just under 18,000sq m (190,000 sq ft) of plush office space, it is about 50 per cent bigger than its previous, dated properties in the capital.
EY is very much in growth mode. When O’Keeffe took over as managing partner in 2018, the Big Four accounting firm had annual revenues of about €250 million on the island of Ireland. In the year to the end of June 2025, its fee income was €850 million.
O’Keeffe won’t be drawn on the figure for the year to the end of June 2026 but it’s expected to nudge €900 million.
“Business is good,” he says. “We are well on our way to reaching our strategic objective of becoming a billion euro turnover business over the next number of years.
“We changed our strategy last year because we were watching the world change, from a geopolitical perspective, from a technology and AI perspective and from a national versus global perspective.
“So we changed our strategy around IQ and EQ, all around behaviours. We have digitalised all of our business.
“We have pivoted around how we go to market. We make sure we have an industry lens and a sector lens in everything we do, not just a service lens.”
He describes how EY goes to “market together” with its alliance partners, namechecking Microsoft, SAP, Service Now and Snowflake.
“We became the Microsoft partner of the year for their full ecosystem. We did the exact same with SAP. We also decided that we would export a lot of our capability in Ireland into other [EY] member firms where they needed our support and our help.”
He cites the Nordic countries and the US as examples of where some of its key staff are deployed to work on projects for big clients of sister firms.
He says the Irish firm has spent a “significant amount of money” on training and upskilling its staff so it can deliver for clients.
This all feeds into a plan to achieve turnover of €1.3 billion by 2031, whichwould represent growth of about €400 million over the period.
[ More than half of Irish business leaders worried over ‘sophisticated cyber attacks’ by AI Opens in new window ]
O’Keeffe estimates that EY is the largest Big Four firm in the market, some 40 per cent bigger than KPMG, in second place.
EY employs 5,600 staff on the island (it has 157 equity partners), with 4,400 in the Republic and 3,500 allocated to Dublin. About 2,000 of its staff were not born in Ireland and some 100 nationalities are represented at the firm.
Which brings us to the impact of artificial intelligence on EY’s business, specifically the potential impact on its graduate programme and overall headcount.
“An awful lot of this has yet to be determined and figured out,” says O’Keeffe, while adding that the firm has the largest AI and data analytics practice of any professional services firm on the island, with a team of 350 people.
Within EY, he says it has “embedded AI tooling in our own methodologies in how we actually perform our work on behalf of clients”.
“In our insurance business, we’ve got very specific tools. You could even go into journal entry testing or predictive analytics and sample sizing right through to diligence and corporate finance and also into tax. They are all our own tools.”
When search engines came out, people said there will be no need for professional services. [AI] is no different and there will be winners and losers ... things will change but we will continue to grow
It is also using Microsoft Copilot and Anthropic’s Claude on a day-to-day basis. “We have nearly one and a half thousand technology consultants that you could tag to being AI ... but everybody else is using AI tools and processes and licenses to make sure that we do the most effective roles to support our clients. And we believe we’re ahead of the our competition.”
Amid tales of hallucination, does he trust the accuracy of AI tools?
“We have very rigorous quality control measures when it comes to anything that we produce for the external marketplace. Everything gets reviewed by a human ... we work together as teams to ensure we’re using the technology in the right way and that we’ve got the right processes and controls and oversight in place to ensure we can stand over everything we deliver into the market.”
[ PwC published ‘thought leadership’ reports marred by AI hallucinations Opens in new window ]
He acknowledges that mistakes can and probably will happen, adding that the firm needs to remain “vigilant” in terms of the quality of information it uses and disseminates.
He says EY took on 400 new graduates in September across the island, a “very similar number” to a year ago. “And we’re currently assessing the business need for 2027.”
He’s not convinced that AI will replace graduates in huge numbers. “We’ve always invested in the next generation of talent an we’ll continue to do that as a significant employer of graduates.”
He says today’s graduates have a head start in terms of their abilities on digitalisation, AI and technology, meaning they could rise up the ranks more quickly than would have been the case in the past.
Will the graduate number always be around the 400 mark?
“Nobody can give you that answer. It has yet to be determined. The market is shifting, the way of work is shifting and we have to determine what that will look like over the next number of years.”
[ Graduate recruitment slowdown by firms like KPMG in UK sends shiver down spine of south Co Dublin Opens in new window ]
Looking out five years, will EY still have 5,600 staff? “At least, he says. “But I also think the ways of working will change and what our people will be doing will be different. If you remember, when the search engines came out, people said there will be no need for professional services. This is no different and there will be winners and losers ... things will change but we will continue to grow.”
O’Keeffe is a glass-half-full person and is confident on the future growth prospects for the Irish economy. EY provides audit or advisory services to many of the big multinationals that operate here.
Does he worry that the recent corporation tax windfalls are at risk by one or more of the tech or pharma giants pulling out?
“That’s something that the Government and the IDA need to be really conscious of,” he says. “They need to stay really close to all of the individual companies and they need to explain the attractiveness of Ireland.
“The Government is very pro-business but they need to stay close to what are the issues that those corporation face globally.”
[ Ireland’s corporate tax advantage is over. So what’s the plan? Opens in new window ]
He also makes the point that Ireland needs to be seen as a welcoming place for senior executives and other “talent” that those same multinationals employ here.
“We need to make clear that we’re a welcoming country with humility, which has brilliant talent. Only six generations ago our people had to be leave this island because there was nothing here for our talent.
“Now we have an opportunity to ... bring people from around the world to Ireland. But we cannot do that if we show any signs of xenophobia within our country, and we’ve seen it in pockets, especially in 2025.”
Is the Government right to tighten the rules on immigration?
“We have to be very mindful of people who have already committed to building their lives here and naturalising themselves. We have to be very clever on who comes here for the benefit of the country. That’s a tricky balance for the Government, no doubt. But we need to attract high-end jobs so that we have the best talent coming to the country, because they will also share their experiences and help others develop and grow to that level of talent. We need to make sure that we’re not losing our ability ... to bring the right people that this country needs to continue its success in the years ahead.”
Unlike most of its rivals, there is no term mandate in place for EY managing partners. O’Keeffe has been in situ for eight years now. Does he intend to see the new five-year strategy plan through?
“I hope so. I have all the energy in the world but that will be determined by my fellow partners. The time has flown by and we’ve had so much change from Brexit to Covid to wars, you name it.
“I wake up every morning with lots of energy and still believe I’ll be doing it [the job] tomorrow, next year and hopefully the year after.”
Family: Married to Susan, four children.
Something you might expect: “Passionate about the interconnected forces of people, business, technology and the geopolitics shaping our world.”
Something that might surprise: “For all the seriousness of my day job, I don’t take myself too seriously and I’m usually happiest when there’s a bit of fun and laughter around.”
Leadership style: “I’d describe it as open, collaborative and straightforward. I try to give people the trust and space to be at their best. I’m a big believer in listening, staying curious and bringing people with me. And I’ve always thought a bit of humour helps, particularly when things get challenging.”

title: ‘It’s been a slow-motion car crash’: Ireland’s postmortems crisis under scrutiny on RTÉ’s Drivetime
description: Radio: Colm Ó Mongáin and Katie Hannon favour sober reporting, as Oliver Callan hears lurid revelations
content:
R TÉ has sought to project an image of itself in recent years as Ireland ’s trusted news source, whether through the network ’s “Truth Matters” campaign or Radio 1’s relentless self-identification as “your public-service media”.
Given these constant assertions of integrity, the promise made by Colm Ó Mongáin on Tuesday’s Drivetime (RTÉ Radio 1, weekdays) may cause some alarm among Montrose mandarins. “Still to come, plenty more gossip,” Ó Mongáin cheerily offers by way of piquing listeners’ interest.
Reassuringly, the presenter isn’t actually peddling salacious hearsay but larking about after his item on the dynamics of gossiping. But by the time Ó Mongáin and his fellow host, Katie Hannon , have finished their discussion with the behavioural psychologist Pádraig Walsh one can’t help thinking that gossip and journalism may have more in common than the presenters would care to admit.
At the very least, Ó Mongáin’s characterisation of the sharing of juicy titbits has a familiar resonance. “It suggests someone is telling you something that’s a breach of confidence, that introduces an element of judgment into a conversation,” he says, in a description that could equally be applied to many a tabloid scoop.
Walsh, in turn, lays out the downsides of spreading tales: “If you get known as the gossip, that doesn’t boost your trustworthiness.” It’s an assertion that chimes uncomfortably with the negative perception that many people now have of “mainstream” media.
Either way, it’s hard to disagree with Hannon’s opinion on the spilling of spicy secrets, whether during a chat or in the media: “The more dangerous the gossip, the bigger the dopamine hit when it lands.”
The week’s news being what it is, however, Hannon and Ó Mongáin lack the requisite scandal to release those feelgood hormones. To their credit, the presenters cover the most dreadful stories without any emotive embellishment; they adopt a sober tone when reporting on the funerals of the murdered English family, in Waterford, or on the tragic deaths of the Bray couple whose two young children died in a fire in 2017.
Other topics are more prosaically sombre, as when Hannon hears Dr Denis McCauley of the Irish Coroners’ Society describe the growing backlog in postmortem services that may delay funerals. McCauley outlines how funding, contract and recruitment issues have led to a fall in the number of pathologists, with often upsetting consequences for the bereaved.
“Even as we speak, there are infants who die, and we don’t know the cause of death, being transported from Dublin to Cork,” McCauley says bluntly.
“That’s very distressing,” Hannon replies, sounding anguished and wondering if the situation has reached crisis point.
“It’s been a slow-motion car crash for a decade,” McCauley responds, his slightly jarring image nonetheless conveying the urgency of the problem. Difficult though the discussion is, it underlines that the Drivetime duo’s strength lies in facts, not rumour.
Not everyone can resist the urge to sensationalise, however. With the arson attack that killed the English family still sending shock waves, the crime journalist Paul Williams appears on The Hard Shoulder (Newstalk, weekdays) to tell its host Ciara Kelly why he wants a new offence of drug-related intimidation on the statute books.
Sounding naturally aghast at the appalling murders – “Four beautiful innocent people were buried yesterday” – Williams outlines the way intimidation over drug debts has become one of the most pervasive crimes in Ireland, along with the consumption of those drugs in the first place.
When Kelly asks if his proposed additional sanction will deter dealers, Williams is under no illusions – “They don’t give a damn” – but says the measure would at least put them in prison for longer. “The best way to describe them – and I don’t care about all this woke nonsense – is the scum of the earth.”
So pointless is his sideswipe about wokeness that it comes across as ridiculous rather than offensive and distracts from his main point. The atrocity has been met with revulsion across the political spectrum, after all, and drug dealers aren’t renowned for cultural sensitivity or progressive beliefs.
Williams returns to the theme, however, undercutting his sensible suggestion for an advertising campaign about the dangers of cocaine by dismissing ads about sunburn as more “woke nonsense”. Now that’s introducing an element of judgment.
Oliver Callan (RTÉ Radio 1, weekdays) displays a capacity for lurid revelations on Wednesday when he talks about a shadowy organisation called the Irish Murderesses.
Disappointingly, Callan hasn’t stumbled upon some sinister homicidal cabal; instead he’s talking about a WhatsApp group of women Irish crime writers who have contributed to a new anthology of “twisted tales”, entitled Fear. The host clearly enjoys his conversation with the volume’s editors, Sam Blake and Edel Coffey , with the two authors describing the origins of their group, as well as revealing their own personal phobias.
Callan also discusses literary matters of a “deep, meaningful” stripe on the same show when he interviews Frank Shovlin, who has just published a biography of John McGahern. Shovlin makes a convincing case for the late novelist as “one of the greatest prose stylists in the English language”, pointing to works such as The Dark, his banned 1965 novel, and Amongst Women, his 1990 bestseller.
[ Claire Coughlan: I’m in a WhatsApp group with female crime writers. It’s called the Irish Murderesses Opens in new window ]
But Shovlin also paints a complex portrait of the writer dubbed “Farmer John” on account of his rural Co Leitrim homestead. McGahern enjoyed working on his farm, he says, but also wrote every morning while teaching at universities for extended periods; Shovlin first met the novelist as a student in Galway. He also recalls their final encounter, shortly before McGahern’s death, in 2006, when he insisted on buying a round in foreboding terms: “I have more money than life.”
It’s a fascinating conversation, with the host asking about McGahern’s “secret son”, Joseph, born after a love affair in the 1960s. Callan’s guest describes how the writer played no part in his son’s life, but, having failed to track Joseph down for the biography, Shovlin doesn’t dwell on the matter.
“I think people’s privacy has to be respected,” he says. “That might sound strange coming from a biographer, but I think there has to be a limit to how far one goes.”
Sometimes there’s a fine line between truth and tittle-tattle.
Anton Savage is long-time motor aficionado, but the host of Newstalk Breakfast (weekdays) knows cars and booze don’t mix, as he makes clear when discussing the Road Safety Authority’s ill-starred plan to install breathalysers in pubs.
Talking to Dr Sheila Gilheany of Alcohol Action, the host sounds perplexed about a scheme that implicitly undoes years of campaigning on the dangers of drinking and driving.
“If you are in a situation where you are checking whether or not you are over the limit, why is your car in the car park outside?”
It’s a fair point; little wonder the plan has been stood down. Still, Savage’s scornful summation of the proposal stands out: “One and a half million quid is a lot to spend on answering the question of golfers who want to see the effect of alcohol.” Fore!

title: Gut feeling drives too many marketing decisions in Ireland, says agency
description: Don’t underestimate the value of customer feedback, Oisin Byrne of iReach Insights tells Dentsu’s Dave Winterlich
content:
If you want to get a deep sense of how your consumer brand is perceived, you can’t beat a survey.
iReach Insights has a panel of more than 40,000 consumers in Ireland, all set to tell it like it is. It also has the first and longest running online omnibus in the country, delivering 1,000 responses from a nationally representative group of adults.
Such omnibuses pool questions from multiple organisations, each of which pays for the privilege of a question or two. It’s why its research is of such interest to anyone marketing to an Irish audience, giving them a valuable alternative to what Oisin Byrne, iReach’s co-founder and chief executive, calls “gut feeling”.
Unfortunately, gut feeling drives too many marketing decisions here, he says. It’s why he set the business up 20 years ago and it’s still an issue today.
“The amount of business decisions made in Ireland through gut feel is still significant, even as our population has changed very dramatically in the last 20 years,” he says. “Even today a lot of brands are making gut feel decisions on ad campaigns, on creative, and on which media to use.”
In comparison, this isn’t the case for the company’s UK clients. “UK brands, especially in the consumer space, do literally nothing without consumer research,” he says.
The residual fear among brand managers here however is, for some reason, that consumers hate doing surveys. But the company’s panellists “really enjoy doing them,” he says.
Willingness to give feedback generally was something the company dug into in its most recent omnibus survey.
One of the questions it asked was, “Do you think companies should get feedback from customers more regularly than occasionally?” and 74 per cent of respondents said they would be very happy to give more regular feedback. “And that’s nationally representative by age, region, gender and socioeconomic groups,” Byrne says.
Extrapolated out, it means more than two million consumers are happy to provide information to brands, a resource that is woefully underappreciated, he says.
“And, going back to my gut feel point, we asked, ‘Do you think businesses rely too heavily on assumptions instead of real consumer feedback?’ and 86 per cent of adults believe that is the case.”
We already know from social media that consumers have strong opinions and a penchant for sharing them. But when the omnibus drilled deeper into consumer attitudes, it found that 92 per cent of consumers have a more positive perception of any brand that proactively asks for their feedback.
“The fear factor for many brands is that they feel they are sending out too many emails. We see this in particular in the retail sector.” However, consumers don’t agree. “Some 92 per cent say they will have a more positive perception of those brands that ask for feedback. That’s stronger than we ever would have expected.”
Leveraging that fact is vital, if only to stave off complacency. After all, one of the biggest fallacies brands fall victim to is that being a customer means being loyal. It doesn’t. “We have seen this in projects we have worked on recently, in financial services. Being a customer of a particular organisation doesn’t mean you are loyal to that brand,” says Byrne.
It’s why keeping in touch with your existing customer base is so vital and could be as simple as putting a survey into your newsletter. Just make sure it’s a two-way conversation.
As part of its own operations, iReach Insights runs what it calls iReach Conversations, which allows its survey-taking panellists – all 40,000 of them – to host discussion forums for ideas generation, suggesting fresh ways brands can get feedback. That might include quirky quizzes and fun polls, as a way to do things differently and keep people engaged.
But when consumers do provide such feedback, it’s vital that you acknowledge it, he says. It’s also not that difficult.
‘People versus AI is the wrong question. It’s people plus AI. That’s the opportunity’
“If someone is reaching out and giving ideas or feedback, show that you are acting on it. It’s not rocket science. Just put it in your newsletter, or go back to the people who took part in your survey and say, ‘thanks for that, we appreciate the feedback, we’re thinking of actioning some ideas and will come back to you when we are’,” says Byrne. “It’s a state of mind, not a technology issue. It’s very easy to do but it’s a simple trick that many brands are missing out on.”
There’s an opportunity cost to not responding to feedback, given that 90 per cent of consumers responding to iReach Insights’s omnibus survey said they are more likely to engage with campaigns or content that is built on their input.
“That’s engagement. That’s traction. And it can be turned into loyalty,” he says. “There are consumers right under your nose that you have access to. So engage with them and make sure they know you want to hear their voices.”
Unfortunately too many brands are “afraid to ask hard questions, because either they don’t want to know the answer or they’re not sure what the answer will be,” he says.
Rather than try to put out large, cumbersome surveys infrequently, brands are much better off doing smaller ones more regularly, he tells Winterlich, particularly as the pace of change in all markets accelerates.
It’s activity that can also help winkle out pockets of potential new customer segments, he says, pointing to a recent project which saw iReach Insights’s data unearth a consumer group – men with an interest in cooking – for a dairy product.
The feedback process is being made easier by new tools that provide iReach Insights clients with AI-embedded reporting, helping them to analyse data even more quickly and easily. It is also launching a new AI interviewer product, which will achieve qualitative surveys at scale.
“People versus AI is the wrong question. It’s people plus AI. That’s the opportunity,” he says.
Discover more Inside Marketing podcast episodes at irishtimes.com

title: Affordable wines: a sauvignon blanc and a malbec, both discounted
description: Wines for the Weekend: This French white would be great as an aperitif, while the Argentinian red would match perfectly with steak
content:
We feature two wines from O’Briens today, both on promotion for the next week.
The Côtes de Gascogne, down in the southwest corner of France, is a great source of light, fresh, fruity white wines, usually at very keen prices. The Combes & Trucs below is one such example.
Argentina is well-known for producing high-quality wines made from the malbec grape . The Mendoza region is responsible for 80 per cent of production. Bodegas Norton, owned by the Swarovski family, is one of the leading producers.
Sprightly and vibrant with lifted floral aromas and zesty green fruit. Enjoy as an aperitif or with lighter fish dishes.
Medium- to full-bodied with smooth dark fruits laced with vanilla spice and a good, rounded finish. The local favourite is steak, but robust bean dishes, venison or grilled lamb chops would all do nicely.

title: Lidl to create 500 jobs with €420m investment in Munster
description: German supermarket chain plans to open 14 new stores and redevelop 10 existing outlets
content:
German discount supermarket chain Lidl plans to create more than 500 jobs with a €420 million investment, which includes new stores and a distribution centre.
Lidl has earmarked €306 million for investment in Co Cork , including €200 million for a new distribution centre in Little Island, as part of an expansion across Munster, launched on Friday.
The chain will spend €420 million across the region, creating more than 500 permanent jobs, boosting its Munster workforce to 1,800, opening 14 new stores and redeveloping 10 existing outlets, Lidl said.
Around 250 of the new jobs will be in Cork. Lidl said it bought €136 million worth of products from suppliers in the county last year, including Keohane Seafoods, Castlecor Potatoes and Irish Yogurts.
Along with the increased employment, the supermarket chain calculates that the investment will support 4,500 construction jobs across the 25 developments that it plans.
The €420 million spend in Munster is part of a wider €600 million investment across the Republic, which will involve opening 35 new stores.
Robert Ryan, chief executive of Lidl Ireland, said: “The €306 million we are investing in Cork alone reflects the importance of the county to our future.”
Ryan predicted the investment in Munster would strengthen Lidl’s infrastructure across the region, adding that the chain works with 120 suppliers across Cork.
Tara O’Connor, regional managing director of Lidl Ireland, said the company’s move would support growth there for “many years to come”.
Taoiseach Michéal Martin welcomed news of Lidl’s expansion.
“Businesses like Lidl play an important role in our economy, creating jobs, supporting local suppliers and making an important contribution to communities right across the country,” he said.
One of the biggest players in the Irish grocery market, Lidl employs more than 6,300 people across its 192 stores, its head office in Tallaght, Dublin, and distribution centres.

title: What’s on show at Nevo this year – a brand-by-brand guide
description: We walk you through the models on display at this year’s Nevo EV show
content:
Cupra was originally established as a brand that would be focused on electric cars, as well as being the sporty, Latin passion arm of the VW Group. We’ve already seen, and been impressed by, the likes of the Born and Tavascan EVs, which mix long ranges with engaging driving experiences.
That all gets kicked up a gear – but down a notch in price – with the arrival of the new Cupra Raval, which is the first of the VW Group’s new affordable front-wheel-drive electric models to hit the Irish market.
The Raval is, in and of itself, nothing too unusual – a compact crossover-style hatchback, with a range of up to 450km depending on the model.
What turns it into a potential game changer is its price – from €23,495, although the cheapest small-battery version doesn’t arrive in the first wave of models – and its sheer sense of fun. Cupra describes the Raval as its ideal of an urban electric car, but with the Raval’s sharp steering and impressive brakes, we’d rather take it on a favourite country road, thanks.
It’s not just about fun – the Raval’s boot and back seat are roomy and practical too – but so far, the smallest Cupra is also one of the most enjoyable electric cars we’ve yet driven.
Having been in the vanguard of the electric vehicle revolution with the original Zoe, Renault has had more practice in making EVs than most others, and it shows. The star of the line-up is, of course, the Renault 5 E-Tech, which with its retro-1980s looks and engaging handling is possibly the most adorable electric car out there, even if it’s a bit tight in the back, particularly in the rear footwell.
Well now it might be about to be usurped in the adorable stakes. The Twingo – specifically designed to both mimic its early 1990s progenitor and to be as cheap as possible to buy and run – arrives with a sub-€20,000 price tag and a range of up to 263km, which isn’t much, but it’s just about enough. What really sells the Twingo, though, is its styling, which isn’t so much cute as it is irresistible.
For an affordable car, there’s not too much sign of cost-cutting inside either, with handy sliding rear seats (as per the original Twingo) so you can trade off boot space against rear legroom, and a dashboard layout so cheerful that it might even brighten up an Irish winter.
Those two cars will be the headline act, but there’s a solid supporting cast of Renault EVs too. The Renault 4 E-Tech isn’t as cute as the 5, but it’s usefully larger in the boot (if only marginally larger in the back seat) and now comes with the ultimate accessory – a full-length “Plein Sud” canvas sunroof, just like a 1960s Renault 4 Plein Air. A shame that the good weather has abandoned this model, but there’s always next year.
Then there’s the electric Scenic, which eschews the MPV lines of its illustrious forebear in favour of an SUV shape, but which is exceptionally roomy, comfy, and long-ranged.
Peugeot now offers a fully electric version of every model in its passenger car range, making it one of the first brands to do so. The E-208 is its oldest electric model now, but while it will be replaced by an all-new car in 2027, the current car is going out with a bang, thanks to the arrival of an E-208 GTi, complete with a 280hp electric motor and much sportier suspension and steering.
The E-308 and E-408 have both been recently updated, and while the sharper styling is certainly no bad thing, the more important aspect for the E-308 is that it now has a little more range, with its slightly larger 55kWh battery giving it up to 452km of range on the official WLTP test. The E-408 is a larger car, but thanks to a low-slung and slippery body, it has a fractionally longer claimed range of 453km, using the same battery as the E-308.
The E-3008 is the star of Peugeot’s electric line-up, though, thanks not merely to its dramatic styling and high-tech interior (that floating screen that sweeps across the dashboard looks fantastic) but also to its truly usable real-world range. The standard model, with a 73kWh battery, can put a genuine 450km between charges, which is useful, but the bigger battery model, with 97kWh, is just starting to become available, and that stretches the official range to a whopping 700km.
The E-3008’s only real flaw is that it’s not the roomiest in the back, but you can fix that by going for the E-5008, a seven-seater which is like an E-3008 with a loft conversion. That’s a properly spacious car, and the extra length and height only exact a relatively small price when it comes to range on one charge.
So far, Xpeng has been a single-model brand in the Irish market. The G6 SUV – updated last year – is a very decent car if you’re just going to have the one, however. It uses ultra-fast-charging lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) batteries which can inhale, at maximum, 450kW of charging power, which is great and all, but it would be helpful if any chargers in Ireland could actually pump out that kind of energy. Right now, they can’t, but it’s always good to be future-proofed, right?
You can choose from standard or long-range G6 models, and there’s a very high-performance four-wheel-drive version with 668hp too.
What’s next from Xpeng? This is a brand with serious expansion on its mind, and Xpeng’s not for scrambling around in the affordable end of the EV market – it wants to take on BMW and Audi for premium buyers’ cash. Which means it’s slightly odd that its next car will be the big X9 seven-seat MPV – surely that’s not chiming with buyers’ SUV obsession? Maybe not, but perhaps the sheer luxury and space of the X9’s cabin will tempt them in.
Beyond that, the sleek L03 SUV-coupe should arrive shortly after, alongside the G9-L, a large, luxurious SUV with eyes on a Range Rover-shaped prize. After that, we’re holding out hope for the next-generation P7 electric saloon, a BMW 5 Series rival with stunning looks and up to 594hp.
Don’t worry – the return of the “real” Smart is imminent with a new two-seat, ultra-compact city car, called the #2 this time around, ready for release later this year. We don’t 100 per cent know that that’s coming to Ireland just yet, but keep your fingers crossed.
In the meantime, Smart has the well-priced #1 and #3 on sale, complete with their wild high-performance 422hp Brabus versions, and while they’re not the super-small Smarts of old, they do offer copious interior space in relatively compact shapes. On top of which, you’re getting an interesting combination of Mercedes design and engineering, and Chinese battery expertise and tech.
Up next from Smart is its biggest car yet, the #5 SUV, which also comes with a high-performance Brabus variant, this time with a whopping 646hp and four-wheel drive, as Smart wants to take on the likes of the Skoda Enyaq RS and the Tesla Model Y Performance.
Beyond that? While we’re waiting for the #2 to be confirmed for Ireland (please) there’s also another new Smart that we don’t get yet, but might – a handsome sports saloon called the #6 that comes with a plug-in hybrid engine. A perfect two-car garage alongside the #2? It just might be.
When Italians do things, they almost always do them much more stylishly than we northern Europeans. Instead of mashed potato, you get pasta carbonara. Instead of jeans and a fleece, you get a Zegna suit. Instead of a dullard hatchback, you get a Fiat 500 or Grande Panda.
The electric version of the Grande Panda is a classic Fiat, and not just in its styling, which takes some very cool cues from the original Fiat Panda of the 1980s and updates them for the 2020s with pixel-brick lights that look like they were designed by Lego, and even a built-in charging cable that winds itself neatly back under the bonnet after you’ve used it.
What we mean by a “classic Fiat”, though, is that you’re getting more than you expect for your money. From just €22,995 you get 320km of range on one charge and plenty of space in the cabin and boot. What’s more, you get style. You get a car that looks and feels 10 times cooler than the cost suggests. This isn’t Lidl-style bargain-bucket motoring – it’s more like finding a 90 per cent off sale at Benetton.
Need more space, more range? Then upgrade to the cute Fiat 600e, which can manage 400km on one charge. Or for the ultimate in style, there’s the gorgeous Fiat 500e, which has the same range as the Grande Panda but which looks more like a Fendi handbag on wheels.
Jeep’s electric Journey started out with the compact Avenger, which was good enough a car to scoop the European Car Of The Year trophy in 2023. You can get it with plain old petrol power or as a mild-hybrid or four-wheel-drive full hybrid, but the electric version is impressive, with 400km of claimed range and plenty of performance thanks to a 156hp electric motor. Recently updated with some interior improvements, the Avenger is nicely priced, with its entry-level electric, hybrid, and petrol models carrying the same €29,995 price tag.
Like the Avenger, the new, larger Jeep Compass also comes in hybrid forms, but you can also get it as a front-wheel drive fully electric version, with up to 500km of range. However, the star of the show is the just-introduced all-electric 4XE model, which will come to Ireland towards the end of this year. This is not just a second electric model; this is the flagship of the Compass line-up and it comes with 375hp thanks to two electric motors, four-wheel drive and the ability to tackle the kind of rough and tumble terrain synonymous with the Jeep name. Oh, and it has a range of 606km thanks to a bigger 97kWh battery too.
Alfa Romeo is on the cusp of an electric revolution, with all-electric versions of the next-generation Giulia saloon and Stelvio SUV currently being worked on. Those cars should have been with us by now, but sadly Alfa bosses decided to hold back on the launch so that hybrid engine versions could be worked into the line-up too, rather than launching with the electric-only version. Pity. Word on the street is that these are spectacularly pretty cars (in the Alfa Romeo tradition) with long ranges thanks to the big-battery “STLA Large” platform, ultra-fast charging, and up to 1,000hp for the high-performance Quadrifoglio versions. Can’t wait for those, but they’ll not be here until 2028.
In the meantime, Alfa’s one and only electric model for now is the compact Junior, a crossover with sharper Italianate looks than most of its rivals, and the choice of 156hp in standard form, with up to 400km of range, or a shorter-range, but much sportier, Veloce version with 280hp and a sports-car-like chassis set-up. You can get the Junior as an “Ibrida” – hybrid – too, but the odd thing is that it’s the two electric versions that feel much more traditionally Alfa to drive – fast, fun, and engaging.
Honda currently doesn’t have an all-electric model in its Irish dealerships, but that’s not to say that batteries have been abandoned altogether. You can get the flagship CR-V SIUV as a plug-in hybrid with an electric range of up to 82km, and the rest of the Honda model line-up – CR-V, HR-V, Civic, and Jazz – are all equipped with super-frugal hybrid petrol engines.
Of these, the Civic, which was recently given a big reduction in price, is unquestionably the best of the bunch. It’s a quietly handsome car, hiding underneath which are a chassis and steering with a rare sense of precision and driver involvement, and a hybrid engine that easily allows you to crack the 4.7 litres per 100km barrier in terms of fuel economy.
Of course, Honda is working on a next generation of electric vehicles, and that’s being spearheaded by the gorgeous little Super-N hatchback. This teeny-tiny car is massive fun to drive, although a bit short on range, which is possibly why Honda hasn’t brought it, officially, to Ireland just yet. Maybe consider writing a letter to your Honda dealer on that score.
Leapmotor is a Chinese car maker, but one with a strong European connection. Stellantis Group (which also owns the likes of Peugeot, Citroen, Fiat, Jeep, Opel etc etc) has taken a stake in Leapmotor and the Chinese company has taken a reciprocal stake in Stellantis.
Why is that important? Synergies. Leapmotor will now be sharing its electric and range-extender tech with other brands in the group, which should speed up development of new EV and PHEV models.
Which is good news – the current Leapmotor B10 SUV, for instance, is one of the most energy efficient electric crossovers we’ve driven, easily able to average 16kWh/100km even in motorway driving.
The arrival of the handsome new B05 hatchback also proves that Leapmotor isn’t just an SUV-focused company, and it’s sharply priced too, starting under €29,000 for a car with 400km of range (and you can stretch that to 482km if you’re prepared to spend a little more).
Nissan pioneered the modern electric car with the original Leaf hatchback, which launched way back in 2010 and which quickly racked up 300,000 owners worldwide and took home a European Car Of The Year prize.
Now, in 2026, the Leaf has been completely reinvented, with a sleek SUV shape instead of a hatchback body, and a choice of two battery sizes, the larger of which can run for up to 622km on the WLTP test. Quite the advance from the original Leaf’s 160km (and that was on a good day).
Of course, Nissan hasn’t stopped making the sleek-looking Ariya electric SUV, but the latest addition to the brand’s electric ranks is the new all-electric Micra, which shares its mechanical and electric components with the Renault 5 (Nissan and Renault being long-time partners). The result is a car that looks like a modern-day update of a classic Micra (check out the cool circular LED headlight rings) but which drives with a sense of fun – and performance – that surely no previous Micra owner would have experienced. It’s well-priced too.
BYD has become the best-selling Chinese brand in Ireland, moving ahead of its biggest rival, MG, and it’s not too hard to see why. None of its cars could be counted as truly outstanding, but all of its cars are at least very good, and the fully electric models in particular benefit from BYD’s beginnings as a battery maker.
Which means that, almost uniquely, BYD designs and makes its own batteries, with no outside supplier necessary. This means it’s “Blade” batteries – which use the more robust lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) chemistry – can form the core of each car’s chassis, rather than being a plug-and-play component.
The downside is the LFP batteries aren’t quite so efficient, so BYD’s electric models generally don’t have the headline-grabbing official range figures of some rivals, but then they are also generally a bit better at being able to hit those claimed figures in real-life conditions, and LFP batteries can be more often charged to full without complaint.
The brand’s best cars in Ireland are its Seal models – the sleek Seal saloon and the almost-as-sleek Sealion 7 SUV – but we have a soft spot too for the upright Dolphin hatchback, which is a solid all-rounder.
And now comes the Dolphin G, making its Irish debut at the Nevo show and delivering the first family hatch plug-in hybrid on the market. Promising up to 105km of full electric driving before the 1.5-litre four-cylinder petrol engine kicks in, it comes with either a 7.4kWh or 18.3kWh battery pack, the latter delivering that impressive range.
Mercedes is currently going through a big change with its electric models, as it moves from a stand-alone EQ-badged range to models such as the CLA, GLC, GLB, and new C-Class which are fully electric versions of more familiar names. Mind you, these aren’t existing models with batteries, but instead are designed around EV-specific platforms, which should future-proof Merc’s electric cars for some time.
The best of the bunch right now is the newly-arrived GLC which, of course, isn’t cheap but then it’s hard to think of a car this side of a Rolls-Royce Spectre that’s quite so quiet at a motorway cruise. The massive full-width “Hyperscreen” is also somewhat less of a distraction than you might fear, and both factors bode well for the incoming new electric C-Class. The sleek CLA four-door coupe (it’s a saloon, really) is rather more affordable, and really good to drive, but suffers a bit from a cheap-feeling cabin. The GLB suffers likewise (it’s based on the same platform as the CLA) but it’s roomy and family friendly, with seven seats on board (the rearmost ones being very much for kids only).
As with many car makers, Mercedes is keeping hybrid and even a few diesel-engined equivalents on sale – the existing GLC and C-Class will remain on sale for a bit yet – for those who are still battery-phobic.
As with its cousins at Peugeot, Opel can now offer a fully electric version of every car in its line-up. When it comes to the Frontera crossover, that’s both good and bad news. The Frontera is, in electric form, spectacularly affordable but it’s limited to a 300km range, and feels a bit to cheap inside for a car boasting German origins.
The updated Astra hatchback and estate are a better all-round bet, especially now that some of the cabin materials have had a quality boost, and the revised 55kWh battery of the latest version gives the Astra a much more useful 450km claimed range. It’s a super-refined car in electric form, too.
Want more fun than that? Opel is reintroducing its classic GSE badge for high-performance electric models, and the first of those, the Mokka GSE, has just arrived with 280hp and a rally-car-style front differential. It’s genuinely fun, but the range takes a hammering.
We’re awaiting the next-generation of Ford’s all-electric models, as the Blue Oval strikes deals with the likes of Renault (it will use the Renault 5’s chassis as the basis for a new electric Fiesta) and Chinese giant Geely (with which Ford is going to share a new vehicle platform and factory space in Spain).
In the meantime the best way to describe the current Ford EV line-up might be “underrated”. The small Puma Gen-E doesn’t have fantastic range, but it is fun to drive.
The Explorer might be VW-based (it’s the same underneath as an ID.4 thanks to a tech-sharing agreement) but it rides and steers like a proper Ford, and has exceptional real-world range performance. The Capri looks too bulky to wear the badge of Ford’s classic coupe, but it’s actually decent to drive and, like the Explorer, has excellent range.
Then there’s the Mustang Mach-E, which – yes – is expensive, and potentially sacrilegious for using the Mustang badge on an electric SUV, but it’s handsome, roomy and really good fun on a twisty road.
Volkswagen is in the midst of evolving its current ID electric car line-up, while also on the cusp of introducing what might be its most important new model in a decade – the ID.Polo.
The ID.Polo is the start of VW bringing together its ID electric models and its more traditional badges, and not only will it be capable of a 450km range (in big-battery form), but the smaller-battery version will have a sub-€20,000 price tag. Oh, and VW is bringing back buttons for the dashboard too. Hurrah!
The ID.Buzz – all cool 1960s styling underpinned by batteries and modern tech – was updated last year, with a long-wheelbase seven-seater model and newer, bigger batteries, while this year it gained a four-wheel-drive GTX high performance version. You can, of course, also have the Buzz as a commercial electric van – the Buzz Cargo – and that is now backed up in the VW electric vans line-up by the recently introduced e-Transporter, which can carry just over one-tonne of payload, and which has a range of up to 320km.
MG has been absolutely killing it in the electric cars world of late. Its all-battery journey might have started slow with the underwhelming original ZS EV, but now MG is making some of the best electric cars around.
That range starts with the small and affordable MG 4 Urban, which actually isn’t that small at all, and which has enough range to do longer runs when you need to. The big-selling MG 4 EV – separate to the Urban, in spite of the similar badge – has just had a big round of updates including a smarter interior, while the S5 EV and S6 EV SUVs prove that MG can do style and sophistication as well as affordable pricing.
Best of all, there’s the Cyberster, which might not be MG’s biggest electric seller, but its sleek shape, cool Lamborghini-style doors, and sense of driving fun prove that MG’s heart is very much in the right place. We can’t wait for the super-cool-looking coupe version of the Cyberster, due very soon.
Hyundai is one of the best-performing electric brands in Ireland, and once you’ve sampled one of its cars, it’s really not hard to see why. That starts with the small, affordable Inster, which has a wonderfully adaptable interior, is good fun to drive, and yet in bigger-battery form has enough juice to do long motorway runs without complaint.
Then there’s the ever-broadening Ioniq range. The Ioniq 6 saloon (just updated) is one of the best-performing EVs in real-world conditions that we’ve ever tried, while the more upright Ioniq 5 still looks great thanks to its slightly retro-70ss sharp-edged styling. The big Ioniq 9 is a luxurious seven-seat SUV, but the best Ioniq may well be yet to come, in the neat shape of the Ioniq 3 hatchback, which will combine affordable pricing with a roomy interior and a surprisingly big boot, not to mention being the first model to get Hyundai’s slick new Pleos digital infotainment system.
DS currently has two fully electric models available, with a third on the way. The DS No.4 is a relatively compact crossover that’s almost a hatchback, and it competes with the likes of the Audi A3.
Arguably better is the DS No.8, which is a low-roofed four-door crossover, and which does a bit of Rolls-Royce impression from the outside. Well, if you squint a bit. It’s a touch Rolls-Royce-y inside too, with proper luxury on offer (somewhat spoiled by too many switches and buttons from lesser Peugeots and Citroens) and a steering wheel that looks like the propeller from a biplane. The No.8 is super-smooth and comfy, though, and with the big 97kWh battery, it has an exceptional 750km claimed range.
Arriving soon is the DS No.7, which will attempt to package some of the distinctive styling and comfort of the No.8, but in a more conventional SUV shape.
Volvos’s all-electric range has already impressed us. The big EX90 seven-seat SUV is a hugely refined BMW X5 rival with luxury to spare, but forgive us for preferring the lower, sleeker lines of the ES90 saloon, which has outrageous (almost stretch-limo) rear seat space, and huge comfort wherever you’re sitting.
The older EX40 and EC40 models are also still impressive, but we’re less enamoured of the compact EX30, which looks great, but which has had too many reliability issues with its software and batteries for comfort. Oh, and it’s WAY too reliant on its big touchscreen for all of the vehicle’s functions and instruments.
About to throw a huge Swedish cat among the premium EV pigeons, though, is the new EX60 electric SUV, which combines pleasantly understated looks on the outside with one of the best modern automotive cabins of all – unfussy layout, clear screens, comfort (but could use a few more buttons, of course).
If Volvo can keep the reliability gremlins away from the EX60, it could be a big hit, not least because the top-spec P12 version has a claimed range of 805km, which will temporarily (at least until BMW’s 900km i3 saloon arrives) make it the longest-range EV you can buy in Ireland.
Mazda dipped a toe in the electric car waters with the original MX-30, the idea behind which was to have a smaller battery, so the car was lighter and more efficient, but you just had to top it up more often. Sadly, Mazda was ahead of the game there, and the charging network just wasn’t up to the job, so for its new line-up of electric models Mazda has turned to the EV experts at China’s Changan Motors.
Which means the sleek-looking new Mazda 6e saloon and CX-6e SUV are based heavily on Changan’s tech, which is good – sturdy LFP batteries and Chinese EV know-how underneath ultra-stylish Mazda bodies – and also not so good – the cabin is too reliant on the touchscreen, with not enough physical buttons.
Neither the 6e nor the CX-6e have class-leading range on one charge, but the 6e saloon is pleasant to drive, and has an exceptionally affordable starting price for a car that looks that good.
For all those who say that electric cars can’t be popular, take a look at the BMW iX3. Not only is it fully electric, it’s also hardly a bargain priced car, and yet BMW has sold more than 100,000 of them in less than a year, and had to put on an extra shift at the factory to meet demand. It’s not much of a surprise, given the iX3’s sharp handling, smart styling, and high-tech interior that includes the clever full-width display screen running across the base of the windscreen.
Better yet, all of that iX3 tech will shortly be available in the lower, sleeker, lighter i3 saloon, which is the all-electric 3 Series we’ve been waiting for, and which will have a potential range of up to 900km on one charge.
