What was that about diesel? If that’s not enough for you, there’s also an all-electric M3 version on the way, with four motors and upwards of 1,000hp.
Does that put the existing i3 and i5 into the shade a bit? Yes, possibly so and the i4 will be replaced next year by a new i3-based model, while the i5 will get a facelift and – hopefully – an upgrade to the i3’s more efficient batteries.
While we wait for those, BMW is launching the bigger new iX5, which looks like a chunkier iX3, has an 845km range, and if you don’t want electric you can buy a plug-in hybrid or even (not in Ireland, alas) a hydrogen-powered version. The heavily updated i7 is also just arriving in Ireland, with new, slightly softer, styling and more range on one charge.
Lexus now has a two-car electric line-up, starting with the sleek-looking RZ SUV, which you can have either in long-range RZ350e form (with up to 558km of claimed range, and a realistic 470km on the road), or the high-performance two-motor RZ500e, which is not only quicker (4.6 seconds 0-100km/h) but which also comes with the “one motion” yoke-style controller instead of a conventional steering wheel.
In theory, you can fully turn an RZ500e without ever taking your hands off the “wheel”. Both models enjoy an exceptionally high-quality cabin.
Just arriving in Ireland is the lower and sleeker ES saloon, which you can still buy as a conventional hybrid, but which in ES350e electric form comes with an almost-600km electric range on one charge. Outside, the ES is definitely marking a new styling direction for Lexus, but inside it’s a little more traditional, which ultra-high quality levels and plenty of space.
Skoda has become a big player in both the Irish and the wider European electric cars markets, and it’s done so with just two EV models – the Enyaq, and the Elroq. To be honest, it’s not hard to see why both cars have been a big success. Both are based on the same MEB electric car platform, and offer maximum ranges of up to almost 600km depending on the model, or you can sacrifice a bit of range for the style and performance of an RS version. Either way, you get great cabin quality and lots of boot space.
Those two electric Skodas are about to be joined by two more, at opposing ends of the price spectrum. The small Epiq (which shares its bits with the Cupra Raval and VW ID. Polo) is a compact crossover with chunky styling, a big boot, and a hint of the classic Yeti about it. It also costs less than €25,000 for a basic one. Much more expensive – but still cheaper than most of its competitors – is the new Peaq, which packs seven seats and a properly luxurious cabin into a sleek-looking large SUV body. Both of these are likely to be catnip for Irish EV buyers.
Audi doesn’t quite yet offer an electric equivalent of every model in its line-up, but it’s getting there. The impressive A6, for example, can be had as a conventional hybrid car, or as a long-range EV in the shape of the A6 e-Tron. Neither car is actually related, bar the badges, so the A6 e-Tron is actually entirely developed as an electric car, and it shows in a long range and engaging driving experience.
Likewise, the Q6 e-Tron offers an all-electric alternative to the combustion-engined Q5, and shortly we’ll have an all-new, all-electric A2 hatchback (based on the same EV package as the VW ID.3 Neo) which will not only be a battery alternative to the A3, but which is promising to match the efficiency of its 1990s predecessor by offering more range for a given battery capacity than most other electric products.
Beyond those, the e-Tron GT – an ultra-sleek four-door closely related to the Porsche Taycan – hasn’t been a big seller for Audi, but it’s utterly fantastic to drive, and recent revisions gave it more usable range, so buy one while you can. Looking ahead, Audi is pushing on with developing a production version of its gorgeous Concept C sports car, which will be one of the very few electric sports cars around when it arrives in 2028.
Polestar is that rare beast – a genuine all-electric brand, with no hybrid nor petrol nor diesel options. In that sense, its only real rivals for now are Tesla, and the single-model Xpeng. It’s just as well then that Polestar’s electric cars are among the best in the business. Certainly the Polestar 2 saloon is. It might be based on decade-old Volvo mechanical bits, but it has an exceptionally long real-world range and is genuinely enjoyable to drive on a twisty road.
Also hugely enjoyable – but rather more expensive – is the Polestar 3 SUV, which is lower and sleeker than you might think, and which has rally-bred genes in its chassis and steering which make it as good to drive as any electric BMW, or even Porsche. In the middle is the Polestar 4, which threads a stylistic needle between SUV, sports saloon, and estate. No rear window? Yup, which is weird, but it’s sharp to drive and looks great.
Coming soon is a second model in the Polestar 4 range, which is a more conventional looking SUV, while about to launch any day now is the low, sleek, expensive, and bullet-fast Polestar 5, a high-performance sports saloon designed to show Mercedes-AMG the way home.
Having had just the one electric model for a long time, Toyota is at last getting serious about EV motoring. That one model – originally called the bZ4X – has been updated and given the simpler bZ name, while at the same time getting a light design makeover and, much more importantly, a better battery, giving it a much more useful real-world range of around 480km.
That bZ has also now been joined by a bZ Touring, which is slightly longer and taller, and is almost an estate version of the standard bZ with a much bigger boot, and a fractionally longer range thanks to an equally fractionally larger battery.
Best of the Toyota electric bunch for now is the C-HR+, which shares (most) of its badge with the smaller hybrid crossover, but which is much roomier inside than that, and which has seriously impressive real-world range. It’s sweet to drive, too.
Up next? An all-electric Corolla, which we may get to see very soon, and which should really shake up the EV market. That and the all-electric version of the Hilux pickup.
Citroen actually has the cheapest electric car currently on sale, although it does depend a bit on how precisely you define “car”. The Ami isn’t really a car, it’s a speed-limited (50km/h) 80km ranged two-seat urban transport solution. A cross between an e-bike and a tumble drier, but it’s adorably cute and fun.
A bit more serious – and still solid value – are the e-C3 and e-C3 Aircross, which have chunky styling and roomy cabins, but which feel disappointingly cheap inside, and you can’t have a seven-seat Aircross with all-battery power.
Rather underrated are the e-C4 and e-C4X which are stylish, roomy, nice to drive, and with decent real-world range. The e-Berlingo is a bit short on range, but has masses of space inside so it’s ideal urban family transport.
Rather more of an all-rounder is the handsome e-C5 Aircross, which is one of the better-looking SUVs around, has an incredibly comfortable cabin, very usable day-to-day range, and which just needs a little more space in the rear seats to be ideal.
If you’re wondering who or what KGM is, it might help to know that it used to be badged as Ssangyong, but was renamed when the company was bought out by the huge South Korean KG Group. It still follows the old Ssangyong template of rugged SUVs and pickups with relatively low prices, but in the electric era it can’t quite seem to offer the bargain prices it once did.
In electric terms, you can choose from the chunky-looking Torres SUV, which looks really handsome on the outside, and is very roomy inside. Batteries from BYD ensure reliability (always a Ssangyong strong point) even if the range isn’t spectacular.
Or you could go for the electric Musso EV pickup, which is still a bit of a rarity in the pickup world. It’s also a bit short on range, but for roughly the same money as the Torres, you get something rather more interesting to look at, even if you neighbours might think you’re moonlighting as a plumber.
Dacia’s relationship to electric power has so far been a bit … mixed. The tiny Spring EV has been a huge seller for Dacia across Europe, and for a time it was Ireland’s most affordable EV (well, one that wasn’t a Citroen Ami) but buyers here didn’t bite, and so it has disappeared from Irish price lists. A shame – in spite of myriad flaws, it had charm.
There’s good news, though – a brand new all-electric Spring is imminent, which borrows the batteries and chassis from Renault’s brilliant new Twingo. That will mean a circa-250km range, but this time mixed with chunky Dacia styling and practicality, plus a price tag that ought to undercut the Renault, even if only by a little.
There’s more to come from Dacia in electric terms too, with an all-electric version of the next-generation Sandero hatchback due to be shown off next year.
Porsche has vacillated a bit when it comes to electric cars. It was early out of the gate with the brilliant Taycan, which remains a high watermark of electric efficiency, performance and styling. We especially loved the estate-style Taycan Turismo, but sadly few others did and relatively poor sales of the Taycan is forcing Porsche into an electric rethink.
The all-electric Macan is also quite brilliant to drive, and pretty efficient too, which is why we can’t understand why buyers are largely staying away and waiting for Porsche to make a petrol-powered alternative. Will it be the same story with the electric versions of the new Boxster and Cayman sports cars? Those have been on-again and off-again in the new Porsche product plan more times than Ross and Rachel, but they do seem to finally be happening and should hit the road – alongside petrol-powered versions – next year.
Farizon seems to be doing all the right things when it comes to making electric delivery vans. The Farizon SV has funkily cool styling (well, by van standards it does) and a cabin that majors on high-tech screens. It’s also notably long-ranged, with a WLTP range of 397km on one charge easily outstripping what the electric Ford Transit Custom or the Volkswagen e-Transporter can manage.
It can even carry up to 1,350kg of cargo, making it one of the most useful vans of all, whether we’re talking diesel or electric. All of that for a starting price of €44,000. Farizon could yet be a big story in the commercial vehicles world in years to come.

title: A rare spirit of innovation
description: Midleton Distillery master distiller Kevin O’Gorman on the nine-year journey behind a world-first Irish whiskey
content:
“I remember looking at it initially with Billy and it stands out as a moment we said ‘Wow, the flavour profile is incredible.’”
Kevin O’Gorman is recalling an early experiment with French sweet chestnut casks at Midleton Distillery, when he and colleague, master blender emeritus Billy Leighton were exploring what an unfamiliar wood might bring to Irish whiskey. More than a decade later, that work has led to Midleton Very Rare Irish Chestnut Edition, the first whiskey finished in casks crafted entirely from Irish sweet chestnut sourced from a single estate. Its provenance, rarity and unique flavour profile combine to make it a collector’s item.
The project began with trials in 2011, eventually producing a French chestnut-finished Method and Madness single pot still whiskey in 2017. Sweet chestnut had been used for centuries for wines and fortified wines in Spain and Portugal, O’Gorman explains, but its use for whiskey was unusual. Encouraged by the results, the team began looking for Irish-grown trees.
“There are a few pockets of sweet chestnut available,” says O’Gorman, who has spent 36 years in the spirits industry, 28 of those at Midleton.
Forestry consultant Paddy Purser, who had worked with the distillery on its Irish oak project, knew of sweet chestnut at Cappoquin Estate in Co Waterford. Built on the site of an old FitzGerald castle, Cappoquin House is an 18th century Georgian mansion within the estate featuring hills, woodlands and gardens on the banks of the Blackwater river. It has been home to the Keane family since 1735. Purser introduced the Midleton team to the estate’s owner, Sir Charles Keane, who welcomed the idea. O’Gorman remembers the date the trees were felled: November 28th, 2017.
Six trees were carefully selected and they were sent to Maderbar sawmills located in Galicia in north-west Spain where they were sawn into staves. The staves then travelled to a cooperage in Jerez de la Frontera, where they underwent air drying before being made into 240-litre hogshead casks with a light to medium toast inside.
Midleton had worked with the cooperage for around 35 years, and O’Gorman stresses the importance of relying on specialists whose work they knew. He also mentions the involvement of Midleton’s master cooper Gerard Buckley, alongside Purser and Keane, in the careful selection and preparation of the timber. Ensuring that the wood was sawn, dried and coopered correctly mattered at every stage.
The casks returned to Midleton, where O’Gorman and master blender Dave McCabe had to choose the whiskey to fill them. They selected light, medium and heavy styles of single pot still whiskey that had already matured in bourbon barrels for between 12 and 19 years.
“We knew chestnut is quite a giving cask. It matures relatively quickly, it is quite giving, and it has a lot of colour, flavour, and tannins. So we wanted a whiskey to stand up to it.” He compares it to the sport of boxing: “You put a lightweight against a lightweight and you put a heavyweight against a heavyweight.”
Sweet chestnut is more porous and less dense than oak, so the interaction between wood and whiskey can be rapid. O’Gorman and his colleagues sampled the casks every few months, watching particularly closely during the early stages. Their previous experience with French chestnut meant they were confident in the flavour potential, although the initial pace of maturation prompted some reconsideration. Chestnut gave the whiskey colour and flavour quickly in the first weeks and months. After a year or two, however, that pace began to ease, and the additional time brought further development rather than an overwhelming influence from the wood. O’Gorman explains that they kept tasting until they judged the whiskey to be in peak condition.
“We were thinking, this is probably going to be a shorter finish than we had planned. But what we found is after year one, year two, it started easing up, slowing down and developing a wonderful complexity with an aroma and taste profile like nothing else.”
They allowed the whiskey to remain in the chestnut casks for five years; O’Gorman says such a lengthy finish could almost be described as a secondary maturation. The resulting whiskey, bottled at natural cask strength of 56.1 per cent ABV, contains whiskeys aged between 17 and 24 years.
Talking through the aroma, he identifies milk chocolate, vanilla and caramel, followed by cinnamon, nutmeg and sandalwood. There are toasted almonds and pecan nuts, honey and honeycomb, red apples and caramelised orange peel. He also explains the chemistry behind those impressions: toasting wood produces compounds associated with roasted, nutty and chocolate flavours, while others contribute spice and vanilla notes.
Science has become an increasingly important part of distilling during his career, although O’Gorman is clear that it complements rather than replaces the senses of the people making the whiskey. “The nose and taste are the primary senses we rely on, but these are supported by a significant amount of analysis, including gas chromatography and other specialised techniques carried out in Midleton.”
He describes the technological changes that have taken place over the 200 years of distilling at Midleton Distillery. “The Old Midleton Distillery which ran from 1825 - 1975, now a visitor centre, would have used coal for heating up the stills and worm-tub condensers for condensing the vapours. These days we have a significant amount of technology and modern equipment to help us run our processes very effectively with the same level of attention to detail and focus on quality.”
Yet tasting and experience remain fundamental, and he continues to learn from younger colleagues. He describes the daily work of assessing whiskeys and learning from the distillers, engineers and scientists around him. “I nose samples every single day, multiple samples, and I’m learning every day,” he says.
Irish Chestnut Edition, limited to approximately 800 case equivalents globally and priced at €440, is the first release in Midleton Very Rare’s Rare Wood Collection. O’Gorman says the distillery is investigating other woods, although he adds that not every experimental wood would suit a Midleton Very Rare whiskey. The selection process, he explains, is deliberately careful, and the team continues to look at the possibilities.
Asked what has pleased him most about the project, he mentions the finished whiskey, which he had followed closely throughout its five years in chestnut, but also the relationships behind it. He recalls Sir Charles Keane’s enthusiasm from their first discussion and the prospect, ahead of the launch at Cappoquin House, of Keane tasting a whiskey finished in wood grown on his estate. Today Midleton Very Rare Chestnut Edition represents a world-first whiskey that is the result of this special collaboration.
O’Gorman is equally as keen to credit the wider team at Irish Distillers and Midleton, and the specialists involved in selecting the trees and making the casks.
“It’s not just me. We’ve got an amazing team in Midleton and everybody contributed to this project, so I see it as a real collaborative effort.”
The result, borne of patience, provenance and innovation, possesses a very rare character indeed.
Midleton Very Rare Irish Chestnut Edition is now available in limited quantities at selected off licences and online at Midleton Distillery Collection, priced € 440

title: ‘It’s not just a loss of money’: Irish restaurants on the most annoying customer habits during Christmas season
description: There are a few things we should all bear in mind before reserving a big table for the festive season
content:
W hisper it, but the Christmas season is approaching. With this happy yet frantic time of year come family get-togethers, catch-ups over brunch and dinners out with colleagues, all of which require advance bookings. As we head into the hospitality sector’s busiest season, restaurateurs would love their guests to keep a few pointers in mind before making a group reservation.
Chef Kevin Burke of Library Street in Dublin 2 says his 33-seater restaurant receives “a fair few late cancellations or no shows a week”, but he adds that “everyone does”.
The Michelin-listed spot does not take deposits when reservations are made, but it does seek card details for each booking.
“We take nothing at the time ... it is just to cover us on a late cancellation or a no-show. It’s a preventive measure to make sure that people are serious about the booking,” says Burke. He notes that Library Street’s relatively small size means a large group not showing up will have a bigger impact than it might in a restaurant with more tables.
“If I am missing 10 guests in a small room of mine, it changes the atmosphere,” he says. “You want the room to be full ... If I have a no-show fee or a cancellation fee it is not because I’m money-hungry and I want your money. We want guests, we want to serve you and we want you to have an amazing time and if it doesn’t happen it’s not ideal.”
The financial impact of empty tables does need to be considered, however.
“I can’t speak for every restaurant but for here, I do a certain amount of customers and I need a certain amount of staff to cater for them, so if I am missing those 10 guests, I can’t just say to my staff, ‘sorry, they were going to pay for your salary that day’,” says Burke.
He says it’s helpful too if guests can advise of dietary requirements before they come to a restaurant, as well as providing an accurate group headcount.
[ Make it special: the best restaurants around Ireland to book for your next occasion Opens in new window ]
“If you book for a table of eight, ideally if that number turns up that is great. If you come with more, we might not be able to fit it, or even less. A lot of groups will book for 10 and turn up and say that there are only five of us and say it as a normal thing.”
Lara Dalla Bona, general manager of the glitzy 180-seater Gloria Osteria in Dublin 2, says the no-show issue has prompted the restaurant to apply a cancellation fee of €20 per person for bookings of more than eight diners if the cancellation is not made at least 48 hours in advance.
“Sometimes people book multiple times and then they show up at their convenience – that is why we decided to put fees on for big groups because it helps us organise when we know we have a big group coming,” she says.
The fee is not just about helping the restaurant recoup money, but to ensure that the tightly planned Christmas season runs smoothly.
“It’s about being secure in how we are going to run the business over Christmas. It’s not just a loss in terms of money, it’s more about organisation, time, people that you prepare on shift, food that you order to make sure you have enough to serve and deliver a smooth experience,” says Dalla Bona.
Another issue when it comes to catering for large groups is timekeeping.
[ Abuse of staff in top Irish restaurants: ‘It was like I had been mugged’ Opens in new window ]
“When it is a very big group, one [person] might come a little bit earlier and then someone else comes after half an hour or 45 minutes,” Dalla Bona says. “We have a sharing concept style and when people don’t arrive all at the same time, they don’t get to eat as much as the other people did, or the food is not warm anymore.”
She says it’s always best to have guests together and on time, especially at Christmas time. This helps with table rotation and with ensuring guests are happy when they leave.
“That’s the aim in hospitality,” says Dalla Bona.

title: Used EV values starting to rise as finance packages evolve
description: The issue of poor used values for electric cars is fast becoming a non-issue, while customer demand will mean finance packages will need to encompass more than just the purchase price
content:
Electric cars have been through their ups and downs when it comes to used values. In the immediate wake of the Covid pandemic, there was an enormous focus on electric cars, and for a brief time, used values spiked.
However, that was followed by a major crash in used EV values as the traditionally conservative secondhand car market raised its doubts over battery life and charging infrastructure. Buyers stayed away, to a large extent, and so used values for electric cars plummeted.
That has certainly changed, especially over the past year, and the upward trajectory of used EV prices seems unstoppable now, to the point where a used electric car is rapidly approaching parity in terms of price with an equivalent used petrol, diesel, or hybrid car.
Canice Fitzsimons is the auction manager at Merlin Car Auctions, where many EVs will begin their journey from their first owner into the secondhand car market.
“I would say we’re definitely over the worst of it, from the perspective of used EV values,” said Fitzsimons.
“It’s definitely levelling off, and the electric vehicles are now starting to depreciate in what you might call the right way, in the same fashion as a petrol or diesel car. Now, if I’m valuing a car coming through the door for an auction, I’d have a fair idea of what it’s worth. That was very difficult to do previously. It was a minefield for a long time, from 2022, all the way up until the middle of last year. I would say the confidence of valuing EVs wasn’t there.”
That process is taking time, though, and Fitzsimons reckons that the next 12 months will see further significant movements in electric car values.
“For instance, you can see Volvo has made a massive leap, and it just doesn’t make diesel models anymore. That kind of thing gives confidence for buyers and from the retailer’s perspective. On the retail side of things, for new electric cars, that’s just surging in a massive way; it’s stratospheric,” said Fitzsimons. “In the used market, we’ve just about found our electric feet.”
There is a warning hanging over all this, however, and Fitzsimons said that’s because “an awful lot of people are still wary of how much it’ll cost if something goes wrong”.
That continuing concern over long-term battery reliability may yet prove a brake on climbing electric car residual values.
However, those used EV values are, for the moment, climbing. According to figures from DoneDeal, electric car values have climbed by 2 per cent this year, outperforming hybrid and combustion cars.
Such a change means that the finance that we use to buy such cars will need to change. In the short term, firmer used values for EVs should mean that more competitive finance offers will be available for them, but there’s more to it than just that.
Martin Cardiff, head of sales for Volkswagen Ireland, said: “Through Volkswagen Financial Services, we offer a range of HP [hire purchase] and PCP [personal contract products] to new and used car customers across all powertrains. PCP provides customers with greater certainty and peace of mind around the future value of their vehicle, which is one of the reasons it remains so popular across all powertrains.
“Private lease customers currently cannot avail of the SEAI [Sustainable Energy Authority Ireland] grant, which represents a missed opportunity. Extending the grant to private leasing could help bring more EVs into the used car market, while giving customers the benefit of predictable monthly payments without the commitment of ownership or the need to consider the vehicle’s future value.”
While private leasing is something of a niche product for now, it seems likely that the more common PCP and HP finance deals will evolve in the coming years, as the nature of car ownership changes. With growing used values, there’s more opportunity for EV-specific finance packages to be created, but beyond that it looks very much as if the nature of electric cars means that buyers might start hanging on to them longer.
Battery longevity has been impressive so far, and that longevity, combined with constant improvements in a car’s functionality thanks to over-the-air software updates, means that car buyers might not feel the need to trade in so frequently in years to come.
Indeed, the likes of BMW are already predicting that car buyers might keep their car for several years and, instead of trading it in for a new car, will instead come back to a dealership for semi-regular updates and improvements, including the likes of replacing tired battery cells and even replacing interior trim and touchscreens to keep a car up to date.
Given that, finance packages will need to change from their current three-year cycle to something quite different. Banking experts predict that in the future, electric car finance won’t just be about buying a car but will need to take into account the total cost of ownership, including long-term servicing and repairs, battery health and replacement, and even charging costs. We’ve already seen the beginning of this, with PCP plans including options for servicing costs and even tyre replacements to be included in the payments.
In the longer term, we could be looking at one of the biggest car finance shake-ups since Ford first introduced the PCP in the 1990s.

title: Seeing What’s Hidden by Manchán Magan: Author’s last words mingle trademark lyricism and rigour
description: Also reviewed: Those Who Listen – New Irish Writing on the Bog
content:
In his introduction to Manchán Magan ’s Seeing What’s Hidden, Robert Macfarlane encapsulates Magan’s relationship with our world. Our existence, Macfarlane writes, “is an ongoing, unfurling, iridescent miracle, happening around and within us every moment”; and our connection with our surroundings can be renewed by being aware of the lives of tree, stone, river, and of the myriad ways in which these lives intersect with our own.
Magan himself – in these, the last words we shall have from him – continues this thread, arguing with his trademark mingling of lyricism and rigour that the Irish have all the tools necessary – language, lore, deep knowledge – to rediscover this miracle.
The experiences of a history of colonisation have traumatised the land, Magan observes, but have by no means ruptured the connections between nature and people. The book was unfinished at the time of Magan’s death, but a sequence of satisfying essays by Merlin Sheldrake, Kerri Ní Dochartaigh and others complete a luminous text.
[ Manchán Magan’s final part of his trilogy: Ireland was believed to be the outer limit of the known world Opens in new window ]
Magan’s ideas are also taken up and explored in the series of moving texts gathered by Alice Kinsella in Those Who Listen. Kinsella’s fine introduction addresses the layered relationship between the Irish and our bog landscapes, with the latter regarded as simultaneously a place of work, nature, secrets, history and potential menace, “as both a living presence and a site of labour, memory, and culture” – and each of these layers is amply explored in the work that follows.
“Oh Christ, it was misery,” writes Belinda McKeon in Endless, remembering the exhausting labour associated with the bog, “I wish I could pretend otherwise, but when I think about the rows of turf and how they stretched out into the future, I can feel it still in my back and in my legs.”
Dean Black’s Bog Bodies addresses directly the tortured relationship between the Troubles and the bog; while other pieces echo Magan’s call for a renewed relationship between humans and world, completing the circle with stirring lyricism. As Jane Clarke reminds us in Large Marsh Grasshopper, all we need do is pay attention: “Somewhere a grasshopper / clings to white beak-sedge. / Yellow-green with red legs / and black knees, he flicks / his tibia against the tips / of flexed wings. Somewhere / a grasshopper sings.”

title: Price is as key as brand heritage in the new car market these days
description: Bank of Ireland says it has seen a clear increase in applications and financed contracts involving emerging brands
content:
There are two evident trends in the new car market. Firstly, electric cars (EVs) are no longer the preserve of technophiles or early adopters. EVs are increasingly occupying the driveways of mainstream buyers, from car fanatics to the A-to-B commuters.
Secondly, an increasing share of sales is going to relative newcomers, particularly brands from China. Where it once took a brand like Lexus a decade or more to establish a foothold in the market, new arrivals are claiming a decent chunk of sales within as little as 18 months.
The lure of these new brands starts with price, supported by a wealth of in-car tech that can be striking to anyone who hasn’t changed their car in the past five years. In that time, there’s been a revolution in infotainment tech, not unlike the leap from blocky mobiles in the late 1990s to the touchscreen smartphones that followed.
For Irish consumers, it appears that price can matter as much as brand heritage. And lending data suggests the newcomers are starting to make an impact.
“We have seen a clear increase in applications and financed contracts involving emerging brands, although it would be premature to describe this as a wholesale move away from established manufacturers,” a Bank of Ireland spokeswoman says.
The bank’s lending data, she says, points to a market that is expanding for both groups. “Established brands continue to command considerable customer confidence and dealer coverage, but emerging brands are now achieving meaningful scale and competing directly for mainstream customers.”
The trends in the bank’s data also suggest that greater choice, rather than one dominant manufacturer, is likely to drive the next stage of EV growth.
“BYD, Xpeng and MG has shown the strongest sustained growth in the bank’s electric vehicle data,” the spokeswoman says.
However, she also points out that financed volumes remain substantial for established brands such as Kia, Hyundai, Ford and Volvo.
“Customers are using a mixture of hire purchase and contract purchase to fund their new or used EV. The data suggests that the EV customer base is widening and the next phase of market growth likely to come from wider mainstream adoption rather than solely from technology-focused early adopters.”
Nor does it appear that the age of buyers is a significant dividing line. Emerging brands have secured customers across all age categories, the spokeswoman says “and there is no significant difference between emerging or well-established motor brands in our data”.
So what’s persuading buyers to take a chance on an unfamiliar badge? Pricing and finance offers are clearly primary drivers, but buyers are also being attracted by high levels of standard equipment, improving range and charging performance, and a wider choice of models, particularly in popular categories such as SUVs and crossovers.
Those choosing newcomer brands don’t appear to be behaving very differently when it comes to borrowing. Bank of Ireland says its data on EV buyers shows customers buying emerging-brand EVs finance a slightly lower euro amount, but it is still a very similar proportion of the vehicle’s cost, compared with the wider financed EV market.
“This suggests that the difference is primarily attributable to vehicle price and product mix rather than different borrowing behaviour,” the bank’s spokeswoman says. “Emerging-brand customers are not necessarily financing a smaller share of their purchase.”
That points us back to price. Rather than attracting a fundamentally different type of borrower, the newcomers appear to be competing by offering cars at prices that bring the monthly cost within reach of more buyers.
And that battle is about to become more intense. Greater availability of lower-priced models should help bring EVs to an even wider mass-market audience.
Next year will see a wider availability of EVs priced at under €30,000, all delivering better range than older models while also loaded with increasingly impressive levels of standard equipment.
Initially in the EV journey, carmakers front-loaded the development costs of their electric tech – which, in fairness, is expensive to develop – into larger, more luxurious, and therefore more profitable models.
Now, though, as batteries and their associated technology become much cheaper, in terms of wholesale costs, and the initial research and development cost starts to get soaked up, we’re seeing a positive glut of very affordable electric cars.
The Hyundai Inster – which is way more capable all-round than you’d think for such as small car – starts at €19,595. A Renault 5 E-Tech, with a 410km range, can be bought for €29,295.
The new Volkswagen ID. Polo will be priced from around €20,000. A Peugeot E-3008 crossover costs pretty much the same as the hybrid-engined version.
Electric cars haven’t just become more affordable, they’ve actually become cheaper than their petrol-powered counterparts in many cases, and that’s before you factor in cheaper running costs. Throw in competitive pricing from new Chinese brands and you can see why consumers who keep a close eye on the finances are starting to see EVs as the sensible choice, regardless of the brand.

title: EVs are rewiring how Ireland thinks about home energy
description: Smart tariffs, solar panels and battery storage are turning the electric car into part of a wider home energy system
content:
For a growing number of Irish households, buying an electric vehicle is no longer purely a transport decision. It is increasingly the moment a family starts paying attention to how their whole home uses power.
“An EV can become one of the largest electrical loads in a home, so suddenly households have a real financial reason to think not just about how much electricity they use but also when they use it and where that electricity comes from,” explains Pearse McHenry, chief revenue officer at myenergi, the home energy technology company. “The EV is often the catalyst that gets a household thinking about its energy as one connected system rather than a collection of separate products.”
An Electric Ireland spokesperson says: “Those with an EV charger installed will often also examine smart meter tariffs to find the best value, which is then creating greater awareness of energy use across appliances, time of use and the home more broadly.”
Customers with a home charger and a smart meter can move on to tariffs such as Electric Ireland’s Home Electric+ Night Boost, which offers a reduced overnight rate and a cheaper “boost” window between 2am and 4am.
“This gives EV drivers a clear incentive to shift charging to lower-cost periods while also encouraging them to think about when they use other appliances and technologies in the home.”
Both energy providers point to the same misconception holding some prospective buyers back: the assumption that charging a car at home will automatically send the electricity bill soaring.
“A common misconception is that home charging will automatically lead to a large increase in the electricity bill, regardless of how or when the car is charged,” the Electric Ireland spokesperson says. “Most drivers do not need to recharge a completely empty battery every night, and a smart charger combined with a suitable time-of-use tariff can move much of that demand to lower-cost overnight periods.”
According to the company’s 2026 Sustainability Index, 76 per cent of respondents with a home charger said they felt they were saving money, with perceived average fuel savings of €91 a month, though the spokesperson stresses that “actual savings will vary by mileage, vehicle efficiency, tariff and charging pattern”.
McHenry identifies a common mistake as consumers reckoning all EV chargers are essentially the same.
“For most Irish homes, charging speed isn’t really the differentiator; domestic chargers will typically operate at up to and around 7kW. The important question is how intelligently the charger manages that energy.” He adds that solar panel ownership is not a prerequisite for savings either.
“You don’t need solar panels to benefit from smart charging. With the right electricity tariff, simply moving a large flexible load like an EV away from expensive peak periods can materially reduce the cost of charging.”
So when do consumers really need to start considering the wider context of their energy supply system and what it might mean to opt for an EV?
For Electric Ireland, it begins at the assessment stage. “Understanding the customer’s driving pattern, current electricity use, smart meter status and home electrical capacity helps identify the right charger and whether a time-of-use tariff could reduce charging costs,” the spokesperson says.
“The objective is not to recommend every technology to every customer, but to identify a sensible sequence of upgrades for that particular home.”
The company’s Superhomes service, they note, offers a “One Stop Shop” covering home assessment, SEAI grants and retrofit works including insulation, solar PV and heat pumps, since “a heat pump works best in an appropriately insulated home”.
McHenry says the first logical step for new EV owners is usually the electricity tariff.
“Once people see the difference between buying electricity at peak times and charging overnight or during cheaper periods, they start applying the same thinking elsewhere in the home,” he says.
“Hot water, heating, solar and battery storage then become part of the same conversation.”
What’s exciting, he says, is how automation is replacing manual management entirely. “We’re moving away from asking consumers to manually manage all of those individual assets. The future has now arrived as the myenergi home energy system can make those decisions automatically, looking at the tariff, solar generation, household demand and the energy required by the car, and deciding the most economical way to manage them.”
Asked whether there is a correct order for adopting solar, an EV and battery storage, McHenry rejects the premise. “I don’t think there is one universal order, because every household is different,” he says.
“Rather than prescribing a sequence of products, I’d start with the household: how much energy do you use, when do you use it, what can you generate yourself and which loads can you move?”
He notes that falling costs are changing the calculation too: “As battery storage costs have now dropped significantly, we are seeing even more scenarios of battery storage being installed, even without solar.”
And there are more exciting changes to the home energy ecosystem on the way. Vehicle-to-home and vehicle-to-grid technology lets an EV’s battery feed energy back into the house or the grid.
“It’s important to separate three technologies that are often grouped together,” says McHenry. Vehicle-to-load, or V2L, essentially allows the battery in your EV to power external electrical devices. Vehicle-to-home, or V2H, goes significantly further by allowing energy stored in the vehicle to supply the home. Vehicle-to-grid, or V2G, adds another layer by allowing that energy to interact with the electricity system.”
V2L is already commercially available, he says, but the other two “require the right combination of compatible vehicles, charging hardware, standards, network requirements and commercial arrangements.”
Even so, McHenry says the potential is “enormous”.
“An EV has a battery many times larger than a typical domestic home battery. If we can intelligently unlock even part of that capacity, the car stops being simply something that consumes electricity and becomes an active part of the home’s energy system.”
For now, though, McHenry is clear about where the actual savings are being made today. “It’s overwhelmingly smart charging and load-shifting,” he says.
“That’s much less exciting to talk about than powering your house from your car, but it’s where consumers can make a financial difference every day.”
Storm resilience is becoming a secondary consideration, he adds, particularly “for those that experienced prolonged outages” during Storm Éowyn, “but I think it’s important to be realistic. Most consumers aren’t investing in home energy technology purely for the occasional outage. They’re investing because it can reduce their energy costs every day.”
Both sources agree that upfront cost remains the single biggest obstacle to wider adoption, but each adds a second, less obvious barrier.
For Electric Ireland, it is a lack of understanding. “Upfront cost remains the most significant barrier, but complexity and awareness are closely linked,” the spokesperson says, citing the Sustainability Index finding that 54 per cent of people named lack of money as their main barrier, while 36 per cent “would like to live more sustainably but do not know how”, and 39 per cent “find sustainability messaging confusing”. Only 15 per cent of adults, the survey found, said they were “very familiar with how much electricity different appliances use”.
For McHenry, the second barrier is a fragmented supply chain. “A consumer might buy the EV from one company, the charger from another, solar from another installer and electricity from a separate energy supplier,” he says.
“Effectively, we’re asking homeowners to become their own energy systems integrators.”
He believes Ireland already has the underlying conditions for the transition to work, with “growing EV adoption, smart meters, increasingly sophisticated electricity tariffs, a strong solar market and significant renewable generation on the electricity system”.
But he says the industry now needs to do the hard part for consumers. “The next step is making all of that complexity disappear for the consumer. That’s ultimately what the smart-energy transition is about: not adding complexity to people’s homes, but removing it.”

title: Nevo EV Show returns bigger than ever as Ireland’s electric revolution gathers pace
description: Returning to Dublin’s RDS Simmonscourt on 7th and 8th November, the 2026 edition promises to be the biggest and most comprehensive yet
content:
Just a few years ago, electric vehicles were still viewed by many Irish motorists as a niche alternative. Questions around driving range, charging infrastructure and affordability dominated conversations.
Fast forward to 2026 and the landscape has changed dramatically. Electric vehicles have become one of the fastest growing segments of the Irish new car market, with registrations continuing to rise as consumers become increasingly confident in making the switch.
Against that backdrop, the Nevo EV Show in partnership with Bank of Ireland has established itself as Ireland’s flagship event for electric mobility, growing year-on-year alongside the market it represents.
What began as an ambitious concept has quickly evolved into the country’s largest automotive event, bringing together manufacturers, industry experts, policymakers and thousands of motorists under one roof.
Returning to Dublin’s RDS Simmonscourt on November 7th and 8th, the 2026 edition promises to be the biggest and most comprehensive yet.
The momentum behind the show mirrors the remarkable progress of Ireland’s EV market. Since launching, Nevo has consistently expanded both its footprint and its audience, responding to growing public demand for trusted information and genuine hands-on experiences.
Rather than simply displaying new vehicles, the event has focused on answering the practical questions that matter most to buyers, from charging and grants to ownership costs and real-world usability. That approach has clearly resonated.
This year’s event expands to two full public days for the first time, allowing even more visitors the opportunity to explore the latest electric vehicles and technologies at their own pace.
It also reflects the growing confidence of manufacturers who increasingly see Ireland as an important market for launching new products.
Leapmotor will headline this year’s event as the official vehicle launch partner, underlining the arrival of another ambitious global brand into the Irish marketplace. Visitors will have the opportunity to experience the latest generation of electric vehicles from across the industry, with no fewer than 140 EVs on display representing 38 leading automotive brands.
Nevo’s Simon Andreucetti says: “As managing director of Nevo, I am extremely proud of how the Nevo event has grown from strength to strength each year. We’re delighted to expand to two full public days for the first time, and we’re expecting around 45,000 guests to join us at the RDS – as always, completely free to attend.
“With more than 140 models on display over the two days, Nevo 2026 is set to be Europe’s largest automotive event solely focused on electric vehicles, and a true reflection of just how far Ireland has come on its EV journey. There is no denying that the Irish consumer is confident in purchasing electric vehicles and EVs are now fully mainstream with a suitable and affordable option for all types of households and families.”
One of the biggest and most popular attractions remains the opportunity to experience electric driving first hand. Reading specifications is one thing, but sitting behind the wheel often changes perceptions entirely.
This year, the dedicated test drive area will operate under the banner of the myenergi Driving Experience, with myenergi sponsoring what has become one of the show’s most popular attractions.
The live demonstration arena also returns following its success last year. Once again sponsored by ESB, it will see a new electric vehicle launched every hour over the weekend of the event. Throughout the event, visitors can watch detailed presentations of the latest electric models while experts explain new technologies, charging innovations, battery developments and the features that differentiate today’s rapidly expanding range of EVs.
Education continues to sit at the heart of the Nevo EV Show.
One of the most significant additions for 2026 is the introduction of the Nevo x Bank of Ireland Meet the Experts Lounge, an interactive education stage designed to remove much of the uncertainty that still surrounds electric motoring. Rather than traditional presentations alone, the new format will allow visitors to submit questions live via an interactive screen, creating real-time discussions with industry specialists.
Expert panel sessions throughout the weekend will cover everything from home charging and public infrastructure to vehicle finance, battery longevity, ownership costs and government supports. It reflects the reality that today’s buyers are looking for practical advice rather than sales pitches.
The show’s growing list of partners also demonstrates the increasingly collaborative nature of Ireland’s transition towards electrification.
Alongside title education partner Bank of Ireland, both The Irish Times and Zevi (Zero Emission Vehicles Ireland) return as supporting partners, while ESB and myenergi deliver some of the event’s most engaging experiences.
Importantly, however, Nevo has never been solely about the cars. Visitors can expect a lively festival atmosphere throughout the weekend, with interactive exhibits, family-friendly entertainment, competitions, technology showcases and a variety of engaging activations taking place across the venue.
The aim is to create an enjoyable day out whether visitors arrive ready to purchase their next electric vehicle or are simply curious about what the future of motoring looks like.
Timing could hardly be better. Ireland’s electric vehicle market enters the final quarter of 2026 in robust health, with EV registrations continuing to outperform previous years and consumer confidence strengthening as model choice expands across virtually every price point.
Improvements in charging infrastructure, longer vehicle ranges and increasingly competitive pricing have all contributed to making electric motoring a realistic option for more households than ever before.
The Nevo EV Show has grown alongside that transformation. In just two years it has become more than an exhibition; it has become a meeting point for the entire electric mobility ecosystem.
Manufacturers can showcase new technology, policymakers can engage directly with motorists, industry experts can answer difficult questions, and consumers can compare dozens of vehicles in a single visit.
As Ireland continues its transition towards cleaner transport, events such as Nevo play an increasingly important role in bridging the gap between curiosity and confidence.
For anyone considering their first electric vehicle, or simply wanting to understand where motoring is heading next, the RDS on November 7th and 8th will once again provide the country’s most comprehensive snapshot of the future on four wheels.
Please visit nevo.ie to get your ticket.

title: Gardaí appeal for information on 40th anniversary of disappearance of Philip Cairns
description: Gardaí renew appeal for information on disappearance in Dublin of schoolboy who went missing 40 years ago aged 13
content:
Gardaí have renewed an appeal for information on the disappearance of Philip Cairns, who went missing 40 years ago aged 13.
On the afternoon of October 23rd, 1986, Philip disappeared as he walked from his home to his school, Coláiste Éanna, in Rathfarnham , Dublin 16 .
Despite an ongoing active Garda investigation into trying to establish his whereabouts, he has never been located.
Philip left the school at 12.50pm and walked the short distance to his home at Ballyroan Road, Rathfarnham.
At 1.30pm he gathered up his schoolbag and left his house to return to school. That was the last his family saw of Philip, who never made it back to school.
[ Philip Cairns: What happened to the Dublin schoolboy who went missing in 1986? Opens in new window ]
Six days after his disappearance, his schoolbag was found in a laneway near the school. This laneway links Ann Devlin Road and Ann Devlin Drive. Some of Philip’s books were missing from the bag.
Philip was described as being 5’2” in height, with short black hair. When last seen he was wearing his Coláiste Éanna school uniform, a grey jacket with black shoulder corners, grey school trousers, grey shirt and school pullover.
On the 40th anniversary of his disappearance, gardaí are renewing their appeal to the public for information.
Over the past four decades, gardaí said they have followed more than 1,600 lines of inquiry.
“The Garda investigation team have received and continue to receive contact and information from the public on a regular basis,” a Garda spokesperson said.
“The Garda investigation team continue to engage with the Cairns family.”
[ ‘It was all the time on my mind’: Mother of missing teenager Philip Cairns dies Opens in new window ]
After “significant media attention” over Philip’s disappearance, recently, gardaí said “new pieces of information” have emerged.
“Similar to all previous information received, this recent information provided to the Garda investigation team is being examined and assessed to determine what, if any, evidential value it may provide.”
Gardaí believe there may be people with information on the disappearance who “were young at the time” and “not in a position to provide An Garda Síochána with information, but may now be able to do so”.
Gardaí are appealing to anyone with information on Philip’s disappearance, “no matter how insignificant they think it may be” to come forward.
Anyone with information is asked to contact Rathfarnham Garda station on 01 666 6500, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111 or any Garda station.

title: Carla Lockhart resigns from DUP position amid row with party leadership
description: MP’s move stems from differing in opinion on withdrawal of Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly from Stormont Executive
content:
Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) MP Carla Lockhart has resigned as a party officer amid a deepening row with the leadership over the future of Stormont .
Lockhart’s move, which was first reported by the Belfast Telegraph, comes amid a difference of opinion between her and DUP leader Gavin Robinson on whether the party should withdraw Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly from the powersharing executive.
Lockhart has argued that the party should remove Little-Pengelly from her post as it would automatically remove Sinn Féin First Minister Michelle O’Neill from her position.
She believes the party should no longer serve alongside O’Neill after the Sinn Féin vice-president took part in an allegedly unlawful protest on the Garvaghy Road in Portadown last month.
O’Neill attended a police station in Belfast on Wednesday for an arranged interview with officers investigating the unnotified protest, which was staged as part of efforts to stop an Orange Order parade proceeding down the predominantly nationalist road.
Robinson was asked about Lockhart’s resignation as a party officer as he appeared on BBC NI’s The View programme on Thursday evening.
“I’m sorry to see that it’s occurred,” the party leader replied.
“I appointed Carla to the party officers. She remains a key part of our team.”
Robinson said his party was democratic and it had come to an “agreed position” not to pull Little-Pengelly out of Stormont.
Asked if he thought Lockhart may ultimately quit the party entirely, Robinson said: “I hope that’s not the case.”
He said he was not going to criticise Lockhart, insisting she still had a “valuable contribution” to make to the DUP.
Earlier on Thursday, Lockhart was asked whether she had confidence in Mr Robinson’s leadership.
She declined to directly endorse him, instead replying to BBC Radio Ulster’s Nolan Show: “I have confidence that the unionist people want action.”
Police are carrying out an investigation into the unnotified protest on the Garvaghy Road on the day the Drumcree parade was meant to proceed and said invitations to attend interviews had been sent to individuals “reasonably suspected of committing offences”.
A Parades Commission decision to allow the Orange Order parade to proceed down the Garvaghy Road for the first time in almost 30 years prompted a two-week stand-off at the site of what was a notorious parading flashpoint during the Troubles.
The parade was ultimately unable to take place because of significant numbers of protesters on the Garvaghy Road, leading Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant to overturn the commission’s decision and ban the procession.
PSNI Chief Constable Jon Boutcher has previously made it clear there would be “consequences” for those found to have broken the law. – PA

title: Raye wins 2026 Mercury Prize for This Music May Contain Hope album
description: Singer beat other nominees including Galway-born singer-songwriter Dove Ellis, Paul McCartney and Olivia Dean
content:
Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for her album This Music May Contain Hope, beating rivals including Paul McCartney , Olivia Dean and Galway-born indie singer-songwriter Dove Ellis .
Her second album came out in March, debuted at number one in the UK charts and includes the singles Click Clack Symphony (featuring Hans Zimmer), I Know You’re Hurting, Nightingale Lane and Where Is My Husband.
The singer beat fellow nominees such as rapper Dave, Florence + the Machine and Suede. The result was announced at a ceremony in Newcastle , the second successive year it has been held in the city.
The prize, created in 1992, is awarded each year to the best album by an artist from the UK or Ireland.
In his five-star review of Blizzard in The Irish Times, Ed Power described the album from Dove Ellis as “urgent and stubborn, full of sharp edges and illuminated throughout by a refusal to compromise”.
[ Dove Ellis: Blizzard review – Thank heavens for awkward outsiders, and for this luminescent Irish album Opens in new window ]
Albums are nominated based on musical merit, irrespective of how successful the record or act have been in the year.
Sam Fender won last year’s prize for his album People Watching.
Along with a trophy, the winner receives almost €30,000 in prize money. – PA

title: Celtic sunk by Celta Vigo as European woes continue
description: European wrap: Bournemouth stun 10-man AC Milan to claim famous win in Europa League
content:
Celtic suffered more Europa League pain as Spanish side Celta Vigo came from behind to win 2-1 at Parkhead.
After defeats by Ferencvaros and Benfica in their first two league phase fixtures, Martin O’Neill’s side struggled to impose themselves on the visitors who were neat and tidy without really testing Hoops keeper Sam Johnstone.
Germany midfielder Mika Baur fired the home side in front just over a minute into the second half to thrill the Celtic fans but Spain defender Javi Rodriguez scored twice in three minutes – a header then an unstoppable drive – to stun the home side who could not find a way back.
It was another damaging Euro night for the Scottish champions, knocked out of the Champions League qualifiers by LASK on a 5-4 aggregate after being 4-0 up at one stage earlier in the season.
Bournemouth scaled giddy new heights in their debut Europa League campaign as 10-man AC Milan were convincingly brushed aside 3-0 at the Vitality Stadium.
The Italian giants, champions of Serie A only four years ago, were wretched, unable to match Marco Rose’s team who pressed them ruthlessly and attacked breathlessly in torrential conditions on the south coast.
The first two goals were penalties scored in the first half, by Justin Kluivert then by Marcus Tavernier, before Amine Adli added a magnificent late free-kick, but the home side ought to have had even more to show for their dominance.
Mike Maignan, the Milan goalkeeper and captain, let his team and his manager Ruben Amorim down badly and inexplicably, swiping at the face of James Hill at a corner, conceding a spot-kick and leaving his side to play for more than an hour with 10 players.
Sunderland remain unbeaten in the Europa League thanks to a 1-1 draw against Lech Poznan at the Enea Stadion.
A thrilling opening saw the Black Cats go in front only two minutes in through Timur Tutierov, who was making just his third competitive start since arriving at Sunderland’s academy in 2023.
The visitors had opportunities to extend their lead when Malick Fofana hit the post and Nordi Mukiele forced a strong save from Mateusz Liz, but Lech responded in the 70th minute through substitute Leo Bengtsson’s low strike.
A point keeps Sunderland unbeaten in Europe this season but ends their winning start, which saw them claim back-to-back victories over AZ Alkmaar and Torreense.
Jean-Philippe Mateta scored on his first start since the opening day but Crystal Palace could not capitalise on a Besiktas red card to produce a winner in their 2-2 Europa League draw in Istanbul.
Palace were looking to bounce back from Sunday’s humiliating 5-0 defeat at Brighton, and were the superior side before Wilfred Ndidi opened the scoring for the hosts in first-half stoppage time.
Yeremy Pino drew the sides level six minutes after the restart and Mateta – who had a first-half goal chalked off by VAR – fired Palace to a first-time lead four minutes later.
Junior Olaitan netted a 73rd-minute equaliser, and Palace could not complete a second comeback after Umit Akdag was sent off for a clumsy 77th-minute challenge on Jorgen Strand Larsen, who was subsequently forced off.
Injury-hit Hearts produced a spirited display in Turkey but ultimately went down to a 2-0 Conference League defeat at the hands of Mohamed Salah-inspired Trabzonspor.
The depleted Jambos were up against it as they arrived in Trabzon without a string of key midfielders and defenders on the back of a 7-1 hammering at Celtic Park on Sunday.
And the Edinburgh side were dealt a further significant blow as it emerged ahead of kick-off that left-back Harry Milne had suffered suspected anterior cruciate ligament damage while training at Papara Park on the eve of the match.
Despite the clear sense of adversity, Hearts acquitted themselves well amid a hostile atmosphere before going down to Salah’s first-half penalty and a second-half strike from Franculino, laid on by the former Liverpool star.
The defeat leaves Wouter Vrancken’s side with one point from two matches ahead of their trip to Swiss champions Thun in a fortnight.
Brighton drew a rare blank as they were held to a goalless draw by Czech minnows Jablonec in the Conference League.
The Premier League’s top scorers, who have scored 23 goals across their first seven matches, misfired badly in the foothills of the Jizera Mountains in northern Czech Republic.

title: Bank holiday travel disruption ahead with Dublin Marathon road closures and rail line works
description: More than 22,000 set to compete in long-running event as Irish Rail puts on extra early morning services to capital
content:
Some sports fans and day-trippers may be left facing disruption in different areas of the country this bank holiday weekend, with the Dublin Marathon and various works on Irish Rail lines taking place.
The marathon, in the 45th year of its running, will lead to a slew of road closures and bus diversions. They will begin on Friday at Merrion Square South where the marathon ends. Some 22,500 people are expected to take part in the race, with many spectators expected along the route.
Leeson Street Lower, Merrion Square South, Mount Street Crescent, Merrion Square East, Fitzwilliam Street and other parts of southside city centre will also be subject to staggered closures over the weekend.
When the start of the race itself approaches, the disruption will become more widespread. The marathon will begin at 8.40am with the wheelchair/cerebral palsy competitors and there will be staggered starts until 9.45am.
Dozens of roads along the route will be closed from 3.30am on Sunday morning to 5.30pm on Sunday evening.
From staging areas in the city centre, competitors will run down Cuffe Street before turning past St Patrick’s Cathedral, up High Street and cross the river Liffey at the Four Courts.
The route then heads through the length of the Phoenix Park and back along its southern wall before heading east along Inchicore Road.
It will pass along part of the South Circular Road and the Crumlin Road, through Bushy Park and along through Milltown. After circling University College Dublin, it will return to town up Stillorgan Road, Merrion Road and Northumberland Road before finishing back at Merrion Square.
Irish Rail will run early trains for those competing in the racewith additional services from Dundalk (6am), Kildare (6.25am), Maynooth (6.50am) and Malahide (7am).
Dublin Bus has also announced a swathe of diversions which come into force from Friday morning to Sunday evening.
The routes that will be disrupted by the closure of Merrion Square to traffic from Friday morning are routes 15a, 15b, 19, 23 and 24.
Diversions begin on Sunday morning from 8am and will effect the following routes: 4, 7, 7a, 11, 11b, 13, 14, 15, 15a, 15b, 16, 19, 23, 24, 27, 37, 38, 38a, 39, 39a, 44, 47, 52, 56a, 60, 65, 65b, 68, 69, 70, 74, 77a, 80, 82, 99, 122, 150, 151.
The following bus corridor routes are also curtailed on Sunday, C1, C2, C3, C4, E1, E2, F1, F2, F3, the G1, G2 and the S2.
Meanwhile, some rail services have been cancelled over the weekend to allow for remedial works on different routes. No Dart services will operate between Grand Canal Dock and Bray or between Howth Junction and Howth on Saturday, Sunday or Monday.
Lansdowne Road Station will be closed for spectators going to the Leinster v Munster game on Saturday evening but fans can make their way to Pearse Station after the final whistle to catch northbound Darts between 7.30pm and 9pm, serving all stops to Malahide.
Train services between Limerick city and Limerick Junction will be replaced by bus services on Saturday, Sunday and Monday as will services running between Limerick and Ennis.
Track improvement works will take place between Athlone and Ballinasloe on Saturday from 6pm for the remainder of the evening with bus transfers in place on Dublin-Galway services but these are expected to be lifted on Sunday and Monday.
Irish Rail spokesman Barry Kenny said bank holiday weekends “afford the opportunity for 76 hours of work (from last train Friday night until 4am Tuesday morning) for projects that require a greater scale of activity” than regular overnight operations allow for.
These larger scale works include improvements to infrastructure such as tracks, overhead wires and bridges and that while most works cause little alteration to services, “some disruption is unavoidable”, he said.
Also on Sunday, there will be a temporary partial closure on Luas Red Line, with no services operating between Heuston and Connolly/The Point from 8.45am to 10.45am to facilitate the marathon.
The Luas Green Line will operate as normal with its Dawson, St Stephen’s Green and Harcourt Street stops near the start and finishing line for the marathon.
The bank holiday will be an exceptionally busy time for Dublin Airport. The airport is expecting 469,000 people travelling during the weekend and the midterm school break. That is up 10,000 on last year.

title: Storm Austen Live: Orange weather warnings for six counties as Met Éireann forecasts intense rain across Ireland
description: Wicklow, Wexford, Dublin, Waterford, Cork and Kerry under second highest alert level for rain until early hours of Friday
content:
Waterford is bracing for the Status orange rain warning which is due to come into effect in the next hour, Darragh Murphy reports.
The local authority are prepared, with crews on call to deal with issues as they arise.
Waterford Fire Service and the Swift Water Response Teams are also ready to mobilise.
Local TD Conor McGuinness said on social media in the last 30 minutes that there is already a lot of surface water on the N25, as well as on regional and local roads across the county.
Waterford City and County Council confirmed that sandbags are available and ready to be distributed at council depots.
McGuinness said that following a visit to the council’s depot in Dungarvan this evening, that there is a good supply of sandbags available.
Meanwhile, gardaí in Waterford city and Tramore have received no reports of serious flooding or damage as of yet, a spokesperson confirmed.
Heavy rain has arrived in Killarney, Co Kerry, Anne Lucey reports.
Cork County Council have issued the following details in advance of Storm Austen, with particular focus on both Midleton in east Cork and Bantry in west Cork, two towns that have suffered serious flood damage in recent years, Southern Correspondent Barry Roche reports.
Preparedness actions in accordance with the east Cork MD Flood Action Plan are in progress and will continue in advance of this weather event including inspections of and cleaning (where necessary) of key drainage assets.
Sandbags have been placed at key locations in flood prone areas throughout the district. River levels are currently low in east Cork. There are over 1,000 sandbags available for use in Midleton.
Cork County Council’s east Cork Roads Operations and Area Services Staff will be carrying out flood watches Thursday evening and overnight into Friday in flood prone areas through the weather event. The Midleton flood pump is mobilised at the lower end of the Main Street. Baby’s Walk will be closed tomorrow.
Forecasts will be continue to be monitored, the county council said.
In Bantry, pumps and sandbags will be deployed in the town centre.
Gardaí in Midleton have received no reports of any flooding on either the town or surrounding villages such as Whitegate, Mogeely and Ladsbridge, which like Midleton suffered extensive damage in Storm Babet in October 2023.
The stormy weather may have been promised by Met Éireann rather than Etta James but that wasn’t going to deter music fans from braving Storm Austen to get the opening night of the 48th Guinness Cork Jazz Festival off to a flying start on Thursday night, Southern Correspondent Barry Roche reports.
Hundreds braved rain to make their way to the opening concert at Cork Opera House where local Leeside based trumpeter, neo soul singer and rapper Diamond began proceedings before London born Yussef Dayes treated fans to his genre-blurring blend of jazz, soul and Afrobeat.
Meanwhile away from the windswept river Lee and up on MacCurtain Street in the Everyman Palace Theatre, American duo of trumpeter Keyon Harrold and saxophonist, Marcus Strickland were celebrating the music of John Coltrane and Miles Davis in a special collaborative tribute.
Back in the heart of the city centre at the Triskel Arts Centre, Oxford born but London based instrumentalist Momoko Gill was treating Cork audiences to her eponymous debut solo album Momoko with its blend of jazzy electronica and spiritual soul search.
Lord Mayor of Cork Councillor Damian Boylan speaking to The Irish Times before attending the opening concert at the Cork Opera House acknowledged the weather wasn’t ideal but said that rain had never deterred either Corkonians or visitors to the city from enjoying “the Jazz”.
“The Stargazers have a song called ‘We All Love the Jazz” that they brought out years back and it’s still true today – hail, rain or shine, Cork people will head out for the jazz – it won’t affect it at all – we nearly expect rain jazz weekend as Cork people, we always do.
“The only thing the rain does is make people sprint from one venue to the next and the city will be buzzing again this weekend with 500 artists performing in over 100 events at 80 venues including concert halls, theatres, hotels, pubs and clubs as well as on the street.”
Tomorrow, any lingering rain will clear to the east by around mid-morning, Met Éireann has said.
Sunshine and well scattered blustery showers elsewhere will follow, mainly affecting western counties.
Sandbags are being distributed in Kerry tonight in anticipation of flooding in the wake of Storm Austen, Anne Lucey reports.
The south of the county is expected to bear the worst of the effects, said Paul Neary, director of climate action and operational services with Kerry County Council.
The whole of Kerry is under an orange warning, he said.
The county council is advising members of the public and all road users to expect disruption and possible flooding tonight, and during the Friday morning commute.
The orange weather warning for rain comes into effect for Kerry at 10pm on Thursday and expires at 5am on Friday. A yellow warning for wind will be in effect from 7pm on Thursday to 10am on Friday.
Kerry County Council is advising motorists to expect surface water and flooding as well as the possibility of fallen trees and debris on many routes tonight and on Friday morning.
Council crews are on standby to deal with any problems which arise. The council’s emergency number will be available overnight for the duration of the weather warning and any weather related issues can be reported to 066 7183588.
Sandbags are being distributed to areas which are vulnerable to flooding.
Council crews and the Civil Defence are on standby.
Rail services are set to face some disruption over the upcoming bank holiday weekend, including parts of the Dart network and regional operations, Glen Murphy reports.
Bank holiday weekends “afford the opportunity for 76 hours of work (from last train Friday night until 4am Tuesday morning) for projects that require a greater scale of activity” than regular overnight works allow for, Irish Rail spokesman Barry Kenny said.
These larger scale works include improvements to infrastructure such as tracks, overhead wires and bridges and that while most works cause little alteration to services, “some disruption is unavoidable”, he said.
In Dublin, works will take place between Grand Canal Dock and Bray, Co Wicklow, as well between Howth and Howth Junction from October 24th to 26th. No Dart services will run between these stations over the weekend, but they will continue operating between Malahide and Grand Canal Dock.
However, additional arrangements have been made by the rail operator to cater for fans attending the Leinster v Munster rugby fixture in the Aviva Stadium on Saturday.
While Landsdowne Road Station will be closed due to the works, fans can make their way to Pearse Station after the final whistle to catch northbound Darts between 7.30pm and 9pm, serving all stops to Howth Junction and Malahide.
Extra early morning services are also being put on to cater for those taking part in the Dublin Marathon on Sunday, October 25th. They will operate as:
Elsewhere, Limerick area services will be disrupted due to works on the Foynes freight line. This involves commissioning the signalling system and affects all trains running to or from Limerick Colbert Station.
Bus transfers will be in operation between the city and Limerick Junction, as far as Ennis on Galway services and on services to Ballybrophy via Nenagh, on Saturday and Monday. No Ballybrophy services will operate on Sunday.
Track improvement works will be taking place between Athlone and Ballinasloe on Saturday from 6pm for the remainder of the evening with bus transfers in place on Dublin-Galway services but these are expected to be lifted for services on Sunday and Monday.
Following a meeting of Waterford City and County Council’s Severe Weather Assessment Team (SWAT) this afternoon, “proactive preparations” are being put in place to deal with the potential impacts of Storm Austen.
As part of these preparations, ground crews are clearing fallen leaves and debris particularly in low-lying and flood-prone areas, where drainage gullies can become obstructed during periods of heavy rainfall.
The crews will be on call throughout the night to deal with issues as they arise, such as blocked drains and gully overflows.
Waterford Fire Service and the Swift Water Response Teams are also on standby.
In the event that sandbags are required, they will be available at Waterford City and County Council Depots in Dungarvan (X35 N793) Carrickphierish in the city (X91 N40T), Tramore (X91 PV08), Leperstown, Dunmore East (X91 YH90), and Tallow (P51 VX71) and also at Clashmore GAA Centre (P36 ET26) and Siopa Nua and Passage East.
“Waterford City and County Council advises the public to exercise caution, heed public safety advice and avoid unnecessary journeys as driving conditions may be hazardous, with surface water flooding expected,” a statement read.
“While river levels currently have some capacity and tides are relatively low, members of the public should stay away from coastal areas as conditions can change quickly during severe weather, heeding the advice of the Irish Coast Guard to ‘Stay Back, Stay High and Stay Dry’.”
Members of the public can contact Waterford City and County Council’s Customer Services Desk on 0818 10 20 20. Outside of office hours calls will be transferred to the Council’s emergency services number.
The Irish Coast Guard, Water Safety Ireland and the RNLI have issued a joint appeal to the public to take extra care around coastlines and inland waterways over the next few days.
They have asked swimmers to avoid the water during the storms and to take extra precautions as the week goes on and daylight hours get progressively shorter.
ESB Networks has warned of possible electricity outages overnight as the first big storm of the season approaches Ireland.
A status-yellow rain and wind warning for Leinster and Munster comes into effect at 7pm on Thursday and will be in place until 10am on Friday.
Wicklow, Wexford and Dublin have a status orange rain warning in place from 2am until 8am Friday.
Counties Waterford, Cork and Kerry have an orange warning for rain in place from 10pm on Thursday until 5am on Friday.
Storm Austen is due to hit Ireland on Thursday evening.
Cloud will increase through the evening as wet and windy conditions spread northwards over the country as Storm Austen tracks to the south of Ireland.
Met Éireann has forecast heavy rain in Munster and south Leinster, spreading into Connacht and the rest of Leinster throughout the evening.
Localised flooding is possible, especially in Munster and Leinster.
Storm Austen will be followed by followed by Storm Boelo on Saturday.
The latter is forecast to coincide with high tides, increasing the risk of flooding from high waves and storm surges, particularly along the west and northwest coasts.
“With two weather events now expected, local response teams will be very busy throughout the bank holiday weekend,” said Keith Leonard, head of the National Directorate for Fire and Emergency Management.
“The National Severe Weather and Flood Coordination Group will meet daily throughout the next few days to ensure the most effective response to any developments arising from the challenging weather conditions.”

title: The Irish Times view on protests in France: uncertainty and discontent
description: A rudderless government looks unable to respond
content:
France is facing a critical period over the next six months as voters prepare for presidential elections in the shadow of student demonstrations for better facilities and wider protests over the cost of living which ended in widespread violence by a small minority last weekend.
