The sense of a rudderless government and an uncertain future has been reinforced as president Emmanuel Macron prepares to depart office without a convincing centrist candidate to replace him. This leaves the field to Marine Le Pen on the far right and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the radical left.
These educational and socio-economic problems are deep-seated. Many French schools, especially in disadvantaged and immigrant communities, have suffered from a lack of investment and teacher shortages. The student movement makes well-founded demands for improvement and has widespread public support, however much it has taken public authorities by surprise. A general malaise over employment prospects and deteriorating life chances among young people has strengthened its appeal. Trade unions and social movements have rapidly taken advantage of this, in classical French fashion.
Delivering reforms in response to such demands is impossible for the outgoing government, already severely constrained economically by an annual budget deficit of 5.4 per cent of GDP, rising national debt and bond market responses to these trends. Politically they are spancelled by Macron’s failed attempt to secure a majority in the 2024 election he called, resulting in a blocked parliament and budget. Against this backdrop, Le Pen’s Rassemblement National party presents itself as the guardian of order, probably boosting its chances of winning next May. Blaming the protests and violence on immigrants and the left, it suits her – along with centrist candidates jostling for position – to claim that Mélenchon is responsible.
This makes for a volatile mixture of political, social and economic uncertainty – for Europe as well as France. Le Pen’s deep Euroscepticism would disable France’s pivotal role in the EU in line with similar policies from the growing far right AFD party in Germany. Mélenchon’s different demands on debt cancellation and taxation of the wealthy would disrupt the EU’s liberal market consensus. The centrist candidates now have to compete against a background of popular activism and discontent, undermining their appeal.
There is far more agreement across the political divides that these problems need tackling than on ways to do it. Huge cuts in state expenditure versus debt cancellations and taxing the wealthy compete for support between right and left, while centrists agonise on how to balance welfare, pensions and increased defence spending with more taxes. This is French politics today.

title: Josie Ray murder accused told her daughter one of them would have to leave, court hears
description: Hasan Ali Gori (52) was living in victim’s home and in a relationship with her daughter
content:
A man accused of murdering a pensioner in her home told her daughter that either her mother or he would have to leave the house due to constant arguing between them, a court heard.
Josephine Ray (89), known as Josie, of St Joseph’s Park, Nenagh, Co Tipperary, was found strangled and suffocated in her bed, on August 4th 2024, the Central Criminal Court in Limerick has heard.
Hasan Ali Gori (52), originally from Chad, Africa, and with an address at St Joseph’s Park, Nenagh, has pleaded “not guilty” to murdering Ray.
At the time, Ali Gori was living in Josie Ray’s home, as he was in a relationship with her daughter, Mary Ray, who it was heard has an intellectual disability.
On Thursday, Mark McGee, a neighbour of Josie and Mary Ray, told the accused’s trial that he “clearly” overheard Ali Gori and Mary Ray talking to one another outside Josie Ray’s house on the night before she died.
McGee told the court that Ali Gori told Mary Ray that “either he had to go or Josie had to leave the house and go”.
Ali Gori told Mary Ray “that he was sick of it” and couldn’t take it any more, he said.
McGee said he walked away then because, he said, Mary Ray noticed him and “whispered” something to Ali Gori.
McGee said that earlier that afternoon he heard “shouting” coming from Josie Ray’s home, and he saw Mary Ray, Ali Gori and Josie Ray arguing with one another outside the front of the property.
McGee said he heard Mary Ray accusing Ali Gori of cheating on her, and Josie Ray was “banging” and “tapping” her walking stick on the ground.
McGee said Josie Ray told Mary Ray and the accused, “I’m tired of ye”, and gardaí arrived to calm the situation.
Ian Donnellan, another of the victim’s neighbours, gave evidence that the accused, Mary Ray and Jose Ray argued with one another “every day”.
“It was angry, volatile, every day,” said Donnellan.
The witness said he contacted gardaí on July 21st, 2024, about two weeks before Josie Ray’s death, to report a row taking place at Ray’s home.
Donnellan told the court he saw Josie that day with a “red mark” on the right side of her face, and that she was “distressed and afraid”.
The witness said he recorded a Snapchat video of the sounds of shouting and roaring coming from Josie’s house on the day before her death and he called the gardaí.
Donnellan said that, at this point, his wife asked the accused to stop shouting as he was “scaring” local children.
The recording was played to the court in which a male voice was heard in the footage shouting “f**k off, f**k off” and the sound of a child becoming distressed.
Donnellan said he recognised the male voice as being the accused.
Ian Donnellan’s sister, Gemma Donnellan, gave evidence Thursday of being one of a group of neighbours that gathered outside Josie Ray’s house after her body was discovered inside the property.
Donnellan told the court she asked Mary Ray what had happened “and she [Mary] said nothing really”.
Donnellan said that it appeared to her that Ali Gori had not wanted Mary “talking to anyone” at the scene.
“Mary was crying, and he [the accused] kept telling her to shut up and to calm down.”
Donnellan said the accused told Mary that Josie was “old and was going to die anyway” and that he “kept walking towards [Mary] to bring her away from us”.
The prosecution case, led by Lorcan Connolly, is that Ali Gori strangled and suffocated Josie Ray.
The trial continues before Judge Sean Gillane and a jury.

title: The Irish Times view on the UNEP climate report: shocking but not surprising
description: The key goals of the Paris agreement will not be achieved
content:
The introduction to the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report this week was blunt. It read: “The chance of holding global warming to 1.5 degrees above pre-industrial levels with no or limited overshoot – a key target of the Paris Agreement on Climate Change – is now gone.”
The best hope the report can offer is limiting the overshoot as fast as possible, bringing temperatures back to the 1.5 degree limit by 2100. This news is shocking but not surprising; it conforms to a trend that has become increasingly obvious.
Even with the lowest possible overshoot – extremely difficult to achieve in the best of all possible political worlds, let alone the one we actually inhabit today – the consequences will be dire.
“Every year spent in a warmer world raises the risk of irreversible damage to the planetary systems that sustain us,” says Anne Olhoff, the director of the UNEP-Copenhagen Climate Centre. “Unless we quickly cut greenhouse gas emissions, our best chance for avoiding a full-blown climate catastrophe will disappear in the rearview mirror”.
The quick cutting of greenhouse gas emissions, however, is far from high on international agendas, just as we approach the 31st UN Conference of the Parties (COP) on climate change in Turkey next month. Ireland’s recent budget went in the opposite direction with its retreat on carbon taxes, while the EU budget proposed by the Irish presidency also proposes cuts to climate mitigation measures. As for the US, it has rejected the Paris Treaty altogether under Donald Trump.
It is troubling that the other major measure UNEP proposes for lowering the inevitable overshoot in heating is the re-capture and storage of carbon from the atmosphere – a technological feat that we are not remotely close to achieving.
We have already seen the disastrous impacts of current global heating in terms of wildfires, flooding, droughts and heat deaths. The UNEP report makes it frighteningly clear that much, much worse awaits us unless there is a truly radical shift in humanity’s approach to this existential issue.

title: ‘Toxic’ Bruno Fernandes is symptom of Manchester United’s culture of entitlement
description: Michael Carrick must now deal with more dressingroom unrest after Lisandro Martínez’s attack on the board
content:
“Toxic”: this is the damning characterisation of Bruno Fernandes from one highly placed Manchester United source after the captain’s incendiary betrayal of Michael Carrick.
There has surely never been a greater anti-leadership act in United’s storied history than Fernandes questioning the man who trusts him to unify the dressingroom and execute his on-field plan. The Portuguese has proved this faith wrong at the precise moment he was required to step up and exude a defiant togetherness.
Nothing could be more dysfunctional than civil war between United’s head coach and captain, featuring Carrick biting back at Fernandes for questioning his tactics as matters hit a new low in the aftermath of Wednesday’s pathetic 4-1 loss to Como. A litmus test for any leader comes when the storm arrives. At the Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium, Fernandes failed miserably, as he squealed about “the staff” deciding the best tactic was not to press Cesc Fàbregas’s bright, emerging team.
For “staff” read Carrick because he decides strategy and bears responsibility for performance. Fernandes is Carrick’s on-field proxy, so his behaviour is the dictionary definition of betrayal. His conduct is not expected to lead to an disciplinary action in the way Lisandro Martínez’s calling out of Jason Wilcox as, perhaps, this is a greyer area.
Discussing tactics may be more within Fernandes’s remit, as captain, than a defender suggesting the director of football’s recruitment failed. Provided there is no damage to the team. But even if Fernandes issues an apology, some acts are irreversible. There is a case for Carrick to strip the 32-year-old of the captaincy and appoint someone such as Harry Maguire or Youri Tielemans.
Carrick is expected to hold his traditional pregame media conference on Friday afternoon and be in charge for Bournemouth’s visit on Sunday, so when the team is announced whether Fernandes has the armband will intrigue. Could he even drop the playmaker? Whatever the decision, Fernandes can have zero excuse for his Como outburst.
Last week Fernandes witnessed how Martínez’s criticism of Wilcox became an extra headache for Carrick, whose sole focus should have been on arresting the direst start to a campaign since 1986. Instead Carrick had to thrash out the most prudent line of action – Martínez is understood to have been fined – then field questions about the episode from the media.
Yet still Fernandes rounded on Carrick after one of United’s poorest displays in continental competition. It was a performance the player was part of, having been on the field until Carrick removed him on 67 minutes. Being replaced by Joshua Zirkzee, who United tried to offload in the last window, shows how ineffective Fernandes was, first as a false 9, then, after the interval, in his favoured No 10 berth.
Fernandes’s comments indicate he is seriously disaffected with team strategy and his role within this. But is there, too, a frustration at still being at the club as his prime years begin to expire? This is a footballer who voiced disquiet last December, during a jarring interview with Canal 11, the Portuguese Football Federation‑owned channel, at “hurt” caused by United’s desire to sell him.
Fernandes was asked whether there had been an offer from Paris Saint-Germain or Real Madrid. He said: “Nowadays, the issue of loyalty is no longer seen the way it used to be. I could have left in the last window and would have earned a lot more. At one point I was going to leave and I would have won many trophies that season. I decided to stay not only for family reasons but because I genuinely like the club. The conversation with the coach [Ruben Amorim] also made me stay.
“But from the club’s side, I felt: ‘If you go, it’s not really that bad for us.’ More than hurting, it makes me sad, because I’m a player they have nothing to criticise me for.”
Now the club, and specifically Carrick, do feel seriously let down by Fernandes. But, it is also relevant to ask how Fernandes (and Martínez) have come to feel so at ease with going off-message.
These are highly remunerated employees. Their job is to play and maintain a united front – whatever happens – and for Carrick to allow a culture of entitlement to fester shows up a serious faultline in his management. For now, Carrick and Fernandes limp on – just like the team.
It will be some act for Carrick to save his job – even victory over Bournemouth may not do so – and for Fernandes to rehabilitate himself, before the head coach and fans. But this is football, a world that can be unpredictable and illogical.
The measure, though, of the debacle at Como, and the wider malaise at the club, can be found in Fàbregas’s post-victory words in which he bemoaned allowing Zirkzee’s added-time strike for United.
“I regret the last 10 minutes because I was the one who told the team to slow down the tempo because there’s another match [Sassuolo on Saturday] and at 4-0 we could manage things a little,” he said. “Their goal hurt me because we dropped our intensity and dropped our defensive block, but it was my fault.”
How Carrick wishes this was what he had to contend with – rather than a mutinous captain and a ship that seems to be sinking deeper on every matchday. – Guardian

title: Advert showing grandparents hugging grandchildren is taken down amid criticism
description: Dublin Rape Crisis Centre removes online video, saying it does not want ‘negativity’ to impinge on its work
author_name: Sarah Burns, Vivienne Clarke, Marie O’Halloran
content:
The Dublin Rape Crisis Centre ( DRCC ) has removed a social media advertisement about consent featuring grandparents hugging their grandchildren.
The video depicted a young girl being uncomfortable receiving a hug from her grandparents.
Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan said the advertisement was “both inappropriate and demeaning” to grandparents and has been removed by the DRCC following engagement with his officials.
In the advertisement, a voiceover carries the message after the girl expresses discomfort at receiving a hug: “Not everyone wants a hug. Even from the people who love them.”
It added: “Awkward? Maybe. Important? Absolutely.”
The Department of Justice said We-Consent is a programme created and developed by the DRCC aimed at informing, educating and engaging the public about all forms of consent.
“Social media videos shared recently as part of this programme were produced by DRCC at a low cost using volunteers and are not part of a Government advertising campaign,” it said.
“The department understands that DRCC intends to review these videos. They are being removed from their social media channels to enable this review.”
DRCC said We-Consent is a long-term campaign as part of its prevention work to increase the awareness and practice of consent in Ireland.
The organisation said it created a video series for its social media channels based on feedback from over 20 consent workshops with younger and older people.
“Part of the workshops involved sharing participants’ own experiences of instances when they felt uncomfortable,” it said.
“The scenarios depicted in the video series came up very frequently in all the workshops. The videos were created with volunteers and staff and reflected these conversations.”
[ Irish comedian Vittorio Angelone apologises for rape joke about content creator Opens in new window ]
DRCC said the series was made on a low budget and promoted online via its social media channels.
“The video was launched exclusively on social media in mid-September but we have removed it from our social media channels due to the negative attention it has attracted in the last 24 hours,” it added.
“We do not want that negativity to impinge on and distract from the vital work that we as a centre do in supporting victims and survivors and improving awareness of these important issues across society.”
Earlier, O’Callaghan said the DRCC video “does not represent the views of the Government”.
The Fianna Fáil TD said: “It goes without saying that having loving grandparents in a child’s life is an incredibly positive thing to be cherished and not something to be campaigned against.”
He added: “While it is vital to ensure that people understand the concept of consent when it comes to sexual relationships, this video did not advance that aim and in many ways was counterproductive.”
Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill stressed the video “is not a Government campaign” and the Government “does not support” it.
Speaking in the Dáil she said there is “a broader question around consent, which is important”, but “that does not extend to this ad or to grandparents in any way”.
“Grandparents are an incredibly important part of family life, incredibly important part of every child’s life” and the advert was “both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents”.
MacNeill said the video “was an error” and did not represent the views of Government. It should be clearly distinguished from an important body of work “around domestic, sexual, and gender violence more broadly”.
Aontú TD Paul Lawless claimed the video was Government-funded and conflated “issues of sexual violence on the one hand and affection exchanged by a grandmother to a grandchild on the other”.
He queried how much the video had cost and asked: “Why is the State asking grannies to second-guess themselves when it comes to hugging their grandchildren?”
Aontú leader Peadar Tóibín said the issue of consent in relation to sexual relationships was “very important”.
However, “for anybody to equate sexual relationships between people and a grandparent hugging their grandchild is absolutely inaccurate and completely wrong”, he said on RTÉ Radio 1’s David McCullagh show.
“Is the State now looking for grandparents to second-guess themselves before they hug their grandchildren or show affection to their grandchildren?”
[ Like Nikita Hand, Cornell case’s Jane Doe is either uncommonly brave or a sadomasochist Opens in new window ]
Independent Ireland TD Ken O’Flynn said he believed the ad “goes too far”, adding that “a lot of decent families will find it insulting”.
Asked about the video on Newstalk’s Claire Byrne show, psychologist John Francis Leader said it was important for people to be able to communicate their specific needs and, as a society, it was important to be supportive of people with different needs.
“People have different norms and different expectations. From a psychological perspective, the key thing that we’re aware is everybody has different needs, and for one person, the hug represents comfort and empowerment and support, and for the other person, it may not represent that,” he said.
“So the challenge is how do you convey a message that suits everybody? To be fair to the video, if you look at it, it does have both. It has a hug and somebody appreciating it, and then it has somebody not appreciating the hug. So I suppose that’s what we all have to grapple with as a society,” he said.

title: Three staff members at school received €1,000 each from free school meals provider, committee hears
description: Financial controls to be tightened on the hot school meals programme amid questions over contract arrangements
content:
Three members of staff at a school received payments of €1,000 each from a supplier of free school meals, an Oireachtas committee has heard.
Department of Social Protection secretary general John McKeon said it has raised concerns with a number schools about contract arrangements under the free meals scheme, which was expanded nationwide in September 2025.
He was speaking at the Dáil’s Public Accounts Committee , which heard that financial controls are to be tightened on the programme after a report by the State’s spending watchdog recommended steps to safeguard public funds.
Responding to a question asked by Sinn Féin TD Cathy Bennett if any suppliers offered incentives to the schools to acquire contracts, McKeon replied “we tell schools they shouldn’t, and that is part of the contract documentation”.
Inspections identified some isolated cases, including football jerseys being provided, “generally” at the school’s request.
There was a case where €1,000 was given to each staff member for doing “extra work” at one school, he said.
The recipients were a caretaker, a secretary and “another” adding, “they were administrative staff”.
He also said payments of up to €1,000 were made to some schools such as one in Co Donegal and Co Galway, for school prizes, hampers and raffles.
He also said a payment of €8,500 was made to a school for a pod to heat the food in the school.
“We’ve raised that with the schools concerned. We’ve told them that we’ll withdraw funding and they’ve stopped it.
“Our concern in these matters is that there are children in the school. If we withdraw funding without giving the school a chance to rectify it, that’s a problem for the children. So we give the school a chance to rectify it.
“We’ve now specifically put it into procurement documentation that no incentives and no payments are to be made to school members.”
A report from the Comptroller and Auditor General (C&AG) was being discussed at Thursday’s committee meeting.
While it found there had been robust governance arrangements, it identified opportunities to strengthen financial controls, procurement assurance and performance monitoring.
It particularly recommended increased use of real-time school enrolment data, having found that enrolment figures submitted by schools were not being routinely verified against official enrolment records, with 1,116 primary schools having applied for funding in excess of their recorded enrolment numbers.
It also identified some schools which held surpluses at the end of the school year due to the assumption that 100 per cent of pupils would avail of a hot meal every day – with this figure approaching €34 million at the start of the last academic year.
[ Hot school meals scheme to be overhauled after reports find poor quality and high waste Opens in new window ]
However, any surplus amounts are deducted from new allocations to schools, it acknowledged.
With five suppliers accounting for 69 per cent of programme provision, the C&AG flagged concentration of suppliers as a potential strategic risk.
The C&AG report outlined that 682,000 children are eligible to partake in the programme across 3,700 schools every week – equating to 3.4 million school meals each week.
With total expenditure rising from €54.3 million in 2019 to €232 million in the 2025/26 school year, the programme is funded and overseen by the Department of Social Protection while individual schools are responsible for contracting out the supply of food.
The C&AG wants a formal check on enrolment numbers to detect any large gaps between the number of pupils enrolled and the number of meals being funded, as well as review the assumption that all pupils eat a hot meal every day.
The department has committed to implementing these recommendations.
In opening remarks, McKeon said improvements had already been put in place around procurement supports for schools.
He said he was confident the process around surplus funding meant the risk to exchequer funds was “very small”.
When asked about students in junior infants receiving the same portion size as a sixth class student, McKeon said, “we don’t believe that it makes sense either”.
“We’ve always said that there should be different portion sizes, and that should be one of the factors that’s taken into account when a school is procuring the meals.”
He said the department was in the process of putting together a “standardised menu” which will operate next year.
A dedicated nutritionist dietitian has been employed “to specifically examine the nutrition”, he added, pointing out that 80 per cent of the meals were found to comply with food standards.
He said foods such as plain pasta, or plain pasta and sauce, were allowed on the menu “to cater for requirements of children who might have special needs in the school, children who might be autistic, who have picky food choices, who don’t want vegetables, who don’t want meat, they just want plain pasta”.

title: Couple allege their Meath home built without planning permission was wrongfully demolished
description: Rose and Chris Murray’s house near Navan was demolished in March after two-decade battle
content:
Meath County Council wrongfully demolished a house built without planning permission in circumstances where the homeowners had an application pending at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in respect of the property, it has been alleged.
After a legal battle spanning two decades, Rose and Chris Murray’s house at Faughan Hill, Bohermeen, Navan, was demolished in March , after the High Court gave the council the go-ahead to knock it.
In an application before Judge David Nolan on Thursday, lawyers for the Murrays sought various reliefs, including court declarations stating the council’s actions, in moving to demolish the building in March, breached obligations under European human rights laws.
The Murrays also challenged a finding last March that they were in contempt of 2020 court undertakings to vacate their property.
Lawyers for the council submitted that the court did not have jurisdiction to grant the reliefs sought by the Murrays, and denied their claims.
Solicitor Neil McNelis, for the Murrays, argued that an application by the Murrays to the ECHR earlier this year should effectively have operated as a stay on the demolition of the house. (The court heard the application was ultimately rejected.)
Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights provides for the bringing of applications to the ECHR alleging a violation of human rights. Under the same article, the State – or in the case of Meath County Council, organs of the State – cannot “hinder” applicants seeking to bring such an application, McNelis submitted.
The demolition in March of the house, the subject matter of the Murrays’ application to the ECHR, was hindrance, McNelis submitted.
The solicitor submitted that Meath County Council should have notified the Attorney General before proceeding with the demolition, in circumstances where the Murrays had made an application to the ECHR.
A situation where an organ of the State can disregard Article 34 and “commit acts of oppression” was “not right”, he said.
[ How a dream family home in Co Meath became a 20-year nightmare Opens in new window ]
Deirdre Hughes, barrister for Meath County Council, told the judge the Murrays’ applications to the ECHR had all been refused.
She submitted that the court did not have jurisdiction, in the context of planning enforcement proceedings, to make the orders sought by the Murrays.
She said the issues raised by the Murrays had already been dealt with by the courts, including in a recent decision of Judge Richard Humphreys in March.
Hughes pointed to Humphreys’ observation that the European Convention on Human Rights Act 2003, an Irish law, does not give effect as a whole to the European Convention on Human Rights. Humphreys noted that an application to the ECHR under Article 34 “does not in itself create domestic legal effects”.
Hughes submitted that even if the court was minded to grant declarations sought by the Murrays, such an order could not restrain a demolition order.
The council is seeking costs of the demolition against the couple, plus its legal costs.
The council’s overall bill across the 20-year process stands at more than €683,000, including costs of securing the property while demolition works proceeded.
The legal saga began after the Murrays, having been refused planning permission in June 2006 for a dormer bungalow at Faughan Hill, built a property on the same site later that year that was 588sq m, twice the size they had originally proposed.
The council initiated enforcement action in 2007 and proceedings ran over some two decades, including in the High Court, Court of Appeal and Supreme Court.

title: Erin King hoping to cap memorable week with victory in inaugural away Test against South Africa
description: Ireland head coach Scott Bemand makes two changes with Stacey Flood and Dorothy Wall named for Cape Town clash
content:
What a week for Erin King to celebrate her 23rd birthday, going on safari with her team-mates ahead of the serious stuff that is a first ever Test game for Ireland’s women in South Africa on Saturday (2pm Irish time).
King, who was appointed as team captain by Scott Bemand ahead of this year’s Six Nations, blew out the candles on the cake on Wednesday.
Back-to-back wins against the Springbok Women over the next week or so will have been on her wish list to cap a whirlwind first two years in green that has included the blow of suffering an ACL injury and subsequently the high of her captaincy selection.
The Wicklow-born flanker has personal ambitions, too, around becoming one of the world’s best at what she does.
“It’s been a bit of a whirlwind,” reflected King. “I was really lucky when I came into the squad to come into such a great group of girls.
“Sam [Monaghan] and Tricky [Edel McMahon] were my captains and they made me feel really at home in the squad, so it didn’t really take long to feel like I belonged.
“The timing was great. When I first started, after my first maul session, I probably cried. I was like, ‘I don’t know if this is for me’. It’s come a long way since then.
“To be the captain is still a bit of a pinch me moment. It’s an absolute honour, and it’s a really exciting time for us.
“Then, my own game, hopefully it’s coming along. I’m constantly working to be one of the best players in Ireland and in the world. I’m lucky to be captain of such an amazing group.”
The safari was part of a collective experience that King believes will help to further bond the group; she is one of the Sevens veterans who have been to the Rainbow Nation a few times and are showing the first-timers the ropes.
Some more activities are planned for next week but, for now, events at the Athlone Stadium in Cape Town are the focus, with Bemand naming a team with two changes from the victory over Japan on October 3rd.
Stacey Flood and Dorothy Wall are reinstated, while Brittany Hogan moves to number eight as the injured Aoife Wafer didn’t travel, and Fiona Tuite-O’Sullivan switches to blindside flanker. Neve Jones wins her 50th cap.
“It’s a great opportunity to get used to touring as a team and how special it can be, the memories that we can make together, while at the same time, not losing sight of the job at hand which is Saturday’s game,” King said.
“We’ve spoken about the history of getting to play in Cape Town – and in South Africa – because obviously, rugby is everything for them. They eat, sleep and breathe rugby. There’s so much history there.
“Not many teams have come to South Africa and won two Test games against them back-to-back – I don’t think any Irish team ever has, anyway. We’d love to create a bit of history.
“There’s a lot of excitement building. We’re playing in the third biggest township in Cape Town, so they’re going to have a huge backing. It’s going to be probably an atmosphere like no other.
“It’s going to be a bit of a challenge. Physicality is what will probably win it and it’s something that we definitely don’t shy away from.”
IRELAND (v South Africa): Stacey Flood (Railway Union/Leinster); Béibhinn Parsons (Blackrock College/Connacht), Anna McGann (Railway Union RFC/Connacht), Aoife Dalton (Old Belvedere/Leinster), Robyn O’Connor (Old Belvedere/Leinster); Dannah O’Brien (Old Belvedere/Leinster), Emily Lane (Blackrock College/Munster); Linda Djougang (Old Belvedere/Leinster), Neve Jones (Gloucester-Hartpury), Eilís Cahill (UL Bohemian/Munster); Jane Clohessy (UL Bohemian/Munster), Dorothy Wall (Exeter Chiefs); Fiona Tuite-O’Sullivan (Old Belvedere/Ulster), Erin King (Old Belvedere/Leinster) (capt), Brittany Hogan (Sale Sharks).
Replacements: Beth Buttimer (UL Bohemian/Munster), Niamh O’Dowd (Gloucester-Hartpury), Sadhbh McGrath (Cooke/Ulster), Kate Jordan (Blackrock College/Leinster), Grace Moore (Munster), Jemima Adams Verling (Galwegians/Connacht), Aoibheann Reilly (Blackrock College/Connacht), Eve Higgins (Railway Union/Leinster).

title: Martina and Ammi Burke lose appeals over two-week jailing for criminal contempt
description: Evidence shows pair were shouting loudly and continuously during court hearing, not ‘speaking up’, judge says
content:
Enoch Burke ’s mother Martina and his sister Ammi have lost appeals over two-week jail sentences they received for criminal contempt following disruptive scenes in the High Court earlier this year.
Both women served the two-week sentences after Judge Brian Cregan found them guilty in March of criminal contempt over their behaviour at a court hearing on February 20th.
The judge said they had engaged in “roaring and shouting” and “intense and venomous” interruptions during the hearing in a “paradigmatic” case of contempt.
The February hearing related to Enoch Burke’s challenge to the membership of a disciplinary panel convened to hear his appeal over his dismissal from Wilson’s Hospital School, Co Westmeath.
In May 2023, the High Court ruled that the school had validly suspended him from his teaching position and subsequently ordered that he be restrained from attending at the school premises.
The school suspended and later dismissed him over his conduct towards the then-principal Niamh McShane at a school religious event in June 2022.
The confrontation arose in circumstances where McShane had earlier requested teachers to address a student by a new name and with the pronouns “they” and “them”.
Enoch Burke, an evangelical Christian, has maintained that this request went against his religious beliefs and his constitutional right to freedom of religion.
He repeatedly breached the judge’s order to stay away from the school and spent more than 700 days in prison for contempt.
He returned again when the school resumed after summer but did not do so last Friday after the court the previous day once again ordered his immediate reincarceration for breach of the orders.
Following the scenes involving them in February, the High Court held an inquiry into whether Martina and Ammi Burke should be jailed for contempt.
In arguments against that application, Martina Burke said she was not interfering in the administration of justice because justice was not being administered in her son’s case.
Ammi Burke had argued, among other things, that she would not “sit silently by while constitutional rights are being denied or while lies are being told in court”.
After they were found guilty of contempt, the pair served their two-week sentences and their appeals over them were heard later.
On Thursday, the Court of Appeal dismissed their appeals.
Judge Tara Burns, on behalf of the three-judge court, said in their arguments in the appeal, the two indicated that their complaint ultimately was that procedural issues arose which rendered their trial for contempt of court an unfair trial which was not compliant with the Constitution or the European Convention on Human Rights.
The judge said they “went as far as submitting that the issue of whether they were guilty of criminal contempt was not an issue for determination by [the Court of Appeal]”.
This revealed a misunderstanding on their part of the jurisdiction of the Court of Appeal in criminal appeals, she said.
The Court of Appeal has jurisdiction to affirm a conviction if it is of the opinion that a miscarriage of justice has not occurred, she said.
Having listened to the digital audio recording of the High Court proceedings, there was no question the High Court judge’s assessment of the conduct at issue as being capable of amounting to criminal contempt of court was correct, she said.
Ammi Burke argued that their actions were “speaking up”, the judge said. Their speaking could not be categorised as speaking up and they were shouting very loudly and continuously, she said.
The Court of Appeal judges were of the opinion that the procedural issues raised by the two did not render their trial unfair. It dismissed both their appeals against conviction and sentence.

title: Appeals over super junior ministers at Cabinet ‘fundamentally flawed’, Supreme Court hears
description: Attorney General says attendance at meeting is being conflated with full ministerial status
content:
Appeals by two Opposition TDs over the attendance of super junior ministers at meetings of Government are “fundamentally flawed”, conflating attendance at meetings with being a full government minister, the Supreme Court has heard.
Attorney General Rossa Fanning made the submissions on Thursday at the hearing of an appeal by Pa Daly of Sinn Féin and People Before Profit-Solidarity’s Paul Murphy over the rejection of their legal challenges to the attendance of super junior ministers at meetings of Government.
A three-judge High Court last December dismissed the challenges by the TDs. They were subsequently awarded 50 per cent of their legal costs against the State because of the importance, novelty and complexity of the constitutional issues raised.
The TDs brought separate but similar challenges, arguing that article 28 of Bunreacht na hÉireann limits the number of government members to 15, and the attendance of super junior ministers at cabinet meetings goes against this.
Ministers of state attending cabinet – or super junior ministers – are appointed by the government on the nomination of the taoiseach. They participate in government meetings, but do not vote.
The High Court, comprising court president David Barniville and judges Siobhán Phelan and Conleth Brady, held that no provision of the Constitution is breached by the attendance and participation of the junior ministers at cabinet meetings.
Both TDs applied to the Supreme Court to hear appeals against the High Court decision on grounds including that it was based on errors of fact and of law. They are also appealing the costs orders, arguing they are entitled to their full costs.
Leading the State’s defence of the cases at Thursday’s hearing, Fanning told a seven-judge Supreme Court that on a narrow view, the case concerns whether the regular attendance of four ministers of state at meetings of Government constitutes a breach of the Constitution.
Viewed in a broader way, the case touches on the separation of powers between the judicial and executive branches of the State, and raises questions about the justiciability of political arrangements underpinning the maintenance of governments in an “increasingly fractious” political landscape, the AG submitted.
Part of the appeal concerned a confusion around the definition of “government”, Fanning said. He said it suited the Daly and Murphy sides to engage in “wilfully simplistic and facile” analysis of article 28 of the Constitution.
“The fundamental error that afflicts both appeals is that the appellants wrongly conflate attending a meeting on one hand with being a government minister on the other hand,” he said.
Fanning submitted that ultimately, ministers of state attending government “are not decision makers”.
This was underscored by the fact that they are not consulted when decisions are taken at incorporeal meetings of Government, he submitted. “That is a vivid and practical manifestation of the fact that although they’re in the [Cabinet] room, they’re not decision makers,” he said.
The appeals, before Chief Justice Donal O’Donnell, Judge Iseult O’Malley, Judge Gerard Hogan, Judge Brian Murray, Judge Maurice Collins, Judge Aileen Donnelly and Judge Brian O’Moore, continue on Friday.

title: Irish Book Awards: Maggie O’Farrell, Vincent Browne, Sally Hayden and Louise Kennedy on shortlist
description: Debutant Djamel White, whose literary crime thriller was longlisted for the Booker Prize, is up for two awards
content:
A strong year for Irish writing is reflected in the expansion of the shortlists in several categories of the 2026 An Post Irish Book Awards from six to eight titles.
Debutant author Djamel White, longlisted for the Booker Prize for his literary crime thriller, All Them Dogs , has been shortlisted for Novel of the Year alongside some of the biggest names in Irish fiction: Maggie O’Farrell for Land ; Sebastian Barry for The Newer World ; Donal Ryan for Where Are the Kings ; John Boyne for The Weight of Angels ; Louise Kennedy for Stations ; Kathleen MacMahon for Other People’s Lives ; and Jan Carson for Few and Far Between .
Sinéad McCorry, chairperson of the awards, said: “This year’s An Post Irish Book Awards shortlist is a wonderful reflection of the depth and diversity of talent across Irish writing. As we celebrate the awards’ 21st anniversary, it is fantastic to see such a strong mix of established and new writers represented across the categories, alongside the publishers, illustrators and booksellers who play such an important role in bringing these stories to readers.”
Biography of the Year is another highly competitive category. Vincent Browne’s long-awaited Charles Haughey: Glory, Greed and Guns is up against another former Fianna Fáil Taoiseach, Seán Lemass: The Lost Memoir , edited by Irish Times journalist Ronan McGreevy. Two late literary titans also feature: John McGahern: A Writing Life by Frank Shovlin and No One Tells You: The Last Years of Edna O’Brien by her son, Carlo Gébler. As well as two very different writers’ memoirs, Home Economics: A Memoir by Caitríona Lally and A Bigger Life by Louise O’Neill, the shortlist also features Talk to Joe: Life, Liveline and Me by broadcaster Joe Duffy; and Not the Perfect Victim by Nikita Hand with Kathryn Rogers.
Djamel White is also in the running for Newcomer of the Year, along with three journalists turned authors, Tanya Sweeney for Esther is Now Following You ; Jen Bray for The Lies Between Us; and Ruth McKee for Wild Iris . Also in contention are Neil Tully for The Visit ; Colin Morgan for The Ballad of Ronan McCoy ; Jessamine O’Connor for Somewhere ; and Edie May Hand for Dirtpickers .
The History Book of the Year category features three books about the struggle for Irish independence, The Plot Against Ireland by Myles Dungan; A Rebel and a Traitor by Rory Carroll; and Catalpa by Michael B. Barry; alongside The Story of Us: Independent Ireland and the 1926 Census , edited by Orlaith McBride and John Gibney; A History of Ireland in 100 Stamps by Max Barrett; and The Fallen: The Magdalene Laundries and Ireland’s Legacy of Silence by Louise Brangan.
Four very powerful books by women are competing for Non-Fiction Book of the Year – Said the Dead by Doireann Ní Ghríofa; The Most Normal Woman: Essays on Appearances by Roisín Kiberd; Opening Night by Sara Baume; and This is Also a Love Story: Searching for Good in a Divided World by Irish Times journalist Sally Hayden – alongside A Sheepdog Named Oscar by Dara Waldron and A Hosting: Interviews with Irish Writers 1991–2026 by Martin Doyle, Books Editor of The Irish Times.
Two Irish Times columnists are competing for Popular Fiction Book of the Year – Paul Howard with A Nation Once Again and Emer McLysaght, along with Sarah Breen, for Our Deadly Summer . They are up against Ardal O’Hanlon for A Plot to Die For ; Cecelia Ahern for Love Unlocked; Lucy Kennedy with The Mini Breakers; Anna Carey for Love Scene ; Vicki Notaro for Anywhere But Here; and Andrew O’Connor with The Expectation.
The Sports Book of the Year shortlist features memoirs by athlete Ciara Mageean; rugby players Peter O’Mahony and Simon Zebo; footballer James McClean; sportswriter Vincent Hogan; and Arthur James O’Dea’s profile of GAA legends, Mackey and Ring.
The crime fiction category is also very competitive this year, featuring the latest books by Liz Nugent, Jane Casey, Steve Cavanagh, Andrea Mara, Edel Coffey, Tana French, Jo Spain and Michelle McDonagh.
Readers are invited to vote for their favourite books of the year on the awards website . Voting closes at 6pm on November 13th. A one-hour television special, hosted by Oliver Callan, will be broadcast on RTÉ One on December 10th, featuring the six finalists competing for Book of the Year 2026 and revealing the winner.

title: Trump says he asked Google CEO to rename Atlantic Ocean on Maps
description: Tech company previously complied with president’s demand to rename Gulf of Mexico as Gulf of America
content:
US president Donald Trump said Google rejected his request to rename the Atlantic Ocean after himself or the United States.
Speaking at a rally in South Carolina, the president said he had called Google’s CEO, Sundar Pichai , to ask whether the company could “handle” his proposal.
“I only like two oceans: the Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean. I’m not going to put either Trump or America on any other ocean but these two. So we seriously looked at the Atlantic Ocean, and I called Google Maps, who were really great with the lake ... They’re still rattled from the Gulf. I said: ‘Sundar, I’m thinking of the Atlantic Ocean,’” Trump said.
Trump referenced his previous executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America , as well as his push to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America amid a trade feud between the US and Canada , for which he also signed an executive order requiring US federal agencies to use his new moniker.
[ The Irish Times view on Donald Trump and Lake Ontario: what’s in a name? Opens in new window ]
According to Trump, Pichai rejected the latest proposal. Trump described the Google CEO’s response by saying, “No, no, no. This time I’m not doing it ... Oceans are different, sir. They cover ... a lot of countries. Please don’t ask us to do that.”
“So I’ll probably pass. Should I pass it?” Trump said, adding: “I think let’s keep it the Atlantic Ocean.”
Google has previously acceded to Trump’s demands for name changes, which triggered public criticism including from Mexico and Canada. On Google Maps, the locations themselves are labelled “Gulf of America” and “Lake America” for US users, while search results display the new names alongside the original names in parentheses. Users in Mexico and Canada, meanwhile, continue to see the original names.
Trump has also previously floated renaming the strait of Hormuz after himself. Last month, amid the US’s ongoing war with Iran, he wrote on Truth Social: “Should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!” – Guardian

title: Russia drops cluster warheads on Kyiv after Witkoff-Putin peace talks
description: Russian missiles bombard Kyiv hours after Witkoff-Putin talks in St Petersburg
author_name: Fabrice Deprez in Kyiv, Katya Arenina in Vilnius
content:
Russia carried out a heavy aerial attack on Ukraine that included cluster munitions, just hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin met a US envoy in St Petersburg to discuss the resumption of peace talks.
Moscow unleashed a barrage of more than 20 missiles on Kyiv overnight that killed two people and injured more than 30, Ukrainian authorities said.
Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelenskiy said three ballistic missiles that hit the capital had been equipped with cluster warheads designed to spread damage over a wide area.
One exploded in the historic Pechersk district in the city centre and damaged several restaurants, shops and monastery buildings.
“The choice of weapon was deliberate, the choice of target area was deliberate, and so was the intent to inflict as much loss and damage on civilians as possible,” Zelenskiy wrote on X.
He added that Ukrainian intelligence services warned that Russia would amplify its air campaign in the coming weeks and was “taking advantage of the slowdown in air defence supplies from our partners”.
Kyiv also launched more than 600 drones towards Moscow, where three people were injured, according to Russian officials
The Russian strikes follow a renewed US diplomatic push, with president Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff meeting Zelenskiy and several European leaders in Oslo this week.
Witkoff then headed to St Petersburg for talks on Wednesday with Putin, whom the envoy hailed as a “humanitarian”.
Witkoff and Putin discussed resuming talks with Ukraine in mid-November, and a possible leaders’ summit between China, Russia and the US in Shenzhen next month, according to Russian officials.
Russia did not commit to renewed talks, while European officials familiar with the Oslo discussions are sceptical the US diplomatic push is making headway.
“Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack,” wrote Zelenskiy on Thursday. “This means there has been no real change in its attitude towards everything that is happening,” he added.
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said the attack damaged an ambulance station as well as metro infrastructure near the city’s South Bridge, a key thoroughfare over the Dnipro river.
Authorities recorded damage across six districts. A shopping centre in the Obolonskyi district was also heavily damaged in the attack.
“Overnight, Kyiv residents heard what Russian ‘humanism’ truly sounds like,” Ukraine’s foreign minister Andriy Sybiha wrote on X.
“Appeasement, servility and flattery will not stop this war. Only strength will.”
Meanwhile, Russian officials said that Ukrainian drones overnight had injured three people. Moscow’s airports suspended operations for several hours overnight, and media reports said a military facility, the 75th arsenal, had been damaged.
The attack was the third largest this year by the number of drones launched towards the Russian capital, according to the tallies reported by Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin.
Zelenskiy told journalists late on Wednesday that Kyiv had “received feedback” that Ukraine, Russia and the US had agreed to revive trilateral talks, which were put on ice at the onset of the war in Iran earlier this year.
Zelenskiy said they hoped the negotiating teams would meet in early November, though no date has been confirmed.
The talks this week failed to deliver concrete progress, even as Kyiv pushed for an energy ceasefire to stop Russia from pummelling Ukrainian power plants and energy infrastructure in advance of winter. Trump has repeatedly demanded that Ukraine cease its own strikes targeting Russian refineries and oil terminals.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said in a Thursday press briefing that Abu Dhabi was being considered as the venue for a three-way meeting between Russia, the US and Ukraine, though he said no decision had been made on who would represent Moscow.
Moscow sees “the increasing activity of certain European capitals trying to understand what is going on”, said Peskov, but added Russia’s interests were not being taken into account.
“It seems we are still a long way from such objective statements,” he said. US media reported that Trump hoped to secure a peace agreement at the G20 summit in Miami in December, but Peskov said no decision had been made on whether Putin would travel to the event.
Ukraine’s air force said 210 long-range drones also took part in the attack on Kyiv overnight and said it had shot down 181 of the unmanned aerial vehicles.
The report did not mention any missile intercepts, highlighting Ukraine’s enduring shortage of sophisticated anti-air missiles even as Moscow expands its campaign against Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Zelenskiy complained to US senators on Monday that “the Pentagon is delaying the delivery” of crucial interceptor missiles Kyiv relies on to protect its cities against Russian ballistic missile launches.
– Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026. Additional reporting: Guardian

title: Man (32) thought ‘shadow men’ were after him during rooftop standoff with armed gardaí
description: Martin Cunningham threw oranges around Lidl in Clonsilla before threatening to kill security guard in separate incident
content:
A man sentenced to a 2½-year prison sentence for making threats and criminal damage thought “shadow men” were after him during a four-hour rooftop standoff with armed gardaí , a court heard.
Martin Cunningham (32), of Sheephill Green in Blanchardstown , pled guilty to three charges for threatening a security guard, producing a knife, and performing criminal damage from the roof of a house in Castaheany in two separate incidents.
A security guard in the Lidl in Clonsilla had called the Garda, noting he had been threatened by a man with a Stanley knife shortly before 10pm on February 22nd, 2024.
The court heard that a woman and a man, later identified as Cunningham, had been observed on CCTV footage throwing oranges around the shop, before attempting to purchase alcohol.
They were denied the purchase as they did not have identification.
The court heard Cunningham then threw a lemon towards the tills before being escorted off the premises by a security guard who he then threatened with a fire extinguisher.
“I’ll bounce this off your f**king head,” Cunningham had said, noted prosecuting barrister Simon Matthews.
He put down the fire extinguisher and proceeded to take a black and yellow Stanley blade from his pocket and was said to have threatened the security guard saying: “I’ll cut you to bits and kill you.”
In a victim impact statement, the security guard said he was left in “fear of his life” and that his partner had asked him to quit his job following the incident. He could not do so, the court heard, as it would financially ruin the couple.
Garda Eva Mahedy of Blanchardstown Garda station told the court that on a separate occasion, on September 15th, 2025, the Armed Support Unit (ASU) and local gardaí engaged in a four-hour standoff with Cunningham who was on the roof of his mother’s house.
At 4am, Cunningham was on the roof of three houses on Castlegrange Avenue and began to throw solar panels and roof tiles at 20 assembled gardaí, the court was told.
During the standoff, he said he would shoot gardaí if he had been in possession of a gun.
He caused €10,200 of damage to the roofs and to a nearby car, before jumping down and attempting to escape from gardaí and being arrested.
During the incident, he had been under the influence of cocaine, vodka and a “few bumps” of ketamine and believed that “shadow men” were after him.
He also thought the ASU had attempted to climb the roof, but Mahedy said they had not.
Cunningham had been awake for two days at this point and previously thought he was being pursued by gardaí while under the influence and had hid in a local river.
Defence barrister Oisín Clarke said his client was “acting the maggot in the store” and had apologised to gardaí for being on the roof of the house and had been under the influence of drugs.
He said Cunningham had begun engaging with professionals for his drug use and was “dealing with his anger issues”.
Clarke said the lighting technician, who also has a forklift driving qualification, had faced “tragedy” as an uncle he was close to had died shortly before these incidents.
The Dublin Circuit Court judge, Martin Nolan, said gardaí took a “very patient approach” with Cunningham during the standoff, and acknowledging his addiction issues, past offending and set a headline sentence of four years.
He reduced the sentence to 2½ years due to the mitigation of his early plea and backdated it to the time of his arrest in September 2025.

title: Ireland still relies on fossil fuel for almost 80% of energy as demand rises
description: Increasing flights, traffic and data centre expansion complicating efforts to switch from carbon-polluting fuels
content:
Ireland is still overwhelmingly reliant on fossil fuels for power, heat and transport despite the climate and cost impacts, latest data shows.
Almost 80 per cent of all the energy used by homes, businesses, industry and travel came from oil , gas or solid fuels, the figures for 2025 show.
The country now has the third lowest share of renewable energy in the European Union , the report from the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) shows.
Growing traffic , increasing flights and data centre expansion are all complicating efforts to move away from the carbon-polluting fuels, it says.
It forecasts that overall energy demand will increase by 10 per cent by 2030 – driven largely by these sectors.
The trend is the opposite of what is required under 2030 energy efficiency and climate targets.
Ireland is already using 15 per cent more energy than those targets allow and the gap is set to widen.
High dependence on fossil fuels not only makes meeting the country’s climate action commitments hard to meet but also costs consumers dearly, the SEAI says.
That is because almost all fossil fuels have to be imported at prices set by markets over which Ireland has no control.
“We’ve seen this year how a secure and affordable energy supply is central to the financial health of our households, the livelihoods of so many of our citizens, and the strength of our economy,” said SEAI chief executive, William Walsh.
“We simply can’t take it for granted any more. With so many worried about their bills this winter, we must reduce our reliance on imported, polluting fuels. It’s the only long-term solution.”
Fossil fuels provided 79.1 per cent of the country’s energy last year which was a small reduction on the 81.4 per cent in 2024.
Emissions from energy also fell last year, by 3.6 per cent, with a further fall provisionally recorded in the first half of this year.
However, those reductions were partly due to an increase in the amount of electricity imported from Britain as Ireland does not have to count the energy usage or emissions associated with the generation of electricity overseas.
A total of 16.3 per cent of the electricity used in Ireland last year was imported compared to 14 per cent the previous year.
The supply of renewable electricity within Ireland is growing but slowly and in circumstances where demand keeps rising.
Gas remained the largest source of electricity generation, accounting for 40 per cent of the total, while wind, the biggest renewable source, provided 32 per cent.
Transport stands out as the sector most dependent on fossil fuels, with 92 per cent of all travel fuelled by petrol and diesel and just 8 per cent by biofuels or electricity.
Despite an increase in sales of electric vehicles, the roads remain dominated by internal combustion engines.
Increased flying is also adding to demand with aviation fuel usage up almost 11 per cent in the first six months of this year, but more private cars and goods vehicles are also on the road.
Data centres used 22.5 per cent of all electricity last year and account for 78 per cent of increase in Ireland’s electricity demand between 2015 and 2025.
William Walsh said while more renewables, more energy storage and more efficient energy use would help, policy decisions also needed to be taken.
“Decisions on the scale and location of major energy users, including large new electricity demands, such as data centres, must also be considered through the lens of energy security, affordability and climate objectives,” he said.

title: Ireland open ODI series with 55-run victory over Namibia in Windhoek
description: Paul Stirling’s half-century and wickets for spinners and Gavin Hoey and George Dockrell help secure win
content:
1st ODI: Ireland 229-9 (50 ovs) (P Stirling 56, C Carmichael 45, H Tector 28, L Tucker 28; JN Loftie-Eaton 4-36, JJ Smit 2-47), Namibia 174 (37.5 ovs) (R Trumpelmann 50, L Steenkamp 26; G Hoey 3-29, G Dockrell 2-22, J Moondra 2-27). Ireland won by 55 runs .
Ireland secured a 55-run victory over Namibia in a low-scoring first One-Day International in Windhoek on Thursday.
Played in temperatures in the mid-30s, Ireland were put into bat in the first of five matches and got off to a fine start as the experienced opening duo of skipper Paul Stirling and Andrew Balbirnie put on 70 for the first wicket.
Balbirnie holed out for 20 but Stirling would go on to make 56, becoming the first batter to pass 13,000 runs for Ireland. The Belfast native has now scored over 3,500 more runs than the second-best Irish batter on the run-scoring list.
Cade Carmichael made 45 at number three, while Harry Tector and Lorcan Tucker both made 28 as Irish batters failed to push on from good starts, with Namibia leg-spinner Jan Nicol Loftie-Eaton taking four for 36 as Ireland’s innings fizzled out on 229 for nine from their 50 overs.
Irish leg-spinner Gavin Hoey would also revel in the conditions, taking three for 29, while left-arm spinner George Dockrell took two for 22 to become the leading men’s international wicket-taker of all time with 327.
Only an enterprising 50 from 43 deliveries from number eight batter Ruben Trumpelmann extended the game, before South African-born Irish opening bowler Liam McCarthy finally ended his resistance and the match by bowling Trumpelmann with the penultimate ball of the 38th over.

title: Spinal surgeon who said he would not practise in Ireland now working in US
description: Dr Connor Green, who was on leave for three years, resigned from Temple Street children’s hospital this year
content:
The paediatric orthopaedic surgeon at the centre of concerns arising from children’s spinal surgeries is now working in the United States , the Dáil has heard.
Dr Connor Green, who was on leave from Temple Street children’s hospital for three years before resigning this year, has been the focus of a number of reports relating to the care provided to children with scoliosis, spina bifida and developmental dysplasia of the hip.
Concerns were raised in 2023 about high rates of post-operative complications, infections in orthopaedic surgeries and the use of unapproved springs in surgeries.
Green is now working in LifeBridge Health in Baltimore, Maryland, with a post on the hospital’s website stating he is “accepting new patients”.
According to the hospital’s website, Green is a “fellowship-trained pediatric orthopaedic surgeon joining the International Center for Limb Lengthening (ICLL) at Sinai Hospital, part of LifeBridge Health, in Baltimore, Maryland”.
“His clinical practice focuses on congenital and acquired limb deformity, limb length discrepancy, limb reconstruction, and hip preservation, including developmental dysplasia of the hip, Perthes disease, and adolescent hip pathology,” the website said.
The hospital outlines his academic training background, detailing qualifications from University College Dublin (UCD), the Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland, as well as a fellowship in Paediatric Orthopedic Surgery and Scoliosis at Texas Scottish Rite Hospital for Children in Dallas.
It does not reference his work at Children’s Health Ireland (CHI).
“His research interests span hip morphology and hip preservation, outcomes measurement in pediatric orthopaedics, and engineering-enabled approaches to orthopaedic care, including image analysis and preoperative planning tools,” the website said.
“He has authored nearly 40 peer-reviewed articles, review papers, and case reports, as well as two book chapters, and actively supervises graduate research at UCD.”
The hospital added that Green believes in “fully involving young patients in their own care and presenting all treatment options to both the child and family”.
“While the approach chosen should always be evidence-based, it should also fit with how the child and family wish for their care to be delivered,” it added.
Green’s work in Maryland was mentioned by People Before Profit TD Paul Murphy during a Dáil debate on the proposed commission of investigation into scoliosis and spina bifida care provided to children.
Green was referred to the Irish Medical Council by CHI in 2023. The investigation is ongoing and no findings have yet been made.
According to the council’s medical register, Green provided a voluntary undertaking not to engage in the practice of medicine.
However, this undertaking only applies to medicine in the Republic of Ireland and does not apply to other jurisdictions. Green was contacted for comment through his solicitors.
The Irish Times understands the regulator in Maryland was made aware of these events when Green decided to work in the US.
A report published last year by the Health Information and Quality Authority found Green implanted non-medical grade springs in three children with scoliosis at Temple Street.
The review described the actions as “wrong”, adding failures in controls meant “children were not protected from the risk of harm”.
Green was not identified in the report, and was instead referred to as Consultant A.
A separate report on his orthopaedic work, conducted by Prof Selvadurai Nayagam, a retired consultant in orthopaedics and trauma in Liverpool, has yet to be published.
However, the HSE earlier this year announced it was going to carry out a wider look at Green’s practice, reviewing patients whose surgeries were carried out between 2016 and 2023 and including all spinal, limb reconstruction and surgical dislocation of the hip surgeries.

title: Fitzwilliam Hotel in Dublin checks in again with a profit
description: Company behind the five-star hotel on St Stephen’s Green made a profit last year of €1.6m
content:
The company behind the five-star Fitzwilliam Hotel in Dublin returned to profit last year, latest accounts show.
Filings for Ampleforth Ltd show that it made a profit of €1.6 million in the year to the end of December 2025. This marked a turnaround on the previous year when the company recorded a loss of €1.3 million.
Turnover rose by 10 per cent to €22.2 million as the business concluded a three-year refurbishment of the hotel in the first half of the year.
“The programme, which incorporated both bedrooms and common areas, has enhanced the guest experience and improved the energy efficiency of the building,” the directors’ report states.
“Trading performance has strengthened during the year, with improved occupancy and room yield reflecting the enhanced offering and the return to full inventory availability.”
The company’s staff numbers declined to 200 from 211 a year earlier, while its total payroll costs reduced by 18.5 per cent to €7.5 million.
Ampleforth is controlled by Michael Holland .

title: Donald Clarke: Booyakasha! Welcome back, Ali G. Sort of. And maybe just this one last time
description: Sacha Baron Cohen has returned to the character who made his name. People are already annoyed
content:
Y ou may well scoff, but the new Ali G film – arriving nearly a quarter of a century after his previous big-screen adventure – looks to have already achieved one of its aims. People are annoyed. There are “calls for a boycott”. NewsCord, a media-monitoring platform, has asked readers to email cinema chains, “asking each to leave the film off its screens”. The last time I checked, more than 56,000 had answered the call. Booyakasha!
There is nothing much new here. Protesters gathered outside the premiere of Ali G Indahouse in 2002 to give Sacha Baron Cohen , creator of the character, a piece of their collective mind. “He is the new Al Jolson,” its organiser Peter Akinti said. “He’s effectively blacked up to take the piss out of a stereotype of young black men.”
As Ali G: Who Iz I? lands for a brief run in cinemas, the same rebuttal will be issued. It is still often forgotten that Ali G – full name Alistair Leslie Graham – was actually a middle-class white kid from Staines-upon-Thames who unconvincingly mimicked the argot of black street culture.
“He is funny because he is delusional,” Cohen said much later. “He lives this boring, white middle-class life in a suburban town, and he deludes himself that he’s living in Compton.”
Maybe offence is still justified. But Cohen, who researched the American civil-rights movement while an undergraduate at Cambridge, undeniably put his invention to worthwhile satirical use.
The character will be best remembered for a series of interviews, carried out in the style of “yoof TV”, with distinguished figures of the millennial years. Too many of them, not wanting to seem fusty, uncertain of the interviewer’s true ethnicity, let him away with comically offensive questions.
Only a few came out of it well. The late Tony Benn , dogged left-wing MP, politely stood up to Ali’s assertion that all strikes were motivated by laziness.
“I decided that the only respectful thing to do was to argue with him and to do so as vigorously as I could,” he later wrote in The Guardian. “At no stage during our talk did I suspect for a second that it was other than a genuine programme.”
Benn was initially angry on discovering the truth, but he mellowed when young people in the street told him “how glad they were that I had stood up to him”.
Cohen moved on to further success with the still-controversial Borat, in 2006, and strong supporting roles in Tim Burton’s Sweeney Todd, from 2007, and Tom Hooper’s Les Misérables, from 2012. Though Ali G made occasional appearance in pop videos and at awards ceremonies, the character gradually receded into the early-century amnesiac mists with the white iPod and Gareth Gates .
What the heck is he doing back in our cinemas? “You wouldn’t get away with that now,” pundits say of anything more offensive than a blown raspberry. If social media is to be believed, cancel culture has annihilated freedom of speech. We cower in terror at the commissars of woke.
You know how this goes. Ali G is a relic, as ancient to current culture as Some Mothers Do ’Ave ’Em was to those attending Ali G Indahouse. Cohen gets all this. He is no fool.
“The fact that Ali G is outdated and problematic is the very reason I resurrected him,” he wrote in Time magazine this week. “The world he’s returned to is, in many ways, worse than the one he left 20 years ago.”
The first thing to say is that few “legacy sequels” have improved so markedly on their big-screen predecessors than has Ali G: Who Iz I? The bad news for Cohen is that this is principally because the earlier film was appalling. A full 24 years ago, Philip French, reviewing in The Observer, declared “the joke has worn thin”.
The new film makes a virtue of Ali’s superannuation as it brings him to the United States for engagement with nutjobs of every calibre. Cohen plays a deluded woke academic who abhors everything Ali G represents. He also plays a buffoonish former Mossad operative who persuades actual right-wingers to don a class of anal cannon.
The willingness of genuine citizens to play along with the madness reaches shocking levels in a closing stunt so hard to credit that it requires a repeated assurance. “Reminder: they are not in on it,” a legend tells us.
None of this is hugely subtle. Nor does it involve the creative cunning that Chris Morris and colleagues brought to the 1990s Channel 4 show Brass Eye. But the film does justify Cohen’s claim that we are living in an even more poisonous media environment than the one his creation skewered during the middle Blair years.
It is, on balance, possible to welcome Ali back. But maybe just this one last time.
Ali G: Who Iz I? is in cinemas from Friday, October 23rd

title: Global stocks dip after AI boom stalls and motor industry slows
description: Stocks on either side of the Atlantic end trading session in the red
content:
Global stocks slumped on Thursday as industry old and new suffered pullbacks in trader confidence. The artificial intelligence (AI) boom in the US is proving to be a dangerous game for investors worried about recent filings from Meta, while the motor industry in Britain dragged its stock indices into the red.
The Iseq All-Share index fell 1.86 per cent to close at 14,026.41, following sizeable drops in the banking sector in particular and little upward movement elsewhere.
AIB saw its stock decrease 4.58 per cent to €10.64 a share, while rival Bank of Ireland fared only slightly better, down 3.81 per cent to close at €18.04 on the day it announced higher interest rates to its fixed-term savings deposit account. Permanent TSB, meanwhile, saw no change in its share price.
Elsewhere, building materials specialist group Kingspan fell 3.90 per cent to €91.20 a share, while Ryanair saw its share price slump 2.59 per cent to close at €22.96.
Nutrition business Kerry Group jumped in share price, up 6.07 per cent to close at €99.60 a share. Its chief executive said earlier in the day the surge in demand for weight loss medications was helping its business to boom.
Stocks in London fell into the red by the close of markets, with the British motor industry slowing down so much that not even a strong showing from real estate companies could drive its stock indices into positive returns.
London’s blue-chip FTSE 100 dipped 0.26, while its mid-cap FTSE 250 index fell 0.93 by the end of trading hours.
Aston Martin’s share price decreased 7.21 per cent as the fallout from legal disputes continues to affect investor confidence that the car brand is a safe bet, while ongoing supply chain issues are also blamed by some. Rolls-Royce fell 5.11 per cent as well to its lowest share price in recent weeks as a technical correction on its valuation pulled its stock lower.
Meanwhile, the online real estate company Rightmove was up 3.63 per cent as buy-backs keep its stock on a consistently upward trajectory.
Elsewhere in Europe, stock indices were not much better, following poor results from the Continent’s luxury goods and energy industries, leading investors to look for safer bets in the telecommunications and pharmaceutical sectors.
The blue-chip Euro Stoxx 50 index closed 1.96 per cent lower on Thursday, with the mid-cap Stoxx 600 index fairly slightly better, down 1.05 per cent at the end of trading.
Luxury goods giant Hermes saw its share price fall after investors lost confidence that the French house can truly compete with Chinese competitors – its third-quarter revenue fell short of analysts’ forecasts and represented the lowest quarterly growth rate it has seen since early 2020.
Meanwhile, German multinational software company SAP’s share price rose after it announced a 12 per cent jump in revenue, which the company largely attributed to increased demand for services supported by AI.
Stocks on Wall Street slid into the negative by midday New York time, as earnings reports from big tech companies in the US rattled investors’ confidence and continued warfare between the US and Iran shot oil prices up.
The Nasdaq index slumped nearly 2.5 per cent, while the S&P 500 fell about 1.25 per cent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped some 0.2 per cent before noon.
Strikes in Saudi Arabia and around the Gulf drove the price of Brent crude oil, the industry benchmark, to $112 – the highest price since May. This only stoked many traders’ inflation worries and pushed the prospect of peace in the Middle East farther away.
Companies at the coalface of AI expansion pulled down many stock indices as investors grew wary of the new technology’s ability to bring in big returns.
Meta reported a sizeable decline in cash flow on Wednesday and indicated it would struggle to fund data centre construction on its current path, leading the company to open more than 5 per cent down at the start of trading hours Thursday. – Additional reporting: The New York Times.

title: Night divers in Cork make rare sighting of long-snouted seahorse
description: It is believed to be the first time a wild seahorse has been filmed in Irish waters
content:
A rare sighting of a live long-snouted seahorse in Irish waters was made by a group of divers in Co Cork.
The seahorse was discovered by a group of divers night diving in the seagrass beds at Oysterhaven, Co Cork, on Monday evening.
They captured the finding on video, and it is believed to be the first time a wild seahorse has been filmed in Irish waters.
According to the National Biodiversity Data Centre, there are eight previous sightings of seahorses in Irish waters, with most occurring more than 100 years ago. The earliest took place in 1837, with the most recent in 1956.
Seven sightings were of the short-snouted seahorse, and the other was of a long-snouted seahorse, which was made earlier this year in Co Cork. However, it was found dead along the Ballynamona Strand.
James Northover, who owns Discovering Scuba dive centre in Carrigaline, was one of the local divers to see the creature along with Martyn Mannion and Luke Cuddihy.
It was Mannion who spotted the seahorse and called Northover and Cuddihy over to see it.
Northover said it was “very exciting”. He said he would often dive in the seagrass beds at Oysterhaven and has seen “lots of marine life” but nothing “as rare” as the seahorse.
Northover, who had previously seen a pygmy seahorse in Indonesia, said he had to look twice upon the discovery on Monday, spotting it and “couldn’t believe it”.
He said the seahorse – discovered about 30 minutes into their dive, before 8pm – was brown in colour and some 4cm to 5cm in length.
Northover took some video footage of the seahorse and has since shared it on his Instagram page.
Ecologist and Cork Sub Aqua Club member Dr Tim Butter described the sighting as “a bolt out of the blue”.
He, who also works with the National Biodiversity Data Centre, said seahorses can usually be found off Portugal, Spain and France. He added that short-snouted seahorses have been found off the south coast of Britain.
He said night diving is popular at this time of year as the water is still warm and many creatures become more active at night as they come out to eat.
The seagrass at Oysterhaven is a popular spot with local scuba divers as it is rich in wildlife but also easily accessible.
He said the seagrass meadows at Oysterhaven have been the subject of research over the past few years by a team of citizen scientists at Cork Sub Aqua Club.
Butter said club members have been working hard over the past few years to study the “incredible seagrass habitat in Oysterhaven and Kinsale and to educate others about this valuable resource”.
Seagrass also has “huge capacity” to absorb atmospheric carbon, supports local fisheries and helps to mitigate the impact of storm events.
He described it as a biodiversity hotspot that supports a diverse range of marine life.
“Not in my wildest dreams did I think we would ever see a seahorse. It is such an iconic species,” he said.
Northover submitted the record to the National Biodiversity Data Centre, which will go through a validation process.

title: Number of young people dying on Irish roads increases by half this year, gardaí say
description: Individuals aged between 16 and 25 years make up one quarter of all road fatalities for 2026 to date
content:
The number of young people dying on Irish roads has increased by nearly half this year, according to new data from An Garda Síochána .
Young people between 16 and 25 years of age now make up a quarter of all fatalities after a new surge in road deaths.
So far this year, 38 young people have died on Irish roads, a 46.2 per cent increase on the 26 fatalities in that age group last year.
The provisional Garda data, accurate to Thursday morning, showed there have been 151 roads deaths so far this year, 12 more than in the same period of 2025.
