There has only been a slight increase in the number of fatalities this year, just six higher than last year, at 134, but there has been a rise in the number of multiple-fatality crashes.
The wrong-way driving crash on the M9 in August was the most fatal incident. The two-car collision killed five teenagers – Kamil Pustkowski (17), Jack Kennedy (17), Jeremy O’Brien (18), Joe “Joey” Carthy (15) and Alex McCarthy (17) as they were driving the wrong way along the motorway in Co Kildare.
The force said that following high-profile crashes, the rate of fatal incidents tended to decrease.
In July and August, 21 and 22 people died respectively, though September saw just 14 deaths.
Just nine people have died this month so far and the Garda is appealing to the public to pay increased attention to pedestrians in the darker months of the year.
With the clocks going back on Sunday less daylight hours are linked to increased pedestrian deaths and injuries, Road Safety Authority data shows.
“As the long evenings draw in, we’re asking all road users to be mindful of each other over the October bank holiday weekend,” Garda roads policing assistant commissioner Denis Ferry said on Thursday.
“Motorists need to be aware of those walking on our streets and roads, and pedestrians should make sure they’re visible, especially as daylight time decreases.”
The number of pedestrians killed in crashes is the same as last year, at 29, with people over 65 making up the largest share of this cohort.
The 151 deaths so far this year are predominantly drivers and their passengers, some 54 per cent of all fatalities – 57 drivers and 26 passengers. Driver deaths increased by two from 2025, but the number of passengers more than doubled from 10 to 26.
There has been a moderate improvement in the number of motorcyclists killed, which has fallen from 28 last year to 22 so far in 2026.
Pedal cyclists (13), e-scooter and ebike deaths (4) and a single uncategorised death make up the remaining fatalities.
A crackdown on Wednesday saw the Garda seize 122 e-scooters, e-bikes, scramblers and Surron bikes.

title: BMWs, Louis Vuitton bags, Rolex watches seized amid charity money-laundering allegations
description: Charity at centre of investigation is based in Dublin and has national reach, dozens of staff and association with national figures
content:
Gardaí have conducted a number of searches and seized assets, including luxury vehicles and designer goods, as part of an investigation into allegations of money laundering at a registered charity.
Liberty Recycling, the charity under investigation, collects clothing via a vast network of clothing banks nationwide. It has a major processing facility in Bluebell, Dublin, and processes a 40ft container of clothing every week.
It has a significant presence in Dublin and also has a national footprint, with dozens of full-time staff and volunteers. Most of its clothing goes to destinations in Asia and Africa, and some is sold via its network of nine shops across Ireland.
The most recent financial records for the organisation suggest its income and expenditure increased significantly in the period just after the pandemic and had reached €5 million in 2024.
The group has also proven adept at attracting well-known figures in politics and the charity sector to become involved in its activities, so boosting its profile and reputation.
Sinn Féin TD Aengus Ó Snodaigh is listed as the current chairman, while Tony Geoghegan, who ran the Merchants Quay drug treatment organisation in Dublin for decades, is also a trustee. There is no suggestion whatever that either man is under investigation.
Liberty Recycling did not reply to a series of queries from The Irish Times. However, as Ó Snodaigh is involved as chairman, and is a prominent TD, Sinn Féin responded, saying it had become aware of the investigation by the Garda and Charities Regulator.
“Sinn Féin fully supports any investigation,” it added. “Deputy Ó Snodaigh has engaged with the office of the Charities Regulator. He has not been contacted by Gardaí, but if required, he will make himself available to assist with their inquiries.”
Some of the group’s expenditure is now under investigation on suspicion it effectively amounts to money laundering.
Specifically, gardaí are investigating if money intended to fund the charity’s services, helping impoverished and addicted people, has been misappropriated.
The assets seized during two days of searches this week were taken on suspicion they had been funded, or part funded, by money from the charity.
Any such activity – converting money into assets to conceal the origin of the funds, and for personal gain – would fall under the legal definition of money laundering.
However, sources familiar with the investigation stressed that no findings had been reached. They added the inquiry was still at the stage of probing allegations and gathering evidence, with no conclusions reached.
Garda Headquarters issued a short statement on Thursday morning confirming searches took place as part of an investigation, in conjunction with the Charities Regular, into a “Dublin-based charitable organisation”.
“As part of an ongoing investigation by detectives attached to the Money Laundering Investigation Unit at the Garda National Economic Crime Bureau, gardaí carried out a number of searches at locations in the Dublin, Eastern and Southern Regions,” it said of the searches on Tuesday and Wednesday.
“During the course of the searches, gardaí seized two BMW X5 cars with a total estimated value of €250,000 and other high value items including Louis Vuitton bags, Rolex watches, and jewellery with a total estimated value of €40,000.”
The Charities Regulator confirmed to The Irish Times that is has been assisting with the Garda investigation and is engaging with the trustees of the charity involved. Neither the Garda nor regulator have identified the charity or the precise nature of the investigation.
The charity has been in operation for more than two decades and while its main presence is in Dublin, it is well established, with centres offering services, in at least counties across the country.
It also has a much higher number of points around the country where people can make contributions to help fund the charity’s work and supply items towards the services it provides.

title: Israel kills at least four people in latest attacks on Gaza Strip
description: Some 1,500 Palestinians have been killed in the enclave since beginning of US-brokered ceasefire one year ago
content:
Israeli strikes and ‌gunfire killed at least four people in the Gaza Strip in separate incidents on Thursday, health ​officials in the enclave said.
In Gaza City, a strike on a car killed at least one person, medics said. They earlier said there had been two ​deaths. A crowd gathered around the burning wreckage, as orange-vested emergency crews sprayed it with ⁠water, photos from the scene showed.
Another strike killed a Palestinian man ‌on ‌a ​bike in the southern city of Khan Younis and ​a man near Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, while gunfire killed a woman near the Jabalia refugee camp, ⁠in the north, the ​medics added.
Israel’s military said it had struck ​Hamas militants in Khan Younis, Nuseirat and Gaza City, but that it ‌was not aware of the reported incident ​in Jabalia.
Israel, which says the ‌ Hamas militant group has been rearming and ​launching attacks in violation of a year-old ceasefire , has stepped up ⁠strikes on the group ⁠in recent ​weeks.
Hamas has denied trying to carry out attacks or rebuild its arsenal and accuses Israel of undermining the Gaza peace deal.
Last year’s US -brokered ceasefire calls for eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made as negotiators have failed to agree terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw ‌its troops.
Israeli air strikes ⁠have continued. At least 1,500 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire, according to the territory’s health officials, ‌while Israel says four soldiers have been killed.
Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people ​have been killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza, launched ​after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel on October 7th, 2023. – Reuters

title: First human case of Shamonda virus is reported in France
description: French authorities say there is no risk to general population ​at this stage
content:
A man in France has become the first human known to have contracted Shamonda virus, with investigations under way to explore whether it contributed to his death.
Shamonda virus is a type of bunyavirus and is spread by bites from infected midges.
Identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, Shamonda was ‌first confirmed in Europe in ⁠late July.
The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said it has since been detected in farm animals in Austria , Belgium , France, Germany , Ireland, Italy , Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands , Portugal , Spain and Switzerland , as well as Jersey.
The French announcement said the ​leading hypothesis was that the patient was ​infected in eastern France, where the virus had circulated among animals this spring and ‌summer.
“Based on the knowledge available regarding ​this virus, no health risk to the general population has been identified to date,” it ⁠said.
The ECDC said the patient ⁠died in early ​October and noted the victim had been receiving treatment for a serious illness that made them more susceptible to infection than the general population.
“Investigations into whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired are ongoing,” it said.
There are currently no commercially available vaccines against Shamonda virus
The ECDC said that in Europe biting midges are generally most active from spring to autumn, with “seasonal patterns varying by species, location and weather”.
“Given the cooling temperatures, the activity of most biting midge species is declining in Europe,” it said.
In animals such as cattle, sheep and goats, the virus can cause diarrhoea, lack of appetite and a decline in milk yield, “as well as abortions and congenital abnormalities in newborn calves, lambs and kids”, according to the Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety.
“In Switzerland and Germany, the presence of Shav [Shamonda virus] genetic material has also been reported in the brains of horses that died from neurological symptoms,” the agency said.
Prof Tom Solomon, the director of the pandemic institute at the University of Liverpool, said the risk to the general public appeared to be very low.
“Shamonda virus has been circulating in animals, particularly cattle, but also sheep, goats, horses and alpacas, for many years, yet this is the first recognised human infection,” he said.
“This suggests that transmission to humans is extremely unusual.”
But unknowns remain, he said: “We don’t know whether healthy people can become infected without developing symptoms, what symptoms the virus might normally cause, or how frequently it might cause serious disease.
“French authorities believe the neurological complications in this patient were very likely linked to the infection, although investigations are continuing. This is clearly concerning, but one exceptional case does not necessarily mean the virus poses a significant threat to the wider population.”
Dr Ben Brennan, group leader and senior lecturer at the MRC-University of Glasgow Centre for Virus Research, said: “This is an important scientific finding, as it is the first reported human infection with Shamonda virus.
“However, it is important to put this into perspective. The patient had a serious underlying illness that left them particularly vulnerable to infections, and we do not yet know whether Shamonda virus contributed to their death.
“Finding a virus in a severely immunocompromised patient does not necessarily mean it poses a significant risk to otherwise healthy individuals.”
“At present, there is no evidence that Shamonda virus causes widespread human disease, although further investigation is needed to understand its ability to infect people.”
Paul Hunter, professor in medicine at the University of East Anglia, said the disease “is primarily a problem in less economically developed countries” and so “we cannot say for certain that no human cases have previously occurred”.
He said severely immunocompromised people can be susceptible to infections that would not cause any problem in other people.
“So, at present we can assume that the risk of onward person-to-person transmission is tiny. But tiny is not zero.” – Guardian/Reuters

title: Shamrock Rovers boss Stephen Bradley claims FAI disciplinary system ‘not fit for purpose’
description: Hoops will have to do without three players in final two games of the season following suspensions
content:
The League of Ireland disciplinary system is “not fit for purpose” according to Shamrock Rovers manager Stephen Bradley .
Bradley’s damning view of the process was prompted by the suspension of three Rovers players in advance of the Hoops’ penultimate match of the Premier Division season at home to Sligo Rovers on Friday.
“The whole disciplinary process and how it is handled is not fit for purpose,” said Bradley. “I think everybody around the league would say that. People within the League would probably say that as well.
“Everything around it needs to change. It is so poor how it is done.”
Rovers winger Danny Grant received a four-match suspension for his role in a fight immediately after the Dublin derby against Bohemians in Tallaght on October 12th.
Grant was injured and sitting in the stand but he ran on to the pitch at full-time. Rovers are disappointed that video evidence was not used to implicate two Bohs players, who allegedly also came from the stand before one of them put Grant in a headlock.
Bohs captain Dawson Devoy and Rovers teenager Naj Razi both received three-match bans for violent conduct arising from the same incident.
Rovers striker Michael Noonan will miss two games, reduced from three following the use of video evidence in his defence. Bohs coach Stephen O’Donnell was also suspended for three matches.
[ League of Ireland permutations: Any Bohemians slip-up could hand Shamrock Rovers title Opens in new window ]
Grant, Devoy and Razi will miss the remainder of the season. There is no avenue to appeal the decision of the three-person disciplinary panel.
The panel is selected from a pool of volunteers, which is independent from the FAI executive and League office. The unpublished list includes legal experts, members of the FAI General Assembly and football representatives.
The process works off the referee’s report, but clubs are entitled to challenge the official account with video evidence. Rob Hennessy was the referee in Tallaght on October 12th.
“Everything around it,” Bradley replied when asked for specific issues with the disciplinary process. “We’ve made great strides [in the League of Ireland] but that is an area I feel we can improve.”
The disciplinary hearing took place on Wednesday, nine days after Rovers beat Bohs 2-1. Rovers are three points clear of Alan Reynolds’s side with two matches to play.
“It definitely can be done quicker,” Bradley added. “But there is so much more. It is maybe a conversation for the end of the season, to go into detail.”
The League of Ireland department of the FAI declined to respond to Bradley’s criticism when contacted on Thursday afternoon.
However, the association did note that their disciplinary process was modernised in recent years and that it is currently in line with other professional leagues. Also, the volunteers undergo training before every season to ensure that they understand the rules and processes.
Any changes to the system would need to be approved by the FAI board of directors.

title: Court grants Rathwood injunction over stock held in warehouse
description: Carlow Warehousing ordered to preserve Rathwood goods it holds pending further order from the court
content:
The Rathwood home and garden furniture company, which recently exited examinership , has obtained a temporary High Court injunction restraining a warehouse company from disposing of furniture which Rathwood says is held for its benefit.
On Thursday, Judge Brian Cregan granted orders to barrister Arthur Cunningham for Rathwood Home and Garden World Ltd, restraining Carlow Warehousing Ltd from disposing of and requiring it to preserve the goods it holds pending further order.
The judge also granted orders permitting the service of proceedings outside the jurisdiction on a company called Paleo Furniture Company Ltd, which the court heard is based in China and has claimed the stock stored with Carlow Warehousing belongs to it. The application was made ex parte, meaning only Rathwood was represented in court.
Earlier this year, on foot of a petition presented by Paleo, along with another creditor of Rathwood, the High Court appointed an examiner to the business. It successfully exited examinership following approval of a survival scheme last July.
In an affidavit, Rathwood managing director Kevin Nolan said that under the terms of that scheme, unsecured creditors were to receive 0.25 per cent of their agreed debts, to include contingent and prospective liabilities due and owing as at the date the dividend is discharged. This was to be in full and final settlement of the creditor’s claims.
[ Rathwood ends ‘working relationship’ with brothers formerly behind business Opens in new window ]
The scheme also provided that a separate category of creditor who had retention of title (ROT) status must make any claim to Rathwood within 14 days of the effective date of the scheme. Failure to do so meant the ROT creditor would be treated as an unsecured creditor.
Paleo had ROT status in relation to a debt of some €258,000 while it was also owed some €2.8 million as an unsecured creditor.
Nolan said no claim was submitted by Paleo within the 14-day period or any time after.
As a result, the total dividend payable to Paleo came to €7,724, and Nolan wrote to Paleo on August 19th, 2026, asking for its payment details so the money could be sent on.
Paleo wrote back saying it had not intentionally waived or abandoned its rights to the stored goods and may have legal remedies to protect its interests. It did not accept its ROT rights had been conclusively surrendered.
In a second email reply, Paleo said its position remained that the stock belonged to it.
Paleo agreed to accept the €7,724 but continued to assert its rights over the stock. It also said it did not consent to the removal of the stock from Carlow Warehousing premises.
Nolan said solicitors for Carlow Warehousing, in September 2026, said they would comply with any High Court order but asserted that a lien against Paleo survived and the goods would not be released until ownership was proved.
Nolan said Rathwood requires its stock before the seasonal upswing of activity in the spring of 2027. The company is in a growth phase and would be severely compromised next spring if it is denied access to the stock.

title: Andy Burnham is removing a Victorian-era law that singled out Catholics and Jews. Why now?
description: House of Commons fast-tracked a Bill related to the prime minister’s religion
content:
There is no separation of church and state in Britain. The Church of England, part of the Anglican Protestant faith, is the state church, answerable to parliament.
One of the constitutional functions of a British prime minister is to advise the monarch – who is also head of the Church of England – on the appointment of Anglican bishops and archbishops. Yet Catholics and Jews are explicitly barred from doing so.
Burnham is the first British prime minister to profess the Catholic faith upon entering office. Under existing British law, if as a professed Catholic he followed his predecessors and advised the British king Charles on the appointment of a bishop, he would be automatically disbarred from all civil and military office.
On Wednesday, the House of Commons debated a Church Appointments Bill to remove the bar on Jews and Catholics advising the sovereign on this specific issue, which arose from discriminatory laws passed in the mid-19 th century.
The path to become prime minister asks if the person “professes” the Catholic or Jewish faiths. Johnson replied “No” when he took office in 2019. As a baby, his mother had him baptised as a Catholic, but he was later confirmed as an Anglican in his teens.
It is accepted, however, that Johnson reverted to Catholicism while he served in Downing Street. While prime minister, he got married in Westminster Cathedral to a practising Catholic, Carrie Symonds and their children were also baptised in the Catholic cathedral, where the couple are now registered as parishioners.
As the existing laws specifically affect only Catholics and Jews, there was no legal bar on advice from Sunak or Keir Starmer, an atheist. Benjamin Disraeli, who became prime minister in 1868, was born into a Jewish family but was also later baptised Anglican.
The existing law only became an issue for British prime ministers in recent years, as Tony Blair converted to Catholicism after he left office in 2007.
[ Branded ‘lazy’ by Trump, a Democrat is mounting an unexpected challenge in a Republican stronghold Opens in new window ]
Not really. Catholic or Jewish prime ministers could delegate the job of advising on bishops. While he was prime minister, Johnson chose to delegate it to his lord chancellor (justice secretary) Robert Buckland. Burnham has also temporarily delegated the power to Alex Norris, the holder of that post in his government.
Also, it is debatable whether the prime minister really “advises” the king at all on church appointments. Under constitutional reforms introduced by Gordon Brown, the prime minister only “advises” the monarch on an appointment after a single name has already been chosen and proposed by the church.
[ Andy Burnham making TikToks about parking tickets seems to be missing the point Opens in new window ]
The advice is just a formality, yet UK government minister Hamish Falconer, who spoke in the House of Commons on Wednesday when the new law was debated, said it was important that the bar was removed so that a prime minister’s faith could never be a bar to them fulfilling all of the duties of their office.
In barely 60 minutes, the new Bill was fast-tracked through its second and third readings in the House of Commons and also committee stage.
There was a short debate, but no party opposed it. The DUP’s Jim Shannon said the removal of the bar affecting Catholics and Jews was to be “welcomed”. The Tories said it was an “anomaly that needed correcting”.
As it has passed all stages in the Commons, the Bill now moves to the House of Lords, where it is expected to pass with no issues. It will become law when it gets royal assent from the king.

title: Macron tightens curbs on protests and accuses far left of ‘seditious acts’
description: Combined yellow-vest and student protest to go ahead in Paris on Saturday as Italy calls in soldiers to patrol Milan streets
content:
There were fresh protests in France as president Emmanuel Macron moved to curtail demonstrations to avoid further unrest and accused far-left groups of “seditious acts” and an intent to overthrow the state.
After meeting intelligence services, Macron announced that protests would be “prohibited” unless organised by trade unions.
Trade-union protests would be directed away from city centres in order to protect businesses and public buildings, he said.
“The general recommendation is that there be no demonstrations in the coming days,” Macron said. “So that calm may prevail.”
After Macron spoke, a student protest massed on a road in the 13th arrondissement of Paris . It received last-minute permission to march as a court overturned an initial police ban. Students also protested in Lyons in defiance of a ban.
Coppélia Moreau of the Interfac student union told media at the Paris rally that the government was trying to “divide the protesters”.
“They told us the problem was the ‘bad’ Yellow Vests versus the ‘good’ high-school students and union members ... but what we’re seeing now is that the government doesn’t want any demonstrations at all,” Moreau said. “It won’t work, they won’t be able to avoid responding to our demands.”
Student and workers’ unions have received permission for a march in Paris on Saturday from Place de la Bastille to Place de la Nation. Organisers of the Yellow Vest movement announced they would join.
“We have a president who remains stubbornly determined to abandoning democracy and the Republic, heading towards authoritarianism,” Yellow Vest organiser Benjamin Ball said. “Everyone in this country has the constitutional right to freedom of expression, the right to protest.”
Macron, freshly returned from a three-day trip to the Middle East, held a talks on Thursday with intelligence services, political parties and student representatives as he sought to grapple with public anger.
“Last Saturday we witnessed political and even seditious acts carried out by organised far-left groups who aim to overthrow the Republic – let’s be clear, they openly admit to this – that were highly dangerous, extremely violent and carefully planned,” Macron said.
“Alongside this, there were acts of delinquency that require a very firm response, but which aren’t of the same nature.”
It came as a second person was arrested in connection with the burning of Limoges city hall. The 66-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of “damage to property by an organised group using means dangerous to persons”, according to the prosecutor’s office.
[ Europe’s angry autumn: what’s driving the wave of protests? Opens in new window ]
On Tuesday a 34-year old associated with far-left movements and reportedly on a security watch list was arrested. He is being questioned on suspicion of organised vandalism and “attempted murder of a person holding public authority”.
Limoges mayor Guillaume Guérin of the conservative Republicans party has blamed events on “anarchist ultra left” people who live in alternative communes in a rural hinterland to the east of the city.
In Italy, the government of prime minister Giorgia Meloni announced tax credits for the haulage, agriculture and fishing sectors to try to quell road blockages and protests by truck drivers angry about fuel costs that have emptied supermarket shelves.
The government has mobilised army troops in a bid to avoid further unrest after rioting in Milan last weekend echoed scenes in France.
Deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini said 500 Italian military paratroopers, many with experience of overseas service, would be stationed in public areas of Milan and would be able to use helicopters and drones to maintain public order.
“They will be prepared to do what a soldier must and can do, within the law,” Salvini said.
A 21-year-old man charged with stealing a dressing gown and a towel during the looting of a Decathlon sports shop in Milan on Sunday told the prosecutor he wanted to “feel something”, according to Italian news agency Ansa. “I wanted to feel alive,” he said.

title: Man (20s) becomes sixth arrest in fatal Waterford arson attack investigation
description: Man and woman previously charged with criminal damage over fire that killed Philip and Kim English and their sons Callum and Jayden
content:
Gardaí have arrested a man in his mid-20s for questioning about the murder of four members of the English family in an arson attack in Waterford city last week.
Detectives arrested the man in Waterford city on Thursday afternoon for questioning and he is being detained in Kilkenny city garda station under Section 50 of the Criminal Justice Act 2007.
This latest arrest brings to six the number of people detained by gardaí for questioning about the murder of Philip and Kim English and their two children, Callum (12) and Jayden (9).
The first two arrested, Jessica Dalton (31) and Cian Stacey (21), were charged with criminal damage in relation to the fire at Birchwood Avenue, Birchwood, in Waterford on October 13th.
Dalton, with an address at Waterford city, and Stacey, of no fixed abode, were also charged with assault causing serious harm to two other individuals who can’t be named for legal reasons.
Gardaí then arrested a man in his 50s and two women in their 30s on October 20th, again in Waterford city, for questioning about the fatal attack on the English family home.
All three were detained under Section 50 of the Criminal Justice Act 2007 and have had their initial period of detention extended by a chief superintendent in line with the provision of the legislation.
However, one of the women has since been released without charge and gardaí will now prepare a file for the Director of Public Prosecutions on her involvement in the deaths.

title: ‘Boarded out’ children must be included in redress scheme, says survivors’ advocate
description: Special advocate for survivors of institutional abuse calls for Mother and Baby Institutions Payment Scheme to be extended
content:
Some children who were “boarded out” by the State were forced to eat from a pig’s trough because they had no food, an Oireachtas committee has heard.
The special advocate for survivors of institutional abuse, Patricia Carey, recalled meeting children who had been boarded out and said their treatment was “heinous”.
Boarded out refers to those children sent from State institutions to farms and families up to the 1970s.
She estimated that 20,000 children, since the foundation of the State, were boarded out, of whom approximately 10,000 were still alive, and the numbers are growing smaller every year.
She called on the State to include them in redress schemes set up to compensate those subjected to institutional abuse as children.
Some of those who were boarded out went in at the age of four and emerged at 16 without support from their biological families, she told the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Children and Equality on Thursday.
“They talk about being dressed up the day the inspector came, and the minute the inspector left, those clothes were taken from them,” she said.
“I’ve spoken to people who were eating from the pig trough because they didn’t have enough food. So this is the reality of these people’s lives.
“Let us be in no doubt that they were treated appallingly, and the State has not responded to them.”
Carey told the committee that thousands of children were sent to work in conditions akin to “slavery on farms and private houses. This system was overseen by the State through inspections and payments were made to the families with whom the children were placed.”
Many endured terrible conditions and others, she told the committee, were subjected to sexual abuse. These were State-run schemes and the families involved received a payment.
She called for the current Mother and Baby Institutions Payment (redress) Scheme to be extended to those who were boarded out.
She said those who had been boarded out feel “invisible within the wider network of institutional abuse” and the response of Minister for Children Norma Foley on this issue to date “cannot be regarded as an adequate substitute for financial redress”.
She referenced an apology from the Taoiseach Micheál Martin in February this year to those who had been boarded out, acknowledging that some of them experienced “heartbreaking exploitation, neglect and abuse within the families and communities in which they were placed”.
Carey added: “An apology from the Taoiseach is one thing, the response to that apology is another.”
The Government’s Mother and Baby Institutions Payment Scheme only includes those who were in residential institutions and not those who were sent to foster families. Despite the apology by the Taoiseach in February, there has been no move by the Government to include them in the redress scheme.
Carey told the Oireachtas committee that the redress scheme has only reached 23 per cent of those eligible, though it has been open for 2½ years.
She also revealed that the Magdalen Restorative Justice Ex-Gratia Scheme , set up in 2013, has had a “very low uptake”.
She said the embassy networks should be used to reach those people who are eligible for redress, but do not know about it.
She said the redress scheme should be extended also to those who were in mother and baby homes under the age of six months and also those who were subjected to vaccination trials.
[ Minister ‘erred in law’ excluding two institutions from mother and baby homes scheme Opens in new window ]
The redress scheme has a budget of up to €800 million. Just 7,500 of the 34,000 people eligible for redress have applied, and the funds could adequately provide for those excluded from the scheme, she believed.
Carey called for a consistent level of support for survivors of institutional abuse. She said a range of benefits exist, with some survivors eligible for medical cards while others are not. The same goes for access to education, housing and wellbeing support payments.
“The fundamental question I have is this: as the Government has apologised and acknowledged the abuse, neglect and exploitation suffered by survivors, why does that accountability not translate into one consistent and equal level of support and redress for survivors?” she said.
“The harm was not hierarchical; unfortunately, the Government response is.”

title: Most Defence Forces personnel fear mental health disclosure could harm careers, study finds
description: Just 22 per cent of respondents indicated they would make such a disclosure to seek medical support
content:
The Defence Forces deputy chief of staff support has said he did “not accept” research presented to an Oireachtas committee that indicated a reluctance among personnel to seek mental health support, saying it was “not my experience”.
A study that identified “significant psychological distress” within the organisation, according to its author, was presented to the Oireachtas defence committee on Thursday morning.
Conducted by Dan Fitzpatrick, who served in the Defence Forces for more than 22 years, the study involved a survey of 687 serving personnel across the Army , Naval Service and Air Corps .
It found that almost all respondents (94 per cent) believed disclosing a mental health difficulty could negatively affect their military career.
Just 22 per cent of respondents indicated they would make such a disclosure to seek medical support.
“This presents a fundamental organisation contradiction. We encourage personnel to recognise psychological difficulties and seek appropriate support, yet the research indicates that many perceive that act of disclosure itself as a potential threat to their professional future.
“A person can recognise their psychological distress, understand the benefits of treatment and still make the calculated decision not to seek help,” Fitzpatrick told committee members.
The survey, which was carried out during the Covid-19 pandemic and was published this year, saw 34 per cent of respondents report having had suicidal thoughts, while 10 per cent reported previously engaging in self-harm.
A quarter also screened positive for probable post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), Fitzpatrick said.
[ Seán Rooney preliminary inquest hearings private ‘to protect safety of Defence Forces’ Opens in new window ]
Sixty one respondents (9 per cent) said they had made a previous suicide attempt, with Fitzpatrick arguing these individuals were “invisible to the organisation”.
He told the committee the medical grading system was one of the “largest barriers” to personnel seeking support, saying they receive an “automatic downgrade” once they present with a mental health issue.
Those who receive such downgrades cannot go overseas and, in some circumstances, are removed from the organisation, he said.
Though he was not asking to “abolish” the system, he said restrictions should be proportionate, periodically reviewed and linked to recovery.
During a separate session on Thursday, Defence Forces deputy chief of staff support Colm Ó Luasa was asked by Independent Senator Tom Clonan, a former Defence Forces member, about the findings.
Ó Luasa said stigma was “not a Defence Forces issue” but a “societal issue”.
[ Minister wants role for Irish Navy in EU mission targeting Russia shadow fleet Opens in new window ]
“We’re doing a lot of work towards stigma reduction within the Defence Forces,” he added, saying the need to reduce stigma was not “unique to us”.
Asked by Clonan if he believed the 94 per cent figure was representative of the general population, Ó Luasa said: “I don’t recognise that figure. It’s not my experience,” adding that he did not “recognise that level of reluctance”.
“It’s not bearing recognition in terms of our experience as an organisation,” he said.
Ó Luasa said the Defence Forces delivers training and education in mental health that is based on “internationally-recognised best practice”.
“I think it’s important [to] point out here that we recognise the issue of stigma and we continue to work to reduce that stigma,” he said.
[ Defence Forces officers earning as little as €4 an hour for working overtime Opens in new window ]
David Lyons, officer in charge of the Defence Forces personnel support services, told the committee he had made contact with Fitzpatrick about the research, saying there was information that was “useful and could inform future policy”.
Separately, Dr Iseult Coolahan, head of clinical delivery, said the purpose of medical classification was “not punitive” but to allow the Defence Forces to “keep functioning, but also allow that person time to heal”.
“The vast majority do not end up being downgraded and losing their jobs,” she said.

title: Tour de France 2027 routes revealed with British stages, time-trials and a volcano
description: Next summer’s men’s and women’s race will start in Edinburgh and Yorkshire respectively
content:
The most ambitious Grand Départ in the long history of the Tour de France was unveiled in Paris on Thursday as race organisers fleshed out the details of next summer’s men’s and women’s race starts in Edinburgh and Yorkshire.
Over six days of racing, Scotland, England’s Lake District and Peak District, Lancashire and Yorkshire, Wales and central London will be taken over by the snaking race caravan on a route that is expected to lure millions to the roadside.
Christian Prudhomme, the men’s Tour director, said he expected “a warm and massive welcome for the champions”. “From the start at the foot of Edinburgh Castle – the northernmost in the history of the Tour – to a team time trial in London, Great Britain offers us a symbol that further ties the two races together,” he said.
The sports minister, Stephanie Peacock, confirmed that £65m (€78m) has been allocated to fund the six stages and said the Tour’s visit would “shine a spotlight on women’s cycling like never before”.
The men’s race starts in Edinburgh on July 2nd and finishes in Paris on July 25th, with a final stage that maintains the tradition of racing up and over the cobbled streets of Montmartre.
Paul Bush, managing director of Grand Depart GB, has big ambitions of his own for the race. “One of my aspirations will be to turn the UK yellow next year, for two weeks, so everybody is in yellow,” Bush said. “Now that would be pretty special.
“Now that would beat 2014. Not that I’m looking to beat 2014, because it’s not a competition. But if we could encourage everybody, workplaces, communities, old age pensioners’ homes, schools, everything to become yellow, I think that would really embrace the thing.”
In fact, the men’s Tour will begin and end on cobblestones. From the Royal Mile to the Champs-Élysées, the peloton will cover 3,479km of racing and take in two individual time trials, three summit finishes and a denouement in the climbs of the Pyrenees.
The first British stage, from Edinburgh to Carlisle, will head through Midlothian and the Borders, while stage two, from Keswick to Liverpool, will cover 223km and take in Lancashire’s Trough of Bowland before finishing on Liverpool’s waterfront.
After the transfer across the Channel, the peloton races across central France, from Cherbourg to the Jura, for the first summit finish on the Grand Colombier, followed by mountain stages to Sallanches and Les Saisies.
From the Rhone Valley, where the furnace conditions that characterised this year’s race are likely to return, the convoy heads into the Cévennes and the Tarn for finishes in Mende and Albi.
The second time trial is centred on Toulouse and comes before two brutal Pyrenean stages, the first crossing the fearsome Col du Tourmalet before a finish on the Col du Portet, and the second, to Laruns, taking in four major ascents and almost 4,500 metres of climbing.
The Tour de France Femmes begin in Leeds on July 30th, 13 years after the men’s race staged its 2014 Grand Départ, with an opening stage from the Headrow to a likely sprint finish on Deansgate in Manchester.
The next day’s challenge, from Manchester to Sheffield, includes both Winnat’s and Snake Pass on a route which features almost 3,000 metres of climbing and which race director, Marion Rousse, saw as the cornerstone of “the hardest opening in the history of the women’s race”.
But the showpiece stage will be in central London, with an 18km team time trial, routed from Westminster to The Mall, taking in Tower Bridge, St Paul’s Cathedral, Trafalgar Square and Buckingham Palace.
London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, said the Tour’s visit would “not only cement London’s status as the undisputed capital of women’s sport, but also inspire more people to take up cycling, as we build a better, greener London for everyone.”
After the transfer to northern France, the women’s peloton heads south, via Calais, Magnanville and Bourges to a first mountain finish at La Loge des Gardes, before a hilly penultimate stage through the Auvergne to Clermont-Ferrand. The nine-day race climaxes on the steep volcanic Puy de Dome, after a stage that includes almost four thousand metres of climbing.
Both routes were unveiled at Porte Maillot even as curfews remained in place in some parts of central Paris, including Place de la République and Les Halles. The French media described the nation as sinking “deeper into crisis”, but in the aftermath of the Covid pandemic and the controversies of climate change, the Tour has become well-versed in facing down adversity and threats.
However, disruption, due to both civil unrest and extreme temperatures, remains possible. Race organisers ASO faced a similar situation in July 2023, when climate activists and rioting threatened the race. That year, Prudhomme said the Tour was “in constant liaison with the state” and would “adapt if needed”. – Guardian

title: Department not capable of ‘great conspiracy’ to oust Labour Court member, official says
description: Unfair dismissal and other employment rights breaches are being claimed
content:
A senior civil servant has said the Department of Enterprise could not mount the “great conspiracy” she said had been alleged by a former Labour Court member to oust him from his seat.
“I have to be honest with you, we’re not that good in the State,” the official told the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).
Tara Coogan, the former head of the department’s industrial relations unit, was giving evidence for a second day on claims of unfair dismissal and other employment rights breaches by Peter DR Murphy, a former business group Ibec nominee to the court.
Coogan told the WRC she felt “unwell” at the suggestion that Murphy was not reappointed because of any connection with a complaint he made against a former Labour Court chairman.
Lawyers acting for Murphy say that when plans emerged to cut back the court, a redundancy situation arose and he was let go with “absolutely no selection process”.
The State says Ibec just didn’t nominate Murphy.
On Monday, the State was directed to produce more documents related to Murphy’s engagements as a Labour Court member between 2005 and 2024, and correspondence coming up to the expiry of his last warrant.
One of the records, a letter dated December 15th, 2023, from then-minister of State at the Department of Enterprise Neale Richmond to Danny McCoy , the head of Ibec, was opened to the WRC on Tuesday.
The letter stated that the minister had received “an analysis by the chairman of the court” to the effect that it had “sufficient resources”.
“It is my intention to suppress the fourth division of the court, reducing the number of divisions from four to three,” the letter continued.
Coogan denied that a redundancy situation had arisen on the Labour Court at the time.
“There is no such thing as a redundancy in the public sector. People move around. If there are vacancies in the system, people aren’t always put in,” she said.
“At this time, Ibec would have confirmed to the department that Murphy was not looking for reappointment,” she went on to say.
She admitted that there was no correspondence stating this.
“There was a lot of meetings in relation to this matter,” Coogan said. “We were informed, and this is orally,” she went on to say.
Lowey said it was hearsay and that his client disputed the assertion.
Coogan said it was relayed to her by an assistant secretary at the department that “Ibec had informed him that Murphy was not seeking reappointment”.
Lowey said the State had produced an “entirely new line of argument that’s not included in any of their three submissions” after being compelled to provide the previously undisclosed 15 December 2023 letter to the WRC.
“It’s grossly unfair, and I’m running out of superlatives to describe the State’s approach to this. It’s outrageous,” he added.
Frances Meenan, for the State, said: “Ibec did not nominate the claimant for reappointment in 2023, it’s as simple as that ... there is absolutely nothing new.”
Under cross-examination, Coogan confirmed that the Labour Court chairman who gave the workflow analysis to Richmond was Kevin Foley.
She denied Foley was involved in the decision to suppress the fourth division of the court, which was a “departmental decision in consultation with the social partners”, she said.
Lowey put it to her that it seemed “arbitrary” that of the two Ibec-nominated warrants set to come to an end in February 2024, the department had sought nominations for only one – the one not held by his client.
Lowey then put it to her that it was “completely and utterly unreasonable” not to think Ibec would not favour the incumbent in the other role for nomination.
Coogan said Ibec could have nominated Murphy, but the department was “of the view Murphy was not seeking reappointment”.
“When you bring in other matters, it all of a sudden looks like a great conspiracy, but I have to be honest with you, we’re not that good in the State,” Coogan said. “I wouldn’t participate in such a process,” she added.
She confirmed that she was denying that a redundancy situation arose when the court was cut from four divisions to three.
Lowey referred Coogan to a letter from the department’s former head of human resources, Denise Kennedy, on July 31st, 2020.
“My client is being informed by the department that an investigation is going to take place into his bullying and harassment complaint,” Lowey said.
“Can you please confirm for me this letter ... confirms that the parties, having sought to resolve matters, ultimately didn’t and that an investigator would conduct an investigation into his complaint?” Lowey said.
Coogan confirmed the letter stated this but said the department’s current HR chief, Pat Phelan, would be in a better position to give evidence on it: “Things like this, I wouldn’t be aware of them,” she said.
Meenan said the complaint was withdrawn by Murphy. Lowey said this was accepted.
Lowey then put it to her that on the same date, July 31st, 2022, the department had for the first time written to Ibec asking it “not to reappoint [Murphy] but to make three nominations”.
“Isn’t it straining credibility to think these matters aren’t related?” counsel asked.
“That’s absolutely the most ridiculous statement I’ve heard,” Coogan said. She said she knew “nothing” about the complaint. “That assertion is actually making me feel a bit unwell,” she added.
Coogan accepted she was aware of High Court proceedings brought by Murphy in which he secured leave for judicial review of the decision not to reappoint him on October 30th, 2020.
An email confirming a new warrant issued “an hour and 20 minutes” after the High Court ruling, Lowey said.
“Is that a coincidence as well?” he asked Coogan.
Coogan said it would be to ascribe “a remarkable efficiency” to the department to suggest “we would be able to draft warrants and have everything ready at the drop of a hat”.
“We’re not as efficient as that,” she said.
Lowey is instructed by McInnes Dunne Murphy for the complainant, Meehan by the Chief State Solicitor’s Office .

title: Prosecutors seek 11-year sentence for John Gilligan if convicted of Spanish charges
description: Previously released footage shows the moment armed officers used battering rams to smash into his Costa Blanca property
content:
Convicted criminal John Gilligan has been warned he faces more than 11 years in prison over drugs and a gun found at his Costa Blanca home in Spain .
The veteran Irish criminal spent more than eight months behind bars following his December 2024 arrest before paying €10,000 bail to leave jail in August last year.
Public prosecutors confirmed overnight they were pushing for a custodial sentence totalling 11 years and three months after Gilligan was charged with three crimes.
In an indictment submitted to a court in Elche near Torrevieja, where the 74-year-old from Dublin faces trial, prosecutors revealed they were demanding an eight-year jail term for the drugs trafficking charge, nine months for belonging to a criminal gang and two years and six months for illegal weapons possession.
The drugs found in the property, which were subsequently sent off for analysis, were also revealed: ketamine, cocaine and marijuana worth nearly €5,000.
Gilligan is set to be put in the dock along with two brothers from North Macedonia who were among the other eight people arrested by police in high-profile raids that led to detectives saying at the time they had held a “man belonging to the Irish mafia”.
Spanish police went public in January last year with the first images of the “drug lab” that led to Gilligan’s December 18th, 2024, arrest and subsequent remand in prison after appearing before a judge.
They released footage showing the moment heavily armed officers used battering rams to smash into the Costa Blanca property where they held the Irish man – as well as the moment they found the revolver wrapped in plastic inside a hideaway on an outside wall.
Public prosecutors say in their indictment, which omits some personal details because of data protection laws: “The defendants, for an unspecified period of time, but in any event prior to December 18th, 2024, conspired to manufacture narcotic substances at the property situated at [redacted] with the aim of obtaining successive and significant quantities of narcotic substances for subsequent sale.
[ Law Society seeks to meet O’Callaghan ‘in person’ to solve legal aid payments impasse Opens in new window ]
“This laboratory was supervised by the defendant, as the property was his own and served as his usual place of residence.
“It was frequented by the other defendants, who were responsible for bringing the necessary materials to the premises for the manufacture and facilitation of the handling and distribution of the narcotic substance.”
The property was also used for “storing the substances, with the profits derived from the sale of the substance subsequently being shared amongst them all”, the documents state.
“Prior to the aforementioned date, acting jointly and in concert, and with the intention of making a financial profit, the defendants possessed at their various addresses illicit substances, in particular, tusi, ketamine, cocaine and cannabis, for their subsequent distribution and sale to third parties, as well as products, equipment and instruments used by them for the manufacture of those substances and their distribution.”
Gilligan was in bed when his home was raided at 5.48am, the documents show. Of the weapon found, public prosecutors said: “A firearm, a six-calibre pistol, model 1938, was also seized at the property.
“This has been the subject of an expert report, which determined it to be a Mondial revolver, model 1938, in 6mm Flobert calibre, with no visible serial number.
“It is in a normal state of repair and functions correctly. It was originally a 7.4 regulated firearm, but as the barrel had been modified and it is capable of firing conventional cartridges containing bullets, it is now classified as a prohibited firearm.
“A firearms licence and a certificate of ownership are required for its possession and use, neither of which the defendant possessed.”
[ Convicted gang rapists say trial was prejudiced by allowing woman to give evidence behind screen Opens in new window ]
A BMW X5 believed to belong to Gilligan’s British ex-partner Sharon Oliver was also seized.
As well as the prison sentence, prosecutors want Gilligan fined €120,000 if convicted as charged. No trial date has yet been scheduled.
The gun found in the pensioner’s back garden during his 2020 arrest was initially linked to Irish journalist Veronica Guerin’s 1996 murder, of which he was acquitted.
The gun used to shoot her by one of two men on a motorbike was never found.

title: Mark Duffy’s Axis to ask court to delay ratifying Bawag’s PTSB takeover
description: Company seeking to put together 11th-hour bid
content:
Axis Capital, a corporate advisory firm cofounded by former banker Mark Duffy, said on Thursday it will ask the High Court next week to delay ratifying PTSB’s takeover by Austrian lender Bawag as it seeks to put together an 11 th -hour rival bid.
Axis said it will seek an adjournment of up to six weeks of the sanctioning hearing, scheduled for October 27 th .
The company said that investment bank Keefe, Bruyette & Woods (KBW) has introduced it to a “large global investment manager”, which is weighing acting as lead investor in the financing of a potential bid.
“The possible funder is evaluating acting as lead anchor investor in the financing of a possible offer, with the balance of the capital to be syndicated to its limited partners and other co-investors,” it said.
KBW has not been engaged by either side. Axis is advised by Berlin-based Quirin Privatbank. Duffy was the chief executive of now-defunct Bank of Scotland (Ireland) .
“The possible funder has indicated that completing its confirmatory due diligence is essential before it can syndicate the balance of the capital to its partners and provide a formal letter of support,” Axis said.
[ Bawag ‘rising above the noise’ as it eyes completing PTSB deal, CEO says Opens in new window ]
“It estimates that it requires four to six weeks from access to the due diligence information to complete that work and seek the necessary internal approvals.”
PTSB, which is 57.5 per cent State owned, has not met Axis or provided access to information to carry out due diligence, Axis said.
The chief executive of Bawag said earlier this week the Austrian banking group is “rising above the noise” as it awaits High Court approval of its takeover of PTSB later this month.
Scotchstone, led by Piotr Skoczylas, is a long-time dissenting PTSB shareholder that has pursued a series of cases in the Irish courts stemming from PTSB’s effective nationalisation in 2011. It also signalled on October 9th that it was considering making an offer for PTSB.

title: Rail IT contract awarded to firm that did not own intellectual property, Minister says
description: Darragh O’Brien says procurement issues around the Irish Rail project are now being addressed ‘very seriously’
content:
The contract for developing the now-scrapped IT programme to manage trains across the rail network was awarded to a company that had never previously delivered such a system and did not own the intellectual property involved, Minister for Transport Darragh O’Brien has said.
“That was crazy,” he told the Oireachtas Transport Committee at a hearing on Thursday.
The Minister said that the procurement arrangements for the information technology programme – known as a traffic management system – was fundamentally where the problems began.
On July 17th last, Irish Rail terminated the contract with Spanish technology company Indra for developing the traffic management system. The project was several years behind schedule and had run significantly over budget.
The State-owned rail company had earlier written down by €50 million the value of its investment in an overall new national train control centre, largely due to problems associated with the traffic management system.
The chairman of the Oireachtas Transport Committee, Michael Murphy of Fine Gael, asked the Minister whether in light of the experience of the traffic management system he had confidence in governance arrangements at Irish Rail.
“Would you commit to a review of the governance structures? Surely this raises serious questions about oversight in Irish Rail and serious questions for the National Transport Authority as well,” Murphy said.
O’Brien replied: “I would agree with you. And that is part of our work programme.
“The IT system, I think it goes back to the awarding of the contract. It appears to me ...it was awarded to a company that had not delivered a system and did not own the IP (intellectual property). That is crazy. I think the procurement was fundamentally where the issue was. And that is being addressed very seriously. I take my responsibilities in managing the people’s money for investment [seriously] and this will be dealt with.”
The Minister said he was waiting for advice from the National Transport Authority on how to proceed.
“This project is needed for efficiency across our train services,” he said.
O’Brien said he was “comfortable with the governance arrangements in place right now”. However, he said there were “absolute learnings that have to be made”.
The Minister said there were no issues with another large-scale technology project being developed by Indra, the new contactless system for buying tickets for buses, rail and Luas.
Indra, in a statement to The Irish Times earlier this week, said its traffic management system had been successfully deployed and was “operating in countries including Spain, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Lithuania, all of which have repeatedly expressed confidence in Indra’s technology”.
“The system contributes to safer, more efficient and increasingly digitalised railway operations. Indra Group is also implementing its traffic management system technology in Estonia as part of the modernisation of the country’s rail network.”
Indra, previously, had blamed Irish Rail for how it has handled the project. It said the State company had relied too heavily on external advisers.
Indra also said that critical knowledge about the unique characteristics and limitations of the Irish Rail network had neither been comprehensively documented nor systematically shared with the project team. It said key Irish Rail personnel who would use the planned system had not been actively involved in the project until its fifth year.

title: Storm Austen: Orange warnings issued as Ireland braces for torrential rain and wind
description: Warnings of possible transport and power disruptions, with ‘blustery’ conditions for Dublin marathon runners
content:
Emergency co-ordinators are planning daily meetings through the weekend as a double dose of storms approaches Ireland.
Storm Austen, due to hit Ireland early on Thursday evening and continue through Friday morning, is expected to be quickly followed by Storm Boelo on Saturday.
The latter is forecast to coincide with high tides, increasing the risk of flooding from high waves and storm surges, particularly along the west and northwest coasts.
“With two weather events now expected, local response teams will be very busy throughout the bank holiday weekend,” said Keith Leonard, head of the National Directorate for Fire and Emergency Management.
“The National Severe Weather and Flood Coordination Group will meet daily throughout the next few days to ensure the most effective response to any developments arising from the challenging weather conditions.”
The Irish Coast Guard, Water Safety Ireland and the RNLI have issued a joint appeal to the public to take extra care around coastlines and inland waterways over the next few days.
They have asked swimmers to avoid the water during the storms and to take extra precautions as the week goes on and daylight hours get progressively shorter.
ESB Networks has warned of possible electricity outages overnight as the first big storm of the season approaches Ireland.
Met Éireann has issued a number of status-orange weather warnings for intense rain and wind from around 7pm Thursday evening, continuing into Friday morning.
The progress of Storm Boelo is being closely monitored and more detailed warnings are due to issue tomorrow.
ESB Networks urged householders and businesses to “take necessary precautions” for Storm Austen.
“Prepare for possible power outages by having essential supplies on hand,” it warned.
It advised having a torch, battery operated radio, extra batteries and a fully charged phone on hand.
During or after the storm, it also warned people never to touch or approach any electricity wires that may have blown down.
Bus Éireann is also advising passengers of possible disruption to services.
“Met Éireann is forecasting difficult driving conditions as strong winds and heavy rain cross the country from this evening, and into the weekend as well,” said chief customer officer Allen Parker.
“There are also warnings about the possibility of flooding, debris and fallen trees on the roads.
“All Bus Éireann services are scheduled to operate as normal, however if any are impacted by the stormy weather, we will post details online as quickly as possible to keep our customers informed.”
Storm Austen is due to hit Ireland early on Thursday evening.
A status-yellow warning for Leinster and Munster for rain and wind will come into effect at 7pm on Thursday and be in place until 10am on Friday.
Counties Waterford, Cork and Kerry will have an orange warning for rain in place from 10pm on Thursday until 5am on Friday.
This warning will be extended to Dublin, Wexford and Wicklow from 2am on Friday until 8am.
People have been warned of flooding, disruption to public transport and difficult travel conditions. Outdoor events may be affected and people have been advised to be alert to debris and fallen trees or branches during the storm.
Weather conditions for the Dublin city marathon on Sunday are going to be blustery, Met Éireann meteorologist Gerry Murphy warned.
He said it is going to be wet “everywhere” in the country on Thursday as rain spreads northwards.
Local authority employees and other union members engaged in industrial action will work as required to deal with the impact of the storm.
Fórsa and Siptu , the two largest unions involved in work-to-rules as part of the public sector pay dispute, confirmed there were specific clauses for automatic derogations from industrial action in cases where there was a serious threat posed to life or wellbeing. Where derogations need to be requested, they are almost always granted immediately.
Dublin City Council said its flood response team was “preparing for the potential impacts of heavy rainfall across the city and has put measures in place to respond quickly should localised flooding occur”.
Storm Austen is the first named storm of the 2026/2027 season.
[ Government wants HSE to cap hospital parking fee at €10 a day Opens in new window ]
The name Austen was chosen by Met Éireann in tribute to Austen H Nagle, who became the first director of the Irish Meteorological Service when he was appointed in 1936.

title: Law Society seeks to meet O’Callaghan ‘in person’ to solve legal aid payments impasse
description: Minister for Justice offers talks to hear Law Society’s viewpoint as four-month withdrawal of services escalates
content:
The Law Society has urged Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan to meet its representatives “in person” with a view to resolving the dispute over a new legal aid payment model for the District Courts .
As criminal defence solicitors escalated their four-month withdrawal of services from Monday to include virtually all cases, including custody cases, O’Callaghan sent a letter to the society offering a meeting.
In a letter to the Law Society’s president, Rosemarie Loftus, O’Callaghan said he had instructed his officials to “organise a meeting in the coming days to hear your viewpoint and specific concerns”.
The dispute is over a €520 “one flat fee” payment model for legal aid work in the District Courts, irrespective of the number of court appearances or separate prosecutions involving a client. The old model provided for €240 for a first appearance and €60 for each subsequent appearance.
The Minister says the new scheme will effect necessary reform, reduce the number of adjournments of cases and address “abuses” of the system under the old scheme, particularly regarding the number of multiple legal aid certificates sought by some solicitors.
Solicitors say the model means they will not be paid for the work they do in complex cases, including involving children, people with addiction and mental health issues and regarding clients facing separate prosecutions.
A withdrawal of services by many criminal defence solicitors, under way since the new model came into operation on July 1st, has caused considerable disruption of the work of the criminal courts across all court divisions and the adjournment of thousands of cases.
[ Jim O’Callaghan reiterates claim that solicitors are targeting rape cases Opens in new window ]
In a letter on Wednesday responding to the Minister’s offer of a meeting, Loftus said the society believes the meeting “should take place without further delay and trust it will address the substance of this dispute and support a meaningful resolution of the matter”.
She said the impasse is having “a real and significant impact” on the administration of justice, noted the High Court had urged the parties to resolve it and the Chief Justice has said the continuation of the dispute is a matter of concern to him and judges generally.
Loftus said the society has been calling for years for criminal legal aid reform and has publicly expressed support for reform and in engagement with the Minister and his officials.
“Our concern has never been with reform but with ensuring any new model is practical, evidence-based and capable of protecting the constitutional rights of accused people, while remaining sustainable for those who provide publicly funded legal representation.”
The society previously set out two core issues, the addressing of which would, it believed, resolve the criminal defence solicitors’ key concerns, she said. Those concern ensuring payment for defence work in more complex cases and ones involving clients facing separate prosecutions.
In concluding her letter, Loftus asked that the Minister “attend in person” and the society would make itself available “at any time”.

title: No link between healthcare staff recruitment and hospital performance, says Minister
description: Jennifer Carroll MacNeill compares Cork to Beaumont, where fewer patients are on trolleys
content:
Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill has claimed there is no real link between healthcare staff recruitment and hospital performance.
Healthcare dominated Dáil Leaders’ Questions on Thursday, with Sinn Féin finance spokesman Pearse Doherty referring to a 21 per cent rise in the number of over-75s who have spent more than 24 hours in emergency departments this year, saying it was “shameful” and “cruel” that an elderly person “would have to go through this”.
Claiming the situation had worsened under Carroll MacNeill’s leadership, Doherty said senior managers in the health system had been unable to recruit since June due to HSE employment restrictions and were warning of risks to the safety delivery of services.
“In the Midwest alone there are 350 posts that are vacant,” he said.
The way senior managers were speaking out was “unprecedented”, he said, and they were doing so because “they’re telling us they have no other choice” and are “very, very worried”.
Carroll MacNeill said demand had increased in every area and every hospital. Giving detailed statistics about a number of hospitals, she added that “the reality is that there are some hospitals that have not improved that need to improve”.
“Tell me why is Beaumont different to Cork [University Hospital] ,” she said to Doherty. “Both of them have recruited. Both of them have the same demand pressures. Both of them have needs for the future into 2027 [which the budget] has delivered.
“But Beaumont have nine people on trolleys, whereas Cork have four. They are using things differently.”
[ More than 70,000 people left Irish emergency departments before completing treatment Opens in new window ]
She said St James’s Hospital , “one of the biggest, busiest hospitals in this country, in an area of particular socio-economic disadvantage”, has 10 people on trolleys, “but Cork has 44”.
“And bizarrely, the ones that consistently don’t improve, ie Cork, have had the highest recruitment,” with 233 people recruited, Carroll MacNeill said.
“So, if there was a correlation between recruitment and performance, I’d agree with you.”
Labour health spokeswoman Marie Sherlock said hospitals “are terrified of what’s in store this winter” as she accused the Minister and the Department of Public Expenditure of failing to properly plan the health budget.
She said Budget 2027 was based on a 2 per cent growth in demand when “actual demand” far surpasses that, with emergency department admissions up 6.75 per cent this year and a 10 per cent increase in outpatient appointments.
Sherlock said she had responses from the HSE that “they’re only forecasting demand for next year now after they get their budget allocation. No wonder the health service is in crisis. No commercial viable business will ever operate like that.”
She added it made no sense that there is an embargo on recruiting graduate nurses when agency staff payments are “surging ahead by €255 million”.

title: Why did huge swathes of the internet suddenly go offline yesterday?
description: A computer programming language supporting an estimated 70 per cent of all websites was found to have ‘critical vulnerabilities’
content:
I t caught countless website developers off guard and has left many wondering how protected their cyber systems really are.
When the team behind computer programming language PHP, which powers an estimated 70 per cent of all websites, warned on Wednesday that its software contained “critical vulnerabilities”, it sent the internet into a frenzy.
“Who is at risk: all PHP installations serving web requests,” the developers put it bluntly, but not so simply – “all installations serving web requests” means, in layman’s terms, a website that you can click on.
Users were advised to update immediately or take their sites offline to avoid a cyberattack. While the vulnerability was largely contained within 24 hours of being identified, the fright it has caused will not be easily forgotten.
“It’s essentially a framework that websites run on,” says Martin Potgieter, the chief technology officer for the South African arm of Integrity 360, a Dublin-based cybersecurity consultancy firm.
[ Revolut’s outage was a warning to us all Opens in new window ]
While it’s difficult to say just how many websites run on it, estimates hover around 70 per cent. “A large number of websites on the internet are using it,” Potgieter says.
“It’s an open source code, that’s why it’s so extensively used,” he adds. “Many people might say ‘oh, well, it’s an open source code so that’s why it’s insecure’, but that’s not really the case – it doesn’t make it less secure, just more available.”
“A flaw was found in the software that renders the websites using PHP vulnerable to an attack,” Potgieter says. “Once that flaw was discovered, it’s essentially a race between the PHP developers trying to create a patch quicker than news can get out and the details to exploit that vulnerability get out to the world.”
[ ‘Critical vulnerabilities’ found in computer code supporting up to 70% of internet Opens in new window ]
A “patch” is a corrective measure used to eliminate errors or issues within codes. “It’s very similar to when you get a little notification on your laptop that says Microsoft needs to do updates,” Potgieter goes on. “It’s essentially a change to the code that renders the vulnerability inoperable.”
“Many people were advising to switch off your website, if you can’t patch it, because patching does take time,” he says.
And thus, countless websites suddenly went offline for fear of a cyberattack. You couldn’t read an article from the Journal, you couldn’t buy a screwdriver from Woodie’s DIY and you couldn’t even access the Finnish government’s land registry records.
“If a hacker successfully exploits the vulnerability, they can take control of that system and do what they want with it. That’s obviously high risk – they could take information off of the system or use it for another attack,” he adds.
“There were reports of attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities ... I’m not sure if there’s any verified reports that they were successful – but it’s only a matter of time,” he says. If successful, hackers could control website operations or harvest users’ data, among other actions.
[ More than half of Irish business leaders worried over ‘sophisticated cyber attacks’ by AI Opens in new window ]
Brian Honan, a cybersecurity expert and chief executive of BH Consulting, says “it’s not rare for a big vulnerability to be found in a piece of software, but I think the impact of this vulnerability will be a surprise due to the fact that the software is used so widely”.
“The vulnerabilities are of a very high severity and would actually enable a potential attacker to remotely control and manage a website to do what they want with it,” he adds.
“The impact of this is huge,” Honan says, “there are websites that are liable to be taken over.”
Honan says “there’s continuous research by security professionals worldwide into looking for weaknesses in software so that they can go back to vendors and recommend to them how to improve the software and make the platforms more secure”.
“With the advent of AI [ artificial intelligence ] platforms and tools, that makes the research much more scalable and, in some ways, easier to carry out. Researchers can find more vulnerabilities than they could beforehand thanks to AI.”
OpenAI , the force behind ChatGPT, was quick to take credit. “We led a coalition of maintainers, researchers and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP,” the company said in a statement on Tuesday.
“Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory,” OpenAI said.
But Potgieter is less convinced. “Sometimes, these AI labs take credit for AI being used as part of this research, but in many cases, it wouldn’t be possible without humans either starting the process or guiding the AI through it.”

title: Seán Rooney preliminary inquest hearings private ‘to protect safety of Defence Forces’
description: Several hearings held ‘in camera’ in advance of  inquest next month
content:
Hearings being held in advance of the inquest into the death of Irish soldier Pte Seán Rooney are being held in camera to protect the safety of members of the Defence Forces , the Dublin District Coroner’s Court has heard.
Rooney (24) was killed in an attack on a convoy of Irish peacekeepers on a United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon ( Unifil ) deployment on December 14th, 2022. His inquest is due to begin on November 17th and expected to last about three weeks.
A number of preliminary hearings have taken place at the coroner’s court in recent months that were held largely or fully in camera, meaning the media could not attend.
On behalf of The Irish Times, Matthew Austin, instructed by Hayes Solicitors, made a submission querying why these hearings were held in private.
Coroner Dr Myra Cullinane on Thursday said certain hearings were held in camera “to deal with sensitive issues where it was understood that public broadcast of those issues was not in the interest of the safety of the Defence Forces”.
Hearings in April, May, June, July and three in October, including Thursday’s hearing, were held partially or fully in camera.
Cullinane said this was necessary as the various parties tried to reach agreement “on what would be heard at the inquest proper in public and where it might still be necessary ... to hear certain elements [in camera]”.
The next preliminary hearing in the case is due to take place on November 6th.
Cullinane said she hoped “final matters around sensitive issues” and practical arrangements for the full inquest could be made on this date.
She said two witnesses due to give evidence at the inquest might need to be anonymous, so the manner in which evidence would be given and questioned needed to be finalised.
The Defence Forces previously argued that “extremely sensitive” information being made public during the inquest would elevate operational risks to personnel deployed to the Unifil mission , which is due to wind down in the coming months.
At a hearing in July, that was partially in camera, it was confirmed Rooney’s family was seeking to address the “conduct” of the military and Garda investigations into his death .
Rooney, who was from Newtowncunningham, Co Donegal, was killed when his armoured vehicle was ambushed as it drove north through Al-Aqbiya, a town controlled by the militant group Hizbullah.

title: Government rows back on promise to hold tribunal into scoliosis and spinal surgery scandal
description: Issues include unauthorised springs implanted in children, alleged waiting list irregularities and unnecessary hip surgeries
content:
The Government previously told advocacy groups it would hold a tribunal of inquiry into the scoliosis and spinal surgery scandal , but rowed back on it last month, documents show.
The Government announced last month the statutory inquiry into spina bifida and scoliosis services would be a commission of investigation, which means it would be largely conducted in private.
However, last year, Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill, Tánaiste Simon Harris , Department of Health officials and advocacy groups held a meeting following a number of controversies at Children’s Health Ireland (CHI).
These included unauthorised implantation of springs in children with scoliosis, alleged waiting list irregularities and unnecessary hip surgeries.
Advocacy groups met policymakers on a number of occasions last year to call for the inquiry, which got significant public attention following the death of nine-year-old Harvey Morrison Sherratt , who had scoliosis and other health issues.
