Minutes of the November 12th meeting, published by the Spina Bifida and Hydrocephalus Paediatric Advocacy Group, show Carroll MacNeill and Harris had “no settled view of the form that the inquiry would take”.
However, intensive discussions continued and, by the end of the meeting, Carroll MacNeill said the “interests of children is paramount”.
“She then stated that she would bring a memo to Government informing them of her intention to establish a statutory public inquiry, that would be, in principle, a tribunal of inquiry,” minutes of the meeting state.
[ ‘Great frustration’ only 19 children treated abroad for spinal surgeries, Dáil hears Opens in new window ]
“She would also appoint a mediator to discuss terms of reference, and that this will have the interests of children paramount. She would then sigh off on the terms of reference. She intends to bring this to Cabinet next week.”
The meeting minutes note that it was agreed a mediator would be agreed by both sides.
Advocacy groups have repeatedly called for the inquiry to take the form of a tribunal, which would be held in public.
However, following the announcement, the Government appointed senior counsel Remy Farrell to lead a scoping exercise for the inquiry.
Last month, he recommended a commission of investigation taken place, and that the inquiry would examine the period from January 1st, 2019, to December 31st last.
It should be divided into four distinct “modules”, the report said: waiting lists, spinal surgery, hip dysplasia and the Crumlin orphans.
A statement from the advocacy group said: “At no point during today’s Dáil statements did the Minister explain why she departed from the pathway agreed with families on 12 November 2025. She had an opportunity to explain that decision, acknowledge the breakdown in trust and bring families with her. She did not take it.
“We are now calling for an independent mediator, agreed by both sides, to be appointed so that meaningful engagement can begin again. Families have spent years fighting for answers. They should not have to fight the Government for a credible inquiry into the harm their children have experienced.”
Speaking in the Dáil on Thursday, Sinn Féin’s health spokesman David Cullinane said the record of a meeting in November last year with groups representing affected families, showed the Minister “intended to bring forward a statutory public inquiry, which would in principle be a tribunal of inquiry”.
He said agreement was reached that a mediator would work on the terms reference and the minutes also state it was accepted the mediator would “be agreed by both sides”.
There was also discussion about an independent clinical expert not connected to CHI, he said but “the families and advocacy group say the facilitator was not agreed with them and the independent clinical expert discussed at the meeting was not appointed”.
He told the Minister “the families say that the further meaningful engagement they expected never happened”.
The Waterford TD said “what is missing here is a requirement for transparent public giving of evidence”.
While some parents may be able to give evidence publicly “what is missing” is that senior decision makers and people under scrutiny for their actions “will not be required to account for account for themselves in the same public way”.
“That’s a real difficulty. If the inquiry is to rebuild trust that can be no hiding places for anybody,” he insisted.
Social Democrats health spokesman Pádraig Rice called on the Minister to appoint a mediator “as there clearly is an impasse”.
The advocacy groups wrote to both the Taoiseach and Tánaiste and want a “constructive way forward and the appointment of a mutually agreed mediator to resolve the impasse between Government and the families” and restore confidence in the process, he said.
Chairman of the Oireachtas Health committee, he urged the Minister to heed that call and appoint a mediator and said “it’s not too late”.
There is a “real strong difference of opinion” between families and the Minister, he said, and “the families and children affected deserve the best inquiry possible”.
In response, the minister said she was “aware of calls for a tribunal of inquiry as opposed to a commission of investigation”.
However, the scoping process found “a commission can deliver the same statutory powers as a tribunal” and “there was a significant risk in his view that children may be identifiable, even where anonymised”.

title: Heated exchanges at Yves Sakila inquest after solicitor questions Garda investigation
description: Congolese man died from cardiorespiratory arrest after period of restraint with a number of contributory factors, court hears
content:
There were heated exchanges at Dublin District Coroner’s Court on Thursday when a solicitor representing the stepmother of Yves Sakila raised concerns about elements of the Garda investigation into the Congolese man’s death in Dublin in May .
Solicitor John Gerard Cullen, representing Angel Issemezey Anzibi, questioned if it was appropriate that gardaí from Store Street Garda station were involved in helping to oversee the investigation as officers from the station allegedly handcuffed Sakila shortly before his death.
Coroner Dr Myra Cullinane took exception to this remark, saying the purpose of the hearing was to confirm Sakila’s identity and cause of death. She said the inquest then needed to be adjourned so as not to prejudice ongoing investigations by An Garda Síochána and Fíosrú.
Cullinane accused Cullen of being “aggressive” and said he had “raised the temperature”; a charge he denied. The coroner said she did not wish for her court to descend into argument, as this would be “extremely disrespectful” to the deceased and his loved ones.
Sakila (34) was suspected of stealing a bottle of perfume from Arnotts department store on Dublin’s Henry Street on May 15th and was pursued by security personnel . When gardaí arrived on the scene, Sakila had been held on the ground by a group of security guards for a period, it was reported.
Gardaí handcuffed Sakila but removed them when they realised he was unwell, and began performing CPR, according to reports. Sakila was taken to the Mater hospital where he was later pronounced dead.
State Pathologist Dr SallyAnne Collis carried out a postmortem on Sakila on May 16th, the inquest heard. His cause of death was listed as cardiorespiratory arrest (a sudden cessation of both heart and lung function) following a period of prone restraint.
Collis’s report said mixed drug intoxication and raised body mass index may have played a role in his death, while schizophrenia was listed as a contributory factor.
[ Congolese community mourns and calls for justice at vigil after Henry Street death Opens in new window ]
Anzibi, who was married to Sakila’s uncle, was not present in court but a statement was read out on her behalf. It said she and Sakila moved from Congo to Ireland in 2004, joining her then-husband via the family reunification programme.
The court heard that although Anzibi was technically Sakila’s step-aunt, she referred to herself as his stepmother and her children referred to him as their brother.
Anzibi’s statement referenced the fact that both of Sakila’s parents were deceased. However, the court heard his biological mother is alive and still living in Congo.
Solicitor Albert Llussà appeared on behalf of Janet Sakila, Sakila’s biological mother, saying she “is very much alive” and wished to be recognised as his next of kin.
Llussà said he could provide her birth certificate and other documents to prove she was alive. Cullinane welcomed this, saying the documents could be used to correct the record.
The court heard Sakila’s family members had not agreed burial arrangements. Cullinane said it would be “very desirable if an agreement could be reached regarding the manner in which Yves’s remains could be deposed”.
Det Insp Ken Hoare from Store Street Garda station sought the adjournment of the inquest so that the separate investigations being carried out by the Garda and Fiosrú could continue.
Cullinane granted a six-month adjournment, though this is likely to be extended. She said the inquest may or may not be reopened, pending the outcome of the two investigations. If it is reopened, she said this is not likely to happen for “a significant period of time”.
The case is next due to be mentioned on April 21st, 2027.

title: Central Bank inquiry made ‘fundamental errors’ in former PTSB chief tracker mortgage case
description: David Guinane wins tribunal appeal against Central Bank sanctioning of him for his role
content:
A tribunal has confirmed that former PTSB chief executive David Guinane has won an appeal against a Central Bank of Ireland inquiry sanctioning him for a role played in the State’s tracker mortgage scandal .
The Irish Financial Services Appeals Tribunal (Ifsat) said that the sole inquiry member, Peter Hinchliffe, made errors of law that were so fundamental that they negated his decision last year that Guinane be fined €80,000 and reprimanded.
The tribunal concluded in a decision published on Thursday that Hinchliffe “erred in law”, acted beyond what was established by case law elsewhere, “failed to give fair notice of certain issues”, and “failed to give reasons for his decision”.
“Moreover, it held that the errors of law in the inquiry decision were manifest from the text and were fundamental so as to deprive the decision of its basis,” said the tribunal, chaired by chaired by former Supreme Court judge John MacMenamin.
Its conclusion still needs to be confirmed by the High Court. The Central Bank said it does not plan to appeal it.
The Irish Times first reported on the conclusion of the appeal last month.
[ Former PTSB chief wins appeal over tracker mortgage sanction Opens in new window ]
“This deeply flawed process, which has cost millions in taxpayer funds, has had a profound effect on my family and on my career,” said Guinane in a statement on Thursday afternoon.
“With this now-discredited allegation, the Central Bank tried to single me out as a scapegoat. It is extraordinary that I was the only individual to be subject to a formal inquiry in respect of the tracker issue.”
Ifsat said that the Central Bank should pay Guinane’s legal costs for the inquiry and appeal, including his €5,000 appeal fee.
It rejected an application by PTSB, a notice party in the case, for costs. PTSB paid a €21 million fine in 2019 for its role in the industry-wide tracker mortgage scandal.
Hinchliffe emphasised last year there was “no finding of dishonesty against Mr Guinane” and that he “did not form an intention to harm or take advantage of customers”. Guinane was also entitled to receive better support from within the wider Irish Life & Permanent Group, of which PTSB was a part at the time, he added.
The inquiry centred on a special condition in some PTSB tracker mortgages offered during the pre-crash property boom. This required customers who moved for a period to a fixed rate to instruct the bank afterwards to put them back on a tracker rate or another fixed product. Otherwise, they would default to a standard variable rate.
The ambiguous wording of the condition led to questions in early 2009 about whether a customer opting to go back on to a tracker rate was entitled to their original margin over the European Central Bank rate, or a higher margin then on offer from PTSB.
The bank adopted a strategy in January 2009, on the basis of legal advice, to only put customers who requested the original rate – or complained – on the more favourable rate. The Central Bank said Guinane signed off on the strategy when he responded to the plan, when advanced by a colleague via email in January 2009, with the words, “okay to that”.
Guinane testified during an inquiry hearing in early 2024 that while he did not remember events surrounding the decision, he understood the email to mean – based on having reviewed documents – that “any customer” coming out of the fixed rate would “go back to their original rate”. The email only contained a summary of the legal advice.
The grounds for the Central Bank’s decision to hold the inquiry were that Guinane knew and understood the strategy.
However, Ifsat said Hinchliffe reframed the allegation by removing “those critical elements of knowledge and approval”.
Instead, Hinchliffe criticised Guinane’s “failure” to ask certain questions, to make follow-up enquiries, or to take other steps which might have shown him what was happening to PTSB customers.
“The meaning of the allegation, as originally notified to the appellant was fundamentally altered in the ultimate decision,” Ifsat said.
The Ifsat decision raises questions about whether the Central Bank will still go after other bankers suspected of having played a role in the tracker mortgage scandal.
Ifsat’s conclusion marks another major setback for the regulator’s post-crisis vetting and enforcement activities.
Ifsat was previously highly critical in 2024 of a Central Bank refusal to approve a board nominee for a fund , saying the decision-making process was “flawed” and denied the individual fair procedures “at every stage”.
The Central Bank was also found in a High Court ruling, published in April, to have badly handled an enforcement investigation into a funds industry executive , saying it was “irretrievably tainted” by errors. The bank committed to learning lessons and changing procedures as a result of both cases.

title: Nobody Wants This on Netflix: Chicken dipper TV – not unpleasant, but eminently disposable
description: Television: This third season bobs along in a pleasant middlebrow haze, with no sense that anything is ever at stake
content:
Does anybody want a third serving of Nobody Wants This ? ( Netflix from Thursday) Kristen Bell’s binge-and-forget romcom has bobbed along anonymously, part of the deluge of middlebrow content the streamer has unleashed in its strategy to woo those of us who watch television with one-third of our brain while devoting the rest of our mental capacity to doom-scrolling or staring into space.
This makes it the quintessential Netflix show, one with huge audience numbers and less cultural impact than a random Twitter meme. But for anyone who wants to tune in and switch off (most) of their cerebellum, this third season bobs along in the same pleasant haze, with no sense that anything is ever at stake or that its cast are real characters you should care about. It’s chicken dipper TV – not unpleasant in the moment, but eminently disposable and sure to leave an aftertaste if you go overboard.
The toothlessness of the whole thing is disappointing given that it tackles the, in theory, serious subject of how couples navigate the challenges of different faiths. In this case, Bell’s Joanne is converting to Judaism, having moved in with love interest/junior rabbi Noah (Adam Brody) – but that potentially deep and meaningful topic is hand-waved away in favour of frothy laughs.
As the action picks up, Joanne and Noah are starting their new life under the same roof, and some gentle friction emerges as they navigate the struggles of sharing their personal space. For instance, Joanne can’t stand sleeping with annoying linen sheets over the quilt (fair), and Noah seems put out when she leaves early to get ahead on her relationship podcast with her younger sister, Morgan (Succession’s Justine Lupe).
The only real tension comes from Noah’s brother Sasha (Timothy Simons), whose marriage to Esther (Jackie Tohn) is crumbling; episode one ends with the devastating reveal that she’s decided to use their trial separation to try out some dating apps. Sasha is shell-shocked, though he is also a hypocrite, given that he only discovered that Esther was dating again when signing up to an app himself.
Interfaith strains and crumbling marriages are topics rich with dramatic promise, and creator Erin Foster is an expert on the trials of dating, having once worked as co-creative head at the app Bumble. But Nobody Wants This is so determined to maintain its frothy, floaty register that it never delivers on that potential and instead lurches harmlessly onward, not actively offensive, but a long way from memorable.

title: Halloween festivals, spooky parades and ghoulish galas to consider this midterm
description: A round-up of the best activities, concerts and family-friendly events to attend around Ireland over the October break
content:
As nights lengthen and days shorten, Samhain, or Halloween , is fast approaching and with it the long weekend and midterm break. We may be hunkering down for winter, but the festive calendar is gearing up with spooky parades, family-friendly festivals and ghoulish galas all around the country. Here is a selection of some of the best events over the October midterm.
At 7pm on Halloween night, a 36-foot dragon will prowl the streets of Cork , journeying from Shandon Bells to the city centre. This year marks the 20th anniversary of the free parade, although organisers are asking for help to “feed the dragon” in the form of donations and participants; face-painters, float-pushers and stewards are required.
Touted as Europe’s largest Halloween festival, the walled city’s spooky itinerary includes artwork in the form of Luke Jerram’s suspended globe Gaia in the Guildhall, circus spectacles as part of the Walled City Trail and live music at the bandstand in the Cathedral quarter. The pièce de résistance, the carnival parade and firework show, will close out the festival, which is ringing in a roundy birthday with four decades of creepy celebrations under its belt.
A more literary take on macabre revelling, this Dublin City Council -organised festival celebrates the legacy of Dracula author Bram Stoker . Talks, workshops, theatre performances and walking tours explore the themes of the Gothic, the supernatural and the Victorian as part of Stoker’s legacy. It all culminates on Monday when Macnas brings its spectacular parade to Dublin’s northeast Inner City.
Flagship events for Samhain in the Heartlands include Longford’s Dead of Night festival (featuring family-friendly entertainment), a “Fire & Shadows Procession” in Longford town, and an aerial acrobatics spectacle, “Samhain After Dark”, at Belvedere House and Gardens outside Mullingar. More than 50 events will take place across the three midlands counties with plenty of free activities for young and old.
Less ghoulish than other Halloween events but still boasting plenty of after-dark mischief, the Cork Jazz Festival will take place across the city over the long weekend. Although in recent years it has strayed from its jazz roots, this year’s line up puts contemporary jazz front and centre with acts like London Septet Kokoroko, jazz house producers Berlioz and English jazz drummer Yussef Dayes.
Christmas pantomimes may be a childhood rite of passage but a Halloween panto is still a novel idea. Designed to be spooky not scary, Creepy Town will run both matinees and evening shows throughout the midterm break and promises to be a family-friendly festivity.
Taking place in Manorhamilton, Co Leitrim, this year’s Samhain Parade is inspired by the legend of the goddess Macha and invites people and artists from the Northwest of the country to contribute skills and talents. The parade is directed by Kíla composer and fiddle player Dee Armstrong who has been at the helm of the festival since 2001.
Paranormal presentations, family-friendly history tours and mask-making workshops for kids make up the Halloween programming for Waterford city’s museums. One unusual event for fans of the supernatural is Paranormal, Past and Present at the Medieval Museum which is headed by Ghost Éire’s co-founder Anthony Kerrigan, who will discuss his 2024 paranormal investigation of the Irish Wake museum.
With events and workshops across comedy, music, circus and procession, Púca offers a pick‘n’mix of activities for everyone. There will be live music from The Coronas, The Waterboys and The Stunning, and comedians including Enya Martin and Shane Daniel Byrne are set to perform. Family-friendly circuses are also on the programme.
The 40th anniversary of the Macnas parade will feature 121 performers, 168 volunteers and a 45 person-strong professional production crew. This year’s theme is Fiáin and includes six sections and 11 individual floats, as well as five giants, puppets and masks from previous parades. If you won’t make it out west to see the spectacle, you can catch it in the Pale at Dublin City Council’s Bram Stoker festival on October 26th.
Footsteps and Folklore on the National Famine Way, a series of evenings of storytelling and traditional music from October 24th – 26th, will take place at Strokestown Park on Saturday, before moving to Mosstown Harbour, Killashee on Sunday, and Coolnahay Harbour, Ballynacarrigy on Monday as part of the Samhain in The Heartlands Festival. Strokestown Park will also offer a family-friendly, self-guided Samhain trail over the midterm where visitors are awarded a “spookalicious treat” upon completion of the trail. Rounding off the week is the After Dark House Tour on November 1st, where guests are guided by candlelight.
Cookery classes, Pumpkins after Dark at Newbridge House, and mask-making workshops are just some of the events on offer at Fingal’s Halloween festival. There are 20 venues taking part and a suite of castles including Howth and Malahide in among the most gothic. A sample of an event taking place in stately and haunted surrounds is Craic from the Crypt at Ardgillan Castle, a ghostly tour for ages eight and up.
[ Why Halloween pumpkins are smaller this year, and three viral hacks to carve them Opens in new window ]
Fabulously fantastical and dinosaur-themed, Kilkenny’s Jurassic Newpark is looking to welcome families with kids of all ages and scare thresholds. As part of its Halloween programme the theme park will offer a daytime Jurassic Haunt featuring witches and wizard classes, spooky trails and live entertainment. For older and hardier guests, the witching hour experience will take place after dark and allow guests to explore the park by night.

title: Leinster’s Sam Prendergast injured for Munster clash as Dan Sheehan starts at number eight
description: Joey Carbery will line up against his old team, marking his first run out in the 10 shirt since rejoining Leinster
content:
Sam Prendergast will miss Leinster’s interpro clash with Munster this weekend due to a reported injury.
While the precise issue yet to be confirmed, or indeed the lengthy of time Prendergast will spend on the sidelines, it adds another potential issue to Andy Farrell’s outhalf situation ahead of the upcoming series of Ireland fixtures. Argentina are first up in Dublin on November 6th.
Farrell and Ireland are already without Jack Crowley (vascular issue) and Harry Byrne (head injury).
Prendergast’s absence means Joey Carbery starts at the Aviva Stadium on Saturday, marking his first run out in the 10 shirt since rejoining his home province. He will be partnered by Jamison Gibson-Park in the halfbacks as the scrumhalf returns to action for the first time this season.
Elsewhere, Dan Sheehan will captain Leinster from the new position of number eight with Jack Conan and Caelan Doris both missing through injury. Jamie Osborne also comes in at 13 in place of Garry Ringrose.
Munster have made seven changes to their side that beat Racing 92 last time out. Seán O’Brien marks his 50th appearance for the province by moving into the centres as Alex Nankivell shifts to 12 and Dan Kelly drops out of the side. Shane Daly also comes into the team at wing while Josh Wycherley, Kieran Brookes, Fineen Wycherley, Jack O’Donoghue and Gavin Coombes all start in a much-changed pack.
Craig Casey and Charlie O’Shea continue their halfback partnership.
Meanwhile, Connacht are set to offer debuts to former Leinster forwards Jerry Cahir and Will Connors in their Friday night clash against Zebre in Galway.
Cahir starts in a frontrow that also sees the return of Finlay Bealham while Connors is on the bench. Mack Hansen returns to the back three as he starts on the left wing but Bundee Aki drops out of the matchday 23. Ciarán Frawley continues at outhalf while Ireland squad members Cian Prendergast, Darragh Murray and Sean Jansen also start.
Ulster have named new Ireland call-up Jamie Benson at 13 for their trip to Pretoria to take on the Bulls. Despite providing outhalf cover in Farrell’s Ireland squad in November, Benson starts in midfield alongside Stuart McCloskey on Saturday.
Tom O’Toole lines out at loosehead while Nick Timoney, Nathan Doak and Jacob Stockdale also feature. James McNabney, another Ireland call-up, is on the bench.

title: Complacency led to energy squeeze in Republic, conference told
description: Data centre industry conference hears of planned electricity grid investment
content:
Complacency created the energy squeeze in the Republic that has ignited controversy over data centres and is hindering investment, a tech industry veteran told a conference on Thursday.
The State plans to spend more than €20 billion tackling bottlenecks in the national electricity grid and energy networks.
The Republic became “complacent” following its success in luring the high-tech industry here in the nineties, Gary Watson, managing director, Stellanor Data Centres, told Digital Infrastructure Ireland’s conference in Dublin.
“There’s no two ways of saying that,” said Watson, who has worked in the Irish tech industry since the 1990s, including on the Global Crossing telecoms connection that tied the Republic to the US, helping to pave the way for the sector’s growth here.
“The grid did not invest on time, at the right time,” he said, adding that it became increasingly challenging to get industry and relevant Government departments to talk to each other as problems emerged.
“After 35 years of spare grid capacity, we saw what was coming and we sat and did nothing,” said Watson.
The resulting “negative narrative” came from Government, which wanted to shift the blame, he argued.
“I think Ireland is a challenging place to invest right now,” he cautioned. “Capital is competitive, it’s not loyal to one nation.”
IDA Ireland executive director, Donal Travers, who took part in the same panel discussion with Watson, noted that the State had a stable grid up to five or six years ago “when it hit the skids”.
He acknowledged that the Republic was beginning to catch up. “It’s taking a long time, we would like it to move faster from an IDA perspective,” he added.
Travers noted that the Government planned record investment in the electricity system, but stressed that there were no easy solutions to the problems.
Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform, Jack Chambers , pointed out that the Government had earmarked €3.5 billion for EirGrid and ESB Networks from National Development Plan funds.
That will be in addition to the €18.9 billion total investment that regulators approved for both companies under a plan that runs from this year to 2030, he added.
“The electricity grid is the backbone of everything we want to achieve in building new homes and investment,” Chambers added.
Meanwhile, the value of business done abroad by Irish building and engineering companies could hit €8 billion this year, with data centres approaching €3 billion of that, according to Fergus McMahon, head of high-tech construction at State agency, Enterprise Ireland.

title: Manic Street Preachers in Dublin review: Masters of euphoric melancholy play an emotionally charged 22-song set
description: Nearly 30 years after they first played the Olympia, James Dean Bradfield and his bandmates are defiant, life-affirming and always uplifting
content:
Manic Street Preachers played the Olympia for the first time nearly 30 years ago, over Easter weekend in 1997, starting a long association with the former Victorian music hall.
The funny thing is that the band didn’t set out to be a going concern as a beloved heritage act a quarter of the way into the 21st century. In 1992 they made the grandiose claim that they would outsell Guns N’ Roses ’ Appetite for Destruction by flogging 16 million albums, then immediately split up.
The Welsh firebrands have now sold 10 million albums, so they’ll need to stick around for a while yet if they want to catch Axl Rose and company.
But it’s a testament to their back catalogue and confidence in their material that they can, audaciously, kick-start the first of two nights at 3Olympia with their 1992 song Motorcycle Emptiness, an anthemic, hands-in-the-air song about consumerism and late-stage capitalism partially inspired by Rumblefish, the 1975 novel by SE Hinton.
Every other bunch of seasoned old pros from the 1990s would reserve a song of this calibre for the encore, but the Manics never do things the easy or predictable way.
The irresistibly melodic Ocean Spray, from 2001, follows, its title lifted from the brand of cranberry juice the band’s singer, James Dean Bradfield , would bring to his mother when she was having cancer treatment.
In stark contrast, they then unleash the blistering fury of Faster, from their album The Holy Bible. It epitomises the Manics’ singular power, with Bradfield barking the refrain, “I am stronger than Mensa, Miller and Mailer, I spat out Plath and Pinter.”
The trio are flanked by their long-time producer Dave Eringa on keyboards (he played on their debut album, Generation Terrorists) and by an additional guitarist from Galway named Ray Murray.
For another song from The Holy Bible, Die in the Summertime, the Manics pare down to their nuclear formation as a three-piece. It’s poignant moment, as they leave empty the side of the stage formerly occupied by the song’s lyricist Richey Edwards , who disappeared in 1995 and was declared dead in 2008. It’s a touching tradition.
They dedicate a cover of Union City Blue, by Blondie , to Clem Burke, the US band’s drummer, who died in 2025. They also preface No Surface All Feeling with a snippet of Total Eclipse of the Heart and a shout-out to the late Bonnie Tyler .
If You Tolerate This Your Children Will Be Next is the perfect parting glass, a stirring song about the Spanish Civil War and, some of us would say, one of the best number-one singles of all time. Confetti is pumped into the air at its rousing conclusion, bringing an emotionally charged 22-song set to a celebratory end.
The most thrilling thing about this remarkably resilient band is that they never sound mournful or despondent, regardless of the subject matter of any of their songs. The Manics’ brand of melancholy is euphoric, defiant, life-affirming and always uplifting.

title: Irish doctors say UK bid to crack down on ‘cosmetic cowboys’ does not go far enough
description: Under new rules, procedures including ‘Brazilian butt lifts’ could only be performed by doctors
content:
Cosmetic doctors have called on the Government to implement “more robust” legislation governing the sector than that which has been proposed in the UK .
The UK government on Wednesday announced new rules on the cosmetic industry in England in a bid to crack down on “cosmetic cowboys”.
Under the rules, fillers injected into parts of the body other than the face, including liquid “Brazilian butt lifts”, would be legally defined as cosmetic surgical procedures, meaning only doctors could perform them.
High-risk non-surgical or wellbeing treatments, including deep chemical peels, “ vampire facials ”, dermal micro-coring and some laser procedures would be restricted to doctors, dentists and some nurses, midwives and pharmacists who have completed an accredited training course that legally authorises them to prescribe medications to patients.
A statement from England’s department of health said new rules would close a “dangerous loophole” that has seen ill-qualified practitioners working out of hotel rooms performing high-risk procedures without regulatory oversight.
However, the Irish College of Aesthetic Medicine said the rules did not go far enough, and stricter legislation was required in the Republic to protect patients.
They took particular issue with the proposals to allow nurses, midwives and pharmacists in England to perform high-risk cosmetic procedures.
“A medical procedure does not become less medical simply because it is performed for cosmetic reasons,” saidICAM president Dr Caitriona Kieran.
“Ireland has an opportunity to establish a clearer and more robust system rather than reproducing regulatory compromises made elsewhere. We urge our Government and the Department of Health to introduce legislation that establishes clear medical procedures for cosmetic injectable procedures. We should not wait for a serious incident to expose weaknesses in the law.”
Dermal filler injections can cause vascular occlusion, or blocked blood vessels, tissue necrosis (cell death) and permanent blindness. Other complications include infections and severe inflammatory reactions. Botox can also cause serious adverse effects, particularly when inappropriate products or techniques are used.
[ ‘I couldn’t open my eye’: the dangers of unlicensed Botox procedures in Ireland Opens in new window ]
“When something goes wrong with an injectable treatment, patients need more than someone who knows how to hold a syringe. They need a medical professional who can recognise a serious complication, make an immediate clinical decision and provide appropriate treatment,” Kieran said.
“That can make the difference between a manageable complication or permanent injury. Botox and dermal fillers are increasingly marketed as routine beauty treatments. Yet these procedures involve prescription medicines or substances injected to human tissue. This can result in serious complications. That’s why we argue that the distinction between medical procedures and ordinary beauty treatments must be reflected in legislation.”
Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill has previously said she is “aware of concerns in relation to the safe administration of dermal fillers”.
The programme for Government 2025 commits to ensuring the administration of dermal fillers is only undertaken by trained healthcare professionals.
“My department is currently conducting research activities with respect to legislative and regulatory options regarding the administration of dermal fillers. This includes a review by the Health Research Board, commenced in 2025, the report of which is expected in the coming months,” she said in response to a parliamentary question in January.
“Once received, the department will consider the most suitable option with respect to administration of dermal fillers. We plan to engage with stakeholders as part of the programme of work to progress this matter.”

title: Judi Dench: ‘I can’t be on stage... I can’t do a film any more. I can’t read’
description: Dench is no longer able to work as an actor due to age-related macular degeneration
content:
Judi Dench has said she is no longer able to work as an actor because of her eye condition.
The 91-year-old actor was diagnosed with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) in 2012, which has made it difficult for her to recognise people’s faces.
“I can’t be on stage. I can’t do a play any more. I can’t do a film any more. I can’t read any more,” Dench told BBC Radio 4’s Today.
“I go up to lots of the wrong people and give them a hug and say, ‘oh sorry, didn’t realise’.”
Addressing interviewer Emma Barnett, Dench said: “I can’t see your face at all.”
The James Bond star also expressed sadness at not being able to see bluebells in the summer, saying: “They said this summer was absolutely sensational with bluebells; I couldn’t see one.
“But I know what my trees look like, and part of it is in my memory and part of it is about hopefully what I can make out.”
Asked how she felt about ageing in general, Dench replied: “Ageing? Rubbish. There’s nothing to say for it at all.
“Don’t think about it too much and just keep on trying to do the roller skates and whatever.
“If you can’t see as well, which I can’t, it’s a whole other ball game. I have to put up with it. My ma had it too.”
Dench previously told how she stopped driving a few years ago because of her deteriorating eyesight.
“A couple of years ago I stopped driving, which was one of the most traumatic moments of my life. It was absolutely appalling,” Dench said.
“But I just know I’ll kill somebody if I get behind the wheel of a car now.”
AMD is a common condition and does not cause total blindness, but it can make reading and recognising faces difficult, according to the NHS.
Dench, whose career spans seven decades, has won various awards including an Oscar, two Golden Globes and six Baftas.
Earlier this year, it was announced The Shaftesbury Theatre, the largest independent theatre in London’s West End, would be renamed the Judi Dench Theatre to honour the actor.
At the time of the announcement in June, she Dench: “The Shaftesbury Theatre has always held a special place in my heart. My relationship to the Theatre of Comedy and to the Taffner family goes back many years and to have this beautiful theatre renamed after me is truly overwhelming.
“Live theatre continues to be so important as a way of telling stories and entertaining audiences, something I have aimed to do all my working life.” – PA

title: International investors give Ireland the thumbs up, ignoring corporate tax warnings
description: ‘Markets are pricing today’s tax windfall, not tomorrow’s risks’, warns fiscal council
content:
Ireland as one of Europe’s safe havens for investors? Something of a milestone was hit this week when the cost to the State for raising short-term borrowings dipped below that of Germany, traditionally the euro zone’s benchmark.
By Thursday morning the quotes were more or less the same for short-term, two-year German and Irish borrowings at just under 3.1 per cent. Looking at 10-year bond yields – the more traditional comparative measure – Ireland at 3.54 per cent was still a bit above Germany at 3.37 per cent.
But as interest rates rise worldwide and investors focus on countries with high debts and deficits – notably France – Ireland remains in a sweet spot. The domestic debate on volatile corporate taxes and the risks ahead is not resonating in international markets.
Long-term interest rates are on the rise worldwide because of fears of rising inflation and increases in central bank rates. As this has happened, the cost of borrowing for countries with higher debt levels - like the US, the UK and particularly France – have taken the biggest hit.
Ireland’s borrowing costs have risen too. The National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) recently borrowed new 10-year funds at a rate of 3.5 per cent. A year ago the rate was 2.5 per cent while back in 2022 the State was raising 10-year cash at 1.5 per cent and there were even some six-month borrowings conducted at negative interest rates.
Market conditions are now a world away from that period, but Ireland is at the right end of the euro zone league and 10-year borrowing costs here compared to over 5 per cent in France, 4.6 per cent in Italy, 4.5 per cent in Belgium and 4 per cent in Spain.
[ Fiscal advisers point out the flaws but Government ignores them. What’s the point of Ifac? Opens in new window ]
Particular concerns surround France, with a debt-to-GDP level approaching 120 per cent, a deficit of 5.4 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP), political paralysis and riots on the street.
Its 10-year bond rate has jumped by 1.3 percentage points since June, sparking fears that the European Central Bank (ECB) might need to step into the market, or that some kind of borrowing shock could lie ahead which could ripple out across the euro zone.
Fears of debt pressures have left big institutions looking for safe havens. And Ireland with its low debt-to-GDP ratio and significant budget surplus is benefiting. Investors seem happy to overlook the risks from the well-discussed reliance on potentially volatile corporate tax revenues from a few big multinationals. Or perhaps in an uncertain world they reckon these dangers are sufficiently far into the future not to worry about.
This issue is on the radar internationally. The KBRA debt agency pointed out in a recent note: “Changes in corporate profitability, investment structures or international tax arrangements could therefore have a sizeable fiscal impact, particularly given the importance of the pharmaceutical and technology sectors.”
And noted US commentator Brad Setser of the Council on Foreign Relations, a long-time critic of Ireland’s tax policies, returned to the fray, saying on X in response to posts on Ireland’s low bond rates: “Sadly, winning at tax competition pays ... Ireland runs a large surplus largely because a small subset of US companies pay more tax in Dublin than in (Washington) DC.”
Setser has called for changes in US tax legislation to combat this. But for now at least bond investors retain confidence in Ireland’s ability to ride out any likely fall-off in corporate taxes.
[ Ireland’s national debt could hit €250bn in 2030s Opens in new window ]
This is supported by strong short-term forecasts for the Irish public finances. Kevin Timoney, chief economist at Davys , argues that the Irish budget was conservative in its forecasts and that the predicted budget surplus would be higher than expected this year, leaving more leeway in 2027. He also points to the strength in tax revenues in areas other than corporation tax.
Ireland’s growth story seems to be reassuring investors. “Economic growth has been about double the speed of Department of Finance budget forecasts since 2022,” Timoney said, another factor which he believes is underpinning support for Ireland’s borrowings on world markets.
He also believes Ireland has significant leeway due to its financial balance sheet – including significant cash on hand – and believes it could continue to attract international confidence even if it had to borrow to fund some future State investment. In other words there is significant leeway in the figures.
The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (Ifac) , the budget watchdog which has consistently warned about the outlook for the public finances, not surprisingly takes a different view.
[ Budget 2027 continues extraordinary rise in State spending Opens in new window ]
“Markets are pricing today’s tax windfall, not tomorrow’s risks,” according to its chief economist, Eddie Casey. “If you strip out the corporation tax we can’t explain, the Government is heading for €20 billion deficits, with three firms paying nearly half of it and nobody knowing how long that will last.”
If the corporate tax receipts fade, then “the surplus goes with them”, warns Casey. " Whether they fade depends on things Ireland doesn’t control: how a handful of tech and pharma products sell, who runs these firms, and tax policy abroad. Nobody knows how that will pan out."
The debate – and the pressure on countries such as France – underlines the importance of Ireland retaining international confidence in its public finances. If something blows up in the markets – and a string of European elections next year, notably in France, will be vital – then the place to be is out of the spotlight.
The Government points out that it is putting cash aside for the future in two funds. However, its own forecasts suggest that while the headline general government balance – the EU borrowing measure – will remain in strong surplus, Ireland is getting to a position where it will have to borrow if it wants to continue to put money into the two funds.
[ Denying our dependence on US firms is like saying Tony Soprano worked in ‘waste management’ Opens in new window ]
The concept of the funds was that they would be putting away excess corporation tax receipts. But, in fact, the vast bulk of corporation tax receipts are being spent, rather than saved. And by 2028, on the Department of Finance calculations, the cash borrowing needed will be quite substantial.
This is like the exchequer taking money out of one of its pockets and putting it in another. You could argue that it would be better to run down the national debt, rather than borrow to put money into two funds. Gross national debt is due to rise from €208 billion this year to €236 billion by 2029, but of course there will be increased cash assets on the other side in the two funds.
The key debate is just how volatile the Irish public finances outlook is. The Department of Finance estimates that “potentially transient” corporation tax now accounts for around half of all tax from this heading – about €18.8 billion this year rising to almost €23 billion next year.
[ Ireland’s reliance on multinationals extends ‘far beyond’ corporation tax, warns watchdog Opens in new window ]
Its longer term forecasts in its Future Forty analysis shows that into the 2030s the Irish public finances could come under serious pressure if the windfall part of corporate tax receipts – the part not explained by activity in Ireland - gradually winds down. The budget watchdog cautions that in addition to this we need to consider other pressures on the public finances, notably from an ageing population.
The debate about the extent of leeway in the public finances is crucial – and it is impossible to accurately predict what will happen with volatile corporate taxes, never mind the many other uncertainties around. For now investors are happy to bet on Ireland’s strong growth and headline public finance figures. We have seen before how quickly this can turn.
But it would probably require an “event” – say a big drop in payments from one or two of the big payers – to draw attention to Ireland.
The benefit of staying in the exclusive club of safe havens is huge – but whether Ireland can make the choices to allow this to happen is the question. Using the surplus to invest wisely and protect the public finances is the formula – but political pressures are in the other direction, to spend the money now.

title: Stryker charged over alleged health and safety breaches after worker’s death at Cork plant
description: John Murphy (41) died from injuries sustained while carrying out at work at company’s plant at Carrigtwohill
content:
A leading US medical devices technology company has been charged with breaches of health and safety regulations over the death of a contractor’s employee who suffered fatal burn injuries while carrying out work at one of its plants in Co Cork more than three years ago.
Stryker Ireland Ltd was summonsed to appear at Midleton District Court on Thursday following a Health and Safety Authority (HSA) investigation into the death of John Murphy (41), a father of three who died from injuries sustained while carrying out at work at Stryker’s plant at Carrigtwohill in east Cork.
Murphy from Condonstown, Watergrasshill, Co Cork, suffered third-degree burns to 75 per cent of his body in the incident while working for facilities management company Apleona, which was doing contract work for Stryker at Anngrove, IDA Industrial Park, Carrigtwohill, on April 18th, 2023.
He managed to make it off the roof where he had been working before losing consciousness and was rushed by ambulance to Cork University Hospital, but he was later transferred to the burns unit at St James’s Hospital in Dublin, where he died on June 9th, 2023.
On Thursday, at Midleton District Court, Stryker Ireland Ltd with registered offices at Earlsfort Terrace, Dublin 2, appeared on seven summonses arising from the HSA investigation into the circumstances of the incident that led to Murphy’s death.
The summons related to alleged breaches of the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 including that Stryker Ireland Ltd failed to manage and conduct its operation in such a way as to ensure non-employees were not exposed to a risk to their safety or welfare at the Anngrove plant.
Specifically, the same summons further alleges that Stryker Ireland Ltd failed to ensure titanium particles did not rise from the production floor and enter the heating, ventilation and air-conditioning system located on the roof, thereby exposing Murphy to risk.
The same summon further alleges this failure by the company resulted in sparks being generated by tools and that this in turn resulted in Murphy being set alight and suffering personal injuries that led to his death.
Another summons against Stryker, which employs more than 5,500 on seven sites in the Republic, alleges that it failed to ensure a suitable and appropriate risk assessment arising from an explosive atmosphere in the heating, ventilation and air-conditioning system on the roof.
Other summonses related to the alleged failure to classify the heating, ventilation and air-conditioning unit on the roof as a hazardous or non-hazardous place and the alleged failure to identify those hazards and have a written assessment identifying the risks to safety, health and welfare.
Emmet Boyle, barrister for the Director of Public Prosecutions, told the court it had directed trial on indictment at Circuit Court level on all seven summons and that the DPP was also consenting to the defendant going forward to the Circuit Court on a signed plea of guilty if it so decided.
Barrister for Stryker Ireland Ltd Alison Fynes applied for discovery of the DPP file in the case and Judge Colm Roberts directed that the file be forwarded to Stryker’s lawyers Arthur Cox LLP and adjourned the matter until December 3rd for the preparation of a book of evidence if it is required.

title: Russell Brand accuser ‘didn’t think she would be believed’, rape trial hears
description: Former comedian denies rape and sexual assault after being accused by six different women
content:
Friends and family of one of Russell Brand’s alleged rape victims told a court she did not go to police at the time because she “didn’t think she would be believed”.
Brand, now 51, is accused of raping a 21-year-old fan after meeting her at one of his Hammersmith Apollo gigs in 2009.
Southwark Crown Court heard evidence from friends of the alleged victim who were told at the time that Brand, a star of British TV and Hollywood films, had forced her into having anal sex at the end of an encounter that started off consensually.
The woman’s parents also told the court that their daughter had told them about the alleged attack, including “screaming out in pain” while telling Brand to stop.
One of the woman’s friends said she told her to go to the police, but she “felt it wasn’t worth it”.
She told the jury: “She didn’t think she would be believed, and she didn’t think it would be worth it to go.
A colleague of the woman recalled being told about the alleged rape by the “ashen-faced” woman, who told her she did not want to come forward at the time.
“I said to her ‘you’ve been raped’, and she said ‘nobody will believe me’”, she said.
The colleague said the woman told her “they are going to think it’s my fault”, and she added: “She said ‘I feel really bad, I feel really guilty’.”
Brand denies three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one allegation of indecent assault, after being accused by six different women.
Jurors have heard he picked out the alleged rape victim in the foyer after the Apollo show, so that she and another woman could have a threesome with the comedian backstage.
The woman told the court on Wednesday that she willingly engaged in the threesome, then agreed to go to Brand’s home a few days later for consensual sex.
She says she said no to anal sex during the second encounter in his bedroom but alleges Brand did it anyway, pushing her down on the bed so that she struggled to breathe.
“I did not consent to that,” she told the jury during Wednesday’s evidence.
On Thursday morning, one of the woman’s friends who was at the Apollo gig recalled her being “excited and flattered” by messages from Brand that she received from the comedian after the threesome.
She told the court Brand “sent a car to collect her” and her friend recalled being told to wait in a room at Brand’s home “until he was free to see her”.
The friend said the alleged victim recalled Brand being “quite aggressive”, and she told her of “forcibly” anal sex which “really, really hurt her” and Brand turning “really nasty” afterwards.
“I asked if she was OK, I told her that was awful and I asked specifically ‘did you say no?’, and she said yes, lots of times.”
The alleged victim had a boyfriend at the time, but their relationship ended after she confessed to the threesome with Brand on the night of the Apollo show.
The court heard the woman went to stay with another friend after the relationship breakdown, and that friend remembers being told of Brand “pressing” the woman to come to his home.
She “eventually gave in” and agreed to go to Brand’s home, but afterwards she told her friend that she had turned down anal sex but he forced her into it.
“I told her it wasn’t right and it was rape,” the friend said, before recalling seeing the woman “on the bed with a hot water bottle laying all scrunched up”.
The alleged victim’s parents also provided witness statements, setting out how their “very unwell” daughter came to stay with them for two months shortly after her encounters with Brand.
Her father said his daughter told him: “They were having sex, she asked him to stop, she kept saying she had been assaulted.”
He told the court in a statement: “I turned to her in the car and asked if she asked him to stop, and she said ‘no’ several times.
“I said ‘you have been raped, that’s rape’.”
Her mother remembers her daughter saying Brand “didn’t stop even when she screamed out in pain and asked him to stop”.
Another friend of the woman told the court she said Brand was “quite cold” and “keen to get her gone” after the alleged rape, while one of her work colleagues remembers advising her to go to the police.
She said: “I said to her you need to tell the police and she said ‘no, they won’t believe me, I went to the house’.”
One of the woman’s former boyfriends also told the court he was told about the alleged rape, telling the court she “didn’t really want to talk about it, but she was incredibly clear about the event – the rape.
“That it was that, that it was rape and that she hated it.”
Brand denies all the charges he faces, and says all sexual encounters were consensual but have since been “reimagined” by his accusers.

title: How Manchester United became a club too big not to fail
description: United’s ongoing problem is that everyone always has someone else to blame
content:
J ust as Christmas seems to come earlier every year, so does the descent of a Manchester United managerial reign into rancour, recrimination and public apologies to supporters.
Winless in seven matches and with his captain in open revolt about his tactics, Michael Carrick is already doomed. The only surprise is the speed at which everything has plunged into crisis.
We are now at the point in the Manchester United life cycle where the demand is for the well-meaning but overwhelmed former player to be replaced by some glamorous tyrant who will show these abject players what real work looks like. (Antonio Conte.)
Conte will add extra running sessions and ban ketchup from the club canteen, after which he will win the Carabao Cup/Europa League while gradually losing the dressingroom. He will be followed in 18 months by the salve of a giddy interim spell by a genial and earnest former player (Johnny Evans), who will beat Manchester City and either Liverpool or Arsenal with an adrenal display of counter-attacking football. This will be followed by a modern coach supposedly capable of playing dominant football, and so they’ll hire an Ineos-coded ideologue with good hair. (Eddie Howe – though we note Fabian Hurzeler’s recent hair transplant.)
And when this fails, because United players are incapable of pressing, José Mourinho might be ready to come out of retirement for one last job to show these abject players what real work looks like. Luke Shaw and Diogo Dalot will still be the full-backs.
The sense of purgatory at United was accentuated this week by the publication of The Athletic’s two-part interview with Erik ten Hag , who reflects on his time at United with an exquisite lack of introspection. “I think I’m always quite self-critical and reflective,” says ten Hag, during an interview in which he blames everyone but himself. In a jarring echo of David Moyes’ complaints that he was unable to sign Gareth Bale, Cesc Fàbregas, Cristiano Ronaldo and Toni Kroos, Ten Hag laments that the club didn’t sign Harry Kane and Declan Rice. (He neglects to mention that the club did sign expensive flops like Antony and Andre Onana for him.)
Otherwise, says Ten Hag, the preseason travel was too long and exhausting; Ineos’ hierarchy broke promises about keeping Scott McTominay; the club’s indulgence of the players created a “toxic culture”; and Antony had to be signed at a king’s ransom because Jadon Sancho refused to play on the right wing.
[ Bruno Fernandes questions Michael Carrick’s tactics as pressure builds on Manchester United manager Opens in new window ]
This is not to say Ten Hag is necessarily wrong about any of this. The hopelessness of Ineos’ offering was summed up after Ten Hag left the club: Dan Ashworth spent as long at the club as he had on gardening leave waiting to join, leaving apparently because he warned against hiring the tactically inflexible Ruben Amorim, whose formation didn’t suit the squad. Amorim was fired just over a year later for being too tactically inflexible. The same people who disregarded Cassandra Ashworth are still calling the shots.
This is the ongoing problem at United: everyone always has someone else to blame. The players blame the manager’s tactics or, in Lisandro Martinez’ case , the transfer acumen of the technical director; the manager blames the players or the hierarchy; the hierarchy blames the players, the managers or each other.
Alex Ferguson’s success was built on the fact he was the only person at the club allowed to throw around blame, and every decision he made was primarily to assert his authority. Ferguson infamously bristled at Channel 4 journalist Jon Snow’s description of his methods as “Stalinist” after he retired from United in 2013, but his was a better charter for success at United than this subsequent democracy of ass-covering.
[ There’s a clear reason the world’s best players are staying away from the Premier League Opens in new window ]
Ineos’ Corporate Camelot precludes any coach building up the same level of authority at United nowadays, but even if they did want to cede control, the noise around United means it’s impossible for any manager to stick around long enough to build any control.
One of the reasons United remains cursed to repeat this cycle is that their travails make such a successful media business plan. Gary Neville’s Overlap has expanded to become a daily podcast, and their core offering remains angry and bleakly comic inquisitions about how This Is Manchester United We Are Talking About. One of the new Overlap hosts is Mark Goldbridge, who made his name with hysterical, Partridgean reactions to United defeats in front of a green screen in his bedroom.
This was once Liverpool’s plight, where a suite of legendary players joined the punditry ranks to scorn the diminished standards at their once-great club. United’s institutional collapse has been greatly exacerbated by its coinciding with social media and a scale and brutality of criticism that no human being is built to endure. When you hear Harry Maguire’s performances mocked in the Ghanaian parliament , you realise it is impossible for anyone to succeed under this level of scrutiny.
[ Too much Overlap? Gary Neville’s podcast empire knows no bounds Opens in new window ]
Everyone at United has calculated that the best means of not being smothered by this avalanche of criticism is by shovelling it in someone else’s direction.
Michael Carrick will be the latest fall guy because Manchester United has become too big not to fail.

title: Man accused of Dublin mosque arson attack has date set to enter plea
description: Saeid Khosroabadi did not enter a plea on Thursday due to the ongoing solicitor strike
content:
A date has been fixed for a self-described anti-Islam activist to enter a plea on charges from an alleged arson attack on a mosque in Dublin city centre.
Iranian national Saeid Khosroabadi (41), of Seville Place, Dublin 1, was arrested following a Garda investigation into a blaze at the doorway of the Faizan E Madinah Mosque, on Talbot Street, at the end of June.
He was originally charged with committing arson, causing criminal damage at the mosque. An additional charge of endangering life was brought in front of Cloverhill District Court in August.
The charges were sent forward for trial, which was due for mention on Thursday.
The court heard that Khosroabadi was “unfortunately affected” by the ongoing solicitors’ withdrawal of services and a date for the arraignment was sought in two weeks’ time.
Judge Martin Nolan of Dublin Circuit Criminal Court set a date for Khosroabadi to enter a guilty or not guilty plea by November 19th. He ordered that the accused will appear in person.
[ Dublin mosque arson accused tells court he fled Iran to escape hanging Opens in new window ]
Khosroabadi spoke only to identify himself and to thank the judge.
Emergency services, including more than 20 firefighters, four engines and gardaí, responded after thick smoke engulfed the mosque on Talbot Street in June.
The premises was safely evacuated with no reported injuries.
The accused previously told the court he was from an Islamic country and had been tortured.
“I did not accept Islam. I said Islam is not my religion,” he said. “They wanted to hang me, the radical Islamic religion of Iran. I escaped in 2016 from prison to start a new life.”
A bail hearing was previously told how during Garda interview Khosroabadi said he was “disappointed” the mosque had not burned down.

title: A town called Schengen: After decades of seamless travel, European border checks are back
description: Creeping reintroduction of checkpoints inside Schengen travel area a nuisance for town where Luxembourg, France and Germany come together
content:
N icolas Ruppert, a 10th-generation winemaker, is chatting to me in his uncle’s vineyard on a small hilltop in the town of Schengen in Luxembourg .
A bridge across the river below brings you to the spot where the German and French border come together. It would take you two minutes to spin between the three European countries in a car. The exact “tripoint” where Luxembourg, Germany and France meet is in the middle of the Moselle river.
It was near this point, aboard the MS Princesse Marie-Astrid, that France, Germany, Luxembourg, Belgium and the Netherlands signed the Schengen agreement in 1985, committing to remove checks when crossing borders within the five countries.
The pact created a European common travel area, or as it’s commonly known, the Schengen area.
The Ruppert family vineyard is spread across 24 hectares of land, split two to one between Luxembourg and neighbouring France. Before the agreement workers transporting grapes or wine could be held up in queues at the border waiting “for hours”, Nicolas says.
The Schengen zone, which did away with the need to flash a passport, expanded over the years.
Today it includes 29 countries; all European Union members (bar Ireland and Cyprus), plus Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein. Border controls still obviously apply to people entering the Schengen zone from countries outside of it.
For a long time the agreement served as a concrete example of the practical benefits closer European integration could bring to the lives of ordinary people, when political squabbling was set aside.
Nicolas, who is 28 and helps his uncle Henri manage the vineyard, grew up in a Europe where seamlessly driving or flying between most countries was the norm, until recently anyway.
Germany reintroduced police checks at all land borders in September 2024, in an attempt to show it was cracking down on illegal immigration.
The restrictions followed the Solingen terror attacks, where a Syrian national who was refused asylum stabbed three people to death at a German street festival. The man, who had ties to the Islamic State group, was convicted and is serving a life sentence.
Spot checks had been in place along Germany’s eastern borders since 2023, a move that had prompted Poland to start checking Germans heading in the other direction.
The “temporary” restrictions have been rolled over every six months. Germany has justified the controls by claiming high levels of irregular migration pose a threat to public security and order.
France followed suit and introduced spot checkpoints on its land border crossings two years ago.
Giorgia Meloni, Italy’s hard-right prime minister, took things a step further in response to the Ceuta “crisis” this summer, imposing passport checks on people travelling by boat and plane from Spain to Italy.
More than 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, the tiny Spanish exclave on the north African coast, over two days this summer, although nearly all later returned to Morocco.
The chaotic scenes sparked panic in European capitals about a sudden spike in arrivals of asylum seekers. Rome and others took pot shots at Spain’s left-wing prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, some going as far as calling for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen travel area for a time.
Relations between Rome and Madrid have been tense since, exacerbated by the fact Meloni and Sánchez are both facing elections soon. However, it seems a detente is in the offing to stand down the Italian checks.
The Dutch government, traditionally another hardliner on immigration, has privately been advocating for greater co-ordination between Schengen countries on border management.
The idea would be modelled on the Eurogroup format that brings finance ministers from EU states who share the euro currency together once a month, to compare notes.
“We always make the comparison to the Eurogroup, which was created after the financial crisis. If one [member] doesn’t perform that has consequences for the others,” one diplomat said.
This is not the first time border stops have been unilaterally thrown back up between countries inside the Schengen zone.
Germany, Denmark and several other EU states started checking passports and papers at internal Schengen borders during the 2015 migration surge, when more than one million asylum seekers crossed to Europe, putting particular pressure on countries along the EU’s external southern border.
National reception systems are not under anywhere near the same pressure. In fact the number of people applying for refugee protection in the EU is at its lowest point in five years.
But many governments are under huge electoral pressure from populist, far-right parties gaining unprecedented support in Germany, France and elsewhere, on the back of promises to fight illegal immigration and keep asylum seekers out.
In Schengen town, the police checkpoints on a busy motorway between Luxembourg and Germany are a real inconvenience for the large numbers who travel back and forth every day.
“People here, they are pissed,” says Nicolas, the young winemaker who makes the journey daily.
The irony of border checks taking place at Schengen was not lost on a group of politicians from Luxembourg’s social democrats, who were on a bus heading across the bridge last month to meet their SPD sister party in Germany’s Saarland region.
The bus was pulled over and inspected by German police, according to parliamentarians who were on board.
“It could hardly be more symbolic: social democrats from Luxembourg and the Saarland are meeting to discuss cross-border co-operation and a strong Europe, and are being checked at the very place where, over 40 years ago, the foundation was laid for a Europe without internal borders,” the two political parties said in a joint statement afterwards.
Ulrich Commerçon, who leads the SPD in the Saarland state parliament, said the holdup his colleagues from Luxembourg faced was “not merely symbolic”, but something that undermined the spirit of cross-border co-operation. “The European ideal is increasingly falling by the wayside,” he said.
Luxembourg is one of Europe’s smallest countries and almost half of its workforce commutes in from neighbouring Belgium, France and Germany.
Out of the 20 staff employed in the Ruppert family vineyard, only Nicolas and his uncle are originally from Luxembourg.
French is spoken front of house, German in the cellars, and English can often be the common denominator between workers who don’t have both.
“I think [that] is a particularity of Luxembourg and also of Schengen that you have a lot of external workers,” Nicolas says.
Luxembourg’s wine region, Moselle, is best known for producing whites.
It is unusual because it’s recognised as a “transnational” wine region that stretches from Luxembourg into French and German territory too. “The Romans brought wine to Luxembourg 2,000 years ago,” Nicolas says.
The area is good for viticulture because the river locks in the heat of the summer sun, making the temperature along its banks warmer than other parts of the country, he says.
The steep slopes traditionally gave a good angle for the rows of vines to catch the sun for longer throughout the day. “Today we are looking to plant areas with a bit less sun ... because of climate change,” he says.
Beyond making or tasting wine, there isn’t a huge amount to do in Schengen.
Walking along the small town’s main street you’ll pass by a beaten-down Chinese restaurant, a petrol station, a pub and not much else. There is a small castle.
And a museum dedicated to the history of the Schengen travel area. The ship where the agreement was signed, the Marie-Astrid, is docked outside for visitors to have a look around.
The ship had been sold to Germany in the early 1990s, but not too long ago the local council bought it back, with financial help from the government.
It was restored as a sort of floating memorial in Schengen, where it’s been for the last year.
In the four decades that have passed since it hosted the signing ceremony the boat has held up well. The same cannot be said about the Schengen travel area itself and the concept of doing away with border checks between European countries.

title: Central Bank fines Irish-based unit of crypto giant Coinbase €3.3m
description: Coinbase Global is the largest crypto exchange in the US and the world’s biggest custodian of Bitcoin
content:
The Central Bank of Ireland has fined a second Irish-regulated unit of Coinbase Global, one of the world’s largest crypto asset exchange operators.
The regulator has fined Coinbase Ireland (CBIE), a licensed electronic money firm, €3.25 million for regulatory breaches as it was found to have had excessive reliance on its US parent for outsourced services, failed to adequately safeguard customers’ funds, and had governance shortcomings. The fine remains subject to High Court confirmation.
No customers suffered financial loss or were unable to access their funds as a result of these issues, Coinbase said in a separate statement. The company has also since “fully resolved” the issues identified, it added.
The sanction followed a €21.5 million fine levelled by the bank last November against Coinbase Europe, a virtual asset service provider (Vasp), for failing to properly monitor more than 30 million transactions for money laundering or terrorist financing over the course of a year.
Coinbase Europe’s Irish Vasp registration lapsed at the end of last year as the group moved its activities to Luxembourg as the EU moved from national Vasp registration regimes to a harmonised authorisation under markets in cryptoassets regulation, known as Mica.
The Central Bank found that for a period of four years Coinbase Ireland allowed its users’ funds to be mixed with funds held elsewhere – despite the Irish entity’s explicit promise at the time of authorisation in 2019 that it would have robust and automated safeguards. The failure increased the risk of loss of these funds, the regulator said.
[ Coinbase asked by SEC to halt trading in everything except bitcoin, CEO says Opens in new window ]
It added that the outsourcing of the safeguarding function and overreliance on the US parent “materially impaired” the quality of the Irish unit’s internal safeguarding controls.
“While outsourcing presents many benefits to industry, when not effectively managed, it can threaten the operational resilience of firms,” said Karen O’Leary, the Central Bank’s director of enforcement.
“Payment and e-money firms have a fundamental obligation to fully safeguard customers’ funds. The Central Bank has made its supervisory expectations in this regard clear: we have no tolerance for weaknesses in safeguarding arrangements.”
Coinbase said in a statement that the issues of the case largely arose as the company took steps “to protect customers during periods of significant disruption”.
“For example, during the 2023 US banking crisis, CBIE directed customers to deposit their funds into alternative bank accounts held by Coinbase to protect them from potential losses arising from bank failure,” it said.
“While this helped protect customers from financial loss and disruption, it involved CBIE customers’ funds being mixed with funds held for other Coinbase entities, which was not in line with regulatory safeguarding requirements.”
Similarly, following Brexit, although the Irish company repeatedly instructed customers to use its Irish bank account for future deposits, some customers continued to deposit into legacy UK bank accounts, which did not comply with regulatory safeguarding requirements, it said.
Coinbase Ireland self-identified and reported several of the issues to the Central Bank in January 2024, addressed the vast majority of the underlying control issues that year, and has since fully resolved them, it added.
Coinbase Global is the largest cryptocurrency exchange in the US and the world’s biggest custodian of Bitcoin. The parent group is led by chief executive and co-founder Brian Armstrong, one of the most influential people in the fast-growing cryptocurrency industry.

title: Aughinish Alumina exports not included in draft EU Russia sanctions package
description: Measures cutting Aughinish Alumina’s exports to Russia not included in draft of EU’s next round of economic sanctions targeting Moscow
author_name: Jack Power, Conor Gallagher, Jack Horgan-Jones
content:
Sanctions prohibiting Aughinish Alumina from continuing to export material to Russia are not included in a draft of the European Commission ’s next package of measures targeting the Russian wartime economy.
The EU’s member states will be asked to weigh in on what will be the union’s 22nd round of economic sanctions, which are intended to make it harder for Moscow to wage its war in Ukraine .
Confidential discussions will take place over the coming weeks between commission officials and senior diplomats from all 27 EU states to sound out support for the draft sanctions package, and make changes, before governments start negotiating between themselves.
The Estonian foreign ministry has said it plans to push for Brussels officials to sanction alumina, a move that would prohibit Aughinish from shipping the product to Russia.
The Co Limerick plant is owned by Russian metals giant Rusal and ships vast quantities of alumina to smelters in Russia, where the raw material is turned into aluminium, a key ingredient in the industrial supply chain.
The plant, which employs several hundred people in the Foynes area, previously warned it could be forced to shut if its exports to Russia were barred by EU-level sanctions.
A draft of the commission’s 22nd package of sanctions does not propose measures prohibiting alumina exports, according to one senior source briefed on the closely guarded details.
However, several sources in the commission’s Brussels headquarters cautioned that changes could often be made following confidential talks, known as “confessionals”, with national diplomats in Brussels.
It is understood the commission had internally debated proposing a quota to limit Aughinish’s exports to Russia, rather than a full export ban. The restriction would have reduced sales to Russia gradually over time, to give the Irish plant a chance to find other markets for its material.
The commission, the EU’s executive body, has privately not ruled out sanctions on alumina, meaning it is possible the proposal features in later packages.
Estonia will ask the commission to target alumina in the coming package.
“We can confirm that yes, Estonia has made such a proposal at the EU level,” a spokesman for the Estonian ministry of foreign affairs told The Irish Times.
Sources said Estonia did not expect the Irish Government to fight the proposal. However, other countries with alumina or aluminium industries, such as France, may have objections. Poland would probably be minded to back alumina sanctions, another source said.
Aughinish Alumina’s exports of alumina to Russia have been in the spotlight after reporting by The Irish Times tracing the shipments to smelters in Russia , where it is made into aluminium that is sold to ASK, a Moscow trading company known to supply the alloy to Russian arms and missile manufacturers.
The Limerick plant’s exports to Russia have significantly increased since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine and account for about half of Aughinish’s business, prompting concerns that material supplied by Ireland was being used to make missiles and weapons for Moscow’s war.
The EU has levied round after round of economic sanctions on Russia since its invasion of Ukraine nearly five years ago. In effect the measures cut off Russian companies, oligarchs and industries from the western economy, by making it an offence for EU entities to sell listed products to Russia, or buy products. Alumina has not been listed as a sanctioned product.
The Government has repeatedly made the case it has not opposed any EU sanctions to date. Ministers point out that proposing sanctions on Aughinish’s shipments to Russia is a call for Brussels to make.
[ ‘Physically we live here, but mentally we live in Ukraine’: Envoy on Russia’s attack on hometown Opens in new window ]
A proposal to levy sanctions on Aughinish Alumina’s Russian business ties would put Dublin in a very awkward position, forcing the Government to choose between possible backlash from European allies for opposing EU-level sanctions, or local backlash in Limerick if jobs were put at risk.
Any new sanctions must be unanimously agreed by all 27 EU states.
Asked about the sanctions package at an EU presidency event in Dublin on Thursday, Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee
said she had not yet seen the proposal from the Commission, but would support “any measures that are being proposed”.
She said Ireland had been “very clear and very open” on the matter of exports from Aughinish Alumina, and that Ireland had commissioned a report on the matter which had been shared with Brussels and Kiev. “We’ve been very clear in saying, if measures need to be taken, that we will work closely with them.”

title: Down two-time All-Ireland winner Kevin O’Neill passes away
description: O’Neill was part of the Down teams of 1960/’61, the first team from north of the border to win Sam Maguire
content:
Down GAA has paid tribute to two-time All-Ireland winner Kevin O’Neill, who died on Wednesday.
