O’Neill was a member of the history-making Down teams of 1960 and 1961 – the first occasions a county from north of the border won the Sam Maguire.
With his brother Seán, he was one of two sets of siblings on those trailblazing Mourne sides along with James and Dan McCartan.
Down GAA stated: “Kevin O’Neill was an astute judge of football, he had a great love of the game, and he had wisdom and knowledge, a trait that he carried not just through his involvement in the GAA but also in his work in local government as Clerk and Chief Executive of Newry and Mourne Council.
“Kevin O’Neill was a part of a very special group of players who made history, he was man of firsts, with school, with club and with county, he was a leader who asked no one to do anything he would not do himself.
“He had many fine attributes but it is fair to say that his steel and determination was a key component in Down winning two All-Irelands in 1960 and 61.
“We in Down GAA value that contribution made by Kevin, he played a vital part in making us the county we are today, he was a man who gave of his best in any role that he was asked to fill, we are only the inheritors of a great tradition left to us by men like Kevin O’Neill.
“We extend our deepest sympathy to his sons Michael, Shane, Donal and Ronan, his daughters-in-law Sophie, Fionnuala and Louise, his grandchildren Grainne, Fearghal, Niall, Naomi, Tara, Natasha, Nalova and Tala, his brother Seán, sisters Maureen, Una, Bronagh and Veronica, whilst also remembering his late wife Mary and brother Brian. To his Club John Mitchel GFC we offer our condolences on the passing of a man who gave great service to his club.”

title: Bank of Ireland and PTSB raise interest rates on products for first time since June ECB hike
description: Changes, which are effective from today, follow recent moves by non-banking lenders
content:
Bank of Ireland and PTSB have raised the interest rates on some of their fixed-rate products on Thursday, making them the first mainstream domestic Irish banks to do so since the European Central Bank (ECB) began raising rates in recent months.
Bank of Ireland increased the interest rate on some of its fixed-term savings deposit accounts, while PTSB has raised fixed mortgage rates. The changes are effective from today, the banks said.
They follow recent moves by non-bank lenders, such as Nua Money, the newest mortgage lender to establish itself in the State, as well as ICS Mortgages, recently acquired by Pepper Advantage.
It comes weeks after the ECB increased its interest rates by 0.25 per cent in early September. The second time it has done so since June, it is expected by many economists to increase rates again in December.
Bank of Ireland said it has increased its six- and 12-month advantage fixed-term deposit savings rate by 0.25 per cent each and its 18-month offer by 0.5 per cent, the bank announced Wednesday morning.
Customers of any scheme can access “up to 25 per cent of their deposited funds during the term, providing flexibility should they need access to some of their savings”, it added.
“Existing fixed-term deposit customers will continue to earn interest at their existing rate until the end of their current term,” the company said in a statement.
Meanwhile, PTSB has raised its four-year fixed rate mortgage 0.2 per cent – the lowest of all its increases. The bank increased its seven-year fixed rate, three-year higher value mortgage, and three-year green mortgage by 0.25 per cent each, and its five- and three-year fixed rate mortgage rates by 0.3 per cent, respectively.
Among PTSB’s largest increases on Thursday were its five-year higher value mortgage, five-year green mortgage and five-year green mortgage of more than €250,000 – all by 0.35 per cent.
Bank of Ireland’s director of everyday banking, Carol Meehan, said: “These increases strengthen the returns available across our fixed-term savings range, while giving customers a choice of six-, 12- and 18-month terms and the option of accessing up to 25% of their money during the term.”

title: The long history of runners taking shortcuts in the marathon
description: There is an extensive track record of men and women somehow cheating their way to the finish line
content:
O f all the guarantees that come with running any big city marathon – tortuous muscle cramps, vicious blistering, hitting the wall, etc – there is no escaping the sense of deep satisfaction when crossing the finish line.
Assuming it’s all been achieved by entirely scrupulous and unassisted means. It may or may not yet have even entered the minds of the 22,500 runners who have signed up for this Sunday’s Irish Life Dublin Marathon , but there is a long history of men and women somehow cheating their way to the finish line, and most commonly by way of a simple short cut.
One of the last examples of someone caught cheating in the Dublin marathon was four years ago, when the organisers announced that a male runner – an off-duty member of the Garda anti-corruption unit – had been disqualified and his finisher’s medal returned when it emerged that he’d likely travelled a latter portion of the 26.2-mile course on the Luas.
The runner himself claimed this was largely unintended, as he’d willingly dropped out around the halfway mark, and only returned through the finish line to collect his gear. At which point he was awarded his finisher’s medal anyway. He might have got away with it too, had someone not pointed out that the second half of his marathon was run almost impossibly faster than the first half.
Dublin Marathon Group, the organisers of Sunday’s marathon and countdown race series, declined to comment on whether cases such as this remain a running concern.
In the meantime, there are now several running watchdog groups set up for the purpose of the protecting the integrity of the marathon. These include the Marathon Investigation website, started in 2017 by former US marathon runner Derek Murphy, and more recently the Official Marathon Time Integrity Unit (OMTIU), set up in Australia last year, who identify suspected unscrupulous runners on Instagram.
Trace the trail of marathon history, and the first recorded example of a cheating runner came at the 1904 Olympics in St Louis. Eight years after the classic distance was first revived for the 1896 Olympics in Athens, Fred Lorz from New York reached the finish line in three hours and 13 minutes and was immediately hailed as the winner.
With that, Lorz was photographed with Alice Roosevelt, daughter of US president Theodore, and was about to be awarded his Olympic gold medal when it was discovered he’d actually stopped running after nine miles, hitched a ride in a car for 11 miles, then started running again (after the car broke down). Lorz claimed it was all just a practical joke, and although initially banned for life, he was back running in time for the 1905 Boston edition. This time he did win, presumably by entirely unassisted means.
More than seven decades later, Rosie Ruiz was also greeted as the winner at the finish line of the 1980 Boston marathon, in an excellent time of 2:31:56. Suspicions about her victory arose immediately after claims that no one had seen her at checkpoints along the 26-mile course, and at least one witness reported seeing Ruiz enter the course at Kenmore Square, about a mile from the finish line.
[ Dublin Marathon countdown: Essential dos and don’ts before Sunday’s classic endurance test Opens in new window ]
Not so easy in the days of modern chip timing and Strava. Still, in last month’s Berlin marathon, the OMTIU reported the case of Yuanyuan Sun, a 30-year-old Chinese fitness influencer with more than half a million social media followers, who had been photographed sitting on the back of a bike during the final 5km. Only then did she admit to her illegal assistance and was later disqualified.
The Marathon Investigation website, which continually exposes runners cutting short or skipping entire sections of several major road running events, is also in the business of verifying some marathon results. One interesting example of that was in last year’s Berlin marathon, when Harry Styles finished in a highly impressive 2:59:13.
Although the former One Direction star was running under the pseudonym Sted Sarandos, Marathon Investigation confirmed his timing chip registered across all official mats, thus perfectly legit.
As for Sunday’s Dublin marathon, Gary O’Hanlon, the top Irish men’s finisher in 2017, who coaches groups of marathon runners every year, says he’s never come across anyone who was tempted to cheat at the distance.
“No, not in my experience,” he says. “There’s an honesty thing about marathon running, and most of that is just being honest with yourself.
“I can understand why some people might cheat on an exam, just to pass it, because they need it for a job. Or something like that. So they might think to themselves ‘if I could just get through this exam’.
[ Definitely a runner: Alan Milton on preparing for Sunday’s Dublin Marathon Opens in new window ]
“But to me, it just doesn’t make sense for someone running a marathon, who maybe wants to break four hours. It’s only you that’s being cheated on. They also think other people might be impressed, but they just want you to be happy. So if anyone is going out there to cheat, just ask yourself, ‘for what?’ Because no one else really cares.”

title: Andy Farrell goes with a tried and trusted formula for Autumn internationals
description: Ciarán Murphy bemoans the loss of Finnbarr Roarty to the AFL; a new book by Siobhán Doyle captures Ireland’s sporting past
content:
On the whole, continuity was the theme on Wednesday when Andy Farrell named his squad for next month’s Nations Championship , Ireland’s head coach largely sticking with his tried and trusted. “It may not be especially exciting,” writes Gerry Thornley of the selection, “but for the most part a relatively settled squad is generally a sign of strength.” There is fresh blood, though, in the shape of Ulster pair James McNabney and Jamie Benson.
John O’Sullivan profiles McNabney, the 23-year-old who has impressed since returning from the ACL injury that ruled him out for all of last season. He’s “some specimen of a man” said Farrell of the 6ft 5in, 18-and-a-half stone Ballymena native who was a member of the under-20s’ Six Nations Grand Slam-winning side in 2022.
It’ll be a busy old spell for our international teams, John bringing news that an Ireland XV will play Fiji A in Cork on November 20th in a double-header which will also see the Irish under-20 side take on Scotland.
It’s busy on the club front too, John previewing the meeting of old buddies Leinster and Munster on Saturday in the URC. “What a difference a year makes,” he says, 11 players from the matchday squads from Munster’s win in Croke Park last season unavailable through injury, and another six no longer contracted to either province.
In Gaelic games, Gordon Manning reports on the findings of the Gaelic Players Association’s Annual Member Survey, one of the more eye-catching ones the 63 per cent of players supportive of playing Friday night games - if certain conditions are put in place.
And in his column, Ciarán Murphy bemoans the ever-increasing loss of Gaelic football’s brightest stars to Aussie Rules , Finnbarr Roarty, the 2025 Young Player of the Year, the latest. “We have had winters where the spectre of our best young players being spirited away from us has loomed large, but this might actually be the time to start panicking.”
In football, what’s the latest on Manchester United? Well, let’s just say, ‘carnage’. As if being mullered 4-1 by Como in the Champions League wasn’t enough to be getting on with, captain Bruno Fernandes, who has been decidedly abysmal of late, had a dig or three at gaffer Michael Carrick in the aftermath. Mikel Arteta’s crew were somewhat more content after their draw away to Bayern Munich .
Finally, make sure you don’t miss David Gorman’s excerpts from a new book by Siobhán Doyle, Irish Sport in 100 Objects . From the 1527 Statute of Galway, which prohibited the sport of hurling, to the saddle Rachael Blackmore used to win the 2021 Aintree Grand National, it’s a very lovely trip through our sporting journey down the ages.
TV Watch: Séamus Power is in the field for the Bermuda Championship, and if he can find anything like the form that won him the tournament back in 2022, he’ll move that bit closer to securing full PGA Tour status for 2027 (Sky Sports Golf, 6pm). Premier Sports and TNT Sports have a bunch of Europa League and Conference League games this afternoon and evening, among them Celtic’s home game against Celta Vigo at 8pm (Premier Sports 1 and TNT Sports 3).

title: US and Israel draw up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after midterm elections
description: Donald Trump has repeatedly cancelled plans for a return to major combat
author_name: Julian E Barnes, Eric Schmitt, Farnaz Fassihi
content:
The US and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for renewed strikes against Iran after next month’s midterm elections , according to US officials and other people briefed on the deliberations.
As planning for a short but intensive operation progresses, the US and Israeli militaries have stepped up exercises, flying planes over Iraq to practice strike manoeuvres.
US defence secretary Pete Hegseth met prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu in Israel this week to discuss new strikes, US officials said.
The targets would likely include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal. Some officials say one more big round of attacks could push Iran’s economy over the brink and force the country to make diplomatic concessions after nearly eight months of conflict.
Still, there are reasons to be sceptical that a renewed war would be any more successful than the first phase of intense US-Israeli strikes between February and April. Those rounds of fighting drove up energy prices and inflation around the world, eroded security in the Middle East and severely strained the Pentagon’s supply of missile interceptors.
It is also far from certain Trump will approve fresh strikes. Repeatedly this year he has vetoed plans for a return to major combat operations, including this month when the US and Israeli militaries were nearly ready to attack.
All of the officials interviewed for this story spoke on condition of anonymity to candidly discuss military planning.
Iranian officials have promised to retaliate this time by expanding their targets beyond commercial ships and energy infrastructure in the region to data centres and underwater internet cables.
They say the fighting will be neither quick nor limited.
While the United States is assembling a large arsenal that will be fully in place by early November, diplomatic efforts have continued, as US negotiators use the potential return to war as leverage with Iran to make progress on their demands on its nuclear program and control over the Strait of Hormuz.
So far, however, Iran’s negotiators have been unwilling to make concessions on the nuclear program, insisting on deferring that issue until later in the talks.
Some US planners are convinced that an intensive three-day campaign could cause enough economic damage to change the Iranian position.
But US officials have frequently predicted Iran’s collapse, and other Western officials noted that Iran’s government has so far weathered the pressures on its economy.
“At this point in the war, what is clear is that the conventional military campaign waged to date, and the current punishing economic sanctions and American naval blockade, have not brought the regime back to the negotiating table in a meaningful way,” said Dana Stroul, who served as the Pentagon’s top Middle East policy official in the Biden administration.
Neither Trump nor Netanyahu “has made a compelling case for how more war would change this strategic dilemma in an increasingly unstable and conflict-ridden region,” said Stroul, who is now with the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
Israel’s election on Tuesday next could complicate the plans. If Netanyahu loses, he will become a caretaker prime minister, and it will be difficult for him to launch a war, experts say.
But some analysts believe that Netanyahu could leverage the prospect of an imminent joint US-Israel strike to pressure his rivals into joining a unity government to manage the war, which would extend his hold on power.
After Hamas attacked Israel on October 7th, 2023, Netanyahu formed a unity government that brought some opposition members into a war cabinet to help make national security decisions.
“He could use this to call for a broad emergency government, but he will face deep suspicion from his political rivals,” said Mazal Mualem, an Israeli political commentator and the author of a biography of Netanyahu.
“If Iran attacks, that’s one thing, but initiating an offensive strike would be extremely difficult for him.”
Officials say there is a small possibility that Trump could decide to begin a campaign this month, but there are many political reasons that he is likely to wait until after the US election, not least his own promise early this month not to strike before the vote.
The United States will not have its full complement of military assets – including three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and Special Operations forces – in place until early November.
The US military prefers to conduct attacks under the cover of night, and there will be increasing hours of darkness over Iran early next month.
There are also concerns that the war could spiral into a larger conflict. On Wednesday, the US state department ordered nonemergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, as the Iran-backed Houthi militia continues to attack sites there.
A White House official said Wednesday that the administration does not comment on military plans “that may or may not exist.” Trump, the official added, was keeping all options on the table to ensure that Iran cannot acquire nuclear weapons.
Some officials say the targeting will avoid refineries and oil infrastructure because Trump is eager to prevent even higher gas prices.
Both the US and Israel militaries are drafting plans for operations against Iran’s nuclear program, according to people briefed on the work. That could include an attack on Pickaxe Mountain, a deeply buried nuclear site that Iranians call Kooh Kolang.
Trump said last week that he was considering using a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, or Moab, against Pickaxe. Officials say Trump is enamoured of the weapon in part because of its nickname, “mother of all bombs”.
But weapons specialists say that the Moab explodes above ground, producing a wide blast, and would not likely destroy an underground site like Pickaxe, which is composed of granite. Military officials also warn that the bomb must be delivered by a slow-flying MC-130 transport plane that would be vulnerable to Iranian anti-aircraft fire.
Israel and the United States came close to striking Iran early this month, but Trump again decided at the last minute to postpone the attack, according to US and Israeli defence officials familiar with the details. The decision came shortly before the operation was to begin, after both militaries had made extensive preparations and placed their air forces on the highest state of alert.
The repeated planning efforts followed by Trump’s decisions against new attacks has caused “day-to-day whiplash” among military planners, said one commander, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters, as they try to stay poised to carry out whatever military option Trump decides in the coming weeks.
In each round of the war so far, Iran’s leadership has become less conciliatory, convinced that the ultimate U.S. and Israeli goal is to topple its government.
Iran’s new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, remains an enigma to US and Israeli intelligence officials. Some officials say he is not as powerful as his father, who was killed early in the war, and that hard-line members of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard make key decisions.
Iranian officials say they are aware of the US war planning and have been developing their own new targets and tactics.
Peiman Salehi, a political analyst in Tehran, said that if Pickaxe is attacked, part of Iran’s plans to retaliate would be to strike major oil refineries in Saudi Arabia, including Aramco, because that would immediately spike oil and energy prices.
“The war has made us understand that the best leverage for pressuring Trump is increasing oil and energy prices because it will hurt the American people,” Salehi said.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

title: Who is Storm Austen named after?
description: Meteorologist at the centre of a storm: Englishman Austen H Nagle was a ‘tough and very capable administrator’
content:
T he first storm of the new season is named after Austen H Nagle, who was an Englishman from Birmingham. He graduated from the University of London and went to work in the meteorological office of the then British air ministry, remaining there until he moved to Dublin.
He was appointed as the first director of the Irish Meteorological Service (IMS), now Met Éireann , in 1936.
The decision to name the first storm of the season after Nagle is in recognition of 90 years of the IMS.
Up to that point, Irish forecasting had been done by the British Meteorological Office, but the State’s growing role as a transatlantic air hub made an indigenous service a priority.
Operations began out of St Andrew’s Street in Dublin under Nagle, but it was not until 1941 that the service’s recruits were trained and it could satisfy increasing demand for weather reports on its own.
And it was not until 1948 that the IMS began supplying its forecasts to Radio Éireann, a service that was extended to newspapers in 1952.
According to the late meteorologist and Irish Times weather columnist Brendan McWilliams, Nagle was a “tough and very capable administrator”.
He stayed in his role at the IMS until 1948 when he joined the US Weather Bureau in Washington. He was succeeded as the head of the Irish weather service by Mariano Doporto, a Spaniard who had been on the losing Republican side of the Civil War and fled to Ireland.
Nagle went on to become the president of the World Meteorological Office Commission for Aeronautical Meteorology.
After retirement, he came back to Ireland to visit the newly opened Met Éireann buildings in Glasnevin. He died in 1984.
Storm Austen is the first storm of the season, which runs from one September to another.
It is coming to a county near you from Thursday night until Friday morning, bringing with it the prospect of heavy wind and rain to all parts of the country. The coastal counties from Clare around to Dublin will receive quite the battering on Thursday night into Friday morning and those counties are under an orange weather warning.
The naming conventions for winter storms are shared between Met Éireann, the UK Met Office and the Dutch meteorological service KNMI.
Met Éireann and the UK Met Office started naming storms in 2015 , with KNMI joining them in 2019. Each weather service gets to name seven of the 21 storms.
Storm-naming is a relatively recent development on this side of the Atlantic, though it has long been in use in the United States.
The convention makes it easier for the public to be warned about the potential dangers involved.
[ Never a dull moment in 75 years of weather forecasting Opens in new window ]

title: Minister wants role for Irish Navy in EU mission targeting Russia shadow fleet
description: Lebanon mission due to wind down early next year, ending five decades of Ireland’s presence in the region
content:
Military planners are examining significantly increasing troop contributions to an EU mission in Bosnia and a Nato -led mission in Kosovo as the UN peacekeeping mission in Lebanon winds down.
Minister for Defence Helen McEntee says she would also like to see the Irish Naval Service contribute to an EU mission targeting the Russian shadow fleet in the Mediterranean.
It comes as the Government progresses a contentious piece of legislation abolishing the triple lock , a legal provision that requires a UN mandate before more than 12 Irish troops can take part in overseas peacekeeping missions.
McEntee argues the triple lock is no longer fit for purpose and that it grants countries such as Russia and China – permanent members of the UN Security Council – a veto over the deployment of Irish troops. Opposition parties argue the triple lock is central to Irish neutrality .
Abolition of the requirement for UN approval would allow Ireland to take part in EU missions that do not have a UN mandate, including Operation Irini, a naval mission in the Mediterranean.
[ Triple lock Bill passes Dáil vote amid Opposition anger Opens in new window ]
Ireland previously contributed to Irini, including sending a ship to the Mediterranean in 2023. At the time, the mission had a UN mandate to prevent the smuggling of arms into Libya.
However, that mandate was withdrawn last May, forcing Irish personnel to pull out of the mission at short notice.
Irini has since been retooled to focus on combating Russia’s shadow fleet, a collection of hundreds of vessels with fraudulent registrations that are used to evade sanctions on Moscow’s oil exports.
Speaking at the annual conference of the Representative Association of Commissioned Officers (Raco) on Wednesday, McEntee said she would like to see Irish personnel return to Irini following the abolition of the triple lock.
“I had an opportunity to meet with some of the serving officers who had to leave immediately once the UN mandate didn’t continue, and what I heard very clearly is that we have not only benefited from our contribution to Irini but also we have contributed significantly.”
“I would like to see if it’s possible our troops reinstated there. There are 23 other countries that didn’t leave that are still part of that operation.”
Raco’s conference heard calls from military officers for the Government to find new overseas missions for the Defence Forces to contribute to. This follows the decision of the UN Security Council to wind up Unifil, the peacekeeping mission in south Lebanon where more than 300 Irish soldiers are stationed.
The mission is due to start winding down early next year, bringing an end to five decades of Ireland’s presence in the region.
Military representatives argue a new mission is needed to drive recruitment and retain serving personnel. However, the UN has not approved a new peacekeeping mission since 2014.
The Government is examining proposals to contribute to a new EU-led mission in Lebanon focused on training the Lebanese Armed Forces. However, any troop commitment would probably be much smaller than Unifil.
[ Triple lock neutrality row fuels fractious Dáil exchanges Opens in new window ]
Officials are also examining other smaller missions where Ireland could send additional troops. One is KFOR, a Nato-led mission in Kosovo where about 13 Irish troops are stationed.
The other is Operation Althea, an EU military mission to support civil authorities in Bosnia. Ireland contributes seven troops.
Planners are examining the possibility of significantly increasing troop commitments to both missions, sources said. Discussions are in the early stages, and no numbers have been confirmed.
Such an increase could occur even if the triple lock remains, as both missions already have a UN mandate.
Defence Forces Chief of Staff Lieut Gen Rossa Mulcahy said the drawdown from Unifil “will be a challenge for us for sure because we’ve been there for almost five decades. But it is not the end of our overseas service”.
He said the Defence Forces was looking for new challenges, and he would advise the Minister on potential contributions to future missions.

title: More than 70,000 people left Irish emergency departments before completing treatment
description: Figures for first seven months of 2026 show issue most prominent at Dublin’s Mater and St James’s hospitals
content:
More than 70,000 people did not wait or left before completing their treatment in emergency departments during the first seven months of this year, new figures show.
The issue was most prominent at the Mater and St James’s hospitals in Dublin.
A further 31,821 waited longer than 24 hours to be admitted or discharged in emergency departments between January and July, the figures show.
The data was obtained from the HSE under a parliamentary question, submitted by the chairman of the Oireachtas Committee on Health, Pádraig Rice.
The Social Democrats TD said he was prompted to raise the issue after speaking to an elderly woman who described overcrowded and chaotic scenes when she brought her husband who had cancer and an infection to a hospital emergency department.
Apart from the extraordinary lengths of time people were waiting to be scene, there was also the concern of the pressure hospital staff were facing, he said.
The 70,000 people who left before completing their treatment was a symptom of a bigger problem, he told RTÉ Radio’s Morning Ireland.
He explained that ‘not completing their treatment’ meant that people left before being admitted to hospital or discharged. These people could still need further treatment, he said.
“It is a huge number of people who haven’t gotten the care that they need.”
Rice called for further capacity within the health system. “We don’t have enough beds in our hospitals. According to Eurostat, we have the fifth-lowest per capita number of beds and we need to build that up.
“The ESRI say we need 300 additional beds per year, just to keep pace with the ageing population and the growing population as well. And last year we fell far short of that with only 196 new beds.
So in the first instance we need to build up those beds and then staff them and that’s a crucial issue.”
There also needs to be more staff and there was “essentially an embargo on hiring staff”, which had led to huge shortages and huge pressures, he added.
“Beyond that we need to build up community services to prevent people going to the hospital in the first place. We have a huge shortage of GPs, particularly in rural areas, commuter areas, and people end up going to emergency departments because they can’t get access to a GP service. People are waiting over two weeks to see a GP,” he said.
With GP visits costing up to €70, many people end up going to hospital instead, Rice added. “We have the most expensive GP system in all of Europe,” he said.
Sláintecare needs to be implemented with more focus on prevention, early intervention and keeping people at home, the TD said.

title: Joanne McNally is every Irish woman’s best friend. The begrudgers won’t make a dent in her
description: This brilliant comic deserves every opportunity coming her way
content:
E veryone I know refers to Joanne McNally simply as “Joanne”. If a Joanne comes up in conversation the assumption is that it’s Joanne McNally that’s being referred to, unless otherwise stated. I have a cousin called Joanne, and in a recent text conversation with a friend about a family trip I had to specify that “Cousin Joanne” was going, “not Joanne Joanne”.
Joanne McNally is every woman in Ireland’s best friend. The comic jokes that when she’s doing gigs she’ll regularly get Instagram DMs from audience members letting her know what pub they’ll be in beforehand in case she wants to join them. The thing is, it feels plausible that she might join you, have four wines while debating if it was obvious that you left your scarf at a lad’s house purely so you’d have a reason to get back in touch, and make it on to the stage to deliver a stunning hour of comedy.
When my best friend Joanne appeared on The Tonight Show with Jimmy Fallon this week it inspired a sense of national pride we haven’t felt since Jessie Buckley won the Oscar. We do so love to see Irish people doing well. Until, of course, it tips over into begrudgery. However, with the women of Ireland behind her, I can’t see the begrudgers making a dent in Joanne even though the higher you climb the harder they’ll try. And she really is climbing.
On top of the Fallon appearance, she’s filming her show Pinotphile for a Netflix special in New York next month, the first stand-alone special on the streamer by an Irish comedian. My Therapist Ghosted Me, her podcast with Vogue Williams, draws millions of listeners every week. She’s in Bill Murray’s BBC golf show A Course Called Ireland (which begins this Friday) and also joined a star-studded cast on this year’s The Celebrity Traitors with the delightful air of someone who’s not in the Scottish castle to catch traitors so much as to enjoy an all-inclusive holiday.
There was some scattered criticism aimed at Joanne when the Fallon appearance was announced, given the calls to boycott the American talkshow after Conor McGregor was interviewed and fawned over by Fallon in June of this year. Joanne was quick and assured with her response: “Imagine every single woman was expected to deplatform/silence/shrink herself from all and any public platform or professional opportunity cos it had previously had a bad man on it … he’s ruined enough women’s lives … I’ll be taking the opportunity.”
[ Lena Dunham’s Girls will be glorious again as long as it sticks to this one principle Opens in new window ]
In Prosecco Express, the show that preceded Pinotphile and ran for a record-breaking 78 nights at Vicar Street, Joanne used McGregor to help explain the class system in Ireland. At the top is Enya “in her panic room in Killiney”, the rest of us are in the middle and “down the bottom is Conor McGregor”. She joked during the show that there was always a twinge of fear that one of McGregor’s sisters might suddenly rise up out of the Vicar Street audience. It’s not beyond the realm of possibility given the numbers who attended.
I ended up seeing Prosecco Express three or four times between the jigs and the reels. Joanne attracts an audience that’s about 96 per cent woman, 3 per cent gay men and a meek minority of straight husbands and boyfriends. She relishes in her female audiences, saying recently in interviews that a male comic had told her that she’s really “found her niche” as if women wanting to laugh is a “niche”. Could you really call four upcoming nights at the 3Arena and a Netflix special a niche?
I do worry that if my best friend Joanne ever gets married or has kids, the women of Ireland will fall apart. Singledom and parenthood are common themes in her shows and she has spoken about freezing eggs or maybe having a “gayby” with her best friend.
Of course, we’d all be thrilled for her if she chooses motherhood, but is she machine enough to raise a chic baby while doing a hundred nights in a row? Joanne’s shows have a distinct and gloriously deranged mams on tour vibe, but where will the mams go if Joanne joins their ranks? Who will they live vicariously through? Can a woman, even our beloved Joanne, really have it all? (Of course she can, don’t be ridiculous, she’ll just siphon off one of Vogue’s nannies.) A funny woman who has it all. How niche.

title: Convicted gang rapists say trial was prejudiced by allowing woman to give evidence behind screen
description: Court of Appeal also told that trial judge did not give clear explanation in response to jury question on rape laws
content:
Three rapists who used a young woman like “an object that they were entitled to” have argued that allowing the complainant to give her evidence behind a screen was prejudicial to their trial.
Barristers for Anthony Hickey (41), Fabio Vicente (43) and Matin Zolfaghari (36) also submitted to the Court of Appeal that the trial judge should have given a clearer explanation in response to a jury question on the difference between recklessness and carelessness in Irish rape laws.
The three men were convicted in February 2025 following a trial at the Central Criminal Court . They had pleaded not guilty to offences which took place in a car and in a Dublin house on August 31st, 2019.
In a victim impact statement, the woman said the three men “watched my movements and took advantage of me and used me and my body as if I was an object that they were entitled to”.
The court heard that the woman went to a nightclub in the early hours of August 31st, 2019, where she encountered the three men, whom she didn’t know. The court heard the woman’s memory of the night was particularly poor and her recollections were limited.
She recalled being in the back of a vehicle, which she believed to be a taxi, with up to four men. The woman remembered being raped in the back of the taxi and thought she may have been raped there a second time.
The woman recalled the car stopping and moving, and that a man, who she believed to be a taxi driver, opened the door, unbuttoned his trousers and raped her.
The woman also remembered lying in a bed and kicking out while a male was on top of her. She woke the next morning and a man, identified during the trial as Hickey, was asleep beside her in the bed.
Zolfaghari, of Marley Court, Rathfarnham, Co Dublin, was convicted of the oral rape of the woman in the house. He was sentenced to 14 years in prison with one suspended by Judge Paul Burns in March 2025.
Hickey, a personal trainer with an address at La Vallee, Bray, Co Wicklow, was convicted of raping the woman in his then address in Dundrum, and of orally raping and sexually assaulting her in a car. He had 10 previous convictions. He was jailed for 16 years with one year suspended.
Part-time stripper Vicente, of Little Newtown, Enniskerry, Co Wicklow, was found guilty of raping the woman in the car and raping her in Hickey’s then home. He was also jailed for 16 years with one year suspended.
In launching an appeal against conviction on Wednesday, Michael Bowman, counsel for Hickey, , said that after the jury began their deliberations, they returned with a question as to whether being careless is the same as being reckless under rape laws.
He submitted that the jury had decided that recklessness and carelessness were linked and couldn’t determine where they overlapped, with the trial judge then repeating verbatim the same charge he had given the jury days before, which may have caused the issue in the first place.
Judge Patrick McCarthy pointed out that the trial judge replied to the jury that recklessness and carelessness are not the same, to which Bowman argued that this was not enough.
“It required an understanding of what each term meant,” said Bowman, adding that somewhere along the line the jury had engaged with the concept of carelessness.
John D Fitzgerald, counsel for Vicente, , adopted a similar submission, saying that after asking whether recklessness was the same as carelessness under rape laws, the jury returned with “an instantaneous verdict”, so the answer they received must have been important.
He said that within law, recklessness and carelessness are a million miles apart, as carelessness does not contain mens rea (the state of mind or criminal intent of a defendant), so the judge could have been clearer in his answer.
Moving on to a second ground of appeal, Bowman said that an application was made for special measures to permit the complainant to give her evidence from behind a screen. He said that an investigating garda had told the court that the complainant had expressed concerns that it would be her “worst nightmare” to give evidence in front of the accused, as she was concerned about anxiety, stress and fear. The woman also told the garda that if she didn’t get the screen, she wouldn’t be able to give evidence.
Bowman said that the evidential basis was not sufficient to introduce the screen, as the witness’s vulnerabilities must be over and above merely being a complainant.
Judge Alexander Owens said that if the garda had expressed his view that the woman would not have been able to give evidence without the screen, the trial judge was entitled to take that on board, as these protections were to enable the witness to give evidence.
Bowman said the woman had vetoed the option of giving remote evidence via video-link, so an artificial barrier was erected between her and the accused. He said that the law only contemplates such a measure when there is no alternative option.
McCarthy said this as this was a case of “a gang rape allegation” in which the woman was to come into court and sit within a close distance of the three accused men, it was bound to be different from many cases and would attract special measures.
Bowman replied that the use of a screen was prejudicial, as it interfered with the presumption of innocence by portraying his client as a man to be feared.
Barra McGrory, senior counsel for Zolfaghari, said he wished to adopt the same submissions as his colleagues.
Counsel for the Director of Public Prosecutions Karl Finnegan said that the definition of recklessness given by the judge in his charge to the jury was word perfect, and when the jury later asked their question, he gave another word-perfect definition.
Concerning the introduction of the screen, Finnegan said the judge did not make “an off-the-cuff decision” to allow it but meticulously thought it out.
McCarthy, presiding over the three-judge court, said that judgment would be reserved to a later date.

title: Irish politics is in a fragile holding pattern, with serious stress tests ahead
description: Inside Politics: From triple lock to public sector strikes, the mood is ill-tempered
content:
Today is the last sitting day for the Oireachtas until November 3rd – as the evenings draw in, a grand stretch of time for trick or treating opens up for the political classes.
There has been no shortage of niggle in Irish politics in the few short weeks since the Dáil resumed sitting after its summer break – including in recent days, with the Opposition and Government going hammer and tongs over the triple lock and reform of the criminal legal aid system. The budget came and went without directly setting off any landmines, but was marred by conflict over RTÉ’s funding package – with whispers that relations between the Taoiseach and Tánaiste were very frosty as the finishing touches were applied.
At the major end of the scale, there were the public sector strikes – while at the minor (nay, petty) end, there was a confusing and bitter row over the timing of an announcement related to sports capital grants.
Polling suggests Irish voters are far from entranced with goings-on in Leinster House, with nobody generating much in the way of forward momentum. Just before the Dáil reconvened, Donald Trump came, rolled a few hand grenades into the room and left – generating much in the way of light, but little lasting heat. The EU presidency continues, without sparking much awareness or enthusiasm among voters.
The overriding mood of Irish politics is definitely ill-tempered – politicians will tell you the discourse remains as curdled as before.
There remains a seam of anger in Irish politics – and yet, compared with the angry autumn described in today’s paper by Europe Correspondent Naomi O’Leary, the pot has not boiled over.
For sure, we don’t have to look far back beyond Easter to know that dissatisfaction can take over the streets in Ireland. But Irish politics – probably for reasons to do with the application of billions of euro in public money – remains in what could be described as a fragile holding pattern, rather than tipping over the edge.
Will that maintain over the winter? Nobody can say. But will it be tested? You can bet your bottom dollar.
Read Marie O’Halloran’s write-up of the Dáil debate and vote on scrapping the triple lock (no Government casualties, but a couple of Fianna Fáil absentees were remarked upon) here .
Mary Lou McDonald and Michelle O’Neill were interviewed by the PSNI over Drumcree protests.
Eoin Drea writes on ideological drift and shapelessness in Irish politics , and warnings for the political centre here from Angela Merkel’s experience.
It’s the little things that trip you up, Albert Reynolds said. But can they also make a political agenda for Andy Burnham or anybody else? Finn McRedmond considers that question .
On the Inside Politics midweek podcast, Hugh Linehan speaks with loyalist activist Jamie Bryson, who spearheaded the campaign to secure a return of Orange Order members to the Garvaghy Road. Listen here .
The long weekend is nearing, and so too is the big autumn Irish rugby derby it brings with it. John O’Sullivan previews Leinster v Munster at the Aviva .
The last sitting day of the week opens with oral questions in the Dáil for Jack Chambers, followed by Hildegarde Naughton. Then it’s an hour of questions (Leaders’, Other Members’ on Policy or Legislation). Simon Harris is still on paternity leave, so Jennifer Carroll MacNeill is in the hot seat temporarily vacated by him.
In the afternoon Government Business will be given over to statements on Children’s Health Ireland .
Topical issues and a report from the justice committee on civil legal aid round out the day.
Here’s what looks lively in the committees on Thursday:
Meanwhile, over in the Seanad, Commencement Matters get under way at 9.30am, with Government Business given over to motions on opting in to EU counterterrorism measures.
Elsewhere, Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee is meeting EU commissioner Maroš Šefčovič in Dublin while former president Mary Robinson will deliver a keynote address on the future of international law in Dublin.

title: Meta ordered to pay $25bn in New Mexico, faces new class action in Australia
description: Company strikes deal with Zuckerberg to keep CEO in California
content:
A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms on Wednesday to pay the state $25 billion (€22.24 billion) after a jury ‌found the company had misled consumers about the privacy of their data, hitting the company with one of the largest financial penalties in US history.
The ruling came in a case stemming from allegations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm involved ​in Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent. New Mexico had sued Meta, accusing it of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data.
“Facebook’s wrongdoing – over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict.
Mathew found that a penalty of ​more than $219 billion was warranted based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion.
In a statement, CJ Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, ⁠makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Mahoney said. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to ‌enforce ‌new ​rules for what people can say online.”
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement after the ruling that the penalty was one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in US history.
Meta is also facing a class-action lawsuit in Australia that alleges its Instagram and Facebook social media platforms exposed ​children to harmful content and kept them addicted through algorithms.
The lawsuit, filed in Australia’s second-highest court by law firm MinterEllison ​this month, could be the first in Australia to blame social media ⁠for harming its users, particularly children and teenagers. It was filed on behalf of eight plaintiffs, who allege they were harmed ⁠by Meta while ​they were under the age of ​18, and are seeking compensation.
Separately, Meta signalled it was getting ready to bet more aggressively on the AI market, with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg telling investors that a pricey wager on artificial intelligence is delivering results.
During its quarterly earnings report Wednesday, the social-media giant boosted its capital spending plans for the year and announced a new class of nonvoting stock that could ultimately be used to help pay for acquisitions and other expenses.
After struggling to persuade investors to accept ballooning costs, Meta has made headway with its technology in recent months, especially with a new AI agent called Muse. Zuckerberg pointed to that progress as reason to keep ploughing ahead.
“Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we’re seeing velocity across the board,” Zuckerberg said in Wednesday’s report.
Capital expenditures for the year will be in the $135 billion to $145 billion range, Meta said, raising the bottom end of the range from $130 billion.
The new class of shares will be distributed to existing investors through a stock dividend. Holders will get one share of the new stock in what will essentially be a two-for-one stock split, Meta said. It expects trading of the new shares to begin in January.
The stock will also be a tool to help further Meta’s expansion. It will be used for capital fundraising, employee compensation and potential takeovers, Meta said.
It will also allow Zuckerberg, who is the sixth richest person according to Forbes, to potentially fund a multi-billion-dollar tax bill in the event voters pass a wealth tax proposal next month. The company struck a deal with Zuckerberg in exchange for a commitment to remain a resident of California, or wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, for ​eight years.
Zuckerberg, who has a net worth of about $240 billion (€213.54 billion), can immediately sell 20 per cent of ⁠the Class C shares he ⁠receives, representing 10 per cent of ​his overall economic stake in the company, allowing him to pay a potential tax bill without losing voting control.
Zuckerberg touted the success of Muse during a conference call with analysts, saying that more than 10 million people have used the service in the US and Canada over its first six weeks.
“Now that Muse has clear product-market fit, we are entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it,” Zuckerberg said.
Over the last year and a half, Zuckerberg has refocused the company’s efforts on advancing in the AI race. The push has included committing hundreds of billions of dollars to build out the infrastructure needed to support its models and overhauling its AI unit under head Alexandr Wang.
Earlier this month, Meta launched Muse Wonder, a long-awaited new AI model with “frontier capabilities” that its leadership said put it on par with OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude when it comes to coding or working through financial or legal questions. If Meta’s claims hold up to outside testing, and Muse Wonder gains traction with researchers and developers, it would mark a significant turnaround for the company, whose models last year fell flat in Silicon Valley.
The Muse personalised AI assistant debuted in September. It is designed to automate a range of tasks for consumers, including shopping, buying movie tickets and scheduling appointments. Muse quickly rose to the top of mobile app charts.
But that success has come with a cost. Meta noted that the AI agent requires a great deal of computing power. That’s one of the reasons the company hasn’t launched the agent globally yet.
Zuckerberg said that Muse should remain free for most people, with Meta making money through transaction fees paid by businesses, subscriptions for heavy users and customers who want access to the most advanced models, and paid tools for companies that rely on Muse at work. “If compute efficiency continues improving quickly for another few years, which we think is highly likely, then Muse will be highly profitable over multiple years,” he added.
Meta still has a lot of spending left to do before the end of the year. Even though the midpoint of its capital expenditures outlook is $140 billion, the company has only spent about $86 billion through the first nine months.
Meta also signalled that it will take longer to see returns from some of its newer AI investments, even as its core business helps absorb the cost.
“While these investments will take longer to generate returns than those in our core business,” chief financial officer Susan Li said, “the breadth of monetisation opportunities and internal efficiencies gives us confidence in their long-term potential.”
Meta is cutting costs elsewhere as it bulldozes money into AI. Headcount was down 15 per cent year over year following significant job cuts, and the company has pledged to narrow losses at Reality Labs, its hardware division.
Meta expects Reality Labs losses of as much as $19 billion this year, before falling to around $15 billion in 2027 as it reallocates spending toward other priorities – “primarily AI”. - Bloomberg, Reuters

title: Clare man (92) on trial accused of indecently assaulting two orphan girls in his care over 50 years ago
description: Alleged offences happened between 1973 and 1975 when orphaned girls were in man’s care
content:
A 92-year old Co Clare man has gone on trial for the alleged indecent assault of two orphan girls who came into his care more than half a century ago.
At Ennis Circuit Court on Wednesday, counsel for the State Sarah Jane Comerford told the jury that it will be alleged that the accused indecently assaulted two girls on dates from July 1st, 1973 to January 31st, 1975.
The man recently turned 92 and, at the time of the alleged offences, the accused was aged between 39 and 40 and the girls between seven and nine.
The man, represented by Patrick Whyms, denies six counts of indecent assault against one girl and two counts of indecent assault against the second girl.
Comerford said that the two girls were born in 1964 and 1965 in Co Clare and their father and mother both died years apart when they were young.
Comerford said that after their mother’s death, the two stayed with a woman they called their “aunt”, who was a good friend of their mother’s. The woman was not a blood relation but was a godmother to one of the girls.
She said that the woman married the accused in the early 1970s and the two young girls moved in to live with the couple in their marital home in Co Clare.
Comerford said that it was during that time when the two girls were indecently assaulted by the accused. She said that one girl recalls two specific instances of being indecently assaulted by the accused when she was around seven or eight: once in the accused’s work vehicle and on a different date in a bed at their home.
As a nine-year-old, the second complainant would wake up in the morning and jump into bed beside the accused and his wife and the accused would indecently assault the girl, the court was told.
Counsel said that the abuse ended when one girl was sent to a school and the second girl went to live with grandparents.
Evidence is due to commence on Thursday before a jury.

title: Weight-loss drug revolution proves ‘accelerator’ for Kerry Group
description: But weaker dollar hits revenues in year to date
content:
The surge in demand for weight-loss medications is proving a boon for Irish ingredients group Kerry, the company’s chief executive has said.
Edmond Scanlon said, contrary to predictions, the GLP-1 revolution was spurring growth across the business.
GLP-1 drugs refer to the new class of anti-obesity medications such as Ozempic and Mounjaro.
Many commentators predicted the advent of these drugs would damage traditional food and drink businesses.
“Three years into the mainstreaming of GLP-1s, I think we can now point to the fact that it has been and will be more of an accelerator to our business,” Scanlon said.
“The prevalence of these drugs, whether you’re taking them or not taking them, ... is driving a narrative around health and wellness that is better for our business,” he said.
Scanlon noted that Kerry’s snacking business grew by 17 per cent between 2024 and 2025 and “we expect further strong growth in our snack business in 2026″.
The reformulation of snack foods to reduce sugar and salt was underpinning the strong performance, he said.
“Consumers are demanding healthier products ... and we are well positioned to help our customers provide that,” he said.
Scanlon was speaking after Kerry reported “strong” volume growth across its three business regions – Europe, Americas and Asia/Africa – while maintaining its full-year earnings guidance of 6-10 per cent growth for 2026.
The company supplies tastes and ingredients to about 25,000 food and beverage manufacturers worldwide.
It recently opened a coffee extraction business in the US, which Scanlon highlighted as a major growth area.
The company said volumes rose by 3.6 per cent in the third quarter – which was ahead of the wider market – as the company’s strategy of targeting high-growth protein and health and wellness markets drove demand.
But the weakening of the dollar against the euro led to a decline in revenue over the year to date, with an adverse currency translation of 2.5 per cent for the period.
However, the company expects the impact of exchange rates to become favourable for the rest of the year.
Kerry reported strong volume growth of 4 per cent across its Americas operation, which accounts for roughly half the company’s annual €7 billion revenue.
“Within North America, strong growth was achieved in snacks through innovations and renovations utilising Kerry’s range of savoury taste profiles and Tastesense salt reduction technologies, as well as new innovations with emerging and retail brands,” it said.
Kerry’s European division saw volume growth of 0.7 per cent, with its Europe Beverage unit seeing “good growth” supported by new beverage innovations and the performance of low- and no-alcohol products.
At the end of September, the company’s net debt was €2.4 billion. The company also announced a further share buyback scheme of up to €300 million following the completion of the current buyback.
“While macro and geopolitical uncertainty continue to impact market conditions, our strong end market outperformance highlights the strength and relevance of our strategic positioning across our markets, channels and customer base,” Scanlon said.
“Our inbuilt business resiliency positions us well through this period, and we remain strongly positioned for volume growth and margin expansion, underpinned by a good innovation and renovation pipeline,” he said.

title: Avant Money profits rise 21% in first nine months of 2026 as loan book expands
description: Spanish-owned bank launched Irish deposit accounts earlier this year
content:
Avant Money , the Irish unit of Spanish banking group Bankinter , saw its net profit for the first nine months of the year rise 21 per cent as its loans grew at pace, driven by mortgages .
Net profit rose to €41 million, even after setting aside €17 million for problem loans and other provisions, according to a presentation from Bankinter that accompanied its latest quarterly results.
A spokesman clarified that the charge relates to the Irish lenders’ year-to-date credit impairment charge across cards, loans and mortgages.
“The overall cost of risk remains in line with our expectations at approximately 46 basis points, compared with 44 basis points in the same period last year,” he said. “The impairment charge is consistent with a growing lending portfolio.”
One basis point equates to 0.01 of a percentage point.
Denis McGoldrick, an analyst with Goodbody , highlighted that the lender’s “asset quality remains strong, with the Irish [non-performing loan] ratio of just 0.3 per cent”.
The company’s loan book rose by 26 per cent on the year to €5.6 billion at the end of September. The presentation did not give a breakdown of Irish deposits. Avant officially launched a deposit offering in February, months after carrying out a soft launch of savings products.
The company, led by chief executive Niall Corbett, became a branch of Madrid-headquartered Bankinter last year, allowing it to venture into deposit gathering with the benefit of the group’s Spanish licence.
[ Avant Money builds up €100m deposit book in first half after entry into savings market Opens in new window ]
Bankinter has previously said it expected the Irish loan book would be almost fully funded by local deposits within eight years of the launch of savings products.
“The strategic objective is increasingly clear: management expects Ireland to finance the incremental growth of its own loan book, progressively creating a more balanced local loan-to-deposit position rather than relying on group funding,” said McGoldrick.
“Alongside deposits, the bank continues to build out its digital banking proposition, with the broader strategy focused on acquiring customers and developing longer-term relationships rather than competing solely on deposit pricing.”
Avant’s interest income increased 21 per cent for the nine months to €103 million.
Mortgage activity also remains supportive, with Ireland and Portugal together accounting for around half of group mortgage origination outside Spain. Management characterised Ireland as continuing to gain scale while maintaining strong profitability and asset quality.
The wider Bankinter group reported 11 per cent growth in net profit for the nine months, to €901 million.

title: Elon Musk sets lower sales target for Tesla as it explores SpaceX merger
description: Carmaker reports flat revenue and falling profits as it pivots from electric vehicles to AI
author_name: Christian Davies, Stephen Morris, Kana Inagaki
content:
Tesla will aim to sell 5 million vehicles a year by the end of the decade as Elon Musk sharply lowers his ambitions for the electric vehicle business and the carmaker prepares for a possible merger with SpaceX.
The target is far from the chief executive’s original aspirations for annual sales of 20 million vehicles, which he first laid out in 2020 and quietly dropped in recent years – and aligns with his strategic pivot away from cars to robotics and AI.
“I think we’ve got a good shot of achieving” the 5 million vehicle goal by 2030, Musk said at an earnings presentation on Wednesday, adding that the company was adding more manufacturing capacity. Tesla last year delivered 1.6 million vehicles.
The company reported that adjusted net income fell 4 per cent from a year earlier to $1.7 billion (€1.51 billion) in the third quarter compared with the year before, slightly above Wall Street’s expectations for $1.6 billion. Its shares fell 3 per cent in after-hours trading.
Tesla has suffered from a drop in electric vehicle sales in the latest quarter as higher demand in Europe, driven by petrol prices, failed to compensate for the loss of EV incentives in the US under president Donald Trump. Revenue was flat at $28 billion, in line with analysts’ estimates.
It earlier disclosed it delivered 486,532 vehicles in the third quarter, beating analysts’ forecasts but was 2 per cent fewer than in the same period last year.
The result came after Musk on Tuesday announced Tesla and his rocket company SpaceX had set up special committees to explore a mega-merger between the two groups with sprawling businesses from rockets, satellites, social media, robots and cars.
Musk, who called the combination “a good idea” on Tuesday, deflected further questions from analysts.
There has long been speculation of his ambitions for a merger. Last week, he unveiled a “flying” sports car called Roadster, which performed backflips and jumps using cold-gas thrusters developed by SpaceX.
The two companies also announced a joint venture earlier this year to build a huge “Terafab” in Austin, Texas, costing tens of billions of dollars to produce chips for Musk’s autonomous vehicles, robots and orbital AI data centres.
Tesla retired its X SUV and S luxury sedan models in January to focus on AI-powered humanoid “Optimus” robots, self-driving golden “Cybercabs” and an electric “Semi” truck.
Musk said he expected to start delivering Optimus to companies outside of Tesla from the end of next year but cautioned that scaling would take time.
Tesla will also aim to deliver Cybercabs to customers by the end of 2026, but the company has thus far only managed a limited robotaxi experiment in a few cities in Texas and California.
The proportion of new Teslas sold in North America with the company’s supervised version of the Full Self-Driving software reached more than 75 per cent, boosting revenues.
Capital expenditure more than doubled to $4.7 billion in the quarter but came in much lower than expectations of $7.9 billion and $1 billion less than the previous quarter.
Finance chief Vaibhav Taneja said the company was cutting its annual capex guidance to about $20 billion from an earlier $25 billion by managing its capital more efficiently.
Musk has said spending needs to drastically increase to compete with its Big Tech rivals that are forecast to spend trillions of dollars on AI in the coming years. Those vast investment needs have also fuelled speculation of a merger with SpaceX.
Dan Levy, analyst at Barclays, said in a note: “While some questions remain on Tesla’s capex, which is tracking well below guidance, nevertheless Tesla’s AI growth initiatives remain intact.”
GAAP (generally accepted accounting principles) net income, which includes stock-based compensation and swings in Tesla’s investments in crypto and SpaceX, was 44 per cent lower at $787 million.
Its automotive profit margin, excluding regulatory credits, improved to 18 per cent while its cost of goods sold fell from last quarter, suggesting an improvement in core profitability.
Coupled with a reduction of capital expenditure for the quarter, that helped Tesla to report free cash flow of more than $1.5 billion, far above Wall Street expectations of a cash burn of more than $4 billion.
Earlier in the week, the company released its proxy statement in advance of its annual meeting on December 3rd. The document revealed that after a fierce, years-long battle over a Delaware court’s decision to rescind a $56 billion 2018 stock award, Musk’s ultimate victory on appeal left him in control of 19.8 per cent of the company’s shares.
The proxy also showed he is yet to achieve any of the milestones in a new historic $1 trillion pay package. Musk needs to increase Tesla’s market value to $2 trillion and hit one of a number of other financial and sales objectives to unlock the first tranche of the stock award, but the shares have fallen 18 per cent this year to give it a value of $1.45 trillion. title: Zimbabwe’s president stays put as succession drama plays out
description: Emmerson Mnangagwa (84) will remain in office after his term ends in 2030, as vice-president accuses him of following Mugabe’s path
content:
Zimbabwe’s 84-year-old president has secured his party’s endorsement to continue in office after 2030 when his current, extended term ends. But attention is already turning to succession.
When the Zimbabwe African National Union-Patriotic Front (Zanu-PF) met for its annual conference last Friday, it postponed the election of party president for two years until 2029. And it endorsed Zimbabwe’s president Emmerson Mnangagwa as its candidate at the next presidential election the following year.
Mnangagwa, who succeeded Robert Mugabe in 2017, signed a constitutional amendment earlier this year extending presidential and parliamentary terms from five to seven years, extending his current term by two. And the president will no longer be chosen in a popular election but by a vote in parliament, where Zanu-PF enjoys a huge majority.
Mugabe resigned after more than 30 years as president under pressure from the military and from within his party. Mnangagwa, who had been in exile after Mugabe fired him as vice-president, returned just before the military intervention.
Constantino Chiwenga, the general who led the military move against Mugabe, is now Mnangagwa’s vice-president. And at last Friday’s party conference, he suggested that the current president was following the same, dangerous path as his predecessor.
“What caused the Second Republic to be in place? It was meant to fix mistakes of the past. Are we not repeating the same mistakes?” he said.
Chiwenga was long tipped to become Zimbabwe’s next president but Mnangagwa has sidelined him and his allies, some of whom have been removed from the party leadership. And as the president has sought to diminish Chiwenga’s status, he has elevated Kudakwashe Tagwirei, a billionaire businessman.
Tagwirei made his fortune selling fuel but his interests have expanded over the past decade to include mining, manufacturing, construction and logistics. Sanctioned by the United States for corruption in 2020 and by Britain the following year, Tagwirei is the main financier for Zanu-PF and he has cultivated business ties with Mnangagwa’s family.
Within the past year, Tagwirei has joined Zanu-PF’s central committee and politburo, become a senator and joined the government as minister for economic development. This rapid ascent has fuelled speculation that Mnangagwa is grooming the billionaire businessman to be his successor.
The president’s patronage may not be enough to secure the succession for Tagwirei, whose lack of political experience leaves him ill-prepared for the intensity of party infighting at which Zanu-PF excels. And Chiwenga’s standing as a party veteran, his military links and his history of toppling a president means that it is too early to write off his ambitions.

title: Darragh O’Brien backs Phil Hogan for key UN post despite pushing for his resignation in Golfgate row
description: Minister for the Environment says Covid-era golfgate controversy that cost EU commissioner his job ‘is done’
content:
Former Fine Gael minister and EU commissioner Phil Hogan is an “excellent candidate” for the post of head of the UN ’s food agency, Minister for the Environment Darragh O’Brien has said.
O’Brien, who as Fianna Fáil minister for housing in 2020 called on Hogan to resign his commissioner role over the Golfgate controversy, said that issue was in the past.
“He did the appropriate thing [by resigning]. That’s done,” O’Brien said.
O’Brien and Hogan, who launched his campaign for the job of director general of the Food and Agriculture Organisation last week , greeted each other warmly at a Global Bioeconomy Summit in Dublin on Wednesday, where both were speakers.
Hogan is the official Government candidate for the post , which could see him return to public life for the first time since 2020.
He has worked in private consultancy since his second term as commissioner was cut short by the controversy over his attendance at a golf dinner while Covid-19 travel restrictions were in place.
O’Brien said this took place at “a very different time”.
“Obviously I was in Government at the time so I was involved in that and I am very aware of it, but I think Phil has extensive expertise, extensive knowledge and real skills and he would excel should he be successful,” he said.
“He’s proven his ability over multiple different roles in the commission and within Government, and he’s a person who knows food, knows agriculture and the food security side.
“He is an excellent candidate, and would be excellent in that role should he be successful.
[ Phil Hogan’s new consultancy offers ‘unique insights’... but you won’t find them on Twitter Opens in new window ]
“I think it would be a very significant statement for Ireland too that he can lead an organisation at global level. He’s of a different political hue than I, but I’ve always been impressed with his work ethic and his track record.”
Asked whether he felt he had the full backing of the Government parties, Hogan replied: “When did I not?”
He said he was “very confident” of his chances of being appointed to the role.
Speaking later to the summit, Hogan said if he got the job, he would seek to improve market access for innovators and entrepreneurs working in agri-food and related industries, particularly among rural communities.
He said the markets needed “clear rules, reliable standards and credible evidence around sustainability”.
[ Phil Hogan insists resignation over Golfgate ‘disproportionate’ Opens in new window ]
This would support business opportunities, jobs and local resilience in regions where the economy was dependent on natural resources, he said.
He called on the agri-food sector to support talent in Africa where, he said, many highly educated young people were seeking job opportunities.
He also said a renewed focus was needed on nurturing healthy soils and careful water management as “the foundation of all this”.

title: Bord Gáis Energy Theatre in Dublin’s docklands posts €5m profit
description: Revenues for 2025 dip compared to year before when hit musical Hamilton helped sales reach record
content:
The company that owns Dublin’s Bord Gáis Energy Theatre posted a dip in revenues and profits last year, accounts show.
Crownway Entertainment Ltd posted turnover of just under €17.7 million for the year to the end of last December, down marginally on income of just under €18 million a year earlier.
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) fell by 11 per cent to €7.2 million. Its pretax profit declined by 15 per cent to €5.02 million.
These declines for 2025, however, followed exceptional trading in 2024 when the hit Broadway musical Hamilton underpinned record sales at the Docklands theatre.
High-profile productions hosted last year included Book of Mormon, Fiddler on the Roof, Moulin Rouge, Dr Strangelove and Nutcracker.
Turnover comprised ticket sales and other revenue of €13.4 million and food and beverage income of €4.3 million. The company employed 56 staff on average during the period with total payroll costs amounting to €3.3 million.
Almost 600,000 people attended shows in the theatre in 2025.
Cash and cash equivalents at the end of 2025 totalled €22.5 million, up from €21 million a year earlier. The company closed the year with accumulated profits of €15.5 million.
A dividend of €18,900 was paid to shareholders, down from €56,400 a year earlier.
The company’s corporate tax bill reduced to €890,000 for the financial year down from €1.15 million in 2024.
Trading this year is expected to be “strong”, according to the accounts, helped by shows such as High Society, Matilda, To Kill a Mockingbird and Mrs Doubtfire, which have drawn big attendances.
Shows listed for 2027 include the West End hit Just for One Day: The Live Aid Musical, authorised by Bob Geldof , which is to be staged here next August.
The theatre is also to host Billy Elliot, Jersey Boys and Grease.
Crownway Entertainment acquired the theatre in 2014 for €29.1 million, purchasing the freehold three years later from Dublin City Council .
In September 2024, Crownway renewed the naming rights agreement with Bord Gáis Energy for 10 years. The sponsorship is worth about €2 million a year.
Crownway is a family investment company owned by husband-and-wife team John and Bernie Gallagher.
Entrepreneur Harry Crosbie had opened the theatre in 2010, but lost control of the property after his loans were transferred to the National Asset Management Agency following the 2008 banking and property crash.

title: Leaving Cert students: What you need to focus on at college open days
description: Curriculum content, college facilities, accommodation and public transport are key issues when sizing up third-level options
content:
Open days offer prospective students a valuable opportunity to sample college life – but preparation is key.
The country’s third-level colleges will bring prospective 2027 students onto campus over the coming months.
The opportunity to physically experience the college environment – even if just for a few hours – can help motivate students to reflect on their Leaving Certificate goals as they consider the next step on their lifelong career journey. It can also bring a greater focus to a student’s interactions with their school guidance counsellor as they work together to identify the most suitable course option to pursue following completion of their school life in June 2027.
The key to successfully making the transition to higher or further education is to concentrate on the suitability of the curriculum content, college facilities and availability of accommodation or public transport links, rather than the desired occupational area or specific job to which they may hope to progress following graduation.
That task can become the focus of attention in four or five years, when college life is coming to an end and the needs of the labour market, which is being rapidly transformed by AI , are clearer.
Whatever the nature of the coming open days, you should undertake some basic research about the colleges you are considering and their course offerings before each event.
After all, depending on the decision you will make, whether it is to start your post-second level academic journey in a local PLC college at level 5 or on a tertiary degree, or in a university via the CAO process, you are committing several years of your life to this next stage of study and learning.
For many, the process is already well under way. More than 28,000 students attended The Irish Times Higher Options conference in mid-September. There they benefited from talks by experts in the field of further and higher education at home and abroad, heard about apprenticeships and other training opportunities, and spoke to representatives of many colleges and courses.
Those considering third-level options in colleges in the Republic will have read the 2027 CAO Handbook online at cao.ie and are now exploring all third-level and further educational college courses on offer on qualifax.ie .
Of course, as outlined above, Leaving Cert students are not only considering courses offered through the CAO. Thousands choose to study at their local Further Education (FE) college, where they can secure level 5 and 6 QQI awards facilitating entry to employment or into those CAO courses that reserve a percentage of their first-year undergraduate places for FE graduates.
[ ‘I got to talk to people who had done the course or were teaching the course’ Opens in new window ]
In 2023, then minister for further and higher education Simon Harris introduced a new option outside of the traditional CAO: tertiary degrees. More than 80 tertiary degrees have been developed to date by the education and training boards and higher education institutions and provide transitioning pathways from further to higher education.
A list of degrees offered in 2027 and the universities hosting these programmes can be found at nto.ie . If attending open days at these institutions, prospective students should inquire about these tertiary degree options.
All FE colleges operate their own open days, often holding several such events throughout the academic year.
Several thousand Irish students will apply for courses in Northern Ireland (particularly those living near the Border), Scotland or, in some cases, England, notwithstanding the £9,790 (approximately €11,500) yearly fees. All general applications to Northern Ireland and UK colleges are made through the UK Universities and Colleges Admissions Service ( ucas.com ).
EU citizens can study in any EU country under the same terms and conditions as in their own country, and thousands of Irish students have in the past 10 years chosen to study at one of the more than 1,000 courses taught through English in continental EU universities.
