There are 2,000 students from the Republic studying in the Netherlands, as an example of the growth in this pathway in recent years.
These EU colleges also host in-person open days that Irish students can attend – low-cost air fares should help minimise the expense involved in going to such events. You can find out more about these events from the European Universities Central Application Support Service , at eunicas.ie .
When exploring college options, be aware that the course is only a small part of what you will experience when you arrive on registration day in early September next year to start college life. You will be entering a community that will help shape you for the rest of your life.
[ College entry system is rigged in favour of comfortable classes Opens in new window ]
In our personal relationships, we take time getting to know other people and every aspect of their personality before we commit to them. Selecting a course that will commit you to living your life within that community for at least three years should be considered just as carefully. The only way to evaluate whether a college is right for you is to explore all aspects of its life as fully as you can on its open day, and see whether it feels like a good fit. This is more than an intellectual exercise.
As a guidance counsellor and teacher for more than 40 years, I have dealt with many students whose minds were full of facts and figures about dozens of courses, but could not differentiate between them. They were lost in a sea of data, with no guiding compass to make the right choice.
On a college open day, you will see the institution put its best foot forward. The glossy brochures, the presentations, smiling student ambassadors, friendly lecturers and goody bags are all designed to present the college in its best light. It can be hard to take in the true nature of college life from such an experience.
You can, however, see through a certain amount of the perfection that a college looks to display on an open day if you take the time to dig a bit deeper.
If you are particularly impressed with a college or course after an open day, and are considering ranking their programme at the top of your CAO application list, then simply try to go back on an ordinary day and wander around to see if day-to-day normality gels with the aura of its open-day presentation.
[ How can incoming students get the best out of their first year at college? Opens in new window ]
It may well take the next six to eight months to clarify your thought processes as to where you want to launch yourself into the post-secondary world, but if you follow the advice outlined above you will probably find clarity by the closing date for final course choices, on July 1st, 2027.

title: ‘I had no idea that being pregnant increased your risk of getting a blood clot’
description: Blood clots can happen to anyone, but pregnancy and birth raise risks for women
content:
T ax consultant Alma de Bruijn was anxious right from the start of her second pregnancy, because her first had ended in miscarriage.
“I had an almost heightened awareness of how my body felt and what was changing,” she says. When she had lower back pain at 10 weeks, she put it down to being pregnant. However, she did drop a urine sample into her GP surgery to check it was not a urinary tract infection and that came back clear.
She recalls lying on the floor while working at home in south Dublin to get some relief from the back pain. But over the course of that Friday evening, “the pain started to travel down from my lower back down into my groin area, down my leg towards my knee. I had a bit of a weird cold sensation in my leg”.
Overnight the pain worsened and there was a little swelling in one calf. The following morning, their out-of-hours GP service sent a doctor to their house who, based on her symptoms, thought it was sciatica. He advised her to walk around as much as possible and make an appointment to see a physiotherapist.
“It didn’t seem like an unreasonable diagnosis,” says Alma.
Over the weekend she struggled to walk up and down the garden using crutches they had in the house. But the pain was getting worse and there was more swelling in one leg.
On the Monday morning she made an appointment with a physio, but also phoned her own GP, who suggested she come into the surgery as soon as possible. “She straight away pulled up the leg of my trousers and said, ‘I think you have a clot.’”
That possibility had never entered Alma’s mind; she associated clots with long-haul flights or extended hospital stays. But her first concern was what it meant for the baby.
[ Sing for joy: ‘One of the best things you can do for your mental health is join a choir’ Opens in new window ]
The GP advised her to go straight to the National Maternity Hospital on Holles Street, where she was already booked in under the care of an obstetrician. There she had an injection of blood thinner before being referred to St Vincent’s for a scan of the suspected clot. Her husband Bastiaan, who drove her there, could not come in because it was November 2021 and Covid restrictions were in place.
“I will never forget that ultrasound because as they moved the probe along and had to press it into the leg, it was just excruciating,” Alma says.
When three or four doctors soon gathered at her bed, she knew it was not good news. “They explained that I had a significant clot, deep vein thrombosis, that had originated in the vein in my right calf. It had travelled all the way up my leg and into my vena cava, which, as I understand it, is one of the major veins that makes its way up towards your heart. Their concern was to try and stop it from travelling any further, or from breaking off.”
Ordinarily, the treatment would be a very high dose of blood thinners, but there was a risk this could terminate the pregnancy. “That was really difficult to hear,” says Alma, who asked if there was an alternative or what would the consequence be of not taking that treatment. “They were throwing stats at me like, ‘If you don’t get rid of this clot or try to resolve it, there’s a risk that you could be immobile for life.’”
A vascular consultant at the hospital, who had been conferring with a haematologist colleague and Alma’s obstetrician, said she knew a radiologist at the Mater hospital who had specialised in clot management in the US and the technique of thrombectomy. This procedure would involve going in the back of Alma’s knee and, in lay terms, sucking out the clot. When she was assured there would be no risk to the baby, it was a “no-brainer”, she says, to opt for that.
“At this stage, it was a week on from my initial diagnosis and my leg was huge. I wasn’t able to walk at all.”
[ GLP-1s in Ireland: How weight-loss medications work under the HSE system Opens in new window ]
She was told it was the first time this type of mechanical thrombectomy, using this particular instrument, had been done in Ireland.
The procedure at the Mater, which was “traumatic enough” for Alma as the pregnancy limited what pain relief she could receive, successfully removed most of the clot. Taken back to St Vincent’s to recover, she was discharged in the run-up to Christmas. “It took me a long time to get back walking longer distances. And there wasn’t just the physical effects of having the clot, there was the psychological as well.”
But the rest of her pregnancy was well monitored and, as she was on blood thinners, a plan needed to be put in place for her labour. “I had a date to be induced two weeks before my due date. I would stop the blood thinners 48 hours before being induced.”
However, after the induction there was concern about the baby’s heart rate. “A decision was made to do an emergency C-section, which again was something I wasn’t mentally prepared for because all along the conversation had been that they wouldn’t want to do a C-section because of the risk of bleeding,” Alma says.
But their son, Zander, was born safely and “it was one of the best days of our lives”.
Alma continued on blood thinners, and also the wearing of compression stockings that go from her toes almost up to her hip for the next six weeks. However, when she stopped wearing the stockings, her affected leg became painful and heavy. “My vein is damaged, so the decision was made that I would wear a compression stocking long term and I still do.”
[ How can runaway spending in the health service be reined in? Opens in new window ]
She takes blood thinners before a long-haul flight and also after any surgical procedure.
Looking back, she says: “I had simply no idea that simply being pregnant increased your risk of getting a clot.” If she had, she does not know if it would have made any difference, but “maybe I might have got an earlier diagnosis”.
However, she considers herself very lucky. “I owe a lot to my own GP who acted so quickly,” says Alma, who is using her experience to raise awareness, as a patient representative on the thrombosis council within the Irish Heart Foundation (IHF).
Blood clots are the leading cause of maternal death in the western world, says consultant haematologist Dr Denis O’Keeffe, national clinical lead for venous thromboembolism (VTE), but such deaths are very rare, he stresses. The risk of developing a clot is raised during pregnancy, but is at its highest after the baby is born. In evolution, the most common reason women died in childbirth was because of bleeding, he says, so their blood clotting system increases in the post-partum period as a protective factor. This elevated risk of a clot issue can be heightened by factors such as a Caesarean section, or if the mother is unwell and immobilised for any reason.
The combined contraceptive pill (ie oestrogen and progesterone, as opposed to the progesterone-only mini pill) is also associated with a higher risk of clots, as is hormone replacement therapy (HRT) in menopause. However, with the newer option of getting HRT through skin patches, rather than orally, the risk is very low, says O’Keeffe, who is based in University Hospital Limerick.
Each year, about 6,000 people in Ireland are affected by VTE, ie a blood clot forming in a deep vein, usually the lower leg, but parts of it may break off and become lodged in an artery in the lungs, causing a pulmonary embolism. It is the third most common cause of death from cardiovascular disease, after heart attack and stroke.
Up to 50–60 per cent of all VTE cases occur during or after hospitalisation. Last year, the HSE launched clinical guidelines to improve diagnosis and care for patients with blood clots. They are known as “Eve’s Protocol”, in memory of Eve Cleary (21) from Corbally, Limerick, who died at University Hospital Limerick in July 2019, just hours after she had been discharged from the hospital following admission for a suspected foot fracture.
An inquest in 2021 found the cause of her death was cardiac arrest, secondary to extensive blood clots in the lung. Returning a verdict of medical misadventure, coroner John McNamara said it was clear that there had been “missed opportunities”.
Once VTE is diagnosed, the treatment is very effective and straightforward, says O’Keeffe. For most people, it would be an anticoagulation tablet; a thrombectomy would be extremely rare. “Here in the Midwest and Limerick we might have four or five patients a year that would meet the criteria for needing that treatment,” he says.
Long-haul flights of more than six hours are a minor risk factor but for people with multiple risk factors, “that may well be the final trigger”, he says. Those other factors include: smoking, being overweight, cancer and a family history of clots.
Women should know their risk factors, particularly going into pregnancy, says Emily Bury, an advanced nurse practitioner specialising in thrombosis at St Vincent’s University Hospital in Dublin. It is really important that they ask their GP or healthcare provider early on, “Should I be worried?”
Up to five in every 1,000 women will have a clot during pregnancy but that rises to 20 in 1,000 post-partum. “The strongest risk is there until the 13 weeks post-partum period and then it begins to abate,” she says.
While there have been strong, public awareness campaigns around stroke and sepsis, says Bury, who is chair of the IHF’s thrombosis council, “I think we’re lagging behind in terms of our thrombosis campaign”.
It is a situation they are trying to rectify, now that the IHF has taken over patient support in this area since the winding up of Thrombosis Ireland last year. “I think a lot of people don’t know that thrombosis is the leading cause of hospital-acquired, preventable death,” she says. Patients remain at increased risk for up to 90 days after discharge. The advice is to stay as mobile as possible, she says, to keep hydrated and wear compression stockings if prescribed.
The IHF has developed a “blood clot alert card”, which details signs and symptoms, to be given to patients leaving hospital.
It is also encouraging people to make sure they are risk assessed for thrombosis within 24 hours of being admitted to hospital. The IHF runs a nurse-led helpline for anybody with a clot-related concern or who is seeking further information.
Meanwhile, after Alma and Bastiaan sought medical advice about having a second baby, they decided not to try. Not only was the risk of getting another clot in pregnancy very high, says Alma, but if it happened in the same leg, she might not be able to have a thrombectomy again because the vein was so damaged.
The risk of permanent immobility was also increased.
“For that reason and for the risks,” she says, “we decided that our one was perfect for us.”
IHF helpline: 01 668 5001; email support@irishheart.ie .

title: Leinster and Munster face the same choice ahead of Aviva Stadium clash
description: Clayton McMillan and Leo Cullen must chose between tried and trusted or twist towards youth on Saturday
content:
What a difference a year makes. Put selection to one side and the most striking aspect of Munster’s 31-14 victory over Leinster in the United Rugby Championship (URC) last season is the turnover in personnel in the intervening 12 months since, which is largely attributable to the physical toll of professional rugby.
The two meet at the Aviva Stadium on Saturday, but as of last weekend, 11 from the matchday squads for last year’s game at Croke Park are unavailable through injury. A further six players are no longer contracted to either province. That’s 36 per cent of the total – albeit based on injury updates from this week, so that figure might come down – but it’s still quite a churn.
Clayton McMillan’s Munster arrive in Dublin off the back of two wins and a draw in their last four fixtures across the URC and Champions Cup , including the win over Racing 92 at Páirc Uí Chaoimh last weekend. There were no legacy injuries after Saturday’s game and there was positive news regarding players being on the cusp of a comeback.
Of those who were in the squad for the game last October, fullback Shane Daly (groin) is nearing a return as are loosehead prop Michael Milne (ankle), secondrow Edwin Edogbo (shoulder) and hooker Lee Barron (neck), who was a replacement 12 months ago. It’s unlikely that all four will make Saturday’s game.
Meanwhile, two of Munster’s key players from the game at Croke Park will certainly be watching from the sidelines this weekend. Outhalf Jack Crowley , who was outstanding in his player-of-the-match contribution in last year’s meeting, is out until the new year , and centre Tom Farrell is rehabilitating following shoulder surgery during summer.
Wingers Andrew Smith and Thaakir Abrahams have since left the province, along with Jean Kleyn and Paddy Patterson, while John Ryan retired at the end of the season.
Ethan Coughlan, a try-scorer in the 31-14 win, is behind both Craig Casey and Ben O’Donovan in the pecking order. If Daly doesn’t recover in time for Saturday, potentially the only returnee from Munster’s starting backline at Croke Park will be Dan Kelly.
JJ Hanrahan and Alex Nankivell were on the bench last October, as was Gavin Coombes and Jeremy Loughman, all four of whom will be vying for a starting role this time out.
Munster recruited South African hooker Marnus van der Merwe and experienced tighthead prop Kieran Brookes during summer. As McMillan has said, there is no arguing about their impact.
Then there is 20-year-old outhalf Charlie O’Shea. Injuries handed him an opportunity initially, but he has demonstrated impressive self-possession to complement his talent and courageous free spirit, rather than trying to fit in unobtrusively. Shay McCarthy shares some of the derring-do DNA. A natural winger, those instincts were obvious in his try against Racing 92.
Munster’s outhalf and three-quarter line on Saturday will be interesting and instructive. McMillan’s selections will be a statement of intent, irrespective of whether he chooses youth, experience or a blend of both.
In Farrell’s absence, Nankivell, Kelly and Seán O’Brien have all had a turn in midfield, the latter demonstrating his versatility by also wearing the 11 jersey. The 29-year-old Nankivell signed a two-year contract extension with Munster during the week to take him up to 2029. By that point, he will be Irish-qualified and has expressed his desire to play Test rugby.
Kelly should get a crack at two of three players from Garry Ringrose, Robbie Henshaw and Jamie Osborne, all of whom are in the squad announced by Ireland head coach Andy Farrell for November’s Nations Championship games. Saturday will be a massive game for him, whether he plays 12 or 13. Versatility is a double-edged sword. Kelly carries hard in traffic, but he also possesses the pace and footwork to break the line.
Brian Gleeson, Coombes, John Hodnett and Alex Kendellen have shared backrow duties. Seán Edogbo has grasped his chance, and his power and pace is likely to see him involved.
Leinster, too, could be much changed this weekend. Jordan Larmour and Jamison Gibson-Park are trying to shake off the remnants of injury, neither having played yet this season, while Paddy McCarthy and RG Snyman are out with long-term injuries. James Lowe has gone to Japan and Ciarán Frawley switched to Connacht , to great success.
Fintan Gunne, Caspar Gabriel, Todd Lawlor, Oliver Coffey, Conor O’Tighearnaigh, Josh Ericson and Alex Usanov have been given decent minutes to date, while Niall Smyth, Stephen Smyth, Alan Spicer, Ciarán Mangan and Hugo McLaughlin have enjoyed varying degrees of exposure in the URC.
For Leo Cullen and McMillan, the choice this weekend is whether to stick with the tried and trusted or to twist towards youthful promise in one or two cases.

title: Ardstone faces another legal challenge to plan for 562 new homes in Dublin 6
description: Residents of South Dublin suburb seek High Court review of planners’ decision on €69m site
content:
Builder Ardstone faces a third legal challenge to its efforts to build new homes on a site it bought seven years ago for around €69 million.
Planning appeals body An Coimisiún Pleanála gave the company permission to build 562 dwellings, including 56 social homes, at Milltown Park, Sandford Road, Dublin 6, in August.
But local group Cherryfield Residents’ Association and Dermot Murphy have asked the High Court to review the planners’ decision, saying it was invalid on several grounds, including that it contravened the Dublin City Development Plan.
This latest challenge is the third legal action taken by the organisation against different Ardstone proposals for the site.
It follows appeals against permission given Ardstone to build 667 dwellings there in 2021 and then to a revised application for 636 homes, which the commission allowed in 2023.
Cherryfield residents’ challenges to those earlier permissions at the site are continuing and at different points in the State’s legal and planning processes.
This leaves it open to the courts or the commission to allow either of those larger developments.
[ A 10-acre site in Dublin 6 exposes the depth of Ireland’s planning paralysis Opens in new window ]
Branding news of a fresh judicial review bid “deeply frustrating”, senior Ardstone director Mark Forrest said the proceeding was the only thing stopping the company from starting work on the new homes.
“We have revised the proposals to address concerns raised during the planning process, reducing the number of homes and building heights, and increasing separation from neighbouring properties,” he said.
“This reflects our commitment to bringing forward a considered development that contributes positively to the surrounding area.”
Ardstone has spent seven years working to bring new homes to Milltown Park, Forrest said.
Planners approved the company’s three applications, but residents have sought judicial reviews of each decision.
The developer has cut the number of apartments it proposes to build in each of the three applications, from 667 originally to 562 this year.
Judicial reviews involve a High Court judge scrutinising decisions of public bodies or lower courts to ensure these conform with the law and follow proper procedures.
Cherryfield Residents’ Association says the commission’s August decision is invalid as Ardstone’s proposals breach provisions governing density as set out in the Dublin City Development Plan.
The group’s lawyers argued in court documents that the planning body reached a conclusion “contrary” to those provisions and/or misinterpreted them.
Ardstone is one of Ireland’s biggest property investment and development companies. Backers include the State’s Ireland Strategic Investment Fund, which has placed €100 million with the business.
The builder bought the site in Milltown in 2019 for a reported €69 million.
It got planning permission for 667 apartments in 2021. Following the residents’ challenge, the High Court sent the issue back to An Bord Pleanála – now the commission – where it is awaiting a new decision.
The High Court is due to set a date for the judicial review of the 2023 grant of planning permission at some point this year.
Dublin City Council approved the current plan, for 562 dwellings, in April.

title: Budget was missed opportunity to provide disabled people with meaningful help
description: Cost of disability payment falls way short of what is needed and cannot be claimed by those who work
content:
Sir. – Since the general election in 2024 this Government has positioned itself as a champion of the disability and caring community, yet its actions do not reflect this.
After a year of protesting against disability poverty and the cliff-edge removal of the additional supports, the Irish Wheelchair Association, the Disability Federation of Ireland and Access For All Ireland held their collective breath on the announcement of a permanent cost of disability payment in the recent budget .
To say we were disappointed is an understatement.
Yes, we welcome a new permanent payment linked to the cost of disability, but at €500 it is €9,500 less than the lowest figure proposed in its own Indecon report on the additional costs of living with a disability in Ireland from 2021.
That official Government report stated a person with a disability needed an additional €10,000 to €15,000 above their nondisabled family and friends just to get by. We are not even close to that.
With winter approaching and the disability community needing warmer homes for their health and wellbeing, we will now see the community fall further into poverty and despair.
It seems no matter how much we protest against this gross inequality the Government continues to look the other way and ignore our pleas for help.
Once again, it proves to us that we really do not matter. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – We are working disabled people who pay tax and contribute to our communities. When the Government announced a €500 cost of disability payment, it left us with a difficult question: why are working disabled people being left out?
We welcome the recognition that disability brings additional costs. But those costs do not disappear when you go to work. Wheelchair maintenance, specialist transport, adaptive equipment, accessible accommodation, assistance and electricity are exorbitant ongoing expenses for us. They are part of our everyday lives, not occasional costs we can avoid.
We have to manage these additional expenses on top of the costs of living everyone is experiencing. Being employed does not reduce these costs or mean that our disabilities are less.
Yet the announced payment is directed at people receiving qualifying long-term disability payments through the social welfare system. Disabled people who work and pay tax are excluded, despite facing many of the same financial pressures.
We believe this is fundamentally unfair. Employment must be encouraged and supported, not become a reason to miss out on help with the additional costs of disability.
We are calling on Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers to meet us and for a cost of disability tax credit of just €500 in 2027 for working disabled people, equivalent in value to the payment announced by the Government.
This would be a practical step towards ensuring that disabled people are recognised and supported whether they are in employment or receiving social welfare.
The Government has acknowledged that disability comes at a cost. Now it must ensure its response does not leave working disabled people behind.
We want to continue working, contributing and living as independently as possible. We should not be financially disadvantaged for doing so. – Yours, etc,

title: Not even Jim McGuinness could persuade Finnbarr Roarty to stay – that’s a bad omen
description: GAA must stem the trickle of top players to the AFL now before it becomes a flood
content:
Finnbarr Roarty’s decision to sign a contract with AFL side Collingwood came out of the clear blue sky last week, one of those stories that genuinely caught you on the hop. He is a magnificent footballer, the 2025 Young Player of the Year and a fella who was going to be a cornerstone of the Donegal team for the next decade.
He may or may not be a better Gaelic footballer in a few years for his time spent as a professional athlete in Australia , but wondering how he might reintegrate to Gaelic football is the best-case scenario for Donegal right now. It is as likely as not that he has played his last game for the county.
Jim McGuinness’s greatest talent as a manager might well be getting his players to believe in him utterly and in his project. If the GAA could have chosen one person to try to plead the case with Roarty that his future would be better served in Ireland then McGuinness might have been the unanimous choice – and that’s before you consider that he and Roarty are clubmates.
That even McGuinness couldn’t convince him to stick around is a potent indication of the appeal of Aussie Rules to young Gaelic football players.
If Kobe McDonald wins Young Footballer of the Year next week, then the AFL will house four of the seven baubles given out in that category this decade after Oisín Mullin won it in 2020 and 2021.
Mullin’s progress in the AFL in the last couple of years, this season in particular, is one of the great Irish sports stories. He has shown an incredible facility as a tagger, a player sent out to try to nullify the opposing team’s best player.
And as James O’Donoghue astutely pointed out on the Football Pod this week, his success in that role is portentous.
Previously Aussie Rules teams would have gone for Irish players with ability in the air, more often than not the biggest specimens they could find. They are not all that common.
But if they see the benefit now in bringing over lads who are around 6ft with unbelievable aerobic ability and work rate, then they could have the pick of about 80 per cent of each intercounty squad and certainly anyone who plays in the “middle eight”.
We have had winters where the spectre of our best young players being spirited away from us has loomed large, but this might actually be the time to start panicking. Where this panic would lead us is another, rather more difficult question.
As usual when faced with these thorny GAA issues, I turn to my colleague Ken Early. His suggestion? “Excommunication. If you sign for an AFL team, then you and your entire family are to be excommunicated from the GAA, never to be allowed become a member again. You’re looking at me like I’m crazy ... you people used to love blanket bans.”
Early’s conviction is admirable, but I can’t help but feel it’s a little heavy-handed. Alternatives don’t exactly jump out at you, though. The GAA is pinning its hopes on recategorising Irish players , who are currently Category B rookies. If the AFL were to deem them Category A rookies then young Irish players would have to be included in the salary cap and take up a slot on the squad roster.
This would, in theory, make an Irish player less of a “shot to nothing” and might make AFL clubs think twice. But as the hit rate increases for Irish players, that may prove a small deterrent.
The GAA is apparently willing to bring back the International Rules as a means of stabilising the relationship, a return that would be regarded with, at best, a transcontinental shrug of the shoulders.
There’s a real hostility towards the AFL in many corners of the country. When Mayo played in Kerry in the league this year, there was a strangely worded banner, visible on the TV coverage, that read “AFL – Hands Off Kobe. Breed Your Own.”
I don’t really need my GAA banners to be quite so eugenics-coded, but they were preaching to the converted in Kerry as discontent over the poaching of their best young players is bubbling barely below the surface.
This is a specific GAA problem in one respect, and a societal fact of life in another. Young people will want to move to Australia, whether or not they have an AFL contract waiting for them on arrival.
There is no leverage the GAA can use to keep them here apart from the same ties that motivate us all: place, family, all that good “emotional blackmail” stuff. It’s not nothing, but it’s also not enough for more and more people.
If the GAA wanted an indication of what the All-Ireland senior football championship might look like in 10 years time then they need look no further than the Ladies Gaelic Football Association . There is no doubt the standard in the women’s game over the last two years has decreased as the number of players in the AFLW has grown.
No competition can bear the loss of nearly 50 of its best players. That’s not happening in the men’s game yet, but we’d be fools not to consider ways to slow the stream, starting today.

title: When red means go
description: Are both cyclists and pedestrians ignoring red lights?
content:
Sir, – Marianne McMullin has had difficulty finding the section of the highway code which exempts cyclists stopping at a red light (“ Seeing red over cyclists’ behaviour on our roads ”, Letters, October 21st). Always happy to assist; might one suggest it is a subsection of the piece that encourages them to cycle on the footpath. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Marianne McMullin (Letters, October 21st) asks which section of the highway code exempts cyclists from stopping at a red light. I believe it’s in the well-thumbed appendix that allows pedestrians to cross when their light is red. – Yours, etc,

title: Regulation of food industry is needed to tackle obesity
description: Drugs like Mounjaro are not the only solution to problem
content:
Sir, – The HSE is considering whether to make the obesity drug Mounjaro available to people with obesity or at risk of obesity with co-morbidities. There is no mention of a single measure to regulate the food industry that has caused this epidemic.
The Lancet Commission on 21st century Global Threats to Health just published its report. What was the biggest threat so far? Obesity.
The lessons from many Latin American countries and the UK are that food policies like taxes on sugary drinks, bans on food advertising to children, front-of-pack warning labels and healthy school food policies can make a real difference to persistently high levels of obesity.
The Lancet Commission also reported that a scaled-up global coverage of GLP-1 agonist drugs, such as Mounjaro, to cover 50 per cent of eligible people, makes only a small difference in projected increases in obesity. The drugs are valuable for individuals, but at a population level their impact is small.
Obesity is the biggest contributor to loss of healthy life years, yet no political party has any policies to tackle this beyond the hot school dinners programme. This has to change. Have Irish politicians the gumption to take on the food industry?

title: Safe as eggs in a Citroën 2CV
description: Apparently its designer said he wanted ‘an umbrella on wheels’
content:
Sir, – My first car was a “preloved” Citroën Deux Chevaux, complete with canvas roof. Though designed originally in the 1930s for the French rural community, who up to then did not have any suitable or affordable wagon, the basic model was still largely unchanged up to the late 1960s.
Apparently its designer said he wanted “an umbrella on wheels” that would seat two farmers, wearing their hats and each holding a basket of eggs and also storing 50kg of farm produce each, and get them over rough roads to market without breaking any of the eggs.
It must have worked. As far as I can remember, I, too, broke no eggs during my shopping trips in that quirky little banger. – Yours, etc,

title: Forgotten pension levies
description: Private sector pensions faced a controversial emergency 0.6-0.75% pension levy from 2011 to 2015
content:
Sir, –Finbarr Dolan ( Letters, October 20th ) refers to “pensioners left behind” and the anomalies between teachers’ pay and the old-age pension with a paltry increase of €10 per week.
During the financial crisis between 2009 and 2011, more than €20 billion was stripped from the National Pensions Reserve Fund (NPRF) to recapitalise lenders such as AIB and Bank of Ireland and support the EU/IMF rescue programme. The private sector pensions faced a controversial emergency 0.6-0.75 per cent pension levy from 2011 to 2015, which raised about €2.4 billion.
How eaten bread is soon forgotten when it comes to the retired people of Ireland who did get up early in the morning. – Yours, etc.

title: Newton Emerson: Were bad landlords partly to blame for race riots in Northern Ireland?
description: Riots drove out three-quarters of Ballymena’s Roma population. One in three left Northern Ireland altogether
content:
“Private landlord failures” bear much of the blame for the racist rioting that convulsed Ballymena in June last year, driving out three-quarters of the town’s Roma population.
That is the finding of a report published this week by Radius Housing, the largest housing association in Ballymena and Northern Ireland . It convened two forums this year, bringing together residents, community leaders, minority groups and voluntary and public bodies. Their testimony makes up the report, although it notes the voices of many victims are absent. One-third left Northern Ireland altogether, according to a survey by Ballymena’s Inter Ethnic Forum.
Witnesses were still able to pass on grim stories: teachers told of struggling to help families evacuate, and of children never heard of again, their belongings abandoned in classrooms.
The violence spread to other unionist-majority towns, and some unionist politicians were criticised for raising “legitimate concerns”. The time to do this is not during a riot. One year on, the report performs that function.
In June 2025, Ballymena was home to around 1,200 Roma, about 4 per cent of the town’s population and half of Northern Ireland’s Roma population. Many lived in Victorian terraced streets in a small area of the town centre.
The trigger for the riot was the arrest of two teenagers over an alleged sexual assault – the charges were later withdrawn.
But long-term residents had seen trouble coming for years. They spoke about rising tensions due to overcrowding, rubbish, neglect, crowds loitering in the streets, fighting and intimidation. Churches and other organisations made valiant efforts to help people integrate, but they were overwhelmed by the scale of demographic change. That change was made possible by the private rental market, as was the squalor that went with it. “Absentee landlords” bought house after house; multiple families lived at some addresses, and properties fell into disrepair.
Residents and community workers repeatedly warned statutory agencies of these issues and appealed for intervention, to no avail.
One resident was so fearful of a landlord buying the property next door that he remortgaged his own home to buy it.
[ Failure by Sinn Féin and DUP to agree Stormont budget ‘beyond alarming’, says NIO minister Opens in new window ]
Stormont regulates the private rental market, with most enforcement delegated to councils. Councils have complained of a lack of power over planning and Houses of Multiple Occupation. However, they scarcely use other relevant powers over building standards, safety and environmental health. Councils are responsible for street cleansing and rubbish collection, yet rarely upgrade services to deal with overcrowding. Noise abatement is another neglected council duty. Residents complained of landlords “profiting from a system that offered little enforcement or inspection”.
These are common failings across Northern Ireland and must be mainly due to budgets and bureaucracy. However, it must also be asked – and the report does not do so – if there is official reluctance to acknowledge problems in immigrant communities, for fear of appearing prejudiced or of stoking prejudice.
In 2018, the leader of the far-right Britain First party was arrested in Ballymena for distributing leaflets intended to stir up hatred. The leaflet complained that “many local houses that could have been given to local people have been handed out to busloads of [Roma] migrants.”
As EU citizens, most Roma had the same rights to social housing as British and Irish citizens before Brexit. Since 2021, EU citizens have been largely barred from social housing, forcing them into the private rental market. This created a worst of both worlds, with festering perceptions of Roma taking social and private housing. Agitators have continued stirring this pot to the present day.
The report identifies causes of the rioting beyond housing, including social media disinformation and lack of political leadership, yet even these tie back to disinformation and lack of leadership on housing. The report recommends reforming the private rental sector, improving communication between communities and establishing a “tension monitoring system”.
[ PSNI feared gun use by dissident republicans if parade went down Garvaghy Road, court told Opens in new window ]
All this may be worthwhile, but it is still no solution to a fundamental housing problem. How should a large migrant population be accommodated in a provincial town?
Buying privately is out of reach for the vast majority of migrant workers. Social housing cannot cope with immigration, even where immigrants are entitled to it. Only 1,800 units were started across Northern Ireland last year.
Care must be taken when regulating private landlords: they remain essential, and their businesses must be viable. Demonising them is dangerous as well as foolish – responsible landlords were threatened in Ballymena simply for renting to immigrants.
Denmark is approaching this issue with laws to prevent the formation of ghettoes, by capping the number of “non-western” residents in public housing estates. It is inconceivable that could happen in Northern Ireland, and indeed it may be struck down in Denmark.
But avoiding ghettoes should still be an aspiration, perhaps worthy of its own monitoring system. Ballymena’s problems had been evident for long enough.

title: GP services should not lose the human touch
description: People need to be heard, understood and valued
content:
Sir, – Dr Joe Loftus’s letter “ Corporatising of GP Practices ” (October 21st) highlights what is so important about the relationship between the GP and the patient.
We should all be concerned about the needs of the patient and not least the community where GPs work so hard and have a respected and special role to play.
The business model has taken over so many areas of Irish life, not least in the NGO sector.
As Theodore Roosevelt once said: “Patients don’t care how much you know until they know how much you care.”
We daily see the importance of giving time to people – people need to be heard, understood and valued. – Yours, etc,

title: Connecting Galway
description: Our gridlocked city cannot wait any longer for the BusConnects corridors
content:
Sir, – Eamon Ryan’s article “ Quiet scaling back of BusConnects is a travesty ” (Opinion, October 20th) states that Minister of State for Transport Seán Canney recently indicated that he wants to hold back on building the Galway BusConnects corridors until the ring road starts.
What an extraordinary sentiment from the Minister. Our city is in gridlock. The planned road is not necessary for BusConnects. To link the projects is to condemn an entire population to years more sitting in traffic.
Whatever about the road, we need BusConnects now. – Yours, etc,

title: No obvious indications mother who died at Bray home had suffered violence
description: Bodies of Bridget ‘Biddy’ O’Brien and Jamie McGinn discovered at their home in Bray
content:
The death of Bridget “Biddy” O’Brien (45), whose body was found with that of her partner at their Co Wicklow home on Wednesday, remains unexplained, as there were no obvious indications she had suffered violence.
Gardaí have not ruled out the possibility she was discovered deceased at the house by her partner Jamie McGinn (38), who may then have taken his own life in the garden, where his body was found.
The bodies of the couple, who are said to have “lived for each other”, were discovered at their home in the Cois Cairn estate, Old Connaught Avenue, north Bray , at about 8am on Wednesday.
The scene was immediately sealed off and the resources of a murder inquiry were put in place, but no clear evidence of murder has emerged. Gardaí believe nobody else was at the property when the couple died and are yet to find any evidence of third-party involvement.
McGinn had suffered wounds that were fatal but which may have been self-inflicted. O’Brien’s remains were discovered in bed at the same time, but gardaí believe she may have died some time before McGinn.
Sources said the results of the postmortems on the remains of both, including toxicology tests, were required before a clear picture would emerge.
The couple had suffered addiction issues in the years since they lost their two children, Jordan (4) and Holly (3), in a fire in Dublin in 2017 . O’Brien had been badly burned in that fire and though she survived, she suffered extensive burns that were life-changing.
The blaze was at a facility for women moving on from domestic violence, which they had been visiting. O’Brien’s cousin Anne-Marie O’Brien (27), her daughter Hannah-Paris (2) and her unborn son AJ also died in the Clondalkin fire.
Biddy O’Brien was the only survivor, and missed the funerals of her two children. She only learned her children had died about six weeks after the incident. During her long stay in hospital, McGinn maintained a vigil at her bedside.
Jim O’Brien, a relative and co-ordinator of the Bray Travellers Community Development Group, said the organisation was “devastated” by the deaths “of two very loved members of the community”.
“All we say at this stage is that we send our deepest, deepest, deepest condolences to both the families. They are both well-respected families and we offer all the support we can to them,” he said.
Garda Headquarters said the scene in Bray would remain sealed off for further examination by the Garda Technical Bureau today.
“The bodies of both have been removed to the City Morgue at Whitehall, where a postmortem examination will be completed by State Pathologist Dr SallyAnne Collis,” it said. “The results of the postmortem examination will assist gardaí in determining the course of the investigation going forward.”
McGinn’s drug habit led him to incurring a debt of €8,000 with a drug gang, which then pressured him into storing cocaine and cannabis at his home in Bray. The drugs, worth almost €200,000, were found during a Garda raid three years ago.
Although a 4½-year sentence was imposed, the final three years were suspended due to the exceptional background and circumstances of his life. The court was told he was a law-abiding person who turned to drugs to deal with the trauma of losing his children.
O’Brien was close to the Lynch and Gilbert families in Fassaroe, Bray, who lost 10 family members in the fire at a Traveller site in Carrickmines, Dublin, in October 2015.
Harry Gilbert, whose daughter Tara (27) and granddaughters Jodie (9) and Kelsey (4) died in the 2015 blaze, lives near the home of the dead couple, and knew them well.
“I would consider myself their neighbour. They were a lovely couple. I would talk to Jamie from time to time. They went through the same thing I went through, losing their two children in a fire.”

title: Finn McRedmond: Andy Burnham making TikToks about parking tickets seems to be missing the point
description: Why does politics feel more parochial than ever at a time when global affairs are king?
content:
I n 1974, Harold Wilson circulated a memo around the Labour cabinet titled Little Things Mean a Lot. The idea was to draft a list of low-intervention policies that would improve the day-to-day of the average British voter. He was concerned with things like the cost of pints and whether Britain needed another morale-raising bank holiday.
It is not the first thing that comes to mind when Wilson comes up – the British prime minister who famously said “the Labour Party is a moral crusade or it is nothing”. But Andy Burnham – who longs to inject the ethos of the 1970s into contemporary Britain – appears to have spent some time thinking about it. On Monday morning he announced a national campaign to crack down on antisocial behaviour on public transport – not violent crime or anything so serious but “headphone dodging”.
He is right to have identified an area of public life that has materially worsened in a short few years; if you are a commuter you will know how maddening it is when other passengers blare music or TikTok videos out loud from their phones. You will also be aware of how prevalent the habit is. I don’t remember that happening, say, five years ago.
Fine. Good thing to fix. But is this really the policy area for a prime minister to be pronouncing on? Ought it not be a little beneath his office? Well, the first thing to note is that Burnham doesn’t care. He is happily taking Britain to a place of parochial politics – he has also announced new measures to protect drivers hit with “rip-off” parking fines.
Then there is the campaign to remove hidden airline fees, to challenge bad customer service, to end auto-renewing subscriptions. All serious annoyances, of course. But I wonder if matters of such quotidian banality ought to be reserved for junior ministers, at least ... What is Burnham’s plan to improve the quality of Starbucks croissants?
The little-things-that-mean-a-lot approach to governing does not exactly meet the moment. Or put another way: why does politics feel more parochial than ever, at a time when global affairs are king? Ireland is not excused from this criticism either, but more on that later. Burnham has long made it clear that the local and the domestic are areas of policy that matter to him; unlike Keir Starmer (or Emmanuel Macron, Leo Varadkar or Boris Johnson), Burnham eschews the international stage. It makes sense for a mayor.
And fortunately for mayors, they needn’t concern themselves with wars in Iran or on Europe’s eastern frontier. Unfortunately for Burnham, he cannot elude big global crises by refusing to care about them. He might have had an idea about how he wanted to run Britain, but Burnham is slave to events just as every world leader is. Announcing a policy about parking fines in a jaunty TikTok video does not communicate that the British prime minister is taking these events as seriously as one might hope.
In this era of parochial politics, we might consider the triple lock debate raging in the Dáil . Commendations to Micheál Martin for acknowledging that the “world has changed” and that Ireland might want to think about adapting. The level of debate, meanwhile, is totally debased by the Opposition – utterly and credulously attached to a policy that is no longer appropriate or even in their own interest (these arch pacifists are rejecting a motion that would allow Ireland to engage in more peacekeeping missions, for reasons logicians will spend years trying to get to the bottom of).
[ The triple lock: What is it and why is the Government trying to change it? Opens in new window ]
In other words, this is parochial politics, too. It is a strange thing for Ireland’s left to do: at once wanting to be seen as a serious global arbiter on matters in Israel and Palestine (rightly or wrongly, the intensity of their posture reads as bizarre to many outside of Ireland) while shirking the actual obligations of being global arbiters. The longer Ireland clings on to the triple lock, the further estranged it will be from any European-wide conversations about the security and future of the continent. And I am afraid placards in parliament and mudslinging about Nazis does not – to repeat myself – really meet the severity of the moment.
As for the Government? It is not totally exonerated from accusations of parochialism. Yes, it is good that Ireland is having a conversation about its international role. But as anxious Lithuanians peer at the Russian border wondering what might happen tomorrow, the debate about the triple lock looks like tinkering at the margins of a policy that is unfit for 2026. What feels gravely symbolic to the nation (and rightfully so) appears navel-gazing from the outside. I still hope the Government is successful. Just as I would rather have a knife at a gunfight than nothing at all.
Martin has rightly – cautiously and sensitively, too – started a necessary conversation. But I look around anxiously and find a British prime minister making TikToks about parking tickets, and a Taoiseach adapting Ireland’s foreign policy 10 years too late. Nothing to worry about then.

title: The Universal review: A little bit of sauce would go a long way in this Michelin-listed Galway pub
description: Provenance is very strong at this cosy city spot and the food is good, but some tweaks would enhance the experience
content:
It’s that kind of semi-drizzly Irish evening that marks the start of autumn. In Galway’s Westend though, it’s cheerful under the street lights with punters enjoying a drink, sheltered under The Universal’s awnings. It’s even busier inside.
A bar runs along one side, with tables opposite. We wait a few minutes before realising that the empty tables are marked with place cards and so we find our reserved spot. It’s at the back, with a direct view into the compact kitchen, and despite being next to the storeroom with a constant flow of staff in and out, it’s pleasingly away from the main bustle.
Mark Gunnip has been head chef here since 2019, having previously spent years cooking in the US. His menu, recently earning The Universal an addition to the Michelin Guide , is strikingly simple, with four starters and four mains. Provenance is immediately obvious and I happily lock in on the most local dishes. The menu has a list of producers and suppliers, most centred around Galway, such as Bia Oisín for organic vegetables and bread from Magpie Bakery just across the river, but also going as far as Lost Valley from Inchigeelagh, Co Cork.
Our server is friendly when taking our orders but there’s a sense that they are overstretched, and this comes into focus when our starters arrive but we have no means to eat them. I manage to catch someone’s eye and napkins plus cutlery are landed on the table without a huge amount of finesse.
A jaunty pile of red and yellow Athenry heirloom tomatoes is as seasonal as it gets, the sweet flesh drizzled with a healthy glug of olive oil (€13). Kalamata tapenade adds the required saltiness, the overall dish staying light and fresh, with abundant sourdough for mopping.
My starter of Doonbeg crab is perfectly picked and lightly bound, without a trace of shell to jar my sensibilities (€19). A touch of espelette pepper, traditionally associated with the south of France and the Basque region, brings a gentle heat but ultimately it’s all a bit too simple, lacking an element of lively crunch or pickle.
After the fast arrival of our starters, the pace slows and we enjoy some people-watching from our corner table. I admire the solo diner a few tables away who is happily doing justice to some spuds and a bottle of red wine, while it turns out that our neighbours, like my companion, have ordered the black sole served off the bone (€36). They have been given a fish knife while my companion, randomly, has to be content with the standard variety. The fish is well cooked, if on the small side, and served simply with a drizzle of sauce vierge, which is just not enough for the fillet.
I figure that as I was in a pub I should order the striploin steak (€37), cholesterol be damned. It’s perfectly decent but could be better seasoned. The small knob of green peppercorn and mustard butter is the best thing on the plate and I just wish there was more of it.
[ Blackthorn restaurant review: Much skill on show at this stylish Galway bolthole Opens in new window ]
Sides are extra so we add a bowl of Kilkenny baby spuds with spring onion butter, which turn out to be a joy (€5.50). I recall many years ago enjoying a sensational bowl of potatoes with ramsons at JP McMahon’s nearby Aniar and I wonder if this is a Galway thing?
We share a dessert of home-made caramel ice-cream with Achill Island sea salt, which is so-so, missing the anticipated bursts of salty sweetness (€6.50).
The wine list is mainly organic, chosen by owner Conor Lynam, starting at €36 and topping out at a reasonable €72. It features a clever section of chilled reds, including cult favourite Eric Texier Chat Fou from the Rhône Valley. I order a glass of Clandestina, a natural Spanish Macabeu made from 80-year-old vines (€11), which is fresh and straightforward and suits the easy-going vibes. My dining partner is delighted to see Wexford’s finest, Yellowbelly Citra pale ale (€7.40).
In general, a little bit more sauce is a good maxim by which to live life. In the case of The Universal it would be the factor that turns good into truly satisfying. A bit more crunch, a bit more tang, an extra spoonful or two. That’s all that’s needed.
Dinner for two with a glass of wine and beer was €135.40.
The verdict: A strong menu of skilfully cooked local and seasonal dishes that could benefit from more oomph.
Food provenance: See above, and beef from Gilligan’s Farm in Roscommon, fish from Four Leaf Clover Galway and Glenmar Seafood, Kinvara lamb from Hickey Meats, game from Gourmet Game Clare, vegetables from Steve’s Leaves Organic Farm, Tribal Foods, Ernie’s Fruit & Veg and Shannon’s Eco Farm, cheese from Sheridan’s.
Vegetarian options: Good – three vegetarian starters and one main.
Wheelchair access : The pub is accessible, but the toilets are not.
Music : Varied with a focus on Irish artists and curated playlists.

title: Bank of Ireland ‘accelerating’ AI’s role in fraud detection and financial guidance
description: Bank says generative artificial intelligence tool has identified €55m in potential tax refunds to customers since April launch
content:
Bank of Ireland is “accelerating” its implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) across its services, with the new technology now embedded in the bank’s fraud detection software and providing customers with financial wellbeing insights.
“It’s a very exciting development,” said Prag Sharma, Bank of Ireland’s chief AI officer since October 1st. “I’ve noticed a real drive within the organisation, from top down and bottom up, to adopt this technology in a safe way.”
He continued: “We’re seeing this transformation across many aspects of how we do business today,” given the bank’s “rich ecosystem in the Microsoft base”.
“A lot of good stuff has already happened and I now need to accelerate that across the board in a safe manner,” Sharma said.
Recent developments attributed to AI’s role in automating processes include “circa 2.9 million customer transactions” being assessed by “AI-powered scam detection technology”, Bank of Ireland said in a statement.
The value of reported fraudulent financial transactions conducted in the State has increased in recent years, rising from €141 million in 2024 to €179 million in 2025, according to data from the Central Bank of Ireland. Last year’s statistics represented approximately one in every 10,000 payments made.
Bank of Ireland pointed to its “benefits finder” tool, a service that uses generative artificial intelligence to help customers identify potential tax credits, according to the disclaimer that appears on screen before accessing the site.
Launched in April, the benefits finder has been used 31,000 times and identified €55 million in potential tax refunds to service users, the company said.
“We use machine learning with data, both internal and external, to make sense of the data for our end users,” Sharma said. Its developers have “spent a lot of time and effort to ensure we have it right”, conducting “a lot of testing around it”, he added.
[ Bank of Ireland invests €10m in ‘tech-for-good’ fund Opens in new window ]
Bank of Ireland, which employed nearly 11,000 people in 2023 and is the country’s largest domestic financial institution based on the value of its assets, said almost 7,000 employees have completed training courses on how to effectively utilise AI services such as Microsoft Copilot.
This comes “as part of a major roll-out across the bank”, it added, estimating these practices save up to half an hour a day for staff who use the technology in their work.
AI-supported services have been credited with “significantly improving the handling of chargebacks”, the process of refunding money when a customer disputes a card transaction. “Over four in five cases are now closed in three days,” the bank said.
The technology has also been implemented across the bank’s contact centre, reducing call transfers by more than 40 per cent and providing “127 million AI-powered spending insights” to customers last year, the company said in a statement.

title: Anti-Semitism is serious enough without conflating it with legitimate criticism
description: Israel is a democracy that claims western values, and so invites the standard that it professes
content:
Sir, – In his letter (“ Being Irish and Jewish: I love my home, but I am so angry ”, Letters, October 19th), Nick Davis writes that he sees anti-Semitism at the core of Ireland’s apparent singling out of Israel for criticism. Without wishing to downplay the seriousness of this concern, it’s important to understand the issue based on the facts.
It is simply not true to say that Israel is singled out for criticism. You need only look at how far Russia has been excluded since 2022: kicked out of the World Cup and the Olympics, with its overseas assets frozen. Or look back to the 1980s to the treatment of apartheid South Africa .
Furthermore, even if we grant that Irish criticism is disproportionately focused on Israel, is this explicable by something other than animus towards Jewish people? I believe that it is. Israel is a democracy that claims western values, and so invites the standard that it professes.
It is also a major trading partner of Ireland and other western countries. This gives the Irish public leverage there that they lack over Sudan , or non-state actors in Nigeria , to mention the other contemporary human rights crises that Davis brings up in his letter.
Anti-Semitism is serious enough without conflating it with legitimate Irish criticism of Israel. – Yours, etc,

title: ‘Some specimen of a man’: Why Andy Farrell has faith in uncapped James McNabney
description: Ulster’s 6ft 5in solid young backrow is athletic and has excellent pace and footwork
content:
Ireland head coach Andy Farrell has described James McNabney “as some specimen of a man”. At 6ft 5in and 118kg (196cm and 18-and-a-half stone in old money), it’s a fair comment.
For those who have watched the 23-year-old play rugby, it doesn’t reveal the full picture, but Farrell was offering a soundbite, not a deep-dive assessment.
McNabney is one of two uncapped players named in the Ireland squad for November’s Nations Championship fixtures, Ulster team-mate Jamie Benson being the other. Ballymena man McNabney would have enjoyed a debut by now but for a series of unfortunate events.
Announced as a development player and brought to a training camp in Portugal in advance of the 2025 Six Nations , he was to occupy a similar role in advance of Ireland’s tour to Georgia and Portugal that summer, only to tear his anterior cruciate ligament in training.
It was a cruel blow for a player who had started 14 of Ulster’s 17 games, featuring as a blindside flanker and number eight, and it ruled him out for all of last season.
[ Andy Farrell names Ireland squad for Nations Championship ]
He played for the Ireland under-20s, part of the 2022 Six Nations Grand Slam-winning side, joined in the backrow by captain Reuben Crothers and player-of-the-tournament James Culhane.
The young flanker started three games in that campaign, featuring off the bench in a fourth, and played in the World Junior Championship last summer. The following season, he won another under-20s Grand Slam, playing 380 of 400 minutes alongside Munster duo Ruadhán Quinn and Brian Gleeson, scoring tries against Italy and Scotland.
He travelled to a second World Championship in South Africa as part of the side coached by Richie Murphy that was beaten by France in the final. Ulster gave him a development contract in 2024, having made his senior debut against Glasgow Warriors in November 2023, and it was upgraded to a senior deal in 2025.
It represents a potted rugby history, but as a sport, it wasn’t his preference growing up.
In a 2024 interview with the Belfast News Letter, McNabney said: “I used to ride horses. I also played rugby when I started Cambridge House [secondary school in Co Antrim ], but I didn’t play any mini rugby.
“I grew up on a farm, had quite a busy upbringing and rode horses until the stage of under-18s and more or less gave it up. I haven’t ridden a horse in ages now. It got to a stage where I had to decide whether I wanted to be skinny and ride a horse or put weight on and play rugby.
“So I didn’t really watch an awful lot [of rugby] when I was younger. I always had far more fun playing it than watching it. I did a sport called ‘Mounted Games’; it’s not that common in the North, but I represented Northern Ireland on a few occasions at Royal Windsor Horse Show, and I was on the GB team for a year.
“It’s a bit like agility on horseback, or relay racing on horses. It was great fun and highly competitive. Michael Black, who was involved with the Under-18s – I’m not sure of his exact role – told me I needed to make this decision or that it was one that was coming up.
“It was influenced by him, but it was also on me and there was no real pressure because at that stage I didn’t know whether I was going to become a professional rugby player or not.”
He stood out at school in rugby terms on account of his stature and strength, and played interpros at under-18s and under-19s before joining the Ulster academy and going on to achieve great with the Ireland under-20s.
Asked if he made the right decision to stick to rugby, he said: “Well, there’s no money in horses, I know that for sure. I’m happy with my decision and I’m really enjoying my rugby so far, so I’ll just see where it takes me.”
Farrell’s enthusiasm for the young backrow, having brought him into an Ireland alignment camp in August, is understandable. He shares many of the traits that made Stephen Ferris a standout with Ulster, Ireland and the Lions.
McNabney is athletic, has excellent pace and footwork, and loves collisions on both sides of the ball. All he needs is a chance, and that looks to be coming his way next month.

title: Eoin Drea: Ireland’s relationship with Big Tech is a bad case of Stockholm syndrome
description: As debate raged in Brussels about dependence on US tech firms, Google celebrated Ireland’s EU presidency
content:
I rish ministers should have paid far greater attention to the cautionary tale of the former German chancellor Angela Merkel . The arc of her cratering reputation since her retirement in 2021 bears an uncanny resemblance to Ireland’s decade of political drift over the last 10 years.
It also offers a warning as to how political stability – dressed up in successive coalitions of centrist parties – can distract from a much more dangerous reality. Namely, how the desire to retain power at any cost can foster an ideology-free approach to government.
This is an approach that favours easy political fixes – preferably with bags of extra cash – over actual economic or political reform.
Take Fine Gael . Its longevity – it has been in power since 2011 – correlates to its abandonment of any discernible centre-right ideology. The party’s last vestiges of financial prudence were pushed out the door along with Enda Kenny in 2017.
Analysis from the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council shows that Ireland has – and continues to spend – close to 90 per cent of its bumper (and highly unstable) corporate tax receipts. Between 2022 and 2025 alone, Ireland recorded €50 billion in budget surpluses, with no discernible improvement in public services.
Irish public spending has doubled in just 10 years. If that’s fiscal rectitude, I’d hate to see us do fiscal prolificacy. But wait, didn’t we already bankrupt ourselves in 2010?
A traditional, soft-right conservatism has been replaced by successive leaders for whom policy development is, and never will be, a policy priority.
The result – as in Germany under 16 years of Merkel rule – is no meaningful economic reform agenda. Just as Merkel doubled down on cheap Russian gas and exports to China to keep the economy solvent, Ireland burrows deeper every year into our financial dependencies on United States technology and pharmaceutical companies. Neither approach was, or is, sustainable in the long run.
Ireland’s lack of vision is all too apparent to onlookers in Brussels, where we are often seen as tax haven opportunists happily in bed with US multinationals. We are increasingly viewed as a freeloader on defence, too.
Our constant preaching about our “Europeaness” barely conceals a lack of vision for Europe’s future. This is a remarkable characteristic shared across Ireland’s political spectrum.
And recently it has led to some paradoxical situations such as the one in early October here in Brussels. As debate was intensifying about how to lessen the European Union’s dependence on US tech companies, Google was busy throwing a party to celebrate Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the EU. On the guest list were a host of digital industry figures. The guest of honour was the Irish Commissioner Michael McGrath .
Outside, across the Rue d’Arlon, academics waved placards and protested against what they saw as Ireland’s incestuous relationship with Big Tech.
“When states become captured by corporations, then of course they can’t take decisions in the interest of citizens,” one – Benedetta Brevini, a professor of platforms and society at KU Leuven, and one of 50 academics who recently signed an open letter to the Financial Times on the theme – told the Brussels Times.
And while EU states debate how to reduce children’s access to addictive social media platforms, Meta’s Dublin office hosts a full-day event on “Ireland as a trusted digital regulatory hub”, featuring, it said, “regulators, government departments, industry and practitioners in one room ”.
As noted by Johnny Ryan of the Irish Council for Civil Liberties , one of the speakers was Ireland’s former data regulator, Helen Dixon, who now works for a law firm that represents Meta .
Where our relationship with Big Tech is concerned, the Irish Government is suffering such a bad case of Stockholm syndrome we don’t even realise we’ve been kidnapped.
The ability of policymakers to ignore likely negative outcomes should never be underestimated. Take the cautionary tale of Merkel again.
When she left office in 2021, she was heralded as one of Europe’s most consequential leaders. After all, even Covid couldn’t distract from the win-win of cheap energy and lots of cars. Yet now, disavowing her legacy is about the only thing that unites all German political parties – including her own.
Like Ireland, across a whole host of issues, Merkel-led governments favoured inaction, delay and prevarication over forward looking, growth-stimulating policies.
Instead of delivering on successive campaign promises to improve Germany’s notoriously dated digital infrastructure, German health authorities faced into Covid depending on fax machines and some of the slowest internet speeds in Europe. Despite a decade of low public debt and zero interest rates, Merkelism failed to invest in Germany’s ageing and decaying physical infrastructure.
The result since she left office was a German recession in 2023 and 2024, declining manufacturing output, some of the most expensive energy prices in Europe, its heavy industry tackling multiple crises and the state belatedly trying to pump the economy with investment. After deliberately starving their armed forces of appropriate resources, Berlin is now attempting to patch up the damage.
Worryingly for Ireland, the Merkel effect illustrates how repeated but slowly diminishing coalitions of the political centre can fuel even more extreme public discontent and distrust. Because as the centrist parties merge into one in the public consciousness, the political extremes may seem to offer the only viable alternative.
The inability to make hard economic decisions has also become a characteristic of Irish coalition governments since 2017. Regardless of the crisis – fuel protests, unhappy farmers or constant chronic overspending in the health service – the default response is more money and no reform.
But the biggest lesson of Merkelism for Ireland is that periods of relative political and economic calm should not be wasted. Germany stood still while China ate its lunch, lack of spending corroded its infrastructure and a failure to plan long-term diminished public support for what passed as an immigration strategy. The question is not why are extreme parties doing so well in Germany in 2026, but rather, why did no one see them coming?
Ireland has similarly squandered the last decade of unprecedented financial health. Most of our corporate tax receipts were spent covering day-to-day spending in areas such as health and education without discernible improvements in service. Delivery on badly needed infrastructure remains slow, expensive and ridiculously bureaucratic.
Not even a pandemic, Donald Trump or war in Ukraine has changed the Irish approach. And this is while Irish citizens suffer from among the highest electricity prices in Europe while seven in 10 of our 18 to 24-year-olds consider emigrating. Every year, the productivity of our indigenous small businesses falls further behind the multinational giants.
This is what politics looks like when all semblance of ideology has long since vanished. It’s also a German warning for Ireland’s coming – and maybe even inevitable – economic crisis.
Eoin Drea is a senior researcher at the Wilfried Martens Centre, the official think tank of the European People’s Party, of which Fine Gael is a member

title: What is the best way to transfer trust fund to our daughter when she turns 18?
description: We need guidance on how to transfer funds to our daughter in a way that best serves her needs
content:
Q: Our wonderful daughter, who has a mild general learning delay and attends a special school, is about to turn 18. I’m struggling with the arrangements we need to put in place for her.
We have used the annual €3,000 small gift exemption for many years and the resulting fund is held in bare trust for her benefit.
We need guidance on how to transfer it to her in a way that best serves her. In our will, she will equally share our estate with her two siblings in time.
A: The parents have used the small gift exemption here to good effect. This is where anyone can give someone else €3,000 a year, tax-free. That’s a potential gift of €6,000 per calendar year from two parents without reducing a child’s lifetime Capital Acquisitions Tax (CAT) threshold.
This money has been accumulating in a bare trust for their daughter’s benefit.
Parents considering gifting money in this way should ensure the account is designated as a trust at the outset, says Greg Flanagan, solicitor, and partner at Lavelle Partners.
If it’s simply in a bank account in a parent’s name, Revenue may refuse to recognise it as being in trust for the child, he says. This will have tax implications.
[ Inheritance tax reform could unlock €170bn sitting on deposit, expert says Opens in new window ]
The beneficiary of a bare trust is the true owner of the assets, says Catriona Coady, head of tax at Goodbody .
“The trustees merely hold and administer the assets until the beneficiary is legally entitled to take control of them, typically age 18 in the case of a child,” Coady explains.
“Some immediate practical steps these parents can take now are to review the bare trust arrangement, confirm the balance and investment ownership, and plan with their daughter how the account will operate when she turns 18.”
Depending on her needs and wishes, the family could consider a supported bank account, proportionate spending controls agreed with her, a decision-making assistance or co-decision-making agreement, and an enduring power of attorney made by her if she has the required capacity, says Coady.
The reader indicates that in time, her three children will inherit the parents’ estate in equal parts.
Using a discretionary trust may be particularly suitable for this future inheritance, Coady says.
Rather than leaving her a one-third share outright, the parents could revise their will so that her intended share passes to trustees who can apply the assets for her housing, care, education, therapies and wider support, while making controlled payments over time, according to Coady.
These trustees would have full discretion about when and how the daughter receives the money, so it is important that trustees are people who you trust.
Typically, the parents would write a “letter of wishes” to guide the trustees. Although the letter is not legally binding, it is an important guide to the parents’ intentions.
But the existing bare trust fund is different. As the daughter is already the beneficial owner, the parents cannot unilaterally transfer her money into a discretionary trust, Coady says.
“If, once she is 18, she has capacity to make this specific decision, she could choose to settle some or all of the fund into a new trust, but she should receive independent legal advice and understand that she would be giving up an unrestricted entitlement in favour of trustee discretion,” Coady adds.
Her agreement must be voluntary and properly informed. Having a mild learning delay does not of itself mean that someone lacks capacity.
“Capacity is presumed and is assessed in relation to the particular decision, with appropriate support,” Coady says.
[ All inheritance tax-free thresholds rise in the budget but no wider reforms Opens in new window ]
“If she lacks capacity to decide whether to place her existing property in a discretionary trust, her parents cannot simply consent on her behalf.”
Advice would be needed on the supported decision-making arrangements available under the assisted decision-making framework.
Any proposal that removes her existing absolute entitlement to the bare trust would require careful scrutiny, Coady says.
‘Payments of trust income may also have income tax implications for the trustees and/or the daughter, depending on how the payment is made and its source’
Before any transfer to a discretionary trust is considered, the family should obtain professional advice to determine the legal, tax and social welfare implications of the daughter’s particular circumstances.
However, one of the major benefits of a discretionary trust created under her parents’ will is that for a child with additional needs, their entitlement to State supports such as social welfare, a medical card and disability benefits may be protected. These supports are means-tested.
While assets retained in a discretionary trust are not generally owned by the child, any money or assets paid or appointed to her could become her income or capital and may affect her eligibility for means-tested support.
Get advice before distributions are made, Coady advises.
A discretionary trust is normally subject to tax of 6 per cent of the capital value of the trust fund in year one, and 1 per cent of the capital value for each year afterwards, for as long as the trust continues. If the beneficiary has additional needs and the trust is set up exclusively for them, a discretionary trust tax exemption may apply.
To qualify, Revenue usually requires a medical report or letter from a doctor confirming the child is incapable of managing their own affairs, says Flanagan.
[ Can I avoid capital gains tax on a rental property by gifting it to my child? Opens in new window ]
When assets are eventually distributed or appointed out of the trust to a beneficiary, standard gift or inheritance tax rules and thresholds still apply at a rate of 33 per cent on amounts above the child’s €420,000 tax-free threshold, regardless of disability, Flanagan says.
However, depending on the nature and purpose of a payment from the trust, it may be CAT exempt – for example, where funds are used for the beneficiary’s qualifying support and maintenance, or for qualifying expenses related to medical care.
Payments of trust income may also have income tax implications for the trustees and/or the daughter, depending on how the payment is made and its source, so specific tax advice should be taken, Coady says.
The parents might also want to consider the dwelling house exemption – this would allow their daughter to receive the parents’ main home, lived in until the time of their death, tax-free if certain conditions are met, Flanagan says.
If the daughter has occupied this as her main home three years before the date of inheritance, and will continue to do so for at least six years after, and she doesn’t have an interest in another residential property at the date of inheritance or the valuation date – in her own right or in her parents’ will – she could inherit the property tax-free.
The name of the reader who submitted the question is not being published to protect the identities of those involved.
