Please send your legal queries to Joanne Hunt, Ask the Lawyer, The Irish Times, 24-28 Tara Street, Dublin 2, or by email to joanne.hunt@irishtimes.com with a contact phone number. This column is a reader service and is not intended to replace professional advice.

title: Storm Austen: Unions confirm council staff on industrial action to carry out emergency work as needed
description: Met Éireann issues status-orange rain warnings for Thursday night when the storm tracks past Ireland’s south coast
content:
Local authority employees and other union members currently engaged in industrial action will work as required to deal with the impact of Storm Austen .
Fórsa and Siptu , the two largest unions involved in work-to-rule as part of the public sector pay dispute, confirmed that there are specific clauses for automatic derogations from industrial action in cases where there is a serious threat posed to life or wellbeing. Where derogations need to be requested, they are almost always granted immediately.
Dublin City Council said on Wednesday that its flood response team was “preparing for the potential impacts of heavy rainfall across the city and has put measures in place to respond quickly should localised flooding occur”.
“As part of these preparations, crews are clearing fallen leaves and debris where necessary, particularly in low-lying and flood-prone areas, where drainage gullies can become obstructed during periods of heavy autumn rainfall. Dublin City Council crews will be on the ground overnight monitoring conditions and responding to any issues that may arise,” it said.
It asked that members of the public refrain from parking over drains and report urgent cases of flooding. Council staff will “continue to monitor weather forecasts and conditions closely and provide updates as necessary through its website and social media channels”.
Asked about its staffing situation, a spokesperson for the council said it relies on a voluntary code of practice agreed with the unions. This is based on a Workplace Relations Commission code that provides for “the maintenance of essential public services the disruption of which could endanger life or health, or cause serious damage to the national economy or widespread hardship or anxiety to the community or large sections of the community”.
Siptu, meanwhile, said it was working with councils and other providers of emergency services to ensure these were maintained without disruption.
“There’s a derogation blueprint,” said Con Casey, an official with responsibility for staff at Kerry and Tipperary County Councils. “We’ve had requests in from those two councils and other officials will have heard from the local authorities they deal with.
“There’s preparatory work to be done in situations like this to limit the damage caused and then there will be work to be done during and after the storm where trees have come down or there has been flooding. In many cases staff will be working with contractors but there is no issue with granting the derogations required as long as the work is directly related to the storm.”
It is understood other unions are similarly co-operative where required in such circumstances.
Met Éireann said Storm Austen will “track past Ireland’s south coast from Thursday evening to Friday morning, bringing heavy rain and strong winds to many areas”.
[ Storm Austen approaches as Met Éireann issues orange warnings for six counties Opens in new window ]
The forecaster issued status-orange rainfall warnings for Cork, Kerry and Waterford, which will be the first counties to be impacted by the heavy rain on Thursday night. Later in the night, a status-orange rainfall warning for counties Dublin, Wexford and Wicklow will come into effect.
“There is a risk of flooding across parts of the south, southeast and east for Thursday into Saturday associated with heavy rainfall,” Met Éireann said. “Small, mountainous, upland and urban catchments are most at risk, as they can respond rapidly to periods of intense rainfall.
“River levels are expected to rise across Cork, Kerry, Waterford, Tipperary, Kilkenny, Carlow, Wexford, Wicklow, Kildare, Laois, Offaly, Kilkenny, Dublin and parts of the surrounding counties, potentially resulting in rivers exceeding their banks and flooding is expected. A nationwide status-yellow rain and wind warning has been issued from Thursday evening through to Friday morning.“

title: This one scientific advance could help reduce energy use and bills. The key is the human heart
description: Small science can beat Big Tech at finding solutions to the real problems facing the planet
content:
I n a world captured by AI tech bros and their cheerleaders, what we really need are the scientists working diligently on simple solutions that make our world work that little bit better.
It might seem like a very small thing, but it really sparked my imagination to learn on a recent visit to the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (Ista) that some of its scientists have turned to the human heart and circulatory system to find a solution to the energy lost by liquid swirling through pipes.
I travelled to Vienna at the invitation of Dublin City University for the collaborative initiative “Media for Future”, which aims to connect journalists and scientists to strengthen communication on the climate crisis.
Reporters and academics from Egypt, Germany, Iceland, Ireland and Portugal came together to learn about glacial melt, land use change, the impact of clouds on global heating and how the world is sleepwalking into catastrophe at faster speeds than ever previously imagined.
Much of that, you have no doubt heard before.
But not in a million years, did I ever think I would be so taken with work on pipes. Bear with me, until I explain.
How many pipes run through your house in terms of heating, bathrooms, the kitchen and even the garden hose? There’d be tens of millions throughout the country and not just in our homes, if we totalled them all up.
Then there’s the pipes used in industrial applications, from our world-beating breweries and bars to dairies, fuel businesses, drinking-water production and wastewater treatment, while they are also prevalent in vehicles.
Apparently, no matter how smooth the inside of a hose, the water swirls. But this tiny movement means 10 per cent more energy is needed to push the liquid through said pipe than if it didn’t.
[ Data centre electricity demand could exceed entire power usage of Republic Opens in new window ]
Pipes are present in just about every part of life and any reduction in the amount of energy needed to push liquids through them could be a huge win across the board.
The human circulatory system has solved this problem and at Ista, scientists are developing ways to mimic its energy-saving pulsing techniques within man-made pipes.
Rather than sucking up 23 per cent of electricity from the national grid and hoovering up almost a billion litres of drinking water in 2025, like Ireland’s data centres, this one scientific advance could actually reduce energy use, bills and climate-harming emissions for everyone.
We need more of these simple solutions to the problems we face – not more energy-hungry AI looming large over humanity with threats of massive job losses and extinction .
As far as I can see, AI’s coup-like takeover of the internet has done very little by way of progressing humanity and finding solutions to the biggest problems of our time.
Surely something that powerful should be used to transform, improve and save lives, solve the climate crisis and progress society, but that’s not what’s really happening, is it?
[ Data centres ‘may have used as much water’ last year in Ireland as more than 340,000 homes Opens in new window ]
In a recent United Nations report Ireland was cited as a “cautionary tale” about the environmental impact of runaway AI-growth.
An Oireachtas committee heard in September how data centres designed for AI each demand more electricity than is needed to power 100,000 homes. Meanwhile, proposed rules to allow them to provide their own electricity are expected to increase fossil fuel use.
I have never seen a breakdown of just how much of Ireland’s data centre capacity is used for AI, nevermind meaningful versus trivial things. It would be good to know, given the breakneck speed at which our Government seems to be pushing them forward regardless of their energy and water use, and the ensuing summer hosepipe bans.
Nor do they appear to be creating that many jobs, with tech giants shedding workers by the hundreds, citing AI.
Outside Silicon Valley’s grip on the Irish Government, however, scientists are still working hard on simple solutions that will move humanity forward in meaningful ways.
Dr Harald Wilkoszewski of Ista says they are trying something new, where staff are free to work across multiple disciplines rather than being pigeonholed into faculties. He says the number of research grants they are awarded are proof they must be doing something right.
I’m just grateful we still have scientists both at home and abroad who are still moving the dial on issues that may appear small but have the potential to become much bigger – even if they involve hosepipes.
Shauna Corr is an investigative journalist and UCD Earth Institute journalist in residence.

title: Axa enters Irish life insurance market through its Laya brand
description: French insurer is targeting further growth in life market through partnerships
content:
French insurance giant Axa has entered the Irish life insurance market, initially as an underwriter of term life and mortgage protection policies through its Laya brand .
The group’s Axa Life Europe business in Dublin has replaced a unit of Swiss reinsurer Swiss Re – known as iptiQ Life – as the insurer behind Laya’s life insurance offering. IptiQ began underwriting the company’s life policies in 2015.
AXA Life Europe is now actively seeking additional Irish partners, including credit unions and non-bank mortgage lenders, to offer its protection products to their own customers, the company said in a statement.
Axa Insurance in Ireland acquired Laya Healthcare in 2023 for €650 million . It subsequently started to underwrite the company’s health policies at the start of last year, replacing another unit of Swiss Re, called Elips Insurance, which had been behind Laya’s health policies for years.
The move by Axa to take over Laya’s life offering coincided with plans to strike distribution deals with more partners in the State to open up a new growth avenue for the French group in the Irish market.
“Axa brings global scale and underwriting expertise, and Laya life already has a reputation Irish customers trust. Over time, we expect to widen how people can reach our products through further distribution and partnerships,” said Eoin Lynam, chief executive of Axa Life Europe.
Life cover with Laya starts from €9 a month for a non-smoking 25-year old taking out a €100,000 policy for 20 years, according to Axa. That price includes a 10 per cent discount for buying the coverage online. It covers up to €750,000 depending on age.
Coverage can be taken out on one life or two, with benefits including early lump sum payments for terminal illness and funeral cover, according to Axa. It can be index-linked over time. Mortgage protection is available on the same single or dual life basis, also with terminal illness benefit, and pays off the outstanding mortgage if the policyholder dies during the term.
[ How much life insurance cover do you need? Opens in new window ]
While Axa is aiming to offer products online, customers can also purchase over the phone.
AXA Life Europe, established in 2005 and headquartered in Dublin, operates across several European markets and has 190,000 in-force policies. Its offering through Laya leaves Laya Life as the regulated insurance intermediary responsible for sales and aftersales services.
The Axa Life Europe spokesman declined to comment on the value of life premiums written in the past through Laya.
Insurance Ireland members paid out almost €14 billion in 2024 in benefits and claims, according to the latest published figures from the representative group.
Axa Insurance in Ireland saw its revenue soar by 53 per cent last year to €1.7 billion as it began underwriting health insurance policies for Laya, the second-largest player in the health market.
Health gross written premiums amounted to €672 million, according to the company’s 2025 solvency and financial condition report, underpinned as Laya increased the cost of plans last year. The three other coverage providers in the market also hiked pricing last year amid rising claims and hospital charges.
Axa Ireland’s general insurance revenue in the Republic dipped by 4 per cent to €744 million in 2025, leaving it as the second-largest general insurer in the market, behind Allianz Ireland .

title: Concerns over living longer
description: I worry about a future full of people succumbing to senility in their 60s
content:
Sir, – My grandfather recently passed away, but not before reaching his 100th birthday. We were amazed by how cognisant he was, but science was on his side; his hobbies included playing piano, learning other languages and the infamously difficult Crosaire cryptic crossword, all activities that help keep the mind sharp.
According to a recent report, an infant born today has decent odds of repeating his feat (“ Society must prepare for one third of children born today living to 100, report argues ”, October 19th). Modern pastimes include letting an algorithm show you short, easily-digestible videos, letting a YouTuber explain why a superhero movie you haven’t seen should make you very angry and, of course, letting an AI tool summarise an email you received that was already only a few sentences long.
I share the report’s concerns that Ireland is not prepared for a large population of people like my grandfather. I worry, also, about a future full of people entirely unlike him – succumbing to senility in their 60s. – Yours, etc,

title: Dublin Marathon: Former drug addict to run 2026 race on ‘the streets where friends died over the years’
description: After overcoming 40 years of drug-taking, Paul Killeen says running helps him to stay healthy
content:
P aul Killeen (61), who has overcome four decades of heroin and later crack cocaine addiction , is “determined” to finish the Dublin Marathon on Sunday.
“It will be emotional to run the streets where I used, where friends died over the years. That will carry me through on the day, thinking of people I grew up with who are gone because of the drugs.”
From the Liberties, Dublin , he has been drug-free for five years, having first used heroin when he was 14. He endured brutality and sexual abuse at school.
“I went to the Christian Brothers , and I was dyslexic; I didn’t know that at the time. I was called ‘thick’ and ‘stupid’ and came home with black eyes. If you were late for school, you got the leather strap.”
“I was an altar boy, and things happened there.” He went on to Bull Alley vocational school – now Liberties College, but got expelled after three months “for fighting”.
He left school unable to read or write but got an apprenticeship in a garment factory in Smithfield. It was around this point that he was introduced to heroin.
Asked if this was a difficult time in his life, he says: “To be honest, I was 100 per cent happier than when I was in school. I had an apprenticeship, and I was accepted. I wasn’t judged.”
He didn’t realise how his drug habit was becoming an addiction, however. He lost his job as a jeans cutter and was soon “in and out of prison” for robberies to pay for heroin. He learned to read and write at St Patrick’s Institution, where young offenders were kept, and found acceptance there.
Still, heroin came before everything: “I was living with my ma, then sofa surfing and eventually ended up on the streets.”
In the 1990s, he met a woman and had two children with her. “I was an addict when they were born. They never saw me clean until five years ago. I would trample over people to get what I thought I needed.”
After he stole his daughter’s Confirmation money, he decided to go to England, “thinking I would get off heroin”.
He lived on the streets of Birmingham, spent time in prison and was introduced to crack cocaine.
His mother, with the help of social workers, tracked him down and brought him back to Dublin. “Crack was only starting in Dublin then. I was injecting. I hadn’t patience to smoke it.”
About 2019 he frequented the Lighthouse cafe on Pearse Street, a drop-in centre for homeless people, run by the Tiglin addiction charity. Its founder, Senator Aubrey McCarthy, and its staff encouraged Paul to think about recovery.
A confluence of circumstances in 2021 led him to apply for a place on Tiglin’s 16-month residential rehabilitation programme.
[ Definitely a runner: Alan Milton on preparing for Sunday’s Dublin Marathon Opens in new window ]
“At an appointment in St James’s Hospital , my doctor, [Prof Colm] Bergin, said, ‘Paul, if you don’t stop the drugs, your immune system is nearly gone. You are gone in six weeks’.
“Something clicked in my head. I’d just had enough. I was tired.”
He was offered a place on the Tiglin’s men’s residential rehabilitation programme in Ashford, Co Wicklow , starting December 2021, followed by aftercare in the charity’s Greystones centre.
A key worker, who ran daily, encouraged him to run with her. He had run for Dublin as a child and had loved it.
After 40 years taking drugs “to block every feeling I ever had out”, he was in recovery, without drugs, and reliving a lot of trauma.
“Running helped me process that. My running is my [Narcotics Anonymous] meetings. I can’t do meetings. I can’t sit in a room. It makes me very anxious. But I love going out on a run. I feel free when I am out.”
He has been training for the marathon for more than a year and he is “excited but nervous”.
The day after the marathon, he travels to South Africa to volunteer for Tiglin in the townships of Cape Town. It will be his fifth trip there. “It’s a way I can give back.”
He has no regrets about life. “It is what it is. I am happy. I am working for Tiglin. I have my children back in my life. My ma is 88, and she’s delighted. My sister, I never got on with her. We are like that now,” he says, crossing his fingers.
“And I will finish the marathon on Sunday if I have to crawl the last miles. I am determined.”

title: Why foreign governments are paying lobbyists to make their case in Brussels
description: More countries are turning to public affairs consultants instead of diplomats to make their case
content:
L obbyists like to keep a low profile in Brussels . In fact, they don’t even describe themselves as lobbyists most of the time. Instead you’ll hear them marketing their expertise in political consulting, public affairs, government relations, strategic communications or “advisory services”.
There are a lot of them here, working for clients to influence the legislative and regulatory beast that is the European Union , often with plenty of success.
In the vast majority of cases, the lobbyists have been hired by a private company or industry group to bat for them in Brussels.
Increasingly, though, the client is a country.
“We are freer to talk about a compromise, or some deal,” says Andreas Geiger, managing partner of Alber & Geiger, a lobbying firm that specialises in representing foreign governments.
The company, which describes itself as a “lobbying powerhouse”, represented Panama in the aftermath of the Panama Papers offshore money laundering scandal . More recently it has done work for the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and India .
Geiger, who started out as a lawyer, explains that it can be useful for sovereign clients to have plausible deniability, or a layer of cover, in political dealings.
A lobbyist from a “local” Brussels-based firm might be better placed to get through to an MEP or EU official, and could have more latitude to wheel-and-deal than a country’s ambassador. “We connect better with the legislators than the clients,” Geiger says.
Foreign governments are paying lobbyists to get in the room with officials and lawmakers that matter. “When we go to our counterparts in the European Parliament, they can be more willing to negotiate,” Geiger adds. Knowing how and when to intervene and exactly who to target is important, he adds.
The work pays well. Alber & Geiger’s contract to lobby for the UAE was worth between €300,000 and €400,000 last year, financial records show.
For countries who have a poor record on human rights, a resolution criticising those abuses passed by the European Parliament could cause a public relations “catastrophe” domestically, Geiger says.
The firm’s work for Panama involved talking up reforms undertaken to push back against its reputation as a tax haven and help keep it off the EU’s money laundering “black list”.
They were hired by the Indian government to make the rounds in the European Parliament and head off concerns MEPs had about an EU-India free trade deal being negotiated.
The UAE was worried that mounting evidence it was backing one side in Sudan’s brutal civil war would complicate efforts to build closer economic links to the EU, and scupper preliminary talks about a trade deal.
So, Alber & Geiger mapped out a plan to lobby the EU institutions to keep “the trade agenda moving”, despite concerns about the fighting in Sudan.
In fairness to the lobbying firm, they are transparent about their business and set out all the above in a section on their website titled: “Wins”.
That’s not always the case. The Irish Times last week detailed how Anders Rasmussen, former Danish prime minister and Nato secretary general, forged a lucrative career after politics advising the governments of Japan, Taiwan, Armenia, Albania and Ukraine .
Our reporting found multiple occasions where Rasmussen did not disclose these contracts while publicly echoing the talking points of governments he was being paid to advise.
Sometimes governments just want to get an accurate read through the political fog.
Glyn Ford, a former British Labour MEP, runs a small company, Polint Ltd, that advises clients on the lay of the land in the European Parliament. “We provide what I call political intelligence,” says Ford. Two of his long-term clients are China and Thailand’s embassies in Brussels.
Ford tracks debates and other goings-on in the parliament to weed out what’s important from “all of the noise,” he says.
There’s a big difference between a statement being made by the leader of the centre-left Socialists and Democrats, the second biggest grouping in the parliament, and an intervention by a nonaligned independent MEP.
Ford, who is in the process of winding down his company, says he wasn’t meeting MEPs to encourage them to vote one way or another on legislation. “We made it very clear to the Chinese, we were not prepared to lobby on their behalf”, he says.
European politics was rocked by a scandal four years ago, Qatargate , that forced the parliament to tighten up its transparency rules. Several individuals were arrested and bags full of cash seized in an investigation that centred on Qatar and Morocco paying bribes to influence MEPs and swing votes. The sprawling criminal inquiries are still trundling away, beset by legal delays and rows over immunity.
The controversy shook Brussels awake to the lengths unscrupulous governments will go to get their way.

title: Sixty years of fighting hunger yielded results but another food crisis looms
description: Nutrition quality rather than calories is now key to food security but conflict and climate change make the task harder
content:
T he world is facing a food crisis in late 2026 and well into 2027. Three key factors are responsible.
Nearly 300 million people suffer from severe food insecurity as a result of protracted conflicts, with Sudan the most notable example, and climate change .
The Russia- Ukraine and Middle East conflicts are disrupting flows of grain, fertiliser and energy which will impact on the production of crops of wheat, maize and rice in 2027.
The coming El Niño is likely to be the most severe in recorded history. The 2023-24 El Nino led to the worst Southern African drought in more than a century, with more than 60 million people requiring humanitarian assistance.
Despite these steadily increasing risks, there has been an alarming lack of political action and resultant preparedness.
In June 2026 the Food and Agriculture Organisation and World Food Programme launched a Joint El Niño Anticipatory Reaction Appeal for the June 2026-March 2027 period, seeking $202 million (€180 million) targeting 22 high risk countries and nearly nine million people. By the end of September only $40 million (€36 million) had been pledged – 20 per cent of their request.
There is a leadership deficit in securing action. The UN is currently in a weakened position given existing geopolitics and with a new UN secretary general due to take up office in January 2027.
There are some similarities, but many dissimilarities, to the situation in the late 1960s when the spectre of mass starvation threatened a number of Asian countries, most notably India. This was averted through a combination of massive food aid shipments from the US and scientific breakthroughs resulting in increased crop yields for wheat, maize and rice nurtured by the green revolution.
The green revolution, a concerted global effort to strengthen agriculture and boost food production in vulnerable countries, allied to other improvements in health and living standards, contributed to a remarkable half century of progress in human welfare.
[ UN agency chief warns of coming food crisis due to Iran war Opens in new window ]
Between 1970 and 2025 world population increased 122 per cent from 3.7 billion to 8.2 billion. The proportion who were chronically undernourished fell over that period from nearly 25 per cent to less than 8 per cent – still a staggering 645 million. Under-five mortality reduced by three quarters to 37 per 1,000 live births in 2025. Life expectancy increased from 59 years in 1970 to 74 years in 2025. Billions of people have been lifted out of extreme poverty.
Looking forward to 2050, we can expect a continuation of certain of these trends, including the improvement in child mortality rates and the increase in life expectancy.
There will be important changes in population dynamics. The world population is projected to grow from the current 8.2 billion to 9.6 billion in 2050. Europe and certain countries in Asia (China, Japan, South Korea) will experience reductions in their populations, necessitating economic and social adjustments.
Africa is the only world region expected to show a significant population increase, doubling its current population to 2.5 billion by 2050.
Global demand for food is expected to grow by 30-50 per cent between now and 2050. In 1970, the Green Revolution faced the hugely challenging but relatively straightforward task of increasing the number of calories to feed hungry people. Today’s challenge is more complex and includes addressing ‘hidden hunger’ – micronutrient deficiencies, as well as overweight and obesity – to achieve nutrition security.
The other huge challenge is the effect of increased climate variability and extreme weather events on food production, as well as the need to reduce carbon emissions from food production systems.
[ Wars and aid cuts fuelling surge in world hunger, report warns Opens in new window ]
In drawing lessons from the past 75 years and in looking to the future, we focus on three areas we believe should be prioritised: political leadership; the potential of science; and the need to invest in Africa to realise its development potential.
The incoming UN secretary general should make global food and nutrition security a personal strategic priority on taking office in January 2027. This should translate into making food and nutrition security a core pillar of the UN‘s agenda for peace, development, climate and human security.
In addition to being the right thing to do, this would be good politics. In a world increasingly dominated by the two superpowers of the US and China, the UN has a strategic interest in promoting a new multilateralism reflective of an emerging multipolar world. Enhanced global food and nutrition security is a big idea around which new coalitions of regions and countries could emerge, seeing it in their best interests to contribute to the initiative.
Over the next two years the UK and South Korea will hold the presidency of the G20. Both should prioritise food and nutrition security.
Given the policy of the current US administration, including the abolition of USAid, the US is unlikely to contribute to such an initiative. But in light of the US’s long-term track record in promoting global food and nutrition security, its continuing strength in leading-edge agri-food research and, importantly, its enduring values and longer-term national interests, a future US government, possibly even the successor to the Trump administration, may revert to playing a positive role in global food politics.
Getting new technologies into the hands of millions of smallholder farmers across the developing world will be crucial to delivering improved food and nutrition security at local, national and global level.
[ Irish farming is unprepared for impact of climate change, says advisory council Opens in new window ]
The range of technologies now available is more advanced than the science that underpinned the green revolution. Advances in genomics, advanced breeding and gene editing are critical for climate adaptation. AI, machine learning and advanced data analytics can provide farmers with relevant, locally specific advice.
The Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research, which played a vital role in delivering the green revolution, warns against dependence on any single technology and advocates bundling digital decision tools with climate-adapted seeds, water-efficient technologies, crop diversification, finance and market access. Its work will underpin future food and nutrition security.
Africa is a continent with high vulnerability but also with huge opportunity. Vulnerabilities include governance challenges, conflict in a number of countries and regions, the impact of climate change and underdeveloped infrastructure.
On the positive side, the doubling of Africa’s population to 2.5 billion by 2050 represents a huge opportunity as well as a challenge. The challenge is how to generate jobs for the 20 million young people annually entering the work force. The opportunity is in reaping the demographic dividend of this increase while leapfrogging part of the development process through widespread adoption of renewable energy and digital technology.
Investment in its people and developing its human capital is Africa’s single most important priority.
Malnutrition-induced stunting is a key problem, with 62 million children under-five in sub-Saharan Africa stunted in 2024. It can cause lifelong physical and cognitive problems. Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for 60 per cent of global under-five deaths. The World Bank’s 2020 Human Capital Index reported that children born in Africa are expected to achieve only 40 per cent of their potential productivity.
For Africa’s potential to be realised, four main conditions must be met: stop the conflicts, get politics and governance right, ramp up agricultural research and development to address food production constraints, and invest in human capital. It is primarily up to African political leadership and its people to deliver on this but the wider international community should play a key role as partners.
[ We’re only ever nine meals away from anarchy. That risk is no longer just theoretical Opens in new window ]
We have both spent many years working and advocating for increased food and nutrition security. Despite the many challenges we are optimistic that hunger can be substantially eliminated by 2050. But this will require sustained political commitment – putting the gains of science into the hands of millions of smallholder farmers and partnering to achieve an economic and social revolution in Africa.

title: Artificial intelligence can’t replace the benefits of nature intelligence
description: As AI changes what and how we learn, real world learning will grow in value
content:
T he “school of life” is used to describe learning outside of the formal education system, involving real-world challenges that stretch capabilities and expand perspectives.
Within a formal university setting we often take students outside of conventional classrooms to experience learning about nature – a broad definition of life – in the real world. We believe that it can be far easier and more effective to learn about the natural world through experience with and within it.
Artificial intelligence can extend our capabilities, but nature intelligence is also critical for understanding and responding to the global challenges we are faced with. We develop nature intelligence through formal learning combined with experience in nature. This is field teaching, with university field courses ranging from an hour or two outdoors on the university campus, to days or weeks in far-flung destinations experiencing very different forms of nature from the perspectives of different cultures.
Field teaching is fundamental to any degree in the natural sciences – from the study of the physical world around us to microbial, plant and animal life and the interaction between people and the natural world.
As AI changes what and how we learn, real-world experiential learning and its application will only grow in value. The combination of human experiences with nature, machines and digital sensors is powerful, but experience in and with nature is not fully replaceable by machines. While in the early days of Covid university educators pivoted from in-person field courses to virtual experiences of nature, this experience underlined the deep value of real field teaching. We were quick to pivot back to include real experiences of nature within our degree courses.
There are challenges to field teaching. It can be expensive, requiring students to pay additional fees for travel and accommodation; it can involve high greenhouse gas emissions through air travel, and it requires a different approach to health, safety and inclusion compared with classroom or online teaching.
There are ways of addressing all of these challenges, which means that field teaching can be incorporated easily and sustainably into degrees. Field courses can be local, use sustainable forms of transport, and be designed to accommodate students with additional needs. Bursaries and hardship supports can be provided to enable students to experience field courses that they would otherwise not be able to afford.
We see an increasing focus on university campuses as locations for climate and biodiversity learning and action, including the incorporation of natural ecosystems into the university infrastructure. More natural areas on campuses are not just useful for field teaching, they contribute significantly to the wellbeing of staff and students and to the protection and restoration of green spaces within urban areas.
Some university campuses include important local ecosystems, an example being University of Galway which supports the initiative to have Galway recognised as a National Park City, and University College Cork which has extensive areas of natural habitats on campus. More natural areas on campus can also signal to the wider community the importance of wilder green spaces in an urban context and provide this experience to visitors and local residents, such as Trinity College’s ornamental wildflower meadows at the front entrance to the college.
Despite the costs and challenges of far-flung field courses, there is considerable value in providing experiences which take students and teachers outside of their education comfort zones, and expose them to real world experiences far beyond what is achievable close to home.
This is why, at Trinity, we offer both local field courses together with overseas field courses such as the zoology field course in tropical biology and conservation in Kenya, taught largely by local land managers and academics. Students experience at first hand the challenges faced by local communities and national park managers, such as human-wildlife conflict and tourism pressures. Students then bring this nuanced and culturally sensitive understanding of people and nature to their formal learning in zoology and ecology.
The real school of life, nature, is all around us. By connecting formal education with experience in, and with, nature we deepen and expand our nature intelligence and our understanding of our place in the world.
Professor Yvonne Buckley is codirector of the Co-Centre for Climate, Biodiversity and Water and is Professor of Zoology at Trinity College Dublin.

title: Understanding Donald Trump
description: The only hope for the United States is for the Democrats (with the help of Independents) to win big in the midterms
content:
Sir, – Understanding Trump is easy enough. He’s been written about for the past 10 years, and more. How he got the mindset he is stuck in, and his greed and narcissism that have exploded with his years in the White House.
We call him a mé féiner. But trying to do something about it is a no-win situation. Trying to reason with him – telling him he is wrong – will get you thrown out of the room.
The only hope for the United States is for the Democrats (with the help of Independents) to win big in the midterms. They then might have a better chance of halting Trump’s tyrannical ways, if not impeaching him, again. On this latter point, I have to believe in the best and that there will be enough Republicans – with so many now turning their backs on him – to make up the two-thirds majority needed to impeach.
[ Emerging Democrat star Jon Ossoff has become a chief thorn in Trump’s side Opens in new window ]
Only then can the United States begin to recover the goodwill of our allies across the globe. I only hope it won’t be too late for Ukraine. – Yours, etc,

title: Top Ires investors sell down stakes below Barings proposal price as deadline nears
description: FMR, Starwood and Janus Henderson have sold most of their shares since bid approach announced
content:
Some of Ires Reit’s largest shareholders have sold down stakes at a discount to the price Barings has indicated it would be willing to pay for the group, locking in recent gains in advance of a formal bid deadline.
Boston-based FMR, Starwood Capital and Janus Henderson have sold most of their shares since the State’s largest private residential landlord announced on September 28th it had received a €726.9 million bid approach from a unit of Barings, the US-based alternative asset manager.
FMR, formerly Fidelity Management & Research, has slashed its stake to 3.34 per cent from 6.98 per cent, raising €22.5 million by selling 17.5 million shares at as much as €1.29. It has also “transferred out of” almost 1.5 million shares, according to a stock exchange filing this week, which did not provide any further details.
Representatives for FMR did not respond to requests for comment.
The price at which FMR has been selling is almost 22 per cent higher than where Ires shares were changing hands in late September, before the landlord announced it had received an approach.
However, it is below the €1.386-a-share Barings has proposed it would be willing to offer. Ires said as it announced the proposal that it “would be minded to recommend” a deal if a formal offer were made by a November 9th deadline set by the Irish Takeover Panel . Ires is led by chief executive Eddie Byrne.
US property specialist Starwood, which started building a stake in Ires in 2024 as the real estate investment trust (reit) was in the middle of a battle with an activist shareholder, has raised €13.7 million reducing its stake to 0.91 per cent from 2.92 per cent. A spokesman for Starwood declined to comment.
London-based Janus Henderson has sold 6.32 million Ires shares since the approach announcement for about €8.21 million, cutting its stake by more than half to 1.05 per cent.
Keyridge has reduced its stake to 3.21 per cent from 5.81 per cent, having been a net seller of shares since news of the Barings bid approach emerged. A spokesman for the firm also declined to comment.
The moves by some of largest Ires shareholders to sell down their stakes have allowed them to capture recent gains by the stock since the Barings approach was revealed while also derisking their positions before the so-called put-up-or-shut-up deadline next month.
Barings has been carrying out due diligence on Ires’s portfolio, which comprises more than 3,600 rental homes, since the announcement.
Shares in a number of other European reits, including Vonovia and TAG Immobilien in Germany and Finland’s Lumo Kodit, have fallen in value since news of the Ires approach, amid mounting speculation about how many more interest rate rises the European Central Bank will push through over the coming year to rein in inflation.
Ires’s largest shareholder, Thames River Capital, a specialist real-estate investment arm of Columbia Threadneedle, owns 8.13 per cent of the company. Its holding has been as high as 9.5 per cent since it disclosed it had breached the normal 3 per cent disclosure threshold early last year.
The Barings proposal, the fifth approach it had made since early August, before Ires made an announcement in September, would give the company an equity value of €726.9 million. Adding in Ires’s borrowings puts an overall value on the deal of almost €1.27 billion.
Barings survived the collapse of its then parent Barings Bank in 1995, resulting from rogue investments carried out by trader Nick Leeson , as Dutch financial giant ING acquired the group for a nominal sum of £1. ING later sold Barings to Boston-based MassMutual Financial Group in 2005.

title: New townhouses and apartments with sleek interior finishes for sale in Shankill
description: Boutique new development by Winterbrook sits between bustling Shankill village and Dart station
content:
The sea has a strong influence on the design of The Poplars, a new development of houses, duplexes and apartments just off Quinn Road in Shankill , south Dublin.
When choosing colours, textures and materials for the homes in collaboration with Kruger Lyons Architects, Kate Rhatigan, director of developers Winterbrook, kept in mind the scheme’s proximity to the coast, adding ideas that subtly evoke the spirit of sea and sand, including the rich navy vertical tiled splashbacks in the kitchen and the distinctive hand-glazed zellige tiles and sandy oak textures in the bathrooms.
The development of just 25 A-rated homes sits between bustling Shankill village and Shankill Dart station and comprises two- and three-bedroom townhouses, three-bedroom duplexes and one-bedroom apartments.
The houses are energy efficient thanks to air-to-water central heating systems with smart-zone controls, and underfloor heating at ground-floor level. The first phase of A2-rated homes are now being released through agents Hooke & MacDonald .
There will be four one-bed apartments for sale, measuring between 57sq m-59sq m and priced at €470,000. Each of these homes are laid out with a double bedroom off the hall and an open-plan kitchen/living/diningroom to the rear, opening to private gardens.
The two-bedroom townhouses, of which there will be two released, are priced at €730,000-€740,000 respectively. They extend to 92 sq m, with a spacious kitchen and diningroom flowing into a rear living area on the ground floor, along with a downstairs loo, and two en suite double bedrooms upstairs.
There will also be one three-bedroom duplex extending to 115sq m for sale, priced at €725,000.
A total of seven three-bedroom townhouses, Extending to 138sq m with two reception rooms and a study, will also be released, priced from €815,000-€870,000.
Inside, the craftsmanship and contemporary modern aesthetic of these homes is apparent in the bespoke finishes, hand-painted cabinetry and fine details, such as the oak shroud enveloping the kitchen units and the dark-brown travertine-effect tiling enhancing the main bathrooms. The developer sourced materials from several countries, and travelled to Italy to ensure that they chose the right bathroom finishes for the project.
The three-bedroom townhouses should prove to particularly appealing to those looking for their forever home in south Dublin.
Downstairs is an open-plan kitchen/dining/livingroom, with the kitchen facing out to the front of the house, maintaining a connection with the world outside. The kitchen is fitted with micro Shaker-style units with vertical tiled splashbacks, bespoke stone worktops and integrated Bosch appliances.
Banquette seating provides a cosy dining area, and the livingroom has large glass double doors opening out to a fenced back garden with patio and lawned area. A guest loo completes the downstairs, and high ceilings make the space feel even roomier.
Bedroom two, a double, is on the second floor, facing out towards the back garden, and next to that is the main bathroom, which is laid out in a luxurious blend of large-format porcelain tiles and small feature tiles. The bathrooms have high-quality satin nickel fittings, and the main bathroom and second-floor en suite have an oak-finish vanity drawer unit.
Next to the bathroom is a handy utility cupboard for the washing machine and dryer, with space to fold and store your linen.
[ Get on the right track at these new homes on Luas and rail lines Opens in new window ]
To the front is the second livingroom, a cosy den to watch TV or hang out.
The spacious main bedroom is on the second floor, facing out to the back, with a sizeable en suite. Bedroom three looks out to the front, and next to that is a small study that could also be used as a nursery.
All the windows are double-glazed AluClad aluminium with satin nickel handles, and the front door is Ultra Tech hardwood. The houses benefit from not being overlooked – the windows look out to mostly mature trees and shrubs, while the duplexes are built at a discreet distance from the houses.
Shankill village, just around the corner, has evolved into a busy, vibrant community, well served by shops, cafes, pubs, supermarkets and leisure facilities. The Dart station is just 800m away at the end of Quinn Road, and the M50 motorway, along with the N11 to Wicklow and Wexford, is a five-minute drive away. Schools in the area include Scoil Mhuire, St Anne’s National School, Rathmichael Parish National School, St John’s National School, St Laurence College, Woodbrook College and John Scottus School.

title: Branded ‘lazy’ by Trump, a Democrat is mounting an unexpected challenge in a Republican stronghold
description: Democrat Josh Turek is mounting an unexpected challenge in Iowa, a traditional Republican bastion
content:
T he late, great David Lynch titled his filmic ode to Iowa The Straight Story, and the local joke is that the terrain is so flat here that you can watch your dog run away for three days. But Josh Turek likes to point out that it was his good luck to be born in the Loess Hills, the gruff hills that straddle the ragged western edges of Iowa and the Nebraska border. The hills in his home city of Council Bluffs made for a gruelling workout as he ferried himself around in his wheelchair looking for votes to join Iowa’s state legislature.
John Turek has occasionally described his son as “a casualty of the Vietnam War”, because the family strongly believes that the spina bifida with which Josh Turek was born in 1978 originated from his father’s exposure to Agent Orange during the 22 months he spent fighting that war. As a fledgling politician, Turek used the wheelchair, and his athletic prowess, as a weapon, physically hauling himself up porch steps, dragging the chair behind him, and then seating himself before ringing the doorbell. The effort at least earned him an open conversation.
“The only way I was able to win was going out and dragging my wheelchairs upstairs and having conversations with Republicans and Independents,” he said of that initial foray into politics.
Now, he is on the cusp of winning a senate seat. Sioux County is a Republican stronghold, but Turek billboards and yard signs have begun to bloom. President Donald Trump is due in Sioux City to campaign for the Republican candidate, Ashley Hinson, on Thursday afternoon, as a series of polls suggest the race is deadlocked.
Turek has termed himself “the prairie populist”, advocating a return to the Democratic Party virtues of John Kennedy and Roosevelt and his personal touchstone Tom Harkin, who served as senator to Iowa for a full 30 years from 1985. Harkin was the lead sponsor of the landmark Americans With Disabilities Act in 1990. In a fitting symmetry, Harkin, now 86, campaigned for Turek in that first election campaign for House district 20, which he won by just six votes out of the 6,800 cast.
“We went to the west part of Council Bluffs knocking on doors, and I couldn’t believe it – this guy dragging that wheelchair up and down stairs,” Harkin said.
“Now that impressed me that he was willing to do that. But what also impressed me was the way he connected with people. It wasn’t just a quick handshake and I’m moving on.”
On Monday night, the upstairs room in Morningside College is full by the time Turek wheels himself in, to loud cheers. He is wearing denims, a black polo top and his customary black Hawkeyes baseball cap, and he apologises for his appearance: he’d been out on farmlands all day. If Turek is to win Iowa, then a mutiny by the state’s farming class will be the essence of the story.
[ Funny, irreverent, cocky: Can Abdul El-Sayed win a vital senate seat in abandoned America? Opens in new window ]
Over an hour-long question-and-answer session, and on the campaign trail, he offers a deft but bleak series of statistics that depict the ways in which life has gone wrong for Iowans. These are that the state lags in 48th place in income growth; is one of only three US states to have its economy contract; that it closed some 842 healthcare facilities in the last six years; that it is second in the national cancer rate only to Kentucky (due, he says, to a combination of nitrates in the water caused by pesticide run-offs and the fact that it is a state with an ageing population dealing with “healthcare deserts” requiring trips to the bigger cities for treatments); that it scores too highly on social problems such as binge-drinking and smoking; and that 70 of its 99 counties are losing population.
It’s difficult to reconcile this vision of Iowa with what you see on the four-hour drive from Kansas City to Sioux City, which runs through the Loess Hills and is a rolling vista of impeccably neat corn fields and tidy, silent towns. It feels like a place that would promote health and abundance. But the cycle of emptying small towns is the backdrop to the acute stresses visited on Iowa farmers, whose corn and soybean produce are highly vulnerable to the Trump tariff policy, as well as the obvious hike in fuel prices.
Turek has the common touch and speaks in the low confiding tones of a Midwest late night radio show. But his candidacy has seen a sharp rise in his profile
“We have arrived at a second farm crisis,” Turek tells the audience. “We had the first one around 40 years ago when we lost half of our small family farms.
“Our farmers need open markets and free trade more than any other group. You are looking at commodities prices tanking, at a complete loss of markets for them. I had a farmer tell me today: ‘the difference between diesel prices this year and last year is $100,000. That is the difference between me making a profit and having to sell land.’ It really is a farmageddon. Our farmers do not want handouts. They do not want subsidies. They want stable markets.”
John Gray, a Sioux City resident, has come along with his friend Greg Peterson. When they attended their first Turek rally, before the primary, just 12 people showed up.
We talk for a while about the transformation of life in Iowa over the past three decades. Gray grew up in Rockwell City, a town of about 2,000 people an hour north of Des Moines.
“Like many of our towns based on agriculture, many people who grew up there have left for college and moved on to big cities,” he says.
“That’s been going on for a long time, but it has accelerated as the farms have gotten bigger. There is more of an emphasis on ‘big ag’. And then the retail stores suffer. And then there is often a consolidation of the schools. And when a town loses its school, that is kind of the end of the town. In Sioux County, a lot of the towns are still successful but the towns in the centre and south and west of the state, not so much.”
The genesis of the Iowa senate election is compelling in its own right. The exiting senator, Joni Ernst, in staunchly defending the Trump administration’s decision to remove some 1.4 million immigrants from receiving benefits at a public event in Parkersburg, was challenged by an audience member who said the policy would cause people to die.
“Well, we are all going to die,” Ernst retorted.
It was one of those soundbites that lit up the information channels and was held up as an example of the heartlessness of the policy. Ernst (56) announced she would not run again that September, leaving an open contest to join Chuck Grassley, the 93-year-old Iowan institution who has held the senior senate seat for the Republican Party since 1980.
Turek brought four years of Iowa state house experience along with an extraordinary and classically Midwestern story. His condition meant a hospital-defined childhood: he went through 21 surgeries before the age of 12, involving painful and solitary recuperations. The family came from what he calls “modest” circumstances. In the hall, he told of a childhood defined by clothing from the Goodwill charity and free summer lunch programmes.
[ The Irish Times view on US midterms: a lame duck Trump is still a danger Opens in new window ]
Like many Iowan kids, he was a basketball obsessive. He found a wheelchair team and excelled, spending eight to 10 hours a day on his way to becoming a two-time gold medallist with USA Paralympian teams before playing professionally in Europe. The wheelchair at once limited his range of movement and was his passage around the world. In Spain, in particular, he took note of the health and social systems.
“I understand your struggle right now,” Turek tells the smattering of college kids in the room. “I come from humble beginnings economically. I say that my story is uniquely the American dream. In no other country on Earth could someone from my economic background, health background, ultimately win gold medals, represent their community in high legislature, or certainly run for the US Senate .
“And I understand that for young people you may be the first generation who may not have the same standard of living as your parents. I understand apathy because you have looked at whether Republican or Democrat is not going to make any difference to your life. My promise and my pledge to every one of you is, I am fighting for this American dream. My north star is what is best for the people, and ensuring this American dream continues for the next generation of Americans.”
Turek has the common touch and speaks in the low confiding tones of a Midwest late night radio show. But his candidacy has seen a sharp rise in his profile: Barack Obama has campaigned with him, and the pair shot hoops. (Turek points out that he won).
Republican attack ads have branded him “America’s favourite liberal” who skipped 58 per cent of Iowa state legislature votes this year while he “schmoozed with wealthy coastal elites in Los Angeles and Washington, DC”.
It’s clear that if Turek is to go to Washington, he will have convinced a significant percentage of Iowan farmers to break with tradition
“Despite missing hundreds of votes, Turek still collected over $20,000 in taxpayer-funded benefits,” one ad states.
Trump, probably not then fully aware of Turek’s extraordinary life story, branded him as “lazy”; he is likely to choose a different attack line on Thursday.
[ US midterms: how likely is a blue wave? Opens in new window ]
The presidential rally will come with the usual security and media carnival. But Turek’s sitdown on Monday night illustrated the berserk way in which donor money has distorted US politics. At one stage Turek remarked, in genuine wonder, that he had stopped on his way to buy a small carton of fresh fruit to keep him going. “It cost eight dollars,” he said, to a low murmur of recognition.
The Turek town hall had the look and feel of a particularly enthusiastic book club: a gathering of pleasant locals. But the Des Moines Register this week reported that $137 million (€122 million) has been spent on trying to influence Iowans in this senate race. The bulk of that figure has been spent on adverts attacking both candidates.
The Iowa Farm Bureau, representing more than 150,000 Iowan farming families, has endorsed Ashley Hinson, a former local television reporter who has represented Iowa in the US House for the past six years. The smaller Iowa Farmers Union has backed Turek. It’s clear that if Turek is to go to Washington, he will have convinced a significant percentage of Iowan farmers to break with tradition.
“Oh, he’s going to need to do that, yes,” Shiela Thompson, a retired union worker, tells me when the event finishes and Turek eases into a meet-and-greet.
“Our farmers are traditional Republicans. I have knocked doors for 20 years, so I know. And I think that it is down to, they do what their parents did. Our farmers are very important. And our children are so important. I think we need to go in the right direction and stand up for Iowans. We have been in dire straits.”

title: ‘People mistake innovation for creating something new’: Apple’s former head of music on keeping things simple
description: New book discusses Steve Jobs, U2’s automatic album download and the culture of secrecy at one of the world’s biggest companies
content:
Neil West, the former head of music for Apple in Europe, feels he is stuck in a moment with U2 .
When Apple decided in 2014 to upload the band’s album Songs of Innocence to the libraries of hundreds of millions of iTunes accounts without permission, it caused a backlash over privacy and overreach . Twitter, Instagram and Facebook exploded.
“Woke up this morning to find Bono in my kitchen, drinking my coffee, wearing my dressing gown, reading my paper.”
Apple was forced to apologise and issue a removal tool while Bono took his share of the blame for a stunt that backfired.
The author of a new book on Apple entitled It Just Works: The Nine Simple Rules of Apple’s Success , West says it’s the issue he is most asked about to this day, and it was a rare example of Apple breaking its own rules.
[ It wasn’t the internet that killed the old cultural order, it was U2 Opens in new window ]
“One of the foundations of Apple is predictability, and with the free U2 album all of a sudden iTunes was behaving in an entirely new and unexplained way. If it’s a U2 album today, what might it be tomorrow?” he tells The Irish Times.
One of the secrets of Apple’s success is simplicity, he says. Simple solutions are more effective, more resilient and easier to understand. They reduce friction and they help cement relationships with customers.
Apple has mastered both simplicity and the “jobs to be done” idea that people don’t purchase products, they hire them to do a specific task. The iPhone packs all the functionality you need daily with a phone, a camera, a music player, a browser and apps. AirPods pair seamlessly and remove the tangle of traditional wired earbuds. Apple Pay removes the need to carry a physical wallet while the App Store makes it simple to add functionality to your devices.
The customer experience is another vital element. Consider unboxing. The iPod was the first mass market product to come fully charged, a small tweak at the manufacturing stage that delighted customers. In the same manner, bundling a little screwdriver into the Nest thermostat removed a friction in what was otherwise a simple installation. As Tony Faddell, the creator of both the iPod and Nest, puts it: “It may not be your fault that the customer doesn’t have the right screwdriver to hand, but that won’t stop them feeling bad about your product.”
[ Apple’s $5tn milestone comes with a hefty price tag Opens in new window ]
Not all additions are welcome, as the U2 experience shows. When the iTunes Music Store launched, West suggested adding a £10 iTunes gift card to the box of every new iPhone and iPod sold. Steve Jobs hated the idea and shot it down. This was a battle of philosophies between a team with a tactical marketing plan versus Apple’s devotion to the user experience.
“It was a distracting call to action that would force the customer to pause their emotional journey with their new product and think about a separate transaction,” West says.
Apple is famous for this type of exceptionalism, and Jobs personified it, with his genius, volatility and creation of a culture of intense secrecy at the corporation. West’s 16-year period at Apple covered both Jobs’ and his successor Tim Cook’s tenures at the top, with their radically different styles.
“It’s no secret that at times Steve could be abrasive, rude and extremely direct,” West says. “At the same time, everyone who worked directly with him will tell you that was almost immediately forgiven because it wasn’t personal; it was in pursuit of greatness and he more than proved that his methods led to greatness.
“I don’t think anyone [now] would hold up Apple under Steve Jobs as an ideal and healthy working culture and Tim very much took steps to make Apple a more supportive, inclusive place to work.”
A frequent critical observation about Tim Cook’s tenure was that it was characterised by incrementalism and a lack of the radical innovation seen under Jobs. West disagrees.
“It’s very easy to look at the headlines about the things that were launched under Steve Jobs and miss the innovations that changed the world, but let’s not forget that Tim raised Apple’s value by around 14-fold,” he says. “It’s a fun game all right to imagine what world-changing products Apple might have launched had Steve still been with us, but I think the more adult business perspective is to imagine what mediocre, unpolished products might have been released by Apple had anyone other than Tim Cook been leading it.
“People mistake innovation for creating something new. Apple has always seen innovation as being about making things better. The fact that so many years after its invention, the iPhone is still the world’s favourite premium smartphone is proof that incremental change is absolutely the best strategy.”
Inevitably, the process of innovation involves developing ideas that ultimately never come to market. A classic example is Project Titan, Apple’s secretive plan for a self-driving electric car, which was reportedly abandoned in 2024 after around a decade of development.
West says that a cornerstone of Apple’s success over the years has been what Jobs used to call “ownership of the whole widget”, and he feels it would not have been feasible for Apple to manufacture its own cars. “Apple was going to have to surrender a great deal of control over how the car was made and that was always going to weaken its ability to develop something great in the same way it can with iPods or iPhones.”
On the culture of secrecy at Apple, West feels that this is a combination of normal competitive practice and Apple’s long-standing desire to make exciting surprise announcements.
“I had absolutely no visibility at all regarding the car project, for example. I didn’t need to know, so I didn’t know. Secrecy can seem arrogant, but it is a very competitive business with other companies looking at your strategy and adjusting theirs accordingly.”
In the area of artificial intelligence , Apple has taken a strategic bet to let others lead in the creation of AI models. West says his hunch is the major battle here may not be about who has the most powerful models but who can use AI to solve the most problems for people and that Apple may be on the money here. “I think it will be a winning strategy. As far as AI in the home is concerned, I think Apple is perfectly positioned.”
Apple has recently appointed a new CEO John Ternus , who comes from a hardware engineering background, in contrast to Cook, who came from corporate operations, and there is much speculation about the direction the corporation will go under his leadership. “I have heard only good things about him from former colleagues,” says West who notes that the new CEO has dampened down speculation about radical new departures from the current winning formula.
West’s book provides some interesting colour about the inside of Apple, while never compromising his relationship with his former employer who he clearly retains huge affection for. He returns constantly to the theme of simplicity. In a world of information overload, this is one of the keys to a winning business strategy, he concludes.
It Just Works: The Nine Simple Rules of Apple’s Success by Neil West, is published by Macmillan Business.
