title: Workplace conflict is said to be costing Irish firms €239m annually. What can be done about it?
description: Value of lost productivity due to conflict more than €239m, with in excess of €187m in the private sector and almost €52m in the public sector, according to NUIG study
content:
W hen I moved here from New York more than three decades ago, I became the default complainer in restaurants. It wasn’t my choice; others expected me to give out for them. I found it strange that even when an Irish friend’s meal was inedible and the service lacking, they’d say everything was okay: “Fine, grand, lovely, thanks.”
If they wanted to express their dissatisfaction with the food, they’d switch plates with me and try to persuade me to gripe on their behalf. Initially, it was amusing, but then it became annoying. Why couldn’t they just complain themselves? Why was this such a big deal to them?
As I only learned after years working and living here – despite being raised abroad by a mother from Carlow and a dad from Dublin – Irish culture is polite and indirect. Avoiding conflict and saving face is a big part of society and often informs how people communicate, or don’t.
Culturally, we know that our strength comes from togetherness and mutual care. Ar scáth a chéile a mhaireann na daoine: as we live in one another’s shelter. Although we’ve become a more individualistic society in the last 50 years, much of our communalist culture remains in our behaviours and attitudes.
William Corless, a workplace mediator and coach, says cultural norms follow us into the office. When it comes to conflict at work or anywhere, he says, the Irish approach is to avoid it nearly at all costs.
“We’re a land of a thousand welcomes, so we have to be nice,” he says. “But it has to seep out somewhere.” It finds its way into the post-meeting huddle where people are whispering to one another and asking ‘what was that all about?’ instead of complaining constructively. Then it might grow into gossip, then later into a culture of ‘quiet quitting’ or people leaving. In many cases, this can feel more comfortable than addressing an issue head-on.
Both head-on avoidance and conflict itself can be very expensive, professionally and personally, if not well managed. Data indicates that workplace conflict, interpersonal mistreatment and work-related distress result in hundreds of millions of euro in lost productivity annually, plus direct legal awards and reduced performance and efficiency across Irish organisations.
The estimated overall value of lost productivity due to workplace conflict is €239.3 million, with €187.6 million in the private sector and €51.8 million in the public sector, according to the Value of Lost Productivity from Workplace Bullying in Ireland, a 2020 study by NUI Galway’s John Cullinan, Margaret Hodgins and Victoria Hogan. Across the entire economy, absenteeism from conflict results in approximately 1.42 million missed days in the private sector and 276,473 days in the public sector annually, says the report.
Employees who reported that they were bullied were considerably more likely to report that they were often or always stressed, while bad and very bad relationships between management and staff were also significantly associated with greater stress, particularly for female employees. That’s according to Bullying and Work-Related Stress in the Irish Workplace, a 2019 study from NUI Galway, by the same researchers plus Michael McDermott and Sharon Walsh.
Remote and hybrid working can also increase the potential for conflict as some of the signals we rely on – body language, physical presence – go missing. Corless likens poor communication and conflict to a screen with missing pixels. We fill in the gaps, but sometimes we fill them in the wrong way and we tend to assume negative intent because we are wired to protect ourselves, he says.
Conflict isn’t always bad and, if well managed, constructive disagreement is the sign of an engaged workforce. High-performing teams aren’t those that never fight – they’re the ones who learn to listen to each other and reset the fastest after disagreements.
When there is an issue, managers carry much of the weight in resolving both indirect and direct conflict. Even so, many find there is little organisational, structural support or training to help them address the problem.
Katie Muldoon, author of Mind Your Self: How Leaders can Integrate AI without Disintegrating Humans, says teams should agree the ground rules together before conflict has a chance to arise.
Start with agreeing on principles, not rules. “A principle is: if we were to do the opposite, would it still be reasonable?” she says. We treat each other kindly is a rule, because nobody would argue for the reverse. Whereas saying we meet in person by default is a principle, because there are good reasons to sometimes do otherwise. When someone wants to break a principle, the team already has a shared reference point for that conversation. Leaders can still make the call, she says, but they should explain it and acknowledge the frustration it may cause.
“You might also ask each individual, ‘what are we here to do as a team?’ You may be surprised to find several different answers, and this may be the original root of conflict in the group.”
Consistency is extremely important for team cohesion too. What unsettles teams is unpredictability, says Muldoon, like “the boss who is warm on Monday and furious on Tuesday”.
She suggests managers think through their communication based on a driving analogy – mirror, signal, manoeuvre. Look in the mirror: what does the team need today? Signal the change in tone. Then manoeuvre and explain why. If, for example, the company’s share price has just dropped, you might be focusing on that when in reality people may be worrying about their jobs and not listening to your plan at all.
Rapport pays off when things get heated. If you know a colleague, Muldoon says, you can tell whether difficult behaviour is a state – a bad day – or a trait. “When we don’t know each other, we avoid conflict. And when it goes underneath the surface, it simmers.” It emerges as missed tasks and skipped meetings. Psychological safety matters here too. “A high-performing team doesn’t make fewer mistakes,” she says. “They learn from them quicker because they can talk about it.”
1. Put formal structures in place for issues like sexual harassment and bullying;
2. Agree team conflict resolution principles and rules from the start. Formal rules are how we work together. Principles can act as guardrails if disagreement arises. Informal structures like weekly team check-ins, shared learning sessions, and one-to-one meetings set us up for success;
3. Repair before resolving: acknowledge the emotions and manage assumptions first so that tensions can decrease and thinking can re-emerge;
4. Determine if it’s a state or trait. Was the engagement you had with someone indicative of a hard day or a character flaw? Someone may just have been having an awful day, so reflect on your assumptions before reacting;
5. Have the courage to speak up. If team members don’t learn how to disagree constructively, then feelings and resentments get pushed down, and this is where real tension simmers. It’s best to speak up and get it resolved early ... and learn how to complain about your own dinner too.

title: Two-bed apartment in grand Georgian building in Ballsbridge
description: Second-floor home on Pembroke Road is one of eight apartments in D4 building with off-street parking
content:
Number 51 Pembroke Road is one of those fine old Georgian grandes dames found so frequently on this stretch of Dublin 4 , extending from the canal at Baggot Street to the heart of Ballsbridge.
The land it was built on in the 1830s originally belonged to the Fitzwilliam dynasty and was passed on to the earls of Pembroke, the Herbert family, through marriage. The 11th earl, George Herbert, laid out Pembroke Road and planned it as a wide, tree-lined thoroughfare, influenced by architectural trends in Europe.
The road retains much of its former gracefulness today, and is home to a mix of residential and commercial premises. Apartment 4, a two-bed, second-floor apartment at 51 Pembroke Road, has come on to the market with Hunters Estate Agents, seeking €695,000. It would make a great base in the city, as it has for its current owner for decades.
Well set back from the road, 51 Pembroke Road is a semidetached four-storey-over-basement property laid out as eight apartments. The front door has an ornate fanlight and is set between doric columns.
Stairs lead up to the second floor. It’s worth noting that there is no lift access. A double-height window illuminates the stairs and dominates the hallway. It has very finely detailed inset stained glass in a rose pattern with a heraldic deer at its centre.
The 102sq m apartment at number 4 occupies most of the second floor. It is Ber exempt and heated by gas. Views from the home stretching to the south encompass the Dublin mountains.
Standing in the hallway, the two bedrooms are to the front of the building, and the living and dining area and kitchen are to the back. There’s a bathroom on the right of the hall.
The living and dining area is a lovely space with the elegant proportions of Georgian architecture, namely high ceilings, simple coving and large windows. A gas inset fire in a marble fireplace takes centre stage in the room, and an attractive recessed arch sits to the right with a capacious storage cupboard tucked away behind it.
It’s a room that would be perfect for entertaining, large enough to host a decent gathering. A feature window will need some attention as some of the glazing is cracked and could prove troublesome in the winter.
There is a small kitchen off the livingroom. It would benefit from a cosmetic refresh, but it has a bright aspect with a large window overlooking the garden. It’s easy to picture a small breakfast table underneath the window.
Both bedrooms lie to the front of the building and overlook Pembroke Road. The windows are high, with original shutters and six-over-six sash windows, and Juliet wrought-iron balconies add further charm. Both feature built-in wardrobes and there is enough space in the second bedroom to install an en suite shower room.
The communal garden outside is another lovely feature of the building; it’s well tended, full of tall, mature trees and has plenty of benches and bistro-style seating. There’s also a designated parking space for the apartment in the front garden.

title: Charming end-terrace Victorian in Dún Laoghaire
description: Spacious Mosaphir Terrace home retains period details such as deep bay windows and ornate plasterwork
content:
When 3 Mosaphir Terrace, Corrig Road, a two-storey-over-garden-level house in Dún Laoghaire , sold around the peak of the Celtic Tiger in 2006, it had a new roof but needed a lot of work, says one of the owners.
They paid €2.1 million for the Victorian house and “did everything” to it, before moving in, in 2007. Nearly 20 years on, with their children grown up, they are placing the home back on the market.
Number 3 Mosaphir Terrace, a 327sq m (3,520sq ft) end-terrace four-bed home, is now for sale through Sherry FitzGerald, seeking €2.35 million. It has a C1 Ber.
The house has retained many of its original features, including ornate plasterwork in the hall and main reception rooms, large marble fireplaces and sash windows with working shutters. Very deep bay windows on three levels at the back of the house are an unusual feature, with the bay on the top floor providing views across Dún Laoghaire’s rooftops to the sea.
Upstairs, the house is decorated in a period style, with sweeping floor-length drapes and handsome period furniture. Downstairs, there’s a large modern kitchen opening on to the back garden, and a large family room. It’s a bright house, decorated in a mix of neutral and bold colours. The part-panelled front hall, for example, has striking red-patterned wallpaper.
The drawingroom at the front of the house, oak-floored like all the downstairs rooms, has two tall sash windows overlooking Corrig Road to the front. It has ceiling cornicing, a centre rose and a white marble fireplace with slate inset. Double doors under an arched glass panel open into a formal oak-floored diningroom with deep red walls. Its deep square bay window at the back overlooks the back garden. There’s also a small study at this level.
Stairs lead down to the garden level, which also has understairs access from the front garden. The kitchen/breakfastroom has white timber units, an Aga with a tiled splashback, a Crema Marfil-tiled floor, a large island with a polished granite top and French doors opening to a patio and the garden. There’s a desk in the deep bay at this level, with floor-to-ceiling glass windows. A good-sized walk-in pantry opens off the kitchen, next to the breakfastroom area.
French doors open into the large, comfortable family room beside the kitchen. The room has two sash windows looking into the front garden, a wood-burning stove in a sandstone fireplace and an oak floor. A good-sized utility room, with cupboards and a sink, opens off it. There is also a shower room off the downstairs hall.
Upstairs, the main bedroom, directly above the drawingroom, is wide and bright, with two tall sash windows overlooking Crosthwaite Park at the front. Like all the bedrooms, it has fitted wardrobes. The en-suite shower room is part tiled and has underfloor heating. Another bedroom has deep blue walls and another has the deep bay window with space to sit and enjoy glimpses of the sea and Howth. A fully tiled family bathroom on the top return overlooks the back garden.
The walled back garden is mostly in lawn with a patio area at the side of the house; there’s also a gravelled patio/parking area at the bottom of the garden beside an electronic gate, accessed off a lane from Clarinda Park. The family has residents’ permit on-street parking and usually park across the road in Crosthwaite Park. The park, a well-tended green space, is open to the public.

title: Old meets new in extended Ranelagh redbrick mere metres from Luas stop
description: Modernised Victorian Villa with period features and contemporary styling occupies excellent location near Beechwood green-line stop
content:
Less than 200 years ago, much of what we now know as Ranelagh was little more than a semi-rural village − as opposed to the leafy suburb filled with period redbrick houses that make it such a sought-after residential location today. The opening in 1854 of the Harcourt Street Railway line from Dublin city centre to Bray in Co Wicklow and the later addition of the Rathmines and Ranelagh station in 1896 made it a particularly attractive place to live for those seeking a home convenient to both the city and the countryside.
Land that was formerly a plant nursery was sold and houses were built in the ensuing decades near what is now the Luas Green Line and Beechwood Luas stop.
One of these , number 9 Beechwood Avenue Lower, a Victorian redbrick villa-style home, was built about 1890. Although from the outside it retains an old-world appearance, the split-level semidetached house has been extended and renovated in a thoroughly modern fashion.
Behind its slate-grey front door, accessed via stone steps, is a hallway with a door to the main sittingroom.
With its high ceiling, coving and ceiling rose, this room has a distinctly period feel. The floorboards and the Victorian fireplace are original and there’s an oval-shaped Victorian-style mirror on the wall above the mantelpiece.
Stairs leading to the ground floor from the hallway reveal a modern extension, in complete contrast to the old part of the house. Here, there’s another sittingroom, which is book-lined; a bedroom that could also be used as an office; and an open-plan kitchen/dining/livingroom with sliding glass doors that open to the back garden.
The kitchen is secreted behind stainless steel cupboards; the floors are tiled in dark grey; and the walls are painted in a calm beige tone, giving it something of a futuristic look. A substantial American-style stainless steel fridge adds to the room’s 21st-century vibe.
Upstairs, the two double bedrooms, which have white walls and the family bathroom, tiled in beige with modern fittings, are equally contemporary in style.
The landscaped, west-facing back garden has a paved patio, a small lawn with a neat, gravel border and fencing on either side.
The house sits within metres of the Luas stop, with regular services taking about 10 minutes to reach St Stephen’s Green in the city centre. Ranelagh, with its wide selection of chichi restaurants, cafes and boutiques, is about a five-minute walk away.
Extending to 124sq m (1,335sq ft), with C1 Ber rating, number 9 Beechwood Avenue Lower is now for sale through agent Mullery O’Gara, seeking €1.375 million.

title: Merz hopes to cash in chips with Nvidia investments
description: Jensen Huang was guest of honour at the inaugural Invest in Germany event
content:
Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang is not just the king of the chips driving AI, he is also a pro at generating headlines.
In London, days before flying to Berlin, the Taipei-born American engineer-executive was broken-hearted over the sorry state of Germany .
“Nothing hurts me more than to see one of the world’s most technologically advanced countries lagging so far behind,” he said.
On Monday evening and Tuesday, managing his hurt bravely, Huang found himself the target of a very public wooing by chancellor Friedrich Merz .
Huang was guest of honour at the inaugural Invest in Germany event, a humbling sign of the times when Germany has to hustle for business.
But Huang was the ultimate get, smiling and nodding in Berlin on Tuesday as Merz insisted – despite ample headlines and economic data to the contrary – that Germany is open for business.
For Merz, lagging in polls with Europe’s largest sclerotic economy, his pitch was plain: in Europe, only Germany has the industrial AI data that Nvidia needs.
“This is a real secret,” he said, “and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies.”
For its part the chipmaker has promised to back four German start-ups, part of a commitment of almost $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in Europe-wide spend on companies, universities and research institutions.
Though the German firm names are known, Nvidia did not disclose the size of its respective planned investments. Agile Robots develops AI-powered robots for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare; Avelios Medical programmes AI-powered hospital management software; Mirelo is behind AI models that generate audio for video; and Reflex Aerospace designs and builds satellites.
Merz and his business minister Katherina Reiche were both tight-lipped about the scale of Germany’s investment in the Nvidia partnership, but informed guesstimates are several hundred million euro.
Germany has some cash spare since last year, when Nvidia rival Intel officially cancelled its $30 billion planned investment in eastern Germany, with about a third in state subsidies.
One year on, Germany’s unpopular chancellor can only hope his chips are down, but not out.

title: What the Philip K Dickens is Marvel up to with VisionQuest?
description: Can the MCU’s latest TV offering match the depth of much-celebrated predecessor WandaVision?
content:
Looking back, it’s clear that WandaVision was an unlikely success. The Marvel Cinematic Universe’s first Disney+ series, from 2021, formed around two of the least-renowned members of the Avengers – Wanda “Scarlet Witch” Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen) and the Vision (Paul Bettany) – was a genre-defying oddity, each episode depicting its heroes “trapped” in a different flavour of sitcom parody, from chintzy 1950s fare such as I Love Lucy all the way up to 2000s-era offerings such as Modern Family.
It was smart and funny and won critics over with a sharp, witty script that cannily teased out its bonkers premise – that Wanda had created this facsimile of family life, including Vision and their two children – to a satisfying, even moving, conclusion.
At the time it seemed as if the MCU’s foray into television might herald a chance to tell stories too big, too small, too bloody weird for the conventions of a three-hour blockbuster. Nearly 20 shows later it’s hard to argue that expectation has been fulfilled.
In the plus column we could place the time-travel romp Loki , the colourful ebullience of Ms Marvel and the retro-exactitude of X-Men ’97. I’d go to bat for Hawkeye , Moon Knight and She-Hulk: Attorney at Law – three shows that I greatly enjoyed and that everyone else seemed to vehemently dislike.
As for the rest, especially the dreary dregs of The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, Echo and Secret Invasion , we shall abide time-honoured tradition and speak of them no more.
Occasionally, Marvel’s latest TV offering, VisionQuest (Disney+, two new episodes each Tuesday), reminds us of the scope and scale of its progenitor.
It is, as the name suggests, a direct sequel to WandaVision, following the titular android superhero reeling from the loss of his love Wanda and wrestling with who he is. (This is literal. After a series of events that I’d be reckless to try to unpack here, this Vision is the original’s clone, resurrected by a grieving Wanda and implanted with memories to which he now has no emotional connection.)
Unmoored in his new reality, he does what anyone would: acquires some shift work in an Edinburgh pub and spends his off-time in an elaborately constructed Mind Palace where a coterie of Tony Stark-created AIs help him uncover the secrets of his past and teach him how to act like a human being.
[ The Marvel Cinematic Universe used to be pretty cool. Why is it sliding towards mediocrity? Opens in new window ]
As always with Marvel projects, a vast catalogue of lore must be parcelled out before one gets started. The MCU had this issue even in its earliest outings, as a decades-long backlog of comic narratives had to be made explicable on screen.
Now those screen offerings themselves form the problem, with their unwieldy plots, their baffling array of heroes, villains, creatures and worlds, their overlapping timelines and their multiple universes.
To engage with every named character in VisionQuest’s first episode alone requires at least passing familiarity with six films and two previous Marvel shows. (I did not have to compile this list myself, as Disney+ cheerily provided these homework instructions on its website ahead of broadcast.)
Marvel’s onboarding process was laborious 10 years ago, but it’s doubly so now, as its biggest hits recede deeper behind the veil of time and its newer outings remain lesser seen and even lesser remembered.
One among those shows mentioned, Agatha All Along, is a series I watched in full two years ago, and whose campy thrills I seem to recall passably enjoying – without, however, a single plot point lodging in my brain.
There’s a temptation to call Vision’s wranglings, as an AI that seeks humanity, “timely”. I do not find this to be the case. The machine-longing-to-be-human trope is the main subject not merely of just about every piece of fiction about robots ever written but also of just about every Pinocchio-style fable of the puppet, automaton or mechanical creature that holds within its unbeating heart dreams of becoming a real live boy.
And at a time when every fleece-wearing goon on Earth is tripping over his feet to tell us that the word-guessing algorithm he has built has gained consciousness, the show’s “Am … I … alive?” moments risk feeling more tedious and annoying than ever.
[ Neil Jordan: In defence of the Marvel Cinematic Universe Opens in new window ]
This is not helped by long stretches of dialogue between Vision and his AI companions. Watching Bettany, Orla Brady, James D’Arcy and James Spader, all innately watchable and interesting actors, trade comically wordy dialogue about humanity, artificiality and the boundaries between the two is often grating.
When Vision tells Spader’s Ultron that he wants to know more about his former self, he says, “We are forever entangled, but he is a stranger to me and therefore I am a stranger to myself.”
That this is how two robots would converse is likely textually accurate, but the result is multiple scenes that resemble those viral videos in which people force a pair of competing LLMs to interact with each other in an infinite loop of inane verbosity.
This sense isn’t helped when human characters so frequently speak arch and heightened dialogue themselves. There was a brief and mortifying clamour among well-meaning Marvel heads to regard one particularly purple quote from WandaVision – “what is grief if not love persevering?” – as one of the greatest lines of poetry ever written. It is, therefore, hard not to cringe when it’s repeated here by another character, verbatim, as a dramatic plot point.
The degree to which viewers can look past the abstruse chatter and the homework will rest on how much joy they can extract from the rest of the show – which is, thankfully, a perfectly engaging action thriller.
Vision is being hunted by a master bounty hunter called the Paladin – aided, in a gloriously unexpected casting turn, by Philomena Cunk’s Diane Morgan – who wants to deliver him to a shadowy figure known as the Client.
To do this they’ve kidnapped – dramatic music – his son, Tommy. Yes, the son who shouldn’t exist because he was a figment of Wanda’s imagination, deleted the second she was apprehended at that show’s conclusion.
He’s now a Scottish man living in London who balances life as a pickpocket with his own psychological struggles about the impossibility of his existence, rendering his backstory an odd melange of Oliver Twist and paranoid science fiction that I am forced to call “Philip K Dickens”.
As a genre caper it more than acquits itself with well-helmed set pieces, some knotty moments of intrigue and able turns from its younger cast, most notably Ruaridh Mollica as the impossible Tommy.
The plot is consistently surprising, as should be expected from an adaptation of Tom King’s seminal comics run. (It may be notable that the year’s great comics telly hit, HBO’s Lanterns, is also a Tom King joint.)
And VisionQuest is simply better shot, with better sets, than many of its peers, suggesting that Marvel has at least heard criticism of the eye-scorching CGI and muddy drabness that have characterised much of its late period fare.
It’s just that, for all its charms, the show still bears a weightlessness that begs to be forgotten. In its first episode we watch as Vision blankly peruses his carousel of implanted memories, scenes from a life he’s not sure he truly lived. In a year or two’s time I expect to read this very review with the same curious, baffled distance. Did any of this, I’ll ask myself, even happen at all?

title: Klara and the Sun review: Aran Murphy is lovely. Otherwise, this film is best forgotten
description: Taika Waititi’s adaptation of the admired Kazuo Ishiguro novel is like an underdeveloped, overly long, candyfloss-swathed episode of Black Mirror
content:
Let’s start with the few positives. Aran Murphy gives a lovely supporting performance in Taika Waititi’s otherwise regrettable adaptation of an admired Kazuo Ishiguro novel. The rising actor’s turn as an eccentric young boffin clarifies that, soon enough, we will no longer feel obliged to note that his parents are Cillian Murphy and Yvonne McGuinness.
What else? The Waititi regular Rachel House raises a few laughs as a terrifying housekeeper. The New Zealand scenery is nice. Help me out. I’m struggling.
We are watching a familiar genre here. Amy Adams stars as Chrissie, a flinty mother in a vaguely postapocalyptic world who, years after her oldest child dies, buys a humanoid robot to keep her surviving daughter, Josie (Mia Tharia), company in the waving wheat fields.
Jenna Ortega deserves our sympathy for heroic efforts to make something appealing of Klara, the titular cyborg, but the irritating feyness of the character will not be resisted. She is forever smiling manically and falling backwards to no comic effect. You have avoided a hundred street performers painted silver doing this act.
The film is treading on ground already covered by films such as AI: Artificial Intelligence, Bicentennial Man and After Yang. In an odd coincidence, Travis Knight’s fine Wildwood, also released this week, features another mother replacing a doomed child with a mechanical one.
Klara and the Sun, alas, features no insights into the potential consolations of a manufactured intelligence, preferring instead to focus on the tedious quirk that has lately become Waititi’s stock-in-trade.
The film is peculiarly uncertain in its world building. Somewhere in the opening 20 minutes, Natasha Lyonne, as the proprietor of the robot store, hurriedly talks us through the planet’s disastrous backstory. Something about the internet. Something about war. Something about what we have lost.
But the film’s Earth – or its New Zealand, anyway – does not seem particularly blasted. City streets are a bit bleak. Technology feels a tad retro. (This Sony film features an old-school Sony monitor.) Everything looks very much as the average 21st-century hipster would like it to look.
Imagine an underdeveloped episode of Black Mirror swathed in candyfloss and stretched out to three times its ideal length. Never as funny as it is annoying, never as touching as it is maudlin, here is a film too misconceived to establish even the most eccentric cult following.

title: Fatherland review: Ravishing-looking final part of Pawlikowski’s trilogy falls short
description: It seems churlish to complain that Fatherland is the weakest of the director’s historical trilogy, but it is
content:
Immaculate surfaces trump uncertain substance in this snapshot of a battered Germany in 1949. Pawel Pawlikowski ’s trademark deployment of sculptural beauty here feels more like tasty trademarked secret sauce than a means of articulation.
Germany is complicated for Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler), the Nobel laureate in literature, returning to his native land after 16 years in American exile. Accompanied by his dutiful daughter, Erika (Sandra Hüller), he travels between West Germany and Soviet-controlled Weimar, accepting honours while a fractured nation competes to claim his cultural legacy.
The journey promises a searching examination of guilt, identity and the unfinished business of Nazism. Too often, however, history becomes an elegant backdrop for portentous exchanges, carefully staged silences and clunky stereotypes. Elliptical editing and sparse dialogue leave psychological connections frustratingly vague.
August Diehl’s Byronic Klaus Mann, the writer’s son, disappears far too early, leaving Sandra Hüller to anchor the film. (No better woman, to be fair.) As Erika, caught between filial loyalty and mounting resentment, she conveys a lifetime of frustration through guarded expressions and snippy exchanges. Her daddy-daughter two-step provides more dramatic force than the broader political parallels the screenplay feints towards.
The film’s most poignant scenes depict two returning refugees struggling to find a shared home and identity following personal and geopolitical catastrophe. Otherwise, the film relies on Bach’s Jesu, Joy of Man’s Desiring to provide emotional heft. (No better man, to be fair.)
The postwar setting teases fecund ground for exploring national denial and moral quandaries. But, at 82 minutes, this vignette feels as if it is only clearing its throat for the aria. Accordingly, the film’s truncated treatment of Germany’s divided postwar identity remains curiously schematic. Historical arguments are annunciated, not dramatised.
It seems churlish to complain that Fatherland is the weakest of Pawlikowski’s historical trilogy. Yet this ravishing-looking film, replete with Lukasz Zal’s crystalline cinematographic compositions and academy-ratio framing, is seldom as engrossing as Cold War and never as impactful as Ida .
Fatherland is in cinemas from Friday, October 23rd

title: Warmer, cosier and cheaper to run – how a home energy upgrade is helping one committed homeowner
description: Warmer, cosier and cheaper to run – how a home energy upgrade is helping one committed homeowner
content:
As a committed environmentalist Deirdre de Burca knew all about the carbon reduction benefits a home energy upgrade would bring before she undertook the work.
What she didn’t anticipate was just how much more comfortable her home would become, and how much money it would save her.
The former Green Party senator retired from politics 16 years ago and today runs an international consultancy specialising in sustainable development.
She inherited her three-bedroom semi-detached home, on a housing estate in suburban Dublin, from her late mother.
“After leaving politics, I moved to Brussels in 2012 and was working and living there when my Mum had a very serious stroke. So, I moved back to Dublin in 2017 and looked after her while she was in hospital and then in a nursing home,” she explains.
It was a difficult time, made harder by an uncomfortable home.
“The house was built in the early 1980s and was extremely drafty. My sister would come to stay and tell me her bedroom was like Siberia. You’d go in and freeze,” she recalls.
The house had oil-based central heating but only some of the radiators worked.
“When my Mum died, in 2020, I stayed on and we were straight into Covid. I was home a lot and had a decision to make about whether to sell and move somewhere else or invest in an energy upgrade with proper insulation. It really wasn’t comfortable and I knew I couldn’t remain living there if I didn’t do something,” she says.
A campaign by the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) caught her attention.
“They were promoting their One Stop Shops for home energy upgrades, so I thought right, I’m going to invest in upgrading this house and make it much warmer and more comfortable to live in,” she says.
With SEAI’s complete home energy upgrade grant route, a registered One Stop Shop provides a complete home upgrade in one go, managing everything from the initial home energy assessment through to the final BER, including the grant application and contractor works. The grants are deducted from the cost of works upfront, which can really help with the financing. A list of registered One Stop Shops is available on the SEAI website.
As recommended, de Burca contacted several One Stop Shops for a quote and chose the one she was happiest with. “I asked around and they had a good reputation,” she says.
The work went smoothly. “I made my first proper contact with them in June 2023, and all of the work was done by March 2024,” she says.
She focused on three key areas. “The first thing I did was replace all my doors and windows, with triple glazed windows, new window frames, and a composite front door. It made the house look newer and because the old windows had a lot of panels, the light coming into the house was much better with the new ones. It transformed the house,” she explains.
Once that was complete, she upgraded her attic insulation and had the house wrapped in external wall insulation. “It was like a facelift for the house. It looked like I had built a brand-new house, it was so unrecognisable from what had been there before. It just looks so modern,” she says.
The final step was to replace her polluting oil burner with a modern heat pump and install efficient new radiators.
Her service provider had made it clear that the house must first be sufficiently insulated to benefit from a heat pump.
“The heat pump has been such a winner,” she says. “As someone who is not very ‘techie’, what I like most about it was that it is self-regulating. Once installed all you have to do is decide what temperature you want, and then just leave it to run itself.”
As part of the work, she had separate thermostats installed for upstairs and downstairs. “I set them for the temperature I want and leave the heat pump to it. I have as little to do with it as possible and it works away quietly and efficiently,” she explains.
But the biggest revelation has been the comfort. “The heat it provides in the house is entirely different from the heat I experienced from the radiators before. What I remember about them is having to sit close to them to get a real sense of heat - and there were always draughts,” she recalls.
“The combination of insulation and heat pump means the heat is dispersed nicely throughout the house. It’s a lovely diffuse kind of heat, warm and toasty, with no draughts and no cold spots. Every room is very comfortable,” she says.
For Deirdre, the consistent warmth gives her a terrific sense of wellbeing. “I go out in the morning and the house is warm and I don’t have to worry about putting the heat back on before I get home. It just stays at a very nice temperature,” she explains.
“It has transformed my experience. The house went from being a draughty place that wasn’t really somewhere I chose to spend time, to something I looked forward to coming home to.”
The work improved her home from a Building Energy Rating (BER) of E2 to A2, a terrific improvement. But it’s the improved ‘liveability’ that really impressed her and de Burca isn’t the only one benefiting.
That’s because, before undertaking the work, she had considered taking a tenant under the rent a room scheme. “But there’s no way most people would agree to rent a room that was draughty and cold. Since getting the energy upgrade, I’ve taken in a tenant and they are delighted with the house,” she says.
The added bonus is that, since doing the work, de Burca’s energy bills have fallen. “We’re in the second energy crisis in four years. Most people I know are paying around €1700 to fill their oil tanks, and they need two fills a year. I feel so lucky that the timing of my energy upgrade was before the current Middle Eastern crisis but it has made us all aware of how dependent we are on other parts of the world for our energy and also that prices are only going to keep going up unless we switch to alternative sources,” she points out.
Separately, since her home energy upgrade Deirdre has also taken advantage of an SEAI grant towards an electrical vehicle charger installed and bought an electric car. She installed solar panels too.
“I don’t have petrol bills for my car anymore and I don’t have oil bills for my heating. What I do have is one electricity bill and I can’t believe how low it is,” she says.
“I’m on a nighttime tariff so I charge my electric car in the early hours of the morning, from a timer on my phone. It’s hard to make direct comparisons, because so much has changed, but I think I’m saving between €4,000 and €5,000 a year on my bills. I’m amazed how much I’m saving.”
She now believes whole neighbourhoods should band together to get home energy upgrades, to benefit from economies of scale.
It isn’t only about being sympathetic to the environment, as de Burca so avowedly is. “As well as making your home warmer and cosier, and being cleaner, this saves you money,” she says. “That has to be a really good reason for people to think about it.”
To find out more about SEAI home energy grants and the different energy upgrade routes available, search SEAI Home Energy Upgrades or visit seai.ie/homeenergyupgrades . Saving energy saves money.

title: Irish company at centre of large energy project for West Bank
description: Energy consulting firm Azorom working to bring two new solar and battery storage systems to Palestinian territory
content:
Irish energy consulting firm Azorom is at the centre of a plan to bring a new solar and battery storage system to the West Bank.
The company has just completed a six-month feasibility study for the Palestinian Energy and Natural Resources Authority (Penra), funded by the World Bank , to assess existing solar generation , electricity demand and the distribution network in the region.
The objective was to determine where additional distributed solar and battery storage systems “can be deployed safely and economically”, the company said.
The need for greater energy independence is crucial for the Palestinian state. The West Bank currently depends on Israel for 87 per cent of its power needs.
And the supply frequently gets caught up in the politics of the region. Israel’s state-owned electric company Israel Electric Corp has in the past imposed power cuts on several West Bank cities for unpaid debts.
Palestinians in Gaza have been without system electricity since 2023 when Gaza’s power plant was forced to shut down due to fuel depletion, leaving the territory in an effective electricity blackout.
The Palestinian Authority has being trying to reduce the region’s dependence on Israel for energy through state and private sector-funded solar projects.
Penra is targeting an additional 1,430MW (megawatts) of solar PV by 2030, nearly five times the current installed capacity across the West Bank and Gaza combined.
[ Arab parties could be kingmakers in Israel’s election. Netanyahu has reason to worry Opens in new window ]
Azorom was selected by Penra following an international tender process. As part of its work, the Irish firm assessed the feasibility of adding the additional power to two pilot electricity networks – Tulkarem Municipality in an urban setting and the Tubas District Electricity Company (TDECO) in a predominantly rural one.
The company “analysed the performance of the networks and their need for storage, to produce investment-ready procurement documentation”.
[ Will French unrest benefit Marine Le Pen’s presidential run? Opens in new window ]
Together, the two electricity networks serve approximately 54,000 customers. Tulkarem has over 12MW of solar PV, while TDECO has over 27MW of existing solar PV capacity.
“The study assessed how much additional solar can be accommodated by each network and how much and where storage is required,” the company said.
The work is intended to provide a replicable model for wider roll-out across the West Bank.
“The West Bank faces significant electricity supply constraints, recurring outages and a heavy dependence on imported power,” Azorom chief executive Conor Lonergan said.
“This project has been about moving beyond analysis and putting the technical, financial and procurement groundwork in place to bring solar and battery storage projects towards investment and delivery in a scalable and sustainable manner.
[ World Food Programme cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza due to funding shortages Opens in new window ]
“The focus is on enabling greater use of locally generated renewable energy while supporting a more secure and reliable electricity supply for communities and businesses.”
On whether the company found it difficult to operate in the region given the continuing violence between Israeli settlers and Palestinians, Longergan said: “We worked in neighbouring Lebanon for many years.
“On this project in the West Bank, because of the present situation, we were allowed to have our international experts work from home base while also utilising local experts on site.”

title: Applications open for Research Ireland Industry Fellowship Programme
description: The overall aim is to strengthen the linkages and interplay between industry and the research community
content:
Applications are open for the Research Ireland Industry Fellowship Programme. The programme provides funding for collaborative research projects, codeveloped by researchers and industry partners, and supports researcher placements in industry.
Researchers spend time working in host organisations, helping to address real-world challenges, explore new opportunities and strengthen connections between industry and the research community.
Research Ireland provides up to €130,000 in funding to support eligible fellowship costs associated with researcher placements of between one and 12 months full-time (or up to 24 months part-time), helping organisations access specialist expertise and develop their collaborative research capacity.
The overall aim is to strengthen the linkages and interplay between industry and the research community. “We are looking to strengthen competitiveness through the development of an innovation-led economy with a focus on attracting and retaining FDI and supporting indigenous industries to scale,” says Dr Aisling McEvoy, head of enterprise partnerships at Research Ireland.
“We want to increase the capacity of the economy to use knowledge, and this requires absorptive capacity in firms but also requires institutions to make expertise easier to find, research infrastructure easier to access and relationships easier to sustain,” she adds.
The Industry Fellowship Programme forms part of a broader portfolio of mobility fellowship programmes being developed by Research Ireland to support the movement of researchers across sectors, strengthening collaboration, knowledge exchange and research impact, she explains. This portfolio includes programmes such as the Research Ireland Fellowship and the Public Service Fellowship.
The programme builds on the success of previous enterprise-facing mobility schemes, including the Enterprise Fellowship Placement Stream and the Industry RD&I Fellowship Programme.
“It aims to support researcher mobility to enterprise to strengthen knowledge exchange, collaboration and innovation, and to accelerate the application of research for economic impact across Ireland,” McEvoy explains.
“The fellow is based in a company working on a codeveloped research project that addresses shared challenges and opportunities,” she continues. “By embedding researchers within industry, the programme promotes the exchange of knowledge, skills and expertise between academia and enterprise.”
The programme is open to late-stage PhD candidates, postdoctoral researchers and academic staff, she adds. These include faculty staff seeking dedicated time to undertake a collaborative project with an eligible industry partner; postdoctoral researchers; and late-stage PhD candidates who will have completed their PhD before the fellowship begins.
Applicants must have the support of both an eligible Irish research body and an eligible industry partner to undertake the proposed fellowship. The research body administers the award and acts as the employer of the fellow throughout the fellowship.
Eligible industry partners are companies, in Ireland or overseas, that can provide an appropriate research environment for an embedded fellow to undertake the proposed project and have the capacity, expertise and resources to support the collaboration.
“Partner companies to date have included large multinationals, SMEs, start-ups and spin outs,” McEvoy notes. “These include large companies whose technical staff might be primarily physicists and engineers, but they are developing or introducing a new product that might need specific skills like polymer chemistry, electrochemistry, nanotechnology to develop the new product.”
There is also an FDI dimension, she says. “The embedding of a fellow can help to develop research capacity and capability in the Irish base of a multinational company which demonstrates the opportunity to do more and can give confidence to the corporate headquarters to invest in R&D in Ireland.”
At the other end of the spectrum the programme can be very useful for SMEs and start-ups who can’t afford to recruit a PhD qualified researcher. “The expertise of the researcher can unlock innovation in the business helping them to grow and scale.”
In an example of a successful fellowship funded by Research Ireland Dr Ayse Kont, a postdoctoral researcher at University College Cork (UCC), worked with Boston Scientific Cork to work on medical device polymer bead process optimisation.
Looking back on the fellowship, she said: “Transitioning to industrial research during the fellowship seemed like learning a new language or putting on a new pair of glasses – you understand, see and gain access to a new world. It truly widened my perspective and enabled me to grow professionally. Beyond professional growth, it also helped me to identify and pinpoint the environment and area I want to continue working.”
“This project deepened our understanding of the existing product, opening possibilities for expanded applications and new features. The methodologies and concepts developed during this work are also transferable, offering a framework for handling newly acquired products within the same space at Boston Scientific,” said Gareth Bell, senior fellow manufacturing engineer at Boston Scientific.
There is no specific closing date for applications, McEvoy says. “Applications can be submitted at any time, but batches of applications will be assessed in November 2026, March 2027 and September 2027.”

title: Make time for Dublin this winter
description: From autumn rugby and city shopping to good food and leisurely mornings, there’s plenty to enjoy a stay at InterContinental Dublin this winter
content:
Winter is a wonderful time to spend a few days in Dublin. The city’s restaurants and bars are buzzing, the cultural calendar is packed and there’s something particularly appealing about wrapping up for a walk before finding somewhere warm and welcoming to spend the evening.
Whether it’s a weekend catching up with friends, a trip to the rugby, an afternoon shopping or simply a change of scenery, there’s no shortage of reasons to visit. And rather than rushing home at the end of the day, why not make a night of it?
Set in the heart of Ballsbridge, InterContinental Dublin offers an elegant base from which to enjoy the city, with the added appeal of having everything you need for a memorable winter stay under one roof.
November brings the Autumn Nations Series to the Aviva Stadium, with three weekends of international rugby adding to the atmosphere around Ballsbridge. Even if you’re not heading to a match, there’s something infectious about the energy of the city on a rugby weekend.
Just a short walk from the hotel, the RDS has a busy programme of exhibitions and events, including Art Source in November, while the winter season brings plenty more reasons to explore the city.
For those who enjoy a little shopping, the independent boutiques and cafes of Donnybrook and Sandymount are well worth discovering, while Grafton Street and Dublin’s city centre are only a short journey away.
And if shopping isn’t on the agenda, a walk through nearby Herbert Park is a lovely way to spend an hour, particularly when the trees are turning and there’s a crispness in the air. The best part of a winter walk, of course, is coming in from the cold.
There’s a wonderful sense of arrival at InterContinental Dublin, where grand surroundings and warm Irish hospitality make it easy to feel at home.
The Reading Room, with its inviting fireplace and comfortable armchairs, is just the place to settle in after an afternoon exploring the city. Order a pot of tea, catch up over coffee or make an occasion of afternoon tea, with a selection of delicate pastries and freshly baked scones.
As evening approaches, the Whiskey Bar comes into its own. Whether it’s a cocktail before dinner, a good Irish whiskey or a nightcap at the end of the evening, it’s an inviting place to spend time with good company. It’s this combination of elegant surroundings and a relaxed, sociable atmosphere that gives the hotel its character. There’s a sense of occasion without the need for an occasion.
Of course, one of the best reasons to stay overnight is being able to enjoy dinner without having to think about the journey home.
At Simmons, the hotel’s restaurant, guests can settle in for an evening of contemporary dining in elegant surroundings. With a focus on carefully sourced ingredients and thoughtfully prepared dishes, it’s a lovely setting for dinner for two, a celebration with friends or simply a night out.
Begin with a drink in the Whiskey Bar, take your time over dinner and enjoy the fact that your bedroom is only a short elevator journey away. While there’s plenty happening beyond the hotel doors, a winter stay is also an opportunity to take a little time for yourself.
InterContinental Dublin’s spacious bedrooms and suites offer a welcome change from the everyday, with beautifully appointed interiors, comfortable beds and plenty of room to unwind. After an evening enjoying the city or dining at the hotel, it’s a chance to switch off and enjoy a night away from the usual routine.
For those who would like to make the most of the hotel’s wellness facilities, the indoor swimming pool and Wellness Area offer another opportunity to slow the pace. A relaxing spa treatment can be the perfect addition to a winter break, whether you’re staying for one night or making a weekend of it.
And the following morning? Breakfast at your leisure, perhaps another coffee, and no particular rush to leave.
It’s all part of the hotel’s winter philosophy: the art of slowing down. Not about doing less for the sake of it, but about making more time for the things you enjoy.
For those planning a winter stay in Dublin, InterContinental Dublin’s Winter Moments package offers a little extra, with an upgrade to the next room category, €50 dining credit and breakfast the following morning.
Available on selected dates throughout November, December and January, it’s an ideal excuse to make a night of it, whether you’re visiting for the rugby, enjoying a weekend in the city or simply taking some time away.

title: More than 50,000 households are being rewarded for flexible electricity use
description: ESB Networks aims to give customers practical and relatable ways to participate in the move towards a more renewable net-zero future
content:
Small changes in when we use electricity can make a meaningful collective difference. That’s the thinking behind Is This a Good Time?, an ESB Networks programme that rewards customers for shifting some of their electricity use to times when demand is lower or renewable electricity is more abundant.
Open to all electricity customers, regardless of supplier, the programme gives households a practical way to take part in Ireland’s energy transition. Participants receive alerts that help them make informed decisions about when to use electricity and can earn rewards for taking action.
While energy costs often dominate the conversation, energy flexibility remains a relatively new concept for many households. Yet simply changing when we use electricity can help make better use of renewable energy, reduce demand on the network during peak periods and support a more flexible and resilient electricity system.
Through initiatives such as Is This a Good Time?, ESB Networks is helping customers play an active role in creating a cleaner, more sustainable energy future, one small change at a time.
“As demand for electricity continues to grow, we need to ensure that the electricity network remains resilient while also maximising the use of renewable energy when it is available,” says Aisling Walsh, customer and strategy manager at ESB Networks. “More than 50,000 customers have already participated in our Is This a Good Time? programme, showing that our customers not only understand the important role flexibility plays, but are willing to take action.
“By making small, practical changes to when they use electricity, their collective efforts are helping to ease congestion on the network, make better use of renewable energy and support the transition to a more renewable, net-zero future. Our aim is to continue giving customers practical and relatable ways to take part and make a real difference.”
The electricity network faces greatest demand between 5pm and 7pm. Like clockwork, everyone begins to use their appliances at the same time. “They are getting home from school or work and putting the kettle on, the dishwasher on, maybe putting a wash on or charging their electric car,” Walsh says. “There’s a massive draw on the network as a result.”
Customers who sign up to the Is This a Good Time? programme on the ESB Networks website receive text and email alerts with helpful information and tips on how to make the most of their home’s energy usage, with suggestions to “flex down” or “flex up”, and updates about peak events.
Small shifts can bring real rewards. Participants in Is This a Good Time? can earn digital gift cards simply by making small, practical changes to when they use electricity. Whether it’s setting the dishwasher to run later, charging an EV overnight or using an air fryer instead of the oven, these everyday actions can add up to make a real difference. Best of all, the programme is open to all electricity customers, regardless of their supplier.
“If there’s lots of wind available, we’ll ask customers to flex up, so to use their appliances at this time instead of their usual time,” Walsh says. Similarly, when there is less renewable electricity on the network, customers will be asked to “flex down”, and delay heavy appliance usage and perhaps look at alternatives such as using an air fryer instead of the oven.
“If we anticipate periods of particularly high demand on the network, participating customers may receive a text message encouraging them to reduce or shift some of their electricity use for a short period,” Walsh explains. “The aim is to make the best possible use of the network capacity we already have. While investment in the network will always continue, flexibility allows us to use existing infrastructure more efficiently, helping to accommodate growing demand and support more customers immediately.”
Essentially, this means that small actions taken by thousands of customers can make a significant collective difference. By shifting electricity use away from the busiest periods, customers help reduce demand on the network and free up capacity when it is needed most.
‘While investment in the network will always continue, flexibility allows us to use existing infrastructure more efficiently’
“These are simple changes that generally do not impact people’s daily routines,” Walsh says. “It could be running the dishwasher a little later in the evening or charging an electric vehicle at a different time. Individually, these actions may seem small, but together they can help balance demand across the network. It is also about making greater use of electricity when renewable generation is more readily available, helping us build a more flexible, efficient and lower-carbon energy system for everyone.”
More than 50,000 customers have signed up already, and those who take action after receiving the alerts are rewarded with digital gift cards. Walsh says the goal is to instigate a “mindset shift” about how and when we consume electricity. It’s already happening, she says, as the drive for sustainability becomes the norm and customers become more cognisant of where their energy is coming from.
“Rewards are about helping to change behaviours, but over the longer term, ideally, people will automatically change their behaviour and begin to time their dishwashers or dryers to run later or change when they charge their electric car,” she says.
The Is This a Good Time? programme is easily signed up to on the ESB Networks website and, while it is suitable for everyone regardless of their electricity supplier, Walsh says ESB Networks is conscious that it also has many customers who may find it more difficult to participate.
“Every household is different and customers are best placed to decide what works for them,” she says. “Flexibility is completely voluntary. For those who choose to take part, it’s an opportunity to make small changes that fit around their routine, earn rewards for their participation, and help create a more efficient and sustainable electricity system. Every contribution, no matter how small, can make a difference.”

title: Food Drink Ireland launches new Food Safety Incident Management Guide
description: Aimed primarily at manufacturers, the new guide is designed to protect and maintain Irish food safety standards
content:
Food Drink Ireland (FDI), the Ibec group representing the food and drink sector, has produced a new Food Safety Incident Management Guide to help Irish food business operators protect and maintain the country’s world-class food safety standards.
Aimed primarily at manufacturers, the guide offers structured, step-by-step guidance covering proactive prevention, rapid early-stage response and continuous improvement.
“The guide is available to both Food Drink Ireland member companies and non-members,” says FDI deputy director Linda Stuart Trainor. “It reinforces that modern food safety is a whole of business issue requiring cross-functional collaboration across operations, finance, legal, commercial and communications teams.”
The overall objective is to support the high standards already in place. “We have a very strict food safety regulatory regime, and the industry is renowned globally for its exceptionally strong commitment to safety standards,” she notes. “This means we have some of the safest food on the market anywhere in the world. But unfortunately, incidents can and do happen, even with all those measures and safeguards in place.”
The guide was produced following consultation with members, according to FDI senior regulatory affairs executive Aoife Moran. “We’re always looking for ways to support our members. We had a look at the food safety side of things to see what we could do there and our members told us that it would be really valuable to have a practical playbook or toolkit to use within their businesses. Because of the really high standards that exist, a lot of businesses may never have experienced an incident. We are trying to harness some of the learnings and some of the best practice that companies would generally only learn by going through an incident and trying to give them some tools and insights to help them to prepare.”
Designed for ease of use, the guide is not intended to be a comprehensive listing of all regulatory requirements. “There’s a huge suite of regulations and we couldn’t include them all,” says Moran. “It’s an overview and a checklist to make sure people are aware of their obligations. It points to additional resources that are available as well.”
The guide focuses on prevention and response. “We hope that companies will never have to use the response part of it, but it is always useful to prepare for every eventuality,” says Moran. “The second part of the toolkit is around preparing a business for a worst-case scenario event. What do I need to do immediately? Who do I need to contact? Who manages that?
“The other important consideration is if there is an incident, it affects the whole business. Everybody needs to be brought into it. A big part of that is identifying the key stakeholders internally. Who’s managing the messaging? Who’s logging what’s happening? Who’s engaging with the regulator? What does your external stakeholder list look like? What are the financial implications of this? And how do we do that in a very structured and calm way so that we’re managing things to the best of our abilities and that we’re not missing anything. There is a checklist at the back of the guide to help people follow the steps.”
One of the recommendations is to carry out a simulation event. “This allows businesses to see how an incident would play out so that they can be as prepared as they can be should one occur. It helps to identify gaps and weaknesses and where additional attention may be required.”
To help businesses to embed the best-practice frameworks contained in the guide, FDI has partnered with the Food Drink Ireland Skillnet to deliver interactive training programmes.
“The training is very practical and hands on,” says Moran. “It’s for anybody within the business because a food safety incident impacts everybody, not just the technical or regulatory teams. Typically, the training gives an overview or a snapshot of the regulatory requirements and what you should be doing in order to prevent an incident from happening. There are also simulated events like a mock product recall where people are assigned different roles within the business. Part of that is getting the business back up and running again after the event and all of that is covered within the training. We’ve run a number of training sessions so far and the feedback has been very positive.”
Training is available both in-house for companies and on an individual basis. “Some companies prefer to do the training in-house and have it focused on their specific business. Others prefer to be in a mixed group where then can learn not only from the trainers, but from the other participants,” says Stuart Trainor who also points out that it is delivered via the Food and Drink Ireland Skillnet and is open to any manufacturer in Ireland.

title: Event guide: Púca Festival, Jazzy and the other best things to see in Ireland in the week ahead
description: October 24th-30th, 2026: Our pick of music, art, theatre and more coming your way
content:
Rooted in Ireland’s significance as a birthplace of Halloween, through the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain, Púca Festival balances tradition (storytelling, heritage, mythology, handicrafts, divining) with contemporary entertainment. Music highlights of this four-day festival include the triple bill of The Stunning, Sharon Shannon and Mundy (Thursday, October 29th, Púca Big Top, Trim, 7pm, €35), as well as The Waterboys (Sunday, November 1st, Púca Big Top, Trim, 7pm, €50). Comedy highlights include Enya Martin (Thursday, October 29th, Swift Cultural Centre, Trim, 7.30pm, €29) and Shane Daniel Byrne (Saturday, October 31st, Swift Cultural Centre, Trim, 7.30pm, €29). Samhain Circus is pitching its tent at the Fairgreen, in Athboy (9pm, €25, over-18s only), for the duration of the festival.
When the Dublin DJ, performer and songwriter Jazzy topped the charts in the summer of 2023 with her debut single, Giving Me, she celebrated by buying everyone at her local pub a drink. This weekend sees the release of her long-awaited debut album, Peace & Patience, and while you couldn’t expect her to buy a drink for everyone at 3Arena, she’ll be celebrating its arrival in fine style. Special guests include two acclaimed tastemakers and floor shakers: the London remixer and producer Route 94 and the Dublin DJ Kayleigh Glynn. Jazzy also plays the Telegraph Building in Belfast, on Saturday, November 14th.
[ Dublin DJ Jazzy: ‘Calvin Harris messaged me on Instagram to say he loved my song’ Opens in new window ]
Two months ago Macklemore was preparing to join Ed Sheeran’s Loop tour as an opening act, alongside the Irish acts Biird and Beoga. On its first night, at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey on September 4th, the Seattle-born rapper gave a two-minute speech calling for a free Palestine and then performed his song Hind’s Hall, which he dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University. By September 14th, Macklemore had been officially dropped from the tour, prompting him to announce this Free Palestine tour, proceeds from which he will donate to numerous charities and other organisations that support the Palestinian people. The line-up of Friends for this show had not been announced at the time of going to print, but we wouldn’t be entirely surprised if he had invited Biird and Beoga to join him on stage.
Solo work by the lead vocalist of an established band can struggle to make much of an impact, but Brandon Flowers , of The Killers, appears to have ignored the memo. With three successful albums to his name – Flamingo, from 2010, The Desired Effect, from 2015, and Thrasher , from August – Flowers has embraced the solo life as if to the manner born. He has enough of his own songs to fill the set list, of course, but we bet that fans are also hoping that he includes one or two Killers classics.
As they mark the 25th anniversary of their influential debut album, Is This It – “the template for rock’n’roll in the modern day”, according to the tastemaker Zane Lowe – The Strokes have had to contend with largely middling reviews of Reality Awaits, the album they released this summer. It’s an awkward reality that their previous two albums, Comedown Machine, from 2013, and The New Abnormal, from 2020, got similarly tepid responses. But Julian Casablancas and his bandmates are as popular live as ever. Their special guests at this sold-out show are the English band Fat White Family and the Australian songwriter Alex Cameron.
To call Haunted Dancehall a Halloween festival with a difference is an understatement. Named after the 1994 album by the English electronic group The Sabres of Paradise, it focuses on boundary-pushing shades of music instead of obvious spooky tropes. Across three rooms and two days, this year’s music acts include Kelela, from Washington; Voice Actor, from Sheffield; Proc Fiskal, from Edinburgh; Nashpaints, from Dublin; and Caitlin Orla Eve, from Cork. A particular highlight is a Halloween staple with a twist: a presentation (on Sunday, October 25th) of FW Murnau’s film Nosferatu, live-scored by Chicago’s Circuit des Yeux and accompanied by Alan Sparhawk of Low.
Perhaps best known for his big public artworks – notably Bláthú, a nine-storey, 750sq m mural at Bolands Mills in Dublin, the largest ever painted in Ireland – the street artist Sean Atmos presents, in his debut studio exhibition, far more intimate paintings that explore and experiment, he says, without any expectations. “This show invites the public in to my own private world and into work you’d never find on the streets of the city.” The artist will be in conversation at the studio on Saturday, October 31st, at 11am, €5.
The actor, comedian, presenter, writer and music-video/film director Richard Ayoade presents a show based on his most recent book, Afterthoughts, or Some Pistachios Won’t Open: Wisdom for the Unreflective. Ayoade’s comedic delivery is deadpan and absurdist; if you’re a fan of axioms such as “It’s very important to listen to people, but we must never underestimate the joy of ignoring them,” then you know what to do.
Since its inaugural outing, in 2022, Keep Her Lit has showcased women in Irish traditional and folk music. This year’s festival features the concert Awe na Mná, with Karan Casey, Clare Sands, Inni-K and Brídín (Saturday, October 31st, 8pm, €25). On Sunday, November 1st, a series of events (some free) in Inistioge village includes trad sessions, sean-nós dancing and singing workshops, and storytelling.
