title: A History of the Novel in Britain: Thrilling tome is an epic of progress
description: The novel ‘was always a form that not only thrived on inequalities but required them’, Philip Hensher says
content:
On the first page of the first English novel, a man rejects the class into which he was born and seeks, as his sceptical father puts it, “to rise by enterprise, and to make [himself] famous in undertakings of a nature out of the common road”. Robinson Crusoe ’s father, “a wise and grave man”, praises “the middle state” and advises Robinson to eschew “the two extremes” and to remain as best he can “between the mean and the great”.
But Robinson Crusoe is the narrator of a novel. The middle state will not contain him. His life, like the novel itself – a form inventing itself before our eyes as Robinson, “on the first of September 1651”, boards his first ship – has been enabled by the root fact of modernity, which is this: the structures of social class will not stay still.
“ Defoe ’s novels are radically new,” Philip Hensher argues, in his thrilling new history of the novel in Britain . “The possibility of social change, of the individual’s ambition, of a transformation based in desire and will and not of a revelation run by a deus ex machina are all fundamental to the novel, as practiced from Robinson Crusoe to our times.”
In other words, the novel arrives at the same time as, and in many ways actually constitutes, bourgeois capitalist modernity. “[C]apitalism defines the form,” Hensher writes, and it is capitalism that “explains how, at the beginning of the eighteenth century, people can make of themselves what they choose”.
This isn’t a new argument – Ian Watt set it forth in The Rise of the Novel (1957) – but Hensher, novelist and Spectator columnist, gives it a Whig spin. That is to say, he makes his history of the novel an epic of progress. For Hensher, the novel is an unmixed good, and the capitalism that enabled its invention and shaped its growth is therefore pretty good, too. Inequality is tolerable at least in part because the novel “was always a form that not only thrived on inequalities but required them, in order to describe the struggle to change and rise”.
An opinionated history, therefore. But there’s nothing wrong with that. Hensher starts with Defoe and ends in the year 2000 – “it seemed very unlikely that a history beyond that point could make an accurate summary of what will prove to be interesting”. Past historians of the novel, Hensher notes, who “tried to sort out their contemporaries” in every case “got things completely wrong”. The living novelists we now adore have no claim on posterity, which will make its own judgments.
Hensher includes Irish novelists up to 1922, which allows him to discuss Maria Edgeworth and George Moore (he admires both), but also allows him to equivocate about James Joyce , who, as Hensher points out, held a British passport until he died but can by no stretch of the imagination be claimed as a British novelist. (Hensher chucks in Elizabeth Bowen later on, mainly because he likes her work.)
But this really is a history of the British novel, and does opinionated justice to that history’s heroes (Richardson, Austen , Thackeray, Scott, the Brontes, Dickens, Eliot, Trollope, James, Woolf , the Amises), to its rebels and eccentrics (Thomas Love Peacock, Henry Green, Ivy Compton-Burnett), to its colonial and postcolonial latecomers, and to its also-rans (Susan Ferrier, Charlotte Elizabeth, AJ Cronin). Hensher defends Arnold Bennett, dislikes Woolf’s The Waves, wants us all to read RS Surtees, who wrote about fox-hunting, though apparently quite well.
[ Dublin Book Festival: ‘I couldn’t believe I’d never heard of this weird historical episode’ Opens in new window ]
A sampling of Hensher’s insights. “The patronage and control exerted over content and publishing format by the circulating library mogul Mudie in the nineteenth century, and the same patronage exerted by the literary prize today may have the same good intentions and make the same ultimately unhelpful contribution to the development of the novel.”
The new can often look like the bad: “When later novels in the [18th] century strike us as quite bad, it is often a sign that something radically new is being tried out. Why not a novel narrated by a coin?” Then again, the bad can just be bad. Ann Radcliffe, the Gothic novelist, “was (and remains) a simply terrible writer […] She doesn’t know anything. In The Mysteries of Udolpho (1794), set in the early sixteenth century, characters drink coffee”.
Hensher praises Jane Austen’s “frail and exact” novels (this is just right). The centre of gravity in English literature shifted from poetry to prose “when Scott did” – that is, when Walter Scott published Waverley (1814) and became the first novelist to become truly rich from the sales of his novels. Dozens more insights, arguments, cranky dismissals, tender rescues of the long-neglected. Hensher’s history of the British novel has energy and exactitude: two things no individual novel can long survive without.
Kevin Power is an author and assistant professor in English at Trinity College Dublin

title: AI start-up aims to cut assessment and feedback workload for educators
description: Irish education technology venture Diotima is preparing to bring its AI-powered assessment platform to market
content:
Diotima of Mantinea was a Greek priestess and philosopher who reportedly taught Socrates all about the nature of love.
Her modern namesake, an Irish AI -powered education technology platform, has no ambitions in that direction.
Instead it wants to change how people learn by giving them feedback while they are still working, rather than waiting until an assignment is finished.
The idea behind this approach, known as “formative feedback”, is that intervening while someone is in the learning phase is likely to lead to better results.
The problem is that while this approach might work with a handful of students it’s almost impossible for an educator to implement it at scale using traditional feedback methods.
This is where Diotima fits into the frame. The platform uses artificial intelligence to carry out the time-consuming aspects of the work, providing individual-specific feedback in a fraction of the time it would take a teacher to do so manually.
Diotima ingests an organisation’s teaching materials, curriculum and desired learning outcomes. It then builds assessments and drafts student-specific feedback based on the approved material. Trainers and teachers review this feedback and can edit or change anything they’re not happy with before signing it off.
“Assessors use the platform for assessments and feedback, and learners use it to access their assessments and review their work before submission,” says Jonathan Dempsey, who cofounded Diotima with Siobhán Ryan earlier this year.
“Learners work through assessments at their own pace and can attempt a question more than once before submitting,” Dempsey says. “As they review their answer, Diotima prompts them to check their own reasoning rather than handing them the solution. The criteria their work is judged against are revealed once they submit, not before. That keeps the assessment honest and keeps the learner thinking rather than working backwards from the answer.”
Diotima is the brainchild of Ryan, a biochemist by background, who spent more than a decade working on the brewing side in Diageo before taking a career break to raise her family.
She subsequently retrained as a teacher and worked in education before starting to tease out an idea she’d had for an AI-related project that would transform exam preparation for students.
At the time Ryan was working on her idea alone and, feeling she could do with some support, she applied for an Enterprise Ireland innovation voucher. This allows entrepreneurs to tap into the skills of third-level institutions.
Ryan used hers with the Learnovate Centre at Trinity College , which specialises in education technology and innovation.
With input from Learnovate and academics in the schools of education and computer science, Ryan shifted her focus from exam preparation to using AI to deliver personalised feedback at scale.
Ryan was introduced to Dempsey during her time working at Learnovate. A 20-year veteran of the edtech sector, he subsequently joined Diotima as co-founder to lead the business side of things.
Following a feasibility study and an injection of just under €500,000 in commercialisation funding from Enterprise Ireland Diotima is now ready to spin out as a stand-alone entity. The company, which is fully funded for now, will begin operations with four employees.
The first iteration of the platform is aimed at the corporate training market and professional education, training and membership bodies.
Diotima will work in any educational setting. However, Ryan says the company is starting with professional education, as it’s easier to manage and less fragmented than the primary and secondary school systems here.
With a successful trial of the system under its belt with the Law Society , Diotima will be ready to sign up paying customers in a few months’ time, and its revenue model will be a subscription linked to the size of an organisation and the number of users.
“Diotima will work for any organisation that runs courses or oversees certification or continuing professional development where their assessors are basically spending too long marking and writing feedback,” says Ryan, who adds that the system is built for educators, not IT departments, so if someone can use everyday online tools, they can use Diotima.
“Essentially, Diotima removes the repetitive manual work so educators can spend their time on the human connection that only they can provide. What’s absolutely key here is that everything we do has human oversight,” she adds. “Nothing reaches a student without an assessor reviewing and approving it first. That’s the core design commitment of our platform and what makes Diotima different from other AI tools, where the output goes straight to the learner.”
Dempsey adds that while AI is a key part of Diotima’s solution, it has to be managed and fully compliant with the European Union AI Act.
“Diotima has been engineered with EU AI Act Annex III compliance at its heart rather than being added after the fact, as compliance is not something that is easy to retrofit. Learner material from our customer organisations is never used to train AI models, and that’s also strictly built into our platform,” says Dempsey, who recently participated in the AI ecosystem accelerator programme run by NovaUCD in partnership with CeADAR, Ireland’s Centre for Applied AI.
“Under the Act there is a high-risk category which includes anything that is deterministic in the future of an individual. An educational result would be an example of this, so there must be a human in the loop,” says Dempsey, who points out that breaches of the Act carry potentially far heavier fines than GDPR violations.
“We empower educators to be their best while ensuring we also protect their organisations from risk,” he says. “This makes it possible for organisations to cost effectively adopt AI for feedback where it is otherwise too risky.”
There has been a lot of debate about AI regulation, with those who oppose any regulation arguing that it will stifle innovation. Ryan disagrees. “I think that’s nonsense,” she says. “The regulations have not held us back. We were still able to build Diotima, and it’s fully compliant. I’m on my soapbox here, but I think it’s a lazy excuse. If the mindset is there, you can do it.”

title: Mary Lou McDonald and Michelle O’Neill attend police interview over Drumcree protests
description: Sinn Féin leaders interviewed as part of investigation into demonstrations that blocked Orange Order march on Portadown’s Garvaghy Road
content:
The Sinn Féin president and vice-president have attended a Belfast police station for interview in connection with an investigation into protests that blocked a controversial Orange Order march at Drumcree .
Mary Lou McDonald and Michelle O’Neill , who is the First Minister of Northern Ireland, were among a number of Sinn Féin politicians who received letters from the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) asking them to attend interviews.
The PSNI is investigating protests that blocked the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown, preventing the Orange Order march from taking place.
The protests were not notified to the Parades Commission and were therefore “unnotified” and deemed illegal.
The PSNI has sent letters to those “reasonably suspected” of having committed a criminal offence in relation to the dispute.
They include other Sinn Féin Ministers, People Before Profit MLA Gerry Carroll and SDLP MLA Justin McNulty.
In a statement on Wednesday, the SDLP confirmed McNulty “has received correspondence from the PSNI and will engage fully with any policing or judicial process.
“The SDLP stands fully behind Justin’s decision to stand with Garvaghy Road community on 27 September,” it said.
A decision by the Parades Commission to give the go-ahead for the Drumcree parade to take place on September 27th for the first time in 28 years sparked a two-week stand off between the Orange Order and Garvaghy Road residents and their supporters.
[ Jamie Bryson: Northern Irish unionists ‘must go on the offensive’ Opens in new window ]
On October 9th, Northern Secretary Chris Bryant intervened to end the stalemate by banning the march following a request by PSNI Chief Constable Jon Boutcher that he review the permission for the march to proceed.
Speaking to the media outside Musgrave police station in central Belfast as they arrived on Wednesday afternoon, McDonald said they had committed to “co-operate with any processes arising from that decision that we took [to take part in the protest], and so we are here today to have an interview and to co-operate fully with the PSNI”.
She defended her participation in the protest, saying “we stood on the Garvaghy Road to support that community at a time of great pressure and vulnerability, at a time when the peace and peace of mind of that community was under real threat, at a time when their right to live free from sectarian harassment was directly under threat”.
“We stood with them shoulder to shoulder because that was the right thing to do, in fact, it was the only thing to do.”
Asked if she would resign as First Minister if she were to be prosecuted, O’Neill responded that she was “going nowhere” and would “keep turning up for the people.
“I am the First Minister and that is my job,” she said.
[ PSNI feared gun use by dissident republicans if parade went down Garvaghy Road, court told Opens in new window ]
Earlier, a meeting of a Stormont committee ended amid heated exchanges after O’Neill left to attend the police interview.
DUP MLA Deborah Erskine said O’Neill had treated the people of Northern Ireland with “absolute contempt” but Sinn Féin MLA Sinéad Ennis said the First Minister had made the committee aware of her time constraints and other commitments.
Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly said she was “more than happy to stay” to answer questions but the committee was advised that, given she shares a joint office with O’Neill, this would not be in line with protocol.

title: Man (20s) dies after being struck by a car in Co Cork
description: Gardaí appealing for information on fatality which occurred on the N20 near Mallow
content:
A man in his 20s has died after he was struck by a car on Wednesday evening in Co Cork .
The incident, which involved a car and a pedestrian, occurred at around 5.45pm on the N20 at Burnfort, near Mallow.
The male pedestrian was fatally injured and his body was removed from the scene to the mortuary in Cork University Hospital where a postmortem examination will take place.
The male driver and sole occupant of the car, also aged in his 20s, was also taken to the hospital for treatment of non-life threatening injuries.
The road will remain closed overnight and local diversions are in place, the Garda said in a statement.
A technical examination by Forensic Collision Investigators will take place on Thursday morning.
Gardaí are appealing to anyone who may have witnessed the collision to contact them. Any road users who were travelling in the area of the N20 at Burnfort between 5.15pm and 5.45pm on Wednesday and who may have camera or dash cam footage are asked to make it available to investigators.
Anyone with any information is asked to contact Mallow Garda Station on 022 31450, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111 or any Garda station.

title: Irish Rail seeks to recover damages from contractor over scrapped software project
description: Rail operator tells Oireachtas committee that Spanish IT firm Indra has issued its own claim over shelved traffic management system
content:
Irish Rail has said it will seek to recover damages from a Spanish IT company over what it says was the failure to deliver key software for a new system to manage trains across its network.
Irish Rail chief executive Mary Considine also confirmed to the Oireachtas Committee on Transport on Wednesday that the Spanish IT firm Indra had issued its own claim in relation to the scrapped project, known as the traffic management system (TMS).
However, she said: “We do not believe we owe anything to Indra.”
The Irish Times reported on Wednesday that Indra had sought payments of potentially about €30 million as part of a final settlement of accounts.
The State-owned rail company had already written down by €50 million its investment in a new national train control centre at Heuston Station, largely due to problems with the planned TMS system.
Considine told the committee that Irish Rail had terminated its contract with Indra for the development of the TMS on July 17th.
Questioned by committee chairman Fine Gael TD Michael Murphy, Considine said Irish Rail had recently issued its final account to Indra. She said it was trying “to recover as much as we can on behalf of the exchequer”.
“At the end of the day, Indra did not deliver a product that was fit for purpose,” she said.
[ ‘Absolutely chaotic’: Passengers frustrated by overcrowding on Irish public transport Opens in new window ]
Separately, Considine told the committee that Irish Rail had seen record passenger levels, with a 20 per cent growth experienced in just two years.
However, she said the rail company did not have sufficient capacity or fleet to meet the demand for its services. She said there was a pipeline of new developments and she asked passengers “to bear with us”.
“The coming 12 months will see the beginning of benefits to our customers from a range of projects. Our new Dart fleet will begin entering service from quarter two in 2027. The first trains will be battery-electric trains, operating on the Drogheda commuter line, with charging facilities having been installed at Drogheda Station.” She said this would allow existing trains on the northern line to be “cascaded” to other parts of the network.
She said other projects that were nearing completion included the new Galway Ceannt Station, which will be completed by the end of this year; a second platform and associated section of second track at Oranmore, which will be completed next year; and the new Foynes freight line that will be commissioned this coming weekend, allowing for services to begin in 2027.
She said the new Waterford Plunkett Station would also open next year.
Several members of the committee expressed concern about overcrowding on trains and questioned whether this represented a safety risk.
[ Eamon Ryan: Quiet scaling back of BusConnects is a travesty Opens in new window ]
Irish Rail head of corporate communications Barry Kenny said the company appreciated that this could be uncomfortable but maintained that trains were designed to accommodate passengers who were standing.
The rail company separately told the hearing that it was envisaged that the second phase of the western rail corridor from Athenry to Claremorris would come into operation in 2031, while it was planned that the Dart West expansion would open in 2032 and the Dart South West scheme in 2034.

title: Declan Rice strikes late for Arsenal to deny Bayern Munich in blockbuster
description: Harry Kane on target from the penalty spot for hosts
content:
It is as if Harry Kane cannot get enough of tormenting Arsenal . The Bayern Munich striker has plenty of form from his Tottenham days. He remains the top scorer in north London derby history with 14 goals. He made an impact yet again here and yet it was not a night when he had the final word. That honour fell to Declan Rice , the Arsenal midfielder storming into the Bayern area in the 82nd minute to guide home a low finish that Kane would have been proud to call his own.
Arsenal were hunting their latest statement result. Only once had they ever won away against Bayern – the 2-0 in the Champions League last-16 second-leg in 2013, although it did not prevent an away goals exit. Mikel Arteta was an Arsenal player that night. When Eberechi Eze, who came on for the injured Bukayo Saka in the 10th minute, gave them the lead in the 25th minute, their hopes surged.
Enter Kane. He wore his playmaker’s hat; some of his passing was sumptuous and it was his assist for Alphonso Davies that helped Bayern to draw level. He wore his finisher’s one, too, scoring from the penalty spot to put his team in charge. It meant he had scored in 10 consecutive Champions League ties; one short of Cristiano Ronaldo’s record. There is a reason why Kane is the favourite to win the Ballon d’Or on Monday.
Rice loosened Bayern’s grip. It was a lovely goal from him and Arsenal even hinted at a late winner, Jurriën Timber drawing a tip over from Manuel Neuer in stoppage time. Bayern had wanted revenge for their 3-1 defeat at the Emirates Stadium last season. They did not get it.
Arsenal knew they were inside a fortress. Bayern had not lost a Champions League group or league phase tie at their own stadium since the 3-2 reverse against Manchester City in December 2013, 40 games ago. The following 39 featured 37 wins and two draws.
Arteta’s idea was to go pretty much as strong as possible with his line-up. He made just two changes, Jurriën Timber for Ben White and Noni Madueke for Eze, albeit the latter was not on the bench for long. Saka had tussled with Davies and it looked innocuous. The alarm bells rang when Saka grabbed his thigh and went to ground, waving his hand in the air.
Was it possible for the Arsenal support to think that Bayern had been stripped of their fear factor in the line behind Kane? Michael Olise was suspended, Jamal Musiala was injured and Luis Díaz was surprisingly a substitute. Bayern were without the midfielder Joshua Kimmich for personal reasons.
Arteta moved Madueke over to his more natural position on the right wing when he introduced Eze on the left and Bayern will still be wondering how the latter was afforded so much space up the inside channel on that flank to put Arsenal in front.
It was a fabulous ball from Martin Ødegaard, who was in the mood at the outset, full of sharp turns and urgency, and Eze had the time to let it bounce before shooting first time into the far corner. An offside flag killed the Arsenal celebrations and there was one of those weird waits before the video assistant referee ruled that Eze was in fact onside.
Kane was booed by the Arsenal fans. Of course he was. He dropped deep to link the play and there was a moment in the 17th minute when he started a move with a pass from inside his own penalty area. There was a glorious ping over Gabriel Magalhães, who was the last Arsenal defender, for Ismael Saibari on 23 minutes, though his team-mate could not control, and Kane’s fingerprints were all over the equaliser. He was on halfway when he sculpted the low through-ball for Davies, which took Timber out of the equation. The Bayern winger’s finish was clinical.
Bayern had other chances in the first half, none better than the one for Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, in the 21st minute. It was Kane who began the attack, taking a quick goal kick – yes, really – and Gnabry was the man over on the right when the Bayern forwards worked it that way. Arsenal were caught cold. Gnabry’s shot was too close to David Raya. Kane also saw Ezri Konsa produce a fine block to keep him out.
It is never anything other than a pleasure to be at the Allianz for a showpiece match. All the staples were present and correct. The en masse scarf waving. The slightly slapstick oompah band notes. The fans at either end of the ground calling to each other. The non-stop drumbeat and song from the Südkurve, who also bounced as one at times.
The pregame surprise had been the sight of Vincent Kompany in the Bayern dugout; the manager made a Lazarus-like rise from his sickbed and the action after the restart kept the blood pumping. Arsenal thought they had gone back ahead when Bruno Guimarães rose to meet Declan Rice’s corner only for Neuer to make an extraordinary save.
The goalkeeper touched the ball up and on to the crossbar and away. Shades of Gordon Banks from Pelé. It was Raya’s turn next; his save to keep out Dayot Upamecano’s close-range header from Gnabry’s cross was of the highest order.
It was interesting to watch Kane after the penalty was awarded for handball against Timber. Bayern had worked the ball back to their No 9 and, when he shot, Timber’s arm was outstretched. Kane went through his mental processes. He could see Raya did not retreat to his line for what felt like an age. Kane then delayed even longer. He was in total control. He stuttered before banging the ball hard into the right-hand corner.
Bayern were close to putting the game to bed. Konrad Laimer dragged narrowly past the far post when well-placed but it was Arsenal who showed their fighting spirit. Eze was excellent. When the opportunity knocked for Rice after a pass from the substitute, Viktor Gyökeres, he made no mistake. – Guardian

title: The Experiment on Channel 4: An unflinching and provocative horror show dressed as satire
description: Television: No punches pulled as connection is drawn between Nazi dehumanisation of disability and modern day demonisation of disabled people as ‘benefits scroungers’
content:
C hannel 4 has been hush-hush about The Experiment (Wednesday, 10pm), revealing only that the documentary will “open the door” to an “experimental new residential home”. What it turns out to be is a provocative reality documentary that draws a direct connection between the Nazis’ murderous dehumanising of disabled people in the 1930s and 1940s and the demonisation of people with disabilities in modern Britain as “benefits scroungers”.
So it’s strong stuff, and no punches are pulled by actor Mat Fraser and rights activist Sophie Morgan, both of whom have disabilities and see proposals in the UK to cut benefits paid to disabled people as the thin end of a very sinister wedge.
In the usual course, a Channel 4 documentary about social welfare cutbacks in the UK would be of little relevance to Irish viewers. But the question asked by The Experiment is whether the prejudices against disabled people that the Nazis tapped into still linger, and that is of course as pertinent in Ireland as anywhere else.
Fraser and Morgan travel to Austria , where they visit nightmarish Hartheim Castle, where disabled people were murdered by the Nazis – an immaculately preserved charnel house which understandably brings Fraser to tears.
Back in the UK, they recreate the essence of that building but soften the horrors by using modern corporate speak. The facility is called “Segrilife House”, and members of the public, unaware that the institution is a set and all the inmates actors – are invited along for a tour.
This is a horror show dressed as satire, the sort of thing that might have appeared on Chris Morris’s scorched-earth satire, The Day Today, in the 1990s. You do feel slightly for the punters as they are walked through the building and invited to interact with patients who are forced to perform menial tasks, sleep in prison-style dorms and are invited to consider the “benefits” of sterilisation and euthanasia.
Initially, the visitors nod and smile politely. The further it goes, the more overwrought some of them become, leading one man to compare the centre to a Hitler fever dream. Others go along with it and observe that the patients seem perfectly happy.
Before it became the home of Bake Off and endless variations of Location, Location, Location, Channel 4 had a reputation as the punk rock alternative to the BBC and ITV. It harks back to those early years with this barricade-rushing call to arms, which asks us to critique our own views toward disabled people. There is a limit to how far its warnings about the weaponisation of the benefits system against disabled people apply to Ireland, but even with that caveat, this is unflinching and provocative television.

title: Bruno Fernandes questions Michael Carrick’s tactics as pressure builds on Manchester United manager
description: ‘I’ve not given my own position any thought,’ says Carrick after 4-1 drubbing against Como
content:
Bruno Fernandes questioned manager Michael Carrick ’s tactics after Manchester United were thrashed by Como on Wednesday.
United’s season sank to a new low as they were humbled 4-1 by the Italian side in the Champions League .
It has been a troubled start to the campaign for United, with just seven points collected from seven Premier League games, defender Lisandro Martinez openly highlighting the club’s shortcomings, and Carrick coming under pressure.
[ Como demolish dismal Manchester United to pile more pressure on Michael Carrick Opens in new window ]
Fernandes, who was substituted after 67 minutes at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia, delivered a damning assessment after the game.
The captain told TNT Sports: “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave a little bit of space in behind, and trying to get the ball in the first moment, to wait for them, to give them the ball.
“Sometimes when you give too much of the ball to these teams, they get confidence. They have so many bodies behind the ball that make you run a lot, make people get frustrated, and then obviously when you recover the ball, the legs and the brain are much more difficult to make it work.”
Asked further about the tactics, he added: “It’s on the manager and on the staff to say it, it is not on me.
“I just said that I think sometimes we have to be more brave under pressure, trying to take a risk of getting that press very high and making them uncomfortable, as they did to us.”
Fernandes felt United’s attitude was wrong from the moment they conceded the first goal after two minutes.
He said: “Obviously it’s not the first time and I think, again, we started on the wrong foot and they scored very early.
“Conceding the goal very early makes us feel, going into the game, already in a mood of a defeat, and it’s very difficult to get out of that at the moment without being ourselves and trying to push and trying to be brave, trying to have the ball, trying to make something happen.
“And if we’re not able to do that, it’s going to be very difficult to get out of this situation.”
Carrick held his hands up apologetically to the largely empty away end after the defeat.
“First of all, I have to apologise to the supporters,” he said after game.
“For us to play in that way is not acceptable. It wasn’t a good performance at all. We wanted to build on what we brought to Leeds and the performance that we had at Leeds. That bit of intensity, that spirit, that aggression, that real willingness to give everything, and tonight was the total opposite of [that] performance. It was tough to watch.”
Carrick sidestepped a question about whether he would quit during a press conference that ended with him being asked if he feared he could lose his job.
“I’ve not given my own position any thought,” he said. “It is the supporters (I am thinking about). I was one of them tonight watching that and I wasn’t happy at all.”
He added of his side’s effort: “We can all play well, we can all have poor performances, but to do it in that manner is really not right at all.
“It wasn’t just the goals, it was the manner and the way we played at times, in the way we went about it, was the difficult thing to watch for me.”

title: Como demolish dismal Manchester United to pile more pressure on Michael Carrick
description: United suffer ugly defeat in beautiful Italian surrounds
content:
In sight of the Alps, a boat ride from George Clooney’s villa, Manchester United will hope, in what has been a terrible start to the season, that things do not get any worse.
They can’t – for the team’s prospects, and Michael Carrick’s job security, because witnessed here by Lake Como was a humiliation of the three-times European champions by Cesc Fàbregas’s competition debutants, as United suffered their worst defeat in continental football since 1994.
By 57 minutes this was over, as Como were 3-0 ahead, and Nico Paz had destroyed Carrick’s men with a scintillating display featuring two goals and the assist for Tasos Douvikas’s strike.
When Como attacked and defended it was as a unit supremely drilled by Fàbregas. Carrick, on this and the evidence of only two wins all term, is a coach struggling at elite level.
Como’s supremacy in the most famous victory of their 119 years came despite having just 62 Champions League appearances to United’s 242. Or, more simply, Como’s men against United’s boys.
At a sold-out Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia, with a capacity of 13,602, the visitors went down to a club whose tagline is “the most beautiful football in the most beautiful location”. For United, though, this was an ugly night in Lombardy.
Disaster hit two minutes in. Carrick’s men snoozed, allowing a Paz curler from the right to beat Senne Lammens, and the local faithful partied.
This was a whole 60 seconds longer than Atlético Madrid were kept out in last week’s 2-0 defeat, as United became the first English team to concede inside two minutes in consecutive major European matches.
The opener came moments after Diogo Dalot spurned a simple opening to dizzy the hosts: Matheus Cunha flipped the ball to his right-back, Dalot’s touch was awful, yet after possession was retained, he ballooned wide.
This was United’s current form crystallised at each end of the pitch: a basic lack of quality. When Paz left Noussair Mazraoui gasping, as the No 10 careered along Como’s right, another example was on show. Cunha, running back, could not stop Paz and if his cross had found a colleague, and not Mason Mount, Lammens might have been beaten again.
Mount lined up alongside Andrey Santos in a midfield that had Cunha, Youri Tielemans and Bryan Mbeumo ahead, with Bruno Fernandes again a false-ish nine.
Como hogged the ball throughout so any United foray needed to threaten Jean Butez’s goal: Mbeumo’s corner from the right patently did not when failing to clear a first defender.
Como had United’s number, penetrating at will, and when the ball was moved into the area and Martin Baturina went to grass, a penalty was claimed. Sven Jablonski, the referee, turned this down.
After a near 24-hour deluge the rain did finally stop but Como’s blue wave, when attacking or closing down, continued relentlessly. United’s press was piecemeal, maybe involving one or two, but was never a group act, unlike Fabregas’s players who hunted the ball in packs.
One more scare in a half studded with these came when Douvikas went clear, then down under Lammens’ attentions, but he was flagged offside. United were impotent and at the interval, Carrick had to earn his corn. In missing nine players due to injury, suspension or illness, there was some mitigation.
Mathijs de Ligt, partnering Harry Maguire in central defence, being thrown straight in for a first appearance in 325 days after a serious back injury illustrated Carrick’s straitened resources. This, too, was shown by Tynan Thompson and Jack Fletcher being on the bench, after each played for United under-19s in the afternoon’s 2-1 Youth Cup defeat to Como.
Carrick’s move was to take off Cunha and Santos for Carlos Baleba and Amad Diallo in a reshuffle that took Tielemans into central midfield, Fernandes to No 10, and Mbeumo leading the line.
The net result: Como’s second. Once more, it was too simple. Paz enjoyed a universe of time to thread in Douvikas, and he ran on and powered past Lammens.
This was a mere four minutes into the second half and thoughts turned to the clock ticking on Carrick’s tenure, before Como netted twice more.
First came Paz’s second, this time the Argentinian skating along the right and beating Lammens for 3-0. Then, on 76 minutes, Como waltzed through for a fourth time.
Up rose Jacobo Ramón to head home Kaiki Bruno’s cross from the left and United’s disintegration was complete, many of their travelling fans already heading for the exit and local hostelries to try and drink away the pain of what they had witnessed. Josh Zirkzee’s stoppage-time goal was not even a consolation.
By the end Carrick was as broken as his team. Next up for United is Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday. Even if Carrick survives until then, who knows how much longer he will remain after this. – Guardian

title: Supreme Court appeal opens in row over super junior ministers attending at cabinet
description: Constitutional challenge by Opposition TDs Pa Daly and Paul Murphy had been dismissed by High Court in December
content:
Influence exercised by super junior ministers attending at meetings of government is not provided for in the Constitution, and represents an arrogation of power, the Supreme Court has heard.
The arguments were made on Wednesday at the hearing of an appeal by two Opposition TDs over the rejection of their legal challenges to the attendance of super junior ministers at meetings of government.
A three-judge High Court last December dismissed the challenges by Sinn Féin TD Pa Daly and People Before Profit-Solidarity TD Paul Murphy . They were subsequently awarded 50 per cent of their legal costs against the State because of the importance, novelty and complexity of the constitutional issues raised.
The TDs brought separate but similar challenges, arguing article 28 of Bunreacht na hÉireann limits the number of government members to 15, and the attendance of super junior ministers at cabinet meetings goes against this.
Ministers of state attending cabinet – or super junior ministers – are appointed by the government on the nomination of the taoiseach. They participate in government meetings, but do not vote.
The High Court, comprising court president David Barniville and judges Siobhán Phelan and Conleth Brady, held no provision of the Constitution is breached by the attendance and participation of the junior ministers at cabinet meetings.
Both TDs applied to the Supreme Court to hear appeals against the High Court decision on grounds including that it was based on errors of fact and of law. They are also appealing the costs orders, arguing they are entitled to their full costs.
Opening Murphy’s appeal before a seven-judge Supreme Court, senior counsel John Rogers said the Constitution clearly defines the government as the 15 members appointed by the president, on the nomination of Dáil Éireann.
Under the Constitution, those 15 members are accountable to Dáil Éireann, whereas the super junior ministers are not, submitted Rogers, appearing with Paul Gunning and Molly Higgins instructed by KM Solicitors.
[ Government accepts ‘super junior’ Ministers are involved in decision-making at Cabinet with no constitutional basis, court hears Opens in new window ]
Rogers argued that the present arrangement, whereby super junior ministers participate in government decision-making, has an “attrition” on “the effectiveness of the people’s government, as ordained by the Constitution”.
The present scenario arises from a “formalisation” of an arrangement whereby the taoiseach invites super junior ministers to attend and deliberate at every meeting of government. The arrangement gives those ministers the authority to debate topics at cabinet, and “assist in the formulation of government policy”.
The super junior ministers’ power to exercise influence at meetings of government is not provided for under the Constitution, Rogers said. The Taoiseach has placed them “in the room”, and in doing so has “arrogated power”, he submitted.
Questioned by the judges on the attendance of the chief whip, attorney general and secretary general at meetings of government, Rogers said their presence was a “functional necessity”.
Arguing Daly’s appeal, senior counsel Feichín McDonagh submitted there was a “crucial distinction” between the taoiseach inviting individuals – including super junior ministers – to attend and brief meetings of cabinet, and those individuals participating in reaching a consensus decision.
“That is the dividing line in the case,” said McDonagh, appearing with Brendan Hennessy and John Biggins, instructed by Rogers Law.
McDonagh submitted that evidence before the court is that at present, government decisions are made by 15 ministers and four super junior ministers on consensus, rather than a decision of the 15 “influenced” by the four.
The judges put several questions to McDonagh as to how the court could “police” the dividing line between non-government members briefing government meetings, and their participation in reaching a consensus decision at government meetings.
The appeal, before the Chief Justice, Donal O’Donnell, Judge Iseult O’Malley, Judge Gerard Hogan, Judge Brian Murray, Judge Maurice Collins, Judge Aileen Donnelly and Judge Brian O’Moore, continues on Thursday.

title: Triple lock Bill passes Dáil vote amid Opposition anger
description: Government narrowly wins vote on proposed legislation removing need for UN approval of Irish troop deployments
content:
The Government has won a Dáil vote on legislation to remove the triple lock, a change that would end the need for UN approval before Irish troops can be sent on peacekeeping missions.
The Defence (Amendment) Bill passed second stage by 79 votes to 71 following a fractious debate.
Minister for Defence Helen McEntee told the Dáil that it was “absolutely crazy” that five countries, the permanent members of the UN Security Council, have a say in where Ireland sends its military personnel.
She was speaking as she introduced the debate on the divisive Bill. The triple lock requires UN approval (from the US, UK, France, Russia and China), as well as Oireachtas and Government support, before 12 or more members of the Defence Forces can be sent overseas with an armed international force or body.
McEntee said the changes contained in the proposed legislation were “necessary if we want to ensure that as a sovereign country, we have the independence and the ability to make our own decisions about where we deploy our troops”.
The Opposition, united against the move, accused the Government of betraying the public and reacted angrily to a guillotining of the introductory second stage debate to under four hours. Green Party leader Roderic O’Gorman said it was not a minor technical amendment but removed a core plank that shaped Irish defence policy for decades.
“Whatever your view we can all agree that legislation of this magnitude warrants careful examination,” he said.
The Minister said the changes were necessary “if we want Ireland to continue being a force for good in the world”. She added: “No other country in the world has this mechanism. No other country in the world allows another country or a superpower to decide for them.”
But Independent Ireland TD Michael Fitzmaurice said Ireland was relying on others for defence and could not operate its own naval vessels in Cork because of a lack of personnel.
“And then we talk about ourselves as if we’re going to be the messiah that’s going to keep peace around the world.”
He also suggested other forces might be at play. He asked “who’s calling the shots. I’d love to know what’s the endgame in all of this. Who’s promised what?”
[ The triple lock: What is it and why is the Government trying to change it? Opens in new window ]
An almost four-hour debate that began quietly became tetchy and fractious as TDs interrupted speakers and Ceann Comhairle Verona Murphy warned hecklers they could watch the debate in their offices.
Earlier, at Leaders’ Questions, Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald called on the Taoiseach to “let the people vote on this because anything else is a profound betrayal”.
She accused the Government of “staggering” dishonesty and warned “the consequences of the legislation, if passed, cannot be underestimated”.
McDonald said “the Government is tearing away current vital safeguards” and “clearing the way for this Government and future governments to send Irish troops into military operations without a UN mandate”.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin said the Government’s “only motivation here is to retain the capacity to participate in peacekeeping” and “in no way does it undermine Irish military neutrality”.
He said “our reform of the triple lock is fundamentally about keeping alive the Irish tradition of peacekeeping and, indeed, keeping alive our capacity to have an independent foreign policy”.
There were repeated reminders it was the Taoiseach who had previously said the triple lock was “at the heart of Ireland’s neutrality”.
[ Triple lock neutrality row fuels fractious Dáil exchanges Opens in new window ]
Social Democrats defence spokeswoman Sinéad Gibney referred to “a schism” in Fianna Fáil, as some members expressed opposition in internal debates. Some “are seeing through the Government spin and recognise this is an absolute nail in the coffin of Irish neutrality”, she said.
Her party colleague Pádraig Rice pointed to Fine Gael members who “openly talk about wanting to join Nato”. He said “that is the direction of travel” and warned the Government would regret the change.
Some Fianna Fáil TDs spoke in favour of the change. Dún Laoghaire TD Cormac Devlin said “nothing in this Bill changes Ireland’s traditional position of military neutrality. Ireland does not join a military alliance” and “any change would require a referendum”.
The Government won the vote by 79 votes to 71, one of the closest in recent months. There were no Fianna Fáil objectors and Independents Gillian Toole and Michael Lowry backed the Bill against a united Opposition.

title: The Irish Times view on the care of vulnerable children: ongoing failure is not acceptable
description: The case of a 14-year-old girl this week again highlights the lack of supports for those most in need
content:
A constant and often valid criticism in the provision of State services is the inability of the system to react at speed to critical deficiencies. Nowhere is this more evident than in the care of the most vulnerable children, an issue again in the news this week when it emerged that there was no place in secure State care for a troubled 14-year-old girl, subject to abuse that a judge referred to as “abhorrent”.
There have been a string of such cases in recent years. Judge John Jordan, who presided over this week’s case, has been highlighting the issue since before the Covid pandemic, consistently pointing to the unacceptable situation where Tusla, the responsible agency, is unable to comply with High Court Orders in this area. A review he undertook in October 2024 underlined the opposition of the Department of Public Expenditure to higher pay for staff at that time; the judge was critical, saying it had failed to take account of the views of experts in the area, including Tusla.
The issue was then examined by a review group appointed by Tusla, which reported in April of last year, against what it referred to as “a backdrop of severe challenges in the service, including critical bed shortages and staffing difficulties”.
The judge was correct to lift the in-camera rule in this week’s case, to bring it to public attention. It underlined then while action keeps being promised, progress is not evident. When the Tusla review was completed, only 14 of the 26 beds in three special units where these vulnerable children are accommodated were open. Now it is 13, and whether Tusla can meet its target of increasing this to 20 beds by the end of 2026 is unclear.
Staffing remains a key issue and the review proposed an increase in pay levels, along with new approaches to rostering and recruitment. Tusla has made significant efforts to address this, opening new routes to recruitment and training. The budget allocation in this area is to rise and Minister for Children Norma Foley said the necessary funding had been supplied to open the 26 beds. Whether this actually happens remains to be seen.
It is easy to say that the answer to problems in the provision of State services is always more money. But resources need to be prioritised and there can be few greater imperatives than looking after the most vulnerable children in society, an area where the State has failed on too many occasions.
It is not good enough for the Taoiseach to reply, when asked about this case, that he will talk to his Ministers about it. The Coalition – blessed with a large surplus on the public accounts – was able to allocate €46.5 million in the budget to cutting capital gains tax and €58.6 million to an extension of a research and development tax credit – a combined amount four times that allocated to emergency care. That says a lot about its priorities.

title: The Irish Times view on motor insurance: needless litigation should be avoided
description: Going to court costs more, but typically leads to the same outcome for claimants
content:
The latest data on private motor insurance claims would indicate that the low hanging fruit in the cost of personal injury claims have been picked.
The introduction of the Personal Injuries Guidelines in 2021 and their subsequent adoption by the Injuries Resolution Board (IRB) has seen average motor personal injury settlement costs fall from €38,008 in 2020 to €36,775 last year. This equates to a fall of almost 20 per cent allowing for inflation. Motor insurance premiums have remained flat on the same adjusted basis.
This may be about as good as it gets as regards a step change in the cost of personal injury claims. Almost two-thirds of motor injury claims under €100,000 are now settled via two routes, directly with insurers under the guidelines or via the IRB.
But the number that are still resolved via litigation remains stubbornly high, even though nearly all of these cases eventually settle outside of court. They also usually result in a similar outcome for the claimant as going through the IRB, yet they account for two-thirds of legal and other costs. Average awards from either channel are at around €19,700, but the IRB charges €791 against average litigation costs of almost €20,000.
Some claims are always going to be litigated, particularly where there is a dispute over liability or the facts, but there is clearly more work to be done to ensure that claimants understand that the court process takes longer and is unlikely to produce a materially different outcome.
Reducing the cost of unavoidable litigation is part of the wider challenge of improving the administration of justice; the difficulty and complexity of this task is demonstrated by the current dispute over criminal legal aid payments to solicitors.
Taken in the round, the introduction of the injuries guidelines and their adoption by the IRB can be seen as a policy success when judged against the goal of reducing the cost of motor insurance claims. The apparent failure of the insurance industry to pass these savings on in full to customers is another issue.

title: Bohs captain Dawson Devoy to miss title run-in after ban over Shamrock Rovers melee
description: Rovers trio Naj Razi, Danny Grant and Michael Noonan also sanctioned
content:
Bohemians captain Dawson Devoy and two Shamrock Rovers players have been suspended for the remainder of the League of Ireland season for their part in a fight that erupted after Stephen Bradley’s side secured a 2-1 win in Tallaght earlier this month.
Devoy and Rovers midfielder Naj Razi both received three-match bans for violent conduct during the incident on October 12th following a disciplinary hearing on Wednesday.
Rovers winger Danny Grant was given a four-game suspension for his involvement in the same incident, while Michael Noonan received a two-match ban. That will see the 18-year-old available for selection for their trip to play Dundalk on October 30th in what would be his last appearance for the club before his move to Nottingham Forest in January.
Bohs assistant coach Stephen O’Donnell will also miss the remainder of the season, with two games left to serve on his suspension, while Rovers’ midfielder Matt Healy will miss their game against Sligo Rovers on Friday due to an accumulation of yellow cards.
Devoy’s absence is a significant blow to Bohs’ title hopes, with Alan Reynolds’ side currently three points behind Rovers ahead of Friday’s Dublin derby against Shelbourne at Dalymount Park. Their last game of the season is away to St Patrick’s Athletic on Friday week.
Meanwhile, Shelbourne will be without Ali Coote after the Scottish winger received a three-match ban having been shown a red card for a foul on St Pat’s midfielder Ryan Sheridan during last Friday’s win at Richmond Park.

title: Josie Ray’s grandchildren had told gardaí of safety concerns before her death, court hears
description: Hasan Ali Gori denies murder of pensioner (89) found dead in her home in her home in Nenagh, Co Tipperary in 2024
content:
Grandchildren of a pensioner allegedly murdered in her home had previously alerted gardaí and social services about concerns they had for her safety, a court heard.
Josephine “Josie” Ray (89), of St Joseph’s Park, Nenagh, Co Tipperary, was found dead in her bed on August 4th, 2024, after she was allegedly suffocated and strangled.
Hasan Ali Gori (52), originally from Chad, Africa , and with an address at St Joseph’s Park, Nenagh, has pleaded not guilty at the Central Criminal Court , Limerick, to murdering Josephine Ray.
At the time, Ali Gori was in a relationship with Josie Ray’s daughter, Mary Ray, who it was heard has an intellectual disability, and they were both living in Josie Ray’s house.
On Wednesday, the court heard evidence of a phone call made by Josie Ray’s granddaughter, Rosie O’Brien, to gardaí on the night before her death.
O’Brien told gardaí that Mary Ray and the accused were “fighting” and “screaming at each other” at Josie Ray’s house, and she was concerned for her elderly grandmother.
Josie Ray’s grandson Daniel O’Brien gave evidence in court that he was a regular visitor in his grandmother’s home, but that he stepped back from visiting her after the accused moved into the property.
O’Brien described his grandmother’s relationship with the accused as “bad”. He said he witnessed a lot of arguments involving Josie, her daughter Mary, and the accused.
Mary Ray, the accused, and Mary Ray’s son were in the house when she was discovered dead, the jury of nine men and three women heard.
[ Elderly woman and man accused of her murder had regularly argued, court hears Opens in new window ]
Answering prosecuting barrister David Humphries, Daniel O’Brien said he had grown “very concerned” that his grandmother was suffering “abuse” in her home.
O’Brien agreed with Ali Gori’s barrister Aidan Doyle that he contacted a social worker and a council housing official and told them that his aunt Mary and the accused were being “violent” to his grandmother at her local authority home.
Sarah Ray, another daughter of Josie Ray, told the court that her mother and the accused were constantly arguing.
Sarah Ray said she saw her mother hit one of the accused’s legs with a “poker” when she was “all over the place” and “didn’t mean it”.
She said her mother paid “most” of her own household bills, but she agreed that the payment of bills later became an “issue” in the house.
Sarah Ray said that, a few months before her mother’s death, she found her on the floor of her own kitchen after she “slipped” and fractured her hip.
Sarah Ray said her mother recuperated at her home for a few months because she had felt safe there.
Sarah Ray said that, on the night before her mother’s death, her sister Mary was telephoning Josie constantly asking her to go back home, telling Josie “there’s trouble in the house”.
She eventually brought her mother back to her home that night because her mother “was worried about Mary”.
Carmel Ray told the court that she did not have a close relationship with her mother growing up, because she lived with her father, while Josie lived with Mary, who required her full attention due to having a learning disability.
Carmel Ray said her sister Mary was a “very kind, shy” girl but that she was “easily led” and her mother “always had to protect her”.
Mary Ray was not a person to normally show signs of “aggression”, Carmel Ray said, “unless something really annoyed her”.
[ ‘She was a great woman for glamour’: Warm tributes to Josephine Ray at funeral Mass in Nenagh Opens in new window ]
Carmel Ray recalled an incident when Mary was a teenager and she struck another of their sisters after she repeatedly refused to do chores.
Carmel Ray also recalled a later incident when, following a traumatic incident, Mary “couldn’t control her emotions” and the situation required five gardaí to subdue her.
Josie Ray didn’t approve of Mary having boyfriends; Mary had children but she was not capable of looking after them, it was heard.
Carmel Ray said Mary’s relationship with the accused was “volatile, disruptive, constantly arguing, and dysfunctional”.

title: Arnotts asks Dublin revamp tsar to move GPO social welfare payments to reduce antisocial behaviour
description: Robert Watt previously said north inner-city Dublin unfairly burdened with services for ‘people on the margins of society’
content:
Management at department store Arnotts has said antisocial behaviour in Dublin city centre could be tackled by ending the use of the nearby GPO as a facility for paying out social welfare entitlements.
The retailer made the suggestion in an email to Robert Watt , the senior civil servant who has been seconded by the Government to the role of Dublin’s regeneration “tsar” and lead the Dublin City Taskforce.
The taskforce is looking at improving the city centre, particularly the O’Connell Street area – known for its long-term antisocial behaviour and dereliction.
As a working post office, the GPO on O’Connell Street pays out social welfare payments in cash to eligible recipients.
The email was sent to Watt by Mark Limby, operations director of Brown Thomas Arnotts Ltd, the company operating the store.
The communication appeared on the Register of Lobbying, which is maintained by the State’s ethics watchdog, the Standards in Public Office Commission (SIPO) .
Brown Thomas and Arnotts, Dublin’s best-known department stores, are both owned by the Selfridges Group.
In a statement, Arnotts management said it had engaged with the taskforce on the use of the GPO for social welfare payments.
“Given the concentration of multiple services at the GPO, we asked that the location for social welfare payments be considered as part of the wider plans for the area,” the company said.
[ ‘Talbot Street is known as Tablet Street now’: Will a €2m makeover be enough to turn things around? Opens in new window ]
“The GPO is an iconic and historic building and an important tourist destination, and we believe its use is a legitimate question to raise in the context of the taskforce’s work.”
Details of the retailer’s lobbying about the GPO were first reported by Dublin Inquirer.
Arnotts said the use of the GPO for social welfare payments was a matter for the Department of Social Protection and An Post .
“We would expect any such review to be guided first by the practicalities and the impact on the people who rely on these services, ensuring a modern, accessible and dignified setting, with no one disadvantaged in receiving their payments,” Arnotts said.
Most An Post staff have vacated the GPO and moved to new headquarters in the Dublin docklands, but the post office facility remains and is likely to continue there even if other uses are confirmed for the building itself.
The Office of Public Works is preparing a public consultation regarding the future of the building, including the possibility of alternative uses by arts groups.
[ Dublin city centre ‘scourged with anti-social behaviour, drug-dealing, gang intimidation’ Opens in new window ]
An Post said it was not aware of the proposal from Arnotts that the GPO cease paying benefits.
“The distribution of Department of Social Protection benefit payments is an integral and valued function of the post office network, including at the GPO, and it is a vital service for customers and local communities,” the post office operator said.
Watt did not respond to a request for comment.
At the start of this month, the former Department of Health secretary-general said north inner-city Dublin had been unfairly burdened with a “large over-concentration” of services for “people on the margins of society”.
He believed services for homeless people, refugees and people with “particular needs” were concentrated in an area around O’Connell Street, “which has been subjected to neglect, a lot of dereliction, a lot of underdeveloped sites and, sadly, a lot of antisocial behaviour”.
Watt told the Irish Planning Institute ’s autumn conference that the area was one where a “large number of various services for people on the margins of society have been located and that has contributed to what is, at times, a very difficult situation”.
Social Democrats TD Daniel Ennis, whose Dublin Central constituency includes O’Connell Street, said “collecting your pension or welfare payment is not antisocial behaviour”.
Ennis said there was an over-concentration of services in Dublin 1, but a “post office serving local residents and people who come to the city centre is certainly not one we should be proposing to take away”.

title: Familiar Ireland squad may lack excitement, but that could be its strength
description: Andy Farrell named his 36-man squad for next month’s Nations Championship northern series games
content:
A 36-man Ireland squad that falls along anticipated lines and with a very familiar look to it may not be especially exciting, nor will it satisfy the desire for freshness, but for the most part a relatively settled squad is generally a sign of strength. Exhibit A: the Springboks at the last World Cup.
All but six of the players named by Andy Farrell on Wednesday for next month’s Nations Championship northern series were among the 36-strong squad for the southern series during the summer. Four of those places have been taken by Andrew Porter, Ryan Baird, Mack Hansen and Tommy O’Brien, all of whom are returning from injury having been sidelined from Test rugby since last November.
This leaves the Ulster pair of James McNabney and Jamie Benson as the two uncapped bolters. Undoubtedly, their promotion is at least partially down to Jack Conan and Harry Byrne joining Caelan Doris, Bryn Ward and Jack Crowley and others on the list of injured absentees.
But if McNabney and Benson are the winners, then Jeremy Loughman and Cormac Izuchukwu are the main losers. With Porter back, Loughman misses out to Billy Bohan despite starting three games in this year’s Six Nations and being named on the bench against Australia and New Zealand in July. It is, however, further evidence of 20-year-old Bohan’s rapid progress and huge potential. Likewise, Sam Illo’s retention ahead of Finlay Bealham looks like a line in the sand.
Ryan Baird return is a significant addition. Athletic and effective in the air, the hybrid lock/flanker being available has contributed to the similarly talented Izuchukwu, and Tom Ahern, missing out.
Baird’s end-of-season form in 2025 would have also given the Lions something different for their tour to Australia, and he had been playing superbly against South Africa last November before suffering a broken leg.
McNabney has evidently jumped ahead of both Izuckhukwu and Max Deegan. It comes as no surprise that the 23-year-old’s strength and physicality appeal to Farrell, and having been a standout for the Ireland under-20s in their Grand Slam-winning campaigns in 2022 and 2023, he would have featured in the senior squad sooner only for an ACL injury that ruled him out last season.
Opportunity knocks for him now, albeit Doris and Conan will return in time for the Six Nations. The same is true for 24-year-old Benson, in the absence of Crowley, Byrne and Joey Carbery.
Benson has built up quite a body of work with the England under-18s and under-20s, as well as Harlequins. Irish-qualified through his mother, he is highly versatile as an outhalf, centre and fullback, but is seemingly most at home at 10.
A skilful, tidy player, with a varied kicking game, he has a low centre of gravity with a nifty step off his left, as well as a creative, passing game.
Twenty of this squad went to the World Cup three years ago, and that’s despite Doris, Conan and Crowley being among those sidelined. The expectation is that all three will be fit and restored for the Six Nations and will be on the plane to Australia for next year’s World Cup.
Granted, there were six uncapped players in the 37-man squad for the 2022 Autumn Nations Series, with Loughman, Joe McCarthy and Jimmy O’Brien among 25 players from that squad who went to the World Cup the following year.
Ten from the squad subsequently missed the cut for the World Cup in France, whether through injury or selection. Eight were later restored, most having recovered from their respective injuries, or in the case of Ross Byrne, having been called in from the wilderness. It demonstrates there is still scope for some fluidity between now and next year’s tournament.
The upcoming three games against Argentina, Fiji and South Africa at the Aviva Stadium, as well as the final playoff in Twickenham, will tell Farrell plenty about his players.
No press conference was held following the release of the squad on Wednesday, giving no opportunity to inquire as to the potential roles of the forwards selected. However, the make-up of the loosehead forwards suggests Nick Timoney will also be an option at seven and eight. Either way, Sean Jansen’s emergence looks even more significant in the absence of Doris and Conan.
The team is still dependent upon a core group of relative Test veterans, including Tadhg Furlong, Josh van der Flier, Jamson Gibson-Park and Garry Ringrose. To some degree, the stability of this squad can be attributed to the lack of obvious alternatives. Aside from outhalf, this is especially true in the backs.
Matty Devine’s impact after his move to Ulster and Fintan Gunne’s growth at Leinster are in the background, but the scrumhalves remain unchanged, as is the case in midfield. They all went to the last World Cup and, barring injury, will likely go to the next one.
Seeing as the outside backs are all fit and healthy, they also pick themselves, even if the departed James Lowe would still offer something different.
As has been the case since the last World Cup, the biggest point of discussion will be around the 10 jersey. Sam Prendergast has continued his resurgence with Leinster, while Ciarán Frawley’s start to life at Connacht as a bone fide outhalf for the first time in his professional career may also prove a positive for Ireland, and perhaps Prendergast too. It’s certainly given Farrell real options in spite of Crowley’s absence.

title: Putin agrees to resume talks on Ukraine war with Kyiv and Washington
description: Stephen Hubbard (74), a former teacher, freed without any ‘swap’ required, says US president
author_name: Katya Arenina, Amy Mackinnon, Max Seddon
content:
US special envoy Steve Witkoff discussed a resumption of peace talks between Russia, the US and Ukraine followed by a possible summit between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping next month, according to Russian officials.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said after the Wednesday meeting in St Petersburg between Witkoff and Putin that establishing a “security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends” was the main issue Moscow was ready to negotiate on, Russian news agency Interfax reported.
Witkoff’s trip, his ninth visit to Russia, is part of a pivot towards Putin in the US’s push to end Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine that has alarmed Kyiv and its European allies.
Russia also released a US citizen on Wednesday, with Trump noting that the US was “not asked to give anything in return”.
Trump’s envoy and Putin discussed resuming the talks with Ukraine in mid-November, and a possible leaders’ summit between China, Russia and the US at the Apec forum in Shenzhen next month, Ushakov said, adding that Beijing, which is hosting Apec, had already begun preparations for a meeting.
On Tuesday Witkoff met Volodymyr Zelenskiy and other European leaders in Norway, with the Ukrainian leader signalling willingness to resume talks with Russia and the US, potentially advancing to a leaders’ meeting if progress was made, according to an official familiar with the talks.
Ukraine and the US also advanced on security guarantees, which are a Kyiv demand for the peace process to move forward. But the official said expectations remained measured given Russia’s limited willingness so far to engage seriously in negotiations.
A US official said Russia accepted a proposal put forward by Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, to hold technical talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine. Ukraine agreed to the idea during the talks in Oslo, they added.
In their talks with Putin on Wednesday, Trump’s envoys updated the Russian leader on the progress made in talks with Zelenskiy, the official said. Witkoff and Kushner, who dialled into the talks virtually, also discussed a postwar economic and prosperity plan, European security architecture and plans for the upcoming trilateral meeting.
The official described the two days of talks as “positive and constructive” while noting that important work still remains.
Images of Witkoff at the meeting with Putin showed him with handwritten notes that read, in part, “I feel momentum. Need to build on that” and “business deal”.
US-brokered talks with Ukraine have been on hold since the war in the Middle East began in late February. Russia has since paid lip service to the US’s diplomatic efforts and rejected Trump’s push for an immediate ceasefire or a moratorium on striking each side’s energy infrastructure.
Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel this month while putting pressure on Ukraine to end its long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries, aiming to tame global fuel prices ahead of US midterm elections next month.
The shift has driven Trump’s relationship with Zelenskiy to its lowest point since their infamous spat in the Oval Office last year.
Putin hailed the diesel deal, which he said had driven global prices down 5-6 per cent. Commenting on the deal, Putin told Witkoff on Wednesday that Russia was preparing to dispatch several tankers, with the first carrying 40,000 tonnes of fuel. It would leave “in two or three days”, he said.
Russia is interested in resuming economic co-operation with the US, Putin said, citing the possibility of sending “large quantities of fertiliser supplies” to the US market.
The Ukrainian president has in the past week wrestled with a brutal degradation of an already-fraught relationship with Trump, who insisted Zelenskiy should “get somebody else to negotiate”.
But Zelenskiy struck an upbeat note following the talks in Oslo, saying he had received “positive signals” from the US and that intelligence sharing on early missile warning had been restored.
However, speed limits on the Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military to fly drones into Russian-controlled parts of Ukraine and to operate interceptors targeting long-range drones remained active on Tuesday, with no changes reported the following day, Zelenskiy said.
Washington has repeatedly denied throttling the crucial communication systems to prevent drones from flying faster than 160kph, but Zelenskiy insisted it was deliberate.
Speaking on Fox News, Zelenskiy said Ukraine would be ready to accept a ceasefire that would freeze the fighting along the current front line, Kyiv’s long-standing proposal that Moscow has repeatedly rejected.
“Freeze, and stop. This is the minimum we need from Russia today,” Zelenskiy said.
The Kremlin on Wednesday said it released a jailed US citizen on humanitarian grounds. Stephen Hubbard, a retired schoolteacher, had been detained for more than four years after being captured by Russian forces in eastern Ukraine.
Trump said on his Truth Social platform that Hubbard “is on his way back home and will soon be with his family”.
“The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return,” he added.
Witkoff told Putin in comments about Hubbard’s release broadcast on state TV: “You talk so much about my president, president Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again.”
Hubbard, who is in his 70s, was captured by Russian forces from Izyum in eastern Ukraine in April 2022, where he had lived for several years while the city was under occupation.
He was sentenced to almost seven years’ imprisonment, accused of fighting on behalf of Ukraine – charges that Hubbard’s lawyer denied. He was deemed wrongfully detained by the US government in 2025.
Separately, Russia’s FSB internal security agency said on Wednesday it had detained a German citizen who had served in Ukraine’s armed forces. The announcement followed last week’s detentions of a Japanese journalist accused of espionage and a Swede whom the FSB also accused of serving in Ukraine’s military.
Earlier this month Dmitry Medvedev, deputy head of Russia’s security council, publicly suggested Moscow might need to detain more Europeans and Americans to secure Russians’ release abroad.

title: ‘My mother asked me to let Evan go’: Murder accused was asked to spare brother with special needs
description: Robert O’Connor says parents wished to discuss his cocaine use and were not comfortable with it happening in the house
content:
A 32-year-old man accused of murdering three members of his family in their Co Louth home described to gardaí how his mother had asked him to let his younger brother with special needs go as he held them at knifepoint, a jury has heard.
Robert O’Connor, of Drumgowna, Louth Village, Dundalk, Co Louth, has pleaded not guilty of murder by reason of insanity, or guilty of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility, over the killings of his mother Louise (56), his father Mark (54) and his younger brother Evan (27) at their home between September 28th and 29th, 2025, both dates inclusive.
The Central Criminal Court jury has been told the accused accepts he caused the deaths of the three victims.
At the outset of Robert’s first interview at Drogheda Garda station at 5pm on September 29th last year, the accused’s solicitor told officers his client has schizophrenia and could not remember the last time he took his medication.
The solicitor explained that the accused had seen a doctor earlier that day, but Robert said he did not remember seeing one. When the accused was asked by gardaí to tell them in his own words what had happened, Robert replied: “I don’t know what to tell you, I really don’t.”
When gardaí asked him to tell them what he remembered, Robert said that the Friday was “normal enough”.
Robert said his father, mother and brother were in the house at the time. The accused said he could not remember what they had for dinner, but he had gone upstairs to “do some cocaine”.
He said his parents then called him back down, as they wanted to talk about his cocaine use and were not comfortable with it happening in the house. “Aside from my mates, they are the only people I had in this world, I don’t know why I did it,” he added.
Gardaí asked the accused what he meant when he said “did it”. The accused replied “murdering them”.
Robert said the conversation with his parents about violence in the house and whether he wanted to stop using cocaine continued. He left the room, went upstairs, took cocaine and watched pornography.
When he returned he saw “them all sitting in the sittingroom” and “got a knife – all angry and sh*t”.
“I went into the sittingroom and walked over with the knife and asked my mother why she didn’t feel empathy and why she didn’t feel the pain,” he said.
Robert said he “slashed” his mother first “on the head”.
The accused told detectives he was pointing a knife at the three members of his family and telling them “not to be opening their mouths at the one time”.
Robert said his mother went for the door. “I slammed it back shut and said get the f**k back in there.”
He said his father charged at him to try to get out the door, but he thought he stuck “it in his stomach or something”. The accused said to gardaí: “Can I please not give details about the stabbing.
“I stabbed them multiple times, I can’t remember.”
He told gardaí he thought his brother’s iPad “changed the reality” and that his brother was “like a programmer”.
“I wanted him to get the iPad and undo everything that happened,” he added.
Asked what had happened “after the murders occurred”, Robert said he thought “they went down the hall” and “it started freaking me out when my dad wasn’t dying, loads of blood was coming out, I don’t want to revisit it”.
When asked whether he wanted to change or add anything to his statement, Robert said: “I wish to add that my mother asked me to let Evan go.”
“Is it fair to say you are telling us you murdered them?” asked gardaí, to which the accused replied: “Yes.”
The trial continues on Thursday before Judge Mícheál P O’Higgins and a jury of six men and six women.

title: Free Show: Frank McNally on the liberating power of prison art
description: Time Well Spent is an exhibition running for a month and including paintings, sculptures, ceramics, textile craftwork and an installation called Reflections From Home
content:
Tom Shortt is a brother of Pat , the comedian. But when, in describing an event he invited me to in Tallaght last Friday night, he used the term “breakout exhibition”, I don’t think it was meant as a joke.
The affable Tom is arts officer with the Irish Prison Service . His reference to a breakout, however, was intended in the cultural sense: describing an event that could be important, even defining, for some of those involved.
Just for the record, the ex-inmates present at the opening night of Time Well Spent, a show of their work at the Rua Red gallery, had left jail in the legal way, after completing sentences.
Other exhibitors, unavoidably absent, are still doing time. But in a message that applied to both, a paradoxical theme of the night was the liberating power of art, even when you’re still locked up.
It featured prominently in the paintings and conversation of Thomas Hendy, for example, a 44-year-old who had spent much of his life in correctional institutions before freeing himself first through artistic expression, then by actual release.
