A tattoo on his neck depicted the silhouette of a swallow: prisoners’ code, he explained, for “resilience, hope and a safe return home”.
The bird also featured in one of his striking, black-and-white compositions: a self-portrait in which he crouches in a prison yard while a hovering swallow forces him to look upwards.
In the background, depicted as graffiti on a wall, are the words “Open your feckin’ mind”. That’s not just a personal mantra, he told me. It doubles as a tribute to a man named Billy Gallagher, the training officer and mentor who first drummed the phrase into his mind.
Another of Thomas’s high-concept paintings is of an office drudge, sitting at a desk with an egg timer, which he constantly refills. The theme there is that you don’t have to be in jail to be a prisoner.
Still, Hendy is happy to be on the outside again and putting a troubled past well behind him. He lost two brothers to drugs (the subject of another of his works, in which he communes with their reflections in prison-yard puddles).
But he was last in jail five years ago. Since when, as he sums up: “I got out, got clean, got married.” Now he’s among those artists for whom the Tallaght show could indeed be a breakout – in the cultural sense – to bigger things.
Another of the speakers on opening night was James Murphy, a former republican prisoner who has become (in Shortt’s words) “a very important artist”, not least for depicting the prison experience.
Also present, although not exhibiting, was Eddie Cahill, whose life may be the ultimate example of the redemptive power of art.
Eddie is a brother of the late and still probably better-known Martin, aka The General , once Ireland’s most notorious gang leader. The siblings had similar trajectories as teenagers, being sent to different reform schools (Letterfrack and Daingean, respectively) and then graduating to lives of crime.
The lesser-known Cahill spent the best part of 30 years in various forms of detention. But in Portlaoise Prison, he discovered art – or art discovered him – and never looked back.
He took to practising it 10 or 12 hours a day at one point: it was a vocation, clearly, however late. And now it’s a career, in which he has had many of his own exhibitions.
Having curated a previous version of the Tallaght show, he was lending his presence to the latest one as a senior fellow of the prison art programme. But as a man of few and well-chosen words, he had to be coaxed into taking to the rostrum and then limited himself to thanking us for coming.
“Near enough,” he told me when I asked if he made a living from his work: “It’s a famine or a feast.” But commercial or not, in his experience, prison art was life-changing, and not just for him. In a world where recidivism is common, none of his fellow art students in Portlaoise from that time went back to jail afterwards.
Time Well Spent, which runs for a month, is curated by Orla McGovern, a young UCD doctoral student “with an interest in prison art as contemporary folklore”. It also includes sculpture, ceramic and textile craftwork, and an installation called Reflections From Home.
[ The Irish Times view on Irish prisons: inhumane conditions Opens in new window ]
Produced by the Portlaoise Prison Education Unit, that comprises music, writing and stone sculpture in the form of a carved “window of memories”.
[ ‘You couldn’t ignore that madness’: The comedians turning the GAA into a laughing matter Opens in new window ]
The installation’s creators were not named or present on opening night. But their teachers were, proudly displaying the work of their proteges. And the work illustrated a poignant point made by Shortt during his speech: that for those still incarcerated, it was important to know that, via their art, “a little part of them at least is out of prison”.

title: Portráidí den ealaíontóir agus den scríbhneoir
description: Bhí pictiúr den údar Gaeilge Pádraic Ó Conaire ar ceant i mBaile Átha Cliath le déanaí
content:
Díoladh pictiúir de bheirt – an scríbhneoir Pádraic Ó Conaire agus an t-ealaíontóir Charles Lamb – a raibh dlúthbhaint acu le Gaeltacht Chonamara ag ceant a bhí ar bun i mBaile Átha Cliath le gairid.
Tugadh €3,738 ar phortráid den scríbhneoir iomráiteach Pádraic Ó Conaire, nó Sean-Phádraic mar a thugtar air uaireanta, ag an gceant a bhí á reáchtáil ag na ceantálaithe Whyte’s.
Agus fritheadh €2,368 ar phortráid den ealaíontóir Charles Lamb a rinne pictiúir go leor de Chonamara is de mhuintir Chonamara i rith a shaoil.
An t-ealaíontóir Harry Kernoff a chruthaigh an dá phictiúr.
Chreid Lamb nár mhór d’ealaíontóir cur faoi i gConamara le go mbeadh ar a chumas an ceantar agus muintir an cheantair a phéinteáil i gceart…
Tá biseach an cheannaitheora de 20 faoin gcéad (agus CBL 23 faoin gcéad ar an mbiseach sin) san áireamh sna praghsanna seo. Is pastal déanta ar pháipéar, 16 orlach faoi 12 orlach, atá sa bpictiúr de Phádraic Ó Conaire agus bhí treoirphraghas idir €2,000 agus €3,000 luaite leis.
Nuair a cuireadh an dá phictiúr seo ar ceant ag Whyte’s i mBealtaine na bliana seo caite, níor díoladh iad. Treoirphraghas níos airde d’idir €3,000 agus €5,000 an ceann a bhí luaite leo an uair úd.
Thug an ceantálaí Ian Whyte le fios go raibh níos mó suime léirithe sa bpictiúr de Shean-Phádraic an uair seo. Tá sé deimhnithe ó shin ag Músaem Cathrach na Gaillimhe gurbh iadsan a cheannaigh é.
Sa mbliain 1933 a rinne Kernoff an phortráid de Ó Conaire, sin cúig bliana tar éis bhás an scríbhneora in 1928.
Deir an staraí ealaíne Kathryn Milligan, ó Choláiste na Trionóide, gur minic a rinne Kernoff portráidí de dhaoine nach raibh aithne aige orthu. Bhunaigh sé iad ar ghrianghraif nó ar shaothair ealaíne eile.
Treoirphraghas idir €2,000 agus €3,000 a bhí luaite leis an bpictiúr de Charles Lamb, chomh maith. 15 orlach faoi 10.5 orlach atá an pastal ar pháipéar seo.
Rinneadh é sa mbliain 1959, cúig bliana sular bhásaigh Lamb in 1964. Bailitheoir príobháideach a cheannaigh é, a dúirt Ian Whyte.
Sa dá phictiúr, tá an bheirt gléasta go snasta, iad ag caitheamh seaicéad le geansaí faoi agus léine is carabhat. Sa gcúlra de phortráid Uí Chonaire tá radharc den fharraige agus faoileán ag eitilt os a chionn.
Rugadh Pádraic Ó Conaire i gcathair na Gaillimhe in 1882 agus nuair a bhásaigh a mháthair in 1894 chuaigh sé chun cónaí le gaolta leis i Ros Muc i gConamara.
Agus é fós ina dhéagóir bhog sé go Londain, áit a raibh sé fostaithe sa státseirbhís ar feadh tamall de bhlianta.
D’fhill sé ar Éirinn in 1915 agus ba ann a chaith sé an chuid eile dá shaol.
Idir na blianta 1901 agus 1927, foilsíodh na céadta gearrscéalta leis in irisí is i nuachtáin éagsúla, agus foilsíodh a úrscéal Deoraíocht in 1910.
Ceathracha a sé bliana d’aois a bhí sé nuair a bhásaigh sé.
Cuirtear suim i gcónaí i saol agus i saothar an cheannródaí seo i scríbhneoireacht na Gaeilge sa 20ú haois.
Le gairid, foilsíodh an leabhar The Lives of Pádraic Ó Conaire, le hAindrias Ó Cathasaigh, agus níl sé i bhfad ó shin ó chraol RTÉ Raidió na Gaeltachta an tsraith clár Blaiseadh de Shaothar Shean-Phádraic Uí Chonaire, chomh maith le píosaí faoin scríbhneoir ón gcartlann.
Níos túisce i mbliana, foilsíodh macasamhail de M’Asal Beag Dubh, Aistí agus Mion-scéalta sa seanchló in éindí le haistriúchán go Béarla déanta ag Peadar Macken.
Ba i bPort an Dúnáin i gCo. Ard Mhacha a rugadh Charles Lamb in 1893.
Péintéir tí a bhí ina athair agus chleachtaigh Charles an cheird sin fhad is a bhí sé ag déanamh staidéar ar an ealaín i mBéal Feirste.
In 1917, fuair sé scoláireacht le freastal ar an Metropolitan School of Art i mBaile Átha Cliath, áit ar chaith sé ceithre bliana.
Deirtear gurbh é Pádraic Ó Conaire a mhol dó cuairt a thabhairt ar an gCeathrú Rua i gConamara an chead lá ariamh in 1921.
In 1927, phós Charles Lamb Katherine Madox Hueffer, iníon an scríbhneora Ford Madox Ford. Bhí an-tionchar ag Madox Ford ar shaol na litríochta i Sasana ag tús na 1920idí agus d’fhoilsigh sé scríbhneoirí ar nós James Joyce, Joseph Conrad, Ernest Hemingway agus Jean Rhys in irisí dá chuid.
Sa mbliain 1935, thóg Charles Lamb teach agus stiúideo ar an mBóthar Buí ar an gCeathrú Rua.
Chreid Lamb nár mhór d’ealaíontóir cur faoi i gConamara le go mbeadh ar a chumas an ceantar agus muintir an cheantair a phéinteáil i gceart, agus b’in a rinne sé.
Ach an oiread le Ó Conaire, tá suim i saothair Lamb i gcónaí. Tá 44 phictiúr leis, a bhailigh Patrick agus Frances Smith thar thréimhse 30 bliain, á gcur ar ceant ag de Veres faoi láthair.
Pictiúir de thírdhreach agus de mhuintir Chonamara atá ina bhformhór. Is féidir tairiscintí a dhéanamh ar na pictiúir seo go dtí an 20 Deireadh Fómhair.
Is i Londain, in Eanáir na bliana 1900, a rugadh an t-ealaíontóir Harry Kernoff. (B’in an mhí is an bhliain chéanna a chuaigh Pádraic Ó Conaire chun cónaí sa gcathair.)
D’aistrigh a chlann go Baile Átha Cliath nuair a bhí sé 14 bliana d’aois.
Shaothraigh a athair a chuid ag obair mar chaibinéadaire agus d’oibrigh Harry leis fhad is a bhí sé ag freastal ar ranganna oíche sa Metropolitan School of Art, áit ar fhreastail Charles Lamb freisin.
Bhí Kernoff lárnach i saol cultúrtha na hardchathrach agus rinne sé portráidí go leor de scríbhneoirí, d’aisteoirí, d’amhránaithe is d’ealaíontóirí eile na linne. Orthu seo, bhí Patrick Kavanagh, Brian O’Nolan (Flann O’Brien), James Joyce, Peadar O’Donnell, Hilton Edwards agus Delia Murphy.
In 2004, íocadh €15,000 (gan táillí san áireamh) ar phictiúr a rinne Kernoff den scríbhneoir Liam Ó Flaithearta in 1933. (Bhain Kernoff agus Ó Flaithearta beirt leis an eite chlé ó thaobh na polaitíochta de.)
Rinne sé pictiúir go leor freisin de shaol na cathrach agus de dhaoine i mbun oibre, chomh maith le radhairc den tírdhreach timpeall na hÉireann.
Tá an-tóir ar phictiúir Kernoff sa lá atá inniu ann agus baineann siad praghsanna arda amach, ach ní hamhlaidh a bhí sa gcuid deiridh dá shaol.
Tuairiscítear go ndearna sé iarracht 42 cheann dá chuid portráid a dhíol le Gailearaí Náisiúnta na hÉireann in 1966, ach nár ceannaíodh iad.
Ní saol éasca a bhí ag lucht an phinn ná ag lucht na scuaibe tráth.
Sa bheathaisnéis nua fhíorspéisiúil, tugann Aindrias Ó Cathasaigh le fios go raibh cuid de leabhair Uí Chonaire,Deoraíocht agus An Chéad Chloch san áireamh, as cló nuair a bhásaigh sé in Ospidéal Richmond i mBaile Átha Cliath.
Nuair a phós a iníon Eileen cúpla lá roimh a bhás, tugadh le fios ar an deimhniú pósta gur “labourer” a bhí ina hathair.
Ach an oiread le Pádraic Ó Conaire, tuigtear gur beag de shaibhreas an tsaoil a bhí ag Harry Kernoff nuair a bhásaigh seisean in Ospidéal na Mí san ardchathair Lá Nollag 1974.

title: ‘Critical vulnerabilities’ found in computer code supporting up to 70% of internet
description: Websites worldwide pulled offline in effort to prevent cyberattacks on companies’ systems
content:
“Critical vulnerabilities” in a computer programming language that supports as much as 70 per cent of the internet have caused multiple websites, from Woodie’s DIY to the Finnish government, to suddenly go offline in an effort to protect their systems from cyberattack.
The coding issues were discovered by digital agents powered by artificial intelligence (AI) , with the programmers behind the code encouraging all its users “to update immediately” after it was informed of the problem.
The European Union ’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) told users “where that is not feasible, organisations should consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix is applied and verified”.
“Technical details are now being discussed publicly,” CERT said in a statement on Wednesday afternoon, adding that “this raises the likelihood that attacks are already exploiting the vulnerabilities”.
OpenAI , which said it “led a coalition” of researchers investigating the vulnerabilities in question, described the “severity of these flaws” as “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory”.
“To our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did, opening a defender’s window for maintainers and security providers to prepare fixes and protections ahead of disclosure,” the company, which operates ChatGPT , said in a statement.
PHP, the programmers behind the code, explained there was “a demonstrated exploit” in its system “where an unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code runs”.
[ Revolut’s outage was a warning to us all Opens in new window ]
“All PHP installations” were “at risk” of a cyberattack, the company warned.
Brian Honan, a Dublin-based cybersecurity expert and chief executive of BH consulting, said “the vulnerabilities are of a very high severity and would actually enable a potential attacker to remotely control and manage a website”.
“We don’t have a lot of details just yet because, obviously, if they were to release details of what the vulnerability is, that would enable criminals to hack in before systems are updated and fixed,” he said.
Hackers could “steal data, change websites, do whatever they want”, he said, with “websites liable to be completely taken over”.
“It’s not rare for a major vulnerability to be found in software, but I think the impact of this vulnerability will be a surprise ... the impact is huge,” he told The Irish Times.
An incident of this scale “makes it really important for companies to ensure that they understand what cyber systems they have in place”, Honan said, “and that they have a process and tools in place to keep themselves abreast of what potential ways there are to fix those vulnerabilities”.
[ Google says its Gemini AI model hacked three other companies Opens in new window ]
Howard Shortt, a cyber partner at Grant Thorton , added “there is a real risk that some IT departments overlook this potential threat as they might not realise that it is being used in their systems”.
“If remediation cannot be arranged urgently, then affected systems should be temporarily isolated from external exposure and be subject to heightened monitoring,” he said.

title: Teenager drove stolen car wrong way on M50 before crashing into garden, court told
description: Michael Maughan (18) allegedly avoided three stinger devices and nearly collided head-on with a bus and Garda patrol car
content:
A young man drove a stolen car the wrong way on a busy dual carriageway and the M50 in Dublin before a 30ft-drop crash into a family’s garden, it has been alleged.
Michael Maughan (18) avoided three Garda stinger devices and sped around the city, nearly crashing head-on with a bus and a Garda patrol car, Dublin District Court heard.
Judge Peter White granted conditional bail pending the Director of Public Prosecutions’ directions.
He restricted Maughan, of Whitechurch Heights, Rathfarnham, Dublin, from being in any motor vehicle save for public transport or one owned by a family member.
Garda Cein Meade told the judge on Wednesday that Maughan was arrested in the early hours of Tuesday and charged with five counts of dangerous driving, driving without insurance or a licence, and possessing a stolen Toyota Aqua, taken on October 17th in the Dundrum area.
The teenager appeared unrepresented in court, as many solicitors, including his, have withdrawn their services due to legal aid payment reforms introduced in July, which have caused widespread disruption to the criminal justice system.
The judge cautioned the accused against self-incrimination, stressed that he still enjoyed the presumption of innocence, and gave him a chance to study the bail objections with help from his older brother.
Meade alleged that at 12.40am, he was on patrol with the divisional drugs unit when his command and control unit informed him that a stolen vehicle had failed to stop for gardaí in the Clondalkin area.
The 2016-registered red car was observed at Sundrive Road heading in the direction of the local Garda station. The garda observed the Toyota Aqua approach the junction at speed, followed by a patrol car with its sirens activated.
A Garda stinger device had been set up on one side of the four-way junction, but the teenager, allegedly caught red-handed, swung to avoid it and kept driving through a red light.
The vehicle continued through the Dublin 12 area along the canal at speed, allegedly breaking three more red lights at Herberton Road, Dolphin Road and Davitt Road, putting numerous road users and pedestrians at risk. The car turned right on to Tyrconnell Road, doing 100km/h in a 50km/h zone, the court heard.
The garda said he watched it cross the white line, go through another set of red lights, and continue on the wrong side for the entire Chapelizod Road.
The youth allegedly passed Islandbridge; another Garda stinger device was deployed just outside the Criminal Courts of Justice building, but it was avoided.
The vehicle later took a sharp left at speed, crossing the river Liffey against oncoming traffic at Frank Sherwin Bridge.
At the Chapelizod Bypass, described by the garda as one of the busiest access routes to the city centre, the vehicle drove on the wrong side of the road, heading outbound along the inbound lane towards the M50, covering a total distance of 7km against oncoming traffic.
The officer did not follow it; however, it was tracked by the Garda Air Support Unit helicopter.
The court heard the vehicle drove in the bus lane and narrowly avoided a head-on collision with an oncoming public bus.
Gardaí deployed a third stinger, but the driver “took sharp evasive action”, evaded it, and went on the M50 motorway at Junction 7, where it continued northbound in the southbound lane.
At Junction 6, it exited on to the Navan Road and continued against traffic before turning on to Parkway Road into a cul-de-sac beside a closed school and turning off its lights to avoid detection. Meade said he drove into the same cul-de-sac and met the accused coming head-on, forcing him to take evasive action to avoid a collision.
The court heard that the teenager allegedly drove back on to the Navan Road, followed by the Garda Air Support helicopter, as it continued outbound on the inbound lane on the N3 at the Dunboyne exit, Co Meath. It turned on to the correct lane towards Dublin again.
Meade headed towards the Dublin Mountains at about 2am to continue patrols in search of the vehicle.
While travelling uphill in Dublin 16, he was met head-on by the accused, travelling downhill at speed, forcing him to take evasive action to the side of the road.
He turned in the direction where he had last seen the vehicle and observed a marked patrol car on the side of the road and the accused’s vehicle, which had gone over a 30-ft drop down into the front garden of a family home, coming to a halt near a cement mixer and the front door of the house.
The accused and two other younger teenage boys, who have not been charged, were located near the vehicle.
The accused allegedly made some admissions about driving, but denied stealing the vehicle.
The judge set bail in Maughan’s own bond, cashless at €500, and remanded him to appear again on December 9th for possible further charges.

title: Relatives express ‘deep gratitude’ to rescue crews after retired couple’s deaths in fire
description: Married couple in their 70s died in blaze at  dormer bungalow in Raheen, Co Cork
content:
Relatives of a retired couple who died when a fire broke out at their home near Innishannon, Co Cork , yesterday have expressed their “deep gratitude” to the fire service, ambulance crews and gardaí.
In a post on Rip.ie, the family of Geraldine (Tina) and William (Willie) Hawkes indicated that they appreciated all of the rescue services ”kindness, care and efforts” at this “difficult time”.
The married couple, who were in their 70s, died in the blaze at their dormer bungalow in Raheen, Crossbarry, yesterday morning.
Willie Hawkes contacted the emergency services at about 7.30am. Units of the Cork City Fire Service, firefighters from Bandon, gardaí and the emergency services immediately went to the scene. The fire had seriously taken hold, however, and there was no possibility of saving the couple.
The bodies of the couple were subsequently located in the property. The remains were transferred to Cork University Hospital for postmortem examinations.
An inquest will be held in due course. The fire is being treated as a tragic incident.
Willie Hawkes had recently retired from his job as a milk recorder with Munster Bovine.
Geraldine Hawkes previously worked as a midwife at the Bon Secours Hospital in Cork city. She had a talent for sewing and taught classes locally in her retirement. The pair were very well known and liked locally.
Local Social Democrats councillor Ann Bambury posted on social media that the loss of the couple was “heartbreaking”. She said they were a community “in mourning”.
“My thoughts and prayers are with their extended family, neighbours and friends as they face this incredibly difficult time.”
Funeral arrangements for the couple are being finalised.

title: Mark Allen reveals he made snooker return after 10-week stay in mental health clinic
description: Former world number one vows to show ‘fighting qualities’
content:
Mark Allen has revealed he spent 10 weeks in a mental health clinic before discharging himself to play in this week’s Northern Ireland Open.
In a statement posted on X, the 40-year-old said he was “not OK” but vowed to show his renowned “fighting qualities” as he continues his recovery.
Allen’s 4-2 defeat against his friend and compatriot Jordan Brown on Tuesday was his first match since he lost the World Championship semi-final to Wu Yize in April, when he missed a black off its spot that would have given him the win.
After losing to Brown, Allen conducted an emotional interview with TNT Sports in which he said he was “really overwhelmed”, and suggested his career could be over. He wrote on Wednesday: “Everything I said in that interview was true. However, rest assured I’m doing my best to turn things round.
“I have been in a mental health clinic for the last 10 weeks, finally discharging so I could attempt to play in Belfast. I owed that to my family, in particular my daughter to see me play for what could be the last time ... I also owed it to the fans who have supported me throughout my 21 years on tour.
“I also owed that to World Snooker who have been amazing from day one in all this, in particular [chief executive] Simon Brownell and [WPBSA Players chief operating officer] Neil Tomkins who have remained in touch regularly, even Simon paying me a visit in the clinic itself.
“I’m not OK, but I’m OK in that itself. I’ve been much worse in the last few months than you saw yesterday. I literally didn’t see a future in anything. My daughter kept me going, the therapists, staff and all the other patients were amazing and helped me through some really dark days.
“I see the light now that I couldn’t see before but I do now. I also know it won’t happen overnight. I’m a work in progress. My fight and determination on the table has always been there for ones to see. I need to show those same fighting qualities off it now for a while.
“Please don’t detract anything from Jordan yesterday, he’s been aware of my struggles and that can’t have been easy to play in but he handled it with grace and skill as I knew he would. I’m proud to call him a friend.
“I hope the rest of the event is a success and I will continue my treatments going forward and then see what’s ahead.”
Since his defeat against Wu, Allen has stayed away from the tour for unspecified personal reasons that are understood not to relate to any repercussions from the manner of his defeat at the Crucible.
Allen has won both UK and Masters titles in 12 ranking tournament wins, and has reached the world championship semi-finals three times. He was ranked world number one for four months in 2024.

title: ‘For the first time we feel we’re being listened to’: New children’s hospice in Castlebar gets go-ahead
description: Following long campaign, planning permission granted for Sunflower Children’s Hospice, due to open in 2029
content:
A children’s hospice may conjure up sad images but confirmation that the first such facility is to be built outside Dublin is being celebrated as a “beacon of hope”.
Planning permission was granted this week for Sunflower Children’s Hospice, due to open in Castlebar , Co Mayo in 2029.
“When we got the news, we were incredibly emotional. It’s like a weight has been lifted off of us, that this is finally becoming a reality,” said Linda Cox, from Lisacul, Co Roscommon, whose son Daire (12) needs round-the-clock care.
She and her husband, Brendan, have two other sons, Aaron (17), and Cathal (15).
Daire, who is non-verbal, starting having seizures when he was just two months old. His mother described him as a very happy boy who “adores” his older brothers but she explains that the six-hour round trip to Co Dublin places a big strain on her family.
“Daire is not a great traveller and he finds the journey to Dublin extremely difficult. It can take him that day and the next day to recover.
“This news has brought a huge sense of relief to us. It’s not even the miles on the road, it’s time and time is precious. It give us more time with him, and gives his brothers more time with him.”
Mayo Roscommon Hospice Foundation is behind the construction of Sunflower Children’s Hospice. The plans were unveiled in November 2025 and €9 million has been raised through community and corporate fundraising, donor support and local initiatives. The final cost of the development is €20 million.
Parents were consulted on the new hospice plans, and Linda Cox is full of praise for Mayo Roscommon Hospice chief executive Martina Jennings and her colleagues.
“For the first time we feel like we’re being listened to ... we feel less alone.”
She says the option to stay with Daire, which will also be available to his siblings, is “such a relief”.
“If we want to come home we can – we’re only 45 minutes away from Castlebar. If they need us, or Daire needs us, when we drop him up to Laura Lynn [Dublin children’s hospice], we’re three hours away.”
Cox says: “When people think of a hospice they think of end of life ... but it’s more than that – it’s the care and support you receive there.”
Jennings says she promised a woman who lost her son at the age of nine that she “wouldn’t forget the children” when the Mayo Roscommon Hospice Foundation was started.
“They lived in Ballina and they used the hospice in Dublin, but they had two other children. While the hospice was great, it was a six-hour round trip. By the time they got there, they were exhausted.
“I made a promise to her that I wouldn’t forget.”
Jennings hopes Sunflower Children’s Hospice will be a “beacon of hope” for families with sick children in the West of Ireland.
It is the first new facility of its kind to be developed in 15 years.
She says siblings will also be at the centre of what the facility hopes to achieve.
“When people say to me about a children’s hospice, ‘that’s so sad,’ I think the sad thing is that we don’t have one yet in the west of Ireland,” she says.
“It gives families time, memories and it creates moments of joy for them.
“When we did the research, one thing that stood out was siblings really suffer too. In this building children will get all the therapies they need, while the families are also minded.”

title: Majority of intercounty players support Friday night fixtures
description: GPA’s annual members survey reveals 63 per cent are willing to play on Fridays under the right circumstances
content:
Over 60 per cent of male intercounty players are supportive of Friday night games if certain conditions were to be put in place.
It is one of the standout findings from the Gaelic Players Association’s Annual Member Survey, while includes responses from 3,555 intercounty players across the four Gaelic codes.
The debate around Friday night intercounty games has been ongoing for several years, with one of the stumbling blocks being concerns over the impact such matches would have on the working lives of amateur players.
Laois and Carlow played on a Friday in the 2013 Leinster football championship, but the subsequent blowback dimmed the idea of such fixtures becoming more widespread.
However, under the right circumstances, intercounty players have now for the first time collectively indicated they would be open to Friday night fixtures.
Some 46 per cent of respondents to the GPA survey said they would be supportive “if players are compensated for time off work”. A further 17 per cent supported the idea, but only on the basis that the matches would be “local derbies, and if players are not required to take time off work”.
Collectively it amounts to 63 per cent of intercounty players declaring a willingness to play on Fridays. A separate 24 per cent said they would be “very supportive in all instances” without caveats. Only 11 per cent of respondents indicated they were “not supportive in any instance”.
Many now counties stage club games on Friday nights but the further distances and extra pre-match preparation involved in intercounty games bring logistical challenges.
However, GPA chief executive Tom Parsons said they would not stand in the way of Friday night games, so long as players are not left with financial implications.
“Players won’t be the blockers if the conditions are right, but it needs really good consultation,” said Parsons. “If there’s a blanket kind of, ‘this is an amateur game, suck it up and play a Friday night match,’ it just won’t be tolerated.
“But it should not be put on players, or certainly their representative body, that we are the resistance to a Friday night game. Sit down, let’s design it, let’s make sure players are protected and aren’t out of pocket.”
Parsons feels it is possible for a workable model to be put in place to facilitate Friday night games, although Croke Park officials must negotiate such an agreement.
“If a player gets injured, the GAA will fund a loss of wages, there is a fund there for loss of wages,” the former Mayo footballer added. “There’s already something there that triggers the reimbursement of a day off work, and it’s an injury. So a Friday night game is a different trigger, but it triggers the need that a person can’t work.
“Let’s say Mayo are playing Roscommon, and we have a few lads that are living and working in Dublin. Leaving Dublin at 12 or one on a Friday is like leaving at five o’clock – the traffic to get out of Dublin is insane. To drive down to play a game, is that fair? No, the player has to take the day off work.
“With a derby game, again if you have Mayo v Roscommon, you have Ryan O’Donoghue coming from Belmullet on a Friday, the day’s gone.”
And it is not just financial renumeration Parsons believes players would look for assurances on, but also the value of their time so that perhaps the rest of the weekend would be left free.
“It’s how it’s looked at and framed. There needs to be a mature conversation about it, a modern form of amateurism that players can be reimbursed.
“There could be a lot of benefits to it but then you need to consult players. What does the cadence of their week look like?
“Would we get a guarantee or a policy that if you play a Friday night game, the rest of the weekend is off? Because if you play a Friday night game and then it’s a case of, ‘let’s use this as an opportunity for a camp all weekend,’ That’s what could happen.”
Among the other findings in the report is that 85 per cent of players are in favour of sharing their data with a centralised database for the purposes of supporting workload, welfare and injury risk.
A total of 74 per cent of respondents reported an injury in 2026 and 49 per cent had two weeks or less rest between the end of the club season and start of their intercounty campaigns.
There is also no major appetite for further football changes, with 76 per cent players in the men’s game wanting no more tinkering with rules, while 23.5 per cent said they would be open only to small tweaks.

title: ‘For four seconds I was a millionaire’: Man charged after accepting controlled delivery of cocaine
description: When asked whether he wished to apply for bail while representing himself, defendant says ‘I’ll give it a bash’
content:
A 36-year-old Dubliner claiming he had €65 to his name told a court he was a “millionaire for four seconds” when gardaí carried out a controlled delivery of cocaine worth €1.5 million at his home.
David Wheelock, of Kevin Barry House, Coleraine Street, Dublin 7, was arrested after accepting a package at his home on Tuesday and charged with possessing drugs for sale or supply.
He appeared before Judge Michele Finan at Dublin District Court on Wednesday, who remanded him in custody with consent to bail in his own bond of €200 with a €10,000 independent surety to be approved.
Solicitors have withdrawn their services in response to legal aid payment reforms introduced in July, resulting in widespread disruption to the criminal justice system. Wheelock was therefore unrepresented in court, but when asked whether he still wished to apply for bail against Garda objections, he told Finan: “I’ll give it a bash.”
He maintained that the package was sent to his home and had his name on it, but that he was innocent, adding, “And I want to get to the bottom of this. Someone has done this to our home”.
The judge cautioned the accused against self-incrimination and stressed he still enjoyed the presumption of innocence. “I am innocent,” Wheelock told the judge.
Wheelock was told he could ask for clarification on any procedural point, would have the opportunity to cross-examine, and that the hearing was solely to determine bail.
Garda Alan Kelly feared the accused would evade justice and cited the seriousness of the case.
The court heard that at 11.20am on Tuesday, gardaí entered Wheelock’s flat with a search warrant “following a controlled delivery”.
They later found the consignment, silver-coloured bricks of cocaine, with a total weight of 15kg.
Wheelock disputed the assertions that he would leave the jurisdiction, saying he had children in Ireland and could not find his passport, which he had lost.
He said he had separated from his partner and began living at his father’s flat, where he was arrested.
He said he would abide by any conditions the court imposed.
“The Garda delivered the package and handed it to me. And then five seconds later they came into the house and found the package. I have €65 in my pocket, but for four seconds I was a millionaire, apparently,” he claimed.
Pleading to be released, he spoke about how his family life would be destroyed if he were denied bail, and detailed how had already suffered injuries in a workplace fall.
Cross-examined by the garda, he agreed the one-bedroom flat was his father’s and explained he had moved there after a break-up.
When asked whether he genuinely lived there, he said gardaí could check with the neighbours, local CCTV and the corner shop, because he goes there every day.
Finan agreed that bail could be imposed with various conditions, including residing at an alternative address, signing in daily at his local Garda station, and surrendering his passport.
She also told Wheelock she was imposing a curfew.
He was in favour of this, explaining that he goes to bed at 10pm, and added: “I’m actually a very boring person.”
The curfew was set for 10pm-7am. Wheelock was remanded in custody to appear at Cloverhill District Court on October 28th, pending approval of his bail person.

title: Paul Mescal and Jessie Buckley sign letter supporting Sally Rooney after UK books withdrawn
description: Cultural figures back Irish novelist after publisher decides to stop distribution of her books in the UK due to anti-terrorism legislation
content:
Actors Paul Mescal and Jessie Buckley and musicians CMAT and Kneecap have signed an open letter supporting Irish author Sally Rooney after her publisher stopped supplying her books in the UK.
The Irish artists have joined dozens of prominent international cultural figures supporting the novelist in the letter published in British magazine the New Statesman over Rooney’s backing of a pro-Palestinian action group.
The signatories – who also include Irish authors Colm Tóibín, Anne Enright and Anna Burns, and actor Sharon Horgan – condemn the withdrawal of Rooney’s books from sale in the UK “on the basis of ill-conceived and draconian anti-terror legislation”.
Rooney’s publisher, Faber & Faber, announced last week that, in agreement with the author, it would no longer distribute her books for sale in the UK because British anti-terrorism legislation means it cannot pass on earnings to her from her book sales.
The signatories say in the letter that the move is “an affront to basic principles of free speech and expression so long taken for granted in this country”.
“We categorically reject censorship – whether direct or indirect – and urge the government to change course, amending the legislation which has led us to this point of repressive absurdity.”
The letter is signed by Daisy Edgar-Jones, Mescal’s costar in the BBC adaptation of Rooney’s Normal People, and Lenny Abrahamson, the director of the drama miniseries.
“Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist,” the open letter starts.
“Her books must be available to the public.”
[ Sales of Sally Rooney books surge in Northern Ireland after publisher stops UK distribution Opens in new window ]
International figures who have signed the letter include Nobel Prize in Literature winners Anne Carson, JM Coetzee and Annie Ernaux, along with authors Arundhati Roy and Ben Lerner.
Other signatories include Booker Prize winners Bernardine Evaristo and George Saunders, Jeanette Winterson, Irvine Welsh, Zadie Smith, William Boyd, William Dalrymple and Naomi Klein and former footballer and presenter Gary Lineker.
The letter is also signed by Mark O’Connell and Seamas O’Reilly , who both write columns for The Irish Times.
Rooney’s Normal People has sold more than one million copies in the UK alone, while her first novel, Conversations with Friends , and Beautiful World, Where Are You have each sold more than 500,000 copies.
Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian direct action group, was proscribed as a terrorist organisation by the UK government in July 2025.
[ Mark O’Connell: Sally Rooney could have made things a great deal easier for herself. She chose not to Opens in new window ]
After the group was banned, Rooney, who lives in Co Mayo, said she would use proceeds from her sales to support Palestine Action.
In August 2025, she wrote an opinion piece in The Irish Times with the headline: “I support Palestine Action. If this makes me a ‘supporter of terror’ under UK law, so be it.”

title: European shares rise on solid earnings but Carrefour slumps after French unrest
description: France’s borrowing costs rise to their highest since mid-2002, ​as widespread protests added to concerns over the country’s fragile finances
content:
European shares rose on Wednesday as a slew of solid earnings reports cheered investors. However, French supermarket chain Carrefour slumped after it issued a profit warning as it counted the cost of trading disruptions caused by unrest across the country.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 index closed 0.9 per cent higher.
Over on the bond markets , euro zone bond market interest rates – or yields – rose, led by another increase in French borrowing costs to their highest since mid-2002, ​as widespread protests added to concerns over the country’s fragile finances and political uncertainty.
A rebound in crude oil prices above $110 (€97) a barrel after a brief retreat the previous day added to pressure on bond markets.
The Iseq All-Share index rose 0.9 per cent to 14,292.67.
Kenmare , which is currently the subject of bid interest from an Abu Dhabi company, jumped 7.5 per cent to €2.86 on hopes that the group will sign a new royalties deal covering its key Moma mine in Mozambique. While local reports have cited Mozambique government officials as saying that a “definitive agreement” had been reached, after four years of talks, Kenmare said on Tuesday it was unable to confirm this.
Banking stocks were in demand, with AIB rising 2.3 per cent to €11.15 and Bank of Ireland advancing 0.7 per cent to €18.75.
Ryanair , the largest company on the Iseq by market value, advanced 0.9 per cent to €23.57. Its chief executive, Michael O’Leary, warned on Tuesday that European airfares are set to jump next year as fuel-hedging contracts, which protected the industry to varying degrees from the full brunt of a spike in oil prices in 2025, peter out.
The UK’s FTSE 100 ‌edged 0.1 per cent higher, supported by gains in oil majors and financial stocks, though hotter-than-expected ‌inflation reinforced expectations of a Bank of England interest rate hike, limiting the index’s upside. UK inflation rose to ​3.5 per cent.
Energy giants gained, with BP and Shell among the biggest boosts to the large-caps index.
Britain approved the Jackdaw North Sea gasfield, ending years of legal and political wrangling ‌as the Labour government seeks ⁠to balance its climate goals with energy security concerns.
Asset manager Aberdeen Group, among the top losers on the ‌FTSE 100, fell 4 per cent after flagging a slower-than-expected return to adviser-segment inflows.
Bicycles-to-car ​parts retailer Halfords dropped about 8.6 per cent, the steepest on ​the FTSE 250, after posting first-half results.
Carrefour dropped 13.8 per cent after the supermarket chain cut its annual earnings forecast, saying riots, looting and curfews had raised costs and disrupted trading at its stores.
The unrest in France has ⁠added to concerns about ​the country’s weakening public finances and slowing growth.
French tire maker Michelin reversed 7.2 per cent after reporting a drop in nine-month sales.
Randstad jumped 20.2 per cent after the Dutch recruitment firm reported organic revenue growth of 3.9 per cent for the third quarter, beating analysts’ estimates.
DSV gained 15.1 per cent after the Danish transport and logistics firm reported a rise in ‌its third-quarter revenue.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq led US stock indices higher in early afternoon trading after quarterly results from SpaceX and Super Micro Computer ‌improved appetite for AI-linked stocks, while Netflix slipped as its forecast failed to impress investors.
Elon Musk’s rocket and space technology firm jumped after he said on ​Tuesday that a merger of SpaceX and Tesla would be “a good idea”.
Super Micro soared to the top of the S&P 500 after the AI server maker forecast quarterly revenue and profit margin above Wall Street estimates, signalling that ​AI demand remained resilient. Peers HPE and Dell also rose.
Investors drew comfort from the reports as concerns over the profitability of the AI buildout triggered a sell-off ⁠in AI-linked stocks last week, with data centre operator CoreWeave at the centre of the storm.
AT&T fell despite beating third-quarter revenue and profit estimates.
Abbott Laboratories declined after the medical device maker cut its 2026 sales ​growth forecast. – Additional reporting: Reuters

title: Family of IRA victim Brian Stack get State apology for flawed Garda inquiry but still seek ‘full truth’
description: ‘It hurts every time you see Sinn Féin representatives at a memorial for IRA men,’ says prison officer’s son
content:
There was a quiet and sombre atmosphere in the Dáil chamber as the Taoiseach formally apologised on behalf of the State to the family of Brian Stack over the flawed investigation into his murder by the IRA .
Micheál Martin said Stack and his family were “badly failed by the investigation into his killing”.
Just 49 years old when he died, the senior prison officer was shot in the neck in March 1983 as he left the National Stadium in Dublin after a boxing tournament. He had been approached from behind by a man in a balaclava.
“Brian survived the shooting but was left paralysed and brain damaged, and, after fighting on bravely for 18 months, he succumbed to his injuries on September 29th, 1984,” the Taoiseach said.
The father of a young family, he served the State “with great distinction”.
His wife Sheila and sons Austin, Kieran and Oliver, who pressed for the apology, sat in the visitors gallery as the Taoiseach spoke.
The apology was offered for the shortcomings of three Garda investigations following the IRA shooting.
Martin said “those who shot him, transported the killer and covered for them in the intervening decades” were the parties “responsible” for the killing. But Stack and his family were “badly failed” by the subsequent Garda investigations.
He was a man providing a “hugely important service” as chief prison officer at Portlaoise Prison, at a time of “great peril for the State”.
The family “campaigned tirelessly” to “uncover the truth of what happened” to Stack, and to keep his memory and legacy alive, Martin said.
An Garda Síochána “continues to pursue live lines of inquiry in the case and is making every effort to bring those responsible to justice”. But he said: “Unforgivably, we still don’t have the full truth of, or any justice for, what happened that day”, a “very dark day in our country’s history”.
He highlighted investigation failings, including a failure to keep a map of the crime scene and a motorbike helmet found nearby, or to keep custody of materials gathered during the investigation.
Other failures included not interviewing prisoners, prison officers in Portlaoise Prison, or Stack’s family and friends.
Gardaí also failed to identify a link to the IRA “until this was admitted to Austin and Oliver Stack by a former IRA commander in 2013 through their own family efforts to uncover the truth”.
Addressing the family, he thanked them and paid tribute to their dedicated campaign for their father. “I share your hope that justice may still come.”
In a personal statement to the Dáil in 2016, Sinn Féin ’s then leader Gerry Adams said the shooting of Stack was wrong but he had “no information” on who carried out the killing.
Labour leader Ivana Bacik recalled that contribution on Wednesday, saying: “It’s very rare for the Dáil to give a member time for a personal statement, and it’s the Labour Party’s view that Gerry Adams wasted that opportunity in failing to provide the Stack family with substantive answers in that statement.”
She said: “As we all know, there are people – there must be people – who know who Brian Stack’s killer or killers were or are.
“Indeed, it’s been alleged that former members of this House either knew who the killer was, or indeed possessed information that would have been material to an investigation into the killing.”
Sinn Féin was represented in the chamber by the party’s Dáil leader Pearse Doherty , who welcomed the State apology on Sinn Féin’s behalf and offered his “sincere sympathies” to the family.
He was standing in for party leader Mary Lou McDonald , who was in Belfast being interviewed by the PSNI over her attendance at a demonstration against the Orange Order march on Garvaghy Road in Portadown.
Doherty said the “hurt caused by republican actions must be acknowledged, and that suffering cannot be disowned”.
“The shooting of Brian Stack was wrong; it should never have happened. His family suffered a terrible loss. The failures in the investigations compounded that suffering and left them seeking answers over many decades.”
He told the Dáil: “I am sorry for all the lives lost during the period of conflict on this island, without exception.”
Other families also sought answers. “Their circumstances differ, but each deserves dignity, compassion and a fair hearing. Families should be supported in seeking [truth] and accountability without having to carry the burden of a public campaign for decades.
“People from all walks of life and every background suffered through the actions of British state forces, republicans – including the IRA – and unionist paramilitaries,” Doherty said.
Speaking on RTÉ’s Six One, Austin Stack said it was a “very emotional” day for him, his mother and his two brothers, and thanked the Taoiseach and Tánaiste “for agreeing to do the state apology”.
Stack said it was “disheartening” for the family when they found out that there were 194 errors and omissions in the original Garda investigation.
“We are hopeful that at some stage, even though the likelihood is growing less likely every day, but we are still hopeful that something will come out of the Garda investigation.
He said it was a “very emotional” day for his 82-year old mother following the State apology over the investigations into Brian Stack’s death
“At the time, she was 39 and myself, my two brothers were were quite young. We were young teenagers, and, you know, she had to bring us up our own … it was a very traumatic time in for her.”

title: Man and woman found dead at house in Bray, Co Wicklow, had lost two children in house fire
description: Bodies of Bridget O’Brien and Jamie McGinn found at residence on Old Connaught Avenue in Bray
author_name: Conor Lally, Kitty Holland, Tim O'Brien
content:
A man and woman found dead in their home in Co Wicklow lost their two children in a fire that killed four people in Dublin almost 10 years ago.
They have been named locally as Bridget ‘Biddy’ O’Brien and Jamie McGinn.
The deceased woman was also trapped in the blaze and, though she survived, she suffered life-changing injuries in the fire that claimed the lives of her young children.
The remains of Jamie McGinn (38) and Bridget O’Brien (45) were found on Wednesday morning at their home at the Cois Cairn estate on Old Connaught Avenue in north Bray .
The deceased woman, who grew up in Bray, suffered extensive burns in the fire almost a decade ago and was in intensive care for a prolonged period.
She missed the funerals of her two children and of two other family members who died in the fire. She only learned her children had died about six weeks after the incident.
She was close to the Lynch and Gilbert families in Fassaroe, Bray, who lost 10 loved ones in the fire at a Traveller site in Carrickmines, Dublin, in October 2015.
Gardaí believe violence was a factor in the events that brought about the deaths in the Bray house. They have yet to find evidence anyone else was present or that there was third-party involvement in the deaths. Sources stressed, however, the inquiry was at a very early stage.
The Irish Times understands the remains of Jamie McGinn were found outside the house, and that he had visible injuries, while Bridget O’Brien was found in an upstairs bedroom.
Sources said the results of the postmortems and the forensic examination at the house would determine how they died and would dictate the direction of the investigation. The resources of a homicide inquiry have been committed to the case.
In a statement, An Garda Síochána said the remains of the man and woman were discovered at the property just after 8am and both were pronounced dead at the scene.
“The scene has been preserved for examination by the Garda Technical Bureau. The local coroner and the Office of the State Pathologist have been notified and postmortem examinations will be arranged,” the statement added.
“A senior investigating officer has been appointed and an incident room has been established at Dún Laoghaire Garda station.
“The outcome of the postmortems will assist gardaí in determining the course of the investigation.”
The couple were said to have “lived for each other” after the deaths of their children almost a decade ago.
Members of the local Traveller community said Bridget O’Brien and her partner Jamie McGinn, were “very well liked” and “very private”.
O’Brien was the only person to survive a fire in the early hours of March 8th, 2017, in which her two children Holly (3) and Jordan McGinn (4) died. The blaze was at a facility for women moving on from domestic violence, which they had been visiting.
Her cousin, Anne-Marie O’Brien (27), her daughter Hannah-Paris (2) and her unborn son AJ also died in the fire in Clondalkin.
Jim O’Brien, a relative and co-ordinator of the Bray Travellers Community Development Group said the organisation was “devastated” by the deaths “of two very loved member of the community.
“All we say at this stage is that we send our deepest, deepest, deepest condolences to both the families. They are both well-respected families and we offer all the support we can to them”
The community had recently marked the 11th anniversary of the Carrickmines fire which killed 10 members of the Traveller community in October 2015. Two of the three families who lost loved ones in the tragedy – Lynch and Gilbert- were from Bray.
Harry Gilbert, whose daughter Tara (27) and grand-daughters Jodie (9) and Kelsey (4) died in the 2015 blaze, lives near the home of the dead couple, and knew them well.
“I would consider myself their neighbour. They were a lovely couple. I would talk to Jamie from time to time. They went through the same thing I went through, losing their two children in a fire.”
In 2018 Amanda Gilbert, Tara’s twin, died by suicide.
“They were quiet. People liked them. People are very upset,” said Gilbert of O’Brien and McGinn.
Another local who knew them but did not want to be named said the couple “were never the same after their children died.
“They were very close, very close to each other. They lived for each other after their children died.”
Jamie McGinn had developed a drug habit, which a court was told was a result of the trauma he had endured after losing his children.
He was later pressured by a drug gang, after he ran up a drug debt, to store drugs at his home. When it was raided three years ago, cocaine and cannabis valued at almost €200,000 were discovered.
He was arrested and made admissions, telling gardaí he took responsibility for the drugs, which he said he had agreed to store to reduce a debt of several thousand euro.
When that case reached the court the judge was told the defendant had turned to drugs, developing a cocaine habit after the deaths of his children, but he had been clean for almost a year by the time of his sentencing hearing.
Although a 4½-year sentence was imposed, the final three years were suspended due to the exceptional background and circumstances of his life.
The judge was told that, but for a very small number of minor convictions, the man was a law-abiding citizen before getting drawn into drugs after the deaths of his children had a profound impact on him.
Residents of the Cois Cairn housing estate were reluctant to speak on Wednesday morning as gardaí erected a blue scene tent and screen in front of one of the semidetached bungalows.
Numerous gardaí were in attendance. Some neighbours stood in their doorways or in small groups outside their houses.
At about 12.30pm members of the Garda technical team arrived at the scene, followed by members of the Garda divisional crime squad.

title: ‘Mania’ for adopting AI to cut costs poses long-term risks, Ibec chief warns
description: Profits could be diverted to the tech giants
content:
Companies that rush into artificial intelligence (AI) adoption with the primary intention of cutting labour costs are at risk of simply diverting any additional profits they generate to the tech giants, business group Ibec chief executive Danny McCoy has warned.
Speaking at the organisation’s annual leadership conference at the RDS on Wednesday, McCoy said many employers currently regard AI as an opportunity while many employees view it as a threat, but both could end up losing out if adoption isn’t well planned with the potential benefits clearly identified.
“I think there’s been a bit of a mania towards AI,” he said.
“In the short term, there are instances where AI could be a negative for both the owner and the employee.
“What you certainly have is cases where employees are becoming fearful. And companies are changing the way they are doing things. But there’s a big question now about whether the investment being made in AI is about doing things better or cutting costs so as to increase profitability.
“And is that all about the short term? I’m sure in the medium term things will work out. But in the short term, are you sure that you’re not actually replacing a dependency on your employees with a dependency on AI?
[ HR bosses predict AI will not cause ‘significant reduction’ in employee numbers Opens in new window ]
“And if your motivation is to shrink your wage bill for more productivity and more profitability, well, the jury is out on both of those things. So are you sure you’re getting the productivity? And are you sure you’re going to hold on to profitability if you become dependent on AI?”
Ultimately, he suggested, there is the potential for employers to go from spending a lot of money on their employees, to replacing the employees and trying to capture the benefit from that “only to hand it on to somebody else”.
“We can replace people with AI. But this kind of thing won’t be linear, and I think there is a kind of a rollback,” McCoy said.
Asked what the solution is, he said it might be “to make hay, slowly”.
He said the power, or knowledge, imbalance between the tech giants and their corporate customers has become an issue that was undermining the proper functioning of the market and that the problems may only grow if the number of systems providers shrinks and the remaining firms are able to exert a monopolistic power over the market.
Companies who adopted AI, he suggested, could be trapped into paying greatly increased costs.
McCoy said he believes the technology will ultimately help to generate more jobs than it will displace while it will also allow the reorientation of the employment landscape so that more work of direct benefit to people may be done but, he added, it is currently causing a big issue in relation to trust, not just around employment relations but in the wider world at a time of geopolitical uncertainty, diminished trust in the US and the threat of bad actors such as Russia.
“It’s not just the trust between employers and employees. That’s all always been there. It’s actually much more fundamental than that: It’s about whether the system we are operating in is fundamentally fit for purpose.”

title: Europe’s angry autumn: what’s driving the wave of protests?
description: Demonstrations from Albania to Spain are largely unconnected, but some common frustrations run through them
content:
Y oung people are at the forefront: angry about education conditions, Gaza and the sense they are getting a raw deal.
In Spain and Portugal , the housing crisis is the main motivation. In Albania , it is opposition to a government seen as corrupt, with students at the forefront.
In Italy and France , autumn student protests have a greater sense of momentum than in previous years. This weekend in both countries a new contingent of people joined protests, apparently intent on destruction and confrontation with the police. Looting followed.
The French government has announced a massive security operation to prevent a repeat this weekend, while Rome has imposed a sweeping emergency security law, clearly concerned about a contagion effect.
In France, online calls for nationwide protest against fuel prices and the cost of living on October 17th began to go viral in September, branded as a revival of the “gilet jaune”, or yellow vest, movement.
Separately on September 17th, students at a high school in Créteil, southeast of Paris, began protesting about teacher shortages.
Protests spread to other secondary schools, with schools emptying and students marching on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Teacher unions declared their support and universities joined too, fuelled by outrage at a heavy-handed response by police. The movement had momentum.
On Saturday, October 17th, the student movement and gilet jaune call-out combined. A small hardcore group on the sidelines of the official marches set about rioting, looting and burning down buildings. Sporadic looting followed on the evening of Sunday 18th.
[ What’s behind the violence shaking France, and what comes next? Opens in new window ]
Unrest diminished as French authorities announced local curfews. All eyes are now on the next protests: the yellow vests have called for an “act two” on Saturday, October 24th, and unions have called a large protest and strike for November 5th.
In Belgium , high school students in French-speaking areas began protesting in solidarity with their peers in France from October 1st. Tens of thousands marched in protest at school conditions and austerity measures on October 9th, and a smaller protest about the cost of living on October 17th saw violent clashes with police.
In Italy, autumn protests and the occupation of high schools by students are almost a seasonal event.
In Rome it began this year with a march by tens of thousands in solidarity with Palestine on September 22nd, which saw students occupy part of La Sapienza university. A high school was occupied next.
On September 24th, the government of prime minister Giorgia Meloni passed an emergency decree limiting the percentage of students in each class who can be non-Italian citizens. Several more high schools began protesting in response.
On October 16th, students marched across Italy under the banner of “No Meloni Day”. Complaints included school conditions, funding for the defence industry, and the government’s school decree. They also expressed solidarity with their peers in France.
A string of further high schools were occupied by their students.
Social media channels “L’Italia in Piazza” and “Movimento 17 ottobre” called for protests against the cost of living in several Italian cities on Saturday, October 17th.
In some cities it was a flop. In Milan, a protest march was confronted by the police and devolved into rioting, disorder and looting, reminiscent of scenes happening simultaneously in France.
[ Italy’s Giorgia Meloni faces a challenge from the right Opens in new window ]
Italian media report that those involved in unrest were disadvantaged young people from the suburbs, a different group to the protesting students, apparently driven by footage on social media.
Further sporadic rioting, again attributed to social media posts, occurred on Sunday, October 18th.
The government announced the deployment of army troops to Milan. Clearly concerned about the possibility of contagious rioting, the Meloni government passed a sweeping emergency decree on Tuesday night.
The decree reduces the presumed age of criminal responsibility to 14, extends powers of preventive detention from the age of 16, introduces fines for the parents of minors involved in disorder, and introduces a new crime of “organised violence at public protests”.
[ Michael McDowell: France is falling to the extremes of left and right. Ireland cannot be complacent Opens in new window ]
Such emergency decrees become effective immediately in Italy, but need to be approved by parliament within 60 days or they lapse.
The “October 17 Movement” have called for protests every Saturday at 3pm. Students and grassroots movements have called a new day of protest for October 30th. Major unions have called a general strike for November 20th.
Spain saw widespread protests about the housing crisis from September. Anger crystallised around the eviction and subsequent death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, a Madrid widow who lost her flat of 60 years after an investment firm bought it and she couldn’t afford the rent hike. Protesters set up encampments in some cities.
After failing to pass measures to ease the housing crisis through a hung parliament, prime minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election for November 29th. The centre-right conservative party is currently leading in polls.
Portugal saw connected protests about spiralling housing costs, with demonstrators setting up encampments in Lisbon and Porto.
Albania saw initial protests in May against the planned development of an ecologically protected island overseen by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son in law. The government of prime minister Edi Rama was accused of cronyism.
Fresh protests co-ordinated over social media broke out on October 13th, with high school students and university students at the forefront.
Their demands focus on high tuition costs and poor conditions on campuses, but the protests are also about broad dissatisfaction with the government, economic stasis and alleged corruption. The last week has seen fierce clashes between police and protesters demanding Rama’s resignation.

title: Pretax profits at yoghurt maker Glenilen Farm rise 56% to €1.6m
description: Sales increase by 25% to a record €15.8m in 2025
content:
Pretax profits at yoghurt-maker Glenilen Farm last year increased by 56 per cent to €1.65 million on the back of record revenues.
Accounts filed by the family-run Glenilen Farm Ltd, based in west Cork, show that profits rose as sales increased by 25 per cent to a record €15.8 million in 2025.
The business started in 1997 with Alan Kingston on the farm and Valerie Kingston in the kitchen, producing and selling products at local markets in Cork.
At the end of December last, accumulated profits had climbed to €4.62 million. In 2025, numbers employed at the firm increased from 73 to 84.
The firm’s post-tax profits of €1.45 million for 2025 follow post-tax profits of €930,826 in 2024.
Cash funds last year increased from €202,442 to €347,071.
Net assets at the company last year rose from €3.43 million to €4.88 million.
Alan Kingston said on Wednesday that growth in 2025 “was driven by strong consumer demand across Glenilen Farm’s core product ranges, continued innovation and expanding domestic and export sales”.
The firm has also expanded its presence in export markets including the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Macau and Singapore, with the total export market accounting for 9 per cent of turnover in 2025.
Kingston said “while we’re very pleased with our 2025 results, and the continued strong performance of the business in 2026, it has not been without its challenges, as rising input costs are having an impact on every business”.
He said “our focus remains firmly on the opportunity ahead. More than half of the yoghurt consumed in Ireland is still imported, which means there remains significant potential for Irish producers like Glenilen Farm to win a greater share of the domestic market.
“As consumers become more conscious about where their food comes from, we believe there is a real opportunity for Irish-made dairy products to continue gaining ground.”
On the rise in profits last year, he said the increase in profitability in 2025 was the result of a long-term growth strategy rather than short-term market conditions or cost-cutting measures.
“Over recent years, Glenilen Farm has reinvested profits back into the business, with significant investment in factory expansion, automation, innovation and operational efficiencies,” he said.
The profits last year take account of net non-cash depreciation costs of €553,514.
Directors’ pay, including pension payments, last year increased from €166,229 to €180,296.

title: Man who punched Brendan Courtney has completed anger management course, court told
description: Ross Deegan (22) pleaded guilty to assaulting Courtney, causing harm, in February 2025 at Usher’s Quay, Dublin
content:
The hearing of a man who punched broadcaster Brendan Courtney several times has been adjourned to allow his suitability for community service to be assessed.
Ross Deegan (22) of An Riasc, Finglas, Dublin 11 , pleaded guilty to assaulting Courtney, causing harm, on February 27th, 2025, at Usher’s Quay in Dublin city centre.
Dublin Circuit Criminal Court previously heard that Courtney was walking home around 9.30pm on February 27th, 2025, when he was beckoned over to a car stopped at traffic lights.
The court heard the front passenger appeared to roll down the window and call him over. Courtney went over thinking he knew the occupants of the car and later described to gardaí that he believed they were ridiculing him. He turned to leave, tapping on the window as he went.
Deegan, who was a back seat passenger, left the vehicle, then assaulted Courtney along with a co-accused, who is also before the courts.
Courtney went to hospital the following day after waking up in pain. He sustained a concussion and a fracture of his eye socket.
After hearing the facts of the case in March, Judge Martina Baxter directed the preparation of a probation report and remanded Deegan on continuing bail.
The case was then adjourned to the next date in July as it was affected by ongoing action by solicitors in relation to the criminal legal aid scheme.
On Wednesday, Oisin Clarke, defending, confirmed the case could go ahead. He said Deegan had completed an anger management course. He said his client is assessed at low risk of reoffending.
[ Driver had ‘no time to react’ to e-biker (24) that died in N11 crash, inquest told Opens in new window ]
The court heard the injured party does not wish to accept €1,500 previously brought to court by Deegan, and Judge Baxter directed it should go to the Mater hospital, as he suggested.
Judge Baxter considered the probation reports that were before the court and said she would adjourn the case one final time to allow Deegan’s suitability for community service to be assessed.
She adjourned the case to December 9th, 2026, for finalisation.
During a previous sentence hearing in March, CCTV of the assault was played to the court. Deegan ran at the injured party, then punched him. He threw two further punches to the side of the injured party’s head.
He voluntarily contacted gardaí on March 5th, 2025, identifying his involvement in the assault. He came forward from the District Court on a signed guilty plea.
A cyclist stopped and helped Courtney, who went into a nearby pub. Nothing was said by the men during the incident, and there was no suggestion the parties are known to each other, the court heard.
[ Female student doctor attending exams in Dublin city centre punched in unprovoked attack Opens in new window ]
When interviewed by gardaí, Deegan claimed it was self-defence. He said that the injured party approached the car aggressively and struck the front passenger window with his fist.
Deegan said he perceived this as an attempt to hit his brother, who was in the front seat.
No victim impact statement was provided to the court.
Garda Shane Monahan agreed with Clarke that the cyclist said in a statement that there had been a knock on the front passenger window.
Clarke said this is an “utterly bizarre offence”, which does not really have an explanation.
Referring to the statement from the cyclist, Clarke said the catalyst appeared to be a “bang of some description on the window” and that Deegan took umbrage. But he added that this was not an excuse for what happened and asked the court to take into account his client’s guilty plea, co-operation and youth at the time.
Two letters of apology, including one written to Courtney, and letters of reference from family members were handed to the court.
Clarke said his client was supportive of his two sisters, who are gay. He noted that his client is adamant that he did not know who the injured party was.
Judge Baxter said the court had concerns as Deegan behaved in “such a reprehensible fashion” on the night and has not come to other negative attention before or since.
She also directed that the €1,500 gesture of remorse should be given to gardaí for transmission to the Mater hospital.

title: Jamie Benson included as Andy Farrell names Ireland squad for Nations Championship
description: Cormac Izuchukwu and Harry Byrne miss out as Andy Farrell names squad for matches against Argentina, Fiji and South Africa
content:
Hookers: Sheehan (capt), Kelleher, Stewart
Props: Porter, O’Toole, Bohan, Furlong, Clarkson, Illo
Backrow: Baird, Cian Prendergast, Van der Flier, Jansen, Timoney, McNabney
Outhalves: Sam Prendergast, Frawley, Benson
Centres: Aki, Henshaw, McCloskey, Ringrose
Outside backs: Hansen, Jimmy O’Brien, Tommy O’Brien, Baloucoune, Stockdale, Keenan, Osborne
There are no real hard luck stories among the 17 backs chosen in this squad, which also has a very familiar look to it save for the uncapped Benson.
Despite Fintan Gunne’s growth this season at Leinster, Matt Devine’s positive impact since joining Ulster and the resurgence at Caolin Blade and Colm O’Reilly at Connacht, they haven’t done enough to force their win into the senior squad and must hope opportunity knocks for them in the ‘A’ game against Fiji ‘A’ in Cork on Friday, November 20th.
At outhalf, Joey Carbery’s delayed return to Leinster colours until last week’s cameo in Clermont also means he has ground to make up, and though this window is now a big opportunity for Benson, his selection also demonstrates that there is still an opening there.
The midfield quartet of Thirtysomethings has a distinctly tried and tested look to it but the four of them are also there on merit and have looked in good nick, not least the 36-year-old Bundee Aki. It would be absolutely no surprise if, barring injury, the four of them are not at the World Cup in a year’s time.
Similarly, the seven outside backs picked themselves, and despite the departure of James Lowe to Japan, this area also has a competitive and healthy (touch wood) look to it. Long may it last.
As ever in these squads, where there are winners, there also have to be losers. This is all the more so given Andrew Porter, Ryan Baird and Mack Hansen are all returning to the Irish squad after protracted absences and having last played Test rugby in the concluding November Test of last year against South Africa.
Porter’s return has resulted in Jeremy Loughman missing out on the squad altogether despite having started three of Ireland’s games in last season’s Six Nations against France, Italy and England, as well as playing as a replacement last summer against Australia and New Zealand.
This is, of course, also testimony to the way the 20-year-old Billy Bohan has grasped his chance with Connacht and Ireland, having made his Test debut against Japan last July.
Similarly, with Sam Illo retained, there is again no place for his provincial team-mate Finlay Bealham.
In light of Baird’s return, the most notable casualty from last summer’s squad for the southern hemisphere leg of the Nations Championship is Cormac Izuchukwu, who made his Ireland debut in the Six Nations against Italy and played against Japan in July. But whereas McNabney makes the cut, Izuckukwu misses out, as does Tom Ahern and Edwin Edogbo, who has yet to feature for Munster this season due to injury.
With injuries having forced their hands to some extent, Andy Farrell and his assistant coaches have picked a 36-man squad along largely anticipated lines.
In particular, the loss of Jack Conan to a shoulder injury sustained in the act of scoring a superb try for Leinster against Clermont last Saturday compounded the absence of Caelan Doris, as well as Bryn Ward, opened the door and through it has stepped James McNabney.
Similarly at outhalf, injuries to Jack Crowley and Harry Byrne, which has restricted him to just 30 minutes rugby this season also opened the door at outhalf. Through this door has stepped Ulster’s new Irish-qualified ex-England Under-18s and Under-20s outhalf Jamie Benson.
Farrell and co like McNabney’s size and physicality. Capped 14 times at Under-20s level in the Irish Grand Slam-winning sides of 2022 and 2023, his breakthrough into the Irish senior squad would probably have come sooner but for an ACL injury after being picked in the Irish squad for the 2025 summer tour and which sidelined him for all of last season.
Benson is a skilful, highly versatile player who has had played plenty of games for Harlequins at fullback and, as in his first three games for Ulster, in midfield, but two-thirds of his starts have been at outhalf, where he played in last Saturday’s Challenge Cup win away to Zebre.
The IRFU press release reports that several players were not considered due to injury, including Jack Boyle, Jack Conan, Jack Crowley, Caelan Doris, Iain Henderson, Paddy McCarthy, Calvin Nash and Bryn Ward.

Props: Porter, O’Toole, Bohan, Furlong, Clarkson, Illo

Dan Sheehan captains the side as Mack Hansen, Ryan Baird and Andrew Porter return. Jamie Benson and James McNabney are two uncapped players selected for the first time.
Six players from the summer tour aren’t included – Jack Conan, Jeremy Loughman, Cormac Izuchukwu, Bryn Ward, Zac Ward and Harry Byrne.

If you’re looking for more rugby chatter, join our Irish Times Rugby WhatsApp community and get our best rugby writing sent directly to your messages inbox.
From Gerry Thornley : Despite James Lowe’s departure to Japan, Hansen’s return makes the stock of outside backs look relatively healthy. Tommy O’Brien is also back after being withdrawn from the summer expedition due to the hamstring injury he picked up in Leinster’s URC final win over the Bulls.
Jimmy O’Brien has carried on his end-of-season form with Leinster which earned him a starting place in all three summer Tests, while Jacob Stockdale and Robert Baloucoune are also in good form for Ulster, as is Hugo Keenan with Leinster.
The official squad announcement is expected about 3pm.
Some Ireland XV news from John O’Sullivan :
The IRFU has confirmed that an Ireland XV will take on Fiji ‘A’ at Virgin Media Park on Friday, November 20th (7.45pm) in a double-header along with the Ireland Under-20 taking on their Scotland counterparts (5pm). It is the first of three outings for the Ireland XV this season.
The Ireland XV will be coached by Mark Sexton (Ulster) who will be assisted by Jimmy Duffy (Munster), Jared Payne (Munster) and IRFU performance pathway scrum coach, Seamus Toomey. The game takes place the night before Ireland’s Nations Championship clash with South Africa at the Aviva Stadium.
The fixture will form part of an important series of matches throughout the upcoming campaign for Ireland XV, with a renewed focus on developing emerging talent and providing players of national interest with valuable match minutes in green and exposure to a national team environment.
[ Ireland XV will take on Fiji ‘A’ in double-header with Ireland under-20s in November Opens in new window ]
From Gerry Thornley : Sam Prendergast’s form and Ciarán Frawley’s impressive start to life at Connacht is timely in the absence of Jack Crowley, but there could be surprise third choice at outhalf given Harry Byrne has only played 30 minutes of rugby this season due to a recent concussion, while Joey Carbery only returned from a lengthy absence last Saturday.
Jamie Benson is a product of the Harlequins academy and has played for the England Under-18s and Under-20s, but is Irish-qualified through his mother, who grew up in Belfast. The 24-year-old is highly versatile, having played at outhalf, centre and fullback for ‘Quins, with two-thirds of his starts coming at 10. After three games in the Ulster midfield following his summer move, he made his first start at outhalf in last week’s win away to Zebre. He looks a real dark horse for inclusion.
[ Ireland boosted by return of Porter, Baird and Hansen for Nations Championship Opens in new window ]
Ireland head coach Andy Farrell will name his squad to face Argentina, Fiji and South Africa in the Nations Championship on Wednesday afternoon, expected about 3pm. Captain Caelan Doris will miss the series with a foot injury, but Andrew Porter, Ryan Baird and Mack Hansen are expected to be back after significant injuries themselves.
