Ireland will play three games at the Aviva, against Argentina (November 6th), Fiji (November 14th) and South Africa (November 21st), before a concluding playoff at Twickenham on the last weekend of the month.

title: Driver had ‘no time to react’ to e-biker (24) that died in N11 crash, inquest told
description: Sam Elliot died 12 days after being struck by a car while crossing the N11 on a red light
content:
A driver who hit a 24-year-old e-bike rider crossing a Dublin road on a red light had “no time to react”, an inquest into his death heard on Thursday.
Sam Elliot (24) of Foxrock Close, Deansgrange, Co Dublin, was dressed in dark clothing on a black e-bike without a light or helmet when he was hit by a car while crossing the N11 road at Cabinteely shortly before 5pm on November 14th, 2024, the court heard.
Elliot died 12 days after the crash in the intensive care unit of Beaumont Hospital on November 26th 2024 due to severe head injuries consistent with the incident.
Coroner Dr Myra Cullinane of Dublin District Coroner’s Court ruled Elliot’s death a misadventure, an “accident, with a risk” caused when he “proceeded on a red light”.
Garda forensic crash investigator Gerard Dowd concluded that Elliot had crossed the N11 on a red light and was struck by a white Toyota Yaris which had entered the junction on a green light at a legal speed for that stretch of the road, 63km/h.
The driver of the car “started to brake shortly before the impact,” Dowd told the court.
No criminal charges were brought by the Director of Public Prosecutions against the driver of the Toyota, a decision which was subject to an unsuccessful judicial review by the Elliot family.
Daniel Hayes, a friend of the deceased, said he and Elliot were cycling to a local Chinese restaurant on the Cabinteely village side of the N11 dual carriageway.
To cross the busy road, Hayes made the decision to cycle his mountain bike up and over the roadway on the Cabinteely Footbridge, whereas Elliot opted to traverse through the junction itself.
“See you on the other side,” Hayes said to his friend, who he recalled replied, “Yeah.”
While cycling over the footbridge, Hayes heard an impact noise and looked down to see Elliot’s “skidding and sparking”. He called another member of the Elliot family while passersby, who rushed to the aid of the injured cyclist, alerted emergency services.
The 24-year-old received treatment from paramedics at the scene before being brought to Beaumont in “critical condition”, one Garda at the scene said.
Dublin District Coroner’s Court heard that Elliot cycled across the road, “with his head down” when a green arrow activated for a slip road on Johnstown Road. It was said he may have misinterpreted the light.
One witness to the crash said she remembered thinking “Why is he trying to cross there?” at the time of the crash, before seeing his electrical bicycle “flying up in the air” and the cyclist being “projected” through the junction before landing on his head.
Another witness recalled that Elliot received medical treatment from passersby while they waited for an ambulance to arrive, with the cyclist having received serious injuries to his head.
The driver of the white car said she had “no time to react” and braked “as soon as I saw him”.
Her vision of the e-cyclist was obscured by the cars in the right-turn lane, but she was travelling within the 80km/h speed limit towards a junction at which the lights were “fully green”.
Cullinane issued her “very deepest condolences” to the family who lost their son and brother in an “instant”.

title: Lions lock Hyron Andrews died from aortic dissection, autopsy finds
description: South African was found ​unconscious in team hotel on Friday ahead of Champions Cup opener
content:
Lions lock Hyron Andrews died due to an aortic dissection, a tear in the body’s main artery, the club have confirmed.
Andrews died at the team hotel last Friday, a day before the ​Lions were due to play La Rochelle in the Champions Cup at Stade Marcel Deflandre. The game went ahead on Saturday evening in honour of the 31-year-old.
French media reported that Andrews was found ​unconscious in a shower cubicle at a hotel on the Île de Ré, ⁠where the team had been staying.
“Lions Rugby Company, on behalf of ‌the ‌Andrews ​family, confirms that, following an autopsy report, Hyron’s death was found to be caused by an aortic ⁠dissection. This dissection most likely ​occurred on an aortic aneurysm,” the club said ​in a statement.
“The French authorities, who conducted the autopsy and in whose care Hyron’s body currently remains, described the cause of death as ‘a tear in the aorta (due to natural causes), which led to a significant accumulation of blood within the sac surrounding the heart’.
“The Andrews family asks for respect, ‌privacy and patience during ⁠this difficult time as the repatriation process begins,” the statement added.
Andrews played for South Africa’s under-20 side and had a spell with ‌the Sale Sharks.
“A timeline for the return of Hyron’s body to South Africa ​has not yet been determined,” the Lions added. “Further ​information will be communicated when it becomes available and under the guidance of the family.”

title: Female student doctor attending exams in Dublin city centre punched in unprovoked attack
description: Woman says assault ‘particularly devastating’ as she had come to Ireland having fled Sudan, where she was ‘targeted as a doctor and a woman’
content:
A student doctor attending exams in Dublin city centre was punched in an unprovoked attack with “troubling racial aspects” by a grandmother with more than 300 convictions, Dublin Circuit Criminal Court has heard.
Jackie McElhatton (51) assaulted the young woman on the afternoon of January 28th, 2025, at Marlborough Street, Dublin 1.
She approached the young woman, shouting at her, and asking her where she was from.
The victim, who is in her 20s, turned to answer, when McElhatton punched her on the forehead while wearing a ring. The injured party sustained swelling to her forehead and a small scratch.
Her friend recorded McElhatton, but not the assault. When gardaí viewed the video, they identified McElhatton.
In a victim impact statement read to the court by prosecuting barrister Sarah Connolly, the injured party said “the suddenness of the unprovoked assault left me deeply traumatised for a long time afterwards”.
She said the attack was “particularly devastating” given how she came to Ireland, having fled Sudan, where she had been “targeted as a doctor and a woman”.
She said she chose Ireland due to its “reputation for upholding human rights and equality”.
She said she has dedicated her life to the work of healing others and never expected to be attacked in broad daylight.
McElhatton, of Gardiner Street, Dublin 1, came forward to Dublin Circuit Criminal Court on a signed guilty plea to assault causing harm.
McElhatton has 310 previous convictions, including 27 for assault, 171 for public order offences, 42 for theft and two for robbery.
She was handed a seven-and-a-half-year sentence for robbery and a consecutive one-year sentence, also for robbery, last April. Her earliest release date is in March 2032 and she was on bail at the time of this incident.
Judge Orla Crowe said this was “a nasty attack on an utterly blameless young woman at an exam centre who had the misfortune of being approached by” McElhatton.
The judge noted that McElhatton was “unknown” to the victim and “had temerity to ask her where she was from”.
“In the view of this court, this has troubling racial aspects to it,” the judge added.
She said McElhatton had “no basis for saying what she said or doing what she did, it was entirely unlawful”.
As the judge noted that McElhatton had moved to Ireland in 2000 from the UK, McElhatton shouted out: “I’m London Irish. My family is Irish.”
Crowe imposed a two-year sentence, suspended in full, on strict conditions including two-year probation supervision. The judge directed that the suspended sentence should run from the expiry of the one-year consecutive sentence.
In her victim impact statement, the injured party said her sense of safety was shattered, and she had withdrawn socially.
She said she was “deeply embarrassed” and “struggled to find the words” to speak about what had happened.

title: Revolut’s outage was a warning to us all
description: High-profile incidents highlight Europe’s precarious position when it comes to who controls tech infrastructure
content:
T uesday was a tough day to be dependent on Revolut . Customers trying to make card payments as normal were refused. Cash withdrawals were also affected, leaving some people with no access at all to their money. If they were lucky enough to be able to log in to the app, the in-app support was unresponsive, and Revolut does not routinely offer phone support to its customers.
It was, in short, a bit of a disaster for the digital bank. Revolut was quick to reassure people that their money and data were safe, but that didn’t help those who were stranded without a way to pay for travel or buy food.
It would be easy to shrug and say that people should always have a backup. A second bank card with a different financial institution; perhaps some emergency cash just in case (did none of us read the Government’s emergency booklet?) to get us through.
There but for the grace of the tech gods go all of us. The problem wasn’t down to Revolut’s systems, or a cyberattack, but a failure at Google Cloud . The company has made a concerted push into the financial services market as it vies for business with rivals Microsoft and AWS.
It could have been any bank; this time, it just happened to be Revolut, a relative newcomer to the banking world that is still treated dismissively by some. This is despite the fact that more than 3 million people in Ireland use the digital bank’s services. A good number of those users were lured away from Ireland’s traditional banks, which have been forced to provide better digital services to customers.
And it wasn’t just Revolut that was affected. Although AIB and Bank of Ireland reported no problems with their services, in the UK, Lloyds and HSBC also suffered the effects of the outage. The UK’s courts video system was taken down too.
[ Why is motor insurance so expensive in Ireland? Opens in new window ]
The issue that Revolut’s outage raised is not that we should turn away from digital banks; it is the fact that we are overly dependent on a small number of tech systems in every facet of our daily lives. Take out one and the cascade effect is terrifying to behold.
These incidents are relatively rare, but they happen. Ironically, it was a year to the day that a big problem with AWS’s services caused apps such as Fortnite and Snapchat to go dark. That was followed only days later by a Microsoft Azure issue, an “inadvertent configuration change” that not only knocked Microsoft’s own services offline, but also affected airlines, Heathrow airport and even An Post .
They are, in a way, a victim of their own success. If Google, Microsoft , and AWS were not supporting as many of the day-to-day services we use, we wouldn’t notice if the service had a minor blip. But they do and, consequently, when things go wrong, the impact is widespread.
It is not just the infrastructure underpinning these services that is out of our hands. A French judge of the International Criminal Court (ICC), Nicolas Guillou, found that his access to many of the services we take for granted has been effectively blocked after US president Donald Trump imposed sanctions on him. Travel bookings made through Expedia have been cancelled. His bank account has been restricted, and booking flights or other transport is almost impossible for him.
Imagine if you could not access your email or cloud storage services. How many mobile numbers have you committed to memory, because you know they are stored safely on your phone? How much of your life would be affected if you could no longer use your bank card?
The sanctions, which were imposed on a number of ICC judges and block US entities and their overseas subsidiaries from providing services to him, came following investigations into alleged war crimes in Afghanistan and Palestine and the issuing of arrest warrants for Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant.
Imagine if you could not access your email or cloud storage services. How many mobile numbers have you committed to memory, because you know they are stored safely on your phone? How much of your life would be affected if you could no longer use your bank card?
More recently, the reported slowdown of Starlink’s satellite communications system in Ukraine affected the country’s ability to defend itself. Ukraine relies on the system to help intercept Russian missile and drone attacks; speed limits that were imposed last week made that a more difficult task.
According to the Wall Street Journal, that slowdown came at the order of billionaire Elon Musk . Musk appeared to point the finger at the White House, but the US has denied involvement.
Regardless of who was responsible, the end result was the same: a powerful billionaire somewhere put a thumb on the scale and ordinary people suffered the consequences.
These incidents all highlight our precarious position in Europe. Whether it is a concentration of business in a small number of tech firms or the shifting geopolitical landscape, Europe needs to get some sort of control over things.
Proposals published by the European Commission in June set a number of targets to help achieve this, from increasing data centre capacity to supporting chip production. Bureaucracy moves slowly, though, and EU bureaucracy is a particular behemoth. The targets set are still a good way off, and Europe is starting from behind.
The alternative, though, is throwing up our hands and giving up. To adapt a phrase, the best time to start developing tech sovereignty was yesterday; the second best time is now.
Europe needs alternatives, and it needs them fast.

title: Youth mental health charity sees almost 40% rise in referrals
description: Jigsaw says figures ‘paint a clear picture’ of growing pressure facing young people in Ireland
content:
Referrals to the youth mental health charity Jigsaw rose by almost 40 per cent in the first half of the year compared with the same period in 2025.
The increase was reflected across all of its 15 local services, with Dublin city recording a 74 per cent rise in referrals and Dublin south west seeing an increase of 72 per cent.
Referrals also rose by 63 per cent in Roscommon, 61 per cent in Limerick and almost 60 per cent in Tipperary.
The charity, which provides early intervention mental health services to children and young people aged 12-25, said it provided 29,004 direct clinical contacts during the first six months of the year. Total referrals increased from 5,241 to 7,270 over the period.
Joseph Duffy, chief executive of Jigsaw, said the latest figures “paint a clear picture of the increasing pressures facing young people across Ireland”.
“Early intervention is crucial when a young person is struggling with challenges like anxiety, loneliness or depression, and ensuring free, timely support is available in their local communities is more important than ever,” he said.
Jim Lyng, clinical lead with Jigsaw, said a growing awareness of the service and reduced stigma around accessing supports had driven an increase in demand.
Speaking on RTÉ Radio 1’s News at One, Lyng said there was also a deterioration in youth mental health globally, which was “more concerning”.
“We can see it in Ireland, but there’s a number of major pieces of work across a number of different countries that show us outside of everything else, youth mental health is deteriorating,” he said.
[ ‘Loneliness and isolation are among the most alarming challenges young people now face’ Opens in new window ]
“It’s of huge concern because I think in some ways you might say the health of a society is in the health of its young people.”
Lyng said there was not “one simple explanation” for the deterioration but that young people were citing worries around housing affordability, job security, climate change and global wars.
“It’s hard to ignore that these things are playing a role in the experiences and the distress that young people are telling us about,” he added.

title: Irish comedian Vittorio Angelone apologises for rape joke about content creator
description: Vittorio Angelone made remark about social media influencer Rebecca Goodwin in Have a Word podcast roast
content:
The Irish comedian Vittorio Angelone has apologised for a rape joke he made about a woman who says her sexual-assault case is being heard in court in the UK.
Rebecca Goodwin, an OnlyFans model and influencer from England, posted a video on her TikTok account earlier this week in which she cried about Angelone’s remark.
In a statement posted to his social-media accounts, Angelone said he “made a joke I shouldn’t have made and I’d like to say sorry”. He also said he had contacted Goodwin privately to apologise.
The Belfast comedian made the rape remark on one of the Have a Word podcast’s roast episodes, which invite guests to mock, tease and insult a particular person. For this programme it was his fellow comedian Freddy Quinne.
The roast was published on the podcast’s subscriber-only Patreon page in December 2025. Angelone then shared a screenshot of himself making the joke to his 498,000 followers on Instagram.
He faced a swift backlash for his joke online, and his comments were condemned by Dublin Rape Crisis Centre .
Rachel Morrogh, the centre’s chief executive, said in a statement: “For survivors, hearing rape treated as a punchline can be deeply hurtful, and it reinforces the attitudes that discourage people from coming forward.
“Reporting sexual violence and going through the courts takes enormous courage, and survivors deserve to know that the process will be treated with seriousness and respect.
“Anyone with a public platform, including performers, promoters and venues, has a responsibility to consider who is listening and the harm this kind of material can do.”
In a video Goodwin posted to TikTok addressing the joke, she said: “I am currently going through a rape trial at the minute. It is active. It is in court. I am really disappointed...
“I just can’t believe that it was not only okayed by the Have a Word pod, but it was also allowed to be aired in front of millions of people.”
Goodwin, who had appeared on a previous roast episode of the podcast, said she was not approached before the episode was released and found out about it from her followers.
Dublin Rape Crisis Centre ’s national 24-hour helpline is at 1800-778888

title: Germany accidentally hikes cigarette prices by €4 a packet overnight
description: A bureaucratic blunder has left tobacco companies wondering whether their products are legal to sell
content:
Cigarettes in Germany almost slipped from guilty pleasure to illegal contraband on Wednesday after a clerical error brought forward a duty hike planned for January 1st.
Last Friday, the Bundestag parliament approved a Bill containing higher duty on tobacco that would increase the price of a packet of 20 cigarettes by about €4 to €12-€14.
Now the federal finance ministry has admitted the new law was published “in error” on Tuesday in the federal gazette.
The publication of any law in that publication activates it the following day: Wednesday, in this case.
“A technical error occurred in the documents regarding the effective date,” acknowledged the ministry in a statement.
Alarmed tobacco companies contacted the finance ministry and state customs offices seeking guidance. They were caught off guard by the publication, and noted how the paper duty stamps and seals – at the new rate – had yet to be printed, let alone attached to their products.
Even worse: the clerical error implied that later tax increases, scheduled to come into effect by 2030, also kicked in on Wednesday – on paper at least.
[ Smokers and vapers could save more than €700 a year on life assurance if they quit Opens in new window ]
“The federal government has to act very quickly to establish legal certainty for the continuation of production,” said Jan Mücke, spokesman for the Federal Association of Tobacco Products (BVTE).
He said members were uneasy about continuing to produce and distribute its products in what he called a legal “grey zone”.
On Tuesday afternoon, the finance ministry issued statements to say that cigarettes already in stores can still be sold off at the old tax rate.
The federal finance ministry alerted the customs authorities – which administer tobacco duty – not to apply the new law until January 1st.
“Words are all well and good,” countered Mücke, “but the law now applicable says something else. Just because the finance ministry messed up, we are in an intolerable situation.”
The slip prompted much head-shaking across the influential German tobacco industry, where firms are furious that months of lobbying failed to halt the duty hike.
The changes are expected to pump an additional €12 billion into the German exchequer in the next four years.
“It is astonishing that such an absurd error could happen within a federal ministry,” said Maximilian van Ackeren, head of the German Tobacco Industry Association. “A ministry drafts a law, only to say the next day, ‘Oops, that’s not what we meant at all!’ This is the kind of amateurism that leaves me completely dumbfounded.”
[ Irish smokers buying more tobacco abroad due to ‘stark’ price differences, say retailers Opens in new window ]
Currently one in four Germans aged 15 and over smoke at least occasionally – roughly the EU average and higher than the 16 per cent of the equivalent population in Ireland who do . An estimated 130,000 Germans die of tobacco-related illness each year.

title: Consumers urged to stop using certain Aldi hairdryers due to risk of ‘electric shock or fire’
description: About 5,400 affected hair dryers were sold, the CCPC said
content:
A warning has been issued to thousands of consumers to immediately stop using a certain type of hairdryer sold by Aldi in Ireland last year.
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission ( CCPC ) said about 5,400 affected hairdryers were sold and the product presents a risk of “electric shock or fire because the power cord may become damaged over time, potentially exposing live wires or causing overheating”.
The product is certain Ambiano Ionic hairdryers sold by Aldi between August and September 2025.
Adele O’Sullivan, director of market surveillance at the CCPC, said: “Anyone who has one of these hairdryers should stop using it immediately and return it to their nearest Aldi store for a full refund.
“We urge consumers not to take any risks with their safety. Even if the hairdryer appears to be in good condition, it is important that they stop using it and return it for a refund.”
The affected products were sold in black, white, yellow and orange and can be identified by the following product codes: 4061462195075 (black), 4061462195211 (white), 4061462195310 (yellow) and 4061462195372 (orange).

title: Corporatisation of Irish GP practices raises serious concerns about primary care
description: There is an inevitable tension between delivering patient-centred care and generating returns for shareholders
content:
Sir, – The proposed €350 million acquisition of Centric Health by a US healthcare group marks another significant step towards the corporatisation of Irish general practice.
General practice has traditionally been built on continuity of care, clinical independence and the long-standing relationship between doctors, patients and their communities. These are fundamental strengths of our healthcare system, not simply commercial assets.
The increasing involvement of private equity and multinational healthcare corporations raises serious concerns about the future direction of primary care in Ireland. When healthcare becomes an investment vehicle, there is an inevitable tension between delivering patient-centred care and generating financial returns for shareholders.
While corporate investment may bring efficiencies and additional resources, we must question whether increasing market consolidation will ultimately improve accessibility, affordability and continuity of care, particularly in rural communities.
Irish general practice should be driven by the needs of patients and communities, rather than the financial expectations of international investors.
The long-term consequences of this transformation deserve far greater public debate. – Yours, etc,

title: Arab parties could be kingmakers in Israel’s election. Netanyahu has reason to worry
description: Opposition parties are discussing an alliance that could strip the prime minister of key powers even if they fail to win an outright majority
content:
T he main opposition parties in Israel , making up the anti- Netanyahu bloc, are unlikely to obtain an overall majority in next Tuesday’s election, so they have formulated a plan B: to take control of the Knesset parliament and push through key legislation after the election, before a new government is formed.
The underlying logic is as follows: right-wing opposition figures are reluctant to sit in a potential coalition with Arab parties, but they may be open to a deal with the Arab parties to form a majority in the Knesset to advance legislation that will undermine the position of prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu , even as the coalition talks take place to form a new government.
Representatives of the four main Zionist opposition parties have already discussed the plan B option, although in public declarations the message is that they are still aiming to clinch an overall majority in next week’s vote. In recent days, according to Israeli media reports, discussions have also taken place with the two Arab parties expected to gain seats in the incoming Knesset.
The Arab parties, which are projected to win around 14 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, realise that entering into a coalition is unlikely but both parties appear open to a deal that would undermine Netanyahu’s grip on power.
In return, the Arab parties are seeking a freeze, or at least a significant cutback, in the widespread demolition of buildings in Israeli Arab communities, deemed illegal by the government. Right-wing opposition lawmakers back the demolitions but may be willing to stop the actions as part of a deal with the Arab parties.
[ Trump’s backing fails to lift Netanyahu as Israel heads for defining vote Opens in new window ]
The first critical step in the opposition plan is to force a vote after the new Knesset convenes on November 10th to replace the Knesset Speaker and the head of the Knesset Arrangements Committee, in order to take control of the parliamentary agenda.
The new Knesset can pass and repeal laws independently of the government. The priority will be bills to dismantle the judicial reforms enacted by the Netanyahu government and the establishment of a probe into the October 7th, 2023, Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, which is likely to ultimately point the finger of blame at Netanyahu himself.
[ Can anyone end the Netanyahu era? Opens in new window ]
Another possibility is that the Knesset could pass legislation to prevent someone under criminal indictment from being prime minister, which would rule out Netanyahu, who is on trial accused of bribery, fraud and breach of trust – charges he denies. Setting a term limit for a prime minister is also under consideration.
The current coalition parties will attempt to block the opposition plans, but the plan B architects believe the high court will allow them to proceed.

title: Cristiano Ronaldo asked for punishment ‘without mitigation’, then fought to cut it
description: Inquiry chose to halve, then halve again his punishment
content:
Cristiano Ronaldo successfully fought to reduce his punishment for walking out on a Portugal training camp after publicly saying his sanction should be imposed “without mitigating circumstances”.
In a lengthy statement on social media after he left the camp in Denmark last month, Ronaldo said he should be punished as the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) saw fit, adding that his role as captain constituted “an aggravating factor”.
However, during the disciplinary council’s inquiry, the 41-year-old put forward several arguments for cutting his punishment. Ronaldo received a 30-day suspension and €255 fine, and the document accompanying the ruling reveals he presented three arguments in mitigation: his disciplinary record this season and in the previous three seasons; his services to football, including recognition for sporting merit; and his contribution to establishing the facts of the case.
To support these arguments, Ronaldo listed the club titles he has won and his achievements with the national team: the 2016 European Championship and two Nations League titles. His individual awards were also highlighted, including his five Ballon d’Or wins. Beyond his achievements on the pitch, he mentioned the honours he had received from senior state officials.
The decision-makers accepted Ronaldo’s arguments concerning his achievements and services to the country, opting to halve his suspension and fine. The punishment was then halved again because Ronaldo accepted responsibility for his actions.
Ronaldo’s suspension will be served in a period during which there are no international matches. It is unclear whether he intends to return to the national team, or whether head coach Jorge Jesus will select him again.
The account of events provides a clearer picture of the circumstances surrounding Ronaldo’s departure from the training camp. After Jesus held a press conference in which he reiterated that he was in charge of the team and that no player would influence his selection decisions, Ronaldo requested a vehicle from the FPF and set off for Copenhagen airport.
During the journey, he called the Portuguese federation’s president, Pedro Proença, and told him he was “not in the right frame of mind” to remain with the team.
“The defendant [Ronaldo] did not inform or provide prior justification to the federation or the men’s national team officials regarding his intention to leave the stadium and the training camp,” the ruling states.
It adds that between September 30th and October 4th, Ronaldo missed more than 30 team activities, including travel, training sessions and meals.
The federation says Ronaldo’s promise on social media, after leaving the training camp, to tell his fans “the whole truth” brought further negative attention to the incident. “Given his prominence as a public figure on a global scale, the defendant could not have been unaware that his conduct, in the circumstances in which it occurred, would be subject to intense media scrutiny, as indeed it was.”
Ronaldo was therefore “expected to exercise particular caution in choosing the timing and manner in which he expressed his dissatisfaction with the manager’s decisions and conduct”.
Instead, he “further fuelled speculation and public curiosity by posting on Instagram on the very day he left Copenhagen, announcing that, ‘in due course’, he would tell ‘all Portuguese people the truth about the reasons that led to his departure from the men’s senior national team’,” the inquiry concluded.
Portugal are scheduled to play Denmark again in their next game on November 14th in Braga. – Guardian

title: Ed Power: A Course Called Ireland review: Bill Murray leaves no cliche unbothered in this schmaltzy Oirish tour
description: Faux-trad diddly-dee muzak, the strategic deployment of the word “feck” and jokes about the Irish and their quirky patois
content:
A few things have been lost in translation as Bill Murray touches down in the old sod for his toe-curling, golf-themed travelogue, A Course Called Ireland ( BBC One, Friday 10.40pm). It really is the worst possible case of Groundhog Day as Murray and his British production crew set off on a tour of the country, filling up their bingo card of musty stereotypes and condescending chestnuts as they go.
No cliche is left unbothered. Faux-trad diddly-dee muzak, the strategic deployment of the word “feck” in a script that clearly did not come within light years of an actual Irish person, and jokes about the Irish and their quirky patois (look at how they spell “Cove” as “Cobh”, lol)… it’s not quite EastEnders go to Wicklow and meet a donkey but it’s not all that far removed either.
Murray is famously an odd fish – with a reputation for eccentricity that for most of his career was regarded as adorable but which, a few years ago, put him at risk of cancellation (there were sexual misconduct allegations against him on the set of a movie in 2022). So perhaps A Course Called Ireland is the latest salvo in his campaign for rehabilitation. Then again it might just be part of the BBC’s historic mission to portray Ireland as a leprechaun reservation, where uncouth locals roam free and uncivilised, forever tipsy on their inexhaustible supplies of whimsy.
The actor clearly wants to be a good sport as the journey begins on the Old Head of Kinsale golf course but he struggles throughout to connect with the people he meets.
A feature of the super-famous in the United States is that they are so removed from ordinary life that they find it hard to interact with everyday individuals and there is some of that with Murray. In his conversations with passersby, there is never a moment where he cannot fathom not being the centre of attention: he’s the famous one so of course it has to be all about him.
The series also has lots of the traditional “othering” of the Irish. Instead of having Murray narrate, they rope in a Cobh woman to read the script and there is an unspoken assumption throughout that we find her and her Irish ways amusing.
Similar forces are at play in a segment where Murray and his American golfing companion Tom Coyne go road bowling in Cork and the producer interviews one of the organisers. He talks to him the way an anthropologist might interact with a member of a “lost” tribe for a BBC natural history documentary in 1965.
Murray is a lively presence but never exactly funny – the most amusing moment is when a passerby confuses him for Bill Cosby (though perhaps that will change when he interacts with celebrities such as Chris O’Dowd and Joanne McNally in later episodes). He is, if anything, at his most engaging when speaking from the heart, such as when recalling how Irish people were marginalised when he was growing up in Chicago. He sits at the harbour in Cobh with tears practically welling in his eyes – very Irish American but nonetheless extremely affecting.
But these moments of heartfelt reflection are eclipsed by the schmaltz and the donkey-staring-over-a-stone-wall vibes. Who ya gonna call if you want a thoughtful meditation on the Irish-American experience as conveyed through the medium of golf? Not Bill Murray, that’s for sure.
A Course Called Ireland is on BBC One, Friday, 10.40pm

title: Australian MP Helen Haines has lost both legs after alleged attack
description: Independent politician’s husband says her ‘her heart and mind are in good shape’
content:
The Australian MP Helen Haines has lost both legs but remains in a stable condition, two days after an alleged targeted attack near her electorate office in north-east Victoria.
Haines, an independent MP, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was struck by a car in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon. Surgeons were trying to save her right leg on Tuesday, but both legs had to be amputated due to the seriousness of her injuries.
Her husband, Phil Haines, provided an update on his wife’s condition at Melbourne’s Alfred hospital late on Wednesday afternoon.
Composed and clear, he said his wife had survived a “horrendous incident” and faced a long road to recovery.
“The good news in all this is Helen is alive and she’s stable,” he said.
“That is the most important thing for our family. And I think when we reflect and talk about and think about Helen, the two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind.
“Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person. Incredibly supportive of all around her – her family, her community, anybody she comes across. And her mind. She has the sharpest intellect.”
Phil Haines described his wife (65) as a fighter. The pair have been married for nearly 40 years and have three children and two grandchildren. He became emotional for a moment at the end of the statement, reflecting on his wife’s strength.
“She is a determined person who will do her best with our support and love to recover, and that is what we hope for,” he said.
“We are grateful at this stage that both her heart and her mind are in good shape.”
Haines asked for donations to Save the Children as his wife recovers. A special appeal has been launched by the charity.
Police allege Monday’s attack was targeted, and have charged Brendan Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official.
Nugent faced Wangaratta magistrates court earlier on Wednesday.
Phil Haines was joined by the governor general, Sam Mostyn. Mostyn said she had relayed news of the incident to King Charles and praised Helen Haines’s work as a local representative, including her commitment to improving the standards of public discourse in Australia.
“This violent attack on a much loved and respected sitting member of our federal parliament must be a moment for us to pause and to choose to be better,” she said.
“We’ve got to hope that that beautiful heart, that beautiful mind will be strengthened every day by our support and our commitment to be more like Helen as part of this great democracy.”
Anthony Albanese and politicians from across federal parliament have expressed shock and anger at the alleged attack on Haines.
The incident has sparked calls for changes to politicians’ safety, with security services including the Australian federal police and Asio briefing MPs on the current landscape on Wednesday.
Speaking at a vigil in Wodonga on Wednesday evening, Cathy McGowan, who held the seat of Indi before Haines, paid tribute to her friend.
“There is another level of grief, different and deeper from the actual violence, from the sorrow, the shame and the hurt,” she said.
“It’s about Helen in her role as our elected representative. In attacking her, we intuit that this is an attack on our political system, on our democracy, and especially so for all the supporters who did the democracy work getting Helen elected.”
McGowan called for the upcoming Victorian state election campaign to be conducted in a positive and constructive way. Voters go to the polls next month.
The community could not let violence win, McGowan implored.
“That we ensure the legacy of this attack on Helen will be a stronger, more vibrant and effective democracy, and from a personal perspective, all candidates and especially women, know they can run for office and be safe.” - Guardian

title: Legal technology start-up Estatemin raises €1m in pre-seed funding
description: Irish-founded company is focused on US market
content:
Irish-founded legal technology start-up Estatemin has raised €1 million in a pre-seed round to help support its growth in the US.
The company, which was founded by Isabella Hughes, Oisín Dolphin and John Noonan, is building a platform powered by artificial intelligence (AI) and focused on trust and estate law firms in the US, helping them to reduce their administrative workload.
The platform can digitise client intake, organise estate information, extract data from documents and support form preparation, helping law firms to save between five and seven hours on an estate-planning matter, with up to 10 hours on estate administrations.
The pre-seed funding round saw participation from NDRC, First Port Syndicate and angel investors Mike Hanrahan, Moira McKenna and Conor Stanley, among other Irish angels.
Enterprise Ireland has also backed the company through its High Potential Startup programme. Now headquartered in New York, Estatemin will use the money to accelerate customer acquisition in the US, expand its engineering and product teams, and support its go-to-market function.
Its engineering operation will remain in Ireland and the UK. The company employs eight people, with one based in the US. However, the priorities for hiring have shifted, Hughes said.
“AI has got so good that you can do so much with so little these days,” she said. “We need more people on the go-to-market front, that’s an area we could hire tomorrow. By the end of next year we are probably looking at a team of around 15 people.”
The company was born from a meeting between Hughes, who is a law graduate, and Dolphin through an NDRC founder weekend at Dogpatch Labs in 2024. Dolphin had been through the probate process, which is paper-heavy, following the death of his father.
Hughes said her experience of working in the industry matched Dolphin’s. That posed a simple question: why are highly trained legal professionals spending so much time retyping information?
The duo founded the company as Simple Probate, with Noonan subsequently coming on board as the third cofounder, bringing his experience of working with legal technology company Clio to the start-up.
Initially focused on Irish law firms, the company changed tack and focused on the US market, which was faster to adopt the platform.
Estatemin partnered with Clio and now supports law firms across all 50 US states. It has grown revenue 20 per cent month on month, with companies using the platform managing more than $770 million (€685 million) in estate value.
“We are growing quickly right now,” Hughes said. “We are always looking ahead and getting ready for that next round.”

title: U2’s Adam Clayton gets green light to build Kinsale ‘retirement home’
description: The first floor is to have two bedrooms and a second kitchen and livingroom
content:
U2 ’s Adam Clayton has finally found what he is looking for after Cork County Council gave the green light for his plans to build a “retirement home” close to Kinsale .
The council granted planning permission to Clayton to demolish a ruined homestead and build a replacement dwelling on a greenfield site at Ringfinnan overlooking Kinsale and the river Bandon.
The floor space of Kinsale House is 795sq m, which is more than seven times the size of an average three-bed semidetached home of 111.4sq m.
Clayton has been busy recently celebrating U2’s 50th anniversary and will soon be preparing for U2’s The Greatest Show on Earth world tour, which starts in Mexico City in February.
No objections were lodged against the planning application, which was submitted in June of this year.
With the granting of permission for Kinsale House, Clayton can proceed to demolish the existing ruined two-storey detached dwelling and associated outbuildings and begin the construction of a replacement six-bedroom dwelling complete with a rooftop paved terrace.
The sprawling home on the lower ground floor is to comprise a games and media room, a kitchenette/bar and three en-suite bedrooms.
On the ground floor there is to be a gym and spa area, a snug TV room, a front and back kitchen and a livingroom as well as a covered patio, an entrance hallway and a principal bedroom.
On the first floor there are to be two more bedrooms along with a second kitchen and livingroom.
The development is also set to involve the erection of 50 photovoltaic panels on ground-mounted arrays and five micro wind turbines.
In a design statement submitted by architects, Rundell Associates said “when the applicant first saw the plot, and recognised that it was an ideal place to create his retirement home, his architectural brief was both clear and ambitious”.
Rundell Associates said Clayton “envisioned a house designed to the very highest aesthetic and environmental standards, that would respond to its local context and become an exemplar for future development in the area”.
The architects said Clayton intended that the new building “would not only be built using local materials drawing inspiration from the existing derelict buildings on site but also that it would integrate itself into the landscape through careful consideration of its massing, rooflines and landscaping”.
Rundell Associates said he “also emphasised his preference for the layout of his home to make direct reference to traditional Irish farmstead typologies, as a way of grounding the architecture in place and memory”.
The design statement by Rundell Associates said the group’s brief was to provide a modern, sustainable and comfortable family home and design a building reminiscent of local farmsteads.
The architect said this involved establishing “step-free” access throughout the main living areas and principal bedroom so that it could serve as a “lifetime home”.
The brief also included providing convenient staff quarters directly linked to the main house with covered parking for staff and visitors.
There were also instructions to minimise the visual impact on the surrounding area by building on the most discreet part of the site and sinking parts of the building into the landscape.
[ U2 podcast: Drummer Seeks Musicians - the story of how U2 began Opens in new window ]
Planning consultants for Clayton, Coakley O’Neill Town Planning, told the council the proposed development represented “a high-quality development that will integrate successfully with the existing and sensitive character of the local area”.

title: Government working on ‘very serious case’ of sexually exploited teen, Taoiseach tells Dáil
description: Martin says fundamental issue is staffing shortages, insisting it is ‘not for the want of funding’
content:
Taoiseach Micheál Martin has insisted the Government is working on the “very serious and deeply worrying” case of a teenage girl subjected to “horrifying” sexual exploitation by a group of men, for whom no place in secure State care is available.
He said the fundamental issue is staffing shortages for specialised care spaces, and insisted “it is not for the want of funding or supports”.
High Court Judge John Jordan directed that details of the case and two others involving sexual exploitation and drug trafficking be sent to three Government Ministers – Minister for Children Norma Foley , Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan and Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers – as a “vivid illustration” of the “consequences” of the State’s ongoing failure to open all special-care beds.
The Taoiseach said Foley “and other Government colleagues are engaging on this case”.
The cases, reported in The Irish Times, were highlighted in the Dáil by Social Democrats TD Liam Quaide, who cited the “horrific sexual exploitation” of a 14-year-old girl with an intellectual disability who is in the care of Tusla .
The Cork TD said the High Court had ordered the girl be moved to a special care setting, “but the Government has failed to ensure Tusla can provide the protection and support she desperately needs”.
The court was also told of another teenage girl being sexually exploited by men and a 16-year-old boy being drawn into drug trafficking by adult criminals.
Nearly half of the State’s 26 special-care beds remain closed because of staffing shortages, and Quaide said it is “utterly shameful that, in 2026, children who have already suffered extreme adversity are being subjected to appalling abuse and exploitation while in State care”.
He asked what immediate action the Government would take “to protect these children and when will all 26 special-care beds be safely operational?”
The Taoiseach told him “the fundamental issue is a shortage of staff in terms of being in a position to open all 26 special-care beds”.
“At the moment, 15 of the 26 special-care beds are staffed. These are for children with particularly complex needs who need sufficient and significant staffing resources.”
Martin said: “Sometimes it can be as high as 14 staff to an individual child or young person. It is not for the want of funding or supports but in a very core, complex number of cases the recruitment of staff has proven to be extremely difficult, but the Government is continuing to work on this and on this case.”
Sinn Féin spokeswoman on children Claire Kerrane said that while the number of open special-care beds has been between 15 and 16, “it is now 13 beds in operation”.
Kerrane said the new pay grade for special care workers “needs to be examined and if more money is needed, this must be provided”.
The Roscommon-Galway TD said Tusla could not open the 26 beds and sustain them “within existing resources”. She said issues “have also been flagged by staff in special care around the new Tusla reforms. Staff need to be heard on this, and their experience needs to be respected.”
Tusla said in a statement “we deeply regret the current situation where we are unable to fulfil our statutory obligations to provide timely access to special care for some young people subject to a High Court order, and the impact this is having for these young people”.
The Child and Family Agency confirmed there are just 13 special care beds in use out of 26 with recruitment and retention challenges “ongoing for a number of years”.
A young person waiting for a special care bed is cared for “in a residential or emergency placement” and has “an allocated key worker, an active care plan and their care is coordinated on a 24-hour basis”, Tusla said.
If there are concerns about exploitation “there is intensive engagement with An Garda Síochána to ensure the young person’s safety”.
The agency said it was using all resources to keep current beds open and hoped that with the creation of the new special care worker grade in 2025, they would “see additional beds opened in the coming months”.

title: Ireland XV to take on Fiji A in double-header with Ireland under-20s in November
description: Game to be the first of three Ireland XV outings this season
content:
The IRFU has confirmed that an Ireland XV will take on Fiji A at Virgin Media Park on Friday, November 20th (7.45pm) in a double-header along with the Ireland Under-20 taking on their Scotland counterparts (5pm). It is the first of three outings for the Ireland XV this season.
The Ireland XV will be coached by Mark Sexton (Ulster) who will be assisted by Jimmy Duffy (Munster), Jared Payne (Munster) and IRFU performance pathway scrum coach, Seamus Toomey. The game takes place the night before Ireland’s Nations Championship clash with South Africa at the Aviva Stadium.
The fixture will form part of an important series of matches throughout the upcoming campaign for Ireland XV, with a renewed focus on developing emerging talent and providing players of national interest with valuable match minutes in green and exposure to a national team environment.
Fiji A will be the visitors to Cork this November, before Ireland XV take on Chile at Queen’s University in Belfast on Friday, February 12th and then travel to Sandy Park in Exeter to face England A on Saturday, February 20th, the same day that Wales host Ireland at the Principality Stadium in the Six Nations Championship.
IRFU Performance Director David Humphreys said: “The Ireland XV programme is an important part of our player development pathway, providing players of national interest with the opportunity to experience the standards, expectations and environment of the senior international set-up.
“These fixtures help bridge the gap between provincial rugby and the senior international squad, allowing players to test themselves against quality opposition while gaining valuable experience in a national team environment. They also give us an opportunity to assess players, build relationships and develop greater depth across the player pool.
“Matches such as the upcoming one against Fiji A in Cork are a valuable part of that process, challenging players in different ways and helping to ensure we continue to develop a strong group of players capable of competing in green at international level.”
Broadcast and ticket details will be confirmed shortly.

title: Woman (28) with stage 4 cancer awarded large sum after radiologist misread scan
description: Michelle Craughwell ‘really disappointed’ with quality of care received at University Hospital Galway in 2023
content:
A 28-year-old woman with stage 4 cancer has received a significant monetary settlement from the HSE after a scan was misread by a radiologist at University Hospital Galway (UHG) in 2023, delaying her diagnosis.
The HSE and UHG have apologised “unreservedly” to Michelle Craughwell “for the deficiencies in radiology care” that led to a delay in diagnosing her with adrenocortical carcinoma, a rare and aggressive cancer.
The case was mediated last week. The compensation covers medical fees, counselling and loss of earnings.
Jonathan Kilfeather, instructed by Damien Tansey Solicitors, told the High Court on Wednesday that if the scan had been “read correctly” in 2023, Craughwell would have “a significantly longer life expectancy”.
“Unfortunately the tumour wasn’t spotted until two years later, at which stage it had become stage 4.”
Kilfeather told the court Craughwell’s prognosis is “bleak”.
Oonah McCrann, representing the HSE, read out an apology on behalf of Chris Kane, general manager of Galway University Hospitals .
“We would like to sincerely and unreservedly apologise for the deficiencies in radiology care in 2023 which led to the delay in diagnosis of your adrenal cortical carcinoma.
“We wish to acknowledge the upset and distress that this has caused you, and we do not underestimate the challenges that you are facing. We deeply regret this and offer you our sincere apologies.”
[ Hospital apologises to woman who had to have a mastectomy when seven months pregnant Opens in new window ]
Judge Paul Coffey sympathised with Craughwell and her parents, Fiona O’Toole and Cyril Craughwell, who were present in court.
Speaking after the hearing, Michelle Craughwell said she was “really grateful” for the apology but disappointed at how her case had been handled.
“I’m just really disappointed that it wasn’t picked up in 2023.”
She said she and her family “had to go through all this turmoil for something that could have been an easy fix at the very beginning”.
Solicitor Damien Tansey said that if the tumour had been detected three years ago, “the outcome would have been totally different”.
He said UHG is a centre of excellence, and Craughwell should have received a higher standard of care.
[ ‘I said I had a headache every day’: Hospital apologises for Mayo woman’s brain tumour diagnosis delays Opens in new window ]
Craughwell, who lives in Tuam, Co Galway , had a history of persistent kidney infections with two prior hospitalisations at UHG in 2019 and 2022, according to documents filed in the case.
On July 16th, 2023, Craughwell presented to the emergency department (ED) at UHG with urinary problems and pain. She had a computed tomography (CT) scan of her abdomen and pelvis. An adrenal mass measuring approximately 2.3cm was missed on the scan, according to the statement of claim.
At this time, Craughwell had stage 1 cancer and the mass was confined to her right-side adrenal gland. As the mass was missed on the scan, no treatment plan was devised.
On June 17th, 2025, she attended her GP with symptoms of a fever and an upper respiratory tract infection. Her GP referred her to the ED, believing she may have had sepsis.
A CT scan of her abdomen and pelvis was carried out on June 19th, and a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan occurred the next day, confirming the presence of the adrenal mass.
In July 2023, the tumour measured about 2.5cm in diameter, court documents noted. By June 2025, the tumour measured about 10cm in diameter and the cancer had progressed to stage 4.
[ At 49 I was a mum, a wife, a runner and constantly tired. Then one day I collapsed at work Opens in new window ]
In August 2025, she underwent surgery at St Vincent’s University Hospital in Dublin and required significantly more surgery than she would have needed in 2023. She also required chemotherapy.
Treatment of her condition is “ongoing”, according to court documents.

title: As Ukraine’s US alliance falters, a bitter dispute with Poland resurfaces
description: Zelenskiy stripped of Polish state award for honouring 1940s Ukrainian militants who massacred Poles
content:
L ast month, like every month since Russia launched its all-out invasion in 2022, barely a day went by without another funeral for another soldier in the main cemetery of Lviv in western Ukraine .
But unusually, at the same time in another part of the city, the bones of men who fell fighting for other nations were being carefully lifted from the earth where they had lain for nearly 90 years.
The remains of 115 Polish and 18 German troops were removed in September from graves where they were buried in autumn 1939, when this city was Lwów in eastern Poland , and the armies of Hitler and Stalin attacked under their secret pact to carve up eastern Europe at the start of the second World War .
Samples of DNA will be taken from the Polish remains, belongings found in the graves will be examined and experts in Poland will try to identify all the dead and find living relatives. Then they will be reburied with dignity. The same will be done for the German soldiers by an organisation that looks after their country’s fallen soldiers.
Meanwhile, work moves on to other graves, on both sides of today’s border between Ukraine and Poland.
It involves quiet, meticulous effort and close co-operation, and it continues despite a recent bitter row over history that put the neighbours at odds, just when Kyiv needs its European allies more than ever amid growing hostility from the White House.
“I don’t feel any enmity between us. We work comfortably together,” Lyubomyr Horbach, head of the Lviv-based Pamyat (Memory) organisation that searches for victims of war, said of its work alongside experts from Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance.
“We are comfortable because there is no politics in what we do. We are historians, archaeologists, scientists doing professional work. We are not politicians.”
Yet disputes over historical crimes, and vandalism of graves and monuments in both countries, delayed and disrupted such work for decades, and can still poison relations – even as Ukraine fights for its survival, and Poland hosts a million Ukrainian refugees and provides Kyiv with crucial military aid and diplomatic support.
The latest row erupted five months ago, when Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy bestowed the title “Heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army” on a unit of his military, to honour its service in the war with Russia and help “restore the historical traditions of the national army”.
The Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) is best remembered in its homeland for waging guerrilla war against Soviet troops in western Ukraine through the 1940s. Its defiance of Kremlin power against huge odds provides inspiration for today’s struggle, and its red-and-black flag is again a symbol of the fight with Moscow.
By contrast, Poles know the UPA for killing about 100,000 Polish citizens in what is now western Ukraine, in a campaign of ethnic cleansing that peaked in 1943. Ten years ago, Poland’s parliament declared the massacres to be genocide.
Kyiv acknowledges that UPA units committed atrocities but rejects the allegation of genocide, and urges Poles to admit that their own forces killed at least 10,000 Ukrainian civilians at the time, following severe interwar repression of the large Ukrainian minority in what was then eastern Poland.
In a video address, Polish president Karol Nawrocki denounced Zelenskiy’s decision “to glorify the UPA” as “outrageous…incomprehensible and deeply disappointing”.
He announced he was stripping Zelenskiy of the Order of the White Eagle, calling it “a symbol of [Poland’s] highest trust”, and then delivered a warning to Kyiv.
“Ukraine’s path toward European structures also requires a willingness to honestly confront the difficult chapters of its own history,” he said.
“A united Europe was built on the rejection of totalitarianism and the cult of violence. These principles must apply to everyone. For those who do not understand this, there can be no place in the European Union , and Poland will certainly not allow it.”
If the nationalist Nawrocki, an admirer of US president Donald Trump, expected contrition from Kyiv, then he was badly mistaken.
Instead, Zelenskiy noted that Warsaw had never seen fit to remove the Order of the White Eagle from Russia’s expansionist empress Catherine the Great, Italian fascist Benito Mussolini or former German chancellor turned Kremlin ally Gerhard Schröder.
[ Gerhard Schröder stirs up ‘uncritical and romantic’ ideas about Russia Opens in new window ]
“Ukraine will remain open to all meaningful formats of engagement with Poland in order to try to avoid conflicting interpretations of the difficult and painful chapters of our shared past and to ensure proper respect for all innocent victims of the 20th century,” Zelenskiy wrote on social media.
“And Ukrainians are doing everything in our power to ensure that Europe does not suffer defeat in this century … We believed that the Order of the White Eagle, awarded in 2023, was meant for the Ukrainian people and our army. That is what was said at the time. Today, I sent the order back to the president of Poland.”
Kyiv felt Nawrocki was trying to humiliate it, having won last year’s presidential election by tapping into growing hostility towards Ukrainian refugees, which has led to several people being attacked in Polish cities.
In a rare show of support for Zelenskiy, three former Ukrainian presidents also sent state awards back to Poland, as did Kyrylo Budanov, the former chief of the country’s military intelligence who now heads the presidential administration.
“Undoubtedly, this is a gift to the Moscow aggressor, who will certainly use it against both of our countries,” Budanov said, calling for “deep reflection” rather than “crude political speculation”.
“Our peoples have long-standing relations and varied pages of history – both heroic and tragic … Ukraine does not dictate to any other people how to teach its history. Therefore, we too reserve the fair right to our own national memory and dignity.”
Poles have also suffered at Russia’s hands for centuries, but Myroslav Marynovych, a Ukrainian former dissident who was jailed and exiled by the Soviet authorities, says the elites of both countries “presume they have a mission to help, rule and raise up Ukrainians to a higher level”.
“In Polish minds, Ukraine must be thankful for that ... And Ukrainians’ gratitude will mean they accept the Polish vision of history. And if not, then they are not grateful enough.”
Marynovych, who founded the first chapter of Amnesty International in the Soviet Union and is now adviser to the rector of Lviv’s Ukrainian Catholic University, has signed public letters seeking Polish forgiveness for crimes committed by the UPA, but sees no willingness from Poland to examine its own historical mistreatment of Ukrainians.
Kyiv fears relations will face more strain during next year’s parliamentary election campaign in Poland, and will hope the liberals of current prime minister Donald Tusk can defeat Nawrocki’s nationalist and populist allies.
“We are not just neighbours,” Tusk said last week after meeting Zelenskiy. “We are friends who can count on each other in difficult times. And no one will ever change that.”
[ ‘The war is getting nearer’: Ukraine’s eastern exodus accelerates as Russia steps up attacks Opens in new window ]
Meanwhile, exhumations of second World War graves continue. In the village of Laskow in eastern Poland, researchers said this week they had found the suspected remains of more than 40 Ukrainian men, women and children who were killed by Polish forces in 1944.
[ Victoria Amelina's Nothing bad has ever happened: a tale of two genocides, the Holocaust and the Holodomor Opens in new window ]
“I don’t think I’m responsible for what my ancestors did, but I can and should ask forgiveness for that. And the Polish side should do the same, even though they are not responsible for what their ancestors did,” says Horbach.
“Our work is about reconciliation. And reconciliation would come sooner if politicians didn’t meddle in this, and make it a political issue at every other election.”

title: Man charged following seizure of €1.7m worth of cocaine in Dublin
description: Separate arrests made in drug intimidation inquiry
content:
A man in his 30s has been charged in relation to the seizure of more than €1.7 million worth of drugs in Dublin .
Around 17 kilograms of cocaine was found as part of an intelligence-led operation involving Revenue’s Custom Service, the Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau and Dublin North Central Divisional Drugs Unit on Tuesday.
Gardaí said on Wednesday that the man arrested during the operation has been charged and is due to appear before Dublin District Court.
A second man, aged in his 50s, who was also arrested has been released without charge. A file will be prepared for the Director of Public Prosecutions .
Separately, a man in his 20s is due to appear before a court charged in connection to a drug-related intimidation investigation.
Members of the Dublin Metropolitan Region North Fógra Investigation Unit carried out search and arrest operations in Meath and Dublin on Monday as part of the investigation.
Two men aged in their 20s were arrested.
Gardaí said on Wednesday that one of the men has been charged and is expected to appear before a sitting of Balbriggan District Court on Tuesday. The second man remains in Garda custody.

title: Man killed in single-vehicle crash in Mayo
description: Incident occurred on N5 at Lisgormin, Bohola, at approximately 5.15am
content:
A man in his 40s has died in a crash in Co Mayo on Wednesday morning.
The single-car incident occurred on the N5 at Lisgormin, Bohola, at approximately 5.15am on Wednesday.
The driver and sole occupant of the car was pronounced dead at the scene.
His body has since been removed to the mortuary at Mayo University Hospital for a postmortem. The coroner has been notified.
The road was closed for examination by Garda technical staff. Diversions were in place at Ballyvary and Bohola.
Gardaí have appealed to anyone who may have witnessed the crash to contact them.
Any road users who were travelling in the area of the N5 at Bohola between 5am and 5.30am on Wednesday, and who may have camera footage, are asked to make it available to gardaí.
Anyone with information can contact Ballina Garda station on (096) 20560, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111 or any Garda station.

title: Booking.com under investigation over fraudulent listings concerns
description: European Commission to carry out ‘in-depth investigation’ as a matter of priority
content:
The European Commission has launched a formal investigation into Booking.com over concerns it has not “effectively mitigated risks” related to fraudulent listings and phishing scams.
The formal proceedings, conducted under the Digital Services Act (DSA), will also assess whether the platform breached the Act’s transparency rules by failing to clearly label as ads listings whose providers paid for a higher ranking in search results.
The Amsterdam-based operator connects travellers with more than 30 million accommodation options across the world and has processed about 6.5 billion bookings since 2010.
It has become particularly attractive to criminals, with concerns over bogus listings deployed to scam users. Earlier this year it emerged it had suffered a data breach, with “unauthorised parties” gaining access to customers’ details, prompting concerns over “reservation hijacking” whereby criminals target people they know have legitimate bookings.
The commission said its investigation would examine whether the platform “has properly identified and assessed the systemic risks linked to the dissemination of illegal content”.
It will focus on fake listings including non-existent properties, impersonation fraud and noncompliant accommodation offers that “may have negative effects on consumer protection”.
It will also assess whether the platform has put in place effective measures to mitigate risks, by removing fraudulent and non-compliant listings and it will investigate whether Booking.com has “diligently assessed and addressed the risks that phishing scams pose to consumers”.
In particular, the investigation will focus on risks related to the way reservation and guest data is shared with accommodation providers, and the design and functioning of Booking.com’s messaging service.
The commission will also examine whether the company has put in place sufficient safeguards to prevent data from being misused to carry out phishing and solicit fraudulent payments.
The last strand of the investigation will look into Booking.com’s compliance with the DSA’s advertising transparency obligations.
“Accommodation providers can make their listings more visible in Booking.com’s search results by paying a higher commission,” the commission noted. “Users should be able to clearly recognise that these ‘boosted listings’ are in fact advertisements.”
It said it would “also examine whether, for each advertisement shown on Booking.com, users can easily see who is behind it, who paid for it, why they are seeing it and how they can change the settings that determine which ads they see”.
Under the DSA, users are entitled to understand when, and on whose behalf, an ad is shown to them.
“Without this, they cannot tell whether a listing appears prominently because it matches their search or because the accommodation provider paid for that visibility,” the commission said.
If proven, the failures would constitute infringements of the DSA, which obliges “very large online platforms and search Engines to identify, analyse, assess and mitigate systemic risk” and requires them to ensure users can clearly identify advertisements and the information about them.
The commission said it would carry out the “in-depth investigation as a matter of priority” and the opening of formal proceedings empowered it to take further enforcement steps, such as interim measures and noncompliance decisions.
It is also empowered to accept commitments offered by Booking.com to remedy the matters subject to the proceedings.
It stressed that opening formal proceedings “does not prejudge any final outcome or decision, nor does it impact enforcement actions undertaken by other authorities under other regulatory frameworks”.
The commission’s decision follows a preliminary investigation that included an analysis of the risk assessment reports submitted by Booking.com in 2026 and the preceding three years, information published in its transparency reports, and the company’s replies to the commission’s formal requests for information.
In a statement, Booking.com said it is cooperating fully” with the European Commission and “engaging constructively on its questions under the Digital Services Act (DSA).
“Security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities at Booking.com. We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to combat cybercrime and online fraud and protect traveller’s and partners,” a spokesman said.

title: Phil Hogan would seek Donald Trump’s help to restore grain corridor
description: Former commissioner bidding to lead UN food agency and increase its involvement in talks with Russia and Ukraine
content:
Former EU commissioner Phil Hogan , who is vying to lead the UN’s food agency , would engage with Donald Trump to seek to reinstate a safe Black Sea corridor for grain exports as part of his drive to put food security at the heart of geopolitics.
Russia has been intensifying attacks on cargo ships in Black Sea ports, blocking Ukrainian exports. Hogan, formerly a Fine Gael minister and Brussels’ top official on agriculture and trade, said he would “absolutely” seek to involve the US president and other world leaders in an effort to revive the route that enabled the export of 32 million tonnes of grain and food in 2022-23 under the Black Sea Grain Initiative.
The deal was negotiated with the help of Turkey and the UN. But despite its specialist remit to promote food security, the Food and Agriculture Organisation, which has been led by Qu Dongyu of China since 2019, stuck to the sidelines at that time. Qu has since cautioned against FAO staff getting involved in political activism.
Hogan said the 81-year-old Rome-based agency needed to become “relevant to the 21st century”.
“There is no doubt FAO needs reform,” said Hogan, who this month launched his bid to lead FAO. Its members elect a new director general next June.
“I would certainly, as director general, be centrally involved in trying to create the political conditions to ensure that food security is seen as just as important as global security,” he added.
One tool would be to use an FAO insurance brokerage scheme, established to help move food amid climate challenges and still “in its infancy”. It could be employed “for the purposes of ensuring that food is able to be transported through corridors in an emergency context”, Hogan said.
Besides the Ukraine war, the US conflict against Iran has disrupted trade through the Strait of Hormuz , pushing up oil and fertiliser prices. This year’s powerful El Niño weather phenomenon also threatens to weaken global food security.
But currently, FAO data “is not being used properly for the purposes of helping to create solutions to problems like we have in conflict zones and areas prone to hunger and affected by El Niño”, Hogan said.
Hogan said he would draw on his experience of dealing with Trump and his administration during the US president’s first term.
“President Trump is a dealmaker. He’s transactional. He likes farmers. He has tried to support farmers with special financial packages themselves during the market crisis and during the tariff wars. And I’ve done likewise with the European farmers during my time as the EU agriculture commissioner. So now we can build on this common ground. We’ve done it before,” he said.
“We found solutions to so-called intractable problems on trade ... So I’m confident we can do the same again,” he added. “President Trump shares the objective of most western countries, which is he wants to see a more effective, efficient and agile UN system and especially around food security.”
Trump is a critic of multilateral agencies and a climate sceptic, but Hogan said the president “actually cares more about farmers and food than about many issues, so I would say on the issue of food security, I would have an open door to having a conversation with the United States government in a positive way”.
Hogan served as environment minister from 2011-14, after the economic crash prompted a European Commission, European Central Bank and IMF bailout.
“I had to reform local government and reduce expenditure and make a lot of tough decisions – I didn’t shy away from doing it,” he said.
[ Phil Hogan ready to ‘serve once again’ as he launches bid for UN food agency job Opens in new window ]
Hogan moved to Brussels as agriculture and then trade commissioner between 2014 and 2020, when he quit after breaching Covid lockdown rules by attending a golf dinner. He has since worked as a consultant and is sinking some €250,000 of his own cash into his FAO campaign to succeed Qu.
Spain, Italy, Turkey and Angola have also nominated candidates for the role. But Hogan was optimistic.
“The vast majority of the European Union countries are supporting my candidacy and the other two European candidates know that,” he said. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited

title: Irish sport in 10 objects: The Liffey Swim, Ronnie Delany’s shoes, Rachael Blackmore’s saddle
description: A new book by Siobhán Doyle captures Ireland’s sporting past through a collection of 100 objects, here is a selection of 10 of them
content:
A statute from the King of England Richard III in 1527 shows an early sign of the suppression of Gaelic sports by the British Crown. The statute forbids hurling from being played, reading “at no time to use nor occupy the hurling of the little ball with hockey sticks or staves, nor use a handball to play outside the walls, but only the great football”. Any person caught playing hurling or handball would be issued a fine of eight pence – the equivalent of about €20 today.
During the 19th century, one of America’s most popular spectator sports was competitive walking, or pedestrianism. Competitors walked around dirt tracks in endurance tests that lasted for several days. Born in Co Cork, Daniel O’Leary moved to New York at the onset of the Great Hunger and became a walker after being determined to prove a theory wrong that only an American could walk 100 miles in 24 hours. O’Leary was declared “Champion of the World” after winning a famous 500-mile race and his likeness was captured on a cigarette packet collector’s card.
This turnstile was used in Lansdowne Road , manufactured in Manchester and made from heavy-duty cast iron. It was designed for durability, which showed, as it lasted for more than 100 years. Now called the Aviva Stadium , Lansdowne Road first hosted a rugby international in 1878. It featured a sealed-in, tamper-proof counting mechanism to record the number of people entering through the gate, and could admit up to 4,000 spectators per hour.
A peak into a different world as artist Jack B Yeats captures the thrill and atmosphere of the Liffey Swim, which has been a big part of Dublin’s sporting calendar since 1920. It invites viewers to see the race as an observer and depicts the crowd leaning forward to get a good view. A year later, Yeats entered this painting in Olympic Arts Competition, an event included in the Olympic Games between 1910 and 1948. The painting was awarded a silver medal, which was the first Olympic medal for the Irish Free State.
A larger than life character, throughout his life Mick Murphy was a cyclist, wrestler, darts player, boxer, runner, farmer, circus performer, fire eater, ventriloquist and bricklayer. The Co Kerry man had an unconventional training regime involving eating raw nettles, raw meat and cow’s blood. Murphy described these weights as the “secret to his success” and made them when he was 12 years old, using a crowbar and stones. Known as “The Ironman”, Murphy later won the Rás Tailteann .
The shoes that helped create Irish history, worn by Ronnie Delany as he won gold for Ireland in the 1,500m at the 1956 Olympics in Melbourne. Adidas began producing running shoes in the 1920s and by the 1950s the company was producing shoes specifically for long-distance running. The shoes were designed with cushioning and support, but lightweight enough not to slow the runner down. Delany only found out he would be selected for the race by newspaper report, but ran an Olympic record. The legendary athlete died earlier this year aged 91 .
In 1989, Dubliner Eddie Jordan invested his personal money to create a Formula One racing team. The 191 was its first car; constructed by a relatively small team of 33 people, they produced an elegant design powered by a Ford-Cosworth engine.
