The car was painted green, in homage to Jordan’s Irish roots, as well as a deal with the Irish tourism office, 7up and Fujifilm. In 1991, they finished fifth in the Constructors’ Championship, and one Michael Schumacher made his debut in the car.
The first woman to represent Ireland in athletics at the Olympics, Maeve Kyle was a trailblazer who saw it all over her career in athletics, cricket, hockey, tennis, swimming and sailing. Kyle’s participation at the 1956 Olympics in Melbourne was met with disdain by some in conservative Ireland, with one letter in The Irish Times describing her as “a disgrace to motherhood and the Irish nation” for leaving her husband and daughter at home when she competed. 44 years later she was back in Australia at the Olympics in Sydney as a coach, and wore this blazer at at the opening and closing ceremonies.
Katie Taylor became a household name when she won gold at the London Olympics in 2012. She wore these shorts in the 60kg final in a close-fought match against Russia’s Sofya Ochigava. Taylor recalls putting on these shorts before the fight: “Everything about putting on the Irish Olympic team uniform was a beautiful, simple pleasure – the small crest on the singlet, the shorts, even the colours and the material – those basic things were just incredible. I was saying to myself ‘this is the dream’”.
This is the saddle Rachael Blackmore used to win the 2021 Aintree Grand National with Minella Times. It was the first win by a woman jockey in the history of the race, which dates back to 1839, and it came three weeks after Blackmore was named top jockey at the Cheltenham Festival. Previously, women had been banned from horse racing in the UK and Ireland until 1972. The saddle weighs 7lbs and was made in the UK. Blackmore’s leather saddles were a favourite as they sat well and gave a close contact feel.
Irish Sport in 100 Objects by Siobhán Doyle is available to buy in book stores in Ireland for €24.99 for a hardback copy.

title: A knock at the door changed everything: how CPR saved a toddler’s life
description: From a lifeless baby to a suspected stroke, Irish Red Cross volunteers reveal the moments that changed lives forever
content:
“I answered a panicked knock on my front door to find a really distressed couple carrying a very young girl, around two years old.”
This is John Kavanagh, a volunteer with the Irish Red Cross in Wexford for more than 40 years.
“The toddler had stopped breathing,” he says. “Her parents had been on route to the after-hours medical service when the child’s condition worsened and they suddenly realised time was against them. Luckily, they knew where I lived and that I was first-aid trained.”
As an emergency medical technician (EMT) he has helped many people in distress over the years.
“I performed CPR on the child and thankfully, within a few minutes, she began breathing again. I’ll never forget how relieved the parents were ... as well as myself. I was so glad I could help and the little girl was okay.”
Kavanagh’s friend Damien Dineen, also a volunteer with the Irish Red Cross, has also been on-hand when someone has been in need.
“Recently at work, a colleague came to me and explained that she wasn’t feeling well,” says Dineen. “She had pain down her arm and couldn’t feel her lips. She was very pale, and her lips were slightly blue. I sat her down and took her pulse and immediately carried out stroke protocol. After ringing for an ambulance, I was able to keep her comfortable in our first-aid room and constantly monitor her until the ambulance crew took over.
“The lady had experienced a minor stroke which could have had much more serious consequences if I didn’t have the experience to read the signs. I certainly would not have been able to deal with that situation without the excellent training we get at the Irish Red Cross.”
Sarah Barker is also an EMT and volunteer with the Irish Red Cross, in its Dundalk branch. “Late one night I was feeding Oisín, my two-week-old new baby, and I suddenly realised that he was choking,” she says. “At first, I was calm. I started giving Oisín back slaps, trying to dislodge whatever was caught in his throat, telling myself he’d cough it up and everything would be fine. I truly believed it would pass in a few seconds. But then it changed. So quickly. He turned blue. His little body went completely limp in my arms, lifeless. That’s when I realised, he wasn’t breathing.”
“I began performing CPR including rescue breaths and compressions, using two fingers. Thankfully, within about a minute, Oisín started breathing again. He started to get sick I quickly rolled him on to his side and then I burst into tears because I was so relieved; vomiting meant that he was okay, his airway was clear and he was breathing again. The relief was indescribable.
“My message to everyone who will listen is: learn CPR. You never know when you might need it.”
Irish Red Cross volunteers, which include Kavanagh, Dineen and Barker, collectively give one million minutes of their time every month to help people in their community by providing first-aid cover, training people in first aid and CPR, responding to medical emergencies and supporting people affected by severe weather events such as storms and flooding.
Kavanagh says being an Irish Red Cross volunteer is a way of life for him: “I’ve been doing this for over four decades now, so I just can’t imagine not doing it. Since I did my initial first-aid course all those years ago, I’ve been hooked. I enjoy meeting new people, working alongside my fellow volunteers and while it has its serious side, of course, it is great craic. Being able to use my skills to help other people and make a difference in their lives – it’s very rewarding.”
Now, as Ireland enters the winter storm season, the Irish Red Cross is calling on the public to help strengthen that vital volunteer network through A Million Minutes, a new national fundraising and awareness campaign.
Extreme weather and other emergencies are placing increasing demands on communities and volunteers. The aim of A Million Minutes is to help strengthen the capacity and capability of the Irish Red Cross network of branches and volunteers across the country, ensuring they are equipped and ready to respond when their communities need them most as Deirdre Garvey, secretary general of the Irish Red Cross is well aware.
“Crises don’t wait until we’re ready,” she says. “We need to be prepared for emergencies, be it a severe storm, flooding, a fire or pandemic. It is our role as the Irish Red Cross to respond when needed and help communities recover stronger. We are preparing by upskilling our volunteers and increasing the capacity of our branches to ensure they can be there when needed. With the support of the public and businesses we can do even more. We are inviting everyone to take the Irish Red Cross one-hour challenge – be that a sponsored run, walk, cycle [or] swim – and help us raise A million Minutes – essentially help us buy more vital preparation time, to train our volunteers, maintain and upgrade their equipment, and make our branch network even stronger and better able to respond to their communities in times of crisis.”
There are countless ways in which Irish Red Cross volunteers across the country support stronger communities in Ireland, including providing first aid cover at events and sporting occasions, enabling people to safely enjoy events such as the Dublin City Marathon, Electric Picnic and the Ring of Kerry Charity Cycle; training community groups and schoolchildren in first aid and boosting life-saving community skills; transferring patients with mobility or transport challenges to medical appointments, ensuring they can receive critical continuity of care; carrying out door-to-door checks on vulnerable people isolated due to storms or flooding, bringing essential supplies and human connection; running community cafes to combat social isolation and foster connection and community cohesion; offering therapeutic hand care massages in community hospitals and nursing homes, easing painful joints but more crucially bringing conversation and connection; and supporting migrants and refugees to rebuild their lives through a range of initiatives including integration cafes and other social outlets.
Tim Kelleher, a volunteer with the Irish Red Cross Clonakilty branch in Cork, is passionate about volunteering, as are all seven members of the family – his wife, Annemarie, and their five children, aged between six and 17 years old.
“My son Patrick was just a toddler when he swallowed some playdoh,” says Tim. “We almost lost him on the way to the hospital and only for the fact that I was trained in first aid and CPR, he wouldn’t be with us today. Ever since that day I swore I would commit myself 110 per cent to the Irish Red Cross and to helping others through first aid.”
To support the training and equipping of Irish Red Cross volunteers so they can continue to help communities in Ireland, get involved with A Million Minutes. Visit amillionminutes.com to kick start your one-hour challenge or to make a donation

title: ‘I’m in a bad place’: Mark Allen says career could be over after Northern Ireland Open exit
description: Snooker player says he has spent the last 10 weeks in a mental health clinic
content:
Mark Allen said he was in a “bad place” and his career could be over after losing to Jordan Brown in the first round of the Northern Ireland Open in Belfast.
Allen was playing his first match since his World Championship semi-final loss to Wu Yize in April, when he missed a match-ball black off the spot at 16-15 in front and went on to lose a decider.
The 40-year-old has since stayed away from the tour due to personal issues that he has kept private but are understood not to relate to any repercussions from the manner of his defeat at the Crucible.
After his 4-2 defeat to Brown, a close friend and compatriot who is also from Antrim, Allen indicated he is set to take another long and potentially permanent break from the sport.
In an emotional interview with TNT Sports, Allen said he was “really overwhelmed”, adding: “I’m in a bad place at the minute, so even just to go out there and try was tough.
This is heartbreaking to watch 🥺💔 Mark Allen admits he may never play snooker again. We’re all rooting for you, Mark 🙏❤️ pic.twitter.com/9v6wvWMflE
“I think if I wasn’t playing Jordan I wouldn’t have come back. I felt like if I was going to play one last time, playing here at the Waterfront, where it all started in 2005, against one of my best mates, I thought that was a better way to sign out.”
Asked if he was serious about his threat to retire, Allen confirmed his view and continued: “I’ve been flooded with support but the problems are within. I just don’t see a future with snooker in it, if I’m honest.
“It’s sad to say, because it’s all I’ve loved to do since I was 12 but the last few months has been really difficult and it’s put snooker into perspective for me. At the minute I’m just trying to survive.”
Allen has won both UK and Masters titles in a total of 12 ranking tournament wins, and has reached the World Championship semi-finals three times.
Brown said: “First and foremost it’s just great to see Mark back playing. He obviously came through a tough time off the table and I’m with him every step of the way, like everybody is.
“We’re all behind him. I miss him and I love him and we all just want to see him healthy and well and playing the game that he loves so much. He’s a great player and a great guy.”
Both World Snooker Tour and the sport’s governing body, the WPBSA, have provided support to Allen and have indicated their desire to continue helping him in any way they can.
Allen released a statement on social media on Wednesday saying he was doing his best to turn things around.
“I have been in a mental health clinic for the last 10 weeks, finally discharging so I could attempt to play in Belfast.
“I owed that to my family, in particular my daughter to see me play for what could be the last time ... I also owed it to the fans who have supported me throughout my 21 years on tour.
“I also owed that to World Snooker who have been amazing from day on in all this, in particular Simon Brownell and Neil Tomkins who have remained in touch regularly, even Simon paying me a visit in the clinic itself.
“I’m not okay, but I’m okay in that itself. I’ve been much worse in the last few months than you saw yesterday. I literally didn’t see a future in anything.
“My daughter kept me going, the therapists, staff and all the other patients were amazing and helped me through some really dark days.
“I see the light now that I couldn’t see before but I do now. I also know it won’t happen overnight. I’m a work in progress!!! My fight and determination on the table has always been there for ones to see. I need to show those same fighting qualities off it now for a while.
“Please don’t detract anything from Jordan yesterday, he’s been aware of my struggles and that can’t have been easy to play in but he handled it with grace and skill as I knew he would. I am proud to call him a friend.
“I hope the rest of the event is a success and I will continue my treatments going forward and then see what’s ahead.
“Thank you to every single message I have received on here, instagram, Facebook, text messages and WhatsApps, I’ve seen them all but a bit overwhelmed to reply right now. Just know that they have helped me a lot but I’m not going anywhere just yet!!!! I have so much to live for and this is only the beginning of my new journey.
“Also, I was not made to do any interviews, I was simply given a choice and felt I owed it to everyone to speak. The media team at WST have been incredible through all this too.

title: Four St Pat’s players named in League of Ireland team of the year
description: Pico Lopes and Tommy Lonergan also among those included in vote by the players
content:
Four St Patrick’s Athletic players have been named in League of Ireland Men’s Premier Division Team of the Year.
The team contains two players who travelled for the World Cup, goalkeeper Joseph Anang for Ghana and most notably centre-back Roberto ‘Pico’ Lopes for Cape Verde, who starred as his team reached the knockout stages.
Anang is joined by Luke Turner, Kian Leavy and Joe Redmond in the team, voted for by the players. Lopes is one of three Shamrock Rovers players in the side, as well as Graham Burke and Tunmise Sobowale.
Bohemians’ Dawson Devoy is named in midfield, with Derry’s Michael Duffy and Dundalk’s Daryl Horgan on the wings. In-form Waterford and Ireland under-21 striker Tommy Lonergan is named as striker.
PFAI Men’s Premier Division Team of the Year: Joseph Anang (St Patrick’s Athletic); Tunmise Sobowale (Shamrock Rovers), Joe Redmond (St Patrick’s Athletic), Pico Lopes (Shamrock Rovers), Luke Turner (St Patrick’s Athletic); Dawson Devoy (Bohemians), Kian Leavy (St Patrick’s Athletic), Graham Burke (Shamrock Rovers); Daryl Horgan (Dundalk), Tommy Lonergan (Waterford), Michael Duffy (Derry City).

title: Tusla plans to reduce the number of children it takes into special care
description: In a recent case, a 14-year-old girl was given drugs and sexually exploited by several adult men
content:
Tusla plans to reduce the number of highly at-risk children it takes into special care in the face of harsh criticism from High Court judges over its failure to find spaces, an internal paper shows.
The paper, dated September and obtained under Freedom of Information legislation, sets out a two-year plan to get all 26 special-care beds open by the end of 2028.
However, it notes that the first target of having 20 beds open by the end of the year is “at risk”, with just 13 open at present.
The document says a target of ending the “no beds list”, which lists children whom the High Court has ordered to be in special care but who cannot get beds, by the end of the year is “on track”.
The High Court on Monday, however, made orders to detain three children for whom there were no beds, including a 14-year-old girl who has been given drugs and sexually exploited by multiple adult men.
Judge John Jordan lifted the in-camera rule, which operates to protect the identity and privacy in such cases, in that case and also in a second involving extreme sexual exploitation of a teenage girl.
[ No special care place available for girl (14) being sexually exploited by group of men Opens in new window ]
He directed that details of the cases be sent to three Government Ministers – Minister for Children Norma Foley , Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan and Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers – as a “vivid illustration” of the “consequences” of the State’s ongoing failure to open all special-care beds.
“It is important they be aware of the appalling predicament of this child and of the absolute urgency in opening up all the three special-care units,” he said.
Asked about the case on Tuesday, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said he did not have the details, but it was “a very serious situation, obviously”. He said he would speak to O’Callaghan, Foley and Chambers about it.
The third order was to detain a 16-year-old boy, considered to be in extreme danger with a drug gang, in special care.
These three teenagers will likely, at the next High Court special care hearing, be added to the no-beds list, which already includes a boy involved in the sale and manufacture of crack cocaine who has been expressing suicidal ideation.
In July, High Court judge Emily Egan found Tusla to be in contempt for its failure to provide beds to children ordered by the High Court to be detained there.
The September strategy document says “staff shortages remain the primary barrier to opening additional beds” in the three units.
It says “considerable efforts are also being made to ensure that young people are only referred to special care when all other options and supports have been provided”.
There are growing concerns among legal sources that children who otherwise would have been recommended for special care by Tusla’s referral committee are being refused, thereby keeping their cases away from the High Court.
Five objectives are detailed in the strategy, including to “increase bed capacity”, “strengthen workforce sustainability”, and “improve system flow to and from special care”.
[ Tusla whistleblower asks gardaí to investigate alleged ‘retaliation and unlawful conduct’ Opens in new window ]
Of 30 actions detailed, eight are described as “at risk” of not being achieved. In addition to the aspiration of having 20 beds open in the next 10 weeks, a plan to open a fourth unit in Cork and another to bring staff absenteeism down to below 20 per cent by the end of the year are deemed “at risk”.
In a statement Tusla said: “We deeply regret the current situation where we are unable to fulfil our statutory obligations to provide timely access to special care for some young people ... and the impact this is having for these young people.
“It is important to note [that] where a young person in our care is awaiting a special care placement, they are cared for in a residential or emergency placement. They have an allocated key worker, an active care plan and their care is co-ordinated on a 24-hour basis.
“Where there are concerns in relation to exploitation, there is intensive engagement with An Garda Síochána to ensure the young person’s safety.”

title: Too much Overlap? Gary Neville’s podcast empire knows no bounds
description: The Overlap has gone daily, with Steven Gerrard and Joe Hart among the latest additions to an ever-growing family
content:
Viewed in 2026, Nathan Barley, Chris Morris’s 2005 sitcom, shows remarkable prescience about the last two decades of metropolitan life, from smartphone addiction and digital derangement to sheer existential vapidity.
When Barley’s character referred to his occupation as “self-facilitating media node”, Morris and co-writer Charlie Brooker were way ahead on the creator economy. What the pair failed to predict was ex-footballers joining the sector in droves. These days, if you are a former footballer without a podcast or YouTube channel, then did you ever really play the game?
Setting aside the Gary Lineker Goalhanger empire, manspreading its centrist-dad agenda into issues way beyond guffaws with Micah Richards and Alan Shearer, there is Gary Neville to rule them all. Manchesterism’s second-most influential practitioner has been on heavy manoeuvres. Unlike Lineker’s productions, the Overlap’s output continues to stick largely to football; a rugby podcast was mothballed in February, though its cricket equivalent continues.
Having snatched Wayne Rooney from the BBC in the summer for a Manchester United-based two-hander with the YouTuber Mark Goldbridge, last week the Overlap went daily, extending the output to 4pm Monday to Friday. An online launch had Jamie Carragher baiting Goldbridge, real name Brent Di Cesare. The former policeman shunned a “no comment” approach during his interrogation, biting back during an exchange that had Neville choking on his Huel in laughter. Clipped up, the send button pressed, job done.
The Overlap has gained a TV family dynamic, a chorus line of familiar characters. Neville and Carragher are mummy and daddy bear, football’s Richard and Judy. Jill Scott is the dotty aunt, Roy Keane the irascible uncle, smirking along with Ian Wright in picking over the latest gossip.
It has been highly popular, occasionally agenda-setting, softening Keane’s image, even making a cultish figure of production hand Kiaran Saunders, supplier of biscuits and blueberries. Neville’s empire-building, though, is boundless, his tanks bulldozing into the already packed football podcast space, with newsletters to follow. The Overkill, anyone?
The family has been extended. Mondays have Steven Gerrard reviewing the weekend’s action with Becky Ives, this week offering a defence of Florian Wirtz: “Don’t give up on him.” Tuesdays have Kelly Cates and Ashley Young in tandem. Tim Sherwood and Jamie Redknapp are Wednesday’s pairing. Not the first time the Sky mainstays, one-time Tottenham midfield partners, have diversified.
In the mid-2000s, they ran Icon, a lifestyle magazine initially only available to professional players. A combination of high-end advertising, onanistic photography and Redknapp’s purring interviews with A-list sportspeople fell flat, even after it became available in airport first-class lounges.
Two decades on, such cologne-fragrant exclusivity has been swapped for the ubiquity of Bury’s most famous son piling it high. The quarter-zipped ex-Spurs duo are not alone as 1990s footballers taking the Neville shilling. Mark Crossley and Duncan Ferguson make an unlikely – but promising – pairing.
Previously most famous for being the only goalkeeper to save a Matthew Le Tissier penalty, Crossley has made a successful after-dinner speaking career of Brian Clough anecdotes and “young man” impressions. “Big Dunc” completely refused to speak to the media when a player but he was a hit within ITV’s World Cup 2026 coverage.
On last week’s edition Ferguson suggested Gianluigi Donnarumma might be over the hill. “He’s 27, actually,” said Crossley before a classic game’s gone discussion of video assistant referees ruining the sacred art of smashing into the opposition at goal-kicks. Just what the listener came for, eating perhaps into the Under The Cosh’s market share of real football man podcasts. Whether Ferguson’s appointment as Glentoran manager breaks up the band is unclear, though management never halted Robbie Savage’s many media ventures.
Two further goalkeepers have signed up. Last week’s Friday edition had Joe Hart and Peter Schmeichel entering the Manchester City charges chat. While admitting to mistakenly burying the lead when Lisandro Martínez was willingly dishing the dirt on Manchester United while serving as CBS’s Champions League interviewer in Madrid last Tuesday, Schmeichel gave Hart a far harder ride.
“It’s tough to be a Manchester City person,” Hart said. “I love the club ... we’re in it together.” Schmeichel stayed insistent on City’s owners: “They’re letting Manchester down, they don’t understand what this place is. They have built a lot of towers and homes and all that but they don’t get this place.”
“I’ve worked closely with Khaldoon [al-Mubarak] and he does get this place, that’s my reference point,” said a hesitant Hart. “He’s an incredible person.” More good, strong, clip-up content.
The City affair will ask former players to intersect with uncomfortable issues for some while yet. That Neville’s further business interests include building projects running parallel to the Abu Dhabi-funded developments in Manchester is another example. Overlaps have become unavoidable in more ways than one. – Guardian

title: Only way to combat ‘drugs intimidation’ is to inform gardaí, Jim O’Callaghan says
description: Matt Carthy calls for ‘immediate, determined crackdown’ on gangs ‘terrorising communities’
content:
The only way to combat the scourge of drugs intimidation is for those affected to inform gardaí, Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan has told the Dáil .
He acknowledged this “may strike some terror” into people because of the fear they have of the person intimidating them.
But he insisted the only way to deal with such intimidation and violence “is through An Garda Síochána being informed and being involved”. He said the State “and the Garda Síochána is there to protect people” and he pledged “I will resource An Garda Síochána to ensure that they are able to meet this threat”.
O’Callaghan also said people who make a decision to use drugs need to be informed that “this is going to bring a load of misery on to them” and “can bring terrible intimidation on their families”.
He was speaking in the Dáil on Tuesday evening during a Sinn Féin motion brought following the fatal arson attack in which Kim and Philip English and their children Callum (12) and Jayden (9) were killed at their home in Waterford. Two other children, Nadia (14) and Elliott (6), are in critical condition in hospital.
The motion called for a wide-ranging response to drugs intimidation and violence, which the Government supported. The Minister said it was “extremely important” to have a united response.
“We need to say together there is no place for such intimidation in this country, in a civilised society, and any persons who seek to terrorise families for their own financial gain will be pursued relentlessly by An Garda Síochána,” he said.
Opening the debate, Sinn Féin justice spokesman Matt Carthy called for a public awareness campaign so that people know where to turn if they face such intimidation and receive the support they need when they do.
He also called for an “immediate and determined crackdown on the criminal gangs responsible for this intimidation” and said there should be a “particular focus on stopping young people being groomed” by these gangs into a life of criminality.
[ Jim O’Callaghan and solicitors face increasing criticism as legal aid stand-off worsens Opens in new window ]
“Those engaged in this criminality have to be identified, they have to be arrested, and they have to be prosecuted and imprisoned. We need to get these people off our streets and out of our communities.”
He said the Criminal Assets Bureau (Cab) should establish a dedicated operation to identify and target those responsible, “seizing the assets of the gangs and individuals who terrorise families and communities”.
Sinn Féin Waterford TD David Cullinane said “those criminal gangs and those thugs thrive on fear and they thrive on silence”. He said he had spoken to hundreds of families who said “that family lived in fear”.
He said the State has to stand up in a really forceful way “and say that we are going to crack down on these criminal gangs, that there will be no hiding place for the people who carry out attacks”, but also “the people who give the orders”.
Waterford-based Minister of State Mary Butler referred to comments at the funeral of the English family by Bishop Alphonsus Cullinan that “anyone taking drugs recreationally is feeding an evil machine”.
She said “the reality that we all must face up to is that the majority of people taking drugs do it by choice. They see it as a weekend or a weekday recreation. They see no harm. But the results are devastating, not just for the English family, but for countless families and communities up and down the country.”
[ Waterford arson victims were ‘a beautiful family who did no wrong’, funeral told Opens in new window ]
Social Democrats justice spokesman Gary Gannon said the Government spoke of this attack being a “watershed moment”. He did not understand, however, why last year was not a watershed moment when four-year-old Tadhg Farrell and his grandaunt Mary Holt were killed in a fire in Co Offaly in December.
“That was a moment when I expected, that the whole resources of the State” would be used to confront “these thugs” because everyone knew this thuggery and terror was happening all over Ireland.

title: The criminal courts are operating, but not ‘effectively’, as Jim O’Callaghan claims
description: Minister has offered to meet solicitors as legal aid dispute sees case backlogs rise
content:
P ressure is mounting on the Minister for Justice and criminal defence solicitors to resolve the bitter dispute over a new criminal legal aid payment model for the District Court .
As case backlogs continue to rise across all criminal court divisions, the Law Society received a letter on Tuesday from the Minister, Jim O’Callaghan , stating he has instructed his department to organise a meeting “in the coming days”.
Solicitor sources expressed some wariness about the invitation, with many still smarting over the Minister’s claim that rape trials listed on Monday at the Central Criminal Court were “deliberately affected” by their withdrawal of services .
Solicitors, and members of the Oireachtas Committee on Justice, firmly rejected the claim after pointing out that all types of cases are affected.
The view among solicitors on Tuesday was that the proposed meeting must involve “meaningful” engagement about the Minister’s reforms and “not a listening exercise”.
The Law Society, which had sought a meeting after the Minister declined its proposal to enter an independent mediation of the dispute, is expected to take up his offer.
Under way since early July when the new payment model came into effect, the withdrawal of services has affected a wide range of criminal cases, including assault, rape, drug offences, arson, burglary, money laundering and theft.
The action escalated this week to include cases involving people in custody and what are known as protocol cases, ones involving young or vulnerable accused and victims.
The Minister, who previously argued the criminal justice system is operating “effectively” despite the withdrawal, told the justice committee on Tuesday he fully accepted there is disruption in Dublin but said the scheme is “working very well” in other districts.
[ Jim O’Callaghan accused of treating solicitors’ pay dispute ‘like it’s a game’ Opens in new window ]
Committee chairman Matt Carthy and other members queried that, telling him of disruption of courts in many locations up and down the country.
O’Callaghan repeatedly stressed his strong belief the criminal legal aid system must be reformed to achieve cost savings and efficiencies.
He stood over the principle of retaining a flat fee – €520 based on an average five appearances – and trying “to cut down on the scandal” of multiple legal aid certificates.
He said people are confusing the words “failing to engage” with “giving solicitors what they want” but he is prepared to “tweak things”, having previously made some changes to the scheme.
The committee generally agreed reform is required, with several stressing the best way to achieve that is by sitting down with the Law Society to hammer out a compromise.
The Chief Justice, Donal O’Donnell, spoke for many court users earlier this month when he said he and the judiciary are very concerned and hoped the dispute would be resolved soon.
Although the criminal courts system continues to operate, few involved believe it is operating effectively. The withdrawal of services has played havoc with the management of court lists, leading to thousands of adjournments. That is fuelling the concerns of complainants about further delays in hearing their cases.
One complainant who contacted The Irish Times on Tuesday about the dispute said it was “very hurtful and insulting” to hear the Minister suggest the dispute is causing minimal disruption when he is full of fear and anxiety that the trial of his alleged abuser, listed for later this month, will not proceed.
In Dublin Children’s Court on Tuesday, District Court president Paul Kelly had a list of 16 cases involving young people on charges including drugs, theft and travelling in stolen vehicles, with solicitors appearing in just three of those.
One solicitor participating in the services withdrawal represented, for no fee, a 17-year-old client who turns 18 in a few days and faced sentencing on six different charges involving different dates and gardaí.
The judge imposed a total sentence amounting to 10 months’ detention and expressed hope the youth, described as very vulnerable, would serve that in Oberstown rather than an adult prison.

title: Minister for Health says onus on everyone to ensure private care bills paid by insurers
description: Public Accounts Committee told €125m of insurance claims written off over four years in HSE hospitals
content:
It is “everybody’s responsibility” to ensure private health bills in public hospitals are paid, Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill has said.
The Oireachtas Public Accounts Committee (Pac) is due to hear that public hospitals are losing millions of euro a year due to unpaid bills from private health insurers.
Over the last four years across HSE -run and voluntary hospitals, €125.1 million has been written off in private insurance claims. In that time, €37.6 million has been lost as a result of the HSE not properly submitting claims to insurers.
Carroll MacNeill said she did not want to “ascribe fault”. “It’s everybody’s responsibility. But if there’s anybody there who hasn’t discharged their responsibility on that today, well, they really should because they really must,” she said.
The situation had come about because of a combination of factors, none of which were acceptable, she told Newstalk Breakfast on Wednesday. If private activity happened in a public hospital, which consultants were entitled to do, then it was important a consultant signed off on the insurance forms.
“It is very important the HSE have processed them and equally important that the insurance company pays them. And anywhere where that falls down is simply not acceptable. That’s taxpayers’ money,” the Minister said.
“You and I as taxpayers have built that hospital. We fund that hospital. And if there’s private activity legitimately happening ... the taxpayer must be recompensed for that”.
She said no one in particular was to blame. “The consultant has to make sure to sign it within a year. It has to be processed by the hospital and the HSE and the insurance company has to pay it,” she said.
On the issue of paid parking at public hospitals, Carroll MacNeill said there was a balance to be struck because it was important to make sure parking was accessible for patients and their families.
“We’ve 45 hospitals of different kinds around the country. Nine are completely free. And the other 36 all have a maximum daily charge,” she said, adding there a review was under way.
“A lot of them are contracted with private entities, including in [St] Vincent’s. And there’s a balance to be struck because we want to make sure it’s accessible and easy for patients,” she said.
“[But] you don’t want it used maybe by people looking for daily parking at a different price than you might get in the city centre.”

title: Ireland’s November internationals squad may contain a few surprises
description: Andy Farrell will announce his selections this afternoon
content:
“The Lord giveth and the Lord taketh away.” So says Gerry Thornley in his preview of the naming of the Irish squad for the November internationals by Andy Farrell this afternoon. The loss of the injured Caelan Doris and Jack Conan will be compensated somewhat by the return of Andrew Porter, Ryan Baird and Mack Hansen for the first time in almost a year. Will there be any surprises in the squad? Well, one “bolter” might well be Ulster outhalf and former England underage international Jamie Benson who qualifies for Ireland through his mother.
Alex Nankivell isn’t available to Andy Farrell just yet , but the Munster centre will be in two years’ time when he will qualify to play for Ireland. John Fallon talks to the New Zealander who has just signed a two-year contract extension with Munster.
Gordon D’Arcy looks back on the opening weekend of the Champions Cup and is encouraged by the tweaks to its format , the competition having struggled with “ugly duckling syndrome” until now. He was heartened too by the performances of all four Irish provinces in Europe, Connacht and Ulster having “the clearer picture” of how they want to play.
In football, Gavin Cummiskey takes you through the permutations for the title race and relegation battle in the League of Ireland with just two games left to play, Shamrock Rovers within touching distance of their sixth crown in seven seasons.
In Gaelic games, Gordon Manning talks to John Meyler, the chairman of the Hurling Expert Advisory Group, about the experimental rules that will soon be trialled in the game . There are plans too for an interprovincial hurling exhibition in Thurles at the end of November to showcase the changes.
Gordon also has word on the retirement from intercounty football of Roscommon’s Ultan Harney , the three-time Connacht senior football championship winner ending an 11-year career with his county.
And in his America At Large column, Dave Hannigan tells us the story of the Manchester City of the NBA, the LA Clippers . After being caught using shadow deals to circumvent spending rules, they were handed their punishment last month - and it’s hefty enough to all but guarantee that they won’t be competing for an NBA title any time soon.
TV Watch : There were goals galore in yesterday’s Champions League games, PSG , Manchester City and Liverpool managing 13 between them. We’ll see how today’s offerings go.
Manchester United are off to Italy where they will play the Cesc Fabregas-coached Como (Virgin Media Two and TNT Sports 2, 5.45pm) and at 8pm, Real Madrid host RB Leipzig (Virgin Media Two and TNT Sports 4) and Aston Villa play Norway’s Viking (TNT Sports 2). The tie of the day, though, looks like being Bayern Munich v Arsenal (RTÉ 2, Premier Sports 1 and TNT Sports 1).

title: All sides primed for a fight in Dáil over plans to scrap the triple lock
description: Inside Politics: Uproar in chamber as debate dredges up old wounds, while Jim O’Callaghan’s long war rumbles on
content:
TDs holding signs in the Dáil chamber proclaiming Save Neutrality! A big argument over the Dáil’s business for the week! Seán Russell and the Nazis!
It was lively stuff in the Dáil when the triple lock came up yesterday – and the main event isn’t even happening until today.
If there was ever an indication of the depth of feeling – or the political theatre, depending how you look at it – over Government plans to scrap the triple lock, it came at Leaders’ Questions on Tuesday. Whatever way you feel about the issue, it’s clear everyone is primed for a fight.
Sinn Féin attacked the Government for wanting to move towards “military adventurism”. The Taoiseach responded by saying he would take “no lectures” from a party that “once supported nazism” during the second World War.
Cue uproar, as Micheál Martin told the Dáil that Sinn Féin leaders “colluded with the Hitler regime and Seán Russell was the key person”, prompting much heckling and denials from Sinn Féin, with Eoin Ó Broin eagerly reminding the Taoiseach of De Valera’s condolences on Hitler’s death.
There followed a spirited row when the Dáil came to vote on its own business for the week – especially the 3½ hour debate on the triple lock legislation scheduled for later today (the Opposition wants more time for debate).
Some hours in the Dáil barely trundle along – this one crackled with energy. You’d only hope they saved some for today’s proceedings.
Read Marie O’Halloran’s write up of yesterday here . And anyone who needs a refresher on the triple lock can find it here , courtesy of political editor Pat Leahy.
Make no mistake about it, the passage of this legislation will be one of the big confrontations as we head into the winter.
The triple lock was one of two political rows punctuating the day yesterday – the second being Jim O’Callaghan’s long war against the criminal solicitors.
The Minister for Justice was before the Oireachtas justice committee, but was so keen on one of his attack lines (that solicitors had deliberately sought to affect rape trials with their withdrawal of services during a row over his reforms to criminal legal aid) that he let it slip on the Six One News on Monday, and in a widely leaked copy of his opening remarks to the committee.
The net effect was that the solicitors (plus Opposition politicians and even some Government ones too) had almost a full day to pillory the Minister .
Where does it leave us all? Well, nowhere closer to a resolution, that’s for sure. Intentional or not, O’Callaghan has shown an ability to stoke tensions around this long-running row – from his “crime doesn’t pay” jibe over summer, to this latest foray.
Who does the public back? In a choice between politicians and lawyers, perhaps neither. But patience for the long-running conflict is probably finite; sooner or later, they’ll want it sorted. And if it’s not, there may be plenty of blame to go around.
Here’s our front page piece on it this morning.
Our editorial points out that while solicitors and O’Callaghan face off, complainants, defendants and their families are caught in the middle.
Cui bono from the unrest in France ? asks Europe correspondent Naomi O’Leary. Michael McDowell is also writing on French disruption.
Kitty Holland writes about the impact of the ending of the Accommodation Recognition Payment for those hosting Ukrainians.
Read Mark Weiss on the Israeli elections here . Hot off the presses – Denis Staunton’s early morning take on Alberta’s hefty rejection of an independence vote in Canada.
Action in the Dáil starts at 9am with topical issues, before the second stage of Ruth Coppinger’s legislation on non-binary and intersex recognition. Leaders’ Questions, Other Members’ Questions and Questions on Policy or Legislation brings us up to lunchtime, when the State apology to the family of the late Brian Stack will take place.
In the evening, it’s hard to look past the debate on legislation scrapping the triple lock (mentioned above) as the main draw. Here’s the full schedule .
The Seanad sits from 10.30am with commencement matters. Government business is given over to legislation on media regulation and labelling of vapes in the afternoon. In the evening, there’s a motion on fuel costs from Sinn Féin senators. Here’s the full schedule .
The committees sit from 9.30am. Here’s what looks most lively:
Away from Kildare Street, a Supreme Court appeal of Paul Murphy’s super junior ministers legal challenge is getting under way.
The Global Bioeconomy Summit is on in the Convention Centre – the Taoiseach, Minister for Climate Darragh O’Brien, Minister for Agriculture Martin Heydon and former minister/former EU commissioner/possible UN food agency chief Phil Hogan will also be there.

title: Case struck out for man accused of taking part in fatal assault on Anthony Long in Dublin
description: Court
content:
A man accused of taking part in an assault on Dubliner Anthony Long, who died after being attacked in the summer, has had his case struck out.
Nathan Kenna (29) of The Nurseries, Mulhuddart, Dublin 15, was charged with assault causing harm to Long at Parslickstown Drive, Mulhuddart, on July 3rd.
The unemployed father was remanded in custody on July 20th after he became the second person charged in the incident.
His case had been adjourned several times for directions from the Director of Public Prosecutions.
However, the case was struck out at Cloverhill District Court on Tuesday when Judge Alan Mitchell noted that directions on the possibility of further charges were still unavailable.
On July 3rd, Long, in his 40s, attended a gathering at a house near his home when a confrontation broke out around 3.55am.
He was discovered with severe injuries and was rushed to hospital in a critical condition but died two days later.
At a bail hearing in August, Garda Sean Ó Fatharta agreed that a postmortem had established the deceased suffered “blunt and sharp force trauma” to his head.
It was alleged that Kenna, who allegedly had MMA training, acted in concert with a second male. The garda maintained that the accused attacked Long with punches and kicks, including a “roundhouse” kick, before the other man struck the victim on the head with a machete, rendering him unconscious.
Earlier, Darren McNamee (42), of Talbot Hall, Riverbank, Swords, north Dublin, was charged with the murder of Long, and he was remanded in custody.

title: Actor Christina Applegate reveals she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis
description: ‘I’m back at square one – I don’t know what’s going on with me’ says the Dead to Me star
content:
A fter becoming a prominent advocate for multiple sclerosis awareness and chronicling her struggles in an emotional memoir published in March, the Emmy-winning actor Christina Applegate has revealed she does not have the debilitating autoimmune disease after all.
Applegate (54) made the stunning announcement in an episode of her podcast MeSsy, recorded with fellow actor Jamie-Lynn Sigler, posted to YouTube on Tuesday.
“I’m back at square one – that I don’t know what’s going on with me,” she said through tears.
Applegate recalled the moment she found out about the misdiagnosis in a visit to her doctor.
“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations – you don’t have MS.’ I was not happy at all.
“You don’t get misdiagnosed, and all of a sudden I’m better. I haven’t gotten better, Jamie. If anything, I’ve gotten worse in some ways.
“I still have to use wheelchairs when I go to the doctor’s office. I can’t walk from the car to the room. I’m still in this. Nothing magical happened when she said, ‘You don’t have MS.’ Nothing magical happened.
“It’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down. It’s this weird feeling of like I became this, you and I, the poster children for MS. All that I did, everything that I was doing, I had a f**king reason as to why my day sucked every day.
“And now I don’t have a reason. It’s very unnerving and it’s really confusing for me.”
[ Celebrity Traitors: Is James Acaster the worst Traitor in the history of the show? Opens in new window ]
Applegate had revealed in 2021 that she was diagnosed with MS. In an interview with People magazine promoting her memoir, You With the Sad Eyes, she said was largely confined to bed because of her diagnosed condition.
She is known for her roles in the TV series Married ... With Children and Dead to Me – as well as the films Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy and Don’t Tell Mom the Babysitter’s Dead.
Applegate also worked on the TV show Friends and won a 2002 Emmy for outstanding guest acting in a comedy series.
She retired from acting two years after the 2021 MS diagnosis, when she wrapped up her role on Dead to Me.
Applegate had also stepped back over the last six months from the podcast with Sigler, who revealed in 2016 her own diagnosis of relapsing MS (RMS).
During that period, Applegate said in Tuesday’s episode, “a lot of interesting things happened to me”.
I’m sure people are saying like, ‘Crybaby, you don’t have MS, you know, that’s a good thing’ – but no, no, no
She recalled originally receiving her diagnosis in 2021, when a doctor showed her images of dozens of lesions on her brain and confirmed she had MS. “That was it, right? That was my answer to everything going on,” she said, saying she began to feel safe and welcome in the MS community as her treatment moved on.
“I had every symptom of someone with MS. Every single one.”
She said a study into her diagnosis began “a couple of years ago” after cell testing produced curious results. Now that she knows she does not have the disease, she said: “That’s going to be an online investigation my doctors are going to get into just to find out what has been happening since 2021. Why did this happen?”
Later in the episode, Sigler and Applegate discuss what they say is a trend of misdiagnoses.
“We have come to learn this is not that rare of an occurrence, especially when it comes to MS,” Sigler said.
Applegate added: “There’s a pretty damn high number of misdiagnoses with MS, and that’s after people have been going through the process of it, with the infusions, for many years.
“It’s clear now they’re finding something different, that something else is going on.”
Applegate said learning she doesn’t have the disease was challenging mentally.
“I’m sure people are saying like, ‘Crybaby, you don’t have MS, you know, that’s a good thing’ – but no, no, no,” she said.
“I’m sitting here having slept all day yesterday, feeling like absolute crap because of the heat. My legs aren’t working. You know, all the same stuff is happening to me, and yet I have this thing of like, well, you don’t have that, so maybe you’re faking it.
“In my head I’m like, what can I be doing differently? This is what I’m sure a lot of people start thinking when they get their misdiagnoses. It’s like, ‘Well, what have I done wrong? What am I doing?’”
Sigler told Applegate that she never let anybody down.
[ Tyson on Netflix: A jump scare during this series may deter some viewers from continuing Opens in new window ]
“Everything you did, and shared, and were, and are to so many people doesn’t go anywhere,” she said.
“Because of this misdiagnosis or this new information that you have in your life, that doesn’t take away anything that you did. You didn’t mislead anyone. In no way should you feel bad or uneasy about your continuing to share your journey with people.”
A 2024 Swiss-led study, published in the Multiple Sclerosis Journal, found “high-level evidence for high proportions of misdiagnosis and underdiagnoses of MS” – including a 15 per cent misdiagnosis rate in cases it looked at. – Guardian

title: Are breathalysers in pubs a good or bad idea?
description: Agency had sought tenders to provide devices so drinkers could test themselves
content:
The Minister who vetoed a plan by the Road Safety Authority (RSA) to install breathalysers in pubs and hotels has said it would have sent out the completely wrong message to road users.
Sean Canney , Minister of State for Road Safety, intervened on Tuesday upon learning through media reports that the RSA had sought tenders for the installation of the devices throughout the State. It is understood the value of the tender was about €1.5 million.
Canney said he was “taken aback” when he learned of the plan because it was not consistent with RSA’s clear message on alcohol – which is not to drink and drive.
“There was no point in spending money on something that was offering ambiguity,” Canney told The Irish Times on Tuesday.
“I know the right decision has been made to take down that procurement notice. The message it was sending out was wrong in my view.
“If the policy is ‘don’t drink and drive’, which is very straightforward, if you are saying to people in a pub or nightclub to take a breathalyser test, you are not being consistent with that message in my view.”
He said the money allowed to the project could be used for other initiatives such as education, communications and on-road safety ambassadors.
The idea behind the campaign is understood to have been to challenge to people on their perceptions of their level of impairment after consuming alcohol.

title: Man wanted in United States for possessing child pornography appeals extradition
description: Appellant, who went on the run in Ireland, claims ‘systematic’ overdetention in requesting state of Louisiana
content:
A US man who went on the run in Ireland after fleeing his home country before he could be sentenced for possessing child abuse material is appealing the High Court’s decision to order his extradition, arguing that prisoners in the requesting state of Louisiana are “systematically” detained beyond their release dates.
John Patrick Navarro’s senior counsel Mark Lynam told the Court of Appeal on Tuesday that the US department of justice had been “scathing” in a report it prepared on the issue.
He said in 2022, approximately a quarter of prisoners in Louisiana were overdetained, some by one or two months and others by more than a year. He said there were a “myriad” of reasons why this happened and it eventually resulted in the attorney general bringing proceedings against the Louisiana department of state corrections.
Navarro’s surrender to the United States is sought for the purpose of sentencing him on 11 counts in relation to the possession of pornography involving juveniles.
The 37-year-old had pleaded guilty to the offences on February 6th, 2018, in the criminal district court for the parish of Orleans, Louisiana. He was legally represented by his attorney at that time.
After pleading guilty, Navarro was granted bail and his case was listed for sentencing in February 2018. However, he failed to appear on that date and a domestic arrest warrant was issued two months later.
The US issued an extradition request to the Irish authorities in December 2024 and Navarro was brought before the High Court on foot of a warrant for his arrest the following April.
His surrender, which had been opposed, was ordered by Judge Sean Gillane in July 2026. He found that Navarro had not established that a real risk of a violation of his fundamental human rights arises.
Appealing this decision on Tuesday, Lynam said the focus of the extradition proceedings had been overdetention in Louisiana, where he said prisoners were systematically being held for longer than they should have been as a result of “defects in the system”.
He contended that Gillane erred when assessing the risk of a breach of his client’s rights if surrendered. Counsel argued the judge was wrong to disregard evidence of overdetention in Louisiana on the basis that a specific assurance had been given that Navarro would not be held beyond his lawful release date.
He said in accepting the assurances given by the requesting state, the court failed to recognise that this must still be weighted against any specific, up-to-date information that Navarro faces a real risk of breach of rights.
The barrister pointed to an expert report from Prof Andrea C Armstrong, a professor of law at Loyola University, New Orleans, which highlighted several ongoing cases aimed at preventing prisoners from being overdetained. Counsel said there was also a class-action lawsuit in Louisiana challenging this, which he said remains a “live issue”.
In response, Ronan Kennedy, for the Attorney General, said the judge hadn’t simply accepted the assurance provided but rather had engaged in a “detailed, factual analysis”. He said the judge carried out a rigorous examination of all the material and information before him in accordance with the law.
Kennedy submitted that the preponderance of the evidence before the High Court related to historic issues of overdetention in the requesting state, which predated numerous reforms implemented by the Louisiana department of public safety and corrections.
Kennedy said the height of Navarro’s case was that there was “no evidence of the reforms”. However, counsel said that while this wasn’t “publicly available”, information about the reforms – including those introduced in February 2026 – had been provided to the court and that information hadn’t been challenged by Navarro.
He said the High Court made a finding of fact, which was open to it to make, that Navarro had not established a real risk of being subjected to inhuman or degrading treatment or would be unlawfully deprived of his liberty if surrendered.
He asked the court to dismiss the appeal.
Judge Patrick McCarthy, sitting with Judge Alexander Owens and Judge Paul Burns, said the court would reserve judgment.

title: ‘Nowhere left to go’: Beluga whale off Ireland amid growing sightings of Arctic species
description: ‘It is mad to think that now we have a species of whale in Irish waters that is the food of polar bears’
content:
A beluga whale, a species that normally lives in the freezing waters of the Arctic and sub-Arctic, was spotted in Donegal Bay on Saturday.
Pádraig Whooley, sightings officer with the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group (IWDG), said “our latitudes are not the natural home for beluga whales”.
On October 17th, Sebastian Szumlański was at Fintra in Donegal Bay, where he recorded drone footage of the whale that was later shared with the IWDG.
There have been at least four previous reported sightings of Beluga whales around the Irish coast, with the first known dating back to 1948 off Clare Island in Co Mayo.
The video from Donegal Bay was the IWDG’s second ever validated record; the first was off Dunseverick, Co Antrim, in 2015.
However, Whooley said the whale’s presence did not mean it was “trying to make Ireland its home”. He said the beluga was an adult, which was known because the whales were “born quite dark and they pale with age”.
He said the whale spotted in Donegal Bay was “absolutely brilliant white”.
Adult belugas can reach up to 5m in length. Whooley said the one spotted looked to be 4m-4½m long.
He said many such whales had scars from polar-bear attacks.
“It is mad to think that now we have a species of whale in Irish waters that is the food of polar bears,” he said. “It is just a little bit of a trend that we’re beginning to see that we are writing more and more of these articles about these Arctic animals that are turning up in Irish waters.
Though “still very infrequent”, Whooley said there were a lot of sightings of the bowhead whale, the walrus, the narwhal and the belugas.
“Sightings of these animals are, you know, becoming more frequent. We’re seeing them more frequently ... the interval gap is narrowing,” he said.
“There are big changes out there ... we’re losing some species that perhaps used to be more common. We’re also starting to see more species that we almost never saw before.
“It’s very dynamic out there. Things are changing and it’s the rapid rate with which things are changing.”
Beluga whales belong to the same family as narwhals. In 2025, a juvenile, female narwhal became stranded on Sweet Nellies Beach, north of Greencastle on the Inishowen Peninsula in Co Donegal.
Whooley said the beluga whale sighting was “coinciding with really bad weather”, citing Storm Austen .
“The big storm won’t make any difference to the whale but it’ll impact our ability to actually observe the animal and to try and monitor it from the shoreline.”
Whooley said the nearest population of Arctic belugas was probably Svarlbard, a northern Norwegian territory – all marine species “are on the move”.
“The trend is that everything is pushing farther and farther north because everything is looking for cooler water because most fish have a preference for cool water,” he said.
“So when the fish are tracking north and I’m talking about, you know, species like mackerel and herring and stuff like that, that are really important for whales, as they’re tracking north, the predators are following after them.
“But what do you do when you live on the top of the world? You can’t go north. There is no north. When you live in the North Pole already, there is nowhere left for you to go.
[ ‘A beautiful animal’: Shark fishing needs more regulation and training, expert says Opens in new window ]
“The only place for you to go, if your habitat breaks down, is to drop south and that is why we are starting to see more of these Arctic species in warmer waters because there is literally nowhere left for them to go and that is a problem of their geography.”
[ What changes in butterfly populations tell us about climate change in Ireland Opens in new window ]
Whooley asked members of the public who had seen any species of whale or dolphin to report their sightings to the IWDG here .

title: Netflix sales growth to slow for fourth quarter
description: Projection amplifies concerns about performance of streaming service
content:
Netflix reported its slowest sales jump in three years and forecast a fourth consecutive quarter of slowing growth, a projection that amplifies concerns about the world’s leading online TV network.
Netflix delivered sales of $12.9 billion (€11.5 billion) in the third quarter, in line with Wall Street’s expectations, and forecast sales of $13.4 billion in the year’s final three months, falling short of what analysts have predicted. The pace of growth has fallen from 17.6 per cent in the final quarter of last year to a projection of 11.5 per cent for this year’s fourth quarter.
The company blamed its sales shortfall on the advertising business, which is on pace to deliver $300 million less than the company expected.
Shares fell as much as 7 per cent in trading after the results were announced.
“I know we can do better,” Netflix co-chief executive Greg Peters said on a call with analysts Tuesday. “That better is our upside.”
Over the past week, Peters and co-CEO Ted Sarandos have overhauled the company’s leadership to address what they see as a decline in programming quality. Netflix fired chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film chief Dan Lin just days after announcing cuts of 6 per cent of the staff, or about 1,000 people. The last time Netflix made such substantial reductions was in 2022, when it reported its first quarterly subscriber loss in more than 10 years.
The company’s operating margin forecast for the fourth quarter of 26 per cent is impacted by costs associated with the job cuts. Earnings of 87 cents per share in the third quarter exceeded analysts’ projections for 82 cents.
Sarandos and Peters are walking a tightrope, seeking to assure investors that the company has a bright future while acknowledging things aren’t going as well as everyone would like. Netflix remains a clear leader in streaming. It has more than 325 million subscribers, which the company says equates to almost 1 billion viewers. It accounts for more viewing than any other Hollywood streaming service.
But Hollywood studios don’t overhaul their programming teams when everything is hunky dory. Netflix has gone months without a large, culture-shaping hit in film or TV and has struggled to lure viewers to both new shows and new seasons of older shows. Netflix’s haul of Emmy Awards fell to a 10-year low in 2026.
Sarandos and Peters brought in Peter Rice, a veteran film and TV executive who previously served as chairman of general entertainment at Walt Disney Co, and before that as president of 21st century Fox, to replace Bajaria.
“We see an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in the US,” Sarandos said, touting Rice’s experience in all aspects of entertainment. Rice has worked in film and TV as both an executive and a producer. He also has deep relationships with top filmmakers.
“We want Netflix to always be the place people want to do the best work of their life,” Sarandos said.
Long a Wall Street darling, Netflix has faced growing scepticism ever since it made a play to buy the streaming and studios businesses of Warner Bros Discovery.
After losing out in its bid, Netflix has struggled to convince investors it has a viable growth strategy. The stock is down about 25 per cent this year and more than 40 per cent from a year ago.
Investors and analysts have pestered Netflix’s leadership about stagnant engagement. Netflix’s share of US TV viewership sits at 7.8 per cent, according to ratings tracker Nielsen, far behind YouTube, which captures about 14 per cent. And Netflix viewers watched only 2 per cent more programming in the first half of the year than a year earlier.
As Netflix has grown from a small US streaming service into a global behemoth, it has evolved from a producer of “prestige TV” shows like House of Cards and The Crown to a broader entertainment platform, competing with everything from sports channels to YouTube influencers.
Bajaria led the division that released hits like Squid Game and Wednesday, and helped shepherd Netflix’s live programming era with sports and an expanded unscripted portfolio.
But Bajaria’s hot touch cooled over the last year, and many began to question the quality of Netflix’s programming.
“Investors will need, in short order, some indications toward confidence in the growth trajectory that this powerful, global platform should be able to provide,” David Joyce, an analyst at Seaport Research Partners, said in a note before the results were released.
Netflix is seeking to increase the amount of time its users spend on the service by expanding into live sports, podcasts and video games while also integrating film and TV programming from third parties like TF1 in France. Peters said the company is open to integrating programming from other companies and will also look to sell other streaming services within Netflix. -Bloomberg

title: SpaceX and Tesla boards explore potential merger
description: Elon Musk says combining his two public companies would be a ‘good idea’ as the world approaches an AI singularity
content:
SpaceX and Tesla are studying a deal to unite Elon Musk’s two public companies in a multitrillion-dollar combination that would be the largest merger of all time.
The world’s richest person on Tuesday said both companies had formed special committees to study a tie-up. It marks the biggest step towards a merger that would create a sprawling conglomerate oriented around AI and potentially worth more than $3 trillion (€2.67 trillion.
“Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes. But at the end of the day the shareholders have to be supportive of this,” Musk said, adding that as chief executive of both companies he cannot participate in the discussions.
“The special committees have not reached agreement on the terms of any transaction, and obviously there is no guarantee that they will,” he added.
SpaceX has a market value of $2 trillion, while Tesla is worth nearly $1.5 trillion. On paper, combining the seventh and 11th most valuable companies in the world would vault Amazon and leave the new entity behind only Microsoft, Alphabet, Apple and Nvidia.
The electric-car maker has deepened its ties with SpaceX in recent years. In March, Musk announced a joint venture called Terafab, a large semiconductor manufacturing plant in Texas that will produce chips for his autonomous vehicles, humanoid robots and orbital artificial intelligence (AI) data centres that could ultimately cost $119 billion.
“There is a lot of merit to combining the two companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” Musk said.
The two companies have also teamed up to produce a “flying” sports car called Roadster, unveiled last week. It performed a series of inverted backflips and jumps using cold-gas thrusters developed by SpaceX. Musk’s AI model Grok is provided for free in many Tesla vehicles.
“There is a lot to be gained from co-operating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab, robotics, mass to orbit with the [Starlink] constellation connectivity,” Musk said. He has previously rolled the social media platform X and his AI lab, xAI, into SpaceX.
Tesla shares rose about 1.5 per cent after hours, while those of SpaceX climbed 8 per cent after it reported strong earnings.
SpaceX said its revenue more than doubled in the third quarter, swinging the company into profit and calming investor nerves about accelerating spending on AI.
Revenue surged 161 per cent to $14.6 billion in the third quarter, up from $5.6 billion a year ago and beating analysts’ estimates of $12.9 billion, the company said.
SpaceX posted a net profit of $4.4 billion in the three months to the end of September, exceeding Wall Street’s expectations of about $2 billion. It made a net loss of $1.1 billion in the same period last year.
The outperformance was driven by sales of cloud computing services, with revenue from AI surging ninefold to $7.6 billion from $813mn a year ago and tripling from $2.56 billion in the previous quarter.
SpaceX continued to spend heavily on AI. Capital expenditure rose to $19.6 billion from $18.4 billion in the prior quarter and more than consensus estimates of $18 billion compiled by Factset.
The vast majority of that investment was on data centres and chips, and Musk said capex would climb again to between $35 billion and $40 billion in the fourth quarter – much more than analysts expected.
Musk has rapidly transformed the company into an AI data centre provider, striking deals to lease its excess computing capacity. Rival model developers, notably Anthropic and Google, have proven willing to pay premium prices to secure access to the chips needed to train and run their models.
Musk said he was being “hounded relentlessly by every hyperscaler and dozens of smaller companies to rent more of our compute. We could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone.”
SpaceX said it had 1.7 gigawatts of installed computing capacity at the end of September. The size of its pair of Colossus data centres now surpasses the 1.5GW of active power that CoreWeave, the largest listed “neocloud”, had online at the end of June.
On a call with investors, Musk said he would be “surprised” if SpaceX did not have 13GW by the end of next year, with a “small, non-zero possibility” that capacity could reach 20GW. That is roughly equivalent to twice the peak power consumption of New York City.
A computer-generated video of SpaceX’s Starship landing back on Earth
Musk’s opportunistic move into renting out data centres has grown into a lucrative business but has led to concerns that SpaceX’s internal AI efforts are failing to gain traction.
The earnings report is the second since the rocket-and-AI group raised $86 billion in the largest initial public offering ever in June at a $2 trillion valuation. The shares initially surged but have tumbled from a peak of $225 in the week after going public to $148 on Tuesday.
Revenue from Starlink, its 11,000-strong network of broadband satellites, rose to $5.2 billion from $3 billion the year before, and it reported net income of $2.4 billion in the quarter.
SpaceX has recently become embroiled in tensions between Ukraine and the Trump administration. Starlink terminals used by Ukrainian forces have been hit by speed limitations that disrupted the ability to deploy drones, which President Volodymyr Zelenskiy blamed on a “planned operation ... to restrict us”.
SpaceX’s launch business rose to $1.8 billion in revenue, but it made a small loss during the period. Last month, its skyscraper-sized rocket Starship reached orbit for the first time, deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites that it says will significantly increase the network’s capacity.
The 400ft rocket is core to Musk’s sci-fi ambitions to build a network of orbital AI data centres, start a lunar economy and colonise Mars. On Tuesday, he said SpaceX would attempt to catch the booster and spacecraft stages with mechanical “Mechazilla” arms during the next test flight in November. -Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Government wants HSE to cap hospital parking fee at €10 a day
description: Minister tells Dáil committee that health service will carry out new national review of charges
content:
The Government wants the HSE to implement recommendations dating back eight years to limit hospital car parking charges to €10 per day.
Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill said the HSE would carry out a national review, due to be completed in the first quarter of next year, of the parking fees, which generated €17.8 million last year.
In a letter to the Dáil’s Public Accounts Committee , she said four hospitals around the country currently charged more than €10 per day for patients and visitors.
Committee chairman and Sinn Féin TD John Brady has previously said St Vincent’s hospital in Dublin has the highest car parking charges, with a daily cap of €17.
In her letter, the Minister said the HSE review would look at “relevant matters including the balance between affordability measures and broader reductions in charges; the financial implications of any proposed changes, and sustainable funding options where required”.
Carroll MacNeill said Department of Health secretary general Derek Tierney had written to the HSE chief executive Anne O’Connor asking that it give effect to key outstanding recommendations arising from a review of car parking charges carried out in 2018.
“This includes progressing the recommended maximum daily charge of €10 and ensuring that flexible passes, multi-entry arrangements or appropriate concession arrangements are available across all hospitals,” she said.
“The Department will continue to engage with the HSE as this work progresses, including in relation to the practical options identified by the review group and any next steps arising from its work.”
Figures provided in response to a parliamentary question last month show that more than €73.5 million has been generated by hospital car park fees since 2020.
Cork University Hospital (CUH) brought in the highest revenues in this period (€11.97 million), followed by St James’s Hospital (€8.83 million) and Beaumont Hospital in Dublin (€5.96 million) and University Hospital Limerick (€5.92 million).
Carroll MacNeill said the HSE maintained that revenue from hospital car parks was used for a range of purposes, including the maintenance and upgrading of parking facilities, repayment of loans associated with such upgrades, investment in site security and, where relevant, support for the overall hospital budget.
The Programme for Government pledges to “explore further ways to reduce hospital car parking charges” and the HSE has said it wants to ensure the recommended maximum daily charge of €10, alongside flexible, multi-entry and concession arrangements, are “in place across all hospitals”.
Carroll MacNeill said the latest review would “build on” the 2018 exercise and “examine relevant matters including the balance between affordability measures and broader reductions in charges”.
It would also assess “the financial implications of any proposed changes, and sustainable funding options where required” and site-specific issues such as “infrastructure, demand pressures and contractual arrangements”, she added.

title: ‘He never saw it coming’: Families of ‘one punch’ victims seek tougher measures
description: Families call for public awareness campaign similar to Australia’s ‘coward punch’ initiative
content:
A public awareness campaign similar to a successful “coward punch” campaign in Australia should be introduced to address the issue of unprovoked assaults, an Oireachtas committee has been told.
Ireland is letting down a generation of young men by allowing the online glorification of violence to go unchallenged, said Bryan Gallagher, whose 26-year-old brother Cian died after he was punched by a stranger in Tallow, Co Waterford, in November 2022.
He was giving evidence on Tuesday to the Oireachtas Committee on Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, which is preparing a report on the issue of unprovoked or “one-punch” assaults, and how those convicted of such crimes are treated in the courts.
“To hear that the man responsible for killing your son and brother boasted about what he had done and compared himself to a well-known Irish mixed martial arts fighter sums up the fundamental issue with unprovoked violence, and gives weight to the very complex issue of the definition of masculinity and the role models men are facing in Irish society,” Gallagher said.
On the night his brother was left lying “on the cold, wet ground”, three young men had stopped to help him, he said.
“They did not walk past. They did not take out their phones, video it and post it online. They showed integrity, compassion and they protected Cian.”
“Those three young men are genuine role models to all men young and old across this country. Yet their names and actions will never be shared millions of times or glorified on social media,” Gallagher said.
“We need to ask ourselves, who do we want as role models for our young men in Ireland?”
Unprovoked violence, he said, was not confined to any one group or social background. Young men from vulnerable backgrounds should not be made scapegoats, as unprovoked assaults were carried out by men of all ages and backgrounds.
Gallagher co-founded a campaign group called Walkaway, Siúil Leat, with Sharon Lynn, whose only sibling, Martin, died three days after being assaulted in Whitehall, Dublin , in July 2023. The group is calling for a public awareness campaign, improved collection of relevant data and greater supports for victims’ families in the courts system.
Lynn, who also addressed the committee, said her brother had come home in a taxi after a night out when he was assaulted outside his home by a man who got off his motorcycle because he thought the taxi had obstructed him.
The man “approached Martin in a rage and punched him, knocking him to the ground. Martin’s hands were in his pockets. He never saw it coming,” she said.
Her family was “devastated” over the sentence her brother’s killer received, which meant he would only serve four years in prison.
She said she would like to see greater consistency in sentencing decisions, greater transparency and stronger recognition of victims’ families within the justice system.
The families should be entitled to access the transcripts of court sentencing decisions, she said.
In her brother’s case, she had been so “overwhelmed” over what happened at the sentencing hearing that she could not recall what the judge said, and yet was told she was not entitled to see the transcript.
Gallagher said changes in the language used to describe unprovoked violence should be part of a public awareness campaign. Such campaigns had been successful in other jurisdictions. “There is no need to reinvent the wheel.”
Reena Sarkar, an academic at Monash University, Australia, told the committee that, in Australia, changing the language around unprovoked assaults had a significant impact. “Nobody wanted to glorify the behaviour.”

title: Two killed by Russian drones near Ukraine’s Kharkiv, governor says
description: US envoy Steve Witkoff due in St Petersburg for talks with Vladimir Putin after meeting Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Norway on Tuesday
content:
Russian drones killed ‌two people near Ukraine ’s second-largest city of Kharkiv ​overnight, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said on Telegram on Wednesday.
Another 11 people suffered ​stress reactions in the attack that struck private ⁠houses and caused other damage, ‌he ‌said.
In ​Ukraine’s capital of Kyiv, a Russian air strike hit ⁠a high-storey ​apartment building and ​transport infrastructure, causing fires, mayor Vitalii ‌Klitschko said on Telegram.
