There ​was also a strike on ⁠a university ⁠in ​Kremenchuk in the Poltava region that injured two, local authorities said.
The ‌Russian defence ministry said ‌on Wednesday its drones had hit ​a cargo vessel carrying military cargo to Ukraine ​en route to the ⁠port of Odessa.
The ‌ministry also said ​its forces had ⁠hit ⁠a warehouse complex ​used for drone storage in the central Ukrainian city of Poltava, and an ‌electric power ⁠substation, which supplies power to Ukrainian ‌defence and industrial sector ​as well as ​logistics centres in Kyiv.
The fresh strikes came in advance of a meeting scheduled between US envoy Steve Witkoff ‌and Russian president ⁠Vladimir Putin on Wednesday.
A US official said Witkoff had “constructive” talks ‌with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Norway ​on Tuesday. – Reuters

title: Oil rises on Middle East supply fears
description: Falling US crude and product inventories lend support to prices
content:
Oil prices gained over $1 on Wednesday as ​escalating Middle East tensions fuelled fears of supply disruptions, while falling US crude and product inventories lent support to the market.
Brent crude futures rose $1.59, or 1.5 per cent, to $110.38 per barrel as of 0350 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude gained $1.36, or 1.4 per cent, to $99.18 per barrel.
Prices fell in ​the previous trading session after Iran’s president discussed mediation efforts in a meeting with Pakistan’s army chief in Tehran, though Brent hit a five-month high ⁠before easing.
“Oil prices have been having a bit of wild ride in the last couple of sessions,” ‌said ‌Suvro ​Sarkar, head of energy research at DBS.
“We believe this is a mix of profit taking and optimistic hopes of a Qatar- or Pakistan-brokered deal, countered by the realisation that ⁠any deal is still very distant ​and compounded further by inventory data from the American Petroleum ​Institute (API), which shows drawdowns continuing in the US for both crude and products.”
Iran told Pakistan’s army chief there would ‌be no talks with Washington until its demands ​were met, Iranian media outlet Nournews reported on Tuesday, adding that a Qatari delegation had arrived in Tehran. There ⁠was no official confirmation of the reports.
Maritime security ⁠risks are also escalating. ​Shiptracker Kpler said on Monday that at least 18 vessel attacks were recorded over the past two weeks, while LSEG analysts warned Iran was targeting tankers well beyond the Strait of Hormuz, reaching into the Gulf of Oman and jeopardising Gulf crude loadings and the ship-to-ship transfers supporting regional loadings.
In Saudi Arabia, the Houthis on Monday claimed responsibility for attacks on a Saudi Aramco site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield and Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh and Abha airports.
The death toll from a Houthi attack on Yemeni government forces ‌on Monday rose to 73 ⁠as fighting intensified.
Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said in a television interview aired on Tuesday that Iran has not received a response from Saudi Arabia or Yemen’s Houthis to its offer ‌to help broker peace talks.
In the US, two Energy Department officials said on Tuesday they were working with refiners around the world to ​boost fuel output as a diesel shortage has raised prices.
According to market sources ​citing API data, US crude stocks fell by 4.9 million barrels in the week ended October 16th. - Reuters

title: Alberta vote boosts Mark Carney but referendum leaves Canada weaker
description: Prime minister gets breathing space to pursue international goals, such as closer ties with European Union
content:
Alberta ’s three-to-one vote to remain part of Canada was an emphatic rejection of independence and a welcome boost for Mark Carney.
But the referendum has left Canada weaker and more polarised.
Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney welcomed the 76 per cent to 24 per cent vote against independence this week as a clear choice by his fellow Albertans.
“They chose unity, to build together and to take care of each other,” he said.
“Canada is greater than the sum of its parts.”
The big margin of victory has taken Albertan independence off the table for the foreseeable future and the province’s premier, Danielle Smith, who called the referendum, said she would not be putting the issue to a vote again. And she acknowledged actions Carney has taken to address some long-held Albertan grievances, including the fast-tracking of approval for a new pipeline.
“I am well aware that not every grievance Alberta has with Ottawa has been resolved. There are still many political and constitutional battles ahead of us,” she said.
“But I am also convinced that the federal government is no longer targeting and trying to phase out and eliminate Alberta’s largest economic sectors as they attempted to do under the previous prime minister.”
The independence vote was one of 10 measures put to referendum in Alberta on Monday and all but one of the others looked set for approval as the final votes were tallied. Those approved included proposals for curbs on immigration , the exclusion of immigrants from health and social welfare programmes and the charging of fees to immigrants with permanent residency for the cost of their families’ healthcare and education.
Other proposals Albertans approved that will require constitutional change in Canada would abolish the country’s senate and give the provinces control over appointments of judges to their courts. The only proposal that looked set for defeat would have allowed Alberta to opt out of some federal programmes without losing access to federal funds for use in social programmes it would design itself.
Some of the anti-immigration proposals were inspired by the example of Quebec , which reached an agreement with the federal government in 1991 to gain exclusive control over the selection of economic migrants. Quebec held referendums on independence in 1980 and 1985 and the proposal was rejected on both occasions.
The pro-independence Parti Québécois won an election in the French-speaking province this month but fell short of an overall majority. The party had promised a third independence referendum but in a minority government it will be unable to fulfil the pledge, which it said would in any case wait until Donald Trump leaves office in the United States.
Independence may be off the agenda for now in Alberta and Quebec, offering Carney the breathing space he needs to pursue his international goals, including closer relations with the European Union. But the result of Alberta’s other referendums suggests underlying grievances and discontent within Canada’s federation will persist.

title: Cheaper HSE drugs, and are women in your workplace earning less?
description: Business Today: The best news, analysis and comment from The Irish Times business desk
content:
Ireland’s health system saves about €239 million annually by using cheaper copies of expensive biological drugs, according to one pharma executive. However, Diane DiGangi Trench, country head and general manager for Swiss drug company Sandoz’s UK and Ireland division, says that greater use of so-called biosimilars could unlock almost another €150 million in savings for the HSE. Eoin Burke-Kennedy reports.
By the end of November, all employers with more than 50 employees must publish data about their gender pay gap to a new public gender pay gap portal. Joanne Hunt writes that the data will lift the lid on gaps in pay and equip you to find out whether women in your workplace are earning less than men.
When developers say that a project isn’t ‘viable’, are they saying it is not profitable or just that another project would be even more profitable? Viability and profitability are not the same thing, writes John McManus in his latest column . Grasping the difference is the key to understanding why developers are pulling resources from Dublin’s office market and pumping them into hotels.
Sticking with commercial property, Irish retail property investor Signature Capital is looking to dispose of two flagship Avoca premises that it acquired for €22 million in 2017 from the retailer’s owner, Aramark. Ronald Quinlan has the details.
Anyone planning to put their money to work through the Government’s new tax-efficient investment account scheme will still pay stamp duty of 1 per cent, Joe Brennan reports , if they want to invest directly in Irish public companies with market caps of more than €1 billion. Currently, there are 11 companies on the Euronext Dublin above the threshold, but it also applies to large Irish companies listed overseas like CRH.
Joe also has the story that Pepper Advantage is planning a rebrand. The UK-headquartered business, which is used by firms that acquired problem Irish loans after the property crash, will become Continuum Credit Group in January, while its Irish loan servicing business will be renamed Engage Credit Ireland.
After their initial plans were rebuffed, a company owned by the family of veteran developer Paddy Kelly has scaled back its plans for a housing development on the site of two cottages in south county Dublin. Stephen Conneely has the story.
Paddy Power owner Flutter will cut 240 jobs from its Irish head office as it grapples with rising British betting taxes, Barry O’Halloran writes. The group said on Tuesday that it planned to cut about 1,400 jobs in its UK and Ireland division to counter the impact of British government tax rises set to cost it $540 million (€480 million).
Meanwhile, Conor Pope reports on stark new figures from the Banking and Payments Federation of Ireland, which reveal that almost half of young adults have been approached to use their bank account to transfer money for so-called money-muling purposes . Some €7 million was laundered through Irish accounts in this fashion in the 12 months to the end of June.

title: ‘I am married with two kids, but I drunkenly embraced a colleague at a work party’
description: Tell Me About It: ‘I get along very well with her, but I had never thought about her in a romantic context’
content:
I am in a job that I really like and have worked here for a number of years. I am married with two kids.
Our workplace recently had an annual summer party, which was held on the other side of the country. It involved an overnight stay. There was a lot of karaoke singing and drinking involved and, long story short, I ended up drunkenly embracing one of my colleagues.
She has a long-term partner. No one else in the team knows about what happened. My colleague is someone I have known for years, and we get along very well, but I had never thought about her in a romantic context. Due to working-from-home arrangements, we don’t see each other very often in person. She hasn’t mentioned what happened between us since that night. I suspect she doesn’t want to make anything of it either. And I don’t want to blow up my life by telling my wife what happened.
This question is really one where context matters – is this event indicative of a lessening of intimate relationships with your wife and so it looms large in your consciousness, or is it something flirtatious that happened as a once-off?
The fact that you are writing about it suggests that this is important and deserving of attention in your life and it feels to you that you are withholding something from your wife. If this feels like a secret that might explode your marriage, then it is worth considering what gives it such power and intensity.
Loyalty and fidelity are recognised as cornerstones of marriage – your vows probably mentioned both commitments – and you are feeling that you have breached one or both of these. But again, it might be worth looking at the context.
In work we meet people who are like-minded, share similar goals and with whom we form strong connections, and it can be easy to misinterpret these good feelings when drink is involved. Indeed, a type of love can exist in the workplace, but it is good to respect it for what it is and not cross boundaries, particularly when other lives are involved. Sex and desire are strong, natural drives, but without the containment of good judgment, they can bubble to the surface, overflow and create havoc.
[ ‘I recently met a fantastic man through work. He is divorced, but I am married’ Opens in new window ]
Your good judgment is required now to ascertain what meaning this event has, what truth needs to be disseminated and what learning or outcome you want to take from it.
Is your marriage in trouble, or sliding towards distance?
Is your body drawing you towards another, or are you surprised by what happened?
It might be important to investigate this with your wife so that you are both participants in creating and shaping whatever future you have together. Of course, there is a risk here – that of questioning the relationship contributing to its demise.
However, all relationships need resetting and engagement to keep them vibrant and alive. You both need to look at secrets and how they impact your relationship; you both get to decide what needs to be disclosed and how the relationship handles these rough spots.
Any relationship can cope with disclosure if the basis is solid and there is a foundation of faith in its endurance and resilience. If the foundation is fragile, care needs to be taken to build trust and confidence, and the starting point for this is vulnerability and openness. You are clearly disconcerted about the work event, and it has perhaps exposed fractures that need to be addressed.
[ ‘My wife, who I love and adore, has emotionally abandoned our relationship’ Opens in new window ]
Pretending or hoping that these can be papered over is a short-term solution that perpetuates the ongoing underlying issue and so you will be confronted with something similar again in the future. With two kids, it might be difficult to find the time to start the conversation, and it might be better not to begin when both of you are tired, late at night when the children are in bed.
Could you organise sitters for a Saturday morning and both of you go for a walk and coffee?
Ask your wife how she thinks the relationship is going, how she sees your current positioning and what she sees as potential rifts. If you can, be honest about your concerns and do not try to fix everything too fast. It is good to tolerate the uncomfortable reality and to trust that solutions will only emerge after ongoing discussions and reflections. If your wife hears your commitment to the long haul, she will have enough faith to engage and see this situation through.
Your work event highlighted a difficulty in your marriage that was below the surface for you. However, there is the possibility that your flirtation was actually a real pull away from your marriage.
If you are giving consideration to this then it would be worth engaging with a psychotherapist to help you unravel what is going on. (Look up the Irish Council for Psychotherapy or the Psychological Society of Ireland for accredited professionals.)

title: Open days: Parents need to know the difference between encouraging a child and deciding for them
description: Guardians can research the multiple choices available and act as a sounding board, but an independent decision is key to success
content:
Deciding which college or course to take at the age of 17 or 18 is one of those life-changing moments. It will likely, but not definitively, affect the trajectory of a person’s 20s, if not their life.
It’s a difficult decision and it doesn’t always come down to the cost and logistics of a commute or rent. While these practical matters will possibly sway opinions on one course over another, it comes down to interest, intent, passion and ultimately career.
How can a school leaver make that choice without it becoming a somewhat pressurised decision?
Parents most often step in and help balance the conversation with their personal insights into college life, affordability and learning ability.
But where is the line between encouraging a young adult to take a course because you deem it suitable to their skills and talents, and supporting their instinct and interest for something else?
There is a significant difference in being a “supporter” for your school leaver and a “decision maker”. A parent’s role is to support them, encourage them to explore and give them the confidence to make their own decisions.
“Parents are the single biggest influence on what a young person chooses after the Leaving Cert,” says Emma McEvoy, commercial director at whichcollege.ie . “We see it every year. Parents researching courses, entry requirements and costs with their teenagers. The challenge is that many parents are going on their own experience of college, and today’s options, from apprenticeships and PLC courses to whole new degree areas, look very different.”
Researching the multiple choices available for your young adult is almost an education in itself, so be prepared to learn about the new dynamics of education. Start early if you envisage it to be as overwhelming for you as it could be for your teenager. McEvoy suggests that the families who do best in troubleshooting this decision, start in fourth or fifth year rather than waiting for the CAO deadline, which allows a decision to be made when calm and relatively unstressed.
A parents’ involvement matters because, as McEvoy says “picking the wrong course is one of the main reasons students don’t make it past first year. The key is to support, not decide. Parents know their teenager’s strengths and temperament better than anyone, so they’re well placed to act as a sounding board and widen the options rather than steer towards one path.”
[ As the class of 2026 begins college, a masked shadow lingers Opens in new window ]
Noya Fernandez del Cotero, director of Student Recruitment at UCD, believes parents should attend college open days with their school leavers, particularly when they are first exploring different colleges and the many course options available. “The college system, vast course choices, qualifications, and the application process can be unfamiliar to both students and parents, so attending together gives parents a better understanding of the options and allows them to provide informed support,” she says.
“I also think teenagers should have the opportunity to explore options independently and with friends at college open days. Friends may ask questions they might not think of themselves, although there is a risk of being influenced by what their peers consider ‘cool’ rather than what suits them personally.”
Camille Rocca, NCAD Student recruitment manager, agrees that college open days are for everyone and that parents and peers alike can bring great questions. NCAD encourages that kind of bold and curious thinking. They host their open day on a midweek so that prospective students can see the studios in full swing.
”Many students visit with their school, led by an Art, DCG, or Guidance teacher,” says Rocca. “Others come alone or with a friend. Everyone is welcome. And many parents step back once their teenager settles in, but still enjoy the day. Open days add something different. You feel the atmosphere and see the facilities. Student life is about so much more than what you learn. You become part of a community.”
Parents are natural worriers when it comes to their children’s future and a decision they may deem risky or unrealistic may in fact be the making of them. Rocca has recognised that “people succeed best if they study what they are genuinely curious to know more about”.
Added to that, every course brings additional, possibly unexpected, skills. As Rocca points out, “every degree builds transferable skills. Students learn to think creatively and solve problems. They learn to analyse, research and collaborate with others. Those skills travel into every career.”
[ ‘They deserve to be on a good wage’: Dublin parents back teachers on industrial action Opens in new window ]
There are plenty of approaches a parent can take when supporting school leavers in making this very difficult but exciting decision. Honest conversations are the best, especially when it comes to finances and the practical matters of transport, accommodation and fees. Equally, a parent can ask their young adult questions about their expectations of themselves, the course, the campus and college life. But ultimately encourage an independent decision.
McEvoy reiterates that parents should “go to open days together, look at what students actually study in first year, and remember the CAO isn’t the only route. Further education and apprenticeships should be on the table from the start.”
She also suggests that when there is a battle of wills, parents and students should “separate the course from the career, and the emotion from the information. Most of the conflict comes from parents worrying about job security and teenagers wanting to do something they love, and those are rarely as far apart as they first seem.”
Agree on the facts together, she advises, which includes understanding the course content, where it leads and where graduates end up.
“Then set out your concerns honestly once and let your child make the call. Nothing is final, and it’s better to back a decision your child owns than win the argument and lose their motivation.”
Rocca says that parents can help their school leavers make a good choice by “listening and talking about their hopes for the future. One piece of advice we hear often at NCAD is worth sharing. Unsure exactly what to study? Choose a broad degree in the area you love. That might be science, literature or design. You can specialise in year two or three, once you know more.”
Personal dreams are important too and shouldn’t be dismissed but accounted for in their choice. Fernandez del Cotero suggests that parents should encourage students to have aspirational choices on their CAO regardless of Leaving Cert points, not to limit their student before they have even begun. “Realistic course choices should follow and finish off with safety-net course choices,” she says. “These preferences should be made regardless of points.”
In all and perhaps most importantly, parents and students should remember as Fernandez del Cotero says: “Their first choice is important, but it doesn’t have to define their whole future, there are many alternative routes available into college and choosing a course at age 17 or 18 does not mean deciding the rest of their life.”

title: Decoding the CAO and your college options: An open days explainer
description: A guide to what you will hear on campus, how entry works and your options if the CAO does not go to plan
content:
Brochures and websites can tell you a lot, but only open days give you a real feel for a college campus.
What size is the college? What are the teaching spaces like? Do you like the atmosphere?
Between entry requirements, access routes and the range of third-level options, there’s a lot to take in – so we’ve put together a plain English guide to what you will hear on campus, how entry really works and what your options are if the CAO does not go to plan.
Ireland’s higher education sector is made up of universities, technological universities (TUs) and other colleges. Universities focus on research-intensive degrees across arts, sciences, business, law, medicine and engineering.
TUs – formed from former institutes of technology – emphasise applied learning, work placement and industry links, though many also offer research degrees.
Colleges include independent, fee-paying institutions such as Griffith, plus teacher training colleges, art colleges and the National College of Ireland.
In further education, “college” can also refer to institutions offering Post-Leaving Certificate (PLC) courses.
On the CAO form, you will see courses described as level six, seven or eight. These refer to the National Framework of Qualifications (NFQ): level six is an advanced certificate, level seven an ordinary bachelor’s degree, and level eight an honours bachelor’s degree. Many students start on a level seven or eight course and may later progress to level nine (masters) or level 10 (doctorate).
The CAO lists both level six/seven and level eight courses in separate columns, and points are published separately for each. It’s worth applying for level six and seven courses as well as level eight, as many institutions allow students to start on level six/seven and progress to level eight if they miss out on points. “Common entry” means you apply to a broad programme (for example, science, business or engineering) and specialise after the first year, once you have sampled different subjects. This is useful if you are unsure which niche to pursue. By contrast, some courses are “direct entry” to a specific discipline from day one.
[ As the class of 2026 begins college, a masked shadow lingers Opens in new window ]
Within degrees, you may encounter “major/minor” structures, where you focus primarily on one subject (the major) while taking a secondary area (the minor).
“Electives” are optional modules that let you tailor your degree, perhaps taking a language, a business module or a creative arts class alongside your core subjects.
At open days, ask how flexible it is to change direction after first year and how electives work in practice.
Grades are not the whole story. Many courses have additional entry requirements. Art, design and architecture programmes typically require a portfolio; music and performance courses may require an audition; teaching, medicine and some health courses may involve interviews or aptitude tests. These are often “restricted entry” courses, meaning you must list them on your initial CAO form and complete supplementary steps by early deadlines.
“Matriculation” refers to the minimum subject and grade requirements you need to be eligible for a course or institution. For example, some engineering degrees require honours maths at a certain grade, while languages may require a specific level in that language. Always check both the general matriculation rules of the institution and the specific entry requirements of the course.
At open days, course tutors can explain how these requirements work in practice and whether there is flexibility for borderline cases.
[ ‘They deserve to be on a good wage’: Dublin parents back teachers on industrial action Opens in new window ]
CAO points are a ranking system based on your best six Leaving Certificate subjects. Courses fill from the highest points down until places are exhausted. Points rise and fall according to supply and demand: more applicants or fewer places push points up; fewer applicants or expanded intakes can push them down. In 2026, overall CAO points rose by an average of 1.5 per cent despite lower grades.
In high-demand courses, points can hit the ceiling of 625. When more students achieve the maximum score than there are places, “random selection” is used: a lottery among 625-point applicants.
In 2026, 35 level eight courses used random selection, up from 25 the previous year, with many in health, medicine and veterinary science. This means even top marks do not guarantee a place in some programmes, which is why some students look to English-taught courses in European universities.
At open days, admissions staff can outline how points have moved on specific courses over recent years.
The CAO is not the only show in town. Post-Leaving Certificate (PLC) courses in further education (colleges offer level five and six qualifications, often with strong links to specific industries and progression pathways into level seven/eight degrees.
Some further education colleges now offer “tertiary degrees”, where students spend a year in further education building foundational skills before moving directly into the second year of a linked university degree. This happens outside the CAO points race, alleviating pressure for many students.
[ Has your child settled in to school? The essential prep has nothing to do with reading or writing Opens in new window ]
Apprenticeships combine paid work with structured learning, leading to nationally recognised qualifications in areas such as construction, engineering, ICT, finance and hospitality. They suit students who prefer hands-on learning and want to earn while they learn.
At open days, further education colleges and apprenticeship providers can explain progression routes and employer links in detail.
See FetchCourses.ie and nto.hea.ie for more information.
Hear (Higher Education Access Route) offers places on reduced points and extra support to school-leavers from disadvantaged backgrounds, while Dare (Disability Access Route to Education) does the same for school-leavers under 23 with disabilities.
Both schemes require you to apply through the CAO and submit supplementary documentation by early spring deadlines.
[ ‘My son has just started secondary school and seems a little overwhelmed’ Opens in new window ]
On average, the points reduction is around 10 per cent, but you must still meet matriculation and any specific course requirements.
Mature students (aged 23 or over on January 1st of the entry year) apply through the CAO but are assessed differently, often based on work experience, prior learning and motivation rather than points.
Some colleges require aptitude tests or interviews, and many reserve places for mature entry.
Access offices at open days can talk you through supports such as tutoring, mentoring and financial assistance.
Every year, approximately 10,000–12,000 Irish students choose to study in the UK, the EU or further afield, motivated by culture, language, specialised courses and, in some cases, lower fees and living costs. For students who miss out on high-points courses in Ireland (particularly medicine, dentistry and some health professions) English-taught programmes abroad can offer an alternative route. Entrance may be based on meeting minimum grades rather than competing on points, though some programmes have their own tests or selection procedures. For help with your application, see eunicas.ie .
Before committing, check how your qualification will be recognised in Ireland, especially for regulated professions like teaching, medicine, engineering and social work. Some Irish students on Italian medical programmes, for example, take their intern year back in Ireland, while UK teaching graduates may need extra coursework or an Irish language test to register.
Many Irish universities also offer Erasmus or linked study-abroad options for an international experience without a full degree overseas.
At overseas open days, international offices can outline exchange opportunities and recognition issues for specific courses.

title: Ireland expected to pay more towards EU asylum solidarity fund in 2027
description: Asylum solidarity contributions
content:
Ireland is expected to increase its contribution to the EU Migration and Solidarity Fund for 2027 from the €9 million pledged in 2026.
The annual report from the European Commission on this matter is expected later this month. It set out the “fair share” contribution each EU member state should make to countries such as Italy, Greece, Spain and Cyprus on the union’s southern borders.
Last year, the commission determined that the Irish Government should pay €9.26 million in lieu of taking an additional 463 asylum seekers.
Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan briefed the Cabinet on Tuesday that the commission’s latest proposal for “fair share” would involve a greater contribution from the Republic to the union-wide solidarity effort.
Countries have a choice of accepting relocated additional asylum seekers or providing financial support to the countries closest to the southern border of the union.

title: League of Ireland permutations: Any Bohemians slip-up could hand Shamrock Rovers title
description: Waterford can avoid relegation playoff ahead of FAI Cup final by beating Drogheda on Friday
content:
Brass tacks. If Bohemians fail to defeat Shelbourne at Dalymount Park on Friday, Shamrock Rovers would secure the Premier Division title if they beat the already-relegated Sligo Rovers in Tallaght.
Only three points separate Rovers from Bohs with two games remaining in the season.
“We are playing to win a league, they are not,” said Stephen Bradley, the Rovers manager, following the 2-1 defeat of Bohemians on October 12th.
The comment sounded premature, especially after Rovers 2-0 loss in Galway last Friday coincided with Bohs winning 2-1 against Waterford.
But Bradley is an expert at mind games come this stage of the campaign. It is the eighth straight season that his Rovers squad have contested the title race. They are on course to capture a sixth League of Ireland title in seven seasons, having finished runners-up to Shelbourne in 2024.
If Bohemians see off Shelbourne in the north Dublin derby and Rovers somehow lose to Sligo, the pressure will build on the Hoops ahead of the trip to Oriel Park to face Ciarán Kilduff’s Dundalk on the last night of the season, Friday, October 30th.
On the same evening, Bohs would need to overcome St Patrick’s Athletic at Richmond Park to have any chance of ending a 17-year wait for major silverware.
Bohs will learn on Wednesday if their captain Dawson Devoy is available for the run-in after the Republic of Ireland international was sent off following a melee on the Tallaght pitch last week.
If found guilty of violent conduct, Devoy can expect a three-game suspension. He already missed Friday’s match against Waterford.
Rovers teenagers Naj Razi and Michael Noonan are also before disciplinary hearings arising from the same incident.
If, as expected, Shamrock Rovers take three points off Sligo Rovers but lose away to Dundalk while Bohs take six points off Shels and Pats, the title will come down to goal difference.
Currently, Bohs and Rovers are level on +19 goals so Bohs 60-goal total to Rovers’ 54, gives them an advantage if the clubs finish level on points.
St Pat’s manager Stephen Kenny admitted on Monday that a second loss in three days to Derry City at the Brandywell, following the 2-1 collapse at home to Shels last Friday, “more or less knocks us out” of the running.
Miracles can happen; if Rovers lose their last two games and Bohs only manage to add three more points while St Pat’s bank six, their current six-goal advantage would leave Kenny’s side as the unlikeliest of champions.
Whatever happens, Rovers, Bohs and St Pat’s have qualified for Europe next season with the Europa League spot reserved for the winners of the FAI Cup final between Waterford and Derry City on November 8th at the Aviva Stadium.
It is possible that Waterford will play European football from the First Division in 2027. Last Monday’s dramatic 3-2 win at home to Galway United put Graham Coughlan’s side clear of the relegation playoff, but only on goal difference.
Waterford’s -10 goal difference is just three goals better than Drogheda United ahead of the clubs meeting at the RSC on Friday night.
Remarkably, Waterford strikers Podge Amond and Tommy Lonergan are locked in competition to top the league’s goal scoring list.
Amond’s brace against Galway this week brought his tally to 13, level with Bohs Collie Whelan. But it was Lonergan’s bullet header in the 89th minute that secured the points and extended his lead to 15 goals.
Lonergan also scored four times in three recent appearances for the Ireland under-21s, including two in the 3-1 win over England to secure a Euros playoff against Finland next month.
Galway are four points clear of Waterford and Drogheda so it is still possible that John Caulfield’s men could drop into the relegation playoff by losing at home to St Pat’s and away to Drogheda.
Cork City earned promotion as the First Division champions, with 19 points to spare over UCD. The students face Longford Town in a two-legged promotion semi-final next Saturday and Tuesday to play the winners from Colin Healy’s Kerry FC and Bray Wanderers.
The First Division playoff final is at the neutral venue on Sunday, November 1st with the promotion/relegation tie set for the following weekend. If Waterford are involved, the match will be pushed into the middle of November.
