title: Sale of GP practices
description: I look forward to a rigorous public debate on this most essential service
content:
Sir, – Should we be concerned about the steady march of privatisation in healthcare at its most crucial and vulnerable point – the local GP practice?
The proposed sale of Centric for a reported €350 million suggests there are massive profits involved. Are these profits being realised at the expense of the ordinary patient?
Setting aside management gobbledegook, can the reason be increased charges for patients and decreased time allocated to appointments?
One must also wonder why so many doctors are walking away from the management of their practices. It is in the GP practices where the rubber hits the road for the vast majority of health interventions in the State.
Should the Government be helping GPs run their own practice? Would a co-op that simply provides finance and admin functions reduce the burden on GPs?
[ Why is rude lateness from doctors universally accepted? Opens in new window ]
Has the Minister for Health, Jennifer Carroll MacNeill , or any of the health unions anything to say about these developments?
I look forward to a rigorous public debate on this most essential service.- Yours, etc,

title: Jim O’Callaghan reiterates claim that solicitors are targeting rape cases
description: Minister faces backlash for saying rape trials were only cases ‘deliberately’ targeted by striking solicitors
author_name: Cormac McQuinn, Mary Carolan, Jack Horgan-Jones
content:
The dispute over changes to the criminal legal aid system has intensified, with criticism directed at Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan and solicitors who have withdrawn their services.
O’Callaghan faced a backlash over remarks claiming that rape trials in the Central Criminal Court were the only cases “deliberately affected” by the withdrawal of services by solicitors protesting over the new legal aid regime.
Meanwhile, the impact of the dispute has continued to be felt in the courts.
At Dublin Circuit Criminal Court on Tuesday, Judge Martin Nolan criticised solicitors , saying it was “astounding” that those participating in the dispute were not attending court to represent clients in custody. He was speaking after adjourning cases of dozens of defendants who appeared without a solicitor due to the dispute.
In July O’Callaghan scrapped a per-appearance fee system in the District Court in favour of a flat-fee approach, leading to a withdrawal of services by many solicitors.
[ Jim O’Callaghan accused of treating solicitors’ pay dispute ‘like it’s a game’ ]
The row escalated on Monday with the withdrawal of services expanding to cases including custody and children’s cases.
On Tuesday morning O’Callaghan came in for criticism after his comments suggesting solicitors targeted rape cases had emerged in advance of the Oireachtas Justice Committee meeting where he was due to deliver them.
The remarks were described as “false” and “misleading” by criminal defence solicitor Eoghan O’Sullivan, who said “there was no deliberate targeting” of rape cases.
The Irish Council for Civil Liberties spoke of “the understandable anger among solicitors” as a result of O’Callaghan’s comments and it called on him to engage in meaningful talks to resolve the dispute.
O’Callaghan defended the comments in response to criticism at the justice committee meeting later in the day.
He told the committee the legal aid scheme was “operating nationwide” and that “solicitors continue to provide representation” while acknowledging that others had withdrawn services.
Fine Gael backbench TD Barry Ward – a practising criminal barrister – told the meeting that O’Callaghan’s comments on rape cases were “grossly unfair commentary”, also saying there was “no evidence to suggest that solicitors were deliberately targeting that [rape cases]”.
O’Callaghan responded by saying he wanted to “set out the facts” that six rape cases in the Central Criminal Court were adjourned on Monday because of the withdrawal of services. He also said other rape cases were adjourned earlier in October due to withdrawal of services.
[ Department of Justice received 78 legal aid invoices for individual’s theft charges ]
The Fianna Fáil Minister said that on Monday “there was also seven cases which weren’t rape cases, which were trial-continuing cases. None of those cases were affected by the withdrawal”.
Ward said this was because they were continuing trials and he asked: “Is it not deeply disingenuous to ascribe a deliberate targeting of rape trials?” O’Callaghan repeated that the seven non-rape cases were not affected by the withdrawal of services by solicitors.
During the meeting the Minister said the “fundamental principle” when it came to the new flat-fee system was trying to cut down on the “scandal” of multiple legal aid certificates being issued for one accused individual.
Labour TD Alan Kelly asked about areas O’Callaghan was willing to negotiate with solicitors on.
The Law Society of Ireland , which represents solicitors, had previously proposed that long-running cases would see a second legal aid certificate issued when cases exceeded 10 court appearances, citing cases involving children among those cases where this could happen.
O’Callaghan told the committee there was an ongoing Department of Justice review on children’s cases. “If it is the case that it looks like the average length of time it takes for a children’s case to conclude is more than the five [court appearances], I will reflect that in changes.”
Earlier on Tuesday the Law Society issued a statement urging O’Callaghan to meet to “try to resolve this escalating dispute”.
The Minister has written to the Law Society to indicate his willingness to engage further, saying he had instructed officials to organise a meeting in the coming days.

title: Global temperatures set to rise far in excess of 1.5% threshold pledged in Paris Agreement
description: Report from UN Environment Programme shows emissions growth has slowed but a turnaround is yet to be achieved
content:
Climate-harming emissions from oil, gas and coal rose globally again last year as countries failed to honour commitments to reduce their use.
The annual Emissions Gap Report from the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) shows while emissions growth has slowed, a turnaround has yet to begin.
In an assessment it calls “sobering”, the report says the only way the world can now minimise the damage is by dramatically scaling up climate action and deploying technologies to remove huge amounts of emissions from the atmosphere – technologies that do not yet exist.
Otherwise, countries must prepare for a global temperature rise of at least 2.1 degrees and more likely 2.6-2.8 degrees within this century. This is far above the global pledge to keep temperature rise from exceeding 1.5 degrees.
The chance to avoid that overshoot is now “lost”, the report says. Even before it officially happens, the extra warming is already causing climate chaos with deadly and destructive extreme weather in all continents.
[ New era of climate obstruction requires pretending things are okay when clearly they are not Opens in new window ]
“Overshoot is not surrender,” UN secretary general António Guterres says in a message in the report. “We can still keep it as small and as short as possible and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees by the end of the century.”
However, the report shows that would entail unprecedented effort.
If all countries honoured their individual pledges, or Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), global emissions would fall by 5 to 8 per cent by 2030 and 11 to 15 per cent by 2035.
To have a hope of minimising the 1.5 degree overshoot, emissions need to fall about three times faster – by 18 per cent by 2030 and 45 per cent by 2035.
In addition, 320 gigatonnes of carbon emissions would have to be removed from the atmosphere and permanently stored. That equates to eight years of global carbon emissions.
Carbon capture and storage technologies are in their infancy and their potential to work at the scale needed is unproven.
The report admits “socioeconomic and technological challenges make the chances of achieving this uncertain”.
[ Here is something you do not often see: an optimistic column on the climate crisis Opens in new window ]
The challenge is made greater by the behaviour of big emitters such as the US, which had the largest emissions increase last year, largely because of a return to burning coal.
Turkey, which hosts the UN climate summit Cop31 next month, had the second highest emissions increase.
The outlook in this year’s report is “worse than last year’s projections”, the report says.
“New NDCs submitted since last year’s report have made a negligible difference for these projections.”
The authors insist that there are still grounds for hope, highlighting progress made since the 1.5 degree pledge was made in the 2015 Paris Agreement.
In the decade since, global renewable electricity capacity has grown three times faster than anticipated, with solar PV buildout increasing seven times faster.
[ It takes collective climate action to fight climate destruction Opens in new window ]
“Growth in fossil fuels has been slower than predictions made 10 years ago, and there is evidence that climate policies have real effects on reducing emissions,” they say.
They also warn, however, that emissions of carbon and the second most common greenhouse gas, methane, “are heading in the wrong direction”.
“While current policy scenarios project that some of these emissions will stabilise by 2030, none show declines occurring at the pace and scale needed to minimise the magnitude and duration of the overshoot of 1.5 degrees.”
UNEP executive director Inger Andersen urged countries to “pull out all the stops” to make “fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions”.
“Every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5 degree increases climate impacts and risks, such as the deadly floods, heatwaves and wildfires that have plagued many nations this year,” she said.

title: Hurling advisory group hope new rules experiment will be broadcast
description: Group chair John Meyler is keen for some of the game’s top intercounty players to roadtest the new rules in front of a large audience
content:
An interprovincial hurling exhibition is set to be staged in Thurles at the end of November to shine a national spotlight on the trial rules.
A series of experimental rules are to be trialled in the GAA’s Higher Education Division One league this month – starting with Tuesday night’s fixture between UCD and Maynooth University.
There will be four more third-level games on Thursday night and data will be collected from matches over the coming weeks before any decisions are made on which, if any, of the trial rules might be brought forward to next year’s Congress.
And the Hurling Expert Advisory Group – chaired by former Wexford and Cork manager John Meyler – are keen for some of hurling’s top intercounty players to road-test the rules in competitive fare while showcasing them to a wider audience, so plans are afoot to host two interprovincial games, either on Friday, November 27th or Saturday, November 28th, in Semple Stadium.
Meyler is currently in negotiations with RTÉ to broadcast the games live.
The Football Review Committee organised an interprovincial tournament at Croke Park in October 2024 to test their rule enhancements. Arising from those games, the FRC decided to abandon plans to increase the worth of a goal to four points – though that particular alteration is now again under consideration by Kevin McStay’s committee.
[ Hurling to trial new rules which include prohibiting consecutive handpasses Opens in new window ]
“We need to get the games out to the public and the more exposure we get the better,” said Meyler when asked about the possibility of an interprovincial series.
“Please God we’ll get the games on the 27th or 28th of November; that’s what I’m discussing with RTÉ at the moment and we’ll use [the gate receipts] for charity for the Dillon Quirke Foundation. We’re just trying to get everything lined up.”
Former Wexford camogie player Ursula Jacob is a member of the HEAG and she believes the more aware hurling fans are of the rules the better informed the committee will be at the end of the trial window.
“I do think the education piece is crucial because people are making certain assumptions about the trial rules without seeing the games taking place,” she said.
“So the more people get to see the rules being applied, the more understanding there will be on what works and what doesn’t.”
Among the trial rules on show in the third-level games this month is the prohibiting of consecutive handpasses, an increase inthe number of steps permitted from four to six, 65s to be taken from inside a team’s own half of the field and the awarding of two points for a converted sideline cut.
The proposals also include a stipulation that three players from each team must remain between the 45m and 20m lines for puckouts and an increase in the number of steps permitted in possession from four to six, while all handpasses will require a clear and definite striking action.
Within the committee’s extensive 170-page interim report, there is also a recommendation to penalise the spare arm tackle. Under the trials, it will now be a foul to “hold an opponent with the hand(s) or arm(s) .”
William Maher, who is the GAA’s National Head of Hurling and also a member of the HEAG, says proposals on tackling and increasing the number of steps are efforts to try avoid the proliferation of rucks developing in games.
“[We wanted] to tackle the spare arm tackle so that players are able to release the ball without being held, that wasn’t in the rule book previously so we’ve put that in now,” explained Maher.
“And we will see if it has an effect on avoiding that melee, ruck area.
“[The same with the steps], we’re trying to see can we get around that piece to avoid rucks, avoid poor tackling, avoid poor execution of handpasses and get more striking ultimately when players get to the open grass.
“Will there be unintended consequences? Possibly, but we want to trial it and see what will happen with six steps. But the main point is to try get around the ruck area and players getting tackled on the fourth step.”
Line umpires will now have more power by acting as ‘assistant referees’ to help the official in the middle of the field.
“We speak about referees as a team of officials,” said Meyler. “We want the team to work together – the three match officials (referee and the two line umpires), the fourth official and four umpires – so effectively we have eight people refereeing a game of hurling.
“American Football has seven, ice hockey three, basketball two, we have eight – so it’s a massive effort from a team there.
“We had romantic ideas at the start and said we’d go with two referees, one in each half of the pitch. There was a certain amount of debate on that issue and what we settled on – maybe because of a shortage of referees and a shortage of referee experience – is that we’d give the line umpires a half each.”

title: Auto-enrolment changing pensions landscape as employers make schemes mandatory, says Ibec
description: Employers also increasingly requiring hybrid workers to attend office, according to survey
content:
The Government’s auto-enrolment scheme has prompted significant growth in the number of private sector employers bringing staff into occupational pension schemes and those making voluntary schemes mandatory, the latest Ibec Trends report has found.
The survey of more than 300 employers, published on Wednesday to coincide with the organisation’s annual Leadership Summit in Dublin , also found that Ibec members are increasingly requiring hybrid workers to attend the office.
“A significant area of focus for this year is the shifting landscape in relation to occupational benefits driven by the introduction of pension auto-enrolment,” said the employers group’s executive director of employer relations, Maeve McElwee.
“We have seen a 12 per cent increase in the number of organisations operating an occupational pensions scheme. There has been a notable 19 per cent uplift in voluntary schemes transitioning to a mandatory structure, as employers align and simplify their retirement offerings in response to legislation.”
The number of firms requiring a minimum amount of service before staff become eligible for occupational schemes halved in a year, the survey found, from 55 per cent to 28 per cent, while 81 per cent said their firm’s scheme was now open to all employees and almost half – 48 per cent – have made them mandatory.
Recent legislative changes in relation to contractual retirement ages (CRAs) have had some impact, with 21 per cent of firms now setting their CRA at 66 rather than 65 to align with the State’s pension age. However, a small majority (56 per cent) still operate on the default basis of staff retiring at 65, with almost the same number – 57 per cent – saying they deal with requests for extensions on a case-by-case basis.
Hybrid working, meanwhile, remains a valued tool in relation to recruitment and retention, but the number of firms wanting to see their staff spending more time on-site continues to edge slowly upwards.
In the 12 months since Ibec affiliates were last asked the question, the number of employers requiring a minimum of two, three or four days in the office had increased from 18, 31 and 9 per cent respectively to 19, 35 and 11 per cent.
The two most commonly cited drivers of workplace policy on the issue were found to be productivity and talent attraction. Cost and collaboration were also prominent reasons.
On artificial intelligence , almost 60 per cent of companies believe the technology will not have a big impact on workplace processes or employee numbers in the short to medium term, but 36 per cent acknowledged they have yet to do any significant modelling of the impact it will have.
By far the most commonly listed issue of concern for the coming year was pay transparency, with many aspects of the EU directive due to come into force in Ireland over the course of 2027.
Only a fifth of firms suggested they feel well prepared for its implementation, while 10 per cent said they had done no preparation and 22 per cent said they have completed very little to date.

title: HSE could be saving nearly €150m annually by using more biosimilar drugs
description: Swiss pharma firm Sandoz highlights potential savings Ireland could make on medicines bill
content:
The Health Service Executive could save €149 million annually by making greater use of lower-cost biosimilars – cheaper copies of expensive biological drugs – the Irish and UK head of Swiss pharma group Sandoz has claimed.
Diane DiGangi Trench, c o untry head and general manager for Sandoz UK and Ireland, said biosimilar competition delivered an estimated €239 million in savings for the Irish healthcare system in 2025.
A further €148.8 million in “potential annual savings” could be realised through the greater uptake of biosimilars already available in Ireland and through the introduction of additional biosimilars already available in Europe, she said.
Previously a unit of Novartis , Sandoz is the world’s largest manufacturer of biosimilars. It acquired Cork pharma firm Rowex in 2024 and was the second-largest supplier of medicines to the HSE last year.
Unlike generics, medicines made from living cells cannot be exactly copied and are referred to ​as biosimilars.
“Ireland could capture a lot more savings ... through greater uptake of the current biosimilars on the market as well as additional biosimilars being introduced,” DiGangi Trench said.
She noted that only 11 of 26 biosimilars (available in Europe) are marketed in Ireland, which represented the second-lowest uptake in Europe. Sandoz produces seven out of the 11 used here.
DiGangi Trench said one of the reasons for the slow uptake in Ireland was the HSE’s best-value biologics (BVB) medicines programme, which identifies lower-cost options within a specific drug class.
The BVB tender process is, however, only triggered when there are at least four competitor drugs, including the originator, and it takes 240 days, considerably longer than in other countries.
She noted that the ustekinumab drug, which is used in the treatment of psoriasis, had the potential to save the HSE almost €30 million annually, but the uptake here is just 30 per cent against a HSE target of 80 per cent.
The same is true of several other biosimilars, she said.
“A lack of control within the system” meant the potential savings “are just not happening”, she said. In practice that means while some parts of the HSE are utilising the newer lower-cost drugs, others are not.
“Ireland is spending more money than ever on healthcare and in trying to manage that growing pressure ... it could capitalise on more opportunities around biosimilars to reduce its medicines expenditure,” DiGangi Trench said.
She predicted the next decade would be a “golden decade” for biosimilars as the patents on many branded medicines expire.
The company forecasts that approximately $650 billion (€597 billion) worth of branded medicines globally ​are due to lose patent exclusivity between now and 2036. DiGangi Trench compared it to the 2011-2016 patent cliff while noting that Sandoz wants to derive biosimilars from 100 products by 2040.
“There is this huge wave of biosimilars coming on the market, and that’s why it is in Ireland’s best interest ... to figure out how do you get uptake quicker, and how do you get more products to enter more quickly,” she said.
In North America, Sandoz’s biosimilar sales grew 47 per cent in the first half of 2026, driven by sales of its new bone disease drug Wyost and osteoporosis drug Jubbonti.
One of the largest opportunities for biosimilars and generics is the diabetes and obesity drug market.
The US Food and Drug Administration recently agreed to review two Sandoz-made tirzepatide drugs ​that, if approved, would rival obesity drugs made by Eli Lilly.

title: Why developers are turning to hotels, not apartments
description: When it comes to deciding between more hotel rooms or much-needed housing, the key is viability. But for whom?
content:
T he cracks are starting to show. After years of defying reality about the Dublin office market’s prospects, developers are now embracing the hotel market as never before.
The latest convert is the German property group KGAL , which wants to knock down an office block on Dublin’s Golden Lane and build a 225-bedroom hotel. They follow in the footsteps of Core Capital’s Derek McGrath and of Johnny Ronan’s eponymous property group, both of which have reversed planned office developments.
The change of heart reflects an anaemic market for office space in Dublin, with CBRE expecting the take-up of office space this year to be roughly in line with last year but below the long-run average. They see a few bright spots on the horizon and tentative signs of the new development cycle, helped somewhat counter-intuitively by demand from artificial intelligence companies.
A more downbeat view is expressed by Peter Keegan, the director of debt and structured finance at CBRE , in a letter submitted to Dublin City Council as part of the KGAL planning application. It can be paraphrased as saying that, notwithstanding the green shoots mentioned above, lenders are wary of office development in Dublin.
Or, as Keegan put it, “there will be much deeper liquidity from debt providers for the development of a hotel on the site versus a new office building ... this is a development which will be received more positively as a hotel project than a speculative office scheme”.
Lenders call the shots in property development, and their enthusiasm for hotel projects is easy to understand. There is a well-documented shortage of hotel rooms in the capital, as evidenced by high occupancy rates. The shortfall is put at 3,600 beds, which equates to 20 or so hotels along the lines of the one planned by KGAL.
The downside with hotels is you have to find someone to run it for you, but if you can get more than 80 per cent occupancy, you will do well. It’s not a one-way bet. About 2,600 new beds are already in the pipeline, according to consultants Mitchell McDermott. The window of opportunity is closing and hence the stampede towards hoteliership by office developers.
From this perspective, their lack of enthusiasm for building apartments is hard to understand given the much larger and open-ended demand – 50,000 homes a year for the foreseeable future.
Again, the KGAL planning application is instructive. It contains an assessment of the site’s potential for an apartment development. The planning report argues that if the various rules and regulations pertaining to apartments – such as access to daylight and minimum open spaces – were to be complied with, then the maximum number of apartments that could be built on the site is between 50 and 60 units. This would not be “viable” even though it is a 10-minute walk from Grafton Street.
The site’s suitability for student accommodation is also deemed not to be “viable”. Urbanest, the student accommodation provider, kindly supplied a letter saying planning constraints “render it not possible” for student accommodation of sufficient scale to be viable. Two-hundred bed spaces would be needed.
Viability gets mentioned a lot in the KGAL planning application, but it is not really defined. Presumably what they are talking about is commercial viability and that is something of movable feast.
It takes a lot of factors into account, including the value of the site for other uses, the costs of construction and the availability and cost of debt financing. It also includes opportunity cost – whether you might make more money using the debt and resources required for Golden Lane elsewhere.
Viability is thus not the same thing as profitability. It may well be profitable to build apartments or student accommodation on Golden Lane, but just not as profitable as building a hotel.
Whether it is “viable” to choose an option that delivers a lower profit is another question entirely. It is perfectly reasonable for KGAL to argue it is not viable for them to choose an option – such as apartments instead of a hotel – that will deliver a lower return to their investors.
But that does not mean it would not be viable for someone else with access to cheaper funding and different objectives, such as the Land Development Agency , to build apartments.
Dublin city planners would be doing us some service if they looked a little deeper into the question of viability. Is KGAL saying it would not be profitable to build apartments or student accommodation on Golden Lane or simply that it would be more profitable to build a hotel?
The planners might then apply their own definition of viability. It would seem axiomatic that if a 60-unit apartment development could be built at a profit, it would be more than viable from the perspective of the Government’s obligation to house people.

title: HR bosses predict AI will not cause ‘significant reduction’ in employee numbers
description: Quarter of HR specialists expect artificial intelligence will cause ‘minimal impact’ on workplace structures
content:
The supposed impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on employment practices and headcount figures is yet to be noticed by Irish human resources (HR) bosses, with only 4 per cent expecting a “significant reduction” in employee numbers within the next three years, research reveals.
A quarter of HR professionals in Ireland indicated that AI should have “minimal impact” on their workplace structures, according to a national survey by business group Ibec . One in three foresaw little to no change in employee headcount, albeit with a “significant redesign of existing roles and responsibilities”.
Only 3 per cent of respondents expect an increase in employee numbers due to the integration of AI-specialised roles within their organisation.
Aside from AI’s impact on those already employed, the survey of 325 HR leaders provided insight on the recruitment process itself: 30 per cent of respondents said AI integration was “not at all” driving a shift from an experience-based competency assessment to a skills-based talent strategy.
A further 34 per cent pointed to only “minor changes or experimentation” with its hiring process as a result of AI, while 17 per cent named “moderate changes” such as individualised departmental approach.
HR leaders listed a number of barriers to full adoption of AI services, with 55 per cent of respondents naming “data privacy and security” as their primary concern. This was a seven percentage point decrease from last year’s finding.
The survey recorded a 13 percentage point drop in the proportion of respondents who pointed to a “lack of internal knowledge or skills” as a factor preventing them from fully embracing the new technology, down from 65 per cent in 2025 to 52 per cent this year.
Maeve McElwee, Ibec’s executive director for employer relations, said: “Unsurprisingly, AI and workforce transition remain front and centre of HR operations, given the scale of organisational change under way.
“However, there is genuine confidence that while some roles may change, the narrative of job displacement does not currently reflect what HR leaders are seeing.
“What we are seeing from the feedback is that the challenge for businesses lies in gaining a better understanding of how they capture and measure the productivity benefits of AI across their business operations.”
Nearly one in five (19 per cent) of survey respondents said they “do not anticipate AI driving significant value” in their HR departments within the 18 months. Three-fifths said it would improve “HR operations efficiency” such as automating administrative workflows, managing contracts and taking meeting minutes.
More than a third of respondents (36 per cent) expected AI practices to improve operational efficiency for “talent acquisition” such as reducing the amount of time it takes to recruit a new employee.

title: Opinion: The Annals of Inisfallen are part of Irish history. They don’t belong in a British library
description: Former colonies are increasingly seeking the return of their ancestral heritage. The Annals of Inisfallen are part of ours – a reminder of a thriving, independent civilisation that existed before colonisation
content:
F or the past two months, the Annals of Inisfallen, a medieval Irish manuscript of immense historical importance, has been on public display at the Glucksman museum, University College Cork. Soon, however, this little book of just 57 vellum leaves, recognised as a priceless national treasure, will leave these shores and return to the University of Oxford’s main Bodleian Library, where it has been kept since the 1750s. The last time the Annals of Inisfallen came home was in 1983 when they were exhibited at Muckross House, Killarney, Co Kerry. Then, as now, there were calls for the manuscript’s permanent return to Ireland. People wonder why such an important Irish artefact should be housed in a British library.
For anyone unfamiliar, the Annals of Inisfallen are a record of important events in Ireland, chiefly Munster, and abroad between the years 433 and 1450. Written on calfskin vellum, the manuscript was created by more than 30 scribes over the course of about 500 years at different locations. It is thought it was initially copied in the monastery of Lismore, Co Waterford, from materials created in the monasteries of Clonmacnoise in Co Offaly and Emly in Co Tipperary, and Inisfallen monastery on Lough Leane, Killarney, was the last place it was worked on. The text includes references to Saxon attacks, celestial phenomena including a comet, inter-monastic warfare, deadly plagues, Norse raids on Skellig Michael, Brian Boru’s Viking campaigns, Norman invaders, Irish king lists, the deaths of feted poets, saints, clergy, heroes, villains and so on. The good and the bad of the Irish medieval past: they’re all in there.
As a result of Henry VIII’s dissolution of monasteries in Ireland, England and Wales (1536-1540), Inisfallen monastery was later abandoned. By the 1590s, the annals had found their way into the collection of Finghín MacCarthy Reagh, a leading nobleman and scholar. Imprisoned in the Tower of London over a period of 40 years, MacCarthy Reagh had little choice but to sell his manuscripts to finance his release. This is probably how James Ware (1594-1666), a senior civil servant and prolific manuscript collector, came into possession of the annals. It is quite possible that it was Ware who gave the book its name, simply as a catalogue entry.
After Ware’s death, the manuscript had different owners until it was bought by Richard Rawlinson (1690-1755), a noted clergyman and antiquarian. Rawlinson bequeathed his enormous manuscript collection, including the annals, to his alma mater, the University of Oxford and the Bodleian Library. The Annals of Inisfallen have been in the Bodleian archive ever since. Undoubtedly, if it were not for collectors such as Ware and Rawlinson, who were genuinely interested in the scholarly study of Irish manuscripts, and without the Bodleian Library’s enduring stewardship, the book would likely have been lost. Their dedication to conservation should be acknowledged.
However, the world has changed, and former colonies are increasingly seeking the return of their ancestral heritage. Museums across the globe, our own included, are examining and engaging in ways to make that process more accessible. Indeed, just this year, the Irish Heritage Council published a report advising the Government on best practices for the restitution and repatriation from Irish institutions of “cultural objects that may have been illegally or unethically elicited or traded”. UK cultural institution have their own way of doing things. The University of Oxford’s museums and libraries, which includes the Bodleian, have procedures in place to deal with claims for the return of cultural objects, stating they will deal with each claim on a “case-by-case basis”. But, this is not as straightforward as it might appear in relation to the Annals of Inisfallen, given that they were purchased legally and given freely to the library.
So, where to from here? This past summer, I spent time in Munster where I asked people how they felt about the Annals of Inisfallen. The overall consensus was that the manuscript should be here, not in some foreign institution. The question of legal ownership didn’t really matter. I realised that, while Irish people might not be aware of the finer details of the book, they feel its absence. When I mentioned that the Annals of Inisfallen are freely available online for anyone to view either in English translation or in the original Irish and Latin, that didn’t seem to matter to them. This really is the heart of the issue. Why does an inanimate object such as a book, written long ago, mean so much? It is perhaps because of what that book represents. The Annals of Inisfallen are a reminder of a thriving, independent civilisation that existed before the colonisation that destroyed so much of Ireland’s culture.
For centuries, there have been calls to bring the book back home to Ireland, but to no avail. In the 1730s, Dean Jonathan Swift tried in vain to obtain them for Trinity College Dublin. Since Swift’s day, many have sought the annals’ permanent restoration. But, artefacts acquired by British cultural institutions during imperial expansion and colonisation are incredibly well protected by law. And even here in Ireland, any calls for the Annals of Inisfallen’s return are often dismissed as opportunistic political stunts. Small wonder that attempts to repatriate the annals to Ireland have fallen by the wayside.
[ Gulliver’s Travels at 300: Did Jonathan Swift predict AI? Opens in new window ]
It is a recognised right of people everywhere to determine what happens to their own cultural heritage. Article 11 of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007) states that “indigenous peoples have the right to ... maintain, protect and develop the past, present and future manifestations of their cultures ...[and] ... artefacts.” The Irish experience of colonisation influences how we feel about our ancestral heritage, especially when that heritage is held outside this country. Our British neighbours may not quite grasp this because they do not share our experience of colonisation.
Chris Doyle is lecturer in m edieval h istory at the University of Galway

title: Gordon D’Arcy: The season has properly started now – let’s see who can keep momentum going
description: Four games in, you can see shape emerging in how the provinces want to play
content:
I t was difficult to escape the feeling that the season only started in earnest last weekend with the first round of fixtures in the Champions Cup and Challenge Cup . There was no fanfare. The budget doesn’t appear to allow for any razzamatazz.
The Champions Cup has struggled with ugly duckling syndrome for quite some time, the format clunky and dull at the pool stage, where there is little jeopardy for those clubs who apply themselves for two of the four matches.
This season’s rule tweaks regarding the qualification for the knockout phases and the try bonus point are a step in the right direction. I found last weekend’s rugby engaging for the most part across a broad spectrum of matches.
Back when I was busy establishing myself in professional rugby after what I will politely term a false start or two – and the wilderness years that ensued – I came to value this time more as each season progressed.
Requirements are different for every player depending on age, physical development and positional requirements. You must keep evolving, and preseason is where that happens. It might be skill development. For some players it’s physical. I was lucky, naturally springy and powerful.
My challenge was usually keeping my weight in check and building the aerobic capacity for which there is no shortcut. Experience comes with time and so does physical development. The ability to last 80 minutes is something into which you grow.
Munster back rows Seán Edogbo and Brian Gleeson came off about the hour mark on Saturday. No problem there. It’s good management from Clayton McMillan , looking after young players and not squeezing too much out of them, even in a game that needed the power they bring.
I can still picture walking out on to the back pitches at UCD, Michael Cheika sitting there with his big ghetto blaster while we ran shuttles. He and Jason Cowman, our head of fitness, had a view on where the game was going. They saw it getting quicker and felt the law changes would bring a higher tempo. They wanted us 5 to 10 per cent lighter, but fitter.
It was a paradigm shift. The running was brutal and it was endless. You’d wake up in a cold sweat knowing what was coming that morning. But it gave the season a focus. Over a few seasons we built mental resilience, then fitness and then the ability to win. It took several preseasons to build up to that first European Cup.
Joe Schmidt brought the same singular focus. We played an incredible amount of drop-off touch: where any time you touched the ball you then sprinted back to your own try line before you could rejoin proceedings. The defence was always short, so the smart attackers went where you weren’t. It was all work-rate and intensity, but it put a huge emphasis on skills too.
The net benefit came out in season. I mention this because, four games in, you can see shape emerging in how the provinces want to play. Connacht and Ulster have the clearer picture. Richie Murphy is building on a longer runway in Belfast, and Stuart Lancaster is into his second year in Galway.
Lancaster’s calling card is high-level skills execution under pressure. If you’re going to play high-tempo, possession-based rugby, it’s a prerequisite. Connacht won’t be the biggest team, or the strongest, or the fastest. What they can control is skill execution.
There were plenty of examples in the 45-36 win over Saracens . Ruck accuracy was good. Decision-making was sharp both in timing and execution.
Ulster’s 40-21 win against Zebre in the Challenge Cup wasn’t as stern a test as those faced by their provincial siblings. It was though a chance to make changes, and after last season’s injury issues that’s no bad thing.
Rotation in personnel and Ireland players returning in dribs and drabs over the first three United Rugby Championship (URC) games brought a level of early-season disjointedness in playing patterns, but that was less evident at the weekend.
Munster honoured Anthony Foley’s memory with a suitably energetic display where Marnus van der Merwe, Edogbo, Gleeson and Dan Kelly led the way in the carrying game, putting their team on the front foot. The quality of the ruck ball was excellent, which brought Craig Casey into the game and let him dictate tempo.
The way they want to play is clear. Charlie O’Shea, Alex Nankivell, Kelly and to an extent, Seán O’Brien, all get heavily involved in sweeping plays off the second and third wave of attack, hunting mismatches. That’s the start of a style of play, maybe even an identity.
Shay McCarthy impressed me. I loved his try. A winger with pace, smart enough to realise that once he’d broken the line with a lovely drop of the hip, he had to go flat out for the try line, which he did, beating three opponents. That’s someone who knows when to be selfish for the team. It’s been a weakness in Irish teams from time to time.
Leinster looked solid and strong up front , the tight five laying a foundation for everything else. Fintan Gunne was sharp. Yes, he made mistakes, but with little game time under his belt at this level those errors are understandable.
The promise was there. His snipe around the ruck and the offload for Tadhg Furlong’s try epitomised modern game values: break the line and keep the ball alive.
There was a lot to like. There is a willingness to explore. Sam Prendergast had a run in the first half and got caught. He didn’t get caught the next time. You don’t only judge the wins. You develop a feel for when to attack and why.
The continuity is developing too. Off a Clermont knock-on, Prendergast broke from deep, and the kick was fantastic. But what matters is that Jimmy O’Brien was ready for it. A yard later and he doesn’t have the space to gather and get the ball back to his outhalf. Every time there was space in behind, O’Brien was there. That is players starting to see the same thing without having to communicate.
I’ve been a big critic of Scotland’s Finn Russell for much of his career. I had a barney with Simon Zebo about it. He defended Russell as creative and awesome. I questioned the outhalf’s ability to navigate big games when the bullets were flying.
Russell has grown into a truly remarkable player. What sets him apart is his all-round game, putting the ball where it needs to be through whatever means necessary.
Prendergast has shown similar qualities, a passing range against Cardiff and last weekend a spectacular kicking game out of hand. This feels to me like a player that has looked at himself over the last year and asked what he needed to do differently.
Clermont’s inside defenders stood off him, not seeing him as a threat with ball in hand. Rather than panic, he watched the outside defence come up and dropped the ball on his foot into the space behind, often with team-mates recognising the opportunity at the same time.
That brings out more in others. Tommy O’Brien will want to try things. Ryan Baird will get into it. The challenge for Leinster is seeing it together often enough for it to become ingrained. Next Saturday lines up beautifully. Leinster versus Munster. Preseason is over. Let’s see who keeps the momentum going.

title: Leaving Cert reforms too risky for student learning and teachers’ health
description: School labs lack adequate facilities for proposed physics, chemistry and biology studies to be done safely
content:
Sir, – Breda O’Brien’s article (“ Farcical Leaving Cert reform must stop now ”, Opinion, October 17th) deserves the strongest support.
As a practising science teacher, I also commend Aoibhinn Ní Shúilleabháin and Prof Pauline Mellon from the National Council for Curriculum and Assessment’s Mathematics Development Group for highlighting the issues as a result of their concerns about the proposed senior cycle reforms. Students, parents, employers and the State should also share this concern.
The proposal to award 40 per cent of Leaving Cert marks for these research projects also poses a serious threat to examination integrity. Does this serve our students well in a competitive points race?
Artificial intelligence (AI) can produce a project report of high standard in minutes. How can we reliably establish that submitted work represents a student’s own knowledge and understanding of the subjects of physics, chemistry and biology?
The credibility and international standing of the Leaving Cert must not be put at risk.
An independent report, written by Prof Michael Watts and based on responses from 351 secondary schools in Ireland, raises alarming health and safety concerns about the proposed laboratory-based research investigations in the new physics, chemistry and biology curriculums.
Analysis of the data showed many laboratories lacked adequate facilities to support such student research investigations. Teachers are expected to supervise different experiments simultaneously without laboratory technician support.
The Watts Report recommended to the Department of Education that implementation of these research projects should be paused on health and safety grounds. Why has this warning not been heeded?
At a time when schools are struggling to recruit qualified teachers of science and mathematics, the increasing workload on teachers, concerns about legal responsibility and increased stress, without adequate laboratory technical support, will make teaching an unattractive profession.
This farcical Leaving Cert reform must stop now. – Yours, etc,

title: Ireland’s relationship with Israel
description: There is undoubtedly a range of feelings among Irish people about what is happening in Gaza
content:
Sir, – Nick Davis writes to say he abhors the way Irish people castigate the state of Israel and finds the land of his birth to be deeply anti-Jewish (“ Being Irish and Jewish: I love my home, but I am so angry ”, Letters, October 19th).
He also asks why real examples of genocide in Nigeria and Sudan don’t receive the same level of attention in Ireland.
The war zone that is Gaza is covered regularly in this country, whereas other war and conflict zones involving mass deaths have not received the same publicity. The placement of Gaza within a wider European context probably explains the greater coverage it receives.
The evidence of what has happened to the people and the physical structure of Gaza is not in dispute, but Davis is disinclined to acknowledge the scale of this tragedy. I consider that Irish people are questioning the tactics of the Israeli Defense Forces ( IDF ) and the political strategy of the Israeli government.
There is undoubtedly a range of feelings among Irish people about what is happening in Gaza, but I believe there is consensus that Israel is acting outside the parameters of what a democratic and civil-rights country should stand for. This is not anti-Jewish, but is rather challenging the behaviour of a state that seems intent on the subjugation of a people they appear to regard as lesser human beings. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Fintan O’Toole is right that principle has a price tag (“ Zionism is not racism, any more than Irish nationalism is sectarianism ”, Opinion, October 20th). Opposing anti-Semitism while defending Palestinian rights is easy to endorse and hard to practise, because each cause is too readily turned into a weapon against the other.
Criticism of the Israeli government is too often dismissed as anti-Semitism. Equally, some supporters of Palestine excuse or minimise Hamas , whose atrocities against Israeli civilians were indefensible. Neither the reflexive charge nor the reflexive excuse deserves a free pass.
A government is not a people, a religion is not a state and a population is not its rulers. The real test is whether we can condemn the slaughter of Palestinians, the murder of Israeli civilians and the demonisation of Jews without qualification. Human rights cannot depend on whose side we happen to be on. – Yours, etc,

title: Love at first sight led me to a whirlwind adventure with my Citroën 2CV
description: Cornering at speed, going roofless and smuggling a TV were all possible in the ‘Deux Chevaux’
content:
Sir, – My first car, purchased in 1976, was an emerald green Citroën 2CV. It was love at first sight.
My father told me it was no better than a lawnmower and offered to lend me the extra money to buy a Ford Escort. I refused.
I’d read that a French farmer would load up his Deux Chevaux with garden produce, eggs and even a pig to transport to the market and I thought that this car could also have a commercial future. The deal was done, and a happy partnership emerged.
I could drive fast around corners with the body of the car leaning over while all four wheels remained firmly on the ground. When the roof was rolled back my friends could hang out and wave at other road users and startled pedestrians.
My most frightening experience though was when I was smuggling a television from Co Armagh , where I grew up, to Dublin where I was working. I’d decided to leave early on a Sunday and take an unapproved road to avoid customs.
In the depths of the south Armagh countryside, suddenly, a young man leapt from the hedge into the middle of the road in front of me. I had to jam on the brakes, the television wobbled in the back seat – the boot was too small to hold it – and the passenger door was wrenched open.
This stranger jumped in and said: “Drive.” I could smell alcohol and began to feel uncomfortable. I was asked where I was from, he named families in my village and then, just as suddenly as his arrival, his departure bore the words: “Stop. I’ll get out here.”
That was the beginning and the end of my side hustle as a smuggler. Although I never realised the car’s full potential as a goods vehicle, I had many memorable adventures the length and breadth of Ireland with my much-loved and treasured 2CV. – Yours, etc,

title: Are women in your workplace earning less? A new Government website lifts the lid
description: Ireland’s national gender pay gap stands at 8.3%
content:
D o women in your workplace have the same average earnings as men? A new Government website will make it easier for you to find out.
Ireland’s national gender pay gap stands at 8.3 per cent, according to figures quoted by the Department of Equality this year. That’s the average difference in pay between all men and all women in the workforce. If you’re a woman working in an organisation on the wrong side of the gap, it pays to know about it.
New data published from next month aims to lift the lid on gaps in pay and equip you to find out how your workplace measures up.
By the end of November, all employers with more than 50 employees must publish data about their gender pay gap to a new public gender pay gap portal.
The gender pay gap is the average difference in pay between all men and all women in an organisation. If you are a woman working in an organisation where there is a big gap, it doesn’t bode well for your finances.
The pay portal has been open for voluntary reporting since last year and viewable to the public since June, but publication by employers is about to become mandatory.
The Employment Equality Bill 2026 will be enacted in the coming weeks, with individual company gender pay gap figures for 2026 available to view by the end of November, Minister for Equality Norma Foley told the Dáil last week.
The Central Statistics Office (CSO) put Ireland’s national gender pay gap at 9.6 per cent in 2022. Mean hourly earnings for men were €27.73 and €25.06 for women, a gap of €2.67.
As age increases, the gender pay gap grows. The biggest gap was in the 50-59 age group at 16.7 per cent, with men earning €33.03 and women earning €27.51.
Sectors such as construction, aviation and finance tend to show wider gaps due to male-dominated senior roles, while education and healthcare often show the opposite trend.
In many cases, it’s less about pay rates and more about representation at senior levels, says UCD’s Professional Academy.
It’s important to note the gender pay gap is not a test of whether men and women in an organisation are paid equally for the same work – that’s already required by law. Rather, it highlights imbalances that influence how opportunities are distributed, according to the academy.
If your organisation has a big gender pay gap, there may be some telltale signs.
There are probably fewer women in senior or higher-paid roles; there is an over-representation of women in lower-paid or part-time roles in a company; maybe there is unconscious bias or barriers to the progression of women; there is a culture where availing of hybrid working is frowned on; or maybe there is a culture where the men who work there never take leave for caring responsibilities.
[ Female participation in Irish workforce jumps 90% since 2000 Opens in new window ]
Some or all of these characteristics can contribute to a workplace where pay between genders is out of whack.
If you work in or are interviewing for a role in an organisation with a big pay gap, the impact can ripple far beyond your pay cheque.
Lower average pay than male colleagues in an organisation can mean women there get a smaller percentage pay rise than male colleagues, receive a less generous pay-linked bonus, are unable to borrow as much their male colleagues can to buy a house, and end up with smaller pensions in retirement.
If you are already in a job or scouting for a new one, the new pay gap portal will make it easier to look under the bonnet and see the reality of the hiring, pay, promotion practices and culture there.
Gender pay gap reporting requires employers to choose a snapshot day in June this year, and use pay information for the previous 12 months for their pay gap calculations. Employers then have five months to publish their report, by the end of November.
Some 1,000 employers have now created accounts on the portal in preparation for publishing their reports by the end of next month, the Department of Equality says.
Some firms have been proactive, voluntarily publishing their 2025 pay gap data to the portal. You’ll find 410 such reports already published.
Searching the portal by company name and looking for the mean, or average gender pay gap, is a useful metric for employees, says Michelle McDonagh, chief client officer at human resource management consultancy Adare.
If you see a large gender pay gap percentage, it doesn’t necessarily mean that the organisation is paying women unfairly, says McDonagh.
“Gender pay gap measures the pay of all men and compares it against all women. There is no allowance for the type of role, length of service, level of seniority or expertise,” she says.
“It’s a blunt instrument in that regard.”
The gender pay gap figure, however, is a useful indicator of hiring and promotion practices, policies and culture in a company.
[ Being a working mother is a horror show at times. The stress can be crippling Opens in new window ]
A zero per cent pay gap is the ideal. That would mean men and women’s pay is perfectly balanced.
A positive gender pay gap, of five per cent for example, means women earn five per cent less on average than men. A negative, or minus gap, means men earn less than women on average.
“Most organisations will have a positive figure because in most organisations, women will earn less than men on average,” says McDonagh.
Comparing companies by sector can provide an interesting perspective.
Take the telecommunications, computer programming and consulting sector in the data, for example. This is one of the most highly remunerated sectors in the country. Consultancy firm Deloitte has been proactive in publishing its data and reports a 5.2 per cent gender pay gap for 2025 in favour of men.
Another useful search in the portal is “distribution of gender by pay quartile”. This requires bosses to segment their workforce by pay band and tell you the balance of men and women in each of four different bands. Looking at Deloitte, there were 10 per cent more women than men in the lower middle pay band in 2025, but 4 per cent more men than women in the very top pay band.
“One of the trends we tend to see in companies is if there are a lot of females coming into lower-paid roles and for whatever reason they are not progressing through the ranks,” says McDonagh.
“Then you see a lot of males in the higher-paid roles and women’s representation drops away as they move through those different pay quartiles.”
[ What top CEO pay and gender pay gap reporting tell us about Irish business Opens in new window ]
Companies are required to publish a statement about what is causing their pay gap and what they are going to do about it.
Deloitte’s statement says the company has met its target of 35 per cent female partners by 2025.
“We aim to increase this to 40 per cent by 2027, with a 50 per cent longer-term goal,” according to the firm.
Data for PwC shows a 1.6 per cent gender pay gap for 2025 in the mean hourly pay of female and male employees.
Women and men are 50:50 in the lowest pay quartile, but there are 10 per cent more women than men in the topmost pay quartile.
‘Women make up at least half of our population. This, in turn, has had a significant influence on the outcome of our gender pay gap analysis,” says PwC.
KPMG , Ernst & Young (EY) or Accenture have not published data on the portal for 2025. They will be required to publish their 2026 data by the end of November.
They were required to publish 2025 pay gap data on their own websites, however.
KPMG reports an average gender pay gap of 11.1 per cent for 2025 – the organisation comprises 51 per cent women and 49 per cent men. There are more women than men in all three lower pay quartiles, but 11 per cent more men at the top pay quartile.
There is a 23.2 per cent average bonus gap between men and women at the consulting firm, its report says.
At partner level, women represent 24 per cent of partners. The pay gap between female and male partners is 5.6 per cent.
[ Pay transparency rules could cause conflict in workplaces, say HR and law experts Opens in new window ]
The mean pay gap at Accenture for 2025 is 9.2 per cent. The number of women and men are almost equal in all pay quartiles – except at the top one where there are 10 per cent more men in the highest pay grade.
The mean pay gap at EY for 2025 is 6.5 per cent. Some 71 per cent of partners are male.
Meta Platforms Ireland , which employs 95 per cent of Meta’s staff here, has a 2025 gender pay gap of 26.5 per cent, and an average bonus pay gap of 37 per cent.
The company employs an almost equal number of men and women. The number of women at Meta is greatest in its lowest pay quartile, where there are 62 per cent women, and the number of women is fewest in the highest pay quartile, where there are 63 per cent men.
Women are better represented in non-tech roles in the company, Meta says. Tech roles, like software engineers, are typically paid more in the market, and this has a disproportionate impact on pay gaps, it says.
The bonus gap is higher than the hourly pay gap, which is primarily driven by higher tech equity, it says.
Hooke & MacDonald is the only large real estate firm to have voluntarily published its gender pay gap data to the Government portal for 2025. It reports a 13 per cent gender pay gap in the mean hourly pay of female employees and of male employees.
“We are clear that our pay gap arises as a result of a greater proportion of males in senior positions in specific areas of the business and on higher pay points within those grades – due to longer service in those roles. This significantly contributes to the pay gap,” the company says.
Government organisations have been busy reporting their data too.
An Coimiusiún Pleanála , for example, had a 6.1 per cent gender pay gap in 2025. It’s an improvement of 9.4 per cent on the previous year.
This is down to a relatively higher share of roles taken up by women in administrative grades, which have a lower average hourly pay than other grades, it says.
There are 8 per cent more women than men in the second-from-top pay band, but 12 per cent more men in the top band.
“A great deal of effort [is being made] in recent years to improve our gender balance at senior manager level, including actively supporting family-friendly initiatives such as hybrid working, work sharing, statutory leave schemes and the shorter working year scheme,” says the commission.
The commission reported its 2025 pay gap in three categories – men, women and non-binary – but says the format of the portal makes it impossible to fully report on pay gap statistics for the three groups.
An Post reports a zero gender pay gap for the fifth consecutive year. Its 2025 data shows a mean hourly gender pay gap of minus 4.85 per cent in favour of women. It has an equal percentage of male and female executive directors.
[ Banking and finance sectors slow to disclose salary information, data shows Opens in new window ]
Gender pay gap stats may be particularly beneficial to women in the middle pay quartile, says McDonagh.
“If you can see the norm in your company is for more male representation at the top, maybe you hadn’t realised that’s the context you are working in – the report will tell you that,” says McDonagh.
“Then you are going to have to take charge of your own career, you are going to have to drive it yourself.
“If the stats tell you that men in your organisation have the majority of the income, you are going to have to drive those conversations with your manager yourself to make sure you are getting the opportunity to progress. Keep asking the question, what do I have to do to move up?”
The data is a very public opening of the kimono for organisations, and at a time when HR headcount and diversity and inclusion initiatives are under fire.
“Some 64 per cent of employers have identified employee perception as their biggest concern about publication of their gender pay gap report,” says Adare’s McDonagh of her company’s most recent HR Barometer data.
While gender pay gap statistics can be a bit of a blunt instrument, the statement employers are required to publish explaining the data can be insightful, says McDonagh.
This self-examination requires them to explain the cause of their gender pay gap and what they are going to do about it.
Work to transpose the remaining parts of the European Union (EU) Pay Transparency Directive is continuing, the department says. This will include the obligation for employers to carry out a gender-neutral job evaluation. This requires employers to examine why they are remunerating some types of work more than others. It involves assessing the value of different types of work in their organisation, putting work of similar value into the same category and ensuring these people are similarly paid.
This means equal pay for those doing work of the same value too – even if that work looks quite different.
In UK clothing retailer Next , for example, the mostly female sales staff were found to be earning less than the company’s mostly male warehouse workers. Even though their jobs seem different, the retail staff contributed work of equal value to the warehouse workers, a tribunal found.
Employers will be invited to training to help them compare work objectively – based on skills, effort, responsibility and working conditions – to eliminate gender pay gaps and bias.
Done right, this could upend old pay structures that have unfairly rewarded some skills over others, for no objective reason.

title: Funding local government
description: Ireland needs a more clearly understood system
content:
Sir, – There has been a lot of correspondence in your columns recently regarding the relative merits of higher or lower local property tax ( LPT ) rates. Most of the arguments base their “facts” in their respective political space.
The big problem, however, is different. The overall funding of local government is understood by few, leading to absurd positions where parties, supposedly on the left, coalesce with parties of the right to oppose capital taxation, while at the same time both demanding that more money is spent.
Ireland needs a more clearly understood system of local government funding, and I have long called for a national forum to be established to agree a system that can be clearly understood by the public and on which all political parties can then base their proposals using the same agreed funding models.
Such a forum, comprised of the social partners, councillor representatives and the political parties, would be given six months to present a report in time for it to be legislated for the 2029 local elections. Not only would it be a more honest approach financially, it also could bring back credibility to our local government. – Yours, etc,

title: Kathy Sheridan: When words fail, we still turn to the priest to find them
description: In some of the loneliest moments of our lives, we trust in the wisdom of a priest, born of years spent attending scenes of human devastation
content:
O n Sunday, the human cost of our cool cocaine culture was laid before us as the remains of Kim and Philip English, and their boys Jayden and Callum, were carried to a Catholic church in Waterford city and placed in the care of a parish priest, Fr Gerry Chestnutt, for their funeral on Monday.
The most remarkable aspect of that handover ritual is that there was nothing remarkable about it at all. It’s generally what we do in times of grief and tragedy. We entrust the final farewell of our loved ones to a man who is part of a tribe often vilified for his calling and who represents a near eviscerated institution. Yet, in some of the loneliest moments of our lives, we trust in that man’s wisdom and empathy, born of years spent attending scenes of human devastation, to bring a sense of the sacred that comes with the comforting old rituals of a Catholic funeral .
That’s if we think about it at all. Maybe we just want a venue and a proven, formulaic way to handle the heartbreak of death. Either way, the Catholic funeral is such a natural part of us that we hardly question it. If pushed, we’ll repeat the accepted line – that Ireland is still Catholic but no longer religious – but we mostly prefer not to dwell on what that actually means. What exactly do we want of the Church now?
Some Catholics argue if a church is reduced to a merely useful funeral venue that priests should stop facilitating them altogether. It’s understandable. It would also be another tiresome example of the church shooting itself in the foot. Leave aside the existential question of women in the church and have a look at the most strongly supported proposals at the first national synodal assembly last Saturday: healing as a priority; pathways of belonging for young people; communion with those struggling to see the relevance of the church. Severing one of the last through lines between the church and those wobbling on the margins will hardly help achieve any of those goals.
After decades of covering Catholic funerals , the memories that linger are of row after row of pale, subdued, awkward young men dressed in hastily-acquired black suits and ties and a photograph of a young face on the coffin. I never pass St John’s Lane Church in Dublin’s Liberties without remembering Anthony Campbell , the 20-year-old apprentice plumber who was working in a house where crime boss “Marlo” Hyland was the target of a double killing in which the boy was an innocent victim. A “mistake”.
More than 2,000 mourners, who included rows and rows of black-suited young men, heard Fr Sean McArdle speak of Campbell’s “cruel and senseless death”, that “what happened to him was terrible and evil and has shocked all right-thinking and decent people”. He prayed “that in some way God will touch the hearts of the men and women of violence in our society”. That was 20 years ago.
Last August, when rage towards the five dead boys in the M9 crash was at fever pitch, it fell to Carlow priest, Fr Tom Little, to tell a congregation of their grieving relatives and many young men that “ what the boys did was wrong ” while couching it in the promise of a merciful God.
[ How drug debt fuelled Waterford arson attack Opens in new window ]
We know the drill. When tragedy strikes, and the media descend on a community deep in shock, the priest will be available and will find the words when no one else can. He would possibly have given the last rites at the scene – or at least know the truth of it – and has been navigating a family’s distress and possibly a community’s divisions, as well as his own haunted flashbacks in the long days since.
It’s when you attend a succession of those funerals and note the celebrants’ exhausted faces, the minefield of names, relationships and sensitivities to be negotiated, and hear the scrupulously worded, often brave homilies, that you wonder what their inner life must be like.
Ten years ago, when eight suicides were recorded in Co Laois within three weeks, Fr Paddy Byrne described the clergy as “ sacramental firemen ” going from one crisis to another. In Belfast, Fr Aidan Troy, best known for defying death threats by walking daily with the girls of the Holy Cross primary school through a loyalist gauntlet of spit, stones, fireworks, blast bombs and sectarian abuse, has written of similar experiences.
These men at the frontline know too much to ask if the victim was an observant Catholic or if the distraught relatives attended Sunday Mass.
[ Waterford arson victims were ‘a beautiful family who did no wrong’, funeral told Opens in new window ]
In 2015, after a balcony collapse in San Francisco resulted in the deaths of six young people – a seventh, Aoife Beary, died in 2022 – an Irish priest serving nearby became the accidental voice and through line of old rituals for broken families and traumatised young people an ocean away. Fr Aidan McAleenan – just 10 years a priest – said, “The families decided what they wanted ... They wanted it to be like home.”
“Like home”. There’s a phrase for the modern church to conjure with – and for all of us, because funerals are not just for old people.
[ Funerals are the only aspect of Catholic life I engage with any more Opens in new window ]

title: Timing is everything as Roscommon’s Ultan Harney announces intercounty football retirement
description: With the primrose and blue reclaiming the Connacht title this year, Clann na nGael player bows out a three-time championship winner
content:
Roscommon’s Ultan Harney has retired from intercounty football .
A three-time Connacht senior football championship winner, Harney made his Roscommon senior debut in 2015 and made 68 appearances for the county.
A physically imposing midfielder, the Clann na nGael club player scored 2-29 during his Roscommon career.
“Roscommon football has been a huge part of my life and representing my county has been one of my greatest privileges,” said Harney in announcing his retirement.
“It’s given me some of the best days of my life. I’d like to thank all the managers, coaches and backroom teams I’ve worked with over the years, but in particular the players I’ve shared this journey with. We’ve all shared the same passion and love for football in this county.
“A special thanks to my family, particularly my parents, Eamon and Kathleen, and especially my wife, Kayleigh. They’ve supported me through all the highs but, more importantly, through the setbacks and difficult days. I couldn’t have done it without them.
“I’d also like to thank all the Roscommon supporters for their incredible support over the years, and everyone at Clann na nGael for their continued support throughout my career.
“I’ll always be proud to have worn the Roscommon jersey and I wish everyone involved with Roscommon GAA all the very best going forward.”
A former Roscommon underage player, Harney won Connacht minor championships in 2012 and 2013. He added provincial under-21 medals to his haul in 2014 and 2015.
Harney’s senior career coincided with Connacht title wins in 2017, 2019 and 2026. He also won four Division Two National Football League titles – in 2015, 2018, 2020 and 2022.
In a statement, Roscommon chairman Thomas Murray paid tribute to Harney for his commitment to the primrose and blue.
“On behalf of Roscommon GAA, I want to sincerely thank Ultan for his outstanding service and dedication to Roscommon football over the years.
“From his early success at minor and under-21 level through to his senior career, Ultan has been a tremendous servant to our county. He was a fierce competitor, a hugely committed player and someone who never took a backward step when wearing the Roscommon jersey.
“His resilience in overcoming injury setbacks and his determination to return to the highest level speak volumes about his character. To finish his intercounty journey in a year when Roscommon reclaimed the Connacht senior title is a fitting way to bring the curtain down on a distinguished career.
“We also recognise the enormous support provided by Ultan’s family, particularly his parents, Eamon and Kathleen, his wife, Kayleigh, and his club, Clann na nGael, throughout his intercounty career.”
“Ultan can look back on his achievements with great pride, and we wish him and his family every happiness and success in the years ahead.”

title: Pensioners left behind
description: The grey vote counts for nothing in the eyes of politicians
content:
Sir, – The recent budget confirms a clear decision to leave State pensioners behind.
Look at the last 14 years in cash, not percentages. I have picked a teacher’s salary as an example of public pay, but the pattern is the same across the public service.
A newly qualified teacher earned €30,702 in 2012. That starting point is now €47,417 – a gain of €16,715 per year.
A person on the maximum State contributory pension got €230.30 per week in 2012. It is €299.30 today. That is a gain of €69 per week, or €3,588 a year over 14 years.
Put that against inflation. Cumulative inflation from 2012 to today is 30.7 per cent. In real terms, a pensioner has stood still, while a teacher – again as just one example of public service pay – has gained 54 per cent and comfortably beaten inflation.
And what did the recent budget offer pensioners? This year we are offered €10 again. The living alone allowance is to be increased by a whopping €3 a week. Will public service unions accept a €10-a-week increase? I doubt it very much. The bodies representing State pensioners failed miserably once again.
Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael promised before the election to bring the pension to €350 a week. At €10 a year, that promise will never be met in the term of this Government .
We are told the State cannot afford to link pensions to wages or inflation, as is done elsewhere in Europe. We can afford to link public service pay to both, and more. The grey vote counts for nothing in the eyes of politicians. – Yours, etc,

title: A scandal or a crisis?
description: Shelter must be viewed as a human right
content:
Sir, – I would have thought that after however many years of a “ housing crisis ”, it might be time to start calling it “the housing scandal”.
I have worked in a healthcare capacity with the homelessness services, and I tell you it is a sobering experience to see grown men fight back tears as they describe the indignity of living on the street. Housing (ie shelter) must be viewed, first and foremost, as a human right, and not a wealth-extracting commodity. – Yours, etc,

title: Politicians and productivity
description: Can anyone remember when, if ever, ‘productivity’ was a sine qua non for the endorsement of pay rises for Oireachtas members?
content:
Sir, – You reported that Taoiseach Micheál Martin has insisted productivity increases would be a part of any new pay deal with the public sector unions (“ Taoiseach rejects Michael O’Leary’s view that he would ‘buckle’ to public sector unions ”, Politics, October 18th).
The Taoiseach is quoted as having said that he is “open to an agreement that is affordable” and “that can advance productivity within the public service”.
Can anyone remember when, if ever, “productivity” was a sine qua non for the endorsement of pay rises for Oireachtas members over the years? – Yours, etc,
