title: Car size isn’t everything
description: Compared to the original Citroën 2CV, today’s cars are bigger, heavier, more powerful – and more wasteful
content:
Sir, – Brian O’Brien’s letter concerning the Citroën 2CV ( October 19th ) raises an interesting question about the evolution of the motorcar.
The original 2CV, introduced in 1948, had just nine horsepower, weighed approximately half a ton and could carry four adults. The original Mini, introduced in 1959, had 34 horsepower and weighed approximately 650kg. Both were designed to provide practical, economical transport. Today’s Mini has more than four times the horsepower and weighs approximately twice as much as its ancestor.
Many modern SUVs weigh two tons or more and possess several hundred horsepower. Undoubtedly modern cars are safer and more comfortable, but have we made comparable advances in common sense?
According to the International Council on Clean Transportation, between 2001 and 2024 the average weight of cars sold in the EU increased by 22 per cent, while engine power increased by 56 per cent.
The environmental consequences are considerable. In its Global EV Outlook 2023 report, the International Energy Agency estimates that manufacturing an electric SUV produces over 70 per cent more carbon emissions than manufacturing a small electric car. Larger vehicles also require more materials and energy to operate.
The motor industry has persuaded us that greater size, weight, power and acceleration represent progress.
From an environmental perspective much of this is simply extravagant wastage.
Perhaps the greatest achievement of the 2CV was not that it managed with nine horsepower, but that its designers understood that nine horsepower could be enough.
One wonders what they would make of a two-ton SUV, equipped with hundreds of horsepower, employed to transport a solitary 75kg motorist to the local gym – Yours, etc,

title: IT firm seeks up to €30m from Irish Rail for scrapped technology project
description: Irish Rail to tell Oireachtas committee it terminated contract for new traffic management system in July
content:
Spanish IT company Indra is seeking payments of potentially more than €30 million from Irish Rail as part of final accounts for an information technology system to manage trains across the network, which has been scrapped.
Irish Rail is arguing there is no money due to Indra.
The State-owned rail company has already written down by €50 million its investment in a new national train control system based at Heuston Station largely due to problems with the technology – known as the traffic management system (TMS).
Irish Rail chief executive Mary Considine has told the Oireachtas committee on transport in advance of a hearing on Wednesday that it terminated the TMS contract with Indra on July 17th, 2026.
She said work was currently progressing to close out the contract in line with its terms and conditions.
The Irish Times understands Indra has sought additional payments as part of the finalisation of accounts that could amount to more than €30 million.
Irish Rail said in a statement on Tuesday that it had “rejected Indra’s position, noting there are no monies due to Indra”.
It is understood that, in turn, Irish Rail is seeking to address the financial effects of what it maintains is the lack of a developed product from Indra.
Indra did not reply to specific questions on Tuesday relating to additional payments.
[ ‘Absolutely chaotic’: Passengers frustrated by overcrowding on Irish public transport Opens in new window ]
It said it “continues to make every effort to pursue constructive dialogue and seek an amicable resolution with Irish Rail”.
Indra said it remained “fully confident in the quality of the work delivered” and expressly reserved all of its rights.
The TMS project to integrate signals, communications and other systems on the railway network was originally expected to cost about €19 million, but was beset by years of delays and cost overruns.
Indra, however, said its TMS had been “successfully deployed and is operating in countries including Spain, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Lithuania” where operators had repeatedly expressed confidence in its technology.
Considine is expected to tell the Oireachtas committee that it was currently proposed to provide a replacement train control system.
Irish Rail is seeking to put in place a system designed by Siemens in the Greater Dublin Area “to improve operational resilience and help mitigate the obsolescence risks for that part of the network”. This work is expected to be substantially completed by late 2028.
[ New battery-electric trains due to arrive next year in bid to relieve overcrowding on services Opens in new window ]
Irish Rail also wants to deploy the Siemens system across the remainder of the network and has sought approval from the National Transport Authority to go outside normal procurement arrangements. It is understood that this proposal has not yet been approved.
“While overall completion is envisaged by 2031, the majority of the project will be substantially complete and operational by the end of 2030,″ it said.

title: Michael McDowell: France is falling to the extremes of left and right. Ireland can’t be complacent
description: There are people of both political extremes who crave street politics just because it has potential for violence and confrontation
content:
The riots in France are a very serious matter for us all. They are not just some minor, routine, explosive geyser – part of a long-standing French tradition of street protest. Nor are the rioters protesting in sympathy with teenagers venting anger at underinvestment in their lycees.
Some violent, destructive rioters appear to have been co-ordinated by extremists on the far left, who saw mass demonstrations organised by more moderate leftists as an opportunity to further radicalise French politics. All these events serve to deliver French political debate into the hands of the left and right fringes of political opinion – at the expense of centrist politics.
Many millions of decent French men and women look on with dismay at the riots and the kind of political instability they are carefully designed to create. The same applies in Italy in relation to the smaller-scale copycat rioting in Milan. French president Emmanuel Macron ’s televised national address in response looked and sounded weak.
Leftist street politics are not a legitimate response to the economic problems facing France, which are chronic and accelerating. Of course, people in democracies have a right to peaceful protest. These are rights that do not exist in the totalitarian states led by despots of the kind that the shameful president Donald Trump claims such warm personal relations with, and mutual respectful admiration for.
In 2024, the French left united to demand earlier retirement ages, increased state expenditure and wealth taxes for the rich, as well as the usual left agenda. While Ireland takes steps to increase economic participation by extending working lives to take account of demography and longevity, left-wing French politicians argue for diminished economic participation, easier economic opt-outs, higher taxation and increased public spending.
On social media, centrist politicians are denounced and mocked as traitors, usually by people availing of online anonymity
It should be no surprise that Marxists favour street politics over democratic means of resolving divisive political issues and determining national politics. The appetite for street politics is not confined to Antifa militants who want physical confrontation to increase their profile, and to radicalise opinion. A craving for simplistic, binary political debate is not the monopoly of the left either.
In Ireland, we see many of the same patterns. On social media, centrist politicians are denounced and mocked as traitors, usually by people availing of online anonymity.
The fuel protests were a case in point. Organisers claimed they were intent on making the State ungovernable by blockading fuel depots. They denied the right of elected politicians to lift their unlawful blockades, which threatened all economic activity and wellbeing.
The protests succeeded insofar as they led to sensible reductions in taxation of fuels as a response to spiralling prices. But the self-appointed leaders wanted more – they wanted to capitalise on the fuel-price concessions made to create some form of incoherent political movement, most probably an alliance of anti-immigration, pro-life, Irexit, religious conservative and anti-homelessness sentiment. So far, that strategy has petered out. Efforts last month to reconvene activists at O’Connell Street in Dublin drew desultory support.
One less obvious element in this would-be political alliance is the cohort of domestic admirers of Trump’s Maga movement. They have recently become muted by the slump in American support for Trump, but they remain admirers and political fellow travellers of Trump in their hearts, often hiding behind social media anonymity.
[ ‘I have never felt anything so painful in my life’: Irish caught in French riots Opens in new window ]
Interestingly, they echo Trump by claiming that his critics suffer from Trump Derangement Syndrome (TDS) . It is deranged, they imply, to see Trump as a threat to liberal democracy, or to the western democratic alliance, or as a destabilising, destructive force in world politics, bent on a new political order where might becomes right, and the world is increasingly to be divided into spheres of influence controlled by a consortium of dictatorships.
Accusations of TDS are a reaction straight out of the Roger Stone political playbook. He and a small group of like-minded Maga practitioners developed the political tactic of immediate, vigorous political response based on counteraccusation, smear and personal invective to criminalise or vilify all opponents.
How near are we in Ireland to the reign of violent street politics? Thankfully, we remain a good distance away. There was a collective recoil from the rioting, burning and looting that were fanned aflame online by extremists in the aftermath of the shocking attempted murder of very young children on Parnell Square.
Attempts in 2025 by masked pro-Palestinian demonstrators to break a Garda cordon protecting Dublin’s Port Tunnel from occupation were forcibly put down without exciting much controversy or misplaced sympathy from the general public.
We should not, however, be complacent. There are people who, whether on the left or right, crave street politics precisely because it has a potential for violence and confrontation; they have their willing pawns, complete with face-masks and hoodies, who would gladly do their bidding if they were given any pretext.
Happily, we are not yet in the position of France, where the centre seems to be crumbling and the people face a binary choice in the election next April between the Marxist Jean-Luc Mélenchon and the far-right’s Marine Le Pen – with the latter the favourite to occupy the Élysée Palace.

title: Pepper to rebrand as Continuum Credit amid expansion of business offering
description: Company agreed in July to buy Dilosk, parent of ICS Mortgages
content:
Pepper Advantage said it plans to rebrand in January as Continuum Credit Group as it continues to broaden its offering following its takeover last year by US private equity firm JC Flowers.
The UK-headquartered business’s Irish loan servicing business, used by investment firms that acquired problem loans in the wake of the financial crisis as well as mainstream lenders, will become known as Engage Credit Ireland.
The Irish unit also agreed in July to buy Dilosk, which is parent to ICS Mortgages, for an undisclosed sum. It plans to continue to run the business under the ICS Mortgages brand, with its existing management team and regulatory framework.
The deal will mark a return by Pepper to providing Irish home loans , having sold its previous mortgage portfolio – amounting to €200 million at the time – in 2018 to Finance Ireland.
The company also plans to retain the sub-brand Harbour Credit, a manager of unsecured consumer credit for banks, utility firms and semi-State agencies that it launched in the Republic in May.
“The launch of Continuum will mark a defining point for our business,” said Fraser Gemmell, group chief executive of Pepper Advantage. “It will be a new identity that brings our capabilities across credit management, access and technology together in a clear and compelling way.”
Pepper Advantage Ireland’s chief executive, Niall Sorohan, told The Irish Times in May that it was developing new lines of business to diversify as the post-crisis era of large non-performing portfolio sales fades.
Pepper Advantage offers a range of services across Asia, Europe, and the UK. The company, with €75 billion in assets under management, operates in multiple asset classes including residential and commercial mortgages, SME loans, asset financing and leasing, credit cards, retail finance and buy now, pay later.
The company was acquired in March last year by JC Flowers from Pepper Global, which was founded in Australia.
The firm entered the Irish market in 2012 and is best known for servicing mortgages secured by collateral.
The most recent set of accounts for Pepper Advantage Ireland shows that its assets – mainly comprising mortgages – under management fell to €20.4 billion at the end of 2024 from €22.8 billion a year earlier, driven mainly by borrowers paying down debt and some portfolio disposals by clients.
Meanwhile, Dilosk has this week raised €441 million through the refinancing of a portfolio of mortgages on the bond market. It marks the company’s 12 th residential mortgage-backed securitisation deal since it started such a programme in 2015.

title: New Premier Inn hotel at Clerys Quarter seeking more than €66m
description: Construction well advanced, with completion set for early 2027 and opening planned soon after
content:
A wide range of Irish and international investors are expected to express their interest in the sale of the new Premier Inn Dublin City Centre Hotel.
Located just off O’Connell Street on Earl Place, the 229-bedroom hotel, now under construction and nearing completion, will form part of the Clerys Quarter scheme. The hotel is being offered for sale on a freehold basis, fully let to PI Hotels & Restaurants Ireland Limited, with Whitbread Group plc as guarantor, at a guide price of €66.6 million.
The guide price reflects a net initial yield of 5 per cent, after standard purchaser’s costs of 9.96 per cent. The lease runs for 30 years from practical completion on a full repairing and insuring (FRI) basis, with no break option, CPI-linked rent reviews with a cap and collar.
The hotel is set to be highly sustainable with an A2 Ber rating and is targeting Breeam Excellent certification. Construction is well advanced, with practical completion set for early 2027 and opening planned soon after. Offers for the hotel are being invited by the sole selling agent JLL on the basis of a completed hotel, with sale completion and lease commencement expected in the first quarter of 2027.
Commenting on the sale, Dan O’Connor, head of capital markets and hotels at JLL, said: “This is a rare chance to acquire a brand-new, freehold Dublin city centre hotel let for 30 years with no break option in place to the UK and Ireland’s largest hotel operator, with a guarantee from the FTSE-listed Whitbread Group.”
Isobel Horan, senior vice president at JLL’s hotels division, added: “Few sectors in Ireland combine a term certain of more than 30 years with inflation-linked income. This will be Premier Inn’s flagship asset, freehold, fully electric and A2-Ber rated, and it is set to open for business in a thriving Dublin city centre market.”

title: Tax-efficient investment accounts still face 1% stamp duty charge on large Irish companies
description: Share purchases of Irish firms valued at more than €1bn will be subject to the levy
content:
People planning to put money to work through the Government’s new tax-efficient investment accounts will still face paying stamp duty of 1 per cent if they want to invest directly in large Irish public companies.
Share purchases of Irish companies valued at over €1 billion are subject to stamp duty at a rate of 1 per cent. This follows a move last year by then minister for finance Paschal Donohoe to remove the charge in relation to companies below this threshold.
In the UK, a rate of 0.5 per cent applies, with rates in other European countries generally lower.
The new personal investment accounts , which will be available from next July, have been flagged by the Government as being exempt from tax on income, profits and gains arising on eligible investments.
However, the new Finance Bill that gives effect to many Budget 2027 measures does not extend the exemptions to stamp duty on shares in Irish public companies.
“There is no specific provision contained in Finance (Number 2) Bill 2026 exempting investors from the 1 per cent stamp duty that applies to the trading of shares of Irish plcs with a market value of more than €1 billion, where such shares are purchased through the new investment account,” said a spokeswoman for the Department of Finance in response to questions from The Irish Times.
[ Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work Opens in new window ]
“However, where the market value is below €1 billion, the relevant exemption continues to apply.”
There are 11 companies listed in Dublin with market capitalisations above that threshold, ranging from Ryanair, which is valued at €23 billion, and the country’s two largest banks to home builder Glenveagh Properties and healthcare services group Uniphar.
The levy also applies to large Irish companies listed overseas, including Greencore and Grafton Group in London and New York-listed CRH, Flutter Entertainment and Smurfit Westrock.
In practice, however, there are ways for investors to avoid the charge on US-listed Irish companies, including trading in so-called American depository receipts, rather than shares, or where the trades are settled through a North American settlement system.
“Although not addressed in the budget, we continue to advocate for the abolition of the 1 per cent stamp duty on shares in Irish companies listed in both Ireland and the US,” said Daryl Byrne, chief executive of Euronext Dublin, which runs the Irish stock market.
“The duty makes investing in Irish-listed shares more costly and less attractive to investors, particularly when comparable share transactions in the US are not subject to stamp duty.
[ We look at four different scenarios that could unfold for different types of investor Opens in new window ]
“We look forward to working with Government and market participants to address this remaining barrier, strengthen Ireland’s capital markets, and support greater investment in Irish companies .”
While the expectation is that most novice investors taking part in the Government scheme will shy away from investing directly in individual shares and bonds, in favour of putting money in investment funds, including exchange-traded funds, the underlying managers of equity funds face the stamp duty when purchasing shares in large-cap Irish companies.
Under the scheme, people will be able to put €12,000 a year tax-free into the new accounts . The accounts will feature a low tax rate of just 1 per cent, levied on any amount in the account over a tax-free threshold of €50,000.

title: Moving from America to Ireland for work? Here’s what you need to know
description: Figures indicate US workers are increasingly interested in a move to Ireland, but what should they look out for before making the move?
content:
The number of US citizens moving to Ireland has more than doubled in recent years , while Irish recruiters have seen “growing interest” from professionals based overseas.
An estimated 10,000 people moved to Ireland from the US in the 12 months leading up to April this year, up from 4,900 in the same period two years prior, according to data from the Central Statistics Office .
More than half (53 per cent) of the overall number of immigrants in that period were of working age, between 25 and 44, while just 3 per cent were aged 65 or older.
Although the majority of job applications continue to come from those already based in Ireland or elsewhere in Europe, Matrix Recruitment has seen a “growing interest” from professionals based overseas, such as in the US.
But what should US citizens know before making the move to the Republic for work?
[ Meet the Americans moving to Ireland for a better life Opens in new window ]
Securing a job offer is the first step, as employers often assess visa requirements early in the hiring process, according to Breda Dooley, head of recruitment at Matrix.
Where permits are required, timelines and recruitment decisions can be impacted, she says.
“Our advice to US professionals considering a move is to research permit eligibility, understand salary thresholds and ensure their qualifications and experience align with occupations currently in demand,” she says.
Dooley adds that experience gained within US markets can often be viewed “positively” by employers based in Ireland.
“That said, employers generally favour candidates who either already have the right to work in Ireland or whose skills clearly justify sponsorship through an employment permit process,” she says.
The two most common routes available to US citizens hoping to move to and work in Ireland are the critical skills employment permit and the general employment permit.
Dooley says the critical skills permit, which targets highly skilled workers, is an “important mechanism” to attract talent into areas where demand exceeds the available domestic workforce.
Such job opportunities are most commonly found in software development, cybersecurity and data analytics, engineering, pharmaceutical and life sciences sectors, as well as finance and certain healthcare professions.
The Department of Enterprise maintains a full list of critical skills occupations while such roles require a minimum salary of €40,904.
Once a worker has completed 21 months on a critical skills permit, they can apply for Stamp 4 permission to work in Ireland without an employment permit.
[ ‘I’m an American, can I live in Ireland for six months of the year?’ Opens in new window ]
General employment permits, on the other hand, are open to all occupations, with the exception of those listed as ineligible by the department.
However, this route is less straight forward as employers are required to undertake a labour needs test first. If no suitable candidate applies for the role, the employer can then apply for a general employment permit.
The role must have a minimum salary of €36,605, though the salary for meat processors, horticultural workers, healthcare assistants and home carers must be at least €32,691.
Workers on general employment permits must complete 57 months before they are eligible to apply for Stamp 4 permission.
Moira Grassick, chief operating officer at employment law and HR firm Peninsula Ireland, cautions that an employment permit does not automatically grant someone the right to enter or live in Ireland.
“Anyone moving to Ireland from outside the EU should also ensure that they have registered with the immigration service and obtained the appropriate immigration permission for a long-term stay,” she says.
Once an employment permit is secured and after moving, US citizens must obtain an Irish residence permit at a cost of €300 for the initial application and for subsequent renewals.
Those who successfully secure employment must also obtain a PPS number in order to get paid and register with Revenue, she says, adding they should also familiarise themselves with their rights and obligations as an employee in Ireland.
