title: Moving back to Ireland, so much is different and so much is still the same
description: But after a year home, there’s still a part that wonders what would life be like if we had stayed in London
content:
I left Ireland in 2018 because that’s what I thought you had to do. I left because I thought there were more career opportunities abroad and I got one: a funded sports science masters and internship at Leicester City Football Club . I was doing what I thought you were supposed to do, leave the nest, leave the home, leave this country , to see if I could stand on my own two feet, to see whether I could make something of myself, to experience the world.
But I didn’t go far, just across the pond. I lived in Leicester for four years. After my internship, I was lucky to get a job there as a strength and conditioning coach in their academy. I’d taken my first step on the career ladder that so many were talking about.
The four years flew by in what felt like an instant; I was head down in work, trying to improve myself, trying to prove myself. My girlfriend (now wife), also from Dublin, moved up to Leicester from London for my final year there, although at the time I didn’t know it would be my final year.
Unaware, I’d let myself get to this place where I didn’t recognise myself. Life was something of a charade. I was able to perform at work, to pretend to be normal, but returning home I felt empty, defeated and drained.
After a year in Leicester, my wife was moving back to London, and I decided to go with her. I felt like I was starting to take back control over my life. I moved to London with no job lined up, just a hope and belief that something would work out.
Luckily after a few weeks I got a role at Arsenal ; the risk paid off. I was back climbing the ladder, living with my wife in a beautiful part of London, life was good. Until it wasn’t. Feelings of old resurfaced, an unhappiness, a lethargy. It felt like my time wasn’t my own, as if life was dictated to me. But the reason wasn’t the environment alone, it was more that I needed to change within me.
So I found performance coaching, a place where you can sit with others through the questions I was wrestling with, and through presence, listening and thoughtful questions, hopefully help another reach their own point of clarity.
We spent another year in London: four years in London, eight years in the UK altogether. And then we felt home calling, to take the next steps, towards finding our own little home, to starting our own little family.
We were of that age now. You go away and then you come back home, like the countless others before us. Was this something we actively chose or something we just felt was the thing you do? Not everyone always comes back. Maybe they find a life that suits them better, or slide into a new sense of normality without questioning if this is what they really want. For those of us returning, do we ask the same question? Or do obligations and unsaid callings influence decisions to come home?
[ The Irish emigrant journey now: Graduate from college, spend 10 years abroad, move home Opens in new window ]
Like so many of returnees our age, we moved in with parents – my kind and gracious in-laws. Being able to call over to my parents to say hello, to see my brother and sister more regularly, to sit more with my grandparents, means the world. And it reminds me why we made our decision.
But after a year home, there’s still a part that wonders what would life be like if we stayed in London. I think these are thoughts we often have when trying to find our own way. We question and reminisce about the old chapters we closed in life. Nostalgia sets in and we only replay the good times and very little of difficult moments, when we felt lost, alone, unhappy. Our memory tricks us like that, it’s never to be entirely trusted.
Being home now, I see so many people who are leaving Ireland or are still away. Each emigrant has their own reasons. Perhaps it’s something they have to do for themselves, or it’s where their only opportunities lie, or a call to adventure or to find meaning is too loud to be ignored. Or maybe it’s for survival, feeling pushed out or forgotten.
Being back, so much is different and so much is still the same. I stand at the same traffic lights on roads I crossed as a child going to primary school. I look in my grandad’s same knowing and believing eyes, when I don’t quite have that same belief in myself.
We each have our own relationship with this country, our own valid reasons for staying, leaving or returning. The question is whether you can live with your decision.
Charlie Norton Sherwood is from Dublin and returned to Ireland from the UK in 2025, working as a performance coach . Charlienortonsherwood.com

title: Seán Moncrieff: I’ve been emailing obscure academics seeking radio interviews. Except I haven’t
description: I’ve been impersonated online, but how long before we can’t spot a fake?
content:
L ike a lot of quotes from world-famous people, Andy Warhol probably didn’t coin the phrase about everyone getting their 15 minutes of fame. Not that it matters: the axiom is irretrievably his and all the more powerful for its prescience. In the online age, it seems as if everybody will eventually get some degree of attention.
It could be “going viral” – in a good or bad way – but increasingly, the 15 minutes consists of someone impersonating you.
As usual, I’ve been way behind this trend. Online impersonation has been going on for years, while I only got into it in the past few weeks. The first email came from an archaeologist in Israel who was, rightly, suspicious that an Irish radio show would wish to interview him about his obscure, academic book on ancient Israelite settlements. He forwarded on the request he received, purportedly from me. It was written in Americanese – almost certainly composed by AI – but did enough to imply familiarity with the archaeologist’s work. If you didn’t look too closely. What made him suspicious was that it came from a Gmail account.
Others followed. A sociologist in Sweden. Another in Australia. A “joy-seeking recovering alcoholic” in the US who had penned a self-help book. A number of emails went to academics in UCD, where they were quickly spotted as fake.
But some of the overseas people were all but convinced that the interview request was genuine, yet wanted it confirmed: not because of the Gmail account or the robotic prose, but because of the sheer unlikelihood anyone would want to interview them.
This was the part of the process where human cunning was involved, and it was almost exquisitely cruel. The scammer, or scammers seemed to have specifically targeted the authors of dense, academic works, or books produced by small local publishers: the sort of thing that won’t trouble the bestseller lists or attract attention from radio stations on the other side of the world.
[ Deepfake Ireland on Virgin Media One: Gráinne Seoige’s distress in this grim film is palpable Opens in new window ]
And the authors, buoyed by the unexpected validation, probably weren’t familiar with how media interviews work. “Sean”, having made the request, would refer them to his colleague, “Nova”, who would prepare an “author spotlight”. Of course, it involved a fee.
Even if the author baulked at this, “Sean” would email them again. “Please feel free to verify the programme and its arrangements independently before deciding how you wish to proceed.”
Presumably, a percentage of the people contacted found this believable enough to not bother checking. And afterwards, when they realised they had been fooled, were too embarrassed to tell anyone about it.
It prompted me to have a bit of poke around online, where I discovered – surprise, surprise – that scams aimed at authors are astonishingly common. I looked at the websites of publishers and literary agents and was unable to find one that didn’t carry a warning that they were being impersonated.
[ Who should we believe on the AI apocalypse? Opens in new window ]
This reminded me that I had received a scam email some months ago. It purported to come from a real publisher in Chicago. It mentioned my radio show, this column and the titles of various books I’ve written, along with a few flattering remarks that seemed to have been scraped from reviews. They were desperate, they said, to “work with” me, though they didn’t specify what that meant.
Luckily, my impenetrable cynicism – and the telltale Gmail address – protected me from believing it. Yet I was impressed by the sophistication. Not just the details the AI had collected, but the way it was all presented: telling me what it calculated I might wish to hear.
You can congratulate yourself when you spot the scam. But how far away is the time when you can’t? When AI develops sufficient subtlety, even a sense of irony? The last request “Sean” made that I heard about was to a writer in New York. He’d published a book about the dangers of AI.

title: More than €7m laundered through money mule accounts in 12 months, banks say
description: Almost half of young adults have been approached by people looking to use accounts to transfer money
content:
More than €7 million was laundered through Irish money mule accounts in the year to the end of June, with almost half of young adults saying they had been approached by people looking to use their accounts to transfer money, according to figures from a bank industry group.
The data from FraudSMART, the fraud awareness initiative led by Banking and Payments Federation Ireland ( BPFI ), suggests that a significant percentage of adults aged between 18 and 34 would consider allowing their account to be used by others, with men far more likely to give the green light for others to access their accounts.
Some 44 per cent of 18 to 34-year-olds said they had been approached or knew someone who had been approached to use their bank account to transfer money, a sharp increase from the 24 per cent recorded in the previous survey in 2025.
Meanwhile, 21 per cent of all adults had been approached or knew someone who had been approached by another person looking to use their bank account to transfer money, up from 13 per cent in 2025.
A total of 37 per cent of 18 to 24-year-olds, and 35 per cent of 25 to 34-year-olds, said they would consider allowing their account to be used to transfer money in exchange for payment.
Across all age groups combined, men were almost twice as likely as women to say they would consider allowing their account to be used to transfer money, with 20 per cent saying they would at least think about it compared with 12 per cent of women.
Knowledge of the consequences of money muling was lowest among 18 to 24-year-olds, with 31 per cent saying they did not know it could lead to a criminal record and 40 per cent unaware it could affect their ability to obtain a visa.
“Money mule recruiters are targeting people of all ages, but particularly young adults, through social media, messaging apps, fake job advertisements and peer-to-peer contact,” said Niamh Davenport, head of financial crime at BPFI.
“Approaches are often disguised as legitimate opportunities with offers of so-called ‘quick’ or ‘easy’ money in exchange for allowing funds to pass through their bank account.”
Highlighting the risks for students, Daniel Walsh, president of AMLÉ, formerly the Union of Students in Ireland, said young people “often face significant financial pressures, making offers of quick or easy money appear tempting”.
“However, allowing someone else to use your bank account can have consequences that extend far beyond the initial payment.”

title: ‘We are abandoned’: Ukrainian family with permission to stay but nowhere to go
description: Fiona Dunne and Anna Polyshchuk have become friends but the Co Laois woman had not anticipated sharing her home for four years
content:
Fiona Dunne, who has hosted a Ukrainian woman and her daughters in Co Laois for almost four years, feels “completely let down” by the Government.
Her guest, Anna Polyshchuk, feels “abandoned” with supports for members of her community, including the monthly €400 Accommodation Recognition Payment (ARP) to hosts like Dunne, being wound down .
Introduced in July 2022, just months after Russia invaded Ukraine , the ARP was initially paid at a monthly rate of €800. This was reduced to €600 in June 2025 and to €400 last month. The payment is due to be terminated next March.
There were 16,300 people hosting 38,300 Ukrainian beneficiaries of temporary protection as of October 11th, according to the Department of Justice .
Polyshchuk arrived in Ireland via Moldova, Poland and Germany on March 31st, 2022, having reluctantly left Ukraine with her mother (now 72) and daughters (now 13 and 19). They initially stayed in Citywest, Dublin, before being moved to a hotel in Abbeyleix.
“It was very difficult all living in just one room, especially for my mother, but we were safe and very grateful. My children started in school,” she says.
Polyshchuk got work as a kitchen porter in the hotel. “I was looking all the time for a house to rent, but couldn’t find any house. I abandoned the search.
“Some local people knew my situation and they looked for a house too. One day in November, I came home and there was message on my phone. It was Fiona. ‘I know you are looking for a house. I think I can help you.’ I couldn’t believe my eyes. Fiona was a miracle.”
A neighbour, whose mother was involved in the local effort to welcome Ukrainians fleeing the war, asked Dunne if she would host a family. She was contacted by the Irish Red Cross (IRC), which co-ordinates pledges of accommodation for Ukrainians, and added her name to its list.
“I was apprehensive to be honest. I didn’t want any long-term tenants. I thought Anna would find another house to rent quickly enough,” adds Dunne, who is “semi-retired” and tends to “come and go a bit”.
Dunne’s home has a self-contained section with its own kitchen, bathroom and bedrooms, which represented a big “improvement” for Polyshchuk and her family after living in a hotel. It also meant they could remain in a community to which they had developed links.
“[The children] could stay in the schools and I can keep my job,” she says.
Unable to use her master’s degree in linguistics, Polyshchuk now has an entry-level administration job with an energy company in Portlaoise.
Dunne receives the ARP directly, describing it as “useful”, while Polyshchuk pays her family’s share of bills and towards the upkeep of the house.
The women have become close friends but had not anticipated sharing a home for four years.
“I never expected the war to be so long,” says Polyshchuk.
After a year in Dunne’s home, she began looking for accommodation for her family.
“I am 50 now. I was looking for a mortgage but at my age and salary and the only person working in the family, I cannot get enough to buy anything,” she says.
“I am not eligible for social housing or any housing support because of my status. The rents are very high and there is nothing to rent in Abbeyleix, completely nothing.
“In Portlaoise, we looked online, there are only five houses to rent. And surrounding [the town] there are 11. The prices are high and also the landlords wouldn’t consider me. They don’t want to accommodate someone without a renting history. To be honest I am lost.”
In the coming months Dunne will need the space in her home back for her own family. Polyshchuk fears for her children’s safety if they were to return to their home city Odesa.
“I am concerned. The war in Ukraine is getting only worse.”
Dunne feels a responsibility to Polyshchuk and her children, but cannot continue housing them.
“I feel we have been left on our own. You step up, you do something good. Hosting has been [a] very good model for integration,” she says.
“And integration is the key. If immigrants can’t integrate, it just becomes a lightning rod for anti-immigration sentiment.
“Government policy now is sabotaging integration.”
Asked what she will do, Polyshchuk says: “I do not have a solution. The temporary protection status is extended to 2028 because the war is still going on.
“If we have the permission to stay but we do not have possibility to rent or to have accommodation ... we are abandoned.
“Almost all Ukrainian people in subsidised accommodation, they are women with kids.”
A spokeswoman for the IRC said it would like to see the ARP scheme “remaining in place for as long as the temporary protection directive” continues.
“The ending of the ARP is likely to lead to a significant reduction in the number of pledges of accommodation received by the Irish Red Cross.”
A Department of Justice spokesman said hosts “can continue to have private arrangements with individuals” following the termination of the ARP scheme.
“People in receipt of temporary protection can also avail of private rented accommodation either through their own means or with the assistance of rent supplement, a means-tested payment administered by the Department of Social Protection,” they said.

title: Avoca’s Kilmacanogue and Rathcoole stores hit the market with €29m price tag
description: Flagship Wicklow and Dublin premises come for sale fully let to popular retailer, with 21 years remaining on lease
content:
Having paid about €22 million to acquire two of Avoca ’s flagship premises from the retailer’s US -headquartered owner, Aramark , in 2017, Irish retail property investor Signature Capital is now looking to dispose of the properties.
The sale of Avoca’s outlets at Kilmacanogue in Co Wicklow and Rathcoole in Co Dublin is expected to provide Signature’s private clients with a healthy return on their original investment. The two properties are being offered to the market by joint agents JLL and TWM, fully let to Avoca until 2047, with Aramark (US) as guarantor, at a guide price of €29 million.
Avoca Kilmacanogue is arguably the retailer’s best-known outlet apart from the company’s original mill in Avoca village. Located just off the N11, the store, which first opened for business under Avoca’s former owners, Donald Pratt and his wife Hilary in 1979, has long proved to be a draw for the affluent and densely populated south Dublin and Wicklow catchment area. It is also hugely popular with tourists and day-trippers travelling to the nearby attractions of Glendalough and Avondale Forest Park.
Avoca Kilmacanogue comprises a distinctive lifestyle and retail premises extending to 2,570sq m (27,663sq ft) on a landscaped site of 6.39 hectares (15.79 acres). Developed over a number of phases, the accommodation includes a large retail offering consisting of convenience, food, homewares and fashion, together with the Sugar Tree Cafe, Fern House Restaurant, a bakery, garden centre, ancillary accommodation and extensive cold-storage facilities.
The site may have longer term potential for residential development, subject to planning permission, according to the selling agents.
Avoca’s Rathcoole outlet is located just off the N7 Naas Road, close to junction 4 of the M7/M50 interchange, and about 16km southwest of Dublin city centre.
Developed in 2007, the property comprises a three-storey building of 3,964sq m (42,668sq ft) on a site of 1.6 hectares (3.95 acres) with frontage to both the N7 Naas Road and Fitzmaurice Road.
The ground floor consists of extensive retail and ancillary space, while the first floor is home to the Egg Cafe and Birdcage Cafe, together with kitchen facilities and balcony seating areas. The second floor comprises modern office accommodation accessed via a dedicated entrance and passenger lift, with a mix of occupiers including Avoca.
Both the Kilmacanogue and Rathcoole properties are let on long-term leases with 21 years left until expiry. The tenant is currently paying total annual rent of €1,680,000. Rent reviews occur every five years and are linked to the Consumer Price Index (CPI), subject to a 3.5 per cent annual cap and -0.5 per cent annual collar, compounded annually.
The rent is guaranteed by Avoca’s parent company Aramark (US). Aramark acquired the Avoca business from the Pratt family in a €66.7 million* deal in 2015.
The next CPI rental uplift is due in September 2027, with the rent payable increasing to €2 million at that time. The vendor is providing a rental underwrite to ensure that the incoming owner will secure a yield of 6.2 per cent based on the asking price of €29 million.
Sean O’Neill of TWM says: “Opportunities of this calibre rarely come to the market, combining the security of such a recognisable tenant with the benefit of long-term secure income. This portfolio offers investors an exceptional opportunity to secure stable and predictable cash flows, making it particularly attractive to those seeking wealth preservation, inflation protection and long-duration income in a premier retail and hospitality asset.”
Max Reilly of JLL adds: “This is an exceptional asset with long-term, inflation-proof income backed by an outstanding guarantor.”
*This article was amended to include the correct price paid by Aramark for the Avoca business. Reports published in 2015 and 2016 suggested the deal carried a lower value of between €51 and €60 million

title: Dublin 4’s landmark Schoolhouse Hotel for sale, seeking €12m
description: Boutique four-star venue comprises 31 guest rooms, gastrobar and 24 car-parking spaces
content:
Having owned and operated the boutique Schoolhouse Hotel on Dublin’s Northumberland Road for nearly three decades now, Galway-based hotelier and businessman Terry Sweeney has instructed agent Lisney Commercial Real Estate to find a buyer for the Ballsbridge landmark.
The 31-bedroom venue is being offered to the market as a going concern at a guide price of €12 million, which equates to €387,096 per key.
Designed by renowned architects Deane and Woodward – whose works famously include Trinity College Dublin’s Museum Building – and built originally in 1859 as St Stephen’s Parochial School, the building was restored and converted into a four-star hotel by Terry Sweeney in 1998.
Numerous of the building’s original features have been preserved, including its distinctive redbrick facade, its arched windows, and high ceilings. The hotel comprises 31 guest rooms, a gastrobar, landscaped gardens and 24 on-site car-parking spaces.
The Schoolhouse Hotel has, over the years, established itself as one of Dublin’s best-known independent boutique hotels. The food and beverage offering is centred around a series of dining and lounge spaces featuring original brickwork, exposed timber detailing and contemporary finishes. There is extensive outdoor seating in the hotel’s mature, landscaped gardens.
Shane Markey of Lisney Commercial Real Estate says: “The Schoolhouse Hotel’s prime setting, strong reputation and distinctive architectural character have seen it attract a loyal mix of corporate, leisure and international visitors.
“This sale provides an opportunity to acquire a well-established hospitality business in one of Dublin’s most sought-after locations, combining strong operational fundamentals with an irreplaceable heritage setting.”

title: Asian food wholesaler secures €7.35m from sale of Dublin 11 warehouse
description: Sale follows move by P&B Foods to new and larger facility within Huntstown Business Park
content:
Having taken delivery of and relocated to a new and larger food storage and distribution facility at Huntstown Business Park, Asian food wholesale distribution specialist P&B Foods, has completed the sale of its former premises at the Dublin 11 scheme. The company, which will be better known to consumers for its Heera, Balah and Rishta brands, secured €7.35 million from the sale of Cobalt House to an Irish owner-occupier company. The price paid equates to a capital value of €2,518.76 per square metre (€234/sq ft).
Cobalt House comprises a detached warehouse of 2,920sq m (31,422sq ft) and includes 453sq m (4,877sq ft) of two-storey office accommodation. The property has a secure, gated and fenced yard with depths of 36-40m, 24 car-parking spaces (including two EV spaces) to the front, alongside freshly landscaped boundaries. Loading is provided via two dock levellers and one level-access door.
The warehouse is of single-span steel-portal frame construction, with a clear internal height of 12m, an FM2 grade floor with a loading capacity of 60kN/m², high-output LED lighting and an insulated twin-skin composite roof with siphonic drainage system. The office accommodation has been finished to a high standard and comes equipped with a curtain-wall glazing system, suspended ceilings with recessed LED lighting and a new air-conditioning system.
Kevin McHugh of industrial specialist agent Harvey represented P&B Foods in the transaction while James Kearney of BNP Paribas Real Estate acted for the purchaser.
Kevin McHugh said: “Cobalt House attracted interest from both owner-occupiers and investors owing to the property’s combination of prime northwest Dublin location, excellent building specification and immediate availability with vacant possession.”
[ Dún Laoghaire business park with scope for residential scheme seeks €3m Opens in new window ]
James Kearney added: “We are delighted to have advised our owner-occupier client on the acquisition of Cobalt House. The property’s modern design, A2 Ber rating and proximity to both junction five and six of the M50 motorway made it a compelling opportunity to service their business in both Dublin and across the island of Ireland”.
Huntstown Business Park is located on the western side of Cappagh Road in Ballycoolin, 16km northwest of Dublin city centre. The property sits equidistant from junctions five and six of the M50 motorway, providing ready access to Dublin Airport, Dublin Port Tunnel and to all the main arterial routes on Ireland’s national road network.

title: Keelings seeking occupiers for latest phase at FoodCentral business park
description: Family-owned food group offering total of 41 acres for sale or lease at 280-acre scheme next to Dublin Airport
content:
Keelings , the well-known family-owned Irish food business, has engaged Finnegan Menton and Cushman & Wakefield as joint sale and letting agents for the latest phase of lands at FoodCentral , the 280-acre food industry park it owns at St Margaret’s near Dublin Airport . The scheme, which is dedicated to companies operating in the food, drinks and flowers sectors, currently comprises more than two million square feet (185,800sq m) of food-industry accommodation and is occupied by a range of companies including Keelings Group, Donnelly Fresh, Dixons, Oakland, Americold, Keoghs Crisps, Mad Flowers, HelloFresh, Flogas and HPP Tolling.
The latest phase of development lands being released for sale or letting comprise 41 acres in total. The available sites range in size from 2.95 acres to 28 acres while permissible building sizes are from 20,000sq ft (1,858sq m) to more than 300,000sq ft (27,800sq m), subject to planning permission . The joint agents are guiding a price of €600,000 an acre for sites of five acres or larger in the current phase. Rental levels for completed buildings, meanwhile, will depend on specification and the overall building and plot size. A range of options are available to prospective occupiers including design and build or lease.
The launch of the latest sites at FoodCentral comes as Dixon Transport nears the completion of the fourth phase of development at its facility since locating there in 2015. The latest phase comprises a fully automated ambient and temperature-controlled distribution centre of 10,200sq m (110,000sq ft) immediately adjoining a slightly larger sized facility completed in mid-2024. Dixon’s facilities at FoodCentral will extend to more than 28,000sq m (300,000sq ft) once the current works are completed.
Derry Group Ireland acquired a 5.7-acre site at FoodCentral in late 2024 and secured planning permission within three months for a new 2,046sq m (22,000sq ft) refrigerated warehouse and truck parking facility. The development is due for completion by the end of this year. Derry Group specialises in the storage, order picking and distribution of chilled and frozen products throughout Ireland with depots in Armagh, Dublin and Cork.
[ French investor pays €15m for Portlaoise logistics facility Opens in new window ]
A Tesla Supercharger station is also under construction at FoodCentral with eight superchargers being delivered in the current phase, with another six spaces to follow in phase two. Keelings Farm Shop and Cafe is also set for expansion, with planning permission recently granted by Fingal County Council to extend the existing space to more than 416sq m (4,480sq ft).
The FoodCentral scheme is well located immediately next to the northern runway at Dublin Airport, and about a six-minute drive from the M1, M2 and M50 motorways. Dublin Port Tunnel is about a 10-minute drive away.
Nicholas Corson of Finnegan Menton said discussions were already under way with a number of parties in relation to the sale of sites and for the development of completed buildings within FoodCentral. A plot of 5.5 acres within the 41 acres now being marketed is already reserved and at legals.
Brendan Smyth of Cushman & Wakefield said: “FoodCentral is an excellent location for both processing and logistics. The scheme is close to Dublin Airport and the road network and offers prospective occupiers flexibility in regard to site size, scale and future expansion.”

title: Subsidies like Help to Buy are no longer needed as homebuyer demand weakens
description: Government is using taxpayers’ money to support property prices as it chases increasingly unrealistic housing targets
content:
C ontinued growth in housing completions and moderating house price inflation have been welcomed as signs that Ireland’s housing crisis might finally be turning a corner.
However, a deep dive exposes problems which are difficult to ignore.
At a glance, both supply and price inflation are moving in the right direction. Nearly 16,700 new dwellings were delivered across Ireland in the first six months of 2026 . This is the strongest first half of the year since before the global financial crisis and it represents an 11 per cent up-lift on the corresponding period in 2025.
This has coincided with a continued slowdown in house price inflation which has almost halved from 10.1 to 5.1 per cent a year over the last two years.
All else being equal, increased supply should dampen house price growth, so it is unsurprising that people have assumed a causal link between the continued uplift in completions and receding inflationary pressure.
However the all-else-equal condition rarely applies in nature and, in the Irish housing market , other things have been happening besides increased supply. In particular, demographic and economic headwinds have emerged which suggest that slowing inflation may be as much to do with weakening demand as strengthening supply.
[ House price inflation slows as demand falls Opens in new window ]
Most fundamentally, population growth is slowing sharply. With the exception of a Covid blip in 2021, the rate of demographic expansion is now back to levels last seen a decade ago. On the economic front, the European Central Bank has raised interest rates twice since June, causing mortgage rates to begin moving up. By impacting debt service-to-income ratios this is imposing restrictions on the amount that home buyers can borrow.
Labour market developments are also dragging on demand. There has been a pronounced slowdown in jobs growth and unemployment has been creeping up, albeit from a low base. Just as importantly, weakness has been concentrated in highly remunerated sectors of the economy which, until recently, had underpinned the property market. Tech is Ireland’s best paid industry, with earnings levels 65 per cent above the national average.
However, whether it derives from a shift in tech firms’ investment priorities or America’s stance on foreign direct investment, tech employment in Ireland has contracted by 6.5 per cent since early 2025. There has also been a shake-out in professional services, another highly paid sector, with 17,800 jobs lost in the last year.
Inevitably, these weaker employment dynamics have impacted earnings growth. Average salaries are now rising at a rate of 3.9 per cent a year, well below the post-Covid norm.
It is hard to be definitive about the respective contributions of stronger supply and weaker demand to the current slowdown in house price inflation. However, several factors suggest that the demand side may be dominating.
Firstly, although residential sales are up by 5.6 per cent year-on-year, this has largely been driven by the heavily subsidised new homes sector where transactions have risen by 15.2 per cent.
One interpretation is that consumers who cannot avail of State supports have hit their affordability limits. Indeed, this interpretation aligns with intelligence from online sales portals which shows that, although the flow of second-hand homes to the market has remained broadly flat, these properties are taking longer to sell and are achieving lower premiums over asking prices.
Also pointing towards the demand side, a tenure shift from home purchase to renting appears to be happening. The growth rate in private tenancies is outstripping that in household numbers, and pricing dynamics suggest that frustrated buyers are being displaced into the rental market; whereas house price inflation has slowed, rent inflation has rebounded from 2.7 to 4.7 per cent a year since the start of the year.
Ultimately, housing costs in Ireland are too high. This cannot be resolved by engineering lower prices. With housing equity appearing on many voters’ balance sheets, and with banks relying on property collateral, attempting to do so would be politically and economically impractical.
Therefore, the least painful resolution would be for earnings growth to exceed modest house price inflation for a sustained period. Welcome as it is, the recent slowdown in price growth falls well short of achieving this. In fact, both property price and rent inflation are still comprehensively outstripping earnings growth, so affordability continues to disimprove.
It should also be remembered that, as property prices and rents build up, inflation rates get applied to a higher base. At the onset of Covid the average house cost €261,240 and today’s 5.1 per cent inflation rate would have represented an absolute price increase of €13,323. The average home now costs €400,201, so that same percentage increase represents €20,410.
Reflecting on recent trends, and the factors behind them, the objective of sustained moderate house price inflation should be within reach. But achieving this would require housing policy to stop working against itself. A good starting point would be for Government to review whether its housing targets are realistic, necessary or helpful.
The current target of around 50,000 completions a year appears to be based on an assumption that the rapid population growth of 2022-2024 would be sustained. This was never likely; the inflow of Ukrainian nationals during this period was inevitably going to slow at some point, just as the magnet of rapid jobs growth was also destined to weaken.
The target also appears to bake-in an assumption that household sizes in Ireland will converge towards European norms. Again, this is unrealistic; Ireland has the highest proportion of children in the EU and children naturally tend to live in larger households.
[ What is behind the slowdown in Ireland’s property prices? Opens in new window ]
Finally, the inclusion of an overbuild target to correct a supposed backlog of unmet housing demand is just plain flawed – the Census measured housing vacancy at almost eight per cent.
Recent evidence only reinforces doubts about these targets. With demand weakening, Ireland’s property market appears to be heading towards equilibrium at a run-rate of approximately 40,000 housing completions a year.
This should be embraced, and the correct policy action would be to drop subsidies like Help to Buy , the First Home Scheme , the Local Authority Home Loan and the Rent Tax Credit .
The aim of these schemes is to turbocharge supply, which is clearly no longer needed. Their mechanism for drawing out the extra supply is to widen development margins by boosting prices. This is exactly the opposite of what is required.
Current demographic and economic trends present a golden opportunity to prioritise affordability over increased housing output.
We are building enough dwellings to meet demand and backing off the inflationary subsidy schemes at this point would allow house price inflation to continue naturally moderating. Unfortunately, however, politics is politics. The Government has staked its reputation on delivering more homes, and it seems determined to do this at any price.
Despite advice from its own consultants to shut down Help to Buy, it extended the scheme until 2029 and doubled-down in this month’s budget by raising the subsidy from €30,000 to €35,000. Simultaneously, it increased the Rent Tax Credit for the third time since its introduction in 2022, while also raising the First Home Scheme price caps in July.
A sustained period of moderate house price inflation is needed to resolve Ireland’s affordability crisis. But, as long as the political system remains shackled to chasing supersized output targets, this will not be achieved. This is because, for a country with overflowing public coffers, stimulating supply generally means using taxpayers’ money to drive up prices.
John McCartney lectures in property economics at TU Dublin

title: Renovated Mount Pleasant Avenue home with design flair
description: Ranelagh four-bed showcases considered design and elegant period features
content:
Number 13 Mount Pleasant Avenue Upper in Ranelagh is a renovated four-bedroom period property overlooking the grounds of Leinster Cricket Club. Its owners have not only extended the ground floor and added new bathrooms, but they have designed the 193sq m (2,077sq ft) home with meticulous attention to detail, and flair for colour and style.
Coming to the market seeking €1.625 million with Sherry FitzGerald , the two-storey-over-basement house is set back from the road behind wrought-iron railings with a well planted and paved front garden. The owners enjoy sitting out here with a bottle of wine on warm Sunday evenings, and many of their neighbours pop over to join them.
Through the front door, topped with an elegant fanlight, the entrance hall is painted in Farrow and Ball’s Worsted grey shade, with dark stained floorboards and a chandelier suspended from an ornate ceiling rose.
The heritage theme continues in the two reception rooms leading off the hallway. The drawingroom is painted red and features a wide sash window and a cast-iron fireplace with a slate hearth.
Behind it lies the diningroom, the dramatic ante is considerably elevated here, with classic period furniture, many pieces of which were family heirlooms, a large gilt overmantel mirror and walls painted in Railings by Farrow & Ball. All elements combine to create a sumptuous entertaining space.
The owners spent the majority of their time in the basement kitchen and livingroom. With the help of architect David Smith, they extended past the original footprint of the house into the garden, considerably enlarging the available space and allowing the installation of a custom-built kitchen by Gallagher’s of Lucan. Underfloor heating and extensive insulation resulted in a B Ber.
A short flight of stairs leading down to the kitchen is adorned on one side by a shelved area that the owners have used as a wine cellar. All the kitchen appliances are Miele and a large island has a sink unit and plenty of seating.
A large roof light over the dining area and sliding doors leading out to the garden contribute to the feeling of light and space. The garden is small and immaculately planted, with acers and lavender and a seating area.
Back inside, a living area in the centre of the basement floor is lit by a stove. The built-in shelving is unobtrusive, slotting in with the high-end design of the entire property. Tiles underfoot are a sleek polished granite.
There’s a utility area tucked away under the stairs with laundry appliances and plenty of storage, and the rest of this floor consists of a bedroom and bathroom, with its own entrance area to the front.
On the first-floor return is a small bathroom and a bedroom, both with underfloor heating. The small bedroom could equally be used as a home office, away from the main activity zones of the rest of the house.
The first floor has two well-decorated bedrooms, both in dark, subdued tones. The main bedroom enjoys great views over the cricket grounds through its deep, tall windows. It has a fine en suite bathroom and built-in wardrobes. The second bedroom on this floor overlooks the garden, has an exterior wrought-iron railing at the window and retains its original cast-iron fireplace.
Somewhat reluctant to move, but with another restoration project in their sights, the owners say they have loved living on Mountpleasant Avenue thanks to their neighbours, the quick access to the city and being an easy distance from Rathmines and Ranelagh.

title: A walk through Dennis the Menace’s troubled hometown
description: Scotland’s comic capital remains rich in character, even as it struggles to overcome deep social scars
content:
I had 24 hours to kill after a political event in Aberdeen and before meetings I had planned in Fife, so I hid out in the east of Scotland on the Tayside in Dundee . There I found a city riddled with contradictions, at once handsome and ugly, funny and sad.
It really is a funny place. Dundonians are known for their deadpan wit while their city is also renowned as the comic capital of Britain. Dundee is home to DC Thomson, publisher of the Dandy, which ceased in 2013, and the Beano, still going after 88 years. This year the city also celebrates one of its most famous sons: Dennis the Menace is 75.
Like many men now blundering into the thickets of middle age, I was raised on comic strips such as the Bash Street Kids, the Beano characters who were originally based on children from the High School of Dundee, which was near DC Thomson’s old offices.
I had heard that Dundee’s city council had, years before, renamed a city thoroughfare as Bash Street in the strip’s honour. I found it just off Marketgait, in an old industrial area to the west of the grimy, run-down commercial centre. The city gave me my first smile.
The councillors had supposedly chosen that specific location for the tribute because it was also the site of a planned children’s soft play centre. They envisioned real-life kids having fun directly beneath a Bash Street sign. The play centre fell through. These days, tiny Bash Street’s only real feature is the not-very-kid-friendly smoking area of a casino.
I walked through Albert Square, with its locally-famous bronze figure of cartoon character Oor Wullie. He sits near another famous Dundee statue: Scotland’s national bard, Robert Burns. In the grand, facetious Scottish tradition of revellers adorning statues, someone had tried to crown him with a traffic cone, but got his quill instead.
There were more Beano and Dandy cartoon-themed bronze statues on High Street: including an eight-foot Desperate Dan and a catapult-wielding Minnie the Minx.
But it wasn’t all smiles in the city centre. Dundee is acknowledged to have the worst drug problems of almost any city in Europe – only Glasgow has recently overtaken it. Ample human evidence of the city’s chronic polydrugs crisis shuffled about the streets.
While the centre is woefully neglected, planners in Dundee, which is long past its textiles industrial heyday, have encouraged development on the waterfront.
It includes a stunning offshoot of London’s design palace, the V&A (Victoria and Albert museum) at one end. At the other is the HMS Unicorn, a preserved 1842 frigate that is one of the oldest surviving wooden ships in the world.
Dundee’s other big landmark is the Tay Road Bridge that spans the Firth of Tay, whose calm estuary waters shimmered all weekend in the late autumn brightness – Dundee is also the sunniest city in Scotland.
As I walked along the waterfront past the point where the bridge reaches out across the Tay, I noticed a large, colourful sign on the wall: “Look out for each other.” The slogan was repeated in the pedestrian lift up to the bridge and various points thereafter.
Ostensibly, it seemed to allude to the need for cyclists and pedestrians to be careful as they shared the path across the bridge. But it could also have had another connotation: bridges the world over spell danger for the most desperate of people. In Dundee too.
Scottish government data indicate Dundee has the highest suicide rate of any Scottish city. Local charities blame the city’s drugs crisis, the ingrained deprivation wrought by decades of Dundee’s industrial decline, and over-strained mental health services.
Police Scotland has a grim official categorisation for call-outs dealing with people who are spotted in situations where they are in danger of acting in such a desperate way. They call them “concern for person” incidents. The Tay Road Bridge is a hotspot.
After a number of high-profile, tragic cases this year, there is an ongoing local campaign to get bigger safety barriers installed on the Tay Road Bridge. Meanwhile, the people of Dundee continue to look out for each other. Local mental health charities and volunteer groups have recently galvanised to collaborate in a “suicide prevention collective”.
That night, I returned to the city centre to find that Dundee’s myriad social problems had multiplied in the dark. Parts of the city centre are quite handsome in the daylight, but there is a far grittier edge to the place at night. This is acknowledged among Dundonians.
[ Two sides to the story in city dubbed ‘Yes capital of Scotland’ Opens in new window ]
Yet the city also retains its indomitable free spirit. Dundee is widely considered to be the ‘Yes’ capital of Scotland’s independence movement. While the nation as a whole voted 55 per cent ‘No’ to 45 per cent ‘Yes’ in the 2014 independence referendum, Dundee returned a 57.4 per cent ‘Yes’ result, the highest of any region.
It is a city embroiled in a difficult transition from its past, still at the heart of the debate about Scotland’s future.

title: Leixlip town centre site with scope for 48 apartments guiding at €1.75m
description: Shingle House occupies high-profile location on Main Street in thriving Kildare employment hub
content:
Developers and investors involved in the delivery of housing for the owner-occupier, private rented sector and student accommodation markets are expected to run the rule over the sale of a prominent property and site in the heart of Leixlip town in Co Kildare .
Shingle House, a distinctive three-storey period building of 258sq m (2,777sq ft), which occupies a 0.5-hectare (1.24-acre) site at the junction of Leixlip Road and Main Street, is being offered to the market by agent Lisney Commercial Real Estate at a guide price of €1.75 million.
The subject property and its site are zoned for the most part as Zone A – Town Centre under the terms of the Leixlip Local Area Plan (LAP) 2020 – 2023, as extended to March 2029. The property is also included in Leixlip’s Town Centre Regeneration Area.
The site’s potential for residential development is highlighted in a feasibility study drawn up by Plus Architecture in advance of the current sale. This suggests that the lands could accommodate an apartment scheme comprising 48 apartments, consisting of a mix of 28 one-bedroom units and 20 two-bedroom units, along with the retention of Shingle House, subject to planning permission.
Shingle House occupies a high-profile location on Main Street in Leixlip and sits within walking distance of the town’s shops, cafes and other amenities. Leixlip is a thriving employment centre thanks to the presence in the area over several decades of the operations of a number of the world’s leading technology and pharmaceutical companies. In the case of Intel, its Leixlip campus is its largest European manufacturing and innovation base and has been in operation since 1989.
Leixlip is also an established commuter town with rail connections to Dublin available at both Louisa Bridge and Confey stations. The M4 motorway is a short drive from the town, allowing ready access to the capital and to the wider national road network. For those parties interested in exploring the site’s potential for student accommodation, Shingle House is situated 10.6km from Maynooth University.
Shane O’Connor of Lisney says: “This property’s central location, zoning and residential potential make it an attractive opportunity for developers looking deliver a scheme within an established and well-connected town centre.”

title: Wildwood review: Five stars for a stop-motion wonder destined to become a classic for the ages
description: In an age of safe sequels and reboots, Laika Studios deserve credit for taking a swing
content:
Even if the latest animation from Laika, the stop-motion home of the diligent Travis Knight, had not turned out to be a wonder, one would still feel obliged to praise the makers of Wildwood for their bravery.
In an era of endless sequels and reboots, here is family entertainment that dares to mark out its own territory. No other mainstream animation house would allow this degree of angst, peril and actual death.
The fantasy begins with something like a suicide and goes on to take in martial slaughter on a medieval scale. Yet, despite its sense of murky jeopardy, it remains an oblique charmer throughout.
The film is set around Portland, Oregon, and it wants you to know it. Young Prue McKeel (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) is living the rough-wool, matted-hair, mung-bean life characteristic of that post-hippie locale with parents who tick every homeschooled box. At one point they note that an emergency caused them to try every mad solution, “even western medicine”.
Prue enjoys a largely untroubled adolescence, but some sort of secret is nagging at the family’s messy idyll. Why are the parents so protective of Prue’s baby brother, Mac? (His cries are those of the director’s own son.) Anyone who has ever heard a fairy tale will suspect that some pact with malign forces is at the root of the mystery.
[ Forgotten Island review: A plot that breaks up into a kaleidoscope of surreal adventure Opens in new window ]
Anyway, one day, defying her mum’s instructions to keep the child at home, Prue brings him to a coffee shop and then on for adventures in the school playground. In a neat allusion to Alfred Hitchcock’s The Birds, the jungle gym (“climbing frame” to us) is soon obscured by a colossal murder of crows.
The animals descend on the children, pluck poor Mac from Prue’s protection and transport him into the looming woods that abut this version of the United States’s most organic city.
Adapted from a popular novel by Colin Meloy, founder of the rock band The Decemberists, Wildwood, as that synopsis demonstrates, is rich with reminders of ancient folklore and more recent fantasy: CS Lewis , JRR Tolkien , Philip Pullman . Dare one suggest there is also (accidentally, I’m sure) a bit of Rupert the Bear in the unsettling anthropomorphic supporting characters?
We soon learn that much of the evil in Wildwood is down to the dominance of a bitter, frustrated presence known as the dowager governess Alexandra (voiced throatily by Carey Mulligan ). She is wicked witch, evil stepsister, Pullman’s Mrs Coulter. She is also convincingly tragic, damaged by believable human catastrophes.
There is a beautiful originality to the animation, the characters moving with a natural dip and bob that stop-motion rarely manages. It helps that Caleb Deschanel, the veteran cinematographer behind The Right Stuff, lights each shot with more creative invention than you would expect from the widest live-action epic. This will almost certainly be the best-looking animated feature you see this year.
The voice cast is also beyond compare: Tom Waits , Richard E Grant , Awkwafina, Angela Bassett and on and on.
Should we worry about who the film is for? Set in an anti-present that, once in the woods, blends Victorian with dark ages – Alexandra’s coyote henchman are dressed like hussars – Knight’s entertainment, stretching past two hours, demands more attention than the vast majority of talking animal flicks.
And there is no getting away from the impressive levels of slaughter. The closing battles dare to stretch out into complex martial symphonies that might gain approval from even Akira Kurosawa .
This is the sort of film that parents might assume will bore or terrify children. Such thinking has too often governed the decisions of panicky studio heads who haven’t bothered to investigate the unsettling tales of the Brothers Grimm (or even the nastier corners of Roald Dahl ). The film may struggle to gain huge audiences on release, but it will surely settle in as a classic for the ages.

title: Possible Love review: A searching, darkly funny film about class, dignity and exploitation
description: This masterclass in dramatic timing over 165 minutes coalesces into a gasping thriller
content:
Possible Love, a searching, darkly funny film about class, dignity and exploitation, was loosely inspired by Krzysztof Kieslowski’s biblically themed Dekalog, specifically the instalment based on the Ten Commandments’ prohibition of covetousness.
This wickedly smart drama’s real target, however, is the unequal distribution of wealth and power. Who gets to chronicle this inequality? And who has to put up with it?
Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong), a dilettante film-maker wearing Gwyneth Paltrow-friendly quiet-luxury brands, arrives at a memorial gathering for a recent corporate lay-off who has died by suicide.
She is making a documentary about workers dismissed after a violently suppressed industrial strike. Her subjects include the traumatised Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), a former factory worker left physically and psychologically shattered, and his wife, Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon, star of Secret Sunshine, the director’s 2007 tragedy), who struggles to hold their family, including their distant young son, together.
An unlikely friendship develops between Mi-ok and Ye-ji, drawing both couples into increasingly queasy proximity. The director’s sharpest insights concern the sleek seduction of wealth and the pretensions of benevolence. Ye-ji masquerades as a campaigner, yet on the ride home from a shoot, her Elon Musk-alike – Musky? – entrepreneur husband, Sang-woo (Zo In-sung), praises her method acting.
He exudes charm and foundation charity wealth. “You remind me of Steve Jobs,” Mi-ok coos schoolgirlishly at Sang-woo over dinner, just before he dashes outside for a phone call that may or may not concern the multinational that has doomed Mi-ok and her husband.
For the wealthier couple, their new friends are exotic poverty porn to be sampled at will; for Ye-ji’s subjects, their world is inescapable. Their “film within a film” director’s gaze becomes equally and absurdly intrusive.
Watching Lee Chang-dong’s films, you feel they must fall under some kind of magical seal. Going in, the subject matter and duration always look formidable: 139 minutes for Poetry, the 2010 Cannes favourite in which a woman struggling with Alzheimer’s disease develops a late interest in literature, or 148 minutes for Burning, another Cannes prizewinner, in which two toxic men compete over a missing woman.
In common with these titles, Possible Love offers a masterclass in dramatic timing over 165 minutes; its meticulous, unhurried rhythms coalesce, miraculously, into a gasping thriller.
The film’s second half moves to the affluent husband’s coastal retreat, where material inequality becomes almost nauseatingly oppressive. Affluence offers its owners a freedom that the workers can scarcely imagine. Their hosts, who whistle to summon their “inherited” butler, remain oblivious to the humiliations embedded in their generosity.
The performances are note-perfect. Zo In-sung and Cho Yeo-jeong are appropriately frictionless as the high-rollers. Ho-seok’s clenched movements flag injuries that language cannot convey, while Jeon Do-yeon channels warmth, desperation and steel in Mi-ok’s every blink.
Lee and his co-writer, Oh Jung-mi, offer neither easy reconciliation nor the comfort of moral superiority. Everyone here is scrambling in opposing directions. This is an end-times fable. There can be no happy reconciliations for this 1 per cent and their many victims.

title: ‘Irish customers want a kitchen that is warm and welcoming, and premium appliances that stand the test of time’
description: The Miele Experience Centre offers Irish customers a premium environment in which to discover innovative appliances that are designed to last, as Miele director and country manager for Ireland Ben Murphy explains
content:
Experiential retail became a buzzword at the end of the pandemic, but Miele had been refining the idea for several years. The German appliance brand had already established Miele Experience Centres in many of the world’s biggest capital cities and its dedicated space at Liffey Valley Shopping Centre in Dublin brings that same sense of occasion to Ireland.
“We wanted to give the Irish consumer a sense of how premium should feel,” says Ben Murphy, Miele’s director and country manager for Ireland. “Premium isn’t just about viewing products, it’s about meeting our teams, engaging, touching the products and understanding the features and benefits.”
Miele has been in Ireland since 1983 and its appliances are designed and tested to last more than 20 years. The centre was conceived to attract long-time customers as much as new ones, giving them a chance to ask questions and to engage with the products in a very practical and tactile manner. The Liffey Valley Experience Centre mirrors those in Milan, Paris, Copenhagen and Stockholm, Murphy says.
“A Miele Experience Centre should feel the same everywhere,” he says. “You’re meeting the same friendly, knowledgeable staff and getting that same Miele feeling.” He believes the Irish market is more than ready for it. Over the past two decades, he says, Irish consumers have become more affluent, more discerning and more comfortable buying premium brands, including premium domestic appliances.
Visitors to the store are greeted by the team – “part of the Miele family” – and offered hospitality before being left to browse without pressure. Staff then pair them with the colleague best suited to answering their questions. “A number of our team members are specialists and we have different age profiles,” Murphy says, “from people with families to younger members just starting out. We try to identify the customer’s requirements and tailor their experience in store by matching them with one of our key employees.”
Demonstrations are central to the concept. A Miele Experience Centre is equipped to host cooking classes as well as intimate masterclasses with some of Ireland’s favourite foodies. The team is ready to cook a meal any day of the week in order to showcase particular features and guest chefs have included Rachel Allen and Mark Moriarty. “If we show you something and it lives up to your expectation, that’s a very positive thing,” says Murphy.
Certain customers come to explore kitchen design ideas; others to learn more about the latest technology. The store showcases a curated edit of Miele’s hero products and highlights include its MasterCool fridge-freezers; Taste Control, a cooking feature that helps automate results; and the new Nova washing machine, which he describes as a world first, designed with Miele’s gentlest programme yet to protect clothes for a lifetime. “One of the tests we often do to demonstrate how delicate the washing machine cycle is involves washing a rose from end to end. It comes out of the machine with its petals still intact.”
Murphy believes that customers want “good, honest advice, that’s truthful and unbiased” and staff are ready to offer their opinions on appliances as well as which companies and partners to consider when designing a kitchen. “In Ireland, we love the kitchen,” Murphy says. “Irish consumers want to create a kitchen that is warm and welcoming. After all, in my home, friends and family come in, they sit in the kitchen, we have a drink in the kitchen, we socialise in the kitchen.” Miele has paid close attention to how the sound, colour and function of its appliances fit the way people live now. “If you want to socialise in your kitchen, having a dishwasher that’s super-quiet is so important,” says Murphy.
‘If you want to socialise in your kitchen, having a dishwasher that’s super-quiet is so important’
One question that often comes up is price. As a premium product, Miele sits at the higher end of the scale. The team responds by walking customers through the value of a product over its lifetime. An appliance built to last 20 years, Murphy argues, should be judged on that lifespan rather than on the sticker price.
Miele is a company built on innovation and at the recent consumer electronics and home appliances trade show, IFA, in Berlin, Murphy saw how the company is focusing on using AI to reduce the time and effort people devote to household chores. Cameras in ovens and dishwashers are central to this. In a dishwasher, the camera assesses what has been loaded and how dirty it is, then chooses the programme and detergent amount using Miele’s PowerDisc automatic dosing system. In an oven, FoodView captures images of the cooking process every minute, so you can monitor its progress at a glance in the Miele app, adjusting the oven settings or switching it off remotely.
Murphy also expects Miele’s advanced steam ovens, already popular in Scandinavia and Germany, to grow in popularity in Ireland. “People of my generation will remember pressure cookers bubbling away furiously on a stove somewhere. Miele has really looked at this whole concept, at how steam cooks fish and meat, and how it retains the nutrients in vegetables. We’ve come up with a concept that allows the consumer to cook with care, safety and precision, but faster, while still holding on to the nutrients in the food.”
The Miele Experience Centre at Liffey Valley Shopping Centre is one part of a wider approach by the company to invest in all of its retail partners throughout the country. “Miele is investing in a training programme that takes the Liffey Valley experience and brings it to our ambassadors and partners in electrical retail. We’re working very closely with them so they understand not only the future trends, but that Miele products are the way to future-proof a kitchen for the next 20 years, meaning they’ll stand the test of time.” The Liffey Valley Experience Centre, Murphy explains, is partly about “setting the standard for our partners to follow”.
Looking ahead five to 10 years, Murphy would like to see more than one Miele Experience Centre in Ireland. But his real measure of success is the fact that what customers are told in the centre holds true once the product is in their home. “The knowledge that’s imparted by our teams to consumers is actually felt long after they walk away,” he says.
Visit the Miele Experience Centre at Unit 15, Liffey Valley Shopping Centre, Fonthill Road, D22 XH28; phone 01 4610710 or email liffey-valley.store@miele.ie . For more, see miele.ie

title: ‘Lessons learned’ as Kelly family scales back plans for housing scheme in south Dublin
description: Kelland Homes-led project has been held up in appeals after initial plans were rejected as ‘overdevelopment’
content:
A housing development proposed on the site of two cottages in south Co Dublin has been significantly scaled back after a previous planning application was thrown out and the project was held up in the appeals process for nearly two years.
The initial plans were deemed to constitute “overdevelopment” of the area, between Foxrock and Blackrock , although the team behind the project says the renewed proposal “is heavily informed [by] lessons learned” from its past experience.
Developer Kelland Homes has applied for permission to construct 22 houses and apartments in blocks up to three storeys tall on a site facing the Clonkeen Road in Deansgrange, documents filed last week to Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council show.
The developer spent more than €2.5 million in total through two purchases more than five years apart from one another, to acquire the site that consists of two two-bedroom bungalow cottages and amounts to a little over a quarter of a hectare in size.
Kelland’s new application has reduced the number of planned units by more than a third. The developer previously sought to construct 35 apartments in blocks up to six storeys tall, planning records from nearly four years ago show.
The local council rejected the initial proposal in April 2022, with its planning office stating the “overall scale, height and form” of the development would be “detrimental” to the surrounding properties. Its “visually overbearing” stature would “unreasonably compromise” the local area, planning documents read.
An appeal was lodged in May 2022 by Kelland Homes, which was established in the 1970s by Patrick Kelly , the well-known Celtic Tiger-era property tycoon. The company is still largely owned by Kelly’s family.
[ Rise and fall of a Tiger tycoon Opens in new window ]
In January 2024, nearly two years after the planning application was submitted, An Bord Pleanála (now known as An Coimisiún Pleanála) upheld the council’s decision.
The State planning authority said the plans “would constitute overdevelopment” and “would seriously injure the residential and visual amenities of property in the vicinity of the site”.
In supporting documents submitted last week to the council, a town planning consultancy firm working on behalf of Kelland Homes said that the “revised proposals” are “substantially different” from the original development and its volume has been “significantly reduced”.
The developer is now seeking permission to construct 10 town houses of three or four bedrooms and 10 apartments of two or three bedrooms, not exceeding three storeys in height, the renewed planning application reads.
The site currently hosts two semidetached bungalows, which Kelland Homes proposes to partially demolish and later refurbish. The two properties sit on a combined 0.43 hectares, according to data from Tailte Éireann , which maintains the State’s official land register.
One of the homes, 21 Monaloe Cottages, was sold in October 2020 for €1,625,000, while the adjoining 20 Monaloe Cottages property was sold in April 2026 for €900,000, according to the Property Price Register. Both cottages had two bedrooms at the time of their sale.
Kelland Homes also proposes “the relocation of the existing bus shelter and associated bus stop on Clonkeen Road”, which services the Dublin Bus L26 route to Blackrock Dart station, to provide space for the development’s entrance.

title: Pensions become part of the talent equation
description: As employees pay closer attention to the full value of their benefits, a good pension is becoming an increasingly important part of the employment proposition
content:
In a competitive market for talent, salary will always matter. But employees are increasingly looking beyond the number that lands in their bank account each month and considering the wider package an employer can offer.
For David Churchill, chief people officer at Version 1, pensions form an important part of that equation. Version 1 is a technology services business employing about 4,000 people, with a significant presence in Ireland as well as global delivery capabilities and customers. In a people-based business like this, Churchill says the employment proposition has to recognise both employees’ immediate needs and their longer-term future.
“Everything we do, our success depends on people, so their expertise, their judgment, the relationships they have with customers,” he says.
Version 1’s employee proposition encompasses meaningful work, career development, fair reward and financial wellbeing. Within that broader concept of total reward, Churchill sees pensions as fundamental. “It’s a tangible investment in someone’s life beyond the work they’re currently doing.”
The challenge for employers is ensuring employees recognise that value. Historically, Churchill says, pensions have sometimes been regarded simply as another deduction from a payslip rather than an important part of compensation. Employers therefore need to make their pension provision visible and understandable, including explaining the contribution they themselves are making.
“Salary is really important. Clearly, it’s the prominent part of anyone’s compensation. But it’s only one part of the total value proposition.”
In a competitive employment landscape, simply having a pension scheme is no longer necessarily enough to distinguish one employer from another. Good pension provision is increasingly expected. “It’s no longer, in my view, a differentiator, it’s a requirement,” Churchill says.
What can distinguish an employer is the quality of the pension provision and the employee experience around it. Different employees will naturally engage with pensions in different ways. Someone approaching retirement may have very different questions from a person in their first job, while some employees want straightforward information and others want to explore their investment options in considerably greater detail, says Churchill. Employers need to accommodate that range.
“It’s not just enough to say a scheme exists,” Churchill says. “Transparency is central. Employees should be able to understand an important element of their reward without having to chase information, while practical questions should be easy to answer: what am I contributing, what choices do I have and who can I contact when I need help?”
Churchill has a 17-year-old son preparing to enter the workforce and remembers his own attitude towards pensions when starting his career. For someone dealing with rent, transport costs or hoping eventually to buy a home, retirement can feel very distant.
“The starting point for this is empathy,” he says. “Rather than ignoring those immediate pressures, employers should acknowledge them while finding ways to make the future more tangible.
“That means clearly showing what the employee is saving, what the employer is adding and what those contributions could potentially mean over the longer term.”
The objective, Churchill stresses, is not to turn every employee into an investment expert. “Our aim here is not to turn our employees into investment experts. But it’s to help them understand the benefit and know where to get support at just the right time.”
Communication also needs to continue beyond an employee’s first few days with a company. Onboarding already involves absorbing large amounts of information. Simply explaining the pension scheme once and expecting an employee to navigate it alone thereafter risks undermining the investment the employer has made in the benefit.
Instead, employees need ongoing access to information, digital tools and appropriately qualified human support.
Investment performance is another important part of the equation. Employees are becoming more interested in where their pension money is invested, Churchill says, including environmental, social and governance considerations.
Employers and pension providers therefore have to balance a number of considerations, including performance, fees, risk, choice and usability, says Churchill. “Long-term performance matters, but so does communicating potential outcomes responsibly without making promises about future returns.”
That combination of transparency and choice allows employees to make informed decisions without requiring them to become investment specialists.
The impact of pensions on retention, however, should not be overstated. “Version 1 does not separately measure the effect of its pension scheme on whether employees remain with the company,” Churchill says, “and therefore cannot attach a specific retention figure to it.”
Instead, he sees pensions as one element of a much broader relationship between employer and employee. People consider whether they are treated fairly, whether they have opportunities to progress, whether leaders deliver on their promises and whether the organisation invests in their wellbeing. “The pension is one tangible element of that picture,” he says.
One mistake employers can make is assuming that investing in a pension scheme automatically means employees appreciate its value.
A company can spend significant amounts on pension provision while leaving employees unclear about what they are receiving. That makes communication almost as important as provision itself.
Employers should clearly show their contribution, explain important choices in plain language and make information and support easy to find, Churchill says.
The importance of doing so may grow as pension coverage expands. With Ireland’s MyFutureFund auto-enrolment system broadening pension participation, workplace pensions are becoming an increasingly familiar part of the employment relationship.
That could make employees more likely to compare what different employers offer, not simply in monetary terms but in the quality, accessibility and flexibility of their schemes.
Churchill believes pensions are therefore likely to become a bigger consideration as people assess employment choices. As pension coverage becomes more commonplace, the opportunity for employers lies in demonstrating what makes their own provision valuable. Ultimately, that comes back to ensuring employees understand what they have.
“It goes back to understanding the quality of the provision,” Churchill says. “And that isn’t just about the monetary value. It is about access and information, and decision-making rights of the individual.”

title: Dublin Book Festival: ‘I couldn’t believe I’d never heard of this weird historical episode’
description: Historical fiction, a genre in which Irish writers have been particularly prolific and influential, is a focus of this year’s festival
content:
W ith its sense of celebration and inclusion, and its anticipation of new developments in Irish writing and publishing, the upcoming Dublin Book Festival has to be one of the most comprehensive arts events of the year.
For its 20th anniversary, books are of course the main focus, but the generous embrace of live performance, cross-arts collaboration and programming for children make it particularly broad-reaching. The current flourishing of writing in the Irish language is excellently showcased and traditional panels and workshops are offset by more cutting-edge sessions, such as late-night open mic and storytelling gigs.
One area that comes into focus is historical fiction. It’s a genre that has metamorphosed and expanded exponentially over this first quarter of the new century and one in which Irish writers have been particularly prolific and influential.
Whereas in the 20th century and earlier, the Irish canon tended to focus on the depiction of Irish history itself, or on Ireland’s political struggles, the horizons of Irish authors have expanded to explore a more international view of our past, with works about our diaspora and extending beyond themes strictly Irish. Their approach is more intimate, more character-focused and often questions the sources of history itself and offers alternative interpretations.
Two historical fiction sessions will take place on Saturday, November 7th, Writing History (1.30pm, National Library) and Macallaí na Staire/the Echoes of History (2pm, Royal Irish Academy of Music).
[ Dublin Book Festival celebrates 20th anniversary in style Opens in new window ]
For Writing History, author Neil Hegarty interviews novelists Martina Devlin, Henrietta McKervey and Emily Hourican.
Devlin’s Glorious Monsters, published by Lilliput, takes us to Rome in 1819, where the artist Amelia Curran (a sister of Sarah Curran, fiancee of executed Irish revolutionary Robert Emmet) meets the passionate trio of artists Percy and Mary Shelley and Mary’s half-sister, Claire Claremont.
The work follows several threads, primarily examining the complex relationship between the three. It also looks at the idea of art itself, and how a painting, such as one painted in the 17th century of Beatrice Cenci (a noblewoman executed for her part in her father’s murder), can influence artists of a different generation. The detail, emotional sensitivity and careful sense of place bring the subject to life and the reader becomes completely captivated by the whole.
“For some writers, history is a faintly defined background, an attractive setting really. But for me that’s not the case,” says Devlin. “I want to understand the texture of daily lives from the period I’m dealing with. And you can get lost in the sweep of large-scale world events: wars, plagues, famines, executions. But I’m trying to home in on individuals and how they are impacted. My hope is to make history feel vivid rather than words on a page, which can happen with history text books.”
[ Glorious Monsters by Martina Devlin: An engrossing novel about Frankenstein author Mary Shelley Opens in new window ]
Certainly, the historical facts could not paint three more colourful figures.
“We are fascinated by the Romantics today – they were dazzling, brilliant, volatile. But underneath the genius they were flawed human beings. I’m interested in how we relate to them when you lift the veil.”
The main protagonist in Hourican’s latest book, A House in Winter, also attracted the author as an intriguing historical figure. The book takes place over the 48 hours in 1965 when Britain’s Princess Margaret accompanied her husband, Lord Snowden, on a visit to his ancestral home in Abbeyleix.
When resentment against the royals’ visit generates IRA violence, the ensuing siege brings to light both the underlying feelings of the local community, the political situation in 1960s Ireland and the personal struggles of the princess.
“I would never have thought of writing about her if I hadn’t come across this weird historical episode,” says Hourican. “I couldn’t get over the fact that I’d never heard of it.” The author of four previous historical novels, Hourican’s passion for historical fiction comes from the challenge it presents to “move us into a different world”. “History doesn’t just tell us what happened back then, it tells us something about now. If it’s not reflecting things that are still important, then it doesn’t work.”
McKervey, whose latest novel, The Woman in The Water, is set in 1937, describes the recreation and interpretation of historical material as something she was reticent to approach at first, but came to love after discovering how much she liked the research.
“I have to go so far away from myself in the writing of it. I love that it’s not my experience, it’s not my life, it’s not that of anybody I know – so the challenge is to really inhabit a complete other world. I can lean on myself, obviously, for emotional responses – but everything else in the world I need to research.”
