Macallaí na Staire/The Echoes of History sees Prof Michael Cronin of Trinity College Dublin in conversation with author and publisher Darach Ó Scholaí, author of Súil an Daill and more recently Bódléar; author and short story writer Réaltán Ní Leannáin, whose novel Cití na gCartaí takes us from Gallipoli to Belfast in the first World War and after, and Liam Mac Cóil, whose historical novels range from a literary detective novel to the Lucás O’Briain series of historical thrillers.
When I was starting out, I found there weren’t that many books that interested me in Irish, but that’s not the case anymore. If someone were to start reading now they would have a wealth of books to choose from
For Ní Leannáin, the extensive geographical nature of her research was a challenge in itself. It involved not only trawling through historical records, but travel to the Mediterranean to research her grandfather’s time in the Great War. “It took a long time to finish the book as I went down rabbit holes of reading and research, but I value authenticity and factual accuracy and wanted it to ring true,” she says.
For Cronin, it’s an area that has traditionally been a staple of Irish-language literature, but has also seen huge expansion of late.
“There has been a whole slew of writers in recent years who have been taking on historical fiction in Irish and amplifying it. What these writers are doing is recreating a society where Irish was the everyday language of all the different social classes of society and they are looking at that both in Irish and in foreign settings – as in the Irish diaspora.”
Darach Ó Scolaí, who is a publisher as well as an author, has seen the steady success of new books in Irish since the turn of the century, and feels that this is very encouraging to see. Leabhar Breac uses a distributor to get books around the country, but Ó Scolaí describes it as “a joy” to ship books not just to Ireland but all around the world.
[ Adventures as Gaeilge: The bestselling Irish-language author who captivated young readers Opens in new window ]
“Some years back, when I was starting out, I found there weren’t that many books that interested me in Irish, but that’s not the case any more. If someone were to start reading now they would have a wealth of books to choose from. This is especially good for bilingual readers. If an Irish reader is not used to reading in Irish, they’ll have to read a few books before they get into it. But you can’t do that unless the books are there, and they are now.”
Both panels promise to deliver some lively conversations between the authors, focusing both on their respective recent books and on the genre and its developments. Elsewhere in the programme, festivalgoers will find other authors of Irish historical fiction, from Sebastian Barry (November 7th, 2.45pm, RIAM) to the more recent genre-bending work of Doireann Ní Ghríofa (November 8th, 12.30pm, RIAM). Michael Cronin’s new book, Ireland: Why It Matters to Be an Island, is also featured during the festival (November 8th, at 11am, RIAM).

title: Partita by Barbara Kingsolver: What keeps people from their birthright in beauty?
description: This story of aspiration, romance, disappointment and reconciliation drags in the middle
content:
Forty years after she documented women’s lives during the 1983 Phelps Dodge miners’ strike in Arizona – an act of witness that led to her first book, 1989’s Holding the Line – Barbara Kingsolver herself held the line in a union work stoppage for the first time. As a member of the Writers Guild of America, she closed her keyboard in 2023 with her fellow screenwriters, striking for improved healthcare and protection against the corporate fetish for AI .
Asking how to create safety and community around both industry and art, those two strikes could be said to parent Kingsolver’s new novel; the offspring doesn’t talk about them outright, but it has their eyes.
Over the past four decades, Kingsolver has proven why her surname would make a damn fine brand name for a guillotine. Her novels can be as large, righteous and billion-footed as a No Kings protest. But years before she took up the sweeping social novel, she was a music student – studying piano, just like the protagonist of Partita – before she left music theory to pursue the sciences and journalism in the American southwest.
Partita is a story of aspiration, romance, disappointment and reconciliation; and though it’s a first-person suite of memories, it seems to take its bearings from structural questions about the instrumentality of women’s artistic ambitions and the creation of art as undercompensated labour. It drags in the middle, but Kingsolver jolts even its most unhurried stretches with aphorism: “Other than relief at escaping a lifetime of debt, I was having trouble locating my feelings.” Or: “You can learn a lot about your belongings from throwing them off the roof.”
In 1989 teenage pianist Livia Bohusz escapes the abuse of her Kentucky childhood home on a scholarship to an Indiana music conservatory. Reflecting on that “year of earthquakes and oil spills and iron curtains starting to crash”, Livia reminisces from middle age that “our options then were different and also maybe about the same” as they are in today’s America.
[ Barbara Kingsolver: ‘The first time I set foot in Ireland I felt so at home. Something about the language, the culture’ Opens in new window ]
While at university, Livia begins a passionate affair with Sigurd, a hot labour organiser resentful of campus indifference, who soon leaves her heartbroken, financially vulnerable and rusticated from the stage by a terrible hand injury. Sigurd heads off to Arizona in his own arc of futility, shortly after his author witnessed the movement there being decimated.
When, in the overture of the novel, Livia hears from Sigurd again after decades, she has one week to decide whether or not to reunite. Those seven days of deliberation each get a chapter titled “Prelude”, alternating with movements into the past titled with (and tutoring us in the musical meanings of) terms such as “Sarabande” and “Fugue” and “Pathétique”. A partita, as Livia explains to Sigurd, is “a composition made of a lot of parts with different paces and moods ... and the artist’s work is to make them all add up to something that feels whole”.
In Partita, Kingsolver relishes classical music as a source of discipline and splendour while recognising the precarity of its vanishing career opportunities. Beyond classical music, it might be more accurate to think of the book’s focus as art and the public domain. Since everyone can possess Bach and Chopin, the question becomes: who has the right combination of deracinated accent and approved upbringing, unbought time and institutional access to a heavy piano that’s required to “stand up among us to play or sing real music, one breathing soul to another”?
What keeps people from their birthright in beauty? Kingsolver dramatises how reproductive rights are artists’ rights – the way an unplanned pregnancy, in a country that routinely torments people seeking abortion, can upend a career and contribute to the suppression of a potential agent of harmony.
Partita is very much a reaction to the maximalist success of Kingsolver’s last novel, Demon Copperhead , which retold Dickens’s David Copperfield in opiate-riddled contemporary Appalachia. When Livia finally marries a stoic, loving man, her sister-in-law can’t decide if the couple are “like a Charlotte Brontë novel or a Thomas Hardy novel. Definitely a novel. I said I wanted to be the one where nobody dies”. Mercifully, in a book that contains a Jude’s worth of severe trauma, they suffer only minor allusions.
That self-consciousness about accumulation and the repetition of prior scripts finds its correlative in a subplot in which Livia must enter her dead mother’s house and dispose of the sedimentation of a lifetime’s hoarding. Here a novel so committed across most of its pages to the intricacy of touch must convince us that the ultimate good is to release your grip. What lingers are frequent moments where Livia practises her fingering of the repertoire on the skin of her partners. This tactile tale finds unity in the proposal that any hand can make music, heard or unheard, from its play along any material surface.
Greg Londe teaches literatures in English at Cornell University and lives in Wexford

title: Chinese cars in Ireland: Here’s our rundown of each brand and what it sells
description: With an ever-expanding roster of Chinese brands entering the Irish car market, here’s our rundown of each one and what it sells
content:
BYD is the 200lb gorilla of the Chinese car brands. It has risen, with frankly astonishing speed, to become one of the world’s biggest car brands, and has been vying with Tesla as the number-one maker of fully electric models .
Right now, depending on whose figures you believe, BYD hovers just outside the top 10 of global car makers, but that has to be taken in the context of the fact that BYD made its first car in 2005. Most of the car makers ahead of it in the charts have been at this since at least the 1920s.
In Ireland, BYD has actually broken into the top 10 list this year, muscling Renault and Dacia aside to take ninth place overall. In fact, BYD is only a few hundred car sales short of overhauling Ford in the Irish charts – something that would have been unthinkable just a decade ago. BYD clearly sees more potential in the Irish market, as it’s splitting from its independent importer Motor Distributors Limited and is taking its Irish operations in-house .
In Ireland, BYD’s bestseller is the big Seal-U plug-in hybrid , but the company is better known for fully electric models such as the Seal , the Sealion 7 and the Dolphin. Fears that BYD would undermine the efforts of European car makers by selling its small electric city car for as little as €10,000 were allayed when that car – called the Seagull in China, but named Dolphin Surf here – arrived with a price tag closer to €20,000 thanks to the need for expensive re-engineering to meet European safety standards.
Nonetheless, when European and Japanese car makers worry about Chinese competition, it’s BYD that’s at the forefront of their minds. Next up are high-end models under BYD’s Denza brand, including a plug-in Land Rover Defender rival, the Bao 5 , and a sleek 1,100hp Z9 GT – and no, that horsepower is not a typo. The latter will be a competitor for the Porsche Panamera and Taycan.
There’s also the big seven-seat Ti7 SUV, the new Atto 8 seven-seat family crossover, which is a rival to Skoda’s new Peaq, and even a pickup truck, the Shark. At the more compact end, there’s the new the Shark hatchback.
The company even makes its own batteries, a rarity in the car world, and it has helped popularise the more rugged lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) battery chemistry. Next up? Ultra-fast charging at up to 1,500kW from BYD’s own-design ‘Flash’ fast chargers. In theory, these can top up your battery from flat to 97 per cent in as little as nine minutes. At that speed, charging stops will see their coffee sales plummet, with not enough time to order a flat white ...
Indeed, BYD has set itself the ambitious target of ‘cooling the planet by 1 degree Celsius’ thanks to its electric vehicle sales, zero-emissions public transport buses and vehicles, and investments in low-carbon manufacturing and battery recycling. It sounds grandiose, but who would bet against BYD now?
[ BYD aims to outsell Toyota by 2031 to become world’s biggest car maker Opens in new window ]
MG is the OG of Chinese brands in Europe. Resurrected by Shanghai Automotive Industrial Corporation (SAIC) from the ashes of MG Rover – the last surviving remnants of the disastrous British Leyland empire – MG’s return to European and Irish markets wasn’t initially all that promising, with cheap-feeling cars such as the ZS and HS. While some MGs still feel cheap inside – step forward the current ZS hybrid and the MG 3 hatchback – as is so often the case with Chinese brands, it has taken big steps forward, and the likes of the MG S5 and S6 look and feel as smart inside as any European or Japanese competitor.
MG was the biggest-selling Chinese brand in Ireland until this year – possibly helped by the brand recognition factor of its classic badge. But BYD has since accelerated past it. Don’t feel too sorry though – MG’s Irish sales are up 77 per cent so far this year, and its line-up runs the gamut from the small and cheap MG 3 hybrid hatchback to the large and relatively luxurious HS plug-in hybrid SUV.
The S6 electric SUV is arguably its best all-round model – classy looks inside and out, and good range – but only the smaller MG 4 EV hatchback and the gorgeous Cyberster convertible demonstrate much of the old-school MG driving brio.
Hopefully the new MG 2 electric hatch – already seen in a very Mini-esque concept form – will have that trait in spades, as will the slick-looking MG Cyber large electric SUV, which looks more than a little like a bargain-priced Ferrari Purosangue. However, MG has a record of not bringing all its models to Ireland – we still don’t get the seven-seat S9 plug-in hybrid SUV, nor the more premium IM5 saloon and IM6 SUV.
Leapmotor only really launched in Ireland last year, and while it’s definitely a Chinese brand, it does have some European connections. Stellantis Group (Peugeot, Citroën, Opel, Fiat, etc) owns a minority stake in Leapmotor in China and a majority stake in its global sales operation, which is why Irish sales are handled by Gowan Auto, home to all Stellantis brands.
Leapmotor first landed in Ireland with the tiny T03 electric city car (surprisingly good, considering it’s specifically designed to be cheap) and the chunky C10 SUV, which comes in fully electric or extended-range plug-in hybrid forms. That C10 has impressive quality inside, but it looks – and drives – rather like a Moomin (those cute cartoon hippos). In general, none of Leapmotor’s cars – the electric pair of B05 hatchback and B10 SUV – have much in the way of driver appeal, but they do tend to have good usable electric ranges on one charge, and a long six-year warranty.
Leapmotor seems to be working closely with Opel on its next generation of cars, so hopefully some of Opel’s sharper chassis engineering will rub off on the Chinese.
[ Leapmotor: China’s no-frills EV maker aiming to become the next BYD Opens in new window ]
Xpeng is perhaps one of the most interesting of all the Chinese brands, but you’d hardly know it from the single G6 model that it sells in Ireland. There’s nothing wrong – and quite a lot right – with the G6 , but while it’s roomy, long-legged, and incredibly fast charging (up to 450kW on DC chargers), it’s also not especially exciting to drive, and looks like a very generic egg-shaped EV SUV on the outside. For a company that yearns to be taken seriously in the European premium car market, that’s not a good look.
More – much more – is coming, though. First up, with the soon-arriving X9, Xpeng will attempt to restart the MPV market with a car that boasts seats for seven, long EV range, and a classy cabin. It will also launch the L03 SUV, and while the current G6 may look a bit like a Tesla Model Y, it’s the sleek and rather more stylish L03 that’s aimed right at the Tesla’s heart, with a potential 600km range. There’s also the big G9L luxury SUV which wants to be an electric Range Rover for much less cash, and the one we’re really waiting for – the P7 saloon which looks as if a 1960s Buick Riviera never left production, but just evolved into something far more high-tech. That car has the potential to be a true game changer in how we perceive Chinese cars and their relationship to high-end European brands.
Oh, and Xpeng is also making its own ‘flying car’ air taxi with a six-wheeled ‘Aircraft Carrier’ truck launcher. Don’t expect to see those in Ireland, but it gives you a sense of the ambition.
Chery has been building up quite a head of steam, especially in the UK market where, with its three brands – Chery, Jaecoo, and Omoda – it has already broken into the top of the sales charts.
Indeed, at various points over the past couple of years, the Jaecoo 7 (known as the ‘Temu Range Rover’ or ‘the Evoque I ordered from Shein’) has been the bestselling car in the UK. Given its Range Rover-y looks and low price tag, it’s not hard to see why it’s been doing well. Clearly, Chery is doing something right.
Will it be as successful here? Well, selling a mid-size SUV with hybrid power and a low-figure sticker on the windscreen is a quick way to Irish buyers’ hearts too. But once you get up close to either a Jaecoo or an Omoda, you really start to see how awkward they look (the grilles and overhangs are totally out of proportion with the rest of the body), and while the cabins look and feel nice, there have been worrying rumblings from the UK when it comes to longer-term reliability. Big things are expected, then, but Irish buyers are notoriously hard to drag away from their favourite brands, so Chery Group might have a bigger fight on its hands here than in the UK.
Geely has taken a different route to the rest of the Chinese car industry, bar SAIC and its purchase of MG. Geely has snapped up brands that are already familiar – Volvo and Lotus, for instance.
When it has created a new brand, Polestar, it’s been diligent in giving that a distinctly European, indeed Swedish, flavour (whatever US lawmakers might think …). Not only is Geely already in-country here with Volvo and Polestar (and to a much lesser extent with Lotus), it also owns the Farizon commercial vehicles brand.
Next up will be Geely’s own-brand cars, which will range from the oddly named Starray-iM plug-in hybrid SUV (a rival to the likes of the Hyundai Tucson and Nissan Qashqai) and its all-electric cousin, the E5, to the smaller Geely E2 hatchback, which will go up against the likes of the Renault 5 and the Volkswagen ID. Polo.
There is also its other premium player, Zeekr, which will enter the mix with its Polestar and Volvo brands.
Geely is also playing it smart with its European efforts by making sure to move production to this side of the world, and so it’s going to start making cars with Ford in Valencia, Spain.
Ford will rent Geely the factory space, and the two brands will share some platforms for new models, which could include the brand’s Toyota Land Cruiser rival, the Galaxy Cruiser 700.
Changan is another Chinese company that’s sorta-kinda already here, because it provides the platforms and batteries around which Mazda builds the new 6e saloon and CX-6e SUV. And very impressive they are too.
Changan has already started selling its own-brand Deepal models in Northern Ireland – the S05 and S07 SUVs, both electric but with the S05 also offering a plug-in hybrid version – so they’re likely to work their way south of the border before too long. As Changans, though, they’re a bit faceless and bland in their styling, so you might be better off sticking with the Mazdas, to be honest. Actually, the Changan name comes from the fact that the company was once the Chongqing Changan Arsenal – not a football team, but literally an armaments maker. It was the first Chinese car brand, though, launching the Changjiang Type 46 in 1959.
China has an oversupply of car makers right now, and the somewhat Darwinian process of winnowing all of the start-ups and hopefuls down to a profitable few is well under way.
For instance, the Hi-Phi brand – which wanted to sell futuristic-looking saloons with gullwing doors – fell quickly by the wayside. Others are seriously worrying ‘western’ car makers, such as Xiaomi , which built its reputation making mobile phones but which now makes the incredibly high-performance SU7 saloon, which has been vying with Porsche for racetrack lap records. It’s also been embroiled in some worrying safety scandals in China, so it may take some time to get to Ireland, if ever.
Nio is more likely to arrive here soon, and its compact Firefly hatchback has been garnering rave reviews, but sadly its battery-swapping tech seems to have been superseded by faster DC charging.
[ Chinese car exports topping one million deepens anxiety in Europe’s automobile industry Opens in new window ]
Li Auto is planning a European debut, but actual sales here could yet be affected by European tariffs on Chinese electric cars – something that has driven BYD, MG, Geely and Chery to set up factories within the EU and Turkey.
The Maxus brand is, of course, already operating in Ireland, but largely in the commercial vehicles sphere, as its MPV models – the Mifa 7 and Mifa 9 – haven’t garnered much attention here yet.
GAC, or Guangzho Automotive Group, is already in the UK market with its all-electric Aion brand, but there are no plans to come to Ireland yet, while Great Wall Motors was, of course, present here for a time with the cutesy Ora brand , but has retreated for the moment to lick its sales wounds. Don’t expect it to stay away forever.

title: Peugeot E-308 review: Who needs an SUV when hatchbacks are this good?
description: With sharper styling, more electric range and engaging handling, the updated Peugeot E-308 makes a persuasive case for ditching the SUV habit
content:
Was life really that much better before we all started buying SUVs in their thousands?
Think back to when the Golf, the Focus, the Corolla, and the 308 were all bestsellers; the planet wasn’t on fire, Donald Trump was just a TV personality, and Formula One cars had proper engines. Okay, so Mayo were still winless, but you can’t have everything.
Trying to sell hatchbacks to a modern audience raised on nothing but a sludgy diet of SUVs is Sisyphean, but at least some are still prepared to make the effort. It probably doesn’t hurt this Peugeot 308’s business case within the broader Stellantis Group that it shares its platform, engines and pretty much everything but the bodywork with a crossover, the Peugeot 408.
For 2026, Peugeot has given the 308 a bit of an update and an upgrade. You’ll notice this most at the front, where the grille that used to be inset into the bodywork now spreads broadly across the face of the car, rather in the manner of a child smearing chocolate cake around its lips (but rather more handsome than that sounds).
The headlights have been split into two units, leaving glowering three-section LED running lights up high, while the main beams shine from separate lamps lower down.
It certainly looks more distinctive than the older version, with its long, drooping “fang” LED lights. Around the back there is a set of slim brake lights, but less in the way of overall newness. Gotta love the new colours, though – this shiny, rich “Lagoa Blue” (which looks much more green to us…) is the standard, no-cost colour option.
Inside, there’s really nothing new here, or at least I thought so until it was pointed out to me that the driver’s digital display has new graphics and view options. They’re nice, but the main touchscreen – set low in the dashboard, with some handy physical shortcut buttons and the customisable “I-Toggle” shortcuts above those – is a bit sluggish and can sometimes take too long to make up its mind.
You can’t fault the comfort in the front of the 308, though, and while many will still struggle with the way the small, hexagonal steering wheel is supposed to more or less sit in your lap, it’s never bothered me.
Material quality is very good, and the cabin looks and feels notably classy – backing up Peugeot’s recent strong showing in various reliability surveys.
In the back, the 308’s case as a “you don’t need an SUV” car does start to fall apart a bit. Legroom is notably on the short side (it’s adequate, but no more than that), while the boot, at 412 litres in the hybrid version, is eclipsed by rivals such as the Skoda Octavia.
It’s worse again in this E-308 – just 361 litres. Happily, you can rectify all that by picking the very handsome 308 SW estate, which has a longer wheelbase than this hatchback model (meaning a little more rear legroom) and a massive boot.
Either way, you’ll have a very pleasant car to drive. You can have the 308 with a 145hp 1.2 litre hybrid petrol engine, which is pretty efficient, but to be honest it’s getting on a bit now and feels a wheezy at times.
It’s far better to go for the updated E-308 electric version. This has just gained a new battery pack, which gives it a critical increase in range. Previously, the E-308 had an official range of 411km and struggled to get much past 350km in real-world driving. The new 55kWh (net) battery stretches the official range to 450km.
[ Kia PV5 is adorable, agile, keenly priced and even fun. Not bad for a van Opens in new window ]
Better yet, in real-world conditions you should pretty easily reach 420km or 430km – this is a seriously efficient car, easily able to duck under the 15kWh/100km efficiency level even with lots of strenuous motorway driving. Charging isn’t quite so impressive (11kW on AC power is okay, but 100kW on DC feels a bit slack) but the genuine range is so good that you probably won’t mind much.
The steering is light and sharp, and so the E-308 is very pleasant to thread along a challenging road, but it’s also reasonably refined on a longer motorway run. The ride quality allows the large alloy wheels of our GT-spec test car to bobble and jiggle around a bit too much at lower speeds, but you could probably cure most of that by picking a more basic Allure version and specifying smaller alloys than the 18-inch rims of our test car.
There is one final hurdle for the 308 to leap, and that’s its price. A starting price of €33,995 for the (admittedly well-equipped) hybrid Allure model is slightly high, but that makes the €39,190 for our GT test car seem quite chunky. Possibly better to go for the Allure E-308 at €36,390 and forego such niceties as heated seats and steering wheel.
Still, either of those cars, or the 308 SW estate, just make so much more sense and are so much better to drive than almost any equivalent SUV model. An SUV certainly can’t transport you back to a happier, simpler time, even if it is only for a fleeting moment, and who could put a price on that?
Power: 115kW e-motor developing 156hp and 270Nm of torque, powering the front wheels via a single-speed automatic transmission.
CO2 emissions (annual motor tax) 0g/km (€120).
Electric consumption: 14.9-15.1 kWh/100km (WLTP).
Price: €39,190 as tested, 308 starts from €33,995.
Verdict: A bit pricey in GT form, but the new battery has unlocked seriously good range, and the E-308 remains pleasing to drive and to look at.

title: More than 300,000 US visas revoked during second term, says Trump administration
description: Rights advocates say crackdown has violated due ‌process ‌and created an unsafe environment, particularly for minorities
content:
President Donald Trump ’s administration has ‌revoked more than 300,000 US visas during his second term, the State Department said on Tuesday, ‌as the federal government continues its sweeping immigration crackdown.
The number shows an acceleration in the ​pace of visa revocations in recent weeks.
In an update issued on August 10th, the State Department had put the number of visa revocations since US president Donald Trump’s current term began in ​January 2025 at more than 175,000.
Trump says his immigration crackdown and deportation drive aim to ⁠improve domestic security. Rights advocates say the crackdown has violated due ‌process ‌and ​free speech rights and has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial ⁠profiling.
In announcing the latest ​number on X, State Department spokesman ​Tommy Pigott said the Trump administration “has revoked more visas at a faster ‌pace than any administration in history”.
[ Trump administration plans to revoke visas of foreigners seeking asylum Opens in new window ]
Pigott said ​the administration had “zero tolerance for foreigners here on visas who break ⁠the law, commit fraud, or undermine ⁠our national ​security”.
Among visa revocations particularly condemned by rights advocates are those of pro- Palestinian foreign protesters demonstrating against US ally Israel ’s attacks on Gaza, and of foreigners over their social media comments about the assassination last year of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk .
In addition to attempts to deport foreign protesters, the Trump administration has enforced tightened social media screening of immigrants ‌and visa applicants.
[ British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos detained by ICE as a ‘visa overstayer’ Opens in new window ]
Rights advocates ⁠say the government has deployed national-security justifications to target critics and used isolated cases of fraud to broadly target ‌immigrant communities such as the Somali-American community in Minnesota.
While Trump campaigned in 2024 on ​stopping illegal immigration, his administration has also made ​legal immigration more difficult – for example by imposing expensive fees for certain work visas. – Reuters

title: Father of triple murder accused Robert O’Connor died after 44 stab wounds in ‘sustained’ attack
description: Chief State Pathologist testifies that there were no obvious defence injuries on bodies of Mark and Louise O’Connor
content:
The father of triple murder accused Robert O’Connor died after suffering 44 stab wounds in “a sustained and violent attack” at his Co Louth home, while his wife was stabbed at least 20 times, the Chief State Pathologist has told a Central Criminal Court jury.
The expert witness also testified on Tuesday that there were no obvious defence injuries on the bodies of Mark and Louise O’Connor.
Robert O’Connor (32), of Drumgowna, Louth Village, Dundalk, Co Louth, has pleaded not guilty of murder by reason of insanity, or guilty of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility, to the killing of his mother Louise (56), his father Mark (54) and his younger brother Evan (27) at their home, between September 28th and 29th, 2025.
The Central Criminal Court jury has heard the accused accepts he caused the death of the three victims.
The Chief State Pathologist, Linda Mulligan, on Tuesday told Roisin Lacey, prosecuting counsel, that she conducted a postmortem on Mark and Louise O’Connor’s remains on October 1st, 2025. The witness said she was aware the three deceased all had multiple stab wounds and there was a significant amount of blood on the bodies.
The witness said she had not attended Drumgowna, but viewed photographs of the scene, where she saw Mark’s body near the entrance gate to the house. Mulligan said the body of Evan, who was found wearing only shorts, was near the patio doors, while Louise was found fully clothed in the kitchen.
The witness said three knives were recovered from the scene.
Regarding Mark, Mulligan said he had heavy blood-staining over the head, hands and clothing. She said he had been stabbed 44 times in total and that the majority of the stab wounds were to the back, head and neck.
She said his shirt and trousers were heavily blood-stained. One stab wound went through the shoulder blade and entered the left chest cavity to a depth of 20cm, but had not damaged the left lung, she said.
Mulligan said Mark’s brain was swollen. She testified that blood loss had compromised respiration because of air in the chest cavities, which would have resulted in Mark’s death.
The witness said the 44 stab wounds and seven incised wounds suggested “a sustained and violent attack”.
She said death had occurred from blood loss and respiratory compromise arising from multiple stab wounds with no contributory factors.
Turning to the postmortem on Louise, Mulligan said her body was discovered with multiple stab wounds and there was heavy blood-staining over her hair, face, hands and clothing.
Mulligan said Louise had been stabbed at least 20 times including to the head, the front and back of the trunk, and the upper left arm.
She said no obvious defence injuries were identified.
In both cases, Prof Mulligan said many of the injuries showed one squared and one blunted end, indicating that the blade of the knife used was a single, sharp-edged weapon.
The trial continues on Wednesday before Judge Mícheál P O’Higgins and a jury of six men and six women, who will be told about the postmortem performed on Evan O’Connor.

title: MPs back Northern Ireland Troubles Bill to deal with legacy of conflict
description: Bill to be sent to House of Lords after MPs vote 330 to 178 in favour of Bill at third reading
content:
Draft legislation to deal with the legacy of the Northern Ireland Troubles has been passed by the House of Commons.
Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant said veterans and those who lost loved ones in the decades of conflict “deserve answers”.
MPs voted 330 to 178, majority 152, in favour of the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill at the third reading on Tuesday. It will now be sent to the House of Lords for further scrutiny.
The draft law was first introduced to parliament last year and is set to overhaul the previous Conservative government’s Legacy Act, with a reformed Legacy Commission.
Bryant appeared emotional in the Commons on Tuesday evening as he said: “This Bill isn’t about one group or another. It’s not about special favours for one group or another.
“It’s about honesty, candour, the pursuit of justice, and most importantly, truth. Because in the end, it’s only truth that can really set us free.”
He had earlier said: “When people say to me that people need to move on in Northern Ireland, my answer is, ‘No’.
[ Chris Bryant had ‘no other decision’ but to halt Drumcree march, court told Opens in new window ]
“No one has moved on more than the victims and survivors of the Troubles. They’re not living in the past, they’re living with the past.
“And if it’s not resolved, if people don’t get answers, that trauma will pass on to the next generation.”
He said: “Veterans and those armed forces families who lost loved ones in the conflict deserve answers.
“It is in the interests of the whole armed forces community affected by the Troubles that steady progress is made to ensure this legislation’s provisions are effective.”
At committee stage, he rejected an accusation from Traditional Unionist Voice MP Jim Allister (North Antrim) that the Bill had been drafted to “spare the sensitivities of the Republic of Ireland”.
Shadow Northern Ireland secretary Alex Burghart argued the legislation will allow, but not compel, the Republic to co-operate with the Legacy Commission.
Bryant said the two governments plan to pass their own legislation to implement the agreement, which will “come into force in lockstep”.
The Irish Government has promised the fullest possible co-operation with UK investigations.
More than 3,500 people were killed in The Troubles from the late 1960s until the 1998 Belfast Agreement , in sectarian conflict largely centred on whether Northern Ireland should remain in the UK or become part of a united Ireland.
More than 150 amendments were proposed by the British government last week, prompting concerns over the ability of MPs to adequately scrutinise the draft legislation over two days.
This included the UK’s attorney general being given the responsibility of deciding whether serious prosecutions related to the Troubles should go ahead.
Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson claimed the involvement of the attorney general would not give more protections for veterans, while Labour’s Andy McDonald (Middlesbrough and Thornaby East) urged the government to reconsider the change.
Alliance MP Sorcha Eastwood (Lagan Valley) also argued the situation in Northern Ireland “is not black and white, it is shades of grey”, as she criticised the new role of the attorney general.
On Monday, concerns were raised over the exclusion of the Omagh bombing from the new Legacy Commission’s jurisdiction.
The Bill states the Commission will only look at events and conduct between January 1st, 1966 and April 10th, 1998 – when the Belfast Agreement was signed.
But the republican car bombing, which killed 29 people, including a woman who was pregnant with twins, took place months after the peace agreement on August 15th, 1998.
MPs voted to reject a bid by the DUP’s Robinson to extend the cut-off to August 30th, 1998.
There is an ongoing inquiry into the Omagh bombing, with a memorandum of understanding signed in April 2025 to secure the co-operation of the Irish government.
In Westminster, pressure was also put on ministers to allow victims of sexual violence during the Troubles to request an investigation.
Bryant pledged to “get that right in the House of Lords”, after Ulster Unionist Party MP Robin Swann (South Antrim) argued victims should not “become an overlooked part of the history of the Troubles”.

title: Doué and Vitinha burn bright as brittle Barcelona come unstuck against PSG
description: Match at Parc des Princes goes ahead despite widespread unrest in Paris
content:
Fire, noise, fury, a sense of empty energy. And across town, a football match too.
Do any of these randomly pitched autumnal Champions League fixtures mean anything? Probably not when you’re Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona , and the only game in town is risk-free TV income and a semi-guaranteed place in the knockout stuff.
But this was still a dazzling occasion at the Parc des Princes as the champions of France and Spain played out a light, open, frictionless, exhibition-style game of football. PSG finished 4-2 winners, having been pegged back to 2-2 at one stage. But this was also a game where the score almost didn’t seem to matter at times, and where the only really hard message was the frailty of the Barcelona backline and PSG’s thrilling attacking energy in these midweek A-games.
“Debris! Debris! DEBRIS!” the insanely loud announcer screamed into his mic before kick-off, what appeared to be a poor-taste tribute to the current state of the nation’s capital, although it may also have been “du bruit”.
In the hours leading up to the game, France’s interior minister had specifically ruled out postponing the whole thing due to the ongoing state of civil unrest, the kind of statement that is no doubt intended to sound reassuring, but which also generates its own kind of whiplash.
Paris is burning. Paris is always burning. No, but Paris really is burning this time. The main site of the violence of the last few days is three miles east of the Parc, which lurks by the ring road in one of Paris’ slightly négligé inner quarters, rising up like a vast concrete alien doughnut in between the town houses.
On matchday, it required a degree of cognitive dissonance to take in these two opposing spectacles. On one hand, the piles of charred bikes and the mass looting which has, in reassuringly Parisian style, seemed to focus on elite high-fashion brands. Chanel will rue the day.
And in the middle of this, Paris also hosted this glittering treat of a game, stuffed with so many throwaway little delicacies, like an elite artisan patisserie. Before kick-off there were leaping tongues of flame, a laser show spectacular, and an awe-inspiringly vast tifo at one end showing a ghoulish PSG serial killer type attacking the Barcelona badge with his blood-soaked chainsaw. The message here seemed to be: we are confident. We believe in our process. And we will hack you to death.
This was a high-grade, disarmingly open game at the start. For Hansi Flick’s Barcelona it represented a genuine test of method, an elite team that plays with a studied disregard for some of the tenets of positional defensive play. We will press forward and trust what lies behind. We will also give up on the basic idea of marking from the kick-off, as it turned out.
With one minute gone PSG should have scored. A quick passing move from right to left put Khvicha Kvaratskhelia in space. His shot pinged off a post and back to an offside Ousmane Dembélé, who shinned wide of an open goal.
There was a fury to PSG in those opening minutes, the front players finding angles and free channels. Pedri and Marc Bernal in central midfield took a while to settle for Barça. Bernal is pure La Masia, a baby-faced 19-year-old Catalan, misleadingly so, as he also has the physique of a rugby union flanker. And Pedri is of course the kind of footballer who glides through these occasions, so casual you half expect to look down and notice he’s playing in flip-flops and holding a Calippo.
Before long Barcelona were making chances of their own, Dani Olmo setting off on a couple of surging deep runs, Anthony Gordon almost getting on the end of a cutback.
João Cancelo was booked with 16 minutes gone for a lunge on Désiré Doué, a disastrous state of affairs for any full-back faced with this nightmare of feints and fast-twitch feet. And two minutes later Dembélé was off, injured chasing the ball, replaced by Ferran Torres. Maybe he should play a bit more, get match fit.
Still the game just zinged from end to end. Raphinha had a close-range shot blocked by Matvey Safonov after a nice pass from Gordon. PSG had three shots blocked or saved in the space of six seconds on 28 minutes, Joan García saving brilliantly low down.
And on 37 minutes PSG deservedly took the lead. The goal was in keeping with the game, expertly high-tech but also oddly easy and open. Lamine Yamal tried a clever chipped clearance. João Neves claimed the ball back. It fell to Doué, and he was able to jink inside, feel the space around him, and shoot low inside the post.
PSG were bossing this by now, Kvaratskhelia running up and down the gears on the left. By the break Barcelona were hanging on, overrun in midfield and straining to contain PSG on the flanks.
The start of the second half was more of the same: mobile, relentless, high grade product, lovely attacking interchanges, large spaces in the Barcelona backline. Doué forced another fine close-range save, played in by Vitinha.
On 54 minutes Barcelona equalised. Xavi Espart got it, galloping through the left side of the PSG defence and smashing a shot into the net off the hands of Safonov. The PA announcer gave the goal to Lamine Yamal, because, well, great branding. But it was Espart’s first in Europe, the second of his career. He’s 19, hyper-versatile, another Catalan youth-team player.
Before long Barça had made a triple substitution. One of those entering the field was Rodri. Would this see order restored? For a while it did feel as though Rodri was the only grown-up on the pitch, as Barcelona did started to dominate possession and territory.
But PSG always have tools to hurt you. Doué sliced open the right hand side again and crossed for Fabián Ruiz to hit the post from six yards out. From the corner Lucas Hernandez was given space to leap and produce a wonderful finish, thumped off the meaty part of the forehead high into the top corner.
Six minutes later it was 2-2. This was a strange goal, scored by Lamine Yamal after a wonderful run in from the right and a lofted near-post finish that in the moment either looked like a mistake from Safonov or a moment of pure invention.
And two minutes after that it was 3-2 to PSG as the game just kept on running to its own speed. It was another brilliant goal, this time a controlled first time shot from Vitinha, seizing on a bouncing ball near the edge of the box. Fabián Ruiz added a fourth four minutes from the end as PSG just kept coming. – Guardian

title: Phil Foden hat-trick helps Manchester City cut through noise to crush AEK Athens
description: Hosts turn on the style when required in front of a subdued Etihad crowd
content:
Enzo Maresca has called for Manchester City to make their own noise on the pitch to drown out the cacophony surrounding them but maybe a quiet night at the Etihad Stadium was what they needed all along. AEK Athens were easily dispatched in a businesslike manner, as Phil Foden announced his return to form with a hat-trick to get City’s Champions League campaign back on track after being pummelled by Paris Saint-Germain.
The match was uneven throughout as Foden shone on the wing and later down the middle, with goals from Elliot Anderson and Rayan Cherki helping to ease City to victory in front of half-full stands. Stavros Pilios’s consolation was more a reward for the boisterous fans in yellow and black than for the overall efforts of the visitors.
Maresca took the calculated risk of eight changes from the win over Ipswich, although that did mean a return to the starting line-up for Enzo Fernández and Elliot Anderson, while Erling Haaland was left on the bench. His replacement, with senior options lacking, was 17-year-old academy graduate Floyd Samba, whose only other senior football came in a Carabao Cup win against Norwich, when he scored twice on debut.
The game had not captured the imagination with the stands having huge gaps of blue, which is understandable amid the constant churn of fixtures for City and the cost of following the club. AEK was seen by many fans as a game that could be missed, in expectation of a simple victory over a team lacking global superstars. The visiting supporters were far more animated, filling a corner of the ground over three tiers where they created a party from two hours before kick-off.
Inspiration was required from those on the pitch with the home faithful subdued, and it was provided by Fernández clipping a free-kick on to the bar and Anderson following up to whack the rebound into an empty net in the 12th minute. The celebrations lacked enthusiasm, acknowledged with a nod of approval.
AEK had no desire to capitulate and created some promising moves without ever threatening the City box, lacking quality when it mattered most. The Greek side had half of the possession in the opening quarter but the hosts, while not at their best, turned on the style when required, going from static to full steam in seconds to create chances.
The Champions League debutant Allan was City’s most entertaining offering, providing direct running and skill on the left wing. The Brazilian was a menace and almost marked his second home appearance with a goal but his vicious shot clipped the bar and flew into the stands. With seven matches in 21 days for City, games like this gave an opportunity for fringe players to impress and Allan was eager to make his mark.
City were able to take control, passing the ball around with ease and holding AEK at arm’s length, while Foden and Cherki tried to work their fleet-footed magic in tight spaces. Eventually the calmness in the final third was rewarded when Foden finished after neat work on the right from Rico Lewis, as the two academy products combined. The full-back has struggled for minutes in recent times and almost left the club 16 months ago but showed he can provide something as an attacking threat from defence.
With City comfortable, complacency kicked in and Abdukodir Khusanov reflected the crowd by drifting off, giving Zini the chance to turn him and slip a pass into Stavros Pilios who thrashed the ball across Gianluigi Donnarumma. The AEK fans erupted, while their counterparts pondered how City had been dragged back into a fight, having previously been impenetrable.
Natural order was restored by Cherki, a neat trick inside the box and a precise shot into the corner did the rest. It was an occasion for the maverick Frenchman to be a leader, making the difference in critical moments and he offered up evidence of his capabilities with the finish, creating breathing space in the process.
If the plan was to test life without Haaland, the loss of Antoine Semenyo to injury for eight weeks created a problem for Maresca. Samba’s deployment ranked somewhere between plan C and D but the teenager was an adept decoy, allowing the more experienced around him to show off their repertoire. Samba acquitted himself well but whether he is a suitable replacement for the Norwegian will remain unknown until City face more competitive opposition.
City were starting to showboat as AEK realised resistance was futile. Cherki knocked it long for Lewis to control into the path of Foden, who provided a sublime first-time finish into the top corner from the edge of the box. The exceptional goals were racking up on what felt like an otherwise mundane night.
On a positive night for City’s academy, Ryan McAidoo came off the bench to send in a perfect cross for Foden to complete his treble with a striker’s instinct, earning the biggest cheer of the night. Foden scored his first goal since mid-December at the weekend but the confidence is clearly flooding back to a player who has spent too long watching on from the sidelines, especially considering the talent he possesses. – Guardian

title: Alexis Mac Allister double sparks thrilling Liverpool comeback against Villarreal
description: Andoni Iraola’s side fight back from a tepid start at Anfield
content:
Andoni Iraola and Iñigo Pérez parked their long and close friendship in the build-up to the Champions League duel between two old Athletic Bilbao team-mates. They will have a humdinger of a contest to dissect when communications are restored. Liverpool, driven by Alexis Mac Allister and ignited by Rio Ngumoha, recovered from two goals down against Villarreal to maintain their 100-per-cent record in the competition in emphatic style.
Mac Allister struck twice as Liverpool fought back from a tepid start to record a third successive win in all competitions. They were given a scare when Tani Oluwaseyi volleyed in a late third for Villarreal, but were well deserving of their latest impressive result.
The regular phone calls between Iraola and Pérez had eased off as their first competitive confrontation as coaches approached. Iraola could have advised his close friend to bring a coat had they kept in touch. It had rained incessantly in Liverpool all day yet the Villarreal head coach opted for a short-sleeved polo shirt on the touchline. A brave move, although he would have been warmed by his team’s potent start against a much-changed host.
Liverpool’s expensive attacking trio of Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola were all on the bench as Iraola made six changes to the side that beat Brentford on Saturday. A fourth game in 10 days explained the omissions of Wirtz and Barcola, who had featured heavily in the previous three, while Isak’s workload was being carefully managed after his recent thigh injury. The rotation resulted in a second successive Champions League start for Trey Nyoni, and Ryan Gravenberch shifting forward into Wirtz’s number 10 role.
Iraola’s rejigged team did not have time to find their rhythm before falling behind. An error-strewn start by Van Dijk was responsible, and also in keeping with a ponderous opening half-hour from Liverpool in which Villarreal passed their way around Anfield with style and precious little resistance.
The Liverpool captain presented Georges Mikautadze with an opportunity as early as the second minute when he misjudged a long clearance out of defence by Renato Veiga. Van Dijk’s poor touch almost released the Georgia international striker through on goal but Jérémy Jacquet was across quickly to close off that route. Van Dijk’s second slip followed moments later, and this time there was no reprieve. The defender attempted to head another Veiga long ball back into the safe arms of Alisson. He found Mikautadze instead and Villarreal’s number nine pounced expertly, controlling well before rolling the ball under the Liverpool keeper. There were apologies all round from Van Dijk.
Villarreal doubled their lead with a goal that encapsulated the start made by both teams – the visitors passing their way through Liverpool’s midfield and picking holes in their high defensive line, with the home side slow to react. Pape Gueye, Alberto Moleiro and Nathan Saliba all combined to send their rampaging left back, Sergi Cardona, clear of the Liverpool backline. Played onside by Kostas Tsimikas, the full-back beat Alisson with a finish a striker would have been happy with.
Cardona’s defending was much less impressive as Liverpool, stung more by their own performance than the groans of the Anfield crowd, clawed their way back into the contest before half-time. The recovery commenced when Mac Allister rose superbly to meet a Tsimikas corner and flicked an unstoppable header into the unguarded side of Peter Gulacsi’s goal. The former Liverpool keeper could only stand and admire the midfielder’s header, while asking where a Villarreal challenge was.
Villarreal had bigger questions to answer when their once comfortable lead vanished entirely with the final kick of the first half. The visitors had dealt with another corner from Tsimikas when Rio Ngumoha gathered possession and clipped a cross towards the far post. Cardona checked his surroundings, then inexplicably let the ball bounce behind him. And right into the spot where Ronald Araújo was lurking. The on-loan defender headed home for the second successive week in the Champions League and celebrated with a mass pile-on with fans in the Anfield Road Stand.
Araújo failed to appear for the second half as Iraola introduced Wirtz and moved Gravenberch once again, this time to right back. The Liverpool head coach must have been sorely tempted to shake things up more, such was the paucity of his team’s first half display, but his half-time switch and demands sufficed. Liverpool improved vastly after the restart with Ngumoha and Wirtz a constant threat. Pérez’s substitutions were less impactful and the former Newcastle forward Ayoze Pérez was the object of his ire on several occasions.
Ngumoha took the acclaim of the Kop after creating Mac Allister’s second of the night with a sparkling run down the right. It was some one-two that brought Liverpool the lead. Mac Allister floated a pass out to the 18-year-old winger, whose first touch brought the ball under control and took him away from Cardona in the same movement. He then left the substitute Juan Foyth in his wake before pulling back a pass from the byline for the incoming midfielder to smash a shot in off the underside of Gulacsi’s crossbar.
Wirtz completed the comeback, continuing his own recent improvement, after Tsimikas and Cody Gakpo had combined to create space for the playmaker inside the area. The Germany international drilled a clinical left-foot finish inside the Villarreal keeper’s far corner. – Guardian

title: US resumes sharing missile intelligence with Ukraine, says Zelenskiy
description: Ukrainian president says country again receiving warnings of ballistic missile attacks, apparently suspended last week
content:
The US has resumed sharing intelligence with Kyiv on Russian missile strikes, Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday after a meeting with US envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway.
Zelenskiy said Ukraine was again receiving advance warnings of ballistic missile attacks, which were apparently suspended last week by the White House. “Now it works. It’s great,” he said, saying the US move would save lives.
He added: “It’s very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic [missiles] is coming. So we are thankful to the American side.”
The talks in Oslo took place amid the worst crisis in US-Ukraine relations since Russian president Vladimir Putin ’s full-scale invasion in February 2022. US president Donald Trump has bitterly accused Zelenskiy of failing to end the war and has said Ukraine needs a new leader.
Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner joined Witkoff and Zelenskiy by video. Norway ’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, also took part, alongside EU and British security officials.
Zelenskiy said he had held a “positive” phone call earlier with the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio . Asked whether Ukraine was now losing the war, after recent hostile US actions, Zelenskiy replied: “Of course we are not losing. But we are losing people because of Russian attacks and time. It’s a pity.”
He said he had raised with Rubio restrictions imposed last week on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk ’s satellite internet service. The slowdown has crippled Ukraine’s ability to launch mid-range drone strikes on Russian battlefield positions.
Zelenskiy said he had offered to stop Ukraine’s long-range attacks on Russian oil refineries – a key Trump demand – if the US provided Kyiv with Patriot missile interceptors. The Pentagon has blocked the delivery of Patriots to Kyiv paid for by other countries, leaving Kyiv more vulnerable than ever to air attacks.
Speaking on Tuesday, Zelenskiy also said he opposed a trilateral summit floated by Putin, which would see the Russian leader, Trump and China ’s president, Xi Jinping , meet next month to strike a Ukraine deal. Zelenskiy would be shut out in such a scenario, the Wall Street Journal reported.
“There can be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,” Zelenskiy said in Oslo. He added: “If it’s about Ukraine and our future, it can only be acceptable when we are at the table of negotiations.”
The Washington-Kyiv crisis began 10 days ago when Trump announced he was lifting US sanctions on Russian diesel, in an attempt to lower fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. He then announced an energy ceasefire, which Kyiv implemented for several days but Russia ignored.
Despite this, Trump has bitterly rounded on Zelenskiy. He has effectively positioned the US as Russia’s ally, favouring Moscow over Kyiv, to the dismay of the US’s pro-Ukrainian European and British backers. The US’s peace proposals have largely echoed Russia’s maximalist demands.
The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas , on Tuesday questioned whether US negotiators had been honest brokers in the peace efforts. Witkoff has held numerous meetings with Putin in Moscow, while so far visiting Kyiv only once.
[ Trump’s pressure campaign on Zelenskiy enters a decisive phase Opens in new window ]
“Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now,” Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin’s terms “because Europe has been supporting Ukraine”, Kallas said.
Tuesday’s talks came after Zelenskiy told a bipartisan group of US politicians that he believed “some political decision has been made to slow down … support for us”.
US officials have denied, this but have failed to explain convincingly why satellite communication services were curtailed or intelligence sharing temporarily cut off.
Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio insisted nothing had changed. He said Patriot interceptors were in short supply and were needed in other parts of the world, as well as for the US’s own defence. “There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” he insisted.
At least nine people were killed in Ukraine on Tuesday, including passengers who were travelling on the Kyiv-Odesa highway. A Russian drone struck two vehicles, killing three people and injuring four. One of the victims was the driver of a shuttle bus, which was on its way from the capital to a military cemetery. - Guardian

title: ‘Massive’ security operation planned in France ahead of  fresh protests on Saturday
description: Fresh curfews imposed on Tuesday after first quiet night since France’s most destructive rioting in years
content:
Fr ench cities were calm overnight under curfews imposed after last weekend’s scenes of chaos, as protest groups announced a new round ‌of demonstrations next Saturday.
Reeling from a weekend of extraordinary violence, the government is scrambling to reassure people it has learned its lesson ​from security shortcomings that left the centres of cities such as Paris, Marseilles and Lyons largely unprotected from post-demonstration rioters and looters.
“The targeted curfews have contributed to the calm of last night,” prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said in a post on ​X, adding that the measure could be extended “where the situation requires it”.
The fresh curfews were being imposed across the city centres of Paris and Lyon on Tuesday after the first quiet night since France ’s most destructive rioting in years.
Lecornu said a “massive” security operation was being planned for new protests on Saturday.
Paris police said the current curfew in two designated zones — around Place de la République and the Les Halles shopping district — had restored “public peace” overnight and would remain in place “for as long as necessary”.
The curfew zones leave out other areas hit on Saturday, including the Champs-Elysées and the area around the Saint-Lazare train station and parts of the Rue de Turbigo in central Paris, where protesters set up barricades and lit fires.
At the weekend, hundreds of thousands of people took part in combined protests across France by students and people angry about the cost of living , in demonstrations accompanied by arson and looting that continued from Saturday into Sunday.
They stoked a febrile political atmosphere as candidates from the far right and far left lead ⁠the field for a presidential election next ​April and May.
The calm after the weekend chaos hands the government a short breather after weeks ⁠of protests that have exhausted police ⁠and public authorities. But new ​challenges await next Saturday.
Representatives of the Yellow Vest movement, which organised Saturday’s protest, declined to disown the violence and declared they would hold an “act two” protest this Saturday.
“We were asked to condemn the violence, the riots, the barricades. To condemn the anger of the people,” the organisers said in a statement.
“We refuse to add our voice to the chorus of indignation. We do not condemn this anger: we applaud it.”
France’s main student union UNEF said in a flyer posted on social media that it planned to keep up the pressure on president Emmanuel Macron and his government to fix what students and pupils say is a broken and under-financed education system.
Coming in the build-up to a presidential election in the spring, the scenes of looting and burning of famous buildings including Limoges town hall led to bitter political recriminations, with calls for Macron to resign or to declare a state of emergency.
After holding a crisis meeting on Monday, Lecornu said he was “absolutely determined to restore order” and did not rule out calling a state of emergency. “If needed, I will do it.”
However, he told reporters that for now targeted curfews were a better solution, and said he had asked local authorities to put them in place to prevent further nights of violence.
[ ‘There’s nothing left’: French businesses count the cost of a weekend of unrest Opens in new window ]
“The chaos, to put it bluntly, is focused in urban centres,” Lecornu said. “We are dealing with a very specific and widespread form of crime: looting and also reselling.”
The economy ministry met representatives of online retail platforms to discuss how to prevent looted goods from being re-sold and to seek assistance in identifying those seeking to sell stolen items.
At least 3,000 businesses were affected, according to the government, with damages expected to amount to hundreds of millions of euro.
Lecornu announced supports for ransacked businesses including furlough schemes for employees as he sought to staunch any wider economic damage.
“We need to get things back up and running very quickly. Obviously, we can’t risk losing jobs, and French businesses are major employers,” Lecornu said. “There‘s a need for cash flow. Many retailers had already stocked up for Christmas.”
Almost 2,400 people were arrested during the weekend unrest and nearly 1,000 police officers were injured, according to the interior ministry.
Interior minister Laurent Nuñez had offered to resign following the violence, admitting police had “lost control”. Macron did not accept his resignation, instead asking for clarity about why there were “intelligence and foresight failings”.
Nuñez announced that additional police forces would be deployed this weekend.
French stocks sank when financial markets opened on Monday. The government now faces the difficult task of passing a budget through a hung parliament, balancing strong public opposition to spending cuts and bond markets concerned about French national debt.
Representatives of the trade unions, which have called national demonstrations to demand pay increases on November 5th, have been invited to meet the government for talks on Wednesday. - Additional reporting: Agencies

title: Elderly woman and man accused of her murder had regularly argued, court hears
description: Hasan Ali Gori (52) denies murder of Josie Ray (89), who was found dead in her home in Nenagh, Co Tipperary, on August 4th, 2024
content:
An elderly woman allegedly murdered in her home in Nenagh, Co Tipperary , regularly argued with the man accused of her murder, his trial heard on Tuesday.
Josephine “Josie” Ray, aged 89, of St Joseph’s Park, Nenagh, was found dead in her home on August 4th, 2024.
Hasan Ali Gori, 52, originally from Chad, and with an address at St Joseph’s Park, Nenagh, denies a single charge of the murder of Josie Ray.
At the time, Ali Gori was in a relationship with Josie Ray’s daughter, Mary Ray, who the court heard was vulnerable after she was born with an intellectual disability, and she often struggled with relationships.
At the time, Mary Ray and Josie Ray shared a close bond and were living together in Josie Ray’s local authority-owned home.
Another of Josie Ray’s daughters, Frances Ray, gave evidence on Tuesday at Ali Gori’s trial, at the Central Criminal Court in Limerick .
Frances Ray told the court that her mother had not liked it when Mary had relationships with men and brought them into her home.
Frances Ray said there were regular rows in the household involving Mary Ray, her mother, and the accused, and that this was causing “stress” on her mother in the weeks leading up to her death.
Frances Ray said the rowing “escalated” the night before her mother was found dead in her bed.
Prosecuting barrister Lorcan Connolly said Ali Gori was dependent on the Ray family for accommodation; that he had motive and opportunity to murder Josie Ray.
The prosecution case is that Ali Gori suffocated and strangled Josie Ray in her bed after they rowed.
Frances Ray told the court that her late mother had wanted Ali Gori out of her house because “she did not like him”.
“I’d say it was the way he treated Mary at times, being grumpy and giving out to her,” Frances Ray said.
“He didn’t like it, she [Josie] was ‘black’ this and ‘black’ that; she was set in her ways. She [Josie] was aggravated by him [the accused] and she doted on Mary,” Frances Ray added.
Frances Ray said gardaí were called to her mother’s house on the night before her death after another row ensued.
Answering questions from Aidan Doyle, senior counsel representing the accused, Frances Ray acknowledged that her mother had a “fiery” personality.
Frances Ray said rows at her mother’s house were often fuelled by her sister’s “jealousy” and “possessiveness” of Ali Gori, and her belief that he was cheating on her – for which the court heard there was no evidence.
Frances Ray said she warned her sister that she and the accused could be evicted from the local authority home if their rows continued.
The court, sitting before Judge Sean Gillane, heard that despite being “frail” and “small” in stature, Josie Ray was fully independent and in good health leading up to her death.
The trial, which is due to last up to four weeks, continues Wednesday.

title: Triple lock neutrality row fuels fractious Dáil exchanges
description: Opposition parties raise signs with Save Neutrality message after Taoiseach and Sinn Féin leader trade political blows
content:
The intensifying row over the legislation to end the triple lock on peacekeeping missions led to disruption in the Dáil as Opposition parties held up signs with the message: Save Neutrality.
The protest followed testy exchanges between Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald and Taoiseach Micheál Martin over the issue, which has united the entire Opposition.
She accused the Government of wanting to move away from peacekeeping and towards “military entanglement” and “military adventurism” with a guillotine on the second stage or introductory debate on the Bill, to be introduced on Wednesday.
[ Opposition parties left and right in Dáil unite to resist shelving neutrality triple lock Opens in new window ]
Under the triple lock, the Government must secure UN approval before 12 or more members of the Defence Forces can be sent overseas with an armed international force or body. The Government wants to remove the UN requirement.
McDonald said Irish people want no part of the “military might is right” agenda.
“Our neutrality keeps Ireland outside this dangerous military race to the bottom. It allows us to speak for freedom, human rights, and justice,” she said, adding the Government’s move is “an enormous step”.
McDonald warned, “it is literally inconceivable any taoiseach or government would push ahead with this without seeking first the permission of the Irish people”.
But rounding on the Sinn Féin leader, the Taoiseach said it was “outrageously hyperbolic” to suggest the State would abandon significant commitments to the rule of law and to many marginalised people in conflict and humanitarian crises worldwide.
He told her, “there is no balance to what you were saying. You use language like military adventurism, military entanglement. Who is going to engage in military adventurism? Do you think Dáil Éireann is?” he asked, angrily.
Martin said he would take “no lectures” from a party “that once supported nazism” during the second World War.
To repeated heckling, he said when Éamon de Valera affirmed the policy of neutrality, Sinn Féin leaders “colluded with the Hitler regime and Seán Russell was the key person” involved.
He said Sinn Féin “haven’t an inch of credibility” on neutrality because “for a long, long time, you saw you saw any conflict that Britain was involved in as Ireland’s opportunity, right beyond World War II, and so therefore you couldn’t have given a continental about Irish neutrality for many, many decades”.
[ Poll: Coalition may face battle to remove triple lock as voters align with Opposition Opens in new window ]
He claimed Sinn Féin was saying Russia “should have a veto on Irish participation in peacekeeping”, and the US and China.
And he warned “the Lebanon Unifil mission is about to end with no prospect of our participation” in a follow-up because of the US decision not to support continuation of the mission.
During the Dáil protest, Sinn Féin, People Before Profit-Solidarity, Labour and some Social Democrats held up the posters, and Ceann Comhairle Verona Murphy had to repeatedly insist they take them down, with Labour and Social Democrats the first to adhere to her call.
Sinn Féin defence spokesman Donnchadh Ó Laoire insisted debate on the legislation not be guillotined tomorrow, a call echoed by Labour’s Duncan Smith, who said it was a “modest ask”.
People Before Profit-Solidarity TD Richard Boyd Barrett said guarantees on the triple lock were made in the Nice referendum. “When we pick up these signs, we’re holding you to account for commitments that were made to the Irish people about neutrality, which is their property, not yours.”
Independent Ireland leader Michael Collins said “the whole of this country is upset and concerned about this” and the debate should not be guillotined.
Government Chief Whip Mary Butler said the Bill would get three hours and 34 minutes of debate tomorrow. But she was repeatedly heckled when she said voting had to be completed by 9pm on Wednesday, as the clerk of the Dáil explained at the business committee “that voting has to be completed at 9pm because of the work-to-rule that we are under orders on”.
Butler rejected Opposition claims that the Government is “trying to rush the Bill”.
Later on Tuesday evening, a proposal to retain some connection with the United Nations as part of a triple lock mechanism was suggested at the meeting of Fianna Fáil TDs and Senators.
Former minister for defence Willie O’Dea suggested at its Parliamentary Party meeting that the general assembly could provide a basis for mandating peacekeeping missions.
O’Dea was one of several TDs who argued that UN General Assembly be explored as an alternative to avenue to the Security Council as a means of achieving UN approval.
The assembly has not given permission for a mission in over 70 years, having deferred such decisions to the Security Council. Vetoes exercised by its five permanent members has resulted in no UN peacekeeping mission being sanctioned since 2014.
One proposal made at the meeting was that decisions and criticism made by the General Assembly on international conflicts could perhaps give some legal basis for a peacekeeping mandate involving Irish troops.

title: The Irish Times view on the legal aid dispute: solicitors should end it now
description: Jim O’Callaghan still has time to show he has the stomach to take on bigger reforms
content:
The four-month dispute between criminal defence solicitors and Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan took a turn for the worse this week, with an escalation in both action and rhetoric.
Solicitors protesting the introduction of a new payment model for free legal aid cases extended their withdrawal of services to include people held in custody and cases involving children. The Minister, for his part, appearing before the Oireachtas Joint Committee on Justice on Tuesday, accused those taking the action of deliberately targeting rape trials, a charge they indignantly denied. Meanwhile, the backlog in the courts continues to build, with thousands of adjournments and a surge in High Court challenges by unrepresented defendants, some of whom have been freed as a result.
None of this reflects well on the solicitors involved, who seem less concerned than they should be by the damage they are inflicting on their clients and on the courts.
Nor does it say much for the Minister’s conduct of his responsibilities. The objective of controlling the cost to the State of the criminal legal aid system, which has risen from less than €50 million in 2014 to a projected 120 million last year, is entirely legitimate. His public handling of the dispute is less so, with unnecessary baiting of the legal profession that has only made a settlement harder.
Caught in the middle are complainants, defendants and their families, who must now wait even longer than before for the justice system to deliver an outcome. That these now include those involved in rape cases, as well as children in the criminal courts, is unconscionable. To have such vulnerable members of society caught up in an argument over fees seems very far removed from the high ethical standards the legal profession purports to represent.
Despite his zeal for savings in this specific budget line, the Minister has shown little appetite for the larger, long-overdue reforms that Ireland’s legal system so clearly needs in order to advance competitiveness, lower barriers to entry and provide better value for money for all.
He was always an unlikely standard-bearer for real reform, given his own successful career as a senior counsel, exactly the sort of insider that the current system has served well for so long. The objective of the fees reform is legitimate and should not be abandoned, but in the context of the wider structural flaws in the legal system, it is relatively marginal. The Minister still has time to show he has the stomach to take on those bigger reforms.
Both sides have claimed they are willing to sit down and discuss the narrow issues dividing them. They should do so without further delay, and the solicitors should end their action immediately.

title: Palestinian student’s visa refusal was unlawful, court told
description: Outcome of challenge may impact 38 similar cases taken by others denied documentation by Minister for Justice
content:
Lawyers for a Palestinian student refused an Irish visa, who sought to pursue an engineering university degree here following the grant of a scholarship, have argued in the High Court that the denial was unlawful.
The outcome of the student’s challenge, which is being heard by Judge Anthony Barr, will potentially impact 38 similar lawsuits taken by Palestinians refused student visas by the Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan .
Opening the 20-year-old’s case on Tuesday, barrister Sarah Jane Hillery said the student was still in Gaza , living in “what remains for her home” following Israel’s assault on the region . Many of her immediately family members, including her mother and sisters, were killed in an Israeli air strike in March 2024, the court was told.
Hillery, barrister for the student instructed by Phoenix Law, said that the only reason she was not at University College Cork (UCC) pursuing an engineering degree on a fully-funded scholarship was because she was refused a visa to come to Ireland. She said her side’s argument is that the visa refusal was unlawful.
It is argued on behalf of the student that the refusal was unreasonable, irrational and in breach of fair procedures.
Hillery submitted the student met various criteria required for the granting of a visa. She said the student had provided a letter from UCC proving her place on the engineering degree, a proof of waiver of her tuition fee and proof of access to money during the period of study.
It is submitted that certain documentary requirements for the granting of a visa – including the procurement of bank statements – are irrational and “set an impossible standard” for Palestinian students seeking visas, with regard to the destruction of infrastructure in Gaza.
It is submitted that the student does not have access to an appropriate, alternative remedy to pursue her complaint, given that an appeal to the visa refusal will not be determined until September 2027.
The State is opposing the student’s judicial review challenge.
Earlier this month, four Palestinian students refused visas settled legal actions, after the Minister for Justice agreed to expedite their appeals to the refusals. Three of the students were subsequently granted visas, while the fourth lost their appeal.
At Tuesday’s hearing, the court heard that no such agreement has been reached in the case currently before the court.

title: The Irish Times view on the electricity market: risks are being dialled down
description: Eirgrid’s winter outlook has pointed to increased leeway in the network, but big investment needs remain
content:
The risks facing the Irish electricity system heading into the winter are markedly lower than they were a few years ago, when supply was on a knife edge. Eirgrid, which operates the network, said in its outlook for this winter that even on days of peak demand there should be a significant safety margin.
New power plants coming on stream, increased battery storage and the availability of emergency generation have helped to create more leeway. The contribution of renewables is rising and even solar panels on people’s homes are helping. Gas remains central to electricity generation and to providing emergency back-up. Temporary generators put in place in recent years – available when the system is under pressure – will be needed until 2028 or 2029, according to the regulator.
Energy security issues remain. Ireland is reliant on the UK for around 16 per cent of its electricity supply. Meanwhile, more than 80 per cent of Ireland’s gas is imported, via pipelines from the UK, though much of it originates elsewhere.
