The Government is planning an emergency storage facility for liquefied natural gas in Shannon, but it is unclear how quickly this will be delivered.
The energy transition – the planned increase in renewables and the phasing out of fossil fuels – remains difficult, particularly given the slow development of offshore wind. Even in an optimistic scenario, this is unlikely to provide any significant power to the Irish grid until into the 2030s.
Eirgrid will thus have to continue its balancing act on annual supply and – along with ESB Networks – get on as quickly as possible with the necessary investment in the grid. The State has committed extra funding and the regulator has given the go ahead. It is now, as in other areas of major infrastructure, all about delivery.
The taxpayer will pay for much of this investment. But some of the burden will fall on households and businesses in another way – through their energy bills. As well as wholesale prices, this is a key issue for competitiveness and affordability in the years ahead.

title: Storm Austen: Met Eireann issues status yellow rain warning for Thursday
description: Met Éireann says heavy rain set to spread eastward across country into Friday with risk of localised flooding
content:
A status yellow rain warning has been issued for Ireland on Thursday, with Storm Austen set to spread eastward across the country.
Met Éireann has warned of difficult travelling conditions and localised flooding. It said outdoor activities could be severely impacted.
The warning comes into effect from 7pm on Thursday and will remain in place until 8am on Friday.
Another status yellow warning has been issued for counties Dublin and Wicklow on Wednesday. The national forecaster had said this would bring a spell of heavy rain with the potential for difficult travel conditions and localised flooding. This warning is valid from 1am until 8am.
Storm Austen is the first named storm of the 2026/2027 season.
Aoife Kealy, deputy head of forecasts at Met Éireann, said Storm Austen will develop in the Atlantic Ocean.
“It’s getting help basically from a strong jet stream. So it’s deepening as it approaches western Europe and the UK.
“As it passes to the south of us, it’s going to bring that strong or the heavy rain and potentially some strong winds.”
She said the strongest winds will be felt in the UK. Warnings could potentially be updated on Wednesday or Thursday as the track of the storm becomes clearer.
Kealy said “even small differences in exactly how the low pressure will track are going to make a big difference to where the worst of the weather is on Thursday night and Friday”.
“It’s hard to pinpoint any one area just at the moment” where conditions may be worse.
[ ‘This keeps me awake at night’: How will Ireland’s climate worsen over the next 20 years? Opens in new window ]
“There’s potential for heavy rain right across the country and potential for strong winds as well. The winds look likely to be in the south, the strongest of the winds, closest to the low [pressure].
“But we could see those strong winds everywhere and as I said, we’re generally going to see a very wet night and even a wet start to Friday.
She advised people to stay up to date with the latest information from Met Éireann.
The name Austen was chosen by Met Éireann in tribute to Austen H Nagle, who became the first director of the Irish Meteorological Service when he was appointed in 1936.

title: Minister for Justice accused of ‘grossly unfair commentary’ over rape cases
description: O’Callaghan criticised for saying ‘only cases deliberately affected by withdrawal of services in Central Criminal Court yesterday were those involving allegations of rape’
content:
Jim O’Callaghan has been accused of “grossly unfair commentary” and a “massive misstep” over his claim that rape trials in the Central Criminal Court were the only ones “deliberately affected” by the withdrawal of solicitors’ services as part of the dispute over legal aid .
The Minister for Justice was defiant, however, in the face of criticism of his remarks during an appearance at the Oireachtas Justice Committee on Tuesday.
O’Callaghan signalled he is open to compromise on issues solicitors may have with how the new legal aid regime is applied to cases involving children.
Many defence solicitors, particularly in Dublin, withdrew legal aid services in July after a new flat-fee system for District Court cases was introduced.
The dispute escalated on Monday with the withdrawal of services expanding to cases including custody and children’s cases.
[ Jim O’Callaghan accused of treating solicitors’ pay dispute ‘like it’s a game’ Opens in new window ]
O’Callaghan has faced a backlash from political opponents and solicitors over comments he made about rape cases in his opening statement to the committee , which emerged in advance of the meeting.
During the committee hearing, O’Callaghan said the legal aid scheme is “operating nationwide” but that “particularly in Dublin, a number of solicitors have withdrawn services which have impacted on court hearings, and that’s regrettable”.
He said: “Despite this, in the Central Criminal Court yesterday [Monday], the majority of cases proceeded without issue.”
O’Callaghan said six rape cases “were adjourned due to the withdrawal of services by solicitors”. He expressed his “deep concern that the only cases deliberately affected by the withdrawal of services in the Central Criminal Court yesterday were those involving allegations of rape”.
Fine Gael TD Barry Ward , a Government backbencher who is a practising criminal barrister, said this was “grossly unfair commentary”. He said there is “no evidence to suggest that solicitors were deliberately targeting that [rape cases]”, and that O’Callaghan should “consider withdrawing that remark because you don’t have the basis for it”.
The Fianna Fáil Minister said, however, that he wanted to “set out the facts”, reiterating that six rape cases were adjourned on Monday because of the withdrawal of services.
O’Callaghan said four rape cases were adjourned on October 12th and another five rape cases were adjourned on October 5th, all on the basis of “withdrawal of services”. He said that on Monday “there was also seven cases which weren’t rape cases, which were trial-continuing cases. None of those cases were affected by the withdrawal.”
Ward responded that this was because those cases were continuing trials, and asked whether it was not “deeply disingenuous” to suggest ”a deliberate targeting of rape trials – it’s hugely emotive, it’s very unfair, and it’s also wrong – because the evidence is not there to support it”.
Sinn Féin TD Mark Ward said there were other cases in the District and Circuit Courts that did not proceed as a result of the withdrawal of services by solicitors, including trials on robbery, arson, fraud, burglary, violent disorder and other offences. He put it to O’Callaghan that he “cherry-picked one court and had a look at one court, because it suits your political agenda at the moment”.
O’Callaghan said he “zoned in on the Central Criminal Court” because “that’s where the [solicitors’] campaign was yesterday”.
He said: “The coverage yesterday was all about disruption to rape cases in the Central Criminal Court. I was perfectly entitled to make the point I did.”
Labour TD Alan Kelly told O’Callaghan that reform of the legal aid system is necessary, but “from a negotiation point of view, to say what you said in relation to a rape trials was a massive misstep. If you’re trying to de-escalate a situation in negotiations, to say something like that was only throwing fuel on the fire.”
Kelly asked about the issues O’Callaghan was willing to negotiate over with solicitors.
During the summer, the Law Society of Ireland proposed that long-running cases would see a second legal aid certificate issued when cases exceed 10 court appearances, citing cases involving children among those where this can happen.
O’Callaghan told Kelly there is an ongoing Department of Justice review on children’s cases. “If it is the case that it looks like the average length of time it takes for a children’s case to conclude is more than the five [court appearances], I will reflect that in changes.”
He said: “I’m not going to go back into permitting multiple certificates, but I’ll keep an open mind. I’m not going to negotiate in here with you now.”
During his opening statement to the committee, O’Callaghan cited an example of 131 certificates being issued in the Dublin District Court in relation to a money laundering charge. He said: “There was only two appearances in the District Court, and the fees payable to the solicitor would amount to €26,800.”
He later said the “fundamental principle” when it comes to the new flat-fee system is “trying to cut down on the scandal of multiple certificates. I’m not going to change that.”

title: Ireland boosted by return of Porter, Baird and Hansen for Nations Championship
description: Andy Farrell to name squad for northern series on Wednesday afternoon
content:
The Lord giveth and the Lord taketh away. Although the absence of the captain Caelan Doris has been compounded by the injury sustained by Jack Conan last Saturday, Ireland will welcome back a trio of frontline players for the first time in almost a year – Andrew Porter, Ryan Baird and Mack Hansen – when Andy Farrell names his squad for the Nations Championship on Wednesday afternoon.
The three last played for Ireland in the final game of last year’s November series against South Africa. In that game at the Aviva Stadium, Hansen suffered a foot injury that required surgery in December, ruling him out for the rest of the season, Baird fractured his tibia, and did so again in Leinster’s Champions Cup quarter-final against Sale in April, while Porter was twice sidelined due to calf issues.
Porter, Baird and Hansen all provide unique abilities and points of difference that will be gladly restored to the Ireland squad. Allowing for the loss of Doris and Conan, Farrell will also have been encouraged by the form of other summer tourists after their delayed seasonal returns.
Ireland will play three games at the Aviva, against Argentina (November 6th), Fiji (November 14th) and South Africa (November 21st), before a concluding playoff at Twickenham on the last weekend of the month.
There could be one or two uncapped bolters included in the squad, such as Ulster outhalf Jamie Benson, while The Irish Times has learned there will also be an A game during this window, possibly against a Fiji XV side, which the IRFU are set to confirm later this week. This fixture might allow Farrell the chance to give some game time to fringe players.
Porter’s return could see Billy Bohan rerouted to the A squad, and possibly Sam Illo as well, to accommodate the return of Finlay Bealham, but then again, the young Connacht tyros were in the summer squad on merit and would have earned their places here too.
The hookers will likely be unchanged, with the usual names in the secondrow to be supplemented by one or two from Cormac Izuchukwu, Darragh Murray, Tom Ahern and Edwin Edogbo, who is on course to return for Munster against Leinster on Saturday having last played in May.
With Sean Jansen set to fill the void as Irelands starting eight in Doris and Conan’s absence, the door is ajar for Max Deegan and one of the younger uncapped backrowers, such as Munster’s Seán Edogbo or Brian Gleeson. But with Nick Timoney another option at eight, a likelier fit might be one of Ulster’s backrowers, David McCann or James McNabney, especially as Bryn Ward has been ruled out of Ulster’s upcoming trip to South Africa in the URC.
A regular at blindside in the 2022 and 2023 Ireland Under-20s Grand Slams, McNabney was a development player for both the Six Nations and the summer tour in 2025, but missed the latter with an ACL injury which sidelined him for all of last season.
In the safe expectation that Jamison Gibson-Park will be named in the squad, despite not yet playing this season but having resumed training, he is likely to be joined by Craig Casey and Nathan Doak, while other contenders such as Fintan Gunne and Matty Devine may feature in the A game.
Sam Prendergast’s form and Ciarán Frawley’s impressive start to life at Connacht is timely in the absence of Jack Crowley, but there could be surprise third choice at outhalf given Harry Byrne has only played 30 minutes of rugby this season due to a recent concussion, while Joey Carbery only returned from a lengthy absence last Saturday.
Benson is a product of the Harlequins academy and has played for the England Under-18s and Under-20s, but is Irish-qualified through his mother, who grew up in Belfast. The 24-year-old is highly versatile, having played at outhalf, centre and fullback for ‘Quins, with two-thirds of his starts coming at 10. After three games in the Ulster midfield following his summer move, he made his first start at outhalf in last week’s win away to Zebre. He looks a real dark horse for inclusion.
By contrast, the old warhorses at centre look set to be named en bloc again, namely Bundee Aki, Stuart McCloskey, Robbie Henshaw and Garry Ringrose, given their form so far this season. The only other players to break into the midfield mix in recent times, Tom Farrell and Jude Postlethwaite, are currently sidelined, while Jamie Osborne is another option, being able to also slot in at fullback or on the wing.
Despite James Lowe’s departure to Japan, Hansen’s return makes the stock of outside backs look relatively healthy. Tommy O’Brien is also back after being withdrawn from the summer expedition due to the hamstring injury he picked up in Leinster’s URC final win over the Bulls.
Jimmy O’Brien has carried on his end-of-season form with Leinster which earned him a starting place in all three summer Tests, while Jacob Stockdale and Robert Baloucoune are also in good form for Ulster, as is Hugo Keenan with Leinster.
Props: Porter, O’Toole, Bohan, Furlong, Clarkson, Illo
Locks: Ryan, McCarthy, Beirne, Izuchukwu, Murray/Ahern
Backrow: Baird, Cian Prendergast, Van der Flier, Jansen, Timoney, McNabney
Outhalves: Sam Prendergast, Frawley, Benson
Centres: Aki, Henshaw, McCloskey, Ringrose
Outside backs: Hansen, Jimmy O’Brien, Tommy O’Brien, Baloucoune, Stockdale, Keenan, Osborne

title: Senior civil servant to take charge of department during Patrick O’Donovan’s sick leave
description: Minister for Communications remains in hospital, but is to return to duties when he recovers
content:
The senior civil servant in Patrick O’Donovan’s department will take charge during the Minister’s absence from Government duties due to illness, it has been confirmed.
Feargal Ó Coigligh, secretary general at the Department of Communications, Culture and Sport , will discharge the department’s administrative functions following the Minister’s admission to hospital last week.
O’Donovan had a health episode when hosting an informal meeting of European Union ministers in Limerick and remains in hospital.
At a briefing on Tuesday, the deputy Government spokesman said O’Donovan’s condition remained “stable” in hospital.
“He is likely to remain in hospital for a further period,” he said.
[ ‘Leave my health out of it’: Anonymous briefings, a defiant response and a dramatic turn of events Opens in new window ]
The department continued to operate as normal, the spokesman said, also saying further decisions would be made by the Minister in due course.
No indication was given as to how long the recovery was expected to take or when O’Donovan would be in a position to resume his duties.
The spokesman said there was a legal provision that allowed a minister to delegate functions to a secretary general for a period if they are on leave.
Tánaiste Simon Harris, a Fine Gael colleague of O’Donovan’s, remains on paternity leave after the birth of his third child, but is due to return to work next week.
In O’Donovan’s absence, another Fine Gael ministerial colleague, Peter Burke , brought a memo to Cabinet in his place last week. The Minister of State at the department, Charlie McConalogue , has also deputised for the Minister for Dáil questions and debates.
In a statement last week, Harris said O’Donovan would continue to serve in Cabinet when he recovered from illness.
O’Donovan was taken to hospital after falling ill on Tuesday last week in Limerick, where he was hosting an informal meeting of EU telecommunications ministers.
At a press conference earlier that day, O’Donovan had criticised internal “betrayal” from some quarters in Fine Gael who had suggested anonymously that his health might preclude him from continuing in Cabinet.
He was previously admitted to hospital during the summer while on an official trip to Brussels. O’Donovan has said he was diagnosed with epilepsy 10 years ago.

title: ‘He was devoted to his band’: Tributes paid to Fontaines DC manager Trevor Dietz at inquest
description: Inquest heard Dietz felt ‘overwhelmed’ by mental health problems and had become ‘increasingly distressed’ by global events
content:
The “intelligent, kind and compassionate” manager of Fontaines DC took his own life in June this year, an inquest in the UK has found.
Trevor Dietz (47) died after a fall from height in East Sussex on June 7th after a long battle with mental health issues.
Fontaines DC called Dietz “the sixth member of the band”, while Irish hip-hop trio Kneecap paid tribute to him during their headline set at Crystal Palace Park later in June.
On Monday, East Sussex Coroner’s Court heard that Dietz felt “overwhelmed” by his mental health problems and had become “increasingly distressed” by global events, particularly in Gaza .
Beyond his impact on the music industry, Dietz was widely known as a campaigner for Palestinian human rights and against genocide.
His sister and partner both attended court while his brother watched proceedings via video-link.
In a statement read out by the coroner, Dietz’s sister Helena Prentice wrote: “Throughout his life he was passionate about humanitarian issues, particularly Palestine, and found it very difficult to accept the suffering of innocent people.”
She added that he was an “exceptionally intelligent, kind and compassionate man” who had experienced “recurrent anxiety” for many years.
[ Trevor Dietz, manager of Fontaines DC and ‘the sixth member of the band’, dies Opens in new window ]
Dietz had been engaging with his GP and other mental health professionals about an ongoing anxiety disorder and suicidal ideation, the court heard.
Assistant coroner Rachel Redman said: “He clearly was really, really dedicated and devoted to his band and it seemed to be a mutual feeling.
“I’m sure that they and all of the musicians he worked with will be lost without him.”
Fontaines DC shared the news of Dietz’s death on June 9th with a heartfelt tribute.
They wrote: “We are utterly heartbroken to let you know that on Sunday June 7th we lost our dear friend and manager Trevor.
“Trevor was beside us from the beginning of our journey as a band, we have never known Fontaines DC without him, the sixth member of the band.
“He cared passionately for us and for what was fair and right in the wider world. He was fearless in his beliefs. We will miss him always.”
[ Trevor Dietz and Fontaines DC emerged in a Dublin that seems to be slipping away Opens in new window ]
The band concluded: “We ask that you kindly respect our privacy and that of his family at this terribly difficult time. RIP Trev.”
Dietz signed Dublin band Fontaines DC in 2016 in advance of their breakthrough debut album Dogrel.
The first photo in the online tribute showed Dietz wearing a Kneecap T-shirt, with the fellow Irish musicians’ official page commenting: “Suaimhneas síoraí dá anam, a chara”, translated from Gaeilge to “Rest in peace, my friend”.
Kneecap rapper Móglaí Bap also wrote: “Suaimhneas síoraí Trev.” – PA

title: Two women and man arrested over petrol bomb murders of English family in Waterford city
description: Man (50s) and two women in their 30s arrested in latest phase of inquiry
content:
The arrests of three people over the fatal arson attack at the home of the English family in Waterford city forms part of a Garda strategy to move closer to the leadership of the drugs gang behind the attack.
Philip and Kim English, and their children Callum (12) and Jayden (9), were killed in the fire. Two other children – a girl (14) and a boy (6) – were rescued from the house and are in critical condition in hospital.
Three suspects – a man in his 50s and two women in their 30s – were arrested on Tuesday in Waterford.
Two other individuals have been charged and appeared before the courts.
The three people arrested on Tuesday are suspected of offences contrary to section 72 of the Criminal Justice Act 2006 in connection with the arson attack, namely aiding the crime gang.
The Garda said all three are currently detained under section 50 of the Criminal Justice Act 2007 at Garda stations in the Garda Eastern region.
“An Garda Síochána continues to appeal to any person: if you have any information on the murderous arson attack, please speak to the Garda investigation team at Waterford Garda station, contact the Garda Confidential Line 1800 666 111 or speak with any member of An Garda Síochána that you know.”
The suspects can be held for up to seven days without charge as they were detained under legislation used in the investigation of alleged crime gangs.
The Garda’s murder inquiry has been focused on trying to prove the identity of the person who threw the petrol bomb into the house on Birch Avenue, Birchwood, just after 5am last Tuesday and anyone who aided them on the day.
[ Waterford arson victims were ‘a beautiful family who did no wrong’, funeral told Opens in new window ]
However, gardaí also believe those involved at the scene were working on the orders of others, and may have been assisted after the crime, especially when it became clear four members of the English family were killed in the fire.
An Garda Síochána has begun examining the network of people, all suspected of having strong links to the Waterford drugs gang that ordered the attack. The gang had been waging a campaign of violence against the English family.
The family’s car was attacked outside their home as far back as August 2023, and just last month a petrol bomb was thrown at the house, though nobody was injured. Threats had also been made against members of the family on social media.
Gardaí suspect Philip English was being pressured to pay a €20,000 drug debt owed by a man he knew. Detectives believe the attacks and threats against him and his family represented a campaign of drug-related intimidation to extort that money from Philip English, even though he had no involvement with drugs.

title: Defence Forces officers earning as little as €4 an hour for working overtime
description: Issue of low cadet starting pay – about €25,000 – also raised at Raco union annual conference
content:
Officers in the Defence Forces are still being required to work overtime for rates as low as €4 an hour, their union’s annual conference has been told.
Representative Association of Commissioned Officers (Raco) delegates unanimously backed a motion on Tuesday calling for security duty allowances – effectively payments for overtime – to be linked to the national minimum wage as this would yield increases of 66 per cent in some instances to the allowances currently paid.
“Overtime payments are generally linked to your actual wage,” observed Raco president Lt Col Martin Ryan. “The fact we are trying to get this one linked to the minimum wage tells you something.”
The organisation has been seeking talks to the Government on the issue since February when the Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers adopted a decision by the European Committee of Social Rights with regard to a complaint made Raco and the Permanent Defence Force Other Ranks Representative Association ( Pdforra ) in relation to working conditions.
About 50 of the forces’ most senior officers receive no payments but have been routinely rostered to work overtime during Ireland’s presidency of the EU. “If you are not going to pay them, that’s fine,” Raco general secretary Lt Col Conor King said at the event. “Just don’t ask them to do the extra work.”
King is expected to call on Minister for Defence Helen McEntee , who is due to address the conference on Wednesday, to address the overtime issue as well as one relating to pensions for officers who joined after 2013.
While Chief of Staff Lt Gen Rossa Mulcahy told the conference that personnel numbers were showing signs of recovery, with 17 consecutive months of growth taking the total above 8,000 for the first time since 2023, delegates heard that more than half of the first army cadet class to join after the pension cuts had already left and “you’d be foolish if you didn’t think the others were planning their escape route”, according to one officer.
Representatives of Air Corps personnel suggested there would be an exodus of recruits to that service from the period too as soon as their initial 12-year contract expires.
Raco wants to see the reinstatement of the supplementary pension cut in 2013. It had previously helped to bridge the gap between retirement from the Defence Forces and the State pension. That gap now lasts four years and the conference heard of officers having to go long before that so as to try to get established in a second career while they still regard themselves as employable.
Cadet starting pay of about €25,000 was also raised, with Ryan among those to suggest raising the age ceiling on recruitment to 39 was a waste of time if pay remained at that level.
There is, however, the potential for someone to join as an enlisted member (private) on about €45,000 then switch to cadet training after six months.
“We don’t get many joining who are over 30,” said King, “We do have people taking the enlisted route, though, and that’s just a colossal waste of resources and money that needs to be addressed as well as leaving people on almost twice the money their classmates are getting.”
King said Raco’s hope is that some of the issues will be raised as part of the public sector pay talks.
Confirmation on Monday evening that the Committee of Ministers had adopted the decision which found the Ireland to be in breach of the European Social Charter in relation to pay for hours worked, overtime and public holidays, meanwhile, meant the Government no longer had any “excuse” not to engage on the issue, King suggested.
He would, he said, be raising the matter with McEntee on Wednesday and writing to the department as soon as the conference is over.
Mulcahy, meanwhile, said he continues “to provide military advice and recommendations to Government regarding possible future overseas deployments”.
A spokesperson for the Department of Defence said: “The Minister has indicated a clear interest in exploring how Ireland might contribute to any future EU supports for Lebanon given Ireland’s long-standing support for Lebanon, where Defence Forces peacekeepers have served in Unifil for almost 50 years.
“At EU level, discussions on the operational requirements of the proposed mission are ongoing. At this stage, no decisions have been taken regarding the nature or scale of any Irish contribution.”

title: Will French unrest benefit Marine Le Pen’s presidential run?
description: For moderate political forces, it is all about preventing the hard-left from getting into the presidential second round
content:
S itting presidentially behind a huge desk, the French flag behind her, Marine Le Pen took the occasion of the unrest in France this weekend to make a grave address to the nation.
“In six months, the French people will be able to choose another path. That of authority and security restored,” the veteran far-right campaigner said. “The path of hope, the path of rebirth. Long live the Republic.”
On the face of it, the chaos and widespread destruction may have benefited Le Pen’s chances in the presidential election next spring, especially as she has been able to link it to her favourite campaign topic, immigration.
However, the picture may be more complex.
The French government and moderate politicians of all stripes have focused on pinning blame for the weekend’s unrest on the hard-left political movement of Jean-Luc Mélenchon , who is the runner-up to Le Pen in polls as a presidential candidate.
Judicial authorities have been more circumspect, avoiding casting blame on any political group.
The Paris prosecutor told French media she “absolutely cannot confirm” that those responsible for violence in Paris were “politically aligned with the far left” and that those arrested were low-profile people who did not make political demands.
Speaking anonymously to French investigative outlet Mediapart cast, police leadership and local officials cast doubt on whether Mélenchon’s France Unbowed (LFI) was to blame and suggested there could be a political agenda at work.
“There were far-left activists at Saturday’s demonstrations, but they weren’t a majority,” a local police chief in an area hit by unrest told the outlet. “The rioters are just kids.”
A local politician in Marseilles told the outlet that Mélenchon’s party “isn’t organised enough in the city to orchestrate anything ... In this instance, I think LFI was the first to be overwhelmed.”
[ ‘I have never felt anything so painful in my life’: Irish caught in French riots Opens in new window ]
It is true, of course, that Mélenchon and members of his party have backed the student protesters, and took part in their vast marches over the last few weeks, including on Saturday.
Mélenchon was also very slow to condemn the rioting and looting, insisting until a late point that whatever violence took place was the fault of the police.
Until Saturday, the student demonstrations were accompanied by the kind of running battles with riot police and minor vandalism that is traditional at such protests. They did not come with the destruction, arson and looting of the sort seen this weekend.
What changed on Saturday was that the students were joined by a revived Yellow Vests or Gilets Jaunes movement, which had called out on social media for nationwide protests on October 17th, long before the student movement even started.
The Yellow Vests are politically diffuse. Past polling has found their supporters vote both for the far left and far right.
Initially angered about the high cost of fuel but with wide-ranging grievances, they called on groups as diverse as farmers, civil servants and climate activists to take part and have declined to disown the violence.
Yet there is a political reason why the current French government and moderate politicians might want to pin the unrest on Mélenchon.
French presidential elections usually have two rounds. If no candidate wins an outright majority, the two leading candidates face each other one-on-one for a second-round run-off, which would take place in May.
Until now, polls have suggested this second-round scenario would be Le Pen versus Mélenchon. They are old rivals who have run for the presidency multiple times and are probably each other’s preferred opponents, each representing everything the other abhors.
Polls suggest that this scenario would lead to a landslide Le Pen victory. This is because while Mélenchon has a strong base of support, he is also sufficiently divisive to drive some voters to choose whoever he is running against.
The political calculation behind attempts to blame the unrest on Mélenchon may therefore be to prevent him from getting to a second round.
If the unrest causes Mélenchon’s support to falter, that may allow space for a more moderate candidate to emerge as Le Pen’s main contender – someone with broader appeal and a better chance of beating her in a head-to-head contest.
[ What led to the eruption of violence across France last weekend? Opens in new window ]
The centre-left Raphaël Glucksmann, the centre-right Édouard Philippe, the “Macronist” Gabriel Attal and the conservative Bruno Retailleau are all less prolific presidential candidates who hope to emerge as the moderate figure who can unite the votes of all those who don’t want president Le Pen.
The first poll out since the unrest showed a boost for Le Pen, now on 38 per cent, with Mélenchon and Glucksmann vying for second on about 16 per cent. All eyes will be on the next surveys to see how it all plays out.

title: Final call for the sky’s most eccentric airliner
description: Lufthansa’s quirky plane, with its extra-long fuselage and toilets down a flight of stairs, has a devoted following. Now, the carrier is taking it out of service
content:
T he Airbus A340-600 is not the world’s fastest, newest or sleekest airplane. Its cabin is dated compared with its modern, high-tech counterparts. It guzzles far more fuel than its rivals and relies on four engines to fly routes that other planes do with two.
Still, the A346, as it is known, has developed a devout fan base that is drawn to its abnormally long fuselage, restrooms that can be configured to be down a set of stairs adjacent to the cargo hold, and the power of its four engines.
“The A346 has been one of my favourite aircraft since about the age of seven,” said Connor Joossens (31), an aviation maintenance student, who lives in Orlando, Florida.
But the plane’s days are coming to an end. Lufthansa, one of only three passenger carriers that still use it, flew the plane for the last time on Sunday, from Washington’s Dulles International Airport to Frankfurt Main Airport. (Of the other two carriers, one is in Iran and the other is in Venezuela, making it unlikely most people will fly on their planes.)
Personal tributes have flooded social media while aviation photographers have travelled thousands of miles to shoot the plane one last time. And some fans have spent thousands of dollars – and shaped entire intercontinental trips – to get on a farewell flight.
Joossens is one of them. For most of his life, the opportunity to fly on an A346 had eluded him. But in June, when his wife had to go to Finland for work, he saw his opportunity. Instead of flying the most direct route from their home in Orlando, which would have taken about 14 hours, they first travelled to Washington, then flew the A346 to Frankfurt, and then connected to Helsinki, arriving in Finland about 24 hours after they departed.
Joossens said flying on the plane for the first and last time was an amazing, yet slightly bittersweet experience. “It’s really disheartening to see these amazing planes retire,” he said.
Charmaine D’Cruz, who runs Lufthansa Group’s ground operations at Dulles, said many passengers are drawn to the downstairs toilets, often taking pictures of the staircase and waiting area. “Passengers always make sure to see it,” she said. “It’s special.”
The jet entered service in 2002, engineered to compete with Boeing’s 747 and connect cities that many thought were too far apart for twinjets to safely fly between and that were out of range for the shorter, underpowered A340-300 (with engines often mockingly compared to hair dryers). For the A346, however, power was not a problem.
But the plane was hardly a success. Fewer than 100 were built, while Boeing’s competitor aircraft saw thousands roll out over generations. After Boeing introduced the 777-300ER in 2004, matching the A346’s capacity and range with half the engines, many considered the Airbus jet an anachronism.
The final four planes Lufthansa has been flying were already living on borrowed time. The carrier originally retired the aircraft after the pandemic flatlined international travel and had already ordered dozens of modern, fuel-efficient jets. But many of those have been delayed for years, so the airline resurrected the A346 to meet the soaring demand for post-pandemic travel.
“It was a special situation for us,” said Francesco Sciortino, a member of Lufthansa’s board and the pilot captaining the aircraft’s final flight from Dulles. It helped that the airline already had pilots certified to fly it, and that the aircraft was reliable. “But this era should be over already,” he said. “It’s time.”
Does he believe that the A346 will be missed?
Pilots will reminisce about the four engines, Sciortino said, but “from the perspective of a passenger who is not an aircraft enthusiast, to be honest, they will miss nothing.”
In a world where most planes are indistinguishable from one another, the A346 does stand out, and not just because of its extra engines. Its 75-metre fuselage – the longest in the world for more than a decade – appears even longer to the naked eye because of its narrowness relative to its length. Passengers sitting in the back have said that, on take-off, they would see the front of the plane lurch toward the sky long before they felt themselves lift off.
“It’s just one of those planes that you see in the air, and there’s no mistaking what it is,” said Cameron Stone (23), a ramp agent in Sacramento, California. Rather than fly with a single layover from Berlin to California in August, he flew from the German capital to Frankfurt, then from there to Dulles Airport on an A346, then from Washington to Los Angeles and finally north to Sacramento. “It’s such an oddball of an aircraft,” he said.
“It was just an incredible beast of a machine,” said Chris Pohl (63), a pilot living in southern France and one of the first A346-certified captains who has flown Airbus jets for 37 years and who runs a popular aviation Instagram. “We used to call it Beauty and the Beast, because it’s beautiful with four big monster Rolls-Royce engines slung under the wings.”
They are so powerful, Pohl said, that even “if you lost an engine flying across the Atlantic, you could actually climb to a more efficient altitude.”
But such power comes at the expense of efficiency, with the A346 burning as much as 40% more fuel compared with Airbus’ most advanced wide-body jets.
Jason Steyn (32), a copywriter from Cluj-Napoca, Romania, flew on an A346 by chance. “I didn’t think I would ever be able to do it,” he said. But when business brought him to New York in August, he was shocked to see one on his itinerary.
“I was geeking out to the ground crew as we were boarding,” Steyn said. “They were kind of looking at me funny, like ‘Come on, dude, it’s just a plane.’”
This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

title: Aviation firm co-founder ousted during sick leave wins €41,000 for unfair dismissal at WRC
description: Legal papers calculate Magellan Aviation Services co-founder’s total losses at more than €1.2m
content:
An aviation maintenance firm which dismissed one of its co-founders while he was out of work sick following a breakdown in relations at the firm during a €1.2 million pay dispute has been awarded €41,000 at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) .
Gerry Burke secured the award against Magellan Aviation Services Ltd on foot of a complaint under the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977, following the termination of his employment in August 2023 after 33 years at the firm.
Burke was a co-founder and managing director of the company prior to its acquisition in 2013 by the Tokyo-headquartered Marubeni Corporation, the WRC heard.
Having been paid an “eight-figure” sum for his shareholding, Burke moved to Malta for tax reasons, and stepped down as managing director to a new post as director of special projects, the company’s lawyers submitted.
His base salary in that job was €80,000 – later increased to €88,000 – with health insurance, pension contribution and a contractual provision for a €305,000-a-year bonus, bringing his total annual remuneration to €369,786, his lawyers said.
A preliminary objection by the company submitted that the Unfair Dismissals Act did not apply, arguing that Burke lived in Malta, carried out his work “entirely outside” Ireland, and had his salary paid free of Irish income tax. This argument was rejected.
The company received tax advice in 2022 that it was unlawful to pay Burke his salary without deducting either Irish or Maltese tax, it was submitted.
It sought to “regularise” the situation with a new contract increasing Burke’s pay and requiring he pay income tax in Malta, but Burke rejected this, the company submitted further.
Burke said in evidence that the allegations of “tax evasion” levelled at him by the firm were “thrown in to discredit [him] and put a cloud over his reputation”. He was “tax-compliant in Ireland and in Malta”, he said.
His position was that he had contacted Marubeni’s compliance department in 2022 with what his lawyers submitted was a protected disclosure concerning the sale of the company, management practices, and certain pay and contract matters, the tribunal was told.
It was Burke’s case that an investigation into the pay and contract matters proceeded first, with a directive issued from Marubeni that Burke receive a 15 per cent pay rise, which was not actioned, his lawyers submitted further.
The company’s managing director, Niall Duggan, said that when he put the proposal to Burke at a meeting in Zurich, the complainant “suggested that he would move to Dubai”.
Duggan added that Burke “intended to sue [the company] if it took action to ensure that it complied with [Malta’s] tax legislation”.
Burke agreed he had threatened an injunction but said that without the firm sharing its tax advice with him, he could not reasonably agree to the company’s plans to establish a company in Malta and make him an employee there.
In 2023, Duggan said, “matters became increasingly fractious”, with Burke initiating a High Court action in Ireland and seeking to escalate the dispute to the leadership of the Marubeni Corporation in Japan.
In March that year, Burke underwent “serious surgery”, his legal team submitted. The actions of Magellan caused him “stress and strain” and delayed his recovery, it was further submitted.
After about five months’ absence due to sick leave, the company terminated Burke’s employment on the basis of disability, the tribunal noted.
There was “an express contractual provision under which an executive is automatically deemed to have a disability following an extended absence from work due to ill-health” in Burke’s employment contract, the adjudication officer noted.
Although Burke sought reinstatement as his preferred remedy for the dismissal, his legal papers calculated his total losses at more than €1.2 million, the WRC recorded.
The WRC noted that Burke had alleged non-payment of salary going back to 2020, and had initiated separate proceedings in the High Court.
Ruling the dismissal unfair, adjudicator Ewa Sobanska wrote: “I cannot accept that other matters, some of them still remaining unresolved, had no impact on the respondent’s decision to dismiss [Burke], Sobanska wrote.
She was not satisfied the termination arose “wholly or mainly” due to any question of Burke’s capability, she wrote.
However, she found she could not order reinstatement on the basis of “fractious relationships” and “tension between the parties”.
Sobanska wrote that €41,434.08, about six months’ base salary, was a “just and equitable” award for the dismissal.
This was because she could not take Burke’s claimed bonus payments into account, and she regarded his efforts to seek new work to be “inadequate”.
Peter O’Brien was for the respondent, instructed by Edward Kelly of Holmes O’Malley Solicitors. Ercus Stewart appeared with Tom McGowan for the complainant, instructed by solicitor Melvyn Hanley.
*This article was amended on 21st of October to make clear that Ercus Stewart appeared with Tom McGowan for the complainant, Gerry Burke, instructed by solicitor Melvyn Hanley and that Peter O’Brien was for the respondent, Magellan Aviation, instructed by Edward Kelly of Holmes O’Malley Solicitors.

title: Mr Nobody and a broken vase: Frank McNally on a British Museum accident with historic resonance
description: In 1845, a young Dubliner visited the museum and committed an act of vandalism that should have earned him permanent infamy
content:
T he mysterious smashing of a Chinese porcelain bowl in the British Museum recently appears to have been the work of a notorious recidivist vandal, celebrated in verse.
The rare, 300-year-old artefact fell from a shelf in its case on October 4th and, so doing, damaged another exhibit below. But according to the museum, CCTV shows that the room was empty at the time and there is no evidence of shelf “failure”.
So although investigations continue, the incident has most of the hallmarks of a well-known folk character who always tops the list of suspects in such cases:
“I know a funny little man, as quiet as a mouse / Who does the mischief that is done in everybody’s house! / There’s no one ever sees his face, and yet we all agree / That every plate we break was cracked by Mr Nobody.”
The accident, if that’s what it was, caused outrage in China . There were also claims there that it had been underreported in England, perhaps due to embarrassment in a country that sometimes justifies its accumulation of global treasures on the grounds of safe keeping.
Either way, it’s a relief to know there were no Irish students involved in the British Museum ’s latest embarrassment, because the case has some echoes of a much more notorious one from nearly two centuries ago, in which there was a clearly identifiable culprit.
One day in 1845, a young Dubliner – who later confessed to have been drinking for a week beforehand – visited the museum and committed an act of vandalism that should have earned him permanent infamy.
That would have been ironic because, until his moment of madness, he had been living under an assumed name in England, as William Lloyd, having left unspecified “family troubles” behind in Ireland, where he was a student at Trinity College .
Before his drinking binge, he must have been trying to keep a low profile. Then he went to the museum and smashed the Portland Vase, a masterpiece of ancient Roman glass that had, until then, survived intact for two millenniums.
[ Conversations on a Homecoming: Frank McNally on returning to the Dáil after a 20-year absence Opens in new window ]
Breaking it wasn’t as easy as it sounds. The vase was itself under thick glass, in a case. Unfortunately, this being the British Museum, there was a large lump of basalt nearby, from the ruins of Persepolis.
So, having first waited for a supervisor to leave the room, “Lloyd” launched the basalt sculpture at the case, shattering the priceless vase into 200 pieces.
Museum investigators later established that his real name was “William Mulcahy” and that his family was poor. Beyond that, posterity has allowed him to return to obscurity. So little else is known about him today that he might as well be Mr Nobody.
In the short term, he benefited from a good lawyer who pointed out that the legislation he was charged under, for “wilful damage”, applied only to objects worth a maximum of £5. He was therefore convicted of destroying the case, not the vase.
Then, an unnamed benefactor bought him out of a two-month jail sentence he had been given in lieu of the fine he couldn’t pay.
A London Times correspondent demanded “severe public flagellation”. But the vase’s owner (it was on loan to the museum then), the Duke of Portland, was more charitable. He didn’t pursue a civil action against the guilty party, not wanting the man’s family to suffer for his folly.
More than a century later, in 1954, an unnamed writer of this newspaper’s London Letter revisited the incident after a conversation in a Wedgwood shop in Piccadilly.
[ Try walking in Patrick Kavanagh’s shoes: one man’s pilgrimage from Inniskeen to Dublin Opens in new window ]
The keeper of the shop was Wolf Mankowitz, later a well-known playwright and screenwriter (and later again to retire and die in west Cork, courtesy of Charlie Haughey’s artists’ tax exemption).
He was then an expert on Josiah Wedgwood, the potter, who had once borrowed the Portland Vase and made 40 copies. Through that, Mankowitz knew a bit about the man who broke the vase: that he had been a “scenic painter” and that his brother was “a lecturer, probably in mathematics, in Trinity College”.
If anyone could tell Mankowitz where or how the museum vandal had ended up, the London Letter added, he would be “overjoyed” to hear. But if there was any response to this appeal, it was not reported.
The job of restoring the vase was a challenge similar to the reconstruction of Humpty Dumpty. A first attempt in 1845 was good enough to make a name for the craftsman John Doubleday, although when finished he still had 37 small pieces left over.
These were then stored carefully in a box but later devolved into the ownership of somebody who couldn’t remember what they were. After they and the vase were reunited, a second restoration was attempted in 1948, adding some of the misfit fragments. But a third and, so far, final reconstruction was required in the 1980s.

title: Construction of new National Maternity Hospital expected to begin next year
description: The €1.86 billion project is due for completion in 2033
content:
Construction of the new National Maternity Hospital is expected to begin early next year, after the Government formally approved the €1.86 billion project.
Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill on Tuesday secured Government approval for the new National Maternity Hospital (NMH) at the St Vincent’s University Hospital campus at Elm Park, Dublin , to proceed to construction.
John Sisk & Son has been appointed as the main contractor, while Designer Group has been appointed as reserved specialist contractor for mechanical and electrical works.
The announcement comes more than a decade after plans were announced to relocate the NMH to Elm Park.
The €1.86 billion budget is more than 10 times the amount originally allocated in 2013 when it was estimated the construction of the hospital would cost around €150 million.
Expected to be completed in 2033, the seven-storey, 54,000sq m building will include 244 beds in single-occupancy en suite rooms, five operating theatres and 24 birthing rooms. It will have capacity for 10,000 births a year.
Prof Jennifer Walsh, master of the NMH, said the move was an “important step forward” for women and babies in Ireland.
“In addition to providing maternity care, the NMH cares for women across every stage of reproductive and gynaecological health, supporting them through the many different stages of life,” she said.
“The new hospital is designed to provide modern, state-of-the-art clinical facilities in which to provide world-class care. Importantly, it will also give our patients the privacy, space and dignity they expect and deserve.”
[ ‘Every maternity negligence case costs us a midwife’, doctors’ group warns Opens in new window ]
The Department of Health said the design of the new NMH has been approved and signed off at each of the project stages by the relevant stakeholders, reducing the likelihood of future changes.
The finalised design was subject to external review and validation before the project progressed to tender.
It added that the budget excludes the impacts of global market fluctuations beyond that provided for in statistically probable worst-case scenarios.
Carroll MacNeill said Government approval was a “major milestone” and will provide “state-of-the-art” services in a purpose-built facility beside St Vincent’s.
“This co-location will ensure that women and newborn babies, particularly those with complex clinical needs, have immediate access to the highest levels of specialist care when required,” she said.

title: European stocks extend slide as French unrest rattles investors
description: Iseq edges up as Ryanair gains 2.6%
content:
European shares ended just ‌a touch lower on Tuesday, as violent protests in France kept risk appetite in check and hammered equities in the euro zone’s second-biggest economy.
The protests , ​which have intensified pressure on a country already grappling with soft economic growth and ballooning government debt, sent France’s benchmark CAC 40 index 0.38 per cent lower.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 index dipped 0.14 per cent to 638.64 points after slipping 0.8 per cent in the previous session.
Investors weary of elevated oil prices ​and high government bond yields have relied on robust earnings to pluck the Stoxx 600 out of the narrow range it has been stuck ⁠in over the past month.
Ryanair closed the session 2.6 per cent up at €23.35 as oil prices eased on news of a potential deal in the Middle East . Chief executive Michael O’Leary had earlier predicted a record increase in European air fares next year linked to higher fuel prices. The Iseq ended the day up 0.6 per cent at 14,161.
Ticket prices are set to increase by as much as 20 per cent next year, O’Leary said on Tuesday during a press conference in Brussels.
Kenmare Resources , which is the subject of a potential bid by a company controlled by the Abu Dhabi royal family, saw its shares fall by 5.7 per cent to €2.66. Insulation specialist Kingspan fell 1.1 per cent to €93.95 while Kerry Group traded flat at €94.50 in advance of results later this week.
Several major European sectors were trading lower, with industrials leading declines, dragged down by ABB’s 5 per cent drop as nervousness about the sustainability of artificial intelligence ( AI ) investments weighed on the Swiss engineering company, which is a major supplier to data centres .
French cloud operator OVHcloud jumped 18 per cent to a near one-month high after reporting its first positive levered free cash flow since its 2021 listing.
Comet Holding jumped 4.7 per cent following an increase in the electronic equipment maker’s third-quarter sales due to expansion of data centres and AI ‌infrastructure.
Schneider Electric fell 3.3 per cent after ⁠the French electrical equipment maker raised €6 billion in an accelerated bookbuild, a fast share sale to institutional investors.
Britain’s FTSE 100 ended lower ‌on Tuesday as banks and commodity-linked stocks weighed, while signs of resilience in the labour market kept expectations ‌alive for a Bank of England rate hike next month.
The blue-chip FTSE 100 index fell 0.29 per cent to ​10,733.00 points, while the midcap FTSE 250 was down 0.06 per cent at 24,364.
Banks eased 0.8 per cent and hit a more than four-month low. Heavyweight lenders HSBC, Lloyds and NatWest fell between 0.8 per cent ⁠and 1.2 per cent.
Energy stocks ​also weighed on the market, with heavyweights BP ​and Shell down 1.7 per cent and 0.7 per cent, respectively
The FTSE 350 basic resources index was ‌down 1.6 per cent, with miner Anglo American ​falling 2 per cent after maintaining its 2026 copper production guidance despite a 5 per cent drop in ⁠third-quarter copper output.
Technology and online grocery firm Ocado rose 6.6 per cent to top the FTSE 250 after JP Morgan raised its price target on the stock to 460 pence from 290 pence.
Wall Street’s main indexes moved higher on Tuesday as ‌a surge in healthcare stocks and softer oil prices boosted risk appetite, building on a recovery from last week’s technology-led sell-off.
Brent crude prices slipped 1.1 per cent after touching a ​five-month high in a choppy session as traders weighed Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf.
Most S&P 500 sectors gained, with healthcare hitting an all-time high. The gains were led by large-cap drugmakers, including Eli Lilly’s 4.7 per cent jump to a record high. Amgen, Pfizer, Johnson & Johnson and AbbVie were also up ​more than 2 per cent each.
The financial index also gained 1.2 per cent.
Energy, however, led the losses, while an about 2 per cent decline in Meta Platforms pulled the communication services sector down.
The market extended ⁠Monday’s rebound, as investors bought the dip in technology stocks following last week’s bruising sell-off, fuelled in part by concerns over ‌CoreWeave’s debt ‌load ​and the cost of financing the AI buildout.
AI-related shares were flat to higher on Tuesday, after early weakness in premarket trading. CoreWeave was last up 2.5 per cent, while the chip gauge Philadelphia Semiconductor index rose 0.7 per cent.
“You’re seeing ⁠some strength in some high-value stocks and the Dow, ​and so that’s helping to sort of lift the overall indexes,” said ​Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth. – Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Jim O’Callaghan accused of treating solicitors’ pay dispute ‘like it’s a game’
description: Taoiseach defends Minister for Justice on issue saying ‘essence of the reforms are here to stay because we do owe it to the taxpayer’
content:
Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan has been accused in the Dáil of treating the solicitors’ dispute “like it’s a game” as calls were made for Taoiseach Micheál Martin to “intervene and show leadership”.
Deputy leader of the Social Democrats Cian O’Callaghan said the “open warfare between your Justice Minister and solicitors has to end” because “victims of crime are being caught in the crossfire”.
Labour leader Ivana Bacik said “victims of crime cannot be collateral damage in a proxy war between Jim O’Callaghan and the Law Society , or indeed a proxy battle for the leadership of Fianna Fáil ”.
The Taoiseach defended O’Callaghan, however, and in turn called on the Opposition to “show some leadership” on the issue after they had repeatedly complained over the absence of legal system reforms.
They should engage in reform rather than “saying it’s all the Minister’s fault, and no one else has any contribution to make”, said Martin. He described the Minister’s changes as a “more sensible reform” with “better value money for the taxpayer who’s paying for it”.
The Taoiseach told the Labour leader the Minister had met the Law Society twice, and is prepared to make further changes, “but the essence of the reforms are here to stay because we do owe it to the taxpayer”.
During Leaders’ Questions on Tuesday, O’Callaghan said the Minister had last met the solicitors in July and it was only this morning, hours before his appearance before the Oireachtas Justice Committee, that “he sends a letter saying he’s open to a meeting”.
He pointed to cases where the accused themselves were allowed to cross-examine “terrified victims” where no solicitors were available. In one case, he told the Dáil, a man who broke into a woman’s home while her children were present and threatened to “rip her teeth out with a pliers” cross-examined the victim, while in another, a mother who took out a barring order against her son was verbally abused by him, and he had to be removed from court.
O’Callaghan also highlighted the rape trial cases that were affected by the dispute over the change in payment to a flat €520 for each case. He said his party leader Holly Cairns had in July highlighted the impact on rape cases, “and nothing effective has been done since then to resolve this”.
The Taoiseach agreed the cases were “harrowing”, but “solicitors should attend those cases. I don’t think the dispute and the nature of that dispute justifies the absence at such cases”
O’Callaghan had suggested that lawyers were deliberately affecting rape trials with their withdrawal of services, comments which were condemned by members of the Opposition and lawyers .
Calling for the Opposition to “show some leadership” on the reforms required in the legal system, Martin said TDs raised “very serious issues at various committees, public accounts everywhere, about value for money”.
“This is fundamentally a money dispute, and multiple payments have been granted for no stated reason,” he said, adding that “multiple solicitors have been assigned to the same defendant for charges heard on the same day, resulting in multiple payments for the same case”.
Martin also said O’Callaghan is “happy to engage” on changes to the scheme, particularly in the area of the Children’s Court”, and has already made changes since the scheme was first introduced.
Bacik said the latest withdrawal of the services of criminal solicitors “is deeply regrettable”, but the Minister “appears to be in denial about his own role in escalating the situation”.

title: Building industry deaths reveal pressing need for closer surveillance of small sites
description: All 23 people who died were men, only one of whom was not an Irish national
content:
Falls from heights were the leading cause of death in the construction industry between 2022 and 2024, according to a review by the Health and Safety Authority (HSA).
Publishing its Review of Construction Fatalities in the Republic of Ireland 2022–2024 on Tuesday, the authority said 23 workplace deaths were recorded in the construction industry during the period.
The review found falls from heights accounted for 15 deaths. It also found that 19 of the 23 occurred on smaller construction sites with between one and four workers.
All 23 people who died were men, all but one of whom were Irish nationals. Self-employed workers accounted for 10 fatalities.
The report also shows age was a factor in construction deaths. Most deaths occurred among workers aged 35 to 64 years. These accounted for 20 of the 23 deaths.
Overall, 96 per cent of those who died were over 35 years of age. The HSA said this “contrasts with the common perception that young and inexperienced workers are at the greatest risk”.
Construction work on farms accounted for five deaths, with single-house upkeep, repair and maintenance also accounting for five deaths.
Housing projects accounted for seven of the 23 deaths, with four of these occurring on single-house projects and three occurring on housing projects consisting of multiple units.
[ Lives lost in the workplace remembered Opens in new window ]
Upkeep, repair and maintenance in commercial settings accounted for three fatalities, while civil engineering projects accounted for two. “Other work” accounted for one of the deaths. This involved a construction worker working at a quarry.
HSA assistant chief executive Eibhlin O’Leary said the findings provided “important lessons” for everyone involved in construction. She said the review particularly showed the need to focus safety efforts on smaller sites.
“Every fatality in construction represents a person who went to work and did not come home. This review shows that falls from height continue to be a critical risk, accounting for 15 of the 23 fatalities. It also highlights the need to focus on smaller sites, with 83 per cent of these fatalities occurring on sites with between one and four workers.
“The findings provide important lessons for everyone involved in construction,” she said

title: Farmer’s estranged wife seeks order freezing his assets after he sold herd without telling her
description: Wife’s solicitor tells judge client has made a court application over dissipation of marital assets
content:
The estranged wife of a dairy farmer who sold off his entire herd with an estimated value of between €500,000 to €600,000 without telling her has applied for a court order freezing the man’s assets.
At the Family Law District Court, solicitor Shíofra Hassett told Judge Catherine Ryan her client has made a Section 35 application under the Family Law Act 1995 to the Circuit Court in relation to the dissipation of marital assets.
A Section 35 “freezing order” application prevents a spouse from selling property, transferring money out of bank accounts, or shifting investments to avoid paying a settlement or maintenance, pending finalisation of a case.
Hassett told the judge about the Circuit Court freezing-order proceedings by the woman against her estranged husband when applying for an adjournment of a hearing for the woman’s separate application for a maintenance order before the District Court.
In September, Judge Adrian Harris granted an interim maintenance order for the farmer to pay maintenance of €300 to the woman and €60, per week, for one dependent child.
The woman was seeking an interim maintenance order of €500 per week pending a full hearing in the case. Hassett told the judge that the hearing into the full maintenance order can be adjourned on consent with the other side in the case.
Hassett said that in the Circuit Court, in response to the Section 35 application, Judge Francis Comerford “has made certain directions and has given time for a replying affidavit to our application”.
Hassett said the Circuit Court proceedings have been adjourned to November 25th.
In response, the judge said Hassett’s client has sought a Section 35 application to freeze assets where there are matters of a financial nature to be addressed in the Circuit Court.
The estranged couple were not present in court for Hassett’s application to adjourn the maintenance order proceedings.
At a hearing in September, the court heard the dairy farmer was “at breaking point” when selling off his entire herd without telling his estranged wife.
At the interim maintenance order hearing at the Family Law Court, the farmer told Judge Harris, “I disposed of the cattle because I was not able to do it any more.” The man said he is at his “wits’ end” since his marriage broke down.
In evidence, the wife told the court her estranged husband had “made a decision to sell the cows without telling anyone”.
She said that, during their marriage, “I worked seven days a week, milked cows twice a day. I did the cooking, the cleaning, and I reared the children.”
She said: “We always made money, despite drought, Covid, rains and storms knocking down buildings.”
The farmer told the court he was not in a position to pay an interim order.
The farmer told Hassett in September that he has “lost everything” with the sale of his dairy herd, “and I did not take that decision lightly, to watch my whole livelihood be brought away in a number of lorries after 38 years of work”.
Solicitor for the husband, Máiréad Doyle, said her client has significant assets but also significant liabilities, with a debt of €1.2 million attached to the farm. She said it costs €244,000 per annum to service the bank debt.
The farmer told the court: “We have come to a point that, if I don’t do something now, we will end up with nothing.”
He said: “This is the hardest time of my life – I have walked away from it. I haven’t slept for weeks – two or three hours every night.”
The man told the court his estranged wife “didn’t want her name on any of the loans. She is not liable for any of the loans – I am liable for all the loans.”

title: Live commerce platform Whatnot to double Irish workforce in 18 months
description: Company to expand European headquarters in Dublin
content:
Live commerce platform Whatnot is to double its Irish workforce in the next 18 months as it expands its European headquarters in Dublin .
The company is also planning to open the platform to Irish sellers in 2027.
Whatnot, which has been operating in Ireland for the past four years, currently employs 130 people. It is targeting close to 300 in the near future, with roles in engineering, artificial intelligence (AI) , operations, strategy, and trust and safety being created.
The platform allows businesses and individuals to sell through live video, demonstrating products and taking orders in real time. The first half of the year saw sellers generate more than €6.8 billion in sales.
The Dublin team plays an important role in keeping the platform working, reliable and secure, working on payments, buying and selling flows and infrastructure. The expansion will see new AI engineering recruits build tools to help reduce admin tasks for sellers, from product listings to post-show tasks.
Cofounder and chief executive Grant LaFontaine said the company had been building quietly in recent years. It also has an office in Berlin, but the focus is on growing the team in Dublin.
“The vast majority of hiring is happening in Dublin, so it is the biggest office outside the US and it will be for a while,” he said.
“Six years ago we had 10 people, so to go from that to 1,400 [globally], it is quite a large sum.”
There are Irish buyers on the platform, with the number of people in Ireland shopping on Whatnot each month has grown almost fivefold over the past two years, but officially Whatnot has not opened to Irish sellers. That has left most orders filled by sellers in the UK, Germany and the US. That will change next year, with Whatnot opening to Irish businesses.
The news of the expansion was welcomed by Minister of State at Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment Alan Dillon .
“The company’s plan to double its team in Ireland, creating high-quality jobs across engineering, AI, operations, and trust and safety, is a strong endorsement of the exceptional talent available here and of Ireland’s attractiveness as a location for innovation,” he said.
IDA Ireland ’s executive director Mary Buckley said the decision demonstrated strong confidence in Ireland’s technology ecosystem and skilled workforce.

title: Elderly couple who died in fire at Co Cork house named as Geraldine and Willie Hawkes
description: Roof of the property near Innishannon collapsed amid blaze, making search operations more difficult
content:
A couple in their 70s have died in a house fire in Co Cork .
They have been named locally as Geraldine and Willie Hawkes. Geraldine Hawkes was a former midwife at the Bon Secours Hospital in Cork city. She taught sewing classes in Knockavilla parish. Willie Hawkes was a retired milk recorder.
The dormer bungalow where the fire occurred is in Raheen, Crossbarry, near Innishannon.
It is understood the couple contacted the emergency services on Tuesday morning after the blaze broke out at their home.
Emergency services, including firefighters from Cork city and county, paramedics from the National Ambulance Service and gardaí, responded to the incident at about 8am.
Firefighters had to wear breathing apparatus when entering the burning building. It is understood the roof of the house collapsed, making search operations more difficult.
The bodies of the victims were recovered by firefighters. Conditions were described as challenging, and firefighters remain at the property.
Investigations will be carried out to determine the cause of the fire. The local coroner has been informed and an inquest will be held at a later date.
Co Cork senior assistant fire officer Leah O’Shea told Cork’s Red FM that crews from Cork city and Bandon had been dispatched to the scene immediately.
“When they arrived at the scene the fire was well established. Sadly, one fatality was initially removed. Some time later, a second fatality was also discovered at the scene.”
West Cork Independent councillor Alan Coleman, who lives in Innishannon, said the couple were well known and liked locally.
“They didn’t have children themselves but they had an extended family. The community will rally around them. They [the couple] were very involved in the community. They both grew up and spent their whole lives here.”
Cllr John Collins of Independent Ireland, who lives in Bandon, said the elderly couple and their relatives were in the thoughts and prayers of the people of west Cork.
Gardaí have issued an appeal to members of the public who may have spotted the fire as they passed the property this morning to contact them at Macroom Garda station on 026-20590.

title: Millions affected by Revolut disruption linked to Google Cloud outage
description: Fintech says data and customer money remain safe
content:
Millions of customers of digital bank Revolut found themselves unable to access financial services after a power outage at Google Cloud caused widespread disruption on Tuesday.
Customers across Ireland and the UK reported problems accessing the bank’s systems, from logging in to the app and transferring funds, to making card payments and cash withdrawals.
The disruption was linked to an outage at Google Cloud, which provides core infrastructure services to Revolut.
The problems began early on Tuesday morning and lasted for several hours, with Downdetector recording a spike in reports between 7 and 8am. Revolut confirmed the outage, but moved to reassure customers that their data and money had not been compromised.
“We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe,” a spokesman said. “We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.”
[ Revolut customers in Ireland affected by ‘third-party’ data breach Opens in new window ]
Revolut has 3.4 million customers in Ireland.
Google later confirmed the problem was caused by a “power event” at Google Cloud’s “Europe-west2-b” region, which knocked services offline early on Tuesday morning and caused intermittent network failures.
“A power event caused an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated,” Google said. It later updated customers, saying the issue with impacted products had been reduced for most of those affected. “It is believed to be affecting currently a very small number of customers and our engineering team is working on it.”
Revolut was not the only company affected. In the UK, Lloyds Bank and HSBC users were also reporting issues to Downdetector, as well as DPD and the courts video platform used throughout the country.
AIB and Bank of Ireland said they were unaffected, and that all services were operating normally.
Google’s cloud division is competing with rivals Microsoft and AWS in providing cloud services to critical industries. This outage has brought the reliance of companies on a small number of cloud services back into the spotlight.
In October last year, a problem with AWS took down major apps such as Fortnite and Snapchat, along with banks, transport and messaging services. That was followed a week later by an issue at Microsoft Azure after an “inadvertent configuration change” caused problems for users.

title: The triple lock: What is it and why is the Government trying to change it?
description: Opposition argues that removing the legal provision will compromise the State’s neutrality
content:
The triple lock is a legal provision which requires that before more than 12 Irish troops are deployed abroad, three tests must be satisfied; there must be a decision of the Government, a vote of the Dáil and United Nations backing. While it dates back to 1960, it was only in 2001 that the phrase entered public use in the context of defence policy.
It was used to reassure the public that the Nice treaty would not compel Ireland to take part in EU military adventures overseas.
Since the Government naturally commands a majority in the Dáil, the UN authority is the point at issue and it is this test that the legislation before the Dáil this week proposes to remove.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin argues that the “world has changed” and that Irish policy must change to reflect that. The stalemate on the UN Security Council means that it has not authorised a new peacekeeping mission since 2014 and there is no sign of that changing anytime soon.
Effectively, the Government argues, the triple lock affords a veto to the members of the council on any Irish peacekeeping deployment overseas.
This is best illustrated by the expiration of the mandate for the Unifil mission in Lebanon , where Irish troops have served since the early 1980s, later this year. This means that Irish involvement in Lebanon will cease under the current rules.
Campaigners opposed to its removal say that a UN General Assembly vote could replace a security council resolution, but in practice this has never happened.
[ Triple lock neutrality row fuels fractious Dáil exchanges Opens in new window ]
It has quite a bit to say on the issue. It says that the triple lock is central to Irish neutrality and that removing it will fundamentally alter the nature of a policy that has been a foundation for Irish foreign policy and which has the overwhelming backing of the public.
It says that the public is opposed to the move (which polls bear out) and that the Government should put the question to the public in a referendum. It warns that Irish troops could be used for all sorts of foreign military adventures.
[ Government may face battle to remove triple lock as voters align with Opposition Opens in new window ]
Well, Martin previously thought so – he said it was “at the core of our neutrality”, something of which pro-neutrality campaigners are fond of reminding him. However, it is true that in the past neutrality has tended to mean whatever the government of the day said it meant.
And one of the ironies of the current argument is that the people who previously said that the triple lock was central to neutrality now say it’s not, and the people who previously said it was meaningless for our neutrality now say it is essential.
The truth is that the world will not take a great deal of notice what Ireland does, though the Government would be able to point at the move to its EU partners, who believe that Ireland is a complete freeloader on defence.
Well, the Government has a majority for sure. There is some unease about it on the Fianna Fáil benches, and TDs who might want to undermine Martin have an opportunity to do so, though whether they are prepared to lose the whip is doubtful.
Much to the Opposition’s displease, there will be only 3½ hours for debate on Wednesday. If passed, the Bill will then move to committee stage. If the Taoiseach gets his way, it will pass through the Oireachtas before Christmas.

title: Gardaí arrest two men and seize drugs worth €1.7m in Dublin city raid
description: Move against organised gang in north of Dublin city follows ‘intelligence-led operation’ by Revenue and Garda units
content:
Two men have been arrested and drugs with a street value of €1.7 million have been seized following a Garda raid on a property in Dublin targeting an organised drugs gang.
The men, in their 30s and 50s, were arrested and detained under drugs trafficking legislation.
The raid in the north of Dublin city was carried out following an “intelligence-led operation” by the Revenue Commissioners , the Garda national drugs and organised crime bureau (GNDOCB), and a divisional drugs unit.
In the property, gardaí found vacuum-sealed foil packages containing 17.35kg of drugs suspected to be cocaine with a street value of about €1.7 million.
The substances will be sent to Forensic Science Ireland for testing, the results of which will inform any prosecutions.
The men are being detained in a Garda station in Dublin under the provisions of Section 2 of Criminal Justice (Drug Trafficking) Act 1996.

title: Murder accused to watch trial by video-link after judge notices ‘humming noises’
description: Seth Whelan (36) has been charged with murdering his father, Michael Whelan (64), at their home in Dublin 8
content:
A man on trial for the alleged murder of his father will watch the proceedings by video-link after a judge noticed the accused was “rocking” and making “humming noises” that might have made it difficult for the jury to listen to witnesses giving evidence.
Seth Whelan (36) responded, “I don’t know”, when arraigned on a charge last week of murdering his father, Michael Whelan (64), at the home they shared in Herberton Park, Rialto, Dublin 8 . His barrister entered a plea of not guilty on Whelan’s behalf.
