Prosecution barrister Anne-Marie Lawlor has previously told the jury of six men and six women that gardaí found Michael Whelan’s body on the kitchen floor of the flat on February 27th, 2024. He had died from blunt force trauma to the head about one week before his body was discovered.
On Tuesday, Judge Caroline Biggs told the jury that it had become obvious that noises were coming from the accused man that might make it difficult for them to hear what witnesses and barristers were saying.
After sending the jury away for a time, Judge Biggs apologised for the delay but said time was needed to figure out how best to deal with the issue. She told the jury there will be no evidence in the trial that Whelan has a mental disorder and therefore insanity or diminished responsibility do not arise.
However, she said there was a reference to Whelan being autistic and some of his behaviours in court, including making humming noises and rocking in his seat, may be related to sensory or communication issues.
She said it is Whelan’s express wish to attend the rest of the trial by video-link. She said he will still be taking part in the trial process but will not be physically in the courtroom. Sending the jury home until Wednesday, she said it will take time to iron out the logistics to put the video-link in place.

title: Alex Nankivell clear on Ireland ambitions as he sticks with Munster to 2029
description: New Zealander will qualify to play for Ireland in two years’ time
content:
A two-year contract extension for Munster centre Alex Nankivell will add real substance to his desire to play for Ireland when he qualifies in two years, the 29-year-old has said, but in the interim, his focus is on achieving success with the province.
Nankivell, who joined Munster in 2023 from the Chiefs, where he also played under Clayton McMillan , signed a new contract this week that will keep him in Limerick until the summer of 2029, by which time he will have qualified to play for Ireland.
“International rugby is still the pinnacle for me,” he said. “Obviously, the opportunity to represent New Zealand has gone on since leaving and coming over here. I never thought I’d be here this long and I guess the prospect of becoming Irish-qualified is exciting because it gives me an opportunity to try and get selected to play international rugby.
“Now, that’s a long way away, and I don’t really get too far ahead of myself, but yeah, it’s a really exciting prospect to try and challenge to play international rugby, because that was a dream of mine as a young fella.
“But, first and foremost, I’m here at Munster and I want to do well for them and contribute as much as I can, both on and off the field.”
Nankivell, who played five times for the Maoris and four games for the All Blacks XV, has made 58 appearances for Munster and reckons they are going places under McMillan.
“I’m really excited about it to be honest. Obviously, with the new coaching group coming in, Clayton coming in, I’ve got huge faith in him having been coached under him in New Zealand. I know what he’s about, and being here at Munster, he suits it to a T.
“I’m really optimistic about the growth that we can have going into the future, [and] that we’ve already had, just over this past pre-season. We’ve got an awesome group of lads who are extremely passionate about this club and we’ve got an awesome province behind us, and to me there’s no reason why we can’t continue to grow and continue to challenge.”
He has plenty of experience of Irish derbies since his arrival in Munster, and is set for another this weekend as they take on Leinster at the Aviva Stadium on Saturday.
“Obviously, I’m not from Ireland, but seeing what it means to the lads here at Munster, and obviously the rivalry has been going on for years and I guess it stays strong as things have been going so well in the recent past.
“We’ve probably got a bit of a chip on our shoulder that we want to compete, and obviously that rivalry is strong, the lads are always excited to face the [other] provinces. Whatever province we face, it’s always a big game because you want tobeat them and get bragging rights.
“There’s something about the Leinster game. Going up there, we always get great support. I don’t know where it starts, but it’s just always intense.”
Munster’s biggest concern ahead Saturday’s clash is at loosehead, with Michael Milne battling his way back from an ankle injury while Jeremy Loughman is in a race against time after suffering a knee injury in the Champions Cup win over Racing 92 last weekend.
Forwards coach Jimmy Duffy said Lee Barron (ankle), Shane Daly (groin), Edwin Edogbo (shoulder) and Will Harrison (knee) are all increasing their training load, with a decision on their availability to be made later this week.
“They’re going through their rehab kind of stuff, and hopefully everybody that’s on that list is available for selection on Saturday,” said Duffy.
The former Connacht player and coach, who joined Munster from Ulster, has more experience than most of what’s involved in Irish derbies, and he’s under no illusions as to the challenge awaiting them at the Aviva.
“We’re up against the defending champions and an international scrum that’s probably coming again on the weekend,” he said.
“It all [goes] hand-in-hand. If you’re stable in your setpiece, then it makes a huge difference. We’re very aware of how strong Leinster are in that department; scrum and lineout.
“We’ll have to be completely on the money for the weekend to be in the fight.”

title: ‘No apology can bring our baby back’: Parents of baby who died two days after birth settle action
description: HSE admitted breach in its duty of care, but denied it caused the death of the baby
content:
A couple have settled a High Court action against the HSE over the death of their son just two days after his birth at Cork University Maternity Hospital ( CUMH ).
Baby George Duggan, from Sweeney’s Hill, Rathpeacon, Co Cork , died in the arms of his parents, John and Aine Duggan, on December 21st, 2022.
On Tuesday, his parents ended a four-year legal battle as they attended the Four Courts for a ruling on the settlement of their case over the death of their firstborn.
The HSE has admitted a breach in its duty of care in the case, but denied it caused the death of the baby.
“We had so many hopes and dreams for George and for our lives with him in it. We never got to watch him grow, see his smile or hear his little laugh. We carry the grief of losing George every day along with the sadness of all the moments and milestones that should have been his,” Aine Duggan said in a statement outside court.
“We hope that by continuing to speak about George and honour his life, our experience might help protect other families from experiencing this heartbreak. George will always be loved, always be remembered and always be our little boy. No apology can ever put right what happened, or bring our baby George back.”
In court, Patrick Treacy, counsel for the Duggans, instructed by Cian O’Carroll Solicitors, said the core of the case was the failure to review and assess the mother during an 11-day window, and the obstetric management of mother and baby during that period up to December 19th, 2022.
It was their case that if there had been proper and continual assessment after the December 8th review and before December 19th, when Duggan’s waters broke, a Caesarean section would have been performed, George would have been better placed and would have survived.
He said George was delivered by emergency Caesarean section on December 19th at 29 weeks and three days, but he said tragically the baby suffered bruising and subgaleal haemorrhage.
[ Boy (8) settles action over circumstances of birth at Cork hospital for €7.5m Opens in new window ]
Counsel read a letter signed by the clinical director of CUMH Ireland South Women & Infants Directorate, Dr Maireád O’Riordan, which said the hospital offered “heartfelt sympathies and deepest condolences to you on the loss of your baby George”.
It added: “We do not underestimate how traumatic this has been for you and your family, but please be assured the maternity practices within the hospital are continuously reviewed and strengthened with the ongoing commitment to ensuring the safety and wellbeing of all patients in our care.”
In the proceedings, it was claimed that there was an alleged failure to deliver the baby by expedited Caesarean section prior to the rupture of the membranes on December 19th, 2022.
It was further claimed that, had proper investigation or surveillance been carried out in an appropriate or timely manner following the December 8th review, the mother’s worsening placental function would have been identified, and she would have been admitted to hospital.
The HSE has admitted it breached its duty of care in not performing more frequent foetal monitoring following the December 8th review. However, the HSE denied it caused the death of the baby.
Noting the settlement and the division of the statutory €35,000 mental distress payment, Judge Paul Coffey conveyed his deepest sympathy to the Duggans.
[ Hospital apologises to woman who had to have a mastectomy when seven months pregnant Opens in new window ]
Outside court, Aine Duggan said their lives changed forever when they lost George.
“On Christmas Eve, a day usually associated with magic and joy, we said our final goodbyes to George and buried him in his little white coffin. It was a day filled with the deepest grief,” she said.
She said the last four years “have been incredibly painful” and that having “to revisit the worst time of our lives through this legal process has added another layer to that pain”.
She added: “His little brother Charlie will grow up without his big brother and we will never get to watch them play together or see their bond develop.”
Duggan disclosed that she had private care, believing it would give the best possible care for herself and her baby.
Duggan said she believed more frequent monitoring could have saved George’s life.
Referring to a lack of foetal movements, she said she specifically asked whether she should be worried.
“I believed my concerns were being taken seriously when we were reassured we had nothing to worry about. Parents should be listened to, and a mother’s instinct should never be dismissed.
“If there is one thing we want other mothers to take from our experience, it is to trust their instincts and never be afraid to speak up and keep asking questions,” she said.

title: Chris Bryant had ‘no other decision’ but to halt Drumcree march, court told
description: PSNI lawyers refute assertions police were considering the ‘feelings’ of the Provisional IRA in security assessments
content:
Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant could have taken “no other decision” than to halt the Drumcree march in Portadown, Co Armagh, the High Court in Belfast has heard.
Legal representatives of the PSNI also pushed back against assertions that police were substantively considering the “feelings of the PIRA [Provisional IRA ]” in security assessments relating to the parade’s ability to proceed.
Members of the Orange Order are seeking a judicial review after Bryant halted the march from going along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road amid large-scale protests by residents opposed to the procession. His decision on October 9th followed a two-week stand-off.
The application for judicial review against that decision is being heard by Judge David Scoffield.
It includes a challenge to the decision by PSNI Chief Constable Jon Boutcher to ask Bryant to review the determination made by the Parades Commission , which had given the go-ahead for the parade.
Barrister Phillip McAteer outlined discussions Bryant engaged in with party leaders over the course of the stand-off, as well as with members of the Portadown District of the Orange Order and the Garvaghy Road residents, which the barrister maintained were “an attempt to facilitate the procession and reach agreement”.
It was said in the course of those talks there was no resolution that was acceptable to the Orangemen that did not involve going down the Garvaghy Road, and none to the residents that involved the Orange Order doing so, leading the talks to end unsuccessfully.
[ PSNI feared gun use by dissident republicans if parade went down Garvaghy Road, court told Opens in new window ]
McAteer highlighted that the Secretary of State said at this stage that his door was still open and it was only when he received updated information of the security situation changing that he intervened.
He outlined the Secretary of State’s position by October 9th that the Parades Commission determination “could no longer be given effect, but it was properly reached on the basis of information before the commission at that time”.
“Which reflects something which was important to the Orange Order, which was the importance of the fact that their determination had been lawfully reached in the first place, a matter which has been confirmed by the court of appeal,” McAteer said.
“So that preserved that position, but also reflected the reality of the situation whereby the determination couldn’t now be given effect.”
Later, arguing the Secretary of State could not have amended the ruling to allow the march to proceed in a different form, McAteer said it was “repeated over and over and over” that the march for the Orange Order “was only about marching the Garvaghy Road”, which the residents were “blatantly opposed to”.
“No other decision by the Secretary of State would have achieved the aims, which was to end that stand-off and therefore mitigate all of those risks and avoid public disorder, crime, and ensure an appropriate balancing of the convention rights,” he said.
On Monday, Richard McConkey, who represents a member of the Orange Order, referred to a senior officer having access to nine intelligence risk assessments and said a police record from the officer included the phrase “the feelings of the PIRA”.
Barrister for the PSNI, Peter Coll, said there were “interests outside the confines of this court” in relation to that line and highlighted there were “other mechanisms” to put concerns around it to the Chief Constable.
[ DUP accuses Bryant of ‘disgraceful appeasement’ on Garvaghy Road march Opens in new window ]
He said it had been suggested that “a commander had been taking account of and working with the feelings of PIRA”, when the log was a description of intelligence information.
He said: “What he’s saying there is: ‘I’ve seen intelligence documents, I’m mindful of their contents’, and then he breaks down what the contents are, and the contents include, as he phrases it, ‘the feelings of the PIRA’, and he’s simply stating that as a fact.”
Coll agreed with the judge’s characterisation of the police position that it is “unfair to read that as: ‘We don’t want to hurt the feelings of the PIRA’”.
A judgment is to be given next week. – PA

title: State’s population surges by almost 800,000 in a decade
description: Net inward migration responsible for two-thirds of increase, official figures show
content:
The State’s population has risen by almost 800,000 in the last decade, with two-thirds of the increase coming from net inward migration.
Figures indicate that the Republic’s population grew by 786,000 or 16.6 per cent between 2016 and 2026 to stand at 5.5 million.
This was the third highest increase in the European Union behind Malta and Luxembourg. It compares to an overall EU population increase of less than 2 per cent.
The Central Statistics Office said the Republic’s population growth was driven by positive net migration and by a natural increase as a result of more births than deaths.
Net migration – the difference between the number of people moving to and from the State – totalled 511,000 since 2016, which accounted for 65 per cent of the overall increase in population here.
“Over the last 10 years, Ireland has consistently recorded positive net migration,” the CSO said.
“However, net migration in 2026 fell by 19.4 per cent (to 48,100) compared with the previous year. Net migration peaked at 79,300 in 2024,” it said.
The agency’s latest Measuring Ireland’s Progress report noted that over the last 10 years the natural increase in the population (births minus deaths) has almost halved, from 35,600 in 2016 to 18,800 in 2026.
During the period, the proportion of the population aged 45 and over rose from 37.1 per cent to 42.2 per cent, whereas the proportion aged under 45 fell from 62.9 per cent to 57.8 per cent.
In 2025, Ireland also had the highest young-age dependency ratio in the EU at 28.1 per cent. This ratio measures the number of children aged under 15 years as a proportion of the “working-age population” aged 15-64.
The State also had the second lowest old-age dependency ratio (the number of people aged 65 or over as a proportion of those aged 15-64) in the EU at 23.8 per cent.
With households in the grip of another inflationary surge, the CSO’s report also noted Ireland had the second-highest price level for consumer goods and services in the EU in 2025 at 36.2 per cent above the EU average, while Denmark had the highest at 39.7 per cent above average.
The figures also indicated that the State’s national debt has fallen to its lowest level since the banking crisis began in 2008.
Total debt fell to just under €210 billion last year, equating to 63 per cent of modified gross national income (GNI*), the agency’s bespoke measure of national income here.
In the wake of the banking bailouts post-2008, Ireland’s debt as a percentage of GNI* soared to 166 per cent.
The State’s improved debt picture since then stands in stark contrast to the trend internationally, with debt crises engulfing several countries, most notably France , the United States and the United Kingdom .
France’s debt – at €3.6 trillion – is currently 120 per cent of the country’s income. The worsening trajectory of its annual fiscal deficit has triggered a surge in French bond yields, hiking up the annual cost of servicing its debt.
Ireland’s debt-to-GDP ratio has been helped more by the rise in national income rather than a reduction in the debt itself.
The State’s GDP has doubled to €602.4 billion since 2015 on the back of huge multinational-led investment.
As a percentage of GDP, Ireland’s debt was 32.9 per cent last year, the fifth-lowest government debt-to-GDP ratio in the EU.
However, it still equated to €37,988 for every person in the State, which is large by international standards.
CSO’s figures also indicated that Ireland recorded the highest annual GDP growth rate within the EU, at 8 per cent.
This represented a reversal from 2023, when Ireland experienced the lowest GDP growth rate in the EU, at -3.3 per cent.

title: Two gardaí injured after crash involving teenagers in stolen car
description: Three teenage males were arrested following the chase
content:
Two gardaí were injured after their patrol car was involved in a crash with a car carrying three teenagers in south Dublin early on Tuesday morning.
Three teenage males were arrested after the car, which was reported stolen, was stopped following a Garda operation.
Gardaí on a routine patrol shortly before 1am on Tuesday on the Nangor Road near Clondalkin spotted a vehicle which had been reported stolen.
The vehicle ran from the squad car before a “managed containment operation” was initiated by the Garda and the car was brought to a stop on Cruagh Road in Rathfarnham.
It is understood the chase continued for a “significant period” across the west of the city through Ballyfermot, Lucan and along the M50.
Three teenagers, two of whom under 18, were arrested by gardaí at the scene.
The adult teenager, who gardaí believe was driving the car, is detained under Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act at a Garda station in south Dublin.
The two teenage boys were released pending further inquiries.
A Garda squad car was hit during the chase and two gardaí were brought to hospital. They have since been discharged.
The vehicle is undergoing forensic and technical examinations.
Niall Hodgins, the president of the Garda Representative Association, said the thoughts of the association are with the two gardaí injured in the crash.

title: ‘It is the most basic duty of a solicitor to represent a client in custody’, says judge
description: Judge Martin Nolan made comments in the context of a number of defendants appearing without a solicitor due to the legal aid dispute
content:
A judge has said he finds it astounding that solicitors are not attending court to represent clients who are in custody as part of the legal aid dispute.
Judge Martin Nolan made his comments in the context of a number of defendants appearing without a solicitor before Dublin Circuit Criminal Court sittings.
In the dozens of cases affected, the court was informed by barristers for the prosecution or the defence that solicitors who were previously “on record” as acting for the accused were not in attendance because of the ongoing dispute.
On Monday solicitors escalated their protest with Justice Minister Jim O’Callaghan over changes to how they are paid under the legal aid scheme by withdrawing most services in court. Since July solicitors had withdrawn their services in “bail cases”, – cases where defendants were out on bail.
A number of cases before Judge Nolan on Tuesday morning involved defendants who were in custody and the judge repeatedly criticised solicitors who were on record but were not in attendance. He said that there is a statutory procedure set out whereby if “people want to come off record they must come to court”.
“I am surprised and taken aback that solicitors adopt this approach of leaving their clients in custody unrepresented. It is the most basic duty of a solicitor to represent a client in custody.
“For solicitors to make a unilateral decision not to represent their clients in custody is ... astounding. If solicitors think their dispute with the (Justice) department is more important than representing their clients in custody ... I find it hard that solicitors would adopt this position,” he said. His comments came in the context of a man facing sentence for theft.
In another case, a defendant appeared via video-link from custody. Judge Nolan said that the solicitor on record “has refused to come to court” and “is failing in her obligation to her client”.
“If you are on record, you must act for your client. The courts have been very very flexible in relation to non custodial cases. It seems solicitors have lost sight of their duty to their clients who are in custody,” he said.
Defending counsel Oisin Clarke BL said that the matter could not progress in any case because the accused needed a psychiatric assessment. The defendant spoke directly to Judge Nolan and said he didn’t need a psychiatric report and that he has been in custody since February and it was “literally breaking” him.
Judge Nolan put the case back into the list for mention next month and asked Mr Clarke to speak to the solicitor.
“This man needs help. He is in custody. He needs someone to talk to him,” Judge Nolan said.
There were 16 defendants up for sentence before Judge Nolan, ten of whom were “custody cases” involving serious violent or drug dealing offending. Instructing solicitors were in attendance for five of these and the sentence hearing went ahead.
There was no solicitor in attendance for the five remaining “custody cases” and the six “bail cases”. These cases were all adjourned for sentence to dates in mid to late November. One of these involved a defendant on bail awaiting sentence having pleaded guilty last June to the sexual assault of a female in Dublin in 2023.
Most of the 32 other defendants up before Judge Nolan for mention or for arraignment – where defendants can either enter a guilty plea or elect to take a trial – appeared without an attending solicitor and were adjourned to future dates.

title: Narrow Water bridge components arrive by barge from Belgium
description: Delivery of part of deck and a pylon for project linking Louth and Down a ‘major milestone’, says Taoiseach
content:
Key parts of the Narrow Water bridge that will link counties Louth and Down next year have arrived in Warrenpoint harbour following a five-day voyage from Belgium .
Welcoming the arrival of the barge, named Caroline , Taoiseach Micheál Martin said it marks “a major milestone” in the construction of a bridge “that will do far more than connect two shores”.
A major part of the deck of the bridge, plus a pylon, were transported by the barge, accompanied by the Multratug 29 tugboat, which left Belgium on October 15th, crossing the North Sea.
A second barge, the Karel Victor, carrying the remaining section of the bridge’s fixed span, left Belgium on Sunday and will take seven days or so to arrive, subject to weather and sea conditions.
Once open late next year, the bridge, which is funded by the Government’s Shared Island programme, will link the Cooley peninsula and the Mournes. It is expected to unlock major economic opportunities.
“Seeing its structures now making their way across the water is a reminder that this long-held vision is fast becoming a reality,” said Martin, who described Narrow Water as “a landmark project” for the Shared Island initiative.
When it is completed, the 195m, two-span, cable-stayed bridge will connect Cornamucklagh, near Omeath in Co Louth, with Narrow Water, near Warrenpoint in Co Down. It will carry vehicles, cyclists and pedestrians.
The installation of the two-part fixed span will be completed within eight to 12 weeks. The shorter northern span of the bridge will be able to open, allowing marine traffic to continue using the Newry river.
Today is a significant milestone in the construction of the Narrow Water Bridge, as major steel components arrive at Carlingford Lough for assembly on site. This project is a tangible symbol of our vision and commitment to deepening connections across this island. pic.twitter.com/ySAGcXbIxE

title: ‘Fanciful’ to assume funds from new dereliction tax will reach local authorities, DCC chief says
description: Richard Shakespeare said local authorities are ‘unhappy’ with the replacement of the levy
content:
The planned replacement of the derelict sites levy has been criticised by Dublin City Council chief executive Richard Shakespeare, who said it would be “fanciful” to assume funds generated by a new tax will be directed to local authorities.
Speaking at the reopening of St Patrick’s Tower in the Liberties as an event and exhibition space, Shakespeare said a €1 million refurbishment of the structure was funded through derelict site levies collected in Dublin 8 .
“Things like this will no longer happen, because the derelict site tax will now go straight to the exchequer,” Shakespeare said.
He noted that local authorities had been able to reinvest income from the levy in to the areas it was generated in.
“Now, that ability will be gone with the derelict site tax,” he said.
Asked if he was unhappy with the Government ’s decision to replace the levy, he said: “You’re never happy when you lose the opportunity to work on good projects like this.”
He said the local government “sector” is unhappy with the move and it would be “fanciful to assume” revenue collected from the incoming tax “will find its way to Dublin City Council or any local authority”.
Accepting long-standing “issues around collection” of the levy, Shakespeare said charges on the properties meant the levies were collected once they were sold or once the issue reached the courts.
Local authorities collected more than €2.9 million last year in levies, with Dublin City Council collecting €1.3 million of this, according to figures published by the Department of Housing earlier this month.
However, more than €35.6 million in levies remained outstanding by the end of the year. Dublin City Council was owed some €9.3 million of that total.
Shakespeare said the council had worked hard to remove properties from the register and tackle dereliction by encouraging owners to bring them back into use.
“I don’t know whether this will be the same in terms of the derelict site tax,” he said, adding that he believed there “won’t be a material link in terms of cause and effect”.
Once the 7 per cent tax comes into effect, local authorities will remain responsible for identifying derelict properties, while Revenue will be in charge of collecting taxes due.
First payments are not expected to be made until June 2028 after preliminary registers of derelict properties are published by councils next September. Any derelict site levies outstanding once the new tax comes in to effect will remain the responsibility of local authorities to collect.
The refurbishment of St Patrick’s Tower, which had been unused since 1860, came at a cost of about €1 million and was fully funded by Dublin City Council.
Noting that the structure, once a windmill, was built in 1757, Fiach Mac Conghail, chief executive of Dublin’s Digital Hub , said conservation works accounted for much of the cost.
Mac Conghail said the Digital Hub was “very proud” to bring the “much-needed” venue back into use.
Lord Mayor of Dublin, Daryl Barron, commended Shakespeare and his team for “the vision to support such a worthy endeavour”.
“St Patrick’s Tower is a wonderful example of how historic buildings can be given new purpose and become an active part of the city once again,” he told attendees.
The venue, which can accommodate up to 50 people, will host its first official event in November as part of the art and technology-themed Beta Festival.

title: Woman describes alleged assault by Russell Brand as ‘frenzied’ and ‘violent’
description: Former comedian faces charges of rape, indecent assault and sexual assault, which he denies
content:
Former comedian and actor Russell Brand laughed after pinning a woman against a wall and kissing her “sloppily” at a radio station, a court has heard.
Brand, now 51, is accused of sexually assaulting the woman in the mid-2000s after encountering her at the Choice FM studios in central London.
She told Southwark Crown Court on Tuesday that Brand appeared to find it funny after grabbing her breasts and forcefully kissing her.
She told jurors that three men and a woman with Brand witnessed the incident and “did nothing”, other than to laugh afterwards to “break the silence”.
When faced with questions about her account, the woman said: “This was a situation I did not want to be in.
“I wanted it to go away. I don’t gain a single thing by saying ‘Russell Brand did that to me’.
Describing the alleged assault, she said Brand was a “perfect stranger” to her and she recalled him saying “aye, aye” before grabbing her face.
She said: “He was kissing me and he was pushing his body against me.
“It was hard, I would say it was sloppy.
“He was kissing me all down my neck. His hands at that time were all over me.
“He touched my bum, touched my breasts, hands on my waist, his other hands were pinning me so his body was pressed up against me.”
She added: “It was rough, it was very, very rough. It was hard, I would say that his whole body was pressed against me, the kisses were hard and sloppy, going down my neck.
“The reason I used the word frenzied is because it was just ... violent.
“It was hard and he just wasn’t stopping.”
She told the court she was “stunned” and “in a haze”, she said she pushed Brand away and told him to “f*** off”, and added: “He kind of stumbled back, then it was just still.”
She said: “I remember he made like a sound, that was like funny – ha ha – like that.”
She recalled a man who “started laughing, almost like it was to break the tension”.
She told the court she looked to a woman who witnessed the assault, but she “didn’t say anything”.
She said the three men also did nothing to intervene.
Brand denies three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of indecent assault.
Jurors have heard he says sexual encounters were consensual and some of his interactions with women have been “reimagined” in recent years.
Among the allegations, he is accused of raping a woman in a hotel room in 1999 and forcing an MTV worker into a sex act in a Soho bar.
A Channel 4 worker also told the court that she was “repulsed” after she was forced to massage Brand and the comedian thrust his head into her lap.
The woman said members of Brand’s entourage shrugged and laughed when he carried out the sexual assault during a recording for a Channel 4 project in 2009.
She told Southwark Crown Court that Brand had been “really lovely” at the start of the recording session, but he grew annoyed as the day wore on.
His associates Jack Bayles and Gareth Roy said Brand would only continue if she gave him a massage, she told the court.
It became “clear that he was quite unhappy about things” and the “atmosphere changed” in the studio, she told the jury.
“They said Russell won’t carry on ... unless you give him a massage”.
Asked how she responded, she said: “I didn’t want to give him a massage, I actually laughed.
“I thought they were joking because I didn’t expect somebody to say that.
“Then I saw by their faces that they weren’t joking.”
The woman said Brand “leaned into my lap – my groin area”, and she told the court: “I could feel his breath against me.”
She said she looked to Bayles and Roy, “hoping someone was going to help me”, but she added: “They just, arms up, as if to say: ‘Come on.’ They were shrugging and gesticulating, to say: ‘Are you going to do it?’”
The woman said she thought: “Oh my god, I have got to do this”, and she placed her fingers on Brand’s shoulders.
She added: “I was so repulsed by the situation and my automatic reaction was: ‘Urgh, you’re so bony.’”
The woman said that Bayles and Roy “laughed”, but then she added in a quieter voice: “Russell didn’t laugh.”
She said Brand made a series of offensive comments, suggesting that he and Roy had been “wanting to know: is it a girl or a boy?”
The woman said Brand then walked to the other side of the room and started to make a joke about a calculator drinking from a glass of water.
“It was just a bit of a charade, just a change of tune, and then he said: ‘Right, are we going to get on with this ... or not?’” she told the court.
The woman said she reported the incident the following day to her line manager at Channel 4, and she believes it was passed on to the head of her department.
Earlier, another woman gave evidence that Brand sexually assaulted her in a radio station corridor, pressing her against a wall and planting “sloppy” kisses.
She tearfully told the court that she had nothing to gain from giving evidence against Brand, and recalls pleading with people with Brand to intervene but getting no help.
“There was a culture of fear,” she said, recalling the atmosphere at the time as “people-pleasing”.
“Russell Brand was an A-lister star, it was Big Brother, people were watching it, we all watched it.”
She also criticised the workplace “banter” from the 2000s, telling the court: “Women were rated by colleagues on what we were wearing, how we looked.
“It wasn’t an environment where management were coming to talk to us about workplace behaviour, that didn’t exist.”
She added that if she had reported the incident to a manager, she thought the response would have been: “Oh, you’re lucky.”
Brand denies three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one allegation of indecent assault.

title: Former rugby player Brendan Mullin represents himself in court due to ‘strike situation’
description: The 62-year-old is charged with theft of a bottle of perfume worth €158 from Brown Thomas on Grafton Street last May
content:
Former rugby international Brendan Mullin represented himself before a judge of Dublin District Court on Tuesday at a short hearing of the shoplifting case against him.
Mullin, of Albert Lodge, Stillorgan Road, Donnybrook, Dublin 4, has been charged with the theft last May of a bottle of Hermès perfume worth €158 from Brown Thomas department store on Grafton Street.
The 62-year-old won 55 caps for Ireland between 1984 and 1995 before going on to work in financial services.
He told Judge Treasa Kelly he wishes to have the case against him heard by a District Court judge, choosing that option over the alternative of going before a jury of the Circuit Court , which has wider sentencing powers.
Mullin stepped forward from the public gallery to represent himself when his case was called, saying his solicitor, John O’Doherty, was not present because of the “strike situation”.
The remand hearing lasted no more than three minutes.
After Mullin indicated his preference for a District Court trial, Kelly directed him to attend the court before another judge on November 2nd to set a hearing date. The case was likely to be taken in the new year, the court heard.
Mullin asked to be excused from that hearing, saying this was his fourth appearance before the court. However, Kelly said he was required to attend and said the judge would have the option of issuing a bench warrant if he did not.
The judge noted “full disclosure” of statements in the case after solicitor for the Director of Prosecutions Prosecutions (DPP) Emma Croydon said a number of statements were sent to O’Doherty on October 16th.
However, a further statement had been presented to the DPP on October 19th, the eve of the hearing on Tuesday.
The judge said the new statement could be handed to Mullin in court but he asked that it be sent to O’Doherty. Kelly directed that the statement be sent to Mullin’s solicitor by email.

title: Opposition, lawyers condemn O’Callaghan over rape trials ‘deliberately affected’ remark
description: Minister’s comments on solicitors withdrawing services in legal aid dispute ‘deliberately provocative’ and an ‘absolute disgrace’
content:
A government backbencher has criticised comments by Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan relating to rape trials as “both incorrect and deeply unfair”.
Fine Gael TD for Dún Laoghaire Barry Ward made the comments after opposition parties and lawyers have rounded on Jim O’Callaghan following a suggestion that lawyers were deliberately affecting rape trials with a withdrawal of services in a long-running battle over reform of criminal legal aid.
Ward, who is also a practicing criminal barrister, said the comment “is both incorrect and deeply unfair to the solicitors concerned”.
He said that all the trials listed in the Central Criminal Court yesterday were rape cases.
“Either the minister doesn’t understand how the trial list works or he deliberately and disingenously sought to blame his opponnents on the legal aid issue for something that was not of their doing”.
The Irish Council for Civil Liberties said the comments “risk further embedding a serious impasse”.
O’Callaghan dropped a per-appearance fee system in the District Court in favour of a flat fee approach over the summer, leading to a withdrawal of services by many solicitors.
The Law Society issued a statement on Tuesday calling on O’Callaghan to “meet and try to resolve this escalating dispute, which now affects every level of our criminal courts: the District Court, the Circuit Court and the Central Criminal Court.
The minister wrote to the Law Society, which represents solicitors, on Tuesday morning indicating that he was open to engaging further and saying he had instructed officials to organise a meeting in the coming days.
Fine Gael TD James Geoghegan, also a barrister and a constituency colleague of O’Callaghan’s in Dublin Bay South, said on Tuesday that the “war of words needs to end”.
He said the focus should move towards tweaking the reforms as outstanding issues have “narrowed”, he said, warning that the people who have the most to lose from the impasee are victims of crime and ordinary citizens.
Speaking on the Leinster House plinth on Tuesday, Sinn Féin justice spokesman and chair of the Oireachtas justice committee Matt Carthy said O’Callaghan was providing a “textbook example as to how not to deal with a dispute”.
O’Callaghan’s comments were “deliberately provocative”, he claimed.
“We’re coming to the stage where we will see people who should be in prison at large,” he said, adding that others would have strong cases to have their convictions overturned due to the dispute.
Social Democrats justice spokesman Gary Gannon said the Minister’s statement was an “absolute disgrace”.
“I think it’s an absolute shame that the Minister chose to pursue that language,” he said.
Meanwhile, O’Callaghan’s statement was described as “false” and “misleading” by one solicitor.
Criminal defence solicitor Eoghan O’Sullivan, a partner at Powderly Solicitors, insisted “there was no deliberate targeting” of rape cases.
“It is beneath the dignity of the office of the Minister for Justice to try to accuse criminal defence solicitors of such a deliberate act,” he said.
“His claim is not only risible but wholly inaccurate.
“This is a full withdrawal of services. There has been no deliberate targeting of rape cases.”
Asked about O’Sullivan’s comments, a spokeswoman for O’Callaghan said he “looks forward to addressing the Joint Oireachtas Committee this afternoon.”
In a statement, the Irish Council for Civil Liberties called on O’Callaghan to engage in meaningful talks with solicitors to identify a lasting resolution.
It said it “note[s] the understandable anger among solicitors after he accused them ahead of his Oireachtas Justice Committee appearance today of deliberately targeting rape cases in their dispute. Such comments risk further embedding a serious impasse, when what is urgently required is constructive engagement and a resolution.”
Taoiseach Micheál Martin said on Tuesday that he will not intervene in the deepening dispute.
Speaking on his way into Cabinet, Martin also said O’Callaghan had an obligation to “say it as he sees it”.
“The Minister will deal with this, and I won’t be intervening in the situation at all,” Martin said.
The Taoiseach said, “I support the Minister in terms of what he’s endeavouring to do, in terms of reform of our courts, and I would share his regret [that] what appeared to be a significant number of rape cases were not heard.”
[ Judge ‘coerced’ into adjourning six rape and sexual offences trials as solicitors withdraw Opens in new window ]
He denied O’Callaghan had escalated the situation with his comments, which the Minister initially made to RTÉ on Monday evening and is expected to repeat in an appearance at the Oireachtas justice committee on Tuesday.
“I don’t think he’s putting fuel on the flames,” the Taoiseach said. “I don’t think the action yesterday is necessary, quite frankly. The Minister has an obligation to uphold the law, say it as he sees it.”
Martin said there had been “significant participation” in criminal cases in the District Courts “across the length and breadth of the country” despite the withdrawal of services.
Martin added that O’Callaghan had already changed some aspects of the reforms and was open to further engagement with solicitors.
Asked about a report in The Irish Times on Tuesday detailing the lack of a special care place for a 14-year-old girl who is being sexually exploited by a group of men, Martin said he did not have the details of the case but it was “a very serious situation, obviously”.
[ No special care place available for girl (14) being sexually exploited by group of men Opens in new window ]
He said he would speak to Ministers, including O’Callaghan, Minister for Children Norma Foley and Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers, who will receive written details of the case following an instruction by Judge John Jordan.

title: Application to unseal Bessborough mother and baby home burial records to be made
description: Location of more than 800 children and 19 women who spent time in the institution remains unknown
content:
The release of records related to burials at the Bessborough mother and baby home moved a step closer on Tuesday.
Minister for Children Norma Foley has secured Government approval to make a High Court application to unseal technical archaeological reports at the former institution. The application will be made to search for and publish technical documents related to burials at the site.
Campaigners trying to stop the building of an apartment development at the Cork city site have welcomed the news. The burial places of more than 800 children and 19 women who spent time in the institution remain unknown.
In a written update provided to survivors and advocates on Tuesday, Foley said: “No evidence or document given to the Commission of Investigation into Mother and Baby Homes can be published by the minister or any other party, unless otherwise directed by a court.”
Foley said she sought Cabinet support to make a High Court application because of the “importance and sensitivity of the issue ... to so many families, and to help support transparency”.
The release of witness evidence given to the commission will not be sought as part of the application.
Patricia Carey, special advocate for survivors of institutional abuse, welcomed the fact Cabinet approval has been granted.
Carey said the commission of investigation into mother and baby institutions “was veiled in secrecy” and the sealing of records was “an affront to an open and transparent response to burial grounds and survivors’ concerns”.
[ Number of mother and baby home redress applications triples after awareness campaign Opens in new window ]
“I have repeatedly called for the opening of records to ensure survivors can have access to their records and to identify burial grounds of all those who died in institutions,” she said.
A motion calling on the Government to release unpublished technical archaeological reports concerning burials at the former institution was passed unanimously by Cork City Council last month. The motion also called on the Government to direct the Attorney General to open an inquest into deaths at the institution “as a matter of moral urgency”.
Labour Party councillor Peter Horgan, who proposed the motion, on Tuesday said he was “glad that the Government is listening to Cork City Council and survivors”.
He called on the High Court to “prioritise” the application once it receives it, given the “emotional toll this has had on people”.
“I hope that the court would move swiftly in unlocking these details, so that all survivors can have a look at the information in the full light of day.”
Carmel Cantwell from the Bessborough Mother and Baby Home Support Group said the potential release of any extra information “is welcome from our point of view”.
“We’re going in the right direction ... It’s about finding out the truth,” she said.
Cantwell’s brother William died in December 1960, when he was six weeks old, in St Finbarr’s Hospital in Cork after being transferred there from Bessborough. She has not been able to find out where he is buried.
Cantwell is among the defendants taking a judicial review aimed at overturning the planning permission granted in July.
In her update, Foley noted that details of the findings of the records in question were included in the commission’s final report in 2021.
“The documents include high resolution Air Corps photographs of Bessborough from 1951; site survey documentation; and the Commission’s cartographic and landscape assessments of possible unrecorded burial sites, carried out by forensic archaeologists,” the statement said.
“Witness evidence falls outside the scope of materials which are proposed to be searched for under this proposal, as evidence was given in private session by witnesses at the Commission on their understanding that their confidentiality and privacy would be respected and upheld at all times.”
In February, developer Estuary View Enterprises was granted planning permission by Cork City Council to build 140 apartments at the site. Horgan and the Bessborough Mother and Baby Home Support Group lodged appeals with An Coimisiún Pleanála (ACP), which in July upheld permission for 106 apartments.
In its ruling, ACP said there was no evidence of unrecorded burials in the area where the development was proposed . Conditions attached to the permission include forensic archaeological monitoring during construction works and the appointment of a liaison officer to engage with survivor groups.
More than 900 children died at Bessborough or in hospital after being transferred from the institution, which operated from 1922 to 1998.
Despite “very extensive inquiries and searches”, the commission of investigation was able only to establish the burial places of 64 children, meaning the burial places of more than 800 children remain unknown.
The inquiry concluded it was likely some of them were buried in unmarked graves but did not consider it feasible to excavate the full site, which amounts to 24 hectares. The entire estate covers about 80 hectares, parts of which have already been built on.

title: Spiorad na gcomhaontuithe in easnamh
description: Tá deacrachtaí arís eile roimh Thionól agus Feidhmeannas an Tuaiscirt ach ní leor forálacha lena réiteach
content:
Tá fiche bliain caite ó Chomhaontú Chill Rímhinn, an comhaontú a thug na struchtúir dhéabhlóidithe ar ais ó thuaidh i ndiaidh tréimhse fhada gan aon Tionól a bheith ag feidhmiú ar Chnoc an Anfa.
Nuair a bunaíodh na struchtúir den chéad uair faoi Chomhaontú Aoine an Chéasta, bhí dóchas forleathan ann go mbeadh siad in ann riar éifeachtach a dhéanamh ar an Tuaisceart agus, de réir a chéile, go dtiocfadh deireadh leis an aighneas domhain idir na páirtithe polaitíochta agus iad ag obair as lámha a chéile. Ní hamhlaidh a bhí. Bhí thuas seal agus thíos seal ag an Tionól ó 1998 ar aghaidh agus nuair a thit sé arís in 2002 bhí imní fhorleathan ann nach dtiocfadh sé ar ais arís.
An difear is suntasaí a bhí ann an uair sin ó thaobh na bpáirtithe polaitíochta de ná go raibh líon na suíochán a bhí ag an UUP agus an SDLP tite, rud a d’fhág nach raibh na páirtithe a bhí lárnach i mbaint amach Chomhaontú Aoine an Chéasta i lár an aonaigh a thuilleadh. Go deimhin, i ndiaidh thoghchán an Tionóil in 2005 bhí an DUP ar an pháirtí is mó sa Tuaisceart, agus níor chuir siad a n-ainm leis na socruithe comhroinnte cumhachta riamh go dtí sin. Ar thaobh na náisiúnaithe, bhí Sinn Féin ar an pháirtí is mó, agus cé go raibh siad anois mar chuid den chóras, bhí fós deacrachtaí ann maidir le tacaíocht an pháirtí don PSNI.
Chuir an t-athrú seo go leor brú orthu siúd a bhí ag iarraidh Cnoc an Anfa a fheiceáil ag feidhmiú arís, Rialtas na Breataine agus Rialtas na hÉireann ina measc. Agus Bertie Ahern ina Thaoiseach agus Tony Blair ina phríomh-aire, bhí suim phearsanta ag an bheirt cheannairí sna struchtúir a bheith ar obair agus ag feidhmiú go maith, agus bhí an ceannach isteach pearsanta sin riachtanach do Chomhaontú Chill Rímhinn óir bhí tuiscint agus tiomantas acu i leith an ábhair.
Go bunúsach, rinneadh leasuithe ar na struchtúir a cruthaíodh i gComhaontú Aoine an Chéasta chun, go teoiriciúil, iad a dhéanamh níos inbhuanaithe. I measc na n-athruithe is mó a rinneadh, bhí athrú ar an bhealach ar ceapadh an Céad-Aire (ón pháirtí is mó in áit ón phobal ainmnithe is mó sa Tionól) agus leasú ar na struchtúir thuaidh-theas agus oirthear-iarthar chun gné níos láidre a chruthú le réigiúin eile sa Ríocht Aontaithe. Agus ba é ceann de na gnéithe is cinniúnaí de Chill Rímhinn ná tacaíocht Shinn Féin don PSNI, rud a deimhníodh ag Ard-Fheis an pháirtí ag tús 2007.
Thug an Comhaontú seo an clúdach polaitíochta a bhí de dhíth ar na páirtithe, go háirithe ar an DUP, chun dul isteach san Fheidhmeannas leis na páirtithe eile. Spreagadh dóchas as an nua go dtiocfadh le polaiteoirí Chnoc an Anfa a róil a chomhlíonadh ina n-iomláine arís, agus nuair a ceapadh Ian Paisley agus Martin McGuinness mar Chéad-Aire agus mar LeasChéad-Aire faoi seach ar an Fheidhmeannas, bhí iontas forleathan ar dhaoine faoin chaidreamh a d’fhás idir an bheirt acu agus iad ag obair le chéile.
Tá tuairim láidir ag teacht i dtreis go bhfuil tuilleadh athruithe de dhíth ar bharr na n-athruithe a rinneadh i gComhaontú Chill Rímhinn…
Bhí go leor míreanna teicniúla sa Chomhaontú ach rud a bhí tábhachtach faoi, mar a bhí le Comhaontú Aoine an Chéasta a tháinig roimhe, ná go raibh na páirtithe, ag an phointe sin, tiomanta feidhmiú laistigh de spiorad an Chomhaontaithe. An deacracht nach raibh daoine ag súil léi - agus atá níos deacra fós lena réiteach - ná cad a tharlaíonn nuair nach bhfuil sé ar leas na bpáirtithe é sin a dhéanamh? Mar gheall ar ghéarchéimeanna éagsúla thar na blianta, thit na struchtúir as a chéile arís cúpla uair. Gach babhta, déantar iarrachtaí leasuithe a dhéanamh ar na struchtúir nó pacáistí infheistíochta a chur ar fáil chun polaiteoirí a mhealladh ar ais, rud a tharla le Comhaontú Chromghlinne, Tús Úr, agus le Ré Nua - Cur Chuige Nua. Ach fós féin maireann deacrachtaí agus constaicí atá leabaithe sa chóras féin.
Is iomaí plé a dhéantar ar athbhreithniú ar na bealaí a bhfeidhmíonn an Tionól agus an Feidhmeannas chun é a dhéanamh níos éifeachtaí agus níos láidre. Tá neart moltaí sa réimse seo faoi láthair, agus plé leanúnach ar an cheist ag leibhéal an Tionóil agus i measc an phobail agus na meán. An deacracht is mó atá rompu siúd ar mhaith leo an Tionól agus an Feidhmeannas a dhéanamh níos éifeachtaí amach anseo ná go mbeadh toil na bpolaiteoirí a bhaineann buntáiste as na struchtúir reatha de dhíth chun na hathruithe siúd a chur i bhfeidhm.
I bhfianaise na ndeacrachtaí atá feicthe againn i bpolaitíocht na Sé Chontae le roinnt seachtainí agus míonna anuas, tá plé athoscailte maidir le seasmhacht na n-institiúidí. Tá tuairim láidir ag teacht i dtreis go bhfuil tuilleadh athruithe de dhíth ar bharr na n-athruithe a rinneadh i gComhaontú Chill Rímhinn agus sna comhaontaithe a bhí ann ó shin.
Fós féin, níor athraigh Comhaontú Chill Rímhinn ná aon chomhaontú eile na bunrialacha a bhaineann leis an chóras comhroinnte cumhachta. An dúshlán is mó ná nach féidir leis na struchtúir sa Tuaisceart feidhmiú mar is ceart mura bhfuil na páirtithe ag obair faoi spiorad an chomhaontaithe chomh maith. Gan an toil sin, forálacha ann nó as, beidh sé deacair mórán dul chun cinn a dhéanamh.
Comhaontú Chill Rímhinn = St Andrew’s Agreement
Comhaontú Aoine an Chéasta = Good Friday Agreement

title: Trump’s pressure campaign on Zelenskiy enters a decisive phase
description: Recent steps by the US president that favour Vladimir Putin reflect his intensifying desire to normalise the relationship with Moscow
content:
H e shunted aside a bipartisan law, signed just weeks ago, imposing new tariffs on Russia . He cut a deal to purchase diesel from Moscow. His negotiators agreed on the vague outlines of a deal for much of Lukoil, a battered Russian energy firm. And he called for the replacement of president Volodymyr Zelenskiy of Ukraine , whose success in taking the fight inside Russia deeply frustrates him.
US president Donald Trump’s intensifying effort in the past few weeks to rehabilitate Russia and usher president Vladimir Putin back into diplomatic society is remarkable for its speed, its characterisation of Zelenskiy as the primary obstacle to peace, and its brazen denial that Russia is continuing the war that Trump says he is trying to end.
“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump said on Monday, speaking to reporters outside the White House as he left for a campaign rally. “They haven’t been doing much,” he said, making no mention of the Russian missiles and jet-powered drones that have been targeting apartment buildings in Kyiv and Ukraine’s surviving electricity grid.
In contrast, he said, “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. They’ve given nothing to us. Remember that.” He repeated the statement for emphasis. The night before, he wrote on social media that Zelenskiy “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” because it brought him a flow of cash and arms from Europe, making no mention that Ukraine is fighting for its sovereignty and even survival in a war that it did not start.
Trump’s disdain for Zelenskiy is hardly new. Nor is his willingness to give the benefit of the doubt to Putin, for whom he has often expressed respect and even admiration.
[ Zelenskiy goes to Oslo for US talks as Trump tensions mount Opens in new window ]
But what is different now is Trump’s increased determination to force a deal on Zelenskiy, telling him that holding out to retain occupied portions of the country’s eastern provinces is not worth it – and that there is money to be made for Ukraine, as well, if it would only drop its objections to an accord, even one written largely on Russia’s terms.
That will be the US message to Zelenskyy on Tuesday in Oslo, Norway, where Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, and his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, are expected to meet the Ukrainian president.
Participating in the discussion, officials say, will be Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, and Alexander Stubb, the president of Finland. (Finland has become an enthusiastic member of the Nato alliance. In the second World War it ceded about 12 per cent of its territory to Russia, and has never got it back.)
The next day Witkoff and Kushner will fly to St Petersburg, Russia, to meet Putin in his hometown. There, Trump’s representatives are expected to take the next step in their efforts to show the benefits of deal making with Putin by securing the release of a long-held American.
Trump discussed the prospect of a hostage release again on Monday, but did not say who was involved. The only American the US state department categorises as “wrongfully detained” in Russia is Stephen Hubbard, who Russia accused of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine when he was seized in 2022. Hubbard, who is in his mid-70s, was sentenced to more than six years in a penal colony.
The timing of the release, if it happens, says volumes about Putin’s strategy. Ridding Russia of an elderly American hostage costs Putin nothing, and does no good for Ukraine. But in the midst of midterm elections in the United States it allows Trump to make the case that he is pursuing an America First foreign policy, complete with the heartwarming images of a prisoner being reunited with his family.
But the larger goal here, for Putin and Trump, is to normalise a relationship that began to go off the rails more than a decade ago, when Putin took Crimea, a territory that was integrated with Ukraine during the Soviet era, and when he began to send Russian fighters into eastern Ukraine.
Europe and the United States responded with sanctions. But a year later, then-chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany signed a deal with Putin to build the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline, calling the Russian leader a “reliable supplier.”
The idea was to reintegrate Russia with the West, in hopes of curbing Putin’s territorial appetites. The effort failed; seven years later Russia launched its full invasion of Ukraine.
Today, that history, and the rationale behind it, is replaying itself. But it is Trump who is taking the role that Merkel once played.
Trump’s ambitions are clearly bigger. There is already talk of a three-way meeting in China between Trump, Putin and Xi Jinping of China on the sidelines of a larger summit of Pacific Rim countries scheduled for next month. Trump said on Monday the goal would be to discuss the three largest nuclear arsenals in the world, and “denuclearisation.” (He likely meant arms control, since none of the three powers seems remotely interested in eliminating their nuclear stockpiles.)
That is exactly what Putin has in mind: expanding the discussion with the United States to other topics, apart from Ukraine, that make the long-running conflict look like just one of many issues to be managed. And should the three-way meeting happen, the image of the leaders of the three largest nuclear powers talking would likely carry the suggestion that they are carving the globe into zones of influence, much as Josef Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt did at Yalta.
A month later the three are scheduled to be together again, this time at a G20 summit meeting at Trump’s Doral resort in Florida. Several months ago, Trump invited Putin to attend, the first indication that the Russian leader was being called back in from the cold.
To get to that point, however, Trump had to abandon all talk of helping Ukraine defend a fledgling, if still corruption-plagued, democracy. While he insists that any settlement of the war would come with “security guarantees” to keep Russia from reinvading, Ukrainian officials say they now doubt that the United States would really come to their aid, at least while Trump is in office.
“The reason it’s hard to think of a precedent of America switching sides in a conflict like this is that there really isn’t one,” said Richard Haass, a long-time diplomat who served Republican and Democratic administrations from the end of the Cold War through the invasion of Iraq 23 years ago.
“What’s unprecedented here is the decision to reverse course and penalise the victim of the invasion – Ukraine – while rewarding the aggressor.”
In fact, as Haass suggests, there is no satisfying analogy in recent history.
Yes, president Richard Nixon shocked allies in 1972 with his opening to China, which led, years later, under president Jimmy Carter, to diplomatic recognition of the People’s Republic, and the withdrawal of formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan. But there was no active war when Nixon made the move, and it came with extensive commitments from Washington to protect Taiwan, a strategy that has worked, so far, for nearly half a century.
The United States pulled out of Vietnam, but while it had extensive disputes with South Vietnam it did not openly side with the North. And Trump, in his first term, and then president Joe Biden, negotiated and executed a deal with the Taliban that quickly led to the takeover of Afghanistan – again, a withdrawal that resulted in the collapse of a government that the US had tried to prop up. But there have been no business deals brewing with the Taliban leadership.
Trump’s aides insist that the war between Russia and Ukraine is now at what they call an “inflection point.” The next move is Zelenskiy’s, they insist, saying he must prove to Trump that he, too, is willing to deal with the Russians, even if it means giving up sovereign territory.
That is something the Ukrainian leader once promised to Congress that he would never do. He got a standing ovation in return, and promises that US support would never flag. On Sunday, appearing on NBC’s Meet the Press, he acknowledged that the atmosphere was different. Asked if his country could survive without US military and intelligence aid, he responded: “Of course, in all the difficult situations, you have a chance. But we will have a low chance – low chance to survive without support of the United States.”
-- This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

title: Hospital apologises to woman who had to have a mastectomy when seven months pregnant
description: Seanagh Rice (33), who had to have chemotherapy after the birth of her baby, sued St James’s Hospital, Dublin over care
content:
A hospital has apologised in the High Court for the failings in care to a mother of two who had to have a mastectomy when she was seven months pregnant after it was discovered she had invasive breast cancer .
Seanagh Rice (33), who sued St James’s Hospital , Dublin, over an alleged delay in the diagnosing of her breast cancer, had to have chemotherapy after the birth of her baby.
Michael Delaney, Rice’s counsel, instructed by Cian O’Carroll Solicitors, told the court it was their case that there was an eight-month delay in the diagnosis of his client’s cancer.
Rice, whose mother died of breast cancer at 48, had the breast cancer BRCA2 gene variant and had been attending St James’s Hospital for reviews.
In April 2023, Rice had a routine breast MRI at the hospital which identified an abnormality measuring over 3cm, and an ultrasound or biopsy was recommended. It was claimed that no ultrasound or biopsy was arranged or carried out.
When Rice, from Ballyfermot, Dublin , attended for her next review at the hospital in January 2024, she was sent for an urgent mammogram and ultrasound and an invasive cancer was revealed.
Rice, while 31 weeks pregnant, had a left breast mastectomy and reconstruction, and required chemotherapy following the birth of her baby.
Speaking outside the Four Courts after settling an action against the hospital, Rice said she had lost precious time with her two children and would never get it back.
“What should have been one of the happiest times in our lives became a time of enormous fear and uncertainty. Instead of enjoying those precious months with my newborn baby, I was undergoing chemotherapy and cancer treatment that should never have been necessary,” she said.
“The physical and emotional consequences have been overwhelming ... While I welcome the admission of liability from St James’s Hospital and its apology, no settlement can ever give me back what I have lost.”
[ ‘Every maternity negligence case costs us a midwife’, doctors’ group warns Opens in new window ]
The hospital admitted liability in the case and a letter of apology from Mary Daly, St James’s Hospital chief executive, was read to the court.
“On behalf of St James’s Hospital, I wish to apologise for the failings in the care provided to you following the results of your MRI performed in April 2023. We recognise that having to receive and cope with this news during your second pregnancy would have made an already difficult situation even more challenging,” it stated.
“We acknowledge that your experience fell below the standard of care that we strive to uphold and we are sorry for the distress this caused to you and your family.”
The letter concluded: “While we cannot change what happened, we are committed to ensuring patient safety and the highest standard of care for all our patients. Please accept my sincere apologies for the impact these events had on you and your family.”
Outside court, Rice said her hope was that “lessons will be learned from what happened to me, and that no other woman or young mother would have to endure the same experience because an important medical finding was simply not followed up”.
She said the settlement brings to an end an incredibly difficult chapter in her life, but she would continue to carry the consequences of what happened to her.
“Having lost my mother to breast cancer and knowing I had the breast cancer gene, I knew only too well the risks I faced,” she said.
“I did everything I was supposed to do, including attending regular screening. Because I wanted to do everything possible to protect myself and be there for my husband and children.
“To discover that an abnormality on my MRI had been identified but not actioned for nine months has been devastating.”
In the proceedings, it was claimed there was a failure to take adequate measures to protect Rice from the risk of developing breast cancer, and her cancer was allowed to develop and spread unidentified, unmonitored and untreated until she was diagnosed in January 2024.
[ Couple settle action against National Maternity Hospital over death of baby girl Opens in new window ]
Rice’s cancer, it was claimed, was allowed to grow and become microinvasive, and she required more extensive treatment than she would otherwise have required.
Had she been diagnosed in a timely manner, it was claimed, she would not have required chemotherapy.
Noting the settlement, Judge Paul Coffey said he was delighted to see the case had been resolved to Rice’s satisfaction.

title: €620k Ferrari and three Lamborghinis among vehicles seized by Revenue last year
description: Trucks and other vehicles with a combined value of €15.6m were seized over tax, fuel and smuggling issues
content:
A black Ferrari valued at €620,000 and three Lamborghinis worth almost €1 million were among the more than 1,000 vehicles seized by Revenue last year.
Trucks and other vehicles with a combined value of €15.6 million were seized in 2025 because of vehicle registration tax (VRT) issues, marked fuel or their use for smuggling.
The haul included an orange Lamborghini with a value of €405,000, which was confiscated in December and listed as being held in a State warehouse.
Another Lamborghini, worth about €200,000, was seized in June and was also listed as stored at the State warehouse.
A third Lamborghini – this one valued at €330,000 – was seized in August but marked as “released locally” in Revenue records.
The €620,000 black Ferrari was confiscated in March but it was also returned to its owner, according to records released under the Freedom of Information Act.
[ Ferrari’s first electric car is courting controversy at 310km/h Opens in new window ]
Revenue also seized a yellow Ferrari 360 worth an estimated €120,000 last September but it too was released.
Not all vehicles were of such value, with three seized cars – a Volkswagen Golf, Vauxhall Astra and Toyota RAV4 – worth just €200 each.
Both Ferraris and all three Lamborghinis were held because of issues with VRT, which accounted for most of the Revenue seizures last year.
A total of 858 vehicles, worth a combined €12.7 million, were seized because of VRT problems in 2025.
Another 127 vehicles, valued at just over €1 million, were confiscated over the use of marked mineral oil or green diesel.
Revenue also logged 66 seizures worth €1.6 million where cars or trucks were used for smuggling of illicit goods.
A further seven vehicles valued at €221,000 were seized because of their use in drug-related crime.
Revenue reported that another 552 vehicles were seized in the first half of this year.
Collectively, those cars and trucks were worth €7.4 million, with most of the seizures related to VRT.
Asked about the figures, a Revenue spokesperson said work on vehicle detention and seizure was about “fairness and protecting the public interest”.
They said: “The aim is to make sure people who pay the correct taxes and duties, and businesses who trade legitimately, are not undermined by those who evade tax or use vehicles to support criminal activity.”
The spokesperson said avoiding VRT or misusing marked fuel gives individuals an unfair advantage over ordinary motorists and legitimate motor traders.
“Similarly, when vehicles are used to transport illegal tobacco, alcohol, fuel or drugs, this harms the exchequer and wider society,” they added.
The spokesperson said that when a vehicle was seized, Revenue followed a set of legal and administrative steps to decide whether it should be returned to its owner or disposed of.
They said in some situations, the vehicle was returned, usually where a person co-operated or agreed to pay a “compromise sum” as well as any outstanding VRT or tax.
If the owner didn’t challenge the seizure within the legal time limit and the conditions for forfeiture were met, the vehicle was treated as permanently taken by the State.

title: Two charged in relation to fatal Waterford arson attack remanded in custody
description: Jessica Dalton and Cian Stacey appear in court after Philip, Kim, Jayden and Callum English killed in petrol bombing
content:
Two people charged in relation to an arson attack on a home in Waterford city that claimed four lives have been further remanded in custody.
Kim and Philip English and their sons, Callum (12) and nine-year-old Jayden, died after their home in the Birchwood estate was petrol bombed on October 13th.
Two other children remain in a critical condition at the children’s hospital in Crumlin, Dublin.
Jessica Dalton (31) and Cian Stacey (21) appeared before a special sitting of Clonmel District Court in Tipperary on Saturday.
Stacey is of no fixed above while Dalton has an address in Waterford city. They were charged with three offences.
At a sitting of Waterford District Court on Tuesday, defence solicitor Ken Cunningham said Stacey was consenting to a 28-day remand in custody pending directions from the Director or Public Prosecutions (DPP).
Judge Caitríona Murray remanded Stacey in custody until November 17th when he will appear before Waterford District Court by video-link.
Stacey, who also appeared in court by video-link on Tuesday, was not required to speak during the short hearing.
Cunningham, who also represented Dalton, said he had considered raising the issue of bail on Tuesday.
However, he consulted with his client and a decision was made to consent to a remand in custody for 28 days.
Dalton has reserved her position in relation to bail. The judge remanded her in custody to appear before Waterford District Court on November 17th next for DPP directions.
Dalton was present in court but was not required to speak.
Dalton and Stacey were previously charged with a single charge of criminal damage on October 13th at an address in Waterford.
They also face two counts of Section 4 assaults causing serious harm. The alleged offences are contrary to the Non Fatal Offences Against the Person Act, 1997.
At the hearing on Saturday, Det Sgt Michael Burke told the court he charged Dalton at 2.45pm on Saturday at Waterford Garda station.
He said she made no reply to each charge. The court heard Dalton was a single mother who was not working. An application for free legal aid was granted.
Det Sgt Brian O’Callaghan said he charged Stacey at 2.44pm on Saturday at Waterford Garda station. He said Stacey made no reply to the three charges when they were put to him.
Defence solicitor Ciaran Murphy said his client was earning €600 per week. However, he applied for free legal aid given the gravity of the charge.
Judge Andrew Gubbins granted free legal aid subject to the submission of a statement of means.
Murphy said Stacey suffered from depression. He asked that he be given a psychological examination while in custody.
Murphy added his client had concerns for his own safety and asked to be remanded in custody to Cork Prison rather than Limerick Prison.
Judge Gubbins said he had no jurisdiction over custody matters. He said they were an issue for the Irish Prison Service.

title: Paddy Power owner Flutter to cut 240 jobs at Irish head office
description: Company has been hit by increase in British gambling taxes
content:
Paddy Power owner Flutter will cut 240 jobs from its Irish head office as it grapples with rising British betting taxes.
The group said on Tuesday that it planned to cut about 1,400 jobs in its UK and Ireland division to counter the impact of British government tax rises set to cost it $540 million (€480 million).
About 240 of those jobs will be lost in its Dublin office, while the group will also reduce numbers in the United Kingdom and in various centres around Europe, according to sources familiar with the business.
Flutter did not comment on the numbers that will be lost in each location.
However, an industry source estimated that up to 550 jobs could go in the UK, with the remaining cuts in Porto, Portugal, and Cluj-Napoca, Romania, Malta and Gibraltar, which service the UK and Ireland division.
Along with Paddy Power, the unit includes Betfair and Sky Bet.
Gaming and betting duty hikes announced by Britain’s Labour government will cost Flutter’s UK and Ireland unit $540 million this year, the group has already confirmed.
Its business in the Republic is suffering as it forms part of the UK and Ireland division, where the impact of the tax increases will be felt.
UK and Ireland chief executive Kevin Harrington said the group was not able to “fully absorb” this without cutting costs.
[ Paddy Power’s long goodbye from betting shops accelerates Opens in new window ]
Plans announced in last year’s UK autumn budget noted the rate of remote gaming duty – the tax on online casino games and slots – increased from 21 per cent to 40 per cent earlier this year.
Firms will also see a new 25 per cent rate of general betting duty for online bets from April next year, up from 15 per cent, as part of the budget changes.
Flutter employs 1,750 people in its Irish office in Clonskeagh, Dublin and 9,000 overall in the UK and Ireland division.
The group plans to begin consultations with its Irish workers shortly. Local management told them of the planned cuts before the group announced the move on Tuesday morning.
Flutter recently confirmed plans to close up to 100 Paddy Power bookie shops in Ireland and Britain in light of growing economic uncertainty.
Its latest announcement comes as speculation grows that British prime minister Andy Burnham’s government could increase taxes on fruit, roulette and other slot machines in British bookie shops at the next budget later this month.
Such a move could spark further betting shop closures in Britain. The Republic’s laws do not permit those machines in bookies.
Flutter said its cost-cutting plan is likely to cost between $80 million (€71 million) and $90 million over the next three months.
Harrington said: “The material increase in betting and gaming duties announced in the UK budget last year has fundamentally changed the economic model of the regulated betting and gaming industry in the UK while helping to fuel the unlicensed, unregulated market.
“As we warned a year ago, we cannot fully absorb a rise of this magnitude without reducing our fixed cost base and therefore must restructure our business so that we can best position ourselves for the future.
“We remain confident that we are well placed to benefit from share gains given our position as the largest-scale operator in the UK.” – Additional reporting: PA

title: Erik ten Hag accuses Cristiano Ronaldo of ‘letting down’ Manchester United
description: Former manager claims club broke promises made to him
content:
Erik ten Hag has claimed Cristiano Ronaldo “let the team down” during their time together at Manchester United . Ten Hag has also alleged that promises made by United’s owners went unfulfilled, leading to his sacking by the club in October 2024.
Ronaldo returned for a second spell at United in August 2021 and was already at the club when Ten Hag was appointed in April 2022 as Ole Gunnar Solskjær’s successor. The relationship between the pair quickly broke down, however, with Ronaldo refusing to come on as a substitute in a win against Tottenham in October 2022 before he then publicly criticised the club in a TV interview. The forward’s contract was mutually terminated the following month.
“He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him,” Ten Hag said in an interview with the Athletic. “He’s one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in.”
Ten Hag claims Ronaldo did not complete the full run that players were set after they were beaten 4-0 by Brentford early in his reign. “I confronted him with this,” Ten Hag said. “Many times I say: ‘Ronnie, everyone wants to work for you to bring you in the right position, but if you can’t bring yourself in the box, you can’t score.’”
Ten Hag was sacked only five months after he won the FA Cup and then signed a contract extension. The Dutchman claimed in the discussions with the club’s owners about his new deal that he was made promises which were not kept, and he was left “embarrassed” when Scott McTominay was sold to Napoli without his consent. He said: “They promised me loyalty, they promised me backing, they promised communication, that we get aligned. We spoke about the issues. But the promises, they didn’t keep.
“I said: ‘No selling Scott McTominay.’ And in the end they sold him. I got, of course, very embarrassed and disappointed.”
