description: Is fuirseoir, aisteoir agus ceoltóir í Síomha Hennessy. Ainmníodh í don ngradam Spirit of Wit ag an Dublin Fringe Festival in 2023 (The Coil’s Lament), agus in 2025 (Building Character). In 2026, chuir sí an seó Gaelmaxxing i láthair ag an bhféile, a ainmníodh don ghradam Bewley’s Cafe Theatre Little Gem.
content:
Cén t-ealaíontóir atá beo is mó a bhfuil meas agat air?
Tá meas mór agam ar aon ealaíontóir atá tar éis airgead nó deiseanna a íobairt ar mhaithe le seasamh a ghlacadh ar son mhuintir na Palaistíne - leithéidí Macklemore agus na n-ealaíontóirí eile a d’fhág camchuairt Ed Sheeran: Aaron Rowe agus Beoga. San earnáil seo, is beag deiseanna nó airgead atá ar fáil dúinne, na healaíontóirí, mar sin tá brú atá ann gan aon rud a rá nó a dhéanamh a chuirfeadh na deiseanna sin i mbaol. Tá an-mheas agam ar dhaoine nach ngéilleann don bhrú sin.
Cad iad na straitéisí a úsáideann tú chun tréimhsí lag trá cruthaitheachta a shárú?
Fanaim go dtí an nóiméad deireanach, go dtí go bhfuil an spriocdháta ag éirí cóngarach agus gur cás éigeandála atá ann i ndáiríre, nuair nach bhfuil aon rogha eile agam ach rud éigin a scríobh ar an diabhal leathanach. Ní mholfainn an modh seo más maith leat do mheabhairshláinte a chaomhnú.
Mura mbeifeá ag gabháil don ealaín atá á cleachtadh agat faoi láthair, cén tallann chruthaitheach ba bhreá leat a bheith agat?
Is minic a bhím ag brionglóideach faoi éalú go dtí pluais áit éigin sna sléibhte, i bhforaois nó taobh le loch, agus leabhair a scríobh. Is dócha go mbeinn ag scrollú ar mo fón gan stad ansin freisin!
Cad é an chomhairle is measa a fuair tú riamh?
Gur chóir dom ‘’branda níos soiléire’’ a bheith agam ar na meáin shóisialta. Ní hé gur droch-chomhairle atá ann don chóras caipitlíoch ina maireann muid. Sa chóras seo, is fíor go gcaithfidh tú tú féin ‘a dhíol’, agus cuidíonn sé go mór má tá ‘táirge’ soiléir agat. Ach is ‘ilcheardaí’ mise - fuirseoir, ceoltóir, scríbhneoir, aisteoir, agus cruthaím ábhar polaitiúil freisin ar na meáin shóisialta. Tá sé dodhéanta dom díriú go hiomlán ar ghné amháin.
Is ‘ulchabhán oíche’ amach is amach mé, ní bhíonn aon smaoineamh amháin soiléir i mo cheann roimh 7pm.
An raibh aon mhúinteoirí inspioráideacha agat?
Chaith mé dhá thrian do mo chuid ama ar scoil i dtrioblóid in oifig an phríomhoide. Bhí múinteoir nó dhó a raibh píosa craic iontu, agus múinteoir deas nó dhó a rinne iarracht mé a spreagadh chun píosa beag oibre a dhéanamh. Is cuimhin liom múinteoir deas amháin, Iníon Nic Anraí a mhúin Béarla dúinn don Ardteistiméireacht. Ar an lá deireanach don scoil, scríobh sí ‘comhairle don saol’ ar an gclár dubh. An pointe a sheas amach domsa ná “Bíodh cuimhne agaibh ar Sylvia Plath, agus seachain fir cosúil le Ted Hughes”. Comhairle thábhachtach a d’fhan liom!
Conas a bhí do shaol cultúrtha mar pháiste?
Labhair muid Gaeilge sa bhaile, agus bhí ceol mórthimpeall orainn. Ba ghnách le mo mháthair a bheith sa bhanna ceoil Na Casaidigh lena chuid deartháireacha. Is cuimhin liom suí taobh léi ag an bpianó, agus mé an-óg. Bhí mo sheantuismitheoirí, Seán agus Nóirín Uí Chasaide, an-cheolmhar, agus bhí béim ollmhór i gcónaí ar an gceol sa chlann. Bhí tréimhse i m’óige nuair a bhí Daid de shíor ag seinm ceirníní de chuid Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan. Tá cuid de na hamhráin ar eolas de ghlanmheabhair agamsa agus ag mo dheirfiúr, cé gur sa Phuinseáibis atá siad agus nach dtuigeann muid focal. Thug Daid dlúthcheirnín den albam Blue le Joni Mitchell dom mar bhronntanas nuair a bhí mé 16, agus mé ag foghlaim an ghiotáir. Ba é Case of You an chéad amhrán a chan mé leis an ngiotár.
An bhfuil saothar cruthaitheach amháin ar mhaith leat tabhairt faoi ach nach bhfuil tosaithe agat fós?
Ba mhaith liom sraith drámaí grinn a chruthú do TG4. Tá mé manifesting anseo!
Is ‘ulchabhán oíche’ amach is amach mé, ní bhíonn aon smaoineamh amháin soiléir i mo cheann roimh 7pm. Díreach agus mé ag iarraidh dul a luí, dúisím agus tosaíonn na smaointe ag teacht. Ansin, coinníonn siad i mo dhúiseacht go mall mé. Déanaim taifead le mo ghuthán nó scríobhaim san aip Notes iad. Is minic agus mé ag déanamh rud éigin eile ar fad a thagann na smaointe chugam. Cabhraíonn Ritalin.
Cad é do thuaraim faoi fhorbairt na Gaeilge sna healaíona in Éirinn?
Ag labhairt mar dhuine a tógadh le Gaeilge sna 90idí, tá sé thara bheith suimiúil an t-athrú a fheiceáil i measc an phobail - go háirithe sa ghlúin óg - maidir leis an nGaeilge. Scríobh mé seó iomlán faoi le déanaí don fhéile Dublin Fringe, Gaelmaxxing, agus déanann sé plé greannmhar ar an nGaeilge mar threocht. Is iontach an rud é go bhfuil suim sa Ghaeilge múscailte sa phobal. Sílim go bhfuil cúpla cúis leis. Go bunúsach, ceapaim go bhfuil daoine (go háirithe daoine óga) ag cuardach rud éigin taobh amuigh de luachanna an chaipitleachais agus an impiriúlachais. Ceapaim freisin go bhfuil nasc idir an ghluaiseacht mhór ar son na Palaistíne atá feicthe againn in Éirinn le cúpla bliain anuas agus an tsuim atá daoine ag léiriú i stair fhrithchoilíneach na hÉireann. Tá an teanga mar chuid de sin, agus is iontach an rud é. Ag an am céanna, cé go bhfuil dearcadh an phobail i bhfad níos dearfaí maidir leis an teanga, tá líon na ndaoine atá ag maireachtáil trí Ghaeilge - nó á labhairt go laethúil - ag laghdú, de thoradh na géarchéime tithíochta sa Ghaeltacht, agus easpa infheistíochta ón stát. Is iontach an rud é go bhfuil an pobal mór ag cur suim sa teanga agus sa chultúr, ach ní leor sin leis an teanga a choinneáil beo. Caithfear infheistíocht cheart a dhéanamh i dtithíocht, sna meáin, agus i seirbhísí trí Ghaeilge.

title: Inside Ireland’s only boarding school offering the Leaving Cert and International Baccalaureate
description: With more than 60 nationalities represented in the student body, Villiers School in Limerick prides itself on a diverse and inclusive ethos
content:
D og-friendly campus notices on the walls and a bright, airy cafe for staff and students , with posters for the film-makers’ club, the art club, the craft club, the book club and the Christian Union, are some of the first signs of inclusivity at Villiers School on North Circular Road in Limerick city .
We are here to meet teachers, boarding-house and catering staff, and students at what is Ireland’s only boarding school to offer the Leaving Certificate and the International Baccalaureate (IB) to senior-cycle day and boarder students.
Introduced into the school in 2017, the IB is a two-year diploma programme in which students take six subjects chosen from arts, humanities and sciences. They also have to write a 4,000-word essay, engage in a module on the theory of knowledge and partake in sporting, creative and voluntary activities. Currently, there are 24 students enrolled in the programme across fifth and sixth years at Villiers.
“When attending Model United Nations conferences [a simulation of the UN in which students role-play national delegates debating global issues] in Europe, the teachers met students attending IB schools and felt it sat well with our ethos,” says Jill Storey, principal of Villiers School.
Renowned for fostering independent learning and critical thinking, the IB is considered to be one of the best academic preparations in the world for third-level education. “There are 10 attributes that an IB student should have – to be knowledgeable, caring, open-minded, reflective, balanced and principled, and to be a risk-taker, an enquirer, a communicator and a thinker,” says Shane Hanna, who leads the IB diploma programme at Villiers School.
“Most of our IB students are thinking of studying in universities outside of Ireland,” adds Storey. Irish students taking the IB also study Leaving Certificate Irish to keep open the option to attend universities within Ireland that require the subject for admission.
With more than 60 nationalities represented in the student body – both among day students and boarders – the international dimension of Villiers extends well beyond the IB programme. Of the 165 boarders from the 550 students, about two-thirds are from Ireland, with the rest from throughout Europe, Asia, the Middle East, South America and the Cayman Islands. Staff members also come from a range of countries including Belarus, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, Lithuania, New Zealand, Nicaragua, Pakistan, Poland, Spain and South Africa.
Historically, the school has had a strong international dimension, reflecting its location near the international free trade zone set up next to Shannon Airport in the 1960s.
Susan Peña, head of admissions and communications, says that since the school became an IB school, it has attracted more families from overseas, as well as Irish and international families relocating to Ireland from places such as South Africa.
“We could fill transition year with Spanish students based on the number of enquiries we get. But we make sure we have a mix of languages and backgrounds among the boarders,” says Peña. The school recruits students through educational agents in Europe, Asia, the United States, Latin America and Mexico. Students with families in Nigeria, Kenya, Zimbabwe and Tanzania also attend.
Boarding school fees for 2027/2028 range from €12,750 for five-day boarding to €22,000 for seven-day boarding for the Junior Cycle and Leaving Certificate Programme. The IB diploma programme costs €17,800 for five-day boarders and €27,200 for seven-day boarders. About one fifth of boarders avail of grants for their fees.
Although the school is open to students of all religions and none, there is an underlying Christian ethos, with the Dean of St Mary’s Church of Ireland Cathedral in Limerick and representatives from the Methodist and Presbyterian churches on the board of governors.
Villiers School was founded in 1821 followed a bequest from Hannah Villiers to provide accommodation for widows and their children as well as education for the children from the aforementioned religious denominations.
The school doesn’t have a chaplain, but Emily Sexton-Consadine, religious education teacher, is the spiritual and religious adviser who leads whole school assemblies. “I also greet students and staff as they arrive in school to set the tone for a happy place and I am around during break and lunch times. It’s about creating empathy, compassion, respect and openness for those who do have faith and for those who don’t,” says Sexton-Consadine.
[ Inside the only girls’ boarding school taught entirely through Irish Opens in new window ]
Diversity and inclusion seems to be a core part of the school ethos with an LGBTQIA+ alliance, a People of Colour alliance and non-competitive extracurricular running and tennis clubs held in a parallel to competitive sports such as rugby, hockey and basketball. “We want to make sure that all students regardless of their race, ethnicity, gender identity or sexual orientation feel they have a voice and a safe place in this school,” says Storey.
Mindfulness meditation, yoga, kindness workshops and Feel Good Fridays (an open-mic student-led music event at lunchtimes on the last Friday of each month) run throughout the academic year. There is also a club for students with additional educational needs, which offers them a space to talk about their concerns. Students for whom English is not their native languages have access to extra English classes.
Janet Woods, academic coordinator, brings her labradoodle, Alfie, to class with her every day. “He relaxes students. When they come into my office for an academic meetings, they talk more when he’s there. Any boarders who have left dogs at home particularly love him,” she says.
[ Life at Ireland’s biggest boarding school: ‘I have so much more independence’ Opens in new window ]
The school campus is compact, with new buildings and extensions supplementing Tivoli House, where the school moved from Henry Street in Limerick in the 1950s, and the adjacent Derravoher House and gardens, which was bought by the school in 2012.
Picnic tables are scattered around what would have been the gardens of these once stylish 19th century family homes on the edge of Limerick city. And the basement in Tivoli House has a games room with darts and table football, brightly coloured couches and beanbags and a kitchen for use by sixth-year boarders at the weekends.
Separate dormitories for boys and girls with bedrooms accommodating four to eight students per room are in Derravoher House and Tivoli House. House parents also stay in on-site accommodation. The principal, Jill Storey, her three children and two dogs (a pug and a whippet – both of whom are regularly walked by boarders) live in Tivoli House.
There are plants in the corridors and the art work on the walls is done by the students themselves. “Students say that the dorms feel like home,” says Vivienne Long, head of boarding.
Amy Clarke, first-year boarder from Co Tipperary: “I share a room with five people. It’s nice. It’s like having a sleepover every night. I also like having a time schedule for my day.”
Phoebe Hodgins, fifth year from Co Tipperary: “It’s calm and relaxing and people can choose to do what interests them. There is a lot of balance and structure, which gives me great routine. I like that there are always people around.”
Evan Mooney, sixth year from Co Tipperary: “I’m the youngest of three so my brother and sister came to school here too. It was a massive change to come from a small rural primary school to a school in the city with 550 students, but I think living with other people in school will make going to university easier.”
Kyle Sabeta, third year from Co Kildare, originally from Zimbabwe: “I was a bit rebellious when I came first as I didn’t care about anything, but I changed quite quickly. The school has helped me take care of my belongings and help other people. My favourite extracurricular activities are rugby and hockey.”
Sunny Chang, sixth year from Taiwan: “I came here in second year and stayed with a host family. I joined the boarders in fifth year and I prefer it to being in a host family because I have other students who listen to me. Studying in Taiwan is very pressurised and I’m not very studious so it’s easier to study here.”
Jenna Kasten, sixth year from Frankfurt: “I came here in fifth year because my brother came here and liked it. He was with a host family but I was afraid of getting a bad host family. Some students don’t like the rules of boarding schools but I think that while it is strict, the staff also trust us. As a sixth year, we can sign out for 90 minutes every day and for four-and-a-half hours on Saturdays and every second Sunday. The disadvantage is that so few students do the IB but we boarders mix with the other students.”
Diego Redondo, sixth year from Madrid: “I’ve always wanted to study the IB. My older brother studied it in the US and my parents gave me that option but it was too far away. My cousins came here and recommended the school. I went to Clongowes Wood College as a boarder in first year to learn English. It was very focused on study and sport. It’s more relaxed here. You make good friends as a seven-day boarder but you don’t get to disconnect from school. Overall, it’s a great opportunity to improve my English. I’d like to study a degree through English when I go back to Spain.”

title: At 49 I was a mum, a wife, a runner and constantly tired. Then one day I collapsed at work
description: What I want after surgery on my brain tumour is simple: to know every appropriate option has been explored for me
content:
I call my brain tumour Boris. Giving it a name makes it feel slightly less like an incurable cancer and more like an unwanted house guest.
Boris arrived, uninvited, last November, just before my 50th birthday, and has long outstayed his welcome. Now he has a little brother. Baby Boris is due for eviction from my frontal lobe on October 21st, three days before International Brain Tumour Awareness Week begins. But brain cancer pays little attention to timing, fairness or good manners.
Until last November, my life was busy in a way that now feels wonderfully ordinary. I was 49, a mum to two beautiful children and director of marketing, communications and public affairs at the University of Limerick. I loved my job and loved to run, often with the dawn. I was the person who planned, organised and got things done. I joke that it took Boris arriving for my husband to join the class WhatsApp group.
I was proactive about my health: an early mammogram, regular check-ups and blood tests. When fatigue, anxiety and brain fog appeared towards the end of October 2025, I blamed hormones, contacted my GP and carried on.
Two days before that appointment, I collapsed at a work conference in Birmingham and woke after a seizure with a dislocated shoulder. A scan had found a large mass in my brain. I was in another country, away from my husband and children. That night, as we all tend to do now with any illness, I googled brain tumours and prayed mine wasn’t a glioblastoma.
I was flown to Cork, where my neurosurgeon at Cork University Hospital (CUH), the wonderful Chris Lim, told me the tumour was operable. In the days before surgery, I bought my children’s Christmas presents and a 2026 calendar, marking our important family dates. I didn’t know what condition I would be in when I woke up, or whether I would still be fully myself. Buying their gifts was one small thing I could be sure of.
On November 19th, Lim removed as much of Boris as was safely possible. Tests confirmed glioblastoma: an incurable grade 4 brain cancer.
I turned 50 on the day of The Late Late Toy Show. We sat around the television that night in matching pyjamas. Instead of looking forward to the year ahead, I wondered whether I would see another Christmas. I lost my own mother young; the thought of my children knowing that same pain was, and is, unbearable.
[ Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international study finds Opens in new window ]
Once the initial shock subsides, you look for hope. I was shocked to discover that the treatment offered to me would have been broadly the same 20 years ago. I completed it all: surgery, six weeks of chemotherapy and radiotherapy, followed by six monthly cycles of chemo. Standard treatment has given me 11 months in which to live remarkably well.
I wanted that life to still feel like mine. Movement has always been my medicine, so I kept running. I flew to Spain with my family this summer and have laughed and cried with extraordinary friends.
Because I’m not allowed to drive, my running girls co-ordinate lifts with military precision. And I threw myself into organising a 50th-birthday festival in west Kerry for my best friend Niamh. Given the choice, the planning part of my brain would much rather obsess over disco balls and personalised face tattoos than bloody Boris.
But last month, I learned the cancer had returned. My MRI suggests Baby Boris is a mix of tumour and treatment damage, again in my right frontal lobe. I’m frightened, but grateful that surgery is possible.
What comes afterwards is much less clear. There is no single agreed standard treatment when glioblastoma returns. Clinical trials offer hope, but even where hospitals are recruiting, patients can be excluded by a molecular feature, an eligibility rule or simply timing.
[ Your Family Treating oesophageal cancer: ‘The service delivered here is on par with the best in the world’ Opens in new window ]
Brain cancer affects fewer people than many other cancers. But small patient numbers should not mean small ambition.
Last month, I took the train to Dublin to address the board of Cancer Trials Ireland as a member of its Patient Consultants Committee. Speaking for myself and others unable to make that journey, I called for brain cancer not to be overlooked in national advocacy, earlier patient involvement in research and a clearer route from tumour testing to clinical trials, including options abroad.
I was told it could take another 10 to 15 years for comprehensive molecular testing, which helps doctors match patients to targeted treatments and clinical trials, to become standard practice across all cancer types.
Living with glioblastoma, I find that timescale difficult to hear.
I’m lucky to have clinical teams in University Hospital Limerick and CUH working with me to explore what comes next. I have the experience and wherewithal to ask questions, chase answers and look beyond Ireland.
Even so, it’s exhausting, and I can’t assume I will always have the capacity to do it. No patient should have to navigate this alone.
I want to be involved in decisions about my care, but I don’t want cancer to take up every inch of my life. One minute I’m googling how to dress an 11-year-old as a giant squishy for Halloween; the next, whether a personalised vaccine in Germany might help keep me alive.
In between, there are dinners to organise, gumshields to find, lifts to arrange and all the everyday chaos of family life.
I’m not asking for false hope. I know an experimental treatment may not work. I’m asking for a fair chance to be considered, and for the system to move with the urgency of the disease.
[ Camille O’Sullivan on her cancer: ‘You have to go further than a smear test’ Opens in new window ]
By the time International Brain Tumour Awareness Week begins, I hope to be recovering in a bed in CUH, Baby Boris evicted and beginning the work of getting back on my feet.
I will still be Laura: mum, wife, friend, runner, reluctant brain-cancer advocate and organiser of things that probably don’t need organising.
What I want after surgery is simple: to know every appropriate option has been explored for me. More importantly, I want that to be the case for the next person who wakes after a craniotomy and hears the word glioblastoma.
In brain cancer, possibility is all about time: another birthday, another Christmas, another school run, another wonderfully ordinary rainy Irish day with the people I love.

title: Open days: Key details for NCI, NCAD, technological universities and other institutions
description: Everything you need to know in advance of undergraduate open days around the State
content:
When is open day? Open days will be held on Wednesday, November 18th from 11am-2pm and Saturday, January 23rd from 10am-1pm.
Registration details: You can register at ncirl.ie/About/News-Events/Events/cao-open-day-november-2026
What to expect: Speak directly to lecturers, meet current students and learn about clubs and societies, learn about the career opportunities related to your course.
Student life: NCI has a number of sports clubs including GAA, badminton and basketball. Societies include dance, film and mental health.
Accommodation: Private student accommodation options nearby include Canvas Point in the Dublin docklands area. Canvas Mayor Square is located on the NCI campus.
When is open day? Open days in Maynooth will take place on Friday and Saturday, November 20th and 21st from 10am-2pm.
Registration details: If you have any queries in advance of the open days, you can email admissions@spcm.ie .
What to expect: Take a campus tour, listen to a dedicated talk on studying at the university, talk to current students.
Student life: As the representative body for students of both St Patrick’s Pontifical University and Maynooth University, Maynooth Students’ Union organises a number of social events for students.
Accommodation : The residence office at Maynooth University manages student accommodation at SPPU. The university village apartments on the North Campus are owned by SPPU. Those who would like to live on campus may make an expression of interest for on-campus accommodation by emailing your name, CAO number and name of school to: villageaccounts@spcm.ie

title: Firms offering new personal investment accounts must register with Revenue
description: Customers will have an expectation of annual statements regarding tax deducted and paid
content:
Investment firms, banks and insurers planning to offer new tax-efficient personal investment accounts under the Government’s planned scheme will have to register with the Revenue Commissioners and provide investors with annual statements of tax deducted and paid on their behalf, according to the Finance (Number 2) Bill 2026 published on Monday.
People will be able to put €12,000 a year tax-free into the new accounts, which will be available from next July, Minister for Finance Simon Harris said in his budget speech earlier this month.
The accounts will feature a low tax rate of just 1 per cent, levied on any amount in the account over a tax-free threshold of €50,000. They will be exempt from tax on income, profits and gains arising on eligible investments.
Any tax due is supposed to be calculated and paid at source by the companies providing the investment accounts. Revenue must be informed of any tax owed by 31st March after the end of the tax year, with the amount falling due from April 14 th , according to the Bill.
However, the draft legislation specifies that in the event an account provider fails to deduct funds from an individual investment account to discharge the investment account tax (IAT) liability, the underlying investor may be required to deal with the payment.
“The legislation also imposes an obligation on qualifying account providers to provide an annual statement to qualifying individuals. Where the qualifying account provider fails to deduct funds from an individual investment account to discharge the IAT liability, the qualifying individual may be required to discharge the IAT,” the Department of Finance said in an explanatory note on the Bill.
Firms planning to offer the new accounts are unlikely to finalise pricing structures for investors until closer to the planned July 1 st launch date.
However, industry sources have estimated that all-in annual fees, including charges by service providers, underlying investments, and trading costs, could range from 0.5 percentage points, for accounts where no advice is offered, to 1.5 per cent, with advice.
“For financial institutions considering offering these accounts, early preparation will be important. Providers will need to consider product design, eligible investments, customer declarations, daily valuations, contribution monitoring, transfers between providers and Revenue reporting,” said Brian Murphy, a tax partner with Grant Thornton.
The planned new accounts are “transformational for retail investment in Ireland, with the potential to change our investment culture”, according to PwC Ireland.
“Irish savers have traditionally favoured holding their money on deposit for security rather than investing in higher-returning investments such as equities, bonds, and other financial instruments,” PwC said. “Investing money on deposit delivers returns that underperform inflation over the long term.”

title: Gerry Thornley: Champions Cup has had its lift-off but one fundamental flaw remains
description: Provinces off to winning start in European top flight
content:
The decision-makers in both the EPCR and IRFU would have been entitled to recline in their office chairs somewhat smugly on Monday morning. The tweaks to the Champions and Challenge Cups largely worked over the course of the opening weekend, and the Irish provinces were evidently not hampered by the instructions imposed on them regarding their frontline players.
Leinster appeared fresh rather than rusty, and the decision to bring 41 players to South Africa, while not playing nine of their Ireland summer tourists, appears to have ben vindicated. Hence, that mini-tour can only have enhanced squad unity and Leinster have also looked fitter than they were at this stage last season when they lost to Munster at Croke Park, their third defeat of their first four games.
Dan Sheehan, Tadhg Furlong and Andrew Porter – scrummaging strongly and for once receiving a fair crack from an English referee – all looked in prime nick. Likewise, Joe McCarthy and James Ryan, while Ryan Baird’s return must be like having a new signing.
Josh van der Flier was true to his word in adding more of a jackal threat at the breakdown, making two clean turnovers at Stade Marcel-Michelin to augment his strong carrying and all-round game.
Revived in the second half of last season, when he was unlucky to miss out on some big games, Jimmy O’Brien is playing the best rugby of his career in making light of Leinster bidding adieu to James Lowe and Rieko Ioane. Hugo Keenan, Tommy O’Brien and Garry Ringrose all looked sharp, while Robbie Henshaw has also had a rejuvenation.
And then there was Sam Prendergast. Critics of his defence will cite the missed tackle on his inside shoulder for Clermont’s first try, but for the second week running he was named player of the match. His decision at the start of the second half to run turnover ball from close to his own line, the execution of his kick on the run for Jimmy O’Brien, and then supporting to score was a pivotal moment in the game. Pure vision and class, albeit after last season’s improvement his goalkicking is an issue..
One hopes the Irish “system” doesn’t curb him, or Munster’s Charlie O’Shea, of his natural instincts as it has done with so many gifted, slightly maverick talents in the past. Seán Edogbo’s performance, some slick handling and good defensive sets against a big Racing side were other positives in another encouraging Munster display.
Former Ireland outhalf Ronan O’Gara was critical of the Munster Branch’s decision to move last Saturday’s game against Racing 92 to Páirc Uí Chaoimh, claiming that playing the fixture at Thomond Park would have been a more fitting way to honour the 10th anniversary of Anthony Foley’s passing.
The Munster Branch, who surprisingly remain somewhat prickly to criticism, issued a statement defending the decision. The attendance of 24,906 on Saturday night was still comfortably the second biggest crowd of the weekend, behind only Toulouse v Exeter, and will be the largest for any pool game played in Ireland this season.
A great city though Cork is, the in-game atmosphere was curiously muted. Admittedly the 8pm kick-off didn’t help, as was the case last December against Gloucester. And disappointingly, there were no flags flying at either end of the ground.
Reading some of the reports out of France, where simmering disquiet among vast tracts of the population have again boiled over, the normal bonhomie of a trek to the Stade Marcel-Michelin was replaced by some truly menacing scenes. This must have been the least enjoyable trip to the Auvergne for Leinster fans, some of whom were forced to seek shelter in a cathedral at one point.
On the pitch, the biggest blemish was undoubtedly the shoulder injury suffered by Jack Conan in the act of scoring a gem of a try. He seemed set for another vintage season but now looks likely to miss next month’s Nations Championship fixtures, compounding the absence of Caelan Doris.
Ireland manager Andy Farrell will announce his squad on Wednesday and didn’t look the happiest bunny after seeing his son and his old team Saracens beaten by Connacht in Saturday’s thriller at the Dexcom.
Yet there was also encouraging news in the performance of the province’s Ireland contingent, not least Sean Jansen, who could become the go-to number eight. And Ciarán Frawley’s move west already looks fully vindicated; talk about hitting the ground running.
It still seems a little ridiculous that Mack Hansen and Finlay Bealham couldn’t play, as Stuart Lancaster had used them in the previous three fixtures.
Hansen, who had been sidelined since last November, only managed three games in total last season so must be itching for, and in need of, game time. Bealham wasn’t part of Ireland’s summer tour, and his three appearances, one of which was off the bench, amounted to a grand total of 130 minutes.
As much as the duo would have loved watching their team-mates perform so thrillingly against Saracens, it must have been a tough game to miss.
But bringing the first round forward certainly achieved its primary aim of igniting the Champions Cup earlier in the season, while weather conditions were still favourable. Overall, it was a positive launching pad for the tournament, beginning with Gloucester holding back-to-back champions Bordeaux Bègles to a 36-all draw on Friday night.
While Exeter also ran Toulouse close in their Sunday thriller, it wasn’t until Northampton’s victory over Cardiff in the final game of the weekend that a Premiership side managed to claim a win. The French were restricted to four wins, which was also no harm.
Another tweak to the competition was a change to the bonus-point system, with a team now having to score at least three more tries than their opponents in order to earn an attacking bonus point.
As a consequence, there were 10 fewer try-scoring bonus points claimed over the first round compared to what would have been the case under the old system. It did seem a little harsh on Saracens and Exeter, having scored six tries apiece away from home, not to mention Connacht and Toulouse, who both scored seven.
Munster also missed out, but then again, so too did Pool 3 rivals Gloucester and Bordeaux Bègles. And as head coach Clayton McMillan noted, the change means losing teams won’t obtain cheap bonus points if winning sides decide to down tools as full-time nears.
Another tweak will be that after the top three teams in each pool (who qualify automatically), the remaining four Round of 16 qualifiers will be determined based on points, regardless of which groups they are in.
Applying both changes in retrospect last season, Munster and the Sharks would have advanced rather than Leicester and the Bulls, although Munster would have been away to Bordeaux Bègles. All in all, they do look like positive tweaks.
The Champions Cup has had its lift-off and, especially on these shores, has injected some life into the season. But now, having had a taste of European rugby, it returns to hibernation until the second round in December. If only there was another round next weekend. Alas, that fundamental flaw remains.

title: Listening to the people
description: The Government needs to start acting to stop Israel’s genocide in Gaza
content:
Sir, – In her interview with Aimée Walsh, Turkish writer Elif Shafak said “literature is one of our last remaining democratic spaces” (“ Elif Shafak: ‘This is the age of anger, anxiety, and AI’ ”, Book Review, October 17th). Well, it should be, but the withdrawal of Sally Rooney’s books from UK bookstores because of her principled stance on Palestine is a harbinger of how democratic freedoms we once took for granted are now under threat.
Mark O’Connell’s accurate characterisation of Rooney’s position on Palestine as “judicious and moral” stands in stark contrast with that of the Irish Government (“ Sally Rooney knows what she’s doing and is willing to pay the price for it ”, Opinion, October 19th).
In her 2025 report on the complicity of third states in Israel ’s genocide, Francesca Albanese cited Ireland for trade in dual-use items with Israel valued at $3.2 billion and the transfer of weapons through Shannon Airport.
The Occupied Territories Bill , a minimal act of solidarity, was gutted through the removal of services, which has rendered the legislation more symbolic than a meaningful sanction.
And, more than 50 students from Gaza have been forced to launch legal appeals against a Department of Justice decision to decline them travel visas to take up scholarships in Irish universities. A callous way to treat third-level students who have endured three years of genocide and scholasticide.
An opinion poll carried out in October 2024 showed that 71 per cent of Irish people agree that the Palestinian people live under a system of apartheid implemented against them by Israel. When is the Government going to act according to the wishes of its people and start acting to stop Israel’s genocide in Gaza and dismantle its system of apartheid? – Yours, etc,

title: ‘We don’t want a repeat of that’: Leinster fuelled by memory of Croke Park loss to Munster
description: Both provinces go into Saturday’s URC derby on the back of morale-boosting wins
content:
Leinster assistant coach Tyler Bleyendaal believes his former side Munster are in “a good place” ahead of Saturday’s derby meeting in the United Rugby Championship at the Aviva Stadium (kick-off 6pm).
Over the course of his 62 appearances as a Munster player from 2015 to 2020, Bleyendaal enjoyed two wins out of five outings against Leinster. Victories for the southern province in this fixture have continued to be few and far between since then, although Clayton McMillan’s charges did secure a 31-14 triumph at the expense of their arch rivals in last October’s URC meeting at Croke Park.
While the remainder of the 2025/26 season was often turbulent for Munster, the current term thus far has seen them record two wins and one draw from four games played – including an emotionally charged Champions Cup pool -stage win over Racing 92 last Saturday.
“I would say [Munster are in] a good place,” Bleyendaal remarked at a Leinster media briefing in UCD on Monday. “I think they’re very hard to beat, they’re having good wins. Maybe their hand is being forced, but there’s a bit of youth being injected in there too, which brings a bit of a different dynamic.
“Our poor performance last year is really sharpening the mind that we don’t want a repeat of that. So we are aware of the challenge that Munster will bring and we were definitely lacking in many departments last year.”
While Leinster are expected to have a relatively strong hand to pick from this weekend, Jack Conan is ruled out. The experienced backrow injured his shoulder in the act of scoring a try in the province’s convincing win away to Clermont Auvergne on Saturday.
Although he is uncertain how long Conan will be sidelined for, Bleyendaal acknowledged it is a big blow for the player as the Ireland squad for next month’s Nations Championship games is set to be named on Wednesday.
“I’m not sure how long [he’ll be out], but definitely not [playing] this weekend and obviously the timing of the Irish announcement is not ideal. I don’t know if they’ll have news before then or within the week,” said Bleyendaal, who added that Conan was being assessed on Monday.
“James Culhane is now back. We’ve got cover, but we lost Josh Ericson as well. He played a few matches with Caelan [Doris] out. So we’ve got cover, but we’re getting stressed as well in that one position.”

title: Giving patients the best care is why doctors are often late
description: Blame for tardiness is on Government for failing to deliver a fair and decent health service
content:
Sir, – Lateness is not inherently rude if you understand the reasons for it. Lateness is not a profession-wide smug, triumphalist tool doctors employ to feel important. Neither is it incompetence nor poor timekeeping.
Perhaps it is simply a reluctant, even pathetic badge of honour worn by the doctors still committed to providing a public health service to those who need it, when they need it, in our almost-collapsed two-tier health system.
Balancing the unlimited chaos of the public General Medical Services contract obligations with the increasing expectations of privately paying “consumer patients” is the context in which doctors working as general practitioners (GPs) will experience Rachel Minogue’s ill-informed grievance (“ Why is rude lateness from doctors universally accepted? ”, Letters, October 16th).
My final GP examination assessed the clinical consultation and time-management skills taught in the core curriculum. A stressful mock clinic of back-to-back short consults across the entire medical sphere, watched by examiners, with actors as patients.
Famous for being the first and last time you’d ever finish a clinic on time, you were saved by a farcical bell that told your patient their time was up, whether their problem was solved or not, whether they were crying or not.
Thankfully, reality allows us to be more humane and reasonable. But we were indeed taught about timekeeping as your letter writer felt we ought to be.
It is incorrect to state that in the context of healthcare provision “things change at short notice from time to time”. Actually, continuous unplanned interruption is the daily norm for a GP. In our clinic, despite being fully booked by 10am, the same-day appointment requests roll in relentlessly all day for issues patients insist “cannot wait”. We believe them and squeeze them in as best we can.
I say “thanks for waiting” when it’s very bad, but I no longer personally apologise for systemic factors that prevent me from being “on time”. My apology is conveyed to my patients by my ability to offer them a calm or cheery version of myself as the daily chaos of under-resourced primary care unfolds. I sense the acceptance of my apology by the kind multitude of cards and gifts at Christmas.
Rather than being hurried towards burnout by vexatious commentary on lateness in the medical profession, many vocational GPs prevail in the “doctor’s world” where we continue to enjoy giving patients the time they need to benefit from our expertise and humanity, with no priority given based on ability to pay.
And maybe some day if we all wait long enough, the Government will apologise for their tardiness on delivering a fair and decent public health service that serves both patient and doctor. – Yours, etc,

title: More market disruption ahead as streamers go after live sports
description: Netflix last week announced it had acquired Spanish rights to 2030 World Cup
content:
P eople have been predicting for a while now that it was only a matter of time before the big streaming platforms got serious about disrupting the lucrative live sports market. Until fairly recently, they seemed more interested in one-off marquee events than in longer-term licences. That’s now changing.
Last week, Netflix announced it had bought the rights to all 104 matches of the 2030 World Cup in Spain , which co-hosts the tournament with Portugal and Morocco . The price wasn’t disclosed. RTVE, the Spanish public broadcaster, reportedly paid €55 million for this summer’s tournament. Netflix already holds the North American rights to the next two women’s World Cups , and it is among a group of streamers preparing to take on Fox for the US rights to the 2030 and 2034 men’s tournaments, a bundle Fifa hopes might fetch as much as $4 billion.
Netflix executives spent years explaining why they didn’t need sport. Their first live forays were deliberately eye-catching: a Mike Tyson comeback fight here, a couple of NFL games on Christmas Day there. Then came a 10-year $5 billion deal for WWE wrestling , a slice of Major League Baseball and now the biggest football tournament on the planet in one of its main markets (Spain holds both the men’s and women’s World Cup titles).
Why the change of heart? Partly because Netflix and its rivals have run out of easy growth in mature markets. Keeping existing subscribers is just as important as finding new ones, and sport is the most reliable antidote for churn. People who binge a drama often cancel when it ends, but people who follow a team tend to stay for the whole season.
Then there’s advertising. Every big streamer now offers a cheaper tier carrying ads, and advertisers will pay a premium for audiences watching live in large numbers simultaneously. Sport is almost the only programming that delivers that any more. The irony is that the streamers did more than anyone to break the habit of collective, scheduled viewing. Now they are spending heavily to buy it back.
[ Watching the Premier League in Ireland is a strikingly costly business Opens in new window ]
The economics of sports rights explains why the price keeps rising inexorably. A league or federation sells something that cannot be replicated by a new entrant (no matter how hard the Saudis try). Rights are carved up by territory, by package and by platform to maximise the number of bidders. Those bidders need the property so badly that they overpay for it. The pay-TV model that Sky built around the Premier League in the 1990s established the principle of sport as the anchor holding an expensive bundle together.
Now the bundle is fraying. According to Ampere Analysis, streaming services will spend about $14.2 billion on sports rights this year. Amazon has overtaken DAZN as the biggest spender, and general entertainment platforms like Amazon, Netflix, Disney+ , Apple and Paramount+ now account for 44 per cent of the total, up from 31 per cent last year. Their advantage over a specialist like DAZN, which has lost billions acquiring and distributing rights across Europe and Japan, is that sport doesn’t have to pay for itself. It only has to make the wider subscription more sticky. And a global platform can spread the cost across hundreds of millions of customers.
But the Spanish deal also shows the limits of exclusivity. Netflix will make one match each day free to watch, and will sub-licence a package to a free-to-air channel that includes every Spain game, both semi-finals and the final. This year’s final in New Jersey drew an average Spanish audience of more than 15 million. No sponsor wants to give up an audience on that scale, and neither does Fifa.
Nor does the law permit it. Under the EU’s audiovisual media rules, member states can draw up lists of events considered so important to society that they must be available on free television. Spain’s 2022 audiovisual law includes the World Cup semi-finals and final. So the Netflix deal recognises that obligation.
Ireland has its own version of these rules. Under section 162 of the Broadcasting Act 2009, designated events include the All-Ireland football and hurling finals, Ireland’s games at the World Cup and European Championship along with the opening games, semi-finals and finals of both tournaments. To qualify, a broadcaster must offer a free service reaching more than 90 per cent of the population. These lists were designed to stop Rupert Murdoch putting national shared moments behind a paywall. Whether they are fit for an era when the bidder is a global streamer, possibly one with a free tier of its own, is a question that can’t be avoided forever.
Irish soccer fans are already feeling the effects of fragmentation. From next year, anyone who wants to follow every Champions League game will need RTÉ, Premier Sports, Sky, Amazon Prime Video and Paramount+, which has taken the bulk of the British rights from TNT Sports. RTÉ has held on to its Wednesday night first pick, but it is now one tenant among many. In Gaelic games, GAAGO has shown how quickly matches viewers once took for granted can migrate behind a paywall and how vociferously the public objects when they do. All of this, of course, is welcome news for dodgy box vendors.
[ Make it easier to watch live sport in one place and you’ll do away with dodgy boxes Opens in new window ]
Free-to-air sport in Ireland is not going away. The designated list remains a protection, and RTÉ still has the reach that rights holders and sponsors value. But the new bidding war is changing the calculus. The streamers are bigger, richer and more strategically focused than the satellite companies ever were, and they’re no longer content to view live sport as an optional extra.

title: Will we use Meath’s new stations as a way to honour Irish women and create local pride?
description: Fifteen stations across the State are named after male historical figures
content:
Sir, – Co Meath is due to see four new stations built at Dunshaughlin, Kilmessan, Navan town centre and to the north of the town.
Fifteen stations across Ireland are eponymous of historical figures, all male and executed republican commanders of the Easter Rising .
Are we to leave the new stations with the neutered and bland names of Navan “Central” and “North” lacking character and pride?
Or are we to use this as an opportunity to commemorate and celebrate the lives of Irish people, particularly Irish women, who have contributed to science, art, medicine, engineering, political life and much more?
Navan town is changing beyond recognition due to new developments in infrastructure. I am both excited and concerned at these possibilities.
Excited at the potential for these investments to improve the quality of life for the people but also concerned at the risk the changes may lead to a homogenised urban environment indistinct from any other lacking any character and degrading our local identity.
I wonder what other readers particularly those in the communities where the proposed new stations will be built feel about this?
I think people should be asked if they were to commemorate the life of a historical Irish figure by naming a new station after them who would it be and why?

title: In case of emergency, keep cash handy as well as a torch and a battery-powered radio
description: Government advice booklet for households fails to plan for a scenario like the great Spanish power blackout
content:
Sir, – I feel the Government’s Be Emergency Ready booklet has a serious omission. It does not emphasise that access to cash may be vital in a situation where regional or national electricity supply has failed.
I happened to be in Spain in April 2025 when there was a power outage for about 12 hours and in some localities even longer. During this time credit cards, mobile phones and internet did not work.
Those without cash were unable to purchase anything in the cafes, shops and other services that remained open or even to hire a taxi. Very distressing for some, particularly families, as with no news updates no one could advise why there was no power or how long the outage may last.
Fortunately I had some cash when all this was going on, meaning I could get some biscuits and the like in the local corner shop. Advice to others would be to have a few notes always handy just in case. Emergencies can happen anytime anywhere. – Yours, etc,

title: Eamon Ryan: Quiet scaling back of Bus Connects is a travesty
description: We will be spending billions building a motorway between Cork and Limerick, bringing yet more traffic into cities that cannot cope
content:
T en years ago, the National Transport Authority launched a BusConnects plan for Dublin . It was designed to combine high-frequency services with 12 new corridors where buses would get priority and cyclists safe passage. Once delivered, it would transform a bus system still running on tram routes from the 1870s, while making Dublin a great city again to get up on a bike.
There followed an extensive public consultation process, which raised opposition from locals understandably concerned that the corridors would take some of their front gardens, cut down much-loved trees or change the character of their village forever. In fairness, the engineers were listening and adapted their designs. Slowly but surely, they won people over, not just in communities but also with a majority of public representatives.
In the end there was widespread support for what was planned, and the officials confidently went into the planning system looking to get the official stamp of approval. Ten years later, we finally have the necessary permissions. Eight of the 12 Dublin corridors have been fully approved and the remaining four are in the last throes of the judicial review process.
Such was the initial success of the approach that it was decided to deliver similar BusConnects schemes for both Cork and Galway . In Cork, the public consultation again raised real opposition, but seven major bus corridors for the city have finally been identified and broadly agreed, with only the planning approvals to come.
In Galway, a corridor planned for the Dublin Road has all the necessary permissions and an important cross-city corridor only awaits a final court decision. That route could be built in double quick time as it requires relatively few major capital works. It would transform the city, linking all the housing on one side with all the offices and factories on the other.
[ As smart cities reduce car use, Ireland goes all in Opens in new window ]
Limerick and Waterford also reviewed their city bus networks and came up with plans to ensure they could provide for their planned population increase. The National Planning Framework is all about promoting better balanced regional development and more compact growth but it won’t work if the public transport systems are not in place first.
After 10 years in planning everything was ready to go – or so it seemed until a review of the National Development Plan last year, which gave no extra money to the Department of Transport, forcing them to choose between the whole raft of transport projects they have in development.
The Government decided to prioritise funding for the Metro, Cork Metropolitan Rail, Dart West upgrade, Finglas Luas, the Galway Ring Road, A5 upgrade and M20 Motorway from Limerick to Cork. The Navan rail line and the other Dart and Limerick rail upgrades will have to wait another decade or two, at the very least.
But it is BusConnects that was the biggest loser. In Dublin, only three of the 12 bus corridors will start construction before 2030, and there is hardly any funding for the new bus services that were due to be introduced over the same period.
In Cork, there is only enough money to build one of the seven promised bus corridors. In Galway, Minister of State for Transport Seán Canney recently indicated that he wants to hold back on building the bus corridors until the ring road starts. And in Limerick and Waterford, work on new bus routes has effectively ground to a halt.
[ What will you say when a child asks: ‘Why are we driving a vehicle that is killing our planet?’ Opens in new window ]
We will be spending billions building a motorway between Cork and Limerick, bringing yet more traffic into cities that cannot cope. We will end up with tens of thousands of houses built around promised public transport services, which are never delivered. Galway, Limerick and Waterford will sprawl further with everyone still driving, continuing a transport strategy that can never work.
There is nothing inevitable about this abandonment of public transport. It is a political choice about what gets priority. Some representatives might think that putting in bus and cycle lanes will be unpopular, while holding back and saying nothing will deliver an electoral gain.
But their silence is doing our citizens a disservice. Councils are failing if they pretend their development plans make any sense without the right transport solutions. Public faith in politics will wane if we keep signing off on climate action plans while pursuing transport strategies that make emissions reductions impossible. At some point, the people who really do want public transport and safe streets will find their voice and demand a more sustainable alternative.
It is time for those people to protest against what is going on. Is car dependency so ingrained in our society that we cannot even imagine better ways of moving around? Are we willing to see BusConnects being abandoned in this way? Are we willing to simply accept that we will be stuck in traffic for the rest of our lives?

title: Bond market turmoil complicates ECB rate decision
description: Frankfurt expected to increase rates again in December
content:
T he European Central Bank (ECB) has raised interest rates twice in the last four months and another hike is expected in December as the bank combats the surge in inflation from energy prices .
That was the holding narrative we’ve been working from for the past number of weeks, but there’s a new weave in the tapestry that is complicating matters.
Turmoil in bond markets is lifting borrowing costs independently of the ECB’s rate hikes, which is also cooling the economy. The bond sell-off and commensurate surge in yields is reducing the need for further rate hikes, placing a question over whether the ECB will opt for a December rate hike.
Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at ING, says the context has changed since September. “The surge in German bond yields since the September meeting has already had roughly the same impact on growth and inflation as an additional 25bp [basis points] rate hike,” he said.
“For France, it’s closer to a 50bp hike. With bond markets doing the ECB’s job, some central bank officials might be less keen to continue hiking than they were at the September meeting.”
[ Looming elections place burden on Ireland to find EU budget compromise Opens in new window ]
ECB chief Christine Lagarde said pretty much the same thing on Saturday, noting that the current bond sell-off was making borrowing more expensive ‌in the euro zone, curbing economic growth and ultimately inflation.
“While ​growth has been resilient, financing conditions have tightened, with long-term interest rates rising notably since our last meeting,” Lagarde told fellow central bankers and finance ministers gathering in Bangkok.
“This will ​slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than projected in our September ​exercise.”
[ Grocery inflation nudging 5 per cent according to fresh data Opens in new window ]
If the ECB opts for a further quarter-point bump in December, that would take the bank’s policy rate to 2.75 per cent, a level financial officials define as restrictive or curtailing of economic activity.
The inflation outlook, and the second-round impacts on food and other items (which have yet to materialise) is being closely monitored.

title: Productivity not a one-way street
description: It is time the Department of Education was held to the same standards of efficiency it expects of others
content:
Sir, – Productivity is invariably raised during public sector pay negotiations , with public servants expected to demonstrate efficiency and accountability. But who holds the Department of Education accountable when its own administrative failures leave newly appointed teachers without pay for weeks?
When I was appointed to a permanent teaching post, I had to wait 10 weeks to receive my salary. Other newly appointed teachers can face delays of up to eight weeks, if not more.
Principals submit appointment forms on teachers’ behalf. Yet the department has reverted to accepting paper forms only, despite having facilitated electronic submissions during Covid . The absence of a reliable way to track submissions or confirm receipt compounds the problem.
Having worked as a senior manager in the private sector, including in human resources, before becoming a teacher, I find this level of inefficiency astonishing. Would a private sector organisation tolerate recurring payroll failures on this scale without demanding answers?
If productivity matters in pay negotiations, it must also apply to the department. Public servants cannot reasonably be expected to meet high standards of performance while the systems supporting them escape equivalent scrutiny.
Electronic submissions, confirmation of receipt and timely payment are basic requirements. It is time the department was held to the same standards of efficiency it expects of others. – Yours, etc,

title: Minister for Gaeltacht has power to alleviate housing crisis in Irish-speaking areas
description: Legislation specifically allows State to give financial help towards building or improving homes
content:
Sir, – David McWilliams draws attention to the long-term damage to the prospects of the Gaeltacht due to lack of housing in Irish-speaking areas (“ From dereliction to Airbnb, the Gaeltacht is being destroyed by the housing crisis ”, Opinion, October 17th).
He states that “the Gaeltacht itself is being destroyed by the refusal to do the very thing that generations of people from the west of Ireland did all over the world: build houses”.
It is worth pointing out that the Minister for the Gaeltacht has powers under the Housing Gaeltacht (Amendment) Act 2001 “to make schemes for the provision of grants or other financial assistance to a person towards the cost of the erection or improvement of a dwelling house in the Gaeltacht”. These powers have not been exercised since the financial crisis of 2008 when they were put on hold but not revoked.
The Minister’s reason for his department’s refusal to use the powers conferred on him by the Oireachtas is that provision of housing in the Gaeltacht is a matter for the local authorities.
But what if the local authority has decided not to provide social or affordable housing in Irish-speaking areas, giving Irish speakers instead the option of moving outside their Irish-speaking community?
This is the policy being implemented by Galway County Council in the strongest Irish speaking area in the country, south Connemara , with a population of about 12,000, with the result that many Irish speakers have to move out of the Irish-speaking area to find suitable housing.
Is it not time for the Taoiseach to ask the Minister for the Gaeltacht why he is not using his powers under existing legislation to help alleviate the housing problem in the Gaeltacht. His refusal to establish schemes under the existing legislation is, in the words of McWilliams, “destroying the Gaeltacht”. – Yours, etc,

title: DAA International to run exclusive Washington terminal
description: Airports company chosen to develop and run premium passenger facility at US capital’s international gateway
content:
State airport operator DAA’s international business has won a contract to run a VIP passenger terminal at Washington Dulles International, the main gateway to the US capital.
DAA International, part of the group that runs Cork and Dublin airports, has operations in North America, the Middle East, Europe and Asia, managing airports and facilities and advising on investment and development.
Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority (MWAA) has hired the Irish business to develop, lease and run a new premium passenger terminal at Washington Dulles International Airport, the pair have confirmed.
[ DAA made more than €1.7m per week from car parks in 2025 Opens in new window ]
The 3,500sq m VIP terminal will cash in on growing demand for premium travel services and will be the first of its kind to serve the US capital, DAA said on Tuesday.
The deal involves a 30-month development phase followed by a 20-year operating term. Facilities will include suites, lounges and bars, transport to aircraft, personalised check-in and baggage services and security screening.
Global architecture firm Corgan will design the terminal building. DAA predicted that the project would create jobs locally and open opportunities for businesses in the region to supply goods and services.
News of DAA International’s appointment by the Washington authority follows the recent award to fellow group subsidiary, Aer Rianta International, of a contract to run the duty-free business in JFK New York’s terminal four.
Welcoming confirmation of the partnership, DAA deputy chief executive Nick Cole noted that Washington Dulles played a “vital role” in connecting the US with the wider world.
“This appointment demonstrates the continued confidence that airport authorities place in DAA International’s ability to deliver complex, high-profile aviation projects,” he said.
Cole, who is also chief executive of DAA International itself, branded the agreement with Washington a testament to the strength of the wider Irish airport operator company.
MWAA executive vice-president Chryssa Westerlund explained that the project would draw on DAA International’s experience in airport operations and terminal development.
Washington Dulles is responding to “traveller demand”, said Westerlund.
“Adding a VIP terminal at Dulles International reflects our commitment to giving passengers the options to choose an airport experience that fits their needs,” she added.
[ Residents seek injunction to force DAA to comply with Dublin Airport passenger cap Opens in new window ]
Minister for Transport Darragh O’Brien described the contract award as a “positive endorsement” of DAA’s expertise in international airport management and advice.
“This contract provides an opportunity for DAA to strengthen its presence in the United States,” he said, adding that this was a key market for Irish companies which were creating jobs there.
DAA International deputy chief executive Clive Power said the project highlighted the international reputation of Irish aviation expertise.
“The DAA Group continues to demonstrate that Irish aviation expertise can compete and succeed on the world stage,” said Power.

title: Don’t forget about one key job at a station Mass
description: Hens in the hall might not have been forgiven
content:
Sir, – Further to Colette Sheridan’s Irish Diary on hosting a station Mass at home (October 13th) and the letters that followed , one key job has not been mentioned.
In some households the hens were kept in boxes in the hall, and before the stations they had to be moved out, boxes and all, and given a new home so the hall could be cleared and cleaned. No house was ready to host the station Mass until the hens had been relocated. – Yours, etc,

title: How can Americans stand by and let this happen?
description: US failures in Ukraine show us why the Trump administration is so dangerous
content:
Sir, - This morning, I spoke to a Ukrainian man delivering bread to Tesco in Rathcoole. He was empty of emotion. He didn’t mention the United States or Donald Trump, but he didn’t need to. His eyes said everything.
While Europe must do more, it beggars belief that Lindsey Graham’s carefully considered bipartisan bill is not being fully implemented and that the US is not providing every possible measure of support to help Ukraine resist Russia ’s aggression.
Trump’s actions are shocking and dangerous. How can Americans, at home and abroad, stand by and allow this to continue? – Yours, etc,

title: ‘We are terrified’: Father calls for son driving at 200km/h into traffic to be detained
description: Boy has been missing from Tusla care for more than two weeks, and is nightly posting videos of himself breaking into cars
content:
A teenage boy missing from care and driving stolen cars at high speeds into oncoming traffic is going to “kill himself or someone else” if he is not detained, his father has said.
The boy has been missing from Tusla care for more than two weeks, and is nightly posting videos of himself and others in cars driving at almost 200km/h, sometimes into oncoming traffic.
“We are terrified about what could happen and no one seems able or willing to stop him,” his father told The Irish Times.
Neither the father nor his son can be identified as the boy is in voluntary care and a minor before the courts on dozens of charges associated with dangerous driving and car theft.
“He’s driving the wrong way up the roads ... He is going to kill himself or someone else. That’s the biggest thing I worry about,” his father said.
“I have no idea where he is or who he is with. He doesn’t have his [ADHD] medication or his epi-pen [for a severe nut allergy].”
In correspondence to the father’s solicitor when the boy was missing from its care, Tusla said: “[The boy] has successfully re-engaged with a structured, intentional weekly plan and is displaying strong motivation to participate.
“He also actively participates in the weekly Tusla wellness programme. [The teenager] has a well-established rapport with his allocated staff team, frequently engaging in shared pro-social activities such as card games, baking, and video games.”
The boy’s father described Tusla’s assessment of his son as “clearly incorrect”.
The Irish Times has seen videos and photographs posted on the boy’s social media of himself and others breaking into, travelling in and driving cars.
One recent video shows a car driving at speed in a housing estate and braking suddenly, causing sparks to fly up from screeching tyres.
In one photo, showing the boy standing out of the driver door of a car, the vehicle’s registration number is clearly visible. In others, speedometers show cars being driven at almost 200km/h.
During an appearance by the boy at Dublin District Children’s Court last month, Judge Brendan Toale heard of the father’s wish for him to be in special care. He has been detained on three occasions at Oberstown Children Detention Campus.
“It seems to me – and has seemed to me for a very considerable time – that this is a case that is crying out for an application to special care,” said the judge.
“I am fully aware of the intervention or lack of to some extent ... on the part of the State. He has been on the radar for quite a considerable degree of time.”
No application for special care has been made for the boy to date. Though there are 26 special care beds, just 15 are open due to staff shortages.
“He loved his primary school but didn’t really settle in secondary,” said his father. “He wouldn’t go back to school after the summer last year. It was murder here in the mornings.
“Even the school secretary was on the phone trying to coax him to come in. Then he was on the social media watching the fellas with the cars and then it started from that.”
The boy then began absconding, sometimes travelling as far as an adjoining county and often overnight. Last year he was picked up by gardaí 20km from his home in the company of known drug-dealers.
“He changed completely in personality, went totally against me,” the father said. “When he went missing – and I told the guards – he’d smash things up in the house.
“I’d tell him, ‘I have to tell the police when you’re gone. I wouldn’t be responsible for you if I didn’t’. There were times I had the guards here four times in a day, at all hours of the night.
“I couldn’t go to work. If I tried to stop him going out he’d threaten me with screwdrivers, vice-grips he’d robbed up in Woodies.”
Supports from several agencies were “promised” but “never happened” – including intervention by Tusla’s education welfare officers, organised day-activities, and counselling for the boy.
“I asked for help with his behaviours and didn’t get it,” the man said. “The end of last year I told him I couldn’t deal with his behaviours any more. I put him into voluntary care.”
The boy has been in several temporary emergency placements, in different parts of the country, but has repeatedly absconded.
“I thought he’d get all the services he needed then but it’s gone downhill since. He has gone from zero convictions a year ago to 38 now. I think the only thing that will keep him safe is special care, or to be put in Oberstown again.”
In its letter, Tusla said it would “continue to work with [the boy] to build resilience, enhance his capacity for safe decision-making, and mitigate community risks. In parallel, the agency will continue to review the necessity of special care”.
In response to queries, a spokesman for Tusla said the agency could not comment on individual children.
“We note a marked increase in the complexity of needs among a small cohort of vulnerable young people, including challenges related to mental health, substance misuse, disability, exploitation, and behaviours associated with criminality,” the agency said.
“Meeting these needs requires an inter-agency and whole-of-Government response, including timely access to services across the HSE, Tusla and in some cases, the juvenile justice system.
“Special care represents a profound intervention involving the deprivation of a young person’s liberty as a measure of last resort.
“Its purpose is as a short-term therapeutic intervention for young people who meet certain eligibility criteria and are the subject of a High Court order.”

title: Government must ensure meaningful progress for workers in private sector
description: Rising costs affect all employees
content:
Sir, – The Government ’s decision to appoint an independent mediator is welcome and should help resolve the public sector dispute. The Government’s change of heart recognises the value of negotiation and collective bargaining in resolving disputes and addressing workers’ pay and conditions amid the cost-of-living crisis.
But this crisis also affects private sector workers. Many face employers who refuse to recognise their trade unions or negotiate collectively, leaving workers with little influence over decisions affecting their livelihoods.
If the Government recognises the value of collective bargaining for its own employees, it must ensure private-sector workers can benefit from it too.
The EU Directive on Adequate Minimum Wages requires countries where collective bargaining coverage falls below 80 per cent to establish an action plan to increase it. The Government must turn that obligation into meaningful progress for workers.
All workers face rising living costs. All deserve the right to organise, be represented by their trade union and bargain collectively for fair pay and decent conditions. – Yours, etc,

title: German model shows how bad Ireland’s transport system has become
description: We remain cut off from each other by meagre public transport offerings
content:
Sir, – I’ve returned to Ireland after 10 years living as a musician in Berlin . Moving to the country, I was prepared for the meagre offerings of public transport available, but only when my film was accepted to be shown at Roscommon Film Festival have I come to realise how abysmal our public transport offerings truly are.
On a Saturday night, if one would want to journey to the capital of our country from a town that has a train station, say, after attending a film festival in said Metropolis, the last bus available is 6:30pm and last train is 7pm.
Now, this may seem normal to people who’ve lived in Ireland their whole lives. But as a touring musician in Germany I was able to get from the most remote, tiniest of towns to any other part of the country 24 hours a day, seven days a week – including public holidays and Christmas, for that matter.
I once played a German music festival whose train stop was a literal field. How can a country so flooded with cultural hotspots, tucked away in nooks and crannies of the country like Dingle and west Cork, be so cut off from each other? And have no possibilities for return, if you ever manage to get there in the first place?
Sipping on a Guinness in Ennis yesterday, my attention fell on an old sign beside my table. It stated: “Enjoy the Western Rails – Journey from Kilkee, Milltown Malbay to Ennistymon.”
If only. How have we gone so wrong? And on an island famous for its craic and ceol, how in God’s name is one to go anywhere other than their local to find any? And if it’s not walking distance, how in God’s name will you get back, if you want to sample a Guinness while you’re there? – Yours, etc,

title: Bloomberg plans to double Irish staff number in pursuit of growth
description: Company has rapidly increased staffing in Dublin, its largest EU office, over the past 12 months
content:
Business information company Bloomberg is expanding its Irish office, planning to double its staff to almost 400 through investment in engineering, technology, product development and data capabilities.
The company employs 190 people in Dublin, a figure that has doubled in the last 12 months to make the office its largest in the EU and a strategic centre for Bloomberg’s engineering, product development, and data capabilities.
To oversee the expansion, Bloomberg has appointed Amanda Brady as director for Ireland, with Richard Norton relocating from the US as head of engineering.
Donegal native Brady said the Irish-based engineers would be involved in the building of critical products for financial professionals, with Ireland a natural home for the operations. Bloomberg is aiming to have 250 people in Dublin by the end of next year, with the remaining staff coming on board in the following two years.
The firm has already secured additional space in its building in Charlemont Square in Dublin, where it moved last year, to facilitate growth. That expansion means the office is now larger than Bloomberg’s office, where it has a large engineering presence, working on trading and market data infrastructure
“We are now the largest in the EU. London will always be the flagship,” said Brady. “But we have big ambitions.”
Norton, who has worked with Bloomberg for 20 years, will also lead the company’s enterprise data delivery platform Data License Plus globally. He said the Irish team’s work was core to the firm’s data and technology offering.
“Last year we made a number of investments here in the team in Ireland, particularly in engineering,” he said.
Bloomberg’s future expansion is being supported by IDA Ireland.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin welcomed the announcement, saying it was evidence of the strong economic offering Ireland has in technology, data, and Stem [Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics]. “The Government is committed to ensuring that Ireland remains a trusted and stable location for critical talent and business alike,” he said. “Digital and technological services are crucial for future-proofing our economy.”
Bloomberg does not publicly report its financial results. According to Forbes, however, it generated revenues of almost $15 billion (€13.4 billion) last year, up from $13.3 billion in 2024.
In a memo to staff in February, Bloomberg Media chief executive said the division’s revenues were up 6 per cent in 2025, with subscription revenues up 10 per cent.

title: Irish motor-claim costs up 10% as inflation drives damage expenses
description: Benefits of insurance reform being ‘eroded by excessive legal costs’, says industry group
content:
Irish motor insurers estimate that the average claims cost per policy rose 10 per cent to €424 last year, driven by an increase in both vehicle damage and personal injury claims costs, according to Central Bank of Ireland data.
The bank’s latest annual report on motor insurance shows that the average cost of damage claims per policy amounted to €197, up 6 per cent on the year, but almost double where it stood in 2019, before the pandemic.
Insurers have highlighted in recent years how inflation has driven up the cost of labour and spare parts, while advances in smart technology have added to the complexity of modern vehicles.
[ Irish motor insurers still pay 50% more than UK peers for third-party injury claims Opens in new window ]
The average cost of personal injury claims is ultimately expected to amount to €228 per policy in 2025, up 14 per cent on the year, but broadly in line with where they stood before the Covid-19 pandemic.
While personal injury guidelines, introduced in 2021, have been “effective in reducing awards for standard claims, insurers now expect an increase in the number of exceptionally large claims, and in the number of claimants going to court, driving up legal costs,” said the bank.
[ Personal injury guidelines result in sharp fall in claims Opens in new window ]
The estimates of costs per policy also take into consideration reserves insurers have set aside for claims relating to 2025 that have not yet settled. The figures are based on the bank’s National Claims Information Database.
Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan backed down in July last year from asking the Oireachtas to rubber stamp the Judicial Council’s plans to increase personal injury awards by almost 17 per cent, following an inflation spike after the awards were initially unveiled. While the Injuries Resolution Board (IRB) remains bound by the original guidelines, judges have more discretion to potentially depart from the guidelines.
