Assessing claims for less than €100,000 – which make up 94 per cent of cases – the bank found that the average compensation for a litigated case was €19,600. That’s lower than the average €19,734 award received from going through the less expensive and quicker IRB process.
However, legal costs for litigated cases averaged €19,902 – more than the average compensation award – while those for Personal Injuries Resolution Board cases averaged €791.
“When average compensation is virtually identical whether these claims are settled through litigation or the injuries resolution board, yet average legal costs in litigation exceed the compensation paid, it highlights the importance of how claims are resolved,” said Tracy Sheridan, a member of the board of the Alliance for Insurance Reform and owner of Kidspace play centres in Rathfarnham and Rathcoole in Dublin.
“We need stronger action from Government to encourage more suitable claims to be resolved through the injuries resolution board, ensuring fair compensation without unnecessary litigation costs.”
Insurance Ireland chief executive Moyagh Murdock said: “It is increasingly disheartening that the benefits delivered by insurance reform continue to be eroded by excessive legal costs.”
The average premium per policy rose 4 per cent last year to €655, bringing the increase from 2022 to 18 per cent. However, the bank noted “encouraging signs” as premiums started to fall in the second half of last year. “This mirrors the trend seen in the [Central Statistics Office] consumer price index for insurance, which has also seen the average price of a premium continue to decrease into 2026,” it said.
The ultimate objective of an insurance company is to pay out on all claims and make a profit, the bank said. In 2025, insurers took in more in premiums than they paid out in costs. This, coupled with investment income, is how insurers mainly make profit.
The net profit of Irish motor insurers amounted to €89 million last year, equating to 5.7 per cent of gross earned premiums of €1.54 billion.

title: Opinion: Varadkar wants the south to apologise to Northern nationalists, but it’s more complicated
description: No Irish nationalist wanted partition. Partition was created by Westminster
content:
L eo Varadkar believes people living south of the Border will one day have to apologise for abandoning northern nationalists after partition a century ago. The former taoiseach’s words in Dungannon earlier this month will be taken as a statement of the obvious by many, or most northern nationalists, since they have believed it for generations.
However, Varadkar’s speech deserves far greater scrutiny than it has so far attracted, especially his argument that southern nationalists “went off and built our State and largely forgot about what happened up here for a very long time”.
Varadkar does not elaborate on what should be on the apologies list. Reconciliation, however, should start with everyone acknowledging – especially northern nationalists – that southern Irish nationalists did not create partition. Nor were they responsible for, or could they have done much about Stormont’s discrimination against Catholics. That responsibility lies with London and a unionist-dominated Stormont.
No Irish nationalist wanted partition. Partition was created by Westminster. With the exception of a tiny number of Irish Parliamentary Party MPs, no Irish nationalist was consulted about the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, nor voted for it.
Northern Ireland was a fait accompli by the time the Anglo-Irish Treaty talks began in late 1921, when London made clear from the off that Northern Ireland ‘s status was not up for negotiation.
Nevertheless, Arthur Griffith won a Boundary Commission to redraw the Border in line with inhabitants’ wishes; it would, the Irish believed, make Northern Ireland unviable. But it proved a disaster for nationalists. The Cumann na nGaedheal government took it seriously, producing thousands of documents to back up its claims. However, it appointed Eoin MacNeill, who proved a clueless interlocutor and inept Free State negotiator.
If Varadkar believes an apology is owed, he should start here. Two critical errors made by Fine Gael’s Cumann na nGaedheal forebears copper-fastened partition in its early days.
Firstly, they reinforced the hard Border in 1923 by establishing customs posts. Customs were governments’ main source of revenues then. Equally, they were intended as a declaration of Irish sovereignty but they made partition a reality for Border communities – on both sides of the religious divide, and on both sides of the Border – who did not want to be where they were on the map.
When the Boundary Commission’s findings were leaked in November 1925, showing only modest adjustments and even ceding parts of the Free State, the Cumann na nGaedheal government sought to suppress it. In return for keeping the Border in place, the British government agreed to write off Ireland’s share of the UK imperial debt, the equivalent then of 80 per cent of the new State’s annual GDP.
William T Cosgrave and his northern counterpart, James Craig, promised a new era. Cosgrave took the debt write-down but they never met again. Indeed, the leaders of both jurisdictions would not do so for 40 years, when Fianna Fáil’s Seán Lemass and the Ulster Unionist Party’s Terence O’Neill met in Stormont Castle in January 1965.
If Cumann na nGaedheal’s attitude to partition can be characterised as one of cynical neglect, the same cannot be said of Fianna Fáil. In and out of office, Éamon de Valera was obsessed with partition. Articles 2 and 3 of his 1937 Constitution refused to recognise it, with Dublin claiming jurisdiction as a matter of law. In 1938, he did make progress with Neville Chamberlain during talks to end the Economic War.
Chamberlain was prepared to state that Britain had “no selfish, strategic or economic interest” in Northern Ireland and that Britain would leave when, and if, a majority wanted.
However, such a declaration was scuppered by the IRA’s 1939 bombing campaign and the second World War. In 1940, de Valera rejected Winston Churchill’s offer to end partition in return for Ireland’s entry into the war, believing it would not be honoured. De Valera continued to campaign against partition after leaving office, but his international tour was a failure. Back in Dublin, the inter-party coalition government led by John A Costello decided to fund nationalist candidates in the North.
Instead of aiding the nationalist minority, however, the action galvanised the unionist majority into coalescing around the Ulster Unionist Party in the 1949 Stormont elections.
Successive Irish governments failed to end partition not because they were uninterested, but because their campaigning to end it was counterproductive.
[ No friends in the North: Partition has become embedded in the daily lives of people on the island Opens in new window ]
Ireland’s second World War neutrality meant there was never any realistic chance of bringing international pressure on London. Meanwhile, Costello’s government was busy creating a confessional Catholic state inimical to Ulster unionists.
Lemass wanted to end partition, but he saw the problem differently to de Valera. De Valera blamed the British for it. Therefore, only the British could end it. Lemass saw it as an issue between unionists and nationalists. “I could see it as almost a disease which would ultimately destroy the nation, and I therefore began to talk about unity as a spiritual and not a political conception,” Lemass remarked.
Lemass and O’Neill parked partition, concentrating on issues of concern. Their lead was followed by Jack Lynch, but Northern Ireland erupted when the Troubles began in 1969. In August 1969, Lynch made his “standing idly by” speech, raising expectations that the Irish army would save northern nationalists from loyalist mobs. In reality, it was in no position to invade anyone, let alone a large military power.
That imbalance in strength was there from the beginning.
Could partition have been overturned in the 1920s? There were attempts, beginning with the IRA’s May/June 1922 offensive, but it was a complete failure.
When a contingent of pro- and anti-Treaty forces captured the villages of Pettigo and Belleek in June 1922, Churchill deployed 1,000 British troops, who shelled the Irish positions.
Churchill’s action was overkill, but it was deliberately done. Any adventurism by Irish nationalists would be met by an overwhelming response. The message was understood clearly in Dublin.
Irish governments in later years were central to one effort after another to bring peace: Sunningdale, the Anglo-Irish Agreement; the 1993 Framework Document, the 1998 Belfast Agreement. Varadkar leveraged EU support to prevent a hard Irish Border after Brexit. Taoiseach Micheál Martin established the Shared Island fund which is backing projects on both sides of the Border. None of these are the actions of bystanders.
The reconciliation sought by Varadkar between southern and northern nationalists must first answer a few key questions: what should, or could the South have done differently? What options did it have?
If Varadkar, and the many others who agree with him, believes there should be a process of reconciliation between northern and southern nationalists, it should be informed by facts.
Ronan McGreevy is an Irish Times journalist and a historian.

title: The power of holy water cannot be diluted
description: Bucket mishap at station Mass in rural Donegal fondly recalled
content:
Sir, – About 1953, a station Mass was held in a house in the townland of Dirlaught, Lettermacaward, Co Donegal . My twin brothers, Karl and Pauric Cannon, were serving as clerks at the Mass.
Among the priest’s first duties was to bless a bucket of water for use as holy water. He then heard confessions and celebrated Mass, after which he was served a meal.
It was while the dishes were being washed afterwards that someone discovered, to considerable consternation, that some of the newly blessed holy water had been used for the washing-up. Only half a bucket remained.
The lady of the house was informed and there was much discussion about what could be done. Eventually, someone offered a practical solution: “Sure, we’ll top it up with ordinary water, and nobody will know the difference.”
“Oh no,” her firm reply came. “We must leave the holy water at its full strength.”
A true story and a fond memory of the Stations tradition. And a lesson on the power of holy water. – Yours, etc,

title: Culture wars in the North
description: Sinn Féin and the DUP need to park their cultural identity issues and take responsibility for running the province
content:
Sir, – At a time in Northern Ireland when cultural identity is displaying minimal tolerance for its neighbour, as highlighted in the Drumcree Orange Order parade dispute and the vandalism of dual-language street signs, surely it is time to consider the “parity of esteem” that was regularly quoted during the peace process.
In Belfast, Sinn Féin controls Belfast City Council. It has invoked a policy whereby dual-language (English/Irish) street signs will be erected if only 15 per cent of residents approve this, even if a majority oppose it. It results in a significant number of streets having to accept a substantial minority verdict.
If a similar threshold (15 per cent in favour) regarding Orange Order parades was then considered, in the interests of equality and tolerance of each other’s culture, the parade should then be allowed to proceed, and this would save finance to the local economy by negating the need for a parades commission.
Unfortunately, our graceless, shameless Sinn Féin and DUP MLAs are more interested in the distraction of culture wars. (These typically include Irish-language signs and loyalist marches where they are not welcome, funding for bonfires, and a big increase in funding for the Casement Park redevelopment.)
These “cultural” issues cost countless millions of pounds. Rather than dealing with the real issues affecting everyone in Northern Ireland (such as the broken health system, potholed road infrastructure, crumbling school buildings, environmental disaster in Lough Neagh and public sector pay deficit), our representatives embarrassingly go whingeing to Westminster to complain that they have been allocated insufficient funds.
They should park the so-called culture issues until we can afford to resolve them and start to take responsibility for running the country. – Yours, etc,

title: Wolfe Tones ‘leaving no stone unturned’ in bid to rectify Meath’s dire Leinster club record
description: Royal County clubs have managed just one Leinster club football title success in 40 years
content:
Wolfe Tones manager Shane McCoy has been putting in the miles as the new county champions set out on their bid to break the bleak record of Meath clubs in the Leinster club Senior Football Championship .
The weekend before the Meath final, McCoy travelled to Aughrim to watch the Wicklow SFC decider between An Tóchar and Blessington. The winners of that game had been drawn to meet the winners of the Meath final in Leinster, so McCoy hopped in his car and headed for the Garden County.
“We’ll be leaving no stone unturned to go as far as we can in Leinster,” said McCoy. “It was a Sunday to myself and the wife wasn’t too pleased but, yeah, I went to Aughrim to see the Wicklow final.”
When it comes to Meath clubs in the provincial competition, a dire recent history demonstrates you can never be too prepared.
No Meath side has won the Leinster club football title since Dunshaughlin in 2002. It is the county’s only triumph in the Leinster club SFC over the last 40 years.
[ Wolfe Tones prove the kicking kings as they secure a third Meath crown Opens in new window ]
No club from the county has even contested a final since Skryne in 2004. The last time a Meath club managed to win consecutive games in the provincial championship was Skryne in 2010. There have been far too many one-and-done campaigns. From 2011 until 2025, Meath clubs have contested 20 Leinster championship games and won only six.
Since Skryne’s appearance in the 2004 final, eight different Leinster counties have been represented in at least one provincial decider – Meath, Wexford and Wicklow are the outliers. Kilkenny clubs don’t play in the club senior football championship.
Wolfe Tones won their third Meath SFC last Sunday with a comprehensive victory over Donaghmore/Ashbourne.
In their previous two forays into Leinster, Wolfe Tones collected just one win – beating St Joseph’s of Louth in a first-round fixture in 2006. That was followed by a defeat to Dublin champions UCD in a quarter-final, while they lost to Kilmacud Crokes after winning the Meath crown in 2021.
An Tóchar collected a first Wicklow title in 31 years with a 0-21 to 1-7 victory over Blessington two weekends ago. The Wolfe Tones vs An Tóchar game will take place in Ashbourne on Sunday, November 15th.
“We’ve got a couple of weeks to prepare for that,” said McCoy. ”We’ll enjoy the next couple of days but, to be honest with you, these boys expect you to be prepared for a couple of weeks’ time. That’ll be the Leinster campaign.
“When you look through the panel, there’s a lot of boys in their mid-twenties so there is definitely a maturity and leadership within the group.”
Thomas O’Reilly is one of those leaders. The 29-year-old was superb in Sunday’s final, finishing the game with 0-3 and causing havoc all afternoon.
O’Reilly played in the 2021 defeat to Kilmacud Crokes and says the current crop of players are determined to make a mark on the provincial championship.
“We want this journey to go as far as we can take it,” he said. “We’ll celebrate this first, but at least we have a bit of a period now before the Leinster championship starts. We want to give a good account of ourselves.”
Summerhill beat Killoe Young Emmets of Longford in the opening round last year but subsequently lost to Athy by 10 points.
In 2024, Dunshaughlin suffered a 13-point drubbing at the hands of St Loman’s Mullingar while in 2023 it was a 10-point loss for Summerhill against Naas.
So, it hasn’t necessarily been a case of narrow losses either for Meath clubs in Leinster.
Dublin clubs have dominated the competition over the last decade. The last time a non-Dublin side won the Seán McCabe Cup was 2018, with Mullinalaghta’s surprise victory over Kilmacud Crokes the anomaly.
Some 14 of the last 15 Leinster senior club football finals have included a club from the capital. Cuala are already installed as favourites to win it this year but the Dublin champions are on the stacked side of the draw.
Their first outing is a round-one tie against Tullamore, who are a seasoned outfit having recently completed a four-in-a-row in Offaly. The winners of that game will then meet the Kildare champions in a quarter-final.
Laois champions Portarlington or Carlow’s Rathvilly will be waiting in a semi-final.
On the other side of the draw, if Wolfe Tones can negotiate safe passage beyond An Tóchar they would progress to a semi-final against either the champions of Westmeath, Longford, Wexford or Louth.
So there is a genuine opportunity for Wolfe Tones to rectify the dismal record of Meath outfits in the competition.
“It’s a special club with a lot of great people,” added O’Reilly. “We’ve been chasing this [county title] for the last number of years, [and] we probably felt like we left one behind us in 2024 when we lost the final to Dunshaughlin.
“It was a bit disappointing the following year. Then Shane and Ciarán [Marks] came in this year and set out their stall early on what they wanted us to go and achieve. They knew we had a lot of potential in the group.”
The challenge for Wolfe Tones now is to prove that potential extends beyond the county border.

title: Fintan O'Toole: Zionism is not racism, any more than Irish nationalism is sectarianism
description: If Israel-Palestine is, for us, a story about Ireland, it ought to be, not a simplistic narrative of good and evil
content:
A ccording to Maurice Cohen, chairman of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland, the Herbert Park Hotel in Dublin cancelled a booking for 70 delegates to last week’s international conference on combating anti-Semitism.
The conference was held here as part of Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the European Union . Some of the delegates are Jewish, some are not – Ireland’s representative, Colm O’Loughlin, is a principal officer at the Department of Justice.
According to Cohen, the hotel manager asked him whether the Israel Defense Forces would be involved. “Nothing I had said had anything whatsoever to do with the Israeli army, yet somehow that was where the conversation had gone.” The booking was subsequently cancelled without explanation.
Whatever the intentions of the hotel (and one suspects that the cancellation was motivated more by a desire to avoid the possibility of protest than by any conscious prejudice), this should be just as upsetting to Irish people as the effective cancellation of Sally Rooney in the UK over her support for Palestine Action.
The difference between virtue-signalling and standing on moral principle is that the latter has a price tag. It imposes obligations. In the case of Ireland’s official and popular stance against the Israeli regime, there is a double duty: we have to be completely consistent in opposing the dehumanisation of Palestinians – and we must be equally unfailing in opposing the demonisation of Jews.
I know that for many readers this second claim may border on the insulting. Why, people may ask, should we have to prove that we are not anti-Semites just because we are horrified by the slaughter in Gaza and the ongoing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank ?
But there are, in turn, two good answers to this question. One is that the State has a duty of care to its small Jewish minority, a community that has every reason to be hypersensitive to signs of threat, of which there have been deplorably many. The other is that anti-Semitism is an ineradicable pathogen that lurks in the subsoil waiting for the right conditions in which to thrive. Those conditions exist right now.
Suffering is not a zero-sum game. It does not diminish our consciousness of the Palestinian catastrophe if we recognise that Jewish people worldwide are having a terrible time.
Most of the Jewish people I know have (to put it mildly) very complex relationships with Israel. But the conjunction of the Hamas pogroms, the appalling scale of the retaliatory violence and the rise of anti-Semitic attacks in Europe has been heart-rending and head-wrecking for them.
In this atmosphere, anti-Semitism is being trivialised in two contradictory ways. Binyamin Netanyahu’s regime belittles it by using it with unabashed cynicism as a moral shield: anyone who objects to the regime’s ultraviolence is an anti-Semite. But some people who take up the Palestinian cause minimise anti-Semitism, too.
Ask a member of one of Australia’s indigenous nations how she feels about the Irish. It’s not overwhelming love
They do so by parroting two stupid slogans. One is “by any means necessary” – a licence for atrocity that justifies the murder and kidnapping of Jewish civilians. Lurking within it is the ancient anti-Semitic trope: the Jews deserve it because they are collectively guilty.
The other is “Zionism is a form of racism”. This is as historically illiterate as, for example, “Irish nationalism is a form of sectarianism”. There are many racist Zionists and many bigoted Irish nationalists. There are also Zionists who put their lives on the line to try to defend their Palestinian neighbours and there are Irish nationalists who believe passionately in a pluralist idea of nationhood.
As Irish people, we have less excuse than most for not understanding that it is possible to be both a refugee and a colonist.
The best study we have of Irish attitudes to Jewish people is one conducted in 2023 by Miceal Canavan, of Queen’s University Belfast, and Liam Kneafsey of Trinity College Dublin . It found little evidence of hostility to Jews. (Islamophobia is much more common.)
But what it did find is that Irish people view the Israel- Palestine conflict through the lens of our own history: “Ireland’s sympathy for Palestine”, as the authors put it “is, at root, a story about Ireland.”
But if that’s the case then we damn well ought to know that people fleeing persecution and discrimination build their sanctuaries on other people’s land. Have you ever asked a member of one of Australia’s indigenous nations how she feels about the Irish? I have – and it’s not overwhelming love.
If Israel-Palestine is, for us, a story about Ireland, then it ought to be not a simplistic narrative of good and evil but a tragic tale in which Palestinians were made to salve Europe’s guilty conscience just as indigenous people in North America, Australia and Argentina paid for the British policies that made Ireland unlivable for so many of our own people.
Jews didn’t just go to Israel because they liked the scenery – or because they fancied a bit of racism. Unthinking sloganeering obliterates the past that led to Israel’s creation. Can we blame Jewish people if some of them hear in it a call for future obliteration, too?
The essential mechanism of racism is collective blame. Every bad act is attributed not to those who commit it but to all those whom they resemble. In the extreme polarisation of current politics, there is a danger that support for Palestine becomes a tribal signifier. It defines membership of “Us” and opposition to “Them”.
The problem is there is a deep history in the West of “Them” being not Israel but the Jews. Not to be aware of that history is to be at risk, through ignorance and thoughtlessness, of repeating it.
We should support Palestinians not because they are Palestinian, but because they are human beings whose humanity is being literally and metaphorically erased. We should oppose Israel’s government not because it is Jewish, but because it is systematically carrying through the logic of that dehumanisation.
The antidote to this poison is not more poison. The worse the Israeli regime gets, the greater the urgency of standing unequivocally against anti-Semitism.

title: Britain supplying 16% of Irish electricity, EirGrid says
description: National grid operator says the Republic will have enough power for winter
content:
Ireland relies on imports from Britain for around one sixth of its electricity, according to national grid operator EirGrid .
The State company estimates that electricity demand in the Republic could peak at a record 6,100 megawatts (MW) this winter, topping a 6,024MW high hit in January 2025.
Newly connected power plants, temporary generators and electricity imports from Britain will aid the system in meeting this demand with supplies to spare, according to EirGrid’s director of system operations, Diarmaid Gillespie.
The Republic and Northern Ireland now import around 16 per cent of their combined electricity needs from Britain via three power lines running under the Irish Sea, EirGrid confirmed.
Britain supplied 15.8 per cent of Irish electricity in the 12 months to July and 16.4 per cent in 2025, according to the State company.
The British National Energy System Operator is due to publish figures this week indicating that there is no risk to those imports, Gillespie noted on Monday.
Gillespie was speaking in advance of the publication on Monday of EirGrid’s Winter Outlook, which assesses whether the Republic will have enough electricity to meet its likely needs from November 2nd to April 4th.
Risks that the system will not have enough electricity to meet demand at any point over those five months are at their lowest for several years, the report shows.
The “loss of load expectation”, which measures the probability of there not being enough electricity to meet instantaneous demand, is less than 50 minutes for the entire five months, down from 1.1 hours last winter and 3.6 hours the year before, according to Gillespie.
[ Ireland can capture the AI dividend while mitigating the risks Opens in new window ]
That is against a standard of three hours set by the Department of Energy, he pointed out.
“That is very good, it’s very low,” Gillespie said. “The day of the highest peak demand, we have a 1,000 megawatt margin.”
The loss of load figure is an assessment of risk, so there is little likelihood of an actual shortage of electricity supplies, he said.
New gas, wind and solar power plants capable of generating 1,084MW of electricity, enough to serve more than 500,000 customers, have connected to the grid since last winter, while 63MW of batteries have also plugged into the system, EirGrid’s figures show.
That includes 275MW of gas-fired power plants built by Lumcloon Energy in Castlelost, Co Offaly, designed to switch on quickly at times when wind and solar power supplies are low, along with 809MW of renewables.
EirGrid maintains temporary generators in Dublin, Offaly and Kerry, as an emergency backstop.
It called on these twice to back up supplies this summer, the only occasions on which they were deployed for this purpose since the grid company commissioned them in 2023.
Industry overseer, the Commission for the Regulation of Utilities, announced last month that they would remain in place until 2028 and 2029 at the latest.
[ Emergency electricity plants to cost customers €1.4bn Opens in new window ]
Electricity customers will have paid €1.4 billion for the temporary emergency generators once they are all shut down.
Turbines at the old ESB Tarbert power plant have been converted from burning coal to heavy fuel oil and can be called on as a last resort.
EirGrid has not used this option, but has occasionally ordered them to be ready in case they were needed, Gillespie said.

title: What are telematics policies, and how can they knock thousands off motor insurance costs?
description: Telematics policies use technology to track a driver’s habits through a small device or app
content:
Young people who agree to allow their driving to be monitored remotely as a precondition of their insurance policy can end up saving thousands of euro a year on the cost of cover, according to new research from price comparison and switching website Bonkers.ie .
However, those who don’t want telematics to be part of their motor policy can end up paying close to €4,000 for annual cover.
Telematics car insurance uses smart technology to track a driver’s habits through a small device or smartphone app installed in the vehicle.
It monitors metrics such as speed, braking, acceleration and cornering, as well as time spent on the road.
The information is shared with the insurer, and safe drivers are then rewarded with lower premiums.
The system can be particularly useful for young or first-time drivers, or those new to Ireland, who are often hit with penal premiums.
Bonkers.ie sought quotes from a range of providers including AIG , Aviva and Zurich under a number of conditions and found that a 20-year-old driver with a full licence was quoted just €570 for fully comprehensive telematics cover.
When there was no telematics cover, the price of the standard policy jumped to almost €3,900.
[ What’s driving up the cost of car insurance in Ireland? Opens in new window ]
Even learner drivers were able to find competitive cover, with a 23-year-old driver with three penalty points quoted €968 for third-party, fire and theft telematics cover, compared with over €2,800 for a standard policy.
“It’s very possible for younger drivers to get on the road for under €1,000 by choosing a telematics policy, especially if they have their full licence,” said Daragh Cassidy from the price comparison site.
He noted that telematics could also benefit drivers who are new to Ireland and don’t have a long record of driving in the country that insurance providers can draw on when deciding on the costs to impose on individual motorists.
Cassidy said that the Bonkers research highlighted how new drivers “shouldn’t automatically rule out getting fully comprehensive cover because they assume it’ll be too expensive. In some cases, a fully comprehensive telematics policy can cost less than a conventional third-party, fire and theft policy.”
He did note, however, that the excesses on some telematics policies can be higher, and he stressed the need to “understand any conditions attached to the cover, including how their driving is monitored and whether there are limits to when and how much they can drive”.
“I’d also encourage parents of young drivers to take note of our findings,” Cassidy said.
“Many first-time drivers will rely on the ‘bank of mum and dad’ to help them get on the road. So for parents worried about facing a four-figure insurance bill for their son or daughter, telematics is certainly worth investigating.”

title: Horror is the main reaction to our decision to get rats as pets
description: We’re now a family with two rats and two cats
content:
I t came down to a choice between the cold-blooded reptile who required a diet of live crickets, and the fast little rodent with sharp teeth and a long tail, notorious historically for spreading the Black Death. It sounds a bit like the end of a dystopian book, but was just a regular old day in our house. We went with the latter.
Responses to our decision to get a pet rat have gone a few ways, and very few of them are positive. Horror has been the main reaction.
Wide eyes and declarations about how visits to our house are now over. Some sadness from my mother-in-law. And confusion. “But ... but ... why? Rats aren’t a pet!” as if I’d accidentally housed two wild rats from the ditch in my kids’ bedroom. That, and: “But don’t you have two cats?!” Which is actually a fair point.
So anyway. We drove to Carlow to get these rats as none were available in Dublin (insert joke here). I thought this was entirely normal behaviour, but the more I told people the more they thought it was a bit odd. It was assumed I was being a martyr mammy. “Aren’t you awful good,” at least one person said to me. The truth is I was quite positively disposed to getting these rats myself. I grew up watching endearing geezer Roland Rat on breakfast telly. As a kid, I had rabbits and hamsters, so I know my way around the furry critter world.
Myself and the seven-year-old ambled around the enormous Davy’s Pets and came across the nest of six rat babies, each cuter than the last. The helpful assistant, an owner of a chinchilla herself, enthused how rats are absolutely her favourite pet. How they have so much love to give and they would crawl inside your skin if they could (insert horror emoji here for 99 per cent of population). She popped a little brown and white fellah into my waiting hands and he promptly pooed on me. His vulnerability won our hearts and we headed off with him and his brother, a white lad with little grey flecks, packed into a shoebox for their motorway trip home.
Later that day, we christened them Pickle and Biscuit and set up their gaff, a surprisingly enormous cage complete with hammocks, staircases and rope swings. The hot tub, large wall-mounted TV, and pool table will follow ...
Rats as a species are more than 60 million years old, but colourful domesticated “fancy rats” started as a thing in Japan during the 17th and 18th centuries. This variety are extremely social (breeders and pet shops won’t sell you fewer than two) and love human contact. They are also smart and apparently able to learn tricks, if the antics seen on various YouTube channels can be believed, but realistically, there are some rats who just can’t be arsed and prefer a snooze and a mooch, like our sensitive and slightly nervy new furry son Biscuit. According to the nice man at Kinsealy Pets, rats are much maligned and misunderstood.
[ Despite having 11 kids and 20 grandkids, my dad’s favourite children are his dogs Opens in new window ]
They unjustly get a bad rap out there. The guy in the petshop on Parnell Street was equally supportive and visibly perked up when I said we had rats at home. “They’re like little dogs!” he said, eyes shining.
Not unlike a pair of students in a stinky 1990s flat, Pickle and Biscuit come to life fully about 3pm and party hard through the night, punctuating the silence of the house with nibbling, nifty acrobatic moves sideways across the bars, and thuds as they drop from the cage ceiling. They do “zoomies”, bombing around at warp speed, like they’ve ingested a bag of amphetamines.
The seven-year-old has declared that they’re better than the telly, which is high praise indeed. Pickle is a big hit, sitting on shoulders and hiding in hoods. Even the 10-year-old, who isn’t that generally keen on animals, gives Biscuit an odd rub. I find myself talking in a ridiculous voice to them, treating them to florets of broccoli and corn on the cob, and lavishing them with kisses on their lovely little heads, quite unlike any other 40-something-year-old woman I know. It’s all fun and games until the place starts to get a bit grubby and needs a big clean (my god, the poo! It’s epic and it’s everywhere, despite furnishing them with a litter tray which for some reason they largely ignore) and we’re reminded again why cats really are the easiest of all pets.
So, a month in and we’re now a family with two rats and two cats. With regard to management of this delicate ecosystem, complete segregation is all we can come up with for now. No mean feat in a small house though. Lately Silvie, the grey tabby, is starting to smell a rat and is sitting outside the closed bedroom door, staring a lot. We live slightly on our nerves.
But helpfully, or unhelpfully, depending on your view of it, rats typically only live about two or three years. So, this will be a brief enough rat run. Then our visitors might return. Until that is, the bearded dragon and his entourage of live crickets moves in.

title: ‘Absolutely chaotic’: Passengers frustrated by overcrowding on Irish public transport
description: Irish commuters face the daily reality of jam-packed journeys, with some describing services as a public health risk
content:
W restling to get on board jam-packed public transport services is a daily reality for thousands of Irish commuters.
Sinéad Hickey, a 25-year-old architect who commutes into Dublin city centre five days a week from Co Carlow , sees the strain it puts on people as she completes her 2½-hour journey from home to office.
Her train from Carlow at 7.05am brings her to Heuston Station for 8.15am, followed by a mad dash via a Luas and bus to make it to Drumcondra for 9am.
“The Luas at Heuston is scandalous,” Hickey said. “It’s by far the worst part. I find myself waiting for the third or fourth tram to arrive before I can get on, the others are all too full.
“Then, people on the Luas are annoyed, they’re trying to push on, and then they end up getting mad at each other,” she added.
The last leg of her journey is the bus. “You just never know when they’re coming – it’ll say two minutes for about 10 or 15, then suddenly a random bus shows up,” she said.
Hickey was one of more than 70 Irish Times readers who responded to a call-out for people to share their experiences of overcrowding on public transport at a time of record demand for services.
Responses ranged from commuters being unable to reach their seat on a train because the carriage was too full, to 30km journeys lasting up to two hours on a bus due to congestion.
[ Commuters to face increased fares on buses and trains Opens in new window ]
Even those who work for public transport bodies voiced their discontent at the services provided.
One Dublin Bus driver spoke of his frustration at being unable to rely on the bus to get to work. His employer “cannot even supply adequate public transport for the people that run” it, he said.
He asked that his name not be published out of concern that it may jeopardise his employment with the company, which undertakes its services under contract with the National Transport Authority.
“It’s crazy,” he said, that a designated staff-only bus service “doesn’t run early or late enough to cover all the shifts for various routes supplied by the garage” he is primarily stationed in. “It means some people are forced to drive or cycle,” he continued.
“It doesn’t make any sense that they’ve decided to run these earlier routes, but the staff service just isn’t there.”
The driver, who only began his job recently, said he understands people’s annoyance at so-called “ghost buses” – services that appear in real-time updates on the Transport for Ireland app or live timetables at bus stops but not in reality.
He explained that overcrowding on earlier routes often considerably slows the service down throughout the morning, meaning operational managers will have to cancel later routes he is scheduled to drive as he is sometimes still completing the earlier one.
Jason Campbell, a 52-year-old from Skerries in north county Dublin, said his train into the city centre most mornings is “absolutely chaotic” and “completely overwhelming” at times because of passengers being “packed like sardines” into the carriage.
“It’s been markedly worse since colleges have started back,” he added, with “a significant increase” in people unable to board the train at stops closer to the terminus.
“Apart from it being unpleasant, it is actually unsafe,” Campbell said, with “commuter trains having no air conditioning” and some people “wilting away, close to collapsing”.
“I don’t want to sound like a whinger,” he said, “but this is only going to get worse” given large housing developments in the area and public transport services not planned to increase alongside the population.
Mark Walsh, a civil servant from Co Kilkenny , travels to the capital twice a week to work from the office. “The train is so crowded,” he said, owing to only six carriages in use, “and you might see very elderly passengers who haven’t pre-booked a seat”.
And on the other end of things, “I see more and more students taking the very early trains,” he said, “probably because student accommodation is so scarce as well”.
“I’ve started to see carriages full of people standing” for the 90-minute journey, “it’s starting to look more like a Luas”, Walsh said.
[ ‘It’s just stressful’: Workers facing two and three hour commutes into Dublin Opens in new window ]
Yasmin Mello commutes by rail from Park West station in west Dublin to Drumcondra and describes her morning journey as “absolutely horrible”.
“The 7.55am train is consistently extremely overcrowded, with passengers regularly struggling to board and being forced to squeeze into already packed carriages. Sometimes people are left behind because there simply is not enough space.
“People should not have to start their working day worried about whether they will even be able to board their train,” she said.
“It raises a genuine question about whether train sizes and capacity are being allocated according to passenger demand.
“In terms of solutions, I believe Irish Rail needs to prioritise longer trains during morning and evening rush hours, ensure services operate at full capacity wherever possible, and review the scheduling and allocation of trains based on actual passenger numbers.”
In Co Kildare , Lori Scanlon has recently returned to work following maternity leave. She speaks of new housing developments adding to overcrowding and “lateness ... or a technical fault with the line” nearly guaranteed.
“Every day I leave the house dreading the commute because I am either wedged into a vestibule or right under someone’s armpit on the Luas,” she said.
Scanlon says it has become “a passenger safety issue” – something reiterated by Peter Moonlight, who commutes from Wicklow town on the Rosslare line.
He said he had seen people collapse in overcrowded conditions, and once witnessed a passenger who had a seizure, during which “there was no response at all from the driver or guard to the passengers pressing the emergency intercom”.
“Passengers were left helpless, and simply had to wait until the train stopped at the next station, having passed through several intermediary stations without stopping, before they themselves got off with the ill passenger to call for help.”
Moonlight said he sent a complaint to Irish Rail.
Some 672 complaints were made to Irish Rail in 2025. Delays in services were the largest single issue, accounting for nearly half of all grievances recorded.

title: An American in Dublin: ‘People are like, okay, maybe she has notions, but she doesn’t know any better’
description: ‘In some ways I get a free pass because I am an outsider,’ says musician Joanna Mattrey
content:
“W e can live a lot better in Dublin than we could in Brooklyn,” says Joanna Mattrey (39), who moved from New York to Dublin in 2024.
Mattrey and her Irish husband, James, decided to move to his hometown after their daughter was born. “I knew no one in this country aside from my in-laws. Then I moved here with a six-month-old. It was very dramatic.”
The couple met through a dating website in New York in 2018. Her husband had graduated in architecture in 2009, right in the middle of the financial crash, which virtually paused all development and building.
“There was a massive movement of Irish architects to New York, because in some ways New York is recession-proof.”
James moved to the city with a lot of his peers. “He had a much different immigrant story than I did. He moved over with a whole support system. He even had some family, with an uncle in the city.”
From the start of their relationship, he was very upfront about his intention to move back to Ireland, she says. Early in their relationship, he even told Mattrey that he thought they should break up because of this, she recalls. However, the couple stayed together, with Mattrey open to one day moving to Ireland.
“I never thought I would leave New York,” she says. Growing up in upstate New York, Mattrey felt like “somewhat of a black sheep, certainly within my own family”. Her father was originally from Lebanon but had to flee in the aftermath of the 1967 Six-Day War. The family settled in upstate New York and have been there ever since.
“I did grow up in a very kind of religious, conservative home. My family has a lot of people who might be supporting Trump, for instance.”
Mattrey began her career as a musician and composer in upstate New York before moving to Boston to train at the New England Conservatory of Music. In her late 20s she settled in New York city, where she felt accepted.
“Brooklyn particularly is the kind of place where kind of whoever you are or however you are, you can find a community to belong to.”
[ From the US to Mayo: ‘They warned of slow internet and tiny roads. It wasn’t a problem for me’ Opens in new window ]
They did not take the decision to move to Ireland lightly. But after their daughter was born, Mattrey realised how difficult it was to be a mother and a performing musician in the city.
“Among the music community in New York city, I know very few who could pull off being a parent, even if they wanted to.”
A lack of affordable healthcare and the exorbitant price of a good college education were some of her biggest concerns about raising her daughter in the US.
“Having a daughter and just being a parent in general lowers the tolerance for the kind of suffering to which you are willing to subject your own child.” Having a daughter made her worried about the repression of women’s rights in certain US states.
There were other reasons for moving to Ireland, aside from her husband’s nationality. Once deciding factor was that Dublin felt like a place where there were strong work opportunities for the viola player. She plays a lot for the National Opera and recently had a show at the Dublin Fringe Festival . She often plays with ensembles in Europe, so being close to the airport is also essential for her work. “I was in two countries last week and am going to Germany this week.”
[ From Boston to Ireland: ‘It’s been almost three years, but I’m still a foreigner’ Opens in new window ]
Two years in to life in Dublin, finding friends and building her own community is an ongoing process, she says. She admitted to feeling quite isolated after they first moved over. Because their daughter was so young, Mattrey was not able to get out and meet many new people.
But more recently Mattrey says she has had more opportunities to socialise, which has helped her to realise that people in New York make friends very differently than they do in Ireland.
In the northeast of the US, people will tell you their whole life story the first time they meet, she says. In Ireland it might be years before people feel close enough to tell you some of the things going on in their inner landscape.
She found the slower Irish process of making friends confusing in the beginning. Her usual approach of being quite upfront and sharing a lot was possibly working against her, she says.
More recently she feels people have got used to her a bit more. “I think in some ways I get a free pass because I am an outsider. They are like, ‘Okay, maybe she has notions, but you know she does not know any better because she is from New York.’”
Most of her family in Lebanon had to leave following Israel’s invasion in October 2024. Fundamentally, however challenging parts of the move to Ireland has been, she feels very lucky that she could move out of choice.

title: No special care place available for girl (14) being sexually exploited by group of men
description: Judge directs that details of cases be sent to three Government Ministers
content:
There is no place in secure State care for a teenage girl who gardaí believe is being subjected to “horrifying” sexual exploitation by multiple men, the High Court has heard.
The girl, who is 14 and has a mild learning disability, is in the care of Tusla and believes these men “care for her”, Judge John Jordan was told yesterday.
She had been approached by men who brought her to a house in another county and gave her alcohol, cocaine and other drugs to “relax her”.
Tusla was seeking a special-care order for the girl, but told the court it was currently unable to provide her with a bed in any of its three special-care units.
Special care is the most secure form of care for children aged 11 to 17 whose behaviour is so disturbed as to put them or others at extreme risk. A High Court order is required to detain a child in special care. However, just 15 of the 26 beds are open due to staffing shortages.
The judge described the abuse as “abhorrent” and said the girl should be provided with a bed in the system “immediately”.
He lifted the in-camera rule, which operates to protect the identity and privacy in such cases, in this case and also in a second involving extreme sexual exploitation of a teenager.
Jordan directed that details of the cases be sent to three Government Ministers – Minister for Children Norma Foley , Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan and Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers – as a “vivid illustration” of the “consequences” of the State’s ongoing failure to open all special-care beds.
“It is important they be aware of the appalling predicament of this child and of the absolute urgency in opening up all the three special-care units,” he said.
Sarah McKechnie, barrister for Tusla, told the judge that the 14-year-old’s family had been, since her birth, known to social workers for antisocial behaviour, drug-taking and verbally abusing their children. The girl had witnessed one of her parents die, the court heard.
McKechnie said the adolescent had been “seeking out males to offer them sexual gratification as a way of feeling wanted and loved”. She was “having sex with numerous males” and complaining of pain in her vaginal area, the barrister said, but “sadly she reports liking this attention”.
Gardaí were “heavily involved” in the “disturbing case”, McKechnie added.
Making the special-care order, the judge said compliance was “not optional”.
The court also heard that a second teenage girl in Tusla care was being “sexually exploited by a large number of men”.
Paul Gunning, barrister for Tusla, said the girl had been seen on social media “clearly under the influence of drugs and distressed”.
She had complained of pain in her pelvic area as a result of what she described as “very rough sex” with these men.
Making an order to detain her in special care, the judge said the girl was “clearly the victim of abhorrent sexual exploitation by adult males”.
He ordered papers in her case also be sent to the Ministers “so that those in authority with the power to open up the beds ... will have a vivid illustration of the consequences of not doing so”.
The court also heard that a 16-year-old boy was taking and selling drugs, and holding large quantities of heroin and crack cocaine for older men. Making an order that he be detained in special care, the judge said the child had “become enmeshed in criminality and drugs”.
The boy saw these older criminals as “his support system”, the court heard, and was “unsafe” in the community.
He had been found by gardaí with a consignment of drugs worth several thousand euro.
“There are concerns now for his safety for reason of his loss of that consignment,” the court heard.

title: Detached Blackrock home offers countryside feel a short hop from the city
description: Single-storey home off Sydney Avenue boasts a wonderfully private setting yet is close to village amenities
content:
It was the countryside-like setting juxtaposed with city convenience that attracted the current owners to buy Priory Bank, off Sydney Avenue in Blackrock , Co Dublin, 11 years ago. The 1970s bungalow occupies a wonderfully private site at the end of a quiet laneway, and is just minutes from Blackrock village.
With an engineering background and a good builder on board, they were able to retain much of the bungalow’s original footprint while removing the interior walls and reconfiguring the layout.
The B-rated house now extends to 155sq m (1,668sq ft) and benefits from an emphasis on natural light and a flow through the rooms that extends out to the garden. Accessed through a gated, gravelled driveway, it feels removed from the surrounding urban setting, with mature trees providing privacy from the outside world.
The front door, to the right of the building, opens into a reception hall where built-in storage helps keep the space uncluttered. From here, the layout leads into an open-plan area that incorporates the kitchen, living and dining spaces. Full-height glazing along the rear opens the room towards the southeast-facing garden, allowing natural light in throughout the day.
In the kitchen, the cupboards reach from floor to ceiling, adding to the sense of height in the room. A large island provides seating for six, and a four-ring hob is positioned opposite it, alongside additional units with a marble worktop.
The living area also faces the garden and opens into a more formal diningroom. A second reception room provides another space to retreat to, with all rooms beautifully designed with a mix of modern fittings and antique pieces.
There are two double bedrooms, one of which is en suite, while the other has exclusive use of the main bathroom. There is also the main bedroom suite, which was created by adding to the floor space of the original house.
“We made it into our little haven so we could decamp into our own studio if the kids had taken over the kitchen,” one of the owners says.
The house wraps around a garden that looks as neat as the indoor spaces. The owners undertook the landscaping themselves, planting ferns and mature shrubs around an artificial lawn. Extensive timber decking provides space for outdoor dining and relaxing, allowing the garden to be a regular extension of the living areas.
During Covid lockdowns, the owners built a small bar to one side of the garden. It has a fold-up hatch at the front and a separate door to the side, adding a bit of fun to the space. The garden is not overlooked from any angle, while a gate provides access to Blackrock Tennis Club, which the family used regularly during their time at the house.
A garden room was also added at the entrance gate, which the owners had as a teenage den and later a home office, offering a degree of separation from the main house.
Despite the sense of seclusion, the property, which is on the market with Lisney Sotheby’s International Realty guiding €1.95 million, remains close to Blackrock village and its amenities. Schools within a short walking distance include Carysfort and Booterstown national schools, as well as St Andrew’s, Blackrock College and Sion Hill.
With the children now grown up and making their own way in the world, the owners are looking forward to their new chapter in life.
“We’re reaching an age where we’re thinking, ‘Do we have one more project in us?’ and I think we do. We’ve done up a few houses before, and we’ve learned so much along the way, so we’re excited about taking on a new challenge.”

title: China’s economic growth picks up but consumers prefer to save not spend
description: Helped by AI, China’s economy grew by 4.5% in the third quarter
content:
China ’s unexpectedly strong third-quarter economic growth suggests that Beijing is on course to meet its 2026 target for the economy to grow by 4.5-5 per cent. But although this figure is enviable for other major economies, it is historically low by Chinese standards and reflects an increasingly unbalanced, two-speed economy.
The 4.5 per cent growth figure was an improvement on the previous three-month period but it was China’s lowest for decades apart from during the Covid pandemic. And with domestic demand still weak, the growth is driven by exports at a time when partners like the European Union are becoming increasingly impatient with their ever-expanding trade deficit with China.
China’s exports are benefiting from the buildout of infrastructure for artificial intelligence and the global demand for microchips and technological equipment for data centres. Chinese AI models such as DeepSeek, Kimi and Z.ai are surging in popularity around the world, and the country is leading in the production of advanced robots and other cutting-edge technology.
But while new industries are flourishing, more traditional drivers of economic growth are struggling, with none suffering more than the housing market. The share of China’s population living in cities doubled this century, and house prices increased sixfold in the 15 years before they crashed five years ago.
Property investment fell by 20.6 per cent in the first nine months of this year and although there are signs of stabilisation in the market in the biggest cities, prices are still falling elsewhere. Consumers are continuing to choose saving over spending, contributing to the deflation, which is accelerated by price wars in many sectors that have cut profit margins to the bone.
This autumn has seen policy measures aimed at boosting consumption, including mortgage subsidies for some borrowers and capital injections for state banks. But Beijing remains shy of introducing stimulus on a large scale, much less of the kind of dramatic steps needed to rebalance the economy towards consumption.

title: Open days: What questions should students ask?
description: Going to open days can help you decide where you want to spend the next few years
content:
Open days are a perfect chance to get a feel for what a third-level institution is really like. They give prospective students an opportunity to explore courses, meet lecturers and current students, and see the campus for themselves.
And, just as importantly, they’re a chance to ask questions.
Before you go, it can help to spend a bit of time thinking about what matters most to you. Is it the course content? Career opportunities? Accommodation? Financial support? Student life?
The answers to these questions could play a big role in where you decide to study.
Try to arrive with a list of things you would like to find out. Take notes as you go, and don’t be afraid to ask follow-up questions if something isn’t clear. Remember, open days aren’t just about colleges making an impression on you, they’re also your opportunity to decide whether a college feels like the right fit.

title: My new landlord wants me to pay a deposit before issuing a tenancy agreement. What should I do?
description: Property Clinic: Is it common practice to request a rent deposit at such an early stage?
content:
After viewing a rental property , I was informed my application to become the tenant had been approved, subject to references. Before the references were checked, I was asked whether I could pay a deposit immediately to secure the property. I was uncomfortable transferring money before receiving a tenancy agreement. Is it common practice to request a deposit at this stage, and what should prospective tenants expect before committing any funds?
From an agent’s perspective, I believe the process should be straightforward and transparent. In our practice, we would fully check references first and establish that this was the tenant we intended to proceed with before requesting any deposit.
After reference checks, we would also agree the key terms of the tenancy, including any special conditions, the proposed lease term and the responsibilities of each party. For example, whether the lease would be a Part 4 or a 12-month fixed-term lease and practical matters such as who would be responsible for grass cutting and garden maintenance, parking arrangements, etc.
Once references are satisfactorily checked, the decision to proceed is made, the terms are agreed and the deposit is then requested, along with written confirmation of the amount and terms of the lease.
I can understand why a prospective tenant would be uncomfortable transferring money before these matters are clarified. My advice to tenants is never to transfer funds without viewing the property first and being sure of the lease’s terms and special conditions. This should ideally be confirmed in writing by email.
The rental market is competitive, and agents and landlords need an efficient process, but tenants should never feel pressured into transferring money without assurances in place. In my view, good practice is about protecting both the landlord and the tenant and setting clear expectations from the outset, ensuring everyone understands the arrangements before money changes hands.
Shirleen Rigby is a property managing agent and an associate member of the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland

title: Boney M: The strange but true story of the Daddy Cool disco divas
description: Warring egos, studio shenanigans and bad blood taken to the grave: after a turbulent career, the band are bringing their farewell tour to Ireland
content:
M aizie Williams sits in her hotel room at Prague airport, fresh off a plane and thinking about another time and another flight. “We didn’t know what to expect,” she says. “We thought, ‘Oh God ... going to Russia ... communist Russia!’”
The singer with Boney M is rewinding to December 1978, when the 1970s hit machine created history as one of the first western acts to perform behind the Iron Curtain, playing 10 concerts to packed crowds across the Soviet Union and shooting a video on Red Square, in Moscow.
They were welcomed with open arms – and a precondition. Boney M were forbidden, upon pain of banishment, from bashing out their hit Rasputin , a four-minute-40-second recap of Russian history that chronicled how, in the early years of the 20th century, the eponymous mad monk inveigled his way into the confidence of the tsarina, bedded half the court and precipitated the collapse of the Romanov dynasty. It was, as the tune astutely observes, “a shame how he carried on”.
“We had 10 shows in five days. Plus recording on Red Square – Mary’s Boy Child. It was amazing,” Williams says. “All 10 concerts were full. All the dignitaries came. We didn’t know how they were going to react. We didn’t know if we should get them out of their seats.”
The Soviet Union took Boney M to its heart, and they retained a loyal following in Russia through their many ups and downs in the decades to follow. If anything their stock was higher there than in the West, where there was, in the 1970s, a tendency to regard Williams and her bandmates as a novelty act, a cash-grab riding through on the coat tails of disco.
But that’s no longer the case. At some point in the past decade, Boney M became inescapable. Today it can be a challenge to sit through an ad break without encountering Daddy Cool, the 1976 stomper now repurposed as the soundtrack of commercials for banks, detergents and soft drinks.
Hand in hand with that tune’s revival has been the comeback of Rasputin, whose Ra-Ra-Rasputin chorus has proved imp-imp-impossible to avoid thanks to prominent placement on the soundtracks to Dr Who and Black Mirror, and which has Cossack-danced its way to 1.5 billion streams.
What a turnabout. Just as Abba went from kitsch embarrassment to beloved pop pioneers, so Boney M have been rehabilitated as first-rank disco geniuses. It’s in this guise that Williams, who is now 75, will bring Boney M to Guinness Cork Jazz Festival and to the National Stadium, in Dublin, this month as part of a farewell Final Curtain tour.
Their rehabilitation is remarkable, and not simply because, as well as being caught up in the homophobic and racist backlash against disco, they were considered forgettable fodder in the 1970s. There is also the soap-opera aspect to their story, one involving warring egos, studio shenanigans and bad blood taken to the grave.
The band’s creative genius and full-time agent of chaos was Frank Farian, an eccentric German producer who assembled Boney M on the fly after chalking up a disco hit in the Netherlands by accident and finding that he needed to put a face to his music. In a certain sense he was Boney M: he wrote and produced all the songs and sang lead vocals on some of their biggest hits.
But he was also a middle-aged Rhinelander, with the complexion of porridge left out too long in the rain, and he knew he couldn’t possibly front a disco group whose music was steeped in reggae and calypso.
Enter Williams, born in Montserrat, raised in Birmingham, and a successful model when she was approached at a nightclub in Hanover and asked whether she would like to front a German pop project.
This was the beginning of Boney M, which would become a unique proposition in 1970s music, a disco outfit led by four singers of Caribbean heritage: alongside Williams were Bobby Farrell, from Aruba, and Marcia Barrett and Liz Mitchell, from Jamaica.
“I’m a Birmingham girl. I wanted to be in the entertainment industry, so I moved to London, because there were more possibilities there for me. I was holding down a nine-to-five job at the same time. That’s where the break came to go to Germany,” Williams says.
“They sent me to Germany to do a show over there, which was really a fashion show. Lo and behold, the rest is history. That’s where they approached me to see if I wanted to be part of a group they were trying to put together.
“At first I was a bit sceptical. Then I thought, ‘Oh, what have I got to lose?’ Whenever I finished what I was doing there, I would have to go back to London and back to my nine-to-five job. I gave it a chance, to see what was going to happen.”
Williams wasn’t exactly blown away by Farian at their first meeting. He had rudimentary English and was quiet and unassuming, though that would change as they became successful.
“He was a very ordinary, easygoing guy. So it was really easy to communicate with him, quite frankly. He spoke very little English. He knew the normal words, like hello and how are you and things like that.”
Williams recalls being the first to meet Farian in the studio and being upfront about what needed to happen if she was to join Boney M.
“I said, ‘If you want me to stay in Germany, then I don’t know how I’m going to survive. I’m running out of money. I have no place to stay.’ He said, ‘No worries. I’ll give you per diems so you can buy food.’ The agent had an office. It had a showroom in the corner and a sofa bed. And that’s where I stayed until I could get my own apartment.”
If Farian was outwardly easygoing, he had a clear sense of what he wanted from the project. He had sung and recorded Boney M’s first hit, Baby Do You Wanna Bump?, from 1975, all on his own. He saw no reason to change the formula. And so, while Williams and Farrell would front the band, and perform when they were on the road, in the studio they were shut out.
As often happens with successful people, Farian altered as one hit followed another, Williams says.
“I don’t know if the right word is ‘control freak’. He became a little bit changed later on.”
[ Christmas hit songs: How much money can you make from a Yuletide tune? Opens in new window ]
His hands-on approach caused considerable tension, especially with Farrell, who was also upset at being denied what he saw as his share of the royalties. “The guy is stinking rich. He’s got a studio,” he protested. “I don’t have millions. Frank Farian’s a stinking millionaire.”
Farian later relented, allowing Farrell to perform on their 1981 song We Kill the World. He also surrendered the spotlight to Barrett, who sang on Mary’s Boy Child – that perennial of shopping-mall Christmas choirs around Ireland – and Belfast, a somewhat starry-eyed appeal for peace and understanding in the North.
The latter went to number one in Ireland, but Farian would later regret its naivety. (It could have been worse: the song’s initial title was Londonderry.)
“We have sung about Ma Baker” – Kate Barker was the matriarch of an American gang of outlaw brothers – “we have sung about Rasputin, let’s do a song about a real problem, Belfast, which was very bad at the time,” Farian told the British media in 2004. “But it was not a big hit. I think this was not the right theme for Boney M – too serious. I think this was a little mistake.”
[ Fighting words: Frank McNally on the best and worst songs of the Troubles Opens in new window ]
Farrell died in a St Petersburg hotel on December 30th, 2010 – 94 years to the day after Rasputin was shot dead in the city.
Farian died in 2024. In some ways his work with Boney M was eclipsed in the late 1980s by that with Milli Vanilli, a fake R&B duo that ended in a lip-syncing scandal.
But Boney M continue, with Williams taking the band across the world. Why does she think the group’s music is still so beloved today?
“There’s something for everyone there. A little bit of Caribbean, a little bit of reggae, a little bit of jazz, a little bit of soul, a little bit of everything. It’s quite commercial, so everyone can relate. And, also, our lyrics are very ‘storytelling’. We tell stories about different characters in the past and all that. We crossed over into a different level, where we were not typical disco, but we were disco at the same time.”
Boney M play Cork Jazz Festival on Saturday, October 24th, and the National Stadium, in Dublin, on Sunday, October 25th

title: Data centre policies risk decline in tech industry
description: Lobbyist says “stroke of a pen” could solve problems
content:
Government policies hindering data centres from using their own electricity supplies risk tipping the Irish technology industry into decline, the head of an industry body has warned.
Recently introduced rules require data centres to have their own backup electricity plants, which can supply the national grid when needed, while they must draw 80 per cent of their energy from renewable sources within six years of starting operations.
However, delays in getting national grid connections are creating problems that deter data centre developers from investing here, says Ronan Kelly, chief executive of lobby group Digital Infrastructure Ireland (DII).
[ How Ireland feels about data-centre construction revealed in new Irish Times poll Opens in new window ]
The Republic has already lost out on the first wave of AI investment, which went to Spain and the Nordics, but could still capture a share of the next if it deals with easy-to-solve problems, according to Kelly.
Many of the 109 centres now operating here are more than five years old, so they are getting close to the point where their systems must be renewed, which is generally at 10 years, according to Kelly.
That could prompt their owners to move those facilities to other countries, if barriers to investing here remain, he explains, leading to an overall decline in the tech industry, with the loss of economic benefits, including corporation taxes.
“In 10, 15 years’ time, when the government comes to raid your pension pot, that’s when the chickens come home to roost,” he warns.
Government can solve most of the problems with “the stroke of a pen”, according to the industry advocate, who adds that they are largely the result of policy.
Data centres are not allowed to start operations without national grid connections, for which they have to wait five years, even while they must have their own electricity supplies, Kelly maintains.
His organisation wants this rule changed to allow centres to start operations using their own power sources, on condition that they immediately connect to the grid once that is possible.
Alongside this, data centres cannot count renewable power supplied through direct connections to wind or solar plants, known as private lines, against the 80 per cent requirement, which can only be met with green electricity from the grid.
Data centres could meet their renewable commitments quickly if they were allowed to count what they buy through private lines, Kelly argues.
This would also provide an outlet for wind and solar plants that are often prevented by a lack of capacity in parts of the national grid from supplying electricity to the market.
[ ‘Big tech’s lapdog’: How can we break free from the sector’s malign influence? Opens in new window ]
DII argues that concerns that data centres will draw natural gas supplies away from new housing ignore the fact that policy dictates that new homes will use electricity.
The organisation has no difficulty with many aspects of the rules now governing data centre connection, stresses Kelly, who adds that the Republic has stricter regulations governing the industry than many jurisdictions.
Their presence here is a result of long-standing policy, he says. Government built the telecoms lines they needed in the late ‘90s. “We built the infrastructure and lo and behold, they came,” he says.

title: Egypt: Notes from the Nile
description: Recently returned from Egypt, Oroko’s head of product and marketing, Emilie Lynam, shares her notes from Cairo, Luxor and five nights sailing the Nile by dahabiya
content:
There are certain places we feel we know long before we arrive.
Egypt was one of those places for me. The pyramids, Tutankhamen, the Nile – stories and images absorbed over a lifetime, until standing in front of them feels strangely familiar and completely extraordinary at the same time.
I had expected to be overwhelmed by the monuments. I hadn’t anticipated quite how absorbing the history would become, or how much of Egypt would stay with me beyond it.
We crossed the Giza plateau by golf buggy with our private Egyptologist, the pyramids growing steadily larger across the sand until we were standing beneath them. Even at close range, their scale is difficult to reconcile with their age.
Our Egyptologist was already drawing us into a larger story, pointing out symbols and beliefs we would encounter again further south. He had a wonderful habit of asking us to remember something. Its significance would become clear days later.
At the Grand Egyptian Museum, it was the smallest objects that stayed with me. Among Tutankhamen’s treasures were his shoes, walking sticks and bed. These intimate possessions brought an unexpected humanity to the golden mask I had known since childhood. Behind one of history’s most celebrated archaeological discoveries was a boy whose life had been remarkably short.
The change from Cairo is immediate. The city gives way to the vivid green of the Nile Valley, with fields and palms running alongside the river.
Our Egyptologists had a wonderful instinct for making connections. A story introduced almost casually in Cairo might return days later, suddenly legible in the stone before us. I began to understand why ancient Egypt could occupy a lifetime of study.
Hatshepsut was the site that surprised me most. Her temple rises in terraces against the cliffs of the West Bank, its architecture almost inseparable from the landscape. But her story is every bit as compelling: a woman who claimed the authority of a pharaoh and ruled Egypt as king. In a history so often told through the achievements of men, there was something particularly wonderful about standing before a monument to one of its most formidable women.
For five nights, we travelled south towards Aswan aboard a dahabiya, a traditional sailing boat with just 10 cabins. Unlike the larger cruise ships, it sits low on the water, close enough to the banks that you feel part of the landscape rather than simply passing through it.
Life on board had its own lovely rhythm. Within a day, the crew knew everyone. Cold towels and drinks appeared after sightseeing, Egyptian dishes were shared around long tables and tea arrived at sunset. One evening, we dined beneath the stars on a small island, ending the night dancing with the crew. Somewhere along the way, the formality of being guests had disappeared.
But it was life along the river that I loved most. In the mornings, there was a wonderful stillness to the Nile. Fishermen worked from small boats, birds skimmed the reeds and water buffalo gathered at the water’s edge. Beyond the impossibly green strips of farmland, the desert began almost without warning.
Then there were the children. As we passed villages, they would swim out towards us or appear alongside in tiny boats, sometimes catching hold of a rope and letting the dahabiya carry them along. Their delight was infectious: enormous smiles, laughter carrying across the water, triumphant thumbs-up before they eventually let go and waved goodbye.
There was such unguarded happiness in these fleeting encounters. They lasted only minutes, yet I remember them with an affection quite disproportionate to their brevity.
At Gebel el-Silsila, sandstone cliffs rise directly from the Nile, carved with shrines and tombs left from the ancient quarries that supplied stone for many of Egypt’s temples. I had only just come back up on deck and could easily have missed it. For a few minutes, I was there alone as the dahabiya sailed slowly past the carvings. The river was almost silent and, as the cliffs moved alongside us, white birds swept overhead.
With our private Egyptologist and more flexibility than the larger cruise ships, we could time temple visits to avoid the busiest periods.
At Edfu, we entered the Temple of Horus with relatively few other visitors. Enormous columns rose overhead, while shafts of light caught the carvings in its darker chambers.
Kom Ombo tells a different story. Our Egyptologist explained how closely the ancient Egyptians observed the natural world, from the behaviour of crocodiles to the seasonal flooding of the Nile and the movements of the stars. These observations shaped their understanding of time and the calendar, a remarkable intellectual legacy still recorded in the carvings.
By the time we reached Aswan, I thought the great temples were behind us. Egypt had saved one more.
Philae sits on an island, reached by a small boat across the water. As we approached, its great pylons rose ahead of us, seemingly straight from the Nile.
As the sun began to fall, we boarded a felucca and sailed between the islands. There was no temple to reach and nothing left to tick off. We simply sailed, watching the light change across the river, the desert beyond and the Old Cataract on the bank.
After days spent trying to take in thousands of years of history, it was a beautifully simple way to say goodbye to Egypt: under sail, as the sun went down over the Nile.
Egypt is entering a new chapter. The Grand Egyptian Museum has given Cairo a remarkable new centrepiece. Mandarin Oriental is restoring the Winter Palace in Luxor and transforming Aswan’s storied Old Cataract. Yet for me, Egypt’s greatest appeal lies in the way you experience it. The right Egyptologist, the freedom to explore slowly and the intimacy of a small sailing boat on the Nile.
The ancient world may be what takes you to Egypt. The journey down the Nile is what makes you want to return.
