title: Social-housing pilot guarantees rent for landlords – but will they sign up?
description: Rental accommodation scheme rules have been updated but property owner lobby still has concerns
content:
A new pilot scheme, aimed at boosting the supply of social housing by offering a “secure, low-risk letting option” for landlords , has been launched by the Department of Housing .
Run by councils across Dublin for now, if it’s a success, it might be rolled out across the State.
Announcing the Dublin Rental Accommodation Scheme pilot scheme earlier this year, Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage James Browne said: “By encouraging more landlords to make their properties available, the pilot will help increase the supply of homes for individuals and families in need of social housing”.
But how does it work? Is it attractive for landlords? And with the rental market so tight, is it going to be enough to get landlords to commit to social housing?
Run on a pilot basis across the four Dublin local authority areas, the new rental accommodation scheme is being pitched as a “flexible, secure and financially attractive way to let residential properties”.
The tenant target is households that have received rent supplement for 18 months or more, and that have an ongoing housing need. The tenant pays an income-based differential rent contribution to the local authority, and the local authority pays the landlord the agreed rent.
The hope is that if more private landlords sign up for the scheme, more properties should become available to social housing tenants.
This is not the first time councils have looked to incentivise landlords to let their properties through local authorities. The rental accommodation scheme has two components – one working through approved housing boards letting their properties to councils and the other a private-sector arrangement whereby private landlords enter into rental agreements with local authorities.
It is the latter that the new pilot scheme is focusing on.
There have been challenges in attracting and retaining enough properties through the previous scheme. According to a review from the Department of Housing back in 2025, there has been a significant decline in the number of private landlords participating in it.
In 2023, for example, 1,004 landlords left the scheme but just 103 entered, leaving 7,010 tenancies. This compares to 11,231 back in 2018.
Three reasons for this are cited in the report: landlords selling the unit; tenants allocated social housing; and the landlord didn’t renew the contract.
And there are fewer landlords signing up, for reasons including rents on offer that are below market levels.
A spokeswoman for the Irish Property Owners Association (IPOA) says the scheme was “disadvantaged from the start” due to the rules set out in rent pressure zones. The maximum landlords could set rents at through the rental accommodation scheme was 92 per cent of market rent but this made it difficult to get back to a market rate, as only specified increases were allowed.
“It ended up that landlords were actually stuck with that sub-market rate due to rent pressure zones, which made the rent accommodation scheme unappealing,” she says.
HAP (housing assistance payment), on the other hand, had no such limits on the level rent was set at, as councils contribute a fixed amount and the tenant tops up the gap. This made it more attractive to landlords.
As a result, the new rent accommodation scheme pilot has been launched with some key differences. Firstly, landlords can charge local authorities up to 100 per cent of market rent. This rent is guaranteed, and will be paid “in full and on time” by the local authority – not the tenant.
And, if a tenant decides to leave, the council will pay the rent until a new tenant is placed.
Moreover, tenants will be sourced by the local authority, which means landlords won’t have to take on the task of vetting possible tenants.
The maximum length of a contract has also been extended, from four-to-six years previously to eight under the pilot scheme.
Rental payments will be front-loaded, so landlords won’t have to wait for their first payment. There will be better damage and compensation arrangements. And applications for the scheme will be more streamlined. Landlords will be responsible for managing the tenancy, and the property.
County councils certainly hope it is. Pamela Kearns, mayor of South Dublin County Council, says the scheme will transform lives.
“Every property made available provides a vulnerable family, individual or senior with a safe, stable home in our community. While Dublin desperately needs housing, it also thrives on collaboration. Landlords now have a meaningful way to tackle housing shortages and build stronger communities. It is a true win for owners, tenants and Dublin as a whole.”
Already there has been “significant” interest in the new pilot, says the Department of Housing, with about 200 applications received by the end of September.
However, while the new scheme may have some key differences, groups representing property owners say it may not be enough to encourage landlords out of the private market and into guaranteed rent through the rental accommodation scheme.
“It looks very well on paper, but once you scratch the surface it’s not really like that,” says the spokeswoman for the IPOA, adding that there are a “couple of hurdles” that are making it unpalatable for landlords.
Firstly, the promise of full market rent is a “marketing strategy”, says the spokeswoman, because under the current legislation, a landlord can only charge market rent if they’re eligible for it, such as at the end of a six-year tenancy cycle. And if you’re not eligible then the council cannot override Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) rules.
Another issue is the length of the contract. A contract of a maximum eight years could mean that smaller landlords (ie those with four or fewer properties) could end up with a tenant for 12 years – even if the council drops out after eight. And larger landlords could have the tenant for life even if the council is no longer involved.
And if the tenancy wasn’t working out, such as if the tenant stopped paying rent, the IPOA spokeswoman says the landlord would need to go down the standard legal route, and issue a notice of termination. But it can take up to two years to get vacant possession of the property, she says.
However, the spokesman for the Department of Housing says tenancies can match up and “a six-year rent accommodation scheme agreement can align with the statutory cycle for small landlords with one to three tenancies, provided the relevant start dates coincide”.
For larger tenants, however, these new tenancies can only be ended for breaches of tenant obligations or because the property no longer meets the needs of the household’s accommodation needs.
Another challenge that might arise is that although the landlord doesn’t select their tenant, if things go wrong, they still have to sort it out. “The main landlord-tenant relationship ultimately remains the same between the property owner and the rental accommodation scheme tenant as it would with a typical private rented tenancy,” the scheme’s documentation states.
Forward payment is just two months, while other benefits can’t really be described as such, the IPOA argues. The offer of “100 per cent mortgage interest tax relief” is something all landlords are entitled to – while property tax is not eligible for a tax deduction.
Another factor, says the spokeswoman, is that the rental accommodation scheme has “very, very strict property standards enforcement”.
If an issue is identified – and according to the spokeswoman it could be something as relatively minor as the width set on window restrictors – rent payments will be suspended until the landlord gets its sorted.
The scheme is being run on a pilot basis until 2029 to see whether or not this additional flexibility will result in an increased flow of properties.
“This pilot allows us to test whether additional flexibility and stronger supports can increase property owner participation and expand the supply of homes available to social housing tenants,” the Minister said, adding that the results of the scheme would guide future national policy.

title: Did the budget help a widow with two young children?
description: Generally, welfare payments will rise and a wider standard income tax band should help, if only a little
content:
I am a widow with two young children, in my second year of widowhood. I am in a good job and lucky enough to be able to support the three of us, even with reduced working hours.
I pay a significant amount of tax through my PAYE as the widow’s pension gets taxed that way. My take-home pay was significantly more when we were jointly assessed as a couple and I was caring for my sick husband.
Does the recent budget help the solo parent families from a tax viewpoint? And, where I lose out as one earner, is there any improvement to the social welfare support for me? Little has changed in our outgoings since four became three, and those kids are getting bigger and hungrier.
Raising children is tough enough. Raising them on your own after having had to care for your husband when he was ill is a daunting challenge.
It’s at times like this that you hope a budget will deal a decisive blow in your favour, but, unfortunately for you and others who are financially vulnerable, this Government has sought to spread its largesse thinly and widely – hardly helped by the hospitality VAT cut last year limiting its room for manoeuvre this time around.
To make matters worse, although an exceptional tax credit is granted to new widows with children to try to ease the blow of two earners becoming one or the loss of joint assessment, the credit is phased down every year. And it does not appear to have been adjusted in the budget.
Although it will have been worth €3,600 to you the year after you were widowed, this drops to €3,150 in the second year of widowhood, €2,700 in year three, €2,250 in year four and €1,800 in year five.
This is on top of the annual widow’s tax credit, which replaces whatever other personal tax credit you might have been on previously. It is payable at €2,000 this year.
[ Leaving shares to a spouse at death can make more sense than a lifetime transfer Opens in new window ]
This credit tends to keep pace with the single person’s tax credit so I am assuming it rises next year to €2,125.
You should also be eligible for the single person child carer credit as long as your children are under 18 or in full-time education over that age. It is worth €1,900 this year, but will rise to €2,025 next year.
You refer to the widow’s pension and you are certainly eligible for that. On the basis of what you say, you will be on the contributory pension – a payment that is available to you because of your PRSI record or your husband’s. In your case, I am assuming it is on the basis of your record.
I should say this pension has now been renamed the bereaved partner’s (contributory) pension. It’s not just because someone in social protection decided the word “widow” needed changing: the pension is, since last year, now available also to cohabiting couples where one partner has died.
If they don’t have children, they must have been together for five years, or, for those with dependent children, two years.
Widows under the age of 66 get between €252.60 and €259.50 weekly, depending on the number of PRSI stamps they have. Those over the age of 66 get a payment of between €286.60 and €299.30.
If, like you, they have dependent children, they get €58 a week for each child under the age of 12 and €78 for older children.
Anyway, along with most other welfare payments, this payment will rise by €10 from January of next year. So, if you are on the maximum payment for someone under 66, it will rise to €269.50 a week. And the payments for children rise by €6 a week – to €64 or €84 depending on the age of your children.
As a result, you will get an additional €22 a week, or just shy of €1,150 a year, unless one of your children turns 12 next year. It’s not nothing, but if, as you say, you are paying tax on this money, it doesn’t really stretch too far.
If your children are in childcare or after-school care with a creche that is signed up to the Government’s core funding model, that cost will come down next year but not until September.
On top of that, you will also benefit from the employee or earned income tax credit, which is rising by €125 a year to €2,125.
[ Is my €1,000 monthly childcare bill really falling to €550? Opens in new window ]
There is also a benefit from the widening of the standard rate income tax band. As a widow, you pay 20 per cent income tax up to €48,000, which is better than the €44,000 for a single person, but short of the €53,000 you would have had as a married couple with one person working.
From January, your 20 per cent band will increase to €50,500, which will cut your tax bill by €500 as long as you are earning above that €50,500 level.
On the flip side, PRSI is rising for all employees although there will be a modest cut in your Universal Social Charge .
All told, you will be around €950 better off next year, leaving aside childcare, which may or may not be relevant.

title: Guilty Pleasure by Patricia Nilsson: Exposing how online porn has shaped our lives
description: An incisive and vital book, with a glaring omission
content:
There is a scene in Adam McKay’s film The Big Short, which charts the US housing bubble and financial crash, where McKay needs the audience to understand what a sub-prime mortgage is. To help, he gets Margot Robbie to explain the concept as she lounges in a bathtub. The hidden infrastructures shaping our lives can be excruciatingly boring to hear about – so sometimes you have to sex up the explanation.
It would be easy to think Patricia Nilsson’s Guilty Pleasure is deploying a similar technique, using sex to lure us into a lesson about the somewhat drier subjects of data harvesting, financial institutions, platform capitalism and the architecture of the internet. But Nilsson’s argument is more foundational, asserting that the infrastructure of pornography helped build our entire online world.
Nilsson, a Financial Times journalist, traces the move of pornography from VHS tapes and DVDs produced and sold by recognisable studios to an industry dominated by free tube sites, obscure conglomerates and algorithmic control. As pornography moved online and much was available for free, users’ attention and behavioural data became immensely valuable.
Tube sites began recording not only what users clicked, but what they hovered over or lingered on – and that information is used to push content towards them. Terrifyingly, all attention is considered equal. The system cannot distinguish desire from disgust, or curiosity from shock. And because extreme material is particularly good at capturing attention, it is rewarded.
Nilsson is compelling on how this focus on extremity can recalibrate sexual norms, noting how practices once associated with BDSM or more extreme pornography – choking, spitting, humiliation – have become increasingly commonplace within mainstream porn. As extreme, shock-value content is fed to consumers, what is novel becomes normal, and soon, consumers can’t distinguish between what they actually desire, what induces actual pleasure – and what they’ve simply been programmed to consume in a never-ending quest to simply feel something.
[ Strangulation porn: How it became mainstream and its distorting impact on Irish teenagers Opens in new window ]
This is the book’s most interesting idea, that the attention economy logic developed by online pornography now shapes our lives, as online platforms encourage constant attention and consumption, but in ways that are increasingly disconnected, disembodied and devoid of genuine pleasure.
In one of the book’s most incisive passages, Nilsson describes how online systems have started edging out reality – we check our friend’s social media instead of hanging out, we swipe through dating apps without meeting anyone, so that consumption replaces interaction. “In this environment,” she writes, “‘porn’ has become shorthand for stimulation without participation or fulfilment. We’ve begun to describe all kinds of online content as ‘porn’, from ‘food porn’ which we salivate over but do not eat, to ‘outrage porn’, which gets our heart racing but offers no closure. Scrolling has trained us to become voyeurs in search of sensation, keeping us in a state of perpetual build-up without release.”
[ Porn before puberty in Ireland: ‘It is horrible, and it’s in every school’ Opens in new window ]
It is a striking framework for thinking about TikTok , Instagram and the wider attention economy – yet frustratingly, Nilsson often fails to fully develop these links, assuming a chronically online reader who can fluently fill in the blanks. More concrete accounts of how behavioural logic migrates from Pornhub to Instagram Reels or YouTube shorts, keeping users scrolling through decontextualised short-form content; or how camgirls’ performance of authenticity later shaped how online influencers monetise intimacy and parasocial relationships, could have made her thesis land more effectively.
Other weaknesses emerge when Nilsson moves beyond business and technology into psychology and sociology. She repeatedly states that young people are increasingly anxious and ill-equipped for real-world interaction, which is why they turn to online interactions and pornography. These claims may feel intuitively true, but are rarely supported by evidence, and needed more input from sociologists and psychologists.
There is also a frankly bizarre refusal throughout the book to name misogyny. At one point, Nilsson astutely draws a parallel between the extremity pushed by mainstream porn-site algorithms, and the attention-economy success of figures such as Andrew Tate and Donald Trump . She argues that both online systems reward spectacle, domination, humiliation and displays of power. Yet she fails to ask the obvious question of who is being dominated and humiliated.
[ Where is Ireland’s manosphere? Opens in new window ]
[ Teenagers in Ireland: ‘I’ve been online for so long. I’ve seen a bunch of stuff. I’m kind of desensitised to it’ Opens in new window ]
And as she writes about the male owners of porn companies, she never interrogates the business model of men owning companies that increasingly rely on images of women being degraded. In a book about how technological systems transform desire and power, it feels like a glaring omission not to explore further the gender of the people building those systems, the gendered patterns they repeatedly amplify and the impact of a largely male-led tech industry.
Nilsson’s work is more confident when operating as an investigative business journalist, with one chapter becoming a mystery story as she pursues the deliberately obscure men behind enormous pornography companies; and another chapter sees her reveal the hidden ecosystem connecting pornography to Wall Street, banks and payment processors.
Opacity, secrecy and a lack of accountability become one of the book’s most disturbing themes. Who knew that Visa and Mastercard were massive, invisible regulators of online sexual expression? Who can name any of the owners of or investors in the porn companies that mine extraordinarily intimate information about millions of users? At least we know who Mark Zuckerberg is, so the US Senate can question him and Aaron Sorkin can make two films about his awfulness. Meanwhile, men making billions pushing videos of women being choked towards generations of young male consumers remain nameless.
[ The Social Reckoning trailer: Aaron Sorkin’s latest take on Facebook’s fortunes Opens in new window ]
Guilty Pleasure effectively shows how the monetisation of attention that emerged with online porn now defines much of our lives and, more vitally, highlights how little we understand about the forces shaping our desires and the world around us.
Roe McDermott is an Irish Times columnist

title: Rising demand raises concerns for ‘fiscal sustainability’ of healthcare system, ESRI says
description: Growing and ageing population will increase pressure on services and public purse in years ahead
content:
The growing demand for healthcare raised “questions about the fiscal sustainability” of the Irish health system, the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) said.
In a report published on Tuesday the think-tank examined the medium-term outlook on health and social care services in the State.
The finances of the health system have received significant attention in recent months with spending overruns for the year predicted to reach €1 billion following a record budget allocation for 2026.
The ESRI report highlighted how the growing and ageing population would continue to increase pressure on health and social care services and the public finances in the coming decades, with action needed to ensure the long-term sustainability of the system.
“The growing demands for health and social care raise questions about the fiscal sustainability of the system,” the report said.
“While Ireland’s population is relatively young (compared to other European countries), already approximately one-quarter of current Government expenditure is allocated to health and social care.
“Even within this budget, access to some healthcare services remains problematic, with long waits for a range of healthcare services, and the majority of the population continues to pay out of pocket for primary care services.”
The report noted that increasing health expenditure requirements were “coming at a time of great uncertainty for Ireland (and the world)”.
“Geopolitical tensions, increased digitalisation and climate change all bring challenges to the Irish economy and society in general and for the healthcare system in particular,” it said.
The ESRI said that continuing to increase the allocation of public funds to healthcare was “likely to be less viable in the Irish context”.
“Increased consideration could be given to policies which positively impact population health, both as a means of improving the quality of life of the population and reducing demand for health and social care services,” it said.
The research also looked at policy initiatives designed to increase access to and capacity of the healthcare system, including plans to reduce waiting lists and the expansion of the GP visit card.
“In general, the included policy reforms had a much smaller impact on projected demand relative to changes in the size and age structure of the population,” it said.
Reflecting Ireland’s ageing population, the ESRI analysed a number of scenarios and in each one long-term care emerged “as the main driver of expenditure growth”.
“It is relatively certain that the ageing and growing population will contribute to a significant increase in demand and expenditure requirements on health and social care, raising the question of how to ensure the financial sustainability of the public healthcare system,” it said.
Report author Sheelah Connolly said Ireland “has begun to plan for higher health and social care demand, but demographic change will require sustained action”.
“Expanding capacity needs to be accompanied by increased efficiencies and a stronger emphasis on preventing ill health,” she said.

title: St Pat’s title hopes in tatters after Dos Santos nets Derry winner
description: Stephen Kenny’s side struggle to find energy after Friday's defeat to Shelbourne
content:
St Patrick’s Athletic ’s title aspirations have been left in tatters after two defeats in three days to put Stephen Kenny’s side third in the Premier Division , six points adrift of Shamrock Rovers with two games remaining.
A subdued contest at the Brandywell came to life in the 62nd minute when Darragh Burns scurried down the right to plant a cross on the head of Portuguese winger Kevin Dos Santos.
The contrast between this game and last Monday’s thrilling Dublin derby between Shamrock Rovers and Bohemians was stark. Flat, slow paced and riddled with miscued passing, St Pat’s looked jaded after their full-court press against Shelbourne on Friday night.
The 2-1 loss at Richmond Park will torture them through the winter rather than what transpired here. The opening 45 minutes last Friday was when Kenny’s side let slip their chance to end a 13-year wait for a League of Ireland title.
Three days on, they were devoid of energy. Even when Kian Leavy tiptoed into the Derry box after just three minutes, his shot lacked any venom and the excellent Patrick McClean sent the ball for a corner. Three minutes later and Leavy burst through again, only for Jamie Stott to get across with another block.
Derry listed Michael Duffy and Adam O’Reilly as injured, but 20 days out from the FAI Cup final against Waterford, interim manager Mark Connolly would be forgiven for taking no chances with his best players. Mired in the mid-table, and with only one route into Europe remaining, there’s no need to risk the pair until November 8th.
Asked if James McClean can return to the Derry squad ahead of the final, his younger brother Patrick said: “I’m not sure. I don’t know. I would love to see it. It would be an honour to share the pitch with him. I wish him well in whatever happens. I’m going to be there to support him. It is obviously a sad after.”
Burns, a former St Pat’s winger, had an interesting first half. Despite looking dangerous dribbling off the right, he was yellow carded for a blatant dive moments before he wasted a clear sight of goal. After Barry Crowe-Baggley was blocked from retaining possession by referee Aaron O’Dowda, Burns exchanged with Tyler Smith only to shoot straight at Joey Anang.
The visitor’s lack of tempo suggested they had nothing in the tank. Kenny has already criticised how the recent international break left his squad idle for 27 days.
Around the hour mark, Derry seemed to realise that some form will be required before they meet Waterford in the Cup decider. Their goal came after St Pat’s skipper Joe Redmond’s bullet header missed the target from a Zack Elbouzedi free kick.
It began with James Clarke switching the play with the outside of his right boot. Brandon Fleming and Dos Santos injected pace into the attack down the left before play went back right where Burns skinned James McClelland and sent a dangerous cross into the St Pat’s six-yard box. Dos Santos had continued his run, keeping hold of Elbouzedi’s shirt, and he let the ball bounce off his head to nestle in the far corner.
Kenny flung Ryan Sheridan and veteran playmaker Chris Forrester into the fray instead of Crowe-Baggley and Leavy. But the damage had been done last Friday, this was just the killer blow to the former Republic of Ireland manager’s plan to bring silverware back to Inchicore in his third season.
Sheridan almost saved the day. The teenager picked up the ball 40 yards from goal, gliding between two Derry players and evading another with a deft back heel before a left-foot shot went straight at goalkeeper Thomas Norcott. The Kildare midfielder could shine at the under-17 World Cup in Qatar next month.
Romal Palmer had two late chances to beat Norcott and secure a point that would have given St Pat’s a mathematical chance of catching Rovers, but the Englishman’s effort hit the goalkeeper’s leg before he put a tap-in wide.
Meanwhile, the top goalscorer in the Premier Division has become a battle between Waterford strike partners Podge Amond and Tommy Lonergan as Graham Coughlan’s side eased out of the relegation playoff spot with a dramatic 3-2 win over Galway United at the RSC.
Amond scored twice before half-time to bring his tally for the season to 13 goals. Galway drew level with goals from Lee Devitt and Stephen Walsh, only for Lonergan to hit his 15th of the campaign in the last minute.
The result brings Waterford level on points with Drogheda United, but ahead of them on goal difference with two games remaining.
DERRY CITY: Norcott; Lyons-Foste (Barr 46), P McClean, Stott, Fleming; Twisk (Dummigan 79), Clarke; Dos Santos (Markey 72), Chapman, Burns; Smith (Doherty 85).
ST PATRICK’S ATHLETIC: Anang; Redmond, Hoare, Turner (Palmer 75); Elbouzedi, Crowe-Baggley (Sheridan 64), Lennon, Breslin (McClelland 57); Leavy (Forrester 63), Keena (Edmondson 57), Olunsanya.

title: The Irish Times view on the Israeli election: the battle to unseat Netanyahu
description: European hopes for a major change of policy direction unlikely to be realised
content:
The weekend endorsement from Donald Trump looks like a belated mixed blessing for the re-election campaign of Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu. The once-close relationship between the two men has become frayed, with many Israeli voters less than impressed with the US president’ s very public insistence that because “I call all the shots “ Netanyahu should accept US leadership unquestioningly.
The sting in the tail of the endorsement was the warning by this most unreliable ally that should Israelis not re-elect Netanyahu “the US would have to take on the Islamic republic (Iran) alone, and I am not inclined to do so”. Is this Trump, with an eye to his looming midterm elections, preparing his off-ramp from an unpopular war?
With a week to go to the election on October 27th, Netanyahu’s position is precarious. The hard-right coalition of his Likud party with its extremist Haredi religious and settler allies, is polling just behind the alliance led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot of the Yashar party, who has a predicted one-seat (52-51) lead in the Knesset.
The bulk of the balance of seats are likely to go to the Arab parties, representing a fifth of voters, Mansour Abbas’s United Arab List and the Joint List, who are predicted, if their leaders can get their reluctant supporters out to vote, to win a combined 13 seats.
That’s enough to hold the balance of power. But with neither the opposition nor Nethanyahu keen to coalesce with the Joint List, forming a majority will be difficult.
If Eisenkot wins the right to form a government, he will have to rely on external support built around the united demand of all the opposition to get Netanyahu out. The Arab parties also strongly support demands for an inquiry into the events surrounding the October 7th 2023 Hamas massacre, likely to focus on the prime minister’s actions, including whether, as some reporting alleges, there was advance knowledge of the attack.
European allies’ expectations and hopes that Netanyahu’s defeat could mean a major shift in the country’s internal and external policies appear to be wishful thinking, however. Political observers believe an Eisenkot government may indeed wish to curb settler violence against Palestinian communities in the West Bank and to improve relations with the Palestinian Authority.
But opposition leaders have maintained that if they win, they will continue striking hard against militant groups across the region. All have attacked Netanyahu for failing to “destroy” Hamas and “eliminate” Iran’s nuclear programme, as he had promised to do.
Eisenkot likes to say he has never said the words “Palestinian state “ and none of his allies support the idea of a two-state solution, still seen by many as the only path to long-term peace.

title: Man (60s) dies after collision involving truck and car in Co Wicklow
description: Gardaí appeal for witnesses to incident which took place on N81 at Athgarvan
content:
A man in his 60s has died following a “serious” two-vehicle collision in Co Wicklow on Monday.
The fatal collision, involving a truck and a car, occurred on the N81 at Athgarvan at around 11.15am.
The driver of the car was pronounced dead at the scene. His body has since been removed to the mortuary at Naas General Hospital for postmortem examination and the coroner has been notified.
The driver of the truck, also a man in his 60s, was brought to Tallaght University Hospital for treatment of injuries believed to be non life-threatening.
The road was temporarily closed with diversions in place but has since reopened.
Gardaí are appealing to anyone who may have witnessed the collision to contact them. Those with relevant video footage are asked to make this available.
So far this year, 148 people have been killed on the State’s roads.

title: Rape trials only cases ‘deliberately’ targeted by striking solicitors, Jim O’Callaghan to tell Oireachtas
description: Criminal defence solicitor Michael Finucane rejects suggestion rape or any specific cases targeted
content:
Rape trials were the only cases “deliberately affected” by the withdrawal of services by some solicitors on Monday, Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan will tell the Oireachtas on Tuesday.
Many defence solicitors, particularly in Dublin, withdrew legal aid services in July after a new flat fee system for District Court cases was introduced.
The dispute ramped up on Monday with the withdrawal of services expanding to cases including custody and children’s cases.
O’Callaghan is due to appear before the Oireachtas justice committee to be questioned on the dispute.
In his opening statement, seen by The Irish Times, O’Callaghan will say six cases were adjourned on the previous day and “every one of these was a case involving an allegation of rape”.
He will express “deep concern that the only cases deliberately affected by the withdrawal of services in the Central Criminal Court yesterday [Monday] were those involving allegations of rape. I believe this committee and indeed the public are entitled to an answer as to why this is the case.”
[ Huge rise in claims of unlawful detention linked to withdrawal of solicitors’ services Opens in new window ]
Criminal defence solicitor Michael Finucane rejected any suggestion rape or any specific cases were targeted by solicitors. “This is a full withdrawal of services in all criminal cases,” he said.
“The Minister was warned by solicitors and the Law Society well in advance [that] this would happen, that complainants could face extended disruption and possible retraumatisation. No one regrets more that this has come to pass than solicitors.”
O’Callaghan insisted he would not revoke the new regulations at the centre of the row and would mount a defence of his changes to the system brought in last July.
He will maintain the system is operating nationwide, that legal aid continues to be granted by the courts, with about 3,400 legal aid certificates issued since July.
He will, however, “acknowledge” that, particularly in Dublin, a “number of solicitors have withdrawn services” which has “impacted on court hearings”, and describe this as “regrettable”.
“Despite this, in the Central Criminal Court yesterday, the majority of cases proceeded without issue.”
On Monday, justice committee chairman Matt Carthy, a Sinn Féin TD, argued the escalation of the dispute was “entirely avoidable” as he claimed O’Callaghan had failed to “meaningfully” engage in resolution efforts.
O’Callaghan said he has engaged with the Law Society on the matter and would do so again.
[ Judge ‘coerced’ into adjourning six rape and sexual offences trials as solicitors withdraw Opens in new window ]
He said he would not revoke the new regulations but said he is happy to “tweak” them “if there’s a necessity to do so” and he would “engage with the Law Society in respect of that”.
Criminal defence solicitor Tony Collier said, while the Minister had indicated the courts are working effectively throughout the dispute, significant backlogs have occurred “to such a point that the Chief Justice has expressed his concern”.
He welcomed O’Callaghan’s indication that he is prepared to examine particular issues but said any “tinkering” would have to be “in the context of a full and proper engagement with the Law Society”.

title: Fears of gang feuds in Drogheda as loaded guns and pipe bomb seized
description: Gardaí discovered loaded handgun and machine pistol during search of open group at Rathmullan Park, Drogheda
content:
Two guns and a viable pipe bomb discovered in Co Louth were being stored by a gang heavily involved in the drugs trade in Drogheda , gardaí believe.
The firearms, including a loaded machine pistol, were discovered during searches in Rathmullan Park, Drogheda.
While a number of senior criminals involved in gun violence as part of the Drogheda gangland feud have close ties to Rathmullan Park, gardaí do not believe the discovery of the firearms is linked to the feud.
Instead, it is suspected the guns are owned by another group, heavily involved in the local cocaine trade, and which is under intense investigation by gardaí in the northwest at present.
However, the discovery of loaded firearms, a handgun, a Rak machine pistol and a viable pipe bomb has raised concerns that they had been acquired for planned attacks by the gang on their rivals in the local drugs trade.
The cache was found on Sunday during a search of open land in the Rathmullan Park area, as part of a pre-planned operation led by members of the Divisional Drugs Unit.
“During the course of the search, a viable pipe bomb was located and subsequently made safe by a Defence Forces explosive ordnance device team,” the Garda said in a statement.
“Two loaded firearms – a handgun and a machine gun – were also located, along with ammunition. The operation was carried out with the assistance of members from Drogheda, the Armed Support Unit and local and national dog units.”
Given the violence that could have been inflicted with the seized guns and pipe bomb, and the fact the Drogheda feud had dissipated in recent years, a major inquiry is now under way to ensure a fresh feud does not erupt.
[ Gardaí believe several people can help with Jamie Bailey murder investigation Opens in new window ]
A number of senior figures on both sides of the Drogheda drugs feud, which resulted in four murders, are either in prison, dead or have left the country.
A number of those who fled abroad, including the Boylan brothers, are believed to remain active in crime and are suspected of having an influence on the drugs trade in Drogheda and the wider region.
However, as a group of senior criminals on both sides of the feud are no longer a force in the area, other groups are vying to secure a section of the local drugs trade, including the gang believed to own the guns found on Sunday.
Josh Boylan, Moneymore, Drogheda, Co Louth, and Keith Boylan, Park Heath, Drogheda, Co Meath, were charged with serious offences alleged to have been committed in late 2018.
[ Boylan brothers: The Irish gang leaders who have been on the run for five years Opens in new window ]
However, in June 2020 a sitting of Dublin Circuit Criminal Court heard the brothers, who are from Drogheda, had “gone off the radar” after being granted bail. Bench warrants were issued for their arrests, but they could not be found. They are still believed to be abroad.
In June 2025, when a number of women appeared before Dundalk Circuit Criminal Court on money laundering charges, the Boylans were named as the leaders of the Boylan organised crime group involved in the Drogheda feud.

title: Dublin council denies St Edmundsbury housing rezoning but gives green light to two other sites
description: Finnstown Castle and Coldcut Road locations approved after Minister instructed authorities to provide more land
content:
South Dublin County councillors upheld the decision not to rezone an area of land belonging to businessmen John Magnier and JP McManus in the Liffey valley following a vote on Monday afternoon.
The St Edmundsbury site, on the southside of the river Liffey, close to Lucan and just west of the Hermitage Golf Club, will not be rezoned.
However, sites at Finnstown Castle, between Lucan and Adamstown, and at Coldcut Road, south of the Liffey Valley shopping centre , will be rezoned for housing after the council vote.
The Irish Times previously reported that the council’s chief executive, Colm Ward, had proposed rezoning the three sites, which combined could accommodate more than 1,700 homes.
It followed an edict last summer from Minister for Housing James Browne that all local authorities must provide significant additional land for housing.
Councillors previously voted against rezoning the land.
A number of councillors on Monday raised the issue that they had to vote more than once on the issue.
Councillor Daniel Loftus of Sinn Féin said: “I understand this policy that we have to have a second vote, but we already voted on this. People have made their points clear.”
People Before Profit-Solidarity councillor Jess Spear said: “The process has created a loss of trust and confidence in democratic decision making. The community feels that the council is just holding another vote to get the outcome that you want, which you are.”
At the beginning of the meeting Ward said: “I do appreciate the challenges and the difficulties and the burden that has been carried by councillors throughout this process.”
He said the second vote on the issue was a “statutory process”.
[ Dublin residents protest against rezoning of land owned by John Magnier and JP McManus Opens in new window ]
“It’s not something we’re trying to do to get people to change their minds or anything else, that’s the process and we have to respect that and we have to see that through,” he said.
The council meeting heard that 1,710 submissions were received, including prescribed bodies, raising “various observations” and were “heavily weighted to St Edmundsbury and Finnstown”.
The Irish Times previously reported that more than 1,600 submissions opposed the rezoning of the St Edmundsbury site.
A demonstration against the proposal to rezone St Edmundsbury was held in Lucan, west Dublin, on Saturday, by the Save St Edmundsbury Protest Committee, calling on local councillors to vote against the proposal.
The land is currently zoned as “high amenity” due to its environmental and natural amenity value.

title: New public sector pay deal could be struck within days, union leader suggests
description: Two sides met for first time for talks proper at Workplace Relations Commission on Monday
content:
The possibility of a new public sector pay deal being struck quickly remains a possibility, union leader Kevin Callinan said on Monday night.
Callinan, who is Fórsa general secretary, was speaking after union and Government representatives met for the first time for talks proper at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).
He indicated before the talks got under way he felt there was the possibility of a deal being struck in days rather than weeks.
After six hours of talks on Monday, he said: “I think one of the positives out of today was both sides are committed to try and do this as quickly as possible.
“The urgency does seem to be shared, so I think that is a positive. So we definitely welcome that.”
The opening session, he said, had been mainly about the two sides providing an “opening outline of positions”.
“We went through in some detail our priorities in relation to pay, the various aspects of it,” he said. “We had a good discussion with the WRC’s facilitators, and we’ve given them some things to think about overnight.
“Obviously, we’re going to start with pay, but there are other things to be discussed as well, from both our perspective and theirs. We’re back in at 10.30am, so we’ll see tomorrow.”
Asked if the unions had received any feedback from the Government side in relation to their opening positions, he said they had not, but suggested they would “get a sense of that tomorrow”.
“We mainly laid out the issues and backed them up with a lot of detail today,” he said. “I think they listened to that and now do have a number of things to reflect on.”
Callinan was accompanied to the talks by Phil Ní Sheaghdha of the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation , John Boyne of the Irish National Teachers’ Organisation and Adrian Kane of Siptu .
He was earlier asked about the Taoiseach’s suggestion that any deal would have to have productivity elements that provided taxpayers with value for money.
[ Any pay deal reached with unions must have productivity elements, says Taoiseach Opens in new window ]
“Any pay negotiation has a cost-of-living element and usually a productivity element,” he said. “We’re prepared to listen to what they have to say.
“But I think if they’ve heard what members said on the picket line, so many of them said that they’ve nothing more to give. That they’re really struggling with the cost of living and under huge pressure and work. Let’s see what develops in the talks.”
One of the 19 unions involved in the dispute, Unite , meanwhile, announced on Monday it too had suspended Wednesday’s strike action after consulting with its shop stewards.
The union, which represents about 4,000 of the more than 400,000 workers in the public service, had voted against the suspension at Friday’s meeting to consider the situation in the wake of Wednesday’s strike.

title: Opposition parties left and right in Dáil unite to resist shelving neutrality triple lock
description: Parties also expected to adopt joint approach in seeking amendments to Bill, especially during committee stage
content:
Opposition parties will launch a high-profile campaign against the fiercely contested Bill to abolish the triple lock in advance of the first big debate on the legislation in the Dáil on Wednesday.
All Opposition parties, including the right-leaning Aontú and Independent Ireland, will co-operate in opposing the legislation. A joint media event will be held outside Leinster House on Tuesday.
The parties are also expected to adopt a joint approach in seeking amendments to the Bill, especially during committee stage next month.
[ Courts will decide on military deployments if triple lock is removed, warns Labour leader Opens in new window ]
The Coalition will also face opposition to the Bill from within its own ranks. Veteran Limerick TD and former minister for defence Willie O’Dea will raise the issue at tonight’s Fianna Fáil parliamentary party meeting. A letter he drafted before the summer questioning, in part, the basis of the Bill, was signed by 20 colleagues and hotly debated at an internal party meeting.
Under the triple lock , the Government must secure UN approval before 12 or more members of the Defence Forces can be sent overseas with an armed international force or body.
The Bill would remove that requirement. Irish troops could instead join a force or body that is sanctioned by the United Nations, the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe, the European Union or any EU institution or body, or by another regional arrangement operating under the UN charter, assuming a decision by the Government and the Dáil.
A spokesman for Minister for Foreign Affairs and Defence Helen McEntee said on Monday the triple lock needed to be reformed if the State wanted to continue its role in international peacekeeping.
“As a sovereign country, the UNSC [United Nations Security Council] members shouldn’t hold an effective veto over where we can send peacekeepers,” he said.
The changes, he said, are “in line with our policy of military neutrality”.
The second stage debate is scheduled for three hours and 34 minutes on Wednesday, with a vote on Wednesday night. The Bill will then go to committee stage.
Sinn Féin defence spokesman Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire suggested that, privately, a majority of the Dáil were uncomfortable with the legislation , particularly in Fianna Fáil.
“It is a foolish and reckless and regressive move that will undermine Ireland’s standing in the world,” he said.
Labour’s Duncan Smith said the Bill exposed the clearest divide between Government and Opposition on a fundamental issue.
“The Government is going to face opposition to this from not just the opposition, but also internally from backbenchers, especially in Fianna Fáil. I think they could be surprised at the kind of force they’re going to come up against.”
Sinéad Gibney of the Social Democrats criticised the plan to guillotine the debate, setting a strict time limit to advance the legislation quickly. “We feel any TD who wishes to speak on it should have the opportunity to do so,” she said. She said the removal of the triple lock would be “a full compromise of our neutrality ... we are not going to be neutral once the triple lock is gone.”
[ Taoiseach Micheál Martin defends plan to scrap triple lock before facing Fianna Fáil TDs Opens in new window ]
On cross-party working, she said the Irish Neutrality League, which was involved in the demonstrations against US president Donald Trump ’s visit to Ireland, had been instrumental in helping cross-party co-operation.
“It’s not just left-wing parties,” she said. “When it comes to the triple lock, this goes across ideology.”
O’Dea said the triple lock had been a particular concern for his party. “Neutrality and the triple lock have been more associated with Fianna Fáil than any other party. It’s an important enough matter for our members,” he said.
He said he expected the Government to be “open to reasonable suggestions to preserve the link to the United Nations if at all possible”. He also wants to know whether troops could be sent on the basis of a resolution of the UN General Assembly, given the logjam at the Security Council. “If it is possible, we should use it. I think. If it’s not possible, I’d like to know why.”

title: Cristiano Ronaldo given 30-day ban and fined €255 for leaving Portugal camp after row
description: Ronaldo left international camp after he was an unused substitute in Portugal’s Nations League fixture against Norway
content:
Cristiano Ronaldo has received a 30-day suspension for leaving the national ‌camp following a rift with head coach Jorge Jesus.
The Portuguese FA’s disciplinary council upheld the charge against the 41-year-old forward in full and imposed a €255 fine.
Ronaldo left Portugal’s base in Copenhagen before their Nations League match ⁠against Denmark earlier this month, accusing Jesus of ‌twice ‌breaking ​his word regarding the 41-year-old’s role in the team after he was an unused substitute against Norway.
Jesus denied making ⁠any agreement with ​Ronaldo but left the door ​open for his return.
The Portuguese FA’s statement did not specify what matches or activities the suspension would cover, or whether time already served under a provisional suspension would count towards the 30-day sanction.
Ronaldo subsequently apologised for failing to acknowledge ‌supporters after the Norway ⁠match and for leaving his team-mates, saying he remained available for selection after serving any punishment ‌arising from the incident.
Portuguese FA president Pedro Proenca said everyone within ​the association wants Ronaldo to return to ​the national team once the matter is resolved.

title: Draws for provincial football championships to take place on November 19th
description: Draws expected to be shown live on GAA+
content:
The draws for the 2027 provincial football championships will take place on Thursday, November 19th.
The GAA have opted to retain the later date following a trial last year which saw the draws pushed back from their usual slot in October.
The draws are expected to be shown live on GAA+, with Croke Park and provincial council officials finalising the details.
The draws were broadcast on the GAA’s streaming platform last year in a change from the previous arrangement by which RTÉ provided live coverage of the event.
The draw for the 2027 Leinster football championship will be of particular interest as several counties will fancy their chances of landing the Delaney Cup.
With Dublin’s era of dominance now over, Louth and Westmeath have been crowned Leinster champions in the past two seasons. Meath and Kildare will also see themselves as contenders, so there should be a stacked field chasing provincial silverware next summer.
The four semi-finalists from this year’s Leinster championship – Westmeath, Dublin, Kildare and Louth – will go straight to the quarter-final stages, while the remaining seven counties – Meath, Offaly, Laois, Wicklow, Longford, Carlow and Wexford – will contest the first round.
In Ulster, teams who feature in the preliminary round receive a two-year exemption from the opening fixture, meaning Donegal, Derry, Tyrone and reigning champions Armagh will begin their respective championship campaigns at the quarter-final stage.
The contentious seeding system is likely to dominate much of the conversation in Munster, where Kerry will be vying for their seventh successive title having won 13 of the last 14 instalments.
In Connacht, two of the quarter-final pairings are already predetermined, with Sligo travelling Stateside to take on New York and Leitrim making the trip to Ruislip to play London.

title: Woman to be awarded damages over alleged rape by employee at hotel
description: Civil action against accused worker and company  over sexual assault, rape, battery, false imprisonment and emotional suffering
content:
The High Court is set to assess damages owed to a woman who claims she was raped by an employee of a hotel at which she was staying, after the alleged perpetrator and hotel failed to respond to her lawsuit against them.
The woman alleges she was raped by the employee at the hotel in Leinster.
The woman brought a civil action against the employee and the company behind the hotel over the alleged rape.
In the claim, she seeks damages over the employee’s alleged trespass of her person “to include sexual assault, rape, battery, false imprisonment, and intentional infliction of emotional suffering”, and over the hotel’s alleged negligence, breach of duty and breach of contract.
In court documents, the woman says the hotel company was the controller of the hotel at the time of the alleged rape, and as such, was either directly or vicariously liable for the employee’s actions.
Neither the employee nor the hotel entered an appearance in the lawsuit against them. In High Court actions, a defendant must file an appearance within a set time period if they intend to defend the action.
On Monday, barrister Alannah McGurk, appearing for the woman instructed by Coleman Legal, asked Judge Paul Coffey to grant her client judgment against the employee, in circumstances where he had not entered an appearance.
Counsel said the employee had been served with the proceedings and had been issued with a warning letter following his failure to enter an appearance.
The court heard that the woman’s lawyers had already obtained judgment against the hotel company in default of appearance.
The judge granted judgment in favour of the woman against the employee.
Coffey said the case should be set down for trial before a judge for the purposes of assessing damages owed to the woman.

title: ‘There’s nothing left’: French businesses count the cost of a weekend of unrest
description: Thousands of shops damaged or looted as protests descended into violence, leaving owners fearing for their future
content:
A s unrest spread across France last weekend, Youssef Khoukha (61) drew down the shutters of his family-run sportswear shop, Footmax.
He and a handful of employees watched tensely from inside as their security camera showed hooded people in black gathered outside on Boulevard de Magenta near Paris’ s Gare de l’Est train station.
Footage on social media shows what happened next: the group forced open the shutters and began smashing the windows.
“We tried to reason with them from behind the shutters, telling them we’re a family business, we have children,” Khoukha recalled.
“It wasn’t possible. They said: ‘listen, it’s very simple, you leave and we won’t hurt you.’”
He could do little but watch as the business he built up over 26 years was ransacked. “All our merchandise was taken, and there was nothing we could do,” he says. “Young, not so young, the general public, vandals, everyone took advantage.”
🔴 Paris 10ème : Magasin Foot Max boulevard Magenta dévalisé. #17octobre pic.twitter.com/tFQHy5ypZS
Videos of the carnage show people ducking in and out of the shop, fleeing with bags or armfuls of looted shoes and sportswear. The shop was left ruined: interior fittings torn down and smashed, the floor littered with broken hangers, shoe boxes, glass and detritus.
Originally from Morocco but living in France since the 1980s, Khoukha worked alongside his wife and brother in the shop and raised two children running the business.
[ ‘It was like having Tabasco poured in my eyes’: Irish caught in French riots recall chaos Opens in new window ]
His daughter launched an online fundraiser to help save the shop.
“Nothing was left. Every jersey, every accessory, every item was taken. Even the refrigerator was emptied and stolen,” reads the fundraiser, which has raised just over €4,000. “The future of the store remains uncertain.”
There was looting in cities including Paris, Lyons, Marseilles and Nice on the sidelines of combined protests by students and against the high cost of living on Saturday. The unrest continued into Sunday as bands of people dressed in black roamed Paris late into the early hours.
Across France, the damage inflicted on businesses amounts to “hundreds of millions of euro”, according to France’s Chambers of Commerce and Industry, which has warned some may shut their doors for good.
“Nothing can justify such violence, such attacks on people and property. Shopkeepers, tradespeople, small and medium-sized businesses and their employees see their livelihoods destroyed in a single day,” the industry body said in a statement.
“This violence is affecting businesses already weakened by years of successive crises, rising costs, and declining foot traffic in city centres. For many of them, this vandalism could be the final blow.”
The French government has said that at least 3,000 business have been affected, and that it will offer them financial support and furlough schemes.
The government has also vowed to expedite a law designed to make those who cause damage – or their parents – financially liable for the cost of repair.
Investigators are set to comb social media footage to find clues about the perpetrators, with prime minister Sébastien Lecornu announcing a “massive judicial operation” to gather fingerprints and images.
Khoukha is preparing an insurance claim. He believes the damage will put him out of business for at least six months to a year.
“The shop is a disaster,” he says. “There’s nothing left.”
[ What’s behind the violence shaking France, and what comes next? Opens in new window ]

title: Sex assault victim challenges refusal of application to compensation scheme
description: Woman says she was not given any information about scheme by gardaí
content:
A woman who was violently sexually and physically assaulted near a football pitch nearly five years ago has brought a High Court challenge over a refusal to include her in a scheme compensating victims of crime.
The woman immediately reported the assault, which occurred on November 7th, 2021, to the Garda Síochána, but she says it was not until this year that she learned of the Scheme for Personal Injuries Criminally Inflicted of 1986 and/or 2021.
She was out of time to make an application under the scheme, as it must be made within two years of the crime.
Judge Mary Rose Gearty on Monday granted leave to Conor Power, counsel for the woman, to bring judicial review proceedings seeking to quash a decision of the Criminal Injuries Compensation Tribunal of April 1st last to refuse her application.
The court application was made with only the woman’s side represented and adjourned to next month.
The proceedings are against the tribunal, the Minister for Justice, the Garda Commissioner, Ireland and the Attorney General.
The woman seeks declarations including that the tribunal erred insofar as it considered itself bound by the scheme so that it could not disapply it.
She also seeks a declaration that the scheme is invalid because the tribunal is not an independent and impartial tribunal previously established by law. She wants a declaration that the respondents have failed adequately to transpose a 2004 EU directive relating to compensating crime victims and in failing to place the tribunal and/or the scheme on a statutory basis. She also seeks damages.
In her action, it is argued she is entitled to rely on the 2004 EU directive and that she has a legal right to compensation as the directive requires that member states shall provide for a compensation scheme.
It is further claimed that because the scheme is not on a statutory footing, it amounts to an administrative practice which can be changed at the whim of the executive.
Under a 2012 EU directive, member states are also required to ensure that victims are offered information about the compensation scheme, it is claimed.
It is argued that this right was transposed into Irish law under the 2017 Criminal Justice (Victims of Crime) Act and provides that gardaí or the Garda Síochána Ombudsman Commission (Fiosrú), as the case may be, shall offer to the victim information on the compensation scheme.
The woman says she was not given any information by gardaí.
It is also alleged the tribunal fettered its discretion by its failure to consider extending the time for accepting the application. It is noted that the Residential Institutions Redress Scheme, which compensates victims of historical abuse, has a longer period for making an application and has an inbuilt discretion to extend the time for making an application.

title: Definitely a runner: Alan Milton on preparing for Sunday’s Dublin Marathon
description: Talk of split times, strides and boomerang runs becomes second nature as do jitters about ‘Heartbreak Hill’
content:
F requency illusion – also known as the Baader Meinhof Phenomenon – is real and is something I can attest to.
It’s the behaviour of thinking something happens more regularly than previously, but only because it has recently become relevant to you. After signing up to run my first marathon at the ripe age of 48, I am now seeing joggers / runners everywhere I go.
Needless to say, they’ve always been there – not least at this time of the year – when the hugely popular Dublin city marathon looms large on the horizon, but when you’ve got a precious entry ticket in your possession they register in a different way.
There’s almost a kindred spirit sentiment to the spotting process.
The fluorescent attire might be the first element to register before a sneaking glance at the ever-growing sponge sole footwear. Then there’s the mental speculation about what type of training or run they are on as you hopelessly attempt to gauge their speed, wondering how they long they’ve been pounding the pavements and how far they’ve journeyed.
On Sunday Dublin city centre and outlying areas will close to vehicular traffic as roughly 20,000 committed souls run, jog and, in some cases, plod their way around the 26-mile 385-yard route passing some of the city’s most recognisable landmarks.
It’s a special club, an assertion that rings through in people’s reaction when you confide in them your plans to attempt to join it.
However, putting one’s hand up for involvement encompasses so much more than the day itself.
After the passing of time retired me from the rigours of Gaelic football , the vacuum had to be filled with something other than coaching and sports administration. And that something became running , an interest sharpened by the additional time that the Covid pandemic granted us.
And so, it starts with 5km and 10km runs before the miles in the legs increase, and the possibility of completing a half-marathon doesn’t seem as far-fetched as it once might have.
You soon discover some of your friends and acquaintances are closet runners, and the addictive and competitive nature of it all kicks in.
When your alarm buzzes at 6.45 on a Sunday as you start squeezing in longer runs whenever possible, you start to see your native city in a different light and at a time of the morning that you sometimes saw as a reveller in younger years.
Of course, there is an inherent beauty to Dublin city on a bright summer Sunday morning with tourists outnumbering locals and even they are in short supply.
Clondalkin village, Inchicore, Kilmainham, Pimlico, The Liberties, O’Connell Bridge, the Quays, Phoenix Park, the Papal Cross, Chapelizod – the clock ticks on and with it grows the number of others stealing a march on the day, banking the kilometres or, in old money, miles.
Naturally, the lexicon has changed over the course of the last four months. Split times, Fartlek, accordion sessions, boomerang runs, floats, strides, electrolytes and any amount of confusing training plans have been deciphered and digested to such a point they now resemble a new norm.
Similarly, an array of apps and gadgets are now commonplace in the running bag, not to mention a collection of blindingly bright footwear only permissible when running.
A tight hamstring led to numerous physio visits and the identification of previously unknown back muscles – not to mention Google searches for solutions to “chest chafing”. There was also a return journey home by Luas when the aforementioned hamstring did not share my enthusiasm for the early Sunday start.
So after running all over the capital city, on the north Antrim coast, International Drive, Orlando, New York and along Lake Michigan in recent weeks and months, the nods and greetings of the runners’ etiquette handbook have been practised and perfected.
The stomach lining has built up a resistance for the consumption of energy gels; the minutes per kilometre needed to record a given target time has been rehearsed.
The giddy nerves have started to kick in and will only increase as you ponder running a distance longer than even your recent “long run” – not to mention the justifiable jitters around “Heartbreak Hill” and, of course, hitting “the wall”.
Of all the things learned on the journey, the bond and respect in meeting fellow runners – friends and strangers alike – has been a major takeaway.
Striking up a conversation with a stranger while running at the same pace on a glorious August morning in Central Park reminded me of the power of sport, swapping stories, discussing footwear and wishing each other well for upcoming runs in Berlin and Dublin.
All told, it has been a big commitment but an enjoyable experience, providing interesting insights into the mindsets of so many who do it year-in year-out. More power to them.
As for the burning question of what follows and are you “one and done?”, that remains to be seen, but if I make it around then there will be satisfaction in being able to say as much.

title: Ex-Labour Court chairman subject to dignity-at-work complaint from senior official, WRC told
description: Member of industrial relations service ‘was unfairly dismissed’
content:
A former chairman of the Labour Court was the subject of a dignity-at-work complaint by an ordinary member of the court who has now claimed unfair dismissed, the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) has heard
The complainant, Peter DR Murphy, who sat as a member of the Labour Court from 2005 to 2024 as a nominee of business group Ibec , is pursuing allegations of unfair dismissal and other rights breaches against the Minister for Enterprise.
The State said Ibec did not nominate Murphy for a further term after his last warrant expired in 2024. Murphy’s legal team has said the department did not seek replacement nominees from the business group when the warrant ran out.
Murphy, a qualified solicitor, had been earning more than €140,000 a year in the role.
He alleged he was subject to workplace bullying during his appointment and he specifically identified a former chairman in a formal dignity-at-work complaint, according to legal correspondence in 2020 opened to a hearing on Monday.
Tara Coogan, a civil servant at the Department of Enterprise who was in charge of the section overseeing the Labour Court and the WRC at the end of Murphy’s last term on the court, gave evidence on the respondent’s preliminary objection to the case going ahead on Monday.
Frances Meenan, for the State, asked Coogan about a legal letter of October 5th, 2020, to former minister for enterprise Damien English from the complainants’ former solicitors.
In the letter, read out by Coogan, Murphy’s then solicitors wrote: “Our client has grave concerns about recent steps regarding the renewal of his warrant.”
The alleged change in practice was “not coincidental and is a direct response to certain recent events and issues raised by our client in respect of his working conditions and the treatment he has been forced to endure in the workplace”, the letter also said.
The letter stated Murphy had raised statutory claims concerning “bullying, victimisation and other related matters” and had “also instituted internal complaint against the chairman of the Labour Court under the Civil Service dignity at work policy”.
At that point, Meenan intervened and said: “We won’t mention any names.”
Coogan said: “I don’t know anything about this letter.”
Meenan said the State would present evidence that the complaints referenced in the letter “were subsequently withdrawn by the complainant”.
Tiernan Lowey, for the complainant, said: “We’re happy for the letter to be read out in full.”
The tribunal has heard how Murphy received one further term on the court before his final warrant lapsed in February 2024.
Meenan said it was position of the State that Murphy was not an employee and therefore had no standing to pursue the claim.
She said appointment to the Labour Court was contingent on Murphy being put forward as a nominee by Ibec, and accordingly Murphy’s 19 years at the Labour Court came to an end, Meenan said.
However, Lowey said: “We don’t believe there ever was any correspondence from the department or on behalf of the department [to Ibec] when Murphy’s last warrant expired.”
Lowey said Murphy “was never regarded as anything other than an employee of the minister”. The complainant’s position is that it had become the custom and practice to renew warrants until a member of the court resigned and only then seek three nominees.
Meenan accepted the State had “a gap” in its supporting documentation as copies of correspondence between the department and Ibec asking the employers’ group to put forward a nominee for the court every time Murphy had been reappointed were not with its legal papers.
She said the documents in question were “old paper files that are hard to get”.
Adjudicator Christina Ryan said it was “unusual” that the State was not ready with the documents in question when it was making the nomination process a “central feature” of its case.
She directed the State to produce the material and said the matter could be revisited when the case resumed on Wednesday.
Murphy’s complaints are under the Unfair Dismissals Act, the Protection of Employees (Fixed-Term Work) Act, the Redundancy Payments Act and the Minimum Notice and Terms of Employment Act.

title: Ulster ‘understand the challenge’ that awaits in South Africa
description: Winless in the URC this season, Ulster’s Challenge Cup victory over Zebre came at the right time
content:
A first win is in the bag, albeit at Zebre in the Challenge Cup , and yet there is simply no let up for Ulster as they now depart for South Africa where the challenging task of facing the Bulls and the Stormers awaits.
Still without a victory after three rounds in the URC , having drawn two games and lost one for an eight-point tally, this is hardly the situation Richie Murphy wanted to find his side in ahead of a match at altitude in Pretoria against the in-form Bulls before they move on to Cape Town to test themselves against the strength of the Stormers.
The bonus-point win over Zebre will at least have made Ulster feel better about themselves ahead of the long trip, though there are concerns over internationals Stuart McCloskey and Nick Timoney, who both missed the game in Parma due to muscle injuries picked up in training last week.
It’s hoped both will be available to feature at Loftus Versfeld on Saturday afternoon, however, there is doubt over Zac Ward after he picked up ankle injury against Zebre.
Locks Ben Donnell and Eli Snyman and Ethan McIlroy also missed out at the weekend and will undergo fitness monitoring in South Africa.
Getting a positive result against the Bulls will be a tall ask for Ulster, as they learned two years ago when they were crushed 47-21 in Pretoria.
“They understand the challenge,” said Ulster forwards coach Clarke Dermody. “We had a show of hands as to who had played there [South Africa] and there were maybe four or five in the room that hadn’t.
“So we’ll make sure that they get a chance to talk to the boys that have played there and what it feels like, because it is different playing at altitude.
“All we can do is be as ready as we can be. We’ve got some good plans in place that we’ll get a chance to have a crack at [in training] and then it’ll be up to them to get their mentality right and go out and execute it.”

title: Warning not to drink water affected by aluminium in Tipperary lifted but boil notice stays
description: Uisce Éireann has apologised for disruption in Tipperary communities
content:
Uisce Éireann has lifted the do-not-consume notice affecting almost 11,500 people served by the Ardfinnan water supply in Co Tipperary , but customers will still have to boil the water before drinking it.
The warning not to drink their tap water under any circumstances was in place for 10 days after high levels of aluminium were found in their supply from the Goatenbridge water treatment plant.
Ardfinnan, parts of Cahir and surrounding communities were affected and had to rely on bottled and tankered water supplied by Uisce Éireann.
“We recognise the disruption this caused for households, businesses and the wider community,” Uisce Éireann said on Monday afternoon.
While the water was declared unsafe to drink for the duration of the notice, the company said the main risk from aluminium in drinking water was from ongoing exposure.
“Following on from concerns raised, the HSE have provided specific advice for the general public indicating there is little known risk from short-term exposure at the levels that were seen in the Goatenbridge water treatment plant,” it said.
“The lifting of the [do not consume] notice follows the completion of critical works at Goatenbridge water treatment plant, an extensive targeted flushing programme across the network and comprehensive water quality sampling at both the plant and across the regional network over the weekend.”
[ Co Tipperary town told not to drink water due to excessive aluminium content Opens in new window ]
However, the boil water notice which had already been in place for the past four months – and for several months last winter – remains.
“We know how challenging this period has been for communities,” said Fionnuala Callery, regional operations senior manager.
“People have had to manage both the restrictions associated with the do-not-consume notice and repeated interruptions to their water supply over recent months.
“We sincerely apologise for that disruption and thank everyone for their patience and understanding.
“Our focus now is on lifting the boil water notice as quickly and safely as possible.
“We will continue the necessary testing and monitoring and work closely with the HSE so that it can be lifted when it is safe to do so.”
Earlier in the day, Ardfinnan community council notified local people that it had sent a complaint to Uisce Éireann on their behalf and asked company representatives to meet them.
[ What Paris can teach Ireland about clean water Opens in new window ]
It comes as anger remains over how people were notified of the aluminium concerns, initial poor organisation around the supply of bottled water and the lack of a clear finish line for the upgrading works.
“We are very aware of the community’s frustration on this issue and the lack of clarity surrounding this whole issue,” the council wrote.
It said it would arrange a meeting for all affected residents and businesses as well as public representatives in the near future.

title: ‘If we do that, we’ll win’: Connacht backs coach clear on what’s needed to beat Zebre
description: Gerard Mullen says the team has much to improve on despite thrilling nature of win against Saracens
content:
Connacht will be aiming to build on their thrilling Champions Cup victory over Saracens when they return to United Rugby Championship (URC) action against Zebre in Galway on Friday.
Backs coach Gerard Mullen is taking nothing for granted against the Italian visitors despite their position at the bottom of the URC table.
“Friday is an opportunity for us to kick on again and hopefully get a win at home,” he says. “Our focus is having a better and higher level of performance.
“Saturday against Saracens was great . . . but we have to be better again.
“We’re still nowhere near where we know we can be and get to. We’ve got to keep pushing the envelope. We definitely left scores out there against Saracens. We could have been more ruthless and we conceded a couple of scores we were unhappy about. It’s just about trying to grow our game the whole time.”
Connacht have been boosted by the return of several key players to full training, including Will Connors, Dave Heffernan and Harry West, who are all available for selection.
However, Shane Jennings and Thomas Connolly are undergoing graduated return-to-play protocols and are ruled out, while there are no updates on Dylan Tierney-Martin, Ben Murphy, Hugh Gavin and Byron Ralston.
Mullen, a former Clongowes player who coached at Harlequins for several years, says Connacht cannot take Zebre for granted.
“In some ways, they are the harder games [against a team struggling] because they’re going to come here and throw the kitchen sink at us, he says. ”So for us, it’s about really sticking to our systems and processes, while also taking it up another level from the win over Saracens.
“If we do that, we’ll win the game. So, in terms of a sharp training week, we need to get our contact skills on point. If we do, we’ll cause problems.”
The Italian side plays an unstructured game, which could cause difficulties for Connacht.
“We know it’s not going to come easy,” adds Mullen. “I wouldn’t be surprised if it’s quite close for large parts of the game. But if we stick in there and keep pounding, we’ll be able to get the job done.”

title: Woman jailed for helping to commission murder by buying petrol to destroy getaway car
description: Ciara Mahony (46) has ‘moral culpability’ in relation to 2017 death of Jamie Tighe-Ennis (24) in Dublin, judge says
content:
A woman who helped to commission the 2017 murder of a Dublin man by buying petrol to destroy the getaway car has been jailed for six years and three months.
Ciara Mahony knew Jamie Tighe-Ennis “from around the area” and phoned and met him on the night he was murdered in October 2017, Dublin Circuit Criminal Court heard.
She then purchased petrol that was used to set the getaway car on fire.
Mahony (46), with an address at Edmondstown Road, Ballyboden, but originally from Artane, was extradited from Birmingham, England, last year in connection with the murder of Jamie Tighe-Ennis (24) nine years ago, which remains unsolved.
She pleaded guilty to the sole count on the indictment of facilitating a criminal organisation in the commission of the murder between October 27th and 28th, 2017. It is an offence that carries a maximum sentence of 15 years.
