Jamie Tighe-Ennis died instantly after being shot in the head as he walked along Moatview Avenue, Coolock, in the early hours of October 28th, 2017. A black Audi getaway car was found burnt out in Finglas a short time later.
Mahony’s involvement included purchasing the petrol that was used to burn out the Audi, the court heard. She was seen on CCTV footage filling a red jerry can in a Topaz petrol station that was later found in the burnt-out vehicle, Det Sgt Domhnall O’Connell told prosecuting barrister Conor McKenna.
Gardaí also discovered her involvement from a phone that was found in the car and a limited edition bottle of wine, which was only sold in about 12 places in the country and which they tracked down to the Priorswood Inn, Clonshaugh.
Jamie Tighe-Ennis was socialising in the Priorswood Inn on the night of his murder and Mahony met him there briefly, the court heard. The pair went outside and spoke briefly before he went back inside and Mahony left.
Gardaí used phone mast data to track Mahony’s movements that night. She phoned Jamie Tighe-Ennis a number of times and again the following morning after he was killed, the court heard.
Mahony, who has no previous convictions except for some road traffic matters, was arrested in October 2018 and released, with a file sent to the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP).
The DPP decided to prosecute in November 2024, at which point Mahony was living in the UK and extradition proceedings began. Her guilty plea was an early one, the court heard.
In a victim impact statement read out by O’Connell, the father of Jamie Tighe-Ennis, Kevin Ennis, recalled arriving on the scene shortly after his son had been shot and seeing the pool of blood around his body.
“My son was dead,” he said. “It’s with me every day and will be for the rest of my life.”
He said he was sickened when he heard Mahony was a mother.
“How would you feel if it was your child?” he said. “You can rot in hell.”
June Tighe said her son’s death was “violent, sudden and devastating” and learning of it was “the worst moment of my life”.
“He was loved,” she added. “He mattered. He had a life, a future. We will never make the memories that should have been made with him.”
Defence barrister Jack Ryan put it to O’Connell that while Mahony knew “a very serious offence” was planned that night, she did not necessarily know Jamie Tighe-Ennis would be killed.
The detective said Mahony was “aware something serious was going to happen” to Jamie Tighe-Ennis.
O’Connell agreed with Ryan when he said Mahony had a severe addiction to crack cocaine at the time and was under the influence of people involved in organised crime, including two previous partners.
Judge Martin Nolan said Mahony “has moral culpability in this particular case”.
He took into account mitigating factors, including Mahony’s early guilty plea and lack of previous convictions and said she had been unlucky in her previous relationships that appeared to involve violence and coercion.
He set a headline sentence of nine to 10 years, which he reduced to six years and three months.

title: France unrest pushes European shares down despite tech rebound
description: Irish market begins week in red amid weakness in banking and some construction stocks
content:
European shares dipped despite a tech rebound, as protests in France continued and weighed on sentiment.
Triggered by rising prices and worsening public services, the protests have soured investor sentiment towards a country already grappling with weak growth and rising debt.
The Irish market started on a negative note, ending the opening session of the week in the red. The Euronext Dublin dipped 0.8 per cent to end the day at 14,069, dragged lower by weakness in banking and some construction stocks.
AIB lost 1 per cent over the day, finishing at €10.84, while Bank of Ireland was 2.46 per cent lower at €18.40. Insurer FBD was also off the pace, shedding 0.5 per cent.
Insulation specialist Kingspan declined by 1.5 per cent, and Cairn fell almost 0.6 per cent. But rival home builder Glenveagh added almost half a per cent over the session, ending the day at €2.34.
Ryanair , meanwhile, was slightly lower at €22.75, a decline of 0.1 per cent.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index ended down 117.21 points, 1.1 per cent, at 10,764.69.
Miners were a weak feature after mixed economic data in China and worries over the demand outlook for artificial intelligence (AI).
Anglo American shares fell 4.1 per cent, Glencore lost 3.3 per cent, while Rio Tinto dipped 1.5 per cent. Barclays declined 3.5 per cent.
The Bank of England is examining whether Barclays traders misrepresented illiquid private credit loans to understate their risk after an insider raised concerns, the Financial Times reported on Monday.
On the FTSE 250, Volex fell 12 per cent despite predicting financial 2027 underlying operating profit will be towards the upper end of current market expectations.
The Hampshire-based maker of power and data transmission products, said trading in the half-year ended September 30th was “excellent”, with year-on-year growth in every end-market.
But it cautioned headline year-on-year growth rates have started to “normalise”.
French equities suffered their worst day in nearly two weeks on Monday, weighing on European shares after rioting erupted in cities across ​the country over the weekend.
France’s blue-chip CAC 40 index fell 1.1 per cent, while the pan-European STOXX 600 index slipped 0.9 per cent to 639.1 points.
French lenders BNP Paribas, Société Générale and Credit Agricole fell between 2.5 per cent ⁠and 3.4 per cent. Retailer Carrefour declined 2.2 per cent and shopping mall ​operator Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield dropped 2 per cent.
Political uncertainty ​also came to the fore in Spain, where the equities benchmark fell 1.5 per cent. A snap election scheduled for next month ‌has left investors wary.
Cyclical sectors led declines across Europe, with banks the biggest laggards following a 2.2 per cent decline. Defence stocks also came under pressure, falling 1.5 per cent.
The technology index was the only big index in positive territory, rising 0.7 per cent. Last week, European shares held up better than US peers during a sell-off in AI-linked stocks over concerns about rising debt to fund infrastructure spending.
The tech-heavy ‌Nasdaq Composite led Wall Street’s gains on Monday as investors returned to AI-related stocks following last week’s bruising sell-off, while declining oil prices lent additional support ahead ​of key corporate earnings reports.
CoreWeave, which was at the centre of last week’s sell-off ⁠after its shares plunged more than 25 per cent on worries over a $50 billion debt load, climbed 3.1 per cent on ‌Monday. ‌Goldman ​Sachs upgraded the neocloud firm to “buy” from “neutral”, saying the recent sell-off offers a buying opportunity.
Chipmakers Broadcom climbed 3.2 per cent and Micron jumped 5.3 per cent. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index ⁠rose 3.7 per cent, putting it on course to end an ​eight-day losing streak, its longest run of declines since October ​2008.
Amazon.com was up 5.2 per cent after Morgan Stanley named the ecommerce and cloud computing firm as its “top pick”.
By midmorning, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 91.03 points, or 0.18 per cent, to 52,093.44. The S&P 500 gained 68.47 points, or 0.89 per cent, to 7,727.91, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced 463.92 points, or 1.78 per cent, to 26,603.96. – Additional reporting by Reuters and Press Association

title: US gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskiy says
description: Ukrainian president accuses Washington of ‘denial of reality’ in ongoing row with Trump over apparent support for Moscow
content:
Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, Volodymyr Zelenskiy has said, reviving concerns that Washington is withholding intelligence in order to bully Kyiv into capitulating to Moscow .
Yuri Ihnat, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, said on television on Monday morning that Ukraine had not received a warning before a Russian missile barrage hit power plants in Kyiv at around 11pm.
Ukraine did receive a warning before a successive strike, at 3am, Ihnat added.
“Once again, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack in multiple waves throughout the night, and once again, there was no warning from our partners,” Zelenskiy wrote in a social media post on Monday morning.
“When the supply of missiles for Ukrainian air defence is blocked, and Russia receives sanctions relief or delays, it is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners,” the president added.
[ ‘The war is getting nearer’: Ukraine’s eastern exodus accelerates as Russia steps up attacks Opens in new window ]
On Friday, US president Donald Trump waived a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia, telling the US Congress the pause on the legislation, named for the late senator Lindsey Graham and passed by both chambers, was in the national interest. Ukraine has also complained of slowed deliveries of PAC-3 air defence missiles from the US.
The US president wrote on Truth Social on Sunday: “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.
“Zelenskiy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”
For years, the US had warned Ukraine before Russia launches ballistic missiles, giving authorities several minutes to sound alarms and allow civilians to reach shelters before the strikes hit. However, Ukraine has said it was not warned on at least three days in the past week before missiles were launched, amid a public quarrel between Zelenskiy and Trump.
[ Europe should consider ‘all options’ to plug Ukraine’s budget shortfall, Taoiseach says Opens in new window ]
Speaking in the early hours of Monday on a trip to Samarkand, Uzbekistan, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “If it happened last night, I don’t know exactly. I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system.”
US officials have not previously mentioned a software glitch in the early warning system. In at least one case, Ukrainian officials had been told that bad weather over southern Russia had obscured preparations for the missile launch. Rubio said the military’s European Command was looking into the strikes.
The US has maintained plausible deniability as services and programmes provided to support Ukraine have suddenly begun to fail. The Trump administration has denied that it throttled services in Ukraine for Starlink, the satellite internet service run by Elon Musk that is used both on offensive drones and anti-air weapons by Ukraine.
Ukraine has also said US weapons delivered through a scheme where Europe purchases US weapons then delivers them to Ukraine, have been delayed. The Trump administration reportedly threatened Kyiv with a slowdown in crucial weapons deliveries unless it stopped striking Russian oil refineries.
Meanwhile, Moscow and Kyiv have been discussing the possible evacuation of the Russian-occupied frontline city of Oleshky, where about 2,000 people have been cut off from food and medical supplies for months in the southern Kherson region, according to a Ukrainian human rights official.
Pope Leo XIV held a phone call on Monday with Ukrainian Zelenskiy, the Vatican said, and urged Ukraine and Russia to cooperate to let ​aid and food into the blockaded town of Oleshky.
Residents of the Ukrainian town, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, have reported a deepening ​food crisis.
Leo “expressed the hope that cooperation between both parties will allow for ⁠the delivery of food and medical aid, and for the ‌voluntary ‌and ​safe evacuation of the civilian population,” the Vatican said in a statement about Monday’s call.
Zelenskiy did not ⁠immediately release a ​statement about the conversation. - Guardian

title: Owen Doyle: Several messages pinged to my phone during Leinster game over confusing decisions
description: During Leinster v Clermont last weekend, many were confused by some of Matthew Carley’s decisions
content:
“Can you please explain what on earth Matthew Carley is up to?”
That was the gist of several messages which pinged to my phone round about the 24th minute of Leinster ’s match against Clermont.
I’ve altered the wording. The messages were angry, invective-laden and would correctly never have passed editorial scrutiny. Here’s what happened: Leinster had just been awarded a penalty five metres from the Clermont line and, quite within their rights, chose to have another scrum.
Scrumhalf Fintan Gunne put in the ball. Carley, standing behind the Leinster scrumhalf, immediately blew for a crooked throw, awarding a clearing free-kick to the home team. My initial thought was, what was the referee thinking, why would he wish to get involved in the scrum put-in? After all, he and all of his peers have persistently, and consistently, ignored this part of the game for aeons.
Leinster put in a great performance and won in style. Had they not done so – the score was just 7-6 to Leinster at the time – Carley’s decision could have taken on significant relevance. Wherever he conjured the decision from, the referee should now clarify that he erred and has no intention of repeating the trick.
He made matters worse by grinning at Gunne and saying “not even close”, whereas the scrumhalf, I’d be absolutely certain, found nothing whatsoever to smile about. We are a long way away from having straight put-ins, if indeed we can ever get back to those, and referee solo runs are confusing and, worse, completely inequitable.
Carley had already pulled up Gunne, as early as the first minute, for not using the ball at a breakdown within the five seconds allowance. An unusual sanction. Referees are somewhat loose on this for the simple reason that it’s easier to allow a little leeway than to whistle it up. I found myself wondering if the absent Jamison Gibson-Park would have been treated the same way in these two incidents, but can’t claim to know the answer to that one.
Leinster did get one big decision which went their way, Carley awarding them a penalty try that was highly debatable. All of these issues confirmed that, in any sport, the referee becoming the centre of attention is a bad idea.
[ Rugby referees need to cut out the first name chummy approach to players Opens in new window ]
The change in the bonus point system for this competition means that both teams will play hard until the end. Even if the winners score four tries it is not automatically enough. Now they must score three more tries than their opponents to get a bonus point. The only bonus point now available to the losers is to finish seven points or less behind the winners. So, referees cannot afford to relax either – they must continue accurately and equitably until the full 80 minutes is played. Going into cruise control is not an option.
France’s glorious Pink City provided an epic, sensational match where 14-man Toulouse just about hung on to defeat Exeter. It went right down to the very last kick, with Henry Slade missing a penalty that would have earned a draw. Exeter left with only one bonus point as the new system kicked in. And Toulouse, despite scoring seven tries, earned none as it was only one try more than the visitors scored.
Referee Hollie Davidson came out of it very well. The straight red card she handed out to Rodrigue Neti, all of 124kg, for a hard shoulder directly to the head of Toulouse’s Ross Vintcent was absolutely correct and calmly explained. No argument could be brooked.
However, the permanent nature of the card probably underlined once again the difference between the two hemispheres in dealing with foul play. Down south, from what we’ve seen, it would have gone to the bunker for a maximum sanction of a 20-minute red. It is a continuing, unwelcome, divisive argument, and a global solution must be found.
It’s a shame that this fractured European competition is now mothballed for a month or so. If anybody can follow who plays who next and why, then please advise. The whole thing needs urgent revision. Its appeal, which really only starts with the knockout stages, will otherwise continue to diminish.
Apart from the put-in, the scrum continues to attract a lot of attention, especially with regard to the hookers’ so-called brake foot. Opinion is divided. Some see it as helping stability, others consider that it’s not safe. In either case, it’s hard to believe that the brake can have much effect in steadying the two packs, both of which come in at around 950kg.
[ Owen Doyle: Someone needs to have a word with some of these referees – and their critics Opens in new window ]
However, there is another part of the law that is not applied: the part that requires all players in the frontrow to support their body weight on at least one foot. Instead, the four props are allowed to have their feet way behind themselves to achieve maximum heft. Quite often, on collapse, a prop is penalised for having his feet too far back so it seems common sense to get them packing down correctly from the outset. Maybe it could be the start of the props actually “propping,” and the hookers “hooking,” which was their role once upon a time. That’s probably too much to hope.
I’ve resisted saying it before, but the referee kit supplied for the European competitions deserves a mention. It can’t be beyond the powers-that-be to find something more suitable than dressing the match officials in fluorescent flamingo pink or canary yellow shirts. It’s awful.

title: Man goes on trial accused of smothering and strangling 89-year-old woman
description: Hasan Ali Gori (52), of no fixed abode, denied a single charge of murdering Josephine ‘Josie’ Ray at her home
content:
A man went on trial on Monday, accused of murdering his then-partner’s 89-year-old mother by allegedly smothering and strangling her.
Hasan Ali Gori (52), of St Joseph’s Park, Nenagh, Co Tipperary, denied a single charge of murdering Josephine “Josie” Ray at her home, which she shared with her daughter Mary Ray and the accused, in Nenagh, Co Tipperary .
Ali Gori, who is using the services of an interpreter in court, replied “not guilty, sir” when arraigned before Judge Sean Gillane, on the charge that he murdered Ray at her home at St Joseph’s Park, Nenagh, on August 4th, 2024.
Prosecuting barrister Lorcan Connolly opened the trial in front of a jury of nine men and three women at the Central Criminal Court in Limerick .
“Josie Ray was killed at the hands of Hasan Ali Gori,” he said. “She was found dead in her bed.
“She died by asphyxiation after external compression of her neck – Josie Ray was smothered and strangled,” Connolly told the jury.
“You’ll hear about inward fractures caused by this compression and DNA matching the accused found on the fingernails of the late Josie Ray.
“The prosecution says there was a close physical struggle – perhaps Josie was trying to defend herself – and the person who did it was Hasan Ali Gori.”
Connolly said that while “nobody saw him do it, so perhaps it is a circumstantial case”, the prosecution case is that Ali Gori “had motive” and that his DNA was “found on the victim’s fingernails”.
[ Two men charged over wrong-way driving incident on M50 denied bail Opens in new window ]
He said Ali Gori also had “opportunity” to kill the victim “who was in her bedroom in her own home”, which she shared with the accused.
Connolly claimed Ali Gori and Mary Ray were involved in “a volatile and tempestuous” relationship at the time of Josie Ray’s death.
Connolly said that before the alleged killing, Ali Gori had “struck up” a relationship with Mary Ray, then 55, who has a “learning disability” and who shared a “close bond” with her mother.
“Hasan Ali Gori was Mary Ray’s cohabitant for social welfare purposes, and he ultimately came to live [with her]. Hasan Ali Gori was dependent on the Rays for accommodation.
“He and Mary shared an upstairs bedroom, and in August 2024, there was a fractious atmosphere in the house, and Josie Ray was killed at the hands of Hasan Ali Gori,” he added.
Connolly said Josie Ray was “a well-known and sprightly lady regularly seen out and about” in her native Nenagh.
[ Paddy McKillen jnr stands over financial statement in personal insolvency bid, court told Opens in new window ]
He said Josie Ray’s marriage had broken down in the 1980s and while four of her five daughters lived with her husband, she and her daughter Mary resided together.
Connolly said that before her death, Josie Ray was not suffering from any acute medical condition. She had been recovering from a broken hip in early 2024, which left her unable to walk upstairs, and so she was sleeping in a downstairs front room in her home.
“She was a small, frail, 89-year-old lady,” said Connolly.
He said Josie Ray left her home that evening to stay with one of her daughters, but, at some stage, “returned to her home, uninjured, well and normal”.
Later on, after 2am, neighbours saw Josie Ray smoking a cigarette outside her house, “and that was her last time she was seen alive”.
Prosecution witness Samuel Abuchie, a grandson of the victim, gave evidence of raising the alarm after finding his grandmother’s body, at around noon on August 4th.
A 999 call the witness made to emergency services in respect of his grandmother was played in court.

title: Odds in Eugenio Chacarra’s favour as Race to Dubai reaches final stretch
description: Rory McIlroy’s pursuit of a record-equalling eighth title hindered by Genesis absence
content:
Europe captain Luke Donald ’s foresight in including Spain’s Eugenio Chacarra among the potential Ryder Cup players invited for a site visit at Adare Manor a day after last month’s Irish Open was, it would seem already, an inspired move.
Chacarra’s victory in the DP World India Championship – his third success of the season on the European Tour – brought with it the twin benefits of leapfrogging him to the top of Ryder Cup qualifying as well as to the top of the Race to Dubai standing with just three tournaments remaining.
Nobody has been on a hotter streak than the 26-year-old in recent weeks having followed up his third-place finish at the French Open with second at the Spanish Open before his victory in India, moving him up to a career-best 39th in the world rankings.
“It makes my job a bit harder going into the last two events,” said Rory McIlroy of his quest to claim the Harry Vardon Trophy for a record-equalling eighth time by winning the order of merit. Adding further difficulty to the aim is the fact the Northern Irishman will only contest the last two tournaments in the United Arab Emirates, opting to sit out this week’s Genesis Championship.
In contrast, Chacarra is intent on maintaining momentum, heading straight on to South Korea, where he will have the opportunity to increase his Race to Dubai lead in the absence of his two closest challengers; Patrick Reed in second and McIlroy third.
Previously ranked second in the world as an amateur, Chacarra joined LIV in 2022 but left at the 2024 season and full status on the DP World Tour after winning last year’s Hero Indian Open.
“I know what I’m capable of,” Chacarra said after his latest success, having also taken wins at the Italian Open and KLM Open earlier this season. “I was one of the best amateurs in the world and I wanted to be one of the best professional players in the world.
“I work really hard. I’ve got a great team surrounding me, they’re always trying to make me better, and I think we’ve been doing a great job. Great, hard work, and it’s paying off, and I’m really thankful for it.”
He added the result in Delhi came in spite of “playing with my B-game and not feeling the best”, with a stiff neck and a recent toe break having little impact on his title charge in Delhi.
“To be able to win against this kind of field is something that gives me a lot of motivation to keep working so we can win bigger and bigger events in the future.
“When I left LIV, I wanted to be in Majors, be in Ryder Cups, win tournaments on the DP World Tour, be on the PGA Tour. That’s what I dream of since I was little.
“I believe in myself. I believe I can be one of the best players in the world, and that’s what I wake up every single morning dreaming of, being one of the best players in the world and contending in Majors.”
Chacarra’s climb up the world rankings will bring with it an invite to next year’s Masters, and likely the other Majors, as well as a PGA Tour card.
“It feels great,” Chacarra said of his place atop the Race to Dubai rankings, leading Reed and McIlroy by 618 and 948 points respectively.
“There are two big events with a lot of points, and I’ve got two of the best players in the world coming against me now. Rory and Patrick [are] behind me, fairly close, so I need to keep working and getting better and hopefully I can get it done in Dubai.”
But suddenly, the odds are stacked in his favour.

title: Stud owned by billionaire John Malone concerned over Mount Juliet expansion plan
description: Planning permission being sought for new suites and spa facilities at five-star Co Kilkenny hotel
content:
A stud operation owned by US billionaire John Malone has expressed concerns over €8 million plans by businessman Barry English to expand the five-star Mount Juliet hotel.
In August, English’s Golden Beam Hospitality Ltd lodged plans with Kilkenny County Council for 19 new guest suites and spa facilities to include 13 treatment rooms including an indoor thermal spa at Mount Juliet estate at Thomastown, Co Kilkenny .
The scheme includes a partial demolition of the existing two-storey extension on the south wing of the Manor House hotel at the resort and the construction of a new two-storey extension.
Planning consultants for Malone’s Ballylinch Stud have told the council that it has concerns over the scheme in relation to impact on protected views.
Ballylinch Stud describes itself as one of Europe’s leading thoroughbred racehorse breeding operations and is located outside Thomastown.
In the submission on the Mount Juliet expansion plan, architect Barry Lynch said that Ballylinch Stud in particular has concerns in relation to the erosion of designated protected views contrary to the objectives of the Kilkenny Development Plan.
Lynch said two of the protected views “are now compromised and seriously affected by this proposal”.
CCH Architects have made a submission “on behalf of a number of property owners on the Mount Juliet Estate”.
On behalf of the firm, Arthur Hickey said that the Mount Juliet was a beautiful 18th century example of a large estate house.
Hickey that the proposal to extend the house would roughly treble the ground floor of the existing house and “totally detract from the integrity of the existing building”.
Hickey argued that large interventions “will make this large country house into something which it is not”.
In response to the concerns expressed, the council has placed the project on hold.
In a letter requesting revised plans, the council said that while it welcomes the continued growth and tourism development of the Mount Juliet estate, “the applicant is invited to consider a more suitable location for the proposal which could be more successfully integrated into the estate while protecting the characteristics of Manor House”.

title: Kenyan cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of almost 200 murders
description: Self-proclaimed pastor Paul Mackenzie was found guilty of 191 murder charges - all but one of them children
content:
A ‌ Kenyan court on Monday found starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and about 30 others guilty of murder over the deaths of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult-related disasters in recent history.
Mackenzie ‌and his co-accused will be given their sentence on November 6th.
He was arrested in 2023 after police received a tip-off, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola Forest near the ​coast in southeastern Kenya.
Prosecutors say Mackenzie and his Good News International Church organised a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered from the Shakahola Forest. Many were severely ​decomposed, with only 26 bodies able to be identified.
Monday’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into the other deaths are ongoing.
Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight ⁠hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie was in court, wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers, ‌sitting ‌alongside ​his wife who is one of the co-accused.
When his name was read out by the judge he stood silently, staring into space.
Family members of some of those who died in the forest gathered to hear the judgment at Mombasa High Court.
Francis Wanje (62) lost ⁠eight family members including two grandchildren to the cult.
Speaking before the verdict, ​he said: “It has been really a heavy thing [for] us as a family, and ​it has really taken us very far in terms of psychological problems, ... I was hoping for this particular day.”
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in ‌the coastal forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions ​over how Mackenzie was able to continue to operate despite having been on the radar of the authorities since 2017 when his premises were searched by police. ⁠In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated to the Shakahola ⁠Forest, police said.
The case has also led ​to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Kenyan president William Ruto said in 2023 that government agencies should have been able to prevent the deaths. He said he took responsibility as president.
People with direct knowledge of the cult’s activities said Mackenzie planned the mass starvation in three phases: first children, then women and young men, and finally the remaining men.
A former taxi driver, Mackenzie forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, branding such institutions as Satanic, some of his followers told Reuters for a 2023 article.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into ‌areas with biblical names like Jerusalem and Judea.
The ⁠plight of his followers began to emerge in mid-March 2023, when a local man told police that his brother and wife had starved their children to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.
Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives say he brought forward the date on ‌which he told his followers the world would end. Police arrested him again in April 2023 and started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths including ​terrorism-related ones, which he has denied.
Prosecutors say while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 ​people in Kwa Binzaro village, which lies about 30km from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case. – Reuters

title: Wexford Festival Opera 2026: Croí na Féile review – Joseph Calleja, Ermonela Jaho, Daniela Barcellona and Giorgi Manoshvili take to the stage
description: The four singers star in the festival’s Croí na Féile fundraising gala on Saturday night, performing Verdi, Massenet and Rossini
content:
This year’s Wexford Festival Opera is the 75th, with only a single year skipped since the first, in 1951, because of the 1960 renovations and reconstruction carried out on its then home, the early-19th-century Theatre Royal.
So on Saturday, in its home since 2008, the altogether more salubrious National Opera House, the festival celebrates old friendships in a Croí na Féile fundraising gala concert that should raise a fair penny, with ticket prices of up to €750.
The festival is a celebrated showcase for rare and neglected operas, and has long been known as an important international forum for young talent – or, rather, stars in the making.
A quick trawl through the performers of the first 50 festivals finds the names of Janet Baker, Daniela Barcellona, Ugo Benelli, Norma Burrowes, Joseph Calleja, Christiane Eda-Pierre, Juan Diego Flórez, Mirella Freni, Bruce Ford, Lesley Garrett, Heather Harper, Philip Langridge, Sergei Leiferkus, Ermonela Jaho, Ann Murray and Matti Salminen.
Saturday’s programme features three of these singers: Barcellona, an Italian mezzo-soprano; Calleja, a Maltese tenor; and Jaho, an Albanian soprano. They are joined by the much younger Georgian bass Giorgi Manoshvili, who in 2022 featured in the Wexford Factory (the festival’s opera studio) and also in a main-stage opera. This makes him the only singer on stage never to have sung in the Theatre Royal.
The flavour of the evening is well set by each singer’s opening offering.
Jaho, who made her Wexford debut as Agnès Sorel in Tchaikovsky’s Orleanskaya Deva in 2000, chooses a very inward approach to Pendant un An Je Fus Ta Femme, the lover’s appeal from Massenet’s Sapho.
Jaho is an exceptional performer whose projection is clear even when she sings almost inaudibly. The effect is a very touching intimacy, as if, from your seat in the theatre, you are being drawn into her innermost sanctuary, vulnerabilities and secrets laid bare.
Barcellona, whose Wexford debut was as Imelda in the 1996 production of Donizetti’s Parisina, is a singer of an altogether more forceful and feisty character. In Cruda Sorte, the putting-the-best-foot-forward aria from Rossini’s L’Italiana in Algeri, she creates a character pushing at the envelope, unafraid of risks or consequences, to the point of pushing her already imposing voice to the limit.
Calleja opens with the arrogant Questa o Quella, from Verdi’s Rigoletto, his tone generous and full, thrusting in what almost feels like heedless ways. The wonderful easy lyricism of his early festival appearances, as Liecrona in Zandonai’s I Cavalieri di Ekebù (1998) and Zéphoris in Adam’s Si J’Étais Roi (2000), is replaced by a burlier, sometimes overstressed delivery.
Manoshvili trained in traditional and ecclesiastical music before turning to opera, in which he graduated from the Vano Sarajishvili State Conservatoire in Tbilisi as recently as 2020. He is a grounded, rock-solid singer, with a resonant voice that might have been created for characters who lay down the law. He handles the reflective sadness of Ella Giammai M’Amò, from Verdi’s Don Carlo, with piercing directness.
Daniele Callegari and the Wexford Festival Opera Orchestra may not always be in the tidiest of form. But, in addition to partnering the singers, they perform two Verdi overtures (to La Forza del Destino and I Vespri Siciliani) with a sensitivity to colour, nuance and instrumental texture that has been all too rare in Ireland outside of Wexford in recent years, Maurizio Benini’s handling of Bellini’s Norma earlier this year an outstanding exception.
Wexford Festival Opera runs until Saturday, October 31st

title: French prime minister calls for partial curfews in bid to quell unrest
description: More than 2,400 people have been arrested after clashes between demonstrators and police
content:
France’s prime minister has said he has asked regional authorities to impose partial curfews in some cities after the government admitted police had “lost control” in several places during violent weekend protests around the country.
Sébastien Lecornu said after an emergency cabinet meeting on Monday he was “fully resolved to restore public order” and had called for “local and partial” curfews if needed. There was “no question” of imposing a full curfew on entire cities such as Paris , he added.
Lecornu told reporters that if declaring a state of emergency was deemed necessary “we could do so”, but ⁠added that at this stage partial curfews seemed “more appropriate”. He did not say which cities, or what form the curfews would take.
His comments came after France’s interior minister conceded police “lost control” in some cities during Saturday’s protests and the president, Emmanuel Macron, demanded a full security review and “new operational methods” to end the rioting.
[ What’s behind the violence shaking France, and what comes next? Opens in new window ]
Laurent Nuñez said on Monday there had been a “lack of anticipation” in preparations for the protests and acknowledged that police numbers had sometimes been inadequate to deal with rioters and looters on the fringes of the demonstrations.
Nuñez said intelligence had suggested there would be 200,000 demonstrators around the country. In the event, there were more than 500,000 and peaceful protests were hijacked, morphing into one of France’s most violent days of unrest in recent years.
He said he had tendered his resignation to Macron because he felt “responsible for everything that happened”. Macron refused it, demanding instead that Nuñez “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over planning and intelligence failures”.
The protests follow weeks of demonstrations by high school students that have been marred by sometimes violent clashes with police, rocking the country six months before a crunch presidential ⁠election and amid mounting economic pressures.
Public buildings including a town hall were attacked and set ablaze and an estimated 2,000 shops were ransacked and looted, authorities have said. Nearly 2,400 people – 70 per cent of them adults – were arrested and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes injured.
Nuñez said 60,000 police and other security forces had been deployed around the country, but acknowledged it had not been enough to control determined, organised groups of violent rioters in major cities including Paris, Marseille and Lyon.
“You couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and say we hadn’t lost control,” the minister told French radio, but added that the responsibility of “rioters, looters and ultra-left militants” should not be glossed over.
The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, also said intelligence failings had left the state vulnerable. “There’s no good policing without good intelligence, he said, adding that many of those arrested had police records and “about 80%” were being prosecuted.
Macron’s office said in a statement on Monday that besides reviewing the security shortcomings, Nuñez had been tasked with “promptly implementing new operational methods for security forces to use on the ground in combating rioters”.
Rioting and looting continued on Sunday. The mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Grégoire, said on Monday that about 30 shops had been targeted in the capital the previous day, with a further 350 people arrested overnight.
“Maintaining public order is the responsibility of the state. It is the state that was at fault this weekend,” Grégoire said. “We have a social movement that is spreading, and no political prospect for a constructive way out. So the protests will continue.”
Marseille’s mayor, Benoît Payan, said not just democracy but “the very foundations of the Republic” had been undermined. Describing the situation as “almost insurrectional”, he said the government’s stance amounted to “petty political manoeuvring”.
On Monday, protesters blocked entrances to the Louvre Museum in support of the nationwide high school student protest movement and to denounce “police repression”. The museum could not open as scheduled because of the protest.
A leaflet displayed outside the museum read: “We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world’s largest museum.”
In a televised address on Sunday, Macron criticised the “ unbridled” violence and said local authorities would be able to ban some demonstrations in the coming days, but stopped short of drastic measures such as declaring a state of emergency or curfew.
Saturday’s protests, by students, teachers, parents, unions and workers, focused on the high cost of living, an issue that also prompted demonstrations in several other European countries including Italy, Belgium and Albania over the weekend. - Guardian

title: Two men charged over wrong-way driving incident on M50 denied bail
description: Daniel Brown (22) and Adam White (25) face charges of being in a stolen car and cannabis possession
content:
Two men charged in connection with a traffic pursuit in Dublin on Sunday evening, in which a stolen car was allegedly driven on the wrong side of the M50 for one kilometre, have been denied bail.
Daniel Brown (22), of Hampton Wood, Dublin 11, was charged with four counts of dangerous driving, being in a stolen Volkswagen Golf estate car and possession of cannabis.
Co-defendant Adam White (25), also from Hampton Wood, was charged with being in the stolen car and possession of cannabis for sale or supply.
The pair are also accused of having a stolen key to a Toyota car.
Garda Dylan Toner, of Coolock Garda station, gave evidence of the arrest, charge and caution, and objected to bail for the pair, who had no solicitors to represent them because of the industrial dispute over legal-aid fee reforms.
They opted to represent themselves and had separate hearings, during which Toner told Judge Karen Dowling both men made no reply when charged.
The garda objected to bail, citing the seriousness of the incident and charges. He said he expected the case would be sent to the Circuit Court, but added that the book of evidence was yet to be completed.
He was emphatic in his assertion that imposing bail conditions would not alleviate his concerns about the accused men.
The garda alleged the pair were arrested following a 40-minute traffic pursuit and were “caught red-handed”. It was stated that the Garda helicopter captured the whole incident on CCTV.
He told the court that Brown drove for more than one kilometre northbound on the southbound lane of the M50 before he was arrested.
In cross-examination, the accused, Brown, asked Toner if he had seen him getting out of the driver’s side of the car.
The judge warned Brown, because he had no legal representation, about the risk of self-incrimination.
Brown maintained that he was being carried in the stolen car.
The judge gave the accused men time to read the bail objections and allowed Brown’s partner and a relative of White’s to sit with them briefly to help them prepare for the bail hearings.
“I had nothing to do with the car,” White told the court.
Both men had seen a doctor in custody to have injuries examined and were deemed fit to appear in court. Brown’s face was bruised, and White, a father of three, said he had a sore ankle.
The garda said White was caught close to the car when it stopped. He was adamant that no bail conditions would satisfy him and said the charges painted a picture in relation to that alleged incident.
The judge stressed that the pair enjoyed the presumption of innocence and lacked legal representation. However, she held that the threshold had been reached to refuse both men’s applications and remanded them in custody to appear at Cloverhill District Court on Friday.

title: Waterford arson victims were ‘a beautiful family who did no wrong’, funeral told
description: Hundreds attend service for Philip and Kim English, as well as their sons Jayden (9) and Callum (12), at Sacred Heart Church
content:
“A beautiful family who did no wrong to anybody.”
The words of parish priest Fr Gerry Chestnutt rang out among the silenced congregation gathered at the Sacred Heart Church in Waterford city on Monday afternoon.
Before the altar sat four coffins; two small white caskets flanked by two larger pine boxes.
In front of the coffins lay four cream candles and a family photograph of the dead: Philip and Kim English and their sons Callum (12) and Jayden (9).
Their other children, aged 14 and 6, remain in a critical condition in hospital following an attack on their home last Tuesday.
The church pews were packed with hundreds of people for the joint funeral Masses; family and friends, classmates from Scoil Lorcain and St Joseph’s, and team-mates from Johnville Football Club.
Aides-de camp for President Catherine Connolly and Taoiseach Micheál Martin were also present, alongside Chief Whip Mary Butler, Minister for State John Cummins, Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald and party TDs David Cullinane and Conor McGuinness.
“An act of total evil” had left a family and community “devastated and heartbroken”, the priest said in his homily.
“The feelings of all are clear: heartbreak, shock, devastation and, yes, anger.”
Mourners had gathered outside the church from early that morning to pay their respects with floral tributes laid outside on the steps.
Philip English was “funny, lovable, sensitive and caring”, said Chestnutt.
“Family always was his priority. Any photograph that you have seen of him sums him up: always smiling.
“Kim had a different personality to Philip: vocal and feisty, but the most loving, kind and caring person. As parents, they adored their children.
“Their life as a family was a journey of love. And there were many journeys as three of their children faced illness. Through all of that they were completely united and dedicated.”
Callum was remembered for his “mischievous smile” and was a “lovable rogue” while Jayden was “a force of love, life and energy”.
“You were full of fun and mischief. Very often you were heard before you were seen.”
Concluding his remarks, Chestnutt said the community were “better people” for knowing the family, as they were “the salt of the earth and lights in this community”.
Kim English’s younger sister Charlene said she was “the light of her life” and was grateful she had told her she loved her in their last call, the night before she was killed.
“I’m going to miss our calls and hearing you say ‘g’wan I love you’. I’ll never forget watching Cinderella every night next to you.”
Philip English’s cousin Raymond urged young people in Waterford city and throughout the country to “please walk away from drugs”.
“Please ask for help when it comes to addiction. Please ask for help if you’ve been led down a bad path. Please choose a life. Choose hope. Please, most certainly, choose a future.”
His words received a loud applause from those assembled.
Bishop Alphonsus Cullinan of Waterford and Lismore closed the Mass stating the four family members had been “innocent victims of a web of evil which is the drugs trade”.
“As a country, we have not really faced up to this problem and it is a fact that in every city, town, village and townland harmful drugs are available. Up and down this dear land people are turning to drugs,” he said.
“Young lives and the lives of the not-so-young are being destroyed by drugs, and those who work behind the scenes need to see the consequences of their dark trade and atone for their sin.”
He added that anyone who thought there was “no harm in taking a line of cocaine on the weekend is utterly mistaken and is also feeding this evil machine”.
Gerry and the Pacemackers’ You’ll Never Walk Alone was played as four hearses carrying the coffins were led out of the church grounds and past the Birchwood estate where the family lived. Burial took place at Kilbarry Cemetery.

title: Union boss set to warn politicians on hazard of mishandling artificial intelligence
description: Ictu general secretary Owen Reidy argues for central role for workers as workplaces change
content:
Ireland could be “a canary in the AI coal mine” if artificial intelligence policy is “mishandled”, Irish Congress of Trade Unions (Ictu) general secretary Owen Reidy will tell TDs and Senators.
On Tuesday, the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Artificial Intelligence (AI) will hear from unions on the topic of AI and work, including the risks and opportunities of the technology.
In his statement to the committee, Reidy will say the technology “will change our workplaces and in potentially radical ways”. And that the union movement is “not a block to the appropriate development and spread of AI” but “workers need to be central to the debate”.
[ AI ecosystem may be booming but at what cost? Opens in new window ]
Reidy is to raise concern that “catastrophising” over the risk of job losses from AI “will undermine attempts to improve job quality”.
There must be a policy focus on maintaining and improving job quality, both for the jobs that will be retained and the new jobs that will be created, he will say
“In contrast to the three previous industrial revolutions, the disruption will manifest most heavily in white-collar sectors and tasks.”
His statement will add: “Ireland is particularly at risk from potentially transformative changes given the high level of knowledge-intensive and professional jobs.
“Ireland could be a canary in the AI coal mine if AI policy is mishandled, with particular concerns for entry-level and junior employees.”
His contribution will continue: “On the other hand, we have high levels of Stem [science, technology, engineering and mathematics] graduates and a high concentration of AI talent which leaves us well placed to potentially benefit.”
Reidy will say workers’ voices and their trade union representatives must be “front and centre” in policymaking on artificial intelligence.
Meanwhile, the Communications Workers’ Union statement will note the discussion on AI must ask who keeps their job; “what happens to those that remain, who controls the technology and how do we share the dividends”.
It will add: “For our members this is not hypothetical. We have seen hundreds of tech-sector jobs lost or placed at risk in restructuring processes where AI and automation have been cited”, though artificial intelligence is not the sole cause.
The opening statement from another union, Fórsa’s representative Ryan McKinney, will note that an interim report by the committee “recommended that trade union negotiation be a precondition for AI driven-change in public services, and that the guidelines for the responsible use of AI in the public service be made mandatory.
“Fórsa supports both recommendations, and our central message today is simple – they can and should be acted on now.”
The Financial Services Union is to tell the committee that artificial intelligence offers opportunities to improve productivity and services but also raises “significant concerns” about job security, changing skills requirements, workplace surveillance, and inequality. It will note that “AI must work for people, not the other way around”.

title: Paddy McKillen jnr stands over financial statement in personal insolvency bid, court told
description: Two lenders owed a combined €11 million by the businessman raised concerns about his disclosures
content:
Paddy McKillen jnr has stood over financial statements provided to the High Court as part of his bid for a personal insolvency arrangement (PIA), after two lenders owed a combined €11 million by the businessman raised concerns about his disclosures to the court.
Last month, McKillen jnr obtained a protective certificate after the court heard he was “firmly insolvent”, with debts of €27.7 million. The certificate, obtained late last month, protects him from his creditors for 70 days.
On Monday, lawyers for lenders Herbert Street Finance and Cabriz Finance – who are owed €2.3 million and €8.7 million, respectively, by McKillen jnr – told Judge Nessa Cahill their clients had issued applications to set aside the protective certificate.
Bernard Dunleavy, counsel for Herbert Street Finance with barrister Niall Ó hUiginn, said his client’s application comes amid concerns regarding an alleged “absence of detail” in information provided by McKillen jnr in his application for a protective certificate.
Dunleavy pointed to a recent judgment, in which Judge Liam Kennedy struck down an attempt by McKillen jnr to set aside a bankruptcy summons issued by Herbert Street Finance over the debts owed to it.
Dunleavy described the judgment as noting “inconsistencies and silence” in information provided by McKillen in the context of that application. He submitted his client had observed this pattern again in McKillen’s application for a protective certificate.
Dunleavy also submitted McKillen jnr’s affairs were “complex”, and said there were “unusual” features to his arrangement with his mother and wife, which elevates them in the list of his creditors. The court previously heard McKillen jnr owes €2.9 million to his wife, Edel McKillen, and €1.8 million to his mother, Maura McKillen.
Dunleavy said his side was seeking directions that McKillen jnr provide further written evidence with “appropriate disclosures” relating to his affairs. He said his side was prepared to reply to such evidence within three days.
Martin Scanlon, barrister for Cabriz Finance, said his client was agreeable to Herbert Street Finance’s suggestion.
[ Paddy McKillen jnr built a hospitality empire – now the man with €270 in the bank owes €27.7m Opens in new window ]
Keith Farry, appearing for personal insolvency practitioner Eugene McDarby, said he was agreeable to the suggested directions. He said his instructions were that McKillen jnr stands over his financial statement provided to the court, and that it was truthful and accurate. He said was happy to engage with further details required by creditors.
The judge made directions allowing for the filing of affidavits, and adjourned the case to next month.
Earlier this month, McKillen jnr, of Torquay Road, Foxrock, Dublin, consented to a judgment against him over the €2.3 million debt owed to Herbert Street Finance.
McKillen jnr’s lawyers told the court that he was conceding the claim for the debt, in circumstances where he was seeking a personal insolvency arrangement.
McKillen jnr was the co-founder of the hospitality group Press Up .

title: ‘I have never felt anything so painful in my life’: Irish caught in French riots
description: An Irish student protester and a Limoges resident share experiences of street violence and tear gas in France
content:
“W e didn’t want to get into any altercation with the riot police, so we ended up just running through the tear gas, and I have never felt anything so painful in my life,” says Clara Conyngham (23), a Dubliner who took part in protests in Paris on Saturday.
Conyngham has been taking part in student protests since she moved to the capital to begin a master’s in cognitive science at the École Normale Supérieure this year.
Her student body joined a movement started by secondary school students “after we saw the kind of violence they were met with for these very reasonable protest demands”.
“If a teacher got sick or was away at maternity leave, these poor students would be left for seven or eight months without a teacher for that subject,” Conyngham says.
“The classroom conditions were terrible: cockroaches, rats, crazy temperatures in the summer and then freezing in the winter, and obviously this disproportionately affected poorer areas.”
At noon on Saturday she went to the official march starting point at Place de la République in central Paris, where student protesters joined a revived Yellow Vests movement including farmers, climate activists, trade unionists united in anger about the cost of living .
There she encountered riot police as she tried to join.
“We were walking down one of the streets when we saw them coming up behind us, the riot police, coming with batons and all, a big line of them,” she recalls.
“We were just gonna leg it in the other direction, but they had already thrown tear gas canisters, about five of them, in front of us.”
Conyngham ran through the gas to get away from the advancing police line. “It was like having Tabasco poured in my eyes,” she says.
She was assisted by protesters and “street medics”.
“Everyone was helping each other out. People had saline that they were giving out, and we were all putting it in each other’s eyes. In the midst of all this chaos, it was kind of a beautiful moment,” she says.
[ French prime minister calls for partial curfews in bid to quell unrest Opens in new window ]
Conyngham eventually managed to link up with the main march as it made its way through Paris. The scene was “night and day” to the chaos at Place de la République.
“People playing music, chanting, singing. Old people, young people. There was a child who was holding up a sign from his apartment, saying ‘Bravo’, and everyone would cheer when they went past.”
The area where she lives was affected by the looting and violence that spread from the initial clashes on Place de la République.
“There’s burned-out bikes and looted shops,” Conyngham says. “Obviously I don’t believe in the burning and the looting, but you also have to understand that no people who are happy with their circumstances are taking these actions.
“I think it is a desperation move. This sort of group desperation, group violence, I think it takes on a mind of its own.”
Originally from Ballina, Peter Durcan (40) has lived in Limoges for 15 years where he runs a 3D-printing company. He was returning from a basketball tournament with his daughter on Saturday when they saw cars “coming up the motorway in the wrong direction” and realised something was wrong.
“The gang of people – I don’t even know how to describe them – they went on to the motorway and stopped all the traffic, then put a cop car over on its roof, and burned it,” he says.
He managed to get to his home in Limoges city.
“You couldn’t see it from where we live, but you could smell the smoke,” he recalls.
The protesters made their way to Limoges town hall, a protected structure from 1883 that stands at the centre of the city.
“It’s this unbelievably beautiful building at the heart of the city. It’s where I got married 10 years ago, it’s where all the kids get their paperwork, where their birth certificates come from, it’s a super important part of the city,” Durcan says.
Local police say that by this point they had run out of tear gas canisters and were overwhelmed by the protesters.
“It was obviously strategically planned,” Durcan says. “They broke in by going in via the basement at the back, and also they had a battering ram.”
Footage of what followed has gone around the globe: flames engulfing the town hall and its spire collapsing in scenes reminiscent of the fire at Notre Dame cathedral in Paris.
[ What’s behind the violence shaking France, and what comes next? Opens in new window ]
On Sunday Durcan went to have a look at the aftermath. “It’s smouldering,” he says. “It’s super unbelievably sad.”
A solidarity rally was held in the square, and the mayor and local officials addressed the crowd. Some sang the Marseillaise. “It was quite emotionally charged.”
Some protesters were peaceful and had reasonable demands, Durcan says. He believes those who caused the damage were a mix of politically-motivated people “who are just against everything that the government stands for” and kids “from the suburbs who are just making the most of the chaos to loot shops”.
“Petrol is expensive, and I can understand their frustration, but that’s nothing to do with the French government,” can says. “After the amount of hatred and anger and violence that was used – it’s got zero credibility, it’s outrageous.”

title: Japan leads mission to make first return trip to Mars
description: Voyage due to launch early Tuesday morning Japan time will be watched for further potential signs of life on red planet
author_name: Michael Peel in London , Harry Dempsey in Tokyo
content:
J apan is preparing to launch the first return trip to Mars’s orbit, aiming to retrieve physical samples from the moon Phobos and search for further possible signs of life.
A H3 rocket is set to blast off from Tanegashima Space Center on Tuesday carrying a spacecraft that will make a five-year voyage that promises to reveal vital data on the red planet’s secrets and the feasibility of human travel there.
The so-called MMX expedition, a collaboration with US and European space agencies, has risen in importance after Nasa cancelled its own Mars sample return programme due to cost overruns and science budget cuts. The MMX module will drop a wheeled exploration rover named Idefix, after the dog who features in the Astérix comic books and is known to English-language readers as Dogmatix.
“We’ve been to Mars a lot of times, but we’ve never come back, so it’s a huge milestone for space exploration,” said Sanjeev Gupta, a planetary scientist at Imperial College London.
The origin of Phobos and its fellow moon Deimos is “one of the big unsolved questions in planetary science” with potential implications for the possibility of life on Mars and elsewhere, he added.
“If Phobos is an asteroid, it’s likely to belong to the fleet of asteroids thought to have brought significant amounts of the water and volatile chemicals needed for life from the outer to the inner solar system early in its history,” Gupta said.
The meteor-gouged moons are named for the twin sons of the gods Aphrodite and Ares, the Greek counterpart of Roman war deity Mars.
Scientists hope to search material from Phobos, the larger of the duo, to settle the long-running mystery of how it and Deimos came to be.
While it is possible the pair are asteroids captured long ago in Mars’ orbit, they could alternatively be debris from a giant collision between the red planet and another celestial body.
If the moons are the product of such a cosmic crash, they may contain Martian matter that includes clues on whether the planet was able to support life.
“Material returned from Phobos could serve as a time capsule of ancient Mars,” said Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, the MMX expedition’s project manager. “Or [it could be] a record of the building blocks delivered to the young terrestrial planets that may have contributed to the emergence of habitability.”
The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency has carved out a niche in returning samples to Earth. It was the first nation to recover asteroid materials, via its Hayabusa – meaning Falcon – expeditions.
Kazuto Suzuki, a University of Tokyo professor, said Japan was “consciously taking decisions to do sample returns as something the US cannot or has not done”. China is more focused on prestige space missions that appeal to the public, Suzuki added.
The MMX mission will take roughly a year each way to travel to and from Phobos, with three years of data collection in between.
The voyage will face multiple technical challenges, starting with the pressure to launch on time. The best window for travelling to Mars comes around only once every 26 months, when the planet and Earth are aligned to allow the most energy-efficient trip.
The H3 launch rocket has failed twice in nine previous attempts, while landing on Phobos is hard because of weak gravity and uncertain surface conditions.
The expedition features advanced technologies including to lighten the craft’s load for the journey home, said Araki Ono, lead engineer at Mitsubishi Electric, prime contractor for the 4,480kg probe.
“What is groundbreaking about this mission is that we will go to the Martian system and then return,” he said.
[ Starship rocket reaches orbit, with SpaceX saying it will pave way for Mars missions Opens in new window ]
The voyage will have a bittersweet quality for planetary scientists as a reminder of an elusive even greater prize. This is the material held uncollected at Mars’ surface, aboard the Perseverance rover dropped there in 2021 as part of the abortive Nasa sample return mission.
While the MMX expedition would be “not a replacement” for the Perseverance trove, it could help build on “tantalising evidence” transmitted back to Earth of potential ancient Martian microbial activity, said planetary scientist Briony Horgan.
“MMX will be a critical step in our understanding of small bodies in the solar system, and may be able to provide some insight into Mars itself as well,” said Horgan, director of the Research Institute for Space Exploration at Purdue University in Indiana. “This could be very helpful for understanding sources of materials needed to support microbial life on Mars.”
MMX promises further crucial insights into possible future crewed visits to Mars, a long-standing dream of some space agencies and billionaires, notably Elon Musk .
A successful voyage would “tell us a lot” about the logistics of a human Martian mission including how to enter and leave the planet’s orbit, said Bruce Jakosky, a planetary scientist at the University of Colorado Boulder.
“It won’t tell us about landing on the surface of Mars and then ascending to orbit again, or the full details of planetary protection required for samples,” Jakosky said. “But the more we can do some of these ‘firsts’ before we send people, the fewer we need to do later – and therefore the lower the risk.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Failure by Sinn Féin and DUP to agree Stormont budget ‘beyond alarming’, says NIO minister
description: Sarah Owen tells British-Irish Parliamentary Assembly that Northern Ireland receives £1.24 for every £1 that goes to her Luton constituency
content:
A failure by Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionist Party ( DUP ) to agree a Stormont budget is “beyond alarming”, and London has made its final offer, the Northern Ireland Office has said.
Speaking in Sheffield to the British-Irish Parliamentary Assembly, Northern Ireland Office (NIO) parliamentary undersecretary Sarah Owen bluntly criticised the two largest parties in the Assembly .
She said both lecture the British government about how it should set its budget, while failing to agree their own – a situation that was impacting public and charitable services.
“Having no budget is beyond alarming,” Owen added.
Sinn Féin MLA for Newry-Armagh Cathal Boylan insisted that Stormont has “lived on austerity budgets for 20 years” and the extra £1.5 billion offered by the Treasury “is not cutting it, it’s just not making the measure”.
Sharply rejecting criticism about the offer, Owen said Northern Ireland gets £1.24 head of public money for each £1 that goes to her constituents in Luton, but Stormont avoids imposing the local taxes that it could.
“Quite often I’m told that Northern Ireland doesn’t get its fair share in comparison to Wales or Scotland . There’s also a country that’s left out of that conversation, which is England,” she said.
“I represent one of the most deprived areas in the UK . Over half of the children in some parts of Luton, because of the 14 years of austerity, are growing up below the poverty line.
“They get £1 for each £1.24 that goes to NI. I do have to go back and explain why that is,” said Owen, who emphasised that London will offer no more. “It’s not like we haven’t gone and asked. There is no more.”
[ Sinn Féin and the DUP are happier arguing over a parade than agreeing a budget Opens in new window ]
Owen said Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant had made clear to Stormont’s political parties that this was the British government’s “best and final offer, and I really urge the Executive to accept it”.
“We will be ready and willing to work with them to do the best for the people of Northern Ireland,” she said. “Do not let perfect be the enemy of good, because people are crying out for progress, crying out for hope.”
She said members of Northern Ireland’s business community “are crying out for some financial stability, for people to take the tough decisions”, while knowing that they would “never get away” with failing to agree a budget.
Alliance Party MLA David Honeyford said “blocking decisions is more rewarding than making them” for many Stormont politicians.
“Bad government is actually rewarded, and failure is rewarded,” he said.
Owen clashed sharply with Sinn Féin’s Ruairí Ó Murchú over the handling of the Drumcree Orange Order parade crisis , following the Louth TD’s declaration that prime minister Andy Burnham “had stepped in” to ban the Orange Order march.
[ Many loyalists are desperate to leave – the only thing stopping some is a £5,000 ‘exit fee’ Opens in new window ]
“The fact is that it took 13 days to reverse a bad decision. That’s always going to be the issue in Ireland, because it will always be a secondary or a tertiary issue for British politicians,” Ó Murchú said.
Owen told Ó Murchú the NIO had “not sat there for 13 days doing nothing” following the decision of the Parades Commission to give permission for the march to proceed. Instead, she said, NIO ministers and officials were “on the phones 24 hours a day” trying to find agreement between the sides.
“Please don’t take my enthusiasm as a sign of weakness, and please don’t patronise me,” Owen told Ó Murchú.

title: Why Europe is giving up on Trump-whispering
description: This new crisis looks different and the bloc’s leaders are preparing to talk directly to Putin
content:
T he latest crisis in relations between the US and Ukraine has strong echoes of the darkest days of 2025. The infamous televised Oval Office confrontation between JD Vance , Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskiy crystallised fears that the US was now on Russia’s side. Those worries flared up again with the Trump-Putin summit in Alaska.
European leaders responded to these previous crises with determined Trump-whispering. They embraced Zelenskiy and coached him on how to sound grateful and conciliatory in his dealings with the US president. And they deluged Trump with phone calls and flattery, in an effort to take the roughest edges off US policy.
This time around things look different. Zelenskiy is much less restrained in his remarks about Trump. He has directly accused the US of throttling satellite services in Ukraine and suggested Trump is attracted to autocrats. The Ukrainians have also defied a US demand to stop hitting Russian energy facilities. This weekend saw some of the biggest strikes yet on oil facilities in St Petersburg.
Zelenskiy’s outspoken statements may be driven, in large part, by anger and exasperation. But there is also probably some calculation behind his change in tone. With Trump weakening in the polls and Republicans apparently heading for defeat in the midterm elections, it could be worth appealing to Americans over the heads of the president and his cronies. On the campaign trail, even some Republican candidates have questioned Trump’s plan to buy Russian diesel. Polls suggest Americans do not share Trump’s admiration for Vladimir Putin .
There is also an important shift under way in Europe’s approach to Russia. There is a growing consensus in European capitals that the continent’s leaders can no longer tolerate a situation where only the Americans are talking to Putin. Channels with the Russians are already open and a call between European leaders and Putin may happen soon.
The change in approach reflects a belief that Trump-whispering is increasingly ineffective — particularly given the president’s preoccupation with the midterms and his anger at what he regards as Europe’s failure to help him in Iran. The Europeans also fear US policy is largely driven by a desire for business deals with Russia, rather than a coherent security vision.
Europe’s own approach currently rests on two props — support for Ukraine and sanctions on Russia. Both policies are regarded as crucial, particularly as US support for Ukraine weakens. But direct European involvement in peacemaking efforts is also increasingly seen as a necessity — particularly since it is European money that is keeping Ukraine afloat, following the cut-off in US financial aid.
The Europeans seem confident Putin will be willing to talk. But the Russian leader himself is believed to be floating the idea of a three-way summit between himself, Trump and Xi Jinping of China. That kind of summit would play to Russia’s great-power pretensions — and would keep Ukraine and its most important supporters out of the room.
Russian wariness about engaging with the Europeans may be increased by the kind of proposals that could be put on the table. If and when European talks with Putin take place, the Russian leader is likely to be presented with two possible paths to peace. The first is to freeze the conflict on the current line of control — and in return get a guarantee that Ukraine will never join Nato. The second option would be for Ukraine to cede the rest of the Donbas to Russia — but then to join Nato.
Both of those choices would be regarded as a betrayal by some in Ukraine. But, given the strong desire for peace in his country, Zelenskiy might be able to sell either idea. The Europeans are much less confident that Putin is ready to accept either. But they still think it is important to start talking directly to the Russians.
Alongside the diplomatic rethink, there is also growing European determination to become less dependent on America for crucial capabilities — in particular, the satellite coverage provided by Starshield and Starlink. Two Finnish companies — Nokia and Iceye — this month announced a partnership to develop satellite communications networks for military and civilian purposes. But the first launches are not expected until 2028 — so that cannot solve Ukraine’s immediate problems.
For the moment, the Zelenskiy government remains very reliant on US satellite capabilities both to defend against incoming attacks — and to provide information for offensive operations. Indeed, the Ukrainians have not given up hope that they can persuade the US to extend satellite assistance, allowing them to target missile launch sites deep inside Russia.
The fact that Ukraine is still so dependent on US capabilities might suggest that it is in Zelenskiy’s interest to continue to be as obsequious as possible to Trump and Elon Musk — in the hope that they will relent and provide Kyiv with the help it needs.
Instead, the Ukrainian leader has gone in the opposite direction. He has even discussed the possibility that the US might side directly with Russia against Ukraine. “He’s gone full Carney” is the verdict of one top European.
That is certainly a risky strategy. But Trump has not left the Ukrainians with many better options.
- Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Gardaí believe several people can help with Jamie Bailey murder investigation
description: Limerick man killed in Dublin at the weekend believed to have been attacked by people in his wider social circle
content:
Gardaí have identified a number of people they believe have crucial information to share about the murder of Jamie Bailey (38), a Limerick man who died after being stabbed in Dublin at the weekend.
Though the victim was known to gardaí, as he had a lengthy criminal record, detectives suspect his murder in the early hours of Sunday was related to difficulties in his personal life. However, it remains unclear if the fatal attack at Blackhorse Place, Dublin 7 , was spur of the moment or if some degree of planning was involved.
Bailey, who had a number of children and had lived in Dublin for some time, had been involved in a bitter personal dispute that had worsened recently. Gardaí suspect he was attacked by people in his wider social circle, or certainly by someone who was known to him.
The deceased man had addiction issues during his life and had been jailed a number of times. He had convictions for a wide range of crimes including burglary, theft, criminal damage, public order and road traffic offences. Bailey had also been caught in stolen cars after they were pursued by gardaí.
The murder investigation team, based at the Bridewell Garda station, believes several people were at the scene at the time of the killing and that they can aid the investigation.
Gardaí have been told by witnesses they were alerted to an issue outside an apartment building close to the scene when a loud argument between a number of people began. This resulted in Bailey being stabbed, with the male suspect fleeing the scene.
However, gardaí believe a person who was living in the area was also present when the dispute broke out and when they are spoken to, they will have a clearer picture of how the events leading to the murder unfolded.
Gardaí have also appealed to anyone who was in the area of Blackhorse Avenue between 2am and 3.30am to contact them. They are especially keen to speak to anyone who was recording footage, including dashcam, at or around the scene at Blackhorse Place-Blackhorse Avenue.
Gardaí also conducted house-to-house inquiries in the area, including in the apartment block close to the scene, on Monday to find more witnesses.
[ Man killed in fatal assault outside Dublin apartment named as gardaí search for weapon Opens in new window ]
Footage recorded by CCTV cameras in the area was being harvested in the hope that the fatal attack, or the killer, was captured. However, no arrests had been made by Monday evening, and the man gardaí suspect carried out the stabbing remained unaccounted for and was being sought.
The victim was discovered injured on the pavement at Blackhorse Place, and the emergency services were called. However, while paramedics attended to him at the scene before he was taken by ambulance to the Mater Misericordiae University Hospital, he was pronounced dead there.
The scene was sealed off and securely preserved overnight before being examined by the Garda Technical Bureau on Monday.
The results of the postmortem, to establish the cause and time of death, would dictate the course of the investigation, gardaí said. However, a murder inquiry was started immediately after Bailey’s death was confirmed.
“This investigation is being co-ordinated from an incident room at the Bridewell Garda station under the direction of a senior investigating officer,” a Garda statement said of the murder inquiry.
Anyone with information is asked to contact the Bridewell on (01) 666 8200 or the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111.
Cabra-Glasnevin councillor Séamas McGrattan said he was shocked by the fatal attack on Sunday morning.
“Knife crime has become a real problem in our city. We need an urgent and serious response,” the Sinn Féin councillor said.
“People must have the right to walk the streets of Dublin safely and without fear.”
He called for increased Garda presence on the ground and policing to deter crime and antisocial behaviour from taking place.

title: Judge ‘coerced’ into adjourning six rape and sexual offences trials as solicitors withdraw
description: Defence solicitors warned by judges they need court permission to cease representing people in custody
content:
A senior judge was “coerced” into adjourning six rape and sexual offence trials involving accused people on bail on Monday as the dispute over the new legal aid payment model was intensified by solicitors.
Many defence solicitors, particularly in Dublin, withdrew legal aid services after a new flat fee system for District Court cases was introduced in July.
This has led to the adjournment of thousands of criminal cases across all court divisions, adding to existing backlogs. The dispute ramped up on Monday with the withdrawal of services expanding to almost all cases.
