Judge Paul McDermott at the Central Criminal Court said the withdrawal meant he had been “obliged” or “coerced” into adjourning six out of 13 such cases before him on Monday.
Those cases were listed for trial but, had he forced the trials on, defendants may have been forced to conduct their own defences and possibly cross-examine vulnerable complainants, he said.
[ Jim O’Callaghan insists he will not go back on new legal aid rules as dispute ramps up Opens in new window ]
The six trials were adjourned to October 27th, when new trial dates will be assigned.
McDermott also said criminal defence solicitors withdrawing services in protest at a new legal aid payment model need court permission to cease representing accused people in custody. A solicitor “cannot unilaterally withdraw”, he said.
McDermott, who manages the Central Criminal Court’s list of serious crime cases, said, when dealing with one case dating from 2020, the court had “limited options” when a solicitor withdraws from a case.
He has said “on numerous occasions how regrettable this is”, and added: “Cases like this with a very long history need to get on.”
Noting the “obvious suffering” this inflicted on those involved, he said he was “obliged/coerced” to adjourn the cases, and apologised to complainants.
Defence solicitors were conspicuous by their absence from the Criminal Courts of Justice on Monday and their withdrawal – replicated in various other courts around the country – resulted in adjournments in the central, circuit and district courts.
Courts Service sources said the adjournments were compounding existing backlogs but the real impact would only become obvious later this year and next year.
The withdrawal began in mid-June but intensified when the new payment model was introduced on July 1st.
[ Judge again urges O’Callaghan and solicitors to resolve legal aid case between them Opens in new window ]
Court presidents were told, in a letter on Friday, the withdrawal was being escalated to virtually all cases, including custody cases and cases involving children, due to the Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan ’s failure to engage in “meaningful” discussions.
The new payment model provides for one flat fee of €520, based on an average five court appearances, irrespective of the number of charges and court appearances.
O’Callaghan said it would achieve necessary reforms and cost savings but solicitors have said it would result in them not being paid for their work in more complex cases, including those involving children and people with addiction and mental health issues.
They said two “narrow” issues, aimed at ensuring they would be paid for their work in more complex cases, separated the sides.
Separately, the work-to-rule action by public sector employees in the Courts Service continues to adversely impact the courts.
The action means, where registrars and other court staff have retired, are ill or on holiday leave, other court staff will not take their place.
Sources said the action has had a particularly serious impact on the Dolphin House family court complex in Dublin.
Just two or three out of the five courts in the complex have been sitting since the work to rule began two weeks ago, causing adjournments of multiple domestic violence, guardianship, maintenance and custody hearings.

title: World Food Programme cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza due to funding shortages
description: Food rations halved and cash ​assistance cut for thousands of families
author_name: Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem, Seham Tantesh in Gaza
content:
This winter is likely to deepen hunger for Palestinians in Gaza , after sweeping aid cuts forced the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) to end support for more than half a million people each month, the agency’s director for Palestine said.
More than a year after a Trump -brokered ceasefire came into force, promised reconstruction has not begun, there are few jobs and the vast majority in Gaza still rely on aid to eat.
This summer, WFP programmes helped feed three-quarters of Gaza’s population, about 1.6 million people, but funding has fallen by more than half from 2025 levels.
As a result, from October, aid has been scaled back to 1.1 million people each month. Cuts to deliveries of ration boxes, cash stipends to buy food in markets, and hot meals at community kitchens have already been rolled out.
The WFP said it ⁠urgently needs €400 million over the next six months to maintain critical operations in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
A year of large aid shipments ended a famine declared in summer 2025 and reduced the most severe hunger, but without steps to rebuild Gaza’s economy, most families still rely on food handouts.
“These are very fragile gains, easily reversed, and the situation is still brutal,” said Shaun Hughes, the WFP’s representative and country director for Palestine.
Two-thirds of the population in Gaza face crisis levels of food insecurity, phase three under the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), which is used to assess if a population is approaching famine.
Food insecurity is at emergency levels for 200,000 Palestinians, which means immediate humanitarian supplies are needed to prevent deaths from hunger, Hughes said. This is IPC phase four, one step away from famine conditions.
Young children and their mothers are particularly vulnerable. After enduring years of food shortages, one in eight children in Gaza are chronically malnourished or stunted, a recent Unicef survey found, and may have suffered permanent damage.
Humanitarian aid will be needed at scale until Israel and the international community launch the large-scale reconstruction promised last year. There is no way for most people to feed their own families at present, because about 80 per cent of Gaza’s population is unemployed, according to UN data.
“We need to invest in recovery. This humanitarian operation isn’t affordable or sustainable in the long term,” Hughes said. “Ultimately that’s also what everyone in Gaza is telling us. They really don’t want to be reliant on these handouts, don’t want to stand in the hot meals queue every day. They want to have some chance of stability and recovery.”
Gaza was self-sufficient in fruit and vegetables before the war, but the vast majority of farmland has been occupied by Israel’s military. The sophisticated greenhouse and irrigation systems that supported agricultural production have been destroyed.
Fish has historically been a key source of protein in the territory, but the Israeli navy bars fishing boats from waters off the coast.
Alaa Sarhan (40) lives with his wife and five children aged between four and 16 in a tent near the “yellow line” the marker of Israeli control. They have already noticed the impact of the WFP cuts.
“In recent days, we have had to plan our meals around what is available rather than what we want to eat,” he said. A former paramedic, he was injured by Israeli attacks nearly two decades ago, and his disability benefits buy very little.
“Often, I give up my share of food so my children can eat. I got accustomed to doing this because the most important thing is that they have something to eat.”
For three years, Israeli restrictions on aid shipments have been the main driver of hunger and malnutrition in Gaza. For months at a time, entry of food was restricted or entirely barred as Palestinians went hungry inside the territory. - Guardian

title: New battery-electric trains due to arrive next year in bid to relieve overcrowding on services
description: French-built units planned for use on Dublin-Drogheda line will allow for reallocation of other trains to different routes
content:
Capacity issues on the Republic’s railway lines will not ease before the arrival of the first order of 55 new battery-electric train carriages go into service next year, Minister for State at the Department of Transport Seán Canney has said.
The new order of battery-electric trains is due to go into service on the Dublin– Drogheda route, freeing up existing intercity and commuter trains for redeployment to Dublin and services elsewhere.
The move is aimed at easing overcrowding on rail services at a time of record demand for public transport.
Almost 22 million rail journeys, excluding the Luas , were taken between January 1st and May 24th, 2026, which was up 13 per cent on the same period in 2025, according to the Central Statistics Office .
Irish Rail said the first arrivals of battery-electric trains will be 11, five-carriage trains and the first of these will begin entering service by June 2027. The deployment of these 55 trains is to be completed by the end of the year
The five-carriage units can be coupled together so they can operate as 10-carriage trains. Each new 10-carriage battery-electric train is equivalent in length to an existing eight-carriage Dart or commuter train.
The 55 new arrivals will allow slightly less than 55 intercity and commuter carriages to be available for redeployment across the network. The redeployed carriages will be used to lengthen existing trains or, in some cases, adding services to the timetable.
Speaking in a recent Dáil debate on rail services into Galway city, Canney said carriages to improve that service would “be available” from the redeployed Drogheda route trains “in 2027″.
However, difficulties have already emerged on some routes, notably the Dublin to Rosslare line, which includes a section of single-track railway that makes scheduling additional services problematic.
Wicklow-Wexford TD Malcolm Byrne, who has campaigned for many years for better rail transport, said conditions were so bad on the line that from the beginning of the year to mid-August, Irish Rail had spent more than €700 on a stock of water for distribution to customers in circumstances that “include times of emergency, lengthy delays or extreme weather conditions”.
Byrne said he had received a commitment that while the first new battery-electric trains will serve Drogheda from 2027, trains from a second order will allow commencement of Dart services to Wicklow around 2029.
A spokesman for Irish Rail said the routes that will benefit from the deployed Drogheda route services is yet to be determined in conjunction with the National Transport Authority .
The timetable for the new trains entering service has been delayed a number of times due to technical issues. Last October it was put at the second quarter of 2027, and Irish Rail said on Monday it was still on course for this schedule.
Spokesman Barry Kenny said overall, 285 carriages have been ordered from French builder Alstom.
Some 100 of these will replace the original 1984 Dart fleet, leaving 185 carriages offering new capacity.
“All trains in 2027 and early 2028 represent new capacity, and then it will be a mix of new capacity and replacement of the original Dart fleet through the remainder of 2028 and 2029,” he said.
“We plan further orders of these trains within the framework contract with Alstom, as the Dart+ programme continues, and in turn continuing the cascade of intercity and commuter trains currently in use in the Greater Dublin Area for other routes,” he said.

title: Rory McIlroy hits back at Kevin Kisner over comments about appearance fees
description: Former PGA Tour player said McIlroy’s comments about growing the game were ‘dog shit’
content:
Nothing acts as fuel for the fire to any player than the suggestion that appearance fees are the primary motive for playing in a tournament, which is exactly what irked Rory McIlroy after player-turned-broadcaster Kevin Kisner implied the Masters champion’s choice of playing in India for a second straight year.
Speaking on the Fore Play podcast, Kisner questioned the real reason for McIlroy playing in Delhi in the DP World India Championship.
“That is such a dog shit comment,” said Kisner of questioning McIlroy’s decision to play, “but I guess for the right price, we could all say that comment. He doesn’t want to globally expand (golf) in India, he wants to get his $10 million bucks and go play in India.
“I know there’s a pile of guys that got paid for that event. How else would you get that event in India with eight billion people in the middle of the city?”
Kisner retired from the PGA Tour to focus on a career in broadcasting with American network NBC, but ironically still plays on the TGL virtual golf league started by McIlroy and Tiger Woods.
In his response to Kisner’s comments, McIlroy observed: “I don’t know why me being in India would be something Kis needs to comment on. ”
“Two things can be true at the same time,” he added. “People can get paid to come play in a tournament but at the same time do it from a place of a genuine interest of trying to bring the sport to another country, a developing country, a country where the middle class in India is larger than the whole population of the United States. It’s a huge market for golf.”
The Irish Times Shield and the Irish Open share one thing in common – they were both played for the first time in 1927!
And hosts Powerscourt Golf Club will have the honour of defending The Irish Times Shield in next year’s centenary edition of the popular inter-club competition after using local knowledge to great effect to fend off Dún Laoghaire in ideal playing conditions at West Course, succeeding Castle as champions.
Confined to four-man teams (with the best three scores counting) and players with handicaps of nine or less, Powerscourt’s team of Donal Hurley (9) Gerard Murphy (5), Mark Kissane (5) and Mark McKevitt (5) claimed the shield, with Murphy producing a superb 41 points in helping his team to success.
Irish international Will O’Riordan from Greystones, playing off plus-4, shot a four-under-par 68 to claim the individual gross prize, while Castle’s Stephen Finlan took the individual nett prize with 42 points playing off seven.
“I think this tournament means everything to me because you have the chance to play in front of all your family and friends and in front of all the amazing fans, it’s just amazing . . . it’s a dream come true to win at home, and I think I’m lucky to win it twice. I hope this is just the beginning” – Ruoning Yin on winning the Buick LPGA event in Shanghai on home turf.
There are two Irish players – Leona Maguire and Lauren Walsh – competing in this week’s BMW Ladies Championship in South Korea on the LPGA Tour.
Peter Oosterhuis was the dominant player of the early years of the PGA European Tour, winning the Harry Vardon Trophy for topping the order of merit in each of the circuit’s first three seasons from 1972 to 1974. He had also topped the money list in 1971, the year before the new tour was founded.
His victory in the weather-affected Italian Open came at Venezia where rounds of 37-72-70-70 for a two-under-par total of 249 gave him a two strokes winning margin over Dale Hayes and Jonny Miller. The first round was reduced to nine holes due to severe weather.
That success was the sixth of seven – his seventh would come with a playoff victory over Manuel Ballesteros in the following week’s El Paraiso Open in Spain – but his appearances on the European Tour would be reduced considerably in subsequent years after the Englishman earned his PGA Tour card at Q-School and effectively committed to the US circuit before going on to a fine second career as a broadcaster.
