title: ‘The war is getting nearer’: Ukraine’s eastern exodus accelerates as Russia steps up attacks
description: Millions could face ‘most difficult time of war’ if Russia continues to destroy critical infrastructure
content:
T he people of Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine have lived in the shadow of war for more than a decade, but many are now fleeing its last Kyiv -controlled cities as Russian air strikes intensify, the civilian death toll soars, and a potentially brutal winter starts to set in.
United Nations data shows that during the first eight months of this year, 400 Ukrainian civilians were killed or injured every week – a 55 per cent increase on the same period in 2025 – and nearly 2,500 civilians in front-line areas such as Donetsk were killed or wounded by Russia’s powerful glide bombs, a 62 per cent year-on-year rise.
Russian attacks are only getting bloodier as winter looms – civilian casualties in Ukraine last month were 85 per cent higher than in September 2025.
For many residents of cities such as Kramatorsk and Slovyansk, the largest remaining links in Ukraine’s so-called fortress belt in Donetsk, the now-constant threat from Russian drones, bombs and missiles has become impossible to bear.
“For a long time the war was somewhere ‘over there’. We could still go to work and try to live as normally as possible. But the war [is getting] nearer and nearer,” says Larysa Solovyova, who fled Kramatorsk with husband Volodymyr this year.
“In the end I just couldn’t sleep at night at all. I felt such fear. It seemed drones were overhead all the time, you heard explosions all around, and people were being killed,” adds the former nurse.
“I can’t imagine what it will be like in Kramatorsk this winter. Life there is so dangerous, even without considering what could happen with water and power supplies. It’s a horrible thought, that people will die there, just trying to hold on inside their own four walls.”
Her husband Volodymyr worked in one of Kramatorsk’s factories and then became a bus driver. He shakes his head as he recalls how a Russian glide-bomb attack killed more than 30 people on two buses in Kramatorsk this month.
“The situation just got worse and worse,” says Olena Kovalyova, who fled the village of Novyi Kavkaz outside Kramatorsk this year.
[ Russia’s new jet-powered drones are fuelling anxiety in Ukraine Opens in new window ]
“If it was more or less okay before, even though you heard [explosions], now drones are literally flying over the fields. It’s like roulette – you go to bed and hear them flying around, and you have no idea where they are going to strike,” she adds.
“Mostly elderly people are left in the village now. They have nowhere to go, and some have animals to look after. For older people in general, it’s hard to leave your home and move to a new place.”
Kovalyova and husband Hryhorii left the city of Donetsk after it was seized by Russian-led militants in 2014, as the Kremlin reacted to Ukraine’s pro-western Maidan Revolution by illegally annexing Crimea and unleashing violence on the east.
The Solovyovs lived through three months of occupation by the militants and their Russian leaders that year, before Ukrainian forces liberated Kramatorsk, Slovyansk and other nearby cities and drove the enemy back to Donetsk, prompting the Kremlin to send in regular troops to halt a potentially victorious counteroffensive by Kyiv’s army.
Twelve years on, and nearly five years into Russia’s all-out invasion, Kyiv holds only about a fifth of Donetsk region and the front line is less than 15km from Slovyansk and Kramatorsk.
Ukraine has heavily fortified the cities and surrounding areas and refuses to bow to Kremlin demands to give them up as a precondition for any peace deal, arguing they are not only still home to tens of thousands of people, but also protect the flatlands of central Ukraine from Russian attack.
Kyiv’s forces have pushed back Russian troops northeast of Slovyansk and Kramatorsk in recent weeks, and say their operation “Vivaldi” has retaken 16 villages and more than 250 sq km of territory.
The counterattack has eased pressure from Russia’s ground forces, but unrelenting air strikes continue, and the authorities in Kramatorsk last week expanded a mandatory evacuation zone for families with young children.
“The safety situation is deteriorating, and waiting until the danger reaches your home is too great a risk. This is especially true when children are involved. I urge parents not to delay. Evacuation saves lives,” said Vadym Filashkin, head of the Donetsk region’s military administration.
Ukraine has essentially halted Russia’s slow and immensely bloody advance on the battlefield, but faces ever-greater threats from the air. The US has stopped supplying the Patriot rockets it needs to down ballistic missiles, and vital satellite internet provision by Elon Musk’s Starlink system was disrupted last week, as US president Donald Trump again strongarms Kyiv to make a deal with Moscow.
“We already see ... that the Russian Federation is renewing its attacks on energy infrastructure. We see it in Kyiv and Kharkiv and the cities closest to the frontline,” says Iryna Tymchyshyn, a spokeswoman for UNHCR, the UN refugee agency, in Kyiv.
“This year the Russian Federation has also started to strike water and sanitation systems, so this is our primary concern, that this year not only energy and heating facilities but also water supplies will be targeted,” she adds.
“Maybe people could endure many hours without electricity, and people already have coping strategies for this, and there are some backup options for heating. But if entire cities, where millions of people live, will be left without water supplies and sanitation services, this will really have a devastating impact on civilians.”
[ Lara Marlowe: Robots have brought a ‘horrifying intimacy’ to warfare Opens in new window ]
The UNHCR and other aid agencies support state-run transit centres that offer displaced people food and shelter, medical and psychological help, assistance with documentation, benefits and accommodation, and other services.
“From the start of 2026 until August, over 111,000 people passed through transit centres and received support there. But that doesn’t show the total number of people displaced, because so many people are self-evacuating,” Tymchyshyn says.
“According to the local authorities, approximately 80,000 people are now living in the Ukrainian-controlled part of Donetsk region. That’s about a third of the population recorded a year ago. So ... we have seen a quite significant displacement from this area.”
Most are staying in neighbouring regions such as Kharkiv and Dnipropetrovsk, to be close to home in case a chance to return emerges.
But the Solovyovs and the Kovalyovs are now living in the western region of Lviv, near the border with Poland. They still hold out hope of going home one day.
“If Ukraine can keep Donbas and rebuild, then we will go back,” says Kovalyova.
Solovyova’s eyes fill with tears as she talks about having to start again as a pensioner 1,000km from Kramatorsk.
“It’s very hard. At night sometimes I dream about home,” she says. “But I feel much safer here. I can finally relax and sleep normally. At home I was always rushing for cover in the basement, even though it wouldn’t have done much good in a direct hit.”
At a time when Ukraine feels increasingly abandoned by Trump’s United States, the UNHCR and other aid agencies are urging the world not to forget its people.
[ Did the internet really get less toxic after Russian data centres went down? Opens in new window ]
“Ukraine could be facing the most difficult time of the full-scale war, and millions of people face very uncertain months,” Tymchyshyn says. “This is when support is really needed, perhaps more than ever.”

title: What’s behind the violence shaking France, and what comes next?
description: As demonstrations spread across France, questions remain over who was responsible for the violence and what it means for Emmanuel Macron
content:
On Saturday two protest movements came together . Secondary school students and their supporters organised a march through Paris , as they have several times a week for the last few weeks.
They were joined by demonstrators who had already called for protests in cities across France on October 17th many weeks ago about the high cost of living and fuel prices.
The second group are hoping to revive the Yellow Vest, or Gilet Jaune , movement that paralysed France at times between 2018 and 2020. Their online calls for protests invited disparate groups, from farmers to trade unionists to climate activists, to take part.
In Paris, clashes between police and protesters began in the early afternoon around Place de la République, the meeting point for the demonstration. A march of tens of thousands of people then proceeded around Paris largely peacefully, with students chanting and marching with placards, sometimes accompanied by parents or grandparents.
At the same time, smaller crowds began attacking shops and buildings and burning cars in a wildcat manner in various points around central Paris. They also built piles of rubbish and electric rental bicycles along the roads and set them alight, causing a potent dark smoke and the batteries to explode.
Place de la République was a focal point. Bus stops were smashed, a newspaper kiosk was burned and shops and buildings attacked indiscriminately. The symbolic central monument representing Marianne, an allegory of the French republic, was badly vandalised with graffiti.
No. Protests had been called for most large towns and cities in France. People thought to be protesters burned down the historic city hall in the small and picturesque city of Limoges.
In Marseilles, demonstrators managed to break open the door of the city hall and ran through the building, trashing some furniture and art.
In Lyons, a tourist information centre on the central square where crowds amassed was sacked and burned. Shops were looted in Marseilles, Nice and Lille.
Some of the initial vandalism was clearly by protesters. They scrawled left-wing political messages on the Marianne monument on Place de la République and inside the Marseilles town hall.
However, it isn’t clear that the later, wider looting and destruction was political.
The Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau, who is responsible for criminal prosecutions, told French media she “absolutely cannot confirm” that those responsible for violence in Paris were “politically aligned with the far left”.
Those arrested are mostly people with no public profile who “remain silent and do not make any political demands”, she told broadcaster TF1.
The instigators appear to have be largely young men, mostly dressed in black, many in hoodies and often with their faces covered.
Once the shutters and doors to shops were forced open, video footage indicates that some people who appeared to be random passersby opportunistically took part: young women with shopping bags, a middle-aged lady in a headscarf, a child running off with a pair of runners.
Adults make up 70 per cent of the 2,331 people arrested in France since Saturday in connection to the unrest, according to the minister of justice.
Protests are set to continue. The Yellow Vest organisers, who have declined to disavow the violence, have called for an “act-two” protest on Saturday, October 24th, to demand the resignation of president Emmanuel Macron .
Unions had already called for a mass demonstration against the proposed budget on November 5th.
School students had until now been protesting on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays; however, the half-term break has begun. Their next large protest may end up being November 5th, when they return to school.
The most immediate concern is whether wildcat rioting and looting could continue this week.
There was sporadic looting in central Paris and Marseilles on Sunday night. Authorities have banned all public gatherings in Marseilles from noon until 8pm on Monday. Macron is reported to have considered imposing a curfew, before deciding against it in case it antagonised protesters further.
France is in full campaign mode in advance of presidential elections in April 2027 and the unrest is widely being seen as a turning point, though the implications are not yet entirely clear.
The front-runner in polls, far-right Marine Le Pen , has used the violence to present herself as a law-and-order candidate. She has been blaming the left wing for causing the unrest, and accuses the current government of incompetence for losing control.
She issued a presidential-style address to the nation from behind a desk on Sunday night, promising to pass new laws and restore order.
Politicians from across the political spectrum are using the violence as an opportunity to attack Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the hard-left candidate and runner-up to Le Pen in polls. He has been marching with the students and on Saturday blamed the police for causing the violence, only belatedly condemning the rioting.
Interior minister Laurent Nuñez has admitted that police resources were misallocated on Saturday and has said he offered his resignation, but that Macron refused it .
The public anger and disorder are a discordant end to Macron’s final term in office, and the president looked uncertain as he delivered an address to the nation on Sunday night. He is due to leave France for a three-day visit to the Middle East.
With his term due to end soon anyway, an early resignation seems unlikely.
French stocks sank on international markets when trading opened on Monday, and the cost that Paris must pay to borrow money will be closely watched.
The French government faces the difficult task of passing a budget through a hung parliament under the watchful eye of market hawks concerned about excessive national debt, while public sentiment is fiercely opposed to cuts in spending.
The government collapsed when trying to pass a budget last year, so watch this space.
[ ‘A bombshell’: French teachers spot something on payslips that reveals scale of funding crisis Opens in new window ]
A protest against the cost of living in Milan devolved into rioting on Saturday. There were protests against the housing crisis and cost of living in Portugal, which follows mass demonstrations about the housing crisis in Spain.
Although there are common themes, the movements in each country are not directly linked. Viral clips on social media could play a role in spreading unrest, but this is unclear.
Within France itself the complaints of protesters are highly disparate. Some young people have very concrete concerns about education policy, but also much broader worries about what future they will have linked to climate change, the effect of artificial intelligence on the labour market and inflation in housing costs.

title: Second public sector strike is off, but legal-payment dispute rumbles on
description: Inside Politics: Criminal defence solicitors withdrew all services for the day this morning
content:
If you’re a parent of school-goers, there’s no need to use up that annual leave day this week it would seem. Peace has broken out and the machinery of industrial dispute resolution is about to work its magic.
As of this morning, the old social partners – who we all feared were poised for a painful break-up – are talking again . The Workplace Relations Commission is playing host to the two sides after weeks of deadlock and will endeavour to weave a spell that reunites them.
Wednesday’s planned second day of industrial action won’t happen and the consensus appears to be that the players will now dance the dance, agree on a big number and do the deed.
The Taoiseach welcomed the commencement of the process yesterday and said it would need to deliver “value for money”. Micheál Martin rejected the suggestion from that cheeky chappie Michael O’Leary that he would be “rolling over” in negotiations.
The unions have also pointed out that trust has taken a bit of a bruising over the last little while and there’ll be no rush to jump into bed just yet.
There is still some trouble in paradise, however.
The criminal defence solicitors have upped their action – and this morning withdrew all services for the day. The dispute over Jim O’Callaghan’s flat-fee payment system has rumbled on all summer and a backlog of cases is rapidly building up within the courts system.
Not only this, but the industrial action has led to almost 90 High Court cases alleging unlawful detention.
But the up and down of the public sector tiff is that the placards can be stowed away while everybody awaits the renewal of vows.
Oh, how Emmanuel Macron must envy such serenity.
The French president and his government have watched as peaceful school protests, calling for more public spending, have been overtaken by wild violence and looting on the country’s streets.
The French cabinet was in emergency session last night as Macron said there was no place for violence in French society. Parts of Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseilles have seen streets barricaded and historic buildings set alight.
More than 2,000 people have been arrested and more than 600 members of the police and emergency services injured.
The government there is blaming the actions on the “ultra-left”. The opposition parties have asked how the state didn’t see this all coming and are demanding that heads roll. Politically speaking, that is.
Macron however is holding the line and, according to the Elysée, has declined the offer of interior minister Laurent Nuñez to resign.
You’d suspect it’ll hardly get sorted out at the French equivalent of Lansdowne House.
One of the items on the agenda at said Lansdowne House in Dublin’s Ballsbridge will be the effect that high fuel costs are having on the cost of living.
There won’t be much relief there for a while – what with Ukraine hitting Russian refineries in St Petersburg with its largest drone attack on the city .
Kyiv sent a very clear signal to Donald Trump and his decision to buy Russian diesel. Russia, meanwhile, again pummelled Ukrainian energy sites. Watch the price at the pumps.
Speaking of the cost of living, the Finance Bill is up for debate this week.
The Bill, which gives effect to the budget (remember that?), is set to include a new derelict property tax.
Owners of such properties will have to show they intend on doing something to tidy up the place if they want to avoid paying a 7 per cent tariff. Local authorities will be required to draw up lists of derelict sites and hand them over to the no-nonsense types that inhabit the offices of the Revenue.
On the matter of properties, councillors in south Dublin could tonight decide to lift a ban on the building of 500 homes .
The plans in question focus on land belonging to billionaire businessmen John Magnier and JP McManus close to Lucan.
The kibosh was put on the proposal after councillors received more than 1,600 submissions opposing the whole thing. But the council chief executive has asked them to reconsider. Standing in support of the plan are the Office of Public Works and the National Transport Authority.
Finally, later in the week it is expected the family of the late Brian Stack, the chief prison officer at Portlaoise Prison who was shot by the IRA 43 years ago and later died in hospital, will receive a formal State apology in relation to the mishandling of three separate Garda investigations into his murder.
The Taoiseach is due to deliver the apology on Wednesday in the Dáil after a meeting with the family.

title: Melanie C in Dublin review: Spice Girl meets teenage raver in night of effortless joy
description: At 3Olympia, Melanie Chisholm exudes likeability, confidence and a sense of liberation on a tour to promote Sweat, her ninth studio album
content:
“Who in the room has never seen a Spice Girls show?” the artist officially known as Melanie C , better known as Mel C and born Melanie Chisholm asks the crowd at 3Olympia on Sunday. After a surprisingly thick smattering of hands fly up, Sporty Spice fuels the reunion rumours anew with a teasing “We need to do something about this.”
But tonight is not about her bandmates or anything as tediously grown-up as diary scheduling and clashing commitments. It’s about rediscovering the teenager who would go to the Costa Brava to lose herself in rave culture as part of a group of friends dubbed the “F**king Yeah Four”.
It’s this exuberant, pre-Spice Chisholm who is resurrected to infectious effect for a gig in which her old hits are a highlight but never the whole point.
She bounds on to the stage in a satin boxing robe, ready to shuffle and jab her way through Undefeated Champion, one of the superior tracks on Sweat, the clubby, cardio-pop album she released to deservedly positive notices in May.
Sweat is Chisholm’s ninth studio album (the next most musically productive Spice Girl is Emma Bunton , with four), and it’s also her best-defined one. You feel fitter just by playing it. Confidence permeates its beats, and she lets it flourish on this tour, delivering all 13 of its songs with their sense of liberation and self-knowledge intact.
During one of them, Pressure, she crouches and springs about in a dance frenzy, her body language alternating between the world’s most likable predator and the epitome of ecstatic abandonment as she covers her face with her flying hair.
She reinvents the delightful What Could Possibly Go Wrong? as an acoustic manifesto for doing whatever she likes, however imperfect, and not overthinking.
And on the album’s title track, which samples Diana Ross ’s Work That Body, she exudes an irresistible 1980s vibe by pulling on the tour merchandise also worn by her keyboardist and drummer: a Frankie Goes to Hollywood-style T-shirt that marries her band and solo identities with the slogan “Sporty says sweat”.
Chisholm recently demurred when Louis Theroux repeatedly suggested to her on his podcast that she had the best voice in The Spice Girls, modestly (and accurately) insisting that it’s down to personal taste. She was, in truth, one of three members, the others being Bunton and Mel B , who contributed distinctive vocals to their hits.
Comparisons are moot in any case. Tonight she shows off her power, dexterity and sincerity, her voice both soft and strong on Emotional Memory and One Track Mind, while on Cashmere, another peak from Sweat, and Never Be the Same Again, her 2000 number one (now shorn of its rap by the late Lisa “Left Eye” Lopes), its textures are just lovely.
But, as Chisholm says, it would be “rude not to get spicy” on this tour, which began in North America and now proceeds to Britain, continental Europe, Japan and Australia. So in the mid-set acoustic section she gives us the 30-year-old Say You’ll Be There, the Spice Girls’ superb second single, the crowd effortlessly harmonising with her breezy vocal ad-libs, and later, after a sojourn behind the decks, a snippet of Nirvana ’s Smells Like Teen Spirit heralds Who Do You Think You Are, with all hands soon in the air for the still-joyous Spice Up Your Life.
By the time she closes the night with the Ibiza-channelling I Turn to You, another solo number one, she has done what she set out to do: make us sweat and sing along – sometimes both at the same time – in a spicy carnival of a show.

title: Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber ‘heartbroken’ over death of ‘sweet’ son Presley
description: The couple paid tribute to their son in an emotional statement posted on Instagram on Sunday
content:
S upermodel Cindy Crawford and businessman Rande Gerber said they were “beyond heartbroken” in a tribute to their “sweet beautiful” son Presley.
Their eldest child died aged 27 at a rehab facility on September 20th, according to Los Angeles County Medical Examiner records.
The cause of his death has not been disclosed.
Crawford and Gerber paid tribute to their son in an emotional statement posted on Instagram on Sunday.
“We are beyond heartbroken to lose our beloved son and brother,” it said. “We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years.
“He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever. We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability.
“We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain.
The message was signed “with love forever” from them both, and their model daughter, Kaia Gerber.
Kaia, who also expressed her support in the comments, shared a message on her own page alongside a carousel of images and videos of herself and Presley through the years.
In a letter addressed to her brother, she said: “Prez, I don’t have the words. Maybe the tiny mercy is that we didn’t need them all along.
“Words fail and words subtract and words summarise and words always lack truth, and how naive of me to believe that language could transcend grief.”
Kaia said she had “none of the answers” and could not articulate the “magnitude” of losing her brother.
“You know how much I loved being your sister. It has always been, and will forever be, my favourite thing about myself.”
The letter described her older brother as “inherently good” and her “ultimate teacher”, recounting childhood memories as she reflected on her grief.
[ Vincent Browne: Haughey loved Terry Keane. She made his life miserable Opens in new window ]
“I am learning how to love you when I cannot see you,” Kaia said.
“How to tell you something without picking up my phone to call you.
“How to be your sister in a world that I can’t reach for you in.
Kaia ended her post: “My best buddy, my great protector, the hardest I’ve ever laughed and the one true love of my life.
“You lit all of my candles and took all of my monsters away, and I love you.”
The post was set to First I Was by Jake Minch, which Kaia described as “the last thing we talked about”.
It was flooded with condolences from fellow stars, including US actors Taylor Lautner and Patrick Schwarzenegger , singer Suki Waterhouse and socialite Paris Hilton .
Hilton wrote: “My heart breaks for you and your family.
“Presley was truly one of a kind, and I feel so lucky to have known him. I’ll always remember him with so much love.”
Presley was signed by IMG Models when he was 15 and modelled for brands including Burberry , Dolce & Gabbana , and Bottega Veneta .
He spoke frequently about his struggles with depression and substance abuse. In March, he posted a video of himself undergoing drug withdrawal treatment known as a “pre ibogaine flood dose” in Cancun, Mexico.
Ibogaine is a naturally occurring psychedelic substance that has attracted attention for its potential use in treating substance use disorders, particularly opioid and alcohol dependence. Its use remains experimental. It is illegal in the US but can be possessed and administered in Mexico. – PA

title: First storm of season could be named in advance of ‘very windy’ conditions
description: Met Éireann forecasts ‘very windy’ conditions and heavy rainfalls on Thursday
content:
The first storm of the season could be named this week amid a “risk of strong winds” on Thursday, according to Met Éireann .
Rain and windy conditions are expected throughout this week before what will be a “blustery” bank holiday weekend, though Thursday is likely to see the windiest conditions.
According to the latest forecast, Thursday is expected to be “very windy” with “strong and gusty” northwesterly winds.
Rain is also expected, with heavy falls likely across the country that day, gradually spreading to “all parts” from the southwest and ultimately clearing to the east overnight.
Noting a risk of strong winds on Thursday, Met Éireann said the strongest gusts are expected to affect the south coast of the country and the southwest of the UK.
“We will monitor the evolution of this system in collaboration with the UK Met Office and if it meets the criteria for a storm, it will be named,” it said.
The first storm of the season will be called Storm Austen, a name chosen by Met Éireann in tribute to Austen H Nagle.
Nagle became the first director of the Irish Meteorological Service when he was appointed in 1936.
Before Thursday, wet and windy conditions are forecast throughout the week, beginning with scattered outbreaks of rain and drizzle in the east and south of the country throughout Monday.
Highest temperatures of 9 to 13 degrees are expected during the day, and Monday will be a “cold night”, dropping to lows of -1 to 3 degrees.
Tuesday will start “cold but dry”, though rain is expected to develop in the southwest, with some “heavy and persistent falls” before spreading east overnight.
Highs of 10 to 15 degrees are expected on Tuesday, before dropping to lows of 5 to 9 degrees that night.
Rain is set to linger in the east for a time on Wednesday while the rest of the country will see sunshine and scattered showers, though it will be a “blustery day”.
Highs of 8 to 12 degrees are expected before falling to lows of 3 to 7 degrees on Wednesday night.
Showers are set to continue along the west coast on Wednesday night though conditions will be largely dry elsewhere.
Following a very windy and wet Thursday, the forecaster said, Friday will see scattered showers and “blustery winds” amid highs of 8 to 11 degrees.
Beyond Friday, Met Éireann said conditions were likely to remain unsettled over the bank holiday weekend, with “more rain” and some blustery conditions expected.

title: Bawag ‘rising above the noise’ as it eyes completing PTSB deal, CEO says
description: PTSB will be the first public-company deal that the Austrian lender has completed
content:
The chief executive of Bawag said the Austrian banking group is “rising above the noise” as it awaits High Court approval of its takeover of PTSB later this month, even as the Irish lender has attracted 11th-hour bid interest from two parties that have criticised the €1.62 billion deal.
Speaking on a call with analysts after Bawag reported third quarter results on Monday, chief executive Anas Abuzaakouk said his group has “spent a significant amount of time communicating with regulators, the PTSB board and leadership team, and many other stakeholders, introducing ourselves and our business”.
This follows the deal agreement in April and subsequent PTSB shareholder approval, led by the Government, with a 57.5 per cent stake, at the end of July.
“Our goal has been to listen, learn and prepare for a smooth and seamless integration. We are confident in having put our best foot forward, being patient, staying disciplined, working constructively and transparently at every stage of the process, all while rising above the noise,” he said.
Bawag’s first deal involving a publicly quoted company has been the noisiest of 15 transactions the group has agreed since it began an acquisitions strategy in 2015.
[ Takeover panel rejects PTSB sale complaints from ex-banker Opens in new window ]
Some minority investors, led by Piotr Skoczylas of Scotchstone Capital, have argued the deal should be ratified separately by non-government shareholders. This is set to come up at an October 27th High Court sanctioning hearing for the deal, which is being carried out under a scheme of arrangement that requires at least 75 per cent shareholder backing and court oversight.
PTSB has said it has “very strong” legal advice no second vote is needed. Some 36 per cent of minority investors voted against the transaction at the extraordinary general meeting (egm) in July.
Scotchstone is a long-time dissenting PTSB shareholder that has pursued a series of cases in the Irish courts stemming from PTSB’s effective nationalisation in 2011. It signalled on October 9th that it was considering making an offer for PTSB.
The intervention came just seven days after a corporate finance firm cofounded by former Bank of Scotland (Ireland) chief executive Mark Duffy, called Axis Capital, said it was considering a bid for PTSB . Neither Scotchstone nor Axis has said whether it has secured any funding for a bid.
The Irish Takeover Panel said last week it has rejected concerns raised by Axis about the PTSB sale process.
Axis helped initiate talks in 2025 between New York private equity firm Centerbridge, the Department of Finance and PTSB over a potential deal for the Irish bank. The US group subsequently submitted a non-binding proposal in September last year for the State’s 57.5 per cent stake in the bank.
Centerbridge was the underbidder to Bawag in April as a formal sales process, initiated in October, concluded.
“PTSB would be our first public company acquisition, with different dynamics, but always staying consistent to our principles,” Abuzaakouk said on the analysts call. “We focus on delivering results through our actions and avoiding empty slogans and self-promotion, as our actions speak louder than our words.”
Bawag reported that its net profit rose 13 per cent on the year to €248 million in the third quarter and that it had started to set aside money during the period to cover dividends, having paused this in the first half of the year as it gathered funds to carry out the PTSB deal.
The Vienna-based group said in July it had accumulated more than €1 billion of excess capital, more than enough to self-fund the Irish acquisition.
The remainder of the €1.62 billion cost of the takeover will come from PTSB itself, including the Irish bank’s surplus capital and the ability of Bawag to book an immediate profit from the deal agreed in April.
The transaction values PTSB at an almost 20 per cent – or €400 million – discount to its reported end-2025 net assets, opening up the prospect of the difference being booked as a negative goodwill, or badwill, gain.

title: Being Irish and Jewish: I love my home, but I am so angry
description: The pride I once had in being Irish is fleeting
content:
Sir, – I have wonderful memories of growing up in Ireland. As Bagatelle taught us, there was nothing quite like a “Summer in Dublin.” Summers meant playing cricket for Carlisle, playing on the rocks in Dún Laoghaire and, when I behaved, a delicious 99. Rugby winters weren’t too shabby either, playing on the wing for Wesley. Dublin was home, and it made me proud. Though I no longer physically live at home, my heart never left.
But there is another part of my identity that I kept more hidden. I am Jewish. I never really felt uneasy about my background. I am Irish and I am Jewish. It wasn’t a contradiction. The lads would often joke, “If Ireland was ever at war with Israel, who would you fight for?”
The answer was easy; “Ireland.” I am Irish through and through.
Today, though, it’s no longer so simple. The pride I once had in being Irish is fleeting. All the visceral hate, anger and animosity shown towards Israel and the claims of genocide are disgraceful.
Moreover, they are completely hypocritical. Where is the outrage towards Nigeria? Sudan? Where actual genocide is occurring. Is this truly about defending those who are suffering, or is it because Israel is a Jewish state? The adage of “No Jews, No News” is horrifyingly true.
How low has the nation fallen when an Irish-Jewish girl is brutally kidnapped by terrorists, but the then Taoiseach Leo Varakar said she innocently got lost? Claiming that they are anti-Israel and not anti-Semitic is false.
Simply writing this letter breaks my heart. I love my home, I love my country ... or at least I want to. But I am so angry. The performative display put on by the men’s football team and the FAI was the disgraceful final straw.
It saddens me that so many Irish people have taken upon themselves to hate and ignorantly cheer on a people’s demise.
The Irish can no longer hide their anti-Semitic ways by hiding behind their pure hate towards Israel. The mask is off.
I want to be proud of where I came from again. Ireland is home and shaped who I am, but I proudly declare that I am, and always will be, a Jew from Ireland. – Yours, etc,

title: Dublin Gallery Weekend announces winners of first Francis Bacon art awards
description: Patrick Graham and Cathy Wilkes named as recipients of new annual Irish prizes worth €40,000
content:
Patrick Graham and Cathy Wilkes have won Dublin Gallery Weekend ’s inaugural Francis Bacon Awards for Irish visual art, worth €40,000. Graham receives the €25,000 lifetime-achievement prize. Wilkes receives the €15,000 mid-career prize.
Graham, one of the first artists in the country to work in the abstract expressionist style, is regarded as one of Ireland’s most influential contemporary painters.
Born in Co Westmeath in 1943, he was awarded a scholarship to the National College of Art and Design when he was 13; he had to wait three years until he was deemed old enough to take it up.
The painter, who is represented in Ireland by Hillsboro Fine Art, came to wider attention when the Hollywood horror actor Vincent Price bought some of work after visiting his exhibition at the now-closed Lincoln Gallery in Dublin. Price also introduced him to the Los Angeles arts scene, launching his international career.
One of the first artists involved in setting up Temple Bar Gallery and Studios , Graham was also one of the first artists to take up residence at the community-oriented Fire Station studios on Buckingham Street in Dublin.
Wilkes, who was born in Belfast in 1966, is based in Glasgow, where she went to art college. She represented Scotland at the Venice Biennale of 2005 and Britain at the biennale of 2019. She was nominated for the Turner Prize in 2008.
Working in painting, collage, installation and sculpture, her art tends to take ideas and memories of domestic scenes but make them troubling and strange.
Dublin Gallery Weekend began in 2023, after 10 of the city’s commercial galleries joined forces as the Contemporary Art Gallery Association to promote artists and their work. The winners of these inaugural Francis Bacon Awards were selected by a panel comprising Emma Goltz, Barbara Dawson, Brian Cass, Caoimhín Mac Giolla Léith and Mary McCarthy.
Praising Graham for paintings “confronting cultural trauma, religious repression and existential angst”, the judges noted that Wilkes’ work makes “overt allusions to the fraught years of her Northern Irish youth” and praised “her unique ability to transform everyday material into profound, lingering meditations on care, memory and loss”.
The Francis Bacon Awards are supported by Château La Coste, the French wine estate and sculpture park owned by the hotelier and property investor Paddy McKillen . Both winners will have solo exhibitions at the Provence chateau, where the collection features works by Tadao Ando, Louise Bourgeois, Alexander Calder, Sophie Calle, Tracey Emin, Frank Gehry, Sean Scully and Ai Weiwei.
Graham will join the gallerist Robert Diament for a Talk Art podcast recording at the National Gallery of Ireland on Saturday, November 7th. Wilkes has a solo show at the Model in Sligo until January 2027.
Dublin Gallery Weekend runs from Thursday, November 5th, until Monday, November 8th

title: Councillors urged to reverse ban on developing John Magnier/JP McManus Liffey Valley land
description: Council chief wants councillors to rezone ‘high amenity’ lands for 500 homes
content:
A ban on the construction of almost 500 homes on “high amenity” Liffey Valley lands owned by billionaire businessmen John Magnier and JP McManus could be lifted by South Dublin councillors on Monday .
Council chief executive Colm Ward is urging councillors to reverse their decision last June to refuse the rezoning of 15 hectares at St Edmundsbury on the southside of the river Liffey, close to Lucan and just west of the Hermitage Golf Club.
The councillors’ decision had followed the receipt of more than 1,600 submissions opposing the rezoning, with Lucan locals branding the proposal “unthinkable”, “baffling” and “an absolute disgrace”. A majority suggested the lands should instead form part of a Liffey Valley park, which had been proposed by the Office of Public Works 20 years ago.
The Office of the Planning Regulator , the National Transport Authority (NTA) and the land owners have all sought the reversal of the councillors’ vote last June so the land can be developed for housing. Councillors will meet on Monday to reconsider the proposal and Ward will call on them to change their position.
McManus and Magnier bought the 110 hectares of land, formerly part of the St Edmundsbury Hospital estate, from Seán Mulryan and Marese Ltd for €4.3 million at an auction ordered by the National Asset Management Agency (Nama).
Successive attempts to rezone the land for housing had been rejected by the council due to the site’s amenity value, and because sufficient sites had already been rezoned in the Lucan area for housing.
However, following an edict in mid-2025 from Minister for Housing James Browne that all local authorities must rezone significant additional land for housing, Ward earlier this year recommended that councillors rezone about 15 hectares at St Edmundsbury.
[ From a dump to a national park to housing: how plans for Liffey Valley Park have changed over the years Opens in new window ]
Following exceptionally strong public opposition to the use of the protected lands for housing, councillors voted against the rezoning.
The O’Flynn Group, development partners of McManus and Magnier, subsequently made a submission to the council arguing the decision should be reversed.
The rezoning process should not be “determined by the number of submissions received but by the planning merits of the issues raised and the planning authority’s assessment of those issues”, it said.
Developer Michael O’Flynn told The Irish Times it was “unconscionable” the development of homes on the land was being blocked “at a time of a national housing emergency”.
Deputy planning regulator Anne Marie O’Connor warned the council it risked “frustrating the implementation of national housing policy” and undermining the delivery of housing targets by failing to rezone enough lands for new homes.
The NTA in a submission said the St Edmundsbury lands should be prioritised for residential zoning due to their “strong accessibility” by existing public transport services.
Ward will this week ask councillors to accept the appeals from the developer and statutory bodies, and his recommendation, to rezone the lands. In his report, which will be presented to councillors on Monday, he said he recognised “that most submissions support the retention of the current [high amenity] zoning on the lands at St Edmundsbury”.
[ Fresh bid to rezone ‘sacred’ lands near Lucan for housing sees vigorous local opposition Opens in new window ]
However, he said, “the strategic justification for rezoning these lands is reinforced by their location” and their “strong accessibility to existing and planned public transport infrastructure and services and facilities”.
The Liffey Valley Park Alliance is appealing to councillors to resist the rezoning attempt and not to rescind their June decision. The campaign group is also calling on the Government and local authorities to implement the 2006 Liffey Valley Park Strategic Plan to develop a park along the river from Dublin city to Kildare.

title: Irish provinces set down a marker on opening European weekend
description: Meanwhile, Ken Early is recovering after viewing a collection of dire Premier League games over the weekend
content:
It was but a month ago that all four Irish provinces lost in the opening round of the URC, a whitewash that hadn’t happened in an entire 17 years. So, come ye and rejoice, all four Irish provinces won on the opening weekend of European competition for the first time in five seasons. “So much for being undercooked,” as Gerry Thornley says in his round-up of Munster, Connacht and Leinster’s Champions Cup victories, and Ulster’s bonus-point win away to Zebre in the Challenge Cup.
It was an emotional evening by the Lee, Denis Walsh at Páirc Uí Chaoimh to witness “a perfect tribute” to Anthony Foley on the 10th anniversary of his death. Munster honoured his memory with a 33-25 win over Racing , Gerry talking to Jack O’Donoghue after the game, the flanker the sole member of the current squad who was in Paris a decade ago when Foley died.
Leinster, meanwhile, got their Champions Cup efforts off to a bonus-point winning start away to Clermont Auvergne , John O’Sullivan reporting on the game and hearing from man of the match Sam Prendergast after.
Linley MacKenzie tells us about “ a dream result for Stuart Lancaster’s side at a sold out Dexcom Stadium”, Connacht’s Champions Cup journey beginning with a 45-36 win over Saracens.
And in his Tipping Point column, Denis looks at how the “dark arts” are slowly being legislated out of rugby with 10 more law changes on the agenda between now and next Autumn’s World Cup, the game’s laws in a perpetual state of review.
In Gaelic games, Malachy Clerkin saw Cuala dismantle Castleknock to win their third Dublin football title and talked to manager Derek Dunne after. Wolfe Tones did much the same to Donaghmore/Ashbourne in the Meath final, Gordon Manning in Ashbourne to see them sail to a 10-point victory . Paul Fitzpatrick rounds up the rest of the football finals , including Crossmaglen Rangers picking up just their 48th Armagh title.
And on the hurling front, Denis was back in Páirc Uí Chaoimh on Sunday for the county final when Glen Rovers sealed their 28th Cork championship with a three-point win over St Finbarr’s. Stephen Barry has news on the other hurling finals around the country , among them Kilcormac-Killoughey making it a four-in-a-row in Offaly.
In football, Ken Early is recovering after viewing a collection of dire Premier League games over the weekend, including the one between Leeds and Manchester United when “neither team could string five passes together” . The English game’s “intensity arms race” has, he concludes, “created an absolute wasteland for imagination, creativity and skill”.
And Paul O’Hehir has word on how the Irish abroad fared over the weekend, Jack Moylan very definitely the man of the moment after scoring his sixth league goal of the season for Cardiff City.
In cycling, Ian O’Riordan reports on Lara Gillespie striking gold in the points race at the UCI Track World Championships on Saturday, to add to the silver she won earlier in the week. A year ago she became the first Irish woman to win a UCI world track title in any event, so she’s making a habit of it.
In racing, Brian O’Connor looks at Aidan O’Brien’s hopes of securing another British trainers’ title , and in athletics, Ian brings you a list of essential dos and don’ts for next Sunday’s Dublin Marathon . We’d just say don’t do it, stay in bed, but Ian is a bit more encouraging than that.

At the same time, Spurs will be looking for their first win of the league season when they play Coventry on home turf (Sky Sports Premier League).

title: Huge rise in claims of unlawful detention linked to withdrawal of solicitors’ services
description: Almost 90 challenges mounted since July at costs ranging from €20,000 to over €40,000 per case
content:
The withdrawal of services by criminal defence solicitors since last July over a new legal aid payment model has sparked a huge increase in High Court challenges alleging unlawful detention.
Almost 90 such challenges have since been taken arising from the dispute, with the legal costs of an individual challenge estimated to range from €20,000 to more than €40,000.
Since the model for the District Courts was introduced on July 1 st , Courts Service data obtained by The Irish Times shows 87 of 116 challenges taken up to last Friday arose through accused persons being unable to obtain legal representation.
In the same period in 2025, a total of 30 challenges over alleged unlawful detention had been taken.
The highest number of challenges, brought under Article 40 of the Constitution, was 52, in July – of which 45 related to the new payment scheme.
Of 38 challenges in August, 33 related to the scheme. There were 13 in September, including seven under the scheme. This month, up to the 16 th , there were 13 challenges, including two under the scheme.
During the hearing of one application, the High Court was told a senior counsel was due a total fee of €16,250; a junior counsel’s fees were €10,565, and the solicitor’s fees were put between €16,000 and €19,000.
[ Judge again urges O’Callaghan and solicitors to resolve legal aid case between them Opens in new window ]
In that case, the judge was told it was almost impossible to provide a final bill of costs at that stage, as the matter was not fully completed. In a different case, a judge was told the fees were estimated at between almost €42,815 and €45,815.
At the end of July last, another High Court Judge, Mary Rose Gearty, ordered the immediate release of 11 people who had been remanded in custody.
The court found they were deprived of access to a solicitor and, without legal representation, their detention was illegal and could not stand.
One of the 11, a woman facing a robbery charge, had told the District Court judge she was worried she would lose her home and access to her daughter if she was not released from prison.
[ Legal aid dispute a matter of concern, says Chief Justice Opens in new window ]
Gearty’s ruling set a precedent that resulted in a number of people, some of whom legal sources suggested would never normally get bail, being released in the lower courts, as judges became aware of the precedent.
In a ruling on a different Article 40 challenge, Judge Garrett Simons stressed the absence of legal representation “does not, of itself, render a bail hearing fundamentally flawed”. He said an unrepresented accused may, depending upon the circumstances, be given “a meaningful opportunity to understand, test and answer the case for detention”.
Some Article 40 applications were converted by High Court judges into bail hearings, and bail was refused in a number of those.
The withdrawal of services by many defence solicitors is set to escalate from Monday with its expansion to virtually all cases, including of persons in custody.
In letters to court presidents on Friday, the solicitors said the escalation was due to the failure of Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan to agree to “meaningful” engagement with their representative body.
Many criminal defence solicitors, particularly in Dublin, have withdrawn services, leading to the adjournment of thousands of criminal cases across all court divisions, adding to existing court backlogs.
[ Confusion and delays at district court as criminal legal aid dispute drags on Opens in new window ]
The new payment scheme provides for a single flat fee of €520, irrespective of the number of charges or appearances. Solicitors say it means they will not be paid for the work they do, particularly in more complex cases involving children and vulnerable clients with addiction and mental health issues.
O’Callaghan has repeatedly said the scheme involves necessary reform of criminal legal aid, will achieve costs savings and is in the public interest.

title: China’s economy picks up pace at 4.5% growth
description: Third-quarter GDP rate puts world’s second-biggest economy on track for full-year target, analysts say
content:
China’s growth accelerated more than expected in the third quarter, boosting the odds of the economy reaching Beijing’s annual target and dimming the prospects for additional easing measures.
Gross domestic product grew 4.5 per cent from a year ago after a gain of 4.3 per cent in the second quarter, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Monday, compared with the median forecast of 4.4 per cent by economists surveyed by Bloomberg. That took expansion in the first nine months of the year to 4.6 per cent — within the government’s annual goal of 4.5 per cent-5 per cent.
“Bigger fiscal spending helped both fixed asset investment and retail sales,” said Xing Zhaopeng, senior China strategist at Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd. “The recovery remains unsolid because the fiscal outlook is not stable. The question will be how much fiscal expansion can do in the future. We still see a downside risk to 2027.”
The improvement in the economy should give policymakers some breathing room, allowing them to hold off on further easing as they remain constrained by thin bank margins and persistent fiscal strain on local governments.
Industrial production growth accelerated to 5.5 per cent on year in September, matching forecasts. Fixed-asset investment shrank 7.2 per cent in the first nine months of the year, unchanged from its drop in January-August.
Retail sales picked up far more than expected to 1.1 per cent, versus a 0.4 per cent rise in August. Excluding car purchases, retail sales grew 3.9 per cent from a year ago, the fastest pace since October 2025.
The yield on the government’s 10-year bonds climbed one basis point to 1.65 per cent after the data release. The yuan held on to its earlier gain, rising 0.1 per cent to 6.6829 per dollar in offshore trading.
China’s currency has advanced over 4 per cent against the dollar since the start of the year to outperform most of its Asian peers, thanks to rising exports and the central bank’s tolerance for a stronger exchange rate.
Even as the slowdown intensified in recent months, officials initially focused on implementing existing pro-growth policies, before dialing up their support three weeks ago with a package of fresh targeted measures.
Growth in the world’s second-largest economy has been marked by a divide between booming exports — stoked by a global investment supercycle in artificial intelligence — and sluggish household spending, with investment stuck in a long slump. The job market has also softened while a years-long property downturn drags on.
Property investment plunged 20.6 per cent in the first nine months, a deterioration from a drop of 19.9 per cent in January-August. The surveyed urban jobless rate unexpectedly improved to 5.2 per cent in September from 5.3 per cent in the prior month.
Frail domestic demand has left China increasingly dependent on exports for growth. And that’s put Beijing under rising pressure from trade partners to address its yawning surplus, which is on pace to hit a new high this year in excess of the $1.2 trillion recorded in 2025.
The European Union is preparing to create new powers that could allow it to shut off China’s access to its single market as part of a dramatic new push to rebalance bilateral trade.
Meanwhile, foreign leaders have called on Beijing to allow for more appreciation in the Chinese currency, which they say is undervalued and gives the nation’s exporters an unfair competitive advantage. The International Monetary Fund estimates the yuan’s undervaluation in the range of 17.3 per cent to 25.3 per cent in 2026, with a midpoint of 21.3 per cent.
“Overall, the latest data suggest growth momentum improved toward the end of the third quarter,” said Zhou Hao, chief economist at Guotai Junan. “While the property downturn and soft domestic demand remain challenging, stronger-than-expected GDP and retail sales figures, firmer manufacturing activity, and an improving labor market point to a more constructive outlook for this quarter.” - Bloomberg

title: Homelessness often a ‘domino effect of compounding circumstances’
description: New DePaul research highlights five common pathways into homelessness
content:
“I never thought I was going to be off the street,” said a man from Co Waterford who experienced drug addiction and homelessness for 20 years.
On Monday, Depaul , a cross-Border charity supporting people experiencing homelessness or at risk of homelessness, published new research that found it is rarely the result of one event.
Homelessness, the report said, is more often is a “domino effect of compounding circumstances that can leave people with nowhere else to turn”.
The research highlighted five common pathways into homelessness – losing a home, relationship breakdown and domestic abuse, family breakdown and bereavement, childhood adversity and care experience, and addiction, mental health and the cyclical journeys through homelessness.
In August, the official number of homeless people in the State was 17,885, including 5,830 children.
Dean, (37) said he became homeless due to addiction. From the age of 12, he started smoking hash and progressed to using “anything and everything”.
He said he came from “good parents” but after “experimenting” as a child a “divide” grew between him and his family and he ran away.
He was addicted to drugs for 20 years and in that time was homeless and spent time in psychiatric units, prison and in and out of hostels.
He said he was “lost” and “broken” adding that he suffered with his mental health due to his addiction.
“I didn’t see any way out of it ... it was very dark for quite a while.”
He said loneliness and addiction led to “all of them situations of homelessness, prison, things I never thought would have happened to me”.
He said things continued to get “worse and worse” as his mental health deteriorated. He attempted suicide multiple times.
He said drugs led him to “total self-hatred” and self-destruction.
“So many people tried to help me, whether it was in the hostels, in the psychiatric units and I just rebelled and rebelled because I just hated what way my life went.
He said he was “so shut off from the services” that he didn’t know anyone who had gotten clean from drugs.
He added that he didn’t think there was any hope or way back from where he was.
Now, he is the “complete opposite of that lost, lonely young man” and has been clean for four-and-a-half years.
At the start of his prison sentence, Dean said he felt like he had “lost everything” and was “really, really angry” with himself.
All he had was a “tracksuit on my back and a pouch of tobacco”, he said.
“I hated myself for it and I used that anger and strength to say to myself that in this prison sentence ‘I’m not going to use any more.’”
He did not use for the entire sentence and completed a six-month residential treatment.
“I tried to rebel in thinking that the services were against me, that was my belief. But it wasn’t that way, like, all these people were trying to help me.”
After engaging with Depaul, Dean has his “first ever forever home” in Dublin where he lives with his partner and two “beautiful” sons, adding that he is “very, very grateful” to the charity.
He hopes to help others in addiction services. “It’s something that I’m very passionate about.”
He said he does not have any mental health issues now and keeps himself “as fit and healthy as possible” by running marathons and “doing all these beautiful things that recovery has given me”.
He urged other people in a similar situation to “share the darkness”.
He advised those people to find someone to open up to and to link in with services. “There is the world of support in Ireland, you need to reach out.”
In the research, carried out by Coyne Research, many of the participants described the difficulties of trying to find a home through the wider housing system, with the private rental market a particular source of frustration.
They also spoke about finding out about important supports by chance, pointing to the need for clearer information and signposting.
Participants identified practical changes that could help such as bringing vacant properties into use, improving access to housing supports and providing greater consistency in the services people rely on.
David Carroll, chief executive of Depaul, said this research is “an opportunity” for the wider public to “understand these issues to a greater extent”.
“There’s such a range of kind of disparate kind of issues that do lead people into the situation.”
He said it is a “huge challenge to get people out of temporary accommodation”.
“They are completely disempowered, mostly from a financial perspective,” he said, adding that they can’t buy a home and “find it really difficult to access private rental accommodation because ... the housing assistant payment ... hasn’t kept pace with private rent, which has gone through the roof”.

title: Why Trump, Putin and Xi are all courting Central Asia
description: US, Russia and China compete for influence in region that is geographically important and has huge resources of oil, gas and rare earths
content:
Washington , Beijing and Moscow are competing for influence in Central Asia with a parade of visits in recent days. But the locals can see them coming.
When Marco Rubio arrived on Sunday in Samarkand, an ancient Silk Road city in the Central Asian republic of Uzbekistan, he was at the head of a delegation of more than 200 business representatives. The American secretary of state’s visit came a day after China’s premier, Li Qiang, was in the Uzbek capital of Tashkent promising more co-operation on everything from critical minerals to artificial intelligence.
More than a century after the British geographer and politician Halford Mackinder identified a vast area of Eurasia as “the Heartland” that was key to controlling the world, Central Asia is back at the heart of competition between the great powers. And for all the economic firepower Rubio is taking with him, every government in the region enjoys important relationships with Beijing and Moscow as well as with Washington.
He is attending a summit of the C5+1, which includes Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and the United States. Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Uzbekistan are also part of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, which held its 25 th anniversary summit in the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek a few weeks ago with Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Narendra Modi among those present.
The Bishkek Declaration that emerged from that summit condemned the US war against Iran and criticised unilateral economic sanctions such as those imposed by the US and the European Union. Central Asian states have been the targets of sanctions from Washington and Brussels in recent years because of their trade with Russia after Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Mackinder saw control of the vast area that stretches from the Kazakh steppes into southern Russia as carrying the possibility of dominating everything around it because it was immune to the threat of sea power. The theory went out of vogue during the Cold War, when the region was under Russian control, and during the heyday of globalisation that followed the fall of the Soviet Union.
But for today’s great powers, Central Asia is not only important because of its geographical situation but also on account of its huge resources of oil, gas, rare earths and other minerals that are essential to advanced manufacturing. China has become an increasingly important economic and infrastructure partner for the region, although economic, political and cultural ties to Russia also remain strong.
The Trump administration has brought a renewed enthusiasm for cultivating relationships with Central Asia and although it no longer bothers to pretend that Washington cares about human rights or promoting democracy, it is trying to bind the region more closely into the western embrace. Central Asian governments meanwhile have become increasingly adept at playing the great powers off against one another while promoting their own interests with a higher international profile.
Kazakhstan pleased Trump by joining the pro-Israel Abraham Accords, buying American aircraft and selling minerals the US needs, but Russia is building the former Soviet republic’s first nuclear power plant and the country offers an important transit corridor for Chinese exports. Kyrgyzstan was elected to the United Nations Security Council this year and will take up its seat in January, while Tajikistan is seeking a seat for the first time in 2028-2029 and Uzbekistan is hoping for a place in 2035-2036.

title: Bóithre na Sinsear
description: Mo thriall go Titley
content:
Bíonn tóir ag an-chuid daoine ar a sinsir, cérbh iad, cad as dóibh, cá raibh cónaí orthu, cad í an obair a bhí acu. Nuair a tháinig torthaí dhaonáireamh 1926 amach i mbliana, bhí daoine réidh ullamh léimt ar an idirlíon ar uair an mheán oíche nuair a cuireadh ar fáil iad. Táim cinnte go bhfuarthas go leor eolais a bhain preab as daoine, nó a chuir iontas orthu.
Daoine eile tá sloinnte uaisle acu agus is maith leo a mhaíomh gur de shliocht ríthe nó banríonacha iad, go bhfuil fuil uasal ag rith ina gcuisleanna. Muintir Uí Néill, b’fhéidir, nó Uí Chonchubhair go raibh flaitheas Éireann acu, nó Uí Bhriain a mhaífeadh gaol le Brian Bóraimhe.
Ní mar sin domsa, áfach, mar ní shílim go bhfuil deoir den fhuil ghorm sin im chorp. De mhuintir Anluain mo mháthair, agus ní raibh acu ach leathacra talún agus teachín i mball sceirdiúil i gcuan Chorcaí. A máthair sise, mo sheanmháthair, ní raibh puinn tailimh in aon chor acu siúd. Maolánaigh ba ea muintir mháthair m’athar agus bhí cónaí orthu sin i mbothán ar imeall na cathrach, í ag fuáil éadaí chun snáth a choinneáil faoin bhfiacail.
Ní fhágann sin ach aon duine amháin eile, an duine a d’fhág an sloinne neamhchoitianta agam, is é sin, athair m’athar, an Titley bunaidh. Níl oiread sin d’eolas againn ina thaobh agus luaití é le cogar mogar folaitheach sa teaghlach. Is amhlaidh gur mairnéalach ba ea é a sheol farraigí an domhain mar chócaire ar longa trádála éagsúla. Is dual go mbeadh mistéir éigin ag baint le mairnéalach, agus cá bhfios cad iad na rúin a bhí aige? Níl aon chuimhne cheart agam air, mar fuair sé bás nuair a bhíos im gharsún agus mé i bhfad níos óige ná mar atáim anois.
Nílimid cinnte cad as dó go díreach, ach áit éigin sa Bhreatain go cinnte. Tá sa seanchas nach foláir gurbh as ball éigin gar don bhaile ónar thóg sé a ainm, óir logainm is ea Titley. Ní raibh ann riamh ach ball ar léarscáil dom, spota ar an teorainn idir an Bhreatain Bheag agus Sasana, idir Herefordshire agus Powys. Is é sin go dtí i mbliana nuair a bhíomar ar saoire teaghlaigh i dtuaisceart na Breataine Bige agus gur shocraíomar ar chuairt a thabhairt ar an áit sin a thug a ainm dúinn.
Turas, n’fheadar, 160 éigin míle ann agus as arís a bhí ann dúinn, ach ba chuma. Ghabhas féin, iníon liom agus a fear céile, mac liom agus a mhac siúd, an bóthar ó dheas, ar mhótarbhealach i dtosach, agus ansin ar bhóithre a bhí ag éirí níos cúinge agus trí cheantair ag éirí níos tuaithe, fad na teorann idir Sasana agus an Bhreatain Bheag, ainmneacha Breatnaise agus Béarla ag malartú a chéile, leithéidí Ivington ansin Llandridrod, Blakemere ansin Pontolgach, Slobdon ansin Llangadfan.
Go dtí ar deireadh gur shroicheamar é. Cad leis go rabhas ag súil? Ní fios, dáiríre. Ní fhéadfaí sráidbhaile a thabhairt air, óir ní raibh aon tsráid ann. Stráice de bhóthar a ghabh thar sheanséipéal ar thaobh amháin, teach nó dhó laistiar d’fhálta ar an taobh eile, agus an t-aon fhoirgneamh a bhfuil aon cháil air, bialann nó teach tábhairne a thuill réalta Michelin. Seachas é sin, ghluaisfeá tríd gan é a thabhairt faoi deara.
Cad a mhothaigh mé mar sin? Ní féidir liom a rá gur oilithreacht de shaghas ar bith a bhí ann. Mar sin féin, sásamh éigin, gur leagas cos ar an áit as a dtáinig duine éigin de mo shinsir, duine a d’oibrigh sna goirt sin mórthimpeall ní foláir, is duine a d’fhág chun tabhairt faoin saol mór, mar a dhéanaimid ar fad.

title: German investor’s Dublin office doubts and John Fitzpatrick’s New York hotel boom
description: The best news, analysis, and comment from The Irish Times business desk
content:
German investor KGAL is the latest real estate investor in Dublin to signal viability issues with property projects in the city, reports Killian Woods.
The asset manager, which plans to demolish a Dublin city-centre office block to build a hotel, told the local council recently that neither extending the office nor redeveloping the site for housing would be financially viable.
US debt group AB CarVal Investors has generated a large gross surplus from the collection and resale of Irish property loans they acquired from KBC Bank and Bank of Ireland for a combined €1.02 billion since 2022.
New York is “booming”, according to Irish hotelier John Fitzpatrick, despite cost-of-living pressures and concerns about travelling to the US.
In an interview with Ciarán Hancock, the businessman who runs two midtown Manhattan hotels says his group recorded turnover of $28 million (€24.9 million) last year and he is spending more than $4.5 million refurbishing his Grand Central property.
In a world where war and political upheaval are wreaking havoc on the international conference circuit, Pilita Clark writes about the reason why London remains a leading destination for business gatherings.
In his latest column , economist John FitzGerald says Ireland has a difficult balancing act on its hands when it comes to brokering agreement on the EU’s 2028–2034 budget.
He writes there is division between member states, and the Irish Government has the tough task of potentially having to trim agricultural supports to secure an agreement.
For this week’s opinion piece , IDA Ireland chief executive Michael Lohan writes about the opportunity Ireland has to turn the AI boom into long-term economic gains.
He says Ireland can capture more investment from AI heavyweights like OpenAI and Anthropic if the State and companies invest in people at every stage of their careers.

title: The best and worst companies in Ireland for customer experience
description: While Irish companies overall seem to be doing better than counterparts abroad, there are recidivist offenders and a notable debutant on the naughty list
content:
T he queries and complaints that come to Pricewatch from those who have reached the limit of their patience have a wearily familiar pattern.
Mary pays for something somewhere and is delighted. She’s full of optimism about the positive impact whatever it is she has spent money on – a phone, laptop, a fridge, a holiday or insurance – will have on her life.
The retailer, the product or the service lets Mary down. Mary is disappointed and contacts the retailer or service provider hoping to have things put right. Mary is ignored or her pleas for help are rejected. So Mary tries again. And again.
Mary might try to get redress for a long, long time before she eventually contacts Pricewatch.
Pricewatch then contacts the retailer or service provider and within hours the problem has magically been resolved and a statement of regret has been issued.
That is not to blow our own trumpet but to express dismay at how slow too many companies are when it comes to righting the wrongs that have been inflicted on their customers, at least until we get involved and promise to expose their shortcomings.
And the frustrating thing is no matter how often we hear from the Marys of the world and no matter how often some operators appear on this page, we know the pattern will be repeated and the same companies will incur the wrath of our readers over and over again.
It is in such a context that we flicked through the customer experience report from the CX Academy published last week.
We couldn’t help but smile at the sight of some very familiar names appearing close to the bottom of the league with the likes of Re-turn , Ryanair and Ticketmaster all faring badly.
[ Credit unions win again as Re-turn, Ryanair and RTÉ fare poorly for customer service Opens in new window ]
But before we get to the bad guys we might have a look at the companies that appear to be serving their customers well.
The Irish credit union movement stands alone. It has been ranked as best for customer service for the 11th consecutive year. But why is that?
“The real strength of the Credit Union model is that members remain at the centre of everything we do,” says the chief executive of the Irish League of Credit Unions, David Malone. “Whether it’s introducing new services or supporting people through important life moments, the focus is always on helping members and serving communities.”
And, he says, as “people’s needs and expectations continue to change, credit unions have embraced new technology and new services without losing the personal touch and community focus that members value so highly”.
After that most benign of enterprises come the pharmacies, with Life Pharmacy finishing in second place and McCabes and Holland & Barrett taking seventh and joint ninth respectively.
Specsavers is in third while Shannon Airport, which was in the top 10 for the first time in the last report, was steady in fourth place. PhoneWatch moves from 11th to fifth while Zurich Insurance has climbed 21 places to sixth. Ikea is up an even more impressive 27 places to eighth while the Irish Passport Service, the highest-ranked public sector organisation, has climbed 25 places to finish joint ninth.
That will come as no surprise to anyone who has been able to apply for a passport online using a picture taken on their phone and have a turnaround time of less than 48 hours.
The Survey was conducted by Amárach Research over a period from June 8th to the end of July, which asked a representative cross-section of Irish consumers to give feedback on their experiences with 170-plus organisations across 11 sectors.
More than 32,500 experiences were evaluated for, among other things, value, preferred channels, how important employees are to the customer experience, how experiences have changed in the Past year, whether customers would pay more for a better experience and how good organisations are at making improvements to meet customer needs.
The annual assessment suggests that Ireland appears to be doing well compared with our peers in other countries. Similar studies in other jurisdictions show customer experience are falling globally but climbing in Ireland, where they have reached their highest level in almost a decade.
The chairman of the CX Academy and author of the report, Michael Killeen, says the main reason global CX scores are dropping while Ireland’s are advancing is down to Irish consumers’ “absolute preference for human touch experience over tech solutions”.
He puts Ireland’s customer experience recovery down to three key factors.
He says it “has been driven by a broad-based recovery, not by a handful of brands. Secondly, brands have improved their performance in the two weakest areas: meeting customer expectations and resolving issues when they arise. Thirdly, we are seeing stability at the top and volatility below. The leading brands improve or barely move year to year, while the middle and lower table see the churn. That consistency is a strength of the best-performing sectors. If you take supermarkets as an example, most brands scored solidly, which helps it outscore other sectors which have both stars and laggards.”
One area that has seen a lot of churn over the past 12 months is fast food. According to the research two of the best performers from the last survey, KFC and Subway have recorded the biggest falls this year, with the former falling 77 places to 92nd and the latter dropping 69 places to 98th.
Their performances, the CX Academy says, are emblematic of a weak performance by the restaurant sector, with a broad retreat particularly noticeable across the fast-food category. Burger King has fallen 45 places to joint 98th, alongside Subway and McDonald’s, down 41 places to joint 113th alongside Eddie Rocket’s.
“Across the main brands customers were saying the same thing; the food quality has dropped, or service has declined or we got the wrong orders or cold food,” Killeen says. “Many customers complained about the prices and ‘shrinkflation’. The sector fell three places from second to fifth this year and was the only one to experience a decline in its average score.”
But while fast food is doing badly, it is by no means the worst.
The bottom 10 is made up of the Department of Social Protection , Ryanair, RTÉ, Re-turn – making its very first appearance on the list – Instagram, TikTok, Uisce Éireann, Ticketmaster, Dublin Bus and – in last place – Facebook, even before the company has to contend with the Social Reckoning on its way to cinemas in the days ahead.
Killeen says that when it comes to the bottom of the barrel, the common thread on the data is that “these are largely services people use out of necessity or habit rather than choice: social platforms, public transport, utilities and nondiscretionary public services, which tend to score low across all areas rather than on any single one.”
Ticketmaster drops 17 places to 160th, third from bottom. It is the company’s lowest placing and the third survey in succession that it has made the bottom 10.
The highest ranking it has ever recorded was 106th, in 2018.
Customer anger and frustration was very much in evidence in the comments directed at the company, according to Killeen, who says tiered pricing and so-called in-demand pricing for high-profile concerts during a cost-of-living crisis have alienated consumers.
“Ticketmaster operates a de facto monopoly on tickets for major events here and provides an excellent example of what happens when there isn’t sufficient competition in the market,” he says.
We are going to interrupt his words for a moment to say that Ticketmaster has on many occasions completely rejected the notion that it operates anything close to a monopoly and it has long insisted that the market is open to anyone who wants to take it on.
He says the platform “consistently put the interest of their shareholders ahead of customers, and indeed the company has the second-lowest score for putting customers first.”
Three years ago, in the wake of revelations surrounding secret payments to Ryan Tubridy, RTÉ found itself in last place in the survey. Over the past couple of years it has moved off the bottom but still finds itself in lowly 155th position, one below Ryanair and above new entrant Re-turn.
Despite this report, co-author Gerard O’Neill, chairman of Amárach Research, says RTÉ has actually made a notable recovery.
“RTÉ’s decline was the sharpest and most compressed in our study, and the only one where trust is unambiguously the leading casualty. But the pattern of recovery is the most interesting feature, and it has also happened over a relatively short time.”
“RTÉ’s scores indicate that audiences feel understood again, though full forgiveness on integrity is taking longer. For RTÉ that is precisely the measure to keep watching.”
He says that “while it’s positive that RTÉ has got its score back to where it was previously – it is one of five customer experience redemption stories in the report – other brands have moved on.”
O’Neill says this is “a key aspect of customer experience. Customer expectations continue to grow apace, and if you are treading water, you are going backwards. That’s why it is so difficult for low-scoring brands to break free from the bottom end of the table. And it’s true to say we are seeing a degree of CX polarisation between the best and worst providers.”
The report provides welcome news generally for the financial sector, which is the second-best-performing sector in 2026, and particularly for AIB, one of the biggest risers, moving up 58 places to 68th.
The bank is also among the redemption stories included in the report because five years ago the picture was not so rosy.
In 2022 the bank announced it was removing cash and cheque services from 70 out of 170 branches. Although it reversed its decision 72 hours later following a customer backlash, the bank’s reputation and score took a big hit.
Killeen says AIB learned some valuable lessons, which other companies and organisations could also learn from.
“Firstly you have to fix the problem and tell people you’re doing it.
