AIB invested substantially in branch cash services after trying to remove them, and other changes such as upgrades for visually impaired customers signalled a new approach to customer experience,” he says. “Secondly when you’re in a CX hole, stop digging. AIB reversed its decision within 72 hours, and its trust score barely moved. What customers punish is not the mistake but the refusal to own it and change.
“Finally it’s really important to lead with convenience and follow with personalisation. If you are trying to build relationships while failing to address major CX issues, you are working against the grain. Customers appear to want to be served competently before they want to be better known. AIB did that and customers can bank easily again. But the data shows that they do not feel individually known, so there is still plenty of room for the bank to improve in that area.”
It is a good report for the banks in general, with Bank of Ireland moving up 29 places to 72nd and Revolut moving up 10 places to 58th. PTSB, whose shareholders have approved its sale to Austria’s Bawag Group, is the backmarker in the sector at 134th, down 38 places, while EBS, which is owned by AIB is 98th, down 44 places.
Killeen says competition in the sector has been good for customers. “People wondered how Revolut and its ‘digital only’ proposition would perform here. The answer appears to be quite well, and it is now outscoring both AIB and Bank of Ireland on CX. In fact you might argue that it has forced the banks to up their game. However they all remain well behind the Credit Unions and An Post Money which lead the sector.”
Permission to use AI ‘has to be earned through confidence and trust’
Another factor addressed in the report for the first time is the demand for AI and usage across all brands.
A recent Red C global survey found Ireland continued to lag global peers across most AI measures, and while progress is being made, the pace of change is not matching that seen in leading markets, particularly in terms of embedding AI into core economic and workplace activity, Kileen suggests.
He says the report finds demand for AI is loudest where service is hardest. It also confirms that AI solutions must be determined by the customers’ need, not by the technology available.
“Appetite for AI is concentrated in high-friction categories like telecoms, insurance and logistics, and within those, the struggling brands hear it most,” he says. “So their appetite is a symptom of the pain, not a vote of confidence in the technology. It’s a sign of frustration as much as enthusiasm. That is not a good starting point.
“If digital or AI applications cost consumers convenience, ease and time – the very thing self-service is supposed to improve – that’s a problem. The business might have moved some of its service online or into an AI ‘solution’, to save itself effort, but that effort does not vanish. It shifts on to the customer, who now has to work though the menu, the chatbot and the online forms. Easy for the business is not always easy for the customer.”
He argues that permission to use AI “has to be earned through confidence and trust. Our findings show customers are not rewarding brands for having AI; they are rewarding brands they trust to deploy it appropriately. While AI has undoubtedly huge potential, the quality of staff remains the strongest single influence on any brand CX score – stronger then every digital and AI measure put together.”

title: Mark O'Connell: Sally Rooney could have made things a great deal easier for herself. She chose not to
description: There are very few writers as famous as Rooney, and almost none as willing to leverage that fame as bravely for a moral cause
content:
Sally Rooney could have made things a great deal easier for herself. Last year, when the UK government proscribed the direct-action network Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation – making it a criminal offence to provide financial aid to the group or to express an opinion or belief in support of it – she could have said nothing. It was clear, by then, where she stood on the question of Israel ’s campaign of slaughter in Gaza : that it amounted to a genocide; that it was happening with the full support of European and American governments; and that it needed to be named and opposed and brought to an end.
But she did not say nothing. She wrote an article for this newspaper about the proscription and its ramifications. In it, she criticised the Irish Government for remaining silent about the Irish citizens arrested in the UK for expressing their support of Palestine Action; Irish citizens who, because of the very legislation they were peacefully protesting against, risked being imprisoned for up to 14 years. She also defended Palestine Action itself, and its direct-action tactics against arms manufacturers whose weapons were being sold to Israel, and which were used in the destruction of Gaza in the wake of Hamas’s October 7th attacks. In the incident that immediately led to the proscription, activists broke into an RAF airbase in Oxfordshire and sprayed red paint on two aeroplanes in protest against the UK government’s military support of Israel.
In this context she felt obliged to state her support for the group. “If this makes me a ‘supporter of terror’ under UK law, so be it,” she wrote. Her books were still available in British bookshops, she pointed out, and she was regularly in receipt of residual payments from the BBC’s television adaptations of two of her books. “I want to be clear,” she wrote, “that I intend to use these proceeds of my work, as well as my public platform generally, to go on supporting Palestine Action and direct action against genocide in whatever way I can. If the British state considers this ‘terrorism’, then perhaps it should investigate the shady organisations that continue to promote my work and fund my activities, such as WH Smith and the BBC.”
She made this claim in the full knowledge it was likely to lead to serious legal consequences. And this was not recklessness; it was a calculated decision. Her aim was to use her fame and the prominence of her books to illustrate the absurdity of the legislation. The consequences, as such, came as no surprise. Her UK publisher Faber was forced to stop paying her royalties, because of the legal risk that it would be held liable for indirectly funding terrorism. (The same situation arose in the UK, with residual fees from the television adaptations of her books Normal People and Conversations with Friends . ) And it was this situation that led, earlier this week, to the announcement that, because of its inability to pass on earnings, her UK publisher Faber will no longer be distributing her books in the United Kingdom.
I should say here that it has not come as a surprise to me either. Rooney is a very close friend. I’ve known her since long before any of this arose, since long before she was a famous novelist, or a novelist at all. My view of this whole business can’t but be influenced by my friendship with her. But my admiration for the way she conducts herself as a public figure – for her judicious and moral expenditure of the otherwise useless currency of celebrity – would, I feel sure, be no less great if I’d never met her.
The decision to stop supplying her books for sale in the UK was one she came to in close consultation with Faber. They would not have done this without her consent. They were not prevented from selling her books, after all, only from passing on royalties for those sales. But as Faber itself put it in a statement released on Wednesday, “to sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher”. So this is in that narrow sense a matter of principle, on which both author and publisher are in agreement.
It is a matter of principle in a broader sense, too: her aim is to force this legal situation to the limits of its own absurdity, at whatever the cost might be to herself. The ruling on Palestine Action was rooted in the UK’s Terrorism Act of 2000. That act provides a very broad definition of terrorism, stating: “a reference to action taken for the purposes of terrorism includes a reference to action taken for the benefit of a proscribed organisation.” And since Palestine Action is a proscribed organisation, any action taken for its benefit could be interpreted as an action taken for the purposes of terrorism. (Earlier this year, the UK’s high court struck down the proscription, ruling it unlawful, but the Keir Starmer government appealed, and the court of appeal overturned the ruling. The case is due to go to the supreme court next month.) Until the Palestine Action proscription, UK governments tended to use the power to proscribe organisations in a less sweeping way, but the potential for this swerve into authoritarianism was always present within it.
[ Naza review: An essential record of the nightmare Israel has engineered in Gaza Opens in new window ]
Last month, Margaret Owen OBE, a 94-year-old Jewish human rights lawyer – and a friend of foreign secretary Ed Miliband’s late mother – was arrested in Liverpool after she wore a placard reading “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action”. Owen knew what she was doing, and why she was doing it. She wanted to expose the absurdity of this cruel and stupid law, and she succeeded. Rooney, in her own way, is doing a similar thing. The withdrawal from sale of her novels is a direct result of this profoundly illiberal legislation, and its absurd application in the case of Palestine Action. This legislation does grave damage to the UK’s image as a nation that values individual liberty and free expression. This is not the conduct of a democratic culture in robust health.
[ Raphaël Glucksmann’s refusal to use the word ‘genocide’ divides France’s left Opens in new window ]
There are very few writers as famous as Rooney, and almost none as willing to leverage that fame as bravely for a moral cause. There are people who resent and despise her for it, of course, just as there have always been those who have resented and despised artists and other public figures – especially female ones – for their strong moral and political commitments. But she understands it is a price worth paying for turning her fame to some moral purpose. And that purpose is, in its more direct and political way, in keeping with the role of an artist in society: to reveal the world as it is to those who are willing to see it.
[ Gaza student with UCD scholarship hopes for reprieve ‘before chance is gone’ Opens in new window ]

title: Sinéad O'Sullivan: Did the internet really get less toxic after Russian data centres went down?
description: A viral theory that online discourse went quiet after Ukrainian drone attacks tells us something about our confidence in data security
content:
O ver the space of four days recently, Ukrainian drones successfully targeted three large data centres in Russia . The Yandex data centre in Sasovo, more than 1,000km from Kyiv, was struck and shut down. Second and third strikes hit data centres in Kaluga, partially disabling operations, and Vladimir, taking the facility fully offline.
Yandex is Russia’s version of Google, providing search, cloud and maps, as well as the plumbing for retail banking. Russian Railways, the state-owned railway company, and MegaFon, a large telecommunications and mobile operator, went dark following the strikes. Yandex has three supercomputers that it uses to train its AI models, and two of those were inside the first building to be hit – and are assumed to be destroyed. Ripple effects from the operation were felt in web traffic anomalies all over the world. Cloudflare, which monitors internet traffic, saw automated traffic from Yandex’s network fall by 35 per cent when Sasovo was hit, going down to 99 per cent after Vladimir was taken out.
Why should we care about a data centre nearly 4,000km from Dublin? What might a sudden drop in Russian web traffic mean for Ireland?
A lot of people think it matters quite a bit, as it turns out. An intriguing theory suggesting that vast armies of Russian bots had suddenly gone silent immediately went viral on the internet. The sudden change in web activity across Europe and the United States sent the internet down into one of its favourite rabbit holes: wondering how much of our furious online discourses we thought we’ve been having with each other has actually been with Russian bots. Here in Ireland, it manifested as a conspiracy theory that one controversial Twitter account, Éire89376, was actually a man called Dmitry using Yandex translate this whole time. A post shared on Reddit , and later removed, made statistical claims showing a huge drop in activity on European political forums, including that the Irish politics subreddit, r/irishpolitics, was 80 per cent quieter than usual.
And while this seems like not much more than a somewhat entertaining diversion, the fact that so many people found the theory entirely plausible is worth paying attention to.
In fact, there’s no statistical proof that what Cloudflare saw was a drop specifically in Russian bot traffic, but that is almost beside the point – in politics, perception is reality. And whatever the reality, the perception in Europe was clear: Zelenskiy said social media had become noticeably less hostile; while in Germany, claims of a sharp fall in online activity around the far-right AfD party spread widely.
This means two things for Ireland. The first is that, despite having no natural enemies, Ireland does have security vulnerabilities – and Russia is a security threat. We have spent a lot of time worrying about Russian submarines and ships in Irish waters, and what they might be doing to our undersea cables and critical infrastructure. Yet somehow, we overlooked the possibility of a just as grave threat to our information sphere. Comparatively little attention has been given to the possibility that we are reading, sharing and arguing with the digital equivalent of those same hostile actors every day. The submarines may be somewhere out in the Atlantic’s vast drawl. But the bots, if that’s what they are, are already with us.
[ These Irish State agencies use password software with deep links to a Russian tech firm Opens in new window ]
In 2018 I was part of a monitoring programme out of George Mason University in Virginia on Russian influence operations on social media in the US midterm elections and the Missouri Senate race. We briefed the US state department and eight federal agencies on what we found – that the SVR, Russia’s foreign intelligence service, was identifying the issues that divided a state’s voters and flooding social media on exactly that issue every time a race narrowed to within a few points. This was later given as evidence to the Mueller investigation, the US department of justice inquiry into Russian interference in the 2016 election, and to the House intelligence committee.
What I learned then is that what might seem like a standard grumpy comments section to you or me can quickly become Russia’s theatre of military operations.
Ireland does not have a secure information environment. We have an independent media struggling for resources and limited independent investigative journalism.
Meanwhile, look at the people surrounding our political leaders. Of the 10 advisers working for Simon Harris , at least three had direct backgrounds in journalism, while several others are from government communications, public relations and digital media. Many of our politicians have prioritised getting better at managing messages than supporting the independent institutions needed to scrutinise them.
[ Ireland retains out-of-date air navigation systems in response to Russian jamming Opens in new window ]
The result is that Ireland sometimes looks like a country governed by Liveline phone-ins, Twitter pile-ons and Reddit threads – and the political priority is to respond to whatever, or whoever, has captured public attention today. Given that public reaction has become a substitute for any sort of analysis, think about how easy it is to influence policies with an artificially amplified controversy and a co-ordinated influence operation.
Ireland is just as susceptible as any other European country to manipulation by outside forces.
And if we accept that Ireland’s superpower is diplomacy – which is often given as a reason for not needing military capacity – then we must accept the consequence: those relationships are exactly the same channels a hostile state might exploit. You do not need to attack a neutral country’s non-existent tanks if you can target its conversations and its trust in its own institutions.
[ Ireland’s whack-a-mole approach to defence is profoundly concerning Opens in new window ]
With Mark Zuckerberg moving to Ireland , perhaps now is a good time to remember that we need to treat information security as national security. Ireland needs to invest further in independent investigative journalism and to build the expertise to monitor and expose co-ordinated influence operations – to highlight manufactured outrage before it gets turned into our public policy.

title: Love is complicated, but neurodivergent people often bond around shared experiences
description: This is the third of a four-part series on neurodiversity and the family by John Sharry, clinical director of the Parents Plus Charity
content:
Seek first to understand, then to be understood – Stephen Covey
In the last article we described how neurodivergence is hereditary and neurodivergent (ND) children are much more likely to have ND parents. In this article, we describe how ND people are more likely than non-ND people to partner with and marry an ND person.
While the process of attraction and falling in love is complex, it seems to consist of two main dynamics.
First there is the attraction of similarity – people seek out partners who they feel comfortable with, who have similar interests and shared experiences. ND couples often bond around the shared experience of being different – many have had similar experiences of feeling misunderstood and some have experienced trauma on account of this. This shared vulnerability can intensify a bond.
The second dynamic is about ‘polarity’ or the attraction of opposites. People are attracted to a partner who possesses qualities or strengths that they would like in their life. The falling in love process is often about finding your ‘other half’ or a achieving feeling of ‘completion’ or ‘wholeness’ with the other person in your life.
For ND couples this is often about being attracted to someone who is ‘neurodivergently’ different from you. An autistic person might be attracted to an ADHD person who they perceive as fun, socially gregarious and spontaneous – qualities that they would like more in their life. An ADHD person might be attracted to an autistic person who they see as thoughtful, balanced, and solid – qualities that they also seek in their life.
As long-term relationships progress, most couples experience a ‘falling out of love’ stage. The stresses and strains of everyday life can burst the ‘in-love bubble’ and you encounter the other vulnerable person with all their flaws and weaknesses. Some of the initial attractions that drew them together can fade and even become sources of annoyance, especially when there are clashing needs. The ‘spontaneity’ quality you so initially loved can become annoying and feel ‘disruptive’. Or the ‘organisation’ that you so admired in the early days can suddenly feel like ‘over-controlling’, etc.
This falling out of love is primarily driven by stress and relationship neglect and nothing drives this more than the arrival of children with the extra demands and decrease in personal autonomy that comes with it. Roles have to be renegotiated and new parents have to find new ways of supporting one another as a couple and meeting their own individual needs as well – this is when the work of creating a real loving relationship begins.
When couples come to therapy they often bring a list of complaints about their partners’ attitude or behaviour. They might be frustrated as to why their partner is ‘lazy’ or ‘inconsiderate’, or they may be perplexed as to why their partner needs to ‘control everything’ or why they ‘freak out’ when plans change. They interpret their partner’s behaviour as unreasonable and sometimes even see it as ‘deliberately chosen’ to hurt or annoy them – ‘He is so selfish, he never notices when I am upset and does nothing about it.’
When I meet these couples I invite them to try to compassionately understand the needs that underpin these complaints. Often these flow from their partner having a different neurotype to them. You partner may have alexithymia and not process feelings in the same way as you and so needs you to say directly what you need – ‘I am upset, can I have that hug now?’ Or your partner might become distressed at the sight of mess or untidiness (that you simply don’t notice) – it might agitate their senses and provoke a negative physical reaction. They can feel relaxed and calm only when their personal space is tidy.
In resolving these conflicts, it is does not help to blame or harangue your partner and expect them to change their basic neurotype – this is simply not possible and will only frustrate you further and damage your relationship. The key is to compassionately understand each other’s different needs and then to seek mutual accommodations that work for you both. One couple I worked with divided out household tasks that played to each of their strengths. She did not like ‘wet’ and ‘messy’ tasks – so her husband cleaned bathrooms, washed dirty pans and after-sport laundry to accommodate her sensory preferences.
She did more of the jobs that her husband didn’t have the attention to detail for – such as tidying, organising and clearing accumulated mess. Each prioritised the parts of housework that were relatively satisfying for them. He liked the proprioceptive input from vacuum cleaning and washing up and she liked listening to podcasts and some quiet time while she sorted laundry or cleared cupboards. Understanding each other’s needs and preferences with curiosity and compassion is what made the difference in their relationship.
Being able to identify your own needs and then to communicate them to your partner are the building blocks to a harmonious long-term relationship. This is especially the case for ND couples when their needs may be less apparent to their partner. For example, one autistic woman I worked with needed to ‘shut down’ for a period of quiet when she arrived home to recover from a stressful day of work.
However, her partner (who was possibly ADHD) liked to chat and connect when he came home – he needed to ‘vent’ and talk through the day’s events to regulate and reduce his own stress. As a result he could find her partner’s shutdown as ‘dismissive’ and ‘cold’ and she experienced his pressure to talk as a stressful demand – this frequently led to rows between them.
In the therapy we came up with a plan as to how she could communicate her needs to her partner such as:
This new direct communication method helped her partner understand what she needed and also get what he needed as well. It also avoided resentment and the misinterpretations that lead to arguments and harm to the relationship.
Viewing relationships through the neurodiversity lens can be helpful for a wide range of couples. Everyone has needs and sensitive vulnerable sides to their personality that are often not validated. Our partner will always be different from us in significant ways and have unique needs that we don’t initially understand. Learning to understand and appreciate our partners needs while articulating our own is the hard work of relationships. Such mutual understanding allows you to connect at a deeper level and creates an enduring bond.
Nurturing your relationship feels effortless in the early ‘in love’ stages.
In mature relationships it takes prioritising and daily effort. Marriage therapists John and Julie Gottman liken a healthy relationship to a bank account – you have to make frequent positive emotional deposits to ensure the relationship has enough credit to sustain the stresses and withdrawals of daily life. Positive emotional deposits include setting time aside for shared passions, trying out fun and novel things together, having daily chatting times, making sure to respond when your partner seek your attention, etc.
For ND couples it is important to consider what represents a relationship deposit for your partner recognising that it could be different from what you initially expect. The Gottmans talk about trying to discover your partner’s ‘love language’, recognising that it could be different from your own. The biggest turn on for one person could be surprising them with an exciting novel date; for another it could be simply cleaning the house before they come home.
Take time to discover what works best for your partner and yourself and find a way to meet in the middle.

title: ‘My son is in sixth year and has no idea what he wants to study’
description: If your son enjoys people, travel, business and exciting international environments, here’s a number of degree options
content:
My son is in sixth year and has no idea what he wants to study. We live in the midwest and he enjoys meeting people, loves the idea of travel and working internationally, and has a strong interest in business.
He is not sure he wants a traditional business degree and is looking for something that could lead to a wide range of career opportunities.
Are there any alternative options he should consider?
Many students find themselves in exactly this position as they progress towards the end of their school life. They know what they enjoy but are unsure how to turn those interests into a career.
If your son enjoys people, travel, business, and the idea of working in exciting international environments, there are a number of degree options he might consider.
TUS offers a number of business studies with events and hospitality management, with an international placement, at their Athlone campus. ATU offers a number of similar hospitality and events management programmes from their Letterkenny and Sligo campuses.
A new degree your son might also consider is the Bachelor of Business Studies in Global Luxury & Experience Management, offered by Shannon College of Hotel Management, University of Galway .
[ Japan working holiday: ‘Lots go to Australia - this is a different experience’ Opens in new window ]
This innovative programme has been developed in response to the growing global demand for graduates who understand not just business, but also how to create exceptional customer experiences and manage premium brands. While the title includes the word “luxury”, the degree opens doors to a much broader range of industries than many students might initially realise.
Students develop core business skills in areas such as marketing, management, finance, digital business, innovation and entrepreneurship. Alongside this, they learn how leading global organisations design and deliver memorable experiences that build customer loyalty and brand value.
One of the key attractions of the programme is its international focus. Students have opportunities to gain global experience through industry placements or international study opportunities, helping them build professional networks and practical skills before they graduate.
The breadth of career opportunities is particularly appealing for students who are unsure of exactly where they want to specialise. Graduates may pursue careers in Luxury brands and fashion, Premium retail management, Hospitality and tourism, Events and experiential marketing, Real estate and property services, Customer experience management, Business development and sales, Brand and marketing management, and Entrepreneurship and start-ups.
In today’s economy, organisations across many sectors are competing on customer experience as much as on product or price. Employers increasingly value graduates who can combine business knowledge with strong interpersonal skills, creativity, commercial awareness and an understanding of global consumers.
The programme is delivered at Shannon College of Hotel Management, which has built an international reputation for producing highly employable graduates with strong industry connections. Its emphasis on professional development means students gain experience that employers genuinely value.
[ What companies are offering competitive, interesting and challenging graduate programmes? Opens in new window ]
For students who enjoy working with people, are curious about the world and want a business degree that offers variety and flexibility, this programme provides an exciting alternative to more traditional business courses. Importantly, it does not lock students into a single career path. Instead, it equips graduates with transferable business and leadership skills that can be applied across multiple sectors and countries.
For a student living in the midwest who likes business but is also attracted to travel, international opportunities and people-focused careers, the programmes at TUS in Athlone and at ATU in Sligo and Letterkenny, alongside the new Bachelor of Business Studies in Global Luxury & Experience Management in Shannon, could be exactly the types of modern degrees that helps turn broad interests into a rewarding global career.

title: When are open days taking place in Irish universities?
description: The key dates and what to expect at Ireland’s university open days
content:
UCC’s open day was held on Saturday, October 10th, but it will hold a spring undergraduate open evening in 2027 (probably in March).
Registration details: If you would like to receive communications from UCC on planned events, you can submit your details at ucc.ie/en/study/undergrad/events/opendays
What to expect: A variety of talks, information stands and opportunities to speak to academic staff and students about studying at UCC.
Student life: There are more than 100 societies at UCC, including accounting and finance, the choral society and the chemical society. Sports include GAA, tennis and rowing.
Accommodation: UCC has full accommodation for the academic year across six complexes, ranging in location, size and price, but all close to the main campus. The applications are put through a lottery system, which opens for one month every year.
UCD’s open day will take place on Saturday, November 14th.
Registration details: You can register at ucd.ie/myucd/visiting-ucd/events/ucd-open-day
What to expect: Attend talks and information sessions across various subject areas; take a tour of the campus; meet current UCD students and academic staff.
Student life : Sports clubs include sailing, football and rugby. Societies include the engineering society, drama society and music society.
Accommodation : There are several on-campus accommodation options with on-site laundry facilities, outdoor bicycle storage and a gym.
Trinity College’s open day is on Saturday, November 21st.
Registration details: Register your interest at tcd.ie/openday
What to expect: Attend course talks, take a campus tour and meet current professors and students.
Student life: Trinity College has more than 120 societies, such as The Women’s Network, Trinity Orchestra and Hispanic society. Clubs include netball, ultimate frisbee and American football.
Accommodation: First-year undergraduate students can apply for Trinity Hall in Dublin 6, while Trinity also has partnerships with the private student accommodation complexes Kavanagh Court and Here! Cork Street.
UL’s open days took place on Thursday, October 15th and Friday, October 16th. A further undergraduate open day will be held on Saturday, January 16th, 2027 for students who could not attend in October or who want a second look before making a decision.
What to expect: Attend subject talks, library tours, faculty tours and student support stands. For anyone who may experience sensory overload or fatigue, a dedicated quiet space will be located in the Glucksman Library, Room GLO 38.
Student life: Societies range from aeronautical society to games development, and fashion to writing. Clubs include hockey, pool and powerlifting.
Accommodation: For incoming CAO first-year students, a lottery system is in place for UL Accommodation. Applicants who live more than 60km from UL will be prioritised.
Maynooth University will hold open days on Friday, November 20th and Saturday, November 21st.
Registration details: You can register at campaigns.maynoothuniversity.ie/ugopenday
What to expect: Meet students and staff in person to learn more about studying at Maynooth, take a tour of the campus and attend talks to find out more about courses that interest you.
Student life: Students can join societies such as the history society, investors society, trad music society, darts and judo.
Accommodation: Maynooth University offers just under 1,200 rooms arranged into apartments on-campus. 50 per cent of these rooms are allocated to new first-year undergraduate students.
The open days at the UG took place on October 2nd and 3rd. The Spring Open Day is on March 13th, 2027.
Registration details: You can register at universityofgalway.ie/opendays
What to expect: Campus tours, faculty tours and student life talks as well as course-specific talks, information on access routes and exhibition stands.
Student life: There are more than 50 clubs and 110 societies to choose from, including botany, musical, astronomy, cycling and athletics.
Accommodation: UG has three student residences on the university campus – Corrib Village, Goldcrest Village and Dunlin Village – providing for almost 1,900 students a year.
DCU will hold an open day on its Glasnevin Campus on Friday, November 13th from 10am-3pm.
On Saturday, November 14th, an open day will be held on both the Glasnevin Campus and St Patrick’s Campus from 10am-2pm.
What to expect: Speak to current students, faculty staff and support units about DCU’s courses and services. Explore the campus and learn about the clubs and societies on offer for students.
Student life: Get involved in a range of clubs and societies such as cooking, creative writing, football and hockey.
Accommodation: Incoming first-year students are allocated rooms on the St Patrick’s Campus, in O’Donnell House on the All Hallows Campus and in Larkfield Apartments on the Glasnevin Campus.
[ Advice for first years: ‘You don’t find yourself at university, you kind of create yourself there’ Opens in new window ]
RCSI will hold an open day on Friday, January 8th, 2027.
Registration details: You can register at rcsi.com/dublin/undergraduate/meet-rcsi
What to expect: Attendees can explore RCSI’s facilities, meet student ambassadors and receive information about access routes, the HPAT exam, the application process and scholarships.
Accommodation: A popular student residence is Mercer Court, encompassing Mercer Court Apartments and Millin House Student Residence, located a two-minute walk from the RCSI Library and main university.
Prospective students are advised to check with individual universities and Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) for further updates and information on open days. The CAO application booklet is available to download from CAO.ie

title: Attracting Irish doctors in Australia back to Ireland
description: Australia’s health system benefits significantly from their expertise and their dedication to patients.
content:
Sir, – As an Australian doctor, I have followed with great interest your coverage of public sector strikes in Ireland. Every Australian hospital is held up by Irish doctors, acting as recipients of their exodus from your shores.
Tea rooms are a cacophony of Irish voices. So much so, that Australian doctors have adopted Irishisms into their own slang. Good things are no longer grouse for Australian doctors but grand, and many weekends – we don’t work all of those here- – are spent in search not of a good time but for craic.
Irish doctors are among the best in the world. Australia’s health system benefits significantly from their expertise and their dedication to patients.
They help us sustain a world class health system with decent conditions for its staff.
Australian doctors are also on strike. Our demands are achievable and include a maximum 12.5-hour workday, four protected days off a fortnight and a 30 per cent increase in pay. They will make our workplaces safer and attract more doctors to Australia. To Irish doctors, they are unimaginable.
It is a catastrophic mistake to force your best and brightest to work in conditions so abhorrent that moving to the other side of the world is the only option. The best Irish doctors are looking after mums and dads in Sydney rather than Sligo because the Irish Government refuses to pay or treat them properly.
Though I would miss working with Irish colleagues, I hope these strikes are an overdue wake-up call that compels the Government to give them a decent life to return home to. – Yours, etc,

title: Any pay deal reached with unions must have productivity elements, says Taoiseach
description: Fórsa chief Kevin Callinan says unions would now test whether Government has understood protesters’ position
content:
Any pay deal reached with public service trade unions in talks beginning on Monday would have to include productivity elements, Taoiseach Micheál Martin has said.
The Taoiseach delivered the blunt message on Sunday ahead of talks starting at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) following a framework agreement reached between both sides over the weekend. This resulted in further industrial action originally planned for this Wednesday being called off .
The Taoiseach declined to discuss suggestions that the €1.2 billion allocated to pay for a new deal in the recent budget could be increased by dipping into a €1.6 billion contingency fund.
“We’re not going to go into what may transpire over the course of the negotiations ... Nothing is decided, no precise figures have even been mentioned yet,” he said at an event in Co Kildare.
The potentially tough talks are set to start with an attempt to deal with the trade union side’s claims in relation to cost-of-living pressures. This included demands that measures be taken to address a shortfall of between 5 and 7 per cent on increases received by most workers since 2021, when taking into account inflation during the period.
[ Analysis: ‘It’s not going to be smooth’ – Government and unions start on long road to pay deal Opens in new window ]
The order had previously been a sticking point between the two sides but engagement on Saturday chaired by WRC chairman Kevin Foley led to progress.
Asked what he thought of suggestions in the media that another €400 million could be added to the €1.2 billion earmarked for addressing pay next year, Fórsa general secretary Kevin Callinan said: “I have no comment on the figures floated in Sunday’s papers other than they appear to be deliberately used to try to get people to forget that the Government was talking about €2 billion a few weeks ago.”
Speaking at the Fianna Fáil Wolfe Tone commemoration at Bodenstown, Co Kildare, on Sunday, Micheál Martin rejected suggestions by Ryanair boss Michael O’Leary that he would “buckle” and “roll over” to the public sector trade unions, and insisted that productivity increases would be part of any new pay deal with the unions.
“Obviously there has to be value for money, there has to be productivity and all of that, and that has always been our position. As someone who is experienced in politics, that’s my approach.”
[ Opinion: Unsustainable pay increases for public sector workers will put Ireland’s stability at risk Opens in new window ]
Martin declined to be drawn on whether he would be open to a lower percentage increase for higher-paid public servants with a higher percentage increase for lower-paid workers, rather than an across the board percentage increase.
“I’m open to an agreement that is affordable, that can advance productivity within the public service, that would look after low-paid workers – but again, let’s allow the negotiations to start. It’s not for me to be getting into the details or precise preferences about the shape of any agreement.”
Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers , meanwhile, welcomed the agreement reached on Saturday evening regarding a basis for proceeding with the talks.
Callinan, who will lead the union side’s negotiating team, said on Sunday evening: “The Minister told me that the Government had listened to the people on picket lines last Wednesday. We’ll now test whether they have understood and back it up in practice.”
The Government side will be represented in the talks by officials from the Department of Public Expenditure . Unions have had a strained relationship with the department in recent times, suggesting that the talks process could prove difficult.
Senior Government sources expect tough negotiations and say they hope the process can wrap up in a matter of weeks, but are prepared for it to last longer.
One union, Unite , voted against deferring a second day of strike action this Wednesday when the Public Services Committee of Ictu met on Friday, arguing that the Government position had not shifted far enough to enter talks. Unite is due to consult its shop stewards on Monday on how it should proceed.
It appeared to remain possible that the union, which represents about 4,000 public sector workers, could push ahead with its strike if it receives support from its members.
Attempts to contact the union for clarification on Sunday were unsuccessful.

title: CarVal generates €310m surplus in four years from loan portfolios bought for €1bn
description: Minneapolis-based group bought Irish property debts from KBC, Bank of Ireland and others
content:
Loan investment vehicles linked to US debt group AB CarVal Investors have generated a gross surplus of €310 million from collections and the resale of Irish property loans they acquired for €1.02 billion since 2022.
In 2022, AB CarVal’s Irish vehicle Braunton Property Finance Designated Activity Company (DAC) bought a portfolio of Irish residential mortgages from KBC Bank Ireland and Premier Homeloans for €610.2 million.
The Minneapolis-based firm’s subsidiary Hartland Property Finance then paid Bank of Ireland €410.4 million in 2023 for a separate portfolio of distressed Irish residential and commercial property loans.
New financial filings by AB CarVal’s firms, which cover the 2025 financial year, show Braunton will be wound up after it “sold its remaining portfolio of loans”, and Hartland has also sold a large portion of the debt it acquired in 2023.
An analysis by The Irish Times of financial statements for Braunton has shown it made €764.9 million from both the collection and resale of the KBC Bank Ireland and Premier Homeloans it acquired for €610.2 million – a surplus of €154.7 million.
Hartland has recorded a surplus of €155.3 million after making €565.7 million from both the collection and resale of loans linked to the portfolio it bought from Bank of Ireland for €410.4 million. The €565.7 million total for Hartland includes €90.8 million of proceeds it made from a sale of part of its portfolio in April 2026.
The combined €310 million surplus represents proceeds above the original purchase costs before financing costs, operating expenses and tax expenses.
The disclosures follow reporting by The Irish Times earlier this year that showed AB CarVal’s Elmscott Property Finance also made a €75 million profit in the space of three years from flipping some non-performing personal and commercial debt, valued at €694 million, that it bought from Ulster Bank in August 2023 for €268 million.
Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings have shown a special-purpose entity linked to the investment bank Goldman Sachs called Penryn Funding 2024 DAC acquired some of the debt sold by AB CarVal’s vehicles, Hartland and Elmscott.
Minneapolis-based AB CarVal was one of the first foreign funds to move on Ireland after the financial crash, and among the most prolific purchasers of distressed Irish debt.
The firm bought non-performing loans valued at billions of euro, including loans connected to the Irish Banking Resolution Corporation’s (IBRC) Project Stone loan portfolio, which was valued at a combined €6.85 billion, and a collection of 5,000 loans called Project Poseidon that included assets such as the Lyrath Estate Hotel in Kilkenny and the Regency Hotel in Dublin.
Following the recovery of the Irish economy, AB CarVal has continued to use its office in Ireland as a hub to manage distressed debt in other parts of Europe.

title: Small Fry has big Australian ambitions as racing’s global perspective increases
description: Cork jockey Johnny Allen enjoys more big race success with former Irish horse Kingswood in Caulfield Cup
content:
Flat racing’s global perspective will go up several notches during the coming weeks and Joseph O’Brien’s immediate focus will be on Geelong in Australia in the early hours of Wednesday morning.
O’Brien was out of luck with the unplaced Starford in Saturday’s Caulfield Cup, but Small Fry is set to line up for the Geelong Cup, one of the final ‘Golden Ticket’ races that gets the winner into the Melbourne Cup on the first Tuesday in November.
Dermot Weld used the Geelong Cup as a stepping stone to glory in ‘the race that stops a nation’ in 2002 through Media Puzzle. The French horses Americain and Dunaden did the same double back-to-back in 2010 and 2011.
Small Fry, a winner at York in August, is part of the OTI ownership and a spokesman told local media: “We probably need to win it to guarantee a spot [in the Melbourne Cup] and if we only run a place, we’ll be on the cusp because Small Fry is currently not qualified. We’ve got to be active there. Small Fry is one of those horses that’s below the radar.”
O’Brien, twice a Melbourne Cup winner with Rekindling and Twilight Payment, as well as having a Cox Plate success through State Of Rest, is set to have his largest raid yet on Australia’s biggest race next month.
He has nine horses left in the Melbourne Cup, including high-class pair James J Braddock and Defiantly. The latter landed one of the ‘Golden Ticket’ races, Deauville’s Prix Kergolay, in August. They, along with the JP McManus-owned Trustyourinstinct, currently dominate ante-post betting on the race.
Saturday’s Caulfield Cup was won by Irish jockey Johnny Allen on board the ex-Irish Kingswood. The grey was formerly trained by John O’Donoghue on the Curragh and was third in the 2023 Gallinule Stakes. It was just the latest big-race success for Allen, an ex-jump jockey in Ireland, who rode State Of Rest to Cox Plate success in 2021.
Separately, Johnny Murtagh’s belief in his filly Believed was vindicated at Ascot on Saturday when the 16/1 outsider found only Minnie Hauk too good in the Group One British Champions Fillies & Mares Stakes. Her jockey Oisín Murphy described her run as a “career best”.
Murtagh sends six runners to Gowran on Monday and might enjoy a first and last race double through Littlepacer and Lord Aus.
The Harty team send last week’s Roscommon winner Zaranakarena for a mile handicap, and she may be up to defying a 9lbs hike in the ratings. It was her first handicap start a week ago and the experience should be of benefit.
Dylan Browne McMonagle is on the newcomer Acknowledge rather than the 88-rated Wo Wo Never in a juvenile maiden and it looks a significant pick.

title: Irish firms lag behind global peers in managing cyber risk, PwC finds
description: Less than a fifth of Irish respondents strongly agree cybersecurity is integrated into overall risk management
content:
Irish companies lag behind their global counterparts in integrating cybersecurity into their risk management, new research by PwC has found.
A survey of 4,000 business and tech executives from 71 countries, including Ireland, found 17 per cent of Irish respondents strongly agreed that cybersecurity was fully part of their organisation’s overall risk management, compared to 41 per cent globally.
PwC Ireland cybersecurity and privacy partner Leonard McAuliffe said that as many organisations are racing to capture the value of AI , preparation for cyber risks “needs to become a business capability”.
“The survey finds many organisations are still underprepared for a rapidly evolving cyber landscape, and organisations that get this right will be better positioned to innovate with confidence while continuing to operate through disruption,” McAuliffe said.
The results of the survey also showed only 23 per cent of Irish respondents strongly agreed their employer regularly conducted incident response exercises, compared with 41 per cent globally.
Against a backdrop of rapid advances in AI, 84 per cent of global security and finance leaders said they expect their cyber budgets to rise over the next 12 months.
Responses from Irish participants also indicated protection against AI-enabled attacks was a lower spending priority, as 34 per cent identified securing against AI-enabled attacks as a cyber spending priority compared with 46 per cent globally.
Irish executives showed they are wary of adopting autonomous AI tools as part of their cyber defence. Only 6 per cent said they would allow AI agents to act fully autonomously to help protect their systems versus 22 per cent globally.
[ How HR teams are combatting AI and other security threats in recruitment process Opens in new window ]
On a global basis, 29 per cent of companies said quantum-computing exposure was a cyber threat that their organisation is least prepared to combat in the next 12 months, and Ireland lags behind global counterparts.
Quantum computing is expected to break current encryption protocols as early as the 2030s, according to the PwC report, and only 6 per cent of Irish respondents said that they are implementing quantum-resistant security measures compared to 21 per cent globally.

title: ‘It’s not going to be smooth’: Government and unions start on long road to pay deal
description: Unions needed ‘day out’ to underline their determination, senior Government figures believe
content:
T he path towards a new public sector pay deal enters a new phase this morning when negotiators from the unions and the Government side sit down together at the Workplace Relations Commission to begin what could be a lengthy process of trying to thrash out a new agreement.
Both sides want a deal; both are keen to stress they don’t want it at all costs. It wouldn’t amaze anyone if there were a few stops and starts along the way. “It’s not going to be smooth,” said one Government insider.
The unions probably start the process on the front foot. In the talks about talks over the weekend, concluded hastily on Saturday evening after just one day, the Government conceded the union demands that pay be dealt with at the start of the negotiations and that this should include the unions’ “claims on cost-of-living effects between 2021–2025, this year, and for the duration of any agreement”, as the agreed statement put it.
The statement also noted that “there is a need to rebuild trust and confidence in industrial relations in the public sector by addressing commitments made in the context of the previous agreement” – code for the local bargaining elements of the last agreement which the unions say have not been honoured in recent years. The local bargaining elements are not popular on the Government side, where they are viewed as just a means to secure top-up increases.
Could the Government have not agreed all this a week ago and avoided the strike last Wednesday? You’d think so. Though there is a view present at the top of Government that the unions needed a “day out” to underline – both to the public and to their own members – their determination and their willingness to go all the way to strike action.
[ Taoiseach rejects Michael O’Leary’s view that he would ‘buckle’ to public sector unions Opens in new window ]
But nobody, it seems, wanted two days out. Or at least, nobody at leadership level did. A protracted period on the picket lines can harden attitudes and make the eventual compromise – if and when it comes – harder to sell. Union leaders are always aware that after any deal is done they then have to go and persuade their memberships that no better deal is on offer. Sometimes that can be harder than agreeing the deal in the first place.
The unions are also likely to face questions about the structure of any deal – does it seek to give the most to lower-paid public sector workers who are feeling the pinch the most from cost-of-living pressures? Asked about this at Bodenstown on Sunday, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said he was keen to see an agreement that would look after lower-paid workers, but stressed that he wanted to see what the unions were looking for. It remains to be seen whether the unions would be willing to trade gains for higher-paid public servants in order to help the lower-paid significantly.
Because of the way public sector salaries are structured, with many jobs subject to incremental scales, older workers tend to be paid significantly more. That means flat-rate percentage increases benefit them much more than the lower paid.
[ How Ireland’s first national public sector strike in 17 years left unions strong and Jack Chambers ‘scrambling’ Opens in new window ]
The Government has put aside €1.2 billion, though it will end up with a more expensive – and possibly much more expensive – deal. But at €1.2 billion, that’s enough to give everyone in the public sector a 3 per cent pay rise.
What that means, however, varies widely. With a 3 per cent increase, the secretary general of a government department would benefit by about €700 a month; a teacher on the bottom of the scale by about €120 a month. It will be interesting to see how the unions address this issue in the talks.

title: Hotel planned on central Dublin site after investor rules offices and housing ‘not viable’
description: German asset manager KGAL is latest investor to signal issues with delivering new office accommodation in the city
content:
German property investor KGAL plans to replace a Dublin city-centre office block with a hotel after concluding that neither extending the office nor redeveloping the site for housing would be financially viable.
The investor’s proposal adds to signs of a shift from office development in Dublin, with Core Capital ’s Derek McGrath and Johnny Ronan ’s development group also pivoting towards hotel construction .
Earlier this month, KGAL’s Irish subsidiary Golden Lane Liffey Limited sought permission from Dublin City Council to demolish 31-36 Golden Lane and build a new midmarket 225-room hotel beside the Radisson Blu Royal Hotel near South Great George’s Street.
The property was extensively refurbished after being let to San Francisco tech firm New Relic on a 20-year lease in 2017, but has been vacant since the company moved out last year.
KGAL said in its application that several options were explored for the site, which included extending the existing three-storey office from 2,800sq m to 6,700sq m across eight storeys and refurbishing the block into 59 apartments or 160 student beds.
[ Aviva seeks operator for new luxury hotel on Dublin’s Clarendon Street Opens in new window ]
It added that demolition of the building and construction of a new hotel was the only viable financial option.
“Given the current high level of office vacancy rates, the emergence of the ‘work from home’ model and the site’s location outside of the core office districts, the redevelopment of the subject site for office use is not financially viable,” KGAL’s planning application said.
Feasibility studies added that a financially viable apartment block would be difficult to build because the site’s “constrained nature” meant it would be difficult to meet residential development standards. Similar constraints “render it not possible” for student accommodation of sufficient scale to be viable.
A letter attached to the submission from student accommodation investor Urbanest said the site would need to house at least 200 bed spaces to be viable to run on a cost-per-bed space ratio.
KGAL’s application added that there had been strong demand for further hotel accommodation in Dublin based on occupancy across seven competing hotels exceeding 90 per cent in the summer of 2026.
[ Tenant exit and flat rents weigh on €300m Dublin office portfolio Opens in new window ]
The new hotel proposal has come soon after Ronan Group sought approval to change its redevelopment plans for the current Citigroup building in Dublin’s International Financial Services Centre and replace 40 per cent of planned office space with two new hotels.
McGrath’s Renmark Property Holdings Limited also plans to change its development plans for a site near the RDS in Ballsbridge , where it has permission for an eight-storey office block.
Last week, McGrath told the Business Post his firm had decided to develop a 244-bedroom hotel and a 194-bedroom aparthotel on the site instead due to uncertainty in the office market.
KGAL, which manages €15 billion of assets globally, acquired 31-36 Golden Lane for €25.5 million in 2018 from Peter Leonard and Derek Pippinga’s Mm Capital . The latest accounts for Golden Lane Liffey Limited valued the property at €20.1 million.
The building was pre-let to tech firm New Relic on a €1.4-million-a-year, 20-year lease deal in 2017 and then went through an extensive refurbishment before the company moved in a year later.
New Relic, which indicated it would grow its Irish headcount from 100 to 300 following the move to Golden Lane, has cut back its Irish office from 117 to 90 staff since 2022 and relocated to new offices on Pearse Street in 2025.

title: Poignant Munster victory caps perfect weekend for Irish rugby
description: All four provinces win on the opening weekend of Europe as Munster honour Anthony Foley before turning their attention to Leinster
content:
S o much for being undercooked. Unlike the first round of the URC a month ago, all four Irish provinces won on the opening weekend of the European competitions for the first time in five seasons.
Despite only welcoming back nine frontliners a week previously, Leinster set the tone with an impressive 43-23 bonus-point win away to old foes Clermont on Saturday. At the same time Ulster were completing a 40-21 bonus-point win in the Challenge Cup away to Zebre Parma.
Back in the Champions Cup after a four-year hiatus, Connacht then treated a throbbing Dexcom Stadium to an 80-minute rollercoaster of Lancaster-ball in their memorable seven tries to six, 45-36 victory over the locked-and-loaded three-time champions Saracens.
Munster completed the quartet with a 33-25 win over Racing 92 on a poignant night in Páirc Uí Chaoimh, where tributes marked the 10th anniversary of Anthony Foley’s passing in a Parisian hotel on the morning of a scheduled match against the same opponents.
Alas, the vast majority of the 24,906 crowd had vacated the stadium when the Munster squad and management formed a circle on the pitch to sing their dressingroom anthem Stand Up and Fight, as they had done after their epic win over Glasgow a day after Foley’s funeral a decade ago.
“For me personally, it was very emotional,” said Jack O’Donoghue, Munster’s one player from both the Glasgow game and last Saturday night.
O’Donoghue believes they can take confidence from this win when Munster face Leinster in the URC at the Aviva Stadium next Saturday (6pm) but, understandably, the magnitude of the past week dominated their focus.
“To be honest, I haven’t given it a hell of a lot of thought,” admitted head coach Clayton McMillan. “A lot of energy went into this week, and we can now turn our attention to Leinster.
“I watched a good portion of their game before coming here. We know the quality that Leinster have. It’s an international side running around, but our guys will celebrate tonight and then turn our attention on Monday to Leinster.
“I imagine after looking at the game tonight, they would have seen a number of avenues that they can look to attack us with,” added McMillan wryly after an imperfect Munster display.
[ ‘I stood in that circle 10 years ago’: Jack O’Donoghue on an emotional night for Munster Opens in new window ]
“We’ll need to make sure that we do our homework and tidy up the areas where I think we were a little vulnerable tonight, but also look at where we can have a crack at them.”
McMillan’s bold selection was vindicated, not least by giving 20-year-old academy outhalf Charlie O’Shea a Champions Cup debut in only his fourth Munster outing and second competitive start. Hopefully, Munster will cultivate rather thancurtail O’Shea’s innate inventiveness.
“I like to think that we encourage all of our players to express themselves and to bring to the table what they’re naturally gifted at. Charlie is a fairly ambitious man. You never want to take that away from him.
“There were some moments tonight that he’ll review himself. He won’t need me or any of the senior players to tell him what he needs to do better. He’ll do the homework and come in and know. Our job is just to keep supporting him, keep being honest with him, keep challenging him and he’ll be a really good prospect for us.”
Munster would have earned a bonus point under the old scoring system but missed out on one under the amended rules by scoring five tries to three.
Even so, McMillan said: “I like it personally. I’d be a big advocate for no bonus points; I think you [should] just win or lose and that’s it.
“This is a format that’s used in Super Rugby, so it’s not unfamiliar to me, and I think it rewards teams that are clearly dominant for scoring three more tries than the opposition and doesn’t allow that team to loosen off late in the game and perhaps give opposition teams an opportunity to walk away with one or two points that they might not have got on another day.”
All four provinces progressed to the knock-out stages five seasons ago, whereas last season Munster began with a 40-14 defeat in Bath, but McMillan paid little store by that.
“I would probably be a big believer that your past is never a great predictor of your future, so just because other teams have won their first game and gone on to make finals is a little bit irrelevant to me.
“We just need to win our home games, and we need to press teams hard when they’re playing at home.
[ Páirc Uí Chaoimh crowd pay perfect tribute to Anthony Foley on emotional evening by the Lee Opens in new window ]
“We literally only focus on the next game in front of us because that’s the team we are at the moment. We’re not good enough to be looking too far in the distance; we’d just get bitten on the backside.
“We celebrate tonight because it was a big week for the club. I hope that our supporters and in particular the Foley family are proud of the performance, and we’ll go to sleep tonight with a little bit of a smile, but we get back to work, and we’ll start talking about Leinster on Monday.
“I don’t even know when the next European Cup game is; a month or so away, is it?”
Close. It’s a trek to Bristol in December, followed by the concluding rounds in January, when Munster go to Bordeaux and host Gloucester. Much to do still.

title: As rugby becomes more sanitised, the ‘dark arts’ are being legislated out of the game
description: Rugby is more concerned with how it is perceived than ever,  and its laws are in a perpetual state of review
content:
In the build-up to Munster ’s Champions Cup game on Saturday, Denis Leamy and Tadhg Beirne both mentioned the “dark arts” and their creeping demise under the rule of law. Leamy is a defence coach now, but he was a flanker in his playing days, so the destruction of nice things has been central to his mission in rugby.
“I think the dark arts have gone out of the game around the breakdown,” said Leamy. “Certainly, the team without possession is getting refereed.”
Beirne spoke about the increasing hopelessness of trying to defend a lineout maul, at least if he must behave himself. “There were a few ways of getting around the laws a little,” he said. “I tended to do it where you have one shoulder attached to the maul and you can reach around, but that’s all gone now … The dark arts are slowly going out of the game, that’s for sure.”
Just like in all team sports, there is a certain, half-suppressed admiration for the “dark arts”. It is an instinctive reaction to dire straits. As a player, or coach, or supporter, if somebody is threatening your tryline or your goal, the means of prevention is suddenly not a matter of conscience. Hymns to fair play are for another time.
The phrase “dark arts” comes from a family of words such as skulduggery and blackguarding, all of which include the concept of cheating, even though that word is deliberately silent. It’s like those food labels that carry the soothing phrase “no added sugar”, which is not to suggest that such products are sugar-free.
Our attitude to cheating in sport, though, is full of contradictions and double standards. We are appalled by the behaviour of Manchester City , for example, or any doping scandal in athletics or cycling, and we cannot countenance the thought of someone cheating in golf, but we have a certain tolerance for the “dark arts”.
Forgiveness for this kind of behaviour is always along party lines. Neil Back has still not been forgiven by Munster supporters for slapping the ball out of Peter Stringer’s hands when Leicester were defending their own line, and a narrow lead, in the closing minutes of the 2002 Heineken Cup final. But Back’s justification for his actions at the time captures the essence of the dark arts: motive, opportunity, a breakdown in surveillance, and a jackpot for petty crime.
“This game is all about little edges – particularly in finals – and doing what you can to win,” he said. “That was a very crucial scrum, and I did what I had to do to ensure a win for Leicester. I am not a cheat, and I would be very upset if anyone accused me of being one. What I did was part of the professional game. I am sure that other backrow players have done it in the past.”
In common with all practitioners of the “dark arts”, Back rejects its association with cheating, even though the difference is only a matter of labelling: no added cheating, in other words.
Hip-drop tackles (which involve a defender dropping their weight onto the legs of an opponent while bringing them to ground) will be banned from November 1st
The “dark arts” is a sidebar issue in rugby’s ongoing reckoning with safety and self-image and how the contact zone is managed. As Leamy pointed out, the breakdown is not nearly as lawless as it once was. The punitive practice of raking the back of a player who had landed on the wrong side of a ruck, for example, was phased out in the build-up to the 1999 World Cup after decades of acceptance. The game, though, was not nearly as conscious of its appearance then as it is now.
The way the lineout maul is being refereed this season is not a law change but a “law application guideline” that emerged from a Shape of the Game conference hosted by World Rugby in February.
[ Owen Doyle: Conflating cheating with ‘character’ will make refereeing rugby impossible Opens in new window ]
It became a lightning rod for competing visions of how the game should be played. It had been suggested going into that conference that rugby was about to be “depowered” in order to produce “rugby league lite”. It has been reported since by Charlie Morgan in the Times that South Africa and France were instrumental in protecting the status of the maul, leading to the current clampdown in illegal interference. According to one source, South Africa “came out swinging”.
Naturally, given their power, the virility of the lineout maul is in the Springboks’ interests. Rassie Erasmus and his assistants reportedly arrived at the conference armed with copious video examples of lineout mauls being disrupted by what Beirne might describe as “dark arts”.
Of course, this is not a joust between rugby’s white knights and dark knights, and it is not a matter of right and wrong; South Africa are only interested in leveraging the direction of the game to their benefit. They are world leaders in the “dark arts”.
Rugby is more concerned with how it is perceived than it ever was, and, partly to that end, rugby’s laws are in a perpetual state of review. Between now and the World Cup in Australia next autumn, 10 law changes are on the agenda. For example, hip-drop tackles (which involve a defender dropping their weight onto the legs of an opponent while bringing them to ground) will be banned from November 1st.
[ Irish rugby bickering is a collision between blowhards and blow-ins Opens in new window ]
As of October 5th, referees were instructed to punish players who drop to one or both knees before making a tackle. Greater protection for scrumhalfs at rucks has also been introduced. All these measures are designed for enhanced player welfare.
Other law changes include less time for kickers to take a conversion, and allowing just 30 seconds to get a lineout set up. There is also more protection for a player trying to move the ball away from a maul. Those interventions are meant to deliver more ball-in-play time and to further enhance the spectacle.
“It’s hard to keep scorelines down now,” said Leamy last week, speaking for all bewildered defence coaches as basketball scores have infiltrated the top echelons of the game. “Attacks and the way the game is refereed allows for a little bit more of a free-flowing product.”
With the sanitising of rugby, the “dark arts” were always going to meet a legislative termination. Take it or leave it.

title: Letters to the Editor, October 19th: On protecting  citizens from hardship, public service pay and buying second hand books from Britain
description: Every sector and group are banging their drums and putting their hands out
content:
Sir, – As a society when did we become so dependent on the State to save us from any hardship? The current severe inflation being experienced and projected is as a result of wars started and continued by big powers who do not care about the consequences.
There is no state in the world that can insulate its citizens from these rising costs. We in Ireland are largely a wealthy country and very many can well afford to tighten their own belts and ride this out.
Instead we have every sector and group banging their drums and putting their hands out.
This makes it harder for the State to help those who really need it. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – One can only agree with Stephen Collins’ assertion that over generous pay increases for the public sector will eventually undermine our economy, (“ Unsustainable pay increases for public sector workers will put Ireland’s stability at risk ” Opinion and Analysis, October 16th).
Having said that, it is blatantly wrong that many civil servants, teachers and nurses in permanent and pensionable jobs can no longer afford to buy a house.
While it is correct to point out that overall numbers in the public sector have risen to dizzy heights, the real focus should be on particular areas of the public sector and individual Government departments that have boosted their staff allocations and pay to levels that merit serious scrutiny.
The Government has never entered into discussions with the public sector unions on foot of the completion of a root and branch analysis in relation to pay and public service numbers.
Such an exercise could legitimise and strengthen the Government’s position and also provide more scope and flexibility in relation to pay.
In the context of the current impasse, there is a clear opportunity and need for such an approach. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Whenever the subject of public sector pay is in the news, we can always expect the public sector “bashers” to come out of the woodwork. However, I was still a bit dismayed by Stephen Collins’s article blaming the public sector workers for the financial crash of 2009.
I was a public sector worker in 2009 and I still vividly recall the burning sense of injustice felt by myself and my colleagues at that time. Many despairingly asked their union reps “Why are we being blamed for this”, as we endured pay cut after pay cut (a fact omitted by Collins). The fact was that we were simply a popular and convenient scapegoat at the time.
Of course, the true facts of what caused the financial crash subsequently emerged and are now in the public records. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I am a simple fellow with limited political intuition and as a consequence, find it difficult to understand why US president Donald Trump appears more sympathetic to Russia than to Ukraine, a country fighting for its survival against an aggressive dictatorship.
He criticises Ukraine for striking Russian oil refineries, while at the same time restricting access to technology that could strengthen its war effort. Meanwhile, Trump wants to purchase Russian oil that will provide revenue to that regime, helping to fund and sustain its conflict against Ukraine. What am I missing?
Amid this grave international situation, Trump finds time to bask in newly contrived awards and honours, apparently generated to compensate for the genuine accolades that have rightly eluded him.
I cannot help wondering if the presidency has become a stage on which one man’s appetite for admiration must continually be satisfied, rather than being a force for good in a world that badly needs intelligent and compassionate leadership. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Somebody needs to sit down with Donald Trump to explain to him why we are experiencing oil and diesel shortages, resulting in higher prices.
As a consequence of his attack on Iran, the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea are closed to shipping bringing oil and diesel and many other products to the rest of the world. We are all experiencing rising prices and inflation, but I believe we all know who is responsible.
Ukraine is currently targeting Russian oil refineries. This is in retaliation for Russia indiscriminate and unprovoked attacks on people and resources in Ukraine.
Trump’s defence of Russia is truly shocking and has all to do with self interest on his part, rather than on justice for the people of Ukraine.
Please, please, can somebody explain this to Trump. Just be aware, he appears to be a slow learner. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Two weeks back we accidentally broke the fibre optic cable providing Wifi and internet to the house. After the initial panic, pandemonium and search for alternative accommodation, things calmed down.
My evenings were spent in the company of John Creedon’s music programme on RTÉ Radio 1 and with a good book – was reading, and enjoying, Leo Varadkar’s autobiography, Speaking My Mind.
To my surprise I survived, and to my amazement I actually enjoyed the two screen free weeks which brought me back to times past. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Recent correspondence to your page suggested that card playing has become less inspiring than video games. Let me assure you as a mature bridge player that there is nothing to compare with the pure pleasure of an evening spent in the company of a hall full of vigorous card players.
Firstly the game is alive, it’s challenging, it’s almost always friendly, importantly it’s competitive and it gives one an excuse to get one’s hair done, to don a sparkly top and to compel one’s granddaughter to paint one’s nails. Is this not more life-giving than sitting in a dark room watching a video game called Grand Theft Auto? – Yours, etc.
Sir, – The recent changes in import and customs charges may have been designed to offset the surge in cheap Chinese goods, but it appears to have had a more damaging and I would hope unintended consequence: the price of second hand books from the UK has now skyrocketed.
This morning I attempted to buy a book online that was priced at £4.78, but when I specified I was in Ireland, the price changed £13.78.
After some investigation, it seems this is common across reputable booksellers.
Shipping, thankfully, was free. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Irish sheep farmers know the distress and financial losses caused by dog attacks on livestock. A compulsory national dog DNA database would help identify dogs responsible and hold their owners accountable. But its benefits would extend far beyond protecting sheep.
The current pre-legislative process for the Dog Breeding Establishments (Amendment) Bill 2026 provides a timely opportunity to demand this change.
While farming organisations and several independent politicians have repeatedly called for a compulsory national dog DNA database, the present debate on the Dog Breeding Industry is too good an opportunity for sheep farmers to pass up.
Without a DNA database the approximately 45,000 people who adopt, purchase or otherwise acquire a dog each year have no reliable way of knowing their new family member’s genetic coefficient of inbreeding.
This is a material fact affecting inherited disease risks and animal welfare. There is no reason to justify consumers being denied access to this information before purchase or adoption.
Over the past decade, Ireland’s commercial puppy-farming industry has reportedly produced around 100,000 puppies annually.
Concerns about inbreeding and the effectiveness of oversight make independent, verifiable genetic information – coupled to microchip registration – increasingly important.
Mandatory DNA profiling, linked to microchip identification and appropriate genetic testing, could help trace livestock attacks, exposé irresponsible breeding practices, improve animal welfare and give responsible breeders a means of demonstrating their standards.
It could also give buyers greater confidence in the dogs they acquire. This measure alone would significantly reduce local authority inspection time and costs.
Sheep farmers have a direct interest in this reform. They should urge their representative organisations and public representatives to seek mandatory DNA certification for every dog in Ireland while the 2026 Bill is under consideration.
This is an opportunity to protect livestock, consumers, and children from dog bite injuries. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – The Citroën 2CV being relaunched can only be good news, as probably only the VW Beetle holds a comparable place in automotive nostalgia. The origin of its name is an elegant encapsulation of the ingenuity of the original car, and its being “designed to reduce costs” as Emmet Ryan says (October 15th).
The letters mean deux chevaux or two horses, a reference in a sense to the vehicle’s horsepower. At the time in France car tax was calculated on the basis of measurement of the chambers within the engine, and what they would be predicted to do.
And those of the 2CV put it in the lowest category, and thus the cheapest for taxing it. Nonetheless the actual power was very much higher, reportedly in the region of 7-9 horsepower when launched.
A miracle of modern engineering then, in the 1940s. Later models were far more powerful but the name was retained.
As a comparison, on a quick search I think the lowest powered car on the Irish market now delivers 45 horsepower, with most being in the hundreds. But few, if any, have the 2CV’s panache. – Yours etc,
Sir, – The Irishman’s Diary (October 15th), about the very popular adventure stories of Reics Carlo, triggered memories from our 1950s Irish class.
