From our modest school library, we had to select an individual Reics Carlo book, read it and present a review/synopsis the following week. While some lads struggled, others, who were more proficient in the Gaeilge, made light work of the reviews.
Soon, those elegant synopses, were circulating gratis among the weaker students, who then copied them in their own handwriting and handed them in. The Brother never twigged what happened. A trouble shared was a trouble halved. -– Yours etc.

title: Futurity likely to prove decisive in Aidan O’Brien’s hopes of another British trainers’ title
description: The Irish trainer takes a narrow lead over Andrew Balding and has Futurity favourite in Noble Exhibit
content:
Aidan O’Brien has labelled it a “a bit of fun” but Saturday’s William Hill Futurity at Doncaster could prove serious in the Irishman’s tussle with Andrew Balding for the British trainers’ title.
O’Brien emerged from Saturday’s Champions Day action with a lead over his rival of £82,494 (about €97,000) having landed the Filly & Mare race with Minnie Hauk. Balding also struck at Group One level in the Long Distance Cup with the 33/1 shot Mount Atlas.
With O’Brien failing to fire in the two major seven-digit prizes, both of which fell to Godolphin, it meant some bookmakers cut Balding’s odds on a first championship to 5/4. O’Brien remains a 4/7 shot to win for a ninth time in all and for a third year in a row.
The championship race runs to the end of the year, although the outcome of Britain’s final Group One of the season this weekend may ultimately prove decisive.
O’Brien has suggested he’s unlikely to have any more cross-channel runners afterwards and should Balding still be within touching distance after the Futurity, a slow accumulation of minor pots through November and December on the all-weather might prove enough for him.
“Andrew Balding is a great fellow, and they are a great family. The very best of luck to them today. It is a bit of fun, and we are all delighted to be here,” O’Brien said at the weekend.
The competitive nature of elite level sport, however, suggests a record-extending 13 th Futurity success will be a priority. O’Brien has 18 of the 32 Futurity entries ahead of Monday’s next acceptance stage. Noble Exhibit, winner of the Beresford Stakes, is already a 5/4 favourite with some firms.
However, he’s likely to distribute some of that depth of talent to the following day’s Saint Cloud fixture in Paris, where both the Criterium International and the Criterium de Saint Cloud take place. The Irishman pulled off the Group One double last year through Puerto Rico and Pierre Bonnard.
The Futurity is worth £155,952 (about €180,000) to the winner and an O’Brien success would make him hard to peg back. Balding has just two entries, the Newmarket maiden winner Royal Quest and the Salisbury debut scorer Gran Dia.
“The Futurity Trophy will be the deciding race. We’ve got enough horses to keep running and some that were always programmed to run in valuable races through the year. We’ll stick with that and hope for the best,” Balding told RTV.
“I almost didn’t want to be in this position, as everyone’s put so much effort into this, but we’re usually quiet in November and December. We’ll play the cards we’ve got and it might be enough,” he added.
It might be a triple-Group One juvenile weekend in Europe but it’s the following week’s Breeders’ Cup that’s the target for another of the Ballydoyle two-year-old team.
Great Barrier Reef was third to his stable companion Darkness Falls in the recent Dewhurst Stakes and is now set to step up to a mile for the Juvenile Turf at Keeneland. O’Brien has won it eight times, including last year with Gstaad.
“He ran very well [in the Dewhurst] and I was kind of surprised and delighted really. He’d had a good break when he ran at the Curragh [Round Tower Stakes] where he got chinned and just got tired. Then we tried to run him back again and he got sick and had a bad scope.
“It was a very serious run in the Dewhurst. We thought if he ran well we’d go on to the Breeders’ Cup Juvenile with him because we thought he was a horse that would get seven furlongs and could get a mile, so that’s where we’re going next with him,” O’Brien commented.
The strength in depth of Ballydoyle’s two-year-old team was underlined with a vengeance again on Saturday through a six-timer at Leopardstown’s all-juvenile programme, repeating the feat at last year’s fixture. All six were ridden by Wayne Lordan. It was the first time a trainer-jockey partnership has won six races at a single meeting in Ireland or Britain.
It included Group Three successes for Wall Street in the Eyrefield Stakes and Capability Brown in the Killavullan Stakes.

title: ‘Nobody ate, nobody drank’: Inside the strange culture of San Francisco’s AI boom
description: Soaring wealth, rising rents and widening social divides are changing the city again
content:
‘Stop Hiring Humans,” declares the billboard. Ava is the AI model pictured in the ad. She is the new hire. Her generically good-looking features are scattered around the San Francisco Bay Area. At first sight they were a bit of a shock. The ads are by now as common as the various brands of driverless cars, or what we used to call taxis.
The historic cable cars still rattle up the steep hills, their bells dinging away, with tourists hanging out straining to get a photo on their phone of a passing Waymo or Zoox. The latter, the new kid on the block, and known locally as a “toaster on wheels”. It also resembles a stagecoach of old, sparing the horses of course. It is weirdly cute.
A crowd gathered recently when one stopped during a street festival, apparently confused by all the walking crowds. The pedestrians cheered – “Go on, go on, you can do it!” – and the toaster on wheels slowly moved forward.
AI and agentic AI are the new shiny gems to be panned in San Francisco, among the 19th century saloons and the historic Wild West mentality. They are bringing their own trappings of wealth.
San Francisco market rents have risen 22 per cent over the last 12 months to more than $4,500 per month for a one bed. The average property price is $1.6 million.
How will anyone afford to live here any more? And shock, they say even tech workers are being priced out of the all-ruling market. There is talk of young beneficiaries of recent AI IPOs turning up at property viewings and offering share options as downpayments. And of those offers being accepted
Every few weeks tens of thousands of these guys descend on the city for giant tech conferences. And they are mostly guys. They are the new cowboys with lanyards as neckerchiefs, but they are far from wild.
A chef I know recently catered a large party for an AI company. He shook his head at the memory of it.
“Nobody ate, nobody drank, they all stood around and barely even chatted with each other. These guys were in their early 20s and looked bored out of their minds. I ended up taking most of the food away. You know what? We need to show them how to party like we did.”
Yet a few weeks ago at the Burning Man festival, 80,000 or so gathered in the Nevada desert’s heat, sun and mud to get out of their heads and dance, with private jets bringing in the tech guys to land on the temporary sand runway. There’s an upsurge in psychedelic drug taking while many shun alcohol.
[ Sublime evenings and empty downtowns: Democrats threaten comeback in America’s heartland Opens in new window ]
Like most US cities, San Francisco still has large numbers of homeless people with addiction issues in certain areas, such as the Tenderloin. There is a drop-in centre called Hope Cafe. My friend Miriam is the baker. “It’s not really a cafe at all, but it has all the trappings of a proper restaurant like taking orders, issuing receipts to customers and serving people proper food. It’s about humanity and dignity,” she says.
The libraries and parks of California are effective day centres for the homeless. There are a few I see regularly down the road here, beside our yoga class. The woman who sits on the steps or inside the library, reading. The middle-aged man in the fashionable yet unclean clothes who walks around talking loudly to himself. And, in the last few weeks a young man, maybe 22, blond long hair, handsome, needs a shower, with rucksack and mat, doing the loop between the park and the library’s free magazines and newspapers. He’s no older than the guys in hoodies putting share options down on houses.
The gap has never been bigger and the midterms are looming. Unexpectedly, rows over data centres have become the new bunfights at the OK Corral. And the sheriffs of AI are suddenly voicing concerns over their posse of robots acting like outlaws .
Downtown they are trialling human style robots dressed in everyday clothes, just to see how we react or if we do at all.
I saw a new AI ad today. The same company as before. Ava is now pictured upside down. The ad says “Ava Flipped for Humans”. The inverted Ava is pictured wearing a T-shirt that says “I Heart Humans”. Right.
Opposite Trader Joes, two young women on scaffolding carefully paint a mural. They are standing on a cherry picker handpainting a huge ad. The wall mural attracts onlookers. It depicts a San Francisco with cable cars on Market Street. With flying cars. The caption reads: “Search For An AI Future.” The two artists take a rest.
Seems there are some things we still need creative humans for. For now.

title: Society must prepare for one third of children born today living to 100, report argues
description: Report finds Ireland ‘remains institutionally organised’ with policy shaped around shorter-life paradigm
content:
One in three children born in Ireland today are expected to live to 100.
The findings are contained in a new report which calls for the development of policies and plans to meet such a future demographic shift.
The 100-Year Lives Project: Longer, Better Lives for All recommends the establishment of a dedicated institute to prepare for the new reality.
Current average life expectancy is 82.9 years – 84.6 years for women and 81.3 years for men. With an ageing population, the report notes that “demand for healthcare services and State pensions will rise significantly, causing huge pressure on government budgets”.
It warns that Ireland is “not fully prepared for the social, economic and policy implications of this profound demographic reality”. Rather than seeing longevity as a burden, it notes, it should be viewed as an opportunity to “reshape how people learn, work, live and take part in their communities throughout life”.
[ Ageing population in Ireland will see rise of up to 58 per cent in need for family care Opens in new window ]
Commissioned by Community Foundation Ireland, an organisation that distributes philanthropic donations to community groups and charities, the 98-page report was written by social psychologist Karen Hand and marketing and strategy specialist Carolyn Ogdens.
It contains interviews with 16 experts in areas such as longitudinal medicine, macroeconomics, leadership, lifelong learning, education and social inclusion.
It also includes data from citizen workshops in Dublin, Cork and Mullingar with people aged 18 to 80, as well as “nationally representative” citizen polling.
Key concerns among those polled include physical health (84 per cent), cognitive impairment (83 per cent) and loss of independence (82 per cent).
Vulnerability, poor quality of life and being seen as a burden also factor, while isolation, age discrimination and end-of-life care are concerns for about two-thirds of respondents.
The potential benefits of living to 100 include seeing younger family members grow up (86 per cent), benefitting from healthcare advances (80 per cent), and providing emotional support to family (77 per cent).
Six in 10 agree social connection and learning new skills are positives of living longer. Respondents also believe maintaining health and fitness is key to ensuring a better life at 100.
But respondents are not optimistic about the State’s ability to develop a cohesive strategy. Of those interviewed, 65 per cent would like to see collaboration between government, businesses, charities and citizens, but are “less certain about government’s capacity to deliver on long-term needs”.
The authors compare Ireland’s approach to those of other countries and note the UK has advanced the concept of multi-stage lives, while Ireland “remains institutionally organised around a shorter-life paradigm, with policy still fragmented across ageing, health, and pensions”.
[ Ireland ‘needs 1,000 new nursing home beds a year until 2040′ for ageing population Opens in new window ]
The report proposes a “cradle-to-grave” approach built around three priorities – connected wellbeing, lifelong opportunities and active citizenship.
It makes a number of recommendations including, at national level, a dedicated institute or existing public body to co-ordinate national action.

title: Lack of access to books adding to impact of poverty on children’s education, ESRI finds
description: Children in poverty twice as likely to dislike school, research think tank finds
content:
Persistently poor children are more than twice as likely to dislike school and have lower educational aspirations with a lack of access to books a key cause, a report by the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) has found.
The research think tank pointed to the need for subsidies to ensure equal access to cultural and sports activities for children and young people of all economic backgrounds, and to ensure positive school environments to mitigate the impact of poverty.
Prior research had identified a link between childhood poverty and worse educational outcomes, but there had been little research to explain why this link existed, the ESRI said. The report, funded by Department of Children, Disability and Equality , attempted to fill that research gap.
About half of Irish children were in poverty at some stage before the age of 13, with one in five children experiencing three or more spells before they became a teenager. Each period in poverty was found to cause a decline in reading level.
Persistently poor schoolchildren in Ireland are more than twice as likely to dislike school than those who have not experienced poverty, the report found.
The gap in test scores was credited by the ESRI report to be down to poverty restricting access to books, a lack of time spent reading to the child by the time they are five, and other home activities that help enhance cognitive development.
“Children living in poverty are less likely to be involved in cultural and sports activities, which plays an important role in mediating the effects on test scores at age nine,” the report reads.
As the child grows older, the influence of home factors is lessened and school and teachers have a greater influence.
[ More children missing school today than before Covid pandemic, says ESRI report Opens in new window ]
However, among children aged nine who were classified as being in poverty throughout much of their childhood, 9 per cent said they ‘never like school’ compared with just 4 per cent of those who were never poor. The report found a similar gap in attitudes among 13-year-olds.
Spending time in poverty also leads children to have a lower expectation of their possible future educational achievements. While nearly four in five (79 per cent) children aged 13 expect to get a degree later in life, this figure falls to just 62 per cent among persistently poor children.
ESRI research professor Emer Smyth, one of the report’s authors, said its findings “point to the importance of providing access to a range of extracurricular activities and promoting parent-child reading”.
She said “better-quality relationships between teachers and students” were found to improve children’s engagement in school and directly with those teachers’ subjects, and enhances their “educational expectations and cognitive development”.
“School climate is key in addressing the impact of poverty on children and young people.”
[ Chronic absenteeism: More than 75,000 secondary students missed 20 days in school year Opens in new window ]
The Minister for Children, Norma Foley , said the findings show the importance of “tackling child poverty given the impact that it has on children’s education and life opportunities”.
“Helping children to access supports at home as well as at school, and providing after-school access to sports, drama, art and music are important parts of giving every child the best possible start,” the Minister said.

title: Manchester City’s inflatable bananas are back. Business is booming for Imre Varadi
description: The story behind them? It all goes back to 1987, when City were rubbish
content:
I nflatable bananas, you might have noticed, have become quite a thing again at Manchester City since they were found guilty of all those charges. Their supporters have been bringing mountains of them to games, with Phil Foden even carrying one to a post-match interview on Saturday.
The story behind them? It all goes back to 1987, when City were rubbish. A supporter by the name of Frank Newton brought a five-foot inflatable banana to a Second Division game against Plymouth. Why? Just for a laugh, and soon enough most City fans were brandishing them. “Gallows humour”, as the Manchester Evening News called it, “it helped fans cope with lacklustre performances on the pitch”.
And, eh, naturally enough, one of their strikers at the time, Imre Varadi, became known as, well, “Imre Banana”. Was he offended? Heck no, he even has a website called ImreBanana.com where, yes, he sells inflatable bananas at a tenner a pop.
Seeing as they had become a thing of the past, you can’t imagine the fellah was earning a whole lot from his business ... until last week. Now? “I’m getting thousands of orders from all over the world – demand has absolutely gone through the roof,” he told The Sun. “They are bringing a lot of joy to the game.” And to his bank balance, hopefully.
Liverpool had a profitable Champions League visit to Austria last Wednesday when they collected three points from their 6-3 win over LASK. And it proved to be a profitable trip for some of their supporters too, after they collected empty beer cups around the stadium in Linz.
According to the Daily Mail, LASK are big in to “eco-friendly schemes” and so offer €3 for every returned empty beer cup (which makes them sound a touch pricey). Naturally then, Liverpool fans busied themselves collecting the empties, with some gathering so many, they covered the cost of their trip to Austria. Mind you, it meant they missed quite a bit of the action. “I think I saw one of the nine goals scored,” as one of them told the paper.
Is there any sign of an end to the aggro between Cristiano Ronaldo and Portugal’s manager Jorge Jesus? Not really. And you can’t imagine the latter’s lawyer, Luis Henrique, has helped. He has been a long-time columnist for the Record newspaper, but announced last week that he’s quitting because Ronaldo is a shareholder in the company that owns it.
His message to Ronaldo in his final column? “You have achieved something that no opponent ever managed: to spoil our ability to remember all the good you have brought us. You surround yourself more and more with those who tell you what you want to hear and less and less with those who tell you what you need to hear. That is the fate of gods and autocrats: they end up alone on Olympus, surrounded by mirrors.” Divil a sign of an olive branch, then.
Stop what you're doing and watch this unreal penalty from the Caribbean Cup pic.twitter.com/iqFdr1gPDL
To be honest, some of us thought this was an AI creation, but apparently Trayvone Reid’s interminable penalty run-up in the Caribbean Cup game between Mount Pleasant and Club Sando was real. The Sun’s headline was most excellent: “Pen will it end?”
“For me, they should start on minus 25 points for the next five years. Also, a transfer ban for five years and a big fine. The ownership should be forced to sell the club, and there should be bans for everyone who has been in on this.” – Apart from that, Peter Schmeichel hopes the Premier League will go easy on Manchester City.
That’s how much Mikel Arteta will earn a day after signing his new contract with Arsenal. A week later? The club announced they were cutting 60 jobs. Timing? It’s everything.
“The executive of Real Madrid has an orchestra of mouthpieces. The script is always the same. It reminds one of the propaganda techniques that Goebbels used.” – How have La Liga president Javier Tebas’s remarks gone down? Not great.
“Personal preference is one thing; you prefer Messi, Pelé or Maradona. I understand that, and I respect it. But saying that Cristiano isn’t complete is a lie.” – Cristiano , of course.
“Yes, we’re a bit fragile, and we concede poor goals, but I’m quite excited – I think we’re actually probably playing the best football in the Premier League.” – Jason Cundy hailing his old club Spurs after seeing the bottom-of-the-table side fail to win any of their first six games and fail to score in the first four. Easily excited, that lad.

title: Did this hawk kill the pigeon in Dublin?
description: Eye On Nature: Éanna Ní Lamhna responds to your notes and queries on mushrooms, caterpillars and hawks
content:
I spotted this hawk feasting on a pigeon. Would it have hunted the pigeon first? He seemed to be taking his time with it, over an hour from when I first spotted it, to when the hawk was sick of his audience and flew off with his lunch. Mairead Slater, Clonskeagh, Dublin
This is a female sparrowhawk, which is larger than the male and has dark grey back feathers and white and brown stripes along the breast. It is an urban predator and feeds on birds by gliding low along hedges and in gardens and then ambushing the unsuspecting prey. It catches its prey with its talons and then uses them to stab and crush it to death. It then plucks and eats most of it unhurriedly on the spot.
Can I have an identification for this spider please. It was found on a flowerpot in my back garden in Ashbourne, Co Meath. Ailbe Kit McFadden, age six
This is a running grass spider – most likely Tibellus oblongus because of the two black spots at the rear of its abdomen. It normally occurs on coarse grasses, rushes and heather and is most commonly seen in July, although females can last into the autumn. It doesn’t catch prey in a web but lies stretched out along grass leaves and rushes, waiting for insects to pass.
I photographed these striking purple mushrooms at Ballynafagh Lake, Co Kildare, at the end of September. What are they? Emma Jane Leeson
There are a lot of mushrooms around at the moment. This one is the violet cobweb – Cortinarius violaceus. These are called cobweb mushrooms because there is a cobweb-like veil beneath the gills . The mycologist Hubert Fuller says that, while this group can be demanding when it comes to identifying species, this one is fortunately readily identifiable with its intense deep violet-coloured cap, gills and stem. The cap is dry and finely scaly, as in the image, 10 to 15cm in diameter, while the stem can reach 12cm in height. The cut flesh is said to smell of cedar wood. This is a mycorrhizal fungus, which forms a close mutual partnership with the roots of poplar, birch and beech trees, and is rare in Ireland and Britain.
This strange little insect crossed my path in the ruins of the Dominican Priory in Carlingford recently. It looks spectacular. I wonder what it is called? Úna Uí Dhuinn, Rathfarnham, Dublin
Wonder no more. This is the caterpillar of the pale tussock moth. It has a magnificent appearance with tufts of yellow, red and white hairs. These are nasty things and cause a rash if handled. Birds keep well away from them. This one was on its way, after a summer of feeding on tree leaves, to pupate in a hairy silken cocoon among leaf litter. It passes the winter like this and will appear as a moth in April.
We observed this very unusual insect with fluorescent-coloured legs in our garden in Donacarney, Co Meath. What is it? Is it an invasive species? Lucy and Chris Sweeney
It is an Ichneumon wasp, which are parasitic insects that lay their eggs in the caterpillars of moths and butterflies. These eggs hatch out into grubs that live inside the caterpillar, feeding on the living, growing, poor unfortunate. It eventually pupates inside the now-expiring caterpillar, and bursts forth as an adult from the shrivelled skin, which is about all that is left of it. This species is Pimpla rufipes – the black slip wasp. The protrusion at the back is the ovipositor of this female. They do not sting and yes, they are a native species, not a recent invasive species.

title: Ken Early: The Premier League’s intensity arms race is killing the art of football
description: Obsession with physical duels is turning the world’s richest league into a wasteland for creativity
content:
Manchester United away at Leeds , the red rose against the white, a classic fixture of English football. Such a game is a big attraction even before you consider the circumstances – the morbid spectacle of the latest out-of-his-depth Manchester United manager crumbling under the pressure of bad results, while struggling to manage the fallout of Lisandro Martinez’s attack on the club’s malfunctioning hierarchy.
The game ended in a draw that did little to improve Michael Carrick’s position. The only thing that really stood out about the match was how bad it was.
All the players were running around too fast – at least, the pace at which they were trying to play appeared to be beyond their technical ability. Neither team could string five passes together. The game was just an endless sequence of scraps and tussles all over the pitch, with both teams’ main attacking idea being to get the break from a lucky bounce and flood forward into the unexpected gaps.
It wasn’t just the two Uniteds at Elland Road that produced absolutely appalling football. Brentford’s game against Liverpool was similar. Arsenal ’s trip to Nottingham Forest was grimmer still.
The demands of the current generation of Premier League coaches for ceaseless physical competition all over the pitch have created an absolute wasteland for imagination, creativity and skill.
Liam Delap’s performance for Forest against Arsenal should be studied in this context. He spent much of the game battling under high balls against Gabriel and Ezri Konsa. Often he won these duels, whereupon he would turn and blast a cross into the stands, or dribble a 20-yard shot at David Raya. He never looked like scoring, but he kept battling as fiercely in the closing minutes as he had in the beginning. He had the energy to run in behind Konsa in injury time, but not the technique to get his shot off early enough to beat Konsa’s recovery challenge.
This is the profile of a £50 million centre forward in today’s Premier League.
Player of the Match was Noni Madueke, another technically limited powerhouse, as he had scored the winning goal past Mats Sels with a deflected shot. This is what the Premier League is now. An ultraphysical league that ruthlessly selects for ultraphysical footballers no matter their other shortcomings.
This is good news for players like Delap and Madueke. Other types of players are taking notice. Think back to Lisandro Martinez. When he chose to open fire on United’s directors, it was plainly because he resents his own situation – a fed-up senior player at a team that stubbornly refuses to improve, now old enough, at 29, to worry he might never get the chance to go somewhere better. It was probably the sight of his international centre back partner Cristian Romero enjoying his new life at Atlético Madrid that pushed him over the edge.
[ As chatter around Troy Parrott lulls, everyone’s talking about Jack Moylan Opens in new window ]
Martinez does not want United to trigger their option to extend his contract by one year; otherwise it expires in summer 2027. United would like to replace him with someone better, but it seems unlikely they will want him walking away on a free transfer, so the unhappy embrace will probably continue until 2028.
He has at least made a lot of money from his association with United, so his time there hasn’t been a complete waste. But considering his attributes as a footballer, it would have been a much better decision to avoid the Premier League altogether.
It’s clear that at the football level, moving to the Premier League has been a disaster for Martinez. Erik ten Hag brought him to Manchester from Ajax because he believed at that time that he was the best defender in the world in build-up play. How often have we seen these qualities in the Premier League? Being a centre back in England is much more about fighting duels than playing nice passes. The demands of the league have been too much for Martinez’s body. He has suffered a succession of serious injuries and has missed nearly as many matches as he has played.
What might have happened if he had gone to Atleti or Inter rather than United? He might have stayed fit enough to play 200 matches and built a reputation as one of the world’s top defensive playmakers. In the Premier League he is just an undersized defender who is liable to be bullied, as he was by Tottenham’s Dominic Solanke last week. Against Leeds, he took a knock in a duel with Dominic Calvert-Lewin and was subbed at half-time, another multi-week lay-off in prospect.
The main criticism of Carrick has been that his team consistently fails to match the intensity they are faced with every week in the Premier League. He was not an “intensity” player, and it appears he is not an “intensity” coach either. In the current Premier League context, his long-term prospects look dim.
[ ‘Like being a s**t celebrity’: Inside the world of top-level football referees Opens in new window ]
But the issue is much bigger than Carrick. Last Wednesday, PSG continued their multiyear project of making a show of all the top Premier League teams by shredding England’s best technical side, Manchester City .
Much has been made of PSG’s ability to rest key players so they are fresh for Europe, while the squad players take care of the relatively undemanding French League program. Ousmane Dembele joked that he had played so well against City he must be due another vacation.
Underlying that is a serious point. Could Dembele have won the Ballon d’Or if he had joined Arsenal and had to fight duels for 4,000 minutes a season? Would PSG be able to slice up the City midfield the way they did last Wednesday night if every weekend they were involved in attritional battles like Leeds v Man United or Forest v Arsenal? Unlikely.
We hear a lot about the Premier League’s incomparable financial advantages, but the clubs have become trapped in the logic of an intensity arms race, and the only solution anyone ever proposes is to add more intensity.
The outcome is that clubs like PSG, Bayern, Barcelona and Real Madrid can make a more compelling offer to top players than their counterparts in England. That’s why they have footballers like Dembele, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, Lamine Yamal and Michael Olise, while viewers of the world’s richest league are watching Delap and Madueke. For the powerhouses, the Premier League remains the place to be. For the best players, the real football is elsewhere.

title: ‘A hovercraft I bought many years ago is still sitting in the same place as the day I got it’
description: Me & My Money: James Hennessy, founder of the National Reptile Zoo, Kilkenny
content:
James Hennessy is the founder of the National Reptile Zoo, based in Kilkenny , which works to advance environmental literacy, conservation practice and curiosity towards reptiles, amphibians, invertebrates and their habitats .
Definitely a spender. I’m also a firm believer that because you can’t take it with you when you’re gone, you need to enjoy it now, live in the moment and bring everyone along on the journey with you.
I worked on a schoolfriend’s farm in primary school. It started out just helping out while hanging out with my friends. Eventually his dad would give me the occasional five pounds. They had a marsh on their land, and that’s probably where my obsession with frogs started to grow into my current obsession with all things slimy or scaly.
Personally, I’d do lots of shopping around and research but equipment for the zoo tends to be very specialised. Unfortunately, there aren’t a lot of options when it comes to shopping around for that.
Two years ago, I bought an electric VW van for almost €60,000. It was a slightly worrying outlay at the time, but 100,000km later, it’s still going strong and is charged mostly by the solar array that we have on the roof.
In 2006, I bought a Toyota Hilux pickup. Almost three-quarters of a million kilometres on the clock later and I still have it. It has dragged building material and equipment around and has taken me on many adventures, and it’s still going strong. While we use the electric van mostly for work, I still have the Hilux for redundancy.
I bought a hovercraft many years ago, which is still in the same condition and sitting in the same position as the day I bought it.
Only when I’m in a region where the culture allows for it. In Ireland, I have a very good grasp of the value of labour and materials; I don’t begrudge people trying to make a living and find it a bit insulting when people try to devalue someone’s labour or skills.
I don’t, mainly because I’ve not had enough exposure to it to have what I would consider a good enough grasp of it. I also prefer to see a more immediate return on any spare funds I might have.
[ Investing in cryptocurrency seems ‘like a more upmarket approach to gambling’ Opens in new window ]
I’ve got a very basic pension plan but I don’t have a plan to ever retire. As I become less able to work, I’d hope to be able to still potter about the place, giving some kind of input.
I bought a vintage three-wheel car in the UK as a project car and drove it back to Ireland. The plan, as it is for a lot of these things for me, is to restore it, sell it and raise some funding. Is it good value for money? So far, I can neither confirm nor deny that.
Yes, quite a few. Big purchases are relative, of course. When I was around 12, I spent two years saving for a guitar, paying money into the guitar shop’s savings scheme each week.
Yes. I blew the engine in that vintage three-wheel car I recently bought.
[ The hard work and satisfaction in restoring classic cars: 'It's a learning process' Opens in new window ]
Not at all. While I will often take chances on purchases and business decisions, I don’t have any interest in betting. I see it as a bit pointless.
My best habit is that I always tend to have a financial backup. While I enjoy living financially for the moment, I’ll always make sure I have that. My worst habit is impulse buying, and the stranger the purchase, the bigger the impulse.
I always try to have some cash on me, so I have €45. It’s a good habit if you travel.

title: Women and children given weeks to ‘uproot our whole lives’ as homeless facility closes
description: Rendu Apartments in Dublin’s north inner city does not meet fire safety requirements, says Depaul
content:
A number of women have said they fear where they will end up after being informed that an emergency accommodation centre in Dublin ’s north inner city will close down next month.
Rendu Apartments, operated by Depaul and funded by the Dublin Region Homeless Executive ( DRHE ), provides self-contained apartments for women and children who are experiencing homelessness .
Eighteen women and children live in the centre at present, Depaul said. A number of residents have serious medical conditions, including cardiac issues.
In a letter sent on September 29th, Depaul informed residents that the building, owned by the Daughters of Charity, does not meet fire safety requirements. The letter, seen by The Irish Times, said “significant levels of work” were required to bring the building “up to regulations in the short term”.
“Depaul worked closely with DRHE to source funding to undertake the work required; however, unfortunately funding has not been secured,” the letter said, adding that the building was being closed on November 27th “with deep regret”.
Residents say they fear being placed in homeless hostels that may not be suitable for children or those with long-term medical conditions. Some of the women have experienced domestic violence in the past and do not feel comfortable being housed with men.
Some residents said they asked if they could stay in Rendu until January, so their children could celebrate Christmas together, but were told this was not possible.
“Santy comes into the building, [the children] love that ... It’s very special,” one woman said, adding that residents were given weeks “to uproot our whole lives”.
[ Children Ombudsman ‘deeply concerned’ about changes to homeless accommodation eligibility Opens in new window ]
“There’s women in there with life-threatening conditions ... It’s the most vulnerable of society,” she said.
This woman has dealt with addiction issues but said she has been sober for years and worked hard to get her life “back on track”.
“All this trauma is after affecting my recovery; I’ve never been so tested.”
The woman and her young child were recently moved to another homeless facility in the area, but some other residents don’t know where they will be sent.
Another woman, who suffered a cardiac arrest in recent months, said she fears being sent somewhere that does not meet her medical needs. She said she has had multiple panic attacks due to the stress of the situation.
“I’ve been fighting, advocating for myself to get properly housed ... I have two more surgeries to do as well.”
Depaul, which has been running the Rendu facility for 14 years, said in a statement: “In recent years it had become clear that the building was reaching the end of its current life and that it was critical and clear that plans had to be made for its longer term future to continue as a resource to serve the community.
“Following a recent statutory fire inspection report of the building, it has become apparent that extensive works must be completed to maintain the current accommodation services in the building.”
Depaul said carrying out short-term remediation works on the building would be “costly” and “would not constitute value for money”.
After consultation with the DRHE and the Daughters of Charity, it was agreed that this approach “was not a responsible use of charitable donations or public funds ... therefore closing the service was agreed as the most prudent course of action”.
Depaul said it was closing the facility “with sadness” and would work with the DRHE to “ensure all current service users are relocated to appropriate accommodation suitable for their needs”.
A spokeswoman said the Daughters of Charity “have been working very closely with Depaul” on the matter.
[ ‘An intelligent, nonconformist man’: Galway’s homeless millionaire Opens in new window ]
In a statement, Dublin City Council (DCC) said Depaul has “support in principle” from the council for “a longer term plan to develop social housing together with community services at this location”.
“As the service cannot continue in its current use without significant capital works, current residents will be relocated to the most appropriate accommodation suitable to their needs.”
DCC said there is “sufficient alternative emergency accommodation available” to find new places for residents to stay.
“We know that the change of emergency accommodation is very disruptive to residents and we are committed to making the most appropriate alternatives available.”

title: Cutting Palestine flag necklace from Cheap Irish Homes episode a ‘mistake’, says RTÉ
description: Show participant wearing necklace was not informed of edit prior to broadcast and lodged complaint with Coimisiún na Meán
content:
RTÉ has said it will review its processes on impartiality guidelines after a Palestinian flag necklace was edited out of an episode of Cheap Irish Homes in post-production, without the consent of the woman wearing it.
Claire Molloy, who appeared in an episode of the property programme last month, has lodged a complaint with RTÉ and Coimisiún na Meán over the issue, claiming “this selective editing compromises the broadcaster’s obligation to fairness and impartiality”.
RTÉ confirmed the footage was edited and said “a mistake” was made “in the interpretation and application of our guidelines”.
“These are judgment calls in a production process, and these edits were made in good faith and in an effort to adhere to obligations on impartiality and RTÉ’s guidelines on the undue prominence of symbols and emblems,” a statement said.
“RTÉ acknowledges that this matter could have been handled differently. With that in mind, RTÉ will review its processes and procedures for the application of its guidelines.
“While RTÉ does not believe there is any regulatory contravention or breach of guidelines arising from this, we do acknowledge an excessively strict interpretation of them.”
Molloy, an accountant based in Dublin, and her partner Peter Foley took part in filming for the programme last May, looking at houses in Tipperary. The episode was broadcast on RTÉ One on September 29th.
While watching the episode, Molloy noticed the necklace she was wearing during filming was no longer visible, while footage of her wearing a blue keffiyeh scarf was also used sparingly and mainly in wide-angle shots.
Molloy said no one raised her necklace or scarf as an issue during filming, and that if she had been asked to remove either, she “probably wouldn’t have gone ahead with the filming”.
She said she was not asked to sign a release form prior to filming. RTÉ and Cameo Productions, the company which makes the programme, did not reply when asked if Molloy had signed a release form.
Molloy, who has previously volunteered in the West Bank, said she regularly wears the necklace and scarf in solidarity with the Palestinian people.
“I was just so shocked that [the necklace] was removed from my person without them telling me,” she said.
Molloy wrote to RTÉ to complain earlier this month. An executive producer with Cameo Productions replied to Molloy and acknowledged the necklace had been removed during post-production.
‘It is important to also acknowledge that some sections were retained; the blue keffiyeh is included in several shots and is part of the thumbnail for the programme on the RTÉ Player’
“The pendant in question was inadvertently overlooked during filming and was not identified as an editorial issue at the time,” an email sent on October 12th said.
“Once identified during post-production, it was considered in the context of RTÉ’s guidelines because it contained imagery associated with a matter of political and public debate which was unrelated to the subject matter of the programme.
“It was felt that there was a reasonable basis to suspect certain parts of the content may be, or may be perceived as being, in contravention of the guidelines.
“It is important to also acknowledge that some sections were retained; the blue keffiyeh is included in several shots and is part of the thumbnail for the programme on the RTÉ Player.”
The producer wrote that decisions regarding editing footage “can be difficult and are not straightforward”.
“RTÉ is responsible for what it broadcasts and at all times retains the editorial control of its content; we as producers and RTÉ as a broadcaster must therefore make every effort to be in compliance with its obligations,” the email added.
When asked for comment, the producer said Cameo Productions did not wish to add anything beyond RTÉ’s statement.
Coimisiún na Meán said it “does not comment on individual complaints”, but noted that members of the public “have a right to complain if they believe that they have seen something broadcast ... that does not meet statutory or regulatory standards”.
“In the first instance, we advise members of the public who wish to complain about broadcast content to complain to the broadcaster concerned,” a statement said.
“If they are unsatisfied with the response they receive from the broadcaster, they can contact Coimisiún na Meán. All complaints received by An Coimisiún will be processed as standard under our statutory complaints handling process.”

title: Dublin Marathon countdown: Essential dos and don’ts before Sunday’s classic endurance test
description: This is no time for any cramming or binge-training ahead of Sunday’s early morning start
content:
The best thing about counting down the last days before the Irish Life Dublin Marathon is that participants have all the hard training already done. At least it should be, because this is no time for any cramming or binge-training ahead of Sunday’s early morning start. No time for any second thoughts either.
For all the 22,500 runners who have signed up, however, there is still time to undo some of that hard training. So, it doesn’t matter if you’re trying to win it, or simply trying to finish it – these are some of the essential dos and don’ts in the week before any big city marathon which can ultimately help make the difference between triumph and disaster.
Do start tapering right back on the training, reducing it down to easy and slow runs only. Then nothing more than a jog on the day before. Do pay more attention to eating well, sleeping well, and hydrating well. Every runner has their own favourite method of carbo-loading, just go easy the evening before. And don’t chance anything different.
Do start familiarising yourself with the Dublin Marathon course, even if you’ve run it before. Whether you’re mapping it out in 26.2 miles, 42.2km, or 138,336ft, the 45th staging of the event will follow the same course as last year. Starting on Leeson Street Lower, shortly before arrival at St Stephen’s Green, it finishes later on Mount Street Upper, just beyond the Pepper Canister Church.
The most testing part of the course comes between miles 20 and 22, around the hilly Clonskeagh and Roebuck Roads. But don’t panic! From there it’s a straight downhill along Foster Avenue, and then a (more or less) flat run to the finish.
Do plan on getting to the start line in plenty of time – at least an hour beforehand, and allow for a gentle 10-minute-or-so warm-up. Each of the 22,500 runners will have their own ambitions, but the same running rules apply to all. There are five different start times beginning with wheelchair participants at 8.40am, followed by four major waves, each at 20-minute intervals. Wave 1 (Orange) starts at 8.45am, Wave 2 (Green) at 9.05am, Wave 3 (Blue) at 9.25am and Wave 4 (Purple) at 9.45am.
Wave positions are allocated by your predicted finishing time, and while moving up to a faster wave is not allowed, do feel free to move down a wave if you’re no longer confident about your predicted finish time.
The four baggage areas will be in Merrion Square North, with access via Merrion Square West or Lincoln Place. Each area has designated opening times according to runners’ colour-coded race numbers. Only bags that show the official baggage label displaying runners’ race numbers will be accepted.
Don’t try parking anywhere near the start or finish areas, as most final approaches will not be accessible by vehicular traffic. All runners and spectators are advised to use public transport where possible, with both Luas lines expected to be operating as normal.
[ It’s not just the Berlin Marathon. Cheating runners everywhere are now being closely watched Opens in new window ]
Do give yourself plenty of time to pick up your race number. This can only happen in person at the Dublin Marathon Expo, set up at RDS Simmonscourt on Friday (12pm-7pm) and Saturday (9am-6pm). Do remember to bring some form of ID (passport, driving licence, student card, etc).
The actual cut-off time for number collection is 6pm on the Saturday, so don’t be late. The Expo will also have lots of different running brands selling their latest super-shoes and fancy gear, but don’t go wearing these on race day. Well-worn running shoes and socks only.
Don’t dare think about giving away your race number. Or go looking for one. Dublin has a strict zero-tolerance policy for number swapping outside the official transfer window, and accurate participant information is vital in medical emergencies. Any runner found to have transferred, sold or swapped a number outside the official period will be disqualified from Dublin Marathon Group events.
Don’t worry about any need to bring your own drinks and gels supply, unless an essential part of your own routine. The Dublin Marathon has ample refreshment stations – 10 in total – but do look at the map and note where exactly they are. Lucozade Sport is provided at the 9.5-, 13-, 19- and 22-mile marks, and High5 energy gels at the 16- and 22-mile marks.
Do consider following one of the designated Dublin Marathon pacers. If you’re confident about your target finish time, the pacers run at a steady effort throughout, aiming to finish a few seconds under each time band. Pacers are allocated to each wave as follows: Wave 1 – 3:00, 3:10, 3:20; Wave 2 – 3:30, 3:40, 3:50; Wave 3 – 4:00, 4:10, 4:20; Wave 4 – 4:30, 4:40, 4:50, 5:00.
[ Seán Ó Riain: ‘We want to say the Dublin Marathon owns the city on the October bank holiday’ Opens in new window ]
There’s no requirement to sign up to any pacing group in advance. Just turn up at your wave start, look for the pacing runners wearing large balloons, then run as steady as they go.
Do make time for breakfast on Sunday morning, leaving ample time for digestion too, ideally about two hours before your wave start. Munching on a banana or two just before the start is grand, but again, don’t chance anything different – regular caffeine consumption levels included.
Don’t forget that summertime ends and the clocks go back one hour at 2am on Sunday , effectively giving you an extra hour in bed before the run. Finally, don’t forget the most important piece of advice for running a marathon: it’s not the distance that kills, it’s the pace.

title: Bittersweet symphony as Champions Cup opens with three Irish wins
description: Munster overcome Racing at on 10th anniversary of Anthony Foley’s death, with a minute’s silence for Johannesburg Lions’ Hyron Andrews
content:
A s Champions Cup opening weekends go, from an entirely parochial Irish point of view, that wasn’t too bad at all. “It’s a tsunami of glorious attacking quality,” said Mark Robson, and he was only talking about Connacht ’s display against Saracens. Throw in Munster and Leinster ’s meetings with Racing and Clermont and we had ourselves three Irish wins, 126 Irish points and 19 Irish tries. You’d take that.
Leinster were up first and even though they helped themselves to a handsome enough 48-23 bonus-point win away to Clermont, Stephen Ferris, back in the Premier Sports studio, only gave them an 8.5 mark out of 10 for their efforts. That was partly because he adjudged Clermont to be a bit rubbish, Rob Kearney not disagreeing, although he was reasonably complimentary about the man of the match, Sam Prendergast.
When he spoke to the French telly man after, Prendergast was labelled a “demi-d’ouverture” on-screen. We’re going over old ground here, so apologies, but the French terms for rugby positions will never not be lovely.
A demi-d’ouverture sounds much more like a half-completed orchestral piece by Rossini or Brahms, of course, rather than the outhalf person who directs traffic on a rugby pitch. Lovelier still, incidentally, is the term for the scrumhalf: le demi de melee.. That’d be kinda like the Gaelic for the position being an leath shemozzle, which it isn’t. But should be.
Any way, le match du jour proved to be the one over in Galway, Connacht welcoming sort of the Manchester City of rugby, Saracens. Not really in trophy-hauling terms, more down to difficulties understanding money rules down the years.
As Mark noted, having been drawn in a pool featuring five former winners of the competition, Connacht were “in with carnivores”, and finding themselves 12-0 down after 12 minutes, it looked like they might be eaten alive.
But? They responded with just the 19 unanswered points, Mark’s companion Darren Cave struggling to keep up. “It’s caught us sleeping in the commentary box,” he said, “we were thinking of our next pun.” Soon after. “It’s Saracens’ turn to throw haymakers back ... you just wonder will Connacht do any form of shadow boxing?”
The tries kept on coming. “We’ve already been treated to nine, all from different areas of the cheese board,” said Mark. Whether this is an actual rugby term with which us non-rugger people are unfamiliar, or whether it was simply a reference to the variety of scores on view, who knows? “It hasn’t just been a Gouda game, it’s been un-Brie-lievably grate – I wouldn’t rule Sars out, though, this is not a feta-compli,” Darren didn’t reply, completely missing a trick.
Saracens wouldn’t lay down, so the west couldn’t rest easy, Mark wondering, even in the dying stages, if they might still “take a bit of air out of this Connacht Hindenburg”. Unlike the Hindenburg, though, Connacht landed safely at the end of a breathlessly tremendous game.
On to Cork for Munster against Racing at Páirc Uí Chaoimh . A poignant evening too, of course, with the marking of the 10th anniversary of Anthony Foley’s death.
“Axel was the embodiment of everything good about Munster rugby,” Simon Zebo had said on The Late Late Show the evening before. “The backs against the wall, the underdogs, doing the impossible, lifting the Champions Cup, the first captain to do so for the province. He means a whole lot to a whole lot of people in Munster and Irish rugby, and I’ve no doubt his legacy will live on forever. It’s cemented.”
And when Premier Sports introduced its coverage of the game, we saw Zebo looking through the collection of photos of Foley displayed at the ground, each of them picking out memorable landmarks in his storied career.
At the best of times, There is an Isle and Stand up and Fight would stir you, but when the Shannon RFC choir sang the former before the game in honour of Foley, and the Munster players gathered in a circle to sing the latter post-match, they were very beautiful tributes.
And before the game, a minute’s silence for the Johannesburg Lions’ Hyron Andrews who died on Saturday at the age of just 31 before his side’s game against La Rochelle. The cruelty of it all.

title: Sex trafficking victims ‘inappropriately’ housed in direct provision, charity says
description: Human trafficking “in every corner of Ireland’ as 284 victims now engaging with charity
content:
Women who have been victims of human trafficking are being housed “inappropriately in direct provision congregated settings”, according to the chief executive of Ruhama .
The charity, which supports women impacted by prostitution, sex trafficking and commercial sexual exploitation, saw a 31 per cent increase last year in the number of trafficking victims engaging with it.
Its chief executive, Barbara Condon, said human trafficking was now “in every corner of Ireland”.
In 2025, 284 used the charity’s services, a significant increase which “reflects how the global epidemic of violence against women is happening every day” and all across Ireland.
Noting that “many victims” were being housed “inappropriately” in congregated settings in direct provision, Condon stressed that “safe, appropriate and specialist accommodation” was needed to protect victims and to allow them recover.
“Without a secure place to live, it is almost impossible for women to rebuild their lives,” she said, calling for their current housing to be “addressed as a priority”.
In total, 1,242 individuals engaged with Ruhama in 2025, representing a 10 per cent increase from 2024; 77 of those victims were male.
Data from Ruhama points to Nigerian women being the largest cohort of women victims of prostitution and human trafficking – making up more than half of the known human trafficking victims in Ireland at 177. Prostitution victims from Zimbabwe (50) and Ireland (46) were the next most frequent.
Ruhama said its case workers recorded a 77 per cent increase in the number of victims seeking suicide prevention assistance.
“Accommodation issues remain a significant challenge, with service users requiring support in relation to Ipas (International Protection Accommodation Service) transfers, the housing crisis, unsuitable accommodation and experiences of homelessness,” the charity said.
Immigration decisions around the right to work, Ruhama said, have left women “more vulnerable to sexual exploitation” and have impacted their mental health .
The service said it had facilitated nearly 1,200 appointments for victims with its trauma therapists and had helped 190 service users to start new education courses within the year.
In the education system, however, the lack of part-time courses and an “increasingly hostile housing environment” for migrants were raised as some of the barriers facing victims.
The charity also trains people working in the Irish immigration system how to identify victims of human trafficking.

title: ‘I never thought I would do my Junior Cert’: Inside the centre helping teens stay in education
description: About 1,000 teenagers leave education each year before they have attained a Junior Certificate
content:
F or Sean Moore (16) from west Dublin , secondary school was “just bad”. He found it difficult to settle, was “getting into trouble” and “just thought [he] wasn’t a school person”.
Around the time of his mother’s death, as he was turning 14, he disengaged from school altogether. He remained out of education for more than a year.
“I felt really down. I was stressed. I was bored. I wanted to be in a school, but I didn’t know if we could find one. I never thought my nanny would find one as good as this,” he says, sitting in a classroom at the Carline centre in Lucan .
Carline, an out-of-school education centre for adolescents aged 12 to 17 for whom all other interventions to get them back into school have failed, gets them to Junior Certificate and supports them beyond that.
Founded in the 1990s by a local nun, it has been managed by the Peter McVerry Trust since 2019.
Like other such facilities, it has a growing waiting list, with referrals coming via Tusla , schools and families. It has 30 places, 15 in a city-centre location. It has to turn young people away every year.
“Generally, every young person referred into us has suffered adverse childhood trauma or has grown up in a very challenging environment,” says Sarah Morrissey, principal and head of youth services with the Trust.
“Since Covid we are seeing more children referred in with significant mental health difficulties .”
Students here are taking seven Junior Cert subjects rather than the usual nine. “Our trauma-informed approach enables the student first and foremost to feel safe and supported by a team. There’s eye contact, smiles, warmth, support,” says Morrissey.
“We have small classes. We don’t have a uniform or books. We don’t do homework. The kids don’t have to bring anything here other than them themselves. We feed them, nurture them. They have a home-cooked lunch every day. That is really important.”
Teaching is at a pace that suits the young people – some are taught individually, and subjects are often taught differently – fewer long texts, and more videos and project work. Maths may be taught through playing dominoes or scrabble, or baking, with ingredients to measure.
“If we weren’t here, I believe not one of the 30 kids here would be in school, not one,” Morrissey says.
Nationally, about 1,000 teenagers leave education each year before they have attained a Junior Certificate – the most basic qualification without which it is “near impossible to progress and thrive in adulthood”, says Morrissey.
Some have been expelled from schools, some are unable to cope with school and “many ... were reported as experiencing severe emotional and social difficulties”, a department of education report, Review of Out of School Education Provision, commissioned in 2018, found.
There is no data on whether all who disengage from school are re-engaged in education.
[ We are walking our way into a fundamentally flawed education system, and we have been warned Opens in new window ]
The report identified 23 out-of-school centres around the State, “managed and staffed by a committed and caring group of educators ... taking a holistic approach ... [providing] wraparound supports ... catering for ... educational, social, behavioural and mental development”.
Each operates slightly differently and is disparately located, leaving children in some areas with few or no options.
“The lack of standardised structures in the current out-of-school provision leaves it vulnerable in terms of governance, funding and staffing,” says the report.
Its 2022 recommendations, including standardised referral pathways, governance structures and resourcing, remain unimplemented.
Founded in 2007, iScoil provides online and blended in-person/online education across the 26 counties.
Referrals from agencies like Tusla are growing: from 105 in the 2018/19 school year to 344 last year. The numbers iScoil has to turn away are also increasing – from 55 in 2023 to 134 last year.
Chief executive Brian Fitzsimons called on the department to implement its own report, saying each child, “no matter the gaps in their schooling, has huge potential and, we must not forget, a legal entitlement to education.
“The reality of having to turn away State referrals and leave highly vulnerable young people with no education options is not good enough. Quality alternative education providers need investment and an adequate policy platform,” he said.
Back in Carline, Nicole Sweeney (16) tells of her delight at completing her Junior Cert last June.
She had left secondary school three weeks into second year and was out of education all that year.
“I was having panic attacks in my old school. There was no support, and I was feeling sick and scared going in. Here, the teachers are different – much more open. They’ll ask, ‘Why are you acting out?’ ‘How are you today?’ There’s always support for you.”
She did “really well” in her exams, including a distinction in English.
“When I was out of school, I never thought I would even do my Junior Cert. I was so overwhelmed when I got my results. I started crying and all; I was so happy. My mam was crying as well, saying, ‘I’m so proud of you. I knew you could do it.’”
[ My son has become disinterested in school. The principal regularly uses the phrase ‘parental responsibility’ Opens in new window ]
She plans to study childcare. Sean hopes to get an electrician apprenticeship.
A spokesman for the department said: “The department is currently finalising the first phase of an implementation plan [for the report] that will be presented to the minister shortly.
“It takes account of the many positive developments in the education space, to support children and young people at risk of disengagement and early school leaving, since the implementation group commenced its work in 2022.”

title: Pilita Clark: Why London looks better than ever for a business shindig
description: In fragile times, it pays to view your own city through the eyes of strangers
content:
As deadly Houthi missiles smashed into Riyadh’s international airport last week , people from around the world still made their way to the Saudi capital for one of the biggest oil and gas industry conferences on the calendar.
When they arrived at the WPC Energy Congress, in some cases having driven for hours to avoid flying, they found a number of prominent names on the agenda had gone missing. The bosses of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell and BP had pulled out after the attacks, which killed at least a dozen people and injured hundreds more .
I expect more big names will skip another international conference due to start in a week in Riyadh – the so-called Davos in the Desert.
This probably won’t be the last time this happens in a complicated world showing no sign of improvement. A string of Middle East trade shows and conventions has already been cancelled or deferred as the Iran war grinds on. The street arrests and travel restrictions by Donald Trump ’s administration continue to drive international academic conferences away from the US to other countries.
As a frequent conference-goer myself, these dispiriting sights have made me wonder: which cities are now deemed the best places for business gatherings?
To my surprise, it turns out I am living in one of them.
London was named the best city in Europe for events and meetings this year for the fourth year in a row in a closely watched ranking by the Cvent conference tech group.
Yet again we beat Barcelona, Madrid and Lisbon. Even Paris only managed fifth place.
I say “we”, even though I am a transplanted Australian, one of the more than 40 per cent of Londoners who are foreign-born. As it happens, that is a higher share than you will find in Paris, Berlin and even New York City – a pleasing reminder that London is one of the most diverse major cities on the planet.
Take the Tube that we all moan about constantly, and is admittedly expensive, but still zips you across the city in a sliver of the time it takes to cover such distances in other big cities
Cvent makes scant mention of this in its list of reasons for ranking London so highly. But the factors it does cite underscore how revealing it is to look at your city as an outsider.
The sprawling conference centres I am occasionally required to trek out to for work are apparently world-class.
London Southend Airport, which I have never technically been to, means we have six airports. There are also more than 80 Michelin -starred restaurants and, by Cvent’s count, 200 museums, 270 theatres, 857 art galleries and four Unesco World Heritage sites. If you are wondering, they are the Tower of London, the Palace (and Abbey) of Westminster, Kew Gardens, and maritime Greenwich.
All this helps to explain why the London Convention Bureau, a division of the city’s official growth agency, is expecting close to 80,000 convention visitors this year. Thousands of rheumatologists and urologists have already been for their latest shindigs. The 44th World Scout Conference is due next year, along with hundreds of port and harbour delegates and a slew of tech conventions.
The striking thing is, the big draws for convention delegates are just a fraction of what London now offers its full-time residents.
As of this year, there is year-round outdoor swimming in, of all places, Canary Wharf. You can get there on the Elizabeth Line railway that has transformed cross-city travel. Or cycle there via the cycle superhighways that have revolutionised two-wheeled transport.
Or take the Tube that we all moan about constantly, and is admittedly expensive, but still zips you across the city in a sliver of the time it takes to cover such distances in other big cities. And you don’t even need to queue up for a ticket. Just swipe a credit card on the turnstile.
Next week, something even more astonishing will begin. After years of wrangling and false starts, a stretch of Oxford Street nearly 1km long will be closed to traffic as the famed shopping street at long last starts to become pedestrianised.
[ Is London ‘lawless’ or the safest big city in the western world? Take your pick Opens in new window ]
As usual, critics are predicting mayhem. Diverted traffic will clog side streets. Bin collections won’t work. People will feel unsafe at night, and so on.
I suspect the doubters will all be proved wrong and the move will be so successful that we will regret it not happening years ago.
At least I hope so. Watching a city brighten and improve is a pleasure for visitors and residents alike. At a time when war and political strife stalk ever more unlikely places, these are gains that should be celebrated – and never taken for granted. – Copyright The Financial Times

title: Joe Humphreys: Fr Dougal Maguire hit on an under-recognised truth about faith and religion
description: Catholic theologian and philosopher Tomáš Halík argues that the difference between belief and non-belief is not as great as you’d think
content:
I f you were looking for someone to give direction to Ireland at this juncture in our history, you probably wouldn’t think of a 78-year-old priest from Prague . But then Tomáš Halík is not an ordinary cleric.
The Catholic theologian, philosopher and author was active in the “underground church” during communist rule in then Czechoslovakia. He has worked as a psychotherapist with drug addicts, supports gay marriage and other liberal causes, and is outspoken on world affairs, describing as “genocide” both Israel’s actions in Gaza and Russia’s war on Ukraine .
But what really makes Halík interesting is his view of faith. The difference between belief and non-belief is not as great as you’d think, so Halík argues. We typically think of faith as acceptance of a set of principles but, he suggests, a non-believer may have more of the “spirit” of Christianity than a pious churchgoer.
Acknowledging the rise of “nones” across Europe – 14 per cent of the Irish population said they had no religion at the last Census in 2022 – Halík boldly states: “The time has come for Christianity to transcend itself.” Its future “will depend primarily on the extent to which Christians relate to the spiritual seekers among the nones”.
How you believe is as important as what you believe, Halík writes in The Afternoon of Christianity. “If we want to understand this world, we must discard dogmatic adherence to the principle that ‘a’ cannot be ‘non-a’ at the same time.”
Halík (who I’d never heard of until a kindly reader of this column recently recommended him to me) is attracted to the notion of “anatheism” promoted by Irish philosopher Richard Kearney . This points to a “god after god”. As Kearney puts it, “anatheism is a radical opening to someone or something that was lost and forgotten by Western metaphysics and needs to be recalled again.”
The key word here is “opening”. The answer to the puzzle of life, Halík and Kearney suggest, is not faith per se – let alone dogmatic faith – but rather an “openness” to something beyond the purely material or measurable.
Halík has gained a strong following among liberal members of the church. But, if – like me – you’re in the “lapsed Catholic” bracket, or otherwise of an atheistic persuasion, you may wonder is there anything in Halík for you?
[ Confessions of a recovering atheist: I now appreciate the allure of faith Opens in new window ]
I believe there is. In Ireland, Catholics are often sneered at for holding contradictory beliefs. Sometimes it’s played for laughs. In Father Ted, Ardal O’Hanlon’s character Fr Dougal Maguire innocently proclaims that basic tenets of the faith are “mad”. In one scene, he tells a bishop: “You know the way God made us all? ... And when we die we’re all going to heaven? Well, that’s the bit I have trouble with.”
But Halík sees no contradiction in Dougal’s doubt. Nor it seems did Pope Francis who famously said good atheists can go to heaven – and perhaps relatedly invited O’Hanlon to the Vatican with other comedians in 2024. It’s not that faith makes no difference. But the line between belief and non-belief is permeable.
Christianity, of course, is not the only option in the marketplace of belief systems – some might look to eastern mysticism, or some to nature, for spiritual nourishment. However, Christianity merits special attention in Ireland due to its link to our ancestors. It connects us to a more ancient way of thinking about moral character and our place in the universe that is both Christian and pre-Christian. And, as the French philosopher Simone Weil , said: “To be rooted is perhaps the most important and least recognised need of the human soul.”
What are these ancient ways of thinking? Three dimensions stand out.
First, the idea that things in the natural world (human included) have inherent value, and are not just valuable because they are useful or because they are means to an end.
Second, the idea that cruelty, envy, pride and other vices are types of self-harm, and that you need to protect your soul from such base instincts.
Third, the idea that there are truths beyond what science or the “knowledge economy” tells us, and that these truths include moral truths.
These beliefs aren’t unique to any one philosophy or religion, which is why Halík sees scope for people across the religious divide to build alliances and to support one other – spiritually and materially – to create a better world.
[ I enjoy going to Mass occasionally, an embarrassing admission for an atheist Opens in new window ]
We have been sucked into religious tribalism and identity politics for too long – the labels we tend to put on one another are largely superficial. The real fault line today – the fault line of most consequence – rests on the issue of power. It lies between, on the one hand, those who believe in the right to exercise absolute power – power without legal or moral constraint – and, on the other hand, the rest of humanity.
Ireland in 2026 is not short of knowledge, nor is the world as a whole, and the promise of future “smart” societies hardly inspires hope. What we are short of is moral courage – the spirit to hold the line against greed and hatred, and to defend what we know deep down to be true. Where to find that spirit is the challenge ahead.

title: ‘They are ashamed to come forward’: Men experiencing domestic abuse reluctant to get help, says charity
description: Men’s Aid Ireland reports more calls about encouragement to suicide by  partners
content:
“W e’ve had guys call us and they’re in a horrendous situation,” says Men’s Aid Ireland (MAI) chief executive Shane Kelly. Some, he says, say they have been encouraged to take their own lives by their partners, and be told “everyone will be better off without you”.
While he cannot say this has actually led to suicide , Kelly says his organisation is hearing more men talk about encouragement to suicide. It is the reason some men contact MAI, but most callers, who range in age from 18 to 80, just hope an intervention by it will improve their relationship, Kelly says.
“A lot of men won’t use language like ‘victim’ or ‘perpetrator’ – they still love their partner. Usually they are saying ‘can you help me help her, she doesn’t mean it’. It’s a desperate plea. We would say, that sounds like coercive control, but they would not hear this language in their everyday life.
“We have some very sad cases. We had a man aged 80, 40 years of an abusive marriage, he talked about being humiliated, made to feel stupid, no confidence, suicidal ideation. We have had men come in and say, ‘I’m going to kill myself, the kids are grown up, I’ve had enough.’”
MAI has existed in different iterations for about 30 years. Its latest annual report, for 2025, shows a total of 8,041 contacts with the service, including 2,876 calls to its helpline, and postal and repeat contacts. Court support is an important part of its work, and 927 court clinic contacts were recorded. It made 20 child protection referrals to Tusla.
Despite rising numbers of callers across every age group, Kelly is concerned that many other men experiencing domestic abuse do not come forward.
He cites a study, MenCallHelp2, carried out for MAI by Melissa Corbally and researchers at the School of Nursing and Midwifery at Dublin’s Trinity College Dublin .
They are overwhelmed. They’re being asked, ‘Where are you, who are you with, what are you doing?’
Published last year, it analysed 7,132 contacts during 2022 to MAI. Of those, 1,232 reported domestic abuse experiences, with about 93 per cent perpetrated by a female partner, and 85 per cent reporting more than one form of abuse.
The most prevalent types of abuse were emotional (86.1 per cent), psychological (69.3 per cent), physical (36.9 per cent), coercive control (30 per cent), parental alienation (26.3 per cent) and economic abuse (20.3 per cent).
[ Male domestic abuse victims ‘largely unseen’ due to embarrassment, shame and fear - study Opens in new window ]
“Men don’t come forward. The number-one reason they say why they don’t is embarrassment and shame,” says Kelly. “That’s why we want to do more awareness-raising.”
MAI has “utmost respect” for Women’s Aid and other agencies working with female survivors and trying to address “shocking” levels of violence against women. “Nothing we do diminishes their work, we’re all about the same thing,” he says.
MAI is seeing increasing numbers of men seeking protection orders against their adult children, often arising from addiction and mental health issues. “That veers into elder abuse,” says Kelly.
It also hears from young men, from 18 upwards, reporting control by their partners.
“They are overwhelmed by it. They’re being asked, ‘Where are you, who are you with, what are you doing?’” he says.
A qualified psychotherapist, Kelly says control “always comes from fear”.
It’s not about men versus women, I think victims are finally getting more recognition
“That does not excuse it. It can become very, very dangerous.”
Men are “terrified” to leave and are often advised by lawyers not to leave their home unless their life is in danger, he says. “The law does not really support men in that situation – it has to get really bad for them to leave.”
Men are more likely to leave when their children are older “or when it is so bad they believe they have to get the children out”.
Victims, whether male or female, should be protected and not forced to leave the home, he says. “It should be the perpetrator who leaves.”
[ ‘Before I would have held my husband’s hand walking around the streets. But now I wouldn’t’ Opens in new window ]
There are currently no refuges for men in Ireland. MAI says it is not calling for these, but believes men should have more “safe spaces”, Kelly says. Some charities have transitional houses that can be used, and Kelly would like to see more of these being set up.
MAI has clinics in the Dolphin House court complex in Dublin and other locations including Drogheda, Trim and Galway.
Karl Heller, a retired Garda chief superintendent, who staffs the Dolphin House clinic four days weekly, was very involved in community policing and the roll-out of victim services during his policing career.
“What I’m doing is a natural progression from my work with the guards,” he says. “It’s not about men versus women – I think victims are finally getting more recognition.”
Controlling behaviour and isolation are recurring themes from service users. “That feeds coercive control – men talk about [being] restricted, or [having] no access to family members.” Some talk of being subject either to “total silence” or being “constantly put down”.
The clinic has about 500 callers annually. Heller says he saw 14 men last year who spoke of being encouraged to take their own lives.
About 6 per cent of the service users are gay men, he estimates. “They can experience higher levels of violence. The community is small and they are in fear of talking openly about their experience.”
[ ‘Once somebody shares the fact they are thinking about suicide, there’s a connection to life’ Opens in new window ]
MAI, stresses Kelly, is a “signposting”, not an emergency service, and works only with victims.
