Its work also includes education on domestic violence, including free training for employers and employees on identifying and dealing with concerns of domestic violence.
Kelly believes there is a growing societal recognition that men can be subject to gender-based violence, noting callers to MAI include mothers worried about their sons, and sisters about their brothers.
The “big boys don’t cry” mentality is still very prevalent, he cautions.
Education is crucial to tackling gender-based violence, he believes. “It’s about getting into schools as early as possible and educating about what is a healthy relationship.”
Battling against toxic masculinity is a challenge. “People like Andrew Tate and similar individuals make our work harder. Men don’t stand up enough to this.”
Despite the challenges, Kelly has “great hope for change”. A father of three children, he says: “I think it is wonderful what they think is not acceptable.”
Alan* estimates he has spent about €100,000 in legal fees since his marriage started to go “very wrong”.
His wife was drinking excessively, leading to her missing work due to hangovers, car crashes and fluctuating behaviour, including screaming and shouting at him and their children, he said. “It got so bad communication was just via WhatsApp and emails.”
Everything “came to a head” several years ago when she served divorce papers, he said. The family lived in a house bought by him before he had met his wife, but she told him if he did not leave, she would say he raped her, he said.
“My big mistake was not to go to a solicitor then.”
After an incident where he suffered an injury when she threw an object at him, he said his solicitor advised him to seek a protection order, and he did so.
After his wife alleged he raped her, which he strongly denied, the matter went to trial and he was acquitted.
Such allegations “are very dangerous for a man”, he said. “All you need is an accusing finger.”
In response to allegations by his wife of mistreatment of her and their children, an assessor nominated by his wife to prepare a report interviewed all of the family, he said.
Alan said his lawyers obtained that report, which included criticism of his wife’s behaviour and findings that the children had been alienated against him.
He has since secured full custody of one of his children, who was deemed to need therapy, but his wife would not agree to that and court orders were required, he said.
He got court-ordered access to another child, but further court applications will be necessary due to his wife’s handling of that access, he said.
“This has been going on 10 to 12 years and I don’t see any end to it.”
* Name has been changed for legal reasons
The Men’s Aid confidential helpline can be contacted at 01 554 3811 or via email at Hello@mensaid.ie

title: ‘Every maternity negligence case costs us a midwife’, doctors’ group warns
description: Prof Gabrielle Colleran, president of the IHCA, said these cases have a huge impact on staff
content:
Every time a maternal medical negligence case is taken, a midwife leaves the profession, according to a union representing senior doctors.
The Irish Hospital Consultants Association ( IHCA ) annual meeting in Killarney on Saturday focused on medical negligence, risk and reform.
President of the High Court , Judge David Barniville, said the healthcare and justice systems “intersect in a whole host of ways”.
He said the courts have made changes in recent years to improve the way in which these cases are handled, “but ultimately they need to be underpinned by legislation”.
“There are all these recommendations going back, in some cases, 20 years. Pre-action protocol is in legislation but requires ministerial regulation,” he said, adding that an implementation group designed to introduce reforms hasn’t met in several months.
Pre-action protocols refer to a set of rules requiring early engagement between claimants and doctors. It is envisaged that this will cut the number of cases reaching the High Court or only being settled after the protracted involvement of lawyers.
In addition to benefiting all parties, such a move could help curb the growth in the State’s liability for medical negligence claims.
“Courts aren’t experts; legislators are supposed to be the experts. We are at the limit in terms of what we can do,” he added.
[ ‘I felt so broken’: Three mothers on the impact of stillbirths and miscarriages Opens in new window ]
Prof Gabrielle Colleran, president of the IHCA, said these cases, and their adversarial nature, have a huge impact on staff.
“Every time we have a medical negligence case in maternity services, you lose a midwife who was involved in it, who then leaves practice,” she said.
“If you think about all that goes into training ... we need to change that.
Eavanna Fitzgerald, a barrister who practised for 20 years, said nobody wants patients or doctors having legal cases “looming over them for five years”.
“They’re losing sleep for five years. Patients who have already had [an] adverse event are having repeated trauma,” she said.
Fitzgerald said, in her experience, between 95 per cent and 97 per cent of cases are settled before the trial; however, she said sometimes this can be on the steps of the court, which is still traumatising.
Prof Rhona Mahony, former master of the National Maternity Hospital , and former chair of the interdepartmental working group on the rising cost of health-related claims, said it is important to remember that patients are at the heart of these claims.
“The big cost of claims is the cost of damages in cases of brain injury, largely cases of cerebral palsy and cases arising from birth,” she said.
[ How can runaway spending in the health service be reined in? Opens in new window ]
“There’s a huge gap between what the courts award and what is available to the patients who cannot take the case and cannot make a claim. There’s huge inequality.”
Mahony called for “early care pathways” for all individuals with brain injury, regardless of whether there was negligence.
Barniville added that the high damages awarded in such cases, which have been as high as €35 million, are largely comprised of the cost of care, with only €500,000 being for compensation.

title: Gugai MacNamara of the Róisín Dubh: ‘There’s a wildness to Galway’
description: Róisín Dubh music booker on the pull of Galway, the importance of grassroots venues to artists, and the negativity around immigration
content:
G ugai is an old Irish word for an egg. My twin sister was born with hair and I was born without it, and the first thing my mother said when I was handed to her was “my little gugai”. It just stuck, and now the only people that don’t call me Gugai are my mother and my twin sister. I have had it longer than my actual name.
I grew up near Castleconnell and I went to school in The Crescent in Limerick City . It was great, a lot of my friends were in bands. If it wasn’t English or history, I had very little interest in school. I tend to be very focused on some things to the detriment of almost everything else.
I went to college in Galway in 1996 and I did arts, studying English, history, politics and philosophy in first year. I definitely loved the student life more than the student work. I had a great time but I didn’t last very long. Once I ran my first gig, that was it for me. A few years later, in 2004, Simon Heaslip, Kevin Healy, Greg Healy and I bought the Róisín Dubh where I have been music booker ever since. I also book the acts for Big Top at the Galway International Arts Festival .
My friends in Limerick had bands, so we were used to going and seeing gigs. When I came to Galway, there just didn’t seem to be any young original bands playing anywhere. Everywhere was a covers band pub. The main reason I started running gigs was to put on something that I would like to see.
We do about 400 shows a year, from 30 to 4,000 capacity including the Big Top. I always try to focus on developing acts. I do a lot of stuff with Strange Brew, an independent music promoter, record label and radio show. On Thursday and Friday night at the Róisín we put on a couple of bands from 12am to 2am and there’s no cover charge, and we pay them. That’s just a really good way of getting bands in front of audiences and getting them to a level where they have fans.
That’s why grassroots venues are so important for artists – you don’t get to play huge venues unless you are an essentially manufactured kind of band, unless you have worked and embarrassed yourself and made mistakes in small rooms. That is where people learn how to perform and how to interact with crowds and sound engineers and build their audiences.
There are so many stadium shows and festivals for a country of this size. But if you want to go see Bruce Springsteen or Taylor Swift in Dublin that is going to set you back €500, or Oasis or Stevie Wonder – that’s going to cost you a lot of money. That might have taken you to 15 or 20 gigs in a smaller venue like the Róisín Dubh or Coughlan’s in Cork City.
It can be hard booking acts, but the one advantage we have is that everybody loves coming to Galway. There’s a wildness to Galway – the weather is insane, but it’s just so vibrant. There is such a mix of people from all over the world who come through here and they stay and never leave, or else they leave and they come back every year. It’s always had this mad artistic energy that permeates through the whole city.
Fifteen years ago, some of the really big successful bands sounded like they could have been English or American. But now if you look at Ireland, all these bands that are huge international successes couldn’t be from anywhere else in the world other than Ireland. And that is incredible. That’s what I really love to see. It’s not a band that you could pick up and put anywhere else. You listen to Madra Salach, Kneecap or CMAT – any of these bands you know straight away that they are Irish.
[ Camille O’Sullivan on her cancer: ‘You have to go further than a smear test’ Opens in new window ]
I don’t think there is anywhere else in the world I would rather live in than Ireland. A lot of Irish people who moved away feel like that. A lot of people I know who moved away are just waiting to move back.
I am proud to be Irish. It’s one of the most beautiful countries in the world. The whole west coast of Ireland along the Atlantic is incredible. I have been to beaches all over the world and there is nowhere as nice as the west of Ireland on a sunny day, the rare amount of them that we get. Someone once told me that we are much better off that way because if the weather was any better it would just be full of English people all the time, so maybe we should be thankful for the rain keeping tourism down.
We’re definitely not like other English-speaking countries. Everyone knows that. When you are in London you can spot the Irish people on the Tube by the people who say hello when they get on. There is definitely a lyricism to the way Irish people think and talk. There are a lot of incredibly talented people in Ireland. Maybe it is just that their talent gets nurtured a bit more and that pub culture/trad session culture is a bit more ingrained in Irish people – we just love singalongs.
There is a lot of negativity at the moment, this “Ireland for Irish people” bullshit, but I don’t think that’s a huge populist movement. I think that is an insane, radical, small and very vocal group of crazy people that don’t understand what Irishness is, or know why Irish people are everywhere around the world. Anyone in Ireland who gives out about immigrants coming into Ireland should take a look at what we did to other countries. We should be the most welcoming country in the world because every country took us in.

title: Broke in Australia, I took a street sales job - but sidelined my better instincts
description: We were taught how to convince strangers you were trustworthy enough to hand you their bank details
content:
On a working holiday visa in Australia , I completed a long (expensive) trip down the east coast and decided to stay in Melbourne for a while.
Finding work was key. After several dozen unsuccessful applications, I broadened my horizons. This is how I ended up working in a multi-level marketing sales job. It would only last a few weeks, but I was left with unforgettable memories (and not for the right reasons).
The recruiter had a way of making me feel special to be selected for this wonderful opportunity. At that stage I would have done almost anything, I just needed money as quickly as I could get it.
The interview was unorthodox. There were 15 of us, mostly on working holiday visas, brought in as a group. The company told us they were a marketing firm selling subscriptions on behalf of charities.
“Here’s the catch though: we are not really just looking for salespeople, we are looking for leaders to build their own team as they move through the ranks here. How do you do that? Simple, just reach your sales targets and you can have your own team under you in weeks.”
[ ‘I feel guilt and rage about living in Australia while my family is in Ireland’ Opens in new window ]
The chief executive was a friendly man who appeared to have made a fortune but also came across as ordinary, giving you the intended impression that if he could do it, so could you.
Then followed discussions that pitted each of us against each other. Some of us knew how to play that game. And four of us would start training the next day.
On my first day out in the field I was paired with my leader, who was also on a working holiday.
I was the only one of the new cohort to get a sale on the first day (in fact I got four, all told). Each time my leader would hype me up, and off I went, talking to older women about a charity that was often very close to their hearts.
We were taught several methods by which to stop strangers and convince them that we were trustworthy enough to hand over their bank details. It was quite similar to fishing: patience, baiting, and a gentle wrestle to keep them with you until you made a catch.
I tried to convince myself that the money was going to charity, but I knew the methods were manipulative
Firstly, you’d offer them a token, such as a fridge magnet, and wait for them to reach for it. Only you don’t let go. Before they’d even make contact, you’d say, “I’m not collecting today, but I would love your opinion.” This often rattled people, and in that moment they’d give you their full attention.
You’d begin this delicate dance by asking whether they had a personal connection to the cause in hand. Almost everyone did, one way or another, and immediately they’d feel part of what you were talking about.
Next, you pointed to your table, spoke about statistics and a lack of government funding – all while keeping the matter light and adding a few jokes to convince them you are not in fact after their money.
Then came the key question: “All everyone’s been doing today is dropping a name and a number, a small amount to chip in for next month, and from there you donate for as long as you like. Sound fair enough?”
In reality, you had often been standing at a shop corner for six hours waiting for your first sale. On top of this, I wouldn’t have actually told them I needed their card details yet.
If they agreed it was “fair enough”, I would begin taking all their details, my heartbeat rising as I got closer to asking for their card information. I would keep looking down at the table as if this were the most normal interaction in the world. “All right, I’m assuming it’s the same name on the card for yourself?”
And just like that, I had their credit card details without directly asking for them.
On my first day, the chief executive told me he thought I would be a very good salesman. The truth was that I simply followed their sales workshops (which felt like lessons in manipulation), and happened to have a friendly smile.
If you advanced far enough in the company, you became a leader, and would take a cut from your team’s sales. I would not be making any commission until I received my first “promotion”. Each promotion required a set number of weekly sales over consecutive weeks.
Boundaries were non-existent in the company, with a phone call every night from my leader to reflect on my day and talk about the next. If sales were poor, I could expect a couple of these calls.
My performance slipped quickly, and eventually I was making only one sale a day if I was lucky. This meant my paid hours would be cut, so I’d end up working voluntarily to make unpaid sales. I began to focus my entire life around the job, even my social life, with free pints to make up for a lack of commission.
Increasingly, the job didn’t sit right with me. I tried to convince myself that the money was going to charity, but I knew the methods were manipulative.
Looking back, it amazes me how many of us working holiday travellers were in the same boat: needing money, and not asking questions once the money came in
I watched others sign up elderly women who warned there might not be funds in their account when the money was collected. I once stopped a woman who told me she was on her way back from her mother’s funeral. As I took her payment details, I realised she was starting to cry. I told her she didn’t have to sign up.
I was planning my way out. I just needed a few more days to survive before I left, when my bosses set me a challenge. Do whatever I needed to do to get three sales the next day, or else.
The next day I pushed every interaction. Shamefully, I even shouted to a woman in her 20s to come back after she had walked away. Nervously, she did, and I made sure she chose the lowest subscription.
By the end of the day, I had my three sales. That night, I was told my paid hours had increased. It hit me then that, even though I knew I was being manipulated, they had succeeded.
The next day I knew I wouldn’t be coming back. I had sidelined my better instincts when food and rent were the priority. What was scariest was how effective I became once I stopped hesitating. My final day was quiet – just me thinking about how many vulnerable people I had convinced to sign up.
Looking back, it amazes me how many of us working holiday travellers were in the same boat: needing money, and not asking questions once the money came in. Were we in many ways just as vulnerable and manipulated as those people we had signed up?
Eddie Ferns, from Co Wicklow, moved to Australia in March 2025. He currently lives in Melbourne, where he works in a school and writes.

title: Who was George Gabriel Stokes? The Irish mathematician whose 180-year-old puzzle has AI giants at war
description: OpenAI claims to have found proof of Sligo scientist’s equations but tech rivals are less than impressed
content:
A mathematical problem is making big news, with AI companies clashing over claims by one tech giant to have found the solution to the Navier-Stokes equations. Regarded as one of trickiest puzzles of mathematics, it has Irish connection.
George Gabriel Stokes was born in Skreen, Co Sligo , in August 1819, the son of the local Protestant minister. After schooling at home, in Dublin, and in Bristol, Stokes entered the University of Cambridge in 1837 to study mathematics.
He held many of the most significant roles in 19th century science, including Lucasian Professor of Mathematics – a position previously held by Isaac Newton and later held by Stephen Hawking – and Member of Parliament for Cambridge University.
While his research interests were wide-ranging, his most significant contributions were to hydrodynamics, and he is best known for the Navier-Stokes equations (French physicist Claude-Louis Navier also did work on them).
Much of Stokes’s work on this topic was inspired by the Irish coastline. Stokes said it was a childhood experience of almost being carried away by a large wave off the Sligo coast that first made him interested in studying waves, and later measurements for his research that lead to these equations were taken at or near the Armagh coast, his wife’s homeplace and the family’s annual holiday destination.
The Navier-Stokes equations – which were published in 1845 – are the fundamental basis of fluid mechanics. They can predict how fluids will behave under certain conditions, and have been used in scenarios as varied as weather forecasting, vehicle aerodynamics and aviation, blood flow in the body – and to explain why the bubbles in a pint of Guinness sink rather than rise.
However, despite the fact that these equations are used in practice every day, the theoretical understanding of how the equations work is far from complete. The primary unanswered question is whether – under certain, specific conditions – solutions to the equation always exist and whether these solutions are smooth (a word mathematicians use to convey a certain type of consistency).
The importance of these equations means they were chosen by Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000 to represent a Millennium Prize Problem, the solving of which carries a $1 million prize (€890,000).
Well, it remains to be seen if the problem was truly solved. In early September, OpenAI announced that it had found a solution to the problem and posted a proof totalling 166 pages.
In order for the Navier-Stokes equations to be considered solved, one of two things has to happen: either the equations have to be shown to exist and be smooth in all scenarios (under the specific conditions outlined), or a counter-example has to be found that therefore proves the equations don’t hold in all scenarios. OpenAI’s solution presents the latter. It shows how the equations can sometimes fall apart, finding scenarios known as “blow-ups” where the speed of part of the moving fluid becomes infinite – a situation that can’t happen in real life.
Approximately 10,000 OpenAI LLM (large language model) agents spent 88 hours constructing a blow-up collectively, which showed that the equations do not, in fact, always hold.
There has been no shortage of contention since the solution was announced last month, with mathematicians still unable to agree on whether the equation was solved, how exactly it was solved if that’s the case, whether the process amounts to plagiarism, and what exactly all this means for the future of mathematics research.
Leading experts in the field of fluid dynamics have found the OpenAI proof difficult to read. Several research groups are now working through the paper and its accompanying programming code to see what’s really going on with the maths in the equation.
In a further twist, it has emerged that OpenAI’s rival Anthropic had also been working on the problem in collaboration with academic mathematicians, and there are allegations that information was passed on to OpenAI – something OpenAI denies.
The row over the equations has become another front in the acrimonious rivalry between OpenAI and Anthropic, which was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI employees who believed OpenAI was putting profits ahead of safety in developing artificial intelligence.
[ Tech leaders outline AI dangers and opportunities at Dublin summit Opens in new window ]
Another competitor Google DeepMind AI has criticised Open AI’s approach to the Navier-Stokes problem. Its co-founder and chair Demis Hassabis told this week’s AI summit in Dublin – an event hosted by Ireland as part of the EU presidency – that his company was examining similar maths problems. But, unlike OpenAI, he said his company believed in “working with the maths community to understand maybe how the answer was arrived at, not just come up with the answer out of the blue”.
OpenAI is undeterred, however, and last week it announced hundreds of new findings, amounting to tens of thousands of pages, claiming to have solved questions across numerous subfields of mathematics and theoretical computer science. The quantity and scale of these solutions has left the mathematical community at a loss, with no clear answer on what the approach should be for verifying and understanding this new mathematics or what it means for the future of the field.
Aoife Kearins is a history of maths PhD student at the University of Oxford, researching 19th century mathematical physics and particularly George Gabriel Stokes

title: Ireland can capture the AI dividend while mitigating the risks
description: The IDA’s role is to work with the 1,800 multinationals already here to expand their mandates and attract the next generation of AI investment
content:
A rtificial intelligence is changing how companies innovate, how they compete, where they invest and how people work. The question for business leaders is whether they can harness it quickly, responsibly and at scale to safeguard their competitiveness.
Global corporate investment in AI more than doubled in 2025 and organisational adoption reached 88 per cent. Generative AI is now being used in at least one business function by 70 per cent of organisations.
These numbers mark the emergence of a new layer of economic infrastructure – one capable of reshaping productivity, research, customer experience, supply chains and decision-making across every sector.
This point in our AI-driven era represents a defining opportunity for Ireland. Our clear ambition must be to harness AI’s transformative potential so as to strengthen competitiveness and productivity, improve enterprise performance and public services, and support education and learning to equip our people for the jobs of the future.
To harness the real potential of the AI opportunity, we must invest in people at every stage of their careers. Ireland ranks fourth globally for both AI engineering talent concentration and net AI talent migration, according to our latest Labour Market Pulse report – a strong indication that Ireland has both the specialist skills base and international appeal needed to develop, deploy and scale AI-intensive operations.
The same report sees Ireland rank third globally and first in Europe for AI adoption.
It’s true that AI will automate some tasks, augment many more and create roles we cannot yet fully define. The correct response to this is not complacency or fear but preparation: AI literacy for every worker, advanced technical skills for specialists, and stronger collaboration between industry, education and government. Human creativity, judgment and leadership will remain fundamental and critical to success.
As Taoiseach Micheál Martin emphasised during his opening address at the International AI Summit hosted by the Irish Government in Dublin last week, Ireland is determined to capture the AI dividend while mitigating the risks. That means pursuing a distinctly European approach – responsible, safe, secure and human-centric – in which innovation is guided by our values and the benefits of AI remain firmly anchored in human agency.
The summit examined AI’s impact on competitiveness, innovation and economic growth at a time when the technology is now moving beyond information generation into the physical world: powering machines; supporting autonomous decision-making; becoming embedded in products, factories, healthcare systems, transport networks and critical infrastructure.
[ Global stocks edge lower as AI and rate fears hit tech Opens in new window ]
AI is also changing the geography of global business. Investment decisions increasingly depend on access to advanced skills, trusted data environments, research partnerships, secure digital infrastructure, clean energy and a clear regulatory framework. Companies are asking where they can develop, deploy and govern AI across international markets – not merely where they can locate a single function.
This creates economic opportunity but also intensified competition. Capital and talent will flow to locations that can bring innovation, regulation and execution together. Support for the regulation of AI in a way that fosters and aids innovation, and where Europe’s competitiveness is enhanced not stymied, will be critical.
Initiatives such as the Trusted Tech Alliance – a global industry coalition between transatlantic technology companies committed to strengthening innovation security – underscores the need for commitment and focus on this.
At the same time, the concentration of advanced compute, chips and expertise in a small number of markets creates new dependencies. Resilience, cybersecurity and trusted international partnerships are therefore becoming central to corporate strategy. Ireland’s track record across all three elements is proven and exemplary.
We enter this new era from a position of industrial strength. We are home to a deeply embedded base of leading global companies, a vibrant ecosystem of indigenous industry, a strong basis in research and education, and a workforce with expertise across technology, life sciences, financial services, engineering and advanced manufacturing.
Furthermore, we prioritise an unwavering commitment to trustworthy innovation, reflective of the views held by our fellow Europeans.
[ Anthropic’s quarterly revenue surges 45% to nearly $17bn Opens in new window ]
Our role in IDA Ireland is not only to attract the next generation of AI investment. It is to work with the 1,800 multinational companies already operating here – employing more than 300,000 people – to transfer, renew and expand their mandates. That means connecting firms with talent, research partners and funding, supporting AI adoption across all sectors, and ensuring that opportunity and benefits are felt across our entire country.
Over the past 12 months, IDA Ireland has supported significant client investment in AI and AI-adjacent initiatives.
OpenAI announced 250 new roles in its Irish operation in July, followed last week by a further 200 jobs to support a new Applied AI Lab. Canadian company OpenText unveiled a €105 million investment, creating 400 jobs across Cork and Galway focused primarily on agentic AI, sovereign cloud and European cyber resilience.
Anthropic announced plans in March to create 200 jobs across engineering, operations, sales and compliance. Earlier this month two leading financial service companies, Stripe and MasterCard , announced big expansions of Irish operations reflecting AI-related growth.
Stripe is to create 200 new roles at its Dublin headquarters while Mastercard’s European Tech Hub in Dublin, where teams are driving innovation in AI, agentic commerce, cybersecurity and next-generation payments continues to grow.
[ Stripe to add 200 jobs at Dublin headquarters in endorsement of ‘Irish talent’ Opens in new window ]
Reflecting our ability to remain agile and responsive as AI continues to evolve, several initiatives have been announced to ensure Ireland is well positioned to harness the opportunity.
Last week, the Government published its Intelligence:Applied programme, which includes a €150 million AI Future Skills programme to support skills and lifelong learning, a €21 million AI Start Up Accelerator Programme, a national Regulatory Sandbox Programme to be established by the AI Office of Ireland, and the selection of 10 AI Sectorial Champions to advocate for transformation across various sectors.
We must be equally clearsighted about infrastructure. AI is energy intensive. Its sustainable growth depends on resilient grids, renewable energy , efficient data centres , secure connectivity and continued investment in cloud and semiconductor capacity. The countries that align digital ambition with energy and infrastructure delivery will be best placed to capture the next wave of investment.
Ireland is well positioned to capitalise on this. We must ensure we bring together our strengths in these areas to succeed.
Success will also depend on how we prepare for and scale these new and emerging technologies. Ensuring that we are not only adopters of these technologies, but leaders in shaping and scaling them for the future, will help us realise our true growth potential in AI.
Ireland has adapted effectively through every significant wave of global change. We have been to the fore of technological advancements throughout the decades and we are positioned to do so again, to help shape what comes next and to drive the global AI opportunity into our own economic advantage.
Michael Lohan is IDA Ireland chief executive

title: John Fitzpatrick: ‘The two hotels are running perfectly. Someone might make me an offer ... but I’m not in any hurry’
description: Irishman’s two hotels in New York City, the Manhattan and Grand Central, have bounced back from Covid to post record revenues
content:
I n the hotel trade, renovation is a constant state of being. No sooner have you finished upgrading a property than it’s nearly time to start thinking about the next refresh.
Irish hotelier John Fitzpatrick knows the feeling only too well. He owns two stylish four-star properties in midtown New York – the Manhattan and Grand Central – having moved there at 29 years of age to expand the family business.
At Grand Central, which has 155 bedrooms and suites, “we’ve been three years doing the bathrooms. We’re down to the last two floors,” he says, adding that each bathroom takes 12 weeks to completely refit.
“I can’t just shut the whole hotel and renovate, I’ve got to renovate as I go along. I’m working now with a company on the interiors for the bedrooms, they all have to be done. They only take four weeks. I’m trying to make them a little bit more up date. It’s small things like putting two different types of USB ports beside the bed, to save people searching around for a socket and pulling things out.
“Manhattan [with 91 rooms and suites] was done about six years ago but by the time I’m finished with Grand Central I’ll be coming back to the Manhattan to start looking at touching it up.
“I’m also going back now to look at the bar in Manhattan. We’re looking at moving it to the middle [of the room]. I want it to be casual but elegant. A hotel bar not a pub. But I won’t get to that until February or March.”
The bill for refurbishing Grand Central will be north of $4.5 million (€4 million), he says.
According to Fitzpatrick, New York City is “booming” right now in spite of all the cost-of-living pressures and geopolitical issues dominating the political debate in the United States , with midterm elections next month, and the fear that many tourists have of US border control searching their social media and stopping them from entering the country.
Fitzpatrick argues that these fears are overblown, citing the Fifa World Cup during the summer when tens of thousands of overseas football fans visited New York.
“People travelled and had a great time,” he tells me over a light lunch at his Irish home in Wicklow, adding that 65 million people will visit New York this year, back to the level it was at before the pandemic.
“There’s a perception that America doesn’t want people to travel. It’s not true.”
There is also a World Cup lament. “It brought us some business” but if Ireland had qualified ”we would have been out the door”.
Last year, his two hotels posted record turnover of $28 million, with earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (ebitda) of about $7 million.
It’s occupancy rate is running at about 90 per cent and the average room rate is $350-$450, in excess of what it was achieving pre-Covid.
There was also a big boost to New York from the Knicks, the city’s basketball team, winning the NBA title for the first time in more than half a century. The title win gripped the city.
Fitzpatrick’s bars in Grand Central (located opposite the famed train station of the same name) took in $22,000 between 4pm and 9.30pm on the night the Knicks secured the title in the fourth of five finals matches, with local workers and tourists packing in to watch the action.
“I was watching the numbers coming in [on an app] and it was unbelievable,” he says. “Knicks winning the NBA championship was really important. All of New York was behind it.”
The annual UN week in September (when world leaders gather in the city) was “very busy” and “Christmas is just jammed”, he says. “I don’t know where the people are coming from but it’s great.”
Fitzpatrick moved to New York when he was 29 to open a hotel for the family, which is best known for the Killiney Castle in south Dublin, now owned and operated by his sister Eithne’s sons Mark and Joseph Scott-Lennon – a third generation running a property that his parents Paddy and Eithne Fitzpatrick bought in 1971 and where John cut his teeth in hospitality. The business is in his blood.
“All I have to do is walk into the lobby and I just know by the employees and by the customers if everything is running smoothly. I will spot something straight away.”
Having sold a hotel in Chicago in 2006, John bought out his family about 20 years ago and wholly owns the New York hotels, including the freeholds on the properties.
Business has not always run smoothly. The 9/11 terrorist attacks devastated the city’s hospitality trade while the Covid pandemic forced him to lay off staff and temporarily close one of the hotels due to lockdown restrictions.
An upside of the pandemic (if there was one) is fewer hotel bedrooms in his neighbourhood. In the area between his two properties on Lexington Avenue there are now 2,500 fewer hotel bedrooms than before the pandemic.
“Some of them changed into student accommodation. And then the Waldorf shut for renovation around the same time. They had more than a thousand rooms and they’re now down to 375.”
“Business is great now in the sense of where we came from in Covid, when we had little or no help from government at all. I paid real estate tax every six months for a hotel that was closed – $1.6 million between the two of them.”
Aside from running the hotels, Fitzpatrick has various investments and is a busy philanthropist. In 1994, he set up a memorial fund (hosting a golf event recently in Druids Glen) in the names of his parents that has raised more than $5 million for good causes, and has been a big supporter of the Ireland Funds (of which he is a former chairman) over many decades, supporting projects on both sides of the Border.
Many who know Fitzpatrick consider him to be a workaholic. “People say that but I don’t know. Maybe I am. I’ve sacrificed certain things in my life to keep things going. But at the end of the day, I’m happy and I love what I do,” he says.
“Some people are happy to retire. Don’t get me wrong, I’d like to slow down, no doubt. Over the last few years I’ve got a really good team around me. I delegate a bit better now. I’m still on the phone every day but I trust the team around me.
“Do I want to work until I’m 80? Absolutely not. Do I want to slow down? Yes. But I do have to get out some time.
“My father worked until he was 72, which wasn’t late, and then died at 75. You think, ‘What’s the point of all this?’ I want to enjoy life as well but I enjoy what I do. I’m not going to work until the end of my time but at the moment I’m happy.”
He namechecks some of the senior Irish staff who have worked with him for years: group general manager Shane Cookman; Chris O’Sullivan, GM of the Manhattan property; Patrick Leyden, GM at the Grand Central; and his finance chief Peter Kidd.
“As long as I have a strong team with me I’m happy. The two hotels are running perfectly, they are within 10 blocks of each other and I can walk between them.
“I have two beautiful properties in midtown Manhattan, and they’re building all around me. Eventually, someone might come in and make me an offer, maybe not for a hotel but for something else. But I’m not in any hurry. I’ve a another good eight to 10 years. I can guarantee that I’m not going to get into my 80s and still be at it.”

title: Inside the plague research labs at the heart of a Russian mystery
description: Health officials worldwide are still waiting for answers over the death of a researcher (28) at a Russian lab from a mysterious infection
content:
M ore than two weeks after a 28-year-old researcher died from a mysterious infection while working in a Russian plague research laboratory, health officials around the world are still waiting for answers.
Darya Shipilova, a lab worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, was initially reported to have contracted pneumonic plague, raising concerns about the kinds of research being conducted at the facility and the safety measures employed there.
The Russian authorities have since ruled out pneumonic plague, a bacterial infection caused by the same pathogen as the better-known bubonic plague, as the cause of Shipilova’s death, but have yet to confirm which pathogen was responsible for causing her pneumonia.
The incident, which led to denunciations by the United States and other governments, has exposed the international community’s lingering mistrust of Russian biomedical research, which harks back to the Soviet military’s once-robust programmes for developing biological weapons.
The institute in Irkutsk never functioned as a military facility, but it was part of the broad yet secretive ‘Anti-Plague System’. At hundreds of field sites and labs across the Soviet Union, thousands of researchers were responsible for tracking emerging strains of plague and other endemic diseases, exterminating disease-causing rodents and developing vaccines. These facilities, experts said, had also provided pathogen samples to the military labs responsible for creating bioweapons during the Soviet era.
Most of these facilities are still functioning, and while those in Russia remain closely guarded, some in former Soviet states have opened their doors to international researchers looking to learn about the fabled system.
Although the Black Death of 14th-century Europe is the deadliest and best-known outbreak of the plague, a disease caused by the bacterium Y pestis and carried by rodents, the illness has haunted Eurasia for thousands of years.
To put a stop to the frequent outbreaks in rural areas, where plague-harbouring animals such as rats, gerbils and marmots are endemic, the Soviet Union established a series of field sites and research institutes early in the 20th-century. They called it the Anti-Plague System.
“The goal of their work was to be a central institute that surveils the vast areas around them, including the steppes that have large populations of burrowing wild rodents,” said Susan D Jones, a veterinary historian at the University of Minnesota who in 2018 visited a former Soviet Anti-Plague Institute in what is now Kazakhstan.
In its early days, the programme was rudimentary. Scientists would venture on horseback into plague hot spots, often staying in tents or renting rooms from local residents, and would spend their days exterminating rodents, digging up their burrows and burning their food supplies in an attempt to eradicate the diseases they carried.
Many of these expeditions were conducted without effective disinfectants or personal protective equipment, making the job of anti-plague workers a very dangerous one. And the eradication efforts didn’t stop the spread of the disease.
Between the 1920s and 1950s, however, the programme shifted its focus from eradication to outbreak prevention, opening up a series of labs in cities around the USSR.
By the middle of the 20th century, as an antibiotic to treat plague was developed, thousands of year-round employees staffed these labs, with hundreds more hired seasonally to collect samples in the field.
The research conducted at these Soviet-era facilities was “hidden behind a curtain of secrecy”, a former anti-plague researcher, Moisey Iosifovich Levi, wrote in a 1994 essay.
To avoid links being made between their work and the bioweapon development programmes in military labs, workers at the plague labs were instructed never to mention anything specific about their work in their conversations.
Furthermore, the lab buildings themselves were built to look like normal housing units. Workers in many facilities maintained gardens, kept the lab windows open and walked around in normal clothing or even pyjamas rather than wear white coats.
It wasn’t until one stepped inside the lab and saw scientific equipment – refrigerators full of pathogen samples, large sterilisers boiling used equipment and long tables dotted with microscopes – that the buildings’ true purpose became apparent.
Because of these unusual working conditions, “biosafety and biosecurity was very different from what we have in western countries,” said Sonia Ben Ouagrham-Gormley, a biodefence researcher at George Mason University who has visited many anti-plague research institutes in former Soviet states.
In a series of anthologies titled Interesting Stories of the Events and People of the Anti-Plague System of Russia and the Soviet Union, edited by Levi, authors describe dangerous conditions that included outbreaks among animals kept in the facilities, lab fires and lost pathogen samples.
In the final years of the Soviet Union, several facilities were provided with safer and more effective lab equipment. Household refrigerators were swapped for more secure versions and fume hoods replaced open windows. But funding for these changes was difficult to come by, so smaller and more remote facilities, including the institute in Irkutsk, struggled to keep up.
“In recent decades, much has changed at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, and not for the better. In contrast with other Anti-Plague institutes, it did not get attention,” a former director of the institute, Igor Valerianovich Domaradsky, wrote in an essay included in Levi’s anthologies.
“Therefore, the institute greatly lagged in acquiring new equipment and technology, which could not but affect the development of the institute,” he added. “What a shame.”
After the fall of the Soviet Union, most labs, from the advanced centres in wealthy cities to financially struggling rural facilities, remained open. And for decades, many were largely unchanged.
Ben Ouagrham-Gormley visited more than 100 former-Soviet facilities in the early 2000s, alongside colleagues from the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies. They found that entering one was like stepping into the past; tracking pathogen samples was done with pen and paper, and many vials were stored in oft-opened refrigerators, with wax seals used to indicate who had last opened them.
Many of the buildings, the researchers said, had no external security measures. And security inside was minimal, as well.
“We got there for a visit, and in the lab there was a table under a window that was wide open, because it was a summer, and there’s no air conditioning, and there were piles of plague cultures on the table,” Ben Ouagrham-Gormley said of one facility.
Over the next two decades, several facilities in former Soviet states were refurbished or rebuilt to accommodate updated scientific equipment, allowing some to become state-of-the-art centres visited by researchers from around the world.
“There are levels of containment within these buildings,” Jones said of the facility that she visited in Kazakhstan in 2018. “Once one is in the most high level of containment, one will be wearing full PPE and all work is done in sealed containment facilities.”
Because Russia has kept its anti-plague system facilities closed to international researchers and government officials, it is difficult to say for certain whether facilities in that country have improved as much as those that benefited from international aid to other states after the break-up of the Soviet Union.
“I would assume that they have not improved much,” Ben Ouagrham-Gormley said. “But they probably had maintained their procedures of Soviet time and their methods, which were good to ensure biosafety and prevent accidents in spite of a lack of equipment.”
About the facility in Irkutsk, little information is publicly available. However, Russian authorities have remained adamant that Shipilova’s death was not the result of unfollowed protocols or lapses in biosecurity at the facility. – This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

title: We want to buy a house in Donegal but are worried it may have defective blocks. What can we do?
description: Property Clinic: The house looks to be okay but the block test shows there is 11% free mica present
content:
My husband and I are trying to purchase a house in Donegal. We’re based in Dublin and now with two young children the time has come to think about moving back home.
We’re not up to speed on the issue of defective blocks in Donegal, but now with our house search we find ourselves having to pay close attention to the potential presence of pyrite, mica and pyrrhotite in the properties we view.
To the best of my knowledge, the science has now shown that mica is not the cause of defective blocks in Donegal – the defects are a result of internal sulphate attack caused by pyrite and pyrrhotite.
We have found a house that we would love to buy. It was built in 1985 and there are no visible signs of defective blocks. However, having said that, the block test has come back with readings of 11 per cent free mica, <0.1 per cent pyrite, and zero pyrrhotite.
The standard underpinning the defective block redress scheme (SI 465) was updated in July this year. This update moves away from identifying mica as the cause of defective blocks and instead highlights the role of internal sulphate attack.
My question is, how should we as buyers view 11 per cent mica as a risk for potential issues down the line? Will banks and other lenders now provide mortgages for houses with mica present, but no sulphides? Will home insurance companies now insure houses with same? We have a block report based on the old SI 465. I am guessing that our first port of call would be to request a new report based on the updated standard?
The defective block issue continues to be very challenging, particularly for properties in Donegal that are directly affected. Unfortunately, and notwithstanding the technical issues, there is almost a stigma attached to the properties, which at a minimum is having a devaluing effect on them.
[ ‘Is it true that Ireland’s new houses aren’t as well built as older ones?’ Opens in new window ]
It is likely that a large proportion of potential purchasers are simply put off by the mere association with the defective block issue, rather than getting involved in the detailed analysis – which to be fair you are endeavouring to do – and will simply walk away. This will reduce the potential pool of purchasers and ultimately the property’s value, so one must proceed with caution.
On the face of it, a test result of 11 per cent free mica is, or at least can be, a cause for concern. However, it is not just appropriate to look at one factor in isolation, and this must be related to whether or not there is evidence of any issues arising from this.
You say that the house was built in 1985 and further say that there are no visible signs of defects. This in itself is very encouraging given that the house is now 40 years old. In simple practical terms, there is unlikely to be a significant problem with the house and no obvious cause for concern.
However, as stated above, the inevitable association with the potential mica problem will result in greater difficulties when seeking both a mortgage and insurance on the property, as the providers will look for some confirmation/certainty that there are no problems.
They will be looking for more than the broad opinion that one might get through a standard building survey carried out as part of the normal purchasing process, which would typically follow best practice recommendations.
This is because pre-purchase building surveys, although comprehensive, do not involve opening-up works or scientific tests but rather are based on a visual inspection.
Accordingly, in this instance it would be prudent to obtain further specialist advice from an engineer and particularly one experienced in and working in the field of defective blocks. A number of engineers have specialised in this field specifically due to the issues in Donegal. This will involve:
This differs from the standard pre-purchase style survey, which as mentioned is generally limited to a visual inspection at a single point in time.
The recommended approach will involve a degree of monitoring to include mapping of any cracks and, perhaps more importantly, sampling and laboratory testing of blocks. This all clearly takes time and more importantly, given that this approach is invasive, can only be done with the consent of the homeowner and thus as a potential purchaser, you lose a degree of control.
[ Only 13% of houses built with defective concrete blocks have finished remediation Opens in new window ]
In fact, it is actually more in the interests of the homeowner/vendor to prove that they do not have a problem. There is a strong case to be made in circumstances such as this for the vendor to commission the inspection and to make the report/findings available to all potential purchasers, so that the facts are clear and to assist in determining the true value of the property for sale having due regard to any inherent defects.
In short, and given the potential for concern here, it is all too easy and more appealing for a potential purchaser to walk away rather than run the risk of getting involved in a complex issue that might or might not be a significant problem.
If, however, in all other respects, the house seems right for you, then you will need to, as you guessed, commission an appropriately qualified engineer to undertake the full specialist report to include not only the inspection but the necessary sampling and laboratory testing and monitoring works.
Val O’Brien is a chartered building surveyor and member of the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland

title: Look inside: Extended 1950s five-bed in Rathfarnham brought bang up to date with A Ber
description: Number 6 Dodder Park Grove extends to a substantial 220sq m following extensive works led by McCann Moore Architects
content:
Dodder Park Grove is a quiet cul-de-sac of 1950s-built homes just off Dodder Park Road in Rathfarnham , and number 6 is a semidetached five-bedroom house that occupies a corner location, with a very large garden to the back and side. The owners of number 6 have completely extended and refurbished the property, almost doubling the size of the house while still retaining more than enough back garden space.
The extension and upgrading work was completed this year, bringing the house from its original 120sq m (1,292sq ft) area to a generous 220sq m (2,368sq m). Behind its unassuming facade is a superb, spacious family home, designed by McCann Moore Architects, and finished to a very high standard, with premium materials and fittings.
A state-of-the-art air-to-water heating system gives the house an exceptional A2 Ber, and underfloor heating enhances the everyday comfort. Number 6 Dodder Park Grove is on sale through DNG seeking €1.9 million.
The central feature of the house is the dual-aspect kitchen/living/diningroom, 80sq m of open-plan living space that spans the entire rear of the house. The flooring is laid in gorgeous tiles by Fossil, the Stone Specialists, and the cabinetry is custom made by The Wood Studio. The room gets lots of light thanks to extra-large glass sliding doors opening out to a wide rear patio, plus a large picture window with built-in seating and another large window looking out to the side patio.
The kitchen area has an extra-large central island, quartz worktops, countertops and splashback, and big open-out pantries. Integrated appliances include Miele double ovens, ceramic hob and extractor, two Bosch dishwashers and a Blanco sink with Quooker tap. The family area has a feature media wall and an extra-large built-in electric fireplace.
While a family will spend most of the time in this bright, open household hub, there is also a large family room and a home office to the front, both with wood flooring. A guest loo has tiled floors, WC and wash-hand basin with brushed brass fittings, and tiled floor. Completing the downstairs is a good-sized utility room, fully fitted with tiled floor, bespoke cabinetry providing ample storage, a marble countertop with sink, and Miele washing machine and dryer. A door leads out to the side garden.
The bedrooms upstairs have wood flooring, and the large main bedroom faces out to the private back garden, and has extensive built-in wardrobes and attractive wall panelling. It has a large, fully tiled en suite bathroom with double walk-in showers and twin wash-hand basins with brushed brass fittings.
There are three more double bedrooms, one with built-in storage. In bedroom three, the original chimney breast has been made a bit deeper to allow for built-in wardrobes to be installed on either side should new owners wish.
The large family bathroom has a full-size bath with shower attachment, and is tastefully tiled.
Outside, the south-facing back garden is fenced on two sides, while a bank lined with mature trees and shrubbery provides a natural boundary along the rear, giving complete privacy. The garden features a large lawn and a wide wraparound terrace, and at the end of the lawn is a large garden room/gym with light and power, built by Shanette, and a separate sauna, its door facing in to the greenery for extra privacy.
[ Look inside: Large and luxurious six-bed home with verdant views in Rathfarnham Opens in new window ]
Dodder Park Grove is close to both Rathfarnham and Terenure villages, with numerous schools in the area including Loreto Grange Road primary school, Rathfarnham Educate Together, The High School and Zion Parish primary school in Rathgar, and De La Salle College in Churchtown.

title: ‘Disco Pigs was the start of everything’: Enda Walsh on 30 years of the play that made his name
description: For the first time, the writer is directing the play that launched his own career and those of Cillian Murphy and Eileen Walsh
content:
Enda Walsh ’s career as a playwright, screenwriter, librettist and installation artist did not begin with the first performance of Disco Pigs at Triskel Arts Centre, in Cork, in 1996. He had worked already with Pat Kiernan of Corcadorca , who had directed his play The Ginger Ale Boy the previous year. But Disco Pigs did set his career in motion.
Its success was a shock, Walsh says at the end of a rehearsal for a new run of the play in the city, this time at the Everyman, to mark the drama’s 30th anniversary. “I didn’t even know if I was a writer. It takes a few plays to be able to settle down to it.”
Just a few years later he had written Misterman and Bedbound; within a decade he had also produced The Walworth Farce and The New Electric Ballroom, which, presented by Druid, became successive winners of Fringe First awards in Edinburgh.
Disco Pigs features Pig and Runt, unhealthily close teenage friends whose intense relationship builds to an appalling climax. At Triskel Arts Centre in 1996, Pig was played by Cillian Murphy and Runt by Eileen Walsh .
It was a riveting production. As we put it at the time, in this writer’s review , the young actors showed total commitment, “building characters from the flow of words, hitting each irony, exposing the danger of lost souls beneath the skin of comedy, revealing with a subversive compassion the need which binds them to each other”. Two schoolroom chairs were their only props.
Des Kennedy, the Everyman’s artistic director, watched the play in Belfast when he was 15. “Seeing these two extraordinary, contemporary, defiant, unapologetic teenagers burst around the stage with such pride, energy and fearlessness changed my life,” he says. “It changed my outlook on the world and on what theatre could be.”
It’s no surprise that Walsh, Kiernan and their cast seemed never to be out of work after that original production of Disco Pigs.
Kiernan continued until 2022 with Corcadorca’s ground-breaking site-specific productions; Eileen Walsh, who has just completed Druid ’s run of the Eugene O’Neill play A Moon for the Misbegotten at Dublin Theatre Festival, has a CV that surges through stage, film and television.
And Murphy, of course, won the best actor Oscar in 2024 for playing the “father of the atomic bomb” in the Christopher Nolan blockbuster Oppenheimer . Since then, Murphy’s films have included Small Things Like These , which he produced and, alongside Eileen Walsh, starred in, and which Enda Walsh adapted from Claire Keegan’s novella.
Apart from its new cast of Aoise Meaney and Séamus McLean Ross, the main difference between this revival and the original production of Disco Pigs is that Walsh is directing his play for the first time.
“In its own small way,” he says, “it did have some cultural significance at the time – but perhaps would have had less importance if I had disappeared afterwards. Instead it was the start of everything for me, for good or bad. I’m still here!”
Indeed, Walsh’s adaptation of Keiran Goddard’s novel I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning , directed by Clio Barnard, has its Irish premiere at Belfast Film Festival next month. A winner at Cannes earlier this year, it features Lola Petticrew, Anthony Boyle, Daryl McCormack and Joe Cole as a group of friends witnessing the destruction of social housing in Birmingham.
“They’re good friends,” Walsh says of the characters. “But they’re hitting 30 and feeling that their life is already exhausted. So it’s political, and I like political work with a small ‘p’.”
Politics with a big “P” had come in 2008, when he collaborated with its director on the script for Hunger , Steve McQueen’s debut feature film, about the IRA hunger strike of 1981.
As well as seeming to move smoothly from book to stage to screen, Walsh’s work has extended to opera: he wrote and directed The Last Hotel , The Second Violinist and The First Child, the composer Donnacha Dennehy ’s trilogy for Galway International Arts Festival .
Walsh also wrote the musical Once, based on the Oscar-winning film starring Glen Hansard and Markéta Irglová. That stage production won eight Tony awards in 2012, including for best musical and, for Walsh himself, best book. (He also collaborated with David Bowie on the jukebox musical Lazarus, which ran on Broadway and in the West End of London.)
At this stage he can’t say which of his many awards were the most important. “I have had very few disappointments in my career,” he says instead. “That’s an award.”
In recent years Walsh has been collaborating with Paul Fahy, artistic director of Galway International Arts Festival, in its series of Rooms installations . Walsh loves returning to Ireland, but home is now London, where he lives with his wife, the journalist Jo Ellison, and their daughter. “London has been very good to me. The balance feels right,” he says.
“The world knows that I think Enda Walsh is a genius,” says Anne Clarke , the founder of Landmark Productions , whose wider associations have been significant in the expansion of Walsh’s work.
“Our first adventure was taking Misterman from Galway to the National Theatre in London and on to St Ann’s Warehouse in New York, with Cillian Murphy as Thomas Magill.
“I remember waking up in New York City that first morning in 2011 and seeing a huge feature in The New York Times, and wondering where it had all gone right.”
Despite such praise, Walsh tends to avoid reviews of his work. His early successes irked some contemporaries, one of whom suggested in the Telegraph newspaper that people should stop producing his output: “Theatre doesn’t need it.” That really hurt, the writer says, “so I don’t go there any more”.
[ Cill Stuifín on TG4 review: ‘We spent our childhoods terrified of seeing Cill Stuifín’ Opens in new window ]
On the other hand, the critic Lyn Gardner declared in The Guardian that The New Electric Ballroom had confirmed Walsh as “one of the most dazzling wordsmiths of contemporary theatre”. “I saw that on a theatre poster in the Tube,” Walsh says. “I felt really, really, really embarrassed. It wasn’t me. It wasn’t what I do. It wasn’t why I do it.”
To watch Walsh with the new Pig and Runt is to be reminded why, and how, he does what he does. The smooth flooring of Grace Christian Church, where they’re rehearsing, at times seems more like a trampoline than a stage, as Meaney and McLean Ross spring together as if their feet are wired.
Disco Pigs tells a sad story, but Walsh can’t quite resist the couple’s animation; his shoulders shake in response to a word, a movement he may not have expected. There is, in fact, a little laughter in the air.
Yet the focus remains acute, and when Meaney’s Runt subsides as if in a dream of music, she mourns herself to tears.
After 30 years, it seems the play remains brilliant.
“I couldn’t write it now,” Walsh says later. “With a mountain of work behind you the naivety of it is visible. But that’s its real honesty.”
[ How to talk to boys about masculinity and the meaning of life Opens in new window ]
Walsh also has a mountain of projects in front of him.
He has been working on a new version of Chitty Chitty Bang Bang with the director Matthew Warchus (who made the film version of Matilda the Musical , starring the young Irish actor Alisha Weir).
[ ‘On the first day I confessed I’d lost my fire. And then they took me on an adventure’ Opens in new window ]
He is also writing a film adaptation of the Edna O’Brien novel The Little Red Chairs, as well as working on a version of the outsider artist Henry Darger’s dauntingly long In the Realms of the Unreal, which, at 12 volumes and more than 15,000 pages, is a strong contender for the title of longest work of fiction ever written.
There’s also a new play, Together, which he expects to do in 2027, not to mention the screenplay he has written for Lineage, a crime thriller starring Isabelle Huppert , which has been filming in London.
As he leaves the rehearsal room in Cork, Walsh is wished a good night. Yes, he says, with a smile. “It will be good. I’m going to my computer, and I’m going to press Send.”
Disco Pigs is at the Everyman Theatre , Cork, from Saturday, October 31st, until Saturday, November 14th

title: Chicken-fed salmon is coming to Irish supermarket shelves
description: Soaring feed prices mean EU’s biggest salmon producers are turning to cheaper protein sources - including chicken
content:
Imported salmon reared on the innards of chickens could already be on the shelves of Irish supermarkets following a change in how international producers feed their fish.
And if it is not there now, it might soon be on the way.
But if consumers believe feeding chicken to salmon is “unnatural and disgusting” – as one recent study put it – they can still ensure that fish and fowl are kept apart by buying locally-sourced salmon.
That is because Irish producers have decided to continue to exclude chicken-based feed from the diets of the fish they farm.
It emerged last week that some of Europe’s biggest salmon producers have started feeding chicken to their salmon, a practice that has not been employed for years, although it is legally permissible.
It is also considerably cheaper than the more traditional proteins salmon have been reared on.
The price disparity between protein-rich fish and chicken feed has worsened over the last two years due to dwindling wild fish stocks and soaring demand for salmon feed in China.
That has seen the price of fish meal almost doubling and as of now poultry feed can be bought for less than half the price per tonne which has made it more attractive to producers if not consumers.
[ Ireland’s wild Atlantic salmon stocks down 80% since 1970s Opens in new window ]
For many years, supermarkets across Europe have shied away from stocking salmon-fed animal byproducts due to concerns about a consumer backlash.
A 2026 study by food institute Nofima found that consumers in the UK and France thought it was “unnatural and disgusting” to feed chicken to salmon.
But the spike in fish meal prices has given pause for thought and led to a significant shift in recent months.
Lerøy Seafood Group, one of Norway’s biggest farmers and a supplier to Tesco in the UK, confirmed to the Financial Times this week that it had introduced chicken byproducts at all of its offshore salmon farms.
The newspaper also reported that Mowi, the biggest salmon producer in Europe, was planning to introduce poultry-based feed at its farms in Norway and Scotland while Norway’s Grieg Seafood introduced chicken meal and oil in July. SalMar, the world’s second-largest salmon producer, started testing poultry’s use in feed in March.
If salmon reared on chicken makes its way into Irish supermarkets, shoppers will struggle to identify it as retailers and brands do not list fish-feed ingredients on packaging.
One way Irish shoppers can ensure their salmon is free of chicken innards is to shop locally. According to Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM), 99 per cent of Irish-farmed salmon is certified organic, and organically grown salmon in Ireland is “fed a diet of sustainable organic feed, that does not include land-based animal products”.
[ Wild salmon are on the verge of extinction. There is not one fish to spare Opens in new window ]
“The feed comes from international feed manufacturers who are certified to produce organic salmon feed. This certification is governed by EU law,” a spokeswoman said.
She added that the feed is “typically made up of fish oil, fish meal, vegetable ingredients, vitamins, minerals, pigments, and amino acids. The antioxidant astaxanthin is added to salmon feed to boost the fish’s immune system and to protect their tissue. It is also a source of vitamin A. Astaxanthin is the substance that gives salmon its pink colour.”
She stressed that the Astaxanthin must be derived from organic sources, such as organic crustacean shells or from natural sources such as the Astaxanthin-rich yeast Phaffia rhodozyma. Wild salmon get astaxanthin by eating crustaceans.
While poultry byproducts are allowed in organic certification, “the Irish salmon industry has taken the decision to exclude this from their diets following customer requests”, the spokeswoman said.
She added that “BIM works closely with seafood producers in Ireland and is familiar with the feed practices in place on salmon farms in Ireland to ensure its organic certification”.
However, the spokeswoman concluded by saying BIM does “not have oversight of feed practices in place on overseas’ farms, or what imported seafood products have been fed on”.

title: AI fever is producing some strange symptoms
description: Some AI researchers reported to have taken up smoking to show conviction that AI will cure cancer
content:
“A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in,” Broadcom chief executive Hock Tan warned this week, saying they set “very extreme expectations” only to discover that the AI trade resembles a casino.
The comments were unusually forthright, although a few critical remarks would not normally be enough to send shares in mega-cap technology giants such as Samsung (down 7.4 per cent on the day) and SK Hynix (down 10.1 per cent) tumbling.
In truth, there was more to the declines than Tan’s comments, with concerns about Chinese competition, the sustainability of AI spending and Samsung’s latest earnings report all weighing on the sector, but the swings certainly highlighted the fragility of AI-related sentiment.
Meanwhile, Tan’s reference to “very extreme expectations” may have been aimed at investors, but extraordinary expectations of AI are apparently evident elsewhere in the industry. Shyam Sankar, chief technology officer of data analytics giant Palantir, claims some AI researchers have taken up smoking to signal their conviction that artificial intelligence would eventually cure cancer – an example, he said, of the “mass psychosis” and “social delusion” around AI.
Then there is Anthropic, which is moving to prohibit sustained cruelty towards its Claude chatbot, despite the absence of evidence that the software experiences suffering.
Clueless investors with extreme expectations are one thing, but researchers smoking in anticipation of a cure for cancer and developers worrying about a chatbot’s feelings suggest the AI boom is acquiring some distinctly unusual characteristics.

title: Looming elections place burden on Ireland to find EU budget compromise
description: Government has the unpalatable task of possibly having to trim agricultural supports to secure agreement
content:
I reland’s EU presidency has the job of brokering a deal on the EU’s budget for the years from 2028-2034. Getting a majority will be difficult between those member states who want a bigger, and others a smaller, budget. There is, however, an urgency to strike a deal before possible changes in government after forthcoming elections make reaching agreement even more challenging.
Marine le Pen , for example, believes in dramatically reducing the EU’s role and returning powers to national governments. If she wins the French presidential election next May, she could seek to upend EU funding.
To judge by the rows over recent decades about the EU’s budget, you might believe it is a major drain on member states’ national resources. However, the budget amounts to only 1.1 per cent of national income, whereas national budgets across the EU average 45 per cent of national income, somewhat higher than for Ireland.
So the fight over whether the budget should amount to 1 per cent or 1.25 per cent of national income is about relatively small sums when averaged across the EU. In national budgets, such a small difference as a share of national income could get lost in rounding errors.
There are a range of public goods that are best undertaken on a pan-EU basis rather than by national governments. Examples include cross-border infrastructure, research and development, climate, security, foreign policy, industrial policy and development aid. These are areas where collective EU spending is more effective than uncoordinated national investment.
[ European Commission unhappy with EU budget but Taoiseach says compromise had to be made Opens in new window ]
The construction of the electricity interconnector between Ireland and France is a prime example that merits the significant EU funding involved. This project will benefit not only Ireland and France, but also the wider EU electricity system.
Interconnection across borders boosts efficiency, provides better matching of variable supply and demand, and minimises wasted power generation.
Other potentially beneficial projects to enable the free flow of electricity across the EU’s national boundaries are only likely to proceed if there is EU financial support.
Food shortages in the aftermath of the second World War were the initial driving force behind the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy. Today, however, it is more difficult to justify rationally why agriculture looms so large in the EU’s budget, or why the EU rather than national governments should fund farm supports.
[ Europe rearms: files reveal extent of plans for a new ‘defence union’ Opens in new window ]
Ireland, of course, has benefited disproportionately from EU payments to farmers over the past half century. Like other EU members, we pay about 1 per cent of national income into the EU budget. However, despite the fact that we are one of the richest EU members, we get back around 0.7 per cent of national income, most of it going to Irish farmers. A great deal.
The modernising of Ireland’s infrastructure has also benefited greatly from EU support to poorer regions over the first decades of EU membership.
Today there are two groups of countries with very different outlooks on the EU’s budget.
The “frugals”, like Scandinavia, Germany and the Netherlands, want a smaller budget, in particular they want to cut back on funds for agriculture, and for infrastructure in poorer states. They want to reallocate funds to other headings.
The “friends of cohesion”, which include Spain, Italy and some poorer member states, want a larger budget, with continuing substantial agriculture and cohesion payments.
The first stab at a compromise by the Irish presidency involved a small cut in the original EU Commission budget proposal. For 2028-34, this proposed that real EU resources, after debt interest, would be slightly lower than today.
[ The Irish Times view on the EU budget: a key task for Ireland’s presidency Opens in new window ]
This draft also largely protected agriculture and cohesion funds. But this compromise got a widespread thumbs down.
In the next round of negotiations, Ireland needs to adjust its proposals to garner more support. Next time, the Bruegel think tank in Brussels suggests, we should propose a slightly larger budget that cuts back on agriculture and cohesion funds, which are unpopular with the frugals, and that reallocates some resources to other European public goods.
A few rounds of proposals may be needed to garner the necessary majority support before year end.
As the honest broker, it may thus fall to the Irish Government to propose a compromise budget that would cut some resources for agriculture, which will be unpopular at home.
However, given the risk that delayed agreement could mean an even more unpalatable outcome, as the political winds shift in France and elsewhere, it is vital from an Irish point of view that agreement is reached on the budget by the end of the year. Better a budget with somewhat reduced funds for agriculture, than no budget and no funds.

title: Monocultural Ireland was always a fantasy
description: At a recent conference, President Catherine Connolly and others warned against the commodification of languages and translation through AI
content:
“O ur civilisation is an immense woven fabric in which very different elements are mixed ... it is pointless searching for a fabric that has remained pure, virgin and uninfluenced by other threads nearby ... What race or language ... can nowadays claim to be pure? No race has less right to make such a boast than the one presently inhabiting Ireland.”
James Joyce made these remarks in a lecture entitled Ireland : Island of Saints and Sages in 1907. They were quoted last week by John McCourt, author of a book on Joyce’s time in Trieste , to argue that recombinations, not zero-sum purity, characterise Ireland’s place in European culture, literature and languages. Ireland understands Europe from within and we are Irish through Europe. Each is a bridge to the other; they are not isolated piers – defined by Stephen Dedalus as disappointed bridges in Ulysses.
McCourt spoke at a conference in Trinity College Dublin to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the university’s chairs in French, German, Italian and Spanish. The papers are based on chapters in a forthcoming book examining the impact of languages across Irish intellectual, economic and political life, looked at from a wide variety of academic disciplines. It is a rich and multifaceted approach, delivering many insights on the creative role of languages in contemporary Ireland.
Joyce’s lecture was an exuberant celebration of Irishness as a pluralist identity open to many cultural influences and languages. It was a pointed case to make in Trieste’s Università Popolare, given its strong commitment to Italian irredentism – reunification with Italy after 500 years of rule by the Austro-Hungarian empire. Joyce stood apart from this type of Italian nationalism, just as he opposed the exceptionalist Catholic and Gaelic version of Irishness championed by the scabrous Irish journalist DP Moran in his newspaper The Leader.
