The German novelist Ulrike Draesner , in an opening address, said national monolingualism is a 19th century invention which “set out to make us forget that multilingualism is our point of departure” – in life as in literature. “Languages are not things but emergent processual weavings: vast fluid spaces of thinking and feeling, of connecting and of generating realities”, grounded in human bodyness. They draw on migration and the exchange of people in which translations transfer and transform human experience.
[ Why do people in Ireland speak so few languages? Opens in new window ]
Her remarks were a warning against commodification of languages and translation through artificial intelligence (AI) controlled by big capital – a false multilingualism of unambiguous speed and flatness. So were those from Yves Citton, the French writer and academic. In his work on curiosity he says that whereas AI’s algorithms instantly generate electronic summaries, mental processes are more like the digestive systems, which move food through our stomachs.
President Catherine Connolly, speaking at the conference, congratulated Trinity for pioneering the study of modern languages 250 years ago. She grounded her thoughtful remarks on languages in a critique of their exploitation by powerful corporations pursuing “endless unsustainable growth, consumption and extraction”, and now using that crude utilitarian ideology to justify their control of AI. Learning a language is instead “a voyage of discovery” in the meaning and use of words.
“Expanding our vocabulary in one language deepens our understanding of other languages” by confronting us with different perspectives and ways of thinking. “One particularly beautiful aspect of language learning is that it invites us into another culture, allowing us to get to know, and crucially, to care about, its people and history ... a profoundly human process of connection that AI can never reproduce.”
And we need “look no further than our own country to see the benefits and opportunities presented by a multicultural and multilingual population”, with more than 200 languages spoken by newcomers, of whom 15 per cent speak a language other than English or Irish at home. The growing gap between the 4 per cent studying languages at third level and the official commitment to the competitive use of languages for economic resilience perhaps reflects that market capture of language, the President said, rather than “a wonderful opportunity to enrich our lives, break down barriers, build bridges and champion diversity”, based on mutual respect.
[ Much of what Irish emigrants prize in Australia can be found in Europe, but lazy logic gets in the way Opens in new window ]
These philosophical reflections on language in Ireland have valuable lessons for cultural shocks that may yet come. Far-right threats to diversity in Ireland and elsewhere in Europe, championing nativist monoculturalism, are one such potential shock .
Another comes from constructive preparation for a united Ireland bringing together very different cultural traditions. The Irish language revival movement has much to learn from these ideas about weaving recent inhabitants’ linguistic energies imaginatively into a new Irish civilisational fabric – drawing on James Joyce, not DP Moran.
Joyce would undoubtedly approve of Seamus Deane’s remark in a 1970 essay: “Irishness will be the result of unity, not the precondition of it.”

title: I enter India, my ancestral home, a stranger and leave a ‘belly-button relative’
description: India’s sprawl of culture may be alienating at first, but soon it all starts to make sense
content:
A t Chittal, a busy roadside cafe en route from the heritage village of Kanadukathan to the bustling markets of Pallathur, I’m waiting for a fresh batch of tendrilled bhajis to fry on a crackling fire outside when I casually enter an existential crisis.
It’s prompted when a friendly staff member strikes up an idle conversation. “How long are you staying for?” he asks in a heavy accent. The question should be innocuous enough – but to a fellow brown-skinned person? Ooof!
Is it that obvious that I’m Indian in heritage only? Doesn’t my appearance suggest someone who’s tried, but hasn’t quite blended in to western culture?
I suspect I’m not the only second-generation immigrant grappling with questions of belonging when visiting the motherland as a tourist. My first trip, to Mumbai in 2009, was a girl-cousins trip, and shopping was the excuse. I flew over excited to see the place from whence the Ganatras came, but it battered all my senses immediately.
The beeps of the tuk-tuks were constant, as was the mortal risk involved when travelling in one. The multisensory pummelling involved in-your-face colours everywhere, constant stares and oppressive humid air.
The kicker was that I was experiencing culture shock with my own supposed culture. I didn’t know if I was too sensitive to the differences, or too westernised, or if India was just not my cup of chai.
It felt like I was the opposite of a “plastic Paddy”, a term I learned soon after moving to Dublin. I saw it in action a couple of weeks in: I vividly remember American tourists in Hogan’s dropping “we Irish” into conversation, as if it were their right from the day they were born in Connecticut. How easily they lay claim to Ireland, I thought a little enviously. How decisively they own their identity.
I wish I could define myself so easily. But how do I parse which parts of me come from my mother country, my family background in Britain, my birth country of Canada, or Ireland – where, with no substantial claim, I felt I found my people? It’s complicated, to put it mildly. There’s friction, and gaps, so I daren’t be so bold as to feel a true sense of belonging anywhere. And that’s always most apparent when I’m a tourist in India. As I return for the fifth time, I wonder if that’s something I’ll just have to live with, like my inherited nose and predisposition for diabetes.
The southeast state of Tamil Nadu is a new destination for me. The state of 80 million people welcomes the second-highest number of domestic tourists in India, thanks largely to its famous colourful ornate temples that make for pleasing pilgrimages. It also includes the embroidery-like tea plantations in the hilly heights of Nilgiri, and the industrial hotbed of Chennai, known as the “Detroit of India” for its soaring automotive industry. Further south, the Bay of Bengal is where nature is at its wildest, with wide stretches of coral-reefed coasts making it worth the trek.
The area of Chettinad, at its centre, is my destination. A loose conglomerate of around 75 villages, it’s the home of the Nattukottai Chettiars: the caste of the money lenders and business owners who made a fortune trading across Southeast Asia and Europe in the heyday of the British empire.
They weren’t shy about it either: during the 19th and first half of the 20th century, the wealthiest families built palatial mansions of pastel-block colours, the finest material from their far-flung travels, and hints of art deco with religious and colonial imagery, which together feel about as expected in these rural plainlands as a brownstone in Brooklyn. About 1,000 of these ancestral homes remain standing across these villages, in various states of repair.
I’m staying in THE Lotus Palace (the capital letters helping to distinguish it from the other Lotus Hotels that exist). It’s a former family mansion built in 1795, which required nearly five years of restoration before reopening as a luxury boutique hotel in 2024.
Painted a creamy light orange and bordered with equally creamy blue, yellow and red, it stands proudly within the village’s main street, along the same stretch as a small temple, an artisan woodcarver and another mansion house opposite, which belonged to the same family and now houses the hotel’s grand streetside cafe, Vaadhyar’s House.
Both buildings offer pristine examples of why the Chettinad mansions have attracted Unesco attention, and become the main attraction in this rural hinterland. The heritage hotel follows the traditional layout to a tee, informed by a balance of the Tamil equivalent of feng shui found in manuals such as the Manaiyadi Sastram, and the practical need to operate as a place of business. The chandelier at the entrance was re-created from black and white photos, using Belgian crystals. It stands before a showstopping ornate door, each frame artfully carved from teak wood over the course of a year. It’s flanked by thinnai – a raised veranda – once where the money lending took place.
Stepping through the door into welcome coolness and quietude, another reception area (the back office of the business) continues into a colonnade-studded inner courtyard, surrounded by two storeys of 15 boldly decorated bedrooms, each fragranced with invitingly fresh jasmine – a common motif in this part of the world.
Of the Chettinad mansions throughout the region, only some are maintained to this original beauty. If they’re not a hotel or tourist attraction, they operate as private properties, like the nearby Chettinad Palace, built by the first Raja of Chettinad in 1912. But most mansions were left to ruin due to emigration, destitution, or plain old family squabbles.
These derelict properties are the opposite of grandeur. Overgrown gardens with weeds reach to the dusty streets, crumbled walls with vegetation push through broken stained glass, and faded colours of religious deities grandly stand at the threshold. But to my eye, the faded glory artfully speaks to Chettinad’s postcolonial history, nature’s prowess and the world’s urbanisation.
For a small sum of 50 rupees (45 cents), I step into a mansion in the village that’s thrown open its doors to visitors. Meenakshi, who lives there as part of eight related families, explains that for their scenario, opening it to visitors was their only choice. “The roof is leaking. We’ve repaired one portion for 2 lakhs (€1,800), and the rest cost 10 lakhs (€9,000),” she says. “Sadly these houses aren’t built for the modern weather system. It never used to rain much here, but we get rain and floods so often now.”
A former medical superintendent in Singapore, Meenakshi is now retired in Kanadukathan and settled into village life, though she’s always considered this home – while abroad, she returned annually for a community-wide reading of the holy scripture of Ramayana. The fortnight-long event took place in the building of THE Lotus Palace, and the hotel continues this ritual to this day: a testament to the traditions that run deep in the village.
I consider Meenakshi’s annual return to her roots as I move on. Perhaps my detachment from India comes from having no close family or connection here – around the 1940s, most Ganatras moved from Gujarat in India to east Africa to help in the British effort to build railroads. They moved again in the 1970s, to the UK, as local resentment built against these immigrants. Colonisers sure have a lot to answer for.
My mixed background at least means I explore THE Lotus Palace and Chettinad with a brush of the familiar. I have a knowledge of the religious customs, and can hazard a guess at the social norms. Some cultural aspects, like parrot fortunetelling – a revered form of divination here – are still full of novelty.
The food is like nothing I’ve tasted before. While Chettinad curries seem to be a trending item in the West, it’s no surprise that it tastes infinitely better at the source. I try it as part of THE Lotus Palace’s 86 Pillars’ raja virundhu, or “feast for the kings”: a 21-item procession of flavours served on a banana leaf – salt and mango pickle first, sweet second, condiments after, then the punchy, fiery depth of the Chettinad curry and rice at the end.
I sightsee with childlike wonder. Kavitha, a local guide brimming with both knowledge and reflections about life in Chettinad, talks me through other prominent mansions, and we learn about Chettinad’s jewellery and tile heritage, and the stunning starch-stiff cotton saris that distinguish Tamil ladies. We amble through the antiques market: a whole area devoted to flea market finds, from pillars extracted from mansion properties, to skilled etched paintings of Hindu deities, to creepy empire-era figurines of British babies. She takes me to lakeside temples such as Sri Kotravaleeswarar Temple, which exudes such a calm that she calls it her “stressbuster”. I can see why. This is the India I resonate with, and it reminds me that India is far from one amorphous mass: each state is country and culture unto itself, and perhaps that adds to the difficulty in feeling a sense of belonging.
As we amble back through its dusty streets, Kavitha shyly asks me about my name. I’m sort of Indian, I tell her, except I’m kind of not. “Ohhh, you’re a belly-button relative!” she says. “I’m so proud when I meet belly-button relatives,” she says. Not quite sure what she means, I add in more nuances and caveats, but she’s more interested in the top line of our shared heritage.
I suspect “belly button relatives” is a colloquial term for the Indian diaspora, like “plastic Paddy” except a term of endearment, judging by her ear-to-ear grin. I leave Chettinad still not entirely sure. But while I attempt to answer the unanswerable, I’ll take it as a definition of our kinship, and indeed, my relationship to India: not plastic, not fake, just tethered. Belly-button relatives we are.
Shilpa Ganatra was a guest of THE Lotus Palace Chettinad and THE Park Chennai. Rooms start from about €188 per night plus taxes. Indirect flights from Dublin to Tiruchirappalli Airport start from €536. theparkhotels.com

title: The Comets by Eoin McNamee: Enlightenment in darkness
description: The title of this collection makes sense as many characters follow strange orbits
content:
In this collection of short fiction, Eoin McNamee takes you to places that feel familiar, and yet you have never visited them, and you hope you will never visit them, but in his masterly hands you are happy to reside there a while, trying to comprehend a little better the human hearts that crush the beauty out of the world into cuts and bruises of stark existence.
The Co Down author, who has written several novels, the best-known being Resurrection Man , places faces in front of you that fell from grace some time ago, if their owners are not already on their knees to begin with, and draws dialogue from them that’s as earthen as the environment that’s shaped it; what sounds like a song one second might slip into a snare the next.
In wrapping these stories in tempestuous weathers, McNamee rattles the windows of his characters’ minds, while smudging their sensibilities so that the line between pleasure and pain is something they stumble over.
You realise the light in the field of vision of The Comets is appropriately streaky when closing its pages, but that’s because McNamee is a writer who’s unafraid to approach darkness. The title of this collection makes sense as many characters follow strange orbits, most have nowhere to call home, nor inner lives to find a moment’s peace.
Most seem to function in high-pressure mode, always watching and waiting for when the pot lid will eventually flip in the futility of bone-crunching violence, bubble over and burn out. Sparks fly in many of the stories, with other recurring images: silk; snow; dust; tables of cigarette burns and drink stains; a magical realism in the weightlessness of wings contrasting the weight of industrial labour’s grind, wearing down the soul; memento mori lurk almost everywhere.
McNamee’s characters are fascinating due to the paradox of how many of them are looking to be found and yet wishing to get lost. A splendid line, of which there are many in this collection, encapsulates the fate of many found within: “If there was a realm of bad choices she would be queen.” His characters feel predestined to a life of pain - from the plain facts of poverty, ignorance and intolerance, religion and sectarianism; or from being other; or from just unfortunately born into it, as he writes movingly in Walking North, Walking Home, of those who have no start in the world.
“There would be children, princelings of destitution in worn-outclothes. There would be care workers, dim figures moving on the periphery of what children allowed themselves to see. All she remembered was that you never looked up.”
In these stories, looking up is likely to get you a smack in the head. In another story we find neglected children with no shoes, leaving beads of crimson after walking through the snow to the local church in search of some food. They are considered forsaken by the Brethren, and turned away hungry. It’s a cold world in every sense, in these tales.
McNamee’s ear for speech is as sharp as ever, as is his materialising menace in the most economical manner (“She knew the look in Eddie’s eye and would get to know it a lot better”) and death is never far from his pages, with its “thick sherbert smell”.
The two longest pieces of fiction in the collection - Love in History at 70 pages, and The Last of Deeds at almost 100 pages - feel the least satisfying from the author’s stretching, compared with his other impressively compact constructions. Among the ragbag cast of characters in the longer works there is no one to truly root for, to lock into with your heart to maintain a reader’s curiosity.
Love in History, set around second World War Belfast, feels overegged with metaphorical description, while The Last of Deeds, with its small-town sectarianism and coming-of-age struggle, is weighed down by its portentousness. Contrasting these are the likes of Quo Vadis, one of the finest in the collection, where McNamee brilliantly delivers dramatic high points in a paragraph in the story, as he does elsewhere, where another writer might overwrite.
A quibble in the turning point of The Road Wife, where a young woman is selling her body to long-haul lorry drivers: at a service station she goes to the toilet and leaves her handbag in the cabin; this is unlikely in almost any circumstances, but especially hers.
Nonetheless, as a collection The Comets leaves a satisfyingly heavy trail on a reader’s mind by its end. With titles such as Corpse Flowers and Sable, you realise you are journeying towards a dark horizon, but there’s a squalling pleasure of being blown around in these stories, like facing outwards for a walk into a stormy night, and not knowing who or what you might encounter.
NJ McGarrigle is a journalist from Co. Tyrone

title: In a Word ... Tricolour
description: ‘Believing there could be a united Ireland before the end of the world is not so far-fetched any more’
content:
A united Ireland is around the corner. Donald Trump indicated this last month at Doonbeg, so it has to be. If he-who-must-be-obeyed says there’s going to be a united Ireland, there’s going to be a united Ireland. Right?
He may even insist it bear his name. Trumpland? It could hardly be called Greenland, there already being that white and cool land he has conquered. Would he insist his united Ireland be called Orangeland, to match his hair? Anything is possible.
Seizing on what he said in Doonbeg, some choose to believe a united Ireland is already upon us . It could happen even before artificial intelligence destroys us, they insist – within a decade, or a little later, depending on which doomsday merchant you talk to.
Believing there could be a united Ireland before the end of the world is not so far-fetched any more.
Would-be emperor Trump might even favour retaining the Tricolour as the flag of his united Ireland. The Orange bit would probably attract.
It might help that the actual bicentenary of the flag will be in 2030, when (sadly?) the US will have a new president, Trump-allowing.
Thomas Francie Meagher is credited with flying the first Tricolour at Waterford in 1848. However, fellow Waterford man, historian John Crotty, says the first Irish Tricolour emerged in 1830, a year after Catholic Emancipation was achieved by Daniel O’Connell in 1829.
In March 1830, at the start of his Repeal movement [for a parliament in Dublin], O’Connell called for: “Orange and green to blend their colours henceforth, and let the general object be to render their country that place of plenty and happiness which God and nature intended.”
A rosette with both colours was soon being worn at Repeal meetings. In September 1830, Dublin woman Emelia Hamilton created the first Irish Tricolour of green, white, and orange inspired by the words of O’Connell and the French tricolour.
It was launched at an event in Dublin that December to mark O’Connell taking his seat at Westminster.
However, because of the Tricolour’s strong association with republican violence in Northern Ireland during the Troubles, it is unlikely to be accepted as the flag of a united Ireland, whenever that happens.
Tricolour , from French drapeau tricolore ( flag of three colours), was first adopted by France (blue, white, and red) in 1794.

title: Three arrested after gardaí chase stolen car on M50
description: Garda helicopter and armed support unit deployed after car spotted by gardaí on patrol investigating burglaries
content:
Three males have been arrested in West Dublin following a Garda chase of a stolen car on the M50 , in which a Garda helicopter and the armed support unit were deployed.
Two of those arrested were in their 20s and the third was a teenager.
Shortly after 7pm on Sunday, gardaí from Dublin metropolitan north division, on patrol as part of a continuing investigation into multiple burglaries, observed a car with several occupants on the Naul Road near Dublin Airport .
The car failed to stop and was pursued by gardaí.
“A co-ordinated response was launched, involving several local and divisional Garda units from across the Dublin region, including the armed support unit and air support,” said gardaí in a statement. ‘’
“The vehicle came to a stop on the M50 near Clondalkin, where three males – two in their 20s and one juvenile in his mid-teens – were subsequently arrested.
“All three are currently detained under Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act, 1984 at Garda stations in north Dublin.”
The Volkswagen Golf car they had been driving was reported stolen during a recent burglary in the Santry area. It has been recovered and brought in for technical examination.
No injuries were reported during this incident.
Investigations are continuing, said gardaí.

title: Male cyclist (60s) seriously injured following incident in Schull
description: The man was found unresponsive on the R592 at Corthna, Schull
content:
Gardaí in west Cork are appealing for witnesses following a serious road traffic incident in Schull on Sunday.
Shortly after 9.30am, local gardaí and emergency services were alerted after a male cyclist in his 60s was found unresponsive on the R592 at Corthna, Schull.
He was treated at the scene before being taken by ambulance to Cork University Hospital with serious injuries.
The road will remain closed, and local traffic diversions will be in place overnight to facilitate an examination by Garda forensic collision investigators.
Gardaí are appealing to anyone who was in the area on Sunday morning, particularly those with camera footage. Motorists with dashcam footage are also urged to come forward.
Anyone with information is asked to contact Bantry Garda station on (027) 20860, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111 or any Garda station.

title: Cuala star power wins the day as Derek Dunne leads his crew to Dublin title glory
description: Manager focused on upcoming Tullamore clash after southside club’s Dublin SFC final win over Castleknock
content:
Derek Dunne would have been forgiven for swerving the Cuala job when it came up last year. Austin O’Malley stepped down after leading the southside club to an All-Ireland title, meaning that regardless of who took over, there wasn’t exactly a whole lot of wiggle room available for improvement. What was he going to do – take them into the Champions League?
But when you’re a lifer, you’re a lifer. Dunne’s father was over the Cuala team that made their first-ever football final way back in 1988. His daughter Jennifer won three All-Irelands for Dublin and over the weekend played her 50th game for the Brisbane Lions in the AFLW. He had the 2002 boys’ team in Cuala when they were kids – five of them played here as they torched Castleknock in the Dublin final by 3-15 to 1-6.
“I would have been involved previously, twice before,” he told us outside the Cuala dressingroom in Parnell Park. “I suppose when you win an All-Ireland, there’s not too many people to step up to take it on ... The bottom line is this is a very experienced group.
“You have people like Michael Fitzsimons in the dressingroom. You have people like Con O’Callaghan in the dressingroom. Peadar [Ó Cofaigh Byrne] obviously is in with the Dubs now. There’s a really, really strong environment there. The likes of Conor O’Brien, who’s been playing football for years with Cuala. It’s a really, really strong group and they drive themselves, you know what I mean? I’m just kind of driving the bus with them.”
Their size and star power won the day for them against a Castleknock side whose challenge fizzled out after making a decent start. Con O’Callaghan ended the day with 2-5 to add a second Dublin football medal to his four hurling ones. Even with the big total against his name, you’d say he’s had more spectacular days. Few more effective ones, all the same.
“Con is class. Con is such a leader within the group. Michael is a leader in the group but Con is ... I didn’t know Con as a footballer. I knew Con as an individual within his family, I know them all very well. But I didn’t know Con as a footballer, as part of a management team. But he’s so, so good.
“When he talks, the stuff he comes out with is brilliant. And then his leadership on the pitch – he scored 2-5 but he probably got four or five turnovers. That’s the part that you don’t see about Con that I think is fantastic. The work rate, the turnovers, the hard hits, the tracking back, that’s the part of Con that I think of and that’s why he’s one of the best in the country.”
Cuala have Offaly champions Tullamore back in Parnell Park in a fortnight now. When the two sides met in the Leinster semi-final a couple of years back, O’Callaghan’s four-point haul was crucial in a scrappy game. Tullamore return to Donnycarney having won Offaly four times on the bounce. But the Dublin champions have won Leinster every year since 2019. Anything short of that will be an upset for Cuala.
“We had Tullamore here two years ago,” Dunne said. “I wasn’t involved but I was here, obviously, and they were very, very good. So it’s a really tough one to start with but we’d like to think that hopefully we can get a bit of a campaign going there.”

title: More than 20 Romanian men with convictions deported on charter flight
description: The 24 individuals were convicted of crimes including burglary, domestic violence, sexual assault, drug offences and organised crime
content:
More than 20 Romanian men were removed from the State on a flight chartered on behalf of the Garda National Immigration Bureau (GNIB) on Sunday.
The 24 individuals, ranging in age from 24 years to 57, are banned from re-entering the Republic of Ireland for periods of up to 10 years.
They were removed on the grounds of convictions and imprisonment for crimes including burglary, domestic violence, sexual assault, drug offences and organised crime.
Under the provisions of the European Union free movement directive EU citizens can be forcibly removed from another EU state if its authorities deem them to be a serious threat to public safety, wellbeing or public policy.
The flight departed Dublin Airport at 4.25pm and arrived in Bucharest, Romania, at 8pm Irish time.
Eighteen of the men were in prison at the time and were removed by the GNIB from the custody of the Irish Prison Service .
The other six were arrested at locations across Ireland and detained before their removal on Sunday.
[ Forty-three Georgian nationals deported from Ireland on Sunday Opens in new window ]
Garda personnel, medical staff, interpreters and a human rights observer accompanied the men on the flight.
Minister of State at the Department of Justice Colm Brophy said: “It is vital that everyone living in the State respects and complies with its laws.
“It is important to acknowledge that the majority of Romanian nationals resident in the State respect our laws and make a positive contribution to Irish society.
“Six previous charter operations this year has seen the removal of 221 people. Today’s operation brings the total removed by charter in 2026 to 245, including 91 EU citizens who were removed on grounds of criminality.”
The cost of chartering the flight was €182,270 (excluding VAT).

title: Macron criticises ‘unbridled violence’ after day of unrest in France
description: Historic public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and more than 2,000 people arrested
content:
French president Emmanuel Macron has criticised “unbridled violence” after one of the most violent days of unrest in years left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and more than 2,000 people arrested in cities across the country.
“Watching these images, we have all asked ourselves, how could French people do this to France ?” he said in a televised address.
Macron said “nothing justifies” violence, and that local state officials would be able to ban certain street gatherings if they deemed it necessary.
He said a distinction must be drawn between what he called genuine, peaceful demonstrators making demands over the cost of living and the state of the education system, and others who “destroy, ransack and loot”. He criticised what he called “factious groups from the ultra-left, joined by numerous delinquents”.
Politicians on the left and right called for the resignation of the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, after the government appeared to have been caught by surprise by the scale of violence on Saturday as state buildings were stormed and torched, bus stops smashed, roads barricaded and shops broken into and destroyed. Protests also took place in Spain, Italy and Portugal.
Crowds clashed with police at Place de la République in central Paris on Sunday afternoon as violence flared for a second day. Electric bikes were piled up in some streets and set alight. Bottles and rocks were thrown and thick plumes of smoke rose from burning bins. Police responded with teargas and stun grenades.
Police and officials faced challenges of different types on Saturday. First, tens of thousands of peaceful protesters attended calm marches through major cities including Paris, supporting schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools.
These gatherings, which came after four weeks of street marches and barricades of schools, were attended by parents, teachers and grandparents as well as students and workers protesting over the high cost of living. The demonstrators carried banners saying the government was not listening to them and calling for more money for public services.
[ France is caught in the politics of emergency, oscillating between nostalgia and extremism Opens in new window ]
But separately to these peaceful demonstrations, different groups caught police and officials by surprise by moving locations, sporadic burning of various objects, barricading of streets and violent behaviour in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseilles.
Finally, masked looters took advantage of what French media called the “chaos” on the streets to smash shopfronts and grab goods. In Paris, groups of looters, some of whom appeared to be children, were seen running through the night with clothes and shoeboxes after masked adult men smashed shopfronts.
In Paris, where police said a record 855 people had been arrested, the burnt-out remains of barricades built using bikes, bins and other materials littered streets on Sunday. Several streets had smashed-up shop windows and the remains of torched cars. The capital had experienced “a level of violence that we have never seen before, I believe”, said the socialist deputy mayor, Lamia El Aaraje.
In Limoges in central France, where the 19th-century town hall was burned down, the mayor Guillaume Guérin said the people who stormed his building “were not demonstrators that defend causes” but “people organised for war”. He said those who stormed and torched the town hall had told a building caretaker he would be killed, and told elected officials they would “burn”. He said there had been a failure of the state to deal with the crisis.
“Around 3.30pm our municipal police, although present in number, found themselves no longer able to fight against the violence of rioters, because they had run out of ammunition,” Guérin said. He called this “a colossal failure of the state”.
[ ‘A bombshell’: French teachers spot something on payslips that reveals scale of funding crisis Opens in new window ]
In Marseilles, where masked groups stormed the city hall and a police station, the socialist mayor, Benoît Payan, told BFMTV: “I have no words … I never thought I’d ever live through something like this. Hordes of rioters and looters attacked our common [state] buildings … with no real demands, but with the sole aim to wreck the demands of those who had demonstrated legitimately.”
Payan said questions must be asked about policing tactics, as other town hall buildings, for example in Lille, were also targeted.
Grégory Doucet, the Green mayor of Lyons, said he had never seen such violence in his city, including the torching of the historic tourist office. He told Le Monde: “I’m stunned by the violence against public and state property. I saw and heard fear and anger. Shop owners felt abandoned.”
Doucet said the government must find a “sense of nuance” in properly examining what happened and “avoiding stereotypes”. He said the government needed to give a political response to long-running societal demands from peaceful demonstrators, and also examine the roots of violence.
Traders’ unions said more than 1,500 shops and businesses had been ransacked, with the cost running into tens of millions of euro. “This had nothing to do with the peaceful protesters,” said one shoe-shop owner in Paris. “These were organised groups who were breaking things and looting. We’d never seen anything like it.”
Opposition politicians questioned the government’s policing tactics, saying there had been a lack of state intelligence.
The interior ministry said there had been more than 2,000 arrests and that about 600 police, firefighters and paramedics had been hurt. A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the eastern-central city of Saint-Étienne. A 17-year-old girl lost an eye in Mulhouse and a policing investigation was opened into the circumstances.
Macron’s centrist government and the far-right front-runner in the presidential election, Marine Le Pen , both blamed what they called “ultra-left” groups for the violence. The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the government would not be “intimidated” by ⁠violence, and blamed the unrest on the “ultra-left” and criminals.
The radical-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who attended the peaceful street demonstration in Paris on Saturday, accused the government of organisational failings that had “opened the door to chaos”.
Lecornu replied on social media: “Laying the responsibility for violence on heads of police is a dangerous and cynical reversal of responsibilities.” – Guardian

title: State apology to be delivered to family of late chief prison officer Brian Stack
description: Taoiseach Micheál Martin will deliver the apology on Wednesday in the Dáil
content:
The family of the late Brian Stack, the chief prison officer at Portlaoise Prison who was shot by the IRA 43 years ago and later died in hospital, will receive a formal State apology in relation to the mishandling of three separate Garda investigations into his murder.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin will deliver the apology on Wednesday in the Dáil . It follows an apology by then Garda commissioner Drew Harris in July 2019. The Stack family has been pressing for a State apology.
Brian Stack (48) was shot in the neck on March 25th, 1983, while returning to his car in the South Circular Road area of Dublin . He died in hospital on September 29th, 1984.
Portlaoise Prison at the time was the highest security jail holding many IRA members convicted under the Offences Against the State Act. As chief prison officer, Stack was known for his efficacy in maintaining security and preventing escapes.
The IRA denied responsibility but in 2013 issued a statement to Stack’s three sons, Austin, Kieran and Oliver, saying its members were responsible but that the murder had not been sanctioned by the leadership.
“In Portlaoise a brutal prison regime saw prisoners and their families suffer greatly. This is the context in which IRA volunteers shot your father,” the statement said.
The family has long been critical of what it said were missed opportunities and delays in investigating who was behind the murder.
In a letter to Austin Stack, dated September 2026, Martin said: “I wish to inform you that following Government approval, over the coming weeks I intend in my role as Taoiseach to offer the Stack family a full and unreserved apology on behalf of the State for the failings in the murder investigations of your late father.”
The family will have a private meeting with Martin and Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan before the apology on Wednesday. The family will arrive at Government Buildings at 11.30am, said Austin Stack in a statement.
The Department of the Taoiseach has been contacted for comment.

title: Extra-time goal by Conor Hand secures Roscommon title for St Brigid’s
description: Crossmaglen Rangers claim record 48th Armagh title while Gowna do a demolition job to get their hands on the cup
content:
On a dramatic day of county finals, last season’s All-Ireland runners-up St Brigid’s retained the Roscommon SFC title for the first time since 2017 with a thrilling extra-time victory over rivals Pádraig Pearses at Dr Hyde Park.
Conor Hand appeared to have won it in normal time before substitute Tom Butler landed a dramatic two-pointer to force extra-time.
Man of the Match Hand then struck a decisive goal as Brigid’s took control, with substitutes Charlie O’Carroll and Eddie Nolan making important contributions.
Declan Kenny’s late penalty offered Pearses hope but Brigid’s held firm to claim their 20th county title and retain the Fahey Cup.
Meanwhile, Crossmaglen Rangers claimed a record 48th Armagh SFC title with a hard-fought five-point victory (1-19 to 0-17) over Killeavy, who were chasing a first title since 1948 and raced into an early five-point lead.
Crossmaglen recovered to lead by two at half-time but the sides were level entering the final 10 minutes before Pearse Blessing, who finished with 1-3, struck the decisive goal in the 47th minute.
Oisín O’Neill (0-6) and Cian McConville also impressed as Crossmaglen held off a spirited Killeavy challenge to secure a first title since 2023.
In Cavan , Gowna also got their hands on the cup for the first time in three years with a 4-17 to 0-14 demolition of holders Kingscourt Stars at Kingspan Breffni.
Vinny Corey’s men dominated from the outset, racing into a 3-9 to 0-7 interval lead with goals from Oisín Pierson, Seanie Hartin and Conor Casey.
Kingscourt, who had beaten Gowna by nine points in last year’s decider, never recovered as the winners controlled proceedings throughout.
Full-back Cillian Brady, who was outstanding, added a fourth goal late on as Gowna, with 13 different scorers, completed a memorable victory – and set up an Ulster clash, incidentally, with Crossmaglen.
Over the road in Louth , Newtown Blues and St Mochta’s must do it all again after playing out a 1-15 apiece draw.
Declan Byrne’s dramatic injury-time two-point free earned St Mochta’s a replay after the Blues had led by five in the second half, with Emmett Carolan netting.
Byrne’s late heroics levelled matters before county man Ciaran Downey was off-target with a two-point free which would have won it.
Ulster champions Scotstown made it 11 county SFC crowns since 2013 as they eclipsed Truagh 1-22 to 0-10 in the Monaghan final.
Captain Rory Beggan landed four two-point frees as Scotstown pulled away in the closing stages. They led by nine in the first half and five at the break; Truagh had reduced the deficit to four points after 40 minutes but failed to score again, with Scotstown registering 11 unanswered points to seal an emphatic victory, Max Maguire chipping in with 0-5.
In the southeast, Kilanerin claimed their first Wexford SFC title since 2008 with a 1-15 to 0-12 victory over St Martin’s at Wexford Park.
Substitute Vincent Higgins struck the decisive goal in the 52nd minute for Pádraig Murphy’s side.
St Martin’s had led by two points early in the second half but Kilanerin turned the contest with three quick-fire two-pointers from brothers Seán, Niall and Páraic Hughes.
Higgins then found the net following excellent approach play from Niall Hughes and Micheál McGonigle, sealing a memorable triumph for the north Wexford club.
In Carlow , Rathvilly gained revenge for last year’s final defeat as they dethroned Old Leighlin with a 0-14 to 1-8 victory at Netwatch Cullen Park.
Cathal Coughlan’s early goal kept Old Leighlin in contention but Rathvilly, who saw an early Conor Doyle penalty go over the bar, led 0-8 to 1-3 at half-time and maintained their advantage thereafter.
Doyle, Liam Gavin and substitutes Brynn Nolan and Eric Molloy made important scoring contributions before Doyle landed the insurance point to seal a deserved victory.
There were emotional scenes as Loughmore-Castleiney claimed their 17th Tipperary SFC title with a hard-fought two-point victory over Clonmel Commercials at Semple Stadium.
Man of the Match Liam McGrath contributed seven points, while late scores from Joey Quinn and John McGrath secured the win.
The 2024 dual champions became the first recipients of the Philly Ryan Cup, presented in memory of the late Tipperary football manager, with Jarlath Burns in attendance as Ryan’s wife, Anna, presented the cup to winning captain Brian McGrath.
It was Loughmore’s third successive county final victory over Commercials, following their triumphs in 2021 and 2024, while Noel McGrath collected his 11th senior county medal.
The Donegal final was again closely contested as Ciaran Moore struck the winning point with the final kick as St Eunan’s snatched victory over holders Naomh Conaill at MacCumhaill Park.
In a thrilling finish, substitute Charlie McGuinness appeared to have won it for Naomh Conaill, for whom Australia-bound Finbarr Roarty lined out, before Niall O’Donnell levelled and Moore completed the turnaround.
Ethan O’Donnell had goaled for Naomh Conaill while James Kelly netted for St Eunan’s in a gripping second half. Moore finished with four points as the Letterkenny side reclaimed the Dr Maguire Cup in sensational fashion.
History was made in Antrim as St Brigid’s claimed their first SFC title with a thrilling two-point victory over Rossa at a sold-out Corrigan Park.
Ronan McGrady and JJ Higgins starred as Brigid’s established a two-point interval lead before Diarmaid Rogan’s second-half goal swung momentum the way of the city club.
The sides traded scores in a gripping final quarter, with Dominic McEnhill drawing Rossa level through a two-pointer. However, Higgins struck crucial late points to secure a historic triumph for St Brigid’s, finishing with seven points as “the Biddies” celebrated their maiden county crown.
Elsewhere, Éire Óg, Ennis completed a historic Clare SFC three-in-a-row with a 2-15 to 1-10 victory over Kilmurry Ibrickane at Cusack Park.
Mark McInerney starred with 1-6 as the champions secured their fifth title in six seasons.
McInerney’s early goal established control before Darren Moroney added a late second, sealing Éire Óg’s place in the history books; the previous most recent three-in-a-row was achieved by Kilrush in the 1970s.
Finally, the Tyrone final also finished in stalemate as Darren McCurry’s dramatic last-gasp two-pointer earned first-time finalists Edendork a replay against Errigal Ciaran.
Errigal, missing Darragh Canavan whose brother Ruairi only came on, led 0-6 to 0-3 at half-time before substitute Fiachra Nelis goaled for Edendork with his first touch.
Errigal appeared to have snatched victory through late scores from Eoin Kelly and Aodhan Quinn, but McCurry’s long-range effort, awarded after consultation between officials, ensured a draw.

title: Adam Screeney’s eight-point haul helps Kilcormac-Killoughey to fourth straight title in Offaly
description: Hurling county final round-up: The Harps claim a first title in Laois while Lough Lene Gaels win for first time since 2002 in Westmeath
content:
Kilcormac-Killoughey made it four in a row of Offaly hurling titles, and eight overall, with a 0-19 to 0-17 victory over Ballinamere at O’Connor Park.
Kilcormac pulled away either side of half-time, with Adam Screeney (0-8, seven frees) helping them into a 0-10 to 0-6 interval lead, before pushing six ahead by the three-quarter mark.
That remained the gap until the closing stages as three Brian Duignan frees made it a one-score game before Aaron Maher zipped an equalising goal attempt over the crossbar.
They will encounter the Kildare champions, Naas or Maynooth, in their Leinster quarter-final.
Years of hurt were washed away in the Westmeath and Sligo hurling finals.
Next door in Laois, The Harps hit the right chord to deliver a first senior hurling title, unleashing a 16-point dismissal of record champions Camross at O’Moore Park.
It’s the second time that former Tipperary goalkeeper and manager Ken Hogan has masterminded a breakthrough success in the county, previously leading Borris-Kilcotton to glory in 2016.
The Harps, who have won the last four Laois under-20 titles, delivered a coming-of-age performance. Their outstanding defence limited Camross to 0-13, while a healthy spread of scorers combined for 2-23.
The Durrow-Cullohill club put daylight between the sides with Ross Deegan’s thunderous finish for a 13th-minute goal.
Tadhg Duggan’s double save kept Camross alive, but only just, trailing 1-11 to 0-8 at half-time.
It was game over on 41 minutes. Zane Keenan’s 21-yard free was saved on the line and The Harps countered, with Justin Duggan collecting Deegan’s delivery to sweep home.
Their Leinster debut will come against the Kilkenny champions, Ballyhale Shamrocks or Tullaroan.
In the Lake County, Lough Lene Gaels won their first senior title since 2002, and eighth overall, with a 1-16 to 0-16 victory over 14-man Raharney at Cusack Park.
The Gaels had suffered seven final defeats since then, including each of the past three years, but David Williams’s 1-10 haul (1-9 from placed balls) guided them over the line.
Killian Doyle (0-8, five frees) led the way for Raharney, who were 0-9 to 0-7 ahead by midway.
It all changed after the restart. Lough Lene reeled off 1-4, with captain Williams slotting the penalty, which saw Jamie Mulkearns dismissed for a second booking.
Noel Conaty denied Doyle a goal, but the forward helped to cut the gap to the minimum in stoppage time.
With Marcus Kennedy’s red card evening out the playing numbers, the Gaels found the insurance scores through Philip Reilly and Williams.
The Leinster campaign will see them meet the Wexford winners, Rathnure or Shelmaliers.
In Sligo, Naomh Eoin put six consecutive final defeats behind them to stun All-Ireland junior runners-up Easkey by 0-17 to 1-13 at Markievicz Park.
Patrick Walsh’s goal got Easkey off to a flying start, but Gerard O’Kelly-Lynch’s freetaking soon had the underdogs ahead. The men from Sligo town led 0-13 to 1-6 at half-time.
Easkey, chasing their seventh title in a row, dug deep with five consecutive points down the stretch. Andrew Kilcullen’s eighth free of the afternoon drew them level in stoppage time.
However, O’Kelly-Lynch’s 10th placed ball proved the winner, wrapping up Naomh Eoin’s first title since their 2019 breakthrough.
The formbook held in Down, where Portaferry completed their five in a row with a 2-28 to 2-17 success against 14-man Ballygalget .
Ciarán Milligan bagged an early goal at Páirc Esler, but the shock looked on at half-time with strikes from Shea Pucci and Cathal Coulter sending Galget into a 2-11 to 1-13 lead.
Jordan Doran was sent off and Eoghan Sands netted to flip the momentum. Portaferry pushed on for a 1-7 streak and they ultimately won the second half by 1-15 to 0-6 with Tom McGrattan’s 0-13 (three from play) leading the way.
Having wrapped up their 26th title, Portaferry will face the Antrim champions, Cushendall or Dunloy, in the Ulster semi-final.
Offaly: Kilcormac-Killoughey 0-19 Ballinamere 0-17
Westmeath: Lough Lene Gaels 1-16 Raharney 0-16

title: The Irish Times view on the EU budget: political compromise will not be easy
description: A draft put forward by the Irish EU presidency has been attacked by all sides, illustrating the problems ahead
content:
The Irish presidency is facing a big challenge in trying to get agreement on the next EU budget, which had been one of its key goals. Its proposal on a new seven-year package was never going to please everyone, in view of the opposing positions among member states, the European Commission and the European Parliament. However, the widespread backlash to the draft budget meant very little, if any, progress was made at the European Council meeting during the week, bar the various sides setting out their objections.
This may have been an inevitable step before real negotiations. EU member states are broadly split into two camps. The “frugals” comprising Germany, the Benelux and Nordic countries want hundreds of billions shaved from the commission’s budget proposal of €1.76 billion. Moreover, these countries want the seven-year budget from 2028 to 2034 to prioritise spending on improving economic competitiveness and defence.
A group of 17 mostly southern member states are opposed to any cut, and want the budget to prioritise agriculture and regional aid. As Taoiseach Micheál Martin put it, the presidency’s job is like “trying to reconcile the irreconcilable.”
The Irish Government proposed cutting the budget by 8 percent, or €141 billion, which has failed to resonate with any of the differing camps. How its plan aims to achieve these savings is equally divisive. It proposed a 3 per cent cut to farming and regional aid subsidies but a much larger 13 per cent cut to competitiveness and defence, as well as reducing funds set aside to respond to contingencies.
The Northern states and the European Commission argue that the proposal would undermine the future viability of the EU. One commission official said that Ireland had drafted a budget fit for the 20th century. There was further criticism of the lack of detail on new sources of taxation that the Commission could use to generate much needed additional revenues.
It is important that progress is made over the coming months. Marine le Pen, the far-right candidate, is leading the polls ahead of the French presidential election next year. She has pledged to slash France’s contribution to the EU budget if she wins. However the politically parlous position of French president Emmanuel Macron, and of his German counterpart, chancellor Friedrich Merz, complicate the search for a solution.
Meanwhile, the EU faces a growing array of threats. It risks being squeezed by the economic might of the US and China and Russia poses a military threat on its doorstep.
A period of drift without a budget agreement would be damaging. Recent years have shown the imperative of European cooperation in response to crises. But politics is making the search for a budget solution very difficult.

title: Glen Rovers turn back the clock to win their first Cork title in a decade
description: Two goals from Eoin O’Leary in a dominant second-half display seal their 28th Cork championship
content:
At the final whistle swarms of Glen Rovers youngsters broke the membrane of stewarding around the packed stands and congregated at a green flare near the City End. In the middle of the throng Glen players were hoisted shoulder high as the music boomed from the stadium’s sound system. “The dog days are over,” sang Florence Welch. The Glen crowd jumped up and down.
Just three years after they were relegated from the top tier of Cork hurling for the first time in their history the Glen were decisive winners of their 28 th title. Only three points separated the teams at the end, and the Glen had to survive a goalmouth scare in stoppage time, but there was no question about their superiority.
Two second half goals from Eoin O’Leary were ultimately the difference between the teams but all told they trailed for no more than seven minutes. St Finbarr’s reeled off six points in a blistering seven-minute spell just before half-time, but their two- point lead at the break was a distortion of the first half.
The Glen recovered from that dizzy spell and surged again. O’Leary’s first goal was a bullish solo effort seven minutes after the break, brushing off his marker along the endline and batting the ball to the net. When he struck again six minutes from the end, he was isolated in so much space 30 metres from the Barrs goal that he must have thought he was in quarantine. He took half a dozen paces at his leisure and smashed the ball to the Barr’s net.
That put them five points clear, 2-18 to 0-19, which was the biggest margin between the teams at any stage of the game. The Barr’s continued to create shooting opportunities and the outstanding Ethan Twomey took his second half tally to five points in the closing minutes, but they desperately needed a goal.
In the final minute of stoppage time a half-chance materialised. A long ball broke around the Glen square, William Buckley was quickest to react, but he couldn’t control the ball first time and Cathal Hickey advanced quickly from the Glen goal. Hickey and Buckley collided and the ball squirted away.
The Barrs and the Glen is the most storied rivalry in Cork club hurling, but the balance of power has shifted away from the city in recent decades, and this was their first meeting in a county final since 1988. Astonishingly, it was the Glen’s first county final victory over the Barr’s since 1967. The significance of the victory was not lost on any of them.
“There was definitely a re-assessment of everything [after the Glen were relegated],” said Rob Downey, the Cork and Glen centre back. “I wouldn’t be slow to admit that as players we allowed standards to drop – in our training and in our preparation. I think in fairness to Tomás Mulcahy [the Glen manager] when we went down he brought in Tommy Dunne [as coach] and he drove things on.
“This year we got in Donal O’Rourke [the former Cork and Waterford coach] and I suppose the club game has gone to a new level now – it’s gone almost like intercounty. You need to be ticking every box. So we had Donal O’Rourke, Ian Jones [the Cork S&C coach], Peter O’Keeffe, along with four or five other brilliant Glen fellas. I don’t know what it is, but we always have this mentality that we think we’re going to win no matter what sort of a team we have.”
They started with that confidence and could have blown the Barr’s away in the opening 10 minutes. Simon Kennefick hit the crossbar from close range, and the Glen shot six wides in quick succession when they were completely on top.
They maintained a two-point lead for most of the first half with Patrick Horgan exerting a greater influence when he drifted towards the half forward line. At the other end, though, there was a similar dynamic at play. Rob Downey started on Brian Hayes on the edge of the square, but the Cork full-forward came out the field as the half wore on and picked off three points to energise the Barrs’ best spell in game.
The Barr’s led by 0-12 to 0-10 at half-time, but the Glen seized the initiative immediately after the break, rattling off 1-2 without reply. Once they wrestled back the lead, they didn’t let it slip. O’Leary took his total to 2-2 and the Glen were home.

title: The Irish Times view on mortgage arrears: a longstanding legacy of the crash
description: Some borrowers who saw their loans sold to investment funds need a way out
content:
A recent study by the Central Bank has shone a light on one of the less obvious legacies of the financial crash. Almost 20 years since the global economic crisis exposed the fatal flaws in the Irish banking system, a small but persistent cohort of Celtic Tiger mortgage borrowers remain caught in a debt trap.
The bank examined more than 20,000 people who are over 90 days behind on their mortgage repayments and concluded that about one third of them have little or no chance of clearing their loans by the time they retire. Most are 50 years or older, which suggests that their problems date back to the crash. They have been availing of the forbearance lenders are required to offer by law, but as they approach retirement age there will be a need for more permanent solutions.
Two thirds of these borrowers already find themselves in the hands of Loan Serving Firms (LSF) who either bought their mortgages from the retail banks rescued by the taxpayer, or act on behalf of investment funds who did so.
LSFs are subject to the same arrears rules as banks when it comes to dealing with struggling borrowers, but they typically charge higher mortgage rates. Because of this, political assurances that borrowers would not be worse of because their loans were sold ring a bit hollow.
The problem will likely manifest first in LSFs as the distressed borrowers on their books tend to be older – 50 per cent are over 56 – and, according to the Central Bank, some 45 per cent of them will not be able to clear their mortgage before retirement. The comparable figure for those with loans with the main banks is 18 per cent.
The issue will crystallise in the coming years as these individual’s approach retirement. The Government would be well advised to move to ensure that adequate alternative arrangements building on the existing Mortgage to Rent scheme and the system of Personal Insolvency Arrangements are in place and are made available. Many funds have already made a decent return on their investment. It is time to give borrowers who really cannot pay a break.

title: Ukraine defies Trump by launching its largest-ever drone attack on St Petersburg
description: Attack on city’s energy infrastructure comes after US president struck diesel deal with Putin and waived new sanctions on Russia
content:
Ukraine carried out its largest-ever drone attack on St Petersburg on Sunday, defying US demands to halt strikes against Russian energy infrastructure.
Fires broke out at the oil terminal in St Petersburg’s port, governor Alexander Beglov said, sending a large plume of black smoke billowing over the night sky. The attacks indicated Ukraine was determined to press on with its campaign of strikes against Russian refineries, which it had paused after US president Donald Trump ’s surprise announcement that the two countries had agreed to an “energy ceasefire”. It resumed its campaign after uninterrupted Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Trump said he had agreed the ceasefire, struck a diesel deal with Moscow and waived a set of new sanctions on Russia’s energy exports last Sunday. But the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskiy , said the energy ceasefire failed to stop Russian strikes, with more than 76 recorded attacks on the country’s energy, oil and gas facilities in the past week, leading to large power outages.
A Russian ‌air strike killed ​one person and injured two ​in Ukraine’s ⁠capital Kyiv ‌on Sunday night, the city’s mayor ​Vitali ⁠Klitschko said ​on ​Telegram. A ​medical facility ⁠and ⁠a ​non-residential building were damaged in the ‌attack, ⁠he added.
“The main targets of these strikes are energy facilities – the Russians are trying to cause a blackout,” Zelenskiy said on X on Sunday. “United States should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements.”
Air defence forces in St Petersburg claimed to have shot down 146 drones on Sunday. One person was killed and nine injured in the attacks, they added.
Parts of Russia’s second city lost power for several hours after the drones hit an electricity substation, according to online media outlet Astra. State-run VK, one of Russia’s largest tech companies and parent company of social network VKontakte, said one of its data centres had also been hit. Online marketplace Ozon said a fire broke out after a drone strike on a warehouse in the city, the first time Ukraine had targeted logistics infrastructure since mid-September.
Airports in Moscow and St Petersburg were closed for several hours during the attack. Hundreds of flights have been cancelled in the past two weeks as Ukraine has expanded its strikes, adding to disruption for Russian travellers who have got used to planning trips considering that they might be severely delayed or land in a different city due to drones.
Alina, a 33-year-old who lives in the Nevsky district in the southeast of the city, one of the worst affected areas, told the Financial Times that she woke to the sound of explosions at 3am and continued to hear them until 6am. Russia’s defence ministry claimed to have shot down a total of 1,015 drones across the country on Sunday, including 512 in the Moscow area, according to local authorities.
The dispute over targeting energy infrastructure has seen Kyiv’s relationship with the White House sink further since the infamous Oval Office meeting between Zelenskiy and Trump in February 2025.
[ Zelenskiy no longer willing to placate Trump Opens in new window ]
The US, which had previously provided crucial targeting data for the strikes, said it had repeatedly asked Zelenskiy to halt attacks on Russia’s refineries, and then allowed Moscow to export diesel amid a rise in prices on global markets.
Zelenskiy told NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday that the US had restored intelligence sharing, which he said had been blocked for three days during ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine.
Ukraine has accused the US of limiting its military support in favour of abruptly embracing economic deals with Russia even as Russia’s president Vladimir Putin has shown no interest in abating his own aerial onslaught.
Zelenskiy said several electricity substations were hit in central and southern Ukraine as Russia launched 180 drones, one ballistic missile and several “Banderol” cruise missiles overnight to Sunday. One hundred and fifty-two drones were shot down, according to Ukraine’s air force.
Speaking to reporters on a WhatsApp chat on Saturday, Zelenskiy said he expected the US to lift more sanctions targeting Russia. Trump’s decision to waive sanctions mandated by a law voted by Congress last month “only helps the Russians”, Zelenskiy said.
In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump said his ‌decision to waive sanctions and tariffs ​related to Russian exports is an effort to ​keep Russia at the ⁠negotiating table.
“My decision ⁠on ​Russia is ​a very simple ‌one,” Trump said ​in the post. “I am in ⁠the ⁠process ​of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want ‌to do ⁠anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away ‌from the bargaining table.”
Kyiv was blindsided this week by unexplained speed limits on the Starlink communication system used by the military to fly drones used to strike Russian targets behind the front line, as well as to strike drones hitting Ukrainian cities. Zelenskiy said the restrictions were “a planned operation”.
A senior Ukrainian official told the Financial Times on Sunday that Starlink remained throttled to prevent its use by the Ukrainian military at speeds above 160km/h. US treasury secretary Scott Bessent told NBC on Sunday that it was “reckless” of Zelenskiy to allege that the Trump administration had intentionally slowed Starlink.
Zelenskiy spoke on Sunday with Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Kyiv is looking to hold talks next week with the US, though the meeting has not been confirmed yet.

title: Man killed in fatal assault outside Dublin apartment named as gardaí search for weapon
description: Gardaí discovered the man with serious injuries on the footpath at Blackhorse Place in north Dublin
content:
Gardaí are searching for the weapon used in a fatal assault outside the Blackhorse Place apartment block in Dublin 7.
A man, named locally as Jamie Bailey (30s) from Limerick, died after the attack. He was found by gardaí on the footpath with serious injuries at the apartment block on Blackhorse Avenue after being alerted by the public.
The man was brought to the Mater Misericordiae University Hospital , where he was later pronounced dead.
Gardaí believe the victim was killed arising from a bitter personal dispute that had worsened in recent weeks and they suspect he knew his killer.
It is understood that gardaí suspect a knife or another bladed weapon may have been used in the assault, which took place between 2.00am and 3.30am on Sunday morning.
Detectives and a divisional search unit were on site searching the area, including drains, for the weapon.
Gardaí viewed CCTV footage from a convenience store on the street, which was not open at the time of the assault.
The force is appealing for witnesses to the incident or those who may have dashcam footage of the area at the time to contact Bridewell Garda station.
The busy road was closed to traffic on Sunday as gardaí carried out a forensic search of the area, with bus routes on the road facing diversions.
The Garda said a postmortem is set to take place and that the coroner and the State Pathologist have been notified.
Cabra/Glasnevin councillor Séamas McGrattan said he was shocked by the incident.
“Knife crime has become a real problem in our city. We need an urgent and serious response,” the Sinn Féin councillor said.
“People must have the right to walk the streets of Dublin safely and without fear.”
He called for an increased Garda presence on the ground and policing to deter crime and antisocial behaviour from taking place.

title: Con O’Callaghan scores 2-5 as rampant Cuala outclass Castleknock to win third Dublin title
description: Dalkey side dismantle the underdogs’ kick-out to register the fourth biggest win in the history of Dublin county finals
content:
Nothing lets the air out of the balloon like a county final blowout. All week, the streets and lanes and backroads around Castleknock have been wallpapered in yellow and blue, the buzz of a second ever visit to the Dublin decider soundtracking daily life around the top of the Phoenix Park. It only took Cuala half an hour to put paid to all that.
The Dalkey side won their second title here at a half-canter. They went after Castleknock goalie John Vahey’s kick-out like it owed them money, grabbing it eight times out of 13 in the first half alone. Their size, speed and dominance around the middle third left Castleknock looking entirely lost at sea. Everything stemmed from that and nothing about it was good for the underdogs.
Con O’Callaghan ended the game with 2-5 against his name without ever having to go Full Con on it. He buried a penalty, scored a second goal after collecting the rebound from another, fisted a couple of points, potted a few frees. It was about as humdrum a county final 2-5 as you’d ever hope to see. He was the tip of a very hefty spear, with the likes of Peadar Ó Cofaigh Byrne, Peter Duffy, Charlie McMorrow and Eoin Kennedy driving things from the middle third.
For Castleknock, it was a chastening afternoon under a blinding October sun. The 15-point defeat was the biggest margin in a Dublin final in a quarter of a century and the fourth biggest in the competition’s 139-year history. They were 10 points down at half-time and 18 behind with three minutes to go. By that stage, the scoreboard was an early Halloween story.
Maybe the worst of it for Castleknock was the fact that they had much the better of the game’s opening exchanges. If you landed into Parnell Park knowing nothing of favourites or underdogs, you’d have guessed that Cuala were the ones who hadn’t been to a county final for a while.
Castleknock were two points up inside two minutes through Lenny Cahill and Conor Chawke and when full forward Eoin Sawyer pounced on a weak Cuala kick-out to bear down on goal soon after, it looked like he might have won Castleknock a penalty. But referee Ian Howley was having none of it, telling Sawyer to get up.
Castleknock didn’t score again for the rest of the half. Instead, Cuala reeled off an unanswered 1-9. McMorrow was at the heart of everything, setting up Niall O’Callaghan for their first score on five minutes, popping the second himself from out on the right and playing a big part in Con O’Callaghan’s go-ahead score on 13 minutes.
At the other end, it was getting late early for Castleknock. Cahill missed a kickable free, wing back Rob Shaw tried a couple of two-pointers that went short and wide. For all that, they were still only a couple of points down in the 20 th minute and had they shown a bit more composure in front of goal, maybe they could have hung in a while longer.
But things were getting ominous for them around the middle, particularly on their own kick-out. Cuala had a red wall between the 45s and every time Vahey put the ball on the tee, his target must have looked like a porthole on a cruise liner.
It was the winning and losing of the game. Kennedy strode forward to swish a two-pointer on 20 minutes, pushing Cuala into a 0-6 to 0-2 lead. And when another one was snaffled by Cillian Dunne – son of the manager Derek – all it took was a quick exchange of passes and Con O’Callaghan was in on goal. Corner back Andrew Hughes panic-fouled him and the penalty was a formality.
It meant that Cuala were 1-7 to 0-2 ahead with the clock about to tick 23 minutes. When Mick Fitzsimons sallied forward for the first of his two points soon after, everyone knew the day was done.
The second half was a scorekeeping exercise. Kevin Stephenson nabbed a goal for Castleknock to get the margin back into single figures on 43 minutes but there was never any serious threat of a comeback. Con coolly slotted home the rebound after his second penalty hit the crossbar, before Jamie Conroy zoomed in off the bench to lorry home a third. But the game had long since been decided.
Cuala go on to meet Tullamore in the first round of Leinster. If anyone shortens their winter, they’ll have earned it.
