title: At least four dead after fire at Canadian military base
description: Prime minister Mark Carney says ‘major fire’ occurred at one of the country’s busiest army posts
content:
​ A weekend fire at an Alberta military base killed at least four people and seriously injured dozens in what prime minister Mark Carney called one of the worst peacetime tragedies ever for Canada ’s armed forces on home soil.
“The nation is in mourning for those brave members ​of our armed forces whom we have lost,” Carney said on Sunday, adding that he had ordered flags on federal buildings across the country to be lowered ⁠to half-staff to honour the victims.
CBC, the government-funded national broadcaster, had previously reported seven deaths at Canadian Forces Base ‌Wainwright, ‌citing unnamed ​sources. Canadian authorities have said the situation continues to evolve and that they will not confirm casualty figures until next of kin have been notified.
CFB Wainwright had 1,310 military ⁠and civilian personnel stationed there as of 2021, ​according to census data. The base, one of Canada’s largest, ​is about 210km (130 miles) east of Edmonton in Alberta. National defence minister David McGuinty said on Sunday he would go ‌to the city for briefings on the situation.
The ​base houses the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which runs training scenarios and exercises for the army. Carney said those ⁠affected in Saturday’s fire came from military bases across ⁠the country.
Few details have ​been released about the cause of the fire, which broke out at about 4pm (11pm Irish time) on Saturday in a training area at the base as winds gusted at 96km/h (60m/h).
The Canadian military said on Sunday there were no indications that the incident was the result of terrorism, but the cause remained under investigation.
Military and civilian firefighters tackled the blaze through the night in “some of the worst conditions imaginable”, Carney said.
Canadian officials are expected to address the public from Wainwright, which is located in a largely rural area, later on Sunday.
Air ambulances from Edmonton and Saskatoon, which is about 300km from Wainwright, flew to the ‌military base on Saturday, Carney ⁠said. Patients are being treated in Edmonton, Wainwright, Calgary and Red Deer.
Health staff in Edmonton said a “code orange”, or mass-casualty event, was declared to co-ordinate the medical response for patients being transported ‌from Wainwright, CBC News reported.
The town of Wainwright, with a population of about 6,600, is just north of the base.
The municipality posted on social ​media that the fire had crossed the base fence into the nearby district, but ​no evacuation orders had been issued. It said on Sunday that the fire is not expected to spread beyond its current boundaries. – Reuters

title: ‘Damaging’ to claim White Paper and Citizens’ Assembly will deliver Irish unity, Taoiseach says
description: Fianna Fáil leader said recent events at Portadown had ‘damaged everyone’
content:
The claim that all that is needed to secure Irish unity is a “White Paper and a Citizens’ Assembly and everything will work itself out” is “damaging” and false, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said on Sunday.
Strongly defending his approach to the unity issue and criticising Sinn Féin , Martin said he and his party would be bringing forward some proposals and ideas on the issue soon.
Speaking at the annual Fianna Fáil Wolfe Tone commemoration in Bodenstown, Co Kildare , the Fianna Fáil leader said recent events at Portadown had “damaged everyone”, and he was sharply critical of Sinn Féin’s behaviour and rhetoric at the Garvaghy Road .
“It is absolutely right to say that there can be no going back to the days of escalating conflict around parades,” he said. “The problem for everyone is that there are those who genuinely don’t seem to understand that how they behave means that, as well as no going back, there is no going forward either. When confronted with a situation like this, people who are interested in uniting communities don’t call for a reckoning; they call for a dialogue.”
The Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald declared that if the Orange Order parade was forced through a nationalist area, there would “be a reckoning”.
Asked afterwards if he was referring to Sinn Féin, Martin said: “If you want unity you have to think really hard about how we unite people, how we avoid going back to the past but also how do we move forward. We can’t just dismiss the imperative of reconciliation ... We need a more substantive approach to the issues than we’ve seen from Sinn Féin and others, whose presentations seem very superficial.
“There needs to be strong objective information that lays it out on the table about what needs to be done – as opposed to coming at it from a very aggressive partisan advocacy perspective like Sinn Féin does, and ignore everybody else, ignore the perspective of others.”
[ Many loyalists are desperate to leave – the only thing stopping some is a £5,000 ‘exit fee’ Opens in new window ]
Martin said that he would be “bringing our thoughts on that to the party and sharing that with my Government colleagues in the time ahead”.
Asked if he would elaborate on this, the Taoiseach replied: “No”, but added: “I’m concerned that a lot of the language that we’ve heard in the last couple of months is the language of the 1970s. We don’t need that language. We need to work with people.”
In his speech, Martin said he would “never accept the demand of angry partisan commentators that we move away from an approach which has delivered and follow their lead in aggressive advocacy.
“It is striking how often people who claim to want to unite the people of Ireland spend their time personally attacking people who disagree with their approach,” he said.
[ Northern Ireland deserves better than rearview mirror politics Opens in new window ]
“If you claim to want to build an inclusive republic which respects diverse opinions and traditions, your first duty is to start showing some respect to other opinions and traditions. Too many people are making casual assumptions about what is required – or are dismissing the idea that there are any hard choices.
“In fact, one of the most damaging developments we have seen recently is the claim that all we need is a White Paper and a Citizens’ Assembly and everything will work itself out.
“This is exactly the type of approach which is unlikely to secure the change of public opinion required to make a vote likely or winnable,” he said.

title: Solemn guard of honour: Waterford residents pay tribute to four family members killed in house fire
description: Johnville football club, where 12-year-old Callum English played, provides guard of honour on Sunday
content:
Four coffins: two small white caskets, flanked by two larger ones, were briefly rested at the entrance to the parish centre in Waterford.
The remains of four members of the same family killed in a house fire in Waterford arrived at the Sacred Heart Church on Sunday, ahead of their funeral.
Philip and Kim English and their sons Callum (12) and Jayden (9) died in an attack on their home in the Birchwood estate on Tuesday.
Hundreds of mourners lined the streets to honour their memory as four separate hearses carried the remains to the church.
Draped across the coffins were a Waterford flag, the Irish Tricolour and a Liverpool FC jersey.
Players from the Johnville Football Club, where Callum had played, provided a solemn guard of honour, dressed in their black and yellow club jerseys. The young members then sat on a low wall outside the parish centre as they waited to go in and pay their last respects to the family. The club has opted to permanently retire the number five jersey as a tribute to Callum.
Inside the church, a photograph of the English family was set on a table, accompanied by two large and two small candles.
Parish priest Fr Gerry Chestnutt blessed each of the coffins in turn before they were moved to a room in the parish centre next door, where a removal got under way shortly after 2pm on Sunday.
Some members of the local community who were too upset to enter the parish centre opted instead to sign the condolence book at the church. A few of them lit candles, while others sat in silent prayer and reflection.
Fr Chestnutt and Bishop Alphonsus Cullinan of the Diocese of Waterford and Lismore spoke to groups of people who approached them outside the centre.
A joint funeral Mass will take place at the Sacred Heart Church tomorrow at 1pm, followed by burial in Kilbarry cemetery.
Two other children, aged six and 14, remain in a critical condition in CHI at Crumlin after the attack. Mourners have been asked to make a donation to the hospital in lieu of flowers.
Two people have appeared in court on charges related to the incident.
Cian Stacey (21) and Jessica Dalton (31) appeared at a special sitting of Clonmel District Court on Saturday charged with one count of criminal damage and two counts of assault causing serious harm.
Both were remanded in custody to appear before Waterford District Court on Tuesday.
Philip English was predeceased by his mother Bridget, his daughter Rachael and his sister Catherine. His ex-wife Anne English was among those who attended the removal on Sunday afternoon. He is survived by 11 children, his father Paddy, his five siblings and grandchildren.
Kim English, nee Companjen, who grew up in Courtmacsherry, Co Cork, was predeceased by her mother Joke Voets, She is survived by her children, her stepchildren, her father Richard, stepmother Teresa, stepfather Marc Voets, and six siblings.
A number of businesses in Waterford will remain closed tomorrow as a mark of respect to the family.
The four family members will be buried at Kilbarry Cemetery.

title: Caveat aware: Ronan McGreevy on the speech that sparked a president’s resignation
description: Paddy Donegan was defence minister 50 years ago when he uttered two words that made political history
content:
Check against delivery is a time-honoured caveat that journalists are asked to observe when given copies of a political speech in advance.
It’s a convention that allows for a speech to change: the politician might talk off the cuff, tell an off-colour anecdote, or two, or omit certain passages.
Fifty years ago, on the morning of October 18th, 1976, an embargoed speech was sent by the Government Information Office to all the national newsrooms. The minister for defence Paddy Donegan would be opening a new canteen at Columb Barracks in Mullingar , Co Westmeath .
He was intending to say how delighted he was to open a new cookhouse and dining hall with its convection oven and servery units extending to 5,000sq ft.
The proposed speech also included a segue in which he stated that the rights of people to be governed by their elected representatives was being challenged across Europe.
A cursory reading of the speech would have understood that this arose out of a decision by Cearbhall Ó Dálaigh, then president, to refer the government’s Emergency Powers Act to the Supreme Court .
The Act arose out of a summer of anarchy with the assassination of the British ambassador, Christopher Ewart-Biggs , on July 21st, 1976, and a successful breakout by five IRA prisoners from the cells under Green Street Courthouse .
Faced with this, the Dáil passed the Emergency Powers Act, which had been in abeyance since the end of the second World War . Detention without charge would be extended from two days to seven. Gardaí could detain a suspect on the basis that the suspect knew about subversive activities even if he or she was not directly involved in that activity. Gardaí would be given powers to search premises without a warrant.
On September 24th, Ó Dálaigh referred this proposed legislation to the Supreme Court. The Bill was later judged to be constitutional and Ó Dálaigh said he would sign it into law on the following day, October 16th.
On that day Garda Michael Clerkin and four colleagues responded to a report of suspicious activity at a derelict house at Garryhinch, Portarlington, Co Laois . They had heard earlier a bomb was being prepared at the house in advance of an assassination attempt on Fine Gael TD Oliver J Flanagan, a ferocious critic of the Provisional IRA.
The officers began a search, during which a booby-trap bomb exploded, killing Michael Clerkin and seriously wounding his colleagues. Det Garda Tom Peters lost his sight and hearing as a result of the blast. This episode of murder and maiming generated revulsion in the Republic, being seen as a direct attack on the police force nationally.
Feelings were running high in government when Donegan travelled to Mullingar to give his speech opening the new canteen, yet the blandness of the proposed speech saw national news reporters staying away from the launch.
Only one reporter attended the event: Don Lavery, then a 23-year-old reporter with the Westmeath Examiner.
Lavery sat across from Donegan at lunch. According to Lavery, when lunch was over Donegan flung the copy of the script he had in front of him down on the table and said to him: “I’ll give you some news for the press.”
Donegan then launched into a tirade against Ó Dálaigh’s decision to refer the Emergency Powers Act to the Supreme Court.
The off-the-cuff speech would give rise to a phrase that entered the lexicon of Irish political life – “thundering disgrace”. Donegan pointed out that previous laws pertaining to the security of the State were not referred to the Supreme Court, so why this one?
Donegan’s words were premeditated. Nevertheless, Lavery was approached to kill the story afterwards, but he refused to do so.
In those days local newspaper reporters were often “stringers” for the national press and would feed copy to the newsdesk that they thought of national interest.
The designated stringer being away, Lavery filed copy to all the major news outlets including The Irish Times.
Donegan attempted to apologise to the president, but his attempts were rebuffed.
He then offered his resignation to the taoiseach, Liam Cosgrave , but pointedly the taoiseach refused it and praised his minister’s contribution to the defence of the State in the face of a Fianna Fáil Dáil motion that he resign.
Cosgrave, who had no love for Ó Dálaigh, chose to take no action against the minister.
Four days after Donegan’s “thundering disgrace” remarks, Ó Dálaigh resigned and published the rather grovelling letter that Donegan had sent him by way of an apology.
In his public comments, Ó Dálaigh stated that resignation was the “only way now open to me to assert my personal integrity and independence as president of Ireland and to endeavour to protect the dignity and independence of the presidency as an institution”.
Donegan remained as minister for defence until a cabinet reshuffle in December 1976; Ó Dálaigh was replaced by Patrick Hillery .

title: Noni Madueke breaks Nottingham Forest’s resistance as dogged Arsenal edge to victory
description: Defeat means Oliver Glasner’s team have still yet to register a goal at home this season
author_name: David Hytner at the City Ground
content:
The theme before kick-off was blanks. Or, more precisely, whether either team could stop firing them at the City Ground. It is a detail to make Oliver Glasner extremely uncomfortable that his Nottingham Forest team had still to score at their home stadium. Arsenal , meanwhile, had drawn 0-0 on each of their previous two visits to this part of the East Midlands.
Forest’s frustrations under their new manager go on. It was another spirited performance from them, bits to like, especially a full throttle performance from Liam Delap in the number 9 position. But, for the fifth time under Glasner in all competitions, there was not a goal to celebrate in front of the club’s home fans.
It was a game that came to feel increasingly set up for the famous terrace chant. One-nil to the Ars-en-nal. Or, as the travelling hordes would have it, one-nil to the champions. Arsenal did not play well. They created little, finishing with just one shot of target. How Noni Madueke made it count.
On as a half-time substitute, the winger took a pass from Declan Rice in the 80th minute and had only one thing on his mind. To cut inside from the left and unload. The connection was pure and that was when he caught a break, which he has worked to earn after a difficult start to the season. The ball deflected off Jair Cunha and flew past the Forest goalkeeper, Matz Sels.
Forest refused to accept the inevitable. Chris Wood, on as a substitute, delayed too long and saw Rice block. Murillo, all of all players, danced inside from the left and curled just off target. And Delap was denied at the death by a thunderous Ezri Konsa block tackle. But it did feel inevitable. Arsenal had not forgotten their previous away fixture – the 3-0 defeat at Brighton. It remains the only blot on their season.
Arsenal had kicked off six points behind Manchester City, who have been perfect on the field in the league this season. Will it matter when the sanctions for their rule breaches are meted out? All Arsenal can do is play the situation as it stands and there was a boost for them here when the teamsheets dropped, and Morgan Gibbs-White, Forest’s key attacking midfielder, was out with a calf injury. He was a big miss.
Glasner said that shooting practice had been a major part of his training sessions during the week and how the home crowd wanted to see something from their team in front of goal. The game was framed from a Forest point of view by the extraordinary number of openings they had blown in the 3-1 defeat at Crystal Palace last weekend; they had eight big chances, according to the statisticians. They were never going to get anything like that number against Arsenal.
Arteta’s team hogged the ball. As they were always likely to do. Bruno Guimarães looked to push up at the outset and combine with Martin Ødegaard, who occupied the number 10 position. Rice was the nominal holding midfielder. Arsenal were determined to be patient but it was flat and predictable from them before the interval.
Arsenal played their patterns. They tried to suck the life out of the home crowd, working on the principle that it is difficult for fans to get animated if their team do not have the ball. The first half drifted by in a lazy Sunday afternoon haze, no shots on target for either side.
Arsenal have been a little barren in first halves this season. This was the seventh time in 10 matches since the Community Shield that they had failed to score. It has not been a problem but they needed to raise their levels for the second-half.
Arteta’s first change was Madueke for Eberechi Eze on the left wing; an admission that the latter had failed to exert an influence. There was also a triple substitution on 66 minutes, the Arsenal manager sending on Jurrien Timber, Mikel Merino and Viktor Gyökeres for Ben White, Guimarães and Havertz. He needed to shake things up because nothing was happening for his team. It was Forest who pushed after the restart, with Delap continuing to put himself about.
The minutes ticked down, the contest narrowing to a fine point and we waited to see whether there could be a moment, one big chance. Ødegaard almost provided it in the 72nd minute when he released Timber with a lovely pass up the inside right. When Timber pulled back, Rice lifted wastefully high.
Glasner’s decision to introduce Ibrahim Sangaré for Dan Ndoye shortly afterwards was telling. Sangaré’s mission was to bolster the Forest midfield and yet he was slow to react to a half-cleared ball. When Rice played the pass, Madueke took over. — Guardian

title: As chatter around Troy Parrott lulls, everyone’s talking about Jack Moylan
description: Irish player tracker: Cardiff City signing can do little wrong right now – and is making the case for regular starting roles with Ireland
content:
Jack Moylan is “pound for pound the best Championship signing of the summer” – or at least that’s according to one Cardiff City supporter on social media, who then urged anyone who disagreed with him to go argue with a wall.
He might have a point. Moylan can do little wrong at the moment and his goal in Saturday’s 2-2 draw at Middlesbrough was his third of the week – after scoring twice in Tuesday’s 5-1 demolition of Watford – and sixth in the league this season.
All of that came on the back of a strong international window with Ireland, where the former Shelbourne player pressed home his claims for regular starting roles under Heimir Hallgrímsson, not just as a relative newcomer to squads. Pity for Cardiff that they seem incapable of profiting off his endeavours as they hover just above the relegation zone.
“He knows the large part of the game he has to improve – and he will, because he has the mentality to do it,” said City’s Irish manager Brian Barry-Murphy. “He’s a very exciting player to watch because of how attack-minded he is, and we don’t want to take away any of that while adding to the parts of his game that he needs to improve.”
Troy Parrott is the only Ireland international talked about more than Moylan right now, but even he is in the midst of a lull, with the hype machine dropping a gear or two having been in overdrive for the last two months.
Another Galactico brought sharp focus to Parrott’s weekend work but, having slain Real Madrid himself with a winner off the bench in September, it was a watching brief at home on Saturday night when Lamine Yamal’s stunner set Barcelona on the way to victory.
Parrott got on for the closing half-hour but his 4/10 player rating in Seville’s leading sports daily told the story of a night of little joy for anyone in Real Betis colours.
“The 2-5 scoreline doesn’t reflect what the match was like,” growled veteran Betis manager Manuel Pellegrini afterwards. “The truth is, I thought the referee’s performance was deplorable, lacking any footballing sense.”
[ Troy Parrott’s Real Betis no match for Barcelona as they hit five goals in Seville Opens in new window ]
Nathan Collins took a step in the right direction by warming Brentford’s bench throughout their 2-1 defeat to Liverpool, having been sidelined with a calf injury since the Sunderland game in early September. It ruled him out of Ireland’s recent Nations League games.
His fellow Ireland defender James Abankwah was named as Udinese’s player of the month for September after good performances against Lazio, Inter Milan (when he scored at the San Siro) and Cagliari, although he was an unused sub in Sunday’s 3-0 home defeat to Lecce, who kept Dubliner Corrie Ndaba on the bench throughout.
Out of sight, out of mind, Josh Cullen is the forgotten man of the Irish squad, having been sidelined since December when he tore his ACL in Burnley’s scoreless draw with Everton. That ruled the midfielder out of Ireland’s World Cup playoff against the Czech Republic in March, the summer friendlies and the eventful Nations League window.
But Cullen is ramping up his recovery and is expected to mark his return by lining out for Burnley’s under-21s when they travel to West Ham this Friday. In his absence, the Clarets have struggled this season following relegation from the Premier League and remain in the bottom three of the Championship.
If the comeback goes well, the 30-year-old could push for squad inclusion when Ireland close out their Nations League campaign against Austria and Kosovo next month, although his position in the side is under threat after Charlton’s Conor Coventry made the most of his opportunities in two games against Israel and also the Austria match.
Ireland newcomer Owen Elding scored a first-half goal for Hibernian on Saturday, but at that stage Hibs were already 2-0 down at home to Falkirk and ended up losing by that 2-1 scoreline. Rock bottom of the Scottish Premiership, there’s been little reason to cheer this season for Elding and his international colleague Jamie McGrath.
“I think we were the thief of our own wallet,” said new Hibs manager Marink Reedijk, appointed shortly after Stephen Bradley ruled out leaving Shamrock Rovers for the Edinburgh club at this late stage of the League of Ireland season.
“We gave away two easy goals. I thought we dominated the game. I have a sick feeling in my stomach but I see progress. We need to look forward and not backwards.”
Up next? A nice, handy one against Celtic, who stuffed Hearts 7-1 on Sunday with Liam Scales assisting their opener.
Gbemi Arubi has endured a frustrating time since swapping life in the League of Ireland for Burton Albion over the summer.
Injury issues scuppered the former Dundalk attacker’s arrival in League One but, after biding his time, the Dubliner announced himself in style on Saturday, scoring an 89th-minute screamer from halfway. Alas, it wasn’t to be the winner as hosts Peterborough scrambled an equaliser deep in injury-time in new manager Robbie Savage’s first home league game.

title: Wolfe Tones prove the kicking kings as they secure a third Meath crown
description: Donaghmore/Ashbourne fail to take advantage of home advantage as they suffer a third final defeat
content:
Wolfe Tones dismantled Donaghmore/Ashbourne’s county final house party with a clinical display of shooting to claim a third Meath senior football title.
For the first time since the 80s, the Meath SFC final took place outside of Páirc Tailteann due to its redevelopment, and with Donaghmore/Ashbourne nominated as the host venue, the Moors had a home decider.
However, the visitors looked far more at home in the county’s showpiece fixture and ran out commanding 10-point victors, the largest winning margin in a Meath final since 2008.
It added to Wolfe Tone’s 2006 and 2021 triumphs, while the wait for Donaghmore/Ashbourne for a maiden Keegan Cup goes on after their third final appearance.
Donaghmore/Ashbourne never once led and from the moment the impressive Thomas O’Reilly put Wolfe Tones 0-2 to 0-1 ahead in the eighth minute, they kept their noses in front all the way to the final whistle.
Wolfe Tones delivered an exhibition of scoretaking in the second half, taking 11 shots and scoring 11 points, with not a single wide or any efforts dropping short. It was a kicking clinic.
They only registered two wides in the first half and their efficiency in front of the posts was one of the main differences between the sides – Donaghmore/Ashbourne had nine wides and the home side’s top scorer on the day was their goalkeeper Andrew Colgan with 0-3.
The venue for the final was selected before it was known Donaghmore/Ashbourne were to be one of the competing teams and Wolfe Tones manager Shane McCoy had no issues with the unusual situation.
“To be honest, it’s credit to Donaghmore/Ashbourne and the facilities they have here. They were always obliging on anything we requested during the week,” he said.
“We’d absolutely no problem with it at all, when the decision was made at the start of the year it’s just something you have to suck up. It could have been any other club in Meath that we were playing against today and it just happened to be a home team.
“It was what it was and we kind of got that distraction out of the way very early after the semi-final and it was never a part of our focus really.”
There was a wonderful atmosphere in Ashbourne but the occasion appeared to spook the home players because they lacked cohesion and allowed the pattern of the game to be dictated by Wolfe Tones.
Wing back Oisín Martin was superb for the Tones in the first half – he won three opposition kick-outs and scored two points with surging runs through the heart of the Donaghmore/Ashbourne defence.
It was from one of those blistering runs that the game’s only goal was scored – Martin rocketing up the field before offloading to Sarán Ó Fionnagáin who in turn fed Tom Gavigan for the finish.
That 27 th -minute goal put Wolfe Tones eight points clear and in firm control.
However, Donaghmore/Ashbourne produced their best period of the game in the brief window before half-time, scoring five points to leave just three between the sides at the interval, 1-8 to 0-8.
That green and white tornado earned Donaghmore/Ashbourne a raucous ovation going off the pitch at the break but within moments of the restart Wolfe Tones had taken control again.
“We conceded those five scores unanswered just before half-time and it probably put us in a tricky enough position then,” added McCoy.
“But we kind of set our stall out, reassessed where the midfield battle had been won and lost and we got that first score after the break, Seán Penny popping up with a point.
“He’s not known for his right-foot shooting, but we’ll take it today. They were asking big questions of us and it probably was a case that we could get ourselves reset at half-time again
“We wanted to get a grip back on the game and I thought we managed the game well in the second half.”
O’Reilly and O Fionnagáin were both superb in the second period but all over the pitch Wolfe Tones had the measure of their opponents. They had the game tidied up well before the end and Donaghmore/Ashbourne failed to score in the last 10 minutes – during which time Wolfe Tones added five points.
An hour after the final whistle there were still fans in purple and gold standing out on the pitch, soaking it all in.
The Keegan Cup was handed from pod to pod as players and supporters posed happily for photographs. Wolfe Tones were champions again and nobody was in a hurry to leave.
WOLFE TONES: Ciaráin Ó Gallachóir; Conor Sheppard, Shane Glynn, Andrew Crawford; Seán Penny (0-0-1), Ross Gallagher, Oisín Martin (0-0-3); Adam O’Neill, Eoin Donegan; Caolan Ward (0-1-4, 2f, 1 45, tpf), Thomas O’Reilly (0-0-3), Sarán O Fionnagáin (0-0-4); Tom Gavigan (1-0-0), Fiachra Ward, Kyle Moran (0-0-2).
Subs: Cian O’Neill for F Ward (15 mins); Adrian Crawford for Penny (54); Padraic Diamond for Crawford (59); Stephen Sheppard for Moran (60).
DONAGHMORE/ASHBOURNE: Andrew Colgan (0-1-1, 1f, tpf); Conor Carton, Seán Curran, Evan Quinn; Kevin Fenton (0-0-1), Shane Melia, Thomas McGovern; Bryan Menton (0-0-1), Jamie Browne; Seán Tyrrell, Zach Thornton (0-0-2, 2f), Kevin Cully; Darragh McGovern (0-0-2), Stephen Carton (0-0-1), Andrew Tormey (0-0-2, 2f).
Subs: Cillian Hegarty for Cully, Evan Kelly for Thornton (both 41 mins); Michael Deegan for Fenton (46); Michael O’Sullivan for Carton (50).

title: Irish childrenswear just got a whole lot more interesting
description: Two Irish children’s clothing labels spurning fast fashion for sustainability and longer life
content:
Children grow fast, so spending on more expensive sustainable clothes for them can feel more like a waste than a wise investment . But two Irish childrenswear brands are making the case for buying better – whatever the age range – with hard-wearing, thoughtfully designed pieces that are made to last and be passed on.
Writer and illustrator Ciara Tinney and her business partner, costume designer Edel McAvoy, founded Wildkind when Tinney first became a mum. “With little people in the house, so much thought goes into what you’re consuming – what you’re eating, watching, reading and putting on their bodies. You cannot really consciously curate one without the others.”
Tinney, who grew up in Co Fermanagh and lives in Belfast, and McAvoy launched a collection of simple gender-fluid pieces in muted tones made from end-of-roll Irish linen sourced at local mills. Each item was designed to grow with a child for three-plus years by incorporating clever design features , such as extra leg-lengths, elasticated waistbands and extendable sleeves. “Our Taoide [tide] dress is designed to fit ages four to 10, so my youngest daughter can wear it as well as my eldest,” says Tinney. “I’m a mom, and I know how expensive life is.”
This commitment to longevity and minimising waste ensures that leftover materials from the collection are repurposed rather than discarded. The pair use handpicked scraps of linen and remnants from the collection for pieces such as its Saor ó Dhramhaíl (zero waste) jacket, while the Starling Patch is a hand-painted quilted square designed to be added to something in need of repair to prolong the life of the garment without compromising the integrity of the Wildkind aesthetic.
This waste not, want not philosophy is inspired by Tinney’s grandmother. “My mom was one of 11 children,” explains Tinney. “There were no new summer dresses until the bag of flour was used and then a dress was made from the bag. I love that story. Even though there was real hardship, I just love that my grandmother took such care not to waste anything.”
Versatility is also built into each design. The Bogha Báistí (rainbow) Collar, for instance, is reversible, offering two distinct looks in one piece. It’s also oversized, so wearable for many years. Adding the Cloud Cuffs to a dress or sweater instantly reimagines it and the Caipín (crest of a wave) Collar can be worn as a collar, wrapped as a belt or draped crossbody to change a silhouette.
Storytelling is as integral to Wildkind as sustainability. “We’ve lost so much heritage in terms of how we dress. People in five different cities could all be wearing the same thing. Wildkind is about awakening our senses and connecting to the wild to nurture a sense of self and a sense of place,” says the mother of three. Tinney handpaints each garment with motifs evocative of the surrounding landscape, while McAvoy uses free-motion embroidery to add a tactile finish that echoes the organic forms and textures of the natural world.
UPA kidswear is another brand rooted in storytelling, sustainability and versatility. Founded by Lithuanian-born, Meath-based Vaida Rasciute, the brand creates seasonless clothes from Irish and Lithuanian linen, which are each made to order. “I don’t design according to seasons,” explains Rasciute. “And if a customer spots an old dress on Instagram that isn’t on the website, I can make it for them. I often revisit past designs in new collections to encourage repeat wear and give existing pieces a longer life.”
Like Tinney, Rasciute draws inspiration from the women who came before her, particularly her mother. “My mother is a very stylish and soulful grandmother to my daughter and she’s my biggest influencer. She knit a dress for my daughter when she was a year old out of silk and mohair wool, which people were constantly asking about, and that’s when I first thought of setting up a childrenswear brand.”
That was 10 years ago. Since then, UPA has been featured in Vogue and Harper’s Bazaar, and it won the prestigious Best Brand Pitti Bimbo 2020 Award; Pitti Bimbo is a premier children’s fashion and lifestyle trade show held biannually in Florence. Rasciute is influenced by heritage and nature, infusing her childrenswear with Lithuanian and Irish influences – evocations of local landscapes and motifs from Lithuanian folklore and culture are imaginatively woven throughout each collection.
Linen is Rasciute’s favourite material because it’s kind to people and to nature. “It’s such a beautiful fabric with amazing qualities that’s great for wearing in winter too. I think you can feel a different kind of energy from it,” she says. Every item is conceived with versatility and wearability in mind. “I introduce features such as exchangeable bows so that one can be swapped out for another in a different colour. You don’t need to buy a whole new dress; you can just change the bow for a different look.”
Some pieces can also be worn back to front, offering two equally considered looks. The Carmen Blouse, for example, features natural shell buttons that can be worn discreetly at the back or as a button-front detail.
This year, Rasciute plans to introduce a new accessories line of ribbons and flowers, designed to be styled across dresses, tops and belts. “This will allow each child to create their own unique look at home,” she says. For both UPA and Wildkind, practicality and playfulness go hand in hand.

title: Martin O’Neill does not believe Celtic made statement with rout of Hearts
description: The Hoops move four points clear of Rangers at top of the table after 7-1 thrashing at Parkhead
content:
Celtic manager Martin O’Neill played down suggestions his side had made a statement in their 7-1 thrashing of Hearts.
The champions moved four points clear of Rangers in the Scottish Premiership and eight above last year’s runners-up, who suffered more Celtic Park misery five months after losing their grasp on the title in the closing minutes of the season.
O’Neill’s side had lost four of their previous five matches and Hearts had arrived in Glasgow as the Premiership’s leading goalscorers.
But, despite the game being fairly even in terms of possession and shots at goal, Celtic were 5-1 up at the break.
Kieran Tierney and Benjamin Nygren netted from corners inside 10 minutes, Callum Osmand struck twice in two minutes and Jamie McCart scored an own goal after Mika Baur had waltzed through the Hearts defence.
Camilo Duran and Nygren completed the rout, with Laurent Mendy netting a consolation.
“It’s probably too early to worry about a message,” said O’Neill, who revealed Osmand had come off as a precaution because of a tight hamstring.
“But I thought we played really well. It’s very early. We were four points behind with about seven games to go last season, so it can be eroded very, very quickly. But it’s nice to win, and winning in the manner in which we did.
“From Hearts’ viewpoint, probably just a bad day at the office, but they’ll still be challengers, they’ve got some really decent players who can play a bit.
“If we lose on Thursday (against Celta Vigo), it’ll be crisis back again. I’ve been here before. You just have to try and win.”
Hearts head coach Wouter Vrancken admitted losing two early goals from corners had made life difficult.
“The mindset and confidence within the group changed, maybe, because what you saw afterwards was us trying to play football,” he said.
“Sometimes it worked, but when I look back at the goals, I think they all came from individual mistakes. We were losing the ball too easily.
“After the game, the most important thing for me is to get into their heads and make sure they don’t lose confidence in what they’re doing.
“I’d rather have players who are willing to take responsibility and make mistakes while still showing confidence, instead of hiding themselves because that doesn’t bring anything to the team.
“Of course, you want to minimise the mistakes, but when they happen, hopefully there are only one or two across the whole game.”
When asked if he would have made tactical amendments with hindsight, the Belgian said: “We have our style of play and the important thing with that style is maintaining the necessary aggression in those moments. We lacked that a little bit in the duels.
“When you’re not aggressive enough and you lose the ball or give it away too easily, it becomes difficult.”

title: Taoiseach rejects Michael O’Leary’s view that he would ‘buckle’ to public sector unions
description: Micheál Martin insists productivity would have to be part of any new pay agreement
content:
Taoiseach Micheál Martin has rejected suggestions by Ryanair boss Michael O’Leary that he would “buckle” and “roll over” to the public sector trade unions, and insisted that productivity increases would be part of any new pay deal with the unions.
Speaking at the Fianna Fáil Wolfe Tone commemoration at Bodenstown Co Kildare on Sunday, the Taoiseach responded to O’Leary’s comments in this morning’s Business Post by affirming his support for public services, but also stressing productivity would have to be part of any new agreement.
“We believe in the public service very strongly,” he said. “It’s essential in any civilised democracy that we have a strong public service to deliver services to people,” he said. “Obviously there has to be value for money, there has to be productivity and all of that, and that has always been our position. As someone who is experienced in politics, that’s my approach.”
Martin declined to be drawn on whether he would be open to a lower percentage increase for higher-paid public servants with a higher percentage increase for lower-paid workers, rather than an across-the-board percentage increase.
“I’m open to an agreement that is affordable, that can advance productivity within the public service, that would look after low-paid workers – but again, let’s allow the negotiations to start. It’s not for me to be getting into the details or precise preferences about the shape of any agreement.”
[ How Ireland’s first national public sector strike in 17 years left unions strong and Jack Chambers ‘scrambling’ Opens in new window ]
Pressed further, the Taoiseach said all such issues would be discussed with the unions first.
Martin also said that previous pay agreements had sought to target lower-paid workers more for bigger increases, but that the Government side would have to hear from the unions on what their proposals were.
“I’m not going to get into specifics in terms of where all that lands, but we’ve always had a view to protect lower-paid workers within the public service,” he said.
Talks between the unions and the Government are due to get under way at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) on Monday morning.
“I welcome the fact that a process has been agreed between the unions and the Government side,” he said. “What now needs to happen is for the negotiations to take place, and we can have a resolution that manifests itself in a new pay agreement, similar to the ones we’ve already negotiated.”
[ Wednesday’s public sector strike called off after unions and Government agree on talks Opens in new window ]
The Taoiseach declined to discuss suggestions that the €1.2 billion allocated to pay for a new deal in the recent budget could be increased by dipping into a €1.6 billion contingency fund.
“We’re not going to go into what may transpire over the course of the negotiations ... Nothing is decided, no precise figures have even been mentioned yet.”

title: Trump endorses Netanyahu in Israeli election
description: US president praises Netanyahu as a ‘great warrior prime minister’ and peace partner
content:
US president Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed his ally Binyamin Netanyahu as the long-time Israeli prime minister struggles for an ‌edge in next week’s parliamentary election.
Trump praised Netanyahu as a “great warrior prime minister” and peace partner, crediting him with joining ​the United States in launching strikes on Iran in February. The conflict, in its seventh month, has disrupted energy markets globally and wreaked havoc across the Middle East, damaging critical infrastructure and destabilising regional economies.
“Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, ​and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself,” Trump wrote in a post ⁠on Truth Social.
“Despite all of that, he has endured and, in fact, he ‌has thrived! ‌I ​have watched Bibi under the most trying of times. Normal men or women in such situations would have wilted under the pressure – But Bibi ⁠did not wilt, he actually got ​stronger, and maintains that same Strength today.”
[ Israel’s former spy chief sues Netanyahu for ‘blood libel’ over October 7th attacks Opens in new window ]
In his ​message, addressed to “the Great People of Israel,” Trump added, “Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete ‌and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in ​his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel.”
The Trump endorsement is not certain ⁠to give Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud ⁠party a boost ​in the October 27th national election, as Israeli public support for Trump has diminished amid Israeli-US disagreements over Iran.
Polls have suggested no candidate has a clear path to power. Israel’s prime minister is chosen through coalition-building in parliament rather than by direct popular vote.
It will be Israel’s first vote since the Hamas attack on October 7th, 2023, that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil, as Israel went ‌to war in Gaza , ⁠ Lebanon and Iran.
The election could determine whether Netanyahu remains in power after one of the most consequential periods in Israel’s history, or is defeated by centrist rivals promising to ‌usher in a new era.
Netanyahu promptly expressed his thanks to Trump on X, saying, “Together we will complete the mission!”
Trump ​has broken with long-time US tradition by endorsing candidates in elections ​in foreign countries, including Hungary, Colombia, Argentina, Japan and Honduras. – Reuters

title: Manchester United held as Calvert-Lewin’s Leeds leveller keeps pressure on Carrick
description: Elland Road display was the latest unconvincing outing under Carrick this season
content:
What next for Michael Carrick and Manchester United ? Game-wise the answer is Wednesday’s trip to Como yet after failing, again, to double the campaign’s league wins tally to two you have to wonder where this already flatlining team are heading.
Sunday afternoon’s display was the latest unconvincing outing under the 45-year-old manager. It featured an odd formation, zero rhythm or control, and the same prevailing sense that the wheels could clatter off anytime.
Bryan Mbeumo’s first-half opener was answered, inevitably, by Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s equaliser after the interval for hosts who were not markedly better but did not need to be, so fragile are Carrick’s side. Elland Road was the scene of Ruben Amorim’s last stand, Carrick’s predecessor reacting to January’s 1-1 draw by demanding his colleagues in the recruitment department “do their job”. The result? He was sacked two days later.
For now Carrick avoids a similar fate but for how long? United remain stuck on a solitary league victory – back at the end of August, versus Ipswich – and so Como, in the Champions League, becomes the next must-win fixture.
Five days after his scathing diatribe aimed at Jason Wilcox – for the director of football’s iffy recruitment – Lisandro Martínez was selected by Carrick, the defender’s Thursday apology enough to clear the way, though his day ended at the interval.
Daniel Farke’s team, unchanged for a fifth consecutive game, were roared on by a crowd who delighted in Martínez’s first contribution, a stray pass hoofed out of play.
The visitors lined up in an “Amorim formation” of 3-4-3, a lesser-seen Carrick configuration. In this, Bruno Fernandes was fielded as the nominal central forward, curtailing the captain’s ability to pull strings from midfield, though his was a free role.
The noise from a febrile home support was dialled up when Carlos Baleba sent Anton Stach to the turf and Darren England saw no infringement. When Fernandes ran though and a clumsy touch caused him to scythe down Tarik Muharemovic, England did act – booking Manchester United’s captain when play next paused, to the delight of Leeds fans.
Gabriel Gudmundsson was also shown a yellow card – for clipping Andrey Santos – in a contest that was full of blood and thunder but lacked regular goalmouth incident.
Gudmundsson, the left wing back in Farke’s 5-2-2-1, did splay the visitors’ defence with a cross that wrong-footed Harry Maguire but it found no team-mate, before Jayden Bogle, the right wing back, repeated the act as Leeds exerted momentary control.
Stach’s free-kick from the right had Nico Elvedi flying at the ball to fashion a header Senne Lammens had to be quick to repel.
At last, the match was alive. Carrick’s men carved a clear chance when Youri Tielemans dropped the ball on to Mbeumo’s head at close-range but he missed – badly.
But next Mbeumo struck via a quick move that sundered Leeds. Along the right Tielamans found Amad Diallo who returned the ball and the Belgian’s cross was slid home by the forward.
Martínez’s removal for the second half brought Noussair Mazraoui to the fray as 45 minutes stood between Carrick and a morale-boosting victory.
They held firm for five. A Mazraoui header sent Bogle’s cross out for a corner on the right. When this was swung in Mazraoui was beaten by Muharemovic, whose flick came to Calvert-Lewin, who outmuscled Mbeumo and crashed home.
With the crowd propelling them forward, Ao Tanaka boomed a volley just over and Farke’s men pinned back Carrick’s side, who lacked ideas: Baleba’s unconvincing long-range effort summed them up.
Better was Fernandes’s turn and shot that spun narrowly wide but he followed this with a weak attempt that the Leeds goalkeeper James Trafford clutched simply.
On 73 minutes Farke took off Noah Okafor for Lukas Nmecha and Carrick removed Baleba for Mason Mount but none of the changes could spark a winner. – Guardian

title: Pope Leo pledges gradual return to duties at first Vatican event since cancer surgery
description: The pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after doctors removed part of his right lung to extract a tumour
content:
Pope Leo told a crowd gathered in St Peter’s Square on Sunday that he would “gradually resume” his activities, at his first appearance before the faithful since undergoing an operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung.
The 71-year-old was greeted with applause as he appeared unaided at the window of the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace to deliver his Sunday angelus. It was his first public appearance since making the announcement at the previous Sunday’s address that a small nodule had been found on his lung.
The pope was diagnosed with the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma – on Tuesday after doctors removed part of his right lung to extract the tumour.
He thanked those who had prayed for him in recent days, saying he appreciated the support, adding that the experience had made him feel especially close “to all those who are going through illness or a state of infirmity”.
“Now that this delicate phase has passed … I will gradually resume ​my ​activities, always with ​the help of God and your ​prayers,” he said.
He left Gemelli hospital in Rome on Saturday, where doctors deemed him “fit for discharge” after undergoing blood tests and a chest X-ray that morning.
Doctors said on Wednesday that his recovery from the operation was progressing normally. They said they were waiting for the results of tests to determine whether the cancer had spread and if more treatment would be needed.
The Vatican had originally estimated a weeklong stay in hospital.
The pope undertook some work duties in hospital, including making a phone call on Friday to Vladimir Putin , during which he urged the Russian president to call a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
[ Landmark Irish Catholic assembly backs further discussion on women’s ordination Opens in new window ]
There have been questions over whether Leo would be able to manage a gruelling 12-day trip to South America in November. However, his surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, said on Saturday there were “no clinical reasons” to prevent him travelling.
“The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery,” Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to fully recover from the operation “in another 10 days or so”.
Before the cancer diagnosis, Leo, who enjoys sports, especially tennis, was generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.
The Gemelli, located in the northwest of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish a high-security papal suite. - Guardian

title: John Swinney versus Andy Burnham: the intriguing new rivalry in British politics
description: Scottish National Party holds its shindig in Aberdeen, while UK prime minister attempts spoiler visit to Motherwell
content:
It is a harbinger for UK prime minister Andy Burnham that the patron saint of Scotland is his namesake, St Andrew: polls show the Labour Party leader is, somewhat incongruously, the most popular political leader in the Celtic nation, which has been run for two decades by his party’s bitter northern rival, the Scottish National Party (SNP) .
All the attention was meant to be on the SNP heading into the weekend, as the independence-seeking party – months after it enjoyed yet another thumping Holyrood election win in May – held its annual conference in recent days in the oil-rich city of Aberdeen.
Instead, Burnham’s spoiler visit to Motherwell in Scotland on Friday in the middle of the SNP’s victory shindig threw a focus on the intriguing rivalry developing between the currently omnipresent UK prime minister and John Swinney , the SNP’s first minister of Scotland.
Apart from the long-dead Tory leader Margaret Thatcher , Swinney was the only other politician namechecked from the stage by Burnham when the Labour leader hosted his own party’s gathering in Liverpool last month.
To boos from the Labour crowd, he complained that Swinney had, on the day Burnham’s father died , predicted the UK leader would be the last prime minister of the union. Burnham, fighting back tears, acknowledged Swinney may not have known he was grieving when he made the quip, but publicly noting it still seemed like a calculated dig.
Senior SNP government sources told The Irish Times in Aberdeen at the weekend that Burnham’s Liverpool outburst, and his decision last week to visit Scotland during the SNP conference, “shows we are getting to them”.
They seemed happy about it, grateful the SNP had another Downing Street rival to use as a focal point on which to project the party’s ire about Westminster. But they felt the dig about Swinney’s comments on the day Burnham’s father died were “below the belt”.
“Everyone knows John is a man of good character who would never want to insult someone grieving his father,” one SNP minister told me. “If anything, it has galvanised us all behind him even more. We’re not afraid of a fight.”
Burnham’s visit to Scotland was, ostensibly, to urge Swinney to join forces with him to devolve powers away from Holyrood into the rest of Scotland. Independence was off the agenda, Burnham said , but they should work together to empower Scottish regions.
SNP sources highlighted that Scotland’s government had already begun this process, independently of Burnham’s intervention. Swinney’s administration has launched a review of proposals to replace Scotland’s 32 councils with six or seven regional authorities, which would sit above about 120 community councils.
The issue was the subject of a Friday morning SNP fringe event, where cabinet secretary Ivan McKee was barracked by some SNP councillors over the vagueness of the plan. He responded that it was still in its early stages and that the government would listen to everyone’s point of view. A report on the issue is due in December.
Later on Friday, a gaggle of photographers gathered at the bottom of the big escalator at the Aberdeen TECA conference venue lobby awaiting the arrival of Swinney, whom they had been tipped off was on his way. Perhaps wary of being compared to the image of the notorious 2016 election campaign entrance of Donald Trump, Swinney eschewed the escalator for a big descent and instead walked the stairs to greet those below.
Having stabilised the once-wobbling SNP since taking over as leader, veteran party stalwart Swinney confidently strode across the TECA exhibition hall. He can present himself as a winner, a man now with his own mandate, after battering Scottish Labour in May.
One of the first stalls he visited was for moustache-themed Movember, a charity that promotes men’s mental health – by getting them to grow soup strainers each November.
“Would you do Movember?” a charity official asked him. The shaven-headed Scottish first minister’s naked pate suggests growing hair may not be his forte. He laughed: “However supportive I am of your objectives, it’s not going to be possible for me.”
All around him, stalls sold merchandise promoting the SNP and its central cause, securing another Scottish independence referendum after losing the one in 2014. SNP members could buy “Aye, Decided!” independence hoodies for £35 (€41.50).
[ A win for the Scottish National Party does not mean the UK is ‘cracking at the seams’ Opens in new window ]
In the heaving bars of Aberdeen that night, however, party rank and file expressed worries that the SNP had no real strategy for forcing Burnham to give them another vote.
Meanwhile, Aberdeen’s raucous student nightlife filled the streets of the city that is the base for the now-fading North Sea oil boom. Many wore fancy dress. The Irish Times mixed with four different Ali Gs in bright yellow tracksuits in the Belmont chipper.
There were sore heads at the TECA next morning, the day of Swinney’s big speech. Yet senior SNP sources told The Irish Times that the party had a plan to give Burnham an independence headache.
They said the SNP’s hope was that the next UK general election produces the mother of all hung parliaments in Westminster, but with Labour as the biggest party. Polls show the SNP could have 40 seats, and possibly the balance of power. It could seek an independence vote as the price for enabling another Burnham UK government.
On Friday night, Swinney had joked at one drinks event that he was “in Burnham’s head and he was in my pocket”. Now, on Saturday, the first minister had a chance to respond to the UK prime minister’s jibes at him.
A grinning Swinney said he sensed “panic on the streets of Manchester”, the English city the UK prime minister used to run. Later, just as Burnham had in Liverpool, Swinney became emotional as he said he wanted independence for the future of his son.
“We build the future on the dreams of those who come next,” he said.
What next for the SNP and its long-held, defining dream of Scottish independence? Swinney and Burnham may yet have more to discuss.

title: Adam Olaniyan impresses again on undercard as emphatic Daniel Dubois defends heavyweight title
description: Promoter Frank Warren plans for the Dublin heavyweight to have ‘15 or 16 fights in the next two years’
content:
Jobstown heavyweight prospect Adam Olaniyan scored the fifth win and stoppage of his professional career with a second round knockout of England’s Dan Garber at London’s O2 Arena on Saturday night.
The former youth world amateur champion was featured prominently on the undercard of Daniel Dubois’s successful defence of the WBO heavyweight world title against fellow Brit Fabio Wardley.
Olaniyan was in control from the first bell, landing sharply with body shots before he hurt Garber (now 14-10) with a straight right hand late in the first round.
The 20-year-old followed up by flooring him with the same punch early in the second and Garber’s corner threw in the towel, but referee Amy Pu elected to let the fight continue, despite having her attention drawn to the towel by Olaniyan.
The Dublin fighter quickly followed up, landing a couple of body shots, before dropping Garber for the second time with a looping right hand, and the fight was waved off.
It proved to be a promising road test for Olaniyan in front of a packed crowd, as only two fighters have stopped Garber quicker, including top contender Moses Itauma.
Promoter Frank Warren confirmed plans for Olaniyan to box on the undercard of Anthony Cacace’s first defence of the WBA super-featherweight title in Belfast on December 19th.
After debuting in March, it will be Olaniyan’s sixth fight in a year, with Warren outlining a busy schedule for the 20-year-old in the near future: “I’m very excited about him. He listens and he does what he should be doing at this stage of his career, which is getting rid of the opponents.
“He’s fighting in Belfast next, and we’re going to keep him busy. I want to get him around 15 or 16 fights in the next two years.”
[ Adam Olaniyan dreams of undisputed success and becoming a cowboy Opens in new window ]
In the main event, Daniel Dubois (now 24-3) blitzed Fabio Wardley (19-2-1) over two rounds to defend his share of the world heavyweight championship in a rematch of their brutal fight of the year contender in May.
Dubois was knocked down twice in their first fight before forcing a stoppage late on, but had a much easier night’s work this time out, dropping the challenger with a hard right hand 20 seconds after the opening bell rang.
Wardley never recovered from that blow, and his corner threw in the towel after a barrage of unanswered blows in the second round.

title: Spain’s Eugenio Chacarra leads Race to Dubai standings after success in India
description: Rory McIlroy slips back to third in the standings after finishing down the leaderboard in Delhi
content:
Eugenio Chacarra claimed his third DP World Tour title of the season at the DP World India Championship in Delhi to replace Patrick Reed at the top of the Race to Dubai standings.
Spaniard Chacarra began the final round at Delhi Golf Club with a five-shot lead after signing for a 63 when the third round was finally completed on Sunday morning following a weather-disrupted start to the tournament.
And although a fast start saw him extend that advantage to six shots early on, Chacarra was left clinging on by his fingernails on the back nine before closing out a two-shot victory over nearest challenger Daniel Hillier.
Chacarra, who seemed to be showing no ill-effects from a recent fractured toe, finished his round with seven pars to card a 70 which also contained three birdies and a bogey.
He now goes into the final three events of the season leading the race to win the Harry Vardon Trophy ahead of Reed in second and Rory McIlroy in third.
Defending champion Tommy Fleetwood finished in a tie for fifth, eight shots behind champion Chacarra on 13 under par, after signing for a final-round 68.
Robert MacIntyre and Tom McKibbin were another shot further back, while Shane Lowry finished tied for 15th on 10 under and McIlroy at four under.
McIlroy is attempting to become an eight-time Race to Dubai winner and knows he will have his work cut out.
“Eugenio is playing well. He’s overtaken Patrick. That makes my job a bit harder going into the last two events,” said McIlroy.
Chacarra stressed how special it would be to put his name alongside Spanish golfing greats such as Seve Ballesteros and Jon Rahm on the list of winners.
“It would mean the world. Those two guys are heroes for me as a Spanish golfer. Seve did everything for European and Spanish golf, and then Jon, it’s a guy that I’ve been looking up to since he went to college and professional golf.
“What he has accomplished, it’s amazing. Hopefully I can put my name on that trophy too. That’s one of the goals.
“I know it’s not going to be easy. Rory in Dubai always plays well and I know it’s going to be a big battle. Patrick too.
“Two of the best players in the world coming for me now, and I know they’re not going to make it easy.”

title: Stuart Lancaster sees hard work pay off as Connacht secure first win over Saracens
description: Connacht went 12-0 behind before finally finding their game to the delight of 12,000 crowd at the Dexcom Stadium
content:
Connacht’s European journey began with a statement victory over three-times Champions Cup winners Saracens on Saturday, their45-36 win the dream result for Stuart Lancaster’s side at a sold out Dexcom Stadium
“A pretty good night,” said Lancaster of his side’s first victory over the English side in four meetings, and also the most points Connacht have scored against an English team in the European competition.
“There was a moment on 70 minutes when the crowd was singing The Fields of Athenry, and it was very special.”
The win came on the back of a “hard training week” when Lancaster pushed his players to the limit.
“We always talked about playing for the full 80 minutes, and when we had an eight-day lead into the game. I put them through the mill on Tuesday, and even on Thursday. But it pays off. I know they can dig deep, and I know they’ve got speed and endurance in them.”
It wasn’t the best start for the home side after conceding tries to Sione Va’eneku and Noah Caluori, but Connacht responded with three first-half tries through captain Cian Prendergast, Cathal Forde and Shamus Hurley-Langton.
“We had to earn the right. We were playing a champion team – full of internationals who had won the competition three times – and we went 12 points down. So we had to find a way. But the three tries in the first half were excellent.”
Although Connacht conceded before half-time, with a resulting yellow card, Lancaster says Prendergast’s second try was “such a big moment”.
Despite the recent disappointing 36-19 URC loss to Glasgow, Lancaster admitted he was always confident in the direction he was leading his players.
“That’s the bottom line. I’m confident in the players. I’m confident in the coaching group. I’m confident in the training we’re doing. I’m confident that if we keep working at it the way in which we do, then we’ll keep getting the rewards.
“The good thing is, as well, I’m looking around the changing room after the game, and there’s a whole lot of lads desperate to play who are really good players.”
Among those missing from Saturday’s victory were Mack Hansen, Seán Naughton, Harry West, Ben Murphy, Finlay Bealham, Dave Heffernan, and Will Connors.
“We’ve got some great forwards to come back. So it’s great to win for the squad, but obviously we need to double down on the URC for five games, and then hopefully we’ll get a good group of players going off to Ireland to play for the national team.”
