title: HSE moves to claw back €30m in undue payments to staff
description: Overpayments to health service workers amount to about €10m a year, figures show
content:
The HSE overpaid its staff by more than €30 million in the space of three years with thousands of employees receiving money they were not entitled to.
A total of €9.53 million in overpayments were identified last year, slightly down on the €9.55 million flagged in 2024.
In 2023, just over €11.1 million in incorrect payments to health service employees were discovered, according to figures released under the Freedom of Information Act.
A total of 3,242 staff were in receipt of overpayments last year, equivalent to an average of almost €3,000 per person.
The HSE said that €5.163 million in money incorrectly paid out was recovered in 2025.
However, more than €4.3 million worth of overpayments remained outstanding at the end of the year.
About 3,700 employees received more money than they were entitled to in 2024, roughly €2,570 per person.
A total of 4,371 staff were overpaid in 2023, an average of €2,540 in each case.
The amount of money outstanding at year end has been falling, however, according to the HSE data.
[ One consultant doctor working for HSE earned more than €900,000 last year Opens in new window ]
In 2023, €5.68 million worth of overpayments were listed as “unrecovered” at the end of the year.
That fell to €4.7 million by December 31st, 2024, and dropped further last year to about €4.33 million.
An information note said the figures covered just “statutory entities” and “HSE staff only.”
A spokesperson said the HSE took overpayments seriously and “works hard to minimise this occurring”.
“The main reasons for overpayments include data entry errors, late entry of unpaid leave, sick leave-related errors, employees not being removed from the payroll in a timely manner, pension overpayments, and allowance overpayments [or] payments made in error.”
[ Health service spent €250m more on ‘higher-cost’ agency staff than budgeted for Opens in new window ]
The spokesperson said once an overpayment was identified, a formal notification issued to the employee outlined proposed arrangements for repayment.
“The HSE will actively engage with the employee on any deviation from this. Where no response is received, the HSE will initiate an automatic deduction where the employee is in receipt of pay.”

title: Landmark Irish Catholic assembly backs further discussion on women’s ordination
description: Archbishop Eamon Martin tells delegates at Co Meath gathering that many Irish parishes will struggle to survive
content:
A significant majority of delegates at a national gathering of Catholics , the first of its kind in Ireland, has voted in favour of a recommendation to bishops that there be ongoing discussion on women’s ordination in the church.
On the question of “women’s ministry, including ordination to the diaconate”, 54 per cent voted in favour, of which 42 per cent highly recommended the proposal and 12 per cent simply recommended it.
Another 19 per cent felt it required further discernment, while 27 per cent were opposed.
The approximately 300 lay and clerical delegates attended the first National Synodal Assembly of Catholics in Ireland, at Gormonston, Co Meath , on Saturday.
The proposal said “the question of women’s ministry, including ordination to the diaconate” should be “engaged with openly, seriously and in a theologically informed way” and called on the bishops “to use their role and influence to encourage discussion and education both nationally and internationally”.
Such advocacy, it said, “needs to be theologically informed by current theology and ecclesiology, with particular emphasis on female theologians who have researched, reflected and written on the history, tradition and role of ordained ministry”.
Conversations about the ordination of women, it said, should “be considered in any discussion on the opening up of all ministry in general to women, so that as we open what is now possible, we are also continuing the conversation about what may be”.
However, delegates voted 56 per cent against the establishment of a national office for women which, it was proposed, would be “a witness to the church’s communal commitment at parish and diocesan levels in Ireland to the full inclusion of women”.
A majority of delegates also recommended to the bishops that the church in Ireland ask the universal church “to develop a more respectful and life-giving vocabulary when speaking about LGBT+ people”.
[ Role of women, married priests and sexuality featured early in the synodal pathway Opens in new window ]
A total of 41 per cent highly recommended this proposal, with 20 per cent recommending it, 26 per cent saying it required further discernment, and 13 per cent opposed.
The day-long assembly, which followed a five-year process, considered and voted on 35 proposals dealing with the future of the Catholic Church in Ireland as recommendations to the bishops.
At the assembly’s conclusion on Saturday evening, Catholic primate Archbishop Eamon Martin told delegates that the bishops’ conference would be meeting next week, and that “we look forward to reflecting together on today’s assembly and all that has led to it”.
“We need this process, because many of our parishes and even our dioceses are unsustainable in the current model and will struggle to survive,” he said.
He also said he had “a personal hope” that at some point over the next seven years, “our holy father Pope Leo XIV might come to Ireland - please God his health will allow for it.”

title: ‘I stood in that circle 10 years ago’: Jack O’Donoghue on an emotional night for Munster
description: Flanker reflects on Anthony Foley’s influence after team secure 33-25 win over Racing 92 in Cork
content:
For Jack O’Donoghue – the one Munster player who was both in the squad due to face Racing 92 a decade and a day ago in Paris as well as the matchday 23 against the same opponents in Cork – paying homage to his former coach made for a particularly emotional night and, indeed, week.
His overriding emotion was “a lot of pride” after Munster’s 33-25 win over Racing 92 in Páirc Uí Chaoimh: “I’m really proud of the performance that we put in to get the result. It was a tough, tough week, with the emotions, to try to keep them down and to focus on your job and to put down a performance like we did.
“I think to come away with the four points is huge and exactly what we wanted to do and exactly what we set out at the start of the week to do.”
Anthony Foley’s wife, Olive, presented the jerseys to the players at their captain’s run in Thomond Park on Friday and reflecting on this, O’Donoghue said: “It was incredibly powerful. She’s an incredibly powerful woman, and she speaks a lot about belief and belief in God and how that has helped her.
“She’s someone I’ve actually stayed in touch with since Axel passing, and it was just great to see her and to show how strong of a woman she is. To be able to stand in front of us 10 years on and to present us with our jerseys, it meant a hell of a lot.
“And to show the strength that she has, it just filled me with massive strength as well, that you know you could go out and face anyone, the way she spoke in the dressing room before our captain’s run.”
As they had done after beating Glasgow in Thomond Park a day after Foley’s funeral in Killaloe, the entire squad and management formed a circle in the middle of the pitch to sing their valedictory dressing-room anthem, Stand Up and Fight.
“For me personally, it was very emotional,” said O’Donoghue. “I stood in that circle 10 years ago as a young fellah just coming through. I was asked after the game what Axel meant to me. You know, he gave me my first opportunity; he put time and effort into me, sitting down with me as an academy player watching videos, watching training and teaching me the little intricate bits of the game.
“To be 10 years on and to still be in that circle, it was very emotional for me because it means a hell of a lot to me.
“It means a hell of a lot to still be in this group and to still be playing and putting in a result and getting a result like that, it meant a lot.”
[ Páirc Uí Chaoimh crowd pay perfect tribute to Anthony Foley on emotional evening by the Lee Opens in new window ]
Munster head coach Clayton McMillan commented: “I didn’t personally know the man, but you actually feel like you know him through the constant mentioning and presence of his name. That’s been really good for me and the other guys that are not necessarily from Munster but want to understand him and the legacy of Munster.
“I thought the players managed the week really well.
“We had some disruptions. We had one day in at UL, a normal training base. They had a big [EU] function there with a whole lot of dignitaries. We weren’t able to go to our own base. We adapted. We changed up the week.
“That, along with everything going on with the memorial around Axel meant it was a different week, but I thought they showed a huge amount of professionalism and just kept their emotions in check.”
Man of the match Craig Casey was in his Leaving Certificate year at Ardscoil Rís when Foley died in 2016. A Shannon player like Foley, he also had the distinction of scoring the final try.
“I was on the East Terrace the week after he died, I couldn’t have been prouder of Munster that day.
[ ‘It never gets easy:’ 10 years on, Anthony Foley is still inspiring Munster Opens in new window ]
“You want to be part of that, how well we rallied around everyone that week and I was only in sixth year, but it drove me to want to be a part of the club.
“It’s a special week, he’s a special man. His legacy will be with every Munster team from here until the very end of time.
“We talk about him constantly, we wrap up every game with ‘Axel’. His family is very special to us, thankfully we honoured him with a win today.”

title: ‘People are afraid it will happen again’: Hundreds protest lack of flooding action in Midleton
description: Storm Babet caused up to €200m in damage to businesses and homes in the Co Cork town in 2023
content:
Close to 500 people attended a protest on Saturday organised by a flood protection group in Midleton, Co Cork , to highlight what they describe as “the lack of any meaningful protections” given to the community since Storm Babet devastated the area in 2023.
Extreme rainfall in Midleton and other parts of east Cork in October 2023 led to flooding of houses and businesses.
The force of the deluge caused the front window of a hairdressing salon in the town to shatter, while flooding was 1.5m deep in some places.
The flooding event caused up to €200 million in damage to businesses and homes in the town.
Members of the Midleton and East Cork Flood Protection Group said they are still years away from full protection against flooding in the region.
[ The floods will overwhelm Irish land. We can’t just sit back Opens in new window ]
Mona Stromsoe, spokeswoman for the group, told Cork’s 96FM that they feel just as vulnerable to flooding as they were in 2023.
“We were expecting the flooding defence scheme for Midleton to go to planning at the end of September.
“As recently as July we were told it was on track to go to planning at the end of September.
“That didn’t happen and we were told by the Minister [Kevin ‘Boxer’ Moran] that it wouldn’t happen until the end of Q4.
Stromsoe said people previously impacted by flooding in east Cork remain fearful of a repeat episode.
“They think, ‘Is today the day?’ We saw in Killarney during the summer that it was just one day of rain and they were flooded.
“People are afraid it will happen again and it will be as bad as Babet.”
The protest took place on Saturday in Midleton and involved groups of people from the town and nearby areas such as Mogeely, Killeagh and Castlemartyr.
[ Is Ireland ready for a monster El Nino? Expect ugly potatoes, transport chaos and widespread disruption Opens in new window ]
Earlier this month Minister of State Kevin “Boxer” Moran announced €1.1 million in funding for interim and flood mitigation measures in Mogeely, Castlemartyr, Ratchcormac and Ballintubber.
The Minister said the announcement was part of an overall €14 million allocation to Midleton and east Cork to address and mitigate the flood risk in the region.
He said a further €5.8 million investment is enabling advance works in Tir Cluain, Midleton, to proceed to construction from spring next year. These works will protect 135 properties.
[ ‘If we flood again, we’re homeless’: Midleton homeowners in crisis without flood insurance after storms Opens in new window ]
Moran said Cork County Council is due to receive the final planning engineering and environmental assessment documents for the overall flood defence scheme from its consultants this month.
He said this will allow the council to make a planning application for the Midleton Flood Relief Scheme to An Coimisiún Pleanála by the end of the year, which would protect 750 properties and all of those impacted by Storm Babet.

title: Historic town hall torched and more than 1,800 arrested as protests spread across France
description: Anti-government demonstrations spiral out of control in many cities, with buildings set ablaze and shops looted
content:
More than 1,800 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protesters supporting high school students clashed with police, with some demonstrations later spiralling out of control as buildings were set ablaze and shops looted.
Tens of thousands of people were estimated to have taken part in protests that spread through viral calls on social media and brought together diverse groups including students, farmers, trade unionists, climate activists and people angry about fuel prices and the cost of living .
While many protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.
Late on Saturday, prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police hurt. On Sunday interior minister Laurent Nuñez announced that the number of arrests had gone up to 1,800.
Nuñez said the official demonstration had been hijacked by casseurs – “opportunistic delinquents who had seen a chance to pillage and loot … we will find them and deal with them firmly”.
He said the government was not planning to declare a state of emergency but added: “I very strongly condemn the violence we have seen.”
In the city of Limoges, the town hall was “largely lost” to a fire set by masked protesters, the top regional official told the AFP news agency.
“The roof has collapsed on to lower floors, except the west wing, and two-thirds of the exterior has already disappeared,” local prefect Maurice Barate said, adding that the extensive damage to the 143-year-old building was a “catastrophe for heritage”.
Protesters burned down the Lyons tourism office, torched cars and built burning barricades on the streets of Paris and broke down the door of Marseilles city hall to storm the building, spraying graffiti and damaging furniture.
Mayor of Marseilles Benoit Payan said the situation was “out of control” and called for national authorities to intervene.
“There are young people who are 16, 17 years old. What’s going to happen this afternoon? They’re going to get tear gas grenades in the face because there are troublemakers in the middle of the marches,” Payan told journalists.
[ ‘A bombshell’: French teachers spot something on payslips that reveals scale of funding crisis Opens in new window ]
“We can’t lump protesters with legitimate demands together with these vandals – they’re morons, imbeciles, thugs ... I want them in prison, I want them brought to justice.”
Some protesters could be seen wearing the yellow reflective jackets that became the symbol of the gilets jaunes movement that ground France to a halt in 2018 with demonstrations initially triggered by fuel costs. “Macron is the vandal,” read one sign.
In some parts of Paris, young people could be seen marching peacefully and chanting the student protest slogan “we’re young, determined and revolutionary”.
Elsewhere in the city centre, protesters, dressed in black with their faces covered, torched parked cars and burned piles of electronic bicycles on the street, their batteries exploding and sending thick dark smoke rising in plumes over the city.
Police attempted to gain control using tear gas and baton charges, and by the afternoon there had been 272 arrests across the country.
Hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon blamed authorities in Paris for the disorder, saying they had been tear-gassing the demonstrators’ gathering point on Place de la République “relentlessly”.
The far-right National Rally blamed “Mélenchon’s far left” for the “disorder”.
“Working France, which is taking the full brunt of inflation and the cost of living crisis, is not in the streets today,” close Marine Le Pen ally Jordan Bardella wrote on social media.
“The real mobilisation of the French for purchasing power, for lowering taxes on fuel, for work that pays decently, will be the vote for Marine Le Pen in the presidential election.”
Before student protests gathered force in September, viral posts on social media had already called for a revival of the yellow vests movement and for demonstrations across France on October 17th.
The protesters came together after a week in which universities shut down and college students joined high schoolers in mass protests in major cities.
[ France’s school protests: What lies behind the anger Opens in new window ]
French president Emmanuel Macron appealed for “calm” and said police forces were facing “difficult times” and “extreme violence”, in a press conference on the eve of the protests in Brussels, where he was attending a meeting of EU leaders.
“There is a constitutional right to demonstrate ... there is a responsibility that comes with it,” Macron said. “The problem is when they are disorganised and there are elements there solely to vandalise and cause chaos, and that‘s unacceptable.” – Additional reporting: Guardian

title: ‘Famous, but without the good bits’: Inside the world of top-level football referees
description: William Ralston’s new book The Impossible Job touches on Thierry Henry’s handball, VAR, death threats and the addiction that keeps referees coming back
content:
J on Moss had the best line to sum up the life of a top-level referee. “Like being a shit celebrity,” the former Premier League whistler told author William Ralston. Famous, but without the good bits.
Moss was a referee for nearly a quarter of a century and made it right to the top of the English game, doing hundreds and hundreds of games. Yet even though he was demonstrably an excellent ref, trusted and respected by enough people who matter to have made a long top-flight career out of it, you still find that almost half his Wikipedia entry is devoted to his mistakes. Why would anyone bother?
Ralston’s new book, The Impossible Job, is a brilliant treatment of exactly that question. For four years, Ralston immersed himself in the world of football refereeing, from qualifying himself to take games in the lower leagues to sitting down with the referee of the World Cup final. The result is one of the best soccer books in years, drilling into every conceivable corner of the world of referees.
“In the beginning,” Ralston says, “a lot of referees go into it because they want to be involved in the game. A lot of referees I spoke to are former players – they either played the game to a reasonably high level and had professional ambitions but injury struck, as happened with Daniel Siebert, the German referee who did the Champions League final this year. Or they simply weren’t quite good enough to make the cut. So they end up falling into refereeing.
“At the higher level, money is obviously a factor. The top referees are well paid, they can make a career out of it. And then there’s the drive to get as far as you can, to get the bigger games, get into the Champions League, do the World Cup and so on. But there was also something deeper which I discovered, which nearly all referees I spoke to mentioned, regardless of the level – it’s the thrill of refereeing a game well.
“Take someone like Clement Turpin, the French referee who is one of the best in the world. His thrill is very precise. It’s that moment of blowing the whistle and that walk from the middle of the pitch to the locker room. Those five minutes are like purely blissful for him. Because the pain of getting a match wrong is so severe that that creates a massive satisfaction when you get it right.”
It seems like a rum deal, all in all. Or at least that’s the conclusion plenty of normal people reading Ralston’s book will surely come to. A few minutes of benign satisfaction after a game doesn’t feel like commensurate reward, given that the downside risks are so severe.
Ralston has stories in his book of referees who’ve had their addresses published, who’ve needed security outside their hotel room, whose families have been targeted. One chap, a second-hand car salesman in real life, had a customer rip up an agreed contract as soon as he realised who he was dealing with.
Not quite at the level of death threats, fair enough. But still surely enough of a pain in the hoop to be better off doing almost anything else with your spare time.
“It’s a fair point,” Ralston says. “But I will say that having refereed myself at the lower levels, that addiction, that thrill really is quite satisfying. I mean, I sometimes wonder why I go out but I do look forward to it. I’m refereeing on Friday and I know that walk off the field after doing it is really satisfying.
“Obviously I don’t have any of the costs of it like you’d get at the top level. My family aren’t threatened or anything like that. I’m doing it at a very low level so the costs are far lower. But that rush is quite severe. I do get it.”
For the book, Ralston interviewed the likes of Anthony Taylor, one of the highest-profile referees in the Premier League. He sat down for lunch with José María Sánchez Martínez a few hours before he refereed the 2024 El Clásico at the Bernabeu. He tracked down some of the referees whose mistakes were among the most notorious in modern football history – Tom Henning Ovrebo ( Chelsea v Barcelona , 2009), Martin Hansson (France v Ireland, the Thierry Henry game). It took a lot of time and effort to get some of them to talk but when they did, he found they were mad keen to tell their story.
[ Ken Early: Thierry Henry, a missed flight, and the invisible hand of history Opens in new window ]
“It was difficult in the beginning because the organisations around them want to protect them as much as possible. Those organisations have a bit of a difficult job because they also want to humanise them. They want to show the skill of their job, but they also don’t want to go and allow journalists to go and ask them scandalous questions that will create headlines about previous decisions. It’s a really difficult balance.
“But, yeah, once they got talking the referees were really open and they were really open about talking about the challenges of their job. And I think generally they want to talk about that complexity. They want people to understand the invisible complexities of their role. But I just don’t think that they’ve really been permitted in the past, and I think that they’ve probably been very wary of journalists.”
It makes for a fascinating read. The chapter on the difficulties faced in the UK by referees of colour is eye-opening and depressing. There’s a wild chapter detailing the crusade by former Arsenal supremo David Dein, now in his 80s but uncommonly obsessed with the concept of Pure Time. And, of course, there’s the mist of VAR hanging over everything, always.
On the whole, referees are pro-VAR. It has particularly improved the lives of linesmen, who no longer have to worry about turning a game on a dodgy offside, since VAR will act as a safety net. But as Ralston shows in the book, while there’s a huge difference between being an on-pitch ref and sitting in a silent room checking for mistakes, we instinctively treat both impostors just the same.
“We do, absolutely. We treat the two jobs as if they’re the same thing. But one of the big things you learn about on-pitch referee is that it’s more about managing the emotions of 22 players sometimes than it is about the laws of the game. There are so many decisions that have a grey area, that are 50-50.
“And if there’s a decision to be made around a yellow card, that takes place in the context of on-pitch relationships that you’ve been forming throughout the game. But the VAR isn’t subject to any of that. Obviously he can hear the conversations but he’s not the one who has to keep control over the players and stop a game from spiralling.
“Sometimes though the VAR will intervene and give a decision that might be technically correct. It might technically be a foul. But realistically, the game doesn’t need to be stopped there. The on-pitch referee has a better feel for what is happening in the game . . . That’s the psychological battle every single referee and VAR is facing.”
The Impossible Job by William Ralston is out now, published by Penguin Books.

title: Lara Gillespie wins gold at track cycling world championships
description: The Wicklow rider adds to her silver medal won on Wednesday’s opening day of competition in Shanghai
content:
Lara Gillespie produced a sensational ride to win the gold medal in the points race on the final day of the UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai, earning herself another coveted rainbow jersey in commanding style.
A year on from becoming the first Irish woman to win a UCI world track title in any event, Gillespie was prominent throughout the 100 laps of the 25km race, which came down to a three-way battle for gold in the final sprint for the line, where double points were on offer.
By taking second in that sprint , Gillespie took her total to 42 points, five points ahead of Amalie Dideriksen from Denmark, with Belgium’s Shari Bossuyt, the early leader, winning bronze on 35 points.
“It’s all sinking in now, I’m just so happy I could pull this off,” she said. “I came really close the other today (in the scratch), and I think that really just pushed me on there today because I was really annoyed with that second place.
“Overall a really good week and I really just can’t thank Cycling Ireland and Sport Ireland enough for all the support over the last few years. And all the people back home who are getting those key sessions in with me, helping me get fast for the track, so I really just want to say thank you to everyone.”
Gillespie was unquestionably the strongest and most astute rider by the end, the 25-year-old Wicklow rider adding to her silver medal won in the scratch race on Wednesday’s opening day of competition.
Points are won in 10 different sprints, after every 10 laps, during the race, with Gillespie, Dideriksen and Bossuyt the only riders to secure the 20 bonus points for lapping the rest of the bunch. Gillespie won the second and fifth sprint, finished second in the seventh and ninth, before her second place in the final sprint earned her the outright victory.
Just one point up going into that final sprint, critically she finished ahead of Dideriksen, the former road race world champion, with Gillespie timing her effort to near perfection.
Defending world champion Yareli Acevedo from Mexico won those final sprint points, but finished up a long way back in fourth, with just 13 points.
Gillespie had finished just inches short of gold in the scratch race, won by Dutch star Lorena Wiebes. She then finished fifth in the omnium on Friday, moving up two places in the final race, but just short of the podium.
Her breakthrough win on the track came in the elimination race at last year’s UCI Track World Championships in Santiago, Chile – and she also won bronze in the points race in 2024.
Since winning in Santiago, Gillespie became the first Irish rider to complete all three major stage races for women – finishing fourth in the points classification in the Giro d’Italia, having taken on both the Tour de France Femmes and the Vuelta de España last summer. She then won two Irish national titles in June (the time trial and road race), before finishing third in the women’s Tour of Poland.
[ Meet Lorenzo Finn, Italy’s teenage cycling super talent with an Irish grandmother Opens in new window ]
Last weekend, Gillespie finished second in the three-day Tour of Chongming Island in Shanghai, with two successive runner-up positions in the last two stages, her best result in a World Tour stage race. She now finishes the season with another rainbow jersey to add to her collection, looking eminently capable of winning many more.
Katie-George Dunlevy has also previously won multiple UCI Para-Cycling track titles.

title: Leaving shares to a spouse at death can make more sense than a lifetime transfer
description: Tax planning can be advantageous financially but families need to be clear on its purpose and its benefit
content:
I own shares in a company which, if sold today, would attract a large tax liability. In one of your articles, you state that “section 1028 of the Taxes Consolidation Act provides that no capital gains arises on assets that are given by one spouse to another”.
So if I transfer my shareholding into my wife’s name, I am no longer liable for capital gains tax (CGT) in that shareholding and my wife’s tax liability commences from the time she receives the shares until the time she eventually sells them. Is that correct? Is the transfer to my wife by way of a gift? Does gift tax arise?
Does the share transfer require new share certificates to be issued in my wife’s name? If so, is this a simple matter? Are there any fees involved in such a transfer?
In the event of my wife’s death, these shares would become part of her estate and would not attract CGT. Is that right?
I understand from your article that if my wife died before me and she left the shares to me, I would again be liable to large capital gains liability. Should my wife indicate in her will that these shares should pass to my daughter, would this resolve the above issue?
Investing in individual stocks is clearly a high-risk game as all your eggs are in one basket rather than being diversified across a number of shares or other assets in an exchange trade fund (ETF). However, stock markets have enjoyed a very strong run in recent years and, for those who chose wisely (or fortunately), their investments have secured strong gains.
And that raises the issue of tax planning.
None of us wants to pay any more tax than we are required to and, as that recent letter to which you refer highlighted, there are potentially valuable exemptions that can help couples do this.
[ When budget changes kick in and how to claim them Opens in new window ]
Irish law determines that gifts (and inheritances) between spouses do not attract any capital acquisitions tax (CAT) liability. So anything your wife gives you or you give your wife is exempt from this tax, which is more commonly known as inheritance tax or gift tax.
You ask whether the transfer you are considering would be seen as a gift? It will, yes, but not one that is liable for gift tax.
At a practical level, you sensibly raise the issue of share certificates or, in more recent times, an electronic record of share ownership.
Registrars are companies that manage the share registers of listed companies. Most particularly, they keep track of who owns how many shares and record changes of ownership when shares are sold or otherwise transferred.
They also keep shareholders notified of company events, such as annual meetings, share placings, rights issues, consolidation, or special meetings to approve things like takeovers, etc.
There are a number of companies that specialise in this work. You do not identify which company’s shares we are talking about here so I cannot tell you which one you need to approach, but the information will be readily available in the investor relations section of the website of the company you’ve invested in.
You can also get the details from any email or letter they may have sent you.
They will send you a share transfer form to formalise the transfer of ownership of these shares to your wife. There will be a charge to do this. I cannot say precisely how much this will be but it tends to be fairly nominal.
If you do not have your share certificate, things can get a bit more costly as you may need to sign (and pay for) an indemnity letter.
The whole thing is a fairly straightforward process though it can be slightly bureaucratic and stressful for people unused to dealing with share registrars, a group which, by the nature of their work, tends to communicate in fairly formal legal terms.
But what about CGT? By your own admission, you have built up quite a CGT liability on these shares over time.
This was the gist of the previous question and, as I said then, the transfer to your wife does not trigger any CGT bill. However, that does not mean that the capital gain you have made disappears; it just transfers to your wife.
While neither of you has any tax bill to pay right now, your wife is deemed to have acquired the shares not on the date you transfer them to her and at their price on that day, but on the date and at the price you originally acquired them for.
If she sells them down the line, all you have really done is transfer your large CGT bill to her.
But what about if she holds them until she dies? Well then, as I said in response to the previous query, the capital gain will die with her. Any capital gain dies with the owner of an asset.
Whoever succeeds her in owning these shares will not have to worry about the legacy capital gain dating back to the time you originally acquired the shares. The only capital gain that will apply for new owners will be the difference in the price when your wife dies and the price at which they eventually sell the shares.
This, as another reader found recently, can create unexpected tax liability as probate generally takes a year and, in strong equity markets, people can find themselves unwittingly with an outstanding capital gain the moment they actually get access to shares. For the new owner, capital gains does not start with when they get control of the shares but when the previous owner dies.
[ Inheritance tax reform could unlock €170bn sitting on deposit, expert says Opens in new window ]
There is one area where you appear to have confused something I have mentioned previously. You understand that if your wife were to leave the shares to you when she dies, the clock goes back to when you originally bought these shares. That is not so.
If your wife were to subsequently transfer the shares back to you while alive, yes, that is the case. But not if she leaves them to you in her will or even in the absence of a will.
Whether your wife leaves these shares to you, her daughter, or anyone else, no CGT issue arises. She can mention them specifically in her will, she can simply leave them to be dealt with under a residuary clause – a clause all wills should have dealing with assets not otherwise allocated to a specific beneficiary – or they can be dealt with under intestacy. In none of those cases will capital gains arise, even if she leaves them to you.
Anything your wife leaves you in her will or anything you otherwise inherit from her is free of inheritance tax but that is not the case for her daughter or any other beneficiary.
The budget raised the amounts anyone can receive in inheritance without paying tax. For a child inheriting from a parent, this threshold is now €420,000. That will cover anything your daughter inherits from either parent and also any gift they may have received from you in your lifetimes over the value of €3,000 in any one year.
But at the end of all this, I have one question for you?
If the intention is not to sell the shares, why bother with this lifetime transfer? If you sell the shares or you transfer them to your wife and she sells them, the same CGT bill arises – and in most families will be paid from the common family financial pool.
And if either of you dies owning the shares, no CGT applies.
[ Inheritance tax in Ireland: ‘The rules are absolutely skewed against the childless’ Opens in new window ]
The only real financial benefit here is if your wife dies before you, having taken ownership of the shares, and then leaves them to you in her will. That would wipe out your CGT liability for sure.
But demographics suggest that a woman will live longer than a man in Ireland, even these days. And it would seem to benefit her more when considering tax exposure to receive these shares from you via your will when she does not have to worry about any tax bill – CGT or CAT.

title: How HR teams are combatting AI and other security threats in recruitment process
description: Fraudulent use of AI in the jobs process is forcing the warm and fuzzy realms of the former to work with the suspicious minds of the latter
content:
W hat would you think if you were asked in a job interview to hold up three fingers in front of your face? Perhaps you’re doing so badly that they’re checking you’re not concussed?
More likely the recruiter is trying to check that you’re not an artificial intelligence (AI) deepfake.
Employers are trying all sorts of things to combat fraudulent AI use in the recruitment process. There are jobseekers who use chatbots to bluff their way into jobs they’re not capable of, or pay “interview mules” to complete assessments for them.
More dangerously, there are hackers who try to get hired with false identities in order to access internal systems, and even remote information technology (IT) workers who turn out to be based in North Korea. The research company Gartner has predicted that one in four candidate profiles worldwide will be fake by 2028.
All this is leading to a culture clash inside companies . The warm and fuzzy realms of human resources (HR) and recruitment are having to learn to work with the suspicious minds of the cybersecurity world.
One example: the HR platform Deel acquired AI cybersecurity company Clarity in August in order to “embed continuous identity security across the entire hiring and workforce life cycle”.
Neev Wilf, who was at Clarity and is now head of product at Deel Security, tells me that “bringing HR and security to the same room is tough” because they “have different interests”. Security teams usually want “every protection, every feature, all the way” but “at the same time, you have [recruiters] who say ‘this enhances friction for the candidate’”.
What sort of security checks are we talking about here? Recruitment platform Greenhouse has introduced a system to allow employers to prompt job seekers for ID verification. “Some do it at the top of the funnel, in the beginning of the process, and some do it further down,” Daniel Chait, Greenhouse’s chief executive, tells me.
Clarity, meanwhile, says it uses AI to examine “facial movements, lip-syncing, eye motions, voice patterns” and other indicators in video interviews, and cross-checks indicators such as “behavioural, identity, and media patterns” to spot signals of deception.
It sounds like a lot of personal data to be hoovered up in a process that might not even result in a job offer. There is surely the potential, too, for “false positives”: for legitimate candidates to be flagged as suspicious and thus denied the chance of getting hired. If a lot of employers start to use the same handful of systems, some unlucky souls might find themselves blocked again and again.
The good news is that the EU’s penchant for regulation has helped pre-empt some of these potential pitfalls. Both the General Data Protection Regulation directive and the European Union AI Act give people protection against being subject to unexplained automated decision-making, for example, especially in high-stakes areas such as recruitment.
[ Interviewing Gen Z teachers: A candidate told me I was in a bidding war for her Opens in new window ]
Both Wilf and Chait tell me their systems have been carefully designed to meet EU regulations and do not lead to automated decisions but only flag information for human review.
That said, these new security features and identity checks feel like a depressing consequence of the AI arms race in recruitment. Already, candidates complain they feel dehumanised by employers’ use of the technology, while employers say they can’t cope with the volume of AI-assisted applications.
According to Gartner’s regular surveys of job seekers, the number of people who had experienced an AI-led interview doubled from 9 per cent in the third quarter of last year to 18 per cent in the second quarter of this year. But only 30 per cent said they felt comfortable with the experience, only 20 per cent felt they were able to get their own questions about the job answered and only 17 per cent preferred the experience to a human interviewer.
Have we reached the point where employers throw up their hands and go back to a much smaller pool of handwritten applications and in-person interviews?
It’s an appealing thought, but it’s worth remembering that way of doing things was hardly perfect either. Indeed, perhaps the worst-case scenario would be a future that contains a bit of both.
A return to more offline, human-to-human recruitment decisions for those who already have personal connections who can vouch for them (or those young people whose parents have connections). And for job seekers without that reserve of social capital? An interview into a webcam with three fingers pressed to your face. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Mother alleges adult son threatened ‘to burn the house down and kill me’
description: Woman among several parents seeking barring orders against adult children with substance abuse problems
content:
A mother who said her adult son threatened “to burn the house down and kill me” after bursting into the family home demanding money from her obtained a barring order against him.
Aged in his 40s, her son is on crack cocaine, and the incident happened shortly after his recent release from prison, his mother told the emergency domestic violence court at Dolphin House in Dublin.
During the incident, he wrestled her phone from her when she was trying to call the gardaí and took money from her purse in front of her, she said.
“I’m afraid to sleep in my own home because he has smashed windows and doors.”
A young relative lives with her, and her daughter regularly visits with her children, the woman added.
Judge Gerard Furlong granted the woman’s ex parte (one side only represented) application for an interim barring order (IBO). The case will return to court later this month when the son can either oppose or consent to a full barring order for a maximum of three years.
The woman was among several parents who came to court on Friday seeking emergency orders, under the Domestic Violence Act, against adult sons with addiction problems.
A father secured a two-year barring order against his son, aged in his late 20s.
He previously got an IBO but, when the case returned to court on Friday, there was no appearance by the son.
“He is unlikely to be here because he runs away from everything,” said his father.
The judge proceeded to hear the barring order application because he was satisfied the son was served with the necessary legal documents.
In his sworn information to the court, he said his son has been an addict, using drink and drugs, since his early teens.
He started on marijuana and moved to cocaine and is living a “chaotic” lifestyle affecting everyone in the family home, said his dad. His son is out four or five times weekly and returns at all hours, often causing disruption, “sometimes violent and always on the edge of it”. He damages the house and the family’s cars and has “threatened my life”, he added.
His son’s personality has altered; he is “clearly mentally ill”, constantly in trouble and does not seem to care for anyone or anything, said his father. “He is descending deeper into addiction, if that is possible.”
The family are traumatised by this “relentless behaviour” and he previously secured a barring order in 2023 against his son.
He was seeking a two-year, rather than the maximum three-year order, he said. “There is always the hope of redemption. We’ll see. I’m here today for my family, but for him as much; he will never change as long as we maintain him in our home.”
The judge said he sees many parents in similar circumstances and always tells them “not to give up hope” and they have the option to discharge the order if circumstances change.
The man thanked the judge, adding he was very thankful to the court for its support over the years.
A mother obtained a protection order against her son, aged in his 20s, whom she said had recently gone into psychosis due to cocaine use and was a danger to himself and others. He had a previous incident of psychosis earlier this year, she said.
Gardaí had advised her to seek an IBO “but I want to give him a chance to get into rehab first”, she said.
In another case, the judge continued an IBO granted earlier this month to a woman against her adult son after he heard the son was in custody over an alleged breach of it.
The woman said, just days after she secured the IBO, her son kicked in her hall door and came upstairs when she was asleep. He had been put out of the house over drinking “and different things going on a long time” and recently “battered” and “choked” her other adult son, she said.
After he came into the house, she rang gardaí who removed him, she said. She is not afraid of her son but does not want to see him, she added.
In another application, a man who left the family home with his children earlier this week got a protection order against his wife. His wife previously agreed to his request to leave their jointly rented home after she was found by her mother and sister with cocaine.
She later returned, promising to stop drinking and to end contact with a man with whom she had been having an affair and repair her relationship with their older children, he said. One evening this week, he said she had driven home drunk and, when their teenage daughter confronted her, said she was leaving with the youngest child and struck the teenager. That was when he left with all the children, and they stayed in his mother-in-law’s house, he said.
The man said he did not want to return with the children unless his wife was barred from the family home.
Furlong said there was insufficient evidence for an emergency IBO, but he would grant a safety order. The barring order application would be heard at a later date when the wife is entitled to be present, he said. If she demonstrated any behaviour before that which put him or the children in fear, he should call gardaí, the judge added.

title: Trump will take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions, Rubio says
description: ‘A lot of you don’t know what my decision is ​yet,’ US president says of controversial waiver move
content:
The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, US president Donald Trump said on Saturday he had yet to ​announce a final decision on the matter, while secretary of state Marco Rubio said officials wanted more time to evaluate the situation.
Rubio said that Trump would use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs that he waived a day earlier.
“A lot of you don’t know what my decision is ​yet, but we’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida.
The waiver comes just weeks before November’s US midterm elections, with Trump ⁠under pressure over high energy prices as war with Iran disrupts global oil supplies.
Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving ‌key sanctions ‌and ​tariffs under the law known as the Graham Act, which he signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine .
The measures, including tariffs on Russian goods and penalties ⁠on countries buying Russian oil and gas, were due ​to take effect next week. Friday’s order did not specify how long the ​waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump opted for a 60-day review.
“I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of ‌analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean ​to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio told reporters on Saturday before boarding a plane for a trip to Uzbekistan.
[ Zelenskiy defies Trump as Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian refineries Opens in new window ]
Complicating matters is ⁠the Graham Act’s call not only for sanctions on Russia ⁠but also for tariffs on goods ​from countries that import Russian energy supplies. Rubio pointed to India, an important US partner that has diversified its energy supplies but remains heavily dependent on Russian oil.
Friday’s executive order drew criticism from Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who warned it would embolden Russian president Vladimir Putin and prolong the war.
[ US snapshot of Donald Trump’s hunger for adulation that has dragged us to this fraught moment Opens in new window ]
Senator Darline Graham, a South Carolina Republican whose late brother Lindsey Graham championed the legislation that bears his name, said she disagreed with Trump’s decision and planned to discuss it with him when he campaigns for her next week.
“Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia,” she told reporters on Saturday. “Because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia.” – Reuters

title: A Dublin woman in Ottawa: ‘Canadians take time to adapt to our humour and way of doing business’
description: Wild Geese: Jackie Gilna, Ottawa
content:
G rowing up in south Co Dublin and attending school in Mount Anville, Jackie Gilna credits her father for giving her the broadest possible appreciation of Irish culture. Wherever possible, the family were exposed to their farming heritage.
“My dad was from Longford. I was that Dublin jackeen. My grandmother would say how awful it was that I was being brought up in the city, and I would be made to drink the milk from a cow. But that brought me closer to an Irish experience than I would not have experienced in Dublin.
“We were also brought all around Ireland, and my dad told me, ‘You will not leave these shores until you know every corner and you are an ambassador for your country’.”
Earlier immersion in Irish culture was a formative influence, she says, in a career that has been shaped around promoting Ireland abroad and bringing the diaspora closer. Gilna, the founder of We Are Global Irish, is on a mission to harness and grow networks of Irish communities throughout the world to support each other, places where businesses and professionals can come together to share information and help each other in practical ways.
We Are Global Irish was launched in 2024 as a private sector company complementing the work of State agencies. As well as networking and introductions, it provides a range of practical business supports and publishes a monthly online magazine called the Irish Exchange.
The business is registered in Canada and, while the largest element of the Irish diaspora is in North America, the venture has a global reach, she says.
“One thing that stands out to me was that the world we live in as the Irish abroad is very fragmented but, when you bring people together, everyone knows someone who knows somebody; there’s only a couple of degrees of separation.
“We have State agencies who do phenomenal work, such as Enterprise Ireland and IDA Ireland, for example – the envy of other countries – and we work closely with them but there needed to be something in the private sector.”
[ ‘There are 30 Irish people in Brandon, Canada. You miss the craic living in a small place’ Opens in new window ]
Gilna’s corporate career took shape in the Netherlands and later Canada, where she moved with her Canadian husband and their familyin 2000. For more than three decades she worked mainly with small and medium-sized businesses, helping them establish, structure and reshape for growth.
“The diaspora didn’t really exist in the Netherlands. It was too close to home. When you come across the pond here, however, the notion of being Irish is very different ... Canada didn’t dilute my Irish identity. It gave me the distance to understand its value, commercially and culturally.”
In a forerunner of what she was to do later, Gilna helped establish the Irish Chamber of Commerce in Ottawa at the invitation of the then ambassador and says that listening to Irish people abroad over the years gave her an understanding of their desire to contribute to Ireland.
She is very grateful to Canada for giving her the opportunity to build an independent career, build new connections, stay connected to Ireland and to add value between both countries. In this, she is in good company: some 4½ million people in Canada claim some Irish DNA, according to census data.
Asked about the current strains in relations between Canada and the United States, and prime minister Mark Carney ’s desire to form closer relations with the EU, Gilna is characteristically diplomatic. She says that, ultimately, the fundamentally strong historic and good neighbourly relationship between Canada and the United States will endure but that forging closer relations with Europe also makes sense for cultural as well as more obvious economic reasons, given the strong European roots of much of the population.
[ ‘We’re an Irish-Canadian-French household. I’m finally getting some return on my Leaving Cert French’ Opens in new window ]
She and her family have enjoyed life in the Canadian capital, where the climate varies enormously. “It can get into the minus-30s in winter but with blue skies and crisp snow. A calmness comes over us in those months. In the summer we enjoy high temperatures from May to September.
“In Ottawa you can be who you are. You don’t have to blend in and be Canadian, so it’s not a melting pot and that’s a cultural difference between here and other places.”
Canadians can be risk averse and polite. There is a different style of doing business from the way it is done in Ireland, she says. Anyone doing business with Canada also needs to factor in the wide regional divergence between different parts of this vast country.
“In Ireland we operate at a fast pace and the craic comes into everything, as professional and all as we are in our engagement. However, Canadians like to take things a bit slower, and they take time to adapt to our humour and our way of doing business.”
While there are economic opportunities for Irish people wishing to find a home in Canada, she cautions anyone interested in this to do their homework thoroughly in advance, not to underestimate the challenges and, most importantly, “don’t arrive without a job”.

title: Message from the Editor: Ireland’s data centre revolt
description: IT Sunday: Ireland has been an enthusiastic host of data centres, but the story of one Co Waterford village shows there are stirrings of local dissent
content:
Politicians, regulators and technology leaders gathered in Dublin this week for the AI Summit, one of the landmark events of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU.
The questions raised by the acceleration of the technology are real, and potentially existential. For Europe, the prospect of being left behind once more is particularly pressing after years in which the EU’s economic growth has stalled and slipped ever further behind the US and China.
Then there is the looming prospect of mass job displacement and the social dislocation that could follow in its wake. Above all of this hovers the prospect, promoted most vociferously by some AI companies themselves, that these systems are advancing so rapidly that they may soon escape human control and threaten the survival of our species.
Meanwhile, the industry’s seemingly insatiable appetite for ever more computing power is driving a data centre construction boom across the world.
Ireland has been among Europe’s most enthusiastic hosts of those centres. But while the Government argues that their continued construction is essential if Ireland is to retain multinational investment, there are stirrings of local dissent in communities next to proposed sites for new centres.
Kilmeaden in Co Waterford was once known for its eponymous cheese. Now, the site of its defunct dairy plant has been earmarked for a 108-hectare data centre. Cian O’Connell meets the village residents who are following the example of towns in the US and resisting the development.
Minister for Culture Patrick O’Donovan was in the news last week when he took ill at a meeting of EU telecoms ministers in Limerick. It came just hours after he had criticised colleagues for anonymously telling journalists that his illness – O’Donovan has epilepsy – could make it difficult for him to continue as Minister. Jack Horgan-Jones and Pat Leahy look back at a dramatic week .
The severe effects of cuts to aid funding from the United States and elsewhere on Irish agencies working in the developing world – and, as a result, on those they assist – has been under-reported over the past two years. Some of the facts and figures reported by Paul Colgan in his review of the funding crisis , including staff cuts of more than one-third and the closure of country offices, are eye-opening.
Public sector workers in Ireland went on strike last Wednesday. A second stoppage planned for next week has been called off pending talks . In France, meanwhile, a row over education funding has pitted students against state authorities, leading to confrontations on the streets of many cities. Naomi O’Leary, our correspondent in Paris, has a revealing story on an obscure line in French teachers’ payslips and what it tells us about the state of modern France .
In the same section, Derek Scally writes about how Germany is losing patience with Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Keith Duggan in Michigan reports on the remarkable rise of Abdul el-Sayed , who is fighting for a senate seat for the Democrats in the Midwest.
Vincent Browne, a celebrated journalist who edited Magill when the news magazine broke some of the biggest stories of the day, has written a biography of former taoiseach Charles Haughey. Browne was one of the most tenacious journalists in pursuing Haughey in the 1980s, but he befriended him in the years before Haughey’s death – a relationship that Browne draws on in his new book. In a fascinating interview with Colm Keena , Browne concludes that “on the balance of his [Haughey’s] achievements and his depredations, I’m afraid the depredations win”. Keena also asks Browne about his own management style - he had a reputation as an employer for being intimidating and a bully – but Browne is much less keen on talking about that. It’s worth a read.
Patrick Freyne and Nick Bradshaw travelled to Alicante in Spain to report on a week-long holiday with a group of mostly retired Irish tourists, six former Eurovision winners and one Marty Morrissey. Read here to find out what goes on during a “Marty Party” package break.
Orla Poole – a survivor of abuse by paedophile swimming coach George Gibney - spoke with enormous courage outside court on Monday, after her tormentor was sentenced to 15 years in prison. Another brave woman, Karen Leach, suffered similar abuse as a child at the hands of swimming coach Derry O’Rourke. She writes here about the day her happy childhood ended.
Elsewhere in Opinion, David McWilliams points out that the Gaeltacht is dying because its people cannot find houses there ; Rachel O’Dwyer writes about shopping without spending money ; and Pat Leahy explains why some public servants need a pay rise more than others .
There are some strong interviews across the site this weekend, including conversations with Ger Loughnane , David Byrne and Elif Shafak . I also enjoyed Denis Walsh’s piece on the flourishing of GAA comedy and Karl McDonald’s minute-by-minute analysis of Mark Zuckerberg’s unconvincing attempt to drink a pint .
Finally, Irish Times journalists this week secured 33 nominations for the 2026 Irish Journalism Awards in categories ranging from investigations and foreign reporting to video, business journalism and arts criticism. All of that work is made possible by subscribers like you.
We like to hear your views. Feel free to send comments, feedback or suggestions for topics you would like to see covered to feedback@irishtimes.com .

title: Dublin residents protest against rezoning of land owned by John Magnier and JP McManus
description: Councillors previously rejected changing the zoning of sites at St Edmundsbury, Finnstown Castle and Coldcut Road
content:
Dublin residents have protested against a final vote on the controversial rezoning of “ecologically unique” land due to take place on Monday.
A demonstration against the move was held in Lucan , west Dublin, on Saturday, calling on local councillors to vote against the proposal .
The Save St Edmundsbury Protest Committee held a walk to oppose the rezoning of the St Edmundsbury site in the Liffey valley, owned by businessmen John Magnier and JP McManus .
The land is currently zoned as “high amenity” due to its environmental and natural amenity value.
Sites at Finnstown Castle, between Lucan and Adamstown, and at Coldcut Road, south of the Liffey Valley shopping centre, have also been proposed for rezoning.
Committee member and Independent councillor on South Dublin County Council Helen Farrell said it was not about “refusing housing in our area”.
“Rezoning has to happen in some places but the lands at St Edmundsbury are ecologically unique,” she said.
She described the area as a “very ancient landscape and an ancient farmland and the two landscapes kind of work together.
“So there’s a very rich biodiversity and we really want to see these lands saved.”
[ Removal of ‘unconscionable’ housing ban on Magnier and McManus Liffey Valley lands urged Opens in new window ]
Residential rezoning for the area has been proposed on numerous occasions over recent decades but refused.
Farrell believes efforts should be focused on “getting high density housing into the city centre on some of the vacant properties that have laid vacant for decades”.
Dereliction needed to be tackled, she argued, rather than building on “highly fertile agricultural lands in the middle of a food crisis and a climate crisis”.
Councillors previously voted against rezoning the land. Now, protesters are calling on them “to vote against residential rezoning, as they did the last time”, Farrell said.
“We really want the Government to notice that this should be part of the Liffey Valley Park going forward and this is what we should leave for future generations.”
Saturday’s protest walk began outside the main entrance gates at St Edmundsbury and finished at the village green in Lucan.
[ John Magnier and JP McManus could see rich returns if €4m Liffey Valley lands are rezoned Opens in new window ]
The Irish Times previously reported that the council’s chief executive, Colm Ward, had proposed rezoning the three sites, which combined could accommodate more than 1,700 homes.
It followed an edict last summer from Minister for Housing James Browne that all local authorities must provide significant additional land for housing.
More than 1,600 submissions opposed the rezoning of the St Edmundsbury site.

title: US snapshot of Donald Trump’s hunger for adulation that has dragged us to this fraught moment
description: In Doug Mills’ photo, here Trump is in a cozy huddle with his most essential type of staff member
content:
S ometimes a candid photograph captures a moment in a presidency, and the essence of the officeholder, so tellingly that you get a penetrating portrait of an era.
It happened when LBJ ( Lyndon B Johnson ) yanked up his beagle by the ears for photographers and demonstrated his domineering leadership style.
It happened when a photographer captured George W Bush being told, while reading to children in a Florida classroom, that a second plane had hit the World Trade Center. His look of shock raised questions about whether, after his decades of winging it, a parlous rendezvous with destiny might be too much for him to handle.
It happened in 2009 when every living president gathered in the Oval office and Jimmy Carter so obviously kept his distance from Barack Obama, Bill Clinton and both Bushes that his sense of superiority was made clear.
It happened when Obama was photographed bending over in the Oval to let a black child touch his hair, to see if it was the same texture as his own, capturing the historic nature of his election.
It happened again when Doug Mills, the New York Times’ dazzling White House photographer, took a picture Tuesday of president Donald Trump on Marine One with his blond aides/acolytes Katie Zacharia, his wobbly new press secretary, and Natalie Harp, his special assistant for floofing.
Mills took the shot from far away with a long lens, but it bristles with intimacy.
The president is leaning in to talk to the two Ivanka knock-offs, who look like sorority-sister clones, four eyes glued on the man they adore, two fervent smiles glazed with pink lip gloss.
[ Katie Zacharia was fired after failing in the one arena Trump cares about: television Opens in new window ]
It is a snapshot of Trump’s hunger for adulation that has dragged us to this fraught moment in the United States.
He desperately craves being the centre of attention and seeing blind devotion mirrored back at him as that devotion wanes with an increasingly disgusted, exhausted public.
Trump was on a trip, part of a self-affirming odyssey to red states, which seemed to be designed not only to boost his unappetising slate of candidates but also to let him bask in applause from the last fanatical members of his dwindling fan base.
In Mills’ photo, marines are at attention beside the curved open doors of the helicopter, giving the impression that we are peering inside a bubble – at the very moment that Trump’s White House bubble is getting smaller and more ingrown and fractious than ever. Here he is in a cozy huddle with his most essential type of staff member: obedient helpmeets who help construct and perpetuate his absurd alternative reality and paranoid worldview.
Zacharia, the inept propagandist, and Harp, the so-called “human printer”, who trails – and sometimes sprints – behind the president with a portable printer, giving hard copies of soft coverage to Trump, offering him validation for his delusions and lies.
Zacharia reposted Mills’ photo with the caption, “Best President in US History!!!” But it really should have been the classic Henry Kissinger line: “Power is the ultimate aphrodisiac.”
[ Trump puts new Russia sanctions passed by Congress on hold amid deepening row with Ukraine Opens in new window ]
Wags on X had their own captions, imagining Harp thinking homicidal thoughts about Zacharia.
But actually, the two women – scorned by colleagues eager to anonymously trash-talk them – were cloistered on the edge of the playground, clinging to each other and to their orange prophet, who told them to hang in there.
But it didn’t last, and by Friday, he was easing Zacharia out. “Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,” Trump told her, as he later recounted to reporters. Soon after, she got the boot.
They were trying to fight back against their in-house critics. Harp showed Trump the Politico Playbook story Thursday reporting that the president is shopping around for a new chief of staff. It also named the advisers who have cashed in. The right to cash in, in Trump’s eyes, is for him and his family only.
“Trump has bristled at recent reports showing several long-time advisers are profiting from foreign consulting business,” Playbook said, noting that Susie Wiles’ daughter Katie is working for a firm representing Republika Srpska, a pro-Russian Bosnian Serb territory.
The Daily Beast headline about the Wiles report blared: “Natalie Harp Knifes Ice Maiden and Sparks Trump ‘Freakout.’”
Tellingly and perhaps prophetically, Susie Wiles is in Mills’ picture but mostly cut out of the frame. You can see her legs in red pants and the Louis Vuitton bag on her lap.
We can’t see the expression on Wiles’ face, but we know that she is no fan of the two gushing young women in the picture.
Alarmed by Harp’s fixation on the president and her emotionally raw letters to him in 2023, Wiles attempted – in vain – to curb her access. Trump’s decision to appoint Zacharia to a critical job where she was doomed to flounder and likely end up in an “SNL” cold open blindsided Wiles, according to news reports.
Even Trump seemed taken aback by the press gaggle after Zacharia’s debut news conference debacle and when the Times’ Shawn McCreesh, before the president and his aides took off for Alaska, asked Zacharia where she had passed the bar.
“When I moved to China,” she said, as Trump – who described her as an attorney when he announced her appointment – snapped his head around. The story unspooled that she hadn’t passed the bar anywhere.
But by the time they got to Alaska eight hours later, she was beaming at her boss and doing damage control.
(She told a far-right Pizzagate conspiracist in an interview that she wanted to be played on “SNL” by “a Scarlett Johansson-type character.”)
Zacharia tried to fight back on “Hannity,” no doubt assuming she would be in friendly territory.
But she wasn’t. Sean Hannity asked her why she had put up 15 media posts identifying herself as an attorney. She lamely protested that they were “retweets of a title that had been given”. (Mistakes were made.)
Hannity pressed on: “Why didn’t you just say ‘I never practised law’?” and asked about her first news conference, “Why only three questions in 14 minutes?”
Zacharia looked unnerved, as though she had been sandbagged by her foes in the White House.
As his hold on the country seems to be slipping through his pudgy fingers, Trump needs the unqualified love from his blond Praetorian Guard.
Not only do Democrats seem headed for success in the midterms, fuelled by a swell of Americans who see Trump as a crook, enriching himself while costs rise for everyone else, but the president’s inner circle is going up in flames. Aides are turning on one another and sinking in a cauldron of corruption and boneheaded policies.
[ Trump’s new press secretary faces mounting questions over her legal credentials Opens in new window ]
The past week has been a cascade of embarrassing stories: Kimberly Guilfoyle getting iced as ambassador to Greece after a donor revealed that just before her Senate confirmation hearing, she tried to shake him down to pay her $100,000 American Express bill; Trump loyalist Ric Grenell, who was the head of the ill-fated Kennedy Center, accused by Trump loyalist Alina Habba Mildon and her new billionaire husband of misallocating a $5.6 million donation marked for the centre; and our ally Volodymyr Zelenskiy saying he felt betrayed by Trump’s sordid deal with Vladimir Putin over diesel oil and the restricted access to Elon Musk’s Starshield amid Russian bombardment. Trump even had to cancel the nitwit plan of his frat boy Pentagon chief to livestream an execution.
Instead of running the country and dealing with the world he has set on fire, the president is focused on settling petty squabbles and a web of corruption in his incompetent – and dangerous – court.
Doug Mills has proved once again that a picture is worth 1,000 words, or in my case, 1,273.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times

title: Israeli settlers attack European diplomats, French mayor and archbishop in West Bank
description: Settler violence surges during the olive harvest
content:
Israeli settler militants have attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of Cambrai in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank , injuring three people and damaging a car, in the latest violent attempt to prevent Palestinians from harvesting olives on their own land.
Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground on Saturday.
The masked militant shouted “Vive la France” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife, and Vincent Dollmann, archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.
The group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.
Settlers first attacked a group working on the lower slopes of hills near Taybeh. As well as stealing olives, they kicked, abused and assaulted a Palestinian woman in her 70s and beat a man so badly he needed six stitches for a head injury.
Then they approached the diplomats and Badoux, who was in Taybeh for the launch of a twinning agreement with his town in northern France. During the attack, the militants smashed the window of an armoured car belonging to the Belgian mission.
Maxime Prévot, Belgium’s deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs, condemned the violence against Palestinians, foreign diplomats and journalists, and said his country would continue to push for European Union sanctions on settlers.
“Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack,” he said. “This violence cannot be separated from Israel’s illegal settlement policy ... the occupation of the Palestinian territory must end.”
Palestinian residents of Taybeh have lived with years of escalating attacks from Israeli militants, but settlers had never targeted foreign diplomats there, said Fr Bashar Fawadleh, the town’s parish priest.
“What happened today is not an isolated incident. It represents a deeply disturbing escalation in settler violence,” Fawadleh said.
Since the start of the annual olive harvest in late September, Israeli militants have used violence to stop Palestinians bringing in a crop that is economically and culturally vital to their communities.
Since September 27th, settlers have launched more than 170 attacks, Israeli rights group Yesh Din said. They killed at least four people, injured more than 100 and damaged thousands of trees, according to Palestinian authorities.
Even the presence of Israeli activists, diplomats, senior clergy and journalists no longer serves as a deterrence to extreme violence.
[ Why Israel fears settlement sanctions are just the beginning Opens in new window ]
“If such violence can take place before international witnesses, one must ask what protection remains for local families and farmers when those witnesses are no longer present,” Fawadleh said. “No individual should have to risk physical assault simply to harvest olives from their own land.”
On Friday, Israeli militants attacked and severely injured Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine as she reported on the harvest in the town of Abu Falah. She required surgery on Saturday morning and is now in “moderate” condition, according to a spokesperson for Israel’s Beilinson hospital where she is being treated.
US secretary ⁠of ​state Marco Rubio said on Saturday that the United States wants Israel ⁠to do more to deter attacks committed by settlers. “We’re very disturbed by those images and ⁠what we’re seeing,” Rubio said. “We’ve asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack ⁠down on that stuff.”
Israel had already severely restricted the harvest this year by imposing new rules barring Palestinians from trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.
Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, condemned the attacks and said police had opened an investigation. He said foreign diplomats risked attacks from Israeli civilians if they travelled in the occupied West Bank without military co-ordination.
Demanding diplomats give advance notification of travel violates both diplomatic conventions and international law, said one western diplomatic source who asked not to be named.
“Israel is in charge of security in Area B and C [the majority of the West Bank], so is obliged to assure safety there for all,” the source said.
A culture of near total impunity for Israeli violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has prompted former prime minister Ehud Olmert to call for the International Criminal Court to intervene.
[ Opinion: Israel’s settlement policy is designed to bury the idea of a two-state solution Opens in new window ]
Gadi Eisenkot, an opposition politician and former general hoping to unseat prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu in elections to be held later this month, described the attack as “Jewish terror under the auspices of the Israeli government”.
Eisenkot backs Jewish Israeli expansion in occupied Palestine but wants militant violence brought under control because the attackers are “harming the settlement enterprise in [the West Bank] and national security”. – Guardian

title: Rachel O'Dwyer: A food delivery site that promises to deliver no food? At first, I didn’t see the appeal
description: It’s bleak when you realise that one of your favourite pastimes is the unrequited scroll, maybe even a little perverse
content:
O ne of the greatest pleasures in my middle-aged life is a Friday takeaway , endlessly debating pizza toppings and portion sizes before buying way too much, watching the little figure bike over the virtual map to our door, only to inevitably get lost in the lane behind our house and need rescuing.
When I heard about a site that allows users to experience the pleasure of ordering without the cost or calories or, well, delivery of anything yummy for dinner, I could not see the appeal. These are so-called dopamine sites, named for the brain chemical associated with reward seeking. Even the name “Food Never Comes” caused a neurological flare of whatever the opposite of dopamine is – deprivation? hanger? – in my hypothalamus.
The trend began in South Korea, where youngsters facing soaring living costs turned to virtual window shopping for the thrill of adding to cart and checking out – minus the bills or buyer’s remorse. Dopamine is released when we expect something – less so when we actually get it. The theory is that clicking a “buy” button – even a fake buy button, even when the wished-for item fails to materialise – yields the same rush as a real transaction. “Craving a getaway too?” a banner ad reads, “Trip never leaves. Book the trip, skip the airport”.
Despite my initial recoil, I have to admit this feels familiar. I’ve come home late and scrolled Deliveroo while eating cereal, just for the giddy notion of summoning my heart’s desire to my door at 1am. Only last night, while my husband read a biography of John McGahern like a good example, I drifted around on Vinted, not even looking for any specific item but looking for an item specific enough to fix my desire to. It’s bleak when you realise that one of your favourite pastimes is the unrequited scroll, maybe even a little perverse, like swiping through streaming apps for 28 minutes instead of watching a 28-minute show; suddenly deferred choice becomes its own empty brand of entertainment.
