I wonder if this shopping that isn’t shopping is all that new? Walter Benjamin wrote about the 19th-century glass shopping arcades, where glamorous Parisians turned out to browse and let their attention drift from stall to stall. To be modern was to enter a capitalist dreamworld, a kind of aimless scrolling with your feet. Shopping has always involved a degree of fantasy, where the object – a new dress or a car – allows us to dream about the person we might become if we only possess it. That’s where much of the pleasure lies. But as I scroll Vinted or the “new in” section of Cos, I wonder if this imaginative hedonism is now less about a specific want than the endless possibility of finding something worth wanting, less a daydream than something that threatens to colonise my attention.
[ Ireland is richer and spending more than 30 years ago but is it making us happy? Opens in new window ]
The internet would say I am deficient in dopamine. Or maybe addicted to dopamine? One of those. One reformed shopaholic I follow on YouTube embraced a minimalist lifestyle several years back. Last week I cleaned my downstairs loo while she spoke about decluttering, before revealing that this too was problematic, as tossing out her old stuff gave her the same high as buying something new. Not shopping, it turns out, can also be addictive. We’re encouraged to frame over-consumption as a dopamine problem, to be remedied by deinfluencers, detoxes, no-spends, Marie Kondo-style clear-outs and even something called “Project Pan” (the revolutionary idea of using up your toiletries before buying more). And now it seems, dopamine shopping is another solution – fantasy retail that cures our urge to shop by allowing us to keep on shopping.
So what are fake sites like Food Never Comes supposed to teach us about real consumption, I wonder, with my finger hovering over a bibimbap, which sits next to some AI slop tentacles labelled “ribs” you could not pay me to eat.
Some of the simulation sites are designed as critique. On Fakehaul, a Microsoft developer, Jack Yang, has built a Temu version of Temu in response to a friend who struggled with impulse spending. Still, I happily add an aromatherapy diffuser and a chilled neck pillow to my imaginary cart. If there’s a bigger lesson, it’s drowned out by the call of stuff. On the checkout page I click on the “place order” button. I am not charged $287.22. I get a fake reference number and watch as my fake items cycle rapidly from an imaginary warehouse, to in transit, to my unspecified delivery address. The whole process, from browsing to not delivery, takes 10 minutes. I didn’t waste money or accumulate cheap things that will end up in landfill, but I wasted data and attention.
[ ‘We’re living in a capitalist hellscape’: The people learning about money on social media Opens in new window ]
Can fake consumption really critique capitalism? I don’t think so. I’m glad I’m not buying real stuff and that Ivan, the DPD driver I’m on first name terms with, is getting a break. But a site for simulated binge scrolling feels less like an incisive critique and more like shopping taken to its extreme, a bleak prospect where our fantasies, desires and leisure have become about what we might consume. We’re still dreaming about stuff we probably don’t need, or the life we don’t have instead of living right now. I’m reminded of a fintech event I attended 10 years ago. A game developer there told me about a failed video game (“for girls!”) where the player could “pretend” to shop. “But it was a stupid idea”, he said, “because women can do that online whenever they feel like adding stuff to a cart.” I can’t help suspecting that I play this game on a regular basis. And I realise what I really want isn’t to be someone who consumes less, but someone who wants less and spends her time better.

title: Opinion: There has been a seismic shift in the way drugs gangs intimidate their victims
description: We can’t allow parts of the country to become no-go areas by the design of drug gangs
content:
I have been working in the area of drug addiction and drug-related intimidation for 30 years within communities across Dublin. The escalation of violence we see now is oceans apart from the ways criminals sorted their differences in the past. There has been a frightening shift in recent times, in which petrol bombs, arson attacks and threats have become the norm; and innocent people and extended family members are being treated as leverage in the violent and intimidating enforcement of sometimes small drug debts.
The ease with which innocent families become embroiled in drug debts is terrifying. A young person gets drugs on credit, or takes some to sell and – for whatever reason – can’t repay the debt. Or they may be asked to sell drugs to pay for their habit. In some cases, a young person has taken some drugs to sell to feed their own habit, and the drugs are subsequently stolen – usually by another young person within the same drugs gang. And then a more senior criminal comes knocking at the door looking for their drugs and their money, and the young person has neither. The threats and intimidation start. Suddenly the whole family is involved.
Parents, grandparents, brothers, sisters, cousins, aunts and uncles are all now apparently fair game when it comes to the enforcement of drug debts. These families face an impossible demand: pay off the debt and support the criminal gang or live in terror of the consequences.
Physical beatings – people with black eyes and other injuries – have always been part of the picture. Now petrol bombs and arson attacks are part of it too, usually intended as intimidation.
The Irish Times reported this week that data gathered from 14 local authorities nationwide revealed there were 113 arson attacks on council properties in the past five years, including 50 in the past year alone. The four local authorities in Dublin had recorded 59 attacks since 2022, 35 of those last year.
Just this week a conference in Portlaoise heard that there were more than 1,000 incidents of drug-related intimidation reported in a two-year period. And those are just the reported instances. Most debts involved ranged from €1,000 to €5,000, though 39 incidents related to amounts of more than €20,000.
In parallel to the physical attacks and arson, social media is increasingly being used as a tool of intimidation. Beatings – and, in some horrifying cases, sexual violence – are carried out and videoed to be deployed as blackmail and humiliation, with the threat that they will be passed around on texting apps or posted to social media. Or young people are threatened with their drug habit being exposed to their family if they fail to pay back a debt, or refuse to commit criminal acts on command by way of repayment. It’s a modern-day form of debt bondage.
In some ways, even more distressing than the bruises or evidence of violence is the shock, trauma, isolation and sheer terror of people who are forced into a prolonged silent battle with their own, or a family member’s, drug dealer. Many young people feel they cannot reach out to family members or trusted adults for fear of reprisal or further violence. They often feel they have no choice but to comply with the orders they are given by the dealers and their cronies.
And it’s not exclusively the very young or people in disadvantaged areas who get caught up in this. In one case I worked with recently, a middle-class man in his 30s with a good job and a cocaine addiction got into debt. He was summoned to a meeting with his dealer, where he was threatened with a gun. He ended up moving out of the family home to try to protect his elderly parents. Ultimately his sister used her savings to repay his debt.
In that sense, he was one of the lucky ones. Most of the young people I meet through my work don’t have those kind of resources – either financial or someone they feel able to ask for help.
Young people’s brains – particularly young males – have underdeveloped impulse control and a propensity to risk-taking. Most young people will thankfully age out of risky behaviours without harming themselves or their community. But for young people who find themselves moving in a circle where drug-taking is the norm, there is a risk they will get involved in drugs and then in antisocial behaviour and intimidation. Couple that with the psychological and physiological grip drugs can have on a person, and their underdeveloped critical thinking skills, and it becomes a perfect storm.
Wherever there are drugs, there is drug-related intimidation – not just in big cities, but in every small town and village in Ireland. We need much more than a policing response to deal with this. We need immediate crisis protocols that include psychological first aid and long-term safeguarding – particularly in schools. Teachers are well placed to observe sudden absenteeism, behavioural shifts that might suggest addiction, or unexplained designer clothes. In a perfect world, these red flags should trigger a multi-agency response, but this doesn’t always happen at a time of overstretched resources.
We need immediate interruption to the violence that we see damaging community cohesion. In some parts of the country, criminal gangs have what we call “a coercive hold” over entire areas. This can’t be broken by policing alone, although as a matter of urgency, violent actors must be made accountable. Periods in custody need to be meaningful and rehabilitative.
Every Garda station has a dedicated member to support victims of drug-related intimidation. Ultimately people need to feel secure that action will be taken and they will be protected if they reach out for help. This means An Garda Síochána need to have the time and resources to provide the confidential supports and guidance needed by targets of drugs-related intimidation at the most terrifying and vulnerable time of their lives.
We need to further invest in local community centres, second-chance education, addiction services, youth clubs and sporting facilities to create safe havens for families, children and communities.
Most of all, we can’t just resign ourselves to a situation where parts of the country are becoming no-go areas by the design of drug gangs.
Trina O’Connor is a criminologist and community activist with master’s degrees in criminology from Dublin Institute of Technology and Maynooth University

title: Mark Zuckerberg drinks pint wrong, leaving his Irish reputation in tatters
description: Plus: Stamp duty slip-ups, literature on the high seas and a Star Wars-related accident
content:
Despite being a strong supporter of the local GAA , Mark Zuckerberg took some damage to his position as an honorary Irishman this week after appearing to drink a pint of Guinness wrong.
Joining Limerick billionaire John Collison in a Two Johnnies-style fake pub he uses to host a tech chatshow, Zuckerberg took what might have been his first ever sips of the national beverage. As Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang described asking his AI agent to source “increasingly obscure teas”, a clip captured the Facebook founder reacting to the taste by making what one might describe as “a face”, taking several seconds to swallow.
“Why did he chew it?” asked one observer, while others suggested that he may accidentally have inhaled a mouthful of foam, a hazard for the inexperienced. A blow to his reputation, certainly.
Cheeky Pint is back! Mark Zuckerberg @finkd and Alexandr Wang @alexandr_wang came to the pub to discuss their new frontier model, Muse Wonder. 00:00:24 Muse’s breakout use cases 00:07:28 The model is the product 00:14:35 Muse Wonder 00:24:56 How frontier models are built… pic.twitter.com/X3lrKFIaPs
It’s not compulsory to drink Guinness performatively any time you’re in public with an Irishman, but it does seem to help. How did Zuckerberg compare with other very famous people offered the chance?
He performed better than Queen Elizabeth II, who drank none, reacting to the pint presented to her at the Storehouse in 2011 with the same passive quarter-smile she might have given to a youth choir, but fared far worse than Barack Obama, who “gave it a right wallop” in Moneygall the same year , to a chorus of local-political yehows.
Overheard’s favourite effort is that of former UN secretary general Ban Ki-moon, who appeared to appreciate his Guinness at Brogan’s, near the Olympia Theatre in Dublin, in 2015: a series of images capturing the pintman’s progress remain on the official United Nations website .
None of these people had a house in Waterford, however, and the standards are higher for Zuckerberg in his new guise as a possible JP McManus-style bazooka of funding for local hurlers.
Overheard scanned the entire two-hour video to seek more information, and neither Zuckerberg nor Wang come close to matching Collison’s pace: the native son’s glass is totally empty around minute 36, with the Meta execs still nursing glasses half full.
The full video does show the contents of Zuckerberg’s pint continuing to diminish, however, and, after being replaced with a new one, his final tally appears to be around 1.4 pints. As thirsty as a data centre, that fellah.
Zuckerberg paid €51,171,155 for Strancally Castle in Co Waterford, a price he could afford 5,100 times over, according to the latest estimate of his net worth. But things aren’t as simple for the Land Development Agency , tasked with turning taxpayer money into taxpayer housing as efficiently as possible.
It’s the dreaded red tape to blame, as the agency’s annual report lays out.
At two sites – Clonmore in Cork and Hollystown in west Dublin – sods were turned, homes built, ribbons cut and members of the public housed, all roughly according to plan.
Delays, cursed delays. All things being equal, the agency would have acquired the houses from builder partners and resold them in time to get the stamp duty back under a recently added legal provision to let providers of “affordable dwelling purchase arrangements” do their work. The cost would have been zero.
But there is a time bar of a year applied to the refund, and the agency crashed into it. At Clonmore, closing the sale of the homes was delayed in 21 of 26 cases. It was left on the hook for €646,789.
Worse was the situation in Hollystown, where it got landed with a €2,751,982 stamp duty bill. It was relying on reclaiming this amount to make the development profitable, but time waits for no State agency, and it wound up being booked as a €1,888,107 loss.
Handily, the stamp duty is paid to the exchequer, so the taxpayer makes out okay.
When it comes to military might, some of Ireland’s neighbours wouldn’t mind if the Government pumped more resources into the defence of Europe’s watery Atlantic fringe. But in soft power terms, we dominate as ever.
The British might have sent HMS Invincible to the Falklands, but we rule the waves with the LÉ William Butler Yeats, the LÉ George Bernard Shaw, the LÉ Samuel Beckett and the LÉ James Joyce. Who needs dazzle camouflage when you have literary modernism?
Whose idea was all this? That of Vice Admiral Mark Mellett, former chief of staff of the Defence Forces and head of the Naval Service , whose forthcoming book Blue Heart recounts bringing the proposal to then minister for defence Alan Shatter in 2012.
“My reasoning was simple,” he said. “Wherever these ships operated, and whenever their names were broadcast over maritime channels, their Irish identity would be unmistakable. The names themselves became a force multiplier for Irish sovereignty, echoing hundreds of nautical miles wherever they were called.”
The eagle-eyed will note that all four vessels named before the policy was reversed were dedicated to blokes, a strategic weakness that might be picked up on by feminist critics patrolling the Rockall Bank area. Not the fault of Mellett.
“Had I my way,” he notes, “names like ... Maeve Binchy would have been fitting.”
Back on dry land, author Colm Tóibín has been having a good time of it lately. Not long after the launch of an An Post stamp commemorating his novel Brooklyn, he was receiving an honorary degree from the 736-year-old University of Macerata in Italy this week, an event that featured someone delivering something called a “laudatio”.
In the midst of all the institutional acclaim, however, he made a misstep. Writer Doireann Ní Ghríofa recounted on her Instagram account an incident that took place as she prepared for an appearance on The Comfort Zone, a culture discussion programme cohosted by Tóibín with presenter Luke Clancy on Lyric FM.
Ní Ghríofa, author of the award-winning Ghost in the Throat and this year’s Said the Dead, suggested “one of my favourite films” to chew over: Phantom Thread, a 2017 film starring Daniel Day-Lewis as a couture tailor whose intense relationship with his muse, Vicky Krieps, gets him into trouble. Acclaimed as one of the best films of the 21st century so far, critics tend to reach for words such as “poignant” and “deft” to describe it.
What did Tóibín think? Hard to know: he accidentally watched The Phantom Menace, the divisive 1999 reboot of the Star Wars franchise featuring double-lightsabered antagonist Darth Maul and Jamaican-coded reptile Jar Jar Binks.

title: My lawn is full of mushrooms. Do they pose a health risk?
description: The recent warm, damp weather has provided ideal conditions for their growth
content:
We have a city centre garden with a small area of grass. We chopped down an old tree a few years ago in the middle of the lawn and the grass has since grown over the stump. Last autumn we noticed some mushrooms growing where the tree had been, which we removed once by hand before mowing the grass. This year the lawn is full of various mushrooms, which we’ve removed several times but keep coming back. It’s usually a play area for our young children. Do they pose any health risk, and is there anything we can do to stop them growing? C Kenny, Dublin
You’re right to be cautious about your young children playing very close to any kind of wild fungi as there’s always a risk of them unknowingly putting them in their mouths, potentially resulting in serious illness or worse. Some fungal species contain poisonous chemicals that can also be accidentally transferred by touch to the mouth, while the spores of others can act as irritants to the lungs.
While it’s not unusual to see wild mushrooms popping up overnight in gardens at this time of year, the recent warm, damp weather has provided ideal conditions for their growth. From what you’ve described, it sounds as if those appearing on your lawn are feeding on the decaying remains of the tree you cut down. So as its stump and underground root system rots away over the next few years, the number of mushrooms appearing each autumn is likely to also decline.
Unless, that is, you’re unlucky enough to have honey fungus (Armillaria ) in your garden, a destructive fungal disease for which there’s no cure. Its honey-coloured mushrooms or fruiting bodies typically appear in dense clusters near the base of affected plants in late summer and autumn and are quite easy to identify, with a distinctive ring around the stem (see rhs.org.uk for a detailed description, as well as the app ShroomID). The tree you cut down was an old one, so I’m wondering if it was also sickly, in which case this fungus may possibly have been the culprit. Sometimes seen in old, established gardens, honey fungus can leapfrog underground from one plant another, making it almost impossible to control.
Let’s assume, however, that your garden’s mushrooms are not a symptom of honey fungus, and are instead one or more of the numerous other species of wild mushrooms that Ireland is home to. Even so, there’s not a huge amount you can do to prevent them appearing.
Scarifying the lawn with a rake to remove any dead thatch and then aerating it by spiking it with the tines of a garden fork may help a little if the ground is inclined to be poorly drained. Keeping your lawn quite tightly mown will also help. But none of these will remove the underground fungal network or mycelium from producing the mushrooms that you’re seeing, and you’ll need to continue to handpick (wear gloves) and then carefully dispose of any that you find to ensure your lawn is safe for your young children to use.
If it’s any small consolation, wild mushrooms can appear on the best-kept lawns and are a sign of soil health and biodiversity.

title: ‘Some of what she told me, she never told anyone’: Finding George Gibney and the long pursuit of justice
description: Mark Horgan’s podcast, co-produced with Ciarán Cassidy, was instrumental in the opening of a new investigation into the now-jailed former swimming coach
content:
W hen justice finally came for the paedophile George Gibney , it arrived as a stark and lonely thing. Since his extradition from the United States, Gibney has had no prison visits, and during his trial he had no character references. The 78-year-old was sentenced on Monday for the sexual abuse of four girls in the 1970s and 1980s, and was wheeled out of the courtroom by a member of the Garda, taken by wheelchair to begin his 15½ years in prison.
The scene on the steps outside the court was a vivid, bustling contrast. Complainant Orla Poole waived her anonymity and stood before the media wearing bright, optimistic clothes, her hair a brilliant auburn. She read a statement encouraging other victims to come forward, assuring them they are not alone.
Nor was Orla Poole. Ber Carley, Tric Kearney and Chalkie White stood with her, more than 30 years after their case against Gibney foundered. Louise Kennedy, daughter of another victim, Lorraine Kennedy, stood there too. Close by were the journalists who did so much to expose the truth about Gibney earlier, Johnny Watterson and Justine McCarthy .
Standing there too was the man who helped bring all of these people together: Mark Horgan.
Horgan presented and co-produced with Ciarán Cassidy the podcast series Where is George Gibney?, which revived national interest and kindled international attention to the story of Gibney, the celebrity swimming coach who disappeared in 1994 after he was granted a Supreme Court injunction preventing the DPP from prosecuting him for the alleged sexual abuse of children.
[ ‘He needs to die in prison’: Survivor of George Gibney child sex abuse reacts to sentencing Opens in new window ]
Few individual pieces of journalism in Irish history can match the podcast’s reach and impact. It is among the BBC’s most successful limited series ever, having been downloaded more than six million times, while Horgan and Cassidy successfully answered their titular question, finding Gibney living in Florida under an alias, John. Once the podcast was broadcast, however, more victims came forward, which led to a new Garda investigation into Gibney and culminated with Monday’s scene on the steps of Dublin’s Circuit Criminal Court.
“To go all the way to where it has, to a woman that came forward on the basis of the podcast standing at the top of the steps of the court with the people we spoke with for the podcast, surrounded by the media, that’s out of this world,” says Horgan.
Horgan is a co-founder and producer of the Second Captains podcast, and following their coverage of abuse cases involving football coach Barry Bennell in the UK and American gymnastics coach Larry Nassar , he turned his attention to the story of Gibney, believing it to be an Irish story with international resonance.
His ambition was to revisit the story in-depth and produce a series that could stand along with any other podcast in the world. He recruited film-maker Cassidy, whose editing qualities, says Horgan, are as good as anyone he knows. Horgan also wanted to partner with an international broadcaster, and so he approached a BBC producer, Dylan Haskins, with the idea. Haskins was enthusiastic, and following a pitch, the commissioning editor of BBC Sounds, Jason Phipps, was fully on board.
[ Where is George Gibney? - Mark Horgan on his quest to find out Opens in new window ]
The first time Horgan and Cassidy pressed the record button was while sitting in a rental car in Florida, outside a house in which they believed Gibney to be living. Evin Daly, a US-based child welfare advocate who remained attuned to the Gibney story throughout the 2010s, tipped Horgan and Cassidy off to this location. Before landing in the US, Horgan and Cassidy phoned local police to tell them what they were doing, while they had looked at images on Google Maps to decide the best location from which to observe the house. They did all of this research at home, fearing that asking too many questions on the ground may alert Gibney, whom they believed to be a flight risk.
Their first task was to confirm they had in fact tracked down Gibney. On their very first day a car emerged from the garage adjoining the house, which Horgan and Cassidy tracked on its way to a supermarket. They followed from a distance but noticed the set of rosary beads hanging from the rear-view mirror. They parked up, and when they saw Gibney emerge from the supermarket, Horgan got out of the rental car and walked in Gibney’s direction, holding his phone close to his face while furtively photographing Gibney as he walked by.
The photographs confirmed they were staking out the right man. From there Horgan and Cassidy hoped to establish Gibney’s daily routine, seeking to ascertain what he did and where he went, and whether he had access to children. Gibney, however, hardly left the house. The rental car was, meanwhile, drawing the attention of neighbours, who began approaching Horgan and Cassidy to ask questions. They changed their rental car and parked elsewhere, near the entrance to the housing estate, fearing the neighbours might alert Gibney to the stakeout and allow him to disappear again. Horgan needed to present Gibney with an interview request as a right of reply, but the BBC’s editorial guidance precluded him from knocking on the front door, given laws in Florida give strong weighting to privacy along with the right to bear arms.
It was on their final day, with hopes fading and suitcases packed into the rental car, that Gibney emerged from the house. Horgan and Cassidy trailed Gibney to another supermarket, at which point Horgan caught his breath and made his move. With his microphone recording, Horgan calmly referred to him by his alias, John, and then explained what he had been doing, asking whether he wished to conduct an interview as a right of reply. Gibney, startled, said nothing.
“We never wanted just a ‘gotcha’ moment,” says Horgan. “It was about finding him, which we did, but it wasn’t really about him. It was about everyone else who was connected to him. His silence was extremely telling and extremely powerful, when compared to the guy that talked for 20 years. I am glad we were able to capture that moment.”
[ A shameless risk-taker and predator: How George Gibney groomed children Opens in new window ]
The first time Horgan would hear Gibney’s voice was more than five years later, when Gibney faced a sample charge from each of the four complainants in an Irish court. Gibney said “Not guilty” four times with his hands joined in prayer, wrapped by rosary beads. (Gibney ultimately pleaded guilty to five counts of indecent assault, and was subsequently convicted of a further 39 counts of indecent assault and one count of attempted rape of children.)
That Horgan ultimately heard Gibney’s voice at all is attributable to the impact of the podcast. Among the victims to contact him after its broadcast was Orla Poole. She and Horgan exchanged emails and then phone calls, usually at around 10pm Irish time, with Orla based on the west coast of the United States.
“It was the most upset I’ve ever heard anybody on any phone call I’ve ever had in my life,” says Horgan. “It was a mixture of extreme anger and fury, but also just tears. She later told me that some of what she told me, she never told anyone in her life.”
They spoke for months, and eventually she agreed to speak on the record for a subsequent podcast episode, initially under a pseudonym. She also proceeded with a criminal complaint against Gibney.
When asked why the podcast series was so successful in encouraging other victims to come forward, Horgan points to a coalition of factors. The testimonies of Ber Carley, Tric Kearney and Chalkie White were the most important, he says, and not only their bravery in detailing the horrors of their experience.
“They were just incredible talkers, people found that highly affecting,” says Horgan. “They also have lives full of love, of success, whether that be from a family perspective or just from a professional perspective. They’ve come forward and they’re survivors, but he hasn’t ruined them or ruined their lives. I feel like there is a sense that ‘Okay, well, maybe it’s okay to be a survivor, I’m not going to be pitied or I’m not going to be put in a box, or feel like I’m damaged. I can still have some power in this moment.’”
The podcast format was vital too, with no limit to the time and space available for the survivors’ stories to be told. The limited technological demands of a podcast without a visual element helped too – the microphones are less intrusive, and Horgan could conduct everything as a one-on-one conversation.
Horgan, meanwhile, found himself drawn into the trial. While on holiday in Spain with his family earlier this year, he took a call from the Garda, explaining that Gibney’s defence had requested he hand over any and all emails, WhatsApp messages, call recordings, interviews, and notes that passed between him and the complainants in connection with the podcast. He said he wouldn’t do so, and subsequently sought legal advice before sending a confirmation letter, explaining that he is “fiercely protective of the obligations I owe to people who spoke to me as part of my investigation, and that it’s not something that I can give up voluntarily”.
The judge subsequently rejected the defence counsel’s request for the communication, and it was not handed over.
“The idea that those early conversations with Orla, or any notes that I’d taken in those conversations or the emails that we shared, that they’d have to be handed over, is such an astonishing invasion of privacy,” says Horgan.
The complainants were requested to hand over notes from counselling sessions – the Government is currently working on reforms to restrict their use in future cases.
“The idea that you don’t hand over medical notes but you’re forced to hand over something like counselling notes is beyond belief,” says Horgan, adding that it “shook confidence” as the complainants endured the challenges of going to trial.
Horgan describes the experience for the complainants as like walking a tightrope. They could not, for instance, reference any other case or incident involving Gibney under cross-examination, lest it lead to the collapse of the trial. (After all of the evidence was presented, the judge told the jury that they were free to draw inferences from the consistency of the evidence presented by the four complainants if they believed them to be truthful and their evidence independent.)
“Some of the exchanges were pretty extraordinary, and it was incredible how they were able to just keep their clarity under the sort of pressure that they were,” says Horgan. He reads from his notes and recounts a scene in which Orla Poole is being cross-examined by Gibney’s legal team, who said to her that there was never any “indecency or molestation” on their client’s part.
“She snapped back, ‘You’re trying to say that I’m lying. Is that what you’re saying?’
“There was a brief pause and the counsel said, ‘Yes.’
“And Orla just stared at him and said, ‘Well I’m not.’”
Horgan says one of the complainants found the trial process extremely difficult, especially the media coverage, which so starkly recorded the nature of her abuse.
“The press have a duty to do that, because it’s really not sugarcoating the depth of the crimes, but it was really difficult for them to tell their stories and then also hear the tap-tap-tap of a laptop,” says Horgan. “I think there’s also a duty there to outline more specifically about what the media do on those days, how this is going to be covered, the reasons why it’s covered the way it is: those sorts of specifics, because it’s a difficult thing. It’s a really sensitive moment in their lives, and they deserve the most privacy to whatever level they can.”
Orla Poole turned to face Gibney directly as she read her victim impact statement, telling him “I’m free to leave today, and you will always be known as a convicted, serial paedophile”, and walked past him on the way out. Ber Carley and Tric Kearney, meanwhile, went to the pretrial hearings with Horgan and eyeballed Gibney. When he smiled back at them, Tric mouthed at him, “F**k you.”
“That was important for them,” says Horgan, “to dress in bright colours and to eyeball him and say, ‘We’re still here.’”
There is one other factor underpinning the podcast’s extraordinary impact: it was heard in 2020s Ireland.
[ A shameless risk-taker and predator: How George Gibney groomed children Opens in new window ]
“Gibney was completely exposed, facing people, sitting in the wheelchair,” says Horgan, recalling the trial. “He didn’t defend himself, he stayed silent. It was striking to see all that love and then on the other side, somebody who was just pathetic and alone and who knows that Ireland today doesn’t pay heed to rosary beads; doesn’t pay heed to clasped, praying hands. It was a younger jury, and I don’t think Ireland listens to that sort of stuff any more.”
There are plans for a follow-up episode with the BBC to ensure all listeners everywhere are made aware of the answer to the question: where is George Gibney? He is where he has long, long deserved to be.

title: Irish health service exceeded agency staff budget by over €250m
description: Employees hired via agencies can cost about 40 per cent more than directly employed staff, HSE tells PAC
content:
The health service spent more than €250 million on higher-cost temporary staff provided through agencies than the amount set out in its official budget in the first eight months of the year, a new internal Health Service Executive report shows.
The HSE’s cost and productivity oversight group report, dated September 25th, says €522 million had been spent on agency staff by the end of August. The budget for agency personnel for the period had been set at €272 million.
The report shows spending on staff overtime was about €52 million higher than the official budgetary figure. However, the bill for staff who were directly employed was about €220 million less than the €7.29 billion provided for in the health service budget to the end of August.
The HSE told the Dáil Public Accounts Committee in September that an employee provided through an agency can cost about 40 per cent more than a conventionally-recruited staff member.
The oversight group’s report says that by the end of August the HSE had a financial deficit of just under €660 million.
This was made up of an overspend on pay of €172.5 million, a deficit on non-pay expenditure of €423.6 million and a shortfall in income of €63.2 million.
Within Government there are concerns the overall HSE deficit could hit €1 billion by the end of the year.
The report indicates the health service is experiencing a significant reduction in income as a result of the abolition of private medical practice in public hospitals. Under changes introduced as part of the Sláintecare health reforms, consultants who had signed up to the public-only contract – which offered higher salaries – could not see fee-paying patients from the beginning of this year.
Previously hospitals as well as doctors received payments in respect of private patients treated in public facilities.
[ How can runaway spending in the health service be reined in? Opens in new window ]
“Income remains a challenge, driven by reduced income from private consultant work as a result of public-only consultant contract implementation. Expected income from private consultant activity is behind August year-to-date budget (€99.0 million/44.2 per cent variance) and total such income for August year-to-date is approximately €91 million lower than the same period in 2025,” the report says.
The report maintains that demand for care in hospitals is also significantly higher than set out in the HSE’s national service plan (NSP) for the year.
“Continued demand growth [above NSP levels] is evident across urgent and emergency care. Over 1.1 million people attended emergency departments by August, representing a 7.2 per cent increase on last year and 4.7 per cent more than the NSP plan allowed for.”
“Admission including over [age] 75-plus remain high year on year.”
The report also says the HSE spent €27 million more than anticipated in its budget to provide what is known as surge capacity to prevent patients having to be treated on trolleys.
“Total surge capacity of 124,288 has been utilised August year-to-date. This is 44.1 per cent more than last year and is necessary to keep patients off trolleys. The incremental costs associated with this are estimated to be €27 million higher than last year.
“Demand has also outpaced targets in other areas such as cancer care and home support (August year-to-date). Demand has risen this year across symptomatic breast and rapid lung clinics with activity running 19.5 per cent and 23.4 per cent above NSP targets respectively. The number of patients having completed radical radiotherapy treatment is 17.5 per cent above the NSP target.”

title: ‘My partner and I have a near-perfect relationship but we are at odds on the question of living together’
description: Ask Roe: ‘With this single issue there doesn’t appear to be any compromise’
content:
We are a couple in our 50s and have been together for two years. We have a beautiful relationship. We love each other, we have fun, we consider each other in almost all aspects of our lives. We live on opposite sides of the country from each other. We see each other every week, sometimes for the weekend and sometimes during the week. We both work full time and have busy lives. We are both divorced and have grown-up children who have left home. The problem is that one of us wants us to eventually live together and the other doesn’t. We are usually very good at compromise and resolving problems between us but with this issue there doesn’t appear to be any compromise. We either live together or don’t. The one (she) who wants to live together sees this as the natural progression of a relationship and important for feeling safe and secure and fully wanted. They feel that a person isn’t “all in” in the relationship if they don’t share their lives fully. They feel very strongly about this and feel rejected by the other person, who can’t even see living together as a possibility in the future. The other person (he) doesn’t feel that living together is important and prefers living alone. They spent 20 years living with someone in a difficult relationship and they now like the peace and autonomy of living by themselves. They can’t see themselves ever living together full time. We have discussed this problem at length and are at an impasse. Neither of us is willing to compromise on this issue but equally neither of us wants to end what is otherwise a near-perfect relationship. Can you help?
Your relationship sounds beautiful. You found each other after other marriages, other lifetimes, you love each other’s company, you have fun, you care deeply for each other and work through conflicts with admiration, consideration and respect. That’s all wonderful, so let’s not lose sight of how gorgeous and important that is as we dive into your question. You have come up against an issue. That doesn’t invalidate everything else that makes your connection wonderful.
It’s clear from your letter that living together isn’t just about the act of cohabitating. It’s become hugely symbolic for both of you. For one partner it’s about feeling chosen, feeling safe, feeling like the commitment between you both is firm and enacted daily. For the other, living independently is about having autonomy, about enjoying personal space for the first time in maybe decades, about actively choosing each other rather than simply being forced to be around each other through your environment.
It’s important to note that neither of these desires is wrong or unreasonable. And it’s also worth exploring the difference between what each of you actually need, and where you’re projecting certain ideas about love and relationships on to this question of living together, when they’re not actually innately true or necessarily applicable to your connection.
For the partner who wants to live together, it’s worth asking whether you actually believe that love has to involve living together. It’s a societal norm for many couples, sure – but not all. Increasingly, the Living Apart Together movement has more devotees, of long-term couples living separately while remaining committed to each other. So do you genuinely believe love and commitment can’t exist outside that? Do you believe that living together automatically equates to love and commitment and lifelong happiness? (I’m guessing your previous marriage has given you at least some reason to question that logic, no?) Are you unduly worried about other people’s opinions? Are you holding on to narratives about what love should look like, instead of trusting the love that is being offered to you, in a slightly less traditional configuration?
And for the partner who doesn’t want to live together, I think it’s very important to separate your feelings about living together generally from your past experience of living with your ex. Living in a house with someone unhappily while also raising children is not the same as living together happily with one person, and it’s not fair to your current partner to conflate the two. Is it not possible to imagine living together while consciously prioritising your needs, so that you have more space than you previously had, so that your boundaries are respected, so that you can prioritise peace and autonomy? Think about where you’re projecting the past on to this relationship, rather than genuinely trying to imagine a future with your partner.
[ ‘My brother-in-law wants to move in with us but I don’t think my marriage will survive it’ Opens in new window ]
Individual therapy and couples counselling will be invaluable here to help think through these questions so that you’re not projecting old, unexamined fears and narratives on to each other and trying to force the other person to heal old wounds they were not responsible for inflicting. And if you both acknowledge and take seriously the core needs behind your individual preferences – her need to feel secure, his need for autonomy – you can start to have more open conversations about whether you can get those needs met in other ways, so that living together or not living together isn’t the only solution. For her, are there other things that could offer feelings of safety and closeness? For him, are there ways to consider living together that could still offer autonomy and independence?
You can get imaginative here. You could consider moving very close to one another – the same neighbourhood, the same street, even the same building, while still maintaining separate homes. (My personal dream is to do what Helena Bonham Carter and Tim Burton once did: buy adjoining houses with a connecting door, allowing for privacy, independence and differing styles of decor, with the option of still having dinner together every night. I’m just waiting on that lotto win.) Could you spend three or four nights together every week, or spend three weeks together a month and a week separately? Could you get a house with enough space for him to retreat when necessary? How could you think about ensuring that he doesn’t feel crowded while she feels loved?
Is getting married a conversation? Why or why not? It does convey commitment and gives you both some legal protection that could allow her to feel safe while still allowing you the option of living separately.
Whether or not you’re considering marriage, you should be considering what the future looks like, and the practical considerations that will arise as you both get older. In both of your ideal scenarios, what do you imagine happening when one of you becomes ill, or develops increased care needs? What happens if travelling across the country every week becomes exhausting or impractical at 65 or 75? What obligations do you believe you have towards each other, and how do you see that playing out practically?
You have been together for two years. It sounds like you want to be together indefinitely. So what if you gave yourself another two years to explore this question together, each committing to asking yourselves: “What am I willing to try?” Is she willing to work on trusting love, even if it comes in a different form than expected? Is he willing to try live together, without judging his partner against a previous relationship? What if you committed to considering these questions for a year, then living together for six months, then living apart for six months so that you can make a conscious, informed decision about how you want your lives to look moving forward?
What you have is special. It deserves special consideration and effort.

title: TV guide: the best new shows to watch this week
description: Women search for medical diagnoses, Bill Murray golfs around Ireland and a new Channel 4 comedy begins
content:
It took broadcaster Katja Mia 14 years to get a diagnosis of endometriosis after suffering from debilitating and painful periods since her early teens. In this documentary, she draws on her own medical history and speaks to other women about conditions like premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), discovering the challenges they faced while searching for answers about their health. With research from Laya Healthcare’s Gender Health Gap report finding that more than half of women aged 25-44 have felt dismissed while discussing health concerns, this documentary is certainly timely. Mia travels across Ireland and even to Greece to speak to women seeking diagnosis and treatment of conditions like PMDD, ADHD and endometriosis, while looking at gaps in treatment and how the internet can lead to the spread of health misinformation. Then she visits researchers at University College Cork ( UCC ) who are investigating medical dismissal and symptom invalidation. It’s sure to be a series of serious interest to anyone who has been looking for answers to health issues, or who has felt stonewalled on their journey.
After last week’s documentary on cardiac issues comes this new short documentary about diabetes . In particular, it looks at how clinical trials are transforming healthcare for people living with the condition. We learn about this through meeting Carmel McDonagh, Tony Marshall and Faye Burke, who share their personal experiences of managing diabetes and participating in such trials. Also featuring on the programme are leading researchers and clinicians like Prof Fidelma Dunne, director of the Institute for Clinical Trials at University of Galway; Prof Seamus Sreenan; Prof Matt Griffin; and Dr Christine Newman. The documentary was filmed in Dublin and Galway, and looks at the day-to-day realities of living with diabetes, as well as how clinical trials (in areas including gestational diabetes and cardiovascular disease) are contributing to progress in both research and care.
Many will either know of or remember the shocking disaster that occurred on October 21st, 1966, in Aberfan, a tiny mining village in south Wales. On an ordinary day, a colliery spoil tip slid down the mountain above Aberfan in seconds, engulfing Pantglas Junior School and a row of houses in its path. Devastatingly, it led to the deaths of 144 people, among them 116 children. This new documentary doesn’t just look at the tragedy in Aberfan, but at the aftermath, when survivors and bereaved families appealed to authorities and the National Coal Board for the other tips above Aberfan to be removed to stave off another incident. Rather than being met with support, they had to fight for common sense to prevail. Members of the community tell their story here and explain the fight for justice on the 60th anniversary of the incident.
Fans of the gamechanging spy fiction author John le Carré will be happy to hear about this new documentary, which looks at the man behind the pseudonym, David Cornwell. Fans and newcomers alike will learn about how he drew on his own childhood and a career in British intelligence to transform the spy genre through his creation of the fictional MI6 officer George Smiley. We’ll learn about the author of The Spy Who Came in from the Cold and Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy and his 60-year career thanks to contributions from his biographer Adam Sisman, Prof Dinah Birch and Prof Christopher Andrew. It’s a good time to swot up before the BBC series Legacy of Spies drops, starring Matthew Macfadyen (Succession) as Smiley.
You might not know the name Leo Reich just yet, but you might have already seen the Gen Z comedian in Lena Dunham’s Netflix series Too Much, or his debut comedy special Literally Who Cares?! The 28-year-old has spent the past four years developing this sitcom for Channel 4, and says “this is a show for everyone who is, has been or will be a delusional and irritating 24-year-old”. Well, a lot of us will resonate with that one. It focuses on best friends Ethan (Reich), Sam (Olive Gray) and Abi (Emily Fairn), who met at university and are now figuring out life in their late 20s after being kicked out of their flat by their landlord. The cast includes our own Andrew Scott, Dunham (who plays Abi’s boss), Amelia Dimoldenberg (of YouTube series Chicken Shop Date) and is narrated by the author Zadie Smith. Sounds like Pulling-meets-Adults, with a contemporary British twist.
Bill Murray is a Hollywood celebrity, but he’s not someone we see on the screen that often. So what’s he up to now, and why has he decided to make a show about Ireland? Well, it’s an intriguing one: in true Murray madcap style, he’s decided to combine a search for his Irish roots with his love for golf. In the first episode, he heads to Kinsale and meets up with friend and golf writer Tom Coyne, who’s by his side throughout. He keeps some interesting company on his trip – future episodes include encounters with celebs like Chris O’Dowd, Joanne McNally and Jason Kelce. The six-part series is being described as a “wildly original and unpredictable road trip”. We know that with Murray at the helm, things are certainly not going to be straightforward, but they should at least be entertaining.
Navy Seal James Reece has some very particular skills, which he demonstrated to devastating effect in the first series of the military thriller based on the bestselling novels by Jack Carr. One of those skills was a talent for uncovering conspiracies that run to the highest level of government, then killing everyone involved. Chris Pratt returns as Reece. Having avenged the deaths of his family and his combat team, he’s given a chance to come in from the cold with a presidential pardon. All Reece has to do is foil a global conspiracy that stretches from the steppes of Russia to the mountains of Virginia. Soon he’s back in combat mode with a crack team, but they might need bigger guns – and cojones – for this job. – Kevin Courtney
When Noah met Joanne, they probably didn’t think their relationship would go all the way to a third series. But here they are, still mismatched and still in love, in this couples comedy starring Kristen Bell and Adam Brody that explores what happens when a sex podcaster and a rabbi find they’ve more in common than either of them expected. In series two, Joanne contemplated converting to Judaism, but Noah didn’t want her to convert just for him. As the new series opens, they’re not only still together but also planning to move in together, which will bring a whole new set of challenges for Joanne and Noah. – Kevin Courtney

title: Cotes Drone? Robotics are being deployed in wine production with impressive results
description: How to Drink Better: Viticulture is adapting to new technological developments along with the rest of us
content:
Yes, it is now quite common for grape growers to use drones in the vineyard. With thermal cameras and other devices attached, they can provide a unique view from the air that provides the producer with all sorts of information throughout the growing season and even before planting a vineyard.
Soils that look the same at ground level frequently vary greatly every few metres. Different soil depth, water-holding capacity and exposure to the sun all have an influence on the growth and health of a vine. Drones can spot differing vigour in the vineyard, helping to separate blocks of vines into parcels that receive different treatments. Drones can also spot zones with uneven growth that may be suffering from disease long before they are visible on the ground. If diseases are present, drones can be used to spray affected vines. In the past this work was done with tractors but that tended to compact the soil. Loss of vigour can also be due to water stress and indicate to the farmer that irrigation is necessary.
In the period before harvest, drones can be very useful in showing varying ripeness levels across the vineyards and allow a producer to plan different picking times for each block of vines.
Grape growers with vines on steep slopes such as German vineyards along the Rhine and other rivers can face great difficulties and high labour costs to harvest their grapes. This year for the first time, a grower in the Saar region is using a drone to carry the grapes from the slopes down to the waiting tractor on the road below. A heavy-duty drone can carry up to 40kg of grapes at a time.
Drones are not the only addition to the winemaker’s tools. Other new technologies being used in the vineyard include robots to prune vines, mow, plough and weed between rows of vines.
So far, the confined space of a winery means that no use has been found for a drone indoors.
Lastly, it is possible that, in the future, drones will be used to deliver wine to your doorstop. However, trials of supermarket deliveries are suspended at the moment.

title: A Belfast designer on making it big in New York: ‘There are still days when I have to pinch myself’
description: Ryan Crown has worked on projects as diverse as a luxury safari resort in Africa, Michelin-starred restaurants in New York and Geneva’s Ritz Carlton hotel
content:
A s anyone who runs their own business knows, life is busy, often chaotic, and can come at you fast. Throw a schedule that requires transatlantic travel into the mix and things get even busier. But this doesn’t faze Ryan Crown, who runs his own design business, Crown Creative, while dividing his time between his home near Belfast and New York City .
The business began in the Big Apple in 2018, but the writing was in the stars two years before that. Crown wet his feet working as a marketing manager for The Dead Rabbit, named “the world’s best bar” in 2016 and founded by Belfast natives Sean Muldoon and Jack McGarry. He then moved to a larger hospitality group as creative director, working across everything from Michelin-starred restaurants and cocktail bars to food halls, Italian restaurants and steakhouses.
The variety of projects saw him fall in love with the job and the city itself, but it wasn’t long before he decided he wanted to branch out on his own. After convincing his employer that “they weren’t losing an employee, they were gaining an entire creative studio”, Crown Creative had its first client.
Now, eight years on, the company has a team of 25 working in Belfast, New York and London, and has grown from a branding and design agency, into a full-service studio offering brand strategy, graphic design, interiors and digital, all under one roof.
“That model came from my own frustration as a client, having to co-ordinate several different agencies on a single project,” he says. “We wanted to offer something more joined-up: a single team which understands the entire vision and behaves like an extension of the client’s own business. We describe ourselves as a creative partner because, on the best projects, that’s genuinely what we become.
“There are still days when I have to pinch myself at the calibre of the clients and projects coming through our doors. To see work created by our team in Belfast, London and New York come to life globally is genuinely humbling. It feels as though we’re not simply designing places – we’re helping to create brands and experiences with a real legacy. In the last year we’ve seen a luxury safari resort open in Africa, a restaurant we designed in Grand Central Terminal in New York and a boutique wine hotel in Oregon.”
The 35-year-old, who has a 20-month old daughter with his partner, Ema, wasn’t always destined to be a designer as he studied drama and English at college, before doing a master’s in drama at Queen’s University Belfast. But, although he never trained as a designer, he says that his background taught him “a great deal about storytelling and how to understand an audience – both of which are fundamental to the work undertaken at Crown today”.
Travel is another great source of inspiration for the designer, who says that being away for “at least one week a month”, and also looking beyond his own industry, helps to get the creative juices flowing.
“Inspiration often comes from somewhere unexpected: the pacing of a theatrical production, the typography on an old street sign, or the way a small neighbourhood restaurant makes people feel completely at home,” he says. “Also, my guilty pleasure is magazines. I subscribe to far too many – Monocle, Bon Appétit and Wallpaper among them – and feel guilty every month when I don’t get through the pile. But I love the discovery involved in print, and the physical experience of holding a beautifully made magazine in my hands.”
The projects undertaken by Crown can vary vastly in size – from the St Regis Cap Cana Resort in the Dominican Republic, where the team created nine individual food-and-beverage brands over the course of two years, to the Neighbourhood Cafe in Belfast, which the founder co-owns with his business partner and best friend, Oisín McEvoy.
Another recent project was The Kithmore in St Andrews, and also a refreshing of the global identity of Peacock Alley, the historic institution associated with the Waldorf Astoria.
But, regardless of the scale, each job is meticulously thought out and executed.
“The budgets and commercial details of many of these projects are confidential, but the developments range from independent hospitality businesses to significant, multimillion-pound international hotel investments,” says Crown. “What matters to us is the same at every scale: finding the story, expressing it consistently, and making every detail feel intentional.
“And there’s something quite surreal about standing in one of New York’s most iconic hotels and seeing a brand developed by our team in Belfast.”
Fashion trends are constantly changing, and the interior design world is no different. But the businessman says while that he and his team are conscious of trends, they “try not to follow them too closely, because if a design is built around a passing visual fashion, it can date very quickly”.
“The strongest movement I see is away from the generic, copy-and-paste international aesthetic and towards spaces that feel rooted in their location,” he says. “There’s a renewed appreciation for character, craft, natural materials and vintage pieces – interiors which can develop a patina over time, rather than looking perfect only on opening day.
“When we began, there was a great deal of emphasis on creating highly ‘Instagrammable’ moments. And while that still has its place, clients are now looking for something deeper. They want comfort, atmosphere, authenticity and a sense that a space could only exist in that particular place.
“Every detail matters, but people rarely leave a hotel remembering a particular wallpaper or bed throw. They remember how the place made them feel. A trend might give you a moment, but a strong narrative gives longevity to a project.”
The design expert says there are many large-scale ideas that can be adapted and work very well in the home, but it is important to be aware of your own style and environment.
“With so many beautiful interiors online it’s tempting to go Pinterest shopping and turn your home into one large mood board,” he says. “But before buying anything, it’s worth understanding your own taste and how you actually want your home to feel. The most interesting homes say something about the people living in them, rather than replicating a nice image online.
“Lighting is the quickest transformation for me. I’ll always choose several small lamps at different heights over switching on the ‘big light’ as warm, layered lighting can change the atmosphere of a room immediately and make even an inexpensive interior feel considered.
“With more of us working from home, it’s also important to create some separation between working and living – even if that simply means a good chair, a dedicated lamp, and being able to put the laptop out of sight at the end of the day. Your home should support the way you actually live, not just photograph well.”
While Crown and his team are currently working on several beautiful Michelin-starred restaurant projects in New York, as well as beginning the interior design of two restaurant and bar spaces at The Ritz-Carlton in Geneva, they have also just launched a Substack called Hospitality Everywhere, which is a home for the team’s “observations, opinions and discoveries – from travel and current projects to the bigger questions shaping hospitality”.
[ A Wicklow mansion rescued from ruin by seven people: ‘I felt sorry for the house’ Opens in new window ]
So the future looks bright as he is looking forward to further success and new developments both in his personal and professional life.
“We have such a breadth of experience within the studio, so I’m excited to give more of the team a platform [with the Substack] and see where it goes,” he says. “But, personally, my next major project is the arrival of our second child in October. And amid the nappies, sleepless nights and chaos of having two children under two, I’m also hugely excited about continuing to grow Crown. I genuinely feel we’re only at the beginning of what the agency can achieve, and I’m incredibly thankful for the people I get to work alongside every day.
[ Why you should choose your furniture before renovating your home Opens in new window ]
“Looking further ahead, I think the word ‘luxury’ has become overused. We’re going to see a return to a more meaningful idea of it – less about marble, thread counts or the size of a bedroom, and more about genuine, authentic experience.
“As our lives become increasingly digital, people will place greater value on experiences that feel human, generous and connected to their location. They won’t necessarily remember every object in a room, but they’ll remember how warmly they were welcomed, who they met and how it all made them feel. To me, that’s the future of hospitality [and design].”

title: Dr Rangan Chatterjee: What will you do with a perfect six-pack if you haven’t someone to share your life with?
description: Dr Rangan Chatterjee on ‘junk connections’, biohacking and why people need to trust themselves
content:
T he last time Dr Rangan Chatterjee came to Dublin , it was for a Bon Jovi concert in Croke Park . He’s a superfan of the band, he tells me during a video call from his home in England. He mentions this because he is a proponent of something called “collective effervescence”, a phrase coined by pioneering French sociologist Émile Durkheim to describe “the special energy we feel when we’re in a room with like-minded people”. That energy is something he’ll be channelling at his Thrive Tour event in Dublin next month.
The Thrive Tour, Chatterjee explains, is his attempt to help people reclaim their own innate health expertise with a two-hour, interactive live experience built around “mindset, values and actions”. A journal is included in the price of the ticket, so people can take notes and, he hopes, go home with meaningful tips to improve their lives. It’s the first time he’s bringing the event to Ireland, but he’s played in front of thousands across the UK , Canada and Australia .
We might be drowning in hacks, longevity gurus and health optimisation strategies, but Chatterjee insists people need to stop outsourcing their wellbeing and learn to trust themselves again. His central argument is that “we’ve outsourced our own inner expertise to external experts”. It might sound strange coming from one of those experts, but he insists his goal is to make people like him redundant.
“I want people to not need me,” he says. “The whole theme of the night is: it’s your life. You get to choose what’s important to you, and everything I do is about giving people tools they can use themselves.”
Over the past decade, Chatterjee has managed to cut through the considerable wellness noise with a common-sense approach that blends his medical background with empowering advice for his more than a million Instagram followers. He first came to prominence in 2015, helping families with their health issues in the BBC TV show Doctor in the House. He has written six bestselling books, and his podcast, Feel Better, Live More, is the most popular health show on Apple Podcasts with more than 300 million listens.
Chatterjee’s approach covers sleep, stress, purpose, relationships, technology and happiness, while increasingly questioning whether modern life itself is making people ill. “We have more health and wellness information than ever before,” he points out. “Yet physical health is worsening, mental health is worse now. If all we needed was more knowledge, we’d be thriving.
“My whole message is about empowerment, trying to show people that it doesn’t matter who you are or where you live or what your perceived problems are. That even if you’re in a dark place, there are still some very simple things that you could do that will make a difference.” His aim with the live event is that “people walk away feeling really inspired and feeling that it’s not as hard as they think it is to thrive”.
What he has learned from seeing tens of thousands of patients in his 23-year medical career and reaching millions more online is that in this hyper-connected world, loneliness is an urgent modern malaise. He’s not surprised when I tell him that articles with “lonely” in the headline receive heavy traffic on The Irish Times website. “A lot of the connection we think we’re getting online is what I call junk connection. It’s like junk food. It’s not real, three-dimensional, nourishing connection.” He quotes one study that says “the feeling of being lonely and isolated is as harmful for your health as smoking 15 to 20 cigarettes per day”.
[ How music, or silence, can help with bereavement, dementia and pain Opens in new window ]
As the son of two immigrant parents from India who faced challenges coming to a new country, he says they were keen that their son excelled. “I took on the message as a child that I was only loved when I got straight As ... but for all my so-called success, I wasn’t actually that happy because a lot of my life had been driven by external achievement and external validation ... I’ve since learnt that happiness is an inside job.”
He is a keen follower of Rose Anne Kenny, Trinity College Dublin’s professor of medical gerontology, who has been a guest on his podcast. “She’s been studying this for years and has shown that 80 per cent of how we age is down to how we live, while only 20 per cent is our genes. So I think the ideology of trying to help us to live well and be independent and mobile until the day that we die is awesome.” But he also thinks we have “a problem with death in western society. We don’t want to face it. We don’t want to acknowledge it.”
This philosophy has developed even more since his father died. He had lupus, and Chatterjee cared for him for years. An awareness of death is crucial for a healthy life, he believes. He has a vivid childhood memory of watching the funeral of Indian prime minister Indira Gandhi in the early 1980s. “I remember seeing her body on the funeral pyre. In India, death is not hidden away; it’s part of life. All of us, at some point, we’re going to return to earth. And I think there’s something in that because if I could live forever, I’m not sure how much of my life would have meaning. I’m not sure if there would be an urgency to do anything, because what makes life beautiful is the fact that we are going to die at some point.”
I bring up the biohacking movement where science, technology and lifestyle tweaks are used to “optimise” the human body and mind. He says he doesn’t like to judge anybody, but that caution is needed. “The risk of the biohacking movement is twofold. One is that we’re trying to cheat death, and I don’t think we can cheat death. And even if you could cheat death, do you even want to? Is a big question.
“The other risk is a world where so many of us are struggling with our relationships, where so many of us are feeling lonely. If we keep pursuing our own health habits at the expense of our relationships, we’re setting ourselves up for some really big problems. You can have the perfect level of visceral fat. You can be the perfect weight. Eat the perfect diet. But if you haven’t got meaningful relationships, is there any point? What are you going to do with that perfect six-pack if you haven’t got someone to share your life with?
“I think some people do [biohacking] really well, but some people give it a bad name. I don’t think we all have to do cold plunges and red light therapy. They have value for some people, but I would just say, be careful you’re not optimising your own personal health at the expense of your social relationships.”
[ Sardinian village where high number of women reach 100 could be new centenarian ‘blue zone’ Opens in new window ]
He also believes screen use in children may be the most pressing health issue of our current time. He has a 14-year-old daughter and a 16-year-old son. “I was never going to allow my children on social media. Knowing what I know, and seeing what I’ve seen, there was no way.”
We’re living in a world now where there’s noise everywhere. Social media reels, news headlines, podcasts
He started playing a regular padel game with his son recently. “Every week we play two games together on a doubles team. It has dropped my resting heart rate, which is great for my cardiac efficiency. It’s made me sleep better. It’s helped me with multiple aspects of my health, but I don’t play for any of those reasons. I play to hang out with my boy and cultivate our relationship.”
To this end, he hopes people make connections at his upcoming event. “People send me messages saying, ‘I don’t have any friends who want to come with me. Do you think I could come by myself?’ I tell them absolutely, and they often end up meeting or making friends, because it’s like-minded people gathered together.”
The podcasts, the books and the events are about him fulfilling his own evolving purpose in life, he says. The book he is currently writing will explore this topic. “If you’re living a life without purpose, you’re much more likely to engage in problematic behaviours,” he says. “One of the reasons I want to do these live shows is because what drives me is a real desire to help people live better lives. I don’t think it’s as hard as we think it is.”
Before he goes, he tells me he’s heard about doctors who informally prescribe his podcast to their patients. If Chatterjee could prescribe one thing to the population of Ireland for their wellbeing, what would it be? “Ten minutes of silence every day,” he says, without hesitation. “We’re living in a world now where there’s noise everywhere. Social media reels, news headlines, podcasts, right?
“The reason we’re so confused is that we stopped listening to ourselves. Ten minutes of silence, or what I would call solitude, literally helps you to start listening to yourself again. I don’t care if that’s a walk round your block, without your phone, or if it’s meditation or journaling.”
[ There is no such thing as ‘resetting’ the nervous system – and we shouldn’t want to Opens in new window ]
Or perhaps, he says, the most revolutionary act these days is having a cup of tea or a lunch break without checking emails or scrolling social media. “If you spend five to 10 minutes a day with intentional silence, you will start to understand yourself better than you have done for such a long period of time and you will make better decisions throughout the day.” Ten minutes of peace? It’s just what the doctor ordered.
Dr Rangan Chatterjee’s The Thrive Tour event is on at the Bord Gáis Energy Theatre on November 15th

title: The curious backlash against Nick Griggs taking up a US athletics scholarship
description: At 21, after four years of running ‘pro’, his signing with Oregon is all within the NCAA rules
content:
The announcement by the University of Oregon earlier this week that Nick Griggs was officially “Flying with the Flock”, a reference to Oregon’s sports teams also being known as the Ducks, certainly appears to have ruffled a few feathers.
In continuing the long history of Irish athletes taking up a US scholarship, Griggs has brought some wider attention to the rules of the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA), the governors of all US college sport since 1906.
Griggs is unquestionably a major catch for Oregon. The Tyrone runner is the reigning European Under-23 Cross-Country champion, and Irish under-23 record holder over 1,500m (3:35.04), the mile (3:52.42), 3,000m (7:32.79) and 5,000m (13:05.75). He’d broken all those records at Under-20 level too.
His exceptional talent has been known about for many years; in 2022, less than three months after turning 17, Griggs became the youngest Irish runner to break four minutes for the mile, clocking 3:56.40 at the Sport Ireland Arena in Dublin.
Although he had received several offers of a US scholarship before, he’d so far chosen to remain close to home, and for the last two years has attended Ulster University in Belfast, studying sport and exercise sciences, while coached by Mark Kirk. Still, the possibility of a transfer to the US was always in the back of his mind and, prompted this summer by fellow Irish runner Abdel Laadjel, who last year finished up his final season of eligibility at Oregon, moves were swiftly afoot.
At 21, Griggs has already run at the World and European Athletics Championships and the Commonwealth Games, although he narrowly missed out on the Paris Olympics. He also signed a professional contract with Puma, back in 2022, and is looked after by Pace Sports Management, among the biggest professional athlete representatives in the sport. On the good days, he might have picked up a little prize money along the way too.
Until relatively recently, all this would have gone against the rules of the NCAA. Then in July 2021, in arguably the biggest change in NCAA history, student athletes were allowed to generate their own income from selling their name, image and likeness – otherwise known as the NIL deal.
This has impacted on US athletes to varying degrees, depending on the popularity of their sport, with Miami Hurricanes quarterback Darian Mensah currently boasting the highest NIL deal, reportedly worth around $6.5 million (€5.79 million).
Griggs isn’t in that league, although his signing with Oregon has been met with some curious backlash, and the cause of some debate on both sides on the Atlantic. Partly because of his age (he turns 22 in December), his considerable international experience, and his “pro” contract with Puma, some believe Griggs has no place in the NCAA, or will at least make things a lot harder on young US or other foreign athletes starting out in their college career.
Things are a little different when it comes to football and basketball, as under NCAA rules, any player who has signed with the NFL or NBA is prohibited from returning to college (although some of those cases have gone to court). The NCAA have also revised their age eligibility this season, so that athletes only have a continuous five-year eligibility period from the time they start college. This means, all going to plan, Griggs still has three years of eligibility at Oregon, which will see him through the LA 2028 Olympics.
[ Nick Griggs takes lessons from finishing ninth as Josh Kerr wins World Indoor 3,000m Opens in new window ]
Some of the backlash on social media has pointed to the fact Oregon is already a powerhouse of US collegiate distance running (and has been going back to Steve Prefontaine in the 1970s), and they shouldn’t be going after an athlete of Griggs’ age or calibre. But again, Griggs isn’t breaking any NCAA rules here, and nor indeed are Oregon, with Griggs himself responding to that with a telling comment: “Don’t hate the player, hate the game ...”
A lot of things have changed since the first Irish athletes went on scholarship to the US, starting back in 1948, with a simple proposition to Jimmy Reardon: “We could sure use you guys at Villanova.”
The story goes that Reardon, a 400m runner and captain of the Irish athletics team at the 1948 London Olympics, was sitting in the dining hall with thrower Cummin Clancy and miler John Joe Barry. They got chatting with US runners George Guida and Browning Ross, both scholarship athletes at Villanova University, just outside of Philadelphia, who reckoned their famous coach Jumbo Elliott would be delighted to snap up these already famous Irish athletes.
In Barry’s autobiography The Ballincurry Hare, a gem long out of print, he recalls how Reardon sparked the idea, before all three sealed the deal: “It was Reardon who put the question to him, ‘George, you’re telling me if you could run or jump well enough, you’d get a scholarship to an American university, which would include full tuition, full board, books, etc?’”
That began what was originally known as the Irish pipeline, with Ronnie Delany soon following in their footsteps, paving the way for the likes Eamonn Coghlan, John Treacy, Marcus O’Sullivan, Frank O’Mara, Sonia O’Sullivan, and more recently, Rhasidat Adeleke. Spreading from the east coast to the west, north and south, and most places in between, the presence of Irish athletes in US colleges, and their success far beyond, has been a constant during those near 80 years since.
Success has never been any barrier to NCAA eligibility in all the years since, and nor was age. Delany, remember, won an Olympic gold medal while in college in the US, his 1,500m triumph in Melbourne in 1956 coming during his last year at Villanova, and in 1978, a 20-year-old Treacy won the World Cross-Country during his final year at Providence College.
Griggs will take any of this backlash in his stride. Currently recovering from a knee injury, he’s used to adversity. After winning silver in the Under-23 race at the 2024 European Cross-Country, he developed a serious knee infection, osteomyelitis.
