Back in 2021, less than six weeks after losing his older brother Josh in a work accident, he won the European Under-20 3,000m gold in breathtaking style, when still only 16.
And as for Griggs now signing with Oregon, Jumbo Elliott would no doubt have approved.

title: Elon Musk’s trillion-dollar pay deal has a convenient escape clause
description: A takeover - even by an affiliated company - could trigger a huge payout while bypassing operational targets
content:
A million robotaxis, a million humanoid robots, and an $8.5 trillion valuation – Elon Musk ’s trillion-dollar Tesla bonus appears to demand almost superhuman performance.
There is, however, an easier (and less-publicised) way for Musk to collect the big bucks: just sell the company.
A recent study of executive pay finds that enormous share awards usually fail to deliver for shareholders and that “milestones are far less demanding than they appear”, with Musk’s 2025 Tesla package offering a striking illustration of the risks.
In Merging to the Moon: Astronomical Option Awards and Corporate Governance Failures, researchers examined 1.24 million insider stock awards between 1996 and 2022. They found that Tesla-style “mega-grants” subsequently underperformed comparable companies by 15 to 30 per cent over following years.
Tesla’s 2025 agreement offers Musk 424 million shares if the company reaches an $8.5 trillion market value and meets 12 demanding business milestones.
Considered in isolation, the package looks like a properly designed pay-for-performance deal. Under the researchers’ modelling, annual growth of 12 per cent in both Tesla’s share price and earnings would leave the company just short of its profits target after a decade.
If only one operational milestone was met (cumulative vehicle deliveries), Musk would get a payout of about $8 billion – a big sum, yes, but a fraction of the headline award.
However, if Tesla is acquired, the agreement completely waives the operational targets. If Tesla were taken over, the same share-price growth could deliver Musk $448 billion to $545 billion at a typical 20-30 per cent takeover premium, or up to about $707 billion at a 50 per cent takeover premium.
In other words, Musk could bag up to 88 times what he would earn on the operational track, without meeting a single operational goal.
[ As Tesla sales tank, Musk gains a trillion-dollar pay day Opens in new window ]
The pay deal “converts a performance award into a transaction bonus”, potentially allowing Musk to engineer a takeover through an affiliated company such as SpaceX, triggering a huge payout while bypassing the operational targets.
Perhaps Musk’s greatest feat of engineering is financial rather than technological: the salesman who persuaded more than 75 per cent of shareholders to back a pay deal that has “essentially no analogue in market practice”.

title: Met Éireann in scramble to save amateur weather watchers’ network from shutdown
description: About 150 private weather stations nationwide feed into the Wow platform, which the UK will soon close
content:
Ask Sean Rima what the weather is like out his way and he will ask: where exactly?
Across the hills, lakes and valleys of Connemara, four seasons in one day doesn’t quite cover the variety of weather Atlantic forces can bring.
A kaleidoscope comes closer to describing the rapid changes that can affect conditions in highly localised patches.
“I can be looking at the Clifden station and it’s pouring with rain and I look out the window here and it’s bright sunshine,” he says of the weather station data coming from less than 20km away as the crow flies from his home in Renvyle, Co Galway. “It’s interesting to watch the way the weather moves.”
Rima is one of about 150 amateur weather watchers in Ireland whose private weather stations feed information continually to Met Éireann on the Wow (Weather Observations Website) network.
The data is not official as there are too many variations in the type of equipment used to quality-control them all.
But Wow is an important supplement to the 25 official Met Éireann weather stations around the State.
Met Éireann says these contribute to “better forecasts, more accurate warnings and a deeper understanding of our changing climate”.
“It fills the gaps in coverage,” says Noel Fitzpatrick, acting head of observations.
“It’s also useful to consult where there is a particular weather event taking place, to check the progress of a weather front or incoming severe weather.”
[ Archaeologists discover and ‘rediscover’ two neolithic tombs in Galway Opens in new window ]
But Met Éireann will soon lose access to Wow after a decision by its UK hosts to discontinue the platform.
The UK Met Office established it and watched it grow into an international network but it says ageing technology means it can no longer be supported and it will shut down in December.
Met Éireann is working with other EU states to develop a replacement platform.
“We are cautiously looking at early 2027 [as a start date],” Fitzpatrick says. “We want to minimise the downtime between the current system and its replacement.”
Wow contributors include schools, sports clubs and some public bodies but mostly they are individuals, often with a combined interest in weather and technology.
PJ Naughter, a software developer from Ballygarrett in Co Wexford, fits that description perfectly.
“It’s not hard to set up a weather station. Anyone can get a good one for a couple of hundred euro – although you can spend thousands if you want,” he says.
“I’ve connected mine to a network in the US and other international ones so you’re feeding information from Wexford all around the world.”
He gets plenty in return too, recalling the Tonga volcano eruption in 2022 that was so violent, it upset atmospheric pressure worldwide.
“You could see the pressure waves approaching Ireland,” he says. “The first wave approached after about five hours and the second one from the other direction came after about 11 hours.
“You could see it happening in real time just by watching the data on the websites.”
[ ‘Powerful storms are more common’: Threat of rising sea levels and coast erosion in Galway Opens in new window ]
Sean Rima is more interested in local phenomena and collates data from 10 stations he and other enthusiasts installed around west Galway.
Posting on the connemaraweather.eu website as well as Wow, they track conditions far from the official stations at Mace Head and Galway city.
“I used to sail on the Killary so I always needed to know what the weather was doing,” he said.
“Now I fly a drone to take photographs so I can look at an area before I head out and see what the last 10 or 20 minutes have been doing.
“I have a station out on Inishturk and one on Inishbofin because whatever happens out there eventually comes to us.”
Met Éireann is working to add extra weather stations to its own network, but Noel Fitzpatrick believes the local stations will always be important.
“We are a very varied country and that affects weather locally even within short distances,” he says.
“You can have substantial variability whether you are in an exposed area, on the side of a hill or in a valley. That’s the kind of information Wow supplies.”
Scientific value aside, the Wow site is also a beacon for weather enthusiasts who just want to prove a point.
If you’ve ever wondered why it feels warmer or colder in your corner of the country than officially forecast, the chances are a check on a local weather station on the Wow website will prove you are not imagining things.
The website wow.met.ie has a map where all the weather stations can be clicked to check current conditions and past conditions – in some cases going back several years.
At the minimum, they record air temperature but many also relay data on humidity, rainfall, pressure, wind speed, direction and gust strength and soil temperature.
The data will not be transferred to whatever platform replaces Wow so Met Éireann is encouraging anyone who wants to archive past information in graph or table form to download it from the site before the network is shut down.

title: Are public sector workers all as badly off as strikes might suggest? This is what the data says
description: Those under the greatest pressure are younger workers who have to contend with high rents and housing costs
content:
“W hat do they expect us to live on?” one striker on the picket lines asked The Irish Times this week. “Nobody can survive on the wages we’re getting.”
“I think it’s important to say this is for everyone,” said another. “The Government are just squeezing us so hard with the cost of living and yeah, we need more money just to survive.”
It was a refrain heard through the extensive and largely positive media coverage of the strike (RTÉ seems especially keen) on Wednesday: it is impossible to survive on public sector wages. Workers have been hammered by increases in the cost of living. They can’t afford to live.
This is a perhaps understandable exaggeration to make a point, though it is also another example of how moderation is disappearing from our political debate. Public servants are not unable to survive, obviously; they may be short of money, but they are getting by. However, one thing that has been absent from much of the debate is what exactly are public servants – teachers, nurses, gardaí , civil servants and so on – actually paid? Are they all as badly off as the coverage might suggest?
It is certainly true that there are many low-paid workers in the public service who are struggling to get by. They have seen their living standards squeezed and – for younger workers – have little prospect of owning their own home and building the life that they might aspire to. But is low pay endemic across the public sector, in the way that the strikers seem to believe it is?
[ ‘My pay hasn’t gone up – and everything else has’: Public sector workers have their say Opens in new window ]
This year’s budget estimates show that the State directly employs 403,000 people funded by the exchequer this year, for which the wage bill is €31.2 billion – giving an average of €77,400 per head. Of course that is a clumsy way of looking at it, and it fails to take account of lots of things. But it tells us something, all the same.
Let’s look at some individual sectors. According to data from the Department of Education, there are 43,451 primary teachers at the end of June, with a total wage bill of €3.96 billion, giving an average of more than €91,000 annually.
Letter writers, hold your pens – this does not mean that a typical primary teacher is earning this much. There are principals who earn more, and young teachers who earn a lot less. Teachers may receive allowances and top-ups for good reasons, though they tend not to shout about this (understandably) during pay negotiations. The primary schoolteachers’ union, the Irish National Teachers’ Organisation , cites a figure from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) for average pay as €70,629 in 2025.
For secondary teachers, the total number is 35,707 and the total pay bill is €3.08 billion, so the average figure is €86,000 – again subject to the caveats entered above for primary teachers. The OECD figure for average secondary teacher pay is €69,747.
What about doctors and nurses? The total figure for nurses and midwives employed is just under 50,000, with a total pay bill of €4.4 billion; an average of €88,000 a year. For doctors, the total bill for 15,631 medical and dental staff is €3.1 billion, giving an average of €198,000.
[ Stephen Collins: Unsustainable pay increases for public sector workers will put Ireland’s stability at risk Opens in new window ]
No, this does not tell us that a typical nurse on the ward earns nearly €90,000. Lots of nurses earn less, and some on higher grades earn more. The averages don’t tell us everything. But they don’t tell us nothing, either.
For gardaí, there is less rooting around in Government budget figures required, as the Central Statistics Office compiles quarterly figures that clearly identify the earnings of gardaí as a distinct category. They show consistently that gardaí are the best paid part of the public service, with average weekly earnings and average weekly paid hours in the second quarter of this year of €1,833.73 and 43.2 hours respectively. It should be said that one of the reasons for these comparatively high garda earnings is that gardaí tend to do a lot of overtime.
Let us leave aside for now three other very important aspects of public sector pay: the value of guaranteed pensions, which are so expensive as to be nowadays unbuyable in the private sector; the value of job security; and the pay premium that many public sector workers enjoy over their private sector counterparts.
Instead, consider another aspect of employment largely confined to the public sector: the system of automatic increments (ie increases in salary), which means that workers are rewarded for getting older, rather than better, at their jobs. These are not, I regret to say, the same thing. Teachers, for instance, have a 25-point scale; nurses have a 13-point scale.
[ The Irish Times view on the public sector strike: mutually agreed obstruction Opens in new window ]
The people in the public sector who are squeezed the most are younger workers who are low on the increments scale, and who have to contend with high rents and housing costs, worst in Dublin. A city where teachers, nurses and gardaí can’t afford to live is a disaster. But the system operated by the unions and the State works to the disadvantage of younger public servants and the advantage of their older colleagues. A flat percentage increase in pay benefits the older public servants more while their younger co-workers struggle.
It follows that the people who should benefit most – or maybe exclusively – from a new pay deal are younger public servants in cities. Older public servants high up the increments scale do not need the help as much as they do. Whatever the total amount of the pay deal, the pay increases funded by it should be targeted towards those who need them most. The increments system should be reformed. The unions should seek and the Government should agree a Dublin or city weighting. That would be a real demonstration of one of the unions’ favourite ideas – solidarity.

title: Gulliver’s Travels at 300: Did Jonathan Swift predict AI?
description: Satirical masterpiece has been irresistible to illustrators, abridgers and adaptors since its sensational arrival - and its lessons on human nature remain prescient
content:
Jonathan Swift was nothing if not cross. August 1725 was a miserable, wet month, and the Dean of St Patrick’s was at the house of his friend Thomas Sheridan at Quilca, Co Cavan . Occupied in “overseeing and ranting at Irish labourers” on Sheridan’s estate, Swift deplored Quilca’s “scanty lodging, want of victuals, and … thievish race of people", an insufficiency of books and an oversupply of the poor: it was a place of “a million of wants”.
Swift was then finishing a book that savagely satirises humanity in general while also taking precise aim at local targets. Published in London in October 1726 as Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World. In Four Parts (1726), and commonly called Gulliver’s Travels, it was an instant sensation and has secured a lasting place among works of world literature.
Its hero, Lemuel Gulliver, an English man of science and a ship’s captain, embarks on a sequence of voyages (supposedly undertaken between 1699 and 1715) that make up the four parts of the Travels. Shipwrecked near Tasmania, Gulliver is chained to a wooden frame by a race of tiny people 12 times smaller than himself. Among other adventures there, he saves their palace of Lilliput from fire by pissing a torrent of water from his giant height, earning the gratitude of the emperor and the displeasure of the fastidious empress.
Gulliver returns to England only to set sail once more, this time arriving in Brobdingnag where the people, now 12 times his size, are as tall as church steeples and he becomes the terrified prey of rats and wasps. The Brobdingnagians love to see and touch him and Gulliver is driven to disgust when some giant noble women go so far as to strip him naked and place him on their breasts. Women’s bodies provoke particular disgust in Gulliver’s Travels: Swift’s misogynism was but a subset of his disdain for mankind.
Next, Gulliver travels to Laputa and on to Balnibarbi, places devoted to scientific advancement and populated by frenetic schemers and projectors. Although located in southeast Asia, the floating island of Laputa might be thought of as Ireland, a kingdom and a colony long and painfully subject to the half-baked plans of improvers. The final book takes in the country of the Houyhnhnms, where the Englishman finds he occupies a place somewhere between the gracious and civilised class of horses and their underlings, the human-like but hairy and savage Yahoos. If Gulliver seems to learn little across these voyages, the conclusion strikes a notably bleak note with the sea captain miserable and back at home, barely able to tolerate the company of those “English Yahoos”, his wife and neighbours.
[ Subscriber Only Books This is a library where the books won’t be read until 2114 Opens in new window ]
The noted critic Samuel Johnson, always keen to knock a reputation off its perch, remarked to his friend Dr Boswell: “When once you have thought of big men and little men, it is very easy to do all the rest.”
But how easy was it for Swift to think up his stories of “big men and little men”? A Co Cavan story claims that he got the idea there, working on the tale while sitting on a pier overlooking Mullagh lake. In the late 1930s, John Lynch, a 55-year-old farmer in Rantavan, told James Drury, a teacher collecting stories for the Irish Folklore Commission’s Schools’ Project, that some of Sheridan’s workmen (also named Sheridan) had been large men (“of gigantic size”) and the learned doctor had a habit of “parading them occasionally before his visitors”. Meanwhile, Sheridan’s neighbours, the Brookes of Rantavan, Mullagh, employed workers named Bradley who “happened to be the smallest men in the whole district, being almost dwarfs”. “Their descendants who live in Rantavan still are of very small stature,” said Lynch.
To amuse his friend Swift, Sheridan supposedly showed him the working men as they brought in the harvest, inviting the Dean to enjoy the spectacle of “seeing the giant Sheridans lift up the dwarf Bradleys in their hands and place them like dolls on the haycocks” – it is a short distance from this story to Gulliver’s Travels .
If the big book came from a small place, it came too from a curious cultural moment. At the start of the 18th century, with Ireland now secured, Ascendancy writers took an interest in the culture of the vanquished – its language and literature, music and monuments – and began to fashion a new Anglo-Irish literature. The Sheridans and the Brookes were involved in literary coteries that cultivated this new writing, along with Swift and his friends.
An exhibition in Trinity College Dublin’s (TCD) Long Room returns Gulliver’s Travels to its Irish roots and reminds us of how the question of scale has occupied the attention of readers across three centuries. The story’s shifts of size and perception have been irresistible to illustrators, abridgers and adaptors since the book’s first publication and it is a delight to encounter versions from Enid Blyton, Padraic Colum and Marvel Comics.
[ Bookshops are lovely places, but they do create this one hazard Opens in new window ]
According to Aileen Douglas, co-curator of the exhibition: “The first readers of Gulliver’s Travels were very taken with its satire of prominent political figures and the machinations of power. For readers today, fearful of being displaced by AI, Swift’s profound satire of human nature, especially pride in rationality and progress, resonates strongly.”
Her reference to artificial intelligence points to the third part of Gulliver’s Travels which sees our hero descend from the floating island to the continent of Balnibarbi below, to visit the Academy of Lagado. Seeking funding for their highly idiosyncratic research projects, the Academy’s scholars aim to extract “Sun-Beams out of Cucumbers” and develop a scheme to build houses from the roof downwards.
The specific attack is on the Royal Society of Swift’s own day, founded in London in 1660. But the chapter stands as a serviceable satire on both the “projectification” of research in modern universities and the illusions of the current AI boom. One of the Academy’s professors has developed a language “Engine” that bears an uncanny similarity to the Large Language Models (LLMs). Here, Swift mocks the fantasy that knowledge can be acquired without effort. Occupying its own room and operated by 40 young students, the engine comprises a large frame strung with slender wires and interchangeable squares covered with pieces of paper featuring “all the words of their Language in their several Moods, Tenses, and Declensions”.
The students operate the machine’s iron handles and each turn creates new linguistic arrangements. Accordingly, boasts the Professor, “the most ignorant Person, at a reasonable Charge, with a little Bodily labour, may write Books in Philosophy, Poetry, Politics, Laws, Mathematics, and Theology, without the least Assistance from Genius or Study”. All that is needed to realise this dream of automatically generated knowledge is a greater supply of books to feed the machine and public funding to advance the experiment. The case hits so close to home that University College Cork’s Mary O’Connell is currently asking English literature students to engage with Swift’s satire in the service of a “thoughtful rejection of gen AI tools” in their own work.
But in addition to its satirical treatment of an instrumental and token-based treatment of language, Gulliver’s Travels added new and indispensable words to the creative and critical lexicon. How might we conceive of miniaturisation without Lilliput? And, in media studies, the term “Gulliverisation” has been adopted to describe a shifting screen landscape, where we find ourselves turning from mobile phones to jumbotrons [large, high-resolution video screens].
In 1980, a computer scientist seeking to conceptualise the storage architecture of computers, hit on the terms “big-endian” and “little-endian” to describe the order in which bytes are stored. The words come from Swift’s classic, where a row erupts between the great empires of Lilliput and Blefuscu when a king, breaking open an egg from the big end in the ancient and approved practice, cuts his finger with the spoon. There follows “an edict, commanding all his subjects, upon great penalties, to break the smaller end of their eggs” and war wages for years. The conflict looks very like the English split from Rome during the Reformation but language leaps across the centuries.
[ John McGahern, A Writing Life: Biography of literary giant who understood the human condition Opens in new window ]
Written at the very dawn of party politics in England and Ireland, with its focus intently trained on its contemporary moment, Gulliver’s Travels retains the capacity to address our own time. Even the book’s long life across three centuries might cause us to speculate on the experiments in life extension beloved of the billionaire class. On the topic of reverse ageing, Gulliver’s Travels once more has something to say. The book’s third part ends in the Kingdom of Luggnagg, where Gulliver meets a tiny population of immortals known as the Struldbruggs and realises the horrifying price that they pay for eternity: an endless lifetime of sickness and decline. Weary of living on, the Struldbruggs resent the young, distort the past and lose their ability to communicate with the world.
The great man himself died in 1745, aged 77, suffering from memory loss and senile dementia. On a final visit to Cavan in 1735, he reported on staying in “the dirtiest place I ever saw, with the worst wife and daughter, and the most cursed sluts and servants, on this side Scotland”.
Dirty and disagreeable as he found it, Ireland fuelled Swift’s indignation at the world at large. But he was a satirist and not a prophet and we should feel under no compulsion to make his dark visions come true.
Claire Connolly is the author of Irish Romanticism (Cambridge University Press). Gulliver at 300 is curated by Stephanie Breen, Aileen Douglas and Ian Campbell Ross and is on display in TCD’s Long Room until the end of December 2026.

title: A generation late: 900,000 children have been denied treatment at the overdue Children’s Hospital
description: My concerns won’t go away once it opens, as it will be expensive to operate, staff and expand
content:
T wo significant things happened in January 2007. Apple unveiled the iPhone to the world. In Ireland, the government formally decided to build a new national children’s hospital , and promised it would be ready by 2011.
So how has that turned out, almost 20 years on? The iPhone has revolutionised how people live and redefined communication; more than three billion of them have been sold around the globe. The children’s hospital – well, we’re still waiting, and we don’t even know when it will open.
How can that be? How can a project everyone supported and desperately wanted be arriving so late? How is it that the hospital is going to cost a multiple of what we were originally promised? What does this mean for other big projects in the offing – the new National Maternity Hospital and MetroLink , for a start? And, more generally, how we run our country?
Stranger still is the lack of outrage at the waste of money. The media has, by and large, switched off on this story; the Opposition too. The public, fed a circular narrative of ‘Bam [the main contractor] versus hospital development board’, shows little interest. As Paul Weller sang so long ago, “the public wants what the public gets”.
But then Irish public life has become pretty surreal in the third decade of the 21st century. Billions of euros flow into the public coffers from international tax arrangements. We hardly have to worry about funding the present, though we’re fearful about the future. What if the tech tax pipeline gets switched off? Will we wait till then to start bemoaning the waste incurred on public projects? And our failure to even start other much-needed pieces of infrastructure?
Public spending profligacy was a recurring theme in my journalistic career, from interminable tribunals to botched IT projects and repeated overspending in health. Small scandals – such as the Leinster House bike shed or the National Gallery printer – seem to catch the public imagination while larger overspends induce a weary shrug of the shoulders.
Like Paul Weller, however, “I don’t get what this society wants”. Overspending at the children’s hospital bugs me; it’s our money as citizens, my money even. So I started digging deeper into the project, trying to understand what happened, interviewing dozens of people involved at various stages of its development. I talked to patients and their families, politicians, policymakers, builders and architects, on and off the record. I didn’t believe anyone deliberately set out to deliver an over-priced, massively-delayed hospital, but I wanted to see if the errors made could be identified and lessons learned.
The result is Billion Dollar Baby, a detailed but by no means exhaustive look at how the hospital is heading for a €3 billion pricetag and being completed a generation late. The problems on this project, I found, have roots going back many decades but which were made worse at nearly every turn through hubris, over-optimism, inattention to detail and institutional infighting. Many could have been avoided, or at least minimised.
I had lived with this story for many years. In 2014, I was the first journalist to tour the proposed site for the facility, which was then a jumble of old buildings and overgrown patches of weeds at the western end of St James’s Hospital. Even by then, the project had had a controversial history, marked by political machinations, resignations and money issues. The location had been changed once, but planning permission to build it southwest of the city centre had been granted two years earlier.
Gazing over the area from an elevated vantage point, the project director and I tried to imagine the giant building that was to arise on this spot. Ireland’s biggest construction project; a cutting-edge hospital for the sickest children. It was hard not to be excited at this impending symbol of the country’s modernisation.
After that visit, the site was cleared and an enormous hole was dug for the foundations of the hospital. But for a long time, and with apologies for the punning, nothing concrete appeared above the hoardings. Something was amiss.
[ Delay of children’s hospital would ‘impose considerable additional costs’, Minister warns Opens in new window ]
In 2018, rumours reached me of money problems at the hospital. Just as construction was due to get under way, I started hearing how the bill for the project was increasing by millions of euro every week. How the final cost of a hospital that started with a €650 million pricetag was now heading for well over €1 billion. How, if this continued, the building could become the most expensive hospital in the world.
While the public remained blithely in the dark, officials in several government departments were aware of the problem, I was told. Some had even given the increasingly grandiose project a nickname – the Edifice Complex.
At the time, I was living nearby. I would often cycle past the site hoardings, gaily decorated with computer-generated images showing happy patients and doctors inside the clean-edged concrete and glass of a brash building. There was a panel illustrating the timeline of the project, which was regularly updated, yet always seemed to be out of date as deadlines constantly slipped.
No one would confirm the rumours. No firm information was available, I was informed. Finally, in December 2018, the exact figures for the overrun were set down in a cabinet memo, which was leaked to this newspaper. In just six weeks, the officially cited cost of the project had grown by €400 million. And further increases were forecast.
These were telephone-book numbers, in an era when telephone directories still existed. Their revelation triggered a political firestorm. A plethora of reports and investigations was ordered. The government of the time tottered but ultimately survived. After all, as Leo Varadkar tells me in an interview for the book, “the hospital was always a ‘hundreds of millions problem’ rather than a ‘billions problem’ like Brexit or tax policy”.
Construction started – and so did further problems. Turmoil in the wider world intruded. Covid-19. The Ukraine War. The aforementioned Brexit. As costs further escalated, the development board and Bam, fell out in the most public manner and ended up suing each other.
Fast forward almost a decade, and the cost is officially estimated at €2.24 billion, though few would be surprised if the final bill reaches €3 billion. There is still no end date for a project that was promised over 20 years ago. The completion date at St James’s has been delayed almost 20 times.
In 1919, Kathleen Lynn founded St Ultan’s children’s hospital in Dublin with £70 in the bank and two cots in a room. Over a century later, the national children’s hospital will open at some point with almost 480 beds and an operating budget likely to exceed €1 billion a year. It is not the most expensive hospital in the world, we are officially told.
I toured the as yet incomplete facility earlier this year. On the day of my visit, the vast interior space was eerily silent save for the sound of beeping alarms. The only people traversing the tiled ground-floor concourse were building workers and delivery staff kitted out in hard hats, high-vis jackets and plastic shoe-covers. The planned shops and food outlets along the concourse remained boarded up and empty.
The architecture is impressive, the materials used top-notch. The design, encompassing generous use of granite, glass and aluminium, shouts ‘no expense spared’. There are generous play areas between each finger of the building, a ‘meadow garden’ sits at the end of the concourse, a state-of-the-art hydrotherapy pool and gyms on upper floors, a rooftop helipad.
Standing above the atrium, the real meaning of the building can be gleaned not from these fancy elements, but from the fresh air in front of me – four storeys of it rising up from the entrance area and three more above me. This is dead space that would never exist in a private facility, the clearest expression that this is a statement building, designed to boost the morale of citizens. As my guide for the day remarked, “this is the sort of thing you see in Dubai”.
The building is a wonder, and I wish it well. But my concerns won’t go away once it opens. It will be expensive to operate, staff and expand. The job of amalgamating staff from different institutions with different work cultures is a mammoth undertaking, as the ongoing scandals at Children’s Health Ireland show. There is little sign that the promised maternity hospital will be built on the St James’s site in the near future, though this tri-location of adult, children’s and maternity hospital is regarded as the gold standard for patient care.
This is the story of a building but with patients at its heart. For many years, children’s care was the Cinderella of Irish health. Extremely sick patients were – and still are – being treated in often crumbling facilities in our existing, dilapidated children’s hospitals. With the hospital being completed almost a generation late, something like 900,000 children have missed out on the chance of being treated in it. Meanwhile, at a rough estimate, about 5,000 social homes could have been built with the over-spend on the project, or more than 1,500 hospital beds. Depending on what eventually happens in the courts between Bam and the development board, the final overrun on this project could be higher than currently projected.
The story of the children’s hospital, in all its twists and turns, its shocks and reverses, fascinates and appals in equal measure. It is a story about Dublin, and great rivalries in a small place. About promises that were made to a generation of children who, ultimately, were let down by the delays that occurred. It touches on medicine and money, obviously, but also politics, religion, academia and business.
Current headlines tell us only part of the story; the project’s problems have their roots in decisions and events from years, even decades, ago. Overspending, delays and underestimation of costs occurred well before Bam got involved. One minister summed it up pithily as “the wrong design, on the wrong site, contracted in the wrong way and built by the wrong main contractor”.
Most of all, this story is about people; families who have been let down too often before, and whose children have had to wait far too long for the world-class hospital in which they were promised they would receive treatment.
Paul Cullen is a former health editor of The Irish Times. Billion Dollar Baby – How Ireland Built Its National Children’s Hospital – At Any Cost, is published by Hachette Ireland

title: Are many Irish homeowners undervaluing the cost of rebuilding their homes by €83,000?
description: Thousands of Irish homes are inadvertently insured for tens of thousands less than it would cost to rebuild them
content:
There’s nothing like a big number to frighten consumers, especially when it comes to them being left out of pocket at a time of crisis.
Insurer Outsurance this week estimated that many homeowners could be undervaluing the cost of rebuilding or replacing their homes by about €83,000
Underinsurance can very quickly turn a drama into a financial crisis. Bad enough to have your home hit by flood, fire or other catastrophe without discovering your insurer will not cover the cost of putting things right.
People assume that if they have, say, €400,000 of insurance cover, any claim up to that value will be met. But that’s not the way it works.
If the cost of rebuilding your home is €600,000 but you only have cover for two-thirds of that (€400,000), the insurer will only cover two-thirds of every claim – even one for say €20,000 to repair flood damage – leaving homeowners thousands of euro out of pocket.
No one actually knows how pervasive the problem is.
Back in 2021, the Central Bank of Ireland sent a shot across insurers’ bows after a study by its staff discovered the level of underinsurance had surged from 6.5 per cent in 2017 to 16.5 per cent – not far short of 400,000 homes.
That figure, like the Outsurance average, emerged only from an analysis of actual claims made. We have no way of knowing how many others are underinsured. That’s not helped by the insurers themselves, Outsurance included, being remarkably coy on the subject.
In answer to a parliamentary question late last year, then minister for finance Paschal Donohoe said the figure had fallen to 10.7 per cent in 2024. Even if that claim reflects the wider market, there are still more than 230,000 homeowners at risk.
As Bank of Ireland noted in 2026, the trend over recent years to invest in upgrading and extending properties, including retrofits, solar panels and the like, could be making things worse.
All increase the rebuilding cost in case of disaster, but the bank found that six in 10 homeowners never update their insurance details after investing to improve their homes.
With winter looming, now would be a good time to make sure you have the cover you think you have ... before anything goes wrong.

title: David Byrne: ‘This last tour equalled and sometimes surpassed what happened with Talking Heads’
description: The art rockers felt they were the next big thing. But tastes change. Who determines what’s popular, and where do the ideas they champion come from?
content:
David Byrne is in the spare bedroom – also a music room – of his apartment in New York.
The 74-year-old writer, musician and onetime frontman of Talking Heads, almost fills my screen with his shock of white hair and a blue shirt, but behind him I can see cardboard boxes piled up on a metal shelf and the headstocks of an electric guitar and a bass.
He pauses frequently as he speaks, but on the page his words turn into perfectly coherent, thoughtful paragraphs. His speaking style reminds me a lot of his singing.
His new book, Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up, is a fascinating look at the way concepts from the worlds of art and science and philosophy can be forgotten for decades, centuries, even millenniums before being rediscovered through pure luck or the vagaries of a changing zeitgeist. (At the start of each chapter Byrne estimates how long each idea was “asleep”.)
It’s meticulously written and researched, and Byrne’s passion for it is infectious. When I bring up artists or scientists from the book he responds with a delighted “Yes!”, as though I were introducing the subject randomly and not because he had introduced me to them in his writing. When I tell him my 13-year-old nephew loved his rain- and windswept Dublin gig in June he looks very amused.
The phrase “sleeping beauties” was first used by the researcher Anthony van Raan in 2004 to describe formerly ignored but consequential science papers.
“I loved the term,” Byrne says. “It seemed to really resonate, and I immediately thought, ‘Oh, this applies beyond science.’ So I started collecting. I’d read about something or hear about something. If I told people that I was working on this, they’d say, ‘Oh, do you know about..?’ I was kind of down the rabbit hole.”
Some artists hate the idea of analysing creative output, thinking it erodes the magic. Byrne, whose earthy grooves have always come with a side order of art-rock intellectualism, does not agree.
“I enjoy asking why something’s popular, why something is the way it is, why it ended up like this and not like something else,” he says. “Delving into that, I don’t think it takes away from the pleasure or the wonder or the awe of listening to a piece of music or reading something or a scientific discovery. I think it actually deepens it. Knowing how a car engine works doesn’t affect how you can drive.”
Sometimes an idea can be discarded because it doesn’t fit the dominant ideology of the time, he says. In the book he writes about the way the biologist Lynn Margulis’s discovery that interorganism symbiosis was a key part of evolution was ignored for decades.
“I’m probably biased towards co-operation as opposed to competition as a valid engine for creativity and things being discovered,” he says. “But for many decades it’s been pushed aside, and in business, science and the arts the idea has been dominant that competition drives things.
“But some of these scientists and sociologists and evolutionary people discovered that sometimes animals or plants or cells co-operate, and sometimes they actually become a new entity by co-operation. They have this symbiotic union that happens, and their odds of survival increase that way.”
Margulis’s idea ran against the grain. “By that time the idea of survival of the fittest got in some ways perverted to survival of the strongest. She was showing us that it’s not the only way. Sometimes something new comes into being because of co-operation.
“Businesspeople like to think, I’m successful because I’m smarter than the others. Sometimes you were just meaner or lucky. They tend not to give luck much credit.”
Luck is another theme of the book. “Sometimes it’s just the wrong thing in the wrong place, and then [years later] someone stumbles on it.”
Another of the reasons innovations get ignored is prejudice, Byrne says. In the 1940s the abstract artist Janet Sobel “started doing work on these abstract paintings. It was just this texture of paint and splatters and all this kind of thing. She’d lay the canvas on the floor of her apartment.”
Her son “connected her with other well-known artists at the time, and she got some gallery shows and was to some extent well accepted. However, with the art world there was a sexism involved, and a sense that she was not part of the boys’ club.
“She was described as a ‘housewife in Brighton Beach’, which was a put-down, like she was not a serious artist.”
Sobel made a painting called Milky Way; shortly afterwards, Jackson Pollock made a very similar work, called Galaxy.
“It’s pretty clear that Jackson Pollock saw her work and within a year or so he was doing almost exactly the same thing,” Byrne says. “He’s held in very high regard. Not to take anything away from him, but it really seems obvious that he got anointed, probably because he was a macho guy. She was kind of pushed aside.”
Some work is sidelined because the creators themselves thought it too odd in the context of their time, such as the dark and fantasmagoric pieces of art that have become known as Goya’s “black paintings”, which he kept on the walls of his own house rather than intending them for public consumption.
“He might have thought: I have to do this – I have to speak to the world as I see it – but I also understand that there might not be any interest from the public. What really mystifies me, sometimes, is where [an artist says]: I’m not going to show it to anyone; I’m going to keep it just for myself.”
“I’ve tended to take the evolutionary point of view that making art or writing or doing any of those kinds of things is a form of display, like a bird’s plumage or a peacock’s tail, and that you make those things and you put them out because it’s your way of connecting with other people and announcing who you are and what you’re about,” he says.
“You exist because they see what you’ve done. But then there’s people who decide: No, I’m never going to show this to anyone.”
“That defeats that whole evolutionary idea.”
Perhaps this approach to art is more a form of processing than display.
“I think so too,” he says. “I think it’s self-processing. I realised that this has its own rewards, and the reward doesn’t have to be public acceptance or putting it out there. It can be internal.
“You’re having a dialogue with yourself and exploring how you feel about things – what interests you, whether it’s literature or paintings or whatever else. And in that case you don’t crave public acceptance. It’s its own reward, which kind of tempts me to revise my thinking.”
Has this changed Byrne’s approach to making art? He chuckles. Not yet.
“A lot of the work that I do is kind of public facing. But, yes, I also realise now that I’m getting my own kind of personal enjoyment out of that creation, whether it’s the creation of a performance, a show, or this book, or drawings I’ve done. There’s an enjoyment in just putting it there.”
Byrne had some experience of this with drawings he made during the pandemic (although he did subsequently release them for public view). “I didn’t know what they were about when I was doing it, and then, afterwards, I realised [I was] talking to myself about what it felt like during the pandemic.”
[ David Byrne: ‘I couldn't write songs during the depth of the pandemic’ Opens in new window ]
Sleeping Beauties is a rejection of the notion that progress is always linear. There’s an idea, he says, that knowledge accumulates, “and once we’ve learned something, or discovered how to do something, that it adds to this vast storehouse, and these stories make it evident that that is sometimes the case. But just as often things get forgotten.
“Sometimes the thing that actually solves the problem or is really wonderful or beautiful or moving existed in the past and needs to be renovated and rediscovered.”
Byrne rejects modernist hubris. He notes that Roman concrete, for example, was longer-lasting and environmentally friendlier than the version revived by the modern world.
“Sometimes there was a better way in the past, and we have to swallow our pride a little bit and go: Maybe we can learn from that.”
The book includes lots of scientific examples. This feels relatively unusual coming from an artist.
“When I was younger I really debated whether I should go into the sciences or the arts,” Byrne says. “The arts seem to promise a more creative reward faster. With the science it seemed like you had to go through many years before you got to actually experiment and try things out and be creative.
“But, at the same time, the sciences are in many ways just as creative as the arts are, but the emphasis on proofs and predictions and quantitative measurements and all this kind of thing – the arts don’t have that, really.”
“People would like it if they did. People would like to maybe judge a painting by how it sells at Sotheby’s.”
But we can’t, Byrne says. In the 19th century, he points out, art dealers could barely give Caravaggio paintings away, but then, in 2019, his work Judith Beheading Holofernes was valued at up to €150 million or so. “And it’s the same painting. It hasn’t changed.”
Popularity or price or sales figures are never a true gauge of worth, Byrne says.
“Something that, on its own, has a very small audience or reaches a very small public can have a disproportionate influence on other people. We all know records that didn’t sell very well but had a huge influence on lots of other people.
“I used Tom Zé” – the Brazilian Tropicália musician whose albums Byrne was involved in reissuing in the 1990s – “as an example, but there were really obvious ones, like The Velvet Underground .” Byrne included their royalty statement in his book How Music Works. “It was pretty miserable, and yet they had a huge influence.”
Has he seen evidence of the sleeping-beauty phenomenon in his own career? He laughs.
“I’ve been doing music for long enough that I’ve seen my career and acceptance or public awareness go up and down.”
“Judging by my last concert tour, which I just finished on Saturday, after a year, the venues we were playing and the kind of reaction that the audiences had, it equalled and sometimes surpassed what happened with Talking Heads.
“So I realise there are moments when something becomes relevant or is accepted or is exciting to the public and moments when ... not so much.”
What does Byrne put his current popularity down to?
“I’m going to give some credit to streaming in my case,” he says. “I have a lot of problems with streaming income and what artists make from all that, but I think it’s had a positive effect in that it doesn’t cost anyone anything to check something out, to try something and see if they like it or not.
“There’s also, in streaming, a lack of contextual information. You don’t automatically know, ‘Oh, when was this done? What’s the context? Did people like it at the time?’ All those kinds of things are missing. It’s just you and maybe some of your friends who are listening and going, ‘Oh, I like that.’ You’ve just stumbled on it. So you find younger audiences.”
In the early, punk-influenced era of his career, Byrne and Talking Heads had a role in putting the prog rockers, his immediate forefathers, to sleep.
“I think there was an unspoken feeling we were going to topple the giants,” he says. “Not that we ever did or would, but there was a feeling: These dinosaurs have to go.”
And now the prog music they were deciding to topple is coming back, like a sleeping beauty. He laughs.
“It’s coming back! It’s really popular again.”
He refers to the Canadian band Angine de Poitrine in this context but adds, “They’re doing it in a more punk DIY way.”
[ David Byrne: ‘I see new chicanery every day’ Opens in new window ]
Punk’s DIY ethos is still at the core of what Byrne does. He never had conventional musical training. “I bought songbooks. I still have a lot of them up there.” He gestures to an out-of-shot shelf to his right. “I have a Burt Bacharach songbook and a Bob Dylan songbook and a Beatles songbook and Cole Porter .
“I’d start with the simple ones and teach myself through other people’s songs. ‘Oh, this is how it’s constructed. Oh, this is how it’s made. You can go from this chord to this one.’ I highly recommend that kind of approach.
“Often when you go to music school you’re playing scales and playing an instrument that might be really difficult, and you don’t get the visceral reward of, ‘Ah, I can sing a song with this.’
“Whereas taking really simple things and learning them, you get feedback and a reward for yourself right away. With three chords or two chords, you can do something. You can express yourself and actually connect to people with very simple means.”
This approach has taken Byrne a long way. He’ll be on the road again in November, doing events around the book. Right now he’s relaxing at home after the long tour. “It’s a big physical and emotional reorientation for me, as it always is.”
What’s that process of post-tour reorientation like?
“Some of it’s very mundane. You come home and find, ‘My printer’s broken!’ There’s a lot of that mundane stuff.”
Will he then start a new project? He nods.
“When I get my printer fixed. When I get the bathroom door to actually lock.” He laughs. “I don’t know yet. It’s early.”
Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up is published by Canongate

title: Menopause and weight gain: What you can do about a ‘frustrating’ symptom
description: Average weight gain in perimenopause is 1.5kg per year, with excess abdominal fat bringing health concerns
content:
Thickening waist, spare tyre, muffin top or meno belly; call it what you will, but body fat changes can be an alarming feature of the mid-life hormone shift for even the most body-positive woman.
“It is the number one symptom that will trigger a woman to call me,” says nutritional therapist Rachel Graham. “She may be dealing with a host of other symptoms, but it is weight gain that is really frustrating and annoying.” This is not just about appearance; excess abdominal fat is a health concern.
Menopause is, technically, only a moment in time: the 12-month mark after a woman’s last period. The average age of menopause in Ireland is 51. But fluctuating levels of oestrogen and progesterone begin to disrupt the menstrual cycle years before that, during the perimenopause . Symptoms can include hot flushes, anxiety, disturbed sleep, reduced sex drive and brain fog, as well as weight gain. Some of these may wane or disappear post-menopause, but from then the impact of low oestrogen on long-term health is of increased concern.
The end of fertility often coincides with other midlife challenges, such as juggling work with caring for children or teenagers and possibly parents too. As stress, anxiety and disturbed sleep morph into continual fatigue, women are bombarded with conflicting social media advice on everything they should be doing to future proof their bodies. If only they had the time and the energy.
“A stressed body is a perfect environment for fat storage,” says Graham, whose mantra is “nourish your body, don’t punish it”. Doubling down on efforts to cut calories is unlikely to work and can backfire, she warns.
“When you restrict, your body reads this as a threat. It is going to hold on to fat rather than releasing it. What your body needs now isn’t less, it’s more of the right things – optimised levels of nutrients.”
Graham did not initially recognise signs of her own perimenopause. At age 43, she was working in the food business but also studying nutritional therapy at the College of Naturopathic Medicine. Frustrated at her inability to concentrate, as well as noticing a sharp increase in appetite while studying, she started to apply some of what she was learning to herself.
[ Mariella Frostrup on menopause: ‘I thought I was losing the plot’ Opens in new window ]
“I was really optimising all of the nutrients and foods that support brain function. It genuinely worked.” On completion of her nutritional therapy course, she trained to be a medicinal chef, learning about required dosages of nutrients and how to use food in the management of lifestyle-related health issues.
“I poured all of that experience into writing my own menopause cookbook.” What was intended to be a short e-book for her clients “grew legs” into a 400-page document, which she self-published. It then came to the attention of Irish publisher Gill Books, which has now brought out a paperback edition of Nourish for Menopause.
Dr Louise Fitzgerald, a GP at Grafton Medical in Dublin with a special interest in women’s health and the menopause, regards diet as an essential part of managing the menopause transition. She too likes to look at what can be added in, particularly fibre, rather than focusing on what might come out.
“The average weight gain in perimenopause is 1.5kg per year – so in perimenopause, you gain on average 10kg,” she says, acknowledging this will not be the case for all women. Doctors can prescribe hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and non-hormonal medications to ease symptoms, but this “is not going to have a direct impact on dropping those kilos”. However, it will help if the treatment improves mood and energy levels. Aside from menopausal symptoms, there is also the long-term effect of underlying changes to consider, such as a rise in cholesterol, higher blood pressure, and increased fragility.
“Oestrogen is our superpower,” says Fitzgerald. Once women go through menopause, they have much lower levels of oestrogen, and are at a higher risk of heart attacks and strokes, as well as osteoporosis, a disease that weakens bones.
She will always point out to patients that a dual approach is needed: what they can do, around diet, lifestyle, exercise, and what she can prescribe. Muscle loss, which not only reduces physical strength but also impairs calorie-burning ability, accelerates through menopause and beyond. This can be slowed down through resistance training, and doctors should cover this in consultations, she says.
“I was at a talk recently, and the doctor rather shockingly said, ‘Who tells people about diet, lifestyle, exercise any more? That’s so old-fashioned’.” The implication was that prescribing the new generation of weight-loss drugs looks after that now.
[ Relationships and ... menopause: ‘Small gestures of love can go a long way during this time of change’ Opens in new window ]
Fitzgerald might prescribe these if appropriate for a menopausal patient who asks about them, but she would rarely suggest them. For a start, to counteract muscle loss, people at this stage of life need to eat at least 1g of protein per kilogram of their weight every day, which is a huge amount for somebody with a suppressed appetite.
Eating sufficient fibre is also a challenge for those on weight-loss medication, says Gillian McConnell, a dietitian registered with the health regulator Coru. Furthermore, lack of desire for liquids as well as food compounds the problem of constipation.
McConnell works at a specialist menopause and women’s health clinic, Rose Clinic Bray in Co Wicklow, and runs Inside Out Nutrition in Sandyford, Dublin. She welcomes how some GPs now refer patients to a dietitian before prescribing weight-loss medication, because overall nutritional adequacy is a big issue.
In managing menopause, Graham is not averse to HRT, which she uses herself, but regards as the “icing on the cake”. It needs the firm foundation of good nutrition , as well as lifestyle measures of protecting sleep, managing stress, staying active, getting daily sunlight, drinking enough water and staying connected socially, she says.
So what should the nutritional priorities be at this stage of life? In her book, Graham outlines “the meno eight”. For every category, she suggests recipes, each of which comes with a breakdown of the 16 main nutrients it contains – and no mention of calories.
“When you take calories out of the conversation entirely and replace them with the nutrients, the calories essentially take care of themselves,” she argues. The theory is that nourishing food is naturally more filling and satisfying. “You will find that you will be able to maintain a healthy weight and/or lose weight, if that is your goal.”
Even if life might seem way too busy for much cooking, never mind tracking nutrients, being aware of food types to focus on for menopause wellbeing is a good start. Here are Graham’s eight:
Why: to counteract muscle loss that is accelerated not only by increasing age but also reduced oestrogen. Protein is slower to digest and dampens down the hunger hormone. McConnell stresses it should be part of every meal and any snack in between. She suggests aiming for between 1g and 1.6g of protein per kilo of bodyweight a day.
Good sources: a small chicken fillet, steak or salmon darne will provide at least 25g; suggested choices for breakfast include eggs (7g each) and Greek yogurt (10g in a 100g serving). Graham recommends increasing plant rather than animal protein; think, for instance, tofu (10g in 125g portion), quinoa, black beans, kidney beans and lentils. For a snack, combine fruit with a handful of nuts.
Why: to improve gut and heart health, as well as blood-sugar regulation. It not only eases movement of food through the gut but also boosts beneficial intestinal bacteria. As oestrogen drops, lubrication in the gut dries up and the bowel is more sluggish, increasing the likelihood of constipation and bloating, says McConnell. Prolonged transit time of faecal matter “also extends exposure to various toxins, waste and cancer-causing compounds in the intestines”, says Graham. Fibre is key to lowering cholesterol, while its “filling” effect helps in weight management.
Good sources: an estimated 80 per cent of people in Ireland do not eat enough fibre, with up to 35g a day recommended. That’s the equivalent of eight apples (with the skin on) but meals should be built around a variety of high-fibre options such as whole grains, beans, nuts, seeds, other fruits and vegetables. If increasing from a low base, take it slowly.
Why: these are plant compounds that mimic the effects of oestrogen and can help regulate body temperature. They also have a mild binding effect on the body’s oestrogen receptors, which “weakens the cancer-causing potential of old circulating oestrogen”, says Graham.
Good sources: soybeans, alfalfa sprouts, flaxseed (also known as linseed), nuts and wholegrains.
Why: these essential fatty acids are “good fats” and an important part of a healthy diet. Omega-3 is particularly linked with brain health; it can also reduce inflammation and reduce the risk of heart disease.
Good sources: oily fish such as salmon, mackerel and sardines; aim for two helpings a week. Also flaxseed, a “superfood” with other benefits.
Why: to “deal with the ‘exhaust fumes’ of life: pollution, toxins, chemicals, nutritional deficiencies and even stress”, says Graham.
Good sources: this is where “eating the rainbow” comes in. Differently coloured plants have different phytochemicals, which help to protect against cancer, so choose a variety of fruit and vegetables by their colours. Other antioxidant foods include nuts, seeds, green tea and even chocolate – the higher the percentage of cocoa solids the better for flavonoids.
Why: to boost beneficial bacteria in the gut. Fermentation of foods enhances nutrient content and makes them easier to digest.
Good sources: live yogurt, sourdough bread, kombucha, apple cider vinegar and sauerkraut.
Why: these very important minerals work together to protect bones. Insufficient calcium contributes to osteoporosis and high blood pressure. Symptoms of magnesium deficiency are similar to those of the menopause, says Graham. They include muscle cramps and twitches, fatigue, anxiety and constipation.
Good sources: in addition to dairy, plant foods with beneficial levels of calcium include seaweed, leafy greens and legumes. Magnesium is found in dried seaweed and herbs, nuts, seeds and grains.
Why: eating vegetables that belong to the cruciferous family helps to reduce the severity of symptoms such as hot flushes and night sweats. A higher intake is linked to lower rates of cancers, such as those of the colon, breast and lung, as they contain compounds that can boost the effect of enzymes on counteracting carcinogens.
Good sources: cauliflower, broccoli, kale and cabbage.

title: Andrew Scott could be unbeatable at the Oscars. Unless this happens
description: Academy Award nerds are already engraving the Elsinore star’s name on the best-actor trophy. All that stands in his way are pesky other actors
content:
A lmost exactly a year ago I wrote about the premiere of Chloé Zhao’s Hamnet at Telluride Film Festival. The adaptation of Maggie O’Farrell ’s death-clouded meditation on the origins of Hamlet went down a storm at the Colorado event, but it was Jessie Buckley , heartbreaking as Agnes Shakespeare, who received the most vigorous praise.
A good five months out from the Oscars ceremony, premature tipsters declared her (correctly, as it transpired) unbeatable in the best-actress category.
The comparisons with Telluride 2026 could hardly be spookier. Andrew Scott , a fellow Irish performer, arrived there last month as the star of another film about Hamlet that also sees the protagonist engage with mortality.
Simon Stone’s Elsinore focuses on Ian Charleson, the Scottish actor best known from the film Chariots of Fire, as he prepares to take over from Daniel Day-Lewis in Richard Eyre’s storied 1989 staging of Hamlet at the National Theatre in London. Charleson, who had Aids, managed 24 hugely praised performances before the illness overcame him.
The reviews for Scott could hardly have been warmer. “Andrew Scott triumphs as Ian Charleson,” Dave Calhoun wrote in Screen Daily. Variety felt he gave “an astonishingly layered and moving performance”.
A starting gun was fired in the Hollywood Reporter. To that point, Scott Feinberg regarded John Malkovich, star of Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, as “the clear front-runner to win the best actor Oscar”. Not any more. “By Friday evening, when Elsinore had its world premiere in Telluride, I was forced to revise my hypothesis,” he wrote.
Art is not a sport. Grading films by their performances at awards ceremonies is a vulgarian’s game. But there is no escaping the attention around the Oscars. Celebrating their centenary in 2028, they remain the gongs that matter the most. Should Scott triumph in best actor he will join a list that includes Clark Gable, Jimmy Stewart, Laurence Olivier, Marlon Brando and on and on.
Who is the greatest film actor never to have won that Oscar? Maybe Peter O’Toole. Maybe Richard Burton.
Scott will have opportunities for some throat-clearing annoyance over the next few months.
“I’m going to make a pitch for getting rid of the phrase ‘openly gay’,” he said with a wry smile during Oscar season in 2024. “It’s an expression that you only ever hear in the media.”
The Guardian, shortly after Elsinore’s Telluride premiere, minded its language as it wondered if he would become “the first out gay man to win the best actor Oscar”. The Independent, alas, had missed the memo . “A win would make Scott the first openly gay actor to win the prize,” it explained this month.
Expect more of this as the weeks progress. Expect nobody to speculate about him being the third “openly Irish” performer to win the lead-actor prize.
So is the win sewn up? Catherine Shoard certainly thought so in that Guardian piece, writing that he is “almost certain to take the prize next spring”.
This is the view of neither the bookmakers nor the quaintly obsessive fanatics who contribute to awards sites all year long. One of our busiest turf accountants has had Malkovich and Scott joint favourites at 11/8. Over on Next Best Picture, a smoothly run awards site, nine of 17 contributors have Malkovich winning and six have Scott taking the prize. (Matt Damon for The Odyssey and Tom Cruise for Digger garner one vote each.)
[ First Look review: In Elsinore, Andrew Scott shows why he’s one of the great actors of our age Opens in new window ]
A lot may change when the critics’ circles and the professional guilds begin handing out nominations in a month or two, but it does look as if we have a gripping two-horse race on our hands.
The shape is deceptively familiar. Malkovich, sly and eccentric in the McDonagh film, is, at 72, the “overdue veteran” who is set to finally get his prize. Scott is the young gun on a first nomination.
Deceptive? Well, yes. Scott, born in 1976, has been delivering strong performances for a quarter of a century. He made his screen debut in Cathal Black’s film Korea, from 1995. He secured worldwide attention on TV as a sprightly Moriarty, in Sherlock, from 2010.
No stranger to the chatshow couch, he has, over that period, showed great capacity to charm and divert interviewers. As the awards season progresses, that charisma will win over more and more voters.
It also matters (though it shouldn’t) that his character in Elsinore is more empathetic than Malkovich’s dying CIA killer in Wild Horse Nine. Mark the Dubliner down as marginal favourite.
Another great Irish Oscar moment might await. The most common practice over the years has been for the previous year’s winner of best actress to present that ceremony’s best-actor award. That would have Buckley passing over the statuette. Not a dry eye in the country.

title: Billion Dollar Baby: How national children’s hospital became a multibillion-euro project
description: Paul Cullen’s book examines the planning mistakes, disputes and spiralling costs behind a hospital that was once expected to open in 2011
content:
Willie Brown, the famously flamboyant mayor of San Francisco, was supremely relaxed about public projects that went way over budget. “If people knew the real cost from the start, nothing would ever be approved,” he claimed. “The idea is to get going. Start digging a hole and make it so big, there’s no alternative to coming up with the money to fill it in.”
Judging by Paul Cullen’s calmly devastating study of the national children’s hospital scandal, some Irish policymakers have taken that advice to heart. Words alone cannot do justice to the scale of this ever-deepening money pit. You have to use figures too, such as a €500 million price tag and a 2011 opening date spiralling into the best part of €3 billion and late 2027 – if we’re lucky.
Paschal Donohoe, finance minister for much of this period, has said “not managing the hospital better” is his greatest regret. Norah Casey, a former member of the development board, calls it “the most dispiriting project I have ever been involved with”. David Gunning, its current chief officer, admitted to an Oireachtas committee in 2023 that “the optimism has been beaten out of all of us”.
As a health correspondent (now retired) for The Irish Times , Cullen covered this story from the days when it was just a twinkle in some doctors’ eyes. Billion Dollar Baby (if only), however, is far more than a rehash of his journalistic output. It contains striking new interviews with medics, politicians (including three former taoisigh) and international consultants, all offering trenchant opinions on how a facility “once set to be named after a phoenix became an albatross” around so many necks instead.
At least this sorry saga begins with a consensus: the hospital is desperately needed. Paediatrics has long been the “Cinderella of health”, Cullen recounts, largely split between crumbling, warren-like buildings in Crumlin and Temple Street with “chronic infighting over resources”. If you could understand Crumlin’s funding structure, its ex-chairman and former archbishop of Dublin Diarmuid Martin tells the author, “you can explain the Blessed Trinity.”
[ Delay of children’s hospital would ‘impose considerable additional costs’, Minister warns Opens in new window ]
While the Royal College of Physicians first proposed a merger of children’s services in 1993, it was Celtic Tiger headiness that made it seem feasible. Cullen emphasises the hospital was to be a symbol of Irish modernity with no expense spared, “payback time” for our historic poverty. “There was a huge amount of hubris around,” recalls the leading paediatrician Gerry Loftus. “People were saying, ‘We have one chance to get it right,’ so they went all in… everything just ballooned after that.”
Even before Bertie Ahern ’s government formally approved the hospital in 2007, its task group had made an ominous blunder. The Mater campus site it chose was widely condemned as too small and inaccessible, while this newspaper’s late environmental editor Frank McDonald nicknamed the ocean liner-like blueprint “The Incredible Hulk”. Accusations of pork-barrel politics and a “northside job” poisoned the atmosphere, although Cullen scrupulously concludes that they had no basis in reality.
Five wasted years later, An Bord Pleanála refused planning permission and development costs of about €50 million disappeared down the drain. St James’s Hospital was quickly drafted as a replacement home, but attracted near-identical complaints.
“We made a bit of a bags of it,” is what Pat Kenny, St James’s biggest media critic, wishes the political establishment would accept. Bertie Ahern doesn’t go quite that far, although tellingly he concedes: “If I had my way, I’d have favoured one children’s hospital on each side of the city. The idea of one location is wrong.”
Cullen’s 367-page narrative compiles a grim litany of design oversights, unexpected bills and board resignations, all dissected with clinical precision. He pinpoints minister for health James Reilly’s creation of the separate Children’s Hospital Group as another key mistake. This split governance model added expertise but also spawned what one insider dubs a responsibility-ducking “pantomime horse… a recipe for disaster”.
“Oh God, not Bam,” was Leo Varadkar’s private reaction in 2016 upon hearing that the building contract had been awarded to the Dutch firm. Since then Bam has lodged 3,407 cost claims worth almost €1 billion, sparking an interminable blame game between contractor and client.
Cullen’s personal inspection of the site confirms that it will be spectacular when finished, but even here experts disagree on whether luxuries such as a “Rainbow Garden” the length of Croke Park are really justified. “Areas where children can look at trees and grass, it sounds nice,” says an HSE communications adviser. “But when you’re sick, you’re sick.”
Billion Dollar Baby ends by acknowledging this is not the final word, since many official documents about the hospital’s progress (or lack of it) remain unreleased. One day, Cullen argues, there must be a full-blown public inquiry. Until then, his own sober, meticulous chronicle of incompetence is the most accurate diagnosis available.
[ ‘My youngest child will probably be bearded before the national children’s hospital opens’ Opens in new window ]

title: The ‘Irish pope’ who was equally disliked by Irish patriots, Protestants and Britain
description: Rite & reason: When Clonliffe was sold, Cullen’s remains had to be moved. This was done quickly and discreetly on the morning of June 25th 2021
content:
W hen Paul Cullen, Ireland’s first Roman Catholic Cardinal, died in October 1878, he was widely understood to have been both the dominant Irishman of his generation and a figure of global importance.
The Times of London declared that for the previous 26 years: “No man in the kingdom has exercised a greater personal influence, or wielded more absolute power”; the New York Times called him “a power in the land” and the Sydney Freeman’s Journal published a six-page supplement commemorating his life. Requiem Masses were celebrated throughout the world, his coffin was drawn through the streets of Dublin in an open hearse, escorted by mounted police, and followed or observed by at least 100,000 people. Trains and trams were halted, flags were lowered, and the city ground to a halt.
Many thousands more paid their respects at the Pro-Cathedral (now St Mary’s Cathedral) in Marlborough Street before the gates were finally closed. When he was buried the next day in a small vault beneath the chapel of Clonliffe College, there could be no doubt at all that his had been a consequential life.
Some 143 years later, it was very different: Clonliffe had been sold, its contents auctioned, and the chapel closed. Cullen would have to be moved. This was done quickly and discreetly on the morning of June 25th 2021.
A brief service was held in the crypt, his remains were moved by van, and another brief service was held in the Pro-Cathedral. It was all over by 9.30am. The Irish Times noted the occasion in a short article. RTÉ’s news website allowed the event 210 words. Paul Cullen was no longer newsworthy.
This did not happen overnight. For many years Cullen’s importance was unquestioned, even if his legacy was contested. James Joyce mocked him as an “apple of God’s eye”, for example, and he is reputedly the only person never to have set foot on the Continent to have received an entry in the Dictionary of Australian Biography.
More than one old Fenian blamed him for Ireland’s continuing captivity. He was, as the Fenian novelist Charles J Kickham put it, “the deadly foe of Irish liberty.” Nor was it just nationalists who hated him.
Cullen accumulated an impressive range of enemies: Irish Protestants blamed him for despoiling their church (and less plausibly for introducing sectarianism to the island); the Catholic seminary at Maynooth loathed him as a Romanising tyrant (and even now does not own a portrait of him); and the two-time British prime minister Lord John Russell, was convinced that Cullen looked “to force as the true mode of restoring the supremacy of the Roman Church”.
As the idiosyncratic Sir Shane Leslie (who had himself briefly considered writing a biography of Cullen in the 1920s) put it: “At one time there was nothing too bad to be said of Cullen, even from his own countrymen.”
If nothing else, it must surely be a singular achievement to have been disliked in equal measure by Irish patriots, Irish Protestants, the British establishment, and St Patrick’s College, Maynooth. Cullen clearly mattered.
Yet, writing about Cullen is hard. There are masses of papers to work from – he is certainly the best documented Irishman of the 19th century – but they are in a formidably wide range of languages. (Cullen could read at least 10, including Arabic.) They are also widely distributed: for my book, The Irish Pope, I consulted more than 130 archives in 12 countries on five continents.
He is also a difficult subject: he had no vices, no lovers and no sense of humour. Only a tiny handful of people called him Paul, only one person could unquestionably be called his friend, and his only discernible hobby was reading about Ireland’s past.
His inner life is almost entirely unknown, even while we know what he did on an almost daily basis. Largely as a result there has never been a satisfactory biography.
Yet coming to grips with Cullen is crucial. He was the most important Irishman in the generation between the death of Daniel O’Connell and the rise of Charles Stewart Parnell.
Among other things, he bent the Irish church to his will, spread his own version of Irish Catholicism around the world, brought (now Saint) John Henry Newman to Dublin, crushed first the Independent Irish Party and then the Fenians, and proposed the formulation that defined the infallibility of the pope.
It was also because of Cullen, the American historian Emmet Larkin argued in 1972, that the “great mass of the Irish people became practising Catholics”.
Mid-Victorian Ireland can never be properly understood without sustained engagement with the man who stood at its political, social, and religious centre. As Leslie rightly noted of his own projected biography, “it would of course be writing the history of Ireland during the 50 years 1823-1878.”
Colin Barr is Professor of Modern Irish History, Keough-Naughton Institute for Irish Studies, University of Notre Dame, USA. His book The Irish Pope: Paul Cullen, 1803-1878 will be published in Dublin next Thursday

title: Páirc Uí Chaoimh crowd pay perfect tribute to Anthony Foley on emotional evening by the Lee
description: Fittingly it was the present-day Munster number eight Brian Gleeson who scored the game’s opening try in Cork
content:
In the municipal space that surrounds Páirc Uí Chaoimh Munster Rugby installed a pop-up exhibition of images from Anthony Foley’s career. Arranged in a montage, there were 24 pictures from each chapter of his rugby life. In every action shot the game was written on his face, just behind the mud flakes and the Desperate Dan stubble.
A middle-aged man stopped and pointed to the fresh-faced picture of Foley in a St Munchin’s jersey accepting the Munster Junior Cup, 27 years ago now. “I played against him for Rockwell,” he said, “and he was a one-man team. He played number eight, but he was taking all the goal kicks and all the kicks to touch. He was that team.”
Honouring Foley’s memory, on the 10th anniversary of his stunning death, had been the words and music of the build-up all week. The montage, though, was a reminder of another anniversary: it is 20 years since he captained Munster to win the Heineken Cup for the first time. The soul of that Munster team was in the pack and for years Foley was its pulse and its conscience.
