In the corner of the montage was an undated quote that must have been from around the time Foley retired. It read: “If I’m going to be remembered, I’d like to be seen as a stubborn player, someone who never gave in. Once there’s something to chase, I’ll chase it.”
In recent years, Munster have not always lived by that credo. This was not a night to break any of the old commandments.
For the pre-match formalities the Munster players took to the field in tracksuit tops adorned with the number eight, and the two team captains exchanged number eight jerseys in each other’s colours. But for the game Munster stood down the jersey, and Brian Gleeson wore number 24.
Munster’s first attack forced a five-metre scrum, and the Munster number eight ran a hard line on the short side, as Foley had done a million times. A minute later, in the eighth minute of the game, the crowd in both stands got to their feet in a choreographed ovation that grew into a heartfelt chorus of ‘Munster, Munster’.
There had been a late consensus in recent days that this game should have been played in Limerick, for understandable reasons. But the sound of an emotional Munster crowd is not pegged to one place.
The crowd of 24,906 was more than 11,000 smaller than Munster’s last Champions Cup game in Páirc Uí Chaoimh last season, but the atmosphere was better. Racing came with a team that was a mix of milk and water, but they had more than enough quality and power to make Munster suffer during those periods in the game when their concentration dropped and their error count spiked.
Munster don’t have the wherewithal to be a force in this competition, but they have the resources to be better than they were last season. There were flashes of creativity and cohesion that suggested the scope for growth.
Charlie O’Shea, on his European debut, and in just his fourth senior appearance, was at the heart of it. On a massive night in his young career, he was spunky and composed and bright. He is only a couple of inches taller than Craig Casey, and his 20-year-old frame is a little coltish and unfurnished still, but every time he was floored he bounced off the ground like a Jack Russell.
He took a hit under one box kick, in front of the Munster posts, but in the next play, when they tried to bomb him again, he made an exceptional catch with Wilfried Hulleu towering over him. It was a moment where he couldn’t afford to show weakness.
Five minutes before half-time O’Shea made a stunning, crossfield break, from one half into the other, and it wasn’t just his surging pace that was impressive, but his bullish desire to take the game to Racing. He wasn’t looking around for support or easing off the gas to allow other red shirts to catch up: everything about it was fast-forward and funded by attitude.
When he was replaced 17 minutes into the second half Munster’s lead was just three points and the visitors had enjoyed their most productive period in the game. The time that remained was a test of Munster’s game management and bottle.
A week ago in Belfast they had thrown away a massive lead and just after half-time here they were 15 points in front. Even at this early stage of the season, another implosion would have been damaging.
They rejected that possibility. When Racing were reduced to 14 men for the last 10 minutes Munster played out the game in the visitors’ half. With a minute left on the clock Casey finished off a lineout maul in the corner for their fifth try.
About seven or eight minutes after the final whistle, all the Munster players and staff gathered in a giant circle in the middle of the field and sang Stand Up and Fight. They only had one person in mind.

title: Champions Cup as it happened: Munster hold off Racing 92 for opening night victory
description: Champions Cup live: Leinster, Connacht and Munster all in action on first day of European competition
content:
Clermont Auvergne 23-48 Leinster ( Report here )
We’ll bid you oíche mhaith with Gerry Thornley’s match report from Cork. Thanks for joining us folks on a day that saw all four Irish provinces emerge victorious.
[ Munster honour Anthony Foley’s memory with victory over Racing 92 at Páirc Uí Chaoimh Opens in new window ]
Craig Casey confirming what was strongly suspected after that maul try that, really, he nabbed it when it should have been hooker van der Merwe’s score...
Player of the match Craig Casey after @Munsterrugby 's win this evening 🔴 "I was a bit greedy at the end, that's a forwards try, but I'll take it" 🗣️ #InvestecChampionsCup pic.twitter.com/WNgNYMaPRt
An emotional and poignant victory for Munster 10 years after the death of Anthony Foley.
The @Munsterrugby squad and management with a rendition of stand up and fight after their win vs Racing 92 tonight 🔴 An emotional night at Páirc Uí Chaoimh 🏟️ pic.twitter.com/ZROmxWIGzE
The last five penalties of the game all came in the final 10 minutes. All were conceded by Racing. Factor in the yellow card for Roche as well.
The overall penalty count was 11-9 with Racing the more heavily pinged side.
There is never just one factor behind a result, but discipline at crucial junctures went a long way to stopping Racing from completing their second-half comeback.
McCarthy spills and then the ball trickles into touch. Karl Dickson blows his whistle to end an enthralling contest.
No bonus point for Munster, but with this new system plenty of teams are missing out on the extra digit.
81 mins: Munster pinch the ball back from Racing and will try for one last attack.
They need one more try for a bonus point...
A driving maul inches towards the line. Instead of letting Marnus van der Merwe at hooker take the score, Casey wrestles the ball free and dives over himself.
Hanrahan pushes the conversion wide. We will have one last play.
Craig Casey to settle the nerves for @Munsterrugby fans 🔴 "Just what they needed, at just the right time" 🗣️ #InvestecChampionsCup pic.twitter.com/QQWuiAmvoY
78 mins: Munster get a penalty as Racing take a decoy runner out off the ball. Do Munster go for points, pad their lead, or kick to the corner and run the clock down?
Option B is taken. This is the game folks.
Beirne barges over the line with a latch from a teammate but Joey Manu gets underneath the ball. He’s been at the heart of everything positive for Racing tonight.
74 mins: I don’t know how Munster haven’t scored there.
It started with a sensational Hodnett offload to Casey, sending the scrumhalf away down the flank.
When Munster look to go the opposite way, going wide after hammering away at the line, they butcher the opportunity. But that was under advantage.
71 mins: Oh no. There’s a nasty collision between O’Connor and Roche in the air.
Both men are down having landed heavily. Replays show that Roche could be in trouble here.
Yep. He was never in a position to catch that ball and he takes O’Connor out. That’s a sloppy howler from Roche, ensuring Racing will finish a tight game down to 14.
68 mins: That was an awful passage of play. Poor kicks. Errors. Ball on the floor.
Until Racing spark into life. One offload from James, then another ball over the top of the defender and Racing break down the right hand side, Manu battling past O’Connor to score in the corner.
Gibert then converts brilliantly from the touchline.
60 mins: Wycherley scores with his first touch of the ball. But that score is all down to Craig Casey.
Running with the ball close to the ruck, Casey just holds the ball long enough to draw the defender, leaving the ball in the air for Wycherley to run onto and no one can stop him from close range.
Fineen Wycherley with the instant impact 💪 @munsterugby 's fourth of the game 🔥 #InvestecChampionsCup pic.twitter.com/HE97QuZ58T
58 mins: That’s a big call. Charlie O’Shea has been pulled a shore just shy of the hour mark.
JJ Hanrahan is being asked to be the experienced hand to bring things home. Wycherley and Brookes also come into the frontrow for Loughman and Aungier.
53 mins: A maul try. The drive is well set and Munster can’t shut it down. Of all people, it’s the scrumhalf Machenaud who got his hands on the ball at the back of the maul.
Munster ring the changes in the backrow, Edogbo and Gleeson making way for O’Donoghue and Coombes.
50 mins: Racing go whooping and hollering after forcing a spill in contact. Sean Edogbo doesn’t like that and comes up trying to take on the entire Racing pack.
I tell you what, the look in Edogbo’s eyes there. Death stare would be putting it lightly.
He’s been good tonight Edogbo. No need to ruin it with an off-the-ball incident.
48 mins: That’s a soft score. Racing initially make a meal of their lineout, the ball falling to Hulleu in the backfield.
Running towards the Munster pack, he puts some footwork on Gleeson, forcing a missed tackle before sprinting off into the corner.
Good footwork, yes. Also a poor tackle attempt from Gleeson.
44 mins: A try created by youth, finished by experience. Edogbo was everywhere in that passage of play, hitting hard angles to break the gain line. O’Shea - surprise, surprise - also had a half break.
After all that momentum, it’s the old head Tadhg Beirne who is on hand to crash over from close range.
41 mins: We’re back underway in Cork, Munster leading by eight points. For what it’s worth, their one try short as it stands of a bonus point under the new rules.
Charlie O’Shea kicks us into the second half.
At times it’s been harem scarem from Munster. But that’s part of the charm. A strong scrum and carry from Brian Gleeson brought the first score, but a dropped pass was how the second fell to Shay McCarthy.
The rest of the time, Charlie O’Shea has been finding gaps, both fielding and dropping high balls and kicking to various pockets of space when he can. He’s been a joy to watch.
A word too for the breakdown. Nankivell and Beirne have both been brilliant at poaching ball.
After kicking to the corner, Munster spill the lineout. That is that for the first half.
41 mins: Munster are swarming. And it’s that man O’Shea again at the heart of everything.
It starts with an O’Brien intercept. He gets caught, but once the ball is recycled, O’Shea kicks in behind.
Racing get back to gather but Munster blitz the breakdown, Nankivell winning a holding on penalty. Was he off his feet? Most certainly. Do Munster care?
36 mins: O’Shea. He is a young man loving his rugby at the moment.
The reason why this time? A line break from nowhere. A long ball to Nankivell on the flank, the only man close to supporting him, does hit the centre but not in stride. So the score doesn’t come yet. But Munster still have the ball.
That is until O’Shea kicks in behind, finding touch inside the 22.
31 mins: Third time lucky for O’Shea with an aerial contest.
This time, despite fierce pressure from Hulleu, the young outhalf gets up well to win the ball. He lands hard on his back, but he looks to be ok.
29 mins: It’s been a tricky few minutes for O’Shea. Tested again in the air from Gibert, he spills just metres from his own line.
Fortunately for Munster, Manu knocked-on while trying to gather. Had he taken it cleanly, try time.
26 mins: Gibert slots the penalty from the O’Shea error. It wasn’t far out but it was a tight angle over towards the touchline.
24 mins: That’s a shocker from O’Shea. Not a phrase we’ve said too many times since he’s burst onto the scene.
With no one contesting with him in the air, he spills a kick forward. What’s worse, after regathering, he holds on while on the floor, prompting referee Karl Dickson to give a penalty rather than scrum.
22 mins: Racing were just starting to build some momentum. A few more strong mauls, Munster penalties to boot.
But then Jordan Joseph spills before he can get anywhere close to contact. A soft error that kills an attack.
17 mins: Munster’s latest attack is ended by a Baudonne breakdown steal.
13 mins: Wow. A try that comes from a Munster mistake.
Nankivell was trying to feed O’Shea with a ball out the back but he throws it behind him. Luckily for O’Shea, McCarthy wasn’t too far away and is able to gather the ball in stride.
Running at pace, the wing bursts through the line and over a helpless Gibert to get over for the score.
"There was something zebo-esque about that finish" 🗣️ Shay McCarthy turns on the burners to grab @munsterugby 's second of the game 🔥 #InvestecChampionsCup pic.twitter.com/BOod8HQthE
11 mins: Oh Munster look to be away through Sean O’Brien but there was a forward pass amidst the series of short, sharp passes.
Munster quickly get the ball back off the scrum as Dan Kelly gets in for a breakdown poach.
As soon as the clock ticks past 8 minutes, the crowd breaks out in applause. Lasting for a minute, the recognition is of course a nod to Anthony Foley’s number eight shirt.
In the on-field action, Munster win a scrum penalty as 3, Kharaishvili collapses.
7 mins: Power from Gleeson. Picking off the base of the scrum, he gets low and forces his way through three tacklers to ground the ball.
O’Shea slots the conversion from out wide.
Fitting, given the night that’s in it, that Munster open the scoring through their number eight wearing 24 on his back.
"Munster's number 8 wearing 24" 🗣️ Brian Gleeson with the opener for @Munsterrugby 🔴 #InvestecChampionsCup pic.twitter.com/w2Mowpgh6M
5 mins: That’s a very promising opening attack from Munster.
Some of the passing is very crisp, the ball fizzing across the backline as Ben O’Connor carries into the 22. Charlie O’Shea tries a chip in behind and, such was the pressure of the chase, Racing were forced to take the ball back over their own line and ground it.
3 mins: Racing hit the front as Antoine Gibert makes no mistake off the tee from that maul penalty.
Just inside the 10m line and 15m in from touch, it was a nice settler for him.
1 min: We’re underway in Cork, Racing kicking off into the Munster 22.
Munster clear through Casey and off the following lineout, Racing maul their way 20m up the park and win a penalty. An early statement from the French pack.
Munster come onto the pitch at Páirc Uí Chaoimh wearing tracksuits emblazoned with the number eight over the heart. That of course was the number worn by Foley.
Neither side is wearing the number eight tonight. Brian Gleeson is instead sporting number 24 while Maxime Baudonne, the racing captain and backrow, has a blank shirt.
It’s a particularly poignant build-up with the Foley anniversary and a minute silence for Hyron Andrews, the Lions lock forward who passed away on Friday.
This is, of course, the 10-year anniversary of the death of Anthony Foley. The former Munster coach passed away in Paris when the province was getting set to play Racing 92.
Gerry Thornley takes a look at Foley’s legacy a decade on from his death in a poignant piece below.
[ 'It never gets easy' - 10 years on, Anthony Foley is still inspiring Munster Opens in new window ]
Next up it’s down to Cork where Munster welcome Racing 92. Kick-off for that one is at 8pm.
On Premier Sport, Jim Hamilton is already starting the conversation on Frawley and the Irish 10 shirt after a performance like that. Nights like this are why Frawley went to Connacht, for chances to start and excel at outhalf on the big stage.
The only problem, as far as he is concerned, is that Sam Prendergast was also excellent today for Leinster. A good day for Irish 10s.
Saracens spill trying to run back the kick-off and that’s all she wrote.
That was a sensational attacking display from Connacht. At times, defence seemed optional on both sides, but in a proper shootout of running rugby, Connacht had the weapons required to see off a strong Saracens outfit.
80 mins: Enough time for a comeback? Playing against 14, Saracens score out wide as Daly coasts over. This conversion is vital if it’s to become a one-score game...
Farrell misses! And with that, Connacht can’t lose this one.
79 mins: That’s bizarre. Brousset looked to be going to his pocket to bin Gilbert after repeated Connacht infringements, but someone in his ear must have said something to change his mind.
Seconds later, though, he does take out the yellow.
Cian Prendergast will end his excellent night on the naughty step after falling on the wrong side of the ruck.
Ciarán Frawley has been named player of the match. He’s been superb, but justice for Cian Prendergast.
Seriously, Prendergast has been outstanding.
75 mins: Prendergast is pinged for a deliberate knock. Is he lucky that wasn’t checked for a yellow?
Perhaps. Saracens kick to the corner but make a meal of the lineout. That faltering set-piece has cost them tonight, both for Frawley’s second try and then here when trying to claw their way back into it.
72 mins: Frawley has been excellent, gliding through the line off a scrum only for the last pass to go awry.
Meanwhile Blade finds a good touch with a box-kick, keeping Sarries pinned in their 22.
A reminder that Connacht have only scored two more tries than their visitors. They need one more for a bonus point.
66 mins: Connacht nearly get that bonus point score as Prendergast’s hands again set up a break down the left.
Ryan is hauled down short of the line. Hurley-Langton lines up a big carry from 5m out but he takes his eye off the ball as he spills forward.
64 mins: What is happening in Galway? It’s bedlam in the Dexcom.
Saracens have a lineout inside their own half but they make a you know what of it. The long throw over the top bounces perfectly into the arms of Frawley who sprints away under the posts through a disorganised defence.
Opportunistic for Connacht, soft for Saracens. Gilbert, this time, converts. Surely that must be victory wrapped up?
The try-count is now 7-5, meaning Connacht need one more for a bonus point.
"Bright lights are shining all around Galway" 🗣️ What a game at The Dexcom as Ciaran Frawley grabs his second of the game in superb fashion 🔥 #InvestecChampionsCup pic.twitter.com/RHvdqiRiWZ
62 mins: That’s another belter. Knocked back phase after phase, the attack looks dead. Then Frawley snaps a beautiful, flat ball to Forde on the flank.
He does brilliantly to stay in play to pop it inside to Ryan who, in turn, finds Blade on the support line. He rides one tackle but still manages to finish.
Gilbert misses the conversion, meaning the deficit is just seven.
Bundee Aki is gone after an hour, Josh Ioane replacing him. This will lead to a reshuffle in the back line. Let’s see how that materialises.
57 mins: Connacht need to be careful here. Two quick penalties inside their own 22 and there are words of warning from Brousset again.
Saracens are hammering awya here AND THEY’VE SCORED.
Va’eneku with another try, screaming onto a short line to power his way ovr. Farrell converts.
Changes for Connacht. Connolly is on for Illo at tighthead while Blade replaces scrumhalf Reilly.
The officials are happy that Gilbert, who bumped into Tompkins on a decoy, as in a position to take a pass and that the contact didn’t materially effect Saracens’ ability to defend that break.
The TMO thinks he’s spotted obstruction in the build-up. Gilbert is the guilty party - if this try is chalked off. We’ve gone upstairs.
52 mins: It’s a game of basketball at the moment, both sides going end to end to score.
Straight off the lineout, Aki feeds Forde who in turn pulls the ball out the back to Frawley. With Saracens’ backline all at sea, cut open by a series of decoys, Frawley feeds Treacy in space before following up in support.

50 mins: That’s a beauty. Farrell throws a stunning offload to Daly who in turn draws th elast man to send Segun over.
Connacht won’t be happy how Farrell shrugged off one tackler, allowing him to free the arms, but take nothing away from the skills on display.
Farrell misses the conversion, meaning Connacht still lead.
48 mins: Another deserved score for the best player on the park so far. Aki holds onto the ball just long enough to create a dogleg, forcing the defence to bite in. That opens up a gap for Prendergast and he doesn’t need to be asked twice.

Gilbert converts as the ball takes a helping nudge from the upright.
46 mins: Reilly nearly opens up a chance with a carry down the blind side of a scrum, catching everyone off guard. Offloading inside the 22, Ryan takes the ball before Connacht build the phases.

Saracens at times look too powerful, too well drilled and playing with a ruck speed that is too quick for Connacht to deal with.

43 mins: That was as inevitable a try you will see. Down to 14 and flying by the seat of their pants defensively, Connacht can’t stop Tompkins from bashing over from close range.

42 mins: Ben Earl thought he was in. A bust through the middle looked set to end under the posts but somehow Connacht haul him down. At the following ruck, Hurley-Langton was never onside and, given it came immediately after a line break, that was always going to lead to a card.
38 mins: Frustration for Matthew Victory as his lineout throw to Prendergast is crooked. That could well be Connacht’s last chance to add to their lead before the break.
Saracens, by contrast, will get a chance inside the Connacht half.
Trying to run back a kick, Treacy’s pass to Forde was just behind the centre and he can’t hang on. Not the most sympathetic ball but, as Joe Schmidt once said, ‘Good players catch those.’
36 mins: A huge roar from the home faithful as Farrell tries to offload off the deck, only for the ball to hit Va’eneku and travel forward.

Gilbert just curls the ball inside the upright for the conversion.

Under pressure, Daly has to clear quickly but barely finds touch outside his own 22.
27 mins: Farrell’s wide ball to Segun almost puts the wing in. It’s a beautiful, flat pass that takes out two defenders but Connacht scramble to get Segun into touch. Actually, he tried to offload before touch but the ball went forward.
24 mins: That is such a well-worked score. It all starts with an Aki bust straight off the lineout, powering through Knight. Phases later, he keeps it alive with a juggling catch to prevent a spill. 22 mins: Connacht’s defence is much stronger than earlier. Swarming over a Daly carry, Forde’s pressure at the ruck forces Farrell into a neckroll, such was his desperation to secure the ball. Connacht win a relieving penalty.
18 mins: TMO time. Connacht are over after a strong drive off the back of the lineout. It’s difficult to see who ultimately bustled over.
Brousset wants a look with the TMO as he’s not sure if the ball was grounded.
Cian Prendergast was the man who got over after a short carry close to the line. Gilbert converts and Connacht are back in it.
17 mins: Oh Connacht thought they were under the stick there, Prendergast’s offload not finding its way to Gilbert who, had he gathered, would have been in. In the end, it’s good defending from Itoje to disrupt that pas.
Connacht had an advantage so to the corner again they go.
16 mins: Treacy is tackled into touch right on the 22. Fortunately for him, Connacht had an advantage as Saracens drifted offside.
13 mins: Connacht will feel hard-done-by there, but it’s brilliant hands from Daly. The initial line speed off a lineout is good as Ryan smashes the ball loose in a collision with Tompkins.

Connacht simply can’t get out of their half at the moment, such is the territorial pressure from Saracens.
Meanwhile Connacht have been forced into a HIA, Daniel Ryan coming off the bench to replace Shane Jennings on the wing.
7 mins: A lovely play off a tap penalty sees Saracens take the lead. Jamie George’s soft hands are what open the gap in the end, allowing Tongan centre Va’eneku to crash over from close range.
6 mins: Five minutes on the clock and referee Pierre Brousset is already having a word with Connacht captain Cian Prendergast. An offside penalty is what prompts this chat which looks to be a warning.
4 mins: Two quick penalties, one off a lineout, another from van Wyk in a maul, have Connacht in trouble close to their own line.
Saracens have a lineout 5m out against a Connacht side that has struggled against the maul so far this season.
3 mins: Connacht look sharp with their first attack, Saracens missing their mark at lineout time. The ball is quickly spread wide to Treacy who links up with Reilly and then Gilbert as play sprints into the 22.

1 min: They’re underway in Galway, Connacht fielding the kick-off and looking to clear their lines early doors.
Right then, time to turn attentions to Galway. Connacht welcome Saracens to the Dexcom Stadium. Here’s how they line out. The biggest point of intrigue? It’s hard to look past that Frawley-Aki-Forde midfield combo.
But Connacht’s weakness so far this season has not been the backline, but instead their scrum and maul. Let’s see how they deal with Maro Itoje et al in that area.
Ready to put the green armour on today 🟢🦅 #CONvSAR | #InvestecChampionsCup pic.twitter.com/am64cB6dAW
As for Leinster, while Clermont were poor, they showed enough today to suggest they are on an intriguing path with their attack.
Sam Prendergast’s counter-attack score, set up by his kick and Jimmy O’Brien’s chase, will be the score of the weekend. You wouldn’t be surprised to see Bordeaux score that one, such was the counter-attacking quality. Elsewhere, the scrum was dominant against a young Clermont tighthead, the lineout was secure and the defence was also solid. A workmanlike performance with flashes of brilliance.
Meanwhile Ulster are looking at securing a Challenge Cup win of their own, they’re up 33-21 over Zebre with five minutes to go.
Leinster are happy to catch a kick in the backfield, O’Brien taking the ball and landing in touch.
A bonus point win over what proved to be an average Clermont side.
81 mins: That feels a needless card to give away with the clock in the red. McCarthy plays the ball cynically at the side of the ruck, denying a break and prompting Carley to go to his pocket.
Clermont have one last attack running at 14 men in a bid to salvage some pride.
Fintan Gunne is back on at 9. I’m not sure if that means Coffey has picked up an injury but we’ll hear more at full-time I’m sure.
78 mins: Leinster finish with a flourish. Osborne, McCarthy and Penny - the latter giving the scoring pass - are all prominently involved as solid handling from Leinster opens up just enough space for their speedster in the corner.

69 mins: Leinster had a penalty advantage but don’t want it. Some incisive attacking play leads to an infringement before Jimmy O’Brien grubbers into the 22.

66 mins: That fightback didn’t last long.

5m out from the Leinster line, Clermont are going to tap here.

61 mins: Leinster’s wait for a maul try this season comes to an end, Sheehan diving over after the catch and drive rumbled towards the line.

57 mins: Wow. The yellow makes sense. Clermont were under warning and Zahouany, the teenage tighthead, has been obliterated at the scrum by Porter all afternoon. When he fell to a knee at that scrum, a penalty and card seemed certain.

55 mins: There’s another penalty as Clermont infringe at the scrum. No card - yet.
54 mins: Prendergast tries to pick out Henshaw with a cross-kick but it bounces just in front of the centre and into touch. However, there was an advantage for Noah playing the ball off his feet.

Leinster call for a scrum 5m from the line.
53 mins: Leinster get another penalty as Clermont infringe at the lineout, tighthead Zahouany taking out McCarthy’s lifter while he was still in the air.
50 mins: Clermont’s attack looks laboured, unable to create gaps. Their kick-chase, however, is excellent, continually winning possession back high up the pitch when putting boot to ball.

At the scrum, Leinster look to play away but an error means they go back for a penalty at the set-piece. Porter continues to have the upper hand on his opposite man.

42 mins: That is sensational. Light the beacons, Leinster have scored a counter-attack, transition score from deep inside their own half.

Sam Prendergast launches the ball down towards the Clermont 22 as Leinster look to overturn this one-point deficit.

Leinster win it back at the kick-off but a Clermont spill means they’re under advantage. Having gone backwards, Carley says there’s no advantage and calls the half to a close.
39 mins: Leinster are caught offside and it’s in kicking range for Plummer. He calls for the tee in a bid to retake the lead with the last play of the half. He’s got it.

37 mins: Carley really isn’t doing much to please Leinster here, not that that’s his job.
Van der Flier is clearly on the ball, to the point that it pops out of the ruck, but the referee says he was latched onto an arm at the ruck. So he doesn’t reward him with a penalty.

35 mins: Oh that’s silly, stupid even. Carley told Clermont to stop competing for the ball with one of their own lying on the wrong side. That doesn’t stop Swain from flying in and clattering into Conan, who was blindsided by the hit.

33 mins: That scrum off the dead kick costs Leinster.

30 mins: Mistake from Prendergast. Looking for a big spiral bomb from inside his own 22, he catches it beautifully. Too well, in fact.

Tadhg Furlong asks Carley to be consistent with his call of crooked put-ins now Clermont have the ball. You have to laugh, really.
28 mins: That’s a gift, an absolute gift. The result of the previous counter-ruck was a charged down clearance going into touch. Clermont lineout close to their own line.

28 mins: Clermont’s defence is good, forcing a counter-ruck that sees another Leinster attack die inside the 22.

23 mins: Andrew Porter has Zahouany on toast at the scrum so far. Up pops the tighthead under pressure from the Leinster loosehead. Penalty, another scrum.

Clermont use the free-kick to clear their lines.
21 mins: Prendergast’s chip in behind goes dead, Keenan in hot pursuit.

Clermont first have to make a HIA, Lanen’s gumshield is flashing a warning. Michaux is on for him at secondrow.
19 mins: Leinster thought they had lost out in attack as Gunne spilled at the base of the ruck. However, the officials have spotted a cynical hand on the floor knocking the ball loose. Secondrow Lanen was the culprit. He’s lucky to not see yellow for that.
15 mins: Now Porter is caught offside trying to get off the line quickly. It’s in a similar spot to the last Plummer penalty but closer to the sticks. No surprise to see the kicking tee come back on.

13 mins: Henshaw slips a bit high in his tackle on Plummer. It’s marginal, but Carley sticks the arm out.

10 mins: That’s an excellent score. IT all comes from a lineout just outside the 22, a dummy pop and switch at the back of a maul seeing Conan send Sheehan away down the short side.

9 mins: Leinster get close again. This time Keenan chases Prendergast’s kick into the 22 and wins the battle for it.

Matthew Carley says O’Brien knocked-on in-goal while trying to dot down. It was an impressive break from Leinster, going wide in a counter-attack before O’Brien’s chip and chase.
7 mins: Prendergast with a rush of blood to the head. Retreating into the backfield to recover a kick, he tries to take on Jurrand - a wing - on the outside. It’s a predictable race that, given the disparity in pace.

5 mins: An early Leinster attack stutters despite a strong carry from Tommy O’Brien. Prendergast goes to the air but overcooks it, allowing Clermont to mark inside the 22.
2 mins: Leinster get away with giving away an early scrum right on their 22.

Given Ulster are in Challenge Cup action at the same time as Leinster, it’s worth reminding us of the squad they’ve picked to take on Zebre. Plenty wondered how seriously Ulster would take this competition, given they went all in for last year’s final and both lost that while missing out on the URC playoffs.

Richie Murphy has named seven of his 10 Ireland internationals - Tom O’Toole, Cormac Izuchukwu, Nathan Doak, Rob Baloucoune, Jacob Stockdale, Tom Stewart and Eric O’Sullivan. As for Clermont, they have avoided the French affliction of picking purely second string teams for European competition. Leinster at home and all the history these two have during the province’s pomp, winning three titles in four years between 2009-12, perhaps it makes sense why they’re going after this one.
Key man Baptiste Jauneau starts at scrumhalf with Bautista Delguy and AJ Lam providing running threats in the outside backs.
Perhaps fortunately for Leinster, the appropriately named prop Regis Montagne hasn’t been named in the squad having featured in last week’s narrow defeat to Bordeaux. Nevertheless, there is plenty of heft in this Clermont pack.
Let’s start with the team news from the day’s first Irish Champions Cup game. Leinster have made six changes to the XV that beat Cardiff in last weekend’s return to the RDS.
Tommy O’Brien replaces Joshua Kenny on the right flank while Robbie Henshaw comes in for Jamie Osborne in the outside backs. At halfback, with Jamison Gibson-Park not yet fit for action, Fintan Gunne swaps in for Oliver Coffey.
In the pack, Andrew Porter replaces Alex Usanov at loosehead, while Ryan Baird and Josh van der Flier come in for Max Deegan and Scott Penny in the backrow.
There is going to be a first Leinster appearance for Joey Carbery since the province’s Champions Cup final win back in 2018. After stints with Munster and Bordeaux, Carbery is back at his home province and provides outhalf cover on the bench, Leinster going with the more experienced option over exciting young 10 Caspar Gabriel.

title: Munster honour Anthony Foley’s memory with victory over Racing 92 at Páirc Uí Chaoimh
description: Clayton McMillan’s side were far from perfect but had enough to hold off French visitors
content:
On the night they honoured the memory of their legendary former number eight and coach Anthony Foley, a decade on from his passing in Paris, Munster did him the ultimate compliment of sealing an emotional night with a win in their opening Champions Cup game.
In truth, Munster played in fits and starts, but there were enough of them to always stay ahead of Racing, who also burst into life occasionally in what was not a vintage encounter, sprinkled with poor kicks and sloppy turnovers.
With Marnus van der Merwe again excellent, the set-pieces went well and there were more of the click strikes plays that have become a feature of the game. There were some magical moments from Charlie O’Shea and despite one glaring error, Craig Casey pulled the strings, finishing the tie with the final try at the end.
Among the tributes to Foley was a rendition of the Shannon anthem There is an Isle. Jack O’Donoghue was the only member of this matchday squad who was due to have played in Paris on that fateful day a decade ago and played against Glasgow a week later. Bearing this in mind, Foley’s wife, Olive, presented the jerseys to the Munster players on Friday and also movingly spoke of her husband to them.
There was also a minute’s silence, as there was at all grounds in the Champions Cup and Challenge Cup matches, to honour the memory of the Lions player Hyron Andrews, who passed away in his hotel room ahead of their match in La Rochelle on Friday.
The two captains then exchanged number eight jerseys, as both retired that number for the night in further honour of Foley, with Brian Gleeson wearing the 24 jersey as CJ Stander had done against Glasgow. His counterpart and Racing captain Maxime Baudonne had no number on his back.
There was something in the air all right. Racing struck first with a monstrous maul and an opening penalty by Antoine Gibert. But Munster struck back more tellingly after one of those sharp strike plays and a wicked chip by O’Shea which led to Joey Manu conceding a five-metre scrum. Gleeson picked up off the base and charged to the blindside, bumping flanker Nicolas Martins, Baudonne and scrumhalf Antoine Latrasse for a fine finish.
O’Shea even converted from the right touchline in his nonchalant way. After a superb defensive maul by Munster, John Hodnett’s chop tackle and Dan Kelly’s jackal led to O’Shea finding touch 40 metres out and Munster struck again.
There was an element of luck, mind, as Alex Nankivell’s intended pull back for O’Shea went slightly behind the outhalf, who inadvertently flicked the ball into the hands of Shay McCarthy. He didn’t even break stride, leaving two defenders for dead with a step and acceleration before bumping Gibert to finish superbly.
Again, O’Shea landed a very difficult conversion before the crowd were becalmed by Racing’s extended ownership of the ball and territory. They were able to stymie Munster’s brief forays, helped by Karl Dickson awarding Jordan Joseph a jackal penalty when not remotely supporting his own body weight.
Munster put O’Shea in the backfield where he was targeted by the Racing halves, a spillage leading to another Gibert penalty when Thomas Ahern came into the maul from the side. But O’Shea made one great take and Racing kept spilling and turning over the ball, as when Seán O’Brien’s read and intercept was backed up by John Hodnett’s superb one-man clear out and Seán Edogbo fed O’Shea for a quick-witted kick into space. Nankivell chased and won the penalty but, Casey having ill-advisedly tapped a previous penalty, this time Munster couldn’t complete the lineout.
So Racing were let off the hook and a fairly average half of rugby, save for the two tries and O’Shea’s highlights reel, ended 14-6.
On the resumption, there was far more intent to the launch plays from which O’Shea carried over the gainline and in the ensuing phases – Edogbo carrying twice either side of Jack Aungier, before Tadhg Beirne took a good line off Casey to score at close-range.
But they coughed up a soft try when a loose Racing lineout was scooped up by Wilfried Hulleu, who sliced through a sleepy Munster pack simply by dint of stepping Gleeson. Racing were a better team with the experienced Maxime Machenaud at scrumhalf, albeit he went beyond his remit by finding himself at the sharp end of a mauled try.
Clayton McMillan turned to his bench and they delivered, Gavin Coombes and Jack O’Donoghue adding oomph to their carries and after Nankivell and Coombes had put them on the front foot, Casey deftly set up Fineen Wycherley to score with his first touch.
Back came Racing, Arthur Roche running back a Casey box kick and Hulleu offloading for Gerónimo Prisciantelli to make ground and release Manu for the try of the match – Gibert adding another fine conversion.
But Roche took out fullback Ben O’Connor in the air and re-energised by the crowd, Munster marched up field, went to the corner and mauled toward the line before, fittingly, Casey went blind and dummied Machenaud to apply the coup de grace.
Like Foley a Shannonman, Casey held up eight fingers and pointed to the skies before the wider squad congregated in the middle of the pitch to sing Stand Up and Fight, echoing the win over Glasgow a decade ago. Alas, by then, the vast bulk of the 24,906 crowd had dispersed.

MUNSTER: Ben O’Connor; Shay McCarthy, Alex Nankivell, Dan Kelly, Seán O’Brien; Charlie O’Shea, Craig Casey; Jeremy Loughman, Marnus van der Merwe, Jack Aungier; Tom Ahern, Tadhg Beirne (capt); Seán Edogbo, John Hodnett, Brian Gleeson.
Replacements: Jack O’Donoghue for Edogbo, Gavin Coombes for Gleeson (both 54 mins); Josh Wycherley for Loughman, Kieran Brookes for Aungier, JJ Hanrahan for O’Shea (all 57); Kieran Brookes for Aungier (58); Fineen Wycherley for Ahern (60); Max Clein for Van der Merwe (79).

Replacements: Demba Bamba for Kharaishvili, Maxime Machenaud for Latrasse (both 45 mins); Sam James for Habosi (49); Lehopa Leota for Jabea Njocke (53); Arthur Roche for Tupou (57); Nathan Hughes for Joseph (59); Yanis Basse for Escober, Soumalia Camara for Lainault (both 78).

title: Aidan O’Brien takes over from Andrew Balding in race to be top trainer in Britain
description: O’Brien and jockey Wayne Lordan team up for six winners at Leopardstown
content:
Aidan O’Brien emerged from British Champions Day with what might prove a decisive advantage over Andrew Balding after wrestling control from the long-time British trainers’ championship leader at Ascot.
The afternoon began with Balding in front by just under £100,000 and when Mount Atlas produced a 33-1 Long Distance Cup shock, hopes were high at Kingsclere that a first championship was on the cards, despite O’Brien’s Queenstown claiming second.
When it was put to him that the win could prove crucial in the title race, however, Balding prophetically said: “I don’t know about that, there’s still a long way to go.”
Balding still had his trump card to play, too, in Kalpana, who was bidding for a third win in the Fillies & Mares Stakes and with over £280,000 to the winner, it would have gone a long way to securing the title.
However, Colin Keane never looked totally at ease on his mare and as she finished out of the money in her final outing before retirement, while in a double blow for Balding, O’Brien’s Minnie Hauk bounced back to her very best.
That took the Ballydoyle man around £80,00 clear and despite O’Brien’s Gstaad and Constitution River coming up short in their respective races, the writing looks to be on the wall.
O’Brien – who is seeking his ninth British title – said: “Andrew Balding is a great fellow, they are a great family – the very best of luck for them today, it’s a bit of fun [the trainers’ championship] and we’re all delighted to be here.”
The Irishman is likely to only have a handful of other runners in Britain before the title finishes in December, but next weekend is the final Group One of the season at Doncaster, the Futurity Trophy, a race he has won 12 times and has the ante-post favourite in Noble Exhibit.
The master of Ballydoyle enjoyed a fabulous day alongside Wayne Lordan on home soil, joining forces for six winners at Leopardstown.
The 213-1 six-timer saw them land all but one of the races on the card and included both Group Three features as Wall Street (4-7 favourite) edged out Zarak Pasha to land the Group Three Eyrefield Stakes and Capability Brown (100-30) made all in the Killavullan Stakes.
It is the second year running O’Brien has won six races at this fixture, but with Lordan partnering all of them the trainer-jockey combination became the first to win six races at one meeting in Ireland or Britain under either code.
Stable representative Chris Armstrong said: “It’s a magnificent day. For Wayne to get six winners, and six winners for the stable, is incredible.
“We were lucky at this meeting last year, we had six as well. The horses are in form, they are running well. We had some lovely winners today with the maidens and the ones in the Group races. It’s a day to savour.
“Minnie Hauk topped it off in Ascot. Across the two tracks, it’s been a stellar day.”

title: Talks on new public sector pay deal to begin on Monday after sides agree framework
description: Negotiations set to get under way at Workplace Relations Commission after agreement on process reached
content:
Talks on a new public sector pay deal will get under way at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) on Monday after a framework for the process was agreed between the sides on Saturday.
Engagement overseen by WRC chairman Kevin Foley with Irish Congress of Trade Unions general secretary Owen Reidy and Department of the Environment secretary general Oonagh Buckley produced an agreement on how to proceed with substantive talks late on Saturday.
After their conclusion, the three person steering committee issued a statement in which they said the two sides were in a position to get negotiations going and they should be started with discussions on pay and related matters, including the union side’s “claims on cost-of-living effects between 2021 – 2025, this year, and for the duration of any agreement”.
Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers welcomed the news of the progress made, saying the statement “provides the basis for a move into constructive dialogue”.
“This is a positive move forward and demonstrates the genuine commitment to dialogue on all sides to ensure an outcome that delivers for our people and our country. I look forward to the formal talks commencing on Monday,” he said.
However, the three person steering committee said there was “a need to rebuild trust and confidence in industrial relations in the public sector by addressing commitments made in the context of the previous agreement.”
This has been a recurring issue raised by the union side which complains that some of the commitments made by Government in that agreement have not been delivered upon.
The three person committee will not run the process itself but have said they will remain available to be help steer the two sides past any “impasse” that might arise during the talks. They said this arrangement was particular to this dispute and had been put in place because of the importance of the talks and the need to reach an agreement.
The process may still have quite some way to go with the WRC phase last time characterised by disagreement early on and a long break in the talks but both sides are likely to be relieved that a basis has been thrashed out on getting them started.
It follows Wednesday’s industrial action by more than 300,000 public and civil servants who were protesting the absence of negotiations on a successor national pay deal to the one that expired at the end of June and the ongoing impact on their wages of inflation due to rising food, fuel costs.

title: Troy Parrott’s Real Betis no match for Barcelona as they hit five goals in Seville
description: Ireland striker plays the final 26 minutes of heavy defeat to La Liga leaders
content:
Ireland striker Troy Parrott came on for the final 26 minutes but could only watch on as Barcelona’s La Liga juggernaut rolled into Seville on ‌Saturday and left with the scoreboard smoking as the leaders beat Real Betis 5-2 to make it nine wins from nine and stretch their blistering league tally to 39 ​goals.
Lamine Yamal lit the fuse with a dazzling opener before Rodri, Gabriel Jesus, Eric Garcia and substitute Dani Olmo joined the party, while Valentin Gómez and Ez Abde replied for Betis, who played much of the second half with 10 men after Facundo Bernal was sent off for headbutting Lamine.
Barca moved to 27 points, five above ​Atlético who won 1-0 at Espanyol, while third-placed Betis have 19 and Real Madrid sit fourth on 18 before welcoming Sevilla on Sunday,
Betis manager Manuel Pellegrini made eight changes ⁠from the side that beat Porto 3-2 in the Champions League, resting several key players including Antony, Marc Bartra, Natan ‌and ‌Isco ​with a midweek European meeting against Feyenoord in mind.
Yet the hosts still made Barca sweat before the visitors eventually found space, rhythm and, after Betis were reduced to 10 men, plenty of room to turn ⁠the match into another attacking exhibition.
Lamine opened the scoring ​in the 10th minute in familiar style, gliding in from the right ​before whipping a left-footed strike from the edge of the box into the top corner.
Betis levelled in the 27th when Pablo Fornals collected a ‌rebound on the right and clipped a cross ​into the middle for Gómez, who rose highest to head past goalkeeper Joan Garcia.
Barcelona reclaimed the lead in the 41st minute when ⁠Spain captain Rodri powered in a header from Fermin Lopez’s ⁠corner.
Betis thought they had equalised ​three minutes later through Gio Lo Celso’s spectacular swivelling volley from outside the box, but the effort was ruled out after Cucho Hernandez was adjudged to have handled earlier in the build-up.
Jesus, signed from Arsenal in the close season, had a goal disallowed for offside shortly after the break but was not kept waiting long. In the 51st, Lamine darted down the right and squared for the Brazilian to finish neatly inside the area.
A minute later Abde pulled one back on the counter, sliding a low shot inside the right post, but Betis’ celebrations turned sour when Bernal was shown a straight red card following ‌a scuffle. Lamine was booked ⁠for his part in the altercation.
Barcelona made it 4-2 in the 63rd minute when Alvaro Valles failed to deal with Lamine’s free kick and Pau Cubarsi headed the loose ball back across goal for Garcia to tap in.
Olmo completed the ‌rout in the 81st minute, curling a right-footed shot into the top corner from outside the box.
Atletico won 1-0 at Espanyol, with Álex Baena coming off the bench to ​deliver the late sting in a cagey match in Barcelona.
Both sides struck the post in a ​tight tactical contest before Atlético’s substitutes combined in the 89th, Julian Alvarez bursting down the left and squaring for Baena, who drove a fierce strike into the top corner from the edge of the box.

title: Lions play through the tears against La Rochelle in honour of team-mate Hyron Andrews
description: Champions Cup round-up: Unbeaten Glasgow impress in big win over Sale; Bristol suffer heavy loss against Stormers in Cape Town
content:
Several of the players from South ‌Africa’s Lions side could not hold back tears as they paid an ‌emotional tribute to team-mate Hyron Andrews ahead of their Champions Cup fixture ​against French side La Rochelle on Saturday.
Andrews, 31, was found unresponsive at the team’s hotel on the Ile de Re on Friday and ​could not be resuscitated. No cause of death has yet been determined.
A ⁠statement from South Africa Rugby said he “died after falling ‌at ‌the ​team hotel”.
The Lions decided to play the fixture in honour of Andrews and put in ⁠a spirited display ​but went down 31-14 to ​Ronan O’Gara’s side.
La Rochelle fans had formed a ‌guard of honour to welcome ​the visitors at the stadium.
Andrews’s number five jersey was ⁠laid out in front ⁠of his ​team-mates as an impeccably observed moment of silence was held at the Stade Marcel-Deflandre.
Ruan Delport, selected to play in the secondrow, instead wore the number 24, leaving Andrews’s number free.
South Africans on the La Rochelle side, Dillyn Leyds and Salmaan Moerat, ‌presented a special number ⁠five jersey to Lions coach Ivan Van Rooyen, while the ground erupted into applause in the ‌fifth minute of the match.
Glasgow Warriors extended their unbeaten start to the new season by pulling away to claim an impressive 47-27 win at Sale.
Glasgow’s winning score might have looked convincing but they only secured victory in the final 20 minutes after Rekeiti Ma’asi-White had temporarily reduced Sale’s deficit to four.
The hosts had made all the running in the early stages and were 12 points up inside the first 10 minutes helped by tries from Ben Curry and Arron Reed.
The visitors hit back through a penalty try and further efforts from Kyle Steyn and Jamie Dobie to carve out a hard-earned 21-15 lead at the interval.
The game looked in the balance until late tries from Rory Darge, Ollie Smith and debutant Otavio Tuipulotu helped Glasgow pull away and wrap up a precious bonus-point win.
Glasgow host Pau in their next Champions Cup encounter while Sale travel to Leinster for a tricky test in mid-December.
The Stormers ran in seven tries in a 49-12 thumping of Bristol Bears. The home side were on top from the start in Cape Town, with Seabelo Senatla scoring their first try in the seventh minute before Leolin Zas added a second eight minutes later.
Joe Owens broke away down the wing for a solo try for Bristol in the 22nd minute but Jonny Roche restored Stormers’ advantage before the half-hour mark.
JJ Kotze was shown a 20-minute red card for head-to-head contact before the break, while a yellow card for Zas – resulting in a disallowed try – gave the Bears a significant numerical advantage that they took advantage of through a first try for the club from Sol Moody.
However, Roche then scored his second and the final 10 minutes was a horror show for Bristol as they conceded three more tries.
First, Warrick Gelant crossed, then Andre-Hugo Venter got in on the act before Vas ended an eventful game with his second – with all seven tries converted by Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu.
Other result: Bulls 56 Stade Francais 20

title: Sam Prendergast shifts credit to Leinster pack after big win over Clermont
description: Players relish the atmosphere at Stade Marcel-Michelin as they deliver bonus-point win
content:
Sam Prendergast picked up a trinket for the second week in succession, another player-of-the-match accolade, on foot of nuanced kicking, passing and running and a 16-point haul, that included a try, which he started and finished in Leinster’s 48-23 victory at the Stade Marcel-Michelin.
The young outhalf was first minded to pay tribute to his pack for giving him a platform, the time and space to bring to bear his talent. “I thought we played quite well. Our forwards were very good. We got a bit of ascendancy in the second half.
“I think a lot of it was just [down to] forward dominance. I thought our pack was excellent. Scrum, lineout defence and maul were very good. That got us into the right areas of the pitch and meant we could convert when we got [there].
“We love it [the Champions Cup]. We’re ambitious but we knew it [would be] such a tough game. We aren’t really looking too far ahead. We knew we had to come here and do a job and play properly, or we wouldn’t get a win.”
He enjoyed every minute at the iconic venue. “It’s pretty special. I haven’t played here before. It’s an unbelievable atmosphere. You could feel it in that first half and coming back out for the second half. The place was hopping. It’s a surreal experience. The fans, it really feels like they’re on top of you.”
Leinster head coach Leo Cullen also touched on one of the most atmospheric grounds in world rugby but first paid his respects to the late Lions lock Hyron Andrews. “It’s a great stadium, a great crowd, [but] a bit of a sad day with Hyron Andrews and what happened to him.
“Our thoughts are with the Lions and all the families connected to them. We only played the Lions a few weeks ago so horrific news to wake up to on Friday.”
He also paid tribute to Leinster’s travelling support. “We have a lot of Leinster fans here which is great. It’s an amazing place to play rugby and we’re delighted to get a win.
“Huge credit to [forwards coach] Robin McBryde and the work the forwards did this week because we stole a lot of lineout, which is great, and then obviously to get a penalty try from the scrum in the second half; it is a big momentum shift in the game.”
He briefly looked forward to next weekend’s game, when Leinster host Munster in the URC. “Yeah, we played Munster in round four last year in the URC and we were well beaten in Croke Park. They’re making good progress themselves at the moment.
“The form book goes out the window. It will be a great challenge for us back in the Aviva Stadium next Saturday.”
Leinster’s pack won the game, and a standout was their openside Josh van der Flier. He too paid his respects to Andrews before returning to the performance.
“We’re very happy with that game. We worked really hard, to be honest. We’ve been training well the last few weeks and it all kind of clicked there. We all really enjoyed playing here. It’s obviously a team we have a huge amount of respect for. I remember watching games here on TV as a kid and it’s always been my dream to play here.
“A lot of lads were the same, it’s one of the great kind European grounds to come to. They are a very good team and we managed to put in a performance we’re very proud of, so happy with that.”

title: ‘Not acceptable’: Les Kiss blasts humiliated Wallabies as All Blacks claim 13th straight Bledisloe win
description: Second thrashing in a week makes a mockery of the hosts’ ambitions for next year’s World Cup
content:
The ruthless All Blacks embarrassed the Wallabies in their final home Test of the year, brushing aside the golden pretenders 43-21 in Sydney, a second thrashing in a week that makes a mockery of the hosts’ ambitions for next year’s World Cup.
The All Blacks were too fast at the breakdown, the ball hardly slowing as the New Zealanders appeared to advance it at will. They spoiled all but three Wallaby attacking forays, aided by errors and execution failures.
Captain Harry Wilson was blunt after the Wallabies’ 13th straight loss against their trans-Tasman rivals. “It’s not good enough for this group, we’ve got to be a lot better,” he told Channel Nine.
“We’ve got to start better. We had a terrible second half in the first game [of the series]. We had a terrible first half this game. We can’t be having terrible halves against the All Blacks. In the second half, we showed a bit of grit, but it’s too late, mate. We can’t be that far behind.”
Two second-half tries by the Wallabies thinned the margin slightly, but could not temper the conclusion obvious to all those who watched. So comprehensive was this defeat, Australia’s standing before next year’s showpiece must now be re-evaluated. From outsiders for the trophy aided by home support, Les Kiss’s side are now utterly irrelevant, likable entertainers at best. Maybe they will provide a good excuse for a party after the victory over Hong Kong in the opener.
The turnaround of the past two weeks is such a disappointment for the long-suffering Australian rugby community after the early promise shown under Kiss. Any momentum has now evaporated and the Wallabies find themselves in reverse.
Kiss was scathing in his assessment of the team’s first half. “There’s got to be a little bit more thinking about what it really means to actually turn up in that first half and make sure we don’t make those errors that we did,” he said. “It’s just not acceptable what was put out there.”
The enduring image of this catastrophe of an afternoon was the second try for All Blacks’ Josh Moorby, when a feigned overhead pass fooled Max Jorgensen and Ryan Lonergan – two of the most impressive Wallabies in recent months. Stationary in the late afternoon sun, the Australian pair were little more than a guard of honour for the All Blacks winger who crossed untouched.
Much of the speculation among the Australian rugby community before the match was how Declan Meredith would fare. The outhalf was responsible for two outstanding moments in the second half, including a near try when put through by impactful substitutes Angus Bell and Josh Canham, and a counterattack from a cheeky Tom Wright short drop-out. But any deep assessment of individuals would be an indulgence after a one-sided shellacking that was over before half-time, even if the contest showed promise in its early stages.
The All Blacks were forced into a late change when Jordie Barrett pulled out with calf tightness. His absence was amplified when Quinn Tupaea left the field dazed after hitting his head on the turf after just one minute.
Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, back at 13 after two Tests on the wing, was influential early alongside Wright and Jorgensen, who twice found space down the right. But it was the movement left off a lineout that almost put Australia ahead. The final ball from Jorgensen went to ground when Harry Potter and Wright both had clear space in front of them.
The inability to make the most of early field position was punished when the All Blacks ventured up the other end for the first time. Wright and Potter made try-saving tackles on the left, but when the All Blacks spread it to the openside the golden line was stretched thin and Moorby crossed.
Within three phases off the restart the All Blacks were back on the Wallabies’ line, their ruck speed like lightning, and in another three Peter Lakai was over for another. A Lonergan box kick drifted too deep, allowing the All Blacks to clear their lines easily, then the hosts lost the ensuing lineout. Within a minute Rieko Ioane was over in the corner and the score was 22-0.
Finally there was something for the home crowd to cheer when Meredith put Jeremy Williams over. His joy was short-lived when at the other end a harsh offside call saw him yellow carded. From the base of the scrum Wallace Sititi snuck over to resume normal programming. A Barrett intercept from a Jorgensen pass, punished with a runaway try, and the conversion from McKenzie, made it 36-7 at the break.
After Moorby’s sleight of hand and try early in the second period, the Wallabies bench players stemmed the bleeding. Jorgensen, Wright and Potter combined twice down the right to record Australia’s second five-pointer, and Filipo Daugunu scored after Meredith and Wright’s quick thinking. The match petered out, as Harry McLaughlin-Phillips relieved Meredith for his debut.
The Bledisloe Cup whitewash restores some pride after the All Blacks’ 3-1 series defeat to South Africa. Their ability to do it with a long injury list including their captain Ardie Savea, their two top outhalves Ruben Love and Richie Mo’unga, and their influential centre Jordie Barrett, confirms their place as the major challenger to the Springboks at next year’s World Cup.

title: Sam Prendergast plays starring role as Leinster secure bonus-point win over Clermont
description: Arm injury to Jack Conan the one downside to a seven-try showing for Leo Cullen’s side in France
content:
Big picture. Seven tries, a bonus-point win in France, a dominant scrum and lineout, the constituent parts of a super pack performance, collectively and individually. Small picture. Leinster will reflect on untidy passages, lack of precision, some wayward passing and, at times, an absence of stickability in their first-up tackling.
On balance, the ledger is appreciably positive, the only material downside that impressive number eight Jack Conan was walking around in the aftermath with his arm in a sling, a legacy of a dunt he received when scoring a second-half try.
Sam Prendergast was the official player-of-the-match for the second week in succession. His repertoire is considerable, some of the touches, passing, spiral bombs and crosskicks were a delight and when afforded any time and space, he tormented Clermont. His try – he started and finished an 80-metre counterattack – showcased that innate talent beautifully.
He still has the odd rash moment but playing on the edge is hardly risk averse; it goes with the territory. Dan Sheehan grabbed two tries and threw superbly; Tadhg Furlong crossed for another and along with the indefatigable Andrew Porter were bedrocks in a Leinster scrum that shunted their opponents from pillar to post.
Josh van der Flier was outstanding in a back five who all contributed handsomely. Clermont hooker Barnabe Massa will see Ryan Baird’s face in his nightmares. Joe McCarthy, James Ryan and Conan were diligent and unrelenting in their work.
Leinster’s first-half performance was a mishmash of the good, sporadic, and the downright careless as the Irish province gift-wrapped points for their opponents. Clermont didn’t have to work for their scores, just piggyback on Leinster mistakes and there was a surfeit of those moments.
Referee Matthew Carley was pedantic, consistently so – TMO Andrew Jackson missed a couple of dangerous clearouts – with Leinster scrumhalf Fintan Gunne incurring the Englishman’s displeasure, penalised for taking longer than five seconds to clear ball from a breakdown and subsequently for a crooked feed. Spooked into playing quickly he was also blocked down on another occasion.
To his credit he didn’t shy away from playing his natural game, a significant contributory factor in Furlong’s try. Gunne will benefit from the exposure to games of this ilk. The O’Briens, wings Jimmy and Tommy, were standouts, in different aspects of the game, the former in a creative capacity, Tommy as a finisher.
Leinster trailed 16-15 at the interval but were hardly panicked because the reasons were obvious, as all of Clermont’s points could be traced to mistakes. The home side were generous in their largesse too, especially in Sheehan’s first try.
The visitors started sharply and might have scored an early try before they did through Furlong, the product of a slick lineout move in which Conan, Sheehan and Baird did the heavy lifting before Gunne’s vision and pop pass sent the prop barrelling over.
Clermont outhalf and captain Harry Plummer is a consummate ball-striker as he demonstrated twice kicking long-range penalties to reduce the deficit before Sheean’s speed and strength saw him quickest to react to a loose Clermont tap into their in-goal area.
The home side grabbed a try after a couple of Leinster errors after Gunne was charged down and Prendergast’s thumping clearance flew 70 metres and over the dead-ball line. Clermont wing Joris Jurand was the beneficiary of his pack’s softening up process in their carries that ensured space out wide for the try scorer.
Plummer kicked the conversion and then exchanged penalties with Prendergast. In the opening moments of the second half Clermont threatened to score another try but the elegant Argentinian Bautista Delguy slipped as he escaped into the Leinster 22. Darcy Swain threw a loose pass and from the turnover, Prendergast sized up the opportunity.
He accelerated out of the 22 and his beautifully weighted diagonal grubber-kick was hacked on by Jimmy O’Brien, who regathered and passed inside to his supporting outhalf, who dotted down and then added the conversion.
Leinster’s scrum dominance was the conduit for a penalty try and a yellow card for Clermont’s 19-year-old tighthead prop Nohem Ez Zahouany. Sheehan’s second try, from another lineout launch play, took the Irish province out to a 36-16 lead heading into the final quarter.
But the visitors retained that capacity for sloppiness and that played its part in a try for Clermont replacement centre Mathys Belaubre. Any thoughts of a revival were dashed emphatically within 60 seconds. Jimmy O’Brien won the kick-off brilliantly in the air and from that point, Conan beat a handful of tacklers to the line but hurt his arm in grounding the ball.
Leinster had the final say on the scoreboard, Tommy O’Brien, showed speed and nous in switching the ball from one hand to the other as he rode contact to power over in the corner. Four minutes earlier Joey Carbery returned after his eight-year or 3,079-day hiatus from his last appearance in the province’s colours.
It’s unlikely that Leinster will sweat too much about the performance imperfections. There was enough for them to take into next week’s return to the URC and a clash with Munster at the Aviva Stadium.
With Caelan Doris sidelined, and Conan, also likely to be out, the fitness of Max Deegan and James Culhane will take on greater import. Before that they can reflect on a mission accomplished.

title: Man and woman charged in connection with fatal Waterford house fire
description: Philip and Kim English, and their children Callum (12) and Jayden (9) died last Tuesday
content:
Two people have appeared at a special court sitting charged in connection with a house fire that killed four members of the same family in Waterford on Tuesday.
Cian Stacey (21) and Jessica Dalton (31) appeared at Clonmel District Court charged with one count of criminal damage and two counts of assault causing serious harm.
Philip and Kim English and their sons Callum (12), and Jayden (9), died in their home on Tuesday.
Judge Andrew Gubbins presided over the special sitting of the court in Co Tipperary on Saturday evening and was told each defendant faced three charges.
Dalton appeared in court wearing a black sports top and leggings. Stacey wore a grey tracksuit top.
Dt Sgt Michael Burke told the court that Dalton, with an address in Waterford city, was charged with the three offences at 2.45pm on Saturday at Waterford Garda Station and made no reply.
Her barrister Ciaran Murphy said she consented to being remanded in custody until Tuesday at Waterford District Court.
He made an application for legal aid, saying she was a lone parent and not in employment.
Dt Sgt Brian O’Callaghan told the court that Stacey, of no fixed address, made no reply when he was charged at 2.44pm at Waterfront Garda Station.
Murphy made no application for bail and Stacey was remanded to appear by videolink on Tuesday at Waterfront District Court.
The lawyer made an application for legal aid.
The funerals of the four deceased are due to take place on Monday. – PA

title: Ulster secure bonus-point win away to Zebre in Challenge Cup opener
description: Richie Murphy’s side secure a first win of the season as they run in six tries in Parma
content:
Ulster got the job done in Parma, claiming their first win of the season and opening their Challenge Cup campaign with the hoped-for five points even though they had to battle to come away with the maximum return.
Last year’s beaten finalists scored six tries and conceding three as Zebre mounted a spirited second-half revival after the visitors had led 26-7 after their most consistent performance of the season.
Hooker Henry Walker scored twice with Jacob Stockdale, David McCann, Michael Lowry and Martin Moloney also touching down.
After a shaky start, Richie Murphy’s side marched down the park and after two penalties encamped them in the red zone, Juarno Augustus’s drive saw the bill ripped from him only to fall to Walker who scored, with Nathan Doak adding the conversion.
Doak crossed the Zebre line five minutes later after some great Ulster handling, but the scrumhalf lost the ball when hit by Giovanni Licata.
The visitors responded almost immediately, Cormac Izuchukwu and Walker carrying hard before Zac Ward put Stockdale through for a run-in. Doak missed from the angle, but Ulster looked comfortable.
Ulster’s ambition carved out number three, Doak’s chip over the top being gathered by Rob Baloucoune who made ground before Doak crosskicked to skipper McCann who kept the ball alive for Walker to step back in for his second touchdown.
Doak’s conversion made it 19-0 and though Ulster didn’t add to their total, they dominated the remainder of the half whether with ball in hand or through some aggressive defence.
Zebre came out with clear intent from the restart and after a scrum in Ulster’s 22, Licata’s surging run set up Jamie Benson to smash through to score with Giacomo da Re converting.
The visitors responded by putting a penalty to the corner and though their maul splintered when heading towards touch, Walker and Augustus drove it on before McCann reached out and touched the line for Ulster’s fourth try, which went upstairs before being confirmed and converted by Doak.
Discipline and accuracy began to fray somewhat for Ulster, with Jack Murphy being yellow carded for interfering with the ball on the deck just after the hour and only moments after coming on.
The result saw Zebre kick for the corner and after moving it away from the maul, Patricio Baronio gave the scoring pass to lock Alessandro Ortombina who dotted down at the posts allowing Giovanni Montemauri to convert.
With just over 10 minutes left, 14-man Ulster came strongly into Zebre’s 22 with the net result being a yellow card for Baronio and ultimately a score in the corner from Lowry to restore Ulster’s bonus point, the try being superbly converted by Benson.
A helter-skelter final 10 minutes then ensued, Montemauri scoring after a kick through had left Ulster short in the backfield and then converting his own effort to, once more, look like denying Ulster of the bonus point under the new rules that require a side to score by three or more tries that their opponents.
Ulster had to find a response and though looking increasingly ragged, they dug another seven points out when a sweeping attack ended with Moloney crossing in the corner off Murphy’s long pass.
Benson kicked another excellent conversion though they still had to withstand a late push from Zebre, with the game only ending after Izuchukwu’s lineout turnover on his own line.

title: Premier League round-up: Alexander Isak seals comeback win for Liverpool against nine-man Brentford
description: Haaland scores twice as Man City hold on to beat Ipswich;  Manzambi scores winner as Aston Villa claim points at Newcastle; Iwobi sinks Hull as Fulham secure first win
content:
Alexander Isak marked his return from injury with the winner as Liverpool came from behind to beat nine-man Brentford 2-1.
The Reds were misfiring as they trailed to Keane Lewis-Potter’s first-half goal, but the match turned on a needless red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk on the stroke of half-time.
Victor Munoz hauled Liverpool level after the break before Isak struck with his fifth goal of the season.
Brentford then lost Vitaly Janelt to a second yellow card in stoppage time.
Swedish striker Isak had missed the previous two matches but was able start alongside Florian Wirtz and recent signing Bradley Barcola in a £350 million frontline.
Erling Haaland struck twice as defiant Manchester City marched on at the top of the Premier League by holding on for a 3-2 win over Ipswich.
Phil Foden was also on target at the Etihad Stadium but City needed to survive a nervy finish after a Zian Flemming penalty gave the visitors late hope.
It was City’s second successive league victory since the club were found guilty of serious breaches of the competition’s financial regulations last month.
It also maintained their 100 per cent start to the campaign under new manager Enzo Maresca and lifted them six points clear of champions Arsenal at the top of the table.
Promoted Ipswich rallied to cancel out Foden’s opener through former Celtic forward Daizen Maeda but Haaland’s double, taking his tally for the campaign to 12 in all competitions, looked to have reasserted City’s authority.
The Norwegian was denied a hat-trick by VAR, and the game ended in frantic fashion, but City had done enough.
Johan Manzambi scored the only goal of the game as Aston Villa clinched a 1-0 win over Newcastle at St James’ Park.
An end-to-end first half saw the visitors go ahead through Manzambi, who had looked set to join the Magpies over the summer before Villa swooped in to sign him.
Newcastle had opportunities to level through Sven Botman and Yoane Wissa after the break, but Manzambi’s header proved to be the difference and takes his tally to two Premier League goals this season.
Victory lifts Villa into 12th in the table, while the Tynesiders slip to back-to-back league defeats.
Fulham’s winless run under Alvaro Arbeloa was finally ended by an entertaining 1-0 victory over Hull at Craven Cottage.
Alex Iwobi struck the winner in the 33rd minute to lift the home side off the foot of the Premier League table and out of the bottom three, though goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis will wonder how he ever let the shot spill through him.
It meant valuable breathing room for Arbeloa whose position had come under scrutiny after failing to win any of his first six league matches in charge, though a red card in the final seconds for Ryan Sessegnon for leaving his studs on Robinio Vaz marred the afternoon.
Fulham had dropped eight points from winning positions this season, including five when they had led inside the final two minutes, and their wastefulness after going in front was alarming, if not ultimately costly.
Gonzalo Garcia in particular spurned a golden opportunity when he headed against the crossbar with the six-yard box to himself. It was the kind of chance the former Real Madrid striker was brought in to bury, and Fulham may yet find their position remains perilous if they continue to give up chances like this.
Hull were a pale impression of the team that had begun the season with such attacking ambition, and the passiveness with which they approached a game against the side propping up the league will have been of concern for Sergej Jakirovic.

title: Dublin march sees dozens of assorted shoes represent healthcare workers in Gaza
description: Irish Healthcare Workers for Palestine group marches in capital
content:
Irish healthcare workers marched silently through Dublin on Saturday in solidarity with their counterparts abducted, imprisoned or killed in Gaza .
Starting from St Stephen’s Green, the Irish Healthcare Workers for Palestine group were accompanied by the The Children’s Blanket. Also known as the Granny Squares for Gaza, each of its 3,000 hand-knitted squares represents 10 children killed in Gaza.
About 130 pairs of white shoes were displayed representing healthcare workers killed or abducted.
Nicola Cantwell, a pharmacist from Co Carlow, said in April 2025, 1,400 pairs of shoes were displayed in the Netherlands. She said that since then the number had increased to 1,700.
“The shoes we have today are to highlight that increase and to focus people on thinking about the individuals that wore those shoes.”
The variety of shoes, from high heels to sandals and runners, served “to remind people that every person who died in Palestine was a person with a life”.
“This idea of raising awareness is fantastic and standing in solidarity is fantastic, but now the world knows what’s happening, so now what we need is for the world to make a collective, concentrated effort to stop the killing,” she said.
“The people in Gaza at this stage are not living. They’re just surviving. We need to give them back the joy and hope so, that’s why we’re here today, is to call on everybody to make changes.”
Two years ago, Cantwell set up the Irish Pharmacists for Palestine group. She has attended the marches since October 2023 to “stand in solidarity with the healthcare workers, the doctors, the dentists, the pharmacists that have been killed while working.
“It’s the first time ever that doctors and healthcare and hospitals have been seen as a target.
“I think that’s what’s throwing us all because traditionally, if somebody came into you, it didn’t matter what side they were on, they were always looked after and that’s our duty of care.”
Usually, she said, up to 1,000 people attended the marches.
Marchers held signs, posters and banners and walked with Irish and Palestinian flags.
Some of the signs said “stop bombing Gaza,” “let the children eat” and “Israel tortures doctors to death”.
Mike Grennan, from Co Offaly, is not a healthcare worker but travelled to Dublin to attend the march and “show bit of solidarity”.
He and a number of marchers held posters with the names of healthcare workers who have been detained.
Dr Caroline Jagoe Sherman, a speech and language therapist based in Trinity College Dublin, also attended the march.
She said she worked largely on disability rights and humanitarian action, describing Gaza as a “political crisis causing a humanitarian disaster”.
“From a disability angle what we’re seeing is the intentional creation of disability through mutilation, which is prohibited under international humanitarian law.”

title: Wexford Festival Opera 2026: L’Equivoco Stravagante review – Maria Barakova is remarkable in a production that hardly misses a trick
description: Rossini was just 19 when he wrote the soon banned Bizarre Misunderstanding, with its critique of nouveau-riche pretensions and stream of double entendres
content:
Ernestina’s hand has been promised to the wrong man. Her nouveau-riche father has his eye on someone rich and thick. She, however, has already fallen for another admirer – poor, of course.
He’s not just smart and good-looking; he also connives with the servants to make his way into the household as her tutor. A forged letter, purposely leaked, claims that Ernestina is actually male, a castrato in disguise, no less.
So far, so operatic. L’Equivoco Stravagante (The Bizarre Misunderstanding), which Gioachino Rossini wrote when he was 19, is one of the myriad of 19th-century operas that struggled to make it to the stage as their creators intended them.
L’Equivoco was first performed at the Teatro del Corso in Bologna in October 1811 only after implementing changes demanded by the censor. Even then it ran for only three nights before being banned.
