Rossini pillaged parts of it for eight other operas, but, although an arrangement for piano solo was published in the 1820s, the opera would not be performed again until 1964.
Gaetano Gasbarri’s libretto is a curious mishmash. It’s a story of outwardly fawning servants outwitting their master, and of true love winning out against a forced marriage, as well as a critique of nouveau-riche pretensions with literary allusions to match.
Oh, and there’s a stream of Carry On double entendres.
In 1811 the opera also triggered sensitivities to draft dodging and desertion, and brought up the subject of castratos at a time when the practice of castrating boys had become seriously frowned on.
And the opera itself? The summary above encompasses one of the work’s major problems. The setup is a long first act, and the fun only takes off in the much shorter second. This production’s director, Max Hoehn, and his designers (Darko Petrovic, set; Massimo Carlotto, costumes; Daniele Naldi, lighting) take us into a storybook cardboard world that sets up the 18th-century buffo atmosphere before a foot has been set on stage.
The Russian mezzo-soprano Maria Barakova is a properly prim Ernestina, but with a style of delivery to die for. Rossini wrote this punishingly difficult role for Marietta Marcolini, a singer who would become his muse. Barakova, with powerful, smoky-toned projection at the lower end, and ringing high notes at the top, sings it with such pinpoint accuracy and effortless projection that the part sounds as if it could have been written for her. And she brings it off with an insouciance that hides all of its difficulties. Remarkable.
The Russian-born German baritone Stefan Astakhov plays her father, Gamberotto, as a wonderfully self-important buffoon, lively without even having to twitch a limb, and with a pleasingly cavernous tone.
As Ermanno, the suitor who wins out, the Polish tenor Sebastian Mach has a manner that is sometimes vocally less than well centred, with tone that is sometimes pinched. His rival Buralicchio is the firm and warm-toned Armenian baritone Gurgen Baveyan, who gets some of the best lines and plays dumb with glee.
The Argentinian tenor Carlos Natale and the Wexford soprano Kelli-Ann Masterson are a class act as the wily servants Frontino and Rosalia, and the singers of the well-deployed chorus are in fine form.
The skill of the ensembles, a Rossini characteristic, was well in evidence even at this early stage in his career. Hoehn’s production hardly misses a trick, and Riccardo Bisatti encourages much sensitive playing from the Wexford Festival Orchestra.
L’Equivoco Stravagante will be performed again on Wednesday, October 21st, Sunday, October 25th, and Thursday , October 29th. Wexford Festival Opera runs until Saturday, October 31st

title: Ellen Walshe strikes gold as Mona McSharry completes remarkable nine-medal World Cup Series haul
description: Walsh won the 200m butterfly final in Astana while McSharry makes the podium yet again with bronze in the 50m breaststroke
content:
Ellen Walshe claimed her first victory of the 2026 World Aquatics World Cup Series on Saturday, while Mona McSharry completed a remarkable campaign with a ninth medal from nine events as the series came to a close in Astana, Kazakhstan.
Already a silver medallist in the 200m butterfly from the opening leg of the series and a bronze medallist in Friday’s 200m backstroke, Walshe went one better in Saturday’s 200m butterfly final with a stunning victory.
The Templeogue swimmer touched home in 2:04.05, a full two seconds clear of China’s Xinyang Zhou (2:06.12), with Mohan Chang third in 2:06.28.
Shortly after securing gold, Walshe was back in the pool for the 200m individual medley final. She finished fourth overall in 2:07.00, her fastest time in the event across the series.
McSharry brought her World Cup campaign to a close with yet another breaststroke medal, this time claiming bronze in the 50m breaststroke.
McSharry has remarkably climbed the podium in all nine events she contested across the series, returning home with a haul of three gold, two silver and four bronze medals.
She clocked 29.89 in Saturday’s final, with Russia’s Ralina Giliazova taking gold in 29.54 and Belgium’s Florine Gaspard silver in 29.71.
Attention now turns to the World Aquatics Swimming Championships (25m) in Beijing, China, from December 1st-6th, where both McSharry and Walshe are set to compete. The full Ireland team will be announced in November.

title: Health budget no longer based on evidence, consultants’ conference told
description: Cork University Hospital CEO says returning to HSE ‘like stepping back in time’
content:
The health budget for next year is “unrealistically low”, creating a high likelihood of further financial overruns in 2027, the State’s fiscal watchdog has said.
The health service was allocated €25.8 billion in current expenditure this year, but a significant deficit has developed which could reach up to €1 billion by the end of the year.
Budget 2027 allocated €27.4 billion for current services, however Niall Conroy, acting chief economist at the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (IFAC) , said that in reality this was only a “modest” uplift.
Speaking at the Irish Hospital Consultants’ Association (IHCA) annual conference in Kilkenny on Saturday, Conroy said the way in which the health budget is calculated was no longer “evidence-based”.
The health service requires a standstill cost of €1.7 billion for next year, Conroy said, but he argued that when the estimated €1 billion overrun this year is factored in, next year’s increase equates to €600 million.
“It’ll be about 2 per cent. That is well below the cost to maintain the existing level of service,” he said.
“If I was giving this talk again next year, I think I’ll be talking about substantial overruns next year as well.”
Conroy said the sector was being budgeted just to “stand still”.
[ How can runaway spending in the health service be reined in? Opens in new window ]
He criticised the recruitment-freeze cycle, describing a pattern in which the health service recruits in the first half of the year, expenditure exceeds allocation, and then tighter controls or a moratorium is introduced.
“That’s a very poor way of doing workforce planning.”
Speaking at the same conference, Jennifer Kearney, chief executive of Cork University Hospital (CUH), said when she returned to the HSE “it felt, in some respects, like stepping back in time, nearly 10 or 15 years”.
Kearney worked in the UK’s NHS for 22 years, and took the top job in the Cork hospital 15 months ago.
Outlining various difficulties the hospital was contending with, she cited to delegates “the infrastructure, the constraints, the funding arrangements, the complexity of pay and number strategy, the limited autonomy available to those responsible for delivering services”.
Kearney came under public scrutiny in August when she wrote to the HSE, stating the hospital was facing increasing patient safety risks due to a shortage of 1,000 staff.
[ Half of HSE regions have ‘eaten into’ next year’s budget due to overruns, Minister says Opens in new window ]
Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill argued against Kearney’s statements, adding that the hospital had hired a significant number of staff this year and had exceeded its pay budget.
Kearney said she “absolutely stands” behind the patient safety concerns she highlighted, adding the situation “is getting worse”.
She told IHCA members that only seven posts have been approved for CUH since letters she wrote to August emerged in the media, adding that the “gap is getting wider” between what the hospital needs and has.
“We lost €15 million [from our budget] at the start of the year due to supplementary budget. We started already in the red,” she said.
“I want to switch on the CAT scanners that are currently gathering dust because I don’t have the radiographers to open them. Diagnostic capacity, 50 per cent of it is switched off.”
The surgical hub at CUH is open but she said it was not operating at full capacity due to employment restrictions in the region.
She acknowledged the hospital was “overspending” but said this was because of inflation associated with the public-only consultant contract as well as increased overtime due to staff shortages.
Carroll MacNeill has been critical of HSE regions overrecruiting. Last week, she described the practice as “unsustainable” and warned that those areas had “eaten into next year’s allocation”.

title: Have you seen Kevin Bacon’s clothes? Actor appeals for help finding outfits shipped to Ireland
description: Actor’s beloved outfits have been to Israel, France and the UK but remain unaccounted for
content:
There seems to be more than six degrees of separation between Kevin Bacon and his clothes this weekend.
The actor has issued a plea for help in recovering his trunk, lost en route to Ireland where he is filming a horror movie called The Summoner.
Bacon shared his own personal horror story – one that will resonate with anyone who has ever had a parcel lost in transit and found making contact with those who lost it impossible – with more than five million users of Instagram on Friday evening.
And he expressed concern that he might never be reunited with the clothes – some of which date back to the 1990s and are infused with sentimental value.
The story started with a brainwave. Rather than packing his belongings into suitcases and being encumbered as he made his way from the US to Ireland, Bacon chose to travel light and shipped his clothes from upstate New York instead.
Instead of coming directly to Ireland, his belongings ended up in Israel not once or even twice, but on three separate occasions.
They then went on and extended tour of Europe before eventually travelling to Ireland.
[ Kevin Bacon: ‘A lot of actors say they’re really shy. That’s bullsh*t. You want people to look at you’ Opens in new window ]
But while he has been assiduously tracking his vintage jeans, boots and hats for several weeks, and has established that the clothes are now tantalisingly close to him, at the time of writing their actual location remained something of a mystery.
“I wanted to pack light, so I decided to ship some old clothes over to Ireland,” he said on Instagram. “I don’t buy a lot of clothes [and] I’ve had these clothes probably since the 1990s so I used the shipping service. I don’t wanna say the name but it rhymes with bread X.”
He said the box left New York on September 26th and went straight to Memphis. From Memphis, it went to France and by September 28th it had arrived in Germany.
For reasons best known to itself, the courier company that rhymes with bread X then shipped his stuff directly to Israel.
On October 4th, it went back to France. It was there only briefly and it was sent to Israel a second time. A day later it went from Israel to Germany and then back to Israel.
“On October 11th, [the package] left the UK and came straight to Ireland, where it has been sitting for five days and they say they’re unable to deliver it,” Bacon said.
[ Kevin Bacon: ‘I was incredibly cocky and unwilling to take any advice’ Opens in new window ]
“I could buy some clothes, but I want these clothes,” he told his followers. “I’ve had them since the ’90s. They have a certain sentimental value.”
The Irish Times contacted the company Bacon refers to as bread X to see if we could help bring an end to the six or so degrees of separation from Bacon.
“We sincerely apologize for this experience. We are in direct contact with Mr. Bacon’s team to deliver the xxpackage,”’a Fed-Ex spokeswoman said. “This outcome should have happened sooner, and we are reviewing what went wrong to help ensure we deliver the level of service our customers expect and deserve.”

title: Women in ministry among main issues at historic Irish Catholic assembly
description: Among proposals is that the Church seeks a ‘more respectful and life-giving vocabulary’ on LGBT+ people
content:
A historic National Synodal Assembly of the Catholic Church in Ireland, the first of its kind, is taking place behind closed doors at a hotel in Gormanston, Co Meath on Saturday.
It is attended by over 280 lay, religious, and clergy delegates from across the island of Ireland, including 23 bishops led by the Catholic Primate, Archbishop Eamon Martin.
Cardinal Mario Grech, from the Vatican’s General Secretariat of the Universal Synod was due to address the event remotely, attended by representatives of the Church of Ireland, the Methodist Church and the Irish Council of Churches.
The assembly is the culmination of a five-year process which began in October 2021, during which seven priorities for Church renewal were established – belonging; co-responsibility and lay ministry; family; formation and catechesis; healing; women; and youth.
Delegates are considering 35 proposals in a working document which, if agreed, will be presented to the full Irish Episcopal Conference.
One of those proposals recommends “that the Church in Ireland advocate for ongoing exploration of women’s ministry, including the diaconate”. It reminds delegates that “a voice for the full and equal inclusion of women in all areas of the life of the Church, including the ordained ministry, has been heard at all moments of the Synodal Pathway” over the past five years.
It speaks of rebalancing “our Church’s unconscious bias” where women are concerned and calls for “a thorough and systematic examination and correction of texts, hymnals, and other materials that do not recognise the baptismal dignity of all persons”.
The language “of the Divine Feminine, as expressed throughout our scriptures, and by women saints, mystics, and scholars” should be “proactively rediscovered and normalised as expressions of God,” it said.
[ Dublin’s Liberties bells ring after 20 years’ silence following revival project Opens in new window ]
The working document also calls for the establishment of “a liturgical season (eg Easter season) [to] be upheld as a season of special focus in which we highlight the discipleship of the women of our scripture.”
It also recommends “the establishment of a national office for women” which would “oversee and support root and branch culture change, which would enable the full participation of women in line with the equal dignity bestowed by Baptism and recognised in the Church’s documents”.
More generally, another proposal calls for “greater recognition and affirmation of lay ministry as an integral part of the Church’s mission. Increased participation of lay women and men in pastoral, liturgical and leadership roles”.
Where LGBT+ people are concerned, a proposal recommends “that the Church in Ireland would ask the universal Church to develop a more respectful and life-giving vocabulary when speaking about LGBT+ people” and says the Irish Catholic Church should “take a lead in calling the universal Church to employ respectful language in relation to LGBT+ people”.
Other proposals being considered call for “real partnership with migrant communities”; for the dismantling of “the systemic prejudice, misunderstanding, and social exclusion endured by the Travelling People within the Church and wider society”; that “the Church at all levels foster appreciation of the principles of Catholic social teaching”; and for all Christians in Ireland “to renew the sense of ecumenical dialogue and accompaniment locally”.

title: Pedro Neto double at Everton leads Chelsea to victory marred by Emi Martínez head injury
description: Chelsea goalkeeper was stretchered from the pitch following collision with Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite
author_name: Andy Hunter at Hill Dickinson Stadium
content:
Chelsea have returned from the international break with an authority that augurs well for Xabi Alonso. Two goals from Pedro Neto condemned Everton to a first defeat of the season as the visitors climbed to fourth on the back of their first Premier League clean sheet since January. A head injury sustained by Emi Martínez, who was carried off on a stretcher after seven minutes of treatment, was the only concern from a mature display in the Merseyside sunshine for Alonso’s team.
There were goalkeeping problems at both ends, with Jordan Pickford unconvincing for the second week in succession as David Moyes’s side suffered self-inflicted wounds. But Everton could have no complaints about the merits of Chelsea’s victory given their contrasting performances in the second half.
There was more needle than quality on display in a first half that Everton edged and they could question why they were still facing 11 men by half-time. Morgan Rogers risked a second yellow card when leaping into a challenge with James Garner shortly before the break. The Chelsea forward caught the ball and the man but, beyond both players feeling the impact of the 50-50, there was no further punishment from Paul Tierney.
Rogers’s tackle was just as reckless as the one that brought an earlier booking for Harrison Armstrong, one of five yellows shown in a half that owed its entertainment to the animosity between the teams. The hosts’ grievance deepened when Rogers played a part in Neto’s breakthrough moments after the restart.
Having denied Chelsea their customary early goal – with Pickford saving from Cole Palmer and Jarrad Branthwaite blocking a goal-bound Jordan Henderson effort – Everton acquitted themselves well in the first half. They should have taken the lead from a corner awarded after Martínez was penalised for holding the ball too long.
Garner’s initial delivery was poor, in keeping with Everton’s crossing for much of the game, but Jack Grealish supplied an inch-perfect cross at the second attempt for Thierno Barry. The unmarked Everton striker steered a tame header straight at Martínez from close range and the centre of the goal. Another big miss from Barry was one of several recurring themes that undermined Everton’s efforts.
The Chelsea goalkeeper tipped over a Grealish volley as the home side maintained the pressure and also saved comfortably from Barry’s difficult attempt inside the box. The visitors began to turn the tide as the interval approached and were inches away from taking the lead in spectacular fashion. Moisés Caicedo pulled away to the back post for a Henderson corner that arrived exactly where the training ground routine required. His thunderous volley flew past Pickford but smacked the bar, leaving it shaking for several seconds.
Neto forced a decent save from the Everton goalkeeper from distance in first-half stoppage time and beat him from much closer range 44 seconds after the restart. As in the draw at Hull last weekend, Ainsley Maitland-Niles and Pickford were found wanting defensively and duly punished.
Rogers was somewhat inevitably involved when releasing Jorrel Hato, Alonso’s one enforced change from the 5-1 defeat of Bournemouth, away from Maitland-Niles down the Chelsea left. Hato’s low cross from the byline took a touch off James Tarkowski and found Neto, whose shot beat Pickford’s weak attempt to save low to his left.
Goalkeeping worries took on a far more serious complexion when Branthwaite collided with Martínez as they challenged for a Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall free-kick. The Argentina international required lengthy treatment before being carried away with his neck in a brace and to the sound of Evertonian boos. Thankfully he did give a thumbs up to Branthwaite when the concerned Everton defender waited to wish him well.
Martínez’s replacement, Mike Penders, on his Premier League debut, was not seriously tested as the Everton threat petered out and Chelsea managed the closing stages well. Victory was sealed in the final minute of normal time when Henderson’s free-kick struck the head of Barry, rebounded off the Everton substitute Tyrique George and Vitalii Mykolenko, before dropping to Neto. The Chelsea winger rolled a confident finish past Pickford’s despairing dive into the bottom corner. – Guardian

title: Rory McIlroy slips out of contention after eight-hole nightmare in India
description: McIlroy’s Race to Dubai rival Eugenio Chacarra leads by two shots with third round to be completed on Sunday
content:
Rory McIlroy slipped out of contention as Race to Dubai rival Eugenio Chacarra led the DP World India Championship at the end of Saturday’s play.
McIlroy is seeking to win the Harry Vardon Trophy for an eighth time, equalling the record held by Colin Montgomerie, but did himself no favours with four bogeys and a double in an eight-hole stretch in his third round.
Chacarra is the nearest challenger to Patrick Reed, who narrowly made the cut in Delhi at level par before ending the day six under, on the season-long rankings, with McIlroy just behind in third.
Round two was completed on Saturday morning following long weather delays earlier in the week, with Chacarra leading by one at that stage on 10 under par after a second successive round of 67 featuring seven birdies.
The Spaniard added four more in the first seven holes of round three and was 14 under, 10 shots ahead of McIlroy, when bad light ended play. He will return with seven holes of his round still to complete, leading by two strokes from Angel Hidalgo and Joost Luiten.
McIlroy birdied the penultimate hole as he wrapped up his second round, then opened his third with another gain to provide some early encouragement.
But things quickly went downhill from there, finding thick rough at the third and sand at the fourth where he missed a short putt to make it back-to-back bogeys.
A double followed at the sixth, where his chip from another tangled lie beside the green travelled barely a yard, and though he birdied the next he bogeyed the ninth and 10th after missing from five feet at the latter.
He holed from a greenside bunker to eagle the 14th shortly before the hooter, at which point he was in a share of 40th place with three holes to play.
Scotland’s Scott Jamieson, who almost aced the par-three seventh, was 11 under, three off the lead and also facing 25 holes on Sunday. England’s Todd Clements and Tom McKibbin ended the day a shot further back.
Reigning champion Tommy Fleetwood was nine under, matching Italian Gregorio De Leo for the best score among those to have completed their rounds. Fellow Englishman Dan Bradbury was a shot further back alongside Scotland’s Bob MacIntyre, who had five holes outstanding, with Shane Lowry and Laurie Canter among the group at seven under.

title: CRH analysts play catch-up as Wall Street braces for rare earnings miss
description: Rising energy costs and slump in US housebuilding have put pressure on building materials group forecasts
content:
T he honeymoon is over for CRH chief executive Jim Mintern .
Shares in the building materials and solutions giant jumped more than 40 per cent from the start of his tenure early last year to an all-time high of $131.55 in early January – valuing the business at almost $88 billion (€78 billion).
The rally was fuelled by Mintern’s strategy, unveiled last September, which pledged $40 billion in investment and shareholder returns over five years, alongside annual revenue growth of 7-9 per cent and higher profit margins. Anticipation of the company joining the prestigious S&P 500 index late last year also boosted sentiment, as did a consistent buyer of its shares: CRH itself.
CRH spent $1.2 billion buying back and cancelling its own stock in 2025. It brought the total spent under a repurchase programme that started under Mintern’s predecessor, Albert Manifold , in 2018 to $9.6 billion.
However, the group’s stock has slumped by 40 per cent from those January highs to a low of $78.60 on Wednesday on the New York Stock Exchange , where it moved its main listing two years ago. North America accounted for more than 70 per cent of its earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) last year.
Consensus analysts’ earnings forecasts have trended lower over the course of the year as the Middle East crisis has driven up fuel costs and had a knock-on impact on US house building.
CRH’s energy costs surged more than 17 per cent in the second quarter and were running at an annualised $2.33 billion. The conflict has also sent mortgage rates higher, compounding the affordability problems that were already weighing on US house building.
The average rate on a 15-year fixed-rate mortgage now exceeds 6.7 per cent, up from 5.5 per cent a year ago, according to Freddie Mac, the government-backed mortgage finance company.
With CRH due to unveil its latest quarterly results on October 29th, a number of analysts are beginning to contemplate something rare: an earnings miss from a company with a strong reputation for delivering on its guidance.
Taking a red pen in recent weeks to his forecasts for a host of US construction materials groups, Truist Securities analyst Keith Hughes now sees CRH’s Ebitda coming in at $7.87 billion. While that would mark 2.5 per cent growth on 2025, it would come in below CRH’s own forecast of a figure between $8.1 billion and $8.5 billion.
“The cut at CRH is particularly notable given a long history of hitting numbers, but we now see the possibility of an estimate range reduction,” Hughes warned.
He’s not alone. Shane Carberry of Goodbody, one of the group’s corporate brokers, recently shaved 3 per cent off his Ebitda estimate and now sees it coming in at $7.99 billion. Still, the consensus among analysts, for now, is that CRH will achieve the lower end of its guidance.
Jefferies analysts have said CRH faces “a significant effort” to reach that lower end of its full-year target as cost inflation continues apace. But, for now, they reckon that acquisitions “may bridge the gap”.
Under Manifold, CRH transformed through a series of large acquisitions – and, as importantly, divestments of unwanted assets – from being a business that essentially crushed big rocks into cement, aggregates and asphalt to become a vertically integrated leading infrastructure player in North America.
Mintern has sharpened CRH’s focus even more on what he calls three mega-trends: continuing investment in the transport system, from roads to airports; a need to develop water management; and the re-industrialisation of the US.
AI data centres are among the hottest re-industrialisation plays, with the Trump administration placing them at the heart of America’s industrial revival – betting that they will power the factories of the future and give the US a competitive edge.
Mintern said on a call with analysts in July that CRH was active on 200 data centre projects, with 85 per cent of all current construction in this area within 25 miles of one of the group’s locations.
[ CRH to buy aggregates operations in Denmark and Finland Opens in new window ]
The world’s largest five hyperscalers – large-scale cloud computing and technology companies, Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle – are expected to spend almost $700 billion this year on US data centres, according to JP Morgan. Construction accounts for about 15 per cent of total development costs.
But while the infrastructure and non-residential construction sectors accounted for more than two-thirds of CRH’s global revenues last year, 32 per cent came from house building, repair and remodelling.
US home completions slumped almost 13 per cent in the first eight months of the year, according to US Census Bureau data. And data for September is due to be reported next Tuesday. With builders grappling with rising interest rates and weak demand, they’re unlikely to provide much relief.
An earnings miss looks more than priced in at CRH, however.
Truist’s new price target of $105 for the stock – after cutting its forecasts – points to about 25 per cent upside.
The group’s enterprise value – its market capitalisation plus net debt – stands at less than 8.8 times the bottom end of its full-year Ebitda forecast. While that is in line with its 10-year average, CRH has spent much of the last two years trading between 10 and 12 times earnings, after enjoying a valuation re-rating following the move of its primary listing to New York.*
The consensus price goal among analysts of $127 suggests more than 50 per cent.
CRH is also poised to tilt further towards infrastructure with the expected completion early next year of its $8.5 billion acquisition of Dallas-based Arcosa – the biggest of more than 1,200 deals in the group’s history.
The honeymoon may be over. But could delivery on the promises of the Arcosa deal woo Wall Street investors again?
*Updates to amend the valuation multiple reference

title: Viral stars Angine de Poitrine at Vicar Street review: Silly, sublime, scintillating
description: Even in the TikTok era a band cannot thrive on huge rubber face masks alone. Angine de Poitrine have the tunes to go with the absurdist threads
content:
Here’s something you don’t see every day: a man dressed as a giant marionette from your deepest nightmares bashing out the toe-curling “olé, olé, olé” refrain on a double-necked guitar.
But that‘s just one surreal highlight as Angine de Poitrine, the surprise breakthrough duo of the year, storm Vicar Street on Friday with a concert that is at once bizarre, breathtaking and boisterously enjoyable.
Guitarist Khn de Poitrine and drummer Klek de Poitrine – possibly not their real names – play intense instrumental rock, with the added flourish of doing so while dressed as terrifying polka-dot-themed Teletubbies.
It sounds like a gimmick, but the Canadians are committed to the bit: on stage they speak in disconcerting R2D2 mumbles, make triangle symbols with their hands and encourage audience participation via two huge inflatable dice that bounce around the room.
In a world of homogenised rock music the Quebecois pair cut quite the dash, having gone viral when a US radio station posted a video session on social media over the summer.
With his big papier-mache nose wobbling and the carton on his head resembling a McDonald’s fry receptacle, Khn looks like an art installation come to life. Klek is a dead ringer for Mr Blobby of BBC Saturday-night notoriety. You half-expect him to remove his helmet to reveal Noel Edmonds gurning beneath.
Even in the TikTok era a band cannot thrive on huge rubber face masks alone, and Angine de Poitrine have the tunes to go with the absurdist threads. Their dazzling musicianship eclipses their novelty as they plunge into their opener, Angor, a piece of sophisticated “math rock” where heavy-metal noodling is played in the style of a jazz virtuoso.
The blueprint stays largely the same through the 80-minute performance. Khn uses Ed Sheeran-style loop pedals to build into the huge, arpeggiated riff odysseys of Yor Zarad and Ababa Hotel; Klek delivers complex drum shuffles while wobbling slightly from side to side.
But, though it’s essentially the same idea recycled throughout the night, the duo somehow manage to never repeat themselves. Whenever it does threaten to become formulaic, they break out the R2D2 bleeps and start with the hand gestures.
It’s enough to have an overexcited concertgoer yelling “olé, olé, olé” with joy, and that’s exactly what happens. At this point in the evening other artists might roll their eyes or call us simpletons, as Matty Healy of The 1975 did a few years back. Khn goes with it, however, playing along to the singing. It’s a sweet moment during a concert that is both silly and sublime, and at full pelt, simply scintillating.

title: Kerry house with couple and three children inside attacked with petrol bombs
description: Tralee property is damaged, no injuries reported after incident involving a number of males early on Saturday morning
content:
A house in Kerry, occupied by a couple and their three small children, was attacked with petrol bombs early on Saturday morning.
The attack took place at about 4.50am when a number of males got out of a car and threw the bombs at the house in the Fortfield area of Tralee .
The property was damaged though no injuries were reported.
Gardaí confirmed emergency services responded to a report of criminal damage by fire at a residence in the areas.
Fire services extinguished the fire and made the area safe. Gardaí said investigations were ongoing.
Garda technical experts were examining the scene and gardaí were doing door-to-door inquires and canvassing for CCTV in the area and approach roads.
Last week, four people died after a petrol bomb was thrown at the front door of a house on the Birchwood estate outside Waterford city early on Tuesday morning.
Philip and Kim English and their two young sons, Callum (12) and Jayden (9), were killed. Two other children, a girl of 14 and a boy of six, remain in critical condition in Crumlin Children’s Hospital.

title: Man charged with murder of Mark Cullen in Dún Laoghaire, Dublin, last summer
description: Father of three was fatally injured in gun attack at Kill Avenue last July
content:
A man (32) has been remanded in custody, charged with the murder of Mark Cullen, who died following a shooting in Dún Laoghaire, Co Dublin, during the summer.
Cullen was fatally injured in the gun attack at Patrician Park on Kill Avenue on Sunday, July 5th. The father of three, from Shanganagh Cliffs, Shankill, in south Co Dublin, was shot in the leg and died at the scene.
Gardaí arrested Edward Andrews of Radharc na Farraige, Wicklow town, earlier this week for questioning, and charged him with the murder of Cullen.
He was held overnight pending his appearance before Judge John Hughes at Dublin District Court on Saturday morning.
Before the case began, solicitor Edward Bradbury told the judge he normally represented Andrews but that he could not act for him in these proceedings because of the ongoing legal industrial dispute.
Solicitors have withdrawn their services in response to legal aid payment reforms introduced in July, causing widespread disruption to the criminal justice system.
The judge said: “It is a very serious charge before the court, murder.”
Bradbury replied: “I am here out of respect to my client and respect to his rights, and the court.
“This places every active participant in the court in an invidious position; it is not acceptable from the profession’s perspective.”
Det Sgt Grace O’Boyle of Dún Laoghaire station gave evidence of arrest, charge and caution. She told the court Andrews replied “no comment” when the charge was put to him at 9.40pm on Friday.
The District Court does not have jurisdiction to consider bail in a murder charge, which requires an application to the High Court, and Andrews was automatically remanded in custody. He will appear at Cloverhill District Court on Friday.
The court granted Andrews a legal aid certificate, but no solicitor had yet been assigned. The judge told him that very few solicitors in Dublin were operating under the new scheme.
Hughes said the accused was eligible because he was unemployed and receiving social welfare.

title: ‘I feel so grateful’: Fine Gael MEP Maria Walsh announces birth of child after fertility treatment
description: Former Rose of Tralee thanks staff at University Hospital Galway
content:
Fine Gael MEP Maria Walsh has announced the birth of her first baby following fertility treatment.
The former Rose of Tralee took to Instagram to share the news.
She said her baby girl, named Nell Brigid Walsh, was “loved beyond words”.
“My bright shining light – the meaning of your first name. My force of nature – your middle name recognising our heroic St Brigid,” she posted.
“Our village has gathered. Mamó (granny) and Daideo (grandad) already showing you the way.”
She thanked her medical team and the staff at University Hospital Galway.
“I feel so grateful, and I am so in love.”
Walsh, who is a member of the LGBTQI community, previously spoke with podcast presenter Róisín Ingle on an episode of The Irish Times Women’s Podcast during the summer.
She said she had always wanted a family. As a younger woman her “dream was to be in a partnership”, when she became a mother, but “that just didn’t happen.”
In late 2024, Walsh, who was 37 at the time, began researching fertility options and the route to solo parenthood.
“If I didn’t do it, I would have deep regret within myself for not even trying,” she told Ingle.
Walsh, who was born in Boston and grew up in Co Mayo, announced her pregnancy in May on Instagram.

title: Pope Leo leaves hospital after lung cancer surgery
description: Pontiff will lead ​prayers from his Vatican apartment in ⁠St Peter’s Square on Sunday
content:
Pope Leo has been discharged from hospital in Rome after undergoing an operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung.
Leo (71), was deemed “fit for discharge”, his doctors, Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement published by the Vatican .
He walked unaided from the hospital on Saturday afternoon, to cheers from well-wishers.
Leo, who in May last year became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic Church , has been in the Gemelli hospital since Tuesday, when doctors removed part of his right lung in order to extract the tumour.
“Considering the blood tests, the chest X-ray done this morning, and evaluating the clinical picture, the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge,” the statement said.
Doctors said on Wednesday that Leo’s recovery from the operation was progressing normally. They are waiting for the results of tests to determine whether the cancer has spread and if more treatment will be needed.
Leo was diagnosed with the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma.
The pontiff celebrated mass in his room on the 10th floor of the Gemelli hospital in the northwest of the Italian capital before being discharged.
The Vatican said he would recite the Angelus prayer on Sunday “from the window of the papal apartment”. It was during his angelus last week, in a rare moment of Vatican transparency, that Leo made the shock announcement to the crowd gathered in St Peter’s Square that a small nodule on his lung had been detected during a check-up.
[ Pope Leo’s cancer diagnosis tests the assumption of a long papacy Opens in new window ]
The pope has worked from hospital, including making a phone call on Friday to Vladimir Putin, during which he urged the Russian president to call a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
The Vatican had originally estimated a week-long stay in hospital. The pope’s appointments had been cancelled until October 20th.
[ Pope Leo asks Putin for ceasefire to allow aid to occupied Ukrainian town Opens in new window ]
It is uncertain if he’ll make an intense 12-day trip to South America planned in November.
Cardinal ​Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s secretary of state, told reporters on Friday that Leo may need to readjust his trip schedule, at least with regard to South America, depending on his health.
Before the cancer diagnosis, Leo, who enjoys sports, especially playing tennis, was generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.
The Gemelli, located in the northwest of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish a high-security papal suite. - The Guardian

title: Ruairí Kinsella on rehab after ACL injury: ‘I didn’t go full Roy Keane on the machine’
description: The forward is among four Meath footballers working their way back from knee ligament injuries, one milestone at a time
content:
We have become something of a Monday club – a quartet of crocked Meath footballers gathering to try to navigate our way back from cruciate knee ligament injuries.
The recovery journey is largely a lonesome one but on Monday evenings we meet in Dunganny with Meath physio David McCrea for a collective gym session.
I tore my cruciate in June, Jack Kinlough suffered an ACL (anterior cruciate ligament) reoccurrence around the same time, Seán Coffey got injured in early August and just a couple of weeks later my Dunshaughlin team-mate Conor Gray suffered the same fate.
It’s not exactly a club with a waiting list of applicants eager to join, but those Monday get-togethers have helped break the monotony of the solitary rehab sessions every other day.
Don’t get me wrong, there are Mondays when lads might not want to see each other – just get in, get the work done and get out. But mostly it has been helpful for us all to have others going through the same recovery process.
It gives you a lift when other lads are encouraging you or notice that you’ve made progress. Ultimately, we’re doing our best to help each other come out the other side of this.
I was at training the night Conor got injured. He wasn’t in massive pain and initially thought he might even be able to run it off, but there was discomfort so the physio looked at him and recommended a scan. We were all shocked by the result.
When I suffered my injury during a Meath training session in the summer, Conor drove me home that night. It’s hard to believe we are both now dealing with cruciate injuries.
The four of us have chatted in recent weeks about the prevalence of cruciate injuries with Gaelic footballers, we’ve thrown out various opinions on what might be contributing to the rise but ultimately we can’t land on any definitive reason.
[ Women and girls in the dark on injuries due to lack of gender-specific research Opens in new window ]
All we really have control of now is our recovery. Outside of Monday, that’s the lonely road we face. I’ve not kicked a football since June. I was only thinking about that this week. I’ve tried the odd solo with my good leg but I haven’t properly kicked a ball in more than four months. I can’t remember another time in my life where that’s happened.
There have been days I’ve been up in the gym looking out at the pitch and I’d find myself drifting off wondering what it feels like to kick a ball. Even saying that sounds strange, but the injury changed so much, so quickly.
For the most part, I’ve been staying positive, getting through the work and I’d be buzzing around thinking: “Yeah, I’m going well here, everything is going to plan.” But then there are still days you’d find it hard to get motivated because you’ve nothing to actually get fit for or aim towards for a long time.
I’ve got a static bike in the house now so a lot of my cardio work is done on it. Getting going can be the tough part but I always feel better after a session.
My go-to workout on the bike is 20 reps of 30 seconds on, 30 seconds off. By the end of that there would be a puddle of sweat under the bike. If I’m not feeling the energy for a hard session I’d maybe do 30 minutes straight in zone two or zone three.
Occasionally I’d notice the stronger leg working harder than the injured leg and I’d inadvertently find myself almost cycling sideways. So I’d have to readjust myself on the saddle.
In general I’ve been staying disciplined and would have something to do in the gym every day – whether it be exercises for the injured leg, the non-injured leg or upper body.
[ Giovanni Leoni’s return from ACL injury delayed in fresh blow to Liverpool Opens in new window ]
I’m back doing a good bit of jumping and working on running mechanics. You are basically trying to train your leg how to run again. I am still using the cold compression therapy machine and recently took my first isokinetic test in Santry – some people know it as the Roy Keane machine because of the viral video of him hammering out the reps during his cruciate recovery. I was happy with how it went, but it’s fair to say I didn’t go full Keano on it!
I’m walking quite freely now, the crutches are gone and I’m able to drive again. That has allowed me resume sub-teaching, which has been great. The original plan was to apply for a permanent teaching position in September but after the injury I decided to sub instead for this school year, allowing me more time to focus on my recovery while also gaining further teaching experience.
Staying busy is part of the plan, to be honest.
I went away with my brothers for a weekend to Rosslare as well, sea-swimming and some golf. We got a few buggies to go around the course but while they were playing golf, I was essentially playing pitch and putt. I wasn’t able to complete a full swing so I’d drive down the fairway in the buggy, drop the ball on a nice smooth patch and chip it towards the green. The lads enjoyed that!
I’ve done some co-commentary for matches during the Meath championship, got accepted to do a GPA emerging leaders course and also graduated from Maynooth, so life has been going on.
With the injury, my next significant milestone is a return to straight-line running. I’m still possibly three or four weeks away but there’s a definite sense it’s getting closer.
The Meath county final takes places on Sunday between Wolfe Tones and Donaghmore-Ashbourne. The winners, and the losers, will no doubt gather on Monday to pour over the details of the game.
And in Dunganny, our alternative Monday club will also reconvene.

title: Deforestation in Brazil’s Amazon falls to all-time low ahead of pivotal election vote
description: Forest clearing reached record highs approaching 30,000 square kilometers per year in the ‌mid-90s
content:
Deforestation in Brazil ’s Amazon rainforest declined to the lowest level on record in the 12 months through July, according ​to data released by Brazilian space research agency Inpe on Friday.
But whether this globally important success is maintained or reversed is on a knife edge ahead of a presidential election run-off on October 25th between two candidates with sharply different visions for the future of the rainforest.
The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , known as Lula, fell behind in the first round of voting despite an impressive record in slowing the destruction of the Amazon while also reducing poverty and food insecurity. He is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro.
Some 3,335sq km (1,287.65sq miles) of Amazon jungle were destroyed in the 12 months through July, an all-time low in the historical series that goes ​back to 1988. It was a fall of about 42 per cent from the preceding period.
The previous lowest level for ⁠Brazil’s Amazon deforestation was reached in 2011 to 2012, when 4,571sq km were destroyed. In the ‌mid-90s, ‌the ​figure had reached a record high of nearly 30,000sq km destroyed a year.
The data released on Friday, which is produced ⁠yearly by Inpe’s Prodes satellite monitoring ​programme, is measured from August to July as there ​is less cloud cover in the middle of the year to obscure deforestation on satellite ‌images.
“The figures released today are a ​historic achievement,” said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima, adding ⁠they show the world that “with political ⁠will, it is ​possible to curb deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions .”
Lula took office in 2023 pledging to end deforestation by 2030, after it soared to its highest level in 15 years during the administration of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
Lula will face Flavio Bolsonaro, in a presidential election runoff on October 25th, after the younger Bolsonaro performed better than expected in the first round.
The ‌senator pledged in his ⁠manifesto to strengthen environmental oversight in the Amazon, prioritising areas under the greatest pressure from deforestation and wildfires. He said law enforcement would focus on organised crime ‌rather than on extractive workers and small farmers.
However, the younger Bolsonaro has followed his father’s example in courting support from predatory landowners in the Amazon and other extractivist interests while ignoring the climate crisis in his manifesto.
Former environment minister Marina Silva has warned that Flávio Bolsonaro will try to finish his father’s “perverse project” to destroy the Amazon.
The 2019-23 term of Jair Bolsonaro saw a 59.5 per cent increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying more than a million trees a day, through cuts to forest protection agencies, reduced implementation of penalties for environmental crimes and verbal encouragement for illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers.
– Reuters, additional reporting: Guardian

title: US judge dismisses child sex abuse charges against actor Timothy Busfield
description: New Mexico judge says prosecution did not act in a fair and impartial manner in case of actor, who denies the allegations
content:
A state court judge in New Mexico on Friday dismissed charges ​of child sexual abuse against actor and director Timothy Busfield, saying the prosecution did not act in a fair and impartial manner during grand jury proceedings.
Judge Joseph Montano said prosecutors could pursue new charges against ​Busfield.
A spokesperson for the Second Judicial District ‌Attorney Office ‌of ​New Mexico said the office was evaluating its options.
The actor has strongly denied allegations of improperly touching two young boys, twin brothers, on the Albuquerque ⁠set of Fox TV drama The Cleaning Lady.
The twins reported that the alleged contact had occurred over a two-year period, ⁠when they were aged ​seven and eight, during breaks in production, prosecutors ​said in a criminal complaint filed in January.
Busfield, a director and producer of The Cleaning Lady, was ‌charged in February in a four-count ​grand jury indictment that accused the actor of groping one of the boys.
He ⁠steadfastly professed his innocence, calling the allegations ⁠against him “lies”, and ​his attorneys asked for the charges against him to be dismissed.
In Friday’s ruling, Montano said the prosecution did not properly instruct members of the grand jury on procedures for requesting testimony from additional witnesses. In part, the prosecutor incorrectly informed the grand jurors that at least eight of them would have to agree to wanting to hear from a witness for that person to be ‌called.
“The prosecuting attorney failed ⁠to act in a fair and impartial manner,” Montano wrote, adding that the lawyer’s actions “had the practical effect of unilaterally withholding witnesses requested by the grand ‌jurors”.
Busfield (69) is best known for his prime-time television roles as a White House reporter on the ​NBC political drama The West Wing and as an advertising agency ​executive on ABC ensemble series Thirtysomething. He also appeared in the baseball film Field of Dreams, starring Kevin Costner. – Reuters

title: Cliff Taylor: A public pay deal will be done - and here’s what it will look like
description: The Government has to make a show of safeguarding public money. Unions have to fight for every last euro. There will be a few late nights - but a deal is inevitable
content:
T he problem for the Government in dealing with the public sector pay issue is that it is about a lot more than pay. Time and again the nurses and teachers, interviewed by the media on the picket lines, spoke about not being able to afford a house , or not finding an affordable place to rent, or about the costs of a long commute to work in a Dublin school or hospital.
Ireland’s housing omnicrisis lurks behind this dispute, squeezing the younger and lower-paid public sector employees who have been front and centre in the media this week and making it hard – or impossible – to live close to where they work. Their older, better-paid colleagues hover in the background, hoping to benefit from the public sympathy for those who are living from month to month and the resulting pressure on the Government to pay up.
A first step towards a deal has been taken with talks to get underway and next week’s strike action called off, though the work to rule continues. A bumpy road still lies ahead. There will be a lot of noise, but a deal will be struck. The €1.2 billion set aside in the budget would “buy” a 3.2 per cent average pay rise, but everyone knows it will be higher. An average increase of close to 4 per cent – halfway between the Government’s initial offer and the likely union opening demand – is the likely outcome. This will increase the exchequer cost to around €1.6 billion in 2027 - there will be a further cost to be paid for the second half of this year, which will be paid out of the 2026 surplus.
Both sides have to be seen to go to the wire in the talks now getting underway and breakdowns along the way are possible. The Government has to give the impression of safeguarding the public purse. The union leaders have to fight for every last euro. The Workplace Relations Commission will lay on the tea and sandwiches for a few late nights. A separate, third-party mediator, Kevin Foley, will try to chart a way forward. He has his work cut out, for two reasons.
One is that inflation is on the rise again and forecasts of an average rate of a bit over 3 per cent next year are looking shaky. It could be 4 per cent and, in a worst-case scenario, according to the Central Bank , reach 5 per cent. The unions won’t want to lock in a below-inflation rise. And they have noted the result of the militancy from farmers and truckers earlier this year. The Government won’t want to pay up for a worst-case scenario which may not happen.
The second reason this is difficult is the wider context; the background of the housing crisis and the resulting squeeze on lower and middle paid public sector employees. Not only are they, in one way or another, paying the price of the housing crisis directly, but indirectly it means that jobs are harder to fill, increasing pressure on existing staff, notably in parts of the health service.
This creates a problem for Government and unions in trying to negotiate a way forward. Getting anything like universal support from public servants for a pay offer is not going to be easy – the more comfortable classes might happily take, say, something close to 4 per cent, but what about those lower down the pile? After tax, it will only help a bit with sky-high rents, or saving for a house deposit.
Public servants are, in the round, not badly paid compared to the private sector. CSO figures – now a few years out of date – showed that at the lower end, public servants are paid a bit more and at the higher end a bit less. Generous public sector pensions and annual increments are hard to measure, but give a significant boost compared to the private sector.
[ Unsustainable pay increases for public sector workers will put Ireland’s stability at risk Opens in new window ]
Over recent years, public sector earnings have broadly kept pace with consumer price inflation. You can argue the exact figures back and forward depending on when you start, what is included and excluded and so on. Since 2019, Central Statistics Office figures show consumer prices have risen by around 26 per cent and average public pay by around 28.5 per cent.
The surge in prices in 2022 hit people across the economy, as price increases averaged close to 8 per cent. And there are worries now about the impact of another rise in the inflation rate in an economy where costs are already among the highest in the EU.
[ ‘My pay hasn’t gone up – and everything else has’: Public sector workers have their say Opens in new window ]
The wide net covered by the public sector reflects the diverse experience of the wider economy. This was well summed up in research from the Irish League of Credit Unions this week that broke Irish consumers down into three groups – the comfortable, the coping and the clinging on.
The survey shows a disconnect in general between rising household wealth and income over a long period and current economic dissatisfaction – “wealthier but more worried,” as its authors put it. Much of this, they speculated, can be put down to current pressures and uncertainties and to the diverse experience at different income levels. And to the housing crisis.
In this context, there is a strong case for any public pay deal to significantly favour those clinging on – and the more stretched members of the coping classes. Previous deals have had a minimum cash increase, guaranteeing a bit more for the lower earners in percentage terms. This one should go further in favouring the lower paid. The cost-of-living “crisis” applies to some public servants, but not to all of them.
A pay deal cannot solve the housing crisis and nor can it guarantee the free passage of fuel through the Strait of Hormuz. It will, nonetheless, probably still get over the line. A resumed strike, and its impact on pay, would cause real problems for many public servants in affording the mortgage or the rent.
[ Jack Chambers ‘hopeful’ of ‘way forward’ to prevent further public sector strike Opens in new window ]
The Government, meanwhile, will face the traditional dilemma of balancing its role as employer with its wider responsibilities of economic management.
A big question, in terms of the public purse, is the expansion in public sector numbers that has been central to a 55 per cent rise in the public pay bill since 2020 to €34 billion, with numbers rising 42,000 to 420,000. Much of this reflects the need to serve a higher population, but controlling this and getting value for money is a big challenge.
Employment in the public sector collapsed after the financial crisis but has since surged, particularly in health, education and non-commercial State agencies. The establishment in the budget of a special taskforce to look at value for money on spending on public pay and services is welcome, though it does beg the question of what all the civil servants in the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform do for their day job.

title: Katie Zacharia was fired after failing in the one arena Trump cares about: television
description: Zacharia’s five days as White House press secretary expose flaws in Trump’s TV-driven hiring
content:
And so Katie Zacharia joins the mayfly ranks of Liz Truss, Anthony Scaramucci, New Coke, CNN+ and Quibi. To say she burned twice as bright and half as long would be too kind. She went out like a firework on a soggy night.
The White House confirmed on Friday that Zacharia was leaving her role as press secretary after just five days on the job. No one was surprised after a lacklustre press briefing debut and scrutiny over her legal credentials.
But even more importantly, Zacharia lived by the sword and died in the one arena that Donald Trump truly cares about: television.
She reportedly got the job by closely monitoring the US president’s public schedule and tracked his active hours on Truth Social to predict exactly when he would be watching TV. She then timed her own appearances on air to make sure she caught his eye. The fact that she fitted the glossy blond aesthetic from what Trump calls “central casting” also helped.
But TV also proved her undoing. On Thursday, Zacharia gave a series of interviews to Trump-friendly outlets in a desperate bid for redemption. Instead, she sealed her own fate with more hapless performances.
She must have expected Fox News host Sean Hannity, who has even spoken at Trump rallies, to give her an easy ride. But even he was sceptical when she admitted she had “stepped up to the plate with very little prep time” for the first briefing. Hannity asked: “Am I hearing that you think the staff should have prepped you better?”
Zacharia rejected the notion that she had only taken questions from conservative outlets, incorrectly asserting that the Daily Mail is “not known to be a conservative outlet”. Hannity also quizzed her about her dubious legal credentials, saying: “Why not just say: ‘I went to Pepperdine law school, and then took a different career path, and I took the bar once and didn’t pass?’”
Zacharia tried again on Fox & Friends but ran into host Lawrence Jones, who said: “You know, Katie, it’s been a tough week for you. It’s not an easy job to be the press secretary and you never want to be the story.”
He also asked: “Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?” Zacharia responded: “I’m standing here,” referring to the fact that she was speaking from the White House North Lawn.
Her exit hours later was met with widespread ridicule – and a measure of human compassion for someone whom Trump had subjected to a very public humiliation.
Scaramucci, who lasted only 11 days as White House communications director during Trump’s first term, tweeted: “Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.”
Joe Lockhart, a former White House press secretary under Bill Clinton, said in a phone interview: “It’s hard to generate sympathy for this woman, but there was no way for her to succeed. It takes years to be ready to do that job. Not days, not hours. I spent 20 years preparing for my first briefing from the very first campaign I did. It was very unfair for her, but very bad judgment on her part to think she could wander out there and smile.”
The fiasco was also a reminder of Trump’s woeful judgment as a manager whose chief criteria are looks and loyalty. During his 2015 presidential campaign, he promised that he would only hire “the best people”, comparing his future administration to corporate boardrooms. His first national security adviser, Michael Flynn, resigned after 23 days.
His second term has featured incompetents such as Kristi Noem, fired as homeland security secretary after multiple controversies; Robert F Kennedy Jr, a health secretary who spent years promoting anti-scientific claims about vaccine safety; and Pete Hegseth, a defence secretary who bungled the Iran war and announced a livestreamed execution only to be overruled by his boss.
Kurt Bardella, a political commentator, said: “It shows the limitations of the president making decisions like this based solely on: ‘Oh, I liked watching this clip of her on this segment in the most friendly environment possible.’ We’ve seen this time and again with this president selecting figures for very meaningful, important and substantive positions solely based on cable news, and just look at how the war in Iran is going to know that ain’t working out too good.”
Trump also entrusted tech bro Elon Musk to take a chainsaw to the federal government. His choice of personnel has had damaging consequences for US institutions. The position of White House press secretary is the latest example.
Lockhart added: “It one more time shows how Trump cheapens everything he touches. He wants everything to be in his image. He tears down the East Wing. He puts his name on the Kennedy Center. Now he has tried to put someone in that job who reflects him, not the country and the values and the power of this country.
“He has cheapened another institution. I hold that room somewhat dear, and it’s sad to watch each of these things get remade in his image because he is cheap, tawdry, corrupt, and he has managed to make the United States reflect those values around the world rather than the ones we knew about for 250 years before him.”
Zacharia will survive and maybe thrive as a “former White House press secretary” in rightwing media, just as Scaramucci still makes the most of his “former” title. Meanwhile, the hunt is on, presumably, for a successor who can at least look reporters in the eye and not get into a tangle about their credentials.
But the cold truth is that the job of White House press secretary is superfluous when Trump is a word machine who holds two-hour campaign rallies, turns social media into a stream of consciousness and takes calls from reporters on his mobile phone. Playing the role of Trump’s spokesperson carries the inherent risk of inadvertently fact-checking him.
“He’s certainly remade the job because all the press secretary does now is repeat what the president says and tell him how brilliant he was in saying it,” Lockhart said.
“It used to be that credibility was the currency in the room. It’s impossible to be credible when you’re working for someone who lies almost every time he speaks.” – Guardian

title: Laois solicitor used client cash to fund Forest Fest music event, court hears
description: Deficit in client funds rose from €450,000 to €1.13m between June and August of this year, says Law Society investigator
content:
A suspended solicitor was found to have used his clients’ money to fund a music festival featuring acts such as Madness and the Fun Lovin’ Criminals.
The findings against Philip Meagher of Midland Legal Solicitors in Portlaoise, Co Laois, were set out in High Court filings from the Law Society, which regulates the profession.
Meagher, who was suspended from legal practice earlier this month, is the founder of Forest Fest, a summer music festival that attracts thousands of revellers to Emo, Co Laois. The Charlatans and Echo & the Bunnymen performed there in July.
In court submissions before Judge Oisín Quinn, Law Society investigator Michael O’Connor said festival cash flow was financed by the money of legal clients over three years.
Money in solicitors’ client accounts is held on trust for clients and can be used only for their benefit, with their authority and in their interests.
At the time of his suspension, Meagher was directed to prepare the orderly wind-down of his practice and hand over client ledgers, computers, hard drives and passwords.
O’Connor, an accountant, swore an affidavit citing his findings from an interim report after he carried out a four-day inspection of Meagher’s office in September.
He found money from other legal clients was put to the benefit of Meagher’s company Forest Fest Ltd, which runs the festival and which itself had client accounts with his legal practice.
“Client moneys that were available in the client account, but not standing to the credit of that client company, were improperly used to assist the business interests of that client company, in particular in the funding of a music festival,” O’Connor said in his affidavit.
“Payments were made out of the client account over a number of years, generating a series of deficits, with the deficits eventually cleared when the proceeds of ticket sales were remitted to the client account through two companies.
“While these deficits were in existence, other client moneys were improperly placed at risk.”
O’Connor found a deficit in client funds close to €450,000 on June 30th 2026 had risen to €1.13 million by August 11th.
In addition, client ledgers associated with Forest Fest Ltd were overdrawn in specific periods in 2024, 2025-2026 and between August and September 2026.
“The deficits were cleared, it is understood, on foot of ticket sale income transferred from a company called Eventbrite that provided a ticket sales platform, through a company called Digimark and then lodged to the client account,” O’Connor said.
“Festival cashflow was financed by way of other clients’ moneys from the client account in the years 2024, 2024 and 2026,” he added.
“There was a risk to client moneys had either Eventbrite or Digimark failed to remit the money that was ultimately lodged in the client account to clear the various deficits.”
Referring to Meagher, O’Connor said: “The respondent solicitor is the beneficial owner of Forest Fest Ltd, the client company in the interests of which other client moneys were applied.”
He went on to say, “no apparent legal service was provided to Forest Fest Ltd in relation to the making of payments for a music festival and the receipt of takings/income relating to same”.
In addition, various payments associated with the staging of Forest Fest 2027 were to fall due in coming months “creating a risk that future deficits could arise on the client account”.
Asked on Friday whether he had any comment on the findings, Meagher replied by text message: “I have commented previously in respect of that matter and in circumstances where issues are still sub judice it would be inappropriate to comment further.”

title: Sales of Sally Rooney books surge in Northern Ireland after publisher stops UK distribution
description: Tómas Kenny, who co-runs Kennys Bookshop in Galway with his sister Sarah, says sales of Rooney’s books have increased tenfold
content:
Customers at a Belfast bookshop have been “panic buying” novels by award-winning Irish author Sally Rooney since her publisher announced it would no longer distribute her work in the UK due to her support for Palestine Action.
By 11am on Friday, Rooney’s books were sold out at No Alibis on Botanic Avenue in the south of the city.
Scenes from the BBC adaptation of Conversations with Friends – the Co Mayo-based author’s first book – were filmed in the independent store.
The text is on a first-year reading course at nearby Queen’s University Belfast. No Alibis owner David Torrans said staff were left “saddened and worried” by Faber & Faber’s announcement on Wednesday.
“We strongly believe this is a freedom of speech issue. As long as we can source distribution of Sally Rooney’s books, we will continue to sell them,” Torrans told The Irish Times.
Stock arrived at the shop from a Dublin wholesaler on Friday afternoon, with copies of Rooney’s Intermezzo and Normal People lining the shelves at 3pm.
“We had people yesterday who were in a bit of a panic and bought the books,” said Lexi Ward, who has worked at No Alibis for five years.
“One woman came in earlier who said she had never been in our shop before – but after seeing that news it made her want to support bookshops more.”
Rooney donated some of the proceeds from the sale of her books to support Palestine Action, which was proscribed in the UK last year as a terrorism-supporting organisation.
According to Faber & Faber, British anti-terrorism legislation means it cannot pass on earnings to her from her book sales.
Torrans said Rooney had attended events at the shop for many years. She visited the bookshop when Normal People – which sold more than one million copies in the UK alone – was first published in 2018.
“These are books of fiction about people’s experiences. They’re not books of a political or polemical nature,” said Torrans.
“As far as we’re concerned, it seems to be an issue where someone’s creative product is being curtailed and restricted. It’s got nothing to do with politics.”
Demand for Rooney’s books at Bridge Books in the market town of Dromore, Co Down, had “gone through the roof”, according to its owner.
Lesley Price said sales at her independent book shop had more than quadrupled since Wednesday. Many were online orders from Britian.
[ Will Sally Rooney’s books now be removed from shops across the UK? Opens in new window ]
Like Torrans, she sources stock from a Dublin-based wholesaler and distributor. “I have just managed to get a little emergency top-up from Dublin to fulfil orders,” she said on Friday. “But I’ll have none left by the end of the day. Percentage wise, sales have gone a bit bonkers.”
The development has also led to a surge in sales at a Galway bookshop. Tómas Kenny, who co-runs Kennys Bookshop in Galway with his sister Sarah, said sales of Rooney’s books had increased tenfold.
Numbers were “still increasing”, with sales “substantially higher” on Friday morning than at the same time on Thursday, he said.
There was a “considerable uptake in orders” of Rooney’s books from “the UK in particular”, Sarah Kenny said.
On Thursday, the bookshop posted on Instagram: “We have seen an upsurge in sales of Sally Rooney’s books to the UK today. Please note that you can still buy her books from Kennys Bookshop and other bookshops in Ireland.”
Following the post, Sarah said they received a “huge response” from people commenting that they were buying Rooney’s books in solidarity with her.
She said it had been “so shocking” for the public as it was “effectively censorship of her books in the UK over her political views”.
“I think that’s why it’s such a mind-boggling story,” she said. “It’s hard to see how this is going to pan out. It’s obviously a wider political issue.
“We shipped to over 100 countries from Kenny’s and her books have international appeal.”
Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee has confirmed she would speak directly to Britain’s foreign secretary Ed Miliband after it emerged that Rooney’s work would no longer be distributed in Britain.

title: Trump puts new Russia sanctions passed by Congress on hold amid deepening row with Ukraine
description: Move comes after Trump publicly criticised Volodymyr Zelenskiy and said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia
content:
Donald Trump has put on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy , telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.
In an executive order on Friday, the US president said he was waiving many ⁠sanctions, restrictions and duties ⁠on Russia, in a move that comes as he has been publicly criticising ⁠Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy, including suggesting that Ukraine needs a ​new leader.
Trump signed the legislation last month, after Congress passed the measure in an act of rare bipartisan agreement. It sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fuelling Russia’s war against Ukraine .
The legislation – whose ‌primary backer in ‌Congress was the late senator Lindsey Graham – sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving and was due to be implemented in two days.
It also directs Trump to impose up to 100 per cent tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15 per cent of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Friday’s announcement comes a week after Trump said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.
Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and one million tons “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional three million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
The president has face widespread criticism after making the announcement, with a dozen US senators – including six Republicans – calling on Trump ⁠to rescind his diesel deal.
A letter from the bipartisan group of lawmakers sent on Tuesday urged Trump to execute the sanctions authorities included in the legislation passed last month, called the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
Under the legislation he signed into law, Trump had until October 18th to impose the sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy, or waive them. The administration had not told lawmakers whether it would impose the sanctions or issue a waiver.
Zelenskiy said on Friday the diesel deal would mean cash “will start flowing back into Russia”, as he met European leaders in Brussels.
Trump ⁠blindsided Zelenskiy last weekend by announcing that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities.
Facing midterm elections next month, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for ​pushing up energy prices that could cost his Republican Party its thin majorities in the US ‌Senate and House of Representatives.
Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 161km/h (100mph). Neither has officially been confirmed.
The US sanctions legislation has also become a campaign centrepiece for senator Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham’s sister appointed to serve out the remaining months of his term, who is also running to replace him in the Senate more permanently.
In a debate earlier this week with South Carolina Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham – who has Trump’s endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week – said she had been “so proud” to help get the measure passed but acknowledged it was Trump’s purview as to how he implemented it.
“It gives the president tools that he can use, if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions,” Graham during the debate in Columbia.
“So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall.”
– Guardian, additional reporting: Reuters and the Associated Press

title: Connacht prepared for ‘serious challenge’ from Saracens in Champions Cup opener
description: Ciarán Frawley will make his home debut for Connacht at outhalf against English Premiership side
content:
Champions Cup: Connacht v Saracens, Dexcom Stadium, Saturday, 5.30pm (Live on Premier Sports)
After a four-year hiatus in the Challenge Cup, Connacht open their Champions Cup campaign against English Premiership side Saracens.
All previous encounters have gone the way of the English side, who will provide a “serious challenge”, according to head coach Stuart Lancaster .
The last occasion was in 2023 at Stonex Stadium, the English outfit prevailing by 55-36, while Connacht came close in 2013, staying in the hunt before Saracens eventually prevailed by 23-17, but then followed up with a whopping 64-6 defeat in England.
History is on the side of English clubs with Connacht’s record in the Champions Cup three wins and five losses at home; zero wins and seven losses away from home. It is a tall order, but Lancaster is taking the competition seriously.
“We are putting out the strongest team we can,” he said. “Saracens is as important as Zebre or Leinster.”
However, Lancaster has made been forced to make several changes to his starting line-up, and will be missing internationals Finlay Bealham and Mack Hansen due to IRFU protocols. Sam Gilbert takes over at fullback, with Finn Treacy and Shane Jennings named on the wings, while Cathal Forde and Bundee Aki form the midfield partnership.
Outhalf Ciarán Frawley makes his first start at Dexcom Stadium, joining Colm Reilly in a new halfback partnership, while Lancaster is putting faith in youngsters, hooker Matthew Victory and tighthead Sam Illo, who will join experienced hooker Francois van Wyk in the frontrow.
Darragh Murray and Josh Murphy form the secondrow partnership, while there is a tried and tested backrow of captain Cian Prendergast, alongside New Zealanders, number eight Sean Jansen and Seamus Hurley-Langton.
[ Connacht daring to dream on return to Champions Cup Opens in new window ]
On the bench, tighthead prop Thomas Connolly could make his first appearance for Connacht, while Academy winger Daniel Ryan is also named.
It is a big ask for Connacht up against a star-studded Saracens outfit, which includes Owen Farrell, Jamie George and captain Maro Itoje.
“Saracens will be bringing their attacking game,” said Lancaster. “They bring a lot of their fundamentals based on their set-piece dominance, their maul and their kicking game.
“We’ve got one or two enforced changes ... We need to be smart about how we coach, but we also need to put our best foot forward in Europe.
“From experience in Leinster and France, if you get a home win first up, you are up and running, and often teams can qualify for the last 16. You just want to be in the fight,” said Lancaster.
“Last year if you saw the Montpellier games and how well we competed, then it’s not beyond the realms of possibility we could quality. We fight for that.”
