Connacht: S Gilbert; F Treacy, C Forde, B Aki, S Jennings; C Frawley, C Reilly; F van Wyk, M Victory, S Illo; D Murray, J Murphy; C Prendergast (capt), S Hurley-Langton, S Jansen. Replacements: E de Buitlear, B Bohan, T Connolly, N Murray, S O’Brien, C Blade, J Ioane, D Ryan.
Saracens: E Daly; N Calorie, N Tompkins, S Va’enuku, R Segun; O Farrell, T Williams; E Mawi, J George, M Street; O Sodeke, H Tizard; M Itoje (capt), T Knight, B Earl. Replacements: E Clarke, P Brantingham, C Weilbach, N Isiekwe, N Michelow, A Barbeary, T James, F Burke.

title: A lesson from Notre Dame
description: Incredible work was done
content:
Sir, – Unlike your reader who was “pipped by the Pope” and unable to get to visit Notre Dame cathedral in Paris , I was more fortunate. What incredible work was done by builders, carpenters and the many specialised people who worked on its restoration and had it opened to the public within five years.
While I was looking at the magnificent vaulted stone ceiling I thought now that Ireland is hosting the Council of the European Union , perhaps Taoiseach Micheál Martin could ask French president Emmanuel Macron to send us some of those workers to get the Children’s Hospital finished.
Then help to get the A5 motorway built so I hopefully will have a safe road to travel home to Donegal sooner rather than later. – Yours, etc,

title: Champions Cup: Pau’s young stars host Leicester Tigers on intriguing opening weekend
description: English champions Johan van Graan’s Bath host last season’s Challenge Cup winners Montpellier in one of the ties of the round
content:
Leinster travel to France on the opening weekend of the Champions Cup but so too do pool one contenders Leicester Tigers as they make the journey to a Pau team that includes French international wing-cum-fullback Théo Attissogbe the 2024 “La Révélation” breakthrough player of the year at the famous French awards night La nuit du Rugby.
The French club, who led the Top 14 at one point this season, boast another young gem in centre Fabien Brau-Boirie and three Pumas in Gonzalo Garcia, Santiago Grondona and Facundo Isa. The Tigers have prop Archie van der Flier, a cousin of Leinster and Ireland’s Josh, summer signing Mako Vunipola and Joseph Woodward, a son of England World Cup-winning coach Clive, also in the matchday 23.
In the other match in the pool, Sale Sharks, who travel to Dublin in December, host the Glasgow Warriors in Manchester. As a neutral pool two offers some tantalising fixtures although the death of Lions secondrow Hyron Andrews puts matches in context this weekend. The fixture against Ronan O’Gara’s La Rochelle goes ahead.
While Connacht host Saracens in Galway, Toulouse welcome the Exeter Chiefs to the pink city on Sunday. Led by scrumhalf Antoine Dupont, the team contains the Ntamack brothers, Romain and Théo, Joshua Brennan, son of Trevor, and in centre Kalvin Gourgues, one of the hottest prospects in world rugby.
Tommaso Menoncello is on the bench for a team that retains many familiar faces. Exeter, a team that housed several Irish players down through the years, has none now.
In pool three, Munster host Racing 92, while the other Saturday game sees the Stormers host Pat Lam’s Bristol Bears. The South African side includes Springbok halfbacks Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu and Cobus Reinach and fullback Damian Willemse. The 23-year-old centre Jonathan Roche is represented by Jay-Z’s Roc Nation.
The Bears are captained by former Ireland international scrumhalf Kieran Marmion and included in the squad is backrow Paddy Pearce who namechecked a former Ireland and Leinster player as a sizeable influence in his rugby career while at school.
He said: “Mr [Ben] Berry, Mr [Lawrence] Evans and Mr Dempsey, Girvan Dempsey who played a fair bit for Ireland, joined when we were in Sixth Form and is a great coach with a great rugby mind.”
English champions Johan van Graan’s Bath host last season’s Challenge Cup winners Montpellier – they beat Ulster in the final in Bilbao – in arguably the tie of the round in pool four.
Beno Obano, Tom Dunn and Will Stuart return to the front row for the European clash as does scrumhalf Ben Spencey for his first game of the season. He will link up with Finn Russell while Charlie Griffin is handed his European debut on the wing after making a first appearance for the club in the premiership last week. Joe Cokanasiga and Santi Carreras complete a fleet-footed back three.
One look at the Bulls bench never mind the starting team underlines why they will be favourites at home to the highly regarded Parisian side Stade Francais.

title: Taxing issue of LPT rates: How a mansion dweller can pay less than an apartment owner
description: Levy for local government is based on property value, leading to disparities between counties
content:
Sir, – Jim O’Sullivan (“ Depressing move on local property tax in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown ”, Letters, October 16th) seeks to draw comparisons between Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown and Sligo as regards the contrasting variation upwards or downwards of local property tax (LPT) to be applicable for next year between these two council areas.
However, this is not a pure like-for-like comparison, as the amount chargeable per household is based upon property values. A mansion dweller in Sligo can thus pay a lower amount of LPT than an apartment owner in an area such as Blackrock or Foxrock, Co Dublin .
Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown’s LPT liability to date for 2026 as published in August was €56 million, whereas the liability for Sligo was only €6 million.
Strikingly, Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown’s liability is, in effect, approximate to the LPT liability for the entirety of Connacht.
Apart from Sligo, the other liabilities for the rest of the province were: Leitrim (€3 million), Mayo (€11 million), Roscommon (€5 million), Galway County (€20 million), Galway City (€12 million), together for the province all adding up to €57 million.
When this is taken into account, a modest discount to LPT payable for Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown residents approved by a majority of local councillors should not be begrudged. – Yours, etc,
Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council Offices,

title: What will become of Irish towns when all the independent shops are closed?
description: As a shopkeeper and employer I feel duped by the Government in last week's budget
content:
Sir, – What is to become of Irish towns?
I am writing to you as a fifth-generation shopkeeper . The shop I run has been in business for over 40 years, my grandfather’s shop is in the next town and has been in business for over 120 years.
We employ 12 fantastically talented and hard-working women on a part-time basis. I sit here on the verge of tears after last week’s budget ; duped by the offer of a reduction in employer PRSI to compensate for the gigantic hike in minimum wage, which in actuality will not support us in any way as it does not apply if you have part-time workers, as most retailers do.
I personally place a tremendous amount of importance on independent shops, vibrant towns and real human interactions. The Government obviously does not. As a nation, do we think we’re too rich to be shopkeepers?
I am absolutely in support of low-paid workers getting more money in their pay packet each week, but the Government’s blindness to the detrimental effect these relentless wage hikes have on small businesses is baffling.
These increases are adding to the supersonic rate at which this Government is driving us towards becoming a rip-off country that no tourist will want to visit, one in which no retail business can keep its doors open, one in which our towns have no soul.
Last year hospitality (which includes McDonald’s and Starbucks) got a reduction of 4.5 per cent in their VAT rate to 9 per cent to help them absorb the spiralling costs of running a business in Ireland – all of which the retail sector also faces. Meanwhile, retail got nothing, left paying 23 per cent VAT.
So where does that leave us? We have all seen the hollowing out of Irish towns across the country. I am just back from Paris where I bought a handmade hairband from a little shop, which makes its wares out the back, and came across streets and streets of independent shops that we don’t see here any more.
Why does the Irish Government not care? There is no value put on what a community looks like. That our doors are always open for anyone to come in and have a chat. That we are the first place teenagers can find a job to ensure they develop the social skills needed for life.
Once we have lost these retail businesses that have been around for generations there is no way to get them back.
What is to become of Irish towns when all the shops are closed? – Yours, etc,

title: Aidan O’Brien aiming for big Champions Day success to seal British trainers’ title
description: Joseph O’Brien and Maurice Regan combine with Starford in bid to land Australia’s prestigious Caulfield Cup
content:
Ascot’s Qatar Champions Day may be a convoluted “climax” to the British flat season, but it’s hard to quibble with the mouth-watering prospect it throws up on Saturday.
Weeks of cross-channel turf action remain, including next weekend’s Group One Doncaster Futurity, so the showpiece event is hardly any sort of culmination in the strictest sense. The British trainers’ title race won’t even be technically complete until the end of the year.
But although 15 years of Champions Day has provided ample evidence of being an unreliable reflection of merit at the end of a long campaign – last year’s Sprint was won by a 200-1 shot and the QEII had a 100-1 winner – it is still a rarefied atmosphere of elite talent.
Just how lofty the stakes are was underlined by the Coolmore team paying out £70,000 (€83,000) to supplement Constitution River into the Queen Elizabeth II Stakes earlier this week only to then not bother to run him in it.
Instead, Aidan O’Brien has opted to keep the French Derby winner at 10 furlongs where he is the sole representative of the classic generation against outstanding older horses such as Ombudsman and Calandagan. It means the Irish Guineas winner Gstaad stays at a mile for the QEII.
Joseph O’Brien runs his own pair of classic winners, with Irish Oaks heroine Johanna Walsh trying to prevent Kalpana’s hat-trick attempt in the Filly & Mare. The Leger winner Highwayman takes on his elders in the Long-Distance Cup.
Robson Auigar’s Power Blue is the sole hope from this country in the Sprint, while Jim Bolger and Johnny Murtagh also take their chances against Kalpana with Sparan Nua and Believed, respectively.
The crucial ingredient is a decent racing surface unlikely to favour anything that needs extremes. Often prone to ultra-testing conditions, this is a shop window that won’t wind up mud-spattered. The focus instead is likely to be on the potential impact of past efforts on current performance.
Arc runner-up Bay City Roller has just 13 days to get over his Longchamp exertions in the Champion Stakes. Kalpana made light of running in the Arc a year ago but will have to be resolute to do so again and boost Andrew Balding’s hopes in the trainers’ championship.
The Englishman, chasing a first title, leads Aidan O’Brien by about £100,000. The Irish man is odds-on to win it for the ninth time.
“I think the Fillies & Mares is probably a must-win in terms of the trainers’ championship. Aidan sets such an incredibly high standard and is going into this crucial meeting with a much stronger hand than us,” Balding has admitted.
He is not represented in the Champion or the QEII, both of which are worth more than £1,000,000, so if O’Brien strikes in those, any hope Balding has of taking the fight to the bitter end may be futile.
The straightforward problem for the Irish man is the quality of opposition. Only the Hong Kong sprinter Ka Ying Rising, who lines up in Australia on Saturday morning, is officially superior to Ombudsman on global ratings.
Calandagan beat him in last year’s Champion Stakes and wound up the highest-rated thoroughbred in the world in 2025. Throw in Almaqam too, and Constitution River faces a daunting task to restore a once towering reputation.
Gstaad’s main threat could prove to be another of this year’s Guineas winners. Rayif landed the Poulains at Longchamp in May in mud. He beat older horses in the Marois at the height of summer. Crucially, Francis Graffard sends him to Ascot for just his fourth start of the season.
Christophe Soumillon steps in for the suspended Mickael Barzalona on Calandagan, Rayif and another Aga Khan Group One winner Samangan in the Sprint. Almeraq looks the benchmark in this, although his stable companion Division is no back number either.
Joseph O’Brien’s Group One Saturday will begin early at 7.15am Irish time when he tries to pull off a superb Australian hat-trick.
Twice a Melbourne Cup winner, and successful in the Cox Plate with State Of Rest, O’Brien attempts to land another of Australian racing’s iconic contests in the 150 th Caulfield Cup.
Starford carries Maurice Regan’s Newtowanner colours in the Aus$6 million (€3.7 million) handicap over a mile-and-a-half. Local rider Lachlan Neindorf rides the horse that won the Alleged Stakes earlier this year.
The sole Irish hope will have to overcome an unfavourable wide draw in 15 of the 18 runners. The English hope Enfjaar, the mount of Irish man Ray Dawson, fared better with an inside slot in one. There has never been an Irish-trained winner of the Caulfield Cup.
Gordon Elliott is on his weekend travels too, back to the Far Hills track in New Jersey where he saddled five winners on the prestigious American Grand National card a year ago. It included the big race with Zanahiyr, adding to Jury Duty’s win for Elliott in 2018.
Zanahiyr is back for another crack at a race due off at 9.05pm Irish time, although Jack Kennedy has opted to ride the Grade One winner Western Fold in the eight-runner contest.
Kennedy will be back to ride at Limerick’s Munster National programme on Sunday. where Anyway could prove the big-race solution under the season’s leading rider Darragh O’Keeffe.
Leopardstown’s Saturday action is an all-juvenile programme where the exciting Wall Street will be expected to score in the Group Three Eyrefield Stakes.

title: Memories of the Citroën 2CV
description: ‘I’ve never seen a car like it, did you make it yourself?’
content:
Sir, – The launch of the new Citroën 2CV reminded me of a memory of my aunt who travelled from Belgium in the early 1960s in her elderly 2CV.
While travelling through Mayo , she stopped to fill up. The attendant took one look at her unusual little car, clearly unable to make out the make or model, asked her with genuine curiosity: “I’ve never seen a car like it, did you make it yourself?”
My aunt must have wondered whether to be flattered that she could create such a machine or insulted that her faithful Citroën looked like a home-made contraption.
The 2CV was never meant to turn heads but they had character, charm and reliability to keep going. If the recently launched new model inspires as many conversations as the original, I am sure it will do well. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – In my hitchhiking days half a century ago, my heart would always lift at the sight of an oncoming Citroën 2CV. There was a good chance of a lift – not least because drivers might need assistance to complete their journey.
In one instance, a driver required an extra pair of hands to hold the 2CV canvass roof down every time a lorry passed. My role was to pull, with all my weight, on the roof, while the driver did the same, steering with his knees.
We both arrived safely at our destinations.- Yours, etc,

title: Poignant and significant night for Munster as they face Racing 92
description: Must-win match for Munster in Champions Cup comes 10 years after Anthony Foley’s death
content:
Champions Cup: Munster v Racing 92, SuperValu Páirc Uí Chaoimh, Saturday, 8pm (Live on Premier Sports)
Time flies, whatever about healing, and a decade on from Munster losing a legend – and the Foleys losing a son, husband and father – tens of thousands will again congregate around a rugby match to pay tribute to Anthony Foley a decade and a day since he died.
It is doubtful any Munster match will generate such an emotionally charged atmosphere as when the home side paid homage to Foley by beating Glasgow 38-17 in Thomond Park the day after his funeral 10 years ago.
His memory and standing as a true Munster legend remained a driving force in their run to a Champions Cup semi-final and Pro12 final that season. They are some way off rescaling those heights but allowing for the many tributes that have been paid in the intervening decade, perhaps more so than in any season since, Axel’s spirit will be tangible for this rematch with Racing 92.
Even agitators from the Rebel County who have called for more Munster matches being moved from Limerick to Cork admit that by rights this game would have been a more appropriate fit in Thomond Park. Be that as it may, this is both a hugely poignant and significant night for Munster rugby.
As of Friday, the actual 10th anniversary of Foley’s sudden and premature passing before a scheduled match against Racing, tickets sales have topped 23,000, which Munster hope will reach 25,000 by kickoff. Munster note this will thus be the best attended pool game in Ireland this season, albeit the previous Champions Cup game at Páirc Uí Chaoimh against Gloucester last December was a 36,208 sell-out.
Munster had an additional two months to sell tickets for that game, which had a more spectator friendly 5.30pm kick-off. The reduced numbers at either end have facilitated the installation of two larger big screens, which will make the occasion visually better.
Undoubtedly, the TV-dictated 8pm kickoff would have inconvenienced a chunk of supporters from around the province no matter which of the two venues paid host.
Even so, Clayton McMillan’s bold selection has heightened the sense of anticipation. Charlie O’Shea, the 20-year-old academy product of Dolphin, PBC Cork and UCC, will start at outhalf on his European debut in just his fourth appearance and his second start following his two-try, man of the match performance in Munster’s win over the Bulls a fortnight ago.
The Cobh Pirates blindside Seán Edogbo (22) will also make his European debut, as will 23-year-old hooker Max Clein, who made his debut last week and was only a supplemented squad player this week, and scrumhalf Ben O’Donovan (22), off the bench.
Hooker Marnus van der Merwe, tighthead Jack Aungier and versatile prop Kieran Brooks, whose demotion to the bench looks more an attempt to stiffen the scrum after wilting again in the last half-hour last week, will also make their first Champions Cup appearances for Munster.
All told there are six changes to the starting XV from last week’s 26-all draw against Ulster in Belfast. Aungier, Tom Ahern, John Hodnett, Edogbo and Brian Gleeson come into the forward pack, with O’Shea the one change in the backline. As CJ Stander did against Glasgow 10 years ago, Gleeson will wear 24, with Foley’s number eight jersey again retired for the day.
Racing are intriguing opponents. Unlucky not to have a star on their famous sky blue and white hoops after losing close finals in 2016, 2018 and 2020, they have been wildly inconsistent since a 71-17 semi-final defeat to Toulouse ended last season’s Top 14 campaign, and they again conceded 10 tries in losing 64-5 in Bordeaux on opening day.
They sit 12th, having won two of their intervening five games, recovering from 10-0 down at half-time to win in La Rochelle and beating Perpignan 55-25. Patrice Collazo, as is his wont, makes nine changes to the XV from last week’s 29-15 loss in Toulon.
Midfield fulcrum Josua Tuisova and winger Selestino Ravutaumada are seemingly rested, thus diluting the Fijian factor, as is Romain Taofifénua, while the ever-present Demba Bamba is moved to the bench and 17-year-old Tongan powerhouse Sione Finau-Tupou makes his debut on the wing.
Gone are the days of the galacticos − Simon Zebo, Finn Russell, Virimi Vakatawa et al − but in addition to a dozen French players they still draw on 11 more who represent nine different countries.
Munster and Racing have a rich history, with four wins apiece in nine previous meetings, and given a sniff the Parisians could be dangerous. What’s more, whereas Munster have won in Toulon and La Rochelle in recent times, they have slipped up at home to Bayonne and Castres.
This has a must-win look to it, ideally with a bonus point. As against Glasgow a decade ago, for all the tributes which will again be paid to Foley, most fitting would be another performance worthy of honouring his name and, of course, a win.
There is a pressure within that, but it almost seems unthinkable that they won’t.
Munster: Ben O’Connor; Shay McCarthy, Alex Nankivell, Dan Kelly, Seán O’Brien; Charlie O’Shea, Craig Casey; Jeremy Loughman, Marnus van der Merwe, Jack Aungier; Tom Ahern, Tadhg Beirne (capt); Seán Edogbo, John Hodnett, Brian Gleeson. Replacements: Max Clein, Josh Wycherley, Kieran Brookes, Fineen Wycherley, Gavin Coombes, Ben O’Donovan, JJ Hanrahan, Jack O’Donoghue.
Racing 92: Gerónimo Prisciantelli; Wilfried Hulleu, Vinaya Habosi, Joey Manu, Sione Finau-Tupou; Antoine Gibert, Antoine Latrasse; Édouard-Junior Jabea Niocke, Diego Escobar, Giorgi Kharaishvili, Thomas Lainault, Jordan Joseph, Lekima Tagitagivalu, Nicolas Martins, Maxime Baudonne (capt). Replacements: Yanis Basse, Lehopa Leota, Demba Bamba, Nathan Hughes, Soumalia Camara, Maxime Machenaud, James, Arthur Roche.

title: Breda O'Brien: Farcical Leaving Cert reform must stop now
description: Leaving Cert has a good reputation internationally. We are in danger of trashing it
content:
A lert eyes spotted at the end of last month that the reformed Senior Cycle timetable had quietly changed. The introduction of the new maths and English subjects has been moved from 2027 to “at least 2028”.
This was in the wake of particular controversy about the proposed reformed maths. Great credit must go to Aoibhinn Ní Shúilleabháin, DCU associate professor of mathematics education, and Pauline Mellon, professor emeritus in the UCD School of Mathematics and Statistics. They resigned from the Leaving Cert maths redevelopment group because of what they characterised as an incoherent reform where both breadth and depth had been sacrificed.
Did the instruction to delay implementation come from the Minister for Education, Hildegarde Naughton ? If so, perhaps she has sufficient courage to halt this whole flawed reform process. She has already demonstrated sufficient steel to secure one of the biggest raises ever in the capitation grant for primary schools even though colleagues were furious about the hole in Department of Education finances . That overspend came mostly from providing special classes for students with autism. Inclusive education is expensive.
Forcing a rethink on the Leaving Cert would make teachers feel heard. Teachers took strike action because they need a pay increase to keep pace with spiralling prices, but also because they are completely fed up with their legitimate concerns being ignored.
At primary level, that looks like 1,251 mainstream classes with 30 or more pupils , crumbling buildings and inadequate support in mainstream classrooms for students with additional needs. It also stems from implementing new curricula, increased bureaucracy and the assumption that schools can cope with everything from junior infants who are not toilet-trained to the fallout from an increasingly fractured society.
At post-primary, teachers have not dissimilar concerns but also feel ignored – first in Junior Cycle and now in Senior Cycle reform. The National Council for Curriculum and Assessment (NCCA) will point to teacher representation on every development committee and to extensive consultation.
The Association of Secondary Teachers Ireland (ASTI) has expressed concerns that instead there is an endemic lack of transparency and a “disregard for the views of group members when they dissented from an established NCCA position”.
The Leaving Cert has a good reputation internationally. We are in danger of trashing it.
[ Leaving Cert results: One of the most beloved subjects proves, yet again, to be one of the hardest Opens in new window ]
The new additional assessment component (AAC) in maths is not a project, but a single-day controlled assessment taken towards the end of fifth year, under exam conditions. While that might seem better than an investigation open to abuse using AI, Foundation, Ordinary and Higher levels will all sit the same assessment. This makes no sense.
The AAC timetable for the reformed subjects during this current academic year neatly demonstrates the additional stress. The physics investigation deadline is in early December, biology in February, business in March and chemistry is in April. Some schools have Christmas exams for sixth years, virtually all have mocks in February and language orals still take place in the Easter holidays in March, followed by final exams in June. Students will be exhausted. And that is before they have AACs in all subjects. Many subjects currently have projects but a mandatory mark of at least 40 per cent for the AACs generates stratospheric stress.
[ Why I walked away from the Leaving Cert maths reform group Opens in new window ]
The science subjects introduced in 2025 were promised a pilot scheme for lab technicians starting in September 2026. Somewhere in the process, it changed to lab support assistants. A lab technician qualification currently requires a two-year diploma but there are rumours that a Level 5 qualification, equivalent to the Leaving Cert, will suffice for a lab support assistant. Health and safety risks are enormous for science students in a lab where eight people will carry out individual investigations at the same time. Lab technicians would have provided an important safeguard but currently, only a minority of schools – mostly private – have them. There is no word of when the pilot scheme will commence. Health and safety training for teachers will eventually be provided by Oide, the department support service for teachers and school leaders, which simply does not have the expertise.
Other subjects are in disarray. Coiste Oideachais of Conradh na Gaeilge, representing all the Irish language groups, asked that the new Senior Cycle Gaeilge should conform to the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR), which is an international standard to describe language ability and fluency. Astonishingly, the NCCA said conformity with CEFR would take five to 10 years but is currently sticking to introducing their version of reformed Gaeilge in 2028.
Accounting has been paused because of problems establishing what software to use for the AAC. The proposed English oral is proving impossible to implement. Even the new drama, theatre and film studies course is running into trouble, with its AAC worth 50 per cent, because of uncertainty about the balance of marks for a digital journal and a two-minute recording of performance. Currently, all AACs in every subject are marked as high, moderate or low but no one knows how that translates to grades.
It is barely credible that rapid reviews are promised in September after the first examinations, which is far too late for the poor guinea pig students. No wonder teachers are fleeing to Australia. Naughton must shout stop.

title: Consultants’ private healthcare in public settings has ‘ceased’, HSE review finds
description: All regions provided assurance private practice in public settings had ceased, HSE says
content:
Consultants carrying out private healthcare in public settings has “ceased” in line with the rules of their new contracts, a review by the Health Service Executive (HSE) has found.
Private care provided by public-only consultants contract (POCC) surfaced as an issue during the summer, when Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill clashed with the board of the Rotunda Hospital in Dublin.
The Minister threatened the hospital’s funding and indemnity if it refused to comply with the terms of the public-only contract as consultants were still treating private care while on public contracts.
The board of the hospital eventually backed down.
However, the revelations sparked concerns among senior health officials and politicians that the practice of private work could be continuing elsewhere in the health service.
Mairéad Ryan, of the national human resources office within the HSE, said an initial “verification exercise” regarding the implementation of the POCC had concluded, with a specific focus around “compliance with clause 24″, which relates to private practice in public settings.
“This exercise found that previously reported non-compliant service arrangements had discontinued, and all regions provided assurance that private practice in public settings had ceased in accordance with the terms of the contract,” she said.
[ How can runaway spending in the health service be reined in? Opens in new window ]
Ryan’s comments were made in response to a parliamentary question from Social Democrats health spokesman Pádraig Rice, who called for “more than assurances”.
“We need to know exactly what steps are being taken to ensure that every public hospital is compliant with the terms of the POCC,” he said.
“This process must be rigorously managed and governed to ensure that reform isn’t blocked by legacy culture or any historic arrangements.”
The POCC was introduced in 2023 as a key part of the Sláintecare reforms, which seeks to provide universal healthcare.
Under the new contract, senior doctors in hospitals received higher salaries in return for the elimination of rights to treat fee-paying patients in public facilities.
Both hospitals and doctors received money from payments made – predominantly by health insurers – in relation to private patients treated in public hospitals.
The previous contract allowed consultants to have up to 20 per cent of their workload in public hospitals as private, with consultants being given a transitional period of two years to wind down the private practice.
A majority of consultants are now on the new contract, with the HSE stating this is having an impact on the executive’s finances.
The elimination of private medical practice in the public system has contributed to hospitals facing a projected income shortfall of nearly €145 million, the HSE said last month.
The impact is particularly being felt in maternity care as there are no private maternity hospitals, meaning women will gradually lose to option of private maternity care in the State.

title: Public sector strikers cannot expect a raise without working for it
description: Agreeing to pay increases for obsolete workflows makes no sense
content:
Sir, – Wednesday’s reporting that unions “argue pay terms must be agreed before other issues are addressed” misses a fundamental transactional reality from the conversation. Surely, before signing a contract for a service, you expect to know what service you’re agreeing to pay for?
We live in an age of rapid technology advancement, artificial intelligence, and the digital transformation of work. These are areas where the public sector continues to lag considerably behind yet is ripe for improvement.
It is entirely reasonable to insist that measurable productivity benefits and modernisation targets go hand in hand with additional pay. These conditions cannot simply be brushed aside to be agreed after pay deals are locked in.
No consumer or business would agree to pay an increasing yearly premium for manual tasks that basic digitisation or online processing can easily automate. Agreeing to pay increases for obsolete workflows simply because inflation exists without demanding modern efficiency makes no economic sense and does a disservice to the taxpayer. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I wish to commend my fellow public servants on the turnout for Wednesday’s strike, as well as the public for their supportive reception on the streets. It demonstrated that collective action can reflect widespread anger over pay and inflation and apply real pressure on the Government.
What struck me most was the number of young workers participating in their first strike. I remain deeply concerned, however, that no one is effectively fighting for them on housing.
Many of my younger colleagues in medical and clerical roles have no realistic prospect of owning a home. They are forced to live with their parents far longer than my generation ever had to, pay exorbitant rents, or emigrate to achieve a decent standard of living.
These young professionals have done everything right – earned their degrees, secured employment, and pay their taxes – yet they are being locked out of a future here. I hope today’s action encourages more young workers to stand up and be heard. – Yours, etc,

title: Sally Rooney books withdrawal should trouble those who care about freedom of expression
description: Suppression rarely weakens a cause, but usually hands it a martyr
content:
Sir, – Britain’s use of terrorism legislation under which Sally Rooney’s books have been withdrawn from sale in the UK should trouble anyone who values free expression (“ McEntee to raise Sally Rooney book sales withdrawal with UK foreign secretary ”, News, October 15th). McCarthyism taught United States how quickly association becomes suspicion, and suspicion silence.
Suppression rarely weakens a cause; it usually hands it a martyr. Democracies are judged not by how they protect popular opinions, but by whether they safeguard unpopular ones.
A confident government prosecutes crimes. It does not chill conscience. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – If Faber & Faber is now in the business of censorship of Sally Rooney for her moral and political beliefs with respect to the plight of the Palestinian people, then might it be timely that the reading Irish public avoid the purchase of this English publishing house’s catalogue in Irish bookshops and online until common sense, on its part, returns? – Yours, etc,

title: O'Connell St retailers hit with legal notices under revamp plan
description: Circle K, Peter Mark and Allcare Pharmacy all face Dublin City Council enforcement cases over alleged non-compliance with planning codes
content:
More than a dozen retailers and restaurants on Dublin’s O’Connell Street are facing legal action over unauthorised signs and shop fronts as part of a drive to revitalise the capital’s main thoroughfare.
The businesses facing enforcement cases include Circle K, Peter Mark and Allcare Pharmacy, Ned Kelly’s Casino and several Asian diners.
It follows the appointment earlier this year of high-profile civil servant Robert Watt to lead the Dublin City Development Company. This was formed to deliver on recommendations from Dublin City Taskforce, which was set up by the Government to advise on how to revitalise O’Connell Street, tackle dereliction and improve security.
Following a review of O’Connell Street premises by Watt’s new group, 13 enforcement cases have been opened by Dublin City Council against traders and building owners on the street since the beginning of September.
The cases relate to changes to shopfronts without proper permission, unauthorised neon displays, digital advertising boards, canopies and flags, which are covered by Special Planning Control Scheme (SPCS) bylaws that cover O’Connell Street.
Businesses named in the enforcement cases include Circle K, Paddywagon Tours, Peter Mark and Allcare Pharmacy, who face enforcement cases over unauthorised signage in their shop windows.
The council case records showed an enforcement case has also been opened into Ned Kelly’s Casino over digital and neon signage, a canopy and outdoor screens which the council said was non-compliant with planning conditions.
Meanwhile, Imperial Entertainment, a casino, faces an enforcement case over “intensification of signage to front facade”. A separate case for 55-56 O’Connell Street Upper, from which casino operator Carlton Entertainment Group trades, was opened over canopies and flags erected without permission.
Asian-style buffet Fortune Terrace Buffet and sushi bar Encha face enforcement proceedings over unauthorised signage in their store windows. Dublin City Council has also said that ramen and sushi restaurant Yuriko put in place its wooden shopfront without proper permission.
Other retailers that face new enforcement cases are Pick & Pay, Arisu Photo Booth and Green Island Supermarket, all over signage on their windows and facade.
[ Plan for O’Connell Street restaurant approved, but it is banned from serving takeaways Opens in new window ]
Further planning enforcement cases were opened earlier this year for the O’Connell Street premises occupied by Smiles Dental, which attached advertisement signs to a protected structure without permission, and Flanagans Restaurant over unauthorised signage. These cases have since been closed.
The Dublin City Development Company, led by Watt, has no power to enforce planning rules. The new body is understood to have flagged the planning breaches with Dublin City Council through its complaints procedure and following a review of the complaints, the council opened enforcement cases.
Failure to comply with the planning enforcement procedure can result in fines of up to €5,000.
Earlier this month, Watt – who has been seconded from the Civil Service to the new role – told the Irish Planning Institute’s autumn conference Dublin City Council had not imposed planning laws properly on O’Connell Street businesses.
There are two SPCS in place at present in central Dublin, which cover Grafton Street, O’Connell Street and their surrounding areas. The SPCS set out a number of policies and objectives on architectural conservation, property uses, building heights, advertising signs and shopfronts, vacancy and civic identity.
Earlier this month, the SPCS was used by Dublin City Council to bar a new restaurant being planned for Ulster Bank’s former O’Connell Street branch in Dublin from operating any takeaway food service .
Long-standing concerns have been aired by city councillors about the concentration of fast-food outlets on O’Connell Street, from which about a dozen provide takeaway services.

title: Leinster to bring evolved attack against Clermont Auvergne as they begin Champions Cup campaign
description: Champions Cup match has the signs of being a similar tussle, one from which Leinster can again emerge victorious
content:
Champions Cup: Clermont Auvergne v Leinster, Stade Marcel Michelin, Saturday, 3.15 (Live on Premier Sports)
Joey Carbery. Conor O’Tighearnaigh. Oliver Coffey. Someone old, someone new, someone borrowed from the academy and all in the blue of a Leinster team beginning a climb which they hope will end atop the summit of European rugby.
Mentally-attuned and physically-primed represent opposite ends in a spectrum of requirements to survive the rigours of winning away in the Investec Champions Cup . There is a neat tie-up to this weekend’s goal in that Leinster’s first-ever tournament win in France was against Montferrand, a previous incarnation of Saturday’s hosts, Clermont Auvergne.
The intervening years have been both kind to the Irish province with four European triumphs, and bleak with a litany of near misses in finals and semi-finals since 2018. That’s the resume. The living, breathing quest begins again this afternoon in one of the great venues of French rugby, a vibrant yellow and blue bouncing castle with the acoustics to match.
It’s eight years since Carbery last wore the Leinster colours, the 2018 Pro14 final win against the Scarlets, but after spells with Munster and latterly Bordeaux-Bègles, the 30-year-old returns with a kitbag full of experiences in life and rugby, something to which Leinster head coach Leo Cullen pointed when discussing the Irish international.
“He’s been inside the four walls of the champion team [Bordeaux] for the last two seasons, accumulated tons of very relevant experience for us, for himself first and foremost, that we can all lean into,” Cullen said.
“A father now and a much more mature person, he’s seen a lot, been through a lot. He’s been great so far but we’re just keen to get him out there, [to enable him] to enjoy himself and play into the potential that he has.
“That’s our job now as coaches, try and help him along the way there, and we’ll see how he goes. This is his first week back and let’s see what that looks like.” Cullen pointed to the fact that Carbery can also play fullback and there’s no shortage in versatility in the Leinster matchday 23.
The absence of Jamison Gibson-Park provides continued opportunities for scrumhalves Fintan Gunne (23) and Oliver Coffey (22), who carried that workload through the early part of the season in South Africa and upon the province’s return to the Laya arena.
Cullen acknowledged: “They got their time in preseason, grafted hard and we pushed them to another level because we just need our young guys to kick on. Fintan started the two preseason games, Ollie got some time and Cormac Foley got some time. Cormac was unlucky, he got a calf injury before we travelled and that opened a door for the two lads with Jamison unavailable.
“We’ll see how they go. It’s another great step in their development. They’ve had good prep over the last three weeks, it’s good for us to get a bit of consistency. Jamison trained this week, so there’s plenty of experience around the two of them and you’d hope the forwards will help them out and make things easier for them.”
Dan Sheehan captains the team in the continued absence of Caelan Doris while Ryan Baird’s presence in the backrow is a fillip across many aspects of the game including lineout. It’s an area of the game in which Clermont caused Leinster huge problems when the sides last met in Europe two years ago at the Aviva Stadium, a match in which the Irish province squeaked home 15-7.
Leinster lost six of 16 lineouts that day. Clermont’s only survivor from that game is their lineout guru and blindside flanker Killian Tixeront. The French club made four changes to the starting team that was beaten 23-22 at home by the two-time reigning European champions Bordeaux-Bègles in the French Top 14 last weekend.
New Zealander AJ Lam is a new partner for Léon Darricarrere at centre, Joris Jurand comes in on the left wing for Alivereti Raka, Kévin Noah is named at number eight while 19-year-old Nohem Ez Zahouany starts at loosehead prop.
Cullen said: “They’re hugely physical. They cleaned us out [in the lineout] that day [in Dublin in 2024], and it was a very tight game, a proper arm wrestle. If you get into those arm wrestle type games, they’re a tough bloody team to play against.
[ Sam Prendergast starts for Leinster against Clermont Auvergne with Joey Carbery named on bench Opens in new window ]
“They’re proud when they play at home. So, what does that mean? It means they’re very good in the contact area. They’ll whack things, carry hard, so you need to be up for that challenge.
“Harry Plummer has been a hugely influential player for them because he’s able to do a little bit everything; carry into contact, a good defender, able to poach, able to kick and able to score tries.” Cullen also mentioned scrumhalf Baptiste Jauneau (22), one of the best young nines on a global scale.
Leinster have yet to score a maul try this season, and given their proliferation in the URC, that’s a statistic that jumps out and one that they’d love to rectify this afternoon. They’ll need to be strong and disciplined across set piece and breakdown and uncompromising in the collisions. The evolution in attack has been notable and noteworthy in qualitative terms.
Clermont may have won two of six matches – both at home – in the French Top 14 this season but a team coached by Christophe Urios will never be less than ferocious in contact. Leinster have won tight games in France against La Rochelle and Bayonne. This has the signs of being a similar tussle, one from which they can again emerge victorious.
Clermont Auvergne: J Bouraux; B Delguy, A Lam, L Darricarrere, J Jurand; H Plummer (capt), B Jauneau; G Akhaladze, B Massa, N Ez Zahouany; T Lanen, D Swain; K Tixeront, A Hemery, K Noah. Replacements: P Narisia, S Lotrian, M Frisach, L Michaux Vargas, A Chalus-Cercy, L Vermeulen, B Germain, M Belaubre.
Leinster: H Keenan; T O’Brien, G Ringrose, R Henshaw, J O’Brien; S Prendergast, F Gunne; A Porter, D Sheehan (capt), T Furlong; J McCarthy, J Ryan; R Baird, J van der Flier, J Conan. Replacements: R Kelleher, A Usanov, T Clarkson, C O’Tighearnaigh, S Penny, O Coffey, J Carbery, J Osborne.

title: Ulster target first win of season in European Challenge Cup opener against Zebre
description: Stuart McCloskey and Nick Timoney absent as Richie Murphy rings the changes for Ulster
content:
European Challenge Cup: Zebre v Ulster, Stadio Sergio Lanfranchi, Saturday, 3.15pm (Streaming on epcrugby.tv)
Even though going all out in the Challenge Cup is certainly not at the top of Ulster’s to-do list, they have arrived at this European opener with a touch more anxiety than had been anticipated.
This is the northern province’s fourth game of the season. They are yet to register a win, having drawn twice in successive weeks at Glasgow and last Saturday when hosting Munster , and lost their first United Rugby Championship (URC) fixture at home to Edinburgh.
It’s certainly not a crisis. They have accumulated eight points, but Richie Murphy’s squad have only played in fits and starts, with inaccuracy, poor discipline and (last week) a crumbling scrum all contributing to a highly visible inconsistency in what is a critical season, as they cannot be seen to fall short of the URC’s top eight for another year.
They made it all the way to last May’s Challenge Cup final where Montpellier eviscerated them in Bilbao’s crushing humidity , but in doing so compromised themselves in the URC, a scenario that left deep scars.
[ ‘We’re playing matches like they’re training sessions’: Richie Murphy frustrated by Ulster’s lack of intensity Opens in new window ]
Another faltering league campaign is not permissible, hence the sense of unease even though, for an opening European round at Zebre , Ulster ought to be capable of producing a decent shift on the way to victory.
The sense that Ulster’s gaze is more firmly fixed on getting something, somehow, from their next two URC games in South Africa against the Bulls and Stormers is hard to shake off with Murphy ringing the changes for his starting side which will take the field in Parma on Saturday.
Stuart McCloskey and Nick Timoney are not involved following their first outings of the season last weekend against Munster while fellow Ireland squad member from the summer Tom O’Toole starts at loosehead prop having been benched seven days ago.
Jacob Stockdale is shifted to full back with the returning Michael Lowry only given a bench spot and Zac Ward, an unused Ireland tourist from the summer, is brought on to the left wing.
Robert Baloucoune continues on the right flank, but the most notable calls Murphy has made involve the midfield and his pick at outhalf.
Jake Flannery and Daniel Hawkshaw (the latter making his competitive debut) form a new centre pairing with Jamie Benson at 10 where he will hook up with Nathan Doak at half-back.
Untried combinations heighten the sense of risk without being sure of the return.
In the pack, Henry Walker gets his first start at hooker while Harry Sheridan is recalled at lock, presumably because of the unavailability of Eli Snyman and Ben Donnell, and packs down alongside Cormac Izuchukwu who moves into the engine room having played flanker against Munster.
James McKillop starts in the number six jersey with David McCann, who was benched for Munster though he played most of the game due to Snyman’s concussion, at openside and Juarno Augustus playing eight.
Lowry, Tom Stewart, Matthew Devine, Jack Murphy and the returning Scott Wilson provide most of the intended impact off the bench.
For all their issues so far, Ulster ought to get this one over the line and nail that elusive first win of the season.
Zebre: G Montemauri, G Bertaccini, M Zanon, D Mazza, T Wade, G da Re, A Fusco (capt), S Pelliccioli, T di Bartolomeo, J Barbotti, F Ruffolo, A Ortombina, G Ferrari, B Stavile Bravin, G Licata. Replacements: G Ribaldi, F Pisani, F Minervino, L Krumov, J Botturi, P Baronio, R Casarin, M Belloni.
Ulster: J Stockdale, R Baloucoune, D Hawkshaw, J Flannery, Z Ward, J Benson, N Doak, T O’Toole, H Walker, K Knox, H Sheridan, C Izuchukwu, J McKillop, D McCann (capt), J Augustus. Replacements: T Stewart, E O’Sullivan, S Wilson, J Hopes, M Moloney, M Devine, J Murphy, M Lowry.

title: Trump’s problems are his own creations
description: How will US president react if midterms go against him?
content:
Sir, – It’s difficult to recall a US president so unhinged and unable to grasp that the problems he faces are all self-inflicted. I’m referring to Ice operatives killing citizens in cold blood, stalemate with Iran and treacherous dealmaking with Vladimir Putin.
As Gerry Prizeman makes clear ( Letters , October 15th), Donald Trump has lost it – his grip on reality is blown for all to see. It leads to more concerns at a time when inflation is heating up in the US, making his Maga following even more uncomfortable with a president who promised no further foreign madcap adventures. What further reckless action may follow if he loses the midterms ? – Yours, etc,
Sir, - Earlier today, I saw a subheadline on Sky News telling me Donald Trump had shared intelligence with Vladimir Putin. I wonder was it his own intelligence he shared? - Yours, etc,

title: Una Mullally: O’Connell Street was always more than a street. Can it start to live up to its potential?
description: Halloween would be a good place to begin
content:
T he Wild Atlantic Way remains one of the great tourist marketing triumphs of our time. The smartest thing about it is that it reframed what was already in existence. The production value is the coastal scenery. All it needed was some signposting, a map and a brand that is instantly graspable. At the time, it felt less like a marketing success and more like a light bulb moment.
While tourist bodies have attempted to capitalise on Ireland’s heritage and traditions of Samhain, there is something incoherent about the approach.
This year marks the second year of Fáilte Ireland , Tourism Ireland and Tourism Northern Ireland’s Home of Halloween programme. The Derry Halloween Festival feeds into this, now in its 40th year. There’s also the Púca Festival in Meath, although it’s hard to discern how some of the programming – top-heavy with concerts – fits thematically with the celebration. A Samhain procession, the lighting of fires, and some events that speak to ancestral traditions are more on point.
One of the issues with what is being rolled out (and sold to tourists) under the Home of Halloween banner is that Dublin city centre doesn’t seem to feature. But there is an obvious opportunity to bring people into the city on Halloween as the nights draw darker, and offer them things to do.
For children in the capital and its suburbs, Halloween is about staying within their own immediate network of streets, flats or estates. It is a hyperlocal, DIY event. There are some small community festivals, such as Otherworld in Ballymun and Darndale After Dark. But the most obvious signs of Halloween around the capital are about what not to do: posters promoting safety, redeclaring fireworks illegal, and so on. One effort this year is the chunkily named Trick or Treat Main Street Market on a part of O’Connell Street, which is a small indication of an attempt to conjure the spirit of Samhain in the city.
But this seemingly inocuous and small gesture presents us with a very interesting question: what would O’Connell Street be like if it was used differently?
How O’Connell Street and the surrounding area will begin to change as part of the Dublin City Taskforce’s remit to “reinvigorate” this part of the city, and ongoing projects which dovetail with the taskforce’s aims, is a live conversation. It raises the old question of how to eat an elephant. The answer is: one bite at a time. Beyond the big-ticket items such as the GPO, and the progress around Parnell Street – with a new city library and the refurbishment of the Hugh Lane Gallery – there are other, perhaps smaller, signs that O’Connell Street might be on the cusp of better things.
Last week, it was reported that a new restaurant planned for what used to be Ulster Bank’s headquarters on the street will be barred from selling takeaway food. This is sending a signal: no more new fast food places or even new takeaway restaurants on this street. This is significant at a time when so-called “landmark” developments, such as Central Plaza, are fast-food-heavy.
Meanwhile, there are more lofty artistic ambitions unfolding in the area. Nearby on Abbey Street, a former Methodist church is to become the headquarters of Irish National Opera, including an orchestra rehearsal area. The week this was reported, the Irish opera, MARS, won the Sky Arts Award for opera, which should considerably raise the profile of Irish opera.
[ ‘The location is brilliant’: Irish National Opera to make former Dublin church its home Opens in new window ]
In recent months in the capital, the city’s theatres were enlivened by the Dublin Theatre Festival and the Dublin Fringe Festival. The former generated the kind of lively conversation about theatre that has been missing from pubs and corners of rooms in recent years.
Music venues were also recently crowded for Ireland Music Week. Last month saw the Dublin Independent Fashion Week and Design Week Dublin. Ireland’s architectural exhibition from the Venice Biennale, Assembly, will take up residence at Busáras this week. All of this is good stuff. All of it is in the city and of the city. All of it is something very important: ambitious.
Open House Dublin, a programme of events in the city, presented a talk last week named O’Connell Street Cultures, with the head of the taskforce, Robert Watt, the architect Denise Murray, and the photographer Rich Gilligan. Open House’s tagline this year is Dublin Is Living. This is beginning to feel less like an aspirational statement and more like something becoming a bit more real.
Perhaps we need to think of O’Connell Street less as a dastardly avenue that is challenging to tackle, and more like an artery from which cultural activity can flow. Populating the street with affordable apartments would be a key aspect of this.
An excellent Dublin cultural touchstone during this time is the Bram Stoker Festival, which starts on Friday and runs for four nights. The festival began in 2012, and is focused on the legacy, through various interpretations, of Bram Stoker . It draws on the Gothic and the Victorian – the architectural, atmospheric and literary qualities of the capital that are rarely featured in festivals. It appears to do an awful lot with relatively little.
O’Connell Street has always been more than just a street. Yes, it’s weighed down by poor design decisions and a lack of vision, but that can change. There is no trick to this. But considering it a treat might be a start.

title: What is the Department of Education’s plan for primary school consultation?
description: The department committed a year ago to drawing up best-practice guidance but says now only that 'work is ongoing'
content:
Sir, – In two weeks, on October 31st, primary schools all over Ireland must inform the Department of Education whether they wish to act on the results of last winter’s Primary School Survey. More than 200,000 parents responded, and four in 10 with children in denominational schools said they would prefer a multi-denominational one.
Schools were given a very short window to consult their communities meaningfully, and there is no way to know whether this is happening, because there is no requirement to report on whether or how consultation was carried out. Ultimately, the decision on whether a school changes patron rests with boards of management and patrons, whose deliberations are confidential.
Meanwhile, children opted out of religious instruction in Catholic schools, which make up 88 per cent of primary schools, have no national guidance to uphold their constitutional rights not to participate in religious instruction.
The department committed a year ago to drawing up best-practice guidance, but in a reply to me this month, it said only that “work is ongoing,” and confirmed that arrangements remain “a matter for the school concerned”.
It looks to me that the State asked hundreds of thousands of parents what they wanted, then abdicated its responsibility for any real reform.
Over the next two weeks, parents, journalists and public representatives should be asking every school, every patron and the Minister herself what their plan is for a meaningfully inclusive school system that upholds the rights of all children. – Yours, etc,

title: Why you should cut a delayed doctor some slack
description: Some day, you might be the patient who needs more of their time
content:
Sir, – I am sure that one day, when needed, Rachel Minogue ( Letters , October 16th) will be grateful that her doctor spends more time with her than was allocated through the appointments system. This will inevitably lead to delay for subsequent patients.
Such delays are stressful for doctors and patients alike. This, however, is the nature of healthcare. Patients often have complex problems that take time to address.
Clinics cannot function like production lines while also delivering the high-quality service we all demand and expect. – Yours, etc,

title: Memories of a station Mass
description: There could be up to 14 men in the house to be fed, and the preparations were every bit as thorough
content:
Sir, – Colette Sheridan’s Irish Diary on the station Mass (October 13th) and Gerry Christie’s letter (October 14th) brought back memories for my mother.
She remembers neighbours giving all the help they could, especially when a house was not as well off. They helped with the painting and decorating and brought in extra cutlery for the day. The oil paint of the time could take up to two days to dry. At one station Mass in a neighbour’s house, a member of the family had to stand by the wall to make sure nobody leaned against it and ruined their good clothes.
The priest said Mass and blessed the house with holy water, but the only thing he brought with him was the host. Everything else came from the house and the neighbours.
In my mother’s home, the threshing was the equivalent of the stations. There could be up to 14 men in the house to be fed, and the preparations were every bit as thorough. All that was missing was the Mass and the blessing with holy water. – Yours, etc,

title: Senior hospital doctors criticise Minister for Health’s ‘closed-door’ approach to engagement
description: Union says if ‘engagement is being systematically discouraged or prevented, that would be a matter of ‘profound concern’
content:
Senior hospital doctors have criticised the Minister for Health over what they describe as her “closed-door” approach to engagement.
The relationship between consultants and Jennifer Carroll MacNeill has grown increasingly tense in the almost two years she has had the portfolio, with the two sides at loggerheads over the evening and weekend rostering of consultants.
The Irish Hospital Consultants Association (IHCA), which represents some 5,000 consultants, said it had been prevented from any engagement with the Minister over the past 20 months.
Prof Gabrielle Colleran, president of the IHCA, will tell members at its annual conference on Saturday that the union had met the Minister only once during her time in office – in March 2025 – despite repeated requests for further engagement.
“We believed then – and now – that the best outcomes for patients, consultants and taxpayers are achieved when we all work together. But relationships are two-way,” her opening address says.
“We can control our intentions and our actions; we can control how we show up. We cannot control the intentions, actions or behaviours of others.”
Colleran will tell consultants that the union went into the March 2025 meeting “with open minds” but came away “deeply disappointed that the collaborative approach we offered the Minister was not accepted or shared”.
“What does it say about the relationship between the leadership of our health service and the medical profession when the organisation representing almost 5,000 hospital consultants cannot secure a discussion with the Minister for Health? This is all the more surprising given her sustained focus on consultants’ weekend rostering over the past year and a half.”
[ Jennifer Carroll MacNeill: ‘I worried whether I had the objectivity to be Minister for Health’ Opens in new window ]
Anne O’Connor , chief executive of the Health Service Executive , was due to speak at Saturday’s conference, but the IHCA said she was “forced to cancel at short notice”.
The association noted that HSE deputy chief executive Damien McCallion and former Department of Health secretary general Robert Watt had also accepted invitations to attend IHCA events earlier this year, but their attendance was withdrawn.
“The IHCA stands ready to work constructively with the Minister, bringing forward clinician-led, sustainable solutions to the many challenges facing our health service. But if engagement is being systematically discouraged or prevented, that would be a matter of profound concern,” Colleran will add.
Colleran will say the association is “not a party” to a case taken by two consultants in relation to the provision of private care in surgical hubs.
“Portraying this case as an attempt by the Association to obstruct these surgical hubs misrepresents both the dispute and our position,” she will add.
Responding to the criticisms, a spokeswoman for the Minister for Health said she has “regular engagements with the trade union that represents doctors, the Irish Medical Organisation , as well as with all other trade unions representing healthcare workers”.
“The Minister would be greatly appreciative of any and all support for the provision of public only services in surgical hubs,” she said, adding that she is unable to attend the conference “owing to existing diary commitments”.
“The secretary general of the Department of Health met the IHCA on 17th September to discuss the implementation of the public-only consultant contract, extended day and Saturday services and the shared challenges the increased demand and demographic pressures present for our health services and the measures being taken to respond to them,” the spokeswoman said.
“Further engagements will happen in the coming weeks.”

title: Recent mergers may face investigation by regulators following Irish Government error
description: Minister’s order increasing value for competition law scrutiny lapsed
content:
Businesses that agreed mergers or takeovers in recent weeks may face investigation by competition regulators as a result of a Government mistake, it has emerged.
Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, Peter Burke , increased the financial values at which mergers must be notified to the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) in July.
However, his department has confirmed that Burke’s order lapsed on September 30th, when it emerged that the Oireachtas had not approved it on time, exposing deals agreed or completed since that date to possible investigation by the commission.
The ministerial order increased the financial threshold at which mergers must be notified to the commission to a combined turnover of €100 million or more, from €60 million.
Competition law obliges the CCPC to investigate deals meeting the threshold to ensure they do not damage competition in their relevant markets, before approving them, often with conditions meant to protect competition.
As the order lapsed on September 30th, the old rules have applied since then.
So mergers or takeovers agreed or completed since then, where the parties’ combined turnover is €60 million or more, and two of those involved have sales of at least €10 million each, may face investigation by the commission.
The CCPC is advising businesses involved in transactions either agreed or completed since September 30th to consider if they meet the old threshold and whether they should notify it of the deal.
The commission pledged not to investigate any parties to deals done in those circumstances for “gun jumping”, that is completing the transactions before getting its approval.
Any mergers completed between July 1st and September 30th were subject to the increased threshold, that is a combined turnover of €100 million or more, and at least €15 million for two of the parties involved.
According to the department, Burke’s order increasing the threshold was laid before the Oireachtas, but did not get the approval of both the Dáil and Seanad within the time set out by the Competition Act, 2002.
“As a result, the order ceased to have effect,” said a spokeswoman, who confirmed that the error emerged following a department review.
The Act requires the CCPC to investigate mergers for their likely impact on competition, but gives the Minster the power to raise the thresholds for such inquiries to keep them in line with inflation and economic circumstances.
Ministerial orders, also dubbed statutory instruments, generally need Oireachtas approval before taking effect.
Burke signed the order on June 10th, branding the move part of his efforts to cut red tape for business.
The Minister said at the time that he increased the financial notification threshold in response to a public consultation that he held earlier this year.
The CCPC favoured an increase as it allowed the regulator to focus resources on deals more likely to have a meaningful impact on competition and consumers.
The last increase was in 2019, before the significant inflation that followed Covid and the war in Ukraine.
The commission has the power to “call in” transactions below the €100 million value where it believes they could affect competition.
The department will work with the CCPC to “progress revised merger notification thresholds at the earliest opportunity in 2027,″ according to its spokeswoman. The law allows only one change each year.

title: Sabena Power, matriarch of Paddy Power bookmaker family, leaves estate valued at €861m
description: Artist Anne Madden le Brocquy leaves estate valued at more than €6.5m
content:
Sabena Power, matriarch of the Paddy Power bookmaker family, left an estate valued at more than €861 million when she died in September 2025, according to papers published by the Probate Office this week.
The estate is one of the largest recorded by the Probate Office, with the fees for the grant of probate alone coming in at more than €678,000. The grant of probate is a legal measure that allows a person’s estate to be divided up, according to that person’s will.
While the Paddy Power bookmaking business is well known internationally, Power herself was a highly successful racehorse owner and breeder. Her distinctive racing colours were carried by two of the modern era’s finest sprint champions. Sole Power was the winner of the 2010 Nunthorpe Stakes, as well as the King’s Stand Stakes at Royal Ascot, and Slade Power was winner of the Diamond Jubilee Stakes and July Cup in 2014. Sole Power was also crowned Horse Racing Ireland’s Horse of the year in 2014.
In tributes following her death, she was noted for her vivacious presence across Irish racecourses and was a keen supporter of the interests of local Irish racecourses.
Power was the widow of David Power, who died in July 2024 leaving an estate valued at more than €400 million, according to media reports. The valuation was said to fluctuate with the value of shares in Flutter Entertainment plc , the parent company of Paddy Power. Flutter Entertainment plc also owns brands including FanDuel, Sky Betting & Gaming, and Sportsbet.
Under the terms of Sabena Power’s will, her assets were to be divided among her children, with one third going to each of her two sons William and Patrick and a sixth each to her daughters Shani and Tessa. She also left €50,000 to each of her 10 grandchildren.
The Power family bookmaking dynasty stretches back to Tramore racecourse in 1895, and David Power’s grandfather Richard Power. David began working in the betting industry in 1970 when he joined Richard Power after qualifying as a chartered accountant.
In 1988, he made a deal with fellow bookmakers Stewart Kenny and John Corcoran, creating Paddy Power, which joined forces with Betfair in 2016 to form one of the biggest betting companies in the world.
In other grants of probate, the Irish abstract painter and a prominent member of Aosdána, Anne Madden le Brocquy , left an estate valued at more than €6.5 million when she died in December 2025 , according to papers published by the probate office.
Madden le Brocquy, who had addresses in Portobello, Dublin, Paris and Co Cork, was widely recognised as one of Ireland’s most important artists, celebrated for her large-scale, luminous canvases that bridged the gap between organic landforms and pure abstraction. She died at her home in Dublin at the age of 93.
Madden le Brocquy was born in London to an Irish father and an Anglo-Chilean mother. She married the celebrated Irish painter Louis le Brocquy in 1958. The two became a highly celebrated and influential couple, dividing their time between France and Ireland. Louis le Brocquy predeceased her in 2012.
In her will Madden le Brocquy divided her assets between her two sons Alexis and Pierre, with monetary bequests to extended family members.
Internationally renowned engineer Nael Georges Bunni of Howth, Co Dublin, left an estate valued at €7.16 million when he died in November 2025, according to the Probate Office.
Over a 50-year career, Bunni became one of the construction industry’s best known global voices for resolving high-stakes disputes, acting as an arbitrator, mediator and conciliator in more than 140 large-scale international cases valued at up to $700 million.
He served as the president of the Association of Consulting Engineers of Ireland (1987-88) and the global president of the Chartered Institute of Arbitrators (2000-01). He was also a member of the Governing Board for the International Council for Commercial Arbitration.
Born in Kirkuk, Iraq, in 1939, he completed his bachelor’s degree at Baghdad University. He moved to the UK to earn his master’s from Manchester University and a PhD in structural engineering from London University. He left Iraq permanently in 1968 and moved to Ireland.

title: Eva Marie Saint, Oscar-winning actor who lived to 102
description: The American actor won an Oscar for her first film and became one of Hollywood’s most memorable leading women, starring opposite Marlon Brando and Cary Grant
content:
Eva Marie Saint , who won an Academy Award in 1955 for her gripping movie debut as the shy love interest of Marlon Brando ’s longshoreman in On the Waterfront, and who proved equally convincing as a stylish siren opposite Cary Grant in the romantic Hitchcock thriller North by Northwest, died on October 6th at her home in Los Angeles. She was 102.
Blonde and delicately beautiful – as a child, she played an angel in school pageants – Saint had been a working actor for eight years by the time she made her first movie. She learned her craft on live television dramas – which, with their three cameras and constant tumult, forced her to learn to concentrate, she said.
Her supporting performance in On the Waterfront, which boasted one of the most impressive casts and crews ever assembled, would alone have assured her a place in movie history; the movie remains near the top of the American Film Institute’s list of the country’s greatest films. It won the Oscar for best picture and director (for Elia Kazan), and Brando took home the award for best actor, for his tormented performance as a former prizefighter who moonlights as muscle for a corrupt union.
Even if Brando had the most indelible lines (“I coulda been a contender”), Budd Schulberg, who won the screenwriting Oscar, said Saint had the riskiest assignment – portraying a convent-educated young woman, Edie, who simmers with passion for Brando’s Terry Malloy. Edie, who discovers Terry played a role in the death of her brother, who had run afoul of union racketeers, plays a critical role in waking his conscience.
Kazan said he selected Saint from among hundreds of actors for her ability to convey the “simplicity and faith that well-brought-up Catholic girls have,” but he noted she also brought an explosive capacity for lust and an ability to keep up with Brando, a master of improvisation.
Nine months pregnant with her first child when she picked up her Oscar at the RKO Pantages Theatre in Hollywood, she told the audience, “I’m so excited I may have the baby right here.” Her son was born two days later.
Stardom beckoned, but Saint decided to raise a family and to make only one movie a year while her two children were growing up. She later recalled turning down a three-picture deal that her agent promised would make her “a superstar.” What she preferred, she reflected in 1996 to the Hollywood interviewers David Fantle and Tom Johnson, was “to be a working actress with a home life that worked.”
[ Eva Marie Saint, one of the immortals, radiated old-school Hollywood glamour Opens in new window ]
Nevertheless, Saint had a fruitful and celebrated career. Almost as acclaimed as her work in On the Waterfront was her performance as a seductive mystery woman opposite Grant in North by Northwest (1959), which is also on the AFI list.
As Grant’s Madison Avenue executive finds himself on the run, falsely accused of committing a high-profile murder, he finds himself seated in a train dining car with Saint. In a twist, and to his delight, she is the sexual aggressor.
“It’s going to be a long night,” she tells him. “And I don’t particularly like the book I’ve started. You know what I mean?”
In later years, she said some of the easiest work in her entire professional life involved the many retakes required to film their kissing scenes.
Most of Saint’s performances were intensely dramatic. She played the steadfast wife of a drug addict (Don Murray) in A Hatful of Rain (1957); the childhood sweetheart who loses Montgomery Clift to Elizabeth Taylor in Raintree County (1957); the widowed American nurse who falls in love with a Jewish warrior (Paul Newman) during the fight to create the state of Israel in Exodus (1960); and the older woman who is bedded and betrayed by a young drifter (Warren Beatty) in All Fall Down (1962).
When given the chance, though, Saint proved a deft comic actor, playing a secretary still half in love with her ex-husband (Bob Hope) in That Certain Feeling (1956) and Carl Reiner’s wife in The Russians Are Coming, the Russians Are Coming (1966), a Cold War farce about a New England town that thinks it’s being invaded by the Soviets.
[ If you want to understand America and politics, read The Godfather Opens in new window ]
In the 1970s, when movie work grew increasingly scarce, Saint, always level-headed and pragmatic, returned happily and successfully to television. She starred in TV movies; played Cybill Shepherd’s mother in the late 1980s on the ABC comedy-drama series Moonlighting; and won an Emmy in 1990 as a nasty dowager in the NBC version of Dominick Dunne’s biting novel about the upper crust, People Like Us.
Eva Marie Saint, the younger of two daughters, was born in East Orange, New Jersey, on July 4, 1924, and grew up in Delmar, New York.
Her father, John Merle Saint, was an executive with BF Goodrich, the tyre manufacturer. Her mother, Eva Marie (Rice) Saint, had been a schoolteacher.
She was a calm, almost grave, child, her mother told Cosmopolitan magazine in 1954; she thought her daughter had inherited her “serenity” from her father, a Quaker.
Becoming an actor was almost accidental. Saint followed her older sister, Adelaide, to Bowling Green State University in Ohio, and almost immediately found herself cast as the lead in college plays. Stunningly attractive, she was also voted “Sweater Queen” and “May Queen” by her fellow students.
She graduated in 1946 with a bachelor’s degree in speech. (The university named a theatre after her in 2012.) New York and television were the next step. Her early roles included playing a singing cheerleader in a tennis shoe commercial and, more notably, making an appearance on Studio One in the Ring Lardner-George S Kaufman play June Moon in 1949, opposite another young hopeful, Jack Lemmon.
Playing the rebellious daughter Claudia for two years on the prime time television version of the radio soap opera One Man’s Family earned her good money but left her discontented.
An equally discontented aspiring director, Jeffrey Hayden, invited her to lunch; they married in 1951. In the fourth decade of her marriage to Hayden, who had a long career as a television director, Saint told The Los Angeles Times: “I really don’t wake up every morning and say, ‘Well, now, isn’t this unusual? I’m sleeping with the same man after 43 years.’ I do say that you work at marriage. It doesn’t just happen.”
Hayden died in 2016 at 90. Saint is survived by their two children, Darrell and Laurette; four grandchildren; and two great-grandchildren.
To a torrent of critical acclaim, Saint starred with Lillian Gish in Horton Foote’s 1953 television play The Trip to Bountiful, as a young woman befriended by an older one on a long bus ride. When The Trip to Bountiful moved to Broadway later in 1953, it was a commercial failure, but Kazan and Schulberg were in the audience at one of its 39 performances.
Foote said her “ability to transmit an inner purity” made her right for the part in Bountiful, and that same quality, Kazan and Schulberg concurred, made her ideal for On the Waterfront.
Well into her later years, Saint was still a working actor. She played Superman’s foster mother, Martha Kent, in the movie Superman Returns (2006) and had a central role as a spinster librarian opposite a 10-year-old girl and a dog in Because of Winn-Dixie (2005). One of her last movie appearances was in the fantasy Winter’s Tale, based on the Mark Helprin novel, in 2014.
Asked in an interview for Vanity Fair in 2011 if she ever watched her own films, Saint replied: “Sometimes I do. And I think, ‘Well, gee. You did that? Good job!’”
This article originally appeared in The New York Times .
[ Eva Marie Saint, star of movies North by Northwest and On the Waterfront, dies at 102 Opens in new window ]

title: The village fighting a data centre: ‘The country has been sold out to big tech’
description: A proposed new development in Kilmeaden village in Co Waterford has got local residents asking pointed questions including: who are data centres good for, and at what cost?
content:
B ehind the shrubbery at the foot of Danny Brennan’s garden, a small stream reveals itself, crossable via a thick branch that the 87-year-old uses as a bridge when he walks his dog.
Ducking under an electrical wire on the other side, Brennan points to the rolling hills surrounding the defunct cheese factory in Kilmeaden, Co Waterford , which closed in 2005. Now, a 108-hectare data centre campus is proposed for development on the site.
