“I think they should never have been brought here,” Brennan says of the plans. “This is agricultural land and they’re claiming that it’s suitable for development [as] industrial land … For the last 50 years that I’ve lived here, this has been cows on it most of the time, the dairy cattle, for milk for the cheese factory.”
“I don’t know anybody that really wants it, maybe one or two people might have said that it’ll give a lot of employment,” Brennan says. “But it’s not going to give employment, because [as with] other places where they have installed them – it’s kind of self-maintained.”
It is hard to miss Brennan’s house on the drive through Kilmeaden, where he has lived with his wife Eithne since 1960. Pinned to the gates outside its pink walls is a large placard that reads “Stop industrial Kilmeaden”. The sign refers to “three data centres, 16 gas-powered turbines, 43,056 PV solar panels” alongside the message “Say NO!”.
These are part of the infrastructure laid out in a planning proposal submitted to Waterford City and County Council in September of last year. Also mentioned is a “village centre” with a gym, cafe, health centre, pharmacy and office space. The application was submitted by a subsidiary of Irish company Echelon Data Centres, and a local property developer, Kent Homes.
A spokesperson for Echelon Data Centres said, in a statement, that the company was “committed to delivering digital infrastructure responsibly and sustainably”.
“All our facilities are designed and developed in line with regulatory guidelines and in consultation with community representatives,” the statement continued. “They create jobs, support the national grid, help bring large-scale renewables on stream, and drive economic activity in communities throughout Ireland.
“A planning submission for a technology park on a brownfield site in Kilmeaden, alongside new residential housing and community amenities in the village, is still under consideration by Waterford City and County Council. It would not be appropriate for us to discuss the application further at this stage.”
Data centres have been in Ireland since the 1990s, growing in significance since the advent of smartphone technology over the past two decades. As of June of this year, Dublin-based data consultancy Bitpower estimates, there are 109 operational data centres in the country , with eight more facilities under construction and a further 51 having received planning approval.
Data centres are synonymous with “the cloud”, a global network of remote servers that store, manage and process data on the internet so that personal devices do not have to. They are large, physical facilities housing racks of servers, networked computers and other data storage infrastructure.
Essentially, everything done online involves an interaction with a data centre, from streaming music and TV to reading this article. The servers themselves require a vast amount of electricity to run, as do cooling systems required to keep them operational. Ireland’s temperate climate is one of the factors that make it an attractive location.
Kilmeaden is a small, rural village with a population of 334 according to the last census, though a couple of housing developments in recent years, built by Kent Homes, have added to that total. Several thousand people reside in the surrounding area.
“You could look at it as a satellite village for Waterford,” says Mary Sue Connolly, who grew up on a family farm in Kilmeaden, “but it’s far enough away that’s it’s still rural. People have moved out of Waterford, people who don’t want to live in an urban environment, to Kilmeaden to get away from the city life.”
Connolly spent 20 years living in New York before returning to the village. She is a central figure in the Kilmeaden Against Industrialisation campaign, which is driven by a core group of seven or eight people. She cites the new houses as evidence that “this is not Nimby (Not In My Back Yard) territory”, and insists locals have no problem with new infrastructure in general. Connolly says no one objected to the new housing developments.
On a local level, noise, emissions, light pollution, strain on water services and depreciation of house value are among the concerns voiced by opponents to the data centre campus.
[ How Ireland feels about data-centre construction revealed in new Irish Times poll Opens in new window ]
Another member of the campaign group, Jane O’Brien, was raised by her grandparents, who live on a road that bisects the land proposed for development. A dozen or so houses are dotted along the road, and a number of its residents are in their 80s.
“I get emotional [because] it means a huge amount to me,” O’Brien says. “I would love to say I would be in a position to buy that house [in the future] and raise my kids there, where I’ve had such amazing memories. But who wants to live beside that? I can’t.”
Both she and Connolly are concerned about national implications too. According to the Central Statistics Office, data centres accounted for 23 per cent of total metered electricity consumption in Ireland in 2025, up from just 5 per cent in 2015. Projections for 2035 suggest data centres “and other new technical loads” will account for a median level of about 35 per cent of all the electricity demand in the State, the Oireachtas was told last month by Jim Gannon, the commissioner for the regulation of utilities.
“Everybody is struggling right now across the country to pay their electricity bill, to live, to survive,” O’Brien says. “You’re looking at data centres that are paying half the rate that we are for electricity as a population, which is a farce when all they’re doing is making big profits.”
Speaking in Washington last year, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said what he described as the “demonisation of data centres” needed to end if Ireland was to be able to keep up in the tech and artificial intelligence (AI) sector. “We do need to step up. We can’t just postpone AI ... We can’t declare a moratorium on AI. We’d be left well behind if we do that.”
[ Garry Connolly, the man lobbying for data centres in Ireland: ‘Disparaging them means you’re effectively demonising the big tax takes’ Opens in new window ]
The United States has seen a continuing wave of protests against data centres, with what broadcaster-turned-entrepreneur Mark Little described as “the biggest wave of civic activism I’ve seen possibly since the 1960s” in a recent interview with The Irish Times .
On a Saturday in mid-July, opponents to the facilities held 142 protests across 42 US states. There, about 6 per cent of the national electricity supply is devoted to data centres, according to the 2026 Global Data Center Report , compared with Ireland’s 23 per cent.
Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment Peter Burke , following the publication in June of a Government-commissioned KPMG report called The Value of Data Centres to Ireland, said it provided “clear evidence of the critical contribution that data centres make to the Irish economy”.
A recent study carried out by academics in Maynooth University (MU), University College Dublin (UCD), and Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona (UAB) suggested the economic benefits of Ireland’s data centre sector had been exaggerated.
Researchers said the KPMG report’s claim that data centres underpinned more than 876,000 jobs in Ireland was “based on spurious methodology”. As the original report itself noted, only 3,300 people were directly employed by data centres in Ireland in 2024.
The Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment this week defended the report, saying it was independently prepared by KPMG and that its methodology, assumptions and findings were published in full and available for scrutiny and debate. “Like any piece of research, its conclusions may be challenged and discussed, and the Department welcomes academic engagement on these issues.”
The Department said the academics’ report “focuses primarily on the direct economic activity associated with the operation of data centres and takes a more limited view of the wider economic activity that can be attributed to data centres.
“The KPMG report, by contrast, considered both the direct economic contribution of data centres and their role as critical digital infrastructure supporting wider economic activity and Ireland’s attractiveness as a location for investment.”
Under the Commission for the Regulation of Utilities (CRU) connection policy, new data centres in Ireland must meet at least 80 per cent of their annual electricity demand with renewable energy within six years.
A technical response to the planning application for the Kilmeadan data centre campus was carried out by engineering consultant Homan O’Brien. It found that the anticipated annual electricity demand associated with the development was approximately 1,781GWh. A proposed solar farm on the site, it added, would generate approximately 35.7GWh.
Essentially, although more than 43,000 solar panels are planned for the Kilmeaden site, their output would constitute just 2 per cent of its annual electricity demand. The expectation is that Tonn Nua, a large, offshore wind farm set to be developed 12km off the Waterford coast, will prop up the data centre’s energy requirements down the line.
[ ‘No stopping it’: Noise from Dublin data centre causing ‘a lot of annoyance’ for residents Opens in new window ]
When he defended data centres in Washington last year, the Taoiseach also acknowledged the facilities could contribute to climate problems because they consumed a large amount of energy. But he added that Ireland would be able to produce more climate-friendly energy, through offshore wind, in the coming years.
Back in Kilmeaden, Connolly describes the proposed solar farm as “tokenism”.
An environmental group, Friends of the Irish Environment, has said “fundamental questions” around the development of the data centre were yet to be answered. In particular, they pointed to a lack of clarity about how the remaining 98 per cent of the development’s electricity demands would be met.
“This is an enormous new electricity demand,” said the group’s director, Tony Lowes. “The applicant’s own figures show that 98 per cent of its power would have to come from elsewhere. Yet the response still relies on future grid connections, future renewable contracts and future electricity-system decarbonisation rather than secured and assessable measures.”
Signs such as the one outside Danny Brennan’s house are commonplace throughout Kilmeaden. More than 500 submissions have been made in relation to the planning application in the village over the past year and Waterford City and County Council is due to make a decision on the development by Monday, October 19th.
In Killala, Co Mayo, author Sally Rooney was among a cohort of successful objectors to a proposed data centre earlier this year. Planning permission for the development was overturned in September on the grounds that it breached national climate policy.
Rooney, who lives in Mayo and has written bestselling books such as Normal People and Conversations with Friends, argued the data centre would be a wasteful use of electricity whose generation would require burning of fossil fuels. Jane O’Brien says there is a greater volume of support for the protests in Kilmeaden than there was in Killala.
“We’re praying and hoping the council will listen to us, but it’s hard when you’re looking farther up the ladder and you see Government policies at the moment,” she says. “You’re looking at a country that’s already been sold out to big tech for profits.”
She references a separate report by the social policy think tank Tasc from April of this year, which said that nearly 90 per cent of data centres in Dublin were located in economically deprived areas .
“Now, the pressure is on because Dublin isn’t able to cope with the amount of them,” O’Brien says. “If it comes to our rural community, whose rural community does it hit next?”
Waterford City and County Council said it is not in a position to comment on live applications.
One of Ireland’s biggest data centre hubs is Blanchardstown in Dublin 15. Amazon and Meta are among the companies with facilities operating in the suburb and nearby Clonee, which is across the county border Meath. In the two counties, data centres consume about 50 per cent of metered electricity, according to figures from the CRU.
Anne Sheeran, originally from Rathmines in Dublin, has been living in Blanchardstown for 48 years. During that time, its population has exploded. “There was nothing here when I came,” she says. “A lot of [the change] is for the better.”
Now 83, Sheeran has two daughters working in “AI and technology”, so she can see the benefits of the sector to Ireland. She is hesitant to offer a strong view on data centres.
“I’m just talking for myself and friends,” she says. “Their electricity and all that type – energy bills, gas and heating – it’s all gone up very, very much. Some people are saying [data centres are] using a lot, and that’s why it’s gone up for the ordinary working person.”
Tighearnan Noonan, who works in the Blanchardstown library, says the number is too high. He mentions another takeaway from the report involving academics in MU, UCD and UAB: that with the capital invested in data centres between 2019 and 2024, nearly 50,000 homes could have been built in Ireland.
“We get people coming in [to the library] talking about the increase in electricity prices, issues they may have with budgets, the increased cost of living and the housing crisis,” Noonan says. “We have a lot of patrons who would be homeless and would come in here to get out of the elements. Those people could’ve been housed for the same cost that was given [to data centres].”
On a local level, Noonan says that once the buildings are constructed, “the jobs don’t come”. He believes that a warehouse of the same size as a data centre could employ hundreds of people.
“Also, as a staff member in a library, I find AI in data centres abhorrent,” Noonan says. “This is essentially a repository of human information; AI does nothing but steal from it.”
IDA Ireland executive director Donal Travers said: “Ireland is a stable, trusted and pro-enterprise environment for the world’s top companies to run their global businesses, and data centres are a critical part of this.
“We depend on data centres to run our banking system, to secure our supply chains, and in our homes, to deliver our consumer entertainment.”
Travers said Ireland’s level of data centre investment was a result of the positive environment that Ireland has built for data centre infrastructure investment over the last 30 years.
“They have added huge value to Ireland’s economy, not just in the export of critical software and IT services, but in the multi-billion euro sub supply that comes from their construction and operation, much of which is done by Irish companies that have in turn built global export businesses.”
Travers said Ireland’s energy regulator had laid down very clear guidelines for how new data centres will connect to Ireland’s grid – “these, and other regulations, set a very high bar for data centres to operate by”.
He said data centre operators were fully supportive of all regulatory requirements in the locations where they operate.
“In addition, Ireland has set very ambitious targets when it comes to the build and adoption of renewable energy, both onshore and off the coast of Ireland. These renewable investments, which will ultimately help to decarbonise Ireland’s grid and reduce the cost of electricity, depend on large-scale electricity demand, much of which is provided by data centres.”

title: I wore my own wedding dress to my friend’s wedding. I felt foxy and fabulous
description: The bride insisted on my wearing it so vociferously that it would have been rude not to
content:
A t my friend’s wedding in London recently, I wore my own wedding dress. Calm down. Hold back just a second on the urge to tar and feather me. Wearing my wedding dress to my friend’s wedding was not, though it may sound like it on paper, a criminal breach of nuptial etiquette. Hear me out.
Your Honour, ladies and gentlemen of the jury, in my defence, I asked the bride in advance if she would mind me wearing my dress in the spirit of recycling and sustainability and because I am increasingly allergic to shopping. I told her I never felt better about myself than when wearing that dress. Not only did she acquiesce, but she insisted on my wearing it so vociferously that it would have been rude not to. So, with her explicit and emphatic blessing, that’s what I did.
I should mention that my wedding dress is not white, which obviously helped. It is deep pink, a dress made for me by Anne O’Mahony, with giant pink sleeves and tulle for miles. It also had a train, which I had the decency to tuck away using an ingenious hidden button and loop method thoughtfully supplied by O’Mahony. Everyone knows the bride should be the only person with a train on her wedding day.
I got my hair and make-up done. Then I changed out of my joggers in a hotel bathroom. It was like a scene from Mr Benn. The hairdresser was a creative Hungarian stylist who gave my grey hair a roll at the front. I was wearing comfy green sandals and a furry green handbag, both by Orla Kiely. The day before, I’d been to the haberdashery department of John Lewis and got myself a roll of velvet green ribbon which I tied around my waist. Pink goes well with green, as anybody who has watched Wicked knows.
Later that morning, I was standing on a corner near Hyde Park, looking at the GPS on my phone to find my way to the church. Some passing tourists took surreptitious photos of me in my dress. If I had been them, I’d have taken one too.
So there I was in London at a wedding. Feeling fabulous. And ... nothing bad happened. This is not a story of how I felt great in my skin, and then it all came crashing down under the judgmental gaze of the smart London set who laughed at me and my giant sleeves. I had an anxiety dream a couple of nights before that exactly this would happen. I even went shopping for an alternative, ordinary dress just in case. I couldn’t find one that I liked, so my wedding dress became my only option. The best option. The option approved by the bride.
In the church, I will admit to feeling a little self-conscious. There were people in other pews wearing gorgeously minimalist slip dresses. I was fully maximalist. My sleeves alone required their own postcode. At one point an impossibly posh-sounding usher came up to me, in morning dress, tails and all, and told me authoritatively that I was the most glamorous woman in the room.
[ In your 50s it feels like time is rapidly running out. Time for what though? Opens in new window ]
Of course the minute the bride sashayed into the church in her full Vivienne Westwood glory, I was instantly surpassed and relegated to possibly the second most glamorous woman in the room, which was only right and proper. She took everyone’s breath away. The London Gay Men’s Chorus sang Bridge Over Troubled Water, and if you think that is not a wedding song, let me tell you it most certainly is. As the bride reminded us later in her speech, it’s a song about friendship. It was a wedding after my own heart. A wedding that followed some traditions and made up its own. One of the readings in the church was a poem I’d never heard of, called A Girl Who Reads by Mark Grist.
The bride was a total fox. And for the first time in my life I felt like a foxy wedding guest. The whole day was a dream. A celebration of love and friendship and caring and sacrifice. Each one of the wedding speeches was like the rollicking plot of a Richard Curtis romcom. We laughed, and we cried. There was chicken pie and green beans for dinner, served family style so we all got stuck in. I got so many compliments on my dress and my look and my vibe that I have stored them all up to replay in my head for days when I need them.
My advice to all future brides: Don’t wear white to your wedding. That way, you can feel as special as you did that day in the same dress, styled in a new way, at the wedding celebrations of your friends.

title: Irish Times journalists receive 33 nominations for 2026 Irish Journalism Awards
description: Annual NewsBrands Ireland awards take place on November 12th in Dublin’s Mansion House
content:
The Irish Times has received 33 nominations for this year’s Irish Journalism Awards.
National news titles will compete across 23 categories covering reporting, investigations, commentary and digital storytelling.
The awards, held in association with NewsBrands Ireland and supported by Google News Initiative, will take place on November 12th at the Round Room in Dublin’s Mansion House.
Last year’s overall winner was The Irish Times foreign reporter Sally Hayden , who is nominated under three categories this year.
Irish Times London Correspondent Mark Paul and Irish Times Investigations Reporter Conor Gallagher are also nominated three times.
The Irish Times has four nominations in arts journalism and criticism – Lara Marlowe , Chris McCormack , Mark Paul and Philip Watson – and four nominations in feature writing: Keith Duggan , Rosita Boland , Mark Paul and Sally Hayden.
It has three nominations in digital innovation: Mark Hennessy ’s Common Ground, exploring the evolving relationship between the islands of Britain and Ireland; Immersive storytelling incorporating The Irish Times investigation into the export of alumina from Aughinish, Co Limerick, to Russia; Head of Audience David Labanyi for developing conversations with young audiences on different platforms.
The Irish Times also received three nominations in video featuring Enda O’Dowd , Alan Betson and a joint project by Hannah McCarthy and Emmanuel Balam.
NewsBrands Ireland chief executive Ann Marie Lenihan said the shortlisted work demonstrated the resources required to produce original journalism.
“The breadth and quality of work on this year’s shortlist is a powerful reminder of what goes into producing original journalism of this depth. Behind every investigation, interview and carefully reported story is significant time, expertise and investment,” she said.

title: Niamh Flatley: Riverdance star who played leading role in troupe’s global success
description: Meath-born dancer who was a member of original Eurovision 1994 line-up was strongly protective of her family’s privacy
content:
Niamh Flatley was part of an extraordinary reawakening of Irish dancing . A member of the original Riverdance troupe that brought an international audience to its feet at the 1994 Eurovision in Dublin , she had been dancing since the age of three.
Raised by schoolteachers Tommy and Monica O’Brien, in Kilbride, Co Meath , her early life showed a passion for Irish dancing, in which she was guided by the world-renowned teacher Marie Duffy-Pask.
Throughout her youth she pursued Irish dancing to the highest competitive levels and by the age of 17 was placed fourth in the World Irish Dancing Championships.
She first met her future husband, Michael Flatley , on the set of Riverdance and was in the troupe that performed the now historic seven-minute dance during the interval of the Eurovision in 1994.
Niamh later joined Flatley’s global stage shows, where she played the lead role of Saoirse in Lord of the Dance. She went on to perform in Flatley’s expanded, stadium-scale version of the show, Feet of Flames, in front of a live audience of 25,000 people, in London’s Hyde Park.
While the part of Saoirse in the Hyde Park performance was played by Bernadette Flynn, Niamh O’Brien Flatley did dance the lead in the Feet of Flames 2000–2001 World Tour. She also played the lead in Flatley’s third, large-scale Irish dance stage production Celtic Tiger, which had its global debut in July 2005, at the Puskás Stadion in Budapest. The show made its US debut later that, at Madison Square Garden in New York City.
Having known Niamh for more than a decade as a close friend and performer, Flatley said everything suddenly clicked on New Year’s Eve 2005. The couple were married in St Patrick’s Church in Fermoy, Co Cork in 2006, with their reception at Flatley’s mansion, Castlehyde.
During the wedding ceremony Fr Aidan Troy read a blessing from Pope Benedict. Niamh Flatley wore a simple pearl necklace and a vintage beaded Badgley Mischka dress said to have cost €100,000. The wedding ring, a band of gold – cost an estimated €360,000. The engagement ring, made of Irish gold and commissioned in Chicago, is thought to have cost at least twice as much.
The couple had a son, Michael St James Flatley, in 2007. She stepped back from professional dancing before the birth of their son although she remained active behind the scenes in Flatley’s professional life.
She gave few interviews about her life in the world of international dance, and seemingly none in relation to her family life. During his emotional funeral eulogy on October 10th at the Church of St Thérèse in Mount Merrion, Dublin, Flatley, himself seldom shy in front of the media, said his wife strongly protected her family. He said she would explicitly warn him not to make comments or share public information, especially about her illness, that would upset her parents.
[ Michael Flatley pays tribute to his wife Niamh O’Brien at funeral Mass Opens in new window ]
Following her death Mairead Egan, one of her best friends, said she was “just one of those people you felt lucky to know”.
Egan said Flatley had “such a warmth about her and was a real lady. She was incredibly kind, very funny, wonderfully generous, and, above all, just a genuinely lovely person.” Egan said people sometimes didn’t see the Niamh behind all the success and her husband’s celebrity.
Egan said “everyone felt welcome around Niamh” who had “a mischievous side to her that people who knew her well will really miss.”
Flatley has also spoken of how he relied on her advice. He said as far back as Riverdance they would talk for hours. He also said when he had been gripped with anxiety before taking the stage at New York’s Madison Square Garden, it was Niamh who calmed and encouraged him. He said her sharp intelligence made his professional and personal life significantly better.
Twelve years ago Niamh Flatley developed the connective tissue disease, scleroderma. It led to difficulty breathing.
At her funeral, Flatley recounted how she had initially been given just two years to live. He told the congregation that over the past year he had tried to reassure her, telling her to “focus not on the storm, focus on the hand of the Lord”.
As recently as late April the family had travelled to meet Pope Leo and she was in Scotland in August while Lord of the Dance was touring the UK.
Sources close to the family said she had suffered stress arising from the acrimonious battle for control of the Lord of the Dance show between her husband and his former business partners.
In an affidavit opened to the High Court in Belfast earlier this year, Denis O’Sullivan, a consultant working with Michael Flatley, alleged one of Flatley’s former business partners was verbally abusive to Niamh Flatley at a meeting last November.
“This was particularly distressing given that Mrs Flatley was seriously ill that day and required an oxygen mask throughout the meeting,” he said. This allegation was later denied.
[ Michael Flatley thanks people for ‘beautiful gestures of sympathy’ after wife’s death Opens in new window ]
Flatley announced his wife’s death in a tribute on social media on October 5 th . He said: “My heart is broken. I have lost my beautiful wife, Niamh, and my best friend. My gorgeous bride of 20 years has gone to the Lord in heaven.”
He went on to describe her as “the most loving mother, wife and person” and noted that “our lives will never be the same without her,” while thanking the public for their support and asking for continued prayers for their family.
At her funeral, her son Michael St James Flatley, now aged 19, paid tribute to the “loving spirit” his mother brought to their home. He said she was filled with inherent generosity and constant kindness.
Colleagues from the world of dance also paid posthumous tribute to Niamh Flatley’s qualities of intelligence and kindness.
Singer and educator Deirdre Shannon who performed with Lord of the Dance said: “I knew her as a deep person with a comedic twist and a natural flair for style,” adding that “she gave her help quietly, confidently and kindly, as was her nature – she is someone l will not forget”.
Among many tributes on social media, actor Victoria Smurfit said Niamh Flatley was “beauty inside and out”. TV and radio presenter Angela Scanlon said: “I’m so, so sorry to hear this terrible news. Sending deepest condolences.”
A statement from Riverdance said Flatley was “a beautiful soul”. “Niamh was part of our story from the very beginning at Eurovision. Her contribution to Riverdance and the Irish dance community will never be forgotten.”
The Lord of the Dance team said Flatley was “beautiful, kind, funny, warm and fiercely loyal. Full of life, with a spirit, a smile and a spark that would light up any room.” The company added: “Our hearts are truly broken.”
Michael Flatley is also taking a High Court action for damages over remedial works at Castlehyde following a 2016 fire. He alleged his family suffered ill health due to the presence of toxins in the air of the house, which he had bought in 1999.
In a sworn statement, he said his family have “all suffered ill health” since moving back to the house after the fire.
In a newspaper interview, he blamed the toxins issue for him developing cancer.
“I was one of the fittest people in Ireland,” Flatley said. “But when we moved back in I never felt right, and all of a sudden I got cancer. All of a sudden I’ve developed asthma too. How did this happen? We must have been breathing in toxins. We were told to leave immediately and we’ve been living in hotels ever since.”
[ Postmortem on Niamh Flatley will influence legal case over alleged toxins at Castlehyde Opens in new window ]
The Flatley family lived in Monaco in recent years.
On Thursday last week, Flatley posted a picture on Facebook of the Irish Tricolour flying at half-mast outside Castlehyde in honour of his wife. He thanked those who left flowers at the entrance gates to the estate.

title: Karen Leach: It’s a relief to see another ‘god’ of swimming jailed, but I still have many questions
description: Swimmers who were abused by Irish swimming coaches have never received an official, public apology from anyone in Irish sport
content:
W hen I was a little girl, I had a dream. That dream was to swim for Ireland at the Olympics. I believed I could do it, and my mam and dad truly believed in me too.
The Irish Olympic swimming coach Derry O’Rourke saw me swimming at the community games in 1980, when I was 10. After that he started calling my home to speak with Mam and Dad, asking me to join his swimming club, saying he was the best swimming coach in Ireland and that he would make my dream come true and get me to the Olympics. You can just imagine the pride Mam and Dad felt: here was the Irish Olympic coach ringing, wanting me to join his team of swimmers.
It must have been the same pride and excitement other swimmers and their families felt when they got the phone call from George Gibney – who was finally jailed this week for more than 15 years for the sexual abuse of four girls in the 1970s and 1980s – promising to make them a star.
Gibney’s reign of terror was in the Glenalbyn swimming pool in Stillorgan, Newpark Sports Centre in Blackrock, and at his home, where girls were babysitting his children.
My circle of hell was the swimming club at the King’s Hospital in Palmerstown, where O’Rourke was treated like God, and later, in his car, in hotels, in the corridors of Newpark swimming pool and, once, while I was having my photograph taken after winning a competition.
The very first time that I swam in the pool, I knew my swimming would never be the same again. I remember realising right away that this was different; this is serious, no more fun. This was about hard training and winning, and nothing less was going to be acceptable. That day was the start of the end of my very happy childhood.
O’Rourke abused me sexually, mentally, physically and emotionally while I was swimming for his club. Whatever he said went. He had total power over everything and everyone. No one answered O’Rourke back. No one even questioned him.
He had total power over me, over my swimming and over my life. Because he was so good at what he was doing, everyone trusted him and believed everything he said. Which meant that what he wanted, he got.
My last couple of years in swimming were terrible. I was swimming very badly. I just had no power in my body at all. I had no energy, I was in constant pain, and I wasn’t sleeping at night either. I would go to training every day and try my best, but I couldn’t get my body to move. I would swim up and down the pool, crying tears into my swimming goggles. What was wrong with me?
O’Rourke told Mam and Dad to take me to different doctors to find out why I was in so much pain. Nobody could find anything physically wrong with me. It was only later I understood the reason I was in so much pain: it was what he was doing to me. I was deeply depressed , there was no life in me any more, even though I was desperately struggling to live. I eventually gave up swimming in 1987, when I was 17.
[ ‘He needs to die in prison’: Survivor of George Gibney child sex abuse reacts to sentencing Opens in new window ]
I never told anyone what O’Rourke did to me until after he was sent to prison for 12 years in 1998 for the sexual abuse of 11 girls. I didn’t even want to tell myself. When I did finally speak out about what he had done to me, the world I had tried so hard to hold together for so long just came tumbling down around me.
When O’Rourke’s story broke in the Irish newspapers, I remember my mam sitting at the kitchen table reading it. She stopped and looked at me. She said: “This is my little girl I am reading about, this is my child.” She was heartbroken.
I have lost so many things in my life over what he did to me. I have paid a very high price for the sport I loved so much. After I went to court in 2000, I ended up being admitted to psychiatric care, and I remained an outpatient for a decade. But my biggest loss is what it did to my wonderful mam, dad and brothers. It broke their hearts and their spirits.
In 2001, my mam told me that she loved me and she was sorry she didn’t look after me when I was a little girl, that all she wanted for me was to be happy. Four days later my mam’s body was taken out of the canal by a fireman. My beautiful mam was gone. She was amazing, a beautiful lady and a wonderful mother.
The pain of my mam’s death by suicide hurt all of us so much. My dad never recovered either. He would say on many occasions, “Karen, I took you there [to swimming], and Mam is dead.” When I sat with my dad as he was dying, I held his hand and thanked him for being the best dad ever. He turned his head, looked at me and started crying. He said, “I don’t know about that Karen,” and I knew exactly what he meant.
Nobody wants to talk about the reality of abuse – how it happens or what the full spectrum of it actually is: the bullying, the power imbalances, the wilful blindness by organisations, the reality that it could happen again
For the past 19 years, I have been working as a SafeSport advocate and an ambassador for the Voice project (Voices for Truth and Dignity: Combatting Sexual Violence in European Sport through the Voices of Those Affected). I am on the Council of Europe/European Union pool of experts on sexual violence in sport. Unfortunately not everyone wants someone like me around; someone with a strong voice. I don’t always get a very warm welcome in Ireland.
Swimmers who were abused by Irish coaches have never received an official, public apology from anyone in Irish sport. When I raised this, I was told by someone in Irish swimming that they would “not apologise daily for what happened”. But we carry our pain with us every minute of every day.
So while it is a relief to finally see Gibney go to jail – more than 30 years after the story appeared in the newspapers, and 50 after his earliest known crimes – there are still too many unanswered questions.
He fled Ireland in 1993 and would likely have remained living there, were it not for the work of Mark Horgan and others on the Where is George Gibney? podcast.
Why did the legal system let him go in 1993? Who helped him to leave and start a new life in Florida? How many more children did he abuse? How many more did O’Rourke abuse? How many did not survive the abuse by the so-called “gods” of Irish swimming?
And, the biggest question of all: are we doing enough to protect children now? Conversations about safeguarding are easy. People are happy to list off policies and procedures and training. But even now nobody wants to talk about the reality of abuse – how it happens or what the full spectrum of it actually is: the bullying, the power imbalances, the wilful blindness by organisations, the reality that it could happen again.
I want people who have been abused to know there is hope. After 40 years of not being able to go near a swimming pool, I am now teaching children swimming. Before they even get into the pool for their first lesson, I teach children what to do if they need help. I am the adult I needed when I was a little girl.
My next challenge is to get back into the swimming pool, to learn to love being in the water again. I haven’t achieved it yet, but I’ll get there.
Karen Leach is a SafeSport advocate and a qualified psychotherapist. She is on the Council of Europe/European Union pool of experts on sexual violence in sport.

title: Former Irish diplomat Denis Halliday dies aged 85
description: Halliday was a passionate advocate for human rights and resigned from the UN over the Iraq sanctions plan
content:
The death has taken place at the age of 85 of Irish diplomat Denis Halliday.
Halliday was born in central Dublin to Irish Quakers who had been founding members of the Foreign Students’ Society in Dublin in the 1930s.
He attended Trinity College Dublin , where he earned an MA in economics, geography and public administration.
Following his graduation, he served as a Quaker volunteer in Kenya from 1962 to 1963. A year later he entered the United Nations system as a junior professional officer in Iran .
Halliday progressed to senior positions, including oversight of UN development programmes, operations and human resources ,
From mid-1994 to mid-1997, he served as assistant secretary-general for human resources management at UN headquarters in New York.
This expertise led to his appointment as assistant secretary-general and humanitarian co-ordinator in Iraq in 1997.
He was put in charge of the oil-for-food programme in which Iraq was allowed to export oil in return for humanitarian supplies. International sanctions had been imposed upon Iraq following the invasion of Kuwait in 1990.
He resigned just a year later over the sanctions, stating that they were wholly unjust for a country of 20 million people. The sanctions were a “totally bankrupt concept” that punished civilians rather than targeting the regime, he believed.
His resignation marked the end of a 34-year career in the United Nations.
He then became an advocate for an end to the sanctions in Iraq and travelled the world advocating for human rights. His work was recognised with the Gandhi International Peace Award in 2003.
In 2004 there were suggestions that he might run for the Irish presidency, but turned it down on the basis that “having lived overseas for 40 years, my knowledge of domestic issues is too weak.
“I try to keep abreast of issues, but it is hard to catch up after that length of time.”
He spent many of his latter years in Ireland and became involved in the issue of Irish neutrality and, in particular, the use of Shannon by the US military.
He believed Ireland should remain neutral and not join Nato, but also that it should bolster its military to take part in peacekeeping missions.
He was critical of the role of the Security Council permanent members in being able to veto peacekeeping missions, and advocated that the role should be one voted on by the general assembly as a whole.
His funeral notice stated that he “lent his voice to countless other causes, and through it all, his commitment to humanity and accountability never wavered”.
His funeral takes place at Churchtown Friends Meeting House, Dublin 14, at 10.30am on Tuesday followed by private burial.

title: Eamonn Casey did good as well as bad
description: Trócaire has and continues to save the lives of thousands of people in the developing world
content:
Sir, – Bishop Eamonn Casey was one of the driving forces in setting up Trócaire in 1970. He was chairman of that charity for many years ( “Bishop Casey’s pastoral works,” Letters, October 15th).
Trócaire has and continues to save the lives of thousands of people in the Third World.
I am reminded of Mark Antony’s speech at Julius Caesar’s funeral: “The evil that men do lives after them the good is often interred with their bones.” – Yours, etc,

title: ‘You couldn’t ignore that madness’: The comedians turning the GAA into a laughing matter
description: From D’Unbelievables to club-match vloggers, each generation of comic talents casts the GAA in a new light
content:
Long before D’Unbelievables and the roles on stage and screen that made them famous, Pat Shortt and Jon Kenny were a pair of jobbing musicians on the pub circuit in Limerick . One night their arms were twisted to perform at a medal presentation for a juvenile team in a village lounge, where, in the spirit of the GAA , they were treated as indentured volunteers.
Shortt played accordion, Kenny played guitar and for the guts of two hours they parlayed a short repertoire into a lively dance floor. It was nearly midnight when the master of ceremonies took the microphone from Kenny, just as they were running out of gas.
“He’s dead since and I shouldn’t mention any names,” says Shortt, “but he was a big, huge man, big hands on him and a soft hat and cursing – the language out of him was shocking. ‘Now,’ he said, ‘will the f***ing women get the f***ing sandwiches and put them up on the counter and we’ll line up the under-16s for their medals and the band are going to play for another two hours.
“And we were looking at each other, ‘what to f**k’. There’d be no money involved or nothing. The crowd didn’t give a damn because there was dancing and sandwiches and pints. But you couldn’t ignore that as a comedian, that madness in the GAA. That’s what I’d call it, madness – which had nothing to do with the sport, just the people around it.”
The character they encountered that night was the inspiration for Timmy Ryan, the salty caricature in the famous dressingroom sketch that launched D’Unbelievables to a national audience, more than 30 years ago. Timmy’s foaming pre-match speech was full of deathless one-liners (“Let every blow be a funeral”, “Hit him hard, he’s no relation”.)
In the early 1990s, GAA comedy was a niche genre that harvested its material from a short spectrum of themes. Under comic licence, hurling was often portrayed as lawless and that had a self-referential quality.
Dermot Morgan appeared on the Mike Murphy Show in 1983 dressed in a suit but wielding a hurley as a weapon. His glamorous assistant was a mannequin decked out in a tracksuit and a hurling helmet and Morgan used this prop to demonstrate an array of vicious strokes. The accompanying lines were clever and topical, but its characterisation of hurling was a well-worn trope.
Around that time, and for many years, Mícheál Ó Muircheartaigh ’s radio commentaries generated a thriving trade in comic riffs. Distinctive voices are always open to impersonation and Ó Muircheartaigh’s uniquely lyrical style lubricated other imaginations. But as a gag it only had one note.
For a long time, GAA comedy was narrow and, in many respects, predictable but that is no longer true. Over the last 15 or 20 years, GAA comedy has developed layers and it has grown an edge. New comedians saw an opening.
“The penny dropped with me that nobody had really done comedy in the GAA properly,” says Rory O’Connor of Rory’s Stories. “So, I dived into that in 2014 and started to do sketches on all the characters of the GAA.
“I did an endless amount of dirty corner back [sketches] and cocky forward and the lad who’s always injured – just based on everyone from my own club or my own experience. It just took off and it was the foundation of Rory’s Stories. On the Facebook page I had 100,000 likes in a few weeks and it just blew up.”
What emerged was a wave of comedians who took a different view. Bernard Casey started doing stand-up in 2011, a couple of years after he had won an All-Ireland junior football title with Skellig Rangers. Much like O’Connor, he recognised the humour that was under his nose, intrinsic to every dressingroom.
“I understand it,” Casey says, “I get it. I understand the language and the characters and the unwritten rules of the GAA. You didn’t want to go down the route of the stereotypical cliches either – people were kind of sick of that. Many others go down that route and that’s fine. I wanted to go down the untold side and the niche side of the GAA – the hopeless character and develop an actual character around it.”
On Thursday, Casey launched a new book, Local Gossip: Tall Tales and Short Stories from Over the Road. Two stories in it are devoted to Casey’s best-known character, Nephew, whose existence is defined by a hopeless dream.
“A lot of people concentrate their humour on the fella that made it,” he says. “Mine is always about the fella that never made it and never was going to make it. I kind of look at the tragic humour in it. Nephew is a big character and Nephew’s whole identity is trying to make the Kerry minors.
“To everybody else except him he has no hope. But he goes to extreme lengths to enhance his chances of even having a trial. Nephew is talking to a documentary crew who are documenting his progress on making the minors and even the documentary crew are questioning – ‘hang on a second, this lad isn’t going to make it at all’.”
Casey and O’Connor made their breakthrough on various internet platforms, but on a parallel track, GAA comedy established a residency elsewhere. Mario Rosenstock ’s Gift Grub on The Ian Dempsey Breakfast Show had been a staple of comedy consumption for nearly a decade before he was seduced by the GAA’s comic potential. Davy Fitzgerald was his gateway muse.
“When he started managing teams (with Waterford in 2008), that completely caught my eye,” says Rosenstock. “He basically turned out to be a hurling Jose Mourinho. What I mean by that is he comes into your county and says, ‘Lads, you’re f***ed, but I can make ye great again’.
“The latest news about Davy is that he’s taking a year out [from management] so I’m currently looking at a sketch [for his new stage show Boom] about what he’s going to do. So, I’m going to have him go hell for leather on the Camino.”
”I need to chill out,” Rosenstock shouts in his familiar Davy Fitz squeak. “Chill the f**k out.”
When Sky Sports were awarded a contract to broadcast GAA matches in 2014 Rosenstock dreamed up an ingenious parody of their Soccer Saturday programme, with Jeff Stelling, Paul Merson and Chris Kamara short circuited by their first exposure to hurling. The clip reached an audience of “millions and millions all over the world”, says Rosenstock. “For a fool like me, when you give me any bit of success, you’re just encouraging me. So, I said, ‘right, I’m going to do GAA’.”
For years, Gift Grub had a Monday morning GAA news slot delivered in the voice of Morgan Freeman, in the smoky style of his Shawshank Redemption voiceover. Apart from Davy Fitz, though, Rosenstock’s richest crossover character was Marty Morrissey. In the history of GAA comedy, the RTÉ commentator was the first to be portrayed as a lothario.
“I just played up that ironic thing that he’s a ladies’ man,” says Rosenstock. “It’s irony. Everyone knows that he’s not a stud, but girls still go up to him for selfies because he’s a celebrity and he’s nice and he’s funny and he’s friendly. But then that backs up the idea that he could potentially be a stud. I just played that up and made him a sex machine.
“In one of my live shows that ran for a whole year I had him turn up as John Travolta in Saturday Night Fever. I was basically just thrusting everywhere and ladies were falling out of me and all this sort of stuff.”
In a busier market, comedians who wanted to peddle GAA material needed to hustle for their audience. O’Connor said he did impressions of The Sunday Game pundits for about three months until Conor Moore came along. “I said, ‘right, I’m not competing with him,” says O’Connor. “Stay in your lane.” For the first time, GAA comedy was a competitive space.
Cornelius Patrick O’Sullivan started doing stuff during the pandemic. He had been running a comedy club in Cork since 2010 without invading the pitch. But he had been immersed in the GAA all his life and coming home from a match one day, he was told a story of a journeyman coach who had pulled out of a club job and accepted another one a day later because the money was irresistible. The dialogue for a sketch appeared in his head.
“ No, I can’t do it, absolutely no way, she’ll kill me, she’ll absolutely kill me … How much? How much? Do you know what, we’ll f** *ing beat them this year. ”
“That was the first sketch,” he says, “and once it took off you get the dopamine hit from the adulation, the likes and the shares and the comments and I was like, ‘Jesus, I didn’t realise there was that much appetite for it’.”
Over the last couple of years, vlogging became one of O’Sullivan’s points of difference. In comedy terms, it was the equivalent of foraging: the material was there in the wild. He would turn up to a club match of no particular significance and film a couple of hundred clips, edit them down and add a humorous commentary.
“It took off like you’d never believe,” he says. “I’ve over 100 of them done now.”
For about the last year he has been touring his show Pull Hard, “which is about my son, who is autistic, and it’s about hurling, and how they mesh together”. It is a comedy, but it has layers and it is designed to prompt responses other than laughter.
“I have had grown men come up to me, who I know in my heart and soul would never have darkened the door of a comedy club and they go, ‘Jesus, that was brilliant, I really needed that’. Men are very slow to let themselves be vulnerable and I think when you’re laughing you are kind of making yourself a bit vulnerable.”
Shortt is appearing in The Abbey just now, but he will soon be on the road again with Shortt Stories, his stage show alongside his daughter Faye. In it, they have a sketch that was written about a year before Mary McAleese walked away from the integration project, but which would have been true at any time in the history of the GAA. Shortt’s character is a direct descendant of Timmy Ryan.
“Faye comes out in a dress, all done up, and I’m telling her, ‘Stand over there’, and I’m telling her what to do. I’m bringing her on to talk about the importance of women in the GAA but every time she is about to speak, I go, ‘And another thing I want to say – sorry now Mary for holding you up’, and I go on a tirade and she makes three attempts to come up to the microphone until eventually we run out of time and she says nothing.”
Some of the best comedy is not a laughing matter. The GAA was full of that stuff too.

title: Withings BodyScan 2 review: Would you spend €500 on keeping tabs on your health?
description: ‘Longevity station’ measures muscle and fat across six zones and flags diabetic or heart issues
content:
You might have thought that the Withings BodyScan 2 is a simple weighing scale, the type that usually gathers dust in the bathroom because no one really wants – or needs – to weigh themselves on a regular basis.
You would be wrong. This isn’t a scale, it declares. It’s a longevity station. Longevity that will cost you a cool €500.
If you are confused, welcome to the club. I mean, it looks like a scale, albeit a fancy one with a retractable handle that has its own display and a colour screen so you can find out how much of your body it deems is muscle, water and fat, and you can keep track of whatever it is that you feel you need to monitor. But what does that have to with longevity?
A lot, apparently. The BodyScan 2 doesn’t just measure your body composition. It has the equivalent of a six-lead ECG, a blood oxygen sensor, the ability to measure muscle and fat across six zones and monitors the nerves in your feet. There is a lot built into what looks like a fairly standard scales, including metabolic measurements that estimate your basal calorie rate, hypertension notifications and flagging diabetic or heart issues before they become a problem.
It measures vascular age, which looks at the stiffness of your arteries. Not only do they stiffen as you age, but that can also happen as a result of heart disease. The BodyScan 2 measures the speed of the blood pressure wave along the arteries and gives you a score – ideally younger than your heart age, although being in line with your chronological age is considered good.
But I’m getting ahead of myself. The BodyScan 2 has two modes. The first is the daily scan, which is a quick check-in on your weight, body composition and a quick check of your heart and arteries.
The second is the longevity scan, which looks at your metabolic and cardiovascular health. That is scheduled for once a week, although you can take it more regularly if you see the need. That adds the ECG in to the mix, along with nerve response in your feet, and generally takes a little longer on the scale.
You can switch between the two by using the electrodes on the retractable handle as buttons, and all the data is funnelled quickly to the Withings app on your phone for tracking trends etc over wifi.
In measuring body composition, Withings says it is accurate for weight to within 50g and the body fat readings had a 99 per cent correlation to a medical Dexa scan, which is a body composition scan usually used to measure bone density.
[ Woojer Vest 4 review: This vibrating vest might be the weirdest gadget I’ve ever reviewed Opens in new window ]
What really made the BodyScan 2 useful for me personally was that it splits your body into six zones – torso, arms, legs and visceral fat – and measures the composition of each. You can see how much muscle and fat is in each area – with the exception of visceral which only measures fat – and see how each has changed over the weeks and months. It avoided labelling me with anything negative (a previous test scale described my body type as “sturdy and obese” and I’ve never recovered from that), instead opting for body profiles that range from “elite” and “powerhouse” to “room to build” and “at risk”. They are colour-coded too, with green, orange and red indicating your rating.
Measuring glucose resilience – a premium feature that comes with a Withings+ subscription – on a scale was a new one for me. The measure reflects how well your body manages your blood sugar, using your visceral fat and nerve response score. The idea is that the Withings system will flag any potential issues before they become a real problem; that is outside the scope of this review, though, as it might take years before it could be tested fully.
All that comes at a stiff price. Withings devices tend to come in at the more premium end of the price scale, and the BodyScan 2 is no exception. But who can put a price on their health? (Withings can, it’s just under €500.)
The BodyScan 2 measures a significant number of data points, from the muscle mass in your legs to your blood oxygen level. Crunch all those numbers into the app and you can get some useful trends and insights that can keep you on the right track to meet your health goals.
It also avoids too many negative labels for body types. “At risk” is the lowest rating for muscle and the highest rating for body fat. Other ratings are “softened” and “robust”, neither of which carry the stigma of the previously mentioned “sturdy and obese” label slapped on my body type by a particularly snarky scale.
[ Litter Robot 4 review: Fed up with scooping cat litter? Try this Opens in new window ]
If you are looking for something simply to measure weight and body composition, this scale is going to be overkill. You can get those measurements from a scale spending less than €50, rather than €500.
Some features are gated behind a subscription, but not any of the essentials.
The six-zone measurement also looks at muscle composition, which Withings is pitching not only to those who want to measure their body composition in detail but also for people on GLP-1s to keep an eye on potential muscle loss.
The battery is rechargeable, which means no searching through the junk drawer every few months, and it uses a USB C cable.
If you have a need for the extra data and indicators the BodyScan 2 provides, this might be a price you are willing to pay. It might save you money in the long run. But for those who just need the basics, this will be a pricey bathroom addition.

title: Patrick O’Donovan: Anonymous briefings, a defiant response and a dramatic turn of events
description: Patrick O’Donovan characterises anonymous Fine Gael party briefings on health as ‘sad day for Irish politics’
content:
“I’ll hold my own with anybody,” the Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan told reporters in the lobby of the University of Limerick’s sports campus last Tuesday.
It was part of a typically bullish response by the combative O’Donovan when the press asked him about reports in the Sunday newspapers which questioned his health and his political future.
He mounted an impassioned defence of the rights of all people to participate in public life, including at the Cabinet table.
O’Donovan, who has epilepsy, was responding to anonymous briefings from within his own party which had raised questions about his temperament, but also whether he was healthy enough to continue in his role.
These briefings, he said, were “the ultimate in betrayal” – not just of him, but of people with disabilities or those with neurological and other life-altering or limiting conditions.
He judged it a “slap in the face” to all these groups, and a “sad day for Irish politics”
[ Patrick O’Donovan remains in intensive care after taking ill on Tuesday Opens in new window ]
Within hours, events had taken a dramatic turn.
About lunchtime on Tuesday, rumours began to circulate that he had left one of the sessions of the informal meeting of European Union telecommunications ministers he was hosting at the University of Limerick.
The Co Limerick TD reappeared for a “family photo” of delegates attending the meeting, after which he went to a private room, where it is understood he suffered a seizure.
Outside, an ambulance appeared at an emergency exit of the sports arena and screens promoting the State’s EU presidency were deputised as a privacy shield.
O’Donovan’s Garda driver was prominent in rearranging the parked motorcade of black luxury vehicles and people carriers that had ferried the VIPs to the event, making room for a second ambulance.
Gardaí said there was a “medical incident” inside.
Shortly after 2pm, officials from O’Donovan’s department confirmed that he had been taken ill, and a planned press conference with visiting EU commissioner Henna Virkkunen was cancelled.
As O’Donovan was transported to hospital, followed by a Garda car and his ministerial car, there was a sense of shock among those left on the UL campus as delegates began to leave. Back in Dublin, where word spread quickly about the events, there was widespread concern and good wishes for the Minister.
O’Donovan was transferred to the intensive care unit at University Hospital Limerick, where he remained seriously ill as of late this week.
The briefings about his health, his reaction to the coverage, and his subsequent illness have raised inevitable questions about political life, the personal health of high-profile people and the participation of those with different abilities in public life.
O’Donovan has had health issues before this year. In 2023, while serving as minister of state, he was taken to hospital by ambulance after becoming unwell while answering a question in the Dáil chamber.
This week’s incident was O’Donovan’s second hospitalisation in a little over three months, after falling ill in Brussels while on official business. O’Donovan reportedly cancelled a planned trip to Strasbourg last week after his team concluded that he was not well enough to travel.
In a statement on Tuesday, after O’Donovan’s comments, Epilepsy Ireland pointedly said people with the condition successfully pursue careers across every sector, including in leadership and high-profile positions.
It is vital, the organisation said, that individuals “are assessed on their abilities, experience and circumstances rather than on perceptions or stereotypes associated with the existence of a medical condition” – adding that nobody should have their professional capabilities “questioned solely because they are living with epilepsy”.
Away from his health problems, O’Donovan has been making headlines. Earlier this month, he found himself at the centre of a series of post-budget controversies, largely of his own making.
Reports emanating from his department of a €100 “culture card” in the budget came to nought – prompting obvious embarrassment for him – while he ended up in a post-budget row over RTÉ funding which annoyed his bosses, Taoiseach Micheál Martin and Tánaiste Simon Harris.
Throughout his career, the Minister has made a habit of a chin-out style of confrontational politics which has endeared him to some – but rubbed others the wrong way. As a Minister, he has locked horns with RTÉ and the Arts Council. He is widely known for a keen political mind and waspish sense of humour – but also a devastatingly sharp tongue.
His public appearances are often reflective of his personality – colourful and memorable – but sometimes feeding cycles of conflict and recrimination, behind closed political doors and in public.
Contemporaries describe him as a socially conservative, outspoken politician who has climbed the ranks with tremendous staying power. An ally says that there are “no layers” to the Minister.
“What you see is what you get ... makes every judgment call in the best interests of the people he serves,” they say.
This person adds that there is “nothing Machiavellian” about O’Donovan. “[He] just goes and does it and to hell with the consequences.”
[ Epilepsy: What is it and what does the future hold as treatments improve? Opens in new window ]
Former taoiseach Leo Varadkar says O’Donovan has “some real strengths” and was a “highly competent” minister.
“He might have ruffled a few feathers at times, but sometimes that was needed,” Varadkar says, adding that he could always be relied on to go to bat for the party.
The benign view is not universal. Many who have worked with him at close quarters bemoan his conflict-driven style of doing politics, seeing it as causing unnecessary difficulties for himself and colleagues.
All of these matters are put aside for now. O’Donovan is seriously ill, and the road ahead will be decided on by himself, his family and his doctors. After that, his future political career will be a matter for him and his boss, Harris.
O’Donovan has already spent more than a month-and-a-half recuperating after he suffered a seizure in Brussels while attending an EU meeting in early July. He returned to work at the beginning of September.
There are various arrangements that can be made while a Minister needs to take time off. He or she can authorise their secretary general to deputise for them, as Harris – on paternity leave following the birth of his third child – has done.
The process for a Minister fully stepping aside from their role for a period of time is entirely ad hoc, extemporised when Helen McEntee became the first Minister in the history of the State to take maternity leave in 2021 (she later did so again in 2022-23).
What happened then is that the Taoiseach allocated her portfolio to another Minister – first Heather Humphreys and then Simon Harris – and she remained a member of the Government, becoming Minister without Portfolio. It is somewhat convoluted, but constitutionally sound.
And of course Ministers have served while dealing with serious illness. Brian Lenihan remained as minister for finance despite a diagnosis of terminal cancer in 2009-10. His father, Brian Lenihan snr, underwent a liver transplant in 1989 while serving at Cabinet as tánaiste and minister for foreign affairs.
Many TDs have stepped aside while dealing with illness – as Richard Boyd-Barrett did last year and Sinn Féin’s Denise Mitchell said this week she would do after surgery for cancer.
Around Leinster House, speculation about O’Donovan’s future is present but muted, with many politicians in all parties expressing sympathy and worry for him when the news that he had taken ill broke.
On Tuesday, his Cabinet colleague, Fianna Fáil’s James Lawless, told RTÉ that O’Donovan was a “solid worker at Cabinet” who made strong contributions on several issues.
“I just wish him and his family the best as they cope with this difficult time,” he said.
The indications are that O’Donovan intends to return to Cabinet. On Friday, a statement was issued on his Instagram account on behalf the “O’Donovan family”, saying his “interdisciplinary team” was “working with him to ensure his return to his department as soon as new treatment has bedded down”. It added that O’Donovan was “heartened by the support for his long-term Cabinet career demonstrated by his colleagues”.

title: In pictures: Historic Dún Laoghaire racing yachts return to the waves
description: A project is under way to revive the entire fleet Dublin Bay 21-footer cruiser vessels, the older racing class in the world
content:
Any attempt to restore a classic racing yacht is fraught with difficulty. A project to revive an entire fleet has to be described as audacious.
Such a project is under way in Dún Laoghaire .
It seeks to revive the entire fleet of Dublin Bay 21-footer cruiser racer yachts – the oldest cruiser racer class in the world.
Designed for Dublin Bay Sailing Club by the renowned Scottish yacht designer Alfred Mylne, seven of these identical gaff cutters were built between 1903 and 1907.
The boats quickly became a feature of sailing life in the harbour and for over 80 years the boats, known as the Seven Sisters, competed in the full racing programme of Dublin Bay Sailing Club as well as in various club regattas along the east coast of Ireland.
In the course of their long life the 21s were also cruised extensively.
For decades the boats were a familiar sight – graceful, powerful and distinctive – however over time they fell into disrepair.
In 1986, Hurricane Charley provided the coup de grace and all seven boats were brought to Arklow for major repairs and restoration in Tyrrell’s shipyard. Sadly, John Tyrrell died in 1988 and following the closure of the his yard, the entire fleet was stored on a nearby farm.
There it lay exposed to the elements for almost 40 years until two long-time champions of Irish maritime heritage, Fionán de Barra and Hal Sisk, came up with this ambitious restoration project.
They were able to source Mylne’s original line drawings and enlist the collaboration of master boatbuilder Steve Morris and his talented team at Kilrush Boatyard in Co Clare .
So far five boats have been returned to the water – Naneen, Estelle, Garavogue, Geraldine and Oola. Maureen and Innisfallen will follow.

title: Vincent Browne: Haughey loved Terry Keane. She made his life miserable
description: Journalist says he shed tears on hearing of Haughey’s death in 2006 but says the former taoiseach would have hated his upcoming book and viewed it as a ‘betrayal’
content:
T he journalist Vincent Browne (82), whose long-awaited book on former taoiseach Charles Haughey is to be published next week, feels “a bit bad” about what he’s written.
Charles Haughey: Glory, Greed and Guns paints a deeply unflattering picture of a man who was a central focus of Browne’s long and high-profile career, with the author’s proximity to his subject one of its key ingredients.
During a lengthy interview in his home in Dún Laoghaire, Co Dublin, Browne says he liked Haughey because he was so intelligent and able, and also because he was funny, mischievous, and a rogue.
“But I got on very badly with him while he was taoiseach,” he says.
“It was only in his last years that I became friendly with him … I was meeting a clever, funny, resourceful, outrageous man, in his last years and on his way to death, and I wasn’t judging him. This was just friendship and that’s it.”
By then Haughey, suffering from cancer, was light-bodied and frail. His reputation had been shredded by inquiries into his personal finances. And he was also, according to Browne, “desolate” because of the absence of his “one true love”, the social diarist Terry Keane. Haughey died in 2006; Keane in 2008.
Haughey and Browne, who had known each other since the late 1960s, would drink white wine and talk about the people they’d known.
“One of his charms was he never spoke well of anybody,” Browne says, smiling. “That was very funny.”
Former taoiseach Bertie Ahern (“there wasn’t much to him,” Browne quotes Haughey as saying) and former taoiseach Jack Lynch (“the biggest sh*t of them all” - again, Haughey, according to Browne) were among those disparaged by Haughey and defended by Browne, he says.
“He had almost a contempt for PJ [Mara, Haughey’s long-time press adviser],” says Browne, who liked Mara. “And PJ did so much for him.”
The book’s prologue, The Final Years, is a moving portrait of a man reduced by illness and age. Haughey, once so arrogant, now dozes off mid-conversation, and needs help from his wife, Maureen, when negotiating the stairs in Abbeville, the 15-bedroom “Gandon mansion” in Kinsealy, Co Dublin, that they bought in 1969.
“I shed tears on hearing of his death on the morning of 13 June 2006,” Browne writes. “He would have hated this book and probably would have regarded it as a betrayal.”
Does he have any contact now with the Haughey family? “I never knew the family,” he says.
The book does not hold back in its condemnation of Haughey. The former leader of Fianna Fáil was taoiseach three times: December 1979 - June 1981, March - December 1982 and 1987-1992. He is described as having, amongst other matters, plotted to use public money to buy arms and ammunition for the nascent Provisional IRA at a time (1969/70) when its leadership – which Browne says included Gerry Adams, although Adams has always denied this - believed Britain could be forced out of Northern Ireland by way of violence and killing. Browne describes their “campaign of slaughter” as having been “futile”.
Haughey also, the book says, lied on oath when on trial for the arms plot (he was found not guilty); lived a life of at times farcical indulgence – shirts from Paris embossed with his initials CJH – using money sourced from the rich and powerful; evaded tax; and was party to a “criminal” offshore banking scheme run by his friend, Des Traynor, the main architect of the secretive Ansbacher deposits system.
And as if that is not enough, Haughey is portrayed as a foul-mouthed (“I don’t f**k fat women”) serial groper and boor prone to losing his temper and being cruel and abusive to others. He once pushed journalist Stephen Collins up against the wall and told him to “f**k off” when Collins, then a reporter with the Irish Press and later political editor with The Irish Times, asked him a question he didn’t like. A photographer had to intervene.
[ Terry Prone: ‘Charlie Haughey grasped me by the knee and told me I was a rude b**ch’ Opens in new window ]
And then there is the detail about Haughey’s relationship with Keane who, in May 1999, gave an interview to the Sunday Times about their 27-year affair. The former wife of chief justice Ronan Keane, she also went on The Late Late Show to talk about it and the hurt caused to Haughey’s family and her own.
“There is no question,” says Browne. “He absolutely loved her. Even after the Sunday Times and The Late Late Show and so on.”
He is not so sure that Keane loved Haughey.
Keane was friendly with the writer June Levine, who was living with the psychiatrist Ivor Browne in an “unprepossessing basement flat” in Dún Laoghaire, according to the book. The two couples socialised in the flat. Browne and Levine “purchased a waterbed for their own enjoyment, but when Charlie and Terry saw it, they insisted on also savouring its delights”.
Ivor Browne, who got to know Haughey “fairly well” via Keane, described him as a narcissist, says Browne. “And I think that’s a proper description … [Haughey] got the idea that he was different, above us all ... He developed a sense of entitlement.
“He was a very talented person, and he abused that talent in ways that were obnoxious. He had the ability to be the best taoiseach we’ve ever had, and he squandered it.”
Haughey, says Browne, may have had no particular political beliefs or interests at all, other than what served his personal ambition. He had no interest in policies to address deprivation. His involvement in the thwarted plot to buy arms (and 250,000 rounds of ammunition) for the Provisional IRA may have been designed to ensure he would not be outflanked by his party colleague, Neil Blaney, when the time came for Fianna F á il to replace Lynch as leader.
Born in 1925, Haughey grew up in poor circumstances but was a bright student. He went to secondary school and University College Dublin on a scholarship. It seems he became involved in politics because some of his school friends were from political families. He trained as an accountant but left the firm of Haughey Boland to pursue a political career.
His wife was a daughter of the then taoiseach, Seán Lemass. Within a year of being elected for Dublin North-East, in 1957, Haughey bought a “sumptuous” property, Grangemore, in Raheny, on 45 acres, and began to live a lifestyle hugely beyond what he could afford on the basis of his income from politics. This was to remain the case for the rest of his days.
Browne believes Keane, and the former Haughey Boland accountant Traynor - the key figure in Haughey’s secretive financial arrangements - encouraged Haughey’s developing narcissism and sense of entitlement. He thinks Haughey, because he was so clever, “had this idea that he was special”.
Browne’s book creates the impression that at the same time as he and Haughey were nominal antagonists, with Browne questioning Haughey’s suitability for high office, they were also sharing a sense of mischief and fun.
“Yes, but at the time when Haughey was taoiseach we were at each other’s throats,” he says. And it was only in Haughey’s last years that they really became friends.
“I think some people, reading the book, will wonder, here you are, almost in love with this fella [in the prologue], and then you do him down in the rest of the book. My wife, Jean, kept saying [when he was writing the book]: ‘But you liked him, you liked him.’ But you have to tell the truth.”
Haughey’s political career was not without achievement, Browne says, but, “on the balance of his achievements and his depredations, I’m afraid the depredations win”.
In the book Browne writes that Keane once came up to him in a bar and said, “I’ve just been f**king a friend of yours for four days.” This man, and another of her lovers, a member of Fine Gael, he writes, told Browne she would sometimes phone Haughey from the bed without revealing she was in bed with another man.
Asked if it was fair to include such details in the book, Browne says he did so “because it influenced [Haughey] quite a bit and he was often terribly upset by her”.
He thought the four days story was funny. “Maybe I took it too far with that. But her influence on him was a huge factor, I think, and she often made his life miserable.”
[ Fearless! Vincent Browne’s Magill and Ireland in the 1980s: Skilful acknowledgment of a valuable legacy Opens in new window ]
Last month saw the publication of Fearless! Vincent Browne’s Magill and Ireland in the 1980s by Kevin Rafter. The book details the excitement around the magazine Browne founded, with its long-form journalism and occasional agenda-setting scoops. Later in the decade, Browne was editor of the Sunday Tribune, and a shareholder. Both were exciting publications with precarious finances.
At one stage, in 1977, desperate for investment, Browne asked Haughey if he would put money into Magill. “That was ridiculous, outrageous, and a terrible thing to have done,” he says. Haughey said no.
Browne edited Magill from 1977 to 1982, followed by Colm Tóibín.
Journalists who worked with Browne in Magill, according to Rafter’s book, variously described him as charming, generous, ambitious, talented, passionate, charismatic, crusading, dogged and funny, but also obstinate, obsessive, contrarian, baffling, inconsistent, destructive, caustic, mad and a bully.
I read out the list and ask if it ever occurred to him that he and Haughey might have shared certain characteristics, or recognised something in each other. “That never occurred to me,” he says. “I thought we were going to talk about the [Haughey] book?”
I say that among the reasons people will find his book interesting is that it is a book about Haughey written by him, Browne. That he was obviously close to Haughey.
He says it is not fair to put to him allegations about him made in Rafter’s book as he has not read it. He appears to get upset and his eyes get wet. We move on to another topic.
Later, when he is expressing the view that Haughey had no interest in improving the plight of the poor, I say that he, Browne, during his career, regularly upbraided the government for not doing more to address inequality. Yet he had a reputation as an employer for being intimidating and a bully, including in relation to young women.
“I thought this [interview] was about the book,” he says. “You want to talk about me.”
Both, I say. He says: “If the contention is that, as a human being, I was deficient. I agree.” Anyone, I say, could say that. Was it the case that he could be mean and bullying with his staff? “Well, I never intended that,” he says.
Later I quote Tóibín’s observation, in Rafter’s book, that Browne was “very much a member of the establishment with huge anti-establishment feeling as well” and that he moved easily in the social world of establishment figures.
Browne says he acquired “social capital” by attending what he described as a “posh” school – Castleknock College. It gave him an ability to move easily in certain circles. “Posh” schools, he argues, impact society and students negatively. “It’s quite insidious, I think.”
Later he returns to the issue of what was said about him in the Rafter book.
“I think what you read from the book is grossly unfair and exaggerated,” he says. He says he remains friends with most of the people from those days. “Not with Toibín, but with most people.”
