He says that as far as he can recall, he only lost his temper once (with Tribune journalist Aileen O’Meara). “I apologised, in public,” he says, within the hour.
Later in his career Browne had a late-night radio show and founded Village Magazine in 2004. He also hosted the Tonight with Vincent Browne show, on what was then TV3, now Virgin Media, from 2007 to 2017, where his abrasive interviewing style made some government politicians loath to go on the programme.
Despite being advised to shut it down, he persisted with the loss-making Village. It ceased publication in 2008 and was relaunched under a new owner.
“I kept it going and my mortgage, all sorts of things” were affected. “I think I lost €1.8 million, which was a huge amount. I would have been in real trouble financially had I not been on TV3 for 10 years.”
One of the factors that caused him not to close the magazine, he says, even though he knew he should, was that “I loved writing. I loved being a journalist.”
Charles Haughey: Glory, Greed and Guns will be published by Eriu

title: Celebrating imperfect gardens in all their glory
description: New book highlights the hard graft, ingenuity and love that 27 well-known people including Nigel Slater and Jimi Blake have poured into plots they tend
content:
Glossy coffee-table books about unimaginably wealthy people’s elaborately planted, expensively landscaped, immaculately maintained gardens can sometimes leave me feeling an unseemly level of cynicism. Much of the reason for this is that the hands that tend those same gardens are often not those of the owners themselves, some of whom may not know a shovel from a fork, but instead those of their hard-pressed, possibly underappreciated, generally not very well-remunerated gardener or gardeners, who typically remain entirely anonymous through no choice of their own.
So to flick through the pages of Stephanie Mahon and her husband John Campbell’s new book, The Creative Gardener: Inspiring People, Remarkable Gardens, is a treat for many reasons – not least because it highlights the hard graft, ingenuity, love and fierce effort that those people featured in its pages have personally poured into the plots they tend. None are household names in the way that a rock star, famous actor, technocrat or billionaire might be, although a few will be familiar to some readers, such as the food writer Nigel Slater; the floral artist Bex Partridge; the Wicklow gardener, educator and social campaigner Jimi Blake of Hunting Brook Gardens, and the Cork-born, London-based garden designer and ceramic artist Declan Buckley.
Of the 30 individuals featured, many came to gardening by a circuitous route, such as the garden designer Sarah Price and the flower-farmer-florist Rachel Siegfried, who both originally trained in fine art; Charlie Harpur, head gardener at Knepp who studied architecture; the landscape designer Thomas Blunt whose CV includes a stint as a dog-sledding guide in Canada and an unfinished degree in biochemistry; the Afghan war veteran turned professional horticulturist and head gardener Joshua Sparkes, and the former rock critic turned garden writer Alice Vincent. Others featured, such as the singer Kyla La Grange, discovered a love of gardening in adulthood, sometimes giving up well-paid, well-established careers to pursue professional horticulture in one shape or another.
What they share is that the gardens they tend are their spiritual touchstones, the places where they go to nurture their creativity and find a soothing, salving retreat from the relentlessness of modern life. By vividly sketching their stories, including the various tribulations along the way, Mahon gives a great sense of the intensity and intimacy of that relationship and how it feeds their life force. Campbell’s elegant, atmospheric photography beautifully reinforces this, providing a rich sense of place and people.
In a world where social media relentlessly markets “perfection” as the bar we all should aim for, The Creative Gardener serves as a valuable reminder of the endless joy that gardening gives if we give up that other, fruitless pursuit. Real gardens, as Mahon says in her thoughtful introduction, aren’t perfect, just as life is never perfect, nor is perfection possible or indeed even desirable. “Every gardener works within limits, whether it’s the size of their plot or budget, their soil or aspect, or having to also manage full-time jobs, young children, illness or grief.”
It’s also important proof of how the best gardens gradually evolve in parallel with those who tend them. One of the oldest gardeners featured in the book is the topiary artist Charlotte Molesworth ( whom I coincidentally mentioned in this column just a few weeks ago ). She and her husband Donald have spent 40 years creating their wonderfully idiosyncratic garden at Balmoral Cottage, a place filled with giant topiary specimens reminiscent of the movie Edward Scissorhands that the couple grew from tiny cuttings and baby plants.
When they bought the property as a young, almost penniless married couple, it was “small and almost derelict, with a leaking roof, wonky foundations, bad wiring, one meagre light bulb, and a Rayburn for warmth”. Unable to get a conventional mortgage, Donald instead agreed a payment plan with the sellers, who also happened to be his employers. Surviving on a tiny household budget, they succeeded in creating a uniquely magical space by dint of decades of hard work, patience, artistry and a deep-rooted love of gardening, honing their considerable skills along the way.
Jonny Bruce, the British nurseryman, garden writer and botanical artist who tends the world-famous garden of Prospect Cottage, the starkly beautiful creation of late film-maker and author Derek Jarman, also features in the book. He too studied fine art as a young man but was considering dropping out of college when he headed to Italy one summer and found work in the gardens of Villa La Pietra. Being surrounded by the beauty of Florence’s historical gardens turned out to be a light bulb moment that led him to Dungeness and a garden he describes as having “grown out of the landscape”. Bruce eventually took on the role of its steward, balancing the responsibility to preserve Jarman’s unique vision with the need of any living garden to continue to evolve and change.
That’s equally true of John Little’s endlessly experimental garden, Hilldrop, where biodiversity and habitat creation is every bit as important as beauty. Campbell’s photograph of Little’s old blue Citroen van half-buried in the ground and surrounded by a drift of hops, sweet pea and teasels tells us a thousand words about the latter’s maverick approach to the art of garden-making.
In short, if you’re looking for a “How to” gardening book, this is not it. Instead The Creative Gardener is unabashedly a “Why to” gardening book, and beautiful for it. To quote Mahon, “the key lessons I have learned from my time with these generous and talented people are these: be curious, be patient, be bold ... and just care.”
The Creative Gardener: Inspiring People, Remarkable Gardens by Stephanie Mahon and John Campbell is published by Quarto/Frances Lincoln.
October brings the likelihood of the first of autumn’s harsh frosts, so place any tender or half-hardy potted garden plants such as pelargoniums, banana, begonia, salvia and bedding fuchsia under cover of a glasshouse, polytunnel or even under the eaves of a roof to protect them. Some will also need an additional layer or two of horticultural fleece.
Reduce watering of food crops growing under cover of glass or plastic to minimise the chance of disease, and only water in the morning for the same reason.
‘From English Borders to Mediterranean Resilience: Rethinking Garden Design for a Hotter, Drier Future’: A talk by Lucie Willan Foxrock Church Pastoral Centre, Dublin 18; Tuesday, October 27th (8pm-10pm), on behalf of Foxrock & District Garden Club.

title: Ger Loughnane: ‘I was on the verge of a massive heart attack, and there’d have been no coming back’
description: The 73-year-old still has an athlete’s ranginess and cleanliness, and he shakes hands with a hurler’s grip
content:
T he best time to visit Clare is in October-coloured weather, with the wind and the light working off each other and the salty tang of the Atlantic on the breeze. When Seamus Heaney wrote of this place, he captured it perfectly – how it catches the heart off guard and blows it open.
So many Clare people bear the marks of the place that made them. Ger Loughnane has long since settled in Ennis, but he will always be a Feakle man, and Feakle gave us the Tulla Céilí Band, the finishing school that produced master fiddler Martin Hayes .
Consider Hayes’ words in an interview with this newspaper in 2013. “When the music is really going well , you feel like you’re just participating in it,” he said. “You feel like it’s just happening to you, with you and out of you. You feel like you’ve made yourself transparent enough for the music to flow.”
It’s how Loughnane, at his lyrical best, talks of hurling . He has just turned 73, but still has an athlete’s ranginess and cleanliness, and he shakes hands with a hurler’s grip.
“Keeping busy is the whole bloody thing when you come to a certain age. You know that you have something to get up for every day. Between going down and getting the grandchildren out of school, and then between the dogs and maintenance of the house and the place around it, there’s always something to do every day. So it’s about having something to do, you know, that’s not artificial either, that’s not fakery,” he said.
“The one thing I always hated was fakery. I won’t say something to somebody behind somebody’s back and say something completely different when I meet them. Maybe I should have a better filter, but I’m happy with that.
“Maybe there’s a directness to people who become managers. I’ll always remember after Kilkenny beat Clare in the 2002 All-Ireland final. Kilkenny’s banquet was in the Burlington and I decided to go in to see Brian Cody. We were chatting away and Henry Shefflin, who’d been named man of the match, came over. Cody turned on him, [saying] ‘You hit that ball in the one spot that gave the goalie a chance to save it; never do that again’. Henry’s face ... he just turned on his heel.”
[ The waiting is over as GAA’s experimental rules go on trial in college matches Opens in new window ]
Loughnane isn’t convinced by the split season, and will wait and see how the new hurling rules work out, but there is that old certainty in his voice when he considers the serial champions and their motivation.
“Next year, the Ryder Cup is going to be in Limerick. JP McManus is going to want the Liam MacCarthy Cup and the Cheltenham Gold Cup to be in Adare Manor . Look at Jim Furyk . He’s already been to Tipp and Limerick; he’s already talking about hurling; he’s nearly a hurling pundit at this stage. This is going to be a massive one for JP and Limerick are going to kill to win it for him because they know they owe him.”
Loughnane was the smiling public man for long enough. By 2018, he’d had his fill of it. It was coming. He’d started to grow weary of the treks to games for RTÉ . Loved the games – don’t do him a disservice – but time started to matter more and more, and too much was being stolen from him.
He craved being out on the mountains with the dogs, and their excitement was always infectious to him. He was also dodging bullets in Snipers’ Alley – the term doctors use to mark the often treacherous terrain of late middle-age.
Loughnane looks well for a man who died 15 years ago. He’d been in treatment for leukaemia in 2011, and word had gone around on Twitter that he’d passed away. It was an early wake-up call to the dangerous and unreliable territory of social media .
“I did have a very narrow escape because, when my immune system went down, it could have been curtains. There was 24 hours when I was dodgy enough, but I had a narrower escape since that I’ve never talked about publicly. Back in 2016. I was out with the dogs one day, way up in the mountain. A fox came across our way, and the dogs went tearing off after it,” he said.
[ Famous photo of Jimmy Barry-Murphy and Christy Ring a powerful reminder of Cork hurling’s lost empire Opens in new window ]
“I took out my phone to video the dogs and when I watched the video back, my breath was croaky and laboured. I had no pain, but I was thinking, ‘Jeez, there’s something wrong’. I ended up in the hospital above in Galway. They did an angiogram and said they’d have to put two stents in. I was lying there, and it was taking ages, and I could see the concern on their faces.
“Eventually, they finished, and your man says, ‘I want to show you something; look up at that screen there’. The image of my heart before the stents had just one vein – the tiniest of veins – getting blood through. He says, ‘That tiny vein kept you alive’. The other image was with the stents, and there was blood flowing everywhere; it was like a Delta. He was shaking his head, saying, ‘You’re the luckiest man alive’. I was on the verge of a massive heart attack, and there’d have been no coming back from it.”
Two years on, in 2018, he was enthralled by what he says was the greatest hurling championship he’s ever seen. He came to a realisation. That’s it. It won’t get better than this. Go back to the dogs and the mountain air. He made the call to RTÉ head of sport Declan McBennett and walked away from The Sunday Game.
“When I was hurling for Clare, I came to a point where I’d had enough of it. The following year, Sean Hehir, who I have huge regard for, was manager, and he asked me if I’d give it one more year. I said no. I never regretted it, never missed it. Leaving RTÉ ... that was the strangest of all because it was great fun, the mixture of people and the interaction we had, it was hugely enjoyable. There was no fakery,” he said.
“Then, in 2018, Limerick won the All-Ireland for the first time in 45 years and, to me, it was hurling’s greatest year. The round robin came in, and it was a massive success, and there were so many brilliant games. Not many would know this, but I covered the 1978 All-Ireland final for RTÉ. I was on with Pat Hartigan of Limerick, and Bill O’Herlihy was presenter. I’ll never forget it, the three of us in a studio, looking up at a tiny television in the corner.
“So 2018 marked 40 years from there. Michael Lyster was leaving too. It just seemed right for me to go. After the broadcast finished, I bumped into Jamesie O’Connor and JJ Delaney, who were there for Sky, and told them they’d never see me near a camera or a microphone again.”
He’d already retired from teaching and the first year in his post-TV life was fantastic. His son Barry and wife Bridget had three kids, and he and Mary loved spending time with the grandchildren. There were holidays in the sun and days at home were often crowded and noisy. Boredom often afflicts the retired, but the Loughnane family would learn the cruel truth that boredom can be a luxury.
[ Eoin Kennedy’s talent has been no secret in Cuala for quite a while now Opens in new window ]
In October 2019, Bridget was diagnosed with bowel cancer . She went through the grinder of all the treatments available but to no avail. She died in August 2022. The following February, the Loughnanes’ other son, Conor, passed away suddenly.
“Jim McGuinness did an interview on The Late Late Show, and I’ll never forget it. He was telling Ryan Tubridy about the first brother he lost, and Tubridy said to McGuinness that it must have been absolutely terrible to lose a second one. McGuinness said they dealt with it because they’d already been through it. That’s a huge thing. I don’t know if you get strength from it or what it was, but we lost Conor only six months after Bridget,” said Loughnane.
“That was very, very soon. For such a tragedy, as well. Bridget’s death was so traumatic that Conor’s death ... it was another obstacle that you had to overcome. It didn’t lessen it in any way, didn’t lessen any of the pain, but if you survived Bridget’s death, you could survive anything.
“The grandchildren have been a massive, massive help in keeping us going, but you’d be worried about any effect on them long term. A priest said to me inside in the hospital that children are very resilient and will be back outside playing in no time. I said, ‘What about in 30 years’ time?’
“So you always have that worry. But Barry is brilliant. He has a fiercely busy job, and then he comes home to the three kids, and he’s so well organised, and they’re such a team together – it’s just amazing, and they have such support from Bridget’s family, and the childminder, and the school is great to them as well. All of that support structure around them is great. All you can do is to do everything possible to limit any long-term damage to them.
“The death of a mother of very young children is in a league of its own as regards tragedy. To see them grapple with the reality of their new life, that’s very difficult. And to see it sink into them that their mother is gone and won’t be coming back. That’s a very hard concept for young kids.”
Loughnane takes a moment and gathers his thoughts. There is one story from the months after they lost Bridget that he keeps coming back to.
“When Bridget died, it was only two weeks after Aaron’s third birthday. The last time he saw her, Bridget had just slipped into a coma in the hospital, so she couldn’t speak to him. A year and a half later, I kept the date in my phone; it was January 2nd, 2024, I was up the mountain with Aaron, and he saw a deer. All the bedtime stories I’d be telling him were about deers and foxes and dogs and hares. He was mad about them and, the next thing, he saw a deer, in reality. He was so excited.
“We had a great day out and, in the van coming down, he turned to me and asked, ‘Did you visit my Mam when she was in the hospital?’ This was out of the blue after all the excitement about the deer. I said, of course I did, and then he asked, ‘Did she talk back to you?’ I copped on straight away what it was. It was worrying him that she wasn’t able to talk to him when he’d gone in to see her. He was only barely three, and he remembered it. Everyone would have assumed he was too young to remember that. A year and a half later, it was bothering him. Never underestimate the mind of a child.”
Aaron, Harry and Neila are the light of Ger and Mary’s lives, and he breaks into laughter when recalling the morning of the 2024 All-Ireland final, when Clare beat Cork to claim their fifth title.
“We parked up the car and started walking with Harry and his cousin, Dillon, and one of them piped up – ‘We’re going to count how many times people say ‘we’re going to do it’ to us.’”
That was a reference to Clare’s breakthrough win in the 1995 All-Ireland final when Loughnane was manager. At half-time, Clare trailed Offaly by two points and hadn’t got into their stride at all. Marty Morrissey was waiting for Loughnane as he headed for the tunnel. People only remember Loughnane’s final line to the RTÉ man: “We’re going to do it.”
“It’s become a meme. People who weren’t born then know it. That morning, we were still a good bit away from Croke Park, and Harry goes, ‘We’re on 25 already’.”
That era with two All-Irelands and three Munsters for Clare? It’s the shared laughter he relishes most, as much as the details of games. There’s always something that acts as a trigger. Ireland head to Vienna shortly to play Austria. Loughnane remembers the morning of the All-Ireland final in 1995, when Jack Charlton’s side were getting ready to make the same trip.
“We flew up to Dublin very early and were staying at the Airport Hotel. Turned out the Ireland soccer team were there as well. Niall Quinn and Denis Irwin had played a bit of hurling, and they came over to wish us well. We had our breakfast in the hotel, and then the players were to go to bed for two hours,” said Loughnane.
“After the players’ naps, they were to go to Colum Flynn for a rub. But I’d spotted Jack Charlton going into his room and thought we’d have a bit of fun.
“So we gave the players Jack’s room number instead of Colum’s. After the third or fourth player knocked on his door, Jack got thick. He opened his door wide and sat with his feet up on the table, watching the television. No matter what kind of commotion was at the door, he wouldn’t look sideways!”
The Loughnane home in Ennis has no shortage of photographs on the walls and on shelves, but you’d never know it’s a hurling house. Loughnane was the first Clare hurler to win an All Star, but he has always been determined not to be a prisoner of the past.
[ Mary McAleese questioned the GAA’s attitude towards women – now they’ve replaced her with a man Opens in new window ]
“I finished up with two All Stars. One of them is down in the Clare Museum. I brought Aaron in to see it because he was asking about it. It looks fairly rattled, I can tell you now. They must have let it fall. I have no idea where the other one is; it got lost,” he said.
“As you see here, there’s no photographs up from when I played or managed. I think if you have photographs up and all that kind of stuff, you start living in the past. That’s the biggest danger. For me, my whole drive was to be in the record books. You know yourself in college, you’d be out in the pub, and fellas would be arguing about players and teams, and you’d be defending your own team,” he said.
“The big put-down for Clare always was ‘right, we’ll have a look at the record books’. You would say nothing because you’d know we weren’t there for a long, long time. To be in the record books is everything.”
It’s why he says something startling. He hopes to see Clare win another All-Ireland in his lifetime, but would prefer a prize closer to home.
“Think of this: John Kiely has won seven Munsters with Limerick. Clare have won six in our history – and one of those was a walkover against Kerry. If it was a choice, I’d rather see Clare win Munster than the All-Ireland,” he said.
“It’s the one thing where we’re stuck in the last century. To win in Munster, it’s a huge thing. Look at the way Limerick celebrate every one of them. My best days with Clare were when we won the Munster Championship. Shane O’Donnell is gone from Clare now. He has two All-Irelands but never won a Munster. For Clare to win Munster would be immense.”

title: ‘We all call him baby Jesus’: Welcome to Marty Morrissey’s Marty Party on tour in Alicante
description: Kindness and community are to the fore at the Alicante event hosted by Marty Morrissey and featuring six of Ireland’s seven Eurovision winners
content:
T here is a small Irish colony in the Diamante Hotel in sunny Calpe, Alicante, Spain . There, by the palm trees, kidney-shaped pools and skinny apartment blocks, around 500 Irish people are holidaying for seven nights with sports commentator and showbiz phenomenon Marty Morrissey , TV personality and hotelier Noel Cunningham , musicians Seán Keane, Johnny Logan, Niamh Kavanagh, Dana, The Newbridge Gospel Choir and a host of others.
The Marty Party is not hard to find. In the airy lobby of the hotel, near a circular bar, there is a small tower of boxes of Barry’s Tea. In the ballroom there are pictures of Marty hanging like “the Stations of the Cross” (according to his friend Noel Cunningham). There are cutouts of him deploying finger guns all over the hotel.
“It’s not a cult,” say the crew members in Marty T-shirts.
“It feels a little like a cult,” says Nick Bradshaw, The Irish Times photographer.
If this is a cult, readers, I promise you I will completely drink the Kool-Aid. I am neither Woodward nor Bernstein. I will totally miss the big exposé..
At dinner, we sit with John and Mary Gillespie who have recently retired from Gillespie’s shop in Tubbercurry, Co Sligo. It was set up by John’s great aunt in 1888 and recently taken over by their daughter Emma. She’s a dab hand at social media, recently coming to the attention of the 2 Johnnies for getting the whole family to do a haka on Instagram. They love the food, but John’s red wine is a little cold. “Normally I stick it in the microwave for 30 seconds. Just on defrost.”
Mairead McDaid, a youthful looking 70-year-old from Buncrana, Co Donegal, passes us some ready poured glasses of wine from her table. She’s a retired teacher and is just back from a cruise but agreed to come here with her 80-year-old neighbour Margaret McCallum.
Donal Bradley, Margaret’s brother, and his wife Denise celebrated their 50th wedding anniversary the week before. Marty gives out prizes to those celebrating anniversaries. “What’s the secret of 49 years of marriage?” he asks one man. “Plenty of drink and drugs,” he replies.
[ Marty Morrissey: ‘I’m an only child of an only-child dad and an only-child mum. I’ve no aunts, uncles or first cousins’ Opens in new window ]
In the ballroom, Noel introduces the evening’s festivities. He tells us about a woman he met on the plane who had, last year, flatly refused to go to hospital because she didn’t want to miss the Marty Party. “She’s here tonight having had the operation and she’s doing fantastic.”
Marty takes to the stage and tells everyone to give the person on their right a big hug. Pat Slattery, a recently retired quantity surveyor from Letterkenny, Co Donegal, throws an arm around me. He’s a nice man. He gives every act a standing ovation irrespective of whether anyone else is doing it. He and his wife came down to Knock the night before and visited the shrine before flying out. He likes Marty because he’s open about his emotions, he says, and he likes the Marty Party “because you talk to someone different at breakfast every morning”.
Marty is an incorrigible flirt. “I’d like to introduce all of my ex-girlfriends,” he says when he introduces the (excellent) Newbridge Gospel Choir.
Noel is also an incorrigible flirt. “When Paul moved his hips, I thought Noel Cunningham would have a heart attack,” says Marty after a performance by the singer Paul Byrom.
“Marty, I’ll see you again in an hour, I’m away after him,” says Noel.
There are rousing performances from the likes of Seán Keane, all-female trad band Cherish the Ladies and a harmonising folk trio made up of Don Stiffe, Trevor Sexton and Ger O’Donnell. A tombola is rolled out with Marty’s face on it. The quiz question: “Who won the All-Ireland?” demonstrates the kind of low-friction event this is.
Marty flirts with all the winners and says they have to take him on the various trips he gives out as prizes. One prize is won by former minister and presidential candidate Heather Humphreys. “I swear it’s not a fix!” says Marty.
There’s a wild panto feel to it all but it’s touching and warm too. Everyone here has lived a bit. Life is full of troubles, says Marty at one point. “I hope everyone can forget their worries for a week.”
Later, Noel says: “If you see someone on their own go up and ask them to join you for a cup of tea or a drink.”
The next morning, a mulleted saxophonist plays Sade’s Smooth Operator as we queue for their breakfast buffet. People were up dancing until 3am. Marty and his friend Angela O’Dwyer make their way through the room pressing the flesh. Angela laments how difficult it is to get Marty from A-to-B because he never refuses a selfie.
Everyone heads down to a square downtown to see the Newbridge Gospel choir sing as the Rock of Calpe looms nearby. Marty is there. He looks freshly pressed at all times. A white jacket over black slacks and a black shirt at night, a black polo shirt and white shorts and runners during the day. That evening at dinner, Mary and Denis Murphy, retirees from Ovens in Cork, are discussing how sharp Marty looks. He comes over.
“Your legs are a lovely shape,” says Mary.
“Leave Marty alone,” says Denis, protectively.
Sitting behind me at the concert is 76-year-old Donnycarney widower David Mehlhorn. He has fallen in with Jersey-resident John Gordon, also a widower, who is here with his sisters Goreti Callaghan and Breidge Kennedy and his brother-in-law, Paddy. John and Breidge are both retired psychiatric nurses. “I fell on my feet there in case anything happens,” says David with a wink. Much later that evening, I find John and David drinking pints in the hotel lobby, laughing together like teenagers. It feels a little like the Gaeltacht for retirees.
Tonight’s performance kicks off with Noel talking about a very expensive shirt he bought by accident. “It’s in a safe in my room.”
“I wouldn’t pay €8 for that shirt,” says Marty. “It glows in the dark!”
Liam O’Connor, the Guinness-certified fastest accordion player in the world, plays a set (“I was worried there’d be heart attacks,” says Deirdre Grant, who organises all this for Killester travel). Later a woman sits at the feet of Paul Byrom as he sings. A fire alarm goes off temporarily when Joanie Madden from Cherish the Ladies is in full flight. “That’s in E flat and we’re playing in D,” she observes.
Some local Spanish staff jig along to the music. Others seem nonplussed by Irish tomfoolery. Irish tomfoolery like cheering whenever their county is named. Irish tomfoolery like a man hanging on to a large tankard he got with his beer earlier, because he noticed it was bigger than the other glasses. Irish tomfoolery like jokingly pretending to haggle.
“Would you take a fiver for the two pints?” says one man to a stonyfaced barman.
For many people this is just what they needed. Siobhan Webb is from Bath in England and when her husband Michael died, her best friend Catherine convinced her to come to the Marty Party with her. Both Siobhan and Catherine are the daughters of Irish nurses. “As someone who grew up in England, I always feel: ‘Am I Irish yet?’” Coming here, she says, “It felt like coming home.”
I see Limerick woman Sharone O’Loughlin perform an energetic step dance to the music of a youthful trio called Plain Sailing (“The others were all from Clare ... They do a battering step in Clare”). She had no strong thoughts on Marty until she met him when she was with her sister, who has special needs. “He knelt down on the ground in order to talk to her,” she says. She has been to the Marty Party every year. The first two years she came with friends. This year she happily came alone.
I sit at a table in the hotel bar with David Punch, the Marty Party floor manager. He’s also Marty’s stats man for his RTÉ commentaries. A crew member shows me a Photoshopped image of Marty on top of the Rock of Calpe “like Christ the Redeemer”. “We all call him ‘baby Jesus’,” he says. They also coin an nickname for Nick the photographer and myself: “The Hairy Bikers.”
Their driver Gerry Howard is also at the table. The first year of the Marty Party in the Costa del Sol, Gerry Howard drove a van full of gear over from Ireland. This year he brought two articulated trucks. His daughter Sophie is, he tells me, the youngest ever female articulated lorry driver in Ireland. Recently,Gerry was driving a truckload of Kerrygold butter to Poland and Sophie was on the same route. “I never had a prouder moment in my life,” he says.
The next morning everyone is up early for the Marty Party Mass. “We’re going to say a prayer for The Irish Times,” Marty says on his way in. His parish priest Father Donagh O’Meara is officiating (frankly, I’m surprised Marty isn’t). The theme is gratitude. Dana sings. So do the Newbridge Gospel Choir. The priest quotes TS Elliot, Kahlil Gibran and Bob Dylan. “We’re used to getting blessed by Bob [Dylan] every second Sunday back home,” says Marty.
Six of Ireland’s seven Eurovision winners are performing tonight. We witness Linda Martin sit on the laps of not one but two members of the Newbridge Gospel Choir. We witness Johnny Logan pelvic-thrusting in a leopard-skin suit. We witness Niamh Kavanagh break three octaves. We witness Noel dancing on a chair.
Outside by a table filled with Marty merchandise (T-shirts, mugs, greeting cards that speak with Marty’s voice) a woman throws her arm around Niamh and says: “Girl, I’d like to lick the sweat off you.” Vera from Tallaght comes up and tells her about her son who died suddenly. “Those songs brought me back to a time I was happy,” she says.
People are remarkably open here. Last year, retirees Sheila and Mike Fox befriended a couple who had recently lost a child. “When people are away, they talk about things they might not talk about when they’re at home,” says Sheila.
[ We’re apparently rolling in money, but everyone feels poorer and nobody is happy Opens in new window ]
Niamh and Noel, who are good friends, tell me how important it is to cultivate a sense of belonging for people. “That’s why I make no secret of the fact I’m gay,” says Noel. “You’d never know who in the hall that might help.”
Niamh raises an eyebrow and says: “You’re gay, Noel? When were you going to tell me?”
It’s The Irish Times’s last day at the Marty Party. At breakfast, Annette Nagle, Isabel Jones and Eileen King (who sat in adoration at the feet of Paul Byrom) recall the night before.
“Johnny Logan told Annette she had beautiful eyes,” says Isabel.
“You have beautiful eyes too, Patrick,” says Isabel, lest I get jealous. “We’ll get Dana to tell you.”
This trio came here alone but they now have a WhatsApp group called the Calpe Cailins.
There’s a lot of kindness at the Party. The day before there was a special event for people travelling solo. “A lot had lost husbands and partners and it was the first time away on their own,” says Marty.
There were tears, says Noel. “It validates the hurt and the pain.”
[ Marty Morrissey: The most famous man in GAA Opens in new window ]
Marty is a busy man. He has a full-time job he loves at RTÉ and this involves a lot of work too. But he really enjoys being with people. “Maybe it’s personal in the sense that I’m the only child of two only children and when my mother died [in 2021], I felt I needed that sense of community,” he says. “People don’t call in to each other anymore and I think there’s a lot of loneliness in Ireland ... They come as strangers but leave as friends.”
And then we head to the airport and Marty and Noel head off to the pier where each of them is captaining a Marty Party-themed catamaran. I believe everyone survived.
The Marty Party is run in association with Killester Travel and costs €1,599 per person sharing, all inclusive (The Irish Times paid its own way).

title: How Ireland’s first national public sector strike in 17 years left unions strong and Jack Chambers ‘scrambling’
description: Negotiating a deal that is good for the Government will still be a challenge once Chambers gets all parties around a table
content:
Perhaps nobody in Government had heard the old sales business adage: the first one to name a price always loses.
But they might reflect now on how outlining a package aimed at public sector workers in last week’s budget ended up putting them on the back foot.
Within the trade union movement, some believe Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers was gambling that the Budget 2027 tax changes, along with the €1.2 billion set aside for public pay increases next year, would give the Government the upper hand going into talks.
Instead, union leaders seized upon the sums as something to publicly scoff at as, on Wednesday, their members took to the streets and formed picket lines in a public sector strike.
Chambers has been left to “scramble”, as one observer puts it, for several days, discounting all that has been offered so far as merely a starting point for the talks that will at some point follow this weekend’s preliminary engagement.
Labour TD Ged Nash suggested on Thursday, as he proposed a private members’ motion on the issue, that the Government had “sleepwalked” into a first national public sector strike in 17 years.
The sight of so many young workers who had never been on a picket line before outside their workplaces will have provided a wake-up call.
From a public relations perspective, the Government could have done without the parade of workers highlighting what they regard as its failings in interviews with the media.
Ciara Loftus, who works in the Mater’s emergency department, said she was still living at home at 25 and feels she has no chance of getting on the housing ladder. This was a recurring theme, along with childcare, among younger strikers.
“I feel like I’m going to be forced to move country by the end of the year or next year,” she said.
Across Dublin , in Dún Laoghaire, Conor Carroll, a porter at St Michael’s hospital, with young children at home, talked about being stung by food inflation whenever he visits the supermarket.
“You see the price of things,” he said, “even the stuff you need to eat. You’re just not earning enough these days.”
Maurice Sweeney, a lab worker at Trinity College Dublin , said he is supposed to be one of the lucky ones on what is considered a decent wage. The reality, he says, is different.
“The weekly shop has you under pressure and we didn’t see much benefit from that budget there last week at all,” he said.
Many expressed frustration to find themselves in this position when politicians keep telling them the country is booming.
During the last strikes, the situation was very different. Back in 2009, following the banking crisis and economic crash, workers walked out over the scale of the cuts made by a Government with no money and little scope for negotiation with unions.
A decade’s worth of talks and deals that followed, from 2010 to 2020, are characterised as “defensive” by one senior trade union leader.
Now, though, he suggests this week’s industrial unrest might have taken place six years ago, when the public sector pay deal entitled Building Momentum was negotiated, had it not been for the Covid pandemic and the huge uncertainty surrounding almost every aspect of work and the economy at the time.
Relations were strained then by what the unions regarded as the continued efforts by Department of Public Expenditure (DPER) officials to approach pay talks as though the country was still broke.
The situation has only been exacerbated by what they see as DPER’s vetoing, or delaying of, spending that unions thought they were entitled to. These frustrations extend to deals they say were already agreed, such as the local bargaining aspect of the last national pay agreement.
What made the situation significantly worse over the past year, contributing to the loss of trust for the unions, was the VAT cut to hospitality . This, they felt, was given based on arguments that would not stand up to the scrutiny their own spending proposals are subjected to. Then there was the Government caving to the demands of fuel protesters .
“What you had there,” says one observer on the union side, “was people who went, parked their tractors and trucks and said, ‘right, we have the country by the balls’.”
Another person with a vested interest points to “unelected people suddenly having access to the highest levels of Government and being able to force changes that in some cases had been agreed with elected representatives or people with a respect for democratic structures”.
“Say what you want,” says the first observer, “but unions are regulated, there are rules they have to observe and they do because of the potential consequences.”
Most workers – many in modestly paid jobs and feeling the pinch of rising grocery, fuel and accommodation costs – were more put out by the expiry of the last pay deal in June.
It came at a time when prices were on an upward trajectory but the Government had not indicated when they might get around to ensuring their wages were raised accordingly.
Predictably, there is now something of a blame game as to why talks on a new agreement were delayed beyond the expiry of the last deal in June. What is undisputed is that a couple of exploratory meetings in June went poorly.
By the time Chambers wrote an opinion article in The Irish Times on July 1st, he was suggesting “all issues of importance to both sides can and should be discussed as part of any engagement”. He also warned that “setting preconditions or barriers to engagement does not assist the process of building consensus and agreement”.
The unions indicated early on that they wanted to change what was regarded as the normal running order in previous negotiations and have pay addressed up front.
Fórsa’s Kevin Callinan and John Boyle of the Irish National Teachers’ Organisation have since said they believed pay increases had fallen between 5 and 7 per cent behind inflation over the previous four years. They wanted an agreed plan to close that gap over the lifetime of any new pay deal.
One of those familiar with the process on the Government side suggests the unions wanted a final outcome on the pay issue before anything else could be discussed.
This, they argue, would have left the negotiators on the employer side with no leverage at all as they sought improved productivity through changes to work practice around artificial intelligence (AI), hybrid working or anything else.
There seems to have been surprise among officials that the unions subsequently disengaged, as they viewed it, and proceeded to balloting on industrial action relatively quickly.
The unions express exasperation that Chambers did not intervene directly, pick up the phone or arrange to meet them.
Those with experience of previous pay-agreement negotiations suggest there would traditionally have been more going on by way of back channels.
Callinan’s repeated calls this week for Taoiseach Micheál Martin to get involved are likely rooted in this, it is suggested by veterans of the pre-crash system of engagement during the “social partnership” from 1987 to 2009. Martin, they observe, is the only survivor on the Government side of how that worked and they would like to see his department reassert the control it used to exert over the negotiations.
Martin taking over might not look good for Chambers. However, Callinan made it clear on Friday that the shape of the preliminary talks process was hammed over a call with the Taoiseach.
The unions believe they are in a good position as the process gets under way, given how well Wednesday’s strike went.
Michael Doherty, a professor of law at Maynooth University and a prominent figure in the industrial relations landscape, suggests “the Government may have got a shock by the number of young, enthusiastic people getting a first taste of industrial action on the pickets and anxious to be heard”.
Having energised this young and important constituency, he says the unions need to ensure they do not leave disappointed and disillusioned.
“They are going to have to be very careful because there is the possibility they won’t want to accept some sort of fudge, that they’ll feel, ‘Hold on, you marched us up the hill here’.”
At this juncture, the unions might have felt it was better to threaten a second strike date than carry through with another stoppage – especially on what is forecast to be a cold and rainy day next Wednesday.
Preventing the second strike should help Chambers and the Government to regain some control over the situation.
To get this far, he has repeatedly said that pay can be talked about at the outset, while the unions have stuck to their position: “Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed.”
Negotiating a deal that is good for the Government will still be a challenge, though.
Both sides point to different time periods, framing the relationship between pay and inflation in recent deals in a way that suits their purposes.
The unions do not want the sacrifices forced upon them in the wake of that strike 17 years ago to be written out of the equation.
Union leaders now talk about insuring their members against future spikes in inflation such as those caused by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
However, such a mechanism would severely undermine the big prize from the negotiations for the Government: budgetary certainty for the coming few years.
The answer, some observers suggest, could be a short-term deal to get over the current impasse and allow everyone to come back when the tensions have eased. An alternative would be an agreement with a robust review clause for pay.
Both sides will likely agree on one thing if there is to be a short-term agreement: they will want to avoid being back in this current stalemate any sooner than they have to be.

title: From dereliction to Airbnb, the Gaeltacht is being destroyed by the housing crisis
description: Young families make communities – and if they have no place to live, the community dies
content:
A s winter looms, the evening is so pitch black on Inis Meáin that the few street lights across the sea on Inis Mór make Kilronan look like Manhattan. In the silent night, voices travel, and the low murmur of people chatting leads to the Halla Naomh Eoin, which doubles as the local community centre and the school – the beating heart of the least populated of the Aran Islands.
Inis Meáin hosts one of the country’s few all-Irish boarding schools and it is full of life, always oversubscribed with teenagers enthusiastically embracing island life and its language . Tonight’s meeting is about what will happen in a few years, when these students – both locals and outsiders – become adults, and whether they can settle on the island, rear families, continue to speak Irish and infuse the community with vibrancy.
The impediment on Inis Meáin is housing . Irish-speaking adults who want to live here have few options as prices have gone through the roof for the tiny number of homes that come on the market. Meanwhile, restrictive planning laws mean locals cannot build new homes for their children on their plots.
Ireland’s islands are an essential part of Irishness, an integral part of our heritage and culture and one of the last bastions of Irish as a living, working, breathing, everyday language.
Tonight’s meeting is organised by a group of young Gaeilgeoirí activists called Tinteán (“níl aon tinteán mar do thinteán féin”), whose basic message is that if young Gaeilgeoirí can’t afford to live in the Gaeltacht, it will die very soon. Ironically, we are just a few hundred yards from the cottage where JM Synge spearheaded the Gaelic Revival.
According to the latest census, the country’s island population has fallen below 3,000 for the first time. To put this into context, in 1841 there were 48,000 people living on the islands off the western seaboard. Today the average age on the islands is 59 - in contrast to the rest of the country, where it is 43 – and more than one in five of the islands’ population are aged 65 years and older.
The crucial age group between 20 and 35 accounts for just 7.9 per cent of the islands’ population, as opposed to 25 per cent for the State as a whole.
Meanwhile, just 5 per cent of the islands’ population is under four years old, compared with an average of 8 per cent nationally.
These population dynamics mean only one thing: catastrophic decline and, along with a disappearing population, a disappearing language and culture. What would Synge think?
It is essential that the population decline is reversed. At a time when the Irish language has rarely been more popular , when thousands of people are learning and in some cases relearning it, the Gaeltacht itself is being destroyed by the refusal to do the very thing that generations of people from the west of Ireland did all over the world: build houses. Young families make communities, and if they have no places to live then the community dies or becomes more like a museum – visited by curious onlookers during the holiday season, but for all intents and purposes, dead.
One of the main issues is that homes have become trophy assets. When a house here comes up for sale, it is marketed online to everyone from London to New York to Mount Merrion. There is a burgeoning national and international market for property in the west of Ireland, and this process elbows out the local people, pushing prices way out of reach for the average islander.
In addition, the tourist market, so long the source of summer income, has changed dramatically.
Airbnb and Booking.com have made it so attractive for property owners to rent out their places short term that these potential homes are taken off the rental market for young Gaeilgeoirí who can’t afford to compete in trophy auctions. In many cases they are being given the option to rent until the summer comes, and then weekly rents skyrocket for the tourist season and the families must find somewhere else to live until September. They are in effect school-year residents, and that oddly nomadic existence rarely encourages people to put down roots.
Naturally, as more and more rural hotels have been turned over to refugees, tourist bed capacity falls, putting more pressure on the existing housing stock.
[ Life on Inis Meáin: ‘Some people will say there’s nothing here, but in fact there is everything here’ Opens in new window ]
Another issue is vacancy – and ultimately dereliction, because an uninhabited house doesn’t stand a chance against Atlantic storms for long. For example, according to the local community office, on Inis Meáin there are 149 houses, of which 65 are uninhabited. Nearly half of all the homes on an island with a housing crisis stand empty.
We know that people respond to incentives, positive and negative. With respect to building houses in the Gaeltacht to enable Gaeilgeoir families to live here, the key is to create the incentives to make the local housing market work. Considering the fact that there are vacant houses on the island, what might make the owners put them on the market?
At the moment, capital gains must be paid if you sell a vacant property. This is an obvious impediment to selling. Why go through the hassle of selling, particularly an old family house split between a few children, if the government gets 31 per cent of the profit? What about specifically cancelling capital gains on the islands in order to lubricate supply? Make it easy to sell. Such a move would change the conversation about selling.
A buyer’s tax break, specifically for Gaeilgeoirí, like the Temple Bar tax breaks for residents in the 1990s, would bias buying to Irish speakers.
On the planning side, what about setting a quantity of homes to be built by locals every year, based on demand and family structure, allowing the residents to solve their own problems? This would give local people the ability to build on their own island, for their own community.
[ ‘It’s just like a match made in heaven’: Family of seven who moved to Inis Meáin urge others to follow Opens in new window ]
Even if these initiatives were embraced, there is still the issue of the cost of island life – which is far in excess of anything on the mainland. Those of us who don’t live on small islands don’t realise that the sea is a big cost driver. Think about getting material to the island, renting the truck to bring the materials to the harbour on the mainland, renting the boat to bring the stuff across, finding the workers to do the job, putting them up while they are working, and so on. All these things cost money, yet the income of Ireland’s islanders is far below the national average.
What about making island life tax-free for Gaeilgeorí, treating the people the way we treat US multinational capital? When we cut corporation tax , activity responded. The same would apply with income tax , excise duty and VAT on islands.
If we are talking about the Gaeltacht and the language, what about making living on the island tax free for Gaeilgeori? The sums of money would be tiny for a country with an annual budget of €147 billion. We are talking about only a few thousand people initially. The cost is minuscule and the prize, the preservation of a way of life and a language that has been spoken continuously in this part of the country for more than 2,500 years, is enormous.
This morning I asked a local about the weather and he responded, “Tá sé leathghlas ceart go leor,” or, “It’s a bit half grey all right.” (Down here glas isn’t green, it’s grey.) The half grey refers to the sea, the sky and heavy clouds, and the colour of the rocks, the limestone and the horizon where the sea and the clouds meet in a misty angry grey haze. This linguistic richness comes from hundreds of generations inscribing their language with colour, significance and their own meaning.
Imagine losing this for the sake of a few pennies.

title: AI ecosystem may be booming but at what cost?
description: The technology’s threat to junior positions could lead to companies creating their own future skills gap
content:
Ireland’s AI ecosystem is booming. That is the message that was broadcast loud and clear this week as the International AI Summit rolled into town.
Nearly €1 billion has been invested in Irish AI companies across 182 deals since the beginning of 2025, according to Enterprise Ireland.
Pitchbook’s latest figures found the amount invested in Irish AI companies by venture capital firms this year was at a near record, at €256 million across 75 deals so far.
On the face of it, it looks like a decline given that 2025 recorded €691.3 million across 107 deals.
But Pitchbook’s report highlighted 2025’s blockbuster performance, when Wayflyer raised almost €162 million, and Tines grabbed close to €121 million in a series C round of funding. The most recent figures for 2026 represent a “normalisation rather than retreat”.
While the money may be rolling in with AI, support for it among workers may be a tougher sell. Attendees at the AI Summit on Wednesday were greeted by protesters loudly objecting to the growth of the technology. Earlier in the week, an event held by the Communication Workers’ Union heard of the narrowing opportunities for entry-level workers and the degradation of work, with staff employed to oversee the output of AI rather than creating on their own.
[ Entry-level hiring in AI-augmented sectors drops by 16% Opens in new window ]
That was followed by a survey from IDA Ireland that backed up the previously voiced threats to junior positions. The Labour Market Pulse for the second quarter of the year found a 16 per cent decline in entry-level hiring in occupations where AI is commonly used to augment human workers. That could lead to a situation where companies create their own future skills gap, as Christopher Paye, country director for the StepStone Group for Ireland, recently warned in an interview with The Irish Times.
If companies are not careful, they may find that in chasing an AI utopia, they have plenty of money to spend, but can’t get the experienced staff that will ultimately grow the company and help justify those significant funding rounds.

title: ‘It never gets easy:’ 10 years on, Anthony Foley is still inspiring Munster
description: That Munster are due to host Racing just a day after the 10th anniversary of Foley’s death is uncanny. But then, so much of the spirit of ‘Axel’ seems to live on
content:
It’s hard to believe it’s a decade since Irish rugby was rocked to its core when the tragic news broke that Anthony Foley had died in his sleep overnight in a Parisian hotel. Sunday, October 16th, 2016. He was aged 42, a father of a young family, and it still seems just as wrong now as it did then.
Munster had been due to play Racing 92 that day and the sense of disbelief outside the gates of the Stade Yves-du-Manoir among the hushed hordes of the Red Army, save for a moving rendition of There is an Isle, remain vivid.
That Munster are due to host Racing just a day after the 10th anniversary of Foley’s death is uncanny. But then, so much of Axel’s spirit seemed to live on in the days and months and years that followed, up to and beyond this 10th meeting between the province and Racing in Páirc Uí Chaoimh this Saturday (kick-off 8pm).
Mick Galwey, a team-mate with Shannon, Munster and Ireland, will always remember the last time he was with Foley, when hosting a party at his home in Kilkenny on his 50th birthday just a week previously.
“Even though Leinster had beaten him that evening up in the Aviva, he still managed to come down to my 50th in Kilkenny. So, my last time with him was just top-class. Little did we know, we wouldn’t see him again, but it’s lovely to be able to look back and say the last time we were together, we had a great time,” Galwey says.
“Eddie Halvey and Frankie Sheehan and boys like that, and particularly Eddie, who hadn’t seen Axel in years, they both made it to my 50th. We had so many good times together, but the last time we were together was a great time and it’s small consolation, but it is consolation.”
In the poignant week that’s in it, few people are better placed to talk about Foley than Galwey. He has the unique distinction of being a team-mate in all three of Foley’s debuts for Shannon, Munster and Ireland.
“Anthony Foley was rare in Shannon because his dad Brendan was there before him. He knew Shannon before he ever came to Shannon. I’ve never seen a young fella just step in so easily.
“We had a good team, we had a good back row with Halvey and a young Quinny [Alan Quinlan] but then this young fella came through and Axel was amazing.”
Galwey wasn’t remotely surprised Foley went into coaching after his playing career finished.
“As a player, he was so intelligent and he had so much to offer. He wasn’t afraid to speak his mind, even in the early days, and he was great at making a decision under pressure.
“Looking back on it, rugby was his life,” adds Galwey, noting how Foley would come back to play for Shannon even when he turned professional, and he was a big part of eight of the club’s nine AIL titles.
Foley played for Munster 201 times, captaining them to their breakthrough 2006 Heineken Cup triumph. He also played 62 times for Ireland, captaining his country three times.
“His reading of the game was immense,” says Galwey. “You can’t coach talent and Anthony had that in spades. He was like a striker at number eight; he just knew where to be at the right time. Having a rugby brain like that is immense. You can often see fellas trying their best, in fact they’re trying too hard. But if you can read the game, if you know where the ball will be in a minute or 20 seconds, you can be there. And that’s very important.”
A week after his 50th, Galwey was at home in Kilkenny, about to go to a hurling game before returning to watch Munster’s scheduled match, when he noticed he had missed calls from Philip Danaher, John Fitzgerald and Peter Clohessy, whereupon another former Munster team-mate, Killian Keane, called him.
“Killian, how are things?” Galwey recalls saying - “and I was talking to him only this week about it.”
He says Keane’s reply at the time was: “Um, not good.”
“He said: ‘Bad news. Are you sitting down?’
“And I said: ‘Do I need to be sitting down?’ He said: ‘You do.’ And then he told me Axel had passed away. And I said: ‘Are you sure it’s not Brendan?’ No disrespect to Brendan, and thankfully Brendan is still with us and in great fettle.
Then Galwey’s phone lit up with constant calls.
“You didn’t need social media when you had friends, because everybody was ringing me. And I do remember it was a shock. None of us could believe it. It was probably the following day, the Monday, that it really hit me.”
There was solace to be had in shared grief for the two days around Foley’s funeral the following Friday, trying to comfort Olive and the boys, parents Brendan and Sheelagh, who has since died too, and his sisters Rosie and Orla, and being among the extended rugby family.
When thousands descended upon Killaloe to bid farewell to Axel, with many outside a packed St Flannan’s Church as Olive’s extraordinary eulogy to her husband was relayed through outdoor speakers, it was akin to a State funeral.
“We kept saying, ‘what would Axel think of this?’ We had to have the craic and that’s what rugby players do. We had two great days in Killaloe, and then we went to the match in Thomond Park, and it was sad when we were splitting up. We missed each other’s company because there was comfort in numbers, and never more so than in that week.
“I can never remember being at a sadder occasion, but to be with friends made it easier, and it’ll be good to catch up again this weekend. I’m meeting some of them in Cork on Saturday night, but it’s going to be a good turnout in Killaloe on Sunday, and rightly so.”
Galwey was one of the pallbearers who carried the coffin from the church. Paul O’Connell and John Langford were at the back, Galwey and John Hayes in the middle, with Clohessy and Keith Wood in front of them.
“Claw [Clohessy] is smaller than me and his shoulder was about 6in from the coffin,” recalls Galwey.
“It never gets easy, but I look back at the funeral, I look back at the sending-off we gave him and I am very proud of the way all his team-mates, all his friends, all his pals, we were all there.
“We have the game on Saturday in Páirc Uí Chaoimh and I’ll be down at that. But his anniversary Mass is on Sunday in Killaloe and there’s a lot of lads coming up to that, and I think that’ll be a day of catching up, and it’s what we all need, and hopefully his family will appreciate it.
“We have a Munster WhatsApp group and it’s been up there for a while and there’ll be a lot of his team-mates there, I can guarantee you that.”
The day following the funeral, without any training after a week of paying tributes and honouring their team-mate and coach, Munster hosted Glasgow in the Champions Cup at a packed Thomond Park. The ground was possibly the most emotionally charged it’s ever been that day.
Guided sympathetically by Rassie Erasmus and Jacques Nienaber, the team went back to Munster basics in many ways, with a performance that was both true to Foley as a player and coach, and one that would have made him proud.
[ Leinster coach Nienaber guided by Anthony Foley’s words ahead of daunting Clermont test Opens in new window ]
Munster played with a generally controlled fury, roaring into a 31-3 lead and earning a bonus point by early in the second half. A 15m maul set the tone, Keith Earls offloading for Tyler Bleyendaal to finish. Blyendaal and Rory Scannell set up Jaco Taute soon after and despite Earls being sent off for a tip tackle on Gordon Brown, a brilliant Simon Zebo finish made it 24-3 at the break.
Relentless scrum pressure earned a penalty try and though Glasgow scored a couple of tries to make it 31-10, Conor Murray set up Rory Scannell for a 75th-minute try to ensure the win. Bringing their dressingroom anthem, Stand Up and Fight, on to the pitch after the full-time whistle, effectively bringing the crowd into the dressingroom, sealed an unforgettable day . A bonus-point win achieved by 14 players for an hour, but then again, they had started the day with 16 men.
[ Craig Casey aiming to maximise Páirc Uí Chaoimh factor on emotional night for Munster Opens in new window ]
“The match was immense,” says Galwey. “And do you know what I loved about it? I love the way on occasions like that players play above themselves. On days like that, it’s not about your coaching, it’s not about your talent, it’s about the X Factor, and I hope we see it again on Saturday.”
That would be another fitting testimony to Foley’s legacy, which Galwey believes will last for ever.
[ Leinster v Clermont Auvergne: The best moments from a European rugby rivalry Opens in new window ]
“That’s basically it. He was a Munster man coming from a Shannon and Munster family, and what his family have done for rugby, and what he has done for rugby, is fairy-tale stuff.
“For as long as fellas can still play for Munster in the number eight jersey, gone but never forgotten.”

title: Rome to consider sainthood for Irish Jesuit priest killed in bloody first World War battle
description: Pope will make final decision on Fr Willie Doyle once panel of theologians satisfied he fulfilled life of heroic virtue
content:
Irish Jesuit priest Fr Willie Doyle died on August 16th, 1917 during the Battle of Paschendaele in Belgium .
It was a catastrophic day for the two Irish divisions, the 16th (Irish) Division and the 36th (Ulster) Division assaulting highly fortified German positions on Frezenberg Ridge. About 1,200 men perished that day in a doomed attempt to take the ridge in the mud and rain.
Doyle went to the assistance of two officers who were dying – Second Lieutenant Arthur Green from Co Down and Second Lieutenant Charles Marlow, a former captain of the cricket team at King’s Hospital School in Dublin.
According to one account, Doyle was anointing one of the men when a shell burst among them. It also killed Pte John Meehan, a winner of the Military Medal, who had taken shelter there. Their bodies were never recovered from the battlefield.
Death was not the end of Doyle’s story. In the 1920s, a former Jesuit priest and polymath, Prof Alfred O’Rahilly, published a bestselling biography of Doyle, who came from Dalkey in south Dublin, which was translated into several languages.
Readers were told of his intense spirituality, his life of prayer and penance, and his selflessness in the service of others. Thousands testified to his intercession in some aspect of their lives. Many wanted him canonised, but the Jesuits demurred and in the 1930s nothing came of it.
The Catholic Church, it is famously said, only moves in centuries. The cause for his canonisation was revived 10 years ago by the Father Willie Doyle Association, founded by Dr Patrick Kenny.
[ Irish priest moves closer to sainthood after being declared venerable by Pope Leo Opens in new window ]
Doyle’s journey to sainthood moves into another phase with solemn vespers at Mullingar Cathedral on Sunday, which marks the end of the diocesan stage of the process.
The cause was opened in 2022 and the Diocese of Meath’s tribunal, which has been tasked with assembling the case for his canonisation, has collected an extraordinary array of material amounting to 11 volumes, or about 4,000 pages in total. The testimony comes from Doyle’s own voluminous writings, theologians and historians.
There is also the testimony from those who had a devotion to him both when the original case was opened in the 1920s and later. The internet has made the process of gathering material much easier. “It is extraordinary how extensive the interest and devotion is worldwide,” said Fr John Hogan, the diocesan postural of Doyle’s cause.
[ The Great War: ‘The heroic dead of Ireland have every right to the homage of the living’ Opens in new window ]
Rome will receive two copies of the material. The first will go to the Dicastery of Saints, the second to the Roman postural who will write the positio, the formal document examining Doyle’s life, virtues and reputation for holiness. If the panel of theologians is satisfied that Doyle fulfilled a life of heroic virtue, it will be brought to the Pope for decision. If the Pope approves, Doyle will be made venerable.
There are two further steps to sainthood, both requiring a miracle. Doyle will need one miracle to become blessed and a second to become a saint.
“Let’s just say that we have some serious favours that are under consideration,” said Hogan of the process of gathering miracles in support of Doyle’s canonisation.
It took just 12 years from the opening of the case of Carlo Acutis, the so-called millennial saint, until his canonisation last year.
Hogan believes Doyle would make an ideal saint for the modern world. He spent much time in prayer and repentance atoning for the sins of priests. As an Irish Catholic in a British army uniform, he could also serve as a symbol of reconciliation.
[ From the archive: An Irishwoman’s Diary on a strange meeting near Ypres in 1915 Opens in new window ]
His death was mourned by many of those in the 36th (Ulster) Division, with one Orangeman writing in the Glasgow Weekly News: “We couldn’t possibly agree with his religious opinion, but we simply worshipped him for other things. He didn’t know the meaning of fear, and he didn’t know what bigotry was.”

title: Ella McSweeney: What Paris can teach Ireland about clean water
description: We’re paying a lot to clean polluted water, while investing little in restoring the rivers, wetlands and farmlands that could keep it pure in the first place
content:
I n 1735, Benjamin Franklin, a young Philadelphia printer decades away from helping found the United States, used his newspaper to warn a fire-prone town about a dangerous habit: carrying live embers from fireplace to fireplace, causing houses to burn. “An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure,” he wrote, urging locals to use a closed warming pan instead.
When it comes to fresh, drinkable water, Ireland is still mostly buying the pound of cure, using vast amounts of public money to pay for it twice: once at the treatment plant, and again in our failing, polluted rivers.
In Budget 2027 , Uisce Éireann was allocated €2.35 billion, an increase of about 40 per cent (€650 million) over two budgets. That is roughly what the Government’s own advisory committee said our Nature Restoration Plan needed annually: €450-€700 million. Nature restoration got no dedicated funding in this budget – not one cent . Yet the EU’s water strategy is clear: nature-based solutions should come first.
It’s not about begrudging investment in pipes and treatment plants. But we’re paying a lot to clean polluted water, while investing little in restoring the rivers, wetlands and farmlands that could keep it pure in the first place. Other countries are doing the exact opposite.
[ Ireland is the last stand for rare coastal machair habitats in the EU – but it’s failing Opens in new window ]
Farmer Jérôme Forgeot grows wheat, barley, alfalfa and lentils on 300 hectares in the Vanne valley, southeast of the city. Every year he gets a payment from the city’s public water utility, Eau de Paris, not to buy his crops but to pay for what no longer seeps from his fields into the water.
A quarter of Paris’s water comes from springs in this part of France, and for decades nitrates and pesticides from surrounding farms leached into it. Rather than spend money on treatment, the utility decided in 2020 to design its own scheme and pay farmers to stop the pollution at the source.
It’s a clever, simple initiative, exactly the kind that brings farmers in and lets them get on with their work. Farmers sign six-seven year contracts and are paid €150-€450 a hectare to cut pesticides, reduce nitrate leaching or farm organically, with part of the payment tied to nitrate levels measured in their fields.
Eau de Paris agronomists advise farmers one to one and also help them with their businesses, finding buyers for their produce. Forgeot went organic in 2012 and helped found a farmers’ group, Terres du Pays d’Othe, that sells lentils, oil and pasta to Parisian school canteens. In 2020 he signed a contract until 2027. The city’s children eat healthy, local food grown to protect the city’s water; farmers are paid to change their approach and, in return, expand their markets.
Most importantly, it works. About 125 farmers, covering 20,000 hectares, are now under contract. Pesticide use on their land fell by 77 per cent in 2023. In the Vanne catchment, organic farmland rose from 1 per cent in 2010 to 28 per cent in 2025, and peak pesticide levels in the water halved.
It’s a responsible use of public money. Treating polluted water costs three times as much as preventing the pollution. When chlorothalonil residues turned up in French drinking water, the pesticide treatment bill tripled.
Last December, Brussels extended Ireland’s nitrates derogation to 2028, which allows 7,000 farms to exceed EU limits on manure nitrogen. We’re the only member state with a derogation, and keeping it depends on measurable improvements in water quality. That’s still not happening. The EPA’s latest report shows that nitrogen in our major rivers is increasing, and agriculture is the main source, mainly fertiliser and manure.
[ Ireland punishes tax evaders. Pollution should be just as risky Opens in new window ]
Uisce Éireann isn’t blind to this. It has planted 121,000 native trees on its own sites and admits that tackling pollution at the source beats treating it. In 2022, it gave 35 farmers in Cavan’s Erne-Larah catchment free advice, pesticide stores and fencing.
But with such a sizeable budget, Uisce Éireann needs to see itself as more than a builder of pipes and treatment plants. Its catchments supply water to half the country, and the cheapest, most effective approach is to invest in resilient waterways. The question is whether Uisce Éireann, and the regulator that sets its spending, will urgently realise that paying for clean water at source is now a fundamental part of its job.
Uisce Éireann does not publish what it spends removing pesticides, but Northern Ireland offers a guide. NI Water told farmers that carbon filters to strip pesticides out cost £5 million (€5.91 million), plus up to £50,000 (€59,145) a year to run at one plant. When it paid for weed-wiping in one Armagh catchment, pesticides fell by three-quarters within two years, and the savings at the treatment works outweighed the cost.
Uisce Éireann’s annual report shows how it sees its job. Its sustainability section says it aims to protect the environment “on which our services depend”. It sets six ambitions, but restoring the catchments isn’t among them. Paris can say prevention is cheaper because it counts the cost of the cure. Uisce Éireann could start by publishing the same comparison.
Irish farming is mostly grass and livestock, and contradictory farm policies, a weak organic market and poor procurement practices make it hard to change. In the budget 2027, the Government gave €31 million for a new fertiliser scheme, which might benefit the fertiliser industry but will keep farmers hooked on polluting activities. Irish households pay no water charges, so a restoration scheme would fall on the taxpayer, though not necessarily alone: the European Investment Bank and the European Commission are keen to help member states with lending and technical assistance for nature-based solutions in water resilience programmes. The EIB has already lent to Eau de Paris for their work.
Forgeot’s lentils are on Parisian school menus. He’s making money from not polluting. The question for us is: who will pay farmers to keep our water clean, and how much longer can we afford not to?

title: ‘We could be facing a dire situation’: Irish aid agencies on the impact on the ground of funding cuts
description: International aid is being cut everywhere – what does this mean for the world’s poor and the Irish charities trying to help them?
content:
“Q uiet deaths” – that’s the phrase used by Ciara Begley.
She paints a bleak picture of the impact of malnutrition from her experience in Liberia, where she works as country director for the charity Concern Worldwide .
“And out there in a rural community, if you are a young adolescent girl with a child that is malnourished, a lot of the time that child just dies quietly in that community.”
Begley arrived in the west African country six years ago and has seen the number of people working for the charity there fall by more than half in that time, from 106 to 51.
Even more troubling for her has been the effective ending of nutritional treatments in Liberia since September 2025.
“There has never been a nationwide stock-out like this for over a year and it’s happening because Unicef is getting squeezed and cut,” she says, referring to the United Nations (UN) agency for children.
The stock she is referring to falls into three categories: the key one is “Plumpy Nut” – a high-energy peanut butter-like paste that quickly builds up malnourished children and prevents starvation. The other two are milk formulas given to acutely malnourished infants.
“You are trying to refer children for treatment but there’s not much facilities can do,” she says.
“It’s grim and really difficult for our staff; they are working to help them use local ingredients to help cases that need medical treatment. It’s not fair on anyone, but it is what we need to do.”
[ Ireland and Spain only EU countries to increase development aid last year Opens in new window ]
Nutritional programmes such as these have failed due to massive cuts in humanitarian aid from the prosperous “global north”, in particular the United States.
Last year, under instruction from the Trump White House, the United States Agency for International Development (USAid) – the US government’s international aid agency – was closed and the budget for foreign aid slashed dramatically.
The Irish Government said last week it is estimated that up to 700,000 people around the world have died as a result of cuts to international aid by the Trump administration.
This past week brought more challenging news for the aid sector.
Ireland’s draft of the EU budget for 2028 to 2034 included a 17 per cent cut from the Global Europe fund compared with the original proposal. The fund covers all the EU’s spend on international development and co-operation.
Defending the change, the Taoiseach said the proposed funding would still be higher than the existing seven-year commitment and the humanitarian budget of €25 billion would be retained.
But when the US has pulled back so severely from funding aid programmes, it was seen as another blow among the groups dependent on such money.
“Just look at Concern last year,” says Concern’s chief executive Dominic Crowley.
“We had to close three country programmes – in Lebanon, Rwanda and North Korea – and we have a very reduced presence everywhere else.
“We went from having 3,000 staff to just over 2,000 and there was a 17 per cent headcount cut here in Dublin. We’ve never seen that sort of cut in the history of aid going back to the 1980s and we are not alone.”
Crowley points to scores of conflicts around the world, with aid workers being killed in Gaza and working in underground bunkers in Ukraine. This, combined with the reduction in aid contributions from the big four donor countries – the United States, the UK, France and Germany – has made it the most challenging period in the charity’s history.
[ Is Ireland ready for a monster El Niño? Expect ugly potatoes, transport chaos and widespread disruption Opens in new window ]
In Africa, the immediate effect on ordinary people has been profound, says Crowley. In Somalia , which teeters on the edge of famine, Concern was forced to close half of its feeding centres and clinics.
In Darfur and Kordofan in Sudan , at one stage it had to shutter all its operations. An injection of funding from the Irish Government has since allowed it to reopen about a third of them.
Concern’s Somalia country director Richard Nunn says international support in 2022 and 2023 helped ensure that the country avoided famine – but that level of backing is no longer available.
“It’s not as serious yet as it was 2½ years ago, but depending on the rains and El Niño we could be looking at a really dire situation,” he says.
“In just the first year of the funding cuts from the US you had around 300 health facilities which closed. NGOs around the country have closed offices and stopped operations. People who need that support can’t find them in their communities – they have to travel – or they can’t find them at all.”
Nunn’s staff numbers have fallen from 170 to 100, and the charity has reduced its geographical footprint. While Concern’s programmes in Somalia were not directly exposed to cuts by the US government, other donors have also pulled back, he says.
“Our facilities and clinics are more and more crowded, and we have fewer staff to support those people,” he says.
