Nunn says supplies of emergency food to treat malnutrition have been promised until the end of the year but there is “no visibility” into next year.
“We have found other sources – private foundations in the US are providing some targeted, select support to Concern – but other organisations are having difficulties,” says Nunn.
“Private foundations are new for Concern. It’s not bad [the funding] – it’s much more than token. But it’s telling that that is now having to come from the private sector.”
All of the big Irish aid organisations say at the same time as funding is being reduced, their workers are facing ever more threats in the field.
“When I started off you were always relatively safe on the front lines, that’s not so much the case any more,” says Colin Lee, Goal’s director of global programmes and operations.
In addition to a rising number of workers being held against their will, the use of military drones has changed the landscape dramatically in certain countries, says Lee.
“Sudan has been a real test case over the last 3½ years with the use of drone technology. We’ve had health facilities targeted specifically.”
[ Sudan food crisis now so bad people are eating leaves and animal feed to survive Opens in new window ]
While aid workers grapple with funding cuts and new threats to their safety, their charities spent much of the past week making their case in Brussels.
As the Irish Government prepared to formally present its revised draft budget plan at this week’s EU summit, charity leaders met EU commissioners and their officials.
Among them was Trócaire’s chief executive Seán Farrell, who met the EU commissioner responsible for global humanitarian policy, Hadja Lahbib.
“We have seen a move to the political right in many European countries,” he says.
“And part of the narrative around many of these political parties was focused on migration. They have dismantled some aid programmes.”
Farrell says humanitarian funding has also been cut by governments to pay for increased defence spending, including countries bordering Ukraine and Russia that have raided this source to bolster their militaries.
They believe a budget that compounds this trend would be very unwelcome.
“There is no question that the Global Europe funding envelope is being reduced more than others,” he says.
Farrell contends that even deeper cuts to European funding could be on the table as the negotiations around the next seven-year EU budget continue into next year.
“At a time when you look at humanitarian aid globally, with the US having gutted USAid and other European states pulling back, if we take very harsh cuts on the European aid budget the very poorest will pay the highest price,” he says.
“We will be giving up on the idea that we can eradicate extreme poverty.”
Some voices within the charity sector hope humanitarian funding may be close to bottoming out, with the prospect of some improvement in the years ahead.
“After a pretty horrific 2025, things have stabilised slightly,” says Colin Lee of Goal.
“We are very good at whinging and telling you bad news stories – but there have been a number of good news stories.
“US funding is coming back in mechanisms we wouldn’t have seen before, like through UN OCHA,” he adds, referring to Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, a UN agency that helps humanitarian organisations assisting people caught up in crises.
[ ‘End of rules-based order’: Irishman who helped end a civil conflict on a world tilting toward war Opens in new window ]
Lee says the shock of the cutbacks have forced charities and organisations to work together like never before with a move to “less competition, more collaboration”.
“We are not going back to the old model of what was there. The last 18 months has been an opportunity to get our heads around where this is going,” he says.
In Liberia, Concern’s Ciara Begley sees some reasons for optimism; the African country’s government has adopted a more serious-minded approach to funding nutrition and has increased its budget for next year.
“Just because it is submitted doesn’t mean it gets approved, but it’s a ray of hope,” she says.

title: From Dart+ West to MetroLink: Why the State is willing to pay millions to settle planning objections
description: Millions in taxpayer money has been paid out to prevent further delay of infrastructure projects
content:
In September 2024, a hardware and electrical wholesaler in west Dublin took a legal case in which it sought to block a €1 billion project to bring the Dart rail network to Kildare and Meath.
The judicial review action by Burke Brothers, based at Navan Road, and a separate but similar case by motor distributor Gowan, a landowner in the same area, were scheduled to be heard in the High Court in June 2025.
At issue was planning consent for the Dart+ West plan, designed to bring the commuter rail service into Maynooth, Co Kildare , and the M3 Parkway near Dunboyne, Co Meath .
This long-stalled project had been in preparation for two decades, the aim being to boost public transport capacity in the growing commuter hinterland of the capital city. Court proceedings were certain to introduce more delays, increasing costs even if the judge dismissed the legal challenge. But the case did not go ahead in the end.
On the day the case was to open, Irish Rail let it be known it had reached a “confidential settlement” with the litigants. The proceedings were withdrawn, clearing the way for Dart+ West to go ahead.
Nothing was declared publicly about the settlement terms, although the deal was similar to recent agreements by two State bodies to buy out objectors to MetroLink and housing in Dublin. Such arrangements were made at significant expense to taxpayers. The State paid €2 million or more for each of five homes whose sale was registered in different Dublin locations this year.
Such cases have drawn attention to something that usually happens without public scrutiny – or in the realm of compulsory purchase orders, where the State compels property owners to sell to make way for a road or other infrastructure in return for payment.
A high-level public official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the calculation made in legal cases is that settlement costs will be far less than the eventual cost of further delaying the project.
At the same time, it was recognised that settling in the legal arena would involve paying “a little over the odds” for the asset.
“I assume they have been given the nod,” the official said, citing the need for “political consent” for such agreements. In other words, ministers with responsibility for State bodies should be in the loop whenever such bodies make unusual transactions.
Court cases can run for years – and that’s often before any appeals. Given rapid construction inflation and the already high cost of building public infrastructure, the official said litigation in a single case can add hundreds of millions of euro to the cost of a project while no actual progress was being made.
For instance, the cost of the long-delayed Greater Dublin Drainage wastewater scheme was estimated in the region of €500 million in 2017-2018. After prolonged legal and planning wrangles, the latest cost forecasts are in a range between €1.9 billion and €2.3 billion.
Such examples are hardly unique. Citing such costs and a political drive to push ahead with big infrastructure projects, the official said buying up houses or company lands to settle litigation was pragmatic.
A business leader who has frequent engagements with Government figures concurred. “At the end of the day, I think it’s a smart investment,” he said, adding that State agencies should be “extremely careful that they are not held to ransom” with settlement costs ballooning.
“If I was faced [with this] in a private business situation, I’d weigh one against the other. If, on one hand, it’s going to cost me €2.1 million and, on the other hand, it’s a problem that’s not going away and it could end up costing me €15 million, it’s an easy decision to make.”
For all that, another observer noted the risk that such deals could encourage potential litigants to initiate action in the hope that the State might pay upfront to settle. That assumes the prospective plaintiffs have money for their own lawyers – and defendant lawyers if they take the case and lose – and that their property stands right in the way of critical infrastructure.
The extent to which State bodies might settle remains unclear.
Uisce Éireann said it has never bought property to settle a judicial review. The water authority faces seven active cases, so would it consider buying property to settle such litigation? “Uisce Éireann is not in a position to comment on existing or apprehended legal proceedings,” it replied.
In the Dart+ West cases, Irish Rail has said the litigants would have been party “in the normal course of events” to a compulsory-purchase-order process.
When three Burke Brothers companies filed financial statements for 2025 in the Companies Office last week, they appeared to cast light on the settlement terms.
The accounts for Burke Brothers Son & Company, signed off in late September, show that the business received €5.28 million for “compensation in respect of anticipated future business interruption that will arise”.
This is because the business will be required to vacate its current location in 2028 “as a result of the sale of the premises from which the company currently operates”. As a result, the company faces substantial relocation costs.
Accounts for a related business known as Burke Capital show that it disposed of €3.5 million in freehold property and €2.1 million in buildings during 2025. Separate Land Registry documents show that Burke Capital transferred ownership of its land in December to State transport group CIÉ, which is Irish Rail’s parent.
On the face of it, Burke Brothers appears to have received some €10.88 million for business interruption, property and buildings when its case was withdrawn.
Burke Brothers had no comment for The Irish Times for this article and Irish Rail provided no information on deal terms.
“After the issuing of those proceedings and prior to the hearing dates scheduled in the High Court, settlement agreements were reached by CIÉ with both parties. These agreements are subject to confidentiality clauses,” Irish Rail said.
There is nothing on the public record in respect of Gowan Group. The business did not reply when contacted by phone and email.
The transactions involving Burke Brothers are the latest to come to light since Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) reached an agreement last December to end judicial review proceedings against the MetroLink underground rail project in Dublin.
TII, a State body, is buying the homes of Dartmouth Square residents near the city centre after they withdrew a High Court case against MetroLink. The purchase of four homes on the square has since closed, with TII paying between €2 million and €2.6 million for each.
After long delays, the Dartmouth Square deal was done to avert the risk that litigation against MetroLink could go on for years.
As part of a separate agreement to advance almost 1,000 new homes at the former Central Mental Hospital in Dundrum, the Land Development Agency spent €2.15 million in April buying a dormer bungalow in Goatstown from a housing objector.
The objector has withdrawn his High Court challenge, the second such case he had taken against the project at the former Central Mental Hospital.

title: Apple’s $5tn milestone comes with a hefty price tag
description: Tech giant has struggled to maintain landmark market valuation but does it matter?
content:
Apple keeps knocking on the door of a $5tn (€4.45tn) market valuation, but has struggled to make the milestone stick.
It first crossed the threshold on July 28th but only for a few hours, falling back below it by the closing bell. The same pattern played out on July 29th, and again on September 22nd and 28th.
Apple hit the valuation twice more on October 12th and 13th, only to close below it on both occasions. Six trading sessions, six failed breakouts, before Apple finally managed to close above $5tn on Wednesday.
Of course, given shares more than doubled since April 2025’s tariff shock and are up over 25 per cent in 2026, the distinction between $4.99tn and $5tn is unlikely to be keeping shareholders awake at night.
Still, investors could be forgiven for being hesitant. There’s nothing magical about crossing a trillion-dollar threshold – indeed, with the S&P 500 now containing 12 trillion-dollar companies, it’s increasingly routine – but Apple is expensive.
The company now trades at almost 11 times sales, notes Creative Planning strategist Charlie Bilello, the highest level in Apple’s history. Apple’s price-sales ratio is more than double where it was in 2022, and nearly 50 per cent higher than its five-year average.
Other valuation metrics tell a similar story. Apple trades on 36 times estimated earnings, well above its five-year average of 27.
Apple is pricey not only relative to its own history but to all but one of its magnificent seven peers ( Tesla , of course). It is a pronounced premium compared with Microsoft , which trades on 27 times estimated earnings, as well as to Amazon (24), Alphabet (22), Meta (22), and Nvidia (14). The next test comes on November 2nd, when Apple reports earnings.
Bulls will hope the shares can build on the $5tn milestone, but Apple’s bulging valuation leaves little room for disappointment.

title: Lena Dunham’s Girls will be glorious again as long as it sticks to this one principle
description: The HBO show’s revival offers an intriguing chance to move on from the woeful way it ended in 2017
content:
G irls is coming back and, according to Variety, this is a “shocker”. I speak fluent journalese: “shocker” is code for “guys, an exclusive would have been nice”.
The return of Lena Dunham’s show for a five-episode series on HBO in 2027, a decade after its grim finale, isn’t all that surprising. The skies above the entertainment industry are crowded with boomerangs. Everything comes back around eventually, even that show from your youth that you steadily drifted away from, have some residual affection for but now firmly associate with a different time in your life.
It could be a coincidence that HBO, also the outlet behind the original 2012-17 run, was only recently a pawn in the Hollywood megatransaction that saw Paramount Skydance complete a $110 billion (€98 billion) takeover of HBO’s previous parent, Warner Bros Discovery.
But these deals don’t happen without generating a whole new suite of executives who enjoy conjuring up targets for other executives, who are then incentivised to make as many noisy commissions as they can.
Girls is one such noisy commission. Some of us have only just stopped rolling our eyes at the takes it spawned in 2012 when, in its pilot episode, Hannah, the aspiring writer played by Dunham, suggested to her sceptical parents that she might be “the voice of my generation”, or at least “a voice of a generation”.
Dunham conceived Hannah as the walking manifestation of comic delusion. In this scene she’s trying to get her parents to reverse their decision to financially cut her off. She will say anything.
None of that humour survived the discourse that conflated Hannah with Dunham herself before tediously ruling it impossible for the creator of Girls to speak for all millennials – something she never claimed to do.
Famesick , Dunham’s 2025 memoir, did its bit to bring Girls back into the conversation, largely by detailing her negative experience of working with Adam Driver , who played her on-off boyfriend, and her professional break-up with her fellow showrunner, Jenni Konner.
Neither will be involved in the revival. But the central quartet of friends – Hannah, Marnie (Allison Williams), Jessa (Jemima Kirke) and Shoshanna/Shosh (Zosia Mamet) – will return, as will Hannah’s gay friend Elijah (Andrew Rannells), now promoted to Wee English Fella status as the token male in the main line-up.
With all of these cast members alive and available, a comeback was always more likely than not.
[ Patrick Freyne’s top TV shows of 2026: Lola Petticrew, a bearded grump and Siobhán McSweeney’s sneaky Irish Opens in new window ]
This is where I declare my indifference on the basis that I’m not a millennial. Girls is not that show from my youth. The six years it was on air did not overlap with any formative period in my life, and my memories of it have no temporal connection to similar experiences of my own.
I admired much of the series and am intrigued by this revival, but watching the travails of Hannah, Marnie, Jessa (my favourite) and Shosh didn’t have the potency for me that it seems to have done for a younger cohort: for millennial women, Girls wasn’t just a funny diversion; it was a mirror in which they could see an imperfect yet compelling reflection of their own desires, ambitions and frustrations.
This week’s news has therefore triggered a spectrum of reactions, from deep investment to nervous curiosity to the conviction that no good can come of it. Congratulations, you’re old now. Everything is bittersweet. The one consolation might well be that the legacy of Girls was already complicated by the dispiriting way in which it ground to a halt.
The penultimate episode was decent, if downbeat, with a pregnant Hannah concluding that New York City has brought her nothing but misery and Shosh announcing that she’s had enough of her self-absorbed friends. There was a sense of lives moving on in a way that was both realistic and dramatically satisfying.
The final episode, by contrast, was lifeless and moribund. Set in the social purgatory of upstate New York, its final minutes firmly equated Hannah’s newfound maturity with her motherhood, which is about as patriarchal a trope as you can get.
[ It’s hard not to have sympathy for Lena Dunham. But there’s a darker side to surrogacy Opens in new window ]
Viewers who made it through six seasons of messy, exciting, tumultuous girlhood were rewarded with a conclusion that linked the emotional capacity to be a selfless mother with successful breastfeeding. The revival, if nothing else, is a chance to obliterate that trite betrayal of an ending.
Some media narratives never die: only last year, while on the red carpet, Dunham had to explain all over again that “the voice of my generation” thing was a scripted joke. Hannah was just being awful, as she almost always was.
Indeed, the freedom for Hannah, Marnie, Jessa and Shoshanna to be awful was, and should remain, the glorious thing about Girls. They can be awful friends, mothers, daughters, wives and girlfriends, exes, colleagues, citizens, anything.
As long as they have the opportunity to be terrible human beings again, this show should be fine.

title: The life-changing work of Alice Maher, an artist to her bones
description: The Irish artist has spent decades making the everyday uncanny. With her work on show at the Venice Biennale, she talks about myth, misogyny and the power of art
content:
A necklace of tongues and another of hearts, a tower of hair and a house of thorns: if you wondered how far, or how close, the uncanny might be from the everyday, just take a look at the work of Alice Maher.
Always surprising, and often mesmerising, it can confound those who think of art as something to be tamed within a frame. It is also currently on show at the world’s biggest stage for art, the Venice Biennale.
It’s difficult to think of anything tame about Maher, who at 70 continues to conjure wonders from her wild imagination. Yet, on closer inspection, those wonders are grounded in something that might be rather real after all.
Take an object as normal as a thorn, a twist of hair, or a tongue. We all have the latter pair, yet, presented with them in the abstract, we can be torn between being fascinated and repelled. Perhaps that push and pull goes to show how far from home we are with the nature of our bodies.
“I don’t think I knew I always wanted to be an artist,” Maher says. “But it was always there, in my person, as a child.”
Coming from a family of five, she recalls not joining in the games. “I was always a little bit separate.” That, she says, is the artist’s stance: separate from the action, but noticing.
She took European studies at college, going to art classes in the evenings. Then, armed with what she describes as a “portfolio of really bad drawings”, she called into the Crawford art college in Cork (which is now part of Munster Technological University).
Barry Maloney took a look and asked if she could start in two weeks.
“The minute I got there, this was exactly where I wanted to be.”
Maher works in parallel on a number of projects until one comes to the fore, and to fruition. But, tongues and hearts notwithstanding, her work isn’t about the ick.
In The Sybils, her series of large charcoal drawings installed at Venice (and the subject of a limited-edition book with poetry by Paula Meehan), female figures climb, carry, recline on and perch atop their Rapunzel-like locks of hair.
The form for all is Maher herself. “I don’t look at models,” she says. “I use myself. If I want to make an image of a figure, a human being, I get into that position and stay in it until I understand what it feels like to be in that position.
“Where is the discomfort, where is the weight? My partner” – her husband, and fellow artist, Dermot Seymour – “takes photos of me, very simply with an iPad or something.”
Maher’s work gets to grips with symbolism: her tower of hair, Keep, from the early 1990s, is part castle, part cage. The hair came from the north and south of Ireland, during an intense year of the Troubles. The hair, stored in bags, is now laid out on her studio floor after curator Jelena Sofronijevic asked about exhibiting it.
“She’s doing a show about hope and hate. She read it in a geopolitical way. It gave me the idea to relook. As one gets older, you start to reassess. How does a work from 1992 be relevant in 2026? That has become really interesting.”
The readings may change over time, but a constant is the way Maher’s work allow us under the skin, and under the veneer of what we like to describe as civilised.
That said, is there very much that is civilised about our civilisation today? In this, her Sibyls, Cassandra and other mythic figures are there not to draw our attention to easily decipherable tales but to remind us that deeper forces are at play underpinning the nature of human nature.
As Becoming, the title of Maher’s mid-career retrospective at the Irish Museum of Modern Art (Imma) in 2012, showed, her work is more closely connected to how images and things can be transmuted to make gateways for understanding.
Look closely and you might catch a revelation or two, an awareness of the beat of your blood, as the senses of the subconscious, and possible connections to half-remembered other lives, well up.
Maybe that’s what civilisation is designed deliberately to dull. Most of us tend to mute the possibilities of uncomfortable epiphanies with a glass of wine or a spot of scrolling.
Yet we are closer to those gateways than one might think. It’s there in literature, particularly in WB Yeats, and it positively dances in Eoghan Quinn’s brilliant play Visions, currently on the Peacock stage of the Abbey Theatre.
The land is steeped in it too. Once, driving Maher back to Dublin after I visited her then-new studio in rural Co Mayo, she suggested we stop at Tulsk. “The gateway to the underworld is just over there, a few fields away,” she said. But Oweynagat Cave wasn’t open that day, so we got some coffee and got back on the road.
That was almost 20 years ago. Today, behind her in the Mayo studio is a card – maybe it’s a beer mat – saying “Later Is Now”. There are boxes and folders, jars and bottles. A can of spray paint, rolls of paper.
A fabulous fake fur coat is hanging from a rail, and a silver jacket. She slips into the coat. It is a wonder. “You tend to stick to jeans in the country,” she says, possibly ruefully.
Pinned to the bottom of a shelf is a cut-out, either a dancing figure or a stylised sheela-na-gig. Somewhere will be a box of dead bees, and another of bones.
The bees are for occasional repairs to her Bee Dress. Made in 1994, the child’s dress, covered with dead bees, is now in the collection of the Ulster Museum. A companion piece, Berry Dress, made that same year, is owned by Imma.
Modelled on Irish-dancing dresses, both of them layer ideas of construction of identity, femininity, armour, pain and, again, that collision of myth with the substance of the everyday.
Although Maher says she had always been separate from the action, just over a decade ago she and a group of artist colleagues were right in the thick of it, helping to change Irish society with the Artists’ Campaign to Repeal the Eighth Amendment. She set it up in 2015 with Cecily Brennan, Eithne Jordan and Paula Meehan.
“It was after an Aosdána meeting,” Maher says. “Cecily came to Paula, me and Eithne and said, ‘Do we want to actually do something about this?’ and we just all immediately said yes.” The group called a press conference at Buswells Hotel, opposite Leinster House, and things took off.
Artists began to meet in Maher’s studio, sewing banners for the Repeal marches.
“We were working out the imagery and talking. And I discovered that talking through things as you work is a way of making that clarifies ideas. It was a new way of working for me. A lot of people were just waiting for this to happen. It was very important in my life,” Maher says. “We were seeing the power of art and culture, and the power of collaboration.”
The banners made by the campaign were deliberately bright and joyful, while also being intensely powerful. They were exhibited in 2016 at EVA International, which was curated by the late Koyo Kouoh, who would go on to invite Maher to participate in this year’s Venice Biennale. The banners have since been acquired by the National Museum of Ireland.
Also shown at EVA, and now at Venice, is an installation of half-submerged heads, Les Filles d’Ouranos. For someone who is utterly serious about her art, Maher is also very funny, with an eye to the self-deprecating, in the sense of puncturing any possible grandiosity rather than actually putting herself down.
It’s a way of being that many of us would love to master. She describes a visit by the team who had taken on the challenge of completing Kouoh’s vision after the curator died mid-project.
Barbara Dawson, the director of the Hugh Lane Gallery, had driven them to Mayo; on their way back to the car, studio visit complete, one had chanced to see a row of orange heads, now holding back the escaping earth and foliage from Seymour’s vegetable garden. They wanted them immediately. “They had weeds coming out of their noses and snails living in them,” Maher says happily.
She remade them for Venice. Also at Venice is The Map, which, made with her fellow artist Rachel Fallon and commissioned by Rua Red in Tallaght, is based on a retelling of the life and legacy of Mary Magdalene.
So, from myth to Mary Magdalene and through to the social-justice campaigns of recent history, what has changed for women?
“Everything has changed and nothing has changed,” Maher says. “Everything has changed in that the silence and shame that was wielded over us like an axe has been smashed to pieces by feminism and grassroots movements. Yet nothing has changed in that a deep-rooted ancient misogyny still seeps into our lives.”
She describes the institutional imbalances that persist in the art world, and across society, and are so enmeshed that it can be hard to see them or, once seen, to unravel them. “The stories and myths I work with, like that of Cassandra, are very often narratives of silencing and entrapment, intervention and transformation,” Maher says.
Thinking of that transformation, I ask what she’s working on next. What might be in one of those boxes neatly packed and stacked.
“My brother, Paddy, sent me a box of bones,” she says. “He lives in Killarney, and they have some sea eagles there. I’m looking at birds, and it was serendipitous that he sent them. That’s the way it works for me. I thought, ‘Bones that eagles stripped – they might be interesting.’”
Indeed they might. Shortly after our conversation, having been thinking about Maher’s compelling self-possession, I have a follow-up question. “I’m wondering at what point you knew who you were,” I say via email. “Or is that a work in progress, like so many things?”
A day later she emails in reply: “You asked when did you know you were an artist?”
I don’t correct the question. Maher is an artist to her bones. It’s impossible to imagine her, in this life at least, being anything else.
The 61st Venice Biennale , which also included works by Rachel Fallon, Alan Phelan, Mark Francis and Isabel Nolan, runs until Sunday, November 22nd. Alice Maher ’s Les Filles d’Ouranos will be installed on the lake at the National Museum of Ireland ’s Turlough Park branch in May 2027, where they will remain for a year. Alice Maher’s book The Sybils, with new poetry by Paula Meehan, costs €25 from kevinkavanagh.ie

title: Mark Moriarty: Let them eat the most simple cakes imaginable
description: No need for loads of equipment or complicated effort here, just basic and gorgeous baking
content:
T his week, I’m turning my attention to the workhorse of the kitchen, the loaf tin. Nothing fancy, no faffy cheffy finishes, and no hard-to-handle ingredients. These recipes are about a tin, a bowl and the promise that, after 40 minutes, the kitchen will smell considerably better than it did when you started.
These two recipes are very different in flavour, but follow the same structure and technique. The carrot cake is indulgent and leads us firmly in the direction of autumn, and dare I say Christmas. Orange, nutmeg, cinnamon, dates and walnuts bring plenty of warmth and comfort at exactly the point in the year when we need it most. The chocolate swirl cake, meanwhile, is simple and to the point – if you have kids, best of luck in trying to get this to last more than a day.
The carrot cake will make you question yourself when you mix it together, and it starts to resemble a pancake batter as opposed to a cake mix – do not fear, this is exactly what you want. Coconut oil gives it a lovely richness, while the grated carrot brings moisture and sweetness and the walnuts and dates add little pockets of texture. But the clever part comes after baking.
Once the cake is out of the oven, it gets soaked in a simple syrup made with orange juice and brown sugar. This is the key step that turns it from a good bake into a great bake. Lemon cream-cheese icing is designed to cut through the sweetness. Finished with walnuts, orange zest and the delicate green carrot tops, it wouldn’t look out of place in a Parisian patisserie.
The swirl cake is also very simple to put together – a basic cake mix is made before being split into two. Half the mix gets hit with cocoa powder to darken the colour; this is then mixed lightly with the plain batter and swirled together in the tin to create the signature design when you cut through it. Maybe not Parisian patisserie, but potentially set for a modern art museum. Either way, it’s delicious.
Both recipes are designed to be brought together in minutes, resulting in something that looks and tastes like it took hours. Perfect for a cup of tea or a dinner party finish, the loaf tin is a piece of equipment that will always clear the stage for you to be the star.
Tip of the week: Soaking a loaf tin carrot cake in a simple syrup after baking will hugely elevate the flavour.

title: Maverick Languedoc wines: ‘The French AOC rules don’t suit us’
description: John Wilson: Jean-Claude Mas is a fourth-generation grower but the first in his family to make wine
content:
T he Languedoc, a large area covering much of the south of France , seems to inspire entrepreneurs. I have featured the wines of Gérard Bertrand and Laurent Miquel here before. Both are sons of vignerons who ignored the rules and tradition to produce good inexpensive wines that were a little bit different. Today we look at the wines of Jean-Claude Mas, another maverick producer who has been enormously successful on the export market.
“The French AOC rules don’t suit us in the Languedoc,” Mas tells me. “They were made to suit Bordeaux and Burgundy.” So, most of his wines are varietal and not all are native to the Languedoc. He produces a riesling, rarely seen in France outside Alsace.
“Argentina is my reference for malbec ,” he says. His ripe rounded wine is aged in American oak barrels instead of the usual French. “They are good for Mediterranean wines,” he says.
Mas is a fourth-generation grower, but the first to actually make wine; his predecessors sold grapes to the co-op. His father gave him 35 hectares of vines in 1987 and, having studied business and worked in various sales positions unrelated to wine, he returned home to set up Domaines Paul Mas in 1999. Readers may remember a wine called Arrogant Frog, one of his first export successes.
The business has grown exponentially. He now owns 14 estates in the Languedoc as well as one in the Rhône Valley, and farms 1,000 hectares of vines. He sells 22 million bottles to more than 70 markets around the world. He describes himself as making old world wines using new world attitudes. “I love things that give you real emotions, and wine does that,” he says.
Dunnes Stores has recently listed some wines from Jean-Claude Mas, including a range of varietal wines. Molloys Liquor Stores also has a long-term relationship with the business and imports a number of different wines.
Broad, rounded pear fruits with intense lime zest, and a good dry finish. Try it with lighter pork and chicken dishes or maybe scallops or crab.
Ripe and rounded with smooth dark fruits and a touch of vanilla. Good with red meats or mushroom dishes.
Rich and textured with tropical fruits and harmonious buttery notes. Try it with salmon or creamy chicken dishes.
Rugged and full-bodied with layers of ripe dark fruits, a touch of vanilla and a good firm finish. Good with substantial red meat dishes. Would be great with cassoulet or an autumnal bean stew.

title: Behind the scenes at Blas: ‘A last hurrah before winter’
description: Blas is when Dingle welcomes Ireland’s food producers as they meet and celebrate with their peers
content:
There is a point on the Wednesday evening before Blas na hÉireann when Gráinne Kavanagh notices Dingle beginning to change, as finalists and buyers start arriving and familiar faces appear at the door of The Coach House, the Irish craft and design shop she has run for more than a decade.
“Blas brings a different dynamic to Dingle,” she says. “This arrival is for their harvest festival of sorts. The producers have toiled hard all year to bring their products to market, many have developed new products, others have expanded on previous ranges and this is their chance to meet and celebrate with their peers.”
By Thursday, producers are calling in to tell Kavanagh what they hope the weekend might bring, with some returning later with good news to share. “It’s lovely to see them return over the weekend with big smiles after their wins or products being picked up by buyers,” she says.
For businesses around Dingle, Blas also brings a welcome lift just as the pace would normally be beginning to ease. Finn Mac Donnell, the fourth generation of his family to run Dick Mack’s pub, where he has been for almost 19 years, says the difference is considerable.
“If you didn’t have anything on, it would be a dud weekend,” he says, explaining that the pub might have four people working on an ordinary Friday at that time of year, compared with around 10 or 11 for Blas. “It’d be in our top four or five of the year, definitely.”
Being opposite the Blas marquee has made Dick Mack’s something of an unofficial headquarters, although Mac Donnell has a practical explanation for its popularity.
“They don’t have far to walk to get here, and they don’t have far to roll back out if they need to,” he laughs. “And we’ll have the fire on for them if we do have a cold wintry day.”
Staffing the weekend involves persuading some of the pub’s part-time crew, many now back at college, to return to work when they might prefer to be enjoying it themselves. The producers, meanwhile, have reached the end of a long year and are ready to celebrate.
“They’re meeting like-minded people,” says Mac Donnell. “They’re able to talk work and then, by nine o’clock at night, they forget about work and enjoy a weekend away from work and home.”
For Róisín Uí Lúing, who runs Siopa Uí Lúing in Ventry, Blas offers something else. Her involvement began with blind-tasting judging and later included a panel discussion at BackYard, the programme of talks and events that runs alongside the awards, while the sight of the Blas village being built now signals that the weekend is almost here.
“Living in west Kerry means we are geographically far from lots of places around the country, so the Blas weekend is an amazing time to meet our producers and touch base,” she says.
Some are people whose produce Uí Lúing has stocked for years without meeting them in person, while Blas has also led to tasty new finds for the shop’s shelves. “We have definitely discovered new products at Blas over the years and we are always seeking to work with new Irish producers.”
Those connections are not confined to organised events. “Whether you’re in the Blas tent or grabbing a coffee in Bean across the way, you’ll be surrounded by people from various aspects of the food and drink industry.”
Justin Burgess co-owns Bean in Dingle with his brother Luke; the pair also run Dingle Coffee Roasters just outside the town. Having the main Blas area opposite the cafe means Burgess gets a particularly good view of proceedings, including one memorable moment last year when the cafe was full of producers and one received a call for a live radio interview, just as Neven Maguire walked in for a coffee and congratulated them on air.
Blas also took Burgess beyond the coffee shop last year, with two podcast interviews and an appearance on Newstalk, although the latter required a little Dutch courage. “I was so nervous I had to have a quick shot of whiskey at 12 o’clock,” he admits.
When so many people from the food and drink industry arrive, Burgess says local businesses want to show what Dingle can do, helped by the close-knit nature of the town.
“Most of the businesses in Dingle are run by families,” he says. “Everybody knows each other.”
Some producers also use the weekend to get ahead on their Christmas shopping before their own busy festive season begins.
Kavanagh describes the economic benefit to Dingle as “huge”, spreading well beyond accommodation and food, while Uí Lúing believes the timing matters too.
“It’s a lovely boost when everyone in the hospitality industry is ready for the last hurrah before winter kicks in,” she says.
Mac Donnell is quick to point to the people behind the scenes too.
“The volunteers are brilliant in Dingle, people that volunteer their time to help on any given big weekend like that. They really are important.”
For Kavanagh, perhaps the best measure of what Blas has become is the familiarity of those annual returns, when producers walk back through the door and simply pick up where they left off.
“We catch up on both how business has been and, more importantly, how their families have been since we met.”

title: Profits jump more than 25% for Shannon Foynes port firm on record tonnage
description: Work continuing on development of deepwater port in addition to enhanced road and rail links, says chief executive
content:
Pretax profits have risen more than 25 per cent for the company that operates the Shannon Foynes seaport, reaching just over €5 million last year, recently filed company accounts show.
The Shannon Foynes Port Company, which operates the State’s second largest seaport (only behind its Dublin equivalent), also saw turnover increase more than 12 per cent in the financial year to end December 2025.
The company generated €5.06 million in pretax profits during the year – a 26.14 per cent increase from the €4.01 million it accumulated throughout the previous year, the filing shows. Its 2025 turnover was €17.63 million, up from 2024’s €15.73 million.
The company pointed to a 2.2 per cent increase in “throughput”, or the volume of cargo and passengers that pass through a seaport, to 9.35 million tonnes last year. Foynes Port “recorded its highest-ever annual tonnage, increasing 10.8 per cent year on year”, the company said in a statement.
It credited “historic highs” in revenue and operating profit for its “landmark financial performance” in 2025. “The result was driven by robust performance across the port’s operations,” it said.
Pat Keating, the port’s chief executive, added: “These results demonstrate the value of our focus on growing revenues, managing costs and making the most of the capacity and assets at our Foynes and Limerick terminals.
“Record activity at Foynes, in particular, underlines the port’s growing role in supporting industry, trade and supply chains across the region and nationally.
“We are continuing to advance the priorities set out in our ‘Vision 2041’ master plan, including the development of Foynes Island Deepwater Port and the delivery of enhanced road and rail connectivity.”
The company added its short-term strategic plan until 2030 “identifies €210 million in planned capital expenditure to develop port facilities and support long-term demand”.
It looks forward to the reinstatement of 40km of railway between Limerick and Foynes in early 2027, which Keating says “will assist with Ireland’s Climate Action Plan for transport to meet its net zero climate obligations”.
Operational costs within the company for the 2025 financial year amounted to €8.05 million, while €3.86 million was marked down to “administrative expenses” in the account filings. The business held €86.12 million worth of tangible assets and €10.24 million in cash and bank balances – an 82.10 per cent increase from the €5.62 million it held the previous year, the filings show.
Michael Walsh, the company’s chairman, said it is “in a strong financial position to continue investing in infrastructure that will support Ireland’s future economic, logistics and energy needs”.
The company employed 53 full-time equivalent staff at year-end, an increase of four people from the previous year, and paid €3.46 million in salaries. A further €135,850 was spent on overtime pay and €276,869 in “performance-related payments”, according to the filings.
The accounts show €1.04 million was paid to “key management personnel” in the company – consisting of members of its board and senior management team – in salaries and employee benefits. €829,000 was paid in shareholder dividends from profits accumulated in the 2023 and 2024 financial years.
Keating received €117,500 in his chief executive role, which he has held since 2008. He did not receive a pay rise between 2024 and 2025.

title: Dublin DJ Jazzy: ‘Calvin Harris messaged me on Instagram to say he loved my song’
description: Naturally modest and down to earth, she is still coming to grips with her changed circumstances – from working in Tesco’s bakery section to touring with Calvin Harris
content:
“I just want to tell you all that my first single went to No 1 in Ireland today and I want to buy you all a drink.”
Announcing her good news in a pub, a Tricolour draped around her shoulders, Jazzy flashed an awkward grin, hugged her friends, and raised a glass to the camera for the recording broadcast on YouTube.
That was in 2023, when her song Giving Me made her the first Irish female singer to top the Irish chart in more than 14 years. House-y, hopeful and expansive, Giving Me was the earworm that clubbers loved, Calvin Harris praised, and radio stations from Spin to RTÉ Radio 1 played.
As she sits in a brocaded chair in a private room in Dublin’s Dylan hotel, Jazzy – born Yasmine Byrne – admits now that the pub round wasn’t as spontaneous as it might have seemed. “My team definitely gave me a little pinch to do it,” she laughs. “It’s not easy to stand up in a pub.”
Jazzy might look the part of an international superstar – today she’s wearing black denim shorts and a tight black top with simple jewellery and dark-framed glasses – but she’s naturally humble and down to earth, and still coming to grips with her changed circumstances.
From working in the bakery section in Tesco in 2021, Jazzy spent this summer touring and supporting Harris, with whom she also released the single Satisfy. She was nominated for a Brit Award in 2024 and 2025, and a MOBO Award in 2026. In 2025, she became the most popular female DJ on Spotify with 10 million monthly listeners. She did a BBC Radio 1 residency and debuted at Coachella festival in the US. Later this month, she will release her first album Peace & Patience, and play the 3Arena on October 24th, her biggest headlining venue to date.
When we meet she’s barely off the plane from Ibiza – she was there to DJ in Pacha nightclub, making her one of the few people on the lively Dublin to Ibiza flight “trying to go to work” rather than party their nut off. “More than likely, someone’s getting arrested when they’re getting off the flight, that’s how crazy they are. They’d be screaming and singing.”
She’ll be back on a plane at the end of the month for another US tour. “I feel the love when I go over. Playing there, people are coming up asking for old Jazzy tracks. But it’s a huge place, so we have to keep going back and keep going back.”
She’s not stressed about her hectic schedule – “In music if you put too much pressure on yourself, you’re not going to get what you’re supposed to be getting naturally out of it” – but she does have a case of impostor syndrome.
“I see all these things I’ve done and all these statistics about me, and then sometimes I’ll still be like, ‘You’re sh …’” She whispers a word.
I lean in. “Shy?” I suggest. She starts laughing. “Shite!” she whispers. “Sorry! No, I’m not over it [impostor syndrome]. It’s something that comes in waves. I think it’s because I’m honest as well. The humble side of me is struggling to be in the spotlight.”
Yasmine Byrne was raised by her single mother, Catherine, on a council estate in Crumlin, with her brother Ian and sister Tasha. Her father is black and her mother white – her father, she says, “was never in the picture”. Her mother noticed early on that her daughter was musical: Yasmine was bopping her head in time to music while in the buggy. “She had CDs on all the time and it was a complete mix,” Jazzy says of her mother. “She loved Joe Dolan. She loved Dolly Parton. She loved Creedence Clearwater Revival. And she loved clubland music.”
In third class, Yasmine was enrolled in a music programme that had started at St Agnes’ Primary School on Armagh Road, created by Joanna Crooks, former general manager of the National Youth Orchestra of Ireland, and Sr Bernadette Sweeney, then principal of the school. The initiative offered free music lessons and instruments for pupils. When Yasmine took up the violin, the pair soon noticed her abilities.
When I phone St Agnes’ Primary School to ask if they remember their former student, Sr Bernadette returns my call immediately. “Jazzy blew people away by her playing because she was so understated. She’s a beautiful violinist, deeply musical. She wasn’t all about herself, and when you’re not all about yourself, your soul speaks through the music. She started with nothing, no music, no nothing, and worked all the way up.
“All the children know Jazzy. She inspired so many here. I go into shops and people say, ‘Is Jazzy one of yours?’”
‘I realised that what I wanted to be was behind the decks. It’s part of my evolution’
Because Yasmine lived a little far from the school, frequently one of the teachers would pick her up, ferrying her back and forth. She was one of 20 in the class.
“We all had a square patch of carpet to stand on,” Jazzy recalls. “Your violin would be there and you’d pick it up and the violin teacher, Pauline, she’d come around the class and scout people who were holding the violin well or bowing nicely. If she thought you were doing well, she’d pull you aside and say, ‘Would you like to join the orchestra? You can come after school and then you can practise more.’ So that’s what happened. She asked me.”
At home, she would sing “to the four walls”. She loved Fugees and 1990s R&B. She’d try out her vocals covering Lauryn Hill’s Killing Me Softly. But she was hesitant about singing in public. When a teacher announced they were creating a choir, “I had to be pushed,” she says. “Physically. My friend said, ‘Go up, you have to audition.’ She pushed me to go up and sing and then I was singing ever since that.” She got more comfortable, singing solos, developing her sense of pitch and melody.
After taking her grade eight exams for violin, she planned to become a music teacher: she left education at 16 and was working in the school as an assistant violin teacher. But another genre of music was creeping into her life: house music. After nights out at Sin on Sycamore Street in Temple Bar, and dancing to DJ gigs headlined by Amine Edge & DANCE, a French house duo, she asked a friend of a friend if he might teach her to DJ. That friend, Ross Mooney, became her boyfriend, and then her fiance.
She started recording and releasing music with the hip-hop group Powerful Creative Minds. About the same time, Sr Bernadette went around the local shops and asked if they’d give Jazzy a job. “I remember going to one of the supermarkets and saying, ‘I would be delighted if you could give Jazzy a job to keep her going. She’s no Mickey Mouse, no ordinary girl coming for a job, she’s very talented.’ So they gave her the job.”
At Tesco, Jazzy was able to fit recording sessions in around work and help out financially at home. Then Mooney introduced her to Conor Bissett and Robbie Griffiths from Belters Only, and they wrote the song Make Me Feel Good together in the studio. “After I met the Belters boys, it all started to kick off,” she says.
When Belters Only released Make Me Feel Good featuring Jazzy’s vocals in late 2021, it went on to top the Irish singles chart in 2022 and became a hit in Britain. It now has 132 million streams on Spotify.
The song was a crunch point. It was now or never. She went home and told her mother Catherine that she was thinking of leaving work. “I sat down and said, ‘What do you think I should do? Will you help me out?’ She gave me the push. My ma was always really confident in me.”
It wasn’t an easy call. “After Tesco, there was a period where I was like, I’m not getting that many gigs. I did have to get another job in a pharmacy for a while.” After her record label Polydor found out, “they were really good”, she says. “I was only there for three weeks and they found out and stepped in and made sure that I had the funds to be able go and do sessions, and everything else I needed.”
When her first single Giving Me, hit the No 1 spot in the charts in 2023, “Calvin Harris messaged me on Instagram telling me how much he loved the song,” she says. “It started everything for me.”
Her debut album may seem like it’s been a long time coming – the word Patience isn’t in the title for nothing – but getting it right is important to her.
[ Irish rapper Reggie: ‘Dundalk’s on top of the world right now. The centre of the universe’ Opens in new window ]
“I don’t want to be looking back and saying, ‘I wish I’d changed that.’ Some of the tracks were started two years ago so it’s been quite a journey. I like being in the studio as much as I can. I’m mostly in a studio in London with Mark Ralph, who produces all my vocals.” Musically the record is a throwback, a closer cousin of Robin S’s Show Me Love than Dua Lipa. “I like that,” she says. “I don’t want to fit in with everything else.”
She knew early on in the making of the record that she wanted to shout out to her community in Crumlin who had supported her. “I wanted to involve them,” she says. But it took her a while to figure out how to bring them on to the record in a way that made sense musically.
Eventually she asked her family and friends to come to a pub, The Stoneboat on Sundrive Road in Kimmage, to talk on the microphone and be filmed. “We had the top room, a little function room,” she says. “When you’re not used to it, a camera can be intimidating, or a microphone. We wanted it to feel as natural and relaxed as possible.” Her friends did an interview together. “And the lads that I used to be in a band with.”
The result is one of the most joyful moments on the album – a spoken word-led introduction of about a minute long that gathers together affectionate sentiments from her friends, her family, even her six-year-old niece Savannah. “To hear your own child on the radio and all the stations are playing her songs,” her mother says. “She’s auntie,” says Savannah. “She makes good music for the world.”
Reggie , the Nigeria-born, Dundalk-raised rapper who had a career-changing moment in 2025 when producer Fred Again remixed his song Talk of the Town, also guests on the song Elevate. “He’s popping off at the moment,” Jazzy says. “I reached out because he’s smashing it. I knew I wanted to have a rap verse on the song and it was just trying to find the right one. To have another Irish artist was great. I had done a few different ones with a couple of rappers from the UK, but Reggie’s was the standout.”
Soulful, uplifting and as easy to vacuum around the house to as to dance to in a club, Peace & Patience is a record that doubles as an endorphin boost. Her fans often tell Jazzy that her music has helped them through hard times. “I’m quite a happy person so I think when I go into the studio, that’s what comes out,” she says. “I’m happy naturally. Ma always taught us to be kind growing up. I think that is just put into me.”
She has experienced racism as she has become more successful, but she tries not to react to it.
“If I’m being highlighted as a certain thing, and the statistic has the word ‘Irish’ in it, sometimes that will pee off the racist people,” she says. “I love chatting to people that like my music, taking pictures, I’d do it all day. But there is the other side to social media. Nasty comments. I’ve figured out not to always go into the comment section. Friends see things and they’d be jumping in to defend me. Some people would be online, pointing out that I’m mixed race. But I choose not to engage.”
Her circle outside of music is small. When we meet she’s about to celebrate her 30th birthday, but she has no intention of doing much beyond a casual night out. “It’s just been so chaotic that I want to have a chill one,” she says. The same is true of her wedding plans. “I don’t think I’m going to have a big wedding. I wouldn’t have the numbers.”
[ Jason Moran: ‘I have a lot of gratitude for Cork Jazz Festival. And I still have that wonderful crystal vase’ Opens in new window ]
She was surprised the day Mooney – who is also her tour manager – proposed, on a trip to Nara Park in Japan last December. But she did know it was coming – the couple have been together eight years and he had given her a promise ring the year before. “I’d be lost without him,” she says. “He lifts me up.”
The pair try hard to give back to their community. Last Christmas, Jazzy popped up on The Late Late Show to surprise a superfan called Dory, aged eight from Tallaght, who had shared a story about Jazzy driving past her car. Jazzy and Mooney also turned up to watch the children of Francis Street School perform their Christmas play two years ago. “Ross used to go there, so one of the teachers texted and said, ‘Is there any chance Jazzy would be around?’” she says. “I was like, ‘Yeah, go on.’ The children dressed up as us. It was really funny.”
The couple have bought a house on the northside, not too far from her mother’s house, where Jazzy’s sister Tasha and her niece also live. “We got the house a little while ago, so we’re trying to finish that, and then we’ll move on to wedding plans,” she says. Is it a doer-upper? “There’s not much to be done at all,” she says. “Thank God, because we wouldn’t be able for a fixer-upper. It’s going slowly because we’re on the road so much, but we’re hoping at Christmas time to put more time into it. It’s great to even have the house bought.”
Touring is the focus for now – and she has learned ways to cut down on some of the more stressful elements. When she started out, she would sing live. Now she focuses solely on DJing. “After trying the whole performance – singing, DJing, and dancers – a couple of summers ago, I realised that what I wanted to be was behind the decks,” she says. “It’s part of my evolution.” It makes sense for an artist who seems shyer than your average pop star. If she’s lying awake worrying about something now, “It’d probably be missing my alarm clock,” she laughs. “If I’m going to sleep late and I have to be up early I probably just won’t go to sleep.”
The travel can be “hard and tiring”, particularly on those Dublin to Ibiza flights. But Jazzy rolls with it. She’s grateful. “It’s a champagne problem,” she says, with a smile.
Jazzy’s debut album Peace & Patience is out on October 23rd. She will play Dublin’s 3Arena on October 24th.

title: Best in Blas 2026: This year’s top three Irish Food Awards champions
description: The 2026 Blas na hÉireann champions paint a clear picture of what Irish food is: rooted in place and created with the best ingredients by people with the confidence to be themselves
content:
For a small business, a Blas award can open doors. It gives a producer more credibility when approaching retailers, reassures their customers of quality, and creates a moment to pause after a demanding year. Attending the ceremony in Dingle is also an opportunity to meet the people behind Ireland’s food industry: producers, buyers, media, consultants and mentors, who collectively make up Ireland’s food family.
This year’s headline honours went to three producers who embody the spirit of Irish food: Arán Bakery in Kilkenny, named Supreme Champion; Second Street Bakeshop in Cork, crowned Best Artisan Producer; Graham Herterich, beloved baker and advocate, named Producers’ Champion.
When Arán Bakery’s name was called as Supreme Champion 2026, the awards ceremony tent erupted. It was a historic moment: Arán is the first producer ever to win the top Blas title twice, having previously taken the Supreme Champion accolade in 2022.
For co-owners Bart Pawlukojć and his wife Nicole Server-Pawlukojć, the award is both validation and vindication. In conversation after the ceremony, Pawlukojć reflected on what it means to be recognised again at the highest level. “In 2022, winning the Supreme Champion changed everything for us. Suddenly people outside Kilkenny knew our bread,” he said.
“To win again, four years later, is insane. It means everything to us. And it feels like proof that we’ve kept our standards where they need to be.”
“I’ll be honest with you, we’re both immigrants; Nicole is Filipino and I’m Polish. And it’s the immigrant syndrome that we always need to prove ourselves. We always think that we need to prove and we always need to push harder. I know a lot of immigrants that have restaurants and that’s what they do. We just compete. Every year we try to go in with something. Even if it’s tiring, even if it’s difficult, we try to do something.”
Arán’s journey began on Barrack Street with a simple mission: stone‑baked sourdough made with few ingredients, fermented slowly and sold daily from a small artisan bakery. Over the years, the team has added so much to that foundation, by expanding and innovating, from seasonal brunch menus in the cafe to private evening dining, while keeping bread at the centre. Blas awards have been a regular occurrence over the years since they first entered, tallying up to almost 30 awards on their shelves, and even with 19 products as finalists in categories this year, it’s safe to say the Supreme title carries particular weight.
“Bread is humble by nature,” says Pawlukojć. “It doesn’t shout. So when a panel of tasters, year after year, keeps coming back to your loaves, it tells you you’re doing something right.”
Carrigaline confectionery business Second Street Bakeshop, founded by Claire Keane, has quietly built a reputation as having award-winning products with bold flavours and meticulous texture. Known for its American‑style toffee brittles reimagined with Irish ingredients – think Cork butter and Achill Island sea salt – the brand has become a favourite to many.
Second Street has collected multiple Blas awards in recent years, including a gold for its dairy‑free mint chocolate brittle, but the Artisan Producer title marks a new chapter.
Recalling winning the award, Keane says: “The first time I went to Blas and won, I didn’t really understand the full extent of it because I was a little bit shell-shocked. But then I got to know people in the industry and the community and they’re just a lovely bunch of women. I got to do mentorship afterwards also.
“It’s really a stepping stone into building out your community in the food industry and knowing who everyone is- media, press, banking, social media, consultants. It’s one good snapshot of getting to know everyone. And then the other part of it was it gave us validation. You could go to the retailers and say, look, we won gold for this product. You suddenly have street cred; you have clout behind you. So that was, that’s really what it gave to us.”
The awards have also created a community for Keane. She has built friendships with fellow chocolatiers and consultants, and has taken part in a women’s business retreat. At other food events, including the National Ploughing Championships, she now encounters people she first met in Dingle.
“Dingle is a celebration,” she says. “It’s a moment in time to stop, check yourself and celebrate, win or lose. But it’s extra nice to win.”
The Blas Producers’ Champion is decided slightly differently to the other awards in that the winner is specifically chosen by the producers themselves. Each year, producers within the Blas network are asked to fill out a survey to select a person, or people, who advocates for Irish food and drink throughout the year, promoting it through their work and social media channels, and who is a true champion of Irish produce, representing it and helping to elevate it in any way they can.
Former Producers’ Champions include last year’s trio of winners: Santina Kennedy, Anthony O’Toole and Caroline Hennessy; and previously, food writer Kate Ryan, chefs Darina Allen, Rory O’Connell, Conor Spacey, and Neven Maguire, and John and Sally McKenna of McKenna’s Guides.
For 2026, Graham Herterich has been honoured as Producers’ Champion for his dedication to everything Irish, independent and sustainable. This is a special milestone as Herterich is the first actual food producer from within the Blas community to hold the title.
He is an award-winning baker, chef and author of two cookbooks: Bake and Cook. He and his husband Daithí own and run their business which comprises of a bakery, The Bakery shop in Rialto, Dublin 8, a local beacon for freshly baked goods, artisanal Irish produce and baking miscellany, and Ernie’s @ Shackleton Experience, Athy, a gorgeous cafe located in the museum.
Years of visible advocacy is one of the main reasons Herterich was honoured as this year’s Producers’ Champion, from stocking suppliers in his cafe and bakery to his “A-Z of Irish producers” on social media. He is also a massive fan of collaborations and is constantly finding creative, and delicious, ways to work with other producers for his bakes and menus.
“I’m genuinely overwhelmed,” he says. “This award belongs as much to the producers I talk about every week as it does to me. If anything, it shows how hungry people are for stories about where their food comes from and who makes it.
“I was told there’d been loads of people that had suggested me this year and I came out on top. I couldn’t believe it.”
His reasoning to support other Irish businesses is so practical. “Why wouldn’t I support an Irish producer when I am an Irish producer? Who will support me except me? It’s kind of a circular economy thing really.”
Asked which new producers to keep an eye out for, Herterich suggests Lushmallows luxury marshmallows by Arlene Hopkins. “She’s amazing. Her flavours are so punchy. Her packaging is gorgeous. I think her timing is spot on for the market and it’s a really good-quality product.”

title: The little sticker that can. Why a win at Blas is a recipe for food business success
description: Being able to put a coveted Blas sticker on a food item is a game changer for producers
content:
Winning three successive Gold Awards at Blas na hÉireann proved transformational for Cass and Nick McCarthy of Lúnasa Farm.
The couple is that rarest of things in Ireland: first generation farmers. They established their regenerative organic farm and whole animal butchery in Co Clare, in 2022.
Today their heritage-breed pigs and pasture-fed cattle are raised on their farm, near Quin, before being butchered and transformed into premium cuts in their Clarecastle butcher shop.
“We’re a whole animal butcher, properly nose to tail, and produce 100 per cent grass-fed and finished beef and pasture raised pork,” says Cass.
“We don’t use any food additives. Our products are not ultra-processed products. We just use real ingredients. You won’t find preservatives, E numbers or colours.”
The couple has found a ready market of people who are just as committed to quality, ethically raised meat as they are, and willing to pay a premium for it, despite the availability of cheap steaks in supermarkets.
“I think there is more awareness now about the provenance of meat and what is being added to it, as well as the whole sustainability of eating meat, which is a really big one for us too,” says Cass.
Winning Blas na hÉireann awards has helped demonstrably.
For example, when Cass began hand making beef sausages, already popular in her native Australia, friends and family here suggested no one would buy them. “But I knew they were great. So I made them and they were really good but they were right, no one was really buying them,” she explains.
Winning Gold at Blas na hÉireann, and being able to put that precious Gold sticker on her delicious garlic and black pepper beef sausages, changed perceptions immediately.
“As a result, people were willing to try them. They’d see that sticker and say, ‘Oh, I’ll try those’,” says Cass.
“Now, every week, our beef sausages sell out and for us as a small business that’s what it’s all about.”
Winning a Blas na hÉireann award made a sweet impact on Richie Greene’s business, Skellig Jam, too.
He and his wife Jackie set it up during Covid, when his work in the construction industry, and Jackie’s bed and breakfast, came to a sudden halt.
Having been working all over the country, Greene was delighted to be home in beautiful Ballinskelligs for an extended period, much of which he spent making jam, ready for when the B&B reopened.
“It was only when everything was stopped for a while that I realised I was actually sick and tired of never being home,” he recalls.
So he suggested making jam full time instead. It only sounds like a massive swerve until you realise the jam making was a serious hobby for Greene, whose earliest memories are of being taught how to make it by his grandmother.
He still makes it “the old-fashioned way using only fruit, sugar and nothing else,” he explains.
Today the couple has a range of 15 jams, marmalades, sauces and ketchups, which they sell in supermarkets and independent stores.
Winning successive Blas na hÉireann awards helped to supercharge sales and, as a consumer himself, he understands why.
That’s because, when faced with a choice in store, both his wife and his wider family of foodies – and two of his brothers are chefs – will always opt for the product with the Blas na hÉireann sticker on it.
Indeed, even if they spot a sticker on a product they weren’t in the market for, they will likely buy it anyway. “They always want to try it because they know it will be good,” says Greene.
Blas na hÉireann, the Irish Food Awards, are open to any food producer on the island of Ireland. As befits Ireland’s development as a “food island”, entries are growing steadily and this year stood at more than 3,000.
According to Fallon Moore, who has run the competition with her father, Artie Clifford, in Dingle, Co Kerry, since its inception in 2008, it attracts both new and mature food businesses.
Producers enter online and then submit products to judges on a category-by-category basis for a blind tasting competition.
With more than 200 categories, from bread to ready meals, it’s a huge logistical undertaking, but one that has, year after year, successfully winkled out the crème de la crème of Irish food.
Even if you don’t win, taking part has enormous value, not least because of the invaluable feedback from expert judges.
“If you get to the finalist stage it means you are in the top five in your category in the country, and that is hard to achieve. The gold, silver and bronze awards are almost the cherry on top,” says Moore.
Jon Geary saw the value of that first hand when he won a Gold Award last year. He set up his ice cream parlour, Little Mamma’s Gelato, in Donegal town in October 2018, making gelato on site.
At the time friends thought he was nuts to be heading into the winter selling that most seasonal of products. In fact Geary, a chef, quickly proved that when a product is this good, people will buy it year-round. Today he produces more than 100 different flavours, with new ones added annually on foot of trips each January to see what’s new in Italy, the home of gelato.
Not alone does his ice cream parlour have a loyal customer base in Donegal, but retailers began asking if he could supply them too, helped by his success at Blas na hÉireann.
“Two years ago we got to the finals with a sorbet, and last year we won a gold for our wild berry cheesecake gelato, which catapulted everything,” says Geary.
Today Little Mamma’s Gelato supplies more than 60 retail customers and, thanks to its win at Blas, was approached to take part in Lidl’s Kickstart supplier development programme, a big step up that has seen it stocked nationwide.

title: The taste of Ireland today
description: Alongside the foods for which Ireland has long been known, Blas entries and award winners increasingly reflect a more adventurous national palate
content:
Dingle is an excellent place to start if you want to know how Ireland is eating in 2026. Each autumn, Blas na hÉireann brings food and drink from across the island to the town, and after 19 years, the awards offer a fascinating snapshot of how our tastes have changed.
More than 3,000 products were entered for the Irish Food Awards this year. Alongside the dairy, meat and baking for which Ireland has long been known are fermented foods and hot sauces, exotic mushrooms, smoked salts and cheeses, artisan breads and a growing range of sauces, condiments and preserves.
Some of what feels current has deep roots. What has changed is the company those older foods and techniques now keep, as ingredients and flavours that would once have seemed unusual have become part of the everyday Irish larder.
Fallon Moore of Blas na hÉireann has watched that shift through the entries. “The Irish palate is more adventurous,” she says. “We are exposed to lots more global tastes and cultures that are coming here, but we’re not losing sight of the really good quality basics that make Irish food so special, which is things like our dairy, our meats, our small producer network.”
Bread is a case in point. Sourdough exploded during the pandemic and, while most of us have long since abandoned our sourdough starters, Moore believes it left us with higher expectations. “People might be buying a little bit less in terms of quantity but expecting more in terms of quality,” she says. Blas judges even talk about their “weekend sourdough”: “They’re getting a really nice bread for the weekend. That’s what they’re going to enjoy, and they’re quite happy to pay for that.”
For Sarah Steen and John Mallon of Baska Bakery, sourdough changed rather more than their Saturday shopping habits. Steen was working from home in IT in 2021, while Mallon, a railway engineer, was no longer making his regular commute to the UK. One of their outings was to the farmers’ market where a baker sold sourdough. The bread was so popular that they regularly arrived too late to get any. Then, one Saturday in December, there were two loaves left. They grabbed them, only to discover that the baker was winding up the business. A few conversations later, Steen and Mallon had bought it and, within a fortnight, they were baking. “It all happened very fast,” says Mallon, while Steen remembers feeling that “it almost felt like it was sent to us”.
There was family history in the mix. Steen is the fifth generation of her family to go into baking; her grandfather ran McCann’s Bakery in Dundalk, a business that had originatedin Newry. Mallon also comes from a baking family, although neither had worked in the trade before. At Baska Bakery in Co Meath, a loaf takes three days to make and is produced largely by hand using organic, stone-ground flour.
The ingredient list is short: flour, water and salt. Steen has noticed customers taking a much keener interest in precisely that sort of detail. “The general customer now is much more aware and focused on the small print on the label and what’s in their bread,” she says. “For us it’s very easy to sell flour, water and salt,” Mallon adds. That simplicity has also done well at Blas. In 2025, Baska took silver for its Organic Multiseed Sourdough and bronze for its Organic Large Sliced Sourdough, while its Organic Country White Sourdough was also a finalist.
The return to older ways of eating is not confined to bread. Moore, whose father Artie Clifford founded Blas in 2007, has recipes belonging to her great-grandmother and is struck by how many are vegetarian. Meat, she points out, was only eaten a couple of days a week. “I actually think we’re returning to a way that we would have eaten before,” she says. Blas is seeing vegetables and produce given greater weight on the plate, with diners quite happy for mushrooms, for example, to be the main event rather than a side dish.
Joe Gorman came to those mushrooms after 29 years growing white buttons, harvesting around 17 tonnes a week largely for export. Brexit and the movement of sterling made that business unviable, so he walked away and started again. Garryhinch Wood Exotic Mushrooms, on the Laois-Offaly border, now grows shiitake, king oyster, yellow and grey oyster, lion’s mane and maitake.
He knows some customers still need persuading. “They look at them and they look fancy and all that, but it’s literally, how do you cook them?” he says. “They’re just a bit afraid of something that they’re not used to.”
Blas has been part of Garryhinch’s story almost from the beginning. Gorman says winning four awards after its first year in business was “massive”, giving the company “the boost to keep moving forward” and an icebreaker with prospective clients.
Irish Smoked Meats is new to Blas this year, although the Albrecht family’s history in food goes back much further. Andreas Albrecht’s father trained as a master butcher in Germany before coming to Ireland and setting up the business in Dundalk.
Andreas remembers smokehouses where sawdust was set alight on the floor. The process is computerised now, although the products are still hand-finished. Smoke is turning up across the Blas entries in salt, chicken and cheese, something Moore puts down to people being more interested in playing with flavour. Albrecht’s explanation is simple. “Smoking puts a lovely flavour to products,” he says. “You eat with your eyes and your nose.”
Kimchi was a rarity among the Blas na hÉireann entries in the early years. Nearly two decades later, fermented foods are a much more familiar presence. “In the very early years, kimchis and fermented foods were kind of very unusual to have entered with us,” says Blas na hÉireann’s Fallon Moore.
Fermentation has long been part of foods such as bread, cheese and yoghurt, but the range now coming through Blas is considerably broader. Kimchi and other fermented foods sit alongside kombucha and alternative drinks, another area where Moore says the awards have seen considerable growth.
The change is apparent not only in what is being entered, but in how those products are received. Moore says there is now “much broader acceptance across the judging palate” for fermented foods, pickles and newer flavours.
“People are far more open to taste ingredients that maybe weren’t traditionally part of our larder, or flavours that we certainly wouldn’t have grown up with, but that we’re more than happy to have on the table regularly now.”

title: Dublin Zoo and Bruges paintings by Walter Frederick Osbourne feature in online art sale
description: Plus 54 works by Connemara-based Charles Vincent Lamb go under the hammer
content:
V iewing online auction catalogues for Irish and international art is a hobby in itself, which is not confined to wealthy collectors of art. Of course art buyers will keep abreast of which paintings come up for sale at various auction houses (particularly if there is a short time period between a purchase and resale), but these beautifully illustrated catalogues also attract art enthusiasts who want to know more about the various styles and periods of work of the artists they love.
Take Walter Frederick Osbourne (1859-1903) for instance. One of Ireland’s best known and most loved impressionist and post-Impressionist landscape and portrait painters, Osbourne spent a good deal of time in his native Dublin, following his art studies in Antwerp, Belgium, and time in Brittany, where he was influenced by the French impressionists.
Morgan O’Driscoll ’s current Irish and International Art Auction, which ends on October 20th, has three Osbourne paintings for sale. These include In the Market Place of Bruges (1882), with an estimate of €70,000-€100,000. Osbourne submitted this painting to the Royal Hibernian Arts exhibition in 1884 alongside other significant paintings – Apple Gathering and Early Morning in the Markets, Quimperlé – both of which are in the National Gallery of Ireland ’s collection of Osbourne paintings.
Osbourne became synonymous with paintings of street markets and the hawkers and flower sellers therein. However, on his return to Dublin in the early 1890s, he produced many paintings from his studio in St Stephen’s Green of the city’s streetscapes (and also a significant number of portraits). A visit to Dublin Zoo resulted in the uncharacteristically brightly painted piece The Parrot House, Dublin Zoo (€25,000-€55,0000), also for sale at the Morgan O’Driscoll online auction.
Scottish-born painter, William Crozier (1930-2011) spent a good deal of his later years in west Cork, after years painting and teaching art in schools of art in Bath, London and Winchester. His bold, colourful abstract landscapes and still-life paintings are instantly recognisable by those who enjoy the emotional intensity of this style of expressionist painting.
