Crozier’s Spring, also for sale at Morgan O’Driscoll’s art auction (€15,000-€25,000), is one of six paintings he created for the boardroom of BNP Paribas headquarters in London in 1998. When he was approached for the commission, he said that he was incapable of painting to order and suggested that he would paint what he was painting anyway. And if the bank liked it, well and good and if not, he would take back the painting and no harm done. As it turned out, his client was pleased with the results. The painting is typical of Crozier’s work from this 1990s period.
London-born Peter Collis (1929-2012), is a contemporary of Crozier, who moved to Ireland in the late 1960s. Strongly influenced by French post-Impressionist artist Paul Cézanne, Collis painted the Irish landscape with strong, expressive brush strokes. His painting Towards Laragh, Wicklow (€3,000-€5,000) is for sale at the Morgan O’Driscoll auction. Viewing of the art works in the auction continues at the Minerva Suite, RDS, Ballsbridge, Dublin on Saturday and Sunday, October 17th and 18th, from 11am-6pm, and on Monday, October 19th from 11am-4pm.
Meanwhile, deVeres is hosting an auction of 54 works by Charles Vincent Lamb (1893-1964) on October 20th at 6pm. A landscape artist who was a contemporary of Paul Henry and Sean Keating, the Portadown-born painter lived for most of his life in Connemara where he ran an art school.
These paintings, which are mainly west-of-Ireland scenes, were part of the private collection of the late Patrick and Frances Smith (née Murphy), and are for sale now by the family.
Wexford-born Patrick Smith worked as a urologist in the UK, the US, Australia, Italy and Greece. The couple collected Lamb’s paintings for more than 30 years and displayed them in their holiday home in Crosshaven, Co Cork. The paintings for sale include A Day in Winter (€2,500-€4,000), and At the Pier, Carraroe (€6,000-€9,000). Viewing in deVeres, Kildare Street auction rooms continues on Saturday, Sunday, Monday and Tuesday, October 17th-20th from 10am-5pm each day.
On a different note entirely, Victor Mee auctioneers is holding a 900-plus lot online auction of antique advertising, pub memorabilia and other branded collectibles on October 21st and 22nd.
One of the highlights of the sale is a large-scale mural by John Gilroy (€80,000-€100,000), the artist behind Guinness’s most iconic imagery. The playful, action packed piece known at Guinness Man, was created for The Dock Green in Leeds, a public house in what was formerly a police station.
Industrial offset lithographic printing plates of leading Irish musicians from Tony Bradfield printing facilities in Celbridge, Co Kildare, are also included in the Victor Mee auction. Examples include a production plate of U2 for their 1987 album The Joshua Tree (€500-€800), and another one of U2 alongside The Dubliners (€500-€800).
An Irish writers portrait advertising board (€30-€60) is a more affordable piece of advertising history, that would fit well in a domestic or commercial space.
Morganodriscoll.com ; deveres.ie ; victormeeauctions.ie

title: New poetry by Lorna Shaughnessy; Philip McDonagh; Ailbhe Ní Ghearbhuigh; and Padraig Regan
description: Catriona Clutterbuck on Throat Full of Feathers; Estuary; This Deep; The Matter
content:
Lorna Shaughnessy’s intricately woven sixth collection, Throat Full of Feathers (Salmon, €14) , explores the shadowy reaches of sorrow. She joins a tradition of contemporary Irish women poets - including Eileán Ní Chuilleanáin and Colette Bryce - who write reverberant elegies for sisters who have died.
Here, the grief of a youngest sister of three for her deceased middle sister is explored with great sensitivity. Shaughnessy vividly communicates the disorientation such loss involves: “Your name, the root word. / Ours, the prefix and suffix / bereft of meaning” (Your Name). Experimenting with typography, textual layout and gapped narrative, she invites readers into the all-out unrepresentable in the experience of mourning.
More broadly, Shaughnessy explores the gendered complexities of sibling relationships, excavating the darker understories of myths and fairy tales such as The Snow Queen, The Six Swans and The Children of Lir.
While her work is always rich in thought, Shaughnessy occasionally unpacks her extended metaphors in too didactic a manner (The Shape of Air; Bury Your Fossils). Much more often, however, her work achieves lift-off – as when our present darkening global moment is epitomised in a persuasive dystopian vision of environmental destruction, via the strikingly developed image of hot rain falling in When the Rain.
Shaughnessy remains attuned to the metamorphosis seeded within inimical conditions. Like the caterpillar’s “deep structure of wings” which survive its decomposition in the chrysalis (Histolysis…), or her aged father’s bones jutting from his “shrunken shoulders”, our potential for transformation persists as “swollen nubs / beneath the skin, waiting to break free” (Spring Auguries).
This engrossing, risk-taking volume not only calibrates the psychic freeze of loss and betrayal, but also activates “the heartwood’s thaw” of recovered trust in our ability to live on and live meaningfully in the wake of such suffering (Return from the Realm of the Snow Queen).
Philip McDonagh’s third collection with Dedalus Press, Estuary (€12.50 pb, €20 hb), likewise tracks “the swerve of hope always unseen” in dark times (Meteõra). For him, the work of art is implicitly aligned with the intricate work of diplomacy - his other long-term profession. “The in-between world of a poem is like / The estuary, its muddy, dragging tide” (Estuary): poetry mediates between the river of as-yet unfulfilled hope in human history and its oceanic promise of realisation.
In poems set in Russia, India, Italy, Uzbekistan, Iran, Turkey, Spain and elsewhere, McDonagh at once maps and seeks alternatives to power-mongering global strife. Throughout, he highlights Christ’s embodied example of mercy and compassion as foundational for authentic freedom, love and community.
This volume foregrounds the urgency, cost and revolutionary impact of exercising moral integrity and non-violent resistance in the face of autocratic power. McDonagh perceptively diagnoses the sin of Adam as “a sudden occlusion of wide-lensed reverence / by rampant privacy” (Paradeisos), which extends into the social Darwinism of imperialism (A Strange Mutation).
Calling into question patriotic hero figures - whether British imperial generals (The Silence of the Moon) or Irish revolutionaries (The Language of the Gun), McDonagh in contrast honours here John Hume and Gusty Spence who – abjuring “the old wolf-law” of binary political antagonism - each envisioned a both/and resolution to the conflict in the North of Ireland through practising the covenants of “ordinary decency” (John Hume, Public Representative; Trojan Work).
For McDonagh, the slow estuarial work of peacemaking also proceeds through opening ourselves to the transformative effects of sudden joy, affirming our capacity to seize the moment and make it inviolable (see November Days: 2010, 1878). Offering a “holdout for harmony, / a new emoji for hope”, as this collection proceeds, “A rhythm picks up that veers towards heaven” (The Mausoleum of the Samanids): the ocean beckons ...
Ailbhe Ní Ghearbhuigh’s This Deep (Gallery, €13.90 pb, €20.00 hb) - her second dual-language volume – proves this poet’s aptitude for tightly-conceived, evocative allegory, in a book with deep roots in the Irish verse and song tradition. Drawn mostly from her 2022 collection Tonn Teaspaigh agus Dánta Eile (Éabhlóid), with facing-page translations by Alvy Carragher, Alan Gillis, Paul Muldoon, Eiléan Ní Chuilleanáin, Michelle O’Sullivan and Billy Ramsell, here, as in other collections reviewed this month, tones of menace and reassurance compete.
On high alert to contemporary retrogressive momentums towards totalitarianism and state-sanctioned misogyny, the opening poem Cró (Byre - translation Gillis and Ramsell) allegorises the curtailment of women’s freedom by virtue of their presumed biological destiny.
Voiced through the bleakly fatalistic perspective of a cow trapped inside a byre watching another animal hesitate on the threshold, that enclosed space - far from one of nurturance and fulfilment - is one of constraint, hunger and torment. Yet, this is a fate to which her younger sister will submit: “slogfar í ar aon nós isteach i ríocht seo an teasa” (“she’ll be swallowed anyway into this kingdom of heat”).
Still, Ní Ghearbhuigh resists historical determinism. Notwithstanding its hurdles, the experience of new motherhood is central to her resolute affirmation of broader regenerative possibility. Rannta do Léan (Verses for Léan - translation Ramsell) celebrates Ní Ghearbhuigh’s young daughter as “foinnse solais” (“a fount of luminescence”): an animating wellspring whose phonetic equivalent is a spurt of alliteration propelling the gamut of vowel sounds – “bogha binn do bheithe / ar uirlis na beatha” (“the sweet bow of your being / on the instrument of life”) – beautifully imparting the child’s vitality.
[ Glorious Monsters by Martina Devlin: An engrossing novel about Frankenstein author Mary Shelley Opens in new window ]
In this collection, human agency is re-energised through a maternal ethics of care. In Fothragadh (Cleansing - translation Ramsell), dehumanising politics is counteracted by all who tenderly honour its disregarded victims: “mé ag glanadh mo mháthar go cúramach, / dubhfhórsa ag druidim le Kabul” (“I’m washing my mother so carefully, / the black forces closing in on Kabul”).
This stimulating collection communicates how to live deeply and hold our own, in very challenging times.
Padraig Regan’s absorbing second collection, The Matter (Carcanet, £12.99), explores with rare precision, reach and courage, the links between tactility, desire, suffering and love. Preoccupied with the ways our material world keeps us guessing, the book is structured in three parts, deliberately recalling the game of Twenty Questions: Objects – Chiefly Animal, Objects – Chiefly Mineral, and Objects -Chiefly Vegetable.
By investigating some of Earth’s stranger natural phenomena - bats, deep-sea sponges, invertebrates, beetles, slugs, algae, fossils etc, these poems playfully mock the presumption that strict category boundaries are a reliable means to knowledge. The leafy sea dragon (yes, a real creature!) is “long-nosing out from the loose / criterion of fishness”, as Regan celebrates the creative energy released when the instability and contingency of “our collapsible significations” is admitted (A Large Photograph of a Placenta by Janie Doherty).
The volume thus tests an art of the real. A Swan’s Nest on the River Great Ouse at Ely suggests that the well-achieved poem, like the nest, operates as “A sort of cauldron, wide & scooped & void / as a coracle. & buoyant too ... // It is pure mouth // & sheer eye: cloacal, lyrical. / It tames the waters”.
Yet, art’s lyrical and figurative capacities also instigate unease in this poet, spurring the remarkable 20-page personal essay Gogotte at the heart of this collection. Here, the drive for order, meaning and clarity of identity emerges as a circular exercise which can disown the real-world plenitude all around us, but also teach vital lessons in self-other relationships.
Exploring the impulse to control through representation is of immediate importance to a poet such as Regan, who interrogates societal rejection of non-normative sexuality. In writing which for the most part stands back from direct social or political engagement, this volume - by probing our intertwined responses of repulsion and attraction to entities we encounter as alien- deconstructs the basis of anti-woke aggression reliant on hierarchical patriarchal power.
Regan’s quest to understand how human and more-than-human identities interrelate generates their evolving poetics of curiosity and receptiveness towards all that is given. Along the way, “the work (& myself)” have been “open[ed] up to new registers of feeling” (Acknowledgements page). So too, Regan’s readers. In every sense of the word, The Matter matters.
Catriona Clutterbuck’s debut collection, The Magpie and the Child, is published by Wake Forest University Press.

title: Ben Barnes: ‘I would extend the basic income scheme to all professionally trained working artists’
description: Theatre and opera director on his new book, Side Stage: Theatre Writing 1984-2025; his wariness of celebrity actors; and his admiration for John Cleese
content:
It’s a collection of essays, articles, programme notes and interviews. I called the book Side Stage because all these pieces were written in the wings of the stage of my directing life and were incidental to it. The profession of theatre directing is a relatively new one and outside the profession itself there is not much understanding of the role, its complexity and the fact that the director ultimately controls the many moving parts of any production. To illustrate that I have included in the book the mises en scène that I circulated to my creative team as a starting point for four separate opera productions. They are not something one would usually make public but they offer an insight into my process both at a conceptual and at a practical level.
I am a text-based director. The things that exercise me are not the ones which animate the current generation of “theatre makers” and perhaps that’s as it should be. I feel as I say in my book that I “dance to music no one else can hear” – the devil is in the detail, a minimalist aesthetic, the importance of what is left unsaid, taking responsibility for everything you put in the frame (proscenium), the audience as the final arbiters ... They are all leitmotifs in this book. And you know fashions change but the fundamentals remain the same.
My first big play, The Silver Dollar Boys, and the last thing I did, Le Trouvère for Wexford Festival Opera, in my hometown, and lots of productions in between of which I’m proud.
In truth, very little. When you’re in the room with the script and the actors and all the support team it doesn’t matter where it is. Give or take, the processes are the same. Except in America, where the stage managers have stopwatches to enforce the breaks!
[ Author Niall Williams: ‘I will always be an outsider, even here after 41 years’ Opens in new window ]
It’s getting stronger. With the prohibitive cost of living in cities and the preponderance of remote working, the regions have an ever more diversified and sophisticated population which is a ready market for the arts. The Arts Council needs to recognise that, get with the programme and resource professional arts in the regions properly.
Chekhov’s Three Sisters (I still might!) and I don’t have a wish list of actors. I’m wary of celebrity actors. They tend to unbalance the room.
It details in diary format my six tempestuous years as artistic director of the Abbey . Many people in the industry tell me they have a copy of it on their shelves and find it indispensable. As a cautionary tale perhaps! It went into a second print run, which is unusual for a niche publication. Through the Abbey building saga and the controversies surrounding Hinterland and Barbaric Comedies we were rarely off the front pages, k and my international colleagues envied that level of media interest in a theatre. For my part, I think I would have preferred a quieter life. More plays and fewer controversies. But you have to play with the hand you are dealt.
Ibsen’s A Doll’s House for the National Opera House and the Pavilion Dún Laoghaire and an adaptation of Der Letzte Satz (The Last Movement) by Robert Seethaler about Mahler’s poignant last voyage from New York back to Europe.
[ Author Ellen Ryan: ‘Ireland is my muse. That’s where my conviction for writing comes from’ Opens in new window ]
Actually, yes. When I graduated from school at 17 myself and three of my schoolfriends hitched to Sligo from Wexford to visit Yeats’s grave. Today I expect we’d be going to Tenerife!
John Cleese for the genius of Fawlty Towers.
I would extend the Basic Income for the Arts to all professionally trained and working artists. Turning it into a lottery system is unfair. How many of them can there be? What could it cost? A rounding error in the billions at the disposal of the Department of Finance.
Book: Golden Hours, Louisa Young’s continuation of her aunt Elizabeth Jane Howard’s The Cazalet Chronicles; Film: Sentimental Value; I don’t listen to podcasts.
The ongoing genocide and ethnic cleansing of the Palestinian people of Gaza and the West Bank. It shames the world.
Cap Bon in Tunisia on a road trip with my daughter, Milena.
A cleverly designed, solid-silver book mark with my name engraved on it in Arabic that my daughter Milena bought for me in the medina of Tunis.
The Good Soldier by Ford Madox Ford. I have many copies; some in languages I don’t even speak!
The three Elizabeths – Bowen, Jane Howard and Day – John le Carré and William Boyd. A balanced table.
I live overlooking Bannow Bay in west Wexford. Best things: fresh air, space, the sea, Grálinn cafe in Fethard on Sea, Baginbun where I swim daily, the absence of traffic and noise. Worst things: no bookshop close by and it can get a bit grim in January, February.
Mrs Ramsay in Virginia Woolf’s To the Lighthouse.
Anything by Flann O’Brien. Probably The Third Policeman.
Small Things Like These by Claire Keegan, a stage reading of which I directed with the actor Andrew Bennett and the composer and musician Eleanor McEvoy. It was an intense and moving experience.
Side Stage: Theatre Writing 1984-2025 is published by Martello Publishing

title: Peck & Peck by Bonnie Garmus: A novel that starts with great promise but falls short
description: Most of the characters are puppet-like, reduced to stereotypes
content:
Bonnie Garmus’s Peck & Peck follows her debut bestseller Lessons in Chemistry, moving us from a 1960s research institute to the inner workings of a poetry journal in the 1980s. Our verse-obsessed protagonist, Batter (named after his mother’s old dog, a fact that becomes quite a feature of the novel), is entranced by renowned publication Peck & Peck, yet on finally securing a job there as their copy assistant, realises that the inside isn’t quite as shiny as it might seem.
One of Garmus’s skills is world building. Her depiction of the Peck & Peck offices is kaleidoscopic; through Batter’s eyes, we glimpse “thousands upon thousands of silvery metals and burnished coppers, perfectly balanced in precarious-looking mobiles all floating from the twenty-foot-high ceiling like the tentacles of a jellyfish, each a complex arrangement of letters”. It is cinematic writing, evoking the wonder-like sense of a dream achieved.
It’s a shame, then, that after a strong start the second half falters. Much like in Lessons in Chemistry , the characters are quirky, yet here they suffer as two-dimensional. The figure who shines the brightest isn’t Batter himself, but his office foil, Dexter, who’s wonderfully snide. However, the rest of the cast are puppet-like, reduced to stereotypes.
No characters are more at risk of this than the editors in chief, twins Salton and Declonius. One is predictably evil, one is invariably good, and the result falls a little flat. Saying that, twins are included throughout the novel, in various iterations, and this is a highlight that makes for some very fun doubling. The plot starts off convincingly – the premise is fantastic – but in a similar vein to Garmus’s characters, it ends up farcical beyond the point of belief, with strings tied together far too neatly with far too little reasoning by the end.
Peck & Peck certainly has its strong points, with scene setting so effective that surely a screen adaptation is in the works. Yet for all that wonder, and a hopeful start, the novel remains hollow; the Peck & Peck offices might be brought to life, but its inhabitants remain cardboard cutouts.
Emily Goulding is a freelance reviewer based in London, and the creator behind Instagram page @thingsthativeread

title: Sinéad Gibney on The Fall of The West by Owen Jones: ‘We all need to read this book’
description: Despite us being brought up to believe the West is a place of democracy and peace, for many it’s justifiably linked only to death, destruction and corruption
content:
The Fall of The West is a bold and brilliant book, meticulously documenting key geopolitical forces and events in recent history. Owen Jones is known as a powerful social media communicator and political commentator. In this book, his attention to detail and presentation of cold, hard facts truly stand out.
Jones’s premise is that the decline began in 1991 when the West claimed victory in the cold war. Everything since then can be traced in a single line to the current rise of fascism and the precipice of world history we teeter upon.
We start with the legacy of British colonialism in Kenya , and Chile ’s attempt to break the cycle of dictatorship. We then tour through Afghanistan, Russia , Iraq, Britain , Greece, Austria, Gaza and the US . Along the way, Jones ties together each new chapter and layer of world history, bringing us right up to Israel ’s genocide in Gaza today and Donald Trump ’s toxic second term. He connects the Iraq War to the EU-IMF troika, and William Rees-Mogg’s Sovereign Individual to the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025. Trump is described as “neoliberalism’s id, articulating the impulses that have fuelled the policies of western elites for decades”.
We see how countries are used as pawns by dominant western powers, and how insiders who speak out end up sacrificing military or diplomatic careers. We see that the West has seeded, funded and enabled the very terrorists we then gloriously take down, and that the application of international law is horribly biased. The phrase “western violence” is used sparingly, but the reality of it is the part of this book you won’t be able to shake off. Hubris, complacency and moral superiority are hard to stomach as the true characteristics of western power.
We all need to read this book. We all need to understand that despite being brought up to believe that the West is a place of democracy, progress and peace, for many it’s justifiably associated only with death, destruction, corruption, arrogance and entitlement.
[ Martin Wolf: The rise and fall of US hegemony Opens in new window ]
If we want to deal with the rise of fascism and dictatorship, if we want to preserve democracy, human rights, peace and social justice, battered and bruised as they are, we cannot look away. This book does not look away.
Sinéad Gibney is a Social Democrat TD for Dublin-Rathdown

title: The Song of Stork and Dromedary: the story of the Brontës reimagined
description: Supernatural a pervasive preoccupation, as is the relationship between sisters, and the circular nature of time
content:
I could never have imagined, as I set out to read The Song of Stork and Dromedary, that by the time I reached the end of this 700-page epic I might be seized by the impulse to go back and start again.
This is a long novel, ostensibly comprised of 11 short novels, but what makes it so propulsive are the tendrils of detail that fasten each section to the next. The author presents 11 characters from birth to death, every one in some way connected to the Drayden sisters, born in a Yorkshire village in the early years of the 19th century, the daughters of a taciturn parson. Their short lives are distinguished by tragedy, but also by tremendous creativity. They each write and publish a single novel and are recognised, though fleetingly, as authors of talent and promise.
If this sounds familiar, it’s because The Song of Stork and Dromedary is based on the story of the Brontë sisters. Although it ought to feel strange that it was originally written in Dutch while being set predominantly in England, this is not so; such is the skill of the author, as well as the proficiency and dynamism of the translation by David McKay.
The plaintive scenery of the moors is poignantly evoked, but there are many settings: a salon in New York City, a château in the Champagne region of France, a smog-stained house in a working-class district of Lancashire. The supernatural is a pervasive preoccupation, as is the relationship between sisters, and the circular nature of time. Daanje published eight novels before The Remembered Soldier was translated into English and long-listed for this year’s International Booker Prize. If this, her follow-up, isn’t nominated for the 2027 prize, I will be astonished.
In one of many moving moments, a young man afflicted by a family curse which foretells untimely death is looking out over a heath when “the realisation crashes over him that his life is an insignificant part of an awe-inspiring whole he does not begin to understand”.
More than perhaps any other novel I’ve read, The Song of Stork and Dromedary attempts, valiantly, to reach just such an understanding, by means of an intricate, illuminative web of storytelling and ideas.

title: Elif Shafak: ‘This is the age of anger, anxiety, and AI’
description: The author reimagines Gustave Flaubert in her new novel, asking what literature can offer us in a time of war, political upheaval and uncertainty
content:
Stories live on all of humanity’s lips, from a mundane report of a day’s work to the terror witnessed in Gaza . We are all storytellers. But what good is creativity during times like these?
Global uncertainty set author Elif Shafak on a search to renew her faith in storytelling. Returning to the work of 19th-century French writer Gustave Flaubert, she found solace in thinking that “the 19th century is not over yet”. Flaubert’s France was a “time of war, civil war, siege, starvation, brother killing brother” though in modern times the “same thing is happening [now]” the Booker Prize shortlisted author says.
“Of course,” she acknowledges, “we have new challenges, but this feeling that the world is unravelling is not a new feeling.”
There is hope, extended from Flaubert to the modern reader, through the medium of Shafak.
In her latest novel In One Brief Moment All Eternity , the Turkish-British author imagines the life of the French writer and how he came to write Madame Bovary – dubbed the most scandalous woman in literature.
Flaubert is a “connoisseur of the female mind”, Shafak said, “but, I wanted to take that premise, turn it upside down.”
The novel’s jewel in the crown is the imaginative exchange between Flaubert and his creation, Emma Bovary. Shafak’s Emma yearns for a life beyond what Flaubert wrote for her. In the book, Emma says she “descended into a nightmare” as Flaubert types “paragraph after paragraph of agony” for her. Speaking back to Flaubert, Emma says he is “arrogant and self-absorbed” and that novelists “fancy themselves as miniature gods”. She then asks: “What if multiple women were to tell the story of one man’s life?”
In a knot of metafictional deliciousness, Shafak sets out on Emma’s wish: to write a novel with a chorus of women who tell the tale of the making of one man.
There are layers upon layers of questions to be asked about this as a premise, yet the most pressing is this: Do novelists have to be a little eccentric or a touch mad to believe they can create an entire world? Shafak’s Emma thinks so, yet Shafak herself says: “We all have inflated egos, and maybe as artists you need that, but you also need to learn to balance that. It’s a struggle. Some days we do it better. Some days we fail miserably.”
[ Elif Shafak: ‘I wanted to honour water. I think water is the story of our times’ Opens in new window ]
In In One Brief Moment All Eternity, Shafak creates a new world to give voice to women – imagined and real – to tell Flaubert’s story. In one chapter, opium speaks, in another a corpse. But it is the real women, who were largely forgotten, that drew me in as a reader. Julie, Flaubert’s nursemaid growing up, gifted him a love of storytelling, while Kuchuk Hanem, a bellydancer, is a woman who is “at the heart of Madame Bovary”. The writer said: “She has been to a large extent forgotten, literally written out of history, reduced to a few lines in some biographies of Flaubert.”
Shafak immersed herself in researching the political and cultural history of the 19th century, unearthing letters and pamphlets that unlocked ideas that became fully fleshed scenes in the book . Through his letters, the novelist discovered that 27-year-old Flaubert travelled through Egypt, where he had a sexual relationship with Hanem, and in his writings he “talks about how they slept holding hands”. Shafak said: “I wanted to hear the voice of [Hanem] and to dig that voice from where it had been buried under the layers of history books.”
Many of these bellydancers – known as ghawazee – were courtesans, who had been exiled from Cairo to Esna due to their erotic dancing in 1834. Ghawazee were often hired to entertain men, and were the subject of scrutiny among those who deemed their dancing improper. Perhaps it was Flaubert’s experience with Hanem and her displays of desire amid the backlash of society that went on to inspire Emma Bovary.
The name ‘Kuchuk Hanem’ translates from Turkish to ‘little lady’, and has been the subject of critical discussion on whether this name was in fact her own or one selected to appeal to colonial western travellers. On East and West relations, Shafak argues for a porous approach, not one fashioning itself to appease and appeal to the other, but rather a melding of the two, as one informs the other.
She says: “We tend to think of East and West as mutually exclusive, monolithic categories. That never was the case, and especially as we go back in time [to Flaubert and the 19th century], they [those from the East and West] were constantly talking to each other, touching each other, influencing each other. Stories travelled beyond borders, people travelled, ideas travelled, and we tend to forget that European literature has also been influenced by Middle Eastern literary heritage and cultural heritage.”
The fluid movement between both narrative voices and geographical locations reflects the novel’s expansive imaginative power. Shafak calls for greater freedoms of authors to write beyond “what they know”. “In the age we’re living in, the autobiographical aspect of literature is overemphasised ... [It] is a very limited way of looking at fiction. We sometimes write what we want to know. We write what we feel in our soul. The heart is always bigger than boxes of identity.”
We should be free to write wherever our hearts [and] our pens take us. Literature is one of our last remaining democratic spaces where we can slow down, have calmer, nuanced, multilayered conversations
When writing and reading, Shafak is interested in the “transcendental” capabilities of literature. She explains that stories should allow both writers and readers to engage in what the author Iris Murdoch called “unselfing”, the process of entering into another person’s psyche through fiction. Yet, she says, “If you happen to be an Afghan woman novelist, almost no one in the publishing industry expects you to write sci-fi or avant-garde fiction. You are expected to write about the problems of women in Afghanistan.”
Strict conventions to “write what you know”, she argues, are counterproductive: “Flaubert wrote one of the most iconic female characters, as did Tolstoy write one of the most iconic female characters. So, we shouldn’t lose sight of how we surpass the limits of the self.”
There is an echo between Shafak’s life and Flaubert’s. Flaubert was put on trial for obscenity in Madame Bovary in 1857, and almost 150 years later in 2006 Shafak faced a strikingly similar experience when the Turkish state brought a case against her over her novel The Bastard of Istanbul. Shafak explained that the mention of the Armenian genocide within the text – which she said is still “taboo” – went against the Turkish constitution, which protects “Turkishness against insults”.
“The truth is nobody knows what that means. So, it’s quite open to interpretation or misinterpretation ... That article had been used primarily against journalists and historians, but never ever before against a fiction writer, so I found myself in a very honestly Kafkaesque situation in which the words of my fictional characters were plucked, were just taken out of the manuscript of the text, and used as evidence in the courtroom,” she says.
“My Turkish lawyer had to defend my Armenian fictional characters. That went on for over a year, during which time there were ultranationalist groups on the streets, burning my pictures, burning EU flags, spitting at my pictures. They were saying that I was the pawn of western powers. You know, I was acquitted eventually, but it was a very unsettling time.”
Another two of her books – The Gaze and 10 Minutes 38 Seconds in This Strange World – have since been investigated for obscenity, the same accusation that was levelled against Flaubert.
[ Elif Shafak: ‘If we want to see how connected we are, we should look at the journey of a single raindrop’ Opens in new window ]
Shafak is a fierce advocate of artistic freedom. “We should be free to write wherever our hearts [and] our pens take us. Literature is one of our last remaining democratic spaces where we can slow down, have calmer, nuanced, multilayered conversations.” Not least as, she said, “This is the age of three As. It’s the age of anger, anxiety, and AI . But if it were to become the age of four As, if apathy were to be added into the equation, it would have been a much more difficult world to live in. Literature is the antidote to apathy.”
In a world where stories are doubted and discredited through disinformation campaigns, there is an urgent need for writers to be what Shafak terms “memory-keepers”.
“Without stories, people are unfortunately reduced to numbers. When we hear the news that 5,000 people died, our minds do not process the enormity of what we’re seeing, and then we just scroll up and down, and we move to the next news, and then the next news. It doesn’t stay with us. We don’t process it. It causes immense apathy.”
She is worried about what a world without stories would look like. She believes writers and literary festival programmers are at the coalface in creating spaces where listening to stories can be an act of resistance against apathy. That means listening especially closely to writers living through conflicts such as Gaza, which an independent UN panel called a genocide.
“So, when it comes to Gaza, it’s so important that we hear the stories. We listen to Palestinian authors today more than ever.” The same, she argues, should apply to writers elsewhere: “We [need to] hear the voices of Ukrainian writers, of storytellers from Sudan . We have to become listeners.”
For Shafak, there are also reasons to be hopeful about the future of literature. She credits the people who help books reach readers. “If books are still being read, if novels continue to somehow survive and thrive, we owe it primarily to booksellers who keep talking about books wholeheartedly. We owe it to librarians. We owe it to translators. They give so much, and they make it possible for books to travel beyond borders.”
Aimée Walsh is a novelist, journalist and book critic.

title: The Silence of October by Sharon Guard: Black humour mixes with mystery and foreboding
description: Rich writing on dealing with grief could have undertaken a slower, deeper exploration
content:
Sharon Guard’s second novel, The Silence of October , opens on a dumbstruck Klara unable to answer an ambulance crew’s questions about her unconscious teenage daughter Olivia. Olivia’s father Hector, a Trinity College lecturer, cannot be reached.
The expositional chapters feel like a thriller, with a deep secret to be revealed about the child’s death. The mystery deepens when, years later, the couple receive an unsettling wedding invitation to their goddaughter Alice’s handfasting ceremony during Samhain, the anniversary of Olivia’s death.
Guard uses slice-of-life descriptions, such as the procedural preparation of breakfast in their affluent south Dublin home, to cleverly capture the sense of detachment in the bereaved couple’s quiet, mechanical routine. The shifting perspective from third to second person adds to the ominous tone.
The month’s eerie silence is disrupted by the unexpected arrival on their doorstep of suitcase-touting Diane, mother of the bride. Diane and Klara have not spoken for years, and Klara worries that Hector will go mad at the sight of her in their home. Fresh from abandoning her New York art gallery and much younger boyfriend, the Marian Keyes-esque realism of Diane’s character feels somewhat at odds with the foreboding world Guard has built so far. While there is black humour throughout, her “fleeting desire for and fear of a fart” from tight shapewear at a dinner is an example of tonal dissonance that clashes with the subtlety and restraint established at the beginning.
Diane’s character is justified in that she acts as a mirror to the couple, reminding former concert pianist Klara of how fabulous she once was, and confronting Hector’s buffoonery, but as the pages thinned on the right, so too did the promise of an explosive, converging narrative closure for all three of them.
[ The Weight of Angels by John Boyne: What if Oscar Wilde had lived long beyond his 46 years? Opens in new window ]
Guard’s writing is rich enough for a slower, deeper exploration of Klara’s experience of motherhood and marriage. There was room for more of what happens on the stage in symphony halls, or under the dark alcoves of Trinity College. The soft prose could have lingered further on the dark stains that spread across the ceilings of Ranelagh’s redbrick houses, and walks in its residential garden squares. Another novel could give Diane’s wily character and transatlantic story its own, more animated spotlight.

title: The Last Good Day on the Internet, and The Internet We Could Have Had: How it started vs how it’s going
description: Books by Mark Little and Christopher M Kelty take radically different approaches to the web’s lost promise
content:
“If I wanted to get there, I wouldn’t start from here,” goes the old joke about a tourist asking for directions in Ireland. On first consideration, that framing might seem an appropriate metaphor for how, in just a few decades, the internet has journeyed towards its current perilously dystopian state. We’ve travelled from cheerful “You’ve got mail!” notifications and Facebook friend pokes to deepfake election videos and AI bots hacking national health systems.
Surely it must have been something in the surprisingly ramshackle way the internet was thrown together in the distant past that has left us in this desolate online arrivals hall? But the answer is no, according to two different takes, entrepreneur and former RTÉ correspondent Mark Little’s The Last Good Day on the Internet, and University of California at Los Angeles professor Christopher M Kelty’s The Internet We Could Have Had.
Both believe the foundations and early ethos of the internet had great promise to take us somewhere different – perhaps radically, excitingly different – than where we are now. But of course, the internet we have emerged out of those early structures. Little and Kelty have divergent views on what happened and why, and what “there” might look like in the future. But both are adamant that we started from an extraordinarily good “here”, in the way-back construction days of the internet. Maybe we can, maybe we can’t, go back.
Little’s book is the more traditional take, looking first at what Kelty might define as the standard version of the internet’s early, erratic history (so many separate projects and intents that nonetheless merged into something coherent, and that actually worked). The meat of Little’s book comprises a close look, with many insider takes, at what has gone wrong, concluding in a set of chapters with ideas about what might be done to counter or remedy this dire situation, including a (perhaps surprisingly accommodating) look at AI.
He offers the insights of his personal experience as a journalist, then tech company founder (Storyful, Kinzen) and big tech employee navigating the impacts of this high-speed, always-on, enthralling, alarming global phenomenon. That professional combination – including his encounters with key business, political, press and technology figures such as Elon Musk and Rupert Murdoch (whose News Corp acquired Storyful) – drives sharp, unique insights into an internet gone increasingly sour.
Little’s framing of the book around the idea offered in his title, a “last good day on the internet” before it became a shocking mess, is risky and will probably work for some but not others. He’s precise about that Last Good Day: February 26th, 2015, a Thursday, when a pair of llamas escaped from handlers on a visit to an Arizona retirement home and were vigorously pursued for 90 minutes as people all over the world followed a live feed of the chase. Twitter users chattered about the llama drama in 220,000 tweets.
[ Mark Little: ‘Protests against data centres is the biggest wave of civic activism since the 1960s’ Opens in new window ]
Hours later the internet was again in a frenzy over whether an image of a dress showed a garment that was blue and black, or white and gold. People argued over its colour at the frantic pace of 11,000 tweets a minute. Buzzfeed called it the “internet’s greatest day” because a global audience lost its collective head, twice. Little agrees, but also invites readers to imagine their own “internet moment that had the feel of an epic night out with new friends”, or introduced an exciting new idea, or changed their perspective. Those moments, he argues, are gone.
Are they, though? People still find community and discover fresh perspectives and exciting ideas online, and the notion of an identifiable day that provides a before and after does not quite work as a structuring device for me in an otherwise solid, perceptive book packed with fascinating insights. Only 18 per cent of Irish people had a Twitter account in 2015. I did, yet missed the llamas, and the dress barely registered. “Once there was a great, big global us,” Little asserts, but “our” experiences online, even on the same platforms, can be wholly different.
That said, his opening third of the book also delves into much else, identifying critical moments in the net’s development, such as the widespread use of free and open-source software, facilitating new features and capabilities, and Tim Berners-Lee’s coding breakthrough that enabled the worldwide web, something he gave to the world, for free. Now anyone could create a web page and link to other pages. A technological revolution rapidly followed.
Unfortunately, so too did the growing privatisation and commercial control of much of the internet. The middle section of The Last Good Day tears into what these forms of containment, manipulation and exploitation are – the algorithms that shape behaviour, the walled-garden tech environments that chain people to particular devices and companies, the tech “innovations” that keep people scrolling, posting and watching, and allow wide-ranging data collection and surveillance.
[ Location tracking: ‘I can easily see where 80% of the people I know currently are’ Opens in new window ]
Where the book really triumphs is whenever Little goes autobiographical. His career and personal experience provide so many penetrating understandings into why the internet is now inseparable from that state formerly known as real life, and how it has come to be dominated by a handful of recklessly powerful companies.
As a journalist with the national broadcaster, covering war zones, and then the US, he could see how the internet was transforming war coverage, protest, democratic rebellion, elections and campaigns. Events such as the Arab Spring were inseparable from the accessible technologies used to organise and report them. Brexit and Trump’s election were beholden to new ways of harvesting personal information from internet users and effectively targeting ads and social media posts.
With his company Storyful, Little and his employees pioneered ways of verifying video and images. Then, joining Twitter just as the platform was in various forms of meltdown, Little gets – and here, gives readers – a front-row seat on big-tech chaos. This is a centrepiece of the book, honest, deeply engrossing and full of “if onlys” as to how this important social platform (and others) might have developed. Little also ends up at Spotify for a time and builds a second internet-focused company, Kinzen. All this enables him to show, not just tell, how the internet veered from “how it started” into “how it’s going” (to utilise a popular meme). The book’s final third looks at where we are now, and where multiple online worlds might be going, from the challenges facing traditional media to that difficult and daunting newcomer, AI.
This tendency for internet and tech-focused books to end with a “how to fix this” conclusion is an approach rejected by Kelty’s The Internet We Could Have Had, in a book that vigorously spurns much received wisdom and standard views.
It’s a very different and challenging read, as might be expected from someone with a joint appointment in UCLA’s Institute for Society and Genetics, Department of Information Studies and Department of Anthropology. Unapologetically academic (in a punkish sort of way), and also delightfully playful and, occasionally, laugh-out-loud funny, this is a book that requires close (re)reading and is unlike anything I’ve read before on the internet and technology. It’s exhilaratingly different.
“It’s hard to argue that the internet has gone to sh*t,” Kelty suggests from the start, but adds that the many diagnoses of what’s gone wrong are “missing a section, like the 18 minutes of the Watergate tape, or maybe just a drunkard’s blackout. It’s just not clear how we got here.” He therefore presents this “forensic” book to look at the internet we could have had, if (such a critical if!) we had gone a different direction with the profoundly inventive, open-ended internet we originally had.
This is not a relaxing, summer beachtowel read, but it’s a terrifically rewarding and unusual one. Kelty namechecks philosophers and theorists from Arendt to Lyotard, Popper to Hayek (even William Morris has a moment). Kelty has an expertly deep knowledge of the net’s building-block technologies and the individuals behind them too, and knows net history inside out.
No surprise there; he has written a widely cited book on the history of free and open-source software and was active in the development of the groundbreaking Creative Commons licences for online content. So we also get Richard Stallman and Donald Knuth, Lawrence Lessig and Linus Torvalds, Eben Mogen and Tim O’Reilly, not simply namechecked and referenced, but understood.
Interestingly, Kelty considers a kind of “last good day on the internet”, offering a selection of moments that might have been when we lost the internet we could have had, but they begin as early as 1993 and end as recently as 2024. “The victim was last seen by hundreds of millions of people, and yet the time of death is uncertain” is his usefully open-ended take.
Kelty’s analysis of the many-headed monster that is Amazon is particularly astute, exposing how it might seem these giant tech companies are doing one thing – selling books or vitamins or garden hoses – when they are turning into online behemoths.
“Amazon created the internet we do have by capturing labor, land, market and infrastructure all at once, and then figuring out a way to quickly rent it back to the people still invested in the promise of the internet we could have had.” From the company’s point of view, “Monopoly was for suckers. Why bother monopolising the market for a single good or service when you can control all the markets for all the goods?”
Perhaps we need new ways to talk about these mammoth companies, too, to begin to address the harm they cause. “The term ‘platform’ is not up to the job … whatever these entities have become, they combine elements of both capitalism and governance in forms we have never seen before,” Kelty says.
Perhaps the most provocative argument in this provocatively stimulating book is that “[w]e killed the internet we could have had … everyone is the murderer.” Not any one individual, company, nor Silicon Valley. Despite so many wanting something else at the start, and building a structure that could – should? – have allowed it to emerge, we got the internet we have.
However, if we pay attention to how that happened, Kelty offers the parting shot that we might stand a chance with the next big promise/threat: AI. But, tough luck: we aren’t getting back the internet we could have had. If it’s any consolation, he’s sure we will eventually get an internet different from what we have. Because we’re all shaping it right now.
The creator of the worldwide web looks back at how it came to be and its future.
A masterly work for understanding the power of the big tech platforms.
A clarion call at a pivotal point, warning that the people would need to take back the net for it to reach its democratic potential.

title: Books in Brief: A revolt against injustice, an artistic coming-of-age tale and a haunting myth
description: Novels by Sorj Chalandon, Alex Hyde and Madeline Miller
content:
This novel by Sorj Chalandon examines a fictional performance of Jean Anouilh’s famous adaptation of Antigone uniting actors from all major ethnic blocs in war-torn Beirut. Appropriately for a novel about the many readings of Greek tragedy, Chalandon does communicate a sense of inexorable, terrible necessity, with a chorus of characters rendered empathetically despite their wildly divergent views.
Chalandon convincingly depicts the political climates of Paris and Beirut through the eyes of an active participant in France’s militant socialist movement, with scenes and characters rendered in a journalistic register of stark immediacy. Like Antigone, we are confronted with the agony of this individual’s revolt against injustice; certainly doomed, but ineluctable. Seoirse Swanton
Memories of the artist as a young woman rise to the surface in this coming-of-age novel set to the sights and sounds of Young British Artists-era London. Following her debut, Violets, Alex Hyde continues her exploration of Britain’s collective memory, this time focusing on Rabble Stone, an androgynous, working-class photography student who forms an intense bond and creative partnership with “the artist”, a painter whose confessional bravado and self-portraiture recall Tracey Emin.
Rabble addresses “the artist” directly, summoning their intertwined lives through oddly exacting descriptions of encounters charged by desire, class differences and an irreplaceable connection. The memories appear fragmented and separated by white space, as if each is a single frame developing in the mind of the photographer. An emotive read shaped by subtlety and constraint. Ferdia Roche
Miller’s Mestra is a beautiful, slim red volume that contains a whole world. Retelling the myth of Erysichthon and his daughter, Miller writes with extraordinary economy, precision and élan, finding the emotional life inside a story of hunger, violence, transformation and survival. Mestra’s ability to change shape might sound like a gift, but Miller makes it something more complicated: a way of escaping the men who try to possess her, while leaving her uncertain where one body ends and another begins.
[ The Glass Cage by John Healy: Stunning record of a life Opens in new window ]
The prose is clean, vivid and quietly funny, and the details do enormous work. There is no wasted motion here. Miller has the confidence to let the story unfold simply, allowing its strangeness to speak for itself. The result is intimate, haunting and utterly delightful. Adam Wyeth

title: Man who delivered ‘final strike’ in death of man on stag jailed for six-and-a-half years
description: Seán Munnelly of Athlone jailed for the manslaughter of Paul ‘Babs’ Connolly (48), who fell three times during sustained attack
content:
A 40-year-old man who delivered “the final strike” before the death of a man on a stag party in Athlone in 2022 has been jailed for six-and-a-half years.
Seán Munnelly, of Irishtown, Athlone, Co Westmeath, received a sentence of seven years, with the final six months suspended, at Mullingar Circuit Court on Friday for the manslaughter of Paul ‘Babs’ Connolly (48), from Edenderry, Co Offaly.
Connolly died in the early hours of August 13th, 2022, on Church Street after falling on three occasions during a number of physical altercations, involving punches and kicks, with two men: Munnelly, and David Higgins of St Paul’s Terrace, Athlone.
Higgins was previously jailed by Judge Keenan Johnson for one year for assault causing harm to Connolly and engaging in violent disorder.
Sentencing at Mullingar Circuit Criminal Court on Friday, Judge Deirdre Browne said the final punch delivered by Munnelly was “unprovoked and entirely unwarranted, very deliberate ... and came out of nowhere”.
She said Munnelly was gesturing towards Connolly, who had earlier become separated from the stag party group, and was speaking in an “animated fashion”.
She said Connolly was in “a very vulnerable” state as by that stage he had fallen twice and was clearly injured. At the sentence hearing earlier in October, video footage was shown where blood could be observed on Connolly’s face.
Browne said a nurse who witnessed the final punch and who attended to Connolly after he fell for the final time, heard Munnelly say, “F**king deserved it, no one pisses me off.”
Garda Kevin Craig also gave evidence at the sentence hearing that Connolly was refused entry to a number of establishments in Athlone earlier on due to his state of intoxication.
Browne said on Friday that after seeing the extensive CCTV footage, she placed Munnelly’s conduct at “a very high level”.
She said that “at all times” during the assaults perpetrated by Higgins and Munnelly, Connolly appeared “vulnerable” and posed “no threat” to them.
Munnelly claimed Connolly made remarks earlier that night in the presence of three other witnesses that he took exception to. Browne said any such remarks were of “minor significance” in the assessment of the offence of unlawful killing.
Browne said that on the CCTV footage from this part of the night, Connolly “lurches, lumbers, is unsteady and appears out of it, not in an aggressive, threatening way, [but] as if he didn’t know what was going on”.
She said that despite the interventions of younger men, an older bystander, and other members of the stag party, Higgins and Munnelly “would not go away”.
Browne did not accept that this was “a one-punch case”, but was one that involved “a final strike” after “a series of assaults” that took place over an “extended period of time” .
Consequently, she placed the offending in the four- to 10-year band of sentencing for unlawful killing.
After setting a headline sentence of eight-and-a-half years, Browne turned to aggravating factors which included that Munnelly was 36 years old at the time, and so was “not a young man”, and he was also on bail.
Browne said that Munnelly had earlier drunk alcohol and taken cocaine and would have been aware of their “disinhibiting effects”.
Mitigating factors taken into account by Browne included Munnelly’s guilty plea, even though it came “very late in the day”.
However, she noted that this was “a complex case” where the pathologist’s report found the cause of death was a cardiac arrest following mild blunt force trauma to the head in the setting of emotional stress in circumstances of alcohol intoxication.
Browne also noted the conclusion of a probation officer who said Munnelly had “a long-standing dependence on alcohol”, was sorry, and that he had made “significant” efforts to rehabilitate in prison.
Browne suspended the final six months of Munnelly’s sentence for one year to allow him to continue this rehabilitation work and directed him to engage post-release with the Probation Service.

title: ‘Hands off’: Brazilians protest outside Meta in Dublin over claims of election bias
description: Brazil’s top electoral court ruled on Thursday Meta must adopt measures to immediately secure equal treatment of the two candidates
content:
Brazilians living in Dublin protested outside Meta ’s Irish office on Friday amid claims the social media giant is influencing Brazil ’s highly polarised election in favour of Flávio Bolsonaro.
Protesters supporting president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the country’s runoff election taking place later this month held signs reading, “Hands off Brazilian elections,” and, “Meta, stay out of it.”
The demonstrators have called for greater transparency from social media platforms after Lula filed a complaint in court accusing the tech company behind Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp of using biased algorithms and AI restrictions to favour his opponent, Bolsonaro.
Flávio is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro , who is serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted over a plot to overturn the 2022 election result.
Brazil’s top electoral court ruled on Thursday that Meta must adopt measures to immediately secure equal treatment of the two candidates in advance of the October 25th election.
“Fake news is becoming normalised, and falsehoods are being treated as the truth. This is worrying,” said protester Erika Normande at Meta’s Dublin’s offices on Friday evening.
“Meta has been changing the reach of posts and interfering in our elections. We are here to protest against interference in president Lula’s campaign,” said another, Maíra Amaral.
Flávio attempted to woo the support of US president Donald Trump and his administration, meeting him at the White House in May. He has received public praise from Trump.
Lula, who is seeking a fourth presidential term, has said the president’s posts have suffered reduced reach and visibility, while his team have faced difficulties promoting content on Instagram. They also allege that Meta’s distribution systems favour Flávio.
[ Can Lula defy history? Brazil’s left seeks unprecedented run-off turnaround Opens in new window ]
Lula’s campaign has questioned why 255 accounts it considers inauthentic, allegedly operated using artificial intelligence, remain active.
It filed a complaint with Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court after the first round of voting. On October 10th, the court gave Meta 48 hours to explain its content distribution practices.
The company blamed the reduced reach on technical problems, denied favouring Flávio Bolsonaro, and said it complies with electoral rules and treats candidates equally.
“It is unfortunate that minor technical issues are being spun into a political narrative,” Meta said in a statement to The New York Times.
However, André Almo, a protester outside Meta’s head office in Dublin, said: “We are now completely controlled by platforms that are based outside our country.
“Brazil is being held hostage by Meta, which is changing its algorithms in favour of a candidate who follows the American agenda.”
Brazil has almost 160 million registered voters eligible to vote in the 2026 election.
[ Brazil turns right: Bolsonaro in pole position as election goes to run-off Opens in new window ]
In the first round of the election, on October 4th, Flávio Bolsonaro finished the first round with 47 per cent of valid votes, compared with 45 per cent for Lula.
Slightly more than 20 per cent of voters did not cast votes, the highest abstention rate in the first round of a Brazilian presidential election since 1998.
There are an estimated 80,000 Brazilians living in Ireland, according to the Brazilian embassy, with more than 16,700 registered to vote here.
One protester in Dublin claims that Brazil was “suffering from American digital colonisation”.

title: St Pat’s falter as Bohs cut Rovers lead to three points
description: Shelbourne punish Stephen Kenny’s attacking approach with two goals on the break
content:
As the real story unfolded across town at Dalymount Park, St Patrick’s Athletic were punished for an overly ambitious approach with two Shelbourne goals in transition.
Both were sucker punches. Sean Moore and Daniel Kelly did the damage, dropping Stephen Kenny’s side from second to third in the Premier Division, six points behind leaders Shamrock Rovers.
Bohemians beat Waterford 2-0 at Dalymount to cut Rovers lead at the top of the table to three points with two games remaining.
St Pat’s can stay in the hunt by winning away to Derry City on Monday night. But, undoubtedly, this was their chance. Five shots on target from 25 attempts tells its own story.
The League of Ireland had been meandering towards its usual conclusion. Rovers 2-1 defeat of Bohemians last Monday appeared to ruin any chance of high drama over the last three Friday nights of the season.
The defending champions were set to maintain their stranglehold on Irish football in the 2020s with a sixth title in seven seasons unless Galway United could fight their way clear of relegation at Eamonn Deacy Park.
A few minutes before Jamie Lennon gave St Pat’s a first-half lead, word filtered around Richmond Park that Aaron Bolger had scored Galway’s second. It finished 2-0 out west.
News of Rovers’ struggles infused the old ground with a rare energy. “Bolger was a Saint!” screamed one long-suffering Pats man. Bolger also started his career at Rovers. But no matter.
The locals were beginning to voice their frustration as St Pat’s were denied five separate goalscoring chances. Shels goalkeeper Eddie Beach deserves praise for denying Anthony Olunsanya and Zach Elbouzedi.
Also, James Norris made a perfect slide tackle on Kian Leavy. It was so well timed that referee Paul Norton pointed to the spot before his linesman set him straight.
The match officials were in agreement moments later when Kameron Ledwidge fouled Leavy in the box, only for Aidan Keena to slam his penalty off the crossbar.
Kenny delved into his bag of managerial tricks this week to take all the attention off his players and heap it squarely on his own shoulders. The St Pat’s manager took aim at the FAI, namely its League of Ireland department, for what he described as a “chaotic” and “undemocratic” fixture run-in that gave Shamrock Rovers an extra day’s rest before they beat Bohemians.
It sounded like Dalymount Park would have been a better Dublin venue to witness the title race when Sam Todd gave Bohs an early lead against Waterford.
But Lennon silenced a small but noisy gang of Shelbourne fans with a shot that deflected off Beach’s heal to give St Pat’s a 1-0 lead two minutes before half-time.
Suddenly, Kenny’s attacking formation had his team three points behind Rovers with a game in hand.
The attacking approached backfired early in the second-half when Kelly put Moore through to level the derby. Before the crowd could draw breath, Bohs had pushed Pats to third in the table with a goal from Ryan Burke.
Kenny reacted by replacing Leavy with teenage attacker Ryan Sheridan before Chris Forrester and Ryan Edmondson arrived for a grandstand finish.
The season was on the line as St Pat’s bombarded the Shels goal. The push for silverware actually lost them the game as Kelly punished them on the break with six minutes remaining.
Ali Coote was shown a red card late on for a heavy challenge on Sheridan, who was lucky to avoid serious injury.
St Patrick’s Athletic: Anang; Redmond, Hoare, Turner; Elbouzedi, Baggley (Forrester 73), Lennon, McClelland (Brown 84); Leavy (Sheridan 62), Keena (Palmer 83, Olunsanya (Edmondson 73).
Shelbourne: Beach; Untergrabner (Lunney 66), Ledwidge, Casey, Norris (Bone 72); Henry-Francis (Coote 72), McInroy; Moore (Boyd 88), Caffrey, Kelly; Odubeko (Martin 65).

title: ‘We all have similar stories’: NBC’s Today show comes to Kerry
description: NBC’s popular morning TV show broadcast clips of Ireland to its 30 million US viewers
content:
In Kenmare at noon on Friday, presenter Savannah Guthrie opened NBC’s long-running Today show broadcast fully for the first ever time from outside the USA with a reference to how lucky they were to have seen two rainbows that morning.
Then it was on to the news of the day in the United States – the Oregon shootings .
The popular US morning show had been transported with crew, presenters and equipment to Co Kerry in a large logistics operation involving 20 pallets of equipment, dozens of personnel and all seven presenters.
Tourism Ireland , which sponsored the operation, would not say how much it cost. But as far as the overseas marketing organisation was concerned, the proverbial pot of gold had already been found at the end of one rainbow. And the second pot would surely follow.
The show had a daily audience reach of 30 million in the US and Friday’s show broadcast with clips from all over Ireland.
The show went out at noon, but it was an earlier start for the crew who had flown in after Thursday’s US broadcast.
The “media pen” in front of the specially built stage on the banks of the Sheen river heard Jenna Bush, daughter of president George and Laura Bush, practise her cúpla focal – in particular how to properly pronounce Coláiste Íde, the girls’ all-Irish secondary school in Dingle.
She also wanted to tell us how near Ireland was to the US
“From the east coast of America to here is a quick trip and I hope our viewers get to see that,” she said of the seven-hour journey she slept through.
This was from New York to Texas, she notes.
Jenna was in green; many of the crew sported wax coats, with the odd sprinkling of an Aran sweater.
Links with Ireland were emerging in surprising places. Al Roker, veteran weather forecaster and the longest anchor with the Today show, said there was an absolute “grá” for Ireland in the US. And he revealed an Irish ancestry few knew about.
Dressed in green cords – he favours the colour anyway – Roker told how his mother’s grandmother was a Smith from Ireland. She had worked as a domestic servant in Boston and married his great-grandfather, a freed slave, in 1870.
“A black man and an Irish woman in Boston in 1870, that was unusual,” he said.
Ireland was very like the US, Roker said. There was the attachment to the land of generations and also the number of immigrants adding to the culture.
“It’s very American. We all have similar stories,” he said.
Crafts, including pottery from Kenmare and local sweets, were being lined up to be showcased during the four hours, which was swinging to clips from all over the country from Doolin to Donegal and Dublin to Belfast.
A large number of Today fans had travelled with the show, and local schools were brought into the audience.
Meanwhile, downtown Kenmare was cordoned off from 1pm to allow a live feed from Henry Street. US flags flew over shop fronts as an off-season autumn bonanza arrived in the heritage town.
This, too, was part of Tourism Ireland’s game plan.
“Doing it in October was really important to us. We wanted to showcase Ireland as a year-round destination,” said Siobhan McManamy, Tourism Ireland’s director of markets.
She paid tribute to the strong local support, where the event has been greeted like the Sam Maguire. “Kerry always pulls it out of the bag,” McManamy said.

title: Wednesday’s public sector strike called off after unions and Government agree on talks
description: Two sides to enter a ‘focused and intensive exercise’ aimed at agreeing a basis for formal negotiations
content:
Trade unions have called off public sector strikes next Wednesday and will enter an intensive process of talks about talks with Government, facilitated by an independent chairman/woman, in an attempt to unblock formal negotiations on a new pay agreement.
The Government announced on Friday evening it would enter a “focused and intensive exercise” with unions, assisted by Workplace Relations Commission chairman Kevin Foley, in an attempt to agree a basis for formal negotiations on a new public sector wage deal.
In a co-ordinated move, the public services committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions said in a statement that following discussions “over the last 24 hours ... the Ictu PSC [Public Services Committee] has agreed to suspend strike action due to take place next Wednesday”.
However, while next week’s stoppage has been suspended, the work-to-rule action will continue.
The talks are likely to begin on Saturday. They will be conducted by Irish Congress of Trade Unions general secretary Owen Reidy, secretary general of the Department of the Environment Oonagh Buckley and Foley
The agreement was brokered after back-channel communications between Government and unions in recent days.
Fórsa chief and PSC chairman Kevin Callinan told RTÉ he had “a long conversation” with Taoiseach Micheál Martin, who phoned him from Brussels, in which it was “impressed upon him the way in which cost-of-living pressures were affecting our members. And I believe now that the Government have been listening. Obviously, we need to test that in practice in a talks process.”
Later, Callinan said: “It’s good to get this much agreed. There has been a lot of hard work done behind the scenes to agree on a way forward. We’ll see now where it goes.”
Tánaiste Simon Harris welcomed the development and said he hoped “we will all be able to find a way forward, which allows for the parties to reach a mutually agreeable outcome”.
Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers said there was a genuine commitment to dialogue and he hoped that “this initiative will now allow both sides to move forward together into meaningful negotiation”.
Siptu organiser Adrian Kane said: “There’s no doubt that 300,000 workers being out in the streets on Wednesday concentrated minds. We’re hopeful now that further strikes won’t be required, but they remain an option … next week’s has only been suspended.”

title: Man advanced towards gardaí and said ‘shoot me, shoot me, shoot me’, trial hears
description: Robert O’Connor fatally stabbed his parents and younger special needs brother at their family home in Co Louth
content:
A detective has told a jury of the moment a man accused of triple murder put his bloodied hands behind his back, advanced at gardaí , and shouted “shoot me”, hours after he fatally stabbed his parents and younger special needs brother.
The Central Criminal Court trial also heard that the accused asked a detective “what kind of time” he could expect on the way to the Garda station.
Robert O’Connor (32), of Drumgowna, Louth Village, Dundalk , has pleaded not guilty of murder by reason of insanity, or guilty of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility, to the triple murder of his mother Louise O’Connor (56), his father Mark O’Connor (54) and his younger brother Evan O’Connor (27) at their home in Drumgowna between September 28th and 29th last year, both dates inclusive.
In her opening address, Roisin Lacey, prosecuting, said the accused had episodes of psychosis from a young age and was diagnosed with schizophrenia in 2018.
The barrister said the “battleground” between the prosecution and defence in the trial was whether the accused qualified for the special verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity.
The panel has also been told the accused accepts he caused the death of the three victims, who sustained a combined 139 stab wounds.
Giving evidence on Friday, Det Garda Gerard Nixon said he was informed at 9.40am on September 29th that two bloodied bodies had been found in the garden of Drumgowna and were possibly deceased.
The detective was informed one of the occupants of the house had schizophrenia.
Nixon said he was travelling in an unmarked patrol car with a colleague through Phillipstown and in the direction of Tallanstown, when they saw a man in a black hoodie and wearing white headphones coming towards them.
[ Psychiatric state of man accused of murdering three members of his family ‘central’ to trial Opens in new window ]
Nixon told the man he was an armed guard. The man said his name was Robert and was looking for them. The accused took his hands out of the pockets of his hooded top and put them behind his back.
The detective said the accused, who was about three metres away, had advanced towards him and shouted: “Shoot me, shoot me, shoot me.” The witness said the accused was aggressive and angry. “I told him no one is going to be shot here today.”
Nixon gave the accused instructions to put his hands up and kneel on the ground, which he said O’Connor had refused to comply with a number of times. When the accused finally put his hands over his head, the officer could see dried blood on them.
The detective said his colleague cautioned the accused and placed handcuffs on him before searching him for a knife. No weapon was found on the accused. When the handcuffs were removed, O’Connor said he wanted to sit down and gardaí offered him the back seat of the patrol car.
The accused then told the officers: “I killed them. I killed my father, mother and brother. I slashed my mother in the face and she gave me a look. I could see the reflection of my dad in her face. My mother wanted to go to the bathroom. My father was behind her. I then killed my father and brother.”
When the detective asked O’Connor why he had done this, the accused said there was a row over drugs and that he only meant to kill his father and brother.
[ Triple murder accused told gardaí he only meant to kill father and brother, not mother, court hears Opens in new window ]
The detective said the accused had asked another colleague, Det Sgt Paul Gill, “what kind of time” he could expect on the way to Drogheda Garda station.
Under cross-examination, the detective agreed with Michael Bowman, defending, that the defendant’s immediate response was to say “shoot me” and that he had continued to advance and shout loudly a number of times.
The trial continues on Monday before Judge Mícheál P O’Higgins and a jury of six men and six women.

title: Patrick O’Donovan will continue in Cabinet when he recovers from illness, Harris says
description: Minister for Communications, hospitalised following medical emergency, had faced speculation about his future in Government
content:
Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan will continue to serve in Cabinet when he recovers from illness, Fine Gael leader and Tánaiste Simon Harris has said.
O’Donovan remains at University Hospital Limerick after being taken ill on Tuesday. He was to hospital by ambulance while hosting an informal meeting of EU telecoms ministers.
Earlier that day, O’Donovan had hit back at “betrayal” in his party following reports of private discussions on whether his health could preclude him from serving in Government.
He was previously hospitalised during the summer while on an official trip to Brussels. O’Donovan was diagnosed with epilepsy 10 years ago.
In a statement on Friday night, Harris, who is currently on paternity leave, said O’Donovan was “a valued member” of the Government and would continue to serve.
“Following an update from Minister Patrick O’Donovan’s family this evening, on behalf of Fine Gael, I want to acknowledge and thank members and supporters for their well wishes for Patrick and his family in recent days,” he said.
“While he remains in hospital, Patrick continues to receive fantastic care from the staff of the HSE at University Hospital Limerick. We are all hoping for his swift recovery and return to work as soon as is possible.
“Patrick is a valued member of Fine Gael and the Cabinet. He has served the people of Limerick and this party with pride for over two decades.
“I have been pleased to appoint him on two occasions to Cabinet and he serves with distinction in a key Government department and naturally will continue to do so.”
Harris said the party – both in Limerick and nationally – was “behind him”, and wished O’Donovan and his family well “during this challenging period”.
“Patrick has been incredibly open about the challenges he has faced with his health,” Harris said.
“I have seen first-hand how, despite those challenges, he has worked diligently and competently in every role he has been entrusted with and it is my firm belief that will continue long into the future.”
Harris added: “Commentary about his health and political future by anonymous sources was hurtful, has no place in the Fine Gael party and will not be tolerated.
“While I am on paternity leave, I remain in contact with his family. l look forward to welcoming Patrick back to his Cabinet duties as soon as possible.”
A statement by O’Donovan’s family on his Instagram page said he was undergoing treatment.
“Patrick’s interdisciplinary team at University Hospital Limerick are working with him to ensure his return to his department as soon as new treatment has bedded down,” it said.
“He is heartened by the support for his long-term Cabinet career demonstrated by his colleagues.”
O’Donovan has previously spoken about his experience living with the condition .
Before being hospitalised on this occasion, the Co Limerick TD had hit back against critics within his own party, Fine Gael, accusing those who commented on his health of “ the ultimate in betrayal ”.
He was responding to briefings against him in coverage of the budget rows he became embroiled in last week.
In addition to questions over his temperament, a Fine Gael TD was quoted at the weekend suggesting that people within the parliamentary party were questioning whether O’Donovan was healthy enough to continue in his role.
A Cabinet source in the party was quoted as suggesting a discussion on whether he was “well enough” to retain his portfolio was likely.
O’Donovan had been at the centre of a post-budget controversy after first failing to secure funding to support his heavily publicised culture card initiative for 16- and 17-year-olds.
Then, he was again in the headlines after providing RTÉ with €20 million less in funding than agreed under the terms of a 2024 deal with the troubled national broadcaster.

title: The Irish Times view on Waterford deaths: a chilling trend  and a tragedy
description: Attacks of this kind deserve the same investigative resources as shootings
content:
The deaths of Philip and Kim English and their two young sons, Callum (12) and Jayden (9), are the most shocking and distressing yet in what has become a wave of arson attacks across the country. Two other children, a girl of 14 and a boy of six, remain in critical condition in Crumlin Children’s Hospital.
Gardaí believe the attack, in which a petrol bomb was thrown at the front door of the family home on the Birchwood estate outside Waterford city, was linked to a drug debt the family did not incur.
Investigators suspect Philip English was targeted over the debt of an associate, even though the debt was not his. The pattern of intimidation, threats and serious violence linked to such debts has become grimly familiar in some communities. It presents a real and complex challenge for the justice system.
The figures are alarming. Fourteen local authorities recorded 113 arson attacks on council homes over five years, 50 of them last year alone. That count does not include private housing. Nor does it capture the wider pattern of intimidation.
