The Drive project, an inter-agency initiative, recorded 1,027 cases in 2024 and 2025, and gardaí acknowledge that many victims never come forward.
Older criminals load teenagers with debts and then send them out to collect from others. Gangs study which households can be squeezed, through credit union loans or a cut of welfare payments.
This month a judge in Mullingar sentenced two 17-year-olds over a shotgun attack, with one of them also convicted of a string of arsons across three counties, and described those directing such boys as a cancer. Gardaí have also warned that gangs are grooming children online. The debts themselves are often a fiction, inflated at will and never settled, with parents and siblings who have nothing to do with drugs or gambling made to carry them.
Arson is treated by those who commission it as a lesser offence, designed to frighten rather than kill. The horror of this week’s events in Waterford shows how false that notion is. Even when they do not cause fatalities or serious injuries, attacks of this kind deserve the same investigative resources as shootings.
There is a role too for the State beyond policing. The English family had reportedly sought a council transfer because they no longer felt safe. Families under this kind of pressure need a route to safety that moves with the urgency the threat demands.
Garda numbers will reach a record high this week. That is welcome, but the measure that matters even more is whether the upward trend in these particular crimes begins to be visibly reversed.

title: Michael Carrick insists Manchester United have moved on despite Martínez’s Wilcox criticism
description: Manager seeks to defuse tensions, with United struggling for results ahead of Leeds trip
content:
M ichael Carrick returned his most impressive performance precisely when required as he took questions in the midst of the first crisis engulfing him as Manchester United ’s manager.
His team are bombing in the league after the club’s poorest start since 1986 and out of the Carabao Cup, and after Tuesday’s Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid, Lisandro Martínez showed up ruptures at United by calling out the director of football, Jason Wilcox.
All of this two months into a first full campaign piloting United after last term ended so rosily for Carrick.
On May’s final match day, United won 3-0 at Brighton and Carrick had secured an impressive third-place finish, 48 hours after agreeing a two-year deal to continue as the number one.
By last Saturday, United had six points from the first six games after drawing 1-1 with Tottenham at Old Trafford, placing Carrick’s job in jeopardy as the walls close in on him a fortnight before the clocks go back.
A game at Leeds in January proved to be Ruben Amorim’s last in charge at Manchester United after he greeted the 1-1 draw by demanding his colleagues in the recruitment department “do their job”. With an uncanny circularity, Carrick heads to Elland Road on Sunday after Martínez made similar comments. Amorim’s team were sixth going into that game; Carrick’s start the weekend 13th.
On Friday, though, came a masterclass from Carrick in dialling down emotion as Martínez’s explosive comments about Wilcox – “I expect more [investment], 100 per cent. I expect more from our technical director” – were addressed and he repeatedly referred to the “really good feeling” at the club.
“It’s really not a drama for us as a group,” he said. “The boys have trained really well. This morning there was a really good feeling around the squad ... so we’ve moved on pretty quickly.”
[ Roy Keane brands Manchester United ‘circus’ following Lisandro Martinez outburst Opens in new window ]
If this seems less than credible, and almost certainly a stance coached by United’s PR mandarins, what else would Carrick be expected to say? More obvious was how the zen-like performance required from the club’s leader was being delivered. Even when he broke from the script to interrupt an inquisitor this strengthened the sense of Carrick being in control – hardly easy given the heightened glare on United since Tuesday evening.
When the positive vibes trope was challenged by a questioner saying, “We’ll have to take you at face value”, Carrick’s interjection came with a smile. “I’m telling you the truth when I say that,” he said. “Do you not believe me, no? The players totally believe me. I’m telling you the truth. The squad today was in a fantastic place, better than I’ve seen it for a while, actually, and that’s it, plain and simple, you know? We’re emotional, we’re passionate, we care a lot.”
When signing on to be the permanent United manager, Carrick had overseen only 21 games at elite level – in two caretaker spells at the club. United had only 17 league games to play when he replaced Amorim, and Carrick has shown signs of faltering this season when having to compete on four fronts.
Elimination by Brighton at the earliest stage of the Carabao Cup was not a great calling card regarding an ability to juggle competitions, and there was a surprising reaction from him after the 2-0 opening day loss at Hull. He bridled at the suggestion United had lacked “passion” during a first-half horror show. “Oh come,” Carrick said. “That’s ridiculous.”
A faulty United rearguard is hampering an attack that is functioning far better and has the most shots (125) and most touches in the opposition box (205) in the Premier League. Nine goals from six matches is not paltry but greater ruthlessness would transform a promising front six into a potent one. Carrick has to find the right blend from Benjamin Sesko, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo, Marcus Rashford, Amad Diallo, Bruno Fernandes, Kobbie Mainoo, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba.
Baleba has sparkled in his first two appearances – against Spurs and Atlético – and might have provided the shield from the number 6 berth to ensure a less leaky defence had he not arrived injured.
This has to be the hope for Carrick. The fielding of Tielemans at 10 at Atlético suggests the manager may doubt the 29-year-old’s legs, and questions have been raised about whether United are putting in enough of the hard yards. Their 671.4km distance covered in the league is the fifth-lowest (Arsenal’s 716.2km is the highest), and their 581 sprints the fourth-lowest (Brentford’s 765 the most).
The trip to an always febrile Elland Road that saves a particular welcome for their cross-Pennines rivals presents a stern challenge. Leeds are ninth and have lost once.
“It’s a great rivalry,” Carrick said, who was full of praise for his Leeds counterpart, Daniel Farke. “There’s big history between the clubs, the areas. That’s what makes these types of games special. You’ve got to embrace the history, what it means.
“I’m sure it will be a fantastic atmosphere on Sunday. It brings an intensity and it’ll be a little bit extra again, on Sunday against us ... Of course, we have to be ready, and the boys will be.”
Carrick requires a positive result, though in denying this, he again sounded the right note. “I don’t need results, we all need results,” he said. “It’s not about me. Manchester United is a lot bigger than any individual, bigger than me, bigger than any player, anyone else who works at this club. It’s not about me, so please ...
“I don’t go into every day at work, in this situation, this game, thinking about me. It’s about what we stand for, what we live for, the history, the things that we need to live up to, and that’s what drives us. So whatever’s best for the club and for the team on Sunday is the most important thing.” – Guardian
[ Manchester United teammates largely side with Lisandro Martínez’s criticism of Jason Wilcox Opens in new window ]

title: Jewish group weighs legal action after Dublin hotel cancels bookings for anti-Semitism event
description: Venue asked if conference had links to Israel Defense Forces, Jewish Representative Council of Ireland says
content:
A group representing the Jewish community in Ireland says it is considering legal action against a hotel in Dublin 4 over its cancellation of dozens of bookings made for delegates attending a conference on combating anti-Semitism.
Maurice Cohen, chairman of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland, said “every angle will be considered” after the Herbert Park Hotel in Ballsbridge cancelled a booking for 70 delegates attending the Dublin conference.
In a speech on Tuesday addressing the Special Envoys and Co-ordinators Combating Anti-Semitism (Secca) conference, Cohen said when the World Jewish Congress began organising the event, a shortlist of hotels offering accommodation for 70 delegates was drawn up.
The Herbert Park Hotel was selected, after which there was “the usual discussion about rates and arrangements, and then came confirmation that the rooms were reserved”.
However, Cohen said the bookings were subsequently cancelled by the hotel without explanation just hours after he and the event co-ordinator met management to discuss the possibility of staging other elements of the conference at the hotel.
[ Ireland players’ actions at Israel football games ‘shameful’, Jewish advocacy leader says ]
He said he was asked by a hotel manager during the meeting what Secca was. In response, he said he “explained that it brought together Jewish community leaders from around the world and government-appointed officials responsible for combating anti-Semitism. Most of those government officials were not Jewish”.
He said he told the manager the conference was “associated with Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the European Union, that Government ministers would participate and that some of those attending would be meeting the Taoiseach as well as other ministers”.
As he spoke, he said, he noticed the manager’s “manner change” and said there was “a tension that had not been there before”. He said he was then asked if the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) would be involved.
“Nothing I had said had anything whatsoever to do with the Israeli army, yet somehow that was where the conversation had gone,” he said.
Cohen said he was then told that the owners of the hotel would have to be consulted ”to determine whether [delegates] would be permitted to stay there”.
A day later he was told the bookings had been cancelled.
In his speech, he said “contemporary anti-Semitism does not always arrive wearing the language of the past. It does not always announce itself with a slur, a threat or a placard”.
“Increasingly, it can present itself as a question, a precaution, a policy, a request for clarification,” he said.
The question about the IDF was “not an innocent misunderstanding”, Cohen told delegates.
“It revealed how quickly Jewish identity can be collapsed into Israel , how quickly Israel can be collapsed into suspicion and how quickly suspicion can become discrimination.”
Cohen told The Irish Times on Friday that the next steps had yet to be decided. One avenue would be lodging a complaint under the Equal Status Acts, which involved the Workplace Relations Commission .
Asked if he was considering legal action against the hotel on discrimination grounds, he said: “Every angle will be considered and action taken, as unfortunately people need to know that while we are a tiny community we have the same rights as others and we won’t be discriminated against.”
The Irish Times contacted the hotel offering it a right of response, but at the time of writing it had declined to comment.
In July, the Powerscourt Hotel, Co Wicklow, cancelled bookings for a “secretive” conference to be hosted in August by a group cofounded by US tech billionaire Peter Thiel, a co-founder of Palantir, which is a defence contractor known for mass surveillance and has been criticised heavily for its “strategic partnership” with the IDF.

title: Retrial ordered for man previously convicted over getaway car used in Lordship Credit Union robbery
description: Court of Appeal had overturned conviction, but James Flynn (35) will face retrial at Special Criminal Court on amended indictment
content:
The Supreme Court has ordered the retrial of a man accused of conspiring to steal a car that was used days later in a credit union robbery during which Det Garda Adrian Donohoe was shot dead.
James Flynn (35) was previously tried at the Special Criminal Court where he denied a charge of conspiring to burgle cars at various locations in 2012 and 2013. It was alleged that he and others conspired to enter people’s homes to steal the keys to their cars and make off with the vehicles parked outside.
However, following his trial, the three-judge non-jury court found the charge was not proven but amended the indictment to find him guilty of conspiring to steal a Volkswagen Passat from a property in Clogherhead, Co Louth , between January 22nd and 23rd, 2013.
That Passat was used two days later in the robbery at Lordship Credit Union in Bellurgan, Co Louth, during which Donohoe, a married father of two, was shot dead by Aaron Brady .
Brady (35), of New Road, Crossmaglen, Co Armagh, is serving a life sentence with a 40-year minimum, having been found guilty in 2020 of the murder of Donohoe at the Lordship Credit Union.
In December 2023 the Special Criminal Court sentenced Flynn to eight years in prison, but two years later the Court of Appeal overturned the conviction . The court found that the decision to amend the indictment after Flynn’s trial had finished and without consulting the prosecution or defence legal teams was in breach of his right to natural justice.
The Court of Appeal went on to order a retrial on the original indictment for the wider conspiracy, having found the charge as amended by the Special Criminal Court had no “legal effect”.
[ Man pleads guilty to commissioning murder of Lee Slattery in 2010 Opens in new window ]
Flynn appealed to the Supreme Court opposing any retrial, arguing that the Court of Appeal decision to retry him on the original indictment was in breach of fair procedures.
The Supreme Court, in a unanimous judgment, said the Court of Appeal had erred in finding that the amended charge had “no legal effect”.
Delivering the judgment, Judge Brian O’Moore said it was legally permissible for the Director of Public Prosecutions to proceed with a retrial of Flynn on the amended charge related solely to the conspiracy to steal the Volkswagen Passat, but not for the wider conspiracy.
O’Moore said conspiracy to burgle was a serious charge, adding: “There is a clear public interest in a retrial that would decide the innocence or guilt of Mr Flynn.”
He ordered that Flynn be retried at the Special Criminal Court on the amended indictment of conspiracy to burgle on the dates of January 22nd and 23rd, 2013.

title: Aer Lingus general counsel denies ‘whitewash’ of alleged safety complaint
description: Evidence concludes in pilot’s marathon whistleblower action
content:
Aer Lingus’s senior in-house lawyer has denied acting to “whitewash” attempts by a pilot to complain about being subject to disciplinary action over calling in with fatigue.
Evidential hearings into Declan McCabe’s complaints under the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 and the Payment of Wages Act 1991 have now concluded after 15 days at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) .
The parties will meet once more in December for closing legal arguments.
McCabe was disciplined for what the airline deemed breaches of his air safety reporting obligations while flying in June 2023 in command of an Airbus A321XLR which failed to link up with a radio navigation beacon coming into Dublin Airport before making a turn to re-establish contact.
McCabe’s case is that the airline had no right to pursue a disciplinary process against him and that it was penalisation for complaining about another senior managing pilot, Captain Colm Wynne, having a safety management role in the airline, on foot of a previous dispute dating back to 2011.
Maebh Gallagher, now the airline’s general counsel, was the company secretary when McCabe brought up the 2011 matter again in 2023, - expressing concern to Aer Lingus chief executive Lynn Embleton that Wynne had taken an interest in the June 8th, 2023 flight.
McCabe’s evidence to the tribunal last December was that Wynne’s email to him some eight days after the flight was the first he had heard from Wynne in 12 years, following what the complainant called an “outrageous” disciplinary process over a decade prior.
This process began after he called in to say he was too fatigued to pilot an A320 jetliner on July 11th, 2011, something he was required to do as a licensed pilot, he said.
The WRC heard McCabe wrote to Embleton attaching 2016 correspondence about the alleged matters in 2011 as “background” to an objection to Wynne’s involvement.
He pointed out that a letter issued by then Aer Lingus chief pilot Davina Pratt dated September 15th, 2011 demoting him from captain to first officer and removing him from flight duties.
However, that disciplinary sanction was deferred while McCabe flew in command of a number of flights on September 15th and 16th , 2011 to destinations in Spain and the Netherlands, the letter added.
McCabe’s contention was that these flights were not compliant with European air safety regulations, invalidated the airline’s Air Operator Certificate, and constituted a “illegal public transport”, a breach of contract with passengers, and a “criminal act”, the letter continued.
Tom Mallon, for Aer Lingus, put the letter to Gallagher when she gave evidence on Friday before adjudicator John Harraghy.
She said she was on leave the first time the letter was sent in, but had considered it again when it was resubmitted in 2023.
She said a screening committee for protected disclosures in Aer Lingus had determined the matters to have been “fully examined and closed”, calling the issues raised “completely baseless and without merit”.
“It is, in substance a grievance, I explained that. It’s an attempt to breathe new life into something that he had raised years before which emerged from his dissatisfaction with the outcome of a disciplinary process,” she added later.
David Byrnes, for the complainant, put it to Gallagher in cross-examination that when McCabe went to the Irish Aviation Authority in 2016 with the same concerns, the regulator “accepted that they were protected disclosures”.
“I can’t speak to how the IAA triaged protected disclosures,” Gallagher said.
She said McCabe was “seeking to reframe” his unhappiness with the 2011 disciplinary sanction as a safety matter.
“It’s called a disclosure; it has to disclose something,” Gallagher said.
Byrnes said Gallagher, in her responses to McCabe, “tried to legalese [McCabe] out of the protected disclosures environment using your training and expertise as a solicitor” in her representations to the Aer Lingus protected disclosures committee.
“The core of his issue is he’s unhappy with the outcome of the disciplinary,” Gallagher said.
Byrnes put it to Gallagher later that his client complained about being subject to disciplinary action in relation to calling in with fatigue “and nothing else”.
“That is a protected act, and you whitewashed that,” he said.
“I don’t accept that, that’s not my evidence,” Gallagher said.
He said his client had approached Embleton with his concerns because she was “a new CEO” who “wasn’t around then” and there was a chance she would listen.
“You went and told the CEO there was nothing to see here,” Byrnes said.
In 2011, a process led by Wynne found McCabe had “shown a total disregard for the commercial interests of the company” and was “not of the standard of an Aer Lingus captain”, the complainant said. The sanction was reduced on appeal to a final written warning, and he recovered his lost pay in a settlement of a Circuit Court lawsuit, Mr McCabe said.
However, the complainant’s evidence was that he had “no comfort that I couldn’t call in fatigued again” and remained in fear of “retribution” from Wynne, who was subsequently promoted to flight operations safety manager.
Byrnes was led by Setanta Solicitors for the complainant, and Mallon by Arthur Cox LLP for the respondent.

title: Disney faces €63m refund demand after streaming service ‘downgrade’
description: Features of its premium Disney+ service have been switched off in certain countries over patent dispute
content:
Disney is facing calls to refund consumers across Europe up to €63 million after it removed some features of its premium subscription plan in response to a court ruling.
Campaign group Euroconsumers, along with Italy’s Altroconsumo, Belgium’s Testachats and Deco Proteste in Portugal , sent formal notice to the US entertainment giant requesting it repay subscribers to its premium streaming plan at least €5 a month.
The group, which represents seven million consumers, said subscribers paid for features they were not getting, such as 4K, HDR10 and Dolby Vision, which improve picture quality and viewing experience. Que Choisir in France has also issued a similar notice.
Disney+ was forced to temporarily disable 4K UHD, HDR10 and Dolby Vision for users in certain European countries as a result of a patent dispute over video compression technology.
The technologies offer different benefits to consumers: 4K UHD brings better resolution and greater detail in video; HDR improves the range between the brightest and darkest parts of the images; and Dolby Vision adjusts brightness and colour and supports higher colour depth.
The move left customers signed up to Disney+’s premium subscription tier in Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, Portugal, Romania and Sweden with lower-quality video than they were paying for.
The downgrade was only implemented on the streaming service, but viewers who downloaded content to watch offline were unaffected.
The consumer groups want Disney to reduce the price of its premium service immediately and repay subscribers at least €5 a month for loss of parts of the service.
If Disney agrees to the refund, it could cost the broadcaster up €63 million per month, with the cost of meeting the demand in Italy, Belgium and Portugal alone at €12 million.
The company has since begun reintroducing 4K in those countries, using an alternative technology unaffected by the patent ruling, but only for certain devices.
HDR and Dolby Vision remain largely unavailable to customers. Customers affected could downgrade their plans to the standard tier or apply for a part-refund.
Marco Scialdone from Euroconsumers said the measures did not adequately address the concerns raised.
“Our position is clear: consumers should not be required to pay the full premium price for a service that no longer provides all the advertised premium features. Any compensation should be proportionate to the actual degradation and should not depend on consumers having to pursue individual claims.”
The notice was sent on October 6th, with Disney given 14 days from receipt of the complaint to respond.
If Disney fails to take satisfactory action then Euroconsumers said it would file complaints with the European Union’s Consumer Protection Cooperation Network and pursue the company for fines of up to 4 per cent of its turnover in the affected countries.
“Based on our experience with comparable cases, we would reasonably expect to receive a response by mid-November,” Scialdone said.
“While it is difficult to predict how long a negotiated or regulatory resolution might take, we are determined to ensure that consumers’ rights are effectively protected and that any remedy reflects both the duration and the extent of the service degradation.”
Disney has almost 12.6 million subscribers paying for ad-free plans across the 11 affected EU countries.
The company, which launched the streaming service in 2019 before coming to Ireland in 2020, has steadily increased prices over the past few years, introducing an ad-supported tier and deals with Sky .

title: Conversations on a Homecoming: Frank McNally on returning to the Dáil after a 20-year absence
description: A return to the Dáil press gallery reveals new security arrangements, familiar political rituals and an enduring dress code
content:
A few readers might recall that during a former lifetime, back around the turn of the century, I used to write the Dáil Sketch twice a week.
But in the 20 years and five-and-a-bit months since becoming Irishman’s Diarist , I had never darkened the gate of Leinster House again until this week. And when I went back last Tuesday, for a sketching cameo , it was not without foreboding.
Irish literature is full of stories about long-delayed returns or homecomings, none of which end well. Anne Enright’s The Gathering, for example. Brian Friel’s Aristocrats. Oisín falling off the horse.
On the plus side, I didn’t feel 300 years older suddenly. Nor did I find the old house crumbling or get into any family rows.
But in some ways, the Dáil had changed beyond recognition in my decades away. Back in 2006, remember, Irish politics was still a two-and-a-half party system: the old Civil War combatants and Labour.
There was also a thing then called the Progressive Democrats – whatever happened to them? And the main opposition party, I seem to recall, was Joe Higgins. All that has been swept away. But in other ways, the place is the same as ever.
The Opposition still sits to the right of the Ceann Comhairle, the Government to the left. This differs not just from the British system but also the whole model of left-right representative democracy, as established in pre-revolutionary France, when the “Second Estate” (the nobility) sat to the King’s right.
Post-Revolution, the Jacobins sat on the left of the chamber, with moderates lower down (on the “plaine”) and radicals up at the back (the “montagne”). In the Dáil, the lefties are all still on the right.
As for the Fourth Estate, as Edmund Burke called it, the press remains where it always was too, seated on what looks like a choir balcony above the Ceann Comhairle’s head.
There, time is forever frozen circa 1993. Or so you would think from the brass nameplates indicating where each media outlet can sit. Featured titles include “The Irish Press” and the “Cork Examiner”. There is still no mention of “Joe.ie”.
[ Micheál Martin’s feathers ruffled by claims he is ‘playing chicken’ with striking workers Opens in new window ]
One alarming new development, as a colleague had warned, was that the gallery door is now permanently locked. You need a fob to get in and out, something not available to day trippers.
So one of the regular reporters had to let me in. Then I had to be careful not to be the last person left – as was often the case before – or I might still be there.
Mind you, unlike the public gallery, the press one is not glassed off. As always, there remains the emergency option of climbing over the desks and jumping down into the chamber, a route famously taken by three Workers Party TDs in 1982 when they found themselves locked out of the Dáil for a crucial vote.
The creaky floorboards of Leinster House haven’t changed either. And wandering through the corridors, with their low ceilings and high carpets, brought a familiar claustrophobia. This seems to have been a common experience even for distant former residents.
In 1794, the ill-fated Lord Edward Fitzgerald wrote home from what was then the family’s city residence complaining about how “melancholy” it seemed: “A poor country housemaid I brought with me [from Kildare] cried for two days and thought she was in prison.”
His sister, returning in 1812 after years of the house’s decline under the Act of Union, was dispirited at how cold and dark it had become. Finding her way by candlelight to the master bedroom, she complained it was “now more like a convent” than a nobleman’s house.
You wouldn’t mistake it for a convent today, if only because of the shortage of women. Still, there are more of those than there used to be: new paintings in the corridors since my last visit include one of 53 women TDs and senators.
Another ancient tradition that hasn’t changed is backbench TDs using the Order of Business debate to raise points of order that aren’t points of order, to the exasperation of the chair.
The prime example on Tuesday was Danny Healy-Rae – sitting up among the montagnards – drawing attention to the chaos caused on the roads of Kerry and elsewhere by wild deer mounting kamikaze attacks on traffic.
Also in keeping with tradition, the Ceann Comhairle had to slap him down verbally like a bold child, but not before he gained the usual 15 seconds of Oireachtas TV fame.
Speaking of which, yet another thing that hadn’t changed since my last visit is that male journalists are still required to wear a tie. Male TDs, meanwhile, can plead conscientious objection to such tyranny, as increasing numbers do.
But I didn’t take any chances, having learned my lesson years ago when dispatched to cover a mere Oireachtas committee meeting once. Rather than offend the dignity of the house with my open-necked shirt, I was banished to watch proceedings on a monitor in what felt like a broom cupboard.
[ Try walking in Patrick Kavanagh’s shoes: one man’s pilgrimage from Inniskeen to Dublin Opens in new window ]

title: Thousands march in Albanian capital as anti-government protests spread
description: Prime minister Edi Rama rejects calls to resign
content:
Thousands of young Albanians marched through Tirana ‌on Friday, breaking windows and traffic lights, on the fourth day of an increasingly violent student-led campaign to force prime minister Edi Rama to resign.
The demonstrations, which ​are spreading through the country, turned into a riot in the capital on Thursday, with protesters smashing windows, raiding a bank and clashing with police. They follow months of mostly peaceful demonstrations that the students say the government ignored.
“They are pushing us to the limits,” said Enea (19), declining to give a second name for ​fear of arrest. He said his message to Rama was: “To resign as fast as possible before everything burns down.”
The students accuse officials of corruption and neglecting education and say ⁠they are angry about the sale of pristine parts of Albania’s coast to a luxury resort development backed by US president ‌ Donald ‌Trump ’s ​son-in-law Jared Kushner .
The unrest is a challenge for Rama, who won a fourth term last year on promises to take Albania into the European Union and is aiming for membership as early as ⁠2028.
“We will not bow to violence,” he said on ​Facebook.
The students, many ​wearing masks, faced off against lines of riot police in front of the education ministry building. Some small businesses had their shutters down and ‌notes on their facades saying: “We are with you. Do ​not damage our business all over the town.”
In the coastal town of Lezha, police clashed with stone-hurling protesters. Protests have also spread ⁠to Elbasan, Skhodra and Korca, where demonstrators broke windows and ⁠set fire to rubbish bins, local ​media reported.
“We’ve been protesting peacefully for 140 days, and nothing was heard. So this is our only chance to be heard and get our rights that we deserve,” a 19-year-old protester who gave her name only as Klea said.
The demonstrations were sparked by the plans to build the resort, which has faced legal challenges.
[ Kushners’ €4bn Adriatic resort is snowballing into a political crisis Opens in new window ]
Political analyst Afrim Krasniqi said younger ⁠generations saw no future in Albania. “They see that all resources in the country, political resources, economic, everything is in the hands of oligarchs,” he told Reuters.
Corruption scandals have tarnished Albania’s image over the years and analysts say the country is ‌a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking, complicating its efforts to join the EU.
Along with Montenegro , Albania is leading the accession process ​among Balkan countries.
The unrest is part of a wave of student activism in Europe. In ​France, high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education. – Reuters
[ Jack Power: Is a happy ending in sight for the Albania-EU tale of unrequited love? Opens in new window ]

title: Katie Zacharia dismissed as White House press secretary after five days
description: Zacharia faced questions about whether she had misrepresented herself as a lawyer
content:
Katie Zacharia will no longer serve as US president Donald Trump ’s press secretary after spending less than a week on the job, thrusting the White House’s communications operation back into a state of chaos.
Zacharia was out of the role as of Friday, according to people familiar with the matter who requested anonymity to describe the decision before it was public. It is unclear if she will take another position in the White House or in Trump’s orbit.
Trump told reporters on Friday that he encouraged her to “reconsider” her position.
“I said to her, ‘honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,’” the president told reporters at the White House.
Zacharia’s tenure was rocky from the start. Her first and only press briefing was widely panned, as she spoke slowly and haltingly from prepared remarks and took questions from only three reporters.
She also faced a plethora of questions about whether she misrepresented herself as a lawyer, despite not passing the bar exam. Trump also called her “an attorney” in his social media post announcing her hiring.
Zacharia’s rapid rise and fall was remarkable, even by the standards of Trump’s White House. It hearkened back to Trump’s first term, when his staff was marked by constant turnover and turmoil. Then, White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci was fired after just 11 days in the role.
Zacharia’s efforts to defend herself also did not go smoothly. She faced tough questions about her legal background in a pair of interviews with Fox News, which is typically friendly to the administration.
In another sit-down with a conservative commentator, Zacharia made a disparaging comment about China lacking “proper toilets”.
The US president blamed what he described as unfair treatment from the news media for her troubles but still suggested the job might not be for her.
“I told her, I think you’re better off being happy and I’m not sure you can ever be happy in this job,” he said. “I said, Katie, ‘do you need this? I don’t think you need this.’”
When asked if he would force her out of the role, Trump replied that he is “talking about doing something” but that “I’m going to let her make that decision.”
The turmoil is taking place just over two weeks before the November midterm elections, in which Republicans are struggling to convince sceptical voters to stick with them amid their frustrations over the cost of living.
With Zacharia out, Trump is again left without a White House press secretary, an official who traditionally amplifies the president’s message in the news media.
Zacharia replaced Karoline Leavitt, a long-time Trump adviser who left as press secretary in August. It is unclear who will fill the role, or when that person would be appointed. – Bloomberg
[ Trump's new press secretary faces mounting questions over her legal credentials Opens in new window ]

title: Gardaí release description of man found dead in Mallow as investigation upgraded to murder
description: Garda Commissioner appeals for witnesses after body of man in his 50s found on Co Cork riverbank
content:
Gardaí in Mallow have begun a murder investigation following the discovery of the body of a man in Ballyellis, Mallow , Co Cork .
The body of Paul O’Connor (56) was discovered at 1.15pm on Thursday on the banks of the river Blackwater at a townland known as Ballyellis, which is on the edge of Mallow town on the Killavullen Road.
An incident room has been set up at Mallow Garda station and a senior investigating officer has been appointed. A family liaison officer has also been appointed.
The man’s body was removed from the scene and a postmortem examination was conducted by State Pathologist Margaret Bolster. Gardaí said the results were not being released for operational reasons.
The man was wearing a dark green hooded jacket, khaki-coloured combats and black runners. It is believed he travelled from Kent railway station, in Cork city, to Mallow station on Wednesday, arriving shortly after 7.20pm.
Gardaí are conducting house-to-house inquiries in the area. CCTV footage is also being gathered from local businesses and houses.
Officers are interested in speaking with anyone who was on the train between Cork Kent station and Mallow, arriving in Mallow shortly after 7.20pm on Wednesday.
They are also interested in speaking with anyone who was in the vicinity of Mallow town between 7.20pm on Wednesday and 1.30pm on Thursday and who may have seen the man.
Detectives also want to speak to anybody who may have been in the vicinity of the banks of the Blackwater at Ballyellis, close to Mallow Golf Club, between 7.20pm on Wednesday and 1.30pm on Thursday.
Any road users or pedestrians who were in the area and who may have camera footage are asked to make this footage available to gardaí.
Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said: “I’d ask anyone, members of the public out there, who have any information in relation to it, they should come forward.”
An examination of the scene by officers from the Garda technical bureau has taken place. Members of the Garda water unit also attended.
[ Net closing on gang that murdered family in Waterford, says Garda Commissioner Opens in new window ]
It is believed the remains, which were found on the Killavullen side of Mallow, were not in the area for a prolonged period.
Local Fine Gael councillor Liam Madden said his thoughts were with the relatives of the deceased.
“This poor person. They no doubt have a family. And you would have to think was the body just dumped there?” he said.
“I don’t know how we are going to combat [such crime]. Too many families are being affected. When you see what was done in Waterford [with the killing of four members of a family] this week, it is just unreal.”

title: Co Tipperary town told not to drink water due to excessive aluminium content
description: Ardfinnan residents angered by ongoing problems: ‘We simply want a safe and reliable water supply’
content:
A Tipperary town left without tap water following the discovery of high levels of aluminium is entering a second week of uncertainty over future safe supply.
Almost 11,500 residents of Ardfinnan and surrounding areas received warnings from Uisce Éireann last Friday night telling them not to drink the water under any circumstances.
It came after four months of being under a boil water notice because of concerns over possible bacterial contamination – a position they were also in for several months late last year.
[ Uisce Éireann pays performance-related bonus to 97% of staff Opens in new window ]
Local people are tiring of the recurring problems and want them fixed without delay.
“It has been a week from hell,” said local Independent Cllr Máirín McGrath.
She said last Friday’s notice was missed by many and followed by fears over what people had consumed.
“The communication was very poor and the first deliveries of bottled water were badly handled. People didn’t know if there was more to come or how long they’d be without, so there were people loading up cars with multiple five -litre drums and others left with nothing.”
Since then, Uisce Éireann has been regularly replenishing supplies of bottled and tankered water and delivering directly to the homes of vulnerable customers.
But upset remains over the repeated disruption and the length of time it is taking Uisce Éireann to upgrade the Goatenbridge Water Treatment Plant that serves the area.
Husband and wife Tom and Carmel O’Mahoney, owners of Tim’s Coffee Shop in Ardfinnan, took the decision to close out of concern for their customers’ health.
“My wife has found the whole situation particularly upsetting,” said Tom O’Mahoney. “Tim’s Coffee is a small community coffee shop ... She has worried about people who may have consumed the water, including pregnant customers ... The uncertainty has weighed heavily on her.”
Aluminium is used in water treatment to bind and draw out impurities, but at high levels it can be toxic, particularly to people with underlying health conditions and young children.
Uisce Éireann said, “process issues at Goatenbridge Water Treatment Plant caused intermittent spikes in aluminium levels in the water”.
This happened in “early September” and experts “worked hard to resolve the issue” but several automatic shutdowns followed.
To prevent further shutdowns and keep water flowing to homes and businesses for sanitation purposes, safety features had to be disabled so the water was no longer safe to consume.
It said it was in close consultation with the Health Service Executive throughout.
McGrath said the problems in early September should have been disclosed to the public. She obtained records under Freedom of Information that showed levels of aluminium well above EU and World Health Organisation limits in the weeks since then.
Uisce Éireann said it had now completed critical upgrades at the Goatenbridge plant.
[ Improving water system to cost €50bn, Uisce Éireann tells Oireachtas group Opens in new window ]
“With the works now complete, our teams will monitor the plant’s performance throughout the weekend,” it said.
“Comprehensive sampling is also under way at the plant and across the regional network. The results will provide the evidence needed to consult with the HSE and decide when the notice can be safely lifted.”
Tom O’Mahony said locals and businesses deserved better.
“We appreciate that problems can occur and that infrastructure works take time, but people need honest communication and realistic timelines. At present, we have neither,” he said.
“We’re not looking for sympathy. We simply want a safe and reliable water supply, clear communication, and some certainty so that businesses and staff can plan accordingly.”

title: European shares notch up strong week as earnings cushion tech sell-off
description: Irish index of shares ends week on positive note
content:
European shares rose on Friday to wrap up their best week since late June, during which strong earnings helped cushion a rout ‌in AI -linked stocks.
The Irish index of shares ended the week on a positive note, with the Euronext Dublin up 0.7 per cent to close near 14,188.
Kenmare Resources, is the subject of a potential bid by a company controlled by the Abu Dhabi royal family, saw its shares rise more than two per cent on Friday, bringing it to a total gain of almost 6 per cent over the week.
Banking shares also ended the week in positive territory. AIB rose 1.25 per cent to end the week at €10.95, a weekly gain of more than 1 per cent. Bank of Ireland , meanwhile, was 3.5 per cent up on the day, with a weekly gain of 2.75 per cent. Insurer FBD also notched up a gain, ending the week at €19.50.
Ryanair also gained on Friday, but the 1.56 per cent it added over Friday’s session was not enough to push it out of a weekly loss.
Food stocks were mixed, with Glanbia down almost 1 per cent while Kerry Group added almost half a per cent.
Insulation specialist Kingspan notched up a weekly loss of more than 3 per cent after Friday’s trade saw shares sink 2.6 per cent.
The ​export-heavy FTSE 100 closed 0.38 per cent higher at 10,881.90 points, logging a weekly gain of 3.1 per cent, the biggest since early April, while the midcap FTSE 250 gained 0.45 per cent.
Consumer staples supported ​gains. Cigarette maker British American Tobacco rose 2.1 per cent, while Johnnie Walker owner Diageo ‌gained 1.9 per cent
The beverages and ​medical equipment and services sectors advanced 7.8 per cent and 6.9 per cent, respectively, in the week.
Home builders jumped more than 6 per cent in ⁠the week but banks were muted on Friday, recovering from early losses triggered by a report that lenders were likely to be taxed in the budget
Defence stocks extended a strong run ‌on the day: BAE Systems and Babcock International rose 2.6 per cent and 3.6 per cent, respectively
The pan-European STOXX 600 index rose 0.7 per cent to 644.74 points, touching the highest in over three weeks. The benchmark was up more than 2 per cent for the week.
A sell-off in high-flying tech names on concerns over increased reliance on debt to develop ⁠AI infrastructure, alongside worries about competition from China, battered tech stocks this week.
However, strong results from computer ‌chip ‌equipment ​maker ASML, chip systems supplier Aixtron and telecom gear maker Ericsson have helped sentiment.
Aixtron advanced 6 per cent after beating ⁠order intake estimates for the ​third quarter and confirming annual guidance.
Nordex soared 12.3 per cent after the onshore wind turbine maker posted a better-than-expected third-quarter core profit and lifted its full-year margin forecast.
Schneider Electric shares reversed earlier gains and were last down 1.8 per cent after the industrial group raised its 2026 core profit and revenue targets for the second time.
Among other movers, Nestle gained 1.7 per cent after JPMorgan upgraded the Swiss food and drinks ‌group to an “overweight” rating.
The final stretch of a jittery week on Wall Street saw stocks falling amid a technology sell-off that has left investors questioning the prospects for the artificial-intelligence trade.
Tech weakness weighed on the S&P 500 despite gains in most of its shares. The Nasdaq 100 slipped 1.5 per cent.
CoreWeave sank 10 per cent, resuming a rout fuelled by worries over whether the massive buildout of AI infrastructure has outrun the ability of companies to get a return on their investments.
A renewed advance in oil prices also weighed on sentiment, lifting Treasury yields.
The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent in early afternoon trading in New York, with the Nasdaq 100 down 1.5 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was little changed. – Additional reporting: Reuters, Bloomberg

title: Man pleads guilty to commissioning murder of Lee Slattery in 2010
description: Family contacted gardaí when they came upon freshly dug grass and spotted the fabric of a blue tracksuit similar to one worn by Slattery
content:
A man has pleaded guilty to the commission of the murder of a man who was shot twice at close range and buried in a shallow grave in Limerick in 2010.
Kurt Ryan (33) went on trial at the Central Criminal Court in Cork earlier this month charged with the murder of Lee Slattery at Delmege Estate, Knocknalisheen Road, Limerick, in 2010.
However, Ryan, of Moylish Crescent in Limerick, was re-arraigned in front of the jury of seven women and five men on Friday.
He pleaded guilty to possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life on May 28th, 2010, at the Delmege Estate. He also pleaded guilty to the commission of a serious offence, namely murder, in association with a criminal organisation.
The particulars of the offence are that Ryan, who was 17 years old at the time, “did commit a serious offence, to wit, the murder of Lee Slattery, in association with a criminal organisation.”
Michael O’Higgins, prosecuting, said Slattery, who was 25 years old when he was killed, was not a member of an organised criminal gang.
He told Judge Eileen Creedon it was accepted Slattery was “well-liked”. He stated there was “no basis for the killing”, adding the deceased was “wrongly singled out”.
Brian McInerney, defending, said Ryan’s plea was “valuable”. He asked that the case be listed for sentencing in Limerick. The judge said the pleas entered by Ryan were acceptable to the DPP.
She said she had some practical difficulties in relation to holding a sentencing hearing in Limerick.
However, she listed the case for mention in the Central Criminal Court in Dublin on October 27th, when a date for the sentencing hearing will be fixed.
The jury at the trial heard the body of the deceased was discovered on May 31st, 2010. His family were concerned for his welfare as they had not seen him in four days.
His brother Ray, his uncle and two friends went looking for him on the Delmege estate, which had fallen into a state of dereliction.
Ray Slattery said they contacted gardaí when they came upon freshly dug grass, poked around in it, and spotted the fabric of a blue tracksuit similar to the one worn by Slattery.
Retired detective sergeant Shane Curran, who was part of the murder investigation, said Slattery was found in a grave on rough ground “face down in a crouched position, knees bent”.
He said one of the gardaí in the search of the wider area alerted him to an item concealed in a sock close to the roof of a disused outbuilding.
“The sock contained a semi automatic pistol ... a nine-millimetre Star model semi-automatic pistol,” he said.
Then-State pathologist Marie Cassidy carried out the postmortem examination. She recovered a bullet from his right arm.
Her evidence was that he died of a gunshot wound which pierced his heart and lungs. She said it appeared Slattery was dead when he was put in to what was described as a trench. He had two gunshot injuries.
One penetrated the body to cause his death, going through his left arm, continuing in to his body, injuring his lung and heart and continuing in to his right arm.
The other bullet grazed the skin and did not cause internal injuries.
O’Higgins said in his outline of the case that Slattery sold drugs to support his drug habit, while Ryan, who was then 17, was also dealing drugs in the area.
Evidence was also heard at the trial that Ryan called to Slattery’s home when he was missing. Ryan said Slattery owed him €80 for drugs and that he was concerned not to see him around.
The killing was reopened by a cold case unit in 2021.

title: Farm labourer who worked 77-hour weeks for as little as €6.83 an hour is awarded €23,000
description: Workplace Relations Commission orders compensation for unpaid wages and rights breaches
content:
A farm labourer who worked 77-hour weeks for as little as €6.83 an hour during calving season at a Co Westmeath dairy farm has been awarded nearly €23,000 for employment rights breaches.
Edward Lattich was awarded the sum in orders for unpaid wages and leave entitlements and as compensation for workplace rights breaches on foot of complaints against his ex-employer, Mount Temple Dairy Farm Ltd in Co Westmeath .
Lattich, representing himself at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC), said took up work with the company as a full-time farm labourer on December 10th, 2024, with a view to gaining experience in dairy farming.
His evidence was that in his first month, he typically started work at 8am and worked to 6pm or 7pm each workday.
His working hours increased in January last year as preparations for calving season began, when he started work at 5.30am and remained there until 8pm or 9pm, he said.
He worked “every day of the week”, he said, with just one day off in January 2025 due to illness and another the following month due to extreme weather, he said.
The 5.30am to 9pm working day continued until the end of his employment on April 21st, 2025, Lattich said.
His evidence was that his pay was fixed at €2,500 a month “regardless of hours worked” and that he suffered “illegal” pay deductions as a result.
It meant his pay was as low as €6.83 an hour in March 2025, according to the findings of fact by the WRC in the case, which noted that Lattich worked at least 366 hours that month.
Although he said in evidence that he did not typically get breaks, he presented a spreadsheet calculating his working hours to the WRC which referred to a 30-minute daily break, the commission said.
He said he had worked 192 hours in December 2024, more than 353 hours in each month from January to March 2025 and 199 hours in April when he resigned.
Kelvin Hyland, for the respondent, argued that Lattich was “a keen young individual willing to gain experience in the dairy sector”, whom the farm had taken on to “learn in the role within a mutually beneficial environment”.
Lattich had agreed to a “set wage” when he started, it was stated. The employer’s position was that Lattich “did not receive the national minimum wage for each hour worked during his employment”, but this was because the complainant’s employment covered only “the busy period without the quieter period serving to reduce the overall hours worked”.
Hyland said the complainant’s working hour calculations were disputed. While the employer accepted the start times presented by Lattich, its position was that Lattich had two full hours of unpaid breaks each day and had meals at the farm.
“At the end of the working day, the complainant would socialise with the family, often remaining for dinner,” it was argued. There was no work done and this was “purely social in nature”, it was stated.
Lattich disputed this and said he was working on these occasions. He also disputed the length of the claimed two-hour breaks.
Although Lattich was required to work every second Sunday, he frequently came in on Sundays and days off “of his own volition” and got to work without being instructed to do so, it was stated.
The WRC noted the evidence of one unidentified respondent witness who said she had told Lattich to go home on a number of occasions. The complainant showed “no motivation” to leave and simply stayed on the premises, it was also stated.
There were also payments for fuel and services carried out on Lattich’s own farm, it was also argued.
The respondent accepted it owed Lattich wages of €4,268.07 and conceded certain breaches of the Organisation of Working Time Act in respect of Sunday pay and annual leave.
Adjudicator Brian Dolan favoured the complainant’s working time calculations, noting it was the respondent’s duty to keep working time records and that this was not done.
He said it did not stand to reason that two-hour breaks would be permitted during days on the farm. It was “not plausible”, he said, that Lattich, being a man with a young family, would spend “excessive time socialising at his place of work”.
Dolan said in his findings that Lattich’s average working week was 77 hours over the course of his employment.
He found that Lattich was underpaid by €10,420.13 during his employment and awarded that sum under the Payment of Wages Act 1991.
Further orders in relation to the non-payment of a Sunday premium, annual leave and public holiday entitlements, along with the failure to give Lattich his terms of employment in writing, brought the total awarded to €22,928.

title: Gen Z protesters are pouring on to India’s streets as dissent surges. What comes next?
description: Gen Z protesters are pouring on to India’s streets as dissent surges. What comes next?
content:
F or the first time in 12 years, Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s political invincibility faces a serious, enduring challenge from large numbers of Generation Z protesters and a resurgent Opposition, now united in taking to the streets to protest alleged electoral malpractice.
Tens of thousands of disaffected young Indians have rallied under the banner of the satirical Cockroach Janata (People’s) Party or CJP, formed in May after Chief Justice Surya Kant likened the country’s unemployed youths to “cockroaches”. Thereafter, the CJP tapped into anger over endemic unemployment and an education system seen as failing their generation.
Its July protests in central New Delhi over widespread irregularities in government medical college entrance exams taken by millions forced education minister Dharmendra Pradhan out of office – the first such departure from Modi’s cabinet since 2014.
The CJP has now joined opposition parties in protests across Delhi over a September Indian Express newspaper investigation that exposed internal dissent within the Election Commission of India (ECI) and alleged voter-roll manipulation to favour Modi’s ruling Hindu-nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in key state elections. The protests have since spread nationwide.
What exactly are these protesters demanding?
They are calling for the immediate resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, accusing him of overseeing a politically motivated voter-list review launched in 2025 — off–cially termed the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — at –he behest of Modi and his powerful home minister, Amit Shah.
The demonstrators allege that Kumar unilaterally oversaw the deletion of over 130 million names from voter rolls, without consulting his two fellow election commissioners, to favour the BJP at the hustings. The ECI denies all political manipulation, maintaining that the SIR was intended to remove the names of deceased or untraceable voters and eliminate duplicate entries.
Is this a turning point in Modi’s political fortunes?
Speculation about the imminent downfall of his BJP-led government is premature, given its comfortable parliamentary majority, but the protesters have dealt a rude blow to Modi’s aura of invincibility and omnipotence. For a PM accustomed to setting and dominating the political agenda, being forced on to the defensive over the integrity of the electoral process that brought him to office is no small setback – and could eventually prove politically calamitous for Modi.
Another measure of relief for the government is the legal protection Kumar enjoys under a 2023 law passed by the BJP government, granting him immunity from prosecution for all acts performed in his official capacity. Removing him would require a lengthy parliamentary process that the opposition lacks the numbers to initiate successfully, leaving voluntary resignation as the sole route to his early departure.
More protests, it seems. The leader of the cockroach youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday as authorities cracked down on fresh antigovernment protests in the Indian capital.
Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in central Delhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag.
India’s supreme court will eventually have a deciding say in this dispute, as legal challenges over the voters’ revision persist. But the larger political battle will focus on whether the government and the ECI can restore public confidence in the electoral process and conversely, whether the opposition and the CJP can convert street anger into sustained political pressure on the government.
[ The unlikely rise of India’s Gen Z rebels Opens in new window ]

title: Another EU summit overshadowed by Ukraine
description: Inside Politics: Another public scolding from belligerent Trump for Volodymyr Zelenskiy; and 15 years for Donaldson
content:
Another week for Volodymyr Zelenskiy and another public scourging by US president Donald Trump , who really seems to hate him. Trump and his cronies again dialled up the rhetoric on the Ukrainian president, only a week after hypocritically striking a deal with Russian president Vladimir Putin to buy his country’s diesel .
The sting in the tail has been the apparent suspension by the US of its policy to share satellite intelligence with the Ukrainian military, to help defend itself against aerial attacks from Russia. The upshot is that Russia has been able to launch its jet-propelled drones at targets in Ukraine with impunity.
Trump and others called for an election in Ukraine, suggesting dictatorial tendencies on the part of Zelenskiy while completely ignoring the fact that Putin has been in a position of unassailable power for 27 years.
The EU has stood four-square behind Ukraine and has pledged vast resources. But Trump’s impetuous decision to withdraw satellite intel shows the real power balance in geopolitics right now.
As Jack Power reports from Brussels, Micheál Martin said on Friday that urgent actions would be needed to shore up the finances needed for Ukraine’s war effort.
He said some sort of “pan-European financial injection” would be required to cover Ukraine’s budget shortfall.
Martin said he was “open” to different ways the EU could finance such support. “We would look at all options for how we can support Ukraine,” he said.
To use a phrase synonymous with the North, the awful and horrendous truth about former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson – as disclosed by his victims who were children when sexually assaulted by him – is an “appalling vista”.
Freya McClements and Seanín Graham reported on the sentencing hearing for one of the most prominent and high-ranking unionist politicians over the span of 40 years.
Donaldson presented himself in public as a devout Christian and a sober, upstanding family man. But the truth was awful.
Yesterday, he was sentenced to 15 years in prison for one count of rape, 13 counts of indecent assault and four counts of gross indecency. He is likely to serve at least 7½ years in prison.
Donaldson was knighted for political services in 2016 and became DUP leader in 2021, before resigning in 2024. He was stripped of his knighthood in July.
Our Inside Politics Wrap of the Week is here .
Pat Leahy and Jack Horgan-Jones will have a substantial report on Minister for Culture and Media Patrick O’Donovan . The Limerick TD was taken to hospital this week after becoming ill at an EU conference in Limerick.
As Power reported on Thursday, O’Donovan remains in intensive care .
It is understood he is being cared for in University Hospital Limerick . He was hospitalised after being taken ill while hosting an informal meeting of EU telecoms ministers.

title: Zelenskiy no longer willing to placate Trump
description: Asked if Trump had made him a scapegoat for the Iran war energy crisis, the Ukrainian leader gave a knowing smirk
content:
Volodymyr Zelenskiy is in no mood to grovel or pretend he thinks Donald Trump knows best any more.
“We will keep living, fighting ... When it is so horrific during a war, it is so important that you preserve your dignity,” the Ukrainian president told a room packed by the European press corps in Brussels on Friday.
The US president’s attempt to force Zelenskiy into halting strikes on Russian oil refineries – by restricting the flow of vital US military intelligence and access to satellite networks – has caused a fresh rupture between Washington and Kyiv.
This row is perhaps more damaging than Trump’s televised Oval Office dressing down of the Ukrainian leader early last year.
The Ukrainians were blindsided last week when Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel , which will involve easing some US sanctions on Moscow.
Ukraine’s access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite system was also temporarily restricted, limiting its ability to shoot down Russian drones.
“We cannot accept diesel deals because then there will be gas agreements, sanctions will be lifted, then this will come to the banking system, certain individuals, chemicals industry,” Zelenskiy told reporters.
This all may mark the beginning of a new, volatile and uncertain break in what had already been a very strained relationship. The White House had been one of Kyiv’s greatest supporters under the Biden administration.
The stakes are nothing short of the “annihilation” of Ukraine, Zelenskiy said on Friday.
[ Pope Leo asks Putin for ceasefire to allow aid to occupied Ukrainian town Opens in new window ]
If Vladimir Putin only had designs on occupying the eastern Donbas region, why, asked Zelenskiy, did Russia’s invading army try to take the capital Kyiv at the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022?
Ukraine’s air defences are depleted and it is short of US-made Patriot interceptors that can shoot down the ballistic missiles and new jet-powered drones hitting cities and infrastructure.
Ukraine is also grappling with a huge budget shortfall for 2027 which is approaching €70 billion , a hole EU leaders will need to help plug.
Those European allies were the reason Zelenskiy was in town to join a summit to discuss the war. “I heard from our European colleagues support and only support,” he told a press conference afterwards.
Had Trump made him a scapegoat for the global energy crisis triggered by the US war in Iran? Zelenskiy paused, thought about it, and then gave a silent, knowing smirk. “This is my answer,” he said, drawing a big laugh.
At least the entertainer turned wartime leader hasn’t lost his sense of comedic timing.

title: Businesses and producers urged to take stand against staggering level of Irish food waste
description: Government-backed declaration calls for sharing instead of dumping surplus food
content:
Ireland is throwing away so much surplus food that saving just three per cent of it could provide 50 million meals annually, according to a new Government-backed initiative.
The initiative, which is called Declaration on Surplus Food Sharing and Redistribution, urges food businesses, farmers, charities and public agencies to collectively take a stand against food waste.
It builds on the work of FoodCloud , the Irish charity that links food producers and outlets with people in need to ensure surplus food is not wasted.
In Ireland last year, FoodCloud redistributed more than 4,000 tonnes of food – the equivalent of 10 million meals – that would otherwise have gone to waste. The charity, though, says much more could be achieved.
“We have about 708,000 tonnes of food waste in Ireland every year,” said Angela Ruttledge, FoodCloud’s head of policy.
“It won’t all be edible but a lot of it would be and a lot more of it should be shared and redistributed.”
The Departments of Environment and Agriculture agree and are asking not only for more concerted efforts in Ireland, but globally.
They intend launching the declaration at next month’s Cop31 climate summit to encourage other governments to take the problem more seriously.
“By turning surplus food into a resource rather than a waste, we can advance climate action, strengthen food security and accelerate the transition to a circular economy,” said Minister for the Environment Darragh O’Brien .
Surplus food comes from a range of sources, including farmers with more produce than they are contracted to supply or with fruit and vegetables that don’t fit the specific size or shape a buyer demands.
“Often they have little choice but to plough it back into the soil,” Ruttledge said. “It needs to be made feasible for them to link in with a redistribution network.
“We also have food manufacturers, restaurants and other food outlets with surplus food and it needs to be an easy choice for them to pass it on.
“A lot of effort went into encouraging them to separate food waste for composting rather than dumping it in the bin, so we realise it’s asking them to take another step to make it available for redistribution instead. But if there’s a good system in place, it would support them.
“We got that system in place for retailers and that’s working really well now.”
The declaration was launched at the inaugural Food Sharing Summit in Dublin on Friday on what is designated annual World Food Day to mark the anniversary of the establishment of the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organisation.
Food businesses such as Aldi, Ballymaloe, BWG, Lidl, O’Brien Fine Foods, Musgrave and Tesco were among the first to sign the declaration at the event.

title: Lions player Hyron Andrews found dead before Champions Cup game against La Rochelle
description: SA Rugby said Andrews fell at hotel in tragic accident as squad will play on Saturday to honour teammate
content:
Tributes have been paid to Johannesburg Lions’ Hyron Andrews after he died in the team hotel on the eve of their Champions Cup game against La Rochelle.
Andrews (31) who also played for the KZN Sharks and Sale Sharks, could not be revived by emergency services after the alarm was raised at the Atalante-Relais Thalasso hotel on the Île de Ré. A statement from SA Rugby said the lock forward had “passed away tragically” after an accident in which he fell.
“This is terrible and distressing news; our hearts go out to Hyron’s family and the whole Lions rugby community,” said Mark Alexander, president of the South African Rugby Union in a statement released after Andrews’ family had been contacted.
“There are no words to adequately convey our shock and the depth of sympathy we feel for his wife Maighlin, and for his extended family, friends, teammates and loved ones during this time of immense sorrow.
“Hyron was a respected member of the rugby community whose contribution to the game and impact on those around him will be remembered with great fondness.
“His untimely passing is a devastating loss, and we share in the grief of all who knew and loved him.”
The Lions had been preparing to make their debut in the top-tier tournament on Saturday having flown to Europe after a heavy 57-15 defeat by the Bulls, their South African rivals. The squad has chosen to fulfil the fixture in honour of their teammate.
European Professional Club Rugby, the tournament organisers said: “In memory of Hyron, a moment’s silence will be held ahead of every Investec Champions Cup and EPCR Challenge Cup match this weekend.”
Andrews, who was born in Paarl and attended Hoërskool Garsfontein in Pretoria, also represented the Junior Springboks in 2015.
The Lions posted an emotional tribute on Instagram, saying: “It is with broken hearts that we mourn the passing of Hyron Andrews, a valued member of our Lions family. Our deepest condolences are with Maiglin, Hendrix, Emerson and the entire Andrews family during this incredibly difficult time.
“Rest in peace, Hyron. You will always be part of our family.”
Sale reflected on the loss of a “much-loved member” of their squad, who had stayed on past his initial short-term deal through to the end of the 2025-26 campaign, making 45 appearances.
“Hyron was just a brilliant guy and a brilliant team-mate. He was so skilled on the field, but off it, he was always someone you would want to have a beer with,” Sharks’ director of rugby Alex Sanderson told the club’s website.
“He was funny and charismatic in his own unique, dry way and the lads, to a man, loved playing with him and being around him. It was a big move for Hyron and his wife Maighlin to come to England but he truly made a second home in Manchester and it was incredible to see how he and his family embraced the club and area.”
The tragic situation comes on the 10th anniversary of the death of the Munster coach Anthony Foley in a Paris hotel room in 2016. Foley, who was 42, died in his sleep on the eve of a European tie against Racing 92 after a heart condition caused fluid to build up in his lungs.
La Rochelle head coach Ronan O’Gara was part of Racing 92’s coaching team at the time of Foley’s death and is believed to be in his way to the Lions team hotel to offer condolences and show support.
Tributes are due to be paid to him before this weekend’s game against Racing in Cork, with the Munster players set to wear commemorative presentation jackets featuring the club crest and the number eight, Foley’s position. – Guardian

title: UniCredit close to completing takeover of Commerzbank after ECB green light
description: The German federal government still holds a 12% stake, a hold-over from the 2009 banking crisis
content:
German finance minister Lars Klingbeil has called for “constructive talks” between Commerzbank and UniCredit, hours after the European Central Bank (ECB) gave the green light for the Italian takeover of Germany’s second-largest bank.
Klingbeil’s remarks marked a dramatic change of tone on a takeover that, last July, he called an “unacceptable ... aggressive and hostile” bid.
Two years after UniCredit initially launched its takeover plan for the bank, Klingbeil met UniCredit chief executive Andrea Orcel for the first time last month. In the mid-September meeting, Klingbeil insisted UniCredit retain Frankfurt as the Commerzbank headquarters and protect the bank’s 40,000 employees.
Those demands, in reality requests, reflect Berlin fears that an Italian job cull to boost profitability will diminish Frankurt’s status as a financial hub and endanger access to financing by Germany’s small and medium-sized business – to date a Commerzbank speciality.
The German federal government still holds a 12 per cent stake, a hold-over from the 2009 banking crisis when it bought 295 million shares in Commerzbank, equivalent to a 25 per cent stake in the ailing institution.
Many suggest Berlin helped trigger Unicredit’s takeover bid in February 2025 after selling the Italian institution a stake of 5 per cent from its holding just five months previously.
On Friday, Germany’s finance min is ter said on the sidelines of the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok that the German government’s position on Commerzbank – on its location, staffing levels and SME focus – was “well known”.
Klingbeil added that, after a “very constructive start” in talks to Orcel a month ago, he “did not perceive any hardened fronts, but believe that all these things could be handled well together”.
Since Milan-based UniCredit officially launched its takeover offer, the Commerzbank share price has doubled. Throughout the battle, the Commerzbank board rejected the Italian offer as financially inadequate, arguing it offers neither an adequate premium for Commerzbank shareholders nor a firm future plan for the bank.
In March 2026, UniCredit announced a €35 billion unsolicited share exchange offer which closed in July. The Italian bank said almost 18 per cent additional Commerzbank shares had been tendered in that process, largely from institutional investors, a purchase requiring regulatory approval.
This approval, granted by the ECB on Thursday, has given UniCredit access to close to 48 per cent of voting rights.
UniCredit said late on Thursday that the ECB authorisation to cross the 30 per cent ownership threshold in Commerzbank allowed it now “to increase its stake further without upper limits”.
It has vowed to take control of Commerzbank by the end of the year after completing the “remaining regulatory processes and conditions” relating to its bid.
In a note to shareholders, Commerzbank insisted that “even with its future stake, UniCredit cannot unilaterally decide on fundamental structural measures”.
“This requires qualified majorities of 75 per cent ... as well as appropriate safeguards for minority shareholders in each case,” it added.
After UniCredit bought the Bavarian HypoVereinsBank (HVB) in 2005, it underwent a radical restructuring, selling subsidiaries and cutting its workforce by more than half to around 9,000.

title: ‘Physically we live here, but mentally we live in Ukraine’: Envoy on Russia’s attack on hometown
description: The home of ambassador Larysa Gerasko’s aunt was destroyed in an assault on Pryluky that killed 22 people
content:
O n the night of October 7th, the town of Pryluky, 150km east of Kyiv, was hit by Russian cruise missiles.
The cruise missiles were not aimed at military targets. One of them slammed into a five-storey block of apartments, killing 18 people in their beds, including three children.
Pryluky is the hometown of the Ukrainian ambassador to Ireland, Larysa Gerasko.
A missile crashed into her aunt’s back garden, destroying her home while she was asleep inside.
“It was around 7am. She woke up to the sound of an explosion and rubble falling down from the roof. It’s a miracle she survived,” Gerasko says.
A whole family, neighbours of her parents, were wiped out in the attack on apartments in the neighbourhood where she grew up.
Her hometown has been targeted before by the Russians, but not with such a loss of life.
Gerasko wakes up many times at night to check Telegram channels to see which places are being attacked. Most Ukrainians living in Ireland do the same.
“Physically we live here, but mentally we live in Ukraine. It’s more painful when it’s personal,” she says.
Ukrainians are facing into a grim winter. The Russians have stepped up their attacks against civilians and against energy infrastructure night after night.
US president Donald Trump has completed a deal with Vladimir Putin to allow Russian diesel back on to the world market .
Without US support, Ukrainian air defence missiles have become depleted and there is doubt about the continuation of US intelligence-sharing. More Russian missiles and drones are getting through and reaching their targets.
The purpose of these attacks against civilians is to intimidate ordinary Ukrainian, the ambassador says. It is a tactic, she believes, that is bound to fail.
“They want to encourage ordinary people to give up or to pressurise the government to surrender,” she says.
“It doesn’t work like that. The resilience and the resistance of Ukrainians is very strong. Putin and Russians, even now, don’t understand that for us, in the case of occupation, Ukraine would be eliminated and exterminated.
“We know the price. None of us want to live under a dictatorship. I grew up in Soviet times. I know what it means to grow up in a closed autocratic country.”
More than 120,000 Ukrainian refugees arrived in the State after the Russian invasion in February 2022 and, as of June, about 85,000 have stayed.
The number of Ukrainians seeking refugee in Ireland slowed dramatically at the start of last year, but Gerasko says the relentless targeting of civilians by Russia is likely to lead to an upsurge of Ukrainians wishing to leave the country.
Some are moving to rural Ukraine for the winter to escape the bombings, but others will not have that choice.
“Those who still live in Ukraine don’t want to leave the country because they have a job or business or family,” she says.
“They want to stay in Ukraine as long as they can, but what I hear from Ukrainians is that those who have children want to leave.”
She suggests there should be an end to tourist visas for Russians within the EU. If Russians believe Europe is the enemy, they should “stay in Russia and enjoy the Russian style of life”.
She asks about Russian people living in Ireland protesting against their own country’s invasion of Ukraine.
“I met two of them in 2022 and that’s all I have seen in nearly five years. I don’t remember any Russians joining the protests outside the Russian embassy,” she says.
She wants an end to the May 9th celebrations in Ireland when people from the former Soviet Union gather in cavalcade to celebrate the defeat of Nazi Germany. She says it amounts to a pro-Russian rally.
She has raised it with the Department of Justice and the Garda Commissioner every year since the invasion.
“I always received the same answer. It is about freedom of speech. I respect freedom of speech and assembly, but you have to go to draw the line between freedom and propaganda,” she says.
The ambassador says she is “very disappointed” with the attitude of the Irish Government towards Aughinish Alumina following revelations in The Irish Times earlier this year that alumina produced in the Co Limerick factory was ending up in the supply chain feeding the Russian war machine.
A Government investigation proved inconclusive and the matter is with the European Commission.
To Ukraine, Aughinish is a “black and white issue, it is clear”, says Gerasko.
You cannot distinguish between military and civilian use of Aughinish’s exports to Russia, she argues. “It’s impossible technically to exclude Irish alumina from other alumina,” says the ambassador.
She compares it to deciding which grain from which barley harvest goes into a bottle of whiskey.
