title: Victoria Beckham’s new homeware range is just what every dinner table needs
description: What is on offer from Brand Beckham’s new collaboration? Fancy stuff for the table, in short, with several nods to bygone days
content:
Brand Beckham is steadfastly relentless in its expansion. Fashion, sportswear, spirits, perfume, Netflix and an upcoming skincare line called Harlo by Harper from 15-year-old Harper Beckham. But before that launch, Victoria, mother of all the Beckhams – the estranged Brooklyn , Romeo, Cruz and young Harper – has whipped out a homeware line.
She has collaborated with the European design retailer Westwing to produce it. “I wanted everything to feel refined, but never overly formal. There’s an ease in the way the pieces live together,” Victoria Beckham said in a product launch statement. “Home is where some of life’s most meaningful moments happen, and this collaboration felt like a natural way to explore that world through the same lens of design, craftsmanship and attention to detail that defines everything we do.”
So what is on offer from Victoria Beckham’s collection with Westwing? Fancy stuff for the table, in short, with several nods to bygone times.
For most people these days, when you say the word “charger” they think of the object you plug your phone into to top up its battery life. But long before mobile phones, there were chargers for tables. Large round, decorative pieces designed to sit beneath dinner plates, much like a version of an upscale table mat. Beckham’s Westwing chargers are made of clear glass and cost £57.99 for a set of two. Not to be mistaken for plates, which have the advantage of being suitable to eat from directly.
And in days of yore, there was a time when people – let’s be honest, almost definitely women – made butter pats shaped into curls for dinner parties. These were presented on small scallop-shaped gold or silver-plated dishes. The Westwing scallop-shaped butter dishes are stainless steel and come in a set of two, along with two dinky little knives, and cost £119.
There are wine glasses, champagne coupes, water glasses, stainless steel cutlery, napkins (white) and tablecloths (white). In case you were wondering, everything in the porcelain line is also white: plates big and small, pasta dishes and serving platters. The porcelain has a name too, the Dover line.
“Victoria Beckham’s signature chain motif takes on a new expression across our Dover collection of plates,” the Westwing website says. Signature chain motif? It was, the blurb continues: “Originally inspired by the strap of a vintage watch belonging to Victoria’s husband, the motif has become a recurring detail across her fashion and accessories collections. Here, its graphic quality creates a striking contrast with the softer, organic forms of the collection.”
So now you know. From a simple vintage watch strap, a fashion, accessories and now homeware brand was inspired.
The reaction to the homeware brand has been thus far positive. Homes & Gardens said that her collection: “Is a study in runway refinement translated for the dinner table.”
House Beautiful enthused: “Victoria Beckham’s new high-street homeware collection looks as luxurious as her clothing designs.”
Harper’s Bazaar (surely some kind of ready-made future platform for Harper Beckham?) said: “Victoria Beckham just launched her first-ever homeware range and it’s perfect for party season.”
So Victoria Beckham now has created a fashionable collection for an elegant family dinner. Including the chargers you don’t plug in.

title: Swords Express operator says it would cost up to €7m to provide off-site housing for staff
description: Company is appealing Fingal council’s to refuse planning retention for modular accommodation at depot
content:
The operator of the Swords Express has told An Coimiúsin Pleanála (ACP) that providing off-site housing for its mainly foreign-national workforce would cost the company between €6 million and €7 million in capital costs and €250,000 in annual recurring charges.
In an appeal to ACP against Fingal County Council ’s decision to refuse planning retention for its modular staff accommodation at its north Dublin depot, planning consultant for Eirebus Ltd, Peter Thomson, said such an outlay “would render the company economically non-viable”.
Last month the council refused a three-year planning retention application for 19 modular accommodation units and six mobile-home units at the depot at Corduff Road, Dublin 15, after finding that the units’ layout and arrangement “represent a serious form of substandard residential living”.
In Thomson’s 11-page submission he told ACP the company was seeking the planning retention for the units in the context of a housing crisis “where there is a chronic shortage of housing for rent in the area”.
Thomson said the workers’ on-site accommodation was “essential” to sustain the existing transport business on the site “and without it the business potentially becomes uneconomical and unviable”.
Eirebus employs 92 workers and has 70 buses on the road.
[ Fingal County Council refuses planning retention for Eirebus modular units Opens in new window ]
Thomson said the foreign-national workers on arrival into Ireland were not in a financial position to buy a vehicle or rent accommodation.
He told ACP that when numbers of overseas workers for Eirebus were low, the company was able to procure local accommodation.
However, due to the increased numbers, the company would require 12 three-bedroom homes or 18 two-bedroom homes.
Thomson said Eirebus and other companies in similar circumstances felt strongly that the only way they could continue to honour their public service commitments was to provide residential accommodation on site.
Sixty-eight members of the Eirebus workforce are foreign nationals and 43 of them benefit from the on-site accommodation.
The planning appeal said the foreign-national workers were recruited from India , Pakistan , Bangladesh and Nepal and “their accommodation needs have to be carefully managed to avoid ethnic tensions”.
Thomson said the three-year planning retention was required and would allow the applicant to look at alternative longer-term accommodation solutions.

title: US group buys largest Irish GP practice network in deal worth about €350m
description: Centric Health operates 90 primary care clinics across the Republic with 420 GPs
content:
Centric Health, the largest player in the Irish primary healthcare market, has agreed a deal that will see it acquired by a US affiliate of Bon Secours Mercy Health , Healthspan Partners.
Founded in Ireland in 2003 by Dr Maurice Cox and Dr Ray Power, with just one practice in Phibsborough, north Dublin, in 2004, it has since expanded and now operates out of 90 locations across the State, with services provided by 420 GPs to more than 700,000 patients.
It established the VHI SwiftCare clinics in 2005 in a joint venture with VHI before those clinics were bought outright by the insurer in 2017.
Since 2018, the business has been owned by Five Arrows, the alternative assets arm of Rothschild & Co. Cox retains a minority stake.
No price has been disclosed by either side in the transaction but industry sources said Healthspan would have paid in the region of €350 million for the fast-growing Irish business.
The deal is subject to approval by the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) and other relevant regulatory authorities.
Bon Secours already runs a number of hospitals in Ireland in Dublin, Cork, Galway, Limerick and Tralee, Co Kerry.
Centric expanded into the Netherlands, where it now has 11 practices, in 2020 and Germany the following year. There are 23 clinics in Germany. However, Ireland continues to account for the vast majority of its business.
In the most recent accounts available, Centric had a private client turnover of €76.2 million in 2024, plus another €67.6 million in medical card business, for a total of €143.9 million, up 13.5 per cent on the previous year. Of that, 80 per cent was generated in the Irish market.
Cox will remain chief executive of the business under the new owners and a shareholder in the business.
“We have significant ambitions for the future and have been looking for the right partner to help us achieve our goals,” he said.
“Healthspan Partners is the perfect partner as it brings expertise and insight, global networks and reach as well as the necessary financial support to help us achieve our ambitious growth plans.
“We see real opportunities to expand our network, both geographically and through digital innovation. As we continue to grow, we will keep investing to make sure the relationship between doctor and patient stays personal and local, because that is the model that best serves our patients.”
GPs and primary care practices in the Centric Health network will continue to operate under the Centric Health brand, “with full operational and clinical independence,” the company said. Many of the GPs operate under a profit share arrangement with Centric.
“Patients will not experience any change as a result of this investment and do not need to take any action,” the company said in a statement.
Centric Health said the acquisition would support its “ambitious growth strategy in Ireland, Germany and the Netherlands, enabling it to drive further innovation within the company while continuing to evolve and grow the range of clinical services that are delivered to its patients from its extensive GP network”.
“It will also help it to further its research work and programmes in population health which have the potential to positively impact future healthcare policy and planning in the countries where it operates.”

title: ‘A bombshell’: French teachers spot something on payslips that reveals scale of funding crisis
description: As students protest over conditions in schools, an obscure pensions transfer reveals how billions earmarked for education are funding retired civil servants instead
content:
L ooking closely at their payslips, teachers in France can spot something strange. The columns of figures show a pension contribution figure, “Contrib PC”, that is greater than their take-home pay.
Once little-noticed, the accounting practice is in the spotlight for what it reveals about a generational imbalance in state spending and France’s deep financial troubles, as hundreds of thousands of young people protest across the country over conditions in schools .
“We think we’re paying for schools, but we’re paying for pensions,” sums up Gabriel Lattanzio, an associate professor at the Panthéon-Sorbonne University who has been posting his payslips online to highlight the issue.
The French pension system is a direct transfer system: current contributions by workers are paid out directly to fund today’s retirees, rather than being saved into a fund.
“Contrib PC” is a transfer from the education ministry into the bank account that pays out the pensions of retired civil servants. The expense is categorised in the French budget as spending on education, but is actually going to today’s retirees.
In August, Lattanzio’s take-home pay was €2,662.27. The direct contribution to pensions by his employer – the French education ministry – was €2,896.08. An additional €351.63 was also deducted from his pay for pensions as well.
Lattanzio published an analysis comparing the French budget of 2006 to that of 2026 and concluded that although spending on education appeared to have risen over time, in fact the vast majority of the increase was to pay for pension payments to retired civil servants.
The issue sheds light on the complaints by protesting school students of teacher shortages and poor conditions, even as France appears to rank relatively well when education spending is compared to other developed economies.
France appears to be “spending more on education than it is actually”, says Todor Tochev, a senior economist at the Institut des Politiques Publiques who began to draw public attention to the issue with a paper he co-authored last year.
“Hiring an additional teacher does not just reflect the expenses incurred by hiring that teacher, but also incurs the expenses of paying pensions for people who are not teachers,” he explains.
[ France’s school protests: What lies behind the anger Opens in new window ]
“The fundamental problem is that there’s a demographic problem,” Tochev says: current retirees now outnumber working people paying into France’s civil servant pensions system.
This has been caused by a decline in the birth rate, but also by government policy.
There has been a shift towards hiring public servants on fixed-term contracts, which means they don’t become contributors into the system.
The privatisation of services, like France Telecom, also reduced the overall number of contributors, while the state retained the responsibility for paying the pensions of their retirees.
Finally there is a “general policy of pay freezes” for public servants, with pay frozen most years since 2010, while pensions are automatically indexed to inflation. This means that salaries and pensions have steadily diverged.
As students emptied from their high schools to march in protest at education conditions this week, the finance ministry published an annex to its proposed national budget for the first time.
The annex contained figures, never released before, showing the percentage of spending on retired civil servants’ salaries per ministry.
It revealed that 32 per cent of the education ministry’s budget, €28.5 billion, is transferred straight back into the bank account that pays out civil servants’ pensions. It was the greatest share spent on pensions of any ministry.
“It’s a bombshell,” ​the economist Maxime Sbaihi, of think tank Institut Montaigne, wrote on social media.
[ France’s school protests: What lies behind the anger Opens in new window ]
The interior ministry, which employs police officers, spends 30 per cent of its budget on pensions, while the justice ministry spends just over 20 per cent.
“So, more than 11 per cent of the central government budget, or almost €50 billion annually, is allocated to pension funding without being recorded as a pension expenditure. Staggering,” Sbaihi wrote.
It remains to be seen whether the revelations will affect France’s presidential campaign ahead of an election in April 2027.
There is an “omertà” about pensions in French politics, according to Renaud Foucart, an economist at Lancaster University. “No politician dares to address the question.”
The front-runners on the left and right are presenting “fantasy budgets”, Foucart says, that “claim to fix everything with vague promises of efficiency, or by ending all kinds of fraud and blaming foreigners and billionaires”.
Some centre-right candidates acknowledge the issue, but their proposed solution is to make “current workers pay for the imbalance”, Foucart says.
They “want to reform the system while preserving the privileges of the boomers, whose pensions are putting the country on the verge of financial collapse”.
[ Inside the school protests in France that have spiralled into arson and street violence Opens in new window ]
Macron abandoned an initial attempt to introduce a points-based pension reform when Covid-19 hit. He oversaw a highly controversial increase of the statutory retirement age from 62 to 64 in 2023, but its implementation is currently suspended.
Foucart notes that students were also at the forefront of protests against the increase to the retirement age.
“They demonstrated to protect pensions and now demonstrate to defend education, and I cannot blame them for not understanding that the former is the cause of most of their problems,” Foucart says. “They are correct to be angry, the adults have failed them.”

title: Porsche offers a glimpse of the new supercar charged with resurrecting its fortunes
description: Mission S will sit above the classic 911 in Porsche’s lineup, but 9,000 job losses also factored in to aid turnaround
content:
Porsche has shown off its Mission S concept, offering a preview of a new supercar that will, uniquely, sit above the classic 911 model in its lineup. The Mission S takes clear design cues from the 911, particularly in its headlamps and front wings, with hints of the brand’s 1990s Le Mans racer, the GT1.
At the rear, there are more historic references, including a wraparound hoop-style rear wing that references the 1980s 959 (a car so far ahead of its time that it still feels quick and sophisticated today). The small, horizontally mounted fan on the rear deck gives a tip of the hat to the wild 917 racing car of the 1960s and 1970s, with its air-cooled flat-12 engine.
Inside, there’s a cabin that very specifically rejects an all-digital layout for a mixture of screens and physical buttons. Even the main instruments feature analogue needles on top of digital projections, for a distinct hint of Porsche’s classic 1960s cabins.
The Mission S, it seems, will be either a hybrid model or just use a petrol engine depending on customer demand. Speaking to Bloomberg at the car’s reveal in New York this week, Porsche CEO Michael Leiters (formerly head of McLaren’s car-making operations and Ferrari ’s chief technical officer before that), said the Mission S, in eventual production form, would be “a super-sports car with a driving focus”.
“The platform, and it’s a mid-engined platform, is very flexible, so regarding the powertrain we can offer hybrid or pure combustion, but at the end the customer will decide what derivatives we offer with this car,” he said.
Reading between the lines, that sounds very much like Porsche will make a primary version of this car with a plug-in hybrid system to keep legislators happy, but then also offer a ‘pure’ petrol-powered version (possibly with access to Porsche’s man-made carbon-neutral ‘e-fuel’ petrol) as a higher-priced model.
Leiters pointed out that unlike previous high-end Porsche sports cars – the 918 hybrid, the Carrera GT with its V10 engine – the production version of the Mission S will be a “normal” Porsche product, with no specific limits on how many will be made, avoiding the Ferrari-style “desire through scarcity” model. That makes for a distinct change in Porsche’s traditional policy, which previously had ruled out a model above the 911 for fear of hurting that car’s halo effect and its profitable sales.
Profits are, of course, the whole point and the reason Porsche is introducing this higher-priced, higher-performance model. It’s part of a plan that will supposedly save Porsche. Dubbed “Sportwagenschmiede ’35″ (Sports Car Workshop ’35), it’s a nine-year plan that aims to boost the profitability of each vehicle the company makes, while simultaneously making fewer vehicles. As Porsche itself puts it, the plan is value, not volume.
“We are pursuing a clear plan with our strategy Sportwagenschmiede ’35,” said Leiters. “The ultimate goal is to further strengthen our unique sports-car brand – across all model lines and with new, highly desirable models in particularly high-margin segments.
“Our strategy will lay the groundwork to make Porsche significantly more efficient, productive and profitable in three phases. At the moment, the main focus is on reducing costs and making the company more financially robust.”
That robustness will involve improving its profit margins from a low of 5.5 per cent per car in 2025 to a much healthier 10-15 per cent, while boosting turnover to €41-€45 billion. Leiters has also committed to reducing Porsche’s break-even production point to less than 200,000 cars (last year the company sold 279,000 cars) and also cutting back on the number of different variants of each model. As part of this turnaround, though, there will be blood, so to speak – 9,000 job losses are expected between now and 2035, most of them coming from management positions, with fewer from production and engineering.
In the meantime, Leiters has confirmed that he wants to see increased prices for Porsche’s models, but not across the board, saying that the top 10 per cent of Porsche’s production will see a roughly 20 per cent price increase, while other models will remain relatively more affordable. “These cars will have a good entry point, and then you can go higher,” he said.
Such models will include the replacement for the current Boxster and Cayman sports cars, which have vacillated between electric-only power and adding in a combustion option. Uneven uptake of electric cars across Porsche’s global markets had led to a rethink, giving the Boxster/Cayman the option of combustion power too, but Leiters has recently reversed that decision again. He says test drives of the new cars showed they were so good in all-electric form that a combustion option would not be needed and that it would cost too much to engineer two versions of the same car for a relatively small sports-car market.
The market may feel differently. Disappointing sales of the all-electric Macan SUV have also triggered a rethink, and Porsche is currently developing a new SUV to sit alongside the Macan, which will have a choice of petrol or plug-in hybrid power. That new SUV won’t arrive until 2029, though, by which time we should also have a better idea of what Porsche is going to do with its saloon models – the combustion-powered Panamera and the electric Taycan.
In spite of the electric Taycan’s excellence, it’s also been a disappointment in sales terms, and so the smart money is on the next generation being a variant of the next Panamera, much in the way you can currently buy a Cayenne SUV in either combustion or all-electric form. Hybrids will be critical too, as Leiters says Porsche’s operations in China do “very well” with hybrid models in that crucial market. Porsche’s sales have plummeted there in recent years.
“Our strategy focuses very much on our medium-term ambition so that the measures and the associated results take effect as early as possible,” he said. “The term ‘Sportwagenschmiede’ was deliberately chosen because it captures everything Porsche aims to stand for in the future: our aspiration to offer the sportiest vehicles in every segment, but also craftsmanship, down-to-earth thinking and entrepreneurial, business-focused action.
“Our goal is to be attractive to all stakeholders: our customers, our workforce, our partners and our investors."
Porsche had to take a painful write-down in 2025, having overextended on its electric car plans, but Leiters said he sees the company as having a “clean table” now, financially speaking.
Porsche has managed already to rebuild some of its profits since the end of 2025, and much of that has been based on the long-serving 911 sports car.
More, and indeed more expensive, versions of the 911 – described as “highly emotive 911 derivatives” – are now promised. Leiters has said Porsche is considering a “super-Cayenne” large SUV to top the range (likely platform-sharing with Audi’s new Q9) and, of course, the new Mission S.
So is Porsche back on track after a period of electric overreach? Or is Sportwagenschmiede ’35 a blip on a long downward track? The Irish Times spoke to Peter Wells, professor of business and sustainability at the Centre for Automotive Industry Research, Cardiff University.
Last year, he told us: “I do believe the business had grown too big, too popular, so maybe what we need is a smaller Porsche in the future.”
“I think Porsche has bought itself some time and will be a beneficiary of the Trump reversal of electrification in the US, tariffs notwithstanding,” said Wells. “However, in my view, the fundamental structural problems have not gone away. Porsche has failed to convince enough buyers in the transition of electric models, certainly at the premium price points it seeks to occupy.
“The performance and quality edge enjoyed by Porsche has been rapidly eroded, most obviously in China, where a slowdown in that economy has accentuated market pressure in the segments where Porsche operates. The system of building in Germany and selling worldwide proved a long-term cash cow for Porsche, but when the IPO was launched, the warning signs were already there.
“As with other German manufacturers, Porsche attempted to compensate for high production costs by developing a wider model range and pushing further upmarket. Now it finds volumes across that model range falling, the upmarket segments contracting, and lower-cost competition entering. The Xiaomi SUV high-performance variant is an astonishing accomplishment for such a new entrant.”
Many Porsche fans have been buoyed up by the fact that, of late, the 911 sports car has been setting record sales figures while the brand’s less-beloved SUVs have stuttered. However, Wells thinks this is more a cause for reflection than celebration.
“If anything, the resurgence of the 911 is a worry. Porsche has repeatedly said this will not be an electric model, but where does that leave market prospects in the future? Backtracking on strategy, especially on electrification, batteries and software, and reducing the numbers employed may cut costs, but it does not cultivate the competencies needed for the future.
“Perhaps Porsche should think hard about the market signals, and reconfigure as a smaller and more focused brand, including an electric equivalent of the 911."

title: Managing your money and your time in retirement
description: On the Money: There is a knowledge gap between what people are putting into their pension fund and how much annual income the fund would deliver
content:
Benjamin Franklin is credited with the assertion that death and taxes are life’s only two certainties, but for many people there’s a third: retirement.
For historical reasons, 65 ended up as the widely accepted retirement age, but for a large part of human history, there was no such thing as formal retirement. People simply worked until they became incapable of doing so.
We have Bismarck to thank for introducing the concept of a modern state pension in the 19 th century, with the retirement age set at 70 – at a time when few enough people lived to see that age. It was also 70 when the Old Age Pensions Act came into force in Ireland in 1908.
The qualifying age was subsequently adjusted downwards to where we are today, although a report produced in May of this year for the Financial Planning Standards Board suggests that while it’s nominally 65, many Irish people now expect to work until the age of 70 to maintain their standard of living.
Almost 80 per cent of those surveyed also felt financially unprepared for retirement, with a critical knowledge gap between what they were putting into their pension fund and how much income they thought that fund would provide when the time came.
Money, or having enough of it, pretty much tops the lists of concerns voiced by those facing retirement. This is closely followed by anxiety about filling the time previously taken up by work.
“Money is terribly important and, in an ideal world, you would start thinking about it long before you retire, maybe seven to 10 years before the planned date, because the sanest and most tax-effective way to save for retirement is by contributing to a pension scheme,” says Paul Kenny, a veteran of the pensions industry and Ireland’s first pensions ombudsman, who now leads courses for the Retirement Planning Council designed to get people retirement fit.
“Things happen that can radically change when people retire, such as illness, redundancy or an accident,” Kenny says. “Then there are those who put things on the long finger and suddenly they’re facing retirement with no financial plan.
“But all is not lost. Last-minute additional voluntary contributions (AVCs) are an option. How much you can put in is limited by your income in the final year and how much you can claim against tax, but they’re worth considering,” Kenny says.
AVCs are supplementary payments into your pension fund. If you’re in your late fifties, you can get tax relief on as much as 35 per cent of your salary if you put it into your pension fund. Above 60, that percentage jumps to 40 per cent.
So if you have just turned 60 and are earning €90,000, with normal pension contributions of 6 per cent, or €5,400, you can put up to a further €30,600 into your pension, assuming you have it. For many, it is a way of beefing up retirement income in a tax-efficient manner if they come into a windfall, such as an inheritance.
“When you’re looking at your overall money picture, an awful lot also depends on what kind of pension scheme you’re in because, in some cases, if you’re already getting the maximum from a scheme, AVCs are not going to do you any good. So, you need to know what you’re in and the benefits,” Kenny says.
“Annuities and approved retirement funds (ARFs) may also come up when discussing retirement financial planning,” Kenny adds. Both are products related to after-retirement income, not saving for retirement.
“An annuity, which will guarantee a payment for your lifetime, will be bought from an insurance company with the money in your pension fund and will very much tie you to what are currently low interest rates. Annuities are based on life expectancy and bond yields, and if interest rates are low, bond yields are low, so you’re locking yourself into a low interest rate for life.
“With ARFs, rather than lock your money into an annuity at a point in time, it remains invested after your retirement, with the retiree drawing down a certain portion of the fund each year.
“It’s crucial how you invest the money because that’s what will determine the capacity to draw down over the rest of your life. So, it’s really important to get good advice.
“ARFs are generally run by insurance companies, and they’re investing in massive numbers of different assets all over the world, something you could never do on your own, and this spreads the risk. They pay you the monies you are drawing down and take care of things like PAYE. An ARF gives you flexibility; if you really need money, you can make a drawdown and pay the necessary tax.”
Kenny says that the one thing to watch with ARF investments is the charges.
“If you’re being offered ‘hello money’ in the form of a bonus allocation, be careful. There’s only one person paying for that. So, the message is to go for the lowest charges. Anything over 1 per cent should be viewed with suspicion.”
Assuming the money side of things is under control, the next burning question for many prospective retirees is what to do with their time.
The psychosocial infrastructure is the term used to describe what a community, such as a workplace, provides to the individual. For better or for worse, this means having colleagues, work to do, and company events to attend. Losing this infrastructure can be a difficult adjustment, especially for those who have been defined by their job (often those in senior positions and the professions) or in whose life work was the dominant feature.
Kenny suggests reframing “all the time I have on my hands” to see it as a bonus, not a negative. “You’re getting back 50+ hours a week and why would you sit there and twiddle your thumbs when there is so much you could do?” he says.
“First of all, some people still want to work, so explore the options. Can you continue to work with reduced hours or part-time at your existing company with less pressure?
“Often people don’t want to keep doing what they’ve done for years, but that shouldn’t be a deterrent to doing something else. It’s really a question of looking for what’s available. If someone is prepared to work voluntarily rather than needing paid employment, then that opens another avenue.
“Sharing your talents, life and work skills with others can be invaluable and it feels good to give back. There are many charitable organisations which would bite your hand off if you had the skills to revamp an outdated system or update a website, for example.”
Retirees often get asked to join a board and, for many, it’s a good way of staying in touch. However, Kenny raises a warning flag. “Check the number of subcommittees because what looks like a once-a-month commitment can suddenly become twice a week,” he says.
Kenny adds age-appropriate exercise into the retiree timetable and also something to keep the brain agile. Both learning a new language and taking up a musical instrument for the first time are seen as particularly good ways to challenge the grey matter.
“The education and training boards offer a huge variety of hobby and other courses, with many of them heavily subsidised and run during the day. Then there are the more formal courses at Third Level for those who want to go the academic route,” Kenny says.
“Then come the hobbies which split into things you do alone and things you do with other people. I know of a gentleman who retired at 76 having known nothing but farming all his life. His son convinced him to go on a retirement planning course, and since then he has taken up horticulture, baking bread, general cookery, hill walking, yoga and line dancing.
“The wonderful thing about any of these activities is that they bring you into contact with new people who have no idea about who you are based on what you used to do,” Kenny adds. “In a sense, you get your personal identity back, and maybe that’s still a 25-year-old trying to break loose.”
You can contact us at OnTheMoney@irishtimes.com with personal finance questions you would like to see us address. If you missed last week’s newsletter, you can read it here .

title: Celebrity Traitors: Is James Acaster the worst Traitor in the history of the show?
description: Television: This tepid second season needs to find a way to raise the temperature in the time remaining
content:
T he territorial and cultural peak of the Roman Empire was also the moment it began its irreversible decline: once you reach the top there is nowhere to go but down. You wonder if this logic also applies to The Traitors and whether, decades hence, historians will trace the downfall of the back-stabbing franchise to the moment Paudie Moloney declared he wasn’t a hugger. It was never going to get any better than that.
That was top Traitors – and since then it’s been down all the way, first with an underwhelming second series of The Traitors Ireland and now with the joyless and thrill-free return of the BBC’s Celebrity Traitors. How did it go so wrong so quickly - and why has the second time out for Celebrity Traitors failed to reach the duplicitous heights of the first year?
The simple answer is that these Traitors seem to have no idea what they are doing – and that most of them don’t even want to be Traitors. First Richard E Grant self-immolated by declaring that he was a Traitor – an admission that not all the back-pedalling in the world could wave away.
Next it became increasingly obvious that James Acaster is the worst Traitor in the history of the show – in that he seems to be of the opinion that getting into the spirit of a ridiculous parlour game would be a stain on his soul. Then he and Maya Jama recruited top telly boffin Hannah Fry – another Traitor who doesn’t want to actually murder anyone.
The Faithful, meanwhile, are in just as big a flap. They are either entirely clueless and running around accusing the wrong people ( James Blunt ) or they are playing the “keep a low profile” game and thus essentially removing themselves from the fun ( Michael Sheen ). Then there is the third category, represented exclusively by Ross Kemp , whose paranoia bubbled straight to the surface so that by the end of episode one he’d turned into Marlon Brando at the end of Apocalypse Now.
[ The Traitors Ireland finale: Final betrayal barely registers as second season fizzles out Opens in new window ]
Week three of the contest has at least advanced the story to the extent that the Faithful have turfed out another Traitor in Fry – using the logic that she’s a professional clever clogs, so of course the Traitors would recruit her. That proved to be exactly the case − but the maths whiz’s number was so clearly up from the outset that there is no dramatic tension.
Will this tepid Traitors find a way to raise the temperature in the time remaining to it? There are indications that token Irish contestant Joanne McNally could be in hot water – because of her habit of nominating completely random Faithful, which Fry, before her departure, identified as the actions of a desperate Traitor.
So maybe McNally will have to face some scrutiny and perhaps The Celebrity Traitors will finally develop a pulse. It will have been a long time coming – to date, this celebration of murder and mayhem has been as dull as the grey cardigan Claudia wore to the latest round table.

title: Man jailed for stag-night killing after 21-minute violent assault
description: Paul ‘Babs’ Connolly’ (48) attacked by two men on night out in Athlone after becoming separated from his group
content:
A man has been given a 6½-year prison sentence for killing a reveller who was “set on” and attacked with repeated punches and kicks while on a stag night in Athlone more than four years ago.
A postmortem found Paul “Babs” Connolly’s death was caused by cardiac arrest resulting from a complex interaction of blunt force trauma to the head in a setting of acute intoxication and the emotional stress of the protracted assault.
The 48-year-old single man, from Edenderry, Co Offaly , was assaulted for 21 minutes along Church Street in the Co Westmeath town in the early hours of August 13th, 2022, after he had become separated from his group.
Sean Munnelly (40), of Irishtown, Athlone, but originally from Co Roscommon, pleaded guilty to manslaughter.
Sentencing him at Mullingar Circuit Criminal Court on Friday, Judge Deirdre Browne stressed that whatever offence had been caused by the dead man’s earlier remarks to people on the street asking if they watched child pornography, there was no provocation.
She recalled video evidence showing how the deceased had been knocked to the ground three times by Munnelly and a co-accused. Several people on the street tried to intervene, but the assault continued.
At one point, members of Connolly’s stag party were present, and Munnelly could be seen back-slapping and shaking hands with them before continuing to confront Connolly despite his vulnerable presentation.
The judge said the victim was “out of it”, struggling at this stage, being both intoxicated and clearly injured, and posing no threat to anyone.
The final piece of video evidence showed Munnelly circling the deceased, gesticulating aggressively before delivering a left-handed punch that connected to the right side of the victim’s head, rendering him unconscious.
Connolly died in an ambulance on the way to hospital. A witness overheard Munnelly saying: “F**king deserved it, no one pisses me off,” as he walked away.
The judge noted there had been a number of kicks and punches and did not regard the fatality as resulting from a single blow.
She commiserated with members of the Connolly family and said their victim impact statements described a much-loved character, and their eloquent testimony spoke of a life well lived.
The judge considered a series of aggravating factors as she imposed a seven-year sentence. Noting the accused’s genuine remorse and the mitigating factors raised in defence submissions, she suspended the final six months for one year.
She backdated the sentence to February 27th, 2024, to account for time served on remand.
An unemployed father of one, Munnelly was out on bail and on a suspended sentence at the time of the incident and had been drinking and snorting cocaine. He changed his plea to guilty in June, just as a jury was about to be empanelled for an anticipated four-week trial. He had 102 previous convictions.
The court heard Paul “Babs” Connolly was initially set on by another man and Munnelly with punches and kicks.
Det Sgt Kevin Craig said the child pornography remark was the catalyst that triggered Munnelly and a co-accused.
Munnelly previously apologised in a letter read out in court, saying: “I’m truly sorry. I never set out to hurt anyone. There are a lot of lives devastated over my actions. I feel terrible. It’s like a nightmare I wake up to every day.”
In a victim impact statement, Diane Lynch said her brother was “like a big kid”. Nieces and nephews adored him, and the family were devastated that they never got a chance to say goodbye.

title: Net closing on gang that murdered family in Waterford, says Garda Commissioner
description: Justin Kelly urged victims of drug-related intimidation to come forward, saying supports are available
content:
Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly has said more arrests will soon be made over the murders of four members of the English family in Waterford , which he described as “an absolutely horrendous crime”.
Kelly said the criminal investigation into the murders of Philip and Kim English, and their children Callum (12) and Jayden (9) last Tuesday morning, had already made very “significant progress”.
Seven homes have been searched – with vehicles and phones seized for examination – while two people had been arrested and remained in custody.
Gardaí locally were “quite satisfied” with the evidence gathered and had firm intelligence on the drugs gang suspected of involvement, Kelly told reporters at the Garda College in Templemore, Co Tipperary, on Friday.
He said drugs gangs could not be allowed to threaten, attack and extort people “with impunity”.
Philip and Kim English died, along with their sons Callum and Jayden, after an arson attack on their home in the Birchwood estate, Waterford City, just after 5am on Tuesday.
Two other children – a girl (14) and a boy (6) – were rescued from the house and are in a critical condition in hospital.
The family had been targeted in the past, including a petrol bombing last month, by a local crime gang trying to extort €20,000 from them to pay a drugs debt incurred by somebody else.
The first arrests in the case were made on Thursday when a man (20s) and woman (30s) were detained on suspicion of being directly involved in the attack and facilitating the crime gang.
Both Kelly and Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan, who was also at the Garda College for a graduation ceremony, said if victims of drug-related intimidation contacted gardaí they would no longer be unprotected.
“They were horrific events that we saw and I think it was a watershed moment,” said O’Callaghan. “We see a family of six people attacked, attempts made to kill, and four of them murdered and two in a critical condition. What’s fuelling this is drugs and this has to be a watershed moment, not just for the Garda or Government, politicians, it has to be for the public as well.
“People who are this weekend taking cocaine need to recognise they are funding organised crime that’s involved in murdering people for debts of €20,000.
“By taking drugs, by funding the drugs industry, you are supporting the horrific events we saw in Waterford . . . funding the criminal gangs that murdered. People would want to get (that link) and they’d want to get it fairly rapidly.”
O’Callaghan appealed to victims of drug-related intimidation to “have faith in the Garda” and report the crimes because “if people don’t report it to gardaí, they are very much on their own”. He said supports are available if they come forward.
Though it was hard for victims, O’Callaghan said if they gave in to the extortion of gangs and paid them, rather than going to gardaí, the gangs “will just keep coming back for more”.
“This was a very difficult crime,” Kelly said of the degree of violence involved and the fact four people, including children, had been killed.
“Drugs-related intimidation is part of the drugs business . . . in every country – this isn’t unique to Ireland,” he said, reiterating the Minister’s call for people being pressured and targeted with violence to reach out to gardaí.
“You can come forward confidentially. You don’t [have to] come to a Garda station if you don’t want to; we will meet you elsewhere. We’ve got dedicated, trained experts, with an inspector in every division all around the country trained to deal with these [cases].”
Kelly implored ”people not to be on their own”, adding a range of options could be pursued and that victims did not have to go to court and give evidence if they did not want to.
But he accepted “people are going to be afraid”, with events such as those in Waterford this week adding to fears around repercussions.
The Garda had prosecuted many criminals for drug-related intimidation and would do so again, he said, while also acknowledging the nature of the violence was changing.
“What we have certainly seen is an increase in use of incendiary devices, petrol bombs. We are very concerned around that. We have increased our targeting, not just against the higher-level drugs and crime groups, but some of the medium-sized ones as well. It’s difficult because often people have outsourced the debt and there’s different layers.”
Kelly and O’Callaghan were speaking to the media at a passing-out ceremony for 207 Garda recruits on Friday at the Garda College. The graduation brought the number of Garda members to 14,825, the highest in the history of the State.

title: Ethiopia’s Abiy names interim Tigray government and calls for election in six months
description: Tigray region is yet to recover from  2020-2022 ‌war
content:
Ethiopia ’s ‌prime minister Abiy Ahmed has named a caretaker government to stabilise the northern Tigray region and prepare for ​an election within six months, after fighting erupted between a rebel alliance and federal troops.
The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) led an offensive last month against Abiy’s government, reigniting a war that killed hundreds of thousands between 2020-22.
Renewed ​conflict has led to the severing of ties between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of ⁠backing the rebels, which Eritrea denies.
The TPLF, Tigray’s ruling party, dominated Ethiopian politics for decades ‌until ‌Abiy ​took office in 2018. Since fighting erupted, Ethiopia’s military and a pro-government militia have made significant advances and taken control of large parts ⁠of Tigray including the regional ​capital Mekelle.
The temporary administration will be in ​office for six months, Abiy’s office said, to create a stable political climate for elections within six months.
“To ​attain the peace that has long eluded them, to secure their right to self-administration, ⁠and to finally enjoy the fruits of ⁠development – which ​have been out of reach for many years – the people of Tigray must break free from this cycle of conflict,” Abiy said in a statement posted on X.
The administration will also repair damaged infrastructure and help displaced people return to their homes, he said.
A TPLF spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Tigray is yet to recover from the humanitarian toll of the previous ‌war, which pushed hundreds ⁠of thousands into famine. Around 750,000 Tigrayans were still internally displaced as of February, according to the UN refugee agency, and the region faces drought linked ‌to El Nino.
There are fears that unrest could spread beyond Ethiopia’s borders in the fragile Horn of ​Africa region where other powers vie for influence.
In addition to Eritrea, ​Ethiopia’s government has accused Egypt and Sudan of supporting the rebel alliance.
They have denied the allegations. – Reuters

title: Tesla unveils ‘flying’ sports car with SpaceX rocket thrusters
description: Roadster makes debut after decade in development as EV maker tries to revive image as brash innovator
content:
Tesla’s chief executive Elon Musk has unveiled a “flying” sports car equipped with thrusters from his rocket company SpaceX as the carmaker tries to revive its image as a brash innovator.
At a launch event on Thursday night at a SpaceX test site in Texas, the electric-car maker showed off the Tesla Roadster. In one stunt, the car launched vertically into the air and performed a mid-air barrel roll over a line of parked Tesla vehicles before landing on its wheels on the other side.
“A friend of mine, Peter Thiel, once said the future promised us flying cars, but instead we got 140 characters,” Musk joked to a crowd of cheering fans, referring to the character limit of social media posts on Twitter before he bought it in 2022. “Well, not any more.”
Musk said the Roadster was “not necessarily a safety-optimised car”, but it would “be an actual car that’s on the roads”.
“I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions,” he said. “But there will be such a car that someone can own.”
Do a kickflip! pic.twitter.com/DJ1Bq1yu8m
The vehicle, which has been under development for a decade and will not enter production until 2028, will be Tesla’s only manual car. With the help of its thrusters, it can accelerate to 60 miles per hour in less than a second and achieve a top speed of 230mph.
The company postponed the launch on at least five previous occasions, originally promising to start delivering the vehicle in 2020. As a publicity stunt, Musk launched a prototype into space in 2018.
Customers – including OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman – paid $50,000 (€44,000) to remain on a waiting list for years. However, a year ago, during a vicious legal battle with Musk, Altman asked for his money back, saying “7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait”.
Musk spent weeks hyping his new product on his social media platform X, calling it “a candidate for greatest product demo of all time”. As far back as 2018, the billionaire had been stoking speculation that the Roadster would be able to fly using cold-gas thrusters developed by SpaceX for its reusable rocket-landing systems.
The Roadster has been a pet project for Musk. Tesla sold a predecessor model as a concept car between 2008 and 2012 to spread awareness of electric vehicles.
[ SpaceX’s wild ride shows how quickly markets can change their minds Opens in new window ]
It will now compete with ultra-luxury electric supercars such as the €550,000 Ferrari Luce and other new offerings from Bentley, Jaguar and Porsche.
However, Musk has played down the Roadster’s significance to his $1.4tn carmaker, saying sales would probably be modest and not “move the needle in a big way financially”.
Tesla has been reducing its number of offered models as it refits its production lines in California and Texas to build robots and autonomous taxis.
In January, Musk discontinued Tesla’s premium S and X models as the group shifted to development of the Cybercab, a gold-coloured self-driving taxi, and a humanoid robot called Optimus.
The vast majority of Tesla’s sales come from its Model 3 and Y, while its Cybertruck has sold poorly since the enormous stainless-steel truck was released in 2023. The company started mass production of the Semi, its articulated lorry, in Nevada this year.
Tesla deliveries fell 2 per cent in the third quarter, hit by a decline in US demand after President Donald Trump ended a $7,500 tax credit for EV purchases.
Tim Levin, a senior editor at the InsideEVs website, said with the bestselling Model Y having first gone on sale in 2020, the Roadster could help revive Tesla’s image as a brash innovator.
But he cautioned that the EV industry had changed since Tesla first announced the Roadster as a concept.
“Maybe back then the world needed convincing that EVs could be these superfast accelerating vehicles,” said Levin. “But maybe now it won’t have the same impact as it would have had in 2020.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Paula Canty killing: Man jailed for 10 years for manslaughter of Cork mother (31)
description: Joseph Butler (43) plunged knife into Paula Canty’s chest but told gardaí he did not feel guilty as it was ‘an accident’
content:
A man who plunged a knife more than 11cm into the chest of a 31-year-old woman and left her to die on an apartment floor in Mallow , Co Cork, has been jailed for 10 years.
Joseph Butler (43) was originally charged with the murder of Paula Canty at an apartment in the Belfry, Bridewell Lane, on January 3rd, 2025. The Director of Public Prosecutions subsequently accepted his plea of guilty to manslaughter.
The mother of two died from a single knife wound to the chest. She had been due to celebrate her 32nd birthday three days later.
Butler, who is a native of Midleton in Co Cork, initially told gardaí he “didn’t feel guilty” about what had occurred as it was “an accident”.
At a sentencing hearing in the Central Criminal Court in Cork on Friday, Judge Eileen Creedon dismissed the account of events Butler had given to gardaí.
She said his claim that the killing had been accidental and arose from a tussle was not in any way consistent with the evidence of the pathologist in the case.
“His account was that he grabbed a knife from her during a struggle and that it was an accident. He indicated that he didn’t feel guilty because it was an accident and he didn’t know she was dead until later when he got a phone call from his niece,” she said.
“The accused’s versions of events were inconsistent with the postmortem and the blood-spatter analysis by forensic scientists. The blood pooling indicates that the deceased bled heavily at that location.
“Paula Canty was a vulnerable person, and was much smaller and physically weaker than Joseph Butler. It is not credible that she posed a danger to him that required him to plunge a knife 11.5cm into her chest. He left the apartment and there was no call to the emergency services. This demonstrates a callousness.”
[ Man (43) pleads guilty to manslaughter of mother-of-two Paula Canty Opens in new window ]
The judge imposed a sentence of 12 years with the last two years suspended with the condition that Butler keeps the peace and is of good behaviour for two years after his release from prison. She said she could only imagine the grief and the hole left in the lives of the family of the deceased following the loss of their loved one. She praised members of the family for their powerful victim impact statements.
Victim impact statements were previously read into evidence.
Darragh Canty, a brother of the deceased, said it broke his heart that she suffered such a brutal death.
“It eats me alive that I could not protect her from that monster of a man. She was left in a pool of her own blood just three days before her birthday,” he said.
Rianna Canty, the dead woman’s sister, said the family had expected to be organising a birthday party for her but ended up having to plan her funeral. She said Paula Canty had been denied the opportunity of seeing her two children mature into adults.
Sinead Canty said her “beloved darling daughter” had been stolen from the family in the “prime of her youth”. She said her daughter had a “soft, pleasant nature” and a creative disposition.
She said she and her daughter had a great bond and that her life had changed forever following her death.
[ From the archive: Gardaí believe 999 call claiming self-harm will help catch killer Opens in new window ]
Paula Canty was in a relationship with Michael John Butler, a brother of the accused, at the time of her death. Joseph Butler, who has a long history of alcohol addiction, lived with the couple in the apartment in which he killed her.
Butler told gardaí he had been fighting with his brother, Michael John, and calling the deceased “bad words” when she pulled a knife. He claimed that she was injured in a “struggle” between them and that she was “grand” when he left the apartment. He stated that he later learned of her death from his niece.

title: Irish exports to US fall by €1.2 billion, CSO finds
description: Elsewhere, the value of Ireland’s total outbound trade also appears to be tightening
content:
The value of exported goods from Ireland to the United States fell by €1.2 billion between July and August this year, the Central Statistics Office (CSO) has found. The total value of exports from Ireland were down €3 billion during the same period.
While the US remained the State’s largest country-to-country trading partner, Irish exports across the Atlantic have steadily declined in recent months and years.
Goods valuing €3.8 billion were exported from Ireland to the US in August, a notable decrease of 24 per cent from €5 billion exported in July, according to CSO research.
While August is typically a lighter trading month, annual comparisons further demonstrate Ireland’s falling trade with the US: €4.1 billion worth of goods were exported in August 2025 and €6.7 billion in the same month in 2024.
Elsewhere, the value of Ireland’s total exports also appeared to tighten: down 15.87 per cent from €18.9 billion in July to €15.9 billion in August. Some €7 billion of August’s exports went to Europe, with €1.8 billion going to Britain and €3.3 billion to the rest of the world.
Among the State’s most valuable export categories in August were: chemical products (€8.6 billion), machinery and transport equipment (€3.4 billion) and “miscellaneous manufactured articles”, which includes, but is not limited to, electrical equipment, travel goods, clothing and professional apparatuses (€1.7 billion).
Imports have also appeared to slip. A total of €12.9 billion worth of goods were imported into the State in August – €1.8 billion of which came from the US, a €200 million drop from the previous month, according to the CSO.
A further €3.7 billion worth of imports came into the State from across Europe and €1.9 billion from Britain with €5.5 billion coming from the rest of the world.
Machinery and transport equipment was the most valuable import (€5.2 billion), with chemical products in second place at €3.4 billion and miscellaneous manufactured articles trailing behind at €1.4 billion.

title: IMRAM Irish-Language Literature Festival line-up revealed
description: Books newsletter: a wrap of the latest news and preview of tomorrow’s pages
content:
The IMRAM Irish-Language Literature Festival once again takes us on a voyage of discovery with a series of multi-media events celebrating the best of modern literature in Irish.
It opens on November 6th with Músaem Na nGréibhlí, featuring stories by Daithí Ó Muirí, inspired by The Museum of Curiosities, a two-floor labyrinth of strange artefacts, eerie objects and peculiar histories, and read to an eerie soundtrack from musician Fergus Kelly.
Na Púcaí Ina Cheann/The Pookahs in his Head (November 9th) is a multi-media celebration of the life of much-loved poet, the late Gabriel Rosenstock, featuring very best of his poetry read by Amanda Bell, Paddy Bushe, his son Tristan Rosenstock and others, with music by Cormac Breathnach and Seán MacErlaine. In Crann Mór/Tree (November 10th) Rosenstock’s translation into Irish of poet Richard Berengarten’s symphonic hymn to a tree – exploring its central place in world mythology and religion – is at the heart of this multi-media choral staging composed by Nick Roth, featuring Chamber Choir Ireland and conductor David Young.
Diamant Agus Meirg/Diamonds And Rust (November 14th) features songs by Bob Dylan and Joan Baez translated into Irish by poets Caitríona Ni Chléirchín and Rody Gorman, and performed by Colm Seoighe and Emma Ní Fhioruisce.
Everyone who lives in Conamara or who has visited knows the road the 424 bus takes west from Galway city. In An 424: An Bus Go Dtí An Ghealchathair/The Bus To The Brightcity (November 13th), poets Laoighseach Ní Choistealbha, Jackie Mac donncha and Cúán de Búrca share new work inspired by their journeys on it, with music from Trá Pháidín.
Ag Seinm Samhraidh/ Singing The Summer (November 11th) rejoices in poet Pearse Hutchinson’s finest work, addressing themes of loss and survival, identity and language.
In The Irish Times tomorrow, Elif Shafak talks to Aimée Walsh about In One Brief Moment All Eternity, her new novel based on the life of Gustave Flaubert. As Gulliver’s Travels turns 300, Claire Connolly considers the lasting impact of Jonathan Swift’s classic. There is an extract from Billion Dollar Baby: The Inside Story of the Hospital that Broke the Budget by Paul Cullen. Vincent Browne opens up to Colm Keena about his new biography of his old adversary, Charles Haughey. And there is a Q&A with Ben Barnes, former artistic director of the Abbey Theatre.
Reviews are Karlin Lillington on The Last Good Day on the Internet by Mark Little and Christopher M Kelty’s The Internet We Could Have Had; Sara Baume on The Song of Stork and Dromedary by AnjetDaanje, translated from Dutch by David McKay; Andrew Lynch on Billion Dollar Baby: The Inside Story of the Hospital that Broke the Budget by Paul Cullen; Céire Sadlier on The Silence of October by Sharon Guard; Catríona Clutterbuck on the best new poetry; Greg Londe on Partita by Barbara Kingsolver; Neil Hegarty on Seeing What’s Hidden by Manchán Magan; Sinéad Gibney on The Fall of the West by Owen Jones; Kevin Power on A History of the Novel in Britain by Philip Hensher; Emily Goulding on Peck & Peck by Bonnie Garmus; Roe McDermott on Not the Perfect Victim by Nikita Hand; and NJ McGarrigle on The Comets by Eoin McNamee.
An Irish writer has won the Sky Arts Literature Award for the second year running.
Belfast author Wendy Erskine received the prize for The Benefactors, her fiercely original and formally ambitious novel that explores class, power, justice and family through a brilliantly polyphonic narrative.
“Set in contemporary Belfast, it captures a community through an extraordinary chorus of voices, creating a vivid and emotionally complex portrait of inequality and privilege. Balancing formal innovation with profound humanity, Erskine brings nuance, empathy and insight to difficult questions of responsibility, parenthood and social power. The result is a novel that feels both urgent and timeless, expanding the possibilities of contemporary fiction.”
Sally Rooney won the award last year for Intermezzo.
Colm Tóibín has received an honorary master’s degree from the University of Macerata. The ceremony, attended by Ireland’s Ambassador to Italy, Elizabeth McCullough, opened the fourth Macerata Humanities Festival.
“Usually, a degree recognises what someone has learned at university. Today we recognise what a university can learn from a great writer,” said Rector John McCourt, a fellow Irishman and an expert in modern and contemporary Irish literature.
McCourt praised Tóibín’s attention to the feelings that often go unspoken in families, in novels including Nora Webster , Brooklyn and Long Island . He also celebrated the range of Tóibín’s criticism, which takes in Henry James, Elizabeth Bishop and Lady Gregory. “He writes about complicated things clearly, without making them less complicated,” McCourt said.
Recalling Tóibín’s answer when asked which traits he most deplores – “humourlessness and laziness” – McCourt added: “Looking at his bibliography, one feels that laziness has never had much opportunity to settle in. His energy is boundless and infectious. And anyone who has spent time in his company knows that humourlessness would be shown the door even faster.”
How well can we ever know the people closest to us? And how far can a lie travel? Bestselling Irish novelist Liz Nugent will explore these questions at Dingle Literary Festival on Saturday, November 21st, discussing her latest novel, The Truth About Ruby Cooper, with crime writer William Shaw.
Nugent’s sixth novel, which topped the Irish charts for seven weeks, follows two sisters whose lives are changed forever by a single incident. Moving between Boston and Dublin, it explores family secrets, sibling rivalry and the lasting consequences of deception.
Shaw, author of The Birdwatcher and the DS Alexandra Cupidi series, joins Nugent for a conversation about morally complex characters, suspense and the darker side of human behaviour. The event takes place on Saturday, November 21st at the Dingle Skellig Hotel from noon to 1pm.
Dingle Literary Festival runs from November 20th to 22nd. Full details and tickets are available at dinglelit.ie .
Actor and audiobook narrator Eoin Lynch has been shortlisted for Best Performance: New Voice at The British Audio Awards for his narration of The Moon Seeker by Dublin-based Irish author Dee Barragry.
Published by Walker Books in 2025, The Moon Seeker is Barragry’s imaginative debut middle-grade fantasy, following Lampwick, a lighthouse keeper, and his faithful sheepdog Humphrey on an adventure to find the missing moon. Blending magical world-building, humour and themes of friendship and community, the book was named one of Children’s Books Ireland’s Best Books of 2025 and received praise from The Irish Times, which called it a “wildly original debut”.
Aosdána, the affiliation of creative artists in Ireland, has elected four new members at its 44th general assembly in the Law Society of Ireland at Blackhall Place, bringing the membership to 249 members.
As well as poet Mark Roper, visual artists Jackie McKenna and Ailbhe Ní Bhriain and choreographer Oona Doherty were elected.
Roper was born in England in 1951 and has lived in Ireland for 45 years. Now retired, he worked in childcare and then taught literature and creative writing. His work includes eight collections of poetry, four collaborative books with photographer Paddy Dwan and two operas with composer Eric Sweeney. His most recent publication is From The Japanese Gardens, a collaborative venture with photographer Margaret O’Brien-Moran. He was Editor of Poetry Ireland for 1999.
Eason has launched a new Book Club with broadcaster Muireann O’Connell, now available in Eason stores nationwide and online at easons.com.
Each month, O’Connell will curate her reading list, recommending two of her favourite titles. Unveiling her picks at the start of every month, Muireann will share in-depth reviews and personal insights into why she selected each book, highlighting her favourite themes and giving readers plenty of inspiration for their next read.
“I’m always excited to talk about a book I’ve loved, and I can’t wait to share two picks each month and explain what stood out to me,” O’Connell said. “I hope readers find a new favourite – or a book they’ll want to pass on to someone else.”
Her first two picks for October are Strange Pictures by Uketsu and Farewell to Eden by Sebastian Faulks.

A poet, a visual artist, an author and an inclusive theatre maker have been presented with Major Individual Artist Awards by the Arts Council of Northern Ireland. Poet Padraig Regan, visual artist and painter Pádraig Mac Cana, author Bernie McGill and inclusive theatre maker and director Andrew Standford will each receive a National Lottery funding award of up to £15,000 to create ambitious new work.
Wexford author Eoin Colfer’s bestselling Artemis Fowl books are to be adapted for an animated television series for Disney Channel and Disney+.
Colfer announced the news at New York Comic Con at an event celebrating the 25th anniversary of the first Artemis Fowl novel.
“I am proud and delighted to be part of the formidable team that is putting the Artemis Fowl animation on screen,” Colfer said. “Everyone is so talented and so positive that I feel certain the fairy world is in excellent hands.”
First published in 2001, the Artemis Fowl books have sold more than 35 million copies worldwide and been translated into 48 languages.
Disney released a live-action film adaptation of Artemis Fowl in 2020, directed by Kenneth Branagh and starring Ferdia Shaw, Colin Farrell and Judi Dench.
Authors Ardal O’Hanlon and Antti Toumainen are in conversation at Carrkickphierish Library, Co Waterford, next Monday, October 19th at 4pm for a special collaboration between Writers at Waterford Libraries and Murder One Festival. City and County Librarian Mary Conway will interview one of Ireland’s best-loved actors, comedians and crime novelists and the Finnish “funniest noir writer in Europe” as they discuss crime writing and combining suspense with humour in a special event to celebrate Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the European Union.

title: Sam Prendergast starts for Leinster against Clermont Auvergne with Joey Carbery named on bench
description: Ciarán Frawley will make his home debut for Connacht in Champions Cup clash with Saracens on Saturday
content:
Joey Carbery will return to Leinster colours for the first time in eight years after being named on the bench for the province’s opening Investec Champions Cup match against Clermont Auvergne in the Stade Marcel Michelin on Saturday (3.15, Irish time). He spent six years at Munster and two at Bordeaux Bègles.
The 30-year-old was due to play against the Sharks in a URC match in South Africa but suffered a tweak in training. Sam Prendergast starts at outhalf following his recent man of the match performance in the win over Cardiff.
There is no Jamison Gibson-Park, but he is back training, so Fintan Gunne starts at scrumhalf with Oliver Coffey on the bench. Garry Ringrose and Robbie Henshaw have been named in midfield with Jamie Osborne among the replacements.
Dan Sheehan leads the team and a pack that’s long on quality. Young prospects Alex Usanov and Conor O’Tighearnaigh are included in the replacements that sees Scott Penny cover the backrow.
Leinster: H Keenan; T O’Brien, G Ringrose, R Henshaw, J O’Brien; S Prendergast, F Gunne; A Porter, D Sheehan (capt), T Furlong; J McCarthy, J Ryan; R Baird, J van der Flier, J Conan. Replacements: R Kelleher, A Usanov, T Clarkson, C O’Tighearnaigh, S Penny, O Coffey, J Carbery, J Osborne.
Connacht welcome Saracens to the Dexcom Stadium (5.30) with Irish international Ciarán Frawley set to make his home debut at outhalf. Prop Thomas Connolly is set for a debut off the bench.
There’s a start for scrumhalf Colm Reilly alongside Frawley, while the centre partnership of Bundee Aki and Cathal Forde is unchanged. There’s an all-new back three from last week of fullback Sam Gilbert, and wingers Finn Treacy and Shane Jennings.
Cian Prendergast captains and is named in a backrow that includes Shamus Hurley-Langton and number eight Sean Jansen. There’s three changes in the tight five from last week’s game in Glasgow, with prop Francois van Wyk, hooker Matthew Victory and lock Josh Murphy coming into the starting XV. Tighthead Sam Illo and lock Darragh Murray complete the pack.
A predominantly young bench includes tighthead prop Connolly and academy winger Daniel Ryan.
Connacht: S Gilbert; F Treacy, C Forde, B Aki, S Jennings; C Frawley, C Reilly; F van Wyk, M Victory, S Illo; D Murray, J Murphy; C Prendergast (capt), S Hurley-Langton, S Jansen. Replacements: E de Buitléar, B Bohan, T Connolly, N Murray, S O’Brien, C Blade, J Ioane, D Ryan.
In the Challenge Cup Ulster travel to face Zebre at the Stadio Lanfranchi (3.15, Irish time) and head coach Richie Murphy has handed young hooker Henry Walker a first competitive start, while Daniel Hawkshaw makes his debut in a new look midfield alongside Jake Flannery.
David McCann captains last year’s beaten finalists for the first time. Ireland international prop Tom O’Toole makes his first start of the season at loosehead, with hooker Walker and Keynan Knox at tighthead prop.
Lock Harry Sheridan starts alongside Ireland international forward Cormac Izuchukwu in the secondrow, while academy forward James McKillop makes his European debut. Scrumhalf Nathan Doak pairs up with Jamie Benson at outhalf for the first time.
Zac Ward returns to start on the left wing this weekend, with Ireland internationals Robert Baloucoune on the right wing and Jacob Stockdale switching to fullback.
Murphy names a 5:3 split among the replacements, with prop Scott Wilson and forward Joe Hopes in line for their first appearances this season.
Ulster: J Stockdale; R Baloucoune, D Hawkshaw, J Flannery, Z Ward; J Benson, N Doak; T O’Toole, H Walker, K Knox; H Sheridan, C Izuchukwu; J McKillop, D McCann (capt), J Augustus. Replacements: T Stewart, E O’Sullivan, S Wilson, J Hopes, M Moloney, M Devine, J Murphy, M Lowry.

title: Wexford Festival Opera 2026: Iris review – Rosetta Cucchi directs a sterling cast, but Mascagni’s music lets them down
description: The Chinese soprano Leyla Gu, a forthright Iris, is the audience favourite, judging by the applause on opening night
content:
Pietro Mascagni peaked early, at the age of 26, with Cavalleria Rusticana, his 1890 verismo slice of Sicilian peasant life. He never achieved a comparable success, a failure that can be linked to his being a bit of a chameleon who wanted to experiment with operatic approaches that didn’t always come off.
His 1895 opera Iris, set in a mythical Tokyo, with a libretto by Luigi Illica, is an extraordinary concoction that opens and closes with a stirring first-person sun chorus: “It is I! I am Life! I am infinite Beauty. Light and Warmth.”
Lured by puppets, the innocent girl of the title, young enough to carry her doll around, falls into the hands of sexual predators. She doesn’t fully understand her abuse. Yet along the way she dreams of an octopus, like the one represented in Katsushika Hokusai’s early-19th-century-woodblock print known in English as The Dream of the Fisherman’s Wife, where the tentacles are focused on multiple erogenous zones.
Her abduction is misrepresented to her blind father, whose rejection (“There! In your face! On your forehead! In your mouth! In your eyes! Mud!”) drives her to leap from a window into an open sewer. She survives the fall and is ultimately borne into the heavens by a sea of blue flowers to a reprise of the opening chorus.
Rosetta Cucchi , the director of this production, lays her cards on the table. Iris is an opera that doesn’t tell a story but asks us to witness a destiny. The Japan of her production is a state of mind. The progress is from innocence cocooned to innocence confronted with real-world destruction and then released from it. She goes many extra miles in trying to support the symbolism of the work.
[ ‘The driver talked all the time for the three-hour journey. I understood maybe 20%’ Opens in new window ]
With her designers (Tiziano Santi, sets; Claudia Pernigotti, costumes; Thomas Achitz, video; and Daniele Naldi, lighting), choreographer (Libby Seward), puppeteers (Caoimhe Dunn, Eddie McCarthy and Dominic Palmer) and aerialist (Hannah Scully), she has animated and fleshed out a fluid and fantastical world.
The cast is sterling, from the forthright Iris of the Chinese soprano Leyla Gu (the audience favourite, judging by the applause), through the thrusting nastiness and vocally impressive strength of the Maltese tenor Joseph Calleja and the British-Irish baritone Jolyon Loy, as the stock villains Osaka and Kyoto, to the solid South Korean bass Jihoon Kim as Il Cieco, the father.
The fly in the ointment is Mascagni’s music, which, opening and ending apart, undermines vocal lines the singers can get their teeth into with colour-rich but feeble writing for orchestra. Nothing is said once but it is heard too often again.
Even the fervent Wexford Festival Orchestra, under Francesco Cilluffo, and the open-throated chorus, trained by Andrew Synnott, cannot generate much sense of connection. It is the chorus, especially at the end, with the singers at the top of the auditorium, that gets the best of the evening.
Iris will be performed again on Tuesday, October 20th, Friday, October 23rd, Wednesday, October 28th, and Saturday, October 31st. Wexford Festival Opera runs until Saturday, October 31st

title: Will Sally Rooney’s books now be removed from shops across the UK?
description: Rooney’s Normal People has sold one million copies in UK while her first and third novels have each sold over 500,000 copies
content:
No, but British antiterrorism legislation means the author and her British publisher, Faber & Faber, have agreed that they are no longer able to distribute her books in that territory.
Nothing. However, in August 2025, Rooney wrote an opinion piece in The Irish Times that was headlined: “I support Palestine Action. If this makes me a ‘supporter of terror’ under UK law, so be it.”
Palestine Action is a pro-Palestinian direct action group that was proscribed as a terrorist organisation by the British government in July 2025. After the group was banned, Rooney, who lives in Co Mayo, said she would use proceeds from her sales to support Palestine Action. Supporting organisations banned under the UK’s Terrorism Act is an offence there and she subsequently cancelled a trip to the UK to pick up an award.
In Rooney’s own words: “Since its foundation in 2020, Palestine Action has primarily organised direct-action protests against weapons manufacturers: defacing buildings, breaking windows and occupying factories. [A]s the UK continued to offer material and diplomatic support for the ongoing genocide in Gaza , activists broke into an RAF airbase and used spray-paint to vandalise two aircraft. The [UK] government responded by proscribing Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation, placing the group on the same legal footing as al-Qaeda and Islamic State.”
Rooney has highlighted that no one was arrested when an Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) mural was recently restored in Belfast, even though the UVF is a proscribed terrorist organisation responsible for the murders of hundreds of civilians. “Palestine Action, proscribed under the same law, is responsible for zero deaths and has never advocated the use of violence against any human being. Why then are its supporters arrested for wearing T-shirts, while murals celebrating loyalist death squads are left untouched?”
No. Faber confirmed that copies of her books currently on sale in the UK market do not need to be returned and will remain on sale.
The same applies. While stocks last, Rooney’s books will still be available to purchase from online sellers.
Potentially. Once copies of the author’s books currently on sale have been sold, customers will have to shop elsewhere. Irish retailers with a strong online presence such as Kenny’s and Eason could plug the gap. However, post-Brexit customs charges will complicate the picture.

title: Drug-related intimidation: ‘When people lose their house or get shot in the leg, then they report it’
description: Drug-related intimidation in Ireland, often with petrol bombings, as in the fatal arson attack on a family in Waterford this week, is getting worse
content:
A well-known family-based drugs gang in Waterford is under investigation this weekend for the petrol bomb attack on the English family home in the city that killed four people, including two children.
Philip and Kim English, and two of their sons, Callum (12) and Jayden (9), were murdered in an attack on the Birchwood estate, just south of the city.
Two other children – a girl (14) and a boy (6) – were rescued by firefighters and remain critically ill in Children’s Health Ireland ( CHI ) Crumlin in Dublin.
John James English, Philip English’s adult son from his first marriage, said the drug debt behind the arson attack had been incurred by somebody else, not his father, and that it had reached €20,000.
The English family home had been targeted before, most recently in a petrol bombing last month. Even Philip English’s first wife, Anne, has had her house petrol bombed, as part of the same campaign of intimidation that has been ongoing for more than three years.
The gang trying to collect the money has cornered a part of the lucrative drugs market in Waterford and the wider southeast region. It also has an intermittent presence in Spain. The group is family-based and has had no profile nationally – until this week.
