The Garda investigation team in Waterford, backed by the National Bureau of Criminal Investigation, moved quickly on Tuesday, carrying out a number of searches across Waterford city linked to the gang. They seized vehicles and mobile phones for examination.
Another vehicle, driven by a woman, was also being sought this week for seizure and examination on suspicion it was used by the arsonist.
On Thursday afternoon came news the first two arrests had been made .
A man in his 20s and woman in her 30s were detained on suspicion of assisting a crime gang in the arson attack on Birch Avenue just after 5am on Tuesday.
Gardaí suspect the attack on the English family home was intended to intimidate them, rather than take lives. The four deaths are now being investigated as murders.
Gardaí believe an associate of Philip English ran up the drugs debt. While Philip English was not involved in crime, and the debt was not his, he was deemed by the gang as someone who could pay the money.
And so pressure was applied to him, resulting in the tragedy that unfolded on Tuesday morning.
Gardaí and people working in community organisations dealing with the fallout from the drugs trade are increasingly familiar with the dynamic Philip English and his family were trapped in.
Over the past decade, gun crime has reduced and has, in large part, been replaced by petrol bombings.
Gardaí believe crime gangs across the State were deterred from reverting to gun crime as a result of the Garda crackdown on the Hutch gang and the Irish-based section of the Kinahan cartel and the subsequent convictions in the wake of the Kinahan-Hutch feud.
Petrol bombings have instead become a tactic of choice. Intended to intimidate rather than kill, they usually result in criminal damage rather than loss of life and so do not draw the same level of attention from national Garda units as a shooting.
The Irish Times gathered data from 14 of the 31 local authorities nationwide showing 113 recorded arson attacks on council properties in the past five years, 50 of them last year.
The four local authorities in Dublin recorded 59 attacks since 2022, with 35 occurring last year. Many were linked to drug-related intimidation.
That intimidation stems most often from a young person running up a debt with a local drugs gang which they are unable to pay back, even after being subjected to extreme violence. The gang then moves on to the people around that person, often parents, threatening and attacking them until the debt is paid.
[ Deaths in Waterford attack put focus on increase in drug-related intimidation Opens in new window ]
Research by the Drive project, an inter-agency initiative, established in 2020 to tackle drug-related intimidation, describes the crime as being “pervasive” and “underreported”, with 1,027 recorded cases in 2024 and 2025.
More than four in 10 cases – 43 per cent – took place in Dublin, but no other county accounted for more than 9 per cent of cases.
[ ‘An everybody issue’: How drug-related intimidation affects all areas, urban and rural Opens in new window ]
Siobhán Maher, national co-ordinator of the Drive project, said people targeted by drugs-related intimidation could be young or vulnerable and forced to take on tasks for drugs gangs, including selling drugs or holding money, drugs or firearms.
As they perform these high-risk tasks in order to pay off a debt, they may also be promised expensive clothing, such as designer jackets.
Ultimately, the people around them, often parents or grandparents, can be targeted with violence to clear their young relative’s debt.
“It manifests itself differently. It could be as extreme as what we know happened this week or it could be where a person is coerced or enticed into selling drugs,” Maher said, speaking at a conference on drug-related intimidation in Portlaoise, Co Laois, on Thursday.
Det Supt Sé McCormack of the Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau told the conference that gardaí accepted the level of reporting of drug-related intimidation was low.
“A significant proportion of people never come to An Garda Síochána, don’t want to come to us, or they don’t come at the first instance,” he said.
“They may build up courage, or things may become too difficult and they may come after the second or third incident. But help is out there.”
The Drive project also carried out interviews with “research participants”, including those with “personal experience” of drug-related intimidation and others working in community-based services supporting victims across the country.
Those interviewed spoke of how local dealers profiled families to establish whether they had the means to pay drug debts on behalf of others who were unable to pay.
“These people aren’t stupid. They know who has money and who hasn’t,” said one interviewee.
“They know who they can squeeze for a credit union loan, but they know they can’t do that again because they’re still paying it off, so they squeeze them for a cut of their weekly benefit payment.
“When you’re paying a debt over time it’s never-ending because they might charge interest or they’re more likely to keep coming back because you’ve demonstrated that you can pay.”
Other interviewees said victims were almost always reluctant to involve gardaí because they feared the local drugs gang so much and did not trust the Garda.
Families were more likely to reach out to local community-run resource centres or other groups dealing with the fallout of the drugs trade.
“Usually when people have ... lost their house, or the car’s been burnt out, or somebody has got shot in the leg ... then usually you’ll hear about it,” said one interviewee from a community-based service.
When locals realise they are unwilling to challenge a local criminal’s child, it lands pretty quick with them the power that criminal has over them
Another said the level of threat posed by gangs was too much for most people.
“Everyone pays,” that person said. “And even though we would say we can put you in touch with the Garda liaison and you can meet them here in plain clothes, not one has ever met him.
“It’s all fear; they have to live in the area and maybe the young lad that’s coming to the door lives in the area too.”
The participants set out the streetwise tactics used by gangs to dominate particular areas, usually housing estates, in a bid to establish the fear they then wield. Groups of street dealers – boys and young men working under gang leaders – take up a controlling posture in communities by “patrolling neighbourhoods, cruising on scrambler bikes or hanging out on corners” to create “no-go areas”.
It soon becomes clear to locals that these clusters of boys and young men are all part of the same group, supporting each other and ultimately working for a senior drug dealer.
Another interviewee made the point that drugs gangs – like the group now suspected of the Waterford arson attack – were often large family-based units.
[ Drug-related intimidation: why petrol bomb attacks are becoming more common Opens in new window ]
And they sought to subtly demonstrate their power by directing their own children to engage in the lowest-level antisocial behaviour, in the knowledge local people would feel they could not challenge the child.
“The younger [family] members are sent off to kick balls at cars, for example – that’s how it starts,” said the interviewee.
One Garda source said that when locals realise they are unwilling to challenge a local criminal’s child, “it lands pretty quick with them the power that [criminal] has over them”.
One interviewee said a local drugs gang could create a “drugs economy”, benefiting and motivating others to protect the gang and shore up its strength by intimidation.
“It’s the Robin Hood effect; drug dealers have a lot of money and they spread it around and then they’re glorified,” said the interviewee.
Once a local drugs gang demonstrated they had the numbers to wield significant power in a community and were the most dominant group there, they could often do as they pleased and people would be reluctant to involve gardaí, participants said.
“They will just choose a house at random, go in and make demands of the family to hold drugs, take their car or demand to be driven somewhere,” said one interviewee.
[ RTÉ’s Kieran Cuddihy calls out cocaine-use hypocrisy after Waterford murders Opens in new window ]
A Garda source said he believed the murders of the English family in Waterford would result in criminal charges.
“For them, this was another low-level incident, or so they thought. This wasn’t a planned murder like a gangland shooting would be; it was supposed to be a threat, but it went wrong,” he said.
“So, they’ll have made mistakes. This is not something that was carefully planned and that’s what will catch them out.”

title: More than €3m of illegal vapes and cannabis products seized in nationwide Garda raids
description: Officers targeting organised crime group also found and removed expensive vehicles and €235,000 cash
content:
Illegal vapes and cannabis-based products with an estimated street value of more than €3 million were seized after gardaí searched properties across the country.
Cash totalling more than €235,000 as well as £3,000 and $3,500 along with high-value vehicles were also seized.
Properties in Longford, Mayo, Roscommon, Wexford and Carlow were searched on Wednesday as part of an operation targeting an organised crime group involved in the sale and supply of illegal vapes and cannabis products throughout the country.
More than 100 gardaí, including members of the Garda National Drugs and Organised Crime Bureau and national specialist units, were involved in the searches.
In a statement, An Garda Síochána said the seized products would be sent to Forensic Science Ireland for analysis.
No arrests were made. Investigations are continuing.
The seizures were part of Operation Tara, a national anti-drugs strategy launched by the Garda in 2021.

title: A 9-19 to 1-9 win and handpass limits: First look at Gaelic football’s experimental new rules
description: Mixed reaction from players of UCD and Trinity to increase in kick-passing
content:
Among the small crowd in Santry on Thursday evening for a third-level league game trialling new experimental rules was a Trinity College masters student attending their first ever Gaelic football match.
The fact the fixture ended up as a cricket score ( UCD 9-19 Trinity College 1-9) might have been puzzling enough, but how do you explain that UCD’s nine goals were worth 36 points in new money but only 27 in old money?
Either way, the GAA newcomer did get to experience a game of Gaelic football in which foot-passing was a dominant skill, present in pretty much every phase of play. The limit of three consecutive handpasses certainly had the desired impact of showcasing a sport with more kicking.
The players were visibly and audibly more aware, and anxious, of that rule than any of the others put forward for experimentation by the Gaelic football Expert Advisory Group (EAG).
They counted handpasses aloud mid-play and, on receiving one, their immediate impulse was to look to make a kick-pass.
So conscious of the rule were both teams that over the course of the entire match there was only one violation – by UCD in the opening play of the second half.
Several early, long kick-passes inside led to scores at either end and players were certainly taking on passes they wouldn’t have under the traditional rules.
However, the increase in kick-passing didn’t massively change the pattern of the game from what would be the norm under the old rules. There was still plenty of lateral build-up play, only, rather than hand-passing across the arc, players were instead moving the ball from side to side by kicking.
On a couple of occasions players were caught on the third handpass and delivered the next offload with an unnatural, popped kick-pass to a team-mate in close proximity.
Aside from the handpass experiment, the other main takeaways were:
Kickouts nearly all went long. Providing goalkeepers with the option of only needing to get their kick-out beyond 13 metres rather than the 40-metre arc actually appeared to stretch the pitch with opposition players tending to loiter inside the arc, prompting the keeper to go long.
Trinity went short with three restarts, UCD didn’t go short once.
There were two backcourt violations – one from each team. No scenario occurred where the ban on a fisted point was tested and yet there were two fisted/palmed goals during the game – when balls were centred across the face of the goal and slapped mid-air by a player into the net. Under the trial rules, those goals are still permitted.
Charlie O’Connor was superb in the middle of the field for UCD while Ben Hanafin, Conor Broderick and Donal Daly were among their goalscorers. James McBreen netted Trinity’s goal.
Overall, it was a generally positive night for the experimental rules but the one-sided nature of the match must frame any analysis. It is impossible to argue the rules received a rigorous road-test over the course of the hour in Santry.
And if the Kevin McStay-chaired EAG hoped momentum would organically grow behind various rules, Thursday night proved how tricky it might prove to gain a consensus.
Because the general feeling of those on the small terrace was that the limit on handpasses had a positive impact on the spectacle – we were treated to some superb long foot-passing and both teams constantly looked to move the ball forward early.
However, after the game several players suggested the game felt stunted and less natural because of the limit on handpasses.
“To be honest I’m not a fan of it,” said Trinity midfielder Tom McCarroll.
“The new rules are encouraging you to try kick forward, but if there’s nothing on you can’t give it. I think there are too many things for the ref to look for, there are too many things going on.
“Even in training, we were working on only doing one handpass at times and just trying to kick it forward, but there is a practical reality to it as well – if it’s not on, you can’t kick it.
“In fairness there was quite a lot more kicking (in the game) than we would normally be used to, but I must say I’m not the biggest fan of it (limited handpass).”
Despite the absence of manager John Divilly, UCD still had a stacked sideline on Thursday night. Current Dublin boss Ger Brennan (who is GAA Executive at Belfield) was in the dugout while former Dublin player Johnny Magee was coaching the team.
“We’ve probably just tried to simplify it as much as we can. We haven’t overly emphasised the new rules because when it comes to the Sigerson it will be back to normal,” said Magee.
“But I suppose the big thing is probably the three handpass rule and being conscious of that.
“It’s about having the lads talking to each other, you could hear them shouting ‘two, two, two’ and letting team-mates know when the kick-pass was on. So, it’s just kind of being conscious of that.”
Experienced intercounty referee Barry Tiernan was the man in the middle and policed the game confidently.
David Coldrick was in attendance as a member of the EAG. Johnny Bradley, head of the GAA’s Games Intellegience Unit (GIU), was also present.
Of all the trial rules, Down native McCarroll feels the four-point goal is one of the most positive – despite it counting against his side on Thursday.
“I’m a big fan of it because it definitely encourages you to go for a goal,” he said.
“The one thing I do like is probably the four points for a goal, it’s more of an incentive now.
“The two-pointers were obviously a big thing this year and it is great to see the long-range shooting in the game now. But I also think it’s a positive that the reward for a goal has gone to four, it encourages players to go for it more often.”
The data from the round-one games this week in the third-level football league – Ryan Cup – will not be central to the review of the experimentation window.
The GIU has identified 15 fixtures in particular to record and analyse – the eight round-two matches, the four quarter-finals, two semi-finals and the final. The round-one matches are being viewed more as an opportunity for players to familiarise themselves with the rules in a match scenario.
“I think you have to let the old new rules settle a wee bit before you start introducing more,” added McCarroll. “But in fairness I did enjoy it there tonight.”

title: Retrial sought for woman who killed abusive partner as he slept
description: Julie Ann McIlwaine (35) had conviction for 2022 murder of James Joseph Crossley quashed earlier this month
content:
Prosecutors are seeking the retrial of a woman whose conviction for murdering her abusive partner while he slept was quashed, the Court of Appeal in Belfast heard on Friday.
But lawyers representing Julie Ann McIlwaine (35) claimed an alternative verdict of manslaughter should be reached over the fatal stabbing of James Joseph Crossley.
Senior judges confirmed they would deal with the competing arguments next month.
McIlwaine, who has been serving a minimum 12-year jail term, remains in custody pending a final determination. Crossley (38) was knifed to death at her former home in the Dunmurry area in March 2022.
She admitted killing her partner but denied the murder charge, claiming to have suffered a temporary loss of control as a victim of domestic abuse.
The pair had been in a relationship marred by emotional manipulation and coercive control.
At the time of his death Crossley was on bail for an alleged assault against McIlwaine and subject to a restraining order prohibiting any contact with her.
Despite a period of separation, they had re-established their relationship by the night of the killing.
Previous courts heard that Crossley took medication and went to sleep following arguments in which he issued an ultimatum for McIlwaine to choose between him and her family.
During police interviews the defendant said it all got on top of her and that she considered taking her own life.
She described taking a knife from the kitchen, returning to the bedroom and moving their young child out of the way before repeatedly stabbing her sleeping partner.
The prosecution argued she made rational choices that demonstrated being in control of her actions.
In October 2024 a jury rejected McIlwaine’s case and returned a unanimous guilty verdict.
However, earlier this month she won a legal bid to overturn her conviction for murder.
Defence lawyers successfully argued that jurors were misdirected and reached a verdict that went against the weight of expert evidence.
Central to the appeal was how the trial judge advised them on the legal test for the loss-of-control defence.
Instead of being asked to decide whether someone of similar characteristics to McIlwaine “might” have reacted similarly, the question posed was “would” that person have acted in the same way.
The wording used was found to have wrongly imposed a higher threshold for establishing probability.
Further issues related to opinions from two consultant forensic psychiatrists on the psychological impact of prolonged abuse and the responses of victims in coercively controlling relationships.
In court on Friday, Chief Justice Siobhan Keegan disclosed: “There is an application for a retrial.”
Prosecution counsel Richard Weir confirmed the request to re-run the case on the charge of murder.
But barrister Eilis McDermott, representing McIlwaine, argued for an alternative outcome.
“Our submission is that the court should consider substituting a verdict [of manslaughter],” she said.
With a number of other legal issues also still to be determined, proceedings were adjourned until early November.

title: Charlie O’Shea and Seán Edogbo to make Champions Cup debuts for Munster
description: Province will play without a number eight jersey against Racing 92, in tribute to the late Anthony Foley
content:
Charlie O’Shea, the 20-year-old Munster academy outhalf, will start for Munster and make his Champions Cup debut against Racing 92 at Páirc Uí Chaoimh this Saturday (kick-off 8pm).
The 22-year-old flanker Seán Edogbo will also make his European debut in the starting back-row and alongside him, in a tribute to Anthony Foley, Brian Gleeson will wear the number 24 jersey - just as CJ Stander did when Munster beat Glasgow 10 years ago.
All told there are six changes to the starting XV from last week’s 26-26 draw against Ulster in Belfast. Along with Edogbo, Jack Aungier, Tom Ahern, John Hodnett and Gleeson come into the forward pack, with O’Shea the one change in the backline.
O’Shea has only played three times for Munster, his sole start being a two-try, man-of-the-match display in the win over the Bulls a fortnight ago, when Edogbo made just his fourth start for the province. Summer signings Aungier, Marnus van der Merwe and Kieran Brookes will all make their first Champions Cup appearances for Munster.
In a youthful and exciting selection by Clayton McMillan, there will be two further Champions Cup debutants on the bench in 23-year-old hooker Max Clein, and 21-year-old scrumhalf Ben O’Donovan. Both of them, like the younger Edogbo, were promoted from the academy to the senior squad ahead of this season.
In the week which marks the 10th anniversary of Foley’s passing on the day Munster were scheduled to play Racing 92 in Paris, there will be a series of special tributes and commemorative activities, in addition to the number eight jersey again being retired for the day.
Head Coach Clayton McMillan said: “The players are determined to put in a performance that Axel would be proud of. He is spoken about every day in our building and we are thinking of him and his family more than ever this week, 10 years on from his shock passing.
“While it will be an emotional day, the players know that the best way to honour his incredible legacy is to play the game with the right mentality and produce a committed team performance that shows how much they care for the jersey and the province.
“It’s exciting to see young players Seán Edogbo and Charlie O’Shea start on their Champions Cup debuts in another step forward in their development.
“Max Clein and Ben O’Donovan are two young men who moved up from the Academy to the senior squad in the summer and are named in a Champions Cup squad for the first time and we have every confidence in them if called upon.
“Marnus van der Merwe, Jack Aungier and Kieran Brookes are seasoned campaigners who have already played at this level. They get to do so with Munster for the first time tomorrow night and we have been really pleased with their contributions since joining in the summer.“
Munster Rugby: Ben O’Connor; Shay McCarthy, Alex Nankivell, Dan Kelly, Seán O’Brien; Charlie O’Shea, Craig Casey; Jeremy Loughman, Marnus van der Merwe, Jack Aungier; Tom Ahern, Tadhg Beirne (C); Seán Edogbo, John Hodnett, Brian Gleeson. Replacements: Max Clein, Josh Wycherley, Kieran Brookes, Fineen Wycherley, Gavin Coombes, Ben O’Donovan, JJ Hanrahan, Jack O’Donoghue.

title: Russell Brand turned into ‘wild-eyed maniac’ during alleged assault, accuser tells trial
description: Brand is accused of rape and sexual assault involving six women from 1999 to 2009. He denies the allegations
content:
One of six women who accuse Russell Brand of sex offences ‌told a London court on Friday that the British actor and comedian turned into a “wild-eyed maniac” when he tried to drag her into a ​toilet cubicle at her workplace.
Brand (51) is accused of indecently assaulting the woman, who told Southwark crown court: “I emerged relatively unscathed. He didn’t manage to rape me.”
The woman, who was working for MTV at the time, said she did not report the incident then because she was “scared” as Brand was famous “and a big asset” to the TV channel.
Brand is facing three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges.
The woman, who gave evidence from behind a screen, said she was working at MTV in 2001 when she met Brand and they had “banter” about a T-shirt he was wearing. She later offered to show him the way to the toilets, where he allegedly assaulted her.
The woman said she felt “bewildered and confused”, telling the court: “This person went from someone jovial and friendly to suddenly turning into this wild-eyed maniac trying to pull me into the toilet.”
Detailing the alleged assault, she added: “His demeanour changed. He grabbed my forearm and he was leaning into the door. It was quite forceful, the grip. It took me unawares, I wasn’t expecting that.”
In response to questions from the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones, the woman said Brand began pleading with her to come into the toilets as she tried to get away.
“I said to him: ‘What are you doing? Are you mad? Let me go.’ Then he started to plead, almost ‘go on, go on, come in’,” she told the court.
She said he had a “wild” look in his eyes and she had to use her strength to escape his “hard” grip in an interaction that lasted about 20 seconds.
The woman said she told two colleagues what had happened but she did not make a police complaint until she saw a 2023 documentary that accused Brand of sexual misconduct.
“It brought everything back,” she said. “I thought I’d managed to get away. It could’ve been very different … I thought it was the right thing to come forward.”
In cross-examination, the defence barrister, Ian Winter, suggested the woman had reassessed her memory of the incident after the documentary, but she said it had not changed her mind.
“I don’t think it’s quite as straightforward as that,” she said. “It would have been my word against his, I had a job to consider, I emerged relatively unscathed. He didn’t manage to rape me. I managed to get myself out of the situation.”
She rejected the barrister’s suggestion that Brand had “invited” her into the toilet for a consensual sexual encounter. She said: “You don’t drag someone by the arm, not in my world anyway. You don’t grip someone to drag them in, that’s not consensual.”
She said he had been “grabbing and pulling” her, telling the court: “That’s not inviting someone in. That’s forcing someone to do something against their will.”
Winter suggested it was “a short-lived, very, very minor incident” and that after the woman declined, Brand “left it there”. The woman responded: “The intent was there. It could have been very different.”

title: Europe should consider ‘all options’ to plug Ukraine’s budget shortfall, Taoiseach says
description: Zelenskiy in Brussels for talks with EU leaders about latest fracture in relationship with Trump
content:
European governments will need to quickly decide how to shore up Ukraine ’s wartime finances until the end of 2028, Taoiseach Micheál Martin has said, as frantic efforts are made to patch up Kyiv’s relationship with the Trump administration.
Ukraine is heading into what will be a cold winter lacking sufficient air defence interceptors to shoot down Russian missiles. More broadly, Kyiv is facing a yawning gap in its budget next year that could be as large as €70 billion.
The EU’s national leaders were in Brussels for a summit on Friday, where they reiterated their support for Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy following the latest breakdown in relations between Washington and Kyiv.
Speaking in Brussels, the Taoiseach said some sort of “pan-European financial injection” would be required to cover Ukraine’s budget shortfall.
Martin said he was “open” to different ways the EU could finance such support. “We would look at all options in terms of how we can support Ukraine,” he said.
He defended the Republic’s financial contributions to Ukraine, after Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten said some EU governments were not pulling their weight.
“We are net contributors [to the EU budget] and through any European mechanism and facility, we will be higher contributors than most ... I think that’s the ultimate way to do it, and it’s the proper and effective way,” Martin said.
Late last year EU leaders agreed to jointly borrow funds as a bloc to finance a €90 billion loan to Ukraine.
Kyiv has been burning through the money quicker than anticipated, due to the intensity of the fighting and changing nature of the war, plus a drop in aid coming from other western allies.
The loan had been backstopped by a €200 billion pile of Russian central bank assets, which are frozen in European financial institutions by the EU’s regime of economic sanctions.
A previous EU plan to use the Russian assets to refill Ukraine’s coffers, in lieu of war reparations from Moscow, ran aground after Belgium expressed concerns about the legality of touching the sanctioned assets.
The last attempt to use the immobilised Russian central bank cash “came to naught in the end”, Martin noted on Friday.
“So I’m conscious of the amount of energy and effort put into that on the last occasion, I would be more in favour of doing something efficiently and effectively and as quickly as we possibly can,” he said.
“In terms of the medium term, over 2027 and 2028, I think we need to focus on that, whether it’s the immobilised assets or other mechanisms, I’m open,” he said.
The Fianna Fáil leader said Europe needed to continue its “outreach” to the US, to stress how Russia had been the aggressor who started the war.
Inside the room national leaders were told proposals to improve Ukraine’s financial position for 2027 would be tabled in the coming weeks by the European Commission, the EU’s executive arm led by Ursula von der Leyen.
Zelenskiy travelled to Brussels to join the European Council summit for the portion of the discussion about Ukraine.
Speaking beforehand, Zelenskiy said European leaders who continued to stand by Ukraine were “real leaders”.
The Ukrainian president said there was no sign at all that Russia was interested in peace. Finding a way to plug the gap in Ukraine’s budget for 2027 was a “key” question that needed to be answered, he said.
“This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine, this is no time to relieve Russian sanctions,” said European Council president António Costa, before welcoming Zelenskiy to the EU summit.

title: Champions Cup stats show hope of breaking French stranglehold is clutching at straws
description: Form book and numbers indicate predictions of another French European triumph are well-founded
content:
It’s six Champions Cup titles on the bounce now for the French clubs. Bookies, pundits and pessimistic provincial fans all tell you that there’s fat chance it won’t be seven. The foreboding sense is that Toulouse and Bordeaux have improved, while La Rochelle eek back towards the top table and Montpellier emerge as a team capable of joining them. Can anyone outside of France break the European stranglehold?
Leinster are looking for a new unpredictability in their attack. If you can’t beat them, join them, then beat them. Northampton have the on-ball threat but probably lack the tight five heft. What of Bath with Mike Prendergast adding some attacking verve to go with their set-piece might?
We are, alas, likely in the straw-clutching business. Factors such as superstar signings (here’s looking at you, Toulouse and Tomasso Menoncello) and undeniable bulk (Ben Tameifuna named at lock for Bordeaux’s opener away to Gloucester) are important. But strip this conversation back to the basics. Where are games of rugby won and lost, and what do recent metrics suggest might happen in these areas?
When it comes to Irish teams struggling for European silverware, the gap tends to be in predictability of attack and speed across the park. The set-piece can come into things as well, particularly if early indications of the maul’s increased value turn into a true trend.
The big, bad French teams can whack you up front and run around you out wide. Granted, we have seen just three rounds of provincial action this season, and only one where the majority of Ireland internationals are available, but there is little evidence to suggest any of that is changing.
Starting with the set-piece, the dominance of French sides is something to behold. Across all of global club rugby last season, the entire top 10 for the percentage of scrums won on opposition put-ins come from the Top 14. Toulouse (23.6 per cent), Stade Francais (23.4) and Montpellier (22.6) made up the top three.
Given the scrum woes of Irish provinces so far in the early season: Leinster away in South Africa even with internationals Andrew Porter and Thomas Clarkson in tow, Connacht against Benetton and Ulster when struggling against Munster, these figures are ominous. Munster, it should be said, have had a solid scrum that excelled against Ulster. Their recruitment focusing on the frontrow, at this early juncture, has looked to had an effect.
The maul is another point of interest given the wider discussion around the new laws. Ahead of this season, World Rugby told referees to clamp down on players disrupting the ball when on the wrong side of the maul but still bound to it. Early signs indicate that this makes it easier for attacking sides, with 32 maul tries being scored across just the opening three URC rounds.
[ Champions Cup has a jeopardy problem: can anyone stop France’s Top 14 giants? Opens in new window ]
While these numbers appear stark, we should proceed with the caveat that it remains early days in assessing the effects of the new law application. Teams will have more time to adapt. Yet if it does come to pass that the maul is a more potent weapon, surprise surprise, the French teams appear better equipped to cash in.
Last season, before the new law application, five of the top 10 “European” (including South African teams) sides for metres gained per maul were French. None were Irish. In the scoring charts, the Irish provinces ranked poorly in the category of mauls required to score. Leinster were the second worst team for the number of mauls required per try scored, Ulster fifth worst, Connacht sixth and Munster 11th.
When it comes to the true superpower of French sides in Europe, namely the unpredictability of their attack, this can be hard to define with pure numbers. But we can look at certain areas and get close.
Speed kills, as Ronan O’Gara once said, and when it comes to ruck speed, French sides dominate. In last season’s league and EPCR action, Bordeaux led the way with 66.6 per cent of their rucks lasting fewer than three seconds. The rankings behind them read Montpellier, Northampton, Toulon and Toulouse rounding out the top five. An Irish point of intrigue is that Munster were the eighth best team in Europe in this category.
Other relevant stats paint a similar French picture. For percentage of line breaks leading to a try, six of last season’s top 10 were French (Ulster were 10th). For gainline carries, four of the top-10 were French. For dominant carry percentage and tackle evasion, three of the top 10 were French. For the most part, English and non-Irish URC sides made up the others on these lists.
[ Leinster’s James Ryan looking forward to ‘proper’ French test at Clermont Opens in new window ]
Even look at style of play. The dominant teams of this era, be it South Africa in the World Cup or Bordeaux in Europe, prefer to play without the ball and strike quickly when they have it. Allow opponents to overplay and punish them when they do. It has proved a mighty effective ploy in knock-out rugby.
Look at the rankings for teams who played for more than five phases in any given attack last season. Of the bottom sides, ie those who tend not to overplay with ball in hand, the entire top 10 were South African and French.
None of which discounts the possibility for slip-ups. Toulouse suffered in last year’s Champions Cup thanks to upsets at Glasgow and Saracens. They were forced into an away knock-out on the same side of the draw against eventual champions Bordeaux. The problems with the Champions Cup format are many, but one of them is that across a shortened competition featuring just four pool games and a series of knockouts, statistical trends are not as relevant given the scope for one-off shocks.
Such upsets, by very definition, are hard to predict. What the form book and the numbers say, though, based on last season’s figures showing few signs of changing, is that predictions of another French European triumph are more than well-founded.

title: Germany is losing patience with Friedrich Merz
description: With economic reforms stalled and industry under pressure, the chancellor faces mounting doubts about his ability to reverse the country’s decline
content:
A ncient Romans kept a sacred eternal flame dedicated to the goddess Vesta, defender of hearth and home, in a dedicated temple guarded by a special priesthood: the Vestal Virgins. Since July the Vestal Virgins on display in Berlin’s Bode Museum, largely 18th century French artworks, have had to share room 257 with a new, popular roommate.
Gleaming blue and gold, the official portrait of Angela Merkel has attracted such crowds – Bode Museum ticket sales are up 85 per cent – that its public display has been extended by two months until January. Germany’s second-to-last chancellor is by far its most popular.
“She was dedicated, a shrewd analyst but at the same time human, who gave us 16 good years,” says Gisela Eggert, a retired university lecturer visiting from Bonn. “But the painting is a bit primitive – the eyes are all wrong – compared to her complexity.”
Angela Merkel’s four terms in office from 2005 were filled with drama – from the banking and refugee crises to the Covid-19 pandemic – but the seven years since have ramped up still further with refugees and rearmament, thanks to Russia’s war on Ukraine, and a persistently flat economy.
That, in turn, has triggered a record wave of insolvencies and compounded serious doubts about Germany’s industrial base. Small wonder, then, that Merkel is being mythologised as a modern-day Vestal Virgin: a defender of hearth, home − and better times.
In room 257, no one has anything good to say about today’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz : too legalistic, too arrogant, a poor communicator, an appalling man.
He is just 18 months in office but only 13 per cent of Germans think he is doing a good job. His centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), hobbled by an identity crisis and daily coalition squabbles, has slumped 10 points in polls since election day in February 2025 to a record low of 19 per cent.
Meanwhile the far-right Alternative for Germany has surged past the CDU to first place in polls and a record 30 per cent support.
You can see Germany’s grim mood on the shelves of a bookshop near the Bode Museum. Half a dozen new books warn about the rise of fascism while the best-selling non-fiction book is called Germany 2033, imagining the rise of the AfD to power a century after the Nazis.
[ Nostalgia and lost pride: the fuel that feeds Europe’s far right Opens in new window ]
“The resistance is far lower than people before imagined, because no one believes any more in its efficacy,” writes author Justus Bender of German election night in seven years’ time. “People submit. They grumble.”
Bender’s version of Germany’s immediate future is not as fantastical as it was in the Merkel era. The greatest danger to his fantasy becoming reality, he thinks, is an army of politicians and officials still in denial. They insist, despite endless proof to the contrary, that their old, trusted political strategies – facts and reality – will work against anxiety-driven politics peddled by the AfD.
After the Bode Museum and bookshop we continue along the bank of the river Spree to the Reichstag parliament building. A fiery debate is happening inside and chancellor Friedrich Merz is struggling on two fronts: with a patchy political record and a scratchy, cold-ridden voice.
After recent state election shocks – and a first AfD-led government looming next month in Saxony-Anhalt – Merz is accentuating the positive: pointing to a 2026 growth forecast of 1.3 per cent, double previous expectations, along with rising foreign investment.
What Germany needs to unblock itself, he says, is the power of positive thinking and “creative efforts proportionate to the dangers which threaten it”, a nod to the sniggering 150 AfD parliamentarians seated before him.
The term “creative effort” originated as “efforts créateurs”, with Robert Schuman, the former French foreign minister, in a May 1950 speech considered a founding text of the modern European Union.
Some 76 years later in Berlin, Merz concedes German voters have “justified dissatisfaction and justified feelings of injustice” and can only be won back through “creative effort” of its politicians.
But creative effort, critics say, is precisely what Merz and his ministers lack.
“Germany is a conservative country but there is too little on offer at the moment for the political centre,” said Prof Klaus Schubert, political scientist at the University of Münster.
The uncertain present, he suggests, is why people are romanticising the recent political past and long for a “Mutti” Merkel or a table-thumping “Basta” chancellor like Gerhard Schröder. A senior Schröder-era cabinet member is happy to speak to The Irish Times about the ex-chancellor, but would rather not be named “so I can speak my mind openly”.
The problem that compounds Germany’s many structural challenges, this ex-minister thinks, is Merz: someone who “offers no perspective or leadership”.
[ If the EU continues to drift, disintegration becomes a more plausible future Opens in new window ]
“Instead you have a chancellor complaining in public that his own ministers have yet to deliver reform proposals,” said the Schröder-era minister. “Where is his authority? That would have been unthinkable with Schröder.”
Another big political difference between now and 2002, when Schröder presented dramatic social and economic reforms, is the sense of urgency. Today’s pressures are palpable – a cost-of-living and housing crises, security fears and record insolvencies – but not unique to Germany. “Back then we had five million unemployed, today it’s two million, so the pressure to act then was far greater,” adds the ex-minister.
Out of sight beneath Germany’s hood, though, everyone can hear the country’s economic engine making worrying noises.
A chronic shortage of new ideas, a national fear of risk-taking and shortage of skilled workers have all brought Germany’s industrial base to the brink. Instead of a leap forward, Merz is being pulled back: lobbying Brussels to water down a proposed 2035 ban on combustion engines.
Back at home, pension and welfare reforms have been stalled for months and, critics say, are of a homeopathic nature. The long-flagged fiscal reform left untouched Germany’s Byzantine tax law and offered instead €10 billion in tax relief.
Munich’s Ifo economic think-tank worries the Merz government seems focused more on plucking low-hanging fruit than the more prickly pears higher up: punitive energy prices, surging non-wage costs, ballooning bureaucracy and a growing AI gap vis-a-vis China and the US.
“Most people know that if the government does not act more decisively than it has so far,” warns Ifo president Clemens Fuest, “that it is putting prosperity at risk.”
[ Germany’s political centre is not holding. It is tearing itself apart Opens in new window ]
Some observers suggest that Germany is beyond risk of – and already trapped in – a vicious circle of decline. In this scenario, mainstream parties’ fear of the political fringes hobbles their own decisiveness, in turn driving increasing numbers of voters to the fringes.
Election numbers tell their own tale: modern Germany’s first grand coalition, lead by Angela Merkel in 2005, controlled 73 per cent of Bundestag seats. Twenty years later, the Merz grand coalition has just 52 per cent of seats.
This dramatic shift from the political centre, and a lack of urgency to reverse it, is a warning signal for many with an eye on the last century. Dr Mark Jones, historian of Germany’s interwar Weimar period at UCD, sees “processes taking place now that overlap with those of the past”.
“The first ‘grand coalition’ was a sort of emergency message intended to create a super stable majority, whereas today’s grand coalition could barely scrape a majority,” he argues.
Nearly eight decades in, he thinks the ongoing drift in Berlin suggests the modern German federal republic is “not as stable and successful a political project as its own history myths would have us believe.”

title: Leinster v Clermont Auvergne: The best moments from a European rugby rivalry
description: From Johnny Sexton’s kicking masterclass to Gordon D’Arcy’s last-minute tackle, a look back at some of the clubs’ Champions Cup encounters
content:
There have been some memorable moments between Leinster and Clermont Auvergne throughout their shared history in the Champions Cup , one that will be renewed once again at the weekend when the Irish province travel to the Stade Marcel Michelin.
Players have stood up and out. Gordon D’Arcy scored a try, was stretchered off and in a different match between the clubs made a game-saving tackle to send Leinster to the 2012 final. Wesley Fofana crossed for a try in one match and was denied another by the D’Arcy tackle. Brock James suffered a kicking nightmare at the RDS on a day when Johnny Sexton couldn’t miss.
Leinster’s first European away win in France was against Montferrand, who later became Clermont Auvergne, a 23-20 success some 24 years ago. Here we look at a few of those tussles in a little more detail.
The game is remembered for the off-colour day that Brock James suffered with the boot. He missed five kicks at goal plus a further three drop goal opportunities, including one at the death that would have handed the French club a victory. It would have been a result that Leinster couldn’t have quibbled with after a game in which Clermont wing Julien Malzieu scored a hat-trick of tries.
Down the road the Australian would go on to atone and enjoy happier days in a Clermont shirt against Leinster. The irony was that Johnny Sexton kicked superbly for the home side (19 points), and coupled with two tries from the man-of-the-match Jamie Heaslip it was enough to allow Leinster to squeeze home.
He said: “It was a see-saw kind of a game and there are mixed feelings in the dressingroom. They dominated at times and there’s a real sense of relief because they could have shaded it at the end.”
Another belter of a contest between the two sides in a Heineken Cup semi-final from which Joe Schmidt’s side emerged. Leinster trailed 12-6 at the interval to four penalties from James before the game spun on its axis with a brilliant training ground move that bore fruition for the Irish province.
Brian O’Driscoll and Rob Kearney laid the groundwork, while Cian Healy scored the try. Minutes later Rob Kearney’s 45-metre drop goal nudged Leinster 16-12 in front. James kicked a penalty, missed another and a drop goal chance before the Australian and Johnny Sexton swapped penalties to leave the game delicately poised at 19-15.
It took a brilliant last-minute tackle by Gordon D’Arcy to force a fumble and deny Wesley Fofana a try at the death, a moment that required a TMO review.
[ Champions Cup pool guide: Leinster, Munster and Connacht’s opponents reviewed and rated Opens in new window ]
A then Irish record for a European pool match of 48,964 watched on as Clermont beat the reigning European champions for the second week in succession. Scrumhalf Morgan Parra was the standout player for the visitors as he kicked eight from nine attempts with the placed ball in a 23-point haul. It ended a run of five successive defeats in Ireland for the French club since 2007.
Fofana scored an early try as Clermont raced into a 25-9 lead and it was only late tries from Shane Jennings and Fergus McFadden that put a modicum of respectability on the final scoreline and earned the home side a losing bonus point. The French side had beaten Leinster 15-12 the previous week at the Stade Marcel Michelin.
Leinster head coach Joe Schmidt said in the aftermath: “It’s very hard to take defeat two weeks in a row with the amount of effort the players put in. The bonus point is handy [for qualification]. Miracles happen in sport, I guess, but mathematical long shots seldom come into being.
“I knew Clermont would come to play, and they’d be better than they were last week. I think we out-thought them last week and they just outmuscled us this week.”
A ninth win in nine games to that point for Leo Cullen’s side but in keeping with many of the matches between the sides it was hard-fought. There were several notable lines from the game, primarily that it was Jordie Barrett’s second match of his Leinster stint.
Following on from scoring a try on debut the previous week against the Bristol Bears, he did likewise from his role at fullback. Leinster’s other try came from Garry Ringrose with Sam Prendergast tagging on five points. The home side struggled at lineout time with six of their 16 throws going astray.
Clermont managed a try from Fijian-born Alivereti Raka – he could be involved again at the weekend – and not even the arrival of Jack Conan and RG Snyman from the bench could provide the Irish province with the impetus to kick on when it came to the scoreboard.
[ Leinster’s James Ryan looking forward to ‘proper’ French test at Clermont Opens in new window ]

title: Third word error in Aer Lingus disciplinary papers, WRC is told
description: WRC is hearing a complaint against Aer Lingus by a pilot who was disciplined for failing to file an air safety report
content:
The case of an Aer Lingus pilot who says he should not have been stripped of command responsibility for failing to immediately file an air safety report over what he considered a “non-event” has heard of a third word error in internal company documents on the case.
Hearings on complaints by Declan McCabe under the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, the Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005 and the Payment of Wages Act 1991 are continuing this week at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).
The WRC has heard for the third time of what is said to be an error in wording in internal company documents concerning a disciplinary process brought against McCabe.
The tribunal was told on Thursday that when the airline’s chief pilot wrote that McCabe had been “indicted” by a safety investigation, he meant to write “indicated”.
McCabe was disciplined for what the airline deemed breaches of his air safety reporting obligations while flying in command of an Airbus A321xlr, which failed to link up with a radio navigation beacon coming into Dublin Airport before making a turn to re-establish contact.
[ Aer Lingus pilot ‘uncomfortable’ at crossing picket line to attend WRC hearing Opens in new window ]
The conclusion in a disciplinary investigation was that McCabe’s aircraft, with 156 passengers and crew aboard, was “flying in the wrong direction ... until air traffic control intervened” on the day, according to Captain Eamon Kierans, the manager who conducted the process.
McCabe said what happened was “a non-event from a flying point of view” and that the relevant Aer Lingus manual left it up to his judgment to decide whether to report it. The company disagreed, and while his actions as a pilot were not impugned, the airline concluded he had failed in his safety reporting duties by not filing a report until he was directed to do so by the airline’s director of safety and security Conor Nolan.
The tribunal heard that Capt Nolan decided in a safety review that the flight crew’s actions prior to the air safety report being submitted amounted to a “reckless violation” – leading ultimately to disciplinary action.
McCabe’s case is that the airline had no right to pursue a disciplinary process against him and that it was penalisation for complaining about another senior managing pilot, Capt Colm Wynne, having a safety management role in the airline, on foot of a previous dispute dating back to 2011.
Yvonne De Silva, who was director of in-flight services at Aer Lingus in 2024, upheld the disciplinary sanction against McCabe when she gave her decision on his internal appeal in March 2024.
David Byrnes BL, for the complainant, said that during the appeal stage his client argued that the entire disciplinary process was prejudged. McCabe cited a letter from the airline’s then-chief pilot, Capt John Kelly, stating before the disciplinary process began that McCabe was “already indicted” by Capt Nolan’s safety probe.
Giving evidence, De Silva said the only role Capt Kelly had in relation to her appeal process had been to ask about her availability, and that she had been assigned to the process by Aer Lingus HR.
“You know what indictment means – charges brought before even a disciplinary investigation to say that a disciplinary hearing is warranted,” Byrnes asked the witness.
“Yes,” De Silva replied. She said she had agreed with McCabe that the word “indictment” was “not appropriate” when he brought it up at appeal stage.
“I read the email myself. My interpretation was that it was a typo,” De Silva said.
McCabe told her at the appeal that Capt Kelly “hadn’t mentioned it”, she said.
“I spoke to captain Kelly and mentioned what was his thinking. He said: ‘Oh, that was a typo; when I wrote back to him I didn’t notice the typo myself,’” De Silva said.
“I wrote in my outcome letter that it was a typo, it was my view that it was a typo,” she said. “The use of the word ‘indicted’ was a typo on the part of captain Kelly – it should have said ‘indicated’” .
Her finding was that “having read the full email, there was no other logical conclusion”.
Earlier this year, Capt Conor Barrett, the disciplinary investigator in McCabe’s case, said he used the word “believe” when he meant to write “belie” in relation to McCabe’s interpretation of the manual’s safety reporting section.
Capt Barrett told the WRC the next day that when he used the word “belies” elsewhere in the report, he meant something different. De Silva said she mentioned the typo in the course of a broader discussion with Capt Kelly – one of a number of conversations she had with senior pilots at the airline during the appeal process, she said.
She told the WRC she wanted “to get a little bit more information” from them.
Byrnes asked De Silva: “Did you document these conversations?”
“I believed it was the right thing to do,” De Silva said.
Byrnes said his client was entitled to “know the evidence and test the evidence from the start to the bitter end” but had only found out about these conversations for the first time at the WRC on Thursday.
Counsel said the information gleaned from such conversations “clearly materially influenced” the appeal process and asked De Silva to show him where the Aer Lingus policy provided for her to have such discussions without notice to the appellant.
“You’re probably going to tell me it’s not there,” De Silva said.
Counsel said De Silva “showed bias toward what people outside the process were telling you”, which she denied.
Byrnes asked her whether she told his client that one of the people she spoke with in this context was Capt Kierans, the disciplinary officer, and “the person you were reviewing in this appeal”.
Byrnes asked whether the HR officer assisting De Silva with the appeal process had warned her that she “ought to be careful” about contacting Kierans during the appeal.
“I can’t remember,” De Silva said. She accepted she did not give McCabe and his representative during the internal process, Capt Padraig Higgins, “a chance to respond to those conversations I had”.

title: AIB cuts four-year fixed mortgage rate for borrowers
description: The move comes following two interest rate hikes by the European Central Bank in the past six months
content:
AIB has made a reduction of up to 0.35 per cent on its four-year fixed rate for mortgages over €250,000.
The reduction, available to those whose homes don’t have a building energy rating of B3 or higher, has been put in place with immediate effect for new and existing customers.
The rate will apply to customers with a minimum mortgage balance of €250,000 and a loan-to-value ratio of more than 80 per cent.
For those with an LTV of more than 80 per cent, the rate will fall from 3.6 per cent to 3.25 per cent.
Rates for mortgage holders who have an LTV of 50-80 per cent have fallen from 3.5 per cent to 3.2 per cent, while those with an LTV of below 50 per cent can avail of a rate of 3.15 per cent, down from 3.4 per cent.
Data provided by AIB said customers on a new €350,000 four-year fixed-rate mortgage, with an LTV of 50-80 per cent over a 25-year term, can save up to €55.52 per month, or €666.24 a year, under the new terms.
It added monthly repayments based on this example would fall from €1,750.82 to €1,695.30.
Based on data from the Banking and Payments Federation Ireland, new mortgages in Ireland were on average €318,000 in the second quarter of this year.
In the period, the average first-time buyer mortgage was €326,000 and the average mover mortgage was €391,000.
In October last year, AIB also reduced a number of its non-green fixed mortgage rates by up to 0.65 per cent, which it estimated could benefit more than 10,000 people each month.
The latest cuts by AIB have come in the wake of two interest rate increases by the European Central Bank in the past six months, which led to more than 100,000 people who hold tracker mortgage facing immediate increases to their repayments .
The new rates are available to new customers buying their first home, or borrowers moving home or switching their mortgage to AIB.
Existing customers on variable rates and those coming to the end of their fixed-rate period can also avail of the new terms.
A statement from AIB said the bank had observed customers increasingly seeking out fixed rates, with almost nine in 10 new customers opting for a fixed rate this year.
AIB managing director of retail banking Geraldine Casey said this fixed-rate reduction would offer security for customers amid the rate hikes.
“We are committed to pricing our mortgages at a sustainable rate for our customers and the bank. And we continue to monitor the mortgage market and the needs of customers, making considered adjustments where appropriate,” she said.

title: Court users face further disruption after criminal solicitors escalate action
description: Criminal defence solicitors to escalate services withdrawal from Monday
content:
Courts face increased disruption from Monday due to some criminal defence solicitors escalating their withdrawal of legal aid services to almost all cases, including people in custody and private law cases.
Court presidents were told, in a letter on Friday, that the escalation arose from the Minister for Justice’s failure to engage in “meaningful” discussions in the dispute over a new legal aid payment model for the District Courts .
While some solicitors have resumed legal aid work, and others never participated in the withdrawal under way since July 1st, sources say most, particularly in Dublin, continue to participate in the action.
Until now, the withdrawal had not affected cases of people in custody before July 1st, when the new one-flat-fee payment model was introduced.
Under the escalation, custody cases and all other cases, with very limited exceptions, will be affected. The escalation will affect protocol cases, those involving young and/or vulnerable defendants, victims and witnesses.
The action has led to the adjournments of thousands of cases, compounding existing backlogs and delays.
The letter sent on Friday from Tony Collier, a partner in Ferrys Solicitors LLP, is believed to reflect the position of a substantial number of defence solicitors.
Collier referred to comments in early October by the Chief Justice expressing the judiciary’s concern over the continued dispute and expressing hope for a resolution.
He also noted comments by High Court judge Mary Rose Gearty encouraging a resolution of a legal challenge over the new payment model. That challenge by Dublin solicitor John Quinn was taken against O’Callaghan in late July.
Gearty’s judgment is due on November 3rd.
In his letter, Collier said the Law Society , the representative body for solicitors, “remains ready to engage with the Minister at a moment’s notice”.
John Quinn had also written to the Minister seeking a meeting but had received “no substantive response”, he noted.
There remains “no indication that the Minister is willing to enter into meaningful discussions aimed at resolving this dispute”, said Collier. That “is both regrettable and difficult to comprehend”.
He said the solicitors’ profession has made “substantial concessions” in an effort to resolve the dispute, with “only two relatively straightforward issues” still outstanding but “fundamental to the proper administration of justice in the District Court”.
In the circumstances, Collier said he regretted to advise his firm will, from Monday, withdraw all criminal defence services, including custody cases, in Dublin and nationally.
The escalation is not due to any unwillingness by solicitors to resolve the dispute but is the consequence of the Minister’s failure “to engage in meaningful discussions”, he said.
The letter comes days after the continuing impasse was discussed by Dublin-based solicitors and solicitors countrywide during Zoom meetings.
The new payment model provides for one fee of €520, based on an average of five court appearances, irrespective of the number of charges and court appearances.
Solicitors say it means they will not be paid for their work in more complex cases, including ones involving children and people with addiction and mental health issues.
In a statement, the Department of Justice said an 8 per cent increase in criminal legal aid fees payable to solicitors and barristers in the circuit and higher courts from July 1st last represented “total restoration” of the criminal legal aid fees cut during the financial crisis, “so it is unnecessary and regrettable that some solicitors are choosing this course of action”.
More than 150 solicitors across the country are “actively working” the new system, with more than 3,000 certificates (invoices for payment) for legal aid issued, with an approximate total value of more than €1.5 million since July 1st, it said.

title: A week in a castle for €99,000: The eye-watering cost of Ryder Cup accommodation
description: Meanwhile, Gavin Cooney on Manchester City and we look ahead to the Champions Cup return
content:
To be honest, we thought there was a typo in Muireann Duffy’s piece on accommodation for next year’s Ryder Cup at Adare Manor. Among the places up for rent is a six-bed house that sleeps up to 26 (so, 4.3 per room) and will cost a mere €19,000 for the week of the tournament. Where is it? Omagh. Yes, as in Tyrone’s Omagh. At the rate petrol prices are going, the renters will pay the same again for the daily eight-hour return trip. Far better to opt for the place in Gort that will cost €99,000 for eight nights. At least it’s only an hour away.
That kind of loot is, of course, small change for the folk at Manchester City, Gavin Cooney looking at how the club is responding to being found guilty of systemically cheating the game’s financial rules.
Gianni Infantino has his own problems, the fella up before a Fifa executive board meeting in Zurich on Thursday, his failure to provide answers to dozens of questions leaving the English FA’s Debbie Hewitt concluding that “he’s not fit to be Fifa president”.
Gavin Cummiskey, meanwhile, previews the latest round of League of Ireland games, St Patrick’s Athletic manager Stephen Kenny none too happy about the “ chaotic” end-of-season match scheduling .
Speaking of chaos. How are things going at Manchester United? “It’s chaos, it’s like a circus ,” is Roy Keane’s verdict.
In rugby, all four Irish provinces are in European action tomorrow, Gerry Thornley talking to Craig Casey ahead of Munster’s meeting with Racing 92 at Páirc Uí Chaoimh and John O’Sullivan hearing from Leo Cullen before Leinster open their Champions Cup campaign away to Clermont Auvergne .
In Gaelic games, Malachy Clerkin rounds up the contenders in each county’s senior hurling championship , taking you through the 14 finals still to come.
And Paul Keane talks to Paudie Clifford about an eventful spell in the life of Fossa , manager Jerome Stack departing the club just five weeks out from their Munster semi-final. Clifford also gives his thoughts on Éamonn Fitzmaurice taking over as Galway manager. He is, he says, “one of the smartest brains in the country”.
Philip Reid reports on the weather-interrupted opening round of the India Championship where Tom McKibbin got off to a flier , his 67 leaving him just one shot off leader Niklas Noergaard. Rory McIlroy is three strokes further back, but Shane Lowry’s 75 leaves him with work to do.
The Irish Guide Dogs assembled a stellar trio of Cork sporting legends last week as part of its celebrations of its 50th anniversary, Sonia O’Sullivan joining Roy Keane and Jimmy Barry-Murphy for a panel discussion. And oddly, considering the three didn’t experience a great deal of it, losing - and how you cope with it - was one of the topics that arose.
And in racing, Brian O’Connor isn’t hugely impressed by the “policy direction” of the sport’s governing body in Ireland, particularly at a time of “increasingly choppy waters”.
TV Watch : Coverage of round two at the India Championship got under way at 7.30 this morning and - weather-permitting - continues until 12.30pm (Sky Sports Golf). At 7.45pm St Patrick’s Athletic host Shelbourne in the league (Virgin Media Two) and rugby’s Champions Cup kicks off at 8pm, the three-in-a-row seeking Bordeaux Bègles away to Gloucester (Premier Sports 1).

title: Rosanne Cash cancels Sligo gig due to public sector industrial action
description: Musician told fans she would ‘miss being in a country I love so much’
content:
Rosanne Cash , the eldest daughter of American singer-songwriter Johnny Cash , has spoken of her disappointment at having to cancel her Sligo Live concert due to the nationwide public sector industrial action.
Cash was due to perform the last concert of her European tour on Sunday October 25th in the Knocknarea Arena at the Sligo Atlantic Technological University campus.
In a statement posted on social media Thursday evening, Cash announced she was “sorry and disappointed” at having to cancel the gig.
“There is a national strike going on by the public sector unions which precludes the use of the theatre on the Atlantic Technological University campus where our concert was to be held,” she wrote. “Ticket holders will be contacted directly by email with information about refunds. I will miss my Irish friends and miss being in a country I love so much.”
“It’s an awful shame,” Sligo Live organiser Rory O’Connor said.
Cash was one of four performances that had to be cancelled or rescheduled due to the ongoing work-to-rule, an aspect of the industrial action that sees some public sector workers refusing to perform duties other than the core ones for which they are contracted.
The sold-out Stephen Wilson Jr concert on October 17th has been moved from Sligo to the TF Royal Theatre in Castlebar. O’Connor said ATU staff “don’t do evening work and don’t do overtime. They’re instructed by the union not to do that and we can’t run it on safety grounds without some college staff present on the night”.
“It takes months and months of work to put all these things together. We’re hoping against hope that Dara Ó Briain ... will still be able to go ahead [on October 23rd].
“We’ve already sadly lost Glen Hansard who was booked for the Saturday night. We’re hoping the talks start preferably before the weekend or there’s a decision and that [strikes] can be called off.”
Cathaoirleach of Sligo Municipal District and ATU integration project manager Labour Cllr Ann Higgins said ATU was “keenly aware” that Sligo Live is the largest event in Sligo and the Cash concert cancellation would come as a blow to fans and the town.
“It’s genuinely regrettable that the concert is cancelled but equally, people need to remember that the cause of this is the industrial dispute. For me the fault lies squarely on the Government’s shoulders who refused to engage in a timely and meaningful way on a national wage agreement. They also failed to acknowledge and to listen to people,” said Higgins.
“I was on the picket line from 9.30am yesterday and the anger and frustration was palpable from so many people in unions who are bearing the brunt of the cost-of-living crisis.
“This is another casualty of the failure of the Government to engage.”
A spokesperson for ATU said: “Regrettably, next weekend’s event cannot proceed due to ongoing national industrial action. While the event’s significant contribution to the region is fully appreciated, these broader circumstances have necessitated the organisers’ decision to cancel. We thank everyone involved for their understanding.”

title: Haughey ‘quietly intervened’ while gravely ill to increase naval funding, ex-chief says
description: Greater investment in ‘larger, more capable ships’ followed from Bertie Ahern government in 2005
content:
The former chief of the Irish Naval Service has said he believes former taoiseach Charles Haughey “quietly intervened” about Ireland needing greater investment in ships.
Vice-admiral Mark Mellett, also former chief of staff of the Defence Forces , said an interaction with Haughey taught him how political influence can sometimes work in “unexpected ways”.
Mellett was speaking about his new book Blue Heart: War, Climate and the Battle for the Ocean that Keeps us Alive at the Institute of International & European Affairs on Thursday evening.
Mellett recalled how in late 2005 while he was commanding LÉ Eithne, he received an unexpected satellite telephone call from the former taoiseach who wanted to know when the ship would next be in Dublin.
“I invited him [Haughey] aboard, but he explained that he was no longer well enough to visit. Haughey was seriously ill at the time,” he said.
“Instead, he invited me with some of the crew to visit his home in Kinsealy. We brought a video tribute from the ship’s company set to the music of Coldplay’s Yellow. Back then our survival suits were bright yellow and the music seemed particularly apt ... We discussed the Naval Service and the need for Ireland to invest in larger, more capable ships, including a multi-role vessel that could support a wider range of defence, humanitarian and national tasks.
“Not long afterwards, a message came from Bertie Ahern ’s office: ‘You did a good thing just there’.”
Mellett said that at a subsequent government briefing, Ahern, who was taoiseach at the time, questioned why naval investment had been neglected and “made clear his view that Ireland needed more ships, and bigger ships”.
“I have always believed that Haughey had quietly intervened,” said Mellett.
“The episode taught me something about how political influence can work, sometimes in unexpected ways. But it also reinforced a frustration that followed me throughout my career: the distance between recognising a strategic requirement, securing political support and actually delivering the capability.”
He added that it is a problem that extends well beyond defence and can be seen today in energy infrastructure, climate adaptation and “many other areas where decisions taken now will shape the country for decades”.
Mellett said one of the central arguments he makes in his book is that “we continue to organise our institutions” around problems that are increasingly interconnected.
“Climate change is not simply an environmental issue. It affects food production, migration, energy systems, economic stability and national security,” he said.
“The ocean sits at the heart of many of these relationships, yet remains remarkably peripheral to political and strategic thinking. That is why I argue for a fundamentally different approach to ocean governance, including the establishment of a department of the ocean in Ireland.”

title: Forecast is for dry and bright weather this weekend
description: A number of weekend train services will be altered due to engineering works.
content:
The weather in Ireland will be dry and bright this weekend but may become chilly at times, with the occasional shower.

In the afternoon, showers will become mostly confined to Ulster and Leinster. In the evening it will be dry and bright with highest temperatures of 10 to 14 degrees.
Friday night will be mostly dry with long clear spells and scattered showers in northern areas.
The lowest temperatures will be between one and five degrees.
Some mist and fog patches will form as well as frost in certain places.

On Saturday night, it will be dry and chilly with patches of mist and fog. Lowest temperatures of one to five degrees, possibly reaching freezing locally, with some frost developing.
