title: Judge tells man caught driving at 184km/h: ‘You would have made mincemeat of a child’
description: Cavan man banned for two years after driving at almost twice legal speed limit
content:
A Co Cavan man who drove at almost twice the speed limit has been told by a judge that if he had his way he would “ban him for life”.
Michael McCooey (25), of Duncollig, Lisboduff, Cootehill appeared before Judge Raymond Finnegan at Cavan District Court on Thursday charged with dangerous driving at Killyduff, Virginia, Co Cavan on September 3rd.
Sgt Damien Galligan told the judge that McCooey had been recorded driving at 184km/h.
Finnegan disqualified McCooey from driving for two years and fined him €500.
He asked McCooey what would have happened if a child had crossed the road at the time of his offence. McCooey said he would have been driving “too fast” to stop in time.
“You would have made mincemeat of [the child],” the judge said. “At 184km/h, you would not have control of your vehicle.
“It’s people like you that [have] road deaths are the way they are. They think the law doesn’t apply to them.
“You were at about two times the speed limit,” he said. “In your hands a car is a very, very dangerous weapon.”
The judge said McCooey, a self-employed electrician working in Dublin, had been caught “this time”.
He advised McCooey to consider using the next two years to think about how lucky he was that he did not kill someone while driving in such a manner.
Defence solicitor Damien Rudden submitted that the offence occurred on “a straight stretch” and that there was no traffic at the time, but that the road conditions were “wet” and that his client was “a bit heavy on the pedal”.
The court heard McCooey has lodged an appeal.

title: First children’s hospice outside Dublin to be built in Co Mayo
description: Sunflower Children’s Hospice in Castlebar due to be completed in 2029
content:
Planning permission has been granted for the first children’s hospice outside of Dublin. Sunflower Children’s Hospice is due to open in Castlebar , Co Mayo in 2029.
The plans were unveiled in November 2025 and €9 million has been raised through community and corporate fundraising, donor support and local initiatives. The final cost of the development is €20 million.
It is the first new facility of its kind to be developed in 15 years.
Mayo Roscommon Hospice Foundation is behind the construction of Sunflower Children’s Hospice.
Located in Moneen, Castlebar, it will provide dedicated support for children with life-limiting conditions and their families across the western seaboard.
The sod will be turned at the Moneen site in Castlebar next month, with construction expected to begin in January 2027. The project is anticipated to take approximately two years to complete, with the hospice scheduled to open to patients in 2029.
Feedback from families was incorporated in the design of the hospice.
The 36,000 sq ft facility will have en suite bedrooms with a private garden or patio access, four family accommodation suites, sensory rooms and gardens, a hydrotherapy pool and dedicated children and young adult spaces.
Teaching and education facilities will also be part of the building, and reflection rooms.
Daire Cox, from Lisacul, Co Roscommon, is 12 years old and needs around-the-clock care. His mother Linda Cox said: “It’s an emotional day for parents of children with life-limiting illnesses in the west of Ireland and we are so thrilled that the Sunflower Children’s Hospice is over the line.”
Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill said: “No family should face additional challenges in accessing the care and support they need because of where they live.
“I want to acknowledge the incredible work of Mayo Roscommon Hospice Foundation in bringing this vision forward and for the dedication, leadership and determination that has brought the project to this stage.”

title: Netflix turns to former Disney executive to revive growth
description: Bela Bajaria was with Netflix for 10 years and became the public face of its content strategy
content:
Netflix is replacing its chief creative officer with a veteran TV and film executive Peter Rice as the streaming giant looks to reinvigorate growth amid a slowdown in viewers and revenue.
Rice previously served as chairman of general entertainment at Walt Disney Company and, before that, as president of 21st Century Fox.
He will assume the new role later this month, with a broad mandate, overseeing scripted and unscripted series, film and live events across all regions.
Rice replaces Bela Bajaria, who had worked at Netflix for 10 years and come to be the public face of the company’s content strategy.
Bajaria was credited with broadening Netflix’s entertainment offerings by expanding its unscripted portfolio and striking a deal with the TKO Group Holdings to bring the WWE’s weekly wrestling show, Raw, to the streaming service. She memorably described the ideal Netflix program as a “gourmet cheeseburger” — something combines quality and broad appeal.
The executive shakeup, coupled with Wednesday’s layoffs of some 1,000 workers or 6 per cent of its staff, are a sign that the streaming industry leader is trying to reinvent itself after seeing its audience growth slow and its stock price tumble.
The service has grown to more than 325 million subscribers globally. But it has evolved from a producer of “prestige TV” shows like House of Cards and The Crown to a broader entertainment source, competing with everything from sports channels to YouTube videos, and doing so on a global basis.
In moving Rice into the role, Netflix’s senior leadership see an opportunity to install an executive with deep relationships to Hollywood talent and experience running a broad portfolio of channels and streaming services. At Fox and later at Disney, he supervised a TV lineup that included hits from The Simpsons to Modern Family.
Recent Netflix shows have seen their audiences decline in their second seasons. The service saw its Emmy Awards wins fall to a 10-year low in 2026. The stock has lost about 23 per cent of its value this year.
Netflix co-chief executive Ted Sarandos, speaking at the Bloomberg Screentime conference in Los Angeles last month, acknowledged that the company isn’t growing as fast as he would like.
While the company has been expanding into live sports and podcasts, the vast majority of Netflix’s roughly $20 billion programming budget goes to films, TV shows and video games.
“Peter is one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry,” Sarandos said in a statement Thursday. “He understands what makes stories resonate, and he’s spent his career helping talent do the best work of their lives.” – Bloomberg

title: Trump’s new press secretary faces mounting questions over her legal credentials
description: Following a rocky debut, Katie Zacharia is facing mounting questions over her legal credentials
content:
US president Donald Trump’s new White House press secretary says it is “unknown” how much she will engage with the press or hold briefings with reporters, as she faces mounting questions over her legal credentials.
In a brief interview on Thursday, Katie Zacharia detailed the whirlwind sprint to replace her predecessor Karoline Leavitt as the US president’s chief spokesperson.
Just six days after receiving a call from the White House, Zacharia stepped behind the podium for her first briefing as press secretary, in a debut that has been widely panned .
Last Wednesday, on October 7th, a White House official called Zacharia and asked her to travel from Los Angeles, where she lives with her family, to Washington for a meeting. (She declined to specify who made the call.)
Zacharia made the trip the following day, before meeting officials on Pennsylvania Avenue on Friday. She was offered the job later that day – and accepted.
“I flew home, packed two bags, said hi to my kids and husband and dogs,” Zacharia said, before returning to Washington on Sunday in advance of her first day on Monday.
But her first briefing, which Zacharia said she was “asked to do” on her second day in the job, was criticised as lacklustre.
And she has since faced intense scrutiny over her claimed legal qualifications. After her debut briefing on Tuesday, reporters asked Zacharia to name the state where she passed the bar exam. “When I moved to China”, she replied.
[ A bumpy debut for Katie Zacharia, the new voice of Donald Trump Opens in new window ]
She later told The New York Times she had “misheard” the question over the sound of Marine One on the South Lawn and thought the reporter had asked: “Where were you after law school?”
However, she did not confirm to the Times whether she had passed the bar exam. According to her LinkedIn profile, after graduating from Pepperdine University’s law school in 2011, Zacharia was an “associate” at the Beijing law firm Zhong Lun from 2011 to 2013.
This week, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing a person familiar with the matter, that Zacharia failed the California bar exam after graduating from law school.
The State Bar of California said it had no record of Zacharia being licensed in the state under either her married name or her maiden name, Katie Black. While Trump has referred to Zacharia as an “attorney”, that title is reserved for those licensed to practice law.
In a different interview with the conservative outlet Human Events on Thursday, Zacharia acknowledged to the rightwing influencer Jack Posobiec that she didn’t pass the California bar.
At the time, she said she was “distracted and overwhelmed and excited” to join her new husband in China, where he was working, after being in a long-distance relationship for more than a year.
A person familiar with the matter said Zacharia “stands by” referring to herself as a lawyer, and that she considered the designation a “valid title”, given her law degree and “international transactional law experience”. She did so after “consulting with other legal professionals and attorneys” about whether it was an appropriate designation, the source claimed, adding that Zacharia had “never given legal advice”; just “legal analysis”.
[ The Irish Times view on US midterms: a lame duck Trump is still a danger Opens in new window ]
However, many legal experts note that “lawyer” and “attorney” are often used interchangeably. On Wednesday, the Campaign for Accountability, a non-profit watchdog organisation, asked the State Bar of California to investigate whether Zacharia misled the public, and potentially violated state law, by describing herself as a lawyer.
After her time in China, there is a 10-year gap on Zacharia’s LinkedIn profile. Wired reported on Thursday that during that period she worked as an “affiliate marketer” for Beachbody, a multilevel marketing company she described to the outlet as “sort of a pyramid scheme”.
She later claims to have served as “general counsel” for Fix California, a conservative group founded by Richard Grenell, a long-time Trump ally and the special presidential envoy for special missions.
Zacharia also said she “did not want to be seen lobbying” for the press secretary role, in her interview with the conservative outlet Human Events. Instead, she said she closely monitored Trump’s social media posts before appearing on conservative talkshows to “audition” for the job.
When Trump announced that Zacharia had been tapped for the post, he described her as a “devoted fan of Maga” who has “an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning”.
[ Trump cancels plan to livestream man’s execution following widespread condemnation Opens in new window ]
Asked what reasons the White House gave for offering her the position, Zacharia – who previously served as an adviser to Trump Media Group, which owns the president’s Truth Social platform, and had a brief stint as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security – declined to comment.
Now the White House press secretary, she also would not clarify on Thursday how often she intended to brief the press. She said that was “unknown at this time” and that Trump “is his best spokesperson, and I will interact as needed”.
“I follow the president’s lead,” Zacharia added. - Guardian

title: Three children and teacher killed by teenager (16) at Oregon elementary school
description: Assailant was shot and killed by a bystander at school in Bend, Oregon
content:
A 16-year-old shooter opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday, killing three children and a teacher before he was shot dead by a community member, authorities said at an evening news conference.
The dead children at Silver Rail Elementary School were aged five, eight and 11, officials said.
A seven-year-old and a 54-year-old were also hospitalised with critical injuries, according to police.
The gunman, who was a Bend resident, has not been publicly identified. Officials said they are still investigating if he had ties to the school.
The deadly shooting has rocked the city of 100,000 residents located on the Deschutes River, roughly 273km (170 miles) southeast of Portland.
“Please hold your children, hold your loved ones tight tonight. Let them talk. Let them cry. Let them know we are going to rally and care for one another in this community,” said Steven Cook, the superintendent of Bend-La Pine Schools.
“We will get through this – but not yet. We must grieve for the loss of our community members.”
At 1.02pm, police responded to Silver Rail Elementary School after receiving several reports about an active shooter. One 911 caller reported an individual armed with a long gun firing at their car. Police did not specify the firearm’s make.
Dozens of callers stated the shooter had entered the school, continuing the attack inside.
He forced entry into the building by shooting at locked doors, according to police.
By the time officers arrived on scene, the suspected assailant had been shot and killed by a bystander, who apprehended him inside.
The attacker used a pump-action shotgun, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting.
In the aftermath of the tragedy, children were taken by bus to a nearby church serving as a reunification centre for families. Parents hugged, kissed and held their kids’ hands as they walked to their cars, with some bringing along favourite stuffed animals or other comfort items from home.
The school serves kindergarten through fifth grade, roughly ages five to 11, and has about 450 students and 40 staff members, officials said.
Oregon governor Tina Kotek praised the intervention as heroic and extended her thoughts to the bystander. “Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden,” she said on Thursday evening.
Classes, sports and extracurriculars were cancelled Friday for all 32 schools in the Bend-La Pine district.
The FBI is helping local authorities investigate the shooting, according to the agency’s director Kash Patel.
The shooting began about an hour before the school day was set to end.
“A school should be a safe place where children can learn and feel secure,” said Bend mayor Melanie Kebler. “Like so many in our community, I’m struggling to make sense of a loss that feels unimaginable.”
Gun control advocate Gabrielle Giffords, ⁠a former congresswoman who survived a mass shooting in 2011, said in a statement she was “heartbroken” by the shooting.
“This cannot continue to be a reality ​in our country. Leaders at every level must step ​up and act,” Giffords said.
Thursday’s shooting is the latest event in a grim history of recurring gun violence at schools across the United States. According to Everytown For Gun Safety, there have been at least 100 incidents of gunfire on school grounds across the country in 2026, resulting in 33 deaths.
Oregon has passed several gun-safety measures in recent years, including a law that requires gun owners to undergo a criminal-background check and safety training before being approved for a firearm permit. – Guardian

title: Hegseth tells UK counterpart that Ukraine’s access to Starlink restored
description: Satellite communications system  disrupted  amid renewed tensions between the US and Ukraine
content:
Britain’s defence secretary said he had been reassured by his US counterpart Pete Hegseth that Ukraine’s access to Starlink had been restored.
Wes Streeting said Hegseth had assured him that the vital Starlink satellite communications system was back up and running, although it remained unclear what had caused the disruption, amid renewed tensions between the US and Ukraine.
He sought to use his first visit to Washington as defence secretary to bolster ties that have been strained by issues including US president Donald Trump’s stance on Kyiv and the widening US-Nato rift.
It came a day after Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy visited London and said Trump had betrayed his country by limiting its use of US-made Starlink terminals which are vital for the Ukrainian military.
Speaking to the BBC after his Thursday meeting with Hegseth, Streeting said: “Unsurprisingly we did discuss Starlink. It’s not yet clear to us in the UK what happened, why the service interruption occurred.
“But I am reassured, and was reassured directly by Secretary Hegseth, that the service has been restored.
“And that is a demonstration, I think, of the importance of the US contribution on intelligence sharing.”
He evaded questions on what caused the disruption, saying instead: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling-out between Washington and Kyiv.
“And as I said to Secretary Hegseth, in the words of St Francis of Assisi, ‘Where there is discord, may we bring harmony.’
“That has been the British approach in moments like this. That’s the diplomacy and the approach I’ve brought to Washington today.
“I’m here to solve problems, and the UK has been Ukraine’s number one ally. We will continue to play that role.”
[ Burnham reaffirms backing for Zelenskiy after Downing Street meeting Opens in new window ]
There have been mounting fears over the United States’ commitment to Kyiv, with the Starlink disruption following Trump’s move to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.
Streeting earlier made the case for continuing American support for Ukraine in a talk held by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies and the Royal United Services Institute.
He warned that if Russian president Vladimir Putin’s aggression was rewarded, “the consequences will not remain confined to Ukraine or to my continent”.
Streeting’s meeting with the US defence secretary also came after Washington withdrew its bombers from RAF Fairford following a suspected terror plot UK prime minister Andy Burnham has said was “almost certainly” directed by Iran.
A Pentagon readout said: “Hegseth also thanked Streeting for communications regarding recent threats to the US military in the UK, notably, a suspected Iran-backed terror plot and security incident at the RAF Fairford airbase in Britain last month.
“The incident prompted the US military to withdraw its bomber aircraft and return them to the United States.” – PA

title: CoreWeave debt scare rattles markets as Asian stocks bounce
description: Reports on Thursday said the Nvidia-backed firm’s bond yields hit levels associated with distressed debt
content:
Asian stocks rebounded on Friday following heavy selling in the previous session when investors dumped tech shares as questions about cloud company CoreWeave’s debt ‌pile fuelled worries about the financing driving the AI boom.
Bond markets stabilised after yields plunged on Thursday as traders bought up Treasuries and other safe-haven sovereign debt. The dollar limped towards its first weekly loss ​in five weeks as lower US yields eroded the currency’s appeal.
Shares of Nvidia-backed CoreWeave recovered some composure on Thursday after starting the session by extending Wednesday’s 15.5 per cent slump amid reports that its bond yields had reached highs associated with distressed debt, triggering a broad, AI-centred equity sell-off globally.
Pressure on chip stocks eased following comments by Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang, who defended the financial position of CoreWeave.
“CoreWeave’s financial strength is improving every day,” Huang told reporters at a Stockholm event, adding he did not see a need for Nvidia to backstop the company. “I’m optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing.”
Analysts ⁠have pointed to pressure on memory-maker shares this week ​after China’s ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) reported progress on a next-generation Dram architecture that could intensify ​competition with established manufacturers.
“Global markets are getting very noisy once again after a period of low volatility: Wall Street is whipsawing, bond yields are swinging, currency markets are ‌doing backflips and commodity prices are running in multiple directions,” Kyle Rodda, ​a markets analyst at Capital, wrote in a client note.
“Global markets could potentially be in for a protracted period of this sort of volatility,” with ⁠tech company earnings announcements due in the coming weeks, and markets also attempting ⁠to discern the trajectory of US ​and other major economies’ interest rates, he said.
Following the slump, Japan’s tech-heavy Nikkei made back some of Thursday’s near 5 per cent tumble as it rose 1.8 per cent. South Korea’s KOSPI climbed 2.8 per cent, following a nearly 8 per cent plunge.
Taiwan’s stock benchmark rose 0.7 per cent and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng added 1.1 per cent. Mainland Chinese blue chips edged 0.3 per cent higher.
Indonesia’s equity benchmark slumped 11 per cent after MSCI said ​the country’s stock market is no longer worthy of “emerging market” status, and is preparing to cut it from a suite of products tracked by global investors, a major setback likely to send money fleeing.
Brent crude futures eased 0.74 per cent to $105.14 (€93.66) a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down 0.6 per cent to $97.33.
Crude oil edged ‌lower as investors weighed Middle East risks and possible US steps to ease restrictions on the world’s “shadow fleet” of tankers.
The Trump administration is considering lifting sanctions on some so-called shadow fleet vessels that ​have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela, in an effort to reduce record-high global ​freight rates, a US official said on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, the escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis and renewed attacks on ships in the region have supported prices. – Reuters

title: Funny, irreverent, cocky: Can Abdul El-Sayed win a vital senate seat in abandoned America?
description: In Flint, birthplace of General Motors, voters wrestling with healthcare costs and economic decline may determine control of the US Senate
content:
T he last of the wasps are dive-bombing through the long line of people waiting outside St Michael’s Catholic Church in the Carriage Town neighbourhood of Flint. Like many parts of the city, the street is a little careworn but the early autumn Saturday is summery and dazzling in its primary colours. Large gatherings of people are unusual here and several cars slow down so their occupants can ask people what’s going on.
“Abdul El-Sayed is speaking here,” people from the line call to them and the faces reflect a carousel of interest, or perplexion or indifference as they roll up the windows and zoom off through wide, empty streets.
The event captures the odd contradiction of the US midterm senate races in that it is both inescapable on social media and almost invisible on the street. Attendees to El-Sayed’s rally are given the precise address just the day before the rally begins. The venue is small, which means it will be full. The vast majority of people in Flint have no idea it is taking place but within hours, the town hall will be spliced and diced and repackaged on social media.
El-Sayed has been wandering Michigan relentlessly with his “It Shouldn’t be This Hard” tour. After Flint, he would head to Saginaw, where Paul Simon famously hitchhiked, and where the trajectory of the city’s fortunes was inextricably linked to the rise and fall of American motorcar production.
But Flint residents take rightful pride in the fact that their city is where it all began and argue that Flint is the true motor city.
“If you go right down here on Water Street where I live, they have the Durant building,” Michele Kelly explains, and talks me through the evolution of Charles Wisner and the “buzz car” and William Durant and the birth of General Motors. Kelly is 67 and has lived in Flint all her life. She’s fizzing with energy and is terrific fun, opening the conversation with a warning that New York mayor Zohran Mamdani is schooling the political classes on both sides on how to get it done.
“There’s no ‘think’ about it,” she clarifies.
When El-Sayed takes to the lectern in the church, the crowd waves placards and cheer as the candidate takes them through a now-familiar address that franks his love of Michigan, and his intentions for major reforms if he wins this senate race.
His ascension to this moment has involved an epic uphill climb, first against the Democratic Party machine, whose favoured candidate, representative Haley Stevens, had the backing of the elders and the funding, outspending El-Sayed’s campaign by ten to one. That election illuminated the internal party chasm between the traditional ideological block of the party and the insurgent socialist democratic left. (El-Sayed has sought to position himself as a capitalist who believes in taxing the billionaire class and advocating universal healthcare for all Americans, rather than a Democratic Socialist.) He defeated Stevens by just under 14,000 votes – less than 1 per cent of the overall vote.
Stevens immediately endorsed El-Sayed and since then, the stars of liberal left, Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, have campaigned for him even as the party machine has thrown its weight behind him. Kamala Harris appeared at an event in Michigan and on Saturday next, former president Barack Obama will join El-Sayed for a rally in Detroit.
The simple equation on El-Sayed’s chances of edging out Republican candidate Mike Rogers – and therefore maintaining a vital senate seat – is that he needs to win over the traditional black, city-based vote. Michigan blows with the wind in presidential cycles but no Republican has won a US senate seat in Michigan since Spence Abraham in 1994.
A recent Washington Post-Schar School poll found that of the 83 per cent of black voters who want the Democrats to win control of the senate, 67 per cent would vote for El-Sayed in the Michigan race. Bridging that gap is essential for El-Sayed if he is to win. The reasons for the wariness among black voters are down to a combination of the ubiquitous attack adverts accentuating El-Sayed as a radical candidate, and a simple lack of familiarity: the communities just don’t know him.
During the series of questions from supporters in Flint, Michele Kelly asked El-Sayed why the campaign, and the Democratic Party, was not actively campaigning in black neighbourhoods in cities like Flint.
“I am 67 years old and I don’t think anybody has directly targeted project people,” she told me afterwards.
“I know they haven’t. Knocking on doors. Calling around. I’m not blaming anybody. I say ‘black community’ because that’s how we talk. But it burns me up when they say, ‘the base’. The base of the Democratic Party is the black community. The base of the Republican Party is the white community. Guess who they cover? Them. Guess who the media covers? Them. Guess who gets to go on TV? Them. So, we don’t see no reason ... El-Sayed needs Detroit, yes. But in order to pull an election win off, he needs smaller cities. Like Flint. Which is a black city.
“This room here did not reflect Flint. At all. Flint is 80 per cent black. White Americans who live in Flint – well, they live in Davison, Burton, Grand Blanc. Most of Flint city itself is black. I thought he did the best he could today. I have been out here trying to encourage family members to pay attention to politics forever. ”
The census statistics on Flint reflect a city still reeling from the rapid contraction of automotive jobs in the city in the 1980s: a median income of $34,000; 34 per cent of residents living below the poverty line; owner-occupier housing at 53 per cent; just 14 per cent with a bachelor’s degree or higher.
It is a startlingly empty place. But any stranger taking a 20-minute walk through its downtown and the main thoroughfare of Saginaw Street will be struck by buildings that hold stories about its former grandeur. The Durant hotel, an exercise in opulence when it opened in 1919, was the social hub for the 50 years of its existence. Frank Sinatra and Glenn Miller booked in there during the years when Flint was automatic on the tour schedule. It fell into disrepair following its closure and now operates as an apartment complex.
The Capitol Theatre, designed in the 1920s to emulate the grand Italian opera house style, has been refurbished. A food emporium is housed in what was the printing press of the Flint Journal. Flint Park is a green area now but in the 1920s, it had its own adventure park. On Saginaw Street there are statues to automobile giants, including Billy Durant, the founder of General Motors before he was squeezed out by the financiers and died, in penury, as the operator of a struggling bowling alley in Flint.
A vast, fenced-off wasteland represents the site of the Buick City along Hamilton avenue, where 28,000 workers clocked in at its peak. Just a thousand jobs remained when the plant closed in 1999. Its premises featured prominently in Roger & Me, the sardonic, evocative documentary by Flint native Michael Moore chronicling the sad closing years of the factory. Michele Kelly graduated from high school in 1977 so she caught the town in its last wave of manufacturing prosperity.
“Yeah, everyone was getting jobs, straight from school. As their parents did. Everyone had new cars, stores everywhere. By the time the next generation came along, General Motors was gone and ten years later, it looked like the Third World. It pisses me off because I remember what it could have been like.”
Flint, then, stands a perfect symbol of Donald Trump’s election promise to somehow reverse the epic monumental decline of the car manufacturing industry. But despite his promises of a resurrection, Flint – and Genesee County – voted for Kamala Harris in 2024.
It should be promising territory for El-Sayed. At 41, he comes equipped with a formidable range of accomplishments: a professor of epidemiology and Rhodes scholar who worked at the Detroit health department before running for governor of Michigan in 2018, when he lost to Gretchen Whitmer. He has developed an easy, streetwise media articulacy and turns up for campaigns in regulation jeans and casual tops.
Mike Rogers, his Republican opponent, is a survivor of his party’s transformation: a former state senator turned US congressman, he ran against Democrat Elisa Slotkin for Michigan’s other senate seat two years ago and fell short by just 20,000 votes. When Gary Peters, who had held this seat for the Democrats for a full decade, announced his retirement, Trump was in office just eight days. But among his flurry of phone calls was a request to Rogers that he should run again.
“Remember Mike Rogers is running for US senate because Donald Trump called him and asked him to. He won’t really break with him on tariffs, on war, because his only pathway to war is through him,” El-Sayed said on television last weekend.
“Now, why does he want that power so bad? Not because he wants to serve as US senator – he doesn’t have any ideas. He wants that power because the last time he had power he was able to retire and make $14 million as an adviser for the very same corporations he had been regulating as a US congressman. He watched the president make 2.2 billion dollars off the presidency and said: you know what, I gotta get while the getting’s good. And you know who gets got? We do. And all he’s got is to point to me and say ... some scary words and it will work. It’s not going to win. Michiganders are too big for that.”
That may be wishful thinking on his part. All polls depict a race on a knife edge: an early October Insider Advantage poll featuring 1,200 voters surveyed had El-Sayed at 48 per cent to Rogers on 46 per cent, with 5 per cent undecided.
In their highly acrimonious televised debates, Rogers has repeatedly sought to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood terrorist group and emphasised his ties to controversial left-wing influencer Hasan Piker. Attack ads on Michigan localised networks introduce him by his full name – Abdulrahman Mohammad El-Sayed before declaring him “the most radical senate candidate in America”.
“When his ally said America deserved 9/11, El-Sayed refused to disavow his remarks,” one advert narrates, referencing Piker, before declaring El-Sayed “too radical, too dangerous, wrong for Michigan”.
Over the course of an hour in St Michael’s Church, El-Sayed roams the room, microphone in hand, trying to debunk the myths and stereotypes. He castigated Rogers for corporate-linked wealth and for owning two yachts.
“Who needs two yachts?” he asks in mock bafflement. He referred to Rogers as a “non-playing character” and referenced Donald Trump’s accented pronunciation of his name.
“Donald Trump can’t seem to take my name out of his mouth. It’s funny because he doesn’t even know how to say it. I mean, to be creepy about Abdul?”
In delivery, he is funny, irreverent and slightly cocky; the northern flipside of the coin to James Talarico’s studied humility.
“This is my first time seeing him live,” Melissa Dugan tells me when the rally ends. “But I did vote for him at the last opportunity I had. Abdul says everything that I am looking for.”
Dugan and her husband run a small business where they live, in Linden, a 20-minute drive from Flint. With one daughter having just graduated from the University of Michigan and their youngest girl currently studying in Michigan State, the last number of years have been a stretch for the family. In addition to running the business, her husband works in real estate while Melissa has a part-time job. Their daughter’s college financial aid was reduced by 30 per cent this year.
“It has made it difficult for us to keep her enrolled. She’s on the dean’s list: she is thriving so we are doing everything we can. We haven’t had health insurance since 2025. Because we can’t afford it. As small business owners we don’t have a company that gives us benefits.
“So, we have to go through the market place and our health was going to cost $8,000 for the year and it didn’t cover anything and had deductibles. So, we self-insure, which means that if something terrible happens, we hope we can afford it. But I can barely afford my groceries and gas.”
That national cost-of-living crisis, and the sneaking sense that billionaire business interests have subtly hijacked the system has formed a crucial part of El-Sayed’s campaign mission. He has built a formidable funding model despite rejecting corporate and political action committee donations, and one of his vows is to try to wrestle the American electoral system away from the clutches of mega-donor influence.
“It is absolutely insane,” Dugan says of the US health insurance system. “I am all for a socialist government, I am all for Medicare for all. It is ridiculous that as one of the wealthiest countries in the world we don’t have health cover for citizens.
“This current administration – maybe this sounds extreme – but I really feel part of their goal is just to eliminate much of the lower and middle class. And they will do that by killing us – by making the cost of living so high that we can’t afford to eat or buy medicine.”
We speak for a while about Flint. The city was still in a drift state after the vanishing of General Motors when it was hit with the water crisis in 2014, caused by the cost-saving measure to switch the drinking supply to the Flint river as a source, which was quickly and lastingly contaminated by lead pipes. That civic disaster lasted a full five years, ending just before the pandemic.
The tragedy of Flint is that the people who arrived to make lives and a city there did everything right. They believed, passionately and with confidence, in its future: the proof is there in the surviving architecture and the residential streets that bloomed when Flint’s population climbed as far as 196,000 in the 1960 census. It is home to about 81,000 people now.
On Saturday afternoon, in gorgeous sunlight, Saginaw Street was completely deserted apart from a lone busker playing guitar and two seniors having a chat on a bench. There are photographs of the same street in Flint’s roaring years: lit up and populated like Sunset Strip and brooking no doubts about its place in the country. Michael Moore’s film drew both lavish praise and considerable pushback for a portrait of a decline that critics felt manipulated the chronology of events to suit the storyline.
But almost four decades later, the arc of time has validated its broad truth. A once-thriving automotive city was devastated by the reimagining and globalisation of the US industry and the people who still live there have to deal with the aftershocks. There’s something brutal and saddening about its story.
“Flint is a great town with great people,” Melissa Dugan says. “What happened here was none of the citizens’ fault. The system is the problem. And we need huge changes.”
Abdul El-Sayed isn’t the first political aspirant to visit Flint in a campaign year. For decades now, Flint residents have been used to candidates breezing through and issuing passionate words. But El-Sayed is adamant that if he is elected as the first Muslim to sit in the US senate, he will carry Vehicle City with him.
“Flint is the canary in the coal mine,” he said, speaking in the church porch to local television crews after the rally was over.
“You look at the failure of our state government to protect just the basics when it came to water. And Flint was also the place that showed the world what a union could do in terms of a sit-down strike. So, when you think about what Michigan is, Flint ... and Detroit ... they are at the heart of it.”

title: Garda regains control of official X accounts after crypto hack
description: Garda warned public not to interact with the Garda Traffic and Info accounts
content:
An Garda Síochána has confirmed it has regained control of social media accounts after a hack which saw “unauthorised access” to two official profiles on X.
The accounts @GardaInfo and @GardaTraffic were taken over in a breach related to cryptocurrency on Wednesday night and members of the public were warned not to interact with them.
The @GardaTraffic and @GardaInfo accounts on X, formerly Twitter, removed some branding and started publishing scores of posts about a cryptocurrency from Wednesday night.
All posts on both accounts have been removed by the platform, but were seen by thousands of people while live.
On Thursday evening, gardaí confirmed they had regained control of the accounts but they will remain inactive while the Garda National Cyber Crime Bureau carry out its investigations.
The Garda said the breach was only on X and that there was “no unauthorised access to any Garda systems and that there is no loss or impact on any Garda controlled data”.
The location on both accounts was changed to Amsterdam, the Netherlands, but the @GardaTraffic account, which has more than 600,000 followers, still claims it is the Garda account for traffic and road safety updates.
The @GardaInfo account, which has almost 300,000 followers, was rebranded to appear to be the support account for a cryptocurrency wallet.
Cybersecurity expert Brian Honan said the incident was “embarrassing” for the Garda as the organisation tasked with tackling crime instead fell victim to it.
However, he said the “hijacking” of corporate accounts is not unusual as attackers often seek out high-profile accounts with trusted names and a large amount of followers.
Olga Cronin, head of policy at the the Irish Council of Civil Liberties, said any hack of a State agency or body’s systems or online accounts is extremely worrying.
“An Garda Síochána is entrusted with extremely sensitive and personal information, and their social media accounts could contain valuable personal information via direct messages for example.
“It’s unclear how these accounts were taken over and the extent of the harm or exposure.”
She added: “But secure collection, storage, use and deletion of data – whether it is gathered through social media, tech like body-worn cameras or people walking into a Garda station to report a crime – are essential to An Garda Síochána’s operation and all of our safety.
“An Garda Síochána and X should explain to the public what has happened as soon as is practicable, in order to address public concern.” – Additional reporting: PA

title: No new takeaway for O’Connell Street and Ireland’s 1%
description: Business Today: The best news, analysis, and comment from The Irish Times business desk
content:
Dublin City Council has barred the owners of a new restaurant being planned for Ulster Bank’s former O’Connell Street branch from operating any takeaway food service. The pushback, Killian Woods reports , comes as a slew of new US takeaway brands, including Popeyes, Wingstop, Dave’s Hot Chicken, Wendy’s and Taco Bell, are expanding into the Irish market.
How much do you need to join the rarefied air of Ireland’s 1 per cent? Around €123,000, according to new research from a Berlin-based data firm. Eoin Burke-Kennedy reports that the Republic also has the EU’s third-largest share of earners in the top 1 per cent across the bloc.
Relatedly, soaring stock markets and asset prices are making Ireland’s - and the world’s - rich even richer. Why is it, then, that most countries are yet to introduce a wealth tax ? Cliff Taylor ponders the thorny policy questions facing Irish politicians in the face of an explosion in household wealth.
Meanwhile, a new survey from an online safety charity reveals that more than half of children under 12 have access to smartphones and other devices in their bedrooms overnight. Parents, it turns out, are equally guilty of being glued to their smartphones, with more than half of young people saying parents were on their devices all or most of the time they were with their children.
The National Treasury Management Agency ended bond market fundraising for the year on Thursday by selling 10-year notes at the highest interest rate since just after the Republic exited its international bailout programme. Joe Brennan has the details.
Barry O’Halloran has the latest on the long-running Dublin Airport passenger cap saga. On Thursday, the EU’s top court ruled that regulators must enforce the 32 million-a-year limit on passengers when allocating take-off and landing slots to airlines. However, the ruling will not affect a recent decision to add 29 new slots at Dublin Airport next summer.
A decade and a half after the property crash, the industry barometers of house prices have crept back into the mix, led by the State’s two main property portals: MyHome and Daft . In his column this week, Eoin Burke-Kennedy asks who’s right about what when it comes to house price data.
Brian Moynihan, the CEO of America’s second-largest bank, with $3.5 trillion of assets, has avoided directly challenging the current White House. That hasn’t spared the Bank of America boss from US president Donald Trump’s ire, however. In our interview of the week , Moynihan sits down with Joe Brennan for a wide-ranging chat about Trump, interest rates and AI.
Joe also reports that Kenmare Resources , the Dublin-listed minerals miner, has lowered the full-year production forecast for its most important product as it continues takeover talks with a company ultimately controlled by the Abu Dhabi royal family.
Revenue is looking at ways to reduce postal communications with taxpayers and expand the use of “robotics” and artificial intelligence to deal with queries. The tax authority is reviewing its postage practices , which cost it around €14.8 million in 2025, and looking to increase the use of its online platform to send out important tax documents to millions of taxpayers each year.
Johnny Sexton has been appointed as an adviser to the Johnstown Collection, the luxury hotel chain behind the Johnstown and Mount Juliet estates, as the group undergoes an investment of almost €40 million across its portfolio. Stephen Conneely has the details .
It’s tempting to wonder what the point of the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council is if governments, time and again, quietly ignore its advice, writes Paul Colgan in Agenda . Still, there are some who believe that it can, and does, influence policy and that State spending would be higher without the body’s critiques.
Effective leadership depends less on who sounds like a leader than on the behaviours and skills they demonstrate, writes Margaret E Ward. When you think back over your career, which manager do you remember first? The boss who believed in you and gave you opportunities or the manager who thwarted and belittled you at every turn?
If you’d like to read more about the issues that affect your finances try signing up to On the Money , the weekly newsletter from our personal finance team, which will be issued every Friday to Irish Times subscribers.

title: ‘The gun jammed and they killed him with bricks’: Réalt na Mara football club and the Troubles
description: A documentary shows how a Belfast youth team brought hope when lives were being ruined by the Troubles, including those of Bobby Sands, Terry Nicholl and Raymond McCord
content:
T he reminiscences of old men about youthful sporting days always carry poignant nostalgic charm, but the stories of the men who were boys in the Star of the Sea junior football club in the late 1960s hold a special type of regret.
The story of the north Belfast club will be told on Tuesday, October 20th, in the TG4 documentary, Réalt na Mara: An Peil, Na Trioblóidí agus An Iarmhairt (Star of the Sea: The Football, The Troubles, and the Aftermath).
The documentary by film-maker James Wynne tells how the Troubles in 1969 brought bitter sectarian divisions into Rathcoole, one of the new housing estates built in the early part of the decade.
Led by an inspirational manager, Dr Liam Conlon, the Star of the Sea club had been formed out of the local Catholic secondary school, but it was open to all.
In its day it was regarded as the finest junior football team on the island. Its young players included the later IRA hunger-striker , Bobby Sands and Terry Nicholl and Michael Acheson, who were later members of the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) .
[ Star turns: The brilliant Belfast boys who defied the sectarian tide Opens in new window ]
However, the documentary does not seek to glorify. “Bobby joined an organisation that murdered 1,800 people. Terry joined an organisation, the UVF, that murdered hundreds of people, as did Michael. They weren’t the guys I knew. They chose to go down that road. They had a choice,” says fellow team-mate, Raymond McCord, whose son, Raymond jnr, was battered to death in a quarry with bricks by the UVF in 1997, fearing he would become an informer.
The lives of each one of the Star of the Sea team was changed by the violence that was unleashed: Denis Sweeney narrowly avoided being killed or injured in a pub bombing and chose to become a doctor.
Best friends, Dessie (Desi) Black, a Catholic, and Willie Caldwell, a Protestant – “you never saw one without the other”, the documentary hears – tried to live their lives apart from the violence.
In the end, however, Black decided after being near a bombing to get out, once he saw advertisements for blocklayers in Guernsey. “It was like f***ing paradise,” he says. “I got married and that and a couple of kids, grandkids and that.”
Soon after, he persuaded Caldwell to join him. It was probably for the best since Caldwell had continued socialising on both sides of the divide in a city that no longer permitted life on both sides of the line.
“I was going to discotheques on the New Lodge Road, which is a Catholic area, one night. The next night, going out with Protestant mates, going to an area just three streets away, Tiger’s Bay, going to loyalist clubs. So, I thought the best thing for me is to get out,” he says in a clip filmed in 1983.
Recently the two came to Dublin from their homes in Guernsey for a screening of the documentary. “They came with their families,” says Wynne. “It was smashing to see them just hanging out all these years later.”
It is not the first time the story of the Star of the Sea has been told. In 1983, many of the team were interviewed for a BBC documentary, Old Scores, but it is one that still rankles with some of the men.
Filmed just two years after the May 1981 death on hunger strike of Bobby Sands, the documentary told the story largely through his eyes and times: “There was too much about Bobby in it, and not enough about what the Star meant,” says McCord.
However, this latest documentary is not just about the Rathcoole club either, since a large part covers the brutal murder of McCord’s son in 1997 – a killing blamed on UVF men who were also police and British military agents.
A later investigation by the Northern Ireland Police Ombudsman in 2002 found “systemic collusion” between the RUC’s Special Branch and loyalist paramilitaries, and that the murder investigation had been deliberately scuppered.
The names of his killers were known within a week: “And young Raymond, the guys that killed him, they were supposed to have been his friends, and they slaughtered that lad there.
“They went to shoot him, and the gun jammed, and they beat him with bricks. I’ll never forget it. The guys that done it were at his funeral,” says another Star of the Sea player, Geordie Hussey.
For Wynne, the documentary tells the story of quiet heroes – the ones who held the line and who helped prevent Northern Ireland from falling fully into the abyss, when it so easily could.
On such a list, the club’s manager, Dr Liam Conlon takes pride of place: “The majority caught in the middle just want a peaceful existence, but that is being disrupted – as we have seen again just in the last few weeks – by divisive rhetoric,” Wynne tells The Irish Times.
Months of research and filming in Rathcoole “reinforced the original idea of the film that shows how Liam Conlon’s ethos was literally 60 years ahead of his time, bringing people together”, he says.
For years afterwards, even when the cross-community make-up of Star of the Sea was but a memory, Conlon continued to help: “He had a holiday home in Donegal that he gave to people. The kind of people who wouldn’t even get the chance of a holiday. It sounds a bit simplistic or glib, but that’s the thing – people willing to do the right thing, regardless of the opposition. He carried that through right to the end,” Wynne continues.
Rathcoole, and so many other places under the sway of paramilitaries 30 years after the Belfast Agreement still need people like Liam Conlon, as one of the final scenes in the documentary reveals, if only in part.
In the scene, McCord is seen visiting his son’s grave in Newtownabbey. However, the film does not show that the gravestone is the fourth put over his son’s grave. Each of the others were desecrated by loyalist paramilitaries.

title: ‘All those years wasted’: Gardaí investigating George Gibney were given Orla Poole’s name 28 years ago
description: Carolyn Brown says she passed Poole’s name on in 1998 but the guards did not contact her
content:
A woman who said she was sexually abused as a child by George Gibney gave investigating gardaí in 1998 the name of a classmate she suspected was also abused by the former swimming coach, but they never contacted her.
The first woman was Carolyn Brown, whose complaints against Gibney did not result in a prosecution against him.
The second was Orla Poole, whose complaint against him in recent years, and court testimony that he attempted to rape her when she was 12 years old, led to the former national and Olympics coach being jailed for more than 15 years on Monday.
Gibney was found guilty in the Central Criminal Court of 39 counts of indecent assault and one count of attempted rape of children for the sexual abuse of four girls in the 1970s and 1980s.
Carolyn Brown attended court to see Gibney being sentenced and recognised Orla Poole sitting in front of her.
Carolyn Brown’s complaint against Gibney, while investigated by gardaí, did not result in a prosecution against the former coach.
Orla Poole was one of the four complainants in the most recent investigation that resulted in his conviction, though the judge referred to them only by the initials of their maiden names.
“Oh, God, I was in the pool with her,” Carolyn Brown said when she recognised Orla Poole in court.
The women started first year together at Newpark Comprehensive School in Blackrock, Dublin, in the mid-1970s but had not met since they both left the school before the Leaving Certificate.
[ For survivors, failed George Gibney investigations were ‘nearly worse than the abuse’ Opens in new window ]
Orla Poole, now living in the US, made a statement to gardaí after listening to the 2020 BBC podcast Where is George Gibney?, produced by Second Captains.
Afterwards, outside the courtroom, Carolyn Brown told Orla Poole she had named her in 1998 to gardaí as a possible victim of Gibney.
“I’m astounded Carolyn gave the guards my name 28 years ago,” said Orla Poole, whom Gibney began abusing when she was eight.
“All those years wasted. How many years of undue freedom did he get?”
Orla Poole said she only contacted the Garda after an online algorithm suggested the podcast might be of interest to her.
“It wouldn’t have been hard for them to find me. My mother [Fiona Poole] has lived in the same house in Leopardstown since 1969. She was not a hard woman to find. She was well known, a former president of the INTO . Her brother was a guard,” said Orla Poole.
[ This is how it ended for George Gibney: a packed court celebrating his demise Opens in new window ]
The Irish Times submitted a request for comment to the Garda but received no response before publication.
Carolyn Brown said gardaí investigating Gibney’s abuse of her from the ages of 13 to 15 asked her if there was anyone else who could give evidence about Gibney.
She said she gave them “a few names, including Orla’s”, but the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) instructed that no charges be brought against Gibney for what he did to her. He was living in Florida at the time.
Carolyn Brown was not contacted for a fresh statement when the latest Garda investigation began on foot of the podcast by Mark Horgan and Ciarán Cassidy.
A second man, associated with Gibney, was subsequently put on trial for abusing Carolyn Brown separately in the same period. That was declared a mistrial after she inadvertently named another victim under pressure of cross-examination.
“Orla and I were in the pool together. We were in classes together,” Carolyn Brown said.
“What bothers me is that she came forward such a long time after me. Nobody told me there was another investigation. I was told nothing.”
Carolyn Brown left school at 15 and never returned to formal education.
“I was shocked when a guard rang and told me the DPP said Gibney was not to be charged. I had gone with them to Newpark, shown them the sauna and his office. He used to lock me in there. I couldn’t understand, after everything I’d told them, how he could go free.”
She said she was not contacted either when a new investigation into Gibney was established in 2015 by the Garda Commissioner in response to questions raised in the Dáil by then Independent TD Maureen O’Sullivan.
[ ‘A lot of people didn’t believe us’: George Gibney victim sees justice done after first prosecution collapsed Opens in new window ]
The first of five successive investigations into Gibney’s crimes against children began 34 years ago, in 1992, when former swimmer Chalkie White made a statement at Blackrock Garda station.
Outside the courthouse after Gibney (78) was taken away in a prison van on Monday, Orla Poole waived her right to anonymity and addressed the media.
“This court didn’t just deliver justice for me but, also I hope, for others,” she said. “It has shown that even after 50-plus years, justice can be got.”

title: Ryder Cup accommodation: €99,000 for a castle and €19,000 for a house in Tyrone
description: A house in Omagh for €19,000: Fans face high prices with official travel provider
content:
Rental accommodation aimed at fans travelling to next year’s Ryder Cup in Adare is being advertised for up to €99,000 as part of the tournament’s official property rental programme.
Ryder Cup Travel Service (RCTS) , the official accommodation service provider for the 2027 Ryder Cup, has over 770 properties listed on its portal (as of October 15th).
The Ryder Cup will take place at Adare Manor from Tuesday, September 14th to Sunday, September 19th, 2027.
The rental accommodation listed by RCTS shows asking prices based on an eight-night stay, and an account is required to make a booking inquiry.
The cheapest option – a one-bed house in Cappawhite, Co Tipperary , 50km from Adare – has an asking price of €2,688 for the week of the tournament.
At the other end of the spectrum, the most expensive listing is the nine-bed Lough Cutra Castle near Gort, Co Galway , which has an asking price of €99,000 for eight nights. The 19th-century castle – which is 75km from Adare Manor, just shy of an hour by car – features six double bedrooms, two triple rooms and one twin room, or space for up to 20 people. The 600-acre wooded estate on which the property is set, as well as the 1,000-acre private lake and a walled garden are included under the rental’s “unique features”.
While 38 of the properties are within 10km of Adare Manor, many leave guests with a considerable journey to see the action. 142 listings are located over 100km away from the course.
Demand for accommodation around the Ryder Cup is likely to be high, with over 250,000 people expected at Adare Manor across the week of the tournament. General admission tickets sold out in July, snapped up by fans from 80 countries.
The property with the longest spin to Adare is a six-bed house outside Omagh, Co Tyrone , which carries a €19,000 asking price. According to the listing, the property can sleep up to 26, and features an eight-seater hot tub, two large lounges, a bar/function room equipped with a full-size professional snooker table, and a BBQ outdoor dining area.
Aware of potential upmarket clientele, access to dedicated helipads/heliports are among the amenities included in a number of listings. Among them is a six-bed house on the seafront in Whiting Bay, Co Waterford , with a €10,000-per-night asking price. For that, guests will have access to the property’s 58-foot swimming pool, steam room, tennis court and cinema room.
Beyond those advertised by RCTS, other booking platforms also have listings geared towards the Ryder Cup. Accommodation for The Event is a third-party website listing properties available to rent in areas near major golf tournaments, including the Masters. The website has 1,260 properties listed to rent for next year’s Ryder Cup.
As with some of the properties on the RCTS site, some rentals are listed as price on application, while many have price points north of €30,000. While almost 300 of the properties are listed as being in Limerick , most are in surrounding counties – Tipperary, Cork, Kerry and Clare – while properties in Offaly, Laois, Kilkenny and Dublin also feature.
Among the Accomodation for the Event listings is a restored 19th-century schoolhouse in Dundrum, Co Tipperary. The six-bed property sleeps 12, with a listed price of €65,000.
There are also some eye-watering prices to be found on Airbnb , where 48 properties in the surrounding areas are listed at over €20,000 for eight nights.
The most expensive is a four-bed property just outside Adare, listed at €75,185, with room for seven guests, while a three-bed cottage in the village is available for €59,560.

title: Plan for O’Connell Street restaurant approved, but it is banned from serving takeaways
description: Former Ulster Bank building acquired by firm linked to businessmen Tommy Kelly and Stephen McCarthy
content:
A new restaurant being planned for Ulster Bank’s former O’Connell Street branch in Dublin will be barred from operating any takeaway food service.
Kingstonway Limited, the new owners of 2-4 O’Connell Street Lower, applied for planning permission to convert the building into a mixed-use restaurant, retail and office development.
Dublin City Council has now granted the company permission to convert part of the old bank into a restaurant, but said it “shall not operate as a takeaway (an outlet that sells hot food for consumption off the premises)”.
In its planning application, the company said it had interest from an international restaurant operator to occupy part of the building, but did not clarify if this operator wanted to provide takeaway services.
Longstanding concerns have been aired by city councillors about the concentration of fast-food outlets on O’Connell Street, from which about a dozen provide takeaway services.
The pushback on new takeaway food businesses on O’Connell Street by the council has come as US takeaway brands , including Popeyes, Wingstop, Dave’s Hot Chicken, Wendy’s and Taco Bell, are expanding into the Irish market.
In 2024, a Dublin City Taskforce led by former An Post chief executive David McRedmond said the Government needed to “revitalise O’Connell Street and environs” through the use of the Special Planning Control Scheme (SPCS).
There are two SPCS in place at present in central Dublin, which cover Grafton Street, O’Connell Street and their surrounding areas.
The SPCS set out a number of policies and objectives on architectural conservation, property uses, building heights, advertising signs and shopfronts, vacancy and civic identity.
In its decision to approve the new O’Connell Street restaurant, the city council cited the SPCS for the area as its reason for banning takeaway services from the venue.
The project to revamp the old Ulster Bank branch is being led by the building’s owners, Kingstonway Limited. The company is linked to eShopWorld founder Tommy Kelly and former BidX1 chief executive Stephen McCarthy.
Kelly, whose wealth has been estimated to be about €1 billion, made a large amount of his fortune from the €600 million sale of ecommerce company eShopWorld.
Following the sale in 2021, he has made a number of investments in property and businesses through CastleGate Investments, including a deal to acquire estate agent Sherry Fitzgerald .
Kelly and McCarthy’s plans for 2-4 O’Connell Street Lower have come a year after the building was put up for sale by Ulster Bank at a guide price of €2.75 million.
The restaurant planned would take up 734sq m across the basement, ground and mezzanine levels of the refurbished building, with 941sq m of office space on the upper floors.
The plans for the building align with a recommendation from the Dublin City Taskforce, which called for more mixed-use buildings on O’Connell Street, including residential, hospitality, cultural and night-time use alongside the existing retail and commercial usage.
A multiyear programme, in partnership with private landlords, to revitalise O’Connell Street and adjoining streets was also required to foster “development of the area as a cultural hub”, the taskforce said.

title: Children Ombudsman ‘deeply concerned’ about changes to homeless accommodation eligibility
description: Minister for Housing was urged to ‘reconsider to prevent any discrimination against children and families in need’
content:
The Ombudsman for Children told the Minister for Housing he was “deeply concerned” about changes to eligibility requirements for social housing and emergency homeless accommodation.
In a letter to the Minister last July, Niall Muldoon said such changes risked excluding vulnerable groups, including “undocumented families with children, Roma families with children and families seeking international protection” from accessing emergency accommodation and housing supports.
“Such exclusions contradict Ireland’s international commitments, as outlined in the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child and other human rights instruments such as the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, which emphasise the rights of all children to access homeless accommodation without discrimination, regardless of their migration status or nationality,” he said.
“I urge the department to reconsider these proposed criteria to ensure compliance with Ireland’s international obligations and to prevent any discrimination against children and families in need.”
Muldoon’s letter, obtained through the Freedom of Information Act, was sent as the Housing and Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill 2026 was being passed through the Oireachtas.
[ ‘Powerful and heartbreaking’: A couch is what Ireland’s homeless children say they want most Opens in new window ]
Under the legislation, each member of a household must be lawfully resident and habitually resident in the State. The lawfully resident requirement will not apply to a member of household who is a child.
Muldoon said he was concerned the provisions would only allow for night-to-night accommodation at the discretion of a local authority for those who did not satisfy the eligibility requirement.
“I also note that consideration of the best interest of child will not apply to these families while their legal and habitual residence is being assessed,” he added.
In his response to Muldoon, Minister for Housing James Browne said the primary motivation for the legislation was to ensure “clarity and consistency” regarding supports provided by the State.
“While applied in practice, there is currently no provision in the Housing Acts requiring residency as an eligibility criterion for social housing or homeless accommodation support,” he said. “This Bill will simply put these eligibility requirements for accessing social housing supports on a statutory footing.”
Browne said his officials liaised with the local authority sector and the Office of the Attorney General to introduce a statutory obligation to ensure anyone eligible was “not simply abandoned” and a “safety net service” would be provided to any household deemed ineligible.
The Fianna Fáil TD also noted that a “number of potentially vulnerable groups” had been listed in the ombudsman’s correspondence.
He said there would be no change to current provisions regarding asylum seekers being entitled to accommodation from the International Protection Accommodation Services .
“Households granted a permission to remain through the international protection process will be entitled to homeless accommodation and apply for social housing - again, there is no change to the current provision,” added Browne.
“Undocumented families from outside Europe who do not have a lawful right to be here, or European families who do not have worker status and/or have arrived in the last 90 days, will be entitled to access the safety net service while they can avail of available assistance, including assistance to return home where appropriate.”
The Ombudsman for Children’s Office said last week that it still had concerns about the impact of the legislation on children but was “engaging constructively” with the Department of Housing and providing advice on impact assessments on children’s rights before the legislation was commenced over the coming months.
“The OCO hope that measures will be put in place to mitigate any potential adverse impact on vulnerable children,” a spokeswoman for the ombudsman’s office said.

title: Mandatory pension deductions and USC tax bands to blame for eroding public workers’ pay
description: Unions should focus on what State takes from salaries rather than pushing solely for wage rises
content:
Sir, – To defend living standards properly, unions must first understand how these are being eroded. Focusing on whether gross pay has matched inflation misses the crucial mechanism that has hit living standards: the State can give an (apparently) inflation-matching increase with one hand but reclaim an ever-growing proportion of that income with the other.
There are two layers. The first affects public- and private-sector employees alike. Although some income-tax bands and credits have received occasional increases, the threshold for the higher (8 per cent) USC rate has remained at €70,044 since 2015.
As salaries rise merely to reflect prices, more earnings become subject to that rate. In effect, the tax rate increases.
Many public servants face a second, even more impactful, layer. Many are subject to pension contributions whereby nothing is charged on the first €34,500, but between 10 per cent and 10.5 per cent is charged thereafter. Those thresholds have been frozen for six years.
For an experienced teacher paying the upper rates of income tax, USC, pension and PRSI , deductions absorb about 59 per cent of an additional pensionable euro.
A €1,000 increase therefore leaves about €410, before ordinary pension contributions. Non-indexation of USC and pension contribution levels means that a teacher’s rate of deduction goes up year after year in effect.
The effect of this in any one year is modest, but over time it slowly but surely erodes net take-home pay and real purchasing power, even when a gross pay increase appears to match inflation.
If the unions and government are going to get this right, they need to start from the correct premise, which is that it has been government policy for a decade to increase, in effect, rates of deduction from pay by failing to apply indexation consistently. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – The strike by public service unions over pay has Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers’ starting offer on the table of €1.2 billion. This pay increase would be divided by about 400,000 personnel.
Do the maths: that’s almost €3,000 per individual, or almost €60 a week. Then add budgetary tax cuts. Then add automatic increments. Now can we please have meaningful productivity for all this dosh? – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Thank you all for going on strike : I had a great day with my grandchildren. – Yours, etc,

title: Diarmaid Ferriter: Feed The World Phil has his eye on a €225,000 job
description: It is not enough to save the state, or Europe. It is time now for multi-options Phil to feed the world
content:
F ormer Fine Gael minister and European commissioner for trade Phil Hogan seems to want to be the new Bob Geldof, keen, he assures us, to “help the millions of people that need help in relation to food security and nutrition”. He wants to do this by becoming the next director general of the United Nations’ Food and Agricultural Organisation. He said he is ready to “serve once again” by obtaining the €225,000 per annum job.
At the launch of his bid this week, where the attendance included several Fine Gael grandees, Feed-the-World Phil dismissed the idea that controversy over his actions in 2020 – when he attended a dinner during Covid-19 restrictions , leading to his resignation as a European commissioner – might impede his chances. He suggested that was only a journalistic preoccupation: “We have gone into the history lesson on that ... I was sloppy in relation to the guidelines that were there at the time. I made a fulsome apology.” Fulsome means excessive or insincere.
To “serve once again”, he said he would spend a “significant six-figure sum” of his own money, but he is also to receive the assistance of two staff from the Department of Agriculture.
Hogan is obviously a very wealthy man: his consultancy firm, Hogan Strategic Advisory Services, earned at least €1 million in 2024, with banking giant JP Morgan Chase and law firm DLA Piper among his larger clients. In March 2022, Hogan paused his work with DLA Piper to ensure there was “absolutely no doubt” about compliance with rules for former European commissioners requiring a “cooling off” period applying to the taking on of clients who were “major stakeholders” in areas covered by an ex-commissioner’s former portfolios. A European Commission ethics committee had contended there was a “substantial discrepancy” between the law firm’s announcement in 2021 that Hogan was advising it and information provided by Hogan, creating “a risk of reputational damage” for the commission.
In pursuit of his current ambition, Hogan will channel his private wealth alongside State resources. He was chosen as a candidate after an interview by a panel that included a former senior civil servant, an industry expert and a human-resources adviser, with the Cabinet then backing his bid.
It might be worth considering other history lessons. As a junior minister on the morning of budget day in 1995, an adviser to Hogan faxed the main points of the budget to a journalist. Taoiseach John Bruton asked him to resign, which he did: “I was the first to break John Bruton’s pane of glass,” Hogan later said, a reference to Bruton’s declaration that his government “must go about its work ... as transparently as it were working behind a pane of glass.”
Hogan’s machinations within Fine Gael in relation to the leadership of the party have been well documented. In Stephen Collins and Ciara Meehan’s 2020 history of the party, Saving the State, they record that when Enda Kenny ’s leadership was threatened in 2010, “Hogan was in overdrive, canvassing almost every member of the parliamentary party, using inducements or threats, whichever he felt was more appropriate to the individual case.”
[ Phil Hogan ready to ‘serve once again’ as he launches bid for UN food agency job Opens in new window ]
As minister for the environment in 2014, Hogan said the decision to set up Irish Water was one of the biggest since the establishment of the ESB. There was trenchant criticism that Irish Water spent €50 million on external consultants in its first year. Hogan responded by saying “€50 million is part of the money that is required to set up this company that will bring €2 billion in savings to the taxpayer over the next seven years.” Plans for domestic water charges became a political fiasco. In 2018, Irish Water spent €683 million on the Republic’s water supply system and received €1.1 billion from the government.
In his 2025 memoir, Speaking My Mind, former Taoiseach Leo Varadkar wrote this of Hogan: “He’s the sort to explore all options, even dubious ones.” Regarding the 2020 controversy, Varadkar records that Hogan “ignored guidelines requiring people coming to Ireland from abroad to stay at home for 14 days. He had met me in the department during that period and been in and out of Kildare for golf trips during the local lockdown, when all non-essential journeys were to be avoided ... he returned to Brussels, leaving the rest of us to deal with the fallout”. European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen sought a detailed statement and timeline of his movements. She said “As Europe fights to reduce the spread of the coronavirus and Europeans make sacrifices and accept painful restrictions”, she expected commissioners “to be particularly vigilant about compliance”. There are certainly no restrictions on his movements now: he has recently been drumming up support for his candidacy in Singapore, Kenya, Rwanda, Ethiopia and south Pacific islands.
It is not enough to save the State, or Europe. It is time now for multi-options Phil to feed the world.
