title: Revenue looks to reduce postal costs and transition to ‘digital-first’ communications
description: Tax authority spends around €14.8m on postage each year
content:
Revenue is looking at ways to reduce postal communications with taxpayers and expand the use of “robotics” and artificial intelligence ( AI ) to deal with queries.
The tax authority is reviewing its postage practices, which cost it around €14.8 million in 2025, and increase the use of its online platform to send out important tax documents to millions of taxpayers each year.
In budget documents published alongside Budget 2027 last week it was stated that Revenue was “developing new systems and processes to transition” some customers to “digital-only” communication methods.
However, a spokeswoman for Revenue told The Irish Times that its work “is focused on transitioning towards a digital-first approach, rather than digital-only communications”.
This means “prioritising digital correspondence where appropriate, while continuing to provide postal communications where necessary”, she added.
Taxpayers who are registered for an account with Revenue’s online service but still receive correspondence by post will be the initial focus of the review.
Some 4.6 million people are registered for the MyAccount platform, according to figures from Revenue.
Tax credit certificates (TCCs) and statements of liability have been “identified as particular areas of focus”, the spokeswoman said. Revenue sent out 1.4 million TCCs in 2025 and more than 600,000 statements of liability, at a total cost of around €3.7 million.
In total, Revenue issued almost 10 million postal items in 2025, equivalent to a little more than 3.4 per cent of the total number of letters delivered by An Post in the same year, according to its annual report.
[ OPW paid large Revenue settlement over renting properties to staff at below market rates Opens in new window ]
Asked about the impact of Revenue’s move towards digital communications, a spokeswoman for An Post said the shift has “been the reality” for more than a decade across Government.
“The commitment to e-government and digitalisation of communications ... has been part of government policy over several administrations,” she said.
“This has fuelled An Post’s transformation to become a major ecommerce parcel and logistics company, digitalising our own processes across the business.”
She said An Post was also reviewing its strategic priorities to decide where to focus future investment. “We are hugely ambitious about taking opportunities to further expand and modernise the business in a digital world,” she said.
Revenue received a budget allocation of €684 million for next year, up around 4 per cent, according to the Budget 2027 expenditure report.
Apart from the review of its postal practices, other “efficiencies” and reforms that the tax authority is expected to deliver include an expansion of its “AI and robotics portfolio of applications into customer service channels”.
[ New public spending efficiency taskforce to be established within three months Opens in new window ]
For several years, Revenue has been using robotics to speed up mundane internal processes and free up staff to do other tasks.
The Irish Times reported in 2019 that Revenue had teamed up with Deloitte for a pilot project using robotic process automation technology to update some 20,000 taxpayer records.
Earlier this year, Revenue commissioner Ruth Kennedy told the Oireachtas AI committee that the authority did not use AI to make “tax-related decisions or carry out its statutory functions”. However, she said Revenue had been using the technology for a long time “to assist in more accurately directing taxpayer queries” to caseworkers, and assisting staff in finding “relevant information” to respond to taxpayer queries, “promptly and accurately”.

title: Brian O'Connor: Stale HRI policy doesn’t inspire confidence it can navigate uncertain future
description: Government funding more vital than ever with gambling industry outlook so uncertain
content:
According to some business types, strategy can sometimes boil down to choosing what not to do. Trying to secure racing’s long-term future is exercising lots of official minds around the racing world, although, it seems, with different degrees of urgency.
At a recent International Federation of Horseracing Authorities (IFHA) meeting in Paris , the splendidly named Winfried Engelbrecht-Bresges, chief executive of the Hong Kong Jockey Club and IFHA chair, was in no mood for sugar coating.
“I would submit that we have the biggest challenges facing the sport ever,” he declared. “This is in the context of significant social, political and economic uncertainties – uncertainties we face in multiple areas.”
Since Hong Kong is one of world racing’s beau ideals for financial clout and popular profile, his warnings on the need to widen the sport’s fanbase, threats to its funding, and what was described as the sustainability of the thoroughbred were stark.
It was little surprise that much of the Paris meeting focused on betting. Money speaks all languages and the rise of illegal betting hits racing bodies where it hurts most – in the pocket.
It’s also doing so right now. In comparison, Engelbrecht-Bresges’s comments on how racing is flirting with losing its popular relevance are intangible. They are vague enough to be put on the long finger by governing bodies busy keeping the bureaucratic carousel turning in the here and now.
That carousel turned in Irish racing’s favour in the recent budget. The Government gave an extra €2.3 million to Horse Racing Ireland (HRI) for 2027, bringing its total funding next year to €81.6 million. On the back of two budgets where the figure stalled, it was a welcome increase for the sector.
Minister for Agriculture Martin Heydon made a point of saying the extra money put into the Horse and Greyhound Racing Fund is linked to implementation of an Indecon review’s recommendations on animal welfare and integrity.
That Indecon report to the Oireachtas last year argued that a stronger public-policy rationale exists for funding of welfare and integrity programmes than for prizemoney, “given the public good” of the former. It even recommended some of the funding be “ring fenced”.
As is the way of such reports, maybe its existence alone is job done, another document to gather dust. Heydon’s reference could even be just a box-ticking exercise. But even at that, it is an indication of the direction of travel when it comes to racing’s broader relevance.
Convincing the public that the four-legged participants at its core are treated properly is the ultimate challenge for racing everywhere. It is existential in a way everything else isn’t.
Failure to invest in mechanisms that provide meaningful reassurance to a wider world ever more dubious about animal sports has the capacity to prove disastrous. Even a cursory look at the online venom generated by the Government’s budget increase to racing underlines the constant balancing act it faces to keep its vital social licence.
Recognising that should be part of the foresight and leadership that is urgently needed, according to Engelbrecht-Bresges’s comments.
It is particularly required in Ireland where racing has both a unique relationship with government as well as major economic status. But welfare continues to be a relative afterthought in a pecking order that seems strategically focused on ploughing on in the same old way.
After 25 years of the Horse and Greyhound Racing Fund, the Government’s funding safety net is more vital than ever since Irish racing’s other great financial pillar, the gambling industry, is in such a state of flux. Not that such upheaval is immediately obvious from HRI’s policy direction.
Much of its current five-year strategic plan is predicated on reaching over €92 million in government funding by 2028, which looks a no-hoper at this point. Another major element continues to be increasing fixtures, at the heart of which is the new Tipperary all-weather circuit due to open in October 2027, for which HRI has borrowed €34 million.
Much of the commercial logic for an increased fixture list is tied up in media rights sales and betting turnover. But the gambling industry reality has transformed. Racing’s significance to bookmakers is declining, betting shops are dying a not-so-slow death, and government instincts towards gambling generally are increasingly more hostile, particularly in the vital UK market.
Declining foal crops, less overall runners and smaller field sizes add up to a questionable rationale for a record 396 fixtures in 2027. If it made financial sense in 2024, the logic of lumping on an ever more uncertain betting outlook when the numbers don’t seem to add up looks increasingly like an old strategy for a new reality.
It certainly doesn’t smack of fresh thinking. Neither does HRI’s perpetual concentration on prizemoney inspire confidence that it’s got the strategic chops to navigate increasingly choppy waters. All of it underlines the potential long-term impact of stale ideas on a sport struggling to recognise that its self-interest is tied up in staying relevant enough for people to care about it.
The weather gods look set to play ball and provide decent ground for tomorrow’s Champions Day action at Ascot. The going doesn’t seem to matter to Rayif (3.20) – winner of the French Guineas and Jacques Le Marois – who will be the freshest QEII runner having had just three starts this season. His trainer Francis Graffard could hardly be in better form and saddled The Revenant to win the race in 2020.
James Doyle has picked incorrectly from a choice of Wathnan runners more than he’d like, but he could have got it right with Division (2.05) in the Champion Sprint. Doyle has overlooked both Paborus and 2024 winner King Of Blue, and the choice looks significant. Division has had little luck this season, particularly on his last start. But a strong pace and midfield draw can help Doyle smuggle him into contention for a late spurt.

title: ‘One of the smartest brains in the country’: Paudie Clifford says Galway have landed a gem in Éamonn Fitzmaurice
description: Kerry footballer says Finuge man will add a lot to Galway
content:
Paudie Clifford, fresh off a historic club success with Fossa, isn’t exactly standing still, but it may feel like that given all the movement around him.
There is Jerome Stack’s decision, for starters, to head for the exit door at Fossa just four weeks after guiding the club to that first ever Kerry intermediate title. Nobody envisaged that departure.
The speculation is that Stack, a hugely experienced coach/manager, took umbrage to training arrangements around the cohort of Fossa players, of which Clifford is one, who play for East Kerry in the senior championship.
“I think they’ll have something in place for next Tuesday,” said Clifford, referencing a replacement for Stack. “We’re just training hard ourselves this week. It’ll be resolved.”
“I’m not really sure. As I said, I’ll have to wait for the club to come to their decisions over the next few days before commenting.”
Fossa are somewhat fortunate that there’s a decent gap until their Munster club semi-final tie on November 22nd, against the representatives from Clare or Waterford.
Éamonn Fitzmaurice , part of the management for Fossa’s All-Ireland junior success in 2023, has also been on the move. Fitzmaurice was recently confirmed as the new Galway senior football manager , succeeding Pádraic Joyce.
At some stage in 2027, Clifford may come up against his old ally.
“When he was with us at Fossa, he just added so much,” said Clifford. “So, unfortunately, he’s going to add a lot to Galway . I suppose he just felt it was an opportunity that he wanted to give a go. I wish him the best because, as I said, I just have massive time for him as a person and as a coach.
“He’s one of the smartest brains in the country. Everyone could see that when he was doing the commentary and the punditry work, how smart he is. But [he’s] also a very good man manager, so he’ll definitely add a lot to Galway.”
Finnbarr Roarty, the Donegal defender detailed to mark Clifford in both this year’s league and championship, is going even further afield, to Australia. The Young Footballer of the Year has taken up a two-year rookie deal with AFL side Collingwood . Considering how tight a marker Clifford found the Glenties man to be, perhaps that is no bad thing?
“He’ll be a big loss for his club and a big loss for Donegal. We’ve been hit hard by it ourselves,” said Clifford, eyeing the drain of young talent from Kerry to Australia. “It’ll be interesting to see how he gets on. He’s a young lad, he could be back after his two-year contract. Or if he gets on well, he might stay there. But he’ll be a big loss for the GAA in the whole country because he’s a top player.”
Clifford was speaking at the launch of the AIB club championships. It was his first proper media sitdown since Kerry’s All-Ireland final defeat to Mayo in July. It was his man-of-the-match performance against Dublin in the semi-final that helped get Kerry there.
They subsequently became a footnote in Mayo’s remarkable All-Ireland story. There was more movement after that final too, Kerry coach Cian O’Neill opting to switch Kingdom football for Cork hurling .
“I think he’ll be well able for that role,” said Clifford of O’Neill’s new position as head coach. “I think he’ll add a lot to Cork. He brings great energy. He brings great ideas, he’s very, very good tactically. So he could be the missing piece that Cork need.”
Back in Kerry, Jack O’Connor is searching for those missing inches too. The Kerry manager has been vocal about the apparent fatigue felt by Kerry players due to the amount of club competitions they participate in each autumn and winter. A work group recommended a guaranteed break of between four and six weeks each autumn/winter for county players – potentially restricting their activity in local competitions – but this was rejected by a county board vote. So the status quo remains.
In Clifford’s case, it means that if Fossa go deep into the Munster and All-Ireland club series this winter, Kerry mightn’t see him or his brother David until well into 2027.
“I’m not exactly sure what went on in the meeting but I do know that they’ll still be aiming to get the four-week break, and hoping that that will pay off later on in the season,” said Clifford.
“However long it goes on for us, the S&C and Jack and all the lads will give us enough of a break that we’ll get a chance to down tools for a few weeks and then build it back up. We’ll get enough of a break that we’ll be ready to go again. It might mean missing a few league games, but I think we’ll be fine.”

title: Urban and more affluent areas have higher proportions of migrants, study finds
description: Research shows 78% of those not born on island of Ireland live in urban settings
content:
Urban and more affluent areas in Ireland have higher proportions of migrants , a new study has found.
Carried out for the Department of Justice by the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI), the research found migrants, defined as those not born on the island of Ireland, are concentrated in urban areas.
It found 78 per cent of migrants live in urban areas, with 43 per cent of the total number of migrants living in cities.
The study, published on Friday, also found the proportion of migrants was higher in more affluent areas. In electoral divisions classified as “very affluent”, 36 per cent of the population were migrants while they comprised just 9 per cent of the population in “extremely disadvantaged” areas.
In Dublin, migrants are most concentrated in the city centre, including the north inner city. Areas located 2km-4km from the city centre have lower proportions, including areas of Ballymun and Finglas.
Migrants are more likely to live in areas with more private rental housing, as opposed to owner-occupied or social housing.
International Protection Accommodation Service (IPAS) centres, the research found, are not evenly distributed across Ireland but electoral divisions with such centres were not any more or less likely to be classified as deprived.
Other key findings include the urban-rural divide among migrants varies according to their country of birth. Those born in Britain and the US were most likely to live in rural areas; those born in some non-EU and western EU countries were most likely to live in urban areas and Eastern European migrants were more likely to live in commuter towns than cities.
Migrant segregation was found to be low in Ireland. Groups of migrants born in non-EU and non-Anglosphere countries have higher average levels of segregation than migrants born in Britain, the US and Poland.
The researchers interviewed stakeholders working in local integration and noted the introduction of Local Area Integration Teams (LAITs) in every local authority was regarded as good practice in migrant integration. Interviewees suggested the remit of LAITs should be expanded to include all migrants or other vulnerable migrant groups and managers of IPAS centres should receive training.
Housing and language were identified as the main barriers to integration. Other challenges included the recognition of qualifications, accessing healthcare, local transport and isolation. Concerns were raised about the availability of English language training in rural areas and difficulties facing migrants living near the border with Northern Ireland, who cannot cross it without a visa.
Evan Carron-Kee, a co-author of the study, noted Irish and migrant populations have different spatial distribution patterns across the country and spatial distribution also differs between migrant groups, affecting their opportunities for integration.
“Ensuring that local stakeholders are empowered to adopt solutions at a local level and to inform national decisions is crucial for effective integration policy,” he said.
The study, Spatial Distribution and Local Integration of Migrants in Ireland, is available on the ESRI website.

title: Funding of universities set to be overhauled, says Minister
description: Operating environment for third-level institutions has ‘changed considerably’
content:
The funding of Irish universities is set to be overhauled significantly, Minister for Higher Education James Lawless is set to say on Friday.
Amid warnings that Irish universities are teetering on a “cliff edge” due to chronic underfunding, the Kildare North TD will deliver a speech to an informal meeting of EU education ministers.
Lawless will tell the meeting that the operating environment for universities has “changed considerably” since the last funding and reform plan for the sector was undertaken in 2022, before the advent of artificial intelligence and accelerating geopolitical instability.
“It is clear to me that the figures and assumptions underpinning our approach to university funding need to be revisited to reflect the realities facing institutions today,” he will say, arguing that the time is right to “take a fresh look at the funding requirements of our university sector”.
Lawless will tell the meeting he plans to bring an updated paper to Government before the end of the year, “examining the adequacy of existing funding arrangements, the changing financial requirements of our universities and the opportunities to develop a more sustainable funding model”.
It will also consider the relationship between future changes to student fees and the Government funding available to institutions, he will say, adding that he wants to ensure the universities have the resources necessary. “But I also expect them to work constructively with me in delivering the reforms required to secure their long-term future.”
An Oireachtas committee heard on Thursday that chronic underfunding by the State over several years has led to a €250 million deficit in the sector.
The 2022 plan – Funding the Future – pledged €25 million annually to bridge a gap of €307 million identified in core funding for universities, although just €10 million was specifically allocated this year amid political pressure to keep spending increases under control.
The director general of the Irish Universities Association, Paul Johnston, told the Oireachtas education committee on Thursday that State funding of higher education per student is 34 per cent less than it was in 2008.
“Government has acknowledged the problem but not moved fast enough to address it,” he said, adding the gap in funding now stands at about €250 million annually.
“Our pre-budget submission thus sought €190 million in additional core funding this year and next to close that gap. Budget 2027 provided only €10 million in new core funding,” Johnston said.
Senior sources said a new funding system may ultimately involve extra allocations from the exchequer, but that third-level institutions would also be expected to concentrate on raising cash through their own internal revenue streams, while also examining their own cost bases.
There is an acknowledgment that the figure required by the sector has grown, but also that funding it is partially dependent on future allocations to Lawless’s department.
Lawless is expected to bring forward a toolkit aimed at bringing costs down in universities while raising revenues – for example, funding some early retirements, alongside engagement on industrial relations issues and staffing.
Sources within the third-level sector want extra money allocated by the Government to cover the total cost of any public sector pay rises, and extra funding to cover older pay increases that they believe have led to a funding gap of €41 million.
The Department of Further Education ’s budget for 2027 included a €34 million student support package, including a €150 reduction in the student contribution fee and a 4.5 per cent increase in SUSI maintenance grants.
The focus on student support comes amid a growing accommodation crisis , with students commuting long distances, couch-surfing and working long hours to afford their educational costs.

title: Is Trump colluding with Putin to damage Zelenskiy?
description: Ukraine was reportedly denied full access to Elon Musk’s Starlink just as Russia launched a missile attack
content:
Sir, – There are two options for ending the Russia-Ukraine war : continue fighting until one side capitulates, which will result in significant loss of life and destruction, or offer Russia terms more favourable than the former.
A precedent for the latter was the acceptance by Joseph Stalin of the favourable terms offered by Finland in the winter war of 1939-1940. Finland ceded about 10 per cent of its territory but retained its independence.
Russia must realise that the cost of occupying Ukraine against a hostile population is futile and would be prohibitively expensive. Offering Russia terms that include the lifting of all sanctions, international help to rebuild their economy and rejoining the G7 group of nations could be a pragmatic solution.
If Ukraine ceded Crimea to Russia it would represent a loss of about 4.5 per cent of its territory or less than half that lost by Finland in 1940.
Terms should include the abdication of Russian president Vladimir Putin and the cessation of all hybrid warfare by Russia in Europe. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – It’s reported that Ukraine military was denied full access to Elon Musk’s Starlink “coincidentally” just as Russia launched a massive missile attack.
Also “coincidentally”, the US failed to warn Ukraine of the Russian attack. Is Trump colluding with Putin to damage Zelenskiy ? – Yours, etc,
Sir, – If it is found that Musk has switched off the Starlink satellite system that helps Ukraine defend itself, how can we as a society buy Tesla cars not to mention tolerate X in our midst? – Yours, etc,

title: Simon Coveney’s consultancy firm made annual profit of almost €150,000
description: Former Fine Gael minister provides advice through his company Waterfront Advisory, including lobbying for developer Johnny Ronan
content:
An advisory consultancy established by former tánaiste Simon Coveney has posted annual profits of more than €147,000 in 2025, its latest accounts show.
Cobh-based Waterfront Advisory Limited provides strategic advice on areas including public policy, marine and maritime affairs, infrastructure, government relations, and defence and security policy.
The other director of the company is Laura McGonigle, who was a special adviser to Coveney in three government departments: Foreign Affairs, Defence, and Enterprise, Trade and Employment.
She was previously a Cork City councillor and also an adviser to Deirdre Clune between 2014 and 2019 when Clune was an MEP for the South constituency.
Waterfront was established in 2025 after Coveney retired from politics after serving as a TD and MEP between 1998 and 2024.
During a long ministerial career, he served in the departments of Agriculture, Defence, Housing, Foreign Affairs and Enterprise.
Coveney’s company disclosed in abridged financial statements that it made a profit of €147,693 in the financial year to the end of February 2026.
At February 28th the company had fixed assets of €39,280 and net current assets of €108,513.
Since leaving politics, Coveney has been involved with several companies. He is a consultant to EY Ireland’s Geopolitical Strategy Unit and is also a director of the Reliance Bearing and Gear Company, a long-established company with headquarters in Cork that supplies components for industrial engineering.
In its most recent return to the Lobbying Register, Waterfront Advisory stated that, on August 26th last, Coveney lobbied Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris on behalf of Bremore Ireland Port Company.
The meeting with Harris, a former Fine Gael ministerial colleague of Coveney, was described in the lobbying return as a “progress briefing on the development of the new port at Bremore”.
In a separate entry for the same day, Ronan Group, the company headed by developer Johnny Ronan, stated that principals of the company, together with Coveney, met Simon Harris and civil servant David Owners “concerning the development of Bremore Port and related ports and infrastructure policy”.
It stated that the intended results were “to gain support, discuss and progress the development of Bremore Port, including relevant Government policy, planning and infrastructure considerations”.
Records on the register show Ronan lobbied Coveney in 2016 when he was minister for housing.
Ronan wrote a letter to the then minister seeing changes in planning laws to allow higher apartments at Spencer Dock, Dublin, and consider new financing models for housing.
[ Simon Coveney: Former minister once lobbied by developer Johnny Ronan, now lobbies for him Opens in new window ]
There were no meetings or further contacts. It was one of 3,000 separate lobbying actions received by Coveney when he was a minister.
Coveney’s profile on the Waterfront Advisory website has stated that his “breadth of experience gives him a rare, joined-up understanding of how economic policy, national security, infrastructure, housing and marine affairs intersect in practice”.
“As Minister for Foreign Affairs during one of the most challenging periods in recent European history, he was a central figure in Ireland’s response to Brexit, helping to safeguard the Good Friday Agreement and protect peace and stability on the island of Ireland,” the website says.
The Irish Times contacted Coveney on Wednesday but he made no public comment.

title: To get into Ireland’s top 1%, you’ll need €123,000 in disposable income
description: Study by DataPulse also found that 134,900 individuals here were in Europe’s top 1% of earners
content:
To rank among Ireland’s top 1 per cent of earners, an individual needs to generate €123,200 of disposable income a year, a new study has revealed.
The threshold or entry point to the elite earners category in Ireland is the third highest in the EU , research by Berlin-based DataPulse found.
Only Luxembourg at €205,420 and Denmark at €135,389 had higher thresholds. Ireland’s entry point is higher than that of Germany (€111,693), the Netherlands (€107,894) and France (€104,743).
The findings, which used Eurostat data on disposable income across member states, are part of a wider “European income ladder” study commissioned by lifestyle and travel magazine AMEXcited.
It found that Ireland also has the third-highest share of its own population among the EU’s top 1 per cent of earners.
Some 2.48 per cent of the Irish population, equating to 134,900 individuals, belong to the EU-wide top 1 per cent category, which has a threshold of €92,200 of annual disposable income per person after taxes and social contributions.
Germany and France together account for about 59 per cent of the EU-wide top 1 per cent by income, with roughly 35 per cent in Germany and 24 per cent in France.
The report also measured “the gap between the middle and the top”. In Ireland, the top 1 per cent earning threshold, €123,200, was 3½ times the median disposable income of €35,138.
This compares to 5½ times in Bulgaria – the highest – and just 2.4 times in Slovakia – the lowest.
[ Household wealth in Ireland hits record €1.4tn Opens in new window ]
The survey also measured how much EU heads of government and members of national parliaments earn compared to people on median gross incomes in those member states.
In Ireland, Taoiseach Micheál Martin ’s gross salary – €256,311 a year – was five times that of the gross median income at €51,781.
TDs, who get paid €119,467 a year, earned 2.3 times the gross median income.
The German chancellor earns €333,704 a year, 6.3 times the German median income at €53,098.
Chief executives in EU markets were found to earn between 100 and 700 times median salaries in their respective countries.
The best-paid chief executive in Ireland in 2024, according to the report, was Kerry Group chief executive Edmond Scanlon on €6 million, which was 117 times median earnings here.
[ CEO pay in Ireland in 2025: One executive earned $237m Opens in new window ]
Separate studies suggest former Flutter chief executive Peter Jackson , who stepped down this year, had a bigger salary than Scanlon.
At the very top of the DataPulse chart was Lucian Grainge of Universal Music Group in the Netherlands, on €41.1 million a year, which was 690 times the national median earnings.
“The best-paid Dutch CEO earns in one year what 690 years of median work would pay,” the report said.
The study only considered regular pay components for a single financial year – base salary, annual bonus, pension and benefits – and not severance or one-off special awards.
When working time instead of salaries is considered, the gap between company chiefs and average workers looks even starker.
Grainge reaches the median Dutch gross monthly earnings in about 11 minutes of work, while the chief executive of the German software giant SAP, Christian Klein, reaches the German median income in about 25 minutes.
A German full-time employee on the minimum wage, by contrast, would need about 576 years to reach the SAP chief executive’s pay.

title: Reward TV licence-fee payers by allowing them to skip ads on RTÉ Listen app
description: Readers agree with Kathy Sheridan’s annoyance about automated commercials ruining listening pleasure
content:
Sir, – I am a huge supporter of Irish public service broadcasting. I spend much time listening to RTÉ Radio – mostly via the recently much-improved RTÉ Listen app.
I feel I get great value for my annual €160 TV licence payment – in quality and quantity.
However, I heartily agree with Kathy Sheridan’s annoyance about the advertisements on the RTÉ Listen app, the pre-roll advertisements in particular (“ I have paid my TV licence long after I needed to. But RTÉ is testing my patience ”, Opinion, October 14th).
You’re listening to a programme, take a phone call and then attempt to rejoin the programme and you’re subjected to the same 45 seconds of ads as when you first opened the app. So annoying.
However, may I offer a solution? And one that might reward Kathy and me and our ilk for continuing to be loyal to RTÉ and continuing to pay the licence fee.
How about having the app opening with a request for the owner’s current TV licence number? Thus, like The Irish Times providing extra online advantages to subscribers who sign in, RTÉ would allow licence holders to bypass the pre-roll ads and all other ads.
Follow the YouTube model. You can watch it free – and you get all the ads. Or you can pay a monthly fee and never see another ad.
Sir, – I wholeheartedly agree with Kathy Sheridan’s irritation on having to listen to the barrage of ads on switching on RTE radio channels on internet radio.
The way I get around this is to switch on the RTÉ channel, but turn the volume down to zero for about 30 seconds until “the coast is clear”.
It reminds of the old PYE radio we had in the 1950s when the thermionic valves had to be switched on for a few minutes to allow the filaments to heat up.
So, despite all the advances in technology‚ I’m back to the same old routine of the good old days.
Plus ça change, plus c’est la même chose. – Yours, etc,

title: Stephen Collins: Unsustainable pay increases for public sector workers will put Ireland’s stability at risk
description: Questions have to be asked about the sustainability of the ever-expanding public sector – especially given that so many civil servants rarely appear in the office
content:
A fter the one-day public service strike this week, the Government , trade unions and the public need to reflect on a painful lesson from the recent past: excessive public sector pay awards in the early years of this century played a central role in triggering the 2008 financial crash.
The popular narrative of that episode is that the crash, the subsequent austerity and the EU / IMF bailout were all the fault of the banks. While there was no excuse for the reckless behaviour of the banks, the focus on their sins has allowed a convenient shifting of responsibility from other players – the government and the public sector unions.
One key element of the public finance crisis that engulfed the country in 2008 was the runaway cost of the public service pay and pensions bill, which fuelled unsustainable growth in government spending from 2000 onwards.
This process was partly driven by a rapid expansion of personnel, with the number of public servants rising by 35 per cent between 2000 and 2008, but it was compounded by a rise in pay of 32 per cent between 2003 and 2008. The cumulative increase in inflation over the same period was 18 per cent.
The dramatic increase in pay was the result of a flawed benchmarking process that developed out of a preordained agreement between government and the trade unions to grant substantial pay increases to public servants regardless of the economic rationale or the long-term implications for public finances.
“The end result was that average public sector salaries were raised to completely unsustainable levels,” according to economists Donal Donovan and Antoin Murphy, who wrote the definitive account of the crash, The Fall of the Celtic Tiger: Ireland and the Euro Debt Crisis.
By 2006, senior public servants were earning 8 per cent more than their private sector counterparts while middle- and lower-ranking grades were being paid between 22 per cent and 31 per cent more than equivalent workers in the private sector.
While social partnership played an important role in helping the country out of the economic depression of the 1980s, it had developed into an out-of-control juggernaut by the early 2000s.
[ Could the public sector strike be a one-off? Opens in new window ]
“Social partnership appears to have placed an exceptionally high premium on avoiding social tension or any outbreak of industrial strife. However, the price was excessive and the consequences far-reaching. Apart from contributing to a loss in external competitiveness, the massive expansion in the public sector payroll bill contributed in a major way to the subsequent financial collapse,” wrote Donovan and Murphy.
Even after the crash, which led to temporary reductions in public service pay, salaries for Irish public servants remained significantly higher than in most other developed countries.
Data from the then 34-member Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development ( OECD ), the grouping of the world’s most advanced economies, in 2011, measured eight categories of public service salaries and put Ireland near the top of the table. We had the highest-paid medical consultants, the fourth-highest-paid nurses, the fifth-highest-paid teachers and the sixth-highest-paid senior and middle-ranking managers. What was really striking was that Ireland was the only country to appear in the top eight in all categories.
A senior British diplomat told me of his amazement shortly after the EU/IMF bailout, to which the UK contributed £3.2 billion, when he learned that the Irish ambassador in London was still paid considerably more than his British counterpart in Dublin, despite the wreckage in the public finances here.
The lesson from the financial crash hardly needs spelling out. The Government simply cannot concede unsustainable pay increases to the public sector without putting the country’s finances at risk once more. This is particularly so given the rapid rise in public service numbers in recent years, which has eerie echoes of the early 2000s.
Replying to a Dáil question from Micheál Carrigy earlier this year, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers conceded that over the past decade the number of civil servants had risen from 35,032 to 53,161, a rise of 52 per cent, while numbers in the wider public service had increased from 301,589 to 417,464, a rise of 38 per cent.
[ Jack Chambers ‘hopeful’ of ‘way forward’ to prevent further public sector strike Opens in new window ]
While some increase was certainly required in light of the rising population, questions have to be asked about the sustainability of the expansion. This is particularly so given that many civil servants now work from home and rarely appear in their offices.
On the issue of pay, it is perfectly reasonable for the unions to seek increases that match inflation, but it is also reasonable for the Government to try to hold the line against excessive demands that are not accompanied by changes in work practices, including a return to the office where needed.
Given the way the unions have begun staging one-day national strikes before talks have even begun, strong nerves will be needed on the Government side to resist pressure for a deal that could blow up national finances yet again when the next downturn strikes.

title: Manchester City finding motivation from their years of systemic cheating
description: Ludicrously, City continue to play matches, and the narrative now taking hold around them is one of defiance against the ‘noise’
content:
In the Premier League , it appears that euphemism is the new hype.
Sky interviewer Patrick Davidson plumped a few verbal cushions in his interviews with Manchester City players and coach Enzo Maresca after the 3-0 win over Liverpool , asking the players how they played in “very difficult circumstances” while referencing the “off-field situation” when speaking with Maresca.
“The Situation”, “The Circumstances” ... this is a jarring bit of restraint from a broadcaster who will sell you, with a straight face, Hull v Sunderland as the stuff of a Super Sunday.
In fairness, Davidson and every other Premier League broadcaster is in a deeply invidious position at the moment, forced as they are to continue covering Manchester City matches in this limbo between guilty verdict and sentencing.
Davidson’s job is to question managers and players and elicit answers to feed the talking points and narrative that sells games, and he is terrific at it. But this is not a normal situation, and City are using their pre-appeal and pre-sentencing pulpit to downplay their transgressions. The club set this tone from the moment the commission’s verdict was published by the Premier League, referring to it in a statement as an “opinion”.
It wasn’t a mere opinion. It was the verdict of an independent commission published 22 months after a 42-day hearing, the transcripts of which run to around 7,000 pages.
The party line among players and coaching staff has been, meanwhile, to dismiss the club’s cheating as “noise”.
Here, for example, is Enzo Maresca to Sky after the Liverpool win: “We need to learn how to deal with the noise because the noise will be with us. In all the away games, there will be noise for the situation, we know. And we need to make our noise, and our noise is to win games ... at the end of the game [it] was just our fans and our noise, and not different noise.”
Maresca is entitled to speak how he likes, but here’s an accurate, alternate version of his comments: “We need to learn how to deal with the consequences of our club’s cheating, because the consequences of our club’s cheating will be with us. In all the away games, we know there will be consequences of our club’s cheating; we know. And we need to make our noise, and our noise is to win games ... at the end of the game it was just our fans and our noise, and not the consequences of our club’s cheating.”
Maresca has already allowed the mask to slip on this act to some extent, saying on Tuesday: “If I am an Arsenal fan or a United fan and you are a City fan, I can tell you: ‘Hey, my friend, you cheat.’”
[ Enzo Maresca says he would describe Manchester City as ‘cheats’ if he was a United fan Opens in new window ]
But City’s cheating is not a matter of differing partisan perspectives: it’s a fact established by the independent commission.
While City are motivated to polish the truth, nobody else has to join with them in doing so. The club continue to insist upon their innocence and have lodged their appeal, but the fact of the appeal does not make invalid or provisional the verdict of the independent commission. They were innocent until found guilty, and now they have been found guilty. They will remain so unless an appeal tells us otherwise in the future.
The process of the appeal should be respected, but the findings of the verdict should not be ignored, as Micah Richards did on Sky last Sunday when he said “if Manchester City are found guilty”.
Jamie Carragher righted him on things: “They’re guilty now. Right now, they’re guilty.”
It’s important to repeat the plain truth that Manchester City have been found to have systematically cheated financial rules by which their rivals have played, because it is important to be continually outraged by cheating. It’s not pearl-clutching to say everyone in sport must play by the same set of agreed rules, because sport ceases to have any purpose whatsoever if someone refuses to do so. Whataboutery as to the fairness of the financial rules City broke is exactly that: the only relevant detail here is City signed up to the rules and then stomped all over them.
Gary Neville has said he is uncomfortable with using the word “cheats” and chafed at Liverpool fans’ chanting the word at City players in the closing stages of Sunday’s game, saying it is the worst thing a player can be called. Yes, it may be unfair on the City players to be tainted by their employers’ cheating, but here’s the thing about cheating: it isn’t fair on anybody.
Ludicrously, City continue to play matches, and the narrative now taking hold around them is one of defiance against the “noise”. City fans gloried in it all at Anfield, and the atmosphere at the midweek Champions League game against PSG was crackling as fans held up a tifo reading City Til I Die.
[ Roy Keane and Jamie Carragher unmoved by ‘devastated’ Micah Richards on Sky Sports Opens in new window ]
Pep Guardiola , embarrassingly, made a point of showing up in wrong-headed solidarity. The City players have spoken all week about sticking together, and Davidson lamentably asked Maresca on Sunday about a “siege mentality”, and whether all of this could make City stronger.
Speaking in euphemism allows this storyline to develop, as if the players were reacting to some quotidian setback like a manager’s sacking. Speaking plainly acknowledges this for what it is: Manchester City finding motivation from their own systemic, years-long cheating. Think of it like that, and you’ll quickly realise it’s time to find something else to watch.

title: Craig Casey aiming to maximise Páirc Uí Chaoimh factor on emotional night for Munster
description: Scrumhalf admits he doesn’t know how occasion will affect him but is focused on delivering a performance to honour Anthony Foley
content:
For a Shannon man like Craig Casey , this is a particularly poignant week. He’s unsure how he will respond emotionally when the tributes are paid to Anthony Foley in Saturday’s Champions Cup clash with Racing 92 at Páirc Uí Chaoimh (kick-off 8pm).
Today marks the 10th anniversary of Foley’s passing in a Paris hotel on the morning of a scheduled match with Racing. Casey was in his final year in Ardscoil Rís and he points out that many of the current squad would not have been coached by Foley, much less played with him.
“It’s probably strange for a lot of lads because with how young the group is, they probably wouldn’t have even been coached or been in Munster at the same time, even in underage groups,” he says.
“I’ll probably be emotional enough, to be honest. I was only in sixth year when he died and I remember being over in the East Terrace when the Stand Up and Fight stuff was on, and that was an emotional day,” recalls Casey of the 38-17 win over Glasgow the day after Foley’s funeral, when the squad sang their dressingroom anthem on the Thomond Park pitch.
“I’d say it’s tough not to get ahead of yourself emotion-wise early on in the week, because it is such a big week. But you have to hold yourself back on that, know that it probably will take you some place. On Saturday night, when there’s a tribute going on, it could take you anywhere. It’s just being ready for that.
“But I think the only way we can really honour him is with a good performance and a win, to be honest. We’ve got to stay on track with that but enjoy it as well. He’s a figure that everyone loved in Munster rugby, and he, Paulie (O’Connell) and Pete (O’Mahony) are probably the three that everyone thinks of as great leaders for Munster and Munster men.
“It’s going to be tough, but I think we have to enjoy the week and bring it to where he deserves, because he does deserve a mighty performance from us. So, we’ve got to concentrate on that first. But hopefully we do bring it.”
Arguably, Thomond Park would have been a more suitable venue than Páirc Uí Chaoimh to mark the anniversary. For the players, though – and even a Limerickman like Casey – playing in Cork ’s GAA stadium is a genuine treat.
“I think GAA stadiums are always cool to play in,” he says. “I’ve really enjoyed going down there the last few times. I only played there once and I thought it was a cool experience to play there. Even when you’re playing in Croke Park , it’s a huge honour to have a game of that magnitude in a GAA stadium.
“Obviously, we love playing in Thomond Park. I don’t think I’ll ever get away from that. That’s our home ground and we love coming here, every chance we get. But I think the Cork lads will tell you how much it means to them and you get some buzz off that.
“I was only down there for a Limerick-Cork game a few months ago and we (Limerick) got absolutely battered – and I was getting abused from all ends. But it will be cool to be on the other side of it and have support down here.”
Casey speaks enthusiastically about the fresh thinking brought to the team by a revamped coaching ticket. He is a nephew of Mossy Lawler, who coached him all through his formative years, including through Ardscoil Rís, which culminated in a Munster Senior Cup semi-final in his final year there. He says his uncle has “been a bundle of energy” with his enhanced role as joint attack coach with Jared Payne.
Much the same could be said of Casey himself, who at 27 has morphed into one of the team’s key leaders.
“I’m really liking it. Throughout the years in underage you’re in leadership groups and I’ve been in the leadership group here for probably seven years. It’s not something new, but I suppose over the last few years there’s been a good few people that have left the building and you really feel like you need to step up.”
Whether in Limerick or Cork, Munster need to start making their homes into fortresses again, as there have been costly slip-ups in Thomond Park in three of the last four seasons, such as the 31-29 defeat by Castres last January that brought their Champions Cup hopes to an end.
“That Castres game was probably still living in a lot of our heads,” he says of the subsequent Challenge Cup exit away to Exeter . “But we let it get to that stage as well. We probably need to have it done by then. If you look at all the other teams that went on to semi-finals and finals, and quarter-finals even, they’ve all that wrapped up before the last game.
“We’ve definitely made a point of making home a hard place to come again because a few times we’ve been scalped at home and that’s never nice.
“You’ve got to play well at home. I think it all comes down to your home games. If you can play well at home and then pick up a good few away wins along the road, you’re setting yourself up well for a good season.
“We’ve talked about it in the preseason, but you wouldn’t really be talking too much about it in the week of a game. I think it’s just about delivering a performance. You can’t really dive too deep into playing at home or where we are. But during the off-season we would have talked about it, yeah.”

title: Memory lane reminds Leo Cullen of the challenge awaiting Leinster at Clermont
description: Province gets Champions Cup campaign under way in France on Saturday
content:
Leo Cullen has participated in all 10 European matches between Leinster and Clermont Auvergne – first as a player, then as head coach. A remarkable statistic.
His involvement dates back to Leinster’s first away win on French soil in what was then the European Cup 24 years ago, a 23-20 succession against Montferrand, a former iteration of the Clermont club before a name change in 2004.
Matt Williams was Leinster head coach, Denis Hickie and Gordon D’Arcy scored tries, and scrumhalf Brian O’Meara kicked 13 points. The night before the game, former Kilkenny hurler DJ Carey gave a little spiel before presenting the jerseys to the team, having travelled at Williams’ behest.
Plucking another encounter from the memory bank, Cullen recalled “an unbelievable epic battle” in the 2012 Heineken Cup semi-final.
“Wesley Fofana [Clermont centre] dropped the ball over the line at the end, and we all thought he’d scored. And then the [replay] came up on the TV and we thought, ‘Bloody hell,’ because it goes from you thought you’d lost the game to, ‘okay we still have a chance now, let’s deal with the exit.’”
After giving away a free at a scrum, Leinster were left “scrambling around our own try line at the end,” said Cullen, but they held out for a 19-15 win.
Also among the “seriously tough battles” between the sides, he pointed to the Champions Cup semi-final in 2017. On that occasion, Leinster lost 27-22 in Lyons, where this season’s Champions Cup decider will be played.
“It’s a great rivalry, great fans. I think about that semi-final in Lyons, just how yellow the ground was on the way in. And even coming out afterwards, there was a respectful arrival, no animosity there.”
Cullen said there has always been a rapport and respect between the two sets of supporters, adding the clubs share a history. Joe Schmidt was an assistant coach at Clermont when they came up against Leinster in Europe prior to him becoming head coach of the province, while players like Nathan Hines and, more recently, Rabah Slimani have donned both jerseys.
Cullen also recalled Clermont beating Leinster over successive weekends in the pool stages in December 2012, first at the Stade Marcel Michelin and then the Aviva Stadium. The results forced the province into the Challenge Cup, which they subsequently went on to win.
There are a few alterations to the rules governing this season’s Champions Cup, including a change to the try-scoring bonus point. Teams now must score at least three tries more than their opponents in order to earn an attacking bonus point, whereas they could previously pick up an extra point by scoring four tries, irrespective of the end result.
The rule has been in place in other tournaments for some time, including the Top 14. Asked about its potential impact on the Champions Cup, Cullen said: “It’s a good question, but there’s definitely a lot more jeopardy for longer in games where the bonus-point structure has come in.
“Watching Top 14 games, it is a more exciting last 10 or 15 minutes because some games can fizzle out. When a team has scored four tries and the other has scored one, it can fizzle out, and a team might come back and score a couple of tries and there’s no actual consequence from it.
“A team that is trying to stay three or four tries in front, you’re encouraged to keep playing and the game continues with much greater competitiveness to the end.
“If it totally blows out, it’ll totally blow out but generally speaking it’s a better system for the fan. This is the first time we’ll be experiencing it but it’s a good little tweak.”
While it may not dissuade clubs from fielding weaker teams, it’s a positive move. “It creates more competition for longer in a game,” Cullen added. “Scoring four tries, you go into cruise control and get the job done.
“You see less games like that in the Top 14, with the way the bonus-point system works, so we’ll see how it plays out in the Champions Cup.”
The Leinster, Munster and Connacht teams for their respective Champions Cup clashes against Clermont, Racing 92 and Saracens will be announced at midday on Friday, as will Ulster’s side for their Challenge Cup opener against Zebre.

title: House prices: Who is getting it right, the CSO, MyHome or Daft?
description: Sometimes they say the same thing, at other times they differ
content:
I n the lead-up to the property crash of 2008 there was – let’s just say – unease about the number of estate agencies publishing what you might call self-interested house-price surveys.
Critics said their reports, and some of the commentary that went with them, were deliberately amplifying positive trends to encourage transactions.
When things began to sour, the “endless growth” narrative around Irish property gave way to the soft-landing narrative: “Okay, things have got a little frothy, there will be a modest correction, but the market is still structurally sound.”
When that thesis collapsed, and Ireland suffered the biggest peak-to-trough property crash of any country, property-price surveys (industry ones) were blamed for exacerbating the problem.
The task of producing an accurate data series on property price trends was given to the Central Statistics Office (CSO). In 2011 the agency began producing the Residential Property Price Index (RPPI), which remains the State’s official indicator of price trends.
A decade and a half later the industry barometers have crept back into the mix, led by the State’s two main property portals: MyHome and Daft . (MyHome is owned by The Irish Times Group).
While both companies’ quarterly reports are viewed as highly credible, they contain structural biases. Foremost, they base their quarterly surveys on asking prices rather than sold prices. In a sellers’ market, where buyers can get into bidding wars, these metrics can underestimate prices. The reverse is true when the market turns.
“From 2024 through to the spring of this year, transaction prices rose faster than list prices, and buyers typically paid well over the list price,” author of the Daft report Ronan Lyons said in the company’s latest survey.
[ Irish house prices are simply too high, and potential buyers have hit a price ceiling Opens in new window ]
“That has now reversed. Nationally, list prices are rising over two percentage points faster than transaction prices, the widest gap since 2023,” he said.
While Daft commands a larger market share of listings nationally, Daft and MyHome are said to be neck and neck (in terms of the listings market) in Dublin and Leinster, with most listings on both portals coming from estate agents.
[ Are we turning a corner on housing? Opens in new window ]
There are also quarterly surveys from Sherry Fitzgerald, Douglas Newman Good (DNG) and the Real Estate Alliance (REA), which use different methodologies.
At the moment they all tell the same story: house prices are still rising but at a slower pace than before because of a combination of affordability pressures linked to higher inflation, higher borrowing costs, enhanced supply and the uncertain economic outlook.
Further interest rate hikes and no resolution to the Iran crisis are likely to accelerate this trend.
Daft’s snapshot of the market in the third quarter put headline annualised inflation (for asking prices) at 3 per cent, half the level that it was a year ago. In Dublin the rate of price growth was estimated at 2.7 per cent.
MyHome’s equivalent report, published on Tuesday this week, put asking price inflation at 3.9 per cent and at 2.1 per cent in Dublin.
The CSO’s official numbers, also published on Tuesday, put inflation (for prices paid) at 5.1 per cent in August and at 3.9 per cent in Dublin.
The CSO’s numbers are based on stamp duty data from Revenue and reflect transactions that took place at least two months ago, so there’s a lag. Because they are based on asking prices, the MyHome and Daft reports provide more of an instant snapshot of which way the market is turning.
The CSO estimates the average price paid for a property nationally in the 12 months to August was €442,512, while in Dublin it was €598,677.
For MyHome, the average price nationally was €461,084 and €585,132 in Dublin. For Daft, the figures were €445,000 and €635,000.
The CSO and MyHome use median (middle value) prices in their reports instead of average prices.
With any property price survey, there is a need to distinguish between quality-adjusted price changes [those controlled for location, property type, new versus old homes, etc] and pure price inflation.
The CSO breaks its figures down by Eircode, which reveals significant price disparities not just between Dublin and the rest of the State but also within the capital itself.
Take, for example, the difference between Dublin 6, which covers Ranelagh and Rathgar, where the average price paid for properties last year was just shy of €1 million (€995,709), making it the most expensive Eircode in the State, and Dublin 10, which includes Ballyfermot and Cherry Orchard, where the average price was €333,391.
[ Irish house price inflation slows as affordability constraints bite Opens in new window ]
According to MyHome, house prices in Tuam in Galway have risen by 10.2 per cent in 2026 while prices in Kilkee in Clare have slumped by almost 13 per cent.
So while the CSO, MyHome and Daft capture the general direction of travel, they can differ significantly because of the disparity between asking prices and actual sale prices.
Put another way, MyHome and Daft measure what sellers want; the CSO measures what buyers actually pay.

title: Ministers and TDs afraid to pass a picket line
description: Why is the Dáil essentially at the behest of unelected trade union bosses?
content:
Sir, – Between June 1922 and May 1923, when this country was enduring a Civil War , Dáil Éireann convened on a total of 97 separate sitting days, passing 25 pieces of legislation.
These sittings took place despite the fact that ministers and many TDs were living under threat of assassination from terrorist insurgents who were, at that time, attempting to overthrow the democratic will of the people as expressed at the general election in June 1922.
What would those men think of our current crop of Ministers and TDs, both Government and Opposition, who decided to shutter the Dáil on Wednesday of this week for fear of having to pass a picket?
It is a mark of the sheer irrelevance of the Dáil to policymaking over the last decade that this decision could be agreed on by Government and Opposition alike, without a single dissenting voice.
It is an affront to democracy that our elected national parliament was shuttered for a day, essentially at the behest of unelected trade union bosses. – Yours, etc,

title: Depressing move on local property tax in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown
description: Can nobody in Government see what is wrong with this?
content:
Sir, – Your story on the decision of councillors in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown to reduce the local property tax (LPT) by 15 per cent must surely bring some scrutiny to the manner in which the Government strains every sinew to provide opportunities for those with the most to reduce their tax liabilities (“ No property tax changes for Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown and Fingal homeowners ”, News, October 12th).
Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown has some of the wealthiest households in the State, with an average income of €85,000, and will have the LPT levied with a reduction of 15 per cent on the base rate. Sligo has among the lower incomes in the State, yet citizens here will face a 25 per cent increase on the base rate.
A tax is being levied at a significantly higher rate on the least well-off. Can nobody in Government see anything wrong with this state of affairs? – Yours, etc,
Sir, – How depressing to read Fine Gael councillor Eoin O’Driscoll’s defence of keeping local property taxes artificially low ( Letters , October 15th). Local government in Ireland is chronically underfunded, our property taxes are low by European standards and we continue to narrow our tax base while relying on corporation tax revenues that could disappear as quickly as they arrived.
At least O’Driscoll’s letter reminds us that Labour, the Social Democrats and the Greens understand the need for a sustainable tax base to fund those services. – Yours, etc,

title: ‘I am having a moment’: Artists welcome new Dublin affordable studios
description: Artist studios
content:
“It is a good time for me,” says Dublin -based photographer and visual artist Conor Horgan. “I am having a moment, as they say”.
Horgan is standing in his new studio overlooking Dublin’s O’Connell Street, which is one of 22 affordable workspaces for practising visual artists launched by the Lord Mayor of Dublin Daryl Barron on Thursday.
The mayor is there because Dublin City Council’s arts office is subsiding rent on the studios. In Horgan’s studio, he admires a close-up photograph featuring vivid pink oyster mushrooms, part of a series titled Disco Vegetables, before he and Horgan move to the large, sash windows overlooking O’Connell Street Lower. “I’ll be selling premium tickets for the [St Patrick’s Day] parade”, Horgan jokes, while the mayor asks about the oriental plane trees lining the street.
In a nearby studio with tall windows also overlooking the streets below, Jen Donnery, who sculpts and draws, stands by two larger-than-life drawings on the wall. “I make large work”, she says, adding the studio is most welcome as she has previously been working in “small, spare rooms”.
Margaret Farrell, who gave up teaching 10 years ago to become a full-time artist, says she is delighted to have a studio to showcase her work – which is inspired by her experiences as an outdoor enthusiast and hillwalker.
[ Inside the Dublin City Arts Office: ‘We meet property developers all the time now’ Opens in new window ]
The collection of 22 studios in Manfield Chambers, on the corner of O’Connell Street Lower and Middle Abbey Street, is a joint project put together by Dublin City Council’s arts office, Visual Artists Ireland and backers Quanta Capital.
The initiative was developed in response to the growing shortage of affordable studio space available to artists, particularly in Dublin.
Dublin City Council contributed €294,000 and sees the venture as a pilot project, one that may help revitalise O’Connell Street and that could be replicated elsewhere. Some €150,000 of the money was invested in refurbishing the building, while the remainder provides revenue support to subsidise studio rents and help keep the workspaces affordable for artists.
Quanta Capital has invested €3 million in restoring the heritage building, while Visual Artists Ireland will manage the programme and support the participating artists.
Visual Artists Ireland chief executive Noel Kelly said the new studios provided additional creative space in the city, particularly since the closure of The Complex, a venue that housed 17 artist studios in the inner city but closed permanently in January after its lease expired.
[ The Complex arts centre to close after final meeting proves unsuccessful in finding solution Opens in new window ]
“O’Connell Street is Dublin’s main street and it should reflect the full diversity of life in our city,” the mayor said. “Having artists working and creating here brings a new energy to the area and strengthens its role as a place for people, culture and community.”

title: Justine McCarthy: For survivors, failed George Gibney investigations were ‘nearly worse than the abuse’
description: As the survivors try to pick up the pieces of their lives, the justice system that betrayed them should not be let off the hook
content:
O ne of the mitigating factors the judge considered in deciding how long George Gibney must spend in jail was that, as he put it, “there is no evidence of subsequent offending” after the 1980s. It was a macabre source of relief that the teenager the former national swim coach raped in Florida in 1991 was unable to be present in the courtroom to hear that. She has been in institutional psychiatric care for most of the years since gardaí informed her in 2002 that the DPP had instructed them not to charge Gibney for what he did to her, resulting in her pregnancy. She had been bracing herself to testify against him face-to-face in court. After the two gardaí left her home that night, she tried to kill herself.
In passing the 15½-year sentence on Monday, Judge Mícheál P O’Higgins was legally bound to deal only with the evidence adduced in the case of four women abused in the 1970s and 1980s and whose testimonies finally secured Gibney ’s conviction nearly 60 years after his first known crimes against children. Gibney’s 1991 rape of the teenage swimmer in Florida was not part of that evidence.
Another mitigating factor the judge cited was that Gibney had “no previous convictions”. That certainly was not for want of his victims’ perseverance in pursuit of justice over 25 years.
Lorraine Kennedy was not in the courtroom either. Her daughter, Louise, attended with a photograph of her remarkable mother who died seven years ago. Lorraine was one of Gibney’s earliest victims. She was a little girl when she joined the Guinness swimming pool in Watling Street. The first time Gibney knelt in front of her and put his fingers inside her was in 1966. Lorraine was unaware the coach was also assaulting her brother Francis, better known as Chalkie White, since he was 11, the year he became the youngest person to win the Liffey Swim.
The siblings were among the complainants in Gibney’s first prosecution on 27 counts of indecent assault and unlawful carnal knowledge. It collapsed in 1994. The paedophile fled the country the day before the High Court stopped the case. Sitting side-by-side in courtroom nine on Monday were Ber Carley and Tric Kearney, who were also part of that abandoned prosecution. In her book, Above Water: A Survivor’s Story, Kearney writes of her “despair forever believing we might find justice” on learning the prosecution had collapsed.
Carolyn Brown was in the courtroom on Monday, too. When the judge said Gibney had no previous convictions, the dejection in her face told yet another chapter in the State’s decades-long failure to deliver justice for the children assaulted and raped by the prematurely frail-looking 78-year-old with his legs casually crossed in his prison-issue wheelchair.
[ ‘He needs to die in prison’: Survivor of George Gibney child sex abuse reacts to sentencing Opens in new window ]
Carolyn was 13 when she started swimming at Newpark Sports Complex where Gibney reigned. He targeted her straight away. The abuse only stopped when, aged 15, she dropped out of school to her parents’ bewilderment and has never returned to education since. In 1998, she made a statement about Gibney to gardaí. They brought her back to her old school at Newpark to show them the office he used to lock her into, alone and scared.
“About six months later, I got a phone call from a garda saying the DPP had decided not to go ahead with my case,” Carolyn told me on Monday. “I was shocked. I thought maybe what he did to me was nothing, after all. That there was nothing wrong with what he did to me. There was a huge sense of not being believed.”
Her case was the third Garda investigation into Gibney’s lifelong spree of child sexual abuse. The 1993 prosecution failed when his lawyers obtained a Supreme Court order for a judicial review and, on foot of it, the High Court ruled that he could not adequately defend himself because some of the crimes were long ago and not specifically dated. The DPP did not appeal against the decision.
The second investigation involved four more of Gibney’s former swimmers, including the teenager he raped in 1991. By then, he was at large in the US and the DPP opted not to apply for his extradition. That same year, 2003, the State successfully sought the extradition from the US of celebrity chef Conrad Gallagher for allegedly stealing paintings from a Dublin hotel. He was returned to Ireland and acquitted.
“If you can extradite Conrad Gallagher for three paintings, why can’t you extradite George Gibney for seven rapes?” wrote Bart Nolan to then Minister for Justice, Michael McDowell. Nolan picketed the national swim association’s AGM year after year in his campaign to get justice for Gibney’s victims. He died before it was delivered.
The fourth Garda investigation began in March 2015. Persistent Dáil questioning by Maureen O’Sullivan, then an independent TD for Dublin Central, culminated in the appointment of a garda detective superintendent to re-examine the 1993 case and any other subsequent and new complaints about Gibney. It petered out without a result. A State report by Judge Roderick Murphy neither named nor blamed anybody.
The fifth investigation started when four more ex-swimmers came forward after listening to the 2020 podcast, Where is George Gibney? by Mark Horgan and Ciarán Cassidy. The testimonies of these women produced the golden key to lock up the former Olympic coach at last.
There has been talk of closure for his victims and whatever consolation Gibney’s belated jailing brings them is to be celebrated. But there should be no closure for the State and its decades-long failure to bring to justice one of the country’s most notorious criminals. Individual gardaí and lawyers have shown commitment and determination down through those years, but their efforts were repeatedly scuppered by the system.
While the survivors try to pick up the pieces of their lives now, the justice system that betrayed them should not be let off the hook.
“The thing about the abuse is that it destroys your trust in anybody, so all those failed investigations were nearly worse than the abuse itself,” Carolyn Brown told me outside the courthouse. “You’ve had to trust again – to put your trust in the system – and then the system lets you down.”

title: Simone Gannon: Six good beauty buys under €25
description: From a €10 eye cream to a revamped foundation, these are the new affordable beauty products to know about
content:
T here has never been a better time for budget beauty . Some of the best formulations I’ve tried in recent years have also been among the most affordable, and I love nothing more than discovering an excellent product that doesn’t cost a small fortune.
These are the latest budget beauty launches that have caught my eye. Each one is €25 or (significantly) less.
First up is one of our own. Hildun Beauty has launched its first mascara and, according to founder Suzy Griffin Dunne, it’s been several years in the making because she wanted to get it exactly right.
Available in two shades, Noir, an intense black, and Pecan, a rich brown. Power Precision Peptide Mascara (€25 from hildunbeauty.com) has a unique curved wand that grabs every single lash from the root – no clumping or flaking in sight. It’s also formulated with peptides to strengthen and condition the lashes and, importantly for me, comes off easily with warm water.
I’ve always had time for Rimmel foundations and remember using them fondly when I was younger. For me, they struck that perfect balance between affordability and a genuinely good formulation.
Match Perfection Foundation (€13.49 from Boots) has been around for a while and it’s a goody, but now it’s even better. The brand has just launched a new and improved version with an expanded shade range, aloe vera to help hydrate and soothe the skin, and SPF20 – all while delivering lightweight medium coverage and a softly blurred finish. It’s still very much a budget buy, too.
PDRN (a DNA-derived ingredient extracted from salmon sperm) has been absolutely everywhere in skincare recently. But The Ordinary being The Ordinary, it has managed to bring this much-discussed ingredient into the budget category, albeit by using a vegan alternative.
Its new Lacto-PDRN 4% + B9 Lifting and Tightening Eye Cream (€10.20 from Space NK) is designed to target firmness and dehydration and help improve the appearance of fine lines around the eye area. It’s a pleasure to use too.
Rhode Pocket Blush has been a bestseller since it launched a couple of years ago, and now the brand has shrunk it and added shimmer in collaboration with Alexandra Leclerc.
Pocket Pearl (€21 from rhodeskin.com) comes in three miniature, metallic shades: Gemini, a shimmery baby pink; Monaco, a rich shimmery terracotta; and Monet, a caramel-hued shimmery apricot. They’re extremely cute, and at €21 each I can see them disappearing into handbags everywhere.
Yet another considered launch from home-grown brand Kash Beauty. A collection of four new eyeshadow palettes with shades you’ll actually use. There’s Baked Basics, Pearl Veil, Golden Heat and Moon Dusk, with a mix of rich mattes and shimmers in each.
As ever, the colour payoff is excellent, the shades are creamy, beautifully pigmented, easy to blend and long wearing. And at €22 a palette, they’re an absolute bargain.
An arguably obvious next step for LanaiBlo, known for its phenomenal professional-level hairdryers, was to launch its own range of styling brushes – and it has done exactly that.
The Professional Hairbrush Collection (from €22.99 from lanaiblo.com) encompasses three styling brushes – small, medium and large – each with a flexible shape and ceramic-coated barrel to give you control, versatility and even heat distribution – helping you achieve the style you want and hold it in place for longer. Better yet, each one is priced between €23 and €25.
Straightforward, no-nonsense advice and tips from one of the most straight-talking skin experts in the industry, Flawless by Dr Sam Bunting (€26 from Amazon) is, as she says herself, “not a book about doing more. It’s a book about doing the right things”.
That means the right ingredients, the right concentrations and, most importantly, how to figure out exactly what your skin needs and build an individual routine around it.

title: After my friend lost his job, he asked AI what came next
description: The fortunes of a laid-off worker reveal how artificial intelligence is becoming the latest vessel for some of China’s oldest beliefs
content:
W hen my friend Wei suggested meeting for dinner, I was expecting an update about the woman he started dating a few months ago, the latest in what had until now been a succession of hopeless cases. But as soon as he arrived it was clear he had something else on his mind.
“I’ve decided to get a new job,” he said.
He was thinking of something that might involve travel, maybe even international travel and more use of his language skills, possibly with a foreign company. I asked him when he had decided to leave his current job at a video games company.
The last time I had seen Wei, he was worried about losing his job, telling me at nearly 40 he didn’t think he would find another one. Now the company had consolidated some of its operations and he was going to spend the next few weeks training someone else to do his work before being laid off.
“If I seem upbeat about it, it’s maybe because I got AI to tell my fortune,” he said.
He didn’t seem at all upbeat and it turned out that although he used Kimi, one of China’s new, blockbuster AI platforms, the fortunetelling was of the most ancient, traditional variety. He asked Kimi to calculate his Ba Zi (literally, eight characters) horoscope, which has been used since the Tang Dynasty in the 7 th century but has its roots a thousand years earlier.
The system is based on the year, month, day and hour of your birth, which form four pillars, each of which produces two Chinese characters. The first is one of 10 characters linked to yin or yang and one of the five elements (wood, fire, earth, metal and water) and the second is also tied to the five elements and to one of the 12 signs of the Chinese zodiac.
[ What a Chinese blockbuster says about Beijing’s view of the world Opens in new window ]
Wei told me to open Kimi on my phone and to ask it for my Ba Zi, which also required the precise location of my birth and my gender. Within a few seconds, it produced eight characters and a detailed explanation, much of which was too esoteric for me but made perfect sense to him.
Then he suggested that I ask it questions, not about my future but about my past and present, which might be easier to verify. We started by asking if travel featured in my life and Kimi told me according to my Ba Zi, I would spend most of my life outside the country of my birth and would live in a number of places.
Wei suggested I ask if I was likely to meet famous or important people and the answer was that I would probably do so but that they would not necessarily be my friends. I was more likely to come into contact with them in an impersonal way, what the horoscope described as sudden, situational encounters.
All of this reflected the life of a foreign correspondent and as we went deeper, the answers seemed uncannily accurate and the analysis of each decade of life rang true. Better still, when I asked about the future, the prognosis was brilliantly optimistic.
When we looked at Wei’s Ba Zi, the picture was bleaker both personally and professionally so it was difficult to see why it should have cheered him up. Then it occurred to me that its main function was to distract him from the news he was dealing with.
He had been laid off a few years ago from a different job and it was a few months before he found a new one, so he said he felt better prepared psychologically this time. But he thought being unemployed might mean the end of his budding courtship, not least because the date had been set up by their families and he feared his prospects were an important part of his appeal.
