[ A police raid on a gay bar, in Asia’s most liberal jurisdiction Opens in new window ]
After he left, I sent him a rather feeble message wishing him luck and offering to ask around about jobs if he told me what he was looking for. He replied right away.
“Kimi told me not to appear as someone eagerly looking for a job but as an experienced professional looking for bigger opportunities,” he said.

title: Séamas O'Reilly: ‘It’s not as scary as you think,’ I tell friends expecting their first child. I’m lying
description: When my kids were babies and we were sleep deprived and generally petrified, I presumed they were in mortal danger at all times
content:
I am staring at a note on my phone. It’s from two years ago, and it’s reminding me just how fearful I was as a new parent . It was typed during one of my daughter’s interminable sleep interruptions, the ones that proliferated in her first three years of life and often left me sitting, bleary-eyed, in her bedroom, trying to rock her back to sleep.
The note is headed “WHY did she say this?” and it prefaces a direct quote from her, after she noticed that her bedroom had no echo, even though the hallway off it did. Before I could attempt a remedial explanation of acoustic physics, she looked at me in the near-perfect dark of a 3am bedroom and uttered the very words I’m reading now: “Maybe there are people who are invisible and can’t hear us, who live in echoes all day long.” Within seconds of saying this she was asleep, leaving me bolt-upright and terrified in a room of silence and shadows, sweat beading from the base of my neck.
I’ve been thinking a lot about the fear and parenting recently, because several close friends are awaiting their first baby, and my advice to them is always: “It’s not as scary as you think.” “You’ll be fine,” I say. But, if I’m honest, being scared stupid is a big part of it.
Reading my notes from this time – in an app I used a lot then but don’t now, for reasons that will soon become clear – reminds me of the first branch of terror: I presumed my children were in mortal danger at all times. I find increasingly unhinged checklists of things to babyproof, from skirting boards and sharp surfaces to the ubiquitous clumps of small objects that tend to accrete on counters and low tables anywhere I’ve ever lived.
Back then, I’d routinely have intrusive thoughts about a button lodging in their throat, a pen jamming in their eyeball. Soon, a vicious cycle asserted itself in which the understandable terrors of parenting were amplified by lack of sleep, which itself made me so muddle-headed and clumsy that feeding a child small, sharp objects seemed all the more possible.
There’s also the fact that my brain was falling apart. I would routinely forget the names and faces of people I’d just recently met. While writing, I’d take many minutes to recall a commonplace word and lose it again if I didn’t immediately jot it down, this since-forgotten notes app becoming just one repository for nuggets I could no longer trust my brain to hold. My motor skills, too, began to flounder, and I became accustomed to tripping on steps and kerbs in public, or watching as any cup or glass I held tumbled helplessly to the floor.
Never one to remain calm and rational about such things, I immediately decided I was in the clutches of a rare and terrifying cognitive disease. It was my wife who suggested that, maybe just maybe, the reason these things were happening was that we were subsisting on almost no sleep, on account of our kids’ nightly schedule. (It should be noted that, despite experiencing less sleep than me in this period, she did not see the need to concoct a brain disease for herself). Soon, she assured me, I’d be fine. “You’ll forget all about this,” she said.
“Yeah,” I said, “that’s what I’m scared of.”
Thankfully, once our kids started sleeping, so did we. Symptoms dissipated. Brains healed. And I’d forgotten about this period of my life until this week, when I opened up my notes app to compose a shopping list and scrolled down to find a grisly cache of demented jottings. A lot of them.
[ Séamas O’Reilly: One of those days that makes you realise parenting is properly hard Opens in new window ]
And now the real fear sets in, as I sit reading hundreds of notes I wrote to myself while sitting half-asleep in dark rooms, when my brain was going 90 with a child purring on my chest. Yes, things my kids had said, and items to babyproof, but also – more terrifying still – a forgotten catalogue of ideas I obviously thought were seeds of great genius. Some are passable riddles – “Would Māori funfairs have more face painting or less?” – others appear to be jokes I’d considered vital to record for posterity – “Something about an immortal eye doctor who calls himself an eternal optometrist???” – before forgetting about them until now.
It’s the internal monologue of a stark raving version of myself, warped by brain fog, hidden from waking hours. An invisible person, you might say, someone who no longer lives in echoes all day long.

title: `What I hear from our customers is that they want to be able to figure their way through on immigration’
description: Bank of America  CEO Brian Moynihan recounts 16 years at the helm, in an interview that took place in Dublin before the bank was hit with a $1.2 billion fine for money-laundering failures
content:
T he surge in US government borrowing costs since the Iran war has given investors plenty to worry about. But Brian Moynihan, the second-longest-serving chief of a major US bank, doesn’t seem to be losing sleep over it.
Bank of America’s chief executive of 16 years, who majored in history at Brown University, pulls out his foldable smartphone and brings up a chart tracking the market interest rate – or yield – on 10-year US Treasury bonds back to 1800.
One of the most important numbers in finance, the yield has climbed by more than a third since late February and reached 5.36 per cent last week, its highest level in 24 years. The increase has been heavily influenced by debate over how the US Federal Reserve will set interest rates in the coming years.
While the yield has swung from nearly 16 per cent in the early 1980s as central banks battled a severe inflation crisis, to just 0.5 per cent in March 2020, amid market panic over Covid-19 , it has averaged about 5 per cent over the past 226 years.
“It gives perspective,” said Moynihan in an interview late last week in Bank of America’s EU banking headquarters in Dublin, adding that his economists were predicting three more Fed rate increases before inflation starts ticking down again in 2028.
[ Global bond sell-off pushes 10-year Treasury yield to highest since 2002 Opens in new window ]
Perspective, however, appears to be in short supply among investors in US banks. Shares across the sector have fallen sharply from record highs in August, partly because investors are looking beyond the boost to interest income from higher rates and worrying instead about rising funding costs, weaker loan demand and increasing bad debts.
Bank of America’s shares, meanwhile, plunged into bear-market territory on Wednesday – marked by a more than 20 per cent slump from their peak – after it reported a 17 per cent drop in third-quarter profit, just days after the interview, amid news of a $1.2 billion (€1.1 billion) fine over failures to detect potential money laundering and other illicit activity.
[ Bank of America profits drop 17% after $1.2bn money laundering fine Opens in new window ]
But despite the turmoil across US bonds and banking stocks, the broader economic outlook remains relatively robust. The International Monetary Fund forecast this week that US gross domestic product will expand 2.3 per cent both this year and next.
Higher market rates “will slow down activity,” said Moynihan. “Does that mean it’ll slow down real fast? I don’t think so. With that market expectation on rates, they’re still saying the economy grows at 2 per cent-plus in the US, which is above trend.
“The good news is that, underlying that, the US consumer is still spending strongly, despite all the statements saying things are not going well.”
The importance of US consumers cannot be overstated. Accounting for two-thirds of the country’s economy, they are expected to spend about $22 trillion this year. That equates to more than the size of the entire Chinese economy, the second largest in the world.
“It doesn’t mean that the absorption of gas prices isn’t on people’s minds,” said Moynihan (67), a fourth-generation Irish American with a face straight out of the Kennedy family album.
Just ask Donald Trump. Concerned that high fuel prices, driven by the Iran war, could trigger a voter backlash in the upcoming midterm elections on November 3rd, the US president has agreed a controversial deal to allow Russian diesel to reach global markets, expanded access to tax-exempt red-dyed diesel, and pressed European allies to release emergency reserves.
Opinion polls point to Democrats regaining control of the House of Representatives and potentially flipping the Senate. What might such a scenario mean for policy direction?
“When you have a split government, people have to work together,” said Moynihan. “It’s hard to predict, because there are a lot of different voices. But it’s generally a structure which in the past has led to compromises on a few core things. We’ll see what happens.”
[ The US’s financial position is deteriorating rapidly. This is bad news for Ireland Opens in new window ]
Immigration is the most obvious potential area, according to Moynihan. While the Trump administration has advanced key priorities such as tax cuts, deregulation, and the use of tariffs as leverage over trading partners, comprehensive reform of the immigration system has proved more difficult, even if it has increased enforcement.
“What I hear from our clients and customers is that they want to be able to figure their way through on immigration. They want to know what the rules are going to be so that they can adjust their business models,” Moynihan said.
“Construction companies all over the country, farmers and hospitals are saying, ‘I need workers. I used to get them this way, but I’m not getting them through this way. So, how are we going to figure this out’?”
While some argue that natural population growth in the US is the answer, Moynihan said: “It takes 18 years to make an 18-year-old. So, you’re not going to have a change in population in the United States of any consequence. It’s going to be an interesting debate.”
He said there was still “a lot of work to be done” on reaching new trade deals with Canada and Mexico. Relations with both neighbours have become more volatile and strained, with Canadian prime minister Mark Carney, in particular, turning more confrontational over the summer.
Major news outlets from Bloomberg to the Washington Post have reported that US business leaders have, by contrast, been reluctant to criticise Trump publicly during his second presidency, fearing retaliation or risking access to the White House.
The CEO of America’s second-largest bank, with $3.5 trillion of assets, has likewise avoided directly challenging the president. Perhaps his most pointed intervention came in a CBS interview last December, when asked about political interference with the Fed as Trump was openly attacking its rates policy . “The market will punish people if we don’t have an independent Fed,” he warned.” And everybody knows that.”
The cautious approach hasn’t spared Moynihan Trump’s ire – or the occasional cold shoulder.
Three days after his second inauguration in January 2025, Trump used a video address to the World Economic Forum in Davos to scold the Bank of America boss and JP Morgan chief Jamie Dimon over allegations that their banks were denying services to – or “debanking” – conservative customers.
“He was saying that people weren’t banking people because they believe X, Y, or Z. We honestly don’t believe that’s correct,” said Moynihan.
Moynihan was the only CEO of a major Wall Street bank not to be invited to a reception honouring Trump when he attended Davos earlier this year, according to a Financial Times report at the time, months after he was left off the list for a dinner of banking executives at a White House event last November.
Asked how history will judge Trump’s economic legacy, Moynihan was circumspect.
“I think it will take time,” he said, noting that tax cuts for workers and new provisions allowing companies to deduct certain investment costs more quickly have boosted economic activity. But it will take years to determine whether the gains are sustainable, Moynihan added.
[ Bank of America’s Dublin EU hub sees profits dip to $1.76bn in 2024 Opens in new window ]
He was keen to emphasise how his group, whose roots date back to the founding in 1784 of The Massachusetts Bank, has helped administrations through the centuries. “We’re here to serve every administration,” he said.
Yet the new $1.2 billion fine marks a low point in the bank’s relationship with the current one. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said as he announced the penalty.
It has left Moynihan, CEO since 2010, facing fresh scrutiny of the bank’s processes and controls, having spent the early years of his time at the helm resolving legal and regulatory claims stemming from the US housing and mortgages bubble that collapsed in 2007–2008.
Asked by analysts during a conference call on Wednesday about “how it gets to this point” and whether there was a misunderstanding of the rules, he said: “I think at the end of the day, we understand what they need us to do. We’re deep in the process of remediating.”
Moynihan, whose ancestors emigrated from Ireland in the 1850s, was born in Marietta, Ohio, where his father worked as a research chemist with DuPont. The second-youngest of eight siblings, he earned a Bachelor of Arts in 1981 from Brown, where he co-captained the rugby team and met his future wife, classmate Susan Berry.
After securing a law degree from the University of Notre Dame in 1984, he took a position at Rhode Island-based law firm Edwards and Angell. One of his clients was Fleet Financial in Boston, which lured him nine years later to become its deputy general counsel.
Moynihan would wear many hats at the company before and after its 1999 merger with local rival BankBoston. He was managing FleetBoston’s wealth and investment management division when it was taken over in 2004 by Charlotte, North Carolina-based Bank of America.
[ The global economy and the art of living dangerously Opens in new window ]
Bank of America’s then-CEO, Ken Lewis, tapped him to become president of the enlarged group’s wealth management business. He appointed him as the group’s general counsel in December 2008, just before Bank of America completed its rescue takeover – albeit for a price of $50 billion – of Merrill Lynch, one of Wall Street’s most storied names. Less than a month after the deal was sealed, Merrill Lynch’s former CEO John Thain resigned and was replaced by Moynihan as president of global banking, wealth and investment management.
Moynihan – who speaks quietly and sometimes mumbles – was a surprise choice to lead the group in late 2009. The board was known to have been searching for an outside star after Lewis resigned amid a shareholder backlash following the disastrous Merrill deal.
Bank of America chose Dublin as its EU headquarters in 2017 in the wake of the Brexit referendum. The unit has two main divisions: global banking and markets, and support services, which includes a global technology and operations centre.
The US banking giant has had a presence in the Republic since 1968. It has more than 1,000 employees in Dublin and about 400 contractors.
The group opened a new office in Belfast late last year and announced last week that it had hired more than 300 staff there, initially focused on anti-money laundering and financial crime compliance. It has a goal of creating up to 1,000 roles in the North.
“We knew the talent was there. We knew that there was capacity, with office space and other things we could get. And it’s a city that’s continuing to grow,” Moynihan said. “We knew we were going to have to expand this business, because it always grows when the business grows.”
All told, Bank of America has about 210,000 employees across 35 countries – broadly the same headcount as in 2007, even though it took on about 76,000 staff through its 2008 acquisitions of Merrill Lynch and mortgage lender Countrywide Financial.
Moynihan has said that Bank of America’s ongoing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) is focused on getting more out of its workforce rather than cutting jobs. The bank has rolled out around 150 AI use cases across the group so far, with “hundreds” more in the pipeline, he said.
He said there is little room for error when rolling out AI to customers, because trust, security and reliability are fundamental to a banking relationship.
“If we used it to make loans, and it turned somebody down, and they alleged we turned them down because of whatever non-valid credit-based decision ... and the [AI agent] couldn’t explain its work, that’s where the agents are going to be tricky to implement.”
Moynihan declined to be dragged into the AI bubble debate, deferring to research last week from the bank’s market strategists, who noted that a narrow group of AI companies has been driving the Nasdaq 100 Index to all-time highs recently. “Low breadth is a classic feature of bubbles building and typically doesn’t stop until they pop,” they said.
Bank of America’s shares surged more than fourfold between Moynihan taking charge in 2010 and mid-August. Its annual profits grew at a similar pace even as total assets rose by only 60 per cent. The $1.2 billion fine – while embarrassing – equates to about 3.6 per cent of the group’s net income for the 12 months to the end of September, and has only brought the stock back to where it was in late May.
The CEO lives in Wellesley, Massachusetts, an affluent suburb west of Boston, and divides his working time between Boston and the group’s headquarters in Charlotte.
Succession planning moved up a notch 13 months ago when the bank promoted two executives – Dean Athanasia and Jim DeMare – to co-presidents of the entire business, and chief financial officer Alastair Borthwick was given the title of executive vice-president.
But Moynihan was coy when asked how long he planned to stick around.
“I don’t talk about it,” he said. “But I expect to serve as long as the board will have me and I’m having fun.”
Family: Married to Susan Berry, whom he met at college, with three adult children.
Lives: Wellesley, near Boston in Massachusetts.
Something you might expect: He is chancellor of Brown University, where he previously studied.
Something that might surprise: He reportedly likes to amuse himself by slipping obscure, archaic words such as “fantods”, “fructify”, “gainsay”, and “concomitant” into calls with analysts.

title: Johnny Sexton to advise Johnstown Collection on ‘culture’ during €40m investment
description: The former Ireland rugby captain will advise the group’s senior management on ‘team behaviour and culture’ to improve standing with corporate clients
content:
Johnny Sexton has been appointed as an adviser to the Johnstown Collection, the luxury hotel chain behind the Johnstown and Mount Juliet estates, as the group undergoes an investment of almost €40 million across its portfolio.
The former Ireland rugby captain’s role is to advise the group’s senior leadership team with a “focus on team behaviours, culture, accountability and continuous improvement” in order to improve its standing among international organisations and corporate clients, the company said in a statement.
“I’m looking forward to sharing my perspective and my own experiences with the team in all these areas, building on what is already there and, together, achieving new levels of success,” Sexton said. “Not just in Ireland, but on an international level, too.”
He will also work to evolve the sporting and training facilities on offer at the Johnstown Estate in Co Meath through providing an “external perspective and high-performance insight” to operations and management, the company said.
The hotel group, which is owned by Winthrop Technologies founder Barry English, said it was experiencing “significant investment and growth” across its portfolio, with “over €39.5 million invested and planned” to be spent.
Some €26 million of this is earmarked for Johnstown Estate, while €8 million and €5.5 million are designated for Mount Juliet Estate in Co Kilkenny and Trim Castle Hotel in Co Meath, respectively.
The Irish Times understands the investment is primarily to increase capacity and expand facilities across the group’s properties.
Proposed developments include a rooftop thermal suite at Trim Castle Hotel and an additional 90 bedrooms and a new restaurant at Johnstown Estate, designed to expand revenues across the collection’s leisure and corporate markets.
[ Johnny Sexton joins private equity firm Exponent Opens in new window ]
Sean Reid, the Johnstown Collection’s commercial director, said Sexton’s appointment “is about aligning our business with the standards and mindset that define elite performance”.
“In hospitality, the difference is often in the small details, and Johnny’s experience will help us sharpen our focus as we continue to strengthen our offering even further for corporate clients and high-performing organisations,” Reid said.
The group’s general manager, Anthony Smiddy, said: “Johnny brings a unique perspective and wealth of experience that will help us realise the ambition we have for the Johnstown Collection over the coming years.”

title: Why is rude lateness from doctors universally accepted?
description: It seems to be a doctor’s world, and we are consigned to accept such avoidable disrespect
content: Sir, – One would think doctors would be taught how to keep time. In all other professions, meeting patients and clients at an appointed time is seen as a bare minimum and common courtesy. We all understand emergencies happen, and things change at short notice from time to time, but the continuous and seemingly universally accepted rudeness of being consistently late for appointments appears to know no bounds among the medical profession. Such lateness can cause much stress for patients, which is not good for one’s health . Alas, it seems to be a doctor’s world, and we are consigned to accept such avoidable rudeness and disrespect. – Yours, etc,

title: Public service industrial action is largely a charade
description: Private sector should take the day off too
content:
Sir, – So now we have it. Civil servants and public sector workers – ie, the Government – won’t talk to civil servants and public sector workers about a pay deal for themselves. Meanwhile, trade unions, with all sorts of different letter salad names ( Siptu , Fórsa , Unite , etc) are agitating and stoking up their members.
The outcome of this has been a national strike , to be followed by another one on October 21st.
Meanwhile, private sector workers continue to go to work to pay for all of this. After all, we in the private sector are unofficial members of the trade union WPFAOT (we pay for all of this).
Most of the industrial action is a charade. It’s predictable. Moaning and groaning mixed with indignation, exasperation, etc, will ultimately result in talks and a bumper pay deal.
After months of no talks, suddenly talks will be convened and they will go on all through the night or nights. (Why they have to go on “through the night” every time is beyond me.) Then news will break that after “mammoth pay talks” a new pay deal has been agreed. The cost will be at least €2 billion, I believe. Sure, why not and whatever you’re having yourself.
Meanwhile, the private sector will continue to go to work.
But how about if the private sector takes a different approach this time? For the second day of public sector strikes how about if the private sector takes the day off as well? This will make the day a national holiday. We’ll all be happy then (at least for a day). – Yours, etc,

title: ‘The location is brilliant’: Irish National Opera to make former Dublin church its home
description: A €9 million renovation of a former Methodist Church on Abbey Street in Dublin will provide Irish National Opera with its first permanent base
content:
D irections to Irish National Opera lead not to a flamboyant Victorian theatre, nor a purpose-built, acoustically considered, modern opera house, but to a grey door, sandwiched between two branches of a well-known Irish gift shop chain on Dublin’s Dame Street .
No harm to the business in question, but it’s not the most salubrious destination.
“ Dublin is one of the very few capital cities, or even big cities in Europe, that does not have an opera house,” says Diego Fasciati, executive director of Irish National Opera.
From the rented offices above the gift shops, Fasciati and his team plan productions not only in Dublin, but across the State, and internationally.
“In the current season, we have big productions, really large scale – Carmen, Turandot, Eugene Onegin. Then we have a touring production, that will tour all around Ireland, then go to London, that’s a baroque piece. Then we have our contemporary piece, on right now in the theatre festival, then smaller scale touring …” The list goes on.
The office work can, for the most part, be done anywhere, and the productions travelling outside the capital are by their nature mounted in hired venues. What the national opera company really needs, Fasciati says, is a home to rehearse and develop performances.
“Performing arts organisations need rehearsal spaces, and in the case of opera, they tend to have to be quite large because of the amount of people involved,” he says.
“For Carmen, for example, at any one point there’s 60 to 80 people in the room. We also have to find spaces to rehearse the orchestra, and not only does it have to be of a certain size, it has to have a certain acoustic quality. Those are difficult to find in Dublin, because there is a scarcity of infrastructure for the performing arts.
“A few years ago we identified a strategic need of the company to have more permanent rehearsal space, while at the same time, also adding some security to the company by actually owning something.”
At the end of last year, Irish National Opera finally bought its first home, a former Methodist Church that housed the Dublin Central Mission on Lower Abbey Street, just off O’Connell Street and almost diagonally opposite the Abbey Theatre.
This large protected structure – almost 1,000sq m – was built in 1820 and remodelled in 1901 to its current appearance as a four-storey redbrick building, but looks can be deceiving.
“From the outside it looks like four storeys, but it’s really two large double-height spaces. Downstairs was the chapel and upstairs the large assembly hall. It’s great for our needs because it’s two large rooms and it’s in the city centre.”
The chapel, not being large enough for an opera stage, will become the principal orchestra rehearsal area, and potentially recital space for a “small ensemble”, Fasciati says. Upstairs would be the main opera rehearsal space.
[ Tenors, baritones and basses losing their voice at Irish National Opera Opens in new window ]
“We don’t need the two spaces full time, because we don’t rehearse all year round, but a lot of other companies and other arts organisations are interested in using it. The location is just brilliant.”
The opera company bought the church for €2.5 million, less than the €2.75 million guide price, and something of a bargain for a city centre property of this size.
“Because it’s a listed [protected] building, there’s only so much one can do with it, which I think is why commercial operators weren’t interested. You probably couldn’t turn it into another hotel.”
The money was raised from private philanthropists. However, for the renovation and adaptation, estimated to cost in the region of €9 million, Fasciati is hoping to secure Department of Culture and Dublin City Council support.
“We are talking to the department obviously, but also Dublin City Council, because this will be something that contributes to their efforts to improve that particular area. Once this is up and running, it means lots of people coming in and out, day and night. That presence on the street will animate the area with people, and people out and about always makes a place feel safer.”
An application for renovation and adaptation will be submitted to the council early next year, with work expected to take two to three years.
The new base will make Irish National Opera visible in Dublin, says Fasciati. “It will give us a physical presence in the city. Part of what we want to do is make sure everyone has access to opera and understands opera. I want Irish National Opera to be really well connected with the performing arts community and the arts community in general in Dublin.”
[ Irish National Opera is showing us how to sing like a pro. Can we pull it off? Opens in new window ]
It is also a first step to delivering on Irish National Opera’s long-term mandate to develop an opera house for Dublin.
“The greater number of productions and performances planned in Dublin cannot be accommodated within existing theatres. There should be a dedicated opera house that can present works of scale and is accessible to independent, Ireland-based production companies. You know, Germany has about 80 opera houses. I’m not saying we have to have that number, but we should have one in the capital.”

title: Dubliner in New York: ‘You have to be on your A-game all the time’
description: Cinematographer Daniel Byrne: ‘Being Irish abroad, I feel like I know how to draw strength from being who I am’
content:
D ubliner Daniel Byrne is catching his breath from a busy morning working on a fashion shoot in a Brooklyn production studio when he speaks to The Irish Times.
Though it’s just 10am in New York , he’s many hours into his day, which often begins early and runs until late. It was one of the adjustments for the 25-year-old on working life in the United States . “People are expected to get up at 5am, go to work and get home at 9pm and get up early the next day.” The demands are “insane” but “there is a sense of community” with colleagues.
“I support shoots for Calvin Klein, Dior and all these crazy brands, it’s fun,” he says of days as a photographer assistant at the fashion studio.
Byrne honed his cinematography skills at the National Film School at IADT Dún Laoghaire and worked on various projects in Ireland, including director of photography for short film Father Brennan Is Having a Breakdown!
But moving to New York last year on a graduate visa has opened up opportunities not available to him in Ireland.
“I’ve been able to achieve some of my dreams, whether I’m just in the room or doing the thing in the room,” he says recalling recent shoots with Cher and Grace Jones.
But in making these connections, Byrne has had to learn to “hustle” and to “make things happen” for himself.
[ An Irishwoman in New York: ‘You can be who you want here if you learn to climb the ladder’ Opens in new window ]
“I’ve been casually asked to shoot video of Hudson Williams from Heated Rivalry for the Met Gala, and to shoot the September cover of Cosmopolitan Italia and shoot for Elle Taiwan,” he says.
The role of video in social media has become a much bigger part of the fashion industry in recent years, and this is where Byrne sees his direction going: “I would consider myself more a fashion or commercial cinematographer.” Byrne has worked on projects connected with the CFDA Awards (the Oscars of fashion), the Bulgari x Hudson Williams campaign, and recently shot Fab Morvan of Milli Vanilli for designer Lorand Coza.
A post shared by Daniel Byrne (@danieldonut)
Byrne’s interest in visual media had its roots in his Glasnevin childhood because his mother was a painter. “I grew up in the arts in that way. Fine art was my thing.” But in secondary school he got “obsessed” with photography and later moved into cinematography, which combined many of the elements he was interested in.
Another influence on him was growing up gay, “it’s a big part of who I am”.
“It makes me strong, because my whole life I’ve dealt with being different or being in a place that, maybe I feel a little bit like the odd one out.”
“Being Irish abroad, I know how to draw strength from being who I am. And being on these sets with these incredible people that are very alien to what I’ve grown up with.”
Compared to Ireland, the celebrity culture in the US is “just mind boggling, you have to be on your A-game all the time”.
Byrne’s Irish perspective means he can see the funny side of situations. “I’m kind of looking around and I’m like laughing to myself like, oh my God, are people actually serious?”
[ I got ‘the call’ from home. Dad’s days of wandering New York’s streets were over Opens in new window ]
“When people hear I’m Irish, they absolutely love it, they almost feel more at home with me.”
He is loving New York, where he shares an apartment overlooking Central Park for less than €1,000 a month (“I am literally on the park”).
But the social scene is “one of the biggest reasons” he enjoys life in New York. “We have Fire Island,” he says of the “gay paradise” off Long Island, which has historically been a destination for the LGBTQ+ community.
“Sometimes Irish people are a little more introverted, they keep their hands in their pockets when they walk. But here, everything’s on the table. And I love that because I’m extroverted.”

title: Look inside: Large and luxurious six-bed home with verdant views in Rathfarnham
description: Carrick on Dodder Park Road extends to 5,543sq ft and is finished to a high standard with features that include a passenger lift and games room
content:
Built in 2006, Carrick is a large, luxurious architect-designed, six-bedroom detached house with a stone-and-copper facade and striking curved roof. Despite its prominent position on Dodder Park Road, it offers plenty of privacy for its residents – along with ample living space. Carrick extends to a very generous 515sq m (5,543sq ft) over three storeys and has a B1 Ber. It is on sale through DNG, seeking €1.995 million.
There is parking for two cars in front, via two large electric gates, and there’s a separate gate for pedestrians. Inside is a wide, sweeping hallway, with striking, round recessed ceiling features with concealed lighting. What’s immediately noticeable is the quality of the materials used for the interiors: the doors, architraves, stairs and banisters are solid oak and the floor is laid in wide, bright porcelain tiles.
The first surprise is that the main living areas are not on the ground floor – doors instead lead into two large double bedrooms, each with its own en suite, while a third door leads into the next surprise: a vast recreation/games room spanning the width of the house, with a fully stocked bar and a snooker table. Off this is the comms room that keeps this lifestyle engine running smoothly.
A passenger lift offers quick access to the upper floors, but it’s worth taking the stairs to appreciate the handcrafted oak-and-glass staircase. The first-floor landing leads to four more bedrooms, and at the centre is a light well with sliding glass doors leading into the walk-in wardrobe in the main bedroom. There are four bedrooms on this level, and the main bedroom runs from the front to the back of the house, with big windows looking out front towards the River Dodder and a large walk-in wardrobe/dressingroom and spacious en suite to the back. Steps lead up from the main bedroom to the very private elevated side garden.
Bedrooms three and four, both large doubles, also have en suites; all five double bedrooms have built-in wardrobes. The sixth bedroom is currently used as a home office.
It’s probably no surprise at this stage to find the main living area on the top floor is vast, and filled with light thanks to its elevated position, large windows and extra-high ceilings. The open-plan kitchen/dining/family room has a Poggenpohl kitchen, with high-end cupboards and fittings, a large central island/breakfast bar with high stools, and a spacious dining area that can easily accommodate a big dinner party. Behind the kitchen is a large utility room.
Another unexpected feature is the mezzanine lounge overlooking the kitchen/dining area, with a large curved picture window giving superb views out over the Dodder. Carrick sits in a neighbourhood abounding with trees and parkland, so no matter which window you look out of, you’re seeing mostly greenery.
Finishing off this floor is a large, light-filled livingroom with a door out to the side garden; doors from the livingroom and diningroom area lead out to a wide balcony that wraps around the front. From the kitchen area, glazed double doors open out to a private south-facing terrace with seated area.
Steps lead down to the private side garden, where you’ll find another unexpected feature: two specially commissioned stone sculptures by acclaimed Irish artist Remco de Fouw. Around the front is a large two-car garage with rolling shutter door.
The owners may have built Carrick almost 20 years ago, but they still made sure to futureproof the house, ensuring in the process that it has continued to deliver both luxury and sustainability. It is equipped with geothermal underfloor heating, a passive air-ventilation system, a central vacuum system and a radon barrier.
Dodder Park Road is close to the cafes, boutiques and restaurants of both Rathfarnham and Terenure villages, and within striding distance of walks in Bushy Park and along the Dodder greenway.

title: Fiscal advisers point out the flaws but Government ignores them. What’s the point of Ifac?
description: Some say that without Ifac’s critiques of budgetary policy, there would probably be higher spending growth and more tax cuts by Government
content:
A ll bark and no bite. If you wanted to be cruel about Ireland’s so-called fiscal watchdog – that would be the obvious cliche to throw its way.
For years, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council ( Ifac ) has advised successive ministers for finance to go easy on the spending increases and tax cuts, put away more money and account properly for the possibility of overruns.
Yet, time and again on budget day, much of the advice appears to be quietly ignored.
The budgetary process now begins several months before the big day itself – with the Stability Programme Update in April, followed by the Summer Economic Statement (SES) in July. Between them, the two documents provide a good sense of what will be at the Government ’s disposal later in the year.
In August, after having a good look at the SES, which outlined the broad parameters for the budget, Ifac said the economy did not need any budgetary support.
It said the economy continued to grow at a “remarkable pace” even when the distorting impact of the multinationals was stripped out of the official figures.
Casting his eye across the SES’s implied net spending growth, its chairman Seamus Coffey said the plans were “not appropriate” for an economy in such a strong position.
Ifac’s position was that if the Government continued down this road, then its policies would only add to an already worrying inflation outlook.
Within hours of the budget’s publication, Ifac said it had put “the public finances on a worse trajectory by repeatedly breaking established spending limits and increasingly relying on high-risk corporation tax”.
[ Budget puts public finances on worse trajectory, watchdog warns Opens in new window ]
Coffey noted that, rather than heed the warnings, the Government was planning on spending €6 out of every €7 in corporation tax it collected.
The Government, as would be expected, defended the €8.7 billion in new measures. Minister for Finance Simon Harris had already defined the respective roles as he saw it.
“We don’t ignore their advice, but they’re not the Government,” he said.
So what is the continued point of having an institution set up in the wake of the 2008 crash to prevent a re-run of that calamity if modern-day governments choose not to take its advice?
Michael McMahon, a professor of macroeconomics, sat on the council for nearly seven years before serving as interim chairman between 2023 and 2024.
“When I joined, I thought we’d actually be advising the Government,” he says.
“That we’d go and meet the ministers involved and say, ‘This is a nonsensical policy; we think this would be better’. I thought it would be technocratic, geeky advice on the highest levels.”
Instead, McMahon quickly realised it was Ifac’s role to assess what was being proposed. “You could replace the word ‘advisory’ in Ifac’s name with ‘assessment’,” he says.
While chairman in 2023, McMahon added his voice to those of his predecessors, warning that the government risked “repeating Ireland’s past mistakes” with its upcoming budget. In particular, the tendency to breach its own spending rule had bothered the council members.
At the time , he said the State was over-reliant on windfall corporation tax revenues in the same way pre-crash governments had relied on property-related taxes.
[ How Budget 2027 will impact families: From renters to stay-at-home parents Opens in new window ]
McMahon also entertained the idea that, at some point in the future, Ifac could hit the “big red button” available to it and refuse to endorse budgetary forecasts. He said the council would be more likely to “wield big sticks” if the spending breaches were going to be repeated year after year.
Looking back, did his words and those of the other Ifac members have any impact?
“The question is not whether the government has always exactly complied with the letter of the recommendations,” he says.
“But rather, what would have happened with spending and tax decisions if an institution like the fiscal council was not endorsing the macro forecasts and criticising the decisions being made?”
McMahon says it is likely, in his view, that government spending would have been higher- and potentially riskier – had it not been for the role played by Ifac over a number of years.
During his time on the council, the government consistently ignored its own spending growth cap of 5 per cent annually, exceeding it each time.
However, the economist claims the cap may not have been introduced at all or, if it had, it would have been exceeded by an even greater margin had there been no independent oversight.
“It’s a very difficult thing to assess,” he says.
“I personally felt over the time I was there, it was a kind of slow beating of a drum of messages that were getting through. Questions were being asked in the media about growing spending at 6 and 7 per cent when their target was 5 per cent.”
McMahon also says it is his belief that the Future Ireland Fund (FIF) – the sovereign wealth fund into which the Government is investing 0.8 per cent of GDP annually – may not have come about had it not been for persistent calls for such a plan from Ifac.
“I think Ifac is useful; it has shifted the debate in Ireland. I don’t think we would have the FIF without it,” he says.
Ifac was established during the bailout years, when the country was picking up the pieces from an economic crash that pushed us into a three-year IMF-EU bailout.
[ Cut costs and abolish Ifac Opens in new window ]
Ireland had narrowed its tax base during the Celtic Tiger era and was badly caught out when the international banking crisis coincided with a collapse in house prices. An over-dependence on elements like stamp duty left public finances cruelly exposed.
Ifac, it appeared, was designed to remind policymakers that the same mistakes could not be repeated. Promoting fiscal responsibility seemed to be its overarching mission.
John Moran was secretary general at the Department of Finance between 2012 and 2014 when Ifac first got up and running. The terms of the bailout hung over the government, and the council was, at times, insistent on difficult medicine.
“We were in a tough position of trying to bring the budget back into order,” he says.
“There would have been moments of disagreement [with Ifac], where perhaps the political judgment of the government at the time was that they needed to do things that were seen as more politically palatable to keep the coalition together and keep the public onside.”
Moran says the economic landscape nowadays, in some ways, is comparable to the pre-crisis years.
“Today’s world is in a different position,” he says. “There are questions about how much extra spending you can do; that’s where the contrast lies [with the bailout years].
“We have some parallels between now and the situation before when we got into financial difficulties, with very concentrated tax sources.”
[ Budget 2027: Big business pays the bills as Coalition rolls the dice Opens in new window ]
The first chairman of Ifac was Prof John McHale.
He believes its importance lies in being able to publicise a counterpoint to government policy. Much of the time, he says, what Ifac is stating is not entirely different from what senior civil servants are telling ministers behind the scenes.
“It is different from [saying] it in public. In a way it helps the government – it helps balance the debate,” McHale says.
“You would never expect the government would take on what we would advise wholesale – it’s under huge political pressure. The council’s role was to take on a longer-term view. We were pulling in very different directions.”
So what was the relationship like between the government and Ifac?
“On the whole, it was good. Sometimes they were a little less forthcoming with information than the council would have liked, and it made our job harder,” he says.
That inability to always get the information it wants from civil servants could be solved, says McHale, by granting Ifac a statutory right. He points out that the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development ( OECD ) has again recently called for this.
That report also highlighted the relative lack of resources available to the council.
Applauding its ability to shape the media narrative here, the OECD said the body “punches above its weight”. It said Ifac ranked highly among similar bodies in other countries and had an ability to “generate influence despite limited resources”.
While winning plaudits from external reviewers, some politicians have eyed Ifac with a little suspicion over the years.
At a time when Ireland was crying out for public investment, particularly in housing, it has been accused of sometimes offering a narrow and needlessly cautious prescription. Yes, the argument went, the economy is doing well, but there are huge gaps where more money should also be spent.
[ How can runaway spending in the health service be reined in? Opens in new window ]
Sinn Féin’s spokesman on finance, Pearse Doherty , says there could be “question marks” over some of Ifac’s warnings down through the years, which were perhaps “too conservative”.
“If we look back at Ifac’s recommendations – and they have gone unheeded by the government in the past – the economy has still continued to grow and continued to have surpluses,” he says.
However, he says the council has played an important role over recent budgets in highlighting consistent spending overruns.
“Ifac have focused – and I think they have been misrepresented in my own view – on the government’s unplanned spending,” he says.
“It undermines the budget day process. You have a situation where the government announces X amount of spending on budget day, but by the end of the year, that has gone up due to unplanned measures.”
Doherty says he doesn’t know what Ifac would have to say about his party’s budget plans. But he believes it would be in line with Ifac’s current thinking on how the funding of extra spending should be done through the raising of additional tax revenues.
“The big difference between us and the Government is that we would increase capital expenditure,” he says. “I’m not sure what view they (Ifac) would take in relation to that.”
The other question that gets thrown at the “watchdog” is whether it is still needed, given that bodies such as the Central Bank of Ireland and the ESRI frequently offer similar criticisms of budgetary policy. The groupthink that prevailed in the pre-crisis period, so the argument goes, is no longer a problem.
[ With so much cash sloshing around, why is there a housing crisis? Opens in new window ]
“It is certainly true that there is a lot of common ground between the ESRI, the council and the Central Bank,” says McHale.
“It makes a difference when you have a body that has a statutory role in assessing these things. The Government has to respond to the council’s report; that is what really makes it stand out.”
McHale, though no longer part of Ifac, believes that budgetary policy is in a “reasonable place”. Despite criticisms around the nature of windfall taxes, he says it remains important that the Government is still running surpluses, though he’d like these to be higher.
This would be wise, he says, “given the underlying risks we face”.
McMahon says Ifac is more about “shaping thinking than shaping policies” and it fits the role of a “town crier”.
“We would all love 10 per cent growth a year, and everyone get free cookies,” he says.
“But we all know the pain that comes from reckless fiscal policy, and there is generally more pain than there is fun on the upside.”

title: RTÉ’s Kieran Cuddihy calls out cocaine-use hypocrisy after Waterford murders
description: Radio review: tetchy exchanges on Liveline; Claire Byrne opts for less contentious coverage
content:
F or all that things have changed on Liveline (RTÉ Radio 1, weekdays) since Kieran Cuddihy took over as host, some elements remain stubbornly, if not quite reassuringly, the same.
The show’s ability to generate bizarrely inappropriate quarrels remains intact, for example, at least if Wednesday’s edition is anything to go by. While the rest of the country reacts to the appalling murders of the English family in Waterford with dumbfounded horror, Cuddihy instead finds himself moderating ill-tempered exchanges on the issues thrown up by the terrible news.
To be fair, Cuddihy doesn’t set out with the intention of creating gratuitous on-air conflict. With the lethal arson attack that killed Kim and Philip English and their sons Callum and Jayden linked to intimidation by a local drug gang, Cuddihy talks to Deborah, who recounts the threats – and worse – that she suffered when her son ran up debts with cocaine dealers.
Speaking in a disguised voice, Deborah tells how, having paid an initial €500, the extortion escalated as her son’s addiction grew, with different dealers turning up to demand money; on one occasion her windows were smashed.
As well as living in constant fear – “You’re being watched all the time” – her grim situation was actually compounded rather than improved by paying the debts, with dealers preferring to pursue easy targets.
Although the menace diminished after her son entered rehab, Deborah’s grim tale underlines the ease with which entire families can get pulled into a cycle of violence over money owed to dealers by drug users.
So far so harrowing. But things turn testy after Cuddihy hears from Robert, a drug dealer turned criminologist who has a novel (to put it mildly) proposal for de-escalating debt-related intimidation before it can turn lethal. With police action ineffective and drug use inevitable, Robert suggests that local “credible messengers” act as go-betweens between dealers and users’ families to settle debts, in order to prevent potentially fatal retribution.
“Violence is bad for business,” Robert says, explaining why gangs would agree to this approach. Cuddihy sounds decidedly dubious about anything that leaves criminals unpunished: “Is this not a version of ‘don’t confront burglars’?”
But the host’s ambivalent attitude is as nothing compared with the reaction of his next caller. “This guy makes my blood boil,” Chris says as he variously blames government indifference and “too many bleeding hearts” for the apparent impunity with which vicious drug gangs act.
If Chris is clear about the problem – “There’s no deterrents in this country” – he’s less specific about the solution, beyond cracking down on crime in robust if undefined manner. “I’m losing my train of thought because I’m so annoyed,” he says.
Robert, in turn, defends his stance, claiming that prison exacerbates criminality in young offenders, but he doesn’t help his case by fudging his response when asked if the killers of the English family should be jailed, no matter what their age. “The answer has to be yes,” Cuddihy says, by way of impatient nudge.
This sourly argumentative tone may be at odds with the wider mood of stunned revulsion, but it’s also understandable given the appalling events in Waterford. Cuddihy isn’t immune to heightened emotions either, as he condemns the hypocrisy of middle-class professionals “tut-tutting” drug-related attacks while consuming cocaine themselves.
“The coke they shove up their noses, they’re buying it from the same people,” the host says. “It’s a bugbear of mine.”
It’s also an authentic – and timely – expression of outrage.
After all that, the opposing opinions aired during Cuddihy’s segment on Wednesday’s one-day strike by public sector workers sounds almost genteel by comparison, if still lively.
Lee phones in to support the strike, highlighting the poor conditions and pay endured by his nurse daughter, while upbraiding the host for saying that thousands had been inconvenienced by the cancellation of hospital appointments.
“I wasn’t weighing in on one side or other,” Cuddihy replies curtly. “It’s a statement of fact.”
Other contributors inevitably take a different view. Robert complains that teachers are on higher salaries than factory workers, while Stephen baldly asserts that there are “far too many civil servants doing nothing”.
Despite the differing stances, the item lacks the fury of the earlier drug debate. But it all adds up to a vintage episode of the long-running show, offering the requisite on-air drama while providing insights into charged subjects. If Cuddihy’s tenure on Liveline can still yield angry jousting, it’s because he knows how to touch a nerve.
Over on The Claire Byrne Show (Newstalk, weekdays), the host covers developments in Waterford and on the picket lines less contentiously, her customary composure ensuring that Liveline-style fireworks don’t suddenly ignite.
But while Byrne’s treatment of these big stories typically avoids extraneous antagonism, she continues to make her mark on her Newstalk show in other ways, by quietly carving out signature themes.
Some of these topics aren’t especially surprising, such as her concentration on health-related items. Byrne is particularly engaged when these dovetail with wider issues such as misogyny; although she remains focused during her discussion on the foul description by the US comedian Shane Gillis of women in gyms as “whores”, there’s no mistaking her strong feelings on the matter.
Less predictable is her interest in the affordability of retrofitting homes, but it’s a subject the host has pursued with notable vigour since her RTÉ days. Having heard Karol Kissane of the Irish Farm Accounts Co-operative claim on Tuesday’s show that low earners are unable to access retrofitting grants, Byrne revisits the issue the next day.
True, there’s a familiar pattern to the arguments of the Sinn Féin TD Pa Daly (who decries the warmer-homes-grant system) and the Fine Gael TD John Clendennen (who defends it). But the host appears to enjoy the occasionally tetchy encounter, overruling the protagonists’ complaints about one interrupting the other. “It’s a debate. It’s okay,” she says.
Byrne’s gently laissez-faire attitude hardly heralds a new era of swashbuckling controversy on her show. But it again highlights how comfortable the host sounds in the comparatively less constrictive broadcasting environment of Newstalk, with the result that even a little argument goes a long way.
While Seán Moncrieff (Newstalk, weekdays) revels in subjects that others might find gross, his item on bedbugs is conspicuously icky even by his standards.
Prompted by the news of a Qantas flight grounded by an infestation of bedbugs, Moncrieff (who’s also an Irish Times columnist ) learns about the parasites from the zoologist Michel Dugon, who brings a witty energy to the itch-inducing discussion.
Dugon describes the ease with which bedbugs travel (“They are fantastic hitchhikers”) and the speed with which they propagate (“When you notice it, it’s already too late”), as well as their sanguinary impact on bed linen: “If you squash one, you have a nice blood stain.” To top it all, bedbugs turn out to be resistant to most insecticides.
By the end, even the usually imperturbable host is seeking consolatory scraps of information. “Can they overdo it?” Moncrieff asks.
“Ah, they’re greedy little things,” his guest answers, with disconcerting levity.
It’s just as well Moncrieff’s show airs during the afternoon: try sleeping after that.

title: Why Halloween pumpkins are smaller this year, and three viral hacks to carve them
description: Get your hammer, your whisk and your biscuit cutters ready before you embark on this year’s pumpkin adventures
content:
A re the Halloween pumpkins in shops smaller this year? You may indeed notice a certain shrinkage in your seasonal gourds as you lift them into your trolley, but why? It turns out that a few factors might be at play.
Pumpkin grower Gerard Toner of Ballymad Farm and Archie’s Acre Animal Farm in Co Meath explains: “You are going to see, depending on where you are in the country, slightly smaller pumpkins depending on how people were affected with the heatwave .”
Toner says the pumpkins themselves tend to enjoy the heat, “which is kind of counterintuitive”, and will grow well in warm weather.
“But when you have consecutive weeks with just heat and no rain ... pumpkins are made up of water, so they need a bit of water to keep them going. In areas of the country, depending on soil pipes, and how they have been planted and whether or not they have been irrigated, that will affect the final size of the pumpkin,” says Toner.
Ireland is not the only country facing this size issue, with England’s record-breaking summer heatwave and prolonged dry spell also resulting in reduced yields and smaller pumpkins .
Outcomes have depended on locality and soil type, with the harvest varying considerably, for example, between Yealmpton and Lifton in Devon, only 50km apart.
“I wouldn’t say they [smaller pumpkins] are harder to carve. I would say different varieties are trickier to carve,” says Toner. He points to smaller varieties with harder skin and “goosebumps”, which he says can be “quite tough”.
Larger pumpkins with a smoother surface can, on the other hand, “be softer inside and then easier to work on”.
Regardless, a smaller pumpkin means less surface area for making mistakes.
Here are some allegedly foolproof hacks from the infinite wisdom of the social media algorithm.
This nifty little trick could work for a pumpkin regardless of size, but it is particularly useful for the smaller ones. Instead of hollowing out your Jack O’Lantern from the top where the stem is, work from the bottom.
Making the place where your tea light sits the base of your pumpkin will leave it easier to light; the carved pumpkin can then be placed back on top like a hat. This trick saves a clawed hand getting licked by flames as you try to carefully lower your candle into the pumpkin.
A whisk can be used for a preliminary scoop-out of the pumpkin flesh in lieu of your hands, keeping them clean.
Once you have extracted most of the stringy flesh, you can run around the interior walls with a spoon to remove any remaining goo.
A well-placed biscuit cutter can be hammered into the face of the pumpkin to ensure your carving has clean cut-outs. It is a handy trick for the artistically challenged, although it is not advisable to use biscuit cutters to which you have a sentimental attachment. And it’s probably best to leave this one to the adults.

title: Affordable wines: a Greek bottle to bid farewell to summer and a French red to greet autumn
description: Wines for the Weekend: The assyrtiko here might just remind you of a Greek holiday, but with better wine
content:
I feature two wines from Aldi this week, one of which – the assyrtiko – was a wine of the week earlier this year. I’m highlighting it again as it’s great value and Aldi still has stocks. It might bring back memories of holidays in Greece, although I am told that this is much better than most of the wine served in Greek restaurants.
If the assyrtiko is a farewell to summer, then the Corbières is a welcome to autumn. This wine, from the south of France, has plenty of power to go with those richer stews and casseroles. At €8.99, it will appeal to those on a budget.
Fresh vibrant citrus and green apple fruits. A great aperitif or to drink with grilled white fish.
Medium- to full-bodied with spicy earthy dark fruits. One to enjoy with something substantial; a beef or lamb casserole?

title: More than half of under-12s have overnight access to smart devices, survey says
description: Most young people say their parents, too, are on smartphones for long periods
content:
More than half of children under 12 have access to smartphones and other internet-connected devices in their bedrooms overnight, a survey has found, with a third saying they faced no restrictions on their online activity.
That rose to about two-thirds for children aged between 12 and 15, the report from online safety charity CyberSafeKids said.
However, parents were also guilty of failing to put their smartphones down, with more than half of young people saying parents were on their devices all or most of the time they were with their children.
“The research highlights the near-constant connectivity of even very young children. Screens in bedrooms, especially overnight, affect not only sleep but overall wellbeing,” CyberSafeKids chief executive Alex Cooney said.
“Children need clear boundaries around device use at home, and the fact that many have no restrictions at all is alarming, given the harmful content and contact inherent in digital environments.”
Most children under 15 reported going online in the evening, with a fifth of eight to 12-year-olds and 37 per cent of under-15s saying they fell asleep with devices.
Almost a quarter of teens were going online as soon as they woke up, and 41 per cent of 12 to 15-year-olds were accessing the internet before school.
The survey, which questioned 1,200 children, also found that young people were finding it more difficult to switch off from products designed to keep them online.
The results were published in advance of CyberBreak 2026, a HSE -supported initiative to encourage families, schools and workplaces to switch off smart devices for 24 hours from 7pm on Friday, avoiding social media , online apps, gaming and non-essential messaging.
More than 25,000 people have already committed to the initiative, which is promoting healthier digital habits.
Psychotherapist Richard Hogan said parents must lead by example.
“This means engaging with our kids before our phones in the morning and during the day – sending the vital message to them that they come first, not our smart devices,” he said.
“It’s our responsibility to help them switch off, unplug and reconnect with what matters most.”

title: What will €954,000 buy in France, Thailand, Portugal, Spain and Co Waterford?
description: One price, home and away: from a coastal home in Dunmore East to a stately townhouse in Hérault
content:
Monda is a small town just inland from the Costa del Sol , about 45 minutes from Malaga. This private, Moroccan-style villa in the mountains outside Monda has four bedrooms, a kitchen, diningroom, lounge, cosy snug area, utility and cloakroom. It is in good condition and rustic in design. There is a large, covered terrace in the front and a heated pool to the side of the property with another dining area.
This property was built in 1996 on an elevated site that overlooks Saleens beach, the Back Strand and Tramore Bay in Co Waterford . It was extended in 2003 and now has a floor area of 215sq m (2,314sq ft). Inside there are five bedrooms, three bathrooms and an open-plan kitchen/living/diningroom with bay windows facing out to the coast. There is a separate family room, a sunroom and two staircases to the floored attic. The C3-rated house is on a one-acre site with seating areas to the front and back.
In the centre of Pézenas in the Hérault region of France is this charming house with high ceilings, stone staircases and historic arches. Hidden behind a gate, the stately home has a courtyard to the front with a lush garden, a pool and separate dining areas. Inside the house is a large living area, kitchen, wine cellar, a reception room that opens out to a terrace on the first floor that runs the width of the house, four bedrooms and three bathrooms.
Located in Rawai on the Thai island of Phuket, this house consists of three connected buildings set out over 400sq m (4,305sq ft) and laid out around a large terrace and pool. The main building has two storeys with an open living space and two bedrooms. The guest building has two bedrooms, and the service building has a kitchen, office and staff sleeping quarters. It is close to Nai Harn beach and shopping areas.
This villa is in a quiet residential area 4km from the town of Loulé in the Algarve . It was renovated in recent years and has a floor area of 200sq m (2,153sq ft). It has a livingroom, diningroom, kitchen, laundry room, three bedrooms and three bathrooms. Outside there are three separate terraces, including a roof terrace with swimming pool. The elevated site has views out to the sea and is 14km to Vilamoura and 20km to Faro airport.

title: A taste of recognition
description: All-Ireland Local Food Hero and Tesco Ireland foodie Eunice Power on celebrating quality Irish ingredients, supporting producers and the impact Blas na hÉireann recognition can have on a food business
content:
On the dairy farm outside Dungarvan where Eunice Power grew up, quality Irish ingredients were not a food trend; they were simply how the family ate.
Beef and milk came from the land around them, new potatoes were eagerly awaited, and September might see her father return from particular fields with a cap full of mushrooms. It is an appreciation she now brings to her role as a Tesco Ireland Foodie and her support for Blas na hÉireann, which celebrates the quality of food and drink produced across Ireland.
“We had a very simple life, and we really embraced seasonality,” she says. “I think the smells of the countryside growing up were a huge thing for us. The honeysuckles, the elderflower, embracing the rowan berries, just embracing seasons.”
Held annually in Dingle, Blas is Ireland’s largest blind tasting of Irish produce, with every product assessed on its own merits. For Eunice, that independent recognition can have a powerful effect on the businesses behind the food.
“Any food or drink business winning Blas na hÉireann recognition for a product, it’ll result in a huge boost to their business profile and to their sales,” she says.
For finalists and winners, the awards offer a national showcase and an opportunity to meet buyers and fellow producers. Tesco buyers across all categories actively encourage suppliers to enter Blas and offer guidance on the categories most suited to their products, helping more Irish producers put their food forward for consideration.
“The premise of the Blas awards is [that] the food has to be produced in Ireland,” says Power. “A lot of the core range and Tesco Finest products, the Irish products, will be Blas na hÉireann award winners. That goes back to the research, the time and the efforts that Tesco put into producing their ranges.”
In all, Tesco products, produced in partnership with 33 different Irish suppliers, came home with a grand total of 86 honours at this year’s Blas na hÉireann Awards, including 29 gold, 30 silver, 24 bronze and three Chef’s Larder awards.
“Last Friday was a proud day for Tesco and the Irish producers it works alongside, with 86 awards brought home from Blas na hÉireann in Dingle. The wins are a celebration of Irish food and, above all, of the producers whose hard work earns the recognition.”
Food has taken Power from catering kitchens to television studios, but the thread running through her work is still the same: an interest in the ingredient and the person who produced it. The Dungarvan-based chef, food writer, broadcaster and entrepreneur runs Eunice Power Catering and the award-winning takeaway AndChips. She is a regular cook on RTÉ’s Today, the author of My Irish Kitchen Table and chief executive of Waterford Festival of Food. In May, she was named All-Ireland Local Food Hero at the 2026 Irish Restaurant Awards.
Her work as a Tesco Ireland foodie, which began in 2025, has brought her around the country to meet growers and suppliers, see their work at first hand and learn more about the relationships that allow Irish food businesses to expand.
“I hadn’t realised that Tesco was the biggest buyer of Irish food in the world,” she says. “I didn’t know how they grow businesses with the opportunities they give them.”
Tesco works with more than 500 Irish food and drink suppliers. Power points to John Dockrell, a lettuce grower who told her that the retailer collected his produce directly rather than requiring him to find his own distributor, as an example of “the support I’ve seen them giving suppliers”.
Another of those businesses is O’Hanlon Herbs, a previous Blas winner and a finalist again in 2026. The business began as a hobby in the founder’s parents’ back garden and has worked with Tesco for 30 years. Power says many of their decisions about growth have been made with Tesco because expansion depends on having a market for the produce.
She was also struck by the approach inside the company’s extensive glasshouses, where large plastic flycatchers trap insects without the use of pesticides. In her own kitchen, she regularly uses O’Hanlon Herbs, particularly the basil, coriander and mint.
The visits have brought home to Power how far many consumers have become removed from food production and how much knowledge that was once commonplace has been lost.
“For us as children, we had much more awareness of where food came from,” she says. “We lost that, but now I feel it’s coming back again, but honestly, not to a huge level.”
A Tesco film made with the Gilpin family, who grow Brussels sprouts in Co Louth, drew surprised reactions from people who had not known that sprouts grow on stalks in fields. More recently, Power filmed with Dockrell, who produces Little Gem lettuce outdoors in Wexford, where every crop remains vulnerable to too much or too little rain.
“People say, ‘how can you run out?’ Well, you can run out because you don’t have enough rain, you have too much rain,” she explains.
The Tesco product development team work closely with the producers in developing their products and their entry into Blas, offering guidance on categories.
Blas recognition can provide a significant boost to a producer’s profile and sales, but she repeatedly returns to the encouragement it offers. For Power, Tesco’s scale offers Irish producers an opportunity to reach more customers, enter new markets and grow their businesses, while Blas na hÉireann gives them independent recognition for the quality of what they make.
“I find that Tesco focusing on the Blas na hÉireann Awards really speaks volumes about their commitment to Irish food culture.”
Picking favourites is tough, as every product held its own, but a few have a special place in my kitchen.

title: Sci-fi and fantasy: Go with confidence into Grace Curtis’s cleverly conceived otherworld
description: Plus new works from Lex Croucher, Adam Simcox, James Islington and Benedict Anning
content:
Dark Academia is having its glow-up moment right now. Lex Croucher’s The Unmagical Life of Briar Jones (Gollancz, £22) offers an irreverent take on the subgenre, which unfolds in the exclusive Temple School of Thaumaturgy, an unholy blend of Eton and Hogwarts where Briar Jones takes up a janitorial position.
A working-class stiff devoid of any magical spark, Briar is disgusted to discover that their sensitive childhood friend Seb has degenerated into a brutal bully, a prefect who employs the dark arts to haze the school’s new intake in a series of ritual humiliations that has in the past proved fatal.
The Temple School, we learn, is a proving ground for an elite and shadowy class that peddles “money, power, influence”, and which employs magic to bend the world to its will; its cadets “look like fairy royalty, wicked princes of something dangerous and uncanny”. Shocked to realise they are now attracted to Seb, but determined to “stop a fascist in his infancy”, Briar joins forces with like-minded rebels in a wryly knowing romp that references Evelyn Waugh, Donna Tartt and Saltburn .
The good news is time travel is possible in Adam Simcox’s Time Jump (Renegade, £22); the bad news is it’s only available to the very rich. Offered the once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to travel to any place and time in recorded history, Rachel opts to time-jump to Camden Town in 1997, where she plans to break all the rules of time travel by saving the life of the boy whose death still haunts her all these decades later.
That rule-breaking results in a complex plot that allows Simcox poke a little fun at the genre: “Time travel doesn’t exist here yet,” says Rachel when she believes her physics-defying jaunt has been rumbled back in 1997. “It’s a plot device for unimaginative movies and hack-job novels.” Meanwhile, readers of a certain age and musical taste will appreciate Simcox’s unashamed wallowing in nostalgia for the sights and sounds of a pre-gentrified London.
Set in the same universe as her previous novel Idolfire (2025), Grace Curtis’s Heaven’s Graveyard (Hodderscape, £22) revolves around Dr Coda Canalluny, a history archivist seeking to ascertain the truth about Tahlia, the Goddess of Wisdom, whom Coda believes was an historical figure 4,000 years ago, long before she was mythologised as the Queen of Heaven.
The quest is urgent, for war is about to break out and the power invested in a god or goddess – its Idolfire – “held endless potential for wonder and destruction”. Aided and abetted by her beguiling but treacherous ex-lover Sparrow, Coda sets out to discover the source of Tahlia’s power before it can be weaponised by the warring factions. “It’s not unusual for people to retreat into fantasy in times of hardship,” observes one of Coda’s travelling companions, but you don’t retreat into a Curtis novel; you advance with confidence into a brilliantly conceived otherworld.
In James Islington’s Scion (Gollancz, £22), wealthy “lifers” can afford to prolong their lives and privilege indefinitely. Azure is a mercenary assassin who preys on lifers for the bounty offered by groups opposed to their genetic meddling, and so he is understandably puzzled and irritated to be assigned to protect Jasa de Alwes, the infamous geneticist who kick-started the lifers’ revolution.
But who is Azure protecting Alwes from if not himself? And why does Alwes believe that Azure is her greatest achievement? The pace is lightning-fast as Azure and the elderly but hilariously pin-sharp Alwes ricochet from one peril to another in a blackly comic novel that pays homage – both in its richly imagined futurism and identity paranoia – to Philip K Dick.
Benedict Anning’s Atomic Coffin (Bantam, £20) opens as a slow-burning cold war spy novel, as Heidi Sperling – code name “Thistle” – escapes from East Berlin with information about TK-15, a Russian nuclear submarine that appears to have gone rogue. The immediate threat is of “thermonuclear annihilation”, but when HMS Viking, the British sub on which Heidi takes refuge, takes a closer look at TK-15, things very quickly get weird.
[ Future lifeforms, ‘Indiana Jones’ in space and a woman’s reluctance to save mankind Opens in new window ]
Sitting deep on the ocean floor off the coast of Iceland, TK-15 is abandoned and empty, according to the Viking’s instruments; so why are the British submariners starting to go mad and killing themselves? As the title suggests, Heidi’s experience of life aboard the Viking is one of suffocating claustrophobia; but the reality is nothing compared with the imaginings of her mental anguish, as she finds herself locked into a kaleidoscopic hell of the mind in a novel reminiscent of Stanislaw Lem’s Solaris and Adam Wiśnewski-Snerg’s Robot .
Declan Burke is an author and journalist. His latest novel is The Lammisters (No Alibis Press)

title: Jhon Durán on the double as Benfica prove too hot to handle for Celtic
description: Camilo Durán offers Celtic’s sole reply in Lisbon
content:
Celtic found clinical Benfica just too much to handle in a 4-1 Europa League defeat in Lisbon.
Colombia striker Jhon Durán scored with a penalty after just five minutes after being fouled by Hoops defender Dane Murray and then helped himself to a second in the 35th minute, after defender Alexander Bah had added a second midway through the first half.
Martin O’Neill ’s side were cut apart at times but could have scored on a couple of occasions before the break.
The Hoops eventually reduced the deficit in the 63rd minute through a brave header from Camilo Durán – who had joined up with the squad late after remaining in Glasgow for the birth of his second child – but they could not close the gap any further before substitute Vangelis Pavlidis fired in a fourth for the home side with two minutes remaining.
Celtic lost 3-1 at home to Hungarian outfit Ferencvaros in their first Europa League game at Parkhead before the international break and will have to pick themselves up again for the visit of Hearts in the Scottish Premiership on Sunday.
Neither side had settled when Murray conceded a penalty. He he kicked through the leg of Durán who had got his foot on the ball from behind him inside the box.
The former Aston Villa player dinked the ball ‘Panenka’ style, with Hoops goalkeeper Viljami Sinisalo diving to his left.
The Scottish champions fought back immediately and Benfica keeper Anatoliy Trubin made decent saves from striker Kasper Hogh and midfielder Mika Baur.
In the 19th minute, Gianluca Prestianni, who was causing Celtic endless trouble down the left flank, curled the ball just wide after coming on to his right foot.
And when the 20-year-old attacker’s cross from the left came over to the back post minutes later, Bah had run away from Sebastian Tounekti and he sidefooted the ball past Sinisalo from eight yards.
Again Celtic reacted well to the loss of a goal. Tounekti’s cross was met by Hogh who hit a post from close range before Camilo Durán curled the ball against the crossbar and Tounekti blasted the loose ball over.
