Benfica were a joy to watch at times but their third goal came after Hogh lost possession, which allowed Prestianni to play in Durán. Despite being under pressure from Celtic defender Auston Trusty and forced wide of the goal, he managed to squeeze the ball low past Sinisalo.
Callum Osmand and Haissem Hassan replaced Hogh and Tounekti for the start of the second half and within five minutes Hassan had a shot saved by Trubin, who then watched Osmand fire an effort over the crossbar.
Celtic gave themselves a lifeline just after the hour when Durán headed in from a Hassan cross.
As the visitors grew in confidence, Durán fired a shot against a post from 12 yards in the 72nd minute before Benfica substitute Andreas Schjelderup did likewise at the other end.
Both sides had more opportunities in the wide open game, but the evening ended with Pavlidis netting a late fourth with a shot from the edge of the box before defender Tomas Araujo sent a header against the woodwork.

title: Witness mistook body for Halloween decoration, Louth family murder trial hears
description: Accused had episodes of psychosis from young age and was diagnosed with schizophrenia, court hears
content:
A carer has told the trial of a man accused of murdering three members of his family at their Co Louth home of the moment she mistook a body lying in the front garden and “drenched in blood” for a Halloween decoration.
Another witness also told the Central Criminal Court on Thursday that when she asked the accused whether the sirens they could hear were for him, Robert O’Connor replied: “Yes, I killed them.”
When rearraigned before the Central Criminal Court last week, Robert O’Connor (32), of Drumgowna, Louth village, Dundalk , Co Louth, pleaded not guilty of murder by reason of insanity, or guilty of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility to the triple murder of his mother Louise O’Connor (56), his father Mark O’Connor (54) and his younger brother Evan O’Connor (27) at their home in Drumgowna between September 28th and 29th, 2025, both dates inclusive.
In her opening address, prosecuting barrister Róisín Lacey said the accused had episodes of psychosis from a young age and was diagnosed with schizophrenia in 2018. The barrister said the “battleground” between the prosecution and defence in the trial was whether the accused qualifies for the special verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity.
The panel has also been told that the accused accepted he caused the death of the three victims, who had sustained a combined 139 stab wounds.
Giving evidence to the trial on Thursday, special-needs support worker Loreto Durrigan told Lacey that she worked for an organisation called Praxis Care which provides support for people with special needs.
She said she had a habit of reversing into the driveway of Drumgowna so it was easy for Evan O’Connor – who had severe autism and an intellectual disability – to put his bag into the boot of her car, which she explained was part of his routine.
When she arrived at Drumgowna at 9.32am on September 28th, Durrigan said she reversed in and thought she saw a Halloween decoration inside the gates. The witness thought this was “very unusual”, as Louise O’Connor would not usually decorate the house for Halloween.
The witness said she remained in the car for about two minutes but did not see Evan or hear anything.
Durrigan said that when she got out of the car and walked towards the gates, she saw a body drenched in blood from head to toe. “At the time I didn’t realise it was a body, I had to look twice,” she added.
The witness said that when she looked past the two cars parked in the driveway, she saw Evan O’Connor lying on his back with his head on a step facing the patio doors.
Durrigan said she then had another look at what she had initially seen behind the gates and realised it was Mark O’Connor’s body. There was a white shoe on the lawn beside him.
She got into the car and drove around the back to a neighbour’s house. The witness was on the phone to gardaí at 9.38am when Martina Malone came out of her house. Durrigan told Malone that Evan and Mark were dead. Malone then brought the carer into her house and locked the door behind them.
The witness said she was quite distressed at the time and had known the O’Connor family for the previous seven years.
Durrigan said she had met the accused three weeks before this and found him very polite. She said Mark and Louise O’Connor were lovely people, but very private.
Martina Malone told the jurors she lived quite close to the O’Connor home and became aware of something “kicking off” at Drumgowna on the evening of September 28th, when she heard “a roar or a shout”.
The trial continues on Friday before Justice Mícheál P O’Higgins and a jury of six men and six women.

title: Roy Keane brands Manchester United ‘circus’ following Lisandro Martinez outburst
description: Argentina defender apologises for comments made after defeat to Atlético Madrid
content:
Roy Keane has branded Manchester United a “circus” following Lisandro Martinez’s outburst against the club’s hierarchy.
The Argentina defender accused the club of lacking ambition and questioned their summer recruitment after Tuesday night’s 2-0 Champions League defeat against Atlético Madrid.
Martinez apologised for his comments following a meeting with manager Michael Carrick and the leadership group after a training session on Thursday.
He admitted his interview “did not help”, adding he is “fully focused on winning together”.
In a statement shared on Instagram on Thursday evening, Martinez said: “Today I met with the club’s leadership and the manager.
“It was a very positive conversation, where we were able to exchange views and speak openly about what happened after Tuesday’s game.
“Everyone knows that I am a passionate person and that I live football with great intensity.
“The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise.”
It is understood United will not make any disciplinary action against Martinez public and consider the matter closed, but he has reportedly been fined.
Former United defender Gary Neville said Martinez’s comments after the defeat amounted to a direct attack on his team-mates and suggested senior players would be “absolutely fuming”, while former United captain Keane described the remarks as symptomatic of the “chaos” at Old Trafford.
“They’re obviously not together,” Keane said of the club, speaking on The Overlap’s Stick to Football podcast. “It is chaotic there from the top to the bottom. We go there on match days and I don’t like the feeling around the club.
“It just seems chaotic – statements can reflect it. It was chaotic with how they got to Carrick as their manager.
“We said from day one there were better options out there, and maybe the players are looking at there’s better options as players out there. It’s chaos, it’s like a circus.”
Martinez hit out at United’s director of football Jason Wilcox and the club’s board in a caustic interview amid their worst start to a league season since 1986.
Neville and Keane shared some of Martinez’s concerns about the state of the club, but also questioned the World Cup winner’s individual performances and whether he had sufficient standing to make such comments.
“When Martinez says they should have brought more players in, he’s directly attacking his team-mates,” said Neville.
“If I was Bruno Fernandes and I was Harry Maguire and the other senior players, I’d be absolutely fuming with him because you’re basically saying that some of us shouldn’t be here and we should be bringing more players in. That’s what I think he’s saying.”
Sky Sports reported Martinez was challenged over his comments by at least one player on the flight back from Spain, but his views are said to be shared by some frustrated team-mates.
“I don’t think it will be a big falling out,” said Keane. “Because I think we’ve question marks over this dressingroom anyway.
“I don’t think there’s enough characters, enough men in there. We know that. But I don’t see him as a senior player at Man United; I see him as a centre half who’s making lots of mistakes.”
“I thought it was really strange to have a go at Jason Wilcox, not because he’s above criticism but the budget is not going to be set by Jason Wilcox; the budget is going to be set by the owners,” said Neville.
“It was obvious they needed more defenders. He [Martinez] would probably be one of the first on the chopping block if players were actually brought in.”

title: The Irish Times view on US midterms: a lame duck Trump is still a danger
description: Most forecasts now favour Democrats to take both houses of Congress
content:
Credible reporting from inside the White House has depicted a president surrounded by sycophants and largely insulated from the cold political winds that every opinion poll shows blowing against Republicans ahead of the midterm elections on November 3rd.
That seems to be changing. Donald Trump’s sudden deal with Vladimir Putin to bring Russian diesel on to the market, defying a 2022 congressional ban and a sanctions law he signed last month, is one of several signs of a renewed tilt towards Moscow on Ukraine. It is to some extent a reversion to type, reflecting the president’s long-standing empathy, verging on deference, towards the Russian leader. It also fits a pattern in which policy and private interest blur. Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have reportedly folded into peace talks a multibillion-dollar sale of Russian-owned assets to a consortium including Gulf investors with business ties to the envoys or their families.
But the shadow of electoral humiliation is a factor too. With fuel prices high, the diesel deal is plainly aimed at voters. Elon Musk, firmly back in Trump’s camp, has poured $276 million into Republican groups since July, much of it into the fight to hold a Senate seat in Texas, where the party is in deep trouble. From Alaska and Iowa to Ohio and Kansas, states that Trump carried comfortably are now in play. Not all will fall, but most forecasts now favour Democrats to take both houses of Congress.
That would change not only the landscape on Capitol Hill, where investigations into the administration would swiftly follow, but the national mood. Trump would be a lame duck, and unpredictable primary contests in both parties to succeed him would begin in earnest.
For Democrats, victory carries its own pitfalls. The party misread the 2022 midterms as an endorsement of Joe Biden’s wish to seek a second term, with disastrous consequences. It must reconcile its warring factions and settle on a leader who can offer a compelling, forward-looking vision to disenchanted voters. The Republican front-runners, JD Vance and Marco Rubio, will struggle to distance themselves from an unpopular president without incurring his wrath, which will still carry weight with the Maga base.
A lame-duck Trump could be extremely dangerous. Presidents in the twilight of their terms have tended to turn to foreign policy, where Congress constrains them least. In Trump’s case, that could mean more decisions like this week’s downgrading of Ukrainian access to the vital Starlink satellite communications network. Regardless of the midterm results , the world should brace itself for more indulgence of autocrats, further ruptures with democratic allies and the relentless pursuit of private profit at public expense.

title: Man and woman arrested over Waterford petrol bombing knew family that was targeted
description: Suspects detained as part of inquiry into attack at home that killed two adults and two children
content:
Gardaí are anticipating further arrests following the detention of two suspects by detectives investigating the murders of four members of the English family in Waterford city.
The man (20s) and woman (30s) being questioned on Thursday night knew Philip and Kim English and their children, Callum (12) and Jayden (9), but are not related to the family.
The Irish Times understands the man and woman are suspected of being linked to a family-based Waterford drugs gang gardaí believe ordered the arson attack, rather than being senior figures in that group. Gardaí believe them to have been centrally involved in the attack, and that they were present at the time.
The attack was carried out as part of a campaign of intimidation, for more than three years, aimed at collecting a €20,000 drugs debt incurred by an associate of Philip English, who was not involved in crime.
“Both individuals are currently detained under section 50 of the Criminal Justice Act 2007 in a Garda station in the Garda Eastern region,” the Garda said of Thursday’s arrests.
Both suspects can now be held for up to seven days without charge as they have been detained under legislation intended for use during the investigation of alleged serious organised crime.
They were being questioned about the assistance they allegedly gave to a crime gang in the commission of the arson attack on the house at Birch Avenue, in the Birchwood estate, just after 5am on Tuesday. It claimed the lives of the couple and their sons.
Their joint funerals are due to be held at the Sacred Heart Church, the Folly in Waterford on Monday, followed by burial at Kilbarry Cemetery.
Two other children – a girl (14) and a boy (6) – were rescued by firefighters and remain critically ill in Children’s Health Ireland (CHI) in Crumlin, Dublin.
Sinn Féin councillor John Hearne said the impact of the fatal fire on the people of Waterford is comparable to the 1981 fire at the Stardust nightclub in north Dublin which killed 48 young people. He called on Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan to go to Waterford and make it clear these crimes would not be tolerated and signal “we’re going to have radical change”.
He added he knew Philip English well, as he had approached the councillor on a number of occasions for help with problems. “He was a lad who would be chatting all the time,” Hearne told RTE’s Six One News.
Waterford had seen intimidation incidents on drug debts of up to €70,000, and urged anyone in a similar situation to contact the Garda. People had had fingers cut off in drug-related intimidation, which led victims into an “absolute fear that smothers them and drowns them”.
In another case, a woman was hit in the head with a hammer and he was aware of an incident where a petrol bomb thrown into a house landed in a baby’s cot, injuring the mother and baby.
He insisted “there is a way out of the darkness” and gardaí were very responsive once a report was made. He knew of cases where gardaí had put suspects under surveillance and were watching them, and arrested them, as they moved or used petrol bombs.
“The community hate these people and everybody hates them and if you get the whole community in a fight like this you can’t lose,” he said, insisting people could not continue paying drug dealers as it would only lead to “a miserable life”.
As part of the investigation in Waterford, a number of vehicles, phones and laptops have already been seized for examination, during searches carried out across the city on Tuesday evening.
Gardaí had been continuing to try to locate a vehicle of interest linked to the case in recent days. It is understood another vehicle was seized on Wednesday, though that was not confirmed by gardaí.

title: Gardaí investigating after body of unidentified man found in undergrowth in Mallow
description: Remains with visible injuries were discovered in middle of the day by person walking their dog on Blackwater river banks
content:
Gardaí have begun an investigation after the body of an unidentified man was discovered in undergrowth by a walkway at Ballyellis, Mallow , Co Cork .
The body, which had visible injuries, was found by a person walking their dog on the banks of the Blackwater river on the Killavullen side of Mallow at 1.30pm on Thursday. It is a popular area for walkers.
Assistant state pathologist Dr Margot Bolster was carrying out a preliminary examination of the scene. It is believed the body had not been in situ for a long period. The area was cordoned off after the alarm was raised.
The remains were kept at the scene on Thursday evening and an examination was due to be conducted by members of the Garda Technical Bureau.
The body of the middle-aged man was due to be removed to the morgue at Cork University Hospital (CUH) on Thursday evening following the technical examination.
A postmortem examination is expected to be carried out by Bolster on Friday morning, which will help determine the course of the Garda investigation.

title: Government and unions inching towards talks but no sign of white smoke
description: Both sides have a distance to travel before averting a second day of national shutdown
content:
Just after 3pm on Thursday, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers stood up in the Dáil to respond to a Labour Party private members’ motion on this week’s one-day national strike by 300,000 public sector workers.
Chambers ran through the well-ventilated position of the Government, arguing that the previous government’s agreement with unions had resulted in cumulative pay increases of 9.6 per cent at a time when cumulative inflation was 6.6 per cent. He stressed the principle of collective bargaining and its principle that nothing is agreed until everything is agreed.
But he also displayed the more conciliatory language and tone evident this week, saying the Government was willing to prioritise pay.
Then, right at the end of his contribution, Chambers dropped a zinger that made everybody in the chamber sit up.
Turning to Labour leader Ivana Bacik and her colleagues, he said: “As this is a sensitive matter and work is ongoing, deputies will understand, I’m not in a position to provide specific or further detail at this time. However, I hope to be able to provide further details shortly and as part of an agreed way forward.”
That was tantalising. Was a breakthrough imminent? Well, not quite. Later on in the afternoon, people on the Government side talked it down a little, saying it was not going to happen that night. But it gave enough hope that both sides could avert a second day of national shutdown next Wednesday.
The all-out national strike that happened this week was once a common occurrence in Irish public life. The 1970s and 1980s were pockmarked by industrial action. In February 1979, for example, there was a crippling 19-week strike involving postal workers seeking 30 per cent increases in pay (inflation was out of control at the time).
A deal struck by incoming taoiseach Charlie Haughey in 1987, with unions and employers on pay increases, formed the basis of the first national pay agreement. It led to industrial peace for a generation.
During his 30-year career as a senior trade unionist, Bernard Harbor witnessed only one big national industrial dispute. It was the public service-wide strike in 2009, following the imposition of the pension levy and pay cuts when the Irish economy tanked.
The atmosphere was forlorn. Public sector workers were angry at their unions after taking an effective 14 per cent pay cut. The public was unsympathetic towards them. The economy was in the doldrums.
When Harbor visited the picket line on Wednesday, the mood was markedly different. It was enthusiastic and there was evident support from the wider public.
Up to 2009, the national pay agreements were economy-wide, involving the public and private sectors. But after the crash, the agreements – Haddington Road and Croke Park – were public sector only. There were some skirmishes from time to time, but generally it restored a long period of industrial peace.
Agreements like this usually take many months to negotiate. Initially, there are the talks about talks, before the substantive engagement begins. This time around it was left very late.
From a union perspective, having everything on the table would mean the talks could be strung out for many months. Hence, the insistence that pay be dealt with first. But the Government was not prepared to do that. If pay was agreed, the unions would have no incentive to concede on productivity or efficiencies.
The process broke down very early and the exchanges during the summer and into the early autumn were testy and gave little indication of a breakthrough. However, after weeks of stand-off, a letter from Chambers to the officers of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions public services committee on Monday gave the first inkling that there may be movement, albeit too late to stop the strike on Wednesday.
Since then, there has been some movement. The Government has emphasised that, in addition to the €1.2 billion it has set aside, there is an additional unallocated fund of €1.6 billion, a portion of which can be deployed. With inflation for the 12 months to September 2026 running at 4.1 per cent, the unions’ chief negotiator Kevin Callinan has indicated the pay increases will have to at least match that.
Union negotiators will not want to bring something back to their members that does not have the pay element up front in negotiations. The Government will have to show it can win agreement on better productivity.
The “sensitive” nature of what is happening right now is trying to find a formula that allows both sides to show they have got a tangible result on the basis of talks.

title: Review of Legal Services Regulatory Authority to follow its first decade of operation
description: Attorney General Rossa Fanning notes ‘limited’ take-up of solicitor-barrister partnerships since 2024 introduction
content:
Terms of reference are being prepared for a review of the Legal Services Regulatory Authority (LSRA) to consider any changes necessary to ensure the Irish legal system “remains modern, efficient, digitally enabled and focused on serving the needs of the public”, Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan has said.
It will draw on a comprehensive statutory review submitted last year by the authority.
O’Callaghan was speaking at an event in Dublin on Wednesday evening marking 10 years since the establishment of the LSRA, the first independent regulator of legal professionals here.
In that time it had delivered “practical reforms that supported transparency, accountability and high professional standards”, the Minister told an audience of judges, lawyers and academics.
The Chief Justice, Donal O’Donnell, noted that the LSRA’s establishment was “not universally welcomed” at the time, with some arguing it was not necessary in light of self-regulation of the professions.
He disagreed with that view, and believes an independent system of regulation was important. The LSRA has proven to be a “good and useful example” of good regulation informed by an understanding of the legal professions.
Attorney General Rossa Fanning said there had been “limited” take-up of an option to become solicitor-barrister partnerships, an option available since 2024.
While survey evidence commissioned by the LSRA had appeared to suggest some appetite for the reform, the LSRA’s register currently lists only two barrister-solicitor partnerships.
The limited uptake suggests the appeal of the independent referral Bar has endured and that the market continued to value the independence, flexibility and specialist skill of the full-time advocate, he said.
Niamh Muldoon, chief executive of the LSRA, said during its first decade the authority established an independent complaints service, introduced new regulatory structures and supported greater transparency in how legal services were provided.
However, during a panel discussion, Noeline Blackwell, human rights lawyer and campaigner, said people continued to face obstacles in accessing the legal system, including a 12-month wait for civil legal aid.
While the Courts Service has made a lot of innovative improvements, the system remained very hard to understand, she said. It is run “for the benefit of the lawyers”, including having many people attend court from early morning when their case may not be dealt with for hours, she said.
There are people whose rights are not being protected because of the structures that have been built, she said. “We could do a lot better.”

title: Sex-offender taxi driver released while he fights deportation case
description: Badruzzaman Masum (48) was convicted of sexually assaulting an 18-year-old girl in his car
content:
A Bangladeshi taxi driver who was due to be deported after being convicted of sexually assaulting an 18-year-old girl in his cab has been released from detention as he fights the legality of the decision to revoke his permission to reside in Ireland.
At the High Court , Judge Conleth Bradley ruled Badruzzaman Masum (48) of Swords , Co Dublin , could be conditionally released while his case is proceeding.
The deportation was due to take place on Monday September 28th.
In his High Court judgment, Bradley said he had previously granted the applicants leave to apply for judicial review to challenge the “making and notification” of the August 2026 deportation order.
The judge said Masum entered the State in September 2003 under a student visa, which was regularly renewed and subsequently upgraded in status, allowing him to live in Ireland for almost 23 years until its revocation in June 2026.
The revocation arose from Masum’s conviction at Dublin Circuit Court, following a guilty plea, of sexual assault, contrary to Section 2 of the Criminal Law (Rape) (Amendment) Act 1990.
On March 11th, 2025, Dublin Circuit Criminal Court sentenced him to two years’ imprisonment, backdated, and directed that he be incarcerated in Mountjoy Prison . He was also placed on the sex-offenders’ list.
[ Taxi driver jailed for sexually assaulting 18-year-old passenger Opens in new window ]
His victim was an 18-year-old female passenger in his taxi in the early hours of November 27th, 2024. The court heard that he groped her.
He had no previous convictions and was imprisoned at Mountjoy Prison until September 8th, 2026.
The Minister for Justice revoked Masum’s residency permission because of the conviction but Masum challenged the validity of his pre-deportation eight-week detention, which began after he completed his jail sentence.
He argued that the pre-deportation detention could not continue after he had commenced separate High Court proceedings objecting to the deportation.
The judge ruled that “a person cannot be detained for more than an eight-week aggregate period, the time period during which legal proceedings have been instituted is not reckonable as part of that eight-week period”.
Bradley wrote that Masum’s leave to apply for judicial review was granted on October 5th, 2026. The judge said this meant the eight-week detention period had been “effectively paused” until the conclusion of the challenge.
The judge granted the conditional release to be dependent on Masum surrendering all travel documents, that he resides at a Dublin address and comply with all requests made towards him by gardaí or immigration officials.

title: The Irish Times view on the sentencing of Jeffrey Donaldson: not one word of regret
description: Judge correct to praise victims for their determination and courage
content:
The 15-year sentence imposed on former Democratic Unionist Party leader Jeffrey Donaldson reflected the seriousness of the sexual crimes, including one case of rape, that he committed against two girls over separate periods from 1985 to 2008, starting when they were both seven years of age.
As the victims, now adult women, sat in court they heard Judge Paul Ramsey praise their “courage, resourcefulness and determination” in bringing Donaldson to justice.
The women provided powerful impact statements. Victim A recounted how her childhood was stolen from her and how “for years I carried shame, anger and guilt, and questioned whether I was worth protecting or worthy of being loved”. Victim B told of how “hope was taken away from me a long time ago” and how “what happened took away my ability to trust people.”
This case still causes shock in Northern Ireland, not least because of Donaldson’s apparent lack of remorse and the fact that since his conviction he had doubled down in his denials .
“There has not been, and doubtless will not be, one word of regret, apology or shame from this man to at least provide his victims with some crumb of comfort,” said Judge Ramsey. As the judge added, Donaldson’s was a “catastrophic descent into disgrace”.
The victims, through their convincing evidence, ensured that justice was served, but the PSNI and the Northern Ireland Public Prosecution Service (PPS) also played their part in making certain that Donaldson would be punished. At a time when many victims of sexual abuse are reluctant to come forward, the bravery of the women and the professionalism and support of the police and the PPS is an important signal.
Catherine Kierans of the PPS’s serious crime unit said that the case showed that sexual abuse can be hidden behind “a facade of respectability”. But thankfully and most pertinently she was able to add, “It also shows that no individual, irrespective of their position, status or public reputation, is beyond the reach of the law.”

title: The €1.6tn battle for Europe: inside the EU’s biggest budget fight in years
description: As member states clash over defence spending and farm payments, Ireland is playing the role of neutral EU presidency dealmaker
content:
I t’s hard to keep track of all the billions and trillions of euro flying around. The European Union’s 27 national leaders are trying to agree on the size of the union’s new long-term budget and how they are going to pay for it.
The negotiations will decide how much money gets set aside for Common Agriculture Policy (CAP) payments, overseas development aid and “cohesion” funding to build roads and infrastructure in poorer EU regions.
The budget showdown rolls around every seven years and grips the Brussels system when it does.
Much has changed since member states agreed the existing joint EU budget in 2020. Many leaders want more cash to be thrown at defence and security, migration control and other “new” priorities. There are plans for a bumper “competitiveness fund” to give Europe’s struggling economy a hand too.
The budget is predominately financed by contributions from national coffers and governments are not keen on increasing the amount they hand over to the European pot.
That makes for an almighty row between different coalitions of EU states, all vying to protect the parts of the budget they feel are most important.
Germany is leading the “frugals”, who want a smaller budget and for cuts to come at the expense of CAP and cohesion funds. The group of net contributors include the Netherlands , Austria , Sweden , Denmark and Finland (though the Finns want to protect CAP).
Speaking at the start of a two-day EU summit, Rob Jetten, the Dutch prime minister, said their plan was to “downsize and modernise” the budget.
Denmark’s prime minister Mette Frederiksen said there was “no alternative” to funnelling much more money towards defence, particularly when the Trump administration was questioning its support for Ukraine.
German chancellor Friedrich Merz and the other belt-tighteners got together for breakfast on the morning of the European Council summit, to co-ordinate their position.
[ ‘No silver bullet’: Energy crunch could bite Europe this winter Opens in new window ]
The European Commission ’s initial proposal for an expansive €1.76 trillion package has been whittled down to €1.62 trillion, in a revision crafted by Ireland, playing the role of neutral EU presidency dealmaker. The frugals – dubbed by one of their own diplomats as the “sensible six” – want deeper cuts.
Europe’s eastern and southern states, led by Spain , Italy and Poland , are fighting to keep the knife away from CAP and other traditional funds.
France finds itself in the middle. Ireland has a foot in both camps too.
The fight has moved up to the level of EU leaders, where it will be refereed by European Council president António Costa , who chairs the summits.
The task at hand was “at times like trying to reconcile the irreconcilable”, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said.
[ EU leaders clash over CAP and military funding as budget talks become fractious Opens in new window ]
“We have a clear end point in mind, which is December,” one senior EU official said.
The final budget will be bigger than the existing €1.2 trillion package that runs out at the beginning of 2028. Any increase may be marginal in real terms when inflation and EU debt repayments are factored in.
The discussion on Thursday was the first real clash over the budget at leader level. They will meet for another summit in Dublin next month and are likely to meet again in Brussels at the end of November.
The distance between the different positions should begin to narrow, culminating in a marathon summit to knock out a deal right before Christmas. That is Costa’s plan anyway.
The prospect of negotiations dragging on into the start of next year and beyond is very real. “We are not in a hurry, we need a good budget. If it’s not done in January, it’s not done in January,” one diplomat said.
[ Ireland in line for a kicking from all sides after publishing EU budget Opens in new window ]

title: Ten children and one adult hospitalised after ‘excess chlorine incident’ at Dublin pool
description: A total of 23 people became unwell at Clayton Hotel Liffey Valley with facility subsequently closed
content:
Ten children and an adult have been brought to hospital after an “excess chlorine incident” occurred at a swimming pool in the Clayton Hotel Liffey Valley in west Dublin .
The Dalata Hotel Group said the incident happened at around 3.35pm on Thursday and emergency services were immediately notified.
“We can confirm that 23 people in total, who were using the pool at the time of the incident, were medically assessed having complained of feeling unwell,” it said.
“Ten children and one adult were brought to hospital and are receiving medical attention. Following the incident the swimming pool has been closed, in accordance with the company’s safety and emergency procedures.
“We can confirm that our emergency plan was activated immediately.”
A “thorough investigation” of the circumstances surrounding the incident will take place as soon as possible, the hotel group added.
“Our immediate thoughts are with those impacted and their families. We are doing everything in our power to support them and the emergency services.”
Dublin Fire Brigade (DFB) said it was called to the scene at 3.39pm after reports of a “hazardous materials incident” at the pool.
Units from Tallaght, Dolphin’s Barn, Donnybrook and Dún Laoghaire attended along with the National Ambulance Service (NAS) and gardaí.
“Firefighter/paramedics in breathing apparatus and chemical protection suits have isolated the hazardous substance and patients are being assessed by NAS and DFB personnel,” it said.
“There is no danger to the wider public and we expect the incident to be scaled back shortly.”
Specialist hazmat appliances from Donnybrook and Dún Laoghaire fire stations are at the scene and have set up a decontamination zone, it added.

title: ‘Scale of our waiting lists remains extraordinary’, Oireachtas health committee told
description: Public and private hospital systems overlap in a way that is ‘complicated, inefficient and unfair’, said Dr Domhnall McGlacken-Byrne
content:
The health system continues to be “a cause for scandal”, with the “spectacle of vulnerable and sick people waiting on hospital trolleys and plastic chairs sadly [still] commonplace”, an Oireachtas committee has been told.
The Health Committee also heard many of the Sláintecare reforms have “faltered”, with the problems in health “inextricable from a political context in which healthcare in this country is not regarded as a basic right of all people”.
There were calls for legislation to make universal healthcare an entitlement rather than a policy aim.
Dr Domhnall McGlacken-Byrne, one of the co-founders of Doctors for Universal Healthcare, appeared before the committee. He said a system that gives everyone access to care when they need it, no matter who they are, was “premised on a conception of healthcare not as an economic good or an item of charity, but a human right of all people”.
He said Ireland did not have such a system, either in policy or in practice.
“In our hospitals, the scale of our waiting lists remains extraordinary,” said McGlacken-Byrne. “Earlier this year, the number of people awaiting specialist hospital care surpassed one million, a remarkable figure for a country of our size. In our emergency departments, the spectacle of vulnerable and sick people waiting on hospital trolleys and plastic chairs sadly remains commonplace. Our public and private hospital systems continue to overlap in a way that is complicated, inefficient and unfair.”
He noted that “half of Irish people feel the need to buy private health insurance ”, adding: “In return, we get systems of care which too often are overburdened, fragmented and difficult to access. This is a bad deal.”
Sláintecare was adopted in 2017 to reform the system and implement a policy roadmap to universal healthcare. He said it has had “some successes, such as the introduction of the chronic disease management programme in general practice, and the public-only consultant contract in our hospitals”.
He added, however: ”Many of the Sláintecare reforms have faltered.”
McGlacken-Byrne pointed to the lack of access to GP care to cover the whole population and “stubbornly high waiting list figures and trolley statistics”.
He called for “sustained, targeted, equitable investment in primary care, in acute services and in prevention”, and said hospitals “urgently require expansion of public hospital capacity”, with universal primary care rolled out swiftly.
Associate professor Sara Burke, director of the Centre for Health Policy and Management at Trinity College Dublin , said a broad commitment to deliver universal healthcare was welcome, but conceded that “despite the policy intent, Ireland is a long way off having a universal health system”.
She said there is “considerable ambiguity about what ‘universal’ actually means in practice and this perhaps has caused the public to disengage with the issue, denying us an important force for change”.
Burke said progress “requires moving beyond eligibility expansion towards a clearer statutory entitlement framework, supported by sufficient workforce and service capacity, public understanding, engagement and support. Universal healthcare will only be realised when quality care is consistently available and accessible in practice, not merely promised in policy.”
The chairman of the committee, Social Democrats TD Padraig Rice, called for a return to the principles of Sláintecare and an “acceptance that reform costs money and that investment will pay dividends later”.
He said there were “enough factors already working against Sláintecare including the strength of private sector lobbying”, adding that the committee had an obligation to “reaffirm our commitment to Sláintecare and redouble our efforts to ensure it’s fully implemented”.

title: Try walking in Patrick Kavanagh’s shoes: one man’s pilgrimage from Inniskeen to Dublin
description: For Frank Greally, this ‘gratitude walk’ has great historic resonance
content:
E ven before Mayo ended their great All-Ireland drought this year, Frank Greally had been in the habit, from time to time, of doing something called the “Gratitude Walk”.
His primary cause for gratitude was just being alive. Born prematurely in June 1951 at the Coombe Hospitalin Dublin, he wasn’t expected to survive. Hence his first ever journey, to an emergency baptism in nearby Francis Street.
But survive he did to grow up in Ballyhaunis and become, among other things, a fine athlete, whose Irish national junior record for 10,000m lasted half a century.
So six years ago, mid-pandemic, he embarked on his first Gratitude Walk, from the Coombe to Ballyhaunis. Then last June, to celebrate his 75th birthday, he repeated the trek in the opposite direction.
By summer’s end, his many blessings would include having lived to see the end of a supposed Mayo GAA curse that began when he was still in a pram. With renewed gratitude for the wonders of life, therefore, he is now walking again.
On Monday, he left the village of Inniskeen, Co Monaghan, at the start of a leisurely stroll to Dublin.
This route is not as long as his marathon hikes between the Liberties and Mayo. But for a devoted fan of Patrick Kavanagh , it has great historic resonance, replicating a walk the poet himself made in 1931 when he set out to visit Dublin for the first time.
[ Autumn reflection: Frank McNally finds poetic cheer in the October gloom Opens in new window ]
Kavanagh took three days to cover the 60 miles or so. Greally is in less of a hurry, partly because he’s taking time out along the route to visit schools and promote the Daily Mile, a scheme encouraging children to do at least 15 minutes’ exercise a day.
Another difference from 1931 is that, unlike his predecessor, he’s not wearing hobnail boots. Kavanagh’s footwear was hand-made by his father, a cobbler. The profession was beginning to suffer then from mechanised mass production. But the young poet who walked to Dublin was a champion of the hand-made product.
On which note, and speaking of All Irelands, his journey to Dublin came soon after what is still Monaghan’s only appearance in a senior men’s final, against Kerry in 1930.
Many reasons were advanced subsequently for their 18-point hammering, but perhaps the least convincing was Kavanagh blaming it on Monaghan’s factory-made boots, which in the wet conditions, he claimed, had “turned to paper”.
A more worrying change for walkers in the intervening decades is the quantity and speed of traffic on Ireland’s roads. There were very few cars in 1931, and Kavanagh would have been far from alone in travelling by foot.
But almost nobody walks in rural Ireland any more, or if they do, it’s an extreme sport. Speaking to me on the phone somewhere between Slane and Ashbourne during the week, Greally confirmed that roads were much scarier for walkers than they used to be.
It might be imagination, he admits, but even in the past few years, traffic seems to have speeded up: “Everyone is in such a blooming hurry now.” This may also be true of life in general: all the more reason for him to take time out and give thanks.
Happily, he has been blessed with some very good company along the route, including Thomas Ruddy, an Inniskeen historian, and more recently Herbie McClelland, an old friend from Donore Harriers athletic club.
Then there is the logistical back-up of Seán Callan, his bagman from Ardee. He has also enjoyed moral and spiritual support from Kavanagh stalwarts Art Agnew and his sister Una, author of one of Greally’s favourite books, The Mystical Imagination of Patrick Kavanagh: A Buttonhole in Heaven.
When he’s not walking, Greally is running, or writing about running, or organising races. In 1981 he founded Irish Runner magazine, which is still – yes – running after all these years, with him now as consultant editor.
And next month he will host his annual Remembrance Run, a 5k in which participants commemorate lost loved ones. It was first held in 2012 to mark the then recent death of his friend Con Houlihan. The latest instalment, on November 8th, will be Houlihan’s and the event’s 15th anniversary.
[ Frank Greally’s startling exposition of the secret self Opens in new window ]
As with his Ballyhaunis walks, the Dublin end of the current route includes a hospital. Not the Coombe this time, but – in keeping with the Kavanagh theme – St James’s.
That was where the poet underwent treatment for lung cancer in 1955, recovery from which inspired one of his finer sonnets, describing an unexpected outbreak of love he felt afterwards for such local banalities as “Rialto Bridge” and “the inexhaustible adventure of a gravelled yard”.
Some of Frank Greally’s inexhaustible adventures are detailed on his website, gratitude.ie . The end of the latest walk, meanwhile, will be at 2pm on Friday, at the seated Kavanagh sculpture near Baggot Street Bridge.

title: EU leaders clash over CAP and military funding as budget talks become fractious
description: Taoiseach Micheál Martin says landing final EU budget deal will be ‘challenging task’
content:
European Union leaders have clashed over the fate of the Common Agricultural Policy and other traditional funds doled out from the Brussels purse, in negotiations to piece together the union’s new seven-year budget.
Governments are split on the size of the overall budget package, and where funds should be allocated or cut.
A summit bringing together EU leaders saw prime ministers and presidents restate their red lines, heading into what will be a fractious number of months to hammer out a deal.
Several leaders repeated calls for the next EU budget to direct substantially more funding towards defence and efforts to “rearm” Europe’s militaries, in light of the Russian threat.
Multiple diplomats and senior EU officials said discussions at the European Council summit on Thursday evening were not expected to lead to any breakthrough, but instead increase the pressure on governments to eventually shift closer towards a compromise.
The negotiations will decide how much money will be set aside for CAP payments for farmers, “cohesion” funding to develop roads and infrastructure in poorer regions, overseas development aid, spending on defence and border control, and a jumbo fund to boost Europe’s economy.
The next EU budget will run from 2028 until 2034, but European leaders are pushing to agree a deal on the size of the package, and how it would be funded, by the end of this year.
“It is a challenging task because there is a real divergence of opinion between those who want a lower budget and those who want a higher budget, and those who want to protect traditional programmes ... and those who want a modern, outward-looking Europe,” Taoiseach Micheál Martin said.
The Government was “never going to please everybody” with its proposed revision to move the budget talks forward, he said.
Ireland, in its deal-making role holding the presidency of the Council of the EU, suggested trimming back the scale of a draft €1.7 trillion budget package .
It is understood European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen told leaders some of the cuts in Ireland’s proposal were hard to understand.
The head of the union’s executive arm singled out changes that would limit the next budget’s flexibility, leaving less room for Brussels to respond to unexpected crises over the seven-year period.
Dublin saw its job as narrowing the gap between EU states who want a bigger, more ambitious European budget, and fiscally conservative governments who favour sweeping cuts.
A coalition of “frugal” states – Germany, the Netherlands, Finland, Denmark, Sweden, Austria – want the draft budget to be cut by several hundred billion euro.
Many of that group favour slashing funding for CAP and cohesion development schemes. That would leave more money to put towards what they view as “modern” priorities such as defence, migration control and economic competitiveness.
A larger group, made up of Italy, Spain, Poland and many eastern and southern states, want CAP and the other traditional planks of the EU budget to be protected.
[ Ireland’s EU presidency proposes budget cut of €141bn for the bloc Opens in new window ]
Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni and Romanian president Nicușor Dan brought this like-minded group together for a pre-summit huddle, where the leaders underlined their demands to “safeguard” CAP and cohesion funding.
They also committed to keep pushing for the joint budget to have “sufficient resources” to address Europe’s common priorities, Meloni and Dan said.
The Irish Government has handed the job of piecing together a final deal over to António Costa, the European Council president who chairs the summits of national leaders.
The joint budget is predominantly financed by national contributions based on the size of each member states’ economy. Governments are separately fighting over ways they could raise additional revenue at EU level to fill some of the shortfall between the bloc’s big ambitions and what member states are willing to pay.

title: Households billed for up to 10 times amounts owed due to Gas Networks Ireland glitch
description: Network operator apologised to customers and said it was trying to establish how many bills were affected
content:
Domestic gas customers around Ireland have been issued with estimated bills that are up to 10 times the amounts owed, as a result of glitch in the Gas Networks Ireland (GNI) system, The Irish Times has learned.
The network operator apologised to impacted customers and said it was still trying to establish how many bills were affected.
It said the cause of the problem had been identified and fixed.
Bills that are issued by all the State’s providers have potentially been impacted. GNI said they had contacted all the providers who had subsequently paused issuing new bills until they could be sure the bills would more accurately reflect the amounts owed.
One customer based in Dublin was shocked when he opened his gas bill on Wednesday and read that he owed 10 times what he had actually used over the billing period.
Other gas users were told that their bill was more than three times the true amount owed based on the gas they had used.
“Gas Networks Ireland was made aware of an issue affecting a number of estimated gas meter readings provided to gas suppliers,” a spokeswoman said.
“The cause of this issue has been identified and fixed. Gas suppliers have been informed and have paused issuing further bills to customers.”
She said the network operator was “now working closely with gas suppliers and the Commission for Regulation of Utilities to address the affected readings and to ensure that the necessary corrections are made to those customer bills”.
The spokeswoman said GNI “apologise for any unnecessary worry and inconvenience caused to any gas customers”.
The latest issue with domestic energy bills has echoes of a glitch that hit users of smart electricity meters earlier this year.
On that occasion a software update led to customers mistakenly being told their usage had soared.
Some customers with smart meters were told they had run up bills of more than €5,000 over the course of a single day. As with the GNI problem, customers of multiple providers were impacted.

title: Irish firm with €2.4m debt to Revenue allegedly diverted business to Gibraltar entity, court told
description: Liquidator alleges company moved money to bank account on the island
content:
An Irish scaffolding company wound up with debts of almost €2.4 million owed to Revenue has allegedly diverted its business to a Gibraltar-registered entity as part of an attempt to place its assets beyond the reach of creditors, it has been claimed in the High Court .
Adrian García Díaz, a liquidator appointed to Instant Upright Ltd, alleges the company – despite its winding up – has moved customer money to a bank account in the name of a Gibraltar entity, also named Instant Upright Ltd.
This week Judge Brian Cregan granted several reliefs to Bernard Dunleavy, counsel for the liquidator with Keith Farry, including an interim freezing order of the company’s assets.
The judge also granted permission for the liquidator to serve the proceedings on several defendants outside the jurisdiction, including the Gibraltar entity and named individuals the liquidator says are linked to the company.
The individuals are: Robert Stowe, with an address in Monaco, who the liquidator says is 50 per cent beneficial owner of Instant Upright Gibraltar; Andrew James Haynes of Cadiz, Spain, who the liquidator says is also a 50 per cent shareholder; Joseph Oxley of Dubai, who the liquidator says is a company director; Serge Marino of Le Cannet, France, who the liquidator says is a company director; and Graham Donald Croot of Melbourne, Australia, who the liquidator says is a company director.
Reporting on the proceedings was restricted for 48 hours to allow time for the liquidator’s lawyers in Gibraltar to make an application to the courts there for an equivalent freezing order.
In a sworn statement Díaz said he was seeking the freezing orders in circumstances where there was “a real and substantial risk” the defendants will “dissipate, conceal or remove” money in the bank account held in the Gibraltar company’s name beyond the liquidator’s reach.
Díaz said he was appointed as liquidator over the company by court order in January, following a petition by the Revenue Commissioners. He said the company is also indebted to the ESB in the sum of €30,831, RFC Security Ltd for €43,405, and Korea South East Power Co Ltd for €2.9 million.
The liquidator said he sought to obtain information from Instant Upright directors about the company’s affairs but no response was received.

title: ‘It’s heartbreaking’: Award-winning Tullamore chocolatier’s stock destroyed by factory fire
description: Extensive damage to Bon Chocolatiers premises in Co Offaly following fire on Tuesday evening
content:
“It’s heartbreaking,” says chocolatier Daniel Linehan surveying the aftermath of a fire in the unit beside his Bon Chocolatiers factory in Co Offaly on Tuesday evening.
“There were one or two orders that day that weren’t out in time. So that’s all wasted. There’s one pallet with 38,000 handmade truffles made by myself and my team. It’s sickening,” he says.
“It’s probably five full days of labour – myself and the team all hand rolling and putting it all in. Usually there’s a huge sense of pride and relief when you pack the pallet waiting to be collected. Certainly it’s a different feeling looking at them now.”
Linehan and his partner, Georgia Quealy, founded Bon Chocolatiers in 2020, and won the top prize at the 2025 Blás na hÉireann Awards . They also supply Dunnes Stores as part of the supermarket’s Simply Better range.
At about 8pm on Tuesday night, as Linehan finished his shift later than usual, he heard a fire alarm.
Initially, “everything seemed to be okay”, but when he exited the factory after checking his premises, he saw smoke “billowing” from a neighbouring unit and called the fire brigade.
Soon after, he opened the door of Bon Chocolatiers. “I couldn’t even see six inches in front of me. It was just black smoke.” The damage to the premises was extensive.
Stock, raw materials and machinery were all damaged in the blaze.
Sharing the news in a video on social media, Linehan says the outpouring of support has been “overwhelming”.
A post shared by Bon Chocolatiers (@bonchocolatiers)
“I must have 40 unread WhatsApp messages there and that is from every type of food producer,” he says.
“A number of what would be considered to be our competitors have said: ‘We only produce five days a week. Our kitchen is empty two days, if you need to come down you can use all of our equipment’,” says Linehan. “These horrible moments sometimes bring out the best in people.”

title: Sally Rooney’s novels are not easy to find in Israeli bookstores despite their popularity
description: Author’s works still for sale from East Jerusalem’s Palestinian booksellers after being pulled from Israel’s shelves in 2021
content:
It’s not easy to find Sally Rooney ’s novels in Israel .
Conversations with Friends and Normal People were translated into Hebrew by the Israeli publisher Modan. But in 2021, Rooney turned down a translation offer from the publisher for her third novel, Beautiful World, Where Are You, citing her desire to support the global BDS (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions) movement.
In response, Israel’s two largest booksellers, Steimatzky and Tsomet Sefarim, pulled all of her novels from their shelves. The two chains, with more than 200 bookshops across Israel as well as dominant online retail platforms, control the Israeli market, making it almost impossible to find Sally Rooney titles save for a handful of independent, progressive outlets.
One of them, Migdalor in Tel Aviv, says Rooney’s books continue to be popular, in particular the Hebrew translations. They have sold hundreds of copies of each title, including her bestselling 2024 novel Intermezzo, which she published through November Books, an independent Israeli publisher that meets conditions set by the BDS movement for exemption from the boycott.
Those conditions include not operating in occupied territory or receiving state funding and expressing support for the Palestinian cause, including the controversial right of return for Palestinian refugees.
Sally Rooney’s books can, however, be found in Palestinian bookstores in East Jerusalem.
[ McEntee to raise Sally Rooney book sales withdrawal with UK foreign secretary Opens in new window ]
Mahmoud Muna is the owner of the Educational Bookshop in East Jerusalem’s main Salah al-Din Street and the iconic Bookshop at the American Colony hotel.
Both stores were selling Sally Rooney books long before she became embroiled in the Israel- Palestine conflict although demand soared after Israeli bookshops stopped selling her titles. Israeli customers now account for about 20 per cent of sales. Muna also distributes Rooney’s books to Palestinian bookshops in Ramallah and Bethlehem and a small store in Hebron.
“This morning we sold another two copies because she’s in the news again. Often, it’s people buying her books as a gift for friends. Normal People is the most popular but we’ve sold hundreds of her books over the years,” Muna told The Irish Times.
“I’m in favour of people who have a platform using it to support voices that promote liberty, freedom and justice. That includes writers, artists and sportsmen and women,” Muna said.
“Every act of art is political at its core and in that sense they have a right to say whatever they want. I would want Rooney’s voice and other voices to be heard.”
The BDS movement said it had evaluated 98 Israeli publishers and found that only November Books met its conditions for exemption.
The backlash in Israel against Rooney was not long coming. One official described the cultural boycott of Israel as “anti-Semitism in a new guise”. Other critics noted that Rooney allowed her novels to be translated in other countries with a record of human rights abuses.

title: Garda technical experts tracking down source of bomb threat emailed to schools
description: Investigation assessed credibility of email attributed to foreign militant group
content:
Garda technical experts are attempting to track down the person who sent a bomb threat to more than 150 schools on Wednesday.
A Garda source said the investigation assessed the credibility of the email – which is understood to have been attributed to a foreign organised militant group – and are now attempting to find the source.
It was not believed there was any immediate risk to students .
Searches were carried out by gardaí in various schools across the country, though reported army bomb disposal unit operations were related to other incidents.
Some searches continued by members of staff on Thursday before schools opened, but the vast majority were operating as normal upon the advice of gardaí .
While no bombs were found, a source said that making false bomb threats remained a crime under the Criminal Justice (Terrorist Offences) act of 2005.
The threats came on the same day as widespread industrial action over public sector pay , when the majority of schools across the country were closed and pickets placed outside.
The Garda previously confirmed it was “aware of a communication” that was sent to a number of schools on Wednesday and that it was assessing the “contents and credibility” of the emails.
A Defence Forces spokesperson said on Wednesday that the Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal Team “deployed twice today to locations within Dublin” but that the deployments “were routine and of no significance”.

title: Ukrainian woman flew to Ireland every fortnight for six months to collect social welfare
description: Tetiana Stakhiv (51)  never lived here and was caught out after a Department of Social Protection check, court hears
content:
A Ukrainian woman has been jailed for flying in and out of Ireland to collect social welfare every fortnight for six months despite never having lived in the State.
Tetiana Stakhiv (51) had been receiving treatment for a serious medical condition, Dublin Circuit Criminal Court heard.
However, that was no longer available when the war broke out in Ukraine, so she began buying her medication on the black market.
Stakhiv was before court on Thursday, having pleaded guilty to the theft of €9,103 from the Department of Social Protection between October 2025 and last April.
Garda Louise Keane told the court how the defendant was living outside Ireland and travelling every two weeks to collect jobseeker’s allowance payments.
When a Department of Social Protection check was carried out, it was found Stakhiv had never lived at any of the addresses she had given to the department.
Keane said several flights between Dublin and Poland aligned closely with Stakhiv’s collection dates and that the woman’s passport also tallied with their records.
She said Stakhiv was arrested in May and told gardaí she came to Ireland in late 2023 to collect her then-underage daughter and return to Ukraine.
The garda agreed with Jennifer Jackson, defending, that Stakhiv had been affected by the war in Ukraine. She accepted Stakhiv had no cash, personal belongings or trappings of wealth when arrested.
Keane also agreed Stakhiv had no English and no family or ties to this jurisdiction and that custody would be difficult.
The garda also accepted Stakhiv was not a criminal mastermind and said she had sympathy for the woman “to a degree”.
Jackson told the court that, once released from custody, Stakhiv was planning to live with her 24-year-old daughter in Bulgaria.
Judge Martin Nolan said it was a serious matter for somebody to come here, pretend she was living here and then fly in and out to collect social welfare.
Jackson said Stakhiv came from a war-torn country and had not committed the offences to go on extravagant holidays.
“Her world was turned upside down. She couldn’t get her medication,” Jackson said, saying Stakhiv was remorseful.
The judge imposed a 10-month jail sentence and backdated it to May 25th when Stakhiv went into custody.

title: ‘Such a lovely person’: Tributes paid to homeless woman who died in tent in Dublin
description: Locals remember Antonia Edgeworth from old library in Dún Laoghaire and seeing her on the city’s streets
content:
Tributes have been paid to former library worker who died in a tent in Dublin ’s city centre last weekend after years of living on the streets.
Antonia Edgeworth, who was in her early 50s and was originally from Foxrock , Co Dublin, was found in an unresponsive state in a tent on Henry Street in the north city centre on Sunday morning.
The mother of one is understood to have been homeless for many years and to have struggled with addiction.
“Gardaí responded to the discovery of a body on Henry Street in Dublin city Centre on the morning of Sunday 11th October, 2026,” a Garda spokesman said.
“A postmortem will determine the course of the investigation.”
Dún Laoghaire independent councillor Hugh Lewis led tributes to her at a council meeting on Monday evening.
In a follow-up post on social media, he said: “Tragically, Antonia was found deceased on a Dublin street yesterday morning. She is another victim of the housing crisis and demonstrates the vulnerability that our homeless and rough sleepers face each night.
“Antonia was ... a well-known face in Dún Laoghaire town and friend to many.”
She is understood to have worked also in the now-closed Magic Carpet pub in Cabinteely and in Supervalu.
A friend, who did not wish to be named for fear of upsetting Antonia Edgeworth’s family, said she had “fond memories” of chatting with her in the old Dún Laoghaire library on Library Road, in the early 2000s.
“She was a lovely girl, a genuinely nice girl who would go out her way to help you find a book. She cared deeply about her family, especially her daughter,” said the friend.
The woman said Antonia Edgeworth had a private rented accommodation in the town which she lost, possibly due to rent arrears.
“I thought at the time: why did no one intervene to help her get a roof over her head? Anyone could see she was struggling.
“I met her by chance last year in Dublin, near the Ilac centre. She was so thin. It was freezing cold and I says to her: ‘What are you doing out here with just a sleeping bag?’ She said she was going to get herself together.
“And then a couple of weeks ago in Dún Laoghaire this girl [Edgeworth] comes up to me, gives me a hug. I told her to look after herself. I thought to myself though: ‘She is going to die if she stays out on the streets.’ It’s very sad. She hadn’t a bad bone in her body.”
Glenda Harrington, who runs the Friends Helping Friends soup kitchen on Tuesday nights in Dublin city centre saw the deceased last week. She described her as “funny” and “very well-spoken”.
“She was loud. You’d hear her coming, but there was no badness in her. The thing you’d always notice was she was so little. She also looked freezing,” she said.
“She was very much a loner, wouldn’t go into the hostels. She was scared of the hostels and to be honest, she was soft. She wouldn’t have done well in the hostels.”
In another tribute posted on social media, a former colleague said: “I worked with Antonia in SuperValu many years ago, she was such a lovely person.”
Another said she thought Antonia Edgeworth was “one of the nicest” she had ever met and that she had “the pleasure of having many chats with her; absolutely heartbreaking the way she passed away on our streets when she should have had a home”.
Antonia Edgeworth’s father Michael died in April 2024. He was described on his death notice as “beloved husband of Siobhan, loving dad of Ross and Antonia and a much-loved grandad of Breanna, Jake and Casey”.
Funeral details for his daughter are yet to be announced.

title: Global stocks edge lower as AI and rate fears hit tech
description: Investors unnerved by ​valuations of firms in artificial intelligence sector
content:
Global equity markets edged lower on Thursday as concerns about artificial intelligence (AI) spending and higher interest rates fuelled a continued sell-off in technology and chip stocks.
Investors have been unnerved by ​valuations of companies in the AI sector as more voices question the sustainability of demand for data centres.
On Wall Street, the tech-heavy Nasdaq was down and the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index was down 2 per cent. The benchmark S&P 500 reversed losses in early trade and was trading higher led by healthcare and materials stocks while the Dow was up ​1 per cent.
Kenmare Resources , the Dublin-listed titanium minerals miner, saw its shares rise 3.7 per cent despite downgrading its production forecasts for the year. The company is the subject of a potential bid by a company controlled by the Abu Dhabi royal family.
Ryanair enjoyed a 1.5 per cent bounce in its shares – they closed at €22.43 – as oil prices slipped. The rise came even though the EU’s top court ruled regulators must take the limit of 32 million passengers at Dublin Airport into account when allocating take-off and landing slots to airlines there.
Airlines, including Ryanair, had challenged the Irish Aviation Authority’s decision to take the cap into account when allocating slots for winter 2024 at the airport, prompting the High Court to refer the matter to the Court of Justice of the European Union.
Bank of Ireland and AIB were down 1.2 per cent and 0.8 per cent respectively amid speculation that central banks globally will raise interest rates again before Christmas, a move that might dampen borrowing.
In European equity markets, the CAC 40 in Paris ended up 0.8 per cent, while the DAX 40 in Frankfurt added 0.3 per cent.
In Frankfurt, semiconductor firm Infineon lost 4.8 per cent. Siemens Energy, which provides power solutions to data centres, shed 2.6 per cent, both well above earlier lows.
A brutal tech-led sell-off had hit stocks in Asia. South Korea’s KOSPI index, ‌whose ‌flock ​of top chipmakers made it one of the main beneficiaries of AI euphoria, plunged almost 8 per cent, while the Nikkei 225 fell nearly 5 per cent.
“I think the sell-off reflects investor caution towards the more vulnerable segment of the ⁠AI ecosystem, with tech chiefs advocating a slower pace of ​frontier model development,” Rong Ren Goh, portfolio manager at Eastspring ​Investments, said.
“Markets increasingly question the sustainability and trajectory of demand for computing capacity. These concerns are compounded by higher funding costs, which raises the investment hurdle rates ‌of capital-intensive AI infrastructure projects.”
The FTSE 100 outperformed global peers on Thursday, encouraged by domestic economic data and lower bond yields, benefiting from a lower exposure to technology stocks, which continued to be volatile.
It ended up 115.49 points, 1.1 per cent, at 10,840.
London’s gains came as investors shifted away from technology stocks amid fears about the future of capital expenditure, Chinese competition and expected returns from AI.
Credit checker Experian led the FTSE-100 risers, up 5.9 per cent, with telecoms firm BT up 4.3 per cent and accountancy software provider Sage up 5.6 per cent.
JD Sports Fashion climbed 4.3 per cent as it hosted analysts in Orlando.
Although there were no updates to financial guidance or targets, management focused the discussion on how they plan to drive growth and profitability in the US sporting goods market.
Computacenter, a beneficiary of strong data-centre spending, led the fallers, down 5.6 per cent. Technology-focused trusts Polar Capital Technology and Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust declined 4.7 per cent and 1.2 per cent respectively.
Antofagasta fell 4.1 per cent as it reported lower third-quarter output and 2027 guidance than hoped.
The London-based miner focused on Chile sees copper production in 2027 between 630,000 and 690,000 tonnes compared to company-compiled consensus of 692,000 tonnes.
CoreWeave, a heavily indebted data-centre operator in the eye of the recent AI storm, fell another 1.8 per cent following a 15 per cent drop on Wednesday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1.07 per cent, the ⁠S&P 500 rose 0.16 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.23 per cent. – Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Stephen Kenny says ‘chaotic’ League of Ireland scheduling lacks professionalism
description: Bohemians end media boycott to belatedly criticise Shamrock Rovers manager Stephen Bradley
content:
Stephen Kenny has questioned the professionalism of the League of Ireland with the St Patrick’s Athletic manager describing end-of-season match scheduling as “chaotic”.
“We’re a tick-box league,” said Kenny. “Can we get a match in the [international] window? Can we tick a box? Certainly, it is not professional.”
The League of Ireland has defended their fixture planning, particularly the decision to give Shamrock Rovers a 24-hour advantage over Bohemians to recover before last Monday’s 2-1 victory at Tallaght Stadium.
As a result, Rovers went six points clear of St Pat’s and Bohs at the top of the Premier Division with three games remaining.
The former Republic of Ireland manager branded the decision as “undemocratic”.
“The people within professional football understand the difference between a three- and a four-day recovery,” wrote Kenny in his programme notes ahead of Shelbourne’s visit to Inchicore on Friday night.
“There needs to be closer scrutiny of these decisions and the impact they have on the fairness of the competition.”
The FAI League department, keen to avoid a clash of televised matches with their broadcast partners, scheduled Rovers’ 3-1 defeat of Drogheda United to last Thursday, which was shown live on Virgin Media, and put Bohemians’ FAI Cup semi-final loss to Waterford on RTÉ a day later.
“For all the resources [Rovers manager] Stephen Bradley has at his disposal, he doesn’t need the league to be giving them another leg-up,” said Bohemians manager Alan Reynolds on Thursday.
“Ultimately, a game was brought forward by the league that gave Shamrock Rovers an extra 24 hours’ rest before a massive game against us. It’s not right. It’s not right for Bohs, it’s not right for St Pat’s, and it’s not right for anyone who believes in a level playing field.”
Rovers celebrated like they had clinched the title last Monday when goals from John McGovern and Dylan Watts sank Bohemians in front of a 10,208 crowd in Tallaght .
“We are playing to win a league, they are not,” said Bradley on Monday night.
Reynolds ended the club’s two-week media boycott on Thursday morning to belatedly complain about Bradley’s comments and Rovers’ post-match celebrations in Tallaght.
“It’s not the first time Stephen Bradley has decided to run his mouth off and insult the opposition to distract from the carry-on of his own club,” said Reynolds.
On Monday, a brawl broke out after full-time in Tallaght, prompting referee Rob Hennessy to show three red cards to players. Crucially, Bohs have lost captain Dawson Devoy for Waterford’s return to Dalymount Park on Friday night, while Rovers must make do without teen duo Michael Noonan and Naj Razi.
All three players could receive three-match suspensions at a disciplinary hearing next week if it is found that violent conduct took place. If that transpires, Noonan will have played his last game for Rovers before his move to Nottingham Forest in January.
Bradley is due to provide an injury update on Victor Ozhianvuna next week. The 17-year-old, who has not played since May, is due to complete a €2-million move to Arsenal in January.
“Victor’s scan was moved to next week,” said Bradley, “so we’ll have news early next week.”
Kenny was also critical of St Pat’s 27-day gap since their last fixture against Sligo Rovers on September 19th due to Uefa’s extended international window.
“These players are brilliant professionals and they’ve been let down by this sort of chaotic planning,” he said. “Whoever came up with the idea [to have FAI Cup semi-finals straight after the international break] has no respect or empathy for players’ efforts, their commitments, their sacrifices. It’s unprecedented.”
Kian Leavy will return for St Pat’s following a hamstring tear, but teenage striker Sam Rooney is out for the season with a shoulder injury.

title: How a former Nato chief cashed in on the big business of lobbying for foreign governments
description: Critics say the perception of a revolving door between politics and lobbying undermines public trust in those who hold power
content:
A fter spending more than a decade at the top of European politics, first as prime minister of Denmark and then secretary general of the Nato military alliance, Anders Fogh Rasmussen walked into the world of lobbying with a big reputation to trade on.
When his term leading Nato concluded in 2014, the liberal veteran of Danish politics established his own political consultancy, Rasmussen Global, advising a roster of high-paying private companies as well as sovereign countries and governments.
While it is common for political leaders leaving office to enter the world of private consultancy, or the lucrative speaker circuit, Rasmussen’s business is unusual for having several countries as clients.
The former prime minister’s remarks on international affairs carry weight.
In one guest opinion article for The Guardian about the tense situation in Taiwan , Rasmussen criticised China ’s aggressive posture and called on Europe to take a firmer line standing up for the small, self-governing island.
However, the 2019 opinion piece did not disclose that the Danish politician’s lobbying firm had a contract to advise the Taiwanese government at the time.
Other opinion pieces written by Rasmussen arguing for the European Union to forge closer ties with Japan failed to disclose that his business also has a long-standing contract to advise the Japanese government.
The Irish Times can also reveal Rasmussen’s past work as an adviser to then-Ukrainian president Petro Poroshenko, part of a contract worth at least €300,000 a year, was paid for by the holding company of a pro-western Ukrainian oligarch.
Rasmussen Global employs a big team to help run the lobbying operation, between Brussels, Copenhagen and Kyiv. Former Fine Gael junior minister Dara Murphy is a vice-president and partner at the consultancy firm.
In Brussels, that work involves helping foreign governments understand and navigate the European Union’s complicated policymaking process, getting in the ear of politicians and senior officials, tracking what way the wind is blowing on certain debates and on occasion, it seems, having Rasmussen himself make the case publicly for a client’s interests.
In one instance, he penned an opinion piece for The Guardian in 2019 describing Taiwan as a “shining city on the hill” for democracy activists.
[ There is nothing more Irish than a former housing minister lobbying on behalf of a developer Opens in new window ]
The former Danish prime minister warned China was building up its military presence in the South China Sea and Beijing’s attitude to Taiwan was increasingly hostile.
In his opinion piece, Rasmussen called on the EU to live up to its values and “defend the largest Chinese democracy from authoritarian pressure” by meeting Taiwan’s leaders and forging closer investment links.
A short biography below The Guardian’s opinion piece stated Rasmussen was previously secretary general of Nato and a former prime minister of Denmark.
Lobbyists in Brussels are required to submit annual declarations to a transparency register, listing their clients and a rough range for how much they were paid for EU-related work.
[ Ukraine to resume strikes on Russian refineries, Zelenskiy says Opens in new window ]
Records show Rasmussen’s consultancy shop has worked for Taiwan since 2019. Initially, the contract was only worth up to €50,000, but increased by €300,000-€400,000 in 2023 and 2024. The work was worth at least €100,000-€200,000 last year.
The declarations are not required to cover lobbying work conducted beyond EU institutions, so they offer a partial snapshot rather than the full picture.
Rasmussen Global has advised the Japanese government since 2018. For a period, it also had a contract with Albania’s foreign ministry, records show.
Rasmussen has counselled Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy’s office pro bono since the Russian invasion, and has been vocal in calling for western powers to support Kyiv in the bitter war.
A spokesman for The Guardian said its code of practice states all guest contributors “must declare any commercial or personal interest, or any affiliations to organisations connected to the topic they’re writing about”.
When asked if the former Nato chief flagged his firm’s Taiwan contract to the newspaper, a spokesman for Rasmussen Global said its email archives did not stretch back to the period in question.
On foot of questions from The Irish Times, The Guardian amended the article to state Rasmussen Global was advising Taiwan’s embassy in Brussels at the time he wrote the piece.
