Rasmussen, chairman of the consultancy firm, has travelled to Taipei, Taiwan’s capital, to make the case for greater western support.
Last year he delivered the keynote address at the Yushan Forum, a conference organised in Taipei by Taiwan’s foreign ministry, where he said Taiwan “stands as a beacon of liberty”.
He first visited the island in 1994 as a member of Denmark’s parliament, he told the audience, according to a recording of the speech. “I will keep making the case for Taiwan and Europe to strengthen our ties politically, economically and culturally,” he said.
In another opinion piece published by Le Monde in 2018, Rasmussen called for the EU and Japan to work closer together to counter the rise of “illiberal” sentiment around the world.
The former prime minister’s article in the French newspaper did not disclose that his firm had been hired by the Japanese government that year.
[ ‘No silver bullet’: Energy crunch could bite Europe this winter Opens in new window ]
The EUobserver, a small publication in Brussels, carried an opinion piece from Rasmussen last December: “The case for EU-Japan ties”. The article made no mention of his firm’s long-term contract to advise Japan.
In the article, Rasmussen pushed for Europe to view Tokyo as “central” to its future strategy. “From satellite systems to missile defence, from industrial innovation to standard-setting in critical technologies, Japan can be both partner and template,” he wrote.
Separate from his for-profit work, Rasmussen was in line for a prominent new role helping to shape European defence policy recently.
Kaja Kallas, the EU’s foreign policy chief, wanted him to chair a high-level group of political and military leaders to report on how governments could close gaps in Europe’s defence capabilities. The idea was scrapped following pushback from foreign ministers, who felt the project doubled up on work under way elsewhere.
The son of a farmer, Rasmussen was elected to Denmark’s Folketing when he was 25 in 1978, and at the time was the youngest member of the national parliament.
He later led the centre-right Liberal party to electoral victory and government in 2001, and secured two further terms in office before he stepped down to become Nato secretary general in 2009.
His reputation as a statesman was burnished when he steered tricky negotiations on the eastward enlargement of the EU, paving the way for 10 new member states to join the union.
After eight years as a prime minister and five years leading Nato, he had a packed contact book to draw on when setting up his consultancy business.
The Rasmussen name helps get the firm’s lobbyists into important rooms. Representatives for the company have regularly met European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s advisers, EU commissioners and senior civil servants to talk about geopolitics, China relations, security, the war in Ukraine and energy policy.
[ ‘He’s with Putin’: Ukrainians recoil at Trump’s pressure campaign Opens in new window ]
Logs of lobbying meetings reported by MEPs show Rasmussen Global staff are also active in the European Parliament.
Records show other private companies, such as global public relations giant FleishmanHillard, law firm DLA Piper and boutique lobbying outfit Alber & Geiger, have previously been contracted to work for foreign governments.
Rasmussen took on the Republic of Armenia as a client in 2022. A small country in the South Caucasus, Armenia is wedged between two old adversaries, Turkey and Azerbaijan. Its government has been carefully trying to shift away from Russia’s orbit and build bridges to Europe.
That contract was worth at least €400,000 in 2023 and 2024, and at least €300,000 last year, filings to the transparency register show.
Nicholas Aiossa, director of Transparency International’s EU office, said the perception of a revolving door between politics and lobbying, particularly when it came to high-profile figures and former leaders, could damage the trust citizens placed in those in power.
Rasmussen Global often promotes its pro bono work advising the Ukrainian government and Zelenskiy’s office. One big project mapped out ways western allies could guarantee Ukraine’s security after a peace deal.
A spokesman for the firm said its efforts in Ukraine, led by Rasmussen himself, were the company’s most significant work with a government.
The company was “fully compliant with all transparency obligations in all jurisdictions” in which it operates.
“Anders Fogh Rasmussen has consistently advocated for the world’s democracies to work more closely together,” the statement said.
“Rasmussen Global’s work is driven by that same goal. That’s why our sovereign clients are, and have exclusively been, democratic governments – and why we frequently highlight our work in bringing them together. This includes pro bono work, most notably with the government of Ukraine as they fight Russian aggression,” it said.
The consultancy work in Ukraine hasn’t always been for free, though. In fact, it was Rasmussen Global’s most lucrative line of business in Brussels for several years.
One of the wealthiest men in Ukraine, Victor Pinchuk made the beginnings of his fortune during the collapse of the Soviet Union, initially in the steel industry, before expanding into oil and gas and the media.
He later married the daughter of Leonid Kuchma, who was president of Ukraine from 1994 until 2005, a period when rampant corruption proliferated through many echelons of the state.
Pinchuk’s wealth grew significantly during Kuchma’s time in power, though the oligarch has always denied accusations that he benefited from insider connections.
In one high-profile privatisation case, the state sold its largest steel plant to a group that included Pinchuk for a bargain rate of about $800 million. The deal caused public outrage.
The sale was reversed after Viktor Yushchenko, who survived a poisoning plot, won the re-run 2004 presidential election. He defeated Kuchma’s man, Viktor Yanukovych, a pro-Moscow politician who would become president years later and fled to Russia after the 2014 Maidan revolution in Kyiv.
The steel mill in southern Ukraine was auctioned for $4.8 billion in 2005.
It was around this time Pinchuk established Yalta European Strategy, a non-profit that organises a high-level political forum once a year to discuss Ukraine’s European path. He held the first event several months before the pro-democracy Orange Revolution protests rocked Ukraine.
[ Trump is blaming Zelenskiy for a problem of his own making Opens in new window ]
One source who had dealings with Pinchuk said the Yalta Forum seemed to have been a way for the oligarch to carve out a new political constituency for himself. The businessman went on to build up ties to western elites over the two decades that followed.
Past speakers have included Bill and Hillary Clinton, Tony Blair, Zelenskiy, Boris Johnson and other prominent politicians, academics and business figures.
UK Companies House records show Pinchuk incorporated a company in London in 2007, EastOne, to hold his sprawling investments. From 2016 until April 2020, EastOne was Rasmussen Global’s biggest client.
The contract to work on Ukraine’s “Euro-Atlantic integration” was worth, at a minimum, €300,000-€400,000 a year, EU records show.
This work involved Rasmussen acting as an adviser to then-Ukrainian president Poroshenko.
Curiously, Rasmussen’s work advising the Ukrainian president was paid for by EastOne.
A spokesman for Rasmussen confirmed the work for Poroshenko was part of the “framework” of its contract with Pinchuk’s firm.
The former Nato head also joined the board of Pinchuk’s Yalta conference in 2017. Filings for Yalta European Strategy Ltd, which is registered in the UK, show Rasmussen resigned from the role this April.
A spokeswoman for Pinchuk said the Ukrainian businessman has long rejected allegations that his companies unfairly benefited from any insider connections in the early 2000s.
The oligarch previously said that, while the steel mill deal was legal, politically it was a mistake to be part of the bid as the then-president’s son-in-law.
He has always maintained he made his fortune before marrying his wife and did not benefit from political favours.
“EastOne engaged Rasmussen Global to support Ukraine’s Euro-Atlantic integration. The engagement, including remuneration, was fully declared in the EU transparency register,” his spokeswoman said.

title: Aidan O’Brien content to stay on familiar ground with Constitution River and Gstaad for Ascot
description: Early-week plans ‘might have been a bit of a knee-jerk reaction’ admits trainer
content:
Aidan O’Brien is optimistic Constitution River and Gstaad will show their true colours on Qatar Racing British Champions Day at Ascot on Saturday.
The three-year-olds have been campaigned over a mile and a quarter and a mile respectively this season, with Constitution River winning the French Derby and Coral-Eclipse and Gstaad claiming Classic glory in the Irish 2,000 Guineas.
But O’Brien had been giving serious considering to switching the pair on Saturday, even going as far as supplementing Constitution River for the Queen Elizabeth II Stakes on Monday at a cost of £70,000 (€82,800).
Ultimately, however, connections have decided to give both colts another chance over their familiar distance.
“We were thinking very strongly of running Gstaad over a mile and a quarter and Constitution River over a mile,” he said. “But the way the week went on and we saw it was going to be a very competitive Champion [Stakes], we just thought it would be tough on Gstaad going into a mile-and-a-quarter race like that for the first time.
“We felt that Ascot suits him very well, he won the Coventry there and we think he’s an absolutely top-class miler.”
Constitution River has had to make do with minor honours in the Juddmonte International and the Irish Champion Stakes on his last couple of starts, hitting the front on both occasions before faltering late on.
While those defeats left O’Brien questioning his stamina, he is keen to try again now his string appears to have recovered from a midseason blip.
“There were circumstances around a lot of the horses’ last runs because the horses were a little bit under the weather at the time,” said the Ballydoyle handler.
“We were going to do it [switch races], but the more we thought of it we felt it wasn’t fair to Gstaad to throw him into a mile and a quarter race of that calibre and it wasn’t fair on Constitution River to go back to a mile.
“It might have been a bit of a knee-jerk reaction. I was saying to myself maybe I’ve been doing the wrong thing with them all year and maybe I was, but especially when it looks as though the ground is going to be nice, we’ll give them another go and we’re going to find out a lot more.”
O’Brien also considered running his star stayer Scandinavia in the British Long Distance Cup, but he has now been put away for next season following his narrow defeat to Caballo De Mar in the Prix du Cadran a fortnight ago.
“Obviously Scandinavia would have been a very strong chance, but the lads felt maybe he’s had plenty of racing this year” O’Brien added.
“He is very well and his last piece of work was very good. We went to France expecting the ground to be gone for Ascot and with the benefit of hindsight maybe we should have skipped France.
“We went to France and ran a very good race, maybe we would have preferred a stronger gallop because he does stay very well and we felt he was a little bit unlucky.
“We just thought looking at the Ascot Gold Cup next year, we just felt it was the right thing to wait.”

title: More than 30 children killed after school roof collapses in Pakistan
description: Victims, mostly aged under 13, died in incident in city of Peshawar along with one teacher
content:
At least 34 schoolchildren and a female teacher were ‌killed on Thursday when the roof of a school collapsed during morning classes in the northwestern Pakistani city of Peshawar, police and rescue officials said.
As panicked parents and relatives thronged ​the school site to search for their loved ones, rescue workers spent hours pulling children from the rubble of the privately run Al-Khair Education Center.
The children killed or injured at the Al-Khair school were as young as six, Lady Reading Hospital spokesman Mohammad Asim said.
Some of the injured were in a critical condition, he said. The hospital declared an emergency as medical staff treated the wounded.
At least 45 children suffered injuries, ranging from minor wounds to severe trauma, said Arif Khattak, regional director of the rescue department.
Television footage showed rescuers clawing through ​debris with their bare hands and carrying bloodied children to waiting ambulances as residents crowded the narrow alley where the school stood.
A higher-floor roof collapsed on to students in classrooms below, crumpling two ⁠storeys of the building, a rescue ​official said.
“The fatalities include 12 girl students and a ​female teacher,” Lady Reading Hospital spokesperson Mohammad Asim said.
Three children were in critical condition, with head injuries, ‌Asim said, adding that most of the ​20 injured brought to that hospital had been treated and sent home.
The incident took place ⁠at 8.48am local time (3.48am Irish time) and the ⁠rescue operation lasted ​for four to five hours, Khattak said.
“It was a weak building structure,” Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed said. “Its roof was overloaded with construction on a weak structure, which caused the collapse.”
Saeed said the school’s owner had been arrested and an investigation launched. ‌A total of 110 students were attending lessons in ​three classrooms when the roof caved in.
Distraught relatives accused the school of ignoring concerns about the ⁠building’s condition and demanded accountability.
“Make an example of them, ⁠a lesson for all, so that ​no one dares open a school just to make money without providing facilities,” said Mohammad Zaman, who lost two nephews in the collapse.
The school was located in a poor, crowded neighbourhood of Peshawar, capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa where Pakistan’s president imposed a state of emergency on Sunday saying the provincial government had failed to tackle Islamist militancy from neighbouring Afghanistan, an allegation it denied.
Pakistan spends less than 1 per cent of its GDP on education, leaving many families dependent on low-cost private schools.
Many of them operate from poorly maintained rented buildings with limited oversight, contributing to recurring safety concerns. In June, at least 14 children died when the roof of a tutoring centre housed ‌in a dilapidated building collapsed ⁠in the eastern city of Lahore.
There was no immediate comment from school officials.
Prime minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the tragedy and offered condolences to the victims’ families, his office said.
Jawad Ahmad, whose son and daughter attended the school and survived, said the ‌news left him devastated.
“It felt as if someone had shot me in the chest when I learned that the school building had collapsed,” he said.
The province, governed for ​years by the party of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan, has frequently been at odds with ​the federal administration.
President Asif Ali Zardari imposed a new governor on the province when he declared the state of emergency on Sunday, sharpening the tensions. – Reuters

title: ‘I couldn’t fight back’, woman accusing Russell Brand of rape tells London court
description: Woman says Brand forced himself on her after they met at a cabaret show at the 1999 UK Labour Party conference
author_name: Tristan Kirk, Ted Hennessey and Josh Payne
content:
A woman accusing Russell Brand of raping her in a hotel room broke down in tears in court as she insisted “I couldn’t fight back”.
Brand, now 51, is accused of forcing himself on the woman after meeting her at a cabaret show at the 1999 UK Labour Party conference.
She told Southwark Crown Court in London on Thursday that she invited Brand to her hotel room believing he was gay and says she did not feel able to flee when he turned on her.
“I know he raped me, I know I said ‘no, no, I don’t want this’”, she said, in a series of exchanges with Brand’s barrister Ian Winter, telling the him: “I am the one who is being silenced.”
She said she struggled to breathe when Brand was on top of her and told the court: “I did not want sex from him ... I couldn’t fight back.”
Raising her voice, she added: “I don’t love him, I don’t find him attractive. Never have.”
Brand has been accused of telling the woman “it’s just fun” as he was raping her that night in 1999.
He denies allegations from six different women and has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault.
In her recorded interview with the police, which was played to the court on Thursday morning, the woman said she talked to Brand at the cabaret show and invited him to continue their conversation at her hotel room when he showed interest in her political ideas.
She says Brand, once in the room, stripped off his shirt and began to “prance around” like an ostrich and perform “goose steps” in the style of Basil Fawlty.
The woman said she first saw Brand as an “intellectual person” when they met and believed she was “sexually safe with him”.
When Winter suggested she “wanted a young man who you met for a short time to join you in a very small bedsit”, she responded: “I thought he was a gay man, very softly spoken, very effeminate.”
She responded angrily to the suggestion that she “fell under his spell”.
“He seemed to have empathy for what I was saying, but all the time he seems to have had something else in his mind.”
She told police Brand had a “snake-like, disgusting” body and she told the court she saw him “as a bit of an ‘ugh’” who made her feel “nauseous”.
Over the course of nearly two hours of heated cross-examination, Winter accused the woman of not telling the truth about her encounter with Brand and suggested she would have left the hotel room if she was in danger of being raped.
She said she was “terrified” as she complied with Brand’s request that she photograph him and baulked at the idea that she could have fled.
She asked: “Where am I supposed to go? Run into the night and him chase after me?
“Of course I wanted to distance myself but I had nowhere to run.”
At one point, Winter also clashed with trial judge Joel Bennathan, who had to “shush” the barrister during a tense exchange in court.
The barrister was grilling the alleged victim on whether she said out loud that she did not wanted to have sex with Brand during the hotel encounter.
When the judge interjected to point out evidence the court had earlier heard on the video-recorded interview with police, Winter said tersely: “Forgive me ... I am conducting a cross-examination.”
When the two legal figures then spoke at the same time, the judge said to the barrister: “Shush. I’m the judge.”
At the close of the cross-examination, the woman referenced Brand’s recent appearance on Piers Morgan’s show “talking about shame and reputation”, and told the court: “I am the one being silenced.”
Faced with the suggestion that she wanted to have sex with Brand at the time, she added: “I can 100 per cent tell you I did not consent, I did not find him attractive.”

title: McEntee to raise Sally Rooney book sales withdrawal with UK foreign secretary
description: Minister for Foreign Affairs ‘shocked’ publisher can no long sell works because of author’s support for Palestine Action group
content:
Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee will speak directly to Britain’s foreign secretary Ed Miliband after it emerged the work of award-winning Irish author Sally Rooney will no longer be distributed in Britain due to her support for direct action group Palestine Action.
McEntee said she was “shocked” when she read the news about the bestselling writer’s work, which will be withdrawn in the UK as publishers Faber & Faber can no longer pass on her royalties because of her support for UK-based direct action group Palestine Action.
Rooney donated some of the proceeds from the sale of her books to support Palestine Action, which was proscribed in the UK in July last year as a terrorism-supporting organisation. It is an offence under the UK’s Terrorism Act to support banned organisations.
“I have spoken quite a number of times to the foreign minister who very clearly has said set out his position in support of Palestine ,” McEntee said. “I’ve engaged with him on steps and measures that they can take as a government to show and reflect that support in terms of this specific decision.”
“I was shocked as well by what I read about Sally Rooney. I like her work. We all watch it and read it as well,” the Minister said.
She added: “I have no problem in speaking directly to the minister, but obviously any decision around their laws or how they’re interpreted by the courts is a matter for the courts there.”
She was responding to Social Democrats arts and culture spokeswoman Sinéad Gibney, who described Rooney as “one of our most prominent contemporary authors” whose books and TV shows based on them “are cherished the world over”.
Publishers Faber & Faber will no longer sell her books in the UK, explaining they can no longer pass on royalties to her because of her support for Palestine Action and the interpretation of UK antiterrorism laws as they apply to that.
Gibney said “she’s not alone. Thousands of people, including older people, disabled people and even a vicar, have been arrested in the UK for merely holding up signs, saying that they support Palestine Action.”
Meanwhile, UK Labour MPs called for the country’s proscription of Palestine Action to be overturned.
Ian Byrne, one of nine Labour government MPs to vote against the July 2025 decision to ban Palestine Action, said the impact on Rooney was “draconian”.
Byrne, who represents the constituency of Liverpool West Derby, told The Irish Times that the decision by Rooney to withdraw her books from Britain was “yet another unintended consequence of that awful piece of legislation”.
“I was completely against the proscription at the time and now I am thankful I voted the right way. This thing with Sally Rooney is just another element of it, targeting an author. It’s like banning books, part of that drift towards authoritarianism we’re worried about.”
He said he had received “no blowback” internally in Labour for his opposition to the ban and added “hopefully the prime minister [ Andy Burnham ] will review it”.
Richard Burgon, another Labour rebel MP who voted against the proscription, said Rooney was “one of the best writers of her generation”.
“This ban [on Palestine Action] needs to be overturned,” he said.
Elsewhere, Downing Street has defended the ban on the activist group, whose members have faced criminal charges and, in a few cases, conviction, for violent incidents before the group was banned in 2025.
Palestine Action initially won a court challenge to the ban, but it was overturned this year in the UK’s court of appeal. While it is proscribed it remains illegal under British law to show support for the group, which has attacked factories in Britain linked to UK military support for Israel.
When asked about the decision made by Rooney, a spokeswoman for UK prime minister Andy Burnham said the court of appeal “found that Palestine Action had committed terrorist acts”.
Burnham’s government has taken a harder line against Israel than the previous Keir Starmer administration, whose government also voted to recognise Palestine as a state. Miliband last month announced Britain would sanction Israeli West Bank settlements over the “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians.

title: Trump cancels plan to livestream man’s execution following widespread condemnation
description: Nidal Malik Hasan killed 13 people at a Texas military base in 2009 and is set to die by firing squad
content:
US president Donald Trump has shelved a widely condemned plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.
In a social media post on Thursday, Trump argued that broadcasting such an execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan” but said that “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device”.
“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” Trump added. “That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose.”
Hasan, who was left paralysed from the waist down after being shot by law enforcement during the shooting at Fort Hood, now uses a wheelchair.
The US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, said last week that the execution of Hasan would be a public event. Hasan’s sentence will be the first military execution in more than 60 years, and would have been the first in US history to be publicly broadcast.
In an interview with Real America’s Voice, Hegseth said he supported the public execution “because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things”.
But since then, the Trump administration has faced sweeping criticism, and comparisons to dictatorships in Iran and Afghanistan. Many US lawmakers, from across the political spectrum, have come out and condemned the announcement, and urged Hegseth to reconsider.
[ Trump and Hegseth’s road to barbarism is a threat to America’s standing Opens in new window ]
Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress, wrote in a post on social media: “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.”
In another post, the senator Lisa Murkowski, a Republican from Alaska, said that there was “no need to livestream any execution, including this one”, adding that she “would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America”.
The representative Rob Bresnahan, a Republican from Pennsylvania, said in a post on social media that “an execution shouldn’t be a live-streamed spectacle”, adding that “the focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment”.
“Their pain deserves respect, not a public show,” he said.
On Friday of last week, the United Nations’ office of the high commissioner for human rights warned that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”, and the president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops also condemned the Pentagon’s plan, saying in a statement that “in no way can Hassan’s actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”.
“The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people,” the statement added.
That same day, JD Vance appeared to cast doubt on whether the Pentagon would actually livestream the execution, telling reporters that “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen” when asked about the plans. The vice-president also said that if it is livestreamed, “I’m not going to be watching it.”
Trump himself had made contrasting remarks in recent days on whether the live stream would happen. On Friday, he told reporters that he “absolutely” approved the plan to livestream the execution, but on Saturday he said that he had not yet made a final decision on whether to go through with it.
“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it” he said. “’Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but I’ll make a decision.”
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian on Thursday about Trump’s announcement. - Guardian
[ The Irish Times view on US executions: a barbaric practice Opens in new window ]

title: U2 to start world tour in Mexico, Brazil and Argentina in spring 2027
description: Announcement comes as U2 gear up to release new album Carnaval De Luz
content:
U2 have announced their return to stadiums. The band’s world tour will kick off in Mexico City on February 23rd, 2027, with further shows in São Paulo and Buenos Aires.
Dates for Europe and North America will be announced in the coming weeks as the band gear up for the release of their first album in nine years, Carnaval De Luz , on November 13th.
The band, who recently played from the balcony of Bewley’s Cafe on Grafton Street to celebrate 50 years together, will be supported by Beck for the dates in Mexico, Brazil and Argentina.
Tickets for the tour, titled Carnaval De Luz presents: The Greatest Show on Earth, will be available first on U2.com. A subscriber presale will open on Monday, October 19th, at 10am local time. Remaining tickets will be available on U2.com from Thursday, October 22nd, at 10am local time.
The tour marks U2’s first return to a stadium setting since they concluded The Joshua Tree Tour in 2019. They last played Croke Park in Dublin in 2017 and the 3Arena in 2018.
The Greatest Show on Earth tour will feature a set list drawn from the band’s 50 years in existence, meaning fans can expect to enjoy classics such as With Or Without You and One alongside material from their forthcoming album.
Carnaval De Luz is U2’s 16th studio album and the band have said it will offer a more back-to-basics approach after a few years where mixes for previous albums ping-ponged between numerous producers.
Helmed by Jacknife Lee, the record features Torn, a duet between Bono and the late Dolly Parton . The album also has a song, The Mirror Maker (Rosalía), dedicated to Grammy award-winning Spanish singer Rosalía.
Fellow Irish band Fontaines DC also have a duet with Rosalía on their new album, Dopamine Chamber, which drops on Friday. Their duet, Where is Gone?, has the same regal languorousness as the 1967 single Some Velvet Morning from Lee Hazlewood and Nancy Sinatra.
[ U2’s new album Carnaval de Luz features Dolly Parton and Bono duet Opens in new window ]
U2’s new single, their third from the record, is the song from which the tour plucks its name: The Greatest Show on Earth. Co-written by U2 and Brian Eno, it’s a sombre, reflective tale of lovers fighting to keep faith in one another.
“We were once the greatest show on earth,” Bono sings, over elegiac, juddering guitars from The Edge.
In recent years, Drummer Larry Mullen jnr was forced to sit out the band’s Sphere shows in Las Vegas due to a neck injury that almost forced his retirement.
After surgery in Dublin, the recovery process meant relearning his drumming technique, a daunting process which took many months. He told Rolling Stone Magazine he will assess his fitness level on tour night by night.
“Even if I can’t play for 2½ hours, if I can play for an hour, that’s enough,” he said. “I’ve had it so good that I’ll accept that.”
Mullen discussed the gratitude he has for his career in a recent podcast series by The Irish Times, Drummer Seeks Musicians , about the origins of the band, back when Mullen placed a note on his school noticeboard at Mount Temple Comprehensive in Dublin to recruit members.
“My parents moved the kitchen table out of the kitchen into the back garden and they facilitated this mad idea with these people showing up in a kitchen in suburban Dublin and playing instruments at high volume,” he told Róisín Ingle.
“That they allowed that is the thing that is most striking to me.”

title: Giovanni Leoni’s return from injury delayed in fresh blow to Liverpool
description: Italian sustained anterior cruciate ligament injury in his debut against Southampton last year
content:
Giovanni Leoni’s Liverpool return has been delayed because of the severity of the knee injury sustained on his debut, Andoni Iraola has revealed.
The central defender had been expected to resume team training during the recent international break but that schedule has been put back by about a month.
Leoni, a €35-million signing from Parma in 2025, sustained an anterior cruciate ligament injury against Southampton 13 months ago. Iraola said the damage extended beyond the 19-year-old’s ACL, adding Liverpool must tread carefully with his rehabilitation as a consequence.
“It is taking more time than we wanted,” the head coach said. “With Gio, the plan was to train with the team in this past international break. It is probably now going to be the next international break [which starts on November 9th], so we have lost one month in the process.
“With Giovanni’s injury, I wasn’t here but talking to the medical department it wasn’t just an ACL. It was a bad injury, a lot of things around the knee were involved apart from the ACL. I think he has to be very confident in the rehab and the process has to be very careful with him.
“We want to make sure once he comes to the team he stays there in a good place. It’s true we’ve had a little bit of not a setback but a delay if you want. The plan now is he starts in the next break. It’s not that far off, but a little bit later than we expected.”
Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak and Cody Gakpo remain doubts for Saturday’s Premier League trip to Brentford having missed Liverpool’s last two fixtures with injuries picked up on international duty.
Iraola had more encouraging news concerning Liverpool’s other long-term injury casualties, Conor Bradley and Hugo Ekitiké. Northern Ireland international Bradley has been sidelined since sustaining a serious knee injury at Arsenal in January, and Ekitiké’s impressive debut season at Liverpool was cut short by an Achilles injury against Paris Saint-Germain in April.
“They are both doing very well and they are in a good place,” said Iraola. “Conor is not so far from training with the group – not full training, but doing some things with the group. Hugo is a little bit behind that, but that was always the plan. He is still doing very well according to the plan.
“When they have been injured for so long it’s difficult to say [when they will be back], but I think Conor is not very far from starting doing things with us.” − Guardian

title: Enoch Burke: High Court again orders arrest and jailing of sacked teacher over school trespass
description: Court had to act to protect Wilson’s Hospital School’s children from Burke’s ‘appalling behaviour’, judge says
content:
The High Court has ordered Enoch Burke ’s arrest and committal to prison over his breach of a court order banning him from Wilson’s Hospital School, his former workplace.
Judge Brian Cregan on Thursday also ordered for the sequestration of a car used by the teacher to travel to the Co Westmeath school.
After hearing evidence of Burke’s repeated trespassing at the school since the beginning of the academic year, the judge said his conduct “amounted to a deliberate and flagrant contempt of court” and ordered his immediate attachment and committal to Mountjoy Prison.
The judge said the court had to act to protect the school’s children from Burke’s “appalling behaviour” and to uphold the rule of law.
Burke was not present at the hearing, because he was in attendance at the school, the court heard.
Burke has already spent over 700 days in prison in different spells for his breaches of the order banning him from the school, made over three years ago by Judge Alexander Owens. He was most recently released from prison in July.
He has also amassed fines of over €208,000 over his breaches.
Burke was formally dismissed from his position at the school in May for gross misconduct. He maintains that he was not validly dismissed and continues to seek his reinstatement through the courts.
The school suspended and later dismissed Burke over his conduct towards its then-principal Niamh McShane at a school religious event in June 2022.
The confrontation arose in circumstances where McShane had earlier directed teachers to address a student by a new name and with the pronouns “they” and “them”. Burke, an evangelical Christian, has maintained this request went against his religious beliefs.
When Burke continued to trespass at the school following his suspension, the school sought court orders banning him from the premises.
The school returned to the High Court this week following multiple instances of Burke trespassing on the school premises since late August.
Moving the school’s application for Burke’s attachment and committal, Rosemary Mallon, counsel for the school’s board with Mark Curran, said the school had done “everything possible” to try to avoid coming back to court. She said the school was conscious of the unprecedented situation it finds itself in and the fact that Burke has spent over 700 days in prison.
However, counsel said the school was in a position where it had no other option but to seek the court’s protection.
Mallon opened a statement sworn by school principal Noel Cunningham, who said Burke’s trespassing was disrupting the normal running of the school.
Cunningham outlined how Burke, on various occasions, waited for security personnel hired by the school – at a cost of €1,200 per week – to leave their position at the school gates before walking on to the school premises. On occasion, Burke gained entry to the school reception, he said.
Cregan said Cunningham’s affidavit made for “lamentable reading” and showed the “great difficulty” the school had in dealing with Burke’s presence.
In a sworn statement replying to the school’s application, Burke did not deny that he had trespassed at the school, the judge noted. He noted Burke’s assertion that the order banning him from the school is unlawful.
The judge ordered Burke’s immediate attachment and committal to the prison. He also ordered the sequestration of a vehicle driven by Burke to school. He placed a two-week stay on that order.

title: Legal profession ‘got away scot-free’ from reforms in wake of 2008 crash
description: Infrastructure taskforce member says interconnector will be first major test of legislation
content:
The State’s legal profession “got away scot-free” from reforms in the wake of the 2008 economic crisis and it still requires change, a member of the infrastructure taskforce has said.
Speaking to the British-Irish Chamber of Commerce, Sean O’Driscoll , however, said many of the concerns he had about the threat of legal blockages to major projects have been overcome by new fast-track legislation.
The legal profession “is a great profession, but like every other profession, there are areas in it that need a bit of cutting up,” he said, in conversation with Marc Lowry, head of growth at Azets Ireland.
The number of judicial reviews being taken to challenge major projects dominated debate a year ago, though a cap has now been imposed on the legal costs that claimants are able to recoup.
“Prior to that, it was uncapped,” said O’Driscoll, the former chief executive of Glen Dimplex. “What has happened? You guessed it – there’s been a significant reduction in the number of judicial reviews that have been brought through. You’ve even seen judicial reviews being withdrawn.
“Last week, three of the four outstanding ones on the Galway bypass were withdrawn."
Others have been withdrawn to Dublin’s MetroLink and the north Dublin drainage system.
The Critical Infrastructure Act, which brings major projects to the top of the planning and courts queue, had significant support from Dáil TDs, who passed it on a vote of 132-15. O’Driscoll says this offers “an indication of the political and public mood”.
However, he said the first major test of the new critical infrastructure list will come once plans get under way to build the north/south 400kV electricity interconnector from Meath, Cavan and Monaghan, into Armagh and Tyrone.
The interconnector, which is unpopular with many farmers and householders along the route, is very important, said O’Driscoll. “It will enhance the security in the country. It will enable the single market.
“So, there are a huge number of positives, but there has been local political opposition to it. It’s now on the critical infrastructure register to be fast-tracked to the very top. The utilities on both sides of the Border are ready to go.
“This will be the big challenge. Is the political system up there when it comes to public acceptance?”
O’Driscoll has repeatedly warned that planning delays are badly hampering the delivery of public projects. He added: “We all talk a good story when it comes to infrastructure, better roads, but none of us like disruption around us either. We all have a job to communicate that infrastructure is good for us.
“That’s why we have 2.8 million people working in this country. We won’t have 3.8 million people working in this country with the same level of infrastructure. So, we have to plan for the future.”
He praised Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers for supporting fast-tracking infrastructure. “None of this would have happened without Minister Jack Chambers,” said O’Driscoll.
“He put his political reputation on the line. He put his career on the line, as indeed did every single member of the Cabinet. Very brave politicians did what they did. Some fantastic, brilliant civil and public servants behaved really magnificently.”
Meanwhile, he said local authorities must operate more consistently by similar rules, rather than having situations where a road engineer in one county takes a completely different view on issues to a neighbouring authority.

title: Israel’s former spy chief sues Netanyahu for ‘blood libel’ over October 7th attacks
description: Ronen Bar has accused Netanyahu of trying to shift the blame on to him
content:
As Israelis prepare to vote in a critical election, prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu is facing fresh questions over the failures that preceded the Hamas-led attack on October 7th, 2023, following a defamation lawsuit brought by the former chief of Israel’s national security agency.
Ronen Bar, who led the Shin Bet security agency at the time, alleges that Netanyahu knowingly published false accusations about his conduct before the attack to shift responsibility on to him.
For the past three years Netanyahu has argued that his military and security chiefs were taken by surprise and failed to warn him. He said if they had only woken him earlier before the dawn attack, he could have ordered an appropriate military intervention.
The €861,000 lawsuit was filed over an X post published by Netanyahu on September 28th, accusing Bar of recognising warning signs but deciding not to call and alert him, concealing intelligence information received before the militant invasion of southern Israel, and attributing “failures” and “criminal” offences to the resigned head of service.
Bar accused Netanyahu of spreading a “blood libel” against him.
Israelis are due to vote in crucial elections on October 27th.
[ Netanyahu faces fresh scrutiny over pre-October 7th warnings Opens in new window ]
The lawsuit lists all the warnings that were presented by the Shin Bet in the months leading up to the attack and details how Netanyahu allegedly rejected recommendations to assassinate Hamas leaders, preferring to maintain the relative quiet and avoid a military escalation.
The Shin Bet also opposed the transfer of Qatari funds, via suitcases stuffed with banknotes, into Gaza, warning that some of the money was going to the Hamas military wing. The lawsuit asserts that Netanyahu ordered the transfers to continue, believing it would keep the enclave quiet.
In response to the action, Netanyahu addressed just one of the allegations: the claim that the intelligence chief did not call him directly on the morning of the attack.
“Ronen Bar, who saw the warning signs on October 7th and didn’t call me, now says he didn’t have my phone number. Ronen, are you serious?”
[ Israel sets date for general election as public support for Netanyahu falls, polls show Opens in new window ]
Bar’s staff did call Netanyahu’s military secretary 16 minutes before the start of the attack, using the accepted communication channel, but he decided not to wake him up.
About 1,200 people, mostly civilians, were killed on October 7th, with 250 taken hostage into Gaza. The ensuing Israeli war in Gaza has to date resulted in the deaths of more than 77,000 residents, according to local authorities.
Despite the magnitude of the catastrophe, Netanyahu has refused to appoint a state commission of inquiry or accept direct responsibility, in contrast to military and intelligence chiefs who have resigned.
Polls show a clear majority of Israelis support an inquiry into October 7th and the main opposition parties have pledged to set up an investigation as a top priority for an incoming government.

title: Zelenskiy defies Trump as Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian refineries
description: Ukrainian president expresses anger at withdrawal of US intelligence sharing as Musk says Starlink military technology is `controlled’ by US government
author_name: Alex Russell and Ben Hall in London
content:
Volodymyr Zelenskiy has said Ukraine will restart strikes on Russia ’s oil refineries as he expressed anger over a “dangerous” withdrawal of US intelligence and simultaneous weakening of Starlink satellite internet service at a time of intense Russian attacks.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelenskiy said in a defiant interview with the Financial Times in London. He also lambasted Washington’s eagerness to strike business deals with Moscow and US president Donald Trump ’s apparent admiration for Russia’s president Vladimir Putin .
Asked to explain the two leaders’ relationship, Zelenskiy said Trump had an instinctive affinity for autocrats and the super-wealthy. “He [Trump] speaks about it openly and loudly that he loves such people and he respects such people. Because for him people who can be leaders 20 years, 30 years, 40 years, it means they can be very strong.”
Washington has piled pressure on Kyiv to stop hitting Russia’s refineries, claiming that a moratorium, alongside a US deal with Moscow to buy hundreds of thousands of tonnes of Russian diesel, is essential to bring down US fuel prices.
Zelenskiy said he had paused energy strikes for three days to comply with US wishes, while Moscow continued to pound Ukrainian energy infrastructure and kill civilians – more than 100 in the last week.
Following Zelenskyy’s comments, Pavel Malkov, the governor of Russia’s Ryazan province, said on Thursday that Ukrainian drone strikes had caused a fire at a refinery owned by state oil company Rosneft, adding that the damage was being assessed.
A Ukrainian official said on Thursday that Kyiv hit a refinery in Russia’s Ryazan province overnight in retaliation for Moscow’s energy strikes. Rosneft did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Ukrainian state energy company Naftogaz said Russia had struck one of its gas production facilities east of Kyiv overnight, halting operations.
Despite Ukraine’s pause, Zelenskiy said his forces had been left without US early-warning alerts for incoming ballistic missiles, while Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite communications service had been slowed down across the country, hampering frontline operations and medium-range strikes against Russian military sites.
Zelenskiy said Ukrainian military officials were told by their US counterparts that “if you will not stop [the energy strikes], we will block intelligence”, although it was subsequently presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch. He also dismissed the idea that failures of the Starlink satellite system might have been caused by a fault. “It was not a technical problem, it was the will.”
Trump earlier denied that Washington had cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Musk posted on X late on Wednesday that Starshield systems, the military-grade satellite network built on Starlink technology, were “owned and controlled by the US government”, adding: “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” referring to Trump.
The breakdown in relations between Kyiv and Washington is the worst crisis between Ukraine and its most important security partner since Trump and his senior aides gave Zelenskiy a public dressing-down in the Oval Office in February last year.
Zelenskiy stressed that Ukraine’s relationship with the US as an “honest” and “strategic” partner was essential in the fight against Russia, comparing it to Kyiv’s relationship with the UK. “Russia can fight ... all of us but only when we are not together.”
But he made clear it was not up to him to mend fences with the White House, saying: “We didn’t destroy any relationship.”
Asked whether Ukraine would halt energy strikes even if Russia continued, as a way of repairing relations with the White House, he said he could only agree if in return he was given more US-made Patriot interceptors. That was the “minimum” that he asked for, he said, adding that when he asked for more air defences the US response was to weaken Starlink’s service.
Zelenskiy said that stopping energy strikes also risked only encouraging the US and Russia to pursue more deals, potentially providing more money for Putin’s war machine.
“The question will be when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas.”
“Business is interesting between the United States and Russia,” he added. “I think that they [America] want to have energy projects and ... [that] of course for them is difficult to have when there is war in Europe.”
But Zelenskiy suggested Trump could face a public backlash. “This politically is not simple [in the US], because everybody will want to ask how it can be when some people are surviving, fighting, dying – and you make ... business with the guys with such aggression.”
The Ukrainian president was speaking in central London after a day of meetings with Britain’s King Charles, UK prime minister Andy Burnham and defence officials.
On Thursday he will address EU leaders in Brussels to plead for more robust sanctions against Russia and a faster release of EU funds to assist Ukraine’s war effort.
Zelenskiy said fighting without the US would be “very difficult” and conceded Europe would be stronger if truly united.
But a spate of elections in Europe over the next 12 months, with possible gains for pro-Russian parties, could bring “a lot of challenges” for Ukraine, he added. Asked about French far-right leader Marine Le Pen’s vow to stop financing Ukraine, he said France had a lot to lose because experience of the Ukrainian battlefield was essential for its defence companies. “It’s a win-win.”
In an implicit response to Trump’s call at the weekend for him to resign, Zelenskiy said it was “rhetoric” which Americans would not like, and which would only boost Putin. “For me, it doesn’t matter. What matters ... is that Putin feels no pressure. When he feels no pressure, he attacks, because he, you know ... got a tremendous kick out of it.”
“The division between Europe and the United States, or Ukraine and the United States, helps him [Putin] to unite his nation. It makes him feel success[ful]. It helps him to feel that he’s not losing, that he is prevailing.”
Zelenskiy went on to say that Putin was not prevailing but that the battle for supremacy in military technology – such as drones – waxed and waned, with Ukraine in the ascendancy one month and Russia the next.
Unfortunately, he added, the cutting off of intelligence and interruption of Starlink by the US have been “dangerous” for Ukraine. “We will find a way out ... but it’s better not to give him [Putin] the new life or the new will to fight.”

title: Mona McSharry seals $10,000 World Cup triple crown title with win in Astana
description: Sligo swimmer earns $10,000 bonus for winning third gold in 100m breaststroke
content:
Mona McSharry earned herself a $10,000 bonus by winning gold in the 100m breaststroke at the World Aquatics World Cup in Astana, Kazakhstan.
The Olympic bronze medallist claimed the triple crown title by completing a clean sweep in the event across the three meets of the World Cup series.
Earlier this month, McSharry won the 100m breaststroke final at the opening World Cup meet in Azerbaijan, and followed that up with another win in the event at the second meet in Uzbekistan last week.
On Thursday morning, the 26-year-old was the fastest qualifier from the heats, placing her in the centre lane for the final.
McSharry clocked 1:04.39 to win gold in what was her fastest performance of the series, with Russia’s Evgeniia Chikunova second in 1:04.76.
“There was definitely a bit of pressure,” McSharry said of going for the triple crown. “You want to be able to get better and swim faster, and I was able to do that, so I’m happy.
“Having the tactics to be able to calm the nerves is really important and just going back to being confident in my ability.”
Meanwhile, Ellen Walshe was just outside the medals in the 400m individual medley, finishing fourth in 4:29.27.
The pair will be back in action on Friday; McSharry racing in the 200m breaststroke, while Walshe will go in the 100m IM and the 200m backstroke.

title: Upgrades to Cork halting site at standstill ‘due to intimidation of contractors’
description: Armed gardaí called in after disagreement over right-of-way led to violence, Oireachtas committee hears
content:
The Garda Emergency Response Unit (ERU) had to accompany contractors on a Cork halting site where a shooting happened during a dispute in summer, an Oireachtas committee has heard.
A disagreement between neighbours about a right-of-way sparked violence at the Spring Lane site, on the city’s northside, on August 23rd.
One man suffered a gunshot wound during the confrontation.
Cork City Council approved plans in 2024 to redevelop the Ballyvolane halting site due to overcrowding and safety issues.
There are also plans for new homes at a nearby site, Ellis’ Yard, and a third site, which is out for tender.
Addressing the Oireachtas Committee on Key Issues Affecting the Traveller Community, council assistant chief executive Brian Geaney said works on the Spring Lane site had been delayed due to “law-and-order issues” and the “intimidation of contractors”.
There were 55 families on site, the committee was told at the meeting on Thursday.
He said contractors attempting to provide electrical upgrades at the site were forced to leave by a number of residents.
Geaney said the council was looking for a new contractor. He also said progress had been made on the third site with a tender going out last week.
He said €557,000 in funding was available for upgrades in electrical funding at Spring Lane, with €518,278 also secured for the upgrading of on-site “welfare units” for washing and toilets for families.
Brigid Carmody, project co-ordinator at Cork Traveller Women’s Network, showed the committee photos of the unsafe living conditions at Spring Lane.
These included photos of overcrowded conditions, potholes, which she said were “more like huge chunks of ground missing”, broken surfaces and sewage spilling out on the ground.
She also showed a photo of a cliff-face at the site, “which could collapse in bad weather”.
Breda O’Donoghue, director of advocacy at Traveller Visibility Group Cork, called for a community liaison officer to be appointed as a “conduit between residents and contractors [and] further security for engineers and contractors if safety was a concern”.
Asked by Senator Malcolm Noonan of the Green Party if long-term planning could not go ahead despite the intimidation incidents, Geaney said: “Funding from the department can’t be spent. The ERU has to go in to help us get on with work.”
Dublin North-West Sinn Féin TD Dessie Ellis said little progress had been made on electrical points and washing facilities since he visited Spring Lane four years ago.
Geaney said some progress had been made, but reiterated the security issues.
“Numerous contractors have refused to go on site due to intimidation of their staff. We want to spend the money allocated,” he said.
“Whether it’s pest control, routine maintenance, Portaloos, I have a litany of incidents where people have been stopped and intimidated and will not go back on site.
“We can’t go to provide the electrical updates.
“There are serious law-and-order issues here. One of the earlier photos showed the burnt mobile home that’s the subject of a Garda investigation.”

title: Murder accused crushed father’s head and repeatedly stabbed him, trial opening hears
description: Jury told no evidence Seth Whelan was suffering from mental disorder at time of alleged killing
content:
A Dublin man is accused of murdering his father by crushing his head and repeatedly stabbing him before leaving his decomposing body in the flat they shared for about one week, a Central Criminal Court jury has heard.
Prosecuting barrister Anne-Marie Lawlor opened Thursday’s trial of Seth Whelan (36) who responded “I don’t know” when arraigned earlier this week on a charge of murdering Michael Whelan (64). Whelan’s barrister entered a plea of not guilty on behalf of his client.
Lawlor told the jury of six men and six women that gardaí found Michael Whelan’s body on the floor of the flat he shared with the accused in Herberton Park, Rialto, Dublin 8, on February 27th, 2024. She said the alarm was raised by a neighbour who asked gardaí to carry out a welfare check after he became concerned that he had not seen Michael Whelan for some days.
When they arrived, gardaí noticed a putrid smell and when they entered the flat, they could immediately see that the deceased had met a violent death, Lawlor said. He was lying on his back and surrounded by extensive blood staining.
Seth Whelan arrived at the flat while gardaí were there and Lawlor said the jury will hear about his demeanour and what he said at that time. She said the jury would also hear there was no evidence of forced entry and when gardaí trawled CCTV footage, they established that Seth Whelan was the only person to enter or leave over the previous week.
Gardaí also established that Michael Whelan was not seen alive after he entered the flat on February 19th, eight days before the discovery of his body.
Counsel said a pathologist would tell the trial that Michael Whelan died from blunt force trauma to the head and two stab wounds that penetrated his heart and lungs. A further 41 stab wounds were inflicted after he died, Lawlor said.
Counsel told the jury that the deceased’s “skull and face were crushed in” and she asked the jury to consider that the injuries he suffered suggest that the person who inflicted them intended to cause death.
The pathologist was also able to say that the body had lain for approximately one week, meaning he died on February 19th or 20th. During the period between when the prosecution says Michael Whelan died and when his body was found, Lawlor said the accused sent a message to an acquaintance telling him his father had died.
Lawlor said this and other messages sent during that time would be relevant when the jury considered that in his Garda interviews, Seth Whelan denied knowing that his father was dead.
Lawlor also told the jury that there would be no evidence Seth Whelan was suffering from a mental disorder at the time of his father’s death. She said the jury may have heard of cases where a person is found to be legally insane and therefore not responsible for their actions.
However, she added: “I want to be clear, lest there be any misapprehension, that does not arise in this case ... That is not something you are going to be asked to look at.”
The trial continues before Judge Caroline Biggs.

title: Jeffrey Donaldson told of ‘descent into disgrace’ as he is given 15-year prison term
description: Former DUP leader noticeably without Christian lapel pin worn during four-week trial for child sex abuse crimes
content:
Jeffrey Donaldson , unlike his two victims who sat a short distance from him in Newry Crown Court, showed no emotion as a 15-year prison sentence was imposed on Thursday.
Hands clasped in front of him, the former DUP leader stood in the dock and tilted his head slightly as Judge Paul Ramsey told him that his “prolonged campaign” of sex offences against young children had led to a “catastrophic descent into disgrace”.
Dressed in a navy suit and pink tie, the 63-year-old was clean-shaven; his appearance unaltered from the weeks before his dramatic arrest in March 2024 when he was the toast of Washington following Stormont’s restoration.
However, gone was the Christian fish pin he had worn on his lapel throughout the four-week trial in June.
The woman Donaldson had raped as a nine-year-old girl almost 40 years ago sat with her head bowed throughout the 30-minute sentencing hearing. It was not until the former Lagan Valley MP was led away that she broke down.
The second and younger victim of the two women sat behind her. She stared at Donaldson throughout the judge’s sentencing remarks.
She blinked away tears as he was returned to custody.
The small, wood-panelled courtroom fell silent while the judge read extracts from the women’s harrowing victim-impact statements.
“Every day I pray to God to let me die,” said the woman he raped, known as Complainant B throughout the trial.
[ Jeffrey Donaldson ‘deserves every day’ of 15-year sentence for sex offences, says DUP Opens in new window ]
She wondered what it is like “not to be afraid at night”, the court heard.
The trauma of the sex abuse she suffered at the hands of Donaldson – he was 25 years old when he raped her – had affected every day of her life and “every relationship I’ve ever had”.
“What would it be like not to wake up shaking, not to have nightmares and not to lock away every feeling I have?” she said.
“What happened took away my ability to trust people and, in all honesty, I don’t think I really know what trust or love truly is. Nothing can ever change what was done to me. I wish it could.”
Ramsey relayed how the younger victim had grown up feeling “ashamed and dirty” with “extremely low self-worth”.
Her childhood had been “stolen” from her.
The impact of sustained sexual abuse had led to her being on medication since her 20s; it was “suffocating and debilitating”.
[ Donaldson victims hailed for ‘courage’ and ‘bravery’ following ex-DUP leader’s sentencing Opens in new window ]
The victim’s husband, who gave evidence during the trial, sat beside her in the public gallery.
They were accompanied by a team of police liaison officers who had been present during each day of the trial.
No members of the public were allowed in the court. The two victims have been granted anonymity for life.
“What was done to me has broken me,” the judge read from Complainant A’s statement.
She wants the court to understand that, he said.
Donaldson listened intently but remained impassive throughout.
Some of the sentencing comments included graphic details of the rape.
Both women gave evidence during the trial from a separate room in the Co Down courthouse, which was streamed on video in the main courtroom.
They underwent days of cross-examination from Donaldson’s barrister, as well as the barrister of Eleanor Donaldson, his wife and co-accused.
Eleanor Donaldson, who was found to have “done the acts” in relation to aiding and abetting charges under a trial of the facts, will be dealt with at a separate disposal hearing next month.
On Thursday, the judge described the devastating impact of the high-profile trial on the victims.
They had been “retraumatised” by the “public nature” of the case and its fallout.
There had been social media scrutiny and intrusion into their private lives, and even friendships had been affected, the court heard.
The reality has been “so much harder to bear than anticipated” and has had a “profound impact”, the younger victim said of her trial experience.
Doing this “so publicly has been horrific”, she added.
[ Woman sentenced to three months for breaching anonymity of Donaldson victims Opens in new window ]
To compound the victim’s trauma, Donaldson has “doubled down on his denials” and shown no remorse, Ramsey told the court.
He has sought leave to appeal his conviction since being found guilty in a unanimous verdict on all 18 sex offences committed between 1985 and 2008.
“There has not been, and doubtless will not be, one word of regret, apology or shame from this man to at least provide his victims with some crumb of comfort,” Ramsey said in his closing sentencing remarks.
It was only through the “courage, resourcefulness and determination of two young women” that he had been brought to justice for the crimes he had committed against them when they were children.
Outside the court, the courage of the two victims was also singled out by the Police Service of Northern Ireland ( PSNI ) and the Public Prosecution Service (PPS).
Their bravery in coming forward to report sex abuse was the “catalyst” for a “thorough PSNI investigation”, Catherine Kierans, head of the PPS serious crime unit, told the media.
An hour before he was driven away in a prison van to Maghaberry prison outside Lisburn to begin his sentence, senior investigating officer in the case, Leah Crothers, outlined how “important” Thursday was for victims.
A former knight of the realm had been brought to justice.
“The police service and our criminal justice system has sent a clear message – no one is above the law.”

title: Uisce Éireann pays performance-related bonus to 97% of staff
description: Water utility’s leadership stand behind ‘tried and trusted’ approach under TDs’ scrutiny
content:
About 97 per cent of staff at Uisce Éireann received a bonus payment last year under its performance-related award scheme, the Dáil Public Accounts Committee has been told.
The water utility said at a hearing on Thursday that 18 personnel did not receive any bonus. The company has more than 3,000 employees.
The committee was told there was also a cohort of staff who had originally worked for local authorities and who had opted to retain their traditional public service system of annual increments rather than a performance-related award scheme.
Uisce Éireann chief executive Niall Gleeson said staff who benefited from a performance-related award received about 90 per cent of their potential payments, which were based on both personal and corporate targets being achieved.
Gleeson was also challenged by Cathy Bennett of Sinn Féin on his €118,000 increase in pay to €391,953.
Gleeson said he accepted he was well paid. He said pay for chief executives across the commercial State sector had been reviewed by a committee established by the Minister for Public Expenditure. He said subsequently and following consultations between the board of the utility and the Minister for Housing, a new salary level for his post had been agreed. He said any future rises would be based on performance.
Uisce Éireann chief finance officer Chris McCarthy meanwhile said the bonus system was tried and trusted in the market and drove performance in the organisation.
Fianna Fáil TD Paul McAuliffe said every year Uisce Éireann faced questions about bonus payments. He said if the utility believed this performance-related payment scheme was more cost effective than the system of annual increments paid across the public service, it should “put the comparative numbers in front of us”.
[ Improving water system to cost €50bn, Uisce Éireann tells Oireachtas group Opens in new window ]
Gleeson said Uisce Éireann’s performance-related system was fair, cost neutral and a driver of performance.
The committee chairman, John Brady of Sinn Féin, said there was a focus on the bonus payments in the utility – which amounted to €17.9 million for 2025 – at a time when it faced penalties from its economic regulator for failing to meet some targets, and it had also been prosecuted by the Environmental Protection Agency and Inland Fisheries Ireland.
Social Democrats TD Aidan Farrelly said Uisce Éireann had only “very reluctantly, after ‘context’”, answered his question about how many staff had received the bonus payment.
Several members of the committee raised a €31 million “negative revenue adjustment” imposed by the Commission for the Regulation of Utilities after it determined that Uisce Éireann had underperformed against targets associated with leakage and with nondomestic billing over a five-year period. The utility argued this was not a fine but a revenue deduction over five years.
[ ‘We have to deliver infrastructure at pace’: Uisce Éireann shifts focus to facilitate housing Opens in new window ]
Sinn Féin’s Bennett asked McCarthy whether he had received a pay increase. He said he had received a 3 per cent raise. She asked about his salary but he did not reply.
Gleeson then said while his salary details as chief executive were published, no one else in the utility had their specific pay revealed, although remuneration bands were set out in its annual accounts.
Gleeson said there was a three-year agreement with unions that provided for a 3 per cent increase in pay. However, payment of the full 3 per cent was also linked to performance.
Gleeson said Uisce Éireann had paid €4,000 for media training for its personnel in advance of appearing at the Public Accounts Committee on Thursday.
He said staff found it “fairly intimidating” to attend such public hearings.
“We receive training to give you the best answers possible,” he said.
“All you have to do is tell us the answers,” Bennett replied.

title: Jack Chambers ‘hopeful’ of ‘way forward’ to prevent further public sector strike
description: Stoppage next week ‘absolutely’ still on as things stand, union leader Kevin Callinan says
author_name: Jack Horgan-Jones, Emmet Malone, Marie O’Halloran
content:
Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers has said he is “hopeful” it may be possible to “find a way forward shortly in the national interest” to prevent further strike action by public sector workers .
Speaking during a Labour Party Dáil private member’s debate, he said it was “a sensitive matter and work is ongoing”. He was “not in a position to provide specific or further detail at this time”.
Union leaders attending a meeting of the Irish Congress of Unions’ public services committee also declined to comment on the scale of progress being made behind the scenes with one expressing the same concern that things be derailed.
Kevin Callinan, who chairs the committee, said there had been “positives over the past 24 to 36 hours,” but added that next week’s strike is “absolutely” still on as things stand.
Other union officials observed the Dáil debate from the visitors’ gallery, as Chambers said: “I hope to be able to provide further detail shortly and as part of an agreed way forward.”
“We welcome the confirmation from the unions that the established principle of collective bargaining will apply. In other words, nothing is agreed until everything is agreed.”
He pointed out that in the last agreement from 2024 to 2026, pay rose by 9.6 per cent compared with cumulative inflation of 6.6 per cent, “achieved through the collective bargaining process”.
He said “that can provide a basis for constructive engagement while ensuring all parties at the opportunity to address the issues that are important to them.”
In the row over union demands to deal with pay first in negotiations, the Minister said “I’ve confirmed Government’s willingness to prioritise pay” in the talks.
[ Union leader warns of ‘long and difficult dispute’ if breakthrough on pay not made Opens in new window ]
Earlier, Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee told the Dáil the Government wants to increase public sector wages but it can only happen if people get into talks.
She was responding to Labour finance spokesman Ged Nash , who warned her the Government had “a maximum of 24 hours to avert next Wednesday’s planned action and the ball is firmly in your court.”
Raising the issue following the 24-hour strike on Wednesday by 300,000 public sector workers, Nash called on the Taoiseach to “make a substantive and substantial proposal to unions to allow the beginning and the end of this dispute to come into view.”
“Will you formally drop your arbitrary preconditions on how and when the question of pay is settled?” he asked. “And will you commit to the principle of keeping public sector incomes ahead of inflation in any putative new agreement?”
As unions warned of a further 24-hour strike on Wednesday, October 21st, the Minister insisted there were no preconditions to further talks, “in the same way that any previous pay discussion or engagement had no preconditions”.
[ Could the public sector strike be a one-off? Opens in new window ]
[ Government seeks ‘negotiation process’ to avoid second round of public sector strikes Opens in new window ]
Striking workers on the picket lines “are hurting because of a pattern of gaslighting and disrespect expressed time and again since this Government took office”, he said.
“They’re hurting because PAYE workers were thrown under the bus in Budget 2026 in favour of chicken chains,” he said of the VAT cut to 9 per cent for the hospitality sector .
“They’re hurting because they saw you write a cheque for those who brought the country to a standstill last April, while they and their unions, people who play by the rules, were told that when their pay deal expired in June, that their lives and their work just didn’t matter as much,” he added.
The Minister said she acknowledged and recognised “the invaluable and the significant contribution that our public sector paid workers make to this country, and indeed the impact that they have on all of our lives.”
McEntee said she had spoken to workers on the picket lines on Wednesday. “And the very clear message that I got is that people want to be around the table. They want Government and the unions to be talking” about pay, conditions and the increased demands on services with a growing population.
She said €1.2 billion had been set aside “specifically for us to be able to start these talks. That’s not the complete picture”, given “what we know from our previous public sector pay agreements”.

title: Sonia O’Sullivan: On a panel with Roy Keane and Jimmy Barry-Murphy you don’t expect to discuss losing
description: We also discussed how to separate our own success in sport from the perceived expectations on our children
content:
When you’re part of a sporting panel with the likes of Roy Keane and Jimmy Barry-Murphy , down on our own home patch in Cork , you don’t expect the conversation to turn towards losing. But maybe this is what’s helped shape all sporting careers, especially in terms of how you react to it.
It was one of the things that came to light last Thursday evening, at the Rochestown Park Hotel, during a celebration of 50 years of the Irish Guide Dogs. This has been a charity close to Roy’s heart for a long time, and some of those in attendance have been enjoying independent living for many years now thanks in part to the dogs that are bred, raised and trained out of the Irish Guide Dogs centre in Bishopstown.
We’d all crossed paths down through the years, although this was the first time sharing a stage. Also joining us was Cork camogie captain Amy O’Connor, who had in hand the O’Duffy Cup for winning the All Ireland , having lost the final the year before.
I’ve been linked with the Irish Guide Dogs as an ambassador since the late 1990s, after we collaborated on a victory run from Cork City Hall to Cobh, when I returned home with two gold medals from the 1998 World Cross Country Championships.
For me, growing up in Cobh in the 1970s, Jimmy Barry-Murphy was a name synonymous with winning. If anything, it felt like we only ever knew success in Cork hurling and football at a time when it wasn’t unusual for players to play both codes, with neither one affecting the other.
It wasn’t until 1998 that I met Jimmy in real life. We were both at Croke Park for the All-Ireland football final, Jimmy being celebrated with the 1973 Cork football team, who had won the All-Ireland that year, and I was honoured by running a lap of Croke Park.
Roy also grew up in that era of winning Cork teams. My first All-Ireland medal was the bronze won with the Cork cross-country team around a muddy field somewhere up in Monaghan. It didn’t matter that I’d finished way down the field, and lost my shoe, this was a taste of winning anything in the red shirt of Cork.
In 1991 when I came back to Cobh after winning a gold and silver medal at the World University Games, I first met Roy on the sidelines of St Colman’s Park, the Cobh Ramblers ground where he’d played before heading off to Nottingham Forest, and he was yet to embark on his leading role with Manchester United.
At that time, we were both back visiting and being celebrated where things first started. But still bright-eyed and youthful, we’d really no idea what lay ahead. Reflecting a bit on that period, one of the things Roy highlighted was that, in sport, we are all so focused on winning.
The reality for most athletes and teams is they will lose more than they win. So maybe we should be focused on losing, managing that side of the narrative. Because it’s only after you learn how to properly deal with losing that you can move on to the next challenge.
[ Irish Guide Dogs at 50: ‘He made the difference of being able to leave the house or not’ Opens in new window ]
You learn so much more from losses if you allow yourself to dig deep and acknowledge the problems. Ignore them and nothing will change. As athletes we can be so focused on winning, we just want to forget the losses and move forward, not realising there’s always a lesson to learn in every defeat.
I think it’s mainly because Irish people still get so excited by the winning part, when that’s only a small percentage of sport. Sometimes when people win, it can also paper over a lot of cracks. Win three or four medals in athletics, for example, and it feels like all the problems go away. But some could still be there, beneath the surface, rarely seen by those watching from the sidelines.
Roy is famous for referencing that old quote “fail to prepare, prepare to fail”, but in this case he meant something different. This is about being able to deal with losing, in terms of finding something positive to come out of it, or some proactive way of dealing with it. Rather than letting it drag you down.
[ Athletics wishes it could scrub the women’s marathon world record – what can be done? Opens in new window ]
Sometimes when people don’t win, it’s hard to see life beyond that. But it’s all part of the process. That’s not just for the athletes and teams, but the diehard supporters, especially when it comes to teams such as Manchester United. And, dare I say, Cork Gaelic games, with just one senior cup returning to Leeside this year.
Jimmy also spoke about our tendency to be a little softer on people now. As coaches, and managers, maybe you’re not allowed to be as hard, when there are so many more things at play now. But to achieve any success, there still needs to be some element of desperation to it. So often that needs to come from within.
Even though Roy and Jimmy played with a team, I think there’s a similarity there in that we were each independent in our own way, to be the best we could be.
