Maybe that’s more obvious in an individual sport than a team sport, but for them it was also about becoming leaders and expecting the best from the people around them.
[ Denis Walsh: You can’t fight luck in sport, you just learn to control it Opens in new window ]
Something else we talked about was the notion of our own children being in the sporting spotlight. It’s one thing I get asked a lot. That’s probably because people assume that I have a big impact on my daughter, Sophie , when it comes to her running, when I really don’t. I have a lot to do with her normal life but not her day-to-day training. But like any parent, you just want them to find something they enjoy doing and are happy in life.
That’s one thing we all had in common, the ability to separate our own success in sport from the perceived expectation on our children. Particularly if they are forging their own path in a sporting career.
We may also be out there in the public eye, sometimes using that to raise awareness and funds for charities such as the Irish Guide Dogs, although deep down we also crave that normal peaceful life, to just head out the door and walk the dog.

title: Apologetic Infantino ‘not fit’ to lead Fifa, claim European FA heads after meeting
description: European leaders expect someone will stand against him in next March’s presidential election
content:
European football leaders are increasingly confident they will find a candidate to stand against Gianni Infantino in next year’s Fifa presidential election, with the heads of the English and German Football Associations questioning his fitness to govern after a three-and-a-half-hour council meeting in Zurick on Thursday.
Infantino began the long-awaited gathering of Fifa’s 37-strong executive board by apologising for failing to consult them over his abandoned World Cup sell-off plan but failed to provide answers to dozens of questions posed by the European FAs on a range of subjects including the Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, Donald Trump’s Fifa peace prize and the Folarin Balogun affair, when the USA striker’s World Cup suspension was overturned after lobbying from the US president.
Council members succeeded in deferring, until they receive more information on Balogun, a Fifa proposal to amend its disciplinary regulations by removing the scope for players shown a straight red card to have it rescinded. Infantino pledged to provide that information by their next meeting in Doha on December 16th, after nominations close on November 18th for March’s presidential election.
The issue of whether the Fifa peace prize will be revived this year or Trump left as a standalone winner has been contracted out to Fifa’s social responsibility committee, and the Asian Football Confederation president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, has been appointed to chair a new committee examining governance reform, but otherwise the meeting broke up without tangible answers, to the frustration of the English FA’s chair, Debbie Hewitt.
“We didn’t get answers to anything that we had specifically requested,” Hewitt said. “I think the man [Infantino] has to answer those questions, and if he doesn’t answer those questions, he’s not fit to be Fifa president. That was what was shared in the meeting.”
The German FA’s president, Bernd Neuendorf, went further by calling for wholesale reforms of Fifa’s administration, which he hopes will fall within the purview of Sheikh Salman’s governance committee.
“The whole administration has to be reformed and the whole governance has to be reformed,” Neuendorf said. “But I’m pretty clear here that this is not possible with Gianni as the responsible person at Fifa. So we need a complete restart, I think, a political restart of persons who represent Fifa.
“Yes he apologised, but I didn’t have the feeling that this apology was because of the FFE project in total. My impression was it was just because it wasn’t brought forward to the council and no one was involved.”
Neuendorf also said he was “very confident” that an alternative candidate would be found to stand against Infantino, a view shared by senior figures at Uefa, who expect a late declaration to limit the amount of time for Fifa to scupper the nomination.
The respective presidents of the three continental confederations who have called for Infantino to go, Aleksander Ceferin of Uefa, Victor Montagliani of Concacaf and Sheikh Salman, have ruled themselves out and suggestions that high-profile figures such as Arsène Wenger or Michele Kang could put themselves forward have been dismissed.
A proposal to distribute $3.5 billion from Fifa’s financial reserves, which would involve each national association receiving €30 million over the next four-year cycle, was approved by council. – Guardian

title: Hybrid deal with surprise benefit eases fears of EU-China trade war
description: Beijing’s concessions to cap hybrid exports have taken the heat out of EU leaders push to get tough on China
content:
T he finer details of an agreement between the European Union and China last week worked out well for an industry that doesn’t usually find itself caught up in geopolitical negotiations: ice cream producers.
European governments have become exasperated at the widening imbalance in their trading relationship with the Chinese economic behemoth.
China is exporting vastly more into the EU market than European businesses are able to sell in the other direction. The difference, known as the trade deficit, has exceeded €1 billion a day.
Europe’s industrial beasts are struggling to compete with cheaper, state-subsidised products flooding in from China, be it electric vehicles, solar panels or consumer goods.
For decades cars, chemicals and manufacturing industries have been the engine of the European economy. So when factories start to close, governments get worried.
That was the backdrop to talks last week between EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and Chinese commerce minister Wang Wentao to prevent tensions between Brussels and Beijing spinning into a trade war.
The two sides reached an agreement, seen as something of a test case: China’s exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid cars into the EU will be capped at 350,000 vehicles a year.
The deal represents a big shift in European thinking. For a long time the focus was on efforts to gain greater access into the Asian market. “We are now more focused on having China sell less to us,” said a senior official in the European Commission.
[ ‘We’re at a tipping point’: EU prepares its toughest weapon yet against China Opens in new window ]
The deal on hybrids includes a couple of add-ons. For example, China agreed to lower tariffs on imports of European ice cream, olive oil, footwear and car parts.
That’s just a sweetener, rather than a solution. “We’re not going to rebalance the [trade] relationship by exporting more ice cream ... The focus is firmly on export moderation,” the same commission official said.
The EU will want to replicate that cap on hybrid car imports and negotiate similar controls to restrain excessive Chinese competition in other manufacturing sectors.
The EU’s 27 leaders met in Brussels on Thursday for a summit to discuss ideas for defensive “tools” that might be used if further dialogue with China goes nowhere. “We have to protect our market,” Luxembourg’s prime minister Luc Frieden said on Thursday.
In the past Berlin acted as a brake, nervous of provoking retaliation from Beijing. But German chancellor Friedrich Merz and French president Emmanuel Macron recently came together to back a tougher line, greatly improving Sefcovic’s leverage in talks. That seemed to work.
The concessions from China on hybrid vehicles have taken the heat out of things for the time being.
[ EU prepares its toughest weapon yet against China Opens in new window ]

title: Rory McIlroy focused on Race to Dubai endgame after solid start in New Delhi
description: Tom McKibbin one shot of leader Niklas Norgaard in joint second at India Championship
content:
Rory McIlroy stayed focused on the bigger picture after an opening round of 70 for two-under-par had him four shots adrift of clubhouse leader Niklas Norgaard in a weather-interrupted DP World India Championship at Delhi Golf Club.
A five-hour delay due to thunder, lightning and heavy rain meant the majority of the field failed to complete their rounds.
The 37-year-old Northern Irishman made use of staying in the hotel on-site to spend time having lunch and utilising some swing practice aids in his room during the pause in play. “Okay. (It was) a solid start, with a lot of golf left to play,” he said after his opening round.
With his three remaining events on the DP World Tour – the India Championship, followed by the Abu Dhabi Championship in two weeks, and the season-ending Tour Championship in Dubai – McIlroy is aiming for yet another top-place finish on the order of merit for an eighth time, drawing alongside Scotland’s Colin Montgomerie. McIlroy is currently third in the Race to Dubai behind American Patrick Reed and Spain’s Eugenio Chacarra.
Of his record-equalling pursuit, he said it’s important “not to force it too much”, adding: “I have to concentrate on myself. I know a good week here, that’ll set me up well for the last two weeks in the Middle East and my track record in the Middle East is really good.
“I don’t need to be leading going into the last two weeks, but if I can just eat into that lead a little bit, I feel like I’ll have a really good chance in those final two events.”
McIlroy had four birdies and two bogeys in his first round, of which he said: “Overall, I felt like it could have been a couple better, but still a solid start. No one’s really getting away. The golf course is playing a little bit tougher than it did last year, just with how long the rough is.”
Norgaard managed an eagle, six birdies and two bogeys in his opening round of 66, earning him the clubhouse lead ahead of Tom McKibbin , Thomas Detry and Chacarra in joint second.
“A goal of mine is to win the Race to Dubai,” said Chacarra. “I will try to make a push the last four events to win it. Rory and Patrick are world class players so I will need my A-game to do it.”
McKibbin, currently 89th in the Race to Dubai having only dipped into the European Tour from his LIV commitments, made a great start in New Delhi with a 67 that featured a sequence of four birdies from the 12th to the 15th on what was his front stretch, having started on the 10th.
“I’m very happy with the way I played,” he said. “The course is very challenging strategically and you have to execute the shots. The course is very tight and the rough is very penal, so happy with today’s work.
“My game has been a little bit off recently, so to have that stretch (of birdies) was nice, especially on a course like this, and it brings a lot of confidence as well.”
A winner of the Hong Kong Open on the Asian circuit last year, McKibbin’s late-year focus on the DP World Tour will see him play the India Championship and next week’s Genesis Championship in South Korea in his bid to move up the standings and secure a place in the Tour Championship, which is confined to the leading 50 players on the order of merit. The top-70 earn a place at the Abu Dhabi Championship.
“They’re events I’ve played the last couple of years and I’ll definitely be giving it my best the next couple of days to try and sneak into at least one of those,” said McKibbin.
Shane Lowry , meanwhile, had a disappointing three-over-par 75 on his opening round.
And at the Buick LPGA Shanghai Championship, South Korea’s Hye-Jin Choi shot an eight-under 64 to take a three-stroke lead over Spain’s Carlota Ciganda, while Lauren Walsh made a solid start with an opening 70 for a share of 12th.
Leona Maguire , kick-starting her Asian swing of events, opened with a 71.

title: Mike Tyson: Is Netflix's new documentary about the boxer even appropriate?
description: Others may choose to sit back, enjoy the boxing and not let all that abuse stuff get in the way
content:
I n the early 1990s, popular culture was dominated by three African-Americans, all born Michael: Michael Jordan , Michael Jackson and Mike Tyson . Each was troubled in his own way, but Tyson was the real unexploded bomb of the trio, and in this absorbing, if at times uncomfortable, new Netflix documentary – Tyson – he remains a volatile and enigmatic presence.
There are several documentaries bound up in one here, and the sailing is smoothest when director Floyd Russ is telling the Rocky-esque story of Tyson’s rise from grinding poverty in Brooklyn to overnight greatness as the most consequential heavyweight boxer since Muhammad Ali .
He hit harder than Ali but lacked his charisma and poetic quality. If Ali danced and floated, Tyson brooded darkly – especially after the death of his mentor, Cus D’Amato, a hard-talking, soft-hearted trainer who made Tyson believe he could be champion.
But there’s a jump scare further into the four-episode series when, out of nowhere, Donald Trump pops up to gush about Tyson and the grand title fight he put on for the boxer in Atlantic City. This was when Tyson was in a public and troubled marriage to Robin Givens, who said Tyson was physically abusive.
He denied those charges then and now – saying that he “pushed” his wife but did not strike her. But there isn’t much pushback against Tyson by the documentary, and the film never interrogates the wider question of whether it is even appropriate for Netflix to make an essentially non-judgmental series about someone accused on national television of being abusive towards his wife (as Givens did when she and Tyson were interviewed by Barbara Walters).
At this point, viewers may wonder if they want to continue with Tyson – and that question raises its head all over again when the boxer is asked about his conviction for the 1991 rape of beauty pageant contestant Desiree Washington.
Washington isn’t entirely discredited, but the documentary gives Tyson a platform to deny he did anything wrong – a “both sides” approach that sits uncomfortably with the fact that he is a convicted sex offender.
[ Lena Dunham’s Girls to return for limited run Opens in new window ]
There are no rebuttals from either Givens or Washington, and you can understand why they would have declined to participate in this largely laudatory profile – but it does make the viewer feel that they are party to a queasy bargain. Sit back, enjoy the boxing and don’t get too distracted by all that abuse stuff.
With the documentary at number two on the most-watched list in Ireland, it is clearly a compromise many are happy to make, though the buck must, of course, ultimately stop with Netflix for giving Tyson a platform in the first place.

title: GAA+ reports 25% surge in profits in the year before RTÉ sold its stake
description: GAA acquired national broadcaster’s shares for €3m in February
content:
Pretax profits at the parent company of GAA+, the pay-walled streaming platform established by the GAA and RTÉ , surged by 25.6 per cent last year to €1.41 million.
New accounts filed by GAAGo Media Ltd show that pretax profits increased to €1.4 million last year from €1.11 million in 2024, as subscription revenues rose by 8.65 per cent from €5.3 million to €5.77 million in 2025.
It is the third consecutive year of strong profit and subscription revenue growth for the subscription platform, originally called GAAGo. The 25.6 per cent rise in pretax profits followed a 28 per cent increase in pretax profits in 2024 and a 7 per cent rise in subscription revenues in 2024.
Earlier this year, the GAA acquired RTÉ’s share of the joint venture for €3 million before rebranding it as GAA+. The deal – which valued the business at €6 million – was completed in February.
Overall revenues at the company rose by 10 per cent for the second year running last year.
Turnover comprised subscription revenue of €5.7 million, sponsorship income and other income.
Sponsorship income increased by 28 per cent from €285,417 to €365,168, while other income rose by 38 per cent from €148,312 to €204,796.
After-tax profits increased by 27 per cent from €978,986 to €1.24 million.
No dividend was paid out last year, after the firm paid a €1 million dividend to its then joint owners, RTÉ and the GAA, in 2024 and a €1.2 million dividend in 2023.
[ GAA embraces new age of streaming as ‘biggest step change’ in match coverage Opens in new window ]
The accounts – signed off by GAA Croke Park stadium director Peadar Mac Cionnaith and GAA director general Thomas Ryan on September 17th – show that the firm had accumulated profits at the end of 2025 totalling €2.56 million.
The directors state that the service streams GAA games to both domestic and international audiences and features more than 100 live and on-demand games over the year.
The broadcast of the games resulted in the company’s operating costs increasing by 6 per cent from €4.07 million to €4.34 million last year, while personnel costs rose from €550,089 to €580,366.
The company directly employed seven people on average last year, up from six in 2024.

title: Addictive online features should be disabled by default, report on use by children finds
description: Blanket social media ban for under-16s would ‘unlikely provide’ comprehensive solution to harms
content:
Addictive features should be disabled by default on online platforms and this should be mandated by legislation or regulations, according to a report by the Oireachtas Committee on Children.
The report on technology, social media and children, with a focus on online safety and wellbeing, follows meetings with organisations representing young people and teachers, the Garda , Coimisiún na Meán and various tech companies, among others.
It contains 45 recommendations including that legislation or regulations “mandate the disabling of addictive features, including infinite scroll, autoplay, algorithmic amplification of harmful content, and behavioural profiling in all circumstances.”
It also recommends a mandatory age classification system be set up for all digital products and services based on the risk they pose to child development – similar to mechanisms for toys and films.
“Regulation and accountability should be strengthened particularly in relation to platform design, recommender systems and algorithmic amplification to ensure the safety of children and young people,” it says.
The committee has welcomed the planned EU Kids Act and set out its belief that “at a minimum children under 13 should not hold traditional social media accounts ” – a measure the European Commission has proposed.
“Based on evidence to the committee a blanket ban alone on social media use for children under 16 would unlikely provide a comprehensive solution to the harms experienced by children online.”
The committee recommends that consideration be given to providing investigative and information-gathering powers to the Irish regulator, Coimisiún na Meán, before a formal investigation is opened.
[ ‘Children are constantly doom scrolling’ Opens in new window ]
It says the same for “establishing a national taskforce including Departments, educators, parents, young people, and civil society groups to co-ordinate a coherent national response.”
Committee chairwoman Keira Keogh said: “Technology is evolving faster than our ability to regulate it, and that is why one of the strongest measures running throughout this report is that we cannot rely on regulation to simply catch up after harm has occurred.”
She said there was a need to ensure children’s safety is built into digital products and platforms from the very beginning, adding: “We need safety by design rather than safety as an afterthought.”
The Fine Gael TD spoke of how the committee heard about the online opportunities for children and young people for learning and communicating but also the “very serious harms” including cyberbullying, exposure to pornography and violent content, grooming, sexual exploitation, harmful algorithms, addictive design features and risks associated with artificial intelligence .
In relation to the recommendation on mandating that addictive features be disabled by default she said: “It was pretty clear to us that the infinite scroll is what’s keeping kids online, you know, far beyond what they would want.”
She said tech companies “can turn this off very quickly if needed”.
Keogh said the committee wanted the Government to consider its recommendation for legislation or regulations in this area while also looking at the planned EU Kids Act – which will seek to limit features that can encourage excessive use, such as infinite scroll.
Sinn Féin TD Ruairí Ó Murchú, also a committee member, said “tech firms are businesses that want to keep you online”.
He expressed his belief that social media platforms “are incredibly dangerous” and they “need to be regulated to a huge degree” with “the enforcement to do that”.
Labour Party Senator Nessa Cosgrove acknowledged that “the idea of safety by design is going to be really hard to implement to get the tech companies to go along with that.”

title: HSE considering reimbursing weight-loss drug Mounjaro
description: State’s approach to weight-loss medications ‘raises important matters of health policy which will require discussions’, says HSE
content:
The HSE is considering reimbursing more weight-loss drugs, known as GLP-1 medications, after receiving a number of applications.
The HSE drugs group met on Tuesday to discuss Mounjaro but has not yet made a recommendation.
“Applications have been made for reimbursement of a number of GLP-1 medications, and these are currently being considered within the HSE’s drugs reimbursement process which encompasses clinical, cost effectiveness and budgetary issues,” a statement said.
The HSE said its corporate pharmaceutical unit – which liaises between the executive and pharmaceutical industry – “will be involved in negotiations with the manufacturers on pricing in line with normal practice”.
“This process can take some time and there may be a number of meetings of the drugs group before a recommendation may be made to the HSE senior management team,” the statement continued.
[ How the rise of Ozempic is reversing the progress on body positivity Opens in new window ]
Weight-loss drugs such as Mounjaro, Ozempic and Wegovy are available privately for type-2 diabetes and weight management. They range in price from about €130 to €600 per month, depending on the brand and dosage.
Sax­enda, which is injec­ted daily, is the only form of GLP-1 ther­apy that is reim­bursed for weight loss by the HSE . This means it is free under the med­ical card or sub­sid­ised for private patients on the Drugs Pay­ment Scheme, which has a cost limit of €80 per month.
More than 45,000 people are get­ting Ozempic for free under the Long-Term Ill­ness Scheme, with more than 8,000 receiv­ing it under the medical card. However, it is only available under these schemes for the treatment of type-2 diabetes.
[ GLP-1s in Ireland: How weight-loss medications work under the HSE system Opens in new window ]
The HSE said the State’s approach to GLP-1 medications “also raises important matters of health policy which will require discussions over the coming months with the Department of Health and other key stakeholders on the potential overall impact on the health budget”.
“The outcome of these discussions will also need to be considered by the HSE in finalising the approach to reimbursement of these drugs.”
In December 2025, the National Centre for Pharmacoeconomics (NCPE) said Mounjaro was not cost-effective but that the HSE should consider reimbursing it if it could agree a price reduction with the manufacturer, Eli Lilly .
[ Inside the Irish factory at the centre of the global weight-loss revolution Opens in new window ]
Prof Michael Barry, who leads the NCPE, said earlier this year that Eli Lilly had made an offer for a significant price reduction that would make the drug cost-effective, or close to it.
However, he warned it could still cost the State between €2 billion and €3 billion over five years.

title: The global economy and the art of living dangerously
description: It would be nice to think the world will become less shock-prone, but it probably won’t
content:
T he past few days have reminded us of one of the two chief contemporary economic realities: the president of the US is a wrecker.
Yet this is consistent with the other reality, which is that despite the disruptions and shocks of our era, the world economy remains a powerful growth machine, driven by remarkable innovations, risk-taking finance and large accumulations of debt. Can this last?
The reason for believing it will is that growth has been the dominant feature of the global economy since the middle of the last century. Yet we must always remember that growth is one thing, but stable growth quite another.
What, then, is the latest US president Donald Trump outrage? First, he started a war on Iran , without a plan, which has raised diesel prices in the US and worldwide. Then, a few days ago, he made a deal with Vladimir Putin to release Russian diesel on global markets, in violation of sanctions imposed after Putin’s illegal invasion of Ukraine.
Trump also told Kyiv to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and threatened to cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine and access to US-made weapons.
This “deal” is both foolish and wicked: foolish, because it is too small to lower diesel prices significantly, and wicked, because it is prepared to sacrifice a country that is struggling heroically to be free from tyranny.
Current US policymaking is not just reckless and immoral. It is also one of the causes of the world’s unpredictability.
Thus, the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) latest World Economic Outlook (WEO) starts with the following comment from Silvana Tenreyro, the new economic counsellor: “In less than seven years, the global economy has been subjected to an exceptional sequence of events.”
Current US policymaking is not just reckless and immoral. It is also one of the causes of the world’s unpredictability.
Yet all but one of these shocks, the exception being the pandemic, are man-made, or perhaps “strongman-made”. The others are the war in Ukraine, the tariff war and the war in the Middle East. Putin launched the first of these in 2022. Trump, of course, began the other two.
These shocks have, as Tenreyro says, “tested the resilience of households, firms, financial markets and governments. Individually, each of these big developments would have been considered unlikely. Their confluence over such a short period of time is even more extraordinary.”
Yet, remarkably, the WEO’s forecasts for growth this year and next, at 3.1 and 3.4 per cent respectively, are “broadly unchanged from April”, despite more persistent energy disruption than was then expected.
Global inflation is, however, expected to hit 4.7 per cent this year, as a result of higher commodity prices, and 4.1 per cent in 2027. But, happily, “the pass-through to core inflation is expected to be limited”.
The explanations for this resilience are familiar. They include adjustment of exports and imports away from direct trade between the US and China. More recently, however, the dominant factors have been the flexibility of the global energy economy, discussed here last week, and the investment boom triggered by artificial intelligence (AI) .
Yet neither is guaranteed to last. As Nick Butler points out, stocks of crude and products are low after six months of drawdowns. Moreover, “product exports of diesel and jet fuel [from the Gulf] remain minimal”. Also at risk are supplies of naphtha, urea and liquefied natural gas (the latter of special importance to Europe).
The AI investment boom also concentrates risk. Even if AI itself works out, the level of investment is likely to stop growing, if not decline, at some point. Moreover, AI might not work out financially on the hoped-for scale at all.
Other fragilities are evident, notably the fiscal positions. Despite the big post-pandemic rise in real and nominal interest rates, most large economies continue to run significant primary fiscal deficits (before interest payments).
It would help if the shocks stopped, too. Alas, given our leaders, I would not bet on that.
The US position stands out, with a forecast primary fiscal deficit of 4.8 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, a share of T-bill issuance in gross borrowing at 58 per cent and an average maturity of a mere 5.9 years.
The WEO rightly emphasises the importance of rebuilding fiscal space. The good news is that, in today’s circumstances, the negative impact of structural fiscal tightening is likely to be offset by lower real and nominal interest rates. But redressing global current accounts imbalances will also be essential. That must, at last, involve China.
[ Ireland is richer and spending more than 30 years ago but is it making us happy? Opens in new window ]
The WEO emphasises other downside risks, including a worsening of the ongoing wars, (probably AI-enhanced) cyber threats and climate catastrophes.
Neither a stock market crash nor a collapse in AI-related investment can be ruled out, should returns on AI disappoint. Upside economic risks include still faster progress with AI technology, though that could also inflict devastating social consequences.
Another plausible upside is an accelerated energy transition, as recent events underline the unreliability of fossil fuels. Given their physical location, these are bound to remain so for many countries.
[ John FitzGerald: Budget reversal of policy on tackling climate change was a mistake Opens in new window ]
The WEO notes that the ability to exploit AI and meet energy needs reliably will be crucial for growth prospects. Sadly, the world’s poorest countries are particularly vulnerable in both respects. Thus, the WEO rightly fears that their living standards are likely to fall still farther behind those in richer countries.
It would be good to believe the world will become less prone to shocks. But it will probably not do so. The best response is to strengthen fundamentals, notably economic flexibility and dynamism, together with energy resilience. In this context, as the WEO notes, it is essential to make support for people vulnerable to shocks targeted and temporary.
The time for throwing public money around freely has come to an end. It would help if the shocks stopped, too. Alas, given our leaders, I would not bet on that. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Ukraine braces for hardest winter yet as Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ unravels
description: Ukrainians believe Trump is playing politics and business with people’s lives by siding with Russia
content:
T hree days into what US president Donald Trump claimed was an “energy ceasefire” between Moscow and Kyiv, 600,000 Ukrainians woke on Wednesday to blackouts after another wave of Russian missiles and drones pummelled power stations.
Ukraine fears it was only a taste of things to come during a fifth full winter of all-out war, with the enemy’s arsenal well stocked with ballistic missiles and new jet-powered drones, and its own air defences stretched thin as Trump cuts US assistance to pressure Kyiv to make a deal with Moscow.
Russia has destroyed more than 60 per cent of Ukraine’s power-generating capacity since 2022, and Ukrainian cities and energy firms are now racing to prepare critical infrastructure for what could be one of the hardest periods of the war, amid daily air strikes, severe economic difficulties and collapsing relations with the White House.
In Lviv, a city of 700,000 people in western Ukraine, local authorities have repaired and strengthened existing infrastructure while making crucial systems more resistant to collapse in the case of attack.
“We have built additional physical protection for heat and water supply, we have worked on creating additional power-generating capacity, we have changed a record number of pipes, and we have introduced more programmes for energy efficiency,” says Andriy Moskalenko, Lviv’s deputy mayor for economy development.
In line with national efforts to reduce reliance on huge, Soviet-era power stations that are easy targets for Russian strikes, Lviv is moving to a more decentralised electricity system, through investments in so-called modular and gas-piston power plants and large-scale battery storage.
At 70 sites around the city, including hospitals and schools, wood-powered boiler houses are being built to ensure heating continues even during blackouts in the coldest months. Emergency plans are also in place to maintain water supply to Lviv even if electricity to pumping stations is knocked out.
Old technology is also being put to good use – the authorities have installed hundreds of pot-belly stoves in shelters and basements around the city, to provide heat during air-raid alerts that can last for hours.
“People laughed at this initiative in 2022, but when we had blackouts they realised it was useful,” says Moskalenko, after returning to city hall from the site of a Russian drone strike that damaged several houses and cars on the outskirts of Lviv.
“We are working, but Russia is also changing its strategy, launching faster jet-powered drones in large numbers,” he adds
“All Ukrainian cities need more protection. At city hall, we can do some things with different brigades, and co-finance some things. We spend about 20 per cent of the city budget on supporting the military - mostly units on the eastern front, but we also give something to air defence, to buy things like pickup trucks and interceptor drones. But we can’t buy Patriots and all our big cities need them.”
A new Patriot battery costs more than €1 billion and each missile costs several million, and it is the only system in Ukraine’s armoury that can shoot down Russia’s most powerful ballistic missiles.
Ukraine is scrambling to source interceptor rockets from European and other states after Trump halted supplies to Kyiv and began a war on Iran, in which US forces have reportedly fired more than 1,700 Patriots, severely depleting their own stocks.
Ukraine has asked for 300 Patriots to help get it through the winter, but fresh deliveries from the US are unlikely amid another sharp souring of relations between Trump and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy .
Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports last week, in a move he claimed would bring down world fuel prices, and demanded that Kyiv halt its damaging strikes on Russian oil refineries, which are a major contributor to the Kremlin’s war chest.
He then offered no criticism of Russia’s latest attacks on Ukraine’s power stations – despite his own announcement of a supposed energy ceasefire – and Zelenskiy said the US had failed to warn his country about the missile strikes and had restricted its access to satellite internet services that are crucial for military operations.
“A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure – the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American president,” Zelenskiy said of Wednesday’s attacks. “The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States.
“The American president has all the effective and necessary tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice, and pressure on the aggressor. We ask for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine. It is entirely fair for us to tell the United States, Europe and all our partners that no country in the world should be left alone to face such a deranged and pro-war actor as Russia.”
In an interview published in the Financial Times on Thursday, Zelenskiy said Ukraine was “done” with its halt on attacks on Russian refineries , and would only consider renewing the pause if the US pledged to deliver more Patriots.
Ukrainians feel Trump is trying to boost Republican chances in November’s midterm elections and line up lucrative deals with Moscow – playing politics and business with their lives as they brace for dark and dangerous months.
“From March until now we have done everything we can to rebuild what was destroyed last winter. We have invested €300 million in this work together with our governmental partners in the US and EU,” says Pavlo Bilodid, a spokesman for DTEK, Ukraine’s biggest private energy company.
“[But] true resilience requires new capacity and a different approach, which is why we are investing in solar and wind generation, as well as battery storage. A key part of our strategy, and the whole country’s, is to invest more in decentralised and distributed assets,” he adds.
“In the last year, we have opened huge battery storage facilities, and they will be particularly important this winter. We are also building wind power plants now and have more in the pipeline. At the other end of the scale, we are putting in smaller substations the size of a phone box to power one neighbourhood block.
“There is also a huge trend among Ukrainian companies and households to add more rooftop solar panels, wind power and battery storage. The war has really accelerated the energy transition in Ukraine.”
Ukraine is beginning to deploy a new generation of interceptor drones that can catch and destroy jet-powered Russian attack drones that can fly at 600km/h – three times faster than earlier, propeller-driven versions.
It is also part of a pan-European project called Freya to produce interceptor rockets to counter ballistic missiles – but delivery is years away.
For now, Ukrainians are bracing for winter under skies that they know are increasingly vulnerable.
“DTEK and other energy companies have repaired as much of the power system as possible. The key question now is how it is protected. So-called passive protection like concrete blocks and cages around assets helps, but can never fully protect against a direct strike by ballistic missiles or new jet-powered drones. That is why increasing our stocks of anti-ballistic ammunition is so important,” says Bilodid.
“We have taken every measure possible to prepare for winter. But the millions of euros invested, the months of work by our crews and the support of our partners could be undone by just one or two massive Russian ballistic missile strikes.”

title: Donaldson victims hailed for ‘courage’ and ‘bravery’ following ex-DUP leader’s sentencing
description: Abuse carried out by Donaldson took place over 20-year period and began when each child turned seven-years-old
content:
The victims of Jeffrey Donaldson (63) have been hailed for their “courage” and “bravery” after the former MP was sentenced to 15 years in prison for child sex offences .
The former leader of the Democratic Unionist Party , was convicted in June of 18 counts of abuse committed against two women when they were children, including one charge of child rape, and was sentenced on Thursday.
The abuse, which spanned a more than 20-year period from 1985 to 2008, began when each woman was around seven years old.
His wife Eleanor Donaldson (60), was found following a trial of the facts to have done the acts in relation to five charges, including four of aiding and abetting her husband’s abuse.
Newry Crown Court was told during sentencing on Thursday that Donaldson had been assessed at medium risk of reoffending, and had “doubled down on his denials” since his conviction.
“There has not been, and doubtless will not be, one word of regret, apology or shame from this man to at least provide his victims with some crumb of comfort,” Judge Paul Ramsey said.
Donaldson was also ordered to sign the sex offenders register for life.
[ Donaldson ‘deserves every day’ of 15-year sentence for sex offences, says DUP Opens in new window ]
Addressing reporters outside the court afterwards, the senior investigating officer in the case, Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Det Chief Insp Leah Crothers, said she wanted to commend the “bravery in pursuing justice” of Donaldson’s victims.
She said they had lived “in silence and fear of the repercussions of telling someone or of not being believed” and “both brave women have suffered immeasurably as they come to terms with what happened to them as children”.
“He robbed them both of their childhood and innocence,” Crothers said.
She said that throughout the case, both women were “subjected to speculation online and in the media, with their legal right to anonymity being jeopardised in the process and yet they remained steadfastly supportive of the criminal justice process”.
Welcoming Donaldson’s sentencing, she said: “The police service and our criminal justice system has sent a clear message [that] no one is above the law.”
The head of the Public Prosecution Service Serious Crime Unit, Catherine Kierans, said the “courage shown by the two victims in reporting the sexual abuse was the catalyst for a thorough PSNI investigation”.
She said she wanted to “pay tribute to the victims in this case”, saying prosecutors “recognise that it took great courage to speak out”.
“Victims of sexual abuse should never feel shame for what was done to them,” she said.
“The shame belongs solely to those who commit these offences.
“We know that the criminal justice outcome will not heal all the hurt these two incredibly brave women have experienced, however, we hope it will be of some comfort to them as they look to the future.”

title: Ireland sells 10-year bonds at highest rate since it emerged from bailout
description: Global borrowing rates have risen this year as Iran war stokes inflation
content:
The National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) has ended bond market fundraising for the year by selling 10-year notes at the highest interest rate since just after the Republic exited its international bailout programme.
The State’s debt-management agency sold €1.25 billion of bonds in an auction on Thursday morning, with the notes priced to carry a market interest rate – or yield – of just over 3.5 per cent.
It was the highest rate the market demanded for new 10-year Irish Government bonds since January 2014, a month after the State exited a three-year international bailout programme.
However, it was not the highest rate the NTMA has paid to raise long-term funding in the post-bailout era. In July, it issued 30-year bonds at a yield of 3.82 per cent, the highest rate for such debt since March 2013.
The auction brings the total value of benchmark bonds issued by the NTMA this year to €12.3 billion, which is above the midpoint of a targeted range between €10 billion and €14 billion set out last December. The agency is led by chief executive Frank O’Connor.
Bond yields have jumped globally this year, mainly as investors bet on the extent to which central banks will increase official interest rates to rein in inflation that has been stoked by the effect of the Iran war on fuel prices .
Still, euro-zone rates have generally come back in from their highs in recent weeks as investors concluded money markets may have got carried away when they were pricing in four more rate hikes by the European Central Bank (ECB) over 12 months. The ECB has already pushed through two quarter-of-a-percentage-point rate increases since the middle of June.
[ NTMA sells €1.25bn of bonds amid market turmoil Opens in new window ]
Other dynamics have also been at play in the European debt markets in recent times. Investors have been increasingly demanding higher rates for French and Italian debt, relative to Germany , the main euro-zone benchmark, amid concerns about their high, and rising, debt levels.
The yield on 10-year French bonds reached 4.9 per cent earlier this week, amid market concerns about political instability hampering efforts to bring the country’s budget deficit under control. France is heading into a presidential election next spring.
The difference – or spread – between the yields on 10-year French and German bonds high 1.59 percentage points earlier this month, the widest since November 2011, at the height of the euro-zone sovereign-debt crisis.
Italy ’s €3-trillion government bond market, one of the world’s biggest, has ​come under renewed scrutiny amid contagion from a sharp sell-off in French debt. Bond yields move inversely to bond prices.
Italian 10-year bond rates hit 4.7 per cent this month and the yield gap with safe-haven German bunds reached its widest in almost 18 months.
Italy’s national election next year throws doubt on Rome’s plans to reverse the rise in ‌its huge public debt, according to analysts. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg

title: Cockroach infestation found at Hopsack Cafe in Swan Leisure Centre, Rathmines
description: Food safety watchdog issues a dozen closure orders in September
content:
Twelve food operators were issued with closure orders by the food safety watchdog last month, with active cockroach and rat infestations, decomposing mice and inadequate procedures for the cooking, cooling and reheating of high-risk foods including sushi among the reasons cited by inspectors.
A pizza restaurant in Rathgar, a smoothie bar and cafe in the Swan Leisure Centre in Rathmines and a Centra in Cavan were among the establishments issued with temporary closure orders by the Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI).
Pizza Petito on Orwell Road in Dublin 6 was closed on September 23rd after inspectors noted “an active infestation of rats” on the premises “and in particular in the kitchen area”.
Rodent droppings were found along the wall on both sides of the kitchen and underneath a food refrigeration unit and inspectors noted that the “kitchen was trading at the time of inspection with one customer seated, eating a freshly cooked pizza. The droppings were noted to be spread widely across the kitchen”.
As of Thursday morning, the closure order had not been lifted.
An active cockroach infestation was observed in The Hopsack cafe @ Swan Leisure in the Swan Leisure Centre in Rathmines on September 10th with “all stages of the cockroach lifestyle from nymph to adult” found.
During the inspection, dead cockroaches were found under the food service area where ready-to-eat food juices were prepared and served and on the floor in the food preparation services area. A live cockroach was also seen under the food service area.
An active cockroach infestation was also seen by inspectors who visited Banadir on Talbot St in Dublin 1, with a closure order imposed on September 16th before being lifted 12 days later.
On September 30th, Furlong’s Bar and Lounge and Nellie’s Takeaway in Curracloe, Co Wexford, was found to have “inadequate procedures to control pests as evidenced by the presence of mice droppings behind the two chest freezers in the kitchen [and] two dead mice observed behind the drinks shelving unit in the food storage room off the bar ... which were at different stages of decomposition”.
An inspection of the pest control company records for the Centra in Ardlo Manor, Mullagh, Co Cavan, on September 22nd “noted that there has been ongoing issues with rat activity and that remedial actions in relation to pest proofing has not been completed to date. The pest control company have stated on their visit this morning that there is evidence of ongoing moderate pest activity on the shop floor.”
On September 9th, J2 Sushi in Swords was found not to have the correct procedures in place for the storage, preparation, production and offering for sale of sushi and sashimi. “The operator could not demonstrate that the food safety hazards associated with these products had been identified and were subject to effective controls, monitoring, corrective action and verification,” inspectors wrote.
They added “adequate procedures were not in place for the cooking, cooling and reheating of high-risk foods, including chicken. The operator could not demonstrate that these processes were consistently controlled by monitoring, corrective action, verification and records.”
The chief executive of the FSAI, Greg Dempsey, said the closure orders “once again highlight the importance of maintaining robust food safety and hygiene practices”.
He said issues such as inadequate pest control, poor cleaning standards and unsafe food storage were “entirely preventable”.

title: Academic and lawyer Maeve O’Rourke to run for Seanad
description: Byelection will be decided solely by TDs and Senators, suggesting she will likely need support from Government parties
content:
Academic and lawyer Maeve O’Rourke is planning to run in next month’s Seanad byelection to fill the seat vacated by Fine Gael ’s Seán Kyne.
O’Rourke, who has built a national profile as an advocate and expert on issues relating to the Magdalene laundries , mother and baby homes , forced adoption and institutional abuse, is currently working as a senior lecturer at the School of Law in the University of Galway .
She will run as an Independent but has secured the backing of the Social Democrats and the Labour Party . She is expected to formally announce her candidacy for the byelection on Friday, once her eligibility to fill the seat on the cultural and educational panel has been confirmed by the Seanad returning officer.
People Before Profit-Solidarity is said to be considering backing O’Rourke, and the Green Party has been approached for support – although it previously signalled it may put forward their Dublin councillor Janet Horner, who performed well in the Dublin Central byelection this year, for the empty seat.
O’Rourke, who was called to the Bar of Ireland this year, is also said to be seeking to meet with the Sinn Féin parliamentary party in an effort to enlist its support.
The electorate for the Seanad byelection will consist solely of the TDs and Senators, suggesting O’Rourke would likely need support from Government parties to be successful.
She said she was looking to meet all TDs and Senators across the political spectrum. She is being nominated by the Law Society, the Irish Dental Society and Comhlámh, the international development workers and volunteers organisation.
O’Rourke, who is married to Labour Party TD Ciarán Ahern and is a daughter of former RTÉ broadcaster Seán O’Rourke, told The Irish Times she was “delighted” to have secured the backing of the Social Democrats and Labour, pledging to continue her advocacy and research if elected.
She also said she wanted to work on the rights of older people in relation to care, as well as their rights and those of disabled people to live independently and on cementing academic links with Palestinian institutions.

title: Jeffrey Donaldson sentenced to 15 years in prison for rape and child sex assaults
description: Former DUP leader will serve seven and a half years in prison, with remission, after he was found guilty in June of 18 sex offences
content:
Former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson will spend seven and a half years in prison after he was sentenced on Thursday for for 18 sexual offences, including the rape of a child.
Donaldson (63) was convicted at Newry Crown Court in June of 18 sex offences relating to the abuse of two women when they were children, on dates from 1985 to 2008.
He had denied the offences but the jury convicted him of one count of rape, 13 counts of indecent assault and four counts of gross indecency.
On Thursday, Donaldson was sentenced to 11 years in prison on the rape charge and the other offences against his first victim, and a further four years for the offences committed against his second victim, to run consecutively – a total sentence of 15 years.
Donaldson qualifies for an automatic 50 per cent remission of his sentence, so he will spend seven and a half years in prison and the rest on licence.
Sentencing Donaldson, Judge Paul Ramsey said that since his conviction, the former Lagan Valley MP had “doubled down in his denials” of the abuse.
[ Jeffrey Donaldson ‘deserves every day’ of 15-year sentence for sex offences, says DUP Opens in new window ]
“There has not been, and doubtless will not be, one word of regret, apology or shame from this man to at least provide his victims with some crumb of comfort,” the judge said.
The judge told Donaldson it was a “disturbing and disquieting case” and “having reached the very heights of public office”, his was a “catastrophic descent into disgrace”.
“It was only through the courage, resourcefulness and determination of two young women that you’ve been brought to justice,” he said.
Donaldson’s victims were in court in Newry for the sentencing, and listened, at times in tears, as the judge read extracts from their victim impact statements which detailed the devastating effect his offending and the “retraumatising” trial process had on them.
One of the victims said it had been a “living nightmare” and the “public nature” of the case had had a “profound impact on my social life and career”.
[ ‘The only person telling lies is you’ – the full story of Jeffrey Donaldson’s abuse trial Opens in new window ]
“My truth, that was deeply private and painful, has become public knowledge,” her statement said.
The other victim, addressing Donaldson and his wife, Eleanor Donaldson, directly, said “you both could have saved me from court ... you both implied not only that none of it happened, but accused me of making it up, and it made everything you did so much worse.
“You took away my ability to trust people.”
The judge said that, having observed the “demeanour and reaction” of both victims while giving evidence, he had “no doubt whatsoever of the permanent mark that this abuse has left on each of them.”
Donaldson stood in the dock, dressed in a blue suit and white shirt, and showed no emotion as the sentence was handed down.
[ ‘Take Mr Donaldson down’: The rise and fall of former DUP star Jeffrey Donaldson Opens in new window ]
The pre-sentence report provided to the court noted Donaldson had “stoutly maintained his denial of guilt” and assessed him as having a “medium” risk of reoffending.
Donaldson was placed on the sex offenders’ register for life and will be subject to a number of other conditions, including a ban on working with children and vulnerable adults.
The former DUP MP has been in Maghaberry Prison in Co Antrim awaiting sentencing since the end of the trial in June. He is appealing his conviction.
Eleanor Donaldson was found to have aided and abetted his crimes after a trial of the facts, which was granted on mental health grounds, and is appealing the outcome.
She cannot be given a prison sentence but could be given a treatment order or an absolute discharge.
The judge said on Thursday he would “deal with her at a later stage, when I am in possession of all the relevant documents.”
Outside the court, the head of the Public Prosecution Service’s serious crime unit, Catherine Kierans, praised the victims’ courage in coming forward to seek justice.
“Jeffrey Donaldson held a prominent public position,” she said. “This case shows that sexual abuse can be hidden behind a facade of respectability.”
Speaking outside court, Det Chief Insp Leah Crothers of the Police Service of Northern Ireland said Donaldson had manipulated his victims and exploited their trust. Police and the criminal justice system had sent a clear message, she said. “No one is above the law,” said Crothers.
During the five-week trial, both victims gave evidence that Donaldson sexually abused them as children.
Complainant A gave evidence of inappropriate touching and kissing by Donaldson and an incident where he used a light to examine her genitals.
Complainant B told the trial she had been raped as a child of primary-school age by Donaldson and later sexually assaulted by him.
At a pre-sentencing hearing last month, prosecution barrister Rosemary Walsh spoke of various tariffs for the offences, several of which carried a maximum sentence of two years. But other offences carried a maximum sentence of between 10 and 14 years under historical tariffs for crimes, she told the court.
She said historical legislation did not differentiate between a child and an adult victim in all the counts, so the disparity in age between Donaldson and his victims should be considered an “aggravating” factor in sentencing. She said Complainant B was “nine or 10” during some of the offending by Donaldson when he was 25 or 26 years old. She had described how she felt “sick” when he abused her and “wanted to scream out” but thought it was her fault.
Complainant B suffered other types of sexual assault by Donaldson when she was as young as “seven or eight”.
[ Woman sentenced to three months for breaching anonymity of Donaldson victims Opens in new window ]
Donaldson’s barrister, Kieran Vaughan, said during that hearing that the former politician was a man of “previous good character” who “did achieve significant things”.
But he added: “These convictions obliterate all those achievements he has made in his life.”
Donaldson was knighted for political services in 2016 and became DUP leader in 2021, before resigning in 2024. He was stripped of his knighthood in July.

title: Patrick O’Donovan remains in intensive care after taking ill on Tuesday
description: Minister has previously spoken about his experience living with epilepsy, which he was diagnosed with more than 10 years ago
content:
Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan remains in intensive care in hospital after being taken ill on Tuesday.
It is understood he is being cared for in University Hospital Limerick . He was hospitalised after being taken ill while hosting an informal meeting of EU telecoms ministers.
A planned press conference was cancelled on Tuesday afternoon and he was taken to hospital by ambulance.
O’Donovan, who is Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport, was hospitalised after becoming unwell during an official trip to Brussels this summer.
He has previously spoken about his experience living with epilepsy , which he was diagnosed with more than 10 years ago.
Before being hospitalised on Tuesday, the Co Limerick TD had hit back against critics within his own party, accusing those who commented on his health of “ the ultimate in betrayal ”.
He was responding to briefings against him in coverage of the budget rows he became embroiled in last week.
In addition to questions over his temperament, a Fine Gael TD was quoted at the weekend suggesting that people within the parliamentary party were questioning whether O’Donovan was healthy enough to continue in his role.
A Cabinet source in the party was quoted as suggesting a discussion on if he was “well enough” to stay in his role was likely.
O’Donovan had been at the centre of a post-budget controversy after first failing to secure funding to support his heavily-publicised “culture card” initiative for 16- and 17-year-olds.
Then, he was again in the headlines after providing RTÉ with €20 million less in funding than agreed under the terms of a 2024 deal with the troubled national broadcaster.

title: Irish universities teetering on ‘cliff-edge’ due to chronic underfunding, committee hears
description: State funding of higher education per student stands at 34% less than in 2008
content:
Irish universities are teetering on a ”cliff-edge” due to chronic underfunding by the State over several years which has led to a €250 million deficit in the sector every year, the Oireachtas has heard.
State funding of higher education per student is 34 per cent less than it was in 2008, director general of the Irish Universities Association Paul Johnson told the education committee on Thursday.
“Government has acknowledged the problem but not moved fast enough to address it,” he said, adding the gap in funding now stands at around €250 million per annum.
“Our pre-budget submission thus sought €190 million in additional core funding this year and next to close that gap. Budget 2027 provided only €10 million in new core funding,” Johnson said.
The Department of Further Education’s budget for 2027 included a €34 million student support package, including a €150 reduction in the student contribution fee and a 4.5 per cent increase in SUSI maintenance grants.
The focus on student support comes amid a growing accommodation crisis , which has seen students commuting long distances, couch-surfing and working long hours to afford their educational costs.
However, the universities themselves now say they too are “treading water”, Paul Farrell, chairman of Trinity College Dublin ’s board told the committee.
“It is incumbent upon us to point to the very real cliff-edge we are teetering upon,” he said.
“The help for students and families is welcome and is appreciated, but the budget day speeches offer no clear commitment to closing the remaining core funding gap.”
Mike Beary, chair of University College Dublin ’s governing authority, said the sector was “now at the absolute limit of capacity” and “cannot deliver a world-class economy and society with one hand tied behind our back”.
Sean O’Driscoll, chairman of the governing authority at University College Cork (UCC), said his institution has become “increasingly reliant” on non-Exchequer income such as philanthropy, international student recruitment, and commercial income to make ends meet.
“UCC’s internationalisation strategy has helped diversify income streams. However, recent Government policy developments affecting visa arrangements, while outside the control of the higher education sector, are having a material impact on recruitment from key international markets, with an estimated financial impact of €3.7 million for UCC for 2026/27,” he said.
The universities called on the State to close this gap in core funding so they can carry out more research and lower student-to-teacher ratios.
They also asked for increased State support in the building of student accommodation in order to close the viability gap they face in building more homes on campus.

title: The rich are getting richer, so why no wealth tax?
description: Choice is whether a levy would be for show – a political sign that the wealthiest should pay more – or for dough
content:
A round the world, the rich are getting richer, with soaring stock markets and other asset values lining their pockets. So why – in most countries – is there no wealth tax ?
True, most tax systems do tax wealth in specific ways, such as charges on property or capital gains. But straight-up wealth taxes – an annual charge on the value of the assets held – are rare.
But with exchequers worldwide searching for cash, taxing wealth is coming back on to the agenda. A new report from the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) crunches the numbers and outlines the key choices facing Irish policymakers.
It shows there is a lot of wealth in Ireland that could be taxed, but raising a significant amount of money requires big political decisions.
For Ireland, as for other countries, the choice is whether a wealth tax would be for show – a political signal that the wealthiest should pay a bit more – or for dough, in other words to raise a significant amount of money for the exchequer.
One of the peculiarities of recent years is that although the wealth of the billionaire class has risen worldwide, the number of countries with wealth taxes has shrunk.
The ESRI report points out that 12 European countries levied an annual tax on net wealth in 1990 compared with only Norway, Spain and Switzerland last year.
Low revenue yields, administrative challenges and concerns that capital would move to other countries are among the reasons cited for countries abandoning the taxes.
France abolished its wealth tax in 2018, citing fears of wealth moving out of the country, and replaced it with a tax on real estate worldwide assets valued at more than €1.3 million. Despite rising wealth, the key message is that full-scale wealth taxes are not easy to design and implement.
Household wealth in Ireland, as measured by the Central Statistics Office household finance and consumption survey in 2023, was €927 billion, about two-and-a-half-times higher than a decade earlier.
That is an average (median) net wealth of just under €256,000 per household, with the family home the main asset for the vast majority. Where a mortgage is still outstanding, this is subtracted from the net wealth figures.
The story of Irish assets over the past decade can be told in a few headlines – rising house prices are the key factor, followed by lower household debt as the Celtic Tiger loans are paid down and a rise in business assets among the better off.
The top 10 per cent still controls close to 50 per cent of wealth. It is worth noting, also, that separate Central Bank of Ireland data , which showed wealth at just over €1 billion early 2023 – a bit higher than the CSO – estimated it at being more than €1.42 billion in the first quarter of this year.
Assets are taxed in Ireland via a few routes, notably capital gains tax and capital acquisitions tax on inheritance and gifts.
However, even if you add the amounts collected via these taxes to stamp duty and local property tax – which operates more like a charge – the total revenue comes to less than €6 billion in 2025 out of total tax revenue of more than €105 billion. Could a wealth tax increase the revenue significantly?
Well, it depends. The key insight from the ESRI paper was that if an Irish wealth tax was going to raise significant money, then it would have to have a wide base – in other words most assets would have to be included. If this happened, then even if the tax kicked in at relatively high wealth levels, significant sums could be raised.
The political problem is that a broad base takes in areas such as businesses, farms and the family home. If all wealth in the State were taxed at 1 per cent, the yield would be €9.3 billion based on the 2023 figures and probably more than €10 billion now. This is not a realistic scenario, but it provides a kind of benchmark.
The researchers go through a range of scenarios, with the widest possible tax base, one excluding the family home and a narrow definition including mainly financial assets and investment property. Cut-off points above which wealth would be taxed range from €250,000 to €2 million, with these figures doubled for a married couple. In all cases the tax rate is 1 per cent and pensions are excluded.
The first – and most striking – lesson is the importance of the range of assets covered. Exempting the family home, businesses and farms cuts the pot significantly.
At a threshold of €500,000 for example – which would be €1 million for a married couple – a narrow base just including financial assets and other investments would raise less than €450 million annually, while one including all assets would raise close to €3 billion.
The second lesson is not surprising: it is that as the threshold lowers for the wealth level where the tax kicks in, the numbers rise sharply.
At the €500,000 threshold, 4.5 per cent of households have to pay. At the lowest one, €250,000, it rises to more than a third. But the share of total national wealth rises less sharply – from 19 per cent to 32 per cent – as the amount of assets held per household falls sharply at lower levels.
The third lesson reflects the importance of the family home as the source of wealth for middle and higher earners. The main residence is only a small portion of wealth at the very highest level – where households typically own businesses or have significant financial asset. For middle Ireland, the family home is the key asset.
For a wealth tax covering everyone with assets over €250,000, exempting the family home would cut the annual tax take from €4.5 billion to €2.6 billion.
The profile of those who pay depends crucially on the rules set. The wealthiest top 10 per cent will always be hit hardest, but a key political decision would be where to draw the line. Too high and you limit the revenue raised. Too low and it ends up as a family home tax on middle earners.
The fact that there are wealthy people with relatively low incomes is another complication.
Overall, an Irish wealth tax would mainly hit middle-aged and older property owners – those aged 55 years of age plus would pay about two-thirds of the tax under most scenarios. If the base of the tax is narrow – excluding the family home – then those aged 65 or more would be in the firing line as those hold higher investments in savings and other financial assets.
They would typically paying close to half or more of the total tax, depending on the rules. On the flip side, younger renters hold hardly any wealth, so would pay little tax.
The report underlines that a wealth tax could raise a significant sum in revenue, but only if it covered a broad base of wealth.
This brings politically sensitive areas of business and farm wealth and the family home into the picture – all advantaged by the Irish tax system at present. An alternative, as recommended by the Commission on Tax and Welfare in 2023, is to increase existing taxes on wealth rather that introducing a separate new wealth tax.
But there is no easy decisions either here for Irish politicians – do they, for example, end the favourable inheritance rules for businesses and farms? Or hike local property tax?
None of these things will happen for as long as there is a budget surplus. But with the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council warning that more revenue will be needed in the years ahead to meet the costs of an ageing population and climate change , sooner or later Irish policymakers will have to consider where it comes from.
Sinn Féin has called for a study on a wealth tax and recommended hikes on capital taxes and pensions. Labour’s alternative budget also calls for a hike in a range of capital taxes, including capital gains tax and the capital acquisitions tax.
The Social Democrats want to tax the “super-wealthy”, likely only to work as part of an international drive in this area, while People Before Profit also want to “tax the multi-millionaires.”
But more taxes on wealth are now creeping on to the Irish political agenda. The comfortable classes are in the firing line – even if they don’t realise it yet.

title: Emma Jeffers finishes 16th in elimination race at Track World Championships in Shanghai
description: 21-year-old Irish rider was the eighth rider to go out in the ‘race for survival’
content:
Emma Jeffers finished 16th in the elimination race at the UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai on Thursday, the sole Irish rider in action on day two of five-day competition.
Also known as the race for survival, as the last rider to cross the line after every two laps is eliminated, the 21-year-old Jeffers was the eighth rider to make way from the 23 starters.
In the final lap sprint for the gold medal, Lotte Kopecky from Belgium easily defeated Yumi Kajihara from Japan, who had crashed earlier in the race but managed to get back into the action after the race was neutralised.
It was a third elimination title for the 30-year-old Kopecky, who took the crown from Lara Gillespie, the 2025 champion, who after winning silver in the scratch race on Wednesday, is next targeting Friday’s omnium.
Unlike the scratch and elimination, the omnium is one of the six Olympic track cycling events at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, and Gillespie is also out to gain some qualifying points towards that target.
The omnium tests the riders over four diverse events, starting with the scratch (5.38am Irish time), followed by the 10km tempo, then the elimination race, and finally the points race (12.40pm). The 24-rider race will again include Kopecky, and also Dutch star Lorena Wiebes, who narrowly beat Gillespie to win a third scratch title.

title: Kenmare Resources lowers production forecast as it continues talks with Abu Dhabi suitor
description: Downgrade a result of ‘continuing commissioning challenges’ at group’s Moma mine in Mozambique
content:
Kenmare Resources , the Dublin-listed titanium minerals miner, has lowered the full-year production forecast for its most important product as it continues takeover talks with a company ultimately controlled by the Abu Dhabi royal family.
The company said on Thursday it now expected to produce 710,000-750,000 tonnes of ilmenite, which is used in the manufacture of everything from paints to plastics and textiles, at its Moma mine in Mozambique , southern Africa, this year. It previously targeted about 800,000 tonnes.
Ilmenite production fell 17 per cent last year to 842,300 tonnes.
Kenmare said the forecast downgrade was a result of “continuing commissioning challenges” at its recently upgraded largest mining plant, known as WCP A, which the group is moving to its largest ore zone, Nataka. Nataka contains about 70 per cent of Moma’s nine billion tonnes of mineral resources, according to the company.
Ilmenite is now well into its fourth year of price decline – driven by Chinese producers, operating at home and in Africa, continuing to oversupply the market. However, Kenmare said its average price for the product rose during the third quarter as it sold more “higher value” ilmenite product.
It said the price of zircon, which accounts for about a quarter of Kenmare revenues and is used to make ceramic tiles, is continuing to improve, having stabilised and started to rise last year.
Chief executive Tom Hickey said the company was continuing to “engage constructively” with the government of Mozambique over a new Moma production and exports royalty agreement and “remains focused on bringing these discussions to a positive conclusion in the near-term”.
The previous 20-year accord expired just before the end of 2024, though the terms were to remain in place until a new one was reached.
The Irish Times reported last week on how Kenmare Resources had attracted bid interest from Abu Dhabi-based International Resources Holding (IRH). Kenmare subsequently confirmed it had received a non-binding proposal from IRH, which has been given a deadline to announce at least a firm intention to make a formal bid by 5pm on November 17th.
IRH is a unit of International Holding Company, which is chaired by sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the United Arab Emirates deputy ruler and overseer of the business interests of Abu Dhabi’s ruling Al Nahyan family.
Shares in Kenmare are up about 25 per cent since news of the bid approach. However, they remain down almost 20 per cent from the level at which they were changing hands a year ago.

title: Jeffrey Donaldson ‘deserves every day’ of 15-year sentence for sex offences, says DUP
description: Ulster Unionist Party confirms its independent safeguarding review into Donaldson’s years in group is ongoing
content:
Jeffrey Donaldson “deserves every day of the lengthy prison service he has to serve”, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) has said.
Donaldson, the former leader of the party and Lagan Valley MP, received a 15-year sentence at Newry Crown Court on Thursday for a series of historical sex offences, including one count of rape, relating to the abuse of two women when they were children.
In a statement, the DUP said: “Today justice has been done with the sentencing of Jeffrey Donaldson for his vile and disgusting crimes against his victims.
“Our first thoughts are again with the innocent victims, who having suffered such evil, were re-traumatised through giving evidence at the trial.
“They deserve our compassion, support and respect. We hope they can find some measure of comfort and can look ahead to a new chapter in their lives.”
The party added: “Regardless of status or position every individual must be held accountable for their actions.
“He deserves every day of the lengthy prison sentence he has to serve following the guilty verdict for preying on innocent child victims.”
Donaldson became DUP leader in 2021, before resigning after his arrest in 2024.
An independent safeguarding review into Donaldson’s time in the DUP is one of several investigations launched in the wake of his conviction.
[ ‘I’ve always voted DUP but never again’: Jeffrey Donaldson’s former constituents on his conviction Opens in new window ]
Separately, the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) said the sentencing of Donaldson reflects the “gravity of his crimes and the lifelong harm he inflicted on his victims”.
In a statement, UUP leader Jon Burrows said: “My thoughts remain with the two brave women whose courage brought him to justice, and with their families.
“No sentence can give back what was taken from them. But today’s outcome is the clearest possible statement that no office, no status and no reputation places anyone above the law, and that the courage of victims who come forward will be met with the full weight of justice.”
He added that the UUP’s own independent safeguarding review into Donaldson’s years within the party continues. “The party will act on whatever it finds,” he said.
Burrows also paid tribute to the “profound service” of charities and support organisations for survivors of historical abuse.
The Sinn Féín MP for North Belfast John Finucane said his thoughts “are with the victims and their loved ones who have shown immense courage in coming forward and seeking justice”.
He added: “We must also increase our efforts to end the scourge of violence against women and girls in our society.”

title: Arson attack: Waterford city ‘as sad as’ Dublin after Stardust fire, councillor says
description: Families in Waterford are under ‘extreme fear’ due to drug debts, said Cllr John Hearne
author_name: Hugh Dooley, Vivienne Clarke, Olivia Kelleher, Marie O’Halloran
content:
The arson attack in Waterford , which killed four people and left two children in critical condition, is having a similar impact on the city as the Stardust fire had in Dublin, a Waterford councillor has said.
A murder inquiry is under way after Philip English (50s), his wife Kim English (30s) and two of their four children died when their home in Waterford city was deliberately set on fire in the early hours of Tuesday.
Two other children – a girl aged 14 years and a boy aged six – remained critically ill in Children’s Health Ireland (CHI) in Crumlin, Dublin, on Thursday.
The impact on the people in Waterford, Sinn Féin councillor John Hearne said, is comparable to the 1981 fire at the Stardust nightclub in north Dublin which killed 48 young people.
“The only way to describe it down here – and I was in Dublin during Stardust – [is that] it is as sad as that,” Hearne told RTÉ’s Today with David McCullagh.
Hearne said he knew Philip English well, as he had approached the councillor on a number of occasions for help with problems. “He was a lad who would be chatting all the time,” Hearne said.
The English family had reached out to several local councillors hoping to secure a council transfer to another home as they felt unsafe.
Gardaí suspect Philip English had taken on a drug debt incurred by an associate in an effort to keep him safe. It is thought the local crime gang which was owed money targeted the family, and was also behind an attack on the home last month.
[ Waterford family ‘murdered by gang in arson attack over €20,000 drug debt’, son says Opens in new window ]
Meanwhile, a manager at a community hub in Waterford city is said she was attempting to place “a blanket of support” around “traumatised” neighbours in the wake of a fatal fire.
Amy McGuire, manager of the Butler Community Centre, said her role involved giving impacted persons “an embrace and a safe space”.
“I want them to be able to come away from everything and just breathe. It can be just having a cup of tea and a talk and a cry. If they want to speak to someone, it is there for them.
