“It is very busy. Boots are on the ground. We have had families in for counselling sessions. We have counsellors, therapists and play therapists.
“Not only do you have a fire and a loss of life, it is the fact that everyone witnessed the fire and tried their hardest to get people out. You can’t fathom how horrific that is.”
[ Deaths in Waterford attack put focus on increase in drug-related intimidation Opens in new window ]
The family were very well acquainted with CHI. The six-year-old boy, who is currently at CHI, underwent open-heart surgery on-site when he was a baby.
Both the boy (6) and Jayden, who died in the fire, had heart defects. Their 14-year-old sister, who is also in hospital in Crumlin, had leukaemia when she was younger.
Local woman Imelda Doherty said Kim was a “a right warrior mum” when it came to advocating for her children.
“She did fight and had to fight to get her kids what they deserve. She was still fighting for them.”
Another friend of the family said the reality of what had occurred was beginning to sink in.
The woman, who declined to be named, said her son was heartbroken at the death of his “pal” Callum.
“Callum was one of his closest friends, and they spent a lot of time together,” she said. “Callum had some wonderful friends, including my son, and it will take them a very long time to recover.”
[ ‘Their kids were their life’: Balloons released as final farewell to English family Opens in new window ]
Waterford Sinn Féin TD David Cullinane meanwhile told the Dáil that “vulnerable families and innocent people” must be protected from violence and harassment.
In the wake of the fire, Cullinane said “other families are looking out their front doors and wondering, could their children be next”.
“No family should have to put their children to bed wondering whether someone will set fire to their home before morning, and yet drug gangs and organised criminals are inflicting precisely that terror on families.”
He said: “They threaten children, they assault people, they burn homes, they murder people and they pursue parents, friends and even neighbours for money.”

title: Aryzta shares rally on appointment of bakery veteran as chairman
description: Urs Jordi has served in a dual role for several years against Swiss codes of best governance practice
content:
Aryzta shares rallied on Thursday as the maker of par-baked breads and pastries cleared up governance questions by deciding to promote its lead independent director, German bakery veteran Heiner Kamps, as chairman at its next annual general meeting (AGM) in May.
The Zurich-listed group, formed in 2008 through the merger of Dublin-based IAWS and Swiss bakery group Hiestand, confirmed that current chairman and interim chief executive Urs Jordi will become permanent chief executive following the AGM next year.
Shares in Aryzta, owner of the Cuisine de France brand in the Republic, rose as much as 5.4 per cent. However, they remain down by more than a fifth so far this year amid declining sales in Europe, led by Germany, its largest market, as consumers have become more price-sensitive.
Jordi was installed as chairman in late 2020 following a boardroom coup and held a dual chairman-chief executive role for several years – against Swiss codes of best corporate governance practice – as he led a turnaround of the business.
Jordi became chairman early last year as Michael Schai, a former managing director of Aryzta’s Asia-Pacific region, became chief executive. However, he took on the additional role of interim chief executive in October after Schai quit after only nine months as the top executive.
“Aryzta has a strong position in the international bake-off market, and I see considerable potential for the business,” said Heiner. “As chairman, I want to focus on our strategic priorities and refresh the board to bring in new experience and perspectives.”
Heiner is best known for founding the Kamps bakery chain in Germany in 1982, before stepping down in 2002 following the sale of the business, which by then had more than 1,000 stores, to Italian food group Barilla. He has also previously served as chief executive of fast-food chain Nordsee and dairy processor Müller Group.
He and Jordi were two of three candidates installed as Aryzta directors at an extraordinary general meeting in September 2020 after rebel shareholders, led by Swiss investor Veraison, secured backing from voters for a boardroom overhaul. The company’s three former Irish directors, including chairman Gary McGann, as well as one Swiss board member, signalled they were stepping down before the meeting.
[ Aryzta’s sales fall more than 2% to €1.06bn, new results show Opens in new window ]
Aryzta saw its centre of gravity move from Ireland to Switzerland following a boardroom shake-up.
Jordi’s reboot has included the sale of unwanted assets, including Aryzta’s former problem North American business and Brazilian unit, reduction of debt and a greater focus on innovation in baked products.
The group said in August, as it unveiled a weak set of results for the first half of the year, that it was “reviewing all options for Germany to maximise shareholder value”. It confirmed on Thursday that it would reveal its plans for that market when it issues a trading update on October 26th.

title: EU’s top court upholds Dublin Airport passenger cap
description: Regulators must take the 32 million a year limit into account when allocating airline slots, ECJ rules
content:
Regulators must enforce a 32 million a year limit on passengers at Dublin Airport when allocating take-off and landing slots to airlines, the EU’s top court ruled on Thursday.
Airlines challenged the Irish Aviation Authority ’s (IAA) decision to include the cap when setting the terms for slot allocation for winter 2024, prompting an Irish judge to refer some questions to the Court of Justice EU (CJEU).
The court ruled on Thursday that the IAA must take the passenger limit into account when setting the terms for allocating slots at Dublin.
The ruling will not affect the IAA’s recent decision to add 28 new take off and landing slots at Dublin for next summer.
Dublin Airport overtook the limit several years ago, while the High Court’s referral of legal points raised by airlines in their challenge stalled its implementation.
The airport handled 36.4 million people in 2025, a number it expects to exceed this year.
Planners capped traffic on Dublin Airport’s terminals one and two at 32 million passengers a-year in 2007.
Minister for Transport, Darragh O’Brien, told The Irish Times that he expected to make an order lifting the limit to 40 million “relatively shortly”.
The IAA is next due to rule on airport slots in April next year, when it will set terms for winter 2027/28.
The Dublin Airport (Passenger Capacity) Act, passed this summer, allows the minister to increase or axe cap.
State airports company, DAA, formally asked O’Brien in August to increase the number to 40 million, kicking off the process required by the law. The minister noted that the process was now under way.
Separately, DAA has also sought an increase to 40 million in an application to planning authority, Fingal County Council, for permission to expand the airport.
DAA said the new law and its €2 billion plan to boost the airport’s infrastructure were critical to the Republic’s economy.
The airports’ company acknowledged that the CJEU decision brought “much-needed clarity” to air travel regulation.
Aer Lingus, one of the airlines that took the original High Court challenge in 2024, argued that the airport capacity act had overtaken the CJEU ruling.
“The priority now is for the remaining statutory process to be completed as quickly as possible so that the passenger cap can be amended, providing the long-term certainty needed by airlines, passengers and the wider Irish economy,” said the company.
Michael O’Leary, chief executive of Ryanair, which was also involved in the High Court case, said the European court ruling highlighted the need for the Government to abolish the passenger cap.
He predicted that traffic at Dublin would hit 40 million next year following the IAA’s decision to cut passenger charges there. Ryanair pledged to add more aircraft to its base there following the regulator’s move.
“It is now time to abolish this stupid cap altogether, and allow the airlines to deliver competition, choice, and lower fares for Irish consumers and visitors,” said O’Leary.
He pointed out that the Government pledged to abolish the cap when it came to power in and had legislation allowing it to do so.
The High Court adjourned the airlines’ challenge after referring it to Europe. The Irish courts must apply the CJEU ruling should the airlines continue their original action. USA carriers joined Aer Lingus and Ryanair in the case.

title: Club hurling championships: Who are county champions and what’s the state of play around Ireland?
description: With county final season up and running, we take a look at who is contending in every senior championship across the country
content:
A couple of the old reliables are still standing, with Dunloy and Cushendall meeting in the final for the fifth time in 10 seasons. Dunloy won their semi-final by 30 points over Glenariffe last weekend and had six points to spare over Cushendall when they met in the group stage in August. That said, Cushendall won the last final meeting between this pair in 2024.
Final : Dunloy v Cushendall, October 25th
Mount Leinster Rangers rattled off their second Carlow title in a row – and their fifth since the start of the decade – with a 3-16 to 1-18 win over old rivals St Mullin’s in late September. They were far and away the best team in the competition throughout, sailing through the group stage with a 100 per cent record. They will play the Dublin champions in Leinster.
It was a long time coming but Inagh-Kilnamona finally won the Clare championship last weekend. Kilnamona won their last as a club in 1908 and this is the first since the amalgamation with Inagh in 2008. Backboned by David Fitzgerald and Aidan McCarthy, they’ll play the Cork champions in Munster.
For such a famous old rivalry, this will be the first meeting of the Glen and the Barrs in a Cork final since 1988. The Barrs last won it in 2022, whereas the Glen have lost their last three finals and haven’t picked up a senior title since 2016.
Final : Glen Rovers v St Finbarrs, October 18th
Slaughtneil made it 14 Derry titles in a row with a three-point win over Dungiven Kevin Lynch’s in mid-September. It was their closest call in a Derry final since 2012 against the same opposition, owing much to a first-half red card for veteran dual star Brendan Rogers. They proceed directly to the Ulster final at the end of November.
Portaferry are chasing their first-ever five-in-a-row in Down and will be well fancied against a Ballygalget side whom they’ve beaten not just in the past two finals but also in the group stage last month. For their part Ballygalget haven’t won the county since 2017, making this their longest stretch without a title since their first one away back in 1959.
Final : Portaferry v Ballygalget, October 18th
With Na Fianna’s three-year hold over the Dublin championship ending last weekend, it falls to the two clubs who monopolised the titles immediately before them to fight this year’s one out. A southside battle between Kilmacud Crokes and Cuala beckons on Sunday week, with Crokes overcoming the luckless Lucan by a single point last Sunday.
Final : Cuala v Kilmacud Crokes, October 24th
Still at the semi-final stage, with favourites Loughrea on the hunt for their first-ever three-in-a-row. There’s a couple of wild cards still in the mix – Tommy Larkin’s have only ever been to one final (winning it in 1971) and Craughwell haven’t won Galway in 96 years. Clarinbridge make up the quartet, 16 years on from their own last title.
Semi-finals : Clarinbridge v Tommy Larkin’s; Loughrea v Craughwell (both October 18th)
Naas have won the past seven Kildare titles in a row and their average margin of victory in this year’s championship is a shade under 40 (yes, 40) points. Maynooth have been their victims in three of the last four finals and though they’d have a decent championship themselves (average winning margin: 13 points), they’ll be huge underdogs in the final.
Tullaroan have been in the doldrums for far too long. They won their last county title in 1994 but still sat proudly on top of the Kilkenny roll of honour until Ballyhale passed them last year. Now’s their chance to go back level with Shamrocks, for whom TJ Reid, Adrian Mullen and Eoin Cody are all fit and firing.
Final : Tullaroan v Ballyhale Shamrocks, October 25th
A first Laois final since 1998 is The Harps’ reward for an epic semi-final win over much-fancied Clough-Ballacolla. They got there thanks to an injury-time goal from wing back Eoghan Murphy and now face perennial contenders Camross in Sunday’s decider. When these sides met in July, Camross came out on top in a game that had 54 scores, including seven goals. Could be a thriller in store.
Final : Camross v The Harps, October 18th
The Limerick championship opened on July 30th with a game in the Gaelic Grounds between Na Piarsaigh and Kilmallock and that’s how it will end. Kilmallock had a single point to spare that night, which is as close as anyone has got to them since. Na Piarsaigh are looking to make it four titles in five years, while Kilmallock last won it in 2021.
Final : Kilmallock v Na Piarsaigh, October 25th
Ballinamere have never won the Offaly championship and have only ever been to two finals. Kilcormac-Killoughey have been in 12 of them since 2007 and are chasing the first four-in-a-row in the county since late-stage Birr in the 2000s. The champions got a big boost when Adam Screeney returned for the semi-final after shoulder surgery.
Final : Kilcormac-Killoughey v Ballinamere, October 18th
Conor Stakelum might have had his tongue slightly in his cheek when he aped his uncle Richie in declaring the famine was over last Sunday. Or maybe not – Thurles Sars had gone nine seasons without a Tipp title, which maybe counts as a famine around Semple Stadium. They have only ever won Munster once, back in 2012. They go straight into a semi-final where they’ll meet either the Cork champions or Inagh-Kilnamona.
Ballygunner carried off their 13th Waterford title in a row last month but it was their closest call yet, with Fourmilewater scaring the life out of them in their first-ever final. The Gunners were a point down with a minute left but an injury-time goal from sub Mark Hartley saw them out the gap. They’ll play the winners of the Limerick final in mid-November.
Rathnure’s place on top of the Wexford roll of honour is secure for a while yet, even though it’s 20 years since their last title. After a spell in the wilderness, they made it back to last year’s final but couldn’t get past St Martin’s. They are favourites against Shelmaliers, who are chasing their third-ever title.
Final : Rathnure v Shelmaliers, October 25th

title: Strike latest: Union leader warns of ‘long and difficult dispute’
description: Taoiseach hopes ‘behind the scenes work’ leads to negotiations to avoid further public sector strikes
content:
Union leader Kevin Callinan has warned the country could be facing a “long and difficult dispute” if a breakthrough is not reached in pay talks after 300,000 public servants went on strike on Wednesday.
The Government has pointed to €1.2 billion set aside in the budget to cover the costs of an agreement increasing public servants’ pay, as part of a broader deal that includes reforms.
However, unions have said they want the pay issue settled first, before discussing other matters.
Callinan, who is general secretary of Fórsa and chairman of the Irish Congress of Trade Union s’ public service committee, said the provisions made by Government for public servants were not sufficient.
He said the €1.2 billion was not just about pay but also had to cover public service pensions and carry-over costs.
[ Could the public sector strike be a one-off? Opens in new window ]
“At very best it would produce a 2.5 per cent increase, possibly even a little bit less than that next year, when inflation is running at 4.1 per cent,” he said.
“So that’s not credible, because we’ve said it’s not just the duration of any agreement next year and beyond perhaps, it’s also this year, where the average increase for public service is 1.5 per cent, again with inflation at 4.1 per cent.
“We’ve identified a very significant gap over the previous five years of at least 5 per cent between wages and prices in the public service.”
Everybody’s struggling with the cost of living , he admitted, but he said it was “particularly severe” in the public service because “after the crash” around 2014-2015, average weekly earnings in the private sector began to improve.
“But for the following six or seven years in the public service, the entire focus was on pay restoration of the pay cuts that had taken place in 2010,” he said.
“So actually there has been a very significant divergence in average earnings in the public and private sector over the last decade or slightly more,” he told Newstalk’s Claire Byrne show.
[ Time to get down to business? Public opinion may shift if second strike takes place Opens in new window ]
Callinan said that at no stage did the unions say they were unwilling to discuss reform such as performance reviews, but cost of living had to be top of the agenda.
The protests on Wednesday had been “really important for democracy”, he said. “Because it was people working through structured organisations, representative bodies in accordance with the law, making their point respectfully.”
Speaking to reporters in Brussels, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said he was hopeful behind-the-scenes work in progress would lead unions to enter talks on a pay agreement.
Public services were brought to a standstill by nationwide industrial action on Wednesday, and a second day of strikes is prepared for next week, putting pressure on the Coalition to get union leaders around the table before then.
“We believe in a negotiated pathway to resolve this issue,” Martin said. “We want the national pay agreement, we have provided substantial funding for that.”
Martin said there was a clear “platform” to begin talks. “I think the most important thing now is for both sides to get into the negotiating process,” the Fianna Fáil leader said.
“Previous agreements were over 2½ years – three years in the past – so there’s a framework there,” he said.
“I hope that the behind-the-scenes work that’s going on in terms of finding a proper process will materialise in a proper process that will yield an outcome that will be beneficial to public servants into the years ahead,” he said.

title: Manchester United teammates largely side with Lisandro Martínez’s criticism of Jason Wilcox
description: Defender’s outburst after loss to Atlético Madrid did prompt at least one teammate to challenge him
content:
Lisandro Martínez’s view that Jason Wilcox is failing as Manchester United’s director of football reflects wider dressing-room frustration over recruitment and squad depth, although the outburst caused at least one teammate to challenge the defender to identify who he believes is not good enough for the side.
Martínez may face internal ­disciplinary action over extensive criticism of the hierarchy made in two broadcast interviews after Tuesday’s 2-0 Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid. The players had Wednesday off so any action would not be taken before their return to training on Thursday.
Martínez directed his anger at Wilcox and what he referred to as “the top” of the club, saying not enough players had been signed and questioning the scale of investment, and that “more ambition” was needed. He said: “We don’t have the best squad at the moment compared with other top teams.”
Martínez’s comments prompted a challenge from at least one teammate before the flight back to ­Manchester and caused a heightening of tension. The Argentinian did not appear to explicitly call out his teammates, saying merely that “as players we have to do more”, and claimed that last season the squad had “created the base to build an amazing team”.
Although the sway of dressing-room opinion is with Martínez, his remarks are also seen as the centre-back considering his future, because he is out of contract next summer.
Defeat at Atlético left United with two wins this season, having taken six points from their first six Premier League matches, the club’s poorest league start for 40 years. The run of form has put the head coach Michael Carrick under pressure, but Martínez took aim at Wilcox and the rest of the hierarchy. “Tonight it is easy to say the coach, easy to say the players, but also we have to see other areas,” he said, pointing upwards.
“I expect more [investment], 100 per cent. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]. I have to be honest, as players we have to do more, but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night.”
Wilcox, the executive in charge of transfers, oversaw £155m of spending in the last window on Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba. The decision to recruit three midfielders while not strengthening other areas has been met with puzzlement among the squad, particularly as Wilcox was looking for a left-back, with Newcastle’s Lewis Hall the prime target. Luke Shaw is United’s only senior player in that position and his 12-year career at the club has been plagued by injury. The 31-year-old missed the defeat by Atlético and owing to a muscular problem. The lack of depth at left-back reflects the prevailing view among players that Carrick has been left without the resources to challenge. United were eliminated from the Carabao Cup by Brighton after making eight changes.
Although Carrick led United to third last season, this came after he took over as caretaker in mid-January with only 17 league games to play with the team out of all the other competitions.
Martínez is understood to favour a move to an elite European club outside the Premier League.
On Wednesday night, Martínez released a statement on social media in an attempt to clarify his comments, writing: “I know that, first and foremost, it’s us, the players, who have to deliver, and I put myself at the front of that responsibility.”
He added: “I believe in my teammates, our manager and everyone working to help this club move forward.” Yet he still maintained his post-match comments “reflect how I feel and how much I want to see this club competing for the biggest honours”.

title: Alan Davies in Dublin review: Confessions of a mature comic can be challenging
description: The QI star hits comedy pay dirt when he asks the audience which decade they are from
content:
If timing is the secret of comedy, ageing is often the subject. Sharon Mannion, who’s Alan Davies’ support act on Wednesday night, is coping with middle-age rage, championing the merits of the harmless man as the ideal partner, epitomised by Taylor Swift ’s Travis Kelce . She is part of the Irish generation whose parents switched channels at public displays of affection, never mind sex.
Davies hits comedy pay dirt when he asks the audience which decade they’re from. The loudest cheer is from the 1960s set, “my people, complaining about the lack of legroom and already needing another piss after going to the toilet at the interval”.
He salutes the 1940s cohort, “conceived in the dark, raised on broken biscuits. They’ve seen bananas but don’t trust them”. There is even one brave soul from 1936, who turned 90 on Monday. Gerry is serenaded with Happy Birthday. When he doesn’t immediately respond, Davies feigns fear and mimes defibrillation. Definitely no bumps, he says. This is all free chat, he adds: the show hasn’t started yet.
The QI star recalls taking his son to see Back to the Future: The Musical, only to be compared to Doc when he’s still channelling Marty McFly. But he’s 60 now, and it turns out the original actor in the film version, Christopher Lloyd, was 47. Worse, Richard Wilson was 55 when he first starred as Victor Meldrew in the BBC sitcom One Foot in the Grave. “I’m five years too old to have one foot in the grave,” Davies says.
Worse still, the Till Death Us Do Part star Warren Mitchell was only 39 when he played Alf Garnett, a character too racist to be shown on TV today. “Racists don’t get irony,” Davies says. “They see the world very much in terms of black and white.”
The comic abruptly changes tack, turning to the subject of his memoir Just Ignore Him , about his mother’s early death and his abuse by his father. Davies jokes about the silence that descends before lightening the mood with reminiscences of his early career. .
He speculates that the love of an audience might have replaced that of his mother, who died when he was six, a loss compounded by his predatory father’s “special cuddles”.
This is more confessional than comedy, but the audience stays with Davies as he talks about how he still gets anxious about noises outside his bedroom door, suffering shortness of breath, a symptom of PTSD, “not to be confused with PTSB”.
When his stepmother found teen porn on his father’s printer, this ultimately led Davies to denounce his father to the police, a line that delivers one of the biggest rounds of applause.
[ Comedian Alan Davies: ‘I talk about what my father did, and how I had him arrested’ Opens in new window ]
Davies then returns to the indignities of age, asking for a show of hands for erectile dysfunction. A significant percentage of men suffer from it, he says, but the funny thing is that none go to comedy shows.
He himself is on a balanced diet of statins and Viagra. The latter is a godsend, he claims, but, rather like ordering risotto in an Italian restaurant, the chef needs 25 minutes.
Despite a sometimes challenging recipe, Davies succeeds in serving up some satisfying comfort food.

title: Jessie Buckley on Oscar campaigning: ‘Maybe we’ve given that too much weight’
description: Buckley suggests there may be greater potential in supporting film-makers at grassroots level
content:
Jessie Buckley has questioned whether the film industry places too much emphasis on Oscar campaigns at the expense of nurturing emerging talent, suggesting there may be greater potential in supporting film-makers at grassroots level.
Buckley, who has made predominantly independent films, won the best actress Oscar earlier this year for her role as Agnes Shakespeare in Chloé Zhao’s Hamnet .
Speaking at the BFI and Chanel film-maker awards in London, the actor was responding to comments by John Malkovich , who said Oscar campaigns were now the only way to get audiences into cinemas.
“I think there’s truth in that,” Buckley said. “You’ve got to take responsibility for sharing your work. It would be so easy to just go and film and then hide. I wish we could all do that. But I don’t think that’s how it works any more.”
She said the industry’s reliance on film promotion affected not just actors and directors but the wider workforce.
“I feel so proud of being part of this community – this affects so many people’s lives. Crews, marketing, everybody. And if you don’t support it, you’re not going to have a job,” she said.
“Maybe we’ve given that too much weight. I wonder if there’s more potential in nurturing at a grassroots level than giving so much weight to a marketing Oscar campaign.”
Buckley called for greater support for film-makers working outside established industry structures, pointing to the success of films “made on shoestring budgets”, including Obsession and Backrooms .
“People went to see them because of their quality, not because of the IP or what was deemed successful beforehand,” Buckley said.
“It’s essential that we support up-and-coming young film-makers. It would be completely selfish if we didn’t. At some point we want to pop off this earth, and we need to support the next generation. I want to know what they’ve got to say, what their world looks like.”
[ Jessie Buckley, a generational talent with acting superpowers Opens in new window ]
The four winning films at the BFI awards explored subjects including political protest, racial profiling, female solidarity and family trauma.
Rich Felgate, director, producer and cinematographer of We, the Hated, was recognised for his documentary about Just Stop Oil protesters and the personal consequences of participating in a polarising movement. The jury described the film as “urgent and brave”.
Buckley said it had prompted her to reconsider the role of protest in society. “In our world at the moment, protest seems like such a dangerous act, when historically it’s been essential to democracy,” she said.
“It realigned me and reminded me of how important protest is, and how we can misunderstand the people within that. That we need to understand more and need films like that more.”
Olive Nwosu won for Lady, her feature debut set in Lagos, which follows one of the city’s few female taxi drivers as she becomes drawn into the world of a childhood friend who has become a sex worker. The jury praised Nwosu’s cinematic ambition and her handling of challenging material.
[ Jessie Buckley profile: From TV talent show runner-up to Golden Globes winner Opens in new window ]
Imran Perretta was recognised for Ish , a black-and-white coming-of-age film set in Luton’s South Asian and Middle Eastern community. It follows two 12-year-old best friends whose relationship is tested after a police stop and search.
The jury praised its exploration of racial profiling and the experience of being British while being treated as an outsider.
Rachel Taparjan won for Something Familiar, her debut feature documentary about her search for her missing sisters after being adopted from Romania and brought to the UK as a child. The jury praised the film’s “naked, unselfconscious revelation of self”, saying it had stayed with them longest. – Guardian

title: Irish provinces gear up for Champions Cup return
description: Meanwhile, Gordon Manning looks at the latest stopover in Mickey Harte’s managerial journey
content:
Rugby’s Champions Cup is back this weekend “if not with a whimper then not with the bang of its halcyon days either”, writes Gerry Thornley. Six-time winners Toulouse and the reigning back-to-back champions Bordeaux Bègles are the joint favourites, but what of the Irish provinces’ hopes? Gerry brings you a guide to each of their pools, Connacht drawing the shortest of straws - they have five former winners of the competition in theirs.
Munster open their campaign against Racing 92 at Páirc Uí Chaoimh on Saturday evening, Gerry talking to Tadhg Beirne ahead of the game. Law tweaks will “potentially reduce his impact” when it comes to the art of winning turnovers in defensive mauls. “The dark arts are slowly going out of the game, that’s for sure,” he says. A “tad wistfully” too.
Leinster also have French opposition for their opener, away to Clermont Auvergne , Michael Scully talking to James Ryan about his first visit to Stade Marcel-Michelin, “one of French rugby’s most celebrated venues”.
In Gaelic games, Gordon Manning looks at the latest stopover in Mickey Harte’s managerial journey , the Tyrone man returning to the club game after his appointment by Down’s Kilcoo this week. He’s still “not ready for the pipe and slippers” just yet.
Football, meanwhile, is losing another of its young stars to Aussie Rules, Gordon with news on Donegal’s Finnbarr Roarty , the 2025 Young Footballer of the Year, signing a two-year deal with Collingwood.
And Ciarán Murphy turns his thoughts to the new hurling and football rules which are about to be unveiled in The Ryan Cup, the third-level tournament. They’re not insignificant changes either.
After brushing aside Kazakhstan in their World Cup qualifying play-off semi-final, the Republic of Ireland’s women face Poland in December for a place in next summer’s finals in Brazil. Gavin Cummiskey gives us the lowdown on Poland, whose star turn is Barcelona striker Ewa Pajor, and hears from Carla Ward about the challenge they’ll pose.
In cycling, Ian O’Riordan reports on Lara Gillespie adding another UCI Track World Championship medal to her collection, the Wicklow rider winning silver in Wednesday’s scratch race in Shanghai - she missed out on gold by less than half a wheel length.
In golf, the India Championship got under way this morning in Delhi, Philip Reid with word on Rory McIlroy opting to leave his driver in his hotel room , such is “the short and tight examination posed” by the course.
And in his America At Large column, Dave Hannigan reflects on the life and times of Mike Ditka , the giant of American football - both as a player and coach - who died last week at the age of 86.
TV Watch : Rory McIlroy, Shane Lowry and Tom McKibbin are all in the field for the India Championship which got under way at 6.30 this morning on Sky Sports Golf, coverage continuing until 12.30 this afternoon. The men’s rugby league World Cup kicks off in Sydney this morning with the meeting of nigh-on perennial champions Australia and New Zealand (Premier Sports 2, 10.05am and repeated at 3pm).
And in football’s Europa League, you can choose from two 5.45pm kick-offs - Lyon v Crystal Palace (Premier Sports 1 and TNT Sports 1) and Torreense v Sunderland (Premier Sports 2 and TNT Sports 2), and at 8pm Celtic are away to Benfica (Premier Sports 1 and TNT Sports 3).

title: UK police force ordered to reopen inquiry into handling of Graham Linehan arrest
description: Writer was awarded a settlement from the Metropolitan Police in July over a civil claim against the force after his arrest for social media posts about transgender issues
content:
British police have been ordered to reinvestigate a complaint over the arrest of Father Ted co-creator Graham Linehan after a watchdog found failings in its handling of the case.
The 58-year-old Irish writer was arrested at Heathrow airport after flying in from Arizona in September 2025, on suspicion of inciting violence over three posts he made on X.
He subsequently received an apology from the Met Police and a settlement following a civil claim .
Britain’s Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) confirmed Linehan later sought a review of how the Met handled a complaint about the investigation into him and his treatment by officers.
The application, received in May 2026, included “an allegation that he was discriminated against due to his gender-critical beliefs”.
The watchdog ruled the Met’s handling of Linehan’s complaint was inadequate and ordered Scotland Yard to reinvestigate the allegation he had been discriminated against.
“In October, we found the outcome of the complaint was not reasonable and proportionate and directed the Met to reinvestigate a number of the allegations made,” an IOPC spokesperson said.
“We found that, during the complaint investigation, the force failed to provide satisfactory explanations for the grounds for the man’s arrest and failed to pursue lines of inquiry regarding a complaint about the man’s bail conditions.
“We also directed them to reinvestigate the allegation that he was discriminated against.”
The IOPC added: “The man will have a further right of review to the IOPC should he be dissatisfied with the outcome of the force’s reinvestigation.”
Conservative politicians and Harry Potter author JK Rowling had criticised Linehan’s arrest.
The Met has been contacted for comment. – PA

title: Could the public sector strike be a one-off?
description: Inside Politics: A second day of action is planned for next week but there is some hope it could be averted
content:
Could Wednesday’s strike by 300,000 public sector workers be a one and done?
The Government – not to mention people impacted by the largest industrial action in almost 20 years – will certainly hope so.
A second strike day is planned for next week , but there is some hope it could be averted.
As Pat Leahy and Emmet Malone report in our lead story , it is expected that contacts between the Government and unions will now intensify as officials seek to find a way forward that could avoid a second strike next Wednesday.
Speaking in Brussels on Wednesday evening, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said there was “a sense of goodwill and a willingness to get a resolution on this”.
The Government is “open for negotiations”, he said. “We will engage and see if we can find a basis and a process that would be satisfactory to all sides that enable negotiations to take place and avoid any action next week.”
There have been suggestions in Government about a possible preliminary process at the Workplace Relations Commission that could see a draft agenda for negotiations agreed, but officials remained tight-lipped on Wednesday night, citing the sensitivity of the issue.
Union sources played down the suggestion of a fresh initiative from the Government, though it is understood informal contacts are continuing.
Fórsa general secretary Kevin Callinan said that recent comments by Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers suggested “there may be a pathway” to negotiations on a new deal. Callinan chairs the public services committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions, which is due to meet on Thursday to review the situation.
Opposition parties all declared support for the strikes and urged the Government to enter negotiations and agree pay increases for public servants.
Unions claimed widespread public support on the picket lines as industrial action shut schools, colleges, local and national Government offices and severely restricted health services across the country yesterday.
Some of the workers who went on strike set out their reasons here .
The coming days will tell whether they will be back on the streets next week.
Wednesday’s Inside Politics podcast looks at how the public sector pay dispute might end.
British prime minister Andy Burnham has reinforced his support for Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy following a meeting in Downing Street. Burnham’s backing came after US president Donald Trump increased pressure on Kyiv and Russia hit the country’s energy plants with a fresh wave of missile and drone attacks.
Philip and Kim English, and two of their sons, Callum and Jayden, were murdered in an attack on their home by a gang trying to collect a €20,000 drug debt, a family member has said. Conor Lally reports .
Martin Doyle has a story about how Normal People author Sally Rooney’s books will no longer be available in UK over her support for Palestine Action.
The Office of Public Works is to conduct an assessment of the legal and contractual implications of terminating or withdrawing from the project to deliver a proposed national children’s science centre, the Dáil’s public spending watchdog has been told .
Ministers have criticised anonymous comments about the fitness of Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan to continue in his role because of health concerns.
The Dáil kicks off with Minister for Rural Development Dara Calleary due to take Parliamentary Questions at 8.47am.
Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill is expected to be up next at 10.23am.
Uisce Éireann will be before the Committee of Public Accounts from 10.30am to be quizzed on its financial statements for 2025. The agency says that sustained capital investment of approximately €2 billion a year over the next 25 years will be required to maintain and transform the water and wastewater networks countrywide and address legacy deficits. Martin Wall has a tee-up story here .
The Committee on Children is launching its report on technology, social media and children at 11am.
There is an opportunity for TDs to ask questions on topical issues at 1.52pm.
Amid the ongoing dispute on pay talks, the Labour Party has a motion on public sector pay, which is to be debated from 2.52pm.
Proposed legislation from Sinn Féin aimed at naming the new national children’s hospital after early 20th century doctor and political activist Kathleen Lynn is to be debated from 4:52pm.
The Committee on Further and Higher Education will hear from representatives of universities on the topic of funding for third level institutions from 9.30am.
The Committee on Defence and National Security meets at 9.30am to discuss building national resilience and national emergency planning. There will be representatives from the Office of Emergency Planning as well as the Civil Defence and local authorities in attendance.
The Committee on Enterprise will hear from employers’ group Ibec on the EU Cybersecurity Act from 10am.
Cork City Council representatives are due to attend the Committee on Key Issues Affecting the Traveller Community to discuss an accommodation site in Ballyvolane. The meeting starts at 12.30pm.
Doctors for Universal Healthcare will be among attendees at the Committee on Health, which is considering Ireland’s progress toward a universal healthcare system at 12.30pm.
The Committee on Agriculture will conduct pre-legislative scrutiny of the planned Deforestation and Forest Degradation Bill 2026 at 2pm.

title: Anthropic’s quarterly revenue surges 45% to nearly $17bn
description: AI company is seeking ​to convince investors that breakneck revenue growth can eventually outrun its enormous costs
content:
Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue rose 45 per cent to $16.8 ‌billion (€15 billion) from the previous quarter, according to an investor who attended a meeting with the AI company’s leadership ‌in San Francisco on Wednesday.
Revenue in the first quarter was $4.7 billion, and $11.6 billion in the second quarter, ​according to the person who attended the investor day meant to familiarise prospective Anthropic investors before its highly anticipated initial public offering (IPO).
The IPO is expected to precede a public listing by rival OpenAI , making Anthropic ​an early test of investor appetite for heavily unprofitable AI developers pursuing massive scale. Its public-market debut is ⁠likely to be pushed until after the November US midterm elections.
Scrutiny ​of AI companies’ finances has intensified as they pour money into chips, data centres and computing power needed to develop and ⁠operate increasingly powerful models.
Targeting a ​valuation of more than $2 trillion, Anthropic is seeking ​to convince investors that its breakneck revenue growth can eventually outrun the enormous costs ‌of building and running AI systems.
The company ​has committed hundreds of billions of dollars in future spending under long-term agreements ⁠for cloud services, computing and infrastructure, Reuters ⁠reported last month.
Founded ​by former OpenAI executives, Anthropic has emerged as one of the leading generative AI developers with its Claude family of models. Its expansion has been underpinned by Amazon and Alphabet’s Google, which are simultaneously investors, suppliers of computing power and important distribution partners, as well as AI competitors.
[ Never mind the ‘risk to humanity’, Anthropic’s IPO raises more prosaic concerns Opens in new window ]
Anthropic has also sought to distinguish itself through its focus on AI safety, warning of ‌the dangers posed by ⁠increasingly capable systems even as it competes in the race to develop and commercialise more powerful models.
Its research has found that its own ‌AI agents have engaged in troubling behaviour in test environments, including leaking sensitive information and sabotaging code, ​though the company has said it has not seen evidence ​of such misalignment in real-world deployments. – Reuters

title: ‘Wave of fear’ in nationalist community in Belfast at proposed Apprentice Boys parade
description: Residents of Lower Ormeau concerned that loyalist march through contentious route will be a repeat of Drumcree standoff
content:
An application for an Apprentice Boys parade through a nationalist area of south Belfast has sent a “wave of fear” through the community, according to a parades’ campaigner.
Hundreds of residents from the Lower Ormeau area have contacted Gerard Rice about the proposed loyalist march along a route that was a parading flashpoint and site of a sectarian massacre during the 1990s.
The Parades Commission is currently considering the application by Belfast Walker Club for a procession on Saturday November 7th.
This is the first proposal at a contentious parading site since the commission ruled that a controversial march could go down the Garvaghy Road in Portadown last month.
Protestant loyal order parades have been prevented from proceeding over the Ormeau Bridge into the nationalist area since 1999.
The latest application would take in the scene past Sean Graham’s bookmakers where five Catholics were murdered by loyalist paramilitaries in 1992.
Rice has represented the Lower Ormeau Concerned Community, a residents’ advocacy group, since violent clashes erupted over parading disputes 30 years ago.
There has been relative peace since then, he said.
The group has lodged a “full submission” to the Parades Commission.
“This community remains resolutely opposed to parades coming down through the area,” Rice told The Irish Times.
“I think the overwhelming opinion, from both sides of the community, is that no one wants to go back.
“Even though the application was made last week, people only found out about it yesterday. It was like a wave of fear going through this community.
“Hundreds of people have contacted me about concerns and apprehension they have around the potential for what happened in Drumcree happening here.
“We have done our best to reassure people that it will not happen.”
Previous applications have been made by the Apprentice Boys to walk to the route as part of annual Remembrance weekend ceremonies.
[ ‘We’re not going back, are we?’: Courts may be the only way to end Drumcree standoff Opens in new window ]
Last year’s bid by the Belfast Walker Club was banned from the Lower Ormeau area – the march still went ahead through non-contentious areas – after the commission ruled there were continuing “sensitivities”.
The fresh proposal is for 80 members to parade from Ballynafeigh Orange Hall before passing through the Ormeau Road, across Ormeau Bridge and onwards to Donegall Pass.
“This is not a new application or response to Drumcree,” added Rice.
He pointed out that residents “never had to go to the Parades Commission about this parade – until now”.
“The commission has always issued a determination,” he said.
“It’s always been the Apprentice Boys come down the road, get on a bus, and go to Donegall Pass and then go on about their parade.
Statements made by Orange Order representatives earlier this week – loyalist activist Jamie Bryson claimed “traditional routes” would be marched once again – have “heightened concerns” among residents, Rice added.
On Monday evening, an unnotified parade took place on Belfast’s Shankill Road in what was the first organised protest by loyalists since the Orange Order’s parade along the Garvaghy Road was banned by Northern Secretary Chris Bryant.
Rice said he hoped that the Parades Commission “would see sense”.
“There hasn’t been a threat of a parade on the Lower Ormeau in 26 years,” he added.
“Work has been quietly going on across the communities over that time.
“The groundswell of opinion is that young people are not for going back. What we are trying to emphasis to people is ‘go about your business and behave normally’.
“In the Lower Ormeau, marching and the hurt caused by it is never far away.

title: Talented James Talarico silences conspiracy theorists in fascinating Senate race in Texas
description: The Democratic candidate, derided by Donald Trump, belongs to none of the traditional American political archetypes and is aiming to win in a state where Republicans have dominated for decades
content:
When he walked into the television studio on Wednesday night, James Talarico was looking fairly hearty – for a ghost. Over the course of 10 maddening days, the whereabouts and wellbeing of the Texan Democratic candidate for the Senate had become the stuff of wild conspiracy theory.
The simple explanation, forwarded by his communications team was that, like Frank Sinatra, he had a cold. The Maga wing of the Republican movement had different ideas, varying from some class of nervous breakdown to an imminent scandal too dark for contemplation to a classic case of the jitters.
“Jimmy appears to be having a full-blown mental Tala-freak-out on the national stage,” ventured his opponent, Texas attorney general Ken Paxton, on his social media platform six days ago.
“My campaign has a simple request: proof of life.”
White House policy deputy chief Stephen Miller, Elon Musk and Maga influencer Laura Loomer soon chipped in with equally mendacious posts.
Talarico resumed his campaign at the weekend, and his ebullient health was confirmed when he participated in a CNN/Jubilee Town Hall in Fort Worth on Wednesday evening. The forum involved the candidate taking questions from members of the public representing Democratic, Republican and Independent factions of the Texas electorate.
Paxton has repeatedly ducked and avoided Talarico’s persistent invitations, or dares, to engage in the kind of live debate formats that are taking place in other toss-up states such as Maine, Georgia and Iowa. When Talarico gave his answer to the very first question – “are you okay?” – from moderator Erin Burnett, it became clear Paxton’s decision to avoid a verbal rumble with Talarico was a smart move.
“I think the responsible thing to do when you get something like the flu is to stay at home and not get other people sick,” Talarico said by way of accounting for his absence.
“And I was able to work remotely from home. But you are right. That decision to stay home for a week sent my opponent and his conspiracy theorists spiralling. I opened up social media to learn that I had apparently dropped out of the race. That I had flown to a mental hospital in Ohio. That I had died. This is crazy. These false claims got millions of views online. And this is an example of what I call the rage economy. Conspiracy theorists can post anything they want on the internet. They get clicks. The billionaires who own these platforms get rich. We all get angry. And nobody’s life gets any better. Conspiracy theories don’t put food on the table. They don’t put gas in the tank. They don’t improve our country. So, I am going to stay focused on the issues tonight.”
The response offered a neat mirror into why Talarico (37) has come to be regarded as a generational, incandescent political talent. He belongs to none of the traditional American political archetypes. Since 2018, having been elected to the Texas state house at the age of 29, he has built a formidable body of state legislative work, introducing 18 Bills that became law before emerging as a national voice. He draws on his life experience as an eighth-generation Texan, a state schoolteacher and pastor as he seeks the seat that will ultimately define whether this autumn surge by Democratic candidates signals a genuine desire for change among Americans or is a midterm mirage in the Lone Star state.
Few candidates have been impugned as savagely by the Republican administration as Talarico. US president Donald Trump routinely refers to him as “Tala-freako”. This week, vice-president JD Vance got in on the act, issuing this slur on the Texan:
“He [Talarico] was asked what he loves in life besides his family and friends and he responded, without skipping a beat, trans children. Now you gotta wonder what the internet search history of a man like that looks like. I don’t want to know – and you don’t either.”
Vance was referring to a remark Talarico made several years ago in an interview.
“I love the trans children who showed up yesterday at the state capital to advocate for their humanity,” Talarico said then.
On Wednesday night, he answered questions from both Democrats and Republican voters who, in the disarmingly earnest way of the American political theatre, stepped under the bright lights to discuss the issues of greatest concern to them. The topics ranged from abortion to education to funding for Ukraine to Trump’s Save America Act to God. In each case, it was clear Talarico’s presence – attentive, always respectful and singularly beatific in aspect – at the very least convinced them they had been heard.
He had one Republican voter, a retired military man who wanted to know his stance on the voter ID issue, applauding his answer before their four-minute allotted conversation had ended. On one of the remarks that the Republicans like to goad him about – that God is non-binary – Talarico had this to say.
“When I said that I was being provocative and I want to admit that and come clean about that. But I think what I was saying was not controversial theologically. The idea that we can’t define God using human categories. Not only did I say that but the late Charlie Kirk said that. The late Pope Benedict said that.”
To a Jewish Democrat concerned about his views on Israel during a period of escalating anti-Semitism, he reminded her he had studied biblical Hebrew as part of his seminarian training and made it clear that his criticisms were narrowed to the government of Binyamin Netanyahu.
Did any of this matter? How many households in Texas counties far beyond the metropolises tune into CNN news in this age of partisan, entrenched media warfare? What did Paxton have to gain by dedicating one of the 22 remaining campaign nights to allowing Texans to compare his communicative limitations with those of Talarico? Trump has been blitzing the state with personal appearances and what has long been marked as a staggeringly expensive regional election is about to become more so.
[ Emerging Democrat star Jon Ossoff has become a chief thorn in Trump’s side Opens in new window ]
Spending for Paxton – favoured by Trump over long-standing Republican senatorial stalwart John Cornyn despite myriad flaws and scandals – has just tipped over the $500 million (€445 million) mark. Regional network television spending is in for a further bonanza as the Republicans seek to extend a vice-grip on the Texas Senate seats they have held since 1994.
It just might work. Talarico has had a profile dating back to his long, dramatic primary election race against Texas representative Jasmine Crockett, whom he defeated in March. Paxton, who finally defeated Cornyn after Trump’s endorsement before a “run-off” election in May, has been playing catch-up. His attempts to catch up have involved avoiding any direct debates with his opponent. But he has the weight of the Texas party machine – and the president – behind him.
[ ‘A lot of people are losing hope’: A state Trump turned red now appears more divided Opens in new window ]
Still, the most remarkable aspect of the night was that as the 90-minute event came to a close, Talarico reminded the audience he hadn’t mentioned “my opponent” just once. You could sense a penny drop: Paxton had been all but forgotten. Then Talarico quietly skewered Paxton, telling voters he has earned $27 million since entering elected office, and owns 15 homes when many Texans are struggling to own one.
Three new polls illustrate just how finely this fascinating race is poised. The Texas Political Project has Talarico ahead by 3 percentage points among likely voters (50 to 47). Marist University has the Democrat ahead by just two points. A new Recon/MR/Siena poll has Talarico four points ahead, narrowing since September. It’s sufficiently narrow for the Republicans to believe that with a rush and a push, the land that they stand on is still theirs. Who knows, they might be right. They’ve been right throughout the century. Talarico is attempting to push against three decades of a formidable Republican institution.
But irrespective of the result, it is clear Texas has unearthed another generational political talent. He was sensational – and over the autumn flu.
[ A visual guide to the US midterms Opens in new window ]
[ Keith Duggan: Lone star Trump believes he can bend Texas and midterm elections to his will Opens in new window ]

title: Oil prices retreat as investors weigh supply outlook, Middle East tensions
description: Iran has threatened to step up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports
content:
Oil prices fell more than ‌1 per cent on Thursday as investors weighed risks to supply from attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz against US efforts to cut petroleum shipping costs by easing sanctions ​on vessels.
Brent crude futures fell $1.64, or 1.6 per cent, to $104.42 a barrel by 0337 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down 98 cents, or 1 per cent, to $94.11, reversing gains from the previous session.
WTI rose to a three-week high in the prior session after the Houthis attacked Saudi Aramco’s headquarters and Iran said it was ​deploying new tactics to target ships in the Strait of Hormuz and keep oil prices high.
A container ship and a dry bulk carrier both sank near ⁠the strait in the past 24 hours after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday.
Attacks around ‌the ‌waterway ​have surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month.
With the Iran war ⁠having disrupted shipping and driven up freight costs to ​record highs, the Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on so-called ​shadow-fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela to help ease prices, a US official said ‌on Wednesday.
The new talks centre on the United ​States potentially allowing “legal oil” to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, the US official said.
Increased output from Russia and the Middle East has ⁠kept a lid on prices. Russia’s crude oil production ⁠rose by 65,000 barrels per day ​in September to 8.43 million bpd but remained down 870,000 bpd year over year, the International Energy Agency said on Wednesday.
The IEA also said crude oil exports from Middle East Gulf producers rose by 4.4 million bpd in September to around 75 per cent of prewar levels.
“While there is little concrete evidence of a near-term peace deal, oil continues to find its way to buyers through alternative routes and logistical arrangements,” said Phillip Nova’s head of market insights, Priyanka Sachdeva, in a client note.
“These workarounds have helped prevent a more severe supply shock, although they come at a higher cost and leave ‌global flows vulnerable to further disruption.”
In the ⁠US, crude oil and distillate inventories fell, while gasoline stocks rose last week, market sources said on Wednesday, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute.
Crude stocks fell by 11.1 million barrels in the week ended October 9, ‌sources said. That was a much bigger draw than analysts polled by Reuters expected.
“Despite the sharp inventory draw, oil prices barely reacted. The failure to rise on ​bullish news suggests investors are cautious about chasing prices higher at current levels,” said Haitong Futures ​in a note on Thursday.
Official numbers from the US Energy Information Administration are due at 12pm EDT (1600 GMT), delayed by a day following the Columbus Day holiday on Monday. - Reuters

title: Serbian students aim to graduate from antigovernment protests to forming new government
description: Anger at establishment led by Aleksandar Vučić has spawned movement that could enable the Student List to form government later this month
content:
Serbia ’s students have been on the streets for two years protesting about the deadly consequences of official corruption. Ten days from now, they could be forming the government.
When Serbia votes in an early general election on October 25th, the main contenders will be former president Aleksandar Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) and the Student List, which was born out of two years of antigovernment demonstrations led by university students. It will be a referendum on Vučić, who resigned as president last month to lead his party in the elections in the hope of returning as prime minister.
The presidency is limited to two terms but Vučić has been either president or prime minister since 2014 and the SNS has been in power in Serbia since 2012. Vučić’s tenure has seen Serbia’s economy growing steadily but he has also presided over restrictions on media freedom, violent attacks on journalists and civil society activists and widespread corruption that has enriched a small circle.
The student protests began in November 2024 after the collapse of a railway station canopy in Serbia’s second-largest city of Novi Sad killed 16 people. Their initial demands focused on holding local politicians to account for opaque contracts with Chinese construction companies and substandard renovation work at the station.
But as Vučić’s government tried to shift the blame on to architects and building workers and refused to conduct an effective investigation into the tragedy, the protests became more political. When police and pro-government thugs violently attacked them, the students started demanding early elections, attracting about 300,000 people to a demonstration in March 2025 and almost 200,000 to another protest last May.
The students started preparing for the election months ago, holding plenaries at their university faculties to select candidates before releasing the list last month. None of the students are seeking office themselves, a decision designed to emphasise their commitment to the common good rather than to secure power.
No member of the parties currently in government were eligible for selection and members of opposition parties could only be selected if they did not hold leadership positions. Most of the Student List candidates are unknown to the public, although former central bank governor Dejan Šoškić is among them and has become a prominent spokesman.
The candidates are ideologically diverse and among the most prominent demands in the Student List’s manifesto are the creation of a free media landscape, safeguarding judicial independence and the introduction of a law to scrutinise the origins of wealth. Other priorities include improving the educational system, extending access to healthcare and making housing more affordable for young people.
Vučić is promising stability and the continuation of a foreign policy that has seen Serbia maintain close ties with China, Russia and the United States while pursuing European Union membership. Amid warnings from the Committee to Protect Journalists that reporters covering the election were subject to violent attack, the EU’s delegation in Belgrade this week warned Vučić’s government that it was watching the vote closely.
“Free, fair and transparent elections in line with international standards are required for Serbia to meet the democratic criteria to advance towards EU membership,” the delegation said.
“We are concerned by several reported incidents of violence which have no place in an electoral process. All instances of violence require swift, transparent and credible institutional follow-up so those responsible are brought to justice. Journalists and civil society should be able to operate in a safe environment. We also expect all relevant institutions to act swiftly in cases of possible irregularities during the campaign and on election day, and to address complaints in a timely manner throughout the electoral process.”
