title: Asian stocks sell off as AI trades crumble
description: Quicker-than-expected increase in US consumer price inflation upped expectations for Fed action
content:
Stocks sold off in Asia on Thursday with the ‌tech supply chain bearing the brunt of the damage, as a quicker-than-expected increase in US consumer price inflation upped expectations for the Federal Reserve to act later this year.
MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan tumbled 3.3 per cent, ​led by a plunge of 8 per cent in South Korea’s KOSPI, while the Nikkei 225 fell 4.8 per cent. S&P 500 e-mini futures were down 0.5 per cent.
“The selloff in Asia looks less like a sudden deterioration in technology fundamentals and more like a repricing of the cost of capital,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Bank in Singapore. “Investors are not questioning whether AI demand exists,” she said. “They are increasingly questioning what price they should pay for ​that growth when interest rates are high, volatile and potentially moving higher again.”
Overnight, stocks on Wall Street logged their third day of declines after US consumer price inflation accelerated by more than expected in September.
The S&P 500 ⁠fell 1.1 per cent, the Nasdaq Composite tumbled 1.9 per cent and a gauge of semiconductor stocks extended losses into a sixth day, as the prospect of higher interest rates pummelled shares ‌of ‌Oracle, ​CoreWeave and other AI stocks sensitive to higher borrowing costs.
“While the initial selloff was triggered by the hotter-than-expected CPI, tech was the main driver of today’s selloff,” JPMorgan analysts wrote in a note. “AI was again the main challenge ... with financing risks and IPO timelines still at ⁠the centre of the story.”
Asian stocks in the tech hardware supply ​chain were hard hit on Thursday. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company fell 2 per cent, Samsung Electronics plunged 9.3 per cent, ​memory chipmakers SK Hynix and Kioxia Holdings plummeted more than 11 per cent each, and AI investor Softbank Group lost 9.4 per cent.
Some strategists found reasons for optimism, noting that volumes were relatively light and October ‌is typically a volatile time of year for markets.
“I’m not worried, ​because stocks are not expensive, there is no sign of a recession, and demand still massively exceeds supply in most parts of the AI story,” said Mark Matthews, ⁠head of research for Asia at Bank Julius Baer in Singapore.
The backdrop ⁠of investor anxiety drove safe-haven buying of government ​bonds, with the yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond down 7.8 basis points at 5.110 per cent.
“We continue to think that yields at current levels offer decent value,” DBS analysts wrote in a note. “We are not convinced that the Fed will have to deliver back-to-back hikes on the back of one set of CPI numbers.”
The inflation data reshaped expectations for the Fed’s rate path, with traders briefly pricing in roughly even odds of a hike later this month before scaling back those bets.
Fed funds futures are now pricing an implied 75 per cent probability the US central bank will remain on hold at its next two-day meeting on October 28, little changed from a day earlier, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool.
“The upside surprise in US CPI and the subsequent rally in bonds is highly counterintuitive,” ‌said Prashant Newnaha, senior rates strategist at ⁠TD Securities. “The cleanest read through is that the slump in AI is repricing growth expectations down, leading to bonds serving as a hedge for stocks.”
Against the yen, the US dollar was down 0.4 per cent at 157.74 yen, while the euro was up 0.6 per cent at $1.1225.
The Australian dollar declined 0.2 per cent to $0.6956 after employment unexpectedly ‌decreased by 39,300 jobs in September, against expectations of an increase of 20,000.
Investor attention turns to speeches from Fed officials speaking in Bangkok, including chair Kevin Warsh, for clues on the US central bank’s next move, ​as well as US producer prices and retail sales data due for release later on Thursday. AI chip giant TSMC will ​also release earnings for the third quarter later in the Asian trading session.
In oil markets, Brent crude was down 1.7 per cent at $104.20 a barrel as traders weighed up the effects of US sanctions relief on supply against attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. - Reuters

title: AI fears, hopes, and high construction costs
description: Business Today: The best news, analysis, and comment from The Irish Times business desk
content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) companies should be “ selling solutions ” in areas like cybersecurity rather than “selling fear”, a conference in Dublin heard on Tuesday. Ciara O’Brien reports from the Government’s International AI Summit at Dublin’s RDS, at which a coterie of top tech executives, including OpenAI chief financial officer Sarah Friar, discussed their hopes and fears for the technology.
Also speaking at the event was Brad Smith, one of the most senior executives at tech giant Microsoft. He told Ciarán Hancock on the Inside Business podcast that AI’s impact on the jobs market could take up to 25 years to play out fully .
High construction costs and planning uncertainty are the biggest barriers to the delivery of properties in Ireland, according to developers, while – perhaps surprisingly – access to finance is down their list of concerns. Killian Woods reports on a new survey from EY Ireland, which also indicates a strong appetite for debt among developers despite recent interest rate increases.
Meanwhile, Stephen Conneely reports from a separate event on creativity and copyright in the age of AI. Ruadhán Mac Cormaic, editor of The Irish Times, told the conference that large-language models have “hoovered up areas of the internet and didn’t ask for any permission”, effectively leading to “billion-dollar companies pretty much overnight as a result of others’ intellectual property”.
Network, regulatory, policy and other costs account for more than half of what Irish people pay for electricity , according to research from a new think-tank, Trifecta Ireland. Barry O’Halloran has the details.
The Irish Government wants more cars on Irish roads to be electric. That makes a lot of sense, but there are barriers to entry, not least the cost. That’s where an old solution may provide a new fix, writes Emmet Ryan . Citroën has relaunched its 2CV model for the EV market. It might be just the shot in the arm that the European market needs.
Not only can money not buy you love, writes Conor Pope, new research suggests it also can’t buy you peace of mind or optimism either. The September 2026 consumer sentiment index shows consumer confidence at 61.1, compared with an average over the 30 years the index has been running of 83. It means that Irish people are richer but they’re also more nervous and gloomy now than back when the Celtic Tiger was starting to purr.
In Ask the Lawyer , a reader asks what happens to her sister-in-law’s share of a family home if she dies or is placed into residential care?
Our Innovator to Watch this week is Aishling Flaherty, who has built Caboodle , an online marketplace bringing small Irish retailers together. She speaks to Olive Keogh about turning a €200,000 problem into an ecommerce platform.
Ciara O’Brien sits down with the European Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation for a wide-ranging chat about the bloc’s attempts to address the challenges raised by the Draghi report, funding for deep tech and digital sovereignty.
In keeping with the AI theme, Eoin Burke-Kennedy reports that entry-level hiring in “ AI-augmented occupations ” in Ireland declined by 16 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, according to a new survey of labour market trends.
Eoin also has the details of new Central Bank of Ireland figures , which illustrate a significant rise in the cost of variable rate mortgages in Ireland, raising concerns that borrowers may be facing into a winter of financial strain.
Finally, Cantillon takes a look at new research that seems to prove the old adage about a happy worker being a productive worker and, separately, some measures the Government could adopt to cut energy bills by the end of the decade.
If you’d like to read more about the issues that affect your finances try signing up to On the Money , the weekly newsletter from our personal finance team, which will be issued every Friday to Irish Times subscribers.

title: Wikipedia is a very odd target for the culture wars
description: If you want to tackle misogyny on the internet, there are better places to start than a website that can tell you as much about the taxonomy of citrus as it can the death of Socrates
content:
W ikipedia – by certain metrics – is the largest “compendium of human knowledge” in the world. It is also a sexist, racist, marginalising, macho endeavour that scrubs women from the history books in favour of the middle-class white men who author it. Didn’t you know? It was news to me too – perhaps I am brainwashed by those same middle-class white men; so captured by their cultural hegemony that I cannot even see my chains. (Agh! The middle-class male strikes again.)
Thank God for Sandi Toksvig, then, here to lay it all out, immune from the internal misogyny that afflicts the rest of us. The British/ Danish TV presenter told a crowd at Cheltenham Literature Festival in the UK last week that Wikipedia, for too long, has been allowed to favour the accomplishment of man; that it approaches women with a mindset more suited to the early 20th century; that it is patronising, merely pretending to be egalitarian in nature. Only 18 per cent of Wikipedia profiles concern women, she says. Because the majority of the volunteer editors are men, she goes on, the gender bias is to be expected.
And so, if Wikipedia is the go-to source for anyone after low-barrier, easy-to-consume information, then the world is in trouble. In fact, maybe the sexual revolution never happened; and all advancements in gender parity were an illusion. Justice will elude women until they achieve proper Wikipedia representation. And so Toksvig is setting up her own venture, “Mappa Mundi”, with colleagues of Cambridge University – “an interactive digital atlas where we can find a home for the vast amount of knowledge that is currently sidelined or deleted”.
It is true that there are not many women featured on the “List of state leaders deposed by foreign powers in the 20th and 21st century” page. “Ancient Roman generals killed in action” and “Roman consuls who died in office” are comparatively weak on women representation too. Cleopatra’s page does not pass the Bechdel test. “List of Catholic martyrs of the English Reformation” might send Toksvig into a swivel-eyed rage. But, pre-empting this accusation of ahistoricism, Toksvig cites one example of a woman physicist denied a Wikipedia page until she won a Nobel Prize.
Fine, justice for Donna Strickland then. Otherwise, this is a culture war from the imagination of Paddington Bear: glib, inconsequential, twee and inflected with the spirit of the Liberal Democrats. I suppose it is the sort of thing Justin Trudeau might have found compelling in 2018.
Who is this for? If you take great interest in gender parity on the internet – and there are better uses of your energy – Wikipedia is an odd target. There are some very dark corners out there. A website that can tell you as much about the taxonomy of citrus as it can about the death of Socrates (white middle-class man) is not one of them.
But this is just what the cultural soft left do – pick the wrong targets, misfire, consume all the oxygen for pointless and self-important reasons and fail to say anything interesting at all. I am reminded of the 2020 push to “decolonise” the classics. The subject was deemed white, obsessed with rape and bloody wars, hyper-focused on words produced by men. The Society for Classical Studies in the US complained of “the complicity of classics as a field in constructing and participating in racist and anti-black educational structures and attitudes”. Whatever that means.
And what else of the classics makes it a worthy target? I suppose it is nice to assume that the absence of women from the historical record is just a clerical error; a problem of reportage that can be amended by some careful rearranging of old primary sources. This is the same fallacy that Toksvig is falling into – that the women of human history carried equal weight and influence (and literacy skills, and tools of production, etc) as men. Same goes for race in Ancient Rome. We know this isn’t true. And we know that acknowledging the realities of the past is not the same as condoning them. But eliding or concealing those realities for contemporary political wins is, meanwhile, dishonest.
[ From quiet quitting to iced coffee: What is Gen Z’s problem with work? Opens in new window ]
Anyone seeking a book deal to redress the apparent gender imbalance of the historical tradition needn’t try hard. Take the reams of contemporary literature retelling the classics from a “female” perspective (Circe, The Silence of the Girls, A Thousand Ships and the 500+ other examples). For decades now, popular historians have sought to illuminate the hidden women of the past – the Suffragettes receive as much historical attention as any Tudor. In my classics degree, excessive concern was dedicated to Sappho (but one woman poet) as some awkward over-corrective measure.
Toksvig’s war on the misogyny of Wikipedia is wrong for two reasons. It’s burdened by an ahistoricism that would not pass the editorial standards of Wikipedia itself. But it has also taken one of the best parts of the internet – that free, sprawling, considered, fair, democratic resource – and used it for navel-gazing and self-satisfied point scoring. Who are the points for? I can’t name a single beneficiary of a crusade against Wikipedia. Toksvig, perhaps.

title: Approach to Leaving Cert mathematics does not add up
description: Syllabuses fail to provide knowledge required for understanding modern technology
content:
A student wishing to study English or a related subject at third level is expected to have a thorough knowledge of the basics of the language, such as the alphabet, grammar and sentence structure.
Likewise, a student wishing to pursue science, engineering, technology or mathematics at third level would be expected to have a solid understanding of the basics required for such programmes.
Modern technology is ultimately based on mathematical concepts. Artificial intelligence (AI) and data science are entirely dependent on topics such as vectors, linear algebra and related structures. Learning algorithms, a fundamental component of AI, are grounded in mathematical principles.
Graphics – including real-time video game graphics – rely intimately on the structure of quaternions, invented by William R. Hamilton, a renowned Irish mathematician. Quaternions extend complex numbers, a topic now proposed for omission from the Leaving Certificate syllabus.
A recent submission by mathematicians and computer scientists to the United States Congress expresses the point succinctly: “Behind every breakthrough technology shaping modern life, from artificial intelligence and robotics to biotechnology, there is mathematics quietly doing the heavy lifting.”
The current and proposed Leaving Certificate mathematics syllabuses fail to provide the basic mathematics required for understanding modern technology. Our reputation as a knowledge-based society would be severely damaged, with consequent and substantial losses to our economy. – Yours, etc
Professor (Emeritus) of Mathematics, University of Galway.
Lecturer (Emeritus) University of Limerick.

title: Actions of Irish footballers were measured but impactful
description: Describing them as ‘anti-Semitic’ and harmful to the Jewish community in Ireland is a denial of the wider truth
content:
Sir, – It is most regrettable that Anti-Defamation League chief executive Jonathan Greenblatt should describe the actions of Ireland’s footballers before their Nations League matches against Israel as “shameful”.
Having decided that the two fixtures had to be played, the FAI made a call on what would be the most appropriate form of protest against the continuing genocide in Gaza and the attacks by illegal settlers on Palestinian homes on the West Bank .
Given the enormity of the issue, the players’ actions were impactful but measured. To describe them as “anti-Semitic” and harmful to the Jewish community in Ireland is a denial of the wider truth – wrong and yes, even shameful. – Yours etc,

title: Eamonn Casey’s work in London
description: It is helpful to get a balanced view of the overall scope of his pastoral works
content: Sir, – I read with great interest and admiration about the practical work of former bishop Eamonn Casey while he was a priest assisting Irish emigrants in London (“ Fr Eamonn refused to buy pints for me in London, long before his reputation was shredded ”, An Irishman’s Diary, October 11th). While we are all familiar with his later misdeeds, it is helpful to get a balanced view of the overall scope of his pastoral works. Thanks to Kieran Fagan for that. – Yours, etc,

title: With so much cash sloshing around, why is there a housing crisis?
description: Why is the HSE underfunded, and why aren’t there decent rail services between Dublin and Rosslare?
content:
Sir, – I don’t get it. According to Fintan O’Toole (“ The blue-green smoothie ruling the country has no plan and even less passion ”, Opinion, October 13th), the Government is spending money like water, but to no great effect. Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael , he tells us, between whose sleek forms it would be impossible to insert a cigarette paper, are throwing tax revenues at existing programmes while, bizarrely, borrowing on the bond markets to beef up the nation’s slimline sovereign wealth funds.
Ireland’s budget surpluses are the talk of Europe. We make so much money from the corporate taxes generated by big pharma and big tech that Brussels is asking if we shouldn’t perhaps share some of the loot with our European partners (which, of course, we won’t).
But with so much ready cash sloshing around, how come there’s a housing crisis , why is the HSE underfunded and why aren’t there decent rail services between Dublin and Rosslare ?

title: Waterford family ‘murdered by gang in arson attack over €20,000 drug debt’, son says
description: Violent dealers are chief suspects after petrol bombing killed man, his wife and two of their children
content:
Philip and Kim English, and two of their sons, Callum (12) and Jayden (9), were murdered in an attack on their home by a gang trying to collect a €20,000 drug debt, a family member has said.
John James English, Philip English’s adult son from his first marriage, said the debt had been incurred by somebody else, not his father.
Two other children – a girl (14) and a boy (6) – were rescued by firefighters and remained critically ill in Children’s Health Ireland (CHI) Crumlin , Dublin, on Wednesday night.
“Debts, drug debts, and I know that for a fact,” John James English told RTÉ when asked why he believed the arson attack was carried out on the home in Waterford city. He also believed he knew who was involved.
“Twenty grand worth of a debt. Is that worth [four] lives, 20 grand? I am not afraid to say it; if I was I wouldn’t be able to die in peace. My family is dead. It’s unreal. Innocent children, the whole lot of them innocent,” he said, saying his father was not involved in drugs or any form of crime.
John James English said that when his mother, Anne, was forced out of her house for about two months after it was petrol-bombed, his father, Philip, and stepmother, Kim, opened their home to Anne. She stayed there for eight weeks.
On Wednesday, Anne said her deceased ex-husband and his wife were a “beloved couple who never had any bother with anyone ... the kids were their life”.
[ Granduncle of boys killed in Waterford arson attack calls on perpetrators to hand themselves in ]
Another member of the family – James English, the granduncle of Philip English – also spoke out, addressing the killer directly.
“We have lost a family now, wiped out,” he said at a vigil for the family at the Sacred Heart Church, Waterford. “Please, whoever done it, be a man and own up to what you done.”
Gardaí believe the arson attack just after 5am on Tuesday that engulfed the home on the Birchwood estate was carried out on behalf of a family-based violent gang of drug dealers in Waterford who also have links to Spain .
Suspects have been identified. Gardaí believe the attacker, a male, was driven to the scene by an accomplice, possibly a woman.
The gang is also suspected of vandalising the victims’ family car with paint in August 2023, throwing a petrol bomb at the house last month and attacking Anne English’s home. The family had also been targeted by rumours and threats online.
The murder investigation was described by An Garda Síochána as being “intense in nature and very active with multiple searches” at properties across Waterford city, linked to members of the suspected gang.
Two people they expected to find were not present in the properties, but a number of phones, laptops and vehicles were seized for technical examination.
Detectives are examining CCTV footage recorded in the area recently to determine if those who carried out the attack had visited the property in advance as part of their planning.
Chief Supt Andrew Pettit, of Waterford-Kilkenny Garda division, said people linked to those responsible needed to consider their positions after the four-fatality murder, urging them to come forward.
The crime scene on Birch Avenue remained sealed off on Wednesday.
Gardaí appealed to anyone who was in the vicinity between 4.30am and 5.30am on Tuesday to contact the incident room at Waterford Garda station on 051 305300, the Garda Confidential Line 1800 666 111 or any Garda station.

title: Building company ceases trading, leaving sports clubs with bills for unfinished work
description: Clearwater Construction & Landscaping ceases trading, calls creditors’ meeting
content:
Several sports clubs face bills for unfinished development work after building firm Clearwater Construction & Landscaping Ltd ceased trading this week.
Clearwater, known to most customers as CWC, is well known for work on pitches and other sports facilities, particularly for local organisations in the southeast.
But the Grangecon, Co Wicklow -based business ceased trading this week, saying it intended to hold a creditors’ meeting on Friday October 23rd, when liquidators will be appointed to the company.
The move took sports clubs for which Clearwater had been working on various projects by surprise.
Statements from some reported that they had not heard from either the company or its director, PJ Norton, in advance of its closure.
One organisation, Bunclody Association Football Club (AFC) in Co Wexford , confirmed it was facing substantial bills to complete work begun by Clearwater that was unfinished.
Club chairman Jamie Farrell confirmed to members that it had paid Clearwater €313,000 to date for work on an all-weather pitch, fencing, ground preparation and lights.
Some of the initial work has been done, but a substantial amount remains to be completed, he confirmed to The Irish Times.
The club estimates that about €180,000 of the contracted work has been completed.
The club had received assurances on Friday September 25th that the work would continue but days later were told that Clearwater was having difficulty collecting debts owed to it.
Farrell said Clearwater’s failure has left Bunclody AFC facing extra financial pressure.
“It’s heartbreaking,” he acknowledged, pointing out that the club does much of its fundraising from supporters in its own community through weekly bingo nights.
Bunclody AFC’s “only hope” is that it can recover the cash lost on the project through the Government’s sports capital grants scheme, Farrell said.
Tramore Tennis Club in Co Waterford emailed members this week to say that it was “finalising an alternative contractor” to complete work on lights for two of its courts originally given to Clearwater.
“Unfortunately, the original building contractor (CWC) is no longer communicating with Tramore tennis club,” said the organisation’s email.
Farrell also said that he was aware of several GAA and soccer clubs in the southeast where Clearwater was working on developments.
Clearwater made more than €299,000 profit last year while it owed €1.4 million to trade creditors, according to its most recent accounts, which Norton signed in May.
The company has nominated Eoin Massey and Anthony Glennon, of Friel Stafford, as liquidators, but they have not yet been appointed, as the creditors’ meeting must decide on this.
Neither Norton nor Clearwater responded to a request for comment.

title: Complex political issues reduced to slogans
description: I sincerely hope there is a change in leadership in Israel on October 27th
content:
Sir – Meaningful progress regarding the Israeli- Palestinian conflict is unlikely to materialise while Israel ’s prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu is in office, and it seems lasting peace, if achieved, will occur only through political agreement.
Since October 2023, many very complex geopolitical issues have been reduced to slogans, social media trends and what is now commonly known as “virtue signalling”.
The loudest voices appear to have a superficial understanding of the historical, political and sectarian complexities involved, and the narrative casts either side as wholly virtuous or wholly villainous. Without minimising the seriousness of the appalling atrocities which have occurred, never before has there been a greater tendency for distant conflicts such as this to attract attention because they are politically fashionable.
Why are we not asking questions about governance and accountability on both sides, including how international aid to the Palestinian territories has been managed over the past several decades?
While I only have immense sympathy for ordinary Palestinian civilians, I do not need to go to a Macklemore concert to affirm this. Public debate has become polarised, and perhaps, due to inertia or fatigue, we have outsourced our judgment to social media algorithms.
This is part of the reason why complex historical and political issues are now reduced to slogans, social media campaigns, concerts, flags and bracelets rather than a vital, informed discussion.
I sincerely hope there is a change in leadership in Israel on October 27th to create the momentum required to begin meaningful negotiations towards peace for both groups. – Yours, etc,

title: Big tax increases should require a compelling justification
description: Tax hikes should not be the default response to budgetary pressure
content:
Sir, – Your report on Monday’s local property tax ( LPT ) decision by Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council (“ No property tax changes for Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown and Fingal homeowners ”, Dublin, October 12th) quoted the chief executive’s warning that retaining the full 15 per cent reduction, at a cost of €10.4 million, will “inevitably lead to [a] reduction in services”. That claim deserves scrutiny.
Last year’s national revaluation increased the council’s LPT intake by €10.85 million annually from 2026 onwards, more than the cost of the discount. The council’s 2026 budget, meanwhile, grew by 12 per cent to €313.7 million, following an increase of more than 50 per cent over the previous council term.
It is difficult to reconcile budget growth on that scale with the claim that services can only be protected by asking homeowners to pay even more, again.
The 7.5 per cent reduction recommended by the executive, and supported by Labour and the Social Democrats , would have increased LPT bills by 8.8 per cent, while the Green Party proposal would have increased them by 17.6 per cent. I voted with the 27-12 majority to avoid tax hikes.
It is all too easy for politicians and officials to spend the public’s money, but every euro spent must ultimately be paid for by someone. Local services matter, but so does responsible stewardship of public money, and big tax increases should require a compelling justification, not be the default response to budgetary pressure. – Yours, etc,

title: Newton Emerson: Many loyalists are desperate to leave. The only thing stopping some is an ‘exit fee’
description: The UDA waives the charge if someone finds religion so it has reportedly been spying on churches for confirmation
content:
Loyalists kept their distance from Drumcree for two reasons. First, they knew it was a lost cause and a disaster for unionism. Second, they had just finished discussing their own disbandment with an expert appointed by the British and Irish governments. They did not want to make a mockery of this at the final moment.
Dutch academic Fleur Ravensbergen published her report on Tuesday, after a year of talking to paramilitary groups, community leaders, victims of crime and terrorism and public bodies. Her team is believed to have included representatives from the Irish Government and the Northern Ireland Office.
The report claims there was significant engagement with dissident republicans, which dissident groups have denied. This confusion is not considered fatal to the exercise – most people have long accepted that loyalism and republicanism present different challenges. Unless or until dissidents do engage, the report is effectively about winding down loyalism.
Its main recommendation is that both governments should establish “an independent, time-bound transition mechanism without delay”.
This should offer a structured process towards disbandment, with credible monitoring and verification at every step. It should operate in parallel with robust policing and prosecution of offences, rather than functioning as any kind of temporary amnesty, given the extent of paramilitary linked crime. No financial inducements should be offered to groups or their members, as this is “ineffective, counterproductive and damaging to public confidence”.
Ravensbergen advises not getting hung up on the word “disbandment”, although it is in the title of her report, as it may be needlessly wounding to paramilitary pride.
“Agreeing the transition process, milestones and end-state of group transition is more important than terminology,” she writes.
The report identifies 11 milestones, including ending recruitment, disposal of weaponry and removal of flags, murals and other physical signs of influence.
After three decades of peace processing, many people will feel they have heard all this before. If it is implemented, loyalism will simply continue stringing everyone along. While this view is understandable, in reality there has never been a structured disbandment process for loyalists or republicans in Northern Ireland, let alone one with a deadline – there have only been deadlines (all missed) for decommissioning weapons.
As to why loyalism would submit to such a process, it is nearer an “end state” than is widely realised.
In 2020, police and intelligence service briefings were leaked to the BBC, revealing loyalist groups were still recruiting and had 12,500 “card carrying” members. This entered public consciousness and continues to be cited as if loyalism remains a 1970s-scale menace.
Leaving paramilitarism behind must be reward enough, with law enforcement providing motivation
However, as the full briefings made clear, recruitment is mainly of young drug dealers, while the vast majority of members have been inactive for decades and are desperate to leave. They are not allowed to leave because their £20 monthly membership fees are the bedrock of loyalist finances, for their local “commanders” in particular.
The Ulster Defence Association (UDA) charges a £5,000 “exit fee”, which it waives if someone finds religion. So many members have been availing of this waiver that the UDA has been spying on churches to confirm regular attendance, according to a Sunday Life report two weeks ago.
The preposterous circumstances of these hollow organisations would be a joke, were they not still all too capable of terrorising their neighbours. Nobody wants or respects them, including most of their members. It should be no surprise that many of their leaders are interested in discussing a way out.
Funding for “community work” has characterised much of the official approach to transition. Ravensbergen has identified this as both a failure and a cause of public cynicism. It entrenches paramilitary control over communities at the taxpayer’s expense, while dragging public bodies – including the police – into a charade of respectability.
Leaving paramilitarism behind must be reward enough, with law enforcement providing motivation. Adding a deadline might seem pointless without a temporary amnesty but experience elsewhere indicates it is crucial.
Most of the world refers to paramilitary transition as Disarmament, Demobilisation and Re-integration (DDR). A model for this has been developed since the 1990s by the United Nations, drawing on lessons ranging from American gang culture to wars in West Africa.
Setting a tight deadline, typically a year, is considered essential to focus efforts, draw a line under conflicts and prevent processes being deliberately prolonged and exploited, as has plainly occurred in Northern Ireland. DDR emphasises dismantling command and membership structures and getting people into lawful employment.
Ravensbergen has worked with the UN on conflict resolution in the Basque Country, Libya, Iraq and Congo – the latter has had multiple DDR programmes, with varying degrees of success. Her report advises learning from “international experience and expertise”.
It is hard not to see this as a mild rebuke to the peace processors of Northern Ireland, who presume they only have lessons to teach the world.

title: Champions Cup pool guide: Leinster, Munster and Connacht’s opponents reviewed and rated
description: Toulouse and Bordeaux Bègles joint favourites to win tournament, but shocks may await Top 14 aces
content:
The Champions Cup is back this weekend, if not with a whimper then not with the bang of its halcyon days either. In a tacit acceptance that the tournament’s profile suffered for its delayed December start since the pandemic, the first round has been brought forward to its traditional October slot of yore for the first time since 2018 and the tweaks don’t stop there .
Previously, the top four teams in each of the six-team pools qualified for the Round of 16, but this season the top three teams will advance, with the top two earning a home draw. The remaining four places will go to the next four teams with the highest number of match points, regardless of their pool.
Furthermore, the bonus-point system will mirror that of the Top 14, with teams only securing a try bonus point if they score three or more tries more than the opposition. This has changed from the four-try system used since the 2003-2004 season.
It seems fitting that the scoring system copies the Top 14, given the tournament has been largely amended to their liking. And in an unprecedented era of French dominance they have won the last six Champions Cups .
The odds are also on this being extended at the end of the final in Lyons next May, with six-time winners Toulouse and the reigning back-to-back champions Bordeaux Bègles the 13/5 joint favourites.
[ Champions Cup has a jeopardy problem: can anyone stop France’s Top 14 giants? ]
Leinster are once again regarded as the biggest threat at 9/2, followed by Bath at 9/1 and Northampton at 10/1, with Montpellier the dark horses at 14/1.
It will be close to a sensation if the winners come from outside those six, and it would be no surprise if Toulouse, who are also seeking a fifth successive Bouclier de Brennus, do not regain the trophy after a two-year absence – a relative famine for them.
The URC’s top dogs in this competition, Leinster (last season’s beaten finalists) and Glasgow (last season’s beaten semi-finalists) appear to have avoided the French and Premiership heavyweights in this season’s draw. Leinster begin away to Clermont, who have had a little bit of a resurgence under Christophe Urios.
The Clermont team is admittedly in the lower half of the Top 14 table with two wins out of six, but the margins have been tight, as was the case last Saturday when losing by a point to Bordeaux at home thanks to a late Maxime Lucu penalty. But if anything, that could make them more dangerous in Saturday’s opening game in the atmospheric Stade Marcel-Michelin.
This rebuilt Clermont team is a younger side than the one Leinster faced a couple of seasons ago, and is built largely around their brilliant young scrumhalf Baptiste Jauneau, a modern-day Morgan Parra. He’s a classy player, has all the skills, generates the tempo and orchestrates their game and it would be no surprise if he’s not soon putting pressure on Nolann Le Garrec and Lucu for that role as understudy to Antoine Dupont at international level.
Pau are a fascinating case, and their opening selection away to Leicester Tigers, and indeed the result, will inform us as to how seriously they will go after this competition.
They have been the coming force in the last two years in the Top 14, also supplying the French team with a gifted crop of talented and exciting young French backs from the Olympic Sevens winning team. The shining light is Théo Attissogbe, who has largely vindicated his selection on the French team ahead of Damian Penaud. If he plays and Pau turn it on against Leicester, that would be a statement of intent and make them intriguing visitors to the RDS.
The Tigers do not look quite the force of old. They have had a little bit of a rebuild under a new coaching ticket, but are missing their man mountain George Martin, who has joined Saracens, and their Lions lock/flanker Ollie Chessum, who is injured. So they’re lacking a little bit of ballast up front, as the traditional Tigers packs had in the past. Again, their opening game against Pau looks to be quite pivotal.
Leicester could be good enough to make the knock-out stages, but unlikely again to make another deep run in the knock-out stages, as has been their lot lately. The same applies to the Sale Sharks, if slightly less so, although Joe Marchant and Courtney Lawes, and their win away to Saracens a fortnight ago was eye-catching. But the Prem is likely to be their priority.
Connacht are back in the big time, and how. They drew the short straw, but a glamorous one all the same, with home games against Saracens this coming Saturday, and Toulouse in January – the three-time and six-time winners, respectively, of this competition.
Indeed, all Connacht’s opponents are former winners as they are away to Exeter in December, and finish away to La Rochelle in January, when Ronan O’Gara welcomes them to the always-packed Stade Deflandre. This is what Connacht wanted: glamour fixtures against the best which, coupled with the advent of the Dexcom Stadium, has swollen pride and enthusiasm out west.
Despite an opening-night loss in La Rochelle to the last kick of the game, Toulouse have hit the ground running and as they seek a record fifth successive French championship are quickly setting the pace again as they invariably do. As well as their unrivalled conveyor belt through their own underage system, the signing of the world-class Tommaso Menoncello has further added to their ridiculous array of imported talent, when one thinks they have the current fullbacks of France, Argentina, Italy and Scotland on their books in Thomas Ramos, Juan Cruz Mallía, Ange Capuozzo and Blair Kinghorn.
O’Gara has made some good signings this season, such as Theo McFarland. Their pack has been bolstered. Le Garrec is coming into his prime and they have weapons everywhere.
Saracens have had something of a reboot, with Brendan Venter returning to oversee the team and Mark McCall moving upstairs. They’ve signed George Martin and Alfie Barbeary. Maro Itoje has been refreshed by a summer’s respite. The Dexcom is in for a treat, of sorts, if Noah Caluori plays, for his is a freakishly gifted 6ft 4in winger who is awesome in the air.
Exeter had a disappointing start to the season when beaten at home by Gloucester, considering they were Prem finalists last season, and then lost to Bath in the Rec before scraping by Newcastle at the weekend. Immanuel Feyi-Waboso would grace any competition, but he appeared to tweak his hamstring last weekend and the Champions Cup may not see too much of him.
Bordeaux, the back-to-back champions, look a cut above the rest in this group and perhaps the whole tournament given their amalgam of power, skill and pace can hurt opponents in any way and in any conditions. They look much the same, and just as strong, more or less, as last season, and when Lucu and Matthieu Jalibert are firing, and Penaud and Louis Bielle-Biarrey are brought into the game repeatedly, they are almost impossible to contain.
Racing do not have the assembly of galacticos of old, and in a crushing semi-final defeat to Toulouse and opening day loss in Bordeaux, when conceding more than 130 points in the two games, they looked like damaged goods. They have since won two of their ensuing five games and will bring a dangerous, Fijian-infused backline to face Munster in Cork on Saturday, with the powerful centre Josua Tuisova and the quickfire Vinaya Habosi and Selestino Ravutaumada on the wings.
Rumours that Gloucester might send out a second-string side at home to Bordeaux on opening night are surely misplaced, for this is a marquee game that demands they put their best foot forward. But George Skivington has regarded this competition as an inconvenience in the past and, under pressure to secure a top-four finish in the Prem, may come to the same conclusion before long again.
Bristol are another to have had a mixed start to the season and Pat Lam’s side appear to be a little bit more pragmatic than maybe they were in the past, and are kicking the ball a bit more, with even Louis Rees-Zammit not counterattacking at every available opportunity. But they will be dangerous opponents at home to Munster in December.
Northampton and Bath look a class apart in this group, whatever about the defensive shortcomings in Franklin’s Gardens last Saturday when the Saints won the match between the sides by 71-48.
Northampton are an unbelievably well coached team under Sam Vesty, which has echoes of Leinster in their pomp under Stuart Lancaster, with everyone knowing their role. They rarely lose their shape and get the ball back incredibly quickly. And in Fin Smith, Rory Hutchinson and Fraser Dingwall, they have three players who excel at the gainline, as well as firepower out wide in Tommy Freeman and Ollie Sleightholme.
They still look the real deal, and probably England’s best bet to win the Champions Cup, given Bath appear to be sorely missing Thomas du Toit, a key figure in their treble win two seasons ago.
Montpellier, Challenge Cup winners and French finalists last season, will make this a three-way tussle for the first two places.

title: Garda numbers set to reach record levels but GRA says growth ‘nowhere near enough’
description: Number of sworn members of Garda set to reach all-time record, likely passing 14,800, this week for first time in history of State
content:
The overall strength of the Garda force will reach record levels later this week when a class of about 200 new recruits passes out at the Garda College.
The swearing-in ceremony in Templemore, Co Tipperary , should bring the number of Garda members above 14,800 for the first time in the history of the State.
The Garda Representative Association (GRA), which represents more than 11,000 rank-and-file gardaí, noted the strength of the force was still far behind the target set by former Garda commissioner Drew Harris .
While the association welcomed the record numbers, it added the rate of growth was “nowhere near fast enough to keep pace with current policing needs”.
GRA president Niall Hodgins said that Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly last week “admitted to the Public Accounts Committee that An Garda Síochána will continue to rely on gardaí to take on overtime and will continue to do so until our numbers reach 16,500, and sadly we are way off those numbers”.
“But what is really concerning is that the commissioner’s predecessor had set a target of surpassing 15,000 in 2021 and rising to 18,000 by the end of the decade, so it seems their sights are getting significantly lower.”
In reply to queries, Garda Headquarters said there were 14,683 Garda members at the end of August, which represented a “year-on-year increase of 500 gardaí”. It confirmed the passing-out ceremony on Friday was expected to increase the size of the force “to the highest number in the history of the State”, subject to the final number of those passing out being confirmed.
The increasing size of the organisation over the past 12 months had “enabled the introduction of high-visibility policing in Dublin, Cork, Limerick and Galway, as well as supporting other units across the organisation”.
[ Waterford murders: Cars and phones seized as two children remain critical Opens in new window ]
As well as Friday’s passing-out ceremony, another intake of recruits will take place next Monday, and before year end, a class that has been in training for some time will pass out.
“Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly [has said] it is the organisation’s intention to meet and exceed the Government target of recruiting 5,000 additional gardaí by 2030. If this is achieved, it is estimated that the overall number of gardaí will be approximately 16,500,” the statement added.
This would bring the “police to population ratio broadly in line with Police Scotland, which polices a similar population to our own”. At the same time, the Garda’s “retention rate is much better than many other UK, European and international police services”.
The GRA has expressed its concern at a “crisis” around the number of Garda members retiring and resigning, saying 400 members had exited so far this year. A significant spike in age-related retirements is expected over the next decade due to accelerated recruitment undertaken 30-40 years ago.
The previous record for Garda numbers, of 14,750, was reached in March 2020, after hundreds of recruits in the Templemore college effectively bypassed training and were sworn in as gardaí with full powers. That unprecedented move was undertaken in a bid to boost numbers for a pandemic-related policing surge.
When those recruits were fast-tracked, the number of sworn members in the Garda jumped by almost 300 overnight. However, the Garda College then closed, due to pandemic restrictions, and the strength of the force steadily declined for several years, as older members retired, and others resigned.
When recruitment recommenced after the pandemic, it was very sluggish at first. Some of the first classes passing out in Templemore were barely above 100 recruits, though 200 members or more should have been passing out in each class.
The Department of Justice said in a statement one of Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan ’s “key priorities is to see more gardaí on our streets engaging in high-visibility policing and the plan to increase recruitment into An Garda Síochána is working”.
O’Callaghan is confident the highest-ever number of serving gardaí will be reached by the end of this year, it said.
