title: A strike should not be the first port of call in a negotiation
description: We need a new legislative framework to ensure proper engagement occurs first
content:
Sir, – Wednesday’s strike was premature and wholly unnecessary. Both sides know that a compromise will have to be reached and both sides know that the public service has a symbiotic relationship with the government of the day.
The fact that both sides have displayed intransigence from the get-go is deeply worrying. The Ministers involved seem to think they can dictate terms in this instance though they ran for the hills when faced with demands from other sectors.
The union negotiators seem to think they are entitled to an ever-expanding pot of money, as if it didn’t have to be earned.
It occurs to me that we need new legislation to cover public sector strikes. A strike is not the first port of call in a negotiation.
We need a legally binding process whereby proper engagement occurs, with both sides required to adhere to a formula. If, for example, we had an agreement that wages would increase by a three-year average of inflation, regardless of other factors, then any other increases could be tied to increased productivity and budgetary constraints. Failure to negotiate in any meaningful way should carry penalties, on both sides, up to and including loss of post. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – There is an inherent contradiction in going on strike for better pay. If workers were genuinely struggling to make ends meet they would not favour a reduction in income via a strike.
Going on strike as a first course of action without meaningful interaction with the Government indicates that workers’ incomes are not as constrained as union leaders proclaim.
Taking action to strike now damages the credibility of their claim. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – David Gordon ( Letters, October 14th ) highlights how effortless it is for a TD to respect a picket line when there is no impact on their pay packet. His observation points to a significant structural flaw facing modern trade unions, especially those that do not issue strike pay.
For example, in the past, nonstriking teachers and SNAs had to walk past colleagues on a picket line to sign an availability register, meaning many chose not to cross and consequently forfeited a day’s pay. (The rights and wrongs of that system are of course debatable.) However, in the digital era, many nonstrikers can declare themselves available for work with a tap on a smartphone from home, drawing full pay while remaining entirely comfortably removed from the conflict.
When public sector unions get to the negotiating table, they must confront this “free-rider” problem. When the personal sacrifice and financial burden of industrial action falls exclusively on those on the picket line – while nonparticipating colleagues enjoy the exact same rewards with no discomfort – the very logic of union membership comes into question. – Yours, etc,

title: OPW to assess implications of withdrawing from proposed National Children’s Science Centre
description: Minister to meet charity behind plans in a bid to identify a way forward for the project while minimising cost to the State
content:
The Office of Public Works (OPW) is to conduct an assessment of the legal and contractual implications of terminating or withdrawing from the project to deliver a proposed National Children’s Science Centre (NCSC), the Dáil ’s public spending watchdog has been told.
Meanwhile, Minister of State with responsibility for the OPW Kevin ‘Boxer’ Moran will meet the charity behind the NCSC plans – Irish Children’s Museum Limited (ICML) – in a bid to identify a way forward for the project, or a way to end any commitment to the project while minimising any cost to the State.
The Dáil’s Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has been examining the NCSC project, which is expected to cost more than €70 million and has been the subject of two arbitration cases since it was first proposed more than 20 years ago.
The OPW is under a legal obligation to deliver a building for the science centre at a site adjoining the National Concert Hall (NCH) on Earlsfort Terrace and it must proceed to tender for the project by the end of 2026.
However, there is no Government department assigned to fund the development of the centre. The PAC published an interim report on the matter in July.
The Department of Public Expenditure and Reform (DPER) has now responded to the recommendations in the PAC report.
The document, seen by the The Irish Times, says that three Government departments – education, higher education and culture, communications and sport, have told the OPW they are “not in a position to provide capital funding for the development of an NCSC”.
The DPER response says that the OPW will “conduct an assessment of the legal and contractual implications of terminating or withdrawing from the project in conjunction with our legal advisors”.
The PAC’s interim report recommended that the OPW, DPER and relevant departments engage with NCSC representatives to identify “a way forward for the project or a way to end any commitment to the project while minimising any cost to the State”.
The DPER response document said the Department is “not a party to the contract in question or the concluded arbitration process and there is no role for DPER in engaging directly with any external parties regarding any legal disputes which may arise”.
It said the OPW continues to engage with ICML and that Moran and his officials will meet NCSC representatives “with a view to identifying a way forward for the project, or a way to end any commitment to the project while minimising any cost to the State”.
A NCSC/ICML statement said: “Ireland needs a National Children’s Science Centre. This has been true for decades, but it is more compelling now than ever.”
It said that since the publication of the PAC report the NCSC sought to engage with DPER but “no response was received”.
The statement said: “Engagement with the OPW is ongoing and we remain committed to working collaboratively with Government to get this much needed science centre for children up and running.”
An OPW statement said that Moran is scheduled to meet representatives of ICML this week. It also said the OPW is preparing to go to tender on the project.
The statement also said “the OPW accepts that there is a binding arbitration award, however, the fact remains that there is no sponsoring authority to fund the development of the project” and the current National Development Plan “makes no provision for any Department to act as the sponsor of the project, and the OPW has no authority to assign that role to another Department.”

title: Improving water system to cost €50bn, Uisce Éireann tells Oireachtas group
description: Piping water from river Shannon to capital and Greater Dublin Drainage Project generational initiatives of national importance
content:
Sustained capital investment of approximately €2 billion a year over the next 25 years will be required to maintain and transform the water and wastewater networks countrywide and address legacy deficits, Uisce Éireann has told an Oireachtas committee.
In a briefing document submitted to the Dáil Committee of Public Accounts, the water utility also said the investment would be needed to improve resilience and compliance, as well as to provide additional capacity required for housing and economic growth.
It said the plans to bring supplies from the river Shannon to Dublin – known as the Water Supply Project Eastern and Midlands Region (WSP) – as well as the Greater Dublin Drainage Project (GDD) were once-in-a-generation initiatives of national importance.
It said big infrastructure projects progressed “through a series of interdependent stages, including business case approval, planning, land acquisition, environmental and marine consents, procurement, construction and commissioning”.
The company said delays at any stage could affect the timing, cost and eventual benefits of investment.
“Greater certainty and efficiency across planning, consenting and approvals would strengthen Uisce Éireann’s ability to progress these projects ... and ensure that essential infrastructure is available when communities and the economy need it.”
In a separate opening statement to the committee in advance of a Thursday hearing, Uisce Éireann chief executive Niall Gleeson is expected to warn that the development of new infrastructure is likely to lead to disruption for local communities.
He is expected to say that it was important to recognise that essential infrastructure works could have a direct impact on communities before the long-term benefits are felt.
“We will continue to seek delivery without unnecessary disruption ... as we deliver these improvements.”
The utility is likely to face questioning at the committee on Thursday about a €31 million “negative revenue adjustment” imposed by the Commission for the Regulation of Utilities (CRU) after it determined that Uisce Éireann had underperformed against targets associated with leakage and with non-domestic billing over a five-year period.
Uisce Éireann will tell the committee that while it accepted the CRU’s finding, its leakage levels are now at their lowest ever levels.
Gleeson is expected to say that water loss had reduced from 49 per cent in 2014 to 36 per cent nationally “and currently at less than 30 per cent for the Greater Dublin Area”.
“We are fixing around 2,000 on average every month across some 65,000km of water network. The task is sizeable.”
Uisce Éireann said the provision of water services for new homes was a priority.
“Providing capacity for housing depends not only on individual connections, but on timely investment in treatment plants, networks and strategic infrastructure. The objective is to translate targeted water services investment into serviced land, housing capacity and sustainable growth in the locations where demand is greatest.”

title: Ciarán Murphy: New proposed GAA rules should have trod the path laid by the FRC
description: Third-level competitions offer a limited test for new hurling and football rules
content:
E very time I’ve heard someone talking about the proposed hurling and football rule changes for this winter, I’ve had to pause and ask myself a question. The Ryan Cup is a third-level tournament in ... hurling, right? So why are we talking about the Ryan Cup in football?
As it turns out, there’s a Ryan Cup in both codes. I’d love to be able to tell you that the Ryan in question was the greatest dual-player in the history of third-level Gaelic games and that this was a co-ordinated plan to memorialise him. This would have a degree of intellectual rigour. But no, it appears as if there is no connection between the two.
The Ryan Cup is the second tier of third-level championship hurling (which has at least merited brief coverage in the past, given the final has been part of the Fitzgibbon final weekend), and the Ryan Cup is also the pre-Christmas football league competition for Division One (Sigerson Cup) teams. I presume that clears it up. Kevin McStay is the chair of Gaelic football’s Expert Advisory Group, and they will be hoping over the coming weeks that their Ryan Cup will give them an indication of what works and what doesn’t.
They are absolutely correct to challenge the accepted wisdom that the 2026 championship was perfect and beyond improvement. There’s nothing as bewitching and attractive as a shock final victory for a universally lauded underdog (even one powered in large part by innovations made possible by the new rules brought into being in early 2025, it should be noted).
But the most important thing for a successful sporting event is competitive uncertainty. Every bit as important as the new rules was the fact that there was drama pretty much everywhere you looked. The only thing shocking about Armagh winning the Ulster championship was the length of time since the last time they’d won it, but it was a culmination of a long-held desire for that group of players. Placed alongside the provincial victories of Roscommon and Westmeath against more vaunted opponents, it was a thrilling roster of winners.
If you have that, the entertainment will often take care of itself. And without it, as we were for much of the last decade due to Dublin’s continued excellence, no amount of rule changes would be able to give us jeopardy, the lifeblood of any contest. So we shouldn’t get too comfortable just because the championship this summer gave us so much.
[ The waiting is over as GAA’s experimental rules go on trial in college matches Opens in new window ]
The proposed changes to both games are not insignificant. The football ‘enhancements’ this winter will ban fisted points, limit the number of consecutive handpasses to three, give us a four-point goal and a backcourt rule, which basically means a team can’t play the ball back across their own halfway line once they’ve crossed into the opponent’s half.
John Meyler, meanwhile, has been in charge of a hurling Expert Advisory Group, and his committee’s suggestions include puck-outs which must go beyond the 45 with three forwards remaining between the 20-metre and 45-metre lines. Consecutive handpasses are no longer allowed, and a clear and definite striking action of the hand is now required for a handpass to be legal. Throw-ins to begin the half will be contested between one player from each team, the number of steps allowed is increased to six, and sideline cuts will be worth two points. These will all be on show in third-level league games from next week.
Both Meyler and McStay are operating in rather strange circumstances. Unlike Jim Gavin and the Football Review Committee, neither Meyler nor McStay can be sure their respective constituencies are crying out for change. Meyler was speaking to Colm Parkinson on the Smaller Fish podcast last month and his rather blase attitude towards the final adoption of these rules was striking. If one or two proposals make it to Congress, then that’s great, but – ‘we’re just spitballin’ here’, basically. He’s going to have to sell them to us a bit more forcefully than that.
These competitions are too small a sample size. And while they are played off without most people noticing every year, it doesn’t mean that the teams involved don’t care about it. Teams are using the Ryan Cup as preparation for the Sigerson Cup, which they care about a great deal.
If you were a manager in that competition, would you really spend much time coaching these new rules if the trophy you’re actually trying to win will be played under different ones? There’s no earthly reason why you’d do that. And the Sigerson Cup will definitely be played under the current (Jim Gavin) rules.
Gavin’s sandbox games existed in their own ecosystem. They meant nothing, which meant they were being played purely to road-test the FRC rules. That, perhaps counter-intuitively, gave them more coherence as a testing ground than what we’re about to watch over the next few weeks.
The ratio of handpassing to kickpassing in Gaelic football is an issue (4.22 handpasses for every kickpass in the 2026 championship), and I like the four-point goal. I think further definition of the hurling handpass is positive, and the throw-in change could be enjoyable to watch. But we all watched the FRC and we all saw how best to trial these things. I’m not sure why we’re not following that template again.
[ Kevin McStay urges patience surrounding further football rule changes to be trialled from next month Opens in new window ]

title: ‘I felt so broken’: Three mothers on the impact of stillbirths and miscarriages
description: On Pregnancy and Infant Loss Remembrance Day, October 15th, three mothers talk about their bereavement – and the long road to healing
content:
A fter the birth of her stillborn baby boy, Anne Marie Gillooley had “such a strong sense of wanting to make memories with him”.
She says she didn’t realise at the time “how important it was to healing”.
In 2014, her son Max was born at 41½ weeks. Gillooley (43), who is from Donegal but lives in Dublin, says she was told her son had no heartbeat following a scan.
“The world changes in an instant,” she says, speaking in advance of Pregnancy and Infant Loss Remembrance Day, which is marked every year on October 15th.
“Everything that you thought you knew and could expect and could rely on, just is swept out from under your feet,” she says.
“The only thing that kept me going through labour and delivery was this stubborn belief that I had in my head that they were wrong.”
She describes the experience as “terrifying”. “I didn’t know if I would be okay to hold him, I didn’t know what he would look like,” she says.
But once Max was born, she felt differently: “He was just so beautiful and so perfect and completely silent.”
Anne Marie and her husband were able to spend a few days in hospital with Max.
“We were parents and we were so proud of him, and we were in awe of having created this little person and there was absolutely the grief of him not living,” she says.
A midwife made them aware of the photography service offered by Now I Lay Me Down To Sleep.
The desire “to remember what he looked like and to hold the proof of his existence” was “so strong”, she says.
The photos with Max are “the most precious photos that we have”, she says.
Since their experience, Gillooley has become the charity’s chairwoman and volunteers as a photographer. Helping to make memories for other families has helped her to heal and is “a huge part” of Max’s legacy, she says.
“I felt so broken and I thought, even if I go on to have other children, every memory with them will remind me of what I’ve missed with Max,” she says. “Now I’m able to say to them 12 years later that this road that is ahead of you is extremely difficult, but you will find joy again.”
Nina Doyle, who lives in Dublin, said she always wanted to be a mother. However, after going for tests she was told she had unexplained infertility and started IVF .
After three rounds of IVF, resulting in two miscarriages , she then became pregnant without IVF but had another miscarriage. Then on the fourth round of IVF, she became pregnant with twins in 2018. Just shy of 23 weeks, labour started and Doyle was told by doctors that her babies would not survive.
“It’s hard to put into words the level of fear, the level of having to give birth to babies that you knew were going to die ... while they were inside me, they were kicking,” she says.
Within hours of receiving the “devastating news”, her babies were delivered. Liam was stillborn and Grace was alive for 31 minutes. The “silence was deafening” after Liam’s birth, she says, but she recalls the “rush of unconditional love”.
“I couldn’t believe he was here. I couldn’t believe we were finally parents,” she says.
She and her husband brought their babies home, “making memories, but it’s heartbreaking to fit a lifetime into such a short amount of time”.
[ Irish women’s birth stories: ‘Women are so vulnerable when they’re pregnant’ Opens in new window ]
“It’s just like an absolute bomb went off and everything changed forever,” she says.
Now in her 40s, Doyle is a regional co-ordinator with Féileacáin , which supports people affected by the death of a baby during or after pregnancy.
She says she wanted their lives to “really matter” and became involved with Féileacáin in memory of her twins. She set up the Féileacáin Wave of Light in 2019, which lights up more than 200 buildings in blue and pink across the country.
Róisín Moriarty (44), who is from Cork, had a miscarriage during her second pregnancy 11 years ago.
She says she was “ignorant” to what could go wrong following her “perfect” first pregnancy.
“Your whole world just falls apart ... it’s just mind boggling,” she says.
Moriarty and her husband named the baby they lost Dessie.
On leaving the hospital, she was handed a booklet put together by the Miscarriage Association of Ireland (MAI). She says the grieving process was “very isolating”, and she contacted the association.
“You definitely feel less isolated when you know you’re not alone,” she says.
Six years after her miscarriage, she became involved with the MAI.
“It probably took me that long to actually go: ‘Oh, I’m actually okay now to talk about my own miscarriage and to talk to other people about theirs,’” she says.
Getting involved was “healing” for her and she is now the secretary of the MAI and a volunteer. Her husband is also involved. It is a “nice way for us to remember our baby”, she says.
Moriarty has two daughters, now 14 and 12. She says she was pregnant with her younger daughter at the time of the due date of the baby she miscarried.
This was “bittersweet”, she says. “The grief comes back for the loss of your other baby. The worry is always there when you’re pregnant after a loss.”
See Now I Lay Me Down To Sleep , the Miscarriage Association of Ireland and Féileacáin (support line: 085 2496464) .

title: Guardians of the public purse?
description: The facts indicate otherwise
content:
Sir , – What a surprise to hear the Minister for Further and Higher Education, James Lawless , announce on national radio that the Government is the “guardian of the public purse”.
Really? The facts indicate otherwise: A bike shelter costing €335,000 and €1.43 million spent on a security hut .
The cost of the national children’s hospital is ballooning, with still no end in sight. A perimeter wall at the WRC doubled from €245,000 to €490,000 .
Approximately €40 million has been frittered on abandoned IT projects.
Approximately €22 million spent on non-functional ventilators during Covid-19. A Dáil photocopier costing €808,000 which was too large to fit into the room allocated for it, thereby necessitating building work.
€530 million spent on the MetroLink and hardly a sod turned. And on it goes.
If this is an indicator of guardianship of the public purse, then I’ll happily eat my bicycle helmet. – Yours, etc,

title: Lorcan Sirr: €43bn should have been enough to build 110,000 homes. Only 27,000 were built
description: Another €9.4 billion was allocated to housing last week. There are questions to be asked about the effectiveness of housing budget spending
content:
C ouncils are the backbone of the vast majority of what happens, or in some cases does not happen , locally. Their work is vitally important for our quality of life from cleaning the roads to running the libraries .
Some form of council has existed since medieval times. Known as Local Grand Juries, these were administrative bodies comprising up to 24 exclusively Protestant “leading men” who were usually large landowners. They were charged with building and maintaining jails, roads, courthouses, hospitals, asylums and, latterly, housing. In 1899, they were replaced by elected county councils.
Today, Ireland’s 31 councils employ 32,500 full-time equivalent staff to carry out their functions in planning, roads, water, waste, fire, youth, economic development and other services. The National Oversight and Audit Commission (NOAC) keeps track of what they do.
Involved in housing since the 1800s, councils today have statutory responsibility for the provision of local authority housing. Four councils directly built fewer than 10 new dwellings last year, with many buying new housing from the market – such purchases totalling 44 per cent of their overall output in 2025 (1,257 dwellings). This is expensive and deals are opaque.
From 2017 to 2025, about €43 billion was allocated to housing in annual budgets. Even accounting for maintenance of existing stock, that is enough to build more than 110,000 council houses. Over the same period, however, the total stock of housing in council ownership increased by just 27,397 new dwellings to 158,772. This sum has also part funded more than 22,000 approved housing body (AHB) houses, but the State doesn’t own them and they could be sold by the AHBs in the future.
In 2017, the combined total of the social housing waiting list and households in receipt of the Housing Assistance Payment (so, overall social housing demand) was 118,609. Nine years – and €43 billion – later and this figure is 121,229, and homeless numbers are up more than 200 per cent over the same period. No real inroads are being made into meeting social housing demand.
Another €9.4 billion was allocated to housing last week.
There are questions to be asked about the effectiveness of housing budget spending, who is receiving it and how much they are getting, and whether it is being used for those who need it most. Increasingly parsimonious Department of Public Expenditure (DPER) officials should ensure budgets are not necessarily cut, but have better outcomes.
Just 2.4 per cent of council housing was vacant at the end of 2025, which is good, but one area for improvement is the variation in the time councils take to re-let their vacant houses.
[ US-backed social housing landlord returned €15m to investors ahead of sale Opens in new window ]
Average reletting of a vacant council house in 2025 took 32 weeks – about four weeks faster than 2024, but 10 weeks slower than 2015.
In urban areas, Cork City Council reduced its reletting time by nearly 10 weeks from 2024, to 23 weeks. Despite a social housing waiting list of 2,101 households, Galway City Council had the longest average re-let time of more than 42 weeks, or 10 months.
In rural areas, Monaghan and Laois had the fastest re-lets at 11 and 16 weeks, and Kerry and Limerick the slowest at 66 (more than 1 year and three months) and 56 weeks respectively. These latter councils have a combined social housing waiting list of 4,901 households .
Councils are required to inspect between 12 and 15 per cent of all new buildings to ensure they meet the minimum required standards. In 2025, that figure averaged 19 per cent. Both Cork City (at 9.5 per cent) and Roscommon (6.5 per cent) failed to meet the minimum last year. Dublin City Council hit 83 per cent of new buildings inspected, but given nearly all new buildings in DCC are apartments, it is much easier to achieve a high percentage as many properties can be inspected in one visit.
Councils are also required to inspect private rented accommodation , again to ensure it meets the required minimum standards. The target here is 25 per cent. Nine councils exceeded this target.
Mayo had the highest inspection rate of 45 per cent of properties; Carlow inspected just 4.5 per cent of private rented properties. In 11 councils, more than 90 per cent of these inspected dwellings were found to be non-compliant with minimum standards. In Louth, this figure was an astonishing 99.87 per cent. If landlords are fleeing the market , it appears to be the wrong landlords.
[ Land Development Agency staff share €2m in bonuses Opens in new window ]
One area in which councils are excelling is energy retrofitting , exceeding the target for last year of 2,500 retrofits by 171 units. Dublin City Council did the most, followed by Cork County and Donegal.
The administration of the planning system is a big part of what councils do. In 2025, councils issued 36,057 planning application decisions, taking a median time of 54 days and granting almost 90 per cent. Three-quarters of planning appeals to An Coimisiún Pleanála confirmed the council’s original decision. This is all part a healthy part of democracy and shows council planning officials are mostly getting it right.
Running this planning system cost €43.20 per capita in 2025. In its recent Homebuilding Horizons Report 2026 , housebuilder Glenveagh called for an increase in planning application fees to “fund a properly resourced planning system” that would enable councils to hire more staff and expertise. Planning is increasingly becoming technically and legally complex – the latest Planning Act is more than 900 pages – so additional funding is a good suggestion.
The top two house building companies in the country made combined operating profits of more than €312 million building and selling 4,933 new houses and apartments in 2025.
It could also be suggested that some or all of the €253 million spent last year alone on the price-inflationary Help to Buy scheme that most recipients do not need , be redirected to improving the planning system. Such money would go a long way towards helping councils employ extra staff and improve their planning processes, systems and overall efficiency.
According to the NOAC report, “housing remains a key area of concern”. And it will remain so until the Government budget strategy shifts from spending on housing to investing in housing, including the critical provision of community facilities. Councils will be the main conduit for this, but their patchy performance needs to improve.
Lorcan Sirr is senior lecturer in housing at TU Dublin, and author of Housing A Nation: seven generations of land, politics and power, available now.

title: Ryanair ‘recognises’ disputed Western Sahara territory in controversial marketing campaign
description: Advertising Standards Authority agrees ‘Moroccan adventure’ advert likely to be misleading
content:
Morocco ’s claim over territory it occupies in Western Sahara is formally recognised by the United States, Israel, France and, now it seems, Ryanair .
The Irish budget airline has been pulled up for advertising flights to Dakhla as a “Moroccan adventure”, because the city is in fact located in Western Sahara, a neighbouring country occupied by Morocco since the 1970s in one of Africa ’s longest-running territorial disputes.
The Advertising Standards Authority , in a preliminary ruling on foot of a complaint from Sinn Féin MEP Lynn Boylan , found Ryanair’s promotional material was misleading, on the basis that Dakhla was “not a part of Morocco”.
Morocco has occupied the majority of Western Sahara since 1976, after Spain withdrew from its former colony on the northwest coast of Africa, near the Canary Islands. A Sahrawi guerrilla campaign by the Polisario Front had separately been fighting for independence.
A United Nations-brokered ceasefire was agreed in 1991 between Morocco and the Polisario Front of the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, which continues to press its claim.
Sometimes referred to as Africa’s last colony, Western Sahara is described by the UN as a “non-self-governing territory” under international law.
Promotional emails from Ryanair in March pushed flights to the coastal city of Dakhla as a place “where ocean, desert, and culture come together”, and offered visitors a chance to surf and “explore Moroccan culture up close”.
Hugh Lovatt, senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations think tank, said Morocco commonly used tourism and trade to “force international recognition” of its claim over Western Sahara.
“Whether you are talking about the European Commission, or Ryanair, it’s the price of doing business with Morocco that you include Western Sahara,” he said.
[ EasyJet to cut 700,000 seats from winter flight schedule amid rising fuel costs Opens in new window ]
Boylan, an MEP for Dublin, complained to the State advertising watchdog that Ryanair’s promotion of the Western Sahara city as a “Moroccan adventure” was misleading and offensive. “This advert erases indigenous people by showing the city as belonging to Morocco,” her office wrote.
In a preliminary decision, dated October 12th and seen by The Irish Times, the Advertising Standards Authority agreed the advert was likely to mislead people.
It recommended the authority’s independent council, which has to give the final sign off to decisions, uphold Boylan’s complaint and direct that the advert should not appear in its current form again.
In its submissions, Ryanair argued that it intended to give passengers an overview of the destination “without expressing any political stance”.
Ryanair, which offers flights to Marrakesh, Rabat and Fez in Morocco, opened the route to Dakhla early last year.
Morocco favours the creation of a Sahara autonomous region that has locally devolved powers but would remain under Morocco’s authority. This is viewed as unacceptable to the Polisario Front, which continues to advocate for full independence and international recognition .

title: Leinster’s James Ryan looking forward to ‘proper’ French test at Clermont
description: Dominating at set-pieces is crucial, Leinster lock says
content:
The proper French cauldrons don’t faze James Ryan .
Although Leinster lost at La Rochelle’s Stade Marcel-Deflandre in a Champions Cup semi-final, they also won a pool game there and Ryan describes it as “very cool” and a “proper rugby ground”. He has a similar regard for the Stade Jean-Dauger, where Leinster beat Bayonne in January.
Saturday will be his first visit to the Stade Marcel-Michelin, one of French rugby’s most celebrated venues, as Leinster open their Champions Cup pool campaign against Clermont.
Ryan knows exactly what to expect. “The Top 14 is such a strong league, isn’t it? The way they get the whole town and the community behind it is very cool,” he said.
“I’ve never played them away. That’s funny, because when I was growing up I felt like Leinster were always playing Clermont away, in that 2011 and 2012 kind of era.
“I remember it was always such a tough place to go, so I can’t wait. It’s a real rugby region, a cool stadium and a nice early kick-off for us. It’s probably going to be bouncing. I can’t wait.”
By virtue of their consistency in Europe, most of Leinster’s playoff games have been in Dublin, so high-stakes trips to France have been relatively infrequent over the past decade.
However, Ryan understands what is required of Leo Cullen’s side to get the job done in hostile territory. As such an established member of the pack, he knows the challenge begins with winning the battle up front.
Dominating at set-pieces, he emphasises, is crucial, but there are other elements that must also go Leinster’s way.
“It’s big, scrum and lineout,” said the 30-year-old. “One thing about Clermont is their lineout maul is very good, very strong, so that’ll be a big one for us as a pack, going after that area of the game and trying to negate their strength there.
“The start is important. They’re a very strong side at home, they’re a very proud club, so we need to start well. And then it’s making sure we take our chances: when we do get into their 22, we have to come away with points. We can’t afford to miss those.”
Ryan insists Leinster cannot use as an excuse the fact that so many of their starters this weekend will have had only one game under their belts, whereas the Top 14 season is already a month and a half old.
“Does it matter? Not really, to be honest,” he said. “That’s the way it is. There’s probably another level in us, to be fair, but we’ve got to get up to speed pretty quickly. We’ve got to make sure we put on a proper performance.
“I know there’s always a lot of noise around the fifth star and the Champions Cup for us. The way we’re looking at this season is not so much about outcomes as about judging ourselves on our performance, because that’s something we can control.
“We know if we are at our best, then we’re going to be in the mix. I certainly think that’s the best approach. We’ll give ourselves a good shot, as opposed to looking too far ahead.”

title: ‘The dark arts are slowly going out of the game’: Tadhg Beirne adapting to law tweaks
description: Munster captain says changes to mauls can ‘clean up the game’
content:
Several aspects of his game have helped to make Tadhg Beirne a truly world-class player over the last decade, including his renowned ability to win turnovers in defensive mauls and over the ball. But two factors have combined to potentially reduce his impact in those categories this season.
Ahead of Munster’s opening Champions Cup game against Racing 92 at Páirc Uí Chaoimh on Saturday (kick-off 8pm), it will be close to one of the wonders of the world if the game does not feature tries off penalties to the corner and resultant catch-and-drives.
Law tweaks have made this the game’s staple diet and for players like Beirne they have become harder to defend than ever this season.
“You’re going to see a lot more mauls for sure, certainly teams going for the corner a lot more,” said the Munster captain, noting that if the attacking teams achieve “any kind of a go-forward, you’re in the shit really. There’s not much you can do, because the penalties, the advantages come quick, and sometimes you get caught in a position where you can’t get out.
“It’s a fine art now to make sure you’re defending the mauls properly and there’s a lot of pressure on you when you are on your own five-metre line to make sure you’re defending them well.”
As to whether this is a positive change for the game, Beirne said: “I think it’ll probably clean up the game in how it’ll be reffed because it might be a bit easier for refs to manage the maul.
“There were a few ways of getting around the laws a little. I tended to do it where if you have one shoulder attached to the maul and you can reach around, but that’s all gone now.
“I’d say refs are probably happier with it because it cleans it up and makes it easier. You’re less likely to have collapsed mauls and turnovers, so maybe that’s good for the game.
“The dark arts are slowly going out of the game, that’s for sure,” said Beirne, a tad wistfully.
“It’s like anything in the game,” he said, noting that defences are under focus and in time it will be attacking mauls and how they’re set up.
“There are laws that have been there for a long time but haven’t been reffed, but they just focus in on them.”
[ Munster aim to honour Anthony Foley in best way possible – with victory against Racing Opens in new window ]
The other factor is Marnus van der Merwe, who has followed the same path as Beirne from the Scarlets to Munster. He’s only played against the Welsh region twice in seven seasons, but Beirne was fully aware of the hooker’s threat over the ball from Munster’s scouting, and there were a couple of poaches by Van der Merwe in addition to his try in last Saturday’s player of the match performance in the 26-all draw away to Ulster.
“He’s a different profile to me over the ball. My opportunities come in different ways than his, but if I see him near the ball, I’ll probably leave it to him before I go at it because he’s a harder object to move than me.
“The big thing I’ve learned over the years is not to chase everything and pick your opportunities. It’s also knowing who’s around you as well, so I’m sure he’ll be getting a few more and maybe mine will go down. But I don’t really care about that.”
The tournament has, sadly, lost much of its lustre from its glory years.
“There’s no going away from the fact that the numbers in terms of attendance around the whole competition is down. I remember first coming here and getting a ticket for a Champions Cup weekend, or Heineken Cup as it was called back then, was near to impossible. We were pleading with each other trying to get tickets off ourselves.
“There’s no shying away from that but that doesn’t take away from how important the competition is to us as a club and us as a team. I think it’s still the pinnacle of club rugby. It’s the competition every team wants to win because I think you’re top of the charts then.
“Every weekend I can guarantee you most people aren’t watching the Top 14 or the Premiership or some people aren’t even watching the URC, but I can guarantee you every weekend when it comes to the Champions Cup, whether you’re in France, England, Scotland, Wales or Ireland, you’re watching the Champions Cup.
“You’re tuning in to watch it and I think that’s the joy of the competition; everyone still loves to watch that competition and I think that’s why it’s so big.
“To us as a club it’s huge for us and we know how big it is for our fans as well. All we want to do is bring them on an enjoyable journey in this competition. The dream is to go the whole way and it starts on Saturday.”
[ Simon Zebo: Joe Schmidt’s double standards drove me mental, made me dislike the Irish camp Opens in new window ]
To that end, Munster haven’t earned a home knock-out tie in the last four seasons and last season went out in the pool stages after three defeats before a tame Challenge Cup Round of 16 loss in Exeter, who they last hosted at Thomond Park in 2021-22 before a quarter-final exit in a goal-kicking competition against Toulouse in the Aviva.
“I’ve been injured as well both times we’ve had knock-out games at home. I’d love to get it, be here, knock-out, full crowd. It’d be some buzz and you can feel it all around. That’s what we’ll be striving towards and, as I said, it starts Saturday which is a huge game.
“It’s class to play in Páirc Uí Chaoimh and hopefully in front of a full Munster crowd again.”

title: People don’t leave jobs, they leave bad managers. What makes a great one?
description: Effective leadership depends less on who sounds like a leader than on the behaviours and skills they demonstrate
content:
W hen you think back over your career, which manager do you remember first? The boss who believed in you and gave you opportunities or the manager who thwarted and belittled you at every turn?
The managerial personality traits and behaviours we observe early in our careers often shape our own management style later. If we liked a boss, we might try to emulate what they did well while avoiding the more negative behaviours of someone we considered a bad leader or a toxic colleague.
In Ireland, many people who are promoted to manager never receive any training on how to manage or even know what good looks like. On a Monday, they’re a colleague and on Tuesday, they’re the boss.
To figure out how to behave as a manager, they might do a little detective work to determine what style is preferred at their company. If Mary was promoted for hitting her targets every month – regardless of staff burnout levels – then that might be someone they choose as a role model.
Or they might look higher up the ladder to the chief executive. If that person is a strong communicator who motivates the team with a clear vision and regular updates then they might choose to focus on developing these behaviours first.
Organisations that value sustainable growth and efficiency should never leave managerial expectations to chance. The cost of this oversight is high when it comes to employee engagement, turnover and productivity.
People don’t leave jobs, they leave bad managers.
Managerial skills continue to be a gap in Ireland, with 61 per cent of HR professionals surveyed identifying insufficient line manager capability and capacity as the top constraint, according to the CIPD Ireland ’s HR Practices in Ireland 2026.
According to Gallup, half of resigning employees cite their manager as the reason they’re leaving. That’s not surprising considering that so much of your compensation, growth opportunities and motivation come from interactions with your manager. This relationship – good or bad – correlates directly with employee engagement.
Employees who leave because of their manager say poor communication, lack of recognition, micromanagement, favouritism and unfairness are the top reasons the relationship breaks down. Companies spend significant sums on hiring employees and training them in only to fail them when it comes to training up their managers.
Thankfully, decades of research on managerial prowess show us what good looks like when it comes to being an effective manager. Academics have identified a set of core traits and behaviours that distinguish effective managers from ineffective ones.
An effective manager is able to integrate certain personality traits (especially conscientiousness, extroversion and openness), interpersonal behaviours (communication, caring, trust building and ethical leadership) and decision-making competence with a people-oriented style.
Individuals like this outperform those who focus on a task-oriented approaches – hitting targets, getting through the to-do list – across most contexts studied.
This ties in with what workers say they value most at work. European workers put a safe environment for mental and physical health (71 per cent) and a trusting environment (69 per cent) ahead of good pay and benefits (66 per cent), according to Eurofound’s European Working Conditions Survey 2024.
[ A beginner’s guide to the 9-5 work week: Minimise your morning, don’t overshare Opens in new window ]
Are managers born or made? How many times have you heard “she’s a born leader” or “he really gets results”?
We assume that certain personality traits or behaviours automatically lead to promotion but research shows they might not be the things that make a manager truly effective. And that’s good news for introverts, more reflective personality types or those who’ve always thought, or felt, they’re not manager material.
An influential study in Personnel Psychology entitled Trait and Behavioural Theories of Leadership, led by Scott DeRue in 2011, was one of the first to explore which useful traits and effective behaviours worked best for managers. Over time, more studies have confirmed and built on their findings.
The most effective behaviours are a mix of transformational, task-oriented, relations-oriented, and change-oriented rather than a single universal style. Within those behaviours, problem-solving stands out as a particularly strong predictor of managerial effectiveness. The good news is that many of these behaviours can be taught and developed.
Managers who are perceived to be extroverts – or who fit stereotypical traits of what a leader looks or sounds like – have a definite advantage when it comes to getting the job but research shows that once they’re in the job, it’s behaviours such as agreeableness and emotional stability that help managers succeed in the role.
Unfortunately, organisations often promote people who put themselves forward or who excel at the technical aspects of the job, then just hope that their managerial skills miraculously emerge afterwards. Research suggests that such an approach can backfire, and that manager quality has a measurable effect on team results.
People who self-select into management perform worse than randomly assigned managers, according to a small study by Ben Weidmann and colleagues in the Quarterly Journal of Economics last year. Selecting managers on their skills rather than desire to lead could substantially improve organisational performance, according to the findings.
Effective leadership appears to depend less on who looks or sounds like a leader than on the behaviours and skills they actually demonstrate. The most influential studies on effective managers have a clear answer: behaviours and skills matter more than demographics or personality traits.
If you’re a new manager, or even a seasoned one, here are some top tips based on research that shows which behaviours have the greatest positive impact.
Margaret E Ward is chief executive of Clear Eye, a leadership consultancy. margaret@cleareye.ie

title: Look inside: A1 energy rated Victorian in Ranelagh where two eras harmoniously coalesce
description: Leeson Park home features bespoke design features and stunning mezzanine overlooking kitchen
content:
To walk through the rooms of 44 Leeson Park is like experiencing a glossy magazine editorial come to life. My first question to the owner was “Wait, you’re living here?” having incorrectly assumed the immaculately furnished Victorian in Ranelagh had been staged for sale.
The two-storey-over-basement building was laid out as six bedsits and an apartment when it was purchased in 2023, and it underwent a thorough renovation over three years, returning it to a single residence. Extensive retrofitting resulted in an A1 energy rating, almost unheard of for a property of its age.
Every care was taken to restore the original Victorian features of the home, from the ceiling cornicing to the original wooden floors, and where original fireplaces had been removed, they were reinstated with others befitting the property’s heritage. It is now a home of two eras that harmoniously coalesce.
Extending to 333sq m (3,584sq ft), 44 Leeson Park is on the market with Lisney Sotheby’s International Realty, seeking €3.95 million.
Entering the property from garden level, you step into an area to hang your coat and tidy your shoes away into built-in cabinets. The layout is open plan, expanding into the livingroom on the left and leading you towards the stairwell straight ahead.
The livingroom is home to a large corner bubble sofa that looks as comfy as it is trendy. The sash windows, complete with restored shutters and the original wavy glass, frame views of the front garden and leafy street beyond.
The room flows into a reception room where a long, curved structure of neutral tiling and dark wood has been erected to house books on one side and a bar on the other. Further storage is supplied by a wall of cabinets, and a plump striped armchair provides a landing spot to relax, whether you’ve opted for a book, a drink from the bar, or both.
From here you step into the double-height kitchen, which is flooded with light from glazing to the rear and overhead. The former outer wall has been retained, meaning the windows and brickwork, now painted white, add period character and interest to the interior of the modern kitchen.
A long island/breakfast bar anchors the space and a La Cornue range cooker in silver and gold sits among the white units. Twin pendants of long vertical lighting strips hang at differing lengths above the island from the high ceiling. Their full impact can be admired from the back garden, where you can take in the entirety of the room.
The ceiling of the substantial kitchen extension drops to single height above the dining area to the rear. The space is dual aspect overlooking the back garden and a Zen garden on the right that is centred by an acer tree and framed by the stone walls of a former shed.
The garden, designed by Bloom-winning designer Alan Rudden, is set up for entertaining and features a built-in barbecue and pizza oven beside the patio and large seating area at the bottom of the garden oriented around an inset gas fire. A private laneway runs to the back of the house.
Back inside, a utility room lies off the kitchen, along with a spacious loo with a bubble onyx stone sink that, like the sinks throughout the home, is a real feature.
On the first floor, the main doorway opens to the lofty entrance hall where the elaborate cornicing has been meticulously restored to its former glory.
The traditional piano nobile room has a piano in situ by the window, made from transparent material. The stark design scheme in white and neutral hues allows the original cornicing and arched cast-iron fireplace to make a statement.
The room flows into a second reception room where doors open to reveal a mezzanine, which looks out over the stunning kitchen below and straight ahead past a rooftop garden above the dining area to the tree tops and redbrick facades of the houses on the street beyond. It was a successful way to make the formal reception rooms connect to the busier living spaces below. Two armchairs here make it a cosy spot for relaxing.
There are four double bedrooms, with one on the first-floor return, another two on the first floor and a fourth on the second floor. The spacious main bathroom sits on the first-floor return with a free-standing bath.
The main bedroom at the front of the first floor is rich in natural light from two arched sash windows with views of the changing leaves in October. It flows into a stunning dressingroom and en suite that has at its centre a bespoke island unit with a glazed top allowing you to see your accessories at a glance. Made in Italy, it is framed in honey onyx and houses a sink of the same material. A bank of built-in wardrobes line the interior wall and a shower is concealed behind a curved partition on one side of the fireplace with a loo similarly housed on the opposite side.
This immaculate Dublin 6 home is sure to appeal to well-heeled buyers looking for a home that is already tastefully designed and offers the highest standard of energy efficiency.
Number 44 Leeson Park is not the only home on the stretch for sale with number 26, another two-storey-over-basement Victorian, on the market with Sherry FitzGerald, also seeking €3.95 million. It extends to 389sq m (4,187sq ft) and has five bedrooms.

title: ‘No silver bullet’: Energy crunch could bite Europe this winter
description: Price-gouging checks at petrol stations and electric vehicle grants for French taxi drivers among Continent’s responses to global energy shock
content:
For the first time in months there’s a nip in the air around Brussels. The hottest summer on record in western Europe, which brought deadly wildfires and heatwaves , has made way for what could be a difficult winter dominated by high energy prices .
European governments are trying to soften the blow from that energy shock. Most interventions were budgeted for on the assumption the world economy needed to weather a short blockade of the Strait of Hormuz , the key shipping artery that brings oil and gas from the Gulf.
The United States has been unable to extract itself from the war Donald Trump started in Iran , or break the chokehold Tehran quickly put on the strait that has sent fuel and energy costs shooting up.
Europe is “not far behind” the US, where a barrel of diesel is up 94 per cent on pre-war prices, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said in a report last month.
The shock has been compared to the 1973 oil crisis but we haven’t seen anything close to the shortages and gas rationing from that period. The IEA says that’s in part because strategic reserves have helped to keep the energy market from really running away, for the moment anyway.
Iran’s strikes on US-aligned countries in the Gulf have done serious damage to the region’s oil and gas production facilities, which will take years to return to full steam.
The European Union’s 27 national leaders meet in Brussels for a two-day summit beginning today. The energy crunch will feature in discussions. “This is one of the main political concerns for the leaders”, said a senior EU official involved in backchannel talks laying the groundwork for the European Council summit.
“There is no one silver bullet to lower energy prices,” the top adviser said.
Leaders also have to contend with the Iran fallout spilling into the fighting in Ukraine. Trump’s relationship with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy has suffered a fresh rupture over Kyiv’s bombing of Russian oil plants.
Closer to home, European leaders know that a sustained spike in the cost of fuel, heating bills, and the wider inflation rate is bad news for their electoral prospects.
More than seven months into the energy crisis, the response from national governments has been a mixed bag, including cuts to tax charged on fuel, subsidy supports and other schemes.
Poland and Croatia put a cap on the price at the pumps and Austria has restricted filling stations to a single price hike a day. Sweden cut public transport fares for the year.
At the start of the crisis Slovenia called in the army to help transport fuel and for a couple of days even instituted fuel rationing, limiting people to 50 litres a day.
France has a €100 fuel allowance voucher for workers who heavily rely on their car and taxi drivers can access a grant to help them to buy an electric vehicle. Czech authorities have been monitoring petrol stations for evidence of price gouging. Italy plans to delay the shutdown of coal-fired power plants by a decade, until 2038.
Others have doubled down on their move away from fossil fuels. Spain, a leader in renewables, wants to designate local areas where green energy projects can be fast-tracked.
Madrid has said future pressure on the power grid from energy-hungry data centres must be offset by additional renewable infrastructure.
Seeking relief for the aviation sector, Irish Minister for Transport Darragh O’Brien privately asked EU energy commissioner Dan Jorgensen to consider suspending tariffs on sustainable aviation fuel imported from the US, in response to “significant and sustained volatility” in the jet fuel market. The April 24th letter was released by his department in response to a Freedom of Information Act request from The Irish Times.
Latvia’s government is exploring a national “solidarity” levy to collect 100 per cent of “excess” profits fuel retailers make above a certain threshold. Portugal is drafting a bill to tax the windfall profits of energy companies.
Germany is leading a group of member states pressing Brussels officials to propose an EU-wide tax on windfall profits booked by oil companies, without much success so far.
The broad thrust of national interventions have been to ease the cost of filling up a motor tank. Heading into the colder period the focus will shift to home heating and electricity bills.
The obvious worry is the pressure on energy costs will stretch well into next year, exhausting what limited fiscal room many European governments have to dig into stretched national budgets. It could turn into a rough few months.

title: Scientists decipher charred ancient scrolls buried by Vesuvius
description: Non-destructive scanning of fragile scrolls will provide further breakthroughs in our knowledge of the classical world
content:
I magine a book arrives by post, packed in a cardboard box. Can you read the book without opening the box? Thanks to advanced technology, AI and the power of mathematics, the challenge can be answered. These techniques are allowing us to read the blackened remnants of some ancient documents.
It is said that an inscription, “Let no one ignorant of geometry enter here”, was carved over the entrance to Plato’s Academy in Athens . Although Plato made no original geometric discoveries, he believed that mathematics provides the finest possible mental training, and regarded it as an essential prerequisite for philosophy.
He formalised the concept of proof, laying the foundations for Euclid’s Elements. When he died in 347 BC, Plato was buried in the large garden of the Academy. But where?
Recently, the precise location of Plato’s tomb has been discovered, not by an archaeological dig, but by analysis of a papyrus reduced to charcoal following the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79.
The volcanic eruption destroyed the cities of Pompeii and Herculaneum, burying them under tens of metres of rock and ash. About 1,800 papyri were found around 1750 at an ancient Roman villa now called the Villa of the Papyri. These scrolls were completely carbonised by the intense heat of the eruption, and quite impossible to read.
Attempts to unroll and flatten some of the Herculaneum scrolls reduced them to dust and ashes, destroying any chance of deciphering them. But recently, scholars have been able to recover the text on some scrolls by non-invasive scanning techniques.
The scrolls have been X-rayed using CT scanners similar to those found in hospitals. 3D images are built up representing the solid spiral scrolls. By clever mathematical transformations, the scans are virtually unrolled to produce flat images of the papyri while leaving the physical scrolls untouched.
The carbon-based ink used on the scrolls has an optical density close to papyrus, so it cannot be “seen” on the flattened surface. However, the writing is raised by a fraction of a millimetre, so that the scroll is slightly thicker where letters have been written.
[ Margaret Hamilton, trailblazer whose software powered Apollo 11 moon landing, dies at 90 Opens in new window ]
This minute difference can be detected by using high-resolution scans, allowing individual letters to be revealed. AI techniques are used to differentiate papyri from ink and also to deduce missing words and letters.
Thousands of words of a document by the Epicurean philosopher Philodemus, The History of the Academy, have been deciphered. They include a description of Plato’s tomb, located close to the Mouseion, a temple in the Academy garden dedicated to the muses. This information lay buried for two millenniums, only to be rediscovered in 2024.
The papyri contain a large number of Greek philosophical texts, some previously unknown. There is also what is believed to be a lost work about Alexander the Great. We may be confident that non-destructive scanning of fragile, unopened scrolls will provide further breakthroughs in our knowledge of the classical world. New decipherment techniques are under development, and perhaps many more charred scrolls lie undiscovered at deeper, unexcavated levels of the Villa.
[ Heads or tails, 3D printing can make fish waste appetising Opens in new window ]
The Vesuvius Challenge is an open international competition to read the carbonised scrolls. It was launched in 2023 by tech moguls and Meta executives, Nat Friedman and Daniel Gross, and computer science professor Brent Seales, to encourage innovation in deciphering.
Numerous cash prizes, some quite large, are on offer for progress in virtually unrolling and reading the scrolls. For information about the Vesuvius Challenge, go to scrollprize.org .
Peter Lynch is an emeritus professor at the school of mathematics and statistics, University College Dublin. He blogs at thatsmaths.com.

title: Emer McLysaght: I adore hearing about friends’ neighbourhood WhatsApp groups. Should I set one up?
description: Anecdotal evidence suggests that package stealing is rare, while package minding is de rigueur
content:
I ’m attempting to buy the Dublin 8 apartment I already live in. Can I afford it? I’m a single-income, self-employed creative. No, of course I can’t afford it. Did I dream of storage heaters and renter-friendly carpet when I imagined purchasing my first home? Also no. However, I have made it my own over the past seven years. I really, really don’t want to move and face finding somewhere else in the current climate and, crucially, my landlord is selling up.
One of my qualms about becoming an apartment owner is having to join the ranks of the management company and paying exorbitant annual fees for things like insurance and upkeep. Currently, such fees are built into my rent, so my eye only slightly twitches when I observe the weekly garden maintenance team blowing leaves around the courtyard. How will I cope with the leaf relocation when it feels like the blower is being fuelled directly by my own hard-earned money?
I’ve been wondering if there’s an owners’ WhatsApp group where I might be able to make inquiries about the necessity of the leaf blower, but I also fear such a thing might become my downfall as I get sucked into the valley of the peeping curtains and go full Rear Window on some cheeky parking or abandoned dog dirt.
The complex doesn’t have a residents’ WhatsApp group. I’ve occasionally thought about starting one (mostly so I can offer dog walking services) but fear that the admin would send me back to the psych ward. I adore hearing about friends’ neighbourhood WhatsApp groups. Nothing fills me with more collateral glee than when it’s kicking off about kids playing football too near the cars or one person being accused of stealing another’s Amazon package.
[ Aerial house photos used to be in all rural homes, but my search for one was no easy task Opens in new window ]
A survey of friends indicates that these groups are, for the most part, helpful. For instance, one pal says that if the power or wifi is down, there will always be an on-the-ball Tech Dad who has contacted the relevant supplier. Another lives in a cul-de-sac where one neighbour has taken on the task of sourcing and delivering local eggs and honey for the entire street. Anecdotal evidence suggests that package stealing is rare, while package minding is de rigueur. One friend who lives on a long street of terraced houses reports that, because the buildings have the same dimensions and layout, there can be a roaring trade in swapping furniture that will definitely fit beside the fireplace or around the awkward bend on the stairs. This also provides ample opportunity for a peek inside a neighbour’s house to get a gawk at any kitchen upgrades or inspiration for a bathroom renovation.
So, that’s the good. What about the bad and the ugly? A friend in a WhatsApp group for her apartment block brings dispatches from a war that erupted recently after one neighbour reported another for having no motor tax. In a different apartment complex, one resident uses the group as their own personal doorbell, constantly sending a mass text asking to be buzzed in. Yet another friend had to leave the WhatsApp group for her housing estate after a rat infestation led to enthusiastic posting of pictures of the rodents in question.
There is conflict in many Dublin city WhatsApp groups because of the council ’s effort to switch all residents from using weekly bin bags to wheelie bins. I can’t say I’m surprised. I suspect that if there were to be a group for my apartment complex, it would go down in flames within a week over the communal bins. Nothing is more starkly revealing about the human condition than the use of communal bins. Many of my neighbours appear deeply committed to misusing the hulking megabins in the basement. My neighbours see an overflowing megabin as a Tetris challenge rather than an opportunity to use the empty one beside it. They love to take their rubbish into the lifts, leaving a trail of fishy bin juice in their wake. Repeated warnings about disposal of furniture in the megabin room appear to serve as a call to action to some, thus increasing the abandonment of chairs, hideous glass TV stands and a truly baffling number of children’s blackboards.
[ ‘There’s nothing wrong with the bags’: inside Dublin’s latest waste war Opens in new window ]
Just writing about the communal bins has sent my blood pressure skyrocketing, which is probably a sign that we are better off as relative strangers; ships that pass in the night carrying bin bags. If I am successful in my apartment purchase and forced to join an owner’s WhatsApp group, I’ll cross that bridge when I come to it, and maybe visit the GP for a beta-blocker prescription.

title: ‘In Ireland I was the English girl, whereas in London I thought I was Irish’
description: Ann-Marie O’Shea on how her Irish grandmother’s use of seaweed remedies inspired her OMALY skincare business
content:
I was born in Cricklewood, or County Cricklewood as it’s known, to Irish parents. That part of London often felt more Irish than Ireland itself.
There were five girls, and we were dragged to every Irish dancing competition known, or to the nearby Galtymore Dance Hall. I loved that feiseanna weren’t just competitions, but were about community. When I later moved to Ireland, I found Irish dancing was a lot more competitive and didn’t have the same feeling.
My father’s from Castletownbere, Co Cork and my mum’s from Belmullet, Co Mayo . So our trips back to Ireland in the summers would be travelling up and down the country for six weeks at a time.
We’d often visit my nan in West Cork. She was originally from Achill but met my grandfather in London before moving back. He was a farmer and fisherman, and they had 11 children.
She was absolutely incredible. For dinner she’d pick all the vegetables, and make her own butter and cream. It was constant work. So at night, she’d sit with seaweed on her legs to ease the pain. Around the fire, she’d tell us many different stories, including about seaweed. When my dad was sick as a child, they’d use carrageen moss and milk to help them recover. These stories made an impact on me.
One summer I had a really bad breakout of eczema. I tried cortisone and all sorts of products, and it wouldn’t heal. It wasn’t until I went into the sea and just had seaweed around me that it began to get better. And that stayed with me.
We moved back to Ireland when I was 12. We bought a pub in Mayo, between Swinford and Bohola. That experience was interesting in itself!
In Ireland I was the English girl, whereas I thought I was the Irish girl all along. I had expected I’d fit in very quickly and easily, but there were cultural changes. In England we really celebrated being Irish, but then in Ireland, that culture was just normal. But we loved being back there, we felt we were home.
So we sold the pub five years later. And then my parents moved to West Cork, to my dad’s family home.
I moved back to London at 19. I wanted to get into fashion – there wasn’t a lot of fashion going on in Dublin. I worked in fashion and beauty for about 30 years, and travelled around the world a lot.
I worked at Gant as buying and merchandising director, and at Fred Perry as global commercial director. They were pretty high-powered jobs, but I didn’t feel as though I was doing enough to fulfil what I wanted to do. So I started to look around, and retrained in beauty therapy and aesthetics.
[ From Famine to feast: the Irish seaweed revival Opens in new window ]
Through those years, I would often try different products on my skin. But nothing seemed as good as seaweed.
Then I set up a clothing and beauty business, Serenity&Grace, with a plan to bring Irish brands global. We had much Irish support, sold occasional and evening wear in House of Fraser concessions, and were about to launch when Covid hit – and the business died a death.
During that time I focused on beauty and seaweed, and tried lots of different seaweed products. It gave me so many wonderful feelings of family and connection, almost as though I had a calling.
At the moment, everything’s made in Ireland from Atlantic seaweed in small batches, a process which can be challenging
Then I found a supplier in Donegal who properly honours seaweed and how to gently extract it, to really make seaweed “a hero”. Seaweeds do so many different things - brown seaweed for anti-ageing, for instance, and green seaweed for detox. This supplier hand-harvests her crop at low tide (often during full moon due to spring tide), because that approach is more sustainable – picking rather than cutting.
The products took seven years to develop and are aimed towards improving overall skin health. They can also help with acne, scarring, rosacea and psoriasis, as well as having anti-aging and anti-inflammatory qualities. It also suits men’s larger skin-pores because seaweed molecules are very big. We’ve also had official MTick approval, showing it supports the skin during menopause.
The product development took seven years, and then we went around in circles with our brand director over deciding on a name. When it came to a name, our brand director said it had to be called after my nan, Mary O’Malley. So we called it OMALY.
At the moment, everything’s made in Ireland from Atlantic seaweed in small batches, a process which can be challenging. It’s a tough industry when you believe in your product and you know it’s good, but you’re competing against so much hype and marketing.
Once people start to use the products, they’re telling other people. It’s not about the story of my family, but that the products make a difference to customers, which keeps them coming back.
I do hope my nana would be pleased with what I’ve done – I feel like the connection is getting stronger all the time.
My children didn’t grow up in Ireland, but have such a strong connection there. They will play on the Irish Korfball (a sport akin to netball and basketball combined) team in Europe next month. They went to Catholic school, so most of their friends are of Irish decent. When Mayo won the All-Ireland final, they suddenly asked me “Did you live in Mayo?”
In conversation with Genevieve Carbery. This has been edited for clarity and conciseness.
Ann-Marie O’Shea is founder of OMALY , which has seven products, including beauty drops and moisturisers. Omaly.com

title: Raphaël Glucksmann’s refusal to use the word ‘genocide’ divides France’s left
description: Splitting the electorate has been disastrous for the left, but their differences appear too deep to repair before presidential election
content:
R aphaël Glucksmann, the MEP who this week decisively won the primary to choose a centre-left candidate for France ’s 2027 presidential election, has worked more than most politicians on the issue of genocide.
In his former life as a documentary maker he made Kill Them All!, a film that argued France held some blame for the 1994 genocide of Tutsis in Rwanda .
He became a leading voice against the persecution of the Uyghur Muslim minority in China after entering politics and winning election to the European Parliament in 2019. His efforts to organise boycotts against goods made with forced Uyghur labour saw him sanctioned by China.
“I hope the National Assembly will rise to the occasion of this historic moment and recognise the genocide targeting the Uyghurs in China,” he said as he campaigned, successfully, for the French parliament to recognise Beijing’s actions as a genocide in 2022.
The topic of genocide is once again prominent, but in a very different way, as he campaigns to become French president in April elections representing a coalition of moderate left parties including the faded but still-powerful Socialist Party.
Glucksmann refuses to use the term genocide to describe Israel ’s killing of Palestinians in Gaza , and was repeatedly cornered on the issue by rival candidates who used the term in the centre-left primary debates.
“It would have been easier if I had used it, honestly,” Glucksmann said after his win, when a journalist asked him whether the young Glucksmann who made Kill Them All! would find his older self lacking in courage.
Glucksmann explains that he takes the stance based on decisions of the International Criminal Court, which has issued arrest warrants for Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes and crimes against humanity – but not for genocide.
“I’ve denounced the Israeli government, I’ve campaigned for sanctions, I’ve campaigned for the suspension of the EU association agreement with Israel ... but regarding genocide itself – and undoubtedly this is linked to my history with Rwanda – I don’t use that term,” he recently said.
“Genocide – it’s the total extermination of a population. That’s the aim.”
The word is likely to continue to haunt his presidential campaign as it will be a dividing line between Glucksmann and his most bitter rival.
The charismatic hard-left veteran Jean-Luc Mélenchon (75), who is running his own, separate campaign in his fourth shot at the presidency, uses the word “genocide” readily. He was one of the first in French politics to do so, raising concerns about a possible genocide in Gaza in December 2023 and declaring that Israel’s actions were “not self-defence, but genocide” as early as February 2024.
The divisions are both highly sensitive and electorally significant in a country that has both Europe’s largest Jewish population and a Muslim minority estimated to number about 10 per cent of its overall population.
Whether to co-operate with Mélenchon’s fiery France Unbowed (LFI) movement is one of the most contentious issues among the centre-left.
[ America has been brought to the brink by Trump’s delusion and Hegseth’s barbarism Opens in new window ]
All sides are aware that splitting the electorate has been disastrous for the French left in the past, but their differences appear to have become too deep to repair.
Glucksmann acted partly from a desire to create a moderate pro-EU alternative to Mélenchon’s movement when, then a columnist, he decided to co-found the Place Publique political movement in 2018.
[ France is caught in the politics of emergency, oscillating between nostalgia and extremism Opens in new window ]
Staunchly pro-Ukraine and a former adviser to the Georgian ex-president Mikheil Saakashvili, Glucksmann has long been the target of ire by Mélenchon and his movement for being too “centrist” for his support of Nato and for a perception he is an out-of-touch Parisian.
The scorn is mutual. “The French left isn’t about playing on Jewish names at rallies to get a cheap laugh,” Glucksmann said last week, a reference to persistent accusations of anti-Semitism against Mélenchon.
Mélenchon joked about the name “Epstein” at a rally earlier this year and later mispronounced “Glucksmann”, a surname that reflects the MEP’s Ashkenazi Jewish heritage on the side of his father, a well-known French philosopher.
Glucksmann ruled out any deals with Mélenchon during the primaries and has said his victory – in which he defeated four other candidates to win with a comfortable 66 per cent – is his last word on the matter.
“There will be no alliance with LFI. That’s decided,” he told French radio after his win. After someone dumped a bag of flour over him on the street in Paris following his victory, he told media that Mélenchon and his supporters were to blame.
[ Crime, terror, immigration: France through the eyes of its 'Fox News' Opens in new window ]
Glucksmann now faces the task of closing the gap in polls, which show him in fourth place on about 11 per cent, with Mélenchon on 15 per cent, the centre-right Édouard Philippe on 16 per cent, and hard right front-runner Marine Le Pen leading the field on 32 per cent.
The candidate has asked the Green party to back him – though his pro-nuclear stance alienates some of their members – saying his campaign will be “deeply ecological”. He has insisted repeatedly that he won’t seek allies to the right.
On one of the other dividing lines of the campaign, immigration, he describes his stance as “realistic”. “Zero immigration means the collapse of the French economy,” he said during primary debates.
Glucksmann believes that his platform of reforms to education, building a strong common European defence, and a rejection of extremes can shake off the pall of the humiliating performance of the centre-left in 2022, when the Socialist candidate was eliminated in the first round after winning just 1.8 per cent.
“We have a democratic left that is regaining strength and vigour, that believes in its principles again, and that can win the presidential election,” he said. “Finally, we are banishing the spirit of defeat.”

title: Two-bed apartment in period building in heart of Dublin 2
description: Dunloe Hall enjoys an central location opposite Government Buildings and Merrion Square
content:
Merrion Street dates from the 1750s, when its construction was commissioned by the FitzWilliam estate and carried out by John Esnor, who also laid out FitzWilliam Square, Holles Street and Clare Street.
Designed to run parallel to Kildare Street, it was originally lined on both sides of the south, or upper part, with Georgian townhouses.
Beginning in 1904, the houses on one side of the street were demolished and the Royal College of Science was built in their place. That building is now part of the fabric of Government Buildings. On the same side of the street, further down, is the Natural History Museum, which is being renovated, and the National Gallery.
Dunloe Hall at number 27 Merrion Street Upper enjoys an excellent location directly opposite the gates of Government Buildings. To its left is the Merrion Hotel, with the award-winning Restaurant Patrick Guilbaud and to its right is Merrion Square, a calm oasis of green in the heart of the city.
The building is laid out in 24 apartments over four floors and number 24 has recently come to the market through Sherry FitzGerald, asking €725,000. Through the old front door, the lobby hallway is well maintained and a short corridor leads to a lift.
