Number 24 Dunloe Hall is at the end of the corridor on the upper floor. Inside, a long, narrow hall has a bathroom at one end, two bedrooms in the centre and an open-plan living, kitchen and dining area at its far end. It extends to 71sq m (764sq ft) and is Ber exempt.
An impressive marble fireplace takes centre stage in the living area, which has laminate flooring. There are two sash windows, considerably shorter than their downstairs equivalents, but nonetheless afford an interesting view over the buildings surrounding Merrion Square, many of which possess that distinctive curved Georgian bow at the rear.
Facing southeast, light pours through the windows on a sunny morning. The kitchen is in good working order, but a little dated, so would benefit from a cosmetic refresh.
The bedrooms are large and bright: the main bedroom has the same two windows as the livingroom, and the second bedroom in is smaller – it would make a great study or home office. There’s scope and space for some refurbishment here, such as adding in storage and built-in wardrobes.
At the end of the hall is the bathroom and, like the rest of the apartment, it is in good nick but would benefit for modernisation. The shower is in the bath, so a separate shower enclosure might be a refurb worth doing here.
The loo is old-school, with a high cistern and a pull chain, and this quirky feature is replicated through all the apartments in the building.
As well as its location, its proximity to the Government and business hubs of the capital, 24 Dunloe Hall comes with its own secure underground parking space.
It’s a sunny, bright city pied-à-terre, that with some relatively minor updates would make a very comfortable home in the heart of Dublin city centre.

title: Two-bed apartment ideal for downsizing in Ballsbridge
description: By leaving a larger house in the area, you could free up equity to bolster your monthly income
content:
It’s one thing to move house, but another to leave an area that you’ve lived in for many years.
It’s hardly surprising, therefore, that many older people choose to stay in the same locality when they downsize .
There’s logic to it: you know where to shop for your groceries; you can continue to take the same route on your daily walk; and you’re still close to your neighbours.
Those living in Dublin 4 who are thinking of downsizing may be attracted to 51 Merrion Village, a two-bedroom apartment in Ballsbridge . But there are additional advantages to downsizing in Dublin 4.
By leaving a larger house in the same area, you could free up equity, which could be used to bolster your monthly income during your retirement . Alternatively, the money could be used to purchase a second property – perhaps a holiday home in warmer climes.
Extending to 50sq m (538sq ft), with a C Ber, the apartment is now for sale through DNG Donnybrook with an asking price of €485,000.
Its location on the ground floor is an added advantage for an older person who may find stairs or a lift difficult to manage.
Built in 1985, the apartment was bought by the current owner in 2006 and has been well maintained. This is an airy, bright residence which is unlikely to feel cramped.
A glass panel cleverly placed in the wall between the entrance hall and the sittingroom lets in the light.
The floor-to-ceiling sliding glass doors in the sittingroom lead to a larger than average balcony which faces southwest. A table and chairs for outside dining would fit neatly here, and if you’re missing your garden, there’s space to grow plants along the wall.
The kitchen has wooden cupboards and a large window. There are two spacious double bedrooms, both with fitted wardrobes. The bathroom has been tiled in beige and has a bath.
All of the flooring is laminated wood, which combines well with the white walls.
Those living in the Ballsbridge area will be familiar with its location, which is just 3km from Dublin city centre and has a number of good restaurants and coffee shops.
The apartment is a nine-minute drive from leafy Herbert Park and just 1km from Sandymount Strand, which is handy if you like to swim or simply want to walk along the promenade and take in the sea air.

title: Well-connected Stillorgan apartment with fresh interior
description: Two-bed ground-floor apartment close to village and bus routes to the city centre
content:
Cedarmount on Stillorgan ’s St Brigid’s Road is a mature, secluded development built in 1989. The development, set behind a security barrier, consists of small blocks of duplex homes over ground-floor apartments, clustered around open green spaces in lovely grounds. Trees abound, both older specimens bordering the enclave and more recently planted trees, which are maturing.
Number 10, a 55sq m ground-floor apartment with two bedrooms and a bathroom, is now on the market with DNG Stillorgan, seeking €425,000. Owners of larger properties who desire to stay in the Stillorgan area might consider this as a downsizing opportunity that would release considerable equity in their home.
It’s easy to envisage this apartment appealing to those who already own a property abroad or those considering investing in one. It would make a great base for anyone downsizing in south Dublin, being so close to the N11.
One of the nicest features of the apartment is that it is dual aspect, so it is bright. From its own-door entrance, a small hallway opens into the livingroom, with a decently deep and large window and an open gas fire. The kitchen is separate from the livingroom and has its own window; there is also something lovely about closing the kitchen door in the evenings.
While small, the kitchen is well-laid out, with a washing machine, oven, hob, extractor fan and fridge-freezer. The wooden units are painted a fresh, pale blue and are in good condition.
A hallway leads from the livingroom to the rest of the apartment, comprising the bathroom and bedrooms. The bathroom has been renovated with a classic large grey tile and modern fixtures and fittings.
At the rear of the apartment are two bedrooms. The main bedroom has French doors opening to the outside patio, and the smaller bedroom has a window overlooking the back of the property. While everything is in walk-in condition, with new laminate flooring laid throughout, a new owner might want to add to the home’s storage capacity in the form of built-in presses and additional wardrobes.
The south-facing patio is private, bordered by a hedge. It is a perfect sun trap for those al-fresco evenings. The Ber is D1, heating is gas and the annual service charge is €2,000. There is plenty of parking throughout the development for residents and their guests.
The location is bound to appeal to a large cohort of potential downsizers, with Stillorgan village just a short stroll away; it has a decent mix of supermarkets, cafes, banking and boutiques. Dundrum Town Centre and Blackrock Village are within easy reach, Deer Park Tennis Club is just behind the development and the coast is a short drive away.
The bus corridor is a two-minute walk from the apartment, offering services to Dublin city centre, Blackrock and south Dublin. The N11 is close by, providing easy access to the M50 and the airport.

title: How to downsize in Ireland: Plan early, sell first, be flexible
description: Despite the challenges, if you plan early and make yourself familiar with the market, the move is very doable
content:
After years spent maintaining a family home, the prospect of downsizing to somewhere smaller, warmer and easier to manage can seem like a sensible next step. It might even release some much-needed equity for retirement, travel or to help the next generation get on to the property ladder.
Yet the prospect of downsizing can seem considerably more straightforward than the reality. For all the talk of older homeowners freeing up family-sized houses, finding a suitable smaller property in the right location is not guaranteed. The finances, meanwhile, are not always as compelling as they first appear, once stamp duty, legal fees, moving costs and the price of a well-located apartment or bungalow are factored in.
Guy Doherty of Sherry FitzGerald is an estate agent in north county Dublin and he comes in contact with many people who are in a house that is too large for their needs. While he would always recommend looking into “rightsizing” for the next phase of life, he can’t guarantee the process will always be smooth.
“I’ve huge empathy with people who are trying to downsize because it’s very hard,” says Doherty. “The main rationale for downsizing is to get a home at a more manageable size. There’s also the desire to get closer to family and facilities, so it makes an awful lot of sense.”
However, in Doherty’s experience, the logistics of lining up the sale of the old home and the purchase of the new home can often become too complicated and has resulted in people changing their mind and taking their home off the market.
“Selling your house and trying to find your perfect downsizer property, and dovetailing the two, is incredibly hard. I find with downsizers that element of risk is too high.”
It is also difficult for homeowners to shift their mindset to apartment living.
“Apartments probably had a stigma and the idea of downsizing to one might be just too much of a move, particularly if they enjoyed their garden and have to settle for just a balcony,” says Doherty.
“But, having said that, I’ve seen it happen and the benefits are huge. If I can get clients to come see the apartments and see how easy apartment living is, they can get their heads around it. There might be management fees, but when you break it down, it means everything is looked after and there’s no maintenance to worry about.”
[ A new home in older age: What are the benefits of downsizing to a new development? Opens in new window ]
Doherty is an advocate for looking at different models of housing for downsizers and feels Ireland is way behind the curve on this. He believes there should be tax incentives to encourage developers to create a more appealing option for downsizers and look at building Florida-style community schemes rather than expecting the older generation to move into an apartment block alongside first-time buyers.
Incentivising this cohort of buyers would also keep the property chain moving.
“There’s the whole circle of life where a lot of families are trying to trade up to these properties but because the older generation in these homes have nowhere to downsize to, that whole circle is incomplete,” Doherty says.
He points out that even small properties in affluent areas, such as Howth, can command prohibitive prices, meaning the equity prospective downsizers had hoped to release to fund a comfortable retirement may be less than anticipated.
However, staying put is not without its costs. An older home with a poor energy rating can prove an ongoing drain on finances, unless owners have the savings to undertake a full retrofit. In some cases, therefore, moving to a more modern, energy-efficient property – even at a higher price than expected – may prove the more prudent option in the long run.
[ RTÉ’s Jacqui Hurley sets up business matching downsizers with those trading up: ‘There’s probably trepidation’ Opens in new window ]
Despite these challenges, Doherty believes if you plan early and make yourself familiar with the market you want to buy into, the move is very doable.
“Speak to your local estate agent and get the lowdown on the area. Describe what type of property you’re selling and what type of property you’d like to move to. From there, we can build on that,” he says.
“We probably already have a string of buyers that would love to trade up to your house, and then we can get you out looking at properties that we think would suit your criteria.”
There are also some things prospective buyers can prepare in advance so they will be ready when they decide to move.
A Ber certificate lasts for 10 years and can be done by an assessor, while it is also possible to get your photos and brochure done by your chosen estate agent without having to commit to putting your home on the market. If you’re sitting and waiting for your dream home, this way you are effectively market ready and could get your house up in 24 hours and be in contention to bid on the property you are after, according to Doherty.
“There will be competition at this level of the market because you’re coming up against first-time buyers and cash buyers,” he says.
“There is a safety net in doing it this way because if you don’t get that property, you don’t have to sell. You can reassess and take the property off the market. No harm, no foul – you don’t owe us any fees. But if you procrastinate, it’s already too late.”
[ What will €315,000 buy by the water in Clontarf and Co Kerry? Opens in new window ]
Financial planning is also an important step. A bridging loan may be required if the timing of the sale and purchase don’t line up. Bank of Ireland has a trade-down equity-release scheme for downsizers that allows owners to borrow up to 60 per cent of their current home’s value to buy a new home. This gives borrowers 12 months to complete the sale of their home and use the funds from the sale to repay the loan with a variable interest rate of 7 per cent.
Legal issues can cause problems at the late stage of any property transaction. William Donovan, a conveyancing solicitor and property law expert at HOMS Assist, says it is always advisable to contact your solicitor as early as possible.
“We need certificates of compliance with planning permission or building regulations, or certificates of exempt development, where a property did not require planning permission,” he says.
“It may be necessary to apply for retention permission which could take six months to a year to obtain. It also takes time to take up title deeds from a bank, where there is a mortgage, or if the title deeds may have gone missing at home. We can reconstitute the title if contacted in a timely manner.”
Donovan says that in some circumstances properties may need an architect or engineer to ensure the physical boundaries correspond with the title map, adding that some houses outside of the city may be met with other setbacks.
“An issue that sometimes arises in the country is that the percolation area servicing the septic tank or a water well may be located on adjoining lands. It may be necessary to have the neighbouring owner sign a Deed of Wayleave or a Right of Way to regularise matters and to facilitate the sale without the purchaser having to qualify the title to the bank.”
It may seem daunting, but with the right planning, there is no reason why you can’t downsize successfully, according to Doherty.
“Sometimes you just have to take a leap of faith. I wouldn’t advise leaving it too late, however. Do it when you have the energy and motivation.”

title: Two-bed apartment with sea views popular with downsizers in Clontarf
description: Seascape scheme was built 10 years ago and continues to draw in buyers looking to trade down
content:
Built by MKN Property Group and designed by O’Mahony Pike, Seascape on Clontarf Road was completed in 2015. The development comprises 59 apartments arranged across two blocks, with some, including number 9, enjoying views directly towards the sea.
When the development first came to the market more than a decade ago, there was considerable interest from people looking to trade down from larger houses in Clontarf. More than 10 years on, that pattern has continued, with a good number of the apartments owned by downsizers.
Number 9 is a first-floor apartment and is being brought to the market through Sherry Fitzgerald , guiding €895,000. Extending to 87sq m (936sq ft), it has a spacious feel, helped by the design which places the livingroom and bedrooms with their oversized windows facing out to the sea.
The apartment is accessed from the lobby by either lift or stairs and opens into a hallway, with the living accommodation to the right and the bedrooms straight ahead.
The open-plan arrangement of the living space allows daylight from the floor-to-ceiling windows to travel deep into the room and through towards the kitchen. The contemporary kitchen is fully fitted with white, high-gloss units by Kube and has a small breakfast bar, which provides a division between the kitchen and the remainder of the open-plan space.
A dining table is positioned to one side, with the main living area across from it. Set into the recess of the window is a second seating area beside the doors out to the balcony.
There are two double bedrooms, both with fitted wardrobes. The main bedroom has an en suite bathroom, and there is a second bathroom for guests. There is a separate utility room.
For anyone considering a move from a house but reluctant to give up outdoor space, the balcony provides a decent substitute for a garden. There is room for plants as well as a table and chairs, while the sea view is a feature that would be difficult to find from most back gardens.
The apartment and the development as a whole have been well maintained and have not dated since their construction. Residents pay approximately €3,745 annually to Greendoor Property Management Company, which looks after the shared areas and landscaped communal garden.
Number 9 has a B energy rating and high levels of insulation, with the sun providing an additional source of warmth. The property comes with an underground parking space located close to the lift, as well as a secure private storage area.
The development is behind secure gates. The location on the Clontarf Road means everything is within walking distance. There is a bus stop directly outside the development, and the cycle path across the road continues into the city in one direction and Howth in the other.
Bay restaurant is on the opposite corner to Seascape and just a few minutes down the road are Póg cafe and Coopers Bottleshop across from the Wooden Bridge, which takes you on to Dollymount Strand.

title: Citroën’s relaunch of a classic could be just what the electric car market needs
description: Price and simplicity are key selling points for the French car-maker’s new 2CV model
content:
At a time when the cost of living and sustainability are competing for attention, one classic is bringing the two together in an innovative way.
The Government wants more cars on Irish roads to be electric. That makes a lot of sense, but there are barriers to entry, not least the cost. That’s where an old solution may provide a new fix.
Citroën launched the 2CV back in 1948 with the goal being accessibility. Not only was it cheap to buy, it was designed to reduce costs for users. The total cost of ownership was factored in, with the aim being to make cars – old-school fossil-fuel-using cars – more accessible to everyone.
The last 2CV left the production line in 1990 as it was overtaken by market forces and greater competition. Now, in the electric era, an old friend is making a comeback.
If the original 2CV was socially transformative, Citroën is out to replicate its effect in the electric car market . With most models being heavy and too expensive to encourage enough drivers to make the switch, the French car maker is out to upend the market with simplicity.
It’s not just a nostalgia play. Citroën unveiled the new model at the recent Paris Motor Show with plans to have it in showrooms by 2028, selling for just €15,000. That’s a price point going to attract a lot of attention.
Electric cars as we know them today are marketed heavily on the bells and whistles that go with them, which involve a lot of computing power and screens. The 2CV, as one might expect, isn’t going down that route.
The plan is for the car to be substantially lighter than the norm, which will mean less energy is required for usage. That facilitates the use of a smaller battery to further reduce the weight. This also means it won’t need to use as much in the way of critical minerals, which would otherwise add to the cost.
Citroën is not the first French car-maker to embrace the past with its electric cars. Renault’s 5 E-Tech is a reimagining of the old Renault 5, another car that was aimed at a wider audience. As it happens, the chap who drives me to and from the pub after going to UCD football games has one, and he’s quite impressed with how much he’s saving as a result.
Yet it still feels like it has more than is necessary to be considered a truly budget option. The more that can be stripped down, the more the gains compound due to reduced weight and the subsequent power requirements.
The electric transition needs cars people can afford. The costs don’t stop once the list price has been covered. That’s why the reimagination of the 2CV, a car targeted at the budget-conscious, is so intriguing.
[ Which EVs won’t make me feel carsick? Opens in new window ]
The Renault 5 E-Tech has a list price of over €26,000, which is hardly terrible, yet what Citroën is proposing is a vehicle €11,000 cheaper. That’s a price point likely to make newly purchased electric vehicles available to a much wider market.
There will obviously be some snobbish mockery; the original 2CV is far more fondly commented on today than in its pomp. When looking to the past for inspiration, there’s also the natural risk that the market has moved on.
Yet I’m confident this can be different. While the original car was designed with farmers in mind, the 2CV was adopted by hippies and counterculturalists as well. Both of these groups could easily be the target markets for the electric version.
The latter group is obvious given that an electric 2CV is the four-wheeled ideal for the eco-conscious. Yet those working in rural areas might well prove just as valuable a market.
When it comes to farming, practicality is paramount. If it works and gets the job done, it’s a winner. If it doesn’t, then it gets left aside. The 2CV was designed with such simple practicality in mind, reducing complications so that it could just work.
These aren’t exactly the most hopeful times in technology. We can barely go a day without a new story about some terrifying way artificial intelligence has been misused, or a new major hack. Even supermarket fridges are no longer safe from cyber threats these days.
That the 2CV, which was born from the postwar slump in Europe where times were tough, could be a shining light in the darkness is truly wonderful.
Citroën isn’t trying to sell the fanciest machine with the most features, yet the car maker has proposed something truly innovative. It’s selling simplicity.
[ Just €109,000 of €3.9m overpaid to car dealers for EV scheme has been recovered Opens in new window ]

title: I feel like picking on myself. And why not? Self-bullying is a core part of Irish identity
description: New version of Carrie burns with cathartic female rage – and sparks some scary school memories
content:
O f all the monsters in the Monster Mash – the werewolf, Frankenstein’s, the vampire, the mummy – I think the most terrifying is the Carrie.
It may be because when I saw the film Carrie and read Stephen King ’s novel I was at an impressionable age, but the moral of that story – “bullying is bad, because the person you’re bullying might be telekinetic and might kill you with their mind” – really landed for me.
“Don’t bully that noodly nerdlinger, Biffo” I would say to my friend Biffo, a bully by trade. “They might be a Carrie.
“Unhand that primping Poindexter. Stop administering sick burns to that doddery dorkmeister. Desist from whaling on that weedy Walter. Potential Carries all.
“We must be vigilant. Yes, any one of these goodie goofballs could have terrifying unearthly powers – this might all end with the school on fire.
“And it’s Ireland in the 1980s, so that would put a lot of pressure on the Department of Education and add to the fiscal deficit. Lest I need to remind you, economic recovery is a good 10 years away.” (Me and the rest of the bullies were in Young Fine Gael.)
It was very clear to me, thanks to Carrie, that bullying was wrong because it might end in my violent death by burning, which would totally suck. It’s something that to this very day I teach my most thuggish nephew. (He knows who he is.)
It was a shame, really, because that whole “pouring a bucket of blood on to the head of the girl that’s been tricked into feeling like she belonged” is a pretty excellent prank, and I would definitely have done it if the movie Carrie had ended with all the hot people high-fiving in a freeze-frame and a girl saying: “That was some pretty cool bullying you did there, Patrick Freyne, you hunk.” Instead, Carrie burned everyone to ash.
The story had such an effect on me that sometimes, indeed, I’d even wonder if I was a Carrie. “Why are you frowning at me like that?” Biffo would say when he had me in an affectionate headlock. “Are you trying to make me go on fire? Do you think you might be a Carrie? Are you trying to make my head explode or is that a different film?”
(Once, while concentrating on making Biffo’s head explode, I thought the lights flickered a little bit. Sadly, I think it was just because the wiring was very old. Poor wiring might also have caused the fire in Carrie, on reflection.)
[ Cill Stuifín on TG4 review: ‘We spent our childhoods terrified of seeing Cill Stuifín’ Opens in new window ]
Anyway, forgetting my aborted bullying career for a moment, both Carrie the book and Carrie the film are excellent works of melancholy horror where the source of terror, as in Frankenstein, is a heartbreaking outcast, not an avatar of evil.
Mike Flanagan’s retelling of the Carrie story on Prime Video seems quite different from the source material. I guess it has to be, because the Carrie story is iconically well known.
The first big difference is that Carrie and her mother are discovered in a sort of cultlike shut-in situation, so Carrie is new to the school. This changes the dynamic somewhat, making Carrie almost exotic rather than simply one of the routine bullyable classes. (That’s anyone who’s different, if you can recall your own bullying days.)
The second difference is that, unlike Sissy Spacek, who plays Carrie in the film as otherworldly and timid, or Carrie in the book, who is overweight and unhappy, Carrie as played by the very charismatic Summer H Howell is chirpy and enthusiastic and well read and clever and surprisingly well balanced for someone who has basically been imprisoned at home and secretly has the power to destroy everything.
[ TV & Radio Sienna Miller: ‘I had to get to a place where I was able to be taken seriously’ Opens in new window ]
There is a sense that with some good career guidance Carrie could, in fact, make a great life for herself. (Perhaps she could become an electrician and fix the wiring in the school.) This does, unfortunately, remove some of the deep sadness from the story.
The third difference is that Carrie’s mother, while filled with righteous rage at the modern world, is not mentally unwell and sex-obsessed like Carrie’s mother in the book or the film. Indeed, it often feels as if Carrie’s mother has some good points to make given the state of the world. (Refusing to leave the house feels like a reasonable response to reality right now.)
[ The Real Rooneys on Disney+: Everything is white. Unlike us, the rich do not fear stains Opens in new window ]
The fourth difference is the idea that there’s a wider world of supernatural conspiracy to contend with. I guess you have to do that if you want a recurring series. This already tends towards overexplanation, whereas some of what’s beautiful about the original film is that gaps are not filled in.
I’m giving it the benefit of the doubt. This is helped by the very good cast – not just Howell but also Alison Thornton, Siena Agudong, Amber Midthunder (who was excellent in Prey ) and Tim Bagley (who was also excellent in Somebody Somewhere). Every character so far is depicted as nuanced and flawed and capable of carrying their own story.
It’s also another show about cathartic female rage, hot on the heels of the excellent crime drama Furious (Disney+) and coexisting with Zoe Kazan’s Steinbeck adaptation, East of Eden (Netflix), which features a terrifying Florence Pugh as a manipulative avenging femme fatale. The female-rage quotient feels necessary. It’s almost as though there are lots of reasons to be angry right now.
The highfalutin notions in the last paragraph make me want to bully myself . And why not? I’d argue that self-bullying is a core part of Irish identity. So much so that while watching the Netflix drama Below, a horror series set in Newfoundland, I just assumed the whole project of Newfoundland was designed to mock the Irish accent.
I know the Newfoundland people are largely descended from Irish immigrants, but it really does feel as if they’re just taking the piss out of us. “Taoiseach asks Newfoundland to just knock it off” feels like the appropriate Waterford Whispers headline.
Nonetheless, Below, which stars Josh Hartnett and Mackenzie Davis, is an excellent slice of humane, thoughtful Canadian horror about a many-tentacled, big-eyed monster lurking beneath the sea.
As in all the best scary stories, more is going on than just a beastie lurking in the deep. There’s subtext . There’s a backdrop of rural depopulation and a frontdrop of disenfranchised men (specifically Hartnett’s character) seeking a new role for themselves in the face of increasing obsolescence.
By the end of the first episode we haven’t quite seen our googly-eyed monster yet, but I’m pretty sure from all the context cues that it’s being bullied into violence by climate change. I feel as if we should introduce him to Carrie. Together they could do the Monster Mash (the Monster Mash). I suspect it would be a graveyard smash.

title: ‘I knew I’d never seen anything like it’: Josh Brolin and Austin Abrams on Whalefall
description: Trapped inside a sperm whale with only an hour of oxygen, a grieving son confronts his relationship with his father in the film adaptation of Daniel Kraus’s novel
content:
When, a couple of years ago, Daniel Kraus wrote his thriller Whalefall, he built the book around an extraordinary premise connected to the strange phenomenon of the title. After a whale dies, its corpse sinks to the bottom of the ocean and forms a new ecosystem, sustaining scavengers, crustaceans and hundreds of deep-sea organisms for many years – decades, in some instances.
In Kraus’s story a 17-year-old scuba diver, Jay Gardiner, is searching the Pacific off California for the remains of his father, a well-known local diver who, in the late stages of cancer, died by suicide. When a giant squid draws Jay into the mouth of a sperm whale, the teenager finds himself inside its stomach with dwindling oxygen and an hour to escape.
As the page-turner races against that deadline, Jay must confront the guilt, anger and unresolved love that shaped his relationship with his father.
A marriage of maritime science, grief meditation, and claustrophobic suspense, Kraus’s adventure earned some rave reviews after it was published in 2023. The New York Times called it “a crazy, and crazily enjoyable, beat-the-clock adventure story about fathers, sons, guilt and the mysteries of the sea”.
So the studio bidding war to win the film distribution rights was no surprise.
The new movie stars Josh Brolin as Mitt, the swallowed diver’s father. The actor read the book while he was shooting Ridley Scott’s film The Dog Stars . He loved it so much that he slowed down, because he didn’t want it to end. The Whalefall story also made him sob, he says, and ultimately prompted him to talk to his own son and father – the actor James Brolin – about their respective relationships.
“I had a massive emotional reaction to the end of that book,” Brolin says. “I’m still trying to figure that out. It took no time – zero time – to say yes to the script. All the elements with the father and the son drew me in.
“Reading it was just something. I knew that I’d never seen anything like it before. And that was a really exciting prospect. You’re reading something and thinking, I don’t know how we’re going to do this.”
Kraus drew the outlandish survival premise from real-world accounts by kayakers and scuba divers who briefly ended up in the mouths of humpback whales.
He and the film’s director, Brian Duffield, also consulted scientists, including Prof Lara Horstmann, director of marine science at the University of Alaska, and Phil Clapham of the Alaska Fisheries Science Center, in Seattle, who advised on every behavioural – and sometimes intestinal – detail.
“I now know where everything is in a whale,” says Austin Abrams , the breakout star of the recent horror films Weapons and Resident Evil , who plays Jay. Be warned: there will be gigantic innards and lakes of acid. Do not bring popcorn to this movie.
As time runs out for the adolescent hero, who has been drawing on Mitt’s salty ingenuity to engineer routes to survival, memories of their turbulent relationship resurface until finally, with oxygen reserves contracting, whale and father speak with one voice. To amplify that point, the whale’s heartbeat is actually Brolin’s.
Something like therapy crept into rehearsals.
“I was in a place in my life where I just wanted to go deeper,” Brolin says. “Can you have a more joyful experience during this process, especially in a movie that is as emotionally difficult as this is? I had an amazing time. During rehearsals we would improvise; we would talk about our families.
[ ‘Build up an extreme well of confidence’: Daniel Kraus on getting in the writing zone Opens in new window ]
“Selfishly, that’s the only reason why you do this. It’s because you’re interested in the human condition and how you fit in – and how you’ve navigated your own raising of your own children,” he says.
“That’s the only way you can sustain this after 42 years of doing this job. You have to have an organic interest in what makes us tick.”
Abrams had already scored a number of hit television shows, including The Walking Dead, This Is Us and Euphoria, before breaking into movies. The star of Paper Towns and Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark won considerable plaudits in 2024, when he held his own alongside Brad Pitt and George Clooney in the glossy thriller Wolfs .
“There’s jitters of working with Brad and George,” he says. “Doubt is definitely something you contend with.”
Before he began filming Whalefall, the 30-year-old actor spent time with sperm whales, the only mammal big enough to swallow a human whole. He scuba-dived alongside them off Dominica, to observe their behaviour in their natural habitat, with Patrick Dykstra, who won a Bafta for his filming of sperm whales for the David Attenborough series Blue Planet II.
Abrams also obtained advanced scuba certification and built his endurance by walking around his neighbourhood in full diving gear.
The training prepared him for the film’s demanding underwater sequences in the Pacific Ocean, where physical stamina and familiarity with diving equipment were essential.
“Diving wasn’t necessarily something I was super comfortable with,” he says. “That was a really important aspect of the discussion. The character needed to be this guy who has been doing it his whole life, so we needed to make it feel and look like that.
“And then there’s also the stunt aspect, where you’re doing all these things with lines, and people are pulling you and twisting you. You have to be as comfortable as you can down there. Learning all that stuff was a really important aspect of it.”
Re-creating the inside of a whale demanded more from the film-makers than computer-generated imagery. Peter Jackson’s Weta Workshop, the Oscar-winning New Zealand effects studio that worked on the Lord of the Rings sequence, created physical sets that make Jay’s predicament particularly nauseous.
The 360-degree stomach set could be rolled, while water was added and drained to alter its contours, approximating the visceral sensation of being trapped in a living, shifting organism. Freaky bioluminescent details provide crucial flashes of light in the darkness.
“I’ve got to say, after seeing a sperm whale, the first thing that comes to mind is: do we even need to sell a fictional story about whales?” Abrams says. “They’re such magical animals in themselves.”
“I agree with Austin,” Brolin says. “They’re incredible animals, and I feel like that’s partly why we keep coming back to whales in mythic stories. There are so many stories about them, and each of them is really affecting.”
Whales have long occupied a space in our collective imagination. In Norse mythology, the sea could conceal monstrous creatures, while Maori tradition reveres whales as ancestral guardians.
[ Why are Ireland’s whales disappearing? Opens in new window ]
In the Book of Jonah, in the Old Testament, the prophet must spend three days praying and repenting inside the belly of a whale, having disobeyed God’s command for the population of Nineveh to repent.
The immortal Moby-Dick has been variously interpreted as an allegory of humanity’s futile struggle to impose order on an indifferent universe, a Marxist critique of industrial exploitation, an ecofable and a warning about authoritarian leadership.
Whalefall perhaps stands out nevertheless: death by gigantic sea beast has rarely seemed as simultaneously revolting and sorrowful a prospect. But the mystique remains.
“There’s a magical quality to whales,” Brolin says. “I think that’s probably why we love telling stories about them.”
Whalefall is in cinemas from Friday, October 16th

title: Naza review: An essential record of the nightmare Israel has engineered in Gaza
description: The most disturbing sections introduce us to a tracking algorithm known, with blackly appalling insensitivity, as ‘Where’s Daddy?’
content:
Much justified praise (and no little condemnation) has already come the way of Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham for their diligent analysis of the mechanisms behind Israel’s ongoing assault on Gaza. It will take more than one viewing to disentangle the reporting on how technology and propaganda distance intelligence personnel from the consequences of their actions.
Not enough has, however, yet been said about the stark, formal brilliance of the project. Naza – the title is a Hebrew acronym for “collateral damage” – largely comprises nocturnal interviews with whistleblowers on the roofs of Tel Aviv. As we hear of escalating horrors, the camera moves to find citizens, shot through picture windows, blithely going about their comfortable business, many ignoring television news on enormous screens.
One can’t help but think of what Jonathan Glazer, an executive producer of Naza, did in The Zone of Interest : the film pointedly tells us that Gaza is just 70km from the Israeli capital.
Szor and Abraham compiled their documentary, winner of a special jury prize at Venice International Film Festival, from conversations with 24 anonymous soldiers and military intelligence officers, their voices digitally altered, their faces appearing in only shadowy silhouette.
The film-makers’ thesis is that the enormous number of civilian deaths “was not simply a byproduct of war, as it was often framed by media outlets, but a premeditated, calculated and intentional action, stemming directly from Israeli decisions”.
To that end we hear much about a programme called Lavender that helps compile a list of potential targets with links to Hamas. We hear how civilian deaths – the titular Naza – are regarded as justifiable in pursuit of supposed military antagonists.
The most disturbing sections introduce us to a tracking algorithm known, with blackly appalling insensitivity, as “Where’s Daddy?” The notion is that the families of those in the crosshairs will, via tapped mobile phones, alert distant Israeli operatives when relatives arrive home.
“You hack her phone and then you kill her,” one says of a 12-year-old girl.
For an attack on one particularly desired target, the authorities approved the death of 500 Naza.
“That’s the population of a small Israeli town,” Abraham chillily observes.
There is little sense here of the film slipping into “shooting and crying”, that dubious genre whereby interviewees ask us to sympathise with trauma suffered while committing atrocities. Some interviewees certainly express regret, but the pervading tone is cold, cynical, analytical.
One explains how indoctrination tells them there are “no innocent people in Gaza”. Another notes that “whoever you decided to kill was considered a terrorist”.
It hardly needs to be said that, after the triumphant Venice premiere, a wall of criticism collapsed on Szor and Abraham. The Israel Defense Forces rejected many of their conclusions. Some pro-Palestinian activists felt it wrong to conceal the identities of personnel involved in such apparent outrages. Miki Zohar, the Israeli culture minister, called for the film-makers’ citizenship to be revoked following what he saw as “treason against the state”. Those debates will continue.
There is no question that Szor and Abraham, who previously worked on the similarly controversial, Oscar-winning No Other Land, from 2024, have, as documentarians will, taken a firm position. After dwelling among the mostly quiet rooftops, the film closes with devastating footage of what an air strike can do to a dwelling in Gaza. Economically scattered archive footage reminds us how Tel Aviv was built on land formerly occupied by just such obliterated communities.
The result is specific disquiet at what is currently happening in that region, but the film, coproduced by The Guardian, also triggers more general horror at how, in the contemporary world, it is too easy to slaughter from a dispassionate distance. An essential record of engineered nightmare.

title: AI’s impact on jobs market may take 25 years to play out, says Microsoft chief Brad Smith
description: Industry must be regulated to ensure safety for people, according to top Microsoft executive
content:
Artificial intelligence ’s (AI’s) impact on the jobs market could take up to 25 years to play out fully, according to Brad Smith, one of the most senior executives at tech giant Microsoft.
Speaking to Inside Business, a podcast from The Irish Times, Smith said: “So far we are not seeing AI displace a lot of jobs, but I think it would be a mistake to just assume that the future won’t create new challenges. We need to double down on giving people the skills so they can put AI to work.
“Really understand how jobs are evolving ... and we’re probably going to need some creative Government policies as well. This is a journey that I think will be ahead of us for the next 25 years.”
Smith, who is vice chair and president of Microsoft, was speaking in Dublin at the International AI Summit at the RDS organised by the Government.
Smith reiterated his view that AI needs to be regulated.
“The power and capability of AI has moved ahead faster than safety. We need safety to catch up, and we need to take the steps to ensure that the benefits of AI accrue across the economy and not just to the AI lab companies on the west coast of the United States.
“Right now, there are more safety rules for a carton of milk than for the most powerful AI on the planet. That doesn’t make common sense in my view. That doesn’t mean we should want regulation to stifle innovation or become bureaucratically heavy-handed, but we need a bit more of the rule of law to keep people safe.”
On whether recent warnings from senior tech executives that AI could kill us all, Smith said: “I always think we’re better off taking things seriously even if we think the risk of something truly awful happening is low.”
Smith said the regulation of AI would probably involve multiple layers involving international collaboration.
He expects national governments to become “fast movers” on AI regulation. “It won’t surprise me if it starts with incident reporting, a legal rule that says that if you create an AI agent and it breaks into somebody else’s network, that you have a legal duty to inform the victim of what happened.
“It won’t surprise me if Australia is the first mover or at least an early mover. They were one of the victims of one of the [hacking] incidents. Australia has a parliament that tends to be capable of moving quickly. It may be them, it may be someone else.”
On the State’s role in regulation, he said: “Ireland quite rightly always thinks about whether for each issue it wants to move at the national level or as part of the EU.
“The thing that gives me hope about Ireland ... is that the Government here tends to be farsighted, tends to develop a vision, have clear goals and actually executes effectively.”
Based on Microsoft research, the Republic ranks number three in the world on the percentage of the population using AI.
“Some 49.9 per cent of the Irish population is using generative AI. That says a huge amount [about] how well positioned Ireland is into the future,” Smith said.

title: Cotton Queen review: Commendably scathing dramatic takedown of postcolonial ‘freedom’
description: Coming-of-age story examines how imperial power survives through new economic arrangements
content:
In Suzannah Mirghani’s Cotton Queen, forces claiming to defend tradition may be more oppressive than those promising modernisation.
Set in a Sudanese village where cotton sustains the local economy, this imaginative coming-of-age story examines how imperial power survives through new economic arrangements and old social hierarchies.
Mirghani centres the story on Nafisa (the magnetic Mihad Murtada), a 15-year-old whose grandmother, Al-Sit (Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud), commands the village through a steely mixture of authority, old legends and fear. Celebrated as a resistance heroine who drove out the British, Al-Sit has somehow become the guardian of a questionable social order.
Her traditional production depends on the exploitation of girls, whose virginity is marketed as a guarantee of quality. These modernised young women watch TikTok tutorials, but the language of heritage disguises a chattel system that polices their bodies.
Meanwhile, Nadir (Hassan Kassala), a businessman of Sudanese heritage raised abroad, rolls up to the abandoned British pile selling genetically modified seeds on behalf of multinational interests. He’s slick and handsome. The locals show far too much deference. But his technological revolution requires the transfer of authority from village elites to corporate capital.
The first narrative feature directed by a Sudanese woman is a commendably scathing takedown of postcolonial “freedom” that has not abolished exploitation; it has merely shifted the mechanisms. Intriguingly, lurking beneath supposed independence are historical mysteries to unravel. Ancient newspaper clippings provide clues to a huge reveal.
Nafisa’s resistance to an arranged marriage becomes the film’s most radical gesture. Her refusal challenges the authority of her elders and a society that treats women as assets to be allocated between competing interests. Sit tight. Her final answer is appropriately brutal.
The film’s shifts between realism, folklore and magical mystery are deft and compelling. Frida Marzouk’s dreamy cinematography, partly inspired by Happy as Lazzaro and The Night of the Hunter, effortlessly transitions between magical realism and village life.
Here is a cousin to Rungano Nyoni’s fantastical reckonings with Zambian traditions in I Am Not a Witch and On Becoming a Guinea Fowl. Here is also a stark lesson about unfinished revolutions.

title: Spend or splurge: Where can you make savings on a home renovation project?
description: Compromises will need to be made when it comes to your renovation budget − but only in certain areas
content:
According to the experts, a home renovation in Ireland can cost anywhere between €1,200 and €2,500 per square metre and can rise to more than €4,000 for high-end projects where significant structural work is involved. For a basic mid-range renovation, that translates into a total of €120,000 to €250,000 for a fairly typical 100sq m three-bedroom home. And €400,000 upwards when you get into the really serious stuff.
But why the wide variation? The first factor to be borne in mind is the condition of the original house. A poorly insulated 30-year-old semi-d is naturally going to cost a lot more to renovate than a younger and fresher model.
Then there is the scope of the project. A basic refresh involving painting and decoration, some new flooring and floor coverings, and maybe some internal doors and light fixtures will be an awful lot cheaper than a renovation where walls are knocked, plumbing is changed, new bathrooms and kitchens are fitted and so on.
Location counts too. Builders warn that labour costs in Dublin are anything up to 20 per cent higher than elsewhere in the country. Bad news for those contemplating a renovation in the capital.
With costs like that, there is a lot of cloth cutting to be done when measuring up a renovation budget. Compromises will have to be made, and homeowners will need to decide where it’s worthwhile paying a bit more for quality and durability and where savings can be made without a negative impact on the overall project.
Seamus Furlong of Brennan Furlong Architects advises people to look at what they don’t actually need to do before deciding on a renovation.
“With our clients, when approaching a renovation project, we start with a really good review of what they currently have,” he says. “If they have an extension that’s not working, can that be reimagined rather than knocking it down and building something entirely new? Very often, we see people demolish an extension and then build one of similar size. Do you really want to knock it down? Is it there not enough light or is there no connection to the garden or the house? These things can be quite easily dealt with, with proper consideration and design. Don’t underestimate what you can do with what you already have with proper professional advice.”
Furlong advises people not to try to cut corners on the building fabric. “If you have a home which is well insulated and performs well, it’s going to save you money in the long term. Make sure it is well insulated, as airtight as possible and properly ventilated as well. That will minimise energy use, improve the comfort of the home and make it healthier for occupants. It is certainly worth investing in those areas, and doing it later can be disruptive and costly.”
He also advises people to take advantage of work being done to make provision for future adoption of technology. “Make it ready for smart home technologies to control heating and so on. For example, you might not be able to afford solar panels now but can put the wiring in for them.”
There are areas where significant savings can be made, however. This includes flooring. “There is no doubting the quality of hardwood floors or polished concrete, but they are expensive,” says Furlong. “You can look at alternatives like laminate that give you the same aesthetic and can be replaced quite easily later on.”
Kitchens and windows are two big-ticket items from a cost perspective, he notes. “If you have a young family the kitchen is going to take a lot of wear and tear in the early years. Maybe the wiser choice is the economical one, and you can it replace later.”
Glazing and windows can have a significant effect on the overall cost of a project, he adds. “Don’t compromise on the performance of the windows,” he advises. “But certain options like bi-folds can be considerably more expensive than fixed solutions. Consider how often you’re going to use a door. There can be significant savings to be made there by having a smaller door with larger fixed glass beside it.”
People often embark on a renovation project with the aim of maximising the value of a home before putting it on the market. That can be a mistake, according to Chris Corrigan, Sherry FitzGerald associate director and Rathmines branch manager. But it is worthwhile making sure a property is in good condition.
“Across all price points, properties in good condition are selling well,” he explains. “Properties in need of refurbishment and renovation are not selling so well because of the costs involved.”
But he doesn’t advise going to massive expense. “A lot of landlords are selling this year because of new rent rules,” he notes. “Quite often, when a landlord gets vacant possession of a house some refurbishment is required. But paint is cheap and if you can do something to improve the Ber, such as attic insulation, do it. But you are not gaining value by replacing the kitchen or bathroom. Clients are being quoted €15,000 to €20,000 for a bathroom. Will you get that money back on the selling price? The answer is no.”
On the other hand, people should take into account the enjoyment value they’ll gain from the investment if they are going to live in the home in the long term. “People often say they have a five-year plan,” says Corrigan. “That goes by in the blink of an eye and the chances are you are going to be there in 10 years. In that sense, you’ll get that value out of your spend on a kitchen, but don’t expect it to add value to the house.
“If you spend €250,000 on a full-width extension at the rear of your home, it will not add €250,000 to its value but we say to clients considering an extension that they need to factor in the time they will enjoy it as part of the value it brings.”

title: Research suggests the old adage is true: Happy employees can boost profits
description: CIPD study says business strategy, employee rewards, career progression and clarity on policies seen as significant
content:
There have been a fair few stabs made down the years at testing the robustness of the old adage about a happy worker being a productive worker. New research from the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development (CIPD) on whether keeping employees chipper is good for the bottom line throws up some interesting angles.
The study, Performance by Design – carried out by Welliba for the HR professionals’ body – weighed up 24 aspects of employee experience in more than 3,000 companies across 23 sectors.
Feedback from workers at companies boasting among the most positive rates of profit growth pointed to business strategy, employee rewards, career progression and clarity on policies being seen as significant.
Less important, it suggests, interestingly enough, are factors such as diversity, autonomy and flexibility.
The sectors that fared best were ICT , biotech and healthcare , while the clothes retail sector proved to be something of an exception to the rule, with strong levels of satisfaction but not such great financial outcomes. Given the challenges from online in that area, however, that is perhaps not entirely surprising.
The authors conclude that, as HR professionals have a big part to play in shaping in employee satisfaction levels, they can indirectly help push profits. CIPD’s director in Ireland, Alison Hodgson, says the findings, which will be unveiled at the Thrive conference in Dublin on Thursday, “clearly show the importance of organisations meaningfully investing in their employees”.
“The end results go much further than culture alone; they have a measurable impact on that company’s profits.”
It would be interesting to dig into the findings more deeply, particularly the suggestion that factors such as diversity, autonomy and flexibility are not seen as being among the keys boosters of productivity and profitability. Debates on their pros and cons are topical and ongoing.
Perhaps even more prescient, though, is the methodology behind the research, with generative AI being used to gauge what employees had said in public commentary including on social media.
Those employees may well not have been aware their views were being noted. It is a lesson that employees everywhere are likely to learn before long.

title: Climate resilient homes: Striking the right balance
description: Our climate may be changing but we do not need to abandon the energy-efficiency progress of the past decade
content:
Is A-rated too much in our changing climate?
For decades, the challenge in Irish homes has been straightforward: keep the heat in. We focused on better insulation, eliminating draughts, more efficient glazing, and reducing the amount of energy required to stay warm. After the hottest summer on record, many of us now find ourselves facing the opposite problem. We’re roasting.
I renovated my small cottage in 2020 and it has been cosy every winter since. It was brought from Ber exempt to a B2 and my gas bills are low. For 11 or so months of the year, everything is hunky dory. My one critical design mistake that has pummelled me this summer was a huge west-facing bedroom window. Combined with a well-insulated room, the effect was suffocating.
Diligent researcher that I am, I went deep down the rabbit hole of cooling solutions. The best advice was not to cool down the room, but to stop the heat getting in in the first place. I closed blinds and curtains, and turned off heat-producing appliances, as my hairdryer looked on forlornly at my expanding frizz. I cracked windows after sunset. On exceptionally hot nights, I rented a portable air conditioner and ran it for an hour before bed.
I got through it, but as Ireland’s climate changes, do we need to rethink what an energy-efficient home means?
Pat Barry, architect and chief executive of the Irish Green Building Council, assured me that we should not abandon well-insulated A-rated homes. “Remember that insulation also keeps the heat out,” he says. A well-designed A-rated home should actually be more resilient against hot weather.
The problem is when other aspects of the design have not been considered carefully enough. South- and west-facing windows can admit substantial solar gain and, once the heat has passed through the glass it can get trapped. Internal blinds help, but Barry says external shading is preferable − awnings, external blinds, shutters, or planting work, although retrofitting can be costly.
Ciara Ahern of the Research Ireland Rinn Energy Centre, and a senior lecturer in building engineering at TU Dublin, also notes that sitting behind closed shutters all day is hardly appealing. Deciduous plants offer a neat compromise, advises Barry, shading in summer and allowing solar gain in winter.
Ventilation is also key. “Vents have to be designed so they can be securely left open at night, and ideally at opposite sides of the house, if the temperature is cool enough at night,” says Barry. Roof windows can create a stack effect, drawing cooler air upwards.
Barry and Ahern both identify single-aspect apartments as particularly vulnerable, because they are difficult to cross-ventilate. Barry believes current overheating guidance for houses could be better. To help, Ahern and her colleagues have developed the Dwelling Overheating Risk Metric, or Dorm, using factors including wall area and orientation to flag homes at risk. She says the team is due to demonstrate the tool to the Department of Housing.
Ahern agrees that the priority should be preventing overheating rather than mechanically cooling afterwards: “We shouldn’t need air conditioning in Ireland.” She also points to one delightfully low-tech solution that I had overlooked: ceiling fans, which are “very, very effective in terms of air movement and comfort.”
In my own home I wanted a more immediate solution, so I investigated reversible heat pumps. Paul O’Sullivan, a lecturer in sustainable energy engineering at Munster Technological University, and also a member of the Rinn Energy Network, says retrofitting cooling to an existing heat-only system “seems to be a non-runner”: the work can be expensive, with no guarantee of good performance.
Designed for cooling from the outset, however, an air-to-water heat pump can provide gentle radiant cooling through underfloor pipework and a floor slab. Radiators, common in retrofits, are less suitable and bring greater condensation risk. O’Sullivan describes the approach as supplementary cooling rather than a replacement for air conditioning, ideally run overnight with water at around 18 or 19 degrees, above the dew point, to cool the building fabric for the following day. He advises anyone buying one now to ask whether the heat pump, and the wider system, is “cooling ready”.
Heatwaves are only part of the climate resilience problem. Barry also points to the urban heat-island effect, where roads and hard surfaces absorb heat. He says French cities are removing paving and introducing planting to cool neighbourhoods. Permeable, planted surfaces also slow rainwater run-off rather than sending it rapidly into drains, helping to reduce the risk of climate-related flooding.
Storms and power cuts are changing how homeowners think about household energy too. Abhilash Borana, founder and chairman of Fáilte Solar, says homeowners increasingly consider the whole household energy ecosystem. “The moment you have a heat pump, you definitely need solar because heat pumps are very heavy on electricity.” He recommends solar paired with batteries to store surplus electricity.
Some modern backup systems can isolate a home from the grid during an outage and switch to battery power, while indicating how long the charge may last. Borana also points to bidirectional EV chargers, which can allow a car battery to supply the home. His advice is to think ahead: systems bought today should accommodate the addition of batteries, heat pumps, EVs or other products later.
Our climate may be changing, but we do not need to abandon the energy-efficiency progress of the past decade. We need to broaden the brief. A climate-resilient Irish home should allow accumulated heat to escape, keep warmth in during winter, unwanted heat out in summer, rainwater moving safely away, and essential systems functioning when weather puts pressure on the grid.
I, for one, will be starting with external shading.

title: Lofty ideas: Making the most of your attic conversion
description: Done well, a converted attic can be the most spectacular space in the home
content:
Most attic conversions are driven by a desire for a new bedroom, a children’s den or a home office. But before you get carried away with the prospect of all that new space, remember, safety first.
“It’s something that has to be considered very seriously,” says architect Georgina Hutton from Nuhaus.
“There are huge rules when it comes to attics, so the best thing for the homeowner to do is get some kind of professional advice, either from an architect or an engineer, because, all of a sudden, you are expecting your two-storey house to act as a three-storey house,” she explains.
When your house was originally built, its attic was likely not designed to be a habitable space. “The original ceiling joists would have been sized for light storage, not live loads,” says Hutton.
Far from simply laying a floor and punching in a roof light or two, there are building regulations to be adhered to, covering everything from structural specifications to insulation, ventilation, and – most importantly – fire safety.
In 2022 the Department of Housing published loft conversion guidelines, Protect Your Family – Fire Safety Guidance, available on its website, to help ensure the public has a greater understanding of the risks involved in attic conversions, which proliferated during Covid, she says.
All habitable rooms in the new storey should be provided with a window or roof light that is suitable for escape or rescue, for example.
There are also special provisions in relation to enclosing the stairs to the new storey and upgrading the protection to the existing stairway. Both the existing and the new stairs should be enclosed in 30-minute fire resisting wall construction.
If the converted space doesn’t comply with building regulations it is not deemed habitable space. “That means that if it was a three-bedroomed house, it cannot be sold as a four-bedroomed house, and people sometimes lose sight of that, which has to do with poor advice,” says Hutton.
Do it right, however, and it’s an opportunity to create what can be the most spectacular space in the home, typically with the best views, she says.
Insulation is key. In a typical attic, the living space is like a box in a triangle.
“The roof space itself outside of the new room or living space is still cold and ventilated in winter, so you want to insulate the walls and ceiling of the living space to retain the heat in there,” says Brian McIntyre from the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI), which administers government grants for insulation.
“Those rooms can also be a bit leaky because they’re made from wall and ceiling panels that all have joints between adjacent panels and they need to be butted together tightly and done properly so they don’t allow a gap for draughts to come in or heat to slip out.”
Internally, clever design can go a long way in attics. Susan McGowan, of interior architecture and design studio Ashen & Cloud, suggests that building single bed nooks under the eaves where the roof is too low to stand can be a very effective use of the space, providing guest accommodation that doesn’t eat into what might otherwise be a children’s den or home office.
When it comes to painting, keep to one colour.
“If you are going to drench the room, whether it’s a dark or a light colour, don’t differentiate the ceiling as it can sometimes feel a bit odd. Because the ceiling comes down quite far, you’ll end up with three quarters of the room in one colour and the rest in another, so it’s better to stick to all the one,” she says.
Similarly, if you are putting in dormer windows, hang the curtains from the ceiling in such a way that they wrap around the space in a u-shape. “It looks better and means that when open, they don’t take light from the room, which will do if stacked on the facing walls,” she says.
Ventilation is vital too. “Heat is a big thing in attics, especially the way things are now. If you are planning to make it an office, you need to make sure you have adequate ventilation in summer because those spaces can get really hot,” she says.
Smart Storage, best known for its understairs storage units, offers a range of bespoke storage solutions for attics too. It can provide both ideas and an estimated quote based on pictures from your phone.
“When you’re converting the attic space you generally end up with these little stubby eave walls along the edge,” says founder Paul Jacob.
“It’s about trying to get storage in spaces that are not high enough for anything else. It’s also about maximising the amount of room in the attic space. The last thing you want is to build out units into the space that you have.”
His units are built back into the eaves. “They go back into that hidden space behind and slide out to give you storage space. All of the units are built into their own boxes under the attic, so when they slide back in. They are not just in open space where spiders or dust can get in,” he says.
The company also designs built-in wardrobes for the gable ends of attics, which typically provide the only spaces where you can hang long garments.
He recommends keeping colour schemes as light as possible, including for built-in features. “With attics you’re always trying to create that feeling of a bigger space,” says Jacob. “It’s all about getting the colour scheme right so that the ceiling doesn’t feel like it’s closing in on you, and light colours will work for that.”

title: Restaurant review: Dylan McGrath’s latest offering delivers an expertly executed pizza party
description: Dylan McGrath’s latest dining proposition is simple, compelling and worthy of praise
content:
Dublin now exists in a state of pizza superabundance. Look around – the city is rife with slice-joints and lousy with pies of almost every persuasion. If you stand still or even slow to a saunter within the precincts between Dame and Stephen Streets, it will likely just occur to you unbidden. You might dodge the Detroit-style squares at Dame Lane’s Doom Slice only to run into Mani’s airy Roman rectangles. There’s a perma-line of tourists outside Bambino waiting for a New York slice.
Beyond the city limits the middle-class suburbs too are being steadily colonised. Rathmines lords Reggie’s over the rest, Ranelagh has both Rita’s and a Sano. Clontarf now has BoCo’s wood-fired specimens to sate its pizza needs. So what’s the deal?
This most democratic of dishes has been repositioned in food culture over the past decade, traversing shifts in perception and quality. Junk-food status and stuffed crusts have given way to a digital discourse around provenance, fermentation-timings and leoparding . Pizza literacy rates have never been higher.
The appeal to restaurateurs and food entrepreneurs is apparent too – there’s dough to be made in those margins.
Dylan McGrath ’s Fade St Tavern opened in early July and occupies the ground-floor space in Fade St Social on Fade Street that had been serving small plates. Electric deck-ovens are now turning out an ambitious three distinct pizza styles, one of which gives its name to the concept. The tavern style is associated with Chicago and distinguished by its thin crust and the manner in which it is served – cut into small squares. “Tavern-cutting” made the pies go further at a point when their purpose was to keep the blue-collar workers drinking. They were often “on the house” to keep you within it.
On a recent Thursday, Fade St Tavern is heaving – there’s a lot of youthful energy in the room and decibels to match. “What’s good?” is commonly used as a salutation in Chicagoland but hereabouts the answer is “pretty much everything”.
You are here for the pies but there’s a concise list of appetisers and sides to round out the menu. Deep-fried lasagne is having a moment just now and the version here, constructed with braised beef cheek, makes a persuasive argument. It is profoundly savoury and sits in a carmine pool of gently piquant and fruity San Marzano tomato sauce.
Our pizza pageant begins with a (red) tavern pie, topped with nduja, lardo and mozzarella, and finished with the sharp sheepishness of pecorino romano. The crust is crisp and light – it’s the perfect thing to take the sting out of a round of strong drinks. Those will be serious cocktails, (€13.50-€16) developed with Dave Mulligan of Bar 1661 to sit at the centre of an impressive drinks programme. There’s also a well-chosen wine list with plenty to interest, along with pét-nats and orange wines for those into that sort of thing. Bottles begin at €30 and top out at €65. The beer-inclined will find a comprehensive collection of suds and the alcohol-averse are unusually well catered for.
If you have yet to try lambrusco (the once maligned, now modish sparkling Italian red) with pizza, prepare to have the scales fall from your eyes. We enjoyed a lambrusco salamino from Emilia Reggiano (€55) that was juicy and refreshing, bursting with sour cherry.
“Grandma pies” are a style most associated with New York (and Long Island in particular), where first-generation immigrant nonnas would bake them in sheet-pans. Our white pie with artichoke and wild mushroom boasts an almost impossibly light and airy crust. It is inches thick – your brain is expecting foccacia’s stoutness and chew, only to encounter an ethereally yielding structure of bubble and crunch. It’s quite the thing.
Grandma’s remains are cleared to make way for “the Daddy”. It’s a New York style pie the size of a manhole cover, made on rye flour and with a natural levain. The pliant, nutty base showcases pepperoni, nduja and a tequila-spiked pepper and tomato sauce. This is a real showstopper.
Bring friends and get a stracciatella gelato soft-serve to finish – it’s a delight. Service is warm and casual without being careless.
Dinner for four with wine came to €188 and we exited with two takeout boxes.
Fade St Social has long seemed like a restaurant (or restaurants) in a state of perpetual flux, cycling through concepts, trying on trends. Pizza (done this well) seems to be a good fit. It’s smart to go casual. In Dublin at least, it would appear that peak pizza has yet to be crested.
The verdict: An expertly executed pizza party.
Music: Handbag house, occasional ‘bangerz’.
Food provenance: Fior di latte, Toonsbridge; potatoes, Ballymakenny; The Fresh Olive Co; Galloni Prosciutto; Italicatessen.
Vegetarian options: Multiple pizzas – marinara, pesto, cheese. Baby gem and radish salad. Fried potatoes.
Wheelchair access: The Tavern is not accessible although the outdoor terrace is. There is an accessible bathroom in the main restaurant.

title: Finishing touches: Interiors trends for winter 2026
description: Deep greens, coffee browns and terracotta, nostalgic prints, tactile fabrics and darker woods are bringing colour, pattern and personality back into homes
content:
After several years when pale neutrals seemed to have the run of the place, interiors are getting more interesting again. Beige isn’t disappearing, but it now has rather more colourful company, fabrics are becoming more decorative and there’s a growing appetite for rooms that feel collected instead of perfectly co-ordinated.
One of the biggest trends Jessica O’Mahony, accessories buyer at EZ Living Interiors, is seeing for autumn/winter 2026 is “modern heritage” or “modern heirlooms”, with nostalgic prints, heavier fabrics, texture and layering all part of the look.
“We’ve gone a lot more earthy,” she says. “Some of our best-selling colour is green, with sages, olives and moss. I’m seeing that an awful lot coming through, and the accessories are deeper coffee browns and greens.”
But that beige sofa doesn’t suddenly have to go; it can serve as a backdrop to complementary shades. O’Mahony sees the new season’s shades as an easy way to give a neutral scheme a lift. “It’s a nice option to add in a tone of brown and a tone of green into your room.”
Cushions are having considerably more fun as well. O’Mahony points to the latest Scatterbox collection at EZ Living Interiors, where William Morris-style prints and shades of green, clay and terracotta appear on heavier, brocade-style fabrics. She likes layering those colours, mixing plains with prints, and playing with different shapes and sizes rather than having everything perfectly matched.
“I think it’s being a little bit more playful and having that little bit of fun in the cushions,” she says. Throws offer another way to mix things up, with faux fur adding a tactile note alongside fabrics such as linen.
Interior designer Caroline Flannery of Interiors by Caroline has also noticed a shift away from homes that look too staged. “We’re definitely moving away from matchy-matchy, perfectly co-ordinated rooms,” she says, towards “a really nice mix of different cushions, different fabrics, different pattern, different textures, different sizes, different shapes.”
Traditional patterns and vintage-style fabrics are appearing in Flannery’s work too, along with tapestry, tassels and fringe, while handmade, inherited or collected pieces bring what she describes as the “human touch”. She is also a fan of colour drenching, carrying one shade around a room rather than stopping at a single wall.
“Colour drenching is huge,” she says. “It’s wonderful for creating character in any room.” Chocolate brown, caramel, ochre, burgundy and dusty blue are among the shades she is seeing, alongside softer oatmeal and beige.
When it comes to curtains, O’Mahony is seeing simple, full-length, floor-to-ceiling treatments, often close to the colour of the walls, allowing artwork or another decorative detail to take the spotlight. Flannery is also seeing plenty of texture at the windows, from velvet to more relaxed French linens, with tassels making a return. “They’re quite nice and relaxed and crumpled,” she says of the linens.
Elsewhere, natural materials are adding another layer, with Flannery seeing grasscloth and jute, along with richer fabrics such as velvet. Lighting is becoming more decorative too, from handblown glass to lampshades finished with tassels. Flannery describes some of the newer pieces as “almost like a piece of art”, while O’Mahony is seeing wood tones including walnut and teak making their way into accessories.
Highly polished metals, meanwhile, are losing some of their shine. Antique bronze is appearing in mirrors, hammered and patinated finishes in lighting, and O’Mahony is beginning to see hints of chrome and silver returning.
“Before, it would have all been shiny brass or shiny chrome,” she says. “Now we’re seeing a little bit more of a hammered finish or a patina finish to it. And I think that’s giving the rooms more depth.”
For a relatively quick update, O’Mahony suggests looking at the walls, where a large mirror or framed print can change the feel of a space surprisingly quickly. She singles out Tropical Twins from the EZ Living Interiors wall art collection, with its browns, blues and greens offering plenty of shades to pick up elsewhere, which “lifts the whole room very quickly”.
Rattan hasn’t had its day either, although the look is evolving. “It’s not over, it’s just changing,” says O’Mahony, who is seeing it move away from yellowish shades towards darker tones in trays and lampshades.
Stark whites are softening, familiar materials are being given a new spin and there’s far more licence to play with pattern and colour. As O’Mahony says, “We’ve definitely softened.”

title: Amid growing concern, a new app aims to curb phone use in schools
description: App restricts access to non-essential smartphone functions during school, while allowing access to vital communications
content:
Three Ireland has partnered with Blackout Education to pilot an innovative app aiming to reduce smartphone distraction in schools. The app restricts student access to non-essential smartphone functions during school hours, while maintaining access to essential communications in the event of an emergency. Longford and Westmeath Education and Training Board (LWETB) is currently participating in the pilot initiative.
“Parents, teachers and school leaders are increasingly concerned about the impact smartphone distraction can have on students’ learning, focus and wellbeing,” says Nicola Mortimer, Three Ireland chief strategy and new product officer. “At Three, our purpose is to simplify how people connect, work and live, and this pilot reflects our ambition to help power people’s everyday lives in ways that are simpler, safer and smarter. Through this partnership, we hope to support schools in creating more focused learning environments, promote student wellbeing, and contribute valuable evidence to inform future approaches to smartphone use in education.”
The technology restricts access to non-essential smartphone functions, including social media, internet browsing, gaming and smartphone cameras, while maintaining access to essential communications, Mortimer adds. “The programme aims to support students’ concentration, engagement and wellbeing throughout the school day.”
Unlike approaches that require students to surrender their devices, the pilot allows students to retain possession of their phones during school hours. While access to non-essential smartphone functions is restricted, students can continue to make and receive voice calls and send text messages for essential communications, including in emergency situations. By removing the need to collect, store and return devices throughout the day, the programme also offers schools a practical and easy-to-manage solution that supports more focused learning environments.
