“It’s an app downloaded to phone with consent of parent,” Mortimer explains. “The app uses core functionality of phone to block everything except calls, texts, maps and the wallet. It uses the phone’s operating system and doesn’t read any data or access any other apps on the phone – it just stops them from working. It’s fully GDPR-compliant. Interestingly, the camera is a key thing people want to see blocked because it can be used in ways they don’t like in a school environment.”
Technology provider Blackout Education is backed by a number of investors, including former Ireland rugby captain Johnny Sexton, who has joined the initiative as campaign ambassador. This is the first time the technology has been used in Irish schools, having already been introduced in schools in England, Scotland, New Zealand and Guernsey. The company expects to be live in four more countries by the end of the year.
Experience from other markets has been encouraging, with schools reporting positive engagement with the programme, and benefits including more focused learning environments, according to Mark Hadley, chief executive of Blackout Education.
“We are delighted to partner with Three Ireland to bring this technology to Irish schools for the first time,” he adds. “Around the world, educators and parents are looking for practical ways to reduce smartphone distraction while maintaining essential connectivity. This pilot offers a simple, effective and collaborative approach that supports students, educators and families alike. We look forward to working closely with participating schools and contributing to a meaningful evidence base around the positive impact that more focused learning environments can have on student outcomes and wellbeing.”
‘At the end of the school year, we’ll prepare a full report on the experience of the schools, students and parents. We will ask if it worked for the stakeholders; did it provide a better environment?’
The technology is simple to operate for schools, according to Mortimer. “There is very little administration to it and it is very simple for the school to use,” she says. “The school sets the times for the app and can set half-days and so on in the administration console. A student can make an in-app request to unblock their phone. They are asked for a reason, and the school is notified as soon as a phone is unblocked. Also, if a child is at home sick for the day or not in school for any other valid reason, their phone can be unblocked.”
The benefits extend beyond education, she points out. “It also enhances the social experience of school. Socialising with fellow students during lunch breaks and other free time is very important, but if your head is stuck in the phone, you are not going to get that experience.”
The pilot programme will be used to gather evidence on the technology’s effectiveness, she adds. “We want to see if it solves a problem. By January we will be able to look at a number of months of use and compile preliminary findings. At the end of the school year, we’ll prepare a full report on the experience of the schools, students and parents. We will ask if it worked for the stakeholders; did it provide a better environment? Did grades go up? We will share all the results with the schools. The plan for this is to see if it is the right solution, and we will look at how it can be rolled out nationwide depending on the results.”

title: Will I inherit my sister-in-law’s share of the family home?
description: Who inherits what depends very much on the wording of a will or the provisions of succession law
content:
My husband inherited part of his family home, along with his sister and brother. His sister has the right to live there. She has a disability and is older than them.
It is likely that she will either go into residential care or will pass away before her brothers do.
In her will, she gives money to her nieces, nephews and to a couple of charities and friends. The rest goes to her two brothers and me.
What happens to her share of the house if she moves into residential care or if she dies before me or her two brothers?
The three siblings have been left the house as “tenants in common”, the will says. This means each owns an equal one-third share, says Helen Ferguson, solicitor and partner in the private client department at Mason Hayes & Curran .
This differs from “joint ownership”, where if one of the siblings were to die, their share would automatically pass to the other two – and so forth, to one owner.
“As these siblings are tenants in common, as and when each of them dies, their one-third share passes to their estate, not to the other surviving owners,” says Ferguson.
The will says the sister has the right to live in the property for life. But this wording is a bit redundant, says Ferguson. It is probably more of an expression of the parents’ wish for how things would go, she says.
“If you own a property as a tenant in common, you have an automatic right to live there for your period of ownership anyway,” says Ferguson. “So, any one of the three of them has the right to live there, actually.
“What the will doesn’t say is that the sister has an ‘exclusive right’ to live there. That would mean she had a ‘life interest’ which would postpone the legal ownership of her brothers,” says Ferguson.
“Because it doesn’t say ‘exclusive’, the other two have an equal right to live there if they want.”
This doesn’t mean that a nephew could just move into the property, for example.
“He is not an owner. I think that would need the consent of the other co-owners,” says Ferguson.
So, what happens to the house if the sister goes into residential care? The three siblings could agree to rent it out, with any profits split in three equal shares. Or the three could agree that a family member moves in as a caretaker.
Alternatively, if the three of them agree to it, the house could be sold.
There are some important things for the siblings to consider sooner rather than later.
“If one of them was to lose their mental capacity to make decisions, then you have a problem because you have a co-owner who cannot sign a contract or take a decision,” says Ferguson.
If there are concerns about the older sister, for example, and she still has mental capacity, talk to her about enduring power of attorney, Ferguson advises.
This is a legal document set up while you have full mental capacity to choose someone you trust, called your attorney, to manage your financial, property and/or personal affairs should you ever lose the capacity to do so yourself in the future.
“If she does that, then she has appointed someone in her place to sell the property, if they all decide that is the right thing to do,” says Ferguson.
If she did lose mental capacity and money was needed to pay for her residential care, for example, but an enduring power of attorney had not been arranged, her brothers would have to apply to court for a decision-making representative to be appointed for her.
Getting an enduring power of attorney in place now will be less time-consuming and expensive.
If the sister were to die before her brothers, her one-third share goes into her estate, to be administered in accordance with her will.
“If she has enough cash to pay the legacies she has made to the nieces, nephews, friends and charities mentioned in her will, then her share of the house would form part of the residue of her estate,” says Ferguson.
This residue is the part the sister says she wants to go to her brothers and sister-in-law. But money left as a legacy in a will takes priority over anything left in the residue – legacies get paid first.
So, if she didn’t have enough cash to pay the legacies, then eventually her one-third share of the house would have to be sold to fund the legacies, says Ferguson.
“The legacies have to be paid at some stage, and the executors won’t want to wait until everyone on the property title has died.
“The executors will look for agreement from the owners to sell the property to pay the legacies, or if the brothers wanted to keep the property, then they would have to fund those legacies.”
If the sister dies, will her sister-in-law, the reader, inherit her one-third share of the property?
“If the sister specifically left her share of the house to her sister-in-law, then that would take priority over the money legacies, but if she doesn’t, then whatever cash is there would first be used to pay the legacies and expenses,” says Ferguson.
If the reader’s husband dies, leaving everything to her in his will, then the reader will inherit his one-third share of the house. If he dies without a will, then two-thirds of his estate, including the house, would go to his wife and one-third to his children.
The name of the reader who submitted the question is not being published to protect the identities of those involved.

title: New ways to invest in your home
description: From modular homes to energy upgrades, this autumn’s PTSB Ideal Home Show reflects the changing ways we are investing in our homes
content:
For homeowners in need of more space, moving house is no longer the only option. Extensions, garden rooms and modular homes are providing practical ways to adapt existing properties to changing family needs and lifestyles.
Modular homes are firmly in the spotlight in 2026, following recently announced changes to planning regulations that could make it easier for some homeowners to create additional living space on their property.
At the PTSB Ideal Home Show, RDS Simmonscourt, October 16th-18th, visitors can see modular homes and garden rooms first hand, step inside different structures and speak directly with suppliers about design, construction, installation, planning and cost.
“Modular homes are generating huge interest because people can see the potential to use the space they already have differently,” says exhibition director Caitriona O’Connor. “Homeowners have lots of questions, particularly around the new regulations and what is possible on their own property. Being able to see the options and speak directly to the companies involved is invaluable.”
The Build, Extend & Modular Homes Zone brings together builders, specialist contractors, modular home companies and suppliers for those considering renovations and extensions, while the Self-Builder Zone offers products, building solutions and specialist advice for anyone planning their own build.
At the PhoneWatch Ask an Expert Hub, visitors can avail of free one-to-one consultations covering architecture, interiors, landscaping, retrofit and energy efficiency.
The Mitsubishi Electric Ecodan Home Advice Theatre will host talks throughout the weekend on building, renovating and retrofitting, with Dermot Bannon among the experts taking to the stage.
At the Electric Ireland Superhomes Home Energy Upgrade Pavilion, homeowners can explore insulation, solar energy, heat pumps and other technologies, while finding out about SEAI grants and supports.
Visitors can also speak with the PTSB team at the PTSB Centre about financing their home plans, while the Drive Electric Zone will showcase electric vehicles and charging solutions.
The Home Interiors Fair will showcase furniture, furnishings, decor and interior design, with ideas for everything from a room refresh to a complete redesign.
At the DFS Interiors Theatre, hosted by Jo Linehan, leading names including Patricia Power, Sarah Twigg Doyle and Claire Rushton will share ideas and practical advice. The Dulux Heritage Interior Design Hub will offer individual colour consultations and advice on finishes and painting schemes.
The Kitchen & Bathroom Zone will bring together kitchen and bathroom specialists, giving homeowners the opportunity to compare designs, cabinetry, sanitary ware, fittings and finishes.
The Home Tech & Security area will feature connected security, home automation, entertainment, connectivity and energy management solutions for modern living.
The Outdoor Living & Garden area will offer ideas for making more of gardens and outdoor spaces, from landscaping and garden rooms to outdoor furniture and entertaining. Visitors can discover Peter and Jessica O’Mahony’s Søw-Sé outdoor lifestyle brand, while award-winning garden designer Diarmuid Gavin will be at the Show on Saturday, talking all things Hampton Luxury Greenhouses.
The Health & Wellbeing Pavilion will showcase the growing trend for wellness at home, with everything from saunas and hot tubs to home fitness, relaxation and recovery products. Home Accessories & Lifestyle will feature homeware, accessories and lifestyle products.
For culinary inspiration, the Dunnes Stores Chef’s Live Theatre will feature live demonstrations from Neven Maguire and Donal Skehan, alongside MC Brian McDermott and Aileen Cox Blundell. The Dunnes Stores Pavilion will showcase collections from Francis Brennan, Helen James, Carolyn Donnelly and William Costelloe.
With up to 230 exhibitors, the show offers the opportunity to explore virtually every aspect of improving a home.
Whether you’re considering a modular home, planning an extension, improving your home’s energy efficiency or simply looking for fresh ideas, the PTSB Ideal Home Show is a chance to explore the options, compare solutions and find inspiration for your next home project.
The PTSB Ideal Home Show takes place at RDS Simmonscourt from October 16th-18th, 2026. For more information and free tickets, visit idealhome.ie .

title: Go big or go clever: Whether to extend or reconfigure
description: Do you need more space or could you make better use of the space you already have?
content:
When your home stops working for you, the obvious solution can seem to be “make it bigger”. Children grow older, working patterns change, and suddenly there’s a queue for the bathroom, nowhere quiet to work, and the kitchen feels cramped.
But before you bulldoze your back garden and plonk down an extension, ask a more fundamental question: do you actually need more space, or do you need to make better use of the space you already have?
For Georgina Hutton, MRIAI, principal architect with Nuhaus, that is the crux of the conversation. She says the first question homeowners should ask themselves is what they really need. Sometimes, clients who believe they need an extension discover that they do not.
A house that worked for a family with toddlers may feel very different when those children become teenagers. The answer might be another bathroom, a study zone, better storage, or rooms that can perform more than one function.
“Sometimes people don’t realise what they need until somebody who has the expertise in making that happen can sit down and talk to them,” says Hutton. Small interventions can have a big impact. A guest bedroom, for example, might incorporate a folding desk behind pocket doors rather than requiring a separate office.
Likewise, a large house is not much use if it’s not well designed. Older homes in Ireland often contain plenty of floor space, but all in the wrong places. For years we had “the good room”, galley kitchens, and layouts designed for a different way of living. Reconfiguration can be transformative: a guest bedroom gathering dust might become a walk-in wardrobe and en suite; or one cavernous room may become two useful ones.
That’s not to say moving walls is always cheaper than building new ones. Once load-bearing walls are altered, structural beams may be required. Rewiring, moving radiators, and replacing flooring all add cost. Even a straightforward opening between two rooms can have knock-on effects for plastering, plumbing, and finishes.
“The biggest mistake that people make, in my opinion, is not seeking professional advice before they make any decisions,” says Hutton.
Her recommendation is to spend money at the outset investigating options on paper. A measured survey and an initial design sketch cost buttons compared with knocking the wrong wall. Establishing what’s possible before committing to a major build is the smart financial choice.
There is also the question of whether you can stay put during the work. For small, contained jobs that may be possible, but Hutton warns that larger remodels can make the house impractical for living due to health and safety, dust, and disruption. If you need to move out, rent should be factored into the budget.
Sometimes, of course, more space is the answer. An extension can create a larger kitchen and living area, another bedroom or additional facilities a family needs. The trick is to not treat it as an isolated box bolted on to the house; consider the overall design.
Daylight, circulation, and the impact on existing rooms should all be planned out. So too foundations, drainage, boundary walls and structural capacity. Hutton frequently encounters homeowners who want to build over an existing garage without realising its original structure may never have been designed to carry another storey.
These are the pesky discoveries that can become cripplingly expensive if they emerge halfway through construction rather than at design stage.
Planning must also be considered early. Hutton points out that a rear extension may qualify as exempted development up to an aggregate 45sq m, but exemptions come with conditions, so under 45sq m is not a free for all. Where permission is required, the standard duration is generally five years, which can make phasing useful.
Extensions don’t have to happen immediately. If your wishlist exceeds your budget, think in phases. A house can be refurbished and reconfigured now while preparing for an extension later. Structure, services, and future openings can be planned in advance such that phase two causes less disruption and does not undo the expensive work already completed.
On one Nuhaus project, the owners wanted a two-storey extension but could not initially afford the whole project. The first phase was therefore designed so the foundations, roof structure, heating system, and internal layout could accommodate the later addition.
Your choice does not necessarily have to be to renovate or extend. With good planning, you can do one now while saving for the other later.
There is another calculation to make: whether the money being spent is likely to come back when you eventually sell.
Estate agent Clare Connolly looks at the decision from the buyer’s point of view.
“If the house has been extended and it’s been signed off and is fully compliant – and the extension is stunning – that is definitely going to add to your market value,” she says. Significant additional floor area can increase value, where it adds useful accommodation.
That does not mean every euro spent will come back at resale. Connolly says homeowners should not expect the cost of upgrading a kitchen or bathroom to be returned in full. A quantity surveyor I spoke to recently estimated that the renovation work I carried out in my own home in 2020 would cost around triple today, making that calculation even harder.
Connolly does recommend smaller interventions that improve how a property presents and functions. Good staging, lighting, and storage all help. Finding room for an additional WC – under the stairs, for example – can make a noticeable difference in a standard three-bed with only one bathroom. Increasing natural light and making existing floor space feel generous also contribute to value in buyers’ eyes.
How long you intend to stay should influence the decision too. If a move is likely within a few years, Connolly would be cautious about a big structural project. A household planning to remain for 10 or more years is different: even if the investment is not recovered on sale, a better-functioning home has the value of improving your life for many years.
There is only one realistic, and deeply frustrating, answer when it comes to renovation costs: it depends. Engineer Kieran McCarthy of KMC Homes describes generic cost-per-square-metre figures as a “misnomer”: every project is different. The age and condition of the house, heating upgrades, structural work, and materials can all dramatically alter the final bill.
Steel in particular can be a big cost. If your dream design requires the removal of load-bearing walls or creating large openings, McCarthy recommends getting structural input early. An architect or a draughtsman can develop the layout, but only an engineer can establish what will be required to make it structurally possible.
McCarthy also cautions against leaving the serious cost conversation until a design is effectively finished. On his projects, designs may be adjusted and costed four or five times with QS input before the solution is settled. He works within a design-and-build model, but the same principle applies on the traditional route with an independent architect, engineer, QS, and builder: design and budget should be tested against each other early and iteratively.
Whether you renovate, reconfigure, or extend, the practical sequence is much the same. Work out what problem you are trying to solve. Get professional advice early. Check the planning and structural realities. Establish a budget that includes extras such as rent. Then test the design against that budget before you start demolishing anything.
Sometimes the answer will be more space, and sometimes it will be a better layout. Often it will be a combination of both, phased if necessary. The goal is not to make your house as big as possible, but to make the home you already have work cleverly for the life you actually live.

title: Letting your garden grow
description: Why the best thing you can do after a renovation might be to slow down and let the garden evolve
content:
There’s a particular point in a renovation when the dust finally settles, the last tradesperson leaves and you can begin to appreciate everything you have achieved. And then you look out the window.
Because while months – sometimes years – have been spent considering everything from kitchen layouts to light fittings, the garden can find itself further down the list – and so by the time attention finally turns outside, budgets have been stretched, decision fatigue has well and truly set in and there can be an understandable urge to just get it finished.
Resist it, says Damien Keane, founder of Damien Keane Garden Design.
“Don’t rush or make rash decisions,” he says. “Look at the space from the inside out and figure out what it is you want from the garden.”
Ideally, Keane believes, the garden should be considered before a renovation even begins. Potential access restrictions or a tree that needs removing, for example, can be dealt with far more easily while building work is under way, he points out. But if that ship has sailed, there is still plenty to be said for doing very little at first.
Patrick Kelly, owner and director of Outdoor Living, agrees. Rather than immediately thinking about paving, planting or furniture, he suggests starting with a much simpler question: What do you actually want to do out there?
“Is it somewhere to entertain friends, a quiet space to relax, somewhere for the family to spend time together, or do you need an additional space for working, hobbies or storage?”
Once you know the answer, the garden can be broken into areas and tackled gradually. More importantly, living with it for a while gives you a chance to discover how you naturally use the space before making expensive decisions you may later regret.
When you are ready to spend, both experts agree that the less glamorous elements deserve attention first. Levels, drainage and the main patio or decking area may not provide the instant gratification of a beautifully planted border but getting them wrong can prove considerably more expensive.
DIY and interiors content creator Paul Rogers discovered this at first hand while finishing the garden following his own home renovation. After laying a lawn twice and repeatedly battling poor drainage, he eventually admitted defeat.
“We were constantly fighting a losing battle,” he says.
Rogers spent around €3,000 installing proper drainage and replacing the grass with Himalayan White porcelain tiles, laid on a slight slope to help water drain away. It was a significant investment, but one that changed how he and his husband use the garden, “It completely transformed how we use the space,” he says. “It genuinely feels like we’ve added another room to the house.”
Kelly takes a similar view when it comes to allocating a post-renovation budget. “I’d rather see someone do one area properly and build on it over time than try to complete everything quickly with compromises that may cost more to put right later.”
Not everything requires a significant investment. If the budget needs time to recover, Keane suggests concentrating first on the area you see and use most.
A simple area of pebble outside patio doors, teamed with planters and a firepit, can create an immediately usable space while you decide what comes next. Painting fences or walls and pruning existing hedges can also make the garden feel far more considered.
Privacy is another consideration, particularly when choosing fencing and screening, but Kelly cautions against simply enclosing the garden without considering the effect on the overall space.
“Ultimately, the best screening is the one that gives you the privacy you need without making the garden feel closed in or out of place,” he says. “The best solutions become a feature with a function.”
For Rogers, paint has been one of the simplest ways to transform his own garden. He painted a newly skimmed back wall a vibrant terracotta, while fencing that went through several shades of grey eventually became black.
“I think people can be nervous about using black in a garden, but against green planting it looks incredible. It makes all the plants pop and gives everything a really clean backdrop.”
It is an approach he carries through the rest of the space, treating the garden much as he would an interior by considering colour, texture and how individual elements work together.
“For me, no garden is complete until it’s heavily planted,” says Keane, who points out that Ireland’s temperate climate gives gardeners enormous choice. The trick is choosing plants for the conditions they will actually live in, rather than simply picking what looks good at the garden centre.
Planting also provides the softness that newly paved, fenced or landscaped gardens often need, and it doesn’t have to mean spending heavily on mature specimens.
Rogers happily admits he is no gardening expert. When it came to choosing plants, he brought a more knowledgeable friend to the garden centre and asked for help. Five years later, hydrangeas bought when they were much smaller are now around four times their original size, while ferns, Fatsia japonica, Japanese maple, geums and campanula soften the porcelain and black fencing.
“My biggest advice with planting is to have patience. You don’t need to fill every gap with a huge mature plant on day one,” he says. “Let the garden grow into itself.”
It is perhaps the most reassuring advice for anyone who finds the prospect of gardening intimidating. Ask questions, choose plants that suit the space and accept that some things will work better than others. Unlike a newly renovated room, a garden isn’t supposed to look exactly the same a year after you finish it.
And autumn needn’t signal the end of the project either. Keane recommends using the coming months to plant spring-flowering bulbs, trees and evergreen hedging, prune established trees and shrubs where appropriate, tidy hedges and, crucially, make plans for next year.
Because, as Rogers discovered while his own garden evolved through different colours, planting and even two unsuccessful lawns, there is no deadline for getting it right.
“Your garden doesn’t have to be ‘finished’ in one summer,” he says.

title: Cutting the extras out of our electricity bills
description: Extra charges make up 55% of household electricity bills and more for some industries
content:
Growing complexity and multiple challenges mean regulations, policy, network charges and a raft of other costs now account for more than half of what we hand over in our electricity bills .
Research just published by Trifecta Ireland, a new think tank funded by the family of industry pioneer Eddie O’Connor, indicates that these extra charges make up 55 per cent of household electricity bills and an even greater share of some industries’ costs, leaving the electricity itself with a minority share.
Trifecta Ireland’s focus is on how the State can develop an electricity system built on three foundations: affordability, cleanliness and security. While its chief executive, Conall Bolger, cautions that there must be trade-offs between these three pillars, he maintains a fair balance between them is possible.
Irish people pay 40 cent a kilowatt-hour for electricity, almost €1,700 a year for a family living in a three-bed semi. That’s 40 per cent more than the EU average.
Figures from the Commission for the Regulation of Utilities earlier this year point to growing arrears, even before increases sparked by the US-Iran war kicked in during the summer.
So Trifecta Ireland’s first report, What Can Move the Needle on Bills Before 2030? which asks how we can cut electricity costs, is timely.
It identifies 17 measures that could help reduce bills by 2030. They include reforming the capacity market, which pays power plants to stay on standby when they are not generating electricity, redirecting the €1.4 million of renewable power lost to network bottlenecks every day to energy-poor homes, mass retrofitting of social housing, and using technology to get existing power lines to deliver more electricity.
While 17 steps seem like a lot, they have been boiled down from more than 180 measures drawn from experts, research and academia, the group says. In essence, what Trifecta Ireland recommends can be distilled to focusing more on electricity customers and getting all elements of the system to work together more efficiently.
The group stops short of saying how much these measures will save, but its report should hopefully spark action on a problem that impacts all of us.

title: Ireland is richer and spending more than 30 years ago but is it making us happy?
description: Optimism of 1996 Ireland has dissipated and outlook to 1956 not very upbeat either, consumer sentiment survey finds
content:
Anyone with even the most passing interest in music knows money can’t buy you love but new research published on Thursday makes it clear it can’t buy you peace of mind or optimism either.
Irish consumers appear to be three times richer than they were 30 years ago and are spending twice as much as they did in 1996 but they’re more nervous and gloomy now than back when the Celtic Tiger was starting to purr.
And they are far, far more miserable than in the halcyon days of 2000 when the nation’s optimism reached its zenith, a report marking 30 years of the Credit Union Consumer Sentiment Index suggests.
The September 2026 consumer sentiment index, published by the credit unions in conjunction with Core Research, shows consumer confidence at 61.1, compared with an average over the 30 years the index has been running of 83. It is less than half of its 130.9 peak recorded at the turn of the millennium.
As part of the expanded research, people were asked to reflect on what has become better or worse since 1996 and what they expected life in Ireland to look like in 2056.
The research lays bare the consequences of living in interesting times with the combined impact of wars on terror, the economic crash, Brexit, a global pandemic, an environmental catastrophe barrelling down the tracks, seemingly endless cost-of-living and housing crises, war in Europe, war in the Middle East, the terrifying march of AI and a whole lot more taking its toll on how people view the world and their place in it.
All told, 75 per cent said the cost of everyday living was worse than 30 years ago, with a similar percentage believing that buying a home was tougher.
Just over half (54 per cent) said their capacity to save money had reduced, with a similar percentage saying the nation’s mental health and wellbeing had deteriorated and 51 per cent of the view that the sense of local community has weakened.
In 1996, consumers in Ireland were experiencing a clear improvement in employment, incomes, migration and inflation following the trying times of the 1980s but today sentiment is affected by markedly higher living costs, infrastructure constraints and concerns about Ireland’s exposure to international policy changes against a backdrop of geopolitical instability and persistent economic shocks.
The research illustrates how an overall increase in wealth in the past decade has not translated into notably stronger spending or a clear “feelgood” factor on the part of Irish consumers in marked contrast to the experience of the Celtic Tiger era, something that reflects psychological as well as financial scarring caused by the crash.
Looking to the next 30 years, consumers were cautiously optimistic about some aspects of Ireland’s future, with almost half of those polled saying Ireland’s understanding of environmental issues would improve and 45 per cent suggesting people would have better education opportunities.
Expectations for overall quality of life were also slightly more positive than negative, with 35 per cent saying they were optimistic compared with 32 per cent who were more downbeat on the subject.
However, financial concerns persist with 47 per cent of those who took part in the research saying housing affordability will worsen by 2056, 46 per cent expecting the cost of living to keep rising and 37 per cent saying the financial security of households and their ability to save would probably come under even greater pressure.
“The past 30 years have seen Ireland build a hugely successful economy, but this has not automatically translated to an increase in consumer confidence,” said economist Austin Hughes. “The sentiment survey suggests that living through periods of boom and bust has made Irish consumers focus more on persistent day-to-day pressures, rather than on wealth that might not be permanent.”

title: AIB’s next-generation app offers better insights and security
description: New app forms part of bank’s broader everyday banking proposition
content:
Two million AIB customers are using the bank’s new app, with about 70 million logins to date. The improved app helps customers spend, save and plan with greater clarity, confidence and security, and supports the everyday financial choices that allow people to manage more of their banking in one place.
“Research and customer feedback showed that our customers wanted more than an updated mobile banking app,” says AIB’s managing director, retail banking, Geraldine Casey. “They wanted a banking experience that was fast, personalised and available whenever they needed it and equipped to respond to evolving security risks. To deliver this, AIB invested in a modern, even more resilient platform that builds on its established security measures while providing better insights, greater self-service options and an enhanced mobile experience, 24/7.”
While customers could complete everyday banking tasks, many wanted greater visibility, control and confidence when managing their money, she adds. “The goal was to deliver a next-generation digital banking service that helps customers make the most of their money. To support our customers to better understand their spending, take control of their finances, build confidence through saving, and achieve longer-term goals such as purchasing a home or planning for retirement.”
The new app forms part of AIB’s broader everyday banking proposition, combining digital-first tools with access to expert support in branch, by phone and online whenever customers need it, Casey explains.
Key improvements include a more personalised, easy-to-navigate experience with a clearer view of everyday banking and account activity; better insights into spending, with categorised transactions and budgeting tools; enhanced security features that build on AIB’s existing protections, including Passkey sign-in, which offers a more secure, quick and easy way to log in using your Face ID or fingerprint; faster and more seamless payments, including Zippay, Sepa Instant and standing order set-up and amendment.
Customers still have access to support where and when they need it, through branches, phone channels and in-app through the Abi digital assistant. “The new app is designed to make it easier for customers to understand and manage their money with confidence, while continuing to offer the support they value,” she adds.
“As fraud risks continue to evolve, the new app builds on AIB’s established security measures with enhanced protections designed for today’s digital banking environment,” she points out. “These include biometric authentication and greater customer control, helping customers bank with confidence while keeping access simple and convenient.”
It is also designed for accessibility. “True to our customer-centric approach to accessibility, we continued our engagement with external advocacy groups and consultancies to inform the design of the new mobile app in a way that meets customers’ needs,” says Casey.
The bank’s partnership with disability-led accessibility and inclusion consultancy Tilting the Lens spanned user experience, web and app design, and was a key focus for feedback and testing of the new app.
“A significant number of enhancements have been made based on these insights, and as part of our ongoing commitment to ensuring accessibility,” she continues. “These enhancements are aimed at meeting customer access needs and significantly improving the experience for those using assistive technologies such as screen readers.”
The new app is built on a modern, flexible platform that enables the bank to invest in and deliver further improvements more frequently. Rather than representing a one-off upgrade, it provides the foundation for the app to evolve continuously in line with customers’ changing needs, Casey explains.
“Continued investment in the platform, informed by data, customer feedback and operational learning, will allow the app to keep evolving and deliver new and improved features over time,” she adds.
Planned future features include enhanced capabilities for children and their parents to support them in managing their daily finances, with a simplified account opening experience, a card for over-12s, and mobile capabilities for children and their parents or guardians, to ensure they have ongoing oversight and control.
Also planned are savings pots and spaces, making it easier for customers to conveniently plan and save for life events, as well as functionality to allow customers to manage their mortgages.
“Our customers told us they wanted a simpler, more personalised way to manage their money. The new AIB app has been designed around those needs, giving customers greater clarity, confidence and control, with convenient access whenever they need it,” says Casey.
“Customer expectations are evolving faster than ever, and meeting those expectations requires more than continuous improvements to digital channels,” says AIB chief operating officer Graham Fagan. “We have invested in a modern digital engagement platform that transforms how AIB can serve, support and engage with customers throughout every stage of their financial lives. The new app is a significant milestone in that transformation, delivering a more personalised, intuitive and secure experience today, while providing the foundation that enables us to rapidly evolve and introduce new capabilities for customers in the years ahead.”

title: The Christmas gift he never forgot: How one shoebox inspired a lifetime of kindness
description: This year, Team Hope is inviting people across Ireland to help reach 200,000 children with 200,000 Christmas shoeboxes
content:
There are some Christmas presents we remember long after the wrapping paper has disappeared. For Adas Rakauskas, one of those gifts arrived in a shoebox.
Growing up in Lithuania, Rakauskas remembers a childhood where money was scarce and his family sometimes struggled to put food on the table.
“I remember sitting at the table as a child for a meal and there was just bread or some carrots,” he says. “At times we relied on neighbours to drop something in, so we were struggling. There wasn’t much money for food and it was pretty bleak.”
Recalling the moment he was handed the gift as an eight-year-old, he says: “I remember all of us gathered in the village and there was a play. At the end, the shoeboxes were given to the children. We were very excited. I think there were pens and pencils and some stationery in the box. What struck me most was that someone had put this together.”
It is a memory that has stayed with him for almost three decades.
Today Rakauskas lives in Drogheda, Co Louth, with his Irish wife Tracey and their three children, Elias, Izabella and Mikayla. Each Christmas the family prepares Team Hope shoeboxes for other children experiencing poverty, passing on the kindness that made such an impression on him all those years ago. Rakauskas also involved his workplace, Guidewire, where colleagues create shoeboxes and volunteer with the Appeal every year.
His story captures something at the heart of Team Hope’s Christmas Shoebox Appeal: a simple act of generosity can mean far more than we ever imagine.
Across Ireland, thousands of children, families, schools, workplaces and community groups take part in Team Hope’s Christmas Shoebox Appeal each year. Each shoebox begins with somebody choosing to pack a simple box with ordinary things such as a hat, a notebook, a toothbrush and a small toy.
But the thought behind those gifts is anything but ordinary. For the child receiving the box, it is a reminder that somebody, somewhere in the world, has thought about them.
“That kindness, travelling across oceans, reminds a child that they are not forgotten – that someone, somewhere cares,” says Team Hope chief executive Deborah Lowry.
“In a world which often highlights what is broken, the Christmas Shoebox Appeal stands as a powerful demonstration that it is also filled with kindness.”
Having now delivered more than three million shoeboxes over the history of the appeal, Team Hope is hoping to reach another 200,000 children this Christmas.
It is an ambitious target, but one built on the extraordinary generosity of communities throughout Ireland.
At FCJ Secondary School in Bunclody, Co Wexford, for example, transition year students have helped co-ordinate more than 30,000 shoeboxes over the past two decades, encouraging younger pupils and neighbouring schools to take part.
The journey of a shoebox has also inspired a beautiful animated film, Kindness Finds Its Way.
Based on a story written by Team Hope’s communications manager Rachel Browne, and brought to life by Ian Downes and Derek Doyle of production company Play Area, the animation follows a little bunny determined to send a shoebox gift to another child.
Along the way, the gift encounters obstacles, unexpected adventures and acts of kindness before finally reaching its destination. It is a charming story, but its message is very real.
Behind every shoebox is a remarkable journey involving families, volunteers, transport and overseas partners, all working together to ensure that a gift prepared in Ireland reaches a child thousands of miles away.
For Lowry, who has witnessed shoebox distributions first-hand, the most memorable moments are often the simplest. “Every box has a child at the other end of it. And when you see the excitement of a child receiving something that has been chosen especially for them, you realise that this is about so much more than the contents of a shoebox.”
While the Christmas Shoebox Appeal is Team Hope’s best-known activity, the organisation also works alongside communities through longer-term international development programmes.
In countries such as Burundi, Malawi, Rwanda, Kenya and Eswatini, Team Hope supports locally led initiatives that help families develop livelihoods, build financial resilience and create opportunities for their children.
Through Community Savings Groups, for example, members save together, access small loans and support one another in developing businesses and improving their families’ futures.
The Christmas Shoebox Appeal and the organisation’s Beyond the Box work are rooted in the belief that every child deserves dignity, opportunity and hope.
As Lowry puts it, “a Christmas shoebox is never the end of the story. It’s where hope begins.”
This year, Team Hope is inviting people across Ireland to help reach 200,000 children with 200,000 Christmas shoeboxes.
Taking part is simple: fill a shoebox with new gifts using the four Ws:
A contribution of €6 per shoebox helps Team Hope transport and deliver the gift to a child.
Shoeboxes can be dropped off at more than 400 businesses and venues nationwide, including all Mr Price stores, which are also supporting the appeal by making official Team Hope shoeboxes and all the four W’s available for less, throughout the country.
And for anyone who would prefer to participate online, Team Hope offers an online shoebox for €25, which is lovingly packed on your behalf.
Thirty years after Rakauskas received his shoebox, he still remembers the kindness he felt from afar. This Christmas, perhaps your shoebox could become somebody else’s unforgettable memory.
Visit teamhope.ie to find out more about taking part

title: When it comes to permanent fixtures, choosing what you really love matters
description: The hard-to-change choices you make during a renovation don’t need to always play it safe
content:
Renovating a home comes with hundreds of decisions, but not all decisions are created equal. A paint colour that doesn’t quite work can be changed over a weekend; a marble worktop, bathroom suite or bespoke windows are a little harder to reconsider. So when you’re investing in things designed to stay put for years, choosing what you genuinely love matters.
For interior designer Geri O’Toole of Geri Designs, one of the biggest shifts is away from the uniform, pared-back interiors that have dominated in recent years and towards homes with more character across permanent fixtures.
“There is much more interest now in character, texture and materials that feel as though they have been there for some time,” she says. “We are seeing a return to natural stone, interesting marbles, aged and antique finishes, handmade tiles and more characterful sanitary ware.”
It is a move that is particularly noticeable in kitchens and bathrooms, where homeowners are increasingly willing to make choices that might once have felt too bold for something so permanent. But bold doesn’t necessarily mean fashionable or a fad that will quickly fall out of favour. “I don’t think timeless necessarily means neutral any more,” says O’Toole. “A timeless interior can absolutely have colour, pattern and personality.”
Interior designer Aoife Maria Tobin of Aoife Maria Interiors has noticed a similar change, but says perhaps the most interesting trend is homeowners becoming less interested in recreating somebody else’s room.
“I’m getting a lot more clients asking what might originally have been in older homes,” she says. That can mean matching original coving or choosing flooring and finishes appropriate to the architecture. “It is really positive to see homeowners becoming more confident in creating spaces that feel personal to them and, importantly, right for the home itself.”
That idea of looking at the house in front of you rather than the one saved to your Pinterest board becomes even more important with windows and doors.
Flooring, natural stone, quality joinery, sanitary ware and brassware are worth prioritising precisely because replacing them later can be disruptive and expensive
Stephen Bonner, director of Vindr VS, says homeowners are increasingly considering glazing as part of the architecture rather than something chosen at the end of a renovation. Full-height windows and doors, large fixed panes and generous sliding doors remain popular, but how they work within the room matters just as much as how they look.
“Glazing determines how daylight enters a room, which views become focal points and how the house connects with its surroundings,” he says. “The aim is not necessarily to notice the window itself, but to notice the light, the view and the space it creates.”
Bonner regularly meets clients armed with images of ultra-slim, steel-style doors and threshold-free systems that may look beautiful online but aren’t always practical in the Irish climate. His advice is to invest instead in quality systems, proper thresholds and multi-point locks – the things you will appreciate long after a particular finish has fallen out of favour.
And while larger openings and striking entrances can make an impact, Bonner says they don’t have to come at the expense of longevity. “Homeowners can be ambitious with a large opening or a striking entrance while keeping the overall design simple and timeless,” he says. “The key is proportion: a beautifully positioned window with minimal visual interruption often makes more impact than a complicated design.”
For Catherine Carton, content creator and author, getting the permanent choices right meant first thinking about how she actually wanted to live in her home. Her small kitchen sat alongside a room that was rarely used, while the layout limited natural light and separated the house from a garden she loves. After years of thinking and saving, she knocked through the wall and added French doors rather than extending and sacrificing precious outdoor space.
“Sometimes we have our homes the way we think they ‘should’ be, rather than making them work for how we actually live,” she says.
The result has made the existing house feel larger, created room for family to gather and brought considerably more daylight into the space. Carton visited numerous showrooms before settling on Crittall-style French doors, one of the elements she refused to compromise on. “Now, when I look out from the kitchen, the doors almost turn the garden into a picture.”
Her approach to trends is similarly personal. Carton describes herself as “a bit rebellious” and prefers to keep the bones of her home warm, neutral and classic, bringing her love of florals, wallpaper and cottage-style interiors through elements that can be changed more easily.
It is an approach O’Toole also advocates when deciding where a renovation budget should go. Flooring, natural stone, quality joinery, sanitary ware and brassware are worth prioritising precisely because replacing them later can be disruptive and expensive. Elsewhere, there is room to compromise.
“You might invest in a beautiful marble worktop or bespoke joinery, but choose a more accessible tile or off-the-shelf basin,” she says. “A successful interior isn’t necessarily about how much you spend; it is about where you spend it.”

title: Growing popularity of solar panels driven by solid returns at a time of uncertainty
description: SEAI recorded a 76 per cent increase in grant applications in first seven months of 2026
content:
With energy costs set to remain a major household concern this winter, Irish consumers are increasingly looking for investments that deliver measurable savings.
For many of us, that means considering doing what more than 200,000 homes across the country have already done and installing solar panels.
The numbers are certainly growing. According to the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) which administers renewable energy grants, the first seven months of this year saw more than 31,000 grant applications for solar photovoltaic (PV), up 76 per cent on the same period last year.
With oil, gas and electricity prices set to rise, not least because of the Iran crisis, it’s little wonder.
Under the Government’s Micro-generation Support Scheme, homes can sell any excess electricity they produce from their solar panels back to the grid, resulting in a payment known as a clean export guarantee (CEG).
The amount you get paid depends on your energy provider, but it’s currently around 19.5 cents per kilowatt hour (kWh). That compares to a standard charge per kWh of between 36 cents and 45 cents.
On top of that, you can earn up to €400 a year from your export payments tax-free.
The SEAI provides grants for the installation of solar PV, which typically cost between €6,000 and €9,000 for an average Irish home, after the grant of up to €1,800 is deducted.
The SEAI website lets you see how much you can save by installing solar panels, and how long it will take to see a return on your investment – typically between five and eight years.
Currently, not alone are more people looking to install solar panels on their roofs than ever before, they are looking to install more panels when they do. That makes sense, says Abhilash Borana, founder of Fáilte Solar in Shannon, Co Clare.
“You have to fill the roof as much as you can, because whether you put on six or 10 or more, the labour costs are nearly the same and you’re getting the VAT free,” he says.
Solar panels come at zero per cent VAT when supplied and installed together under a single contract by a professional. That rate applies for the entire package, including ancillary kit such as inverters – which convert the electricity produced by solar panels to energy that can be used by devices – as well as controllers, wiring and batteries, and labour.
SEAI grants for batteries were withdrawn in 2022 but prices have fallen since then, making them compelling regardless. Once you have a battery, you can store up energy generated by your solar panels and use it later.
Given the difference between the cost you pay per kWh, and the amount you get under the CEG, the most economical thing you can do for your household is use as much of your own energy as possible.
It’s why Borana reckons householders shouldn’t worry too much about speculation that the CEG may be reduced, or even abolished as happened recently in the Netherlands. “You’re better off ensuring every bit you use is stored and reused at a time that you don’t want to take from the grid,” says Borana.
Ronan Power of Solar Ireland, a representative group for the industry, agrees. “My recommendation to people is to always consume as much as you possibly can onsite. Once your system is paid down, in and around the five-year mark, you’re then generating at zero cost,” says Power.
He believes the Government would be unwise to diminish the CEG in any way. If anything, he believes it should be increased, given the value it has as an inducement.
“My own father has a WhatsApp group with all his other buddies who have solar and during the summer months these men, who are all in their 70s and 80s, text to slag each other off about the fact that their system did better than the others,” he says.
Ditto with his father’s electric vehicle (EV). “On sunny days he’ll ring me up and say, ‘I’ve just got 500km for free’,” says Power.
Installing heating controls in your home, which match your heating and hot-water schedules to the way you live, is another good investment, and one for which the SEAI will provide a grant of €700. It can help you prioritise specific zones for heating, for example, rather than heating the whole house in one go.
A combination of app-based information from your energy provider, and time-of-use tariffs, also help you save money by identifying big energy users and simply changing the times you use them at.
As demand for solar grows, so too is demand for batteries. According to Alan Burns of ePower, a nationwide installer of Solar PV and EV chargers, the batteries being sought are getting bigger too. “Just 18 months ago the average size of a battery we were installing was 6kWh. Now it is 9.6 kWh, a more than 50 per cent increase,” he says.
He believes the best way to view such investments is as just that, investments, ones that won’t show a return for some time, but which, compared to leaving money in the bank, add up. It also gives homeowners more control over both costs and supply, in an uncertain energy environment.
Burns also believes it makes economic sense for people to put up as many panels as they can. “I’ve never had someone come back to me saying they wish they got less panels. But I’ve had plenty say they wish they had put up more,” he says.

title: EU innovation chief optimistic on Europe’s ability to play central role in AI
description: Simpler regulation and access to funding for growing companies are priorities for Ekaterina Zaharieva
content:
“I believe we have everything we really need to lead.”
Ekaterina Zaharieva has an optimistic view of European innovation and its potential. As European Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation, her brief is to drive the European Union ’s innovation ambitions and keep innovation at the heart of the EU’s economy.
“We have excellent research and technology infrastructures, [and] we are the biggest single market in the world with a quite wealthy Continent as well,” she says. “We are very good in advanced manufacturing, we have the best deep tech engineers in the world and we still have more AI engineers per cap[ita] compared with the United States .”
But there are challenges, not least the perception that Europe is falling behind. Various multinationals have accused the EU of hampering progress through regulation. There have been warnings that Europe risks becoming the “museum of the world” by chilling innovation.
The Draghi report, published in September 2024, was another blow, as it pointed to a competitiveness crisis facing the region, with Europe lagging behind the US and China. What was needed was sweeping change to boost innovation and competitiveness, it said.
There have been some moves to address the challenges raised by that report. Simplifying regulation, with proposals for an EU-wide regime for registering companies, known as EU Inc, that would make it easier for firms to operate in the EU, and harmonising legislation with the European Innovation Act, are part of the response.
Closer to home, Enterprise Ireland this week announced a new start-up accelerator aimed at replacing the National Digital Research Centre (NDRC) programme that was given a stay of execution last year. The new Startup Ireland programme will include accelerators aimed at early stage companies, AI and founders, along with the establishment of a start-up hub for early stage companies.
The Guinness Enterprise Centre, meanwhile, is targeting growth for Irish start-ups and scale-ups in the UK through a series of partnerships with innovation hubs there. The idea is that small enterprises will have easy access to local networks, workspace, universities and market-entry support as they build their businesses.
[ Mark Zuckerberg says Meta has reached AI ‘frontier’ Opens in new window ]
Europe has a good track record of supporting innovation with funding in the past, helping to finance deep tech start-ups through the Horizon Europe programme. The successor to Horizon 2020, the flagship research and innovation funding programme from the European Commission, is due to run until 2027. Its €95.5 billion budget to fund grants for research and innovation projects makes it the largest transnational research funding programme in the world.
Aside from funding collaboration between universities, research institutes, companies and public bodies across multiple countries, it also funds individual researchers, start-ups and SMEs.
Ireland has done well from the Horizon Europe programme. Last September, the State officially passed the €1 billion mark in funding receiving by projects here, with the target of €1.5 billion – 1.6 per cent of the programme’s €95.5 billion budget – in its sights. The amount awarded to Irish researchers and innovators by September was more than 2 per cent of the overall funding allocated; not a bad metric for a small state.
“Ireland is a strong innovator and you have really a really good performance in Horizon Europe, which is a very competitive programme,” Zaharieva says.
But one area where innovation is suffering is in access to capital. The commissioner points to a recommendation that Ireland increase investment in research and innovation, and also improve the range of finance sources open to growing companies.
[ Will Dublin-headquartered Accenture survive or thrive in the age of AI? Opens in new window ]
It is not just an Irish problem. While there are plenty of supports for early-stage companies at seed capital level, access to growth capital within Europe continues to be an issue.
“We are still fragmented, especially when you talk about capital, for example. We still don’t have a capital market union,” she says. “There are many, many innovative companies [that] were created in Europe”, but when companies have to grow and become global, they are often turning to investors outside the EU.
Zaharieva wants companies to have a choice when it comes to capital.
“It’s really important to find the needed capital in Europe,” she says. “It doesn’t mean I’m against capital outside the European Union. But they should have a choice.”
Public money will never be sufficient to adequately fund innovation to the level needed long-term, she acknowledges, whether it is in Ireland or the EU as a whole. “We have to engage with private capital as well as private big companies and foundations.”
With that in mind, the European Commission has created the Scaleup Europe Fund, a €5 billion late-stage growth fund to support deep tech companies.
Created under the European Innovation Council Fund, it is a public-private partnership, with a €1 billion commitment from Horizon Europe and €4 billion from the private sector. Among the investors are pension funds, insurance companies, sovereign funds – institutional investors giving their backing to the fund.
“The goal of this fund is to help [European] companies become global from Europe,” she says. “The second goal is to show this is good, that it is profitable, to give signals to the market and hopefully to more and more private investors who may start to invest in venture capital. That is something that we really need.”
Another aspect that has come to the fore in recent months has been the issue of tech sovereignty. With Europe dependent on the US for some essential tech services – cloud services, financial technology – the move could help European companies to catch up.
But it is not the only move we should make in Europe, Zaharieva says. Procuring from European companies and innovators should be on the agenda, for both the public and private sector.
“The public sector should lead by example, and we should start procuring innovation in general much more in Europe,” she says.
The European Innovation Act may help here, harmonising legislation and making it more user friendly for public procurement.
She acknowledges the difficulties, though.
[ Anthropic warns rogue AI agents may soon hijack your smart TV or oven Opens in new window ]
“The big American companies have a track record. You are taking a chance on a newer company, or it might be that they can have huge economies of scale and can offer things cheaper. That is often a huge thing for the public sector in particular, the perception sometimes that big companies sell cheaper. But it’s not always the case.”
Smaller companies and those that are newly established may also find the procurement process more complex, something the European Innovation Act is hoping to address, making it easier for European businesses to grow in the single market.
Looking ahead, the plan is to increase the budget for Horizon Europe, ideally doubling it, creating a pool of funding for deep tech. The plan is also to continue to develop European AI, with investment in AI factories and gigafactories – public-private supercomputing infrastructures that can handle the life cycle of frontier AI models – a key component.
The EU is investing in an ecosystem of 19 AI factories that will offer subsidised or free computing power for European start-ups and SMEs.
“A lot of commitment coming from national governments, the commission and the private sector for infrastructure is so key,” she says.
“We talk about AI but without compute power and affordable compute power for our innovative companies, they’re not going to develop their models. They’re not going to train their models. So this investment from the European Commission, together with the member states, first in factories and now in gigafactories, is something that is also very positive.”
That will help boost digital sovereignty, an issue that has been increasingly on the agenda in recent times as geopolitical tensions show.
The change in the US administration may have focused attention on the topic, but Zaharieva points out the debate did not start with the most recent change in the White House. It has been ongoing for some time.
“Europe has started to realise more and more that it’s not good to depend on only one source of supply,” she says, pointing to gas and oil, and basic items that were lacking during the Covid-19 pandemic – masks, ventilators and so on.
[ Subscriber Only Your Money Ireland’s new investment scheme: What will I make if I put €20, €200 or €500 in a month? Opens in new window ]
With the increasing importance of AI, the debate has now shifted to AI sovereignty and the importance of developing it for Europe in Europe. But the drive to make things simpler for European businesses does not mean the push for regulation in this area will be relaxed.
The challenge posed by AI is becoming increasingly evident, both in Ireland and abroad.
The International Monetary Fund this week warned it was one of three risks to the financial markets, with a “reassessment” of efficiency gains and financial benefits expected from the technology potentially triggering a big correction in equity markets.
The incidences of “rogue” AI agents have also caused understandable concern, with calls for stricter rules and regulations overseeing the technology to prevent real harm from being inflicted on society. But, Zaharieva says, regulation should be smart and easy to implement.
“Some of the models are really very powerful. They can be a threat even without the intention to be a threat,” she says.
“It’s not going to disappear. I believe that if AI is developed as we believe in Europe – it’s trustworthy, it’s human-centric, safe – it will help the citizens and the private sector of Europe.”

title: Design essentials for the hardest-working room in the house
description: Good kitchen design starts with making the space you have work for the way you actually live
content:
The kitchen has always been a busy place, but the way we use it has changed. Cooking and eating are still central, of course, but for many households it is also where homework gets done, laptops come out, friends gather and much of family life takes place.
That does not mean it has to be enormous. A compact kitchen can work just as hard as a large open-plan space if it is planned well, and making the most of the room you have is more useful than trying to squeeze in every item on a wish list.
For David Dempsey, a kitchen designer and specialist with Rathnew-based House Kitchens, the starting point is finding out how the people who will use the kitchen actually live.
“You have to get an understanding of the number of people in the household,” he says. “Do they have specific requirements for that kitchen? It’s not just the parents that actually maybe want to make the decision, but they’re considering the rest of the family and how they use it.”
One of House Kitchen’s recent projects involved a family with a nine-year-old girl who was keen on baking and the family wanted a cupboard where her mixer, baking trays and ovenproof dishes could all live together. It is a simple idea, but one tailored to what happens in that particular home rather than to a standard picture of how a kitchen should be used.
Storage is inevitably part of the conversation. Dempsey is seeing more concealed pantry units, coffee docks and even small desk areas that are out of sight when they are not in use. “Everything opens up and reveals the storage behind it, but then when you’re not using it, it just closes away and everything’s hidden,” he explains.
When floor space is tight, looking upwards can help. Dempsey suggests reserving the easiest-to-reach cupboards and drawers for items used regularly, while party platters, Christmas dishes and other occasional items can go higher up. “The big party platters that you might use once a year, you’re putting them up in a high unit as opposed to taking up a drawer that opens every day,” he says.
The popular and covetable island remains high on many wish lists, but it is not necessarily right for every room. Dempsey recommends leaving around a metre to 1.2m of circulation space around one. If that leaves only a small island in the middle, he says, it may not be worth having. Where there is sufficient room, though, an island can add worktop space and give people somewhere to sit while somebody else dons the apron. “It is a nice place, a more social place to kind of sit at,” he says. “You can cook and you can be chatting away to people while you’re in the middle of prepping food.”
Open-plan living has brought its own practical questions. Dempsey points out that having the kitchen, dining area and television in one room does not suit every family, particularly when several people are trying to do varying things at the same time. Where an open-plan layout does work, furniture and lighting can help to give each part of the room its own purpose. Pendant lights can mark out an island or dining table, while the position of a sofa or sideboard can help define the living area without putting up a wall.
Noise is easy to forget on a floor plan. In a room where the dishwasher may be running a few metres from the television or dining table, quieter appliances can make a noticeable difference. Dempsey says he is seeing people pay more attention to dishwasher decibel levels for that reason.
The surfaces chosen also have to stand up to ordinary life. The kitchen designer says porcelain worktops are popular for their durability and resistance to heat, scratches and stains, although he notes that edges can be more prone to chipping than quartz. Quartz remains, in his view, a good middle ground, while among natural stones he favours quartzite over marble where durability is a priority.
Technology can be genuinely useful, but only if people actually use it. Wifi-enabled ovens can be controlled remotely, allowing an oven to be stopped or paused if plans change. Dempsey has one at home and finds the function handy, although he acknowledges that many people never get around to using everything their appliances can do. Boiling-water taps and induction hobs with integrated extraction are among the other features he is seeing regularly. The attraction is practical: one removes the wait for a kettle, while the other can make it possible to position a hob on an island without an overhead extractor.
For households with the room, a pantry or “back kitchen” can take some of the pressure off the main kitchen, with food, fridges, freezers or some preparation moved into a separate space. Dempsey is clear that this depends on having the space in the first place. The broader idea, however, works in kitchens of any size: keep what you use most where you need it and find sensible homes for everything else.
When deciding where to spend, Dempsey advises paying attention to the less eye-catching parts of the kitchen as well as worktops and appliances. “The quality of the cabinetry, the hinges, the drawer systems, they determine the life of your kitchen,” he says. Strong cabinetry can also make it easier to refresh a painted kitchen later without starting again from scratch.
It is worth thinking a few years ahead too. When designing for older homeowners, Dempsey considers the height of frequently used cupboards and appliances, keeping everyday items accessible and ovens at a comfortable level so hot dishes do not have to be lifted from too high or too low.
For all the finishes, appliances and decisions involved, the most useful starting questions are fairly ordinary ones. Who uses the kitchen? What do they do there? What needs to be close at hand, and what can be tucked away? Is there room to move comfortably once the doors and drawers are open? And, however much you may want one, is there really space for that island?
A kitchen that answers those questions well is already doing much of what it needs to do. The details will be different from home to home, and that’s why the best place to start is with the people who live there.

title: Got a smart meter? Time to unlock its value with an ESB Networks online account
description: Having an account turns your data into insights you can act on, offering ways to save money
content:
If you want to save money, make smarter energy decisions, and cut your household’s carbon footprint, chances are the key to doing all of this is already sitting in your home.
That’s because, over the past six years, ESB Networks has installed more than two million smart meters in homes, farms and businesses across Ireland.
“Every household wants to keep its energy bills under control, and a smart meter is one of the most practical tools available to help do that,” says Pat Eccles, ESB Networks’ senior manager of distribution markets and system operation.
But simply having a smart meter isn’t enough, he points out. To unlock its value, you also need to set up an ESB Networks online account.
Setting up an account couldn’t be easier. It takes just a couple of clicks to deliver real gains in terms of lower bills, personalised tariff decisions with your supplier and a lower carbon footprint. Simply by accessing your smart meter data through your account, you can start to find the best energy tariff for you.
You can even upload your smart meter data into independent price comparison sites such as Bonkers.ie, Switcher.ie, PowertoSwitch.ie or EnergySwitch.ie, all of which are approved by the Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU), to help you pick the best supplier and best value price-plan for your household.
In addition, sites such as EnergyPal.ie, Kilowatt.ie and Elec-tariffs.ie can analyse your smart meter usage file to find you the best-value tariff for your home. In some cases, you can even make the switch on the comparison site, making life even easier.
Having an account turns your data into insights you can act on, whether that means swapping suppliers, changing tariffs, or simply improving your energy usage behaviour. All offer ways to save you money.
Think of your online account as a window to your electricity use, allowing you to see exactly what you are consuming, when you are consuming it, and where easy savings can be made.
You only have to register for an online account once to view or download all your detailed usage data, regardless of who your electricity supplier is.
‘With a smart meter, customers can take more control of their electricity usage’
Doing it pays dividends in two ways. First, you get help to make personalised tariff decisions. Your account shows your half-hourly usage data, precisely the information that price comparison sites need to help you find the cheapest option for you.
It’s an individualised recommendation tailored for your home, rather than based on the national average household.
What’s more, if yours is one of the more than 200,000 homes and businesses that generates its own solar electricity, typically from rooftop panels, your account includes data on the surplus electricity you export to the national grid.
And not only does signing up take just minutes, at myaccount.esbnetworks.ie , but you’re also helping to move the dial on Ireland’s climate targets.
Since ESB Networks began its National Smart Metering Programme in 2019, working alongside the CRU; the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment; the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland and every electricity supplier in Ireland, the numbers have added up fast.
These form the backbone of Ireland’s digitally enabled network, one that can absorb far more renewable energy and which supports the electrification of transport and heating.
“We are really proud of the progress of the National Smart Metering Programme and reaching the milestone of over two million smart meters installed,” says Eccles. “With a smart meter, customers can take more control of their electricity usage, and we are increasingly seeing this happen thanks to the roll-out of the programme. This is a vital component of ESB Networks’ Networks for Net Zero strategy, enabling a smarter, low-carbon electricity network that will ultimately benefit all customers and help deliver national climate targets.”
With the National Smart Metering Programme nearing completion, households and businesses in every county can see exactly how and when they use electricity. “That gives customers what they need to compare smart tariffs with confidence and choose the one that suits them, so they can get better value,” says Eccles.
“By checking their usage data, customers can see which smart tariff matches the way they actually live. I would encourage everyone to take a few minutes to look at their data and make sure they are on the best-value option for them,” adds Eccles.
Registering for an account is helping to fuel Ireland’s energy transition. “Completing the smart metering programme is a major step in building a cleaner, more flexible electricity system for Ireland,” he says. “As more renewable power joins the grid, smart meter data will help customers shift their use to cheaper, greener times of day. The result is lower bills for them and a lower-carbon future for everyone.”

title: ‘I don’t feel like myself any more’: Why Irish women are missing the signs of menopause
description: Brain fog, broken sleep and a loss of identity: perimenopause and menopause can affect women’s mental health in many ways, meaning it’s time to learn more about the signs and how to manage them
content:
Menopause may have finally entered the chat, but it appears that many women may be failing to connect the dots between the signs and this natural stage of life. Despite more information on menopause being available than ever before, cutting through the noise can pose a challenge of its own.
A recent survey* commissioned by women’s intimate health brand CanesMeno found that 92 per cent of women affected by perimenopause or menopause experience symptoms, with hot flushes, lack of energy and difficulty sleeping each affecting over half. Yet only 39 per cent say enough trusted resources exist, and just one in 10 say their workplace is genuinely supportive. The gap is not in what women know, but in the support they get.
To help bridge this support gap, CanesMeno developed the CanesMeno Hub, a free-to-access comprehensive digital service offering accurate information, expert guidance and a helpful symptom tracker.
Dr Louise Fitzgerald is a GP with a special interest in menopause, leading menopause services in several clinics around Dublin. She agrees that while the enhanced dialogue on menopause is heartening, many women that she sees in her practice report feeling blindsided by the onset of factors including brain fog, insomnia, anxiety and exhaustion.
