“What I often hear from women in a menopause clinic is, ‘I don’t feel like I’m myself anymore’, and that’s really upsetting,” Fitzgerald says. “But if we understand what is going on with our bodies, we recognise the signs, and we have the knowledge to support ourselves through that, it’ll be a much more positive experience.
“As women, we have oestrogen receptors from the top of our head all the way down to our toes, and oestrogen is the primary hormone that causes problems in the menopause, so that’s why people report things like dry hair, or hair loss, dry eyes, itchy ears, metallic taste in their mouth, frozen shoulders, joint aches and pains, as well as the symptoms that we’re really familiar with of hot flushes and sweats,” Fitzgerald explains.
Fitzgerald is keen to emphasise that menopausal symptoms are due to real hormonal changes. Oestrogen levels plummet, in turn prompting a cascade of effects, from hot flushes to itchy ears, as well as vaginal atrophy, a thinning and drying of the vaginal wall. Vaginal dryness is common and can affect up to one in three women as falling oestrogen levels reduce the body’s natural vaginal lubrication.
Over the counter products can help; CanesMeno has formulated its vaginal Hydration & Comfort Gel to help provide fast and long-lasting relief for up to five days from vaginal atrophy symptoms associated with menopause such as dryness, itching and burning. It can be used alongside systemic HRT. CanesMeno Hydration & Comfort Gel is made from 100 per cent natural ingredients and is available from pharmacies nationwide.
Another important physical sign can be weight change, and more specifically weight gain. Again, this is not imagined; Fitzgerald says the average weight gain in perimenopause and menopause is 1.5kg per year. “This is phenomenal, and unfortunately, it tends to deposit around our midriff, so we hear people talking about the ‘meno belly’.”
These hormonal fluctuations may also cause emotional and cognitive changes. Fitzgerald says that while these may often be the first signs that women experience, it can be difficult to link them directly to the menopausal transition given the often-hectic reality of everyday life.
“Brain fog and verbal recalls were actually one of the first symptoms a lot of women will experience in perimenopause, so possibly even around 40, 41, 42, people might find they go to the supermarket and they can’t remember what they were there for, and that’s confusing,” she says. “Is it that you’re not getting sleep because you’re taking care of elderly relatives or children or is it that you are at the peak of your career and you’re really busy, so that’s what’s impacting these cognitive changes?”
Sleep, or lack thereof, can underpin these cognitive symptoms but Fitzgerald says “huge disruptions” in sleep are themselves common during perimenopause and menopause.
“Some women find it difficult to get to sleep, or other women find they’re waking up overnight and are awake for hours and then can’t get back to sleep, which obviously is very disruptive when you’re trying to work and take care of other people.”
Tracking periods around this time is also crucial, she adds. “Periods change as you come up to the menopause and your periods stopping. And I think we actually don’t expect that. We assume our periods will just keep going the way they are and suddenly stop.” The reality is that some women will experience more frequent or much heavier periods, or both.
Fitzgerald also explains that a woman will only be said to have gone through the menopause when she has had no periods for 12 consecutive months. “Once the periods have stopped, oestrogen drops down to a very low level. So we can still have menopausal signs at this stage related to that very low level of hormones, but the good news is our body will get used to this and those signs will eventually disappear.”
It’s no wonder that joining the dots can be difficult when the picture is as complex and multifactorial as this; Fitzgerald urges women to keep a “menopause diary”, to track the patterns.
“I say to people, track your signs. How severe they might be exactly, and when are they happening - is it cyclical? Is it coming in times of your period? Or is it something that’s there all the time?”
The CanesMeno personalised menopause tracker will do this for you, Fitzgerald adds.
“You input your signs into this tracker and then it gives you free, private, and personalised insights,” she explains, adding that it’s one of her favourite resources.
“It’s not a replacement for your GP and I still say to people, try and have a trusted GP that you can get information from and share your signs with and feel comfortable with. But it’s always important for us to have other resources that we can dip into on our own time.”
CanesMeno’s menopause hub also hosts a comprehensive library of articles that answer many commonly asked questions about menopause, as well as an information video. The hub complements a range of scientifically formulated products launched under CanesMeno including food supplements and a vaginal dryness gel available from pharmacies only nationwide in Ireland.
“This is a fantastic free hub that is there to support, educate, and empower women through the menopause,” Fitzgerald says.
When it comes to the menopause, the overarching problem, the GP believes, is a knowledge gap. The good news is that gaining knowledge can have a transformative effect.
“What I find really powerful is that when you help someone through the menopause transition, whether it’s self-management strategies or combination approaches, they come back to you and say, ‘I feel like myself again’. And that’s really, really moving.”
* Research conducted by Empathy Research on behalf of Canesten, August 2025.
CanesMeno® products are available in pharmacies nationwide and the CanesMeno® Hub is completely free to access.
CanesMeno ® Hydration and Comfort Gel is a medical device. The CanesMeno® Hub provides education on menopause, it is not intended to be a substitute for advice from a doctor and it is not a diagnostic tool

title: Event guide: Cork Jazz Festival, Manic Street Preachers and the other best things to see in Ireland in the week ahead
description: October 17th-23rd highlights: Our pick of music, art, theatre and more coming your way
content:
Sift out the pop/rock acts and there’s a very solid core to this year’s Guinness Cork Jazz Festival. Highlights include The Music of John Coltrane and Miles Davis, with Keyon Harrold and Marcus Strickland (Thursday, October 22nd, Everyman, 7.30pm, €46.50), Jason Moran (Friday, October 23rd, Triskel Arts Centre, 8.15pm, €39.50), Kokoroko (Sunday, October 25th, Everyman, 10.30pm, sold out) and Trygve Seim and Tord Gustavsen (Sunday, October 25th, Triskel Arts Centre, 6.15pm, sold out). Dance-floor pleasers include the double bill of Annie Mac and Tara Kumar (Friday, October 23rd, Cork Opera House, 11.30pm, €32.50). And kudos to the festival for including a decent Irish line-up across the weekend, including The Boomtown Rats, The Stunning and the emerging artists Tolü Makay, Zaska, 49th & Main, Ezra Williams, Winnie Ama and Muireann Bradley.
Husband and wife Kieran McGuinness and Emily Aylmer arrange babysitters so they can play gigs to support their very fine second album, Mother of Christ. Driven Snow’s gentle pop songs are so “perfectly structured, deft and, in their way, wise that calm immediately arrives”, as we noted in our review. So leave your worries behind as you enter the venue. The duo will also perform songs from their sublime 2024 debut, A Kind of Dreaming. Also, Thursday, December 3rd, Sugar Club, Dublin.
Simplicity is at the core of the music of Paahto & the Bull, the stage name of the traditional musicians Patrick Cummins and John Francis Flynn. Long-time friends and former bandmates in Skipper’s Alley, Cummins and Flynn teamed up during the pandemic to experiment with a no-vocals/acoustic guitars set-up. The result is one of the year’s best Irish albums, The 123, plus a series of shows in cosy venues. Also, Saturday, October 24th, Pot Duggans, Ennistymon, Co Clare, 8pm, €17, potduggans.com ; Sunday, October 25th, Connolly’s of Leap, Co Cork, 8pm, €21.50, connollysofleap.com ; Monday, October 26th, Prims Bookshop, Kinsale, Co Cork, 7.30pm, €20, eventbrite.ie
Every road comes to an end, and so it is for the veteran English singer-songwriter Ralph McTell, who embarks on his final tour of Ireland. He will return for one-off concerts, but these shows are an opportunity to experience the man’s storytelling skills up close. The tour concludes on Sunday, November 8th, at the Town Hall Theatre, in Galway.
For a band that promised to split up after the release of their 1992 debut album, Generation Terrorists, Manic Street Preachers are showing no signs of flagging. The Welsh musicians – James Dean Bradfield, Nicky Wire and Sean Moore; original member Richie Edwards disappeared in 1995 and was declared dead in absentia in 2008 – aren’t plugging a new album, so expect a best-of set featuring classics such as Motorcycle Emptiness, A Design for Life, If You Tolerate This Your Children Will Be Next, Your Love Alone Is Not Enough and Autumnsong.
For more than 20 years Shane Mitchell and Rory O’Connor, its founders, have positioned Sligo Live as a festival that highlights the county’s artistic heritage. Music highlights include the Americana performer Stephen Wilson jnr (Saturday, October 17th, Knocknarea Arena, 7pm, €45/€38, sold out), roots royalty Rosanne Cash (Sunday, October 25th, Knocknarea Arena, 7pm, €52) and up-and-coming Irish trad/psych group The Wran (Saturday, October 24th, Hawk’s Well Theatre, 7pm, €28). Comedy highlights include two of Ireland’s best exponents of the art: Kyla Cobbler (Sunday, October 18th, Knocknarea Arena, 7pm, €31.80, sold out) and Dara Ó Briain (Friday, October 23rd, Knocknarea Arena, 7pm, €42, sold out).
It’s elegant, it’s swellegant, and if you have any inclination for some of Cole Porter’s best songs, including Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? True Love and Well, Did You Evah!, then this musical comedy is a must-see. The production adapts Porter’s score for the 1956 film of the same name (itself based on the stage comedy The Philadelphia Story), telling the story of entitled jet-setter Tracy Lord and how best-laid plans for her wedding fall apart. Helen George, Freddie Fox and Nigel Lindsay feature.
Based on the journalist Nicola Tallant’s bestselling book, The Witness tells the remarkable true story of Joe “the Lips” O’Callaghan, the youngest person ever to be placed in witness protection in Ireland. Rex Ryan features, writes and directs. Following this brief run, the production opens at 3Olympia Theatre, Dublin, from February 14th.

title: Putting Stephen Hawking’s life under a microscope has a demystifying effect
description: While the author clearly admires his subject, this is no hagiography
content:
Dara Ó Briain was among the many high achievers who felt deeply inadequate in the presence of Prof Stephen Hawking. “It’s very difficult not to talk like an idiot in front of you,” the Bray comedian (and UCD maths graduate) admitted when making a BBC documentary about his childhood hero in 2015. After several meetings with this “impish, geeky, flirty, curious, stubborn” character, however, Ó Briain declared “the greatest achievement he has is his humanity”.
Graham Farmelo’s suitably heavyweight authorised biography reaches a similar conclusion. Few of us completely understand Hawking’s groundbreaking discoveries about general relativity and quantum mechanics, but everyone knows he communicated them through an American-accented synthesiser while confined to a wheelchair by motor neuron disease. Given just two years to live at 21, he clocked up another 55 that included appearing in Star Trek, performing The Galaxy Song with Monty Python and boasting, “I’ve sold more books on physics than Madonna has on sex”.
As well as being granted access to Hawking’s family archives, Farmelo has carried out wide-ranging interviews with his friends and colleagues. This allows him to construct a warm, intimate, slightly plodding narrative full of revealing domestic details. His research extends to how much Hawking’s “misfit” parents paid for their first London house (£1,100 in 1943), what curry he most enjoyed (chicken jalfrezi) and which Beatles album made him dance (A Hard Day’s Night).
While Farmelo clearly admires his subject and calls him “Stephen” throughout, this is no hagiography. He cites many examples of the scientific genius displaying “annoyingly haughty” behaviour, humiliating his stoical first wife Jane and stealing ideas from fellow researchers. “I do wish [Stephen’s two sisters] could have some good fortune as well,” his mother once wrote. “They really are much nicer people!”
Eddie Redmayne played Hawking in the 2014 biopic The Theory of Everything and recalled his verdict as: “There should have been more physics, fewer feelings.” Happily, Farmelo’s book has plenty of both. Tactful accounts of Hawking’s two messy divorces are interspersed with rather more user-friendly guides to our expanding universe than can be found in his widely bought but little-read A Brief History of Time.
Like Hawking’s beloved black holes, putting his life under such a powerful microscope inevitably has a demystifying effect. This sensitive but by no means starry-eyed portrait still leaves his towering reputation largely intact.

title: How an academic turned a €200,000 problem into an online marketplace
description: Aishling Flaherty has built Caboodle, an online marketplace bringing small Irish retailers together
content:
Aishling Flaherty has always believed in buying local and trying to support Irish-owned businesses through their e-commerce sites. What she found frustrating, however, was having to shop across multiple sites for what she wanted instead of being able to buy from a range of different Irish retailers in one place.
Having looked and found nothing that approximated the kind of marketplace she thought was needed, Flaherty took matters into her own hands. In 2021, she began working on what has since become Caboodle, an e-commerce platform designed to make it easier and more affordable for consumers to shop directly from small Irish businesses.
“Caboodle’s technology is not about creating yet another online shop. It’s designed to solve a bigger problem,” Flaherty says. “It gives dozens of independent businesses some of the shared infrastructure, convenience and economies of scale enjoyed by much larger e-commerce players without taking away their independence.”
Flaherty is a scientist by background who works in academia, but she’d always had an interest in starting a business. That said, she wanted it to be a “passion project”, and building a platform that offered shopping convenience while also supporting Irish SMEs ticked the boxes.
What stood between Flaherty and making her idea happen was money. A platform on the scale she envisaged was going to cost in the region of €200,000 to develop.
One option was to put her idea out there and look for investors, but that didn’t sit well. Instead, she decided to take the much slower, bootstrapped route that involved teaching herself how to build an e-commerce marketplace from scratch.
“I wanted to understand the technology, so I started small, working on building a site using WordPress,” she says. “I gradually learned all about APIs (application programming interfaces), databases, e-commerce integrations, payments, product synchronisation and order routing. What began as learning to tweak eventually became learning how to build an entirely standalone marketplace, and there is now a significant technology platform operating behind the scenes.
The businesses, founders and stories behind the products remain central to the platform
“This learning process took several years, and Caboodle was only officially launched in January this year, but it means the platform has been developed from the ground up to do exactly what I wanted it to do. Global marketplaces have made discovery, checkout and delivery incredibly simple, and I wanted to replicate this for Irish retailers.
“However, unlike the very large international marketplaces, the intention is not for the individual business to disappear behind the marketplace. The businesses, founders and stories behind the products remain central to the platform.”
All of the product information displayed on Caboodle is linked to a retailer’s existing online presence, which means small businesses joining Caboodle don’t need to have a separate catalogue or e-commerce system. Caboodle acts as an additional sales channel. It doesn’t replace a retailer’s existing e-commerce infrastructure.
Caboodle has two sets of “customers”: retailers looking for another way to reach buyers and consumers who want a convenient way to buy local. The platform now hosts in excess of 2,500 products from over 60 small Irish businesses.
The company is making its money in three ways: by taking a commission on sales, by offering businesses the option of having their products promoted on the site for a monthly fee, and through its consumer membership model, which costs €12 a year and unlocks lower prices and free delivery. Over 1,000 members are now active on the site.
The platform is making money and having spent a huge amount of time building Caboodle, Flaherty is in no rush to secure outside investment. However, this may change when she starts looking at applying the Caboodle model in other markets, which is the long-term plan.
In terms of hard cash, she estimates investment to date at around €70,000 between personal funding, new business idea prize money, and State support.
“One of Caboodle’s most distinctive features is its multi-business checkout,” Flaherty says. “A customer can put products from several small Irish businesses into one Caboodle basket, complete a single checkout and pay no delivery fees. Caboodle separates and routes each part of the order to the relevant business.
“For the partner there is very little, if any, additional administration. The Caboodle order appears inside their existing online store in much the same way as an order placed through their own website, allowing them to process and fulfil it through normal workflows, with the payments automated through Stripe .”
A big issue for small businesses selling online is the cost of delivery, and Flaherty has done a deal with An Post that allows her supply partners to send orders at a preferential rate. “We are using Caboodle’s collective purchasing power to make logistics more economical for smaller businesses, and An Post has been very supportive,” she says.
It would be very easy to chase growth too quickly, but I have tried to build Caboodle slowly and credibly
Flaherty combines all of this with her full-time academic job and caring for two small children, so she deliberately structured the platform to require the minimum amount of daily input. “This is another reason it took so long,” she says. ”Any manual type of system was going to take constant updates and it would never scale to the level I wanted. The only solution was complete automation.
“I wanted the whole process to be seamless for members and easy for me to administer. We don’t hold any stock, for example. Products remain with individual businesses. Only their catalogues are synchronised with Caboodle for ordering purposes. My input now is primarily on the marketing side, promoting the platform and bringing new retailers on board.
“Building a marketplace requires patience because both sides of the network have to grow together,” Flaherty says. “It would be very easy to chase growth too quickly, but I have tried to build Caboodle slowly and credibly, make sure the technology works and learn from the businesses and members using it.
“I have had an extremely positive experience with the supports available to early-stage entrepreneurs, particularly through the Local Enterprise Office and programmes supporting female founders, but if I were to suggest one improvement it would be greater provision for companies that sit between a traditional local small business and a high-growth export start-up. Some businesses need time to prove a model domestically before their international potential becomes obvious.”

title: ‘Grand Canyon-esque’: Atlas of the unseen brings Ireland’s deep sea wonders into the light
description: Project pieced together maps of the country’s extensive seabed at depths of up to 5km
content:
D eep in Irish waters lies a string of extinct volcanoes that once spewed molten rock on to the trembling seabed and gushed gasses into the convulsing waves.
In another part of Ireland’s marine territory, remarkable canyons have formed that plummet to abyss-like depths of 5.5km.
Elsewhere, there are mounds, cliffs, escarpments, ice age troughs and etchings and other geomorphological marvels so far down, their existence has taken decades to uncover.
It is all evidence of a terrain formed by tremendous forces and so rich in variety that, if it could be seen, would allow Ireland’s seascape to rival some of the most dramatic landscapes on the planet.
“A lot of people think the deep sea is dark and muddy and not a lot goes on there, but that could not be further from the truth,” says Andy Wheeler, professor of geology at University College Cork (UCC). “It’s a wonderful world down there.”
That wonderful world has now, for the first time, been comprehensively mapped and all its features added to the Irish Marine Atlas.
This atlas of the unseen was already a vast resource that captured in detail Ireland’s extensive coastal waters, which themselves can reach a not inconsiderable depth of 200 metres.
But mapping of Ireland’s deepwater seabed has been piecemeal.
Carried out on individual sites at different times over the last 25 years using assorted technologies, it lacked the consistency needed to produce a full, detailed, reliable picture.
The Marine Institute and the Marine Geosciences Research Group at UCC which Wheeler heads, have been working to rectify the situation.
It was not an easy task as Ireland’s marine territory is vast. Ten times the size of the country’s land territory, it stretches at its furthest point to almost 1,000km from shore and at its deepest to more than 5km.
Some of the existing, limited maps dated back 25 years and were of low quality by today’s standards.
The teams from the Marine Institute and UCC had to pull all the pieces together, enhance them to high resolution, reinterpret them, identify any gaps in the jigsaw and make the final product look seamless.
The result of their work is, says Fabio Sacchetti, team lead in advanced mapping services at the Marine Institute, “a major scientific achievement”.
It is also, he says, “a valuable resource for Ireland’s sustainable development ”.
He’s referring to the fact that the sea and the seabed are increasingly featuring in Government policies and international developments.
Ireland has big ambitions for offshore wind energy and while the five offshore wind projects now in planning will be relatively close to shore and fixed to the seabed, there are longer-term hopes that floating wind farms will be developed far out to sea.
Further into the future, there are aspirations to develop accompanying refuelling platforms that would use the vast power of floating wind energy to produce green hydrogen that could fuel passing ships, almost like a motorway petrol station.
Knowing exactly what would lie beneath such infrastructure is essential.
Already Ireland’s marine territory is crossed by telecommunications cables, pipelines and electricity interconnectors and there are plans for many more. Decisions on their routing will also depend on seabed conditions.
Apart from marine-based infrastructure, the sea is increasingly the focus of concerns around preserving and restoring what remains of the Earth’s struggling nature .
[ European maritime law aims to tighten collective security and environmental focus Opens in new window ]
The issue is increasingly urgent as awareness grows of the vital role healthy seas can play in sequestering carbon and cooling our overheating planet .
Ireland has precious deep-sea habitats, including cold-water coral reefs a kilometre down that suffered badly over decades of bottom trawling by supersized commercial fishing vessels.
These and other natural wonders need protection – and accurate mapping is a critical first step.
Ireland’s long-promised Marine Protected Areas legislation remains a work in progress , but here too, designation and management of protected areas requires good mapping.
At EU level, discussions are also under way on the creation of a European Ocean Act to co-ordinate marine protection from a nature, defence and commercial point of view.
Undoubtedly, there will also be interest from some parties in studying the maps from a seabed mining perspective to gauge the potential for underwater mineral extraction.
The atlas is publicly funded and open to everyone to use.
But setting all that aside, what does the mapping exercise actually reveal about the parts of Ireland we know the least?
Andy Wheeler has difficulty containing his excitement as he lists some of his favourite features.
“There are some incredible submarine canyons at the very south of Ireland’s territory from 200m to 5.5km down,” he says.
“Anything similar on land is ground down and eroded but these are huge. They are Grand Canyon-esque.
“There are also quite a surprising lot of mounds at the far western edge of Ireland’s territory. They’re a series of extinct volcanoes.
“They were last active about 60 million years ago, so similar to the period when the Giant’s Causeway was formed.
“What you also see as you go west is a series of banks and rift valleys, and at the top of the banks there are scours carved into the seabed by icebergs.
“When there was a glaciation, there were icebergs and their keels scoured the rock as they moved.
“When you consider the depth of these marks and that nine-tenths of an iceberg is below water, some of these must have been enormous – hundreds of metres tall.”
Wheeler’s enthusiasm is understandable. He has spent much of his career exploring the treasures of the deep sea and trying to metaphorically bring them to the surface for the public to enjoy.
“There is also a whole series of escarpments, some caused by erosion, some by submarine landslides,” he says. “Some of those landslides may have been tsunami-inducing but we don’t know for sure.
“We don’t think there are any likely to go off at present.”
Work on mapping Ireland’s seabed began in earnest in 1999 with the Irish National Seabed Survey and then its successor, the Infomar programme.
Infomar is due to run until 2029, with the final few years focused on expanding and updating the maps in some shallow zones.
It is a joint programme of Geological Survey Ireland and the Marine Institute and has involved numerous surveying vessels, the deep-sea Holland remotely operated vehicle, and remote sensing technology.
It has been funded by the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment , and has drawn what the department likes to call “the real map of Ireland” – the island and its seas.
Anyone who wants to delve into it can log on to atlas.marine.ie and start making their way around it.
The datasets are extensive and it takes a bit of time to work out how to select specific areas or features to examine, but the latest additions from Sacchetti, Wheeler and their teams can be found under the heading Irish Deep Seabed Geomorphology 200m-5000m.
Although Wheeler has the benefit of being an expert who knows the maps intimately, he urges novices to give it a go.
“Ireland punches above its weight in ocean exploration and we have a huge territory to explore,” he says. “It’s quite wonderful.”

title: ‘Big tech’s lapdog’: how can Ireland break free from the sector’s malign influence?
description: Resisting data centre sprawl can be a key step in ending the outsize influence of tech firms
content:
A t a packed Dublin Book Festival event, authors Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor warn about the impunity of the tech bro billionaires who are simultaneously preparing for – and accelerating – the climate apocalypse.
Despite the depressing title of their new book, End Times Fascism , their message is surprisingly hopeful. To end the impunity of big tech, they call for collective action, political organising and data centre resistance. Because data centres are critical infrastructure at the core of the industry’s socially destructive and ecologically devastating AI race, this is where people power can shift the trajectory.
To the enthusiastic audience, Klein and Taylor acknowledge a big contradiction in Ireland. While they expressed deep appreciation for Ireland’s courageous solidarity with Palestine and applaud how Ireland stands up for human rights and international law on the world stage, they also mention the consequential presence of big tech companies and their data centres in Ireland.
Although they do not elaborate on Ireland’s complicity in protecting the impunity of the big tech companies, many in the audience are surely connecting the dots. International concern for how the Irish State and economy have been captured by big tech has been growing, especially with Ireland hosting the presidency of the Council of the EU.
[ Naomi Klein: The super rich need to be abolished and ‘prescribed a middle-class life’ Opens in new window ]
Embarrassingly, the headline of a recent Guardian opinion article referred to Ireland as “Big Tech’s lapdog”, and an open letter by 60 leading academics called on Ireland to recuse itself from tech-related EU negotiations because of corporate capture.
Corporate capture means private industry strategically uses its power to influence public institutions, laws and regulations so that corporate profits are prioritised over the public good. Corporate capture is dangerous, not just because it weakens policies and regulations intended to protect the environment and public health, but also because it undermines the ability of the public sector and civil society to hold organisations accountable. Without accountability, democratic backsliding occurs and authoritarian regimes take hold; powerful people have reason to believe the laws don’t apply to them.
In Ireland, the prevalence of corporate capture is linked to many societal problems where the profit-seeking interests of the private sector are prioritised over the public good. Ireland’s failure to comply with climate law , and its chronic underfunding of public education, public housing, public health and public transport result from its corporate-friendly approach. The public sector workers labour dispute exposes how corporate capture deprioritises the public sector.
[ ‘They’re getting electricity for way lower prices’: Few regrets in Mayo over data centre refusal Opens in new window ]
As a scholar who studies corporate capture, my research contributes to efforts to rein in corporate impunity and hold industries accountable for the harm they are causing. From the tobacco industry to the fossil fuel industry, from agri-food to big tech, corporations strategically invest in university research to generate and disseminate knowledge that expands their profits.
While many governments around the world commit to evidence-based policymaking, industry-funded research often supports policy-based evidence-making – that is, corporations support research to strengthen their business interests and legitimise their policy positions.
The dangers of corporate capture in universities extends beyond the societal impact of industry-friendly research. A new study to which I contributed (led by US-based professor Noel Healy) shows how decades of corporate capture of universities in the US has made higher education institutions vulnerable to the current onslaught of attacks by the Trump administration. Our analysis highlights how corporate capture erodes democratic governance and the ability of public institutions to stand up against authoritarian control.
[ University education has become meaningless – and now it doesn’t even promise a job Opens in new window ]
Just as the fossil fuel industry made strategic investments in research to deny the severity of the climate crisis and promote fossil-fuel-friendly climate “solutions”, the tech industry strategically invests in universities to incentivise and legitimise the uncritical adoption of AI in research and teaching; a strategy that distracts attention from its societal and environmental harms.
But with independent research revealing the societal, economic and environmental costs of data centres , communities are now mobilising against data centres joining in the fight to end big tech’s impunity. As the global backlash expands , Klein and Taylor’s visit to Dublin reminds us that Ireland is an influential country with power on the global stage that is disproportionate to its small size.
Ireland may be economically dependent on big tech, but big tech is also economically dependent on Ireland. Just as Ireland stands strong in solidarity with Palestine calling out the genocide in Gaza, Ireland needs to now stand up to the tech companies, hold them accountable for the harms they are causing and end their impunity.
Jennie C Stephens is professor of climate justice at Maynooth University and co-convener of the Climate Justice Universities Union .

title: More than 150 schools receive bomb threat email on same day as public sector strike
description: Schools in the Dublin and Kildare regions understood to be operating as normal while taking the advice of gardaí
content:
A number of schools received threatening emails warning them of potential attacks on Wednesday.
It is understood over 150 schools in the Dublin and Kildare regions received the bomb scare email.
The schools are understood to be operating as normal while taking the advice of gardaí .
This comes on the same day as widespread industrial action over public sector pay, where the majority of schools across the country were closed and pickets placed outside.
The Department of Education said it consulted with gardaí on the issue, who advised any school in receipt of the email to contact gardaí.
“The department communicated this advice to schools and boards of management, management bodies, and unions,” it said in a statement to The Irish Times.
“On this basis, the department anticipates that Boards of Management will have regard to the advice from An Garda Síochána, and schools can continue to operate as normal unless otherwise advised by An Garda Síochána.”
Gardaí said they are “aware of a communication” that was sent to a number of schools on Wednesday.
A spokesperson said gardaí are assessing the “contents and credibility” of the emails.
Gardaí are engaging with the schools involved, they said, adding that no further information is currently available.
Sources had suggested that the bomb squad had made callouts to schools, but it’s understood this related to other incidents.
A Defence Forces spokesperson said: “The Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal Team were deployed twice today to locations within Dublin. These deployments were routine and of no significance. Óglaigh na hÉireann has no further comment.”

title: Quick-fire Doué and Dembélé inspire PSG to wild win at Manchester City
description: Pep Guardiola watches on as his former charges suffer 4-2 defeat
content:
A penny for Pep Guardiola ’s thoughts. The legendary Manchester City manager was back at the Etihad Stadium for the first time since his departure at the end of last season and, well, the announcement of you-know-what.
Sporting a flat cap, Guardiola took his seat in the stands behind the City chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, and the chief executive, Ferran “Not” Soriano, and, certainly, the TV director seemed intent on scrutinising him – if the number of cutaway shots to him were any guide.
Everybody knows where Guardiola stands on the great City scandal; the numerous guilty verdicts handed down to them on the 100-plus charges they have faced for breaking the Premier League’s financial rules. He has backed his former employers to somehow disprove them. But what did he make of his old team here against the might of the defending European champions, Paris Saint-Germain?
Not much in the first half would have been a reasonable conclusion. PSG played football from a higher plane and might have led by more than the three unanswered goals they scored. But if defiance has been the theme for City – and it fed into Guardiola’s presence here – they produced plenty more of it during a wild second half.
City refused to accept the inevitable. They threw everything at PSG. Erling Haaland ran on adrenaline as City created a fistful of clear openings. Haaland finished with two goals and a couple of near misses. City were close to worrying PSG.
The problem for Enzo Maresca and his players was the goal from Maghnes Akliouche for 4-1. It was a blast from outside the area that Gianluigi Donnarumma appeared to have palmed up and away. Except that the ball dropped back down and into the net. PSG even had time to miss a late penalty from Ferran Torres; the kick was weak and too close to Donnarumma. Are you missing it all, Pep?
The City support booed the Uefa anthem, as usual, due to their long-standing grievances with the European governing body, albeit they have surely been overtaken by issues closer to home. Perhaps they can coexist unhappily?
Their team’s idea had been to measure themselves against the best and there were reasons why PSG shimmered with such menace. One was that Luis Enrique’s starting XI featured seven players who are on the 30-strong Ballon d’Or shortlist. He had another three from it among his substitutes, including João Neves and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.
PSG were slick and sharp at the outset. There was the trademark assurance on the ball; the beautifully grooved combinations. It does not matter how tight the spaces are. They back themselves to get out of them. Witness the opening goal and a scintillating piece of team play that began deep on the right-hand side of their defensive third.
In the blink of an eye, PSG were surging up the flank and then opening out the move, Fabián Ruiz playing the final pass to Doué on the left. The winger cut inside and shot low for the near corner from outside the area. It was the precision that did for Donnarumma, although the former PSG goalkeeper had to do better at his post.
When PSG landed the follow-up punch just 75 seconds later, City were reeling, the home crowd stunned. The travelling PSG fans were beside themselves. It was a goal that featured two crosses, the first from Dembélé after some nice footwork out to Doué on the left. He took the ball down and crossed back for Dembélé, who had stolen in behind Marc Guéhi. The striker was unmarked; the run was too cute. Dembélé’s header was straightforward.
It was no exaggeration to say that PSG could have had five by the interval. City had no defence to their cut and thrust; the sheer pace of it. The positional fluidity, too. What was the right-back Achraf Hakimi doing marauding up the inside left? Causing major problems.
Hakimi popped up inside the six-yard box in the 32nd minute only to send a free header against the post but City were swiftly disabused of the notion that the danger had passed. Almost immediately, PSG seized on a lofted Donnarumma clearance and went for the jugular. Akliouche was involved and Warren Zaïre-Emery got the assist with a lovely back-heel. Vitinha lashed a low drive home. The PSG support turned their backs on the pitch to perform a perfectly synchronised Poznan. It was a Parisian spectacle on and off the pitch. When Hakimi blew a one-on-one with Donnarumma on 39 minutes, his team were toying with City.
Maresca made a triple change at the interval, introducing Matheus Nunes, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye; an acknowledgment of how the first period got away from his team. The pickings in attacking terms had been slim. Antoine Semenyo blazed high at 0-0 after Matvei Safonov punched a corner against his own crossbar but there appeared to have been a foul on the PSG goalkeeper. There was not a great deal else from City.
They were better after the restart, playing with abandon. Semenyo crackled to life. Enzo Fernández blew a gilt-edged headed opportunity and Ndiaye worked Safonov before Haaland pulled one back. It was a whipped ball in from the inside left by Ndiaye, which Haaland redirected into the far corner with a flex of the neck muscles. He was not close in, either.
Could City take the lifeline? Semenyo ran through and dinked against the crossbar. The offside flag was raised, although he looked to have been level. City needed the next goal to make it interesting. Instead, they lost the initiative after another Donnarumma lapse. – Guardian

title: Donegal star Finnbarr Roarty joins AFL side Collingwood on two-year deal
description: GAA met with AFL this week to discuss potential recruitment protocol
content:
The GAA met with AFL officials earlier this week to discuss the possible introduction of a protocol around the recruitment of Gaelic footballers by Aussie Rules clubs.
The meeting took place in Ireland just days before it emerged that Donegal ’s Finnbarr Roarty had signed for with Collingwood.
The issue of AFL clubs recruiting Gaelic footballers has been a sticking point in negotiations between the two organisations over a possible revival of the International Rules Series.
It is understood the meeting was “positive and constructive” and although nothing was finalised, GAA officials are hopeful meaningful progress will be made in the near future on a recruitment protocol.
One of the possible options would be to reclassify Irish players as category A rookies. They are currently classified as category B rookies, meaning they do not count towards their club’s salary cap or take up a roster place on the draft, making them a low-risk option for clubs.
If Gaelic footballers were redesignated as category A rookies, AFL clubs may be more minded restrained in their recruitment efforts.
If the GAA and AFL can reach an agreement on the issue, the renewed goodwill could bring about a return of the International Rules Series, which the AFL are keen to resurrect.
Roarty has signed a two-year rookie deal with Collingwood as The 2025 Young Footballer, Roarty a two-year rookie deal with Collingwood as he prepares to feature in this weekend’s Donegal senior football final with his club, Naomh Conaill.
Mayo’s Kobe McDonald, who is among the nominees for this year’s Young Footballer of the Year award, is signed to St Kilda, while Oisín Mullin, a two-time Young Footballer of the Year (2020 and 2021), is signed with Geelong.
Roarty started all of Donegal’s championship games this summer, building on a remarkable debut season in 2025 when he finished as an All-Star defender. The 20-year-old was the third Donegal player to pick up the Young Footballer of the Year award, following in the footsteps of Michael Murphy and Ryan McHugh.
Roarty spent much of the summer playing football in the United States, where he helped the Padraig Pearse club to a Chicago senior football title. He has since returned home and has played a leading role in Naomh Conaill’s county title pursuit.
Collingwood has previously looked to Irish players, with Down’s Martin Clarke, Derry’s Anton Tohill and Cork’s Mark Keane all spending time at the Melbourne club.
In total, there were 14 Irish players contracted to AFL clubs last season, eight of whom saw game time.
Tyrone’s Conor McKenna made 21 appearances for Brisbane Lions, including last month’s AFL Grand Final win over Fremantle.
Mullin had the most appearances of any player across the league, featuring on 25 occasions for Geelong, while team-mate Mark O’Connor of Kerry played 22 times. Derry’s Callum Brown played 18 games for Greater Western Sydney Giants.
Cork’s Mark Keane returned after a five-month recovery from a broken leg to make 11 appearances for Adelaide Crows. Another Cork man, Liam O’Connell, played 13 times for St Kilda.
Meath’s Conor Nash made 10 appearances for Hawthorn before a neck injury ended his season, and Kilkenny’s Darragh Joyce made three appearances for the Lions.
The other Irish players contracted to AFL clubs were Kerry trio Rob Monahan (Geelong), Cillian Burke (Geelong) and Ben Murphy (Brisbane), Offaly’s Cillian Bourke (Essendon), Meath’s Eamonn Armstrong (St Kilda) and Longford’s Matt Duffy (Carlton).
Duffy confirmed in August that he was returning to Ireland and in recent weeks has helped his club Dromard progress to the semi-finals of the Longford championship.
McDonald has spent a brief spell in Australia familiarising himself with the St Kilda set-up and will be return to Australia ahead of preseason training in early November.
Ireland under-20 rugby player and former Dublin minor footballer Noah Byrne recently turned down an offer of a contract with Leinster to sign for Brisbane.

title: ‘Nobody can survive on the wages we’re getting’: public sector workers strike across the country
description: Coalition ‘open for negotations’ with unions, says Taoiseach, following action by more than 300,000 workers
content:
That’s a wrap from us this evening after 300,000 people took part in nationwide protests seeking a new public sector pay deal.
The Government has indicated they are willing to negotiate with trade unions, but it remains to be seen if another strike next week will go ahead with no talks currently planned.
A number of schools received threatening emails warning them of potential attacks on Wednesday, Education Correspondent Niamh Towey reports.
It is understood over 150 schools in the Dublin and Kildare regions received the bomb scare email .
The schools are understood to be operating as normal while taking the advice of gardaí.
This comes on the same day as widespread industrial action over public sector pay, where the majority of schools across the country were closed and pickets placed outside.
Gardaí said they are “aware of a communication” that was sent to a number of schools on Wednesday.
A spokesperson said gardaí are assessing the “contents and credibility” of the emails.
Gardaí are engaging with the schools involved, they said, adding that no further information is currently available.
On the eastern outskirts of Athlone on Wednesday, three groups of public sector workers were striking for better pay and to show solidarity to their fellow workers, reports Stephen Farrell.
Sheltering from the blustery conditions at Cornamaddy Community National School were special needs assistants (SNAs) and teaching staff, including Lauren Holmes (28).
“It’s frustrating that it had to come to this, the [the Government][ knew it was coming in June. We’d prefer to be teaching inside,” she said.
The public service Agreement 2024-2026 expired in June and there has been no agreement on any new deal.
Holmes, like most of the teachers in the school, she says, began teaching after 2011, when austerity pay cuts and lower entry salary scales were introduced for newly appointed teachers.
Holmes adds that many teachers in rural areas are on sub-maternity contracts due to the lack of fixed-term contracts and for them “it is even more difficult”.
Holmes said that “the backbone of the school” is the SNA staff, one of whom is Caroline McManus, who said she is looking for “equality and fair play” for all public sector workers.
McManus was particularly mindful of young people already working in the public sector or who may enter the sector in the future: “I would like young SNAs to be treated and respected in their job, fair play for the work they do. So many are leaving the country.”
Another teacher at Cornamaddy is Kate O’Connor who remarked on the public backing throughout the day.
“It’s all been very supportive, people passing by [beeping their horns], there hasn’t been anything negative,” she said.
She too was frustrated at the Government’s approach and that she and her colleagues did not want to be “standing here” on October 21st, the next planned strike date, if the unions demands are not met.
A two-minute walk from the school, to the junction of Woodville Road and the Blyry Industrial Estate, which is the home of the Athlone Ambulance station, a number of ambulance service personnel were on strike including Paul McCabe (63) and Darren Mulledy (56).
Ambulance personnel provided reduced cover, said Mulledy.
“We are out here in solidarity with our colleagues in the public service,” said McCabe.
The cost of living was a big motivating factor for both McCabe and Mulledy in taking part in the strike.
“A number of people are living on the bread line,” said Mulledy, with McCabe imploring the Government to “just sit down and talk to the unions”.
“If reasonable people sit down and talk, they will come to a reasonable conclusion. It’s like the old saying, ‘if you put your head in the sand’,” he said.
The cost of home heating oil was a particular concern for both men.
“It costs €2,000 to fill a tank, I can’t afford that,” said Mulledy, who has had to supplement his fuel with bags of turf.
Less than half a kilometre West, about 40 Department of Education civil servants were also on strike outside their place of employment.
Dearbhla Sargent works as a Higher Executive Officer in the pensions section and is hoping that workers will get some sort of remedy to the cost of living.
“The cost of diesel has increased, the price of food is extortionate, we need some sort of compensation,” she said.
“I don’t have anything for saving out of my weekly take-home pay – and I’m close to retirement.”
She also pointed to a recent increase in her PRSI which has cancelled out any additional money she received as a result of Budget 2027.
“Obviously I’m hoping that they [the Government] will call us back in to talks and offer us something substantial. People who are working never seem to gain,” she added.
“I am a pensioner and my medical appointment was cancelled today but I support the strikers 100 per cent,” Johnny Cloono, from Co Waterford, told The Irish Times.
“They are right to strike for better pay, we are all suffering from the cost-of-living crisis and public service workers deserve wage increases that address it.”
He said the level of public support for the strikers was “heartening to see”.
“I hope that they continue to take action until their demands are met.”
Martina Callanan, an education administrator from Co Galway, said she is angry that “my husband and I, both in full-time employment, have a lower standard of living and worse pensions than our parents”.
“I’m angry that the Taoiseach and senior ministers have spoken disparagingly about me and my public sector colleagues. I’m beyond angry that the Government refuses to nationalise a fully public childcare and creche system, or hire healthcare workers on decent contracts to provide necessary support to children and people with disabilities.
“And I’m furious that blockaders with big trucks got cash in a week ... yet trade unions are held at arms length by Government.”
Ger Moane, a retired lecturer, said: “When over 90 per cent of public employees vote for strike, there is something seriously wrong. It’s not just about pay ... it’s about squeezing more work with less resources.”
Salters Sterling from Co Offaly is nearly 90. He feels the strikes reflect “inequality in our society”.
“The contrasts between mansions and homelessness, between professional and pensioner; between abundance of food and not enough to go round ... are blatant to the point where obvious injustice motivates protest and conscience demands the implementation of a vision of fairer, more equal ways of allocating resources and sharing wealth.”
Speaking in Brussels on Wednesday evening, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said the Government was “open for negotiations and open for dialogue” with the trade unions, Europe Correspondent Jack Power reports.
There was “substantial funding” set aside in the budget for a pay deal. “I believe there’s a platform there for negotiations ... We want to get into a negotiating process,” Martin said.
“So we will engage and see can we find a basis and a process that would be satisfactory for all sides to enable negotiations to take place and avoid any action next week,” Martin said.
He was speaking at an EU press conference in Brussels, where he will attend a two-day summit of EU leaders starting on Thursday.
The strike is having an impact on weather forecast reports and there were disruptions to updates on met.ie on Wednesday.
The last update was posted on Met Éireann’s site at 10pm on Tuesday evening. Meanwhile, there is a yellow weather warning in place for five counties overnight.
The HSE has said hospitals “remain very busy” amid today’s strike action.
“Engagements with unions during the day have been positive and helped us to make sure that emergency and critical care services are being prioritised.
“Rescheduling of impacted appointments and procedures will be prioritised and rescheduled as soon as possible. We ask patients to bear with us as there may be further delays until there is greater certainty regarding future industrial action.”
Minister of State John Cummins has said there is a window of opportunity for talks in advance of a second day of strike action planned for next week.
He told Newstalk: “I do welcome the fact that union leaders have said today that they do see a pathway to talks. I would encourage that to happen.
“I’m a former teacher myself, I’m a former union rep for the school myself, all disputes are resolved by discussing things around the table.
“There’s a window ahead of next Wednesday for those intensive talks to take place.”
Aoife Brady, curator of Italian and Spanish art at the National Gallery, said the strike “could have been avoided” and was “a real last resort for us as union members,” Órla Ryan reports.
“We’re not being paid for our day today. We would rather be in work, getting on with the various responsibilities, which are only going to pile up and be there tomorrow morning, but it’s a necessary evil in our eyes. Unfortunately, in order to get the Government’s attention and to ask them to negotiate fairly as they should have earlier in the summer, this is what we’ve been brought to.”
Brady, a Siptu member, said many public sector workers are “paid under the national average”.
“The cost of living has gone out of control ... We’re looking for a pay raise in line with inflation. So I think it’s only reasonable at this stage.”
Brady said it would be “ideal” if a pay agreement was reached in the coming days so a further strike was avoided next week.
“We have no desire to disrupt the public any more than it has been, but we are prepared to strike next Wednesday, as planned, if the Government don’t sit down at the table and engage fairly in negotiation as we’ve been requesting.”
Catherine Ryan, who works in communications at the National Gallery, said employees are “just looking for fairness of pay, the increments that should be paid to keep us in line with the rising cost of living”.
“Nobody wants to be out striking ... We love our jobs. We’re very proud of the work we do here at the National Gallery, as is everybody here on this picket line ... but our hands are being forced. Basically, we have to do this.”
Ryan said cultural institutions like galleries and theatres “mightn’t be life and death, but it really is a thing that makes your life worth living and enriches your life in all these ways”.
She added: “Ideally, we won’t be here next week, but we’re very willing to be here again and out in great numbers.”
Catherine Boothman, traditional arts officer at the Arts Council, said she and fellow Siptu members were striking “because we really want qualitative engagement with the Government about pay and investment in the public services,” reports Órla Ryan .
“We’ve known forever that the previous [pay] agreement was going to come to an end in June. Public servants are very used to long-term planning, we’re always looking ahead ... So it’s incredible that the Government wouldn’t be coming at the start of this year with substantive engagement - not only about pay, but also about the vision for the public service.”
Boothman was critical of the fact Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers this week told RTÉ News that “strike action should be a last resort, not a first resort for trade union leaders”.
She said: “When Chambers says strike shouldn’t be the first option, actually there were hundreds of first options many months ago. We knew the end date of the previous agreement, and it’s incredible that [the Government] wouldn’t be coming with an actual quality proposal...
“I’d like to see them committing to pay rises, immediately working on an agreement that is going to go from July 2026. We shouldn’t be working outside an agreement.”
Boothman said she hoped the issue would be resolved soon, but added: “I think we’ll be out next Wednesday.”
David Parnell, a manager with the Arts Council, agreed that a new pay deal should have been finalised before the Public Service Agreement 2024–2026 expired in June.
“I suppose the feeling among workers is, ‘Why has it taken this long?’ I think it is a shame that it’s come to this point,” he said.
“No one wants to be inconveniencing people. No one wants to be on strike if they don’t have to be, but it got to the point where there was a feeling that we have to show that we’re serious about this.”
Parnell said he hoped the 24-hour strike planned for next Wednesday could be averted.
“This can’t go on indefinitely. There has to be some agreement at some point. So one would hope that that would happen sooner rather than later.”
Leaders of Ireland’s main teaching unions have called for Taoiseach Micheál Martin to intervene in order to prevent further strike action on the first day of industrial action over pay, reports Education Correspondent Niamh Towey .
Speaking on a picket line outside Hartstown Community College in Dublin 15 on Wednesday, the General Secretaries of the Irish National Teachers’ Organisation (INTO), the Association of Secondary Teachers Ireland (ASTI) and the Teachers Union of Ireland (TUI) all indicated a lack of trust between their members and the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform.
Almost all schools, colleges and universities across the country were closed on Wednesday in the biggest public sector strike seen here for almost two decades.
Approximately 100,000 teachers and lecturers who are members of the INTO, ASTI, TUI and the Irish Federation of University Teachers (IFUT) went on strike over what they called a lack of meaningful engagement from Government on a new public sector pay deal.
In total there were over 300,000 public sector workers including teachers, doctors, nurses and civil servants taking part in the strike today.
“I think it’s fairly evident there’s been a breakdown of trust, and I think really we’re going to need somebody to bring the parties together,” Linda Kelly, general secretary of the ASTI, said.
“I think it was too little, too late from the Minister [Jack Chambers] last night to have his epiphany around pay being a central part of a pay deal, and I think that needs to be addressed. I do think there is a role here for the Taoiseach,” Kelly said.
Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers told RTÉ’s Prime Time on Tuesday night that pay could be dealt with first in any negotiations.
“The question is, can we trust that now?,” general secretary of the INTO John Boyle said.
“This is the same Minister who told the general public only three weeks before the budget that there will be €2 billion available for public service pay, and yet on budget day, he only made available €1 billion, plus point two of a billion for pensions. And within the 1 billion, a lot of that money is already spent on carryover costs.
“So we are going to have to get assurances from the Taoiseach who needs to step in here that whatever negotiations are going to commence, and I am confident that they will commence after last night’s change of heart from the Minister, but the Taoiseach is going to have to convince us that if pay is going to be spoken about at the beginning of the talks, that it’s all aspects of pay,” Boyle said.
Stephen who works as a library attendant in Cabra says at 46, he’d like to be able to move out of his mother’s house in Ballymun, reports Dublin Editor Olivia Kelly .
“At my age I don’t think I should be still living at home, but there’s no way I could afford not to. I’ve worked all my life and I can’t afford to house myself. I’d probably need two jobs that pay the same amount of money that I’m on to move out.”
He says he is on the picket line to highlight the impact of rising costs, not only on library staff but across the public sector.
“I think it’s important to say this is for everyone. The Government are just squeezing us so hard with the cost of living and yeah, we need more money just to survive.”
Courts and court public offices nationwide, were cancelled with very limited exceptions on Wednesday due to the public sector strike, reports Legal Affairs Correspondent Mary Carolan .
Given the level of involvement in the strike, the Courts Service said earlier this week it had decided, after consultation with trade unions and staff, it would be unable to support courts and open public counters on Wednesday.
It said that meant courts and public counter service would not be available on Wednesday except for emergency domestic violence and childcare applications; Garda applications to remand an accused person in custody where station bail was not granted; and injunctions to dela with the protection of life, health, safety or welfare.
In granting these derogations, the trade unions recognised “the particular importance and sensitive nature of the work carried out by the Courts Service, as well as the potential severe consequences for the community and vulnerable individuals should urgent, critical matters arise”, the Courts Service said in a statement.
Those looking for emergency domestic violence or childcare supports on Wednesday were advised to contact An Garda Síochána who have access to the local courthouse/ court office emergency on-call number.
Acknowledging there would be “significant disruption” to court users who may have had a court date on Wednesday, the Courts Service said it would notify all parties when rescheduled court dates are available.
A one-day strike by more than 300,000 public and civil servants got under way countrywide overnight.
Employees are seeking a new public sector deal, with trade unions arguing that pay terms must be agreed ⁠before other issues are addressed.
Schools, colleges, libraries, council offices and many parks are among the publicly run facilities that are closed on Wednesday because of the action. Health services are disrupted, with all elective procedures and thousands of appointments postponed.
The Irish Times would like to hear your views on the strike. Do you support the striking workers, and what is your view of the dispute? Are you striking today, and if so, what has your experience been like? If you are not striking today, have you been impacted by any public services being unavailable?
Josh Graves (31), is one of the more than 150 civilian members of An Garda Síochána striking outside Garda Headquarters in the Phoenix Park and feels the action is the only way to get their point across, reports Hugh Dooley .
From north Dublin, Graves and his partner both work in the civil service; “We’ve just had enough, to be honest. We’re both in our early 30s and we are struggling through life. We can’t afford a house and can barely afford to put the petrol in the car at this stage, never mind groceries and bills.”
He said that the people who work on the ground and keep the country running deserve better.
“We’ve played ball long enough with the Government at this stage in terms of past agreements,” he said, but feels the attitude from Leinster House has been different this time around, “not positive”.
“This is our last option. None of us want to be here. I’d much rather be in work today. We’re not getting paid for today. We don’t want to cause the disruption to the rest of the community, but, unfortunately, we’ve got to the stage where we feel this is the only way we can get our point across.”
The Garda civilian staff work behind the scene, performing administrative labour, consoling the victims of crime, vetting people working with children and working as dispatchers in the control room.
“We take the administrative burden off Garda members so that they can concentrate more on their frontline duties; protecting communities and responding to emergency calls.”
The action is popular among staff, with more than 99 per cent of those who responded to Fórsa’s poll supporting the decision, the trade union said.
Graves said these staff are not looking to be “wealthy or rich” and just want their pay to “meet the requirements of the cost of living and inflation”.
He encouraged Government figures to come out to Garda stations to speak with staff and see how they are struggling.
“We just want to get by. We just want to [be able to] afford a house. I want to get married. I want to have children. But at the moment, none of those are feasible for me.”
Jamie Carroll (32) also works for An Garda Síochána and is in a similar position. He still lives in his parents’ home and “can’t afford to rent or move out”.
He feels the cost of living crisis “doesn’t look like it’s getting better anytime soon”.
“We want better pay that helps to deal with the cost of living crisis, but the Government aren’t sitting down to negotiate and cross their hands,” Carroll said, noting he feels taken for granted by the Government.
“We’ve tried, they haven’t, so we’re trying to force their hand onto the table.”
Teachers do not want to be on strike today and are anxious to see negotiations on a new pay deal begin, one secondary school teacher has said, reports Education Correspondent Niamh Towey .
Anthony Keane is an English teacher and counsellor at Hartstown Community School in Dublin 15.
“I don’t want to be on strike. I don’t know anyone who wants to be on strike today, and it’s unfortunate that it has come to this,” he said on the picket line outside his school on Wednesday morning.
“I think it’s unfortunate that we’re outside the school building rather than inside where we want to be today, inside it, and so I just hope it’s an encouragement for the government to engage in meaningful dialogue,” Keane said.
The cost of accommodation has put huge pressure on teachers in his school, particularly younger staff, and people are “really feeling the pinch on multiple levels,” he said.
Many of the staff at Hartstown are commuting very long distances, some from Kilkenny, Cavan, Westmeath and Offaly, Keane said.
Many are “not able to afford accommodation, not able to get on the property ladder,” he said, meaning “massive commutes are the only option for a lot of people, and all the expense and reduction in quality of life that that entails”.
Part of his reason for being on the picket line today is to show a sense of solidarity with these younger staff members who are “really struggling” on the current wages they receive.
“Let’s appreciate what makes life better for people in this country and they are the basic services, so that people can live and be educated and have basic needs looked after,” Keane said.
He urged those on both sides to sit down and find a resolution through dialogue, sooner rather than later.
“Those of us that are around a long time know that ultimately resolution is the only way through. So why delay? Let’s just get involved in meaningful negotiations.
“It’s unfortunate that taxpayers are being affected today. That taxpayers are on strike today. That people who are providing public services have to be on strike outside their places of work, rather than inside doing what they want to do,” Keane said.
“There is a sort of stereotype around university staff and university lecturers, in particular, being well paid, but it’s oversimplified,” says Trinity academic and Irish Federation of University Teachers activist John Walsh, reports Work Correspondent Emmet Malone .
“The perception really fails to capture the large number of precarious staff in universities. More than 30 per cent of all university staff are on fixed-term or precarious contracts. And even a lot of people who would come in on the assistant professor scale wouldn’t be particularly well paid.
“So a lot of our members would have insecure contracts and poor terms and conditions, much of which is a legacy of the economic crash and of government underfunding of higher education since the crash.
“We want fair pay and also decent public funding.”
Most of the people filing past the pickets at College Green barely give the various unions’ protests a glance as they try to get to somewhere else but those who had been intending to visit the university grounds have generally taken the realisation they have picked the wrong day well.
“We’re very pleased with the level of support we’ve got from members of the public. There’s a lot of people dropping by to express support and even tourists who couldn’t get into see the Book of Kells were saying they support the strike,” Walsh says with a smile.
“They’re a bit surprised, they didn’t seem to have heard about it but it’s all been good. We’ve had a really positive experience.”
Teachers feel “disregarded” by a Government which does not “have our best interests at heart,” one protester said on Wednesday morning, reports Education Correspondent Niamh Towey .
Kai Monahan (25) is a Spanish teacher at Hartstown Community School in Dublin 15.
“There’s a shortage of teachers and they know what they need to do, but it just doesn’t feel like they’re actually doing the best for us,” Monahan said on the picket line outside his school on Wednesday morning.
“If you look at different aspects in life, if you’re looking at the cost of rent, the cost of living in Dublin, it’s increasing every year and we’re not seeing that being reflected in our pay by the government,” he said.
Buying a house feels very far from his grasp on his current salary, but also at any point in the near future.
“I would definitely struggle to buy a house at this point, it just doesn’t seem like something that’s feasible, even in the long term. It’s not something that I’m really considering right now,” Monahan said.
He wants to see a “fair public sector pay agreement” that “reflects the work we do and also the rise in inflation and the cost of living”.
Patrick Burke, a physiotherapist at the Mater hospital, said staff “don’t want to be here today,” reports Health Correspondent Shauna Bowers .
“The cost of food in your food shop is increasing regularly. Even transport to work as well and ability to buy houses. It’s a big pressure on everyone here working,” the 29-year-old Sligo man said.
“A lot of my friends went abroad to Australia. I decided to stay. Now that we’re here now, we’re trying to get better working conditions and pay to encourage more people to stay in Ireland.
Ciara Loftus, who works with the frailty team in the Mater hospital’s emergency department said, “I’m still living at home. I should be saving for a mortgage by now but I’m living with my mam.
“I’m 25 and I feel like I’m going to be forced to move country by the end of the year or next year,” she said.
“It’s not sustainable anymore. I don’t want to leave but I might have to because if something is not done about the cost of living crisis, about our pay, our future, I’m just going to suffer here.”
Emer Kearney, a nurse in the Mater hospital, said protesters are asking the government to “help us”.
“We’re looking to equate to the cost of living. We want our salaries to reflect that. We don’t want to be out in the picket here today, we want to be in looking after our patients,” she said.
“It’s a very real struggle and we have very real costs. We are asking the Government to meet us at the table. We want to be able to do our work and we want to be able to come to work.”
“It’s going very well,” says Maurice Sweeney, a chief technical officer for hazardous materials at Trinity College as he stands with colleagues from Unite at the Leinster Street entrance to the university on Wednesday, reports Work Correspondent Emmet Malone .
“Support for it from the staff has been very strong. I represent Unite, and I think all our members are out today, regardless of childcare issues or whatever. People have made it happen. In some instances, people have brought their children to the picket lines so that (they) could be here.
“There’s unbelievable public support and you can see that the mood of the people here is very boisterous,” he says as large group of mainly young female members of Fórsa and Siptu sing and dance a few feet away and enthusiastically acknowledge each toot of support from passing motorists.
“Everyone’s having fun,” says Sweeney, “but there’s an underlying seriousness to what’s going on.”
There’s people in here and across the public sector, that are on not much more than the minimum wage, he said, adding that he is “struggling”.
“I’m just a family man with a wife and one daughter and a home and a mortgage to pay for. But your weekly shop is putting you under pressure. I would be considered to have a good wage for the type of work that I do. Some days we are coming in here for 5am, so we are the people that Simon Harris says get up early in the morning.
“But we didn’t see much of the benefit from that budget there last week at all. Not that I could see. It’s a couple of pence here and there, a couple of cents. They give it to you on one hand, but on the other hand, they might be taking it away with other bits of taxation or whatever.”
Independent Ireland leader Michael Collins blamed the Government for the public sector strikes and also warned renewed fuel protests are possible, reports Political Correspondent Cormac McQuinn .
Speaking outside Leinster House he referred to last April’s fuel protests and said: “This is the second time in less than 12 months that this country has ground to a halt by a Government inside in that building that are no longer in touch with the ordinary man and woman in this country, especially the working people in this country.”
He said of the strike: “yes services are being lost and put off which is a huge difficulty for many, many people.
“But these people have no choice. At the end of the week there’s little or nothing left in the pay packet to pay the bills that need to be paid.”
He argued that measures to support people with fuel costs in last week’s Budget did not go far enough.
“We have a major cost of living crisis. We have been pleading with the Government for months and months to make changes and unfortunately they haven’t listened,” the Cork South-West TD said.
Collins said the unions “saw how effective” April’s fuel protests were and “they’ve now got to sit up and start fighting for their people because their people aren’t going to survive the way things are”.
Asked by reporters if the farmers and contractors who protested earlier this year should talk to the unions about coming together for a larger protest Collins replied: “Absolutely. I think that’s very, very important.
“Because they’re hungry here and I know by talking to them that they’d love to be involved in this as well – not to disrupt anything – just to make sure they have a voice and people are listening to them.”
He said the fuel protesters are “watching this protest today” and he has been talking to them.
Collins said he was at a pre-budget meeting with the fuel protesters in Moate and he was “pleading with them to try to negotiate, to see can we bring the Government with us.”
However, he added: “The budget last week proved that that’s not possible, so it’s quite possible there could be further protests.”
Jane Culligan, a medical scientist at the Mater hospital, said there was “no need for us to be out here today,” reports Health Correspondent Shauna Bowers .
Protesting alongside her two colleagues Laura Dempsey and Grainne O’Grady, the trio said they are there to support all public sector workers.
“We are annoyed with the Government that the public pay talks have fallen through. There’s no need for us to be out here today, it could have been sorted beforehand,” Culligan said.
“Inflation is going up and our pay hasn’t gone up in line with that. I think the unions involved in negotiations have made efforts to avoid this and I don’t think the Government has listened.
“We feel the pinch and we will remember this when it comes to election time.”
Spirits are high at the @DCU picket today. Solidarity ✊💙🩵 #IFUT #PublicSectorPay #HigherEducation pic.twitter.com/FZKA86oq0X
The Irish Federation of University Teachers (Ifut), the only dedicated trade union and professional association in Ireland for third-level academic and research staff, posted photos and videos on X from picket lines outside universities and third-level institutions across Ireland.
They shared photos from Dublin City University, University of Galway, Maynooth University, Trinity College Dublin, University College Cork and others.
Mark Prouse, head groundsman at the Iveagh Gardens in Dublin, described the provision of €1.2 billion for public sector pay in the budget as “an insult”, reports Órla Ryan .
“Micheál Martin comes along and brags about this €1.2 billion that he’s giving us over the next three years – when you break it down, it’s actually only €3.50, €3.40, a day or something. It’s crazy. You couldn’t get a cup of coffee with what he’s offering us, so it’s not a genuine offer. He thinks we’re all stupid when we’re not,” Prouse said.
“When you mention those types of figures, people automatically think, ‘Oh my God, these guys are going to get a massive money’. But when you break it down between 300,000 people over a couple of years, it’s actually nothing. It’s only pennies that they’re offering us.”
Prouse, who is also a Siptu shop steward, said today’s strike could have been averted if the Government engaged in negotiations with trade unions months ago.
“It got to this point because the Government wouldn’t sit down and talk to us ... We should have sat down in January because our last [pay] agreement ended in June, so we should have been sitting around the table last January to discuss the new agreement for the next three years, and they didn’t. And here we are in October and they still haven’t sat down.”
Prouse, who was striking outside St Stephen’s Green in Dublin, said workers are really struggling amid the cost-of-living crisis.
“My gas bill has doubled, my electricity bill has doubled, my diesel has doubled. I mean, what do they expect us to live on? ... Nobody can survive on the wages we’re getting.”
Prouse thinks the dispute can be resolved in the coming days – in order to avoid another 24-hour strike next Wednesday – if the Government “stop insulting us, sit down and give us a proper [offer]”.
“They give themselves these big wage rises. You don’t see us complaining about how much they’re giving themselves ... We’re not asking for the money that they’re giving themselves every week. We’re just looking for a bit of respect ...“It’s always the unions, it’s always the working class, that have to go to them with our hand out begging, and we’re tired of it.”
The Iveagh Gardens and St Stephen’s Green are among the many parks closed today due to the strike.
