Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald claimed the Government has “played a really terrible and disrespectful game of chicken with 300,000 workers that we all rely on”, reports Political Correspondent Cormac McQuinn .
She made the remarks outside the gates of Leinster House where there was about 150 workers from the Houses of the Oireachtas, the National Museum and the National Library on picket lines.
McDonald argued that the industrial action is “a reflection of the failure of Government”.
She added: “It beggars belief that they have known now for months that they needed to engage and negotiate a new pay agreement and they have failed to do that.”
The Dublin Central TD said there is a “really strong sense of public support for all of the workers” and “these are pay negotiations that need to happen”.
“The very idea that the Government is playing a game of semantics or a game of chicken or brinksmanship with workers and refusing to acknowledge that pay will in fact be the core item and the first item for discussion is absolutely incomprehensible to me.
“So we are calling on the Government to act. I think at this stage the Taoiseach needs to intervene. The phone needs to be lifted.”
She said there must be “clarity” given to workers that “they have been heard, that the cost-of-living crisis that they face is real, that their need for a pay settlement is honourable and deserved and that the talks will happen with pay at their core” and as “the first item for discussion”.
“The bottom line is pay,” said Emma Tyrrell, a District Court clerk on the picket line at the Criminal Courts of Justice, reports Legal Affairs Correspondent Mary Carolan .
“The cost of living is rising and our wages are not. I’m just back from maternity leave, I’ve two young kids, I’ve a mortgage to pay. I’ve childcare costs, petrol, all them things. Inflation is rising, so should our wages.”
Pay, housing and the cost of living are huge concerns for Ian Temple, who was recently promoted to the rank of executive officer, having been a clerical officer for four years. He works in the Phoenix House courts complex.
Housing and energy costs are up 10 per cent, transport 7.5 per cent and it is to go up again, diesel is up 22 per cent, home-heating oil is up 60 per cent, said Temple as he stood on the picket line. “I think it’s very disingenuous to say to people with a straight face that things are okay. Come out to the north inner city.”
He and his wife are renting in a rent pressure zone, paying €1,500 monthly. “That’s 50 per cent of my wages gone, there’s no chance of any mortgage because of the systemic rules laid down after the banking crisis 20 years ago.”
Housing costs are a huge burden for him and many others, he says. “That’s where all my money is going, it’s also going to Electric Ireland. And there’s no grants for renters, there’s more than half a million of us.
“I absolutely love helping people every day, I deal with claims in the accountants’ office, every day I answer that call and help people I know I’m helping citizens. I ask citizens today to support us to get that extra bit of money. We’re looking for what we deserve.”
Ciarán Lyons, an executive officer in the Phoenix House courts complex, said because of the housing crisis, he, at the age of 38, is living at home with his parents.
His pay is around the level of the medium industrial wage, meaning buying or renting a house would be very difficult, said Lyons.
“The pay deal for the public service expired at the start of June and the Government had not meaningfully engaged with the union leadership for us and the other unions involved since then,” said Lyons.
Pay should be the first item discussed and agreed on the agenda, but it has not been in the past two pay deals, he said.
“Even including the 1 per cent from the last pay deal, workers are worse off than we were at the same time in 2023.”
Lyons, a Forsa local workplace representative, said clerical officers had approached him coming up to the strike saying their pay is so low they could not afford to lose a day’s pay.
“One of the most common queries I’ve had is clerical officers saying we want this better deal, we want to be out with our colleagues, but they are scared and anxious of even losing a day’s pay.”
Emma Courtney and Gillian Teehan, both members of the Association of Higher Civil Public Servants, said they were on the picket line at the Four Courts primarily in solidarity with colleagues on lower grades struggling with housing and cost-of-living issues.
“I was an EO [executive officer] and a CO [clerical officer] and I know how tough it is for them, and the nurses, the guards, the younger people” said Courtney. “We’d love a few more quid but if it came to the lower paid workers, getting it, that’s fine.”
“Twenty, 30 years ago, you wouldn’t have younger people living at home with their parents, they would have left, but they have no choice now,” she added.
“There is an inequity in the system,” said Teehan, citing teachers on lower pay grades as an example.
Community nurses were protesting outside the Summerhill primary care centre in Dublin 1 on Wednesday morning, reports Health Correspondent Shauna Bowers .
The nurses said they provide a cradle-to-grave service, often visiting patients in their homes, while using their own cars.
Anita Ennis said the protest was not just about pay, but also about the impact the cost-of-living crisis was having on staff.
Andrea Kelleher, a member of trade union Fórsa who works in BreastCheck Western Unit to the rear of University Hospital Galway campus, said health workers “feel like we have no choice” but to strike, reports Dara Bradley .
“With the cost of living, we are all just struggling to manage on a day-to-day basis. We need hope that we are going to get some pay increases.
“Over 5,000 people have joined Fórsa in the last few days. The next scheduled strike is the 21st of this month. We all hope we won’t have to stand out here again but if we have to we will,” said Kelleher.
More than 150 staff are gathered on strike outside Garda Headquarters in the Phoenix Park on Wednesday morning, reports Hugh Dooley .
“Nobody wants to be on strike. Nobody wants to lose a day’s pay. We just want proper negotiations to start,” Garda control room operator Sinéad Mason (33) told The Irish Times.
“We’re all struggling. The cost of living is rising drastically. It’s very simple.”
Mason was joined on the picket by her daughter Megan (12) and her one-year old Maltese-Shih Tzu, Felix – the cost of food for dogs and teenagers is rising too, she said.
“I didn’t think we would get to this point, but here we all are,” Mason said, gesturing at the assembled protesters buoyed by a passing car blaring its horn to the crowd.
“Civil and public sector workers keep the country going. I myself work in the control room answering emergency calls from the public day in, day out.”
Much like doctors, nurses, midwives and the uniformed gardaí, Mason said the staff assembled with their placards are “essential” and “should be protected” from the rising pressures of the cost of living.
The sight of protesters outside Garda HQ is not new, but as civilian staff strike, the frontline gardaí are legally compelled to continue working.
Both Garda unions have come out in support of the strike, and that solidarity manifested in Garda members activating their sirens momentarily while leaving HQ.
The Government will do “everything we possibly can” to reach agreement with public sector unions, the Taoiseach has said.
Micheál Martin said Public Expenditure Minister Jack Chambers and his officials are “working very hard” to enter dialogue and negotiations.
He said: “I think we can move this into a better space in terms of getting a resolution to all of the outstanding issues.
“I understand fully the pressures public servants are on and workers are on so our focus is on trying to get a process going that can lead to a satisfactory outcome in terms of a new national pay agreement, which is what we want to put in place.”
Martin said budgetary decisions provided “a very strong foundation and platform” for public service pay talks, adding that he detects “good will all round”.
Speaking at the Government’s AI summit, he said: “I think the foundations are there for a very substantive engagement between unions and Government, and we certainly will be doing everything we possibly can.” – PA
Taoiseach Micheál Martin has said he is open to the idea of an “honest broker” to resolve the public sector pay strikes, reports Ronan McGreevy .
The suggestion was made by Forsá general secretary Kevin Callinan on RTÉ Radio 1’s Morning Ireland programme.
Martin responded that the Government “is open to negotiation, we want dialogue”.
He said he detected a “spirit of goodwill all round” to get the public pay issues resolved.
“I know the Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers is working hard on this and his officials in the department are well-practised in relation to public service pay negotiations,” he said
Martin said he noted a change of tone among trade union leaders towards further engagement and a process that could lead to a resolution.
“With goodwill on all sides, I think we can move into a better space in terms of getting a resolution to this dispute,” he told reporters at an AI summit in the RDS.
When asked if he thought a second day of strikes could be avoided, he responded: “I would hope so. That’s a matter for the trade union movement. We will spare no effort to get talks going. We will continue to try and open a process of dialogue.”
“I would like to think that without overstating it. I understand fully the pressures public servants are on and workers are on.
“Our focus is on trying to get a process going that could lead to a satisfactory outcome and a new national pay agreement.”
Labour Party leader Ivana Bacik said she has been visiting picket lines in her Dublin Bay South constituency and she has been “struck by the high levels of support from members of the public from cars honking as they go by” to people bringing the striking workers doughnuts and coffee, reports Political Correspondent Cormac McQuinn .
She said: “People understand that many public sector workers are very lowly paid and that in particular there’s a real concern with the rising cost of living, with rising inflation that public sector pay is not protected against inflation and that’s why the Government need to engage on national pay talks.”
She accused Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers of “recklessly” letting the last public pay deal lapse “for several months before making any sort of positive signs that he’s willing to engage and put pay squarely on the table”.
Speaking to reporters outside the gates of Leinster House – where there is also a picket taking place – Bacik said: “Pay talks must do what they say on the tin. Pay must be first and foremost in the negotiations and we really hope that last night’s glimmer of hope from Government will move things on.”
This was a reference to Chambers telling RTÉ’s Prime Time that pay can “absolutely” be the starting point for negotiations.
Bacik said she had spoken to Fórsa union boss Kevin Callinan and “he’s also said publicly that he believes there is now a pathway to resolving this”.
“Nobody wants to go on strike for a second day. Nobody wanted to be out today but they were left with no choice.”
She said the Labour Party will table a motion in the Dáil on Thursday “calling for Government again to engage meaningfully in talks ... to put pay first and foremost and we really hope we see things moving over the next two days before the weekend”.
Bacik said: “The ball is in Jack Chambers’ court and the Taoiseach’s court.”
Wednesday’s protest is about a “breach in trust” and a “lack of confidence” in the industrial relations system, union leaders have said, reports Health Correspondent Shauna Bowers .
Fòrsa’s Kevin Callinan, Phil Ní Sheaghdha from the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation (INMO), Adrian Kane from Siptu, and John Boyle from the Irish National Teachers’ Organisation (INTO) attended the picket line at the Mater hospital in Dublin on Wednesday morning.
“It’s over to the Government now to try and address those things if this dispute is going to be resolved,” Callinan said.
He added that if Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers is “sincere” in his comments to discuss pay first then “it’s possible that there may be a way in which a framework can be built on that”.
“I’ve indicated that the Taoiseach needs to intervene. Consider that. Obviously, if that’s possible, we’ll work with it. If it doesn’t happen, we’re gonna have another strike next week and so on,” he said.
Asked if they are open to an independent mediator, Callinan said they will consider “anything that is reasonable”.
About 200 Dublin City Council workers gathered on the steps of the Civic offices, reports Dublin Editor Olivia Kelly .
“I think we need to be heard at this stage. We provide such a vital services for the public. We keep the city going and we deserve to have a pay rise going with inflation rates,” said Audrey Lambert, secretary of the Fórsa Dublin city branch.
“We have young people that come in and join us and they cannot stay because the pay is not enough. They can’t get housing. They can’t support themselves.
“We have people, mothers, that are struggling to go to work, to pay childcare and it’s essential that we have a fair pay for everyone here.”
At the Fórsa picket outside the Irish Lights building at Dún Laoghaire harbour, civil engineering technician Colin Ball sounds slightly exasperated that the public service pay dispute has come to him and his colleagues picketing from early morning, reports Work Correspondent Emmet Malone .
Workers from admin, procurement, facilities management and diverse array of other roles stand close by and nod in agreement as he suggests “they [the Government] have had a long time to sort this”.
“They’ve had months but they haven’t really done anything so we’re just standing here, supporting each other, trying to get a better deal,” he says as drivers of buses and cars beep their horns in support of the strikers while passing by.
Asked about the suggestion by James Lawless earlier on Wednesday morning that public servants tend to be better paid than their private sector counterparts, Ball seems surprised.
“I don’t think that’s fair to be honest. But the issue is that the agreement expired in June, and they’ve had plenty of time to sort a new one out. The rate of inflation’s gone up so much but our pay hasn’t gone up. That’s why we are here.”
People Before Profit-Solidarity TD Richard Boyd Barrett joined the Fórsa picket outside the Irish Lights building in Dún Laoghaire and said he hopes there will be talks to end the public sector pay dispute over the coming days as he visited various pickets in his constituency on Wednesday morning.
“I think the Government has been playing a game of chicken with the unions but what they are seeing this morning is an enormous show of strength and I hope that leads to talks now,” he said.
“People are telling me they don’t want to be out on strike but they say they will do it again if they have to and it’s very obvious as you travel around just how strong public support is for the action,” he continued.
“There’s a lot of anger with Jack Chambers, that it has come to this.
“People of all ages, but a lot of young people have been talking about how they are struggling with cost of living issues, things like the cost of accommodation.
“It’s all very inspiring, I’m hearing a lot of people have been joining unions in the last few weeks and it’s inspiring to see how many people are out this morning, how high their morale seems to be.
“Hopefully other people will be inspired too because it’s not just public sector workers who are struggling with the cost-of-living crisis.”
Martina Burke, a healthcare assistant at one of the country’s busiest emergency departments at University Hospital Galway, has a 40km commute to work in Galway city from her home in Kilmaine, Co Mayo, reports Dara Bradley .
A mother of adult children, like hundreds of workers on the picket line at UHG, she’s feeling the pinch of higher fuel prices and the cost-of-living crisis.
“I work three long days. I’m up in the morning at half five; not home ‘til quarter past nine. It’s a long day. It’s busy in the ED. It’s hard work. But the work isn’t the problem, it’s the pay. We want fair pay,” she says.
A rep with trade union Siptu for 20 years, this is Burke’s second strike and she feels the public is backing the industrial action.
“People who filter through the hospital see the hard work we do. The public are very supportive of us,” says Burke, who adds that workers agreed cover in the wards and emergency department to “make it safe” for patients during the strike.
“Our message to the Government is sit down, talk and listen to the unions. We don’t want to be here today, no one does. We had a 95 per cent vote to strike, which was overwhelming – it means everyone wants the same thing.
“If they don’t sit down with us, we will 100 per cent be back here again next week,” says Burke.
Fintan Hourihan, chief executive of the Irish Dental Association (IDA), said the protest was about more than just pay but also about supporting the service to meet the needs of its special care patients as a group of public dentists picket outside the Roselawn health centre in Blanchardstown, Dublin.
Wednesday marked the first ever strike action by members of the IDA since it was founded in 1922, reports Health Correspondent Shauna Bowers .
Conor Carroll, a porter at St Michael’s Hospital in Dún Laoghaire, says Wednesday’s strike is all about wages and the increased cost of getting by, reports Work Correspondent Emmet Malone .
“We’re just out looking for fair play,” he says, as he pickets alongside colleagues from Fórsa, the Medical Laboratory Scientists Association and the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation at the hospital gates on the town’s main street this morning.
“It’s just about the cost of living. Every time you go to the supermarket you feel it,” he says, gesturing towards the Tesco shopping centre across the road.
“Everything’s gone up, even the cost of eating, and whatever you’re earning doesn’t feel like enough these days.
The hospital, he says, is a good place work, a community operation where “everyone gets on”. And it has good to him since he switched from bar work eight years ago to be around more for his then young children.
“Management are good, they are always helpful with rosters when you need it,” he says, explaining that he commutes from Lucan and tries to work shifts that allow him do a school run.
“I have no complaints, really, except that my pay hasn’t gone up,” he says, “and everything else has.”
Jason Dee, a visitor service officer at Dublin Castle, described the strike as “very necessary,” reports Órla Ryan .
“There should be a natural transition from when a pay deal expires into the next deal,” he said, referring to the fact the Public Service Agreement 2024–2026 expired in June and a new deal has not yet been reached.
Dee said “everyone is feeling” the impact of inflation, especially lower paid workers.
He said the strike is “an inconvenience to people and to tourists and to everybody, so I think it’s in everyone’s interest that it’s resolved”.
At Dún Laoghaire’s Intreo Office on Cumberland Street, staff who are used to dealing with other people’s employment issues were outside having to explain to the occasional service user that they are having some of their own, reports Emmet Malone .
“We’ve had a few people along this morning, and when they’ve seen us and they’ve asked a couple of questions about why we are striking,” said Lyndsay McGlynn, the centres manager, as she stands with a handful of her co-workers. “But we’ve had no negative feedback. It’s been very understanding and supportive.”
She said she wants to see talks between the unions and hopes the industrial action can be sorted out before the second scheduled one-day stoppage next Wednesday.
Asked if it should have been sorted out before today, with Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers having effectively said last night pay could be dealt with up front, she says the comments came too late.
“It’s something that came out the day before the strike, the night before it, I think it should have happened a lot earlier.
“I do hope that in the next little while it will get resolved. Hopefully, we don’t have to do another strike date next Wednesday.
“But people are very united, all of us here and across all the grades, you saw over 90 per cent voting for the strike everywhere.
“Missing two days’ wages would be a big commitment for all of us but we are doing it because the wages need to be increased, particularly for those on the lower pay.
“We are very united and I do think if it continues people will be determined enough to see it through.”
Lisa Walsh McAuley, a visitor and security officer at the National Museum, said workers “haven’t had a decent pay rise in forever”, reports Órla Ryan .
“I don’t see anything in my pay packet. I really don’t because they give with one hand and they take with the other.”
Walsh McAuley said she deals with thousands of people every week in her role and, like many workers in the public sector, has been “double jobbing” – ie, doing extra work that does not fall under her role.
“It seems as if this Government wants to push us as far as we can possibly go. We have role creep in our jobs. Some of us are double jobbing, and that’s taking a toll.”
She called on Jack Chambers and other members of the Government to help workers who have been badly impacted by the cost of living.
“Jack seems to be the kind of person – and I can understand where he’s coming from because of his position – that he has to guard the money. But we have a pot there already. How big does he want this pot to be? It has to be spent somewhere ... Either start giving something back or just watch out for the next election because I ain’t happy.”
Walsh McAuley said she hopes the issue is resolved soon, but “we’ll be here next week, if needs be”.
Workers from some of Dublin’s best-known cultural institutions and tourist attractions have called on the Government to engage with trade unions to avoid further strike action, reports Órla Ryan .
Brian Rice, digitisation programme manager at the National Library, said comments by Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers – who on Tuesday night told RTÉ’s Prime Time that pay can “absolutely” be the starting point for negotiations – came too little, too late.
“The Government had the opportunity to engage earlier; they didn’t take it, and now we’re out because of that,” Rice said.
“They should have engaged with workers earlier on this, and I think it’s time to sit down now and it’s time to listen to what workers have to say rather than just arrive at a fait accompli, and to come to some agreement that both parties are happy with.”
Rice said workers are struggling with the cost of inflation and “pay really needs to catch up with where prices have gone”.
“There’s lots of levels of pay in the Library, and I think we’d like to see the lower paid helped more, so they’re proportionally lifted up higher because it is much tougher for them.”
Fine Gael TD Barry Ward has warned: “If people are not sitting down around the table, this won’t be resolved,” reports Vivienne Clarke.
There had been “a concerted attempt” by Government in recent weeks to get people around the table to talk about it, he told RTÉ Radio’s Today with David McCullagh show.
“That hasn’t happened because of preconditions that have been laid down. And I don’t really think you can approach a negotiation by saying to people, well, we’ve got to agree this before we even talk.
“If people are not sitting down around the table, this won’t be resolved. And whatever about honest brokers or whether somebody mediates the discussion or somebody else is brought in to do that, that doesn’t matter. If people are not willing to sit around the table, it won’t be resolved. And what’s really important for ordinary people all over this country is that it is resolved and they get their services back,” he said.
However, People Before Profit TD Paul Murphy told the same programme that he expected to be back on the picket line again next Wednesday.
“What we’re hearing so far from the Government is not a commitment to seriously engage on pay. And therefore the workers are left with no choice. And when you talk to workers, they’re clear. Look, I don’t want to be on a picket line, but they voted overwhelmingly to take strike action. They’re doing so because they’re in a desperate situation.
“Because they see their income being eroded year after year. Where from 2021 to now, the total increases they’ve had in pay is just under 16 per cent. And the inflation rate over that period is about 22 per cent.
“So they’re struggling. And I would say, the beeps from people coming by all the picket lines I’ve been on this morning are incredible. The level of public support for this strike should make the government think again.”
Bags of rubbish left outside the closed Grangegorman recycling centre in Dublin 7 as workers at the centre are on strike.
Fórsa members John FitzGerald and psychotherapist Evelyn Newell holding her dog Alfie were among the hundreds of striking health workers on the picket lines at University Hospital Galway this morning, reports Dara Bradley .
Doctors, nurses, medical laboratory scientists, physiotherapists and other healthcare staff have gathered outside the Mater hospital in Dublin in protest over pay, reports Health Correspondent Shauna Bowers .
The large crowd of healthcare workers is greeted by horns of support by passing cars, trucks and bin lorries as they call for a better pay deal.
“What do we want? Fair pay. When do we want it? Now,” the protesters chanted.
The gathering comes ahead of the four officers of the public services committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions uniting outside the healthcare facility to outline their demands to Government.
Kevin Callinan from Fórsa, Phil Ní Sheaghdha from the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation (INMO), Adrian Kane from Siptu and John Boyle from the Irish National Teachers’ Organisation (INTO) are in attendance.
Strike action is taking place abroad as well, writes Europe Correspondent Jack Power
A small Fórsa picket is set up outside the Republic’s largest diplomatic mission overseas, the Permanent Representation of Ireland to the EU.
About 300 diplomats, civil servants and officials are working in the Brussels office, which has greatly expanded to shoulder the extra workload during Ireland’s six month EU presidency.
Civil servants and temporary staff working in Brussels were unsure to what extent they were covered by the industrial strike action, with conflicting advice and guidance coming from Dublin.
The picket nearly didn’t happen, but for a different reason.
The local council, or commune, of the Belgian capital that hosts the EU’s institutions and embassies, requires 10 days’ notice for a protest or public demonstration.
Fórsa got in the paperwork a week ago and the local Belgian administration isn’t known for its flexibility, but they showed a bit of leeway on this occasion.
Two passersby shouted encouragement for the strike as they walked by, and they didn’t even sound French.
Stephanie Goggins, a primary school teacher at Pelletstown Educate Together primary school in Ashtown, Dublin 15 said, she is “living pay cheque to pay cheque”, reports Education Correspondent Niamh Towey .
“I’m earning the most money I’ve ever earned in my career, and I’m still struggling,” Goggins says.
Goggins, who was among dozens of protesters in Ashtown this morning, says there is “a strong feeling among the staff that we want to fight for this and we deserve a fair wage”.
She feels teachers need a pay increase that is “in line with the cost of living, that we can live comfortably on. You know, many of us are well-educated people. We’re dedicated to our work, and we deserve a wage that reflects that.”
Kevin Callinan, the general secretary of Fórsa and chair of Ictu’s Public Services Committee, has called for the appointment of an independent mediator in the public sector pay dispute, reports Vivienne Clarke .
The Taoiseach needs to take the initiative to try to break the impasse and the appointment of an independent mediator would be a way to do that, he told RTÉ Radio’s Morning Ireland.
It was “disrespectful” to suggest that more than 300,000 people had gone on strike “as a first resort rather than as a last resort”, he said.
“Nobody wants to be on strike, there is a way that we can resolve this but we need a shift in the Government position. I’ve made clear this morning, I think that there is a way in which that can be done.
“I think the Taoiseach needs to take an initiative to try and break the impasse and I’ve suggested how that might be done. If there was an honest broker perhaps assisted by a representative from the employer side and a representative from the union side, it has worked before and I think it’s worth trying.”
Adrian Kane, Siptu deputy general secretary, has called for “senior political intervention” in the public sector strike, reports Vivienne Clarke .
There had been “a rupture in the social contract” between the Government and public sector workers, he told Newstalk Breakfast with Anton Savage.
It would be helpful if the Taoiseach intervened, he responded when asked if Micheál Martin should get involved.
The onus was now on the unions to take the next step to ensure “a deal is done”, said the Minister for Higher Education James Lawless, reports Vivienne Clarke.
The Taoiseach had invited the unions to discuss social partnership, but the unions had “effectively said no thanks, or not right now”.
“I think that’s regrettable, because I think if we did get around the table more often, we’d be in a better place to make progress on these kind of issues,” he told RTÉ Radio’s Morning Ireland.
“And again, my heart goes out to the workers on the ballot today, the parents who had to take children out of school, the hospital appointments being cancelled, the driving test and all the disruption.
“I respect the process, absolutely, but let’s try and not have this again next week and on into the future. The Taoiseach was open to discussion, he had made that position very clear.
“He said pay is always the central issue. He said let’s get on with it. He’s open for discussion.
“No deal was ever done by one side staying outside the room. I think the onus really is on the union now to take the next step.”
In letters to the editor, Irish Times readers had mixed opinions on Wednesday’s strike by public sector unions:
Sir, – The public servants taking industrial action are not available for work and consequently have to forego a day’s pay. However, many TDs, who have a salary of just under €120,000, have indicated over the past week that they would not pass the picket at Leinster House and therefore make themselves unavailable for work, writes David Gordan.
Sir, – I believe the public sector unions are making a major strategic error in their approach to the negotiations with Government on the new pay deal, writes Paul Kilcullen.
In an employment environment increasingly dominated by artificial intelligence (AI), the tactics adopted against Government and the public are ill-advised. The next agreement will be dominated by AI productivity and job losses. The public sector, particularly the Civil Service, is full of opportunities for its use.
Fórsa general secretary, Kevin Callinan, said Jack Chambers’s comments on the potential to discuss pay at the start of any negotiations is “promising” but is not in itself enough to call off next Wednesday’s second one-day strike, reports Work Correspondent Emmet Malone .
He told Morning Ireland he would like to see the Taoiseach seek to appoint “an honest broker” with experience of industrial relations to bring the two sides together.
“It’s worked before and I think it would be worth trying,” he said.
Callinan reiterated that one of the issues is the “breakdown in trust” relating to problems over the payment of “local bargaining” aspects of the last pay deal and the Government’s failure to honour a commitment to repeal Financial Emergency Measures in Public Interests (Fempi) legislation. The legislation was introduced after the financial crash to prevent local deals being done in the public service and to tighten the Government’s control of its finances.
Trade union Siptu said Wednesday’s strike action was its largest mobilisation of its members in a generation.
“More than 60,000 Siptu members will take part in the strike, manning up to 2,000 picket lines across the country alongside tens of thousands of other trade union colleagues in the public sector,” it said in a statement on Wednesday.
Picketing by Siptu members began at midnight at local authority facilities.
Emergency cover will operate under agreed local arrangements to protect life and public safety.
Siptu deputy general secretary, Adrian Kane, said: “This mobilisation demonstrates the determination of our members to secure a better deal for workers struggling under a worsening cost-of-living crisis and a Government which is dismissive of their concerns.
“The €1.2 billion announced in the budget for public sector pay claims is an offer of a pay increase of approximately 2.5 per cent in 2027 once pension costs and previous commitments are included.
“With annual inflation currently running at 4.1 per cent this provides no credible starting point for talks aimed at protecting living standards,” he said.
If you’re curious about today’s weather, Met.ie might not be the most up-to-date place for information.
“Due to industrial action, there will be disruptions to updates on met.ie on Wednesday 14th October,” a post on Met Éireann’s site reads today.
However, Met Éireann previously published two yellow weather warnings for Wednesday.
A yellow wind warning is in place for counties Donegal, Galway and Mayo from 6am to 6pm on Wednesday.
A yellow rain warning is valid from 6pm on Wednesday to 6am on Thursday in counties Donegal, Galway, Leitrim, Mayo and Sligo.
Industrial action should be the last resort, Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke has said as he urged unions to enter talks with the Government. Vivienne Clarke reports.
“A strike should be the last resort. That’s the way the industrial relations architecture has worked because we all know here this morning that this issue will be resolved. All industrial strikes, in my memory, have always been resolved,” he told Newstalk Breakfast with Anton Savage.
“But how they are resolved is by dialogue, by sitting around the negotiating table, trying to get strands of commonality and agreement and getting a sustainable agreement for, first of all, their members.
“And that has been the case, as I pointed out, that over the last pay agreement, we’ve had pay increases of about 9.6 per cent cumulatively, which outpaced inflation of 6.6 per cent. So that’s real wage growth for employees who are in the public service. And the Government wants to be a good employer.
“We want to offer better pay, better conditions, but we also have to get better services for the public,” he said. “We’ve been very clear that we want to improve paying conditions for all members of the public and Civil Service right throughout our country. We want better conditions, but we also need a sustainable agreement for the taxpayer. And that’s Government’s obligation.
“We can’t negotiate an agreement that ultimately will leave our country exposed or that won’t be sustainable. I think that’s only responsible of any government to take that approach.”
Micheál Martin had a tetchy exchange with a metaphor-chucking Mary Lou McDonald in the Dáil chamber on Tuesday.
She accused him of “playing chicken” with the public sector unions. Now, McDonald implied, the chicken games were coming home to roost.
Whatever about the chickens, he remained unflappable throughout. Only his innocence seemed injured. More than once, he spoke of the “enhanced social dialogue” he had offered trade unions in vain.
Frank McNally details the exchange in his Dáil sketch here.
The Taoiseach should intervene to get a talks process started if further public sector strikes and disruption are to be prevented, Fórsa union leader Kevin Callinan has suggested.
As Emmet Malone and Pat Leahy report, he was speaking after the union side rebuffed late efforts by Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers and the Government side to engage and prevent Wednesday’s one-day strike .
Callinan was responding to a suggestion by Chambers that while the Government wanted talks to begin at the Workplace Relations Commission on Tuesday, he would consider other ways to achieve progress if that could not be done.
Asked about what might break the deadlock, Callinan, who also chairs the public services committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions, said it would take “an intervention. And I think that intervention has to come from ... the Taoiseach”.
The Government is likely to make a push to bring the unions into a talks process after the stoppage as it seeks to avoid further strikes scheduled for next week.
According to sources familiar with the Government’s position, renewed efforts to start negotiations in the coming days may include seeking an independent mediator or facilitator to bring the two sides together. Coalition sources stopped short of saying they would agree to the unions’ demand to deal with pay first in the negotiations.
It is likely that informal approaches will be made with a view to repairing relations that have become strained in recent days.
The Taoiseach urged trade unions yesterday to engage in further dialogue ahead of the strike.
Micheál Martin expressed concern around the disruption that could be caused and said the €1.2 billion the Government set aside in the recent budget for a pay deal provided a strong foundation for talks.
“We did appeal (on Monday) for the unions to come in for talks, and I would say in the recent budget, the Government made a number of efforts, and took a number of initiatives, that were important for workers – significant tax cuts, continued expansion of public service numbers and specific initiatives on reducing the cost of childcare,” the Taoiseach said.
“In my view, there is a strong foundation there laid by the budget and other measures to facilitate productive negotiations on a new national pay agreement. We have negotiated previous pay agreements in good faith, there is no reason why anyone should doubt our bona fides in respect of negotiating a new package.
“My real concern is the disruption that will be caused to many people, particularly patients who were expecting operations and procedures and indeed in terms of school days being lost.”
Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers had called on the unions to postpone the strike and instead enter talks at the Workplace Relations Commission.
However, the Irish Congress of Trade Unions’ Public Service Committee said there was “no basis” for the strike to be postponed.
Órla Ryan has a comprehensive piece detailing the background to the strike action and the impact it will have on public life today.
Here is what you need to know about the strike and its expected impact.
Good morning. Hundreds of thousands of public sector staff go on strike today on what could potentially be the first day of a long winter of discontent.
About 300,000 public sector workers, including nurses, doctors, teachers and civil servants, will engage in the national strike following earlier work-to-rule action.
Schools, colleges, universities, libraries, council offices and many parks are among the publicly run facilities that are closed because of the action, which involves some 300,000 workers.
Health services are severely disrupted, with all elective procedures and thousands of appointments postponed. The HSE has warned of “significant and widespread” disruption” to its services.
Members of Fórsa, Ireland’s largest public sector union, as well as Siptu had voted in favour of industrial action including strike.
The major teachers’ unions as well as collective bodies for nurses, midwives and doctors also voted in favour of action.

title: Government seeks ‘negotiation process’ to avoid second round of public sector strikes
description: Union sources play down suggestion of fresh Government initiative, though informal contacts continue
content:
Efforts are under way to unblock the path to negotiations on a new public sector pay deal after public services were brought to a standstill by nationwide industrial action on Wednesday.
It is expected that contacts between Government and unions will now intensify as officials seek to find a way forward that could avoid next week’s scheduled second day of strikes.
Speaking in Brussels on Wednesday evening, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said there was “a sense of goodwill and a willingness to get a resolution on this”.
“The Government is open for negotiations and open for dialogue, we want to get into a negotiation process,” he said. “We will engage and see if we can find a basis and a process that would be satisfactory to all sides that enable negotiations to take place and avoid any action next week.”
There have been suggestions in Government about a possible preliminary process at the Workplace Relations Commission that could see a draft agenda for negotiations agreed, but officials remained tight-lipped on Wednesday night, citing the sensitivity of the issue. Union sources played down the suggestion of a fresh initiative from Government, though it is understood informal contacts are continuing.
Fórsa general secretary Kevin Callinan said that recent comments by Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers suggested “there may be a pathway” to negotiations on a new deal.
Callinan chairs the public services committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions (Ictu) , which is due to meet on Thursday to review the situation.
Some individual unions whose members participated in the strike action met on Wednesday night to take stock and consider how to proceed if no agreement is reached and next week’s strike goes ahead.
Chambers, though, told RTÉ there was “intensive work that’s going on in the background”, and “that in the next day or so we’ll be able to set out a further context”.
[ Public opinion may shift if the second strike goes ahead Opens in new window ]
“I’m conscious that we have to progress that in the coming hours and, indeed, in the next day or so,” he said.
He continued to strike a more conciliatory tone, saying he understood the “significant pressure” that public sector workers were under, adding, “They need a new pay deal delivered.”
He said the aim of Government was for a new agreement that is a “fair, meaningful and credible deal” for workers, but added that any deal had to be “sustainable and affordable” for the State.
He said he was “absolutely” happy for the issue of pay to be dealt with as a priority in any negotiations – a key demand of the unions – but he noted that union leaders had accepted that “nothing is agreed until everything is agreed”.
Chambers praised public sector workers for doing “an incredible job” and said he hoped “we’ll find a way forward” in the “next day or so”.
Unions claimed widespread public support on the picket lines as industrial action shut schools, colleges, local and national Government offices and severely restricted health services across the country yesterday. The HSE said that appointments cancelled yesterday would be “prioritised and rescheduled as soon as possible”.
[ Health service workers claim no choice but to strike Opens in new window ]
However, it indicated that uncertainty about next week’s planned stoppage would impact its plans. “We ask patients to bear with us as there may be further delays until there is greater certainty regarding future industrial action,” the HSE said in a statement.
More than 150 schools in the Dublin and Kildare regions received threatening emails warning of potential attacks on Wednesday. The motive was not clear and the schools continued to operate as normal while taking advice from gardaí.
Opposition parties all declared support for the strikes and urged the Government to enter negotiations and agree pay increases for public servants.
Speaking outside a closed Leinster House, Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald said the Government had “played a really terrible and disrespectful game of chicken with 300,000 workers that we all rely on ... I think you can feel the really strong sense of public support for all of the workers”.

title: Waterford murders: Someone else’s €20k drug debt behind attack, family member believes
description: No arrests have been made in first wave of ‘intense’ searches
author_name: Hugh Dooley, Conor Lally, Olivia Kelleher
content:
Gardaí investigating the murder of four people in an arson attack in Co Waterford have seized a number of mobile phones and several vehicles, as two children remain in a critical condition in hospital.
Philip and Kim English, and two of their sons, Callum (12) and Jayden (8), were murdered by a gang trying to collect a €20,000 drug debt, a family member has said.
John James English, Philip English’s adult son from his first marriage, said the debt had been incurred by somebody else, not his father.
Two other children – a girl aged 14 years and a boy aged six – remain critically ill in Children’s Health Ireland (CHI) Crumlin, Dublin.
“Debts, drug debts, and I know that for a fact,” John James English told RTÉ when asked why he believed the arson attack was carried out.
“My family is dead, it’s unreal. Innocent children, the whole lot of them innocent,” he said, adding that his father was not involved in drugs or any form of crime.
John James said that when his mother, Anne, was forced out of her house for about two months after it was petrol bombed, his father, Philip, and stepmother, Kim, opened their home to Anne. She stayed there for eight weeks.
Anne English later gathered in the Birchwood estate at a vigil for the family. She said that she had ten children with Philip prior to their breakup. The former couple were lucky to have had such an amicable relationship.
Anne emphasised that she was “best friends” with Philip and Kim. She admitted she was “in disbelief” that anyone would knowingly harm the “very well liked” family. “We were one big happy family. We were very close. Their kids were their life.
Another member of the family – James English, the granduncle of Philip English – also spoke out, addressing the killer directly. “We have lost a family now, wiped out,” he said at a vigil for the family at the Sacred Heart Church, The Folly. “Please, whoever done it, be a man and own up to what you done.”
Searches on Tuesday, which included some properties with possible links to the local drugs trade, were aimed at gathering evidence, rather than seeking people for arrest. No arrests have been made, gardaí confirmed.
Detectives have established lines of inquiry and have identified suspects quickly as the campaign of intimidation against the family – by a local drugs gang in Waterford city – had been ongoing for some time .
The house at Birch Avenue remains a crime scene and subject of a technical examination by the Garda Technical Bureau.
Postmortems on the deceased are continuing at University Hospital Waterford by Chief State Pathologist Linda Mulligan and State Pathologist SallyAnne Collis.
Garda family liaison officers continue to engage with the family.
The Garda team also believes the family had shared their concerns and information about their situation with people in their social circle, who may now be able to aid the inquiry.
“There are people in the community who know the person or persons who carried out this arson attack in which four people have been murdered,” Garda Chief Supt Anthony Pettit said.
The family had approached local representatives in recent weeks in the hopes of securing a council transfer to another home as they felt unsafe.
The family’s home, on the Birchwood estate just south of Waterford city, had been attacked before, most recently last month, when a petrol bomb was thrown at their car.
In 2023, the same vehicle was vandalised with a bucket of paint, but it is unclear whether this was directly linked to the arson attacks in recent weeks.
[ Nine-year-old boy killed in Waterford arson attack had heart surgery two weeks ago Opens in new window ]
The latest attack, which happened just after 5am on Tuesday, involved a petrol bomb, which was thrown at the front door, causing a fire that spread through the two-storey semidetached house.
In addition to the two adults and two children who died, two other children suffered critical injuries.
They were initially taken to University Hospital Waterford but moved to Children’s Health Ireland in Crumlin on Tuesday. They remained in critical condition on Wednesday morning.
Though the investigation is at an early stage, gardaí suspect Philip English had taken on a drug debt incurred by an associate in an effort to keep the associate safe.
Gardaí strongly suspect the local crime gang that was owed money targeted the family on Tuesday morning, and was also behind last month’s attack.
The Taoiseach said on Wednesday the Government will put in place all resources needed for the Garda investigation, and for community supports, as he thanked the first responders for dealing with “what was a very traumatic situation”.
[ Deaths in Waterford attack put focus on increase in drug-related intimidation Opens in new window ]
“Our thoughts are still very much on the shocking murder yesterday of the members of the English family,” Micheál Martin said.
“The situation is extremely shocking in terms of the level of violence and the consequences of an entire family to be impacted in this manner, and I think we, as a Government, will ensure that the full resources are behind An Garda Síochána.
“It’s also a period [when] we have to really examine and reflect on this phenomenon of arson attacks on innocent people, and with absolutely no consideration for human life and for the impact of such actions, and I know the Minister for Justice and others will be working extremely hard to stamp this out and to deal very resolutely and robustly with this.”

title: ‘Their kids were their life. People should come forward’
description: Parish priest appeals to those behind fire to ‘stand up, admit what you did and face the consequences’
content:
Pink and blue balloons were released into the sky outside the home of the English family in Waterford city today as relatives and friends hugged and wiped back tears, just beginning to absorb the finality of their loss.
Anne English, the ex-wife of the late Philip English, was among those gathered in the Birchwood estate.
She said she had 10 children with Philip before their break-up and they were lucky to have had such an amicable relationship.
Anne said she was “best friends” with Philip and Kim and was in “disbelief” that anyone would knowingly harm the “very well liked” family.
“We were one big happy family. We were very close. Their kids were their life,” she said. “People should come forward if anyone knows anything. It is a devastating loss.”
Anne had not spoken to the couple very much in recent weeks. She said Kim and Philip were kept busy at the children’s hospital in Crumlin as their son Jayden had been undergoing heart surgery.
On Wednesday night, two of their children were still fighting for their lives at the very same hospital.
Family friend Amanda Powney said Philip and Kim had “gone through hell” over the last few years and were trying to get a transfer out of their home amid concern for their safety.
When Powney heard there was a fire in Waterford, she instantly felt the English family had been targeted. “I knew because of [a] previous attack on the car. The guards knew long ago [what was going on],” she said.
The perpetrators “deserve to be locked up and never let out again. I hope they rot in hell,” Powney said.
As the people gathered for the 5pm vigil on Wednesday evening, four candles – two big and two small – were placed in front of a family picture at a table in the Sacred Heart church.
Parish priest Fr Gerry Chestnutt told the several hundred people gathered that the couple had gone to bed expecting to take their children to school the following day.
An “innocent family” had been robbed of their lives in a horrific manner, he said. “What happened yesterday should never, ever have happened.
“I want to say that even though they are not here, the persons responsible need to have the courage to stand up, admit what you did and face the consequences of what you did.
“If you know anything whatsoever about what happened, please contact An Garda Síochána .”
Members of the congregation laughed as the priest spoke about Philip being “a great man for a chat”. He said you would need time to spare if you bumped into him at the shop. Everything the couple did was for their children, he said.
Bishop Alphonsus Cullinan offered prayers for the two English children who remain in critical condition in hospital.
He also paid tribute to the “heroic neighbours” at the scene and praised the emergency services for their professionalism.
The Sacred Heart church has extended its opening hours in the coming days to give members of the community additional time to pray.

title: ‘Something could have been done’ to prevent Omagh bombing, Nuala O’Loan tells inquiry
description: Former police ombudsman says co-ordinated investigation of previous Real IRA bombings may have hindered organisation
content:
The inquiry into the Omagh bombing has been told “there must be something that could have been done” to prevent the atrocity.
Asked by the lead counsel to the inquiry, Paul Greaney, if it continued to be her view “that the Omagh bombing could have been prevented”, Northern Ireland ’s first police ombudsman, Nuala O’Loan, replied that this was “now for the inquiry to decide”.
But she added that her understanding was that the Real IRA bombings which preceded the attack on Omagh “were individually investigated, there was no linking of them ... and I think if that had happened, it’s possible that the activities of the Real IRA at this stage could have been hindered very definitely”.
She added that, when taken together with mobile phone evidence, “it seems to me that there’s a very cogent argument for saying that there must be something that could have been done”.
A total of 31 people, including unborn twins, died and hundreds were injured when a car bomb planted by the dissident republican group the Real IRA exploded in the centre of Omagh on August 15th, 1998.
The public inquiry, which opened in 2024 under Alan Turnbull, is examining whether the atrocity could reasonably have been prevented by British state authorities.
Its third chapter, which opened in Belfast last month, is examining how the bombing was carried out and who was responsible.
On Wednesday, it heard evidence O’Loan launched an inquiry into the original RUC investigation into the Omagh bombing following a newspaper report in 2001.
The article, in the Sunday People, claimed undercover agent Kevin Fulton told his RUC handlers a car bomb was being prepared three days before the attack on Omagh.
[ Warning to Defence Forces night before bombing ended with ‘Omagh, Omagh, Omagh’, inquiry told Opens in new window ]
O’Loan’s report found police received an anonymous telephone call on August 4th, 1998, which contained detailed information that an attack would be made in Omagh on the 15th, but it was not acted upon.
In her evidence to the inquiry, O’Loan outlined problems with the police’s co-operation with her investigation, describing it as “profoundly difficult ... we were trying to almost draw teeth in terms of getting information out of the police”.
She described difficulties with the provision of material, including intelligence material, by the RUC, and her “astonishment” that “in one case we haven’t even been told about this very significant document”.
The inquiry heard a copy of that document – an RUC review of its investigation into the Omagh bombing by chief superintendent Brian McVicker – was later personally delivered to O’Loan by the then chief constable, Ronnie Flanagan.
In her evidence, O’Loan described meeting Flanagan before the publication of her final report in December 2001, and “he, among other things, told me that I was going to destroy the peace process, that my office would never recover”.
“I said to him, ‘All you have to do, Ronnie, you have to admit there’s a problem with the Omagh bomb investigation, and really get it going and resourced, and you have to set up systems for the dissemination of intelligence,’” O’Loan said.
The former police ombudsman described it a “very unpleasant” meeting and she was “shocked” afterwards, and added Flanagan subsequently urged her not to publish the report.
Greaney also referred to attacks of a “personal nature” on O’Loan at that time, including comments made by the former Ulster Unionist MP Ken Maginnis on the BBC’s Newsnight on December 6th, 2001.
O’Loan described it as “a very serious attack, and I was called a suicide bomber, and it was said that I’d outlived my usefulness, which was dangerous.”

title: The Irish Times view on the AI Summit: who controls the machines?
description: The questions raised by the acceleration of the technology are real, serious and potentially existential
content:
Politicians, regulators and technology leaders gathered in Dublin yesterday for the AI Summit, one of the landmark events of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, where they heard the Commission’s tech chief, Henna Virkkunen, set out a vision for Europe, and executives from Google, Microsoft and others make their case.
It is a sign of how far AI has moved from the margins to the centre of political debate that Micheál Martin will chair a new Cabinet committee on the subject, covering its effects on society and work as well as its regulation and use in the public service.
The questions raised by the acceleration of the technology are real, serious and potentially existential. For Europe, the prospect of being left behind once more is particularly pressing after years in which the EU’s economic growth has stalled and slipped ever further behind the US and China.
Then there is the looming prospect of mass job displacement and the social dislocation that could follow in its wake. Meanwhile, the industry’s seemingly insatiable appetite for ever more computing power is driving a data centre construction boom that strains local resources and is sparking opposition in affected communities.
Above all there is the prospect, promoted most vociferously by the AI companies themselves, that these systems are advancing so rapidly that they may soon escape human control and threaten the survival of our species.
All of this is far beyond the capacity of a one-day summit to address, but some things are clear. This is an industry that warns of catastrophe while asking governments for rules, though often on terms of its own choosing. Europe, for its part, is delaying some of the high-risk obligations in its own AI Act until 2027 and 2028.
One part of this complex jigsaw is already the subject of intense legal and political argument. A parallel conference in Dublin yesterday, held by the news publishing and recorded music sectors, represented groups experiencing the real consequences of displacement and disruption. To train their models, AI companies have used vast quantities of copyright material produced by authors, journalists, composers and other creators. One company, Anthropic, has agreed to pay $1.5 billion to settle claims over pirated books, without admitting wrongdoing. OpenAI and Microsoft await the outcome of their court battle with The New York Times. AI-generated answers are replacing clicks on search results, depriving websites of traffic.
These are important questions for the survival of the creative industries but also for how we define the future relationship between human capabilities and these immensely powerful, privately-owned machines.

title: Bradley Barcola’s clinical hat-trick inspires Liverpool to 6-3 rout at LASK
description: Andoni Iraola’s side quick to shake off Sunday’s defeat to Manchester City
content:
Liverpool cleansed themselves from the stains of defeat by Manchester City at the earliest opportunity. A rampant performance in Austria, where Bradley Barcola opened his account for Andoni Iraola ’s side with a hat-trick, maintained Liverpool’s 100-per-cent start to the Champions League and shattered LASK’s big night on the elite European stage.
Iraola defended the majority of Liverpool’s display against City, the club’s £123-million signing from Paris Saint-Germain and the effectiveness of Florian Wirtz before the return to European action. His faith and confidence were rewarded as his team routed limited opponents who may have surprised themselves to score three in consolation. Barcola hit his stride in a Liverpool shirt with Ronald Araújo also scoring his first goal for the club on a restorative evening in Linz.
The home end was full and in strong voice over an hour before kick-off as LASL supporters came to savour their club’s first home game in the Champions League proper. The LASK team proved to be much less impressive though, in fairness to the Austrian crowd, their support rarely wavered even as a rout unfolded. Liverpool revelled in their superiority and the invitation to recover from Sunday’s first defeat of the season.
Iraola rested Virgil van Dijk, delaying the defender’s 200th game as Liverpool captain, and Alexis Mac Allister as he managed workloads ahead of Saturday’s visit to Brentford. A new-look central defence of Araújo and Jérémy Jacquet were given a physical test by the LASK strikers Samuel Adeniran and Krystof Danek but handled the hosts’ rudimental approach comfortably.
Araújo also showcased his attacking talents. It was the on-loan defender’s ball that Wirtz took in his stride before gliding between two LASK players and testing the goalkeeper, Lukas Jungwirth, with a low shot. Araújo then headed wide from a Kostas Tsimikas corner. He would find his range from the stand-in captain’s next set piece.
Liverpool were utterly dominant against an opponent that struggled to retain possession in all areas of the pitch. The breakthrough was inevitable but also a result of uncertainty in the LASK defence. Alemão had to concede the first of two successive corners after his keeper failed to come off his line to collect a routine through ball. From the second corner, conceded by Alemão’s headed clearance, Araújo towered above his marker to head home Tsimikas’s delivery.
Merely 96 seconds later it was 2-0 as Barcola also opened his account for Liverpool. The summer recruit found himself under scrutiny ahead of the game, along with Wirtz, having gone six appearances for his new club without a goal or an assist. That issue was put to bed when Rio Ngumoha weaved in from the right and, after the teenager had stumbled, Lewis Koumas laid the ball back to the lurking winger. Barcola swept a first-time shot inside Jungwirth’s far post. Liverpool were enjoying themselves.
Wirtz soon found himself with a much-needed assist for Barcola’s second goal of the evening. The Germany international has looked more at home for Liverpool in the Champions League than Premier League and this was no exception. Wirtz picked out his fellow big-money signing’s run into the LASK area and Barcola rolled a cool finish beyond the exposed keeper.
LASK could have been seriously embarrassed before half-time. Koumas had a fine finish disallowed for offside and, following another neat exchange between Wirtz and Barcola, Ryan Gravenberch saw his shot kiss the inside of the far post and rebound clear. Liverpool’s 19 attempts on goal were the most by an away side in the first half of a Champions League game since records began in 2003-04.
There would be no let-up from Iraola’s team after the interval. Jeremie Frimpong morphed into an old-fashioned centre-forward to rise above Yvan Dibango and bury a textbook header into the bottom corner when Tsimikas floated a delightful cross over from the left byline.
Koumas had a second goal disallowed for offside before Alisson’s clean sheet was ruined by the LASK substitute Robert Ljubicic sweeping home inside his near post. The Brazil keeper’s disgust washed over his team-mates. Barcola was presented with his hat-trick when Ngumoha released Frimpong down the right and the full-back flashed a low cross through the LASK six-yard box. The unmarked Barcola applied a simple finish at the back post.
Frimpong also supplied the assist for Koumas’s deserved goal, converted from close range after the home side were caught playing out from the back. The LASK substitute Florian Flecker brought a touch of respectability to the scoreline with two goals in four minutes, both from Dibango deliveries from the left, but there was no disguising the emphatic manner of Liverpool’s victory nor the surge of confidence it should give to Barcola. – Guardian

title: The Irish Times view on the National Drugs Strategy: incremental change
description: A fudge on decriminalisation brings policy a bit closer to reality on the ground
content:
The National Drugs Strategy 2026-2030 has been published. It moves Ireland incrementally closer to decriminalising the possession of small amounts of drugs for personal use as recommended by the Oireachtas Joint Committee on Drugs Use earlier this year. The committee reviewed the recommendations of the 2023 Citizens’ Assembly on Drugs Use which also advocated decriminalisation through the adoption of a health-led approach.
The new strategy advances this goal somewhat by elevating “health supports to people coming into contact with the criminal justice system due to drug use” to the status of a core goal, while de-emphasising the use of criminal sanctions.
It is a fudge but does go some way towards closing the gap between Government policy and the reality on the ground. The Garda are increasingly availing of existing alternatives to criminal prosecutions. These include the use of adult cautions and District Court warnings or fines. A health referral scheme introduced last month offers another alternative to prosecution.
The approach is reminiscent of what used to be termed Irish solutions to Irish problems. The phrase encapsulates a continuing hesitancy to address politically fraught social issues.
Despite the clear recommendation of the Citizens’ Assembly – which found its way into Fianna Fáil’s general election manifesto – and the equally clear view of the Oireachtas committee, it is apparent that many in Government still feel the public are not ready for even partial decriminalisation.
Fine Gael leader Simon Harris and Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan appear to be the most vocal opponents. Taoiseach Micheál Martin is firmly on the fence, while Minster for Health, Jennifer Carroll MacNeill – who has previously supported the move – appears to be biting her tongue.
The reality is that the limited decriminalisation of small-scale personal drug use is now the reality in many cases, while the State will continue to crack down on their trafficking and sale. Given the huge costs to society this, too, must continue and not be seen to be diluted in any way.

title: Daktronics to close Clare facility with the loss of over 100 jobs
description: Decision ‘has not been taken lightly’, company says
content:
US -headquartered electronic display system firm Daktronics is to close its manufacturing facility in Ennistymon in north Clare with the loss of over 100 jobs.
In an announcement on Wednesday, Daktronics said the closure is anticipated to be substantially complete by the middle of 2028.
The move follows Daktronics’s decision to exit the portion of the business which serves rail, bus, and roadway customers outside of North America.
The company said the action was “intended to reduce fixed costs with a low or negative return outlook and improve manufacturing utilisation across the company’s global manufacturing network”.
President and chief executive officer (CEO) of Daktronics, Ramesh Jayaraman, said “exiting Ireland and aligning our manufacturing capacity will help us manage factory utilisation across the network more effectively, improve workforce productivity, set the stage for further automation, and streamline procurement initiatives”.
“We are taking these steps to meet the evolving needs of our customers,” he said.
The company’s vice-president for international markets, Judd Guthmiller said the decision to cease manufacturing operations in Ireland “has been a very difficult decision and has not been taken lightly, but market realities have made it unavoidable”.
“It does not diminish the enormous contribution our Ireland colleagues have made to the company and to our customers and our focus now is on supporting the team through the closure process in the best way possible.”
[ AI companies should ‘sell solutions’ rather than ‘fear’, conference hears Opens in new window ]
Wednesday’s announcement followed the company confirming at the start of September that it was entering a collective redundancy consultation after it informed its employees that their positions were at risk.
In its statement, the company said leaving Ireland was expected to result in $13.5 million (€12 million) of cumulative pretax charges, including employee-related costs, facility wind-down and equipment-transfer costs, and also potential asset impairments.
Daktronics said, when fully implemented, the closure was expected to generate $7.7 million of annualised pretax savings which, it said, will fully offset the associated implementation costs in less than two years “while contributing to the company’s broader structural cost reduction and margin improvement objectives”.
The most recent accounts for Daktronics Ireland Co Ltd showed that the company was profitable.
For the 12 months to the end of April 2025, the firm recorded a pretax profit of €586,003 as revenues decreased by 8.5 per cent from €17.98 million to €16.44 million.
The company at the end of April 2025 employed 116 and staff costs for the year totalled €6.49 million.
