title: Burnham reaffirms backing for Zelenskiy after Downing Street meeting
description: US president denies intelligence sharing has stopped in row over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil plants
content:
British prime minister Andy Burnham has reinforced his support for Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy following a meeting in Downing Street on Wednesday afternoon.
Burnham’s backing came after US president Donald Trump increased pressure on Kyiv and Russia hit the country’s energy plants with a fresh wave of missile and drone attacks.
“The last few days, the last few hours, have been very dark and difficult days for Ukraine,” Burnham said in his meeting with Zelenskiy. “In these moments, Britain will continue to provide you with whatever support that we can.”
The meeting was called after Trump last week announced a deal with Russian president Vladimir Putin for Moscow to release diesel fuel to the global market, and the US sought to force Ukraine to halt its drone attacks on Russian oil refineries. Trump also announced a “ceasefire” concerning energy infrastructure, but Moscow has continued to attack Ukrainian energy sites.
Burnham commended Zelenskiy for the “leadership” he showed in saying he would be prepared to discuss what an energy ceasefire would look like. “Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine,” said the British prime minister. “It’s clear to the world, again, who the aggressor is in this conflict.”
Zelenskiy said he was “thankful” for the UK’s backing, adding that there had been a “continuation of escalation” from Russia rather than a ceasefire.
He also appeared to criticise the US for “difficulties” Ukraine had experienced with Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network, which is providing services to allow Ukraine to guide drones to attack Russia, and with intelligence sharing, issues he said he would discuss with Burnham.
Speaking in parliament earlier on Wednesday, Burnham said that rather than criticise Trump’s actions, he would “try and repair bridges so that the support comes back”.
Burnham announced an increase in British military support – including missiles – for Ukraine and new sanctions aimed at Moscow.
Earlier on Wednesday, Zelenskiy said Ukraine had not received some early warning information from its partners about Russian ballistic missile strikes in the previous 24 hours.
The Ukrainian president said 26 power facilities had been damaged. About 600,000 Ukrainians were reported to be without power on Wednesday morning.
Ukraine is seeking answers from the US and Nato allies about a sudden restriction of SpaceX’s Starlink service for military use. SpaceX limited terminal connections that complicated Ukrainian drone interceptions and mid-range strikes, according to a person familiar with the situation.
The top priority for Kyiv’s allies, including Britain, is to ensure the US does not stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine, and in particular that US early warning systems continue to be used to protect civilian life.
The developments have increased pressure on Ukraine and its European allies to demonstrate that they have a strategy to continue to fend off Russia’s full-scale invasion, which is in its fifth year.
While the US did not contact Britain in advance of the Trump-Putin deal, London saw signs in the weeks preceding the announcement that Trump was once again moving away from the European position, said British officials.
Ukraine retains some leverage even as it comes under renewed pressure from Trump, said the officials. It is able to strike Russian oil refineries without US intelligence by using European targeting data instead. If Putin does not adhere to Trump’s ceasefire, Britain would back Ukraine to keep striking Russian energy infrastructure, they added.
Any cutting off of US intelligence, which briefly happened last year, would be most damaging regarding Ukraine’s defences because it is reliant on a US early warning system to defend against Russian attacks, the officials said. Kyiv’s allies would lobby the US not to stop sharing intelligence, they added. – Bloomberg

title: Adventures as Gaeilge: The bestselling Irish-language author who captivated young readers
description: English-born Cathal Ó Sándair wrote 160 books in Irish, many featuring the suave sleuth Réics Carló
content:
C athal Ó Sándair sold more books in Irish than anyone else. Over a 40-year period, Ó Sándair wrote about 160 books in Irish , mainly adventure stories destined for a teenage audience. In total, he sold more than 500,000 copies.
He was born Charles Saunders in Weston-super-Mare in 1922 to an Irish mother and an English father; the family moved to Ireland when he was two years old. They went to live in Dublin, his mother’s home county. His father, Simon, was a professional boxer who joined the Irish Army when they settled in Dublin.
Cathal attended Scoil Treasa on Donore Avenue and the Christian Brothers school on Synge Street . He was encouraged by his teachers to take an interest in Irish, and a trip to the Gaeltacht at Cois Fharraige in Connemara at age 10 cemented his love of the language.
When he was 16, his first short story in Irish was published in the Christian Brothers’ bi-weekly magazine An Gaedheal Óg. After school, he joined the Air Corps and also became a member of Conradh na Gaeilge. He started writing articles in Irish for different newspapers.
His first book for children, Tríocha Píosa Airgid, came out in 1942. In April that year, not yet 20 years old, he contacted the publication branch of the Department of Education, An Gúm. He told them that he wanted to play his part in supporting the language by writing a few light stories for young people in Irish.
Na Mairbh a d’Fhill was published in May 1943. It was an instant success, with 1,000 copies sold in the first month. It recounted the story of the kidnapping of a professor who was working on a top-secret project for the Irish government.
When the scientist and all his papers went missing, the gardaí called in star private detective Réics Carló to help solve the case. It was here that readers were first introduced to the Mercedes-Benz-driving sleuth who was the principal character of many of Ó Sándair’s volumes.
At the time, a reviewer in the Donegal News newspaper welcomed Ó Sándair’s books as he predicted that they would give fresh impetus to the language among the youth of the country. Judging from what the journalist had read in the early editions, he believed that the books would provide young readers with “racy thrillers with pulsating action in every page and a fresh mystery in every paragraph”.
The initial print run for Na Mairbh a d’Fhill of 3,000 was sold out by the autumn of 1943. Another 3,000 were printed in September that year and yet another 3,000 copies were printed the following September.
[ Cathal Ó Sándair: laoch litríocht Ghaeilge na n-óg Opens in new window ]
This success rate was unusual for an Irish-language book at the time, according to Róisín Adams, who has researched the area of Irish-language publishing for children. A typical print run of a new book would have been 1,000 copies and this would usually have been enough to satisfy demand.
In a sign of how popular his tales of adventure were among young readers, teachers reported seeing schoolchildren reading Ó Sándair’s books under their desks in English class in the 1950s. It was not all plain sailing, however, as An Gúm rejected him a couple of times early on, judging that his Irish was not up to scratch. They soon saw merit in his writing and, by the late 1940s, sales of his work would reach 30,000 copies.
The books were cheap at sixpence each and the colourful cover artwork by artist Victor Penney would have attracted the attention of schoolchildren. Réics Carló featured in about 100 of Ó Sándair’s books. The Dublin investigator was in great demand from private citizens, along with various arms of the State, both locally and internationally.
The fictional detective’s reputation spread worldwide and there were books set on almost every continent, with cases to solve in London, the Isle of Man, China, Mexico and Egypt, to name just a few of the foreign locations. In one book, Carló claimed that he could “have up to 20 cases to solve at the same time”.
In Ireland, Réics Carló was asked to help solve cases in Cork, Waterford, Donegal, Monaghan and Wicklow. Ó Sándair had knowledge of the country. After working in the Air Corps and in the Civil Service during the second World War, he worked in the customs and excise service for a number of years. He was stationed all over the country and this would have been invaluable to him to get to know local geography and customs for the locations in his novels.
Ó Sándair has not been completely forgotten. In 2022, 100 years after his birth, An Gúm republished the first two books in the Réics Carló series. In recognition of all he did for the language, there is a prize awarded at An tOireachtas each year for the best children’s book in Irish called Gradam Réics Carló – a fitting tribute for the writer who did so much to keep young readers reading as Gaeilge.

title: Teaching unions urge Taoiseach to intervene and prevent further strike action
description: Frustration with Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers triggers call around ‘role here for’ Martin
content:
Leaders of the main teaching unions have called for Taoiseach Micheál Martin to intervene in order to prevent further strike action on the first day of industrial action over pay.
Speaking on a picket line outside Hartstown Community College in Dublin 15 on Wednesday, the general secretaries of the Irish National Teachers’ Organisation (INTO), the Association of Secondary Teachers in Ireland (ASTI) and the Teachers’ Union of Ireland (TUI) all indicated a lack of trust between their members and the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform .
Almost all schools, colleges and universities countrywide were closed on Wednesday in the biggest public sector strike seen here for almost two decades.
[ ‘Nobody can survive on the wages we’re getting’: Live updates Opens in new window ]
Approximately 100,000 teachers and lecturers who are members of the INTO, ASTI, TUI and the Irish Federation of University Teachers (IFUT) went on strike over what they called a lack of meaningful engagement from Government on a new public sector pay deal.
In total, there were more than 300,000 public sector workers, including teachers, doctors, nurses and civil servants, taking part in Wednesday’s strike.
“I think it’s fairly evident there’s been a breakdown of trust. And I think really we’re going to need somebody to bring the parties together,” said ASTI general secretary Linda Kelly.
“I think it was too little, too late from the Minister [for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers] last night to have his epiphany around pay being a central part of a pay deal . And I think that needs to be addressed. I do think there is a role here for the Taoiseach,” said Kelly.
Chambers told RTÉ’s Prime Time last night that pay could be dealt with first in any negotiations.
“The question is, can we trust that now?” said INTO general secretary John Boyle.
“This is the same Minister who told the general public only three weeks before the budget that there will be €2 billion available for public service pay, and yet on budget day, he only made available €1 billion, plus point two of a billion for pensions. And within the €1 billion, a lot of that money is already spent on carry-over costs.
“So we are going to have to get assurances from the Taoiseach, who needs to step in here, that whatever negotiations are going to commence, and I am confident that they will commence after last night’s change of heart from the Minister, but the Taoiseach is going to have to convince us that if pay is going to be spoken about at the beginning of the talks, that it’s all aspects of pay,” said Boyle.
Meanwhile, TUI general secretary Michael Gillespie said there is a “feeling that the industrial relations machinery of the country is not being taken seriously by one department [of Public Expenditure].
“Unions need to see some sort of wording from both the Department of Public Expenditure and the Cabinet that acknowledges the cost of living crisis and that public sector workers need a pay rise. Then we could go into talks.”

title: AI firms should ‘sell solutions’ rather than ‘fear’, OpenAI executive tells Dublin summit
description: Cybersecurity could be future growth driver for OpenAI, executive tells tech summit in Dublin
content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) companies should be “selling solutions” in areas such as cybersecurity rather than “selling fear”, OpenAI executive Sarah Friar told a summit in Dublin on Wednesday as the firm targets future growth.
The company may also find more opportunities in areas such as life sciences, drug development and the microchip industry, she said.
Friar, OpenAI’s chief financial officer, was speaking at the International AI Summit at the RDS in Ballsbridge, Dublin .
The event, organised by the Government as part of Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the European Union , brought together leaders from industry and government across the region to discuss the opportunities and challenges brought by the technology.
The executive told the summit that AI had a role to play in shoring up systems, discovering vulnerabilities in older code and patching them at “machine speed”.
“Selling fear is not a good way to come to the world. We have to sell solutions and solutions that feel transparent, open and honest,” Friar said.
There have been fears that the technology will eliminate many jobs, even in the tech sector.
However, she told The Irish Times the number of software developers had increased globally rather than fallen off.
“If you look at the amount of code that can be developed, it has gone way up,” she said. “So if software has eaten the world, to quote [US businessman] Marc Andreessen, we are now just having that happening at an even faster rate.”
What may change, she said, was how people learned to develop software, and new jobs would be – and were being – created through and because of AI.
The AI company has seen significant growth in Ireland, with more than 2.5 million people here using ChatGPT every week, out of 1.2 billion globally.
OpenAI has yet to turn a profit and has raised more than $180 billion (€161.8 billion) in funding, including $122 billion in the first quarter of the year. Recent reports put overall annualised revenues for the company at $50 billion, around $20 billion below previous reports.
OpenAI began selling ads on its ChatGPT platform this year. It recorded an annualised revenue run rate of $1 billion for the ad business as of the end of August. But Friar said trust in the technology was key.
“You have to have trust with your user and be very clear what are your principles off the bat. We’re very clear that you get the best outcome from the model, not the sponsored outcome,” Friar told The Irish Times.
“I think we are a very interesting ad platform because we’re kind of this beautiful meld of high contextual relevance.”
In a speech at the event, Microsoft president Brad Smith called for stricter safety rules for AI, saying there were more safety rules for ovens and cartons of milk than there were for AI.
“Let’s be devoted to the progress of technology, but let’s be even more devoted to the advance of humanity,” he said.
“Think about your kids. Think about our neighbours and remember this: people are more important than AI.”
He said he was optimistic about what AI could do for Europe, with a new generation of technology that created more important opportunities and responsibilities than before.

title: Mickey Harte’s remarkable managerial career takes him back to club scene with Kilcoo
description: Three-time All-Ireland-winning manager takes charge of the Down side after spells with four counties
content:
D eep in the bowels of Croke Park last June, in the aftermath of Offaly’s Tailteann Cup exit, Mickey Harte briefly considered a question on whether he intended to return to the Faithful in 2027.
“Please God, if they’ll have me,” he smiled back.
But just over two weeks later, the Offaly County Board released a statement announcing that joint managers Harte and Declan Kelly had decided to step down.
In explaining the departure of their management team, Offaly GAA stated: “Once Declan had made his decision to step down, Mickey felt it was also the appropriate time for him to move on.”
And so as he entered the winter of his managerial career, so began an autumn of Harte getting routinely linked with various intercounty positions. As recently as last weekend, there were WhatsApp messages bouncing around that Harte had been spotted at the Longford county final. You get the idea – manager wanted, manager available.
But as each vacancy was filled, the more it felt like Harte was moving out to pasture. Or punditry.
And then the Magpies swooped. On Tuesday night, Kilcoo confirmed Harte was to be their new manager – succeeding Martin Corey in the role.
The Down club announced: “Mickey was unanimously ratified at a club committee meeting this evening and the club are over the moon that the Tyrone man has agreed to become our manager.
“Mickey is renowned as one of the top managers in the GAA. He led Tyrone to an unprecedented three All-Ireland senior football championships, six Ulster titles, a National League and 12 Dr McKenna Cups.”
It was one of those ‘let me read that again’ announcements. But perhaps the surprise should not have been that Kilcoo had appointed Harte, but rather that nobody had seen it coming.
In the days after he stepped down as Derry manager in 2024, Harte had said he was “not ready for the pipe and slippers yet”.
[ Mickey Harte takes up club managerial post with Down side Kilcoo Opens in new window ]
That sentiment was all but echoed with his comments at the end of Offaly’s campaign a few months back. Managing teams is all he has known for over three decades now. And he’s clearly not ready to close that particular door behind him yet.
By taking on a highly regarded club team at 72 years of age, Harte will see this as rolling back the years rather than stepping off the stage.
He has a record of continual involvement managing teams every year that stretches back to a time when most current intercounty players weren’t even born.
His intercounty trek has taken him from Tyrone to Louth to Derry and to Offaly – with no gap year. Throughout it all, Harte has stuck to his managerial principles and coaching convictions.
And he garnered silverware in every county he managed, including a clean sweep of winning all four league titles over the last decade. He won Division Four with Louth (shared with Antrim) in 2021; Division Three with Louth in 2022 and also with Offaly in 2025; Division Two with Tyrone in 2016 and Division One with Derry in 2024.
Harte’s last direct club involvement was managing his home team of Errigal Ciarán to Tyrone and Ulster SFC glory in 2002.
Errigal Ciarán won the county final that September before adding a provincial title with victory over Enniskillen Gaels in December. Harte had already been appointed Tyrone manager by that stage but remained at the helm for Errigal Ciarán’s All-Ireland club semi-final the following February when they lost to Nemo Rangers at O’Moore Park in Portlaoise.
“It was a once-in-a-lifetime chance to get to an All-Ireland final and we probably came up against one of the best club sides ever,” he said in the aftermath of that defeat.
“We did that in 1994 and they went on to win the title. I think they are no mean side at the minute either.”
Now, 23 years later, Harte is back on the club beat and he has taken charge of ‘no mean side’ in Kilcoo.
They have been the dominant force in Down football for well over a decade and were this year bidding for an eighth consecutive county title. They came up short in that goal, losing to Burren at the semi-final stages, but if others in Down had hoped that defeat signalled the end of an era, the appointment of Harte demonstrates Kilcoo’s ambitions remain lofty.
Before this year, they had won 13 of the previous 14 Down senior football crowns. But the jewel in their crown was the 2022 All-Ireland club final victory over Kilmacud Crokes.
Kilcoo have won more Down senior football titles than any other club in the county – 23. Harte is the latest high-profile manager to take on the role with Mickey Moran and Karl Lacey among the previous incumbents.
But Kilcoo haven’t appointed Harte in the hope he will merely add another county title or two to their haul.
Burren are Down’s most decorated club when it comes to national honours – the only Mourne side to have won two All-Ireland club titles.
Kilcoo might not stick it up on the club noticeboard, but in appointing Harte their aspirations are clearly signposted towards a return to Croke Park.
The Tyrone underage years. Harte managed the Tyrone minors between 1991 and 1998, leading the county to one All-Ireland title and three Ulster triumphs. He then stepped up as under-21 manager, where he won a further two All-Ireland titles at that grade, plus three provincial crowns.
Harte managed Errigal Ciarán to victory in the Tyrone SFC final over Killyclogher.
He was appointed Tyrone senior football manager, succeeding Art McRory and Eugene McKenna.
Harte’s Errigal Ciarán beat Enniskillen Gaels in the Ulster club final.
Nemo Rangers overcame Errigal Ciarán in an All-Ireland club semi-final. The game marked Harte’s last as the club’s manager.
Harte remained Tyrone senior manager for 18 seasons – during which time they won three All-Ireland titles. He stepped down in November 2020.
Just 10 days later, he was appointed Louth senior football manager.
Harte quit Louth and immediately took over as Derry senior football boss.
His stint as Derry manager proved to be a short one, and Harte stepped away after their championship campaign ended.
Offaly GAA announced that Harte was to join Declan Kelly as the county’s joint senior football manager.
Offaly GAA confirmed Harte and Kelly were stepping down.
Kilcoo announced Harte as their new senior football manager.

title: Wall Street slips after inflation shock as ASML lifts European tech
description: Kerry Group continues to make gains as share price now up more than 4%
content:
Battered by weeks of elevated oil prices and government bond yields, European investors had pinned their hopes ⁠on corporate earnings to breathe life into equities, but results have been uneven so far.
Now, on Wednesday, hotter-than-expected inflation readings in the US have revived fears of higher interest rates.
The news sent Wall Street lower following a rally in shares among European technology firms earlier in the day, led by chipmaking equipment group ASML.
The Iseq All-Share index fell by 0.9 per cent to close at 14,084.62 on Wednesday afternoon.
Kerry Group continued its advance, with shares up 0.8 per cent to €91.30. Since the beginning of the week, its shares have risen more than 4 per cent.
The next biggest riser in the day was property developer Glenveagh , which saw its price up 0.6 per cent to €2.35, followed by Glanbia , which was up 0.6 per cent to €20.10.
Larger losses were recorded by companies at the other end of the index, with shares in Ryanair down by almost 2.7 per cent to €22.10.
Gene Murtagh’s Kingspan group saw its share price fall by close to 1.5 per cent to €101.50, while Mincon Group slipped 1 per cent to €0.99.
The FTSE 100 ended up 0.7 per cent at 10,724.86 on Wednesday, lifted by consumer and defence stocks.
Among consumer staple firms to rise were Unilever and Burberry, which gained 2.5 per cent and 3 per cent respectively. British American Tobacco was up 0.7 per cent, while spirits maker Diageo was up 1 per cent.
Elsewhere, following a call from activist investor Ancora for a strategic review, the self-storage firm Big Yellow rose 5.4 per cent.
Financial services firm Admiral slipped 2.6 per cent after Peel Hunt ‌cut its price target, warning ⁠the insurer’s UK motor policy growth could slow as it raises rates to protect margins.
Defence products maker Chemring climbed 2.4 per cent after its Roke unit secured a partnership with a major US contractor, including an ​initial $16 million order and a minimum $170 million (€152 million) agreement over five ​years.
European shares notched slim gains after robust earnings from ASML reassured investors concerned about AI demand.
The pan-European STOXX 600 index gained 0.43 per cent to 637.75 points on Wednesday. The healthcare index was the biggest gainer on the benchmark, rising 2.3 per cent to hit its highest since early September.
Shares of semiconductor firm ASML rose 1.2 per cent after it said customers were already ​looking to place orders for its advanced chipmaking tools for 2029 and 2030, illustrating that demand remains sturdy.
Among other movers, Orsted dropped 3.9 per cent following a report by Bloomberg News that the US ‌would re-evaluate the permit for its ⁠wind farm near Rhode Island.
Wall Street stocks fell on ​Wednesday after data showed US consumer prices rose more than expected last month, reinforcing expectations the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates as soon as this month.
US Labour Department data showed the core consumer price index (CPI) was up 0.3 per cent in September versus economist expectations for a rise of 0.2 per cent. On ​an annual basis, core CPI, which strips out food and energy prices, rose 2.6 per cent, above forecasts for a rise of 2.5 per cent. The headline rate ⁠rose 3.7 per cent, above estimates for a rise of 3.6 per cent.
On Wall Street, all three indexes were trading lower, with technology and industrials driving losses while healthcare, consumer staples and energy stocks were higher.
In early afternoon trading, the Dow Jones was down 0.3 per cent, the S&P 500 fell 1.1 per cent and the Nasdaq was 1.62 per cent lower.
Large US banks reported earnings on Wednesday, with Bank of America saying profits fell in the third quarter and Morgan Stanley showing it beat expectations for its third-quarter ‌profit thanks to strong equity ⁠trading.
The S&P 500 technology index traded at a two-week low, as chip stocks came under pressure again. They lost ground on Tuesday after reports pointing to progress in chip design by China’s CXMT fuelled competition concerns.
Shares of Intel and Micron fell 2.6 per cent and one per cent, respectively, while Nvidia slipped 1.7 per cent.
Most Magnificent Seven stocks declined, barring Alphabet and Apple, which rose 0.2 per cent and 0.9 per cent, respectively. – Additional reporting: Reuters

title: Dominic Cummings stuns peers with rant about Britain’s ‘duff’ political system
description: Boris Johnson’s former top adviser re-emerges from obscurity to give abrasive performance before a House of Lords committee
content:
B ritain has moved on from the rancorous days of Covid lockdowns and the chaotic UK government of the time, led by Boris Johnson . Dominic Cummings , it seems, has not.
The arch Brexiteer Cummings was Johnson’s conflict-prone chief adviser in Downing Street for most of 2020. He now works as a consultant and occasional Substack author. On Wednesday morning he also appeared in front of a House of Lords committee to opine on the functioning of the UK’s unwritten constitution and its arms of government .
Cummings gave a typically abrasive performance, a throwback to the old days when he prowled Downing Street while lambasting civil servants and Westminster journalists.
He stunned the peers listening on Wednesday in the wood-panelled surrounds of committee room one with a litany of rants about Britain’s “duff” system of “shitshows” and his belief that Russia’s Vladimir Putin is not the main enemy, before aiming a series of digs at his political foes, including former UK health secretary Matt Hancock .
“Do you really want Hancock making decisions?” he asked, seconds after subtly referencing the former politician’s pandemic-era marital affair with one of his aides.
The Lords constitution committee was holding an inquiry into the UK’s balance of powers and its constitutional safeguards. It invited Cummings in to speak as a long-time critic of the system. He arrived displaying his characteristic sartorial style, clad in a crumpled shirt with sleeves rolled up, crumpled green anorak and red baseball cap.
He launched into a lament about the “fake charade” of the existing system, in which an independent civil service is meant to serve UK governments of all hues. Things were better before 19th-century reforms ushered in the modern civil service and, he suggested, ministers were truly accountable to the UK parliament
“That is the system under which the British Empire grew and we took over the world. Why can’t we have that system back?” he said.
Cummings said “elite talent” no longer wanted to work in government, while the UK’s cabinet office, he suggested, had become too powerful and was now setting policy.
[ UK MPs vote to continue progress of Northern Ireland Troubles legacy legislation Opens in new window ]
“If you’ve got duff people, then the institutions will be duff,” he said. “Great people have options. They’re not going to go and sit in stupid meetings with PowerPoint after PowerPoint with no one actually taking responsibility for anything.”
He suggested that all the “great people” he had encouraged into the cabinet office in 2020 had since been “pushed out” or “left in disgust” to work in fields such as artificial intelligence. Government had been left with “the worst kind of HR people”.
At one point he cupped his ears while being questioned by a peer. “I’m sorry, my ears don’t work so well,” said Cummings. The peer was trying to ask him if the felt the UK’s constitution was “under threat”.
“Yes it is under threat,” Cummings replied, because of a “general collapse” in the UK public’s trust in institutions.
“Because of the internet, people can now see the lies they have been told [by government],” he said.
Putin, he said, was “a tiny problem” related to civil servants in the ministry of defence (MoD) and cabinet office lawyers investigating UK troops.
[ Sally Rooney’s books will no longer be available in UK over her support for Palestine Action Opens in new window ]
“It’s not Putin who’s launching lawfare against the SAS; it’s not Putin who’s destroyed procurement inside the MoD ... It’s not Putin who’s stopping the MoD learning from drones in Ukraine. It’s the civil servants who tell the people who come back from Ukraine: ‘Don’t tell anybody senior what you see in Ukraine about drones because that will jeopardise all our budgets.’”
He said ministers didn’t want to take responsibility for anything and civil servants believed MPs were “thick”. So the civil service ended up running everything instead.
As Cummings ranted on, a few of the peers grimaced while others smirked.
“Dominic, I sense you’re warming to your theme,” said committee chair Thomas Galbraith, Lord Strathclyde.
“These things have all been said before,” said another lord.
“Yes, it’s all in Yes Minister,” said Cummings, referencing the cult 1980s television show.
He said people believe politicians “govern like they hate us”.
“This building must start taking responsibility,” he said, punctuating each word with a tap on the table as he lectured the peers in front of him.
Meanwhile, he said, the role of the civil service should be to “follow orders”.

title: Woman allegedly tortured for 13 hours, drugged and had head shaved, court hears
description: Alleged victim ‘screaming for help’ but ‘whimpering’ as she was placed in car boot, Dublin bail hearing told
content:
Two men and a woman have been charged after a woman reported she was “tortured”, beaten and burned during a 13-hour violent ordeal in Tallaght, Dublin .
Paul Walsh (39), Sarahanne Smith (36) and 44-year-old James Colton, all from Tallaght , appeared before Judge Treasa Kelly at Dublin District Court on Wednesday.
It follows a Garda investigation into a woman’s complaint that she was bound and placed in a car boot, attacked, gagged, drugged and had her hair shaved, after the incident commenced in the early hours of October 7th.
All three defendants were charged with false imprisonment of the complainant at Colton’s home, at Fortunestown Close.
Walsh and Smith face additional charges of assault causing harm and production of various articles as weapons.
It was alleged that Smith, a mother of three, instigated the violence, which was suspected to have been caused by the loss of a handbag and a “paranoid” accusation that the complainant was seeing her partner.
A bail hearing proceeded after gardaí brought them to an emergency court sitting to object to their release.
Garda Aaron Melinn told the court that Colton, who did not apply for bail, “made no reply to charge”.
Det Garda Niamh O’Connor and Garda Brian Law objected to Walsh and Smith’s bail, citing the seriousness of the case and fears of witness intimidation.
They gave evidence that the injured party turned up at the Tallaght emergency department and contacted gardaí and said she had been tortured for 13 hours.
She told gardaí she had been “kidnapped, tied up, struck with metal bars, repeatedly assaulted and burned” and that she knew her attackers.
She said she had attended Colton’s home and was “forcibly restrained with zip ties to her wrists and ankles and severely beaten with kicks and punches to her body, and that she was burned by means of boiling water to her head, and by heated instruments to her face.”
She also alleged that clumps of her hair were removed by force with a head shaver and her hand was crushed forcefully using a mastic sealant gun tool.
The complainant alleged her attackers “poured ammonia on to her head”.
The woman claimed that Walsh and Smith “sustained this assault for two to three hours, during which they punched and kicked her as she lay on the floor.”
The alleged victim told gardaí that Smith heated a builder’s trowel until it was hot and then placed it on her face.
The woman alleged Walsh said: “This is where the pain is going to start.”
She maintained that the pair forced her to consume Tranax tablets, which she did out of fear.
CCTV footage obtained by gardaí showed the defendants at the house, the court heard. She was “screaming for help” but “whimpering” when placed in a car boot, the court heard.
It was alleged James Colton and Walsh spoke to the driver, an unknown person, and placed the woman in the car.
It was alleged that the car brought her away, but returned shortly afterwards with Walsh driving and Smith, who lived 180m (200 yards) away at Fortunestown Crescent, in the passenger seat.
The court heard the woman passed out and could not recall how long she was in the car but woke back in Colton’s house with a tourniquet around her arm and Smith holding her arm and uttering: “I told you to stop doing that”, implying that the injured woman had been injected with heroin.
She later stumbled from the house about hours later in “an extremely disoriented state”.
Walsh, of no fixed abode in Tallaght, said he had no legal representation but asked that the hearing proceed even though he said he found it “strange”.
He denied the claims, saying he was not a violent person. The court denied his bail application.
He and Colton are to appear at Cloverhill District Court on Tuesday.
Smith’s solicitor, John Shanley, said his client would live outside the area and abide by strict conditions. The judge held that the female accused could be granted bail, with a cashless €1,000 bond but would have to provide an alternative address outside Tallaght.

title: Pope Leo XIV faces further tests to determine extent of cancer
description: Pontiff eating regularly and has begun walking following surgery to remove cancerous mass from his lung
content:
Pope Leo XIV was eating regularly on Wednesday and began walking and doing respiratory exercises, and his post-operative tests are normal following surgery to remove a cancerous mass from his lung, the Vatican said.
Leo’s two doctors, Dr Luigi Carbone and thoracic surgeon Dr Stefano Margaritora, provided a medical update on Wednesday. Blood tests and a chest X-ray confirmed a normal post-operative recovery, with levels within the norm, they said.
“The holy father underwent respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking in his room. He resumed his regular diet and had breakfast and lunch,” they reported. “Recovery is proceeding as planned.”
US president Donald Trump said ​on Wednesday he hoped ​that Leo ⁠would “get ​better fast”.
“I ​want to ‌see Pope ​Leo get well,” ⁠Trump ⁠told ​reporters. “I just want to wish him well, ‌get better ⁠fast.”
Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said late on Tuesday in a medical bulletin after the surgery.
It said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.
The medical bulletin made no mention of future treatment, and the Vatican said doctors were not currently speaking of chemotherapy or other therapies pending the results of other tests.
The Vatican press office noted the medical statement spoke of the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors removed all suspect tissue in hopes of removing any lingering traces of the cancer.
Leo’s lymph nodes also would have been removed and tested, to determine if the cancer had spread, and there was no word yet on those test results.
“Adenocarcinoma is the most common [type of lung cancer], also with the most favourable prognosis,” said Dr Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Centre.
“While we know the diagnosis we now need to know the stage.”
“We now need to know how big it is, how many spots in the lung are involved. Is it just one nodule, or more than one, and the lymph nodes, are they cancerous?” Liu said.
If the cancer has spread, more tests will be needed to determine what kind of therapy to pursue, he said. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy or targeted therapy, which involves oral pills for specific cancers.
The pope (71) was in the operating room for about three hours, the Vatican statement said. The surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes.
“The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the statement said, adding that the pope later returned to his room.
The right lung has three sections or lobes while the left has two. After one lobe is removed, the remainder of the lung can gradually compensate, especially in otherwise healthy and physically active people.
Leo had walked into the Gemelli hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of wellwishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Stefano Margaritora.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the localised nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and said he would have it removed.
Oncologists said before the operation that even if the nodule turned out to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis would be “excellent” since it would have been removed at an early stage.
The Vatican on Monday cancelled all of the pope’s audiences until October 20th.
While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will stay in a nearby room since the papal apartment is undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.
There was no word on whether Leo would be able to keep his planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru next month. – AP

title: Status yellow rain warning issued for five counties overnight
description: Met Éireann issues rain warning for Donegal, Galway, Leitrim, Mayo, Sligo
content:
A status yellow weather warning is in place for five counties overnight and into Thursday morning, with the possibility of localised flooding Met Éireann has said.
Heavy spells of rain are expected in Donegal , Galway , Leitrim , Mayo , Sligo with poor visibility and impacts on travelling conditions.
A separate yellow wind warning was in place for Donegal, Galway and Mayo, with the potential of wave overtopping on coastal regions. Southwesterly winds were expected to be particularly strong at times along the coasts, according to Met Éireann. However, this warning expired at 6pm on Wednesday.
Thursday will begin with widespread rain and will develop into heavy downpours across the country, which could lead to localised flooding, especially in Atlantic coastal counties.
“The rain will become mostly confined to southeastern and eastern areas by the evening, and winds near Atlantic coasts will freshen at times,” according to Met Éireann’s website.
“Highest temperatures of 12 to 16 degrees.”
Any rain or drizzle will clear early on Thursday night and Friday is anticipated to be a bright day with sunny spells and scattered showers.
The outlook for the weekend is for dry conditions with temperatures between 11 and 14 degrees.
Due to industrial action among public sector workers, there were disruptions to updates on met.ie on Wednesday.

title: Armagh’s Aimee Mackin named LGFA Player of the Month for September
description: All-Star nominee helped Shane O’Neills to maiden senior county title
content:
Armagh forward Aimee Mackin has been named LGFA Player of Month for September after her impressive efforts for her club, Shane O’Neills on their way to winning a first senior county title.
The All-Star nominee, who is also up for the Senior Players’ Player of the Year award, contributed 1-12 for Shane O’Neills as they defeated Crossmaglen 2-18 to 0-10 in last month’s decider.
The 29-year-old also had a standout performance in the semi-final, registering 3-5 in their win over Carrickcruppen.
Mackin is one of six Armagh players nominated for the 2026 All-Star Senior Team of the Year, alongside her sister Blaithín, who is nominated in midfield.
The sisters claimed an Ulster title with Armagh in May, beating Tyrone 2-13 to 1-15 in the provincial final. In the All-Ireland series, they topped Group 1 to set up a quarter-final clash with Kildare, running out three-point winners at the Athletic Grounds.
Their season was brought to an end by eventual champions Galway, who took a comfortable win over Greg McGonigle’s side in the semi-final.

title: ‘My pay hasn’t gone up – and everything else has’: Public sector workers have their say
description: Teachers, health workers, civil servants working in parks and tourist attractions say enough is enough as they take to pickets
content:
M ore than 300,000 workers held a one-day work stoppage on Wednesday, seeking a new public sector deal, with trade unions arguing pay terms must be agreed ⁠before other issues are addressed. Here, some of them share their stories.
Teachers do not want to be on strike today and are anxious to see negotiations on a new pay deal begin, secondary schoolteacher Anthony Keane said.
Keane is an English teacher and counsellor at Hartstown Community School in Dublin 15 .
“I don’t want to be on strike. I don’t know anyone who wants to be on strike today, and it’s unfortunate that it has come to this,” he said on the picket line.
“I think it’s unfortunate that we’re outside the school building rather than inside where we want to be today – inside it. I just hope it’s encouragement for the Government to engage in meaningful dialogue.”
The cost of accommodation has put huge pressure on teachers in his school, particularly younger staff, and people are “really feeling the pinch on multiple levels”, he said.
Many of the staff at Hartstown are commuting very long distances, some from Kilkenny, Cavan, Westmeath and Offaly, Keane said.
Part of his reason for being on strike is to show solidarity with younger staff members who are “really struggling” on the wages they receive.
“Let’s appreciate what makes life better for people in this country, and they are the basic services, so that people can live and be educated and have basic needs looked after,” he said.
He urged those on both sides to sit down and find a resolution through dialogue, sooner rather than later.
“It’s unfortunate that taxpayers are being affected today. That taxpayers are on strike today. That people who are providing public services have to be on strike outside their places of work, rather than inside doing what they want to do.” Niamh Towey
Martina Burke, a healthcare assistant in the emergency department at University Hospital Galway , has a 40-kilometre commute to work from her home in Co Mayo.
A mother of adult children, like hundreds of workers on the picket line at UHG she is feeling the pinch of higher fuel prices and the cost-of-living crisis.
“I work three long days. I’m up at 5.30am, not home until 9.15pm. It’s a long day. It’s busy and it’s hard work. But the work isn’t the problem, it’s the pay. We want fair pay,” she said.
A representative with trade union Siptu for 20 years, this is Burke’s second strike, and she feels the public is backing the industrial action.
“People who filter through the hospital see the hard work we do. The public are very supportive of us,” she said.
“Our message to the Government is: sit down, talk and listen to the unions. We don’t want to be here today, no one does.
“We had a 95 per cent vote to strike, which was overwhelming – it means everyone wants the same thing. If they don’t sit down with us, we will 100 per cent be back here again next week.” Dara Bradley
Josh Graves (31), from north Dublin, was one of the more than 150 civilian members of An Garda Síochána on strike outside Garda Headquarters in the Phoenix Park on Wednesday.
Graves and his partner both work in the Civil Service, and he feels striking is the only way to get his point across.
“We’ve just had enough, to be honest. We’re both in our early 30s and we are struggling through life. We can’t afford a house, and can barely afford to put the petrol in the car at this stage, never mind groceries and bills.”
We just want to afford a house, get married and have children. But at the moment, none of those are feasible for us
He said people who work on the ground and keep the country running deserve better.
“This is our last option. None of us want to be here. I’d much rather be in work today. We’re not getting paid for today.
“We don’t want to cause the disruption to the rest of the community, but, unfortunately, we’ve got to the stage where we feel this is the only way we can get our point across.”
Graves said staff just want their pay to “meet the requirements of the cost of living and inflation”.
“We just want to afford a house, get married and have children. But at the moment, none of those are feasible for us.” Hugh Dooley
Paula Morrin is a midwife manager at the Rotunda Hospital in Dublin who believes the cost-of-living crisis is having a significant impact on the health and safety of staff.
“The budget came and went and there was no reduction in the cost of fuel. We have members here who are travelling from Monaghan, Kerry, Wicklow, Wexford. I’m lucky, I live on the south side of Dublin, but it takes me two hours to get here. That’s a lot of petrol,” she said.
“The prices have affected all of us. We have members who have fallen asleep behind the wheel of a car and died on the roads in the last couple of years. We have members who have lived in their cars. People are impacted and our salaries haven’t risen in line with inflation.”
Morrin said she adores her job, wants to be in the hospital caring for her patients, and that staff “work tirelessly”.
“We have a loyalty to our patients, we care for them, but we also have to care for our families and care for ourselves. We’re all affected as individuals. And there’s been so many broken promises. It’s enough.” Shauna Bowers
Mark Prouse, head groundsman at the Iveagh Gardens in Dublin, described the provision of €1.2 billion for public sector pay in the budget as “an insult”.
“ Micheál Martin comes along and brags about this €1.2 billion that he’s giving us over the next three years. When you break it down, it’s actually only €3.50, €3.40 a day or something.
“It’s crazy. You couldn’t get a cup of coffee with what he’s offering us, so it’s not a genuine offer. He thinks we’re all stupid when we’re not.”
[ Public opinion may shift if the second strike goes ahead Opens in new window ]
Prouse, who is also a Siptu shop steward, said the strike could have been averted if the Government engaged in negotiations with trade unions months ago.
“My gas bill has doubled, my electricity bill has doubled, my diesel has doubled. I mean, what do they expect us to live on? Nobody can survive on the wages we’re getting.”
Prouse thinks the dispute can be resolved in the coming days to avoid another 24-hour strike next Wednesday if the Government “stop insulting us”. Órla Ryan
Wednesday’s strike is all about wages and the increased cost of getting by, said Conor Carroll, a porter at St Michael’s Hospital in Dún Laoghaire.
He switched from bar work eight years ago to able to spend more time with his children.
“We’re just out looking for fair play,” he said, picketing at the hospital gates on the town’s main street.
“It’s just about the cost of living. Every time you go to the supermarket you feel it,” he said, gesturing towards the Tesco shopping centre across the road.
“Everything’s gone up – even the cost of eating – and whatever you’re earning doesn’t feel like enough these days.”
The hospital, he said, is a good place to work, categorising it as a community operation where “everyone gets on”.
He commutes from Lucan and tries to work shifts that allow him do a school run.
“Management are good, they are always helpful with rosters when you need it,” he said. “I have no complaints, really, except that my pay hasn’t gone up and everything else has.” Emmet Malone

title: Netflix to cut 1,000 jobs as growth concerns mount
description: Streaming group faces pressure to boost viewer engagement after shares fall more than 40% in a year
content:
Netflix is cutting about 1,000 jobs, its largest lay-off in four years, as the streaming group grapples with a declining share price and mounting pressure to boost engagement on its platform.
The cuts, equivalent to about 6 per cent of its global staff, will primarily impact employees in Netflix’s product, technology, legal and human resources divisions.
According to an internal memo, Netflix co-chief executives Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters told staff the company needed to be more “disciplined”.
“Our mission – to entertain the world – is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources,” they wrote.
The cuts come as Netflix faces rising questions about whether it can sustain its rapid growth. The company’s stock has dropped more than 40 per cent in the past year, as investors worry about slowing engagement. Its failed attempt to acquire Warner Bros Discovery prompted concern that it did not have enough strong content of its own.
Sarandos acknowledged the challenges at a Bloomberg conference last month. “Overall, we’re not growing as fast as I want us to, and we’re working on making that move faster,” he said.
Netflix has been experimenting with new programming to try to get subscribers to spend more time on its service, expanding into live sports, video podcasts and shows featuring YouTube creators.
Investors have been disappointed with the company’s film and television slate, despite Netflix regularly notching multiple shows at the top of Nielsen’s most-viewed streaming titles. The company has not had a hit that has broken through to audiences in 2026 in the same way Stranger Things, Squid Game or Wednesday have in recent years.
Despite spending enormous sums to attract top directors and actors, its straight-to-streaming approach has often meant Netflix’s movies fail to become cultural events that draw in new subscribers.
Hollywood’s success at the box office this summer, with Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey both raking in more than $1 billion (€900 million) globally, underscored the enduring power of the big screen and its ability to command audiences’ attention.
Netflix has started to shift its distribution model, wagering theatrical releases can help establish its platform as a destination for tent-pole films.
The company plans to release Greta Gerwig’s Narnia in cinemas worldwide in 2027, breaking with its long-held model of releasing movies directly on its streaming service.
The job cuts come a week before Netflix is due to report quarterly earnings. Sarandos and Peters told employees the company was still on track to meet its full-year financial forecast.
The last time Netflix announced significant lay-offs was 2022, after reporting its first quarterly decline in subscribers in more than a decade, a shock that prompted a sweeping reassessment of both its business strategy and the streaming model across Hollywood.
Brian White, an analyst at MCH, said Netflix was “nearing the end of an unfulfilling year”, pointing to the growth and intensifying “video-driven engagement across the leading social media platforms.
“Consumers have an ever-expanding array of services competing for their time,” he added. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Yemen’s Houthis vow more attacks on Saudi targets after hitting oil giant’s headquarters
description: Iran-backed militants retaliate after Riyadh-led coalition strikes sites in Yemen’s capital
author_name: Timour Azhari, Jana Choukeir, Tala Ramadan
content:
Yemen ’s ‌ Houthis said on Wednesday they would continue to attack airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia , a day after a strike that sources said caused extensive damage to the headquarters of oil giant Saudi ​Aramco .
The Houthis said the threatened locations were legitimate targets and described their attacks as retaliation for Saudi strikes on Yemen – threatening to escalate a conflict reignited by the US-Iran confrontation in the Gulf.
Saudi Arabia has faced widening Houthi strikes over the past week, including an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people.
Tuesday night’s attack on Saudi Aramco’s base in the eastern city ​of Dhahran caused a fire that spread across several floors, three people with knowledge of the matter said. The Saudi energy ministry had said the strike caused a limited fire.
Operations at Aramco were continuing normally, ⁠with employees working from home, according to two of the sources. Aramco did not immediately reply to a Reuters request for comment.
The ‌escalating ​conflict has dealt a blow to Saudi Crown prince Mohammed bin Salman’s ambitious plans to transform and diversify the Saudi economy and reduce its reliance on oil.
The Houthis say they have been retaliating for the kingdom’s backing of Yemeni government forces ⁠in the Yemen war that restarted last month.
The Saudi-led coalition said ​it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh on Wednesday ​and several loud booms were heard in the Saudi capital.
[ Why can’t Saudi Arabia stop the Houthi attacks? Opens in new window ]
Saudi authorities earlier issued an alert for a possible aerial threat in Riyadh on Wednesday before the warning was lifted, ‌a witness said.
It wasn’t immediately clear what caused the booms ​and there was no immediate comment from the authorities on their source.
The Saudi government media office didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment about the ⁠cause of the booms.
In their statement on Wednesday, the Houthis said ⁠they had launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles ​and drones at the Saudi Aramco facilities in Dhahran, Riyadh airport and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh.
In a broad threat, they urged “international shipping companies”, civilians and workers to evacuate Saudi airports and oil facilities.
[ Is it safe to fly through the Middle East? Advice for Irish travellers after Saudi airport attack Opens in new window ]
The Dhahran complex hosts a major operations centre for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals.
Riyadh’s international airport has come under attack four times, including Saturday’s attack which was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade.
Authorities have closed the airport until October 17th and airlines have cancelled flights to Saudi Arabia.
Fearing the rise of Iranian influence and the prospect of chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen’s civil war in support of the government in 2015 after the Houthis seized the capital ‌Sana’a.
The UN brokered a 2022 truce ⁠between the warring sides in Yemen that kept a fragile peace until this year.
Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis’ sudden gains last month, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to ‌the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Red Cross said on Wednesday that hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties as fighting intensified along multiple front lines.
The UN ​World Food Programme warned that life-saving assistance had been cut off to the government-held city of Taiz, which was ​encircled by Houthi fighters earlier this month.
“WFP and its partners cannot access more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance, including more than 200,000 women and children,” WFP said in a statement. – Reuters

title: Poland’s breakthrough generation await Ireland in World Cup playoff
description: Poles come to Aviva in December with aim of qualifying for Brazil 2027, their first time on football’s biggest stage
content:
Woman’s football in Poland is experiencing its breakthrough moment. Having reached their first major tournament at last year’s Euros, Nina Patalon’s side can qualify for the Women’s World Cup next summer by beating the Republic of Ireland over a two-legged playoff in December.
Only one global star will make it to Brazil : will it be Ewa Pajor or Katie McCabe?
Gdansk is to host the first leg on December 1st before a return to the Aviva Stadium , Dublin , on December 5th – the scene of Ireland’s deflating loss to Wales two years ago in a Euros playoff.
“Forget Wales,” Ireland manager Carla Ward said following the 12-0 aggregate defeat of Kazakhstan on Tuesday. “Honestly, forget Wales. We have come a long way since then.”
So have Poland. Anything seems possible after they outlasted Belgium this week, when a penalty shoot-out was settled by Spanish-born striker Natalia Padilla-Bidas.
The higher ranked Belgians had been expected to hold on to a 1-0 first-leg lead and give their record goalscorer, Tessa Wullaert, the international stage that her outstanding career deserves.
But Pajor had other ideas. The Barcelona striker is giving Robert Lewandowski a run for his money as the most impactful Polish footballer. Pajor netted twice in the Champions League final defeat of Lyons last May, and she hit another brace to force penalties against Belgium.
The 29-year-old has scored 79 times since signing for Barcelona in June 2024, displaying the lightest of touches in front of goal.
Pajor’s dramatic second on Tuesday, in the 116th minute, would have Brian Kerr describing her as a “barreller”. She willed the ball into the net after bumping off two Belgian defenders and rounding goalkeeper Lowiese Seynhaeve.
“Ewa is a top, top player, but they have a lot of those,” Ward said before the two World Cup qualifiers in April. “It would be naive to concentrate on one player.”
Sure enough, Poland only saw off Belgium after Pajor’s poorly struck spot-kick was saved by Seynhaeve.
Afterwards a relieved Patalon said: “It was the most exciting match of my coaching career. I’ve never had to go to extra-time or penalties before. It’s not like me, but my emotions were certainly visible – and they’ll stay with me for another week.”
The Polish coach has seven weeks to recover before her well-rounded squad face Ireland at home. This moment has been promised since Paris Saint-Germain defender Paulina Dudek and AC Milan midfielder Ewelina Kamczyk were team-mates with Pajor on the under-17 team who beat Sweden in the 2013 Euros final.
Dudek and Kamczyk remain key figures alongside Bayer Leverkusen winger Paulina Tomasiak and Bristol City defender Oliwia Wos.
Kinga Seweryn was an unlikely hero over the two Belgium games as the reserve goalkeeper replaced the injured Kinga Szemik to guess correctly in the shoot-out – twice saving to her left – and she denied Wullaert from the spot in the first leg.
Ward said: “I’ll be honest, I watched it.” Which was some achievement considering the shoot-out only finished in the 12th minute of Ireland’s 4-0 defeat of Kazakhstan.
“I watched it out there [on the pitch in Páirc Uí Chaoimh]. I watched the whole game,” she said.
“They were very good, Poland were, but we’ve played them. We know what to expect. They played a similar way to when we played them first time [in April]. I’m not so sure what they’re going to take away from our two games.”
Ireland were involved in a 3-2 thriller in Gdansk six months ago when there was also a missed penalty by McCabe. Indeed, early goals by Emily Murphy and a sublime McCabe volley had Ward’s side in control throughout.
A brilliant header by Tanja Pawollek made it 2-1 before Marissa Sheva secured all three points for Ireland, although Pajor’s late lobbed finish over Courtney Brosnan kept it interesting.
Another excellent strike from Sheva proved the difference four days later at the Aviva. There were some aggressive exchanges in Dublin as McCabe was smothered whenever she tried to attack down the left and Denise O’Sullivan was kicked from minute one. “I’m used to it, I like to get on the ball,” the Gotham FC midfielder said.
Ward said: “They’re going to want revenge. They’ll look at it as an opportunity to put right what they got wrong.
“What I would say is if you have a look across both games [in April], I think we were dominant. I think we were very unlucky not to walk away with a bigger scoreline away. At home, Denise hit the bar. [Emily Murphy] hit the post.
“I actually think we’re a better team now as well. We’re getting better all the time. We’ve got depth now.”
(Uefa countries already qualified are Spain, Germany, France and Denmark.)

title: Bank of America profits drop 17% after $1.2bn money laundering fine
description: Morgan Stanley posts $2bn of fixed income revenues, worse than analysts had expected
content:
Profits at Bank of America (BofA) fell 17 per cent year in the third quarter, after the second-largest US bank took a $1.2 billion (€1 billion) hit from a regulatory fine for money laundering and sanctions violations. BofA said net income dropped to $6.9 billion, down from $8.3 billion a year earlier.
The bank reported its results less than 24 hours after the US Treasury said it had fined BofA more than $1 billion for “egregious and continued” money laundering and sanctions violations, concluding the bank failed to properly report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions. BofA has around 1,200 employees in Ireland.
The action from regulators – which included a consent order that requires the bank to work with a third party to identify and report undetected suspicious transactions – raises questions about how much BofA needs to spend on remediation to prove to regulators that it has meaningfully improved its compliance programme.
Shares in BofA tumbled more than 8 per cent in morning trading.
In a statement on Tuesday, the bank said it “already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base”.
On Wednesday, BofA’s chief financial officer Alastair Borthwick told reporters that BofA had dedicated “thousands” of employees to remediation work linked to a consent order first imposed in 2024. The bank did not plan to make substantial further hires to address it, he added.
“We staffed up overtime and we feel like we’re meeting all the obligations in that consent order at this point,” said Borthwick. BofA was hit with an additional consent order on Tuesday.
BofA’s performance fell short of analysts’ expectations even without the impact of the fine. Revenues increased 3 per cent to $30 billion, weighed down by lower trading revenue and investment banking fees.
Fixed income revenues have been weak across Wall Street in the wake of the US Federal Reserve raising interest rates last month, including at Morgan Stanley, which also reported on Wednesday.
Morgan Stanley posted $2 billion of fixed income revenues, worse than analysts had expected. At BofA, the figure was 17 per cent lower than a year ago, at $2.6 billion.
But other parts of Morgan Stanley’s business helped make up for it, with revenues in equities trading – which have continued to benefit from clients’ stock market bets around artificial intelligence – up 41 per cent to $5.8 billion, well ahead of estimates for $4.9 billion.
That helped lift Morgan Stanley’s third-quarter profits 6.5 per cent higher than a year ago, to a better than expected $4.9 billion.
Morgan Stanley reported net new assets in wealth management of $232 billion, well ahead of estimates for about $112 billion. The figure is closely tracked by investors as a measure of future growth, and beat the record set last quarter when inflows were boosted by SpaceX’s IPO through Morgan Stanley’s work managing the company’s employee stock plan.
Morgan Stanley said just over half the inflows were tied to IPOs. Its shares fell 3 per cent in early trading. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Tech leaders outline AI dangers and opportunities at Dublin summit
description: Recent incidents ‘early warning shots’ of tech’s potential for harm, says Google DeepMind co-founder
content:
The artificial intelligence (AI) industry needs strict guardrails and standards to ensure the technology is safe, the International AI Summit in Dublin heard on Wednesday.
Tech leaders from Microsoft, Google, Stripe and IBM gathered at the RDS in Ballsbridge, Dublin 4, alongside policymakers to discuss the opportunities and issues facing the industry.
Cofounder and chairman of Google DeepMind Demis Hassabis said recent incidents of AI agents going “rogue” and hacking third-party systems were “early warning shots”.
[ AI will not bring about ‘displacement’ in public service, says Taoiseach Opens in new window ]
“The systems aren’t that powerful yet, so the incidents aren’t that major, but they could be looking into next year and the next couple of years if we don’t do more work as an industry and individually as companies and governments,” he said.
“There’s a lot of work that we can bring best practices from other sectors that have dealt with safety-critical systems, whether it’s biology or nuclear. I think there’s a lot of lessons that can be learned about containment systems, and I think we need to start taking that seriously and bring experts in from those areas.”
Hassabis has backed the establishment of a standards body that would help develop the technology in a “nuanced and nimble and dynamic way”, and put more responsibility on so-called frontier labs who were developing new areas of the technology to make sure it was safe.
“We don’t want to stifle the innovation, all the amazing things that come out of it. We want those things, but also there’s no complete consensus even [among] people working on this – the scientists and the researchers working on this – [about] what exactly the risks are and how big they are,” he said.
He said a framework that could quickly adapt to test critical elements of the systems, keeping up with the technology in a way that regulation would struggle to do, would be needed.
Speaking at the opening of the event, European Commission vice-president with responsibility for tech sovereignty Henna Virkkunen said incidents of hacking and so-called rogue AI undermine trust in the technology.
[ AI systems should adopt safety lessons from nuclear industry Opens in new window ]
“The commission has been loud and clear: AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control, and we stand ready to take all necessary steps to ensure companies follow AI Act rules so that European people can trust AI models and innovations.”
Stripe’s Eileen O’Mara said the technology also presented an opportunity for economies.
“What we are seeing is a complete replatform of the economy. AI companies are going global faster than any other cohort of any in [software as a service] land in history. That’s really unique,” she said.
“AI in this economy should be one that brings everybody with it. This is an opportunity for everybody to have an opportunity to drive productivity and growth, and most importantly for Europe to drive meaningful entrepreneurship and drive business.”
The event was opened by Taoiseach Micheál Martin, who said there was a desire for “responsible, safe and secure AI” with AI benefits “guided and guarded by human agency”.
The technology has the potential to improve services, he said, but there was a need to cut through the noise, hype and rhetoric to zero in on the opportunities that could answer many of the challenges facing Europe today.

title: Rubbish and broken glass line capital’s streets with no one to clean up after Dubliners
description: Council’s plea to the public to bring litter home falls on deaf ears as bins overflow
content:
Dublin city’s public bins were overflowing by midmorning on Wednesday and by the early afternoon many streets in the centre looked like the St Patrick’s Day parade had just passed through.
Burst refuse bags disgorged their contents on to footpaths and broken glass glinted along the length of cycle lanes.
Dublin City Council’s desperate 11th-hour plea on Tuesday evening to residents and visitors asking that, for just one day, they clean up after themselves and not discard their waste on the streets, appeared to have fallen on deaf ears.
“Staff will not be available to empty litter bins or to clean streets,” the council statement said. “We ask the public to help keep the city clean during the strike by taking litter home where possible and not leaving waste beside bins that are full.”
On Thursday morning Alex Kelleher was sweeping the path on South Great George’s Street outside Dublin Ink Tattoo, where he works, as well as the adjacent restaurants and takeaways, some of which had yet to open for business.
“Someone’s got to do it, and if we don’t do it, no one will,” he said as he lifted the empty takeaway boxes, restaurant kitchen waste and household waste spread across the width of the path.
“For a tattoo studio, cleanliness is the upmost important thing. Being sanitary is very important. Having litter anywhere near the studio is not acceptable for our clients.”
As he lifted another catering tub of sauce, he said he supported the striking council workers. “I have no problem doing this today, I think we should all treat our surrounding areas with a small bit of respect and love, and maybe think of the people who are doing this every day. It’s tough work and they deserve to get compensated for that.”
[ Dublin City Council intends to press ahead with bin bag ban in February Opens in new window ]
Audrey Lambert, a Dublin City Council staff officer and Fórsa branch secretary, was picketing outside the Civic Offices on Wood Quay, standing beside a bin, stuffed to capacity by 10am.
“We provide such a vital services for the public. We keep the city going and we deserve to have a pay rise going with inflation rates.”
The bin, she said, illustrated the often unnoticed work council staff do in the city.
“It’s just one bin, but it’s the perfect example of the impact when council services stop. It shows the amount of work we are doing, not only to the public, but to the Government, because if you listen to them, we’re not doing much for the pay rise, but if you look around you, the city is not clean today.”
The gates of the Grangegorman Bring Centre in Dublin 7 were locked on Wednesday. Bags of rubbish and stacks of cardboard were left outside, or squeezed through the railings, next to the sign warning of consequences for illegal dumping.
A man pulled up in his car and hauled out a bulky bag of recycling material. He slowly read a sign on the gate that said: “Official Dispute” and another “Fair Play Decent Work Stronger Services”. “I didn’t know this was part of the public services,” he said. He hesitated, then said “fair enough” and put the bag back in his car before driving away.

title: Pope Leo’s cancer diagnosis tests the assumption of a long papacy
description: Leo suddenly faces the same sense of urgency and questions of longevity that had hung over his predecessor
content:
W hen Leo XIV was elected pope less than 18 months ago, he seemed to have years ahead of him to shape the Catholic Church . At 69, he was young by recent papal standards, and the faithful marvelled at his energy and apparently robust health. He was known to play tennis regularly and had no reported medical problems. He reintroduced summer vacations to make sure he remained fresh and rested.
Leo, the first pope born in the United States , marked a break from his predecessor, Francis , who started his papacy at age 76 but had already had a lung condition at a young age. A year into his papacy, Francis told reporters that he thought he would serve as pope for only two or three years before going “off to the house of the Father”. In the end he lasted a dozen years, but in his later years suffered from a bad knee, intestinal problems and finally, pneumonia in both lungs.
Now, Leo, who was diagnosed with lung cancer on Tuesday , suddenly faces the same sense of urgency and questions of longevity that had hung over Francis.
The diagnosis poses a lurching shift in the outlook for a pope whose relative youth and health indicated he had decades to reign. It casts uncertainty over his travel schedule, his agenda and his efforts to unite the Church. And in the worst-case scenario, it raises questions about succession that most thought would not have to be addressed for years to come.
“The common consensus was he’s young, we’re in for a long papacy,” says Christopher White, a senior fellow at the Initiative on Catholic Social Thought and Public Life at Georgetown University and the author of Pope Leo XIV: Inside the Conclave and the Dawn of a New Papacy.
While Leo was not as young as Pope John Paul II, who was just 58 when he was elected in 1978, Leo’s apparent healthy lifestyle added to an impression of his vitality. “Leo has the profile of someone who takes care of himself,” White said. “So that has added to the shock.”
[ Pope faces further tests to determine extent of cancer Opens in new window ]
At his weekly general audiences in St Peter’s Square or on international journeys, he showed no signs of impaired health and kept a hectic schedule. In Rome his agenda was packed with meetings and over the summer he released a significant document on artificial intelligence.
From the beginning of his papacy Leo, born Robert Francis Prevost in Chicago, behaved like someone who believed he could take his time. In the early months he was considered slow to act. He made few personnel changes and did not immediately grab headlines with dramatic pronouncements or policy moves. He seemed more interested in soothing tensions and listening.
And even when Leo became more strident, as when he criticised the Trump administration’s war in Iran, he responded only when the president specifically attacked him, and then retreated, saying he did not want a fight. With his quiet, steady demeanour, he gave the sense that he was in no rush.
After Francis’s tumultuous papacy, during which conservative Christians baulked at the progressive Catholicism he elevated, Leo was seen as a leader who could calm the church. Leo has been popular not only with both progressive and conservative Catholics, but with people outside the faith who see him as a moral leader in troubled times.
[ ‘Leomania’: How secular France fell for the Pope Opens in new window ]
His illness will inevitably unsettle the church, particularly depending on how transparent the Vatican continues to be about the pope’s progress through treatment. “This kind of thing just creates disquiet,” says David Gibson, director of the Center on Religion and Culture at Fordham University.
For now, the pope, who recently travelled to Spain and France, has said he will keep to his plan to travel to Latin America in November. Inevitably, any changes to his schedule will be scrutinised closely.
The pope’s doctors announced that the surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung was successful and had no complications. Information released by the Vatican suggested the cancer was caught at an early stage.
If Leo makes a strong recovery, Gibson says, the cancer could become part of a heroic narrative that buoys his reputation. Pope John Paul II, who started out in excellent health, was seriously wounded by an assassination attempt in 1981 and spent three months in hospital. His recovery became part of “the mythology that grew up around him”, says Gibson.
And while few people face assassination attempts, many people live with cancer. Leo’s illness and how he behaves during treatment could serve as an inspiration to others suffering from disease.
“There’s also an opportunity for him in this vulnerability to be as great a comfort to many people as he was in the first year and a half of his papacy,” Gibson says.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

title: Nord Stream pipeline sabotage may not have been a crime, say accused’s lawyers
description: Ukrainian ex-military officer alleged to have led personnel in operation to destroy sub-sea gas infrastructure
content:
Lawyers for a Ukrainian ex-military officer accused of plotting the September 2022 bombing of Russia’ s biggest gas pipeline to Europe argued at the start of his trial in Hamburg on ‌Wednesday that blowing up Russian infrastructure may not have been a crime.
Serhii Kuznetsov is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents, including divers and an explosives expert, that blew up the Nord Stream pipeline in one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations ​of modern times.
The case provides the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the bombing.
[ Germany puts Ukrainian ex-officer in the dock over Nord Stream sabotage Opens in new window ]
Moving to have the case dismissed, Kuznetsov’s lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline – which provided half of Germany’s imports of natural gas before Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine – was a “Russian weapon” and therefore potentially a legitimate target.
“Is ​it unlawful to destroy an aggressor’s infrastructure without harming any human beings?” Canestrini asked.
Prosecutors have alleged that Kuznetsov, who was arrested under an international warrant in Italy last year, worked with members of the Ukrainian military to plan the ⁠clandestine operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities.
