Arguing there was no incentive to flee because the EncroChat evidence could be ruled inadmissible, he questioned the reliability of alleged messages sent on devices anyone could have used.
Stressing the defendant’s right to be presumed innocent, he also highlighted how three co-accused have all been released.
Bail was refused, however, due to the risks of flight and reoffending.
Remanding Drew in custody until November 11th, the judge told him: “You are facing allegations of very serious organised criminality.”

title: AI will not bring about ‘displacement’ in public service, says Taoiseach
description: Martin urges critics of technology to focus on positives as he announces new forum on workplace effects
content:
A new forum involving the Government , employers and trade unions is to be established to explore the impact of AI on the workplace.
The Government’s Labour Employer Economic Forum (LEEF) will be convened to address concerns AI will wipe out many professions and make it harder for entry-level graduates to get jobs.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin announced the forum at the AI summit in Dublin ’s RDS on Wednesday, part of the Irish presidency of the Council of the European Union .
He conceded some “work functions may not survive AI”, but other additional work functions will be created.
“We have seen this with technology before. There is an open book on that at the moment. We are certainly looking more at the opportunity side than the negative side.”
Martin said Ireland needed to embrace the possibilities of AI without “compromising on our core values”.
He delivered a robust defence, saying the technology would improve the delivery of public services, assist in health screening, improve customer service experience in the tax system and help with fire and flood forecasting.
He said there was an “open question in terms of displacement”, but it would not be happening in the public service.
“There will be a transformative impact, that could mean changing of roles, redeployment and assuming new roles within the public service. We are not necessarily looking at displacement,” he said.
[ AI systems should adopt safety lessons from nuclear industry Opens in new window ]
“The tasks will change; for example, mathematicians in the research and private sector will be doing different things.”
European Commission executive vice-president Henna Virkkunen , who is also the commissioner for Digital and Frontier Technologies, said Europe will have to triple its data centre capacity in five to seven years.
She acknowledged concerns of citizens across the bloc given the energy the centres consume.
“We are now supporting our member states to build also AI factories, and we have now an open call for gigafactories that we should have even more powerful supercomputers in the coming years and months than we have today,” she said.
During her speech, she said the EU’s AI Act would already regulate high-risk AI systems and models whether developed within the EU or in countries such as China or the United States .
She enumerated the risks of losing control of AI, including biological weapons, mass manipulation that could affect elections, and cyberattacks.
[ Mark Zuckerberg says Meta has reached AI ‘frontier’ Opens in new window ]
The AI Act prevents “overlapping regulation across member states, keeping the European space predictable and simple for our start-ups and industry”, she told the conference.
The commission was “loud and clear” that AI must remain under human direction, she said. And the commission “stands ready to take all necessary steps to ensure that companies follow the AI Act rules, so that European people and companies can trust AI models and systems.”
In the last year, she said, AI was already showing many signs of improving people’s lives, including progress in flagging early signs of cancer.
In energy, AI was helping predict electricity demand and optimise power distribution. In June, the commission launched the AI grids initiatives framework to develop, train and deploy a pan-European AI model for power grids.
About 1,500 leaders in the AI world attended the conference. There was a small demonstration outside protesting against the amount of energy used by data centres to process AI.

title: US inflation jumps to 3.7% as Iran war drives up prices
description: Rebound in fuel costs has piled pressure on voters ahead of midterm elections
content:
US inflation jumped to 3.7 per cent in September as the war in Iran drove a rebound in fuel prices , piling pressure on Americans ahead of the midterm elections and prompting traders to raise bets on Federal Reserve rate rises.
Wednesday’s annual consumer price index figure was up from 3.4 per cent in August and ahead of the 3.6 per cent forecast in a Bloomberg poll of economists.
Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, also came in ahead of Wall Street expectations, rising to 2.6 from the previous month’s figure of 2.4 per cent.
Wednesday’s data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics marks the first time US annual inflation has risen since May. It underlines how the energy shock triggered by the war in the Middle East continues to reverberate across the world’s biggest economy, weeks ahead of November’s midterm election.
US President Donald Trump has tried to contain the economic fallout from the conflict and douse fuel prices, as Democrats tap into voter frustration at the cost of living and seek to wrest control of Congress from his Republican Party.
But Wednesday’s data suggests that less affluent Americans in particular are being increasingly squeezed. Hourly earnings rose by just 3 per cent in September versus a year earlier, marking the sixth consecutive month of declining real wage growth.
[ Energy prices drive Irish consumer price inflation to highest level since January 2024 Opens in new window ]
“Inflation simply isn’t coming down quickly enough,” said Eric Winograd, chief economist at AllianceBernstein. “The bottom part of the K-shaped economy is losing ground, as anybody who has seen campaign ads on TV the last few weeks has heard.”
The inflation data increased bets that the Fed could raise rates again as soon as this month after it lifted borrowing costs for the first time in three years in September. Expectations of an October increase had faded in recent weeks after central bank officials indicated they were not in a rush to act again.
Following the data release, traders in the futures market were pricing in a roughly 45 per cent chance of an October rise, up from 22 per cent before.
Jeff Schulze, head investment strategist at the Franklin Templeton Institute, said that the latest data “bolsters the case for additional rate hikes, but recent dovish Fed-speak . . . suggests that the bar is high for an immediate hike”.
“I don’t think there is going to be urgency to react to this one report and raise interest rates six days before midterms,” added Joe Lavorgna, chief economist at SMBC Nikko Securities. “The Fed doesn’t want to put itself into a political fight unnecessarily. But they will almost certainly go again in December.”
Treasury yields jumped following the figures, with the two-year rising as much as 0.16 percentage points to 4.95 per cent, approaching the 28-month high it hit in September.
The months-long sell-off in the Treasury market had abated in recent days, as bond investors began to snap up government debt. But the recovery in bonds was almost fully erased by Wednesday morning’s move.
The US dollar strengthened 0.6 per cent against the euro to its highest level since May 2025.
The sell-off in bonds was poised to cascade into the equities market, with futures tracking the tech-focused Nasdaq 100 falling almost 0.8 per cent and those for the blue-chip S&P 500 down 0.2 per cent.
The September inflation rise was largely driven by higher fuel prices, with the BLS’s index tracking petrol prices up 34.2 per cent year on year and 9.1 per cent higher than August’s figure.
Petrol and diesel costs eased during the summer from the initial highs after the war broke out. But they have bounced back in recent months as tensions flared in the Middle East, sending the price of diesel to record highs and prompting a flurry of policy interventions by Trump.
Analysts noted that the rise in core inflation suggested price pressures were becoming more entrenched, with rises in everything from cars and airfares to education and toys.
“Today’s CPI report stands out as the first of the year in which price pressure appeared to be showing up in most corners of the consumption basket at once,” said Jason Pride, chief of investment strategy and research at Glenmede. - Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Why can’t Saudi Arabia stop the Houthi attacks?
description: Lethal strikes show growing military power of Iran-backed militia
content:
D espite spending hundreds of billions of dollars assembling one of the Middle East’s most powerful militaries, Saudi Arabia has struggled to stop a wave of Houthi attacks.
Day after day this month, strikes have hit targets deep inside the kingdom, including Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, exposing the limits of that vast investment in stark fashion.
Analysts say the Houthis have used a four-year ceasefire with Riyadh to rearm and hone their tactics. For example, they have been using drones to identify gaps in air defences before launching cruise missiles. In doing so, they are drawing on lessons learned by Iran and its allies.
They are a Shia religious, political and paramilitary organisation founded in Yemen by Hussein al-Houthi in the 1990s in opposition to then president Ali Abdullah Saleh, who was accused of corruption and aligning with the US . As the Houthis sided with Iran, they are part of the “Axis of Resistance”, which also includes Iran, Lebanon’s Hizbullah and Iraq’s fundamentalist factions.
The Houthis have only ground forces. They have no navy and air force although they employ explosive-laden aerial drones, drone boats and domestically-manufactured medium-range ballistic missiles that can reach targets 2,000km and have struck Israel .
Houthi troops grew from about 30,000 in 2015 to 350,000 by 2024. As many have been fighting for multiple years, they are experienced in warfare.
Yemen is gripped in a complex conflict fuelled by a domestic power struggle and regional rivalries that have drawn in outsiders, disrupted international shipping and threaten to precipitate global disorder.
The United Nations had imposed a truce that had frozen the war since 2022.
The current confrontation began in July when Saudi Arabia was blamed for bombing Sana’a airport as a flight carrying an Iran-allied Houthi delegation was due to land after consultations in Tehran.
The Houthis responded by declaring a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, and mounted attacks on Saudi oil refineries, tankers and pipelines carrying Saudi oil .
It had hampered its ability to get its oil to customers at a time oil and gas exports had been reduced due to Iran’s restrictive hold on the Strait of Hormuz , where the normal flow of oil last month but storage facilities must be refilled.
In the near-term, it wants to secure control over all Yemen by seizing territory in the north and west and along the Red Sea coast, including the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, Perim Island and Mocha port.
Control would enable the Houthis to dominate vital global maritime trade routes, project power and exert economic and political leverage.
In the longer term, it wants to weaken Iran’s chief regional rival, Saudi Arabia, which supports Yemen’s recognised Government.

title: Dealing with new uncertainties in a volatile world
description: ‘What we are hearing ... is that uncertainty itself has a cost, making investment decisions more difficult’
content:
Perhaps the most tangible benefit of US president Donald Trump’s visit to Ireland in September was his announcement in Doonbeg Golf Resort of a decision to abolish tariffs on Irish whiskey.
That this sudden policy change was influenced, at least in part, by a word in his ear at the resort by Irish Open winner Shane Lowry, is a reflection of the turbulent and rapidly changing nature of international trading environments and how they can be influenced in great part by the economic and foreign policy whims of the leader of the United States.
Businesses tend to like certainty, especially those dealing with the challenges of navigating overseas markets. But many of them have had to deal with changing tariff rules, geopolitical crises and rising global energy costs in recent years.
Aebhric McGibney, director of public and international affairs with Dublin Chamber, says the impact of global trade tensions extends well beyond Ireland’s big exporters. Dublin Chamber research in Q2 2025 found that 81 per cent of businesses in the region expected to be affected to some degree by escalating international trade disputes, while more recent findings from Q1 2026 show that global trade and geopolitical instability is now the second most significant challenge facing Dublin firms, he points out.
“What we are hearing from businesses is that uncertainty itself has a cost, making investment decisions more difficult, creating supply chain concerns and weighing on confidence, even where firms are not directly exposed to tariffs. Some businesses are responding by exploring new markets and export opportunities and looking at ways to strengthen supply-chain resilience.”
One company that found itself hugely exposed to changing tariff rules was start-up Emerald Ice Cream, cofounded by Eoin Kennedy and Janet Miley.
Buoyed by the success of Irish dairy, its 2025 launch centred on the US market where it has secured listings in several hundred stores. “In our business plan we looked at the rates and duties applying to dairy in the lead-up to our launch,” says Kennedy.
“On the week of our launch, the US administration launched reciprocal tariffs, and we were hit with an additional 10 per cent going on top of an already high rate. The first thing that we did was reach out to the organisations in Ireland that could help us, such as Enterprise Ireland and Bord Bia. We got great support. It was daunting at the start as we were bootstrapping a business, and this wasn’t going to help us.”
During the following months, additional tariffs went through a see-saw of changes. As a nimble start-up it was possible to micromanage the impact of these changes Kennedy says, with constant contact with customs brokers, for example, as the product transitioned from Ireland to the US. Eyes were always on the big prize, but the roller-coaster experience has been a challenge, he says, compounded by significant increases in container price due to rising global energy costs.
The larger and more complex the business, the bigger the challenges. Biosynth, a producer of critical raw materials for the pharmaceutical and diagnostics industries, employs just under 10 per cent of its global workforce in Ireland. It is part of a wider organisation with manufacturing plants in 10 locations worldwide.
“When the new tariffs were introduced, we had to consider the impact for our products that were made in China and imported into the US and what the impact would be on the products we manufacture in the US going into China,” explains Philip Noone, executive vice-president of diagnostics.
The response was to set up an internal “war office” group drawn from a cross-section of senior leaders in diverse positions across the group. In the end, Trump backed down on the proposed new tariffs for China but not before considerable work had been put in to model how the organisation would react.
“We’ve kept that war office open if that issue jumps up again and we’re also aware that we are in a hotspot being in the pharma biotech industry with so many leading companies manufacturing here.”
The significant increase in US tariff rates, from an average of 3 per cent pre-2025 to a minimum 15 per cent baseline on the majority of EU goods, has had a significant impact on Ireland’s export volumes. Irish goods exports to the US plunged 72 per cent year-on-year in January 2026 and 82 per cent in March 2026, partly reflecting the unwinding of 2025’s pre-tariff stockpiling, says John O’Loughlin, partner, global trade & customs, PwC Ireland.
“The biggest impact has been uncertainty, making it difficult for firms to plan P&L [profit and loss], cash flow, pricing and competitiveness. Pharma, Ireland’s dominant export sector, faces the threat of up to 100 per cent tariffs, while SMEs, already resource-stretched, lack the in-house teams to navigate this complexity,” he notes.
Diversification remains a key strategy for Irish exporters looking to sustain and grow their business in this challenging trade environment, he adds. However, add to that the higher energy costs associated with the conflict in the Middle East, and the headache compounds.
“The Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz blockade drove a sharp oil price spike in early 2026, with bunker fuel costs nearly doubling on some shipping routes, fuel costs per container rising from $155 to $269 on the newest vessels and from $360 to $626 on older ships,” McLoughlin adds. “Surging fuel prices place increased strain on the Irish export market, with higher transport costs leading to potentially higher export prices, reduced competitiveness compared with local producers and margin pressure.”
Increased tariffs don’t just affect companies doing business with the US. Tariff increases by the EU this year are affecting steel reinforcement manufacturer Midland Steel, which supplies the construction industry in Ireland, the UK and other parts of Europe. The Mountmellick-based business has traditionally sourced much of its steel outside the EU but is now restricted by rates jumping from 25 per cent to 50 per cent on non-EU material.
Founder and chief executive Tony Woods says that this will lead to pricing and capacity issues in the coming months. Like many other businesses, he says, this pressure is coming on top of the huge increases in energy associated with the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran.
So how can businesses best prepare for this increasingly volatile environment?
“One of the most practical steps any exporter can take is to strengthen due diligence across their supply chain and customer base,” says Laura Fannin, partner, commercial, at Eversheds Sutherland.
“Having detailed knowledge of your counterparties is essential. This includes analysing where they are based, what regulatory regimes they fall under, and whether they are exposed to sanctions or restricted-party lists. Robust due diligence not only helps businesses identify legal and compliance risks before they crystallise, but also enables them to react more quickly to changing trade restrictions and avoiding costly disruption to their operations.
“Importantly, once a particular risk has been identified, businesses are often in a position to mitigate it contractually, whether through tailored compliance obligations, enhanced termination rights, alternative sourcing arrangements, or other risk-allocation mechanisms.”
Another area to be considered is commercial contracts. A well-drafted force majeure or material adverse event provision can protect an exporter where tariff increases, trade embargoes, or regulatory changes make performance commercially impracticable or impossible. Where a supplier can no longer provide goods or services due to trade restraints or supply shortages, companies need flexibility in their contracts to shift suppliers quickly, she advises.
Mary Kiely, partner, corporate at Eversheds Sutherland, meanwhile, says that a more fractured global trade environment is forcing companies to rethink where and how they grow. As a result, cross-border merger and acquisition (M&A) deals have fallen globally.
“Unsurprisingly, buyers are more focused on domestic resilience amid trade/tariff uncertainty,” she says.
“In the first half of this year, we continued to see resilience in the domestic M&A market in Ireland. Companies with strong balance sheets and resilient cash flows continue to command strong buyer interest, demonstrating there is clear appetite for the right assets, especially those insulated from regulatory and trade risks.
“For any Irish company which is considering a sale process in the near future, where possible, they should focus on relocating resources geographically to mitigate geopolitical and trade uncertainties and address energy and supply chain security.”
While global trade and geopolitical uncertainty have made Irish M&A more cautious and valuation sensitive, the outlook remains positive for the remainder of 2026, particularly for mid-market Irish M&A activity, she adds.
Despite the challenges, Irish exporters have demonstrated remarkable resilience over the past decade, having successfully navigated Brexit, Covid-19, supply chain disruption and energy market volatility. These experiences have strengthened their ability to respond quickly to external shocks and build more resilient business models, says Aidan McKenna, regional director, Americas for Enterprise Ireland.
“Companies are increasingly adopting a dual-track strategy: protecting and growing market share in established markets such as the United States, while actively diversifying into new markets across Europe, the Gulf and Asia. This aligns closely with the Government’s action plan on market diversification and reflects a growing focus on reducing concentration risk while maintaining momentum in key export markets.
“Importantly, businesses are continuing to invest through uncertainty rather than retreating from it.”
Despite the uncertainty, Enterprise Ireland supported almost 100 client companies to establish new presences in the US during 2024 and 2025, reflecting the continued strategic importance of the market, he adds.

title: Europe at ‘critical moment’ to regulate AI, conference on ethics and media copyright told
description: Irish Times editor calls for level playing field where media is fairly compensated for the original, creative work it produces
content:
Europe is at a “critical moment” in effective regulation of artificial intelligence (AI), the chairman of the Oireachtas committee on AI warned. “Countries that get ahead will stay ahead” and those “that fall behind will stay behind” in the race to master the new technology.
The comments by Fianna Fáil’s Naoise Ó Cearúil came at a conference on Copyright and Human Creativity in the Age of AI which focused on how to implement copyright claims ethically and protect intellectual property rights as the AI sector encroaches on the creative and media industries.
The conference hosted by NewsBrands Ireland, a representative body of news publishers, and the Irish Recorded Music Association, was organised as part of the State’s six-month presidency of the Council of the European Union.
Journalist and broadcaster Dearbhail McDonald, who moderated the discussion, said this balancing act had “created an extinction-level event for many news publishers”.
Ruadhán Mac Cormaic, editor of The Irish Times, said the large language models (LLMs) that support AI-powered chatbot services “hoovered up areas of the internet and didn’t ask for any permission”, effectively leading to “billion-dollar companies pretty much overnight as a result of others’ intellectual property”.
“To me, and I think to most ordinary, reasonable people – that looks like theft,” he said.
“I think a fair summary of what the industry, in general, wants is a level playing field, a situation in which we are being fairly compensated for the original, creative work that we produce,” Mac Cormaic said.
AI more broadly “is really exciting technology for us and it is transforming the way that we work”, he said. Journalists “spend a lot of time working on very mundane tasks, on our website tagging and that sort of back-end information work”.
“We hope to eliminate a lot of that work so as to enable journalists to engage in original, creative work,” Mac Cormaic said.
However AI’s rapid development has “forced us to rethink basic understandings we have of what knowledge means, what news means, what information looks like”.
“These are fundamental questions that we don’t yet have answers to, but we’re grappling with everyday,” Mac Cormaic said.
Ó Cearúil, who has chaired the Oireachtas joint committee on AI since June, called for global participation in piecing together regulatory guidelines. “We’ve seen instances in the past of international treaties on the likes of nuclear energy; we do need some sort of agreement when it comes to artificial intelligence,” he said.
“If we don’t get it right now, it’ll be a freight train,” he said. “Now is the moment for us to actually push towards regulation, to push towards adoption on an individual and organisational basis.”
On a global scale, “we have completely failed [to regulate effectively] with social media”, Ó Cearúil said. “We need to ensure that there is some sort of global or international agreement ... when it comes to how AI is being developed.
“What we really need to be looking at with AI”, he said, is “how we can relieve ourselves of administrative burdens to allow us to be creative, to allow us the freedom of thought […] and do what separates us from machines”.

title: Just transition projects in midlands delivered a sixth of expected jobs
description: Fund designed to help midlands recover from closure of peat-fired power stations created only 183 jobs
content:
A report on a fund designed to help the midlands recover from the closure of peat-fired power stations found that just a sixth of the hoped-for jobs materialised.
Projects supported by the National Just Transition Fund (NJTF) had been expected to create up to 1,094 full- and part-time jobs. However, just 183 resulted.
An analysis said it was also hoped the programme could lead to as many as 1,600 indirect jobs.
In this area, the project worked better, but it was still well short of estimates, with 956 full- or part-time roles created.
The report by Indecon said the fund had a positive impact on the midlands regarding community resilience, training supports, environmental sustainability, tourism infrastructure and small business growth.
[ ‘Fear and regret’ in the midlands after shift from peat Opens in new window ]
However, it noted, “some issues are likely to exist around the long-term sustainable impact of the fund”.
The report explained that “limited employment impacts” were evident and that the jobs that were created came at a relatively high cost.
“There appears to be a disconnect between the overall strategic objective of the fund and the KPIs [key performance indicators] used to measure its impact and contribution, which were largely focused on employment impacts,” it said.
“A significant number of projects were not completed as per the original application.”
The report was published by the Department of the Environment after a formal request for it was made under freedom of information legislation.
The fund was administered through the department, with 56 projects chosen after a competitive process.
It was intended to help midland counties recover from the loss of employment caused by power plant closures in Lanesborough and Shannonbridge and the resulting fall in peat production.
The Government allocated €22.2 million, of which about €16 million was drawn down.
“The level of funding drawdown by the size of the project shows that the 11 largest projects that were awarded NJTF funding were only able to draw down 55 per cent of the funding that had been awarded to them,” the report noted.
“Typically, smaller projects were able to draw down much higher percentages of their initial award.”
[ ESB to close two peat-powered generating stations Opens in new window ]
The analysis indicated that if judged only as an employment measure, the scheme would be considered expensive compared with others.
It indicated this worked out at “total cost per full-time equivalent direct employment of €106,726 and a total cost per full-time equivalent direct and indirect employment of €17,658”.
It added the fund had a wider role, though, in investing in sustainable businesses, getting new projects started, and providing opportunities for things like remote work.
“However, it is clear that the fund did not deliver as initially set out in the project applications in terms of employment supported,” it concluded.
As part of the research, the authors contacted project organisers, with 39 per cent of those who responded saying they would continue in some form.
However, the report concluded: “The majority of projects that responded to Indecon’s survey of beneficiaries indicated that they do not plan to continue with their projects through their funds, ongoing support and other public funding.”

title: Boy (9) killed in Waterford arson attack had heart surgery two weeks ago
description: Callum (12) died in the attack, alongside his nine-year-old brother Jayden, who had heart surgery two weeks ago
content:
A close relative of four members of the family who died in an arson attack in Waterford city on Tuesday has called on the perpetrators to hand themselves in to gardaí .
The murders of Philip and Kim English and two of their sons, Callum (12) and Jayden (9), are linked to a pattern of violent intimidation by a local drugs gang, gardaí believe.
James English, who is a granduncle of the English children, travelled to Birchwood estate on Wednesday.
English, who is also the godfather of Callum, said the person or people responsible for the callous act “should be ashamed of themselves”.
“Whoever done it should hand themselves in,” he said. “Whoever done this should own up, own up whoever done it. At the end of the day, we have a lot of a family wiped out.”
He was visibly emotional when asked about the medical condition of the two surviving children who were transferred to the children’s hospital in Crumlin in Dublin following the incident.
“They are not too good. She [the girl] is not too good, or the little fellow not too good at the moment. Both of them are not too good.”
Jayden (9) had an operation on his heart just two weeks ago. He and his six-year-old brother previously featured on the social media of Bumbleance, Ireland’s official dedicated children’s ambulance service.
In a social media post by Bumbleance in 2020, the two brothers were described as having been born with heart defects. It further stated the brothers shared the same “chromosome disorder”.
Áine Phelan, a Waterford -based paramedic who previously worked with the service, said she had the “absolute privilege” of travelling on ambulance journeys with Kim English and her children several years ago.
When contacted, she said she had fond memories of her trips with the English family.
“Over those trips to and from their hospital appointments in Dublin and the time spent with them, we got to know each other so well,” she said. “They were always brave and full of fun and they brought so much light and laughter to every journey.
“There was always great excitement when the Bumbleance arrived back and a welcoming committee with Callum, Philip and whichever of the children that hadn’t travelled.”
She said she was trying to comprehend what had happened and added her thoughts were with the family in the “sad, sad days ahead”.
[ Waterford house fire: Family targeted had suffered other vandalism attacks in recent years Opens in new window ]
Meanwhile, Jayden featured on the Bumbleance Facebook page in 2021. He was pictured watching Peppa Pig in an ambulance on the way to Crumlin.
His six-year-old brother appeared on the site on a number of occasions for various journeys to Dublin for appointments and surgery. The youngster was also pictured on a Bumbleance fundraising calendar.
In 2020, Kim English paid tribute to the service in a post on the Bumbleance social media page.
She said she had “so much respect” for the staff and crew of Bumbleance and appreciated them bringing her and her children to hospital “safe and sound”.
Speaking after laying flowers at the house on Wednesday, the principal at Jayden and Callum’s school said it would do everything to make school life normal for the rest of the pupils.
Surrounded by a group of teachers who also brought flowers, Caroline Douris described one of the children as “a lovely young fella” and said the other “lights up the school every day with that smile as he comes through the door”.
“We just want to extend sympathies to the community and to the family,” she said.
“We have a very strong staff. We’re very united, and everybody’s willing to talk openly about the whole situation.
“So we’re lucky from that perspective that we do have a wonderful staff, and the boys will be at the forefront of everything.”
A community hub has been set up in the nearby Butler Community Centre, where councillors are available to speak to locals.
Six psychologists have also been allocated to local schools to help support children.
A prayer vigil will take place at Sacred Heart Church in The Folly, Co Waterford, at 5pm on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, more than €32,000 has been raised on a GoFundMe page set up by a member of the extended English family.
[ Waterford arson attack: Gardaí carry out multiple searches Opens in new window ]
All money raised will go directly to the grandfather of the deceased children to help cover the funeral costs and to support the family through the days and weeks ahead.
Shannon Brazil, who is organising the fundraiser, posted that Philip, Kim, Callum and Jayden will “forever be loved and never forgotten”.
“We pray for strength for our family and hold on to hope for the two siblings still in hospital.”
Callum’s soccer coach at Johnville FC, Alex O’Sullivan, said he would be remembered for his bright smile and his work ethic.
“He always put in the hard work. He was always a great listener. He always put in his absolute best.”
He said Philip and Kim would also be remembered for being very helpful, for always turning up on time for training and games, and for being “absolutely lovely people”.
[ Drug-related intimidation: why petrol bomb attacks are becoming more common Opens in new window ]
Callum’s parents had always said if club officials ever needed a hand “to give them a shout”, O’Sullivan added.
“They always had a smile on their faces. They’re absolutely lovely people; you wouldn’t think for a second that anything like this happened anywhere, especially to anyone’s family.”
The club is currently considering how best to offer support to its members. “This is still very fresh at the moment for us,” O’Sullivan said.
“Club activities are going to have to be cancelled for the next coming days,” he told RTÉ Radio.

title: Gianni Infantino faces grilling at potentially ‘explosive’ Fifa council meeting
description: World Cup sell-off, Balogun and peace prize on agenda of Thursday’s meeting in Zurich
content:
Gianni Infantino will be questioned by Fifa council members over his involvement in the aborted World Cup sell-off plan, the Folarin Balogun affair and the decision to award Donald Trump the inaugural Fifa peace prize at what is expected to be a heated meeting at the world governing body’s headquarters on Thursday.
The Fifa president rejected repeated calls for an extraordinary general meeting of council during the summer after the emergence of the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposals, but will meet his critics for the first time since in Zurich with one attender predicting that the talks could be “explosive”.
Aleksander Ceferin, Victor Montagliani and Sheikh Salman Bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, the presidents of Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation respectively, all of whom have all called for Infantino to resign, will be in attendance to press home demands for an independent review of Fifa’s governance.
In response to letters from Ceferin, Montagliani and Salman sent last month Infantino pledged to commission an external review of Fifa’s future governance, but no details have been forthcoming and there remains scepticism over whether it will be truly independent.
In addition to FFE, Balogun and the peace prize, which featured on an agenda circulated by Fifa last month, Infantino is also likely to face questions about a report this week that he received a “second salary” in 2024 on top of his salary declared in Fifa’s accounts.
US Internal Revenue Service filings show a Fifa subsidiary in charge of running last summer’s World Cup paid Infantino $1.76 million, which was not mentioned in Fifa’s annual report, where his salary is recorded as 4.27m Swiss francs (€4.58 million).
Fifa statutes state that “the individual compensation of the Fifa president ... shall be made public”. The governing body has denied wrongdoing.
“Fifa does not pay a second salary to the Fifa president and complies with all reporting requirements in relation to compensation,” it said. “The Fifa president’s annual compensation, as well as other contractual benefits, are decided by the independent compensation subcommittee.
“Fifa strongly rejects any claims that it has failed to disclose any financial information and has violated Fifa’s statutes. Fifa accounts are independently audited, and all declarations are in line with tax regulations in Switzerland, the United States and elsewhere.”
Despite these controversies, and the public opposition of the European, Asian and North and Central American and Caribbean confederations, Infantino is on course to be re-elected unopposed in March’s election.
Montaglini has rejected calls to stand against Infantino to focus on being re-elected as Concacaf’s president and Uefa has yet to find an alternative candidate despite tentatively sounding out high-profile footballing figures including Arsène Wenger and Michele Kang, who owns clubs including London City Lionesses.
The deadline for candidates to declare their intention to stand is November 18th, with the election to be held at Fifa congress in Rabat on March 18th. – Guardian

title: Sally Rooney’s books will no longer be available in UK over her support for Palestine Action
description: Faber blames UK antiterrorism legislation for decision to stop distributing bestselling author’s works
content:
Sally Rooney , the bestselling and award-winning Irish author, will no longer be distributed by Faber & Faber due to her support for Palestine Action, the author has said.
According to Faber & Faber, British antiterrorism legislation means it cannot pass on earnings to her from her book sales.
Rooney’s Normal People has now sold more than one million copies in the UK alone while her first novel, Conversations with Friends, and Beautiful World, Where Are You have each sold more than 500,000 copies.
Palestine Action is a pro-Palestinian direct action group that was proscribed as a terrorist organisation by the British government in July 2025. After the group was banned, Rooney, who lives in Co Mayo, said she would use proceeds from her sales to support Palestine Action. Supporting organisations banned under the UK’s Terrorism Act is an offence and she subsequently cancelled a trip to the UK to pick up an award, for fear of arrest.
In August 2025, Rooney wrote an opinion piece in The Irish Times with the headline: “I support Palestine Action. If this makes me a ‘supporter of terror’ under UK law, so be it”.
In a statement on Wednesday, Rooney said: “In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK. The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland.
[ Sally Rooney: I support Palestine Action. If this makes me a ‘supporter of terror’ under UK law, so be it Opens in new window ]
“As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence. After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK.
“I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences. I have no further comment at this time.”
In a separate statement also issued on Wednesday, the publisher said: “Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.
“As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format. We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories. We have no further comment at this time.”
Books currently in the UK market can sell through and do not need to be returned.
Rooney had previously warned her books could disappear from UK stores and the publication of new works in the UK could be prevented.

title: Russell Brand ‘a ruthless, calculated and manipulative’ sexual predator, UK prosecutors say
description: Actor faces rape and sexual assault allegations, which he denies
content:
Actor and comedian Russell Brand , once one of Britain’s most high-profile broadcasters, was a ruthless predator who raped or abused six women despite their protestations to satisfy his ‌voracious sexual appetite, prosecutors said on Wednesday.
Brand (51), the former husband of US singer Katy Perry , is on trial facing three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault relating ​to six women from 1999 to 2009.
He denies all the accusations and will set out his defence in court at a later date.
“Today I feel blessed,” he said as he arrived at London ’s Southwark Crown Court. “I feel of course concerned but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved.”
Opening the case against him, prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said some of the six women who ​had made the allegations had protested, while others had no opportunity to react to his advances. It had made no difference to Brand, she said.
“His desire, his strong desire, for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate ⁠and voracious,” the prosecutor said.
Although he could be funny, charming and likeable when he wanted something, he also had a childlike expectation his every desire should be ‌met, ‌she ​added.
“He was ruthless, he was calculating, he was manipulative and, the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator,” Karmy-Jones said.
The alleged offences took place over a decade as he progressed from gigs as a stand-up comedian to a television presenter, actor and Hollywood movie ⁠star, she said.
The first is ​alleged to have occurred in 1999 when he was performing in a show on the ​fringe of the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth.
The first complainant, who had watched the show and had assumed Brand was gay, said he had raped her in her hotel room where ‌she had invited him because she thought he was interested in ​a cause she had been talking to him about.
One of his co-performers at that show said Brand had bragged that he had wanted to bed 5,000 ⁠women in his lifetime, the prosecutor said.
In 2001, he is accused of ⁠trying to drag a woman into a toilet ​cubicle at MTV Europe where she worked. Three years later, a woman said he had dragged her into a toilet cubicle in a bar before orally raping her.
Around the same time, in 2004 or 2005, a woman working at a media company said he indecently assaulted her at her office.
The fifth complainant, a fan, had consensual sex at his home in 2009 but then he anally raped her, the prosecutor said. The sixth complainant, who worked for Channel 4 , alleges Brand had demanded a massage and then pressed his face into her groin area, in the same year.
When interviewed by police, Brand declined to answer questions but provided written statements in which he said he did not remember the incidents, had never engaged in non-consensual activity and accepted that he had had sex ‌in toilet cubicles during parties, Karmy-Jones said.
The women involved did not know each other and had not taken the matter to the police at the time for various reasons, but came forward with complaints following a TV programme and a press report in 2023 in which anonymous allegations were made by other women, ‌the prosecutor said.
Brand’s trial, expected to last about six weeks, has attracted huge media attention, with a second court opened ​to allow more journalists to attend and many outlets running daily podcasts.
The comedian, known for his flamboyant style and ​appearance, became famous in Britain before starring in a number of films including Get Him to the Greek in 2010, the same year he married Perry. They divorced in 2012.
More recently Brand has appeared in online broadcasts discussing US politics, religion and free speech.

title: Can Lula defy history? Brazil’s left seeks unprecedented run-off turnaround
description: Students, activists and social media organisers have mobilised, but polls still show Flávio Bolsonaro ahead before this month’s decisive vote
content:
A fter its unexpected loss in a first round of voting earlier this month, Brazil ’s left is furiously mobilising as it attempts an unprecedented comeback win in presidential elections against the far right.
Just as the ruling Workers Party looked set to plunge into despondency over its defeat, students and grassroots activists have re-energised its campaign as president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva looks to overturn a 2.22 million vote deficit to senator Flávio Bolsonaro in a run-off on October 25th.
Since Brazil adopted a two-round system in presidential elections in 1989, the second-placed candidate in the first round has never come from behind to win the run-off.
Following the first-round defeat, left-wing activists have organised a series of increasingly large demonstrations in support of Lula around the country including two huge rallies in Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro over the holiday weekend. Sunday’s rally in Sao Paulo was the biggest staged by the left in years, filling almost 3km of the main avenue in Brazil’s biggest city with the overflow spilling into side streets.
Speaking at it, Lula acknowledged the importance of young people in his efforts to win a fourth term. “I’m very happy that this rally is mainly young people. Either you take part in political life, or it can’t be fixed,” the 80-year-old leftist told the crowd.
Lula called on supporters to try to convince as many as possible of the 33 million voters who abstained in the first round to vote in the run-off. Among those in attendance at Sunday’s rally who say they have already been trying to spread that message was university student Laura Oliveira. “It is difficult to debate with the other side, they are very fanatical. So the strategy is to reach out to those who didn’t vote to make clear to them what is at stake,” she said.
Like many Brazilians, Oliveira said she and her friends have depended on state support to study at university. She fears Flávio could slash education budgets as did the government of his father Jair Bolsonaro, the former president convicted of a failed coup attempt following his defeat to Lula in the 2022 presidential election.
The Workers Party is also trying belatedly to compete better with the far right on social media. For years the Bolsonaro family has used its mastery of the medium to provide it with a crucial advantage against opponents. Since its first-round defeat Lula’s campaign has sought to give more space to young activists with large online followings who won election to state legislatures and the national congress on what was otherwise a bad night for the left.
The most dramatic expression of this rapid online mobilisation is the new “ Lula’s Army” WhatsApp channel with more than 4.2 million members, created by congressman André Janones, one of the Brazilian left’s first social-media stars. As the channel grew exponentially and attempted to better co-ordinate online activity among Lula’s supporters, it became a target of Flávio’s campaign.
Claiming it was spreading fake news against its candidate, his Liberal Party petitioned Brazil’s electoral court to close it. In response the court’s president, supreme court justice Kassio Nunes Marques, twice ordered the channel off air. The Workers Party eventually thwarted his efforts by registering Lula’s Army as an official channel of the campaign.
Nunes Marques was appointed to the supreme court by Flávio’s father and is embroiled in the Banco Master banking scandal that has also implicated the Bolsonaro family. The judge’s circle is suspected by investigators of negotiating lucrative legal fees in return for sentences beneficial to Master, which collapsed last year after being exposed as a Ponzi-like scheme that allegedly used bribery of senior politicians and judges to avoid exposure.
Messages found on the phone of Master’s imprisoned owner Daniel Vorcaro indicate he organised a party at a Sao Paulo apartment attended by Nunes Marques and a number of prostitutes. The judge denies the accusations.
On Monday another judge on the electoral court ordered Flávio and his brother, senator-elect Carlos, to remove a video they posted that claimed to show open drug-taking by Lula’s supporters at Sunday’s rally in Sao Paulo. The video was recorded in Chile and the court described its sharing by the Bolsonaro brothers as “severe manipulation through decontextualization”.
The court also recently fined Flávio for posts falsely associating Lula with Brazil’s two biggest organised crime organisations.
While Lula attempts a historic comeback, Flávio and his supporters have not concealed their euphoria at what they see as his inevitable victory, with polls showing him maintaining his lead over Lula. “Lula’s campaign is playing catch-up but it has very little time left. Flávio is still favourite but a victory is still possible for Lula,” says political analyst André Pereira César.

title: Aer Lingus pilot ‘uncomfortable’ at crossing picket line to attend WRC hearing
description: Hearings were picketed by union members as part of a one-day strike by public sector staff
content:
Lawyers for an Aer Lingus pilot pursuing rights complaints at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) have said he is “simply not comfortable at all with having to cross a picket line” for his hearing.
Hearings into complaints by pilot Declan McCabe under the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005, and the Payment of Wages Act 1991 were due to resume on Wednesday for the 14th day at Lansdowne House in Ballsbridge, Dublin 4.
However, hearings at the WRC were picketed by union members as part of a one-day strike by 300,000 public sector staff across the country as part of a pay dispute with the Government.
“My client is a member of Fórsa through Ialpa , the pilots’ wing of it ... and he’s just simply not comfortable at all with having to cross a picket line, and remain across it,” said counsel for the pilot David Byrnes, instructed by Setanta Solicitors.
“He wants to return to where he came from, as do I as a professional who respects the constitutional right to strike, as does my instructing solicitor,” Byrnes said.
Applying for an overnight adjournment, he said, “My client does not wish to proceed with the hearing today in these circumstances.”
Byrnes told adjudicator John Harraghy that the WRC administration had confirmed separately to his client, his solicitor and himself: “Yes, everything was going ahead.”
“We had interpreted that as ‘going ahead as normal’. We were taken by surprise, to say the least, to be met this morning by a picket line, and regrettably, that picket line had to be crossed this morning,” he said.
Byrnes said he had discussed the matter with counsel for Aer Lingus, Tom Mallon, instructed by Arthur Cox for the respondent, and said that the hearing of evidence in the case could still conclude by Friday, with closing submissions next month.
[ Psychiatric state of man accused of murdering three members of his family ‘central’ to trial Opens in new window ]
Mallon said: “I understand the concerns of Mr Byrnes and his client. It would be inappropriate for me to say anything further.”
Adjudicator John Harraghy said: “I understand the concerns and I think it might be prudent to adjourn if people aren’t comfortable being in the room today. I’d much prefer people are at ease attending a hearing such as this. I’d like to continue in the spirit we have so far.”
McCabe was demoted as a disciplinary sanction following a company probe into an incident at Dublin Airport , when an Airbus A321XLR, flying from Munich with 156 passengers and crew aboard, failed to link up with the radio navigation beacon for the new north runway.
The complainant said what happened was “a non-event from a flying point of view” and that the relevant Aer Lingus manual left it up to his judgment to decide whether to report it.
Two other WRC employment rights cases are proceeding before other adjudicators at Lansdowne House, though another hearing scheduled for Wednesday morning has not proceeded and the Labour Court is not sitting.

title: Flour beetles prompt recall of Ready Brek and Tesco porridge products
description: The small red insects are frequently found in dry foods such as flour and cereals
content:
Consumers have been advised not to eat some batches of Ready Brek Original and Tesco Super Smooth Porridge due to the possible presence of flour beetles.
The advice comes from the Food Safety Authority of Ireland , which has asked retailers to remove the specific batches from shop shelves.
The authority said the presence of flour beetles would render the products unfit for human consumption, prompting the recall.
Flour beetles are very small insects, appearing red, shiny, flat and elongated, but only 3-4mm long. They are frequently found in dry foods such as flour, rice, pasta, cereals and spices.
The recall covers 750g batches of Ready Brek Original with best-before dates ranging from July 8th, 2027, to September 16th, 2027.
The notice also covered 450g batches of Ready Brek Original with best-before dates ranging from July 1st, 2027, to October 1st, 2027.
Tesco Super Smooth Porridge batches (750g) with best-before dates between June 30th, 2027, and August 15th, 2027, are also covered by the recall.

title: Irish borrowers ‘facing tough winter’ with mortgage costs on rise
description: Average cost of new variable-rate loans is up, meaning higher repayments
content:
A significant rise in the cost of variable rate mortgages in Ireland has raised concerns that borrowers may be facing into a winter of financial strain .
Central Bank of Ireland figures indicate that the rate attached to new Irish mortgage contracts rose marginally to 3.53 per cent in August, against a euro area average of 3.62 per cent.
But the average rate attached to new variable-rate contracts rose by seven basis points to 4.16 per cent, a move that was described as pronounced.
August’s figures also did not take into account the European Central Bank’s (ECB) latest rate increase in September. The bank is expected to hike rates again in December in a bid to quell inflation.
“The ECB’s September increase has yet to show up in these figures, but borrowers may well still be feeling it,” Sorcha Timoney, mortgage team manager at advisory firm NFP Ireland, said.
[ Retirement crisis looms for those in mortgage arrears, new analysis shows Opens in new window ]
“Anyone on a tracker mortgage will see that increase passed on directly.”
Timoney also said mortgage borrowers coming to the end of a fixed-rate contract now face paying higher interest rates .
“With the next ECB announcement due on October 29th, there is a real possibility of a further rise,” Timoney said.
Rachel McGovern, deputy chief executive of Brokers Ireland, said: “While today’s figure is 0.58 per cent lower than a year ago, with rising inflation in Ireland and across the EU, together with a more intense geopolitical scenario the period ahead is looking less optimistic on interest rates, unfortunately.”
She advised any mortgage holders who had not already done so to review their options now, to take advantage of the best available value, “now that we’re clearly in an upward cycle on interest rates”.
McGovern said consumers were already showing caution, which we’re seeing in slowing house-price increases.
Several house-price surveys, published in recent days, point to a slowdown in price growth linked to higher borrowing costs.
Central Bank of Ireland data indicate that euro area average mortgage rates, on new deals, exceeded the weighted average rate here by nine basis points.
[ Pepper rate hike to heap more misery on distressed borrowers Opens in new window ]
Ireland had the 11th highest weighted average rate in the euro area at the end of August, down from the ninth highest in July.
The weighted average interest rate on new fixed rate mortgage agreements, which constitute 94 per cent of the volume of new mortgage agreements, was 3.49 per cent in August, up one basis point from the previous month, the regulator said.
The figures also indicated the weighted average interest rate on household overnight deposits stood at 0.22 per cent in August.
Irish households are estimated to hold up to €175 billion on deposit with Irish banks, a substantial portion of held in overnight deposit accounts, which pay very low returns.
Retail banks here have been criticised for failing to increase their deposit rates in line with ECB levels while reporting big annual profits.

title: AI systems should adopt safety lessons from nuclear industry
description: Balance needs to be struck between regulation and opportunity, Google DeepMind chair says
content:
The artificial intelligence industry must adopt safety lessons from critical industries such as nuclear and biology, a senior Google AI researcher has said, amid concerns about the potential harm that the technology could inflict.
But the cofounder and chair of Google DeepMind, Demis Hassabis, said the right balance needed to be struck between regulating the technology and seizing the opportunities presented by it.
He said recent incidents of AI agents going “rogue” and hacking third-party systems were “early warning shots”.
“The systems aren’t that powerful yet, so the incidents aren’t that major, but they could be, looking into next year and the next couple of years, if we don’t do more work as an industry and individually as companies and governments on security systems and building secure sandboxes to test them,” he said. “We can bring best practices from other sectors that have dealt with safety critical systems, whether it’s biology or nuclear.
“I think there’s a lot of lessons that can be learned about containment systems and I think we need to start taking that seriously and bring experts in from those areas, but also just from cybersecurity in general.”
He said AI could be used to bolster defensive systems, fixing the vulnerabilities in software systems before attackers can use them. “We’ve got to asymmetrically power up our defensive side to keep ahead of the attackers,” he said.
Hassabis has backed the establishment of a standards body that would help develop the technology in a “nuanced and nimble and dynamic way”, and put more responsibility on so-called frontier labs who were developing new areas of the technology to make sure it was safe.
[ Entry-level hiring in AI-augmented sectors drops by 16% Opens in new window ]
“We don’t want to stifle the innovation, all the amazing things that come out of it; we want those things. But also there’s no complete consensus even in people working on this, the scientists and the researchers working on this, on what exactly the risks are and how big they are,” Hassabis said.
“We know that they are out there and we need to quantify them. But there is a lot of uncertainty around it.”
He said a framework would be needed that could quickly adapt to test critical elements of the systems, keep up with the technology and be proportionate with the risk.
“One of the problems with regulation is it is very slow-moving by its very nature and I think governments have to catch up with how fast the technology is moving,” he said.
“If you legislate for something three years ago, it will be out of date today and probably won’t address what the real problems are.”
He also highlighted the growing role of AI in scientific discovery. Despite concerns over the environmental impact of AI, including the power required to run data centres and the water that cools them, Hassabis said the technology could be used to develop a solution to the climate crisis.
However, human creativity and judgment would remain irreplaceable, he said.
“The hardest thing in science is actually asking and articulating the right question. That’s even harder than finding the answer, and I think coming up with the right hypothesis, the right conjecture and the right question to ask requires creativity and judgment,” he said.
“So far, our AI systems are maybe good at helping solve things. But it’s the human scientist and artist that brings the creative process and the question to bear on it… For the moment it looks like there will always be a kind of real-world loop.”

title: Wicklow’s Lara Gillespie claims silver medal at UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai
description: The 25-year-old was narrowly beaten to the rainbow jersey by Dutch star Lorena Wiebes
content:
Lara Gillespie has finished inches short of winning another rainbow jersey at the UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai, just edged out in the final push for the line in the scratch race by Dutch star Lorena Wiebes.
The 10km bunch race was effectively decided on the last of the 40 laps, after Wiebes first launched her powerful finishing sprint, with only Gillespie in hot pursuit. Although the Irish rider made up ground around the final bend, Wiebes held on to strike gold by less than half a wheel length.
It was the third successive title in this event for the 27-year-old Wiebes, who had also got the better of Gillespie by the closest of margins in the final two sprint stages of the Tour of Chongming Island last weekend.
A year on from becoming the first Irish woman to claim a UCI world title in any event, winning the elimination race, the 25-year-old Gillespie adds a silver medal to her collection, having also won a European title early last year.
“I wouldn’t normally say scratch is my favourite race, but I’m really proud of how I rode today, representing Ireland as best I could,” said Gillespie.
“Of course it was so close, and I don’t think I’ve ever been so angry to take silver at a World Championships. But I think I can be proud of how I raced. It gives me confidence for the races coming up.”
She will next take on the onium on Friday, a combination of four events, where Wiebes is also the defending champion.
Gillespie had arrived at the Shanghai Velodrome on Chongming Island with confidence soaring, and although riding Wiebes close the line once again, the experience of the Dutch rider was enough to see her collect her now fourth rainbow jersey.
It also makes it a 10th second-place finish for Gillespie this season – along with two victories – after also finishing second in the omnium at the Three Days of Aigle in Switzerland earlier this month.
The Wicklow rider will also take on Sunday’s points race, which covers 25km, having won bronze in that event in 2024.
Earlier, in the team pursuit preliminary qualifying round, the quartet of Fiona Mangan, Emma Jeffers, Aoife O’Brien and Esther Wong finished in 16th place, clocking 4:27.239, the fastest qualifiers being Great Britain, who clocked 4:08.055.

title: Entry-level hiring in AI-augmented sectors drops by 16%
description: Latest Labour Market Pulse survey highlights risk posed by advent of new technology
content:
Entry-level hiring in “AI-augmented occupations” in Ireland declined by 16 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, according to a new survey of labour market trends.
While IDA Ireland’s latest Labour Market Pulse report indicated that Ireland was entering the artificial intelligence (AI) era in “a position of strength”, ranking fourth globally for AI engineering talent, it warned there were “some emerging risks”.
Chief among them was the risk to graduate-level or junior recruitment.
It found that entry-level hiring in occupations that were using AI declined by 16.2 per cent (on an annual basis) between April and June this year, compared with a 10.8 per cent decline across those occupations overall.
“Within roles such as software engineering and data analysis, there are signs of a sharper pullback in junior recruitment, although the extent to which AI is driving this remains unclear,” it said.
The survey, produced in partnership with Microsoft and LinkedIn, was published to coincide with the International AI Summit taking place in Dublin this week, the flagship AI event of the State’s European Union presidency.
[ Oracle to cut another 70 jobs in Ireland in AI cost-cutting push Opens in new window ]
With more and more firms adopting AI, the survey found the State ranked fourth globally for AI engineering talent concentration, with 1.31 per cent of LinkedIn members in the Republic classified as AI engineering talent.
“Only Israel, Singapore and Luxembourg rank higher, with Ireland ahead of Germany, the UK and France,” the report noted.
The Republic also ranked fourth globally for net AI talent migration, indicating that the State continues to attract AI talent in an increasingly competitive global market.
While hiring here has moderated in line with international trends, the Irish labour market continues “to demonstrate greater resilience than selected European peers”, the report said.
In September, the LinkedIn hiring rate for the Republic was down 6.7 per cent year on year, compared with declines of 11.3 per cent in the UK and 18.1 per cent in Germany.
The report concluded the data showed “no clear evidence that the hiring slowdown is concentrated in jobs most exposed to AI or is disproportionately affecting entry-level recruitment”.
It noted that entry-level hiring declined by 8.3 per cent year on year in September, broadly in line with the 6.7 per cent decline in overall hiring.
“Ranking fourth in the world for AI talent sends a powerful signal to investors, and our focus now is on building on that advantage through continued investment in talent, infrastructure and adoption,” said IDA Ireland chief executive Michael Lohan .
Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke said: “The Irish labour market is performing well with employment levels and rates remaining high, and unemployment low at close to 5 per cent. Ireland has moved quickly in adopting AI, with strong AI usage and diffusion across our economy.
“We need to stay ahead and build on this momentum to fully reap the benefits from AI, a core theme of this week’s International AI Summit as part of Ireland’s EU presidency.”

title: Claire Williams takes top honour at Women in Facilities Management Awards 2026
description: The awards programme drew 45 entries across 10 categories, with 145 guests attending the ceremony at the Crowne Plaza Hotel in Santry, Dublin
content:
Claire Williams, HR manager at Flexéir Facilities Services, has received the overall leader award at the Women in Facilities Management Awards 2026, held at the Crowne Plaza Hotel in Santry, Dublin.
Previously known as K-MAC, Flexéir is a member of Flexim Group, which provides FM services in 17 countries. The Irish operation is based in Shannon and the firm also has an office in Dublin. Flexéir is active in the pharmaceutical, healthcare, electronic, heavy industry, call centre and printing sectors as well as property and commercial building management.
The judging panel said Williams exemplifies outstanding leadership, demonstrating a consistent commitment to excellence, professionalism and the people at the heart of facilities management. “Her approach combines strong commercial awareness with a genuine commitment to developing people and creating positive working environments,” said the award citation. “She continues to set an impressive example of what effective, forward-thinking leadership can achieve.”
Claire Williams commented: “There are fantastic people across all the categories, women who are excelling in different sectors of the industry. It’s an absolute privilege to be here amongst them all today.” Now in its second year, the awards programme attracted 45 entries across 10 categories. Some 145 guests from across the facilities management sector attended the ceremony, which was hosted by Fiona Buckley.
Derek O’Boyle, managing director of MKF Property Services , said the company was proud to support awards that champion the remarkable talent shaping the sector. “These awards encourage new voices, attract future FM professionals, and ensure we continue to collectively build an inclusive FM Industry,” he added.
Anthony Walsh, managing director at Flexéir Facilities Services, said the company was proud to support the awards and celebrate the talent, leadership and contribution of women across the facilities management sector. “The awards inspire others, encourage collaboration and celebrate achievement, reflecting our own commitment to supporting growth, development and opportunities for women,” he said.
Judging co-ordinator Eileen Slamon praised all the shortlisted entrants for participating in the awards scheme. “Putting your head above the parapet isn’t always easy so thank you,” she said. “For too long our work remained almost invisible but now we have a seat at the table and these awards represent another wonderful opportunity to showcase the wonderful career opportunities that exist within the facilities management sector.”
Award winner Nina Haller of Eurofins Scientific encouraged her peers to enter the awards next year. “Whether you’re very confident or doubting yourself, put yourself forward as there is nothing to lose,” she said.
Award winner Michelle My Lee of Novartis noted that there are many talented women in the industry and said she was “proud of everyone”.
Blackrock Facility Management was shortlisted in the team award. “This was Blackrock’s first year at the awards and the team came away genuinely inspired,” said Niamh O’Neill, chief executive of the company. “Hearing from so many women making facilities management cool was a real highlight. We’ll definitely be back next year.”
The legacy award was presented to Margot Slattery, global group head of DIB and social sustainability at ISS World Services . The judging panel commended Slattery for leading initiatives focused on inclusion, equality, diversity and social sustainability for 350,000 ISS employees worldwide.
Kevin O’Driscoll, director of partnership programmes at awards organiser Business River, said: “Events like this are made possible through the support of sponsors. We are thankful to our 2026 sponsors, MKF Property Services, Honest Elevator Company , ISS Ireland and Flexéir Facilities Services. I also want to recognise our supporter, Amárach Research. Their investment in the awards underlines their commitment and support of this key business area.”

title: The steep rise and sudden fall of US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle
description: Donald Trump cut her loose after damaging news reports about her tenure as ambassador to Greece
content:
I t started out so well for her. Kimberly Guilfoyle , the US ambassador to Greece until she was effectively fired on live television on Tuesday when the new White House press secretary said that US president Donald Trump had asked for her resignation, was at one point engaged to Donald Trump jnr, the president’s eldest son. The couple owned a $9.7 million home in Florida, appeared at Trump rallies together and sent each other adoring posts on Instagram.
“Falling in love with my fiancé more and more every day,” Guilfoyle posted on Instagram on Valentine’s Day 2022. “@donaldjtrumpjr, you’re my best friend, my support system and my forever guy.”
“Thanks for always being there no matter what the haters are throwing our way,” he posted in 2024. “I love you.”
Today, the junior Trump is married to a Florida socialite and model. And Guilfoyle, who was nominated as ambassador to Greece by the president soon after her engagement to his son was broken off two years ago, is out of a job after a series of damning reports in The Wall Street Journal, including that she asked a Republican donor to pay off $100,000 (€89,000) on her American Express credit card just before her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025.
The rise and fall of Guilfoyle (57) was not a surprise at the White House, where many saw her as a flamboyant party girl with questionable judgment.
Her supporters said she was in fact a substantive person underneath the glitz. Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host and a former prosecutor in San Francisco and Los Angeles, was once married to Gavin Newsom, who would go on to become governor of California and one of the Democratic Party’s most outspoken critics of the president.
Either way, Guilfoyle was a Trump insider with a prominent role in the family and its political operation. The president’s swiftness in firing her showed his willingness to cut off anyone who becomes a liability and an embarrassment. But it also left her with little reason to remain loyal to the president and his family at a time when Trump’s political authority is ebbing.
In announcing her resignation, she decried what she called false accusations and said she would vigorously defend her reputation. Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Trump did little to suggest he would continue to keep her close.
“She wasn’t a member of my family,” he said. “She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago.”
Guilfoyle, who arrived in Greece less than a year ago, was a highly unusual choice for the role to begin with.
In a sense, it was Donald jnr who got her the job, indirectly. In December 2024 he and the socialite and model, Bettina Anderson, were seen holding hands as they left a Palm Beach restaurant. The next day, then-president-elect Trump announced that Guilfoyle was his pick to be ambassador to Greece.
The timing suggested the president wanted her out of the country at an awkward time for Donald jnr, who married Anderson this year. Guilfoyle’s allies said that was not the case, although Greeks at the time wondered whether they were simply getting the woman who had been jilted by the president’s son.
In Athens, Guilfoyle became a sensation as soon as she arrived, on the private jet of a multimillionaire Greek-American businessman. She wore a partly sheer black evening dress to a Thanksgiving week dinner, joked with the Greek president when she presented her credentials that she was working on finding a new husband and stayed out until the small hours of the morning at Athens nightclubs.
“Oh, I wasn’t late, it was like before three,” Guilfoyle said in an interview with The New York Times last year, referring to how she had turned up at a nightclub for the 1.30am premiere show of her friend and one of the country’s most famous pop singers, Konstantinos Argiros.
Paparazzi followed her everywhere, but Greeks at the time said Guilfoyle worked as hard as she played. By the nature of her position and what they saw as her access to the White House, they viewed her as one of the most important people in the country. Mostly forgotten were her words on Fox during the Greek financial crisis in 2015, when she called Greeks “freeloaders” who should be punished like a dog that “pees on the rug”.
Early on, Guilfoyle announced two important business deals, the development of a US-backed port near Athens and the exploration for natural gas off the island of Corfu. Both were in the works long before she arrived in Athens, but Greek officials said she had jumped into the plans months earlier and wanted them announced on her watch.
Adonis Georgiadis, Greece’s health minister and a vice-president of the governing conservative party, was among those impressed. “When she was first named, the people were, ‘What’s that?’” he said. But if she delivers, he said, “who cares if she has a see-through dress?”.
Her downfall began last month, after the Journal reported about Guilfoyle and her potential conflicts of interest over energy deals in the Balkans.
It is unclear what Guilfoyle will do now. Once a legal analyst for CNN and ABC in New York, her career at Fox ended in 2018, when two people familiar with her exit told the Times on condition of anonymity that she had been forced to leave over questions about inappropriate workplace behaviour.
She was immensely proud of her ambassadorship. At the end of the interview, she pointed out a framed document near the entrance to her official residence, Jefferson House, that listed all the American ambassadors to Greece since 1948. Every one until Guilfoyle was a man.
“Here I am,” she said, pointing to her name. “I almost cried.”
This article originally appeared in The New York Times .
