title: Background costs comprise more than 50% of consumers’ electricity bills
description: Minister pledges that work on north-south power line will start next year
content:
Network, regulatory, policy and other costs account for more than half of what Irish people pay for electricity, new research shows.
The Republic has the most expensive electricity in the European Union, with households paying 40 cent a kilowatt-hour, almost €1,700 a year, on average, for their power, 40 per cent more than the European average.
Network charges, the cost of incentives to lure investment in new power plants, the impact of policy and regulations, and other expenses now account for 55 per cent of what households pay for electricity, research by a new think tank, Trifecta Ireland, shows.
And the non-electricity costs can make up an even greater share of bills paid by some industries, Trifecta Ireland chief executive Conall Bolger noted at the launch of the organisation’s report titled What Can Move the Needle on Bills before 2030, on Wednesday.
The report proposes 17 measures that could cut electricity costs in the shorter term while investment in power plants and long-term improvements to the national grid and distribution networks are under way.
Bolger noted that the changes focused on aiding electricity customers. “We need to use existing networks more efficiently, we need to make the system more flexible, and we need to get more out of what we have,” he said.
The proposals include mass retrofitting of social housing, reforming the system for paying power plants to remain on standby when they are not generating electricity, more focused supports for families in energy poverty, and various measures to encourage electrification and to give homes and businesses flexibility to use electricity at times when it is cheaper.
Work on a long-delayed cross-Border power line that could cut €150 million a year from electricity bills will begin next year, Minister for Energy Darragh O’Brien pledged at the launch.
Planning and political controversies have delayed construction of the North-South Interconnector, a high-voltage electricity line running from Co Meath to Co Tyrone that was first proposed 20 years ago.
O’Brien said on Wednesday that work should begin on the project next year as it now has full planning permission.
“It’s going to be built,” the Minister emphasised. He told a conference that the power line would be subject to “no more reviews” and noted that four studies had weighed whether it was possible to run the line underground rather than on pylons.
“It will deliver reductions in energy bills of up to €150 million annually,” added O’Brien.
Trifecta’s Ireland research drew on more than 40 State, civil society and energy industry organisations. Funded by the family of Irish renewable energy industry pioneer, Eddie O’Connor, Trifecta Ireland focuses on how to provide an electricity system that is affordable, clean and secure.

title: Time to get down to business? Public opinion may shift if second strike takes place
description: With some of the unions not paying any strike pay, the strikers will feel the impact of their own action in their pockets
content:
S eventeen years after the last public sector shutdown, Wednesday’s strike was a reminder to anyone who might have forgotten how central public services are to our lives and what happens when the people staffing them walk off the job.
Tens of thousands of workers stopped at their workplace gates and joined the action at schools, hospitals, courts, council offices and hundreds of other public buildings. As expected, there was huge disruption, including in the private sector, with many parents having to stay at home to mind children, thousands of hospital appointments cancelled, and court cases adjourned, as well as driving test centres and many other Government services closed for the day.
The background to this strike is different from the one in November 2009 , when the government was reeling after the financial crash and workers were protesting over severe cuts, some already made and others being flagged for the budget to come.
This time, the public finances are in good shape, even if they are unhealthily reliant on corporation taxes , and unions say their members have some catching up to do, due to spikes in inflation and substantial increases to the cost of daily basics like housing, food and fuel.
Acrimony has also been building behind the scenes. The unions contend the Government is still doing business as if the country is in a financial crisis, with the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform, only established at the time of the crash, regularly curtailing their ability to negotiate locally with line departments and agencies, or vetoing deals they think are over the line.
[ What services will be affected by the public sector strike and what will be closed? Opens in new window ]
There is also the issue of local bargaining, a component of the last pay deal, which was due to be worth 1 per cent of pay with a further 2 per cent to come.
The unions felt they should have wide-ranging latitude to address outstanding issues in their own areas but even where their departments agreed, the department intervened to stop the payments being processed. More than a year after the money was supposed to be due, thousands of staff have yet to receive it. For others, it has been processed on the eve of the current industrial action.
[ Unions urge Taoiseach to intervene in bid to avert public sector strike Opens in new window ]
That seems to explain some of the union side’s reluctance to attend the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) in recent days, while there is a frustration among the unions’ leadership with the failure of Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers to address their position directly before the last deal expired, or in the almost four months since.
There is lingering anger too over the Government’s decision to proceed with a VAT cut for hospitality that the unions argued was unjustified and its reaction to the fuel protests.
The ballots held by unions suggested very high levels of support for action, although there is an element of members wanting to give their negotiators the strongest possible hand. With some of the unions not paying any strike pay, and others paying only very modest amounts or waiting for the dispute to progress before doing so, the strikers will feel the impact of their own action in their pockets.
Public opinion, supportive to a substantial degree if the picket lines are anything to go by, may also shift if next Wednesday’s second strike and further actions proceed.
[ Live updates: ‘Living pay cheque to pay cheque’ – public sector workers on strike across the country Opens in new window ]
Moreover, the apparent move by Chambers on the issue of when pay can be discussed has made it harder for those driving strategy to continue refusing invitations to get around a table and discuss their grievances.
That the unions will have to compromise on some of their demands as part of that process seems inevitable, but the Government did not help itself by setting aside €1.2 billion for pay increases next year, a figure that is hard to reconcile with what appears to be required to address the situation.
Obviously, the Government, already the target of criticism for its increased spending, could not reveal how much it is prepared to devote to addressing the dispute. Chambers, however, acknowledged this evening that this too should now be regarded as no more than a starting point for negotiations.
Getting those started remains the first challenge, but Chambers repeatedly hinted on Wednesday night that work is going on behind the scenes. And he sounded hopeful, almost confident, that some sort of framework will be announced soon, whether it involves the WRC or mediation by a different third party.
The Government had been hoping it would become easier to move things forward once the unions had made their point about the anger of their members.
After what was a good day for those unions, the feeling might well now be that it is a good time to get down to business.

title: Mike Ditka: The ‘ultra-ultra-ultra conservative’ coach who transcended the NFL
description: Super Bowl-winning coach of the Chicago Bears opted not to run against Barack Obama for a vacant US Senate seat in 2004
content:
I n the summer of 2004, the Republicans were in serious bother in Illinois. Midway through the campaign for a soon-to-be vacant US Senate seat, their chosen candidate Jack Ryan was alleged to have coerced his ex-wife Jeri, an actor who played Seven of Nine on Star Trek, to accompany him to sex clubs in New York and Paris. A scandal damaging enough back then to force him from the race, party apparatchiks scrambled for a replacement, desperate to prevent the Democrats’ rising star, some state senator called Barack Obama , from punching his ticket to Washington.
For a couple of weeks, Mike Ditka was in the frame. A self-described “ultra-ultra-ultra conservative”, pro-life and anti-gay marriage, he had famously warmed up a crowd for George W Bush during the 2000 election. Across 11 years coaching the Chicago Bears, he also helmed the legendary Super Bowl-winning team of William “The Refrigerator” Perry, the first NFL outfit to capture the Irish imagination in the mid-80s. In the Windy City, hero worship of him was so excessive it even spawned a recurring skit on NBC’s Saturday Night Live called The Superfans.
“Who would win in a fight?” asks Bob Swerski of the Bears-loving quartet. “Coach Ditka or a hurricane?” After his colleagues inevitably plump for their hero, he confounds the table, which includes Michael Jordan moonlighting as himself, by pondering, “What if the name of the hurricane is... Hurricane Ditka?”
Adoration on that scale is why Obama openly admitted the gridiron legend would immediately become favourite to take the Senate spot. A bellicose character permanently chomping on a stogie, Ditka wore a trademark bushy moustache (Ted Lasso’s entire look is a homage) and ubiquitous Bears sweater, spoke without filter and didn’t suffer fools. Among other enterprises, he owned an eponymous steak house on Chicago’s Magnificent Mile and reporters flocked to the joint as speculation grew that “Da Coach” might enter the political arena.
“Biggest mistake I’ve ever made,” said Ditka of his subsequent decision not to run and perhaps alter forever the course of American history. No Obama means no Trump. A monumental “What if?” revisited this past week following his death at 86.
He opted out, citing burgeoning business interests; his new clothing line was about to be launched, and, rather lucratively, he had become one of the first sportsmen to advertise an erectile dysfunction drug, leading one snarky Chicago hack to christen him “Limp Ditka”. Despite thinking Obama was “the worst president we’ve ever had”, Ditka still brought his Bears squad to the White House in 2011 and gifted his putative adversary a jersey with his name on the back.
“Somehow the guy seemed immortal, like an Easter Island statue, like a high rift in the granite mantle of the Earth itself,” wrote Rick Telander, the great Chicago sportswriter and sometimes Ditka ghost. “Every Chicagoan is diminished in some way with Mike Ditka not here any more. Was the guy perfect? Ha! Not even close. But, brother, was he a competitor, a character, a warm, caring, nasty, walking, talking whirlwind of ferocity, tenderness and crazy contradictions. Kind of like this city itself, the Chicago he adopted despite his roots in Aliquippa, Pennsylvania.”
[ Why was coach Bill Belichick snubbed from the NFL Hall of Fame? Opens in new window ]
Ditka grew up in steel country, his birthplace a convenient metaphor for somebody whipcord tough enough to become the first tight end to break 1,000 yards receiving in a season. Having won an old NFL championship with the Bears and one of the first Super Bowls with the Dallas Cowboys, he became the first in his position to reach the Hall of Fame. And all of that was just a prelude to an epic coaching career that turned him into such a pop culture icon he had cameos as himself in LA Law, Cheers, and Entourage before busting the chops of Robert Duvall and Will Ferrell in the classic children’s soccer flick, Kicking and Screaming.
These past few days, former players, team-mates and colleagues have unfurled short stories and tall tales about every aspect of his life. From his decades working on CBS’s NFL Today, Jim Nantz recounted Ditka arriving to film in New York each weekend with a wad of 50 hundred-dollar bills in his pocket. He peeled one off every time he needed to tip somebody who crossed his path, figuring this largesse was the least somebody of his wealth could do to make the day of some barkeep or barista.
That was superannuated, almost cuddly Ditka. In his pomp running the Bears, he had been a saltier prospect. Contractually obliged to participate in a weekly radio show on 670 The Score, a caller once accused the coach of holding back tears during the press conference after a defeat.
“I’m 53 years old and my office is at 250 North Washington,” responded Ditka. “Anytime you want to meet me there, you tell me what time and I’ll whip your ass. You got that, wonder boy? It’s easy to hide behind a microphone. Let’s get out in public and see who the gutless wonder is.”
In the week of his firing from the Bears in 1993, Saturday Night Live had the overwrought Superfans drafting an angry letter to the club about “the most monstrous act of betrayal ever committed in the annals of man.” Soundtracked by mournful piano, backgrounded by a framed photo of their deity, they wrote, “We do not fear for Ditka, we know Ditka will rise again. Ditka is like the sun, only smarter…”

title: Lena Dunham’s Girls to return for limited run
description: The HBO sitcom premiered in 2012 and follows the lives of four millennial friends in New York City
content:
Lena Dunham’s hit series Girls will return for a limited run.
The HBO sitcom, which made stars out of the cast, including Dunham, Adam Driver and Allison Williams, premiered in 2012 and follows four millennial friends as they navigate their lives in New York City.
The series will return for a five-episode special starring Dunham as Hannah Horvath, Williams as Marnie Michaels, Zosia Mamet as Shoshanna, Jemima Kirke as Jessa and Andrew Rannells as Elijah.
Production is set to begin in 2027, nearly a decade after it wrapped.
News of the show’s revival was announced on Tuesday with a video released by HBO featuring the original four on a video call.
Dunham said: “Okay. So we used to spend like every summer together, you know, doing this thing that we do, making this show. And is it something that you would want to do again? Are you are you free next summer?
As they all agreed, Rannells popped up in the video call and said: “I’m in, but only because you trash cans need constant supervision.”
Dunham ends the call with a final question: “Seriously, can we still call it Girls? Cause we’re like old as f…”
[ ‘Girls’ returns: less important, more enjoyable, just as funny Opens in new window ]
The series ran for six seasons and also starred Driver as Adam Sackler, Hannah’s on-again-off-again boyfriend, however, it was not confirmed if he will return for the revival.
The show was controversial at the time for its frank depiction of sex with Dunham frequently appearing nude or partially clothed in the show.
Dunham was also behind the Netflix series Too Much about an American woman in her 30s who relocates to London and falls in love with a British musician – mirroring her life and romance to her husband, who she married in 2021.
It comes weeks after Dunham welcomed her first child with husband musician Luis Felber via surrogate. – PA

title: Poland stand between Ireland and a place at the World Cup
description: Meanwhile, Malachy Clerkin looks at the state of play in club football championships around the country
content:
Now we know who stands between Ireland and a place in next summer’s World Cup finals in Brazil: Poland. Gavin Cummiskey was at Páirc Uí Chaoimh on Tuesday evening to see Carla Ward’s team wrap up their play-off semi-final against Kazakhstan with a 4-0 win, making it 12-0 on aggregate. Meanwhile, Poland got the better of the higher ranked Belgium in a penalty shoot-out in Gdańsk.
An upbeat Ward pointed to Ireland’s two wins over the Poles as recently as April, but she wasn’t losing the run of herself. “ We know we got the toughest draw . Even England didn’t want Poland or Belgium, but our team is growing all the time.”
In Gaelic games, with county final season up and running, Malachy Clerkin takes a trip around the entire country to see who is contending in each county’s senior football championship , with plenty of trophy-laden clubs taking on sides seeking their first ever titles.
Cuala have been no strangers to success in recent times, both in football and hurling, and on Sunday they meet Castleknock in the Dublin football final. “Con O’Callaghan v Ciarán Kilkenny, basically.” Eoin Kennedy scored Cuala’s winning point in the 2024 final , Gordon Manning talking to the player who made his competitive debut for Dublin back in January.
In rugby, Gerry Thornley hears from Munster’s defence coach Denis Leamy ahead of what will be an emotional day at Páirc Uí Chaoimh on Saturday when the 10th anniversary of the death of Anthony Foley will be marked. “Poignantly,” Gerry writes, Munster host the same opponents, Racing, as they were due to play in Paris when Foley died. “His memory and presence will, no doubt, linger over this Champions Cup first-round tie.”
In cycling, Ian O’Riordan previews this week’s UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai where Lara Gillespie will attempt to emulate last year’s achievement when she became the first Irish woman to claim a UCI world title in any event.

And at 8pm, the three-in-a-row seeking PSG are away to Manchester City (RTÉ 2, Premier Sports 1 and TNT Sports 1), Roma host Real Madrid (Virgin Media Two and TNT Sports 4) and Aston Villa are at home to Fenerbahçe (TNT Sports 2).

title: Ministers criticise anonymous comments relating to Patrick O’Donovan’s health
description: O’Donovan was hospitalised on Tuesday after being taken ill at a European Union presidency event
content:
Ministers have criticised anonymous comments about the fitness of Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan to continue in his role because of health concerns.
On Tuesday, O’Donovan hit back against critics within his own party, accusing those who commented on his health of “the ultimate in betrayal”.
He was responding to briefings against him in coverage of the budget rows he became embroiled in last week.
Later on Tuesday O’Donovan was hospitalised after being taken ill at a European Union presidency event in Limerick .
On Wednesday, Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke criticised comments attributed to members of Fine Gael about O’Donovan’s fitness to continue in his role.
Burke defended O’Donovan’s performance in his brief, saying he had “performed exceptionally well” in many areas.
“Patrick is a very valued colleague. He’s doing exceptional work in his department. Every department can be challenging from time to time, but never should anyone reach to issues like someone’s health as a reason where discussions would come forward,” he told Newstalk Breakfast.
“My thoughts are with his family, it’s been a difficult time since this illness. But he’s been so open about it, and he’s really encouraged others right throughout society who have a disability or have an illness that there is a place for you at the very top level of government.
“That should absolutely continue to be the place, because if we’re a society that’s closed to that, that would speak very poorly for us.”
Elsewhere, Fianna Fáil Minister for Further Education James Lawless said that speculation on someone’s health and ability to do their job was “a new low”.
He said: “My thoughts are with Patrick and his family. I haven’t heard any reports overnight since he was taken ill yesterday. Patrick is a solid worker at Cabinet. He makes strong contributions on a number of issues.
“This job is never easy for any of us, regardless, and I think bringing someone’s health into it is really a new low. I think that’s something that’s not really appropriate to be speculating on someone’s health, particularly in a political manoeuvring situation,” Lawless told RTÉ Radio’s Morning Ireland.
Lawless said it was important “to rise above” the anonymous comments and to wish O’Donovan well in his recovery.
A Fine Gael TD was quoted at the weekend suggesting that people within the parliamentary party were questioning whether O’Donovan was healthy enough to continue in his role, with a Cabinet source in the party quoted as suggesting a discussion on whether O’Donovan was “well enough” to stay in his role was likely.
On Tuesday, O’Donovan criticised an “anonymous source on the front page of a reputable Sunday paper last week calling into question my health ... that source was attributed to my own party”.
He fell ill later in the day and a spokeswoman said: “The Minister became unwell during the EU informal meeting at the University of Limerick and has been taken off site for assessment and treatment.”
O’Donovan, who is Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport, was hospitalised after becoming unwell during an official trip to Brussels during the summer.
He has previously spoken about his experience living with epilepsy , which he was diagnosed with more than 10 years ago.

title: Lisandro Martinez launches scathing attack on Manchester United’s leadership
description: Defender says club lack ambition and pointed finger at United’s director of football Jason Wilcox
content:
Lisandro Martinez called out Manchester United’s lack of ambition as the defender doubled down on his withering criticism of the club’s hierarchy.
Michael Carrick’s 10 men fell to a 2-0 loss at Atletico Madrid in the Champions League on Tuesday but the only talking point afterwards revolved around a player nicknamed “The Butcher” wielding his cleaver.
Martinez criticised United’s director of football Jason Wilcox for a lack of summer transfer business during an interview with Prime Video.
But the Argentina international did not stop there as the outspoken centre-back reiterated his stance when speaking to former United goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel on CBS Sports.
“We are trying to be positive and trying to be honest,” Martinez said. “We have to change, we have to do more because I think we are capable to do better.
“We have the players and, yeah, we expect but also, for sure, when you watch the television and you watch the games, you see the players and the manager and you point the finger, which is right.
“We take the responsibility but also as a club I expect more, you know. I expect more. I’m not going to close my mouth.
“I expect more. We need more and we need more ambition. We need to talk more about winning the Champions League, to talk about winning the Premier League in terms of other things.”
When Schmeichel pointed out that it was only October, the frustrated United defender said: “Yeah, but every season we are talking the same thing.”
After the 1999 treble winner interjected to say clubs did not win or lose anything at this stage of a campaign, Martinez said: “No, no for sure. For sure. But if we don’t say the truth, nothing will change.”
Martinez’s interviews will dominate the build-up to Sunday’s eagerly-anticipated Premier League trip to rivals Leeds as pressure mounts on Carrick.
The 28-year-old suggested there should also be focus on the Ineos-led boardroom as United travel to West Yorkshire with their worst points tally after six games since 1986 and fresh from a fruitless night in Spain.
United reacted well after falling behind inside a minute to an avoidable Pablo Barrios goal, with Atleti substitute Ademola Lookman completing a 2-0 win shortly after Leny Yoro was sent off.
“I think the belief, the energy [are issues],” Martinez said. “We are not playing well as a team. You can see the disconnection.
“We can’t do sometimes three, four passes together and the body language. We miss some chances and we are negative.
“And, yeah, when you play against these teams, especially in Champions League, you can’t miss [the] opportunity and you can’t concede in the first minute the goal we concede and, yeah, that’s it.”
Asked whether the disconnect he mentioned was down to a lack of confidence, fitness or understanding, the United defender said: “Yeah, for sure the confidence and also the rotation in the team, you know.
“Because we have many, many games and you have to rotate players and, for me, we don’t have the best squad at the moment compared with other top teams.” - PA

title: Grim reality of war sends Shakhtar Donetsk to London for ‘home’ Champions League clash
description: ‘This team need support and need emotion, because we are living under sirens and bombs,’ said director of football Darijo Srna
content:
The morning has thinned out into low, wispy cloud. Beneath it, Shakhtar Donetsk’s players are going through their paces. Arda Turan observes from the side, watching with the director of football, Darijo Srna. A stray ball zips towards them and Srna, after juggling it up, bends it into the goal with a familiar right-footed arc. “Modric!” exclaims Turan. But the two men are football legends in their own right and, as they continue to joke, the thought occurs that this happy scene could be played out almost anywhere else. Nearby, just beyond the team’s accommodation, a lake shimmers under the emerging sun.
It masks the fact that, around dawn, air-raid sirens disrupted the peace for everyone in view. Even here, in Shakhtar’s bucolic spa hotel base 15 minutes outside Lviv, nobody is safe from the threat of Russian rockets and drones. In Rivne, three hours’ drive to the northeast, another alarm had sent the players and staff down to the stadium’s shelter. The second half was delayed by 20 minutes and that, no matter the corner of the country or the vividness of the autumn colours, is a weekly reality.
So is a travel schedule any other Champions League club would recoil at. Shakhtar are about to hit the road yet again, because there remains no chance of playing European games in Ukraine. This season they will host matches in England for the first time, Stamford Bridge the winner in a beauty contest of three venues in London. If the border crossing into Poland is unforgiving, the journey could take anything up to 18 hours. I’ve been invited to join their trip to London for Wednesday night’s game “at home” to AEK Athens.
“It has good feelings for me and, Inshallah (God willing), it will for our players too,” a beaming Turan says, a few hours before making a journey that starts via a convoy of people carriers. He has wrought a transformation at Shakhtar since his appointment as head coach in May 2025 and has been reminding anyone who will listen of his semi-final goal against Chelsea in 2014, when an Atlético Madrid side at the peak of their powers produced a classic away performance. “It’s an iconic stadium but it’s not our home,” Turan says. “If you don’t have a home stadium at this level it’s very difficult, ask any other club. But we have a dream and inside we have great power.”
They will need all of it for the trip. Shakhtar have become used to packing up, regrouping and taking their roadshow to locations in Poland, Germany and Slovakia for their “home” matches on the Continent. But it does not become easier and, with parts of Ukraine under intensified attack from Russia, there is no immediate prospect of a happy ending.
“In the first year playing games away we felt more enthusiastic,” says Vitaliy Khlivnyuk, Shakhtar’s director of sports management. “And we continue, but with each year it becomes harder and harder for everyone. Physically you can get over it but mentally it’s really tough.”
Kyiv, where Shakhtar were based more regularly until three years ago, is an increasingly dangerous place. “Now it has the kind of atmosphere where the birds don’t sing,” says Khlivnyuk, drawing an unhappy parallel with the early days of the invasion of Donetsk in 2014.
At lunch, one of Shakhtar’s bus drivers, Oleksandr, readies himself for the task ahead. He has set today’s departure time for 1pm. Three of the squad playfight by the dessert buffet and then, realising time is tight, hurry downstairs to collect their belongings.
The players and coaching staff travel in a group of smaller vehicles, four or five to each. Shakhtar introduced that extra concession for comfort a year ago, receiving a favourable response. Other club employees follow on a larger coach, the vehicles winding through low-slung villages and past glinting domed churches. Crumbling Soviet signs are reminders of a complex past; a couple of modest cemeteries bring the present starkly into view.
Passengers’ names are taken before arrival at the Krakovets border crossing, which is reached in just under two hours. Many of the players leap out to stretch their legs. Kaua Elias, among the brightest talents in Shakhtar’s modern crop of exciting Brazilians, has been playing Fifa video games with a carload of his compatriots.
In Lviv, they all meet once a week to cook churrasco; Marlon Gomes has the best knack for it, according to Elias. The prospect of Stamford Bridge is plenty to chew on. Tonight’s match is, at least in part, the culmination of a lifelong ambition. “Since I was a kid I dreamed of playing there for Chelsea,” Elias says. “So going there with Shakhtar is a dream in the same way. We’re very happy to play in London this year.”
Border formalities on the Ukrainian and Polish sides take an hour and a quarter. The buses begin coursing through the corn fields of southeast Poland and arrive at Rzeszow Airport four hours after leaving Lviv.
Turan makes a video call while waiting for the flight; one of his assistants is watching Chelsea play Bournemouth and another is clipping up action from the win at Veres. “There’s time to do it on these trips,” Turan says. He is working through episodes of MobLand when downtime is called for.
This magnetic, emotional figure has thrown himself into Shakhtar. “I feel 100 per cent part of this family and this story,” Turan says. “It’s something more important than football. I want to raise the voice of the people here. We live in war but we will never accept it and I will always continue bringing it up. Football is sometimes everything in life, but sometimes it’s nothing.”
Shakhtar hope at least 25,000 fans will attend the AEK game, perhaps the lowest-profile home match of a quartet that will conclude with Real Madrid’s visit in January. The club’s connections with London extend beyond football: Metinvest, its sister company, provided 5,000 tonnes of steel that built the Shard. On the pitch, they will wear shirts highlighting the “Invest in Ukraine” campaign driven by their owner and sponsor SCM.
“If you come along and support Shakhtar, you’re supporting Ukraine,” Srna says. “This team need support and need emotion, because we are living under sirens and bombs. We’re here to show the world that we are alive, strong, united and will fight to the end.”
At the back of the plane, Shakhtar’s Ukrainian contingent are playing cards.
Midfielder Dmytro Kryskiv thinks there is “something special connecting the team”, driven by the mercurial Turan. They disembark after a nine-hour expedition and, within 90 more minutes, will be settled into their west London hotel. For modern-day Shakhtar, it gets no easier than this. On Thursday, they must make the return journey before preparing for Saturday’s league game with Kolos Kovalivka.
“But we have to continue to play,” Khlivnyuk concludes. “Many of our citizens are struggling more than us. When you know that a win or draw can be a spot of light in this darkness, you will always do it.”

title: Deaths in Waterford attack put focus on increase in drug-related intimidation
description: Inside Politics: Public sector workers strike, with Government and unions yet to agree on talks process
content:
Ireland’s political leaders are united in horror at what President Catherine Connolly described as the “appalling attack” in Waterford that led to the deaths of Kim and Philip English and two of their children, Callum (12) and Jayden (9).
In Leinster House, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said the “thoughts and prayers of everybody in this Dáil and across Government are with the family, the wider community in Waterford and also with the first responders”.
Earlier, as news of the incident was breaking, Martin said it was a “very worrying and deeply disturbing situation”.
Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald said: “This community needs every support possible. We stand with them at this desperate, desperate time.”
Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan condemned the arson attack and said “there is no place in a civilised society for such a heinous act of violence”.
In today’s lead story Conor Lally, Barry Roche and Hugh Dooley write that gardaí believe the murders of members of the English family in a petrol-bombing attack on their home is linked to recent violence they were subjected to by a local drugs gang.
Two other children were rescued from the burning house but were in critical condition in Crumlin children’s hospital in Dublin on Tuesday. They were described locally as “a lovely family”.
The Irish Times understands the English family was hoping to leave the property as part of a council transfer because they felt unsafe.
Gardaí carried out searches in the Waterford area on Tuesday night and it is understood they have identified a number of suspects in the murder investigation.
Though the investigation is at an early stage, gardaí suspect Philip English had taken on a drug debt incurred by an associate in an effort to keep him safe. However, gardaí strongly suspect the local crime gang that was owed money targeted the family on Tuesday morning and was also behind another attack last month.
Roche reports from the scene that neighbours were awoken just after 5am to the smell of smoke and immediately alerted the emergency services, running to the house to try to help.
Our Security and Crime Editor Conor Lally writes about how the deaths in Waterford have brought into focus an increase in drug-related intimidation, often in the form of petrol bombings, in recent years.
The first wide-scale strike by public sector workers in 17 years is happening today, with schools, hospitals, local authority services and even proceedings in Leinster House all affected.
It comes amid a row over how to approach talks aimed at achieving a new public sector pay deal after the last one expired at the end of June.
As Emmet Malone and Pat Leahy report , Fórsa union leader Kevin Callinan has suggested the Taoiseach should intervene to get a talks process started if further strikes and disruption are to be prevented.
He was speaking after the union side rebuffed late efforts by Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers and the Government side to engage and prevent today’s strike.
Callinan was responding to a suggestion by Chambers that although the Government wanted talks to begin at the Workplace Relations Commission on Tuesday, he would consider other ways to achieve progress if that could not be done.
The Government is likely to make a push to bring the unions into a talks process after the stoppage as it seeks to avoid further strikes scheduled for next week.
In his Dáil sketch , Frank McNally writes that Martin’s feathers were ruffled by claims he was “playing chicken” with striking workers.
Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan was hospitalised on Tuesday after being taken ill at a European Union presidency event in Limerick. Jack Horgan-Jones reports .
Former minister and European commissioner Phil Hogan has formally launched his bid to become the next director general of the UN’s food agency, saying he is ready “to serve once again”.
On the Opinion pages, Kathy Sheridan writes that she has paid her TV licence but RTÉ is testing her patience.
The actions of the Ireland players in the two Nations League were described as “shameful” by the chief executive of the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) at an event in Dublin on Tuesday. Jonathan Greenblatt spoke on behalf of the J7, a coalition of advocacy groups in countries with large Jewish communities. Katie Mellett reports .
There are no proceedings in the Dáil, Seanad or committee rooms today as staff in Leinster House join other public sector workers in strike action. We will keep you updated on events with a live blog today. Follow the action here .
Elsewhere, Taoiseach Micheál Martin will deliver the opening address to the International AI Summit being held in Dublin as part of Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the European Union. Attendees will hear from various European commissioners, ministers and representatives of artificial intelligence companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic as well as tech giants Google and Microsoft.
Panels include one entitled The European AI Advantage: Leadership, Innovation and Global Competitiveness and another on AI Transforming Health: From Discovery to Patient Care.

title: Germany puts Ukrainian ex-officer in the dock over Nord Stream sabotage
description: German prosecutors say a Ukrainian military officer led the operation that destroyed the Baltic Sea gas pipelines in 2022
content:
A Ukrainian military officer goes on trial in Hamburg on Wednesday, charged with masterminding the explosions that destroyed two Russian -controlled undersea gas pipelines in September 2022.
Seven months after Russian troops invaded Ukraine , the three detonations severed a key energy source for western Europe – and income stream for Moscow – with ongoing economic and political aftershocks.
The Ukrainian defendant, identified in extradition documents as Serhii Kuznetsov, is being charged with acting on behalf of Ukrainian security services to cause an explosion. In addition, Kuznetsov faces a war crime charge because German prosecutors have classified the Nord Stream pipelines as civilian infrastructure.
In a 136-page indictment, the 50-year-old is accused of leading a team that rented a German yacht called Andromeda. Four deep-sea divers in the team allegedly planted “high-performance” explosives and timer detonators on the pipelines 80m under the sea, southeast of the Danish island of Bornholm.
Investigators reportedly found traces of high-grade military explosives both on the ruined pipelines and the boat. A member of the team also reportedly left DNA material on the Andromeda.
During the trial prosecutors will present photographs taken by a curious holidaymaker in a German seaside town, allegedly showing the defendant and others loading up the Andromeda with equipment including deep-sea diving gear.
[ Nord Stream saga shows German leaders’ magical thinking and economical approach to the truth Opens in new window ]
A trail of sightings indicate the Andromeda took a zig-zag course through the Baltic Sea from Germany to Poland and south Sweden in advance of the explosion in Danish waters on September 22nd, 2022.
On the suspect’s smartphone, investigators found documents on the two pipelines, Baltic Sea maps, information about known sea-wrecks in the region and general pipeline technical documents.
Kuznetsov, a father of four with an address in Kyiv and a 25-year military record, denies all charges. Two previous attempts by German prosecutors to have him arrested under a European arrest warrant failed, most notably in neighbouring Poland where he was tipped off by authorities in time to escape back to Ukraine.
In August 2005, Kuznetsov was arrested during a camping holiday with his family in Croatia.
“That was not very smart of him,” said Bojan Pancevski, a Wall Street Journal correspondent and author of The Nord Stream Conspiracy.
“Perhaps he felt safe because, for a long time, there was no evidence against him. But he underestimated the German police.”
A second Ukrainian man is currently fighting extradition in Croatia. In total, German investigators say they have tracked down seven suspects in connection with the explosion.
Defence lawyer Jes Meyer-Lohkamp will push the court to examine whether the attack was justified under humanitarian law, arguing the pipeline income helped finance Russia’s war against Ukraine.
He told the Bild tabloid: “It’s important to me to draw attention not just to criminal code paragraphs but look, too, at the political dimension.”
The first pair of 1,200km-long Nord Stream pipelines was approved in the last days of the Schröder administration in 2005. It and a second set were built during the subsequent Merkel administration.
The second pipeline set was completed but never entered operation as Berlin, responding to the Russian war on Ukraine, refused a permit.
[ Were the Nord Stream pipelines among the biggest strategic errors of the 21st century? Opens in new window ]
The five-judge Hamburg court has refused an application by Russian energy giant Gazprom, majority owner of the pipelines, to join the trial as co-plaintiff.
A verdict is not likely before February and, in intervening testimony, observers expect the trial to highlight the contradictions of Germany’s recent energy and political interests.
“It is a funny situation,” said Pancevski. “Germany is both Ukraine’s largest [military] supporter in Europe yet now it is also prosecuting a Ukrainian offer because of alleged war crimes against their common enemy.”

title: A bumpy debut for Katie Zacharia, the new voice of Donald Trump
description: US president’s newly appointed spokeswoman stumbled through her first White House briefing, leaving reporters with more questions than answers
content:
US president Donald Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, made her debut behind the White House lectern on Tuesday.
“Good morning!” she began. “I want to thank president Trump for his trust that he has placed in me. I have wanted to work for him for a very long time.”
She spent the next eight minutes reading nervously from a script, looking up at the cameras every couple of lines. Then she said she was ready to take some questions.
She called on only three reporters, dropped one wild piece of news, made a slip mixing up her husband and her president, then darted out of there after just 5½ minutes, leaving the White House press corps to scratch its collective head.
All told, Zacharia picked only a few outlets from a list she was holding: Breitbart, Fox News and The Daily Mail.
The White House press secretary gig is a tricky one that, when practised well, involves more than reciting talking points on cable TV, which is what Zacharia was doing as a commentator on Fox News when she got picked for this job.
Of the few questions she allowed on Tuesday, the most substantive one was also among the most predictable: “Has the US stopped sharing intel with Ukraine?”
WH Press Secretary Katie Zacharia on maintaining the job while having four children: "I think this job is not one you necessarily balance...though my work will be demanding they will always be a priority." pic.twitter.com/dRFM8pddIM
For days, the breakdown of US negotiations with the Ukrainians has been front page news – certainly it is the dominant storyline in Washington this week – and yet, Zacharia was not prepared to answer the question.
“I’ll have to get back to you on that,” she said.
One of the few questions she took was about how she hoped to “manage” her new job with a husband and four kids at home (hard to imagine a male press secretary getting that one). There was a moment of levity in the room when she caught herself in a funny slip, and was able to laugh about it. “So, my president, excuse me, my husband,” she said, “that’s a good one.”
She did come armed with one special surprise to drop. When a reporter asked about the fate of the US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, Zacharia said: “We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign.”
Reporters in the room lit up – news! – but before they could ask more about this development, the new press secretary announced that she was ready to “end it,” because it was nearly time for the president’s departure. Reporters pelted questions at her as she prepared to edge out of the room toward the little sliding door painted blue.
“Did the president speak with ambassador Guilfoyle?”
“What about the Russian diesel! Will the diesel come into the States?!”
Having not yet mastered the hard exit, she replied: “He will answer those questions out at Marine One.”
In the history of White House press secretaries, the ones who tend to do best have direct access to the president and therefore feel comfortable speaking on his behalf. Those who don’t end up having trouble in the job. Under president George W Bush, that was Scott McClellan. Karine Jean-Pierre, the press secretary under president Joe Biden, did not often give the impression that she had been in the room with her boss.
Karoline Leavitt, Zacharia’s predecessor, really was part of Trump’s inner circle, and because she was with him on the campaign trail when he was mounting his comeback, she could speak for him with some authority.
Zacharia (41) is not only new to the president but also to a lot of the people who work for him in the White House.
At 27, Leavitt was the youngest person ever to hold the job. Behind the podium, she could be lacerating, vitriolic, dissembling. But she didn’t seem scared, exactly.
Reporters are animals. They can smell fear. Leavitt used to post photos of herself on Instagram sparring with a packed briefing room set to the soundtrack of Welcome to the Jungle by Guns N’ Roses.
Not long after the briefing, Zacharia walked out of the White House with the president on to the South Lawn, where a massive, gnashing press maw was waiting.
Zacharia stood off to the side while her boss prowled the pavement, fielding questions about Iran and Ukraine and the midterms and the end of Guilfoyle’s chapter as Greece ambassador.
The president was asked how he thought Zacharia had fared in her first briefing, and why she had taken so few questions.
In the social media post he made last week announcing her appointment, he called her “an attorney,” and she identifies herself as a lawyer. This reporter asked the president in which state Zacharia had passed the bar exam? Trump turned to look at his new press secretary. She took two small steps closer. “When I moved to China,” she said.
Asked later for clarification, White House officials would not say whether or where Zacharia passed a bar exam.
Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, provided this statement over email: “Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team. She is uniquely qualified and whip-smart to help inform the American people about all the great things president Trump and his administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as press secretary.”
Trump finished taking questions, turned and traipsed toward his helicopter. Zacharia was left standing alone. The reporters began shouting in her direction.
They waved her over. She just smiled and stared straight ahead.
After another moment, the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles, appeared with two of the president’s most trusted aides, Natalie Harp and Walt Nauta. Zacharia joined her new co-workers and together they all walked silently across the South Lawn and climbed into Marine One to begin a long day of travel to Alaska followed by Las Vegas.
Plenty of time for everybody to get to know each other a little better.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

title: Paris Motor Show 2026: Europe comes out swinging against China
description: European brands flex their styling muscles in Paris, but is China still ahead on tech?
content:
N ot only does the 2026 edition of the Paris Motor Show feel like the most vibrant and significant European motor show for some time – possibly even as far back as when the first barrage of Covid holed the now-departed Geneva motor show below the waterline – it also feels like the setting for a big pushback by European car makers against their Chinese rivals.
The headlines so far this year have mostly been about ever-swelling Chinese brand sales across Europe. Chinese brands now account for around 12 per cent of total European car sales, and that combined with falling European brand sales in China has led to the various financial crises we’ve seen at the likes of VW Group and BMW recently.
At Paris, though, the pushback began, and in stylistic terms this was led by Renault and the Stellantis group. Stellantis let its French brands – Peugeot , Citroën and DS – take most of the limelight and, of those three, Citroën probably scored the biggest hit with the concept version of its new 2CV.
This compact, affordable electric car – it is set to cost between €15,000 and €20,000 when it goes on sale in 2028 – comes with a small battery and a small electric range, but big appeal thanks to styling both inside and out that apes the classic original 2CV.
The free-standing headlights are present and correct; so too the corrugated bonnet and the rollback canvas roof. The interior is a riot of retro styling, with a fabulous push-pull gear selector and cut-outs in the glovebox for holding eggs – the original 2CV was, of course, designed to carry a basket of eggs across a ploughed field without breaking any.
If anything, the commercial version of the 2CV concept, the Fourgonnette van, with its boxy back end and instant appeal to mobile coffee providers up and down the land, was even more adorable. How much of either car’s neat design details will make it through to final production remains to be seen, but the hope is that the answer will be “lots”.
Across the Stellantis hall at Peugeot, things were still retro, but focused on the 1980s and 2010s. The E-T16 concept is the clearest look yet at the next-generation 208 hatchback, albeit with the new car’s dimensions and style slightly disguised by a wide-boy rally car bodykit that pays homage to the 40th birthday of the astonishing 205 T16 Group B rally car of the 1980s.
The E-T16 looks incredible, and goes pretty incredibly too thanks to an 816hp electric motor set-up, four-wheel drive, a hydraulic handbrake for tight turns, and a 0-100km/h time of just 2.5 seconds.
[ Peugeot’s electric E-208 GTi proves that fun still lives. This is a real 1980s throwback Opens in new window ]
There’s a faint chance that Peugeot might actually put this wild machine into production as a riposte to Renault’s equally wild R5 Turbo 3E limited-edition model but, more importantly, the E-T16 previews the interior of the next 208 with its odd “Hypersquare” steering “wheel” which isn’t a wheel at all, but an oblong device with four internally rotating sections mounted at its four corners.
It’s a steer-by-wire system which means you can turn the car fully without crossing your arms, and which Peugeot reckons will allow it to unleash the next-generation of its small-wheel, high-instruments ‘i-Cockpit’ layout.
Also getting the Hypersquare wheel, but looking rather more smooth and sophisticated on the outside, is the Peugeot RCZ Vision concept, which mashes up the styling of the 2010 RCZ coupe with that of 2018’s E-Legende concept (which revived the styling of the old 504 Coupe) and creates something rather sophisticated and handsome.
Like the E-T16 concept, the RCZ gets Peugeot’s new “face” with three horizontal LED lights (supposedly the claw marks of the Peugeot lion badge) and it previews the next-generation STLA One electric car platform with solid-state batteries, 500hp, 600km range, and ultra-fast charging. Production chances? Slim, but Peugeot is speaking of it as a potential BMW 4 Series rival.
DS’s neat F3ver concept was less dramatic but more closely related to the next-generation DS No3 premium hatchback, and if the production car looks this good, then perhaps DS’s sales prospects just went up a notch.
Across at Renault, we were seeing two extremes of styling. The Renault 8 Gordini concept revises the look of the classic R8 Gordini rally cars from the 1960s, but mixes it into a modernistic two-seat coupe, with all-electric power and a sporty interior.
Sadly, this one’s not going to make it to production, but Renault seems a little more serious about its striking E-Space concept which – surprise, surprise – riffs on the TGV-like styling of the original 1984 Espace, but which is now all-electric and which has a hugely flexible six-seat cabin layout.
It’s a truly stunning thing to look at, the E-Space, and you can see how relatively easy it would be to productionise. Renault is neither confirming nor denying for now, but the chance is there. In the meantime, enjoy the built-in Connect 4 board game which goes with the multiple 12.3-inch screens in the back to keep your passengers happy on a long journey.
[ Renault Twingo has everything going for it - except one crucial detail Opens in new window ]
More striking again was what Alpine had in store – the Alpine A310 Vision, which looks very much as if an original 1971 V6 rear-engined A310 sports car passed through a time tunnel and turned into a futuristic spaceship on the way.
It’s a stunner of a car, and gives us some idea of what Renault and Alpine might do in the way of a future Porsche 911 rival.
Alas, it too seems unlikely for production, but underneath is the same APP electric car platform which will underpin the new, smaller, A110 sports car. That platform is hugely flexible, so the battery can be split up and moved around in the chassis to get an ultra-low driving position, and combustion power can be added in if the market demands it, but even so the A310 Vision is likely to remain on the concept car shelf. For now.
Elsewhere, Opel’s sleek STX concept, with its lights that seem to fade into the front bodywork, seemingly previews the next-generation Astra estate (or possibly a single Astra model that mixes and matches estate and hatch cues) while Alfa Romeo’s Cuorerosso concept is gorgeous, and a clear hint at the next-gen Giulia saloon, but which seemed a bit of a disappointment given that the Giulia ought to be on sale already, and that the concept comes with a hybrid V6 petrol engine instead of the BMW iM3-rivalling all-electric Quadrifoglio powertrain.
Fiat’s Multiplay concept is probably the oddest, and yet somehow coolest, car at the show. It previews a possible seven-seat MPV-SUV-type thing but the show car can turn into a pickup truck at the push of a button (yes, really) and comes with a dedicated seat for your dog. Mad, but adorable.
What of China, though? There was clear intent, even aggression, in the air as European brands started to push back against their Chinese rivals. In advance of the show, Volkswagen held a conference that extolled the value – in literal and figurative terms – of its European production, and at which Sébastien Martin, France’s minister delegate for industry, pointed out how effective higher European tariffs on Chinese electric cars had been.
With the EU and China trying to thrash out a deal that would limit Chinese exports, that seemed rather timely, as did VW boss Thomas Schäfer’s call for the EU to give more financial support to electric car production.
As far as new cars went, the Chinese brands had a bit of a quiet Paris show. The new Leapmotor B03 hatchback and D19 SUV models will doubtless be impressively priced and equipped, but both looked bland and couldn’t hold a candle to the European metal on show. Changan’s new flagship Avatr, a big, luxury SUV, looked as if someone had melted a Volvo EX90 in the same pot as a Rolls-Royce Cullinan with unpleasant results.
More interesting was the new BYD Atto 8, a roomy seven-seat all-electric rival to the likes of the Skoda Peaq, which piqued interest not so much for its predictable styling inside and out, nor its mad 775hp maximum power output, but because it’s the first BYD coming to Europe – early next year – that’s compatible with the company’s ultra-fast 1,500kW “Flash” charging points.
These can, potentially, top up the Atto 8’s 115kW battery (giving it a 635km range) in as little as five minutes, from 10-70 per cent, or nine minutes for a 10-97 per cent charge. Alas, for Irish customers, the roll-out of the 3,000 Flash chargers expected for Europe has only just begun and none have come to Ireland just yet.
What will sway Europe’s car buyers more? The style of the 2CV, RCZ, STX, E-Space, A310, and Cuorerosso? Or the tech, and pricing, of the Atto 8 and its countrymen? Or will further European tariffs, or a new trade deal with China, have a bigger effect than any of this? Whatever the answers might be, the Paris motor show certainly saw the European brands coming out, Rocky-style, swinging hard.

title: Obama tells Belfast event ‘democracy not inevitable’ but keeps Trump criticism subtle
description: Former US president talks about the Middle East, democracy, journalism and his regular theme of hope during a speaking event
content:
On the way into the O2 arena in Belfast on Tuesday night one man, possibly reflecting the views of the majority of the 7,000 people who turned up to listen to former US president Barack Obama , hoped he would “tear into” the incumbent Donald J Trump .
But there would be no such headline. Obama was interviewed in Belfast by writer and journalist Susan McKay as part of a three-stop speaking engagement that also takes in Glasgow and Manchester. And while he touched on a number of subjects such as the Middle East, democracy, journalism and his regular theme of hope, there would be no verbal assault on Trump.
Rather, what criticism the audience heard was implicit and that was when he was talking about Israel and Palestine, where that main hallmark of his political career, hope, largely was absent. He said the basic point was that seven million Jews in Israel and the seven million Palestinians in the region “aren’t going anywhere”.
People should be conscious that not everyone in Israel supported prime minister Binymain Netanyahu. “The citizenry of Israel has to rethink, to reimagine,” Obama advised, “how are your children and grandchildren going to live in this region? Are you just going to be behind walls and wipe out everybody around you, or are you going to find some just way of defending yourself while still acting in an ethical, moral way?
“And conversely, the Palestinians are going to have to recognise we are not going to outkill, outweaponise the Israelis, which means that we have to look to other examples of how change comes about based on moral claims and ethical claims and ... nonviolent strategies, and that’s going to take some time.
“So I don’t want to offer any false hope here,” he added. “My immediate goal I would like to see right now would be simply relieving suffering, an actual end to violence, and my hope would be at the bare minimum to stop the current ongoing encroachment into the West Bank, alongside helping Gaza to rebuild.”
Here he was subtly critical of Trump. “And even that right now is going to take quite a lot of work, and frankly it will require a US government that is willing to engage in that creative work which may not be forthcoming for a while.”
And even if many in the O2 crowd were hoping for something more red-blooded in relation to Trump, they all seemed well taken with Obama. Tickets for the event ranged in price from about £60 to a £1,000 (€71-€1,183) for a VIP admission that involved a photograph with the former president, a seat in the first 10 rows of the O2 arena and a copy of his book, A Promised Land.
Earlier in the day Obama received an honorary degree from Queen’s University Belfast. Speaking to university staff and students, he said the Belfast Agreement was “still a shining example of what can happen when people put aside old wounds and choose peace”.
And in what possibly could be construed as a careful dig at Trump, he warned: “But as we have seen in many countries, including in my home country the United States, peace and democracy are not inevitable.”
In the O2 arena McKay noted that some people were disappointed Obama was not accompanied by his wife, Michelle. “Michelle is doing wonderfully and she sends her regards,” he said.
“And you promise you’ll bring her next time,” said McKay.
“I will promise to ask her to come next time. She calls the shots,” he replied.
In the O2 he stressed that democracy must “not be taken for granted”, while adding: “If we abdicate our role as citizens, somebody fills the void.” He referred to the importance of large institutions such as the United Nations and the European Union but also pointed to the need for reform. People, he said, “don’t want to feel as if there are five layers of bureaucracy before a decision is made”, adding: “You have to deliver the goods.”
He spoke of the necessity for responsible journalism, saying: “If you look at why it is that democracies seem under attack, why things are so unstable, why everything is so polarised, if I had a sort of a blame pie and I wanted to figure out how big of a slice to allocate, a big piece would be people getting their news from social media.”
It was notable there were many young people and children with their parents in the audience. Resuming his theme of hope, he said he made a particular effort when speaking around the world to talk to young people.
“Nothing inspires me more than spending time with these young people. They’re way ahead of how I was or of where I was when I was their age. Anytime I’m feeling a little mopey and sad I spend some time with them, and that that raises me back up.”
He said: “I feel better with myself, I feel better for my daughters, I feel better for my friends and my neighbours and my community when I assert and insist the possibility that we can do better than we are doing right now.”
“Why not,” Obama offered when McKay reminded him of Seamus Heaney’s epitaph “walk on air against your better judgment”.
“Yeah, let’s walk on air,” he said, concluding the night.

title: Public sector pay theatrics and IKEA’s new marketplace
description: Business Today: The best news, analysis and comment from The Irish Times business desk
content:
With more than 300,000 public sector workers participating in a one-day work stoppage today, John McManus wonders why all the theatrics? Everybody knows that the Government will eventually agree to a pay increase in line with inflation and get some concessions to offset the bill. However, both sides have their reasons, he writes.
Meanwhile, some positive news for the around 65 per cent of Irish adults who say they have at least one piece of Ikea furniture in their home. The Swedish furniture giant is unveiling a new second-hand marketplace that will allow customers to sell and buy preloved Ikea items locally. Joanne Hunt answers the key questions – how will it work, can you make money off of it, and is it actually good for the environment?
A slowdown in the rate of Irish house price inflation is being linked to a shrinkage in real wages as the cost of living and interest rates continue to rise. Eoin Burke-Kennedy reports on the latest official figures from the Central Statistics Office, which reveal a marked slowdown in the rate of annual house price growth in August.
The Irish Times media group saw its revenues decline by 2.5 per cent last year and recorded a loss of €800,000, accounts filed on Tuesday showed. The Irish Times DAC – which includes the Cork-based Irish Examiner, a number of regional titles, and digital assets MyHome.ie and RIP.ie – posted revenue of €112.7 million, down from €115.6 million a year earlier.
Fiachra Gallagher writes that the Supreme Court will hear an appeal by the Data Protection Commission (DPC) relating to certain preliminary matters arising in LinkedIn’s challenge to the imposition of a €310 million fine . The regulator handed out the fine to the Microsoft-owned company in 2024 for breaches of European data protection laws.
Speaking of Big Tech, Ciara O’Brien reports that Google’s philanthropic arm will spend up to €4.46 million on high-tech weather forecasting and climate research in Ireland, including €2.5 million in funding for UCD’s Aimsir Centre and the Climate + Co-Centre.
On a less encouraging note on the tech front, Anthropic has warned that rogue “ AI worms ” will soon be able to hijack smart home devices, such as ovens and TVs, creating a new cybersecurit y threat that will be difficult to contain. The developer of Claude said in a blog post that AI agents may be months away from “self-replicating” across everyday household devices.
The company behind Irish fashion and homeware retailer Kilkenny Design reported an almost 17 per cent jump in pretax profits to €1.5 million in 2025, despite rising labour costs and the negative impact of “global uncertainty” on consumer confidence. Stephen Conneely has the story.
Stephen also reports that McDonald’s has launched a four-month-long “operational pilot” for hand-breaded chicken products in Ireland. It comes amid the recent arrival of a slew of US quick-chicken brands has Ireland – including such as Popeyes, Wingstop, Dave’s Hot Chicken and Chick-fil-A.
Greencore, the biggest producer of pre-packed sandwiches in the UK, is now forecasting annual profit ahead of market expectations after reporting faster-than-expected fourth-quarter volume growth in a trading update on Tuesday. Eoin Burke-Kennedy reports.
Gordon Deegan reports on the latest accounts for Godolphin’s Irish thoroughbred stud operation , which reveal a 42 per cent surge in revenues to €44.29 million last year on the back of a sharp rise in nomination fee income.
If you’d like to read more about the issues that affect your finances try signing up to On the Money , the weekly newsletter from our personal finance team, which will be issued every Friday to Irish Times subscribers.

title: Pope Leo has lung cancer and had lower lobe of right lung removed, Vatican says
description: Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma
content:
Pope Leo has lung cancer and had the lower lobe of his right lung removed during surgery in Rome, the Vatican has said.
The tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin, after Leo XIV had an operation on Tuesday.
It said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during the operation.
The 71-year-old was in the operating theatre for about three hours, the statement said.
The surgery, which itself lasted approximately 90 minutes, has been completed “successfully, on schedule and as planned”, the Vatican said.
Leo XIV returned to his room after the surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, according to a statement from the Vatican spokesman.
Leo had walked into Rome’s Gemelli hospital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of wellwishers who had gathered to greet him.
The Vatican said the surgery would be performed by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr Stefano Margaritora.
[ Pope Leo says he will undergo surgery for small growth on lung Opens in new window ]
The operation got under way as medical staff recited the Rosary prayer in the hospital chapel Tuesday evening.
“Let us join together in prayer, asking the Lord to sustain our bishop, Pope Leo, and to comfort all those who are hospitalised here,” said the vicar of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, at the start of the prayer.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy.
The surgery, which is usually performed under general anaesthesia, will require a weeklong hospital stay and the Vatican on Monday cancelled all Leo’s audiences through until October 20th. – PA, Reuters

title: African countries look beyond the big three credit ratings agencies
description: Global Briefing: Continent’s leaders hope the new African Credit Rating Agency can help them save tens of billions of dollars in interest payments
content:
African countries have long complained they are being held back by unfairly high borrowing costs shaped by international credit ratings agencies. Now they are doing something about it.
It may have drawn little attention outside Africa but the continent’s leaders hope the launch last week of the African Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA) could help them save tens of billions of dollars in interest payments each year. Backed by the African Union , the agency is part of a drive for greater financial sovereignty in Africa and an attempt to address the shortcomings of the big three global ratings agencies there.
Moody’s, Standard & Poor’s (S&P) and Fitch, all of which are based in the United States, issue ratings that determine the borrowing costs for more than 95 per cent of the world’s rated debt. But African governments and firms have long complained that the big three agencies consistently give them poorer ratings than they apply to other parts of the world.
A report by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in 2023 estimated that excessive risk premiums were costing African countries almost $75 billion each year in interest payments and foregone credit. Some African countries pay more to service their debt each year than they spend on health or education and high interest payments are also a drag on economic growth.
“Reducing interest rates paid by African countries on both domestic and foreign debt could greatly decrease the debt service burden they face,” the UNDP said.
“This, in turn, would enable them to repay the principal faster and free up funds for more investments in development.”
Twenty-three of the African Union’s 55 member states are not rated by the big three agencies at all, and others complain that their credit ratings are shaped by a lack of knowledge and expertise. When Moody’s downgraded Ghana’s debt in 2022, its lead analyst had not even visited the country and the government said the agency overlooked important data on fiscal consolidation.
African companies are also neglected by the international agencies with fewer than 4,000 firms across the continent covered by credit ratings. This compares with more than 800,000 in the EU and more than two million in the US.
AfCRA will be privately funded and independent of African governments and its backers are stressing the importance of independence to building its credibility. Mauritius minister of financial services and economic planning Jyoti Jeetun said it was not about getting more favourable ratings for African countries, but to ensure their economies were assessed more accurately
“Africa does not become more prosperous because we change the way we measure it. But the way we measure African economies and its enterprises can influence the way the world perceives its risk, its opportunities and its potentials,” she said.
“Because for too long, too much of Africa’s economic story has been viewed through the lenses designed elsewhere, using assumptions and frameworks that do not always capture our realities, our specificities. AfCRA is in part about ensuring that Africa’s economic reality is accurately understood.”
AfCRA is not the first attempt to establish an alternative to the American ratings agencies, and an initiative to create a pan-European rival to the big three more than a decade ago ended in failure. But the African move may have had an impact already, with Moody’s and S&P expanding their presence across the continent since planning for AfCRA began.

title: I have paid my TV licence long after I needed to. But RTÉ is testing my patience
description: When it comes to RTÉ, we are paying, we are the product and it has the platform to advocate for itself
content:
A s crazy as it sounds, I have continued to pay the TV licence fee well beyond the point where it was lawfully required. This munificence is not because the €160 is burning a hole in my puny bank account, but because it represents a civic effort to preserve a safe-house of reliable, accountable broadcast news and cultural sovereignty.
Even to its haters, the need for RTÉ must be obvious. We know what happens when television audiences are split into parallel warring universes. Have a look at the US if you can bear it, or try to imagine Britain without the BBC .
But RTÉ is trying my patience. Like many radio listeners, I access it by smartphone via the Listen app. Just how many of us there are is shrouded in mystery for some reason, but one calculation puts smartphone and smart speaker listeners at under 12 per cent of total radio listening. This is an indicator of the number who feel a fresh surge of rage every time they are greeted by the so-called pre-roll advertisements. They cut into live programming, and that could be six times a day if you tend to tune in just in time for the news headlines. If there’s a pause or a brief disconnection, the service is interrupted to play the ad all over again. Sometimes, maddeningly, the ad is a plug for RTÉ itself.
Yes, we know RTÉ derives its dual income from the licence and advertisements and that there are more important things to rage about. But for a broadcaster that rightly prides itself on the calibre of its news and current affairs programming – already punctuated with numerous, lengthy advertising breaks – the pre-roll ads feel cheap. They play more like a Del Boy bilking the last drop from a dopey audience than an introduction to Ireland’s authoritative, national public service media organisation.
It’s all part of the relentless hustle. Most of us have learned to be wary of the requirement to “sign in” or register on any website, knowing that by doing so, our data is probably red meat to be segmented and pitched to advertisers. RTÉ has made no secret of a plan to phase in compulsory registration across its video and audio services. It makes sense at several levels. Registration would provide proof of use and relevance of a kind useful (or not) to a publicly-funded organisation. It would provide significant information, such as users’ age bands, locations and preferences and, for audiences, a more personalised service with options such as “continue listening”, recommendations and queues.
But of course there’s more to it. RTÉ’s own rate card tells advertisers that compulsory registration will yield richer information about audiences and better-targeted advertising. That’s what commercial organisations do, of course, and if we give it any thought at all, we put up with it for the most part. But RTÉ is still largely funded by the mandatory licence – “It’s The Law”, as the ad tells us over and over and over – in addition to large chunks of taxpayers’ cash disbursed by the Government (of which a promised but unforthcoming €20 million hijacked the news last week).
So even the heart-sinking phrase “if you’re not paying for the product, you are the product” falls short in this case. We are paying – and we are also the product. It gets harder to feel much affinity with an organisation that views our personal information and behaviour as just another data grab.
After several years of it, the recurring headlines featuring RTÉ in the news as opposed to RTÉ reporting the news are also getting wearisome. At one point last week it inserted itself as the lead in its own news headlines and Morning Ireland newspaper segment, reasoning no doubt that the financial health of the national semistate broadcaster is always in the public interest and that it has a duty to cover it as it would any other important public entity. It could also be argued that it skated close to confusing that brief with the use of its powerful, publicly-funded platforms to defend RTÉ’s corporate interests. No other entity has that level of pervasive air power to put its own chief executive/director general out front of the main news programmes to advocate for itself against a Government Minister.
[ Credit unions win again as Re-turn, Ryanair and RTÉ fare poorly for customer service Opens in new window ]
Even when – or especially when – the Minister concerned, Patrick O’Donovan , has a history of howlers (his choice of RTÉ as the budget patsy was always going to win the headlines against a low-key budget), it was surely possible to stall the predictable news storm with a calm announcement of an efficient two-day investigation and a couple of grown-up meetings. Instead, with even more tiring predictability, the Public Accounts Committee is gearing up for another “grilling” of RTÉ executives about who knew what and when about the withheld €20 million, amid emotive speculation about compulsory redundancies and the impact on small independent producers.
Meanwhile, Wednesday’s Dáil sitting has been cancelled due to a countrywide public sector strike . For what it’s worth, my €160 hangs in the balance.

title: We are walking our way into a fundamentally flawed education system, and we have been warned
description: The fourth ResearchEd conference in Ireland tackled big questions, including: Why are students bad at learning and why do conferences have bad coffee?
content:
W hy do conferences always have such bad coffee?
This was my first thought as I sat down recently, waiting for the education conference ResearchEd to begin.
This is the fourth time ResearchEd has come to Ireland, the first taking place in 2019 in St Columba’s College in Dublin. A conference aimed at both primary and secondary level teachers, it began in England – founded by Tom Bennett with the help of Helen Galdin-O’Shea in 2013 – and aims to bring “the best evidence available” into the classroom in practical ways.
This year’s event took place in Bandon Grammar, on the west side of Bandon, with its tree-lined entrance and sign pointing to the “boy’s dormitory” hinting at its private school status, but without the ostentation of other such institutions.
After recovering from my coffee, I headed to the keynote speaker, Bradley Busch, chief psychological officer at InnerDrive. The conference was taking place in a typically chilly gym, and with the stage flanked by some green mood lighting, it felt like I was about to watch a school musical. Thankfully, the presentation was a bit more professional than that, but with the same level of enthusiasm.
Busch promised us “transformational” research. In a fascinating talk about how memory works, and how we can help transfer information from students’ working memory to their long-term memory, he made some observations that teachers, students and parents consistently ignore – students will probably be upset that highlighting doesn’t mean learning; teachers that dense PowerPoint presentations aren’t helping; and parents that checking the number of pages their child has read doesn’t mean anything.
Learning is about reading and then quizzing, checking repeatedly to see what you know and what you don’t know.
Oh, and he reiterated that we really can’t spot AI in students’ writing, not to any consistent level, once again calling into question the value of not only homework, but of the AACs (project work) that are being brought into the new Leaving Cert specifications.
We are walking our way into an education system that is fundamentally flawed, and we have been warned.
[ One in five Irish children and teens use AI for schoolwork, survey suggests Opens in new window ]
From the gym I went to a tiered lecture hall to listen to Amarbeer Singh Gill, assistant director of London-based Greenshaw Research School. His talk posed a question, “Why are students so bad at learning?” It centred on how students forget, and the inevitability of forgetting.
