Singh spoke about how short-term performance does not reflect long-term retention, how doing well in an assessment straight after instruction doesn’t mean students have learned the topic. A lower performance can lead to improved learning, once we keep returning to assess the topic.
Study was one of the focuses of the talk, highlighting the misconception that long periods of studying one topic is beneficial. Instead, it’s better to distribute study. Shorter, 30-minute sessions are more helpful. Added to that is the notion of interleaving your study. Move from one area to a separate yet connected area – that way students can see connections and stay focused.
From there, I moved to the safety of a traditional classroom for a talk by Julian Girdham, deputy principal at St Columba’s College in Dublin, an English teacher and the organiser of the first Irish ResearchEd. Speaking to a packed room about the importance of “attention” in the contemporary classroom, his talk was about how we can teach our students to focus on the task at hand and encourage them to think closely about the minutiae of our subjects in a deliberate manner.
Girdham’s belief in students, his dismissal of “it was better in my day” rhetoric, spoke of an optimism in our basic humanity. The human impulse to pay attention and think deeply is still within us all.
[ Students are screen hostages. They’re losing the ability to switch off and knuckle down Opens in new window ]
Mutterings of “yes, true” accompanied his presentation. We all left the room wishing we could have been his student, wishing we could teach like him.
His talk contrasted with Tadgh O’Donovan’s in the same room later that day. O’Donovan, a science teacher at Carrigaline Community School and a TikTok creator, spoke about how to grab students’ attention and interest by using content creators’ tactics, such as being punched by the room’s student assistant, as O’Donovan was – with his consent, of course.
Generations apart, Girdham and O’Donovan have fundamental similarities: their love of the job, their appreciation of the possibilities within each student and their understanding that getting students to pay attention doesn’t have to be confrontational.
The use of a “three, two, one” countdown by a couple of English presenters, with raised arm and fingers lowering one by one, to get our attention before and after asking us to chat on a topic, was an unconscious example of how to frustrate a class rather than bring them together with warmth.
The closing talk was by Mark Roberts, director of research and an English teacher at Carrickfergus Grammar School. He spoke about the importance of failure, but in the context of a safe environment. Errors are natural and beneficial once the student feels safe to make those mistakes.
Which made me pause and reflect on my reaction to the bad coffee that morning. Maybe I shouldn’t have gone straight to the organiser of the event, and made my complaints. Maybe I should have simply thanked her for a day of invigorating, positive talks, and then hinted at the coffee issue by including a bag of locally roasted beans.

title: ‘I don’t get on with my husband’s sisters, and it’s affecting our marriage’
description: Tell Me About It: ‘At one get-together, his sister described me as mean and selfish to my face’
content:
It may sound like a common complaint when I say I’m having problems with my in-laws, but I am feeling very cornered in the situation I find myself. And, to me, it’s unique and something my friends do not seem to understand .
I’m a woman and grew up as an only child. I’m married to a man with four sisters. He is the youngest of five children and has been doted on by all of them since he was born. When I first met him, I was charmed by the whole situation of a big family and so much love around.
However, as our relationship progressed and then led to marriage, the trouble began – particularly with one of his sisters. I can’t describe all the details in this letter but, short form, I quickly began to feel that every meet-up with his family was cast as some form of audition where I was to prove myself on some level, which left me exhausted and down after each meeting. He constantly reassured me they were well-meaning towards me, but my gut felt very different, to the point I started to feel unsupported and not at all understood.
Things started to deteriorate from there.
I excused myself from a number of his family occasions but, at one get-together, his sister described me as mean and selfish to my face. I left at that point.
The tension between myself and my husband has continued to grow since our wedding. It’s affected us so much that we have put on hold our plans to start a family, as I feel this has to be sorted before we can take that step.
I can’t see a way forward for us at the moment, as every discussion ends with him feeling hurt and, in my opinion, taking his sisters’ side.
When we get together in close relationships, our families of origin and their patterns and traditions begin to surface in ways that can be challenging. This is why being in a committed relationship is a developmental challenge: the love we feel can stretch us out of our comfort zone into acknowledgment and acceptance of our loved one’s habits and foibles.
This is particularly challenging in your situation where an only child joins with a large family setting and all the learned attachments come under scrutiny. So, when you withdraw from the exhaustion of dealing with your partner’s family, they can read that as rejection and accuse you of selfishness. In their world, battling for position and attention is probably the accepted norm whereas, in yours, attention might always have been given as a right.
Both you and your in-laws might be misinterpreting the situation and then acting on those misinterpretations. The danger here is that your husband might end up in a situation where he is forced to choose between his adoring family and his chosen life partner. This should be avoided as there is a long way to go to achieve mutual understanding and compassion before such a crisis is reached.
[ I absolutely dread going to my husband’s parents’ home for Christmas Opens in new window ]
What you both bring to your relationship is unique and valuable, but it will require each of you to really step into the other person’s shoes so that you know fully where the other person is coming from.
At this stage, it is unlikely you and your partner will work this out on your own, so contact a couple’s psychotherapist who will help you to negotiate this difficult terrain. It might be good to let your partner’s family know you are both committed to seeking help and ask for their support in this. Your husband’s family want what is best for him and they are likely to want to be part of the support system. This will require that you trust them enough (in their love for him) to speak honestly of your desire to make this marriage and larger family work, for the benefit of all. As this statement is true, it should garner a supportive response and then you and your husband can engage with your therapist with the backup of your wider support system.
The reason we get married in front of our communities is so they become part of the support needed when times get tough. If you and your husband are willing to get into the trenches now, and work out the family-of-origin struggles, you will emerge not only stronger, but wiser and closer as a result. Silence and withdrawal will feed into what your husband’s family interpret as uninterest and criticism and they cannot know it is a survival tactic for you, unless you find some way of telling them.
This is what therapy will help you with so that you are not alone and you as a couple can develop new lines of communication and understanding.

title: Northern Ireland deserves better than rearview mirror politics
description: Difficult to ignore how Garvaghy Road conveniently shifted attention from the everyday responsibilities of government
content:
Sir, – The recent events surrounding the Garvaghy Road have left me asking two questions. Why, after 28 years, was a parade through one of Northern Ireland ’s most historically contentious areas authorised? And why did it take almost two weeks of confrontation before the Secretary of State intervened?
Chris Bryant has described how he spent the intervening fortnight seeking a settlement. But was it necessary to allow tensions to escalate before recognising the obvious risks?
There is, however, another question worth considering: who benefited politically? Recent opinion polls show Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionist Party ( DUP ) losing support. Meanwhile, Northern Ireland faces serious problems with public services, hospital waiting lists, public finances and the delivery of effective government. Then almost overnight the political conversation returned to familiar territory: flags, parades, identity and constitutional loyalties. For Sinn Féin the dispute offered opportunity to demonstrate its defence of nationalist communities. For the DUP it provided an equally familiar platform from which to assert unionist rights.
I am not suggesting collusion. But it is difficult to ignore how conveniently the controversy shifted attention from the everyday responsibilities of government.
I suspect many people across Northern Ireland, regardless of background, watched these events with a mixture of embarrassment, frustration and disbelief. After decades of painful progress, must every political difficulty send us retreating into the arguments of the past? The greatest tragedy would be if political parties discovered that reopening old divisions remains easier than solving today’s problems. Northern Ireland requires better than another generation of politics conducted through the rearview mirror. – Yours, etc,

title: Munster aim to honour Anthony Foley in best way possible – with victory against Racing
description: Province have several gestures prepared to mark the tenth anniversary of head coach’s death
content:
It still seems scarcely believable that Anthony Foley died so young and that it was all of 10 years ago when the news broke on the morning that Munster were scheduled to play Racing in Paris. Poignantly, Munster host the same opponents in Páirc Uí Chaoimh on Saturday (kick-off 8pm), the day after the 10th anniversary of Axel’s passing. His memory and presence will, no doubt, linger over this Champions Cup first-round tie.
There will be nothing like the emotional turmoil endured by the Munster squad that following week, when Foley’s funeral took place in Killaloe the day before they beat Glasgow 38-17 in front of a packed Thomond Park.
The Munster Branch have organised several tributes around Saturday’s game to commemorate their former player and head coach’s immense contribution to the province.
For the squad and management, their best form of tribute will be in their performance.
“We’ve spoken about it briefly,” said defence coach Denis Leamy after the squad’s Tuesday morning session at Thomond Park. Leamy’s playing career overlapped with Foley’s for six seasons, including packing down in the same backrow in the breakthrough 2006 European triumph over Biarritz in Cardiff when Foley was captain.
“I spoke about it this morning myself in my own presentation,” he said. “I think that’s going to be very much there. The players are very much aware of it. I think we can’t get too emotional on a Tuesday. That would be wrong, but we’re drip-feeding that in.
“There’s loads of different things that are going to honour the Foley family and Axel in an appropriate way.”
Jean Wallace and Shannon members will sing There Is An Isle before the game, while home players will be wearing commemorative jackets with Foley’s number eight on the back. Munster Supporters Club will lead a round of applause in the eighth minute and both captains will exchange number eight jerseys.
Munster and Racing have a rich and respectful history, having met nine times previously in the competition, with four wins apiece and one draw.
“For us, the biggest honour we can give him is to go out and perform and win the game and do our jersey and his memory justice,” said Leamy.
“That’s definitely to the forefront of the Munster players and the Munster squad and the Munster management at the moment. We don’t want to use it too much as an emotional tool or go too far down that rabbit hole. We have to think about performance and how we get the best out of the 23 players we have.
“As I said, the result and hopefully the win will be a way of showing our care and our love for Axel.”
Munster let slip a 26-5 lead away to Ulster last Saturday, on foot of which Leamy said: “Ultimately the big message was loads of good, loads to build on and loads of strong performances.”
There were no injuries arising from that game, and at a push Edwin Edogbo and new summer signing Will Harrison could be involved on Saturday after returning to training this week.
“He’s a guy that covers a good few positions,” said Leamy of the 27-year-old Harrison, formerly an outhalf/fullback for the Waratahs. “He’s a left-footer and definitely comes with a big reputation. We’re just getting him back to full strength around that knee. He’s looking good, so hopefully we’ll see him back in the next couple of games.”
Defence coaches such as Leamy have it tough in these modern times – witness Northampton’s 71-48 win over Bath last Saturday.
“You look at some of the scores in other leagues and in our own league, it’s hard to keep scorelines down now. Attacks and the way the game is refereed allows for a little bit more of a free-flowing product. I think the dark arts have gone out of the game around the breakdown.
“Definitely breakdowns are cleaner, mauls are cleaner and the speed of ball is quicker. Attacks are really well put together in how they overload you with numbers,” said Leamy, who added, “certainly the team without possession is getting refereed”.
A flip side of Munster only providing three of Ireland’s 34-man squad in the summer is that they’ve had comparatively little disruption, with Craig Casey and Jeremy Loughman having played the last two weeks, while Tadhg Beirne returned against Ulster.
“We should be up and running really,” said Leamy, believing that their three opponents have provided different challenges. Besides which, he added: “In this day and age, what’s a settled 15? I think the game has changed an awful lot. It’s not like 20 years ago where you could roll out the same Munster pack or the same Munster 15 every European Cup game.
“If you rolled out the same 15 every weekend, there wouldn’t be too many fellas walking around here. They’re going to be pretty busted up. We’ve used 37 players,” he added.
“I think if you get into playoff rugby and you’re in the semi-finals and finalists, that’s where you probably see a settled 15 more so than not.”
Ticket sales have only topped 20,000 so far, compared to the 36,208 sell-out at the same venue for last December’s clash with Gloucester. Munster, though, point out that they had asked for a December home game and that even with a shorter window to sell tickets, this game is on course to be the best attended of the pool stages in Ireland.

title: Windfall wealth
description: Politicians strive to reinvent the wheel themselves, which, to date, remains decidedly square
content:
Sir, – Fintan O’Toole expertly exposes the failure of successive modern Irish governments to maximise the opportunities presented by the “embarrassment of riches” that currently populate the fiscal purse (“ The blue-green smoothie ruling the country has no plan and even less passion ”, Opinion, October 13th).
Observers regularly draw comparisons with other countries and how they have handled their modern wealth windfalls to benefit current and future generations. Whatever about prospective Irish citizens having to display an intimate knowledge of their adoptive country, perhaps it should be made compulsory for aspiring/sitting politicians to study how other countries have dealt with windfall wealth so they can apply that learning in their functions.
Otherwise, they strive to reinvent the wheel themselves, which, to date, remains decidedly square. – Yours, etc,

title: Eoin Kennedy’s talent has been no secret in Cuala for quite a while now
description: Kennedy scored winning point in 2024 Dublin SFC final, and will be looking for a Cuala win against Castleknock on Sunday
content:
Eoin Kennedy’s football career is having a moment. At 26 he has become something of an overnight success after making a Dublin breakthrough this season, but his talent has been no secret in Cuala for many years now.
In fact, Kennedy has already etched his name in the club’s annals as the man who scored the winning point in their first, and still only, Dublin Senior Football Championship final victory.
Cuala will on Sunday contest their third Dublin SFC final, having lost to Parnells ind 1988 and overcome Kilmacud Crokes in 2024. They will meet a Castleknock side appearing in only their second final, having lost to St Vincent’s in 2016.
The historic 2024 triumph was achieved by a single point, with Kennedy fisting over the winning score deep in injury-time, his 65th-minute effort sealing a famous victory for the Dalkey outfit.
He can justifiably dine out on that score for the rest of his days. Yet among the experimental rules currently being trialled in the third-level leagues is a ban on fisted points. Unsurprisingly, Kennedy is having none of it.
“Keep them in, keep them in,” he smiles.
“I think a fisted point is a skill in itself at times. [Banning fisted points] probably promotes more goal-taking because in certain circumstances as a spectator you want to see someone roof the ball when they’re through on goal, but the fisted point has its place as well.”
Kennedy found a place for himself in the Dublin team this year. Despite having not played underage for the Dubs beyond under-16 level, a decade later he earned a senior call-up from Ger Brennan and effectively became a mainstay in the side.
After impressing during the O’Byrne Cup, Kennedy was handed his competitive debut in Dublin’s National League opener against Donegal at Croke Park in late January.
The versatile defender subsequently featured in all eight of Dublin’s championship games. He started in six of those fixtures, including the All-Ireland quarter- and semi-final.
“The season probably exceeded expectations in terms of I didn’t expect to be brought into the Dublin panel,” says Kennedy.
“[Playing for Dublin] probably wasn’t really on the radar. Getting in for a Dublin trial was cool, being brought in further was cool and staying on the panel was cool.
“I was a bit older when I got my first run-out playing competitively for Dublin, so that was a massive privilege. Being in a set-up like that, you definitely improve physically and skillwise, and your football smarts improve tenfold.”
It came as little surprise to his Cuala team-mates, though, that he held his own at the top level – he was voted the club’s senior footballer of the year in 2025.
[ History-making Cuala crowned All-Ireland club senior football champions: As it happened Opens in new window ]
Still, Kennedy would be lying if he claimed to be a bastion of calmness taking to the field for his league debut against Donegal.
“My heart rate probably had me as dead at one stage,” he laughs.
“You’re representing Dublin in Croke Park, which is a childhood dream. It is a step up and I don’t think I played the best that day. I lasted about 45 minutes and I was blowing afterwards. But as I said it’s just a privilege to play for Dublin.”
Then again, playing for the county runs in the family. Michael Fitzsimons, the Cuala full back and one of the most decorated players in the history of the game with nine senior intercounty All-Ireland medals, is his cousin.
“When you look at his career, he’s still performing at such a high level and it genuinely doesn’t make sense how he keeps doing it. Long may it continue,” says Kennedy.
“He’s been a massive inspiration to me and a huge help in terms of football knowledge. His understanding of the game is second to none, and you can always go to him with questions. All he wants to talk about is football.”
But around the parish right now the talk is of both football and hurling. For the first time ever, the club will contest both senior county finals in the same season.
There are four dual players across the two panels – Eoghan O’Callaghan, Conor Groarke, Jamie Conroy and Michael Conroy.
And Kennedy was in Parnell Park last weekend to support the club’s hurlers.
“There’s been so much excitement around the club the last month and hopefully it continues,” he adds.
“It’s such a huge opportunity [on Sunday]. You never know how often these chances will come around, especially when the championship is so competitive.
“We’ve worked hard to get here. We know how good Castleknock are, their transition and kick-passing are excellent, so we’ll have to be at our best.”
– Kennedy was speaking in advance of Sunday’s PTSB Dublin SFC final between Cuala and Castleknock at Parnell Park, 4.15pm .

title: A little compassion goes a long way
description: Distressing clamping experience in Dublin
content:
Sir, – Your recent report on clamping in Dublin included accounts of aggressive enforcement outside the National Maternity Hospital (“ ‘I was distraught’: Motorists share clamping stories as Dublin moves to new ‘tow and fine’ regime ”, News, September 16th).
Recently I attended the National Maternity Hospital, where my appointment ran long and I topped up my parking every hour. I missed one top-up while with the doctor, paid again as soon as I came out (eight minutes past the grace period), but was clamped before I could get back to my car.
What stays with me is not the fee but the treatment. The operative walked away as I tried to explain and ignored my tearful pleas to wait a moment so I could pay and release the car immediately so I could collect my young children. Passersby stopped to comment on his behaviour. The interaction was so distressing I could not drive for half an hour once it was released.
Dublin City Council is changing its enforcement contractor on November 1st. A new contract on its own will not fix this. Rules should be clear for people attending hospital appointments, including grace periods and discretion for maternity patients, along with enforceable standards of conduct for operatives and a complaints process that is fair and quick. Outside a maternity hospital, a little compassion goes a long way. – Yours, etc,

title: Ireland players’ actions at Israel football games ‘shameful’, Jewish advocacy leader says
description: Jonathan Greenblatt spoke at event at Herzog Park, Dublin, highlighting ‘hostile environment’ for Irish Jews
content:
The actions of the Ireland players in the two Nations League football games against Israel were described as “shameful” by the chief executive of the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) at an event in Dublin on Tuesday.
Former Barack Obama aide Jonathan Greenblatt, who has led the Jewish advocacy organisation since 2015, said Ireland players bowing their heads for the Israeli national anthem, wearing black armbands and not looking Israeli players in the eye was “dehumanising, it was demonising and it was disgusting and it was an affront to sports fans everywhere”.
“People are entitled to have their opinions,” he said. But sport was considered the “sacrosanct sphere, where people can come together and just play the game”.
Greenblatt spoke on behalf of the J7, a coalition of advocacy groups in countries with large Jewish communities, to reporters in Herzog Park, Dublin, on Tuesday as the group gathered there.
The delegation of the J7, the Large Communities’ Task Force Against Anti-Semitism, visited Dublin to meet politicians and representatives of Ireland’s Jewish community.
[ ‘People afraid to say they are Jewish’: Dublin event marks October 7th attacks on Israel ]
Greenblatt said “the Jewish community is being targeted here at a rate that exceeds all of the other J7 countries by a wide margin”.
Maurice Cohen, chairman of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland, said 143 anti-Semitic incidents were recorded between July 2025 and last January.
“A deeply troubling number for a community of our size,” he said, as the Jewish community in Ireland consisted of “just 2,200 people”.
Greenblatt said even though Ireland was not one of the J7 member countries, “we felt is was crucial for our annual J7 report ... to include a special chapter on Ireland this year”.
The J7 brings together the leadership of representative Jewish organisations from Argentina, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States.
“Anti-Israel rhetoric in Ireland, however, is creating an increasingly not just uncomfortable but hostile environment for Ireland’s Jews, directly affecting the safety and daily lives of this small, historic community,” he said.
“Jewish people are an indivisible element of Ireland. Removing them is removing a piece of this country itself.”
Greenblatt said 2025 was globally the “deadliest year for anti-Semitic attacks in the diaspora in more than 30 years”.
He is calling on the Government to introduce measures “before it is too late”, such as dedicated security funding for Jewish communal and educational institutions and consistent enforcement of hate-crime legislation.
He advocated for political accountability when rhetoric demonised Jews, when it attacked Zionism or crossed the line into anti-Semitism.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin has previously denied suggestions that Ireland was anti-Semitic.
Asked about the matter in late September in the context of the football fixtures, he said: “We are not anti-Semitic – as both Foreign Affairs Minister and then Taoiseach I have been very strong in terms of firstly affirming the role of the Jewish community in Ireland. They have made an historic contribution to Ireland and continue to make it to our society.”
Cohen said he could not think of “a more fitting place” to welcome the J7 delegates than Herzog Park.
He said the attempt to remove Chaim Herzog’s name from the park last year was “deeply hurtful to our community and is typical of the ubiquitous, ambient anti-Semitism that reflects a growing hostility that Irish Jews increasingly encounter”.
“No Jew in Ireland should ever feel they must choose between being proudly Irish and proudly Jewish,” Cohen said.
“We are not asking for special treatment. We are asking to live openly and safely as Jews in the country we call home.”

title: Mixed views on Wednesday strike by public sector unions?
description: Surely, the question is what the Minister is prepared to negotiate
content:
Sir, – The public servants taking industrial action are not available for work and consequently have to forego a day’s pay. However, many TDs, who have a salary of just under €120,000, have indicated over the past week that they would not pass the picket at Leinster House and therefore make themselves unavailable for work.
Easy to stand on principle when it has no consequences on your pay packet. Maybe they should consider donating their days’ pay to the union strike funds to show real solidarity. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I believe the public sector unions are making a major strategic error in their approach to the negotiations with Government on the new pay deal.
In an employment environment increasingly dominated by artificial intelligence (AI), the tactics adopted against Government and the public are ill-advised. The next agreement will be dominated by AI productivity and job losses. The public sector, particularly the Civil Service, is full of opportunities for its use.
A Government, bruised by the current union attitudes, is unlikely to show much sympathy for their members. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Your report on the planned public-sector strike says the Minister’s offer of talks was “swiftly rebuffed” by union leaders (“ Public-sector strike by more than 300,000 workers set to go ahead ”, News, October 13th). That risks making this sound like a willing Government facing unions who simply refuse to talk.
Surely, the question is what the Minister is prepared to negotiate. Is the €1.2 billion allocation a starting point, or a limit? Can the unions negotiate the amount, or only how it is divided?
I am not arguing that every union demand should be met. But before readers are invited to judge their refusal, I would expect The Irish Times to establish what is actually on offer. – Yours, etc,

title: ‘Don’t be going on too much’
description: Be careful with your old talk
content:
Sir, – Colette Sheridan’s Irishwoman’s Diary (“ ‘Fancy’ food and the ‘priest’s sugar’: hosting a station Mass at home ”, An Irish Diary, October 13th) transported me back 40 years. Station Mass was not a feature of my Meath youth, but moving to Kerry , my mother’s county of origin, acquainted me with the tradition.
My aunt’s turn to host the event saw the house smelling of paint, polish and porter. She informed me I’d be sitting beside the priest for the subsequent feast. Knowing of my fractured affiliation with religion , she cautioned me: “Don’t be going on too much; be careful with your old talk.” Knowing my station, I complied. The hum of genial talk in that hillside house is still a pleasant memory. – Yours, etc,

title: ‘Little bit of magic’: The Dublin hairdresser training recovering addicts and ex-prisoners in hair
description: Hair Together helps to train young carers, ex-prisoners and recovering addicts in hairdressing and confidence skills
content:
Eileen McHugh, who grew up in the “chaos” of 1980s Ballymun, is using her experience of addiction and trauma, and her profession as a hairdresser, to run courses for marginalised groups facing barriers.
Since opening her salon Hair Together in the north Dublin suburb in February, she has more than tripled the amount of training she can offer to those such as young people in care, former prisoners and recovering addicts to help them gain skills and confidence.
“I’m feeling really good,” says the 47-year-old, sitting in her salon.
“Ballymun is very special to me. I have great memories from growing up here of a really close and caring community. But I have, equally, extremely traumatic memories,” she says.
She recalls witnessing a man jumping to his death from a balcony as she was running to buy sweets. “I just carried on to the shop, got my sweets, and went back and then told everybody ... Things that weren’t normal were normalised,” she says. “It was chaos.”
“I was 12 when I started dabbling in drugs. We were smoking hash. I think it was 15, 16, the first time I smoked heroin. And then that was it until I was 29.
“I had learning difficulties and later was diagnosed with ADHD ... I suppose heroin, it just kind of shut all that anxiety, [and] my brain constantly turning, down. I remember the first time it was like somebody putting a big, warm blanket around me.”
She never injected; she was “too scared” as people she knew injected had overdosed and died.
[ Rachael Keogh’s story of heroin addiction, survival and spirituality Opens in new window ]
Describing herself as a “functioning addict”, she completed her Leaving Certificate “completely addicted to heroin”, but found a new perspective during several stays with an older sister in Greece. “I still found drugs, but I felt safe there. My nervous system was starting to relax.”
On returning to Dublin, still smoking heroin, she “just caught a bug then for hair. I always loved doing my own hair. I knew I was good at it and knew good hair could make people feel good.”
When working on hair, she noticed she was “zoned in ... I wasn’t thinking about nothing else. My brain got that same break heroin gave me”.
She trained with a city centre salon. “I was good, hyper-focused, and they kind of spotted that and nurtured that.” She suffered with huge anxiety, however, spent time in hospital and was still using drugs.
Recovery began when she became pregnant with her daughter more than 20 years ago. She was in a number of rehab centres and lived and worked for a time in Waterford, before moving back to Ballymun with her daughter, and working in a local salon.
Her involvement in a local GAA club saw her first use barbering to engage young people – boys in particular – at risk with drugs and of dropping out of the club.
There’s something really magic about when you’re distracted and you begin to open up
“There was probably four or five boys that first night. We were supposed to be there for an hour and a half. Two and a half hours later, they didn’t want to go. We were having a chats about everything. And they were doing hair. There’s something really magic about when you’re distracted and you begin to open up.”
From there McHugh continued, with support from local businesses, to run Best (Bringing Education and Sport Together). Hair Academy started around 2019 – in youth clubs, local schools and community centres.
Meanwhile, she was working in a city-centre salon where one of her clients was Dara Connolly, chief executive of the social enterprise Common Purpose. He encouraged her to participate in its emerging leaders programme in 2021.
Founded in post-Thatcher Britain, Common Purpose has operated in Ireland for 30 years. Its mission is to bring together leaders from disparate sectors – public and private sector and community – to learn from, challenge and mentor each other, and ultimately understand and work with each other towards a common purpose of improving society.
“I was terrified,” says McHugh. “I thought: ‘I’m going to be so out of place. But I really want to do this’. So I pushed myself.”
“I gained confidence and the ability to pause and look at myself. I used to be really rigid in how I thought. Coming from Ballymun I had a bit of a chip on my shoulder. I learned what values to stick to and when you’re able to like flex them a little bit to work with different people.
“Skills in me that were never developed or looked at emerged. And the peer support I have gained is incredible.”
These skills helped in her mission to get a premises. Following two years’ fundraising, to a total of €125,000, Hair Together opened in a bricks-and-mortar home in February.
Funding from Rethink Ireland, a charity that backs non-profit and social enterprises tackling pressing social challenges, has enabled her to take three full-time and three part-time staff.
It operates as a working salon as well as a training venue. The courses vary in length, from day courses to one night a week for up to eight weeks.
“Between 2020 and February, since we opened, we had 260 people go through the programme. Today it’s 600 plus.
“You see people go from not being able to make eye contact, to standing up in front of everybody, so proud of what they’re after learning. It’s a little bit of magic what we do here.”

title: State’s doomsday funding crisis is inevitable
description: Government should focus on making itself ‘emergency ready’
content:
Sir, – Mark Fox is correct to question whether the Government itself is “emergency ready” (“ Is the Government emergency ready? “, Letters, October 13th). When, not if, the billions in corporation tax paid by US multinationals shift back to the United States or are carved up among the European Union member states, the State will be plunged into a funding crisis like 2008. If the excess tax had been expended on capital projects, the impact might be limited, but with current expenditure absorbing much of the windfall, the impact will be lacerating.
Instead of lecturing the public on being “emergency ready” for events beyond their control, the Government should be preparing its own plans for the additional taxes and expenditure cuts for the State’s inevitable doomsday funding crisis. – Yours, etc,

title: Core funding for third-level is stalling despite Simon Harris’s promises
description: In his previous role as minister for higher education he committed to tackling €307m shortfall
content:
Sir, – Your editorial accurately calls the Government’s approach to third-level funding “contradictory and short-sighted” (“ The Irish Times view on third-level funding: the shortfall remains ”, October 8th). The Government’s failure is measurable by their own standards.
In 2022 Simon Harris , then minister for higher education, launched the Funding the Future Framework for higher education, accepting a €307 million shortfall in core funding and committing to closing the gap this decade.
Yet progress has stalled. Core funding rose by €40m in Budget 2023, €65.2m the following year and €58.7m in 2025 – but by just €9.6m in 2026. In his first budget as Finance Minister, Harris found a mere €10m for 2027. The Irish Universities Association (IUA) had asked for €190m.
Irish universities punch above their weight. It is significant that University College Dublin this year joined Trinity College Dublin in the QS world top 100: a credit to UCD’s students, academic, research and wider staff and their leadership team.
But the reality is that publicly funded Irish universities underperform in faculty-to-student ratios, directly impacting our global competitiveness. Addressing this requires sustained core funding.
The Government’s progress on the Student Contribution Charge is welcome, but too slow.
The Green Party agrees with Harris’s 2022 assertion that fee cuts shouldn’t come at the expense of core funding. However, portraying a choice between the two is a false dichotomy. Abolishing fees widens access; core funding raises quality. We can sustain both if we make higher education a genuine fiscal priority, an investment strategy for our nation’s future prosperity.
Although the exchequer shows a significant surplus, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council , the Economic and Social Research Institute and the Tánaiste himself repeatedly warn against overreliance on corporation tax windfalls. Graduates, research and Irish spinouts widen the domestic income tax base and keep our economy resilient for when the winds of fortune change.
The IUA estimates Irish universities add €10 billion a year to the economy. Ibec asked for €110m core funding in its pre-budget submission while the Irish Federation of University Teachers sought a “significant and sustained” increase, comparable with well-performing Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries.
The universities, Ibec, the lecturers’ union, this newspaper and politicians across the Oireachtas share the same view: this sector must be adequately sustained through core funding. It’s high time this Government made it a priority. – Yours, etc,
Green Party spokesperson for Further and Higher Education,

title: Traditional card games may become a thing of the past
description: Shift to the screen cannot replace gathering around a table for social connection
content:
Sir, – As the long nights draw in and the eagerly awaited card games resume after the summer break, it is hard not to notice fewer tables occupied in the local community centre and the increasingly older profile of those who are present. Face-to-face card games are declining as younger generations turn away from cards in favour of the instant enjoyment and variety of digital games and video-streaming entertainment.
Although the shift from table to screen has made card play accessible to people who can no longer attend in person, it cannot replace the relaxation of gathering around a table or the social connection that comes from being with others. The traditional card game, once a vital source of companionship through the long, dark winter months, may soon become a thing of the past. – Yours, etc,

title: Drug-related intimidation: why petrol bomb attacks are becoming more common
description: Criminal gangs believe arson is less likely than a shooting to draw attention of Garda’s national units
content:
The deaths of Philip and Kim English and two of their children in their home just outside Waterford city has brought into focus an increase in drug-related intimidation, often in the form of petrol bombings, in recent years.
With shootings in decline over the past decade, arson has become the attack of choice within the drugs trade. It appears the clampdown on the Kinahan and Hutch gangs in Ireland was so successful that most drugs gangs are reluctant to engage in serious gun attacks for fear of drawing Garda attention.
Those same groups have opted instead to pay young criminals, often teenage boys, to carry out attacks on their drug-dealing rivals or on people who owe them money. The result has been an upsurge in petrol bomb attacks.
“You’re talking about [criminals] who are just looking at it as leverage to extort people,” said one Garda source. “Somebody might buy drugs on credit and haven’t paid it back. Or they may have taken a consignment [of drugs] to sell and it’s seized by us, so now they owe the cost of the drugs.
“But you could owe these guys €1,000 and they might demand €5,000. And you could pay it off and they’d want another €5,000. They’re just using the initial debt as an excuse to extort families.”
Another source familiar with drug intimidation said the criminals demanding the money often target parents, or other family members, in a bid to extort money.
“So, you have people who had nothing to do with the original debt, nothing to do with crime at all, getting death threats,” he said. “Or it’s their cars being targeted, petrol bombs thrown at their houses. Their lives are made hell by groups [of young boys] sent by older criminals to just keep hammering away at them until they pay.”
The Irish Times gathered data from 14 local authorities nationwide revealing they had recorded 113 arson attacks on council properties in the past five years, 50 of which were recorded last year. The four local authorities in Dublin had recorded 59 attacks since 2022, with 35 of those recorded last year.
These figures do not include attacks on private-rented or owner-occupied homes.
[ Waterford house fire: Family targeted had suffered other vandalism attacks in recent years Opens in new window ]
Gardaí said arson attacks on houses are rarely, if ever, designed to kill. Instead, they are seen as a violent intimidatory attack that is several levels below a shooting, which draws the attention of national Garda units that deal with organised crime.
But the targeting of the English family on the Birchwood estate in Waterford in the early hours of Tuesday demonstrates how arson attacks designed to intimidate rather than kill can spin out of control.
Most petrol bombings are not fatal, but only because occupants manage to scramble to safety. They are intended as a frightening act of intimidation, usually designed to force the settlement of a drugs debt. Gardaí believe the attack on the English home was drug related.
While there is no suggestion whatsoever Philip or Kim English were involved in the drugs trade, gardaí suspect Philip English may have taken over a drug debt run up by an associate. Detectives believe he was trying to protect his younger associate in perhaps promising to pay the money he owed to local criminals.
The Englishes’ house was attacked in August 2023, with the family car destroyed when paint was thrown over it. The family were attacked again last month when a petrol bomb was thrown at the car, while some threats were also made on social media. In a big escalation, the property was petrol bombed just after 5am on Tuesday.
The flames engulfed the house, killing Philip and Kim English and two of their children, while leaving the other two children in a critical condition in hospital.

title: Psychotherapy groups must be heard to ensure the safety of vulnerable clients
description: State must step up to its responsibility and listen to representative bodies
content:
Sir, – In her article “ Psychotherapy group files complaint to EU against Minister ” (Health, October 12th) Shauna Bowers highlights the concerns of the four accrediting bodies that the standards set out by Coru – which is tasked with the statutory regulation for psychotherapy and counselling – will lower the quality of training and create risks for the safety of clients as well as the employability of therapists outside Ireland.
I have worked as a psychotherapist and group analyst for more than 30 years and with many of my contemporary colleagues have spent years working together on a voluntary basis, ensuring Ireland’s training and accreditation of psychotherapists and counsellors is in line with international best practice.
During this time we continued to call for statutory regulation because we were acutely aware of the damage being done to patients/clients who had bad experiences with people who had no training. Today in Ireland, anyone can set themselves up as a psychotherapist and/or counsellor, and the standards Coru is requiring do not have the basic three prongs that are essential for any robust training of psychotherapists/counsellors. These are personal therapy, clients under supervision and didactic input.
The four professional bodies that are leading the challenge to Coru continue to build on the strong foundations that were laid down in the early days of these professional bodies and are doing so on a voluntary basis, such is the commitment to ensuring the safety of the vulnerable members of the public who seek the services of the registered psychotherapists and counsellors by the current accrediting bodies.
It’s time that the State stepped up to its responsibility and listened to these four representative bodies when it comes to the development of statutory regulation, so that we don’t have to deal with further abuses of the most vulnerable in our society. – Yours, etc,
Psychotherapist and former chief executive of Dublin Rape Crisis Centre,

title: Sir Allen seeks to continue on an upward curve at Punchestown
description: Andrew Slattery hopes Sir Allen can continue a burgeoning love affair with fences
content:
Sir Allen bids to continue a superb year for Andrew Slattery’s stable with victory in the Grade Three Matchbook Betting Exchange Novice Chase at Punchestown on Wednesday.
Fresh from his best-ever season on the level, with his Thurles yard sending out a best-ever 41 winners to date, Slattery bagged a Grade Two chase with Fleur In The Park landing the PWC Danoli Chase at Gowran Park earlier this month.
Now he is hoping Sir Allen can continue a burgeoning love affair with fences against the might of Willie Mullins , Emmet Mullins and Gordon Elliott in the extended 2¼-mile contest at the Kildare track.
Sir Allen is making up for lost ground after missing 15 months with a serious leg injury, recording a comeback win on the Flat and bouncing back to form over jumps, putting up an improved showing to win a Gowran beginners’ event by 4¼ lengths.
“We weren’t surprised by Gowran as he was a good juvenile hurdler and he was always jumping hurdles too big,” said Slattery. “He seemed to take to fences very well, and hopefully he keeps taking to them. He loved fences from the first time he saw them.
“He has been a very versatile horse. He was out for two years with a leg injury, and he is back, and they don’t often come back from them. But he just seems to love jumping fences so we are hopeful they might eke a bit of improvement out of him as well.”
Sir Allen does not have too much to find with Bunting, who won at Ballinrobe before posting a decent effort on the level in the Irish Cesarewitch at the Curragh. Elliott fields two runners in Sligo chase winner Chanceawetmorning (Jack Kennedy) and Miss Fourie (Danny Gilligan). Emmet Mullins’ Vitorio Piel rounds up the five-strong field.
A second Grade Three on the card over the larger obstacles, the Matchbook Betting Exchange Chase looks set to feature an odds-on favourite in Henry de Bromhead’s experienced chaser Gorgeous Tom, who was 12th in the Grand National at Aintree in April and third in the Galway Plate.
The presence of Elliott’s well-travelled eight-year-old Croke Park, rated 4lb below the favourite on official ratings, ensures a stiff test for the remaining two runners.
But Barry Connell is happy to take on the pair with Apple’s Of Bresil, who won a beginners’ chase at Kilbeggan in May by 11 lengths and took a step forward in terms of bare form when second at Listowel on his seasonal reappearance.
“At Listowel, he was stepping up to more experienced company. I think he had one run going into it and the first and third had seven or eight runs,” said Connell. “The trip was probably a little bit shorter than ultimately he would like, so in the circumstances I thought he ran well.
“It is not a novice race, and there are two horses in it that are rated 30lb higher than him who are Grade Two horses, so the reality is if he collects prize-money we will be delighted because it’s another step up the ladder. But the ground and trip will suit.”

title: Republic ‘not some sort of neutral player’ during Troubles, says NI Veterans Commissioner
description: David Johnstone insists there is no question that soldiers who committed crimes while in uniform should be prosecuted
content:
David Johnstone, Northern Ireland ’s Veterans Commissioner, has a message he believes few in the Republic want to hear.
Now extended in office for another three years, Johnstone has been vocal – very vocal, in the view of some – in the role, where his job is to be a voice for British military veterans living in the North.
Sitting in a Dublin hotel after meetings in the nearby British Embassy, the softly-spoken Johnstone is angry on two fronts.
He is unhappy about the failure on the Republic’s part to face up to its sins or omissions during Northern Ireland’s Troubles, along with its attitudes towards legacy questions facing British veterans, many of whom are in their 70s.
“The Irish Government was not some sort of neutral player. It was arguably an active participant, or, at the very least, turned a blind eye to the terrorism coming from the south,” he tells The Irish Times in an interview.
Johnstone claims the “vast majority” of the IRA’s gelignite in the early 1970s came from the Irish Industrial Explosives factory in Enfield, Co Meath, with a British explosives expert warning as early as 1972 that it was possible “to get a case a day out without it showing up”.
“Of course, the Irish State knew what was happening,” argues Johnstone, who claims that Irish politicians and officials do not want to rake over the past, while the southern public has never shown interest.
The vast majority of the 500 killings along the Border – soldiers, Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) and “ordinary Protestants and ordinary Catholics” – were planned in the south where killers “hopped over the Border and hopped back into a safe haven”, he says.
The amendments to the legacy legislation published by the Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant on Monday will take time to study, though London has “clearly” listened to some of the veterans’ concerns, but not all.
[ British attorney general to approve future prosecutions of former UK soldiers under legacy law changes Opens in new window ]
Today, he argues that Dublin’s pressure has played a role in London refusing that would see veterans’ prosecutions taking place only if “new and compelling evidence” emerged that was not available at the time.
Under a deal last year, Dublin will put €25 million behind a new Garda unit that will “endeavour to answer questions that victims or family members may have” about past Garda investigations, but not carry out fresh investigations.
“In three years, the money’s gone unless more’s found. On the other side of the Border, it’s a five-year process that’s going to cost about £2 billion [€2.4 billion] – and that’s conservative.”
Throughout his interview, Johnstone insists there is no question that veterans who committed crimes while in uniform should be prosecuted.
“That is not at issue – at all,” he says with emphasis.
However, cases should not be reopened unless there is “clear and compelling evidence” not available when the first investigations were carried out by the British military before 1976 or afterwards by the RUC.
Not every investigation would stand up today, Johnson concedes.
“Some would fall short, yes. In west Belfast, they couldn’t cordon off a spot, spend three days sifting through rubble. They had, maybe, half an hour, 40 minutes. Or else they were the target,” he says.
“That’s what really frustrates veterans. The idea that we can look through today’s lens and demand that what happened 30, 40, 50 years ago is investigated again is absolute folly. It’s totally unacceptable.”
They include, in particular, the June 1991 killings of three IRA men – Tony Doris, Peter Ryan, and Lawrence McNally – in Coagh, Co Tyrone, when they went to kill a part-time Ulster Defence Regiment soldier.
A coroner’s inquest ruled that the lethal force used was “reasonable, justified, and proportionate”, while the Court of Appeal in 2026 dismissed an appeal by Roisin Nugent, the daughter of Tony Doris.
However, she has been granted legal aid to take an appeal to the Supreme Court in London, challenging the legality of the actions of one of the SAS soldiers, Soldier B, who is now in his 70s.
“I’m pretty familiar with this one,” says Johnston
“He’s had three legal cases. Every one said he used lawful actions. It was proportionate and yet here we go again. He has had seven years wondering if he will be charged with murder.”
The same goes for the 1992 SAS killing in Clonoe, Co Tyrone, of four IRA man – Kevin Barry O’Donnell, Sean O’Farrell, Peter Clancy and Daniel Vincent – after they had attacked Coalisland RUC station with a lorry-mounted .50 calibre heavy machine-gun.
This case was referred in February 2025 on to Northern Ireland’s Public Prosecution Service by Judge Michael Humphries after he ruled that the killings were “unjustified and unreasonable”.
The soldiers did not hold an honest belief that lethal force was necessary, they had made no attempt to arrest and firing up to 570 rounds without warning or challenge was unreasonable, he says.
Equally, they lied when they said they were fired upon, while the operation was not planned, or controlled properly by the military and police commanders to limit the need for lethal force.
Johnstone, a former Royal Irish Regiment officer, is withering about the judgment.
“The idea that you can stand up in a car park against people with a DsHK .50 calibre [machine gun] and go: ‘Excuse me, guys, can you lay down your weapons?’ That is suicide.”
Then, there is the 1987 killing of eight IRA men as they tried to destroy the RUC station in Loughgall, Co Armagh, the biggest single of life suffered by the IRA during the history of The Troubles.
Johnstone bridles even at its mention, especially its return to the Coroner’s Court.
“If ever there was a clear-cut case, it’s Loughgall. The idea that you could arrest James Lynagh and Patrick Kelly is just insane. Please do not insult our intelligence,” he says.
Operations such Coagh, Clonoe and Loughgall were “planned by senior military, signed off by the chief constable, signed off by the general officer commanding [GOC], and, usually, signed off by the prime minister”, says Johnstone.
“This is where veterans say enough is enough. They were there under lawful orders,” he says.
“So, if there’s a problem, it’s not the soldiers’ fault. Put the prime minister in the dock, put the GOC, or the chief constable.”

title: Unions urge Taoiseach to intervene in bid to avert public sector strike
description: Fórsa leader Kevin Callinan calls for ‘intervention from top of Government’ to break deadlock on talks
content:
The Taoiseach should intervene to get a talks process started if further public sector strikes and disruption are to be prevented, Fórsa union leader Kevin Callinan has suggested.
He was speaking after the union side rebuffed late efforts by Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers and the Government side to engage and prevent the one-day strike by more than 300,000 public and civil servants that got under way countrywide overnight.
Schools, colleges, libraries, council offices and many parks are among the publicly run facilities that are closed on Wednesday because of the action. Health services are severely disrupted, with all elective procedures and thousands of appointments postponed.
[ What services will be affected by the public sector strike and what will be closed? Opens in new window ]
Callinan was responding to a suggestion by Chambers that while the Government wanted talks to begin at the Workplace Relations Commission on Tuesday, he would consider other ways to achieve progress if that could not be done.
Asked about what might break the deadlock, Callinan, who also chairs the public services committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions, said it would take “an intervention. And I think that intervention has to come from ... the Taoiseach.”
The Government is likely to make a push to bring the unions into a talks process after the stoppage as it seeks to avoid further strikes scheduled for next week.
According to sources familiar with the Government’s position, renewed efforts to start negotiations in the coming days may include seeking an independent mediator or facilitator to bring the two sides together. Coalition sources stopped short of saying they would agree to the unions’ demand to deal with pay first in the negotiations.
It is likely that informal approaches will be made with a view to repairing relations which have become strained in recent days.
Callinan was critical of Chambers for failing to speak directly to union leaders. “If he was serious about trying to reach an agreement, at some point over the last four months, he would have either met us or picked up the phone to talk to us and try, first of all, to understand what it is that’s required, and secondly, to respond to it.”
The hope on the Government side is that once this stoppage is out of the way, the union side may become more amenable to entering talks. Other sources, however, warned of underestimating what they say is the anger of public servants.
Callinan echoed this point. He said the focus from the Government side on the union leaders ignored the strength of feeling among members who had voted by huge margins in every participating union to take action. “It continues to be dismissive of our members’ concerns,” he said.
At Cabinet, Chambers reiterated his position that the previous pay deals had delivered inflation-beating increases for the State’s more than 400,000 public servants. But unions have accused him of “cherry-picking figures”.
Unions will meet over the coming days to consider what action to take if the dispute runs beyond next Wednesday’s strike in order to meet the required notice periods to employers. But Callinan said on Tuesday they were already focusing on next week’s stoppage “and beyond”.

title: Industry greenhouse gas emissions forecast to rise, says climate council
description: Factory emissions
content:
The Republic’s industries are forecast to increase their climate-harming greenhouse gas emissions over the next few years, when they are meant to be falling.
Milk and dairy factories are of particular concern, with a report from the Government’s advisory body, the Climate Change Advisory Council , showing emissions from milk production grew by 4.8 per cent last year and dairy processing by 3.6 per cent.
Industry overall had a modest reduction in emissions, possibly as much as 3.9 per cent, according to provisional figures.
But anticipated growth in activity in several sectors, including construction, is expected to wipe out that progress.
“It is not expected that emissions are going to reduce between 2025 and 2030. In fact, they are expected to increase slightly,” the council said.
“Industry has missed its reduction target for 2025 and is projected to miss it again by 2030.”
[ Do data centres pay their own way? The answer is not straightforward Opens in new window ]
The 2030 target is a 35 per cent reduction in emissions compared with 2018. Industry is at 15.9 per cent below 2018 levels, but that is expected to slip to 11.6 per cent by 2030.
The State as a whole has a 50 per cent reduction target but is on course to achieve at best 29 per cent.
“The projections are a clear warning that the measures currently planned are not enough to deliver the change needed by the end of this decade,” said council member Jillian Mahon.
“We need to remove the barriers that are slowing transition.”
Barriers include a lack of renewable energy options for industries to switch from oil and gas.
Electricity cannot produce the very high temperatures needed for many industrial processes, but little of the alternative – renewable gas in the form of biomethane – is available.
Plans to build scores of anaerobic digester plants to produce biomethane from agricultural and food waste are far behind schedule.
The council said “immediate and sustained action” was needed to get biomethane production on track.
Another issue is insufficient regulation to ensure low-carbon cement and concrete – achieved by using less clinker in its manufacture – is used in construction.
Cement producers make up four of the country’s five largest emitting industrial plants after the largest emitter, Aughinish Alumina .
[ From the Shannon to Siberia: How alumina from a Limerick refinery enters Russia’s weapons supply chain Opens in new window ]
Their emissions dropped by 3.6 per cent last year but production is forecast to grow to 2030, potentially cancelling out those reductions.
A similar lack of regulatory support for the use of timber in place of concrete in construction is highlighted. Although more timber-framed houses are being built, timber is still rare in large construction projects.
The council also expresses concern at the levels of waste generated from Irish industry, with waste volumes growing 20 per cent in a decade, recycling rates flatlining and landfills adding to greenhouse gas emissions through the release of methane.
The report also says the Government needs to introduce regulations to allow for carbon capture and storage (CCS).
CCS uses technologies that capture carbon emissions at source before they enter the atmosphere and convert the gas to storable forms.
Various technologies are under development worldwide, although they have yet to prove large-scale effectiveness.
The report also assesses how prepared industries are to deal with the impacts of climate change, especially drought affecting water supplies.
[ Opinion: It takes collective climate action to fight climate destruction Opens in new window ]
It says the Department of Enterprise, Enterprise Ireland, the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland, the Sustainable Banking Corporation of Ireland, employers’ group Ibec and Uisce Éireann should do more to help small and medium-sized enterprises become climate resilient.
It adds that the Government should begin a dialogue with industry associations on the risks facing the Irish economy from supply chain disruption due to climate impacts in other countries.

title: Michael McDowell: Trump’s barbarism and delusions have brought America to the brink
description: The US president claims to have done a deal with Vladimir Putin, who appears more and more to be his puppetmaster
content:
Last week, Donald Trump was addressing a campaign rally in New York state at Syracuse. He told his audience that the current attorney general for New York state, Letitia James, who has held office as the state’s 67th attorney general since 2019 and who is black, was “disgusting” and a “dog”.
Should that kind of language surprise us? In another rally speech in Youngstown, Ohio, the week before, he urged Republican voters in the midterm elections to get out and vote to defeat the Democrats and “shove it up their ass”. Trump has resorted to using the F-word on his Truth Social website to threaten Iran with annihilation.
His bizarre attack on the Nobel committee for denying him the peace prize came in the same fortnight. Failure to make him the peace prize honoree was, he said at Syracuse, “an indelible stain on Norway”, a Nato ally of the United States. The decision was brought about by “radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and actually enemies of civilisation”. Trump ridiculously claimed again to have ended eight wars, telling his audience that he was about to “end or win” two more wars.
You may recall that a previous prize winner from Venezuela, María Corina Machado, former speaker of the Venezuelan national assembly and long-time critic of kidnapped president Nicolás Maduro (who is now languishing in a New York prison), offered Trump her Nobel medal to enhance her chances of leading the restoration of democracy in Caracas. But Trump cast her aside in favour of Maduro’s vice-president, who has agreed to act as a pliant US puppet.
As the consequences of Trump’s war in the Gulf – the interruption of oil supplies resulting in all-time-high prices for US gasoline and diesel – have become apparent across the United States, Trump has begun a flailing, desperate campaign to cut domestic diesel costs by boosting world supply. But he appears to have left this electoral gambit far too late for November 3rd – even without the impact of the activities of the Houthis.
Trump claims to have done a deal with Russian president Vladimir Putin – who appears more and more to be his puppet master – to relax Congress’s statutory embargo on Russian diesel exports. His threats earlier this year to seize Russia’s shadow tanker fleet have been forgotten. Now Trump hopes that Russian diesel will flow across the globe in sufficient time to swing votes on November 3rd.
In pursuit of that delusional aim, Trump wants Ukraine to desist from any further attacks on Russia’s oil refining capacity. Kyiv is supposed to let oil sanctions collapse while Putin attempts to annihilate Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. The absurdity of that strategy has led Trump to endorse Putin’s demand that Volodymyr Zelenskiy should be replaced as Ukraine’s president for refusing to capitulate to Trump’s demands. Trump then threatened another arms embargo on Ukraine.
[ ‘He’s with Putin’: Ukrainians recoil at Trump’s pressure campaign Opens in new window ]
Now Trump has resorted to hallucinatory misinformation. He announced last weekend that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an energy ceasefire. Strangely, neither Putin nor Zelenskiy had heard of this agreement. Asked by a US reporter how he could claim to have brought it about, Trump replied that the two parties had agreed “because I said ‘you agree’”.
The US constitution has been warped and usurped by the Trump clique to an extent that should shock and shame thinking Americans who still revere the ideals of the founding fathers. That a sizeable proportion of them still support the Maga conspiracy worldview is a wonder in itself.
Some commentators warn that Trump may still attempt on some pretext of emergency to cancel the holding of the midterm elections on November 3rd – or seek to set aside any result that denies him control of the houses of Congress from January onwards.
Some Republicans, though, are willing to query the proposed livestreamed public execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the former US army psychiatrist who murdered 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas in 2009, and who is a Muslim. Pete Hegseth, self-styled secretary for war in the would-be Nobel peace prize winner’s cabinet, has Trump’s full backing for such a spectacle – hardly surprising for a president who celebrated the American Revolution by staging a cage-fighting show at the White House.
Like all public executions, the livestream will doubtless draw a huge audience online if it proceeds. But the Fort Hood execution has all the macabre attributes and implications of the Roman Colosseum’s spectacles of cruelty. It would also create a potent martyr figure.
Hegseth’s plan echoes the myopic barbarism of Israeli far-right minister for national security, Itamar Ben-Gvir, who is intent on reintroducing hanging – but only for Palestinians. Do none of these people understand that, where barbarism is concerned, what goes around comes around? Can America yet awaken from its shame?

title: Ireland’s Lara Gillespie targets another UCI world cycling title in Shanghai
description: Wicklow rider will again come up against Dutch rival Lorena Wiebes in her first event
content:
Lara Gillespie will face a familiar rival in her first of three attempts to win another rainbow jersey at this week’s UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai. A year on from becoming the first Irish woman to claim a UCI world cycling title in any event, the Wicklow rider has arrived at the Shanghai Velodrome on Chongming Island with confidence soaring, by her own admission riding faster and stronger than ever before.
The first test of that will come in Wednesday’s scratch (11.59am Irish time), arguably the simplest of track events, a 10km bunch race where the first rider across the line wins. The favourite is Dutch star Lorena Wiebes, who last Sunday completed her clean sweep of stage victories on stage three of the Tour of Chongming Island, the last stop on the women’s World Tour this season.
Gillespie, however, pressed Wiebes right up to the finish line in those last two stages, earning her second position on general classification – her best result in a World Tour stage race. The 25-year-old afterwards described those two close finishes as her “best sprint efforts ever”, and there’s no doubt she’s getting closer to Wiebes following those efforts.
Her breakthrough win came in the elimination race at last year’s UCI World Track Championships in Santiago, Chile. This time, Gillespie will also ride the omnium on Friday (a combination of four events, starting at 5.35am Irish time), before finishing up with Sunday’s points race (7am Irish time), which covers 25km.
Since winning in Santiago, she has become the first Irish rider to complete all three major stage races for women – finishing fourth in the points classification in the Giro d’Italia , having taken on both the Tour de France Femmes and La Vuelta Femenina last year. She then won two Irish national titles in June (the time trial and road race) and finished third in the Tour of Poland.
She leads a five-strong Irish team in Shanghai that also includes Aoife O’Brien, returning to her best after an injury-dented 2025, who is focusing on the elimination race (11.30am Thursday).
Emma Jeffers will contest the kilometre time trial, one of the four pure sprint events (qualifying 4am Saturday), with Fiona Mangan taking on the individual pursuit (qualifying Saturday 6.25am). O’Brien, Jeffers and Mangan will also feature in the team pursuit (first round Thursday, 10.05am), joined by Esther Wong, who took silver in the individual pursuit at the recent Aigle 3-Day event in Switzerland.

title: Vincent Durac: For Houthis, war in Gaza is a chance to strengthen role in Iran’s ‘axis of resistance’
description: The attacks raise the obvious likelihood of Saudi retaliation with the concomitant danger of escalation into wider conflict in a region that has known little else for years
content:
O n October 10th, a missile attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, launched by the Yemeni Houthi movement, killed 13 people and injured hundreds more. This was followed the next day by another attack, this time on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam in the east of Saudi Arabia . Previous attacks in September targeted fuel tanks at the airport in Riyadh, destroying a passenger plane and damaging several others. The attacks raise the obvious likelihood of Saudi retaliation with the concomitant danger of escalation into wider conflict in a region that has known little else for years.
The attacks must be seen within the broader Yemeni context.
The Houthi movement – a Shia Zaydi militia – came to power in Yemen in 2014 when they seized control of the capital, Sana’a, from the internationally recognised government that followed the fall, three years earlier, of the country’s long-time autocratic ruler, Ali Abdullah Saleh. In response to the expanded influence of an Iranian ally on its southern border, Saudi Arabia, under the effective leadership of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, led a coalition to expel the Houthis.
However, things did not go according to plan, and the war was effectively stalemated by the time a ceasefire was agreed in 2022. Since then, both sides largely refrained from major escalatory actions, and the level of conflict remained low until earlier this year.
The Houthis responded to Israel ’s war on Gaza with attacks on Israeli shipping and on Israel itself. These were met with air strikes by the US , the UK and Israel, followed in May of last year by a ceasefire agreed between the US and the Houthis. However, this was limited to these two sides. In July 2026, an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation that had attended the funeral in Tehran of Iran’s supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, was attacked at Sana’a airport. The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia, and a series of tit-for-tat attacks ensued. In late July, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and later attacked two Saudi oil tankers. The Saudi response prompted Houthi attacks on a Saudi oil refinery and the port of Yanbu – the first direct Houthi attack on Saudi territory since 2022.
In early September, the Houthis seized control of the Red Sea port of Mokha from Yemeni government forces, giving them a foothold close to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, through which approximately 10 per cent of global oil supplies transit.
The advance of the Houthis alarmed the Saudis for several interlocking reasons. Saudi Arabia has been more reliant than ever on access to Bab al-Mandab since the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, following the outbreak of war between the US, Israel and Iran earlier this year. Equally alarming to Riyadh is the close alliance between the Houthis and Iran, which means that Tehran now has the potential to control the two most important chokepoints for the transit of global oil supplies from the region.
[ ‘They’re not just guys in flip-flops’: Houthis show military reach with deadly missile strikes on Riyadh Opens in new window ]
The advance represented a military setback for the Saudis and the forces they support in Yemen. For the Houthis, the renewed fighting constitutes part of a strategy to force new concessions from opponents inside and outside the country in any future negotiated settlement to end the conflict. The Houthis want recognition of their sovereignty over the territory that they control in the north of Yemen. In the broader region, they have exploited the war in Gaza to enhance their status as a key element in Iran’s “axis of resistance”, having demonstrated their capacity to disrupt the transit of oil and other goods.
The dilemma facing the Saudis now concerns the possible impact of further escalation of conflict. The Houthis have survived air strikes by Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, the US, UK and Israel in recent years and appear to have emerged stronger in many respects. They control mountainous territory across which fighters and weapons are dispersed, with the capacity to threaten major oil infrastructure and shipping routes. While there is uncertainty regarding their stock of weapons, some reports suggest that they possess an array of missiles and drones that can reach the Gulf States and Israel. A report in 2024 by a UN panel of experts documented extensive links between the Houthis, Iran and its regional allies. Iran denies arming the Houthis, which would be in breach of a UN embargo. However, the panel of experts found that support from Iran, as well as Iraqi militias and Hizbullah, had transformed the movement. According to the report, the number of fighters increased from some 30,000 when the war began in 2015 to an estimated 350,000 today.
For Saudi Arabia, its enormous expenditure on the military cannot guarantee complete protection from Houthi missile attacks. The threat to the Saudi economy is clear. The most recent attacks coincided with its hosting of a major international energy summit from which the chief executives of ExxonMobil, Shell and TotalEnergies were missing.
[ Is it safe to fly through the Middle East? Advice for Irish travellers after Saudi airport attack Opens in new window ]
The US also faces a dilemma in determining its response to the attacks. Having declined an earlier invitation by Mohammed Bin Salman to launch air strikes on the Houthis in September, president Donald Trump now appears to be shifting position. He described the attack on Riyadh airport as “not acceptable” and stated that he would “look at” the possibility of joining air strikes. The Houthis, in turn, have made clear that this would end the ceasefire with the UN and vowed “a swift and painful response targeting the US and all its interests in the region”.
US intervention could lead to a halt in shipping through the Bab al-Mandab, further restricting the flow of oil from the Gulf. Over the last two months, in advance of midterm elections in the US, Trump has sought to blame Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy for rising oil prices in an attempt to evade responsibility for the economic consequences of US involvement in conflict in the Middle East. However, if the US becomes further embroiled in conflict in Yemen, he may find it more difficult to escape the consequences of his war of choice on Iran.
Dr Vincent Durac is an associate professor in Middle East politics at University College Dublin

title: Micheál Martin’s feathers ruffled by claims he is ‘playing chicken’ with striking workers
description: ‘Enhanced social dialogue’ offered by Taoiseach more suited to AI summit than public sector unions’ pickets
content:
I t was a balmy October day outside, with a gentle breeze still in the early stages of negotiating severance terms for the leaves left on trees.
But inside the Dáil , the looming strike of 300,000 public service workers provoked chilly exchanges at Leaders’ Questions, during which the Opposition predicted “a winter of discontent”.
Evoking the now-distant days of summer, a rueful Mary Lou McDonald told the Taoiseach he had had four months to avert the crisis – ever since the last pay agreement expired in June.
Instead of “statesmanship”, however, he had chosen “brinkmanship”. That and “playing chicken”. Now, McDonald implied, the chicken games were coming home to roost.
Whatever about the chickens, Micheál Martin remained unflappable throughout. Only his innocence seemed injured. More than once, he spoke of the “enhanced social dialogue” he had offered trade unions in vain.
[ Government renews calls for unions to enter talks ‘immediately’ ahead of planned strike ]
On the eve of Wednesday’s other big event, the International AI Summit, the Taoiseach’s enhanced social dialogue (ESD) sounded like a next-generation chatbot.
But the unions were not interested in access to his superintelligence, apparently. And unimpressed by Martin’s smooth replies, the Sinn Féin leader wanted to be put straight through to a human, too. This was the “11th hour”, she said.
Such was the sense of urgency that, for once, the first item on the agenda of Irish politics was no longer the split. “The first item on the agenda is pay,” McDonald said. “That’s always the case with pay talks,” Martin agreed.
