Most party leaders concentrated their Leaders’ Questions on the strike. The exception was Aontú’s Peadar Tóibín , whose question was not so much a question as an attempted drive-by character assassination of the entire Cabinet.
It was Tóibín who predicted a discontented winter. But starting the storms early and gusting to Force 10, he blasted the Justice minister (for the Garda whistleblower controversy), the Health minister (for the children’s hospital debacle), the Children, Disability and Equality minister (for an “omnishambles”) and the Social Protection minister (for wasting 100,000 school meals a day).
There may have been others targeted in the three-minute fusillade, but it was hard to keep up. Even the Taoiseach’s advanced ESD software struggled to cope.
Remarkably, though, Tóibín had also somehow found time to mention Drumcree . He accused Martin of having “stood idly by” during the standoff, then basking in the glory afterwards.
The reference to a previous Cork taoiseach, circa 1970, and a time when the split really was the first item on the agenda, may or may not have been deliberate.
Either way, this was the nearest Martin came to sounding annoyed. “No one stood idly by in Drumcree,” he said. His cautious approach had been dictated by concern about future relations. As he summed up his Garvaghy Road strategy, semi-cryptically: “I looked around the corner.”
That may have been more of his ESD. Conversely, he accused the Aontú chatbot of an over-reliance on SDS: “simplistic derogatory soundbites”.
Back on the main theme, The Social Democrats’ Cian O’Callaghan also characterised the strike in poultry terms. The Taoiseach had been “playing chicken” with the unions and now the game was “down to the wire” (the chicken-wire, presumably).
All party leaders prefaced their questions with words about the tragic events in Waterford. In expressing sympathy with the “first responders”, Ivana Bacik said theirs were among the professions driven to strike.
Her claims of the Government’s disregard for public servants, however, provoked a religious response from the Taoiseach.
“For God’s sake,” he said, stopping just short of claiming credit for the size of the strike while pointing out that public service employment had expanded by 80,000 in five years. Eschewing chicken metaphors, meanwhile, the Labour leader told him it was time to lose the poker face and put “cards on the table”.

title: Seán Moncrieff: Bono has failed to give Irish people any of the things we demand of our stars
description: We still don’t know what to make of our most famous person – that’s some achievement
content:
I f, a couple of weeks ago, you had been hoping to do some leisurely shopping on Grafton Street, you might have been a bit miffed to find it absolutely jammed: because U2 were playing on the balcony of Bewley’s cafe . And when you got home, having bought nothing, you could be forgiven for suspecting that, not content with ruining your day out, the band were also mocking you. Because, suddenly, U2 was everywhere.
As you know, this was because of the band’s 50th birthday : an event that probably prompted many weary groans across the country, even from people who weren’t thwarted shoppers. And that’s because of a long-embedded view that Bono , in particular, is a bit of a dose.
Doseyness, apart from not being a proper word, is impossible to measure in any objective sense. And we can all have our dosey days. Anyway, I suspect that for the Bono-allergic, that isn’t really the issue at all: it’s more that he doesn’t fit the template of what we expect from our musical stars.
In interviews, he likes to trot out the line about “four guys from the northside of Dublin”. If that is an attempt to appear more ordinary and relatable, it doesn’t work. Bono popped into the world stadium-ready. It’s almost impossible to imagine him any other way.
And that would be grand if he was from Chicago or Manchester. It’s just weirdly un-Irish. We like a bit of the tragic poet to our stars; something to ground them. A drinking problem. Drug convictions. Maybe an early death. Bono has singularly failed to give us any of that. He’s been married to the same woman for more than 40 years. His kids seem to like him. And for someone who can generate considerable animus, he has evaded any serious controversy. Yes, there was the thing with the tax . He was a bit slow to say anything about Gaza . But compared with many of his musical peers, he’s been Teflon.
Anyway, these are minor gripes. The main problem is that if Bono stands still, a pool of sanctimony forms beneath him. Any U2 gig will contain a homily masquerading as a piece of performance art, or just a straightforward homily.
But while a lot of artists might consider themselves “activists” because they wore a T-shirt or shouted a slogan or chucked a few bob towards a charity, Bono has got down and dirty with politicians. In the early 2000s, a series of meetings between him and the then US secretary of state Condoleezza Rice had a direct influence in the formation of PEPFAR, the US’s plan for HIV/Aids relief in Africa. By all accounts, Rice, sceptical at first, was deeply impressed by Bono’s grasp of the issue: the policy wonk stuff. She was meeting a rock star, but also a man channelling his inner Paschal Donohoe.
His understanding of politics also demonstrated his ability to be pragmatic. To get the issue over the line, he had to play nice with then US president George W Bush . They appeared on stage together, and since then have met up many times. It may have antagonised a few U2 fans, but Bono obviously felt it was a price worth paying.
[ Bono on U2’s first days, 50 years ago: ‘Edge and Larry could play. Adam and myself were bluffing’ Opens in new window ]
None of this is very rock’n’roll. Neither is his lifelong Christianity and social democratic inclinations: a set of beliefs that belong more in an off-the-peg suit than a pair of leather trousers. But that’s Bono: a bewildering mess of contradictions. Or more precisely, someone who doesn’t feel the need to be one easily categorisable person.
And he knows it. He leans into it. He’s a preening, egotistical often pompous star mixed with an international development lecturer. The world’s most famous Irish person: one-word-name famous. And he’s delighted about it. Bono loves being Bono, and after five decades, we still don’t know what to make of him. That’s some achievement.
[ From Madison Square Garden to Yankee Stadium, U2 left an indelible sporting footprint in the US Opens in new window ]

title: ‘AI is challenging, the risks are real, but ignoring how it will change your business is foolhardy’
description: Deloitte’s Lynn Guilbaud on getting comfortable with uncertainty, learning by doing and true experimentation
content:
The first thing Lynn Guilbaud remembers building was a cardboard ship.
She was just six or seven years old, sitting at the kitchen table at her childhood home near Clarecastle in Co Clare. She can still remember being frustrated while focusing on getting the unco-operative bow of the ship to fit perfectly.
“One of the girls from the neighbourhood called to the house and was a bit flummoxed why I didn’t want to go out on my bike,” she remembers, smiling. “As a child, I was always reading, drawing or working on some project. I wasn’t necessarily one of those kids who had a great vision of what I wanted to be when I grew up. But I loved the challenge of working on a big problem. I did know I wanted to build though, and I was always curious about where things might lead.”
She couldn’t have known it then, but Guilbaud would spend much of her career doing a more complex version of the same thing, examining the pieces in front of her, working out how they connect and building stronger businesses from the pieces.
It was that same curiosity that led Guilbaud to study Commerce and Spanish at University College Dublin, followed by an MBS at Smurfit Business School. She then spent 16 years at Microsoft in global programme, product and leadership roles. Today as a partner in organisation and work transformation at Deloitte Ireland, she helps business leaders understand how technology and artificial intelligence (AI) can improve what they do, how their organisations may need to change and bring their people with them, and to realise that the opportunities worth taking are not always the ones you can plan for.
Guilbaud is also very comfortable with that level of uncertainty. “Every day, I see that AI is developing faster than many organisations can make decisions,” she says. “Boards want a plan; employees want to know what it will mean for their jobs. CEOs and CFOs are being asked to make expensive choices about technology that’s constantly evolving. There is no well-trodden path here, and you should be sceptical of anyone who tells you they have all the answers. No one has every answer. This technology is changing far too quickly for that kind of certainty.”
So, what’s the one thing businesses can do amid these choppy economic seas? “You have to look at your whole organisation,” Guilbaud says. “The technology is just one part. You have to ask – where will growth come from now? How should we operate now given this incredibly powerful technology? What experience do you need to create for your customers that will not leave you behind. How do you know whether something is delivering value? Unless you deal with those questions together, you end up with lots of expensive activity and very little real change.”
“We’ve been walking the walk ourselves, and in fact, one of the first things clients ask us is how we are transforming ourselves at Deloitte, where we are seeing value and what we have learned? It’s a fair question. There is a lot of talk about AI and transformation across professional services and the disruption we will experience.”
But first goes first, and if the world’s number one professional services firm is asking clients to make bold decisions, rethink established ways of working and tolerating uncertainty, Guilbaud believes Deloitte must be prepared to do the same.
“We can’t ask clients to take that journey while we stay safely on the sidelines,” she says. “We have to try these things ourselves, push beyond what is familiar and be honest about the results. That experience means the advice we give is grounded in what actually happens when an idea meets the reality of an organisation.”
‘Ireland has the talent, experience and international outlook to lead in applied AI. And Deloitte also has an important role to play in helping convene the people shaping that future’
“We operate under an AI-first, human-powered priority,” Guilbaud says. “It might sound glib, but to us, it means using AI where it can help us work faster, spot patterns, remove repetitive tasks and truly transform elements of our business, while also recognising that our teams – some of the most brilliant minds across our global network – bring the challenge, curiosity, judgment and cutting-edge thinking. The technology is powerful, but the real value comes from how people use it. So if we are to be credible, we have to use the technology and develop the scar-tissue that comes from using it.”
Guilbaud admits that approach requires a degree of audacity. “We’ve used AI in the creative process behind our most recent brand campaign, NeverStop, putting the technology to work rather than simply talking about its potential. Our Clarity Incentives Platform is also helping supporting businesses to claim R&D tax credits, freeing up more time for innovation. AI fluency is also critical. Our research found that 66 per cent of organisations report productivity and efficiency gains from AI, yet only 34 per cent are using it to reshape how they work. We’ve seen huge gains by introducing Solaria, an AI tool we’ve adopted widely across our organisation, freeing up our people to focus more on critical thinking, professional judgment, and the work that builds trust.”
Internally, Deloitte’s regular hackathons also allow people to take an idea from conversation to something they can demonstrate within hours.
“There is something very energising about saying, ‘Let’s try it and see what we learn’,” Guilbaud says. “You have to challenge familiar ways of working, measure the result honestly and change course if something is not delivering. We are then able to bring our clients much more value as a result.”
In her role, Guilbaud understands some of the darker conversations that has recently surrounded AI. “Models need proper oversight, organisations must remain accountable and somebody has to question an answer that sounds convincing but may still be wrong. We have to use this technology in a responsible way.” she says. “People need to understand the technology well enough to challenge it, see its limitations and take responsibility for what happens next.”
Ireland is also extremely well placed to influence what happens next. Its mix of international technology companies, regulators, researchers and skilled talent pool gives the country influence beyond its size. It can connect the pace of global innovation with Europe’s focus on trust and accountability.
That opportunity comes into focus at the International AI Summit taking place in Dublin this week which ensures some of the foremost voices in AI come together to talk about developments, trust and responsibility. Run by the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, Deloitte has also been helping to bring together leaders from business, technology and government to consider what responsible progress should look like.
“It is an extraordinary opportunity to have this level of expertise gathered in Dublin,” Guilbaud says. “Ireland has the talent, experience and international outlook to lead in applied AI. And Deloitte also has an important role to play in helping convene the people shaping that future.”
Leaders naturally may still worry about choosing the wrong technology or backing an idea that fails but Guilbaud says that must be weighed against the cost of waiting.
“The first risk in transforming your business is getting it wrong,” she says. “But the greater risk is doing nothing at all. You do have to start somewhere. The businesses making progress are the ones willing to begin.”
The scale of her cardboard creation might have changed, but Guilbaud’s instinct remains on steadying her client’s ships via businesses transformation, ready for a future that can’t be predicted with certainty.
“People ask me what careers will matter in the future,” she says. “There are so many opportunities now and people can change direction, pivot and reshape their careers in ways that were much harder in the past.
“My parents always encouraged me to stay curious, keep an open mind and do what I loved. That is the same advice I gave to my son recently who is in fifth year in school. I tell him to double down on what he loves. It has served me well. You can always build from there.”

title: PTSB’s support for 88-year-old widow leaves family unimpressed
description: Is the bank ‘altogether more human’, as its marketing claims?
content:
A reader called Louise recently lost her father and has started helping her mother, who is in her 80s, with some of the life admin she needs to do. She has ended up with some questions about how her mother’s bank, PTSB , manages the financial affairs of older customers.
“What person in their 80s can register for online banking, answer seven security questions, set up a temporary password, six-digit pin, new password of eight digits – including capital and lower-case letters, numbers and symbols – register a smartphone device, access a one-time passcode, log on to a PC and then download a banking app for an approved device, and all without help from a family member?” Louise reasonably asks.
Louise’s father had online banking with PTSB on an iPad device he set up with her help in 2020.
“He used it very successfully up to the time of his passing earlier this year,” she says. “Despite the fact that the three accounts were held jointly with my mother, the access to online banking did not transfer to her after his death.
“She was required to start from scratch. Over a period of eight weeks, six phone calls (two of which were abruptly ended as the bank agent said I was prompting her or she had answered the security questions incorrectly), two letters to the bank and email correspondence with a regional manager, she was unsuccessful in accessing online banking,” Louise adds.
[ PTSB customer given the runaround trying to access virtual money Opens in new window ]
The reason she was given by PTSB was that she did not have a smartphone registered in her name.
“They would not add a third-party phone number (mine) even though it was the registered phone for my father’s online banking,” she says. “We registered my phone to ensure that neither he nor she would be getting any fraud/scam text messages or cold calls where they might inadvertently give their bank details via a website link or over the phone. He only ever used online banking when I was with him for his own peace of mind.”
Eventually her mother “abandoned all attempts to access online banking and following a personal appointment in-branch she has resorted to transferring money between accounts by standing orders to ensure that she has sufficient funds in her current account to set up direct-debit payments where necessary. In order for her to attend the branch, I had to take an annual leave day from my job and arrange accessible transport for her at her expense.”
[ ‘Our children will in all likelihood lose their mother. We didn’t want to spend precious time calling PTSB’ Opens in new window ]
Louise points out that the PTSB website states under its Enhanced Customer Support section: “Looking for someone to withdraw money on your behalf? If you are unable to visit one of our branches, we have a support in place to allow you to nominate a family member, a friend or carer to withdraw money for you.”
She says her mother “was keen to avail of this support. In practice they do not offer this service and have not for some time. The alternative offered by the bank manager was that I be added as joint account holder on my mother’s accounts. As this has far-reaching and long-term legal and financial consequences for myself and my mother, I politely declined and am surprised that it was offered as an option by a bank manager considering he could not offer any help with online banking, which would be a much simpler solution to her banking needs.”
[ Alarming letters and hoop jumping over paltry sum not actually owed to PTSB Opens in new window ]
Louise says her mother is nearly 90 “and fully compos mentis, and is a customer of PTSB in all its iterations since 1957. She laughs sarcastically when she sees PTSB describe themselves as the ‘human’ bank in advertisements.” Marketing materials refer to the bank as “altogether more human”.
We contacted PTSB, and this was the statement we got back in response:
“We sincerely apologise to our customer and her daughter for the poor customer experience they received at such a difficult time. We have since been in touch with the customer and her daughter to offer any further support that may be required.
“We have an enhanced customer support team in place and offer a range of additional services for customers who may need extra assistance, including help with setting up online banking services. While some of these supports were offered in this specific instance, including an offer to call to the customer’s house to assist her, the process of getting access to these supports was not at the standard it should have been. We will review this specific case to ensure we learn from it.
“To ensure our customers’ funds are protected, we do not permit third party mobile numbers to be given access to another customer’s online banking. Unfortunately, we have seen many cases of attempted financial abuse and fraud by third parties attempting to gain access to individuals’ account details. For customers who require family assistance in managing their financial affairs, we do have procedures in place to enable this, including third-party mandates and other solutions. These supports can be accessed via our enhanced customer support team, who can be contacted on 0818 818721 or by visiting one of our 98 branches nationwide.”

title: ‘I reluctantly signed a severance agreement after being given 24 hours to. What recourse have I?’
description: Work Q&A: I was hesitant to sign agreement because I felt my employer did not make a genuine effort to consider alternative positions I had applied for
content:
I reluctantly signed a severance agreement earlier this year after my former employer underwent restructuring, rendering my position redundant.
I was hesitant to sign the agreement because I felt that my employer did not make a genuine effort to consider alternative positions I had applied for.
All affected employees had an opportunity to apply for different roles during the restructuring and before redundancies. I applied for several positions, all of which were within my skill set. I had been advised by HR that impacted personnel would be given priority before external hires.
I was not called to interview for the majority of applications, and no feedback was given. I applied for a junior role within my organisation and was not invited to interview, and was advised Ireland as a location was not preferred.
During a consultation meeting, I shared my concerns to my manager and HR – that I saw no meaningful engagement or effort to consider alternative employment and was considering initiating a grievance.
I was then advised I had 24 hours to sign the severance agreement and if I did not, I would be made redundant regardless and the severance package would be off the table. I considered taking it to the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) but decided to sign the agreement, as I had no time for counsel. The signed agreement prohibits my taking further action.
I was advised verbally there were no performance issues on my part. My full bonus confirmed this. I believe there has not been due process and that I was coerced into signing an agreement before due process was completed. What recourse have I?
The main issue here is that you do not appear to have been given sufficient time to seek legal advice before signing a legal document, which is “problematic”, according to experts in employment law and human resources.
Moira Grassick , chief operating officer at employment law and HR firm Peninsula Ireland, says employers have an obligation to provide workers with the right to seek counsel before signing legal documentation.
[ Workplace wrangles: Staying on the right side of your HR department Opens in new window ]
“While a severance agreement is normally considered to be legally binding, the document may be null and void if the employee can prove that it was signed under pressure, that there was insufficient time to seek legal counsel, and that it was therefore signed with naivety,” she says.
Should the reader submit a claim with the WRC, they must do so within the timeframe set out in the specific employment legislation relevant to their complaint, she says.
“It’s also important to note that if the WRC did allow a case to proceed, and the employee were to win a claim, it is possible that any enhanced pay they have received may be taken into consideration when determining the value of the award.
“In other words, if the employee received a lump sum as part of the settlement agreement, the WRC could, at the discretion of the adjudicator, deduct that value from any successful reward,” she says.
‘If the employee can prove they were given 24 hours’ notice to sign a severance agreement, that it was ‘sign now or it’s off the table’, then they would have a case’
Grassick adds that employers have an obligation to seek alternative employment for staff members affected by a redundancy process.
“Best practice in this situation would have been to invite the employee to interview for available roles, even if those roles were at a more junior level.
“For the roles based outside of Ireland, the employee should also have been asked if they would be happy to relocate or work remotely,” she says.
[ ‘I returned to work after maternity leave and was issued with a notice of redundancy’ Opens in new window ]
Michelle Halloran , independent HR consultant and workplace investigator of Halloran HR Resolutions, says it would be “problematic” if the reader was given 24 hours in total to sign the agreement.
“I’m surprised if an employer would do that,” she says, adding that employees in similar circumstances are commonly given a week.
She says employers can sometimes add a provision to a document, often where an enhanced redundancy package has been arranged, that agrees the party will not lodge a grievance with the WRC.
“A key requirement on that, and a key requirement on redundancy packages, is that you’re allowed enough time to get independent advice,” she says.
Most WRC time limits are six months, though this can be extended in some circumstances, Halloran says.
“If the employee can prove they were given 24 hours’ notice to sign a severance agreement, that it was ‘sign now or it’s off the table’, then they would have a case,” she says.
[ A charity made me redundant and hired someone else. Does this sound right? Opens in new window ]
She adds that employers must make every effort to relocate, redeploy or retrain an employee whose role is being made redundant.
“Redundancy is the last option,” she says.
If you have work-related questions, from how to deal with burnout to running your own business, The Irish Times Work Q&A column is here to help. You can use the form below to submit your question. Please limit your submissions to 400 words or less and include a phone number. Your name and contact details will be confidential and only be used for verification purposes. Any details about your employer will also be anonymised.

title: My oldest friend is about to turn 40. He tells me he feels good about this
description: Dinner with him after a long absence requires no warm-up. It reminds me why making new friendships is worth the effort
content:
I remember the shy, painfully self-aware boy from the country, but now his big laugh is ballooning out to fill the little Manhattan restaurant he has chosen for our dinner. We’re having Italian food. I’ve gone for spaghetti alle vongole. It’s something of a stretch from when I was 17 and we would eat Supermacs out of the bag while sitting on the floor round someone’s house.
We met at school, which makes him – I believe – my oldest friend. There is no other person I knew back then who I still keep in touch with, let alone whose spare room I’ll still visit to stay in, or who I’ll meet for dinner whenever I’m passing through. He’s one of those people I could call and ask to stay with if it all fell apart, and we’re all incredibly lucky if we have one or two of those.
Neither of us felt comfortable at home, which I suppose is true of many teenagers. My friend was the most self-contained adolescent boy I’d ever met: quiet, straight-backed, buttoned up.
He left for New York in his 20s, where it was easier to live how he wanted to live; easier to be a gay man. This evening, despite the excitement of New York, I’m not really in the mood to socialise. I’m here for a week for work and I’m jetlagged. It’s been a difficult few weeks and I’m anticipating the formulaic catch-up ritual that is much of modern friendship – when you don’t see one another for extended periods, every meeting becomes an exercise in narrative storytelling.
They fill you in on what has happened in their life since you last saw them, and you do the same. By virtue of this upload/download information exchange, you are considered to be “caught up”. The best elements of a friendship – in which you enjoy or do something together or actually connect meaningfully in the present – are often omitted. Then you return to your respectively overwhelming lives and promise to see one another in a few months. I often leave those sorts of lunches or dinners harbouring a small feeling of loss, as though an opportunity has been missed, or I’m aware I’ve been talking past someone I care about.
This evening doesn’t go that way. My friend fills the space across the table between us with warmth. He doesn’t ask probing questions about the recent changes in my life. He doesn’t volunteer unsolicited advice. This in itself is such a rare and restorative quality that I feel myself regenerating softly at the table just thinking about it. Warming up and leaning in. A spring bud feeling the sun.
My friend is about to turn 40, he tells me. Something shimmers between us – an awareness of passed time. So much of it. I ask him how he feels about that number – 40 – and he tells me he feels good. I believe him. He was an old young man when I met him all those years ago. He’s finally moving into the time of his life that always felt like home to him anyway. I can see by his face that he means this.
There is something about that number – 40 – that relaxes something inside him. I think again of the impossibly tense, sombre boy with the straight back. He held in so much. This man across the table from me appears to hold nothing back at all. He laughs constantly. He makes the sort of appalling, maudlin jokes we’ve always bonded over. He bought his own place so now he can finally get the dog he has always wanted, since he grew up with dogs. “I pick her up from the shelter on Wednesday,” he says. “Her name is Noodle. I don’t think I’ll change it. She has a brother called Squidge.”
[ Laura Kennedy: Lessons my snippy friend has taught me Opens in new window ]
So much has changed for us both. The man I’m eating pasta with has transformed in the more than 20 years I’ve known him. I suppose I have too. We’ve witnessed most of the iterations of one another. We’ve spent very significant periods not seeing one another at all. We’ve lost touch a few times. But it’s one of those friendships. It requires no warm-up for reimmersion. Once you are back in one another’s company, it just picks up again. It goes by itself. There is no judgment, no comparison. There is primarily a sense of alignment that allows you to move past the surface-level information exchange very quickly, and to see one another in a deeply reassuring way. These friendships take significant time to build, and as a result they become much harder to develop from scratch with age.
I recently had lunch for the first time with someone new, a person who could perhaps be a good friend with enough time and investment. She and I made tentative social moves across the table, attempting to figure one another out; to find the differences and commonalities. It really is harder to make new friends as you age – you’re thrown together with people more when you’re younger and closeness is given freedom to emerge naturally through proximity.
[ It’s no wonder so many of us are lonely. Friendship has become harder and more complex Opens in new window ]
And yet my oldest friend, who is such a vast presence in my life now, was once an awkward boy who wouldn’t quite look you in the eye. He’s been many different people between that point and this, and I’ve found value in all of them. All of them have borne witness to my own failures, the progress I’ve made, the versions of me between the girl he met at school and whoever he sees across the table now. All of them have been my friend.
His company reminds me why making new friendships is worth the effort at every stage of your life. Not every friend will be like him, but we all need people around us who will turn a bad day around just by sitting near us. We have to work to find them.

title: Gaza student with UCD scholarship hopes for reprieve ‘before chance is gone’
description: Ahmed Abuhassan (22) was refused a visa for ‘financial reasons’ despite full scholarship
content:
A computer science student from Gaza said the refusal of his visa appeal “broke him” after a three-year process of seeking escape from the “genocide that took my house, my street, my university”.
Ahmed Abuhassan (22) had his study visa application rejected due to “financial reasons”. He holds an offer of a full scholarship to study computer science from UCD .
On Friday, he challenged the Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan ’s refusal of visas in the High Court along with three other students, but he lost the appeal.
The other three students’ visas were granted.
Speaking to The Irish Times, he said “timing is everything” as UCD is holding his place until November 2nd.
If his situation is not reconsidered in the next few days he will lose the opportunity to study in Ireland, he said.
Phoenix Law has been acting on his behalf.
He was enrolled in a degree course in Gaza before “the war interrupted” his studies.
He said he reached this point after three years of applying and “being pulled out from under the rubble of my own home with the clothes on my back, after chasing every charging point for a borrowed laptop and every signal steady enough to reach the world, through a genocide that took my house, my street and my university”.
[ ‘Every day we wait is a gamble for us’: Palestinian students continue to face visa rejections Opens in new window ]
“I gave my hope to Ireland because Ireland knows what hunger and rule by force do to a people and because a university here looked at my work and gave me a place.”
He said the letter refusing his visa “broke” him.
Abuhassan is asking the Government to act so his name “can be added to the next group leaving Gaza, before the chance I spent the years of this genocide building is gone”.
Following the refusal of his visa, he said his mind shut down. “There is a human being behind that case and refusing it there, this way, would have an effect. They didn’t handle it the human way.”
He said his home in Gaza was hit by an air strike in October 2023.
Two years later, after being displaced “multiple times”, he was allowed to return to his neighbourhood and now lives in “what’s left of that house”.
[ Refusal of Irish visas for Palestinian students is ‘trapping’ people in Gaza, court hears Opens in new window ]
He said he hopes O’Callaghan will reconsider the decision “because there is no reason” for his visa to be refused, and that UCD sponsored him in “full”.
He said he had placed his “hope and trust” in Ireland.
“All the Irish people were supportive, it was very helpful,” he said. “They were dealing with us in a human way. They were seeing the humans behind the case.”
A spokeswoman for the Department of Justice said it “does not comment on individual cases”.
UCD and Phoenix Law have been contacted for comment.

title: Club football championships: Who are county champions and what is the state of play around Ireland?
description: With county final season up and running, we take a look at who is contending in every senior championship across the country
content:
One way or another, history will be made next weekend in the first all-Belfast final since 2017. Either O’Donovan Rossa will win their first football title since 1991 or St Brigid’s will win the first in their history.
Final: O’Donovan Rossa v St Brigid’s, October 18 th
Managed by their hero of heroes Stevie McDonnell, Killeavy have run up four double-digit wins in a row. Crossmaglen stand in the way of a first title since 1948. Rian O’Neill is available after his suspension was thrown out on Monday night.
Final: Crossmaglen v Killeavy, October 18 th
A repeat of last year’s final, with Old Leighlin looking to go back-to-back for the first time since 2010/11. They’ll have their hands full against a Rathvilly side that demolished them by a gaudy 19 points back in August.
Final: Rathvilly v Old Leighlin, October 18 th
Kingscourt and Gowna meet in the final for the second consecutive year. Kingscourt’s win in 2025 was a big shock but with Jordan Morris (Meath) and Niall Sharkey (Louth) in their ranks, they’re a known quantity now.
Final: Kingscourt Stars v Gowna, October 18 th
No club has done a three-in-a-row in Clare football since the Kilrush Shamrocks in the late 1970s but Éire Óg have the chance to treble up here. Having Keelan Sexton back has done wonders for Kilmurry-Ibrickane, who last won Clare in 2020.
Final: Éire Óg Ennis v Kilmurry-Ibrickane, October 18 th
Nemo have lost the last three finals in a row – before 2023, they’d only lost four finals ever. The Barr’s beat them in last year’s decider but have been shakier this time around, only just scraping through their group.
Final: Nemo Rangers v St Finbarr’s, October 24 th
Another repeat pairing from last year’s decider, which Newbridge won by a couple of points. Magherafelt have had trouble getting over the line, losing three finals since their breakthrough win in 2019.
Final: Magherafelt v Newbridge, October 25 th
Naomh Conaill rarely do it the easy way – of their five titles in the past seven years, two went to extra-time, another went to penalties, another needed two replays. Final opponents St Eunan’s have been the only team to knock them out since 2018.
Final: St Eunan’s v Naomh Conaill, October 18 th
Backboned by various Carrs (sons and nephew of former Down great Ross), Clonduff ended a 26-year drought with a four-point win over Burren last Sunday. It was the first non-Kilcoo final since 2011, the Magpies having fallen to Burren in an epic semi-final.
Cuala are chasing the first leg of a football and hurling double this Sunday against Castleknock. They were champions in 2024, whereas Castleknock are making only their second appearance in a final. Con O’Callaghan v Ciarán Kilkenny, basically.
Final: Cuala v Castleknock, October 18 th
Beleek’s Erne Gaels have won the past two Fermanagh titles but only after a replay both times. Perennial contenders Derrygonnelly owe themselves big time for last year, after being five points up with five minutes to go in the drawn game.
Final: Erne Gaels v Derrygonnelly Harps, October 25 th
The 2025 final between Moycullen and Salthill-Knocknacarra was a thriller and the two sides reoppose on Sunday. Salthill have lost four finals since their last title in 2012, Moycullen have won three and lost two since 2020.
Final: Moycullen v Salthill/Knocknacarra, October 25 th
Spa are the story of the championship, having knocked out All-Ireland champions Dingle and favourites East Kerry to be one game away from their first ever final. Dr Crokes beat Austin Stacks in the game of the year/decade/lifetime last weekend.
Semi-finals: North Kerry v Kenmare; Dr Crokes v Spa (both October 18 th )
Still at the semi-final stage. A huge weekend for Maynooth, who haven’t been to a county final since 1916 and beat champion Athy last time out. Naas and Sarfields have looked fairly rampant from the start though.
Semi-finals: Maynooth v Naas, October 17 th ; Sarsfields v Celbridge, October 18 th
Mullinavat won their eight title in 10 years when they beat Tullogher–Rosbercon in the final back on May 2 nd . It will be six months later, more or less to the day, when they face the Meath intermediate champions next month in the Leinster championship.
Portarlington made it three titles in a row and six in seven years when they routed Courtwood in O’Moore Park on Sunday. Big Kildare flavour on the sideline, as they’re managed by Ronan Sweeney and coached by Johnny Doyle.
Fenagh were so close to a first title since 1932 last Sunday, only for Tom Prior to grab a draw for Ballinamore with a goal in the third minute of injury-time. Ballinamore are trying to avoid a third final defeat in a row.
Replay: Ballinamore v Fenagh (replay), October 24 th
Still at the semi-final stage, where Kildimo-Pallaskenry are in rarefied air, at least for the football side of their house. Mungret stand in the way of a first ever final, having beaten them well back in August. Fr Casey’s are the only unbeaten team left.
Semi-finals: Mungret v Kildimo-Pallaskenry, October 17 th ; Fr Casey’s v Monaleen, October 18 th
Under club maestro Dominic Corrigan, Clonguish closed off a 17-year gap as they romped to victory in last weekend’s county final against holders Emmet Óg Killoe. That’s county titles with six clubs in four different counties for Corrigan. Some man.
St Mochta’s haven’t won a county title since 1914 so they’ve got it all to do against traditional kingpins Newtown Blues this weekend. Managed by Down man Kevin McClorey, who stepped up after being in Steven Poacher’s backroom previously.
Final: St Mochta’s v Newtown Blues, October 18 th
Two sides at the opposite end of the Mayo size scale – Garrymore are definitely the smallest club in the senior championship, Castlebar aren’t far off the biggest. Garrymore were last champions in 1982, a campaign that took them all the way to the All-Ireland final.
Final: Garrymore v Castlebar Mitchells, October 25 th
The rebuild of Páirc Tailteann means the Meath final is a home game for Donaghmore-Ashbourne. They’re chasing a first title since 1942 against a Wolfe Tones side who were in the final two years ago and were champions as recently as 2021.
Final: Wolfe Tones v Donaghmore-Ashbourne, October 18 th
Scotstown’s hold over the Monaghan championship is unrelenting – they’re going for their 10 th title in 12 seasons. Truagh have never won a senior title and were beaten by six points – by Scotstown – in their last final five years ago.
Final: Scotstown v Truagh, October 18 th
Tullamore won their 31 st Offaly title – and their fourth on the bounce – by beating Ferbane last weekend. It was also Ferbane’s fourth final defeat on the bounce, so they must really hate the sight of them by now.
After a replay was needed to separate St Brigid’s and Pádraig Pearses last year, the same pair have made it back again this time around. The two sides have shared six of the last seven Roscommon titles.
Final: St Brigid’s v Pádraig Pearses, October 18 th
St Mary’s mopped up their first Sligo title since 2015 last weekend when they had two points to spare over Shamrocks Gaels. Managed by Sligo stalwart Mark Breheny, they still have former Leitrim star Emlyn Mulligan featuring off the bench.
Holders of 13 out of the past 14 Tipp football titles between them, Clonmel Commercials and Loughmore-Castleiney meet again in the final this weekend. Although they’re the holders, Commercials have lost two finals in five years when facing Loughmore.
Final: Clonmel Commericals v Loughmore-Castleiney, October 18th
Famously a hellishly difficult championship to win, Edendork have made it to their first ever final. With Niall Morgan, Darren McCurry and Conn Kilpatrick leading them, they have blue bloods in the shape of Errigal Ciarán standing in their way.
Final: Edendork v Errigal Ciarán, October 18 th
Down to the last four, with Rathgormack chasing a four-in-a-row. Gaultier have never won a county title and were last in a final in 1996 so they’re up against it here.
Semi-finals: Rathgormack v Gaultier; The Nire v Abbeyside/Ballinacourty (both October 18 th )
Led by a rejuvenated Luke Loughlin, The Downs knocked off their 12 th Westmeath title last weekend with a dramatic one-point win over St Loman’s. They face Longford champions Clonguish on November 1 st .
Martin’s were fighting on two fronts up until last weekend, when they lost their Wexford and Leinster hurling titles after extra-time. They’re chasing just a second ever title, while Kilanerin haven’t won one since Matty Forde’s glory days in 2008.
Final: St Martins v Kilanerin–Ballyfad, October 18 th
An Tóchar won just their third ever Wicklow title last weekend when they blew Blessington away in the second half in Aughrim. The Roundwood side hadn’t been champions since 1995 but with Conor Fee in sparkling form, they prevailed and will play the Meath champions next month.

title: Fine Grain Property seeking €15m for fully let Kildare office investment
description: Irish real estate company acquired Block C at Maynooth Business Campus for €6m in 2019
content:
Having paid about €6 million to secure ownership of Block C at Maynooth Business Campus in Kildare in 2019, Irish-owned real estate company Fine Grain has instructed agent Avison Young to find a buyer for the property at a guide price of €15 million.
Since acquiring the building seven years ago, Fine Grain has undertaken a comprehensive asset management programme. At the time of its purchase, about 3,716sq m (40,000sq ft) of the building’s 6,274sq m (67,532sq ft) of office space was let to global financial services firm, Link Asset Services, while the remaining space was in shell-and-core condition.
Now known as the Campus Atrium, the property, which was built originally by Ray Grehan’s Glenkerrin Homes in the early 2000s, has been finished and upgraded to a high standard, and has a B2 Ber rating. The accommodation, which is distributed across three floors, and complemented by 290 surface car-parking spaces, is now fully let and generating annual rental income of €1,423,114 from three tenants.
Dublin-listed housebuilder Glenveagh Properties is now the anchor tenant for the majority of the property while the remainder of the space is let to ASML, a supplier of semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and BCM Global, a European-wide loan-service provider. Should a sale proceed at the €15 million guide price, the incoming owner would be in line for a net initial yield of 8.63 per cent, assuming standard purchaser’s costs of 9.96 per cent.
Maynooth Business Campus is located on the south side of Maynooth and sits adjacent to the M4 motorway. The scheme is positioned in close proximity to Maynooth University, Intel’s advanced manufacturing facility, and the Kildare Innovation Campus (formerly HP).
The immediate area continues to benefit from significant levels of foreign direct investment, which includes Intel’s recent €5 billion campus investment. Other occupiers in Maynooth Business Campus include Applied Materials, Tokyo Electron, AQMetrics, FANUC and An Post.
Commenting on the sale of Block C, Artem Makarevitch of Avison Young says: “This is a high-quality office building backed by a diverse mix of institutional-grade covenants, in a strategic location where there is pent-up demand. We expect to see strong interest from both domestic and international investors.”

title: Landmark Clare hotel where Christy Moore wrote hit song Lisdoonvarna seeks €1.25m
description: Royal Spa Hotel in Lisdoonvarna, Co Clare, for sale as going concern as long-standing owners the Doherty family retire
content:
Having been owned and operated by the Doherty family for the past 46 years, Lisdoonvarna’s Royal Spa Hotel, a venue synonymous for just as long with the performances of singer-songwriter Christy Moore , is being offered for sale as a going concern.
The hotel, which has 12 bedrooms, a bar, cafe/dining facilities, along with a function room with capacity for up to 200 standing or 160 seated guests, is being offered to the market by agent Sherry FitzGerald McMahon at a guide price of €1.25 million.
Commenting on his long-standing association with the Co Clare hotel, Moore said: “So many great memories garnered over 45 years since I first played a gig at the Royal Spa Hotel in Lisdoonvarna. Back then I was singing with the band Moving Hearts ... it was a great night in a thronged hall. It was to be the first of numerous gigs played in that great venue.
“I also rehearsed and gigged there with Planxty , with The Trad Outfit and with The Compañeros, and across the decades I wrote and recorded many songs in the Royal Spa including Lisdoonvarna and Joxer, my work blessed by the power of the local, sacred and sulphuric spring waters.
“I attended many great gigs there by artists as diverse as Luka Bloom, John Martyn, Dexy’s Midnight Runners, Ronnie Drew , Natalie Merchant, Stockton’s Wing, The Stunning, De Danann, Bagatelle, Eddi Reader. Wonderful nights were spent there before, during and after gigs. I’ve stayed a hundred nights or more, with the best of accommodation, hospitality and top scran.”
But while the Royal Spa is arguably best known – among music aficionados at least – for hosting Christy Moore, the hotel has been welcoming visitors to Lisdoonvarna for generations. The hotel’s own records trace the property deeds to 1832, while the building is included on the National Inventory of Architectural Heritage and is recognised for its architectural and social significance. The hotel was developed originally alongside Lisdoonvarna’s emergence as a Victorian spa destination, when visitors travelled from across Ireland and further afield to experience the recuperative benefits of the town’s mineral-rich waters.
[ Christy Moore at All Together Now: A rousing Auld Triangle is dedicated to the late Glen Hansard Opens in new window ]
The hotel extends to a total area of 1,051sq m (11,309sq ft), and comprises 12 guest bedrooms at present. There is potential, according to the selling agent, to increase this room count through the conversion of a number of currently vacant rooms into an additional four to five en suite bedrooms, subject to planning permission.
The property has 16 dedicated car parking spaces to the rear and is located a short walk from a large public car park. Significant refurbishment works were carried out in the 1990s, including extensive roof improvements.
Commenting on their decision to sell the Royal Spa hotel, the Doherty family said: “When we took over the hotel in 1980, it was in a very poor state of repair. Over the years we have enjoyed renovating and sensitively restoring it to its original character. We have met some wonderful people along the way, both customers and staff. Now it’s time for someone else to put their stamp on this historic property as we look forward to our retirement.”

title: Modernised Blackpitts terrace in Dublin 8 walking distance from city hotspots for €525,000
description: Two-bed terraced home features two-storey rear extension and courtyard for entertaining
content:
Part of the beauty of retirement is the free time it allows you to pursue your interests. For those with a cultural leaning, living close to the city centre provides easy access to museums, art galleries and theatres.
Number 23 St Michaels Terrace in Blackpitts, Dublin 8 , could be just the ticket for a culture-conscious downsizer.
Just south of the Liberties, the terraced home is about a 20-minute walk from St Stephen’s Green on the south side of Dublin city centre. Within about a half an hour you can walk from St Michael’s Terrace to the National Gallery on Nassau Street, the National Museum of Ireland on Kildare Street and Trinity College.
The modernised two-bed, which extends to 65sq m, is on the market through DNG, with a guide price of €525,000.
The Victorian redbrick was built in the late 19th century and was purchased by its current owner in 2019. The previous owner had carried out an extensive renovation and added a two-storey extension at the back in 2015. It was rewired, replumbed and reinsulated, and a new heating system was installed.
“The extension was perfect and they’d done everything possible to update the house,” says the owner. “It’s what attracted me to it in the first place.” He did, however, paint the walls white and add his own furnishings.
On entering, you walk straight into the sittingroom, which has wooden floorboards and shelving on either side of the fireplace. It’s one of three original Victorian fireplaces in the house.
The kitchen has modern units in black and white, a white tiled white splashback and grey tiles underfoot. Floor-to-ceiling glass sliding doors here open to a north-facing paved courtyard. “I often entertain there and it’s a lovely peaceful spot which is not overlooked,” says the owner.
The house backs on to the Warrenmount convent schools and garden. “You’re in the centre of the city, but it’s very quiet and the views at the back provide a sense of space.”
There’s on-street parking and a strong sense of community in the area. “I can’t say enough about the neighbours,” says the owner. “They’re friendly and everyone looks out for each other.”
He likes the locality so much that he’s moving to a bigger house in the same area. “I’ll be sorry to say goodbye to this one, though. It’s really something special.”

title: Retail investment on Dublin’s Exchequer Street guiding at €950,000
description: Ground floor and part-basement levels of Nos 2 and 4 are leased to strong tenants and generating €78,500 in annual rent
content:
Private investors looking for immediate rental income from strong tenants in a proven location in Dublin’s south city centre may be interested in the sale of the ground floor and part-basement levels of numbers 2 and 4 Exchequer Street. The properties are being offered to the market by agent Savills at a guide price of €950,000, which reflects a net initial yield of 7.5 per cent.
The ground floor of number 2 Exchequer Street extends to 32sq m (344sq ft) and is leased to Brown Sugar Hair Dressing Ltd trading as Sugar Daddy Barbers, with a lease guarantee provided by O’Keeffe Hairdressing Holdings Ltd. The tenant recently renewed their lease for a new term of 10 years effective from August 18th, 2025, subject to a passing rent of €28,500 a year.
The unit at number 4 Exchequer Street comprises the ground floor, including rear ancillary accommodation of 71sq m (764sq ft), while the basement level extends to 8.5sq m (91.5sq ft). The upper floors are excluded from the sale. The subject property is leased to Nimbee Designs Ltd trading as The Loft beauty salon for a term of 10 years from January 2024, subject to a tenant break in year five of the term, a passing rent of €50,000 a year and a fixed uplift to €52,500 in year five of the term.
Interested parties should note that all rent is exclusive of rates payable to Dublin City Council, Dublin BID (Business Improvement District) levies and landlord insurance.
Both units occupy a high-profile location across the street from the newly opened Hoxton Hotel, and are within a short walk of Drury Street, South Great Georges Street, South William Street, Wicklow Street and Grafton Street.
Stephen McCarthy of Savills says: “This is an opportunity for investors to acquire two self-contained retail units in a highly coveted part of Dublin’s south city centre. Both units are occupied by long established and highly regarded businesses. This will be of particular interest to private investors and approved retirement fund holders seeking a foothold in a prime Dublin 2 retail district.”

title: Former Galway hospital and lands set for auction with €500,000 guide price
description: St Brigid’s Hospital complex sits on 163-acre site on the edge of Ballinasloe town
content:
Knight Frank and O’Donnellan & Joyce have been engaged as joint agents to find a buyer for the former St Brigid’s Hospital in Ballinasloe , Co Galway .
The former psychiatric facility, which sits on 163 acres, will be offered for sale by way of online public auction with a guide price of €500,000 on December 3 rd next.
Located on the edge of Ballinasloe town, the subject property comprises a number of historic buildings extending across a total area of 22,297sq m (240,000sq ft). Designed by architect Francis Johnson, the buildings, which date from 1832, are listed on the Record of Protected Structures and form part of the St Brigid’s Hospital Architectural Conservation Area. The complex sits on a 163-acre site which is distributed across seven plots and has direct access to the M6 motorway.
The lands have a range of zoning designations under the terms of the Ballinasloe Local Area Plan 2022-2028 . These include regeneration, residential, business and technology, community facilities, open space and amenity uses. This choice of zoning offers flexibility, according to the planning permissions.
Prospective purchasers should note that the Local Area Plan includes a specific policy objective supporting the regeneration and reuse of the St Brigid’s complex through appropriate master planning and stakeholder collaboration, which recognises the strategic importance of the site.
Full details of the sale and upcoming auction are available through the dedicated dataroom at www.st-brigids.com Viewings are strictly by appointment through the joint selling agents.

title: French investor pays €15m for Portlaoise logistics facility
description: Fund in line for €1.37m in annual rental income from its first industrial investment in Ireland
content:
Having only recently completed the purchase for €24 million of Citywest Shopping Centre in Dublin , French investor Iroko has acquired a fully let logistics facility in Portlaoise, Co Laois . Iroko is understood to have paid about €15 million to secure ownership of Ballymacken Logistics Facility for its Iroko Atlas SCPI investment fund.
Located just off the N80, and about 4km from Portlaoise and 3.5km from junction 16 of the M7 motorway, the property comprises 16,445sq m (177,000sq ft) of warehouse and office space across four buildings on an 11-acre site. The facility is generating annual rental income of €1.37 million from a diverse tenant line-up consisting of Tirlán, Graphic Packaging Ireland, Courts Service and Cool Springs. Approximately 50 per cent of the rental income is derived from Tirlán, a company that operates a dairy and chilled-food distribution hub at the site.
The acquisition is Iroko Atlas SCPI’s first industrial portfolio investment in Ireland. The €15 million sale price reflects a capital value of approximately €84 per sq ft, which is substantially below the build cost of the facility.
Michele McGarry of Colliers handled the acquisition on behalf of Iroko while agent Sherry FitzGerald Davitt & Davitt represented the vendor.
Commenting on the completion of the deal, McGarry said: “This investment will provide Iroko with secure income from a strong tenant base. The property benefits from a strategic location close to the M7 and Ireland’s wider motorway network. The acquisition represents another significant addition to Iroko’s growing Irish portfolio.”

title: Sutton Cross site next to Marine Hotel zoned for residential development guiding at €2.4m
description: 1.1-acre holding next to Marine Hotel has scope for 42 apartments according to feasibility study
content:
Developers and investors involved in the delivery of homes aimed towards the upper end of Dublin’s owner-occupier and private rented sector markets are expected to run the rule over the sale of a prime site zoned for residential development at Sutton Cross on the city’s northside.
Located on the Dublin Road and immediately adjacent to the landmark Marine Hotel, the subject site – occupied at present by a large period home known as Corona – extends to a total area of 0.46 hectares (1.1 acres) and is being offered to the market by agent CBRE at a guide price of €2.4 million.
The site is zoned “RS – Residential” under the terms of the Fingal Development Plan 2023 – 2029. The aim of this designation is to “provide for residential development and protect and improve residential amenity”. Permissible uses under this zoning objective include residential, residential care home/retirement home, retirement village and sheltered accommodation.
A feasibility study conducted by Plus Architecture, in preparation for the current sale, points to the site’s potential to accommodate a scheme comprising a mix of 16 apartments and duplexes or the development of 42 apartments with approximately 20 car-parking spaces at surface level.
The subject site occupies a prominent corner location fronting on to Sutton Cross and is accessed from the Dublin Road. The property sits immediately beside the Marine Hotel and across the road from a range of shops and cafes at Sutton Cross. Sutton Dart station is located about 500m away and the area is served by a number of Dublin Bus routes. Sutton is convenient to both the M1 and M50 motorways, allowing for quick access to Dublin Airport, the Greater Dublin Area and wider national road network.
Cliona Lenehan of CBRE said: “The Corona site offers an excellent development opportunity in one of north Dublin’s most established locations.
“There is considerable scope here for residential development, and we expect to see strong interest given the property’s location within walking distance of Sutton village and its Dart station.”

title: Kilcoole lands near Glenroe Farm rezoned for residential development guiding at €9m
description: 25-acre holding near Glenroe Farm includes 11 acres that have now been designated for the delivery of new homes
content:
Housebuilders involved in the delivery of new homes in Dublin’s commuter-belt counties may be interested in the recent decision by Wicklow County Council to rezone lands on the outskirts of Kilcoole for residential development.
Located just off Lott Lane and within proximity to the well-known Glenroe Farm, the 10.1-hectare (25-acre) holding includes 11 acres now zoned for housing and is being offered for sale through agent Cushman & Wakefield at a guide price of €9 million.
The subject property, which is mostly greenfield in nature, is bounded by mature hedgerows and surrounded by existing residential estates. According to the recently decided Variation No 4 of the Delgany & Kilcoole Local Planning Framework, a total of 6.6 hectares (16.3 acres) of the lands have been designated by Wicklow County Council as a mix of residential development (4.4 hectares/10.9 acres) and active open space (2.2 hectare/5.4 acres). The remaining 3.5 hectares (8.7 acres) of the subject holding remains unzoned.
Interested parties will note that the lands are also subject to Specific Local Objective 10, which specifies the framework they would need to follow on the delivery of residential development alongside community sporting facilities and associated infrastructure. An examination of the objective shows for example that no dwelling units permitted and developed on foot of the site’s zoning may be occupied until a community sports facility is fully developed and available for use.
A feasibility study prepared by HKR Architects in preparation for the site’s sale suggests the lands have the potential to accommodate approximately 168 homes, consisting of a mix of housing types, with an emphasis on family homes.
[ Five homes on view this week in Dublin from €275,000 Opens in new window ]
The subject site is located on the outskirts of the village Kilcoole and is situated 5.1km from the nearby town of Greystones, 11.5km from Bray, and 35km from St Stephen’s Green in Dublin city centre. The area is well connected by road thanks to its proximity to the N11 and M11 motorway, while commuter rail and Dart services are available at Kilcoole and Greystones respectively.
Ross Harris of Cushman and Wakefield says: “Kilcoole continues to establish itself as one of the most attractive residential locations within commuting distance of Dublin. The feasibility study highlights the potential to deliver a significant new residential scheme, making this a compelling opportunity for developers seeking scale in a well-established and growing community.”

title: Killiney three-bed house a short walk from the beach
description: Former bungalow built in the 1970s has been revamped and boasts many attractive modern features
content:
Swimmers may be attracted to a house not far from Killiney Beach in Killiney , Co Dublin: it’s about a 15-minute walk from Sans Souci, a three-bed nearly at the junction of Killiney Hill Road and Military Road, to the beach. The dormer bungalow, built in the 1970s, has been revamped by its owners, and has attractive modern features like wide plank oak floors, wall panelling and a smart Neptune timber kitchen.
Sans Souci, Killiney Hill Road, Killiney, Co Dublin, a 130sq m semidetached three-bed, is for sale through Sherry FitzGerald for €1.095 million. It was sold for €650,000 in 2011 and for €665,000 in 2014, according to the Property Price Register. It has a C Ber.
High electronic timber gates lead off Killiney Hill Road into the front garden of Sans Souci. It’s entered from the side of the house, the door opening into a furnished entrance hall. French doors open down two steps into the standout room in the house, a wide, bright livingroom/diningroom. A large corner window wraps around a corner in the livingroom end of the space, which like all the downstairs rooms, has wide plank oak floors.
French doors open from the diningroom side of the space into the front garden, and wall-to-wall bookshelves line the wall beside the dining table. The room has a marble open fireplace between the French doors that lead from the hall and another set of French doors the lead up to the kitchen.
The wide galley-style kitchen is lined with timber cupboards painted duck-egg green: it has pale Silestone quartz countertops, a double Belfast sink, overhead unit with a plate rack and a black Lacanche range with a mottled glass splashback. There’s a separate good-sized utility room off the kitchen and a downstairs toilet off the front hall. A door opens from the kitchen into the back garden.
Steep stairs lead past panelled walls to a landing made bright by a wide window. An under-eaves dressingroom with a large skylight off the main bedroom has fitted wardrobes and a desk. An en suite shower room is fully-tiled with subway tiles; a family bathroom has twin wash-hand basins and a bath. Two other bedrooms are fitted out as children’s rooms.
The back garden is curved, with a circular raised patio that steps up to a semicircular lawn bordered by high walls that are lined with bamboo. There’s room to park several cars in the part cobblelocked/part pebbled front garden which has illuminated raised flower beds.

title: Neighbours were ‘beaten back by the flames’: Waterford estate numb with shock at horror fire
description: Phil and Kim English, along with two of their children, died in the house fire on Tuesday morning
content:
P eople huddled in groups and pairs, some still in dressing gowns, seemingly numb with shock as the scale of the tragedy of four lives lost and two more critical following a house fire in Waterford .
The scene unfolded in Birchwood, a 25-year-old estate of private and social housing, where families had begun preparations for Halloween, houses decorated with witches brooms and spectral ghosts.
Neighbours were awoken just after 5am to the smell of smoke and immediately alerted the emergency services, running to the house to try to help. Several fire brigade units were scrambled from Waterford Fire Service, the National Ambulance Service and gardaí, but they all arrived at a well developed fire.
Local parish priest, Father Gerry Chestnutt from nearby St John’s Park knew the victims well – husband and wife, Philip and Kim English and their four children. Callum (12) and Jayden (8) were both killed while their siblings remain in critical condition in Children’s Health Ireland, Crumlin.
Callum was in first year in St Paul’s, Jayden was in St Joseph’s Special School.
Chestnutt said he was at several of the children’s confirmations, communions and baptisms. An experienced pastor, Chestnutt, like everyone else in Birchwood and the Sacred Heart Parish and indeed the entire city of Waterford, was struggling to comprehend the full enormity of what had happened in the quiet estate.
“I know the community really well and people are just absolutely devastated – to wake up this morning to discover this tragedy here among a family that they all know so well because while it’s a big parish, here is a very tightly knit community, it’s beyond words.”
Bishop of Waterford and Lismore Alphonsus Cullinan returned from a diocesan retreat in Cork to extend his sympathy and show his solidarity with the local community. He too seemed to be struggling for words as he sought to address the enormity of the loss.
“Four lives lost, kids should have been going to school today, instead two are dead and two more are in hospital and their parents are dead – it’s just a huge tragedy and you can see from the reaction here that the local people are just numbed.
Something we never thought we would see on our doorsteps
“Several of them made a heroic effort to try and get into the house to see what they could do to for the family but were beaten back by the flames but we gather as a community and it’s great the local community centre is open below for people to gather and comfort each other.”
Many public representatives were also in attendance to show their solidarity with the residents and among them was Waterford Sinn Féin TD, David Cullinane who spoke of people’s shock and revulsion when their suspicions were confirmed that gardaí were treating the deaths as murder.
“We were dealing with what was a tragedy and a loss of life and now to learn that it is being treated by gardaí as a murder investigation is adding to the shock and the trauma that residents are facing – it’s something we never thought we would see on our doorsteps here in Waterford.”
“There’s an added element of shock gone through this community with this latest news – hearts are broken and this has added to the trauma people are feeling,” said Cullinane as he urged anyone with any information to come forward and assist gardaí in their investigation.
News of the tragedy was greeted with dismay by the local Sacred Heart Family Resource Centre in nearby Kilcohan, which expressed sympathy over the deaths and said that counselling services would be available for anyone deeply affected by the incident.
“Sacred Heart Family Resource Centre is shocked and deeply saddened to hear of the tragedy that occurred this morning in the Birchwood Estate. Kim, Phillip, and their children were well known and much loved within our community.
“Their children attended our childcare service, Tiptoes Community Childcare Centre over the years, and the family was known to many of our staff, children, and families. Our thoughts and heartfelt sympathies are with all those affected by this devastating loss.”
The Sacred Heart Family Resource Centre said it would be holding a dedicated drop-in support service for families and children who have been impacted by this tragedy and people would be welcome to drop in any time even if they simply wished to be with others at this difficult time.
“The service will be available from 9-5pm on Friday October 16th and they will be able to avail of the services of our Family Support Worker, Mary Lyng, and Creative Arts Therapist, Nóirín Hennessey,” said the centre which is contactable on 051-306728.

title: ‘You hack her phone, then you kill her’: What Israeli intelligence officers told Naza director Yuval Abraham about their tactics in Gaza
description: Naza has incensed the Netanyahu administration. That means the documentary’s revelations have frightened it, says the film-maker
content:
“We didn’t expect this backlash,” Yuval Abraham tells me. “We expected some backlash, but such an intense backlash from the highest levels of Israeli government has been not easy.”
One can only imagine. A little over a month ago, Naza, a chilling documentary by Abraham and Rachel Szor, premiered to acclaim at Venice International Film Festival .
Abraham, an investigative journalist raised in southern Israel , knew he was dealing with dangerous material. The formally daring film, comprising interviews with 24 Israeli military-intelligence officers and soldiers, investigates the systems behind the massed slaughter of civilians during the continuing assault on Gaza .
It deals in horror throughout. We learn about the tapping of civilians’ phones. We learn about the computer programs that help determine targets. We hear about loose standards as regards the deaths of non-combatants in air strikes. “Naza” is an acronym, in Hebrew, for “collateral damage”.
Miki Zohar, the Israeli minister for culture, called for the directors’ citizenship to be revoked, accusing them of “treason against the state”. Protesters surrounded the home of Szor’s parents, waving banners that read “traitors”.
Just this week, news emerged that Binyamin Netanyahu , the Israeli prime minister, had ordered his attorney general and the Shin Bet security service to uncover the interviewees’ identities and prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.
“On the one hand there is fear – fear for our families and for our ability to go back home to Israel, which is where our home is and where we derive a sense of meaning to our work,” Abraham says. “On the other hand, there is also a sense of power.
“I think this unhinged reaction from the Israeli government – from Netanyahu – speaks to the fact they’re also afraid of the revelations.”
Abraham, a fluent Arabic speaker who has spent much time among Palestinians in the West Bank , has been here before. In 2024, when No Other Land, the Oscar-winning film that he directed with Szor, Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal on Israel’s destruction of Palestinian villages in occupied territory, took best-documentary prize at Berlin Film Festival, he delivered a speech noting a “situation of apartheid” and calling for a ceasefire in Gaza.
A frenzied response in Germany saw some politicians accuse the film-makers of anti-Semitism.
“You can disagree with anything that I say, but to weaponise anti-Semitism against me, the descendant of Holocaust survivors, felt sick to me,” Abraham says. “It felt wrong. It’s concerning because anti-Semitism is real. And it’s on the rise. It’s more relevant than ever.”
Such is the nature of modern discourse that, after the awarding of a special jury prize to Naza at Venice, there was much complaining from people who had not seen a second of the project.
Not all of it came from a pro-Israel direction. Some objected to the anonymity granted to interviewees revealing atrocity after atrocity.
“This film would not have been made in any other way,” Abraham said last month. “Because the crimes are ongoing, we felt that it was important to make it. And we understand there is a complexity there.”
There was also concern that the interviewees were asking for absolution or parading their own trauma (the so-called shooting-and-crying genre). There is none of that in Naza. Some contributors do express regret, but the tone is mostly one of icy, distanced analysis. The soldiers and intelligence operatives, interviewed on the roofs of Tel Aviv after dark, sketch the systems on sheets of paper, as if offering directions to a lost traveller.
“You find in the same soldier an intuitive sense that they participated in something horrific – and that they should be speaking out about it and that they should be agreeing to answer my questions as a journalist,” Abraham says.
[ Netanyahu faces fresh scrutiny over pre-October 7th warnings Opens in new window ]
“But, on the other hand, the events are so recent that the same person, when you were talking to them, could just as easily put on their cap of intelligence officer or soldier and then speak not from a place of regret but in a place of being back in that chair in front of the screen, operating a drone strike or calculating how many innocent civilians will die in a house.”
The film – and this may disturb as many viewers as it satisfies – is not much about how these operatives were feeling.
“What is more interesting for me as a journalist and a film-maker is to investigate the opposite question: how can you do that and not feel regret?” Abraham says. “How can you do that and continue doing that? This is not shooting and crying, which is a genre of Israeli film. This is shooting and not crying.”
Naza packs an enormous amount of information into its 77 minutes. A good portion of the film is about a computer program, called Lavender, that assists operatives, all at a safe distance, to select supposedly legitimate targets.
“Lavender is an AI-based program that gave almost every individual in Gaza who has a phone a rating of one to 100 that indicates how likely it is that this individual is a member of the Hamas or Islamic [Jihad] military wings,” Abraham says.
“The film really goes into the details we uncovered in the past in our investigative reporting about how it works and how this AI system makes decisions.
“Soldiers speak about how it had an error rate. The Israeli army knew that in some cases they were marking people who had similar patterns to a Hamas operative but were not actually Hamas operatives.”
Abraham speaks about a baker whose premises were near a Hamas training compound. He may have had numbers for Hamas operatives in his phone, but he was not a member.
“You could see how it could mark this person as a target,” he says. “People marked by Lavender – just generally people who would be suspected of being Hamas operatives – would be bombed not while they are in combat, in most cases, but when they are inside their homes, killing not only them but their entire families.”
[ In pictures: Three years of war in Gaza Opens in new window ]
The most disturbing parts of Naza concern the deaths of non-combatants, particularly children, in air strikes on Gaza. The phrase “Where’s Daddy?” creeps in to describe the intelligence services’ habit of tapping a child’s phone to discover when his or her father, a suspected Hamas operative, may be in the family home.
“You hack her phone, and then you kill her,” one interviewee says about a 12-year-old.
Another is content to use the word “genocide” about the mass killing.
It is at moments like this that one wonders why we don’t see a little more unambiguous contrition. Surely nobody can happily live with such sombre responsibilities.
“It is definitely one of the only moments where intelligence officers – who largely view Palestinians as a number on an Excel sheet, or look at them from a drone as tiny little dots – had a more direct exposure to the people, to the children, to the families they were killing,” Abraham says.
“A protocol that was often in place – not always but often – was, if possible, to open the microphones using spyware on cell phones that are in the house, in the building. And, before the room is bombed, to hear who is inside the room.”
They hear civilian life. They hear a man talking to his wife before they go to bed. They might hear a baby crying.
“It is one of the most horrific aspects,” Abraham says. “It breaks this image that we have of the intelligence officer as an individual who doesn’t necessarily know who is behind the screen. You do get into some kind of intimate knowledge of the people you are bombing.”
[ ‘People afraid to say they are Jewish’: Dublin event marks October 7th attacks on Israel Opens in new window ]
Naza is, to some extent, a film about Tel Aviv. While Abraham and his sources talk on the moonlit roofs, the interviewees’ voices digitally altered, the camera peers through windows to find residents going about their typical evening business.
One cannot help but think of Jonathan Glazer’s The Zone of Interest . That director was, indeed, an executive producer of this film.
“That’s one way to look at it,” Abraham says. “Another way to think about it is that it’s an image of Tel Aviv as a city. Tel Aviv is considered to be Israel’s liberal centre. It’s a city that people usually do not associate with Netanyahu and not with the far right.
“It’s like the Israeli centre of the secular population – the population that is more liberal, that is in opposition to Netanyahu. Many of the intelligence officers and soldiers, if they could choose a city that would be most associated with who they are, it would be Tel Aviv. They are also part of Israel’s liberal elite, intellectual elite.”
That seems something of a contradiction. Here they are engineering slaughter on a medieval scale.
