“Gaza is primarily, first and foremost, the responsibility of Netanyahu’s far-right government, who was in power when this was all happening,” Abraham says. “So, this is not to let them off the hook, but what was so striking for me and really important to look at with this film is the extent to which Israel’s so-called centre left – the more liberal elements of Israeli societies – have played uncritically a role in the destruction of Gaza.
“Most of the Israeli pilots and most of the Israeli intelligence officers and most of the senior commanders signing off on air strikes generally come from that liberal side of Israeli society.”
These are insights you rarely get from news reports on this sprawling catastrophe. Abraham knows whereof he speaks. I had read that, at the age of 19, he was assigned to a position in the Israeli intelligence corps.
“I was supposed to be there,” he says. “I was assigned in the mandatory military service, as it says online. That’s true. I left. It’s not something that I’ve done. I left very early on. I never assumed my role.
“It was interesting for me also because, doing this film, it’s like the road not taken. This happened a long time ago. When I was 18 or 19. But when I was talking to some of these officers, it was, like, oh, I maybe could have become one of them if I hadn’t taken a different choice earlier on in my life.”
“There is always an alternative, even if it’s really difficult,” he says. “Israeli society is a very conformist society. When you grow up, it’s like the water you swim in, the military service. That’s part of why criticising the military, as we are doing in this film, is considered a taboo in Israeli society. That’s part of why the reaction against us is so harsh.”
Naza is in cinemas from Thursday , October 15th

title: ‘I ain’t nicked nothing ... yet’: British retailers at a loss over shoplifting epidemic
description: From the infamous ‘Hamster’ of Greggs to my local Sainsburys, Britain has seen a surge of low-level thefts
content:
I was next in the queue on Monday evening at my local Sainsbury’s on a garage forecourt near Clapham Common.
I recognised the man behind the counter as one of the managers, a friendly south Asian who was often up for banter. Just not on Monday.
As the customer in front of me left, the manager beckoned me forward and I plonked my basket down. Just then, he glanced down at the bank of screens below, then sprinted out from behind the counter.
Two aisles away, just out of sight of the rest of us in the queue, we heard the scene unfolding like a radio play. The manager had clearly spotted a suspected shoplifter on the screens and ran out to make an interception.
We heard him loudly remonstrating with a person out of our eye line. “You’ve got to leave, you’ve got to leave,” he shouted, over and over. “Go, go. Out!”
Then we heard a woman’s mock-surprised response, sounding almost comedically indignant in her south London patter: “Wait, what? But I ain’t done nuffin’ yet!”
Grinning, I caught the eye of a woman behind me in the queue, before she, now smiling broadly, glanced at the teenage girl with her. Between us, we mouthed the suspected shoplifter’s unintentionally humorous defence: “But she hasn’t done anything ... Yet.”
Britain has experienced a shoplifting epidemic in recent years. Recorded offences have doubled since 2021. But this is an epidemic that doesn’t just exist in the office-bound realm of statistical reports. Anybody can see it any time they go to the shops.
[ Forty-one people due in court following Garda shoplifting crackdown Opens in new window ]
I have become inured to seeing people stuffing items down their fronts and marching out of stores in London and elsewhere in Britain. It’s as common a sight as a black cab.
Statistics suggest the problem began to spike during the cost-of-living crisis and inflation spiral that swept through Britain after the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The issue has since been adopted by the more excitable elements of Britain’s press as yet more evidence of the country’s moral and social decline.
The sentencing this year of the Greenford Hamster was a case in point.
Greenford is a nondescript west London enclave, a working suburb with row after row of Edwardian terraced homes. It’s the sort of place that has few pretensions but plenty of high-street footfall, ordinary people going about their business.
Like other towns of its ilk, Greenford also has a Greggs, the oft-maligned but more often-visited UK fast food chain. It is most associated with sausage rolls, but sells everything from pizza slices to breakfast baguettes and cake. In Britain’s cultural lexicon, Greggs is the closest thing to Ireland’s obsession with the breakfast roll delis of Centra and Spar.
Greenford’s Greggs was targeted early this year by a prolific local shoplifter, Adam Gosling. In a six-week period from last December 30th to February 10th, Gosling stole from the same shop at least 38 times. Weary staff nicknamed him the Hamster.
In February, he appeared at a local magistrates’ court, where he admitted the 38 offences. Prosecutors said he sometimes visited Greggs several times a day. Over six weeks, he stole at least £1,800 worth of goods. He walked free with a suspended sentence.
The case of Greenford’s Hamster became national news. The story included several cultural touchstones: the widespread belief that Britain’s social fabric is fraying, the even wider belief that courts are “soft on crime”, the stereotypically British setting of a Greggs, and typical English banter about the thief’s furry rodent nickname.
It was rarely mentioned that Gosling was homeless and, clearly, living a chaotic life. He stole food, sometimes hot items, which would have limited sell-on value. He may have been consuming much of it himself. The Hamster was no criminal mastermind.
UK police forces and the government have suggested lately that the shoplifting epidemic has peaked. The rate of growth in recorded offences has slowed. The British Retail Consortium says recorded offences barely scratch the surface of what is happening.
The industry traces the genesis of the current situation to a 2014 law that made shoplifting of items under £200 a low-value summary-only offence. Retailers say this gave virtual impunity to low-level but prolific shoplifters such as the Hamster.
The Labour government has now updated the 2014 law to abolish the £200 clause. Shoplifters can, theoretically, now face sentences of up to seven years for thefts which were previously dealt with summarily under a maximum six-month sentence cap. In practice, it is often just fines.
Yet Britain’s Home Office has yet to sign the commencement order for the new rules, because the courts and prisons are clogged up and the justice system is unprepared for a raft of new shoplifting prosecutions at crown court level. About 650 prisoners were let out early on Tuesday alone, under a government scheme to relieve overcrowding.
Back at Sainsburys on Monday, the woman, who also looked as if she lived a chaotic life, left the store while being videoed by the manager. He said he was ringing police.
“Ring the police,” she shouted as she backed out the door.
“I ain’t nicked nothing. Wasting police time is illegal too, you know.”

title: Francesco Turrisi: ‘I don’t belong to anything, exactly. In a good way’
description: Francesco Turrisi’s musical life had mirrored his family background, divided between Turin and Sicily. Then, 20 years ago, the multi-instrumentalist added Ireland to the mix
content:
The pianist, multi-instrumentalist and “musical polyglot” Francesco Turrisi was born in Turin to Sicilian parents – and grew up belonging fully to neither place.
As a child in his native city, where his maternal grandparents still spoke Sicilian at home, he was taunted as a “terrone”, a slur for southern Italians that roughly translates as a “person of the earth” – in effect, a poor farmer or backward peasant.
During summers with his family in Sicily he faced a similar fate: detecting his northern accent, local kids would mock him as a “polentone”, or “someone who lives on polenta”, an insult implying a certain coarseness and lack of culture.
In many ways, Turrisi’s boyhood experiences have echoed throughout his personal and musical life. Now 48, he has lived in Ireland for 20 years, though, as he wrote in the liner notes to Northern Migrations , his panoramic solo piano album from 2018: “Like every other migrant in the world, I don’t belong where I came from any more, and never will fully belong where I go.”
Turrisi’s open and egalitarian music is similarly rootless and caught between classifications. Equally at home performing jazz, baroque and early music, Irish trad, Mediterranean folk, and Balkan, Turkish and Arabic music, he is primarily interested in exploring the connections between these disparate forms, not just in elements such as improvisation, melody, counterpoint, repetition and rhythm, but culturally and historically too.
The unparalleled range of instruments he plays also reflects his voracious curiosity and widescreen approach. As well as piano, accordion, harpsichord and organ, Turrisi makes music on various tambourines, frame drums and hand percussion instruments, as well as on guitars, lutes, banjos and mandolins. He is a sui generis one-man orchestra, a paragon of the idea that music can exist beyond taxonomy, that it doesn’t have to be just one thing.
“I mean, the languages of all these genres and instruments are different,” Turrisi says, in his impeccable English. We are sitting in the livingroom of his home in Greystones, in Co Wicklow, surrounded by CDs, high-quality hi-fi equipment, a Shigeru Kawai grand piano and several string instruments and their cases.
“It’s like speaking in English and Italian: I can learn both, and express myself in both, and still be myself. I’ve been exposed to so many musical languages, though, that I struggled for a long time with: ‘What is it that I’m doing actually?’ And then I realised that it goes back to that original idea: I don’t belong to anything, exactly. In a good way. And I’m trying to tell that story in everything I do.”
Not being wedded to any one instrument, style or orthodoxy has led to Turrisi releasing an impressive range of albums as leader and co-leader, all compellingly different and created with a wealth of collaborators and fellow travellers, from the Irish cellist Kate Ellis to the Italian trumpeter Fulvio Sigurtà and the Portuguese drummer João Lobo.
He has also appeared on two duo albums with the peerless American singer-songwriter, banjoist and fiddle player Rhiannon Giddens , the second of which, the appropriately titled They’re Calling Me Home, won the 2022 Grammy for best folk album.
In addition, Turrisi has had a long association with L’Arpeggiata, Christina Pluhar’s popular and pioneering early-music ensemble. More recently, he joined the Silkroad Ensemble, the multinational musical collective founded by the star American cellist Yo-Yo Ma and now led by Giddens – who also lives in Ireland, in Limerick, and was for almost seven years, until 2024, both Turrisi’s musical and relationship partner. Previously he was married to the Irish stone sculptor Helen O’Connell; they have a daughter together.
“I think the way my neurodivergent brain works is that it’s always trying to find patterns,” he says. “It also means that I get really, really obsessed with something and want to learn everything about it. But when I get to a place where I can really do that thing, I always get interested in something else.
“The way they teach you in jazz and classical music, however, is that you have to be a master of your instrument, that it’s a lifetime of dedication, and for a long time I used to get frustrated that I was too much of a jack of all trades. I sometimes thought I should quit and do everything through one instrument – the piano or guitar or whatever.”
Turrisi says he had an epiphany when he started working with Giddens. “Because she trained as an opera singer, and then as a folk musician, and because she’s also played so many different types of music, Rhiannon’s the only musician I’ve ever met where I could wear all my different musical jackets and totally be myself,” he says.
“It was the first time that I realised there is this space where I can be everything that somehow lives within me. I started to make sense of things and crystallise who I am.”
He was brought up by parents who may not have had a strong interest in music but who were encouraging and hard-working. His father, Orlando, came from “a very humble family” and often went hungry as a child, yet he “made himself out of nothing” by getting to university in Palermo; he later started a successful computer-software company. Francesco’s mother, Nina, was employed by a telephone company in Turin; after his older sister was born, she worked in the home.
At 11, Francesco had music lessons at school and “started noodling around” on the piano at home. Spotting his talent and enthusiasm, his mother arranged classical lessons. Turrisi found both the teacher and lessons boring, and he later quit and taught himself guitar; at high school he played electric guitar in student hard-rock bands.
[ Jake Xerxes Fussell: Why I’m bringing my Napoleonic sea shanties to Ireland Opens in new window ]
When he was 15, Turrisi heard the music of Charlie Parker, Sonny Rollins and Ornette Coleman on CD through a magazine partwork on the history of jazz, and he “fell in love with the sound of the saxophone”. He saved money, brought a second-hand tenor and “got completely obsessed”, transcribing solos and having lessons at a jazz school in Turin.
When Turrisi left school, one of his tutors recommended that he study jazz at the renowned Royal Conservatoire in The Hague. “At first my parents were, like: ‘Oh no, no, no, no. That’s insane. We just meant you to play for fun. Being a musician is not a job,’” he says. “But, in the end, after they’d spoken to various people, and I passed the entrance exam, they were very supportive.”
During the summer holiday after his first year, Turrisi suffered a serious setback: every time he went to play the saxophone, the muscles around his mouth shook uncontrollably and he couldn’t hold a note. Eventually diagnosed with a neurological disorder called focal dystonia, he was told to “think about another instrument – or job”.
[ Jason Moran: ‘I have a lot of gratitude for Cork Jazz Festival. And I still have that wonderful crystal vase’ Opens in new window ]
He chose the former, recommitting to the piano and, remarkably, continuing his studies by passing the conservatory entrance exam for the second time. Increasingly feeling that jazz, as an African-American art form, was not really his history or language, he had by his third year discovered the beauty of 17th-century baroque music on harpsichord and organ, with its strong links to Italy, counterpoint and the improvisatory practice of basso continuo.
Turrisi went on to earn a master’s degree in what was then a highly unusual combination: jazz and early music.
“Jazz is my first love and my mindset; it’s the way I think I approach everything that I do,” he says. “I’m not trying to mix or add things for the sake of it, as often the music doesn’t need that. I’m trying to create colours that show a song or a style in a different light.”
This month, as well as continuing to post on his engaging music and food Substack, Cooking by Ear , Turrisi brings his considerable experience and imagination to bear on his most autobiographical work yet, Vuci: Voices from Sicily.
Partly the result of a trip he made on his own to the island two years ago, during which he visited relatives and his parents’ hometowns, the mostly solo piano album features original compositions, archival field recordings and Sicilian poems, one of which is read in English by the Italian-American actor John Turturro.
The live performance, which was premiered at this summer’s Kilkenny Arts Festival, also features video projections by the Irish artist Laura Sheeran.
Vuci is Turrisi’s “homage to Sicily, its language and its voices”, in particular “the voices of the people who came before us [and] of the emigrant who struggles to return”.
“There’s definitely a lot of similarities between Ireland and Sicily,” he says. “Not just because both are small isolated places, with a large influence of the Catholic Church, at the edges of Europe. But also in terms of migration, memory and identity. Belonging is a pretty complicated feeling.”
Francesco Turrisi performs Vuci: Voices from Sicily at Project Arts Centre , Dublin, on Thursday, October 22nd; the album will be released digitally and on vinyl via Bandcamp the following day

title: Helen A Pritchard review: Rich work that is lively, engaging and invigorating
description: The London-based artist displays a wonderful sense of proportion, balance and composition in this exhibition to mark the fifth birthday of the Horse gallery in Dublin
content:
The Horse, an unassuming gallery tucked down a side street near the Rotunda in Dublin, is marking its fifth birthday with a solo show by the London-based artist Helena A Pritchard.
A rough-and-ready white cube, minimally interrupted by a bright-yellow staircase, the exhibition space has an improvisatory feel ideal for the scale and tone of Pritchard’s work.
Spanning sculpture, assemblage and painting, the works on show are varied and delightfully promiscuous in their use of materials.
A Painting About Something Smoking (2015) is a small canvas framed behind glass with what looks like an metal ashtray cover sitting in an abstracted colour field of burnished red and blue. The cigarette butt resting within gives it the appearance of a mouth, while a hole just above it distorts the resulting visage in the manner of a lo-fi cubist portrait.
Nearby, an amorphous black sculpture entitled Crow *BF 3 (2026) sits on a roughly gessoed wooden shelf, its form determined by the evident incorporation of a toilet duck resting at a jaunty tilt.
The BF of that title and a number of others in the show refers to the studio of the late sculptor Barry Flanagan, where Pritchard recently completed a residency and from where she has drawn some of the materials she uses in her work.
Free Form *BF 11 (2026), a snaky upright arrangement of rope and rebar, has the delicate balance of an Al Taylor construct; both Block Head Series; Found, Foam, Form, Coelacanth *BF 9 (2026) and Free Form; Fire Works Series (2019-2026) bring to mind the playful papier-mache sculptures of Franz West.
Three pieces, each subtitled as public sculpture proposals, offer absorbing investigations of scale.
Talking Heads Having a Yam; Sound Mirror, Hythe (Public Sculpture Proposal 1) (2026), comprising three upright aluminium ice-cream scoops cradling a ball of yarn, seems to hover between folly and monument, like some parody of Soviet modernist architecture.
Likewise, in Free Form *BF 1 (Public Sculpture Proposal 2) (2026) miniature human figurines stand beneath a vertical assemblage of wood, silver leaf and a single pool ball – tiny tourists visiting some postapocalyptic Las Vegas landmark.
But the works here are not merely humorous or playful diversions. Throughout the show Pritchard displays a wonderful sense of proportion, balance and composition, a sense that is perhaps most clearly seen in the few paintings that punctuate the exhibition.
Here we see colour and line interacting in ways redolent of the geometrics of early minimalism and late modernism’s interrogation of the flat plane.
Yet, like those of contemporaries such as Matt Connors or Fergus Feehily, the paintings here are also defiantly sculptural in their three-dimensional insistence.
Ultimately, Pritchard seems to allow herself to be led by the materials at hand, resulting in a rich body of work that is lively, engaging and invigorating.
Helen A Pritchard is at the Horse , Dublin, until Saturday, October 24th

title: Forgotten Island review: A plot that breaks up into a kaleidoscope of surreal adventure
description: The animation has the sort of heterogenous psychedelic zip with which early-1970s kids’ TV drew in class-skipping hippies
content:
You sense that the latest, hugely attractive film from DreamWorks Animation is covering a few bases. Here is a rare Hollywood production that relishes the rich culture of the Philippines . Forgotten Island also has a case to make about young women in Stem (or science, technology, engineering and mathematics).
If the more sensible of the two leads tells us she is going to Caltech once, she tells us once by 10 to the power of 19 times. That’s the California Institute of Technology. Right?
The sassy Josephine “Jo” Yuson (voiced by the musician H.E.R.) and the studious Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), students in the Philippines, meet up when sent to their school principal’s office in disgrace.
They quickly form the classic odd-couple partnership that has been powering comedy since slovenly caveman moved in with uptight caveman. Raissa works hard; Jo is more at home making noise.
Both of them, now linked by matching charm bracelets, enjoy the company of the latter’s grandmother Fatima, whose tales of a mystical island called Nakali seem likely to resonate in the film’s later stages.
Sure enough, come school graduation, magic forces make their presence felt. Raissa has won a scholarship to study at some distinguished US college. Is it MIT? Is it Stanford? It is neither. Partying on the beach one last time, they come across a sand dollar that transports them to hectic, colourful Nakali.
Here the plot breaks up into a kaleidoscope of surreal adventures. Jenny Slate voices a Batibat – is it dumb of me to be unfamiliar with that winged demon? – who longs for the charm bracelets that harbour all the girls’ friendly memories.
Dave Franco speaks for a weredog named Raww who bears an uncanny resemblance to the 1990s video game icon Crash Bandicoot. Lea Salonga growls as the appalling fanged demon known among folklorists as the Manananggal.
There is an admirable embrace of bad behaviour here – the heroes get tattoos, Raww is a devil for weeing everywhere – that is rarely embraced in US family entertainment. The animation has the sort of heterogenous psychedelic zip with which early-1970s kids’ TV drew in class-skipping hippies.
Forgotten Island is certainly here to do you good, but it’s not afraid to bust up the furniture in the process. A blast, man. An absolute blast.

title: Forever Is Now: Portrait of Eamon Ryan’s political demise shows how hard it is being Green
description: Neasa Ní Chianán’s documentary on the former Green Party leader charts the travails of the larger environmental movement
content:
It’s not easy being Green. Just ask Eamon Ryan . The leader of Ireland’s Green Party from 2011 to 2024 and minister for the environment, climate, communications and transport in the 2020–25 government was consistently criticised for coalition compromises, insufficient progression on transport alternatives and a failure to sell big-picture emissions goals to voters trying to make ends meet.
The film-maker Neasa Ní Chianáin followed Ryan during his final 18 months in power. It’s an apocalyptic reckoning for the Green Party , which would lose 11 of its 12 TDs in the 2024 election. Don’t expect grillings. In common with the Green Party, this clever fly-on-the-wall documentary is working on a macro scale as a portrait of the travails of the larger environmental movement.
Ryan wonders how to get “27 countries to agree on aviation tax, maritime tax” before a European conference. That is small change beside the Cop 29 summit, in Azerbaijan, where goals are derailed by representatives of the Global South who feel they have not been heard. “It’s a bad deal because it allows developed countries to walk away without providing finance to the developing world,” says one delegate.
It’s an impossible standoff. Things are no easier at home. Is there any place for green-branded diplomacy amid the Irish Lives Matter protests?
The lack of progress exasperates younger party members at a conference in Ballina. In the Dáil, Mary Lou McDonald , the Sinn Féin leader, is among the most measured critics we hear. “Just tell us that this madcap, half-baked and unfair notion advanced by Eamon Ryan is now officially ditched,” she says. Ouch.
Important supporting players include Edel Hackett, Ryan’s formidable media adviser, who’s a series of TikTokable moments, whether briskly brushing his shoulders before a press conference or looking appalled by a social media campaign by Michael O’Leary , the Ryanair boss. Please put this woman on a celebrity edition of The Traitors Ireland.
Other dilemmas include the impossibility of being a parent and full-time carer: work and you’re leaving it to your partner; stay at home and there are no breaks. The most affecting scenes feature Ryan and his autistic son, Tommy, as they roam around the countryside and waterways. A vignette in which Ryan coaxes his son to draw the family dog (and scene stealer), Sooty, is a delight.

title: Artificial intelligence tokenisation takes its toll
description: ‘The number I like is cost per correctly completed task. One of the most commonly missed costs is human supervision’
content:
Organisations are starting to learn that there’s no such thing as an artificial intelligence (AI) free lunch. Businesses attempting to embed AI in operations have turned to token-maxing strategies where they require employees to use AI for a certain proportion of their time or a percentage of tasks.
However, as the cost of AI tokens mounts, the value of the outputs is increasingly called into question, forcing those businesses to calculate whether it would be cheaper to use human labour instead.
We look at the pushback against token maxing and ask if it is likely to be a significant constraint on AI adoption.
AI adoption is accelerating across Dublin businesses, but the next phase will increasingly be about demonstrating value rather than adoption for adoption’s sake, says Mia Finnegan, public affairs manager, Dublin Chamber. “Dublin Chamber research shows that businesses are primarily deploying AI to improve efficiency and automate processes, but businesses also report a range of barriers to greater adoption, including skills, internal resources and funding.
“As AI becomes more deeply embedded in day-to-day operations, businesses will become increasingly focused on the return they are getting from that investment. The question should not be how much AI an organisation is using, but whether it is improving productivity, reducing costs or enabling employees to focus on higher-value work. For many firms, particularly SMEs, successful adoption will depend on having the right skills and internal capability to identify where AI can deliver genuine business value.”
AI can be cheap to try and expensive to run at scale, says Mark Kelly, founder, AI Ireland. “A single interaction costs almost nothing. But then usage spreads across hundreds or thousands of employees, agents start performing multiple steps, and you add integration, monitoring, security and human review. That is when the economics change.”
Across more than 1,000 artificial intelligence projects that Kelly has reviewed through the AI Awards, the technology itself is rarely the only issue. The bigger challenge is often the total cost of operating the solution reliably at scale, he says. “The mistake is looking only at the price of the model rather than the cost of the complete process.”
We are increasingly seeing artificial intelligence being priced and consumed through tokens, the units of text and data processed by AI models, says David Lee, chief technology officer, PwC. “Every prompt, response, document summarised or workflow automated consumes tokens, meaning that as AI usage grows, so does the associated cost. However, the real challenge for businesses is not controlling token consumption, but ensuring that token spend delivers measurable business value from the AI.
“The most successful organisations focus on the outcomes and value gained from the AI consumption. Rather than only measuring how many tokens are used, they also track the outcomes generated, such as productivity gains, time savings, revenue growth, improved customer service and operational efficiencies. This allows businesses to understand the true cost per outcome and determine whether AI investment is delivering a return.”
There are dangers in focusing solely on AI costs and usage, Lee says. “Uncontrolled usage can lead to rising costs without corresponding business benefits, while blanket deployment of premium models for every task can create unnecessary expense. Organisations also risk generating productivity gains that never translate into financial value if workflows, governance, accountability, and the right guardrails are not redesigned around AI.
“As AI becomes more widespread, competitive advantage comes from using AI for positive disruption, re-imaging how the business can work differently, efficiently and for specific uses and outcomes. Businesses that combine strong governance, visibility of token consumption and a clear link between AI spending and business outcomes will be best positioned to maximise value while keeping costs under control.”
Tokens become important when volume increases, the information being given to the artificial intelligence becomes larger, or the AI starts performing multiple steps on its own, says Kelly. “As you move up those levels from basic chats to agents, the amount of computing and AI usage generally increases dramatically.
“A simple question to a chatbot might involve one interaction. An AI agent might search information, call another system, analyse the result, retry something and then produce an answer. One business task can therefore create many AI interactions behind the scenes.”
That is why something that looked extremely cheap during a pilot can become material when it is running thousands of times every day, says Kelly. “The key measure should be cost per successful task, not cost per token.”
The value challenge is clear in Ireland, says Lee. “PwC’s 2026 CEO Survey found that only 17 per cent of Irish CEOs reported higher revenue from AI in the previous 12 months, while 23 per cent reported lower costs. PwC’s AI Agent Survey shows a similar gap: 53 per cent of Irish respondents saw measurable productivity gains from AI agents, but only 38 per cent said these gains had turned into real cost savings.”
Artificial intelligence is a positive disrupter and does not come cheap, Lee says. “The findings show you need to use AI to disrupt and reinvent your business to really get value from it – turning higher productivity into financial returns.
“Productivity improvements only create value when businesses reinvent their businesses, redesign workflows, strengthen governance, and link AI spending directly to measurable business outcomes.”
At the same time, artificial intelligence introduces new costs, particularly through token consumption, which can reduce or offset savings if usage is not well managed, explains Lee. “As a result, companies need a disciplined approach that focuses on cost per outcome and return on AI, rather than simply increasing AI adoption or usage.”
The most important number is not what artificial intelligence costs, says Kelly; it is what a good outcome costs. “An expensive AI model can be the cheaper option if it completes a task correctly without intervention. A cheap model can be extremely expensive if its work has to be checked, corrected and completed again by a person.
“After training more than 10,000 leaders, the pattern I see is that the organisations making progress are moving beyond experimentation. They can increasingly answer three simple questions: What problem are we solving? What does it cost us? What are we getting back? That is where the AI conversation is heading: from adoption to economics, and ultimately to business value.”
Rising artificial intelligence consumption costs could become a constraint if organisations fail to manage them effectively, says Lee. “As AI usage grows, token consumption and associated costs can increase rapidly, making it essential to link AI spending to measurable business outcomes. The real challenge is not the cost of AI itself, but whether organisations can demonstrate value from that spending.
“Leading organisations are responding by focusing on cost per outcome, using governance and monitoring to control consumption, and matching workloads to the lowest-cost model that can deliver the required result. In the long term, rising AI costs will drive greater discipline around how AI is deployed, measured, and governed, rather than preventing adoption.”
“If I showed you a shortcut that saved five minutes on your drive home, you could immediately measure the benefit because you know how long the journey normally takes,” says Kelly.
“AI should be evaluated in exactly the same way,” he continues. “Measure the current process first: how long it takes, what it costs, how many mistakes happen and how much rework is required. Then run the AI process beside it and compare the same measures.”
Importantly, Kelly says to include the full cost of the AI process: software, model usage, integration, supervision, mistakes, security and human review. “The number I like is cost per correctly completed task. One of the most commonly missed costs is human supervision. If someone has to check every AI output, their time is part of the business case.”

title: The personal investment account: A simpler way to invest in your future
description: AIB aims to help customers translate Ireland’s strong savings culture into long-term investing habits
content:
The Government’s proposed personal investment account has the potential to offer a simpler, more accessible and more tax-efficient route into long-term investment, according to Adrian Moynihan, head of consumer banking at AIB.
“Ireland already has a strong savings culture,” he says. “Cash savings remain essential for everyday expenses, emergencies and near-term commitments, while deposits also support lending into the Irish economy. The opportunity presented by the personal investment account is not to replace saving, but to give people an additional option for money that can be committed towards longer-term goals.”
Those goals will differ from person to person, he adds. “They may include buying a home, supporting education, preparing for later life or building greater financial security. For money that may not be needed for five, 10 or 15 years, investment can offer the potential for it to work harder over time. It’s so important that customers come to the scheme with a longer-term mindset, as all investment involves risk and volatility over shorter periods.”
Moynihan believes the personal investment account could help address some of the complexity that has traditionally discouraged people from investing. By combining straightforward access, a simplified tax structure, a broad but regulated range of investments and provider-managed administration, it could provide a practical bridge between keeping all long-term money in cash and navigating the existing investment system independently, he notes.
“A simpler tax framework will be central to the account’s appeal,” he adds. “The account will include a tax-free threshold, with a low flat annual tax rate applying to the average value above that threshold. The account is intended to make it easier for people to begin investing. There will be no minimum contribution, enabling customers to start with a modest amount and build confidence over time.”
Eligibility will initially be broad and straightforward. The personal investment account will be available to Irish tax-resident individuals aged 18 or over who have a PPSN, with one account permitted per person. There will be no minimum holding period or lock-up requirement, meaning customers can access their money when needed, subject to the value of their investments at that time.
Customers will have access to a regulated range of investment choices. Eligible investments are expected to include listed shares and bonds, regulated financial instruments, suitable investment funds including exchange-traded funds, and insurance-based investment products. Crypto assets and derivatives will be excluded, and the framework will not impose geographic investment restrictions.
Administration should be simpler for the customer. Providers will calculate, report and pay any tax due to Revenue on the customer’s behalf.
A broad provider framework can help make the account widely available. Eligible providers are expected to include MiFID (Markets in Financial Instruments Directive) authorised firms, regulated fund managers, insurers and relevant EEA (European Economic Area) authorised providers.
“AIB welcomes this approach and the opportunity to support customers who want to consider investing as part of a wider financial plan,” says Moynihan.
“A co-ordinated financial literacy campaign will be essential to the account’s success, helping customers understand the difference between saving and investing, assess risk and time horizons, and make informed decisions that reflect their individual circumstances and long-term goals.”
Advice will be particularly important for customers who are new to investment. “Recent nationally representative research conducted by Amárach Research on behalf of AIB found that 81 per cent of adults had not sought financial advice in the previous three years, including 57 per cent who had never done so,” he points out. “The same research found that six in 10 parents lacked a clear plan for funding their children’s education. While education is only one possible goal for investment, the findings illustrate the wider need to help people turn long-term ambitions into clear, affordable plans.”
The account will work best when it forms part of a balanced approach, Moynihan continues. “Before investing, customers should retain accessible savings for emergencies and near-term costs, identify their objective and time frame, assess what they can afford to contribute and understand their attitude to risk. The first step should always be a plan rather than a product.”
AIB National Savings Week, which runs until Friday, October 16th, should therefore be about more than encouraging people to hold more cash, he adds. “It is an opportunity to promote purposeful saving, informed investing and earlier engagement with advice. The personal investment account could give people a clearer route to put long-term money to work while retaining the protections, transparency and support needed to invest with confidence. As we celebrate National Savings Week, customers can learn more about the range of savings and investment options available to help them achieve their financial goals.”
Every AIB branch has a dedicated savings and deposit adviser who can help customers with any initial questions on the personal investment account and their wider savings needs.
“As a bank serving around half of the Irish retail market, AIB has both an opportunity and a responsibility to make investing more accessible,” says Moynihan. “Our intention is to offer customers a seamless digital route to open a personal investment account, without the need for a lengthy advisory process for straightforward set-up, helping them translate Ireland’s strong savings culture into long-term investing habits. Customers who require more tailored guidance can also meet with AIB’s Financial Planning team in branch, by phone or via video call to explore how personal investment accounts and other savings, investment, protection and pension solutions may fit into their overall financial plan.”

title: Can tech innovations lower your energy bill?
description: A competition backed by ESB and international power companies is generating improved efficiencies and relations
content:
What kind of a difference can a spray-on coating make to your electricity bill? Well, that’s exactly the question asked, and answered, by a UK-based start-up, AssetCool, which last year won the Free Electrons contest, an annual innovation lab backed by ESB and five other international energy suppliers.
AssetCool has developed a system whereby high-tension power lines can be coated with various materials that improve their transmission of electricity. The coating is applied by an autonomous device that rolls along on wheels attached to the power line itself, rather like a drone riding an upside-down bicycle.
“We hadn’t come across anything like this before,” Donal Phelan, ESB’s head of strategy, innovation and transformation tells Business Ireland magazine. “Their technology is a coating that can be applied to overhead power lines so that they can carry more power − as much as 10-30 per cent more power.”
Essentially, the coating means that the power line can radiate excess heat out to the surrounding air more efficiently. Heat is the enemy of power lines and electrical transmission – ramp up the power too high, according to Phelan, and you’re in danger of causing components to melt.
This is exactly the kind of innovation that the ESB is looking for through its engagement in Free Electrons. The idea is that start-ups are invited to present their projects, which are whittled down to a final shortlist through a series of online meetings, and finally meetings in person. The ESB runs Free Electrons in conjunction with Hong Kong’s CLP, DEP in Portugal, E-On in Germany, Canada’s Hydro Quebec, and Origin Energy in Australia.
The thing is that there is no actual prize for Free Electrons. The only thing the winner takes home is the plaudits for finishing on top. “There’s huge benefit to the start-ups by being in the programme, to the extent that we no longer offer a prize to the winner,” says Phelan. “The prize is you’ve won, and that’s worth huge amounts of money to them. They can take that literally: they can take that to the bank and raise finance as a result.”
So, what’s in it for the ESB, which, along with the other major utilities involved in the programme, has sunk around €16 million into the various innovations provided by nine years of the Free Electrons competition? “It gives us exposure to what is coming into the marketplace, and therefore what products we might be able to offer our customers, and how we might be able to change some of our technological focus,” says Phelan. “Some of the utilities – and we’ve only done a little bit of this – actually take up investments in the start-up companies when they’ve been really impressed by the ideas.”
Which is great – innovation needs to be encouraged, and start-ups incubated – but what does it mean for the average Irish punter, looking aghast at yet another hefty bill for electricity? And it’s worth pointing out at this stage that Irish consumers pay considerably more for their power than our EU cousins. In fact, only in Germany is electricity more expensive.
“It’s very difficult to put a monetary value on what Free Electrons does” Phelan says. “What I can say is that it definitely allows us to offer new services to customers that we couldn’t previously offer. It allows us to carry out works and improvements on the system at an efficiency that we couldn’t have previously procured. Equally, although we don’t advertise it, the cost of running the Free Electrons programme is incredibly cheap. It’s a very, very low-budget programme because the start-ups bear their own costs for taking part in it, and the utility’s costs are quite small.”
That might be cold comfort for some, but there is definite potential in the list of Free Electrons innovations for savings to be made and, one hopes, passed on to consumers down the line.
For example, there’s the arduous task of physically checking Ireland’s network of power lines. “Every year we used to have to carry out an inspection of the entire transmission network. And you would do that by putting up a helicopter with a technical specialist on board, and they would have to fly over the entire network,” Phelan explains.
“And we’ve reduced that down now, because we don’t use helicopters; we use drones. You still have a drone pilot, but you don’t have a technical specialist up there. The drone has high-definition video so it records, and a specialist can look at that in the days and weeks afterwards. And we’ve also, through the Free Electrons programme, actually found companies that can provide AI inspections of the same thing. So instead of going to a specialist who has to spend hours looking at it, you can send the footage to an AI engine, and it will carry out inspections of the headgear at the top of every pole and mast, and we have trained it to recognise the kind of faults that we’re looking for. So, at a fraction of the time and a fraction of the cost, we’re now able to do that same inspection.”
Another Free Electrons boost was from a company that created a “digital twin” of the national grid and predicted – with great accuracy – where faults would occur in stormy conditions, meaning that repair crews could be warned in advance about the most likely spots where they’d be needed.
Speaking of storms, one of the big benefits of the Free Electrons tech extravaganza is a purely human one. “There’s a phenomenal set of personal relationships that we’ve established through Free Electrons,” says Phelan. “After Storm Eowyn, we were bringing in utilities from around the world to help us to rebuild the network, and an awful lot of that comes back to the personal relationships that people have built up.
“We didn’t need to spend six months trying to establish legal contracts between the utilities. We simply phoned somebody that we know well in the other place and said: we need help. And it works the other way too – ESB has sent technicians to other countries to help them when trouble hits.”

title: Is it time to take a fresh look at annuities?
description: Rising interest rates and increased life expectancy mean it may be time for a reassessment
content:
When it comes to retirement options it’s fair to say annuities have received a bad press over the years. They are usually portrayed as extremely poor value in comparison to approved retirement funds (ARFs), with scant attention paid to their advantages. But with interest rates on the rise and global economic volatility increasing, maybe it’s time for a reassessment.
It may be difficult to fathom now, but it’s not so long ago that annuities were the only game in town for defined contribution scheme members and personal pension plan holders. Until 1999, when the then finance minister Charlie McCreevy introduced ARFs, the only flexibility open to those people was how much they wanted to draw down in their lump sum – the remainder had to be invested in an annuity.
That wasn’t always a terrible restriction, however. Back in the good old bad old days, annuity rates were very attractive, or appeared so at least. In the late 1980s and early 1990s rates of around 10 per cent were available. That meant a person with a €500,000 pension pot to invest would get a €50,000 annual pension guaranteed for life.
Hands would be bitten off for a similar deal today.
Like all these things, however, this must be placed in the context of the time. Interest rates were sky high – in double digits for long periods − and inflation was even higher at times. That meant the real value of your retirement income was going to diminish quite significantly over time.
The other thing that has changed is life expectancy. It must be remembered that an annuity is an insurance contract that converts your pension fund into a guaranteed income for the rest of your life. How long you are likely to live, therefore, has a profound influence on the income you’re going to be offered.
Back in 1990, the life expectancy for the average Irish person – if such a being exists – was 74.8 years. In other words, someone retiring at 65 could expect to be receiving a pension for 10 years.
Life expectancy today, on the other hand, is 82.9 years, meaning that the same individual can expect their pension to be paid for almost 18 years. That’s a very big difference.
With interest rates plunging in the late 1990s and early 2000s and again in the post-crash period, annuity rates fell to around 3 per cent in the worst cases. Instead of €50,000 a year, our individual with a €500,000 pension pot could expect €15,000. Not very attractive at all.
Further compounding the loss of appeal is the fact that annuities die with you. Payments from a standard annuity cease upon death, with any residual amount reverting to the insurance company. If you die within a few years of retiring, you’re on the wrong side of the deal. Of course, if you beat the actuaries and live on into your 90s, you’re on a winner.
Things aren’t so extreme today, and rates of 6 per cent and above are available in the market. That leaves the €500,000 pension pot holder with a choice of a guaranteed €30,000 pension for life or taking their chances with an ARF which is a personal investment account offering tax-free growth but subject to normal market rises and falls.
Munro O’Dwyer, who leads PwC Ireland’s retirement and pensions consulting business, agrees that annuities appeared to offer “really poor value” at one stage. That is no longer the case, however.
“Today, with higher interest rates, they are much more plausible,” he says. “Annuities can be thought of as almost like a bond. It was rational when bond yields were really low that you mightn’t invest in an annuity, but that factor has been removed. So, they need to be relooked at. That’s probably the best way to think about it.”
The fact that the annuity dies when you do is a “brilliant property”, he believes. “You can consider that a positive or a negative. But to my mind, if your objective is to spend all of your money, it’s a positive. We can catastrophise and say, what if I get run under a bus? And that can happen. But it’s far more likely you’ll be alive at 100. And the annuity carries on as long as you do. You can spend what you get every week because you know it’s coming the next week if you’re alive. With other products, you can never spend it all. People don’t always think about this that carefully.”
It’s very hard to spend all the money with an ARF. In fact, the great majority of people work very hard at avoiding that eventuality – known as the “bomb out” scenario in the industry – because if it does happen, there will be no pension payments after that.
O’Dwyer says people need to understand the fundamental difference between the two products and contends that people will get lower income from an approved retirement fund. “I know people won’t agree with me, and I know people in the advice community won’t agree with me, because what they’ll say is you can invest and get higher returns and get a higher income from an approved retirement fund. But what they have done is introduce risk into the system without properly explaining it. It does not make sense that you can have an approved retirement fund and a higher income and not have introduced risk into the system.”
In other words, if you take the risk out of the ARF and invest accordingly, you’re going to get a lower income than you would with an annuity. And while you’re paying for the certainty of an annuity through perceived lower returns, you also pay for the potential of higher returns from an ARF through higher risk.
“You can take more risk, but your adviser should be very clear with you that that is what you’re doing,” O’Dwyer points out. “And risk works in two directions. It can bring more income, but it can bring less income and there’s no guarantee of greater income. You’re giving up guarantees and you’re taking on risk.”
Bernard Walsh, head of investments and pensions at Fairstone Ireland, believes annuities still have a role to play. “They hark back to the days of defined benefit pensions when people had a sense that someone was looking after them. They like the feeling of their salary, or part of it, continuing. You can pick the payment date, and many people select the same date as their salary used to be paid.”
Along with that sense of comfort, higher bond yields are making them a bit more attractive, he adds. “Also, you need to look at the totality of pensions. If two people in a relationship are retiring, one can choose an ARF and the other can choose an annuity. That gives them a mix of growth potential and certainty. Also, if someone retires with a number of pension pots from different employments, they can put one of them into an annuity and the others into an ARF.”
Flexibility is an important consideration, he adds. “One of things a lot of people don’t necessarily realise is that they can decide to buy an annuity later with some or all of the money they have in their ARF. However, if you buy an annuity at retirement, it’s game over. The decision is made for all time.”
And when it comes to purchasing an annuity, shopping around is very important. “Most pension schemes will allow you to choose from the open market,” says Walsh. “You can purchase an annuity from a range of providers.”
He notes that on one day in September, one insurer was offering a rate of 6.2 per cent. “That would give someone with a €500,000 pension pot an income of €31,000 per annum for life. Another insurer was offering 5.71 per cent, which would translate into €28,475 per annum.” Over 20 years that’s a difference of €50,500.
O’Dwyer concludes by advising people to think ahead to the longer term when making their decision. “Don’t just think about the 60-year-old you, because you’re not buying these products for the 60-year-old you. You’re buying it for the 70, the 80, the 85-year-old you. With an annuity, there’s no management to it. The big attraction of an annuity is you don’t have to deal with financial advisers any more. It just works and you don’t have to deal with people like me.”

title: ‘It isn’t an easy task to turn a social issue like homelessness into a purpose’
description: The Lighter Side: Alpana Delaney, managing director, Change Please Ireland
content:
Cemal Ezel, founder and volunteer chief executive of Change Please. It isn’t an easy task to turn a social issue like homelessness into a purpose. But especially turning that purpose into a commercially viable global company commands admiration, with the impact now being rolled out across the UK, US, Australia, France and Ireland.
When I set up my own consultancy working with charities in 2010, Andrew Simpson, my business adviser through the Small Business Start up Scheme, Isle of Man, gave me some advice that has always stayed with me. He said: “Have a good think about how far you want to go before you hit the glass ceiling of work-life balance.” It made me pause and think about what success meant to me and how far I wanted to take my career without compromising my family life.
Work-life balance is a top priority for me. It is one of the reasons I started working for myself in 2010, when my babies were young. I built good habits protecting that balance; they have stayed with me now that I work in the social-enterprise sector.
Hamnet. Well deserved Oscar for Jessie Buckley.
Handwritten letters from my grandad when I first left Bombay in 2002.
Slea Head on the outskirts of Dingle has a very special place in my heart. We always brought good weather with us enjoying the breathtaking scenery and crystal clear waters of Coumeenoole beach.
Homes by the sea where I could dip my toes in all oceans of the world.
Complete early bird. I love my sleep. A day with a nap is a good day.
I’d make the accelerated infrastructure plan a priority, with a particular focus on building more homes for both private and social housing, and especially on getting families out of emergency accommodation and into a home of their own.
My darling husband. He is a complete family man and has an uncanny ability to switch off from the work day which I am working towards. He is a true Dub, who was raised very well. We are lucky to have each other and our gorgeous babies.
Dún Laoghaire. Anywhere by the sea is beautiful, but Dún Laoghaire is extra special to me. it’s the first place we’d visit whenever we come over from Isle of Man to visit family. It was the first place in Dublin that I fell in love with.
I’d love to plug Change Please Ireland. We are a wholesale coffee company that put 100 per cent of our profits into employment programmes for people at risk of homelessness.
Our aim is to build an ecosystem of businesses coming together to empower people out of homelessness through the power of coffee, support and employment. Businesses can be part of this local impact simply by serving our coffee as part of their offering.
The question I’d like to ask your readers is: what if your cup of coffee could change someone’s life?

title: Taking female leadership in Irish business to the next level
description: When it comes to increasing the proportion of women in senior roles, companies in Ireland have had mixed success
content:
Grant Thornton’s latest Women in Business report showed women now hold 41.4 per cent of senior management roles in Irish mid-market companies, significantly ahead of the global average of 32.9 per cent. But the Central Statistics Office (CSO) Gender Balance in Business report published last year clearly illustrated that getting to the next level is where the glass ceiling really comes into play; Ireland has zero women chief executives leading publicly listed companies on the Euronext Dublin exchange, while women hold just 19.2 per cent of chief executive roles across large Irish enterprises of more than 250 employees.
When women are chief executives, the companies they lead are significantly more likely than companies led by men to name women to boards and senior leadership positions, according to the 2026 Corporate Women Directors International Report. Observers say the key is ensuring that the next generation of women leaders are ready to assume these roles at the top of the food chain.
Elizabeth Sheehan is country executive of the 30% Club Ireland, a global movement that seeks to increase gender diversity at board and senior management levels. She says Ireland – and other countries – have seen “significant progress” at board level. “But the biggest challenge today is not necessarily the boardroom, it is the executive pipeline that’s seeding into CEO, senior leadership roles, and then subsequently the boardroom.”
Last year the 30% Club Ireland carried out a piece of research called the Courage Dividend, which involved surveying around 130 chief executives, chairs, and senior leaders across Ireland. One of the clearest findings, Sheehan says, was that 43 per cent of those surveyed agreed there is a limited senior female pipeline.
“There are multiple factors; it can never be one single thing, obviously,” she says. “But there is definitely a mid-career ‘squeeze point’, as I am calling it, and it is referred to at other times as the ‘broken rung’.”
Sheehan is adamant there is “no shortage” of talented women coming through the pipeline. “Rather, there is limited visibility of what the pipeline actually is, and what the succession plan is for women,” she says. “Our challenge is ensuring that talented women who are already there within the leadership pathways, that they’re visible, that they’re supported, and that they’re given ample opportunity.”
Companies must consider who is sponsoring women through their leadership journeys. “It’s not just about mentoring − they need the same mentoring opportunities − but we need to ask, are women finding sponsors who can talk for them when they are not in the room, when it comes to issues like succession planning and pay, etc?”
Mary Rose Burke is chief executive of Dublin Chamber. She notes that the purpose of the chamber since its inception 240 years ago has been about social and economic progress. “So, while there’s certainly a social aspect to a female leadership, it’s very clearly a business issue.”
Burke echoes Sheehan’s point about sponsorship, saying she believes it is “far more important” than mentorship. “Sponsorship is the senior person in the room when you’re not there saying, ‘I know who has capability and high potential’ and getting them involved in projects and getting them visibility in front of other senior leaders.” This can also lead to “stretch assignments” – where women are pushed out of their comfort zone to help them learn new skills and gain vital experience.
But for sponsorship to actually “move the dial”, it must be intentional, Burke adds. “It needs to be structured so that people are there advocating for young female talent and highlighting their talent, because we don’t have a talent issue, it’s not a merit issue, it’s purely a progression issue.”
Jillian O’Sullivan, partner in corporate compliance with Grant Thornton, says the Women in Business report shone a spotlight on how far Ireland has come in terms of gender parity in business. “We saw a sharp decline in organisations with all-male leadership teams, which is a very positive indicator of cultural change across Irish business.”
But for O’Sullivan, by far the most encouraging aspect is that this progress has been sustained over time. “When our research began in 2004, women accounted for just 15.6 per cent of senior leaders in Ireland,” she notes. “Today, that figure is more than 41 per cent, which shows that organisations have recognised that they need to make deliberate efforts to improve representation and create opportunities for women to advance into leadership positions.”
Yet the same research showed that while women are holding more senior leadership positions, they are simply not reaching the very top roles in the same numbers. “Women in Ireland are still four times more likely to be CFOs or HR directors than CEOs, and chair positions remain particularly elusive, with women occupying just 2 per cent of those roles,” O’Sullivan admits.
Lorna Conn is chief executive of recruitment form Cpl and chair of the 30% Club Ireland. She points out that women are now the most highly educated segment of the Irish workforce, with 63 per cent of women in employment holding a third-level qualification compared with 51 per cent of men.
“The issue is not whether there are enough capable women; unequivocally we have the smarts to progress to the very top of organisations,” she asserts. “The issue is ensuring that talent continues to progress all the way through to the most senior levels.”
According to O’Sullivan, the focus now needs to shift from setting diversity targets to cementing leadership pathways. “That means looking closely at succession planning, sponsorship, access to high-profile commercial opportunities and ensuring women are gaining the operational and strategic experience that is often viewed as a prerequisite for top leadership positions,” she says. “Organisations need to be identifying future leaders earlier, investing in their development and ensuring they gain the broad commercial, operational and strategic experience that boards typically look for in CEO candidates.”
Melrona Kirrane, an associate professor in organisational psychology at Dublin City University Business School offers a different view. She believes that when it comes to women stepping into chief executive roles, it is the selection process that needs drastic reform and not the pathway. “Pipeline-building is a good thing but that locates the work in HR programming rather than considering how executive committees make decisions,” she says.
Ireland’s own data makes this obvious, Kirrane adds. “Senior executive representation grew nearly two points to 32.3 per cent in 2025 according to the CSO, but CEO representation was essentially flat. If pipelines were the binding constraint, that gap would be closing, but it’s not.” A well-stocked pipeline feeding into an unreformed selection process simply produces more qualified women who still don’t get picked, she says.
The issue is no longer simply getting a seat at the table, O’Sullivan agrees; “It’s making sure women have an equal opportunity to progress from the table to the head of it.”
All agree that caregiving responsibilities is a burden that tends to fall disproportionately on women – the world of work must be cognisant of this. “Resulting career gaps or refused relocations may be read as ‘lack of ambition’ rather than a structural bind,” Kirrane says. “Unequal domestic load still functions as a tax on the years that matter most for executive readiness.”
“There is little value in building a strong pipeline if talented women leave before they reach the roles they have been preparing for,” Conn points out. “Supporting people through different life stages, particularly those involving caring responsibilities, is a critical part of keeping that pipeline intact. Industry absolutely has a role to play in that, and it’s very important that we play it, but broader governmental supports are also needed to help keep women in the workforce and keep them progressing for longer.”
Kirrane is programme director of Let’s Lead!, DCU Business School’s flagship executive leadership programme for senior women. “Our programme surfaces the above issues, and others like them, for frank and honest examination in the context of women’s professional experiences,” she explains. “Above all, it develops courage, visibility, self- and other-awareness so women can translate their ambition into reality without losing sight of the goals they set and the values they hold.”
Burke warns that any complacency could see recent progress reversed; it emerged earlier this year that female representation on the boards of Ireland’s largest listed companies had taken a small dip, standing at 40 per cent last year, compared with 42 per cent the previous year.
“A lot of organisations are navigating economic uncertainty, workforce pressures, technological change and a changing global environment.” Maintaining the momentum of recent years is crucial, she says. “We need very intentional leadership to keep us going on this journey – I would be nervous that if we were to take the eye off the ball on female leadership that it would regress.”

title: Cars for simpler times
description: It is still possible to buy cars without hybrid or electric power, and even with a manual gearbox. Strike fast, though, because the window is closing
content:
Sometimes, you just want a car. Along with the electric car revolution (which is, don’t get us wrong, a good thing) car makers have taken the opportunity to try to give their products some of the same appeal as our mobile phones, tablets and laptops. Every car company, at some point or another, has said it wants to be considered a tech brand that just happens to make things with wheels. Cars have sprouted massive touchscreens (sometimes more than one at a time), full-width displays, digital cameras instead of mirrors (best avoided – they’re really not worth the hassle), and the ability to use your phone as the key thanks to NFC technology.
Sometimes, though, you just want a car. You just want to be able to sit in, switch on and drive off, maybe even changing gears for yourself, without having to plan charging stops, nor go through a whole series of on-screen menus to silence the beeps and bongs before departing the kerbside.
The good news is that you can still buy cars like that. The bad news is that, a) many of them are wildly expensive and, b) of the ones you can actually afford, they’re not going to be around for much longer, so you’d better get your skates on.
While electric cars have stolen the headlines this year, becoming for the first time ever the most popular choice of “fuel” among Irish car buyers – leaving petrol, diesel, and hybrid behind – there has been a much bigger change happening in the background. The manual gearbox is dying, with only 35 per cent of Irish new car buyers, so far in 2026, choosing a gearbox controlled by human hand.
Ireland is not alone in that respect. In the UK, there are now proposals to phase out manual gearbox driving instruction unless someone specifically seeks it out. Obviously, electric cars have played their part in this – there are currently no EVs with a manual box – but it’s broader than just that. Car makers have phased out manuals because automatic gearboxes are now smart enough to be able to trim a car’s CO2 emissions, and equally, it’s cheaper to just build a car with one gearbox, rather than a choice of two, and so manuals are on the way out.
On the way out, but not quite dead yet. You can still buy a Mazda MX-5 sports car, for instance, and you really should if you can. It remains one of the very best cars you can drive, it’s not over-priced, it’s frugal, and it comes with both a small dashboard touchscreen and a manual gearbox that feels so perfectly machined and precise that you half expect to find a Rolex label on the gear lever. You don’t have to go for a two-seat sports car either – the same basic gearbox features in the likes of the Mazda 3 hatchback and saloon, and the Mazda CX-30 crossover, both of which come highly recommended in both the driving pleasure and simplicity stakes.
Elsewhere, the manual gearbox clings on. Skoda still offers the Octavia saloon, in its basic 1.5 TSI form, with a manual as well, while the smaller Kamiq, Scala, and Fabia all also come with “proper” gearboxes. In fact, the basic 95hp Kamiq and Scala actually come with a mere five-speed manual, if you really want to recreate that 1990s feel. Thankfully, those three smaller cars also have smaller, simpler touchscreens too, which makes life on board feel rather wonderfully less complicated.
You can also still buy the Seat Ibiza, Arona, and Leon with a manual transmission, while the Volkswagen Polo, Golf, and T-Cross are all still manual-equipped in basic form. Audi is pretty much the last holdout of the manual gearbox in the premium-badge market, with the basic version of the little A1 hatchback still available with a self-shifter, as is the A3 hatchback and saloon. If you go looking for a manual ‘box with Audi’s rivals over at BMW and Mercedes, you’ll be left disappointed.
Opel, Peugeot, Citroen, Fiat, Jeep, Dacia, Ford, Hyundai, Kia, Renault, Suzuki, and Toyota also all still offer at least one model with a manual, but the available choice really is either narrowing down to bargain-bucket basic models or, as in the case of Toyota, wild and expensive enthusiasts’ cars such as the high-performance GR Yaris (another car, like the Mazda MX-5, that totally nails the brilliant, polished, mechanical feel of a great manual gearshift).
In a few years, even these might be gone, as the mainstream of motoring leaves the manual gearbox behind altogether. Or will it? Actually, there are some rumblings that the human-controlled gearbox might not be quite dead after all.
At the highest possible level, it’s definitely not. McLaren has just shown off the McL6 GT, a superfast supercar, with a multimillion euro price tag, that has at its heart a traditional six-speed manual gearbox, complete with an exposed shift mechanism in the cabin so you can see all the delicate linkages at work. Ferrari, having given up on its traditional “open gate” manual boxes more than a decade ago, is now kind of bringing them back, offering its 12Cilindri V12 grand tourer with an odd gearbox that’s technically an automatic, but which can be shifted manually through one of those traditional “clack-clack” shifters if you like.
Back at a more potentially affordable level, Toyota says that it’s working on a manual gearbox that will work with future electric cars, bringing back a level of entertaining tactility to a type of car that so far, for the most part, hasn’t technically had a gearbox at all – electric cars usually just have a single reduction gear, which slows down the wild spinning of an electric motor to a speed that’s compatible with tyres and tarmac.
Actually, we’ve driven an electric car with a manual gearbox. A few years ago, Opel showed off a concept car called the Manta GSe ElektroMOD. That car used a modern set of batteries and an electric motor but built them into the restored body of a classic 1960s Opel Manta coupe, which oddly kept its original four-speed manual gearbox. It was a strange sensation, as you could just leave it in any gear you wanted and drive it like a modern EV, or you could shift gears yourself, at a whim, making the driving experience more engaging.
And that, it seems, is the trick to all this, and the reason why car makers have still not quite abandoned the idea of manual gearboxes. While electric car sales are growing fast, there is still a strong sense that they’ve not been designed for fun. Quite the opposite – electric cars are sold on their combo of silent running and frugal cost base. But car makers know that car enthusiasts – petrolheads if you prefer – are also opinion-makers, and if at least some EVs can be turned into something rather more fun and enjoyable, then more happy vibes might be in the air regarding battery power, which might convince a few more people to make the switch sooner. Equally, with car ownership as a basic concept under pressure from legislators and environmental advocates, car companies are scrambling for reasons to actually buy and own a car, knowing that few, if any, car purchases are truly rational.
Of course, you could go completely the other way. Recently we drove a tiny Morgan Super 3 sports car, which not only doesn’t have any hybrid assistance, it also doesn’t have power steering. Or a touchscreen. Or even a windscreen or a roof. It’s even lacking a fourth wheel, but it’s one of the most spectacularly enjoyable cars we’ve driven in years. There’s a lesson in there somewhere – you can try to turn a car into an oversized mobile phone all you like, but for fun, enjoyment, and engagement there’s no substitute for simplicity.

title: Addressing Ireland’s data centre dilemma
description: Ireland’s digital economy needs data centres but their energy demands raise difficult questions about infrastructure, investment and climate targets
content:
Few pieces of infrastructure have become as contentious in Ireland as data centres. To supporters, they are critical infrastructure underpinning cloud computing, artificial intelligence and the multinational technology sector. To critics, their growing electricity demand exposes tensions between Ireland’s industrial policy and climate ambitions.
The question is, how many can the State accommodate, and under what conditions?
Data centres form an important part of Ireland’s foreign direct investment proposition, says Matt Kennedy, global head of client transformation at IDA Ireland.
“Ireland’s FDI performance over the past year demonstrates that the country remains highly competitive, but that competitiveness is increasingly shaped by the availability of enabling infrastructure across energy, digital connectivity, talent and innovation.”
IDA Ireland’s Adapt Intelligently strategy identifies digitalisation and sustainability as mutually reinforcing growth drivers, particularly in sectors such as AI, cloud services, semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, life sciences and financial services.
Kennedy acknowledges that data centres are large energy users and says their development must align with Ireland’s climate, energy security and infrastructure objectives.
“The issue is therefore not whether Ireland should pursue unlimited growth, but whether Ireland can support strategically important digital infrastructure in a planned, sustainable and regionally balanced way.”
Patrick Brodie, assistant professor in UCD’s School of Information and Communications Studies, takes a different view. “The importance of data centres to Ireland’s economy is drastically overstated,” he says.
Brodie points to the government-commissioned KPMG report The Value of Data Centres to Ireland, which argued that 876,000 jobs, or 32 per cent of national employment, were dependent on the sector. “This basically asserts that a huge proportion of jobs that require frequent use of cloud services are dependent on hyperscale data centres being located in Ireland – an irresponsible claim that was widely called out in the media.”
Brodie claims data centres are a symptom of the privileging of digital and industrial policies that support immense wealth concentration and the disproportionate allocation of ecological resources towards one sector of the economy.
“Developmental trade-offs assume that there is also a notable proportion of jobs supported. However, as the KPMG report shows, direct employment is only in the order of a few thousand jobs, and most are exhausted after the construction phase.”
Technology can make a meaningful difference to the environmental footprint of data centres, says Grit Young, EY Ireland technology, media and entertainment, and telecommunications industry leader.
“More efficient equipment, better cooling and smarter management of workloads can all reduce energy and water use,” she says. “There is also scope to remove waste, such as servers that consume electricity while doing very little. Innovation needs to be matched by cleaner energy and continued investment in the grid.”
For Ireland, she says, developing offshore wind is particularly important, with big technology companies able to provide long-term demand through power purchase agreements.
Brodie says focusing on efficiency risks overlooking how resources and economic power are distributed. “The global cloud market is dominated by three US monopolies, all of whom have major data centre locations in Ireland: Amazon Web Services, Google, and Microsoft together control around 65 per cent of the global market share.”
These tech hyperscalers, he says, account for a large proportion of energy and water demand in Ireland, including 23 per cent of our electricity. “These are resources that are being directed towards the profits of just a few companies. This is not to mention research showing that data centres’ electricity usage will be directly responsible for Ireland missing its binding climate targets.”
Brodie argues that policy is focused on adapting Ireland’s infrastructure to accommodate continued expansion by large technology companies.
“The problem is thus a shortsighted and reactive industrial policy, which relies on large-scale industrial investment by US FDI companies.”
Kennedy rejects the idea that Ireland faces a straightforward choice between economic development and environmental responsibility.
“Ireland needs a more integrated discussion about the total energy system, the pace of renewable deployment, grid reinforcement, demand flexibility and the role of digital infrastructure in supporting productivity and decarbonisation across the economy.”
Data centres have substantial electricity requirements, he acknowledges, but support services across the economy, including cloud computing, AI, public-sector digital services, financial services and enterprise software.
Digitalisation can also contribute to decarbonisation through smarter grids, improved demand forecasting, more efficient industrial processes and environmental monitoring.
“The priority should be to move from an ad hoc debate about individual electricity users to a plan-led approach that balances economic opportunity, climate commitments, affordability, and security of supply.”
In Young’s view, rather than approaching data centre development on an individual country basis, Ireland “should link into a collective European strategy on digital infrastructure and AI”.
