Europe cannot afford to fall too far behind in AI development, she says. Instead, it should identify the most appropriate locations for digital infrastructure based on climate, energy and technological considerations.
Kennedy believes a complete halt to further large-scale data centres would send a significant signal to international investors. “A risk is that investors would interpret it as a constraint on Ireland’s ability to provide the digital and energy infrastructure required for long-term growth.”
The consequences, he argues, could extend to other technology-intensive industries and weaken Ireland’s proposition for FDI.
“The more balanced approach is to ensure that policy and infrastructure keep pace with the urgent need for decarbonisation, while enabling strategically important investment where it is aligned with renewable energy, grid capacity, regional development and national competitiveness.”

title: Ikea is coming for your unwanted furniture – and your wallet
description: That Billy bookcase gathering dust? The Swedish retailer wants someone else to have it and it might just pay you
content:
H ow many Ikea items do you have in your home? For the 65 per cent of Irish adults who say they have at least one, the launch last week of a new second-hand online marketplace here by the Swedish giant will be good news.
Irish fans of the world’s biggest furniture retailer are legion. Its Ballymun shop was its best performing store globally in 2023, with some 3.2 million customers walking through the door. Total retail sales here reached €247.3 million last year, with Irish customers buying more of Ikea’s moving boxes and red wine glasses than any other country in the world.
Now, you will be able to flog your old Ikea furniture and buy preloved items on the cheap through the retailer too. So how will it work, can you make money, why is Ikea doing it – and during this Climate Action Week, is it really any good for the environment?
The launch of Ikea’s second-hand marketplace means customers who have signed up to the company’s Ikea Family membership scheme can connect to buy and sell pre-owned Ikea items locally. Think eBay , Vinted or Facebook Marketplace – but only for Ikea goods.
The new digital second-hand shop will make it easier for people to make some money from old Ikea furniture they no longer need, while helping others to find discounted, pre-owned items, including those no longer available in stores, says Ikea.
The only things you can’t resell are kitchen accessories, mattresses and food.
The launch here follows successful trials by the Swedish company of online second-hand marketplaces in Spain, Norway, Portugal, Poland, Sweden and Belgium.
In those countries, demand has been strongest for bedroom furniture, storage solutions and livingroom sofas and chairs. The company’s Kallax storage cubes and its Malm chest of drawers have emerged as two of the most popular items being traded second-hand to date.
Items are being listed for less than half of their full retail price, says Ikea.
“When we look at the average reduction in price for items listed, it’s 60 per cent or less,” says Greg Lucas, sustainability manager, Ikea UK and Ireland.
Got your eye on the popular Malm Storklinta chest of six drawers? These had been retailing new this summer for €160; now you could nab a set second-hand and in good nick for just €96.
That Besta TV unit that was retailing for €255? If the retailer’s predictions are correct, you could now secure a preloved model from another Ikea Family member for about €100.
Ikea has already cut its prices on about 1,500 products by between 15 and 25 per cent in 20 European countries, including Ireland, since September 1st. The move was an attempt by the flat-pack furniture retailer to counter the cost-of-living crisis as consumer confidence continues to remain depressed.
So, if you are selling products second-hand that you bought before the price drop, you may not recoup quite so much of your original spend.
Unlike some second-hand marketplaces, sellers on Ikea’s site can sell for free, at least for now. Selling through some competing third-party sites can attract fees.
For example, a second-hand Ikea Kallax for sale in Ireland on Vinted right now is priced at €25, but a fee of €1.95 is charged to “cover the cost of providing a safe smooth experience for our community”, says Vinted.
Posting a product for sale on the Ikea site is arguably easier too. Sellers simply tick the product they are selling from Ikea’s vast library, and their ad will pre-populate with the exact description and dimensions, with links to spare parts. Some small spare parts are free. Sellers can also post photos of the item they have taken themselves.
“It’s down to the buyer to highlight what condition it’s in today,” says Lucas.
Helpfully, buyers can post reviews of sellers too, which should help to keep community members honest.
You can choose to receive payment by bank transfer or opt for an Ikea digital refund card – which will give sellers a 15 per cent bonus.
Sellers accepting payment via the refund card can use the credit against new Ikea products. You can also use it to buy other second-hand products in store through the company’s Buyback and Resell service.
[ The pleasures of Vinted have often little to do with money, although the cash is nice Opens in new window ]
This service enables customers to sell eligible products back to Ikea in exchange for in-store credit. By enabling this, Ikea may be countering criticism that the 15 per cent bonus incentivises us back into the shop to buy yet more new stuff on a planet on which there is already too much stuff.
You can also use the card to buy food at Ikea.
When an item is purchased, payment is held securely by Ikea’s payment service provider until the buyer has collected or received the item and confirms acceptance through the marketplace. At that point, a 48-hour buyer protection period begins.
During this period, the buyer can raise an issue if the product does not match its listing. For example, buyers can contact support if there are missing parts, undisclosed damage, or if the item is not an authentic Ikea product.
If there are no issues, payment is automatically released to the seller.
If there is an issue, the payment remains on hold while a refund request is reviewed in line with the marketplace’s buyer protection policy. Ikea says it can support dispute resolution where needed.
While there are no fees on the Irish site for now, the company has introduced a “buyer protection fee” in Spain, which it says supports “safeguards”, like ensuring only authentic Ikea products in usable condition are advertised and only by Ikea Family members.
Sellers and buyers will have to arrange delivery and/or pickup between themselves. But with Ikea products so ubiquitous in Irish homes, you probably won’t have a hard time finding a Billy bookcase or Kallax cube near you.
Indeed, after just 10 years in the State, some 65 per cent of Irish adults say they have at least one Ikea product in their home, according to research the company published in July 2019 to mark that 10th anniversary.
One in four people in Ireland surveyed said that Ikea was their go-to when moving into a new home, with another 21 per cent saying they visited the furniture giant when planning their first home with their partner. Some 70 per cent of Irish parents said they had Ikea products in their home.
Despite the lack of a delivery service, buying second-hand could prove more convenient than buying new. Finding a good-as-new Poang chair for sale in your own town will spare you the schlep to Ballymun, where a tour of the gargantuan shop has been known to test the most solid of relationships.
[ What Irish shoppers love to buy in Ikea Opens in new window ]
Ikea says it is “exploring” a “convenient, affordable and sustainable” delivery service for bulky items, says Lucas.
It piloted the use of TipTapp in Sweden and Lisbon this summer. This is a peer-to-peer mobile app that matches people who need help moving or delivering items with people who have a car and spare time.
“Once the Ikea online marketplace purchase is completed, the buyer can post a ‘delivery task’, set the price they are prepared to pay for delivery and receive offers from available ‘helpers’,” says Ikea.
They can compare helper ratings and reviews, choose a helper, track delivery in real time and pay securely once the item arrives. For those who just can’t wait for that Poang chair, collection and delivery may even be available on the same day.
Ikea’s timing in Ireland is something to behold. Maybe it’s not so much the Scandi-inspired aesthetic that resonates with us so much as its ability to meet the moment. And we’ve had our moments.
Ikea opened its big blue Lego-like superstore in Dublin 11 in 2009 at the height of Ireland’s financial crash. Yes, its furniture was mass-produced and everywhere, but it was also affordable at a time when roughly 150,000 mortgage borrowers had plunged into negative equity, according to estimates from the Economic and Social Research Institute think tank, with house prices dropping from their early-2007 peak.
The higher-end furniture retailer Habitat had shut up shop in Dublin and Galway in 2008 due, it said, to a “severe” deterioration in sales.
[ ‘Vinted is a wolf in sheep’s clothing’: Ireland’s vintage stores on facing down online challenges Opens in new window ]
Now, almost 20 years on from the crash, we find ourselves punch-drunk from another cost-of-living crisis and an ongoing housing crisis, and with further economic clouds scrambling on the horizon. The launch of Ikea’s second-hand selling website here on the day Budget 2027 was unveiled is well timed, or portentous.
Being able to furnish your entire home and garden affordably and from one retailer, using new or second-hand products, is not to be sniffed at. Even if everyone in your estate has the same Billy bookcase.
Second-hand shopping has become big business, and Ikea knows it. It has emerged as a “quiet but significant shift” in Irish consumer behaviour, according to analysis by RedC.
It’s no longer a niche trend confined to charity shops, vintage enthusiasts or bargain hunters. Increasingly, it is becoming a normal part of everyday consumer behaviour in Ireland, says RedC.
It’s not just a way to save money but part of a broader move towards more sustainable and circular patterns of consumption. Second-hand shopping is becoming an established part of life here.
Brands are having to rethink how they compete in a world where new products increasingly sit alongside refurbished, reused and preloved alternatives.
More than nine in 10 adults in Ireland say they shop for second-hand goods, according to research commissioned by Ikea in September. Some 45 per cent of adults said they buy pre-owned furniture.
[ Are you a fool to pay full price? From paint to phones, buying second-hand can slash your costs Opens in new window ]
No doubt Ikea has been watching established second-hand marketplaces like eBay, Facebook Marketplace and Vinted steal its Swedish meatball lunch. Those platforms are full of listings of second-hand Ikea items, likely hitting sales of new Ikea products while returning nothing to the retailer.
So now, Ikea is getting in on the act. By launching its own second-hand marketplace here, it is harvesting something back from this thriving second-hand market of its own products. By incentivising payment through an Ikea digital refund card, money from transacting its products second-hand gets directed back to Ikea.
Buying second hand is great, says the Rediscovery Centre, the National Centre for the Circular Economy, but buying less overall, and repairing what you have, is better.
“The bigger challenge is that, in Ireland, we simply consume too much,” says Claire Downey, chief executive of the Rediscovery Centre, which is headquartered just over a kilometre from Ikea’s Ballymun outlet.
Irish homes contain an average of €531 worth of unused home and garden furniture, according to Ikea’s research, and unused home decor and accessories worth an average of €347. Yikes.
That baby changing table you bought new, and used only for a few short years, could have been borrowed.
“Many of the things we buy are not needed for long. Borrowing, sharing and renting are great alternatives to buying and they help to reduce the amount of stuff we accumulate in the first place, as well as saving money and space in our homes,” says Downey.
[ Ikea’s tantalising promise is that we are all just one good shoe rack away from nirvana Opens in new window ]
Circular.ie and Repairmystuff.ie are digital platforms that support communities to reduce consumption and waste by sharing, reusing and repairing, she says.
Many of the things we spend money replacing could easily be repaired, says Downey.
“We’d love to see a shift in mindset where people automatically consider repairing, renting and borrowing, or buying second-hand before buying new.”

title: Style counsel: Building brands in a notoriously tough business
description: Irish fashion designers and graduates offer insights on making your mark in a sector that is constantly in the spotlight
content:
Many young designers aspire to be the next Jonathon Anderson, Sean McGirr or Simone Rocha, but how do our young creative fashionistas go about establishing themselves and their brands in a notoriously tough and competitive business? We spoke to some of the people behind Ireland’s recent fashion success stories and to those graduating into the business.
Faye Anna Rochford is the founder and director of the sustainable fashion label FéRí. She graduated from NCAD in 2009 with a BA degree in fashion design. She found support for creating her label and networking opportunities by joining the Council of Irish Fashion Designers and the Design & Crafts Council of Ireland, plus a working group called Acorn 7.
Rochford’s sumptuous styles was in the spotlight this summer when Sarah Jessica Parker of Sex and the City fame wore a stunning fuchsia asymmetrical dress from her collection to the Abbey Theatre. The high-quality fabric and eye-catching shade caught the attention of the international paparazzi.
The designer’s commitment to ethical, sustainable fashion is integral to her success.
“My experience includes working with Andrea Crews in Paris, Diane Von Fürstenberg in New York and milliner Philip Treacy,” she says. “I returned to Ireland to pursue my dream of creating FéRí and to become a mother.”
FéRí collections are designed in an array of colourful prints and embroideries which are hand painted in her studio in Wexford. “Every piece is made using natural certified organic fabrics.”
Rochford believes young designers need more enterprise assistance. “The fashion industry is given a more serious platform in other EU countries, but the designers of Ireland are not giving up. Huge changes at government level, including Ireland’s upcoming recycling scheme for textiles, are happening in our industry and more than ever we need to support each other. We need to help emerging designers to stand up for what we believe in.”
Rochford also believes in the power of mentoring younger college students. “I have recently been approached to do this by a fashion college, and I am surprised it hasn’t happened sooner. This is a wonderful way for students to learn and avail of our advice on their journeys.”
Award-winning designer Charlotte Carvill (23), from Stepaside in Dublin, went to NCAD Dublin to pursue her love of fashion design. “I started out with basically zero knowledge of sewing and pattern cutting and the amount I learned over the course of my degree is crazy,” she says. “I felt grateful to be in an environment with my amazing friends in my class where we got to create whatever we liked with the support and guidance from the tutors and technicians.
“In semester one we did a project with River Island who chose one student to receive a bursary and paid internship opportunity. This initiative was a great opportunity to secure a job after college and also to work towards a commercial brief.”
Charlotte Carvill’s collection won the prestigious annual graduate Brown Thomas Designer to Watch Bursary 2026. “I got to display my work as part of the Brown Thomas Create exhibition for six weeks in store over the summer. I also won a cash award, which I am using to help me move to London to find a job in the industry.
“In my You Are Here capsule collection I chose themes of comfort and functionality to create a sense of safety and preparedness for hiking or festival goers to enjoy the experience, regardless of weather or circumstance.”
The collection colours were inspired by the landscapes around Three Rock Mountain. Her outfits include a unique twist on the camouflage theme – ultra baggy trousers with splashes of colour and functional matching jackets.
Carvill advises aspiring designers to utilise the strengths of social media. “It’s impossible not to be influenced by social media as a designer in the modern world. My other biggest inspiration is my friends and current trends. I reimagine the clothes that my friends and I wear at festivals.”
Her role models include Irish fashion designer Robyn Lynch. “Not only do I love her as a designer, but I admire her as a businesswoman. What she has achieved in such a short space of time is so impressive. I also love her ready-to-wear pieces − beautifully made, with quality fabric.”
She wants to gain experience and work for a brand in London before returning to set up her own label in Dublin. “I would prefer to work for a small team to get involved in all aspects of the business and learn more skills. I worked as a design intern in Paris during my Erasmus year alongside the creative director every day and I learned so much observing him doing his work.”
Róisín Heffernan is the designer behind the So Roe label. Her fashion brand became a runway success last year at Irish Fashion Week which provided a launch pad for her ethereal and feminine looks. She is a graduate of fashion design at Limerick School of Art and Design (LSAD), completed a postgraduate in entrepreneurship at Trinity College Dublin and a Diploma in Innovation for Sustainability at UCD.
“Sustainability was a key area that I felt increasingly important to understand. As a designer, I feel a responsibility to educate myself as much as possible, both for my own knowledge and for the future of my business,” she says.
“Looking back, the combination of fashion design, entrepreneurship and sustainability has been hugely important to my journey. They became the three core pillars of my education and ultimately of developing my own business.”
So, what would Heffernan advise those trying to launch a brand? “For me, the most important skills I learned were pattern drafting, sewing and design development. Learning to use industrial sewing machines and understanding how to draft a garment are fundamental. You are essentially constructing something around the human body, but it starts very simply with a pencil and paper, mapping out the individual pattern pieces and working out how to create the original garment. Those technical skills gave me a strong foundation as a designer and allowed me to translate a sketch into an actual, wearable garment.”
One of her favourite projects was a coat commission in college. She sourced 100 per cent Irish Magee wool to create a full-length coat. “I absolutely love the finished coat and still wear it all the time. It was really rewarding to create something from a beautiful Irish fabric and end up wearing it years later.”
She says supports such as the Design Council Ireland Future Makers Awards have been helpful, as fashion design courses can be expensive to take part in. “The ongoing costs of materials, fabrics, trimmings, sewing machines, tools and other equipment rise throughout the duration of the course.
“New events such as Ireland Fashion Week are playing an important role in creating a platform for Irish designers, she says. “For emerging designers, financial support is necessary to cover the costs of developing collections, sourcing materials and putting on shows. Having access to a catwalk could make a real difference in helping designers.”
From So Roe’s business perspective, the financial side of setting up a fashion business was very challenging. “I worked part-time in Brown Thomas for two years alongside running my studio. I worked three days a week in my part-time job and the rest of the week working in the studio.”
Heffernan recently started her So Roe Bridal side. “I am also currently stocked in The Slow Concept in Dingle. The owners stock solely Irish-made fashion for more than 20 Irish designers. The quality of the pieces is absolutely worth the trip down.”
She would like to hear more from mentors in the industry. “I’d love to see more specialists from across the industry talk about their roles in college, from experienced pattern drafters to alterations specialists, to give students a better understanding of the business. Being a content creator is an important part of running a fashion business too. For many people, social media is where they first discover a designer, so having a strong presence is necessary.”
What advice would she give young graduates?
“To emerging talented graduates – I would say focus on your own designs rather than designing what you think other people will like. Stay true to your vision. Invest in good-quality tools that you use regularly in your work. Do post on social media consistently and put yourself outside your comfort zone.”
As Ireland’s new generation of emerging and acclaimed designers hone their skills and make waves on domestic and international catwalks – the future of our fashion industry looks like it’s in safe and talented hands.

title: How Tesco is helping to keep the west’s motorcycle medical service safely on the road
description: Blood Bike West helps to deliver life-saving consignments to hospitals and healthcare sites such as hospices, clinics, care homes and laboratories
content:
For the past 14 years, Blood Bike West’s motorbikes have criss-crossed the country delivering life-saving blood, breast milk, and urgent medical supplies to where they are needed.
The Galway based charity provides a vital out of hours service for this most precious of cargo, in the evenings and at weekends.
“The HSE provides a fantastic service but after-hours things can get awkward, so if we can help carry that burden, that’s what we are here to do,” says Noel Boyhan, chair of Blood Bike West.
He and his team deliver their life-saving consignments between hospitals and healthcare sites such as hospices, clinics, care homes and laboratories. In some cases, deliveries are made to and from a patient’s own home, freeing them from having to make a journey while unwell.
Incredibly, all of this vital work is done on a voluntary basis.
“It’s about trying to give something back, to help the community, and you tend not to want to be paid for that,” explains Boyhan.
Indeed, such is the generosity of its volunteers that very few even claim reimbursement for expenses such as fuel.
“Like all volunteer organisations, we attract a certain type of person,” he says with pride. “It means that, of the money that comes in as donations to us, 100 per cent goes to the running of the organisation.”
Blood Bike West is extremely efficient operationally too, thanks to a rostering app developed by one of its members.
As a result, each volunteer can choose shifts to suit their lifestyle and, typically, their day job.
“During the week it’s from 7pm to 7am, and for those 12 hours you’d be expected to be available to collect, deliver and do whatever is needed,” explains Boyhan.
Blood Bikes, with their distinctive livery, emergency lights and narrow profile, can get through busy traffic to reach their destination quickly and safely. A Blood Bike West van is used for larger packages and in very bad weather conditions.
Each volunteer’s shift starts with safety checks on their bike.
“We have a duty of care to our riders and to make sure we provide the system in the safest and most reliable way possible,” he says. “We also demand that people take an advanced driving course, pretty much the same qualification as the Garda riders have.”
Currently Blood Bike West has a team of 40 volunteer riders, six van drivers and six volunteer controllers.
Each is there to help the organisation deliver on its central mission: to assist positive patient outcomes through the efficient and reliable transport of medical consignments – at no cost to patients.
While it provides this service primarily across the western region, if a longer journey is required, Blood Bike West’s volunteers will not be found wanting.
The organisation was founded by Mike Carty in 2012, after seeing a TV programme about a similar service in the UK.
Together with four friends, he set about creating the first such service in Galway. While it initially took time to introduce hospitals and healthcare providers to the concept, demand quickly grew, and today the distinctive Blood Bike vehicles are a familiar sight across the region.
The service operates between 7pm and 7am during the week, 24 hours a day at weekends, and the aim is to respond to each call out within an hour.
Whether collecting blood samples from a hospice, transporting urgent medical supplies between hospitals, or delivering a forgotten medication to a recently discharged patient, every journey helps healthcare professionals to provide timely care.
Blood Bike West’s volunteers simply collect and deliver sealed packages, allowing medical staff to focus on treating patients.
That includes children undergoing cancer treatment. Rather than having to make weekly trips to Dublin for blood tests, for example, families can now take blood samples at home, and have them collected by Blood Bike volunteers, for delivery to the hospital.
“It saves a family having to drag their child into the hospital to get a blood sample taken and is one of the most satisfying things we do,” says Boyhan.
It’s especially joyous when their young patients recover. In one case a child cancer survivor invited the team to their school to celebrate their recovery.
The charity also plays an important role in supporting the Human Milk Bank, an initiative that collects donated breast milk from mothers and transports it for screening before it reaches neonatal units and paediatric wards caring for premature and critically ill babies throughout Ireland.
Since it was established in 2000, the Human Milk Bank has helped deliver precious donor milk to thousands of vulnerable babies all over the country.
During Covid-19, Blood Bike West expanded its service to deliver medications from pharmacies directly to people’s homes, a service it still provides when needed.
Blood Bike West has received support from the Tesco Ireland Community Fund on more than one occasion, through the familiar blue donation tokens made available at stores in Athenry and Knocknacarra.
Being one of the local choices available in store helps the charity not just to raise money but also grows awareness of the service, which helps with wider fundraising too.
The Tesco funding helps the charity meet essential day to day running costs, including fuel, vehicle maintenance and insurance. Safety gear is also vital for the team, including helmets and air vests, all of which are costly.
Powered by volunteers and backed by its local community, the money from Tesco’s Community Fund is helping Blood Bike West to continue expanding its life-saving service.
“We can use it for our day to day running expenses, which is absolutely fantastic. It costs in the region of €30,000 to keep the five bikes and the van on the road, so the money is an absolute godsend for us,” he says.
“The funding from Tesco helps keep the wheels turning.”
Tesco’s Community Fund is a core part of the retailer’s ‘That’s Every Little Helps’ campaign. Blue Tokens have helped more than 27,000 community projects secure €10 million since it launched in 2014.
For more information on the Tesco Community Fund, or to nominate a cause close to your heart to receive funding, visit tescoireland.ie

title: When it comes to climate change, no company is an island
description: The impact of climate change on business is about investing in resilience as well as reducing emissions
content:
Adapting to the changing climate isn’t simply about reducing emissions. Naturally, that aspect is important for businesses for both ethical and regulatory reasons, but the work doesn’t stop there.
Mitigation alone doesn’t get the job done when it comes to external factors. Severe weather can hit Irish businesses in a range of ways, from droughts to floods through to storms causing infrastructure interruptions.
Then there are the indirect aspects to bear in mind. It’s not just your business being hit but those of suppliers, distributors, and utility providers.
This is why businesses need to take a much broader approach to addressing the climate change question beyond merely meeting their own emissions reduction targets. Disruption is becoming more frequent and more expensive; that can’t be ignored by any business that hopes to thrive.
“Climate change is a direct balance-sheet and operational risk,” says Barry O’Dwyer, climate change lead at KPMG in Ireland. “Severe weather events like Storm Éowyn in January 2025 generated over €301 million in insurance claims, with business claims accounting for a significant 55 per cent of the overall cost. The average business claim stood at €17,000, compared to €5,745 for household claims.”
All of that was from just one storm. Businesses in Ireland are becoming increasingly exposed to both direct physical damage and a wider interruption of services.
“Climate change is already a significant business risk for Irish companies. Businesses are facing both physical risks, such as flooding and other extreme weather events, and transition risks arising from changing regulations, technologies and customer expectations,” says Kathleen O’Regan, senior executive for sustainability solutions at Enterprise Ireland.
“These challenges can disrupt operations, affect supply chains and increase costs.”
That’s why any business taking on a strategy built around resilience needs to consider not only the company itself but also the suppliers and systems it uses.
That, unfortunately, is where gaps begin to emerge. Businesses have become better at working out what impact climate change has on their operations but less so at making the changes required to deal with it.
“While EU reporting standards like CSRD [the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive] have driven progress in adaptation planning, a significant gap remains between understanding exposure and taking physical adaptation measures,” says O’Dwyer.
“Many Irish firms still lag in proactive climate adaptation, often treating sustainability as a regulatory box to tick rather than a core commercial strategy.”
There’s a substantial difference between reporting a risk and actually reducing its potential impact. It’s all well and good knowing a vulnerability but that won’t help if that knowledge doesn’t change the decisions being made.
“Many Irish businesses have made progress on climate mitigation but climate adaptation has generally received less attention,” says O’Regan.
“The biggest gap is often a lack of understanding of how climate risks could affect operations and supply chains and the financial impact this could have on the business.”
That’s why there is a need to move from merely identifying the risks towards taking the necessary steps to address them. Of course, it’s best to actually know what those risks are in detail so you can make the best choices.
“Irish businesses cannot afford to take a wait-and-see approach to climate risk. Companies should assess how extreme weather and other climate impacts could affect their operations and supply chains and put plans in place to reduce their vulnerability,” says O’Regan.
“This may include improving resource efficiency, investing in new technologies or diversifying suppliers.”
Think about the actions you need to take. This should involve assessing key locations and partners. From there, work out where there are potential points of failure, what could still work in the event of an interruption, and where you need to invest to limit your exposure.
“Companies should increase their understanding of where and when impacts may occur by executing climate risk assessments to map exposure and vulnerabilities to physical climate risks across facilities and supply chains,” says O’Dwyer.
“Practical actions include upgrading asset infrastructure, diversifying supplier networks to reduce single-point failures, and establishing emergency operational continuity plans.”
There is no one size fits all and a successful approach to adaptation will vary from company to company. Flood protection could be a priority for some, while others may have greater vulnerabilities located with international suppliers.
Whatever the case, climate resilience should become part of everyday operational planning rather than being siloed. Indeed, no company should treat itself as an island in this scenario.
“The impact of climate change on business is increasingly about resilience as well as reducing emissions,” says Stephen Browne, head of public affairs at Dublin Chamber.
“More frequent severe weather events can disrupt transport networks, energy and water supplies, and digital connectivity, with knock-on effects for businesses, their employees and supply chains.”
Browne says businesses need to think holistically, taking in the needs of their partners in the supply chain but also the work done at a national level around infrastructure.
“Companies can take steps to protect their operations and strengthen their supply chains, but they also depend on reliable national infrastructure,” he says.
“That means building greater resilience and additional capacity into our energy, water, transport and communications networks.”
No matter how prepared a business is, there will always be risk. That goes all the way down to employee level, where they may face challenges getting to work or accessing basic utilities like power and water.
That’s why resilience isn’t just a question for a company in isolation but one where it must consider how the infrastructure it depends on operates. Browne says there have been clear signs of progress in this regard.
“For Dublin, the delivery of projects such as the Eastern and Midlands water supply project and the Greater Dublin drainage scheme will be critical. These are not simply projects to accommodate future growth,” he says.
“They are essential to building greater resilience into the region’s water and wastewater systems and ensuring that Dublin can continue to function and compete as the impacts of climate change become more pronounced.”
Of course, any plan will depend on a company’s ability to invest in it, and that requires convincing the board to back it. There is, thankfully, already a strong case for businesses to take this approach.
“Investing in climate resilience is a fundamental strategy for protecting long-term enterprise value, not an optional overhead,” says O’Dwyer.
“Adaptation should therefore be viewed not only as a response to climate risks, but as a strategic investment in resilience, economic stability and long-term prosperity.”
While the upfront costs in such a plan may be off putting, the cost of not acting should something calamitous occur is much greater.
“The question is no longer whether businesses can afford to invest in climate resilience, but whether they can afford not to,” says O’Regan.
“The cost of disruption, whether through extreme weather, supply chain interruptions or business downtime, is often far greater than the cost of preparing in advance.”
Think back to those numbers from Storm Éowyn earlier in this piece. The risk is too great to defer investment. Fortunately, companies don’t have to act alone when taking on this challenge.
“Enterprise Ireland provides a range of supports to help Irish businesses take a proactive approach to managing climate risks, strengthening resilience and enhancing competitiveness,” says O’Regan.
It’s important that companies treat resilience as an investment to secure their futures. That’s no longer a long-term question.
“Resilience is essential not only to long-term viability, but also to maintaining short-term operational and financial stability,” says O’Dwyer.
Don’t wait for the next storm or flood. The best time to make resilience at the core of everyday operations was yesterday. The second best is right now. The risks won’t wait around for you to make up your mind.

title: Out to lunch: Foodie getaways, supper clubs and a new southside restaurant
description: Ireland’s latest dining experiences include pop-up events in the capital and at a luxurious B&B, plus a swish new Dublin restaurant
content:
Give up yer oul’ Airbnbs. If you’re looking for a traditional and yet elevated B&B, the original of the short stay species, get down to Barnahown, Ciara O’Brien’s boutique B&B in Mitchelstown, north Cork, with wonderful views of the Galtee Mountains.
This autumn/winter season will see her host a series of intimate Taste the Golden Vale pop-up dining experiences. Diners will have the option of turning their visit to Mitchelstown into a memorable foodie weekend getaway by booking into one of Barnahown’s seven luxurious rooms for the night in either the lovingly restored 1800s farmhouse, or its sleek new Kildrum wing accommodation.
Each of the chefs will craft fine-dining menus that showcase seasonal locally grown and sourced produce from across the region, including chef patron of 505 Seafood Restaurant & Wine Bar in Dingle Damien Ring; YCYW Young Chef of the year 2022 winner Ciara Kenneally and TV chef Jack O’Keeffe (The Village Table).
Bryan Rudd (aka Sunshine Primo) will share his passion for Mexican cuisine with a Tostada Boy night, while Praline Pastry & Chocolate Shop’s Norma Kelly will serve up a sumptuous afternoon tea experience and Sinéad Delahunty (Delalicious and Little Deer) will host the next of her hugely popular Barnahown brunches.
Pop-ups are popping in Dublin too, with Landlover Food’s popular supper club concept set for a packed programme. The Landlover Supper Club began in 2024 by former yacht chef Aideen White and passionate host Sheena O’Byrne.
White spent more than 20 years cooking for clients such as Martha Stewart, Leonardo DiCaprio, and Cindy Crawford on super yachts all over the world. O’Byrne brings her signature style of home-made pottery, floral installations and service to the table.
The duo are set to announce five-course fine dining pop-up events in Lilliput Stores in Stoneybatter, Dublin (September 25th, October 15th and November 20th) and The Studio in Galway (October 22nd and 23rd and December 18th).
They will also offer a more casual family-style pre-theatre three-course meal consisting of sharing plates in the Smock Alley Theatre, Dublin in conjunction with shows running there on dates from October to December.
Brothers Marc and Conor Bereen have partnered with Amsterdam-born hospitality brand The July to launch Onóra, a new restaurant on Dublin’s Capel Street, with an October opening date.
The bros’ portfolio already includes Coppinger, Orwell Road, Row Wines and Charlotte Quay, so the new all-day neighbourhood restaurant represents their first experience north of the Liffey.
“Developing Onóra in partnership with The July has allowed us to introduce their team to the incredible culinary scene we have here in Dublin, and across the island,” explains Marc.
Leading the kitchen at Onóra will be Northern Ireland-born head chef Lauren Shimmin, working closely with The July and the Bereen Brothers team to bring the restaurant’s food philosophy to life.
At lunch, dishes range from salt cod croquettes and mussels with fries to roast porchetta with salsa verde. By night the menu moves towards dishes such as Carlingford oysters with shallot vinaigrette, tagliolini with sweet crab, chilli and lemon, and whole grilled brill with capers and brown butter.
After dinner, its music up and plates away for late evening drinks and cocktails. Meanwhile The July aparthotel upstairs means you’ve somewhere to stay over, with an on-site barber shop, co-working spaces, meeting rooms, sauna, gym, and on-site laundry room. Quite the menu.
If you’re looking for somewhere new on Dublin’s southside, check out Simmons, the new restaurant overlooking the terrace gardens at the five-star InterContinental Dublin in Ballsbridge.
Named after one of Ballsbridge’s most historic families, (think Simmonscourt) it takes its design cue from the glamour of the classic European grand cafes, with a warm, sociable atmosphere.
Following a significant investment and completely new design over the past six months, Simmons opened in September, Tuesdays to Saturdays, from 5.30pm.
At the helm is head chef Abhimanyu Behl, whose CV includes The Merrion, The Conrad and most recently Carton House. Front of house is led by restaurant manager and maître d’ Nick Munier, known for his TV roles in Irish MasterChef and The Restaurant, as well as restaurant Pichet. Event organisers take note: there’s private dining too.

title: New campaign highlights home-grown Irish success stories around the world
description: The success of Ireland’s home-grown businesses spreads far beyond the bottom line
content:
Enterprise Ireland’s Growing Home campaign highlights how Irish-owned businesses’ success in international markets translates into job creation and social and economic contributions to local communities across the country.
“The success of Ireland’s home-grown businesses spreads far beyond the bottom line,” says Anne Lanigan, divisional manager, local enterprise and regions with Enterprise Ireland. “With backing from Enterprise Ireland, businesses across the country are reaching international markets while continuing to build, invest and create opportunity in the places they call home.”
The aim of the campaign is not only to celebrate the international success of these businesses but to highlight their importance to local communities as well. “It’s brilliant to see that raised up, to give these companies recognition for what they’re doing. It’s good to have a sense of pride about our home-grown companies. I’ve spent 23 years in Enterprise Ireland, and I’ve worked with companies of all shapes and sizes and I never fail to be impressed with the commitment and the hard work that goes into their success and what they deliver for their communities.”
She points to some impressive statistics in relation to the several thousand companies supported by Enterprise Ireland. “They employ 232,000 people across Ireland, and 69 per cent of the new jobs created in 2025 were outside of Dublin. Those companies are also delivering €38 billion in exports, growing by 8 per cent in 2025.”
In terms of direct contribution to the Irish economy, the companies spend €42 billion in the State every year. “If you work that out, it’s €115 million a day,” says Lanigan. That’s an incredible contribution. Another thing that people don’t realise is that Irish companies employ 1.3 million people outside of Ireland.”
The Growing Home campaign is directly linked to Enterprise Ireland’s overall ambition for Irish-owned exporting companies to be the primary driver of the Irish economy, she explains. “That’s where we’re trying to get to. But we need to recognise what we already have. And it’s much stronger than many people realise. Our first aim with this campaign is to draw attention to that. We have really good, really strong, really innovative companies who are making a great contribution to Ireland.”
The campaign is also aimed at highlighting the supports offered by Enterprise Ireland. “The first aim is to draw attention to those companies and give them credit for what they’re doing,” says Lanigan. “We’re also trying to draw attention to what Enterprise Ireland can do for Irish companies.”
While the organisation has a very broad remit, she says it can be boiled down to support for Irish companies to succeed on export markets. That support takes may forms. “One of the key areas for us is increasing the level of R&D and innovation in our companies. To have a sustainable company into the future, you need to invest in R&D.”
She points out that one of the companies featured in the campaign, Dublin-based fintech Fenergo, has centred all of its R&D activity here in Ireland. “The message that we give to foreign multinationals about Ireland being a great place to do R&D needs to be delivered clearly to Irish enterprises as well,” she says.
She mentions the availability of talent, the R&D tax credit regime, and the funding supports available through enterprise Ireland as key factors. “When you take the funding that’s available, plus the R&D tax credit, it’s really very cost effective to carry out R&D in Ireland. That’s a message that foreign multinationals have understood for a long time. And we’re trying to ensure that Irish enterprises benefit from that as well.”
Companies also have access to Enterprise Ireland supported technology centres and technology gateways around the country. “The R&D ecosystem here is very attractive to any enterprise that is going to put innovation at its heart.”
She also highlights the importance of Enterprise Ireland’s network of 42 overseas offices which provide a range of market intelligence and other services and help put client companies in front of buyers.
The companies featured in the campaign are Fenergo, Mullan Lighting, Croom Medical, Merenda and Revive Active.
Founded by Mike and Edel Treanor in a corner of an old boot factory in Co Monaghan in 2009, Mullan Lighting now employs 100 people across skilled roles including design, welding and ceramics, creating bespoke lights that hang in homes, hotels and restaurants around the world. Today, 90 per cent of its output is exported.
Croom Medical in Co Limerick was established by Paddy Byrnes 40 years ago and has grown to employ 170 people in the development and manufacture of advanced orthopaedic technologies for customers around the world – proof that world-class manufacturing can start, scale and compete globally from rural Ireland. Its engineers continue to advance precision and metal additive manufacturing, including a 3D-printed titanium femoral implant that travelled to the edge of space.
Fenergo continues to call Dublin home, having grown into a global business working with some of the world’s largest financial institutions. Some 98 per cent of its work comes from outside Ireland and the company now has clients in 34 countries. As it continues to scale, the company is also investing at home, bringing roles back to Ireland and strengthening its Dublin hub.
Based in Manorhamilton, Co Leitrim, and led by Ronan Haslette, Merenda was founded in 1984 and employs 20 people in the design and production of high-quality timber products for the global fit-out and furniture industries, with 70 per cent of its output exported.
Revive Active was founded in Galway in 2011 on a simple belief that better health starts with better nutrition. Today, the company employs almost 100 people across Galway and Mullingar, with around 40 working in manufacturing and operations in Mullingar. A new 21,000-square-foot facility is supporting its next stage of growth, while its products are stocked in more than 2,000 pharmacies and health-food stores across Ireland, and reach customers in the UK, Spain, Portugal, the UAE and Nigeria.
“Enterprise Ireland is there to help companies to start, scale, innovate and succeed globally,” says Lanigan. “It’s in that context that we’re saying, here are the Irish companies that we are working with who are delivering great things. The Growing Home campaign is recognising how they support their communities, create jobs, are creating opportunities for the future and are strengthening their communities. In the world we live in now, that’s very important.”

title: Why now is ‘a really important moment’ for Ireland’s screen industry
description: A €1 billion economic engine, the Irish film and television sector is at a critical inflection point
content:
If Screen Ireland were a movie, it would be The Invisible Man. Though audiences can’t see it, it’s the star of the show. As the development agency charged with growing Ireland’s indigenous film and TV sector, attracting overseas productions and promoting Ireland’s cultural expression abroad, it’s also one of those versatile actors that can turn their hand to anything.
Increasingly, it’s being asked to do more with less. What started out as the Irish Film Board was rebranded in 2018 as Screen Ireland, tasked with developing the animation sector, TV drama and documentary and, as of last year, digital games too.
The sector was worth €544 million to the economy in 2025, a record level of production spend, up 26 per cent on 2024. It has a gross value-added tally, or boost to the overall economy, of more than €1 billion.
But perhaps the larger part of its value, in terms of soft power and the tourism generated by people visiting Ireland to see locations such as Skellig Michael – now a significant character in Star Wars – is incalculable.
From 2021 to 2024, Screen Ireland invested more than €120 million, supporting 116 features, 64 TV series, and 120 short films, driving job creation and skills development too.
The result has been the development of what is now one of the Irish industry’s key strengths – talent.
“So often what’s cited by international partners is that the creative talent coming from Ireland is remarkable,” says Désirée Finnegan, chief executive of Screen Ireland.
“Obviously that includes all the actors we’ve seen in recent years and their incredible success in the Academy Awards, and across international awards in general, but also the screen writers and directors, across both cinema and TV.
“The other area we are very strong on in Ireland now is our independent producers, who are among the best in the world. Their competence in raising complex financing and managing multiparty co-production structures for film and TV is remarkable.”
It goes for crew too. “Whether it’s cinematographers, costume designers, editors or visual effects, we have an incredibly strong mix of both creative artistry and technical skill in the craft as well.”
All of this has been underpinned by innovative skills building within the industry. Since 2019, qualifying film and television productions looking to avail of the Section 481 tax relief have had to submit an approved skills development plan to Screen Ireland as part of their application.
This is paying dividends, providing entrants to the industry with the structured learning that helps to build careers.
“We were one of the first in Europe to do that and it has been incredible. We have had more than 6,000 skills-led placements in the last year alone,” says Finnegan.
“And it’s at all levels, both entry level coming into the industry and upskilling for people who are in different crafts or departments.”
Having trained people up so well, keeping them employed is now key.
That has not been helped by the turning off of the spigot by streamers such as Amazon and Netflix, whose “streaming wars” of the 2010s and early 2020s led to a splurge in production as a way to win market share.
“It has caused a really significant disruption and contraction across the industry globally. Ireland has been in a very strong position, having had all the activity we’ve had in screen production, but this has been an unprecedented transformation which is reshaping how film and TV is created, how it is financed, how work is distributed and how audiences are discovering it,” says Finnegan.
Then there is the jump scare of AI, a subject with which the industry is still coming to terms. While keen to use it for greater process efficiencies, the race is on to ensure the intellectual property that underpins the sector is protected.
“We’re all in agreement that the purpose of any technology related to the screen industry is to serve human creativity,” says Finnegan.
“This is a really important moment for the industry. We have grown significantly over the last few years but we can’t be complacent,” she says. “It’s a very competitive area to be in.”
It’s a juncture that requires a step change in support.
“Ireland’s screen industry is a €1 billion economic engine supporting 16,000 jobs, but world-class storytelling, high-quality production capabilities and our existing tax incentives are no longer enough on their own in an ever more fragmented audience market,” says Nicola Cooke, director of Audiovisual Ireland.
“We are at a critical inflection point – global streaming platforms are consolidating, production costs are surging, and without targeted State support or legislative policy, domestic producers risk being forced to surrender the IP rights to their own creative work.”
In that same vein – and in an age where disinformation and misinformation are rife – Ireland needs to follow the lead of many other European countries and provide multiannual funding to public service media, she adds, to safeguard media plurality and independence.
Currently European Broadcasting Union data shows Ireland’s public service media funding stands at just 0.08 per cent of GDP - significantly below the EU average of 0.14 per cent, and among the lowest in western Europe.
History has proven that the right state supports are transformative for the industry. Back in the 1990s Aebhric McGibney, director of public and international affairs at Dublin Chamber, was an economist working for what was then Ibec’s audio visual production federation, helping to develop the economic multiplier model for the industry that made the case for the Section 481 tax relief.
The problem the sector faced at the time was the fact that, by their nature, film productions came and then left, taking their local spend with them.
“The goal was to leverage the tax relief to bring in FDI and to get to a level of activity that meant people could go from project to project and stay in employment,” he says.
It worked. And from that came the realisation of the importance of not just attracting productions from overseas, but of developing our own IP and retaining it.
“Owning the intellectual rights is the ultimate goal, because the IP is where the value added is, and it tends to also influence where productions are set,” says McGibney.
Right now the industry is looking for the Government to establish a Content Stimulus Fund to support high-end productions, ensuring Irish producers retain intellectual property and maintain competitiveness with the UK and other international bases
But other challenges include concerns that the EU’s new €8.6 billion AgoraEU culture budget will not be fully ring-fenced, as the bloc looks to retain budgetary wriggle room in a difficult geopolitical landscape.
For Ronan McCabe, chief executive of Animation Ireland, that’s a concern that couldn’t have arisen at a worse time for his members, who rely heavily on public service media, the importance of which can’t be overestimated when it comes to children’s screen content.
What’s more, if public sector broadcasters “don’t get those audiences when they are young, they are never going to get them when they are older,” he points out.
Given the disruptive impact of AI on animation, he too believes the focus now is on building indigenous IP. “The only way you can build companies of any value is to retain IP,” says McCabe.
The introduction of a content levy on streamers, a move media minister Patrick O’Donovan has dismissed, would help the animation sector, creating a multimillion Euro pool for local productions.
“If you bring in the levy, it gives Irish producers more heft. When we’re going overseas to sell a project, or get further finance, the more funding we can bring to a project, the greater the amount of IP that we can retain,” he explains.
“That gets you into a whole virtuous circle. If we can retain IP, that IP generates revenue, and that revenue goes into the development of new shows.”
Right now the industry is also keen to see the introduction of a “regional uplift”, of 8 per cent, to Section 481, to give productions located outside of Dublin and Wicklow a better chance to compete.
Paul Ryan from Film In Limerick, the regional film office that supports film, television, and digital media production across the midwest, is clear about its value.
“The vast majority of film and TV production in Ireland is in Dublin and Wicklow and that’s something we all, as a country, can celebrate and be proud of. But there is an opportunity to grow it beyond that,” he says.

title: Delivering a secure, clean electricity grid now and in the future
description: EirGrid’s strategic focus is firmly on renewables and resilience
content:
Having marked its 25th anniversary, EirGrid recently launched its Strategy 2026, which outlines how the organisation will deliver a secure, clean and affordable electricity system while managing rising demand and Ireland’s transition to renewables.
“For the past 25 years, EirGrid has been ensuring the safe and secure supply of electricity to homes, businesses and communities across the country,” says EirGrid head of network projects Ireland Jason Kenna. “During that time, we have built a transmission system that has supported national and regional economic growth and a resilient society, while our national control centre has kept the lights on, balancing supply and demand every minute of the day.”
The focus is firmly on the future, he adds. “That’s all about renewables. The grid has undergone a major transformation to enable the integration of renewables, and we are now about to allow up to 75 per cent of electricity to be generated from variable renewable sources such as wind and solar at any one time and brought on to the grid. We now have a programme of work to increase that to 95 per cent. That’s pioneering stuff; not many electricity systems in the world can reach that level.”
That progress supports the Government’s target for 80 per cent of the State’s electricity to come from renewable sources.
It’s been a very good year for renewables generation, Kenna notes. “April saw a new record for solar power, as the country reached a peak of over 1 gigawatt (GW) of electricity provided by grid-scale solar power for the first time. In May, another new peak for grid-scale solar was achieved, with 1.22GW of electricity provided by solar. To put that in context, it is estimated that 1GW is enough to power around 500,000 homes. Wind has grown greatly over the past 25 years and a new record for wind generation was set in February, reaching 3.89GW.”
Although EirGrid is not responsible for generating electricity or building wind farms, the organisation is responsible for connecting electricity generation infrastructure, such as offshore and onshore wind farms, into the grid.
EirGrid is now also involved in developing Ireland’s offshore wind resources and has a new role owning and being responsible for offshore transmission assets. Powering Up Offshore – South Coast is the organisation’s programme to build the new transmission grid infrastructure necessary to bring power generated by offshore wind farms into the grid.
The East-West Interconnector (EWIC) has played a critical role in the transformation since coming online in 2012, Kenna notes. “It links the electricity grids of the island of Ireland and Britain via submarine cables running between converter stations in Ireland and Wales. It is capable of providing capacity of 500 megawatts (MW), flowing in both directions.”
More recently, large battery storage units have been playing a bigger role on Ireland’s electricity system. Up until November 2025, grid-scale batteries mainly supported stability on the power system, but these units are now fully integrated into the real-time electricity market, helping to manage supply and demand more efficiently. “Battery storage will be key to integrating renewable power in future,” says Kenna.
Another key piece of infrastructure is the Celtic Interconnector which will connect the Irish and French electricity grids. “Significant progress has been made on the project,” he says. “Five hundred people are working in Irish and French waters to deliver it. Burial and protection of the previously laid 84km submarine cable was completed in Irish waters this summer, with the route reopened for fishing. In French waters, burial and protection of the installed 97km cable section has continued through the summer. All onshore cables for the project in Ireland have been successfully installed on the 44km route.”
Construction of the converter stations in both countries is substantially complete, with cable terminations also complete, and all equipment installed.
Another significant piece of infrastructure currently being developed is a new 110kV transmission grid reinforcement project in the Laois-Kilkenny region, with construction on many aspects of the project ongoing or complete. In addition, construction has recently begun of the North Connacht 110kV Project, which will add a new underground cable to the electricity system in counties Mayo and Roscommon
An ambitious programme of projects and investments will be undertaken as part of PR6, or Price Review 6, the funding provided to EirGrid by the Commission for the Regulation of Utilities (CRU). These projects include customer connections, transmission reinforcements, and asset upgrades to deliver on social and economic growth, security of supply and further penetration of renewable energy on the system.
“As part of PR6, we will develop and deliver 381 transmission infrastructure projects across the country in partnership with ESB Networks,” says Kenna. “This programme includes 29 priority projects which will provide most benefit to the grid in terms of security of supply, unlocking additional electricity capacity to meet future demand, and facilitating renewables integration.”
EirGrid’s Strategy 2026 is designed to meet the challenges facing Ireland’s energy system in terms of decarbonisation as well as increasing demand from a growing economy and population, he explains.
The strategy is based on four pillars: Keeping Ireland powered – ensuring a safe, secure and resilient electricity system every minute of every day; building the backbone – delivering grid infrastructure at pace and at scale; transforming for clean energy – enabling much higher levels of renewable electricity, clean technologies and a more flexible power system; and unlocking new frontiers – advancing offshore wind and interconnection to strengthen Ireland’s long-term energy independence.
“The strategy is designed not only to deliver an energy system capable of meeting the needs of today and the next wo years, but also to put in place the foundations to build on for generations to come,” says Kenna.
Investment in people will be key, he adds. “We are going to double staff numbers from 1,000 to 2,000 by 2030. We will need the right people on board to help us deliver on our mission. We will also work closely with all stakeholders to deliver at the scale and pace required to ensure the grid is able to meet future needs.”
The overall investment in the distribution and transmission networks is €18.9 billion, with a further €2 billion devoted to offshore wind, he says. “We have a lot of projects to develop and a very good delivery framework for them. A key part of that is working with communities, engaging with the public, seeking feedback and acting on it. Public engagement is at the heart of what we do. It helps shape our decision making and how projects are developed.”

title: O Now! by Niall Williams: A short story can contain immensities
description: A tale about listening and attuning oneself to signals from the air
content:
“In Faha everyone is a long story,” writes Niall Williams at the start of History of the Rain. “The narrative voice that I recognise as the one I am most drawn to is made for longer fiction,” he told Marlene O’Brien in an interview last year. “I want the reader to settle into the armchair of the narrative voice.”
So how would he write the first short story set in his imaginary Irish village? Naturally, by focusing on a man sitting dead in an armchair for a long while.
Two old friends, Bat Considine and Mossie “Ganga” Crowe, spend most evenings in a thatched farmhouse “that had not taken the electricity when it was passing”, “waiting to see which of them would die first”. When Ganga goes, Bat stays with the body and awaits word of the soul’s destination. He’ll try to sustain the pause in time before parish ritual resuscitates the hours.
Ganga’s funeral was already promised as “a famous day” in Williams’s lovely novel This is Happiness, narrated by his grandson Noel, but this story is all about holding off from that flooded cemetery plot for as long as possible. Between Samhain and All Souls’ Day, a spirit might seep “through the aperture” that opens up in the ordinary.
O Now! began as a radio serial in five episodes and is still companionable in print: a book of nightly visits, paced for the revivable pastime of evening recitation. Williams used broadcast as a prompt for a story about listening and attuning oneself to signals from the air, a story about how small places contain immensities, about the “equivocal” little title phrase’s Swiss-army-knife versatility. The story is equal parts specificity and schmaltz: Patrick Kavanagh as directed by Frank Capra.
To fill out the volume, the short story is followed by an essay where Williams maps his regionalist project: “a series of books set in Faha, covering all that happened to the parish during the second half of the 20th century, the time between the coming of electricity and the coming of the internet.” The fantasy of these books – written about “a population … in many ways cut off” – is to redeem connection, together with a cosy and very contemporary desire to unplug.
[ Author Niall Williams: ‘I will always be an outsider, even here after 41 years’ Opens in new window ]
Greg Londe teaches literatures in English at Cornell University and lives in Wexford

title: BYD’s Dolphin G plug-in hybrid delivers impressive range but disappointing road manners
description: Timely PHEV supermini promises up to 105km of electric driving, but its ride, steering and refinement disappoint
content:
BYD may claim its Dolphin G has been developed for Europe, but if that’s the case, they need to spend more time on the roads of Sligo and Stockholm.
True, the Dolphin G is a compact hatchback with a decent boot and an intriguing powertrain that offers plug-in hybrid power, which is a first for European buyers in the supermini category.
BYD is the giant of Chinese car brands . Since its first self-developed car in 2005, it has risen with astonishing speed to become one of the biggest car brands in the world, vying with Tesla for top spot in the EV market . And it’s not shy about its ambitions, name-dropping Toyota as a target it wants to overtake. Here in Ireland, where it has overtaken the likes of Renault and Dacia, the brand is set to fall under direct control by the parent company instead of via a local distributor, a decision driven by a desire to wring out ever more sales volume.
When you hear warnings from European car executives about the threat of Chinese competition, it’s BYD that’s at the forefront of their minds. So, they are right to be concerned when it expands its offering in a favourite category of car for European buyers.
So, let’s assess the positives of this new car. Certainly, the addition of a plug-in hybrid option in the supermini market is to be welcomed.
The front-wheel drive hatch comes with a total output of either 129kW or 156kW depending on the specification you choose. The lower output version has a 7.4 kWh battery pack delivering electric-only range of 40km, while the more powerful version has an 18.3kWh battery pack and boasts an electric range of 105km. Add in the power of the 1.5-litre petrol engine to the mix and it claims a combined range of up to 1,040km from a full battery and petrol tank. BYD claims a combined fuel consumption of 4.5l/100km.
Those are impressive statistics to trot out when considering a supermini. And the new car sales figures show that a sizeable cohort of buyers like the reassurance of an EV driving with a petrol engine backup when the battery runs out.
But there is a reason why rivals in this category have opted to forgo the tech. Partly, that’s down to costs, where the Chinese clearly have advantages in low-cost production these days. But it’s also down to market demand.
Tax changes may change that. The Dolphin G was gifted an edge over non-EV rivals in the recent budget, with CO₂ emissions of 60g/km for the smaller battery version and 32g/km for the larger battery. That means it evades the rise in Vehicle Registration Tax by 1 per cent, which is being applied to new cars with emissions over 80g/km, and which hits non-electric rivals and even regular hybrids like the Toyota Yaris.
Many in this category don’t have off-street parking or else live in apartment accommodation where private charging simply isn’t available. For them, the smaller 7.4kWh battery, which can only take AC charging, is hard to justify without convenient regular charging access.
The larger 18.3kWh battery does support CCS DC rapid charging, but only to a 39kW limit – regardless of whether the charger capacity is 150kW or 360kW. That said, given its relatively small size, BYD claims it will charge from 10 per cent to 80 per cent in 26 minutes.
If the charging options for the smaller battery version are slightly negative, there are more to come. For a car intended specifically with European motorists in mind, the ride and handling are well behind its French and German peers.
We tested the bigger battery Dolphin G in both the mid-range Boost and higher Comfort specification on a wide variety of roads in northern Denmark. In pure EV mode, the car is as quiet as you’d expect, with the odd intrusion of wind noise in the cabin at times.
However, once the engine kicks in, it proves itself tuned for fuel efficiency over performance, with a delayed response under acceleration that’s compounded by a strained engine note.
That could be forgiven in the same way we accept the set-up for other fuel-conscious hybrids like the Prius. However, it’s compounded by a ride quality on the Comfort’s 18in wheels that struggles to cope with the speed bumps that litter Europe’s urban streets and the potholes of rural roads. We forgave it the initially unsettled drive over country roads, but even in towns at slow speeds, the Dolphin G felt ill at ease.
Then there is the steering, which is both heavy and vague, making driving a chore. All this is topped off with the usual concerto of beeps and bongs from the over-anxious safety systems.
On the open motorway, you find yourself regularly correcting the steering line, while on the rutted back roads or broken urban streets the suspension gets out of sorts quite quickly. Some of that is down to the wheel choice, and the ride does improve slightly if you opt for the Boost specification’s 16in wheels. But it’s just enough to soften out the rough edges, certainly not enough to give the car itself any competitive edge.
Then there is the practicality. The boot space is deep and decent, though it has a big lip that can impede loading, but the rear seat headroom and legroom are just average, and the cabin’s hard plastics contrast with the much-improved cabins on offer by rivals these days. The touchscreen controls are quick to respond, but it suffers from the same muddle of menus that curses many modern cars.
Amid a wave of exciting new arrivals in this category, the Dolphin G’s shortcomings are even more apparent.
Due for introduction at the Nevo Electric car show at the RDS in early November, the Dolphin G is targeting 271 registrations. BYD says it will confirm prices closer to launch but “it will be a competitive price for a model kitted out with all the specifications”.
Given the ultra-competitive landscape into which it arrives, pricing will be critical.
Just to recap on what’s coming in this class, at the same time as Dolphin G lands, there will be the new – and really impressive – Volkswagen ID.Polo, delivering Golf-like interior space and the sharp handling and well-honed ride qualities that epitomise the best of the German’s traits. And its starting price is just below €20,000 after grants.
Alongside this comes a fleet of its siblings like the Cupra Raval with its sportier and more engaging handling, and the practically minded VW ID.Cross and Skoda Epiq. And that’s just the new arrivals from the VW Group stable.
Aside from these are the likes of the new Renault 5, Nissan Micra, and the impressive Yaris hybrid, whose Yaris Cross variant is Ireland’s bestselling new car. There are too many more to list.
The Yaris represents a useful contrast to the Dolphin G, and a potential lesson for BYD. This original Yaris supermini was designed in Europe primarily for European tastes, while drawing on its Japanese engineering expertise. They got the mix right. BYD needs to more closely take note of that recipe.
European motor executives are right to be frightened of BYD. Its progress to date is simply astounding when compared to the gradual growth of its European counterparts. Even when it stumbles, it quickly recovers.
And it has some impressive models in its line-up, like the big Seal-U plug-in hybrid, the all-electric Seal and Sealion 7. But it has shown that its mammoth spending on research and development doesn’t always deliver a win. This Dolphin G brings a new powertrain format for buyers in this class, but its road manners need more work. While aggressive pricing will help, on first impressions this seems to be a swing and a miss.

title: Carla Ward strikes only positive notes ahead of World Cup playoff against Poland
description: ‘I think we are a better team now, better than the team that beat Poland twice earlier in the year’
content:
The upbeat feeling around Carla Ward’s Republic of Ireland squad continues apace as only Poland stand in their way of reaching a second successive World Cup in Brazil next summer.
Ireland travel to Gdańsk on Tuesday, December 1 st before the second leg at the Aviva Stadium on Saturday, December 5th.
The major tournament breakthrough for women’s football in Ireland happened at the 2023 tournament in Australia, under the guidance of Vera Pauw, when the sparks of inspiration seemed overly reliant on Katie McCabe and Denise O’Sullivan.
Both McCabe and O’Sullivan remain vital to the cause but others, like Abbie Larkin and Marissa Sheva, seem more important than ever before.
“Ten goalscorers across two games [to beat Kazakhstan 12-0 on aggregate], find me another country that has done that?” Ward asked. “Everybody is contributing now.”
Momentum stalled two years ago under Eileen Gleeson, who had replaced Pauw, with a crushing defeat to Wales at the Aviva Stadium to miss out on the Euros. That low point, which prompted a raft of retirements, can be addressed in the second leg back at the Aviva against Poland in December.
“Forget Wales,” Ward insisted, “we have come a long way since that game. Let’s forget about it!
“What you are seeing now is a completely different type of football. I think we are a better team now, better than the team that beat Poland twice earlier in the year.
“Why wouldn’t you want to come and support this team?” she added about the move from Cork to Dublin. “The team has been superb all year. We are good on the ball now.”
O’Sullivan, the deserving player of the match, concurred: “I think players are stepping up massively now. We’ve a really good team with players all over the pitch stepping up.”
Ireland beat Poland on two occasions last April, 3-2 away and 1-0 at the Aviva, but in Ewa Pajor they have a world-class forward who is a star at Barcelona in La Liga.
“I saw them beat Belgium tonight,” said Ward. “We can have a good look at them now. We know them, they know us. We know we got the toughest draw. Even England didn’t want Poland or Belgium, but our team is growing all the time.
“Let’s be really honest, Poland will want revenge but I thought we were dominant home and away to them. I do think we are a better team now. We got depth now. We got competition in every position.
“It could come down to that added edge and togetherness that we now have.
“We prepared in this camp as if we were playing a top 10 team in the world.”
The question now is how Ward gets Abbie Larkin, Emily Murphy, Kyra Carusa and Marissa Sheva into the same starting 11.
“We can’t pick the team but this camp has answered some questions about players and positions. Now it is about keeping them fit and hopefully they put themselves first in the coming weeks. I shouldn’t say that, but it is true.”

title: UK MPs vote to continue progress of Northern Ireland Troubles legacy legislation
description: Opposition MPs criticised the lack of time being given to examine the more than 100 amendments
content:
UK MPs have voted to continue progress on Northern Ireland Troubles legacy legislation, while opponents have branded the mass of amendments to the Bill “a mess”.
Scrutiny of the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill began in the previous parliamentary session, but it did not pass all its legislative stages.
On Tuesday, MPs were asked to approve a carry-over motion to continue its progress in the Commons, with British prime minister Andy Burnham appearing in the chamber for the debate.
It passed 304 votes in favour to 179 against – majority 125.
However, opposition MPs criticised the lack of time being given to examine the more than 100 amendments that have been put forward by the Government, with the shadow Northern Ireland secretary Alex Burghart branding the Bill “a mess”.
The shadow minister said: “That mess is attested to by the fact that we are still debating it when it was introduced a year ago tomorrow, and we have yet to breach committee stage.
“It is attested to by the fact that we are debating a carryover motion tonight for the second time.
“It is attested to by the fact that the Government in April told us that it was going to submit its amendments after six months of delay, but only published them yesterday, after another six months, and just look at them: 144 Government amendments now making a pack of about 300 – 119 pages.
[ British attorney general to approve future prosecutions of former UK soldiers under legacy law changes Opens in new window ]
“This is a mess in the process of becoming a bigger mess.”
Paul Kohler, the Liberal Democrats’ Northern Ireland spokesman, said only giving the House one week to examine the amendments before discussion at committee stage raises “serious concerns about scrutiny”.
DUP leader Gavin Robinson also said: “I think it is deeply unfortunate for victims, for innocent victims, and for veterans to have but a week to consider and to comprehend the import of the amendments, scores of them, 60 additional pages in this book, and to understand the impact that will have on their quest and their rightful quest for truth and for justice.”
Tory former minister Sir David Davis demanded the Government “drop this evil Bill and start again”.
