“This vexatious use of lawfare is designed with one intent: it is to represent the behaviour of IRA killers, murderers, vicious psychopathic murderers, as somehow liberators, heroes, by destroying the reputations of our own soldiers,” he said.
However, Alliance MP Sorcha Eastwood (Lagan Valley) called for politicians to “stop playing games”.
[ More Troubles legacy probes due to be published shortly, says commission head Opens in new window ]
She said: “This is not perfect. The matter in which it’s being done is far from perfect.
“But people have died. People have died waiting. We have been at this in Northern Ireland for at least 20 odd years. I’m not going to stand in the way of any family.”
Opening the debate, Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland Secretary, said the Bill was needed to allow families who lost loved ones in the Troubles to get answers.
He said: “I don’t think we can ever really build a strong future for Northern Ireland unless we fully understand the past, and understanding the past means making sure that we get answers for people.”
Amendments put forward by the Government include one giving the UK Attorney General final say on whether Troubles-related prosecutions should go ahead.
This will bypass the devolution settlement, meaning Stormont’s own Attorney General, Dame Brenda King, will have no role in any decision. Northern Ireland has appointed its own attorney general since 2010.
The UK government said there was “precedent” for the approach including on national security matters.
The Northern Ireland Office said it would reduce the chances of “rinse and repeat” duplicate investigations.
The Bill overhauls the previous Conservative government’s Legacy Act, which aimed to draw a line under the conflict and legal cases which have followed.
The Act established an investigative body aimed at uncovering information and giving closure to the families of those killed in the Troubles.
However, it was widely panned by different communities in Northern Ireland for offering conditional immunity from prosecution to those who shared information about crimes they were involved in. – PA

title: Pressure on Michael Carrick grows as 10-man Manchester United beaten at Atlético Madrid
description: Champions League round-up: Arsenal produce second-half blitz to ease past Lille at the Emirates
content:
Manchester United’s winless run extended to a fifth match as Michael Carrick’s side made a nightmare start and lost Leny Yoro to a red card in a 2-0 defeat at Atlético Madrid.
The feelgood factor that came with the Red Devils’ surprising return to European football’s top table under their former midfielder has been replaced by growing questions over the head coach’s future.
United were booed after conceding a stoppage-time leveller at home to struggling Tottenham on Saturday and three days later it was a slow start that proved costly as Pablo Barrios scored after just 50 seconds.
Johnny Cardoso saw a goal ruled out for handball and Atléti twice hit the woodwork as Diego Simeone’s side attempted to see off a spirited response from Carrick’s men.
Bruno Fernandes crashed an effort off the crossbar as United pushed for a second-half leveller, only to be reduced to 10 men as Yoro was adjudged to have brought down Jonathan David as last man.
Substitute Ademola Lookman quickly added a second to end the contest, with this loss increasing the spotlight on Carrick ahead of travelling to rivals Leeds with their lowest points after six league games since 1986.
Jurrien Timber, Eberechi Eze and Bukayo Saka all scored in seven scintillating second-half minutes to fire Arsenal to a comfortable 3-0 win against Lille at the Emirates Stadium.
Timber opened the scoring for the home side shortly after the hour mark before Eze doubled their advantage just three minutes later.
Substitute Saka then added a third in the 71st minute as Mikel Arteta’s side cantered to a second win from two matches in Europe, and their ninth in 10 across all competitions so far this season.
The Gunners’ victory here was remarkably their 14th in a row in the group stage of the Champions League as they bid to go one step further than last season and secure their maiden title on Europe’s grandest stage.
It is now almost two years since the Gunners last dropped points in the league phase – a 1-0 defeat to Inter Milan in November 2024.

title: Waterford house fire live updates: Gardaí begin murder investigation as adults who died are named locally
description: Emergency services are at the scene of the house fire in the Birchwood estate, near the city
content:
The murders of Philip and Kim English and two of their sons Callum (12) and Jayden (8) in a petrol bombing attack on their home is linked to recent violence they were subjected to by a local drugs gang, gardaí believe.
Two other children were rescued from the burning house but were in critical condition in the children’s hospital in Crumlin, Dublin on Tuesday. They were described locally as “a lovely family”.
The English family was hoping to leave the property as part of a council transfer as they felt unsafe, Conor Lally reports.
Gardaí have a number of clear suspects after launching a murder investigation earlier on, Conor Lally reports.
They have carried out a number of searches in the Waterford area on Tuesday night.
Just moments from the estate, a community centre has been providing a safe space for locals to access supports, Darragh Murphy reports.
Organisations and businesses have been providing groceries to the centre all day, while community groups and professional services have been on hand to help grieving neighbours in any way they can.
Amy Maguire, manager of Butler Community Centre, said the centre has been transformed into a hub for those impacted by the incident.
“If all we can do is offer a place where people can escape this chaos and grieve together, then that’s what we’ll do,” she said.
Maguire said there has been a steady stream of locals coming through the doors of the community centre throughout the day.
Others, she said, choose to remain in the estate.
“We have had quite a few members of the community in here today, but support is also being brought to the estate itself, and my car boot is open this evening and filled with tea, coffee and sandwiches for people who decide to stay here.
“It’s about the community today, and if people can’t come to the centre then we’ll bring it to them.”
Maguire said the Birchwood Estate is tightknit, and that residents are in deep shock.
“Everybody knows everybody here and the sense of community is very strong.
“It’s devastating, it’s just a surreal situation. Everybody here will grieve, and we all have to grieve together.”
Minister for Mental Health Mary Butler attended the community centre this evening to speak with locals affected by the incident.
She said there is a sense of “stillness, shock, trauma and disbelief”.
“It’s the worst thing we’ve ever had to deal with in Waterford. It’s unbelievable,” she said.
The minister confirmed that six psychologists have been made available to local schools in the area.
The son of Philip English has paid tribute to his brothers Callum (12) and Jayden (8) as “kids who enjoyed fun” and liked their friends”.
Meanwhile, Johnville Football Club said that club members were absolutely devastated by the news.
“Kim and Philip were familiar and friendly faces around our club, always there supporting Callum at his matches. It is incredibly difficult to comprehend that a family we knew so well has been taken from us in such tragic circumstances.”
Separately, an online fundraiser was set up to help arrange funerals for the four victims. It had raised over €7,000 by Tuesday evening.
“There are no words to describe the heartbreak of losing four precious lives in such devastating circumstances,” it said.
“As our family tries to come to terms with this heartbreaking loss, we are faced with the task of arranging four funerals and giving Phillip, Kim, Callum and Jayden the loving farewells they deserve.”
Father Gerard Chestnutt, who is parish priest at Sacred Heart Church at The Folly in Waterford, said it was a “day of immense sadness”.
“People are devastated, in particular here in the Birchwood estate, because the family are well known,” he told reporters at the scene of the fire.
“The community is well established, it’s a very tight-knit community. As you can see, there’s many people out on the street here, and they’re all absolutely heartbroken.
“But it goes beyond here as well. The wider community is absolutely devastated. Our school communities, the primary schools are absolutely heartbroken, both the staff and students.
“And I would know the family very well. It’s a day of immense sadness for this entire community.”
He added: “There’s no words even that people can find to try to grasp or try to understand what’s happened.”
A prayer vigil for the family will take place at Sacred Heart Church, The Folly, Co Waterford at 5pm on Wednesday.
A statement from the Diocese of Waterford and Lismore said: “We invite the people of Waterford to come together in prayer for those who have lost their lives, their grieving families and loved ones, and all those affected by this terrible tragedy.”
Philip English’s adult son has said he is “lost for words” and “devastated” following their deaths, Emma McMenamy reports.
English’s son from a previous relationship, John James English, said one of his brothers rang him on Tuesday morning to tell him about the news of the deaths of his family members.
“I’m devastated, it’s heartbreaking and cruel,” said the 33-year-old in messages after being contacted through social media.
“No one deserves what those little kids, my brothers and sister and Dad and his wife had happen.
“They had their whole lives ahead of them. It’s just crazy carry on; it’s out of this world knowing that innocent children got this cruel act of evil.”
He added: “I loved them and I’m lost for words and in a state of shock. I’m just heartbroken and don’t know what to do or say because nothing will bring them back.
“I hope the people who are responsible feel the full force of the law. Devastation is an understatement.”
President Catherine Connolly has expressed her shock at the “appalling attack”.
In a statement, the President said: “As President of Ireland, may I join with all of those who have expressed such shock following the horrific killing of a couple and two of their children this morning in Waterford and express my deepest condolences to the family and friends of those who have lost their lives.
“This was an appalling attack and all of our thoughts are with the two children currently in critical condition in hospital for a full recovery and with the first responders who have been on the scene and treating them.
“I know that An Garda Síochána have already commenced a murder investigation and I urge anyone with any information to bring it to their attention.”
A neighbour who rang the emergency services when the fire broke out has spoken of her sadness.
“It’s just devastating – a whole family nearly wiped out,” the woman, who did not want to be named, told the Press Association.
“At quarter past five this morning I rang the fire brigade.
“I could hear it all unfolding behind me. The dog actually woke me up barking.
“I’m just so upset. I think the council are offering some kind of counselling down in the community centre there. I might go down.”
The woman said she knew the family who lived in the house well, describing them as “nice” people.
She said the community would now have to rally together, adding: “We just have to stick together now and just look after each other.”
Sacred Heart Family Resource Centre, where Kim and Philip English’s children attended, has paid tribute to the “much loved” family.
In a statement, Sacred Heart said it was “shocked and deeply saddened to hear of the tragedy that occurred this morning in the Birchwood Estate.
“Kim, Phillip, and their children were well known and much loved within our community. Their children attended our childcare service, Tiptoes Community Childcare Centre over the years, and the family was known to many of our staff, children, and families.
“Our thoughts and heartfelt sympathies are with all those affected by this devastating loss.”
The “thoughts and prayers of everybody in this Dáil and across Government are with the family, with the community, the wider community in Waterford, and also with the first responders,” Taoiseach Micheál Martin has told the Dáil, Sarah Burns reports.
Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald said: “This community needs every support possible. We stand with them at this desperate, desperate time. We think of those lives that have been lost.”
The family targeted by the arson in Waterford had suffered two other vandalism attacks in recent years.
There were also threats made against members of the family in recent weeks on social media.
The most recent incident was the attempted firebombing of a black Seat car owned by the family about three weeks ago.
Gardaí investigated the arson attempt, which happened at about 2.20am on Friday, September 18th.
Philip English, who was killed in Tuesday’s fire, had spoken to WLR in 2023, seeking public assistance in finding the perpetrators of a vandalism effort against the same vehicle.
He said gloss paint was thrown on the vehicle shortly before 3am one night in August 2023.
More than one person could be responsible for the arson attack in Waterford, as gardaí are searching for “person or persons unknown”.
Anthony Pettit, Garda Chief Supt for Waterford and Kilkenny, said gardaí believe the house was “attacked by a person or persons unknown and that the fire was started deliberately”.
The force is “appealing to any person who has information on this multiple murder and arson attack to speak with investigating members”, Pettit said in a statement.
Gardaí confirmed that two of those killed in the arson attack in Waterford were the children of the two adults who died.
Anthony Pettit, Garda Chief Supt for Waterford and Kilkenny, said that two adults “and two of their children died in the fire”.
“Two more of their children are currently admitted to Children’s Health Ireland (CHI) Crumlin where they are receiving treatment for critical injuries,” he said.
Pettit said his thoughts are with the family and community.
Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan has condemned the arson attack in Waterford, noting it “resulted in the loss of four lives including two children”.
“I want to express my deepest condolences to the family and friends of the bereaved. My thoughts are also with the two young children in hospital,” he said, noting the attack has had a “very significant impact” on the whole country.
“There is no place in a civilised society for such a heinous act of violence.”
The Minister said he had spoken to Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly about the attack.
“I am confident those responsible for this brutal and heinous act will be brought to justice to face the full rigour of the law.”
Gardaí believe some accelerant was used to set the front door alight but could not confirm pending a full technical examination whether a petrol bomb was thrown at the door, Barry Roche reports from Waterford .
Residents of the Birchwood area made “heroic efforts” to try to get into the burning house to save victims of fire, the Bishop of Waterford has said.
Alphonsus “Phonsie” Cullinan, the Bishop of Waterford and Lismore, said the four children affected by the fire, two of whom have died and two remain in critical condition, “should have been going to school today”.
He said there would be a gathering in the local church to pray for those who have died in the fire and for “the healing of the two kids who are in really condition in hospital”.
Cullinan said he had not come across a tragedy like this fire in the 11 years he has served in Waterford and that gardaí considering the investigation as a murder inquiry “adds to the tragedy”.
The start of the murder investigation into the fire has added to the “shock and trauma” that the community near the fire are feeling, a Waterford TD has said.
“We are dealing with what was a tragedy and a loss of life, and for it to now be confirmed as a murder investigation is adding to the shock and trauma that residents are facing,” Sinn Féin TD David Cullinane said to The Irish Times.
“It is something we would never have thought we would see on our doorsteps here in Waterford. People are holding each other and people are comforting each other as the day as gone on.”
The deaths of four of the six residents of the house, including Kim and Philip English, have sent a “shock wave” through the community, he said.
Gardaí are “doing everything to preserve the scene”, Cullinane said, noting that the community will support the investigation.
The two adults who died in the house fire in Co Waterford on Tuesday morning have been named locally as Kim and Philip English. They are a well-known family in the area.
Waterford councillor Jason Murphy, who lives close to the scene of the fire, said there was a sense of “devastation” in the community.
“I’m just numb, like everyone else around here,” the Fianna Fáil councillor told the Press Association.
“I think there’s an eerie quiet around here. This estate would usually be a busy estate. You’d probably see kids up here playing on the green here, but there’s nothing happening here this morning – only people looking into space trying to, I suppose, make sense of what happened here late last night and early this morning.”
Murphy said local people who witnessed the fire would require professional support and counselling.
“The sounds and what they heard this morning and what they seen, it’ll take a lot of recovering, and they’ll need a lot of support,” he said.
“It’s coming now from the community, and that’ll be ongoing. But they’ll need professional support as well. And I was glad to see that the Taoiseach came out this morning, Micheál Martin said the community will get whatever supports it needs.”
The inquiry into the fire in the Birchwood area of Waterford city has been upgraded to a murder investigation, the Garda confirmed.
The incident is now being considered as an arson attack, which began shortly after 5am on Tuesday morning.
An investigation into the incident is being led out of Waterford Garda station.
The two mayors of Waterford have appealed to the public to give gardaí at the scene of the house fire in the south of the city time and space to investigate.
“We are devastated and heartbroken by the tragedy that unfolded in Birch Avenue this morning,” the mayor of Waterford Liam Brazil and metropolitan mayor Lola O’Sullivan said in a joint statement.
“Our sympathies, thoughts and prayers are with the family and loved ones of those who lost their lives so tragically in the fatal house fire,” they said.
“We appeal to the public to give An Garda Síochána the time and space needed to fully investigate this incident.”
The mayors also extended their thoughts to emergency services workers attending the “disturbing scene”.
Waterford Metropolitan District Mayor Cllr Lola O’Sullivan said the city was devastated to wake up to the news of the tragic fire in the Birchwood estate, Vivienne Clark reports .
“Our thoughts and prayers are with the family and the friends. This doesn’t just affect the family and their friends, it affects the neighbourhood, it affects the greater community of Waterford.”
O’Sullivan said the estate is in a “quiet area of Waterford”.
The situation was also “unspeakable” for the fire service, the gardaí and the national ambulance service, she added.
“I can only imagine the scenes this morning were absolutely horrific for every emergency service who came upon it. It’s awful, it’s life-changing.”
O’Sullivan called on the public to give gardaí space to investigate the incident, saying it upset her to see people commenting on social media when they did not have firm facts.
“I would ask people not to be commenting on something that they don’t have factual information on,” she told RTÉ Radio’s Today with David McCullagh show.
“The community will come together, they always do, and particularly John’s Park is a beautiful old part of the city, and is a wonderful older community, and everybody will rally around to help this family.”
Four people have died in the fire, including two adults – one male and one female – and two children, the Garda has confirmed.
Two other children suffered “critical injuries” in the fire and are receiving hospital treatment.
It is understood the children were initially brought to University Hospital Waterford before being moved to a better-resourced hospital in Dublin.
Gardaí are “investigating all the circumstances” and are appealing to the public for video footage.
Sinn Féin TD for Waterford David Cullinane has called for the public to stop speculating about the cause of the fire, saying it is not helpful.
The family involved were well known and had deep roots in other parts of Waterford, he told Newstalk’s Claire Byrne show.
“So you can only imagine what the wider family members are having to go through, and also people who live in the estate. And I’ve seen people hug each other, people in tears and people just devastated beyond belief.“
Cullinane said he was unable to “put into words that grief that I’ve seen and the trauma” he had seen on Tuesday morning.
“It’s just something that you never wish to wake up to and to hear about. But unfortunately, we’re dealing with that trauma here.
“Communities are resilient, they always rally around, but I think it will take a long time for this to heal. And it’s very raw and very difficult. And given that I know the family, I’m just utterly, utterly heartbroken myself.”
Waterford city is feeling a “real shock” following the news of the fire, Minister of State John Cummins has said.
“This is really, really tragic situation that is still unfolding this morning,” the Fine Gael TD for Waterford, who lives in the south of the city, told WLR FM’s Déise Today with Damien Tiernan.
“I really want to pay tribute to the emergency services who have been attending what is a really tragic situation there in Birchwood.
“I think we’re all shocked this morning, all of us are thinking of the family, friends, neighbours and wider community. There’s no words that describe the grief that we are experiencing.
“We always rally together as a community in Waterford, we always roll up our sleeves and get behind families that have experienced tragic circumstances, and I know that this will be no different,” he said.
The house fire is now subject to a criminal investigation, The Irish Times understands.
While that inquiry was only beginning on Tuesday morning, the possibility the house was deliberately targeted in an arson attack is one line of investigation at present, Conor Lally reports.
A support hub to provide refreshments and facilities to those affected by the fire has been set up by Waterford City and County Council.
The hub is at the Butler Community Centre in St John’s Park in Waterford city.
Sinn Féin’s health spokesman, David Cullinane, who is a TD for Waterford, said he was heartbroken at the news.
“It’s just utterly heartbreaking and there’s such devastation in the housing estate itself, as you can imagine, but also in the wider community in Waterford city.
“Obviously there is shock but people will know the family and there is absolute heartbreak when you have children involved as well so it’s obviously very emotional.”
Cullinane told RTÉ Radio’s Morning Ireland that he knew the family well and had met one of the family members recently.
He said the number of fatalities remained unknown, “but we do know it’s very high and obviously if anybody does survive we wish them our best wishes”.
Cullinane went on to pay tribute to the first responders. He said he had spoken to paramedics and firefighters and knew how traumatic it had been for them when they arrived at the scene.
He asked that An Garda Síochána and first responders be given space.
“My heart goes out to the family members and the relatives and all of the neighbours and friends of the family involved and I’m just utterly heartbroken and devastated.”
The community would rally around, he said. “All they can do is stand in solidarity at this point, there’s no words really, no, and I’m lost for words myself, I know many of the neighbours, it’s a very close-knit community and I know there is tears on that road as you can imagine and just people absolutely devastated and just still in shock.
“It just sends a shiver down your spine. It’s just so heartbreaking particularly when there’s children involved so I think that heartbreak will be felt right across the island when people hear what happened and hear of the fatalities,” said the Sinn Féin TD.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin said he was shocked at the news and asked that emergency services be given time and space “to deal with what clearly is a very worrying and deeply disturbing situation”.
A number of people are feared dead, including children, following a fire at a house in Waterford city.
Gardaí and other emergency services attended the scene in the Birchwood estate, about 3km south of the city centre, after the alarm was raised shortly after 5am.
A couple with several children lived in the home, and at least two people are believed to have died.
Waterford Fire Service received an emergency call about a house fire at Birch Avenue, Kilcohan, at 5.13am, a spokesperson said.
They said several fire units went to the scene from surrounding stations and found the “well-developed fire” at the house.
“Firefighting operations commenced immediately, and a number of casualties were removed from the two-storey house. The fire was extinguished and the scene handed over to An Garda Síochána.”
A Garda spokesman said it was “an ongoing evolving incident” and no further details were available yet.

title: Waterford family’s deaths in petrol bomb attack linked to local drugs gang
description: Philip and Kim English killed in family home alongside two children, Callum (12) and Jayden (8), with two others in critical condition
author_name: Conor Lally, Barry Roche, Hugh Dooley
content:
The murders of Philip and Kim English and two of their sons Callum (12) and Jayden (8) in a petrol bombing attack on their home is linked to recent violence they were subjected to by a local drugs gang, gardaí believe.
Two other children were rescued from the burning house but were in critical condition in the children’s hospital in Crumlin, Dublin, on Tuesday. They were described locally as “a lovely family”.
The Irish Times understands the English family was hoping to leave the property as part of a council transfer as they felt unsafe.
It is understood neighbours heard the fire and alerted the emergency services. A number of local people tried to intervene as they could see the children trapped inside, though the smoke and heat was overwhelming. They urged the couple, who were trapped upstairs, to throw the children out the windows to them.
The family’s home, on the Birchwood estate, just south of Waterford city, had been attacked before, most recently last month when a petrol bomb was thrown at their car. The attack yesterday just after 5am involved a petrol bomb thrown at the front door, which caused the family home to be engulfed in flames.
Gardaí carried out searches in the Waterford area on Tuesday night and it’s understood that they have identified a number of suspects in the murder investigation.
Though the investigation is at an early stage, gardaí suspect Philip English had taken on a drug debt incurred by an associate in an effort to keep him safe. However, gardaí strongly suspect the local crime gang that was owed money targeted the family yesterday morning, and was also behind last month’s attack.
An arson attack in the nearby area in recent weeks, as well as threats made on social media, are also believed to be part of the campaign of drug-related intimidation.
More than three years ago the couple’s car was destroyed when paint was thrown over it outside the house on Birch Avenue. However, it was unclear if that attack, in August 2023, was directly linked to the four murders.
[ Waterford house fire: Family targeted had suffered other vandalism attacks in recent years Opens in new window ]
President Catherine Connolly led tributes to the victims on Tuesday, saying she joined those “who have expressed such shock following the horrific killing of a couple and two of their children”.
She described the murders as “an appalling attack”, adding her thoughts were with the two children in hospital and urging anyone with information to come forward.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin told the Dáil the “thoughts and prayers of everybody in this Dáil and across Government are with the family, with the community, the wider community in Waterford, and also with the first responders”.
Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan has condemned the arson attack, adding he had spoken to Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly about the attack.
“I am confident those responsible for this brutal and heinous act will be brought to justice to face the full rigour of the law,” he said.
Bishop of Waterford and Lismore Alphonsus Cullinan said the English children “should have been going to school today” but, instead, two had died and two were critical despite the “heroic efforts” of local people to save them.
[ Gardaí investigate as four people die in fire at house in Waterford city Opens in new window ]
Sacred Heart Family Resource Centre, a community centre that the children attended, has paid tribute to the “much loved” family. It said it was “shocked and deeply saddened” to hear of the attack.
Chief Supt Anthony Pettit, of the Waterford and Kilkenny division, said gardaí believed the house was “attacked by a person or persons unknown and that the fire was started deliberately”.
Gardaí were “appealing to any person who has information on this multiple murder and arson attack to speak with investigating members”. The investigation was being aided by the National Bureau of Criminal Investigation, the force’s serious crimes squad.

title: Ireland set up World Cup playoff against Poland in December
description: Aviva Stadium set to host the second leg on Saturday, December 5th
content:
The Republic of Ireland must outlast Poland over two legs, to be held in Gdańsk, and at the Aviva Stadium on December 5th, to qualify for the World Cup in Brazil next summer.
Poland are familiar opposition, having narrowly lost twice to Ireland in four days in April to finish bottom of a qualification group that also included France and the Netherlands.
Ireland managed to figure out the Poles, but the threat of Barcelona forward Ewa Pajor remains a serious concern if Carla Ward’s team are to join the 18 countries that have already qualified for the 32-team competition.
The attendance of 10,344 inside Páirc Uí Chaoimh will be disappointed to lose the next international to the Aviva as it has become a popular destination for young fans.
The steady flow of fathers and daughters, who stalled for food in the Marina Market on the easy walk to the home of Cork GAA, might be tempted to catch a train to Dublin on the first Saturday in December.
Framing this playoff semi-final, second leg as a training ground exercise in the match preview was inaccurate. If that had been the case, the Ireland head coach would have blown her whistle long before Jessie Stapleton made it 9-0 on aggregate in the 40 th minute.
The previous 39 minutes elapsed without a proper chance being created as the girls in green took turns putting angled crosses into a crowded Kazakhstan box.
Abbie Larkin and Emily Murphy led the line but Ireland lacked a target woman, namely Kyra Carusa, whose benching should work to her advantage come the playoff final.
Ireland cannot do without the San Diego-born striker. They also lacked urgency and motivation, which was understandable after the 8-0 result in Astana last Friday all but guaranteed progress to a playoff final with Poland.
The first leg is expected to be played at the Polsat Plus Arena in Gdańsk on Tuesday, December 1 st , with the second leg set for a 5pm kick-off at the Aviva on the following Saturday.
Earlier on Tuesday, Pajor scored twice against Belgium in a 3-2 win that forced a penalty shoot-out as the sides finished level 3-3 on aggregate. Pajor missed Pland’s second spot-kick but, for a change, her team-mates covered for their star turn with Natalia Padilla hitting the fifth penalty to surprise the higher ranked Belgians.
Ward was gushing in praise of Pajor before the sides met six months ago, when Ireland won 3-2 away and 1-0 at home, but Belgium would have been a tougher assignment.
Meanwhile, back in the Páirc, Denise O’Sullivan had a valid claim for a penalty waved away by the Czech referee Michaela Pachtová. The Cork midfielder showed her quality to spin away from Aida Gaistenova only to be sandwiched off the ball by Gaistenova and Karina Zhumabaikyzy.
Eventually, five minutes before the break, Ireland cracked the Kazakh low-block when Stapleton rewarded Anna Patten’s curling cross to send a bullet header beyond Angelina Portnova.
McCabe struck her 35 th Ireland goal early in the second half. The arrival of Marissa Sheva was immediately visible; the versatile Sunderland player initiated the attack that invited McCabe to rifle a shot into the bottom corner from outside the box.
Lucy Quinn showed her enduring value to the squad by coming into the contest to curl a third goal that made it 11-0 on aggregate.
Having missed the famous 3-2 defeat of the Netherlands in Cork last summer, O’Sullivan was determined to leave an impression on her latest trip home from Gotham FC in New Jersey. When Stapleton surged into the box and drew a save from Portnova, the local midfielder made it 4-0.
The goal helped her to be named player of the match, but it was her relentless work rate that continues to inspire her team-mates.
Ward also made use of this fixture by starting Shanade Hopcroft and Hayley Nolan. It was instructive and while nobody had a poor game, Sheva and Larkin are becoming too important to be held until the second half of the first leg in Gdańsk. Carusa and Caitlin Hayes also look certain to return to either end of the pitch.
REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Brosnan; Mannion (Quinn, 63), Patten (Toland, 46), Nolan, Stapleton, McCabe; Hopcroft (Sheva, 46), O’Sullivan, Connolly; Larkin (Barrett, 63), Murphy (Carusa, 81).
KAZAKHSTAN: Portnova; Burova, Viasspva, Nurusheva, Nizamutdinova (Sadykova, 63), Babshuk; Gaistenova, Zhumabaikyzy (Norbayeva, 46), Turlybekova (Shustova, 79); Satygaliyeva (Popova, 63), Bibossynova (Rakhatzhan, 88).
Referee: Michaela Pachtová (Czech Republic).

title: Ireland beat Kazakhstan 4-0 at Páirc Uí Chaoimh  – as it happened
description: The Republic of Ireland lead 8-0 following first leg of playoff semi-final in Astana last week
content:
Hello all , welcome to our live updates from Páirc Uí Chaoimh where Ireland will play the second leg of their World Cup qualifying play-off semi-final against Kazakhstan this evening (live on RTÉ 2, kick-off 7.30).
Now, seeing as Carla Ward’s crew won the first leg 8-0 in Astana last Friday, we’re not anticipating a nerve-shredding evening. Indeed, with the return of captain Katie McCabe and midfielder Denise O’Sullivan to the team, this could prove to be the very longest of nights for the visitors.
McCabe and O’Sullivan are among four changes Ward has made to the side that began the first leg, Shanade Hopcroft coming in for her first start for Ireland after making her debut in Astana and Hayley Nolan taking Caitlin Hayes’ place in defence. Kyra Carusa, Jamie Finn and Chloe Mustaki also drop out.
Ireland : Brosnan; Mannion, Patten, Nolan, Stapleton, McCabe; O’Sullivan, Connolly; Hopcroft; Larkin, Murphy.
STARTING XI | Ireland v Kazakhstan Our eleven to kick us off at The Páirc ☘️ #COYGIG pic.twitter.com/jl0B3ct2ag
If Kazakhstan were to win, say, 10-1 tonight, we’d be left with egg on our faces because we’ll soon be telling you who Ireland will face in their play-off final: Poland or Belgium. They’re in to the closing stages of the second leg of their play-off semi-final in Gdansk and it’s all square on aggregate. Belgium won the first leg 1-0 in Leuven last Friday, but it’s 2-1 to Poland this evening with 10 minutes to go.
We’ll update you on that soon, for now you can read Gavin Cummiskey’s match preview.
[ Carla Ward urges Ireland to build on eight-goal lead over Kazakhstan Opens in new window ]
Player of the match Denise O’Sullivan : “It’s always special to play here in Cork, it’s where I grew up, it’s where the people supported me through my whole career, and it’s how I got to where I am.”
“It was a different game tonight, Kazakhstan did really well, they probably learned from the other night, they sat back, they were seven deep at times. It posed a different challenge for us, but we got the job done.”
“Poland are a good side, they have a world class striker [Barcelona’s Ewa Pajor], but we have great players, we’re up for the challenge, we’ll be fully ready in six weeks.”
[ Ireland set up World Cup playoff against Poland in December Opens in new window ]
Job done. True, pre-match predictions that Ireland would top their record win - 11-0 against Georgia in 2021 - were wide of the mark, this not being quite the ruthless performance head coach Carla Ward had demanded. Still, she’ll hardly complain about a 12-0 aggregate victory that puts Ireland through to a play-off final against Poland. Two games away, then, from World Cup qualification for just the second time. Poland have never qualified for a World Cup, so you’d imagine they’ll be rather eager to break that duck.
80 mins : Kyra Carusa is on for Emily Murphy. It’s now 12-0 for Ireland on aggregate with 10 minutes to go, so it might be safe to assume that they’re through to a World Cup qualifying play-off final against Poland in December.
72 mins: Ireland 4-0 Kazakhstan (12-0 agg) Denise O'Sullivan fires home from the rebound to make it 4-0 in Páirc Uí Chaoimh Watch live on @rte2 and @rteplayer pic.twitter.com/Dbpy8S0T4M
The hometown girl makes it four. A lovely one-two between Amber Barrett and Jessie Stapleton sends the latter through, her shot is saved but O’Sullivan buries the rebound.
69 mins: Ireland 3-0 Kazakhstan (11-0 agg) Tyler Toland's cross finds its way to Lucy Quinn who slots the ball in the far corner Watch live on @rte2 and @rteplayer pic.twitter.com/gmGNa8x5PE
The neatest of footwork from Emily Murphy just inside the box, she then played it left to Tyler Toland who was a bit twinkle-toed herself before her cross fell to Lucy Quinn after a deflection or two - and she rifled it in to the bottom left corner.
61 mins : As ever, Marissa Sheva has been lively, adding some much needed energy to Ireland’s efforts after she came on at the break. Karen Duggan wondered at half-time if a bit of complacency had set in. Could be, it’s been the flattest of performances so far. Amber Barrett and Lucy Quinn are on for Abbie Larkin and Aoife Mannion.
Emily Murphy sets up the Irish captain at the edge of the box and she sends a left foot shot in to the bottom right corner. We withdraw our praise of the Kazakhstan goalie.
Two changes for Ireland at the break, Tyler Toland and Marissa Sheva are on for Anna Patten and Shanade Hopcroft.
You’d imagine that the Irish players will receive quite a stern talking to from Carla Ward at the break after she had urged them to be ruthless in this second leg. They’ve been far from that. It doesn’t matter tonight, they’re 9-0 up on aggregate after all, but it sure as heck will against Poland in December.
45 mins : Shanade Hopcroft’s header from Megan Connolly’s corner grazes the outside of the left post. Really gutsy defending - and goalkeeping - from Kazakhstan tonight after the mullering they suffered in Astana.
40 mins: Ireland 1-0 Kazakhstan Ireland finally have the lead on the night as Jessie Stapleton powers home a header at the back post Watch live on @rte2 and @rteplayer pic.twitter.com/uN8LXZhmlr
Clearly, the key to prompting Ireland in to scoring a goal is to whine about the non-clinical nature of their attack tonight. And with that, Jessie Stapleton powers home Anna Patten’s cross.
38 mins : Abbie Larkin still proving to be Ireland’s chief threat, but the Kazakhstan goalie does well to turn away her effort - and then she tips over an Emily Murphy shot. Those anticipating an avalanche of goals are, so far, disappointed.
28 mins : Cripes, still scoreless in Cork, not too many of us saw Kazakhstan holding out this long. No end of industry from Ireland, but they’ve yet to find a way through the visitors’ back eleven. Carla Ward is sporting a bit of a ‘what the heck?’ face on the sideline.
19 mins : Still scoreless in Cork, Ireland proving decidedly less clinical thus far than they were in Astana.
Bar Kazakhstan producing the greatest comeback in the history of association football, Ireland will be through to a World Cup qualifying play-off final where they will play .... Poland. They produced a sizeable enough upset by beating Belgium 4-3 in a penalty shoot-out in Gdansk.
The provisional dates for that two-leg final are December 1st and 5th, Ireland at home in the second leg at the Aviva Stadium (5pm). Lest ye need reminding, the prize for the winners will be a place in next summer’s World Cup in Brazil.
7 mins : It’s all Ireland so far, Abbie Larkin having an effort cleared off the line after she was picked out by a beaut of a pass by Anna Patten. And Patten came close herself when she had a goal-bound header from a corner scooped clear by a defender.
Meantime, over in Gdansk, it’s gone to penalties.
They’re about to get up and running in Páirc Ui Chaoimh - and it’s a zinger in Gdansk. Jarne Teulings’ extra-time goal looked like putting Belgium through, but Poland are now 3-2 up on the night, making it 3-3 on aggregate.
They’re in to extra-time in Gdansk , Poland and Belgium still level on aggregate.
Who would Ireland like to prevail? Poland, probably. And that’s not because they’re ranked eight places below Ireland in the Fifa list, whereas Belgium are three places higher - you should never really pay much heed to rankings. It’s more down to Ireland having beaten the Poles home and away as recently as April, in their World Cup qualifying group. Mind you, both wins were only by one-goal margins.
Ireland and Belgium last met in the Nations League play-offs a year ago, Ireland winning the first leg 4-2 at the Aviva Stadium before losing the second 2-1 in Leuven. But Abbie Larkin’s injury time goal gave Ireland a 5-4 aggregate win.
Either way, it’ll be a somewhat sterner test than the one poor Kazakhstan have offered.

title: Mickey Harte takes up club managerial post with Down side Kilcoo
description: Kilcoo’s bid for eight-in-a-row was ended at the semi-final stage this year
content:
Mickey Harte has returned to club management with Down outfit Kilcoo.
Kilcoo have been the dominant force in Down football for well over a decade but their bid for eight titles in-a-row came up short this season at the semi-final stage. Prior to this year they had won 13 of the previous 14 Down senior football crowns.
Martin Corey stepped down soon after their semi-final loss to Burren and the 2022 All-Ireland club champions have moved swiftly to bring in Harte, whose last role was as joint Offaly senior football manager.
Harte, who guided his native Tyrone to three All-Ireland senior titles, will be hoping to lead Kilcoo back to major silverware in 2027.
On Tuesday night, Kilcoo stated: “Mickey was unanimously ratified at a club committee meeting this evening and the club are over the moon that the Tyrone man has agreed to become our manager.
“Mickey is renowned as one of the top managers in the GAA. He led Tyrone to an unprecedented three All-Ireland senior football championships, six Ulster titles, a National League and 12 Dr McKenna Cups during his record 17-year tenure.”

title: The Irish Times view on the public sector strike: mutually agreed obstruction
description: Both sides have a duty to make every effort to avoid further disruption
content:
There has been a sense of inevitability for some time about Wednesday’s strike by public sector employees. More than 300,000 workers in health, education and the civil service are taking part, which means schools close, non-urgent hospital care is cancelled and a wide range of public services are suspended for 24 hours. The stoppage, described by one union leader as only the second national public sector strike in 40 years, is an escalation in industrial relations, where relative peace has generally been the norm.
It has long been clear that union leaders felt a show of strength was necessary, both to reflect concern among members that wages are not keeping pace with the cost of living, and to demonstrate that they are just as prepared as other sectoral interests to flex their muscles in advance of pay negotiations.
Those negotiations have not begun, even though the previous public pay agreement expired at the end of June. The nominal reason for the delay is the Government’s refusal to accede to union demands that pay be addressed before discussions on other areas such as productivity or value for money.
Jack Chambers, the Minister for Public Expenditure, said on Tuesday that the unions were being unreasonable and that pay could be treated as a priority. The unions say the €1.2 billion set aside in the budget falls well short.
Today’s action follows a work-to-rule in place since the end of September, under which nurses, special needs assistants, social welfare staff and teachers have refused overtime and unscheduled cover.
If the impasse is not broken, a second one-day stoppage is scheduled for next Wednesday, October 21st, and union sources have spoken of further escalation in November. These actions are not without serious consequences. Tens of thousands of cancelled medical appointments will add to waiting lists and put pressure on hospitals later in the winter. Closed schools affect educational outcomes and cause difficulties for families. For all these reasons, the parties have a duty to make every effort to avoid further disruption.
It is hard to avoid the impression that what is happening is more a piece of choreography than the sort of dispute that could develop into all-out action.
The unions know the Government will bend on its budget allocation for pay. The Government knows an accommodation can be reached on the sequencing of talks. Public sentiment appears more on the side of the strikers, although that may be tested if the dispute drags on for weeks. Now that this day of action has taken place, it is time for all concerned to bring real urgency to the task of finding a workable and acceptable solution.

title: Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan taken ill at event in Limerick
description: Fine Gael TD earlier accused party colleagues of ‘ultimate betrayal’ for comments on his health
content:
Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan was hospitalised on Tuesday after being taken ill at a European Union presidency event in Limerick .
A planned press conference was cancelled on Tuesday afternoon after he was taken to hospital from the University of Limerick , where he was chairing an informal meeting of EU telecoms ministers.
A spokeswoman for O’Donovan said on Tuesday: “The Minister became unwell during the EU informal meeting at the University of Limerick and has been taken off site for assessment and treatment.”
O’Donovan, who is Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport, was hospitalised after becoming unwell during an official trip to Brussels this summer.
He has previously spoken about his experience living with epilepsy , which he was diagnosed with more than 10 years ago
Earlier in the day, O’Donovan hit back against critics within his own party, accusing those who commented on his health of “the ultimate in betrayal”.
O’Donovan was responding to briefings against him in coverage of the budget rows he became embroiled in last week.
In addition to questions over his temperament, a Fine Gael TD was quoted at the weekend suggesting that people within the parliamentary party were questioning whether O’Donovan was healthy enough to continue in his role, with a Cabinet source in the party quoted as suggesting a discussion on if he was “well enough” to stay in his role was likely.
O’Donovan reportedly cancelled a planned trip to Strasbourg last week after his team concluded that he was not well enough to travel. He met RTÉ executives the following day.
On Tuesday, O’Donovan criticised an “anonymous source on the front page of a reputable Sunday paper last week calling into question my health ... that source was attributed to my own party”.
“Not only was that commentary a slap in the face of me, but it was also a slap in the face of the people who have to live with conditions far worse than mine and conditions far more difficult than mine.
“I have no difficulty what people think of me on a political basis – don’t get me wrong, I’ll hold my own with anybody, but leave my health out of it.”
He added: “Last Sunday wasn’t anything to do with epilepsy. Last Sunday was the ultimate in betrayal.” He said it was a betrayal not just of him, but of others with disabilities or neurological conditions.
[ Planned strike by public sector workers ‘really unfair on the public’, Chambers says Opens in new window ]
O’Donovan has been at the centre of a post-budget controversy after first failing to secure funding to support his heavily-publicised “culture card” initiative for 16- and 17-year-olds, and then providing RTÉ with €20 million less in funding than agreed under the terms of a 2024 deal with the troubled national broadcaster.
After the budget, it emerged that O’Donovan had written to Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers warning him that without extra funding allocated to his department, several spending areas would suffer from cutbacks or shortfalls – including that the Government faced reneging on its agreement with RTÉ.
He ultimately secured an extra €21 million in funding for his department, but still left RTÉ short relative to the 2024 agreement that had guaranteed the broadcaster €260 million in funding next year – sparking a furious reaction in Montrose and an intense period of controversy, which had to be defused by the intervention of Coalition leaders.
This in turn spawned much media coverage and commentary over last weekend about O’Donovan, and other recent clashes he has had with stakeholder organisations or political colleagues.
[ Fintan O’Toole: The blue-green smoothie ruling the country has no plan and even less passion Opens in new window ]
O’Donovan told reporters on Tuesday that he was answerable to the voters of his Co Limerick constituency and to the Government. “Any day that I feel that I can’t continue in the role that I’m in, I’d gladly hand back that seal of office.”
Asked about the controversy with RTÉ, O’Donovan said he was not personally involved in the matter at present, leaving it to officials whose work is ongoing. He said he had “no notion of going anywhere” following the controversies of the last few days.

title: Duane Keith Davis sentenced to 40 years to life over 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur
description: 'You don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him and just walk away from it,' judge says
content:
Duane “Keffe D” Davis, the former California gang leader convicted of murder for orchestrating the 1996 fatal shooting of rapper Tupac Shakur , has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison.
“For three years, I’ve heard you say some variation of the same thing ... ‘Yeah, I was involved in this. But I’m different. I’ve moved on. I got out of Compton. I’m a grandfather now’,” Judge Carli Kierny said on Tuesday as she delivered the sentence.
“You don’t get to take a man from his family. You don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him and just walk away from it.”
On September 7th, 1996, Shakur was gunned down near the Las Vegas strip shortly after a Mike Tyson boxing match. He succumbed to his injuries days later.
For decades, his murder remained unsolved and one of hip-hop’s most enduring mysteries. Davis is the only person to be convicted in connection to Shakur’s murder.
A confluence of several factors hindered the investigation. The code of silence within street culture made some witnesses averse to police co-operation. Las Vegas police were sceptical about leads from their Compton counterparts, given that the head of security for Shakur’s record label was a former Compton cop.
Orlando Anderson, a gangster and Davis’s nephew, was on law enforcement’s radar as the possible gunman. The night Shakur was killed, the young rap star got into an altercation with Anderson. Las Vegas police interviewed Anderson, but he was never arrested. Anderson later died in 1998.
But then, in 2023, Davis was arrested on a murder charge.
[ ‘I didn’t tell nobody’: How Duane Keith Davis’s words helped convict him of Tupac’s murder Opens in new window ]
It was Davis’s own media tour, touting his status as one of the last surviving eyewitnesses, and a 2019 “tell-all” memoir that led to the breakthrough.
Davis had felt emboldened by a 2008 backdoor deal he brokered with police. He spoke candidly to investigators about Shakur’s shooting, who had actually been seeking information about the death of Christopher Wallace, known as Biggie Smalls or The Notorious B.I.G. Under a proffer agreement, Davis was not to face charges for any offences he shared.
In his memoir, Compton Street Legend, Davis wrote that he and a group of other men targeted Shakur and his entourage, seeking retribution for the scuffle with his nephew.
The memoir and the interview became central to prosecutor’s case. They argued the details amounted to a confession and that his public remarks voided the proffer agreement.
During Davis’s murder trial, his defence team maintained that these details were embellished. They also argued, during the trial, that there was no physical evidence, such as a murder weapon, tying Davis to the Las Vegas slaying.
Ultimately, jurors sided with the state.
Attorneys for Davis have indicated they want to appeal the conviction. – The Guardian
[ Jury convicts former gang leader of murdering rap star Tupac Shakur Opens in new window ]

title: ‘Cruel act of evil’: Son of Waterford man killed in suspected arson says he’s devastated
description: John James English, son of Philip English, says his two siblings killed in fire had ‘their whole lives ahead of them’
content:
The adult son of a man killed in a suspected arson attack alongside his wife and two children has paid tribute to his siblings as “kids who enjoyed fun and liked their friends”.
Philip English, who was in his 50s, his wife Kim English, who was in her 30s, and two of their four children died in a blaze in the Birchwood area of Waterford City at around 5am on Tuesday.
Philip English’s son from a previous relationship, John James English, paid tribute to his half brothers Callum (12) and Jayden (8) who were killed in the devastating fire.
“They were very funny, smart and beautiful,” he said.
The familywere in the house in the early hours when the alleged arson attack took place.
The couple, who have been described as well known and liked in the area, may have been targeted over a suspected debt as gardaí are probing a recent attempted arson attack on the family home.
English’s son from a previous relationship, John James English, said one of his brothers rang him on Tuesday morning to tell him about the news of the deaths of his family members.
Philip English had a number of children from a previous relationship, prior to his marriage to Kim English.
“I’m devastated, it’s heartbreaking and cruel,” said the 33-year-old in messages after being contacted through social media.
“No one deserves what those little kids, my brothers and sister and Dad and his wife had happen.
“They had their whole lives ahead of them. It’s just crazy carry on; it’s out of this world knowing that innocent children got this cruel act of evil.”
“I’m just heartbroken and don’t know what to do or say because nothing will bring them back.
“I hope the people who are responsible feel the full force of the law. Devastation is an understatement.”
Separately, an online fundraiser was set up to help arrange funerals for the four victims. It had raised over €7,000 by Tuesday evening.
“There are no words to describe the heartbreak of losing four precious lives in such devastating circumstances,” it said.
“As our family tries to come to terms with this heartbreaking loss, we are faced with the task of arranging four funerals and giving Phillip, Kim, Callum and Jayden the loving farewells they deserve.”
Johnville Football Club paid tribute to Callum, who played with them for five years.
“Everyone at Johnville FC is absolutely heartbroken and devastated by the tragic events in Waterford,” it said in a statement.
“Kim and Philip were familiar and friendly faces around our club, always there supporting Callum at his matches. It is incredibly difficult to comprehend that a family we knew so well has been taken from us in such tragic circumstances.”
“All his team mates and coaches are absolutely devastated by the news, this pain of this tragedy will take a long time to heal.
“Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with all the family, their relatives and friends following this unimaginable loss. We are also thinking of those who are still fighting for their lives in hospital, and we sincerely hope they can pull through.”

title: Rory McIlroy feels LIV was ‘half a good idea’ and would welcome players back
description: World No 2 believes the breakaway tour is no longer a threat to the traditional game
content:
Rory McIlroy believes LIV Golf was “half a good idea, executed poorly” and the breakaway is no longer a threat to the traditional game as it tries to relaunch after filing for bankruptcy.
Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund ploughed in $5 billion over four years, luring the likes of Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau away from the PGA Tour, before withdrawing its support this year.
That led to Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in the United States with a view to relaunching as LIV 2.0, having received a potential $300 million backing from BC Partners Capital providing a specified number of players re-sign for the new venture.
Rahm has already announced he will not be continuing and news this week that any player signing up for LIV will be barred from DP World Tour membership and Ryder Cup eligibility has delivered a crippling blow.
“LIV had probably like, half of a good idea that was executed pretty poorly,” McIlroy told the Bloomberg New Economy forum in Delhi, where he is playing this week in the DP World India Championship.
“They had a lot of capital but I think a lot of that capital was wasted in some ways. And I think they could have used that money a lot more strategically and could have partnered with some of the governing bodies of the game and certainly could have done better things with it instead of just enriching tour pros who were already making a lot of money.
“BC Partners have come in and seen an opportunity [but] it looks like every day that goes by there’s another player that was on LIV who is not going to join LIV 2.0. So I think it is going to be very difficult to get out of this Chapter 11 bankruptcy and go forward.
“But if they do it is certainly not going to be a threat to the traditional order of the game as it once was.”
A more pertinent issue now seems to be what happens to those players quitting LIV.
The PGA Tour invokes a one-year suspension, denying them access until August next year, and while the DP World Tour has stiffened its rules its membership remains divided.
“I’m sure some members who stayed loyal would feel hard done by if these guys can just walk straight back in but, on the other side, having these players back on the tour is good for business and it can drive revenues up and everyone can benefit from that,” added McIlroy.
“I would vote for them to come back. A rising tide lifts all boats and I think having some of these players back is beneficial for the business of the tours.”
It is not a view shared by six-time DP World Tour winner Joost Luiten.
“Four years ago they didn’t give a s**t about the DP World Tour,” he told Today’s Golfer.
“They made a decision to go after the money and now all of a sudden, the money is gone and they want to come back and act like nothing happened. I don’t think that’s right.
“If they think they are that good then show it at Q-School and beat the guys. That’s how every other guy that wants to play on this tour has to go.”

title: The Irish Times view on the IMF economic forecasts: the limits of resilience
description: High government borrowing worldwide and the risks from the AI bubble are concerns
content:
The latest forecasts for the world economy from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) grapple with the central dilemma in trying to work out what happens next. Economic growth is holding up better than expected, particularly in the context of high energy costs. But the risks continue to grow, with the IMF highlighting the scale of government budget deficits and the damage which could results from a bursting of the AI bubble.
The fund has nonetheless edged up its forecast for global growth to 3.1 per cent this year and expects a lift to 3.4 per cent in 2027. Despite the fall-out from the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, growth remains surprisingly steady.
“The global economy has been resilient” said IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro, “but that resilience is reaching its limits.” This may or may not be correct – the US economy, in particular, and its stock market, have defied many predictions of trouble.
That said, there are warning signs. The most obvious is the sharp rise in interest rates as a result of higher-than-expected inflation. This is pushing up the cost of borrowing, with the IMF underlining the exposure of governments, which on average have a deficit over 5 per cent of GDP.
It also points to the risk of upheaval in the financial markets if earnings from AI prove to be disappointing, leading to questions about sky-high market valuations of many of the big players. As well as supporting markets, the AI investment boom is boosting international economic growth, albeit that the gains are relatively narrowly shared.
In the context of the IMF’s research, Ireland’s budget surplus stands out as a peculiarity internationally and one offering the State some financial resilience. The reliance on corporate tax revenues to create this surplus, however, creates a much-discussed exposure of its own. And the bursting of the AI bubble, were it to happen, would leave Ireland doubly exposed – on corporate taxes, as well as investment and growth. Ireland is resilient up to a point, but key vulnerabilities remain.

title: Retirement crisis looms for those in mortgage arrears, new analysis shows
description: Half of those in arrears will pay off less than 50% of debt by retirement, Central Bank study finds
content:
One in two of those in mortgage arrears are unlikely to clear even half their outstanding loan balance by the time they retire, according to a fresh Central Bank of Ireland analysis.
While the number of mortgages linked to family homes that are in arrears of more than 90 days has fallen from a peak of 12.9 per cent of all principal dwelling home mortgages back in September 2013 to just 3.1 per cent at the end of last year, that still amounts to more than 21,000 home loans.
And three-quarters of those in arrears now have their loans managed by loan servicing firms rather than the banks.
The Solution Waterfall: Insights from Irish Mortgage Distress Cases examines the arrangements put in place for close to 5,400 people in 2024 by banks and loan servicing firms.
Based on what they are paying and the time to retirement, the report’s authors suggest that 31 per cent of those in arrears will not be able to make any headway in clearing their mortgage balance.
A further 19 per cent will clear less than 50 per cent of the amount outstanding.
[ Pepper rate hike to heap more misery on distressed borrowers Opens in new window ]
The figures are worse for those whose loans are held by loan servicing firms than by banks. More than two-thirds of those at loan servicing firms will clear less than half of what they owe by the time they retire, the authors project, compared to just over a third of bank customers.
In the 2024 sample used in the report, loan servicing firms’ customers are older – 56 on at the median – compared to 51 at banks and have been in arrears for longer with larger outstanding loan balances.
Customers of loan servicing firms are more likely to be on higher variable interest rates – a premium of about 1.4 percentage points in 2024, according to the report – and less likely to be meeting the terms of the restructured repayment arrangements, write Patrik Gorše, Thomas Joyce and Paul Lyons.
“The ability to repay mortgage obligations by borrowers in long-term arrears who are now approaching or at retirement age remains a concern,” the authors say. “Finding sustainable restructures within the financial system for engaged borrowers in long-term mortgage arrears may not be possible.
“Many of those in long-term mortgage arrears today are now in their 50s or 60s, are mentally exhausted and need a permanent viable solution,” said Stephen Curtis, chief executive of mortgage-to-rent specialist Irish Homes.
“These people have had mortgage arrears hanging over them for decades and, in turn, the worry that they could lose their home.”
Curtis noted that central bank mortgage arrears data for the second quarter of this year showed that the number of accounts in arrears that are being brought before the courts had jumped by 6.6 per cent over the previous 12 months.

title: Psychiatric state of man accused of murdering three members of his family ‘central’ to trial
description: Robert O’Connor pleaded not guilty of murder by reason of insanity, or guilty of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility to the triple murder
content:
Jurors will hear differing evidence from expert psychiatrists for the prosecution and defence in the trial of a man accused of murdering three members of his family in their Co Louth home last year, the Central Criminal Court was told.
Robert O’Connor (32), of Drumgowna, Louth Village, Dundalk, Co Louth, pleaded not guilty of murder by reason of insanity, or guilty of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility to the triple murder of his mother Louise O’Connor (56), his father Mark O’Connor (54) and his younger brother Evan O’Connor (27) at their home in Drumgowna between September 28th and 29th 2025.
In her opening address on Tuesday, prosecution counsel Roisin Lacey SC said the jury will hear evidence that Robert O’Connor had episodes of psychosis from a young age and was diagnosed with schizophrenia in 2018.
Counsel said the special verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity is not one that a psychiatrist engaged on behalf of the prosecution would support.
Whereas the defence position is that the accused does come within the criteria of the Criminal Law Insanity Act 2006, she said.
The jury panel also heard the prosecution psychiatrist will give evidence that the accused’s mental disorder of schizophrenia had substantially diminished his responsibility for the three killings.
Prosecution counsel previously told the jury that O’Connor accepted he caused the death of the three victims in the case.
The jurors have already been told they will hear evidence that the three victims sustained a combined 139 stab wounds. Last week in her opening address, Lacey said that the accused told gardaí that he had a row over drugs, lost his head and only meant to kill his father and brother, but not his mother.
Lacey told Judge Mícheál P O’Higgins and the jury of six men and six women that they would hear from forensic scientist Georgina Daly, who examined a number of items taken from Drumgowna.
Counsel said Daly examined two knives, the accused’s clothing and door handles from inside and outside the patio door area.
Lacey said forensic scientist Andrea McGrath examined a three-seater couch in the sittingroom, which had a considerable amount of blood-staining.
McGrath, counsel said, will tell the jury that blood-pooling on three areas of the sittingroom floor and on a two-seater couch matched Mark O’Connor. The lawyer said McGrath found that Mark was actively bleeding in those areas while he was in an upright position.
Lacey said the jury will also hear psychiatric evidence during the trial, which will be “critical”. The barrister said in this case, the issue of the intention for murder must be interpreted in the context of psychiatric evidence.
Lacey said there will be evidence from two expert psychiatrists; Dr Fiona Toal engaged on behalf of the defence and Dr Ronan Mullaney engaged by the prosecution.
The barrister further stated that the jurors have already heard the two pleas put forward by the accused; “not guilty by reason of insanity or the alternative plea of guilty of manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility”.
The three criteria for a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity under the Criminal Law Insanity Act 2006 are that an accused did not know the nature and quality of the act, or was unable to appreciate that what they did at the time was wrong or would have been unable to refrain from their actions.
Counsel said the court will hear that Toal is of the view that the accused “does come” within the second two criteria of the Act; namely that he didn’t know what he was doing was wrong or was unable to refrain from committing the act.
Counsel said the prosecution’s position is that Mullaney disagrees with Toal. She said Mullaney accepts that the accused was in a state of psychosis and was having a psychosis relapse of schizophrenia. “Mullaney does say, like Toal, that Robert O’Connor did know the nature and quality of the act, where he disagrees is in relation to the two other elements; that he didn’t know what he was doing was wrong or was unable to refrain.”
The barrister said the court will also hear evidence from Mullaney that the accused’s ability to regulate his conduct was substantially impaired, but not fully impaired. Lacey said the special verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity is not a verdict Mullaney would support from a psychiatric point of view. The barrister said the alternative plea entered by the accused is guilty of manslaughter by diminished responsibility.
She said legislators had provided for this in section six of the Criminal Law Insanity Act 2006 and that this was the second potential verdict open to the panel. “Diminished responsibility is where a mental disorder is operating at the time of the killing and you will hear evidence that the person is criminally responsible but it is substantially diminished.”
Lacey said Mullaney will give evidence on behalf of the prosecution that on the balance of probabilities, the accused was suffering from schizophrenia at the material time and that his mental disorder substantially diminished his responsibility for each of the three killings.
Essentially, she explained, the “battleground” between the prosecution and defence is the verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity. The trial continues on Thursday.

title: LNG critical to energy security, conference told
description: Infrastructure task force member warns of risks
content:
Liquefied natural gas (LNG) is critical to the State’s energy security, a member of the Government’s infrastructure taskforce warned on Tuesday.
The Oireachtas passed legislation this year giving Minister for Energy Darragh O’Brien power to bypass planning laws to approve a proposed State LNG storage project.
Businessman Seán O’Driscoll, a member of the Government’s Accelerating Infrastructure Task Force, told the Institute of Directors annual conference that he had heard arguments in the media that the Republic does not need LNG.
“Thirty per cent of our primary energy is gas,” he said, adding that it came through a pipeline from Scotland.
“If anything happens those pipelines, our economy shuts down in three or four hours. For people to peddle the line, and get away with it, that we don’t need LNG facilities, is complacency,” O’Driscoll argued.
He remarked that the State took a lot of risks with its energy system. While it depends on imported oil for 50 per cent of its energy, its strategic reserve amounts to just 90 days’ supply, O’Driscoll added.
Speaking afterwards, he said the enactment of the Critical Infrastructure Act and new planning laws showed the Government’s commitment to overhauling the State’s system for planning and building infrastructure.
The infrastructure legislation means that key projects move to the top of the planning system’s queue. Government has since earmarked nine projects in transport, energy and water as critical infrastructure.
Those projects include the MetroLink, Shannon-Dublin water scheme, and North-South Interconnector, a high-capacity electricity line between the Republic and Northern Ireland.
That project was announced 20 years ago and has made it through the planning systems on both sides of the Border, but is not expected to be completed until 2031.
O’Driscoll said it was up to local and national politicians to win public acceptance for the project, which has met strong opposition from locals and landowners along the proposed route.
“These things have to be built; political leaders will have to step up,” he insisted.
The absence of the long-delayed project costs electricity users North and South €100 million extra a year, he said.
O’Driscoll is a former chairman of industrial group Glen Dimplex and of the Economic and Social Research Institute.
The infrastructure taskforce identified four key areas that Government needed to tackle to speed up the construction of projects vital to the State: legal reform, regulatory reform, co-ordination and public acceptance.
O’Driscoll said he concurred “100 per cent” with Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers’ remark last week that Government was working on unprecedented levels of change on the State’s systems for planning and building infrastructure.
Actual building of the MetroLink, tying Dublin’s city centre with its airport, could begin in February 2027, while State utility Uisce Éireann hopes to begin construction of the €1.3 billion wastewater project, the Greater Dublin Drainage scheme, shortly. That should be completed in 2030.

title: ‘Doubly endangered’ Dublin fanlight horse discovered
description: The Ringsend property where the figurine stands is up for sale
content:
T he discovery of a third surviving Dublin fanlight horse, this time in Ringsend , might have persuaded me to take the species off the endangered list. But as reader Conall (surname withheld) – who found it – suggests, that would be premature.
“This particular specimen could be considered doubly endangered,” he warns, “because the house is up for sale.”
Sure enough, it is. And describing the Bath Avenue property as a “double-fronted, Victorian residence dating from the 1870s”, the estate agents say it requires “complete refurbishment and modernisation throughout”.
So I fear for the horse: an unusual example of the genre in that it has all four hooves on the ground.
This appears to contravene what Seumas O’Sullivan said in his 1917 essay on the subject, at a time when the white fanlight horse was a classic feature of Georgian Dublin : that the figurine invariably had a raised foreleg, as if awaiting an order to charge.
Conversely, in his childhood mythmaking, no doubt influenced by the story of Oisín and Tir nan Óg, he imagined some great or terrible change overcoming the city if this occupying army of horses ever dropped the hoof.
Perhaps, he suggested in the more optimistic scenario, the raised foreleg “was but a symbol of that uncertainty of purpose, that ineffectual grasp on the things of earth, which had left his native land so many ages behind all other modern countries, and the setting down of it would be the signal for the release of a great and long-latent force of national character, which, once roused, would place it in the forefront of the world”.
That’s a lot of responsibility to place on a mere figurine. But whatever happened when the horse on Bath Avenue put its foot down has happened already, clearly. I’d be more worried now that the sale of the house will be the signal for the release of a great and long-latent force of refurbishment, in which there may be no place for an old-fashioned equine statue.
[ Another sighting of the lesser-spotted Dublin fanlight horse Opens in new window ]
Mention of Monto, Dublin’s former red-light district , last week evoked memories for a Cork reader of days, long past, when he was a foot soldier in the Legion of Mary.
The flood of recollection was prompted party by his confusion as to where Monto is or was, and my mention of its proximity to the Loopline Bridge (the one that crosses Amiens Street from what is now Connolly station).
Because by the time he joined the fight against vice, it seems, the front line had followed the Loopline across the Liffey to the south quays, operating there in the shadows of other bridges.
Anyway, his email is a reminder that, although the legion and its founder Frank Duff famously closed Monto down in the early years of Irish independence, the battle then and later was not all one way.
My correspondent was a “young, impressionable lad” when a friend persuaded him to join the organisation in (he thinks) Dún Laoghaire , from where they launched occasional forays into Dublin: “When we weren’t reciting prayers and imploring God to right the wrongs of the world, two of us were tasked with taking the bus into the city to try to rehabilitate some of the ‘Ladies of the Night’ who plied their trade in the dark lanes behind Tara Street train station, as it was then.
“One night we approached what to us at the time seemed to be an elderly lady lurking in the shadows, to try to convince her to mend her ways. Her response was to tell me to ‘go home to your mother, son’.” He thinks she may also have told him that this was the only way she could put food on the table for her family. This “was certainly food for thought for me and made me look at the bigger picture”.
Another night, he and his comrade were dispatched to Benburb Street, which predated Monto as a red-light area, thanks to the enormous Royal (now Collins) Barracks, and lingered on a smaller scale well into the last century.
[ Take a tour of Monto, Dublin's one-time notorious red light district Opens in new window ]
It lingers no longer: the only echo of red lights there now is the Red Line Luas, which speeds along the street on the stretch between Smithfield and Heuston Station.
The Dún Laoghaire missionaries’ work in Benburb Street was more convivial but no more successful: “We had a great chat with two young ladies and a good laugh too. They told us that they couldn’t afford their lifestyle by working at anything else.”
No conversions resulted, or at least not among the women. The reader’s email concludes: “We wished them a good night and good luck and took the number 8 bus home. I suppose it was part of my education about life and the end of my relationship with the Legion of Mary.”

title: Liverpool boss Iraola has ‘100% trust’ in Wirtz and Barcola but tells others to step up
