description: Liverpool face Lask in Austria without Isak, Gakpo and Szoboszlai
content:
Andoni Iraola has said he trusts Liverpool’s big-money signings Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola “100 per cent” but needs players to step up in the absence of his three leading goalscorers.
Liverpool will again be without Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai when visiting the Austrian side Lask in the Champions League on Wednesday. Iraola said he did not know when any of the trio, all of whom are carrying minor injuries sustained on international duty, would be available.
Their absence heightened the responsibility on Wirtz and Barcola against Manchester City on Sunday but both struggled as Liverpool suffered their first defeat under Iraola. Barcola is yet to produce a goal or an assist in six appearances since his £123 million arrival from Paris Saint-Germain, or even win possession in the final third, while Wirtz has one assist this season and continues to underwhelm in a Liverpool shirt.
“Cody, Alex and Dom are our top scorers this season and now we don’t have them. We need other players to give us those numbers,” said Iraola. “We trust the players we have now to play in those positions. With Bradley and Flo, they have had good games and bad games this season like everyone else. We know their level and we know they will give us good performances.
“The other day, if [Lewis] Koumas scores the goal that he connects with really well, then it is one assist for Bradley Barcola. His performance would be exactly the same but we will all say: ‘Oh, he played really well with an assist’. Sometimes we focus only on the numbers. With Bradley, the other day he had good situations and we did not finish them. Bradley and Flo are players that I trust 100 per cent.”
The Liverpool head coach confirmed he was likely to make changes in Linz, with several players taking knocks against City. Iraola insisted he was happy with the team’s spirit, attitude and work rate against City, “including from the offensive players”, but not with the collective response to Ryan Gravenberch’s harsh dismissal.
“A lot of what happened after we went down to 10 men was because we conceded straight away,” Iraola said. “We were making adjustments and then you go 1-0 down and it’s different, because then you have to go [for it] and you get caught in-between.
“The goal we conceded straight away hurt us. If we had made the adjustments earlier and been more compact at 0-0, it becomes a lot easier. But once you concede it’s not enough to just be compact. You need to go a little bit more and then spaces open.”
Virgil van Dijk is in line to captain Liverpool for a 200th time in all competitions on Wednesday. – Guardian

title: Workers have no ‘collective responsibility’ for business losses, WRC tells catering firm
description: Employee secures order for €2,300 in unpaid wages after working more than 100 hours before and during Forest Fest 2025
content:
A worker left unpaid for over a year after her ex-boss claimed she had “collective responsibility” for poor catering trade at a music festival last year has secured an order for €2,300 in unpaid wages.
“This may come as news to the respondent, but where a business loses money, there is no ‘collective responsibility’ for these losses,” an adjudication officer wrote in a decision published on Tuesday.
Belfast-based Nord Events Ltd has been directed to pay the sum to the worker Martina Tierney after being found in breach of the Payment of Wages Act 1991 by the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC).
Tierney, a secondary schoolteacher, told the WRC that she took up short-term temporary work doing administration for the firm before and during Forest Fest 2025, a three-day music and arts event in Co Laois .
At the time she was hired by company co-owner Aaron Cleary, she was told it was one of a number of festivals for which Nord Events was the catering contractor, she said.
Her duties were in preparation and administration for the catering operation, and she performed “many days” of work between July 18th and 28th, 2025, she said.
Tierney wrote to her employer seeking payment for 119.5 hours on August 8th, 2025, with Cleary having undertaken to pay her no later than 28 days after doing so, she said.
She filed a WRC complaint under the Payment of Wages Act five weeks later on September 15th, 2025 and confirmed at a hearing in September 2026 that she had still yet to be paid – over a year later.
Adjudication officer Pat Brady noted that Tierney wrote to her employer setting out the hours she worked and seeking payment.
In reply, the employer set out a list of issues stated to have arisen at the festival, including reduced turnover and complaints about food.
They blamed these alleged trading difficulties on “a failure of the team put together by [Tierney] to run the operation” Brady wrote.
“He stated that there was what he described as ‘a collective responsibility’ for these poor commercial outcomes. This may come as news to the respondent, but where a business loses money, there is no ‘collective responsibility’ for these losses,” Brady added.
He wrote that businesses had no right to present trading losses as a justification for failing in their legal duty to give staff their properly payable wages.
He upheld Tierney’s complaint and directed the firm to pay her the €2,321.75 in outstanding wages.

title: European shares hand back gains as tech valuations return to haunt
description: Iseq bucks trend with slight rise
content:
European shares closed lower on Tuesday – after handing back earlier gains – as concerns about artificial intelligence (AI) spending weighed on chipmakers and investors looked ahead to more US corporate earnings for clues on whether big technology firms ​can justify their heavy spending and high valuations.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 ended the session down 0.1 per cent.
The Iseq All-Share index reversed the broader trend to rise 0.6 per cent to 14,212.69, as heavyweight banking stocks, Kingspan and Kerry Group advanced.
AIB gained 0.7 per cent to €10.95 and Bank of Ireland edged 0.8 per cent higher to €18.59, benefiting from a knock-on effect on fresh interest by investors in UK banks.
Kingspan gained 1.2 per cent to €103, while Kerry Group added 2.1 per cent to €90.55, benefiting from strong results from Swiss peer Givaudan.
Ryanair lost 1.4 per cent to €22.71 as investors weighted the impact of ongoing elevated energy prices. Oil traders are currently assessing ​supply risks following attacks on Saudi Arabia and weighed the prospect of additional diesel supplies from Russia .
Of Irish interest, Greencore rose 1.9 per cent to £2.67 as the Dublin-based but London-listed sandwich and ready-meals maker again increased its profit guidance for its full financial year that ended in September.
The FTSE 100 index ended down 0.1 per cent, at 10,650.33. It had earlier traded as high as 10,762.01.
Aerospace technology company Melrose Industries rose 3.5 per cent as it said US authorities had begun the process of winding up their investigation into one of the company’s sites in California, after a major safety incident in May.
NatWest rose 2.1 per cent as Barclays Capital upgraded its rating to the equivalent of a buy.
Barclays analyst Aman Rakkar sees scope for earnings per share upside from higher interest rates, continued growth, and from the acquisition of Evelyn Partners.
Elsewhere, advertising giant WPP advanced 4.2 per cent after slightly better-than-expected results from French peer Publicis , which added 2.2 per cent.
But London Stock Exchange Group fell 4.7 per cent after confirming it is in talks to buy financial data firm Octus for $3.5 billion (€3.1 billion) from private-equity firm Permira.
Gambling group Entain rose 4.7 per cent as its joint venture BetMGM reiterated full-year guidance after a “strong” third quarter.
Technology stocks, tracking a ⁠global sell-off after ​reports of rapid tech progress by ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) fuelled concerns that China is narrowing the technology gap with established rivals.
European chipmakers STMicroelectronics , Soitec and Infineon slid between 1.7 per cent and 5.9 per cent, while ASML dropped 2.7 per cent.
LVMH closed 0.1 per cent lower – but well off its earlier lows – as the ‌world’s largest luxury group posted ⁠weaker-than-expected third-quarter sales, as deteriorating consumer sentiment in China weighed on demand for its Louis Vuitton and Dior brands.
Givaudan added 9.4 per cent after the fragrance and flavour maker’s third-quarter organic sales beat expectations.
Wall Street ’s main indexes were lower in early afternoon trading as chip stocks came under selling pressure again while investors parsed a mixed bag of quarterly results, including those from big US banks.
Healthcare shares were the biggest drags, with Johnson & Johnson losing ground despite topping quarterly profit estimates.
Financials added to the gloom as Wells Fargo fell after its net interest income missed estimates and JPMorgan Chase swung between gains and losses following a rare profit miss.
Citigroup dipped but Goldman Sachs rose after both ​topped estimates.
Hopes of a strong earnings season had been propping up the broader market amid geopolitical tension, surging bond yields and inflation worries.
Information technology stocks slid. Chip stocks bore the brunt after reports ​of technological advances by China’s CXMT.
Memory chipmaker Micron Technology dipped while data-storage companies Western Digital , Seagate and SanDisk also dropped.
This has brought the September reading of consumer and producer prices and retail numbers, slated for this week, under greater scrutiny.
Domino’s Pizza fell after scaling back its full-year ​sales outlook. – Additional reporting: Reuters, PA

title: Boy (2) settles case over alleged failure to identify heart abnormality with €1m interim payment
description: Court hears that Ollie Roche’s heart condition could and should have been diagnosed before he was born
content:
A two-year-old boy who is now on “borrowed time” after a serious heart abnormality was allegedly not detected in a hospital ultrasound scan before he was born has settled a High Court action against the HSE .
Ollie Roche was six weeks old when he was diagnosed with complex congenital heart disease and his parents thought he could have life-saving surgery. Within 24 hours, however, they were told that it was too late for surgery and palliative care should be considered.
Oonah McCrann, counsel for the boy, instructed by Cantillons Solicitors, told the High Court on Tuesday that Ollie, from Gorey in Co Wexford, had already defied medical expectations and was a remarkable little boy.
“He is living his best life on what is borrowed time,” counsel told Judge Leonie Reynolds.
The boy, along with his mother Leonie Kinch, father Sean Roche and his grandparents, was in court for the ruling of an interim settlement of more than €1 million in the case against the HSE over his and his mother’s care at Wexford General Hospital before and after his birth in November 2023.
It was their case that the heart defect should have been picked up in an ultrasound scan of June 2023, counsel said, and if identified Ollie would have been able to have surgery.
In a statement outside court, Ollie’s mother said that in a matter of six weeks, they went from the elation following Ollie’s arrival to learning that he had a serious heart condition, but believed it could be fixed with surgery, to then learning that it was now too late for the life-saving surgery.
Kinch said: “The shock and heartbreak of that moment have never left us. The heartbreak was compounded when, following our solicitor’s investigations, we learned that Ollie’s heart condition could and should have been diagnosed before he was born.”
Kinch said her son had defied all the odds and kept fighting, but “our family lives with the uncertainty of not knowing what the next day or even the next few hours may bring”.
[ Teenage girl allegedly raped, strangled and thrown out of car, court hears Opens in new window ]
She said they “live in fear and trepidation that we may see the signs in Ollie of deterioration that we have been advised to be vigilant for. Our days are shaped by caring for Ollie and doing everything we can to give him the best quality of life.
“It is heartbreaking to live with the fear of what the future may bring. We try to make the most of our time together and take life day by day. Nothing can take away what Ollie and our family have been through, and what we have lost, but it means so much that Ollie has finally got justice.
“Hopefully lessons will have been learned that the mistakes in my pregnancy with Ollie won’t be repeated.”
It was claimed in proceedings that, following Ollie’s delivery, there was also a failure to perform accurately or at all a pulse oximetry screening, which detects critical congenital heart disease in newborns.
The HSE has admitted that by failing to obtain a clear four-chamber view of the baby’s heart and not identifying suboptimal ambiguous images for follow up, the assessment conducted by the June 27th, 2023, scan in Wexford General Hospital was incomplete and fell below the standard of care expected.
[ Supreme Court to hear appeal in LinkedIn challenge to €310m DPC fine Opens in new window ]
It further admitted that the failure to identify the baby’s cardiac condition antenatally had adversely affected his survival rate into early childhood years.
The HSE contended that Ollie’s diagnosis of complex congenital heart disease would have adversely affected his life expectancy beyond mid-childhood, notwithstanding the failure to identify this diagnosis antenatally.
Approving the interim settlement, the judge wished Ollie well and hoped he continued to thrive. The case will come back before the court in 2029.

title: Judge again urges O’Callaghan and solicitors to resolve legal aid case between them
description: Situation will continue unless Minister for Justice agrees to engagement, lawyers say
content:
The withdrawal by many criminal defence solicitors from legal aid services seems set to continue unless the Minister for Justice agrees to engagement with a view to resolving the dispute over a new payment model.
That was the message on Tuesday from solicitor sources after the Minister, Jim O’Callaghan, and solicitors were both reminded by a High Court judge that her colleague had urged them to try and “use their own endeavours” to resolve a legal challenge to the new model.
Judge Siobhán Phelan noted Judge Mary Rose Gearty made that call in late July when hearing a challenge by Dublin solicitor John Quinn to the new payment model for legal aid work in the District Courts, introduced by O’Callaghan on July 1st.
Gearty’s judgment was due on October 13th but the sides were told last week, due to “unforeseen circumstances”, it was being deferred to another date.
On Tuesday, Phelan, who was managing the High Court judicial review list in Gearty’s absence, said judgment will be delivered on November 3rd.
Gearty, when hearing the case, had urged the parties to try and resolve matters through their own endeavours and was reminding them of that, said Phelan.
On Tuesday, the Law Society welcomed the “significant” comments of the High Court, noting they came after the Chief Justice last week said the continuation of the dispute was a matter of concern to him and to judges generally.
The Society “agrees that this matter needs to be resolved without any further delay and again calls on the Minister and his officials to meet directly, as the Minister has previously ruled out mediation,” it said.
[ Courts facing further disruption as judicial review of new legal aid model delayed Opens in new window ]
Later on Tuesday, the continuing impasse was discussed by Dublin-based solicitors, and solicitors from around the country, during Zoom meetings.
While refusing to be drawn on the content or outcome of the discussions when contacted by The Irish Times, Tony Collier, a partner in Ferrys LLP, said solicitors in Dublin “remain resolute in their opposition to the new scheme and in their desire to resolve the matter quickly”.
The dispute has seriously disrupted the work of the criminal courts in all divisions since July and has led to the adjournment of thousands of cases, adding to existing backlogs.
While some solicitors have resumed legal aid work, sources say most, particularly in Dublin, continue to participate in the withdrawal.
The new payment model provides for one flat fee of €520, based on an average five court appearances, irrespective of the number of charges and court appearances.
Solicitors have complained it means they will not be paid for their work in more complex cases, including ones involving children and people with addiction and mental health issues.
The Law Society had urged the Minister to agree to an independent mediation of the dispute but O’Callaghan has said that would not be appropriate in a situation where Gearty’s judgment was pending on a challenge to the regulations establishing the new scheme.
The Minister has also repeatedly said the new payment scheme will achieve necessary reform of the criminal legal aid system and is in the public interest.
In a letter to the Society on October 4th, O’Callaghan, while declining to enter mediation, said he remained open to engagement, his officials are available to discuss “operational” issues and were finalising a “preliminary review” of data related to the children’s courts.

title: McDonald’s uses Ireland to test  hand-breaded chicken in Europe
description: Fast food giant facing growing competition from new arrivals specialising in chicken
content:
McDonald’s has launched a four-month “operational pilot” for hand-breaded chicken products in Ireland, the fast-food giant has announced.
Available to customers from Tuesday across a small number of Dublin restaurants, McDonald’s said the scheme “will test both the product and execution, evaluating how restaurants can deliver each menu item consistently at scale while keeping kitchen complexity to a minimum”.
“Customers will be able to enjoy hand-breaded versions of existing favourites,” the company continued, such as chicken wraps and strips. Come February, when the pilot project is set to conclude, McDonald’s plans to initiate larger-scale testing that will benefit from “advertising support”.
The Chicago-based company, which has nearly 40,000 restaurants in more than 100 countries, said it had identified a “strong customer demand” in Ireland for chicken products, complimented by “the country’s chicken leadership”.
This makes the Irish fast-food scene “an ideal market to introduce hand-breaded chicken to Europe”, McDonald’s said.
The new initiative comes as a slew of US quick-chicken brands has recently arrived in Ireland - including such as Popeyes, Wingstop, Dave’s Hot Chicken and Chick-fil-A.
Popeyes has expanded rapidly since arriving here, opening four outlets in three months.
KFC, the longest-established fast chicken player in the Irish market, has pledged a £105 million (€124 million) investment to grow its presence in Ireland over the next decade
McDonalds has already implemented the hand-breaded technique to over 10,000 restaurants across Asia.
Tim Kenward, the chief marketing officer of the fast-food giant’s UK and Ireland subsidiary, said “this is about much more than introducing a new way of preparing chicken.”
“Ireland’s strength in chicken makes it the ideal market to help us understand what it takes to deliver this at scale and support our ambition to become the first choice for more customers, more often.
McDonald’s operates 96 restaurants across the State and employs more than 7,000 people as of April 2026.

title: Cúrsa Ullmhúcháin don Ghaelcholáiste forbartha ag COGG
description: Na Ceithre hAirde: Cúrsa ullmhúcháin COGG; “An-díomá” ar TG4 faoin mbuiséad agus Comhdháil ar Litríocht agus ar Chultúr na Gaeilge.
content:
Tá cúrsa úrnua fógartha ag an Chomhairle um Oideachais Gaeltachta agus Gaelscolaíochta (COGG) le cuidiú le daltaí i Rang a Sé atá ag smaoineamh ar dhul chuig Gaelcholáiste nó chuig scoil Ghaeltachta i mí Mheán Fómhair 2027.
Mar chuid den chúrsa ceithre oíche seo, fanfaidh na daltaí i dteach le teaghlach Gaeltachta i Ros a Mhíl i gConamara, foghlaimeoidh siad teanga agus téarmaíocht na scoile a bheidh de dhíth orthu sa mheánscoil, agus cuirfidh siad le muinín agus cumas s’acu sa Ghaeilge. Beidh deis ag na daltaí bualadh le daoine nua agus cairde a dhéanamh sula mbogann siad ar aghaidh chuig an Ghaelcholáiste i mí Mheán Fómhair, agus beidh spraoi acu lena gcairde nua ag na himeachtaí a reáchtálfar i gColáiste Chamuis san oíche.
Beidh an cúrsa seo ar siúl le linn shaoire na Cásca (29 Márta – 2 Aibreán 2027) agus beidh sé oscailte do pháistí beag beann ar an leibhéal Gaeilge atá acu. Costas €560 atá ar an chúrsa ach cuirfidh COGG €300 ar fáil do gach páiste agus mar sin ní bheidh le híoc ag tuismitheoirí ach €260 do gach páiste ar an iomlán.
An bhfuil suim ag do pháiste sa chúrsa seo? Tá foirm um léiriú spéise ar fáil ar shuíomh gréasáin COGG anois. Is é an 20 Samhain spríocdháta don léiriú spéise agus beidh Coláiste Chamuis i dteagmháil le gach duine a líon an fhoirm faoin 11 Nollaig. Má tá tuilleadh eolais uait, déan teagmháil le Conchubhar ag conchubhair@cogg.ie .
“An-díomá” ar TG4 faoi leithdháileadh maoinithe i mBuiséad 2027
Deir Deirdre Ní Choistín, Ard-Stiúrthóir TG4, gur “cúis mhór díomá” é don stáisiún nach bhfuil ardú ar bith ar an mhaoiniú a gheobhaidh siad faoi Bhuiséad 2027. Is é seo an chéad uair le 10 mbliana nach bhfuair an stáisiún aon ardú sa bhuiséad.
Dar le Ní Choistín, is ionann an cinneadh seo agus “deis curtha amú chun infheistíocht a dhéanamh i seirbhís a chuireann spriocanna cultúir, sóisialta agus eacnamaíocha i gcrích”. Deir sí fosta nach bhfuil an cinneadh “ag teacht ar chor ar bith leis an luach a bhaineann an pobal as TG4, luach atá cruthaithe leis an ardú leanúnach atá ar an lucht féachana, ná leis an méid a chuireann TG4 leis an ngeilleagar.”
€65.4 milliún a bheidh ag TG4 an bhliain seo chugainn, an maoiniú céanna a tugadh don stáisiún do 2026. Deir Ní Choistín go mbeidh “impleachtaí” ag an chinneadh seo ar TG4 in 2027 agus go mbeidh ar an fhoireann “é a mheas anois i dtaobh ár gcuid pleananna agus spriocanna straitéiseacha don bhliain amach romhainn.”
I bpreasráiteas a d’fhoilsigh TG4 an tseachtain seo caite, deir siad go mbíonn “teorainn leis an bpleanáil agus leis an infheistíocht fhadtéarmach ó tharla go bhfuil TG4 ag brath ar chinntí buiséid bliantúla. Cruthaíonn sé éiginnteacht don earnáil léiriúcháin neamhspleách sa nGaeltacht agus ar fud na tíre, ar comhlachtaí beaga iad den chuid is mó.”
Comhdháil ar Litríocht agus ar Chultúr na Gaeilge in Ollscoil na Gaillimhe ar na bacáin
Beidh comhdháil shuimiúil ar siúl in Ollscoil na Gaillimhe an deireadh seachtaine seo ina ndéanfar “comóradh, cur agus cúiteamh” ar Forbairt na Gaeilge, leabhrán tábhachtach ar nádúr, ar fhoirm agus ar chultúr na Gaeilge a scríobh Niall Ó Dónaill sa bhliain 1951.
Tá clár ar dóigh beartaithe arís i mbliana agus is iad Peadar Ó Muircheartaigh (Ollscoil Dhún Éideann), Nóirín Ní Ghrádaigh agus Mícheál Ó Mainnín (Ollscoil na Banríona, Béal Feirste) a bheidh mar aoichainteoirí na comhdhála. Chomh maith leis sin, beidh scoth na gcainteoirí ag teacht le chéile ar champas le roinnt cainteanna agus cur i láthair a chur os comhair an lucht spéise.
Beidh díospóireacht oíche Aoine maidir le dearcadh agus le prionsabail a bhaineann le forbairt na Gaeilge agus is iad Máire Ní Neachtain (Fóram Chois Fharraige um Pleanáil Teanga), Noel Ó Murchadha (Coláiste na Tríonóide, Baile Átha Cliath), Antain Mac Lochlainn (scríbhneoir agus aistritheoir) agus Pádraig Ó Mianáin (Príomh-Eagarthóir an Fhoclóra Nua Béarla-Gaeilge) a bheidh i mbun plé le Séamus Ó Coileáin (Stiúrthóir ar Oifig an Choimisinéara Teanga) sa Téatar in Áras na Gaeilge. Labhróidh an chéad aoichainteoir, Peadar Ó Muircheartaigh, ar fhorbairt agus neamhfhorbairt na dteangacha Gaelacha 1750–1850 ina dhiaidh sin.
Seolfar leabhar úr Ar Lámh Shábhála? Coimisiún na Gaeltachta 1926 le John Walsh oíche Aoine fosta agus cuirfidh Gormfhlaith Ní Thuairisg ó RTÉ Raidió na Gaeltachta agallamh ar an údar le clabhsúr a chur ar an chéad oíche den chomhdháil.
Beidh réimse leathan cainteanna agus cur i láthair ar siúl le linn an lae Dé Sathairn agus is féidir teacht ar an chlár iomlán ar shuíomh Roinn na Gaeilge, Ollscoil na Gaillimhe.
Labhróidh an bheirt aoichainteoirí eile le linn an lae fosta. Amharcfaidh Nóirín Ní Ghrádaigh ar Thaighde Feidhmeach Pobalbhunaithe ar shealbhú agus scríobh na Gaeilge i measc cainteoirí dúchais ár linne, agus déanfaidh Mícheál Ó Mainnín plé ar Éiris, Albais, agus Forbairt na Gaoidheilge.

title: US ambassador to Greece resigns after reports she asked Trump donor to pay bill
description: Kimberly Guilfoyle, former finacée of Donald Trump Jr, is alleged to have accepted improper gifts
content:
Kimberly Guilfoyle is stepping down as US ambassador to Greece , after weeks of reports that she sought payment from a Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials.
The decision, announced by the White House on Tuesday morning, ends the diplomatic career of one of Trump’s longest-standing political allies. It came after Trump and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, were reported to have grown furious over the allegations.
“We have asked ambassador Guilfoyle to resign, she has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well,” said Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary, during her first briefing on Tuesday.
Guilfoyle – the former fiancee of Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr – later confirmed her departure from the post, which she described as the “honour of a lifetime”, and denied what she described as “false” allegations.
Pledging to “vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity” in a post on social media, she wrote: “While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end.”
The most serious claim, first reported by the Wall Street Journal on 8th October, centres on the donor Eric Deters.
Citing Signal messages, the paper reported that in July 2025, days before her Senate confirmation hearing, Guilfoyle pressed Deters to pay off a $100,000 American Express bill, assuring him the transfer would not show up anywhere. “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today,” she wrote, according to the report.
Guilfoyle offered to use her influence on his tax and legal problems in return and told him she had contacted the IRS commissioner and the justice department on his behalf.
He has also said he paid Guilfoyle about $300,000 over the years without receiving “one favour”, and told MS NOW the request “absolutely was a quid pro quo”.
In a series of stories, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official and accepting improper gifts and services.
After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday last, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”
But after another report appeared late on Wednesday, Rubio berated journalists for asking about the allegations, saying he did not know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them.
“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.
Guilfoyle (57), a former San Francisco prosecutor who was married until 2006 to Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, became a fixture of Trump’s political orbit after leaving Fox News in 2018 as she began dating Trump Jr. The couple became engaged in late 2020, and she was a prominent speaker at Trump’s campaign events, including the 2024 Republican national convention, before breaking up soon after in September 2024.
Trump, as president-elect, then named her for the Athens post in December 2024, weeks after his election win, calling her “a close friend and ally”. That month, Trump Jr had been photographed holding hands with Bettina Anderson, a Palm Beach socialite, and Guilfoyle was absent from the family’s post-election portrait, which did include Trump Jr’s ex-wife and their children. Trump Jr married Anderson in May.
The nomination stalled for months in the Senate until Republicans used the “nuclear option” in September 2025 to overcome a Democratic filibuster and confirm her by simple majority. She was sworn in as the first woman to represent the US in Greece, succeeding the Biden appointee George Tsunis, and arrived in Athens in late October 2025. - Guardian

title: Surge in stud fees help Godolphin cut losses sharply at Irish operation
description: Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum’s Irish business comprises five farms across three counties
content:
Revenues at Godolphin’s Irish thoroughbred stud operation surged by 42 per cent to €44.29 million last year on the back of a sharp rise in nomination fee income.
That helps Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum’s Godolphin Ireland Ltd dramatically cutting pretax losses to €1.93 million from €11.34 million previously, a fall of 83 per cent.
Godolphin’s operation in Ireland comprises five farms in Kildare, one in Meath and two in Tipperary.
The Godolphin displayed its financial muscle in recent weeks when it outbid Coolmore to pay €1.3 million for Churchtown House Stud’s Modern Games filly at Goffs’ Orby Sale on September 29th.
The rise in revenues coincided with a strong year on the track by Godolphin-trained horses globally.
In May last year, Godolphin created history with four Classic winners in three days, including the Kentucky Derby victory in the US for Sovereignty.
The headquarters of the Irish operation, which embraces stud, arable and livestock farming, is Kildangan Stud, just outside Kildare town.
Ruler of Dubai and vice-president of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Al-Maktoum is one of the world’s richest leaders and one of the most famous names in the world of horse racing, pouring billions of euro into the industry over the past 40 years.
The Irish operation recorded the €1.93 million losses after incurring €18 million in lease costs and non-cash depreciation costs of €1.89 million.
Numbers employed at Godolphin’s Irish operation were down slightly at 203 people, from 209 the previous year as staff costs increased 7.7 per cent to €14.7 million. Directors shared pay of €758,915 in 2025.
Nomination fee income – the stud fee that owners of mares pay to have their horses covered by a Goldophin horse – last year surged 55 per cent to €36.99 million as accommodation, or “keep fee” income remained flat at €5.8 million.
Accumulated losses at Godolphin Ireland rose to €212.38 million at the end of last year with a shareholders’ deficit of €184.52 million.
The firm’s cash funds increased from €5.46 million to €12.77 million.
On the company’s going concern status, the directors state that Godolphin Ireland had received written confirmation of continued support from a group company, Reliance Holdings Ltd and that it will settle all third party liabilities.
At the end of December, Godolphin Ireland owed €269.7 million to Reliance Holdings Ltd.

title: Man who replied ‘I don’t know’ to charge of murdering his father two years ago pleads not guilty
description: Seth Whelan (36) is charged with the murder of Michael Whelan (64) at a flat in Dublin 8
content:
A not guilty plea has been entered on behalf of a man after he replied, “I don’t know” when charged at the Central Criminal Court with the murder of his father two years ago.
Seth Whelan (36) is charged with the murder of Michael Whelan (64) at a flat they shared in Herberton Park, Rialto, Dublin 8 on a date unknown between February 19th and 27th 2024, both dates inclusive.
He is also charged that on February 20th, 2024 at a flat belonging to another woman at Herberton Park, he damaged a Ring doorbell camera without lawful excuse, intending to damage such property or being reckless as to whether such property would be damaged.
He replied, “I don’t know,” to each charge.
When the indictment was put to him a second time, defence barrister Philip Sheahan SC replied on his client’s behalf, telling the court and jury that Whelan pleads not guilty to each charge.
Judge Caroline Biggs swore a jury of six men and six women to hear the trial, which is expected to take up to four weeks.
Biggs asked the jury to return for the opening of the trial on Thursday. She also asked the jury not to discuss the case or do any research of their own as they are required to consider only what they hear in court.

title: Ban on public sale of nitrous oxide being considered over damage to young people’s health
description: Separately, gardaí to refer first-time offenders found with ‘small amount’ of drugs to health services
content:
The Government is considering legislation to ban the sale of nitrous oxide to the public due to health and safety concerns for children and young people, the Minister of State for Public Health has said.
Recreational abuse of inhaled nitrous oxide, commonly known as laughing gas or whippets, has increased significantly in the last 10 years, particularly among younger age groups. The gas is used in healthcare settings for anaesthetic and analgesic reasons.
But the HSE has said there has been a 130 per cent rise in people presenting for treatment for misuse of nitrous oxide since 2022 alone.
Irish studies have highlighted an “alarming” spike in the number of young people in Ireland ending up with spinal cord damage and lasting injuries from the substance.
Minister of State at the Department of Health Jennifer Murnane O’Connor acknowledged the State needed to do more to protect young people and children from the risk of this substance, which she described as a “worry”.
“I have set up an interdepartmental group within my own department, the HSE and working with [Minister for Justice] Jim O’Callaghan . We are now looking at, do we need legislation or how will we go forward,” she said.
“What I will say is the EU now is introducing what’s called the Reach regulations. So from February 1st, 2027, nitrous oxide will no longer be allowed to be on sale to the general public. Working with our EU colleagues we would be looking at that as well. We will look at all options.”
Fianna Fáil’s Teresa Costello held a meeting with experts in Leinster House on Tuesday on the issue, raising concerns about addiction and the neurological and public health implications of its misuse.
The senator said the use of the substance was at epidemic levels, saying she recently collected more than 550 discarded nitrous oxide canisters in two hours at two clean-ups in Tallaght , southwest Dublin .
Murnane O’Connor was speaking following the launch of the new national drugs strategy, which will run until 2030.
The strategy does not decriminalise drug-use, as had been recommended by the Oireachtas health committee and the Citizens’ Assembly , but instead focuses on a “health-led approach”.
Under the strategy, gardaí can refer a person who has been found with a “small amount” of drugs for the first time to the health services as an alternative to prosecution through the courts.
Murnane O’Connor said gardaí would lead in this regard and would receive training. She did not define what qualified as a “small amount”.
“That will be up to the gardaí. So when the gardaí find someone with a small amount of drugs for personal use, then that will be up to them to decide whether they need to take a health-led approach,” she said.
“If it’s first time, if you’ve gotten drugs for personal use for first time, then it will be led through, as I said, with our gardaí. They will put you in what will be the health-led approach, which is really important.
“Then after that, as we said, it’s up to the gardaí then on a second time, and they will then have that choice if they want to look at it this way.”
A pilot scheme began on September 1st and will be reviewed after a year to “see how its working, do we need to change it a bit, and we are open to that, too”, she said.

title: Supreme Court to hear appeal in LinkedIn challenge to €310m DPC fine
description: Levy imposed for breaches of European data protection legislation
content:
The Supreme Court will hear an appeal by the Data Protection Commission (DPC) relating to certain preliminary matters arising in LinkedIn’s challenge to the imposition of a €310 million fine by the commission.
In October 2024, the DPC fined LinkedIn €310 million for breaches of European data protection legislation.
Microsoft-owned LinkedIn claims that the fine was a sanction that is “criminal or penal in nature” due to its magnitude. The company subsequently initiated High Court proceedings challenging this decision.
LinkedIn asked the High Court to quash the DPC’s decision of October 2023, which came on foot of a 2018 complaint originally made to the French data watchdog by a French non-profit organisation called La Quadrature du Net.
In a statement at the time of its decision, the DPC said LinkedIn had obtained the consent of its users for their personal data to be sent to third parties for generating targeted advertising. However, it found the consent was not “freely given, sufficiently informed or specific, or unambiguous”, as is required under the GDPR.
LinkedIn Ireland said the DPC initially proposed imposing administrative fines of between €430 million and €490 million. That figure was reduced following submissions from the company.
The social media group focused on professional networking claims the severity of the fine entitled it to a fair and public hearing before an independent and impartial tribunal and to the presumption of innocence, as provided for in the Charter of Fundamental Rights.
In a judgment handed down in April, the High Court determined several preliminary issues in the proceedings. The DPC has appealed to the Supreme Court on three of the issues decided on by the High Court. LinkedIn is also looking to bring a cross-appeal on another preliminary issue.
Granting permission for the appeal, a three-judge Supreme Court panel noted that parties to the dispute agree that the issues raised in the High Court determination are matters of general public importance, a prerequisite for any case heard by the Supreme Court.
“[The case] will likely affect the approach to other statutory appeals. The DPC is the lead supervisory authority for GDPR [General Data Protection Regulation] purposes in this respect. The complaint in this case was initiated by a French non-profit organisation,” the court said.
“The number of subscribers to LinkedIn runs to hundreds of millions and the number of persons affected by the GDPR infringement found by the DPC was very significant indeed. And, finally, the State had been permitted to participate in the hearing in the High Court precisely because of the significance of the issues involved.”
The panel also decided that the issues raised warranted a leapfrog appeal from the High Court.
In those High Court proceedings, LinkedIn alleges the DPC, in inflicting such a severe fine and other reprimand, was not exercising limited functions and powers of a judicial nature within the meaning of the Constitution.
The company claims various sections of the 2018 Data Protection Act related to the commission’s powers are contrary to the Constitution, the Charter of Fundamental Rights and the State’s obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights.

title: ‘He’s with Putin’: Ukrainians recoil at Trump’s pressure campaign
description: Residents of wartime Lviv feel the US president’s actions are undermining Ukraine’s struggle against Russia
content:
T he historic city of Lviv in western Ukraine is nearly 1,000km from the front line, but the war with Russia invades the lives of its 700,000 people every day.
Air-raid sirens wailed over the Unesco -listed old town before dawn on Tuesday, and explosions shook people awake as air defences downed jet-powered attack drones on the edge of the city. Several houses and cars were set on fire, but no one was hurt.
During nearly five years of all-out war, Lviv residents have reluctantly grown accustomed to sleepless nights, days spent with a weary eye on news from the battlefield, and the slow procession of funeral cars through the city as another fallen soldier is laid to rest.
Like all Ukrainians, including president Volodymyr Zelenskiy , they have also got used to the tirades of Donald Trump as he repeatedly wields the stick against Kyiv and dangles carrots before Moscow in his flailing attempts to end the Russian invasion.
In recent days, Trump has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports, ordered Kyiv to stop bombing Russia’s oil refineries and told Ukrainians to “get a new president”, before announcing an “energy ceasefire” between the warring neighbours that neither of them appeared to know anything about.
Helena, walking past the Lviv city hall that dominates Market Square, says it is impossible to rely on Trump.
“I don’t think that I, or European leaders and people, can trust him. He says one thing today and another thing tomorrow,” she adds. “He should choose what he wants, and which side he is on.”
Trump has consistently piled pressure on Ukraine – lambasting Zelenskiy in the Oval Office last year, blaming him for the war, replacing US military aid for Kyiv with a purchasing scheme funded by other Nato states – while repeatedly backing down on threats to tighten sanctions on Russia.
[ Ukraine backs Trump’s energy ‘ceasefire’. But is Russia on board? Opens in new window ]
Andriy (48), standing on Market Square in the middle of old Lviv, lets fly a stream of invective at the mention of Trump.
“He is together with Putin,” he fumes, referring to Russia’s president.
“They are friends. It’s all about money – just business,” he adds, admitting he has no idea what to expect from Trump. “Who knows? God knows. He’s a stupid man.”
Mariya, wheeling her sleeping child past a Lviv flower market on a damp autumn morning, says the latest policy spasm from the White House leaves Ukraine “in a bad situation”.
“I am completely not agreeing with what he said,” she says of Trump’s demand that Zelenskiy should go.
“I hope some miracle will happen and [Trump] will change his mind. Also, I hope different politicians in the US and in Europe will help him understand. I hope he will change his mind and be a better man than he is now.”
Zelenskiy pointed out what energy analysts say is obvious – that Trump’s war on Iran is to blame for the spike in world fuel prices, and that Russian diesel exports will be too small to dramatically affect the market, but will help replenish Putin’s war chest.
He also said Ukraine would hold presidential elections if Russia adhered to a full two-month ceasefire.
“In Ukraine, there is a lot of criticism towards the government. There is depression, even devastation because of the war and bombings, and also the corruption scandals of recent years. Of course, people are unsatisfied,” says Vitaliy, an IT worker in Lviv.
“But – and I don’t think this is just a Ukrainian thing – we don’t like pressure and interference in our internal affairs. So I would even say that [Trump’s attack] gave Zelenskiy and his government more internal legitimacy,” he adds.
“In fact, it’s the same thing that Putin wants ... So we feel they are actually on the same side ... When and why and under what circumstances we have elections is for us to decide.”
“Of course Trump is not pro-Ukraine. The question is whether he is pro-Russian or even pro-American. It looks like he is pro-gain – maybe even personal gain or the gain of his allies,” Vitaliy says.
“It seems like it is simpler for him to talk to dictators like Putin or [North Korea’s] Kim Jong-un or the Chinese government ... and Ukraine and smaller countries are just like coins in his game. So I don’t trust him. Yesterday he supported us, and today he says we should surrender because he needs cheap oil.”
Trump’s fear of Republican defeat in next month’s midterm elections for Congress, and his continued failure to end a war that he said he could stop in one day, make for a volatile combination that could destroy the already badly frayed ties between the White House and Kyiv.
Ukrainians fear a furious Trump could pull the plug on Nato purchases of weapons for their country, and on its use of US intelligence and Starlink satellite internet services.
Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukraine had received “no early warning from our partners” the previous night about a “particularly vile” Russian ballistic missile strike on civilian infrastructure in Kyiv. It was not immediately clear why no signal came.
“I think we could survive,” Vitaliy says of the prospect of fighting on without any US help. “It would be hard for us. But Ukraine would remain.”

title: Teenage girl allegedly raped, strangled and thrown out of car, court hears
description: The 17-year-old was described in court as ‘one of the most vulnerable children in Northern Ireland’
content:
A vulnerable teenage girl was allegedly raped and strangled before being thrown out of a car in Co Down , the High Court has heard.
Prosecutors claimed a 37-year-old Belfast man also threatened her with a knife after being told she was pregnant with his baby.
A so-called “good Samaritan” discovered her lying by the side of a road in Bangor following the incident on September 26th.
Details emerged as the accused was refused bail on charges which involve plying the teenager with crack cocaine as part of a campaign of sexual and physical violence.
He is not being named to protect the identity of the 17-year-old girl.
She made a 999 call in the early hours of September 26th, claiming the defendant had just attacked and raped her in his car.
The girl alleged that he then threw her out of the vehicle and drove off.
The girl, who was intoxicated, claimed the man had raped and grabbed her by the throat, striking her head off the dashboard.
She said he had a knife and threatened to use it on her, and that she told him that evening that she is pregnant with his baby.
[ Gardaí ordered to bring two youths at ‘extreme’ risk to special care despite Tusla protest Opens in new window ]
The pair had been in a relationship for a number of months after meeting online through Snapchat , according to the injured party’s account.
He allegedly supplied her with crack cocaine, which they used to smoke together.
The court heard they also had consensual sex on multiple occasions at the defendant’s home and other locations.
But he also recorded those encounters on his phone without her permission, it was claimed.
On the night of the alleged rape, she said he picked her up in the Bangor area, took a shot of neat rum and supplied her with the rest of it.
She was taken to the Ulster Hospital for treatment to injuries on her neck, forehead and arms.
Based on her wider circumstances, the prosecution barrister submitted: “The injured party is deemed to be one of the most vulnerable children in Northern Ireland.”
[ Investment vehicle sues over financing plan for apartment scheme in Leopardstown Opens in new window ]
The defendant denies charges of rape, non-fatal strangulation, voyeurism, possession of an offensive weapon, having indecent images of a child and supplying class A drugs.
During interviews, he claimed the girl’s injuries were self-inflicted following consensual sex in his car.
The man said he pushed her out of the car near a roundabout when she started banging her head off the dashboard
He admitted they had been in a sexual relationship for up to four months but insisted those activities were never recorded.
Defence barrister Sean Devine highlighted how the girl has not yet made an official statement of complaint.
“The issue is one of consent in a relationship which was in place for some time,” he said.
Refusing bail, Judge Doherty cited the risks of reoffending and interference with a vulnerable alleged child victim.
The judge stated: “I am concerned that, at its height, this is an absolutely horrendous incident.”

title: Phil Hogan ready to ‘serve once again’ as he launches bid for UN food agency job
description: Former minister dismisses suggestion that Golfgate-era resignation would impact his chances
content:
Former minister and European commissioner Phil Hogan has formally launched his bid to become the next director general of the UN’s food agency saying he is ready “to serve once again”.
Hogan dismissed any suggestion that his resignation as commissioner during the fallout from the pandemic era-Golfgate controversy would impact on his chances of securing the role, telling reporters on Tuesday: “nobody has mentioned it, only you.”
The former Fine Gael politician is “very confident” he will have the support of the majority of European Union countries as he seeks the role and said he has commitments of support in “all regions” including from Barbados and New Zealand.
The Rome-based agency, the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), which has 194 members – 193 countries and the EU – aims to “defeat hunger” and its top job comes with a salary of $265,000 (€225,000) a year.
The election to replace the current director, Qu Dongyu, a Chinese politician and administrator, will take place in late June 2027.
The Government has strongly backed Hogan’s candidacy with Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee, Minister for Agriculture Martin Heydon and junior agriculture ministers Noel Grealish and Timmy Dooley all speaking at the launch event in Dublin.
Hogan’s nomination by the Government as a candidate for the job earlier this year came after expressions of interest were sought and what has been described as “a high-level independent selection board” assessed applications received.
Spain and Italy have also put forward candidates, leading to fears Europe will split its support and dash its chances of securing the post. There are also candidates from Angola and Turkey.
[ Phil Hogan’s UN job race: Decision on EU candidate unlikely during Irish presidency Opens in new window ]
Hogan resigned as European commissioner for trade in 2020 in the wake of controversy over his attendance at an Oireachtas Golf Society dinner in Co Galway and scrutiny of his movements to and from the event during Covid-19 restrictions.
He insisted at the time that he did not break any law or health regulations and that exemptions for essential work meant he was permitted to break a local lockdown in Co Kildare.
In 2022 a District Court judge dismissed charges against four other individuals accused of organising the Oireachtas Golf Society dinner in breach of pandemic restrictions.
During a press conference on Tuesday, it was put to Hogan that he lost the Irish public’s trust in 2020 and he replied: “I didn’t break the law, didn’t break any regulations. I was sloppy in relation to the guidelines that were there at the time. I made a fulsome apology.”
He added: “I disappointed the people for sure, and I disappointed myself in the way I responded.”
The Irish Times previously reported that Hogan’s consultancy firm – Hogan Strategic Advisory Services – earned at least €1 million in 2024 from work in Brussels according to filings to the European Union transparency register.
Hogan was asked on Tuesday about why he hopes to switch from this lucrative work to the FAO job. He said he was “very passionate about the opportunity to lead” the FAO and he wanted “to spend the next few years in my public service trying to help the millions of people that need help in relation to food security and nutrition”.
Hogan said he expected to spend a “significant six-figure” sum from his own resources on the campaign. He said the State has assigned him two staff from the Department of Agriculture and “they’re putting the embassies at my disposal, and that’s it”.
“All other expenses associated with the campaign – travel, subsistence, accommodation” and promotional material including a campaign video “are being paid for by myself”, he said.
Hogan told the event that he was ready “to serve once again” and requested that ambassadors present to ask their countries to support his candidacy “so that together we can build a new FAO for a new world”.

title: Enzo Maresca says he would describe Manchester City as ‘cheats’ if he was a United fan
description: Manager claims City fans suffering more than players who can focus on games
content:
Enzo Maresca has admitted he would describe Manchester City as “cheats” if he were a Manchester United or Arsenal fan. The manager’s comments came as he suggested it had been harder for City’s supporters to deal with the scandal surrounding the club than it had been for him or the players.
Maresca guided City to an impressive 3-0 win at Liverpool on Sunday in their first game since the club were found guilty of more than 100 charges related to breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules. He was asked whether the performance was down to the team being brought closer together by the guilty verdict.
“It probably has been more tough for our fans than for the players or for me as it’s more complicated,” he said, “because if I am an Arsenal fan or a United fan and you are a City fan, I can tell you: ‘Hey, my friend, you cheat’ – or this kind of thing. But we were happy at the end of the game and inside the changing room. We were very happy celebrating the three points because we know how difficult it is at Anfield.”
City, who have appealed against the independent commission’s ruling and continue to protest their innocence, have drawn criticism for the exuberant manner of Sunday’s celebration. Maresca defended the revelry but is conscious of the need to focus on Wednesday’s visit of Paris Saint-Germain in their second Champions League game of the season, following their 2-0 victory at Porto.
“We won 0-3 at Anfield,” Maresca said. “Even if it was 0-1 it would be exactly the same. We are here today to win tomorrow’s game and we work every day to win games. It’s the only thing that we can think; we can be focused. The rest is just things from outside that we need to deal with but we were so happy inside the pitch and you cannot imagine inside the changing room.
“I promise you that I stress a lot about the game plan and how we can train every day but I don’t stress about things I don’t [control]. The message to the players will be the same. We know how serious the situation is but at the same time it’s not something that we can do [anything about].”
Rúben Dias, City’s captain, echoed his manager. “When you build yourself as a player, you build yourself against any noise,” the defender said. “Personally, and I feel like I speak for the whole group, we’re very calm. We trust the club, and we’re very focused on enjoying football. People don’t love us winning and we love to win.”
Pep Guardiola is expected to be at the Etihad Stadium on Wednesday in a show of support for City’s owners. “In case he’s coming, it’s a nice feeling,” Maresca said of his predecessor. “Especially for him, because this has been his house for 10 years. It’s exciting for everyone.” – Guardian

title: Champions Cup has a jeopardy problem: can anyone stop France’s Top 14 giants?
description: But Leinster could be left-field candidate to challenge predictable stranglehold of Toulouse and Bordeaux
content:
The world is awash with uncertainty, but not, sadly, in the case of rugby’s Champions Cup , which begins on Friday. This season’s winners will be either Toulouse or defending champions Bordeaux Bègles . Next question?
Such is the French stranglehold on the tournament – six consecutive years and counting – that it grows harder, given the existing structure and regulations, to see anyone upsetting the increasingly lopsided odds.
Bookmakers are quoting the Top 14 powerhouses at 13-5 each for the title, with Leinster, Bath, Northampton and Montpellier just about visible in the distance behind them. There might be an argument for adding the Stormers and Glasgow to the chasing peloton, but that’s about it.
A 24-team competition reduced to a handful of serious contenders before a ball is kicked? It is not the greatest of portents.
There are even whispers out of Gloucester suggesting a rotated Cherry and White team will be sent out against two-time champions Bordeaux on the opening night. Which really would tip a large bucket of cold water over an already-lukewarm format. When you remember that Gloucester famously won 26-17 in Bordeaux less than four years ago, a low-key first Friday night at Kingsholm would be properly anticlimactic.
[ It’s death by a thousand tweaks for the once-great Champions Cup ]
The organisers will be desperately hoping otherwise. Apart from anything else they have deliberately shifted the opening weekend forward to October, chasing better weather and greater visibility than in the post-international December gloom. The snag is that a single round generates little momentum, particularly when wedged between busy domestic league weekends.
Let’s try to locate some positives. Who would not want to watch Toulouse, Bordeaux or Northampton fizzing the ball around at the moment, regardless of their opponents?
Those complaining about a surfeit of tries in the Prem and using the dismissive term “basketball” are not factoring in the skill levels required to tie defences in weekly knots. Time was when a single offload from a tight forward prompted talk of expulsion from the “front row union”. Now virtually everybody on the field can give and take a killer pass flat to the advantage line.
To some degree more teams are simply catching up with the way the best French and All Blacks sides have always sought to attack, ruthlessly targeting space and soft shoulders at pace and punishing the slightest defensive hesitation. Players out wide are bigger and better equipped to break tackles than ever before, while the laws relating to the aerial contest have created far more broken-field rugby.
Add in stricter tackle height regulations and more regular yellow cards and there is greater scope even for sides lacking a Louis Bielle-Biarrey, an Antoine Dupont or a Tommy Freeman.
There is, however, an accompanying broader issue. Rugby is built upon jeopardy; the moment it starts to become predictable, either in terms of the result or the way in which the game is played, everybody loses.
It is why the obsession with the increasing volume of tries is something of a red herring. It is the repetitive manner in which so many are being scored that is arguably the bigger turn-off.
Take the close-range rolling maul. Give away the softest of penalties on halfway and teams will invariably kick to the corner. More times than not, they duly come away with seven points. Dull and formulaic? Perhaps not in the last minute with the scores level. But if one pack is significantly stronger than the other it becomes as much fun as watching a bulldozer do battle with a blancmange.
So what to do? The time must be approaching when the defending side are awarded the throw-in when their opponents kick direct to the corner. That at least would force teams to think more and to contemplate other tactical avenues.
The proposed reduction of the Champions Cup to 16 teams should also help reduce the number of routine outcomes, albeit while concentrating even more power in the hands of a decreasing few.
This time around, either way, it will be the same old story unless teams can somehow stop Toulouse and Bordeaux at source. No one is going to outflank them – if sides opt to play them at their own game they will still probably lose 70-40 – but teams who can retain their discipline, get ahead on the scoreboard and pick off the aerial crumbs will at least be in the game.
But how many, in reality, have the squad depth to do that for long enough? There is an argument that only two of the eight English entrants – Bath at home to Montpellier and Northampton at home to Cardiff – will be favourites to win their opening matches.
Even Sale, at home to Glasgow Warriors, and Saracens, away at Connacht , may have to dig deep and the same is definitely true for Exeter in Toulouse and Bristol at Stormers, though the Bears’ Argentina lock Pedro Rubiolo is a rising force.
Complicating everyone’s task further is the amended try bonus point system which, à la Top 14, now requires teams to score three tries more than their opponents. It threatens to make it even harder for less-stacked squads to pick up priceless extra points and sneak into the last 16 by the back door.
If there is a left-field candidate it might conceivably be Pau, second behind Toulouse after six rounds of the Top 14. There or thereabouts will also be Leinster , whose long, winding crusade towards an elusive fifth star on their jerseys is starting to resemble Munster’s pursuit of their first Heineken Cup crown.
Brace yourselves, nevertheless, for a Toulouse v Bordeaux finale in Lyons on May 22nd. By then, hopefully, we will finally have some genuine jeopardy. – The Guardian

title: Public sector pay can be discussed as ‘priority’ with unions ahead of strike, Minister says
description: More than 300,000 workers set for one-day work stoppage over prioritisation of pay in talks
author_name: Pat Leahy, Cormac McQuinn, Jack Horgan-Jones, Emmet Malone
content:
Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers has said pay can be discussed as a priority with trade unions ahead of Wednesday’s strike action.
“Pay can be discussed as a priority. I’m very clear that this is going to cause massive disruption to the public tomorrow,” he said on RTÉ’s Prime Time.
When host Miriam O’Callaghan asked him if pay could be a starting point in talks, he replied: “Absolutely.”
When it was put to him that rising costs meant workers “cannot afford to live”, Chambers pointed to tax reductions and additional funds for childcare and disability in Budget 2027 .
He also criticised trade unions for going ahead with the strike. “The fact they’re not willing to negotiate … not willing to engage, is regrettable and disappointing. I’d ask them to think of the public disruption.”
Earlier on Tuesday, the general secretary of the largest union involved in the dispute dismissed renewed efforts by Government to get trade unions into talks on a new public sector pay deal as “too little, too late”.
More than 300,000 public-sector workers are set to participate in the one-day work stoppage scheduled for Wednesday, with another scheduled for Wednesday 21st. Unions representing the workers want pay issues to be dealt with first as part of any engagement. The last public-sector pay deal expired in June.
General secretary of Fórsa trade union Kevin Callinan said the union side was already looking beyond tomorrow’s strike: “We’re as much focussed on next week’s strike as tomorrow’s and, indeed, beyond that.”
[ Q&A: Who is going on strike on Wednesday and why? Opens in new window ]
The Garda Representative Association expressed its “solidarity” with public-sector colleagues and “their right to protest”.
“It is extremely disappointing that the Garda Representative Association has received absolutely no contact from Minister Chambers or his officials regarding attendance at any pay talks,” the GRA said in a statement. “Once again we have been sidelined, excluded, and taken for granted. We cannot and will not allow this to continue. Our National Executive are meeting tomorrow to discuss the blatant disregard shown to our members by this Government.”
Speaking at lunchtime on Tuesday, Chambers criticised union leaders, saying that “strike action should be a last resort, not a first resort”.
He said that the Government was willing to agree pay increases for public servants but that the “only way we can deliver this if trade union leaders get around the table”.
“The public pay and pensions bill has grown by over €12 billion in a six year period … The last pay agreement delivered over 9 per cent for public sector workers,” he said.
“The public will see such levels of disruption because the trade union leaders won’t negotiate,” he said, appealing to union leaders to “reflect on this and not put the country through this”.
Asked about suggestions that the Government might appoint an independent mediator, Chambers said he was “open to wider suggestions to move forward”.
In a statement early on Tuesday afternoon, the Government had said it was “available” to “immediately enter intensive talks” at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) and Chambers subsequently said this is where he would like to see talks take place.
After a briefing by Chambers and discussion among Ministers at this morning’s Cabinet meeting, the Government said that at a “time of great uncertainty”, the best way “to reduce uncertainty for public servants is for public service unions and associations to enter talks to reach a clear agreement on public service pay”.
[ Who is affected by the public sector strike and can it be averted? Opens in new window ]
Callinan dismissed claims in the Government statement and by Chambers that pay increases over the past six years had broadly matched inflation with lower paid workers receiving increases above it.
“Between 2019 and 2025,” it said, “public servants received pay increases of 22.5 per cent, broadly matching considerable price increases over the period. The lowest-paid public servants saw increases of 36 per cent over the same period, significantly ahead of inflation. The most recent agreement, the Public Service Agreement 2024-2026, delivered cumulative pay improvements of 9.6 per cent against inflation of 6.6 per cent.”
Responding, Callinan, who also chairs the public sector committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions said Chambers and the government side were “cherry picking figures”.
“If he wants to do that we can identify figures that show clearly the pay of civil servants has fallen behind not just inflation but the workforce generally and the broader economy by a long margin.”
Efforts by the Government in the wake of the budget, including a letter by Chambers to union leaders on Monday calling for an “intensive process of engagement as soon as possible”, had been swiftly rebuffed.
Chambers said in his letter that the provision of €1.2 billion for public-sector pay in the budget was “significant” and “pay issues can and should be discussed as a priority alongside other matters as part of the pay talks”.
[ The blue-green smoothie ruling the country has no plan and even less passion Opens in new window ]
The unions promptly rejected the contention that the figure provided a basis for progress and have accused the Government of contributing to the dispute reaching this point by taking so long to start preliminary talks on a new pay deal when the previous one expired in June.
The Taoiseach separately outlined measures in the budget for workers including income tax cuts, expansion of public-service worker numbers, a planned cut in the cost of childcare and supports for people with disabilities.
“That’s a very strong platform upon which to build in terms of public-service pay negotiations.
“My real concern is the disruption that will be caused to many people, particularly patients and those who were expecting operations and procedures and so on like that, and indeed, in terms of school days being lost.”

title: Edwin Edogbo and Will Harrison likely to return for Munster’s clash with Racing 92
description: Tom Ahern and Fineen Wycherley may also be back for Champions Cup opener at Páirc Uí Chaoimh
content:
Munster could have Edwin Edogbo and summer signing Will Harrison back in the mix for Saturday’s eagerly-awaited Champions Cup opener against Racing 92 at Páirc Uí Chaoimh (kick-off 8pm).
Edogbo and the 27-year-old former Waratahs outhalf/fullback Harrison, a summer signing from Kintetsu Liners in Japan, “have started reintegrating into on-pitch training” according to the province’s weekly squad update after overcoming shoulder and knee injuries.
Furthermore, Tom Ahern (neck spasm) and Fineen Wycherley (shoulder) have not been ruled out for the weekend after missing last Saturday’s 26-all draw away to Ulster and will be assessed as the week progresses.
Munster had no fresh injury concerns following that draw, as a result of which Munster picked up three points, while Michael Milne (ankle), Diarmuid Barron (neck) and Shane Daly (hamstring tightness) “are progressing well”.
Munster’s first Champions Cup game in Páirc Uí Chaoimh against Gloucester last December drew a 36,208 capacity and this game appears a more glamourous tie. But although sales have picked up in the last week and could continue to do so between now and Saturday, disappointingly only 20,000 tickets have been sold thus far for Saturday’s game against Racing 92.

title: Cill Stuifín on TG4 review: ‘We spent our childhoods terrified of seeing Cill Stuifín’
description: Television: A wonderfully eerie story about a Co Clare village that seemingly vanished beneath the waves
content:
When Aindrias de Staic gazes out the window of his home in west Clare , he sees a sward of green leading to the sea and, beyond it, the white crests of waves. But what really commands his attention is what he cannot see: a sunken village that supposedly lies beneath the ocean surface and which has historically struck fear into the hearts of locals.
“We were always told as kids if we ever heard the bells, we were to turn our backs to the sea and run for home,” says de Staic, a folklorist and son of the late storyteller Eddie Stack. The bells belonged to a clock tower in Cill Stuifín – a lost village, which, if glimpsed even for a moment, doomed you to an unhappy fate. “You were sure to die within the year.”
The story of the village and de Staic’s family connection to it is told in the wonderfully eerie documentary Cill Stuifín (TG4, Tuesday, 9.30pm), a deepwater plunge into the mythological hinterlands of west Clare, where ancient history meets modern memory and old stories are reborn for the 21st century.
Was there ever a village called Cill Stuifín? Nobody knows for sure, but a recent geographical survey has identified features beneath the waves that may once have been above sea level, including the outline of an old riverbed. So how did Cill Stuifín – or whatever it was – end up lost at sea?
That question was answered – at least partly – when a small earthquake struck the locality in 2010. While it didn’t cause any damage, a similar geological event millenia ago might have been sufficient to condemn a settlement to the bottom of the sea.
“Who’s to say there wasn’t a larger one in the past?” says Martina McCarthy, a geophysicist who, like de Staic, grew up on stories of the lost settlement. “It was the most exciting day of my life.”
But the film is less interested in the origins of Cill Stuifín – we may never know the truth of what it was and where it went – than in the hold it exerts over imaginations to this day.
“We grew up with that folklore,” says McCarthy as she stares out to sea, lost in memories of the deep past but also in recollections of her own childhood and how it was shaped by the invisible shadow of Cill Stuifín and its unsolved mystery. “We spent our childhoods terrified of seeing Cill Stuifín.”

title: Kilkenny Design group records €1.5m in pretax profits
description: Chief executive Evelyn Moynihan credited group’s profitability to ‘tighter stock management and careful cost control’
content:
The company behind fashion and homeware retailer Kilkenny Design grew pretax profits by 17 per cent last year, ahead of the 12.9 per cent rise in revenues, according to company filings published Tuesday.
Clydaville Holdings reported €1.5 million in pretax profits in the financial year to January 25th, 2026, and €36.33 million in turnover in the same period.
The company owns 16 Kilkenny Design stores across the State as well as a number of gift shops and cafés associated with the retail brand. It maintains five outlets in Co Dublin, four in Co Cork and one each in counties Clare, Galway, Kerry, Kildare, Kilkenny, Meath and Tipperary.
“We have protected profitability through tighter stock management, careful cost control and more joined-up planning across stores and online,” said Evelyn Moynihan, Kilkenny Design’s chief executive.
“Rising labour costs also mean we must be disciplined about how we operate and grow. We value our teams enormously, so our focus is on ensuring the business can sustainably support those jobs,” she told The Irish Times.
The group employed an average of 241 workers last year, up from 216 employees the previous year. It paid €7.04 million in wages and salaries, with an additional €780,000 allocated to additional staffing costs, the filings show.
The retailer said it was affected by “global uncertainty on consumer confidence, fuel and transport costs and the reliability of supply chains”.
“Trade uncertainty, including around tariffs, also makes planning more complex,” Moynihan said. “These pressures can affect both the cost of bringing products to customers and what customers feel comfortable spending.
“Our response is to manage carefully the areas within our control: stock levels, buying decisions, costs and co-ordination across the business. Maintaining close relationships with suppliers and planning ahead are particularly important in an uncertain environment,” Moynihan said.
“We are continuing to invest in new and up-and-coming Irish makers, backing their talent and giving them a platform to build their businesses,” Moynihan said.
“Customers want distinctive products and meaningful purchases, and supporting Irish businesses and local communities continues to give them a strong reason to shop with us.”
Pretax profits grew from the €1.28 million the company recorded for 12 months up to January 2025, and were up significantly from its “total comprehensive profit” of just under €70,000 in the year before that.
Turnover was up €4.15 million from the previous period’s figure of €32.17 million, the filings show.
The company held €4.06 million in cash at the end of January 2026, a 35.74 per cent increase from the €2.99 million it held 12 months previously, as well as €8.76 million in fixed assets – most of which stemmed from computer equipment, software and motor vehicles.

title: Why we must have this performative strike by public sector workers
description: Game theory wonks will be fascinated by this week’s industrial action while the rest of us will just be angry
content:
Years ago – in the days of social partnership – I remember an industrial correspondent of this newspaper telling me that on one occasion after an amicable arrangement had been reached in the early evening on the latest national pay agreement, all sides sat around Government buildings until the early hours of the following morning before announcing it. They needed to convey the impression to their respective constituencies – the public and private sector workers, their bosses and the rest of us – just how tough the negotiations had been and how close they came to failure.
Apocryphal as this story probably was, it highlights a truth about the public sector strike on Wednesday. Everybody knows that the Government will eventually agree to a public sector pay increase in line with inflation and get some concessions from the public sector to offset the bill. There is no other possible, sustainable outcome.
So why all the theatrics? Both sides have their reasons. Some are about optics; others are more substantial.
The union representatives obviously need to be seen to be earning their dues. From that simple perspective, arriving at predictable agreement after some ritualistic bloodletting in the form of strike – or a couple of strikes – makes sense.
As well as letting public sector workers blow off some understandable steam, it also makes the eventual and ultimately disappointing outcome in some way more valuable because it has been fought for.
The Government also needs to be seen to fight for the taxpayer – although what seems to get lost in these fights is that public sector workers pay tax. Some of them pay quite a lot of tax.
In much the same way as the unions need to be seen to have fought for every fraction of a percentage point of an increase, the Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform Jack Chambers needs to be seen to have shown a willingness to die in the ditch for the exchequer.
But if it was just about optics, you would expect this biennial process to evolve into some sort of ritualised combat akin to the World Wrestling Federation’s WrestleMania. We know it’s pretence but enjoy it anyway. To a certain extent, this is what happened between 1987 and 2010 under eight successive social partnership agreements, including the one referred to above.
The model broke down in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crash when the cuts sought by the government were too big for the unions to wear and ended up being imposed unilaterally.
An interesting question is why the unions have not tried to put social partnership back together again and have instead adopted a much more antagonistic approach that has brought us to this strike. Rather than enter negotiations without precondition – social partnership style- they have demanded the Government first agree the pay element before then moving on to terms and conditions.
This is where the game theory wonks come in. There is plenty of research to suggest unions can have the upper hand in antagonistic negotiations of this sort in certain circumstances.
These include a tight labour market where the Government finds it hard to recruit and retain employees. There also has to be a credible threat of industrial action and significant consequences for the Government from the resulting disruption, such as damage to its fiscal credibility with electoral consequences.
The final ingredient is significant public support for public sector workers, such as nurses, teachers etc.
It all sounds very familiar. It also explains why the unions are trying to split the talks into two. They want to use their pretty significant leverage where it matters most – pay increases – rather than fritter it away fighting over tea breaks and the like.
The Government can of course see them coming and will not fall into the trap. Not yet at least.
It has given an indirect indication of what is on the table by including a figure for the impact of public pay increases next year in the budget that has just been passed. It can be seen as a reasonable opening bid and has already been upped with the indication that more is available from a €1.6 billion contingency fund.
This reflects the interest of the Government to avoid the strike. But the unions seem confident enough in the strength of their hand to stick to their maximalist position.
Much will now hinge on the blame game that will follow the 24-hour strike and any subsequent ones should they materialise.
Eventually public support or sympathy for the strikers will run out. The disruption of 150,000 medical appointments will erode it. As will the headaches involved in organising someone to look after your children. Both sides know this. They just don’t know when it will happen.
At some point the deal will be done and it will not be very different from the one that could be hammered out this morning. Social partnership for slow learners.
