title: Tadhg Morley calls time on Kerry intercounty career ‘after many proud and unforgettable years’
description: Templenoe defender won two All-Irelands and was named as an All Star in 2022
content:
Kerry’s Tadhg Morley has retired from intercounty football. The two-time All-Ireland winner made his championship debut in 2016 and was an All Star defender in 2022.
He made 57 championship appearances with the Kingdom and also managed to register 1-3 during his Kerry senior career.
“After many proud and unforgettable years, I’ve decided the time has come to bring my Kerry football journey to an end,” said Morley.
“Pulling on the green and gold has been a privilege I’ll always be proud of. One of the greatest honours of my career was bringing the Sam Maguire back to our small club of Templenoe and home to Blackwater. Occasions I know my late father would have been immensely proud of and memories I’ll treasure forever.
“I want to thank everyone who has been part of my journey, particularly my mam Therese, brother John and my wife Ciara, for all their love and support throughout the years.
“To my extended family, thank you for always being there and for the encouragement you’ve given me along the way. To my team-mates, coaches, management and everyone involved with Kerry GAA, thank you for the memories and friendships that will last a lifetime.
“Finally, a special thank you to my club, Templenoe, for everything it has given me over the years. Representing our club on the biggest days has always been a huge honour for me and I look forward to many more years of making memories in the blue and white.
“I’m excited to take my place back in the stands to support Kerry amongst the great supporters I have met along the way, this time with my little son Teidí by my side.
An All-Ireland club junior winner with Templenoe in 2016, Morley also won 10 Munster senior titles and five National Leagues with Kerry.
Kerry boss Jack O’Connor paid tribute to Morley for his commitment to the Kerry cause over the last decade.
O’Connor said: “Tadhg Morley was one of those players who made a manager’s job easier. As well as being versatile he was very dependable and he was a great leader in the dressingroom.
“He was the linchpin of our defence in my first year back in 2022. He organised boys around him and had the respect of everybody on and off the field. He also came on in the 2025 All-Ireland to see us home.
“Tadhg has a career as a coach/manager ahead of him because he has the presence and leadership qualities in abundance. I wish him well in his retirement and I’d like to thank him for his massive contribution to Kerry over the past 11 years.”

title: Sienna Miller: ‘I had to get to a place where I was able to be taken seriously’
description: Miller’s work has often been overshadowed by an eventful personal life. In War, a new HBO series, she hopes to complicate things
content:
Actor Sienna Miller stepped from the lobby of a Lower East Side hotel into the path of an animated woman professing love and fandom. The woman, who held a video camera, had been sent by tabloid site TMZ.
Miller walked on. An actor since her late teens and a paparazzi fixation for just as long, her work has often been overshadowed by an eventful personal life and an obsession with her style.
At 44, and even recently post-partum, Miller remains effortlessly cool, a whirl of wide-leg jeans, swingy blond hair and nicotine pills. Yet she has always been more than an It Girl, even if directors and producers were slow to notice this. She has a desert-dry sense of humour, a casual frankness and an irresistible gift for intimacy. Let’s just say that within 10 minutes of meeting, we were in the otherwise empty basement of an Orchard Street vintage shop, in our underwear, trying on past-season couture.
“I don’t get out much,” she said, laughing as she took off her jeans. The pantsuit she tried on, a 1990s Gaultier houndstooth number, looked as if it had been sewn just for her.
Miller’s career has been variable in quality, if not in type. In addition to her many girlfriends and wives, she has played actors of one kind or another in more than a dozen films, series and plays.
This casting is obvious – Miller has the Hollywood glamour and, for better or worse, the fame. But this stereotyping also suggests that she is seen more for her glossy surfaces than for anything underneath. The irony is ugly: she is repeatedly asked to play actors even as she has struggled to be taken seriously as a performer. (That TMZ camera operator wasn’t there to talk craft.)
“It’s funny, because I have no interest now in playing an actress or somebody who has paparazzi,” Miller said.
In War, a new HBO anthology series from showrunner George Kay (Criminal, Lupin, Hijack), Miller plays another actor. But this time, by leveraging the gap between public performance and private pain, and by bringing the force of her charisma and sympathy to what might otherwise have been an unlikeable character, she hopes to complicate that role.
Her character, Carla Duval, has been served with divorce papers by Dominic West’s tech mogul Morgan Henderson. Carla is, like Miller, a famous actor and a subject of media criticism. Unlike Miller, she girds herself in a thick sheen of narcissism. “I found it would be interesting to play someone who operates in the world that I exist in with a very different personality,” Miller said.
“I spend a lot of time with a thermometer up everybody in any room, just gauging how everybody is,” she continued. “I don’t think she’s at all invested in the feelings of others or their responses to her, which was really relieving.”
Miller became an actor because she has never been able to imagine anything else. As a schoolgirl, she rarely had good parts and wanted them desperately. “Maybe I was too eager,” she said.
After graduating at 17, she spent a few months in New York, studying at the Lee Strasberg Theater and Film Institute, which she recalls as “very therapeutic and strange and kind of embarrassing”. Within a few years, she had a part on a TV show, and soon after she was cast in multiple films, picking up a little more technique with every job. It wasn’t until the 2006 film Factory Girl, in which she played Andy Warhol muse Edie Sedgwick, that she felt confident as an actor.
“I realised that this is what I was supposed to be doing, and I had access to things I didn’t know I could access,” Miller said.
But in those years she was better known as a party girl, a famous girlfriend (she had relationships with actors Jude Law, Tom Sturridge and Balthazar Getty) and an avatar of bohemian chic. The paparazzi were relentless, so invasive that she eventually sued them, accepting a settlement.
She describes that time as “a very hazy blur, wrapped up in all sorts of chaos and trauma”. Paradoxically, it made her even more committed to her career.
“I had to get to a place where I was able to be taken seriously,” she said.
At 30, while engaged to Sturridge, she gave birth to a daughter, which seemed to quiet some of the attention around her. She resented what this implied, but she welcomed the reprieve.
“I was suddenly able to be seen as someone with some substance, because I was a mother now,” she said.
Gradually the roles became better ( Foxcatcher , American Sniper , 21 Bridges ), including a starring turn in the Netflix limited series Anatomy of a Scandal (2022). She played the embattled wife of a politician accused of assault, a crisis compounded by media scrutiny.
The role echoed certain aspects of her own history, which wasn’t lost on her. While she took the part for its depth, “I probably was also curious in a slightly sadistic way to revisit that,” she said.
We were back at the hotel by the time she said this. A woman lunching nearby came over to gush about how much she had loved that show. This was a real fan, not a paparazzo, and Miller was perfectly friendly. “I paid her,” she said drily, as the woman left.
[ Sienna Miller: ‘People think they know me. You think you know me. Trust me, you don’t’ Opens in new window ]
Since Anatomy of a Scandal, Miller has had two children with her partner, actor Oli Green. The youngest, five months old, came with her to New York. (Before lunch, she took time to give him a cuddle.) Though her pregnancy is invisible in War, which shot near her London home, she was more than eight months along by the time filming ended.
Kay, who created the series, knew he needed a film star to play a film star. “Camera presence is not something you can act,” he said. He had written the character of an actor to emphasise how a divorce plays out both in public and in private, and he was impressed with Miller’s ability to play the role on at least two levels.
“You can see her keeping her head held high but having a private stress in her eyes,” Kay said.
War is ambivalent as to Carla’s talent, and even Miller is uncertain of Carla’s gifts. “I don’t know that there’s a huge depth to her,” she said. But while Kay had conceived the character as mannered, narcissistic and high-strung, Miller made her softer, more human.
“Sienna brings this naturalism without losing any status,” Kay said.
West, who first worked with her 20 years ago, in a production of As You Like It, recalled the frenzy back then. (While the play was running, Law, then her fiance, admitted to an affair.)
“She was pursued by paparazzi the whole time, and there was quite a siege mentality, even in the theatre,” he said. Now “there’s a wonderful freedom to her and a real naturalness and a playfulness”.
Miller is thankful to be mostly free of that siege, but she knows it has coloured her career. It’s not an accident that she is so often offered the role of a woman in the public eye, a woman who exists to be seen. She spoke feelingly of making the upcoming film Madden, from director David O Russell, in which she plays the part owner of an NFL team.
“That reinvigorated a passion for what I do in a way that I needed,” she said.
Miller plans to return to the theatre and is proud of a craft that is “ever-evolving and deepening as I become an ever-evolved, deeper person,” she said. She craves deeper roles to match, but even if the offers to play actors keep flooding in, she can accept it.
She pointed to a tattoo on her upper arm of three stars, which she had acquired on a beach in Mexico in early 20s, one for each child she hoped to have. Professional discontent seemed small in comparison.
“Without sounding schmaltzy, life is pretty wonderful,” she said. – This article originally appeared in The New York Times

title: Mark Zuckerberg says Meta has reached AI ‘frontier’
description: Company is committed to further vast spending to challenge rivals
content:
Mark Zuckerberg says Meta has caught up with rivals at the “frontier” of artificial intelligence (AI) , committing to further vast spending to challenge Anthropic and OpenAI and downplaying warnings about the risks of the technology running out of control.
Speaking as Meta released its Muse Wonder AI model on Monday, the billionaire chief executive claimed the new system was “going to allow much more sophisticated behaviours that are at the frontier of what is being done in the AI field”.
The Silicon Valley group claims Muse Wonder performs better than comparable models released by Anthropic and OpenAI in some tasks, according to technical benchmarks.
The release marks a big milestone for Zuckerberg, who since last year has committed billions of dollars to shake up Meta’s AI leadership, build vast data centres and hire star AI researchers on multimillion-dollar salaries – all in a bid to keep pace with OpenAI, Anthropic and Google .
“Getting to this point both required a large amount of compute and investment, and a lot of very rigorous scientific work by the group working on it over an extended period of time,” said Zuckerberg.
The AI push initially unnerved investors, but the company’s share price has risen almost 10 per cent since early September when Meta launched the Muse personal AI assistant, which uses autonomous bots to carry out everyday tasks such as ordering groceries and booking travel.
The Muse app quickly became – and remains – the most downloaded on both the Apple and Android app stores in the US. The $1.8 trillion (€1.6 trillion) company intends to integrate its new model into Muse. Meta said Muse Wonder outperforms Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on some technical benchmarks.
It said the new model can be used to carry out complex tasks from “understanding a lease to making sense of financial or health information”.
The launch was tarnished by a bug that affected how use of the model counted against usage limits for Meta’s Code subscription. Meta’s AI chief Alexandr Wang said it was “working to resolve” the problem.
“There’s a bunch of bugs right now that we’re looking into,” he said later on Monday on X.
Muse Wonder will be a “closed” model, with its best versions sold directly to businesses. That pits it against Anthropic and OpenAI for corporate AI contracts in a serious test of its ambitions.
Zuckerberg signalled further spending as Meta was “already working on the next step up”, adding that its model development would “probably feel like it’ll go quite a bit faster from here”.
[ Who’s hiring and who’s firing in Ireland’s technology sector? Opens in new window ]
However, he shrugged off mounting fears that the tech was advancing at a rate that would soon surpass human control. In one of many high-profile incidents, more than 1,000 OpenAI autonomous “agents” escaped a test environment in July to hack the start-up Hugging Face .
The Meta chief declined to be drawn on his figure for “P (doom)” – a much-discussed Silicon Valley term to describe the probability that AI will lead to mass destruction. Instead, he argued that responsibility should fall on the individual lab to ensure model safety.
“I’m much closer to the belief that AI is a technology that can be engineered with normal guardrails and built responsibly than the anthropomorphic vision of AI, which is that it is just going to go do its own thing,” he said.
Zuckerberg has previously rejected calls by AI chiefs such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman for an industry-wide “slowdown” in AI development. He noted that Meta had at times slowed its internal AI work to ensure its products were safe.
He also played a key role in crafting US president Donald Trump’s White House “Accord on Super Intelligence”, setting out principles for self-regulation of the industry, which critics say falls far short of a formal global AI governance regime.
Zuckerberg has instead pushed a vision of “personal superintelligence” for individual consumers, setting Meta apart from OpenAI and Anthropic, which have ambitions to build “AGI” – artificial general intelligence that can surpass humans at most tasks.
“Everyone else is focused on more knowledge work, automation-type cases, and we’re much more focused on personal empowerment,” Zuckerberg said, adding that he wanted to build “things that are good in the world”.
Zuckerberg said he believed Meta needed to be at AI’s frontier to deliver this vision, noting a “dichotomy” where models are rapidly advancing in certain academic fields but “still don’t have enough common sense to be the ideal personal assistant”.
OpenAI last month claimed that one of its unreleased internal models had made a mathematical breakthrough, solving one of the greatest problems in the field.
[ Anthropic warns rogue AI agents may soon hijack your smart TV or oven Opens in new window ]
“I don’t know what that means, like, sociologically that you know that we got AI systems that could do these advanced mathematics stuff before we got something that could handle customer support reliably for everyone,” said Zuckerberg. “But I think that there’s obviously a lot more to do there.”
Meta’s AI strategy came under scrutiny in April 2025 after its Llama 4 model fell short of expectations, prompting Zuckerberg to spend heavily on talent and infrastructure. As part of the push, Zuckerberg hired Wang, founder of data labelling group Scale AI, to head up its “TBD Lab” at the heart of the company’s AI plans.
Muse Spark, the first model offering since TBD was assembled, was released in April but still lagged the rival offerings.
Meta said Muse Wonder was more capable with challenging tasks, such as advanced coding capabilities, while having improved capacity for remembering relevant information across different conversations with users – more in line with state-of-the-art models.
Muse Wonder also represents a move away from Meta’s prioritisation of open-source models, with users or companies needing to pay for access. There would be a tiered offering, Meta said, with the company charging as little as 20 cents per million tokens for basic usage, or as much as $200 a month for a more powerful premium offering called Muse Wonder Full.
While Meta’s Muse app is helping to popularise AI agent assistants in the US, problems could remain with wider adoption. Shortly after its launch, Amazon blocked Muse agents from shopping on the website, limiting the usefulness of the system and signalling that tech groups could use their market power to limit the abilities of rival AI offerings.
Meta must also overcome concerns about user privacy, with a small number of users accusing Muse of accessing or sharing private information without permission.
[ International Monetary Fund warns of AI-driven market correction in global economy Opens in new window ]
There have long been doubts about the company’s commitment to user safety, having previously been entangled in scandals about its use of data. In August, the company agreed to pay up to $18 billion to settle its blockbuster legal battle with US states over alleged failures of child protection and social media addiction , in one of the largest legal settlements ever made by an individual US company.
“Most of the ways in which people might not trust the company can lead to technological innovations that could be quite productive,” said Zuckerberg. He pointed to the company’s promised “Muse Confidential VM”, an upcoming version of Muse where a user’s data and conversations with their agent would be inaccessible to the company.
Zuckerberg’s recent transformation of Meta has led to internal turbulence. Over the past few years, employees have faced a rapid succession of job cuts, restructuring and executive reshuffles.
After coming under pressure to justify Meta’s ballooning capital expenditure spending to Wall Street, in May the company cut 10 per cent of its workforce – or 8,000 jobs. According to staff, the lay-offs, combined with company plans to install employee-tracking software to capture mouse movements and keystrokes in order to train AI models, have led to low morale.
“A company like Meta is going to do way more things than it does today, but each thing may potentially be able to be done with somewhat fewer people,” Zuckerberg said. “I would guess that in the future, way more people are going to have the job of working with technology to make things than [they] do today.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Revenues decline 2.5% at The Irish Times media group
description: The Irish Times DAC posts revenue of €113m for 2025, down from €116m a year earlier
content:
The Irish Times media group saw its revenues decline by 2.5 per cent last year and recorded a loss of €800,000, accounts just filed show.
The Irish Times DAC – which includes the Cork-based Irish Examiner, a number of regional titles, and digital assets MyHome.ie and RIP.ie – posted revenue of €112.7 million, down from €115.6 million a year earlier.
Some €2.4 million of this related to the sale of a radio asset (WKW FM) and the wind-down of Irish Times Training. A €3.5 million fall in publishing revenues was offset by a €3 million increase in non-publishing turnover.
The company slipped into the red having made a €4 million profit in 2024, which was largely due to a €3.9 million gain on the disposal of WKW FM.
The accounts show termination payments of €741,975 during the year. These relate to former group managing director Deirdre Veldon, who stepped down in September 2025 .
The accounts show that the annual salary of the chief executive, Garry Moroney, and the editor, Ruadhán Mac Cormaic, rose to €281,000 from €275,000. The deputy editor received €162,000 while the chief financial officer was paid a salary of €182,000.
As chairman of the board, Shay Garvey received a fee of €67,000 while John Hegarty received €31,000 as chairman of The Irish Times Trust, which is effectively the company’s shareholder.
The average fee per director in 2025 was €13,023.
The group had an average of 802 employees during the year, down 35 on the previous 12 months. Staff payroll costs amounted to €60.7 million, down marginally from €60.9 million in 2024.
The group’s investment portfolio increased in value to €29.1 million during the year, up from €27.4 million, while net cash fell to €7.1 million from €7.9 million.
In spite of being loss making, the company’s tax charge amounted to €683,212, largely due to the impact of paying tax on its investment income of just under €1.1 million.
Commenting on current trading, chief executive Garry Moroney said he expects revenues to rise by about 2 per cent this year despite a continued decline in print revenues.
“Digital advertising has been good. It’s up over 10 per cent year-on-year. That’s a positive. In terms of digital licensing, we are seeing some more engagement from the tech platforms. It’s one that we can grow.
“In terms of subscriptions, we will probably have similar growth to last year but we had set a big target this year and haven’t managed to hit that acceleration. It’s been steady growth.”
He acknowledged that print sales continue to decline, albeit that the group is performing ahead of the market and had secured new print contracts from other publishers last year.
On whether The Irish Times might consider ceasing print production on certain days of the week, he said: “No, we have no plans to do that. It’s not something we’re planning.”

title: Paramilitaries should receive no financial rewards for disbanding, report says
description: Victims of paramilitary attacks, representatives from affected communities and those from a policing background took part
content:
Paramilitary groups who engage in formal talks about transition should receive no financial rewards, according to a new report.
The report was authored by Fleur Ravensbergen, who was hired by the British and Irish governments to explore the prospect of paramilitary disbandment in Northern Ireland .
She said a “window of opportunity” exists and recommended the establishment of an “independent, time-bound transition mechanism without delay”.
The Dutch conflict-resolution expert has held private talks with loyalist and republican paramilitaries as part of a scoping exercise over the past year.
Victims of paramilitary attacks, representatives from affected communities and those from a policing background also took part.
No individual or organisation is named in the report as “engagements were carried out on a confidential basis”.
Ravensbergen’s report, published on Tuesday, concludes there is “sufficient merit in and support for a formal process of paramilitary group transition”.
However, it cautioned that such a move can happen only “provided certain conditions are met”.
Credible monitoring and verification of progress, “robust” law enforcement and “no financial awards for paramilitary groups” were cited as key conditions in the Independent Report on Paramilitary Group Transition to Disbandment.
The willingness among loyalist and republican paramilitary groups to discuss transition and its implications was singled out as a “significant finding”.
In the case of loyalists, there was “often a clear appetite for it”.
Engagement with dissident republican paramilitary groups was “more mixed”, with some “more open than others to engagement”.
No group brought up “direct financial payments or early release from prison” as a condition of transition or accelerating progress towards it, the reports notes.
“Engagement was overall constructive and serious,” it states.
[ Loyalist paramilitaries ‘community workers by day, terrorists at night’ – former PSNI chief Opens in new window ]
The 74-page document will be laid before London and Dublin governments on Tuesday.
Neighbourhood policing should also be strengthened so that Police Service of Northern Ireland officers can maintain a “sustained focus on their core role within the communities they serve”, the report recommends.
Targeted initiatives aimed at benefiting young people in communities affected by paramilitary harm should also be rolled out.
Those who engaged in the scoping exercise expressed a range of views on the prospect of a formal process of group transition, from “strongly opposed to fully supportive”, according to Ravensbergen, a lecturer at the University of Amsterdam.
“On the whole, I found that the majority were willing for the governments to explore something new, including direct engagement with paramilitary groups via a formal process, provided certain conditions were met,” she said.
There was “limited support” for the term “disbandment” among paramilitary groups to describe the endpoint of the transition process.
“However, objections to disbandment appeared to be less about what transition should achieve and more about the wording,” Ravensbergen said.
“In my view, agreeing the transition process, milestones and end-state of group transition is more important than terminology.”
Drug-related crime, extortion, illegal money lending and exploitation had an “increasing prominence” in communities where a paramilitary presence remains, the report found.
A growing anti- immigrant sentiment was also found in some areas.
Many of those interviewed acknowledged that “although good work has been done and progress made, something more is needed to advance progress towards ending paramilitarism”.
“I believe that the risks of the persistence of paramilitary structures, continued drift and unmanaged fragmentation outweigh the risks associated with attempting a structured and time-bound transition process,” added Ravensbergen.
“My consultations suggest that a window of opportunity exists to pursue further progress, but that this may weaken over time.
“For these reasons, I recommend the establishment of an independent, time-bound transition mechanism without delay. The UK government and the Government of Ireland should work together to develop this mechanism.”
The report warns that any formal transition process would face “significant implementation challenges”.
Success is “not guaranteed” as progress is “unlikely to be linear or uncontested”.
“Different paramilitary groups may participate at different times, move at different speeds and encounter different challenges,” it states.
“A future process would therefore need to manage uneven participation, fragmentation, internal disagreement, unexpected developments, legal complexities and changing political circumstances while maintaining confidence in its overall direction.”

title: Will Dublin-headquartered Accenture survive or thrive in the age of AI?
description: The technology consultancy seeks to calm jitters with an investor day this week
content:
In the space of three months, Accenture ’s shares have suffered the steepest one-day fall and their second-largest one-day gain since the consultancy listed on the stock market a quarter of a century ago.
The wild swings reflect investors’ inability to decide if artificial intelligence (AI) is an existential threat to the world’s largest IT consulting firm or a once-in-a-generation boost.
Investors fret that the technology will allow clients to replace consultants for many tasks. Accenture is betting that companies will desperately need its help to roll out the new technology.
The company, whose market capitalisation has recovered from $76 billion (€68 billion) in June to about $130 billion, hopes it might settle the argument at an “investor day” event on Wednesday.
Here are the metrics investors are watching as they try to assess Accenture’s ability to reinvent itself for a new era.
Technology shifts such as the introduction of cloud computing have typically boosted revenues for information technology (IT) consultants as companies seek help to adapt.
But the dawn of the generative AI era has coincided with historically weak growth at Accenture, a slowdown partially masked by so-called inorganic revenues from acquisitions.
“AI is so radically different and transformational [from other technologies] that some companies are hanging tight on some of the bigger transformational work that Accenture does while they figure it out,” said David Grossman, an analyst at Stifel.
Accenture, which reported sales of $74.2 billion last year, has blamed economic uncertainty for the sluggishness. Companies have also diverted IT budgets away from smaller consulting projects and towards AI experimentation.
Some investors worry that organic growth could evaporate entirely because of the deflationary effects of AI.
As the technology reduces the effort required by consultants, it may significantly reduce the number of hours Accenture can bill clients for. It has also raised clients’ expectations about cost savings, potentially contributing to the pricing pressure the IT consultants have been reporting in recent months.
“Some of these projects with 1,000 people in India , at some point your competition is going to come and reprice that to be 20 per cent of what you’re getting paid today,” said Nate Singer, chief executive of Heron Intelligence, a due-diligence firm that monitors professional services. “You can’t infill with new business fast enough.”
Accenture executives lay out a much more optimistic view. They hope to secure years of lucrative work advising companies on how to prepare for AI, for example by improving the way clients manage data so they can use the technology more effectively.
[ Accenture reports earnings of $93bn in Ireland, more than Apple and Microsoft combined Opens in new window ]
They also argue AI will unlock new services they can sell, from transforming how insurance companies process claims to monitoring what AI agents are getting up to behind their corporate owners’ backs.
For its new fiscal year, which started in September, Accenture has hedged its bets, forecasting a modest decline in organic growth to about 2 per cent this year. Wednesday’s investor event will be a test of whether the company has the confidence to make projections for growth further in the future.
Professional services firms’ product is the expertise of their people. As a simplistic proxy, revenue per employee shows firms’ pricing power and profitability.
The figure is being used as an indicator of two things: whether the new technology is making staff more productive, and whether firms are successfully moving away from hourly billing to supplement revenues with AI-related product, software and agent sales.
Accenture’s revenue per employee fell in the 2010s as it built its labour-intensive outsourcing services for clients. Impatient investors now want to see a step change in the other direction.
“If you draw the conclusion that one of the main benefits of AI is that it makes companies more efficient, you would be hard-pressed to think they won’t participate in that,” said Kevin McVeigh, an analyst at UBS .
[ Consultants head for a showdown with their own clients as AI upends industry Opens in new window ]
The effect on overall staff numbers is mixed. Accenture ended August 2026 with a record 814,000 staff, despite two rounds of job cuts over the previous four years.
“You would think headcount would decline, given the agentic capabilities [of AI]. Coding, for example, is 40 to 50 per cent done now through AI ,” said Bryan Keane, an analyst at Citi . “We’re just scratching the surface on AI capabilities in terms of implementing it through the enterprise.”
There are changes beneath the surface. Accenture’s last job cuts were focused on people who could not be retrained to use AI, and the company boasts 110,000 of its staff are now “AI and data professionals”, almost three times the number three years ago.
Chief executive Julie Sweet indicated that hiring will skew towards cheaper, entry-level staff – in other words, AI-native young people.
“Those entry-level people are well positioned to take advantage of the AI tools,” said Jason Kupferberg, an analyst at Wells Fargo . “The need for mid-level managers has probably decreased across the industry, so I think the shape of the staffing pyramid is widening out at the bottom.”
Accenture has kept up with advancing technology partly by making dozens of acquisitions a year, adding specialist capabilities that it can roll out to its more than 9,000 clients around the world. When the pace of technological change is higher, so are the stakes. Often, so are the prices.
Accenture is not alone in wanting to bolster its business in the face of disruption, intensifying competition for deals. Venture capital is also pouring into AI start-ups, raising valuations. Despite doing fewer deals in the past 12 months than in recent years, Accenture paid more for them overall.
[ Accenture links top-level promotions to use of its AI tools Opens in new window ]
Consulting firms are all trying to add more software-like products to the mix, such as AI tools they can sell at fixed prices that can act as insurance if their model of billing for human labour erodes significantly.
In an age of AI agents, there is a blurring of the line between software and services, said Citi’s Keane. Services companies will have to get used to paying the higher multiples typical of software companies in their deal making.
“You have to pay up for higher, faster-growth acquisitions,” Keane said.
An open question is how those acquisitions will be funded and whether there has to be a trade-off in the form of lower share buy-backs and dividends, or higher debt.
Accenture points out that the right deals can quickly prove their worth. In January, it bought UK start-up Faculty at a valuation of more than $1 billion. Last month, it said Anthropic had hired it as an independent evaluator of the safety of its models, using Faculty technology to help tackle concerns that AI was running out of control – and in the process illustrating Sweet’s claim that AI will lead to entirely new kinds of consulting work.
Accenture is “a bit like the Borg”, said Singer of Heron Intelligence. “They buy the thing that’s going to be cool, and then they plough a ton of resources behind that. They can transform themselves. They can absorb the new hot thing.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Anthropic warns rogue AI agents may soon hijack your smart TV or oven
description: Claude maker suggests models could act as ‘worms’ in future cybersecurity threat
content:
Anthropic has warned that rogue “AI worms” will soon be able to hijack smart home devices, such as ovens and TVs, creating a new cybersecurit y threat that will be difficult to contain.
The developer of Claude said in a blog post that AI agents may be months away from “self-replicating” across everyday household devices to create potentially uncontrollable networks of AI agents.
Anthropic’s warning is the latest in a series of cybersecurity alarms raised by AI researchers as capabilities increase and models become more difficult to control.
The San Francisco-based company said if AI models continued to improve at their current pace, the technology would be capable of spreading itself around the internet like computer “worms” – malicious software that can spread automatically from one device to another without human intervention.
“We’re seeing signs of life for AI worms,” Anthropic said in a research post, likening their slow spread across insecure devices to “digital slime mould”.
The warning suggests that the kind of attack that stunned researchers investigating the Hugging Face hack by “swarms” of OpenAI agents this summer could be launched against devices owned by unwitting homeowners and businesses.
Anthropic’s latest warning refers to so-called “internet of things” devices which have proliferated over the past decade, as consumers use devices that control lights, plugs, thermostats and security systems.
Many of these internet-connected devices have historically offered poor levels of security because they were cheaply made by commodity hardware manufacturers, used for illegal streaming of TV services, or the companies that originally created them have gone out of business.
The insecure hardware creates fertile ground for hackers, who are already using AI’s coding proficiency to accelerate and personalise their attacks.
Worms have long been a popular and effective way for hackers to distribute malware because they are able to replicate and spread quickly across a large network.
Prominent examples include the ILOVEYOU virus that spread across Windows PCs in the early dotcom era, 2010s Stuxnet that originally targeted Iran’s nuclear programme and the widespread WannaCry ransomware that hit organisations including Deutsche Bahn, the UK National Health Service, Telefónica, Renault and FedEx.
AI-powered worms would combine these examples’ ability to spread themselves around the internet with the advanced capabilities of AI models.
“We expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control,” Anthropic said. “While it’s true that IoT [internet of things] devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute.”
At first, these AI worms would propagate slowly, akin to “slime mould or a swarm of fruit flies, which replicate over days”. But as consumer electronics become more sophisticated and models become more efficient, this could accelerate.
“We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain,” Anthropic said. “We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Enoch Burke faces jail again as school lodges fresh High Court application
description: Lawyers for Wilson’s Hospital School say sacked teacher trespassed multiple times, in breach of court order
content:
Enoch Burke faces the prospect of being jailed again after Wilson’s Hospital School lodged a fresh High Court application over his alleged trespassing at the Co Westmeath school.
Burke was formally dismissed from his position at the school in May for gross misconduct. He maintains that he was not validly dismissed, and continues to seek his reinstatement through the courts.
Lawyers for the school told Judge Brian Cregan on Tuesday that Burke had trespassed on various occasions since the beginning of the academic year, in breach of a court order.
Rosemary Mallon, counsel for the school’s board, said the school had done “all in its power” not to return to the courts, contacting gardaí and employing security personnel at the school premises.
Mallon said Burke had for some time confined his protest over his dismissal to outside the school gates.
However, since late last month, it appeared Burke had “changed his mind”, and continued to trespass on the school premises, counsel said.
She said the school had been placed in an “invidious” position, as it had been since the start of the long-running dispute.
The judge granted the school permission to serve Burke with its application for his attachment and committal to prison over his contempt of the court order. The case will return later this week.
Burke was not represented at the hearing.
[ For all his delusion, Enoch Burke comes strangely close to acknowledging something real Opens in new window ]
Wilson’s Hospital School suspended and later dismissed Burke over his conduct towards its then-principal at a school religious event in June 2022.
The confrontation arose in circumstances where Niamh McShane had earlier directed teachers to address a student by a new name and with the pronouns “they” and “them”.
Burke, an evangelical Christian, has maintained this request went against his religious beliefs.
When Burke continued to trespass at the school following his suspension, the school sought court orders banning him from the premises. Burke has continuously breached the order banning him from the school.
He has spent more than 700 days in prison in separate spells, arising from his contempt of the court order.
Cregan ordered Burke’s release from prison in July, despite his refusal to give a court undertaking not to trespass at the school.

title: Solicitor Ammi Burke went on ‘frantic rant’ over lunch invite email, court hears
description: Burke has ‘worst case of victim mentality’, former partner at Arthur Cox told the Labour Court
content:
Solicitor Ammi Burke went on a “frantic rant” after receiving an email inviting her to lunch, the Labour Court has heard.
A former senior partner at law firm Arthur Cox said Burke exhibited “the worst case of victim mentality I have ever witnessed”.
Burke, from Castlebar, Co Mayo , was dismissed by Arthur Cox Solicitors of Earlsfort Terrace, Dublin 2 , in November 2019 and is now on her third challenge to that dismissal.
She had previously taken cases against her dismissal at the Workplace Relations Commission ( WRC ), and there were two judicial reviews arising out of those.
She has now begun the case against her dismissal in the Labour Court, which is the appeal court for the WRC.
Giving evidence to the court, Gráinne Hennessy, a senior partner in the finance department, said she had sent a lunch email invitation on January 14th, 2019, to two new associates who had joined her department. It was intended as a celebration of them becoming associate solicitors.
She had realised that evening as she was leaving that she had not invited Burke, who was the third new associate within the banking and finance sector. The omission was inadvertent, as she had not worked with her before, Hennessy told the court.
She sent a two-line email to Burke at 6.27pm, inviting her too. Hennessy told the Labour Court that within five minutes Burke was standing over her desk in a physically intimidatory manner.
“She was offended, disgusted, and felt that her work was valued less than the two guys who were included in the invitation,” she said.
Hennessy said she apologised repeatedly and stated that she hadn’t meant to cause offence, but “nothing was landing”.
“This was the worst case of victim mentality I have worked with in my career. Nothing was going to undo the offence. I have never witnessed anything more shocking in a work context.”
Hennessy said she resolved after that not to work with Burke again, but did not raise it with HR because Burke had only been made an associate two weeks before.
“I did not want a black mark against her so early in her career,” she said.
Burke denied acting aggressively towards Hennessy in their exchange over the email. Burke said Hennessy appeared to take offence when she (Burke) raised the fact that she had been originally excluded from the lunch.
[ Ammi Burke to blame for damage to her reputation since Arthur Cox dismissal, court told Opens in new window ]
Hennessy said she did not dispute that Burke had been given good reviews as a trainee solicitor, but that was expected of Arthur Cox trainees who were recruited from the best law students in Ireland.
Arthur Cox managing partner Geoff Moore said the decision to summarily dismiss Burke was made by him, following consultation with other partners in the firm.
Moore said he had met with senior partners and HR on November 9th, 2019, and had come to the conclusion that the relationship between Burke and the firm had been “completely and utterly sundered at that point in time”.
He had opted against a disciplinary process because he had come to the conclusion that she was “incapable of seeing any other perspective, incapable of compromise or finding a sensible middle ground on issues like this”.
Moore said he took “no joy whatsoever” in sacking Burke and the ex gratia payment of €70,000 was an attempt to set her up so she could find another job.
Burke suggested to Moore that her dismissal was an act of “gross unfairness and injustice”.
She claimed to have been “ambushed” by being presented with her coat and handbag which had been on the back of the chair and ordered from the building.
Burke rejected Moore’s belief that she would not have been amenable to compromise. “You made a judgment on my character without ever having spoken to me,” she said to him.
She suggested to Moore that Arthur Cox had not followed its own disciplinary procedures in dismissing her – there had been four stages beginning with a verbal warning which were not followed.
Moore agreed, but he said he felt strongly that dismissal was the correct decision for the firm, and “though you don’t agree with me, the best decision for you, Miss Burke”.
Burke said her dismissal was “grossly destructive” of her prospects of getting a job as a solicitor elsewhere. Moore disagreed and said it was her subsequent conduct not the dismissal itself which impeded her career.
He said the almost seven years of litigation that Burke was now engaged in against Arthur Cox over her dismissal vindicated the original decision to sack her.

title: What services will be affected by the public sector strike and what will be closed?
description: More than 300,000 public sector workers are due to strike in the biggest industrial action of its kind since 2009
content:
M ore than 300,000 public sector workers are due to go on strike for 24 hours on Wednesday, barring a last-minute intervention.
Employees are seeking a new public sector deal, with trade unions arguing that pay terms must be agreed ⁠before other issues are addressed.
An attempt by Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers to initiate talks at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) was swiftly rebuffed by union leaders on Monday , meaning the strike appears almost inevitable.
Here is what you need to know about the strike and its expected impact.
Much of Ireland’s public sector is set to go on strike on Wednesday in the biggest industrial action of its kind since the height of the financial crisis in 2009.
More than 300,000 workers including teachers, doctors, nurses and civil servants are due to take part.
Widespread disruption is expected, with picket lines outside hospitals, schools, courts and many other work places.
The Public Service Agreement 2024–2026 expired in June and a new deal has not yet been reached.
The strike is happening because of an impasse between trade unions and the Government ​on the basis for entering talks to finalise a new agreement.
Unions ​are arguing that pay terms must be agreed ⁠before other issues – such as productivity – are discussed, as workers continue to be adversely impacted by the cost-of-living crisis.
The Government has rejected this condition, saying it represents a break from previous deals.
Chambers briefed his Cabinet colleagues on Tuesday on what were described as “substantial efforts” to engage with union leaders and emphasise the Government remains ready to attend talks at the WRC in the hope of averting the strike.
In a letter sent to the officers of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions (Ictu) public services committee on Monday, Chambers described the provision of €1.2 billion for public sector pay in the budget as “significant” and said “pay issues can and should be discussed as a priority alongside other matters as part of the pay talks”.
In its response to the Minister, Ictu accused the Government side of failing to honour commitments made in the agreement that expired in June .
Trade unions have indicated they will seek increases to address what they say was an earlier gap between pay rises and inflation of between 5 and 7 per cent, in addition to a settlement for the second half of this year, and an undertaking that their members’ wages will not be undermined by the cost of living increasing over the term of any deal.
The €1.2 billion, they contended, is not nearly enough to address those demands.
Tens of thousands of medical appointments are expected to be cancelled on Wednesday with the HSE warning of “significant and widespread disruption”.
All non-urgent healthcare services and outpatient appointments in hospitals and community settings are expected to be cancelled. Patients should have already been informed about the cancellations.
Some 32,000 public sector nurses will be involved in the strike, and the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation (INMO) said staffing levels broadly equivalent to overnight rosters would be provided , with the action only affecting hospital day shifts.
“We have already said we’ll cover all life-preserving services, dialysis, chemotherapy, all of those services; there’s just no debate about that kind of stuff,” INMO general secretary Phil Ní Sheaghdha said.
Dentists working in the HSE will also join the strike.
About 2,000 laboratory scientists are also due to strike, causing the postponement of, or delays to, patient tests.
Emergency departments, urgent cancer care and dialysis, and GP services will be available on Wednesday. Ambulance services will also be available, though curtailed.
Siptu has said fire brigades will operate with reduced services.
Schools, colleges and universities are all expected to close on Wednesday.
About 90,000 teachers are due to strike.
The main teaching unions – including the Irish National Teachers’ Organisation, the Association of Secondary Teachers Ireland, the Teachers’ Union of Ireland and the Irish Federation of University Teachers – are all taking part in the industrial action.
Special needs assistants, who are represented by Fórsa trade union, will also be on strike.
The Courts Service said, if the strike goes ahead as planned, it would have no option but to close the vast majority of courts countrywide on Wednesday.
Some exceptions have been agreed with unions to ensure emergency applications related to domestic violence or child-safety issues could be heard.
An Garda Síochána will be able to apply to have accused people remanded in custody where station bail has not been granted.
All driving tests scheduled for Wednesday have been cancelled because staff from the Road Safety Authority will be taking part in the strike.
Cancelled tests will be rescheduled for later dates.
Many libraries across the country will be closed as local authority workers are due to take part in the strike.
The National Library, National Gallery and National Museum are among the institutions that will be closed.
Dublin City Council said on Tuesday that its staff would not be available to clean streets, parks or public spaces, and that bin collection in the city would not take place. It asked the public to bring home rubbish where possible.
🛑Closure Notice Please note that the National Gallery of Ireland will be closed on Wednesday 14 October 2026 due to industrial action. We apologise for any inconvenience caused and thank you for your understanding. pic.twitter.com/x3rxUEcGqR
Civil servants will be on strike, meaning all heritage sites and parks operated by the Office of Public Works are expected to close on Wednesday. However, roads in the Phoenix Park in Dublin will remain open.
The Cliffs of Moher Experience, in Liscannor, Co Clare, will be open, Clare County Council said.
Gardaí and members of the Defence Forces are public sector workers but are legally prohibited from taking part in the strike, meaning they will be working on Wednesday.
Public transport services are also expected to operate as normal.

title: Athletics wishes it could scrub the women’s marathon world record – what can be done?
description: People in the sport talk about Ruth Chepngetich reluctantly, like a family member who has joined a mysterious cult
content:
When Ruth Chepngetich annihilated the women’s marathon world record in Chicago two years ago today, NBC’s commentators compared it to the moon landing. “Bring it on, Neil Armstrong!” cried one. “She has done things in this sport that we have not seen,” said another. “Unbelievable!”
That was a word others reached for too after the Kenyan had crossed the line in 2:9:56, a time that not only smashed the world record by 1:57, but her personal best by a staggering five minutes. Afterwards, she was asked by Robert Johnson of Let’s Run what her response was to those who believed she must be doping. “People must talk,” she replied. “I don’t know.”
We know a lot more now. Because five months after that epic run, Chepngetich’s star came crashing down to earth. First she failed a doping test . Then she was banned for three years . These days people in the sport talk about her reluctantly, like a family member who has joined a mysterious cult. Yet her world record still stands because she passed a test after the race itself.
What should we think of this? What are we allowed legally to say about this? And what, if anything, can be done about it?
A couple of weeks ago, I spoke to Brett Clothier, the head of the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU), which prosecuted the case against Chepngetich, to ask about her world record. “It is not satisfactory, to be frank,” he admitted. “But the world anti-doping code is pretty clearcut on the rights athletes have, even if they’re found guilty of a doping offence.”
That much is true. But while legally, Chepngetich was clean when she broke her world record, the fact it stands surely damages the sport’s credibility.
True, there are plenty of highly suspicious records from the 1980s and early 1990s, given what we know about state-sponsored doping behind the iron curtain and in China. And if you believe Florence Griffith Joyner knocked more than half a second off her 100m and 200m times in 1988 by doing 5,000 sit-ups a day and drinking water, I have some magic beans to sell you.
Griffith Joyner, of course, never tested positive. But before her death, aged 38, her fellow American sprinter Darrell Robinson claimed in a paid interview with the German magazine Stern that he had sold her human growth hormone for $2,000.
He also alleged that she had told him: “If you want to make a million dollars, you’ve got to invest a couple of thousand.” Yet as much as Flo-Jo’s records make us uneasy, they are seen as coming from a bygone and more lawless era.
Also, what makes Chepngetich unique is that no other athlete has been hit with a lengthy ban so soon after a world record.
The Kenyan’s defence for having 20 times the legal limit of hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) in her system? That she had taken her housemaid’s medication after feeling hot and having a rapid resting heartbeat. It was, the AIU noted, a “hardly credible” explanation.
The AIU also found screenshots on Chepngetich’s phone about the banned drug testosterone and “messages related to unidentified third parties working on ‘programs’ possibly related to doping”. The Kenyan has insisted that she has never used testosterone and the messages were from a group chat, but they hardly inspire confidence either.
So what can be done? The short answer, having spoken to the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), is very little. As a Wada spokesperson pointed out to me, removing her results before her positive test “in the absence of any evidence or reasonable inference that the athlete was doping before or at the time of the earlier results, might well breach a number of legal principles including proportionality and human rights”.
But what about Lance Armstrong, who was stripped of his Tour de France titles despite not being convicted of breaking any doping rules while competing? Could this not apply here? Not according to Wada.
“He had procedural avenues open to him to contest the sanction but ultimately chose not to use them,” a spokesperson told me. “That makes his case a relatively weak precedent for establishing how far retrospective disqualification could legally go.”
One idea I floated to various experts was that athletes could be asked to sign a social contract, which pledged they would accept losing their world record if they tested positive within a year of that world record or winning an Olympic medal.
In theory, one anti-doping expert put it to me, it was possible to do this. But he felt it would require everybody – from sports federations and governments to athlete bodies and human rights groups – to buy in and to agree to change the Wada code to allow retrospective punishments. And that is not going to happen.
At least track and field can point to many significant victories over doping in the last decade, given that Chepngetich is one of 317 elite Kenyan athletes the AIU has caught since it was set up in 2017. Many sports pay lip service to catching cheats. Athletics actually does. And the AIU does it on a modest budget of $11.9 million (€10.63 million) a year.
There are also positive signs that prominent athletes realise more must be done when it comes to anti-doping. Before Sabastian Sawe set his men’s marathon world record in London , for instance, his sponsors, Adidas , paid $50,000 for extra testing. Nike did the same for two of their athletes, Jacob Kiplimo and Brigid Kosgei, before Chicago.
Sawe’s agent, Eric Lilot, wants to go further by making his athletes sign a contract that will require them to give up any money still owed to them if it is shown they intentionally tried to dope. All that points to brighter days ahead, however much Chepngetich’s record makes us feel queasy. — Guardian

title: Planning permission for service station beside site of Creeslough explosion refused
description: Bereaved families objected to the ‘profoundly insulting and disrespectful’ application
content:
Planning permission for a service station adjacent to the site of the Creeslough tragedy in Co Donegal , in which 10 people were killed, has been refused.
Donegal County Council had granted permission for the service station last March. However, that decision was appealed to An Coimisiún Pleanála by a number of family members of those who died.
Several families bereaved by the October 7th, 2022, explosion had objected to the application, saying it would be “profoundly insulting and disrespectful”.
An Coimisiún Pleanála has now upheld the appeal and refused permission for the service station after considering submissions on the file and the planning inspector’s report at meetings in August and September.
The commission found that a significant portion of the appeal site is designated as an “Amenity Area”, with an objective “to reserve and enhance” the locality.
The decision can still be challenged by way of judicial review in the High Court.
The bereaved families have welcomed the decision to overturn the original planning permission.
Donna Harper, who lost her 14-year-old daughter Leona in the tragedy, said the families had never been against a new service station being put in the village. She said it was the location of both applications that they objected to.
“We are fully aware that Creeslough needs a shop and service station, everyone can see that,” she said. “We just felt that the location of both of these locations was insensitive and that is why we objected to them.”
[ Health and Safety Authority sends file on Creeslough tragedy to DPP Opens in new window ]
This is the second proposal by siblings Annette and Danny Martin Lafferty for a service station.
The first application centred on the site of the original explosion, and was granted by Donegal County Council but refused by An Coimisiún Pleanála.
This second application sought to demolish an existing dwelling and construct a new building incorporating a shop, post office, off-licence, store and deli.
Plans also included a forecourt, underground fuel storage tanks and pumps, toilets, staff facilities, a car wash, outdoor launderette kiosk, fuel bunker storage, ATM and associated signage.
Donegal County Council granted permission for the development on March 26th, subject to conditions.
The decision to turn down the new application comes less than a week after more than 200 people gathered at the site of the tragedy to mark its fourth anniversary .
Bereaved families once again spoke of their continuing grief and renewed their calls for truth, justice and answers to their questions as to how the tragedy happened.
The names of the 10 people who died were read out by Fr John Joe Duffy at 3.17pm, the time the explosion occurred.

title: Jury sworn in for trial of Russell Brand
description: Comedian accused of rape and sexual assault in allegations which date from 1999 to 2009
content:
A jury has been sworn in for the trial of Russell Brand on charges of rape and sexual assault which span 10 years of his showbiz career.
Brand (51) is accused of groping women and forcing them into sexual acts, in allegations which date from 1999 to 2009.
On Tuesday at Southwark Crown Court, judge Joel Bennathan oversaw the selection of a jury.
Jurors have been sent away until Wednesday morning when prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones is expected to set out the full details of the allegations against Brand.
Eight men and four women have been chosen at random as jurors, with one reserve selected to sit through the prosecution opening.
They were all warned by the judge on Monday to ignore past reporting about Brand and the allegations of sexual misconduct he has faced in recent years.
“Don’t carry out any research”, judge Bennathan told them on Tuesday.
“If you want to, you could go and have a look – but only once you have returned your verdicts.”
As he arrived at Southwark Crown Court at just after 9.20am on Tuesday, Brand said “blessed, thank you very much” in the direction of photographers and members of the press.
Flanked by his security guard, Brand looked at the cameras pointed at him before taking off his sunglasses as he walked up the steps towards the central London courthouse.
His wife Laura Gallacher, who was by his side for Monday’s hearing, did not accompany Brand to court on Tuesday morning.
On Monday, the judge started with 50 prospective jurors, before swiftly excusing six who said they had either seen a Channel 4 documentary or read a newspaper article in 2023 concerning allegations about Brand, which he denies.
In the second stage of the selection process, 20 possible jurors were selected and sent away for the night to check that they are free to sit on a trial that is expected to last six weeks, but could stretch to nine weeks.
Brand denies three charges of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one allegation of indecent assault, made by six women. – PA

title: Disabled Ukrainian woman in hotel accommodation loses appeal over loss of welfare benefits
description: Supreme Court rejects claim that law excluding temporary protection applicants in State accommodation from benefits is unconstitutional
content:
A disabled Ukrainian woman and her husband have lost an important Supreme Court appeal over a law excluding temporary protection applicants in designated accommodation centres from social welfare benefits.
In dismissing the appeal on Tuesday, the seven-judge Supreme Court rejected arguments the 2024 law permitted unlawful arbitrary treatment of the couple in breach of the equality guarantee in Article 40.1 of the Constitution.
Under the law, the woman lost her disability allowance and the man his carer’s allowance because they remained in their designated hotel accommodation.
The couple, who cannot be identified, have lived on a full-board basis in a hotel in Dublin since they arrived in the State in 2022 after fleeing the Russian war on Ukraine.
The woman, a wheelchair user, had from 2022 received a means-tested disability allowance of €208 per week. Her husband, who has medical needs and is unlikely to return to work, received a means-tested weekly carer’s allowance of €224.
Amending legislation in 2024, aimed at freeing up space in designated accommodation centres (DAC), stated displaced people granted temporary protection here “shall be disqualified” from social welfare assistance, other than supplementary welfare allowance, while in a DAC.
When the couple’s hotel became a DAC in September 2024, they lost their disability and care allowances. If they moved out, they would be entitled to the allowances.
Their senior counsel, Feichín McDonagh, argued the 2024 amendments meant the couple were being “pushed out” in a situation where it is “very difficult” for a woman in a wheelchair to get alternative accommodation in a housing crisis.
After the High Court rejected their challenge, they secured an appeal directly to the Supreme Court on grounds it raised a “serious issue” with implications for many – whether the distinction drawn between temporary protection recipients and international protection candidates, on which the legislative changes were based, is constitutionally valid.
Giving the Supreme Court’s unanimous judgment, Judge Iseult O’Malley said the appeal involved a “pure” equality claim in that the couple argued they were unlawfully excluded from a benefit extended to people in a similar position.
Such a claim is governed by legal principles including the court will show deference to the Oireachtas in relation to legislation dealing with matters of social and fiscal policy, she said.
The claim the couple were treated differently solely on the basis of their place of residence failed to recognise their legal status is different in nature and arises from a different source, and the distinctions drawn by the legislature relate to those differences, she said.
A constitutional claim for financial equality would require them to identify other social welfare recipients similar to them who were treated favourably, which they had failed to do, she said.
They had disregarded the financial value of the full board accommodation provided to them and had “not realistically estimated” the living expenses of persons not receiving such a service.
The issue does not arise from where they reside but rather the different forms of service available to people in different forms of accommodation, said O’Malley.
Article 40.1 is not engaged where a claimant is offered a choice between two forms of assistance and fails to establish disproportionately unfavourable treatment of persons claiming either form, the judge held.
The Oireachtas policy to reduce the number of people in State-provided accommodation facilities is not illegitimate once proper alternative assistance is provided, and the State’s obligations under the EU temporary protection directive are complied with, she held.
The Oireachtas may also alter initial reception policy to ensure particular forms of assistance, designed to be temporary, do not become permanent.
Noting the couple are “particularly vulnerable” because of their health needs, the judge said they remain entitled to be given access to suitable housing, or the means to get housing and other assistance for persons with special needs, if they lack sufficient resources.

title: Trump is blaming Zelenskiy for a problem of his own making
description: US president cannot forgive Ukrainian leader for showing up his deal-making impotence
content:
“I want to thank president Putin , to be honest with you,” Donald Trump said last weekend. It should have been the other way round. Trump had agreed to pay Vladimir Putin billions of dollars for Russian diesel that will have a negligible effect on US prices.
Such asymmetry is also known as something for nothing. Trump’s nothing is that the cost of diesel is unlikely to fall before the US midterm elections. Putin’s something is a breach in US sanctions and more money to bomb Ukraine.
I am unqualified to make psychological judgments but an amateur can see that Trump is blaming Volodymyr Zelenskiy for a problem of his own making. The chief driver of rising diesel prices is the impact of Trump’s Operation Epic Fury. Iran and its proxies have knocked out big chunks of Gulf refining capacity, which has sharply reduced global diesel supply. In defiance of Trump’s requests, Ukraine has further disrupted supply by striking Russian refineries. Zelenskiy is thus a ready-made scapegoat for a problem largely caused by the US president.
Things could get still worse for Ukraine. On the day that Trump announced the Russia deal, his son-in-law Jared Kushner and chief envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Ukrainians in Florida. They threatened to block weapons sales and end US intelligence sharing if Ukraine continued to strike Russian refineries. This would deprive Zelenskiy of the last useful bit of US support against Russia’s escalating assault.
In the week before Trump’s diesel deal, more than 100 Ukrainians, including at least 20 children, were killed by Russian missiles. Another US president would be pressuring Russia to stop killing innocents. Trump is instead giving them the means to kill more. He is also giving Russia a green light to keep helping Iran, which it has been supplying with satellite and tracking data to target US bases and allied installations in the region. In a very real sense, therefore, Trump is assisting attacks on America.
Whenever Trump is asked about Russia’s support for Iran, he downplays or ignores the question. On one occasion, he said Putin had reassured him that no such help was being given. But Putin is helpful to Iran, which means he can dangle the promise of brokering an end to the Gulf war.
Zelenskiy, on the other hand, is a constant reminder of Trump’s deal-making impotence. No matter how much US allies urge Trump to back Ukraine, he is unable to forgive Zelenskiy for what he represents. Trump vowed to end the Russia-Ukraine war within 24 hours of taking office, which would have entailed Ukraine’s capitulation. Zelenskiy was predictably unwilling to do that. Nor is he now.
We are thus left with a mixture of bluster and threat. On bluster, Trump said on Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an energy ceasefire in which Russia stops targeting Ukraine’s energy grid and Ukraine lays off Russia’s refineries. This was “effective immediately”. Zelenskiy said that this was the first he had heard of it.
On Monday, Zelenskiy said Russia had attacked power and gas facilities across Ukraine on Sunday night. He insists Kyiv is still willing to observe a ceasefire if Moscow does the same. But he has little incentive to do so. Russia has already taken out most of Ukraine’s grid. Zelenskiy’s imperative is to deprive Russia of the revenues to keep attacking.
On threat, Trump said on Saturday that Ukraine needs a new president. He could go a step further and make America’s intelligence support contingent on Ukraine holding elections. No country can carry out orderly elections – a quintessential peacetime activity – while another nation occupies a fifth of its territory and is randomly targeting the rest. It would be reckless for Zelenskiy to agree to Trump’s demand and there is scant chance that he will.
Ironically, Trump’s ire is boosting Zelenskiy’s support among Ukrainians. They have plenty to complain about, including corruption in Zelenskiy’s circle. But he is getting a “Trump bump” in the polls that has helped sway elections in Canada, Australia, Denmark and arguably the Vatican. Nations tend to close ranks when outsiders try to choose their leaders. Trump has called Zelenskiy a dictator while saying Putin is his friend. No prizes for guessing which of the two is on display in a gold-framed photograph at the White House.
The election that matters to Trump is the US midterms. Should he have been serious about reducing US energy prices, he would have started months ago. But nothing he is trying, including Russian shipments, is likely to lift his party’s bleak prospects. Zelenskiy’s headache is that Trump is preparing to blame a Democratic victory on him. The iron law of Trump is that nothing is ever his fault.
