title: Pygmalion 26: casadh comhaimseartha Gaeilge ar scéal GB Shaw
description: Is i gCorcaigh ar an tseachtain seo chugainn a chuirfear tús leis an léiriú nua de chuid Aisling Ghéar
content:
Is gearr anois go mbeidh leagan úrnua Gaeilge den dráma Pygmalion le George Bernard Shaw le feiceáil ar ardáin náisiúnta, agus €400,000 de mhaoiniú faighte ag an chomhlacht amharclannaíochta Aisling Ghéar chun casadh an lae inniu a chur ar an scéal.
Ba é an gníomhaí teanga Feirsteach agus scríbhneoir aitheanta Gearóid Ó Cairealláin a smaoinigh ar leagan Gaeilge den dráma clúiteach a chur os comhair lucht féachana. Ar an drochuair, cailleadh Gearóid sa bhliain 2024, ach is í Bríd Ní Ghallchóir, stiúrthóir ealaíne Aisling Ghéar agus bean chéile Ghearóid, a chuirfidh craiceann ar an bhunsmaoineamh agus a bheidh mar léiritheoir an dráma ar an chamchuairt náisiúnta.
Deir Nuala Ní Néill, stiúrthóir Pygmalion 26 agus bean atá ag obair agus ag aisteoireacht le hAisling Ghéar le beagnach 25 bliana, go bhfuil sí ag “dúil go mór” leis an dráma seo a chur ar an bhóthar.
Bhí an smaoineamh seo ag Gearóid níos mó ná fiche bliain ó shin. Duine iontach tiomanta a bhí ann ar ndóigh agus bhí a chroí go hiomlán sáite sna healaíona.
“Bhí an smaoineamh seo ag Gearóid níos mó ná fiche bliain ó shin. Duine iontach tiomanta a bhí ann ar ndóigh agus bhí a chroí go hiomlán sáite sna healaíona. Thagadh an smaoineamh seo aníos achan chúpla bliain, ach nuair a d’éirigh linn an maoiniú suntasach sin a fháil ón Chomhairle Ealaíon anuraidh, bhí muid ábalta amharc ar an phlean i gceart,” arsa Nuala.
“An smaoineamh a bhí ag Gearóid é féin ná go mbeadh tuismitheoir ag foghlaim na Gaeilge sa phríomhról, Eilís, ach smaoinigh muid ansin nach mbeadh sin chomh hábhartha céanna don lá atá inniu ann. Mar sin de d’athraigh muid an bunsmaoineamh le go mbeadh duine óg a tháinig tríd an chóras Gaelscolaíochta anseo i mBéal Feirste mar Eilís.”
Cathair cheannródaíoch in athbheochan na Gaeilge is ea Béal Feirste agus is sa chathair sin a chaith Gearóid an chuid is mó dá shaol ag obair agus ag troid ar son na teanga. Ba dheacair smaoineamh ar shuíomh níos fóirsteanaí do Pygmalion 26, ach mar a deir Nuala í féin, is cinnte go raibh athruithe áirithe le déanamh ar script a scríobhadh níos mó ná céad bliain ó shin.
“Nuair atá tú ag iarraidh ábhar tábhachtach a phlé os comhair lucht féachana comhaimseartha, caithfidh tú a bheith ag éisteacht leis an chomhrá atá ag dul ar aghaidh thart ort. Tá rud ar leith ag tarlú anseo i mBéal Feirste. Tá an Ghaelscoil is mó sa tír againn anseo agus tá beagnach míle páiste ag fáil oideachas dara leibhéal trí mheán na Gaeilge i gColáiste Feirste.
“Thosaigh mé féin amach mar aisteoir beagnach tríocha bliain ó shin agus is cinnte nach raibh mórán aisteoirí a raibh Gaeilge acu ag an am sin. Nuair a chuaigh Aisling Ghéar timpeall na tíre do na héisteachtaí d’Eilís, stop muid i mBéal Feirste, Baile Átha Cliath, Gaillimh agus Corcaigh. Bhuail muid le 68 mbean óga a raibh bua an cheoil, Gaeilge líofa, agus aisteoireacht den scoth acu. Ní raibh sé sin ann 20 bliain ó shin. Is léir go bhfuil fás ollmhór ag tarlú.”
Is ag na héisteachtaí sin i mí Iúil a bhuail foireann Aisling Ghéar le hEithne Carson, bean óg as Baile Átha Cliath a bhfuil dúil mhillteanach aici sa cheol agus san aisteoireacht. D’éirigh le hEithne an phríomhpháirt mar Eilís a fháil.
“Is í an Ghaeilge mo chéad teanga agus labhair muid Gaeilge sa bhaile. Tá sé go hiontach anois deis a bheith agam rud éigin mar seo a dhéanamh as Gaeilge agus an grá atá agam don teanga a choinneáil beo i ndiaidh na scoile,” a mhínigh Eithne.
“Sílim go bhfuil Eilís an-chosúil liomsa mar charachtar. Tá sé an-éasca tuiscint a bheith agam ar an scéal mar sin. Is ceoltóir agus Gaeilgeoir í agus foghlaimíonn sí a cuid Gaeilge óna seanathair. Sílim go bhfuil sé go deas páirt a bheith agat atá cosúil leatsa mar go ndéanann sé an scéal níos pearsanta agus bíonn tú in ann tú féin a aithint sa duine.”
Ar ndóigh, cé go bhfuil an Ghaeilge faoi bhláth cois Lagáin, tá easaontas ar dhá thaobh na deighilte sna Sé Chontae go fóill agus conspóid atá go mór i mbéal an phobail ag leanúint ar aghaidh i bPort an Dúnáin. Tá teachtaireacht láidir le cur in iúl ag Aisling Ghéar agus scéal greannmhar sultmhar le cur i láthair ag an am céanna.
“Tá muid ag baint úsáid as an chreatlach a scríobh Shaw in 1912. Bhain sé sin le haicme agus leis an dearcadh a bhí ag daoine faoin airgead agus faoi na daoine áirithe a raibh cumhacht acu sa tsochaí. Sa dráma s’againne, ní hionann aicme agus cumas teanga. Tá an Ghaeltacht, áit a bhfuil Gaeilge bhinn i measc an phobail, suite faoin tuath agus is minic nach gcuirtear maoiniú ná tacaíochtaí cearta ar fáil do na ceantair sin i gcomparáid leis na cathracha móra. Bhí muid ábalta íoróin a úsáid sa script leis sin a chur in iúl,” arsa Nuala.
“Tá líne sa dráma a phléann an uair a cuireadh an teanga faoi chois – is rud polaitiúil a rinneadh orainn, agus mar sin caithfidh go bhfuil an athbheochan polaitiúil fosta. Tá tú ag seasamh suas in éadan an choilínithe agus ag iarraidh teanga a baineadh uainn a thabhairt ar ais ar comhchéim leis an Bhéarla. Is rud polaitiúil é sin gan dabht agus mar sin is deacair é a bhaint ón dráma.
“Ag an am céanna, sílim go bhfuil bealaí áirithe againn le bheith ag déileáil leis. D’fhás mise aníos le linn na dtrioblóidí anseo sna Sé Chontae agus cé go raibh rudaí uafásacha ag tarlú, bhí muid ábalta greann dubh a úsáid. Sin an dóigh a gcoinníonn daoine an misneach go fóill. Thuig muid go mbeadh orainn greann a úsáid sa script leis na carachtair uilig a choinneáil réalaíoch.”
Is léir go bhfuil ceisteanna móra féiniúlachta agus polaitíochta fite fuaite leis an Ghaeilge ach ní hionann é sin agus a rá gur le dream ar leith í. Má tá an teanga le fás agus le forbairt ó thuaidh sa lá atá inniu ann, caithfear fáilte a chur roimh gach duine ar mhaith leo í a labhairt agus a fhoghlaim.
“Is le hachan uile dhuine againn an Ghaeilge. Baineann sé le féiniúlacht s’agat agus cuireann sé go mór le d’fhéiniúlacht féin nuair a bhíonn tú ábalta tú féin a chur in aithne i dteanga eile. Is le hachan duine ar mhaith leo í a fhoghlaim í.
“Tá rud ar leith ag tarlú in Oirthear Bhéal Feirste faoi stiúir Linda Ervine. Protastúnaigh, dílseoirí agus Aontachtaithe is ea tromlach an phobail sa cheantar sin ach deir Linda í féin gur linne uilig an teanga. Tá an teanga ag athrú chomh gasta agus atá an tsochaí ag athrú.”
Níl ach sé lá fágtha anois go mbeidh foireann Aisling Ghéar ag bualadh an bhóthair go Corcaigh le Pygmalion a chur ar ardán an Everyman. Deir Nuala go bhfuil sé “galánta” go bhfuil an fhís a bhí ag Gearóid Ó Cairealláin fiche bliain ó shin á fíorú anois.
“Tá mé cinnte go mbeadh sé linn dá mbeadh sé anseo go fóill, le hata s’aige air, bualadh bos mór dúinn agus pionta ina lámh ag deireadh na hoíche. Bheadh an méid sin bróid air as an fhoireann iontach seo atá againn.”
Agus Eithne ag ullmhú dá céad dráma le hAisling Ghéar, deir sí go bhfuil sí “ar bís” tús a chur leis an chamchuairt.
“Cabhraíonn sé linn beocht a chur sa dráma nuair a bhíonn muid ar fad ar bís, agus tá muid ag súil go mór le bheith os comhair an lucht féachana. Sílim go bhfuil go leor rudaí sa dráma a chuirfidh daoine ag smaoineamh agus ag comhrá ina dhiaidh freisin.”
Cuirfear tús le camchuairt Pygmalion 26 san Everyman i gCorcaigh an Luan beag seo, an 19 Deireadh Fómhair 2026. Rachaidh an chliar ar aghaidh ansin go Gaillimh, An Muileann gCearr, Port Láirge, Béal Feirste, Gaoth Dobhair agus Baile Átha Cliath. Tá ticéid ar fáil anois.

title: What are the US midterms? A visual guide
description: Democrats hope to take advantage of Donald Trump’s declining popularity and reclaim the House and Senate from the Republicans
content:
V oters in the United States on November 3rd will elect members of Congress, which is made up of two parts – the House of Representatives and the Senate .
These elections happen midway through the term of the US president – two years after the presidential elections – and determine which party controls Congress.
The outcome is important because if the president’s party does not hold a majority, it becomes difficult to pass legislation.
A key task of Congress is to create and pass federal laws – laws that apply nationwide.
The outcome will determine which political party – Donald Trump’s Republicans or opposition Democrats – controls Congress and how easy the US president can advance his agenda.
The results are also seen as a barometer of public opinion on the US president’s performance to date.
Trump’s overall approval rating has been falling for months, according to data from Real Clear Polling, down from a high of 48 per cent when he was inaugurated.
A key factor behind his successful 2024 presidential election campaign was his pledge to tackle the cost of living, posing with eggs and other household staples.
Two years on, many voters are struggling with the price of fuel, groceries, housing and healthcare. Data from the polling site Strength in Numbers shows Trump’s approval ratings have been trending in a negative direction on these issues for some time.
All members of the House – which is the lower chamber of Congress – will be elected. The 435 representatives serve fixed terms of two years.
To gain control of the House, a party needs a minimum of 218 seats. The Republicans hold a narrow majority after winning 219 seats in the 2024 elections.
It will only take a few seats to flip and the power dynamics of the House will look very different.
Latest polling indicates that Democrats are likely to win the House.
In the Senate – the upper chamber of Congress – just 35 out of 100 seats are up for grabs.
The Republicans hold 22 of these seat and Democrats 13.
To take back control of the Senate, the Democrats must flip at least four seats, including two in states where the president won by double digits. They also need to keep all of their seats.
Each of the 50 states has two senators. Office holders are elected for six-year terms on a rolling basis. Every two years, one-third of the senators come up for re-election.
Democrats are growing increasingly bullish about their chances of winning seats, even in red states such as Texas and Iowa.
Many seats in both chambers are not competitive because they are located in Republican or Democrat strongholds.
Most observers believe that between eight and 10 states will be competitive and could prove pivotal once the results are tallied after polls close on November 3rd.
They include Alaska, Georgia , Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, North Carolina , Ohio and Texas .
Keith Duggan, our Washington Correspodent, has been visiting many of these swing states. You can read his articles here .
Voting has been made more unpredictable this year because of redistricting, with several states redrawing congressional maps to swing the balance of power in House races.
Other unusual factors include Trump’s pledge to pay voters $5,000 if Republicans maintain control of Congress, as well as eye-watering sums of money being spent on campaigns in some toss-up states during the final weeks.
Since the start of 2026, most polls have given the Democrats a lead nationally.
Polling, however, has tended to understate support for Trump. In 2024, for example, most polls pointed to a Kamala Harris victory in the presidential elections. In the end, Trump won comfortably. Polls also underestimated Trump’s support when he beat Hillary Clinton in the 2016 presidential elections.
Many betting sites or, increasingly, prediction markets have been more accurate.
According to one of the market-leaders, Polymarket, most people who have placed bets are confident that a Democratic sweep of the House and the Senate is the most likely outcome.
If the Democrats win either the House or the Senate then Trump will find it difficult to get laws through Congress.
While some of his domestic plans could be frustrated, the US president has found ways to exercise executive power without his wider party.
Democratic control of either chamber would mean they could use committees to investigate aspects of the Trump presidency.
This could have knock-on effects for the Iran war, funding for Israel and Trump’s political future. Democrat control could mean investigations into the Trump administration.
If the Republicans continue to control Congress, Trump will be able to continue with his plans and policies for the remainder of his time in office.

title: Three injured, one seriously, after four-vehicle crash in Sligo
description: Collision involving three vans and a car occurred on the N15 at Carns, Grange, on Monday
content:
Three men have been hospitalised following a four-vehicle crash in Sligo on Monday.
The crash, involving three vans and a car, occurred on the N15 at Carns, Grange, at around 10.20am.
The driver of one of the vans, aged in his 70s, was taken to Sligo University Hospital with serious injuries.
The other two van drivers, aged in their 20s and 50s, were also taken to Sligo University Hospital with non-life threatening injuries. No other injuries were reported.
Garda forensic collision investigators conducted an examination of the scene and the road has since reopened.
Gardaí are appealing to anyone who witnessed the collision to come forward.
Road users who may have camera footage, including dashcam, and were travelling on the N15 near Carns, Grange, Co Sligo, between 9.45am and 10.20am on Monday, are asked to make this available to investigating gardaí.

title: Is it safe to fly through the Middle East? Advice for Irish travellers after Saudi airport attack
description: Attacks are limited to Saudi Arabia and Yemen
content:
Saudi authorities on Monday extended the suspension of operations at the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, after two deadly attacks over the weekend by Yemen ’s Iran -backed Houthis.
Are other airport in the region under threat?
For now, the attacks are limited to Saudi Arabia and Yemen and travel is continuing without interference to other Middle East destinations, including neighbouring United Arab Emirates (UAE), where the popular Dubai holiday resort is located.
Operations at King Khalid international airport, Saudi Arabia’s second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended ​until next Saturday to “allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of ​the airport’s facilities”, the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement.
The airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded ​more than 300, including an Irish citizen, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another ​attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.
Ireland joined many other countries in issuing a travel warning for Saudi Arabia. Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee said on Monday that Irish citizens should avoid travel to King Khalid airport, saying they should seek updates from their airline, monitor local media and follow official safety advice. Qatar Airways ​said on ‌Monday it ​had ​temporarily suspended flights ⁠to ​and from ​Riyadh and Dammam in ​Saudi ​Arabia.
Is there a chance that attacks in Saudi Arabia and Yemen could widen to the Middle East?
The conflict could escalate and US president Donald Trump said on Sunday that the US “may” join Saudi Arabia in its retaliation against the Houthis, promising that he would speak “shortly” with Saudi leader crown prince Mohammed bin Salman. Such a scenario could trigger a wider regional conflict and lead to the Houthis targeting US targets and allies across the Middle East.
Have other airports in the Middle East been targeted in recent months?
Yes, airports in Israel, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Yemen have all been hit since the US and Israel attacked Iran in June 2025.
Saudi Arabia’s energy minister has said there will be a “serious” response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom’s airports and oil and gas facilities.
“ The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious,” prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told an energy conference in Riyadh on Monday.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they say is a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sana’a airport that they blamed on the kingdom. They warned airlines to avoid Saudi airports, with the exception of the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina.

title: Greencore signals stronger annual profit on back of ‘monumental year’
description: Irish convenience giant says fourth-quarter volumes grew ⁠at faster pace than wider market
content:
Shares in Dublin-headquartered convenience food group Greencore jumped in early trading after the company forecast annual profit ahead of market expectations. ‌
Greencore, the biggest producer of pre-packed sandwiches in the UK, said in a full-year trading statement that its fourth-quarter volumes grew ⁠at a faster pace than the wider grocery market.
The London-listed company, which acquired rival British supplier Bakkavor in January, ⁠forecast 2026 ​adjusted operating profit for continuing ​operations at £248 million, ahead of analyst expectations of £238 million.
Shares were up ⁠4.5 per cent at 274 ⁠pence ​in early trading, before easing back to 268.4p
In a trading update, Greencore said its fourth-quarter revenue increased by 4.5 per cent to £1.04 billion. The company said the integration of Bakkavor was progressing ‌well with a ⁠fast start on “central reorganisation, procurement and distribution synergies”.
Greencore said it ‌had entered the new fiscal year with ​good volume momentum despite wider market ​uncertainties.
Greencore’s £1.2 billion acquisition of Bakkavor created an entity that is the UK’s largest manufacturer of convenience foods. Bakkavor’s retail customers include Tesco, Marks and Spencer and Waitrose.
“Greencore has had a monumental year and we finished it with a strong performance in Q4,” chief executive Dalton Philips said. “We grew volume ahead of the market, drove strong profit growth and we continue to make strides in our integration with Bakkavor.
“That performance means we are in a position to further upgrade our full-year guidance,” Philips said.
“Our focus in FY27 remains simple: producing high-quality, innovative fresh food, ensuring we deliver for our customers and progressing our ambitions for our larger business,” he said.
In its latest update, Greencore said it launched 167 new products launched during the fourth quarter.
“These included two ranges of premium Italian ready meals, new summer-focused grab-and-go sandwich and salad ranges, and a range of limited-edition diner-style mac and cheese products,” it said.
Goodbody analyst Patrick Higgins said the numbers represented underlying growth of around 24 per cent, “is circa 4 per cent better than our and consensus estimates, and well above the top-end of the £234-£242 million guidance range”.
“This is an excellent update from Greencore which we expect to be well received by the market,” he said, adding that word of new business wins “is particularly encouraging”.

title: Bulgaria points to Russia as drones hit more cargo ships
description: Six crew members rescued and 10 others missing in attack near Nato territorial waters
content:
Drones struck two ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, the country’s prime minister said on Tuesday, in the latest in a string of attacks near Nato’s territorial waters that have frayed nerves in the region.
Six crew members were rescued and 10 others are missing, according to Bulgaria’s defence minister Dimitar Stoyanov, after it went down 30km east of the village of Krapets having sent a distress signal.
Bulgaria’s prime minister Rumen Radev acknowledged that it was not clear who had launched the drones but said in a statement that “logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation” and that he had summoned Moscow’s ambassador to seek an explanation.
The uptick in drone strikes on the Black Sea, including attacks on ships in Romanian waters, comes as Russia steps up threats to Nato’s eastern flank and seeks to sow division among Ukraine’s allies.
“The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine,” said Ursula von der Leyen , president of the European Commission. “This is unacceptable.”
One of the ships attacked off Bulgaria’s coast sank, Radev said. Six people were rescued from its crew, according to Lyubomir Nikolov, the Bulgarian interior ministry’s chief secretary. He did not provide details on the whereabouts of the other crew members.
Radev said the other vessel was “in the immediate vicinity of Bulgaria’s territorial waters” when it was struck by three aerial drones. The ship, known as the Chelsea 3, was sailing under Malta’s flag but registered in Odesa, a large port city in Ukraine. Its crew of seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis were rescued and taken to a Bulgarian port, Radev said, where five received medical treatment.
The strikes are under investigation, and “we do not have clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility,” Radev said. However, he summoned Russia’s ambassador to Bulgaria, Eleonora Mitrofanova, for a meeting on Tuesday that lasted less than an hour.
A readout of the meeting, released by the Bulgarian government, cited Mitrofanova as saying she did not have any information from Russia’s defence ministry about the recent spate of drone strikes in the Black Sea.
She suggested that a third party might have been involved, and Radev told her that “there is no logic for Ukraine to destroy its own ships,” according to the readout.
Russia has not commented on the strikes off the Bulgarian or Romanian coasts.
Radev said he would ask allies to help with Bulgaria’s air and sea surveillance, as well as its response to future threats. Nato officials are already on alert; warnings were recently issued to commercial shippers transiting the Black Sea.
Mark Rutte, the Nato secretary general, said the military alliance would respond as needed with deterrence and defence measures.
“We have already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank and will continue to monitor the security environment,” Rutte said in a statement on Tuesday.
Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii ‌Sybiha ‌said ​on X that the strike “once again demonstrates Moscow’s deliberate disregard for civilian lives”.
“The Black Sea is a lifeline for global food security. Russia is attacking it to weaponise hunger and hold the world hostage,” he ⁠said.
More than four and a half years into the war that Moscow launched with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Black Sea shipping has increasingly been drawn into a ‌prolonged battle of economic endurance.
Ukraine and Russia are both among the world’s largest exporters of grain.
Russia has been bombing Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, forcing Ukraine to rely increasingly on river ​ports on the Danube and shipping routes close to the coasts of Nato members Bulgaria and Romania.
Ukraine, ​for its part, has increasingly targeted Russian grain-exporting ships in other parts of the Black Sea and the Azov Sea at the mouth of the Don River.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

title: ‘Young people are being put in jail for nothing’: Inside Kenya’s battle over cannabis
description: Rastafarians are seeking a religious exemption from cannabis laws they say criminalise worship and devastate lives
content:
O ff a busy thoroughfare in Kibera, an impoverished suburb of Nairobi in Kenya , is a small narrow room filled with artwork depicting Pan-African figures and drums. The modest meeting house serves as a gathering point or “temple” for local followers of Rastafari.
The Afrocentric movement which emerged in the 1930s sees black people as oppressed by “Babylon”, an umbrella term for unjust power which is often applied to western capitalism and colonialism. Rastafarians embrace mysticism and revere the former Ethiopian emperor Haile Selassie I as their messiah, with their movement named after his pre-coronation name, Ras Tafari Makonnen (although the emperor remained a devout Orthodox Christian).
Rastafari has been recognised as a protected religion in Kenya since 2019, when a court ruled the expulsion of a pupil from school for her dreadlocks was discriminatory.
Kenyan Rastafarians place a particular importance on dreadlocks due to their historical association with the Mau Mau, who often wore their hair matted and unkempt as they waged a guerrilla campaign against colonial British forces in the 1950s.
Gigi Spice (42) wears a badge of the leading Mau Mau leader, Dedan Kimathi, “who fought against the Babylon, the British”.
The consumption of marijuana, a cannabis derivative, is viewed in Rastafari as a sacrament which enables followers to connect more deeply with a higher power.
While many religious and ethnic communities in Kenya have been granted legal exemptions to brew small batches of alcoholic drinks like honey and palm wines for special ceremonies, Rastafarians face up to five years in jail or a €700 fine for possessing cannabis for personal use. Meanwhile, cultivating cannabis carries a hefty fine of at least €1,670 and up to 20 years in jail. “The wrong people are going to the Babylon,” says Boby Achoky (27).
In 2021, the Rastafari Society of Kenya filed a court petition seeking an exemption for Rastafarians who cultivate, possess and use the cannabis plant as part of a sacrament or ceremony, arguing that the lack of exemption violated the freedom of religion and right to equality.
In July, a Kenyan judge dismissed the petition, saying the community failed to demonstrate a violation of their constitutional rights but that a national debate on cannabis was warranted.
[ Recycling boom forces Kenya’s waste pickers to fight for their future Opens in new window ]
This continuing legal ban on cannabis leaves many Kenyan Rastafarians, who are often unable to pay fines or bribes of up to several hundred euro, facing unpredictable sentences, depending on “the judge or the magistrate you meet”, says Spice. “If you meet the magistrate and that day he is in a bad mood, that day you are going to see fire.”
A few years ago, Spice served two years in jail for carrying 125g of cannabis. “It was too long,” says Spice, “Everything stopped in my life.” The Rastafarian says the police used a local informer in Kibera to bring the charges against him.
Human rights groups have routinely criticised the use of plain-clothes police officers, paid informants and physical force to police slum neighbourhoods like Kibera, which are home to large, economically vulnerable populations who often propel anti-government protests.
“My house has been visited with police several times,” says Jahill Olwenyi (37), a member of Kibera’s Rastafari community.
Rastafarians who find themselves in prison face overcrowded, unsanitary and often dangerous conditions. “Young people [are] being put in jail for nothing because of a small spliff,” says Spice.
The Rastafarian served his prison sentence in the Nairobi Remand and Allocation Maximum Security Prison, which in recent years has held around twice the number of inmates its capacity was designed for. “The situation there is tough,” he says. “You have to be strong, and you have to be a rude boy.”
In jail, Spice says inmates face the risk of violence and sexual assault at the hands of other inmates. “If you’re not serious, if you’re not hard, they’ll turn you into a woman,” says Spice. “There are many people suffering inside in these cells just because of marijuana.”
Spice sees the continuing legal ban on cannabis as “hypocrisy”, alleging that government officials are involved in trading the illicit substance.
Sitting beside Spice is Ismael Jaffar (39), who is originally from Uganda, where the climate has made it a leading producer of cannabis in east Africa, despite recreational use of the substance remaining illegal. A joint venture between an Israeli and Ugandan firm has allowed the country to export medicinal cannabis in recent years.
Spice says the Kenyan government should be looking at cannabis in a constructive way: “Millions of young people can be employed through ganja, and that’s why we want the people and the religious sector to look at it in a different way.”

– Hannah McCarthy’s reporting was supported by the Simon Cumbers Media Fund

title: Property price inflation slows to three-year low of 5.1% as market cools
description: Latest official figures from CSO come amid a marked slowdown in prices in certain segments
content:
House price inflation slowed to its lowest level in nearly three years in August, according to official Government figures, as a combination of increased supply, higher borrowing costs and geopolitical uncertainty cooled the market.
The latest Residential Property Price Index from the Central Statistics Office indicated that prices nationally rose at an annualised rate of 5.1 per cent in August, down from 5.4 per cent in July.
This was the lowest level of price growth in the Irish market since December 2023.
Property prices in Dublin rose by 3.9 per cent while prices outside Dublin were up by 6.2 per cent compared with August last year.
The latest assessment comes amid a marked slowdown in prices in certain segments of the market.
The trend, which was also reflected in property website MyHome’s latest report this week, has been linked to a contraction in real wages on the back of inflation and two European Central Bank interest rate hikes.
The bank is expected to raise rates again in December in a bid to quell the current pickup in inflation.
The CSO’s figures indicated that the median price (middle value) paid for a house in the 12 months to August was €400,000.
The highest median price was €685,000 in Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown, while the lowest price was €199,000 in Longford.
High prices at the upper end of the market tend to distort the average which is why statisticians consider median prices – the point at which half of all homes sold were more expensive and half cost less – more reflective of the overall market.
“There’s no doubt that the heat has been coming out of the housing market since the start of this year and today’s report confirms that this trend is continuing, with the rate of house price growth slowing further,” Sorcha Timoney, mortgage team manager with NFP Ireland, said.
“Despite the cooling in the housing market, national house prices are still 28.2 per cent above the peak of the Celtic Tiger years, meaning that for many people, house prices are still unaffordable,” she said.
“The cooling in house price growth has been more pronounced in the capital, which suggests that many first-time buyers continue to be priced out of Dublin and [have] to look further afield,” Timoney said.
“The Help-to-Buy scheme’s €500,000 price ceiling means that many first-time buyers have no choice but to look beyond Dublin,” she said.
In the 12 months to August, the latest CSO numbers indicate that house prices nationally rose by 4.9 per cent while apartment prices increased by 6.6 per cent.
In Dublin, house prices grew by 3.3 per cent, and apartment prices were up by 5.7 per cent. Outside of the capital, house prices were up by 6 per cent while apartment prices rose by 8.6 per cent.
The regions outside Dublin that saw the largest growth in house prices were the Border (Cavan, Donegal, Leitrim, Monaghan, and Sligo) at 9.1 per cent, and the Midlands (Laois, Longford, Offaly, and Westmeath) at 8.8 per cent.
MyHome, which assesses trends in asking prices via a select sample of properties on its website, estimated that headline price inflation slowed to 3.9 per cent between July and September.
It also noted that asking prices nationally fell by 1.4 per cent in the third quarter compared with the previous three months.

title: “Síleann daoine áirithe go bhfuil litríocht do pháistí simplí, éadrom agus éadomhain. Ní thuigeann siad gurb í an litríocht is tábhachtaí dá bhfuil againn.”
description: Is scríbhneoir do dhaoine óga í Máire Zepf. I measc a cuid leabhar tá Míp, An Féileacán agus an Rí, Nóiní, an tsraith Rita, agus a leabhar is déanaí, Dearg. Is í a chóirigh Rita don scáileán agus a scríobh an tsraith anime Lí Bán.
content:
Cad é an chéad phíosa ealaíne is mó a d’imir tionchar ort mar dhéagóir?
Thit mé i ngrá le ceol an bhanna Capercaillie mar dhéagóir. Bhí mé ag taisteal i gcarr ar bhóithre casta Thír Chonaill le mo chairde nuair a chuala mé an t-amhrán, Fear a’ Bháta, den chéad uair, agus cuireadh iomlán faoi gheasa mé ag guth Karen Matheson. Cuireann an ceol sin drithlíní tríom go dtí an lá atá inniu ann.
Cad iad na straitéisí a úsáideann tú chun tréimhsí lag trá cruthaitheachta a shárú?
Cuardaím éagsúlacht seachas gnáthamh. Athraím rudaí thart go minic. Oibrím le peann agus páipéar má éirím bréan den ríomhaire. Téim amach sa ghairdín, suím i gcaifé nó bím ag obair sa leabharlann. Agus mura n-oibríonn sin, téim ag rith.
Cén t-éacht gairmiúil is mó a bhfuil tú bródúil as?
Tá mé fíorbhródúil as na cláracha teilifíse, Rita, a rinne muid do Cúla4. Ghlac muid an chéad sé leabhar den tsraith pictiúrleabhar agus rinne muid beocháin astu. Ní hamháin sin, ach bhí mise mar láithreoir ar an tsraith – rud a bhí fíordhúshlánach dom. Ach go minic is iad na rudaí is deacra a dhéanaimid a thugann an chúis is mó bróid dúinn.
Cad é an rud is deise a dúirt ealaíontóir eile leat riamh?
Tá an t-ádh orm go mbíonn deiseanna agam castáil ar ealaíontóirí iontacha go minic – scríbhneoirí, ceoltóirí, filí agus fís-ealaíontóirí a bhfuil mé mar fan-girl ceart acu. Cuireann sé idir iontas agus áthas orm arís agus arís eile nuair a admhaíonn siad liom go mbíonn siad féin mímhuiníneach faoina gcuid saothar, go mbíonn siad imníoch nach bhfuil siad maith go leor agus go dteipeann ar an spreagadh go minic. Is deas an rud domsa a chloisteáil go mbíonn na mothúcháin sin acusan fosta – nach bhfuil mé liom féin – agus b’fhéidir go bhfuil an t-amhras ina chuid nádúrtha den phróiseas cruthaitheach. Cuimhním air sin nuair a bhím in ísle brí agus mé i lár tionscnaimh.
Agus mé i mo pháiste beag, bhí amhrán ag mo mhamaí do gach ócáid; amhrán don ghlanadh, amhrán don fhearthainn, amhrán don siúl…
Cad é an chomhairle is measa a fuair tú riamh?
Dúirt go leor daoine liom gur chóir dom díriú ar sheánra nó ar stíl scríbhneoireachta amháin. “Roghnaigh na pictiúrleabhair” a dúirt siad, nó “scríobh do dhéagóirí amháin”. Dá n-éistfinn leo, bheadh mo shaol oibre níos boichte, gan amhras ar bith. Ní bheadh seó anime scríofa agam don teilifís, Lí Ban; ní bheadh seó damhsaíochta déanta agam le mo leabhar, An Féileacán agus an Rí; ní bheadh úrscéalta véarsaíochta, gearrscéalta, dánta agus gearrscannáin filíochta déanta agam. In amanna is fearr éisteacht le do chomhairle féin.
Conas a bhí do shaol cultúrtha mar pháiste?
Bhí mo shaol mar pháiste lán d’ealaín. Bhí mo mhamaí mar chuid de ghrúpa teiripeoirí ealaíne a tháinig chun tí go rialta. Phéinteáil siad le chéile, rinne siad dealbha as cré, agus labhair siad go líofa faoina gcuid mothúchán agus iad ag cruthú. Dar leo, bhí an próiseas níos tábhachtaí ná an toradh. Bhí an t-ádh dearg ormsa go raibh cead agam suí suas ag an tábla leo, ag úsáid an ábhair chéanna leis na healaíontóirí gairmiúla seo agus ag smaoineamh orm féin mar ealaíontóir. Bhí ceol linn i gcónaí, clasaiceach agus traidisiúnta ar dtús, agus ansin mar dhéagóirí, ceol pop, ceol domhanda, punc agus rac-cheol. Bhí uirlis ag gach páiste agus jeamáil muid le chéile go minic. Agus mé i mo pháiste beag, bhí amhrán ag mo mhamaí do gach ócáid; amhrán don ghlanadh, amhrán don fhearthainn, amhrán don siúl, amhrán don trá, suantraí ag am luí. Fuaimrian álainn grámhar Gaelach s’againn féin.
Dá mbeadh sé ar do chumas taisteal siar tríd an am agus tú féin a thabhairt ar ais chuig ceolchoirm amháin ar ar fhreastail tú cheana, cén ceann a roghnófá, agus cén fáth?
D’fhreastail mé ar cheolchoirm Nirvana i mBéal Feirste in 1992. Bhí mé cúig bliana déag d’aois, bhí mé i m’aonar agus (mar a bheadh amadán ann) shocraigh mé dul ann gan mo chuid spéaclaí orm ar eagla go mbrisfí sa log maiseála iad. Sílim gur chaith mé an cheolchoirm iomlán leathdhall ag iarraidh mo bhealach a aimsiú in áit a bheith ag baint sult agus tairbhe as ceol Kurt Cobain. Rachainn ar ais agus mo spéaclaí orm an uair seo.
Cad é an mhíthuiscint is mó atá ag daoine faoi do shaol mar ealaíontóir?
Síleann daoine áirithe go bhfuil litríocht do pháistí simplí, éadrom agus éadomhain. Ní thuigeann siad gurb í an litríocht is tábhachtaí dá bhfuil againn. Tá scéalta do pháistí lán fírinne agus dóchais, samhlaíochta agus grá. Bíonn meas os cuimse ag údar do pháistí ar a c(h)uid léitheoirí, mar go dtéann na scéalta sin i bhfeidhm ar an léitheoir óg ar bhealach mór millteach a mhaireann ar feadh a s(h)aoil iomlán.
Cad é an comhthéacs is aistí ina raibh tú de bharr do chuid oibre?
Mar scríbhneoir do dhaoine óga, téim go dtí domhain aisteacha go rialta i mo chuid samhlaíochta. Bím ag plé le dragúin agus róbait, le maighdeana mara, ollphéisteanna, eachtráin agus arrachtaí. Ach bíonn na himeachtaí do pháistí lán iontais chomh maith! Go dtí seo, rinne mé drumadóireacht Afracach, cuairteanna naíscoile i mo chuid pitseámaí, thraenáil mé ninjaí ar fud na tíre agus thaistil mé Slí an Atlantaigh Fhiáin le Laureate na nÓg Patricia Forde agus bus lán scríbhneoirí agus maisitheoirí.
Níl aon tóin tinn mar do thóin tinn féin.
Is é Dearg an leabhar is nua ó pheann Mháire Zepf. Úrscéal véarsaíochta do dhéagóirí faoi bhean óg darb ainm Fionn agus í ag seasamh ar son cearta teanga agus ag foghlaim cén dóigh le bheith dílis di féin.

title: Man (40s) hospitalised after gun fired into car in Co Clare
description: Injuries are not life-threatening and Garda investigations are continuing
content:
A man in his 40s is recovering in hospital after he was shot in Co Clare early on Tuesday morning.
The man sustained a gunshot wound after a gun was fired inside a vehicle at Coolreagh at about 5.15am.
Gardaí said the man’s injuries were not life-threatening and that Garda investigations were continuing.
A dark coloured Volkswagen van that gardaí suspect is linked to the shooting was subsequently recovered at a filling station on Corbally Road, Co Limerick .
The van was cordoned off by gardaí, and an initial forensic examination took place at the filling station. The van was later removed by a tow truck to a yard for a further forensic examination.
Gardaí designated two separate crime scenes, including one scene at Coolreagh where they believe the man was shot, and at Corbally where the van was recovered, a distance of 32km away.
A Garda spokesman said: “Gardaí and emergency services responded to a discharge of a firearm inside a motor vehicle that occurred near Coolreagh, Co Clare, on Tuesday shortly after 5.15am.
“A male aged in his 40s was conveyed to hospital for treatment of injuries believed to be non-life-threatening at the time. A technical examination of the scene is being conducted. Investigations are ongoing.”

title: Gardaí investigate as four people die  in fire at house in Waterford city
description: Possibility the house was deliberately targeted in an arson attack is one line of inquiry
author_name: Hugh Dooley, Vivienne Clarke, Conor Lally, Barry Roche
content:
Two adults and two children have died following a fire at a house in Waterford city.
Two other children are in a critical condition in hospital.
A couple with four children lived in the semi-detached house in the Birchwood estate, about 3km south of the city centre, where the fire broke out early on Tuesday morning.
The Irish Times understands the fire is subject to a criminal investigation. While that inquiry is at an early stage, the possibility the house was deliberately targeted in an arson attack is one line of investigation at present.
Waterford Fire Service received an emergency call about a house fire at Birch Avenue, Kilcohan, at 5.13am, a spokesperson said. They said several fire units went to the scene from surrounding stations and found the “well-developed fire” at the house. The fire has now been extinguished.
“Firefighting operations commenced immediately, and a number of casualties were removed from the two storey house. The fire was extinguished and the scene handed over to An Garda Síochána.”
A Garda spokesman said it was “an ongoing evolving incident” and no further details were available yet.
Sinn Féin’s health spokesman David Cullinane, who is a TD for Waterford, said he was heartbroken at the news.
“It’s just utterly heartbreaking and there’s such devastation in the housing estate itself, as you can imagine, but also in the wider community in Waterford city.
“Obviously there is shock but people will know the family and there is absolute heartbreak when you have children involved as well so it’s obviously very emotional.”
Cullinane told RTÉ Radio’s Morning Ireland that he knew the family well and had met one of the family members recently.
He said the number of fatalities remained unknown, “but we do know it’s very high and obviously if anybody does survive we wish them our best wishes”.
Cullinane went on to pay tribute to the first responders. He said he had spoken to paramedics and firefighters and knew how traumatic it had been for them when they arrived at the scene.
He asked that An Garda Síochána and first responders be given space.
“My heart goes out to the family members and the relatives and all of the neighbours and friends of the family involved and I’m just utterly heartbroken and devastated.”
The community would rally around, he said. “All they can do is stand in solidarity at this point, there’s no words really. No and I’m lost for words myself, I know many of the neighbours, it’s a very close-knit community and I know there is tears on that road as you can imagine and just people absolutely devastated and just still in shock.
“It just sends a shiver down your spine. It’s just so heartbreaking particularly when there’s children involved so I think that heartbreak will be felt right across the island when people hear what happened and hear of the fatalities,” said the Sinn Féin TD.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin said he was shocked at the news and asked that emergency services be given time and space “to deal with what clearly is a very worrying and deeply disturbing situation”.

title: Scéal dhá oileán, scéal dhá theanga
description: Tá an Ghaeilge agus an tSicilis faoi bhrú ar chúiseanna éagsúla ach tá an inspioráid chéanna ar fáil don dá phobal teanga
content:
Sin an cur síos allabhrach a rinne Máirtín Ó Direáin ar Inis Mór Árann tráth agus é ag machnamh ar ‘sceirdoileán’ álainn úd a óige agus a chuimhne.
Is cumhachtach an íomhá í a d’fhóirfeadh do go leor áiteanna ar fud chósta thiar na hÉireann ach is ar oileán níos faide i gcéin a bhí mé féin nuair a tháinig an frása chugam arís ar na mallaibh.
Iarthar na Sicile an ceantar a raibh mé ag fánaíocht ann, áit a mbuaileann sléibhte loma aolchloiche agus cnoic scrobarnaí ghaineamhchloiche le cladaigh chaola agus le bánna bogthaise. Is dúiche aoibhinn í gan amhras, fíniúnacha agus crainn ológ ag fás ar na machairí, spéir ghléghlan os do chionn, agus an ghrian ar dhath an oráiste dheirg ar thitim di isteach sa mhuir le clapsholas.
Labhair le muintir na háite áfach agus gheobhaidh tú amach gur ag coraíocht leis an tsaol a bhí a sinsir go minic. Tá an talamh creagach, an chré tanaí, agus an t-uisce gann. Agus ní gá a rá nach i bhfeabhas a rachaidh na dálaí sin sa tréimhse atá le teacht. Ní dhearnadh an oiread céanna infheistíochta sa tSicil is a rinneadh i gceantair eile san Iodáil i gcaitheamh na mblianta agus cé gur foinse mhór fostaíochta í an turasóireacht inniu, go háirithe le linn an tsamhraidh, ní leor í le gach duine a choinneáil sa bhaile.
Fágann na gnéithe sin uilig gur fada fairsing an taithí atá ag bunadh an oileáin ar an eisimirce agus gur beag Sicileach nach bhfuil gaolta aige nó aici sa Róimh nó in Buenos Aires nó i mBaile Átha Cliath nó i Nua-Eabhrac.
Mar sin de, cé gur mór idir uiscí gormghlasa na Meánmhara agus farraigí fiáine Fódla, tá cosúlachtaí ann, ó thaobh tírdhreacha agus sochaí de, a thabharfadh lón machnaimh duit lá ar bith den bhliain.
Réimse amháin áfach ina bhfuil difear spéisiúil idir an dá oileán ná cúrsaí teanga. Tá teanga dhúchais ag Éirinn agus ag an tSicil araon ach is mór idir a stádas agus a staid.
Teanga Rómánsach í an tSicilis, nó sicilianu , atá gaolta leis an Iodáilis ó thuaidh ach a d’fhorbair go neamhspleách uirthi thar na céadta agus atá aitheanta ag UNESCO mar theanga ar leith inti féin. Is iomaí dream a leag cos ar thalamh ársa na Sicile ó thosaigh an duine daonna ag treabhadh na dtonnta - Féinícigh, Gréagaigh, Arabaigh, Normannaigh, Catalónaigh - agus tá an éagsúlacht cultúr sin le cluinstin i bhfocail agus i bhfuaimeanna na teanga inniu. Cé go bhfuil sí faoi bhrú ag neart na hIodáilise caighdeánaí, tá suas le cúig mhilliún duine a bhfuil labhairt na Sicilise acu i gcónaí agus tá dlúthbhaint idir an teanga agus féiniúlacht an oileáin. In ainneoin an phobail shuntasaigh cainteoirí áfach, sin agus traidisiún saibhir litríochta a théann siar go dtí an 13ú haois, níl aon stádas oifigiúil ag an tSicilis. Níl áit bhuan aici sa chóras oideachais; níl láithreacht cheart aici sna meáin chumarsáide; agus ní úsáidtear í i dtionól réigiúnach na Sicile ach oiread. Tá grúpaí feachtasaíochta teanga ann go deimhin, agus tá dul chun cinn áirithe déanta, ach is teanga bhaile í go príomha a labhraítear idir baill teaghlaigh, le comharsana agus le cairde.
Is ag an taobh eile den speictream atá muidne Gaeil ar ndóigh. Tá an stádas againn, go náisiúnta agus go hidirnáisiúnta; tá an infheictheacht againn; tá an maoiniú stáit againn; tá na stáisiúin raidió agus teilifíse againn; tá earnáil na foilsitheoireachta agus an aistriúcháin againn; tá an Ghaelscolaíocht againn. Tá tuilleadh le déanamh gan amhras ar bith, go háirithe sna Gaeltachtaí agus sa Tuaisceart. Is ceart agus is cóir agus is cuí cur leis na codanna sin ar fad de shaol na teanga - iad a chothú, a mhéadú, a leathnú - ach ar a laghad tá siad againn. Is é an rud a bhfuil muid gann air ná trúpaí ar an talamh.
Os a choinne sin, tá na cainteoirí ag an tSicilis - an tairseach chriticiúil sin a bhfuil ríthábhacht léi agus a dtabharfadh muidne an leathchuid de Chontae na Mí féin uirthi - ach fágann an easpa cosanta agus an díth aitheantais agus an ganntanas polasaithe gur ag snámh in aghaidh easa a bhíonn pobal a labhartha go minic.
Dhá theanga áitiúla ar dhá oileán Eorpacha ach iad beirt leochaileach, beo ach faoi bhagairt, ar chúiseanna éagsúla.
Agus na gaotha saobha thart orainn ag borradh agus ag bogadh - ó thionchar creimneach na mórchultúr domhanda ar aghaidh go dtí an éiginnteacht pholaitiúil agus an anachain aeráide a deir saineolaithe atá ag teannadh linn - ní deacair a shamhlú go gcuirfear leis an leochaileacht sin thuasluaite sna blianta agus sna glúnta atá le teacht.
Níl réiteach simplí ar na dúshláin atá roimh aon phobal atá ar choimirce na haimsire athraithí nó a bhfuil a dteanga dhúchais i mbaol, ach seans go bhfuil ceacht éigin le fáil i gcur chuige Uí Dhireáin féin. D’fhág an file Inis Mór ach níor fhág Inis Mór a chroí riamh. Tabharfar ár ndúshlán agus cuirfear féachaint ar ár seasmhacht ach cibé áit a mbeidh muid - sa bhaile nó i gcearn eile den chruinne - beidh muid i gcónaí in ann an teanga agus an talamh, na focail agus na fréamhacha, a thabhairt linn agus a chothú inár n-anam istigh. Ní leor é le teanga ná le saol oileáin a shábháil, ach b’fhéidir go dtabharfadh an muintearas sin an t-uchtach agus an tsamhlaíocht dúinn le léim thar an chéad chliath eile ar an chosán.

title: Banba first look: Local produce and seasonal flavours at Dublin’s newest restaurant
description: City centre eatery offers a variety of homemade brews while championing Irish winemakers
content:
“You would be amazed how good the produce is a 15-minute drive up the M50,″ says Ross Bryans, executive chef of the Dean Group, ahead of the opening of its newest restaurant, Banba.
Nestled inside a Georgian townhouse beside The Dean hotel on Harcourt Street , Dublin 2, Banba promises to serve seasonal plates with a focus on Irish ingredients.
One dish exemplifying this approach for Bryans is the Archer’s Farm – in Rush, Co Dublin – gem salad, served with goats curd from Bluebell Falls and preserved strawberry vinaigrette (€12).
“I created a dish specifically for this restaurant where I have taken three farms that are relatively quite close to each other,” says Bryans.
“So I use baby gem salad from Archer’s, beautiful cress and leaves from McCormack’s (in Co Meath ) and then I got some strawberries back in May from Kelly’s (in Co Meath) and they were kind of yellow-green just before they were ripened, so I had them picked and I preserved them.”
What does preserved pre-ripened strawberry taste like?
“It tastes almost like a savoury strawberry because it hasn’t had the sugars develop inside yet,” says the chef.
Opening this Friday, October 16th, the hotel restaurant hopes to attract a wide range of clientele beyond guests staying at The Dean.
Entering the restaurant, diners are greeted by a kitchen island rather than a bar. The room itself is decorated with neutrals – natural woods and warm, earthy colours used judiciously where colour is deployed. Think amber banquettes, earthy-red chairs and warm lighting.
There is also an emphasis on Irish-made details, such as the extensive suite of Nicholas Mosse pottery, artwork by Irish artists and underlit jars of pickles, creating a pantry-style feel.
“The decor itself, we wanted it to feel like you are going to somebody’s home,” says Bryans. “The lounge is very relaxing with the open fireplace, the bar itself looks like a kitchen counter in somebody’s home when you walk in.
“When you go to somebody’s house, you don’t go there to have the same meal twice, so we want to rotate the menu. At least one or two dishes every two weeks to keep things relevant and really work with the growers and the seasons.
“We might have four seasons in a year, but for a good product you can have a couple of different seasons within a season, so we really wanted to tap into that part of it.”
Kicking off the seasonal menu is chicken liver foie gras parfait, spiced apple chutney, Killahora apples and ice wine, which is priced at €14 for a starter. There’s a vegetarian main in the form of roasted cauliflower served with nuts, seeds and gremolata. Another vegetarian option is roasted pumpkin with a spiced honey glaze, both priced at €14.
Other mains on the menu are the pork chop tomahawk, charcutière sauce and creamy scallion mash for €35. Meanwhile, the wild clams, sweetcorn, mushrooms and Madeira Velouté is priced at €24.
“Every season’s change is always welcomed by a chef,” he adds. “I don’t know a chef who wouldn’t welcome it or say otherwise. We have that opportunity to really mix around and play with the produce, not only in a food aspect but also with the drinks.”
Drinks operator for the Dean group is Fergus O’Leary, who says the design of the restaurant’s kitchen island influenced the cocktail menu.
“That bar shaped the style of drinks that we needed to produce,” he says. “I remember when I saw the plans, I was scratching my head like, ‘How am I going to produce a top-class cocktail menu from this?’. But it actually made me rethink how I would normally make a cocktail menu.
“So pretty much 90 per cent of our prep is done before the shift. Everything is bottled, pre-batched, ready to go, and carbonated so you can literally just pick up a bottle and pour the full cocktail over the ice.”
Necessity has led to the creation of multiple in-house brews, such as a line-up of homemade sodas including the Banba Cola.
“I’m really proud of that one,” says O’Leary.
“We have made our own Coca-Cola using a couple of different spices and herbs. We are using figs, perilla, cinnamon, vanilla, some smoked oak and then we balance it with some citric acid and some saline solution. Some caramel as well.”
All cocktails have been made with at least one Irish ingredient, be it the liquor or the aromatics.
“We are using Valentia Island Vermouth in our espresso martini, which is a little bit different,” he says. “We are using Móinéir fruit wines – all three of them as a blend for a New York sour where you have a red wine float up at the top of the cocktail.
“The first page of the wine menu is going to feature Irish winemakers; some in Ireland and some abroad. We will actually have a map of Ireland highlighting where these people are from just to highlight how many cool, amazing winemakers there are from Ireland in all these other countries. You would be blown away.”
Among the Irish winemakers are David Llewellyn of Lusca Wine from Lusk, Co Dublin, Andrew Eakin and Naomi Murtagh’s Château Puynard in Bordeaux , and the Horgan family of Leeuwin Estate in Western Australia .
The restaurant might have a clear line on produce, seasonality and Irishness, but where does the name come from?
“Banba comes from the Irish word Banbha, it’s a mythological Irish woman,” says O’Leary.
Bryans adds: “She was the goddess of the fertility of the land.
“From a food perspective, we want to make sure we are sourcing the best Irish products possible. So we spent a lot of time working with these producers to really showcase the beautiful products that are available in Ireland.”
Banba will open for service on Friday, October 16th. For further information go to banbadublin.com .

title: Buillí na síoraíochta
description: Cuireadh na céadta i Reilig an tSlé, Co. Phort Láirge, le linn an Ghorta Mhóir
content:
Ceiliúradh aifreann amuigh faoin spéir i bpáirc bheag tuaithe i nGaeltacht na nDéise thart ar mhí ó shin. Sheas grúpa daoine áitiúla in éineacht le ceithre shagart san áit chun paidreacha a ofráil. Meastar go bhfuil thart ar mhíle duine curtha in uaigheanna ollmhóra anseo i dtalamh atá suite taobh leis an N25, an príomhbhóthar idir Port Láirge agus Corcaigh. Tiomáineann na carranna, na busanna agus na leoraithe faoi luas thar an reilig a osclaíodh le linn an Ghorta Mhóir ar chósta an deiscirt.
Glaoitear Reilig an tSlé ar an bpaiste talún stairiúil seo atá cúpla míle siar an bóthar amach ó bhaile Dhún Garbhán. Tá na huaigheanna i bhfolach faoin chré inniu, clúdaithe ag féar glas an fhómhair, ach is féidir marcanna míchothroma agus gleannta na n-umar a fheiceáil i gcónaí, iad greanta sa talamh.
Tá rachmas sofheicthe i réim sa cheantar inniu. Déantar dearmad ar an áit uaigneach seo don chuid is mó den bhliain. Tá líonmhaireacht le brath sna siopaí.
Mar a tharlaíonn i dtír atá mar chuid den Chéad Domhan, tá an bhochtaineacht tríd is tríd faoi cheilt agus níl snoí colainne le feiscint in aon áit. Tá na blianta idir 1845 agus 1849 tite go mór siar, siar sa stair. Sleamhnaíonn na míonna go réchúiseach tharainn, an mhórchuid againn ag maireachtáil faoi shuain. Anseo, taobh leis an bhfarraige, bímid ag siúl ar na tránna, ag freastal ar ócáidí sóisialta, an tsiopadóireacht sheachtainiúil á déanamh againn sa mbaile mór gan teip. Sa reilig seo atá as seirbhís anois, tá olagóin na n-íobartach balbh ach amháin ag bomaití áirithe le linn an aifrinn - tá sé éasca a cheapadh go bhfuil an pobal ag éisteacht le buillí na síoraíochta.
Tháinig titim 28% ar dhaonra Dhún Garbhán ó 1841 agus 1851 agus titim 20% ar phobal na Rinne féin.
Ní chuimhnítear rómhinic ar an nGorta Mór, an tubaiste uafásach a tharla breis agus 180 bliain ó shin. Bhí cúrsaí chomh dona go raibh gá leis an reilig seo a oscailt d’aon ghnó i mí na Samhna 1847. Thagadh lán trucaile leis na mairbh trí huaire in aghaidh an lae chuig an áit, na corpáin leagtha amach anuas ar a chéile ar leaba na trucaile. Thiomáintí iad amach ar bhóthar an chósta ó Thig na mBocht. Chuirtí iad isteach sna trinsí aolta a bhí tochailte ann dóibh. Ba mhinic a chuirtí daoine a bhí lag leis an ocras ag deanamh na tochailte. De réir tuairiscí, chaití go leor dos na daoine a bhí fós beo isteach sna huaigheanna chomh maith. Is chuige sin a bhí an sagart Pádraig Ó Tuama a d’fhan i láthair chun beannacht a chur lena n-anam agus chun a chinntiú go raibh gach aon duine acu marbh sula gcuirfí iad.
Tháinig titim 28% ar dhaonra Dhún Garbhán ó 1841 agus 1851 agus titim 20% ar phobal na Rinne féin. Deir staraithe gurb é an Gorta Mór an tragóid ba mhilltí agus ba scanrúla dár tharla do shaol Gaelach na tuaithe. Ceaptar inniu go bhfuil sé aisteach nach bhfuil mórán cur síos ná tagairtí don Ghorta sna hamhráin. Is é tuairim na scoláirí ná go raibh ar thit amach ró-uafásach agus róphianmhar chun a thabhairt chun cuimhne ina gcuid amhrán. Is é an t-amhrán atá fágtha againne i nGaeltacht na nDéise ón uair sin ná Na Prátaí Dubha - ba í Máire Ní Dhroma ó Bhaile na nGall i bparóiste na Rinne a chum an t-amhrán timpeall na bliana 1850. Gríosóir cumhachtach agus misniúil, saghas provocateur a linne, ab ea í, bean a bhí sásta agus réidh labhairt amach go feargach i leith na héagóra agus na fulaingthe a chonaic sí. Níor shéan sí cur síos ar na radhairc a chonaic sí ar na bóithre agus ar shráideanna an bhaile mhóir i línte loma, uafásacha:
Tá na bochta so Éireann ag plé leis an ainnise,
Leanaí bochta ag béiceadh is ag screadadh gach maidin,
I véarsa eile deir sí nár thoil Dé an fhulaingt ar fad, agus chuir sí an milleán go neamheaglach ar lucht an rachmais. Cháin sí go neamhbhalbh córas Thithe na mBocht.
Daoine bochta a chur le fuacht is le fán,
Iad a chur sa phoorhouse go dubhach is glas orthu,
Lánúineacha pósta is iad scartha go bás.
Nach trua móruaisle go bhfuil mórán coda acu
Fearaibh bochta an tsaoil seo ná fuair riamh aon saibhreas
Gan amhras níl aon ghrianghraf againn de Mháire Ní Dhroma ach caithfidh gur bean neamhspleách ab ea í, bean chróga, mhuiníneach agus phaiseanta. Ní raibh na húdaráis róshásta lena dearcadh agus cuireadh an t-amhrán faoi chois ar feadh i bhfad. Inniu, cloistear é á rá le mórtas agus babhtaí i Reilig an tSlé. Bhíodh sé ag an amhránaí ar an sean-nós Nioclás Tóibín, agus bhíodh sé á rá ag Peig Bean Uí Réagáin ag ócáidí babhtaí chomh maith.
Inniu agus talamh na sean-reilige ag dul le fána, ag síneadh síos i dtreo uisce na bá, agus dá seasfá ag féachaint amach ar áilleacht na cruinne ón reilig ní cheapfá go bhféadfadh aon olcas nó brón nó éagóir titim amach sa cheantar álainn seo.
Inniu tá na tromluithe scaipthe, agus an áit fáilteach torthúil. Tá sé de nós ag muintir na háite bailiú uair amháin gach bliain chun paidreacha a rá sa reilig. Bhíodh Bantracht na Tuaithe go mór chun tosaigh in eagrú na cuairte traidisiúnta seo. Déarfaidis an Choróin Mhuire ar thaobh an tsléibhe agus chuimhneoidís ar na daoine a fuair bás de dheasca an ocrais.
Nuair a bhailítear inniu chun paidreacha a rá agus chun cuimhneamh ar an méid a d’fhulaing na daoine a d’éag, snámhann guthanna an phobail ar an aer cumhra agus cuimhnítear ar spioraid na ndaoine atá imithe ar shlí na fírinne agus iad ag éisteacht ón taobh thall.

title: Gardaí ordered to bring two youths at ‘extreme’ risk to special care despite Tusla protest
description: Judge brands agency ‘disgraceful’ over plan to meet and decide priority for children awaiting beds
content:
“Search and deliver” orders for two children deemed to be at “extreme” high risk were issued by the High Court on Monday in the face of protestations by Tusla .
Judge John Jordan issued the orders empowering gardaí to find the teenagers and convey them to special care despite concerns other children may need beds more urgently than they did.
Two beds became available during the hearing when the judge issued discharge orders for children deemed ready to leave special care.
The judge said it was “wholly unacceptable” that Tusla was not moving to “immediately comply” with orders already in place in respect of two children whom he ordered be detained several weeks ago.
Special care is the most secure form of care in which children aged between 11 and 17 can be detained by High Court order, where their behaviours put their lives or those around them at risk.
Just 15 of the 26 special-care beds are open, however, due to severe challenges recruiting and retaining staff.
Sarah McKechnie for Tusla told the court there were up to seven children who urgently needed special care.
[ Tusla in breach of High Court special care direction again over capacity issues Opens in new window ]
When the two beds became available the judge said he expected the two waiting since last month to be taken into special care immediately.
“I very much regret to inform you that [Tusla] intends to have a prioritisation meeting in the morning,” said McKechnie.
Among the other children, she told the court, was a young teenage boy who is manufacturing, selling and using crack cocaine, and swallowing packages of the drug to avoid being caught by gardaí. A new order was granted in respect of the boy whom the judge said was “completely out of control”.
Other cases included a child “in a hospital bed close to death after a suspected overdose” and another subjected to ongoing and repeated sexual assaults in her community, said McKechnie.
The judge said there was a “situation” where two children subject to orders were waiting for beds and two beds were available.
“If these two children are not received into special care this evening I want an explanation filed by way of affidavit from the director and assistant director of special care. I want it sworn by 9.30 tomorrow morning and filed in the central office in each of these cases.
“How it can be that the CFA [Child and Family Agency] can flout a court order, having been declared in contempt?” he said referring to a High Court ruling in July that the agency was in contempt by failing to provide special care to children whom the court has ordered be detained.
“They [Tusla] now have two beds and have decided: ‘We’ll leave it over until we have a chance to discuss it in the morning.’ That is disgraceful ... It’s quite offensive. It is wholly unacceptable,” he said.
“In both cases I will grant search a delivery orders,” he said, adding he expected the children to be in special care by the morning.
Subsequent to the hearing Tusla confirmed the two children awaiting beds would be located by gardaí and taken into special care.

title: Which EVs won’t make me feel carsick?
description: Practical advice on your motoring queries, from buying and selling to issues with your current car
content:
We don’t know for certain if electric cars are actually, scientifically, more likely to make people car sick than a conventional car.
A professor at the University of Pittsburgh has called the available data on the subject “sketchy” but there was a study carried out a couple of years ago by the Université De Technologie De Belfort-Montbeliard in France which found that, whether or not the actual number of cases is higher for EVs, there are almost certainly some reasons why electric cars might trigger car sickness.
In short, we’ve become used to petrol and diesel cars, and now electric cars have come along and we’re not used to them yet, and that makes them harder for those prone to car sickness to deal with.
Braking certainly seems to be part of the issue. This is partially down to how an EV’s regenerative braking is set up. As soon as the driver’s foot comes off the accelerator pedal, the car can slow down quite sharply.
Previously our vestibular system – the combination of nerves, inner ear, and more that helps us locate our bodies relative to the world around us – was used to a fraction of a second pause while the driver moved their feet from the accelerator to the brake.
With “one-pedal” braking systems, that pause can be eliminated almost entirely, and surprisingly sharp “braking” can occur straight away as the car uses its electric motor as, effectively, a traction brake (while also using it to regenerate power that can be fed to the battery, like a dynamo).
The good news is that things don’t have to be this way. Many electric cars – albeit not all – will have adjustable regenerative braking which can be set up from sharp to none at all and many points in between.
The Peugeot E-208 GTi , which has regenerative braking that can be set up to be very gentle, is actually quite like the sort of engine braking with which our vestibular systems are more familiar, so it feels far more natural.
[ Peugeot’s electric E-208 GTi proves that fun still lives. This is a real 1980s throwback Opens in new window ]
Many other cars will be similarly capable, so it might just be a case of trying out a few on test drives to arrive at one you both feel comfortable with.
There are other potential pitfalls when it comes to EVs and car sickness. The lack of noise from the engine is, according to the French study, a crucial factor. Over the decades of combustion engine driving, our vestibular systems have adjusted to subconsciously listening to what the engine of a car is doing and using that as an audible cue of what’s going to happen next.
[ Does going electric still save me money if my fuel is VAT-refundable? Opens in new window ]
Without the engine sound, that cue is gone, and so our bodies are being taken by surprise by the subsequent movement or change of direction, and that can be a problem for anyone prone to motion sickness. Being prepared for a movement is key to fighting motion sickness, and it’s why it’s very rare for a driver to become motion sick – because the driver usually knows what’s going to happen next.
Another potential cause of car sickness with EVs is the electromagnetic field given off by the car’s battery and motors. We know from other studies that these fields aren’t strong enough to present any danger in a health sense, but there’s potential for them to trigger inner ear issues that cause motion sickness, while the faint vibrations given off by electric devices which have a current running through them – try lightly resting your fingertips on a metal-bodied laptop while it’s charging to see what that’s like – might also be an issue.
The sudden torque delivery of electric cars can also be problematic, as the “step-off” performance of most EVs is far, far sharper than that of a combustion engine.
A combustion engine needs time, revs, and space to produce its highest power outputs. An EV is at its most potent at 1rpm, hence the sudden acceleration from standstill that even relatively humble EVs can produce, and which even for those of us hardened to high performance can find discombobulating.
For instance, I swore that the Audi e-Tron GT RS accelerated so hard from a standing start that I could feel the blood draining out of my toes.
Thankfully, cars are developing and changing, and we’re now much more likely to come across electric motors that are tuned to deliver their power and torque more progressively, more in the manner of a petrol engine. Equally, most EVs will have an “eco” driving setting that reduces the power of the motor at low speeds, which can smooth out that initial sudden power deployment.
[ Why are we only supposed to charge EV batteries to 80%? Opens in new window ]
Passengers sitting in the rear seats will likely have a worse time than those in the front, which has always been the case for people prone to car sickness, but in EVs that is exacerbated by the fact that electric cars are, by and large, much heavier than their combustion counterparts. That heaviness means that the suspension has to be tuned to cope with the weight and that tuning can lead to unpleasant movements such as a “head-toss” sensation when driving over sharp bumps or speed ramps.
As with conventional motion sickness, there are some things you can do to ameliorate the worst effects of EV car sickness.
Try to eat relatively light before travelling, and make sure you’re hydrated (having some cold water in the car to sip on can also help). Don’t look down at a book or your phone – keep your eyes up and looking out of the car so that you can see the horizon, which allows your vestibular system to keep a better check on your position relative to the car and the world outside. Crack open a window for some fresh air, or turn an air vent on a cool setting towards your face, and sit as upright as you can, with your head held high.
Given enough time, we’ll all adapt to electric cars and their wily ways, and the potential for car sickness will fall. Human beings are nothing if not adaptable, after all. There will always be a certain cohort of individuals, those who are very sensitive to motion and movement, for whom travelling in a car – any car – will always be an issue, but for most of us these problems will likely fade away given more time and more experience with electric cars.

title: Emotional scenes among victims as George Gibney receives his sentence
description: ‘It has shown that even after 50-plus years, justice can be got’, said survivor Orla Poole
content:
Emotions ran high at the Criminal Courts of Justice on Monday when justice was finally served on George Gibney , the former swimming coach sentenced to 15½ years for the sexual abuse of four girls in the 1970s and 1980s. Malachy Clerkin was there to witness the relief of many of those who fought long and hard for this day. Among them was Orla Poole, one of Gibney’s victims. “This court case didn’t just deliver justice for me but also, I hope, for others,” she said. “It has shown that even after 50-plus years, justice can be got.”
In football, Gavin Cummiskey previews tonight’s game in Páirc Ui Chaoimh between the Republic of Ireland’s women and Kazakhstan . You never, of course, want to indulge in chicken-counting, but seeing as Ireland are 8-0 up from the first leg, there’s a reasonable chance that they’ll progress to the final World Cup qualifying round.
Back in Dublin, Shamrock Rovers took a giant leap towards sealing the title by beating Bohemians, although a dampener on their evening was the red-carding of two of their players after the aggro that broke out at the end of the game. In total four red cards were shown with Bohs captain Dawson Devoy and assistant coach Stephen O’Donnell also sent off.
In rugby, the Champions Cup returns next weekend , but Gerry Thornley is less than impressed by “yet another unconvincing tweak to a format that, once upon a time, was carved in stone”.
Leinster open their campaign with a daunting trip to Clermont, Michael Scully hearing from coach Jacques Nienaber ahead of the game. One man who is very much in Nienaber’s thoughts this week is his old friend Anthony Foley , Friday marking the 10th anniversary of his death.
Connacht, writes Linley MacKenzie, are daring to dream on their return to the Champions Cup. “ Why can’t a club like Connacht ever potentially win it ,” asks Stuart Lancaster.
Owen Doyle, meanwhile, recently attended a reunion of international referees at the Titanic Quarter in Belfast. And it couldn’t have been a more appropriate venue, he says, because “everybody present had struck at least one major iceberg during their career”. What of today’s game? They had plenty to mull over, not least the new tackling laws and the dreaded illegal lineout driving mauls.
In Gaelic games, the widely discussed trial window for experimental rules in football and hurling has arrived, Gordon Manning previewing their introduction in the third-level leagues from this week.
Philip Reid brings you the latest from the golfing world in his Different Strokes column, and in athletics, Ian O’Riordan talks to Sarah Healy about her decision to leave her training base in Manchester , where she had been stationed since late 2022.
And in racing, Brian O’Connor looks ahead to Saturday’s Champion Stakes at Ascot which is “shaping into a fitting climax to the official British flat racing season with a potentially vintage field set to line up”.
