title: The push towards childhood language learning: ‘For primary-aged pupils, it opens minds’
description: Combination of skilled teachers and a Department of Education programme at the forefront of a new approach to languages in Irish schools
content:
As soon as they enter the education system, children in Ireland begin learning their mother tongue. But while almost 40 per cent of adults have some ability to speak Irish , only 1.5 per cent of the population speak it on a daily basis outside of the education system.
These figures, from Census 2022 , also revealed that we are lagging behind our European counterparts when it comes to speaking foreign languages, with only 15 per cent of the Irish population proficient in a second language, compared to up to 59 per cent of Europeans. In fact, according to Eurobarometer data from May, 2024, between 25-28 per cent are capable of speaking two or more additional languages.
Amy Kelly, a teacher at Gaelscoil de hÍde, Roscomáin, has been teaching German to fifth- and sixth-class pupils for 17 years, having started “under the old Modern Languages in Primary Schools Initiative”. For the past two years, she has been involved in the Say Yes to Languages (SYTL) programme, which is celebrating its fifth anniversary and is funded by the Department of Education and Youth . It has allowed her to share her knowledge with younger children, in third and fourth class.
She says the initiative is hugely beneficial to young people and could make all the difference to their proficiency in the future. “It is an excellent programme, which also funds visiting language tutors and provides lots of opportunities for existing school staff to upskill in their chosen language,” she says. “I have found that the pupils are excited before the German lessons as there is a lot of focus on developing their aural and oral language skills, so this makes the lessons fun.
“There are lots of games, interesting videos, songs and rhymes. The lessons are very inclusive, as children from other countries who already speak a home language can also be talented language learners, and really shine during these lessons.
“The pupils learn about the German culture too. At the end of my last set of 10 weeks teaching German, I asked them why they liked learning it and answers included, ‘it will help me on my holidays’, ‘it will help me to write to my German pen pal’, ‘it will help me if I meet a professional German soccer player like [Florian] Wirtz’, and ‘it will help me in secondary school’. So, yes, they really enjoyed the lessons.”
Kelly says the SYTL programme gives children “a fantastic headstart in another language”.
“They have already been learning Irish and can apply some of those skills to learning the new language,” she says. “Pupils in Ireland start learning a second language (Irish) in junior infants, so by the time they are in the senior classes in primary school they are ready to start learning a third and fourth language.
“Then, when they get to choosing their subjects for secondary school, they’re more likely to keep on the language they’ve started, which is the overall aim of the SYTL programme. I think it’s beneficial as it will really give them a confident start in that language, if they choose to continue with it, in secondary school. Most of their European counterparts are learning at least one extra language in primary school.
“English, we are told, is the language of the global economy. However, competency in other people’s languages is also hugely important. It opens doors and job opportunities and for primary-aged pupils, it opens minds.”
The Roscommon-based teacher says schools should “apply directly to SYTL if they wish to avail of upskilling courses for existing staff”. She adds: “If they’re looking for a tutor to come to their school, the SYTL team will find them one also.”
Clare Dunne, a teacher at Griffith Barracks Multi-Denominational School in Dublin, says the initiative, which was set up in 2021, has had a very positive response from students in her school.
“With around 25 different languages spoken across our school community, it provides a wonderful opportunity to celebrate, not only the languages students may continue studying in secondary school, but also the rich variety of languages spoken at home and throughout our local community,” she says.
“Beyond the known cognitive benefits, learning to communicate in different languages from a young age is key to language acquisition later in life. It helps children to grow in confidence, develops their communication skills, encourages them to take risks without fear of making mistakes, and deepens their understanding of sentence structure and grammar.
“These skills are transferable to the learning of any language and I can already see how this strengthens students’ understanding of other languages, including Gaeilge and indeed the patterns and rules of the English language itself.”
Dunne, who is teaching second class, says there is a huge appetite for both teaching and learning languages within Griffith Barracks. “It’s such a lovely part of school life to be greeted with a ‘salut’ on the stairs, or to hear children happily singing a French song in their classroom,” she says. “Through song, drama, games and hands-on activities, language learning is brought to life in a very natural and joyful way.
“And it’s not just the older students who benefit from this wider language culture across the school. In our second class, for example, singing ‘Happy Birthday’ in all the different languages the children know or are excited to learn can take quite a while, but it’s a wonderful, shared experience which celebrates everyone’s backgrounds and curiosity.”
Ten-year-old Alice Ardiff is a fourth-class student at Griffith Barracks Multi-Denominational School. Her mother, Louisa Carroll, says Alice is now in her second year of studying French. “By making language learning so much fun, Alice is keen to continue her studies so she also takes extra-curricular French classes,” she says.
“Doing French lessons in class also means learning some games in French or French traditions,” says Alice. “So, from bonjour to bonsoir, French classes are very enjoyable.”
Kelly, who started learning German when she was 11 after meeting a child from Germany who was on holidays in Ireland, says an early introduction to languages can be transformative.
“I met a German tourist who was on holidays in my village and we became pen pals and are still in touch to this very day,” she says. “I continued with German in secondary school and went on to get my primary degree in commerce with German from NUI Galway. I completed my post-graduate teaching qualification with a specialisation in Italian at Canterbury Christ Church University.
“In 2018, I took part in the Erasmus-plus programme, where I taught and shadowed a teacher in the Herigoyen Grundschule, Sulzbach am Main, Germany. We are still in touch and last year our language classes exchanged Easter cards, written in the language being taught, and got the chance to start a pen friendship with a pupil in the German school.
“I’d like to see the introduction of a modern foreign language in all primary schools across the country, using existing staff to teach it or bringing in a language tutor. After all, as many studies around the world have shown, the younger a child starts learning a third language, the better.”

title: I had my first breast check in my mid-thirties – here’s how it went
description: I’ve now made it my mission to incorporate regular breast checks into my routine
content:
T he day I decided to book in for my first breast check , I rang ahead to see about getting a female GP. Not that I have any qualms about having a male doctor for intimate exams; in fact, when I lived in France many moons ago, I had a male gynaecologist.
But when you’re explaining irregular symptoms in a language that isn’t your own – as I would have done when I lived abroad – the words tend not to carry the same weight. As a matter of fact, it dampens any level of embarrassment you would otherwise feel.
So, you can imagine how much more awkward it felt when I stepped into the appointment room of a local walk-in clinic, only to come face to face with a GP who was, in fact, a male. It certainly didn’t help that I was assured several times over the phone that I’d get a woman. But alas, I persevered.
When he asked what brought me in, I sheepishly told him that I was in for my first breast check before providing my reasons.
As bad luck would have it, a friend of mine had contacted me earlier that week about a lump she had found in her breast, so I was able to tell him that was part of what prompted me to make an appointment.
Also, it had recently dawned on me that I had never done even the bare minimum of health checks required for a woman, and was – quite rightly, mortified by that. But I kept the shame that brought me through his doors closer to my chest (no pun intended).
The first thing he did was check my vitals. After seeing that both my blood pressure and temperature readings were normal, he presented me with a consent form for the physical because there wasn’t a chaperone available.
In clinical settings, a chaperone is an independent person who acts as a witness for both sides during an intimate exam. If there isn’t someone available, you can reschedule the appointment, or provide informed consent to be assessed without one.
After scribbling my name on the consent form, I made my way to the other side of the curtains to change into the gown he gave me, and in true fashion of someone who’s never had such an examination, I almost wore it the wrong way around – with the opening on the back, as you normally would in a hospital setting.
[ Living with breast cancer: ‘I’ve possibly had one of the best years of my life. I’ve got rid of anything that didn’t matter’ Opens in new window ]
We weren’t exactly off to a great start, I thought.
Ignoring the twinge of humiliation that hit me for a millisecond, I geared myself up for an awkward few minutes of nervous toe-wiggling and desperate attempts at filling my mind with anything but the present.
Much to my surprise, it was over before I knew it, and soon after, I discovered he was quite thorough in examining the three main points.
First, he checked for changes in the skin. As he examined me, he explained that changes in skin texture are usually what they begin to look for. It could be anything from redness to inflammation, or dimpling and puckering – none of which he detected on me.
The second focus was around breast tissue. He pressed down around my chest area to see if he could identify any lumps under the skin. A breast lump is the most significant sign of breast cancer, although nine in 10 lumps are not cancerous, according to the HSE .
Finally, he checked my lymph nodes, those small bean-like organs that help the body fight infection. He started by pressing down along the sides of my armpits before moving on to my collarbone.
[ Almost 90% of urgent breast cancer referrals to Letterkenny not seen within target time Opens in new window ]
He explained how the lymph nodes tend to enlarge during a sign of an infection.
After my physical, we returned to his desk and he informed me that there was nothing alarming. Nevertheless, he offered me a referral for a mammogram if I had any concerns, but I politely declined.
While I turned down the opportunity to get a mammogram, I was still interested in hearing more about it. So I reached out to Aisling Hurley, chief executive of Breast Cancer Ireland .
She describes a mammogram as an image taken by a mammography system that is 90 per cent effective. It involves using metal plates to flatten each breast at a time for an X-ray examination, while standing up.
For those getting what she calls a “triple assessment”, it is the next step after a physical exam and a crucial X-ray before an ultrasound.
BreastCheck , Ireland’s national breast screening programme, offers free mammograms to women aged 50 to 69 who have no symptoms of breast cancer, while those under 50 have the option to go private.
[ ‘Life was busy and full, then everything stopped,’ says mum-of-four diagnosed with cancer Opens in new window ]
For example, the Beacon Hospital Breast Centre offers screening mammograms for women aged 35 and over at €200, but prices vary depending on the provider.
Hurley explained how mammography can detect cancer. Generally, women under 50 have breast tissue that is active and alive and usually white in colour. Since cancer also shows up as white, the disease can be hard to detect in younger cohorts.
For women over 50, breast tissue becomes grey, and as we get older it becomes inactive and turns black. The difference in colour can make the cancer easier to detect in older women.
We also discussed an app called Breast Aware. Among many other features, it contains a video of how to do a breast examination properly at home, and options for setting monthly reminders.
After downloading it, I felt a sense of achievement. Then, I wondered about other women and whether or not regular breast checks were part of their self-care routine.
I contacted Dr Ali Ahmeda, medical director at Webdoctor.ie , who is also a GP with a special interest in women’s health, and she had some eye-opening insights.
Ahmeda says it is becoming increasingly common for younger women to seek a breast check, even if they haven’t noticed a specific symptom. Some seek out reassurance, while others book in because they realise they don’t know what is normal for their own breasts.
She encourages women to be breast aware from early adulthood, and advises us to check our breasts about once a month. She says those without symptoms do not need routine breast examinations by a GP, and self-assessing at home will suffice.
In particular, checking for changes in breast size, shape or appearance, and feeling the skin in and around the armpits, and collarbone. But being familiar with our baseline really is key when it comes to picking up on changes.
Helen Forristal, director of nursing services at the Marie Keating Foundation , says anyone who notices a new breast lump, nipple discharge, persistent pain, skin changes, or any other concerning symptom, should always contact their GP first.
They can then be referred to the public symptomatic breast service or, if preferred, to a private breast assessment clinic for further examination.
Thankfully, I did not find myself in that position. However, it is the reality for approximately 3,500 women who are diagnosed with breast cancer each year in Ireland.
I’ve now made it my mission to incorporate regular breast checks into my routine. While I may be quite late to it, it’s still a step forward, and anything towards better health, education and awareness is a step in the right direction.
After all, it’s often the smallest steps that lead to the biggest life changes.

title: Leinster coach Nienaber guided by Anthony Foley’s words ahead of daunting Clermont test
description: Province returns to European action one day after the 10th anniversary of Munster coach’s untimely death
content:
The last message Anthony Foley imparted to the Munster squad remains imprinted on Jacques Nienaber’s mind.
They were coaching together at the province until Foley’s tragic death in Paris before Munster’s Champions Cup encounter with Racing 92.
The 10th anniversary of that awful day falls on Friday, and Nienaber has never forgotten Foley’s final address to the players. Munster had lost to Leinster the previous weekend and, after taking Monday off, the man lovingly known as Axel addressed the group.
“I remember because his passing was on my birthday, October 16th, 2016,” Nienaber said. “The last message Axel had to the squad was, ‘you create your own reality’. That’s probably something I took into my career.
“Whatever you say, it’s going to be. If you say you’re not going to make it, you’re not going to make it; if you say you’re going to make it, you’re going to make it. So you create your own reality, whatever that is.”
The words resonated for Nienaber. It was 13 months later when he and Rassie Erasmus left Munster to coach South Africa. After forging a team that won back-to-back World Cups, Nienaber joined Leinster three years ago.
So his mind is on Foley this week. He is also focused on Leinster’s return to European action. With nearly all of Leinster’s frontline players having just one match under their belts this season, they must take on Clermont at the Stade Marcel-Michelin in their opening pool game on Saturday.
It is Leinster’s first Champions Cup outing since their disappointing performance in last season’s final in Bilbao in May. With Leo Cullen now in his final season – and Nienaber’s future also expected to lie elsewhere – there is an added layer to the province’s motivation to win that elusive fifth star.
However, Nienaber is keen to stress that nothing is guaranteed, not with the quality of the opposition hoping to go deep in the competition.
“You’re not entitled to go all the way, and nobody is entitled to go all the way,” he said. “Leinster have a good squad, but so do Bordeaux, Toulouse and the Bulls.”
The soon-to-be 54-year-old offered a hypothetical: ask a Bordeaux fan whether they would take Jamison Gibson-Park and the answer would be yes. But would they give up Maxime Lucu in exchange? No. The same applies to Matthieu Jalibert and Sam Prendergast.
“That’s why I say it’s such a great competition, with the best players playing against each other,” Nienaber said. “Every club is working extremely hard to go all the way, but nobody sits in a press conference and says, ‘Listen, we’re confident we will go all the way this year’. I don’t think there’s a coach thinking that way.”
The hugely influential Gibson-Park returned to training last week, although it remains to be seen whether he will be risked after a calf injury. Caelan Doris and RG Snyman remain long-term absentees, while Harry Byrne is still going through concussion protocols.
So Leinster are well stocked with available frontline players. They are undercooked, however, as was evident after a lightning-fast start against Cardiff last Saturday was followed by a flatter second-half display.
Nienaber has no problem with the IRFU’s player-welfare system that meant Leinster’s Ireland internationals were largely kept out of action during the opening two URC weekends. He is also satisfied that there is greater cohesion within the setup after a “disjointed” start to last season.
Although Leinster beat Clermont at home in the pool stage in 2024, this is their first game in Clermont for 14 years. Their last meeting on French soil was won by Les Jaune et Bleu in 2017, in a semi-final in Lyon.
Nienaber is among the many in the Leinster camp who have never visited one of Europe’s most authentic and atmospheric rugby stadiums. He is excited about the prospect.
“That’s one ground that, when I spoke to Daan Human, who played for Toulouse and spent seven or eight years in the French league, it always came up: ‘Clermont in Clermont, tough’.
“It always pops up somewhere. Pieter de Villiers, who played for France, said it’s a nice place to go to, to be tested, and that it’s tough.
“When you coach, you always want to coach a game at Eden Park or play at the Aviva or Croke Park, so this is one of those. I’m looking forward to it. It’s always a good challenge. We’ve lost to two French sides in the four years I’ve been here, and unfortunately both were in the final.
“But it’s lovely playing against French sides. It’s lekke . . . a good contest,” said Nienaber, using a South African slang word for “enjoyable”.

title: Alan Eustace: The ‘Liveline effect’ will be crucial to the resolution of the public sector strikes
description: A strike is not a popularity contest: it’s a cold, hard caluclation about which side can outlast the other. But the public mood does matter
content:
O n Wednesday, unless there is a last-minute breakthrough in the public sector pay dispute, thousands of workers like me will be standing on a picket line outside our workplaces. This will be a new and unwelcome experience for most of us, and an unfamiliar sight for the majority of the Irish public.
Strikes are very rare in Ireland: we routinely record single-digit days not worked due to industrial action per thousand workers annually, when the EU average is more than 30 days. Even during the depths of the financial crisis, the European Commission reported itself pleasantly surprised by how quiescently Irish workers, both public and private, swallowed the privations of austerity, pay cuts, lay-offs and hiring freezes. Negotiations around the Croke Park (2010) and Haddington Road (2013) agreements were traumatising for a trade union movement which had become complacent during social partnership in the 1990s and 2000s, having allowed its capacity to organise and mobilise workers on the ground to wither away.
As the economy roared back into life over the past 10 years, wages increased dramatically – but so did inflation, particularly for essentials such as housing and utilities. Workers feel like hamsters on a wheel, running to stand still. Since the Lansdowne Road agreement of 2016, successive governments recognised that providing the level of public services that the Irish people, in the context of a growing population and economy, rightly demand requires more public sector workers; and that stability in the delivery of public services creates the certainty for private sector (especially multinational) investment.
Those workers often need high levels of education and training to deliver complex services and infrastructure, and the State is competing for workers with the private sector and internationally. Remember, this benefits private sector workers, too, when their employers in turn have to compete with public sector conditions.
For the past decade, pay has broadly gone up in line with inflation – until this year, when negotiations on a new agreement broke down. The bottom line is that if you don’t pay people enough, they won’t work for you. The disruption of a strike is simply compressing into a single day, week or month the long-term process of attrition, staff shortages, deskilling and lost expertise that arises when workers move jobs, or choose a career path outside the public sector in the first place.
Private sector employers fully understand the problems of attracting and retaining skilled workers; they just don’t usually have to face up to the stark reality of compressed labour shortages in the form of a strike, because only 14 per cent of private sector workers are organised into trade unions. In the public sector, the majority of workers are union members. That gives us bargaining power to resist the prospect of losing money for doing our jobs, as inflation devours our wages.
There has been minimal industrial unrest in this country for a very long time (the last big public sector strike was 2009). Most people in Ireland have no real experience of prolonged industrial action. I was on strike during the UK’s mini-winter of discontent in 2022-23, when the country was roiled by strikes in transport and public services. Workers spent weeks on picket lines, on and off, watching public sympathy ebb and flow.
Strictly speaking, a strike is not a popularity contest: it’s about how long the employer can keep its operations going without the striking workers’ labour, and whether that is longer than the workers can last without their wages. It’s a cold, hard economic calculation. But the lower trade union membership is, or the less well-organised the workers are, the more they rely on public sympathy to exert pressure on the employer. So part of what both sides in this current industrial dispute are looking for is a read on the public mood.
On Monday afternoon, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers invited unions to negotiate with the Government at the Workplace Relations Commission, but if the strike does go ahead tomorrow, as seems almost inevitable, schools will close, the Dáil will not sit and non-urgent healthcare services will be cancelled. A second strike is planned for October 21st.
[ Winter of discontent looms as public sector workers prepare for stoppage Opens in new window ]
The question being asked right now in both Liberty Hall and Government Buildings is, who will bear the blame for disruption caused by these strikes, should they go ahead? Actual trade union membership in Ireland is low (25 per cent), but sentiment is relatively favourable: stripping out undecideds, 55 per cent of non-union members would support a union in their workplace.
Crucial to the resolution of this dispute will be the “Liveline effect”: whose story will cut through to the public – the nurse who can’t make rent in Dublin and plans to emigrate, or the parent who has to take a day off work because schools are closed, or the elderly patient whose hospital appointment is cancelled? And will the narrative shift depending on how long the strikes go on for?
One unexpected factor in the UK strikes was the emergence of charismatic trade union leaders such as Mick Lynch and Pat Cullen (now a Sinn Féin MP). Will trade union leaders become household names in Ireland again, like they were during social partnership? And what about the significant energy Irish trade unions devote towards campaigning on other issues, from housing to Gaza to breast cancer awareness? These are worthy causes voted for by their members but will they help in attracting broader solidarity, or distract from pay demands and confuse the message?
Strikes tend to increase union membership, as workers see the value in an active organisation on the ground. Trade unions have an opportunity now to make the case, not just for their position in this dispute, but for their value generally, to an Irish public broadly unfamiliar with how unions and collective bargaining work. Closing schools and hospitals will be both a learning experience and a health check for Irish workers.
Dr Alan Eustace is an assistant professor at the School of Law, Trinity College Dublin. He is a trade union member but writes here in a personal capacity

title: Hotel chain iNua weighs strategic options after revenue tops €74m
description: Chief executive Sean O’Driscoll says the company, which has almost €70m of debt, is still exploring a sale
content:
Operating profits at hotel group iNua rose marginally last year as the company was being touted for sale, but interest payments linked to almost €70 million of debt dragged the company into the red, new accounts have shown.
Last year, the group – led by chief executive Seán O’Driscoll – that owns eight hotels recorded a rise in turnover from €71.1 million to €74.5 million.
During the period, operating profits marginally rose from €3.9 million to €4 million. The company also disclosed that its earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation rose by 5 per cent to €11.3 million.
Despite the higher operating profit, a loss of €2.5 million was still recorded by iNua in 2025, compared to the €2.8 million loss the previous year, which led to a rise in accumulated losses to €43.2 million.
The loss was driven by €6.3 million of interest costs linked to €69.7 million of debt owed to lenders, down from €70.8 million the previous year.
The hospitality group previously secured backing from Earlsfort Capital Partners and Blackbee Investments to expand its portfolio of four- and five-star Irish hotels. In 2023, iNua refinanced its debts through an arrangement with lenders Alliance Bernstein and Earlsfort Capital Partners.
The debt has been used by the iNua group to build a portfolio of properties, including the Radisson Blu Hotel & Spa in Limerick, and the Muckross Park Hotel & Spa in Killarney, Co Kerry.
In December 2025, The Sunday Times reported the company would trigger a “liquidity event” early in the new year. It was reported that a sale price of more than €120 million was required for investors to secure a return.
When asked about the sales process, O’Driscoll told The Irish Times the iNua Hospitality board “continues to look at strategic options to realise investor value but are obviously still mindful of the geopolitical situation in terms of timing”.
He added he was “very pleased” with the 2025 financial results and its occupancy level for the year was 85 per cent.
Last year, iNua Group’s staff fell from 1,132 to 1,088, but salary costs rose from €25.8 million to €26.1 million. The company also paid out more than €91,000 to staff last year for “loss of office”.
Businesses in the hospitality sector have raised concerns in recent years about the cumulative impact of measures like minimum wage increases and sick leave entitlement on staff costs.
Last year, the value of the company’s tangible assets, made up largely by properties in the group, fell 3 per cent to €83.4 million. At the end of the year, iNua booked total assets of €93.8 million, down from €97.9 million in 2024.

title: ‘We want to be better’: Carla Ward urges Ireland to build on eight-goal lead over Kazakhstan
description: Katie McCabe and Denise O’Sullivan return for World Cup playoff semi-final, with Belgium or Poland up next in the final
content:
Mostly good problems lie ahead for the Republic of Ireland . Carla Ward’s coaching staff can begin to prepare for next month’s World Cup playoff final against Belgium or Poland before their semi-final second leg even kicks off in Cork on Tuesday night.
Kazakhstan are not a competitive international team, as seen during the 8-0 loss in Astana last Friday.
Belgium take a 1-0 lead to Gdańsk after a goal by Elena Dhont in Leuven gave them a slight advantage over a Polish side led by the exceptional Barcelona striker Ewa Pajor .
The 5pm kick-off in Poland means the Irish players will know the opposition blocking their path to the World Cup in Brazil next summer, even as they engage in what amounts to a training-ground exercise against part-timers.
The Kazakhstan game holds some value for Ward, mainly because Abbie Larkin is growing into a vital player for her country as well as her club, Crystal Palace. The 21-year-old’s form demands a start, yet Marissa Sheva is equally important to how Ireland operate under their English coach.
It was Larkin’s late finish that secured promotion to Nations League A, at Belgium’s expense, in October 2025, but it was Sheva who scored in the two victories against Poland during World Cup qualifying in April.
If they both start, then Emily Murphy or Kyra Carusa will have to make way.
Sheva and Katie McCabe were suspended for last Friday’s victory in Kazakhstan while Denise O’Sullivan’s knee was spared the long-haul flights to Central Asia.
“Katie and Denise will play,” Ward confirmed. “Let me be really clear, we are going to try and step up again. We want to be front-footed, we want to be better. Them two, arguably, are two of Ireland’s greatest ever players. Why wouldn’t they go back in?”
Presuming McCabe will play at left wing back, Chloe Mustaki would shift to centre half as Jessie Stapleton drops to the bench. That in itself is a tough call on Stapleton but Mustaki was superb in Astana.
As O’Sullivan returns to midfield alongside Megan Connolly, Sheva and Larkin appear to be challenging for the remaining position in behind Carusa.
Someone has to give way. Sheva is the engine within Ward’s system, where every player is expected to cover every blade of grass without possession before springing into rapid counterattacks.
Having Sheva or Larkin and Crystal Palace midfielder Shanade Hopcroft to come off the bench brings genuine strength in depth to an Ireland squad that was beginning to grow old together.
“I was saying to the group this morning that it is good now to have really strong competition everywhere,” said Ward. “Jamie [Finn] came [into midfield for O’Sullivan] and did tremendously well.
“We’ve got a really good group. They want to drive and push each other all the time. We are not just a team built on culture any more, we are a bloody good football team.”
O’Sullivan was devastated to be suspended for the last international at Páirc Uí Chaoimh, a 3-2 victory against the Netherlands in June when Amber Barrett scored a late winner.
“I love playing here,” said O’Sullivan, who recently returned to America with Gotham FC in New Jersey after a brief period at Liverpool.
“It is really, really special, my family being here. The whole of Cork has supported me throughout my career. In particular, people from Knocknaheeny. They always come down to watch the games.”
Ireland’s two-legged playoff final against Belgium or Poland will be played between November 26th and December 5th, with the second leg at home.
IRELAND (possible): Brosnan; Patten, Hayes, Mustaki; Mannion, Connolly, O’Sullivan, McCabe; Murphy, Larkin; Carusa.

title: Taoiseach to chair new Cabinet AI committee on regulation and impact of technology
description: Plans for new committee come as AI summit takes place in RDS as part of EU presidency
content:
Taoiseach Micheál Martin is to chair a new Cabinet committee on artificial intelligence (AI) that will focus on the impact of the technology on society, economy and labour market as well as its regulation and deployment in the public service.
Martin will bring plans for the new committee to Cabinet today as he and Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke update colleagues on the International AI Summit taking place in Dublin on Wednesday.
The summit at the RDS is being held as part of Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the European Union.
The Taoiseach will deliver an opening address and attendees will hear from various European Commissioners, ministers and representatives of artificial intelligence companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as figures from tech giants such as Microsoft.
It is understood that initiatives will be announced at the AI Summit to showcase Ireland’s AI ambitions to an international audience.
The Digital Ireland strategy, published in February, outlined the Government’s ambition to strengthen Ireland’s position as a digital leader and a global hub for AI innovation. The new AI Office of Ireland was established in early August.
Separately, Burke is expected to brief Cabinet colleagues on the Start Up Ireland initiative which is to be formally established by this week and aims to create 1,000 new Irish start-up companies. So-called high-potential start-ups will be awarded €100,000 investment and all supports will be co-ordinated from a new hub, co-located with Enterprise Ireland’s new Dublin city centre headquarters. Under the plans, there will also be a specialised AI accelerator programme, matching promising Irish AI companies with global leaders in the field.
Meanwhile, the Minister for Transport is to bring plans to extend the Road Transport Support Scheme (RTSS). The RTSS initially involved payments for hauliers and bus and coach operators for March to May as part of the Government’s response to spiralling fuel costs caused by the Iran war. The scheme is being extended to September and October with some €73 million allocated for this purpose.
[ Ireland’s EU presidency proposes budget cut of €141bn for the bloc Opens in new window ]
Elsewhere, Minister for Housing James Browne is to seek Cabinet approval to launch the Defective Concrete Blocks Social Homes Scheme 2026.
The scheme enables local authorities or approved housing bodies to remediate damage to social housing caused by defective concrete blocks.
Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill is expected to bring the National Drugs Strategy 2026-2030 to Cabinet before a launch event for the publication alongside Minister of State Jennifer Murnane O’Connor.
It is understood that the strategy includes an action plan with 33 actions, including measures on prevention, emerging drug threats, services for women and minority groups, family and community supports, and stigma reduction. Some €7 million was allocated in the budget to begin the implementation of the strategy.
Minister for Higher Education James Lawless is to bring a memo to Cabinet on the commencement of an independent review of doctoral education in Ireland. The review will examine how Ireland can increase the number of PhD students and graduates and strengthen the research workforce that is said to underpin economic growth, enterprise development and public innovation.
Minister for Rural Development Dara Calleary is to ask the Government to approve a five-year strategy to support the community and voluntary sector in advance of its launch this week.
