title: Dublin AI start-up Dubsof raises more than €5m in round led by BlueYard Capital
description: Tech entrepreneurs and execs, including Meta’s David Singleton and Dylan Collins, have backed the company
content:
Irish AI start-up Dubsof has raised $6.5 million (€5.8 million) from a group of European and US technology investors, including Berlin venture firm BlueYard Capital and a fund linked to Irish entrepreneur Dylan Collins.
The Dublin-based company, cofounded by Aidan McNeill, George O’Leary and Bastien Saidi, is helping companies to develop bespoke software infrastructure to help artificial intelligence tools into their existing workflows.
New filings by Dubsof Limited shown the company raised almost €5.4 million in funding from a number of large venture capital investors. McNeill told The Irish Times the total size of the round was $6.5 million.
Dubsof, with a staff of 25 based on Merrion Square in Dublin, was set up last year. It has already tested its platform in beta and live with a number of customers.
A statement from the company said it has plans to use the funding to double its headcount over the next 12 months by hiring further software engineering and machine learning experts.
“Dubsof exists to build a better economy, to solve co-ordination between people and companies. Most working time goes on admin and co-ordination, and we want people to spend it on the work only they do best,” McNeill said.
The largest contributor to the round was BlueYard Capital, the venture capital fund cofounded by Germany-based Dubliner Ciaran O’Leary in 2016, which provided €2.6 million.
Other notable backers to the seed round were Backed VC, which has invested €1.85 million, Project Europe and Cocoa Ventures.
[ The cost of social awkwardness and Ireland’s AI funding boom Opens in new window ]
Project Europe, which contributed €400,000, is a fund backed by more than 200 tech executives and founders in Europe, including entrepreneurs behind Klarna, Shopify and GitHub. Early-stage backer Cocoa Ventures, a fund founded by Carmen Alfonso Rico and Anthony Danon, invested €350,000.
A newly incorporated UK company controlled jointly by technology investors Collins and Maximilian Regner-Bleyleben called 10xHumans Limited also invested €30,000, the documents show.
The company said Collins, best known for selling gaming software start-ups Demonware and Jolt Online Gaming, and Stripe’s former chief technology officer David Singleton, who now works for Meta’s AI unit, were early angel investors prior to this deal.
Another early angel investors was Matt Fitzpatrick, the chief executive of US AI firm Invisible Technologies and former head of QuantumBlack Labs, McKinsey’s AI software unit. Fitzpatrick has invested a further €10,000 as part of the latest round.

title: GAA continue to prove Mary McAleese right
description: Integration discussion needs the strong voice of a well-recognised woman
content:
Sir, – I agree with Malachy Clerkin (“ Mary McAleese questioned the GAA’s attitude towards women – now they’ve replaced her with a man ”, Sport, October 9th). If the steering committee wish to prove Mary McAleese wrong in her criticism of their vision for the GAA and their unwillingness to get integration done quickly, then they have gone the wrong way about it.
We needed the strong voice of a well-recognised woman to show that integration is needed now, not 10 years down the road.
Sadly, I have to concur with McAleese’s criticism and thank her for all her trojan work. – Yours, etc,

title: In making a mess of the budget, Patrick O’Donovan may have done us a favour
description: If public service broadcasting is to retain public trust and integrity, it must be insulated from political pressure
content:
It’s been a turbulent few days for the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport, Patrick O’Donovan . It was bad enough that his heavily flagged proposal to introduce a €100 culture card for young people was conspicuous by its absence from last Tuesday’s budget .
Worse was to follow when it emerged, to widespread surprise, that RTÉ would not be receiving the €20 million increase in funding agreed as part of a multiannual restructuring deal in 2024. The surprise seemed to be shared by the Taoiseach and Tánaiste, whose intervention reportedly led to an emergency meeting between the Minister and RTÉ’s chair and director general on Thursday.
While all concerned were tight-lipped afterwards, it has been clearly signalled that the Government will stump up the €20 million, subject to RTÉ satisfying the Minister on the progress of its reform and redundancy programme. Given that these were always the terms on which the multiannual payments were based, there is as yet no clear explanation as to why the money was withheld in the first place.
None of this is good for O’Donovan’s political reputation, and there were mutterings from various unnamed Government figures over the weekend that he might not keep his Cabinet seat when the midterm reshuffle takes place at the end of next year.
The Limerick TD seems to have an unfortunate knack for losing friends and alienating people, but last week’s embarrassments and the subsequent clean-up may have forced the question of how RTÉ is funded back on to the agenda, and that would not be a bad thing.
The current arrangement was agreed by the previous government in the summer of 2024. It guaranteed RTÉ €725 million in public money over three years, rising from €225 million in 2025 to €240 million this year and €260 million in 2027. The licence fee was retained, and the Exchequer committed to making up the difference between what it brought in and the agreed total. The lower amount raised from licence revenue, the bigger the cheque from the State.
That difference is growing quickly. Licence sales have fallen every year since the 2023 payments scandal. Figures released by O’Donovan last week show sales down 6 per cent in the first nine months of this year, putting full-year income on course for about €114 million, compared with more than €150 million in 2022.
Less widely understood is how much of the licence fee the State already pays. The Department of Social Protection funds free licences for everyone over 70 and others who qualify for the household benefits package, a bill in excess of €80 million a year. That is more than 500,000 licences, set against roughly 715,000 bought by households this year.
Free licences grow by up to 20,000 a year as the population ages, while paid ones keep falling. Remarkably, if current trends hold, licences paid for by social protection will outnumber those paid for by households as early as 2029. This seems untenable.
[ Does Patrick O’Donovan’s explanation for €20m RTÉ funding cut add up? Opens in new window ]
Add the direct top-up and the picture is starker still. In 2025, about 54 per cent of RTÉ’s public funding came from the Exchequer in one form or another. By 2027, that share is likely to be above 60 per cent. The licence fee survives in name, but the money increasingly comes directly from Government.
European law now has something to say about this. The European Media Freedom Act requires member states to fund public broadcasters through transparent procedures based on objective criteria set in advance, and to ensure they have “adequate, sustainable and predictable” resources. The point is to protect editorial independence by making sure money cannot be used as a political lever. The Broadcasting (Amendment) Bill now before the Oireachtas is meant to give effect to those rules here.
Last week’s episode looks much more like political incompetence than a deliberate act of interference. But cutting an agreed sum at a few hours’ notice, without explanation, is clearly not in keeping with the spirit of the EU rules. Whatever its cause, it has shown how easily the money can be turned on and off.
Nor should the role of ill-will be underestimated. Members of the Oireachtas media committee have indicated they intend to question RTÉ director general Kevin Bakhurst about a newspaper column by radio presenter Oliver Callan, which questioned Simon Harris’s credentials as Minister for Finance. One source described Callan’s piece as “antigovernment”. Whether a presenter’s newspaper column should be a matter for a committee examining RTÉ’s finances is debatable. That the two are being raised alongside each other is telling.
The new legislation will strengthen the role of Coimisiún na Meán, which will assess RTÉ’s needs and recommend a level of funding for each three-year period. But the regulator’s role will be advisory. There will be no legal obligation on the minister of the day to follow its recommendations, nor, as far as can be seen, any requirement to explain a decision not to. The final call will remain where it was last week, with a politician putting together a budget.
The licence fee has many faults, including the fact that it is now collapsing before our eyes. But it was based on a sound principle. Money paid directly by citizens to a public service broadcaster, at arm’s length from the government of the day, gave that broadcaster a degree of independence that an annual grant cannot.
If public service broadcasting is to retain public trust and integrity, it must be insulated from political pressure, whether born of malice or just haplessness. If nothing else, we can thank O’Donovan for reminding us of that.
[ RTÉ funding snub not a good look for Patrick O’Donovan Opens in new window ]

title: The punishment or the crime?
description: US planned execution by firing squad
content:
Sir, – Oscar Wilde wrote, in The Soul of Man Under Socialism: “One is absolutely sickened, not by the crimes that the wicked have committed, but by the punishments that the good have inflicted; and a community is infinitely more brutalised by the habitual employment of punishment than it is by the occasional occurrence of crime.”
Let US defence secretary Pete Hegseth , on his own, pull the trigger of his firing squad rather than brutalise a group of young soldiers. – Yours, etc,

title: We risk finding the carcasses of rare birds across the countryside in the coming months
description: We risk finding the carcasses of rare birds across the countryside in the coming months
content:
Sir, – As winter approaches, the scandal of rare birds being shot looms once again.
While I don’t like the idea of any birds being shot, the prospect of red-listed (deemed to be of high conservation concern) and amber-listed ones (medium conservation concern) remaining on the open seasons’ order – meaning they are fair game for shooters – is deeply upsetting.
Unless the Minister removes these vulnerable species from the “license to kill”, we’ll be finding the shattered carcasses of golden plovers, snipe, woodcock, red grouse and shoveler strewn across the countryside in the coming months, along with amber-listed birds such as tufted duck, mallard, teal, gadwall, wigeon and greylag goose.
These species are already reeling under the impact of climate change and habitat loss.
Ireland is failing in its duty under EU environmental law – which specifically requires us to protect rare or endangered birds – by allowing the shooting of these species.
I appeal to the Government to put compassion and conservation before the blood-sport lobby, and take all the above-named bird species off the open seasons’ list. – Yours, etc,

title: Cancelling Wednesday’s Dáil sitting is step in wrong direction
description: Parliamentary principles are important and should not be set aside so readily
content:
Sir, – Undoubtedly, the Dáil business committee, chaired by the Ceann Comhairle last Saturday, would not have taken the decision to cancel Wednesday’s sitting lightly (“ Dáil sitting next Wednesday cancelled due public sector workers’ strike ”, News, October 10th). Holding a sitting in the circumstances would have presented logistical difficulties with unionised staff on the planned work stoppage.
That being said, cancelling a sitting in these circumstances is unprecedented and a step in the wrong direction.
In 2009, if I recall correctly, in similar circumstances, the Dáil sat as scheduled but on a reduced programme, served by a skeleton, non-unionised staff. The scaled-back programme allowed for the industrial dispute to be debated on the day.
Members of the Dáil are effectively office holders as duly elected members under the Constitution and while they are free to exercise their democratic mandate on the streets if they so wish, that should not mean a sitting of the Dáil should be cancelled.
Traditionally, sittings of the Dáil are sacrosanct and in troubled times in the past, when bomb alerts were not infrequent, the sitting was never suspended, adjourned or cancelled. The sceptic or cynic might say what difference would sitting on the day of the work stoppage make, but that misses the point of principle. When a coach and four is being driven through one of the largest western democracies almost on a weekly basis, parliamentary principles are important and should not be set aside so readily. – Yours, etc,

title: Conflict began long before 2023
description: Thousands of Palestinians killed by Israel in the decade before October 7th attacks
content:
Sir, - The core of Ed Abrahamson’s article seems to be that people are critical of Israel because they are essentially anti-Semitic and he references the Holocaust as part of a continuum of behaviour (“ October 7th was a piercing, shrieking alarm call for all Jews ”, Opinion, October 9th).
To repeat what is often said but ignored by Abrahamson in his piece, the conflict in Israel/Palestine did not begin on October 7th, 2023. Thousands of Palestinians were killed in Gaza before then. Israeli human rights group B’Tselem has reported that in the 10 years before 2023 there were 3,837 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces, 2,929 in Gaza.
Moreover, even if we accept the figure of 119 children dying of malnutrition in Gaza, as he references, it is truly shocking that a doctor says this provides evidence of “food-delivery efficacy” while thousands of tonnes of aid are a few kilometres away and barred from entry to Gaza by Israel.
Turning to the West Bank, Abrahamson repeats the view that settler violence there is down to a small number of extremists when all the evidence shows it is supported and financed by the Israeli government. - Yours, etc,
Sir, - Ed Abrahamson writes that “while there have always been some Jews who do not support the Zionist construct . . . for most Jews it is a core belief”.
Research carried out by the Jewish Federations of North America last year, however, showed just 37 per cent of American Jews identify as Zionist. In Britain, a similar picture is painted by research carried out last year by the Institute for Jewish Policy Research, which found that anti-Zionism has increased among all age groups of British Jews since 2022.
Conflating Zionism and Judaism is intellectually dishonest and ties the Jewish religion – which has a rich and proud history of standing for justice, equity and humane values – to the actions of a state that tramples on the dignity of Palestinians by bombing civilians and expanding settlements.
Such a conflation also ignores the reality that Zionism has far more non-Jewish adherents than Jewish ones. In the United States, Christian Zionists outnumber Jewish ones, largely evangelical Christians who believe that a Jewish state in the Holy Land is necessary to usher in the second coming of Jesus.
The reality is that millions of Jews worldwide explicitly reject Zionism and view it as a failed project because of settler violence and the dispossession of Palestinians. - Yours, etc,

title: This is how it ended for George Gibney: a packed court celebrating his demise
description: The former Ireland swimming coach was sentenced to 15 and a half years in prison for attempted rape and indecent assault of children
content:
T his is how it ended for George Gibney: a packed court, giddy with tangled knots of happy people, all hugging and sobbing and congratulating each other on his demise.
Within those knots were the victims, their families, their friends, the journalists who exposed him and the gardaí who investigated him – all united in joy and relief at the road’s end.
In another part of that courtroom was Gibney, the 78-year-old paedophile in grey, rolled-up tracksuit bottoms, carted off to prison in a wheelchair to spend the next 15½ years.
In his sentencing inside Court 9 at the Criminal Courts of Justice, Judge Mícheál P O’Higgins noted that since he arrived back in Ireland in July 2025, Gibney hasn’t received a single prison visit.
“This may be reflective of his notoriety and lonely station in life,” the judge said.
[ Former swimming coach George Gibney jailed for 15½ years for abusing four girls Opens in new window ]
Outside court, one of Gibney’s victims waived her right to anonymity. Orla Poole was the victim of Gibney’s most serious crime, an attempted rape when she was nine years old.
For that, he was sentenced to 10 years, with the rest made up of consecutive sentences for 39 charges of indecent assault.
“His actions have had far-reaching repercussions on people beyond just me, my family, friends and my own child,” Poole told reporters afterwards.
“This court case didn’t just deliver justice for me but also, I hope, for others. It has shown that even after 50-plus years, justice can be got. Historical offenders can be held to account for their actions and choices.
“To all survivors out there, speak when you are ready, reclaim your agency and remember you are not to blame; only the offender is to blame.”
The George Gibney who swanned around as Ireland’s first celebrity swimming coach in the late 1980s and early 1990s is long gone. Here, he presented as a shrivelled, diminished thing, stripped of all power, seemingly unable even to stand up.
Dressed in a red zip-up jacket over a blue polo shirt, Gibney sat with his legs crossed, his Velcro-strapped black runners in the footrests of his wheelchair, his hands clasped on his knees.
When the clerk announced the judge’s arrival with the customary “All rise ...” Gibney made a grimacing effort to lift himself up on to his feet but he didn’t get more than a few inches off the chair before sitting back down.
Whether this was for effect, only he knows. In any case, he had come to the wrong room for sympathy.
Sitting 15 feet to his right was Chalkie White, himself a victim of Gibney when he was a boy and later, as Gibney’s assistant coach with the Ireland swimming team.
He was also the first person to lift the veil of silence around Gibney.
A conversation between White and Gary O’Toole on a flight to Australia in 1991 tipped the first domino in Gibney’s downfall; 35 years later, Chalkie White made sure he was here for the last one.
In the public gallery were victims of Gibney’s crimes going back half a century.
Tric Kearney and Ber Carley were there, 33 years after the Irish justice system had failed them in the original case against Gibney.
Johnny Watterson was there , three decades on from going out on an unprecedented legal limb as a reporter with the Sunday Tribune to name Gibney as the man who abused them.
[ A shameless risk-taker and predator: How George Gibney groomed children Opens in new window ]
Most of all, the four complainants in this case were present, either in person or by video-link, to hear the sentence finally being read out.
O’Higgins took his seat and delivered a 33-minute address that was forensic, comprehensive and stark.
“The offences committed by the defendant were grave,” the judge said, “being part of a pattern of systemic offending that violated the rights of four young children over a lengthy period.
“The offences were predatory in nature and involved a gross abuse of the defendant’s position of authority as a swimming coach. He used his coaching role to access and then assault defenceless children in his care.”
Gibney made no particular reaction at any stage. His face is slightly folded and gummy now, as though he has lost a lot of his teeth.
He appeared throughout to somehow be chewing on something and nothing at the same time. Occasionally, he pushed his black-rimmed glasses back on his nose.
The sentence delivered, the judge took his leave of the court.
This time, when the clerk said, “All rise ...”, Gibney didn’t even make a token effort to get up. He sat back in his chair and waited to be wheeled away to whatever remains of his life.
As his Garda minder backed out of the door, he turned Gibney to navigate a corner, showing to the body of the court for the first time the white letters on the side of his wheelchair: “Property of The Irish Prison Service.”

title: Future of Irish horticultural sector
description: While economic viability is a challenge for growers, it is also shaped by agricultural policy and public investment
content:
Sir, – Cian O’Connell’s article on the Irish horticultural sector notes that a substantial portion of fruit and vegetable imports cannot be produced in Ireland due to our climate (“ Why doesn’t Ireland grow more veg ”, News, October 10th).
While true for bananas and citrus fruit, my analysis of CSO trade data shows that eight of the 15 crops with the highest import volume could be produced domestically. These include apples, onions, cabbages and brassicas, carrots and other root vegetables.
While economic viability is a challenge for growers, it is also shaped by agricultural policy and public investment. Substantial public support is accepted for the economic sustainability of other agricultural sectors, yet the economic difficulties facing horticulture often appear to be treated as simply an inevitable barrier to domestic production.
The future direction of the Irish horticulture sector is not just a function of what we can produce and how much of it, it is also an outcome of policy: which crops and production systems do we choose to promote and support, and therefore who can make a viable living from growing them. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I remember learning, in my first geography lessons in national school in the 1960s, how agriculture was carried on in this country.
In the sunny southeast they grew grain. In the Golden Vale it was milk and dairy products. In the midlands it was beef and the drumlins of Cavan and Monaghan produced the pigs and poultry. As for the rest of the country, west of the Shannon it was subsistence farming. The food producers in the different areas of the country used their land for what it could do best.
I went to the supermarket recently to buy some fruit. The first three packets I picked up came from Portugal, Poland and Peru. – Yours, etc,

title: The waiting is over as GAA’s experimental rules go on trial in college matches
description: Higher-value goals, a ban on fisted points and a seismic alteration to 65s among the stand-out amendments
content:
And so it begins – the sports of Gaelic football and hurling are now on trial. Well, kind of.
The widely discussed trial window for experimental rules in both codes has arrived, with the opening round of matches in Division One of the third-level football league – the Ryan Cup – taking place this week.
The first round of matches in the corresponding hurling league are due to take place on October 22nd, albeit college fixtures are susceptible to change at this time of the year.
Still, on the football front, the first official game took place in Sligo on Monday night when ATU Sligo hosted Dublin City University at Knocknarea Arena.
There have been several challenge matches recently as some teams tried to familiarise themselves with the rules before playing under them in competitive outings.
There are further Division One football league fixtures scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday of this week too.
Members of the Kevin McStay-chaired Gaelic football Expert Advisory Group (EAG) will be in attendance at the round-one games this week, but the data from these contests will not be central to the review at the end of the competition.
The GAA ’s Games Intelligence Unit has identified 15 fixtures in particular to record and analyse – the eight round-two matches, the four quarter-finals, two semi-finals and the final.
The round-one matches this week are being viewed largely as a bedding-in period for players and managers to get accustomed to the rules. And the EAG do not intend putting too much focus on round three either as, depending on results, there could be several dead-rubber matches in that round.
The higher education competition is played on a round-robin format with four groups of four teams. The four table-toppers and runners-up will advance to the quarter-final stages.
The final is due to be played on the week beginning November 23rd.
Among the rules being trialled in football include a ban on fisted points, increasing the worth of a goal to four points, limiting consecutive handpasses to three and implementing a backcourt rule whereby a team cannot play the ball back across the halfway line once they’ve entered the opposition half of the pitch.
John Meyler’s Hurling Expert Advisory Group will see their recommendations officially trialled from next week. There are also some challenge games taking place this week.
Among the hurling ‘rule enhancements’ to be road-tested include awarding two points for a converted sideline cut and a regulation that on puck-outs, three players from each team must remain between the 45-metre line (nearest the player pucking out the ball) and the 21-metre line.
Dublin hurler Conor Burke believes the trial rules should be given a chance in the upcoming third-level games before any definitive pronouncements are made.
And the St Vincent’s clubman is particularly interested to see how the alteration to 65s will impact matches. During the trial, 65s will be struck from a player’s own 65-metre line rather than the opposing team’s 65-metre line.
“There are no free-takers in the country that have an issue scoring 65s these days,” said Burke.
“But I did hear John Kiely raise a good point that the 65-metre line on every pitch is different, the distance between them, so they’re going to land differently. That’s a very valid point, so there are arguments for and against everything.
“The evolution of hurling has been brilliant and we want that to continue, but we also don’t want to bring in rules that go against the great stuff that’s already happening.
“I think you need to be open to change but also appreciate that the game evolves in a way that we don’t want to disrupt that as well.”
One of the more interesting trial rules will see consecutive handpasses outlawed. Instead, if a player receives a handpass he must then strike the ball with his hurl rather than move it on with his hand.
“The game is so quick that instinctively you do things from playing for 25 years,” added Burke.
“So, it’s hard to know until you’re actually in that environment, when you’re in getting tackled by three or four lads from the opposition, what your first instinct is.
“So that’s why I’m saying obviously you need to have a bit of time to get used to things.
“There’s no question if some of the rules come in that they’ll definitely change the way the game is going.
“The rule changes have been great [in football], so that’s why I think it’s important to stay open-minded to potential change, but just hope that the changes do make sense.”
Both committees will complete a review at the end of the third-level competitions before further trials could take place in the pre-league intercounty tournaments next January.

title: Irish house price inflation slows as affordability constraints bite
description: Asking price inflation softens to 3.9%, according to property website MyHome
content:
Irish house price inflation slowed to a three-year low of 3.9 per cent between July and September as affordability pressures and higher interest rates weighed on demand .
That’s according to the latest survey from property website MyHome , which is owned by The Irish Times Group.
It found that asking prices nationally declined by 1.4 per cent in the third quarter compared with the previous three months.
The company said “affordability remains stretched” with the median (middle value) sold price for properties listed on its website now at €412,000. This was 7.7 times average annual pay of €54,000.
The Irish property market is undergoing something of a reset in the face of higher borrowing costs, persistent supply shortages and changes to the rental rules.
[ David McWilliams: The numbers in the Irish housing market don't add up Opens in new window ]
MyHome’s latest barometer, compiled in conjunction with Bank of Ireland, found asking prices in Dublin rose at an annualised rate of 2.1 per cent in the third quarter while those outside the capital rose at a rate of 4.8 per cent.
The median asking price for newly-listed properties nationally was €390,000 in the third quarter while in Dublin it was €480,000.
There was a modicum of good news for prospective buyers with MyHome noting that homebuilding in Ireland hit a new post-crash record of 38,000 homes built in the year to June, enough to accommodate 100,000 people.
[ Ireland records one of lowest rates of house price inflation in euro zone Opens in new window ]
This exceeded population growth, which was 67,000, for the first time in the series.
“This – along with a 12.5 per cent year-on-year increase in homes listed for sale on MyHome – is positive news for homebuyers,” it said.
The number of properties listed for sale on MyHome at end of last month was 14,630. It also noted there have been 10,400 new listings for sale on MyHome since June, which is up 5.3 per cent year-on-year.
However, it predicted that existing home sales was likely to contract for a fourth consecutive quarter.
“The rate of asking price inflation continues to slow, the number of properties for sale on MyHome is rising, and homebuilding has picked up,” Bank of Ireland chief economist Conall MacCoille said.
“All of these factors point to positive news for homebuyers. It still makes more financial sense to buy rather than rent, with rental yields still outpacing mortgage rates,” MacCoille said.
[ What is behind the slowdown in Ireland’s property prices? Opens in new window ]
The typical joint income of first-time buyers in 2025 was €95,000, purchasing a property worth €408,000, equivalent to four times’ their income, he said.
MacCoille forecast 39,600 new home completions in 2026, rising to 42,000 in 2027.
“This is still a far better outlook than many commentators had suggested just 12 to 18 months ago,” he said.
The report also included an analysis of the impact of Building Energy Ratings (Ber) on price, compiled in conjunction with the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland.
It showed that the value of a typical home rises by 2.7 per cent for each step on the scale – with maximum increase of 10-13 per cent going from C-rated to A-rated home.
MyHome managing director Joanne Geary said the report represented good news for homebuyers but noted that there was still a wide discrepancy between the first-time buyer and mover markets.
“First-time buyer transactions are up by 12 per cent year-on-year while mover transactions have fallen by 1.2 per cent,” she said.

title: Public-sector strike by more than 300,000 workers set to go ahead
description: First stoppage on Wednesday by more than 300,000 workers appears almost inevitable
content:
The Government is increasingly resigned to Wednesday’s public-sector strike going ahead after an attempt by Jack Chambers to initiate talks at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) was swiftly rebuffed by union leaders on Monday.
Chambers, the Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform, is to brief Cabinet colleagues on what are described as “substantial efforts” to engage with union leaders and emphasise that the Government side remains ready to attend talks at the WRC in the hope of averting the strike.
Both sides, however, seem to regard the first scheduled one-day stoppage as almost inevitable at this stage.
The strike will see more than 300,000 public-sector workers, including healthcare workers, teachers, courts staff and many others, undertake a 24-hour work stoppage, although essential services will be maintained.
An independent mediator may be approached by the Government side in the hope of getting negotiations started, but sources suggested this is unlikely to happen until one or even both of the single-day stoppages scheduled for the next eight days have taken place and there is more pressure from the public for a solution to be found.
On Monday, Chambers said in a letter to the officers of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions public services committee, which is chaired by Fórsa ’s Kevin Callinan, that the strike would cause “great disruption to the public, especially the most vulnerable in our society, and also result in an avoidable loss of earnings for public servants”.
But, he wrote, an agreement could be reached without delay if both parties were willing to enter an “intensive process of engagement as soon as possible”.
The Minister again described the provision of €1.2 billion for public-sector pay in the budget as “significant” and said “pay issues can and should be discussed as a priority alongside other matters as part of the pay talks”. This has been a key sticking point in getting talks started so far.
[ Unions reject effort to avert Wednesday’s public sector strike Opens in new window ]
In a response sent less than an hour after the proposal had been received, however, Callinan and the other officers said the union side “cannot see how it represents any change in your stated position”.
There was no reference to the suggested meeting at the WRC, but he said: “We believe that the Government needs to respond to the seriousness of the situation by acknowledging that the specific pay issues that we have identified will be addressed in any talks that may be arranged.”
The letter also accused the Government side of having failed to honour commitments made in the national agreement that expired in June. Two sources involved in the process on the Government side acknowledged the relationship between Chambers’s department and unions had broken down.
The unions have indicated they will seek increases to address what they say was an earlier gap between pay rises and inflation of between 5 and 7 per cent in addition to a settlement for the second half of this year and an undertaking that their members’ wages will not be undermined by the cost of living increasing over the term of any deal.
The €1.2 billion, they contended, is not nearly enough to address those demands. The Government argues the budget provided a range of cost-of-living measures in addition to the funding explicitly set aside to meet increased pay.
Despite this, Callinan told Chambers: “We regret to say that your letter doesn’t provide a basis for the strike action scheduled for Wednesday to be postponed.”

title: British attorney general to approve future prosecutions of former UK soldiers under legacy law changes
description: Legislation is intended to replace contentious 2023 Legacy Act passed by then British Conservative government
content:
The British attorney general will approve future prosecutions of former British soldiers and others under long-awaited changes to Troubles legacy legislation going before the House of Commons.
Northern Ireland Secretary of State Chris Bryant said the changes would offer “robust, permanent safeguards” and “fairness, dignity and respect” to former British soldiers and the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
Meanwhile, almost 200 former IRA members holding so-called “on the run comfort letters” between 2000 and 2014, which said they were not wanted, will not be able to use them to block new prosecutions.
This change was something the British government has been clear on for quite some time, but the “on the run” amendment would reinforce the point in legislation, sources told The Irish Times.
Irish Government sources welcomed the amendments, though they said Ireland’s European Court of Human Rights challenge would not be withdrawn until the legislation passes in Westminster.
Once in law, the final decision on prosecutions will be made by the British attorney general on foot of a prosecution recommendation from the Northern Ireland Public Prosecution Service.
However, the Public Prosecution Service and the British attorney general will judge the merits of taking a case by the same rules where cases must have a 50 per cent, or better, chance of success, and where they are in the public interest.
The legislation is intended to replace the deeply contentious 2023 Legacy Act passed by the then British Conservative government, which banned inquests and civil claims for damages for killings during the Troubles.
[ ‘Let them live in peace’: Protestants and Catholics alike express relief in Drumcree Opens in new window ]
In a bid to soothe military and police veterans’ anger about the legislation, they will not be contacted “unnecessarily” until the British state has disclosed all of the information it has on file on cases.
The legacy commission and coroners “must not regard lawful conduct” of soldiers as “equivalent” to those who carried out “acts of terrorism”, said a British government statement.
In addition, the new Legacy Commission, which will replace Independent Commission for Reconciliation and Information Recovery (ICRIR), the body established in 2023 to investigate deaths and cases of serious injuries dating back to Northern Ireland’s Troubles, will not contact other witnesses unless it first assures itself that “compelling new evidence” is likely.
The new legacy body must first get all possible information from the police, the ministry of defence or elsewhere and “only after that” can it consider whether it needs to approach a witness.
In addition, investigators must judge whether new and compelling evidence that is not already on file is likely to come from a witness before approaching them.
However, demands from serving and former British army generals that prosecutions should not happen unless there is “new and compelling evidence” at the time of the killing has been rejected.
The batch of amendments includes one that will recognise the operational pressures facing soldiers and police “during violent unrest” where judgments had to be made in dangerous circumstances.
[ Carmel Heaney obituary: Diplomat who took on dissident Irish republicans and sympathisers in US Opens in new window ]
Once it replaces the ICRIR, currently headed by the former chief justice of Northern Ireland Declan Morgan, the new legacy body will now be able to work with all United Kingdom police forces, not just the Police Service of Northern Ireland.
Former paramilitaries will be barred from being appointed to the Victims and Survivors’ Advisory Group and there will be a requirement for at least one veteran or veterans’ representative to be on the panel.
Because the legislation has been so long on the books, it will be given an extension of time – a so-called “carry over” motion – when it comes before the House of Commons on Tuesday.
However, its passage through Westminster faces challenges, since even with the extension it must pass through all stages in the Commons and Lords before the next King’s Speech, expected to be in late spring next year.
Even with Monday’s amendments, it will face strong opposition in the Lords from former senior military who fear the effect the legislation will have not just on Troubles’ veterans, but also those serving on Monday.
The Committee stage takes place in the Commons on October 19th and 20th, along with its other final stages, though there are so far 150 government amendments and others those tabled by opposition parties.
*** The copy has been amended to make clear that the ICRIR will end with the introduction of the new legislation, and that it will be replaced by a new Legacy Commission

title: Gerry Thornley: It’s death by a thousand tweaks for the once-great Champions Cup
description: Changes to the calendar only weaken a competition that has never been truly loved in England and France
content:
Roll out the bunting and sound the trumpets, the Champions Cup and Challenge Cup return next weekend with the introduction of a one-off first round before the tournaments go back into autumnal hibernation. They will then return with another one-off round in December before, finally, the two competitions are granted back-to-back pool matches for the concluding two rounds in January.
This is yet another unconvincing tweak to a format that, once upon a time, was carved in stone. The tweak is seemingly borne of a vain hope that it will increase interest in the Champions Cup by giving it an earlier presence in the season.
This is also an acceptance that the December starts of the last five seasons have inflicted further damage on the competitions, which the insular French and English have often used as political footballs while prioritising their domestic leagues. The English, along with the Scots, boycotted the inaugural 1995-96 European Cup, while the English did so again in 1998-99.
From the third year of what was then the Heineken Cup in 1997-98 there were pools of four teams and thus six games, played on a home-and-away basis. Even when the number of participants changed from 24 to 20 in 2013-14, pools of four teams and six games remained enshrined until 2019-20. The competitions also started earlier.
Back in 1997-98, it’s incredible to think that the pool stages were actually run off on six consecutive weekends from early September to mid October. From 1999-2000 onwards, the competition began in October in non-World Cup seasons and November in World Cup seasons.
[ Champions Cup has a jeopardy problem: can anyone stop France’s Top 14 giants? ]
But Covid changed everything, reducing the pool stages to two rounds and delayed December starts in 2019-20 and 2020-21. The tournament organisers deserve huge credit for managing to complete both competitions in those seasons despite the prophets of doom that said tournaments featuring teams from six countries could never be completed in a pandemic. The 2019-20 French championship, by comparison, was cancelled, with no winner.
But that was the window of opportunity for the French clubs, who were supported by their English counterparts, in reducing the pool stages in 2021-22 to four games before a two-legged round of 16, with two rounds in December and two in January.
The following season, the round of 16 became a straight knock-out and the Champions Cup was reduced from nine to eight weekends. The shortened and delayed four-game, December/January pool stages have served to further diminish the competitions.
During the period of stability and growth from 1997-98 onwards, all participating teams were guaranteed three home games. Now they have only two. For the French clubs, who are also guaranteed 13 home games in the Top 14, this is not an issue.
But following the demise of Wasps, Worcester and London Irish, the Premiership clubs are only guaranteed nine home games in their domestic league as well as two in Europe – the same amount as URC sides. You’d think they too would want the additional revenue of more home games, but evidently not.
Perhaps it’s not surprising that Irish rugby has been the most enthusiastic and pro-European of the participating countries. Tom Kiernan and Vernon Pugh of Wales were the driving forces of the original European Cup. Whereas the French had their own championship since 1892 and the Premiership had been in existence since 1987, in the first six years of the European competition and professional rugby, Ireland did not have a league to play – in save for the interpros – until the creation of the Celtic League in 2001-02.
Perhaps, too, Ireland’s biggest mistake was winning five Heineken Cups in seven years between 2006 and 2012. That compounded the resentment surrounding the old ERC offices being based in Dublin and, in part, prompted the very Anglo/French coup of 2014. That saw the creation of EPCR and the setting-up of base in Switzerland.
There were also a host of promises about sponsorship and television deals, with accompanying claims that the football equivalent would be emulated. Such promises have largely been unfulfilled.
But perhaps Irish rugby’s adoration of European rugby is also a weakness, in that we don’t rate the URC as much as we should do, even with the advent of South African sides participating, who actually have far more buy-in to the competition, be it the franchises themselves or their fans.
Leinster , after all, have just won back-to-back URCs . If a French team won back-to-back championships there’d be open-top bus homecomings, mayoral receptions and widespread media recognition of their greatness. Instead, if Leinster don’t win the Champions Cup outright , their season is regarded as a failure by many.
The French and the English never appreciated what the Irish teams brought to European rugby. Granted, they never rated European rugby as highly as we did, and still don’t, all the more so as the Top 14 has grown into a juggernaut and their television deals with Canal+ not only dwarf all other leagues, but leave little left in the kitty for European rugby.
For Castres and others, maintaining Top 14 status is imperative or else they could go the way of Biarritz. Save for Toulouse, especially, it’s still hard to compete in both competitions for French clubs, as Bordeaux Bègles were reminded last season.
But there’s never been a period of such French dominance in Europe. Toulouse accounted for four of the first five triumphs until a generational Toulon won three in a row from 2013. But Toulouse, La Rochelle and Bordeaux Bègles have each won two of the last six Champions Cups.
The reduced, quickfire format evidently suits the French, but it also has become the biggest flaw in the two competitions, because unlike the six-game, home-and-away format of yore, there is simply not enough jeopardy in the pool stages.
Sure, every point matters in the jostling for positions, which have ramifications deep into the knock-out stages. But two wins out of four pretty much ensures advancement to the knock-out stages, while a solitary win has been enough for one or two teams in each of the last four seasons.
This is plainly ludicrous, and no amount of tweaks will change that.

title: Fintan O'Toole: The blue-green smoothie ruling the country has no plan and even less passion
description: Civil War politics energised the Government parties. Now they’ve nothing left to do but pump out money
content:
T he Drifters went through a lot of different line-ups: the Classic Drifters, the Original Drifters, the New Drifters and the Drifters Legends. And then there is the late tribute act known as the Merrion Street Drifters. Adrift on a sea of money, the Government moves with the tide of affairs, rudderless, directionless, concerned only to stay afloat.
This is surely the most aimless Government since the dog days of Éamon de Valera in the mid-1950s. Back then, there was the excuse that the chief was 75, the Cabinet was mostly populated with old men of the revolutionary generation and the economy was so flaccid that the young were leaving in droves. What Samuel Beckett called “a lingering dissolution” was general all over Ireland.
But now, the Cabinet is relatively young, made up of men and women on average in their late 40s. The economy is booming and the exchequer has an embarrassment of riches. The population is rising rapidly and the flow of migration is inward rather than outward. The mismatch between the lassitude of the Government and the dynamism of the country is astonishing.
Learned helplessness is the Government’s chronic condition. The nearest thing to a plan it seems to have is to keep pumping out money. It treats windfall corporation tax revenue as though it were a tidal wave of moolah washing over the sides of the ship of State: get rid of it before it drowns us all.
In Budget 2027 , €6 out of every €7 earned in corporation tax is to be spent immediately. To grasp how mad this is, the Government will be borrowing money at high interest rates to put into its own savings fund for the costs associated with the ageing of the population.
It also, comically, can’t even anticipate the arrival of Christmas: the budget has no allocation for the Christmas bonus that will be paid to all welfare recipients in 2027, as every year. Simon Harris and Jack Chambers pretend not to know that Santa Claus is coming to town. Too far ahead, apparently.
There is no narrative, no vision, no set of priorities, no burning ambition to solve long-term problems, no ability to imagine or innovate. Just keep working the money pump, stay afloat and drift, drift, drift.
How do we explain this extraordinary listlessness? We can say it’s a failure of leadership and a paucity of political talent, and both of those things would be true. But I think there’s a deeper problem, one so absurd that I hesitate to suggest it: they miss Civil War politics.
[ Are Simon Harris and gen Z about to turn Ireland into a nation of investors? Opens in new window ]
For about a century, the dynamic of centre-right politics in Ireland was the narcissism of small difference. The real distinctions between Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael evaporated over time. They were never very far apart anyway: both were Catholic nationalist parties committed to only as much social and economic change as was compatible with the interests of those who already had power and money.
There were minor differences of emphasis in relation to Northern Ireland, but these were largely performative. There were different reactions to the rise of feminism and the so-called liberal agenda, but it should be recalled that, for example, Garret FitzGerald committed Fine Gael to what became the Eighth Amendment before Charles Haughey followed suit. Fianna Fáil was more flagrantly corrupt, but Michael Lowry was no beacon of political virtue and, in the warping of the planning system, both parties joined the feeding frenzy.
The paradox is that the very absence of substantive policy or cultural disparity made tribal passion all the more important. Each party needed the other to bolster its own self-image. Fianna Fáilers could tell themselves that they must be great social radicals because they weren’t as pigheadedly conservative as the Blueshirts. Fine Gaelers could convince themselves they must be sea green incorruptibles because they weren’t as sleazy as the other shower.
All of this was indeed absurd. But it was also, for a time, hugely successful. It created a binary choice and an apparent moral drama that reached its climax in the endless Garret v Charlie title bouts of the 1980s. And, as I think we can now see by virtue of its absence, it gave politicians in both parties their sense of purpose.
[ The remaking of Jack Chambers Opens in new window ]
This is what put fire in their bellies. The sibling rivalry of the identical twins made for an incestuous kind of democracy, but it was nonetheless intense. And now it’s gone.
It’s not just that Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael are truly indistinguishable as parties – though it is certainly the case that even the old minor points of disagreement on the North or reproductive rights or styles of corruption have vanished. What’s striking, though, is that they are now so personally homogeneous as well.
In manner, attitude and comportment it makes not a whit of difference that Harris is in Fianna Fáil and Chambers in Fine Gael – or should that be the other way round? They are identikit professional politicians. In the Coalition blender they make the same blue-green smoothies.
The only competition between them all now is in the eternal arena of clientelism. It tells us everything that last month Fianna Fáil TDs held “an emergency meeting” because they believed Fine Gael TDs were getting in ahead of them to announce grants for local sports clubs. The world is on fire, but the only thing that gets these people fired up is the thought that a constituency rival might be pulling a fast one.
[ Paternity leave shouldn’t be a privilege only the likes of Simon Harris can afford Opens in new window ]
That’s what passes for passion now. The climate crisis ? Child poverty? The whittling away of the tax base? The housing disaster ? Just rocks invisible beneath the surface of the money ocean as we merrily drift along.
I never thought we’d miss red-faced oul’ fellas roaring at church gates about the bloody Blueshirts or the Effing Effers. But it seems that that was the only energy our governing parties ever really had.

title: Rory McIlroy’s Order of Merit push takes him to Delhi
description: Patrick Reed and Eugenio Chacarra stand in the way of a record-equalling eighth title
content:
Rory McIlroy will play three of the four remaining tournaments on the DP World Tour as he pushes to match Colin Montgomerie’s eight European Tour Order of Merit titles. It starts with this week’s India Championship in Delhi.
The Northern Irishman is currently third in the Race to Dubai standings, behind long-time leader Patrick Reed and Eugenio Chacarra, who followed up a third-place finish in the French Open with a runner-up finish in the Spanish Open to leapfrog McIlroy.
As things stand, McIlroy, on 3,115.86 points, trails American Reed by 307.76 points and is 142.03 points behind in-form Spaniard Chacarra.
McIlroy has committed to playing the India Championship along with the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship and the Tour Championship in Dubai as part of his push, but has opted to miss the Genesis Championship in South Korea.
Three Irish players are competing in Delhi, with Shane Lowry – who moved up two places to 16th in the updated R2D standings following his tied-13th -place finish in the Spanish Open – and Tom McKibbin also competing.
Leona Maguire , who had a rest week last week, and Lauren Walsh, who missed the cut in the Aramco Korea Championship, are both in the Buick LPGA Championship in Shanghai, which starts on Thursday.
Liam Nolan has moved ever closer to securing a full DP World Tour card for next season. The Galway native followed up his win in Abu Dhabi on the Hotel Planner Tour with a top-five finish in the Hainan Open in China to move up three places to ninth on the updated order of merit. The leading 15 players graduate to the main tour.
Nolan is again in the field for this week’s Hangzhou Open as the circuit remains in China. It will be the penultimate event of the season, with only next month’s Grand Final in Mallorca left before those cards are dispensed.
Gary Hurley is also competing in Hangzhou and is in need of a strong performance. The Waterford man is currently 61st on the order of merit with only the top 45 after this week’s tournament moving on to Mallorca.
“I’m in shock, honestly, pure shock right now . . . that’s fairytale stuff. I’ve played two Opens and to be going to Augusta, I just can’t get my head round it. You can have a great career in this game and never get to go to Augusta, so I cannot believe it.” – Grant Forrest on learning his win in the Spanish Open came with invites to both The Open at St Andrews and the Masters at Augusta National next year.
Blades Brown – at 19 years of age – became the youngest Korn Ferry Tour (KFT) graduate to earn a full PGA Tour card. The KFT season concluded at The Federal Club in Virginia, where Ross Steelman finished as number one to earn a full card and invites to The Players and the US Open. Brown finished ninth in the standings, with 20 players securing their playing rights on the main circuit.
All eyes were on a young Tiger Woods – playing in just his sixth event as a professional – but David Ogrin would claim the headlines by winning the Texas Open at La Cantera in San Antonio. It would prove to be his only victory on the PGA Tour.
Ogrin fired a final-round 72 for a total of 13-under-par 275, which gave him a one-stroke winning margin over Jay Haas with Woods a shot further back in third.
But Ogrin didn’t make it easy for himself, shooting a triple bogey on the 16th hole of his final round, which wiped out his three-shot lead in one fell swoop. His tee shot on the par-three hole hit a cart path and rolled into a creek.
“God wanted it to be exciting for me,” Ogrin would remark of that near-disaster so close to the winning line, but he managed to close the deal and claim a $216,000 payday. Though he didn’t win again, he would manage 32 top-10s.

title: Turning a blind eye to homelessness
description: We are saying I hear you, but we are not really listening
content:
Sir, – It seems that Ireland’s capacity for turning a blind eye hasn’t gone away.
A generation ago the problem was the children who were born to unmarried girls and unknown fathers, and the mother and baby homes. Today, the problem is families with nowhere to live, thousands of homeless children, many of whom are attending school burdened by the shame of their situation.
Politically, these children have been converted into statistics, meaningless numbers not unlike the occupants of hospital trolleys who must wait patiently for their turn.
As Jennifer O’Connell says in her excellent piece: “We suffer not so much from compassion fatigue as shame fatigue” (“ A playground for the living built over the bones of the dead ”, Opinion, October 11th). We are saying I hear you, but we are not really listening. We would prefer not to know. – Yours, etc,

title: Are we turning a corner on housing?
description: There are some positive signs in the latest MyHome report and mood music in the industry
content:
After a decade of surging prices, record rents and persistent supply shortfalls, is the Irish property market finally turning a corner?
There are some encouraging signs. The State’s two largest home builders, Cairn and Glenveagh, have reported record output and enhanced delivery targets in recent weeks, noting an upswing in construction.
This was confirmed by property website MyHome in its latest report, published on Tuesday. It noted that homebuilding in Ireland hit a new post-crash record of 38,000 homes built in the 12 months to June.
It said this was enough to accommodate more than 100,000 people, which exceeded population growth (67,000) for the first time in the series, marking what MyHome described as a “milestone”.
“This – along with a 12.5 per cent year-on-year increase in homes listed for sale on MyHome – is positive news for homebuyers,” the company said.
New home completions are expected to hit about 40,000 this year, still well below the Government’s target level of 50,000 but headed in the right direction.
The Government’s main aim in reforming the rent rules earlier this year was to entice institutional investors back into the Irish market. These are considered crucial to getting annual output up to 50,000.
PRS (private rental sector) investment here stalled in 2022 amid a hike in borrowing and construction costs, leading to a marked slowdown in completions. Tough rent regulations were also cited as a factor.
While it’s too early to say if these changes have had the desired result, investor sentiment countrywide appears to be positive. Several industry leaders, including the bosses of Cairn and Glenveagh, claim the Government has got its policy mix right.
They point to the positive mood music around the State at the recent MIPIM real estate conference in Cannes.
The positive story is still punctured by the fact that prices continue to rise – at a rate of 3.9 per cent in the third quarter, according to MyHome – posing a big challenge for buyers.

title: International Monetary Fund warns of AI-driven market correction in global economy
description: Annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank take place in Bangkok under the shadow of war and AI-driven investment
content:
A “reassessment” of the financial returns and efficiency gains expected from artificial intelligence (AI) could trigger a big correction in equity markets, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.
In its latest Global Financial Stability report, the Washington-based fund said that while financial markets remain resilient in the face of war and inflation, there were “three salient risks ahead”.
These included an “AI-driven market correction”, another sharp rise in sovereign bond yields and further cyber threats.
[ IMF chief alarmed at AI threat to jobs and taxes Opens in new window ]
The annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank are taking place in Bangkok, Thailand, this week under the shadow of war in the Middle East, the ongoing energy supply shock and rising interest rates.
“Weaker or less durable investment and profitability in AI would not only undermine a key engine of growth that has helped offset the economic drag from the war in the Middle East and heightened policy uncertainty, but also lead to a correction in AI-linked equities and credit, which now account for a large share of both markets,” the IMF said.
It also warned that “resurgent inflation” and tighter fiscal conditions could spark a further jump in sovereign bond yields and “broader market turmoil”.
Global bond yields, including the State’s, have rocketed in recent months as persistent inflation and ballooning government debt unnerves creditors.
Pressures from a prolonged war in the Middle East and persistent fiscal concerns could further drive up yields in a “fragile bond market”, it said.
Market confidence could also be undermined by “severe cyber incidents” that had the potential to disrupt “critical financial market infrastructure and operations”.
In its World Economic Outlook report, published alongside the Global Financial Stability report, the IMF said the global economy was in the grip of two competing economic forces.
While the energy price shock continues to stoke inflation and weaken demand, the rapid investment in AI is acting as a counterweight, producing what the fund described as a “demand impulse”.
The global economy, it said, was “split” between these forces, with some countries faring better than others.
The IMF said activity in the first half of 2026 had held up better than expected despite these three challenges.
“Flexible supply responses, rerouting of shipments, inventory drawdowns, fiscal support measures, and lower energy intensity than in previous decades have helped contain the hit to activity from the war,” it said.
The AI-driven technology cycle was also providing a boost to demand, it added.
However, the IMF warned that further trade fragmentation and prolonged uncertainty related to the war could eventually weigh more heavily on activity and confidence while “constraints on energy could impair the AI-led impetus”.
“Financing conditions could [also] change abruptly for any number of reasons, including fiscal sustainability concerns,” it said.
Global growth was forecast to be 3.1 per cent this year, unchanged from its previous projection in April, and 3.4 per cent in 2027.
Global headline inflation is projected to increase to 4.7 per cent in 2026 before easing to 4.1 per cent in 2027, marking a cumulative upward revision of 0.7 percentage points “with the temporary increase driven mainly by energy and food prices”.
A reassessment of AI-related prospects could sharply reduce investment, trigger equity market corrections, and tighten financial conditions, with global spillovers.

title: Right to a home in our own city
description: Latest instalment of Glass Bottle scheme a worrying development
content:
Sir, – Mark O’Connell’s article is an enlightening insight into a very significant social issue in Ireland today (“ A developer needs a lobbyist. Call the ex-housing minister ”, Opinion, October 10th).
It details the 2017 agreement in relation to the Irish Glass Bottle site in Ringsend, in which a consortium led by the property developer Johnny Ronan is building up to 3,800 apartments.
The deal stipulated that 25 per cent of the homes would be allocated for social and affordable housing. The housing minister at the time was Simon Coveney.
Dublin City Council has now obtained legal advice that the inclusion of so-called cost-rental units could satisfy the affordable requirement, despite the fact that such a category didn’t exist at the time of the original agreement. The lobbyist for Ronan is now former minister Coveney, a man well placed to give good advice in this regard.
This is a flagrant attempt to undermine the protections within the initial agreement, which were there to protect citizens trying to buy a home in their own city. This change will result in greater profits for the developers and less opportunity, if indeed any, for ordinary citizens to own their own place. It is, in my view, profoundly undemocratic.
It is also ironic that some of the people, saved by Nama and who I and my fellow public servants continue to bale out every week through our payment of the never-ending Universal Social Charge, are the ones who will benefit most from this.
O’Connell wonders what Government is actually for. Might I suggest an answer that seems radical but surely is just common sense: to protect the welfare of our citizens. – Is mise le meas,

title: Is the Government emergency ready?
description: Recent events would suggest otherwise
content:
Sir, – Most households have received the Be Emergency Ready booklet. However, I wonder if our Government is emergency ready.
The impact of the invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the Iran war in 2026 has a single feature in common: a sudden and sharp reduction in the supply of fossil fuels that forces up energy prices and is causing an indefinite cost-of-living crisis .
Facing into winter, one in seven households are in arrears with their electricity bill. Ireland already has the most expensive household electricity rates in the EU, which is about 40 per cent above the EU average.
It is almost certain that fossil fuel prices will remain high. The fuel protests in April brought the country to a standstill and briefly threatened the stability of our democracy.
This energy crisis is a national emergency and should be treated as such. The priority for Ireland must be to do everything possible to develop and roll out a plan to become energy independent (focused on wind and solar) and quickly reduce our dependence on the importation of fossil fuels. – Yours, etc,

title: Sadhbh O'Neill: When did children stop playing outside?
description: One in six Irish parents don’t think it’s safe for their five-year-old child to play outside at home during the day
content:
W hen was the last time you saw children playing in the street? Or even on footpaths?
Growing up in the 1970s and 1980s in Dublin , it was completely normal for children and teenagers to play on side streets. We played all kinds of games, solo and group ball games, chasing, hopscotch and countless variations that involved complex and ever-shifting rules. Fewer households owned a car, so there was a much lower risk of being hit by one within residential areas. Kids were expected to be outside, and most parents forbade watching too much television because it was generally considered to be bad for a child’s development.
Data from Growing Up in Ireland found 30 per cent of parents reported heavy traffic on their street or road, while one in six Irish parents don’t think it’s safe for their five-year-old child to play outside, even at home, during the day. Conversely, in neighbourhoods parents regard as safe, more children routinely play outside, with a ball, playing games or riding a bike.
There is no doubt that there has been a dramatic transformation in childhood over recent decades, and it has a lot to do with the loss of independence and freedom to play, explore and move about our environment. Perhaps the most visible impact is on how children get to and from school.
By the time my own children were going to primary school in the 2000s, hardly any children were cycling to school and few were walking independently. After I conducted a travel survey of a primary school in one of Ireland’s regional cities, the principal installed some cycle racks. However, it turned out these were obtained from a neighbouring girls’ secondary school where cycling rates had plummeted to zero. There are now more girls driving themselves to school than cycling, though the An Taisce #AndSheCycles campaign is working to reverse this trend.
While there are 600 schools involved in the Safe Routes To School programme funded by the National Transport Authority , this is a fraction of the nearly 4,000 schools in Ireland. According to the 2022 Census, fewer than 20 per cent of primary schoolchildren walk to school, and even in urban areas, this figure does not exceed 40 per cent. In 1986, by contrast, 45 per cent walked to school while just one in four travelled by car.
Some of this may be explained by changing times but, in the Netherlands, about 75 per cent of children walk or cycle to school. While there are other factors involved, it is perhaps no accident that Dutch children were found to be the happiest in the world in a 2025 Unicef report, while Ireland trailed behind at number 24 – and yet ranked first for “skills”. Do we put more emphasis on reading and writing than outdoor play and freedom, perhaps?
[ My son has become disinterested in school. The principal regularly uses the phrase ‘parental responsibility’ Opens in new window ]
Independence is not just about school journeys. By focusing too much on purposeful trips like travelling to school, we risk overlooking the importance of children being able to move around their neighbourhoods to play, socialise and just be out and about. There is a feedback loop at play: the more traffic there is, the more concerned parents are about safety, so they drive instead, adding to the number of cars on the road. What sort of society have we created if childhood now consists of moving from one indoor experience to another throughout the day, and where screens have become a substitute for social interaction, physical activity and fun?
Before we shift to blaming parents, though, we should ask ourselves who and what streets are for. Are they for the free movement and storage of motor vehicles, or are they for the free movement of people?
Children do not get a say in how their environments are designed and shaped, but their lives are profoundly affected by those decisions – and non-decisions – nonetheless. Researchers have noted that as informal play in public places becomes more and more constrained, it is necessary for parents, communities and local authorities to actively intervene to disrupt social practices in the urban environment to “allow” playful activity in public space. Dublin City Council is a pioneer in having had, for a time, a play officer, along with a 126-page play strategy.
Strategies are only impactful when they are implemented. What would make a difference to children is support – and even pay – for those who lead cycle buses and walking buses of children to school, a practice which is common in Britain, more parks and playgrounds and a general improvement in the quality of our public spaces.
[ I routinely have intrusive thoughts about horrible things that could happen to my children Opens in new window ]
Slowing speeds and reducing the volumes of traffic is key to removing the hazards to children. Numerous studies have found that road safety messaging that focuses on training children will not make a difference to injury or fatality rates without interventions to reduce the biggest hazards: driver behaviour, speeding, road design and the weight and size of vehicles.
Children have no power over the policies that would make the biggest difference to their local environment and their wellbeing. But if they could vote, I’m sure they would vote for more play and less traffic.
