title: ‘Cork is like Wellington – people distinguish themselves as not being from the bigger city’
description: New Zealand lawyer Fintan Walsh: ‘In my circle there’s an idea that if you stay and don’t leave to have adventures, you have kind of failed’
content:
Fintan Walsh (30) does not feel that he experienced any kind of culture shock when he moved to Ireland from his native New Zealand last year.
He feels the Kiwi and Irish senses of humour are very similar.
After living here for 18 months, he believes these similarities come from both Ireland and New Zealand sitting next to economically bigger nations. The UK and Australia frequently draw people to move there from their smaller neighbours.
“Australia is so much bigger,” says Walsh. “They have so much more money and people are always moving there.”
Ireland played a big part in Walsh’s childhood. He is from Rotorua on New Zealand’s North Island. In the 1970s his dad, his grandmother and great-aunt Betty emigrated to New Zealand from Ringsend in Dublin .
“From talking with Betty and Dad, growing up in Ringsend at that time was quite difficult. They lived in a council house and had some distant relatives and friends who had moved to New Zealand.”
Walsh’s grandmother figure was his great-aunt Betty, as his grandmother died not long after the family moved. Growing up, he knew Betty was Irish. But now, having lived in Dublin, he recognises that she was a “proper Dub”.
“I remember one time when I was young, I went to visit her and she said, ‘What do you know about Oliver Cromwell?’. She was so funny. She adored Ireland. She would always be playing rebel songs like The Men Behind the Wire.”
When he was 16, Walsh spent a summer in Ireland with a host family after winning an essay competition run by the Irish Embassy in New Zealand. By the end of that summer, he had decided that one day he would move here.
[ ‘I arrived in Arizona to 48-degree heat; being Irish, I decided to go for a cycle’ Opens in new window ]
In the meantime, he studied law at university and qualified as a solicitor, spending four years working in New Zealand before moving to Dublin aged 28. With so many young people leaving New Zealand, he was one of the last in his peer group to move abroad.
“I was feeling like I’m the only one still here. I don’t know if this is a universal experience, but in my circle the idea that if you stay in New Zealand and don’t leave to have adventures and seek your fortune elsewhere, you have kind of failed in a sense.”
Walsh got a job at a law firm in Dublin and then moved into a house share he found on a Facebook group for New Zealanders in Ireland. Coincidentally, the house share was in Ringsend.
“Ringsend, I think, has completely changed. I have had conversations with my dad about it. I think that goes for Ireland in general. So much of it has kind of transformed since the 1970s.”
Walsh feels he got very lucky with finding friends and community. His housemates embraced him and introduced him to their social circle.
“It was exactly what you want when you are moving to a new city.”
He feels that his career has really benefited from his decision to move. In the legal field, Ireland is prospering from being the only English-speaking country in the EU since Brexit. “There’s a huge amount of opportunities,” he says.
Today, Walsh admits he had a very rose-tinted view of Ireland before he moved over. He had never experienced an Irish winter, having only previously been here during the summer. He arrived in mid-winter and colleagues told him that even for Irish standards, he had moved over during a particularly cold one.
“I remember I was catching a bus into town in my first week and people were getting off the bus and slipping on the ice on the footpaths,” he recalls.
He describes the vision of Ireland that his great-aunt Betty painted as “rolling green fields and people having craic all the time in lovely pubs, a very picturesque kind of fairytale”. Such a view of Ireland is, in his opinion, very common for the Irish diaspora.
However, the reality of things like public transport and bureaucracy quickly shattered such notions.
Despite this, he still believes that Ireland is an “amazing place” and sees himself staying here long-term.
He met his now-girlfriend on a dating app not long after arriving. She is a doctor and a year into their relationship, she was told her next posting for completing her training would be in Cork . When Walsh heard the news, his automatic reaction was to think, “looks like I will be moving to Cork”.
The couple have since settled into life in Cork city. He compares Cork to Wellington back in New Zealand, which is the country’s third-biggest city where he lived for a few years. “It’s very hipster, all kind of cool bars and cafes, and people in Wellington like to distinguish themselves as being not from the bigger city, Auckland.”
Walsh says he has been enjoying Cork’s slower pace of life but that he is often back up in Dublin for work, so he is still able to see his friends there. The couple also enjoy hosting their friends in Cork, where, thanks to lower rents in the Leeside city, they can afford a flat with a spare bedroom.
We would like to hear from people who have moved to Ireland in the past 10 years. To get involved, email newtotheparish@irishtimes.com or send us two lines about yourself using the form below.

title: Aer Lingus flight cancellations leave readers raging
description: Airline’s policies create web of confusion and frustration
content:
F lying is a complicated business with many variables, from weather and volcanoes to engines and human beings able to derail the most carefully laid plans in an instant. But how an airline manages things when they go wrong is key and two readers have found their dealings with Aer Lingus after their flights were cancelled to be endlessly frustrating.
A reader called Sofie had a plan to travel to London in early September but ended up in a web of confusion and time changes as a result of Aer Lingus.
Her flight from Cork to London Heathrow on September 3rd was cancelled at short notice. “After the cancellation, Aer Lingus’s rebooking system offered me the 7:10am flight the following morning at £0.00, but the system repeatedly failed when I tried to confirm it,” she writes.
She has “timestamped screenshots showing repeated attempts over the course of the evening, including the flight being available at £0.00 and the Aer Lingus system returning booking errors”.
Eventually, Aer Lingus rebooked Sofie on to a flight the following day leaving Cork just after 4pm. “This was far too late as I needed to be back in London for work that morning. With the early flight showing limited availability and the rebooking system continuing to fail, I booked the 07:10 Aer Lingus flight myself and paid €174.12.”
She was subsequently refunded €66.43 for the cancelled flight and was paid £220 (€260) in EC261 compensation.
“However, they are refusing to reimburse the additional cost of the replacement flight, arguing that I purchased it independently and should have contacted customer service instead,” she says.
“This is the part I find particularly frustrating. I did not simply decide to make my own arrangements. I was repeatedly trying to accept the exact Aer Lingus flight they were offering me at no additional cost, but their own system would not allow me to complete the booking. Had their rebooking system worked, I would not have incurred the €174.12 cost at all. I remain approximately €110 out of pocket.”
She contacted us having had “several exchanges with Aer Lingus, but they continue to repeat that because an alternative 16:10 flight had been allocated and because customer service was available, they will not reimburse me”.
[ Reader couldn’t believe it when she was charged €13 for ‘free’ Vanity Fair tote Opens in new window ]
We have one more story from a reader who is also in dispute with Aer Lingus over a cancelled flight.
Before sharing his “ordeal” with us, David says he is really “just looking to see if my experience chimes with anyone else you’ve come across. The whole process has been trying, to say the least.”
David and his wife were due to fly Dublin-London Heathrow at 5.30pm on Friday, May 29th. They arrived at the airport, checked in their bags in and after passing through security got an email, at 4.15pm, informing them the flight was cancelled “due to operational reasons”.
Around 30 minutes later he received another email, stating that the itinerary had changed and he and his wife had been automatically booked on a 7.30am flight the next morning to Manchester – a fine city for sure, but certainly not London.
“We would then have to wait in Manchester for a 4.40pm flight to LHR, arriving at 5.50pm on the Saturday evening,” David says. “The Aer Lingus staff member at the departure gate could offer no further information, other than to direct us back out to departures to queue at the service desk.”
David points out that there were probably 100 people in that queue “many of whom I suspect were arranging accommodation for the night as there were no flights available that evening. We live in Dublin, so instead I called the customer helpline and spoke to an Aer Lingus agent. In fairness to him, he tried to get us on a direct Aer Lingus flight to LHR on the Saturday, but told me no seats were available.”
[ Can the AA justify a 300% jump in travel insurance prices in under five years? Opens in new window ]
David says he explained that he was not keen to “spend the whole of Saturday sitting in Manchester airport. The best he could do was a direct flight on the Sunday, which wasn’t much use to us either. My wife was checking Skyscanner on her phone at the time and there seemed to be some seats on Ryanair flights to London on the Saturday. He explained he couldn’t book us on one of those flights, but he advised me that if I went ahead and booked the flight, I could submit the cost of the flight as an expense through the online portal, and Aer Lingus would cover the cost of those flights.”
When David got home from the airport on the Friday evening he too went on to Skyscanner and “actually found two seats on an Aer Lingus flight direct to LHR for the Saturday morning, arriving into LHR at 11.15am”.
He says they went through a third-party vendor called Vayama “which probably explains why the Aer Lingus agent on the phone couldn’t access them. They weren’t cheap (€850), but I took a chance and booked them based on the conversation I’d just had with the Aer Lingus agent.”
“After returning to Dublin the following week I submitted both the compensation claim and the expenses claim as instructed. You can probably guess what happened next. Aer Lingus paid the compensation for the cancelled flights (€250 per person, €500 in total) promptly. They did also reimburse the €52 for return bus tickets to and from the airport, but refused to pay for the rebooked flights.
“They maintained they had provided us with acceptable alternative flights (the Manchester layover option). There then followed a series of back and forth emails. I had just gotten a new phone which had a recording of their agent advising us to book the flights ourselves. I sent them a copy of the audio recording, but they refused to back down and told me they felt they had discharged their obligations to me.”
[ Man paid about €400 on Booking.com for hotel that turned out to be closed Opens in new window ]
He says that while the airline “acknowledge that you considered this itinerary unsuitable and chose instead to purchase alternative flights directly, Regulation (EC) 261/2004 does not require reimbursement of independently purchased flights where the airline has already provided an alternative rerouting option. Having reviewed the circumstances of your journey, we remain satisfied that rerouting was provided following the cancellation.”
David accepts that they did provide alternative flights, but says EU laws state that it is required to provide rerouting “under comparable transport conditions, to their final destination at the earliest opportunity”.
“I’ve made a complaint to the Irish Aviation Authority and also lodged a case against them in the Small Claims Court. Am I wasting my time?”
There is no need for the Small Claims court any more.
When we highlighted both of these stories the airline came back to say it “has reviewed the cases of the customers who purchased alternative flights. We have now issued refunds in both cases.”

title: Oil falls as Russia diesel supply prospects counter Gulf supply risks
description: But US politicians warn agreement ‌with Putin may violate US law barring ​imports of Russian energy
content:
Oil prices fell on Tuesday and were on track for their first decline in nearly ​a week, as traders assessed supply risks from attacks on Saudi Arabia while weighing the prospect of additional diesel supplies from Russia.
Brent crude futures fell $1.30, or 1.2 per cent, to $105.35 a barrel by 0329 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $1.25, or 1.3 per cent, at $92.49 a barrel.
Both ​benchmarks climbed nearly $2 a barrel in the previous session, with Brent settling at its highest since September 15th.
US president Donald Trump said Russia ⁠had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel ‌designed ‌to ​deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine.
Additional supplies could help alleviate tightness in global fuel markets, tempering some of the supply concerns that have supported crude prices ⁠recently.
However, “there is considerable scepticism over the Russia-Ukraine energy ​ceasefire, particularly with reports that Russia has hit Ukrainian energy ​targets since Trump announced it,” ING analysts said in a note.
Lawmakers from both parties in the US complained Trump’s agreement ‌with Putin appears to violate US law barring ​imports of Russian energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine.
Concerns over the vulnerability of Gulf energy infrastructure and ⁠shipping lanes remained in focus after Iran-aligned Houthis struck ⁠Riyadh’s international airport over the ​weekend, while tanker attacks were reported near the Strait of Hormuz.
The incidents threatened to derail a recovery in Middle East supplies seen in September, and have reinforced fears of further disruptions along one of the world’s most important energy transit routes.
“Fresh diesel supply from Russia and steadier Saudi flows are offering some relief, yet the market still looks more worried about the risk of further hits to ships or pipelines in the Gulf than it is reassured by extra barrels,” said Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM ‌Trade.
“Until we see clearer signs ⁠of de-escalation, the path of least resistance still leans higher,” he said.
Ministers of OPEC and non-OPEC Participating Countries in the Declaration of Cooperation said shipping and insurance costs have surged to unprecedented levels ‌of over one-third of the commodity value, impeding efficient movement of crude oil and products.
OPEC has revised down its oil demand growth forecast for this ​year to 400,000 barrels per day from 1.4 million bpd at the start ​of the year, in line with developments throughout the year, Haitham Al Ghais, secretary general of the organisation said on Monday. - Reuters

title: TG4 set to pay for ministerial messing
description: Allocation almost 17% lower than broadcaster had targeted for the year in its most recent strategy paper
content:
Spare a thought for TG4 , which has found itself caught in the crossfire of the farcical post- budget row over funding allocations for public broadcasting.
The Irish language station, which will celebrate its 30th birthday later this month, received none of the additional funding it had requested from the Government in last week’s budget.
Some 24 hours after the budget ministers, Simon Harris and Jack Chambers, took their seats last Tuesday, Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan confirmed that TG4’s allocation for 2027 is being left unchanged.
The broadcaster received €65.4 million for 2026 in last year’s budget, an increase of 9 per cent or €5.4 million on the previous year. However, that was almost 17 per cent lower than TG4 had targeted for the year in its most recent strategy document. It’s also almost 26 per cent lower than the €88.6 million the document, published in 2023, envisaged for the 2027 financial year.
It’s worth noting that there has been a step-change in TG4’s funding levels since the start of the decade. Under the previous arts and media minister, Catherine Martin, it grew by 60 per cent over five years to €60 million in 2025. However, the targets TG4 outlined in its strategy document would, at the time, have only brought State funding for TG4 up to the level of Welsh-language public broadcaster S4C.
[ TG4 and Screen Ireland budget funding amounts to ‘cut’ in real terms, industry warns Opens in new window ]
Leaving aside the antics of the past week and the important question of funding adequacy, the fact that TG4 or any large State-funded body should have to wait until budget day – or even after it – to find out what it’s getting seems absurd in 2026.
TG4 commissioned 910 hours of programming from independent producers last year, spending €36.4 million in the process. That is a complex exercise in juggling resources and competing production schedules at the best of times.
Given the last-minute nature of the ministerial decision and you have a lot of plans that have to be reassessed or thrown in the woodchipper altogether.
After RTÉ secured a landmark multiyear settlement from the previous government in 2024, there was some hope in broadcasting circles that this would become the norm. After all of the Coalition’s messing around in the past week, the need for that kind of medium-term funding certainty has never been clearer.

title: ‘I was wary about finding a PA and building a connection’
description: Independence is very important to me – I can plan my days around the hours I have my PA and confidently accept opportunities to do things outside my hometown
content:
S ince 2019, I’ve had many personal assistants (PAs), from educational PAs who would assist me in college to social PAs who tag along on all my adventures because I just love my independence and hate having to drag a family member with me (they’d do it in a heartbeat, but as a mid-20s young girl with a disability, I like my independence).
Amy had been my personal assistant for almost four years, and I struck gold when the Irish Wheelchair Association (IWA) matched her and me.
A PA is somebody who supports people with disabilities to live as independently as possible. It’s one thing finding a willing PA, but it’s another figuring out whether it would be a good and lasting working relationship. Amy and I are similar – we are both extroverts, we read and we can have a conversation about anything. So that really helped us bond.
Our working relationship had to end temporarily recently because Amy is pregnant (I am so happy and excited for her and her family).
I enlisted Amy in helping me find a new PA. “I think when people hear PA, they think of someone in a corporate office and that we’re better paid than we are,” she says. “People also think I say what you can and can’t do, but that’s not the job; it’s much more leader-led and about what you want from the service. It’s about helping to get you out into your community, to work and just supporting the person to be more independent.”
Back when this was a brand-new experience for me, I was wary about finding a PA and building a connection, because I’m an Irish Traveller and was afraid they might be biased in their opinions towards me. Thankfully, with the two social personal assistants I’ve had, that was never an issue. They saw me as a person first, not as an Irish Traveller or a disabled person, which really helped my confidence.
“It’s about making sure that the person is comfortable,” says Amy. “At the start, you get some information from the office. This could be about some of the service users’ interests, and this is what they would like from the service. When you meet the service user in person, it’s about being really relaxed, open, friendly and finding out what the service user wants from the service. I think that’s the most you can do.”
It’s all about the personal relationship, she says. “You won’t gel with every person you meet. You might meet a service user and after an hour, they’d be like, ‘I don’t want her’, and you have to learn not to take it personally. I am lucky to have a good support network from the IWA.”
Independence is very important to me. As a disabled person, I like knowing I have control when making basic decisions and I love not having to rely on my family. I can plan my days around the hours I have my personal assistant and I can confidently accept opportunities to do things outside my home town. This year, I went to Dublin five times within six weeks.
“It’s one of those jobs where you want to become obsolete,” says Amy. “In an ideal world, if the world were totally accessible to you as a wheelchair user, you wouldn’t need me. PAs are very important for those reasons.
“Independence is living your life the way you want to live it despite your limitations. We all have limitations, and to be able to reach your goals with PA support – which is why I think PAs are very important – because we can help service users to do that.”
I ask Amy if she realises the impact her work has on me?
“I’ve had many service users over the years achieve a goal or do something, but it’s not like other jobs where I can go home, and someone could say: ‘How’s work?’ I cannot chat about it because you’re bound by confidentiality, but a moment that really stuck with me was the first time you spoke in Dáil Éireann. To see how much your confidence had built from the first time I met you to being able to do that really showed me how much my work impacts a person.”
[ Changing the world of organ transplants while fearing he could die waiting for one Opens in new window ]
One day, we were in a cafe, and the waiter looked at me, then at Amy, and said: “What would she like?”
Amy just looked at me and said: “Oh, I don’t know, what would you like, Emma?”
The waiter just looked at both of us in surprise and said sorry. That simple act showed I was well able to speak for myself. There are still people who treat disabled people like children.
I’ve had educational PAs who were quieter, so as someone who loves to chat, I really wanted someone I could chat with, and thankfully Amy is very similar to me.
“In those early days, I could tell you were nervous to go out without a family member, which was understandable because you were essentially putting a lot of trust into a stranger, and you could tell your mam was quite nervous, so my main goal was to have both of you at ease.
“At the start, you can be very quiet and shy, but once you get comfortable, you don’t shut up, hah! You really love your independence and are a great advocate for people with disabilities. You have a great personality, are fun, and have a great sense of humour. We could chat about anything. It’s definitely an adventure with you, Emma; no two weeks would look the same.”
[ Has your child settled in to school? The essential prep has nothing to do with reading or writing Opens in new window ]
How does Amy think we could improve the PA system in Ireland?
“They need to look at the structure of the funding because one of the things we face that is difficult is the lack of wage stability. Our wages can go up and down very easily and if you’re applying for a loan or a mortgage, it’s very difficult. If the funding model, coming down from the HSE to your not-for-profit organisation, allowed us to have better wage stability and better hours, it would also positively impact service users because they would get better hours.”
[ Séamas O’Reilly: Am I a soft, overprotective dad bringing his own childhood traumas to bear? Opens in new window ]
What does Amy hope the future of PAs will look like?
“A better funding model and funding for not-for-profit organisations. The Irish Government needs to recognise how important PAs are and how important it is to give a person the right to live in their own home for as long as possible or until they die. That’s what the future of PA and homecare services should look like. Better accessibility. When they’re designing towns, engineers should bring disabled people and their lived experiences into the conversations about whether their plans would work for disabled people.”
What would Amy say to somebody who was considering this career path?
“I would say, do it. It is a very rewarding job even with the challenges. All jobs have their challenges. Somebody with kids would love the flexibility in the hours; it might take you a while to get hours perfectly suited to what you need, but that flexibility suits me perfectly. I can work my hours around childcare. I enjoy my job, I get to experience many things, meet many people, and, to me, it’s just a rewarding job. I would say to others, don’t knock it until you’ve tried it.
“I first became a PA because of the flexible working hours and because I like helping people, the job just suited me. Twelve years later, I’m still here.”
And I’m glad she is. I wouldn’t have done half as much without her support.

title: Home extensions: Four questions worth asking before you decide
description: Before adding square metres to your home, it’s worth figuring out what isn’t working
content:
When a home starts to feel cramped, the obvious conclusion is that you need more space. Perhaps it is time to extend, convert the attic or even to start looking for somewhere bigger. Sometimes more space is exactly what you need, but before adding square metres, it is worth figuring out what isn’t working and whether building is the best way to fix it. A surprisingly large house can feel too small if the layout is poor, while a modest home can work brilliantly when the space is used well. Here are four questions worth asking before a decision on whether to extend.
Start by working out exactly why your home feels short of space. Sometimes the answer is clear. You may genuinely need another bedroom or bathroom, the kitchen may be too small or there may be no room for a utility space. In those cases, additional floor area may be the only solution.
But sometimes it is less obvious. You may simply feel the house is cramped or no longer works as well as it once did. If so, try to identify the particular pinch points rather than jumping to a conclusion.
One useful exercise is to track a typical week at home and notice where things become difficult. Is storage an issue? Is everyone competing for the same space at certain times of the day?
Thinking about how you actually live can reveal a lot. Simply saying you need more space isn’t much of a brief to work with. Knowing that you need enough room for six people to sit comfortably around the table every day is much more useful. Once you know what is missing, you can work out whether you genuinely need additional floor area and what that space needs to achieve.
It is surprising how often people feel cramped in houses with relatively generous footprints because everyday life is happening in only part of them. Everyone might be squeezed into a kitchen and family room at the back, while a spacious sittingroom at the front is rarely used. You may have a diningroom used only occasionally, or even an entire room that has gradually become storage space.
Look at these areas with fresh eyes. Could a little-used room take on a different function or be incorporated into an adjoining room? Small changes, such as moving a doorway, changing how two rooms connect, or swapping their functions, can change how a house works without adding a single square metre.
[ Make the most of your attic space and the value of your home Opens in new window ]
There is rarely just one way to solve a problem. The same brief might be achieved through reconfiguration, a small addition or a more substantial extension, so explore the options before committing to one. This can be difficult when you have lived in a house for a long time and become fixed in your views on how each room is used. It is equally easy to become attached to a solution you have seen elsewhere and try to force it into your own home.
Impartial professional advice can be useful at this stage. A fresh pair of eyes may identify possibilities you hadn’t considered and uncover a simple solution.
Sometimes the problem isn’t that the house is too small, but that it is being asked to accommodate too much stuff. This comes up particularly when planning utility rooms, bootrooms and storage spaces. The list of everything that needs to be accommodated can quickly become very long, and the obvious response is to design a room large enough to fit it all.
Before doing that, ask what genuinely needs to stay. This isn’t about extreme decluttering. Homes contain stuff, everyone needs storage, and good storage makes an enormous difference to how well a house works. But before creating more space to store everything you own, it is worth considering how much of it you need. A good clear-out at the start of a project may not only make the house feel less cramped, it could also change how much additional space you actually need.
A substantial renovation or extension is likely to exist much longer than the stage of life that prompted it, so think first about how your needs might change down the line.
A family with several teenagers may feel desperately short of space now, but if they are approaching college age, the household could look very different within five or six years. The last thing you may want then is an enormous house with two people rattling around in it.
The reverse is also true. Young children who happily share bedrooms and play together today are likely to want more privacy as they get older. Nobody can predict exactly what life will look like in 10 or 15 years, but foreseeable changes are worth considering. The aim isn’t to design for every eventuality, but to avoid investing heavily in additional space to solve a problem that may only be temporary.
By the time you have worked through these questions, you should have a much clearer idea of whether you need more space, and how much of it. The answer may be a substantial extension, a smaller addition combined with reworking the existing layout, or no extension at all. Don’t start with a preconceived idea of what you should build. Start with how you need your home to work: then find the simplest, most effective way to achieve it.

title: ‘On the first day I confessed I’d lost my fire. And then they took me on an adventure’
description: Patrick J O’Reilly of Tinderbox was worn out. Going back to his theatre roots sparked the flame that has become a new take on The Glass Menagerie
content:
W hen approaching a new Tinderbox production, under its artistic director Patrick J O’Reilly , it’s usually best to expect the unexpected.
In 2024 he removed Federico Garcia Lorca ’s play Yerma from the steamy heat and exotic passion of southern Spain and relocated it among a gaggle of tipsy christening-party guests in the car park of a Co Louth hotel.
Earlier this year he reworked George Orwell ’s political allegory Animal Farm into a fiery debate on propaganda and freedom of speech , using as his mouthpiece a group of feisty female protesters banged up in a detention cell.
In 2023 he called upon dazzling gaming technology to pitch Eugène Ionesco ’s absurdist play Rhinoceros into an unsettling, neon-lit virtual environment peopled by a community of automaton-type avatars. His new take was named that year’s best revival of a play at the UK Theatre Awards.
O’Reilly is now in the process of immersing himself and his cast in a cinematic revival of a 20th-century American classic, calling on the world of the movies as an escape route, a refuge, a retreat for its troubled central character, Tom Wingfield, played here by Thomas Galashan.
In his magnificent memory play The Glass Menagerie, Tennessee Williams created Tom as a thinly veiled version of himself. As the audience settles into an alternative reality, cocooned inside the safety and darkness of the performance space, on stage Tom’s regular trips to the cinema disguise the brooding demons bedevilling his claustrophobic home life, with his mercurial mother, Amanda ( Úna Kavanagh ), his introverted, physically frail sister, Laura (Louise Parker), and her precious collection of small glass animals.
O’Reilly did his professional training at the Jacques Lecoq International Theatre School in Paris. Its distinctive style of carefully calibrated physical theatre exerts itself, time after time, in his work. He recently stepped into the rehearsal room at the Mac in Belfast, where Tinderbox is the resident company, fresh and re-energised after completing a two-week intensive training programme at Lecoq’s new premises in the historic French walled city of Avignon.
“Being back at Lecoq these past couple of weeks has given me the final piece in my professional jigsaw,” O’Reilly says. “I hadn’t been there for 14 years, so to do the whole two-year training again, in just 10 days, alongside former alumni from all over the world, has been incredible. It’s given me the official accreditation to teach Lecoq technique, which kind of closes the circle for me.
“Under the same tutors as before, we did tragedy, comedy, melodrama, clowning ... all the things you do in the course of your training. Then they ask you why you do it. What’s your motivation? It’s like you lay all the secrets of your art on the floor and question your own motives, your decisions, your performance choices. Essentially, you confront yourself. It reinvigorated me.
“On the first day I stood up in the room and confessed, ‘J’ai perdu mon feu – I’ve lost my fire.’ That’s why I’m here. And they said, okay, we have to help you find it again. I told them, ‘Je suis fatigué – I’m tired.’
“And so I was, tired of doing of two shows a year, four-week rehearsals for 10-day runs. I’d lost the spark. I was thinking that I’m 45 years old now. What do my next 20 years look like? And then they took me on an adventure.
“It was as though my career didn’t exist inside the school; it didn’t matter. We were being returned to our creative roots. I had a few moments of breakthrough, when I said, ‘Yes, this is the fire, this is the theatre, this is the thing that’s transformative.’
“They are brutal in their honesty. You’re sitting on benches, barefoot, and then you begin the voyage, the cataclysm, in silence. You perform a complete theatrical experience, alone and behind a mask.
“At the end you remove the mask and ask yourself what has changed. The answer is, I’ve changed. Getting back to those roots, silently, deep inside your own head ... it was terrifying – but magic.”
Filled with new resolve and artistic determination, O’Reilly has returned home to The Glass Menagerie, a play he describes as incredible, complex and breathtaking.
Drawing on his rediscovered techniques of rhythms and movement, introspection and questioning, he is encouraging his characters to focus their performances on the four natural elements: earth, wind, water and fire. Amanda is fire, Tom is wind, Laura is water and Jim, Tom’s ambitious friend (Jacob Baird), who offers Laura a brief moment of release, is earth.
The Lecoq mantra is all about the mechanics of movement, what they call the “tout bouge”, the “everything moves”. Its poetic discourse in theatre-making is all about movement.
O’Reilly explains how this philosophy works in practice.
“With Amanda we’re playing a lot with fire. One moment she’s explosive, she’s got sparks; the next she’s ash, then she’s flames. We’re using poetic metaphors and objects to look at the physicality of each character’s development.
“I’ve brought back with me a realisation that each movement has to be clear; each decision has to be clear. Every movement has a beginning, a middle and an end, and it’s my job as a theatremaker to make the performers see and achieve those beginnings, middles and ends.”
When he was developing ideas for reviving and revising Yerma, O’Reilly was disarmingly frank about the parallels between the christening-party scenario and the chaotic family get-togethers he had experienced while growing up in the Co Louth borderlands.
Once again he’s bringing a sharp sense of personal identity to his choice and treatment of The Glass Menagerie.
“I love doing memory plays: The Man Who Fell to Pieces [which he wrote], The Upside Down House, even Ubu, with its flashbacks and looking to the past,” he says.
“I find with Tennessee Williams, and especially with this play, it is obviously semi-autobiographical. You can feel it in the room. As a queer writer, you can feel his need to leave his mother and his sister, Rosa. He just couldn’t stay.
“I can see lots of parallels and similarities with being a young, queer man, needing to leave a very small town, leaving a family behind, fleeing the nest.
“But how do we look back on those memories? How do we reconcile any differences of remorse or shame or regret? That became very much a centre point for choosing the play.
“To be very honest, in the current financial climate we have to do a classic play in a contemporary way so that we can bring in the audiences. But then that gives us the freedom to do new or lesser-known work in the next part of our programme.”
We don’t need tricksy effects or a complicated set when you have a play like this, with such multilayered lives and characters
Director and cast are revelling in the textual and dramaturgical perfection of Williams’s play, which they will perform at Belfast International Arts Festival exactly as it is on the page, starkly and simply, without special effects or script changes.
Through Paul Keogan’s staging and lighting, the audience will be brought directly into the world of 1940s American movies. As in those old black-and-white films, a live pianist will be on stage, in the shape of the composer Daniel Quigley, whose score incorporates a motif for the glass menagerie, mixed in with sounds from the American movie playbook and snatches of southern smooth jazz.
“The reason I chose the prism of the movies is that there is such an importance in Tom’s need to escape his life through film,” O’Reilly says. “When I read and reread the play, I felt it needs a second space that is poetic. It’s not realism. Tennessee Williams very much gives you the invitation to be poetic and symbolic and to play with memory in a way that doesn’t feel limited.
“It’s all in there but interpreted through a different lens. The idea of editing memory is, for me, really interesting, especially the memories we choose.
“Tom’s escapism, his need to move into fantasy, can only last for so long until reality catches up, and he is only able to look at his reality through the lens of film.
“We don’t need tricksy effects or a complicated set when you have a play like this, with such multilayered lives and characters.
“Amanda is the driving force, the fire. She’s a struggling single mother, abandoned by her husband and in danger of loving her children to death. Tom’s perspective is about the conflict of desperately wanting to leave and be free, while being pulled back by the family. When they release him, he has to go.
[ ‘We can all see you’: Gillian Anderson addresses ‘distracting’ fans in front row Opens in new window ]
“Laura is all about water, seeing the world through the clear glass of her miniature menagerie, drowning under the suffocating love of her mother. Jim, the gentleman caller, is earth. He is rooted; his branches are extending throughout the space. He is the light that the family are looking towards.
“I think that Tennessee Williams has done an incredible job in enabling us to have sympathy and compassion and frustration and anger and hope for every family member.
“If those characters had had the ability to articulate their feelings, it would have been a very different play. So it has been a very beautiful and moving journey thus far, in exploring the physicality of the world of the play and then allowing the exquisite text to be the thing that drives that world.”
The Glass Menagerie is at the Mac, as part of Belfast International Arts Festival , from Tuesday, October 20th, until Tuesday, October 27th. The festival begins on Wednesday, October 14th, and runs until Sunday, November 8th

title: Cáineadh ar an gCáinaisnéis
description: Bhí Buiséad na seachtaine seo caite ina údar mór díomá d’eagrais teanga
content:
Táthar ag súil go dtiocfaidh soiléiriú go luath ar cá háit go díreach a ndáilfear an t-airgead a fógraíodh d’earnáil na Gaeilge i mBuiséad 2027 an tseachtain seo caite.
Tionólfar cruinnithe an tseachtain seo idir oifigigh Fhoras na Gaeilge agus státseirbhísigh chun caiteachas Bhuiséid 2027 a phlé.
Agus an t-éileamh poiblí agus beartais Stáit don Ghaeilge de shíor ag fás, bhí díomá nach beag ar ghníomhaithe agus ar eagrais Ghaeilge an tseachtain seo caite nuair nár fógraíodh ach ardú níos lú ná €1 mhilliún (€160.8 milliún ina iomláine) don earnáil.
Cháin Conradh na Gaeilge “an t-ardú is lú in aon cháinaisnéis le dhá Rialtas anuas”. Dúirt Julian de Spáinn, Ard-Rúnaí Chonradh na Gaeilge: “ní hamháin go bhfuil deiseanna caillte ach beidh ceist ciorruithe i mbuiséid eagraíochtaí Gaeilge agus Gaeltachta áirithe ag teacht chun cinn arís.
“Beidh an Rialtas ag caitheamh céatadán níos lú de mhórchiste an Stáit in 2027 (0.16%) i gcomparáid le 2026 (0.17%). Is ionann sin agus céim siar in áit céim chun cinn. Níl sin sásúil. Níl sin dearfach.”
Tháinig laghdú suas le 50% ar mhaoiniú Fhoras na Gaeilge ó 2008 i leith ach tá fás suntasach tar éis teacht ar chúraimí an eagrais ag an am céanna.
I mí Eanáir 2025, bhí ar an bhForas ciorruithe tromchúiseacha a fhógairt de bharr ghéarchéim mhaoinithe na heagraíochta.
Faoiseamh mór a bhí ann anuraidh nuair a fógraíodh ardú 30% sa bhuiséad don bhliain seo. Cuireadh €25 mhilliún sa bhreis ar fáil do Roinn na Gaeltachta agus cuireadh €2 mhilliún breise ar fáil don Fhoras.
Chuir Foras na Gaeilge aighneacht réamh-bhuiséid faoi bhráid an Rialtais i mbliana inar dúradh go bhfuil “riosca córasach” cruthaithe de dheasca easpa maoinithe. Cé gur chabhair a bhí san €2 mhilliún a fuair an Foras anuraidh, tuigtear nach raibh a dhóthain ann ach a ligfeadh don eagras ‘anáil a tharraingt’.
Cé go bhfuil uaillmhian agus dualgais an stáit ag méadú i bhfianaise reachtaíocht cearta teanga, d’fhógair an Foras go bhfuil “acmhainn an chórais seachadta ag laghdú”.
D’éiligh an Foras €2.6 milliún le haghaidh mórscéimeanna teanga i mbliana ach ní bhfuarthas fiú leath an mhéid sin agus tuigtear, i bhfianaise rátaí boilscithe agus costais eile, go bhfuil buairt áirithe ann i dtaobh an infheistithe a bhí beartaithe.
I measc na mórscéimeanna teanga ar chlár oibre Fhoras na Gaeilge tá scéim d’Ionaid Phobail Ghaeilge, scéimeanna féilte agus ealaíon, deiseanna úsáide do dhaoine óga, maoiniú do na sé cheanneagraíocht Ghaeilge, pleanáil teanga agus feachtais feasachta.
Beidh ar oifigigh an Fhorais a mheas anois cá háit ar féidir an t-airgead atá ar fáil a chaitheamh ar na forbairtí a leag Foras na Gaeilge amach ina n-aighneacht bhuiséid.
Ní Foras na Gaeilge amháin nach bhfuair an t-airgead a éilíodh. Anuraidh, ceadaíodh €5.4m sa bhreis do TG4 agus d’éiligh an stáisiún €11 mhilliún sa bhreis i mbliana (€76.4 milliún san iomlán), ach nuair a tháinig an crú ar an tairne níor ceadaíodh pingin rua sa bhreis.
Dúirt Deirdre Ní Choistín, Ard-Stiúrthóir TG4, gur “cúis mhór díomá” é nár fógraíodh méadú don stáisiún sa cháinaisnéis.
“Tá Éire cheana féin i measc na maoinitheoirí is ísle san Eoraip ó thaobh na meáin seirbhíse poiblí a mhaoiniú.”
Dúirt sí freisin go mbeidh “impleachtaí” ag an gcinneadh ar TG4 in 2027.
Bhain an Buiséad stangadh freisin as gníomhaithe teanga nuair nár luadh géarchéim thithíochta na Gaeltachta.
Ba thráthúil mar sin, ar oíche Aoine na seachtaine seo caite, gur fhoilsigh taighdeoirí ó Choláiste na Tríonóide páipéar taighde a thug foláireamh go bhfuil an ghéarchéim thithíochta ag bagairt ar inmharthanacht na Gaeilge mar theanga phobail i nGaeltacht Chorca Dhuibhne.
Dúirt na taighdeoirí gur léiríodh difríocht shuntasach idir teacht isteach na ndaoine agus praghsanna na dtithe sa cheantar ina ndearnadh an taighde.
“Nuair a chuirtear é seo le heaspa tithe buanchónaithe mar thoradh ar thithe samhraidh agus ar thithe ar cíos gearrthréimhseach is bagairt é do thodhchaí phobal labhartha na Gaelainne in Iarthar Dhuibhneach,” a dúirt an Dr Ann Nolan, príomhthaighdeoir an tionscadail.
Ag tagairt don airgead a cuireadh ar fáil sa Bhuiséad le daoine a chumasú sa Ghaeltacht chun feabhas a chur ar a gcuid scileanna teanga, dúirt lucht an taighde nach leor idirghabháil teanga amháin chun creimeadh na teanga a aisiompú. Tá gá le cur chuige comhtháite chun tabhairt faoi na dálaí struchtúrtha atá mar chúis leis an gcreimeadh sin.
Chuir Conradh na Gaeilge fáilte roimh an taighde agus dúirt go léiríonn na torthaí go bhfuil “géarghá le freagairt chuimsitheach, tras-rialtais, chun todhchaí na Gaeltachta mar phobal beo Gaeilge a chosaint.”

title: House building slides in September
description: Construction industry grew only narrowly last month but companies optimistic for future
content:
House building fell last month even as activity in construction accelerated marginally in the Republic, new figures show.
The Government wants 300,000 homes built in the State by 2030, while it has pledged billions of euro to infrastructure projects meant to pave the way for residential construction.
But a report on Tuesday shows that house building activity fell in the Republic in September, even while other parts of the construction industry expanded.
AIB’s construction purchasing managers’ index (PMI) registered 50.4 last month, indicating slight growth in activity on August.
Any reading below the benchmark 50 signals a slowdown on the previous month, while a result above that figure indicates growth.
Building activity has increased for three months running, AIB said in a statement, having slowed sharply earlier in the year as high energy prices hit the industry.
Companies surveyed last month cited rising demand as the factor behind the increased activity. However, the house building index slid to 47.2 in September, showing that the rate of residential construction fell during last month.
September’s fall in residential construction followed a drop in August, the index states.
Growth continued in the other categories that make up the index, the figures show.
[ There is nothing more Irish than a former housing minister lobbying on behalf of a developer Opens in new window ]
Commercial construction, which monitors the building of factories, shopping centres and other business premises, increased to 52.4. September was the third consecutive month in which commercial building grew, the PMI shows.
Civil engineering, which includes State-sponsored infrastructure building, returned to growth, with that section of the index hitting 52.3.
Builders continued grappling with rising fuel costs, a consequence of the US-Iran war, last month, according to AIB senior economist John Fahey. High prices “remained a key challenge” for the industry in September, he said.
Increased fuel bills have hindered construction growth since the war’s outbreak in February.
[ Residential property: All you need to know Opens in new window ]
“At the same time, the construction sector saw a fall in staffing levels, with employment numbers dipping in September following a sustained period of growth over the past year,” Fahey added.
September’s fall in employment ended 10 consecutive months where builders hired more staff, the index indicates.
But other data suggest encouraging signs. New orders, which indicate future work, rose for the third month in a row, said the economist.
“Meanwhile, construction firms’ level of confidence in the prospect of higher activity levels over the coming 12 months remained resilient,” said Fahey. “Positive sentiment was underpinned by rising new orders and a healthy pipeline of new projects.”

title: Credit unions win again as Re-turn, Ryanair and RTÉ fare poorly for customer service
description: Customer experience scores fell globally but hit highest level in Ireland in almost a decade
content:
The Irish credit union movement has been ranked as best for customer service for the 11th consecutive year, but Re-turn , RTÉ , Ryanair , Dublin Bus , Ticketmaster , Irish Water and a host of social media have all found themselves at the wrong end of the league of companies, new research suggests.
The annual assessment of Irish brands from the CX Academy suggests that while customer experience scores are falling globally, they are climbing in Ireland, hitting their highest level in almost a decade.
The improved performance was, the CX Academy said, driven by companies in the supermarket, retail and financial space, with those sectors making up six of the top 10 and 21 of the top 30 rankings.
By contrast, companies and organisations in the entertainment and leisure sphere, the public sector and utilities were among the poorest performers.
Ireland’s undisputed customer experience champion remains the Irish credit union, which topped the overall survey as well as the financial sector.
Pharmacies and wellness continue to lead from the front for customer experience in the retail sector, making up three of the top 10 companies, with Life Pharmacy coming in second place, McCabes in seventh and Holland & Barrett joint ninth.
Specsavers maintained its strong recent performance, moving up from sixth to third, while Shannon Airport, which landed in the top 10 for the first time in the last report, has maintained its fourth position. PhoneWatch has moved from 11th to fifth this time round.
[ ‘I find it obscene’: Aer Lingus response upsets family dealing with terminal illness Opens in new window ]
Several brands recorded significant improvements to move into the top 10. Zurich Insurance climbed 21 places to sixth, Ikea jumped 27 places to eighth, and the Passport Service, the highest ranked public sector organisation, climbed 25 places to finish joint ninth.
The news was not so good for two of the best performers from the last survey, KFC and Subway. They recorded the biggest falls this year, with the former falling 77 places to 92nd and the latter falling 69 places to 98th.
CX Academy said their performances were emblematic of a weak performance by the restaurant sector, with a broad retreat particularly noticeable across the fast-food category. Burger King fell 45 places to joint 98th alongside Subway, and McDonald’s fell 41 places to joint 113th beside another fast-food brand, Eddie Rockets.
The bottom 10 was made up of the Department of Social Protection , Ryanair, RTÉ, Re-turn – making its very first appearance on the list – Instagram , TikTok , Irish Water, Ticketmaster and Dublin Bus, with Facebook finishing in last place.
[ Man paid about €400 on Booking.com for hotel that turned out to be closed Opens in new window ]
Michael Killeen, the head of the CX Academy and author of the report, said the common thread in the data is that “these are largely services people use out of necessity or habit rather than choice: social platforms, public transport, utilities and non-discretionary public services, which tend to score low across all areas rather than on any single one”.
The survey is conducted on behalf of the CX Academy by Amárach. It presents survey respondents with a list of companies from which they choose the good and the bad.

title: More segregated cycles lanes, please
description: The overwhelming answer would be protective infrastructure
content:
Sir, – ​Your report on the Road Safety Authority’s ( RSA ) latest helmet campaign highlights the devastating, lifelong reality of traumatic brain injury (“ One fall without a helmet changed my life forever ”, News, October 9th).
​Yet if the RSA asked people who cycle regularly what would make them safe, the overwhelming answer would be protective infrastructure.
​The RSA regularly commissions observational surveys on compliance with helmets and high-visibility clothing, despite neither being required by law for people using pedal cycles. Absent from its research, however, is any evaluation of how much of an average commuter journey takes place on segregated cycle lanes. On my own daily 7km commute through Dublin city centre, it amounts to less than 50m of flexible wands.
​The persistence of this blind spot reflects an outdated mindset. Rather than urging vulnerable road users to armour themselves against increasingly heavy vehicles, we should look to countries like the Netherlands. There, the safety of children cycling to school is achieved by providing them with high-quality segregated routes, not plastic coatings. – Yours, etc,

title: ESRI report examines options around taxation of wealth
description: Report comes as Irish household wealth grew dramatically over 10 years to 2023
content:
Wealth taxes are back on the Irish agenda, with the Department of Finance funding a joint study with the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) , published on Tuesday, of different ways of taxing wealth.
It comes as Irish household wealth has grown rapidly. In 2023, total net household wealth in Ireland was two and a half times the amount it had been just 10 years earlier, according to the report.
Although the share of that wealth held by the poorest half of households has increased in that time, almost half of all wealth continues to be controlled by the wealthiest 10 per cent of Irish households.
The structure of household wealth has also changed, the report found, with business assets accounting for a larger share “particularly among households at the top of the wealth distribution”. Further down the wealth chain, the family home continues to account for the largest share of household wealth.
The study found that, to maximise revenue, all assets outside pension funds should be taxed, with no exemptions for things like family homes, farms or businesses.
“Our wealth tax scenario analysis shows that the breadth of the tax base matters more for revenue potential than the threshold at which liability begins, with broad-base scenarios consistently generating larger aggregate tax liabilities than those with extensive exemptions,” write authors Rachel Slaymaker and Chi Tran of the ESRI and Department of Finance economists Federica De Blasio and Emmet Ryan.
Doing so, the research paper showed, would allow the tax to be set above a very high threshold where only the richest 1.5 per cent of Irish households would be affected.
It accepted that including business wealth, farms and the family home would be politically sensitive. As they are less liquid, such assets would also be harder to value on an ongoing basis.
[ Tax-rich Ireland at one remove from debt zeitgeist Opens in new window ]
If you allow fairly wide exemptions, the paper argued, you need to dramatically lower the threshold, bringing many more households into the wealth tax net to secure reasonable tax revenue.
The report cited the 2022 Commission on Taxation and Welfare recommendation for a gradual shift from taxing work towards taxes on wealth, capital, property and consumption, to meet the increased costs of an ageing population, public services and the climate transition, “while maintaining fiscal sustainability”.
However, it accepted that, all households, even the wealthiest could have trouble finding the cash to meet wealth tax liabilities from cash income.
Wealth taxes fell from favour in the early years of the century, the report said. Twelve European countries levied an annual tax on net wealth in 1990 but by this year, only Norway, Spain and Switzerland do so.
Limited yields, administrative and valuation difficulties, avoidance and evasion, were cited as reasons for the tax’s diminishing popularity, alongside concerns of governments around capital mobility.
Concerns around the concentration of wealth, together with pressures on public finances and the limitations of tax systems that rely predominantly on income flows, have contributed to renewed international interest in net wealth taxation in recent years.
“Recent research has increasingly emphasised that the effects of a wealth tax depend not only on whether wealth is taxed, but on how such taxes are designed,” the report said.

title: A timber support is getting in the way in our attic. Can it be removed?
description: Do I need an engineer or building surveyor, or will the contractor be able to advise me?
content:
In our attic space, there is a vertical timber support running down from the roof towards the floor level, which is obstructing how we would like to use and finish the space. From what I can see, the support appears to be tied into the surrounding roof structure, but it is not clear whether it is acting as a structural stud, a support for the dormer cheeks or rafters, or simply a trim or finishing piece.
Various online discussions about attic rooms suggest that these timbers often form part of the load ‑ bearing arrangement transferring roof and dormer loads back into the main structure, and that altering them without proper design can affect the stability of the roof or dormer.
I want to remove this timber down to floor level or replace it with a less intrusive arrangement, but I am aware that any change to existing structural members in an attic conversion needs to be approached very carefully. I’m trying to understand what the typical attic room framing practice is, so I know if it’s a big job or not. Do I need an engineer or building surveyor to review, or will the contractor be able to advise me?
The timber should be treated as structural unless and until a competent inspection establishes otherwise. Its appearance or position alone is not enough to determine its purpose, and even a relatively slender member may be carrying load or providing restraint.
A roof window is normally formed within the existing rafters. Where a rafter must be cut, the opening may require strengthened side rafters and horizontal trimmers to transfer the interrupted roof loads around the opening. A dormer is generally more complex and may include cheek studs, a front frame, headers, trimmed rafters and connections to the roof or floor structure. A vertical timber in this location could therefore be supporting a dormer cheek, a rafter or trimmer, transferring load to a beam or joist below, restraining the frame against movement or merely supporting plasterboard. This cannot be confirmed without seeing how it is connected at the top and bottom and what lies behind the finishes.
The scale of the work could range from straightforward removal of a nonstructural lining support to a significant structural alteration. If the member is load-bearing, a replacement arrangement might involve strengthened timberwork, a new beam, revised connections and temporary propping while the work is carried out. Cutting it first and assessing the consequences afterwards could result in movement, sagging, cracking or local instability.
An experienced contractor may offer a useful initial view and can assist with careful opening up, pricing and construction. However, the contractor should not be the sole person deciding that an apparently integrated roof member is redundant. I recommend an inspection by a chartered structural engineer with experience of domestic roof alterations. The engineer should examine the member’s bearings and fixings, the adjacent rafters, dormer framing, floor structure and any available drawings, and then confirm in writing whether it can be removed or provide a suitable replacement detail and temporary works sequence.
[ I’m worried that our 1990s attic conversion may not be safe. Should I do something about it? Opens in new window ]
A chartered building surveyor can review the wider attic conversion, identify defects or compliance concerns, prepare a scope of work and oversee the project. Where a new load path or structural substitution is required, the detailed design should normally come from the engineer.
The proposed alteration may also have implications under the building regulations, particularly Part A relating to structure. Planning, building-control and certification requirements should be checked separately. If the attic is used, or intended to be used, as habitable accommodation, the review should extend beyond this timber to matters such as floor strength and compartmentation, wider fire safety issues such as detection and escape, compliance of the stairs, insulation, ventilation and condensation risk.
[ Why can’t I enlarge the rooflights in my apartment? Opens in new window ]
As no photographs, drawings or site inspection have been provided, no definitive conclusion can be reached about this particular timber. It should remain undisturbed until professionally assessed.
Damian King is a chartered building surveyor and a member of the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland

title: Is my €1,000 monthly childcare bill really falling to €550?
description: Calculating your childcare costs requires navigating a series of interconnected fees and subsidies
content:
I pay €1,000 per month for creche (full time). What is the Budget 2027 impact here? I saw a headline suggesting childcare was being reduced to €550 per month up to senior infants but I can’t imagine that’s right. I hope so but that’s a crazy decrease.
Getting your head around childcare costs can be fiendishly complex. There are different subsidies depending on your financial status and the age of the child and different bands depending on how long the child is in care.
And if it is any consolation, it is not just you and other parents who get confused. In his speech, the Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform, Jack Chambers , did say he was “reducing the maximum childcare fees paid by parents, from €735 to €550 per month for children up to senior infants”, putting €2,200 a year back into parents’ pockets.
Not quite – at least not for everyone, including you. But that does not mean there was not good news for you on childcare in the budget – at least from September of next year when the budget childcare measures kick in.
The Minister was referring to the maximum amount a parent of a child receiving between 40 and 50 hours of care a week can be charged in a creche that has signed up to the Government’s “core funding” scheme, where Government subsidises the cost of care. This is called Band E.
If you are paying €1,000 – or more accurately €959 – a month, you will be in Band F, where your child is receiving care for more than 50 hours a week.
And you are far from alone in having been taken aback by talk of the €735 and €550 maximums.
The Minister’s team insist that Band E is the one most commonly used by parents across the State. That may be so; the statement was not accompanied by figures. What does seem certain is that most parents in Dublin and some surrounding commuter counties, as well as areas of Cork and Galway, are paying Band F fees like you.
[ Budget 2027’s childcare package has triggered storm of protest from parents. Here’s why Opens in new window ]
The net cost to you is determined by two things: fee per band and the personal subsidy to which each child is entitled, depending on your income.
Under the budget measures, the fee for Band F will fall from €336 a week to €300. And, for those on the universal subsidy (anyone with family income of more than €73,000), the subsidy for children up to senior infants will rise to €2.50 from €2.15 per hour up to a maximum of 45 hours.
If your income is below €73,000, the subsidy may be higher and, if it is below €36,500, that could be as high as €5.10 an hour.
When they say household income, they mean income minus any pension contributions you pay. You also do not include certain welfare payments and, if you have more than one child, there are further income disregards.
Anyway, back to the numbers. That €2.50 an hour universal subsidy amounts to €112.50 a week. Taking this from your €300 “fee”, you are left with €187.50. From September next year (11 months in the future), that will be your weekly fee, amounting to €750 a month.
That means a fall of at least €209 in your childcare cost per child each month, or somewhere between €2,300 and €2,500 over the year. So good news, if not quite a drop in charge to €550.
Of course, that is only if you are in a creche that operates under Government core funding. If not, they are free to charge what the market will bear.
