title: New build, renovation or replacement? Seven window and door decisions to make before comparing quotes in Ireland
description: If you’re planning to build a warm home, you can explore Fenbro’s services in Ireland
content:
I got a text from a friend a few weeks ago. She is mid-renovation, and was in a state of mild window-induced panic.
“The price difference between the quotes is mad!” One was over twice the price of the other. The frame materials were different, but on paper it all looked fairly similar. Her question to me was: “Is there an enormous difference ... or is it all kinda the same?” How was she supposed to know? Most of us buy windows once or twice in our lives, and suddenly we’re expected to be fluent in frame materials, glazing, and U-values, while trying to compare quotes that may not even cover the same things.
My short answer to my friend was: “No.” It’s not all the same. But the more expensive quote is not necessarily the right one either. Before you choose based on numbers, make these seven decisions first.
Installing a full set of windows in a new-build is a different job to replacing the windows in an existing house. And if you’re in a protected structure or an ACA, you may require additional planning or conservation consideration.
Pin down the scope before you ask for a price. Are you replacing everything, or just the worst offenders? Are you going for sliders or French doors? A vague brief will get you a vague quote.
Much earlier than you’d think, is my short answer. Windows and doors crucially impact many of your design decisions. Lead times can vary – always ask how long it takes from signed order to delivery.
Fenbro has supplied windows and doors for projects across Ireland, particularly in Dublin, from replacements to full new-build packages. You can discuss your window and door project with them here .
The size and position of every opening affects structure, insulation, layout, lighting, sightlines, and furniture placement. A low window can stop you running units along a wall. Choosing French doors over a slider may dictate where the dining table goes. If you want a flush threshold to your patio, that has to be designed in from the very start.
Decisions are more practical here. Who will survey the opening? Can the work be done room-by-room if you’re still living in the home? This being Ireland, it’s also smart to ask what will happen if it starts lashing mid-fit.
This was the heart of my friend’s question. Is there really an enormous difference between frame materials?
There is, but it’s not a simple ladder from “cheap” to “good”.
uPVC can offer strong thermal performance, requires little maintenance, and is generally the more budget-friendly option. Aluminium is the one to look at when durability and a crisp contemporary finish are the priority. Personally, I went with aluminium sliding doors in the back of my home. I was averse to uPVC at the time; my perception was that they were chunky and plasticky looking. But my mind has changed in recent years. Good quality uPVC that is well installed can be an excellent option, one I would happily choose for plenty of projects and put the savings elsewhere.
This is the technical part, so bear with me. “Double” or “triple” glazed is not enough information; you need to ask for the U-value of the whole window – the frame and the glass together. The lower the U-value, the less heat escapes. It’s not the only performance figure that matters; with a large opening, solar gain and summer overheating can matter just as much as winter heat loss.
In recent history, we as a nation have tended to opt for as much glass as possible. Think this through carefully, and consider the orientation and how exposed the opening is. The right glazing and frame for a sheltered north-facing bedroom may differ from a large south- or west-facing livingroom.
For homeowners in Dublin and other busy urban locations, acoustic comfort, ventilation, and security can be just as important as thermal performance.
Your decision is not simply which is most technically impressive, but which will perform best for your home.
Generally, yes, especially on a new-build or major renovation. That doesn’t mean every window and door needs to use the same material or have exactly the same specification. Different openings may call for different solutions depending on their size, orientation, exposure, and use.
The important thing is to plan the overall window and door package as a cohesive whole. Consider how the frame depths, positions, heights, sightlines, and colours work together, as well as the performance required from each product, and how delivery timings will be co-ordinated.
Fenbro supplies made-to-measure uPVC and aluminium windows, entrance doors and sliding systems to homeowners across Ireland, allowing the complete package to be planned as one project. As the Fenbro team puts it: “For a new build or major renovation, we recommend treating the windows, front door, and sliding doors as one project. It makes it much easier to co-ordinate design, performance, colours, and timing.”
You can see Fenbro projects completed in Dublin here .
This is far more important than most people realise.
Before accepting any window quote, agree who is handling measurement, technical checks, order approval, signoffs, delivery, removal of old windows, fitting, making good, disposal, warranty, and after-sales. Do not assume something is included – check and confirm, in writing.
Arrangements vary and can impact the price. Fenbro, for instance, supplies and delivers the products, while measuring and fitting are handled by an installer: either your own, or one of the independent fitting teams Fenbro can connect you with, under a separate agreement. You can discuss your window and door project with Fenbro early on to see what suits you.
Which brings us back to my friend’s conundrum: a lower quote doesn’t necessarily mean a lower overall cost. Go through quotes line by line.
Start with the specification: frame material, glazing, U-values, number and type of openings, colours (inside and outside), hardware, trickle vents. Then the scope: delivery, fitting, removal, making good, disposal. Finally, review lead times, warranties, and after-sales service. If one quote includes specific details and one doesn’t, you’re not comparing the same job.
Fenbro’s advice here is simple: “The biggest mistake we see is homeowners comparing only the final figure. Two quotations can look similar while covering very different specifications, glazing, delivery, and fitting arrangements.” Don’t compare glazing values alone – ask for the Uw value of the complete window, not just the Ug value of the glass.
If you’re hoping for an SEAI grant, do your homework separately and before you commit to anything. Eligibility and contractor requirements are set by the SEAI, not by suppliers, and you should always check the latest at SEAI.ie.
If you already have quotations, Fenbro can help you compare the specification and explain where the main differences come from before preparing its own proposal.
You may still decide that the cheaper quote is right for you. Or you may finally understand what the extra money buys, and decide it’s worth it. Either is a much better outcome than picking blindly on a figure.
If you’re planning a new-build, major renovation, or full-home replacement, you can explore Fenbro’s window and door services in Ireland , or request an initial quotation request an initial quotation tailored to your home.

title: Ballsbridge one-bed offers convenience and an homage to celebrated Irish artist for €695,000
description: Ground-floor mews apartment with peaceful garden prioritises living space over bedrooms
content:
“I love being able to walk out the door without a plan and decide, I’d like a coffee, where will I go? There are so many options around here,” says one of the owners of 73 Pembroke Lane, a one-bedroom mews apartment in Ballsbridge , Dublin 4.
The couple bought the home as a city base eight years ago, and they have since divided their time between there and the countryside. Now that they have sold their country home, they are consolidating and hoping to buy a larger home in the area, placing this well-located ground-floor mews on the market with Sherry FitzGerald , seeking €695,000.
The owner says she would like to remain living nearby as she has loved being able to walk to restaurants when they weren’t in the mood to cook, or take a walk in Herbert Park, or hop on a bus to the city centre. The home also has off-street parking for two cars to lie in wait for when you want to drive further afield.
A distinctive feature of 73 Pembroke Lane is the rectangular stained-glass window set into its facade. The home was once owned by the founder of the Oriel Gallery, Oliver Nulty, who had the same glass as appears on the facade of the Clare Street gallery installed here. Its vivid design is based on the paintings of Markey Robinson , who produced many of his works in the gallery’s framing room.
As well as its convenient location, the C-rated 77sq m (829sq m) home would suit prospective downsizers as its layout prioritises living space over bedrooms, meaning you have plenty of space for daily life and visits from friends and family without having empty bedrooms going to waste.
Entering from the front door, you step into the open-plan kitchen/living space. The kitchen features a tiled floor, white units and a breakfast bar, with a window overlooking the back garden. It flows through to a living space centred on a big log-effect gas fire that would make it extremely cosy on autumn evenings. This space had been a dining area, and could be again, but the owner thought it was a shame not to have comfortable seating around the fire.
Descending two steps past a flat arch is a second livingroom that opens to the back garden. It is a large room flooded with natural light and is home to the dining table and a pair of sofas. There is also a wall of built-in cabinetry adding storage space.
There is also built-in storage in the bedroom, comprising wardrobes and drawer space on two walls. A fully tiled bathroom completes the accommodation.
The paved back garden is low maintenance and features a large old pear tree that blossoms in spring. It is extremely peaceful here, especially on the weekends, the owner says, when you feel as though you could be in the countryside.
An apartment sits above the mews, with separate access.
This is her favourite time of year to walk around the neighbourhood, the owner says, bested only by Christmastime when the homes are festooned with lights.

title: Ireland’s new investment scheme: What will I make if I put €20, €200 or €500 in a month?
description: We look at four different scenarios that could unfold for different types of investor
content:
T here may have been some disappointment that investors will have to wait until next summer to open the much discussed new investment product. However, the personal investment account (PIA) will have its attractions when it finally launches.
Once you abide by the limits set out, your gains will be able to grow without capital gains tax (CGT), exit tax or dividend withholding tax – and you won’t have to worry about the dreaded issue of deemed disposal. Moreover, it will be up to the product providers to settle any tax bill where it arises – so no juggling with Form 11s either.
We should learn more about the new product when the Finance Bill is published later this week, but, given that we already have tax free savings products through the State Savings scheme, it’s likely that the new products will be most attractive to those who are willing to take on some element of risk for a greater return.
Now that we know how much we can invest in these new products – up to €12,000 a year with a tax charge of 1 per cent on any amount in the fund over €50,000 – how much might we actually make?
Anyone can open an account once they are 18 and have a PPS number. And, as no minimum investment applies, it’s expected that you’ll be able to start investing from as little as €20 or so, though the product providers that will launch products next year may impose their own minimums.
In the UK, for example, some ISA providers allow you to invest as little as £1 a month, although many do apply minimums of £50-£100.
Young investors could look to the new product to build up their knowledge of investing; to save for big future purchases such as a house (especially if this is at least five years or more away); or for a rainy day or trip around the world.
The big advantage they have is that time is on their side – which means it makes sense to open an account, even if what they can invest is limited. Once open, the amount invested can always be increased and the benefits of compounding mean that even small amounts can grow into significant sums.
[ Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work Opens in new window ]
Saving €50 a month, for example, will give a return of about €1,291 after two years, based on an annual return of 7 per cent. But keep investing for longer, and you could have €8,704 after 10 years, or more than €26,000 after 20.
If you hadn’t started the account, saving €50 a month in your current account would give just €12,000 after 20 years. The potential upside is clear, although you do need to bear in mind that markets can fall as well as rise, so there is a risk. And product provider charges, which will only become clear next July, will reduce these gains.
And what about tax? Well, in a PIA your investment can grow tax free for quite a long time if you’re only investing small amounts. This is a significant advantage. As a comparison, if you held your money outside a PIA, and cashed your savings in after 10 years, you would pay tax on your “profit” of €2,704. Based on the current exit tax rate of 35 per cent, that could cost you almost €1,000 to Revenue.
Possible investment choice Vanguard S&P 500 ETF
Possible tax bill €0 until the fund reaches €50,000, which could take 28 years, all things being equal
If the thought of losing your money outweighs any potential joy from making gains, you might be looking for a lower-risk product such as a multi-asset fund.
These are available from providers such as Zurich, through its Prisma range, or Irish Life’s MAPS suite of products, and will probably form part of the new PIA product range.
These funds aim to diversify your investment across a range of products – such as cash, bonds, equities and property – and smooth returns through volatile stages of the markets. However, they may have higher charges than some competing funds.
But again, investing and holding for the long term can deliver strong returns.
Someone investing €200 a month, for example, with an average annual return of 4 per cent, would have a fund worth about €5,000 after two years, almost €30,000 after 10 years and close to €75,000 after 20 years.
Possible investment choice Irish Life Multi Asset Portfolio 2 (MAPS)
Possible tax bill This saver could hit the €50,000 mark after about 15 years (although that limit could have increased by then). Once they pass the tax-free threshold, they will start paying tax at a rate of 1 per cent on the balance of their account over €50,000. So a possible bill of about €38.46 a year, based on assets of €53,846.
If you’re one of the people with a share of the €170 billion on deposit in Irish banks, earning a negligible return, you might want to transfer some of your savings directly into the new product.
While the full details of the new product have yet to emerge, it’s expected that you will be able to fund your new PIA with a lump sum, up to the annual limit.
This means you could seed your new PIA with a €12,000 lump sum, and so could your spouse (so €24,000 per couple), with lump sums made every year thereafter. On this basis, tax would kick in from year five or so.
Remember, however, while your investment will be allowed to grow tax free in the new PIA product, if you’re moving it from somewhere else, tax may apply at that location when you cash it in. If it’s in a savings account, you’ll be paying Dirt each year, at a rate of 33 per cent, capital gains tax at 31 per cent if it’s directly invested in shares, or exit tax at 35 per cent if moving out of a fund (provided you encash after January 1st).
Possible investment choice iShares Global Equity ETF
Possible tax bill €0 until the fund reaches €50,000
Not everything must go up. While the S&P 500, which tracks the top 500 listed US companies, has returned about 6-8 per cent on an inflation adjusted basis every year over the past 20 years, there have been periods of extended bear markets. In 2008, for example, the index fell by almost 39 per cent due to the financial crisis, while it was down by almost 20 per cent in 2022, due to surging inflation.
And if you need to cash in your money when markets are down, you face the risk of losing your money.
As our example shows, if you invest €500 a month over 10 years, but your average return is minus-1 per cent, you will end up losing almost €3,000. And, as you have tipped over the €50,000 mark, you will also have a tax bill – even though you have been losing money.
Possible tax bill After 10 years, when the fund is worth €57,072, an annual tax of €70.72 will apply.

title: Santry housing scheme takes top honour at Business Energy Achievement Awards 2026
description: More than 200 energy practitioners gathered as the programme marked its sixth year with 21 trophies, led by an overall win for the Whitehaven development
content:
A Dublin housing scheme of 255 ultra-low energy homes has been named overall winner at the Business Energy Achievement Awards 2026, held at the Crowne Plaza Hotel, in Santry, Dublin.
The Whitehaven scheme in Santry, developed by Tuath Housing, Cairn and MosArt, was officially opened in November 2025. It includes 161 cost-rental homes, which attracted 7,200 applications.
The award citation described Whitehaven as a standout collaborative project demonstrating how ambitious energy performance can be achieved through innovative design and strong partnership.
“Through energy-efficient technologies and careful design the project sets a strong standard for modern housing,” said the judging panel. “It demonstrates that sustainability, quality and practical delivery can work together to create lasting value for residents and the wider community.”
Jennifer Whitty, sustainability manager of Tuath Housing , said: “As Ireland accelerates its decarbonisation journey the focus must be on buildings that combine ambitious energy performance with real-world results for residents, demonstrating that sustainability, affordability and quality can be achieved together.”
Now in its sixth year, the awards programme drew 102 entries, with 21 awards presented before a gathering of more than 195 attendees. Jude Torley, group chief executive of awards gold sponsor Shabra Group , said: “True industry progress demands accountability and measurable results. These awards highlight the operators transforming ambition into practical, scalable solutions, raising standards across the entire supply chain, and driving long-term economic resilience.”
James O’Regan, associate director, facilities engineering and sustainability, Gilead Sciences Ireland, received the energy leader 2026 award. The award citation noted that O’Regan transformed energy management at the Cork manufacturing site into a strategic programme supporting growth, resilience and long-term competitiveness.
The citation noted: “His leadership has driven major advances in energy efficiency, renewable generation, electrification and sustainable infrastructure, while also strengthening data-led decision making. James combines technical expertise with a commitment to developing talent, empowering teams and delivering sustainable business performance.”
Accepting his award, O’Regan told the gathering: “Being a leader means that you’re empowering individuals to achieve their full potential and reduce energy on-site. The future is bright for Ireland’s energy sector. We have the best of the best with us here tonight. Everybody is mingling and sharing information, and it’s a great event for us to share experience with each other.”
Hosted by Colm O’Regan, the gala ceremony brought together Ireland’s leading energy practitioners, sustainability leaders, and industry decision-makers to celebrate achievement in energy management, decarbonisation, and innovation. Judging coordinator Brian Norton noted that the awards programme brings recognition to teams and individuals who have led from persuasion, to action their organisations to introduce new policies, systems and behaviours.
Irving Oil was presented with an award for energy optimisation at the Whitegate oil refinery. “It’s good to see that we’re being recognised for the hard work we’re doing to make sure everything we do is of the highest efficiency and as sustainable as possible,” said process engineering manager Wen Ning Ching.
Lidl Ireland received an award for innovation in decarbonisation – large. “It was great to get recognition against some of the industry leaders in sustainability and renewables,” said construction manager Jack Fitzgerald.
Seamus Shealy of Kepak described their award in the water usage category as well-deserved recognition for the work done on site and a boost for all Kepak’s employees.
Eamonn Murphy, head of marketing at Activ8 Solar Energies, said the awards are a celebration of companies coming together to mark their decarbonisation wins and goals. He said that Activ8’s partnership with Gyproc Ireland, Saint-Gobain and SSE Airtricity had been a great journey. “It’s always an honour to win any award and this is a great collaboration between all three parties, which is a win for everybody.”
Adam Kane, senior community lead at awards organiser BusinessRiver, said: “Events like this are made possible through the support of our sponsor. We are thankful to our 2026 sponsor, Shabra Group, and I also want to recognise our supporter, Amárach Research. Their investment in the awards underlines their commitment and support of this key business area.”

title: New Irish albums reviewed and rated: Basht, Meryl Streek, Morgana, Wasps vs Humans, Whozyerman?
description: October 2026 releases include Poor Advice, Stories They Don’t Teach You at School, The Whole Thing Was Very Very Emotional, The Day Homo Sapiens Destroyed the Earth, Belly of the Beast
content:
Ah, now. Here we go! Basht – Jack Leavey on vocals/guitar, Lughaidh Armstrong Mayock on lead guitar, Ryan McClelland on drums and Louis Christle on bass – have been around for a few years, but it’s in the past 15 months that they’ve coalesced into a unit whose vibrating elevator pitch approximates Radiohead crossed with Nirvana. Across 10 tracks, nervous intensity dwells beside quiet-loud-quiet manoeuvres, making the likes of Dive, Terror TV, Vermilion Reptilian, Circadia, Kids vs Guns and the title track among the most rock-solid and politically vital of the year.
Bursting with righteous anger, brutal stabs of punk rock and melody-driven outbursts, the third album by Meryl Streek (aka Dave Mulvaney, whose father was the drummer in the acclaimed 1980s Dublin band Guernica) mirrors not only the title of Damien Dempsey’s 2000 debut but also the Dublin songwriter’s defined social conscience. In a recent piece for Rolling Stone UK, Streek wrote, “You either get what I do, or you don’t, and that’s the beauty of it. This music doesn’t fuck about.” He is correct. This is a terrific collection of meaningful statement songs, as eloquent as they are visceral.
Formerly of the duo Saint Sister (with Gemma Doherty), Morgan MacIntyre may have taken some time to find her feet creatively, but her debut solo album sees her land so firmly that you can sense the impact. Several years have gone into the making of The Whole Thing Was Very Very Emotional, but you’d never guess it from the vibrancy and immediacy of the songs. We’re not sure if there’s a template for psychotropic sad-pop with operatic hints (Make It Hot Make It Cool, Win Once), dramatic Giorgio Moroder moods (I’m Not Going Anywhere), momentum builders (Fix Your Heart for Free, You Are Never Gone from Me) or sublime heartbreakers (Car Lot in Montana), but if there isn’t, then Morgana should patent it pronto.
As abrasive as four-day stubble and as ready to ruck as a spiky hybrid of The Ruts/The Clash and Patti Smith/Siouxsie Sioux, the Cork-based band Wasps vs Humans release their second album at a time when the world appears to be burning to a crisp. Husband and wife Carl and Linda Plover present DIY postpunk with self-explanatory titles (God Is Not on Trump’s Side, Concrete Ugly, Shooting Drill and My Country’s Like a Broken Pen), most of which are rugged examples of call-to-action bangers. The album closes on a personal note with the poignant Dead Volcanoes, a song that is more tribute than diatribe but just as potent.
Whozyerman? is Paul Savage, formerly of the Waterford-Cork group O Emperor, who won the RTÉ Choice Music Prize for 2018 and then promptly split up. What Savage did next was intriguing and not necessarily in keeping with his former band’s creative waywardness. He follows Blink, his debut solo album, from 2022, with a far more textured collection of songs that weave their way between playfully woozy psychedelic pop and swaying Krautrock like a skilful skateboarder avoiding cracks in the road. This album needs time, however. One listen isn’t enough; more than two and songs such as Someone’s Waiting, the title track, Book Reader and Coming Alive will have you hooked.

title: The Glass Cage by John Healy: Stunning record of a life
description: A blistering honesty defines the prose, a willingness to present the author in an unflattering light
content:
I had never heard of the writer John Healy until my neighbour, the film director Paul Duane, sent me a documentary he had made about him in 2011. Duane had become fascinated after reading Healy’s 1988 memoir The Grass Arena, the account of 15 years spent as a homeless alcoholic on the streets of London, and of the discovery that helped him escape that life: chess, taught to him in prison by a Brighton burglar. Healy pursued the game with such intensity that he became a professional player and stayed sober, replacing one addiction with another.
It is not irrelevant that I had never heard of him. Healy was once famous. The Grass Arena won literary acclaim , was adapted into an award-winning film, and brought its author into the upper reaches of British literary life, rubbing shoulders with the likes of Harold Pinter and appearing on television talkshows. Then he disappeared almost completely. Faber let his book go out of print.
One of the questions Duane’s film asked, and which Healy returns to in this new memoir, is why the literary establishment picked him up so eagerly and then cast him out so completely. The answer reveals something of the deep and powerful machinery of class.
The book begins with Healy working as a kitchen porter in a filthy cafe frequented by pimps, prostitutes and addicts. His council flat in King’s Cross is in a neighbourhood where “a couple of murders now and then kept the population down, relieved the boredom and, while the killings were fresh in my mind, took the sag out of my shoulders, put a spring in my step”.
That sentence contains much of what makes Healy such an unexpected and delightful writer. His subject is human degradation, the almost uninhabitable reality of certain lives, yet his way of describing it is aggressively plain, amoral and often startlingly funny. There is a blistering honesty to the prose, a simplicity and a willingness to present himself in an unflattering light.
The book is a picaresque (then again, so is life) following Healy as he gets and loses jobs, money, fame, and relationships. Some characters recur across years; others are caught for a moment in the light before receding back into darkness. He has a poet’s eye for the resonant detail.
There is Smithy, a talented forger so accustomed to swallowing pills that, when prescribed suppositories, he takes them orally. The Dipper, from Belfast, loses a foot to frostbite while sleeping rough and turns up carrying a chipped chalk statue of the Virgin Mary for his mother and a pair of gloves for Healy, “probably nicked from Oxfam”.
His relationship with his dying friend Jo is particularly difficult and moving. She loves him, champions his work and stands by him. She is also needy; he cannot return her desire, and her insistence on intimacy naturally breeds disgust. Affection, obligation, and contempt accumulate. They love each other, and keep letting each other down. Healy’s description of these competing emotions is a true achievement.
Publication abruptly deposits him among another class. One of the revelations of the book is how much of the brutality of his former life survives in this supposedly more civilised world. The jargon of publishers begins to sound strangely like that of jailers; the glass case of the title suggests both the prestigious display of his book and Healy himself, exhibited and contained.
He is suspicious of this new world and flattered by it, and, crucially, honest about how much it gratifies him. Of publishers he writes: “If, God forbid, you were to drop dead on the carpet in front of them, they might show vague concern for the rug while you were being dragged out by the heels.” His rage is cosmic in scale. “It would hurt you, it would hurt me, it would hurt the whole world.”
The mystery of Healy’s personality runs through every page. Here is a man with a will strong enough to pull himself, with almost no help, from the depths of addiction, to master chess, write books and meditate for hours, but whose need for recognition and connection has been compressed for so long that, when it bursts out, other people often cannot recognise or respond to it.
It is a stunning record of a life, honestly told: of a vanished London and the people who survived at its margins, of the strange and sinister workings of the establishments and of what can happen to an artist once they decide he’s no longer useful to them.

title: Ireland’s infrastructure shortfalls hit firms’ finances
description: Most businesses expect to grow next year but many warn on competitiveness
content:
Ireland’s infrastructure shortfalls are damaging businesses’ finances by driving up costs or hindering efforts to hire workers, most managers believe.
Government plans to spend €250 billion tackling gaps in the State’s water, energy and transport systems, and to speed up house building.
But the challenges posed by poor infrastructure are hindering business and pose a threat to growth, a survey by the Institute of Directors (IoD), showed.
More than 70 per cent of members said that deficits in housing, energy, water, transport and broadband are damaging their organisation’s finances, according to the study.
A third of members said the problems hinder their ability to hire or keep staff. Housing and energy are the leading causes of concern, followed by transport, the survey showed.
Businessman Seán O’Driscoll, a member of the Government’s Accelerating Infrastructure Taskforce, who will address the institute’s conference on Tuesday, welcomed the Budget 2027 pledge to invest in the State’s infrastructure.
But he cautioned that the Republic still faced “deep-seated” challenges when it came to completing vital infrastructure projects on time and within their budgets.
“Our infrastructure deficit isn’t a lack of ambition or talent; it is the result of two decades of failing to plan for our own success,” he said ahead of the conference.
[ Confusion in business about looming State rules on AI Opens in new window ]
O’Driscoll branded as worrying business people’s fears that shortfalls are hitting the finances of their companies.
“If we want to safeguard Ireland’s long-term competitiveness and deliver the housing, energy, water and transport systems a growing economy requires, we need clear accountability, faster decision-making, and a willingness to accept and manage risk, rather than being paralysed by it,” he argued.
The IoD’s survey of 427 directors and managers found that more than three in four of them expected growth next year, with 37 per cent of them planning to hire staff and half intending to maintain current employment.
IoD chief executive Caroline Spillane argued that Government should match managers’ plans to grow by cutting the cost of doing business and lowering barriers that hold firms back.
“As we digest the impact of Budget 2027, it is very striking that well over half of business leaders do not feel the business provisions outlined in the previous budget last year have been able to boost competitiveness a full year on,” Spillane said.
About two thirds of business people do not believe that the State has become a more competitive location in which to invest since Budget 2026, the study showed.
O’Driscoll, a former chairman of industrial group Glen Dimplex and the Economic and Social Research Institute, will address the conference, titled Leading in Governance, in Dublin’s Intercontinental Hotel.
Other speakers include Kara Owen, British Ambassador to Ireland, and Prof Stephen Kinsella, economic adviser to Tánaiste Simon Harris.

title: Supreme Court will hear Brazilian woman’s case over Irish naturalisation
description: Danielle Caroline Cordeiro Sousa Diniz was born in Brazil in 1995 and came to Ireland in 2006
content:
The Supreme Court will hear the appeal of a Brazilian woman, whose father is an Irish citizen, regarding the Government’s denial of her application to become a naturalised Irishwoman.
Danielle Caroline Cordeiro Sousa Diniz (31) sought permission from the court to appeal a judgment of the Court of Appeal, dismissing her appeal against an earlier decision of the High Court.
Diniz had appealed the decision made by the High Court and delivered in March 2023, refusing her application for a certificate of naturalisation under the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956, on the basis that she did not have a “compelling” discretionary case before the minister.
The court heard that Diniz was born in Brazil in 1995 and came to Ireland at the age of 11 in 2006.
She lawfully lived in the State as a dependant of her father and completed part of her primary education and all of her secondary education here, before returning to Brazil in 2012.
Diniz’s father, who had lived and worked in Ireland, became a naturalised Irish citizen in late 2012. Diniz also has two paternal uncles, a paternal aunt and two cousins who are Irish citizens resident in the State.
Diniz married in Brazil in 2017. She sought to return to Ireland and, following difficulties in securing a permission for her citizenship enabling her to reside in Ireland on a long-term basis, applied for naturalisation in January 2019. The court heard that the minister for justice denied her application, however.
Diniz invoked Section 16 of the 1956 Act, which expresses discretional permission for naturalisation in “rare, exceptional or compelling circumstances”.
The minister had accepted in the impugned decision that the applicant had “strong Irish associations” but said after considering her family associations, immigration history and residence, there were no “sufficient exceptional and compelling reasons” to warrant a recommendation that another element of the 1956 Act be waived, called Section 15 (1).
Section 15 (1) states that the Minister may, in his or her “absolute discretion”, grant naturalisation where the specified conditions are met.
In its determination to hear the matter, the Supreme Court wrote that Diniz relied upon the final sentence of article 2 of the Constitution, which provides that “the Irish nation cherishes its special affinity with people of Irish ancestry living abroad who share its cultural identity and heritage”.
The Supreme Court determined it was “satisfied that the application raises a matter of general public importance and that the interests of justice favour its determination”.

title: Man in his 60s dies in Meath crash
description: Collision between truck and a car occurred after 3pm on N2 north of Ashbourne-Rath Roundabout
content:
A man in his 60s was killed in a road crash in Ashbourne, Co Meath , on Monday.
The collision between a truck and a car happened shortly after 3pm on the N2, north of the Ashbourne-Rath roundabout.
The driver of the car was pronounced deceased at the scene, and his body was removed to the mortuary in Navan.
The driver of the truck, a man in his 40s, was uninjured.
Gardaí have appealed for anyone who may have witnessed the crash, particularly those who were in the area between 3pm and 3.45pm or those who may have dashcam footage, to come forward.
Gardaí can be contacted at Ashbourne Garda station on 01 801 0600, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or at any Garda station.

title: Stephen Bradley says four red cards shown after Shamrock Rovers’ win over Bohemians
description: Dismissed players at risk of missing title run-in
content:
Shamrock Rovers manager Stephen Bradley has said three players and the Bohemians coach Stephen McDonnell were red-carded by referee Rob Hennessy after the Dublin derby at Tallaght Stadium on Monday night.
Rovers beat Bohemians 2-1 , thanks to a 76th-minute winning goal from Dylan Watts, to go six points clear of St Patrick’s Athletic and Bohs at the top of the Premier Division with three games remaining in their campaign, while St Pat’s have four left.
At the full-time whistle, a fight broke out on the pitch as players from both teams came together.
“What I am being told is one of the players threw a dig at young Michael [Noonan] from behind,” said Bradley. “I think that is what started it.
“The ref [Hennessy] just informed me that a few players have been sent off from both teams after the game.
“For Bohs, I think Dawson Devoy and [assistant coach] Stephen O’Donnell. For us it was Naj [Razi] and Michael [Noonan].”
The suspension for violent conduct is three games, so it is possible any dismissed players will not play against this season.
“We are playing to win a league, they are not,” Bradley added. “We need players, we need people ready for the next three games, we don’t need to get dragged into that.
“A lot of talking went on there, in terms of silly stuff. There seems to be a pattern, every time around the pitch the same people are involved in it. Even when it is different clubs, like Shels and Pats, the same people are involved.”
Bradley would not say who he was referring to.
“Look at the pattern, it is quite clear to see. I am not the first one to say this, it is the same people.”
Bohemians manager Alan Reynolds was not available to respond to Bradley’s allegation as the north Dublin club are boycotting the media to protest against fixture scheduling by the FAI.

title: Shamrock Rovers take giant leap towards title as Dylan Watts downs Bohemians
description: Rovers six points clear at the top of table with three matches left
content:
Dylan Watts’s 76th-minute winner ensured Shamrock Rovers took a giant leap towards winning a sixth League of Ireland title in seven seasons.
Tempers flared at the full-time whistle. Two skirmishes broke out on the pitch. The first had Rovers manager Stephen Bradley dragging his assistant coach Glenn Crowe away from the Bohemians manager Alan Reynolds.
The other saw a coming-together of players that fizzled out when the Rovers squad realised the significance of their achievement. Six points clear with three games remaining, they spun away from the melee, towards their fans in the south stand.
In any title race, especially amid the blur of Rovers’ dominance throughout the 2020s, only the special moments are remembered.
Watts’s goal should stand the test of time.
With a record attendance of 10,208, for a competitive match at Tallaght Stadium, supporters were gripped by a Dublin derby that the evergreen Watts settled by ghosting behind the cover to stretch and score off a long throw by Will Fitzgerald.
Twelve months ago, it was Watts, the quietly efficient midfielder, who whipped in a free-kick against Galway United to capture a fifth Premier Division title in six seasons. Their remaining matches are against Galway, Sligo Rovers and Dundalk - and they may need two wins and a draw from those fixtures, depending on results elsewhere, most particularly in the four matches that nearest rivals St Pat’s have left.
This was Bohemians’ chance to catch Rovers cold.
It initially seemed like John McGovern’s 14th goal of the season was going to settle a tense contest. McGovern struck for the fifth time in three games. That was not enough to see off Bohs.
Watts took care of that in a stunning reply to Ross Tierney’s scrappy equaliser five minutes earlier.
Bradley’s men rediscovered their groove when it really mattered. Pico Lopes, clearly over his World Cup hangover, looked sharp and mean at the heart of the defence. Matt Healy stood out in a midfield that included the recently capped Bohs captain Dawson Devoy. Even the European meltdown of late August is consigned to the Bradley notebook of lessons learned.
McGovern’s headed finish on the Bohemians goal line, 10 minutes before half-time, was created by Graham Burke’s rapid movement, a pirouette to freeze seven red shirts and the neatest cross imaginable from the Ireland international’s left toe.
For McGovern it was rapid redemption as moments earlier he had sidefooted a glorious chance wide of Paul Walters’s goal. The movement of the former Down Gaelic footballer and Burke, as they cut Bohs open to reward Daniel Cleary for unburdening Colm Whelan of possession in the Rovers box, deserved a goal.
Rovers may be hoping referee Rob Hennessy forgets to mention what happened between the 25th and 27th minute in his match report; the Dublin Fire Brigade had to extinguish multiple flames down the south end following an explosion of fireworks. As green smoke blanketed the pitch, hiding players and officials, Hennessy blew for a hydration break.
The sheets of rain cleared up with the smoke as the derby eventually restarted.
It was the ultimate spectacle for the league; a crowd made up of a hefty number of fans of both clubs was transfixed by the football, with St Patrick’s Athletic manager Stephen Kenny the most interested spectator.
The fading hope of the title race being revived depends on St Pat’s beating Shelbourne at Richmond Park on Friday and Rovers, somehow, losing away to Galway and at home to the almost relegated Sligo.
This was the chance for Reynolds, Devoy and Bohs to strike a blow against Bradley, Lopes and Rovers. But it was Burke’s class that shone through; the man of the match took the ball at the end and shielded it when his team needed him the most.
“It was a huge game,” said Burke, “the ones you want to play in. It’s a huge three points for us, Bohs played well. Three more games to go, three huge games, we need to keep going.”
Shamrock Rovers : McGinty; Cleary, Lopes, Grace; Sobowale, Byrne (J O’Sullivan 65), Grace, Watts (Razi 85), Fitzgerald (C O’Sullivan 80); Burke (Greene 80); McGovern (Afolbai 80).
Bohemians : Walters; Power, Hickey, Todd, Flores; Devoy (Parsons 63), McDonnell (Burke 15, Diallo 81); Parsons (Vaughan 81), Tierney, Rooney (James-Taylor 60); Whelan (Strods 60).

title: John McEntee confirmed as new Monaghan football manager
description: Antrim native has managed Inniskeen for the last four years and won a county championship as Clontibret boss
content:
John McEntee has been appointed Monaghan senior football manager, the former Armagh player succeeding Gabriel Bannigan in the Farney County role. At a meeting on Monday night, Monaghan GAA also confirmed Antrim native Tony Austin as their new senior hurling manager.
McEntee has managed Inniskeen for the last four years, guiding them to senior final appearances in 2023 and 2025. He previously managed Clontibret to a Monaghan SFC in 2019.
Details of his backroom has not been announced, though former Monaghan midfielder Darren Hughes and ex-Offaly forward Niall McNamee have been mentioned as possible coaches.
Monaghan GAA stated: “John McEntee brings a wealth of experience, leadership and commitment to the role and we look forward to working with him as preparations begin for the challenges ahead.
“Details of John’s full backroom team will be announced in the coming week. In the interests of respecting current football commitments and ensuring there is no distraction to ongoing club activities, those appointments will be confirmed at a later date.”
McEntee’s twin brother Tony managed Sligo for five years and is currently part of the Down senior football management team under Conor Laverty. John and Tony were key players on Armagh’s 2002 All-Ireland winning team.
John has got the nod for the Monaghan job despite speculation linking Séamus McEnaney with a possible return for a third stint.
His appointment means there will two Crossmaglen clubmen managing a senior intercounty football team in 2027 with Oisín McConville remaining at the helm in Wicklow.
Bannigan’s surprise departure at the end of August created the vacancy. Despite two encouraging seasons at the helm, Bannigan felt he did not have the backing of the board to continue for a third campaign.
Announcing his resignation, Bannigan stated: “Over the last number of weeks, I worked hard on my plans for 2027 to build on the excellent foundations now in place.
“During this period, I have come to realise that the goalposts have moved, and the conditions are not right for me to continue and therefore I believe a new management team and fresh voices are now required to take Monaghan football forward.”
Meanwhile, Doheny GAA Club has announced a series of commemorative events to mark the centenary of the death of Sam Maguire.
Born on March 11th, 1877 in Maulabracka, Dunmanway, Maguire spent much of his adult life in England. He was a prominent figure in London GAA – first as a player and then as an administrator. After his death on February 6 th , 1927 a cup in his honour was presented to GAA Central Council for the winners of the All-Ireland senior football championship.
The cup, inspired by the Ardagh Chalice, was first presented in 1928 to Kildare. It was replaced by a replica in 1988, with the original on display at the GAA Museum in Croke Park.
A series of commemorative events are planned by Doheny GAA clubs between Friday, February 5 th to Sunday, February 7 th , 2027.
Among the events will be an unveiling of a specially commissioned bronze bust of Sam Maguire, creating a permanent tribute to one of Dunmanway’s most famous sons.
There will also be a commemorative football fixture between representative teams from Cork and London GAA, recognising Sam Maguire’s lifelong connection to both Cork and London and his pivotal role in the promotion of Gaelic games abroad.

title: Court dismisses Garvaghy Road residents’ legal action against march at Drumcree
description: Portadown Orangemen seek to add PSNI chief constable to judicial review over decision to revoke permission for march on Garvaghy Road
content:
A Belfast court has dismissed an appeal by the Garvaghy Road residents against the Parades Commission’s decision to allow a controversial Orange march at Drumcree.
In the summary of the judgement delivered at the Court of Appeal on Monday afternoon, the Lady Chief Justice, Siobhan Keegan, said she was satisfied that a judge in a lower court was “correct” in his assessment and the residents’ application for leave to apply for a judicial review had “no reasonable prospect of success.”
She said the outcome of the appeal was “as a result of the application of the law” and she and her fellow judges “make no comments on the merits of the [Parades Commission] decision itself, as that is not our function.”
The appeal was dismissed, as was the application for leave to judicially review the decision.
The residents were challenging an earlier High Court decision to refuse leave to apply for a judicial review of the determination by the Commission to permit the Orange Order to parade from Drumcree church along the Garvaghy Road on September 27 th .
The court heard the judges made their decision before an intervention by the Northern Secretary on Friday night that banned the controversial Orange Order parade.
Speaking outside the court, loyalist activist Jamie Bryson described the Court of Appeal judgement as “seismic”, saying the “lawlessness and the law breakers have been defeated.
“The law is clear, the Portadown District has a legal right to walk the Garvaghy Road,” he said.
However Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition, said the judgement was “fairly academic given that the Secretary of State has already banned the march in question.
“The ban is in place, that’s what we sought, we’ve prevented the march, and we’ll be back again to prevent future marches.”
Earlier on Monday, a separate challenge to Chris Bryant’s decision was adjourned at the High Court in Belfast.
During a brief hearing on Monday morning, the court was told that the case will proceed on October 19th.
The judge will consider whether to grant leave for a judicial review and, if permission is given, the merits of the case during the same session.
The court heard there had been an application on Sunday to widen the case to include Police Service of Northern Ireland chief constable Jon Boutcher as a respondent, and to challenge his request to the Northern Secretary to review the permission for the march to proceed.
The Portadown District of the Orange Order applied for leave to take a judicial review of Friday night’s decision by Chris Bryant to intervene and revoke permission for the parade.
It followed a two-week stand-off between members of the Portadown District of the Orange Order and nationalist residents on the Garvaghy Road.
The march on September 27th was blocked by residents and did not go ahead.
In a statement on Friday night, the Northern Secretary said he had been advised by the PSNI chief constable that the march could not proceed without a “major” police intervention, which “would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect across Northern Ireland” and he had therefore decided to ban the march “in the interests of wider public interest and safety”.
[ ‘Let them live in peace’: Protestants and Catholics alike express relief in Drumcree Opens in new window ]
Meanwhile, a motion of no confidence in First Minister Michelle O’Neill was defeated in the Northern Ireland Assembly.
Similar non-binding motions against Sinn Féin Finance Minister John O’Dowd, Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald and Infrastructure Minister Liz Kimmins also did not pass.
The votes were brought by unionist parties in the Stormont Assembly over their participation in protests in support of the Garvaghy Road residents.
O’Neill is among a number of MLAs who have received letters from the PSNI inviting them to a voluntary interview as part of the police investigation into the protests.
The motions contended they “no longer enjoy the confidence of the Assembly” after they allegedly “participated in the unlawful protest” and claim they “failed to observe their pledge of office”.
O’Neill has repeatedly defended her participation in the protests, saying last week that she would “continue to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents” because “it is always right to stand up for what is right and there can be no going back”.
The motions – which carry the sanction of excluding a Minister from holding office for 12 months – were not expected to pass, as this would require cross-community support in the Assembly.
[ Siobhán Fenton: Sinn Féin might have an ulterior motive for its actions at Drumcree Opens in new window ]
At a press conference on Monday morning, Traditional Unionist Voice leader Jim Allister, called on Boutcher to resign, claiming the PSNI chief had “failed to uphold the rule of law”.
The DUP leader, Gavin Robinson, said the UK government had “bent the knee” to “threats of violence and disorder” and he would speak to the Northern Secretary to “ensure that there are sanctions and that there is accountability.”
O’Neill criticised the “very ugly” language used by some politicians, saying it was “dehumanising” but also “dangerous and actually can lead on to sectarianism and violence in our streets.”
Alliance MLA Eoin Tennyson described the motions of no confidence against Sinn Féin as a “wrecker’s agenda designed to destabilise and bring down these institutions and we will have no part in that.”

title: No property tax changes for Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown and Fingal homeowners
description: Green councillor says owners of ‘millionaire mansions’ and private investment funds would reap benefit of vote
content:
Homeowners in both Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown and Fingal will see no increase in their local property tax (LPT) bills next year after councillors voted to retain the rate at 2026 levels.
LPT, which is charged on the value of a property, has a base rate that can be raised by up to 25 per cent, or lowered by up to 15 per cent, by each local authority on an annual basis.
Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown was last year the only local authority in the State to apply the full 15 per cent discount to household’s LPT bills and has repeated the move this year.
Councillors voted by 27 to 12 to implement the full rate reduction, against the recommendation of the council’s executive, which had urged them to rein in the cut to 7.5 per cent to help maintain council services and cope with rising inflation.
Labour councillors had supported the 7.5 per cent cut, while Green councillors put forward a motion to keep LPT at the national base rate and implement no reduction. However, the majority of councillors supported Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil motions to implement the 15 per cent cut.
Council chief executive Frank Curran said the reduction of 15 per cent represented a €10.4 million loss to the council. “We’re not even standing still with inflation, and it will inevitably lead to [a] reduction in services.”
Fine Gael councillor Jim Gildea, who proposed the 15 per cent rate cut, said: “Increasing the cost to our citizens is not the way to bridge the gap of €10 million. We have to look elsewhere.”
Green Party councillor Oisín O’Connor said the average homeowner would only be saving a “few euro a month” from the 15 per cent reduction.
Those who would benefit were owners of “millionaire mansions” and “private investment funds, who own blocks of apartments, who stands to gain hundreds of thousands of euro from tonight’s vote”.
Meanwhile in Fingal, 29 councillors voted in favour of retaining the 5 per cent reduction to LPT, with nine voting against.
It was the same LPT rate as last year, meaning there will be no change in the bills of those resident in the council area.
Sinn Féin councillor Angela Donnelly had proposed a 15 per cent cut to the rate, saying thousands of people were already struggling with the cost-of-living crisis.
“We get very few opportunities to make decisions that will directly impact the residents in Fingal. Today is one of those rare occasions to do the right thing and give people a break,” Donnelly said.
However, her proposal to cut the rate by 15 per cent was voted down by 27 to eight votes.

title: Ammi Burke to blame for damage to her reputation since Arthur Cox dismissal, court told
description: Route solicitor took ‘could not have been more damaging’ to her professional standing, former employer argues
content:
Solicitor Ammi Burke has only herself to blame for the damage to her reputation since her dismissal from one of Ireland’s leading law firms, the Labour Court has been told.
Burke from Castlebar, Co Mayo , was dismissed by Arthur Cox Solicitors of Earlsfort Terrace, Dublin 2, in November 2019 and is now on her third challenge to that dismissal.
She had previously taken cases against her dismissal at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) and there were two judicial reviews arising out of those.
She has now begun the case against her dismissal to the Labour Court , which is the appeal court for the WRC.
Peter Ward, the barrister representing Arthur Cox Solicitors, said Burke had attempted to tie up her former employer in litigation for many years and had disrupted several hearings.
She had been given a “generous” ex gratia payment of €70,000, a year’s salary, when she was dismissed.
Senior partners in Arthur Cox had attempted to resolve the issue by helping her get a new position in a different firm following her dismissal.
Had she taken that route, there would have been no damage to her professional reputation. Instead, she took a course that “could not have been more damaging to herself,” Ward said.
“The course she and her family took couldn’t have brought more publicity on herself.”
The damage to Burke’s reputation was entirely her own fault and not that of Arthur Cox, he suggested.
Her family had picketed outside Arthur Cox offices, engaged in protracted litigation and had made “extremely false and damaging” allegations against the firm.
He cited a judgment in the Court of Appeal in 2024 by Judge Seamus Noonan who described her behaviour as “utterly appalling and egregious”.
It would be “absurd” and “entirely unreasonable” for Arthur Cox to take her back, Ward added.
He told the Labour Court that Burke exhibited a “superiority complex” and was condescending towards colleagues.
Burke began as a trainee solicitor with the firm in May 2016 and became a solicitor with the banking practice group in November 2018 on a salary of €70,000 per year.
Burke told the court that she was dismissed without warning and without cause on November 12th, 2019. Because of the close-knit nature of the legal profession, she claimed her dismissal had resulted in the end of her career.
Before that she claimed to have had an “unblemished” record and was noted for her work ethic and her status as a team player.
She recalled that when she was told she was being dismissed, her HR director informed her that it was a no fault dismissal and she had done nothing wrong.
She went on to state that her dismissal had been “procedurally unfair” and in complete contravention of the employment practices of Arthur Cox. There was a “complete absence” of documentary evidence backing up her dismissal.
Her dismissal had a “devastating” impact on her ability to find alternative employment and therefore the only just remedy would be her reinstatement.
Giving evidence, Ultan Shannon, a former partner in Arthur Cox Solicitors, said he had worked in the banking and finance section and had agreed to take her on rotation into his department.
Burke was made an associate solicitor. Issues later arose with two senior partners in the finance section. Burke had taken offence to a lunch invitation extended to two new associate solicitors in the firm by senior partner Gráinne Hennessy. Hennessy was “shocked and surprised” by Burke’s reaction.
“I got a kick in the stomach,” said Shannon. “I had supported Ammi and this was her first interaction with Gráinne. I had pushed for her to be taken into our group.”
There had also been an encounter with another partner Kevin Lynch after he thanked Burke for working late on a project.
Burke allegedly replied; “I wouldn’t have to do this if your team was doing what they were supposed to do.”
Lynch had spoken to HR about it, Shannon recalled.
There was a third interaction with a fellow associate, Sinéad Cantillon, with whom Burke shared an office. Cantillon requested to be moved as she had been called a disgrace by Burke over a legal question. She had broken down in tears in front of Shannon at a meeting in the boardroom. He went to HR after that about Burke’s behaviour.
“There were just so many issues. I could not see any possibility of her continuing in the firm,” he said. “The trust and confidence was gone. There was no awareness of how to engage with your colleagues, with partners or people in the firm.
“You have to get on with people and you have to be able to engage with them. You have to some nous as how you deal with an issue.
“At that stage I couldn’t see in any circumstances of how we could deal with Ms Burke.”
Burke said that the issues around her interactions with Hennessy and Lynch had not been raised at her appraisal in the July before she was dismissed.
Shannon said he did not have a problem with Burke’s legal skills, drafting or knowledge of the law. It was her behaviour and lack of judgment that was the problem.

title: The Irish Times view on George Gibney: a dark and devastating saga
description: His abuse cast a dark shadow over the lives of his victims
content:
The sentencing of former Irish Olympic swimming coach George Gibney to more than 15 years in prison brings an end to a legal saga that began with a court appearance in Dún Laoghaire District Court in 1993 and ran for more than 30 years.
For those swimmers who were sexually abused by the most powerful figure in Irish swimming at the time, Gibney cast a dark shadow over their lives. Their emotional journey has lasted for 50 years and more.
The 77-year-old former coach was found guilty of 39 counts of indecent assault and one count of attempted rape of children. The sentencing by Judge Micheál P O’Higgins will perhaps give some sense to his victims of justice being served, but the impact of his actions has been enormous.
Not all lived to see Gibney finally face imprisonment. Others, who were deeply damaged by his predations, were unable to take the stand. Those individuals continue to face their own demons and serious life challenges.
The four women who made complaints and triggered his arrest by US marshals before his extradition from the US last year were victims of Gibney’s abusive and criminal conduct through the 1970s and 1980s.
His assaults were largely against young swimmers who trained at Newpark and Glenalbyn swimming pools in south Dublin and the offences for which he was convicted were against children aged 8 to 14-years-old.
Gibney originally faced criminal charges in 1993. However, he was released when the Supreme Court ruled in his favour, after his lawyers said there was a lack of specificity in the charges and an undue delay since the events referred to had taken place. The subsequent halting of the investigation against Gibney caused consternation and outrage.
The original group of swimmers who made complaints never had their day in court, although they undoubtedly paved the way for his eventual conviction, involving a different set of individuals.
What remains deeply troubling is how Gibney remained at large for so long over the following years. When he was originally freed, he fled to Scotland and then to the US, finally settling in Florida, where he lived freely until last year.
Gibney was not alone. For many years, swimming was riddled with scandal. Prominent individuals in the sport, Derry O’Rourke, Fr Ronald Bennett and Ger Doyle were all imprisoned for sexual assaults against young swimmers.
In recent years Irish swimming has enjoyed a golden period, winning medals at Olympic Games and bringing so much joy. But the impact of the years of scandal cannot be forgotten. George Gibney, once the sport’s figurehead, was a central figure in a dark and devastating period in Irish sporting history.

title: Trial date for man accused of murdering Denis Donaldson to be fixed next month
description: Donaldson (55) was shot dead at remote cottage near Glentie, Co Donegal after being exposed as MI5 agent
content:
The trial date of a man charged with the 2006 murder of British spy Denis Donaldson is to be fixed next month.
Antoin Duffy, who is in his 40s, of no fixed address, appeared before the non-jury Special Criminal Court on Monday via video-link from prison.
He is charged with the murder of Donaldson in Cloghercor, Doochary, Co Donegal, between April 3rd and 4th, 2006, after being extradited from Scotland earlier this year.
He was also charged with possession of a shotgun and ammunition “with intent to endanger life” at the same date and location.
He was also charged with the attempted murder of a second man, Liam Copeland McGinley, at Meenaboll in Co Donegal, on November 19th, 2007, and with possession of a shotgun and possession of ammunition on the same date.
Donaldson (55) was shot dead at a remote cottage near Glenties months after he was exposed as a paid agent for Special Branch and MI5 since the 1980s.
In 2009, dissident republican group the Real IRA claimed the killing.
Donaldson was also a former administrator for Sinn Féin’s Stormont Assembly team.
Appearing before the non-jury court on Monday, a barrister representing Duffy confirmed he had been served with the book of evidence.
He said his client would be seeking legal aid, adding that the solicitor for the defendant was Cormac McDonnell.
Judge Caroline Biggs gave the defendant the alibi warning, and said that if he in any way relied on an alibi, then all details of it should be supplied within 14 days.
The case has been adjourned until November 9th, when a trial date is expected to be set. – PA

title: What services will be affected by the strikes?
description: Thousands of schools will not open and hospitals will be disrupted if action is not averted before the due date
content:
A lmost all of the Republic’s courts will close on Wednesday if strike action by more than 300,000 public-sector workers proceeds, it was confirmed on Monday.
The announcement follows discussions between the Courts Service, its staff and unions to establish what level of disruption would be caused.
On Monday, the Courts Service said it would have no option but to close the vast majority of courts in Dublin and countrywide, while counter services will also be suspended for the day.
Some exceptions have been agreed with unions to ensure emergency applications related to domestic violence or child-safety issues could be heard. An Garda Síochána will be able to apply to have accused people remanded in custody where station bail has not been granted.
The High Court will also deal with injunctions sought to protect life, safety or welfare, said the Courts Service.
It had already been confirmed that thousands of schools would close if the action was not averted or postponed, with some 90,000 teachers set to strike and picket their workplaces.
Teachers’ unions, including the Teachers’ Union of Ireland, whose members joined the ongoing work-to-rule on Monday, were working to get placards and other strike-related materials out to members countrywide in advance of Wednesday morning.
[ Late push to avert imminent public-sector strike Opens in new window ]
Special needs assistants and other school staff will also be staging a stoppage.
About 32,000 public-sector nurses will be involved, and the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation (INMO) said staffing levels broadly equivalent to overnight rosters would be provided, with the action only affecting hospital day shifts.
“We have already said we’ll cover all life-preserving services, dialysis, chemotherapy, all of those services; there’s just no debate about that kind of stuff,” said INMO general secretary Phil Ní Sheaghdha.
She said the union was meeting the Health Service Executive on Monday afternoon to finalise some of the cover arrangements but suggested patient numbers were not being appropriately reduced where possible to limit disruption.
“We’re going to provide night duty levels, but part of [the expected procedure] is that the hospitals should be reducing admissions. But that doesn’t appear to have been happening and there seems to have been no change to the discharge numbers this weekend compared to the previous weekend.”
Non-consultant hospital doctors who are members of the Irish Medical Organisation will provide Sunday levels of staffing through the day shift. Areas including palliative care, cancer care, maternity services and sexual assault units have either been exempted or are subject to higher levels of staffing agreements.
Hospital consultants will be on-site during the day but will only work on tasks directly related to the provision of patient treatment and care, the union said.
About 2,000 laboratory scientists are also due to strike, causing the postponement of, or delays to, patient tests.
In addition to the Courts Service, several Government departments and agencies, including the Revenue Commissioners and Department of Justice, are expected to close offices.
[ Who is affected by the strike and can it be averted? Opens in new window ]
Local authority services are also expected to be severely disrupted, with many libraries and public offices among the facilities set to close.
Talks have been continuing about the derogations required to operate some essential areas, with senior civil servants involved in buildings management, human relations and industrial relations all exempted from the action by their union, the Association of Higher Civil and Public Servants, which will have about 2,500 members on strike.
The numbers involved from other unions vary from about 360 for the Veterinary Officers Association up to 100,000 for Fórsa, which organises across a huge number of roles and grades. Many unions report substantial recruitment in recent weeks, a common phenomenon in advance of strikes prompted in part by non-members seeking to avoid having to pass pickets run by colleagues.
Derogations were refused in relation to the Government’s AI Summit on Wednesday at the RDS, but the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment said the event was being organised by an outside company and will go ahead.

title: Connacht daring to dream on return to Champions Cup
description: ‘Why can’t a club like Connacht ever potentially win it?’ asks Stuart Lancaster
content:
Connacht are preparing to return to the Champions Cup when Saracens visit the Dexcom Stadium on Saturday, but head coach Stuart Lancaster has yet to settle on his starting XV.
Shayne Bolton has passed HIA protocols, experienced hooker Dave Heffernan is back training, while talented youngster Harry West may be available, as may David O’Connor. But Lancaster has yet to decide whether Irish internationals Finlay Bealham and Mack Hansen will be in action after playing in the first three fixtures this season.
Lancaster could look to the likes of Finn Treacy, Shane Jennings and “standout” under-20s player Daniel Ryan, while new signing Will Connors is also a possible starter.
“We signed him for a reason because he’s an international-quality player. So getting him back available to train and be available to play is huge,” said Lancaster of the former Leinster backrow.
Connacht have been “rewarded with an amazing pool” that includes Toulouse, La Rochelle and Exeter as well as Saracens, whom he encountered when coaching Leinster.
“It’s a serious challenge. Obviously we watched the game from the weekend. They had a very good win against Bristol ... it’s going to be a hell of a game.”
“To kick off the Champions Cup with a home game, and if you can get a win, it sets you up well, and then obviously you lead into Exeter away, and then there is the excitement of the two French teams in January.”
Lancaster insists Connacht need to put their “best foot forward in Europe” and that last season’s results provided real hope.
“You just want to be in the fight, don’t you? I thought last year, if you saw our Montpellier games and then Montpellier losing in the Top 14 final, how well we competed, it would not be beyond the realms of possibility that we can qualify. So we fight for that.”
Connacht, he insists, are not there just to make up the numbers.
“I’ve seen other teams pay lip service to it. I’m too respectful of the competition to ever do that. I’ve had amazing times in the Champions Cup. You know, I’ve been involved in huge playoff games, in finals, in semi-finals, in amazing pool games.
“So I love the competition personally ... it worries me when there is talk about reducing it to 16 teams in the next couple of years.
“Where does that leave a club like Connacht to have ambition? Why would you rule out a club like Connacht – to have their day in the sun, to play against the teams that won the Champions Cup in the past, and why can’t a club like Connacht ever potentially win it? I’m not saying it’s doable every year, but there’s no reason why a club like Connacht couldn’t come through.”

title: Inland Fisheries chief had right to revert to another role, ex-chairwoman tells WRC
description: Senior officials would not apply for leadership positions if they could not go back to substantive roles, adjudicators hear
content:
The former chairwoman of Inland Fisheries Ireland (IFI) has said her understanding was that the organisation’s chief executive could revert to another role when his term ended.
Prof Frances Lucy, who served on the board of the State agency for 10 years and was appointed chairwoman in May 2022, said this was based on precedent.
Former chief executive Francis O’Donnell is pursuing complaints under the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, the Payment of Wages Act 1997, and the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977 against the State agency, where he was employed as chief executive from September 2020 to July 2025.
Giving evidence at the Workplace Relations Commission on Monday on his behalf, she said her understanding was that his predecessor had gone back to another role based on an employment entitlement.
Questioned by O’Donnell, who is representing himself, Lucy said: “My understanding is that you took up the [chief executive] role for an initial five-year period. My understanding of normal public sector [practice] is that you might or might not have been going for another five years. Alternatively, you would be reverting to your previous position as a director,” she said.
Adjudication officer Michael McNamee asked how she came by that understanding.
“Based on precedent. I was a member of the founder board [of IFI] and the previous chief executive served two terms. Then, in my absence [from the board for a period before being reappointed] he became director of logistics. ”
Counsel for IFI Tiernan Lowey maintained O’Donnell’s predecessor had had a number of fixed-term contracts which had crystallised into a contract of indefinite duration. He contended O’Donnell’s situation was different.
However, Lucy argued there was also custom and practice. She said in public sector organisations people in their 40s and 50s would not apply for chief executive positions if they could not revert to the substantive posts.
Separately, IFI director of finance Suzanne Campion said she had been informed by the agency’s former head of human resources that O’Donnell, in a car park, had given her a prepared letter to sign setting out that he had a right to revert to a post as a regional director. O’Donnell has denied this claim.
Campion said former IFI head of human resources Roisin Bradley showed her the letter when she stayed with her in January 2023. Campion said Bradley was very disturbed by the letter. She said she didn’t want to sign it and feared for her career. Campion said providing an unsigned letter to Bradley was “inappropriate and unacceptable”.
O’Donnell had previously maintained that details of a protected disclosure containing allegations made against him had been leaked and aired in the Oireachtas.

title: Former swimming coach George Gibney jailed for 15½ years for abusing four girls
description: Jury found him guilty in July of 39 counts of indecent assault and one count of attempted rape
author_name: James Cox, Isabel Hayes, Eimear Dodd
content:
Former Olympic swimming coach George Gibney has been jailed for more than 15 years for the sexual abuse of four girls in the 1970s and 1980s.
In July, a Central Criminal Court jury found Gibney guilty of 39 counts of indecent assault and one count of attempted rape of children.
The jury acquitted him of one count of indecently assaulting one of the complainants on a date between 1976 and 1977.
Sentencing Gibney on Monday, Judge Mícheál O’Higgins imposed an aggregate sentence of 16 years and eight months, with 14 months suspended. This results in a sentence of 15 years and six months in prison.
Gibney (78) had only been referred to as a “sports coach” during the trial due to reporting restrictions, but these were removed after the guilty verdict, meaning he could be named.
In sentencing, the judge said he took note of the young ages of the victims, and the predatory context whereby Gibney took advantage of his authority to assault children in his care. Mitigating factors included Gibney’s age, his failing health, the fact that he did not oppose extradition from the United States and his guilty plea, the judge said.
The judge said Gibney “insinuated himself into the friendship group” of his victims’ parents.
He said the “systemic and repeated” abuse and “predatory nature” of Gibney’s actions all placed the attempted rape offence – the most serious offence – on a “higher plane”, leading to the sentence of 12 years, which he reduced by two years to give a net sentence of 10 years.
He said the indecent assault charges were complicated by the “sheer number” of counts. The judge said he regarded each of these offences in the “highest range” of due to the “severity of the assaults”.
He set a headline sentence of two years, reduced to 20 months for each assault. Together, this resulted in a collective sentence for the assaults of six years and eight months, to run consecutively to the sentence for attempted rape.
The judge backdated the sentence to when Gibney first went into custody in July 2025.
Gibney was in court in a wheelchair on Monday for the sentencing.
[ George Gibney: paedophile finally faces accountability after long and harrowing journey for victims Opens in new window ]
After a previous case involving abuse allegations against Gibney was halted in 1993, he left Ireland and took up a role at a swimming club in Edinburgh. Later he moved to the US, first to Colorado, before settling in Orlando, Florida.
While Gibney had been a high-profile figure in Ireland, he lived in relative anonymity in the US.
A 10-part podcast series made by the Second Captains production company in conjunction with the BBC, Where is George Gibney?, put his name back in the spotlight. Four complainants, who were not involved in the early 1990s case, subsequently came forward and made complaints to gardaí.
After 30 years in the US, Gibney was extradited to Ireland to face charges last year. His defence expressed concerns about jurors who had listened to the podcast.
The abuse took place in Glenalbyn swimming pool, Stillorgan, and Newpark Sports Centre, Blackrock, both in Co Dublin .
The trial heard how some of the victims, aged between eight and 13 at the time, were abused by Gibney in his car when he gave them lifts to swimming practice.
Further abuse of two sisters happened in his home when they were babysitting his children.
The abuse included kissing, inappropriate touching and forced sex acts.
Gibney had initially been charged with 79 counts. He pleaded guilty to five counts of indecent assault at the beginning of the trial, while the judge threw out 33 charges after the prosecution’s evidence was heard.
After the verdict, Gibney indicated he would not appeal against his conviction.
In a post sentence statement, Det Chief Supt Thelma Watters of the Garda National Protective Services Bureau said Gibney’s “heinous crimes” were aggravated by the fact he had been in a position of trust.
