“Parents entrusted their children in the expectation of care and safety, this trust was egregiously broken. Children had their childhood and adult lives forever changed,” she said.
She appealed to anyone who experienced historical sexual abuse, and anyone who may have information relating to such offences, to come forward.
“We acknowledge the profound and lasting impact that sexual abuse can have on individuals and their families. For many victims and survivors, disclosing their experiences can be extremely difficult, particularly where the abuse happened years ago,” she said.

title: The Irish Times view on Trump’s move on diesel: an imaginary ceasefire
description: The US president has again shown himself to be an unreliable ally for Europe
content:
US president Donald Trump announced on his Truth Social account over the weekend that “both sides have agreed” to an immediate energy ceasefire. It was news to Ukraine and, it appears, also to Russia. “No, we did not know about that,” Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskiy responded when told about the “ceasefire” by the media. It would be acceptable, however, in the unlikely event it was mutually agreed, he said.
Russia’s response was unambiguous - to bomb a Kharkiv power plant. Trump has eased pressure on Moscow by suspending sanctions against diesel exports and demanding that Ukraine end its effective strikes on oil installations. Putin followed by suspending peace talks indefinitely.
Once again Trump has announced as fact a deal that is no more than wishful thinking, hoping to bounce Ukraine and European allies into accepting it as a fait accompli. His preoccupation is not with ending the war, but entirely about placating angry US voters ahead of the midterm elections next month, with what he claims is a decisive move to reduce diesel prices at the pumps.
It looks unlikely to do so. On Monday there was a only a small downward tick in prices on news of the “deal”. Although, according to Trump, “Russia will … deliver, within a short period of time, three million tons of diesel fuel,” this represents only 7.5 - 8 per cent of a single day’s global consumption. The impact on prices may be limited, although Russia will receive badly needed cash to help to pay for its war in Ukraine and Trump will appear to an increasingly dubious support base to be responding to their concerns.
On Monday, EU ministers correctly made clear their continued solidarity and opposition to the sabotage of Kyiv’s most effective weapon. They refused to countenance following suit by easing sanctions on diesel and agreed to 1,600 new sanctions against individuals and companies in Russia’s military industrial complex.
Trump’s message to Europe is clear once again – the US is no longer the reliable ally on whom the postwar peace was built.

title: Downing Street trying to play down Andy Burnham comments on Russia’s role in Brexit
description: UK prime minister seemed to suggest on politics podcast that Putin influenced outcome of Brexit referendum
content:
If Brexit dominated the past decade for Britain, many in the halls of power in Westminster believe asymmetric conflict with Russia may dominate the next one.
UK prime minister Andy Burnham managed to combine both issues at the weekend by appearing to suggest that Russia had influenced the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum.
Downing Street spent much of Monday trying to walk his comments back.
Burnham gave a Monday afternoon statement on global affairs to the House of Commons, in which he welcomed efforts to secure a so-called “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine preventing them from attacking each other’s energy infrastructure.
Donald Trump had – seemingly prematurely – announced such a ceasefire at the weekend, although Ukraine accused Russia of continuing to hit energy targets. Burnham, meanwhile, suggested he gave the US president the idea for the ceasefire when they met last month in New York.
The prime minister told the Commons on Monday an energy ceasefire would be the “quickest” way to calm events “without rewarding the aggressor”, a deft admonishment of Trump for his recent deal with Russian president Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply 1.8 million tonnes of diesel to the US.
Most of the questions from MPs after Burnham’s statement, however, focused on his comments about Russia and Brexit on The Rest Is Politics, the podcast hosted by former Labour communications chief Alastair Campbell and former Tory politician Rory Stewart.
“I asked the question coming to Downing Street: ‘Was there interference in the 2016 [Brexit] referendum from Russia?’” Burnham told Stewart in podcast excerpts released on Sunday. “And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.”
The remarks immediately caught the attention of the Westminster milieu as, for the first time, a UK prime minister appeared to openly suggest the result of the referendum and Brexit itself may have been swayed, at least in part, by Putin’s Russia.
[ Why Andy Burnham says ‘Brexit has done more harm than good’ Opens in new window ]
That opened up the obvious question of whether Burnham believed the result of Brexit vote was legitimate, given the possibility of Russian interference.
Stephen Doughty, a minister in the foreign office, was sent on to the airwaves first thing on Monday morning to douse the burgeoning story created by Burnham’s comments. He said Russia had “certainly” attempted to influence Brexit, but insisted it had not succeeded.
Later on Monday morning at Downing Street’s daily briefing for Westminster journalists, an official tried further to water down the clear suggestion from Burnham that Russia had a hand in Brexit. A spokesman said that on past form, it was “inconceivable” Russia had not tried to meddle in Brexit, but played down there being direct evidence that it had actually done so, which is what Burnham had implied on The Rest Is Politics.
So what, then, did the prime minister mean when he said he had been told of “clear” interference? The spokesman would not address this point.
Later in the afternoon, after much haranguing from opposition MPs in the Commons, Burnham eventually declared his “respect” for the Brexit referendum result.
The Tories, meanwhile, accused him of trying to “unpick” it.

title: Sandymount flood defences: Walls and rock armour among proposals to protect coastline
description: Dublin City Council publishes four options to safeguard ‘people, property and infrastructure to the greatest extent possible’
content:
Flood defences, involving the construction walls up to 1.5m higher than the current coastal promenade, and rock armour up to 15m wide on the beach, are being proposed to protect Sandymount in South Dublin .
More than 20 years since the coastal suburb was hit by extreme flooding, Dublin City Council has published plans for defences on the beach and promenade along Strand Road, from the Merrion gates to Sean Moore Park, a distance of just over 2km.
Defences are needed to protect more than 1,000 homes in Sandymount identified at risk of flooding since 2002. However, their construction has been beset by delays.
The council has published four options to protect “people, property and infrastructure to the greatest extent possible” from “wave overtopping and coastal flooding”, Gerry O’Connell the council’s senior engineer with responsibility for flood protection said.
The first option involves construction of a new seawall which would be about 5m wide and 1.2m in height, on the seaward side of the existing promenade. The would be accompanied by a “large amount” of new rock armour or “revetments”, large boulders which would extend from 10m to 15m in width, being placed on the beach for part of the 2km length.
The second option would see similar revetments installed, but running continuously along the entire length of the beach. In addition to being 10m to 15m wide, the rock armour could reach about 1m above the height of the existing promenade.
[ Sandymount to Salthill: Five of Ireland’s coastal exposure hotspots Opens in new window ]
The third option would also be for a continuous revetment, but it would be stepped. The top of step would incorporate a path that could be up to 10m wide to reduce wave over topping at the road. The existing rock armour would be removed and replaced with the concrete steps. The top of the new revetment could be 1.5m higher than the existing promenade level.
The fourth option involves putting additional sand on the beach to create a higher and wider beach in front of the seawall. “The larger beach acts as a natural coastal defence absorbing the wave energy before it reaches the seawall which reduces flood risk and protects the existing seawall from wave impact,” O’Connell told councillors on Monday.
Extensive repairs to the existing seawall would likely be required and “groynes” timber structures, which would stretch out towards the sea for about 65m out from the existing sea wall would also be built.
This would be “quite a large increase in the level of the existing beach area. Also, with this, there would be significant maintenance on the structure of this size and significance,” O’Connell said.
“But it would be considered more environmentally friendly, possibly than some of the other options.”
Several councillors asked why a cycle route was not included in any of the four options.
Plans for a cyclepath on Strand Road were the subject of a five-year legal challenge which was resolved last year when the Court of Appeal overturned a High Court judgment that had blocked the implementation of the six-month trial of the path on the roadway.
However, there has been no progress on the development of the cyclepath in the road, which would have involved reducing the width of the carriageway and making it into a one-way route for traffic.
O’Connell said while the flood defence plans did not include provision for a cycleway they “would not conflict” with the development of a cycleway by the council’s traffic department in the future.
The four options will be presented to Sandymount residents later this month. The final option is expected to be selected early next year, with a planning application for the work due to be submitted by the start of 2028. The work could be completed by 2030, O’Connell said.
Costs for the project were not yet available, he said.

title: ‘Fancy’ food and the ‘priest’s sugar’: hosting a station Mass at home
description: A rural tradition where the woman of the house complied, the clergy had to be appeased - and there was to be no scrimping
content:
I f it wasn’t for the now moribund rural tradition of hosting a “station Mass” in households, many of the old houses in the Irish countryside would have fallen down.
That was an observation made by a woman in the audience at Cork ’s Butter Museum where, on Culture Night recently, the history of what was known as “the stations” was recounted by the writer of nostalgia, Alice Taylor , and culinary historian, Regina Sexton .
This high-pressure sacred and social event, whereby Mass was celebrated across the four yearly quarters in different houses in parishes all over Ireland, was an occasion for frantic deep-cleaning, carrying out repairs inside and outside, as well as painting the host house – both the interior and the exterior. (Sometimes, furniture would be stripped of layers of paint to be freshly painted, revealing mahogany.)
With neighbours and friends invited to the Mass, followed by a feast and bottles of stout consumed by the men later that night, the stations demanded a pristine house and “fancy” food. What was known as “priest’s bread” (purchased from a bakery) and “priest’s sugar” (sugar cubes) as well as little balls of butter were served at the breakfast table where the priest and his curate, after Mass and confessions – the latter often held in a bedroom – enjoyed the hospitality on offer.
There was nothing “fancy” about the fare on offer at the Butter Museum on Culture Night, where a breakfast table was set up in the style of what would have been served at the stations. Dressed in a starched linen tablecloth, with chinaware and silver tongs for the sugar, the table’s modest spread comprised sliced pan, hard-boiled eggs and barm brack. And there was of course a pot of tea. Not terribly exciting – until we were given slices of brack covered with butter, churned on the premises. The moist sweet bread and the creamy unsalted butter went down very well. Our hosts said that back in the day there was a lot more food at the stations, with dishes like sherry trifle on offer.
Another woman in the audience recalled how her mother served the priest at her stations in Mitchelstown chicken with grapes. This was apparently a recipe from one of those Cordon Bleu magazines popular in the 1970s. The priest was not impressed and asked that he be served a full Irish fry instead. No doubt, the woman of the house complied – the clergy had to be appeased. And there was to be no scrimping. After what might have been the mortification at the amount of the “dues” donated by each person during the Mass being called out, parishioners all over the country must have been relieved when anonymous envelopes for the money were introduced.
As someone commented at the Butter Museum, the stations were not for the poor. They were all about putting one’s best foot forward, with the notion of plenitude being closely allied with piety. Did genuine piety come into it at all or was it all about show? What if there was no woman of the house to act as host and chief organiser? What if money was tight? Did the rota of houses hosting the stations exclude those of the impoverished?
And God only knows what really went on at the stations once the religious ceremony was over. The legendary seanchaí, Eamon Kelly, used to regale radio and theatre audiences with tales regarding the gossip and drama that unfolded at a village station Mass.
The stations went on all day and at night, there were musical instruments produced, and sing-songs ensued
The term “station” (from the Latin “stationem” meaning a standing or a post) was borrowed by the early church in Rome to describe the movement of the pope between the different station churches to celebrate community-based Masses on feast days and saints’ days. In Ireland the station Mass was linked to Penal times, when travelling priests moved around their communities to Mass stations in farmhouses and outbuildings. Even after Catholic emancipation, the stations continued, making the Mass an important feature of religious rural practice until the recent past.
Originally from Newmarket in Co Cork, Innishannon-based Alice Taylor (88), dressed in cardinal red, said the stations were the highlight of the year. “You’d prepare a year in advance. It was an opportunity for the woman of the house to get things done. The man of the house in his good suit would be at the door, welcoming his neighbours.”
The stations went on all day and at night, there were musical instruments produced, and sing-songs ensued. “The gramophone was a huge thing,” said Taylor. She reminisced about the sense of community that the stations celebrated, mentioning the combination of the “divine” and the social .
But as a man in the audience remarked, there was a “huge distinction” between farm owners and people who only had small cottages. Not everyone felt part of the more privileged class system where religion and prosperity went hand in hand.

title: Toxic Threads review: ‘I was getting all this hate for wanting to be a dad’
description: Television: Brian Dowling Gourounlian chronicles his experiences of social media abuse in moving documentary
content:
Brian Dowling Gourounlian veers between anger and tearful distress as he chronicles his experiences of social media abuse in the unflinching and moving documentary Toxic Threads (Virgin Media One, Monday, 9pm).
The TV presenter and his husband, choreographer Arthur Gourounlian, have been the target of horrific cyber abuse for being a same-sex couple.
What’s especially hurtful, Dowling Gourounlian says, is the vitriol directed at their young daughters: “They get to act out all their rage online. Then they go home, and they have normal lives.”
The trolling compounded the insecurities Dowling Gourounlian felt because he did not have a direct biological connection to his kids: “What happens when my children are born? Am I going to feel weird holding them? I was really paranoid [and] I was getting all this hate for wanting to be a dad.”
Sometimes it went further than just invective. The family’s address was published online and someone made the spurious claim that he was an alcoholic. “They had a link to the house we rented on Daft. I thought, hang on one second – they know our address.”
Dowling Gourounlian sets out to unmask the trolls and, as he does, Toxic Threads becomes an unlikely detective story. He meets a husband-and-wife private eye team in Dublin, though data protection legislation ultimately means they cannot name his abusers.
He also discovers he is not alone. Journalist Aoife Moore talks about how, as her profile increased, the abuse she experienced escalated to death and rape threats. One important breakthrough, she says, is that she became comfortable with acknowledging that she was a victim.
Dowling Gourounlian agrees. “In the job that we do, we’re not allowed to have feelings,” he says.
He also meets Senator Eileen Flynn, who says that as a Traveller, politician and a mother, she has received every imaginable sort of hate. “Thousands of racist, nasty messages. Attacked because of how I look, how I speak.”
Who are these people and why do they spend their spare time attacking strangers? Part of the answer, says cyberpsychology researcher Dr Nicola Fox Hamilton, is the phenomenon of “online disinhibition”. “If they say it to you, they have to deal with your reaction. Online, they say something, someone else agrees with them and they get to feel good about themselves,” she says.
Dowling Gourounlian invites his abusers to meet him and explain why they hate him so much – but nobody takes him up on his challenge. There is a moderately hopeful conclusion, however, insofar as the details of his home address are finally taken down.
Yet this breakthrough comes far too late – by which time the toll on his psychological wellbeing has been devastating. He says that he is at some level “still that kid in Rathangan back in the 1990s that was a gay kid – I think that shame, not being accepted, never really leaves you”.
He tries to stay in a positive frame of mind throughout this brave and compelling documentary. Above all, Dowling Gourounlian says, he wants to be present for his family. “I know I’m a good person,” he says, becoming overwrought. “I want to be the best version of myself for them.”

title: Aviva expands flood insurance access to 13,000 properties following ‘granular’ map update
description: General insurance provider said recent ‘severe weather events absolutely inform our decisions’
content:
Aviva has increased access to flood protection insurance for an additional 13,000 homes and businesses across the State following reforms to its “extremely granular” flood risk map, the insurer said.
The enhancement comes two months after the Government established its Flood Insurance Protection Gap Working Group, of which Aviva, one of the largest general insurance providers in the Irish market, is a member.
This move “is a positive example of the progress being made through investment in flood protection measures, improved understanding of risk and greater collaboration across stakeholders,” said Joanie Hughes, managing director of personal lines at Aviva.
Julie Frazer, head of product, underwriting and intermediary within the personal lines division, said Aviva was “constantly updating its risk assessments” and “regularly reviews data” to do with flood risk.
She said recent “severe weather events”, such as Storm Chandra and Storm Eowyn , “absolutely inform our decisions” on the matter.
The insurer has since updated its “extremely granular maps ... based on the probability of a flood event occurring” at any given property, she said.
The 13,000 additional properties are “very much widespread right across the country.
“Flood risk can be really localised”, with the rock type, hill incline, and proximity to a body of water all factors that can result in “one property being able to access flood protection and another one ‘just up the road’ not,” Frazer continued.
[ ESB battens down the hatches for storm season Opens in new window ]
“Needless to say, the flood protection gap is something we’re very conscious of and would like to help to close,” she went on, “it’s very much at the forefront of our minds.”
Market research conducted by 3Gem Research & Insights on behalf of Aviva “reveals growing awareness among homeowners of the risks posed by extreme weather”, the insurer said.
While it found one-in-10 homeowners have experienced flood damage in the past five years, 24 per cent have experienced “storm-related damage”, and 62 per cent are “concerned” of extreme-weather damage over the next five years.
“Despite high levels of awareness and concern, almost half of homeowners (46 per cent) have not made any improvements to protect their property from extreme weather over the past two years,” Aviva said.
Common actions taken include upgrading gutter systems, repairing roofs, purchasing emergency kits and improving drainage systems, the research of 1,000 homeowners found.
Aviva advised homeowners to inform themselves of weather warnings and local flood risks through alerts from Met Éireann and to consider implementing “practical reliance measures” such as flood barriers to their properties.
The Government established in August a flood insurance working group. Tánaiste Simon Harris said “it will bring together the key public and private sector stakeholders needed to identify practical solutions to one of the most challenging issues facing the insurance market”.
“We have been very much involved with this alongside all of our peers in the industry,” Frazer said. “We’re very determined to find a way to deal with the flood protection gap – we understand and appreciate the difficulties it can create for homeowners and business owners,” she said.

title: Hackers heat up hundreds of French supermarket fridges, causing fires and food loss
description: Danish software firm says affected units ‘were running outdated firmware’ as temperatures were forced up to 50 degrees
content:
Hackers forced the temperature of many French supermarket fridges up to 50 degrees overnight, ​causing fires and food losses at several hundred shops across the country in a large cyberattack .
The Paris prosecutor’s office said a “large-scale” attack was “affecting connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France” and reported damage included “food losses and fires”.
Meanwhile, the country’s prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) to investigate, ​a spokesperson said.
They said France “was co-ordinating with its European counterparts, as other countries may also be affected” while also investigating whether any other French ⁠firms were at risk.
Les Mousquetaires, the co-operative that retailer owns Intermarche, said about 150 of its stores had been affected, ‌with ‌fridges ​heated up to 50 degrees for six hours. It had thrown all the food away to avoid any sanitary risks, a spokesperson said.
Coopérative U chief executive Dominique Schelcher said his supermarket ⁠had also been targeted by the attack.
“Targeting ​equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the ​food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” he wrote on X.
Carrefour said 80 of ‌its supermarkets had been affected but that the vast ​majority of its 6,000 stores had not been hit.
Several other supermarket chains, including Monoprix, E Leclerc and Auchan, did not respond ⁠to requests for comment.
Dutch supermarket operator ⁠Ahold Delhaize, which operates the ​Netherlands’ largest supermarket chain Albert Heijn, said it was also dealing with a “security issue” in its network, and had taken several systems offline to protect them.
A smartphone app for the retailer told clients that due to a “cybersecurity incident” it was unable to deliver groceries.
Online orders represent around 10 per cent of sales for Albert Heijn. Physical stores remained open and Dutch news agency ANP reported that rivals had seen an influx of delivery orders.
It was not clear if there was any link between the French supermarket ‌attack and the problems flagged ⁠by Ahold Delhaize.
Ahold is the fourth-largest grocery retailer in the US, where websites for its Stop & Shop, Giant, Hannaford and Food Lion stores all had notices saying “site temporarily down”.
It was unclear if other operations were ‌affected.
The spokesperson for Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss.
Danfoss said it was “aware of incidents in ​France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems”.
The affected units “were running outdated firmware”, ​Danfoss said, adding that it had “long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions”.

title: ‘The monster that haunts our nightmares’: Child victims of Parnell Square attack tell parents of trauma
description: Mother whose daughter suffered a head injury described Riad Bouchaker as a ‘monster’ who ‘haunts our nightmares’
content:
A mother whose young daughter is severely disabled after being stabbed during the attack at Dublin’s Parnell Square said her family’s life has changed “unrecognisably”.
The woman was among five people affected by the attack on November 23rd, 2023, whose victim impact statements were read at the Central Criminal Court .
She and her husband will be caring for their daughter, now aged eight, for the rest of their lives “and we need to be sure she will be looked after when we are gone”.
“Learning about disability has been eye-opening, but I wouldn’t wish this on anyone,” she added.
Her statement was read by Det Garda Shimna Ní Mháirtin during a hearing on Monday to decide the sentence to be imposed on Riad Bouchaker (52), a native of Algeria of no fixed abode who was convicted of eight offences , including the attempted murder of three children.
Another mother whose daughter suffered a head injury described Bouchaker as a “monster” who had “stolen the innocence” of the 13 children who had witnessed his “evil and cowardly” attack. “He is the monster that haunts our nightmares,” she said.
Childcare worker Leanne Flynn, who suffered serious injuries when stabbed while trying to protect the children, said her life and that of her partner and two young children had changed drastically.
Addressing Bouchaker directly, she told him “harming innocent children is unforgivable”.
Judge Tony Hunt will rule on November 16th on the sentences to be imposed. There was serious rioting in Dublin on the evening of the attack in 2023.
The three attempted murder charges against Bouchaker relate to the severely injured five-year-old girl and to a six-year-old girl and a five-year-old boy.
The six-year-old girl was discharged from hospital a day after having surgery to repair a non-penetrative laceration to her scalp and dislodging of a skull fragment. The boy had a nick to his neck treated with paper stitches and three holes in the hood of his jacket.
Bouchaker was found guilty of intentionally inflicting serious harm on Flynn and will also be sentenced for assault causing harm to two other children.
One was a six-year-old girl who had a bump on her head, a nick behind her ear and a clump of hair cut.
In a victim impact statement, her mother said her daughter had told her, when she was lying on the ground on Parnell Square, the attacker “looked like a real man but he was actually a bad man” and that day was “more worser than any bad days”.
Her daughter continues to be afraid of crowds and loud noises,
The other child was a five-year-old boy who had a small cut and a graze under his arm as well as slashes to his clothing.
His mother, in her statement, told Bouchaker he had left her son and the other children with “terrifying memories that haunt them to this day”.
Addressing Bouchaker in Irish, the woman said she, like him, was an immigrant to Ireland and she and her son loved Ireland, “the best country in the world”.
“I have such a depth of dread that you will ever walk the streets of Ireland again,” she said.

title: Warning to Defence Forces night before bombing ended with ‘Omagh, Omagh, Omagh’, inquiry told
description: Former BBC investigative reporter said call urged gardaí to ‘check the back roads’
content:
A telephone warning to the Defence Forces ’ Finner Camp in Donegal ending with the words “Omagh, Omagh, Omagh” was made the night before an explosion ripped through the Co Tyrone town, the Omagh bombing inquiry has been told.
Details of the telephone call were given to the inquiry, led by Andrew Turnbull, by the former BBC investigative reporter John Ware, who has produced a number of programmes about the bombing.
The telephone warning urged that An Garda Síochána and Defence Forces “check the back roads” for an explosives-laden car travelling across the Border from the Republic, finishing with the words “Omagh, Omagh, Omagh”.
The call came just hours before the Real IRA attack on August 15th, 1998, killed 29 people and injured 220 others, the worst single attack in Northern Ireland during the Troubles, and the second deadliest overall.
The warning was relayed in a note headed “BDS Finner”, which is understood to stand for barracks detachment staff at Finner Camp, the administrative office in the Donegal camp, though it is unclear to whom it was sent.
The caller had “sounded sober”, Ware told the inquiry, on the back of information given to him by a confidential source who was “reliable and well-placed”, but whom he could not name.
The Omagh inquiry, which began last year, must decide on whether the Omagh attack more than 28 years ago could reasonably have been prevented by the British government and its agencies.
It is not known if this warning was passed on to the Police Service of Northern Ireland. A 2009 inquiry by the UK’s intelligence services commissioner Peter Gibson found “no evidence whatever” that warnings were received from the Garda.

title: Investment vehicle sues over financing plan for apartment scheme in Leopardstown
description: Dispute relates to a site at Leopardstown Park, where it was proposed to develop apartments
content:
A corporate investment vehicle set up to acquire a residential site in south Dublin is suing a company over alleged misrepresentation as to projected returns and non-disclosure of an aggregate promoter fee.
Merleview Ltd has brought Commercial Court proceedings against Burton Carman Ltd, a special purpose vehicle set up to acquire, hold and develop a property at Leopardstown Park with a view, it is claimed, to develop around 145 build-to-rent apartments. It is also suing Elkstone Capital Partners Ltd, which was the promoter and manager of the investment in Burton Carman.
The case was entered to the fast track Commercial Court on Monday by Judge Eileen Roberts on consent between the parties.
It was adjourned to next month after the judge was told there may be mediation or alternatively, the defendants say, the dispute may be covered by an arbitration clause.
In a sworn statement seeking entry of the case to the commercial list, Andrew Murphy, a director of Merleview, said that in February 2022, Elkstone director and chief revenue officer Ruairí O’Neill presented him with an “equity opportunity pitch deck” and a “debt opportunity pitch deck” concerning the development of the Leopardstown property. It was proposed to develop it as a private rental sector scheme of around 145 apartments.
Murphy said the pitch decks forecast an exit value of €14.9 million, an equity return of 42 per cent IRR (internal rate of return) and a 2.01 times multiple on a €2.9 million equity investment over 24 months along with a senior debt coupon of 10 per cent a year.
On the strength of these representations, Murphy said, Merleview subscribed for ordinary shares in Burton Carman and advanced an accompanying senior debt facility, together totalling €446,969.
In July 2023, Merleview advanced a further amount of some €303,000 as a loan note.
Murphy said the executed loan note certificate stated an interest rate of 7.5 per cent per annum even though the “debt deck”, and O’Neill’s own representations, had put the rate at 10 per cent.
In August, the defendants’ solicitors sent a corrected certificate showing an interest rate of 10 per cent on the loan note from March 2023 and acknowledging the original cert had been wrong in relation to that.
In April 2026, Merleview raised 10 categories of complaint against Elkstone including misrepresentation as to projected returns and the interest rate and non-disclosure of an aggregate promoter fee entitlement of some €781,000, which Murphy said was equivalent to 15.5 per cent of the total capital raised of some €5 million.
There was also an unauthorised material change to the investment strategy from a private rental sector scheme to a build-to-sell scheme without the investor majority consent required, Murphy said.
There was also a breach of ongoing reporting obligations under the subscription and shareholders agreement (SSA), he added.
The defendants’ solicitors denied liability and that Elkstone owed Merleview no duty of care given the disclaimers in the pitch decks and the SSA.
Merleview issued proceedings last August claiming recovery of the €303,000 principal sum under the loan note, damages for breach of duty, and for intentional interference with Merleview’s economic interests.
Murphy said it was important the proceedings be resolved without delay as Merleview’s senior debt and loan notes have been in default since July 2025 and no principal has been repaid to date. Interest continues to accrue, he said.
Despite repeated requests, he said, the defendants have not produced audited accounts, management reports or verified fee accounts and the parties are in dispute as to Merleview’s entitlement under the SSA to withhold consent to certain proposed transactions pending provision of the information.
The defendants’ solicitors have also indicated an intention to apply for security for costs against Merleview. However, Merleview says it is a fully solvent company.

title: ‘A lot of people didn’t believe us’: George Gibney victim sees justice done after first prosecution collapsed
description: Chalkie White, one of the first to speak out about paedophile’s abuse more than 30 years ago, welcomes sentencing
content:
Two of the people abused as children by George Gibney expressed their relief on Monday as the former swimming coach was finally jailed.
Chalkie White, who was one of the first to speak out about Gibney’s abuse more than 30 years ago, praised the bravery of the four women who came forward despite the collapse of an initial attempt to prosecute Gibney in the 1990s.
White, a former Irish swimming champion, told RTÉ’s Liveline nobody believed him when he initially came forward.
“When we went initially, I was told I should put it behind me and get on with it. There were a lot of people who didn’t believe us, now it’s a case of saying: There you go ... he’s a convicted paedophile and he’s in jail.”
White was a complainant in the prosecution case taken against Gibney in the 1990s that collapsed after a Supreme Court challenge. He was abused by Gibney when he was aged 11 and Gibney, then starting out on his coaching career, was in his late teens.
Speaking on the steps of the Central Criminal Court after Gibney (78) had been jailed for 15½ years , Orla Poole waived her anonymity as one of Gibney’s victims to speak about the case.
She said other victims of sexual abuse should not feel alone.
“If there are any, and I believe there are many, others who suffered at the hands of Gibney ... know that you do not have to carry this burden alone. You are not at fault, the only guilt for what we went through lies with the convicted paedophile,” said Poole.
[ George Gibney: Paedophile finally faces accountability after long and harrowing journey for victims Opens in new window ]
“There are people, organisations and authorities who will listen, who will offer support, and will act.
“The times of sweeping things under the rug, turning a blind eye, or holding that children should be seen and not heard are gone.
“To all survivors out there, speak when you are ready, reclaim your agency and remember you are not to blame. Only the offender is to blame. You are not alone. There is support. There are people that will be of help to you.
“You will be heard and you will be believed.”
[ ‘A little bit of utopia’: Victim of swim coach George Gibney speaks on abuser’s conviction Opens in new window ]
Poole thanked her mother for keeping records and documents, her sister for her support, others who had offered support, and former Irish Times journalist Johnny Watterson, who first reported on abuse claims against Gibney in 1994.
She also thanked An Garda Síochána , specifically Sgt Amy Kelly, Det Sgt Jonathan Hayes and Det Sgt Dave Connolly for their “compassion, kindness and commitment shown towards me throughout the years of this case”.
Dublin Rape Crisis Centre chief executive Rachel Morrogh said: “Half a century since the abuses took place, the court has sent an unambiguous message that George Gibney’s victims are believed, that it was never their fault and that all the shame and blame lies with the perpetrator – the paedophile George Gibney.
“Although he evaded justice for far too long, his day of reckoning has come thanks to the tireless, courageous and determined efforts of survivors and their supporters.”
Morrogh added: “The conviction and sentencing is down to the endurance and determination of the survivors, the swimming community and all their family and friends who sustained them over such a long period of time.”
One of the victims of George Gibney has called for other individuals abused by the former swimming coach to “unburden” themselves by speaking to someone about the abuse when they are ready.
Swim Ireland said no “swimmer, child or family should ever experience such harm within our sport”.
A spokesperson for the organisation said: “Our thoughts are with the survivors and their families. We recognise the immense courage shown by those who came forward, shared their experiences, and participated in a lengthy and difficult legal process.”
The organisation’s support “remains available” to Gibney’s victims, and highlighted the Here to Listen section on the Swim Ireland website, the spokesperson said.
“These supports remain available to any survivor, family member, or member of the swimming community affected by this case, whether or not they have engaged with the legal process.”
In July, a Central Criminal Court jury found Gibney guilty of 39 counts of indecent assault and one count of attempted rape of children.
The jury acquitted him of one count of indecently assaulting one of the complainants on a date between 1976 and 1977.

title: European stocks rise with banks proving a safe bet
description: Stocks in Ireland’s Iseq All-Share index largely began the week on a positive note
content:
Stocks across Europe largely rose on Monday, bolstered by investor confidence in the banking sectors and strong returns by drinks and luxury giants.
Close to home, banking also proved a safe investment as Dublin’s stock market saw positive returns from financial groups, manufacturers and construction companies alike.
Across the Atlantic, however, many traders were hesitant to begin the week with a strong start as key inflation data looms later in the week, seen to be pivotal in shaping the Federal Reserve’s economic forecasts and the trajectory of interest rates.
The Iseq All-Share index rose 1.60 per cent to start the week in the green, closing at 14,123.87 following positive results in the banking and manufacturing sectors.
Strong gains by the building materials and insulation manufacturer Kingspan, whose share price rose 2.41 per cent to €101.80 by close of business, were among the day’s top results.
Elsewhere, home builder Glenveagh Properties was up 1.77 per cent to close at €2.30 a share, while Cairn Homes grew by 0.03 per cent to close at €2.64. Food technology company Kerry Group also saw strong returns, up 1.45 per cent at €88.70 a share.
Both major banks traded on the index saw their share price increase. Bank of Ireland was up 1.79 per cent to close at €18.46, while rival AIB lagged slightly behind, up 1.68 per cent to finish at €10.86.
Agri-services group Origin Enterprises and healthcare company Uniphar also saw their share prices increase, 3.95 per cent and 3.26 per cent to €3.95 and €3.97 a share, respectively.
Insurer FBD Holdings saw its share price drop, down 1.84 per cent to €18.65 by the end of the trading day.
The London stock market saw stocks largely rise across the board, with its blue-chip FTSE 100 index increasing 0.99 per cent and the mid-cap FTSE 250 up 0.47 per cent as well.
Investors put their trust in British banks, with Lloyds Banking Group rising 2.36 per cent and Barclays not far behind, up 1.85 per cent by close. Meanwhile, Lion Finance also jumped 2.75 per cent.
Guinness-brewer Diageo, who also owns Smirnoff Vodka and Don Julio tequila, ended the day up 2.14 per cent on Friday’s closing price.
Telecommunications group Vodafone, however, dipped 1.39 per cent by close – as did publishing and exhibitions group Informa, whose share price fell 2.41 per cent.
Elsewhere in Europe, investors in banking portfolios and luxury goods suppliers helped the continent’s two major indices also close the trading day with growth.
The Stoxx 600 index was up 0.65 per cent, while the Stoxx 50 followed, up 0.45.
Spain’s Santander bank increased 1.80 per cent, while German Deutsche Telekom rose 1.13 per cent.
Elsewhere, France’s luxury good giant Hermes International soared 2.10 per cent by close. Car manufacturer Mercedes Benz Group, however, saw its share price dip 0.82 per cent.
Early trades on Wall Street pointed to a slightly less positive trend compared with global indices.
Some stocks fluctuated near their all-time highs while others faltered as traders looked ahead to the start of the earnings season.
Before midday New York time, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.43 per cent, meanwhile the S&P saw little change and the Nasdaq fell some 0.60 per cent.
Most companies in the S&P 500 rose despite renewed losses in chipmakers and looming inflation data to be released later this week that will be key in shaping the Federal Reserve’s outlook. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg.

title: Workers as well as employers need to feel AI benefit, union leader tells conference
description: HSE’s AI strategy featured input from 30 organisations, but not one represented works, Callinan says
content:
Artificial intelligence has become a key workplace issue, but the terms of its use need to be negotiated to ensure workers as well as employers feel the productivity benefits it presents, a union event on the subject heard on Monday.
Fórsa general secretary Kevin Callinan said the union’s 100,000 members across public services “are not afraid of the tools” the technology will bring “but of the terms” on which staff will be asked to work with them.
The meeting was attended by politicians, union officials and leaders of a number of NGOs.
He said those working for the State had to be authors of the coming change in work practices and not just audience members for a process exclusively driven by management.
“When the HSE published its AI for Care strategy, covering imaging, clinical-decision support and clinical documentation, it consulted a stakeholder group of more than 30 organisations. Not one of them represented workers,” he said.
“Patients were consulted. The people who will work with these systems every day were not consulted at all.
“Let me be clear about Fórsa’s position. We do not stand in outright opposition to this technology. We stand for frameworks that are negotiated before the technologies are deployed; against AI adoption that is premised on cutting jobs; for a named, accountable person being in command of every consequential decision; and for the sharing of AI’s productivity benefits through time and flexibility, through pay and reinvestment in services.”
AI consultant Shaadi Valadkhani said unions were ensuring they were better equipped to deal with the issues arising around the deployment of the technology as “AI is not an act of nature, it is a series of decisions” and staff needed to have a voice in how those were made.
She said the union would have red lines around any attempt to use AI in hiring or firing, surveillance and ongoing governance.
Joe O’Connor, a former official with the union who advises businesses and unions on work practices, said companies such as Ikea had shown how AI could be integrated into systems while the roles of displaced staff displaced were developed to bring benefits to them and the employers.
More commonly, however, management and workers tended to have very different views regarding the potential impact of the technology, he suggested, with one survey indicating 76 per cent of leaders felt their staff were enthusiastic, whereas just 31 per cent actually were.
In relation to negotiations on a new pay deal, Callinan said there were provisions in the last one for consultation on technological change but Fórsa had not been involved in any centralised consultation on it.
“It’s an extraordinarily important issue,” he said. “And we have seen after other technological transitions ... work has been devalued, often that of women. But not this time.”

title: Abusive parents and car park crashes among litany of incidents faced by driving testers
description: Log of 161 incidents recorded by RSA also included cases of irate candidates and accusations of racism
content:
Driving testers were abused by parents whose children had failed their tests or could not take them because of invalid insurance discs.
One candidate became aggressive with a staff member after failing to “understand the rules around traffic lights” and refusing to listen, according to an incident report.
Another candidate crashed their vehicle in a car park at the end of their test.
The incidents were among more than 160 recorded by the Road Safety Authority (RSA) over a 15-month period. In about a quarter of the incidents, staff were subjected to verbal abuse, threatened, attacked or accused of racism.
There were multiple cases of aggressive parents, including one mother who became verbally abusive when a driving examination was cancelled due to expired car insurance.
A note of the incident said: “Her daughter was not taken out on test as there was an issue with the insurance. It was out of date.”
The RSA listed one case of “extreme verbal abuse” and threats of violence after a man’s partner failed to pass her exam.
In another case, staff were verbally abused by a person who showed up with an insurance disc that was “printed in black and white”.
A note said: “Applicant had previously gotten a ‘non-conduct’ for no proof of insurance.”
Another became threatening after showing up 15 minutes late for their test, only to return an hour later to abuse staff.
One case referenced a “direct physical assault” when a test was not conducted, according to the RSA records.
[ Only 14 driving test centres hitting wait-time target Opens in new window ]
The log of 161 accidents and incidents from the authority covered the period from April 2025 to June 2026.
There were other cases where people crashed during their exams and one where a person bumped their head on a door while leaving a test centre.
Another incident report said: “Test applicant illegally driving to their driving test at 10.05 at Finglas driving test centre, unaccompanied and not displaying L plate.”

title: Brother of murdered Gillian Curran tells court ‘beyond evil’ killer inflicted more than 140 injuries
description: Central Criminal Court sentences killer of ‘kind and vivacious’ Waterford woman to life in prison
content:
The brother of a Waterford woman who was “brutally” beaten to death by her partner has said it was “beyond evil” that the defendant has taken no responsibility for the “140-plus injuries” he inflicted on her.
In an emotional victim impact statement delivered to the Central Criminal Court on Monday, the deceased’s family said 47-year-old Gillian Curran, “like many vulnerable women across Ireland, did not deserve her violent end”.
The deceased’s brother, Michael Curran, told the court their sister’s murder and the subsequent trial had a “profound effect” on the whole family. “As a family, we did not deserve to be dragged through the awful details of her death because of the cowardly decision of her killer not to plead guilty.”
He said what their sister went through in her last 24 hours constantly played on his family’s minds and they found this “extremely distressing”.
The court heard during Monday’s sentence hearing for Marcus O’Neill (36), who was sentenced to the mandatory term of life imprisonment having been found guilty of murder last July, that the deceased suffered from chronic alcohol addiction.
O’Neill had told gardaí at the scene that his girlfriend had fallen multiple times from intoxication. However, there was evidence O’Neill had moved her body and changed her clothing. The nature of the injuries she suffered were so severe they were akin to those experienced in a serious road traffic collision.
Gillian Curran, who was 47 and originally from Sweetbriar in Tramore, was found unresponsive at O’Neill’s house on the morning of January 25th, 2025, and pronounced dead a short time later.
O’Neill had denied murdering her at his home on O’Brien Street in Waterford city. The court heard on Monday that Gillian Curran, who was in a relationship with O’Neill, did not permanently reside there but had regularly stayed at his property.
On July 30th last, a jury of five men and seven women found O’Neill guilty of murdering Gillian Curran by a majority verdict of 10-2.
Defence counsel Roisin Lacey told the court on Monday that her client did not accept the jury’s verdict and it would be wrong of her not to indicate that to the court.
Handing down the mandatory term of life imprisonment for murder, Judge Caroline Biggs thanked the Curran family for giving her an insight into the type of person their sister was.
“The evidence I received today is entirely consistent with [that] heard in the trial from her many work colleagues, who held her in such high esteem and who discussed her in the same terms as her family; clever, capable, kind and a funny person, who was undoubtedly very trusting and sadly very vulnerable”.
The judge said the defendant had brutally beaten his partner to death, that she had sustained 143 injuries over the course of that night and early morning and that those injuries had included lacerations to her chin, tears to her kidney and internal injuries to her stomach. She had suffered “what was described by the pathologist as brain damage, thereby causing her body to stop functioning leading to her death”.
She said the pathologist had also given evidence of strangulation marks on the neck area and that the deceased’s body was almost entirely covered in bruises.
Micheal Curran described his sister as an “intelligent, loving, kind and vivacious woman” in the family’s victim impact statement.
“Trying to blame Gillian for his actions resulting in her horrible death was doubly cruel. His complete lack of remorse and taking no responsibility for the 140-plus injuries he inflicted on her is beyond evil. It was incredibly difficult attending court every day and seeing first hand his complete indifference”.

title: GLP-1s in Ireland: How weight-loss medications work under the HSE system
description: Ozempic and Mounjaro are not available for free on medical card or subsidised by the Drugs Payment Scheme
content:
Weight-loss medications such as Ozempic , Wegovy and Mounjaro have become more widely-discussed and available in recent years. But which drugs are accessible, who can get them, and is there any potential for availability of the drugs increasing?
Sax­enda, which is injec­ted daily, is the only form of GLP-1 ther­apy which is reim­bursed for weight loss by the HSE . This means it is free under the med­ical card or sub­sid­ised for private patients on the Drugs Pay­ment Scheme, which has a cost limit of €80 per month.
The HSE has con­firmed that more than 45,000 people are get­ting Ozempic for free under the Long-Term Ill­ness Scheme, with another 8,348 receiv­ing it under the med­ical card. However, it is only available under these schemes for the treatment of type 2 diabetes.
It is not available under the Drugs Payment Scheme, although people can buy it privately for weight loss purposes, at a cost in excess of €200 a month.
The HSE’s expert drugs group is to meet on Tuesday to discuss the potential reimbursement of the drug for weight loss purposes.
A spokeswoman for the HSE said the process can take some time and that there may be a number of meetings of the Drugs Group before a recommendation is made to the HSE Senior Management Team.
The spokeswoman added that discussions will be required with the Department of Health on the “potential overall impact on the health budget”.
They are all known as GLP-1 medications, but often the active ingredient differs.
Ozempic and Wegovy are both manufactured by pharmaceutical company Novo Nordisk. Meanwhile, Mounjaro, a once-weekly injection, is made by Eli Lilly.
The active ingredient in Novo Nordisk’s jabs is a molecule called semaglutide, while Mounjaro uses tirzepatide.
As is the case with decision-making for reimbursing all drugs under the public system, it comes down to cost-effectiveness.
Before being made available through the public system, drugs are assessed by the National Centre for Pharmacoeconomics (NCPE) which looks at the evidence to support its efficacy, as well as the cost of the product and the impact it would have on those who take it.
The NCPE assessment is used as a discussion point among the HSE drugs group, who then make recommendations to senior HSE management around reimbursement.
In December 2025, the NCPE said the drug was not cost-effective but said the HSE should consider reimbursing it if it could agree with a price reduction with the manufacturer.
Prof Michael Barry, who leads the NCPE, said earlier this year that the manufacturer Eli Lilly had made an offer for a significant price reduction that would make the drug cost-effective or close to it.
However, he warned that even with this reduction, it could cost the State between €2 billion and €3 billion over five years. Ireland’s total drugs budget will top €4 billion next year.
There will be clinical criteria that must be met for a patient to be able to access the drug under HSE schemes.
Clinicians will discuss this criteria with patients, with eligibility typically identified through a number of factors including BMI, obesity-related co-morbidities, lifestyle and diet.
Some studies have indicated weight loss medications could be beneficial for other conditions, including lowering the risk of cardiovascular disease, slowing the progression of kidney disease and sleep apnoea, among others.
As with all medications, there is a risk of side effects. The Health Products Regulatory Authority said there have been over 1,500 reports of suspected adverse reaction from weight-loss medication since 2023.

title: Ilhan Omar: US immigration authorities raid Democratic congresswoman’s home
description: Somali-born Omar is an outspoken critic of ‌US president Donald Trump
author_name: Nolan D McCaskill, Andrew Goudsward, Doina Chiacu
content:
US authorities conducted a predawn raid on Monday on the Washington-area home of Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, an outspoken critic of Donald Trump ​who has been the target of political insults by the Republican president, as part of a continuing investigation, the US justice department said.
A person familiar with the investigation said it is related to alleged immigration fraud, and part of the inquiry concerns the Somali-born politician’s immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child.
Omar wrote in a social media post that the US government is being weaponised to target a political enemy of the president.
“For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns,” Omar said. “This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”
Other Democrats accused Trump and his administration of abuse of power. Omar (44), ​is seeking a fifth two-year term in the US House of Representatives in the midterm elections on November 3rd.
In announcing the raid, a justice department spokesperson said: “Today in the Washington, DC area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured ​by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation,” a US justice department spokesperson said in an email.
Homeland Security Investigations is part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (Ice).
Tom Homan, the Trump administration’s “border tsar”, told Fox Business Network that the justice department is leading the investigation with ‌the ‌department ​of homeland security. Homan declined to get into the specifics of an ongoing criminal investigation.
Homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin, a Trump appointee, said last month that “something’s gonna happen” in the investigation into Omar’s family’s entry into the United States.
“If we can prove that you shouldn’t have been here in the first place, we’ll deport you,” ⁠Mullin told conservative podcaster Benny Johnson at the time.
The raid was carried out a little more than three weeks before the midterm elections, when Trump’s party will be trying to defend its narrow majorities in the US Congress. Omar, ⁠a prominent progressive who is running for reelection, represents a safe Democratic ​district. She won reelection in 2024 by a margin of 50 percentage points.
In a joint statement, US House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and other members of the party’s leadership in the chamber said the ‌raid was “deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the” weaponisation of the federal government against ​Trump’s enemies.
Republicans have “relentlessly targeted” Omar, said Jeffries, joined by Representatives Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar. Trump’s “mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family,” they added, and they ⁠said they would “deliver full accountability” for what they called a “rogue abuse of power.”
Minnesota Democrats ​also condemned the raid.
“Americans see this for what it is,” Minnesota governor Tim Walz , a Democrat, wrote on social media. “President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an ‌election.”
Justice department policy bars federal prosecutors and agents from timing any action ​to affect the outcome of any election or benefiting a candidate or political party. The department has historically avoided taking investigative steps against political candidates within about 60 days ⁠of an election.
The US justice department during Trump’s second term ⁠in office has investigated and brought charges against ​a range of Trump’s perceived political enemies.
It has charged former FBI Director James Comey, New York state attorney general Letitia James and Trump’s former national security adviser turned critic John Bolton. It also has investigated Democratic politicians who urged the US military not to follow illegal orders, Democratic senator Adam Schiff and Federal Reserve officials Jerome Powell and Lisa Cook.
The case against James and one of two brought against Comey were thrown out by a federal judge. Bolton pleaded guilty and is scheduled to be sentenced later this month. Grand juries and federal judges have stymied several other probes.
Omar has faced political insults from Trump, who has cast the Somali American community as a threat to Minnesota in a burst of anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric. Omar has called Trump’s focus on her an “unhealthy and creepy obsession.”
Last week, ‌Trump called Michigan’s Democratic nominee for US Senate – ⁠Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim – a “RADICAL Extremist” and “Terrorist Sympathizer” while offering support for El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.
Civil rights advocates have criticised Trump’s rhetoric toward minorities and immigrants, including when he previously called Somalis “garbage”.
In February Trump said Omar and Democratic representative Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, who is also Muslim, should be “institutionalised” and ‌sent back to “where they came from”. Both had criticised Trump during his State of the Union address as he touted his administration’s hardline immigration crackdown and its immigration enforcement actions.
Omar has said she and her family ​have faced death threats, which she attributes to “hateful political rhetoric,” especially from Trump.
Last month, a Minnesota man who squirted vinegar on ​Omar was sentenced to one year and two months in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a federal official. Anthony James Kazmierczak admitted to attacking Omar because he disagreed with her progressive political views. – Reuters
