title: Sky Ireland revenue rises with help from Rory McIlroy 2025 Masters win
description: Sky’s Ireland business rose by £35m to £539m last year
content:
Rory McIlroy ’s winning putt in the 2025 Masters at Augusta last year helped the Irish arm of Sky to increase revenue by 7 per cent to £539 million (€637 million).
Accounts lodged by Sky Subscribers Services at Companies House in the UK show Sky’s Ireland business rose by £35 million from £504 million to £539 million last year.
Sky Sports recorded its highest ever Sunday viewership in April 2025 when McIlroy clinched his Masters win in dramatic circumstances .
Sky’s Irish revenue relates to revenue from direct-to-home pay television, broadband, mobile and telephony subscriptions in Ireland.
The revenue increase was also helped by Sky Ireland imposing a 4.5 per cent price hike on average for Sky customers here.
Sky Broadband has about 280,000 customers, giving it a 17 per cent market share with Sky Ireland’s market share across fibre-to-the-home broadband reaching 21.4 per cent based on the latest ComReg figures.
Sky Broadband has now delivered more than 50 consecutive quarters of customer growth.
Earlier this year, in its battle against the piracy of Sky channels through so-called dodgy boxes, the company issued about 200 cease-and-desist letters to individuals.
[ Details of 300 ‘dodgy box’ users to be provided to Sky, High Court hears Opens in new window ]
The vast majority of the individuals who were served letters are in Co Wexford and it is understood that the compliance level has been high on receipt of the letters.
A spokesman for Sky Ireland said today: “Sky invests significantly in protecting our content, which can include taking action against those who watch Sky without paying the proper subscription fee.
“For those individuals who received cease-and-desist letters earlier in the year, who did not return undertakings, we are moving towards further action. This may include, where necessary, seeking court injunctions to prevent continued use of illegal IPTV services and pursuing damages for copyright infringement and legal costs.”
Overall revenue at Sky Subscribers Services Ltd in 2025 increased by 5.6 per cent from £1.012 billion to £1.069 billion as pretax profit declined by 12 per cent to £97 million.

title: Unions reject effort to avert Wednesday’s public sector strike
description: ‘Pay issues can and should be discussed as a priority’, Minister Jack Chambers said in letter to unions
content:
Unions have rejected a Government attempt to commence talks on a new public pay agreement and avoid the scheduled strike by more 300,000 public and civil workers on Wednesday.
In a letter sent to the officers of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions (Ictu) public services committee, Jack Chambers invited the unions to attend talks at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) on Wednesday in an effort to avoid the disruption to health and other services as well as the closure of all schools.
The Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform again described the provision of €1.2 billion for public sector pay in the budget as “significant” and suggested an agreement couldstill be reached if talks were held.
Chambers told the union leaders in the letter that “pay issues can and should be discussed as a priority alongside other matters as part of the pay talks”. This has been a key sticking point in getting talks started so far.
In a response sent less than an hour after the proposal had been received, however, Ictu public services committee chair and Fórsa general secretary Kevin Callinan said the union side “cannot see how it represents any change in your stated position”.
There is no reference to the suggested meeting at the WRC but, he said “we believe that the Government needs to respond to the seriousness of the situation by acknowledging that the specific pay issues that we have identified will be addressed in any talks that may be arranged”.
The unions have indicated they will seek increases to address what they say was an earlier gap between pay rises and inflation of between 5 and 7 per cent in addition to a settlement for the second half of this year and an undertaking that their members’ wages will not be undermined by the cost of living increasing over the term of any deal.
The €1.2 billion, they contended, is not nearly enough to address those demands.
“Accordingly,” Callinan told Chambers, “we regret to say that your letter doesn’t provide a basis for the strike action scheduled for Wednesday to be postponed.”

title: The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring in Concert sweeps 3Arena off to Middle-earth
description: Review: Howard Shore’s music for Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings movies is one of the great achievements in film scoring in the 21st century
content:
Howard Shore ’s music for the Lord of the Rings movies ranks as one of the great achievements in film scoring in the 21st century, and at 3Arena in Dublin a live performance of the soundtrack to the first of those films, The Fellowship of the Ring, sweeps the audience far away from a grey, rainy October night and off to Middle-earth.
Ludwig Wicki receives a welcome fit for an all-conquering warrior as he emerges to conduct the 100-piece Irish Philharmonic Concert Orchestra through all three hours of Fellowship. The applause is particularly enthusiastic from those who have arrived dressed as elves or hobbits or whose bared arms reveal Tolkien -specific tattoos: rings, flaming eyes, even the haunted features of the tragic anti-hero Gollum.
This year is the 25th anniversary of Fellowship. In 2001 it surprised and delighted sceptical cinemagoers by niftily bringing to the screen a work that many had deemed unfilmable, because of its complicated lore and vast scope. Peter Jackson ’s trilogy has grown in stature in the intervening quarter-century. It is today regarded not only as one of the outstanding adaptations of a classic novel but also as a masterpiece of epic film-making.
Just how essential Shore’s soundtrack is to that magic is made clear as singers from Dún Laoghaire Choral Society intone hauntingly during the prologue. Goosebumps spread around the room as the evil Sauron is defeated by the Last Alliance of Elves and Men. Next, brave Prince Isildur takes the Ring and ... very sensibly casts it into Mount Doom. End of story.
That isn’t what happens, of course. The Ring endures, evil returns and we are transported to Middle-earth as Wicki introduces us to Shore’s strongly Irish-coded pastoral Hobbit theme, with its use of harps, fiddles and tin whistle.
Then it’s on to the heavy stuff as Frodo and the gang set off for Mount Doom. As they do, the swelling title refrain comes stampeding through, making you want to don a cape, grab a broadsword and head straight for the Misty Mountains.
If the evening has a centrepiece, however, it comes in the Elvish domain of Rivendell as Arwen and Aragorn gaze into one another’s eyes and the soprano Grace Davidson performs Enya ’s Aníron. With lyrics entirely in Sindarin Elvish, the song is a gateway to another world.
At 3Arena on Sunday night the audience briefly get a sense of stepping through a portal and then following the road, ever on and on, to somewhere wilder, weirder and infinitely more wondrous.

title: Irish hopes face major task against older stars in potentially vintage Champion Stakes
description: French Derby winner Constitution River looks like taking mile route after being supplemented into QEII
content:
Saturday’s Qatar Champion Stakes at Ascot is shaping into an fitting climax to the official British flat racing season with a potentially vintage field set to line up.
The first three from 2026, Calandagan, Ombudsman and Almaqam, are on course to clash again, presenting a major challenge to Irish hopes with Jessica Harrington’s Hotazhell joining an Aidan O’Brien team likely to be headed by Gstaad.
The Ballydoyle trainer, chasing down Andrew Balding in a race for the British trainers’ title, has left a handful of entries among the 11 left in the Champion Stakes, including another Classic winner in Constitution River.
However, the latter has been supplemented into the Queen Elizabeth II Stakes, the mile highlight on a lucrative programme featuring five Group One events.
O’Brien had proposed some time ago an end of season discipline switch, with the miler Gstaad upped to 10 furlongs and Constitution River doing the reverse. However, the standard set by the older horse brigade looks formidable.
Calandagan beat Ombudsman by over two lengths last year, with Almaqam back in third. Calandagan finished 2026 as the world’s highest rated thoroughbred but earlier this year Ombudsman exceeded his old rival’s mark when reaching a heady rating of 131 after beating Daryz in the Prince Of Wales’s Stakes at Royal Ascot. Only the Hong Kong sprinter Ka Ying Rising (135) is rated higher anywhere in the world.
Having failed to fire on an easy surface in York’s Juddmonte International, it looks like the elements will work in favour of Ombudsman lining up this weekend.
Ascot returned an official description of “good” going on Monday, with just 2-5mm of rainfall predicted before Saturday. Racing will take place on the normal round course. Testing conditions have previously forced a switch to the National Hunt circuit.
Since Champions Day was introduced 15 years ago, just two horses have completed the Irish-English Champion Stakes double. Harrington’s Hotazhell will bid to emulate Almanzor (2016) and Magical in 2019.
The colt sprang a 50-1 shock when just beating Wimbledon Hawkeye at Leopardstown last month in a controversial contest that saw jockey Shane Foley pick up an 11-day ban for careless riding. Saturday’s race will be his final start before retiring to stud in France.
“Winning a big race, a big Group One race like that, which features all over the world, it’s fantastic for the owners. The yard really gets an unbelievable kick out of it and everyone came in on the Monday morning with a large grin on their face,” said Harrington.
“He came out of the race really well, he lost very little weight, he’s done a bit of work at the Curragh since and we were very happy with him – it’s all systems go for Ascot.
“He’ll go in there a little bit under the radar because they’ll say he was lucky to win it at Leopardstown, but looking back on the race, I think he won it fair and square.”
Christophe Soumillon will be on board Calandagan for the first time due to regular jockey Mickael Barzalona being suspended. The Belgian jockey will also team up with the Aga Khan’s French Guineas winner Rayif in the QEII.
Godolphin also paid out a supplementary fee to get Talk Of New York into the QEII. The colt impressed on his last start in Newmarket’s Joel Stakes.
Aidan O’Brien has made 20 entries in total for Saturday’s action where he will hope to overhaul Balding. The championship runs to the end of the year, although this will be final major prize money opportunity for both.
Balding’s main hope is likely to be the King George-winning mare Kalpana, who will bid for three in a row in the Filly & Mare Stakes. Sparan Nua and Joseph O’Brien’s Irish Oaks winner Johanna Walsh are likely to be among her opposition.
O’Brien jnr has supplemented his St Leger winner Highwayman into the Long Distance Cup. He could face the older pair of Scandinavia and Caballo De Mar, who fought out a memorable Prix Du Cadran finish earlier this month.
“I’m happy with him and he’s trained well since Doncaster,” O’Brien said. “It’s a step up to go against the older horses and up further in distance. Hopefully, he can cope with it.”

title: Trump’s squeeze on Ukraine exposes Europe’s strategic weakness
description: EU leaders are confronted with the limits of their own support for Ukraine as Washington pressures Kyiv
content:
D onald Trump has found an unlikely culprit for the energy crisis that has followed the war he started in Iran : Volodymyr Zelenskiy ’s attacks on Russian oil refineries (in a war started by Vladimir Putin ).
Heading into what look to be painful midterm elections , Trump announced a deal last weekend that will see Russia supply the US market with diesel. At the same time, he has demanded both Moscow and Kyiv stop targeting each other’s energy facilities. He singled out Zelenskiy for criticism, going as far as saying Ukraine should get a new president.
Ukraine has had considerable success hitting Russian oil and gas production sites far from the front lines. It may be left with no choice but to curtail that “deep strike” campaign.
The Trump administration plans to get its way by applying force to pressure points where Ukraine still relies on the US.
During Joe Biden’s time in office the US donated huge amounts of military equipment to Ukraine. That help dried up when Trump returned to the White House.
Since last year US-produced arms and equipment shipped to Kyiv have been paid for by Europe and other Nato allies, through a scheme called Purl.
Washington has reportedly threatened to halt this vital supply line and stop sharing battlefield intelligence.
That would place a huge strain on Kyiv’s defences. Other western allies do not have a satellite network that can provide the same level of intelligence and Europe’s defence industry is already at full tilt filling orders to arm its own militaries.
There are some weapons systems that only the US produces, such as Patriot air defence batteries, that can shoot down Russian missiles.
[ Ukraine backs Trump’s energy ‘ceasefire’. But is Russia on board? Opens in new window ]
Against this backdrop, EU foreign ministers on Monday agreed to expand the bloc’s regime of economic sanctions to cover a further 740 individuals and 820 Russian companies. Most have some link to Moscow’s military industrial complex.
“Russia has started this war, we should not forget about this,” said Kaja Kallas, the EU’s foreign policy chief. “If we want to end this war then [the] only way we can do this is putting more pressure on Russia,” she said.
The list had been in the works for months and to some extent papers over the fact Brussels is coming up against real sanction fatigue.
Latvia’s foreign minister Baiba Braže said European governments needed to “look in the mirror” before rushing to criticise the US.
She pointed to a recent decision to lift EU sanctions in place on two Russian oligarchs, at the request of France and Luxembourg.
The European Commission is not rushing into negotiations on what will be its 22nd round of sanctions targeting Russia’s wartime economy, which are separate to the measures this week hitting individuals.
The process of putting the previous package together was a bruising one. Several governments blocked certain sanctions to protect national businesses and industries.
Zelenskiy will have a chance to address EU leaders at a summit in Brussels later this week. He will no doubt make the case that Ukraine needs more help, not less.

title: OpenAI to create 200 jobs in Dublin
description: This latest move will bring to 450 the number of roles OpenAI will have in Ireland
content:
Artificial intelligence company OpenAI is to create 200 jobs in Ireland, with plans for a new applied AI lab at what is its European Union headquarters.
It brings to 450 the number of jobs the company has committed to create here in the coming months. OpenAI, which announced in July that it would create 250 jobs in Ireland over the next couple of years, is recruiting engineers to work with customers on AI applications, along with privacy engineers to build safeguards and tools to protect data as the new systems are developed and used. The company is also hiring sales and user operations staff, among other roles.
The new jobs will help bolster the company’s technical and operational expertise locally, giving European businesses the opportunity to deploy advanced AI solutions.
OpenAI already employs 120 people in Ireland. It is planning to move its headquarters to Dublin’s Tropical Fruit Warehouse from December.
“Since we opened our EU headquarters in Dublin three years ago, Ireland has been critical to our success in Europe. I’m delighted we’re deepening our investment here, creating 200 more jobs and helping turn advances in frontier AI into local opportunity,” said Sarah Friar , OpenAI’s chief financial officer.
[ OpenAI tells investors revenue run rate is $20bn below earlier indication Opens in new window ]
“Through our new Applied AI Lab, expansion of our partnership with Dogpatch Labs and wider roll-out of the SME Academy, we want to help Irish businesses grow, support founders in turning ideas into thriving companies and equip more people across the country to benefit from AI.”
Taoiseach Micheál Martin welcomed the investment.
“This further investment by OpenAI is a vote of confidence in the strength of our people, economy and ecosystem, which sets Ireland apart,” he said. “These factors combine to make Ireland a leading destination for applied AI research, innovation and commercialisation and this is a position the Government will build upon in the years ahead.”
OpenAI’s investment here is being supported by the through IDA Ireland . Michael Lohan , chief executive of the State agency, said the investment highlighted the strength of Ireland’s technical talent and business environment.

title: Andrew Balding reckons he has ‘a squeak’ of beating Aidan O’Brien to trainers’ title
description: Willie Mullins fined and Final Demand disqualified from Cheltenham festival second place after positive drugs test
content:
Top trainer Andrew Balding reckons he will have “a squeak” of beating Aidan O’Brien to the British trainers’ title if he’s in front of him after Saturday’s lucrative Champions Day action at Ascot.
Balding leads his Irish rival by just under £75,000 (about €88,000) in a race that goes on until the end of the year, although it’s likely to be decided by this weekend’s final big prize money engagement.
Kalpana’s bid for a hat-trick in the Filly and Mare is the Englishman’s main hope of a big dividend as he chases a first title. O’Brien has won it eight times.
“Everyone couldn’t have done more than they have done. Now it’s really sort of out of our hands. It depends on what happens on Saturday – not with our runners especially, but with Aidan’s runners.
“He’s always got the [Futurity] Trophy coming up as well, to have any chance we’d have to be on top after Champions Day and then we’d have a squeak in it,” Balding said.
“At the end of the day, winning a race like the King George, and the Juddmonte International at York [with Kalpana], they are two I’ve always wanted to win. So I feel like that’s sort of as big an achievement as anything else, so that’s what we’ve got to keep doing ... try to win important races and the rest should fall into place,” he also told the Nick Luck podcast.
O’Brien is an odds-on favourite to win the cross-channel title for a third year in a row.
Separately, Willie Mullins has been fined £1,100 by Britain’s racing’s authorities and his Cheltenham Festival runner-up Final Demand has been disqualified after failing a drugs test.
Final Demand finished runner-up to his stable companion Kitzbuhel in the Grade One contest at Cheltenham in March but was subsequently found to have a prohibited substance in his system.
The British Horseracing Authority said on Monday that Final Demand ran with mepivacaine, a local anaesthetic commonly administered for therapeutic purposes.
A BHA disciplinary panel reported on Monday, following a fast-track referral for admitted rule breaches, and found that Mullins “failed to declare use of mepivacaine on the horse in its medical declaration forms submitted prior to the race”.
The BHA has a published detection time of 72 hours for mepivacaine and its judicial panel chair, Sarah Crowther, said: “The BHA and Mr Mullins have agreed the proposed sanctions, which in my judgment are appropriate having regard to the table of penalties.”
Crowther also said “the BHA accepts that the failure was accidental and a one-off”.
Tuesday’s jumps action at Punchestown sees Saturday’s Fairyhouse winner Granlahan bid for a quick follow-up in a handicap hurdle under a 7lb penalty. His jockey Darragh O’Keeffe tops the championship table on 43 winners.
Live To Laugh can exploit a lower handicap mark over flights in an earlier three-mile handicap. Rated 112 over fences after a pair of victories last March, a 94 mark over flights looks exploitable now he’s upped in trip from a good third at last month’s Listowel festival.

title: Supreme Court rejects application to appeal plan for data centre in Ennis
description: Development of data centre in Co Clare had been approved by An Coimisiún Pleanála in 2024
content:
The Supreme Court has dismissed an application by opponents of a 200MW €1.6 billion data centre on the outskirts of Ennis for leave to appeal against a High Court decision , clearing all legal hurdles faced by the project.
In its determination, the Supreme Court has dismissed the three grounds put forward in the application by opponents of the data centre, namely Colin Doyle, Friends of the Irish Environment CLG, Futureproof Clare, Martin Knox and Christine Sharp.
The Supreme Court found the application did not meet the constitutional threshold required for leave to be granted to appeal the High Court upholding the planning permission granted by An Coimisiún Pleanála (ACP) to Art Data Centres Ltd.
In its determination, the Supreme Court found that “no point of general public importance arises” in the grounds put forward by the appellants.
ACP granted planning permission in April 2024 to Art Data Centres Ltd comprising six data halls covering 145 acres or 1.3 million sq ft on lands adjacent to the Tulla Road on the eastern outskirts of Ennis near Junction 13 on the M18 motorway connecting Galway to Limerick.
The project is set to generate up to 1,200 jobs during construction, and up to a 1,000 permanent jobs and the underpinning of thousands more in digital industries.
On Monday, the joint founders of Art Data Centres, Tom McNamara and Vincent Fogarty, said the ruling “recognises that there is a future for environmentally-sensitive data centre developments like ours, where there is responsible use of renewable energy, grid-supporting generation technology and heat-recycling for both agri-food and local heating schemes”.
They described the Supreme Court ruling as “great news for this data centre campus and for Clare as the project will be a key pillar of the Ennis 2040 Economic Plan for the area”.
The project’s 200MW scale “will be attractive to the largest technology partners in the world and the project represents the culmination of more than ten years of preparatory work”, they said.
They said the connection applications could be finally processed following the Supreme Court ruling “and work will commence in 2027 as soon as all is in place”.

title: Owen Doyle: Only one thing is certain about new tackling laws
description: World Rugby must show some gumption and ensure lineout driving mauls do not continue dominating games
content:
We met in the Titanic Quarter in Belfast, and it couldn’t have been a more appropriate venue. Everybody present had struck at least one major iceberg during their career. Warm, firm friendships were re-established within moments, the banter and the humorous insults flowed.
Maybe you’ve guessed, it was a gathering of international referees, those of yesteryear. There was also a welcome sprinkling of TMOs at the party, in case we couldn’t agree. It was a great evening, impeccably organised by former Test referee Brian Stirling, who can still claim fame – as the father of international cricketer Paul. The Irish contingent was led by Stephen Hilditch, Dave McHugh and Alan Lewis. The visitors from the UK included Derek Bevan (Wales) and Ed Morrison (England), both World Cup final referees, and Jim Fleming (Scotland). How the game today would benefit from that little group.
When the conversation turned to rugby, it was clear there was a huge amount of knowledge in the room, allied to common sense, of which there is precious little about these days.
Here’s one very interesting common-sense thought: when the referee delivers a yellow card for repeated infringements, that should wipe the slate clean, rather than the next infringement automatically getting yet another card. If that had been in operation, then Andrea Piardi would have avoided the excoriation that followed Australia v South Africa last month, when four yellows were issued, reducing the Wallabies to 11 players at one point.
Having reflected on it during the train journey home, I think the suggestion has real merit, but with a necessary adjustment: the warning remains alive, but another yellow would only follow if the next offence was cynical, such as a maul collapse or a deliberate knock-on. But other offences, such as a mistimed offside blitz defence or a mistimed poaching attempt, would be penalised but not carded.
We saw common sense go completely Awol when New Zealand referee Ben O’Keefe gave a card warning to Argentina (v Australia) for a lineout offence. Shortly afterwards he penalised Argentina again, for a different issue, but did not produce a card, saying the warning only applied to lineout offences. Whichever hat he pulled that rabbit out of, he needs to put it back.
In the last few months, we have seen refereeing that hasn’t been up to scratch. Better is needed as we head into Europe and part two of the Nations Championship. Irish referee Andrew Brace is not included in that comment: he gave a fine, assured display last weekend in the New Zealand-Australia game. And, mercifully, he was not verbose, his communication was measured, and all the better for it. From time to time I’ve been on his case, but certainly not on this performance, which hopefully will become his permanent template. He can further help himself by becoming intolerant to backchat, which went on for too long.
We have also watched the officiating of breakdown side-entry all but disappear. The majority of referees seem happy to ignore it, even though its intent is to clear out a legitimately-placed opponent who has the right to contest possession. To execute an “effective” side-entry, the first offence is offside, but strangely that’s never a consideration. Maybe it’ll need a couple of serious knee-ligament injuries for this to be put back on the agenda; it really does need to be addressed by World Rugby.
After all, World Rugby recently told us the “knee-drop” and “hip-drop” tackles were to be banned on the grounds of player safety. They have actually introduced new laws to cover these, so why not reaffirm side-entry at the same time?
The knee-drop provision means a player cannot drop on to one or both knees to execute a tackle. At first sight it seems as if a good technique has been outlawed. It has caused quite a stir, prompting World Rugby to tell us that a player on the ground is already out of the game; but that if the knee drop happens simultaneously with the tackle, then it’s all okay. There will be some tight calls needed.
The hip-drop is when a tackler, coming from behind or from the side, pulls the ball carrier to the ground so that the tackler’s body weight falls on his lower limbs. It seems straightforward on paper but, in reality, it won’t be easy to adjudicate, a very tough one to referee.
When New Zealand’s Leroy Carter was injured in the act of scoring, the question arose as to whether the Australian tackler, Rob Valentini, was guilty of the hip-drop technique. This new law doesn’t take effect until November but it is already being hotly debated and there is no consensus as to whether Valentini’s action was dangerous or the injury was caused accidentally, which is my view. But one thing is pretty certain: both of these will lead to more delays and more TMO involvement, just when we’d all like to see less.
Lineout driving mauls have become the prevalent play in rugby union, with a staggering total of 10 tries scored from this tactic last Friday evening in just two URC matches. These mauls, formed illegally, are dominating the game, apparently with the full blessing of match officials.
Added to recent law directives that make defending it much more difficult, the driving maul is now a nightmare for defences. World Rugby must surely show some gumption and instruct officials to apply the law. They should pay no attention to excuses that it is difficult to referee – that is no more than a smokescreen, illegal formation is easy to spot. Otherwise, just give any good courier a shout – they’ll be happy to deliver the World Cup to South Africa.

title: Man charged with raping woman in her home while posing as TV technician denied bail
description: ‘Violent pornography, including rape and forced entry’ found on man’s phone 23 years on, judge noted
content:
A man charged with raping a woman twice in her own home while posing as a TV technician more than 20 years ago was denied bail in what the judge described as “one of the most difficult bail applications” she had ever considered.
A hearing of the District Court in Dún Laoghaire on Monday was told that the Irishman (68), based in Dublin , has been charged with two counts of rape, one count of false imprisonment and one count of aggravated burglary.
All the charges arise from an attack on a woman, then in her 30s, in her own home in a housing estate in south Dublin in March 2003.
A previous court hearing last week heard that he replied “not guilty” as each of the four charges was put to him.
Appearing before Judge Anne Watkin in a navy sweatshirt and light grey tracksuit bottoms, the accused, who cannot be named under court rules covering sexual crime cases, did not say anything.
The State objected to his bail application on multiple grounds, including the so-called O’Callaghan principles, which are based on the likelihood that someone will evade justice by not showing up to court, the likelihood that property that could be used as evidence will be disposed of and interference with witnesses.
Andrew Vallely, the solicitor representing the defendant, told the court that his client had never come to the attention of gardaí or appeared before the courts charged with any crime.
He said his client had agreed to sign on at a Garda station twice a day and would live at an address deemed suitable by the courts while on bail.
[ Judge who said ‘it kills me’ to fly Ryanair urged not to deal with any of airline’s cases Opens in new window ]
His arrest followed a Garda investigation into the attack on the morning of March 31st, 2003, during which the victim was allegedly sexually attacked in an ordeal that lasted a long time.
The State alleges the man, who would have been aged about 45 at the time, was the attacker on the day, though no findings have been reached.
At a previous hearing, gardaí said an extensive investigation took place in 2003, with “hundreds of investigative jobs undertaken and over 100 statements taken”.
The investigation had remained open despite the passage of more than 23 years. In 2023, a Garda peer review of the inquiry was initiated by a new investigation team attached to the Garda’s Dublin Metropolitan Region East Serious Crime Unit under a senior investigating officer.
The work carried out on the case since then resulted in the suspect’s arrest and court appearances.
During Monday’s hearing, the court was told that pornographic videos and photographs connected with rape and forced entry into private homes had been found on the accused’s phone after his arrest last Wednesday.
There was also evidence that the man’s DNA had been linked to the alleged assault and there were witnesses who put him at the scene on the day it happened.
[ Eight men charged with violent disorder at horse fair in Ballinasloe Opens in new window ]
The hearing was also told there was evidence that the woman’s hand had been bound by cables during the assault, which, it is said, took place while her six-month-old child was in the house.
“This is one of the most difficult bail applications I have ever had to consider,” Judge Watkin said, as she noted the seriousness of the charges and the “huge” consequences if the man were to reoffend while out on bail.
She accepted that the man had never come before the courts before but said, “We know that he has not been charged; we don’t know that nothing has happened. I have no evidence, one way or the other, and I am not suggesting there may be other cases. All we can say is he has not been charged.”
Judge Watkin noted that “23 years after the events were said to have taken place” the fact that “violent pornography, including rape and forced entry” were found on his phone “was of concern”.
The judge said the case was “far from open and shut” and said that, ultimately, it would come down to consent.
The court heard the man was estranged from his wife and had family living overseas, but the judge said that he had clear ties to Ireland.
“The charge is so significant and so serious. We are talking about life and death,” she said as she denied the bail application and remanded him in Cloverhill District Court in advance of a fresh hearing on November 10th.

title: Sarah Healy to leave Manchester training group after four years
description: The Dublin athlete is already targeting the defence of her European Indoor 3,000m title next March
content:
Every off-season brings some period of reflection, and for Sarah Healy it’s also prompted her decision to leave her training base in Manchester and consider a fresh approach to what lies ahead.
Healy first moved from Dublin to Manchester in November 2022, joining the M11 Track Club coached by the wife-and-husband team of Jenny Meadows and Trevor Painter, and built around British stars Keely Hodgkinson and Georgia Hunter Bell.
“That was definitely the right move for me, obviously I developed a lot, and just learned so much from being around those athletes,” says Healy. “And I’m proud of myself for making that move at the time.”
It did bring some memorable success too, highlighted by Healy’s European Indoor title over 3,000m in March of last year. At 25, she’s now second fastest on the Irish all-time list across the women’s 1,500m, mile, 3,000m and 5,000m, and although not yet decided on a new training group, she is likely to remain in the UK.
After running her first serious 5,000m this summer, Healy is also considering her event options ahead of next year’s World Athletics Championships in Beijing, and ultimately the LA 2028 Olympics. Her fourth-place finish over the 5,000m at the European Championships in Birmingham in August, just .30 of a second off bronze, demonstrated her clear potential in the longer distance, although she’s not quite finished with the 1,500m either.
“I definitely didn’t finish the season feeling very satisfied, but if I do look back, there were still some good moments. It was up and down, one of my more challenging seasons to date, for a number of reasons,” she said.
“It’s interesting because I was fourth in Europeans by such a small margin. But if I’d come third, my whole outlook on my season would probably be different, just because I would have a medal. I know everyone says it, but the difference between third and fourth is just huge.”
Five days later, Healy also finished a close fifth in the 1,500m in Birmingham. On further reflection, she certainly believes there was a medal for the taking in the longer race.
“For sure, on the back straight, it was definitely a mistake not to go wide. And I think had I got into the home straight in a medal position, I would have held on. But I’d literally zero experience of 5k, so it’s not too surprising I made some mistakes. But I did believe I could win a medal. That’s positive.
“I know there’s a lot more left in the 1,500m, but I’m sure, at some point, I’ll be doing the 5k more seriously. But I kind of lacked momentum the whole year, I was injured for a lot of the winter, missed indoors. Which is always quite important for me. Then in the summer I felt I never hit my stride that well, and I’m definitely someone who races well with confidence, and momentum.”
Home in Dublin last weekend to attend an athletics camp supported by Davy, for which Healy is a brand ambassador, she also made clear her first target for 2027; the defence of her European Indoor title in Valencia next March. And after running 14:48.88 on her 5,000m debut, she’s closing in on Sonia O’Sullivan’s national record of 14:41.02, clocked when winning silver at the 2000 Sydney Olympics.
“I don’t have any outdoor senior records. I’d love to hold one, at some point. And I’m sure I can get one of them, if I get everything right. It’s not to break records, I personally want to run fast, but they’re nice targets to have.”

title: DP World Tour to deny LIV Golf players memberships for 2027 season
description: CEO Guy Kinnings has said players, which include Tom McKibbin, must now ‘make a choice’
content:
Players will be barred from playing on the DP World Tour next season if they choose to join LIV Golf in 2027.
Some of the world’s top players were given conditional releases by the European tour in previous seasons, allowing them to compete on both circuits.
But DP World Tour chief executive officer Guy Kinnings has said players must now “make a choice”.
In order to be eligible for Europe’s Ryder Cup team, players must be members of the DP World Tour.
Kinnings told BBC Sport: “Players need to make a choice. We have rules and regulations which are there to protect our tour and which our members must all abide by.
“Players who are not willing to comply with our rules and regulations should not be seeking to join our tour.”
LIV’s future is in doubt after Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund withdrew support at the end of the season and is going through Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in the United States.
The breakaway series has secured an initial funding commitment for a potential $300 million (€268m) investment from BC Partners Credit to help relaunch LIV 2.0 in 2027.
Deadlines for both tours fall next month and players will be asked to disclose which they intend to play on.
LIV players such as Jon Rahm, Tyrell Hatton and Victor Perez and Tom McKibbin are currently eligible to play on the DP World Tour under one of its membership categories.
Rahm is set to quit LIV Golf after refusing to accept new terms offered for its proposed relaunch and is reported to be owed up to $150m (€134m) for the remainder of the contract he signed almost three years ago.

title: Sentencing of Isis supporter who stabbed garda and set fire to McGregor pub put back
description: Abdullah Khan (24) pleaded guilty to Black Forge arson attempt and Capel Street attack
content:
A supporter of Islamic State who stabbed a garda and set fire to a pub owned by Conor McGregor has been remanded into custody before his sentencing next month.
Abdullah Khan (24), whose address cannot be published because of a court order, appeared before the non-jury Special Criminal Court in Dublin on Monday, via video-link from prison.
Judge Caroline Biggs told Khan the sentencing would be put back as the judge who had been dealing with the case was not available due to being unwell.
Khan pleaded guilty to stabbing Garda Gary Lynch on Capel Street in Dublin city on July 29th last year and to the arson attack on the Black Forge Inn, a bar owned by former MMA fighter McGregor, days earlier on July 25th.
An Garda Síochána said Khan shouted “Allahu akbar” before stabbing the garda and expressed support for the terrorist group Islamic State, also known as Isis, during subsequent interviews.
Khan’s defence barrister previously told the court he had been in a “mental health crisis”.
He was remanded in custody for sentencing on November 2nd. – PA

title: ‘He needs to die in prison’: Survivor of George Gibney child sex abuse reacts to sentencing
description: Orla Poole says the swimming coach attempted to rape her when she was 12 – a half-century later she faced him directly in court
content:
A s a nine-year-old girl growing up in Dublin in the 1970s, Orla Poole’s concerned mother sent her to see a psychologist.
She noticed that her daughter’s behaviour had altered. She had become aggressive, angry and volatile. She cut her hair short and she self-harmed.
The reasons did not emerge at the time to explain the transformation that took place almost overnight.
Orla Poole moved from school to school around the country and after graduating from UCD, she left Ireland permanently to live in the United States.
Her work there was inside the American justice system and in 2020 an algorithm sent her a recommendation directing her towards an Apple podcast that had run for a few episodes: the BBC series Where is George Gibney?
She contacted one of the makers of the podcast, Mark Horgan, and subsequently made a statement to An Garda Síochána. Gibney was extradited from the US last year.
Orla Poole’s was one of the testimonies from four women who convinced an Irish jury in July that the 78-year-old former Irish Olympic swimming coach was guilty of 39 counts of indecent assault and one count of attempted rape of children in the 1970s and 1980s.
On Monday, Gibney was jailed for 15½ years . Judge Mícheál O’Higgins described Gibney as a “manipulative predator”, and his abuse as systematic, predatory in nature and a gross abuse of his position of authority as their swimming coach.
[ ‘You are not alone’: Woman abused as child by George Gibney urges other victims to come forward Opens in new window ]
The most serious allegation of attempted rape was made by Orla Poole, who was attacked by Gibney in Newpark Sports Complex in south Dublin. He also assaulted her in a hospital car park in Leopardstown and in the driveway of a ruined old house in the locality.
By 2020, when the algorithm suggested that the Apple podcast “might be of interest” to her they were on episode three of Where is George Gibney?
“My reaction? It was shock. It, Gibney, was a name I had not heard in years,” she says.
“I listened to episode one, two and three, and ended up calling my sister Deirdre. She had been at summer camp with me in August 1975, when the attempted rape took place.
“The more I listened to the podcast the more that I heard of the other people ... I didn’t think he would be charged or extradited but I wanted a record of what he had done to me. I wanted this nine-year-old to have a voice. I wanted to say this is what happened to me. This is my reality.”
She says she had been sent home from the summer camp “for pushing a member of staff into the swimming pool after I had been assaulted by Gibney in the changing room”.
[ A shameless risk-taker and predator: How George Gibney groomed children Opens in new window ]
“But the letter outlining my suspension, which my mother had kept, was all lies,” she says.
After the attempted rape, he says she was taken to what would become Gibney’s office, “locked there until the end of the day and sent home with the letter in a sealed envelope”.
“My mother had kept folders for each one of her five kids, even kindergarten report cards. Folders for everything. If I didn’t have that letter, it would not have given the prosecutor the date of the summer camp in Newpark Sports Complex,” she says.
“Coming from the US criminal justice system I was expecting the worst in court. I found it very uncomfortable. I was expecting that he would ask where hands went and things like that,” she says, referring to the questions she was expecting from Gibney’s defence barrister Patrick Gageby.
“Mentally I was giving myself up for that. I found the Irish system to be a very cold, a heartless, faceless system. You never get to meet the DPP [Director of Public Prosecutions].
“In the US system, you meet with the prosecutor. The DPP here makes the decision about filing charges. It is like a headless body. You don’t know them as people, and they are the ones that make the decisions.”
[ Former swimming coach George Gibney jailed for 15½ years for abusing four girls Opens in new window ]
When Orla Poole took the stand to give her witness impact statement, her chair faced out towards the judge, Mícheál P O’Higgins, to her left and the legal teams to her right.
Her first act was to turn the chair around and face Gibney directly. With her back to the judge, she delivered a powerfully impactful statement as he sat impassively in a wheelchair a few paces away.
“I knew exactly what I was going to do,” she says.
“Because it’s he, Gibney, that did it to me. I don’t understand the idea that you sit facing the judge. The judge didn’t do it to me. He did. What I found disgusting was that he [Gibney] didn’t even raise his head once, not only to me but to any of us.
“He never acknowledged ... he never graced us with even an apologetic look on his face. Just nothing. There was no sorry. Accepting his guilt would sound something like: ‘I am sorry for what I did to you as girls.’
“The only thing we heard out of his mouth was guilty five times at the start of the trial and not guilty 74 times. They are the only words the man spoke. This has been 54 years in the making and that’s all he spoke.”
At the beginning of the trial, Gibney pleaded guilty to five charges of indecent assault against one of the complainants. The four women were aged eight to 14 at the time of the offences.
“There was nothing from him like: ‘I have seen the error of my ways’ or ‘I understand what I put you through and I apologise’. There were no words. It was horrible.
“When I walked into court, he wasn’t even paying attention. He wasn’t listening. He wasn’t hearing. There was no contrition. None. Discarding us like we were a nuisance to him.
“That’s how I felt at 12 years old in August 1975 after his attempted rape – him speaking, him telling me: ‘You are due back in the gym’. Cold. Dismissive.”
Gibney’s indifference was apparent during the trial. He sat in the wheelchair throughout the two weeks without expression. Sometimes he would haul himself on to a bench and other days remain seated in the chair.
“If he’d looked at me, I think I would have had more satisfaction,” says Orla Poole.
“If he had acknowledged that I am a human being and that he did this to me, that would have been something else.
“This was not about sex but about control and manipulation and torture, whether it was emotional, psychic or physical. If I came home from a bar fight with a broken nose and a black eye you can see the physical damage.
“Because it is childhood sex abuse and because most of the time it doesn’t come out when it’s occurring there is no visible physical damage, but it carries lifelong repercussions,” she says.
“At 80 years of age, he can still hurt someone. He doesn’t deserve to be out on the streets. He has avoided culpability for over 50 or 60 years, and he has never taken responsibility.
“For me, I think he needs to die in prison.”

title: DAA says staff in Saudi Arabia ‘safe and well’ after latest airport attacks
description: Dublin Airport operator provides management and consultancy services to Riyadh hub
content:
Dublin Airport operator DAA has said that all of its staff in Saudi Arabia are “safe and well” after Yemen’s Houthi forces launched more attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh in recent days.
The Irish commercial semi-state company provides airport management and consultancy services to the operator of the Saudi international travel hub.
An attack on the airport on Saturday, the third in a week, killed 12 people and wounded more than 300, part of a tit-for-tat military escalation by the Houthis against the Saudis.
Separately, an unidentified projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport on Sunday, with authorities tackling a blaze, the Saudi-led coalition said in a statement.
In a statement on Monday, a spokesman for DAA said: “We are aware of the incidents at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh over the weekend and can confirm that all our team members in the region are safe and well. We remain in close and continuous contact with our colleagues and are monitoring the situation closely.”
DAA declined to say how many staff it has in Saudi Arabia due to commercial sensitivities and security considerations.
The blast at the Riyadh airport on Saturday brought travel to a near-standstill. It also forced the capital’s financial hub to shift to remote work until further notice and prompted executives from BP and Shell to pull out of a big energy event in the city this week.
The Department of Foreign Affairs “strongly advises Irish citizens against all but essential travel to Saudi Arabia until further notice” due to the security situation in the Middle East and Gulf.
[ ‘They’re not just guys in flip-flops’: Houthis show military reach with deadly missile strikes on Riyadh Opens in new window ]
Irish citizens already in the region are advised to avoid “unnecessary journeys, remain vigilant, closely monitor developments and local media, and follow the advice of local authorities”.
The UK government warned on Sunday against all but essential travel to Jeddah and Dammam, as well as to all Saudi airports except for Medina. It suggested British citizens consider departing Saudi Arabia via land to neighbouring countries.
Saturday’s strike came less than a week after Saudi-backed forces in Yemen launched a campaign to retake Houthi-held areas and “eliminate” the group. The militants, who frequently claim attacks on Saudi oil facilities, had recently seized more Yemeni territory and bolstered their control over the Bab el-Mandeb, a global shipping chokepoint.
The Saudi-led coalition called “the cowardly terrorist attack” on the airport on Saturday “a full-fledged war crime” by the Houthis.
The victims included four Saudis, a Palestinian, two Bangladeshis and one person each from the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria and Sudan, according to authorities. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg

title: Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack
description: Governor of Taiz says Yemeni city will soon run out of surgical services and medicine because of Houthi siege
content:
Saudi Arabia was forced to extend the suspension of all flights to and from its main international airport in Riyadh until next Saturday after a further round of Houthi missile attacks caused more damage and left one person dead.
Some airlines, including Gulf Air and Bahrain Air, had already said they were cancelling flights until next Saturday. More missiles were fired at Saudi Arabian cities by the Houthis on Monday, Saudi Arabia’s military spokesperson said.
The Gulf nation announced it was suspending flights from Riyadh, its second busiest airport, after Houthi missiles killed 13 people on Saturday and left more than 300 injured. Saudi state television broadcast CCTV footage that showed passengers deluged in smoke and falling masonry as they queued at the airport terminal to board a plane just as the Houthi missile struck.
The country has pressed ahead with the 25th WPC Energy Conference in Riyadh, hoping to project an image of normality. But some senior oil executives did not attend or appeared virtually.
An urgent review is under way as to how Houthi missiles are repeatedly penetrating badly stretched Saudi air defences. Schoolchildren and some office workers were advised to work from home. The Houthis have also targeted the city of Khamis Mushait, and the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
Interceptor missiles are needed to protect Government buildings, oil facilities and infrastructure hubs across a wide geographic area. The Houthis have said they will attack Saudi airports across the country.
Houthi attacks since last month have targeted fuel tanks at Riyadh airport and its affiliated warehouses, destroying a parked Airbus A320 passenger plane and damaging at least five other aircraft.
Saudi Arabia’s predicament comes after it re-entered Yemen’s civil war to push the Houthis from the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait oil route and stop the ​group from making further gains after its sudden advances in September.
[ ‘They’re not just guys in flip-flops’: Houthis show military reach with deadly missile strikes on Riyadh Opens in new window ]
Fighting has continued in and around Taiz, Yemen’s third city and the most populous governorate, with Saudi planes mounting eight separate strikes on any assembly of Houthi forces. As many as 60 fighters died on Sunday from both sides.
The governor of Taiz, Nabil Shamsan, on Sunday issued an urgent call to lift the Houthi siege and warned that a shortage of medicines meant the city would soon run out of emergency surgical and intensive care services.
Overall, the Houthis claimed the Saudis had mounted 124 raids on Sunday. The Saudis are seeking to locate Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, with rumours of his assassination repeatedly circulating, but Saudi Arabia does not seem to have contemporary intelligence on his precise whereabouts either in the capital Sana’a or in its stronghold of Saada.
On the diplomatic front, Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, spoke to the Saudi foreign minister, Faisal bin Farhan, on Sunday to see if there was a way iIran could act as a mediator between the Saudis and the Houthis, a group Iran has trained and armed.
Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthi Political Bureau, claimed Saudi Arabia accepted the mediation offered by Iran and proposed first a one-month truce, and then a two-week truce, but the Houthis had rejected both offers.
A meeting of the UN security council in New York on Tuesday is expected to debate a resolution calling the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation. – Guardian

title: Jury selected for trial of Russell Brand
description: Comedian accused of rape, sexual assault and indecent assault relating to six women from 1999 to 2009
content:
Jury selection took place on Monday for the ‌trial of British actor and comedian Russell Brand over alleged historical crimes including rape and other ‌sexual offences.
Brand (51), once one of Britain’s most high-profile broadcasters, ​faces three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault relating to six women from 1999 to 2009.
Brand has denied all the accusations. He arrived at London’s Southwark ​Crown Court accompanied by his wife. During the hearing he sat in the ⁠dock, mostly staring straight ahead or with his eyes closed.
“We are about ‌to ‌start ​the trial of one Mr Russell Brand,” the judge Joel Bennathan told potential jurors. “Many of you will have heard of him.”
The ⁠judge excluded those who ​said they had watched a documentary aired about ​three years ago or had read a long newspaper article from the same ‌time in which allegations of sexual misconduct ​were made against Brand.
“Those are allegations he firmly denies,” the judge said.
He ⁠later told those who had ⁠been initially ​selected: “The defendant is clearly someone very well known. You absolutely must not carry out any research at all about this defendant Russell Brand.”
The trial is expected to last about six weeks, Bennathan said, with the jurors formally sworn in on Tuesday while prosecutors will open their case later in the week.
The comedian, known for his flamboyant style and appearance, was a ‌regular on British television ⁠screens in the 2000s and also worked as a radio presenter for the BBC.
He went on to star in a number of ‌films including Get Him to the Greek in 2010, the same year he married US singer Katy Perry. They divorced in ​2012 after 14 months of marriage.
More recently Brand has ​largely appeared on online programmes, with content often focused on US politics, religion and free speech. – PA
Essex-born Brand started out as a stand-up comedian in the UK and his showbiz career took off when he was picked to front Big Brother spin-off shows by Channel 4.
He became one of Britain’s best-known comedians in the 2000s and won presenting roles including the 2007 Brit Awards, Comic Relief and the MTV Music Video Awards, and hosted his own show on BBC Radio 2.
He made the move into Hollywood films with roles including an Arthur remake, comedy Forgetting Sarah Marshall and 2012 musical comedy Rock Of Ages.
In recent years, he has pivoted to podcasting and online influencing, and now lives in Florida in the United States.
Brand, who pleaded not guilty to the charges during pre-trial hearings, is on bail.
His case is being overseen by Judge Joel Bennathan. – PA

title: ‘They’re not just guys in flip-flops’: Houthis show military reach with deadly missile strikes on Riyadh
description: Yemen’s Iran-backed militants have evolved from insurgency into potent armed force
content:
L ethal missile strikes on Riyadh’s international airport over the past week have demonstrated the growing military power of Yemen’s Houthi rebels, who have evolved from an insurgency into one of the Middle East’s most formidable non-state armed forces.
The latest attack on Saturday, the third on the airport in a week, killed 12 people and wounded more than 300, part of a tit-for-tat military escalation by the Houthis against the beleaguered Saudis, who support Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
The Houthis have also targeted Saudi oil infrastructure and seized more territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast in recent weeks, including the port of Mocha, and secured control over the entrance to the Red Sea by taking Perim Island in the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait — although the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces have now launched a counteroffensive.
The Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ports in July and have repeatedly targeted Saudi ships attempting to sail through Bab al-Mandeb, strangling Saudi oil exports.
“Everyone continues to underestimate the Houthis’ military power,” said Farea al-Muslimi, a Yemen expert at London’s Chatham House think-tank, adding that Houthis were routinely dismissed as little more than “guys in flip-flops”.
“Suddenly these guys in flip-flops can double or triple your winter heating bills.”
“They’re not just guys in flip-flops, they’re actually geeks,” he said, and they had spent a decade building military capabilities with Iranian assistance and producing their own weapons.
“They were importing weapons from Africa a decade ago, and now they are manufacturing and supplying weapons to the people they used to buy from.”
Having mostly sat on the sidelines after the US and Israel launched their war against Iran in February, the Iran-backed Shia movement entered the Gulf conflict in earnest in the late summer, after Saudi forces struck Sana’a airport as a Houthi delegation was travelling to Iran for the funeral of the country’s assassinated supreme leader.
The attack broke a truce between Riyadh and the Houthis that had largely held since 2022, and plunged the two sides back into war that culminated with the Houthis’ seizure of Mocha last month.
Yet analysts say the Houthis’ success reflects not only their increasingly sophisticated weapons but their superior organisation and the weakness of Yemen’s Saudi-backed internationally recognised government.
The Houthi group’s military foundations were laid when it captured Sana’a in September 2014, inheriting much of the Yemeni army’s arsenal, including the Republican Guard’s ballistic missiles and the navy’s anti-ship weapons.
“They didn’t start from scratch, they had a foundation,” said Mohammed al-Basha, head of the Basha Report, a specialist security consultancy in Washington. The Houthis also acquired experienced officers, missile technicians and military units, which they subsequently reorganised into a more consolidated force.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Lebanon’s Hizbollah provided training and technical expertise, while a generation of Houthi specialists subsequently travelled to Iran to improve their capabilities, particularly in anti-ship missiles and drone boats, which have been used against shipping in the Red Sea.
Al-Basha said the Houthis could now manufacture their signature Samad attack drones largely independently, using locally produced fibreglass and commercially sourced components, many imported from China.
More sophisticated ballistic and cruise missiles, however, remained heavily dependent on Iranian components and technology, he said.
Extensive air strikes by the US, UK and Israel have largely failed to degrade the Houthis’ missile capabilities.
While the Houthis depend largely on Iran for their missile knowhow, they have apparently also begun to rely on AI. According to a security report published by Anthropic, users in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen tried to exploit its Claude AI model to develop and refine sophisticated missile systems.
Their growing sophistication was demonstrated by the fall of the Red Sea port of Mocha, the gateway to the Bab al-Mandeb Strait from the Yemeni side, where forces loyal to Tariq Saleh, a member of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council and nephew of former president Ali Abdullah Saleh, collapsed within days.
