title: Pupil shoots and wounds two teachers in France
description: Police say no apparent link with recent protests
content:
A French middle-school pupil shot and wounded a head teacher and a ​female staff member with a hunting rifle at a school near Marseille on Monday, causing panic as children ran for cover, the local mayor and a student said.
A supervisor at Joseph Lakanal college disarmed the 14-year-old before police arrived, Aubagne mayor ​Jean-Pierre Squillari told reporters. Both victims were hospitalised but neither suffered life-threatening injuries, he added.
There was no immediate indication that the shooting ⁠was linked to a three-week wave of protests, some violent, at high schools across ‌the ‌country. ​French president Emmanuel Macron condemned those incidents of violence on Monday.
BFM TV said the pupil entered the school with the rifle hidden in a ⁠guitar case. He was later detained ​by police.
“It’s a kid who goes to that school. ​He entered with a rifle, the investigation will determine how, and fired twice in a corridor toward the ‌principal and a teacher,” Squillari said.
One student said her maths teacher had played down the bang ⁠of the first gunshot blast as noise ⁠from nearby construction works. ​A subsequent blast was followed by an alarm and classes emptied into the corridors.
“We were panicking, we ran,” the student said. “There were two ways out: one passage to the sports hall and one passage to go outside. Survival instinct took over and I ran towards the outside.”
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen , front-runner in the race to replace Macron next spring, said the government was losing control of security in schools.
“Schools, which should be sanctuaries, are now ‌places where people risk their ⁠lives. Insecurity has entered the school. Many pupils and teachers go there with a knot in their stomach.”
Macron’s education and interior ministers are due to travel to the ‌college later in the day.
Eddy Sid, spokesperson for the SGP-FO police union, told BFM TV there was no apparent link ​between the shooting and high-school protests against understaffing and lack of funding for ​schools.
There had been no blockades at the Joseph Lakanal college, he added. – Reuters

title: ‘Our children lost years with their dad’: Engineer Robert Pether home after detention in Iraq for five years
description: Irish resident had been  under travel ban in Baghdad after being let out of prison a year ago
content:
Australian engineer Robert Pether, who was held in prison in Iraq for five years, has returned home to Ireland.
He was welcomed at Dublin Airport by his wife and children, who said they have been “living in hell” since Pether was arrested without charge in April 2021 in connection to a business dispute.
The 51-year-old, who had been living in Ireland for a number of years, had been working as a mechanical engineer on rebuilding the Iraqi Central Bank when he was arrested with a colleague from CME Consulting, the Dubai-based company they were working for.
There was a contract dispute between his employer and the Central Bank of Iraq, which led to him and his Egyptian colleague being imprisoned.
Pether was released from jail last year due to his deteriorating health, but was banned from leaving the country until last week when an Iraqi court dismissed proceedings against him and lifted the travel ban, citing a lack of evidence.
He was allowed to board a flight on Monday to Ireland, via Turkey, after negotiations involving officials in Ireland, Australia, Egypt and Iraq – and Pether’s international pro-bono team at Slaney Advisors, a consultancy specialising in international arbitration.
Pether’s wife, Desree, who lives in Co Roscommon, said she was “hugely relieved”. She was there to welcome him home, along with sons Oscar and Flynn.
“It’s been an absolute nightmare, especially these last few months,” she said. “So many obstacles and plot twists right up to the last minute.”
Speaking at Dublin Airport, Pether said his family has always fought for him, but that it has had an “enormous toll” on his wife.
“There will be time to talk about what happened. Why it happened. Who was responsible. And why nobody should ever be allowed to do this to another person or another family again,” he said.
“But today, more than anything, I want to talk about the people who carried us through it.
“My wife and my children have lived this every single day with me. Our children lost years with their dad. They watched their mum fight every day to try and bring me home.
“They grew up with uncertainty, fear and circumstances that no child should every have to carry.
“I’m so thankful to my wife, Desree for always fighting for me, while at the same time holding our family together. All while dealing with a situation that took an enormous toll on her too. She truly is incredible.”
Pether was released from prison last year because of poor health, but was prevented from leaving the country. Last week, a court in Iraq dismissed proceedings against him.
Pether and his Egyptian colleague Khalid Radwan were detained in Baghdad in 2021 after flying in for a meeting with bank officials to resolve a dispute they were having with CME Consulting.
Pether was later sentenced and fined over allegations that his firm spent money that should have gone to an architect and a subcontractor.
In a report in March 2022, the UN working group on arbitrary detention found Pether had been arbitrarily detained in breach of international law.
[ Irish resident released from Iraqi prison is deteriorating rapidly, wife says Opens in new window ]
The UN body also found the arrest constituted an “enforced disappearance” and may have involved forms of torture.
The working group said it had received complaints that Pether was exposed to extreme cold, threats of death, humiliation and various forms of psychological abuse.
“Mr Pether was detained in a [2x2 metre] cell with the lights permanently on,” the working group said in its report. “He was reportedly blindfolded, interrogated, screamed at, threatened, insulted and shown torture rooms.”
Following her husband’s release from jail in 2025, Desree Pether said from Ireland she was “grateful to everyone who contributed to this happening”.
She had previously been critical of the efforts of Australian officials to secure her husband’s release. The Australian government said it had raised the case with Iraqi authorities more than 200 times.
In a statement, Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee said she was “delighted” at the news.
“This brings to an end an extraordinarily difficult period for Robert, his wife Desree and their children,” she said. “I would like to thank the Australian government for all their support to Robert and in securing his release.
“I want to acknowledge the efforts of the Iraqi prime minister al-Zaidi, Iraq’s foreign minister Hussein and the hard work and coordinated approach of the Irish Government who have been liaising on Robert’s release for some time. I would also like to thank Irish diplomatic officials for their work on this case.”

title: ‘The monster that haunts our nightmares’: Parents address Bouchaker in sentence hearing
description: 52-year-old convicted of eight offences, including attempted murder of three children at Parnell Square
content:
A mother whose young daughter is severely disabled after being stabbed by Riad Bouchaker during an attack at Dublin’s Parnell Square in 2023 said her family’s life had changed “unrecognisably” and she “wouldn’t wish this on anyone”.
“A child is forever but every parent’s hope is that you build up their strength to take on life once they are old enough,” the woman told the Central Criminal Court in a victim impact statement on Monday.
She and her husband will be caring for their daughter, now aged eight, for the rest of their lives “and we need to be sure she will be looked after when we are gone”.
“Learning about disability has been eye-opening, but I wouldn’t wish this on anyone.”
Her statement was read by Det Garda Shimna Ní Mháirtin during a hearing to decide the sentence to be imposed on Bouchaker.
A CCTV recording of the 15-second attack on the children and a childcare worker was played in court. Bouchaker (52), a native of Algeria of no fixed abode, was convicted by a jury at the Central Criminal Court last July of eight offences, including the attempted murder of three children, connected with the attack.
Judge Tony Hunt, who heard several impact statements, said he would give his sentencing decision at a later date. The maximum for attempted murder is life imprisonment.
Another mother whose daughter suffered a head injury described Bouchaker as a “monster” who had “stolen the innocence” of the 13 children.
“He is the monster that haunts our nightmares,” she said.
Childcare worker Leanne Flynn, who suffered serious stab injuries while trying to protect the children, said her life and that of her partner and two young children had changed drastically.
She had been called “a hero” but should never have had to be one, and hated that her name “will forever be tied to Riad Bouchaker”, she said. Addressing Bouchaker directly, she told him: “Harming innocent children is unforgivable” and she hoped his God “will never forgive you”.
Det Sgt Padraig Cleary said the prosecution case was that Bouchaker intended to kill the children.
The offence relating to Flynn should be considered in the higher range of the maximum sentence – life imprisonment – prosecuting counsel Karl Finnegan said.
Bouchaker’s barrister said his client’s “very clear cognitive limitations” and intellectual limitations should be considered, including in relation to why he contested the case. Bouchaker was unable to understand the concept of legal guilt, counsel said.
The three attempted murder charges related to the severely injured five-year-old girl and to a six-year-old girl and five-year-old boy. He will also be sentenced for assault causing harm to two other children.
Bouchaker was found guilty of intentionally inflicting serious harm on Flynn, who underwent life-saving surgery.
In a victim impact statement, another mother said her injured daughter had told her while lying on the ground at Parnell Square that the attacker “looked like a real man but he was actually a bad man”. Her daughter continues to be afraid of crowds, loud noises, the sight of blood and noise of sirens, and the family have had to stop visiting places such as Croke Park, she said.
Another mother, in her statement, told Bouchaker he had left her son and the other children with “terrifying memories that haunt them to this day”. Addressing him in Irish, the woman said she, like him, was an immigrant to Ireland, which she said was “the best country in the world”.
Bouchaker had also been convicted of assault causing harm to a French teenage chef, Alan Lorena Guille, who had minor scratches to his hand and face after wrenching the knife from Bouchaker’s hand; and of producing a 36cm kitchen carving knife, including a 24cm blade, capable of inflicting serious injury.
During a pretrial hearing, two psychiatrists disagreed on Bouchaker’s fitness to plead arising from an acquired brain injury, caused by pre-existing cognitive impairment combined with injuries suffered during interventions by members of the public. He spent about three weeks in hospital after the incident.
Hunt ruled he was fit to stand trial with assistance of an interpreter and an intermediary.
On Monday, Cleary said gardaí did not know a lot about Bouchaker’s background. He had some relations in Ireland and had not worked since he arrived in the country. He had no previous convictions.
Cleary agreed with counsel that Bouchaker had said a number of times he was grateful nobody had been killed.
“He brought it back to himself every time,” Cleary said. He agreed Bouchaker had made statements that did not make sense and were “completely at odds” with his actions that day.

title: George Gibney was a shameless risk-taker and predator: How the ex-swimming coach groomed children
description: Former swim coach is jailed for more than 15 years for indecent assault and attempted rape, over three decades after earlier court case perished
content:
W hen the forewoman leaned over the bench in court 20 of the Criminal Courts of Justice just after 3pm on July 6th and handed Judge Mícheál O’Higgins the verdict, he thanked her and began to read.
The counts were then read out: guilty, guilty, guilty.
Former Olympic swimming coach and television pundit George Gibney , who was extradited to Ireland from Florida last summer, was found to have committed 39 counts of indecent assault and one count of attempted rape against four children.
The current generation of six men and six women jurors finally gave the victims of Gibney a sense of justice, something a previous generation were unable to do following hearings in 1993.
They delivered their guilty verdict on a man whom barrister James Dwyer described as “a powerful figure in swimming in the 1970s” and a “predatory abuser taking advantage of young girls with impunity”.
Inside the courtroom, Tric Kearney sat among the benches. Outside in the corridor, Ber Carley sat with her family.
Both women were there to support the four who gave evidence this time and to bear witness to justice finally unfolding for them after their case had perished in the Supreme Court 33 years ago.
Both were also instrumental in bringing international attention to Gibney’s long-standing crimes against children and were – along with swimmers Chalkie White and European medal winner Gary O’Toole – central witnesses in the initial case that began in Dún Laoghaire District Court in 1993. All those years ago, Gibney’s first appearance in court began with a bang.
The car transporting him to court that day was involved in a crash on Dún Laoghaire’s main street and the ensuing chaos ensured anything but a quiet arrival.
That trial finished later that year when the Supreme Court concluded that because of the length of time that had elapsed and the lack of specificity of charges, Gibney should go free.
The decision was not appealed by the Director of Public Prosecutions.
The guilty verdict this time involved an entirely different group of women who had made complaints to the Garda. It highlighted how times had dramatically changed with the gradual alteration of the law over the years and the acceptance of decades-old evidence.
It is highly likely, too, that the current case would not have been heard but for the podcast series – Where is George Gibney? – in 2018 from the Second Captains podcasting team in conjunction with the BBC.
Following the initial 40-minute podcast, there was such a positive reaction that 11 episodes were made, which were downloaded millions of times in 160 countries.
Not only did the series bring the issue sharply into a global public gaze as Gibney lived life as a free man in the United States, but it drew out new witnesses who had not before come forward.
The podcast did what all the other coverage about Gibney could not do: it moved the dial, allowing the Garda to build a brand-new case.
Those women who came forward and presented Gibney with a whole new legal challenge were the individuals who finally got him back to Ireland and put him in prison.
However, during the criminal trial at the end of June and early July, it was not always straightforward.
On day four of the trial, defence counsel Patrick Gageby brought up the lapse-of-time issue. One of the complainants, abused in the 1970s, made a first disclosure to her fiance in 1993 when she was 31 years old.
The prosecution argued case law that a lapse of more than 20 years was admissible if it was made on the first reasonable opportunity as opposed to the first possible opportunity.
It continued that a hastier complaint may carry more weight, but lapses are legitimate and the courts recognise that it takes victims time to make a complaint.
In 1993, the court system did not accept the 27 counts against Gibney of indecent assault and unlawful carnal knowledge of minors, yet in 2026 it accepted similar charges, some of which happened in the 1970s and were 50 years old.
Gibney pleaded guilty to five charges of indecent assault at the beginning of the trial, an admission that took the prosecution by surprise. He had initially faced 79 counts that were whittled down. Importantly, the more serious charge of attempted rape remained.
Throughout the trial, it became clear there were many stunning similarities between the complaints first made in 1993 and those made weeks ago. They concerned Gibney’s modus operandi, his favoured places to bring the children to assault them and his cold indifference afterwards.
What was his demeanour, one complainant was asked after Gibney had attempted to rape her.
“Nonchalant – no different whatsoever,” she replied.
The same words, places and phrases repeatedly cropped up: Trojan Swimming Club; Glenalbyn Swimming Club; babysitting at his house in Killiney, south Dublin; stopping to give lifts to the girls leaving school; or walking and cycling home from swimming.
“Gibney would stop and offer a lift,” said one complainant. “The bike went in the back.”
He would then molest her less than a mile up the road.
There were places he returned to over and over again: the changing rooms by the swimming pool in Newpark Sports Complex, his office adjacent to the pool, the sauna, an old nearby derelict building called Avonmore, a car park in a local hospital.
He also charmed the children’s parents; one remembered how he helped decorate her house along with her father, papering a difficult part of the wall.
Then there was his brazen, calculated nature and almost casual deviance as he strolled through the changing rooms while the girls were undressing.
A risk-taker and predator, he continuously groomed the children by playing with their minds.
He moved them into different groups up and down the ladder, suggested they could one day compete in the Olympic Games if they followed his guidance. He lavished attention on them.
They were in his good books one day and his bad books the next. The power disparity was immense; he was in his late 20s and they were as young as nine.
“I was in [school name] national school,” said one complainant. “I believe it was fourth class, halfway through fourth class.”
Gibney was shameless and audacious. One claimant on day eight of the trial described how her mother had enrolled her in a sports camp in the summer of 1975. On one of the days, Gibney ordered her out from the large group in the school gym to a different location in the changing rooms at the swimming pool.
“I went with him thinking it was to clear things up, pick up floats,” she said.
In the changing room, he ordered her to take off her clothes before performing sexual acts, including attempted rape – an offence for which he was found guilty.
“I was 12 years of age. It wouldn’t fit. Whatever,” she said.
“He pulled his trousers back up and left. I was very angry and confused and felt disgusting.”
When he had finished the assault, he ordered her back to the gym but instead she ran from the changing room and in a petrified dash pushed a teacher from the school into the pool.
Noticing she had not returned to the group, her sister went to look for her and found her alone, vexed, greatly agitated and unable to speak, mumbling incoherently.
She was suspended from the camp for pushing the teacher into the pool. Her mother kept the letter of suspension and it was used in evidence.
Another claimant described how Gibney worked his way into the affections of her mother and father. During a visit to her house one summer evening, he left the company of the parents, who were in the sittingroom below, and entered her bedroom upstairs.
Despite her sister sharing the double bed, Gibney molested her before returning to the company of her parents. She saw a silhouette coming into the room, she said.
“The body of an adult. I recognised his voice,” she said.
“I’m certain I was in secondary school, 13 or 14. He put his hands on my breasts and down to my legs. I was lying on my back.”
The defence took this incident as being so utterly audacious that it could not have been true.
Gibney casually molested the children in the changing rooms, repeatedly putting his hands under their swimsuits. He did the same in his car after they accepted lifts, then grossly assaulted them.
“Good Catholic Ireland. What was I doing to Brona [Gibney’s wife]. How dare I,” recalled one witness explaining the self-recrimination she felt and her confusion over the sense of guilt and that she was somehow to blame.
After he assaulted her in his office, she went home and never swam again.
A figure climbing in stature in Irish swimming – Gibney was later to become an Olympic coach at the Los Angeles and Seoul Olympic Games in 1984 and 1988 – his sense of being untouchable was so bloated that some weeks later he inquired after the girl he assaulted in his office through her parents, wondering if she was ever going to come back to swimming.
While he was molesting her in that attack, the young girl could see her mother through the threadbare curtains that covered the windows on one side of the office. She was sitting in the car waiting to drive her daughter home.
Family connections were not a barrier. Gibney molested a brother and sister who testified in the terminated trial more than three decades ago. He also abused two sisters who gave evidence in this trial.
During the evidence, Gibney sat at the side of the court each day, in the same place, facing the jury. The judge sat to this right. Gibney’s expression remained blank, unchanging.
Wearing the same red shell-suit top and grey tracksuit bottoms for each hearing, the 78-year-old paedophile appeared dissolute, looking like a beaten docket.
In summing up, Dwyer, the prosecution barrister, asked the jury to imagine what he called “an extraordinary image”.
He relayed what one of the complainants had said in evidence: of walking around the rugby pitches of the school she attended during break-time with two of her close friends, who both gave evidence.
Without having the vocabulary to explain – or the comprehension to understand what Gibney was doing to her – the three children discussed whether you could get pregnant from having sperm in your mouth and it travelling into your stomach.
At the end, when O’Higgins uttered the words, “Mr Gibney, I remand you in custody until sentencing”, there was a palpable sense of a long and harrowing journey concluding, but also of justice being done and accountability being delivered.
On Monday, the judge delivered his sentence, jailing Gibney for 15½ years .
Gibney’s jailing won’t scrub clean the pain of what happened. It was clear from the evidence and cross examinations that the cost to the women, now in their 60s, of reliving the assaults took an emotional toll.
But like those who preceded them in 1993, none of the four complainants faltered, but they instead brought painful endurance, courage and agency to a jury that heard them.
That was their superpower. This time, there was a better outcome.

title: Cork scientist wins top international physics prize
description: Professor JC Séamus Davis honoured for pioneering work in quantum physics
content:
An Irish physicist has won the prestigious Institute of Physics Faraday Prize for his outstanding contributions to science.
Prof JC Séamus Davis of University College Cork (UCC) was honoured for achievements that include inventing advanced microscopic instruments.
His instruments capture images of quantum matter with what his award citation said was “unprecedented precision”.
“Before we pictured in our minds what we believed quantum matter looked like, but we never knew for sure as we could never see it,” Davis said.
“Our instruments are like a superpower that have revolutionised how we see quantum matter.”
The award commemorates the 19th century British scientist Michael Faraday, inventor of the first electric motor.
It was one of several announced by the UK-based Institute of Physics, whose president Paul Howarth said the recipients represented “the very best of physics”.
“Through their curiosity, expertise and dedication, they are expanding knowledge, driving innovation and inspiring the next generation of scientists,” he said.
[ Did Anthropic’s artificial intelligence really make a scientific discovery on its own? Opens in new window ]
Davis was also congratulated by UCC president, Prof John O’Halloran.
“His pioneering work has enabled us to see the fabric of all matter at its most fundamental level, enhancing our understanding of quantum physics and laying a foundation that will pave the way for the technology of tomorrow,” he said.
Davis, who is also professor of physics at the University of Oxford, said he was focused on the “new frontier” in quantum physics with the help of artificial intelligence (AI).
He said AI could process and analyse data in days that for humans, would take years.
“The amount of data we produce with our instruments is huge – going over all of it alone would be almost impossible,” he said.
“Imagine taking 10 million photographs of the night sky, and trying to identify all the stars in each image, that is the scale of the challenge we face.”

title: Zelenskiy blames Russia for breaking ‘energy ceasefire’
description: Zelenskiy says Russia continues to strike Ukraine’s power facilities despite Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ announcement
author_name: Henry Foy and Raphael Minder in Warsaw and Christopher Miller in Kyiv
content:
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy has blamed Russia for breaking a purported “energy ceasefire” announced by Donald Trump , signalling that Kyiv will continue its strikes unless Moscow halts its attacks.
The US president wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire”, in a claim that blindsided officials in Kyiv.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Zelenskiy said Trump should have come to him to cut a “diesel deal”, adding that Russia had used drones and missiles to strike power and gas facilities across Ukraine overnight.
“Immediately after [Trump’s] post, Russia launched a targeted strike ... It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social,” Zelenskiy said.
“We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same,” he added, including “to sign guarantees” as proof of Ukraine’s commitment.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov did not comment on Trump’s ceasefire announcement, telling reporters on Monday that “contacts” between Russia and the US “continue”. Peskov rejected Ukraine’s offer of a 60-day truce and presidential elections. He said Moscow was willing to halt attacks only for a day to allow Ukraine to hold elections. “They need 60 days of ceasefire not for elections, but to regroup, heal their wounds and continue the war,” Peskov said.
Despite Moscow’s overnight strikes, European diesel prices fell on Monday as traders responded to Trump’s latest effort to drive down fuel prices in the US before November’s midterm elections.
His announcement of an “energy ceasefire” came after the US president on Friday struck a deal with Vladimir Putin for Russia to release more diesel.
The price of diesel – a vital fuel for industry and agriculture – has soared as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine knock out infrastructure and strain global supplies.
Speaking in Warsaw, Zelenskiy said: “Last night, Russian oil refineries were not burning. But at midnight a Russian jet-powered Shahed drone hit a gas plant in Ukraine ... This is Putin’s answer to Trump.”
Parts of Kyiv and other cities across Ukraine were plunged into darkness on Sunday night into Monday morning following the Russian strikes. Water was knocked out in much of the Ukrainian capital.
Russian drones continued to attack Kyiv on Monday after Zelenskiy’s conference speech, with heavy air-defence fire and explosions reverberating throughout the city.
Sergii Fedorenko, acting chief executive of Ukraine’s state gas company Naftogaz, said critical equipment was damaged by a Russian jet-powered drone.
Vitaliy Bunechko, the governor of Zhytomyr region west of Kyiv, said Russian drones had struck energy and railway facilities there.
Zelenskyy told the Warsaw Security Forum he did not believe the volume of diesel Russia would export as part of Trump’s deal would affect the price.
“Moreover, we see they can export from 300,000 to 500,000 tonnes a month today. Meanwhile, global consumption stands at 120 million tonnes a month,” he said. “What kind of impact can that have? I don’t think it would have any.”
“If some people think otherwise, so be it,” he said in an apparent reference to Trump. “If this is the approach, then why isn’t America making a ‘diesel deal’ with Ukraine? Let Ukraine propose a ‘diesel deal’.”
Ukraine, Zelenskiy said, through its long-range drones that have attacked Russian oil and gas facilities and shadow fleet ships, had “influence over whether these ships can sail or not, whether these refineries can operate or not”.
He added: “If that’s the case, then let’s do it.”
The Trump administration had also threatened to stop the procurement system that provided Ukraine with weapons to pressure Kyiv to halt its strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, officials told the Financial Times.
That followed a warning on Friday from the Trump administration to Zelenskiy’s peace negotiators in Miami that Washington could cut off vital intelligence sharing with Kyiv unless it halts the air attacks against Russian oil refineries.
“We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians,” Zelenskiy said. “Putin is so shamelessly trying to sell his refineries to the world as a solution.”
EU foreign ministers meeting in Luxembourg on Monday agreed to impose sanctions against about 1,600 additional individuals and entities from Russia’s military-industrial complex.
“If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is putting more pressure on Russia,” said Kaja Kallas, the EU’s chief diplomat. “We would call on US to put the sanctions in place so that actually we could finish this war and all these effects of attacks on refineries would not be there.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Winter of discontent looms as public sector workers prepare for stoppage
description: Inside Politics: Unions want shortfalls in pay to be addressed up front and a guarantee that wages will not slip behind inflation during any new deal period
content:
There’s less than 48 hours to prevent a potential winter of discontent.
With hundreds of thousands of public sector workers readying not to go to work on Wednesday, even the Dáil won’t be sitting as a result. The Seanad and the committee rooms will also be locked up.
The Taoiseach had said the sitting should go ahead, but with Sinn Féin , Labour and Social Democrat TDs all saying they wouldn’t be passing a picket to get to the chamber, Government chief whip Mary Butler confirmed over the weekend that Wednesday was off the week’s agenda.
There are some suggestions that all could be avoided.
The Government is expected to say again that it wants talks with the unions – but with the unions insisting that pay should be negotiated upon first, there was no indication this morning that such a position would be deemed acceptable.
Perhaps in an effort to sweeten the offer, sources have been hinting that there is plenty of money available beyond the €1.2 billion mentioned by Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers last week.
The unions are demanding that existing shortfalls in pay be addressed up front – and a guarantee that wages will not slip behind inflation during the period of any new deal.
But a collision seems all but inevitable despite the last-minute throwing of shapes.
With a further one-day stoppage planned for next week, union bosses are suggesting even more industrial action could be coming in the absence of proper progress.
Speaking of deals and proverbial carts being put before proverbial horses, Donald Trump’s weekend ‘ENERGY CEASEFIRE’ between Ukraine and Russia might not actually exist.
With Trump keen to get some diesel refineries back online ahead of the US midterms, he is keen for the two sides to stop pummeling each other.
Announcing the supposed ceasefire yesterday , Trump appears to have struck the deal in the absence of one of the participants.
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskiy said it sounded like a good idea – but was news to him. And then reports started coming in that the Russians were still striking Ukrainian energy targets. Zelenskiy said the skies above parts of his country were still full of Russian drones and that power plants in Kyiv and the east had been struck since Trump’s big announcement.
Trump, it has been pointed out, made a similar announcement last month.
Amid this ‘deal or no deal’ carry-on, Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee is in Luxembourg with the rest of her European counterparts – many of whom are very concerned with Trump’s poor treatment of Zelenskiy of late.
First there was an agreement between Trump and Russian president Vladimir Putin to allow Russia to export diesel to the US – and then Trump’s comments that Ukraine needs a new leader.
McEntee says Europe needs to “redouble” its efforts to support Kyiv and has described Trump’s comments about Zelenskiy as “concerning”.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas will be at the meeting. She has said the EU would welcome any energy ceasefire “if it holds”.
More sanctions are up for discussion today – it’s not obvious whether Irish alumina exports to Russia will come back under the spotlight.
An Irish delegation will be heading to Brussels later in the week with the EU summit scheduled for Thursday. There’ll be more Irish interest than usual, what with Dublin’s suggested revisions to the draft EU budget.
The Irish proposal would see €141 billion slashed away, a scaling back of overseas aid spending and an economic “competitiveness fund”. No further cuts to agriculture subsidies have been mooted, however.
The European Council president wants agreement among member states by December and the Irish-devised compromise will be put through the wringer before then.
Whatever about the “frugal” members and their concerns about rising budget contributions, Irish farmers don’t seem happy. The Irish Farmers Association says the new Irish proposal does nothing to restore suggested cuts to payments and is a “huge let down”.
Separately, Andy Burnham is fluttering his eyelashes at Brussels again. He’s due to tell the House of Commons that it would be a “dereliction of duty” for London to turn its back on the EU.
Burnham has been distancing his Labour Party from the whole Brexit business – saying last week it had caused “more harm than good” .
He will tell MPs that a fresh deal with the Europeans could mean more economic growth and make it easier to deal with illegal immigration – the very things the Brexiteers promised that separation would achieve.
With Nigel Farage of the Reform Party promising a five-year ban on asylum seekers should it win the next general election, Burnham is in a right old bun fight.
Meanwhile, the Saudis and the Houthis spent the weekend attacking one another’s airports. The Houthi attack on Riyadh on Saturday killed 12 and injured 300.
The ability of the Houthis to wage war further complicates the whole mess that has ensued since the US and Israel attacked Tehran back in February.
With the Houthis managing to exert all manner of pressure on Saudi oil production and exports, they are helping to ensure the price of oil remains firmly lodged above $100 a barrel.
Plenty to consider for any pay talks here at home, if they are to happen.

title: Jack Rice of Comet restaurant named young chef of the year
description: Euro-toques ceremony also announced Aengus Moloney of Aniar in Galway as rising pastry chef
content:
Jack Rice of Dublin’s Comet restaurant was named young chef of the year on Sunday at the Euro-toques Ireland annual gala dinner.
Rice, who is originally from Limerick , previously worked at Michelin -starred Galway restaurant Lignum and was winner of the WorldSkills Ireland cookery competition in 2022.
Rice was crowned young chef of the year after a final in which six chefs were challenged to design two original dishes: a main course and either a starter or dessert.
The other five finalists included fellow Comet chef Áine Budds; Shannon Caulfield of Ashford Castle ; Aymeric Decourval who represented Lady Helen at Mount Juliet ; Chapter One’s Sam Nourse and Simone Tamilio of Bar Pez.
The brief asked the six chefs to use a centre-cut of Dexter beef sirloin on the bone from Brave Herders in Co Cork, alongside organic rye, spelt and wholemeal flours from Dunany Flour in Co Louth, and butter and yoghurt from Saltrock Dairy in Gorey, Co Wexford.
The ingredients were selected as part of the competition’s 40th anniversary theme Community at the Table, and Rice’s main course, The Past and Present of Beef in Ireland, followed by his Mum’s Apple Tart, bagged the top prize.
As winner Rice takes home a Kenwood Chef Titanium XL; a one-day knife course with Sam Gleeson; a voucher for sharpening knives; a bottle of Two Shores Superior Irish Rum as well as a chef’s stage at one of the judges kitchens: either Da Terra restaurant in London with chef Rafael Cagali or Restaurante Maca de Castro under Macarena de Castro Martín in Mallorca.
As well as competing in the final, the six chefs also received mentorship as part of the programme, visiting the kitchens of Keelan Higgs’ at Variety Jones in Dublin , Rafael Calgari’s two Michelin-starred Da Terra in London and Nomos alumni Cuán Greene’s recently opened venture Ómós in Abbeyleix, Co Laois. The young chefs also visited Dunany Flour and Carlingford Oyster Company over the six-month mentorship period.
This year’s judging panel included Michelin-starred chef Lewis Barker of Terre at Castlemartyr Resort in Co Cork, fellow Michelin-star holder Keelan Higgs of Variety Jones, and Domini Kemp of Lottie’s in Rathmines, Dublin.
The ceremony also announced Aengus Moloney of Aniar in Galway as rising pastry chef of the year, who won the honour ahead of four other finalists: Aoife Comerford of Liath in Dublin; The Merrion Hotel’s Alena Pazitna; Ashford Castle’s Francesca Kearns; and Masha Campbell of Carrick-on-Shannon’s My Kitchen by Sham Hanifa.
The pastry category’s judging panel included Lali González of the recently opened Glover’s Alley in Dublin; Lady Helen at Mount Juliet’s Tom Phelan; and Orna Larkin who represented the InterContinental in Dublin.
Moloney’s prize includes a trip to visit specialist food decorator PCB Creation in Strasbourg, France, a stage with one of the category’s judges, a Kenwood Chef Titanium XL and a bottle of Two Shores Superior Irish Rum.

title: Plant-based dairy alternatives not recommended for teens, says food watchdog
description: Protein powders, shakes and supplementary drinks were unnecessary to meet protein goals, it said
content:
Plant-based dairy replacement foods and drinks are not recommended for teenagers due to their nutritional composition, and teenage girls should take folic acid supplements, according to new dietary advice from the food safety watchdog.
The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) on Monday published the first scientific report outlining food-based dietary guideline recommendations for adolescents aged between 9 and 18 living in Ireland.
The report was commissioned by the Department of Health in recognition of the specific nutritional requirements during puberty, which is believed to be greater than during any other period in life due to intense growth and development.
It also consider sustainability and climate change when making the recommendations.
According to the report, teenagers have high energy requirements but that this varies quite significantly when considering age, sex, body size and physical activity level.
Carbohydrates, which includes cereals and breads, potatoes, pasta, and rice, are the most important food group for fuelling physical activity, with average requirements ranging from 6 to 10 servings and requirements reaching up to 13 servings for some adolescents.
Teenagers should have four servings from the milk, cheese and yoghurt category per day are if they are sedentary to lightly active, but this should increase to five servings per day for moderately to very active adolescents. Low-fat or reduced-fat options should be chosen.
In general, the FSAI said plant-based dairy replacement foods and drinks are not recommended due to their nutritional composition and the need for the addition of calcium and other micronutrients.
[ How much protein should I eat in a day? Opens in new window ]
Where plant-based dairy alternatives are required, a calcium-fortified soya beverage represents the best choice for teenage boys, and calcium- and iodine-fortified brands represent the best choice for teenage girls, it added.
A reduction in lean red meat consumption to between one and two times per week did not lead to inadequate iron intakes among teens, and mixing plant-based food protein with animal food protein enhanced the overall quality of protein in a meal.
The watchdog said protein requirements were easily achieved, despite the reduction in the amounts and frequency of meat consumption.
“Protein powders, shakes and supplementary drinks were unnecessary to meet protein goals,” it added.
All women of childbearing age, including adolescents, who can become pregnant should take a 400µg folic acid supplement every day.
The report highlighted concerns about current health trends in teenagers.
[ How to tackle Ireland’s unhealthy food environment: Experts on changes they want to see Opens in new window ]
A quarter of adolescents are classified as body mass index-defined overweight or obese, it said, adding that significant numbers of teenagers having higher than recommended intakes of saturated fat, free sugars and salt, and significant numbers of teenagers having inadequate intakes of several micronutrients.
Prof Kevin Cashman, chairman of the FSAI Public Health Nutrition Subcommittee during the development of this report, said adolescence was a life stage where nutritional requirements are particularly high.
“Adolescence is a key developmental window of opportunity for nutrition. During this time, children lay down 40 per cent of their bone mass, protecting them from osteoporosis in later life. In addition, they gain 50 per cent of their adult weight and 20 per cent of their adult height,” he said.
“It is important to note that there is a significant variation in nutritional needs among adolescents, including those of the same age. These differences relate to body size, for example tall versus small; physical activity levels, from sedentary to very active; and maturational timing, such as adolescents who are early versus late developers.”

title: Daniel Kinahan to apply for bail ‘in due course’, court told
description: Kinahan (49) will seek the disclosure of all files in two foreign investigations, Special Criminal Court hears
content:
Alleged crime gang leader Daniel Kinahan will apply for bail “in due course” in the coming weeks, and will seek disclosure of two foreign investigations, a court heard.
Kinahan (49) appeared before the Special Criminal Court on Monday, having been brought to the court by armed escort from Portlaoise Prison .
He is facing a single charge of “directing the activities of a criminal organisation” between October 18th, 2015, and April 6th, 2017, contrary to section 71a of the Criminal Justice Act 2006, as amended.
The prosecuting barrister Dominic McGinn applied for an adjournment until December 21st to allow for the preparation of the book of evidence.
He said there is a “complex factual matrix” behind the single charge, noting that the “statement of fact” used to secure to extradition of the Irish citizen from the United Arab Emirates ran to 189 pages.
The prosecutor said that statement of fact would need to be reduced to a legally submissible document.
“We anticipate the book will be prepared by that date,” he said of the December 21st date.
Judge Caroline Biggs, presiding at the three-judge court, granted the adjournment for the book of evidence to be prepared.
Solicitor Darragh Mackin of Phoenix Law raised three issues before the court, noting that the timetable of any trial would need to factor in the examination of digital evidence by experts instructed by his client.
Mackin said he was seeking disclosure of all of the information behind two other international investigations which he said his client was “acquitted” of.
His solicitor said Kinahan will apply for bail at the High Court “in due course”. It is understood he will apply prior to the December 21st appearance.
“We look forward to a trial,” Kinahan’s solicitor said outside the court and pledged to “vehemently defend” the case against his client.
Mackin said he hoped the trial will be “in the early part of next year”.
“We are anxious to make progress. We are comforted that the Book of Evidence will now be served before the end of the year,” he said. “The rule of law applies to everyone. Nobody is above the rule of law and, equally, nobody is below the rule of law.”
Kinahan was not asked to speak during the court and appeared wearing a dark grey suit and black shirt.
He was the first Irish person extradited from the UAE under a new permanent extradition treaty, which came into force last year. He lived in Dubai with his wife and five children for the last 10 years.
He was arrested in April on foot of an extradition request from Ireland and was in custody there until he was extradited.
Kinahan was flown to Ireland onboard the Government’s Dassault Falcon 6X jet, landing at Casement Aerodrome before being driven to the courts for his first appearance.

title: Woman sentenced to three months for breaching anonymity of Donaldson victims
description: Donna Toman (55) pleaded guilty to publishing material on social media that was likely to lead to identifcation
content:
A Co Down woman has been sentenced to three months in jail for breaching the anonymity of a victim of Jeffrey Donaldson.
Donna Toman (55), from the Lord Moira Park area of Ballynahinch, appeared before Downpatrick Magistrates’ Court on Monday after previously pleading guilty to breaching a lifetime ban on publishing information likely to lead to the identification of the victims.
Toman was released on bail pending appeal.
Donaldson, a former Lagan Valley MP and Democratic Unionist Party leader, was convicted in June of 18 sex offences, including one count of rape, relating to the abuse of two women when they were children.
The offences were committed between 1985 and 2008.
The two victims at the centre of the Donaldson trial were referred to as Complainant A and Complainant B and both are entitled to lifelong anonymity.
No details of the offence by Toman, which was committed on June 26th, were revealed to the court when she pleaded guilty in August.
She faced a charge of publishing material on social media that was likely to lead members of the public to identify a victim.
District Judge Peter Magill asked whether Toman, who was for many years a popular Dolly Parton impersonator, had “breached a lifetime ban on identifying a victim” and it was confirmed that she was pleading guilty.

title: Ukraine backs Trump’s energy ‘ceasefire’. But is Russia on board?
description: Kyiv says it supports the proposal despite being blindsided, while Moscow’s silence casts doubt on whether a truce is viable
content:
U S president Donald Trump announced on Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed an “ energy ceasefire ” effective immediately, and warned the warring neighbours not to break it.
The statement came after another torrid 48 hours in relations between the White House and Kyiv, during which Trump ordered the suspension of sanctions on Russian diesel exports, again blamed Ukraine for failing to end the war, and said it was time for the embattled country to “get a new president”.
In short – with bewilderment. Volodymyr Zelenskiy called it “news to me”, and other Kyiv officials also said they had been blindsided by the development.
Zelenskiy was quick, however, to say Ukraine “supports the ceasefire” while “awaiting details from the American side”.
At the same time, Zelenskiy said Russia struck energy infrastructure in Kyiv on Sunday, and bombed a large power station in Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second city, shortly after Trump announced the supposed truce.
Speaking in Poland on Monday, Zelenskiy said Russia launched an attack on gas and power facilities in Ukraine.
On Monday in Moscow, there was no official Russian reaction to Trump’s announcement. In its morning briefing, the Russian defence ministry made no mention of its forces’ attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov would not say whether Russia had agreed to an energy ceasefire, saying only: “Contacts are ongoing.”
Russian president Vladimir Putin has previously linked any possible partial ceasefire to the removal of international sanctions on all Russian oil and oil products, not just diesel.
But while it has been slow to respond publicly to Trump’s announcement, Russia remains keen to negotiate with the US administration. It would ideally like to agree with Trump on terms to end the war in Ukraine, sidelining Kyiv and European capitals.
Russian state news agency Tass said on Monday that an unnamed source had denied that US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had cancelled plans to visit Moscow due to developments over the weekend. The source said they still intended to come to Russia once they had “a clear understanding” of Kyiv’s position.
Russian missile, bomb and drone strikes on Ukraine’s energy grid have destroyed more than 60 per cent of its power-generating capacity since the start of full-scale war in February 2022. This has subjected millions of people to blackouts and problems with heating, water supply and public transport, all of which are most severe in winter. Analysts say this winter could be the most difficult of the war, and large-scale power cuts have begun in many areas, including Kyiv.
So, Ukraine would welcome any respite in attacks on its power stations. At the same time, Russia would benefit from a halt to Ukrainian drone strikes on its oil refineries and storage facilities.
The energy sector accounts for about a fifth of Russian tax revenue, making it a crucial replenisher of the Kremlin’s war chest as military spending spirals and its budget deficit widens.
Ukraine says its long-range drone strikes have disabled half of Russia’s refining capacity. Western experts put the figure at between 20 and 40 per cent. According to Russia’s own figures, its energy revenue is down 17 per cent this year, despite world crude prices hitting their highest levels for more than a decade.
[ Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war, but Zelenskiy says deal is ‘news to me’ Opens in new window ]
Surveys suggest Trump’s Republican allies could lose control of Congress in midterm elections on November 3rd, and that rising fuel prices are a factor in their declining popularity. The high cost of diesel – which is important for US farming, transport and other sectors – is a particular irritant.
US diesel prices have soared by about 70 per cent since the US and Israel attacked Iran at the end of February, and show no sign of falling amid continued severe disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz .
Energy analysts say the volumes of diesel that Russia could supply in the near future will not have a significant impact on world prices, and that Trump’s war on Iran and instability in the Middle East are – as data shows – the crucial factor in this.
Trump and his supporters insist, however, that Russian supply will bring down US diesel prices, so Ukraine must stop attacking Russian refineries.
The upshot is that Trump is likely to blame Ukraine and Zelenskiy if the energy ceasefire does not take hold, if fuel prices at the American pump remain high and, ultimately, if the Republicans fare badly in the midterms.
Zelenskiy, like all Ukrainians, is somewhat inured to Trump’s tirades. He has learned to speak positively about the US leader even under extreme duress. He quickly backed the energy ceasefire and said Ukraine would gladly hold presidential elections if Russia adhered to a full, two-month ceasefire. He says he is ready for peace talks at any time, but Russia has declined – without facing any of Trump’s wrath.
Ukraine’s arms industry is advancing apace, and is a world leader in drone technology. But the country still relies on US intelligence-sharing, Patriot air defence systems and Starlink internet provision, and would struggle if Trump cut them off.
[ US president Donald Trump says it is time for Ukraine to get rid of Zelenskiy Opens in new window ]

title: The Browns are still the Browns. And Deshaun Watson is still Deshaun Watson
description: After three straight game-winning drives, Cleveland’s quarterback was sacked eight times in a dismal defeat
content:
I guess the New York Jets didn’t get the memo. This was supposed to be a Deshaun Watson lovefest kind of day. A day where, much to the chagrin of those of us with a moral compass and a functional memory, football fans worldwide could declare Watson was “so back” and that the Browns were in some blinkered, alternate universe, a Super Bowl contender. No such luck, as the Browns looked like the Browns – reminding an otherwise jubilant city of Cleveland that they are trapped in the sports equivalent of the Backrooms.
Limping along for 155 passing yards and one touchdown, Watson fell to Earth harder than David Bowie in a Nicolas Roeg film. He completed fewer than 50% of his passes and ended the day with a 69.6 QBR. I should also probably mention he got sacked eight times. Yes, eight times. EIGHT TIMES. He only completed seven more passes than he received punishing hits behind the line of scrimmage. It was a performance NBC NFL writer Patrick Daugherty called “unspeakably bad.” Actually, I think the performance was very much speakable, as I’ve demonstrated here. Stick around for another 400 words.
The thing that has defined Watson’s run as a potentially viable NFL quarterback has been his ability to march down the field and win a game in the dying embers of the contest. After three game-winning drives to start the season, it seemed like the Browns were poised to pull out another improbable victory from where the sun don’t shine, but no. Not today.
On 4th and 11 – with less than a minute left in the 4th quarter, down by five – Watson dropped back, only for his pocket to evaporate faster than spilled water in the middle of the Mojave. Ejected violently from the pocket, Watson begins to scramble. On 4th and 11, remember. He’s unceremoniously tackled near the line of scrimmage, putting the game on ice.
Starting off Sunday, these seemed like two teams going in the opposite direction, but the reality on the field was more like the Spider-Man pointing meme. Offensive ineptitude, with both the Jets and Browns recording fewer than 300 yards of total offense, giving away two fumbles, and failing to convert touchdowns twice in the red zone.
The New York Post might have called this game “tense” and “gritty”, but I’m sure many viewers could think of more apropos adjectives to describe what they witnessed – a game that hinged on a botched snap sailing through the hands of Browns punter Corey Bojorquez. That wayward punt turned into a game-winning touchdown for Jets RB Braelon Allen.
This loss, dropping Cleveland to 3-2 on the year, felt like a necessary corrective to the hyperbole and early extension talks around Watson’s early successes. American sports fans love a comeback story, but this one is mired in issues that are far more important than football. It certainly makes everyone’s life easier when he plays like this.
Cam Little, K, Jacksonville Jaguars: Sure, there’s probably more splashy statistical performances from today. You could make a strong case for Drake Maye, whose 374 yards and four touchdowns gave the Patriots a resounding win over the Raiders. But I’m not going to do that, because we ride for placekickers when I’m around. In a bleak, dystopian ending that felt more like the final five minutes of Digger than a football game, the Eagles went up 17-16 with a mere eight seconds left in the contest. Philadelphia Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni, misplacing his copy of Football for Dummies, decided to have his kicker boot the ball in play rather than ice it with a touchback. A 53-yard return by Ameer Abdullah perfectly set up a gargantuan field goal to win the game for the Jags.
“I didn’t make the right decision, and I lost us that game, and that’s what I said to our guys,” Sirianni told the media after Christmas came early in London for Jacksonville. Now, a 57-yard field goal with nearly no time left on the clock isn’t exactly a gimmie. One could maybe forgive Sirianni for thinking the chances of a field goal from distance to steal the game was unlikely. Except, the Jaguars’ placekicker is Cam Little – the man who holds the record for the longest made field goal in NFL history. A record he set almost a full year ago. The Eagles gave Little a dagger. He should be commended for knowing how to use it.
The Texans won their first game of the year, demolishing an equally troubled, still-winless Titans team 26-3. CJ Stroud dropped 261 yards, a passing touchdown, and a running touchdown on Tennessee, cementing a bounce-back moment that has the NFL buzzing about just how much money he’ll command on the free-agent market. More importantly, the result is coupled with news of Houston getting Stroud reinforcements. WR Marvin Harrison is on the way to the Texans from the Cardinals and Houston coach DeMeco Ryans was more than happy to officially drop the bomb in a brief post-game presser:
Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans ended his press conference by announcing his team just traded for Marvin Harrison Jr. pic.twitter.com/74JcW3zdau
Before their drubbing by the Patriots, the Raiders had scored at least 26 points in all four of their games this season. Here, they didn’t score a touchdown until the fourth quarter, managing 17 meagre points on the road at Gillette Stadium. Las Vegas had a chance to keep pace with the AFC West leading Chiefs during KC’s bye week, but Kirk Cousins was sacked three times and couldn’t convert scoring opportunities into touchdowns. Cousins was replaced by rookie Fernando Mendoza in garbage time, showing how thoroughly the Raiders were handled today. They certainly didn’t benefit from giving up 165 rushing yards, spread across multiple New England players (including 25 yards on the ground for Maye). The Pats grabbed 8.1 yards per play, as efficient and deadly as it gets.
♦ After a World Cup in North America, I hope everyone here has gotten used to the concept of a tie. The Giants and Commanders certainly have. In an example of hopeless, foggy-eyed game management, Washington blew a chance to win the game in overtime. A Cam Skattebo turnover handed the Commanders the ball with enough time for QB Jayden Daniels to march down to the New York 24-yard line. A luxurious 12 seconds remained on the clock. More than enough time to plunk in a field goal to win it. Except, the Commanders wandered around the line of scrimmage for exactly 12 seconds and never did snap the ball, let alone spike it to stop the clock to set up for a kick. Commanders coach Dan Quinn, like Nick Sirianni in the Eagles-Jags game, took the blame for the mistake. For once, I’d like to see a coach just completely throw his players under the bus. “Hey man, I’m not playing. Don’t look at me.” Just for variety.
♦ Put the phone down. No need to call the authorities on your friends who are Steelers fans. After a game with visible tension between Aaron Rodgers and head coach Mike McCarthy on Thursday Night Football on October 1st, the ship was righted in Steel City, USA. Rodgers looked tidy and comfortable, connecting in the end zone with Pat Freiermuth twice to defeat the Colts 34-22.
♦ The Vikings are still undefeated, dropping the Saints to 1-4 on the year. The game was not as close as the 23-13 score, with Minnesota dominating every major team category. New Orleans finished with a paltry 142 total yards. Only 55 of those came on the ground. The Saints only recorded one offensive touchdown, with the other coming on a fumble recovery by safety Jonas Sanker. The story was far different for the Vikes. Minnesota RB Aaron Jones gobbled up 113 yards and one touchdown in front of moribund Saints fans in the Superdome. QB Kyler Murray benefitted greatly from Justin Jefferson’s return to action, throwing for 229 yards and a touchdown. Can anyone beat this Vikings team? They’ve got a bye in week six, then the 2-3 Colts, back at US Bank Stadium. That doesn’t seem promising for Indy.
♦ The winless Dolphins almost pulled off a last-second miracle against the Bengals, pulling within a touchdown with less than a minute left in the game. But kicker Riley Patterson missed the extra point before an onside kick attempt to recover possession was unsuccessful. Cincinnati took the win 31-24 off a splashy four-touchdown day for Joe Burrow. Can anyone lose to this Dolphins team? They’ve got a bye in week six, then the 2-3 Jets, on the road at MetLife Stadium. That doesn’t seem promising for viewers.
♦ The NFL’s oldest rivalry continued, with the Packers tossing the Bears in a meat freezer and locking the door. Metaphorically speaking. Green Bay danced away with the win in the two teams’ 214th ever matchup (including playoffs), 31-7. Bears QB Caleb Williams, perhaps the most hated man in Wisconsin after his ruthless comeback win against Green Bay in last year’s playoffs, remained out. In his stead, Tyson Bagent looked worse than anyone could have imagined, 12-of-21 for 87 yards and two interceptions before being benched for Case Keenum. At most, Bears coach Ben Johnson would say that Williams is “on track” to return, but with no definitive date set. NFL reporter Ian Rappaport did suggest that there’s a chance he can play in week six against the Atlanta Falcons. Perhaps the Chicago faithful should place a call to Pope Leo to speed this thing along.
♦ As a Rams fan still smarting from our disastrous Australian drubbing, the last thing I want to talk about is the 49ers looking like the class of the entire NFL. But San Francisco’s trip to Lumen Field to face Seattle might have been the most consequential matchup of week five. The NFC West has three legitimate Super Bowl contenders (and the Cardinals), and two of them faced off here on Sunday. Seattle and San Francisco traded punches all day, but the game came down to rare, crucial mistakes, as matchups between good teams often do.
Seahawks QB Sam Darnold threw two pivotal interceptions, RB George Holani fumbled right before halftime, leading to a touchdown that put the 49ers up by eight. Seattle exploded for a touchdown and two field goals in the third, tilting the scales back in their direction. But a seven-yard TD pass from Brock Purdy to Brandin Cooks flipped the script yet again. A successful two-point conversion gave the Niners a three-point lead. Seattle kicker Jason Myers tied it up with a little under seven minutes to play, but the Seahawks couldn’t get a stop to force overtime. A 44-yard Eddy Pineiro field goal gave the 49ers a slim advantage. Darnold linked with WR Cooper Kupp, who nearly converted a fourth-and 10 at the 50, which would have given Seattle one last crack at the ballgame. But a controversial spot of the ball left Kupp short and handed San Francisco their fifth win of 2026. And they did it without ace receiver Deebo Samuel, who left the game in the third quarter with a hamstring injury. Niners fans hold their breath. And I put another pin in the voodoo doll. — Guardian

title: Man to appear in court charged over 2005 murder of Eoin McCarthy (27)
description: The Dublin man’s remains were found in a wooded area of Ballinagee, Hollywood, Co Wicklow
content:
A man is due to appear in court charged in relation to the murder of Eoin McCarthy more than 20 years ago.
The remains of McCarthy (27) of Ashwood Park, Clondalkin, Dublin 22, were discovered in a wooded area at Ballinagee, Hollywood, Co Wicklow in November 2005.
The postmortem into his death concluded he died by a gunshot wound to the back of the head.
In March, nearly 21 years after McCarthy died, gardaí said they had arrested a man in his 40s, who was held for questioning before being released without charge.
Gardaí said this man is expected to appear before Bray District Court on Monday.

title: Tusla whistleblower asks gardaí to investigate alleged ‘retaliation and unlawful conduct’
description: Ciarán Kenneally’s solicitor wrote to Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly on October 5th
content:
A Tusla whistleblower has asked gardaí to investigate alleged criminal offences carried out after he submitted a protected disclosure related to the child and family agency.
Ciarán Kenneally resigned from his role at a Tusla aftercare service based at Liberty Street House in Cork city in January 2019, shortly after making a protected disclosure related to procurement and financial procedures at the centre.
He alleges Tusla engaged in “retaliation and unlawful conduct” after he submitted his protected disclosure.
Tusla did not wish to comment on the specific allegations made by Kenneally but said “due process must apply”.
Kenneally, via his solicitor Kevin Winters at KRW Law, lodged a complaint with Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly on October 5th.
This letter, seen by The Irish Times, made a number of allegations related to the actions of several Tusla employees.
It alleged that a number of criminal offences may have been committed, including “retaliation or penalisation for making a protected disclosure” under the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, and “unlawful obtaining, processing, or misuse of personal data” under the Data Protection Act 2018.
“Following the disclosure, our client was subjected to severe workplace bullying, work-related stress, and ultimately the termination of his employment. He was left without income for a prolonged period and suffered significant deterioration in his health, as confirmed by medical evidence,” the letter said.
“Tusla management undertook unauthorised inquiries into our client’s previous employment history, including background checks and attempts to discredit his credibility. These actions were undertaken after our client had already successfully completed Garda vetting and reference checks as part of his recruitment.”
[ Tusla in breach of High Court special care direction again over capacity issues Opens in new window ]
Winters wrote to Tusla in late September informing them about the complaint to the Garda Commissioner. The letter asked the agency to “enter into discussions to resolve this matter lawfully and transparently” and “compensate our client for the losses suffered”.
“We write in advance of issuing proceedings, in the hope that the matters set out below can be resolved without recourse to the courts,” the letter said.
Winters told The Irish Times that, if he does not receive a satisfactory response from Tusla within the next two to three weeks, a plenary summons will be issued.
Ken O’Flynn , an Independent Ireland TD for Cork North-Central, last week asked Minister for Children Norma Foley to examine the case as Tusla falls under the remit of her department. Kenneally has worked for O’Flynn since last year.
A spokesman said Tusla “cannot comment on individual cases”.
“We respect the right of an individual to engage legal representation and engage fully and appropriately in such processes,” a statement said.
[ Additional cost-saving measures would significantly impact frontline services, Tusla warns Opens in new window ]
“It must also be noted that in any circumstances where allegations are made about the agency or individuals within the agency, these must be considered, as such, and due process must apply, and caution should be exerted in the publication of any such information.”
The statement added that all protected disclosures received by Tusla were assessed under the agency’s protected disclosure policy .
An Garda Síochána said it was “precluded by law from commenting on any matter that may relate to a protected disclosure”.
The Irish Times has contacted the Department of Children for comment.
Kenneally settled an unfair dismissal case with Tusla at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) in November 2019. Records released to Kenneally after the WRC case was settled confirmed Tusla had carried out a background check on him.
Earlier this year, the Data Protection Commission found Tusla failed to demonstrate a lawful basis under General Data Protection Regulation for its processing of Kenneally’s personal data.
Documents released in January showed an internal review, carried out in late 2018, raised several issues about financial management at the Liberty Street service. The facility supports service users, often young people experiencing homelessness, via cash and vouchers.
The review found there was an absence of guidelines for staff regarding financial management, inconsistent record-keeping and “a practice of withdrawing cash without regard to combined known requirements and contingency funds”. The review was released following a Freedom of Information request submitted by O’Flynn.
Kenneally submitted a second protected disclosure to Tusla last November, saying another former employee of the agency had contacted him with information that supported his initial disclosure.

title: Takeover panel rejects PTSB sale complaints from ex-banker
description: Former Bank of Scotland (Ireland) chief Mark Duffy separately mulling late bid for Irish lender
content:
The Irish Takeover Panel has rejected concerns raised about the PTSB sale process from a firm cofounded by boom-time Irish banker Mark Duffy, which has also indicated it is considering an 11th-hour bid for the bank.
Axis Capital, an advisory business cofounded by former Bank of Scotland (Ireland) chief executive Duffy, sent a letter to the panel on July 27th that consolidated “a number of matters” it had previously raised in relation to the proposed €1.62 billion acquisition of PTSB by Austrian banking group Bawag .
The panel said that “having carefully considered the substance of all of the matters raised by Axis”, it has ruled there was no case laid out that amounted to any breach of Irish takeover rules.
The announcement comes just weeks before the High Court, which is overseeing the so-called scheme-of-arrangement deal for PTSB to be sold to Bawag, is due to hold its sanctioning hearing on October 27th.
Axis made an intervention on October 2nd saying it was considering making a bid for PTSB. Last Friday, a long-term dissenting PTSB shareholder, Scotchstone Capital, led by Piotr Skoczylas, also said it was weighing a bid for PTSB. Neither has confirmed whether it has secured any funding for a bid.
Axis is being advised by Quirin Privatbank in Berlin and law firm Belmont Legal in Frankfurt.
Axis helped initiate talks in 2025 between New York private equity firm Centerbridge, the Department of Finance and PTSB over a potential deal for the Irish bank. The US group subsequently submitted a non-binding proposal in September last year for the State’s 57.5 per cent stake in the bank.
Centerbridge was the underbidder to Bawag in April as a formal sales process, initiated in October, concluded.
Axis was reported by the Business Post in July to have been urging minority shareholders to vote against the planned Bawag deal at an extraordinary general meeting (egm) later that month. Axis said in a note circulated to shareholders it had become “increasingly uncomfortable with the way the process has developed”, claiming there had been “inordinate involvement from one shareholder, leaving others effectively as bystanders”.
In July, Duffy said in a post on LinkedIn, the professional social networking platform, that the panel should reopen the sale process to allow “all credible bidders to make their best and final bids to all shareholders”.
PTSB secured backing from 91.3 per cent of shareholders – led by the Government – for the Bawag takeover at the July egm. However, some 36 per cent of minority investors voted against the transaction at the meeting.
It is expected the High Court will be asked by some minority shareholders to order the holding of a separate vote of minority investors. PTSB has repeatedly said it had “very strong” legal advice that only one vote was necessary.

title: Hostile Anfield welcome does little to deter ruthless City
description: Meanwhile, Dara O’Shea rounded off an eventful spell in his life and there was a first-time victor in the Clare senior hurling championship
content:
That was a strange old day at Anfield, Liverpool fans giving a rather heated welcome to the club “found guilty of the biggest systematic cheating scandal in English football history”. After winning 3-0, Manchester City’s players and fans celebrated “ like the crew of a pirate ship, brazenly revelling in their plunder ,” writes Ken Early. ”The days of living a lie are over. Finally City can openly be who they really are.”
Paul O’Hehir rounds up the weekend for the Irish abroad, Dara O’Shea completing a rather eventful spell in his life - captaining Ireland against Israel and then celebrating the birth of his daughter - with an injury time winner for Ipswich against Fulham.
In Gaelic games, there was no fairytale finish for Moycarkey-Borris in Tipperary, Denis Walsh witnessing their first appearance in the county hurling final in 42 years end in defeat by Thurles Sarsfields.
But in Clare, Inagh-Kilnamona secured their first ever hurling title when they got the better of “their nearest and dearest neighbours” Kilmaley, Eoin Brennan in attendance for what proved to be a “cracker”. And Paul Fitzpatrick rounds up the football weekend, among the standout results Clonduff ending a 26-year wait for a Down senior title .
Ahead of Sunday’s Cork county hurling final between St Finbarr’s and Glen Rovers, Denis dusts down a photo from 1978 featuring a legend from each of the clubs and two of the greatest of them all, Jimmy Barry-Murphy and Christy Ring . It is, he says, a powerful reminder of Cork hurling’s lost empire.
In rugby, it was another mixed weekend for the Irish provinces in the URC, all of whom, writes Gerry Thornley in his round-up, looking “decidedly undercooked compared to their French and English opponents”.
Gerry was in the RDS for Leicester’s snazzy/clunky 29-5 win over Cardiff , Leo Cullen just relieved to see his team “up and running” in the competition , while John O’Sullivan saw “a game of two halves” between Ulster and Munster , the former fighting back for a draw after trailing 26-5 at the break. After, there were, need it be said, mixed emotions from the coaches , Richie Murphy and Clayton McMillan. And on Friday, poor discipline against Glasgow proved costly for Connacht.
In motorsport, Hannah Kate Costello reports on more than 10,000 people taking to the streets of Cork city to see local boy Conor Shanahan close in on the Formula Drift title , the two-time champion now just a fortnight away from securing another crown.
And in racing, while Aidan O’Brien has plenty left to do in 2026, “the man who has won and done practically everything else in racing has a fresh Triple Crown project waiting for him in 2027 ”. Brian O’Connor looks at Darkness Falls’ chances of achieving the feat.
TV Watch : There are highlights from the GAA club weekend at 7.30 this evening on TG4, and at 8pm Shamrock Rovers will attempt to stretch their lead over Bohemians, three points behind in the table, when they meet in Tallaght. At the same time, Coventry City host Newcastle in the Premier League (Sky Sports).

title: The brown bat’s ears are three-quarters the length of its head and body combined
description: Your notes and queries for Éanna Ní Lamhna
content:
This little chap was on the floor of my workplace for a day before we concluded that he had gone to meet his maker. What type/species of bat is it ? Leo Ó Seanáin, Droichead Nua
Your excellent photo shows a brown bat whose ears are three-quarters the length of the head and body combined. What great use of the imagination therefore to call this the brown long-eared bat, Plecotus auritus . In fact, in life when the bat is at rest, the ears are tucked under the wings and are less obvious. But your specimen is truly aimsir chaite so the ears are on display in all their glory.
I spotted this strange clear gooey substance hanging from the leaves of a beech tree in a wooded area in Limerick. You can clearly see a ball of what I presume are eggs inside some of them. Can you tell me what it is? Vivienne Kiernan, Limerick
I consulted with the Irish expert on caddisflies, Jim O’Connor, for this one. These are egg masses of the caddisfly Glyphotaelius pellucidus. The caddis is predominantly found in ponds, ditches and slowly flowing streams, especially those that dry up totally or partially over summer. When mature, the jelly liquefies, often activated by rain or dew and has been described – charmingly – as tree snot. The little larvae then drop directly into the water, where they start to make cases for themselves. The larvae eat tree leaves and make very distinctive-looking cases of discs of leaves. The species is very successful and is widely distributed in Ireland and the rest of Europe.
In my local park there is this interesting bonding of two trees, a Scots pine and an ash. Is there a special term for this? Ken Mawhinney, Balally, Co Dublin
The seed of the ash – which is windborne – must have dropped into a cavity in the pine tree where there was decaying wood, which acts like a compost. The two different trees do not graft together. The ash is an epiphyte growing on the pine, but it is not in any way parasitic on it.
I was recently reminded of my country childhood when I met this little fellow as he strolled along the sink outlet pipe in the sun. The roadsides were alive with the whirring and leaping of grasshoppers in my distant youth. I had forgotten just how much I have missed them. Maybe he has taken up residence and will entertain me in the future. Deirdre Concannon, Raheny
This is the field grasshopper, one of five grasshopper species native to Ireland. They mature in June and July, and adults may live until November. Males produce so-called normal songs to attract females, while rival males near to each other take it in turns to produce songs – a rivals duet as it were. If herself responds, then it becomes a courtship song, which is quite elaborate and different from the normal song. But it is getting quite late in the year now for that sort of carry-on.
I saw this false widow tackling a sandhopper – Gammarus – on a wall in Courtmacsherry, Co Cork. It was across the road from the beach – I’m intrigued. Richard Hollinshead
Sandhoppers would be far better off if they stayed in their natural habitat among the dead seaweed on the high tide strand-line on the beach. Other readers have reported that they actually can come indoors into houses beside the sea. The false widow spider is a very successful opportunistic carnivore and will have a go at anything. A juvenile lizard and a baby bat are among its recorded prey.
