title: ‘A slow-moving tsunami’: IMF chief alarmed at AI threat to jobs and taxes
description: Georgieva warns technology risks tilting economy toward capital and away from labour
content:
The head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned of the disruptive threat from artificial intelligence to the labour market and taxation, urging policymakers to rethink education and act now to help society adapt.
“It is a slow-moving tsunami, but [a] tsunami nonetheless,” managing director Kristalina Georgieva said Monday during her first appearance at the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok.
Speaking at a session on artificial intelligence’s (AI’s) impact on employment, she said the technology is already hollowing out demand for many human workers by taking over routine, repetitive tasks. At the same time, it is increasing low-paying jobs in sectors like construction, which she said is “not a story to celebrate”.
It is a transformation with far-reaching consequences for public finances, Georgieva said. The risk is that AI strains government revenues by tilting the economy toward capital and away from labour – traditionally the main source of tax income.
The comments are the latest warning about the potential shock from AI on jobs and the global economy. Young workers in AI-exposed fields have already seen a slowdown in hiring, leaving new entry-level applicants far more vulnerable. Concern is also growing that the technology will widen inequality, with its gains so far concentrated among a narrow set of workers and economies despite a global investment supercycle.
“We cannot today imagine what exactly the world of work will be five years from now,” she said. “But we can be disciplined and carefully assess what is happening, and then draw lessons, but – most importantly – act on them now.”
Despite the employment headwinds, the technology can ultimately prove a positive for growth overall. The IMF estimates the spread of AI can add up to a percentage point to growth in advanced Asian economies.
Such a growth boost “is a very big deal,” Georgieva said, adding it will “more than offset” the drag from ageing in rich countries across the region. – Bloomberg

title: Tech company Tines to create 100 jobs in Ireland over two years and open new facility
description: More than half will be entry-level positions
content:
Irish tech company Tines is to create 100 jobs in Ireland over the next two years, with more than half of the roles earmarked for new entrants to the jobs market.
The new roles will be across its product, engineering, sales, customer success, marketing and operations teams.
The company said more than half the roles would be entry-level, giving graduates and those early on in their careers a way to get a foothold in the AI sector .
“It’s an exciting time for Tines as we build and grow an AI company from Dublin. We believe every employee and every team should be able to use AI to build the software they need, and that’s the opportunity we’re going after with Tines,” said co-founder and CEO Eoin Hinchy.
“These 100 new roles are an important part of scaling our business and supporting customers as they put AI to work across their organisations.”
“As we grow, it’s important that we open the door to talented graduates and early-career professionals to build career pathways in this new space. AI is changing the world of work, but we believe that it will create new and interesting careers, including in companies like ours.”
Tines said the new roles would support the company’s next phase of growth for its Tines 3B platform, which is an artificial intelligence-native platform for building, running and governing enterprise workflows, applications and agents. The platform was launched during the summer.
The company also plans to open a new Dublin headquarters later this year to house the growing team.
[ Cornering the market for machines that make Nvidia’s AI chips Opens in new window ]
The news of the expansion was welcomed by Minister for Enterprise and Employment Peter Burke. “Tines is one of a new generation of rapidly scaling Irish technology companies competing successfully on the global stage,” he said.
“These 100 new jobs demonstrate the strength of opportunity from Ireland’s AI talent and innovation base, while the strong focus on graduates and early-career professionals will create new pathways into a sector that will be increasingly important to our economy.”
Enterprise Ireland chief executive Jenny Melia said the new roles would open career pathways into AI and help build a talent base for Ireland’s next generation of technology companies.
Founded by Hinchy and Thomas Kinsella in 2018, Tines developed a workflow and AI platform to help businesses operate more efficiently and mitigate risks.
Tines Stories, which will continue to be available to customers, connects different software tools and can automate repetitive tasks. It counts companies such as Coinbase, Mars, Reddit and SAP among its clients.
The company has steadily grown in recent years, with its most recent valuation at $1.125 billion (€1 billion), following a Series C round last year.
[ Google fights EU attempt to open Android to rival AI Opens in new window ]
Co-headquartered in Dublin and Boston, it has raised $272 million from investors that include Goldman Sachs, SoftBank, Felicis, Addition, Accel, Blossom Capital and Lux Capital.
Earlier this year, the company announced 100 jobs in the US earlier this year and opened a new hub in Boston, and a formal hub in Sydney.

title: AI being used by employers to more closely monitor their staff, Dublin conference hears
description: Moves are also afoot in some sectors, such as the legal profession, to ‘completely eliminate’ a lot of  entry levels roles and work
content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is being used by employers to more closely monitor their staff to make them more productive, a trade union organised conference in Dublin has heard.
The event was organised by the Communications Workers Union (CWU) in response to what was felt to be a lack of union or civil society voices at this Wednesday’s Government-organised AI Summit in the RDS.
Canadian critic and author Paris Marx told the conference AI technology was often used for surveillance of one type or another on staff, while the quality of work being done by workers was being degraded with consequences for pay.
“What’s happening varies across different sectors,” he said. “We see in graphic design settings and translation settings, it’s not always that people are being actually replaced by AI but often it’s that people who would have done the initial work – and been paid well – are now being relegated to editing an AI-generated piece of translation or image.
“Because they are not the original creator they are being paid a lot less despite the fact that the work can take just as long or longer to do.”
Marx said moves are also afoot in some sectors, such as the legal profession, to “completely eliminate” a lot of entry level roles and work.
He said this was occurring “without much thought for what will happen in 10 to 15 years when the people who would have done that work will be needed to replace more senior lawyers who are retiring”.
“So we need to be concerned not just about the jobs that are being or might be lost but also about the way jobs are changing,” he said.
[ Who’s hiring and who’s firing in Ireland’s technology sector? Opens in new window ]
Commenting on the AI-related findings in the Working In Ireland survey, Demitrios Argyros said the results suggested a majority of people using AI at work felt it resulted in them doing more complex or creative work.
A consequence of this, he said, is they felt the parts of their day when they were doing easier tasks or basic admin had been reduced and so their working day had become more intense, leaving them more drained by their day’s work.
[ AI bubble? Nvidia is now bigger than Japan, but valuation looks modest Opens in new window ]
“They feel they work more and do higher value work but they are not getting more pay or time off so there is a sense the productivity gains are all going to the employer when they could be shared through shorter hours, reduced workloads or investment on worker development,” he said.
The event was also told State agencies here and public bodies were becoming too dependent on a handful of huge American corporations at a time when Donald Trump has suggested he regards their AI and software products as a tool of his foreign policy.
That tech, Abeba Birhane of Trinity College suggested, was built on what even a Microsoft insider had described as a massive theft of other people’s work.
Patrick Bresnihan, of Maynooth University, said the construction resources employed to build data centres in Ireland since 2019 would have been sufficient to provide 50,000 houses.
Ian McArdle, of the CWU, said: “You cannot have a serious conversation about the future of AI and work without the people who do that work.
“The conference was about ensuring workers have a voice in the shaping of the future of AI rather than simply having to live with the consequences.”

title: Pedestrian dies after being hit by car while crossing street in Co Roscommon
description: Woman (70s)  pronounced dead at the scene and gardaí are calling for witnesses
content:
Gardaí are appealing for witnesses to an incident on Sunday in which a pedestrian was killed in Co Roscommon.
The woman in her 70s was struck by a car as she crossed the road at St Patrick’s Street, Castlerea.
She was pronounced dead at the scene and her body was taken to Roscommon University Hospital. The coroner has been notified and a postmortem will be arranged.
The scene has been preserved for technical examination and the road is closed, with diversions in place.
Gardaí are appealing to any witnesses to the crash to contact them.
Any road users who were travelling in the area of St Patrick’s Street, Castlerea, Co Roscommon, between 6.45pm and 7.45pm on Sunday and who may have camera footage, are asked to make it available to investigators
Anyone with information is asked to contact Castlerea Garda station on (094) 9621630, the Garda Confidential Line on 1800 666 111, or any Garda station.

title: Na tubaistí atá ag teacht
description: Deir an rialtas linn gur gá dúinn a bheith ‘ullamh’
content:
Isteach tríd an doras an lá cheana tháinig an ghnáthdhramhaíl. Pizzeria nua tamall uainn a raibh rogha de phiazzana an tsaoil á tairiscint níos saoire ná aon dream eile; fógra go raibh gátar le fuinneoga glónradhúbailte anois teacht an gheimhridh agus na laethanta dul i bhfuaire; tairiscint go bhféadfaí tarramhacadam nó leacracha a chur sa chabhsa gluaisteáin; dream ag moladh grianphainéil toisc go raibh an ola ag dul i ndaoire mar go raibh an Trumpa fós ag ionsaí na hIaráine (bhuel, níor dúradh an chuid deiridh sin); an siopa sceallóg áitiúil ag insint go raibh bia Indiach anois á dhíol acu toisc oiread sin imirceach a bheith timpeall; agus bialann Indiach ag rá go raibh sceallóga anois acu oíche Shathairn toisc ocras a bheith ar an bpobal ag fágaint na bpubanna.
I measc an mhiodamais seo go léir bhí paimfléad beag ón rialtas seo againne. De ghnáth nuair a thagann bileog ó pholaiteoir in aice láimhe is d’fhonn a rá gur éirigh leis nó léi bóthar a dhúnadh nó soilse tráchta a fháil nó gur labhair sa Dáil ar do shon. Ach ní polaiteoir aonair uaigneach a bhí anseo ach paimfléad lándéanta clómhóir ildathach ó Rialtas na hÉireann. Is chuige a bhí ná go bhfuil éigeandáil romhainn agus iad ag gairm amach i litreacha nach bhféadfaí gan a fheiscint go gcaithfimis a bheith ULLAMH.
Mar a tharla, cheapas go raibh éigeandáil cheana againn, éigeandáil tithíochta agus athrú aeráide, ach nuair a scrúdaíos an paimfléad lua ná tagairt ní bhfuaireas d’aon cheann acu. Ina ionad sin, dúradh linn go gcaithfí a bheith réidh le haghaidh éigeandála ar bith a d’fhéadfadh teacht uair ar bith i lár an lae, i gcoim na hoíche, nó tú i do thoirchim suain féin.
Níor ainmníodh na héigeandálaí, ach tugadh le fios go bhféadfadh “stoirmeacha, tuillte, cibir-ionsaithe agus cur isteach ar shlabhraí soláthair criticiúla” a bheith i gceist.
Is fíor go bhfuil stoirmeacha ag gabháil steallaidh orainn go rialta anois agus ainmneacha breátha Éireannacha ar chuid acu chun sinn a chur ar ár suaimhneas – Ailill, Breasal, Cairbre, Dúnlang, Eachmharcach, Fionnghuala, Gormghiolla, Haigha, Ionnrachtach, Jeápurs, Keápars, Leabharcham, Mochaomhóg, Neadar, Ólchobhar, Parthalán, Quárhác, Ríoghbhardán, Slíbhín, Tailefhlaith, Uallgharg, Vinny, Wally, Xaxier, Yobbo, Zozimus, in ord aibítre.
Ina choinne sin, ní súnámaí aon cheann díobh, agus bím féin go faichilleach ag déanamh bolg le gréin ar thrá san iarthar, leathshúil i gcónaí ar oscailt ar eagla go bhfeicfinn tonn tuile ag éirí le fearg amuigh ar íor na spéire agus iad ag téarnamh mar chnoc uisce im dháil. Go deimhin, b’fhada ó bhí súnámaí againn, má bhí riamh. Cuid den eagla nach foláir a ghiniúint?
B’fhéidir, áfach, go raibh sé i gceist gur anuas seachas aniar a thiocfadh an spéirling. Ach an oiread le bheith ag faire na trá, níl oíche dá dtagann ná go mbím ag grinneadh na spéire. Tá a fhios againn go bhfuil ar a laghad aon trilliún réalta eireabaill ag scairdeadh soir siar suas síos fiarthrasna in aon chúinne amháin den chruinne nach bhfuil rófhada uainn, agus go dtiteann siad go léir áit éigin. Níl aon chúis nach dtitfeadh ceann uaigneach amháin den trilliún orainne inár n-oileáinín glas féinig, ná go deimhin isteach ar mo ghairdín cúil. Tagann seo idir mé agus codladh na hoíche go fiú nuair a bhím im dhúiseacht.
Ait go leor, ní luaitear an chontúirt eile is mó ar fad. Cogadh núicléach. Iad gann ar chomhairle d’aon tsaghas maidir leis an mbagairt seo. Faraor, sa chás sin, ní bheadh le déanamh ach cromadh síos, do chloigeann a chur idir do dhá chois, lúbadh siar agus slán a fhágáil ag do phrumpa. Sin uile.
Ná bac le haon chomhairle eile ar do sheicliosta.

title: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war, but Zelenskiy says deal is ‘news to me’
description: Britain and Canada say they would back an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv
content:
Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia , apparently without consulting with Volodymyr Zelenskiy who said the deal to stop long-range attacks was “news to me”.
Despite the announcement, Russian overnight strikes hit multiple Ukrainian power plants, Zelenskiy said.
The Ukrainian president said on social media that a drone had hit a power plant in Kyiv on Sunday night, leading to power outages in the capital. Shortly after, he said there had been a strike on the CHP-5 power plant in the eastern city of Kharkiv, adding:“Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ [drones] all day.”
On Sunday, the United States president claimed in a social media post that the two sides had reached an agreement. “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social.
He offered no further details. Zelenskiy said he was surprised by the announcement, but would agree to it if Vladimir Putin did the same. “If President Trump negotiated it with Putin – please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready and we will accept it,” Zelenskiy told the Axios website.
Both Britain and Canada said they would back an energy ceasefire.
“Russia has intensified its strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure over the weekend,” Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, said on Sunday.
“This is an attack on Ukrainian civilians, plunging them into cold and darkness.
“The UK strongly supports President Trump’s call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now.
“I discussed this with Volodymyr Zelenskiy yesterday: Ukraine is ready if Russia stops its attacks. This is the best route to get energy and fuel back into world markets.”
Separately, reports on Sunday said the US was threatening to stop the procurement system that provided ‌Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep ​strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
Officials in Europe, who received calls from US officials ​or were briefed on them, said the US was lobbying European ⁠capitals and Kyiv to try to end the attacks ‌on ‌Russian ​oil refineries, the Financial Times reported.
The message from the US included threats to cut ‌off intelligence sharing and Purl (the ​Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism for procuring US weapons for Ukraine, ⁠the report said.
“They ⁠are calling ​Kyiv . ... They are calling everyone [in Europe],” said an official who received a call from a US defence official.
Earlier, Ukraine’s president had rebuffed Trump’s demand made on Saturday that Kyiv stop bombing Russian oil refineries. Zelenskiy said that Moscow has to first halt its own “brutal” attacks on his country’s energy infrastructure.
Any deal to end long-range drone strikes by Ukraine on targets inside Russia would have to be “reciprocal”, he said. It should be backed by “real guarantees” – meaning punitive measures against Moscow from Ukraine’s allies, including the US.
This is not the first time Trump has announced an energy ceasefire deal. He made the same claim in September, which turned out to be untrue. Ukrainian officials said Russia was still bombing Ukraine on Sunday, with several energy sites damaged.
The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports . He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.
A furious Zelenskiy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump warned that Zelenskiy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.
Responding to Trump, Zelenskiy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.
The bitter public feud is the most serious between the US and Ukraine since last year, when Trump berated Zelenskiy in the Oval Office .
The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported, some with “business ties” to US negotiators.
On Saturday, Trump berated Zelenskiy and said he had refused to make a deal to end the fighting. In response, Ukraine’s president laid the blame for Europe’s biggest war since 1945 on “Russia and Russia alone”. “It is possible to stop strikes on energy infrastructure as early as today, but Putin does not want to do so,” he said.
Ukrainian officials point out that the White House is demanding Kyiv give up its most effective weapon, without demanding any corresponding concessions from Russia. In recent weeks, Kyiv has dealt a major blow to the Kremlin’s economy, striking oil complexes, warehouses and data centres.
Russia’s own bombing campaign has been relentless. Zelenskiy said Moscow’s aerial campaign involved thousands of aerial bombs and jet-powered drones. It continued “unabated”, he said.
Russian attacks killed ‌six people in two Ukrainian cities ​on Sunday, including a strike on a ​grocery store in Kharkiv, Ukraine’s ⁠second-largest city, where three people ‌died ‌and ​20 were injured, officials ⁠said. Regional ​governor Oleh ​Syniehubov said two children ​were among the injured.
In a separate ‌attack in ⁠western Ukraine, officials said a Russian strike ‌killed three people.
The head of Ukraine’s foreign affairs committee, Oleksandr Merezhko, said Trump’s “bullying” demand for Zelenskiy to quit had strengthened him at home “paradoxically”, after recent damaging corruption scandals. “Putin’s plan is to decapitate Zelenskiy and remove him as a wartime leader. Trump is siding with Putin,” Merezhko said.
“I’m afraid that behind this situation is Trump’s worldview. He wants to do business with Putin. For him, Ukraine seems like an obstacle to be removed. Both Trump and Putin wish to pressure us into capitulation.”
Referring to the notorious 1939 agreement between Nazi Germany and the USSR, Merezhko said: “We are moving to a new Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and to a world of strongmen and spheres of influence.”
Merezhko said Ukraine would continue to destroy enemy oil refineries, against US wishes, because these funded Russia’s war machine and he acknowledged that a cut-off of US intelligence sharing with Kyiv – threatened by the Trump administration – would “blind” Ukraine’s air defence systems. “This would be an act of complicity with Putin’s genocide. It would mean more dead civilians and dead children,” he said.
Ukrainian negotiators had been meeting in Florida with their US counterparts, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, when Trump announced the US was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel. Blindsided, the Ukrainians went home early. “It felt like a trap,” one Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent newspaper. – The Guardian, Reuters and Press Association

title: Emerging Democrat star Jon Ossoff has become a chief thorn in Trump’s side
description: Georgia senator verbally pummeled his ‘bigot’ Republican rival in recent debate and has become a chief thorn in Trump’s side ahead of midterms
content:
C onsigned to drift through the afterlife of boxing notoriety, former heavyweight champion Mike Tyson showed up at a Donald Trump rally in Syracuse, New York, on Friday offering a bashful wave and meaningless praise in his familiar soft lisp.
“There’s no way in the world I would ever be here if it wasn’t for a president like Donald Trump,” Tyson said.
“Ah, I watched him get in the ring so many times. He was a scary guy,” Trump said, watching as Iron Mike left the stage with his pit-pull steps.
The pair are both New Yorkers and go back decades, with Trump promoting several of the heavyweight’s prize fights in the decade when he dominated the boxing scene, prior to Tyson’s rape conviction in 1992. Who knows how closely Tyson follows the US political scene but if he caught any of the midterm Senate debates that aired during the week, one brawl would have caught his eye.
The toss-up states of Michigan, Georgia and Texas have been defined by personality-driven contests that are openly hostile and filled with barbed accusation.
But it was the relentless and almost cruel verbal pummelling of Republican candidate Mike Collins by Georgia senator Jon Ossoff that delivered a series of swift, pulverising blows that Tyson might have recognised. For over 40 minutes, Ossoff stood beside his opponent on the stage and repeatedly called him a “bigot” before delivering an argument that was so deliberately paced and sustained that it almost became uncomfortable.
“Georgia has voter ID and that’s good. Mike Collins and Donald Trump? They’re still obsessed with turning over the 2020 election. Mike Collins still believes the 2020 election was stolen. Mike Collins has supported Donald Trump’s effort to overturn the election and he wants to give your tax dollars to the violent thugs and criminals who sacked the US Capitol on January 6th.
“Mike Collins is attacking your voting rights. But that’s not a surprise when you consider who Mike Collins is. This is a man who cheered on a group of young men who were mocking a black woman on a college campus with monkey sounds. If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club.”
The boxing ring would have at least held the mercy of a white towel. Given Georgia’s complex racial history – cradle of the civil rights movement, as Ossoff contended, yes- but also birthplace, at Stone Mountain, of the 20th-century iteration of the Ku Klux Klan, there was something shocking about the charge.
It was the latest in Ossoff’s knack for delivering a succinct, quotable line that has seen him move, over the course of four months, from the periphery to the forefront of predictions on Democratic presidential candidates.
A day after the debate, it was announced that Trump would visit Georgia at least twice before the November 3rd midterm elections to campaign for the flailing Collins campaign. While other Republican aspirants – including Georgia gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson – are campaigning without mentioning the president’s name, Mike Collins is tethered to Trump.
If Collins is to flip the seat that Ossoff holds – a seat essential to Democrats’ ambitions to take control of the Senate – then it will be as an ever-Trumper. In a television interview he gave hours after Wednesday night’s debate, Ossoff said that Collins championing Trump was predictable.
“No, I wasn’t surprised because bless his heart, Mike doesn’t have too much of a mind of his own,” he told Jen Psaki.
“He’s been doing the president’s bidding thoughtlessly now for a year and a half,” Ossoff said, before sliding into campaign mode, reminding viewers of high prices, spiralling healthcare costs, coffee up 30 per cent, ground beef up 30 per cent.
In mid-September, a Quantus Insights poll had Ossoff leading Collins by four points. This week, a series of polls has the Democrat opening up anything from an eight- to 11-point lead. It was reported that the Republicans had begun to reduce their television advertisement bookings within the state. Ossoff has amassed a formidable campaign war chest, with some $40 million available from a total campaign fund of twice that.
Trump’s appearance in Georgia, along with his renewed pledge for $5,000 for every American voter should the Republicans hold the balance of power, will reposition the Senate race as a de facto vote between the president himself and the emergent prosecutorial star of the Democratic Party .
Georgia is the state that will torment Trump after he leaves office. Although he defeated Kamala Harris there two years ago, he continues to brood over the 2020 election loss to Joe Biden by fewer than 12,000 votes, leading to his infamous phone call to Georgia’s secretary of state demanding that he “find” votes.
Now Ossoff, considered a vulnerable re-election prospect when Trump returned to office on a wave of Maga ebullience in January 2025, has emerged as a chief thorn in his side, merciless not only in his coursing of his opponent in the Senate race, but also of Trump himself.
In flightier moments, Ossoff has drawn comparison to the late JFK – mainly for his youth and preppy-conservative wardrobe. If he possesses, within his performative repertoire, his version of Kennedy’s regal sunniness or Obama’s folksy turns, the Georgia senator is keeping it under wraps.
For the moment, Ossoff’s message has been delivered with a steely, sombre gravity to reflect the prevailing mood. He is presenting himself as an antidote to what he would present as the frivolity and unseriousness of the Trump administration.
Having finished with his immediate opponent in the debate, he offered equally sharp appraisals of leading figures within Trump’s administration. On Pete Hegseth’s announcement that the execution of Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people in a 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, would be publicly livestreamed, Ossoff said: “I think Pete Hegseth is, frankly, a deeply unwell person who seems to relish this kind of brutality. All the while he is running a department that is falling into chaos. The guy cannot run the United States military competently and is spending his time on this obscene medieval spectacle.”
Critiquing a recent address by Marco Rubio in Athens, he described it as an attempt “to try and soft launch his presidential campaign”.
“These people are not focused. JD Vance and Marco Rubio are already looking past Donald Trump, jockeying for position in the future Republican primary while the administration’s obscene policies failures have made the world and our country less safe and are immiserating [sic] the American public in a cost-of-living crisis.”
Ossoff dismissed the idea of running in the 2028 election back in April but his profile has begun to fill the political sky since then. If the polling numbers alchemise into a comprehensive victory, then the speculation about his future will intensify.
For now, he remains locked into a riveting and ugly regional election framed not just by the prevailing cost-of-living issues but the spectres of race and white supremacy. This week’s debate was preceded by a report in The Daily Beast, amplified by Ossoff, that two of Collins’s campaign leaders have ties to American Patriots USA, founded by Chester Doles, a former Ku Klux Klan leader.
It’s an unpromising scenario for Trump as he prepares to visit the Peach State.
“I think the last thing that Georgia Republicans want right now is for Donald Trump to come to Georgia,” Ossoff said of that visit. “If he wants to come to Georgia, that’s fine with me.”
Early voting begins in Georgia on Tuesday.

title: Trump’s energy ceasefire is unfair to Ukraine but could it bring something better?
description: A comprehensive energy ceasefire beyond oil refineries could perhaps follow and open the way to a full ceasefire before winter
content:
The energy ceasefire Donald Trump announced between Russia and Ukraine is heavily lopsided in Moscow’s favour and robs Kyiv of one of its most effective tactical measures. But it could be a step towards something better.
When Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskiy was asked on Sunday about Donald Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, he said it was “news to me”.
After speaking with Nato secretary general Mark Rutte, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney and Finnish president Alexander Stubb, Zelenskiy voiced support for the proposal.
[ Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war, Zelenskiy says deal is ‘news to me’ Opens in new window ]
“Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side,” he said.
Kyiv would support a ceasefire that halts attacks on all energy infrastructure, including the energy grid but Trump’s initiative is limited to both sides agreeing to stop attacking each other’s oil refineries. Ukraine has just one refinery, which has been hit numerous times, while Russia has 38, of which 21 have been targets for Ukrainian drone strikes.
Kyiv’s long-range strikes on Russian refineries have been among its most successful operations during the war, disabling up to 30 per cent of Russian refining capacity according to independent analysts. The strikes have led to fuel shortages in Russia and Vladimir Putin acknowledged this month that they had cost the country 1 per cent of its annual gross domestic product.
Trump last Friday trumpeted an agreement with Putin for the immediate release of 300,000 tons of Russian diesel, with a further 500,000 next month and one million tons in December. Trump hopes that the move will lower the price of the fuel, which has doubled since last year because of his war against Iran and has become a burden for Republican candidates facing midterm elections three weeks from tomorrow.
The day after he made the diesel deal, Trump told Zelenskiy to stop attacking Russian refineries, adding that Ukraine needed a new president. But while Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were meeting Ukrainian negotiators in Miami, Russia reported another strike on one of its oil terminals in Rostov-on-Don.
During the Miami meeting, which also included national security advisers from Germany, France and Britain and representatives from Nato and the European Union, the Americans reminded Ukraine that the US shares the intelligence that facilitates its drone targeting, according to Axios. And the Financial Times reports today that the US threatened to halt the sale to Nato of weapons for Ukraine if Kyiv did not stop attacking Russian refineries.
Witkoff and Kushner were due to fly to Moscow after the Miami meeting but they postponed the trip while they waited to see if Ukraine and the Europeans could get behind a new, unified proposal to put to Putin. This could see the halt on refinery attacks extended to all energy infrastructure, a step that would ease some of the suffering of Ukrainians as they face into winter with their electricity grid already depleted by Russian attacks.
Russia’s attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities and Ukraine’s long-range strikes inside Russia cannot move the line of contact on the battlefield, something that would require the kind of mobilisation of manpower neither side is planning. The kinetic phase of this war may be now entering its final weeks and the primary function of the drone and missile strikes is to gain advantage in the negotiations that will follow.
Trump’s unfair, unilateral and brutally imposed halt to strikes on refineries may be the first step, with a comprehensive energy ceasefire the necessary next move. That could open the way towards a full ceasefire before winter sets in, leaving Ukraine and Russia far from a negotiated peace but sparing the lives of many of their people.
