title: The cost of social awkwardness and Ireland’s AI funding boom
description: Business Today: The best news, analysis and comment from The Irish Times business desk
content:
What is the cost of social awkwardness ? Around €600 million each year, according to new research from AIB. Conor Pope reports that Irish consumers are losing €150 on average to a “politeness premium” which sees them overpay on shared bills and fail to collect personal debts.
Meanwhile, new research from Pitchbook, the global private capital markets intelligence firm, found that Irish artificial intelligence (AI) companies have raised an additional €256 million across 75 deals so far this year. Deal volumes and values are down from last year; however, this appears to be a case of “normalisation”, with median deal values still well ahead of historic levels.
On a related topic, researchers have uncovered a worrying trend around the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in hiring processes. It appears that AI agents have a bias towards CVs and cover letters that seem to be written using generative AI. That is disturbing news at a time when AI is already driving a dismal hiring arms race, writes Pilita Clark in her latest column.
A deal last week between EU governments on long-stalled capital markets reforms was anything but certain. Jack Power takes us inside the last-minute negotiations that finally got the agreement over the line.
Where Budget 2027 is faulty is the reversal of the policy on tackling climate change , argues economist John FitzGerald in his latest column. It sends all the wrong signals, and it also means there will be significantly fewer resources to protect those who are energy poor and to fund important climate investment, including flood protection . The proposals would shift more responsibility for regulating the architecture that makes the financial markets tick from national central banks and authorities to a European regulator.
Ireland does not need a completely new economic model , argues Paraic Burke, head of tax at PwC Ireland in this week’s opinion piece. However, we’ve reached a point where what set us apart feels less different, and we need to future-proof our economy.
If you’d like to read more about the issues that affect your finances, try signing up to On the Money , the weekly newsletter from our personal finance team, which will be issued every Friday to Irish Times subscribers.

title: ‘I find it obscene’: Aer Lingus response upsets family dealing with terminal illness
description: Couple in their 80s booked flights to Algarve before cancer diagnosis, daughter writes
content:
F ar too many people reading this will know how hard it is when a family member receives a terminal diagnosis . At the very least we should expect that the companies we have to deal with in the wake of such a diagnosis will be compassionate and supportive. We would certainly expect them not to make things hard. A reader’s recent experience would suggest that, at least on this occasion, Aer Lingus have been found wanting.
“My parents are in their 80s and up until this spring were both fit and healthy,” begins the mail from a reader we shall call Jane – although that is not her real name. “They had travel insurance in place, as an add-on to their home insurance policy, until this March, when the insurance company withdrew it,” she says.
The couple planned to travel to the Algarve in April to spend a month at a friend’s apartment, something they did every year for a long time. They booked their flights almost exactly one year ago and paid a total of €450, Jane explains.
Just a week before their trip, her mother was diagnosed with an aggressive form of cancer and was unable to travel as her treatment had to start immediately. Four days before the scheduled departure date, the family submitted a claim to Aer Lingus, including a letter from the consultant.
“The letter was on hospital headed paper, handwritten and included the consultant’s registration etc. Aer Lingus responded the same day confirming a voucher would be offered subject to provision of supporting information (which we had already submitted). Unfortunately in the turmoil we missed the email – we had submitted from my mother’s email address, which was no longer being monitored,” Jane continues.
[ Paula was ‘disappointed with Ireland’s premier airline’ but Aer Lingus followed the rules Opens in new window ]
The family called Aer Lingus and it “kindly agreed to reopen the case [but], following resubmission, demanded that the consultant’s letter be typewritten. As reluctant as we were to disturb the busy public consultant for a second letter, we did so, and it was duly issued, however this time with the date of dictation rather than the original date,” she says.
The new date on the new letter was past the travel date.
“We were then refused a refund or voucher, with reference to the date of the letter being after the date of travel and on the basis that the people on the booking were not the same people referenced in the medical certificate. However, when we replied, we got an auto response to say the case had been closed.”
So the family called Aer Lingus and explained the situation and again it was confirmed that the case would be reopened “and an email would be sent. We didn’t receive an email, so I called again and I was told the only option was to make an online complaint to customer service.”
Jane says that at this point Aer Lingus clarified that there was an issue with her mother’s name. “My mother is typical of her generation, her passport shows her given name whereas her medical information shows the name she is known by. Despite being instructed to follow the customer service link online, I was unable to submit anything as the original booking reference number no longer worked. I had to call again – each call involving lengthy wait periods and explaining the whole thing from scratch each time.”
[ A ‘cold, spreadsheet-driven’ Aer Lingus response to a young woman’s ‘freak accident’ Opens in new window ]
She says she was “eventually” given an email address and resubmitted the entire set of details including the two letters from the consultant – the handwritten one which was dated prior to travel and the typed version that had a later date. There was also a copy of her mother’s passport, and confirmation that she is one and the same person.
“I can’t fathom how much time was spent trying to sort this out and while I realise Aer Lingus is not under strict obligation to refund, they had agreed to do it on the first contact. I would have preferred to spend all that time looking after my mother and father, who are going through a terrible time. She is very ill. So it was the worst kind of sickening response to get Aer Lingus’ newest request: that I provide proof that my mother’s diagnosis is terminal. They even felt it worth writing this in bold,” she points out.
She includes the quote from the airline which reads: “A doctor’s letter confirming you are unfit to travel again for the foreseeable future due to a terminal diagnosis .”
Jane tells us that it is “difficult to convey why this is so upsetting – money aside, just how callous Aer Lingus is to ask us to go to her doctors and ask for this. It seems that they have come up with a series of new reasons at every turn and I find it obscene that they have stooped this low. I replied to ask whether this new requirement was just because I had indicated that a refund if possible would be preferable over a voucher, as I didn’t see a scenario where she would be able to travel again in the future, but I haven’t had an answer since September 18th.”
She contacted Pricewatch in the “hope you can share the type of ‘customer care’ we have received from Aer Lingus with your readers,” she concludes.
We contacted the airline and a spokeswoman said Aer Lingus “recognises the difficulties experienced by our customer in this case and is sincerely sorry that these circumstances arose during an already challenging time”.
She said the “documentation requirements for such requests are to ensure that refund applications can be assessed fairly and consistently. While we understand that obtaining documentation from medical professionals can sometimes be difficult, particularly during periods of illness, these documents are required so that our teams can assess requests.”
She added that “having reviewed the circumstances of this case, we will provide a full refund. We sincerely regret the upset and frustration caused and extend our best wishes to our customer and their family during this difficult time.”

title: Rachel O'Dwyer: Will generation rent follow the Government’s advice and invest?
description: If the SSIA citizen believed hard work and savings brought security, most young people today probably don’t
content:
I recently came across a post by a money influencer Ann-Marie Gaynor, who goes by @Irishbudgetingmammy on Instagram. Against a typical hectic morning scene where a mother feeds one child while line managing another, a curling pink script reads “62 per cent of Irish women aged 30 to 50 handle the family finances alone. Only 18 per cent of women are investing.”
I thought of this figure when details of Simon Harris ’s new personal investment account (PIA) were floated in February – and subsequently announced again and again in the run up to Budget 2027 . Now we finally have the details. The Government scheme aims to encourage citizens to invest their savings. Many of us are excellent savers, it turns out; there is currently nearly €175 billion sitting idle in deposits.
We’re less confident when it comes to navigating the market: as things stand, just 2.3 per cent of Irish households’ financial assets are held in shares, bonds and other securities.
The new scheme will allow citizens to invest idle wealth in listed shares, bonds, ETFs and other retail funds ( cryptocurrencies and derivatives will not be included). There will be no minimum contribution or lock-in period, but deposits will be capped at €12,000 annually. The accounts will have a tax-free threshold of €50,000. Above that, the Government plans to apply a flat annual charge of 1 per cent based on the value of the account, rather than taxing each capital gain or dividend separately. The accounts are due to launch on July 1st, 2027.
As another financial behavioural incentive, the obvious parallel is with the Special Savings Incentive Accounts (SSIA) , launched by the then-government in 2001. Some 1.1 million Irish people took part in the scheme, which saw the government add 25c to every euro saved, up to a maximum of €254 a month. The stated aim at the time was to divert Irish citizens away from spending and to foster good savings habits. Another ambition was to curb inflation, taking billions temporarily out of circulation during the height of the Celtic Tiger.
In 2001, saving was framed as desirable and financially prudent. Today, it’s seen as financially passive – even unwise. What does it say about an economy when the State first pays its citizens to save and then, 25 years later, tries to persuade them to stop saving so much, and to invest in a product in which, as several commentators have pointed out, they stand to have to pay tax even in years when they have lost money ?
Maybe what has changed is the emphasis we now place on financial investment as opposed to time and graft when it comes to building wealth. In the 25 years between the ideal saver and the ideal investor, two generations have come of age through a financial crash, a pandemic and increasingly shaky assumptions about work, housing and upward mobility.
If the SSIA citizen believed that hard work and savings brought security, most young people today probably do not. They might still go to college and save for a house and act as if that system still works, but there’s a covert sense that this is no longer enough.
Financial security now also calls for a degree of speculation – hence the global popularity of retail trading among gen Z. Irish people may be incredible savers by international standards, but it’s likely that a younger generation will also need to be incredible speculators, willing to wager on an uncertain future. A survey carried out in June by Royal London Ireland found 50 per cent of 18– to 34-year-olds said they would “definitely” invest, in comparison to a more cautious 17 per cent of 45– to 54-year-olds.
[ Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work Opens in new window ]
And where will the younger investors be getting their advice?
If you take to social media and type in “money” or “financial advice”, you’ll find millions of posts on building passive income, smart investment and how to put your money to work. There’s “@herfirst100k” (Tori Dunlap), who introduces her followers to building a retirement fund, or Delyanne Barros (@delyannethemoneycoach), who argues that strategic investment and not simply hard work is now required to build wealth.
“Minorities have always known the system was rigged,” Barros writes. “Now that the majority [sees] that the American dream is a fantasy, we’re starting to see the bootstrap mentality ... crumble.”
Irish financial influencers such as Gaynor, by contrast, have tended to focus more on tried and tested principles including budgeting, cash stuffing and meal prep than markets and retail investment. But maybe that’s beginning to change. “Investment is a different psychology,“ Gaynor tells me. Her followers are predominantly in the 30-50 age bracket, so they “still remember the crash. They like to put €100 in the bank and see it there the next day. But the new government accounts might make investment simpler and safer for the average citizen when it comes to different products and negotiating our tax system.”
Much of the narrative around the new investment accounts has glossed over the fact that citizens are now being encouraged to expose themselves to risk in order to build security for the future
The new scheme is coupled with a financial literacy campaign led by the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission . A website walks consumers through topics such as shares and bonds and the role of inflation. A “get started” quiz asks potential investors whether they can live comfortably within their means, are debt-free, have at least a three-month buffer, a pension plan and what some retail traders might call “diamond hands”, and also calls for comfort with risk and asset fluctuation.
Investment can be empowering. Barros is not wrong when she says that interest, not hard work, are what drive real gains in today’s economy. Greater literacy could empower everyday citizens to take control of their money and make better choices.
But the new claim that everyone can grow their wealth through investment replaces bootstrapping with another fairytale. There are risks involved in any investment, and that’s particularly true for younger and novice investors.
“What happens if 100,000 people go into this and the markets collapse and they lose money? There’s going to be pressure on the Government to bail them out,” Peter Brown, managing director of Baggot Investment Partners, said on RTÉ Radio last week.
[ Ireland’s new personal investment scheme: ‘What happens if I put €10,000 straight in?’ Opens in new window ]
Much of the narrative around the new investment accounts has glossed over the fact that citizens are now being encouraged to expose themselves to risk in order to build security for the future. One unusual feature of the PIA, when the aim is to empower risk-averse investors, is that tax will be charged, not only on profits, but on the average value of the investment account over the €50,000 threshold – meaning that account holders could pay tax on their savings in some years, even while making a loss on their principal. And not everyone can hedge their bets. Not everyone has the same capital, time or cushion if the wager goes wrong.
Dr Rachel O’Dwyer is a lecturer in digital cultures in the School of Visual Culture at NCAD

title: Una Mullally: No, you don’t need AI to read your child a bedtime story
description: Sam Altman’s self-satisfaction about utilising an LLM to raise his child wouldn’t even make the top 20 of his all-time nonsense
content:
I have spent too many hours this week thinking about a single tweet, but some things stay with you. It was posted by a man called Alvin Sng who works in a San Francisco AI company: “My wife: Can you read our baby a book? Me: I can just play an audiobook from my phone. My wife: But then it won’t be in your voice. Me: I can train a voice model. Parenting hits different when you work in AI.”
He later deleted the tweet and claimed he was joking. But the reason it attracted a backlash was because it seemed almost too perfect an illustration of the detachment from the human experience that only those honed by the weirdness of Silicon Valley and the hubris of San Francisco could ever think clever. Or too perfect a satire.
He might have been joking, but parenting does seemingly hit different when you work in AI. Last year, OpenAI boss Sam Altman appeared on an American chatshow. “I cannot imagine having gone through figuring out how to raise a newborn without ChatGPT ,” he said.
On to the Mount Rushmore of AI spoofers and grifters shall Altman’s face one day be carved. Or for expediency’s sake, 3D printed. He is a man famous for telling people what they want to hear, a trait catalogued in Karen Hao’s book, Empire of AI . His self-satisfaction about utilising an LLM to raise his child wouldn’t even make the top 20 of his all-time nonsense.
Here’s one of my favourites: “Number one: We are close to creating a genie that can grant any wish. Number two: we are going to make sure that our first wishes broadly benefit humanity, and that we kinda get the world to a place where a lot more people have a lot more wishes,” Altman said with a straight face on a podcast earlier this year. If you said that deep in the grips of an acid trip at 5am at a music festival you would be gently escorted back to your tent by the medical staff.
“We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology,” he said on a Politico podcast last week. How about: no?
That there are many people out there who don’t want to think for themselves is not a revelation. That there are those who believe AI as a replacement for thinking is cool is nothing new either. That there are billionaires pushing AI as though it’s a drug – these people who have sweeping powers over how we live our lives, who influence policy, whose technology keeps doing dodgy things it should not do , and who are narrating their glorious missions while sounding like utter lunatics – is, however, of considerable concern.
The harvest of such attitudes does not merely reap small beans. Of course, there’s the money at stake; the venture capital funds and banks and lenders and debt ploughed into AI companies – a growing black hole at the heart of the US economy so deep that it could eventually necessitate the bailout to end all bailouts. There are the hyperscale data centres juicing every electricity grid to the max, sucking up drinking water and burning diesel and gas to power the apparently infinite mission of AI for everything (whether people want it or not).
[ Legal risks pile up for Altman as OpenAI uncovers dozens of hacks Opens in new window ]
But the frenzy to offload human connection and thought to machines is bigger than even those things. It’s existential. It’s about not understanding the beauty of attention as a form of care – even though so many tech people work within the attention economy. It’s a mindset that views human interaction as an unnecessary friction that needs to be smoothed over. It invents engineering “solutions” to “problems” that don’t exist and internalises the neoliberalist message of outsource everything. It is this: how can I replace me? And then high-fiving oneself when that has been achieved.
This worldview promotes misguided concepts around efficiency and strives to “invent” hacks and workarounds, while actually adding more steps to a basic gesture. You cannot just sleep; you must track it. You cannot experience a moment; you must document it. You cannot do the work to create, you must offload such a process to a “tool”. This is framed as efficiency, this shedding of all the pesky and awkward states of what it is to be a person with a mind. What you’re left with is not AI becoming human, it’s humans becoming AI.
[ ChatGPT maker OpenAI scraps release of new AI model over safety concerns Opens in new window ]
This tech mindset around “efficiency” is also coming for democracy, as analysed in Gil Durán’s book, The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy . The two trends reinforce each other. Frankly weird tech overlords, prancing along a spectrum from libertarianism to techno-feudalism to outright tech-fascism, champion tech that offers the masses a workaround for thinking, connecting and interacting. If the collective capacity for critical thinking is diminished, how much easier would it be for the anti-democratic goals of, say, Peter Thiel to be achieved?
It is not enough to brush off an aversion to the messy joy of the human experience as brainless and depressing. Stupidity is dangerous, sure. But there exists something more perilous: stupidity that considers itself smart.

title: How music, or silence, can help with bereavement, dementia and pain
description: New book shares personal stories of how music helps in circumstances ranging from imprisonment and bereavement to coping with dementia or chronic pain
content:
In the year since my husband died, I have stopped listening to music at home. Not just “his” music or “our” music but “my” music too.
Silence has, de facto, become the sound of choice.
It was not a conscious decision and something I only started to recognise and question when a new book came across my desk. Avoidance of his beloved film scores and 1960s classics is understandable. However, why also the choral music that I had thrived on long before I met him, and had since loved to play in the kitchen on my own, even if it induced eye rolls in every other member of the family?
The book that prompted me to reflect is The Role of Music in Health and Wellbeing Journeys (Routledge), an Irish-edited, academic publication that includes a collection of first-person stories exploring the transformative role of music in people’s lives. It was the idea of Prof Hilary Moss, professor of music therapy at the University of Limerick .
“It was trying to turn on its head the idea that as music therapists, or any clinicians really, all the textbooks are written about what we should do for people and how we can help them. Very few people are asking the person: ‘Well, how do you use music for your health and wellbeing?’ It might be completely different to what we’re expecting.”
She invited PhD colleague Katie Fitzpatrick to collaborate, who in turn suggested they also needed a therapy participant on the editing team, as it was about professionals taking a step back to listen to individual stories, before adding commentary. Patricia O’Shea, a member of Chronic Pain Ireland, became the third editor of a publication that includes the work of nearly 20 authors, not just from Ireland but also countries including the UK, Finland, the US, Canada and Australia.
It offers glimpses of the power of music to communicate, to comfort, to motivate, in circumstances ranging from imprisonment and bereavement, to coping with dementia or chronic pain, and at end of life. Yet, several of those struggling with emotional turmoil talk of initially retreating into silence, before beginning to find a way out through music.
It is different for everyone but maybe there is psychological safety in quietness; it is easier to keep thoughts under linear control. Put on some meaningful music and who knows what emotions might bubble up and where they might go? Harnessing this potential for a positive impact is what music therapists are trained to do. To ensure benefit, it’s about “the right music at the right time and the right place”, as the editors explain at the outset of the book. That is what needs to be figured out, on a case-by-case basis.
“A lot of the work I’m doing at the moment is around how music might cause psychological harm or distress because nobody’s been asking that question,” Moss tells The Irish Times. “Everybody thinks it’s good.”
During 30 years of working in arts in healthcare, she has seen a “do-goody” tendency among some people. For instance, during a professional stint in a Dublin hospital, she observed “the amount of choirs that wanted to come in and sing Christmas music … and they didn’t want to come in January”.
Well-meaning musicians might want to spread good cheer but it is not always appropriate. “Sometimes people don’t want to listen to music, so it’s the wrong time. If they’re recovering and they’re in pain, they don’t necessarily want a banjo at the end of the bed. But they might …”
She recalls working at that hospital with members of the Irish Chamber Orchestra. One man, who had a stroke and thought he would never be able to get to a concert hall again, was uplifted by being able to hear playing of that calibre live from his hospital bed.
“You give someone a moment of hope,” she says. To be effective, does it need to be pieces or a genre of music with which an individual is familiar?
“Most of the research is that your preferred music is the music to use and that will be most beneficial. But we would improvise with people, making music that neither of us has heard before. Sometimes the arts challenge us to think differently about life.”
Songwriting, singing and participative improvisation are common techniques. Fellow editor O’Shea wrote a joint paper about her own music therapy, in which she talked about creating cacophony to sum up her pain, says Moss.
Quite apart from engaging in therapy, there is scope for everyone, she agrees, to use music more purposefully for health and wellbeing.
“I would work with people with dementia and I’d often be saying to relatives, ‘make a playlist of songs’. We would call it a life review, but it’s basically putting together songs that are significant to the person and having that playlist available for them. That’s a simple thing that anybody could do.”
Therapists work with playlists, as a way of motivation, say, for somebody with chronic pain. It moves them out of particular feelings, she explains, as the pain is so grinding and frustrating.
Anna Bertha Dakudzi, who came to Ireland from Ghana many years ago, was left in serious pain after a car crash. After some negative experiences within the medical system, when at times she felt she was not being believed and multiple medications had made her drowsy, she was referred for music therapy.
“It was a godsend to me during a tough time,” Dakudzi writes in the book. “I have really come to a good place through it. I love music. I love gospel music. It helps me to forget pain and release stress.”
When using music therapy in palliative care, there may be no obvious treatment path, says Moss, but it’s about enhancing quality of life. She becomes very frustrated when she sees nursing homes that don’t offer residents quality recreational activities.
[ Changing the world of organ transplants while fearing he could die waiting for one Opens in new window ]
Even with extreme brain injury, there can still be reactions to music, she says, praising the very specialised work of music therapists at the National Rehabilitation Hospital in Dublin. “There’s a validated tool for assessment, which the team use, and it’s music based because somebody might turn to the sound and that tells them they have some recognition when other things aren’t happening.”
Moss recommends that everybody should think about how music can help their health and wellbeing. “How they could use it to supplement what’s happening for themselves; it’s not going to be a cure. How it can help their mood or help them get motivated.
“Just noticing how they use music in their lives and maybe doing it more intentionally. For some people it’s putting background music on all the time because they feel anxious if they don’t have it on.”
Participation in music can be beneficial for patient and carer alike in the case of chronic illness such as Parkinson’s and dementia, as reflected in choirs formed for this purpose.
“I worked with a man in hospital, and his wife would visit every day and do things like brushing his hair. He couldn’t talk at all, and he was quite disruptive. Then he started singing with us in a group, and she was able to just come and sit with him and hold his hand and sing songs,” says Moss. “It changes the way you can have some time together.”
[ My husband has been cold and distant since I told him about my Alzheimer’s worries Opens in new window ]
She would encourage family members to consider whether music or music therapy is available for a person they might be caring for at home and, if not, to question that.
“We desperately need to recognise the importance of music in child and adolescent mental health and for people with dementia. In German care homes, there is a music therapist in every facility and this is a requirement under care quality indicators there.”
Moss also invites readers to email her ( hilary.moss@ul.ie ) if they have any experience of using music as part of their own health and wellbeing. Meanwhile, I for one am taking tentative steps back to Bach, Handel and Fauré …
A young male prisoner, “Southsider#1”, discovered the power of songwriting at the age of 21, after years of improvising rap lyrics in his head.
“It was the first time I felt I was able to talk about things that I didn’t speak about. The unspoken words were suddenly right there on the page in front of me,” he writes in The Role of Music in Health and Wellbeing Journeys. “I haven’t stopped since.”
But “when I came to prison, I lost everything. I had to leave my life, my family and my music behind.” It was a place he had never expected to be and found it hard to adjust. “All I wanted to do was write. I had things I needed to say and I knew that songwriting would give me a chance to speak, even if the words were never heard.”
[ How psychoeducation can help with depression, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia Opens in new window ]
He grabbed that opportunity when he discovered the music class in the prison’s education unit. A group there was playing a song they had been working on in previous classes but there were still a few empty bars.
“I was immediately inspired and wrote a few bars in response,” he says. “I remember their reaction to my lyrics, the energy in the room, and the sense of achievement I felt. The encouragement and validation that came from my peers was unmatched and immediately built my confidence.”
He started to attend music class three times a week, has achieved a QQI certification (the equivalent of Junior Cert) in it, has learned to play basic chords and scales on guitar and piano and understands enough now about music technology to produce his own songs. He hopes to work towards completing a university degree in music.
“For me, songwriting allows me to escape. I am not thinking when I am writing; it allows me to get everything off my chest. I write about love and relationships, people I am missing, and the pain I am feeling … I write to remember the good times that will never be again, how I can’t change what’s been done, and I write to say sorry.” He also uses songwriting to protect himself from deeper thoughts.
“It distracts me from my sentence; it gives me a focus and a purpose … I do wonder had I gotten into music earlier, if I would be sitting here today. I can get through my hardest days with music: just give me a pen, paper, and a beat.”

title: My son has become disinterested in school. The principal regularly uses the phrase ‘parental responsibility’
description: As a single mum, it’s not easy trying to control a 15-year-old boy who seems to have lost all interest in his school life
content:
My son has become very disinterested in school. I have had numerous interactions with his year head, who has invested huge time and effort to get him to conform to expected behaviour. The phrase “parental responsibility” is regularly used in my interactions with the school principal.
As a single mum, it’s not easy trying to control a 15-year-old boy who seems to have lost all interest in his school life. I am finding it progressively difficult to manage his behaviour as he refuses to conform to my directions - no phone in his room at night, etc.
I try to ensure he is up and ready for school before I leave for work each morning, but he often refuses to comply.
Your dilemma is replicated in homes throughout the country, where a proportion of young men rebel against the societal expectations of how they should conduct themselves.
It is absolutely no reflection on the love and commitment that you have invested in your son that his behaviour has deteriorated to the extent it has.
A recent survey of opinion following the tragic loss of five young men’s lives on the M9 showed a strong societal belief that parents should be held responsible for the behaviour of their teenage children. This view is reflected in the use by school authorities of the phrase “Parental Responsibility”, when a student’s behaviour makes teaching and learning impossible for his fellow students.
It’s ironic that we have spent the past 20 years in Ireland redressing the treatment of women who became pregnant and were forced into institutions where their children were often taken from them shortly after birth. Today, women in those circumstances are free to choose to keep their child if they so wish, and will receive State financial support in raising them.
[ Ireland now: anxious, jumpy and no country for young men or women Opens in new window ]
During my own teaching life and in the privacy of my guidance counselling office, many a mother raising a teenage boy on her own revealed the extent of the daily struggle they faced in trying to control behaviour. Some described being physically assaulted by their own child as they attempted, for example, to take a phone off them at night time.
Who are the adult males in your son’s life outside of his teachers at school? How actively involved are male members of your own family in your son’s life?
There is compelling evidence that the unlimited access to social media that our children are now encountering from their pre-teens onwards is generating a wave of school refusal, loss of interest in studies, exposure to bullying, utterly unrealistic expectations around body image, etc, and is hugely destructive of their healthy development.
The phrase that it takes a village to raise a child possibly contains a clue to supporting mothers such as yourself in bringing your son’s behaviour back under control. As a society, it is not sufficient to congratulate ourselves that we no longer stigmatise women who bear and raise children on their own.
[ ‘TikTok keeps me up all night’: Ireland’s teenagers on their relationship with the social media app Opens in new window ]
Young men need positive male role models. Sadly, some of those they are now encountering in their daily experience online are giving them misogynistic images of what a man should be and a very regressive perspective on the role of women, which may be feeding into your son’s treatment of you.
Who are the adult males in your son’s life outside of his teachers at school? How actively involved are male members of your own family in your son’s life? Are there men at youth or sports club level locally, that he might look up to?
Right now, until he completes his second-level education, you could try reaching out to that proverbial “Village” to assist you in guiding his actions and behaviours.

title: Irish AI firms raise €256m across 75 venture capital deals in 2026
description: Deal volumes and values ‘settling’ after bumper year in 2025
content:
Irish artificial intelligence (AI) companies continue to attract near-record levels of funding from venture capital firms, despite a fall-off in the value and volume of deals in 2026 compared to last year.
New research from Pitchbook, the global private capital markets intelligence firm, found that companies in the Republic’s AI sector have raised an additional €256 million across 75 deals so far this year.
The 2026 figures represent a decline from the record €691.3 million across 107 deals in 2025, the firm said.
It meant that the median deal value has fallen to €1.6 million in 2026 compared with €2.4 million last year. However, this is still above the median for any year before 2025.
Pitchbook said in the report that after a blockbuster year in 2025, the drop-off in 2026 reflects “normalisation rather than retreat”. It said the market was “settling after a banner year for investment” in 2025, in which several large-scale deals exceeding €100 million each were recorded.
The 2025 total includes, for example, Wayflyer’s €161.8 million fundraising round and workflow software platform Tines’ €120.7 million Series C round.
Highlights of 2026 so far include Fonoa’s €94.1 million fundraise to expand its tax compliance automation capabilities. Meanwhile, CameraMatics raised €49 million for its vehicle safety and fleet management software.
Enterprise Ireland, which says it has participated in 392 Irish AI funding rounds since 2020 in nearly two-thirds of Irish AI deals in 2026 to date, published the research on Monday morning in advance of the International AI Summit in Dublin on October 14th.
[ AI bubble? Nvidia is now bigger than Japan, but valuation looks modest Opens in new window ]
The event, which is part of the Republic’s presidency of the EU Council, takes place at the RDS in Ballsbridge, Dublin 4.
“PitchBook’s independent analysis shows the scale of investment now going into Irish AI companies, with almost €1 billion raised since the beginning of 2025,” said Jenny Melia, chief executive of Enterprise Ireland.
“The level of investment reflects the calibre and growing maturity of Irish AI companies, the breadth of sectors they are operating in and the strength of the intellectual property being developed in Ireland.”
Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence Niamh Smyth said: “The International AI Summit will focus on how Europe can turn advances in AI into economic value, while building the skills, infrastructure and trusted regulatory environment needed to support adoption and investment.”
Global M&A and fundraising activity has been mixed so far this year. While deals worth a record $2.8 trillion (€2.5 trillion) were agreed in the first half of the year, according to recent data from the London Stock Exchange group, European transaction volumes tumbled 14.2 per cent as the region faced an outsize impact from the Iran war.

title: Desperate late push to avert public-sector strike on Wednesday
description: Despite 11th-hour bid for talks with unions, both sides feel national stoppage is now all but inevitable
content:
The Government will make another attempt on Monday to convene talks with trade unions in an 11th-hour bid to avert a planned strike across the public service on Wednesday.
The Government is expected to restate that it wants negotiations on a new pay agreement for about 400,000 State employees.
Despite the intervention, there is still a mood of pessimism in both Government and trade union circles that the national stoppage – and the attendant widespread disruption – cannot now be avoided.
[ Explainer: Who is affected by the strike and can it be averted? Opens in new window ]
The strike would see more than 300,000 public sector workers undertake a 24-hour work stoppage, although essential services will be maintained.
On Sunday, Minister for Further and Higher Education James Lawless conceded the strike “probably will go ahead at this stage” , but he also urged unions to engage with Government as a means of preventing it.
The invitation will not set a specific time or date for prospective talks. Contact is expected to be made through the public services committee of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions (Ictu), with the Government side making clear that it wants to hold talks on a new pay deal.
Government sources gave no indication, however, that they would accede to the precondition laid down by unions – namely that pay needed to be negotiated and agreed first before other issues such as productivity were discussed.
Last Tuesday, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers said a total of €1.2 billion had been set aside in the budget for public-servant pay increases.
Lawless on Sunday repeated Taoiseach Micheál Martin’s assertion that the fund could form the basis for negotiations. Unions have argued that the amount mentioned is insufficient.
Government sources pointed on Sunday to another €1.6 billion contingency fund earmarked for as-yet unallocated spending. Speaking on condition of anonymity, senior figures with knowledge of the process said a portion of that fund could be earmarked for any agreement on pay. Some unions have indicated that more than €2 billion will be required to resolve the pay issue.
Some of the unallocated contingency fund will be used to address the overspend in the health sector for 2026.
A further one-day stoppage is scheduled for Wednesday week, with senior union figures privately warning that there could be escalation of industrial action in November if there is no progress on negotiating a new public service pay deal.
The most recent agreement covering pay for groups including civil servants, nurses, teachers, gardaí, local authority staff and Defence Forces personnel expired in the summer.
The chair of Ictu’s public service committee, Kevin Callinan, told The Irish Times on Sunday that staff would be seeking pay increases for this year, as well as assurances that wages would not fall behind living standards over the duration of any new deal and rises to cover the gap of at least five per cent between pay and inflation over the period 2021 to 2025.
“All we have at present is an effective pay cut for next year, nothing for this year [to cover the period since the expiry of the last deal] and a leap of faith after that,” he said.
Phil Ní Sheaghdha, the general secretary of the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation , said it did not look like the Government was serious about a cost-of-living agreement that could be put to ballot and accepted.
She said there was “a lack of trust among our members” who had been subject to unimplemented agreements in the past.

title: Frantic behind-the-scenes talks delivers deal on EU capital markets reform
description: Political agreement had long proved elusive when it came to reforms of the EU’s capital markets
content:
When the EU’s finance ministers sat down for a working dinner in Luxembourg last Thursday evening, Simon Harris warned his counterparts they could be about to face another day of newspaper headlines bashing Europe for again ducking a big decision.
Or, they could strike a deal, even if the compromise on the table wasn’t perfect, the Irish Minister for Finance said.
Finance officials had been toiling for months over a contentious package of reforms intended to break a decade long logjam. The proposals would shift more responsibility for regulating the architecture that makes the financial markets tick from national central banks and authorities to a European regulator.
Simplifying this layer of oversight would hopefully make it easier for investment cash and funding to flow across national borders, ideally creating a bigger pool of European capital that businesses could tap to raise investment and expand.
The Irish Government had set itself a tight deadline when taking over the Council of the EU presidency in July. It wanted to agree a deal on the hugely technical package of financial legislation by the October meeting of EU finance ministers.
Harris, who would be chairing discussions during the EU presidency, had gone back and forth with his advisers about tying himself to a firm date. Ultimately they decided it would help put the pressure on everyone.
The Council of the EU is the body where the member states, either at the level of officials, ambassadors, or ministers, shape policy coming from Brussels. The “presidency” rotates from country to country every six months, and for that period you are expected to be a neutral broker, steering the debate towards a common compromise.
Political agreement had long proved elusive when it came to reforms of the EU’s capital markets.
[ EU governments agree on long-stalled capital markets reform Opens in new window ]
The idea has been knocking around for a long time – a very long time in fact.
“Though a European capital market ought to be the result of spontaneous developments, it will nonetheless require constructive efforts on the part of governments and financial institutions,” Italian economist Claudio Segré wrote in a 1966 report for the then-European Economic Community (ECC).
An expert group chaired by Segré, a commission official, said creating a “broad” European capital market made good economic sense.
Brussels officials took a proper stab at it in the years that followed the financial crash.
Jean-Claude Juncker, then-European Commission president, spoke about creating a “capital markets union” in 2014. The changes would involve greater regulation at EU rather than national level, and aligning things such as insolvency regimes and other financial rules.
Building on banking reforms in the post-crash period, the president of the EU’s lawmaking body said the changes would “increase the attractiveness of Europe as a place to invest”.
[ Ireland’s EU presidency proposes budget cut of €141bn for the bloc Opens in new window ]
Everyone agrees in principle, but individual national capitals had traditionally been nervous that they would lose out in the shake-up.
France has been a big fan of the plan. That’s no surprise given the reforms would expand the remit of the existing European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), which is based in Paris.
Ireland and Luxembourg, two small member states with big financial services sectors, eyed plans to hand extra powers over to a European regulator with great suspicion.
The pair had teamed up in the past to oppose a shift towards a souped-up European regulator, fearing companies and firms would be tempted to set up shop in Paris in the future, rather than Dublin or Luxembourg.
Concerns about Europe’s sluggish economy, and a creeping sense the EU was falling further behind the United States and China, reignited the debate.
A 2024 report by another Italian economist, Mario Draghi, said the EU needed to push through the long-stalled capital market reforms to jump-start growth. The former European Central Bank chief warned the alternative would be a slow, painful economic decline.
[ EU’s big six push to centralise financial oversight in move that will worry Ireland Opens in new window ]
Breaking down national barriers that were stopping capital and investment from flowing throughout the 27-state union was key to that, Draghi said.
Ursula von der Leyen rebranded the capital reforms the “savings and investment union”, part of which would significantly expand ESMA’s remit to oversee financial markets.
The sprawling piece of complex legislation, the Market Integration and Supervision Package was kicked on to the member states, to see if they could land a deal everyone could live with this time.
Securing that deal by a self-imposed October deadline was ambitious but doable, Harris wrote in a letter to his fellow finance ministers after a meeting in July.
There was broad support around the room to get the thing done, subject to the shape of compromise.
A huge amount of the heavy lifting took place in Brussels at official-level.
A working group, chaired by Irish finance attache Emma Moyles, met more than a dozen times in the following months to knead out the sticky details. Department of Finance colleagues in Dublin were heavily involved too.
Irish negotiators got an honest sense of the red lines and the space for a “landing zone” in separate one-to-one discussions with officials from each of the other member states.
When talking to fellow finance ministers, Harris often mentioned Ireland didn’t need unanimous support to approve a deal, only a qualified majority of EU states, a much easier bar to clear.
A compromise text was drafted and redrafted by the Irish presidency that ran to several hundred pages.
The reworked proposal, seen by The Irish Times, included several big changes aimed at bringing reluctant countries around.
The confidential text shows Luxembourg secured leeway in the oversight of asset management groups. Malta opposed ESMA taking over the regulation of crypto platforms, so European oversight was limited to large platforms.
More broadly, representatives of national authorities and central banks would retain a role in ESMA’s governance too.
It was the carveout to accommodate the Germans that kicked off the biggest storm.
We have achieved more in the last 10 months than we have achieved in the last 10 years
Deutsche Börse Group, who run the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, would not come under the supervision of the EU-level authority, but remain regulated locally.
The German government argued the carveout was justified on the basis Deutsche Börse only operates in Germany, rather than across EU borders. BME, who run the Spanish Stock Exchange, were also exempt from ESMA oversight, following lobbying by Madrid.
Several member states, and the commission, were unhappy with the way Germany bagged an opt-out for its stock exchange, while others were being pressed to hand over decision-making authority to a European supervisor. “If we are doing this, we have to do it altogether,” said a diplomat from one country annoyed at the German carveout.
“If it’s a German sausage at the end of all this, what’s the point of it,” one industry source remarked, a reference to the ugly business of policymaking.
Belgium complained about the need to have a “level playing field”. The Belgian government had unsuccessfully pushed for Euroclear, a major central securities depository in its back yard, to remain regulated at national level.
Ambassadors from each member state, who are their governments’ eyes and ears in Brussels, picked up the debate last Wednesday.
Several sources briefed on the closed-door discussion said about 10 member states intervened to register their annoyance. The European Commission were also frustrated the ambition of the reforms had been “significantly” watered down.
[ Harris wants deal on contentious EU capital market reforms by October Opens in new window ]
Officials continued to negotiate deep in the weeds of the massively technical package of reforms, as finance ministers made their way to Luxembourg for their October 9th meeting.
A dinner had been arranged the evening before, where Harris again made the case. They could all spend another six months debating the finer points and they’d probably be in the same position, he said. “No compromise is perfect,” he told the room.
By breakfast the following morning, it seemed clear the other ministers agreed. Word filtered out shortly after they took their seats for the actual EU council meeting: deal done.
“We have achieved more in the last 10 months than we have achieved in the last 10 years,” Dutch finance minister Eelco Heinen later said.
All member states – bar Belgium who abstained – voted to back the compromise crafted by the Irish presidency, faults, carveouts and all.
That’s not the end of things though. MEPs in the European Parliament will have a chance to amend the package, before national governments give their final sign-off.
Speaking at a press conference afterwards, Harris cautioned against waiting around and letting the perfect become the enemy of the good. “That’s not how the European Union works,” he said.

title: The signs are AI prefers AI-written CVs, and one law firm’s experience is revealing
description: The signs are that it does, and one law firm’s experience is revealing
content:
E arlier this year, in the depths of summer, the Addleshaw Goddard law firm found itself in a slight pickle.
In what was becoming a familiar pattern, an advert it had placed for an IT job in its human resources department had drawn a slew of applications.
A year ago, only a couple of dozen people might have sent in a resume for a position like this one. But AI has made the job of applying for a job much faster and easier, and this time 178 applications arrived.
The problem was, the longer it took to sift them, the higher the chance that good candidates would find work elsewhere. Like a lot of organisations, Addleshaw has been encouraging its managers to test ways that AI can safely improve its processes, so the firm’s HR department decided to do an experiment. It would see how well an AI agent could assess the applications compared with humans.
An agent was duly set up, using the firm’s internal Microsoft Copilot system, and told about the role that needed to be filled, as well as the experience applicants would need with certain HR systems and programming languages, and with AI itself.
Humans at the firm sorted the applicants into a shorter pile of about a dozen and asked the agent to score them.
The agent whipped through this task and presented a list of what it deemed to be the top contenders. The humans did the same thing.
Alas, the two lists did not match. The agent was impressed by glossy applications from candidates who claimed to have achieved exceptional IT feats in record time at a previous employer, or worked on big projects despite scant levels of experience. In short, they were too good to be true – and smacked of having been written with the help of AI.
[ Who’s hiring and who’s firing in Ireland’s technology sector? Opens in new window ]
Katherine Rathbone, Addleshaw Goddard’s head of HR, told me her team had theories about why this might have happened.
For one thing, AI tools can make it a lot easier for candidates to tailor a CV to match a job description. But that was not all. “One possible explanation is that, because AI capability was itself one of the criteria, the agent may have interpreted signs of AI use in producing the CV as evidence of AI capability,” she said.
There is another, more disturbing possibility. The AI agent may have actively preferred CVs purely because AI was involved in writing them.
If so, it would confirm the findings of an eye-catching working paper that has analysed the behaviour of AI hiring tools.
The researchers simulated what they said were realistic hiring processes for 24 jobs ranging from teachers and consultants to chefs and engineers. They discovered that candidates using the same AI large language model as the recruiter were between 23 per cent and 60 per cent more likely to be shortlisted than those who relied on CVs produced by a hapless human.
[ AI bubble? Nvidia is now bigger than Japan, but valuation looks modest Opens in new window ]
This human handicap was highest for business roles such as sales and accountancy and lowest for fields such as farming and automobiles.
The paper is still being revised for publication in a peer-reviewed journal, meaning some of its findings may change. But one of its authors, Jiannan Xu, told me that updated analyses continue to provide evidence that AI models “exhibit self-preferencing behaviour”.
That is disturbing news at a time when AI is already driving a dismal hiring arms race. On one side are job hopefuls who, convinced they are battling a wall of soulless recruitment tools, are fighting back with an explosion of AI applications that are swamping recruiters.
If AI is biased towards AI, it adds a fresh dimension of jeopardy. Imagine being the candidate using the wrong type of AI, or no AI at all.
Fortunately, Xu’s paper suggests AI bias can be more than halved with two relatively simple strategies: telling models to ignore the origin of résumés and focus on their content, and using a number of assessment models to dilute the bias of any single tool.
Meanwhile at Addleshaw Goddard, I was pleased to learn that the successful candidate for the IT job was chosen by humans, and was not the one the agent ranked highest.
And as for using AI for recruitment, it is still a work in progress. The tools clearly have potential if used correctly, says Rathbone. “But human judgment remains important. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Postmortem on Niamh Flatley will influence legal case over alleged toxins at Castlehyde
description: Michael Flatley has sought €30m over allegations that remediation work left toxins that made his family sick
content:
A postmortem was carried out on the remains of Niamh Flatley last week over concerns that her lung condition was caused by inhaling toxins in Castlehyde, the mansion in Cork she shared with her husband Michael Flatley and their son Michael St James.
Niamh Flatley, née O’Brien (52), died in the Beacon Hospital in south Dublin last Monday after suffering from a lung condition in recent years which meant she regularly had to use an oxygen mask.
There had been plans to fly her from Dublin to Cleveland, Ohio, for a possible double-lung transplant but she had been deemed too ill to fly to America before her death.
The funeral of Niamh Flatley, who was originally from Kilbride in Co Meath, took place in the Church of St Thérèse in Mount Merrion , Dublin, on Saturday.
Michael Flatley paid an emotional tribute to his wife , saying her long illness and death was the worst pain he had ever experienced.
He described her as the “love of his life” and “my dream girl”. His wife had been diagnosed 12 years ago with scleroderma, an autoimmune disease, and given two years to live at the time.
“Every day of her life she fought it. The last two years were very difficult,” Flatley said in the eulogy. “I told her, ‘focus not on the storm, but focus on the hand of the Lord’.” .
The last year was “particularly difficult” and the last three weeks “were torturous and unbearable for her because she could not breathe”, he recalled.
She was a dancer with Riverdance, the show that received its big break as the interval act for the 1994 Eurovision Song Contest and subsequently propelled Michael Flatley to fame.
She was later a lead dancer with Flatley’s Lord of the Dance show before they married in 2006 in St Patrick’s Church, Fermoy in Cork.
Niamh Flatley had travelled with her husband and son to meet Pope Leo in late April and she was in Scotland in August while Lord of the Dance was touring the UK.
Sources close to the family said she had suffered stress arising from the acrimonious battle for control of the Lord of the Dance show between her husband and his former business partners.
In an affidavit opened to the High Court in Belfast earlier this year, Denis O’Sullivan, a consultant working with Michael Flatley, alleged one of Flatley’s former business partners was verbally abusive to Niamh Flatley at a meeting last November.
“This was particularly distressing given that Mrs Flatley was seriously ill that day and required an oxygen mask throughout the meeting,” he said. This allegation was later denied.
The results of the postmortem carried out last week will influence how a High Court claim for damages that Michael Flatley has brought over remedial works on his Castlehyde mansion in Cork proceeds.
Flatley has alleged that the remedial works left chloride residue in their family home after a 2016 fire. He alleged his family suffered ill health due to the presence of toxins in the air of the house, which he bought in 1999.
In a sworn statement, he said his family have “all suffered ill health since moving back to Castlehyde”.
Flatley has sought €30 million in damages from the insurance company and builders responsible for carrying out the restoration work after the fire. He and his family moved out of the house in October 2023.
In High Court filings, Flatley has claimed that unsafe levels of chloride residue were detected arising from PVC combustion in the 2016 fire.
He has alleged that the main contractor, Austin Newport Group Ltd, was aware of a residue issue. The company has denied the claims.
Ronnie Hudson, Flatley’s former barrister in the case, previously told the court that Flatley was not told about the PVC residue issue.
In the proceedings, Flatley claimed the remediation works carried out were defective, done in a negligent manner and that defects, including the PVC residue, were hidden from him.
In a newspaper interview, he blamed the toxins issue for him developing cancer.
“I was one of the fittest people in Ireland,” Flatley said to the Daily Mail in 2024. “But when we moved back in I never felt right, and all of a sudden I got cancer. All of a sudden I’ve developed asthma too. How did this happen? We must have been breathing in toxins. We were told to leave immediately and we’ve been living in hotels ever since.”
The Flatley family lived in Monaco in recent years.
On Thursday, Flatley posted a picture on Facebook of the Irish Tricolour flying at half-mast outside Castlehyde in honour of his wife. He thanked those who left flowers at the entrance gates to the estate.
Flatley is suing Austin Newport Group and five insurance underwriters: Lloyds Insurance Company SA, Hiscox SA, MS Amlin Underwriting Ltd, AXA XL Underwriting Agencies LTD and Hamilton Managing Agency Limited alleging negligence, endangerment, misrepresentation and breach of duty and contract.
He is also suing David Cushion, an accountant and broker who allegedly arranged the insurance. Flatley claims that unknown to him, Cushion was paid commission and acted as an agent for the insurance firms.
Flatley is represented by Creed McStay solicitors in the legal action. The same firm represents Maurice Regan in an ongoing case against John Magnier.
Regan is one of two billionaires – the other being Luke Comer – that have backed Flatley financially in a series of legal actions over the last two years relating to Castlehyde and Lord of the Dance.

title: Dublin’s Liberties bells ring after 20 years’ silence following revival project
description: ‘You don’t have to be musical and it is not complicated; you just need to do simple things well,’ says veteran bell ringer
content:
The Liberties bells have started calling Catholics to prayer again after ringers from the other Dublin church towers cleaned up the belfry of the St Augustine and St John Church on Thomas Street after it spent more than 20 years silently gathering dust.
So alarmed and confused were some locals when they heard the practice peals from half a dozen campanologists last week that they raced into the church to tell the priests they feared the bells were about to come crashing to earth.
Far from falling down, they were springing into life again following a revival project led by Michael Ryan, a man who was first drawn to bell ringing while serving as an altar boy in the church, known as John’s Lane, more than 50 years ago.
While sitting on the altar in the early 1970s, his eye would often be drawn to the small spiral staircase at the back of the church that seemed to reach towards the heavens.
Eventually curiosity got the better of him and he climbed the stairs where he met the bell ringers.
“They told me they didn’t get many people up in the tower and showed me around,” he says. “They took me on to the roof where I saw views of Dublin that I’d never seen before.”
They also taught him the ropes – literally – and he has been ringing bells in churches around Dublin – and further afield – ever since.
While the bells have tolled occasionally for funerals and other major church events, they fell silent for routine prayer services in the 1990s. “Some of the bell ringers died and there was no one to take over. I had moved away by that point,” Ryan explains.
But although he had left John’s Lane, it never really left him and when the prior of the church, Fr Pat Gayer, gave him the chance to lead a restoration project earlier this year he jumped at the opportunity.
The church, which was built in the 1860s, has the tallest spire in Dublin, and while it doesn’t quite tower over the twin cathedrals of Christ Church and St Patrick’s, and St Audoen’s, nearby, it can lay claim to being taller than all of them.
The Catholics of Dublin 8 didn’t exactly lord this over their Protestant neighbours but it was definitely something they wore as a badge of honour for donkey’s years, Ryan says.
On Sunday morning last, he and a team of six others climbed the vertiginous spiral staircase which snakes past the stained glass of a large Harry Clarke window and into the belfry before the 11:30am mass.
The team ran through a reading from the book of numbers, the bell ringer’s bible which contains the sequences needed to get specific sounds.
“They are called methods but I call them tunes,” he says. “It’s not musical, it sounds musical because all the bells are differently tuned, but it’s just moving numbers around in your head.”
One of the reasons he wants to shout about the restoration project from the rafters is to encourage more people to consider taking up the art of campanology.
He stresses that a religious affiliation of any kind is not a requirement – like other bell ringers he moves seamlessly between Protestant and Catholic churches and is entirely agnostic as to where he goes as long as there are bells that need pealing. In all his years bell-ringing, no one has ever asked him his religion or even if he has one, he says.
Ultimately, he suggests, it is about community. It is also, he says, “a mild form of exercise and it is great for your brain. You don’t have to be musical and it is not complicated; you just need to do simple things well”.

title: How are Munster, Leinster and Connacht looking ahead of Champions Cup openers?
description: Leo Cullen says Leinster need to improve attacking cohesion, although the form of Sam Prendergast is a bright spark
content:
In yet another change of format to the season, for the first time since 2018 the opening round of the Champions Cup has been shunted into October next weekend and as anticipated, through no fault of their own, the Irish provinces look decidedly undercooked compared to their French and English opponents.
Following Connacht’s mauling in Glasgow , Ulster’s comeback draw with Munster , and Leinster’s patchy 29-5 win in their RDS homecoming on Saturday night , the Irish quartet all sit in the bottom half of the table before this first of nine interruptions to the URC season. What’s more, the provinces have only been permitted to use the bulk of their Ireland summer tourists over the weekend’s third round of matches.
Next Saturday, Leinster are away to Clermont and Munster host Racing 92 in Páirc Uí Chaoimh, two sides who are also in the bottom half of the Top 14. Clermont lost 23-22 at home to Bordeaux Bègles and Racing were beaten 29-15 in Toulon on Saturday, but they have each played six, winning two apiece.
Meanwhile, a rebooted Saracens sit third in the Premiership after beating Bristol 30-7 at home ahead of their Champions Cup game against Connacht in the Dexcom next Saturday.
“That’s just the hand that we have,” said Leo Cullen after Saturday’s win. “We just need to do what we can. Hence, why we brought the wider group [41 players] to South Africa as well.
“We’d love to get more wins on the board, but it’s been a bit of a slow start from the four provinces in many ways. We’ve had three wins between us over the first three rounds. It’s not a great return,” he admitted.
“Listen, we are where we are now. We just need to get fully focused on the challenge, which is hugely exciting.
“It’s one of the cooler places I’ve played,” said Cullen of the Stade Marcel Michelin, one of European rugby’s most iconic grounds. “It’s been a long time since we’ve been there, so most of our guys won’t have played there previously. You’d be surprised if any of them maybe have played there previously. But it’s a great rugby ground and it means a lot in the town, so it does. It’s a proper test for us now.”
There’s plenty to work on in the week ahead. After a three-try salvo in the opening 21 minutes in front of an expectant 20,000 full house on an ideal autumnal night for the Laya’s grand reopening, Leinster went the next 55 minutes without scoring.
“The cohesion around attack combinations there is probably the big thing, where we just coughed the ball a little bit too cheaply,” said Cullen. “It’s just making sure we value possession properly and we look after it and make opposition teams work harder defensively for longer.”
Hugo Keenan and Jimmy O’Brien looked sharp in opening the scoring, and O’Brien clearly liked being back home, for in adding a second he repeated his brace the last time Leinster played at the RDS when beating Connacht n May 2024.
But the brightest spark of all was Sam Prendergast. His cameo in Durban a week previously when setting up a late bonus-point try has caught the eye. Here, a striking feature of the 23-year-old outhalf’s performance was his desire to be a running threat in addition to his usual array of passes, and after missing his first three kicks, he finished with a flourish, creating and converting the last two tries.
“It’s probably something that I’m trying to work on personally, being a bit more of a run threat,” he admitted afterwards. “There’s still a few opportunities where I probably ran when I should have passed, and I probably could have done better when I was running. There’s probably a lot of improvement on it but yeah, it was promising.”
Prendergast was equally self-critical when reflecting on last season’s “mixed bag”, even when returning to outhalf for the successful URC knockout stages.
“I just learned to take it week by week,” he added, and fully aware of his critics out there, likewise he admitted there is still more room for improvement in his defence.
“Maybe I’ve been criticised in the past about it but I’m trying to evolve that part of my game. There were still missed tackles out there tonight so I’ll still keep working on it. It’s 50 per cent of the game so I need to keep working on it.”
Looking ahead to his third game away to a French club next Saturday, Prendergast said: “They’ll be flying and it’s always tough going away there.
“I’ve limited experience over there, but it’s always pretty hostile. It’s also very cool. It’s always very hard. I remember Bayonne last year was exceptionally difficult. La Rochelle the year before was difficult. It’s never easy over in France. It won’t be easy over there.
“Leinster and Clermont have a lot of history so it’s a really exciting week for us. The chat in the dressingroom already is we’re really looking forward to it.”

title: Tribunal upholds complaints against solicitor Declan O’Callaghan over mishandling of funds
description: O’Callaghan had represented Brian Colleran, who received a €5.2m insurance settlement in 2011 to cover his lifelong care needs
content:
Seven complaints of professional misconduct have been upheld against the suspended Roscommon solicitor Declan O’Callaghan.
It is understood that the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal, which upheld the complaints, will ask the High Court to strike O’Callaghan from the Roll of Solicitors, the ultimate professional sanction that can be taken against an errant solicitor.
The new findings against him are the latest in a lengthy career. The first professional red flag about him was raised in 1990, though he remained free to work as a solicitor until he was suspended by the High Court in July 2018.
That action followed multiple complaints from clients in the north-west where O’Callaghan, who lived in Ballaghaderreen, Co Roscommon , was a pillar of the local community. He practised at the law firm Kilrane O’Callaghan in the town, the offices of which were run by his wife, Mary Devine O’Callaghan.
Since his suspension, he has moved residence and is also understood to have spent time in Portugal .
Following the complaints about him and an investigation by the Law Society, in December 2018 the High Court ordered that the firm be wound up. In the same year, the High Court referred matters to An Garda Síochána , who have been investigating O’Callaghan since but with no known conclusion.
The latest findings against him came last week when the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal upheld seven separate complaints. All seven complaints related to his handling of the case of Brian Colleran of Ballaghaderreen, who was severely injured in a car crash in December 2009, when he was 21.
Colleran sustained serious spinal injuries in the crash which left him profoundly physically disabled. He is reliant on assistance from family members and professional carers.
An insurance claim to help pay for his lifelong care needs was settled in 2011 for €5.2 million. O’Callaghan went personally to the insurance company offices to collect the cheque and then withdrew €136,000 of the funds, which he used to pay a VAT bill with Revenue.
The VAT bill owed to Revenue was O’Callaghan’s responsibility and had nothing to do with representing Colleran.
Shortly after the settlement was reached, about €4.8 million was given to Colleran, which meant approximately €400,000 of the settlement was not handed over by O’Callaghan.
Neither Colleran nor his parents, Mary and Thomas Colleran, ever received a satisfactory explanation from O’Callaghan for the shortfall. Their repeated requests for proper financial accounts were never satisfied.
Following reporting on the case in The Irish Times, Sligo solicitor Damien Tansey offered to help the family. This culminated in their lengthy and detailed complaint to the Solicitors Tribunal.
The tribunal, whose members are appointed by the president of the High Court, is separate to but works with the Law Society, the representative and lobbying body for solicitors. The tribunal operates to the standards of the criminal justice system, which means the bar of proof is set at “beyond reasonable doubt”. This is different to the civil justice system, which operates “on the balance of probability”.
Using this standard, the tribunal found O’Callaghan guilty on all counts and last week delivered its verdict to him and to the Collerans. The next stage in the process is for the tribunal to ask the Law Society to refer its findings to the president of the High Court.
In their complaints to the tribunal, the Collerans alleged O’Callaghan had “wrongfully appropriated and misapplied” €341,285 of the €5.2 million awarded to Brian Colleran, which the family asserted had been “unlawfully deducted [and] retained” by O’Callaghan. The tribunal agreed.
Several other sums were referenced, but this was the bulk sum.
Two other complaints related to O’Callaghan failing to hand over €1,400 in travelling expenses for hospital visits, despite being asked to do so for seven years.
A further complaint alleged that O’Callaghan made “false and misleading statements” to two Dublin hospitals, namely the Mater and the National Rehabilitation Hospital. This related to O’Callaghan’s assertion to the hospitals that just €200,000 had been recovered by Colleran for medical charges and therefore, the hospitals would have to accept this sum despite billing for €360,000.
O’Callaghan did not tell the hospitals Colleran had in fact been awarded €5.2 million.
It was also complained that O’Callaghan charged the family €12,730 for what was described as “very little work”. He had failed to give a proper breakdown of how such costs were arrived at, it was stated.
Apart from representing Colleran at the Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal, Tansey also succeeded in recovering the misappropriated funds, plus interest, from the Law Society’s compensation fund.
The case against O’Callaghan was heard by the three-person tribunal (two solicitors and a lay member) on May 19th and 20th, but their judgment, in which all complaints against O’Callaghan were upheld, was handed down last Tuesday.
No date has been set yet for the president of the High Court to consider the tribunal recommendation that O’Callaghan be stripped permanently of his right to call himself a solicitor.

title: Denis Walsh: Famous image remains a powerful reminder of Cork hurling’s lost empire
description: Rebel clubs dominated the landscape in the 1970s, but that was then and this is now
content:
There is a photograph of Jimmy Barry-Murphy and Christy Ring from the summer of 1978 that is evocative and magnetic still. It was taken at a Cork training session in Páirc Uí Chaoimh before the Munster hurling final and published in the Cork Examiner on July 26th, four days before the match.
In the black-and-white shot, Ring is dressed in a suit and tie and JBM is wearing the jersey of his club St Finbarr’s. Neither man is looking at the other. JBM is staring at the ground, with his hands on his hips, which was his default posture when the ball was nowhere near. Ring is looking up at the City End.
“Dual star Jimmy Barry-Murphy and maestro Christy Ring ponder a point of tactics during a Cork training session,” ran the caption in the paper.
The body-language detectives would have copped that the reality was not so banal. JBM has been answering questions about this photograph for nearly 50 years. In an interview with Off The Ball on stage at the Cork Opera House three years ago, he said, playfully, that he had given “50 different versions of the story over the years, but this is the truth”.
“He was giving me a proper dressing down, in a nice way,” said JBM. “He said I wasn’t playing to my potential. I was playing football and hurling, and I was cruising through matches. If we were to win another All-Ireland, I literally needed to pull my socks up.”
JBM says that he has signed more copies of that photograph than any other piece of memorabilia from his career. It hangs in pubs all over Cork and in other pubs around the world where Cork people have left a trace. If you were never curious about the words that passed between them, it is an image of two of the most cherished sportspeople in Cork’s history, frozen in another time.
Photographs that live independently of digital devices still have that power: not just as a public portal into a dreamy past, but as safe houses for nostalgia.
It comes to mind now because JBM’s club St Finbarr’s and Ring’s club Glen Rovers will meet in the Cork county final on Sunday. Around the time the photograph was taken, the Glen and the Barr’s captured four club All-Irelands between them in five years. It was a staggering period of Cork dominance during which the three big city clubs – including Blackrock – reigned supreme.
When the Glen and the Barr’s met in the 1977 county final, the Glen were reigning All-Ireland champions. Just a fortnight earlier, Cork had completed the middle leg of what would become three-in-a-row and the old Páirc Uí Chaoimh was only a year old, a model of modernity. All of it reeked of what is now a lost empire.
Parts of it are vivid in my memory still because it was the first county final I was brought to and first impressions on a child are often visceral. The official attendance in the Páirc that day was 34,151, which remains a record for a county final anywhere in the country, but the real figure must have been closer to 40,000.
So many people arrived late that a gate was forced open at one end of the ground and it was estimated that 2,000 people flooded in.
