The official figure also didn’t include schoolchildren, who were admitted for free, and 1,200 five-year ticket holders, who had put their hands in their pockets to help service the debt on the new stadium.
The gate receipts were £23,193, and according to the Examiner, it took six hours to count the money, “under top security”.
The match programme was a thin pamphlet by modern standards, but its centre piece was an article written by Jack Lynch, the taoiseach of the day and a former Glen player. It must be the only time that a sitting head of government has contributed a piece of personal reminiscence to a county final programme, but Lynch was so embedded in Cork GAA that it probably didn’t seem at all remarkable.
The Barr’s routed the Glen that day, holding them scoreless in the second half, and six months later the Barr’s succeeded them as All-Ireland champions.
The landscape of Cork hurling, and its place in the wider scheme of things, is much different now. The Barr’s and the Glen have won just five Cork titles between them since 1989, and they haven’t met each other in a final since 1988. In the last 38 years, only two Cork clubs have won the club All-Ireland, a staggeringly miserable record.
But none of that will matter on Sunday. County final season is in full swing now and every county final, at every level, everywhere, has a self-contained importance. It doesn’t matter how many people are there, or how many people care; it doesn’t need a context other than itself.
In the GAA calendar, the All-Ireland hurling and football finals are the big feast days, and those occasions have a uniquely national appeal. All-Ireland final day, though, has never been inclusive. County finals have a different nature. Clubs find their level and the prospect of glory has a sustainable existence. Year in, year out, that’s enough.
Anyway, the photograph. By 1978 Ring had made a personal investment in JBM’s Cork career. A couple of years earlier, when the Cork footballers seemed more interested in JBM than the hurlers, Ring championed his case.
There is a famous story from the 1976 All-Ireland final. With 10 minutes left, and the game in the balance, Cork switched JBM on to Mick Jacob, who had been cleaning up at centre back for Wexford. The legend is that Ring made a unilateral decision to move JBM and in the time that remained he scored four points, precisely the difference between the teams.
When Barry-Murphy took off on one of his solo runs, Ring paced him in a parallel run down the Cusack Stand sideline and when the final whistle blew, the RTÉ cameras captured Ring making a dash for JBM and wrapping him in a bearhug. “I knew you’d do it boy,” he said. “I knew you’d do it.”
Five weeks after the photograph was taken at Cork training, Cork beat Kilkenny in the All-Ireland final and JBM scored the goal that broke the game open, 13 minutes from the end.
He may have been looking at the ground, but he was listening.

title: Letters to the Editor, October 12th: On Wednesday’s strike, prisoner rehabilitation and growing fruit and veg
description: Government’s approach reflects ‘staggering disconnect from frontline realities’
content:
Sir, – There will be no Dáil sitting on Wednesday as more than 100,000 public sector workers prepare to take part in a nationwide strike over pay (“ Dáil sitting next Wednesday cancelled due public sector workers’ strike ”, News, October 10th). Let me get this one right: the Government has decided they won’t turn up for work on Wednesday because of the strikes? I find it difficult to comprehend that our politicians have made such a decision.
Our TDs should display leadership by turning up for work, especially when a lot of this imbroglio is of their own making. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I have just read Malachy Clerkin’s article on the GAA’s attitude to women (“ Mary McAleese questioned the GAA’s attitude towards women – now they’ve replaced her with a man ”, Sport, October 9th). Please readers, save it and pass it around.
It should be compulsory reading and subject for discussion for all GAA club members and, indeed, for the public. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Ireland’s dependence on imported fruit and vegetables, as described by Cian O’Connell, reflects a food system that makes it difficult for growers to earn a living and leaves too many people disconnected from how their food is grown (“ Why doesn’t Ireland grow more vegetables? ”, News, October 10th).
Global shocks and a rapidly worsening biodiversity crisis should prompt us to rethink our export-focused model that leaves us short and that hurts both farmers and nature. Such a rethink requires an honest assessment of who benefits, and at what cost, from our current food system.
A resilient and sustainable food system is about more than farming. It is about our relationship with food, nature and each other. Community gardens, for example, help people develop practical experience of how growing food together can promote wellbeing and resilience. These gardens cannot replace commercial horticulture, but they can help grow the connections and culture that make good food more accessible, and our communities more resilient, in an uncertain world.
As we mark National Community Gardens and Allotments Week this week, maybe we can go beyond its stated aim of raising awareness of the benefits of urban growing spaces and initiate a nationwide debate on what food, not just agriculture, means to us all? – Yours, etc,
A chara, – I appreciate it is important to listen to all perspectives. However, hearing a consultant paediatrician (“ October 7th was a piercing, shrieking alarm call for all Jews ”, Opinion, October 9th) state that 119 children dying of malnutrition is a “thankfully low” number and due to “food-delivery efficacy”, when the Israeli government continues to block life-saving food and medical aid entering Gaza in a direct breach of international humanitarian law and basic morals, is deplorable. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – You report on the gross proposal of livestreaming of a military execution in the United States (“ Trump administration condemned for plans to livestream execution ”, World News, October 9th). It is mentioned in the report that “the last known cases of a military firing squad in the US was in November 1945″.
It is worth noting that the soldier in question was Private Eddie Slovik, whose crime was desertion. He killed no one, in battle or elsewhere. His story was the subject of a moving film The Execution of Private Slovik (1974), with a young Martin Sheen as Slovik and giving one of his best performances. Though thousands deserted, he was made an example of even though the second World War had ended a few months before.
I welcome the statement of the president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, Archbishop Paul S Coakley, who described the livestreaming idea as “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death”. He went on to say: “The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people.”
Prophetic voices like this are sorely needed at this time. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – As the US is now sanctioning the International Criminal Court (“ US sanctions International Criminal Court, hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize ”, World News, October 9th), is it not time for those who support the ICC to sanction the US? By standing by and doing nothing, do we share their shame? – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Having spent some time in Dublin city centre recently, it is clear that aggressive begging is more widespread.
This is a complex problem requiring myriad interventions. But it has become normalised and accepted here on a scale that you simply would not see in any comparable European city.
Surely, the capital city of a country of our wealth and means can do better.
Whatever the answer, the current approach – or lack of – is certainly not working. Yours, etc,
Sir, – Eoin Burke-Kennedy writes: “Norway knows when its tax windfall will end, Ireland doesn’t – yet we spend it anyway” “ There’s a good chance Ireland will come to regret this boomtime period as a missed opportunity ”, Business, October 9th).
Two of the biggest contributors to our tax windfall could be hugely affected by the onward march of artificial intelligence (AI), yet our Government continues to live in this nirvana bubble.
The Government has an obligation to those that elected it to spell out the consequences of continuous budget deficits and the probable impact of the disappearance of these tax windfalls.
Necessary infrastructure spending needs to be clearly spelt out and how it is going to be financed and priorities need to clearly identified. So many areas need to be addressed – water, power, transport, health, housing, agriculture – and all these projects seem to be managed in a haphazard manner. There doesn’t appear to an integrated plan to identify timelines and resource requirements and how they are going to be financed.
Yes, the Government is in a difficult political situation, but future generations will not forgive them if they ignore what the experts are telling them. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Donald Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin to buy Russian diesel undermines the integrity of the US as a peace mediator, removing any illusions that it acted as an honest broker between Ukraine and Russia (“ Trump agrees diesel supply deal with Russia ”, World News, October 9th).
It is also the antithesis of the role that the US played in the process leading up to the Belfast Agreement . Back then, top-level political commitment by former US president Bill Clinton, combined with the competence of former US senator George Mitchell, played a constructive role in reaching the agreement and making peace.
It was a prime example of the US exercising soft power rather than Trumpian bullying and threats. This chapter of US history deserves to be remembered and highlighted, not merely as a thing of the past, but as an inspiration for what is still possible. It is a message that Irish people on both sides of the Border could amplify by reminding the world of the time when America actually was great. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Donald Trump says Ukraine needs a new president (“US president Donald Trump says it is time for Ukraine to get rid of Zelenskiy”, World News, October 10th)
If any country is in need of a new president it is the US and Russia; not Ukraine. Vladimir Putin continues to bomb civilian targets while Trump, not only turns a blind eye, but offers him support via this diesel deal.
The EU needs to increase sanctions on Russia and the Irish Government needs to show its support by backing any effort to ban the sale of alumina from Aughinish to Russian smelters. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Barry Walsh (Letters, October 10th) should not have been surprised that Coimisiún na Meán issued a statement about the decision of the Minister for Media to renege on the Government’s three-year funding commitment to RTÉ .
As the statement reminds us, article five of The European Media Freedom Act 2024 (EMFA) requires EU member states to put in place funding procedures that guarantee public service media adequate, sustainable and predictable financial resources while safeguarding their editorial independence.
The EMFA, which became law in Ireland in August 2025, requires EU member states to put in place an independent authority, free from political influence by governments, to monitor the application of this requirement and that the results of such monitoring should be made public. Coimisiún na Meán was merely fulfilling its obligations under the EMFA by issuing the statement.
Predictable (and therefore multiannual) funding is essential to the editorial independence of RTÉ and TG4. The Broadcasting Amendment Bill being guided by the Minister for Media through the Oireachtas requires Coimisiún Na Meán to undertake three-year appraisals of RTÉ and TG4, starting in 2027, and to recommend levels of funding for RTÉ and TG4 for those three years.
However, the Bill does not require the Government to offer three-year funding to either RTÉ or TG4.
The events of last week in relation to RTE’s funding could be repeated without apparently breaching the provisions of the Bill. Whether the Bill complies with the EMFA (which the Bill says it is implementing) will be a matter for Coimisiún na Meán to monitor and report on. I think we will be hearing from Coimisiún Na Meán again on this. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Breda O’Brien’s article on our penal system was most disturbing and sad and a shocking reflection of the lack of compassion in our society (“ Ireland may not have the death penalty, but we have no reason for complacency ”, Opinion, October 11th).
We have read so many reports on the overcrowding and the absence of attempts at rehabilitation, but her article detailing the treatment, or mostly lack thereof, starkly emphasises a cruel indifference to our fellow men and women. How can we continue to tolerate such disregard of basic human rights?
As someone who writes to prisoners on death row in the US, I deplore the death penalty and find the case of Christa Pike horrific, but, as O’Brien points out, “even in the absence of the death penalty here, we are still far from a penal system that respects the rights of everyone”. It is well past time we sought to rectify this and to rehabilitate prisoners. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – James Joyce wrote in a university submission in Padua in 1912, when asked to write about the progress made by mankind since the Renaissance: “The much-trumpeted progress of this century consists largely of a heap of machines the very purpose of which is to gather in haste and fury the scattered elements of utility and knowledge and to redistribute them to each member of the collectivity who is in a position to pay a slight tax.”
He could well be talking today about the utility of AI. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Will anyone join me in a class action to sue US president Donald Trump for all the worry, stress, anxiety and insomnia that his erratic words create around the world? – Yours, etc,

title: Irish consumers fuelling ‘fast tech’ trend leading to rise in discarded electronics
description: Purchases such as mini fans, festive lights and power banks totalled 91 million items last year
content:
Irish consumers are fuelling a “fast tech” trend of low-cost, small electronic items, leading to a mountain of discarded electrical goods, known e-waste, data has revealed.
In the 12 months to last July, almost half of Irish people (44 per cent) discarded a fast-tech item – usually bought on impulse or as a novelty – unused, after a single use or within a month.
A third had thrown at least one item in a bin and a quarter kept them at home, with fewer than half using a recycling centre.
The major European online study, conducted in July, found that nearly nine in 10 Irish consumers purchased fast-tech electronics such as mini fans, festive lights and decorations, wireless headphones and speakers, and power banks and chargers in the previous 12 months.
“Because they are usually inexpensive, bought on impulse and easy to replace, fast-tech products can be treated as if they are disposable,” Elizabeth O’Reilly, of Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) Ireland, said.
“One product improperly discarded may seem insignificant, but when that behaviour is repeated across millions of purchases, these gadgets can become a growing waste problem.”
The findings, for the international WEEE Forum, form part of a consumer survey carried out for International E-waste Day on Wednesday across 12 European countries, including Ireland.
It also showed that the number of people buying fast tech in Ireland is higher than the average across the 12 nations – 89 per cent versus 78 per cent.
Separate research by WEEE Ireland showed that fast-tech purchases last year reached 91 million items.
The bigger study, meanwhile, highlighted the low quality of fast-tech products and points to an appetite for longer-lasting alternatives.
Among the 776 respondents in Ireland who answered why they had stopped using these products, 52 per cent cited breakage or a defect, while 83 per cent said they would be willing to pay more for at least some similar products if they lasted longer.
Asked what they had done with unused devices, fewer than half brought at least one item to a recycling centre or in-store recycling point, more than one in three said they had binned them and more than one in four hoarded them at home.
“People may not even realise that even small novelty products can contain electronic components and materials that should be recovered,” O’Reilly said.
“We’re urging people to treat these items as they would any other electrical product. If it can be repaired or reused, that can extend its life.
“When it reaches the end of its life, it should be recycled through the free take-back options at participating retailers and civic amenity sites, so its materials can be recovered for use again as part of the circular economy.
“Many of these products also contain lithium batteries that, if discarded in household bins, can be damaged during waste processing, leading to fires in bin trucks or at recycling centres.”
WEEE Ireland encourages people to bring unwanted fast tech to their nearest recycling point. – Press Association

title: No national risk assessment published for more than two years despite geopolitical changes
description: Report, produced by Department of An Taoiseach, identifies most significant strategic and natural risks facing Ireland
content:
A national risk assessment has not been published by Government for more than two years despite its last report emphasising that new risks were emerging from global insecurity, terrorism and hybrid threats.
The report has been published annually by the Government each September since 2014, aside from a period disrupted by the Covid-19 pandemic .
No report was published in September 2025, however, and neither was a report published in September 2026.
The report, produced by the Department of An Taoiseach , identifies most significant strategic and natural risks facing the State.
The 2024 report identified 24 strategic risks across five categories: geopolitical and global risks; economic risks (including infrastructure deficits and more than concentration in particular sectors); societal risk, especially housing; environmental risk, especially climate change; as well as technological risks, particularly from artificial intelligence.
The absence of a new assessment comes amid a period where there are wars in Ukraine and in the Middle East and where energy costs have soared throughout the EU. There is also a recognition of the increased vulnerability of communications and energy infrastructure.
In September, Cabinet decided it would review the current national risk assessment to see if it adequately captured all the risks facing the State. The Government has now proposed a public consultation, and has invited Oireachtas parties to make submissions. It also intends to set up an interdepartmental group to oversee the development of an updated report.
It has promised that a finalised National Strategic Risk Assessment 2026 will be published by the end of the year.
[ Government has not published risk assessment since 2024 despite rising global tensions Opens in new window ]
In reply to parliamentary questions, Taoiseach Micheál Martin has insisted that the most recent assessment from 2024 remains valid.
Green Party leader Roderic O’Gorman, who has followed the issue, has criticised the delay in updating the assessment, given the emergence of new forms of threat in recent years.
He said the delay in publishing what is meant to be an annual report was not acceptable.
“The profile of risk that Ireland faces has continued to change. Examples include the appearance of drones in our skies on the past year. There is also the impact of the second cost of living spike caused by our dependence on fossil fuels,” he said.
“All of these things need to be understood and assessed by Government. And yet, the Government has now failed to publish a risk assessment for two years in a row.”
He said that obligations laid out for Government in legislation were being ignored, in the same way as climate change legislation was being ignored.
“Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael see no benefit in long-term planning. Everything is in the here and now.
“The idea of taking a step back, looking at the wider situation, just seems to be too much work for them these days,” he said.
Among the other risks identified for Ireland in 2024 were potential infrastructure deficits, weakening competitiveness, pandemic risk, biodiversity loss, plus the effects of extreme weather.

title: What’s in a name? Well, Tottenham have some thoughts
description: Piers Morgan sticks by his pal Cristiano Ronaldo, Ireland young guns give Conor McManus a winning high
content:
Wouldn’t you think Tottenham Hotspur /Tottenham/Spurs had enough to be thinking about after the start they’ve had to the season? You would.
You might recall that in early 2025, the club emailed Premier League broadcasters to inform them that after they had “remastered” their “brand identity”, they wanted the club to be referred to as “Tottenham Hotspur, with Spurs being the preferred short version”. “Tottenham Hotspur Football Club” and “THFC” were also acceptable, but “never refer to our club as ‘Tottenham’, ‘Tottenham Hotspur FC’ or ‘TH’.”
The club not wanting “Tottenham” to be used as a moniker left their supporters bamboozled, but The Athletic had good news for them last week: “The club has been keen to lean into the T-word again, recognising how much it means to fans. There is a clear desire to reassert the importance of this word, and this aspect of the club’s identity.”
In short, you can now call them anything you want (except “relegation contenders”).
“Honestly, I can’t describe it. It’s the closest thing to what I imagine drugs would be like.” – Conor McManus on a high after the Ireland under-21s beat England 3-1 on Tuesday.
The number of games PSG’s Fabián Ruiz has now played for Spain. How many has he lost? None (excluding a penalty shoot-out defeat to Portugal), putting him just five games off the world record. A decent run.
“I think that we will reach a conclusion but, being in my 60s, I will have to be lucky enough still to be here when the final verdict arrives. Now a ruling will come, then an appeal ... I’ll be 80.” – José Mourinho reckoning he’ll be antiquated by the time the whole Manchester City business is resolved.
“I know ... the weight [Cristiano] has in the world ... I made a mistake by putting someone of the stature of Pelé or Maradona on to warm up and then not putting him in the game.” – Part of the statement Cristiano Ronaldo , eh, instructed Portugal’s manager Jorge Jesus to read out at a press conference. Note the mention of Pelé and Maradona, but not Messi.
“I’ve lost my peace and tranquillity. I no longer have any privacy. There’s always someone who wants to take a photo with me or, worse, film me. If I was offered the life I have today or the life I had before, I’d choose the one I had before.” – Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha , who sounds like a man regretful of becoming famous at the World Cup.
Riposte of the week? Well, Cristiano Ronaldo didn’t pick up many accolades after his carry-on during the international break, so we’ll award him this gong as a consolation.
His cheerleader-in-chief Piers Morgan had a bit of a run-in with former Crystal Palace owner and current TalkSPORT presenter Simon Jordan over Ronaldo’s behaviour while on duty with Portugal, Jordan labelling Morgan as “sycophantic, biased, one-dimensional” who was “sucking up to Ronaldo because you think he’s your friend”.
Morgan subsequently sent a clip of the aggro to Ronaldo. His reply? “That blonde guy, tell him to stop with the Botox. He looks like an apple.” Oooh.
All we can hope is that Arsenal fan Stephen Power was jesting when he revealed how much he paid for his breakfast at the Emirates’ WM restaurant on Saturday morning ahead of their game against Leeds.
Incidentally, if you’re wondering what WM means, according to the interweb, it represents “the pioneering 3-2-2-3 (“WM”) formation introduced to Arsenal in the 1920s by manager Herbert Chapman. Your education is complete.
Any way, Stephen’s breakfast featured one fried egg, two semi-cooked sausages, one underdone rasher, one very sad mushroom, one mushy tomato, a teeny tub of beans, and what looks suspiciously like a bit of watercress.
The cost? “£50 fry-up with all the trimmings,” he said. So, that’s almost €60.
Among the replies: “Is there £35 change hidden inside the yolk?” “All what trimmings??? Do they come ‘round and cut your hair??” “£50 for a fry up? And it has salad on it? Game’s gone.” “That’s a bigger scam than Man City have pulled.” True.

title: O’Brien has fresh Triple Crown ambitions with Dewhurst winner Darkness Falls
description: Champion jockey Dylan Browne McMonagle returns to action at Roscommon after Bellewstown fall in August
content:
Aidan O’Brien has plenty left to do in 2026, but the man who has won and done practically everything else in racing has a fresh Triple Crown project waiting for him in 2027.
It’s almost a quarter of a century since O’Brien first voiced ambitions to emulate Nijinsky’s epic 1970 English Triple Crown accomplishment.
Hawk Wing was the first of his horses to spark thoughts of a singular talent with the speed to win the mile-long 2,000 Guineas, the middle-distance class to win the Epsom Derby and the stamina to complete the treble in Doncaster’s gruelling St Leger.
The horse still officially rated the best O’Brien has ever trained ultimately finished runner-up in both the Guineas and the Derby and wound up being defined by a monstrous Lockinge success over a mile.
The Leger test of a mile and 6½ furlongs has long since made it an anachronism in elite bloodstock terms. Nashwan (1989) and Sea The Stars (2009) won both the Guineas and the Derby but never remotely came within contention to try and complete the classic hat-trick.
The irony is how John Magnier ’s Coolmore Stud has driven much of the commercial imperative that has reduced the Leger’s relevance and yet he apparently continues to be consumed by a desire to pull off a Triple Crown.
Camelot defied all business sense and started a 2/5 favourite to equal Nijinsky in the 2012 Leger only to come up short against Encke in a notorious race that appears to be still reverberating.
The following year, it emerged that Encke was among 11 other horses that tested positive for anabolic steroids which resulted in Godolphin ’s trainer Mahmood Al Zarooni being banned for eight years.
Now Camelot’s son, Darkness Falls, is the latest colt being lined up to scratch Magnier and Co’s Triple Crown itch next year.
A recce to Newmarket’s Rowley Mile on Saturday saw Darkness Falls make light of a two-furlong drop in trip to beat Godolphin’s big hope Desert Castle by a neck in the Darley Dewhurst Stakes. It was a record ninth Dewhurst for O’Brien.
The real significance, however, could prove to be what occurs in seven months’ time should Darkness Falls return to the Rowley Mile and win the Guineas.
Since Camelot, there has been ‘TC’ talk surrounding other Ballydoyle stars. City of Troy and Auguste Rodin, however, fluffed their lines in the Guineas. Saxon Warrior flopped in the Derby. None of them subsequently went near the Leger.
Darkness Falls is an incredibly stingy 12/1 with some firms to pull off the feat and O’Brien is far from playing it all down.
“The Triple Crown is out of fashion at the minute because you simply can’t get a horse to do it,” he said. “How can you do it? It’s a very difficult thing to do, but it’s only when you get one you think is capable you then realise exactly how difficult it is to do. It’s the total test of the thoroughbred.
“You are testing every bone in their body. It’s the ultimate test and if they can pass that, they are special. They are more than unusual.
“This horse has an awful lot of class and a lovely mind. He’s very uncomplicated, he’s very classy and Ryan (Moore) felt he had plenty left. At least now we can sleep over the winter, see what happens in the Guineas and go from there."
More immediately, the Irishman will hope to put his stamp on a ninth British trainers’ championship with a lucrative performance in Saturday’s Champions Day action at Ascot.
O’Brien is odds-on to overhaul Andrew Balding in a title race that goes to the end of the year, but which could be decided by this weekend’s big-money pots.
Balding’s prizemoney haul of £8,733,326 (about €10.3 million) is marginally ahead of O’Brien on about €10.2 million.
Ascot will also be a target for Irish champion jockey Dylan Browne McMonagle, who finally returns to action with two spins at Roscommon on Monday.
The 23-year-old rider has been on the sidelines since sustaining a bad fall at Bellewstown in late August. At the time he looked like reeling in Billy Lee in the race for the title but will now hope to regain lost momentum ahead of some major international targets.
Talented apprentice Patrick McGettigan enjoyed the biggest success of his career when Tony Martin’s Alphonse Le Grande repeated his 2024 success in Saturday’s Newmarket Cesarewitch. McGettigan has three rides at Roscommon and Minaun View could prove the best of them.
The veteran Mogwli will have the 100th start of his career in one of the seven-furlong handicaps. Despite being ‘wrong’ on ratings, a combination of soft ground and an inside draw could see Willie McCreery’s stalwart mark the landmark with a ninth victory.

title: Ken Early: No longer forced to live a lie, Manchester City fans embraced their club for what it truly is
description: Their titles now mean nothing, yet still they taunted Anfield with a song declaring: ‘Cheating bastards, we know what we are’
content:
T he victorious, banana-festooned Manchester City section at Anfield was a darkly magnificent sight. As the players and fans celebrated, they were like the crew of a pirate ship, brazenly revelling in their plunder.
The days of living a lie are over. Finally City can openly be who they really are.
Many of those fans have spent years furiously insisting, in spite of all evidence to the contrary, that their club had never broken the rules. The mental contortions must have been tiring.
Now that the verdict is in and City have been found guilty of organising the biggest cheating scandal in English football history, the same fans have flipped to insisting that it doesn’t matter that they are guilty. Actually, they are exulting in their renegade status. They taunted Anfield with a song that declared: “Cheating bastards, we know what we are.”
“We didn’t break the rules” was always a tough position to take seriously, given what we all know about City. “Yes, we broke the rules – but they deserved to be broken!” is a position you can get behind.
[ Roy Keane and Jamie Carragher unmoved by ‘devastated’ Micah Richards on Sky Sports Opens in new window ]
The message coming loud and clear from City’s fans and players is: it was all worth it. They won title after title during the years for which they’ve been found guilty, they kept winning titles in the later years not covered by the investigation, they’re still winning. This is the Premier League , where crime pays.
On Friday, Enzo Maresca claimed he still absolutely trusts his employers, despite the text of the recent judgment suggesting that might not be very wise. Maresca even said that his representatives had never discussed the question of the looming 115 charges in the negotiations to take him to City (negotiations which began while he was still the manager of Chelsea).
It was Friday when he introduced the word “noise” to the discourse and at Anfield, he repeated the word 16 times in a 5½ minute post-match press conference. It was one of those moments when a word gets repeated so much you find yourself beginning to lose your grasp on what it means.
“My message is that the noise will be there because, if I say no the noise is not there, [it] is not true. The noise will be there.
“So it’s how we learn to deal with the noise, but at the same time it’s our duty to make our noise – and our noise is to win games in the way we won today and be happy at the end of the game.”
“Noise” is something sportspeople often say they are ignoring and they usually mean things like media froth, excessive criticism or praise, speculation about their chances of winning or losing, “pressure”, etc.
You have to remind yourself that Maresca is using this word, “noise”, to refer to his club being found guilty of the biggest systematic cheating scandal in English football history.
Some ex-City players and coaches are now saying that whatever the final outcome, “they can never take our memories away”. And maybe it does give them genuine pleasure to think back on all the titles they won on easy mode, with Abu Dhabi’s thumb on the scales, cantering away from all the poor saps who were playing by the rules.
[ Tension, ‘cheat’ banners and inflatable bananas: Manchester City’s welcome to Anfield Opens in new window ]
Outside the defiant banana-waving City pirate bubble, those titles no longer mean anything to anybody.
In the 40-page document giving details of the judgment against Manchester City, a table catches the eye. The first column shows Manchester City’s reported sponsorship income every year from 2009/10 to 2017/18. The second shows the actual amount of said income that was paid by Abu Dhabi sponsors. The third column shows the amount of money that the club’s owners, Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), paid in to make up the difference.
We see that ADUG topped up the sponsorship income by £22.5 million in 2010, £28.5 million in 2011, £70.75 million in 2012.
What’s interesting is that the top-up sums just keep getting bigger. £107 million in 2015. £120 million in 2016. £129 million in 2017. £134 million in 2018.
And that’s where the table cuts off, as the recently-concluded investigation did not go beyond the 2017-18 season. (The Premier League announced the investigation in December 2018, following the Spiegel/Football Leaks publication of City’s internal emails).
We are left to wonder: what happened in 2019? Are we to assume that City abruptly changed their whole way of doing business that summer – that ADUG’s contributions went from £134 million in 2018 to £0 in 2019, that everything from that point on was totally legitimate and above board?
In the absence of the sort of evidence Rui Pinto provided on the earlier period, we can only observe that City’s reported sponsorship income continued to grow and grow post-2018. In 2024-25 they reported the highest sponsorship income in world football: £4m more than Real Madrid, £109 million more than Manchester United, £151 million more than Arsenal. A truly extraterrestrial performance by the hardworking commercial department.
That City ran away with the game at Anfield only after Liverpool were reduced to 10 men following Chris Kavanagh’s decision to send off Ryan Gravenberch only heightened the pleasure for the City fans.
As Erling Haaland clubbed in the opener, you had to wonder again, why were City the only club clever enough to sign him for £51 million from Dortmund? Rivals only have themselves to blame for once again being outsmarted by “the Apple of football”.
Admittedly, it doesn’t take much these days to outsmart Liverpool , a club that has been run in a clownish fashion for the last couple of years. Who spends £230 million on Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz, then appoints a manager who plays 100mph rushball that doesn’t suit either of them?
The supposedly “Premier League proven” Isak is actually the bigger of the two flops, but he gets less criticism because he plays fewer games.
Liverpool at least will get most of their money back on Wirtz, who will go to Bayern and be a superstar. It’s clear that joining Liverpool in the summer of 2025 was the wrong move at the wrong time.
Still, it could be worse. He could have joined City.

title: Roy Keane and Jamie Carragher unmoved by ‘devastated’ Micah Richards on Sky Sports
description: A couple of hours later and the City faithful were celebrating their 3-0 win at Anfield
content:
It can’t be an easy time to be a Manchester City ambassador, especially when you have to appear on live telly sandwiched between Jamie Carragher and Roy Keane . But fair play to Micah Richards, he gave it his all on Sky on Sunday.
Micah: “What if they was to win the appeal?”
Micah: “They’re saying they’re innocent.”
Granted, if you were in need, you wouldn’t be hiring Micah as your barrister any time soon, but he still put up a more cogent defence of City than the one Joe Cole presented on TNT Sports on Saturday morning ahead of Arsenal’s lucky win over Leeds.
“The only pure thing about football is what happens on the pitch,” he said. “For me, what they achieved is not tainted. It’s not right to class it in the same way as match fixing. That is the pits. I don’t think they should be punished retrospectively.”
Martin Keown was speechless, which is never a good thing for a pundit. If his mouth had worked at that moment, it might have pointed out that City weren’t actually being punished retrospectively because they actually broke rules that actually existed.
[ Manchester City win at Liverpool in face of Anfield taunts Opens in new window ]
Clinton Morrison kinda went down the “but City won on the pitch” route too on Soccer Saturday, which had Paul Merson hyperventilating. Due to financial shenanigans, he pointed out: “THEY HAD ALL THE BEST PLAYERS – THEY HAD THE TWO BEST PLAYERS IN EVERY POSITION!”
You know the way you can sometimes wonder about how the same body of evidence can be presented to a jury and six of them say guilty and six opt for not guilty? You can but hope that if you ever find yourself in the dock, having being caught on CCTV committing your crime, that Micah, Joe, Clinton and four-ish like-minds are among the 12 good and true. They’d be like, “not proven.”
“I feel devastated,” Micah had said when Sky opened its inquest in to the City business. “I put my neck on the line for this club ... came through the youth team ... I’ve literally got one knee from giving 100 per cent for Manchester City Football Club.”
Roy was moved. Kidding. “There’s all these lovely stories, ‘I came through the youth team’, lovely, it’s lovely,” he said, doing a bit of a rolly eyes thing while Carra chuckled. “But there are other clubs, other people out there doing their best – all you want is a bit of honesty.”
[ Tension, ‘cheat’ banners and inflatable bananas: Manchester City’s welcome to Anfield Opens in new window ]
Micah was clinging to the hope, though, that City’s claim that they had “irrefutable evidence” that they were innocent would win out. Carra asked him why they didn’t present said evidence in their defence. “Em,” said Micah.
Daniel Sturridge was caught between a boulder and an unbreakable place. He had started his footballing life at City, and might have won a league title at Liverpool only for them. “What could have been,” he sighed. But he didn’t want to entirely hang City out to dry.
Roy, meanwhile, noted how English football was always quick to point the finger at supposedly dodgy leagues, like Italy’s at times, priding itself in its integrity. But here we are. City’s owners might not be English, but they were allowed join the party. “They are so powerful, so rich, they’ve never been told no before in their lives,” said Carra.
“Have we thought about how we analyse every City win from now on?” asked our host Mark Chapman. “Let’s hope they get beaten,” said Roy.
A couple of hours later and the City faithful were celebrating their 3-0 win at Anfield, waving their inflatable bananas triumphantly in the air. “And after all, you really robbed us all” and “All of your stars are fading away” read the banners around the ground, but the show goes on.
The mood in the Sky commentary box was funereal. Carra couldn’t decide which was more gutting, his team being so hopelessly blunt or City being City. Gary Neville, who’d had to endure watching United the day before – and Lord above, what an ordeal – was speaking in those hushed tones that always signify something really bad has happened. “A beautiful goal, not necessarily beautiful for the game,” he said of City’s second, scored by Jérémy Doku.
All week, the debate had been about what City’s punishment should be. Gary, you suspected, was feeling the ultimate sanction would be them having to swap their squad for United’s. Having to exchange, say, Doku and Erling Haaland for Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo would cure them.

title: Joe Humphreys: How to talk to boys about masculinity and the meaning of life
description: First, let go of any attempt to impose your view. Accept the risk that you might hear things you don’t expect
content:
Boys are not great talkers when it comes to serious stuff. Speaking as one myself (let’s face it, most men are just adult boys, right down to the laughing at fart jokes), we are great at deflecting. Avoiding deep questions is our stock in trade.
Add to that a general reluctance in society towards acknowledging specific problems facing boys and men.
Boys are falling behind in education, and men in lower socio-economic groups have been particularly badly hit by reduced incomes and rising job insecurity. As economist Richard Reeves writes in his book Of Boys and Men, these problems are “structural in nature, rather than individual” but they tend to get sidelined in modern debate on gender.
“We can be passionate about women’s rights and compassionate toward vulnerable boys and men,” Reeves points out.
So how do we break down defences against discussing men’s issues. How do we conduct necessary conversations with boys about their purpose in life and their ideas of manhood? This is a serious challenge for parents and educators.
For advice, Unthinkable turned to Robert Grant, founder of Hearlisten, which brings the practice of philosophical dialogue to schools and community groups. Between 2020 and 2025, he ran different sets of dialogues with boys and young men for a project called What Does He Need?, which was hosted by artist and educator Fiona Whelan, Rialto Youth Project, and Brokentalkers, an artistic project exploring societal influences on men and boys.
Grant, who holds a PhD in philosophy from TCD and advocates for philosophy in schools, has some lessons for the rest of us from the experience:
What questions would you use to start a conversation about masculinity with boys?
“When discussing masculinity with boys and men, we found it best to approach the subject obliquely, to come at it indirectly. To ‘tympanise’, as French philosopher Jacques Derrida put it: the tympanic membrane is stretched at an angle over the ear drum, creating a greater surface area and finer precision in hearing.
“So, instead of going head-on into ‘What is a man?’ or ‘What is masculinity?’... we generated a set of philosophical provocations used to spark dialogue. For example, ‘It is a man’s responsibility to protect those he cares for’, or ‘Men are not as strong as they used to be’, or ‘To be a man is to act like a man’, along with themes of violence, identity, and power.
“These statements invite participants to take an initial stand on a particular issue. But once the conversation starts to flow – with careful guidance – the focus inevitably shifts to the assumptions behind those ideas: what is strength? What is care? Where does responsibility come from? Is showing weakness a sign of strength? Is masculinity a performance? Who protects the protector?
“Through these more abstract discussions a view of masculinity emerges, but not in a reductive or prescriptive way. Rather, the dialogue creates space for contradictions, complexity and nuance to emerge. We are not seeking to arrive at a definition of masculinity, but creating an opportunity where boys, or men, can question their assumptions together.”
What are the things to look out for – or to guard against – to ensure it’s a healthy dialogue?
“The health of a dialogue is in direct proportion to the quality of listening that takes place. Too many of our conversations in life, and specifically with young people, tend to be one-way ... ‘Anyone who listens is fundamentally open’, as German philosopher Hans-Georg Gadamer put it.
“This involves letting go of control, of predetermined agenda, of any attempt to impose your view, and taking the risk that you might hear things you don’t expect, you don’t fully understand, you don’t agree with, or that you find uncomfortable.”
[ Unthinkable: Is science being skewed by a gender bias? Opens in new window ]
How do you deal with a conversation if someone says something problematic?
“This can happen just as easily with fully grown adults as with young people. In our practice, we err on the side of openness. We try to avoid moralising or policing thought, which can lead to defensiveness or shutting-down ... It may push people back into those reductive, simplified, echo chambers where views are reinforced.
“But deciding not to moralise is not the same as allowing ideas go unchallenged. Within the methodology of philosophical dialogue lies the obligation to justify your views with reasons. Our approach allows the burden of proof to fall back on those ideas by asking deeper questions: What do you mean by that? How do you define that term? Are there any exceptions? Where do those ideas come from? What if everyone thought that way? Who benefits from people believing that?
“Often times, strongly held views find themselves on shaky ground in the face of genuine critical investigation. This exchange is not done to ridicule or humiliate either. It’s not about winning or ‘gotcha’ moments. It is about taking someone’s ideas seriously enough to warrant thoughtful critique so you can get closer to truth, rather than simply dismissing.”
What else have you learnt from the work?
“I am aware that the potential of philosophical dialogue to reach young boys and men is limited. We are dealing with young, intelligent, vital, energetic boys with access to an infinite amount of mesmerising, exploitative content streamed directly into their consciousness.
[ ‘Young men aren’t just b****rds running around on their bikes ... everyone has their own dreams’ Opens in new window ]
“They are caught at a historical moment where late-capitalist, hyper-individualised society has left them with a dwindling sense of community, purpose, and meaning. The world is literally burning thanks to the adults who’ve been managing it. These boys need much more than just conversations, but it is definitely a good place to start.”

title: Fianna Fáil councillor in Co Clare ordered to pay €5,000 after ‘unlawful’ rent review
description: Rita McInerney, a well-known figure in Doonbeg who was mentioned in the White House by the Taoiseach, said the property was ‘underperforming’
content:
A Fianna Fáil councillor has been ordered to return more than €5,000 to her tenants in overcharged rent after a Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) tribunal deemed a rent review, which more than doubled the amount, unlawful.
Rita McInerney, who has been a Fianna Fáil councillor in Co Clare since 2024 and previously served as chief executive of the Ennis Chamber, sought to increase Bartosz Milinski and Marta Kostanowicz’s rent from €650 to €1,500.
McInerney told the tribunal the previous rent of €650 was “well below market value” and that the “asset was underperforming”, according to a tribunal report published on Friday.
Milinski, who received the rent review notice in 2025, said the amount was “disproportionate”, arguing that similar properties in the area were being rented for between €700 and €1,000. He had been renting the house on Doonbeg’s Main Street since 2016.
The tribunal heard McInerney issued a notice of termination to the tenants in January this year on rent arrears grounds. It followed a warning letter which gave them 28 days to pay €5,100 following the rent review, which came into effect in June 2025.
However, Milinski said the sum had been paid within the 28 days provided.
McInerney, who also ran in the 2024 general election for Fianna Fáil, coming seventh in the four-seat constituency, claimed she was entitled to serve the eviction notice. She alleged Milinski “continued to default in paying the new rent” for several months.
In the rent review notice, the tribunal heard McInerney, who owns McInerney’s shop in Doonbeg, used an apartment in Kilkee as one of the comparables.
Milinski argued this was “not comparable”, saying Kilkee was a holiday village with a population of “1,000” while Doonbeg had a population of “300” and “had no beach”.
McInerney said it was difficult to find comparable properties rented within four weeks in Doonbeg, saying it was a “highly sought-after area”.
The tribunal heard she issued a subsequent notice of termination in March this year as she required the property for her own use.
Her tenant questioned her intention to occupy the property, claiming it had “always been a rental property and the landlord had not lived there”.
However, McInerney explained the property was built in 2005 and she rented it out after she had moved into her parents’ home several years ago to care for them, telling the tribunal they were both now deceased.
Under the terms of father’s will, she said her brother owned the family home, and she needed to vacate “as soon as possible”.
The tribunal deemed the rent review invalid, saying McInerney did not include “adequate comparables” to support the rent sought, though it accepted it was difficult to get “exact comparables” due to the lack of properties being advertised.
However, it said the rules were “clear”, and it deemed the rent review “unlawful” before ordering her to refund the tenants €5,100 in overpaid rent within 28 days.
It also deemed the notice of termination issued on rent arrears grounds invalid, reiterating there was “no lawful rent review”.
It separately deemed the eviction notice issued in March valid, saying it was satisfied McInerney required the property for her own use. It said the tenants should vacate before or on the termination date in December.
McInerney, who is a well-known figure in Doonbeg, has regularly commented on US president Donald Trump’s ties to the local community.
During his visit to the White House in 2025, Taoiseach Micheál Martin passed on a message Trump from McInerney, to “thank his family for the way they have worked with the local community, and for the work they they’ve done”.

title: Psychotherapy group files complaint to EU against Minister for Health over sector standards
description: Formal complaint ‘not an action we have taken lightly, says IACP chief executive
content:
An organisation representing counsellors and psychotherapists has filed a formal complaint to the European Commission against the Minister for Health over new standards for the sector.
Last year, Coru , the regulator for health and social care professionals, published new training standards for psychotherapists that will be brought into law after years of the sector calling for Government regulation.
However, four representative organisations have raised concerns that the new standards will lower the quality of training, creating risks for the safety of clients as well as the employability of therapists outside of Ireland.
The organisations are: the Irish Council for Psychotherapy, the Irish Association of Humanistic and Integrative Psychotherapy, Irish Association of Counsellors and Psychotherapists (IACP) and the European Association of Psychotherapy.
The four organisations raised concerns that under the new standards, there is no requirement for personal therapy, no clinical supervision, that clinical practice of only 200 hours is required and that there is no minimum education course length.
The IACP said its complaint to the European Commission relates to its view that the “legally-required proportionality assessment was not properly carried out”.
Lisa Molloy, chief executive of the IACP, said the formal complaint was “not an action we have taken lightly”.
“The IACP has consistently supported robust statutory regulation of counselling and psychotherapy, but regulation must strengthen public protection in practice, not inadvertently weaken established standards or reduce access to services,” she said.
[ Should therapists be in therapy? Unpacking the rift over psychotherapy standards in Ireland Opens in new window ]
“Our legal advice raises questions about whether the EU proportionality requirements were properly addressed in the development of the standards and criteria.”
Molloy warned that if the requirements proceed unchanged, there is a “real risk” of reducing future practitioners “at a time when access to counselling and psychotherapy is critically important”.
“The consequences for accessibility, quality and public protection could be significant and long-lasting,” she said.
“We are calling on the Minister and Coru to pause further implementation while the complaint is examined, engage meaningfully with the profession, educators and placement providers, and ensure that the regulatory system strengthens, rather than destabilises, Ireland’s counselling and psychotherapy services.”
A spokeswoman for the Department of Health said it was aware the IACP has submitted a complaint in relation to the proportionality test and will “engage with the commission as required”.
The spokeswoman said Coru submitted an assessment report to the department, which was then sent to the Department of Further and Higher Education “in line with the proportionality test directive”.
[ Psychotherapy regulator cited ‘wider implications’ in rejecting personal therapy proposal Opens in new window ]
“Throughout its work to regulate designated professions, Coru has continued to work with the Department to ensure compliance with EU requirements under the Directive,” she said.
“Coru and the board are now moving into the next phase of work to introduce regulation of both professions, with a focus on preparing for the approval and monitoring of education and training programmes.”
Coru has consistently defended its standards in response to criticisms from the professional bodies, describing them as “robust” and adding they ensure those entering the profession have the qualifications to provide “safe and effective care”.
“Coru has extensive experience in introducing regulation, having already done so for 12 professions. This has been a universally positive development,” a statement by the regulator previously said.
However, it also noted that concerns regarding the length of education programmes reflect “a misunderstanding of Coru’s role” as it does “not dictate how courses are delivered”.
Furthermore, Coru said that concerns that the standards will make it harder for practitioners to move between EU countries is “inaccurate” and the “opposite is true”.

title: Trump and Hegseth’s road to barbarism is a threat to America’s standing
description: The decision to livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan is a sign of profound moral decay
content:
A raucous crowd of 20,000 gathered in Owensboro, Kentucky, in 1936 to watch the hanging of Rainey Bethea, a 22-year-old convicted rapist. Revulsion at the media frenzy and carnival-style atmosphere led to a US ban on public executions that has stuck for 90 years. This week, Pete Hegseth , America’s self-named “secretary of war”, broke that taboo when he said the Pentagon would livestream the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, a military psychiatrist who shot and killed 13 of his fellow soldiers. “People need to understand that there are serious consequences for these type of things,” Hegseth said. As a public service, Hasan’s death by firing squad would be available to all.
Edward Gibbon, the 18th-century historian who attributed Rome’s fall to the “triumph of barbarism and religion”, might have felt a pang of recognition.
Hegseth has devoted his time at the Pentagon to re-establishing a culture of “lethality”. This has included championing testosterone as the ultimate warrior quality and the purging of women and minorities from the military’s senior ranks. Last week, he created the Pentagon “office of religious affairs”, which would lift spiritual health to the same level as physical. “Our department is, you might say, putting on the full armour of God, because while we wage physical war, we all know the real battle is spiritual,” Hegseth said.
It is unclear whether Hegseth’s morbid gimmick would be a one-off or open a new chapter in America’s fraught history of crime and punishment. Hasan’s lawyers are expected to argue it would amount to constitutionally banned “cruel and unusual punishment”.
Should it go ahead, the United States would join Iran, Afghanistan and North Korea in the small group of countries that stage public executions. Most democracies have long since banned capital punishment. Britain’s last executions were in 1964. Its last open-air hanging was in Victorian London. The Quakers were key to bringing in the ban by arguing that it “brutalises a society that kills”.
Hegseth and Trump are unlikely to be swayed by such qualms. It is conceivable Trump will reverse Hegseth’s decision if public revulsion takes hold. Thom Tillis, an outgoing Republican senator, called it “beyond disgusting”. But Trump’s fascination with televised spectacle goes deep. On his 80th birthday in June, he hosted a UFC ultimate fighting match on the White House lawn, which had a viewership of 34mn.
Though there is no suggestion Hegseth will set up a pay-per-view scheme for Hasan’s execution, Trump would undoubtedly pay keen attention to the ratings. He is a lifelong enthusiast for capital punishment. On his first day in office, Trump lifted the moratorium on federal executions and said it should automatically apply to illegal immigrants convicted of murder and anyone who kills a law enforcement officer. He also added firing squad, electrocution and nitrogen gas to the permitted menu of options alongside lethal injection. Hasan would be the first person to be executed by a US military firing squad since 1945.
[ Trump administration condemned for plans to livestream execution Opens in new window ]
What would Hasan’s staged execution do to America’s soft power? Recent polling shows that a majority of countries, including US allies, now view China more favourably than the US. The long-standing image of the United States as a society with an egalitarian temper that welcomes all comers is fast receding. The world has become familiar with footage of masked Ice officers snatching mothers from day care centres. They see a US president releasing one fake AI video that depicts Barack and Michelle Obama as monkeys. Another showed a crowned “King Trump” piloting a plane that splatters excrement on the “No Kings” marches below.
Other than opinion polls, it is difficult to put a metric on the scale of America’s reputational harm. Nor would this be likely to influence Trump or Hegseth. The latter has staked his career on kinetic displays of hard power and a contempt for soft. But a contemporary Gibbon would surely take a stab at evaluating the harm. The historian placed greater emphasis on Rome’s internal moral decay than on the menace of barbarians from without. A society that loses its civic virtues wastes its vital sinews, he observed. Bread and circuses kept Romans entertained. Yet they sapped the republic of all that was noble.
