title: From Ireland to New Zealand and back again. Twice
description: As a child moving back to Ireland, my classmates welcomed me as if I had never not been sitting beside them
content:
W hen I returned to Ireland from New Zealand at 11 years old, I was so happy. Before I had ever heard the word nostalgia, it was filling my insides, choking me up like a great glug of accidentally swallowed seawater.
We moved into a rented house in Cregmore, Galway , down a narrow boreen flanked by bare fields. At school, I held a hurl in my hands for the first time (it didn’t remain there for very long).
I felt at home with my new after-school minder, whose easy warmth and fondness of Aromat sparked deep-rooted associations from earlier life before we had left; half-memories of my granny and grandad’s kitchen, the radio blaring, dinner smells at lunchtime.
I lay in bed at night with my door slightly open, listening to the Father Ted opening credits drifting up from downstairs. This easy tune, Songs of Love, had me high on the feeling of safety, the feeling that I was finally back in the place I was meant to be.
My school, which at the time consisted of two rooms, taught fifth and sixth classes together. My classmates welcomed me in a way that felt like I had never not been sitting beside them.
I did a quick job masking the Kiwi accent I’d picked up until I didn’t have to emulate the other kids anymore, it became natural. My teacher spent extra time helping me learn all my prayers before Confirmation, and even this new religious knowledge, while completely removed from my personal interests, made me feel comforted, in on it; whatever it was.
As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end, Amen
Slowly the phone calls to my best friend back in Wellington fizzled and I buried that temporary home, so far away from my real one, 12,000 miles away from all conscious thoughts.
[ A message for Ireland from one of the lesser-known Irish-American Kennedys Opens in new window ]
This year, I went back with my husband, on our honeymoon. He had also lived in Wellington, but as a 28-year old. So our experiences had been very different: boogie boarding vs bars.
We drove out along the coast to Ōwhiro Bay, salt wind whipping against the windshield, an old quarry visible in the distance. We walked right up to my old house facing the water. It surprised me how like itself it still looked. It had been painted but the steps up to the rounded, wooden side door were the same, the dark post smooth under my palm.
[ If my granny saw me reading a novel, she’d tell me to do something useful Opens in new window ]
I could see a woman working inside at the kitchen table but I didn’t feel like disturbing her. I stood in front of the garage, underneath my old bedroom, and looked for a long time out on to the sea, at the view I had stared out at for three years as a child. Sometimes there’d be nothing but wind and waves, other times a couple of dolphins would glide by.
I crossed the road, jumped across a couple of rocks and crunched my way through mounds of dried seaweed, taking pictures of broken paua shells and rubbing their shiny iridescent skin.
We went for a walk through the old quarry, the Red Rocks, where in the distance, around a sharp corner, stands the Devil’s Gate. Sometimes at the weekend we would come here for a drive. I have no memory of what lies beyond the Devil’s Gate, only that maybe it’s more of the same, just grey stones and ominous open space. My husband skipped a few stones into the water. No seals lounged on the rocks, but they must have been close; their smell was as thick as their skin.
I experienced a certain loneliness in New Zealand as a child. I’m not sure what I was expecting to feel this time, but it was nothing dramatic. It took me a while to place it, but I think it was a sense of peace.
Jordan Lillis is doing a PhD in creative writing at University College Cork .

title: Garda overtime bill for Russian embassy security to exceed €1m
description: Overall cost of protecting Moscow’s south Dublin mission since Ukraine invasion now several million euro
content:
An Garda Síochána’s security operation at the Russian embassy compound in south Dublin has cost the State millions of euro since it began in 2022, with overtime expenditure alone now about to reach €1 million.
Sources said overtime spending “supplemented” the main operation, which is mostly run on rostered Garda hours. As a result, the overall cost of the security operation has now reached several million euro, they said.
Information obtained by The Irish Times suggests overtime spending this year has been higher than at any point since the round-the-clock Garda operation at the embassy in Rathgar began just after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
In the first half of this year, the overtime bill was €123,907. Garda sources said that due to the policing pressures of Ireland’s presidency of the Council of the European Union since July 1st, it was likely more of its operation outside the Russian embassy would need to be funded with overtime in the second half of this year.
Between March 2022 and the end of June this year the Garda had spent €875,000 on overtime ensuring a full-time Garda presence at the embassy, the main entrance to which is off Orwell Road . It means the overtime bill is soon expected exceed €1 million.
The Garda commenced a large-scale security operation at the embassy in the weeks following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. While patrols around the embassy were stepped up immediately the invasion began, a much larger, full-time and static security presence was put in place within weeks.
This happened after an ecclesiastical supplies lorry was reversed into the embassy gates in March 2022 in protest at the invasion, raising concerns that other forms of direct protest could take place. The Office of Public Works was forced to repair the damage to the gates, at a cost of €13,250. The driver was acquitted in court of dangerous driving.
Russian ambassador to Ireland Yury Filatov complained at the time that gardaí were not doing enough to keep him and his staff safe.
After that incident, uniformed gardaí were posted outside the embassy on a 24-hour basis with security barriers also erected. A Garda command-and-control centre was put in place for a time. Garda Headquarters was keen to deter any future criminal forms of protest, though peaceful protest has been facilitated.
As part of the operation, which remains in operation, Garda members open and close a security barrier to allow staff enter and exit in vehicles. Just behind them, inside the grounds, Russian security staff are posted.
Although the embassy is in a quiet suburban setting, it is a vast complex bounded by residences and streets, which poses additional challenges for gardaí. Aside from the main property, which is visible from the road, a number of large buildings have been constructed behind it, including two three-storey over-basement apartment buildings.
It includes underground car parking for staff. The compound also has its own ESB substation and satellite dishes and antennas.
While concern has been expressed about the scale of the embassy, now a mini campus, gardaí and the Government have been keen to deter any attacks or incursions as the war on Ukraine continues.
They fear an incident, even one planned as a non-violent protest, may spin out of control and they want to avoid adverse international media coverage that may arise from a breach of security.

title: ‘Shoes and beds are the two things I won’t skimp on. If you’re not in one, you’re in the other’
description: Me & My Money: Brendan Harte, residential director, NorDan Ireland
content:
Brendan Harte is the residential director at NorDan Ireland, the local unit of the Norwegian window and door company, which is marking its centenary this year.
A saver, but only because I got a fright. I was 24 when the recession hit, and it scared the spending out of me almost overnight. Before that I was a shocking spender.
What was the first job you received money for, and how much were you paid?
Working for my dad on attic conversions in the UK when I was 11. I got £20 a day for sweeping up the site and carrying tools. The homeowners used to slip me a few quid on top because they thought I was cute.
For anything big, yes. For the small stuff, I’m a creature of habit, and do the same food shop every week without thinking about it. Holidays get the full treatment, however. We choose five or six places, put them into a spreadsheet with flights, accommodation and what there is to do, and we select on value. I love buying houses and doing them up, so furniture and interiors get the same scrutiny.
What has been your most extravagant purchase, and how much did it cost?
Suit shoes. In the last few years, I’ve spent €400 or €500 a pair, and I can justify it on cost per wear because they last. My grandfather looked after his shoes, paid for quality and kept them polished, and that stayed with me without my noticing. I’m careful about spending on myself otherwise, but shoes and beds are the two things I won’t skimp on. If you’re not in one, you’re in the other.
‘I was 24 when the recession hit and it scared the spending out of me almost overnight’
What purchase have you made that you consider the best value for money?
My dog’s food. It’s expensive but it’s human-grade, the dog is healthier on it and it saves on vet bills. A close second is a dehumidifier. I can’t stand looking at a clothes horse. In an old house it dries the washing in no time and keeps the damp down.
Is there anything you regret spending money on?
The carpets on the ground floor of my house. It was the quick option, and I knew it at the time. I should have put the time and money into hardwood floors, done right for the age of the house, but I ended up with a space that was just finished rather than the space I wanted.
Mostly no. I find it awkward, and I’d rather buy something that’s worth what they’re asking.
Do you invest in shares and/or cryptocurrency?
Shares, yes. A slice of my salary goes into them every month, mainly to have something outside of pay and pension. Crypto? No, and I’ve earned the right to wince at that. Around 2012, a customer in America wanted to pay for a $26,000 order of windows and doors in Bitcoin, and I turned him down. Bitcoin was about $5 at the time. I’ve stopped doing the sum, but the last time I looked, it was the guts of $400 million. Not my finest hour.
[ ‘On Room to Improve everyone goes miles over budget - I just can’t’ Opens in new window ]
Do you have a retirement or pension plan?
Yes. I max out my contributions for the tax relief, and the plan is to retire somewhere warm with my husband Tom.
What was the last thing you bought, and was it good value for money?
The weekly shop. With prices the way they are, I’m not sure any big shop counts as value for money any more, but planning the meals and cooking in batches is the closest I get.
Have you ever successfully saved up for a relatively big purchase?
Our first home. We saved for it during Covid, which was easier and harder at the same time. There was nothing to spend money on and we were lucky that construction kept going, so there was enough coming in to put something away every month.
Yes. I went to America at 25 as a part-owner of a business, and, at 29, I tried to buy out the other owners. It didn’t happen and I lost money in the process. What I got instead was perspective. I realised there’s more to life than work and I’ve built things around that since.
Are you a gambler and, if so, have you ever had a big win?
I’ve never set foot in a betting shop; I’m too afraid of losing the money. The closest I’ve come was a day at the races where I put a tenner on 10 races and lost every one of them. The luck you make yourself is worth more.
[ We bought the bank, and now we live in it Opens in new window ]
What is your best habit when it comes to money? And your worst?
My best habit is that I divide my wages up at the start of every month and give each category a limit. Pension, investments and the mortgage first, then socialising, clothes and the rest. That way I know exactly where the money is going, and if there’s anything left over at the end, I get a treat.
My worst habit is subscriptions. I’ll sign up for a free trial of Disney Plus or ClassPass and forget it exists until it turns up on a statement months later. All the planning in the world and I still get caught by a monthly €12 direct debit!
Nothing. I run almost entirely on cards. The only cash I could lay my hands on is the €2 coin I have for the shopping trolley. And for all that, I still don’t have Revolut.

title: ‘If it’s lost it will be lost forever’: What future for Galway Airport?
description: Joint owners Galway City Council and Galway County Council are looking at potential sale of 118-acre site
content:
Fifteen years after Ireland’s economic crash led to the demise of commercial flights at Galway Airport, local businesspeople and aviation advocates are campaigning to save its runway and air travel infrastructure.
Joint owners Galway City Council and Galway County Council are contemplating selling the valuable 118-acre site at Carnmore, which has huge potential due to its proximity to the M6 east-west and M17/18 north-south motorways, just 8km outside Galway city.
The Galway Aviation and Innovation Advocacy (GAIA) group is, however, adamant that the airport’s strategic assets – its runway and two hangars – should be protected in any sale to safeguard the region’s economic future and emergency medical capabilities.
“Galway Airport should be viewed as an investment in the future rather than a legacy of the past,” said the group’s chairperson, former senator Fidelma Healy Eames.
“Once a runway is removed and aviation capability is lost, it is exceptionally difficult and costly, if not impossible, to recreate.”
The airport dates to the 1970s, when German industrialist Ernst Steiner developed an airstrip opposite his factory that supplied materials to the capacitator industry.
It was later acquired by Galway Chamber of Commerce, whose investment attracted commercial flights, mostly to Dublin and London. It proved popular for time-poor business executives in a pre-motorway time when getting to Dublin Airport involved lengthy road journeys with bottlenecks at Kinnegad and Enfield.
In its Celtic Tiger heyday in 2007, Galway Airport handled a record 309,000 passengers to 16 European destinations. Four years later, it succumbed to the turbulence of the economic crash.
The airport was delivered a double blow in 2011 when the Department of Transport withdrew public service obligation (PSO) funding on Aer Arann’s Dublin-Galway service, and a value-for-money review of regional airports recommended its closure on economic grounds.
The then minister for transport Noel Dempsey, his successor Leo Varadkar, and department officials argued the need for the airport was negated by improved rail and road networks, and also by proximity to Shannon and Knock airports, with larger runways that could handle larger aircraft.
Galway was a “sacrificial lamb”, according to Dr Eamonn O’Donoghue of GAIA group.
“A critical, reflex decision was made 15 years ago in a specific group of circumstances that are not relevant now,” he insisted.
Galway Chamber offloaded the site to the two local authorities for €1.1 million in 2013.
They piloted a park-and-ride facility there later that year, but it did not work out without a bus lane to the city. It fared better in 2020 as a temporary HSE drive-through Covid-19 testing centre.
Danú Media, with Údarás na Gaeltachta and the Western Development Commission, was granted planning permission in 2021 for a multimillion-euro TV and film studio at the airport. That did not proceed, however, after temporary planning permission granted for the development limited its operation to five years.
Last year, both councils invited expressions of interest (EOI) from prospective purchasers of the airport site.
[ County council to investigate buying out city’s stake in former Galway Airport site Opens in new window ]
Galway Ladies Gaelic Football Association announced earlier this year that it wanted to build a “centre of excellence” there, but it did not make a submission before the EOI deadline.
Separately, Atlantic Flight Training Academy offered to lease the site for use as a commercial flight training centre. This option – not part of the EOI process – would keep the asset in public ownership.
Eighteen months after EOIs were invited from organisations interested in buying the site, the councils last week confirmed that none of the six proposals met the criteria to progress the future development of the site.
The councils said they have now decided to “examine the establishment of an appropriate delivery entity to lead and co-ordinate the future development of the site”.
Meanwhile, support for the advocacy group’s cause gathers pace.
Representing more than 500 businesses, Galway Chamber said the region was well-served by Shannon and Ireland West airports, but it wanted a feasibility study to establish Galway Airport’s opportunities.
“We believe it is important that the site’s full potential is understood before decisions are made about its future,” said outgoing chamber president Cait Noone.
Management at the five-star Ashford Castle sees potential for growth in VIP tourism through Galway Airport. Managing director Niall Rochford said the luxury destination’s “growing cohort of high-net-worth international guests” expect “direct, discreet and personalised travel access”.
“Direct aviation connectivity to Galway would significantly enhance our ability to attract and retain high-value visitors, reduce surface transfer times, and elevate the overall visitor experience,” Rochford said in a letter to the group, which emphasised the potential “substantial economic multiplier effect” on tourism.
Elsewhere, former minister for defence Michael Smith highlighted the airport’s national security potential. He said transatlantic subsea fibre-optic and digital cables off the west coast were “vulnerable to sabotage or direct attack by malign actors”, and the airport was a “major asset” that could serve as a national security and surveillance hub for “monitoring and patrolling our maritime domain”.
A spokesperson for the Department of Defence , however, said: “No consideration has been given by the Department of Defence to the purchase of the former Galway Airport site.”
[ Galway Airport could become film industry hub, study says Opens in new window ]
O’Donoghue, a GAIA member and consultant ophthalmologist, emphasised the facility’s potential aeromedical benefits.
Close to the region’s only model 4 – or highest acute public – hospital, University Hospital Galway, it could “help save many lives” by reducing response times if used as a base for helicopter emergency medical services, he said.
It could also support air ambulances, urgent medical supplies, organ transport and emergency response during floods, fire and major incidents, O’Donoghue pointed out.
Jarlath Conneely, former managing director of Aer Arann Islands, which operates daily flights between the three Aran Islands and the small Aerfort na Minna airport in Connemara, insisted GAIA was not seeking a return to scheduled commercial flights in the short or medium term.
He said removing the runway would be like the modern equivalent of closing the Clifden-Galway railway in the 20th century.
“We can have the best of both worlds. Keep aviation and develop the site for business,” he said.
Healy Eames, who served on the board of the airport when she was a county councillor, pointed to Station F in Paris – a train station turned innovation centre with more than 1,000 start-up companies – as an example of what Galway Airport could become.
“Before any irreversible decision is taken, every opportunity should be explored to preserve the runway, retain aviation zoning, invite expressions of interest from aviation operators and position Galway Airport as a centre for aviation, innovation, education and emergency services,” she said.
Throughout the airport’s history, Galway Flying Club has been a constant. Last month, 50 aircraft from flying clubs across the country attended a charity fly-in at Galway Airport to celebrate the local club’s 80th year.
[ Derelict Galway Airport site should be used for ‘regional stadium’ Opens in new window ]
Founded in 1946, Ireland’s oldest flying club is a voluntary, not-for-profit organisation with more than 100 members, seven flying instructors and two single-engine, four-seater Cessna 172s.
Since 2013, it has operated from the airport by lease agreement, renewed annually by vote of elected members of both local authorities.
Chairperson Ian Fennell said if the airport is sold, the club “would work with any organisation with a view to maintaining our presence on site”.
Fennell conceded the club would be “in difficulty” if the runway was dismantled by prospective buyers, as “there is no ready alternative available to us for what we do”.
Elsewhere, Peter McKenna, chief executive of Aer Arann Islands, said Galway Airport is a “significant infrastructural asset for the region”.
[ Galway Airport decision too hasty, says city councillor Opens in new window ]
“We are on the cusp of a revolution in private air travel ... The ambition should not be to compete with Shannon or Knock but rather be a next-generation airport for smaller, sustainable aircraft.
“If it’s lost it will be lost forever, just like the railways in the last century,” McKenna said.

title: Mater Hospital has banned 33 patients so far this year, including one for knife threat to staff
description: Fourteen exclusion orders by Dublin hospital were for physical assault, with the other 19 for verbal abuse or threatening behaviour
content:
More than 30 patients have been barred from the Mater Hospital in Dublin so far this year for abusive or threatening behaviour.
In at least two cases, patients who had been admitted to wards were subsequently arrested by gardaí and removed from the hospital.
Management at the Mater said, in a report to its board, that these two incidents related to “violent behaviours towards staff and other patients”.
The Mater Hospital told The Irish Times 33 exclusion orders had been issued between January and the end of September.
“Of these, 14 related to physical assault and 19 to verbal abuse or threatening behaviour,” it said.
The hospital said “excluded patients cannot attend the hospital for a set period based on severity, but emergency care for life- or limb-threatening conditions is always provided”.
It added: “Before exclusion, the care team ensures immediate treatment, arranges follow-up with community services or GPs, and advises patients on accessing care elsewhere.”
The Mater Misericordiae University Hospital, which is based in Dublin ’s north inner city, said it recently updated its policy on dealing with antisocial behaviour, “in recognition of how seriously it takes its duty of care to all who use or work in the hospital”.
“Violence and aggression towards our staff are not acceptable and the hospital will continue to take firm action to keep everyone in the hospital safe,” it said.
The exclusion orders are issued by the hospital, not the courts, under the hospital’s policy on the prevention and management of challenging behaviours.
“The decision to exclude a patient is taken by a senior hospital manager and reported to the office of the chief executive,” it said.
“Exclusion is a last resort, typically following warnings, unless immediate action is required for severe cases like violence or weapon use. It applies only to patients with decision-making capacity, while those with underlying clinical conditions are managed clinically. The hospital involves An Garda Síochána when staff are assaulted or threatened.”
In a report to the board of the Mater during the summer, management at the hospital said antisocial behaviour “remains a challenge”.
Management said at that point (in June), there had been a total of nine exclusion orders issued since the start of the year.
“One exclusion is for a 12-month period where a patient threatened staff with a knife. The remaining eight exclusion orders range between one- [and] two-month periods. Three of these patients had to be removed from the campus by the gardaí.”

title: Áine Lawlor’s new podcast needs to abandon the safety net and take strong positions
description: Ex-RTÉ presenter’s podcasting partnership with former Newstalk host Chris Donoghue has substance but lacks sizzle
content:
If there’s one easy takeaway from State of Affairs, the new politics podcast featuring Áine Lawlor and Chris Donoghue, it’s that while it may be easy to run away to join the media circus, it’s harder to leave it behind. Less than three months since retiring from RTÉ after more than 40 years at the network , Lawlor has rapidly pivoted into the podcasting sphere, while Donoghue, who first made his name as a presenter on Newstalk , returns to the microphone after spending most of the past decade as a government adviser. Despite their differing career paths, the lure of the big top clearly remains the same for both erstwhile broadcasters.
It will take longer to determine whether their somewhat unexpected partnership is enough to persuade listeners to roll up, however. In terms of popular appeal, Lawlor is the marquee name on the independently produced podcast (which drops on Monday and Friday mornings), thanks to her long-time role as presenter on Morning Ireland. But her reputation on Radio 1’s news programme was largely down to her skill as a formidable interviewer of public figures, an option not (so far) available on her new discussion-based podcast.
Donoghue, meanwhile, has an impressive radio pedigree; indeed, as co-presenter of Newstalk Breakfast, he once was Lawlor’s rival in the morning timeslot. But having left broadcasting in 2017 to work as an adviser to then tánaiste Simon Coveney , Donoghue’s experience as an erstwhile political insider is now his main selling point, even if he downplays his capacity for gossip: “I know nothing about this year’s budgetary process, because I’m outside,” he admits, with admirable, if possibly ill-judged, candour.
So while the duo’s talents might appear complementary on paper, effectively meshing them together is another matter altogether. The most obvious Irish template for such political podcast pairings is Path To Power, which featured Today FM presenter Matt Cooper and former minister Ivan Yates bantering away to high chart-ranking results, at least until Yates’s contentious exit last year. Going by the opening episodes of State of Affairs, however, Lawlor and Donoghue have yet to develop a similar chemistry.
This is partly down to the pair’s on-air personas. Lawlor is an authoritative yet reassuring presence, but she isn’t the kind of instinctive provocateur so prized in the digital space. (After years of working as a public service broadcaster constantly scrutinised for bias, such restraint is unsurprising.) And while Donoghue’s deceptively low-key demeanour masks his slyly observant qualities, he’s not naturally a dominating figure; on Newstalk Breakfast he played the sensible sidekick to the blustering opinions of his co-host, the aforementioned Yates.
It’s notable that the pair’s most lively edition features Yates, who recalls his ministerial days in typically swaggering, if insightful fashion. Perhaps wisely, Yates has been signed up as a regular guest; a “commis chef” in his own description, though Donoghue underscores the new pecking order by calling his former colleague “busboy”.
Other guests, such as Euronews reporter Shona Murray, are promised as the series progresses. The podcast also features recorded segments, such as a telling report from the recent fuel cost meeting in Moate, Co Westmeath , where many attendees effortlessly segue from complaints about rising prices to disturbing expressions of anti-immigrant prejudice.
[ Radio: Aine Lawlor gives women’s voices a rare sporting chance Opens in new window ]
But ultimately the podcast rests on the hosts’ ability to generate captivating conversation and acute analysis. At this early stage, the omens are mixed. On the plus side, there’s no shortage of substance. Lawlor and Donoghue dissect topics such as the budget , Drumcree and the latest RTÉ funding crisis in accessible fashion, as befits such seasoned broadcasters.
Further positives include the odd flash of the stiletto – Donoghue describes Minister for Arts Patrick O’Donovan as “a person who can have a fight in an empty lift” – and the occasional personal touch, such as Lawlor’s revelation that she has neuropathy: “I’m oversensitive to the cold.”
So far, however, State of Affairs is more like a good radio current affairs show than an essential appointment-listening podcast. Possibly thanks to their years in mainstream media and centrist politics, neither presenter seems inclined to cut loose with strong opinions, while their approach is collegial rather than confrontational, whether between themselves or with others.
For instance, though Donoghue expresses alarm at rising racism in Ireland, a sentiment also shared by Lawlor, neither host explicitly decries the disquieting views heard in the Moate report. Airing overtly partisan positions so early in their podcast venture is of course a risk, particularly given the reasonably limited market for Irish politics podcasts. But abandoning the safety net by staking out a strong position might equally attract a passionate audience, adding impetus to Lawlor and Donoghue’s fledgling brand. After all, when it comes to thrills, balancing acts can never match trapeze artists.

title: ‘Each piece must be timeless, and bring joy’: Joanne Hynes on her 10-year collaboration with Dunnes Stores
description: The acclaimed fashion designer works on instinct rather than formula, exploring both newness and nostalgia
content:
I n watchmaking, “complications”, highly valued for their craftsmanship, are intricate functions that go beyond just telling the time in hours, minutes and seconds. In the same way, Joanne Hynes ’ complicated fashion designs go far beyond just clothing. Everything she does comes from deep thought and consideration to the point of obsession, making her signature strong and identifiable as a designer. There is always something unexpected, some exuberant detail or embellishment. And there is always an explanation, a raison d’être.
Her latest collection marks a successful 10-year relationship with Dunnes Stores , spanning 20 collections, from which she kept “what was memorable or important or something that would have future stories”. We are meeting in the Atrium at Trinity College Dublin , where her exhibition Always the Weird Girl took place last month, featuring her latest collection along with pieces from her extensive archive.
“I work on instinct, 100 per cent, what is around me, on the floor, on the table. There is no formula. I am always interested in playing around with aesthetics and I have always experimented with newness,” she explains in her usual thoughtful, deliberate way, as she shows me a working patchworked toile as an example of her creative practice.
Included in the display was one of her very first designs after graduating from Central St Martins in London – an Aran sweater studded with salvaged Waterford chandelier crystals. Crystal also featured in a waistcoat she once made for Daphne Guinness, one of her many fans. Others include Lady Gaga , CMAT and more recently Katie Taylor .
The 14 pieces in her latest collection – in limited editions, like all those for Dunnes – are not quite as colourful as usual, another deliberate choice, though there are bold chartreuse velvet opera coats, pink collars and cuffs, fake fur panelling and silvered blue shirts and pom-pom decor. Shapes are pared back, but the material combinations are more structured and allow for more elaborate surface applications.
Sequins, mirror embroidery and chain embellishment reflect the light – a tailored grey trousersuit has bold sequinned sleeves, a shirt is panelled with triangular glass motifs, and she demonstrates how sequinned jeans can be rubbed one way to get a different colour. An intricate black top made from laser-cut nylon on mesh is layered with green velvet chainmail, while a pinstriped jacket has pinched and draped organza sleeves with storm flaps at the front and back. Knitwear is jacquard Lurex, and waistbands are elasticated.
“I am thinking about something that will last through the seasons and yet is what I want to wear today – what a woman wants to wear with reference to the past,” she says. “I am such a nostalgia freak, so this is also about looking back and it felt complete. I always feel grounded in clothes that are big and complicated.”
A standout piece is her two-in-one skirt with a crinoline underneath, attached with a silver skater chain and worn with a PU black jacket with faux marabou shoulders. “Each piece must be timeless and necessary when it’s viewed on its own in isolation. And it must bring joy.”
A mother of six living in Wicklow, Hynes has also been working for the past four years on a book about grief, after a stillbirth in October 2013. Writing it was a means of processing the experience in her own way, and she has already completed 140,000 words. In November she will be taking part in a residency at the Museum of Literature Ireland with an exhibition of the book and mementoes and objects associated with the experience.
Three years ago at the Kevin Kavanagh Gallery, her creative practices were explored in an exhibition entitled What We Carry With Us , which she described as an ongoing dialogue with clothing, writing and self, arguing that “the process of writing and the act of making have similarities”.
Ultimately whatever she does is uniquely personal, and “not about what I should do, but what I should not do”.

title: Budget reversal of policy on tackling climate change was a mistake
description: While its capital investment plans are welcome, more should have done to mitigate the impact of rising fuel prices for those on low incomes
content:
T here are three crucial tasks for any budget : does it implement a long-term economic strategy; is the trajectory of the public finances sustainable; and will it manage aggregate demand in the economy so that economic activity remains close to capacity?
This year the strategic priorities for the Government should be to enhance the economic security of the State and promote long-term growth, tackle climate change , and reduce poverty, especially child poverty.
The budget has further increased our dependence on corporation tax as indirect taxes are reduced, increasing the economy’s vulnerability. However, unlike many other economies, we will still run a small surplus next year; it is just that it should be much larger.
This budget scores well on growth, committing increased resources for infrastructural investment. Government investment, which is €20 billion this year, will increase by almost 15 per cent in 2027. This is more than 5 per cent of national income, much higher than in other countries, reflecting our rapid population growth.
Some of this investment will go on the start-up of MetroLink and other projects, but the fruits of this investment will only be fully apparent many elections hence. Jam today would have been easier for the Government, but this is the right answer.
Where the budget is faulty is the reversal of the policy on tackling climate change . The carbon tax was due to rise gradually to 2030 to encourage us to reduce emissions and to fund investment in key climate projects, such as retrofitting and protecting those on low incomes. This budget has reversed this, cutting the tax rate on certain fuels, with a commitment to leave it at this low level to 2030. This sends all the wrong signals, and it also means there will be significantly fewer resources to protect those who are energy poor and to fund important climate investment, including flood protection .
The number of children in poverty is increasing, despite our run of economic success. Research by the ESRI has shown that the best way to tackle this problem would be to introduce targeted income supports for children living in low-income families. An opportunity to do this was missed last week.
Dealing with the effects of higher inflation on living standards is best done in a number of ways. The income tax system should be indexed so that the tax take does not increase by stealth. In contrast to last year, this budget does this.
The exceptionally high energy prices pose particular problems for those on low incomes, with higher expenditure on heating. This clearly needed to be addressed, and the best way of doing it would have been to increase welfare payments and introduce targeted support for the energy needs of the most vulnerable.
[ The Government won’t raise carbon tax again but promises to decarbonise the economy – how? Opens in new window ]
Instead, Government expenditure on social payments will rise by only 2.7 per cent next year, less than inflation, and there is no significant targeted support for those who need it most.
More of the reduction in excise tax on fuel goes to those on high incomes, reducing the incentive to cut our emissions of greenhouse gases. None of it goes to those who cannot afford a car. An unsatisfactory outcome for the climate, and for those on low incomes who will suffer from the cold this winter.
If the Government sticks to the numbers in the budget it looks likely that it will be neutral, neither stimulating nor deflating the economy. While some tightening would have been better, the stimulus largely arises from the very desirable increase in public investment.
The budgetary numbers published last week also show the share of public expenditure in national income next year will remain roughly unchanged compared to this year. If this proves to be the outcome, it would be satisfactory. However, as with recent budgets, this one carries the seeds of another overrun.
It is no surprise that Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers did not put a precise number on the provision for public service pay next year. He is beginning a negotiating process, and anything he provided would be taken just as the starting point by trade unions. Thus, there is likely to be some overrun to provide for the final outturn of the pay talks.
The provision for social payments looks like an underestimate of what will be spent. Also, once again in some departmental budgets, it looks as if the estimates do not provide for expenditure that will prove unavoidable, for example in health.
While on paper the budget numbers look moderately prudent, as in previous years, they may prove a poor guide to the eventual outturn.

title: More needs to be done to help home-grown companies scale and offset reliance on FDI
description: There are several ways Ireland can enhance its supports for indigenous private businesses
content:
I reland’s economic model has been one of the great success stories of modern Europe. Our multinational sector has transformed employment and public finances. But we have come to a point now when what made us stand apart feels a little less different and we need to look at future-proofing our economy.
At the same time, Ireland’s private sector continues to underperform when it comes to scaling indigenous companies into globally competitive multinationals. Ireland needs to enhance its offering to FDI as well as putting measures in place to help its home-grown businesses scale into global companies.
Ireland’s corporation tax receipts rose from €4.7 billion in 2014 to €32.9 billion in 2025, now accounting for about 31 per cent of total exchequer tax revenue, compared with just 8.3 per cent in 2014.
This concentration is more than 2.5 times the OECD average (12 per cent). Revenue analysis shows that foreign-owned multinationals generate almost 90 per cent of these receipts, while the three largest companies accounted for 46 per cent of all corporation tax paid in 2024.
While it is unlikely that there will be a significant reduction in corporation tax receipts over the next few years, the picture is far less certain over a 10- to 15-year horizon. The challenge for policymakers is that decisions about future investment are being made today. If Ireland waits until corporation tax receipts begin to decline before responding, it may be too late to attract the next wave of investment required to sustain our spending commitments and economic success. The Government needs to act now.
There are several ways Ireland can enhance its offering to international companies as well as doing more for home-grown private businesses.
Firstly, Ireland needs to invest now for the future. This is not simply about protecting existing industries; it is about identifying the sectors that will drive economic growth in the decades ahead and putting the policies, infrastructure and incentives in place now to attract them.
Ireland should be reinvesting part of today’s corporation tax revenues to develop domestic businesses, support innovation and secure the next generation of FDI. The objective should be clear: act while the tide is still coming in, not after it has turned.
Secondly, Ireland needs to become a more compelling location for high-value research, development and innovation activities. The current R&D tax credit, despite small enhancements in Budget 2027 , would benefit from expanding the range of activities covered.
[ State’s tax take boosted by €3bn as multinationals ‘front-load’ payments Opens in new window ]
The relief should be expanded to increase the benefit for advanced manufacturing investment opportunities. Budget 2027 missed an opportunity to introduce a separate innovation incentive for broader innovation activities, supporting investment in areas such as digitalisation and decarbonisation. These reforms would strengthen Ireland’s attractiveness as a global innovation hub while further supporting private companies.
Thirdly, too many promising private businesses are acquired before they reach scale. Irish firms face systemic barriers that limit their ability to grow and scale. Three things are needed to help – capital, capabilities and culture.
The Government has begun to recognise the capital challenge through its proposed €1 billion Scaling Fund announced in Budget 2027. This is a welcome start, but much will depend on the accessibility of funds. Scaling an Irish business towards a public listing should be more attractive and achievable – Euronext Dublin has only about two dozen actively traded equities, compared with nearly 2,000 listed companies across European markets.
The introduction of the State investment account is also a welcome step towards mobilising pools of capital in Ireland, with the potential to channel significant household savings towards active investment and broaden participation in capital markets. The next challenge is ensuring that a meaningful proportion of those funds is channelled into promising Irish companies, helping to create the next generation of indigenous businesses.
While the budget announcement to reduce Capital Gains Tax to 31 per cent is positive, a larger reduction to 20 per cent would have gone a lot further towards encouraging further investment. Furthermore, revised entrepreneur relief should be enhanced and retirement relief expanded.
Irish businesses need the talent, leadership and expertise to help them scale from successful start-ups into global enterprises. The announcement of funding to the National Training Fund to build skills and resilience fit for an AI -enabled workforce was a practical step and a sign that the State can provide supports to nurture these capabilities. But more of this is needed. Finally, Ireland must create a culture that rewards ambition, celebrates success and makes scaling indigenous businesses a national priority.
[ Budget 2027: Measures put public finances on worse trajectory, State watchdog warns Opens in new window ]
Not every competitiveness issue requires money. Often, smaller businesses face administration burdens that consume valuable time and resources without delivering meaningful economic benefits. Simplification has minimal cost to the exchequer but can have a significant impact.
For example, in our pre-budget submission, we suggested pre-populated simplified tax returns for small businesses. The budget move to allow enhanced reporting requirements to be submitted monthly rather than on a real-time basis is a welcome step. However, there remains a strong case for moving to an annual reporting requirement.
The announcement of a holistic assessment of the various grant schemes, enterprise tax incentives and business development programmes now on offer will hopefully lead to meaningful simplification. However, this will only truly deliver impact if a cross-departmental approach is taken, as success is measured by a reduction in form-filling and hours saved processing applications.
Ireland does not need a completely new economic model. The foundations of our success remain strong. However, maintaining success in a changing world requires enhancing our offering to FDI and the private sector – reinvesting for competitiveness. The real question is whether we are prepared to invest today in what will make us attractive tomorrow.
Paraic Burke is head of tax at PwC Ireland

title: Strength tests from around the world: Mallakhamb, Highland Games, arm wrestling and stone lifting
description: Communities across the globe have devised an intriguing range of fitness benchmarks steeped in their heritage
content:
The bench press has been a default measure of strength in many parts of the world for nearly half a century, said Conor Heffernan, a lecturer on the history of sports and physical culture at Ulster University and the author of When Fitness Went Global.
“It’s a shortcut for a whole cultural idea of strength: upper-body power, muscular masculinity, gym credibility and a number that can be understood by lifters and non-lifters alike,” said Heffernan.
But in centuries past, many other tests of strength were more practical: Communities needed to identify and train their fittest members for military service or employment. “Some tests of strength were just job interviews,” said Heffernan.
Many of these strength tests are still practised around the world, and some are more accessible than lifting at the gym. The equipment is often publicly available in parks or in nature and sometimes all that’s required is your body or an opponent.
Think of the most challenging yoga pose you’ve ever held. Now imagine attempting it at the top of a smooth wooden pole 25cm wide, 2.5m tall and polished with oil, and you’ll be getting close to mallakhamb, an ancient sport in India that combines yoga, gymnastics and martial arts.
“Mallakhamb is a sport where you have to play against gravity,” said Ravi Gaikwad, a trainer and the founder of Mallakhamb India, an organisation that teaches and promotes the sport.
Sometimes called “the mother of all Indian sports,” mallakhamb tests grip strength, total body stamina and balance and was once used as a training regimen for soldiers and wrestlers.
It trains your body “from top to bottom,” said 26-year-old Abhishek Prasad, a mallakhamb athlete in Mumbai.
[ ‘Lymphatic workouts’ and the latest social media wellness hype Opens in new window ]
In a mallakhamb competition, athletes have 90 seconds to perform. They are judged on five categories, including acrobatic feats and poses they perform on the pole, catching the pole after performing a skill in mid-air and balancing during static poses. Athletes can compete individually or as a team, with multiple people on the pole at once.
The sport is part of the curriculum in many schools. Vinayak Dhamne (40), a former athlete, learned about it as a student when he was 14. Not everyone is cut out for mallakhamb, Dhamne said. “You get rashes. Sometimes it burns your legs.”
May through September is the Highland Games season in Scotland, when bagpipe players, dancers, runners, cyclists and strength athletes gather to take part in a 1,000-year-old tradition.
More than 60 annual Highland Games take place across Scotland each year. The “heavy events” are a centrepiece of the games. The most famous events are the hammer throw and the caber toss, in which athletes flip a long wooden pole (which can weigh up to 80kg) end-over-end. Depending on the contest, entrants may also have to toss a 9-12kg stone, throw a 25kg metal block backward over a high bar or use a pitchfork to pitch a burlap sack stuffed with straw.
Anyone can participate in the games, regardless of their skill or strength level, but participants often spend months training, said Elizabeth Elliot, (46), who lives near Glasgow and has been competing for 20 years. Many athletes will spend their off season in the gym building power and endurance, she said.
Technical prowess is also important. “You can be very strong and pick up a caber,” Elliot said, “but you might not be able to do anything with it.”
[ A Wicklow woman in Marbella: ‘I would make friends in the summer and they would then go home. But I found my tribe’ Opens in new window ]
The Highland Games began in the mid-to-late 11th century as a way for King Malcolm III to find his messengers and bodyguards, said Alan Pettigrew, an official with the Royal Scottish Highland Games Association. Long after Malcolm’s reign ended, the tradition continued. “We weren’t going to war as much, but they kept the Games,” Pettigrew said.
Today, most of the festivals across Scotland also include cultural practices, such as Highland dancing and bagpipe playing. The Games have now also expanded to other countries, including the United States and Canada, as well as Australia and New Zealand, said Pettigrew.
Arm wrestling may be one of the simplest ways to settle a debate over strength. “You just go to the table and then you pull,” said Charles Osei Asibey, president of the Armwrestling Federation of Africa.
Becoming a competitive arm wrestler takes a bit more work. Grace Minta, (41), who in 2024 became the first African woman to win a gold medal at the World Armwrestling Championship, trains using dumbbells to build wrist and shoulder strength, squatting to build lower-body strength and running to build stamina.
Minta is a member of Ghana’s national team, the Golden Arms. She is one of a growing number of athletes in Ghana to specialise in competitive arm wrestling, Asibey said. The sport is a pastime that has long been part of the country and the continent’s culture, and it was often used to decide who was the strongest in the community or in school, Asibey said.
[ Dua Lipa to Dior: How books became fashion’s hottest new accessory Opens in new window ]
Arm wrestling “doesn’t have an established birthplace”, Heffernan said, and versions of the practice have existed around the world for centuries in places like North America, eastern Europe, Japan and Brazil.
Last May, Ghana hosted the Africa Armwrestling Federation Championship with 450 athletes from 22 countries. Their team placed first.
When Yuta Sakamoto wants to build strength, he doesn’t head to the gym. Instead, he goes to his local shrine. There, he selects a chikara ishi, or a “power stone”, weighing around 90kg, lifts it from the ground and hoists it up to his shoulder. For Sakamoto, the practice is less about getting fit and more about reconnecting to a long-forgotten cultural practice.
Stone lifting has been used as a measure of strength around the world for thousands of years. In Japan, stones were lifted in community rituals, religious ceremonies and performances of strength, by everyone from samurais to labourers, Sakamoto said. Around 200 years ago, one’s ability to lift a stone 60kg – roughly equivalent to a bale of rice – often determined whether they were strong enough to work in manual labour, he said.
Stone lifting was a significant part of Japanese culture, but after the Industrial Revolution, the practice largely disappeared from daily life, said David Dunlap, director of Tenka Musou, Japan’s international strongman federation.
Thousands of lifting stones now sit largely dormant in shrines across Japan, he said. Many are engraved with the names of the men who lifted them.
Tenka Musou holds annual strength competitions in Japan to help carry on stone lifting traditions. At this year’s event, in March, about 70 athletes from 12 countries hoisted stones that ranged from about 34kg to 159kg.
Sakamoto said he continues to lift stones to connect with his ancestors. He hopes that by documenting his journey on social media, he can help breathe new life into the practice.
His goal is to have more people lifting these ancient stones, he said, and “also lifting up Japanese history”. – This article originally appeared in the New York Times

title: This is a library where the books won’t be read until 2114
description: Inside the silent chamber of the Future Library, in Oslo, unpublished manuscripts by some of the world’s most celebrated writers are being sealed away for a century
content:
I take off my shoes at the entrance to the Silent Room, on the top floor of Deichman Bjorvika, Oslo ’s main library, and pad in stockinged feet across the smooth wood of the winding hallway that leads to a central chamber, curved like a belly, created by rows of smooth, undulating honey-hued wood, the air rich with the scent of timber.
I feel as if I’m in a forest. It also reminds me of stepping into the inner sanctum of a megalithic tomb – Newgrange, maybe, on the morning of the winter solstice, waiting for the light to penetrate the chamber.
The light in the Silent Room comes from slim glass compartments in the walls. They are lit from within, as if sunlight is spilling into a clearing in the forest. There are 100 compartments. So far, 12 of them hold manuscripts by some of the world’s best-known authors.
This is the Future Library . The plan is to add one manuscript a year; each will be stored here, unread, until the year 2114, when the compartments will be opened and the 100 manuscripts will be printed, a century after the first contribution, by the US author Margaret Atwood , was deposited here.
Each manuscript – a short story, a poem or a novel – is presented to the library by its invited author in a ceremony in the Nordmarka forest, on the outskirts of Oslo. Trees in one area of it were felled to provide the wood to build the Silent Room; in the clearing that resulted, 1,000 spruce trees were planted to in turn supply the wood that, in 2114, will become the paper to print the manuscripts.
[ Book of Lives by Margaret Atwood: a literary titan on the art of writing – and art of living Opens in new window ]
In August, Laurie Anderson was announced as the next writer to deposit a manuscript in the Future Library.
The 13th contributor, she’ll follow the Indian-American author Amitav Ghosh, who gave the Future Library his piece this year, as did the novelist Tommy Orange, a member of the Cheyenne and Arapaho tribes of Oklahoma. (He had been unable to attend, as originally planned, in 2025.)
[ Laurie Anderson on Lou Reed: ‘He said, I’ll get on a plane right now. We got married the next day’ Opens in new window ]
Rather than choose authors years in advance, the Future Library Trust has an organic selection process that is influenced year to year by world events and other considerations.
Authors who have already contributed to the project include the Cork resident David Mitchell, the Nobel laureate Han Kang, the Icelandic writer Sjón and the award-winning British-Turkish novelist and activist Elif Shafak .
I sit in the room and wonder what the words held here will mean to future generations when they are finally revealed. In a world where literacy rates are declining, where AI aims to do our reading and writing for us, will people even be able to read them? With wars raging and nature struggling, will anybody be left?
The project was conceived by the Scottish artist Katie Paterson , who had been on a train on England, “just doodling on a piece of paper, looking out the window and letting my imagination run free. I drew a piece of a tree, with concentric growth rings clearly marked, and as I looked at it I had a vision of trees being future books, and I saw a forest growing books over a lifetime.”
The idea might have remained just that had Paterson not been invited to an artists’ conference in Oslo with the theme of imagining public art commissions that step outside the usual format of dropping external objects into public spaces. She realised her idea could meet that vision.
Her proposal was taken up by Anne Beate Hovind, an urban developer and curator who specialises in art in public spaces, and has worked on several creative projects for the riverside development in Oslo where the library sits.
[ Amitav Ghosh: ‘Ireland is where the British created all their colonial methods, it’s where they tried it out first’ Opens in new window ]
This is the most ambitious to date, given its geographical stretch, from the library to the Nordmarka forest, and 100-year time span, which means it will outlive all its creators.
“With this project Katie has expanded my principles of time and space,” Hovind says. “But what is art for if not to challenge and expand us?”
Norway is the perfect place for the Future Library, Paterson believes. “I struggle to think of any other countries that would take this on. In Norway there is more of a drive towards future thinking. And there’s a great connection to forestry – and, unlike many other countries, they’ve taken care of their forests. And then there’s the literary tradition.
“I just felt like they really got it and embraced it. In many other places this project wouldn’t even have been considered, because it’s too risky and unknown.
[ Gunnar Staalesen on the mystery of novels and nature Opens in new window ]
“There are so many unknowns for this – things like climate change , will our forest still be standing in 100 years, and also changing societies, changing languages. Like our Icelandic author, Sjón, pointed out that Icelandic is a minority language, given the country’s small population, and of course we don’t know what it will be like in 100 years.”
According to Hovind, the project has been guided by themes of trust, rituals, hope, climate and nature crisis, democracy, community and resilience, among others.
“We need to produce something different or else nothing new will ever happen,” she says. “We can’t just do more of the same. We see art as a force for achieving something new and ask can art make the world a better place.”
Hovind travels all over the world to speak about the Future Library. Earlier this year she took part in a Sydney Writers’ Festival discussion of radical hope. ”In India they called this a slow march for peace. And everywhere I travel to, I am reminded how similar we all are. There are differences too, of course, but we have a shared core.”
This is a time for radical action in a world that is unstable and chaotic, she believes.
“This is about the brain’s capacity to imagine. If we stop imagining, we lose hope. That’s why art and culture are so important in our time. Art and culture come from the core of our imagination: it is so important to keep using this muscle.
“Young people must exercise imagination and create. It is important that young people can experience their dreams. I feel I’m on a mission. This has been life-changing for me.”
[ Does Ireland have the will to undo the disaster of plantation forestry? Opens in new window ]
In the part of the forest where the trees for the books have been planted, the project’s saplings are growing near soaring pines. I stroke one of them, thinking that one day it might become the words of an Irish author, maybe even somebody from Sligo, my home.
What sort of a world will receive it, and what in that world will remain of today’s literature, art and creativity? What in that world will remain, full stop?
Back in my hotel I touch a screen outside the lift to select the floor I want to go to. In a world where it can feel as if we’re no longer trusted to push buttons on a lift, how magnificent it is to imagine a forest slowly growing a library of unseen words, an act, surely, of radical hope and autonomy.

title: Dáileadh an sparáin
description: Léiríonn an Buiséad nach féidir brath ar ghealltanais ilbhliantúla
content:
Bhí am ann nuair a tugadh ‘cáinaisnéis’ as Gaeilge ar Bhuiséad náisiúnta na seachtaine seo caite. Ós rud é anois go bhfuil níos mó béime ar athruithe caiteachais ná cánach (ardú €6 bhilliún ar chaiteachas reatha in aghaidh laghdú €1.6 billiún ar cháin), tá níos mó ná cáin ag baint leis na gcáinaisnéis.
Agus níl an oiread faisnéise le déanamh roimh ré ach oiread. Tráth dá raibh, bhíodh cinntí cáinaisnéise faoi rún daingean ar eagla go ndéanfaí idirbheartaíocht astu roimh réidh. Sa lá atá inniu ann, pléitear mórán roimh an bhfógairt féin, idir fhíorscéalta agus eitleogacht. Taitníonn sin uaireanta le polaiteoirí – leis an Aire Airgeadais s’againne – mar go mbíonn an dea-scéala á fhógairt agus i mbéal an phobail níos minice. Taitníonn sé le hiriseoirí freisin mar go mbíonn deis trácht air níos luaithe.
‘Buiséad’ mar sin atá againn seachas ‘cáinaisnéis’. Cé go mbraitheann sé go dtagann sé ón mBéarla, is cosúil go bhfuil bunús sa Ghaeilge leis an bhfocal ‘buiséad’. Dar leis an tsanasaíocht go dtagann sé ón tSean-Fhraincis ‘bouge’, focal ar oscailt púitse, ‘bougette’ a chiallaíonn sparán nó púitse beag, agus é sin ón Laidin ‘bulga’ (mála leathair), focal de bhunús Gallach agus Gaeilge (‘bolg’).
Más fíor sin, bhí an bolg lán i mbliana ach ní raibh a sháith ag chuile dhuine. Agus dar le mórán saineolaithe neamhspleácha, tá an caiteachas iomarcach, agus muid ag brath an iomarca ar fhoinsí cánach atá sealadach a dhóthain, gur cheart níos mó a chur i leataobh sa phantrach d’am an ghátair - a thiocfaidh cinnte - seachas inár mbolg inniu.
Tá an rogha pholaitiúil - agus brú an phobail - le feiscint áfach san ardú 6 faoin gcéad ar chaiteachas reatha na bliana seo chugainn. Agus tá an rogha - agus an brú - sin le feiscint freisin sna rannóga Rialtais ina bhfuil an t-ardú is suntasaí: tithíocht (10.5 faoin gcéad), leanaí, míchumas agus comhionannas (7.1 faoin gcéad), coimirce shóisialach (7 faoin gcéad), cosaint (6.3 faoin gcéad) agus sláinte (6 faoin gcéad). Tá ardú 4.4 faoin gcéad (níos lú ná an meán) le bheith ar chaiteachas reatha na Roinne Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail agus Gaeltachta, agus gan aon ardú ar chaiteachas caipitil na Roinne.
Más ón nGaeilge féin ar bhealach casta a thagann an focal ‘buiséad’, ní raibh mórán don teanga i mBuiséad na bliana seo. Ina óráid ar an mBuiséad, d’fhógair an tAire Jack Chambers go gcuirfí “€161 mhilliún ar fáil chun tacú le pobail na Gaeltachta, chun an Ghaeilge a neartú agus chun seirbhísí agus naisc iompair do phobail na n-oileán a fheabhsú”. “Cabhróidh milliún euro breise”, dar leis, “le tuilleadh daoine i bpobail na Gaeltachta a gcuid scileanna Gaeilge a fhorbairt agus a choinneáil”.
Dar le ráiteas ón Roinn Forbartha Tuaithe agus Pobail agus Gaeltachta “airítear ar na méaduithe ar mhaoiniú reatha €0.75 milliún sa bhreis do Scéimeanna Tacaíochta na Gaeltachta, €0.8 milliún sa bhreis do Scéimeanna Tacaíochta na Gaeilge, agus €0.75 milliún sa bhreis don Phleanáil Teanga”. Beidh méadú ar an maoiniú reatha - suas le €1 mhilliún - ar fáil don chomhar Thuaidh-Theas chun tacú le hobair Fhoras na Gaeilge, níos lú ná mar a bhíodar ag súil leis. Ardófar leithdháileadh reatha agus riaracháin Údarás na Gaeltachta €0.8 milliún, go dtí maoiniú dar luach €41.96 milliún ina iomlán. Is ionann sin agus ardú thart ar 2 faoin gcéad, ardú atá faoi bhun an ráta boilscithe agus ar fíorghearradh é dá bharr. Beidh maoiniú €2.17 milliún ar fáil don Choimisinéir Teanga. Lena chois sin beidh €1.5 milliún níos mó ar fáil do sheirbhísí iompair na n-oileán, á ardú go dtí €13 mhilliún.
Ina iomlán, sin breis caiteachais reatha i bhfoisceacht €6 mhilliún, níos mó ná an milliún euro glan a luaigh Jack Chambers lá an Bhuiséid. Dar leis an Aire Calleary, aistreofar €5 mhilliún ó chaiteachas caipitil na Roinne chuig an gciste reatha toisc “deacrachtaí” leis na tograí caipitil a chiallaíonn nach gcaithfear an tsuim chaipitil iomlán a bhí curtha i leataobh.
Deir sé go bhfuil súil aige go mbeadh an obair ar Ché Inis Oírr curtha i gcrích an bhliain seo chugainn. Tá sé ráite san athbhreithniú ar an bPlean Forbartha Náisiúnta go bhfuil súil go mbeidh an obair ar Ionad Gaeilge agus Cultúir Shráid Fhearchair réidh ag tús 2029. Maidir leis an Ionad Oideachais agus Óige in Indreabhán atá le tógáil ar shuíomh Choláiste Lurgan, dúirt Roinn na Gaeltachta an mhí seo caite go bhfuil na tairiscintí tógála “fós á mheas”.
Méadú ar an gcaiteachas reatha agus cúlú ar an gcaiteachas caipitil mar sin a fhágann an t-ardú glan €1 mhilliún atá luaite ag an Aire Chambers in aitheasc an Bhuiséid.
Leis an ráta boilscithe mar atá agus mar atá tuartha, ní haon ardú é seo ach fíorlaghdú. “Faic” dar leis an bhfreasúra, “céim siar” dar le Conradh na Gaeilge agus an tAire féin “ag súil le hardú mór” an bhliain seo chugainn. Ciallaíonn sé freisin go gcaithfear níos mó airgid ó Thuaidh (€200 milliún) ar Thionscnamh an Oileáin Chomhroinnte, peata-thogra de chuid an Taoisigh, ná chun tacú le pobail na Gaeltachta (€161 mhilliún).
An t-iontas is mó ná nár tugadh ardú ar bith - pingin ná puinn - do TG4 ón Roinn Cultúir, Cumarsáide agus Spóirt. Maíonn an tAire Patrick O’Donovan nach bhfuil aon chiorrú déanta ar an gcionnroinnt acu ach leis an ráta boilscithe ard mar atá - agus ardú ar chostas pá níos airde fós seans - tuigeann an domhan mór gur fíorchiorrú atá i gceist le heaspa ardaithe airgid. Tá sin le feiscint freisin sa leithdháileadh do Roinn an Aire O’Donovan (€22 mhilliún, nó 2.7 faoin gcéad), fiú tar éis €20 milliún breise tugtha ag deireadh an phróisis, más fíor do na tuairiscí. Má tá aon Aire ina ábhar cainte – nó cáinte agus conspóide – ó lá an Bhuiséid agus roimhe, is é an tAire O’Donovan é.
Tá roinnt rudaí le feiscint mar sin sa Bhuiséad. Easpa ardaithe le haghaidh na Gaeilge, roghanna an Rialtais maidir le tosaíocht tacaíochta agus nach bhfuil cúrsaí cultúrtha i gcoitinne ina measc. Ach tá sé le feiscint freisin nach féidir brath ar dháileadh ná ar ghealltanais ilbhliantúla. Tá sin feicthe sa chóras ardleibhéil maidir leis an gcoimitmint a tugadh in 2022 i dtaca leis an maoiniú €307 milliún a d’eascair as an tuairisc Funding the Future; tá sé feicthe ag RTÉ maidir leis an ngealltanas €725 mhilliún thar thréimhse trí bliana; agus ag an nGaeilge maidir leis an tabhairt le fios gur ‘chéad chéim’ a bhí san ardú maoinithe anuraidh.
Luíonn sé sin le réasún ar bhealach amháin. Is próiseas dáileacháin bliantúil é an Buiséad agus athraíonn cúinsí na tíre ó bhliain go bliain. Ach ar an taobh eile den scéal, ní féidir pleanáil go straitéiseach ná mór-athruithe a chur i gcrích ar bhunús bliana. Agus tá dainséar don chóras polaitiúil – agus brú ar phróiseas an Bhuiséid – go ngealltar, muna bhfuil maoiniú ar fáil faoi láthair, go mbeidh sé ar fáil amach anseo.
Más bolg – agus oscailt sparáin – atá i gceist le Buiséad, ní bhíonn an sparán ariamh gan teorainn agus is cosúil nach bhfuil a sháith ag chuile dhuine.
Cuntasóir cairte is ea Ciarán Ó hÓgartaigh, iarOllamh sa Chuntasaíocht agus iarDhéan Gnó in UCD. Tá sé ina Chathaoirleach ar an Institiúid um Thaighde Eacnamaíochta agus Sóisialta. Is i gcáil phearsanta a scríobh sé an t-alt seo.

title: Retrofitting: My daughter is reluctant to go the one-stop-shop route advertised by SEAI
description: My daughter is reluctant to go the one-stop-shop route advertised by SEAI
content:
Many owners of older properties find themselves in this situation. Before deciding on insulation, windows, heating systems or grants, she should focus on establishing a clear brief and budget.
The starting point is to ask two simple questions: What do I want to achieve and how much can I afford to spend? Is the target a warmer and more comfortable home, lower energy bills or a particular Ber rating, or is it to address potential concerns with the electrics or other existing issues? Her answers will help shape the scope of works.
[ ‘Is it true that Ireland’s new houses aren’t as well built as older ones?’ Opens in new window ]
With a house of this age, and the issues you mention, I would recommend obtaining independent advice from a chartered building surveyor. A condition survey will identify any issues with the property from a safety and compliance perspective, highlight any defects and help prioritise works.
For example, you mention rewiring. If this is required, it may take precedence over other improvements. Equally, opening up walls to carry out electrical works may create an ideal opportunity to undertake complementary upgrades such as replumbing, insulation or drylining at the same time, improving comfort and cost effectiveness and minimising longer-term disruption.
A survey and initial professional advice can help establish:
Once the budget, scope and objectives are defined, the next steps are usually much clearer.
Before committing to any works, it is also important to understand the requirements of any grant scheme being considered. Grant eligibility criteria, qualifying measures and target energy-performance improvements can influence the scope and sequencing of works. Taking professional advice early can help avoid spending money on works that may not align with a future grant application.
[ We don’t qualify for retrofitting grants to convert a garage for a relative. What can we do on a budget? Opens in new window ]
The SEAI one-stop-shop model can work very well for some homeowners, particularly those who want a single point of contact to manage assessments, grant administration, contractor co-ordination and certification. However, it is not the only route. Some homeowners prefer to appoint their own consultants and contractors and manage works in a phased manner, particularly where budgets are limited or specialist advice is required for an older property. There is an administrative or project management burden your daughter will need to consider if going the direct route.
Craig Potter is a chartered quantity surveyor and a member of the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland
