title: Gold rush cemetery in California bears names of Armagh and Tyrone prospectors
description: It struck me that, wherever gold was found, the Irish had usually got there first
content:
Sir, – Frank McNally’s piece on Shamrock, Texas, and Route 66 reminded me of my own encounter with the Irish diaspora in California ( An Irishman’s Diary , October 9th).
As principal of St Joseph’s Grammar School, Donaghmore, Co Tyrone, I was invited to visit Marin Catholic High School, with whom we had a link. While their team played an away match, I wandered through the cemetery in Grass Valley, an old gold rush town, and found the graves of prospectors from Armagh and Tyrone.
It struck me that wherever gold was found, the Irish had usually got there first, and left a headstone behind. – Yours, etc,

title: ‘Politeness premium’ costing Irish consumers €600m each year, research suggests
description: Fewer than one in 20 Irish adults will always ask for money they are owed back
content:
Irish consumers lose an average of €150 each year as a result of a “politeness premium” which sees them overpay on shared bills and fail to collect personal debts, according to research published by AIB on Monday morning.
The study suggests that fewer than one in 20 Irish adults will always ask for money they are owed back, with as many as 90 per cent saying they would let as much as €50 slide rather than have a conversation they consider difficult.
All told, about €600 million gets lost to social awkwardness every year, AIB said.
And as if to prove the Shakespearean wisdom about never being either a borrower or a lender, the unspoken debt has “soured a relationship” among almost 50 per cent of those surveyed.
The research also highlights how consumers handle peer-to-peer debts varies dramatically depending on county, age and gender.
The geographical divide in financial assertiveness indicates that people from Galway have Ireland’s highest ‘threshold of asking’ and willingly absorb up to €32.50 in unpaid amounts before speaking up.
By contrast, people living in Wexford draw the line much earlier by refusing to let more than €12.50 slide.
Adults from Limerick are the most likely to insist on itemising group bills line by line, while those living in Dublin prefer splitting bills evenly among the group.
When asked why they hesitate to chase small debts, Irish adults often frame their silence as kindness and say things such as “they’d do the same for me”, “it evens out over time”, or “I’d rather be generous than keep score”.
[ Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: How does it work if I have €1 or €12,000 to put in? Opens in new window ]
However, behavioural data reveals the underlying tension when payments arise, with 40 per cent saying owed money left unspoken has soured how they feel about a relationship and two thirds admitting to a level of discomfort when someone suggests itemising a group bill.
Nearly half said they regularly overpay on shared bills or rounds to keep the peace, with 25- to 34-year-olds feeling the greatest pressure and 74 per cent overpaying regularly, according to the survey of 1,009 adults conducted by Bounce Insights on behalf of AIB and Ogilvy.
Close friends and colleagues were deemed to be the hardest groups to ask for money back from, with women saying they found it particularly difficult to reclaim money from close friends.
“People rarely describe their silence around money as awkwardness,” said Dan Bennett, global head of behavioural science with Ogilvy Consulting. “They describe it as generosity. But the cost of that politeness is real, showing up both in people’s bank accounts and in their relationships. In Ireland, the fear of appearing impolite leads many of us to pay a ‘politeness premium’.”
“The behavioural science research that AIB’s new Everyday Banking campaign is rooted in highlights how social dynamics impact our daily finances, create social friction and can even cost people money,” said the bank’s chief customer officer Orlaith Ryan.

title: The best gigs abroad in 2026-2027: Who to see and where to see them
description: From Berlin to Barcelona, New York to Reykjavik, these are the great cities to visit for a gig this autumn and winter
content:
I n an era when tickets sell out quicker than you can say “how much?” a recent report by marketing agency Dentsu found that more than one in 10 Irish adults was partial to “gig-jetting”: travelling abroad specifically to catch a concert. That figure rises to three in 10 under-35s.
It’s a canny move: tickets are often cheaper, it’s an excuse to soak in new and loved destinations, it makes a special concert unforgettable – and it gives serious bragging rights. Here’s where to catch some hotly anticipated gigs over the next six months, if you fancy a trip out of Ireland.
Few cities radiate a sense of cool like Berlin . It’s a superb city to people-watch, shop, soak up history, go clubbing, try karaoke and watch brilliant bands.
Stay at the Michelberger, the hotel beloved by The National (Bryce and Aaron Dessner of the band played a residency there in 2016), or try The Circus overlooking Rosenthaler Platz, which is centrally located and has delightfully retro touches and smart design. Bedrooms have old-fashioned rotary-dial telephones but no enclosed wardrobes, just a set of hangers (in fairness, how often do you need those big old things?).
Kreuzberg is always a good option for a casually cool evening out (try Buya Ramen Factory for noodles or Tacos El Rey for tasty burritos). For hard-core clubbers, meanwhile, Berghain remains one of the city’s most famous spots – just make sure you have a back-up plan if you don’t get in; it has a famously opaque door policy.
Over the coming months, indie rock fans will be well served with music in Berlin – Fontaines DC, Interpol and Bloc Party all play here, while next year sees rising electropop star Adéla – of Ain’t in LA fame – pirouette on to Berlin’s stage. There’s something for everyone in this city.
Fly to Berlin with Aer Lingus or Ryanair
The US’s cultural capital is peppered with world-famous venues that anchor a tour schedule, whether small and storied like The Bitter End, or extravagant like Madison Square Garden – which means almost every big tour in 2027 will pass through.
As an ever-evolving metropolis, repeat visitors to New York can pad a concert trip with their favourite activities (an amble along Brooklyn Heights Promenade is always nice) and peruse the city’s newer draws. The Museum of Broadway invites guests to delve into the history and backstage magic of Broadway productions, or indulge in the cutting-edge of cuisine by seeking out New York fusion food. In Tribeca, the underinvestigated hybrid of Portuguese-Chinese cuisine is on the menu at Macao Trading Company (try the artfully piquant lobster noodles, a signature dish). Or Elephant Ear whips up contemporary Thai cuisine, and the presentation is as bold as the taste.
Artists already booked to play in 2027 include Bright Eyes, Death Cab for Cutie, Gracie Abrams, Niall Horan, AR Rahman, Gloria Estefan and Ghostface Killah, Ashanti, Dinosaur Jr and Ibeyi.
Chief among them is artist of the moment Olivia Rodrigo. She’ll set up a residency at the Barclays Center in Brooklyn throughout February in support of You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love . Set to bother many an end-of-year list, the album has harnessed her alternative sensibilities (she has covered Fontaines DC and CMAT, lest we forget) to breathe new life into the angsty teen pop genre. With all eyes on Rodrigo, this show, part of The Unraveled Tour, should be one to remember.
Fly to New York with daily flights from Aer Lingus, Delta and United
The Dutch capital’s canals make for a pretty backdrop while en route to its many world-class museums or galleries in the daytime (don’t leave Amsterdam without a visit to the Van Gogh Museum).
Yet when evening descends, the shimmering reflections of the network help bring the city to life. Head to De Pijp to veer away from the tourist throngs and revel in a neighbourhood feel – nab a seat at the social beer emporium Café Gollum or cosy natural wine bar GlouGlou.
As a city built for a night out, gigs are abundant: Editors, Ezra Collective, James Blunt, Rush, Amble, Bonobo, Trentemøller, Teddy Swims, Thirty Seconds to Mars, Weezer, Jorja Smith and Passenger are on the cards in 2027.
It’s also the right place to catch 365 party girl Charli XCX as she tours her latest album Music, Fashion, Film. The tour matures her stage show since she went full Brat: out is the visceral DIY effect of stripped-back production and Charli as the sole focal point; in is a monochrome set design and gang of backing dancers that bring the steamy-warehouse-club vibe to life.
Carry on that vibe at Shelter, A’DAM Tower’s underground club with revered DJs, a state-of-the-art sound system – plus a rare (and dangerous) 24-hour licence. Feeling delicate the next day? Fuel a recovery with a brunch at Bakers & Roasters. At their Kadijksplein and DePijp locations, signature dishes like the Navajo Eggs (served with pulled pork, avocado, mango salsa) are reliably comforting. Boozy milkshakes optional.
Fly to Amsterdam with daily flights from Aer Lingus, Ryanair and KLM
As a shining example of a sustainable city, in the happiest country in the world, a visit to Helsinki is an enriching trip in its own right.
Hop on the easy-to-navigate metro and explore the linden tree-lined streets of Art Nouveau architecture, Nordic-chic boutiques and independent coffee shops with perfect rows of pillowy cardamom buns in their windows, all while uncovering Helsinki’s history – keep an eye out for Moomin paraphernalia as Helsinki was home of its creator, Tove Jansson.
Its concert venues are equally accessible. Find Tavastia (a legendary haunt that hosted The Pogues, Nick Cave, and Tom Waits) by Kamppi metro station at the city’s heart. Next year it hosts intimate shows from Saul Williams and Young Gun Silver Fox.
The 15,000-capacity Veikkaus Arena is a direct four-minute train ride from the centre, and rising pop star Sombr performs there in May. The show is part of a mammoth world tour in support of his debut album I Barely Know Her, which continues to Dublin and Belfast the following month. Those who caught the 21-year-old’s set at Electric Picnic know there’s nary a dull moment on his stage, so – as with the city itself – expect a solid dose of the unexpected.
Fly to Helsinki with daily flights from Finnair
Who needs an excuse to visit Portugal, a country so full to the brim of culture, coast and cuisine it draws 900,000 visits from Ireland a year – that equates to one in six of us.
Any visit to the capital should allow time for ever-popular draws (the Time Out Market is a low-hassle way to eat your way around Lisbon’s specialities), while taking in ephemeral attractions – namely the seasonal menu at A Cevicheria and an exhibition at the always-fascinating MUDE (Museu do Design).
It’s also home to a strong music scene, which helps NOS Alive attract one of the best line-ups in the festival calendar.
Already slated for July 2027 are The Neighbourhood and Tame Impala, who is approaching headline status after Kevin Parker’s electro-psych fifth album, Deadbeat , shifted him further into mainstream territory.
The festival takes place on the city’s west coast, with transport links to whisk music-lovers back to the centre within 20 minutes – and trains run until 4.30am to tie in with its finish time (take note, Primavera Sound Barcelona).
Fly to Lisbon with daily flights from Aer Lingus, Ryanair and TAP
Barcelona is a fun spot to visit, and even more so if there’s a gig in the offing. Go to Primavera, the city’s fantastic indie and electronica-led festival, and revel in the sunshine, the incredible line-ups and the novelty value of not having to worry about how you’re going to get back to your accommodation: the transport links – from shuttle to metro to taxi – make an easy job of it.
Even if you’re just in the city for a weekend gig, it’s a lovely place to spend time, whether you’re wandering through the Gothic Quarter, people-watching on Las Ramblas, or oohing and aahing at the Sagrada Família, the world’s tallest church, designed by Gaudi in the late 1800s.
Speaking of venerable institutions, Oasis will play in the city in July as part of their hotly anticipated 2027 tour – tickets are sold out, but you could strike it lucky closer to the time and persuade someone to part with theirs.
Whether you’re cheering in a bucket hat by a stage or just shopping for Adidas trainers on Portal de l’Angel, keep a watchful eye on your possessions – Barcelona is well-known for its pickpockets – and enjoy the city’s reasonably priced street fare, from cheap and tasty pizza to paellas and pastas. Buzzy, lively and diverting, Barcelona is a city that feels alive.
Fly to Barcelona with Ryanair and Aer Lingus
Many artists over the years have made Reykjavik in Iceland their home, from John Grant to Damon Albarn: the Gorillaz and Blur frontman became an official Icelandic citizen in 2021.
It’s no surprise artists love the place: there’s a sense of the otherworldly as you land at Keflavík airport and take in the spare volcanic landscape at the edge of the Arctic Circle.
Music pilgrims often head to Reykjavik in early November for the much loved Airwaves Festival, which takes place across the city over three days.
It’s an ideal time of year to view the Northern Lights and perhaps take a bus tour to well-known sites such as the 8km-long Solheimajokull glacier. Stay a little longer and you can attend Iceland Noir, a four-day literary festival held from November 11th in various venues across the city centre: this year George RR Martin (author of Game of Thrones) is one of the big names attending.
Fewer international music acts might make it to Reykjavik for their tours, but this gives indigenous artists a chance to shine – Björk, GusGus, Of Monsters and Men, Sigur Rós and Úlfur Úlfur are some of the country’s leading lights. Once you get into the city and check out the local record shops, you’ll leave with a lighter wallet, but some newfound musical treasures.
Everything is expensive in Reykjavik (sometimes shockingly so): so you’ll need to factor that in, but if you love nature and music, it’s a remarkable place to visit. Just make sure you’ve got your thermals packed.

title: The subtraction effect: How AI is making leadership more human
description: The Ibec HR Leadership Summit will take place in the RDS on October 21st
content:
On October 21st more than 450 human resources (HR) professionals will gather to discuss the fundamental importance of trust building in a rapidly changing environment at the Ibec HR Leadership Summit in the RDS, Dublin.
The premier event on the HR and people leader calendar, the 2026 summit’s theme – Trust: The human capital imperative – will explore how HR leaders can build and protect that trust and why in a new technological age it matters more than ever.
“As organisations navigate relentless change, trust has become the foundation for strong leadership, engaged teams and sustainable growth,” says Ibec executive director, employer relations Maeve McElwee. “The challenge for HR leaders extends far beyond the traditional boundaries of people management at a time of heightened global volatility and accelerating artificial intelligence (AI) adoption. Cultivating internal trust is no longer just a cultural goal but a critical strategic shield against external instability and HR leaders are on the front line in that battle.”
AI, with its capacity to generate misinformation and deepfakes as well as to reshape roles and organisational structures, is at the core of this challenge, she says.
“As organisations adopt AI there is a need to build confidence that the guardrails are in place to ensure its ethical use,” she says. “Employees need to be able to trust the AI they are working with and how their managers and leaders are using it.”
Interestingly, the impact of AI will probably make leadership more rather than less human as a result of something called the subtraction effect, according to keynote speaker Julien Jourdan.
Prof Jourdan is professor of management and human resources at HEC Paris, and his research examines reputation, legitimacy and other social evaluations of organisations. The subtraction effect, identified by Jourdan and colleagues in research carried out over the past 18 months, is the result of AI taking over elements of current roles and allowing leaders more time to devote to other aspects.
He contends that AI actually elevates the importance of leadership by taking over an increasing share of routine managerial work, from monitoring performance to co-ordinating workflows and generating analysis.
‘Why are employees turning to AI for advice and guidance instead of their managers?’
In a world where machines can increasingly co-ordinate and control, the capabilities that matter most are the ones they struggle to replicate – creating trust, exercising judgment, developing people, shaping culture and setting direction, he says. “The organisations that succeed will not be those that simply adopt AI, but those that redefine leadership around what remains uniquely human.”
He explains that technology has been automating tasks and roles for a long time. “Look at the accountant’s role for example,” he says. “Thirty years ago, they spent a lot of their time doing things manually that are now automated, yet when you look at the jobs market today, accountants are among the most sought after professionals. It’s not that managers will be replaced by machines, they will be assisted. The job will remain. The challenge is to look at what is and is not being automated.”
And the question is what managers will do with the time freed up by the assistive technology. “There is a distinction between management and leadership,” he explains. “Management is all about co-ordinating, bringing order to complex and chaotic situations, setting up processes and procedures and make sure they are followed. Leadership is about creating change, setting vision, creating culture, making difficult decisions, liaising with stakeholders.”
But managers and leaders are usually the same people. And this is where the choice in relation to what to do with the time saved comes in. “You can use it to micromanage, bring in more procedures and so on, or to invest more time in leadership. This is the subtraction effect. The technology is augmenting people at an individual level by subtracting elements of their roles.
“Should you become better at micromanaging and doing things that can be done by AI or be stronger as a leader and spend more time with teams motivating them, building culture and networking with stakeholders?” he asks.
Another speaker at the summit, Marinela Profi, will address the issue of trust drift. “Why are employees turning to AI for advice and guidance instead of their managers?” asks McElwee, of Ibec. “Previous generations probably went to colleagues, but people are now asking AI for advice not just in relation to work but on personal things like what clothes to wear.”
But with AI tending to tell people what they want to hear, Profi will examine how this trust gap can be bridged.
“The mental health implications of overuse of AI and technology will be explored by Colman Noctor,” McElwee adds. “Trust is really important from a mental health perspective. How do you build confidence in the work you are doing, that the information you rely on is trustworthy, that it has been obtained ethically and responsibly? And how do we educate people to know when information may not be correct? We need to ensure people are able to spot hallucinations. We need to find new ways of training people and that brings us back to the National Training Fund. It’s more critical than ever to release money to organisations to train people not just on the technical aspects of AI but in the leadership and management aspects as well.”
To learn more about the Ibec HR Leadership Summit 2026, go to hrleadership.ie

title: Brian Cowen: Anatomy of a Taoiseach -  A ‘political life’ with little on the life of the politician
description: Well-paced account of Cowen’s public life leaves no clear picture of the man behind the decisions
content:
Forty years ago, in The Party: Inside Fianna Fáil (1986), Dick Walsh, political editor of The Irish Times, tried to get the measure of the “slightly constitutional party” that had dominated southern politics for more than half a century. Fianna Fáil had set out, he averred, “with the hope of founding a republic and ended up a partitionist party in a 26 county state. But those who imagined it would die or be rejected by the electorate if its deepest ambitions were not achieved are confounded by its strength and resilience as it celebrates the 60th anniversary of its foundation”.
In the four decades since then, people have repeatedly predicted that Fianna Fáil would be rejected by the electorate and they too have been confounded. Among the horrors that its cumainn have swallowed are burying the hatchet with the Progressive Democrats, a succession of tribunals, crashing the economy, going into coalition with Fine Gael and failing to resolve the housing crisis.
For sure, some of the faithful have departed – to the left and right – and its election workers are not young. But, as Brian Cowen, first elected to the Dáil two years before Walsh’s book appeared, asks rhetorically on the cover of Gary Murphy’s Brian Cowen: Anatomy of a Taoiseach, “Fianna Fáil isn’t f**king dead yet, is it?”.
No, it is not. It climbed out of the electoral grave it dug for itself with the financial crash: 20 seats in the 2011 general election, 44 seats in 2016, and clawing its way back to 48 seats in 2024 – a far cry from the 81 it held in 2002, but no mean achievement for Micheál Martin. “He is not the great survivor of Irish politics for nothing,” as Cowen remarks in the book.
Will ceding to Fine Gael the prudent position that the State should start planning for reunification be a bridge too far? Probably not. The Soldiers of Destiny have trooped across many bridges. They will likely march over this one kicking that rusty tin can before them. But the young people might ask, “What are they marching for?”
Cowen himself was taoiseach when the economy hit the buffers and he had been minister for finance when economists’ warnings that the government needed to catch itself on went unheeded. And then Cowen took over and the crash came and the end of his political career was, in large part, a consequence of that crash and his handling of it.
No fair-minded person would deny that Cowen was an unfortunate taoiseach, nor would such a person dispute that much of his misfortune was of his own making. “Events, dear boy, events” doesn’t get you far when you have been architect, builder and concierge of those “events”.
Anatomy of a Taoiseach is a puzzling subtitle. It suggests that Cowen’s tenure as taoiseach is the concern. But the book offers “an examination of his political life and legacy”, that is, his 27-year political career, from his ascent to the Dáil in 1984, and not simply his 1,036 days as taoiseach.
Curiously, it is a “political life” with little on the life of the politician. Yes, there are some facts. His father, Ber, was an auctioneer, butcher, publican and undertaker, leading some wag to quip that the Cowens would house you, feed you, water you, and bury you. And he ran these businesses while serving on the county council and in Leinster House. The middle child of three, Brian attended primary school in Clara, and boarded in Roscrea. He excelled academically and in debate. And he excelled too on the sports field, making the Offaly senior football panel and coming close to playing schoolboy rugby for Leinster. After studying law in University College Dublin, he opened a solicitor’s practice in Tullamore before being elected TD, after Ber’s death aged only 51.
Those details are in the first 36 pages of a book that runs to more than 360. Missing is what shaped Cowen. What was it like growing up in a well-to-do family in a provincial town in the 1960s and 1970s? What was the political culture of his father’s house? What were its values and how did they change as Fianna Fáil changed through the arms trial, the Jack Lynch years and Charles Haughey years?
Murphy describes the household as “nationalist”. How did the Cowens’ nationalism express itself? By singing songs? He writes of Cowen’s “devotion” to Fianna Fáil and insists that it “means everything to him”, but nowhere does he explain how the party came to mean so much to him. And one scarcely glimpses the constituency politician; how did Cowen win votes?
Anatomy of a Taoiseach is a well-paced account of Cowen’s public life. Future historians, with recourse to more sources, will offer a deeper analysis of his leadership. But na gnáth-daoine – the ordinary people whom Cowen purported to serve – would benefit from a book that looks less at the end and more at the beginning, a book about the making of the man that might explain, at least in part, some mistakes that the man made. And mistakes too made by ourselves, na gnáth-daoine, the electorate.
Breandán Mac Suibhne is an author and professor of history at University of Galway

title: Ireland goes Swedish on investment, but deemed disposal remains a problem
description: The Savings and Investment Account is arguably a welcome attempt to make investing simpler
content:
Earlier this year, Stocktake suggested Minister for Finance Simon Harris might be tempted to borrow Sweden ’s model for encouraging people to invest.
It turns out he was. The Savings and Investment Account (SIA) announced in Budget 2027 is not a carbon copy of Sweden’s ISK, but the resemblance is clear.
Investors can put up to €12,000 a year into the account, with the first €50,000 of investments exempt from tax , while amounts above that will face an annual 1 per cent charge.
Some will be irked by that charge, especially in years where stock markets have fallen. However, a UK-style tax-free wrapper, allowing savers to invest up to £20,000 a year completely free of tax, always appeared excessively generous and politically indefensible.
For the Government, a Swedish-type approach offers a predictable tax stream while encouraging people to put their savings into shares and funds (and a €50,000 tax-free limit is more generous than many expected) rather than leaving them in cash.
However, the new account also highlights the problem with the system outside it. Investments held in the SIA will escape deemed disposal, while investors buying ordinary ETFs will continue to face an eight-year tax charge on unrealised gains, albeit at the reduced rate of 35 per cent.
The Government says it intends to move beyond deemed disposal during the lifetime of this administration, but substantive reform has again been deferred.
And there is a second, less discussed problem. The Funds Sector 2030 review recommended limited loss relief, but the Government’s roadmap says it will not be introduced. As Stocktake previously noted, an investor who makes €5,000 on one ETF and loses €5,000 on another can therefore have no overall gain but still face tax on the €5,000 profit.
[ Is the State’s new investment account going to be a good deal? Opens in new window ]
That is less of an issue for someone holding one broad global ETF, but it matters for a portfolio of separate funds.
Some will have issues with the SIA, but it’s arguably a welcome attempt to make investing simpler. The harder task is making the wider investing tax system equally sensible.

title: In a Word... The Irish
description: For a full analysis of who we were – and still may be – we must obviously go back to the 12th century, no less
content:
Scottish poet Robbie Burns pleaded for the gift “to see oursels as ithers see us!” [to see ourselves as others see us]. On this island, we have always been keen to know what others think of us.
Londoner Dr Samuel Johnson just might have been impressed when he said: “the Irish are a fair people; – they never speak well of one another.”
It is certainly a more elegant phrase than Donald Trump ’s in Dublin last month when he said certain of us were “vicious bastards”. It was meant as a Maga USA compliment.
For Winston Churchill , it was simpler: “We have always found the Irish a bit odd. They refuse to be English”, while we just bewildered Sigmund Freud , who said the Irish were “one race of people for whom psychoanalysis is of no use whatsoever”.
But, for a comprehensive analysis of who we were – and still may be – we must go back to the 12th century and Welshman Giraldus Cambrensis. He was not impressed.
He found us “a rude [primitive] people, subsisting on the produce of their cattle only, and living themselves like beasts - a people that has not yet departed from the primitive habits of pastoral life.” We held “agricultural labour in contempt” with “little coveting the wealth of towns, as well as being exceedingly averse to civil institutions”.
We did not bother with “any kind of trade or mechanical art”, instead abandoning ourselves “to idleness, and immersed in sloth”, while our “greatest delight is to be exempt from toil”, and our “richest possession the enjoyment of liberty”.
But there was a compliment. “The only thing to which I find that this people apply a commendable industry is playing upon musical instruments, in which they are incomparably more skilful than any other nation I have ever seen. For their modulation on these instruments, unlike that of the Britons to which I am accustomed, is not slow and harsh, but lively and rapid, while the harmony is both sweet and gay.” How awful!
[ Let’s have a competition for a new national anthem Opens in new window ]
“Averse to civil institutions”, their “richest possession [was] the enjoyment of liberty” while “incomparably more skilful than any other nation” at playing musical instruments.
Sounds like the very definition of craic.
Let’s be grateful we’re not like that any more.
The Irish, from Old English Iras, for “inhabitant of Ireland”, itself from Old Irish Eriu.

title: Dopamine Chamber is the sound of Fontaines DC becoming megastars. Is bigger always better?
description: The Irish band’s new album lacks the poetic intimacy and postpunk punch so long a feature of Fontaines at their best
content:
Not since Bono first put on a cowboy hat and fixed his gaze on the United States has an Irish band conquered the world with the velocity and ferocity of Fontaines DC .
But while many in Irish music will take justifiable pride in what the group have accomplished, their latest album raises thorny questions about the compromises involved in becoming the biggest Irish rock story of the 21st century.
Dopamine Chamber is an LP made for a mass audience. It booms from the speakers and, at full throttle, has the bulldozing, resistance-is-futile quality of an accelerating Cybertruck. But is bigger always better?
That’s something the album wrestles with over and over, and there’s no glossing over the fact that it lacks the poetic intimacy and postpunk punch so long a feature of Fontaines at their best.
The LP’s monster-truck rumble is its most striking quality: there are moments when you could be listening to Christy Dignam fronting Muse . And while that’s not at all a bad thing, it’s certainly a different thing.
One of the stranger aspects of Dopamine Chamber is how hard it leans into pastiche. There are lots of compelling tunes here, but, gripping though they are, they do suggest songwriters lost in a maze of references.
As the tracks glide by, you may be variously reminded of the dystopian throb of Björk ’s Army of Me, the synth dirges on Joy Division ’s Closer and the doomy disco of Section 25’s Looking from a Hilltop. On Mimesis, Fontaines are so keen to channel New Order ’s The Perfect Kiss that they’ve crowbarred in Peter Hook’s bass solo.
All of that said, few artists today can pull a sublime pop moment out of nowhere like Fontaines DC. That they’ve retained this muscle memory is confirmed by the stadium-indie avalanche of Tongue and the Oasis -style jangle of Demolition, where Grian Chatten ’s boyish lilt splinters with emotion.
They have also perfected the art of writing songs that are thoroughly ho-hum for the first 90 seconds and then become the best thing you’ve ever heard: Happy for You ambles along anonymously before a riff kicks in and blasts everything sky-high; the Chatten- Rosalía duet Where Is Gone? shifts from glum to sublime as the chorus arrives.
Oddly, the album falls down in the very qualities that once made Fontaines so distinctive. The lyrics are among the most generic they have committed to record. Nothing here rivals the cinematic spark of “Dublin in the rain is mine” or the vivid sensation of a panic attack of Starburster, a tune that catches you up in its anxiety as it steamrolls over you.
[ Fontaines DC on their new album: ‘There’s a lot of anxiety. Everyone is looking for something to escape into’ Opens in new window ]
Sadly, it’s also impossible to talk about the record without mentioning the upheavals that have shaken the band. When they take to the stage at Slane in June 2027 it will be just over a year since the death of Trevor Dietz , their manager, and it is difficult not to listen to Dopamine Chamber in the context of those two events: the loss of a mentor and their simultaneous ascent to the biggest stage in Irish music.
The album was largely complete when Dietz died, so it would be an injustice to his memory to comb the lyrics for references to the bereavement. As for their ascendance to venues of the scale of Slane, I’m not sure how well the album’s slower numbers will go down in such vast settings.
Early in their careers, Fontaines DC blew away live audiences with the electrifying brilliance of songs such as Boys in the Better Land. Dopamine Chamber standouts such as Marianne and Intimate are synth-rock behemoths, yet they go about their business with a glacial grace that may not translate to, say, a vast field in Co Meath next summer.
If there’s an additional disappointment for the Irish listener, it’s the loss of specificity. The band have long since moved abroad, and Dopamine Chamber has none of the diaristic detail of earlier Fontaines moments: no screeds against Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil; no ground-level portrait of Dublin in all its romantic grit and bruised beauty.
Dopamine Chamber is an ambitious and earnest attempt to acknowledge the group’s fast-expanding fanbase by supersizing their sound. But, as it stands before us shiny and new, it is as a lesser Fontaines LP – perhaps their weakest since their difficultish second album, A Hero’s Death , and well short of Skinty Fia , their third, and the record that, in hindsight, may prove their masterpiece.
Dopamine Chamber also comes across as deeply uneasy with itself. This is the sound of Fontaines DC becoming megastars, yet it is stalked by the memory of the band they once were but no longer wish to be.

title: ‘People afraid to say they are Jewish’: Dublin event marks October 7th attacks on Israel
description: Jewish community ‘told whether we belong in Ireland depends on how we feel about Israel’, synagogue hears
content:
Jewish people in Ireland are being constantly told their right to stay in the country depends on how they feel about Israel , an October 7th commemoration has been told.
Three hundred people turned up to the gathering in south Dublin to mark the third anniversary of the Hamas -led attacks that left 1,200 Jewish people in Israel dead and 250 taken hostage to Gaza .
The subsequent war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 people, according to the Hamas-controlled Gaza health ministry,
Sunday night’s event was the subject of tight security with a Garda presence outside and was not publicly advertised.
Orli Degani, the incoming chair of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland, said they had to close registration such was the demand for the event. Degani said interest in the event was not surprising.
“We all feel the need to be together, to be somewhere where we don’t have to explain ourselves, where we don’t have to defend our grief or justify our fears,” she said.
“After October 7th, hostility for Jews had already begun spreading and it has never stopped. We have watched Jewish people being pushed out of ordinary life, social spaces, workplaces, cultural activities and public conversations.
“We have watched people become afraid to say they are Jewish. We watched our community being told, again and again, that whether we belong or not in Ireland depends on how we feel about Israel.
“It has become normal now, three years later, that we are asked to put October 7th into context, to qualify our grief.”
The event also heard from Alexandra Herzog, the granddaughter of former Israeli president Chaim Herzog, who was born in Belfast and raised in Dublin.
She said the fraught relationship between Ireland and Israel was “particularly painful” to her as “Ireland is woven into my family history”.
She said her great-grandfather, Rabbi Yitzhak Herzog, had been a friend of Éamon de Valera ’s and a supporter of Irish independence.
Her grandfather Chaim had come back to Ireland in 1985, as president of Israel, to the country “that had shaped him. When my grandfather returned to Ireland at a time when Ireland and Israel had serious disagreements, he said Ireland was not merely the country in which he was born.
“It represented a set of values which he acquired and remained with him throughout his life.
“Ireland and Israel do not have to agree, but political disagreements should never be permission to demonise a people. It should never lead to hostility to Israelis or to Jewish people in Ireland having to answer for the government thousands of miles away.”
The event also heard from family members of those killed in the October 7th, 2023, attacks and from the Irish-born chief operating officer of the World Jewish Congress, John Malkinson.
Malkinson said the attacks on Jewish people in October 7th shocked the world, but in many places by October 8th “sympathy had evaporated – we here in Ireland felt that more than most”.

title: The Irish Times view on the EU and China: a fragile peace on trade
description: EU leaders should approve last week’s deal, but there is more work to do
content:
The European Union and China have averted a trade war with an agreement that saw Beijing agree to limit exports of hybrid cars, facilitate the supply of rare earths and cut tariffs on a range of European products. But as trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic acknowledged in Beijing on Friday night, this is only a first step in rebalancing a trade relationship that is running at €1 billion a day in China’s favour.
Sefcovic said the deal could see Chinese exports of hybrid cars to the EU cut in half over the next four years, a promise that should ease the anxiety of EU car manufacturers, some of whom fear for their future. Producers such as Volkswagen, which is cutting 100,000 jobs, blame lower priced Chinese imports for their difficulties in the European market and around the world.
The details of the deal have yet to be published but it is likely to involve China limiting the number of vehicles exported to Europe, as opposed to the imposition of higher EU tariffs. This has the benefit of predictability for the EU but it could also give Chinese producers a boost by increasing their profit margin on European sales.
Other elements of the agreement include the facilitation through a green channel system of the supply to the EU of rare earths and permanent magnets used in advanced manufacturing. And China has agreed to reduce tariffs on €4 billion of European goods, including car parts, olive oil and footwear.
Sefcovic said that the savings on tariffs were equivalent to a quarter of the value of the EU’s high-profile trade deals with Japan and Australia. But €4 billion is an insignificant sum in comparison with the €370 billion trade surplus China enjoyed with the EU last year.
In advance of Sefcovic’s talks with Chinese commerce minister Wang Wentao in Beijing last week, Germany and France called for tougher trade measures to counter competition from China. These included a “kill switch” that could shut off access to the European single market in response to a coercive measure from Beijing such as denying access to critical minerals.
EU leaders will discuss the trade relationship with China when they meet in Brussels next Thursday and they must approve Sefcovic’s deal before it can go ahead. They should do so because an escalation in trade tensions between China and the EU could have painful consequences for Europe as the continent faces into winter with high energy prices and a turbulent international environment.
But the EU should make clear to China that it is ready to adopt effective trade instruments if Beijing fails to follow through on its promises. And it is in the interest of China as well as the EU to rebalance the trade relationship so that it is more mutually beneficial, sustainable and exemplary for the multilateral trading system.

title: Inagh-Kilnamona secure maiden title against neighbours Kilmaley in Clare cracker
description: David Fitzgerald points add late energy to combo’s Canon Hamilton pursuit
content:
The Clare Senior Hurling Championship continues to be the Disneyland of childhood dreams as Inagh-Kilnamona remarkably became the 13th different title winners in just 23 years in getting their hands on the Canon Hamilton Cup for the first time at Cusack Park in Ennis.
The fact their breakthrough came at the expense of their nearest and dearest neighbours Kilmaley, who started that proud statistic back in 2004, added to a historic day for the combo, who only became a permanent amalgamation in 2008.
Having suffered more than their fair share of heartbreak over the past 18 years, including a late final reverse against Ballyea in 2021, Eugene Cullinan’s side finally found redress with a powerful finish to sink Kilmaley.
With the tense derby decider still level entering the final 10 minutes, at 1-12 apiece, David Fitzgerald put incremental daylight between the sides with three timely points from halfway, while captain Aidan McCarthy and playmaker Sean Rynne stretched their newfound advantage to four before 2026 All-Ireland under-20 winner Fred Hegarty put the result beyond doubt with a spectacular clinching goal at the death.
Outscoring their flagging neighbours 1-6 to 0-2 in the final 15 minutes, the merits of victory for Inagh-Kilnamona were clear, while Kilmaley will rue missed opportunities.
With the wind at their backs for the opening period, Kilmaley started confidently and were 1-3 to 0-1 clear by the end of the opening quarter when Sean O’Loughlin broke through for an opportunist strike in the 14th minute.
Inagh-Kilnamona’s jitters were wiped away when Aidan McCarthy snatched an Eamonn Foudy monster free out of the air before kicking to the roof of the Kilmaley net to slash the arrears to the minimum by the 20th minute.
A timely hook by Mark Callinan on the raiding Cian Moloney denied Kilmaley a reprieve, and while they managed to keep their noses in front by the break, 1-8 to 1-7, it didn’t seem enough with the strength of the wind.
Kilmaley defiantly clung on, but Cian Moloney was denied another goal in the early stages of the second half when his shot was superbly tipped away by Foudy.
Two minutes later, Hegarty inched Inagh-Kilnamona into the ascendancy for the first time, and while the neighbours would be locked together on three further occasions, the tide was slowly turning towards the green and gold as the half progressed.
Three inspirational points from Fitzgerald gave huge energy at the right time, and while Colm Killeen made an impact off the bench for Kilmaley, including a shot cleared off the line by James Hegarty, the gap only widened as the clock ticked down.
O’Loughlin was twice denied a second goal by Foudy, but Inagh-Kilnamona had no such issues at the other end. Despite only scoring two goals in their previous five games, they made up for it with Fred Hegarty’s last-gasp major to seal their maiden title.
INAGH-KILNAMONA: E Foudy; S Woods, K White, C Rynne; K Hehir, J Hegarty, D Cullinan; M Callinan, S Rynne (0-1); D Fitzgerald (0-5), K Guyler, J Guyler; F Hegarty (1-5), A McCarthy (1-5, 3f), D Mescall (0-1). Subs: G Barry for J Guyler (38), N Mullins (0-1) for Mescall (43 mins), J McCarthy for Cullinan (54), J Mescall for Callinan (56), B Foudy for White (63).
KILMALEY: B O’Loughlin; C McGuane, J Casey, C Carmody; A McGuane, M O’Malley (0-2f), D Keane (0-1); T Barry (0-1), S Kennedy; B McNamara (0-1), M O’Neill (0-3), C Moloney; T O’Rourke, C Cleary (0-1sl), S O’Loughlin (1-3, 1f). Subs: E Cahill for Kennedy (43 mins), C Killeen (0-2) for O’Rourke (44), E Enright for O’Neill (57), J Fitzpatrick for Moloney (58).

title: Dara O’Shea’s winning goal against Fulham the latest episode in his whirlwind few weeks
description: Irish player tracker: Goals for Adam Idah and Sammie Szmodics, as Azaz impressed for Southampton
content:
We have grown accustomed over time to hearing Republic of Ireland players remark how a sojourn with the international team can offer a safe house of sorts from the rigmarole of club life, especially if minutes are scarce and the love is not being shown.
But after an international window like no other, where the mental fatigue attached to events off the pitch in Hungary and Serbia was as draining as exertions on it across four games, you suspect the players would have traipsed across hot coals to escape it all.
For most, they have had the comfort and, ahem, purity of the even-keeled, nowt-to-see-here Premier League to nestle back into over the last week, as they restore some normality to their day-to-day lives in the shadow of Manchester City’s pickle.
Dara O’Shea is only coming up for air after a whirlwind time of it since missing Ireland’s second game against Israel as his partner, Louise, was about to give birth. A daughter, Vayda, duly arrived and O’Shea was back on the pitch at the weekend, scoring Ipswich’s come-from-behind winner against Fulham.
He headed home in stoppage time and said: “It’s been a mad time. There’s been a lot going on and to welcome my little girl into the world was amazing. I haven’t really had enough time to spend with her and my family, so I’m really looking forward to that. I’ve a day off [yesterday], put my feet up, help my missus around the house with her and just spent some time together, which we haven’t had a lot of time to do.”
Finn Azaz also caught the eye on his re-emergence in club colours yesterday, providing the delicious assist for Southampton’s winner in their derby success over Portsmouth, while also picking up the Player of the Match gong for good measure.
Gavin Bazunu didn’t have the same good fortune in his first outing since generating global headlines for boycotting both Nations League matches with Israel. His Bolton Wanderers side lost 2-1 at home to Stoke City, where fellow Ireland squad man Bosun Lawal stepped up his return from injury off the bench.
“If Gavin needs anything from us, we’re here for him, he’s got our support because he’s our player, and that’s all we’re really concerned about,” said Bolton manager Steven Schumacher. “He’s in good spirits, he’s fit, he feels nice and sharp, and he is just desperate to get playing again.”
Adam Idah made the most of Ireland’s four-game window and the Corkman maintained his good form by scoring Swansea City’s winner against Norwich City on Saturday, making sure to celebrate the moment against his former club following a spiky enough departure from Celtic.
While Jack Moylan is Ireland’s new kid on the block and a hot ticket because of it, Callum Robinson is the forgotten man of Irish football having last featured for the national team two years ago. But he was back among the goals for Cardiff, with Moylan providing the front-footed assist in a 2-1 defeat away to Blackburn Rovers that leaves the Bluebirds hovering just one place above the relegation zone.
Sammie Szmodics is another Ireland striker with a fight on his hands to get back into favour with Heimir Hallgrímsson but with two more Nations League games to come next month, he did his cause no harm with a brilliant long-range goal for Derby County who were then pegged back by Wrexham at the death in a 1-1 draw.
Keith Andrews’ Brentford continue to pick up points, with Caoimhín Kelleher to the fore in Saturday’s 2-2 draw with Aston Villa but Bees and Ireland captain Nathan Collins missed the game with the calf injury that ruled him out of all four of Ireland’s recent games.
John Egan got 90 minutes in Hull City’s 2-2 draw at Everton yesterday where Jake O’Brien came off the Toffees bench with 12 minutes remaining. Liam Scales played all of Celtic’s 2-0 win at Motherwell but should probably avoid searching his name on X as the reviews were a tad brutal.
Troy Parrott has no such concerns. He remains the darling of Real Betis’ social media handlers but was only an 81st-minute sub in last night’s 5-2 win at home to Osasuna, suggesting he is being kept fresh for Wednesday’s Champions League date with Porto.

title: The Irish Times view on Ireland’s climate policy: rhetoric sounding hollow
description: Last week’s budget raised worrying questions about policy
content:
In 2019, the Dáil declared a “climate and biodiversity emergency”. In the 2027 Budget there is very little sign that this emergency, now surely much more evident than ever, is being addressed.
On the contrary, most environmental experts and NGOs have read the budget measures – and the lack of them – as very retrograde steps. They make the rhetoric about the vital importance of a stable climate and healthy ecosystems to Ireland’s economy and society sound hollow indeed.
The Government does face grimly exceptional pressures on energy prices due to the Middle East conflict. But the U-turn on the carbon tax trajectory sends completely the wrong signal to the public about the urgency of weaning consumers and businesses off fossil fuels.
Meanwhile, the failure to commit any ring-fenced funding for the forthcoming Nature Restoration Regulation seems a drastic blow to the credibility of the most important effort to reverse landscape degradation that the EU has attempted. This funding had been vocally championed by the Minister of State responsible for nature, Christopher O’Sullivan. He has now indicated that this may materialise at a later date. But it is still necessary to ask why such a crucial package for biodiversity did not figure in the budget.
The Government is pausing carbon tax increases due on petrol and diesel this month. It has promised increases in 2027, but given the unpredictability of the US-Iran war, coupled with the Government’s willingness to capitulate to transport protests, these are not done deals. Meanwhile, it has reduced carbon tax on home heating oil and gas, and committed to no further increases whatsoever in this area during its term.
Given the degree to which other climate-friendly initiatives, such as retrofitting homes, depend on carbon tax revenues, it is hard not to see these moves as a double disregard for climate mitigation, regardless of how the Government tries to spin them. All in all, there are many more questions than answers to urgent environmental issues in last Tuesday’s speeches.

title: Gardaí in early stages of investigation after woman’s body found in Wexford
description: Body of the deceased removed from Coolcotts housing estate to University Hospital Waterford for a postmortem
content:
Gardaí are carrying out investigations following the discovery of a woman’s body in a house in Co Wexford .
A large Garda presence had gathered at Coolcotts Court in the Coolcotts estate on Sunday morning after the body was found. Four Garda cars were at the scene, as well as unmarked cars.
Locals were told that officers were responding to “an incident”. A Garda forensic team arrived at the scene and entered the property with cameras. Officers also carried out door-to-door inquiries.
The body of the woman was removed to University Hospital Waterford where a full postmortem examination will be carried out. It is understood that she was a mother of two young children.
“We are investigating all the circumstances in relation to the discovery of the body of a female at a residential property in Coolcotts, Wexford this morning,” a Garda spokesperson said.
The Garda said the results of the postmortem would dictate the course of the inquiry.

title: Club football finals: Clonduff end 16-year wait in Down, Portarlington reign again in Laois
description: Late goal sends Leitrim decider between Ballinamore and Fenagh to a replay
content:
On a day filled with club drama, Clonduff ended a 26-year wait for a Down senior football title with a 1-14 to 1-10 victory over neighbours Burren at Páirc Esler in the first Mourne final not to feature Kilcoo since 2011.
Charlie Carr’s early goal helped the Hilltown side establish a 1-6 to 0-4 half-time lead, while Man of the Match Eamon Brown contributed 0-7, including three two-point frees.
Burren, who dethroned Kilcoo in the semi-final, rallied with a Niall Toner goal after 40 minutes, but Clonduff held firm to secure a famous triumph.
In Longford, Clonguish claimed their first county title since 2009 with a comprehensive 14-point victory over reigning champions Killoe at Pearse Park.
Killoe made a flying start, with Gavin Farrelly netting inside two minutes, but Clonguish recovered to lead 0-10 to 1-2 at half-time. Michael Flynn was outstanding, finishing with 1-9, including two two-pointers and a late goal, while James Hagan contributed 0-5 as Dominic Corrigan’s side secured their 13th senior title in emphatic fashion.
Meanwhile, Portarlington’s dominance in Laois continued as they defeated Courtwood by 1-19 to 0-8. The sides were level at 0-5 apiece at half-time and Courtwood led by a point after 40 minutes but failed to score thereafter. Colm Murphy was to the fore, with his 43rd-minute goal breaking Courtwood’s resistance as part of his 1-5 haul.
Portarlington dominated to the finish, Rioghan Murphy and Ronan Coffey landing two-pointers as they powered to another title.
Next door in Offaly, Tullamore claimed the Dowling Cup for the fourth successive year with a 2-16 to 1-13 win over Ferbane.
A Harry Plunkett goal on 24 minutes helped his side to a 1-6 to 0-6 advantage, but a Leon Fox point and a two-pointer from Patrick Clancy helped level the sides for the break.
Cian Johnson found the net to move Ferbane three ahead on the restart, but a 40th-minute goal from Declan Hogan ignited the champions and they pushed on to win by six.
In the Leitrim decider, an injury-time goal from Ballinamore’s Tom Prior snatched a draw against Fenagh. The Sean O’Heslins lost the final in a penalty shoot-out after a replay in 2024 and fell at the last fence in 2025, but when Luke Murphy put them two up with six minutes to go, their chances this time were looking good.
However, five points unanswered for Fenagh, in search of a first title since 1932, saw them lead by three before Prior’s goal forced a draw. Ballinamore had led 0-8 to 1-4 at half-time, Ryan O’Rourke having netted a penalty for Fenagh in the seventh minute.
Meanwhile, St Mary’s earned a first Sligo title in 11 years after they dethroned Shamrock Gaels 1-12 to 1-10 at Markievicz Park.
An early goal from Robert O’Kelly Lynch got St Mary’s off to a great start, and further scores from Nathan Rooney, Eli Rooney, Fionn O’Hehir and Kyle Cawley helped the Sligo Town team to a 1-9 to 0-4 lead five minutes into the second half.
But a 50th-minute Patrick Kenny goal sparked a revival for the Gaels and they cut the gap to the minimum by the hour mark, with Nathan Rooney’s injury-time free steering the ship home for St Mary’s.
The Westmeath title went to the Downs for a 12th occasion after they defeated St Loman’s by 1-18 to 0-20 in a high-quality decider.
A goal in first-half injury time from Niall Mitchell, who finished with 1-6, helped the Downs to a 1-10 to 0-10 half-time lead, with Luke Loughlin also chipping in with 0-5 in the opening period.
John Heslin kicked 0-12 for St Loman’s, including four two-point frees, but the strong start for the Downs laid the foundation for their title retention.
And there was another famine ended in Wicklow as An Tóchar claimed their first senior title since 1995 with an emphatic 0-21 to 1-7 win over Blessington. The sides were level, 1-6 to 0-9, at half-time, with Patrick O’Connor landing an early goal for Blessington, but Tóchar dominated after the break.
Conor Fee was outstanding, finishing with 0-10, as the Roundwood men pulled clear. Remarkably, every score in the final came from play.
Down SFC final: Clonduff 1-14 Burren 1-10
Laois SFC final: Portarlington 1-19 Courtwood 0-8
Leitrim SFC final: Ballinamore Seán O’Heslins 1-14 Fenagh St Caillins 2-11
Longford SFC final: Clonguish 1-20 Killoe Young Emmets 1-6
Offaly SFC final: Tullamore 2-16 Ferbane 1-13
Sligo SFC final: St Mary’s 1-12 Shamrock Gaels 1-10
Westmeath SFC final: The Downs 1-18 St Loman’s Mullingar 0-20
Wicklow SFC final: An Tóchar 0-21 Blessington 1-7

title: Slick Thurles Sarsfields beat Moycarkey-Borris to win Tipperary SHC title
description: No fairytale finish for Moycarkey-Borris as Thurles win 37th title
content:
Fairytales can be heartless. They suck you in and spit you out. Moycarkey-Borris had waited 42 years to return to the Tipperary senior hurling final, but the dream was just too heavy. From beginning to end only one outcome looked likely.
For Thurles Sars it was their 37th title, but they had lost a couple of finals in recent seasons, and it was nine years since their last title. For a club with their history, not winning had grated on them for too long.
Their hurling was slick and smart and all over the field they had an edge. Thurles built a seven-point lead inside 15 minutes and after that their advantage never slipped to a number that threatened danger.
Eoin Purcell, the man of the match, scored the Thurles goal after 11 seconds, and whatever nerves they must have felt simply dissipated. Instead, Moycarkey were left to cope with a game that was moving faster than they could manage. They landed just point in the opening quarter and in the whirlwind of Thurles pressure they replaced one of their corner backs after just 16 minutes. Their gallant firefighting never entirely put out the blaze.
“Unfortunately or fortunately whichever way you want to put it when you put on a Sarsfields jersey there’s expectation on you every year,” said Padraic Maher, the Thurles Sars manager. “And when you don’t win, and it keeps going and going, and there’s no cup coming back the expectation grows and the jersey can weigh heavy on some lads.”
If that is the case, there was no trace of it here. Purcell racked up 1-3 before half-time, Aidan Stakelum landed a couple of points from wing forward and they moved the ball with such thoughtfulness that they had a flood of shooting opportunities.
To their credit, Moycarkey steadied themselves as the half wore on and they manufactured a terrific goal seven minutes before the break. Joe Maher made a direct run from the wing, played a one-two with Joe Egan, and rifled the return pass to the roof of the net.
That briefly cut the deficit to five points, but with the aid of the wind Thurles kicked again and they were seven clear at the break, 1-12 to 1-5.
Moycarkey needed a fast start to the second half, and though they scored the first two points, Thurles responded with the next three and by the three quarter mark Thurles had stretched their lead to nine. Paul Maher, their corner back, surged down the wing, and after a couple of intricate passes the ball came back to him. From near the sideline he hit a shot that cannoned off the post and over the bar and even though there were 15 minutes to go it already felt like the coup de grace.
“We didn’t probably play to our best and we probably weren’t allowed either,” said Denis Kelly, the Moycarkey manager. “They got the early goal, which was a killer and then they’re a good team to sit back and soak up pressure and get you on the breaks so it was tough.
“They kept the scoreboard ticking throughout whereas we struggled to get our scores and that was the difference in the finish. I’m disappointed for the lads but it was a great experience for them too, their first time in a county final for 42 years.”
Moycarkey had been direct in their approach and it sometimes worked. Jack Hayes and Max Hackett picked off three points and their veteran forward Kieran Morris caused a fuss every time he got his hand on the ball, but the goals they needed in the second half never materialised.
THURLES SARSFIELDS: P McCormack, P Maher (0-1), D Maher, H Fogarty, K Loughnane, Conor Stakelum, Cian Stakelum, D Rossiter (0-1), E Murray (0-2), A McCormack (0-4f), D Stakelum, A Stakelum (0-2), K Rossiter (0-2), P Creedon (0-2), E Purcell (1-4). Subs: S Maher for Fogarty (32 mins); J Armstrong for Cian Stakelum (51); R Maher (0-1) for Creedon (52); T Maher for McCormack (54); R Stapleton for Rottier (59).
