title: Manchester City win at Liverpool in face of Anfield taunts
description: City cut loose after Ryan Gravenberch sent off for Liverpool
content:
It is a soundtrack that Manchester City have heard before but never for such sustained bursts during a match. It came from the Liverpool support, first ringing out around Anfield before kick-off and coming at regular intervals thereafter.
It was always going to be like this as City feel their way into a new reality, one conditioned by the guilty verdicts handed to them by an independent commission on virtually all of the 100-plus charges they have faced for breaking the Premier League ’s financial rules. City continue to maintain their innocence and have appealed.
[ Tension, ‘cheat’ banners and inflatable bananas: Manchester City’s welcome to Anfield Opens in new window ]
The Kop wanted to tell City what they are. And where they are going. According to them, they are cheats, who are set to be relegated. It was not exactly a bear-pit of an atmosphere; it was not really intimidating. It was more of an outpouring and it was impossible to ignore.
City did not care. They rolled with the invective. And after a slow-burn contest turned on a 62nd-minute second yellow card for Liverpool midfielder Ryan Gravenberch, City cut loose. All that their players can do is blot out the noise. They did so here, running all over Liverpool’s ten men to maintain their 100% start to the Premier League season.
It was Erling Haaland, inevitably, who lashed them in front and Jérémy Doku, on as a gamechanging substitute in the 56th minute, who curled them further in front with an absolute beauty. The best was still to come. Again, Doku was involved. Rayan Cherki dummied a pass from Elliot Anderson and ran on to a back-heel from another substitute, Josko Gvardiol. Cherki then cut away from Jeremie Frimpong, on as a Liverpool substitute, before shooting home. It was a team goal marked by individual brilliance. Liverpool were broken and en route to a first defeat under Andoni Iraola.
City had reason to curse the timing of this fixture. Apart from Manchester United at Old Trafford, it could hardly have been worse than a visit here. And not only because Liverpool were one of the clubs most seriously undermined by City’s accountancy practices. The visitors snuck their team buses around the back of the stadium on the way in, avoiding the jibes from the streets but it only postponed the inevitable. It was always going to be lively.
When the Premier League published the document that provided the first raft of details about the decision against City on the Tuesday before last, it hit hard. It was the weight of the language – how it dripped with contempt – as well as the sheer extent of the transgressions. Proven misconduct. Sham arrangements. Concerted attempts to frustrate the investigation. How some of the club’s witnesses gave evidence that they knew to be untrue. It served to frame this game. It will continue to frame each one that City play for the foreseeable.
The Liverpool supporters turned up the decibel levels sharply in the minutes before kick-off. It was frantic. It was fractious. For both sets of players, it was about mastering the occasion. The home fans in the Sir Kenny Dalgish stand did not need Ronald Araújo to whip them up in the second minute after he crashed into a slide tackle on Antoine Semenyo. You can imagine the reaction shortly afterwards when Marc Guéhi was penalised but not booked for going to ground too easily. Araújo got the yellow card for demanding that Guéhi be shown one.
The City fans came armed with scores of inflatable bananas. Some of them wore old-school match shirts. There was a message in there somewhere. Maybe to say that their club predates the Abu Dhabi takeover. It was also possible to spot banners in support of Khaldoon al-Mubarak, the club chair.
You want banners? The Kop had that boxed off. There were some that riffed off Oasis lyrics, including one with the line that “after all, you really robbed us all.” The most eye-catching was unfurled before kick-off, featuring the word ‘cheats’ and a very long sequence of pound signs. The Liverpool crowd had the chants, too. From the get-go. Inside the ground, it was hard not to wonder how clearly they came across on TVs around the world.
There was very little first-half action to report. Even the melee that broke out in the 12th minute after Alexis Mac Allister tussled with Anderson was the definition of handbags. There were no big chances; the precision on the final ball was frequently absent. Liverpool had lost their best three best players of the season so far to injuries during the international break – Dominik Szoboszlai, Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak. Which plainly did not help their rhythm.
Iraola gave Lewis Koumas a full league debut up front and it was the 21-year-old who had the first decent effort of the game straight after the restart. Gianluigi Donnarumma stood tall to save. Liverpool upped the intensity and they had a spell where they pushed and the Kop felt the breakthrough was coming. Gravenberch worked Donnarumma. Mac Allister volleyed wide.
Haaland blew a glorious chance from a Semenyo pass on the hour, dinking past the far post but City had otherwise created little. Then everything changed. Gravenberch had caught the eye with his surging runs but he was on the wrong side when he challenged Doku, who was ready to spark a counterattack.
It was clumsy from Gravenberch, the contact on Doku not exactly strong. But having been booked at the start of the second half for a foul on Anderson, Gravenberch was running an almighty risk. He did not get away with it.
City had their opening and how they pilled through it. The way that they overwhelmed Liverpool was really something; a demonstration of their strength. It was not a game for the neutral. Are there any such viewers where City are concerned any more? Doku almost teed up Nico O’Reilly and City were on their way when Haaland swept home from a deflected Doku cross. A new reality? Same old City on the pitch. – Guardian

title: Mother appeals for help to find Irish man (30) missing in New York
description: Jordan McGrath arrived in New York in mid-August and has not been heard from since
content:
An Irish woman whose son has been missing in New York City for almost two months has appealed to the public for information about his whereabouts.
Fiona McGrath, from Clarecastle, Co Clare , told The Irish Times that her son Jordan (30) arrived in New York in mid-August and has not been heard from since.
Jordan McGrath had previously travelled to the city in June, but returned home to Ireland after less than a week.
“That time, he only stayed a few days. He spent a night with the homeless community, and three nights in hotels. He didn’t say too much about it, just that he really liked the New York people but after his fourth night, he called to say he was coming home. Then, two months later, he was off to New York again,” McGrath said.
The last transaction on her son’s bank card was made at the 101 Hotel in Manhattan’s Bowery district in August.
“He spent $350 for a one-night stay on August 13th, but there’s been no action on his bank cards since then. So we’re very worried that he may have become homeless,” she said.
Jordan’s father Brian, his siblings Michael and Chelsea, and several aunts and uncles have been trying to contact him since and are seeking information from anyone who might know where he is.
“The thing is, to go to America, he’d have had to book a return flight, but we can’t find out what date he was supposed to have come back,” McGrath said.
“We spoke to the NYPD as well, and they’ve checked hospitals and mortuaries, but he never showed up there, thank God.”
Jordan is described as being about 5ft 7in tall, of slight build, with light brown, shoulder-length hair and a beard. He has blue eyes and a piercing at the back of his neck.
Anyone with information about Jordan McGrath’s whereabouts is asked to contact the NYPD’s 5th Precinct on (+1 212) 334-0711 or the Consulate General of Ireland (New York) at (+1 212) 319 2555.

title: Fr Eamonn refused to buy pints for me in London, long before his reputation was shredded
description: The ebullient young priest who had impressed me so much is now dead
content:
T he pub door opened, and a familiar figure came barrelling in. “Heavy shower out there, lads. I’m soaked.” He shrugged off a black anorak revealing a grey cardigan and an almost invisible abbreviated version of a clerical collar.
“Right lads, who’s for a pint?” He looked at me: “You’re new. I haven’t seen you before. Do you have a trade?”
I looked back at him puzzled. “A trade?”
One of the other lads explained. “He means – are you a brickie? Or a sparks, or a plasterer?”
“I’m a kitchen porter, at Mike’s Café in Blenheim Crescent.”
“No good to me then,” said my inquisitor as he moved on, buying pints for the lads who worked on the buildings. I’d see Eamonn often in the months to come. Usually on a Friday evening in the pubs where we Irish lads gathered, around the Portobello Road, Latimer Road and Shepherds Bush in west London. He was always Eamonn to us, one of the lads.
He was working for a housing charity, getting short leases on houses scheduled for eventual demolition, making them habitable for homeless families. In the long term those clearances led to the construction of blocks such as Grenfell Tower . In the short term they were a godsend for poor families, newly arrived in London, looking for jobs and places to stay while they got their names on the council housing list.
The deal was this: on Friday evening Eamonn bought pints for the lads, then on Saturday mornings the lads put in a few unpaid hours painting, plastering, wiring up second-hand cookers and fridges. Very often families moved into those previously derelict flats and houses the following Monday.
[ London is a city where Irishness gets shouted out, rather than smoothed over Opens in new window ]
And each time we met, he would greet me with a broad smile and “No pints for you boy, you’ve no trade”. It was our little ritual. Then one night in Henekey’s pub on the Portobello Road, he appeared in the usual way. Before he opened his mouth, I shook my head. “Look. I don’t drink with curates, not any more.”
“I wasn’t offering”, he replied,” but I wonder if I should take offence?”
“No offence meant. It’s just that yesterday Cardinal Heenan bought me a pint.”
Eamonn’s jaw dropped. “What do you mean?” He just about managed to get the words out. “How did that happen?”
“You know the big pub on Commonwealth Avenue in White City? There’s a new church just being built there.”
Eamonns’s face began to clear. “Our Lady of Fatima, I heard he was giving a blessing there now the church building is finished. I suppose there was a reception afterwards. How did you blag your way in?”
“The parish priest, Gerard Daniel, is my cousin.”
Eamonn was off bustling out the door calling over his shoulder “Tomorrow morning 10 o’clock lads, outside Latimer Road tube station.”
I was disappointed that Eamonn left so soon that night. I wanted to know more about John Carmel Heenan, Archbishop of Westminster. That was the year he was made a cardinal. An Essex boy, he’s best remembered nowadays for reminding us that a church that is half empty is also half full.
[ London’s Irish pubs aren’t hip, but they’re hard to beat as ambassadors for the diaspora Opens in new window ]
At White City he mixed well, chatting to the mostly women and children present. Next year perhaps there would be an official event with pomp and circumstance. For now it was very informal. Later that morning in the local pub I was introduced to him as the parish priest’s Irish cousin. “You’re not having a drink?” he asked. I said it was a bit early for me. “Today is a good day. Good days are important,” he said and moved on to talk to somebody else. He left shortly afterwards.
A little while later I was about to go. The barman called me over. He was pulling a pint of foaming lager, which was a bit of a luxury item in those days. “Yer man left this for you,” the barman said. “He told me to remind you not to forget to celebrate the good days.”
The lives of young Irish men and women in London in the 1960s were transitory ones. We were birds of passage and most moved on. For me, children, marriage, what passed for a proper job lay ahead, but not in London. I lost sight of the energetic young Kerry priest whose ministry was expressed in bricks and mortar, slates and window frames, putting roofs over the heads of the poor and needy. I lost sight of Fr Eamonn Casey , the ebullient young priest who had impressed me so much. In years to come, I would wonder where all that good-hearted energy and enthusiasm had gone.
[ When the Annie Murphy revelations came out, people wore Eamonn Casey T-shirts. How little we knew Opens in new window ]
Now, with Eamonn Casey dead, and his reputation shredded, and my own days numbered, I remember the Cardinal Archbishop of Westminster’s words to me half a century ago, about how important it is to celebrate the good days.

title: Tension, ‘cheat’ banners and inflatable bananas: Manchester City’s welcome to Anfield
description: Incendiary atmosphere greets City in first game since being found guilty of breaking financial rules
content:
Fans lined the streets to Anfield in preparation for the arrival of the Manchester City team bus, pyrotechnics and pure vitriol adding to the tense prematch atmosphere. Every vantage point was taken, with spectators standing on walls to get a glimpse of the enemy, only for the coach to sneak in from the opposite side of the ground to avoid confrontation.
The subterfuge defused a volatile situation that could have turned into an incendiary one. Tensions were high on Merseyside. Since the City takeover in 2008, Liverpool have finished second to their rivals on three occasions, although only one of those falls within the parameters of the investigation into City’s financial breaches of Premier League rules. Liverpool supporters are aggrieved, feeling they would have won more trophies had City not circumnavigated the rules to help sign elite players.
Liverpool were punished in 2018 after supporters launched missiles at the team bus as City players were driven to Anfield for a Champions League clash. The animosity has only been heightened by the independent commission’s guilty verdict.
References to the verdict were not difficult to find at stalls outside. For £15 – haggling took it down to £10 – it was possible to buy a “Guilty 114” flag, including an AI image of City’s squad in prison uniforms, or a “Cheats” banner in the style of the Oasis logo.
Many supporters, however, were content with the traditional – and much maligned – half-and-half scarf to commemorate such an occasion. The fashion conscious could pick up T-shirts with a similar motif. There were more frugal offerings, with home-made banners carrying the blunt message being paraded around the ground.
There was a sense of injustice, and thousands wanted to express it. A solitary City fan, clad in sky blue, stood among the sea of red. He was unbothered by the commotion around him but was left alone because he is not at fault.
Social media chatter suggested City merited a “bus greeting” on Anfield Road, and police were prepared for such an eventuality. There was toxicity and hostility on both sides in the build-up, with away supporters chanting their anthem of “City’s going down with a billion in the bank” while waving inflatable bananas, the latter a tradition that goes back to the 1980s.
It provides a reminder that City existed for 114 years before Sheikh Mansour’s investment and will continue to do so regardless of what happens in relation to potential sanctions. Many have witnessed City drop to the third tier and win the Champions League, so have experienced both ends of the spectrum already.
The police flew a drone above the route the City bus planned to take into the ground, while officers walked up and down filming those in attendance as the decibels and anger grew.
Every vehicle was treated with suspicion, as theories of subterfuge from City, not for the first time, were discussed. The prospect of sneaking the players and staff into the ground were gossiped about among the crowds, but there was no Trojan horse. Instead, the official team bus, with full livery, came up the other side of Anfield Road and around the back of the stand that bears its name.
The Liverpool bus arrived to cheers, chants and plenty of red smoke just before 3pm. The eyes stung as the wind blew. The police presence grew closer to the anticipated arrival time on the bus.
Around an hour before kick-off, after City’s coach was whisked up to the ground with its police motorcade, the visiting supporters were given their own escort across Stanley Park. The message was a defiant one, backing chair Khaldoon al-Mubarak with verses of “We’re Man City, we’ll cheat when we want”. There was mild heckling from home fans in earshot but, like with the bus, it passed without incident. The cheering and jeering carried on while the travelling fans waited to enter the ground, but it was nothing out of the ordinary for a football match between two rivals. Calmness had descended.
As City walked on to the pitch for their warm-up, they were loudly booed by the majority inside the ground, with every player’s name mentioned on the public address system receiving the same treatment. City took solace in the bunch of bananas bouncing around the away end in one small corner before football finally took centre stage. – Guardian

title: Shane Lowry finishes tied 13th at Spanish Open as Forrest wins with birdie at last
description: Scotland’s Grant Forrest birdies final hole to snatch victory in Madrid
content:
Shane Lowry gained more qualifying points for the Ryder Cup with a solid tied-13th finish at the Spanish Open in Madrid, as Scotland’s Grant Forrest birdied the final hole to win in a thrilling finale.
Lowry shot a three-under-par of 68 and will be pleased to have gone bogey-free in his final round in the first of four tournaments in five weeks in his schedule at the end of the DP World Tour season. His final total of eight-under-par was six shots off the winning score.
The Offaly man enjoyed his week in Spain, taking in Real Madrid against Villarreal in the Bernabeu last night, and will now head to the DP India Championship in form, where he will be joined in the field by Rory McIlroy.
Forrest avoided a three-way playoff and snatched a one-shot victory by sinking a four-foot putt on the 18th at the Real Club de Campo Villa de Madrid to deny home favourite Eugenio Chacarra and France’s Victor Perez by one stroke on 14 under.
Forrest, who shared a one-shot lead with England’s Joe Dean going into the final round, sealed his third DP World Tour title and a place at both next year’s Masters and The Open.
On the HotelPlanner Tour, Liam Nolan had another successful week, finishing tied fifth at the Hainan Open, a week after winning in Abu Dhabi. The Galway golfer is up three places to ninth in the standings as he chases one of 15 available DP World Tour cards for next season.

title: Irish man among 300 injured as 12 die in attack at Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia
description: EU chief Ursula von der Leyen described the ‘murderous attack on civilians’ as a ‘dangerous escalation’ in the wider war
content:
The latest attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia ’s capital of Riyadh killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others, civil aviation authorities said early on Sunday, with some in a critical condition. A Saudi-led coalition blamed Iran -backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen.
A missile struck a King Khalid International Airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorised to speak to the media.
Those injured in the airport include an Irish man, although no information was available immediately about his condition or his identity.
“The Department of Foreign Affairs is aware of this case and is providing consular assistance,” the department said in reply to questions on Sunday evening.
“As with all consular cases, the department does not comment on the details of individual cases.”
Earlier, Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee said Irish citizens should avoid travel to King Khalid airport, saying they should seek updates from their airline, monitor local media and follow official safety advice.
“Our Embassy in Riyadh continues to monitor the situation and Irish citizens in need of urgent assistance or advice can contact them,” McEntee said.
McEntee condemned the airport attack, saying she and European counterparts will discuss the situation at a meeting on Monday of EU ministers.
“I will underline that Iran’s attacks on its neighbours must cease and that safe and toll-free shipping through the Straits of Hormuz must be restored,” she said.
“This is critical not just for regional peace and stability but also for the wider global economy. It is in all our interests that there is a return to meaningful, good-faith negotiations.”
She added: “I am deeply concerned by the escalation of attacks by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia. These have included the deliberate targeting of civilian infrastructure.”
A Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said the injured were being treated at several hospitals.
The US president, Donald Trump , said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen. “We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”
The US secretary of ⁠state, Marco ⁠Rubio, called the attacks “​reprehensible” and said “they must ​stop ‌now”.
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the European Union stands “in solidarity with Saudi Arabia”, noting the “murderous attack on civilians” as a “dangerous escalation” in the wider war.
She said the “attacks by Iran’s proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence”.
“They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shockwave sent through the world,” she said.
One witness at the Riyadh airport reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded.
“I was on gate 403,” at the domestic terminal, the witness told the Agence France-Presse news agency. “I saw [gate] 401 hit, I saw injured [people] in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”
The relative of one injured person said they had been wounded in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass and taken to hospital.
[ Saudi Arabia confirms that Houthi strikes on Riyadh airport killed three Opens in new window ]
A projectile also fell near the King Fahd international airport in Dammam, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis. The Dammam airport has become an important alternative to Riyadh amid the recent spate of attacks.
There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sana’a international airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.
Schools in Riyadh will move to remote learning for a week, according to the education ministry, following the deadly attack.
Saturday’s incident comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis ⁠on the kingdom. The airport has already been attacked twice this ​week, leaving four people dead and ‌others wounded, and ‌badly damaging an aircraft.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.
The attack came as forces allied to the UN-recognised government in Yemen claim to have mounted a successful offensive to retake the Bab al-Mandab strait from Houthi rebels, but accounts vary as to whether the push has been repelled.
A Houthi spokesperson said forces from the Saudi-backed government based in Aden “were targeted with a large number of ballistic missiles, artillery support and heavy weapons, resulting in the destruction of more than 22 armoured vehicles and the killing and wounding of dozens, including a number of commanders.
“More than 30 ambulances arrived in Aden to transport the dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations.”
By contrast, the Saudi ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed al-Jaber, said: “Blessed Friday and victory for every Yemeni and Arab. Bab al-Mandab has been cleared of the remnants of the Houthi terrorist militia.”
The exposed 5sq mile (13sq km) Perim Island straddles the strait, acting as a lookout point for all traffic from the Red Sea into the Gulf of Aden and towards the Indian Ocean. Aidarous al-Zubaidi, the president of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), one of the main political forces in the south of Yemen, claimed the island and coastal area had been recaptured from Houthi hands.
An official military spokesperson for the UN-recognised government forces qualified the claim, saying only half the area had been recaptured so far. Waddah al-Dabish said newly established Houthi defensive lines had been broken on the land next to the strait, leading to the death of thousands of Houthi fighters.
It is thought that as many as 500 Houthi fighters are stationed on the island, and Saudi Arabia is desperate to be able to report the strait has been reclaimed to show that the land counteroffensive it launched at the beginning of the week is advancing.
The report came as the United Nations’ special envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, admitted to the UN security council in New York that Yemen – one of the poorest countries in the world – had lapsed back into full-scale war and said the first victims would be women and children.
The Houthis seized control of the strait two weeks ago and said no Saudi-linked commercial traffic would be permitted to go through the narrow waterway. The Houthis are waging a war to remove Saudi influence from Yemen, and have been mounting missile attacks on Riyadh in support of this objective.
[ Netanyahu faces fresh scrutiny over pre-October 7th warnings Opens in new window ]
There have been previous premature reports of military breakthroughs by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government since it launched its counteroffensive at the start of the week, but the recapture of the land by the strait and Perim Island (also known as Mayyun Island) is a military prize western governments desperately need. – Guardian

title: Former Court of Criminal Appeal judge Declan Budd leaves estate worth over €3.5m
description: Elsewhere, former mayor of Kildare left €2.1m, Propate Office papers lodged this week show
content:
Former Court of Criminal Appeal judge Declan Budd left an estate worth €3.58 million when he died in August 2025, according to papers published by the Probate Office this week.
Budd, of Blackrock, Co Dublin, came from a prominent legal family. His father, Frederic Gardner Orford Budd, was a judge of the Supreme Court .
A foundation scholar of Trinity College Dublin , Budd was called to the Bar in 1968, appointed senior counsel in 1981, and to the High Court as a judge in 1991.
He was appointed to the Court of Criminal Appeal in 2008 before retiring in 2011.
He was president of the Law Reform Commission from 2000 to 2005. During his time at the commission he was credited with overseeing vital modernisations of Irish statute law.
He was also an early advocate for allowing family law cases to be heard in public to increase institutional transparency.
In a landmark legal contribution, his rulings were instrumental in preventing the privatisation of the Blasket Islands off the coast of Co Kerry, protecting them as elements of national heritage.
He was a dedicated member and former club captain of Three Rock Rovers Hockey Club. He also spent many years volunteering locally as a member of the Dún Laoghaire association of An Taisce.
[ Founder of Peploe’s in Dublin leaves more than €2.8m in will Opens in new window ]
In other grants of probate, Rainsford Hendy, former mayor of Kildare and Fine Gael stalwart for almost two decades, left an estate valued at €2.1 million.
Hendy was first elected to local government in 1991 and served for nearly two decades representing the Athy electoral area until his political retirement in 2009.
Hendy also ran a business making garden sheds. He was a keen fundraiser for the Irish Cancer Society and a member of the Diocesan Synod for the Church of Ireland.
Following his death in September 2024 aged 73, Hendy was the subject of many tributes from high-profile political leaders, including Leo Varadkar. The former taoiseach said the two had met when they were both councillors and kept in touch over the years. The Hendy family could be proud of his contribution to Co Kildare, Varadkar said.
Racehorse breeder Duncan McGregor of Newtown Lodge Stud in Kildare left an estate valued at €1.49 million when he died aged 84, in February.
Originally from Falkirk, Scotland, McGregor relocated to Kildare with his wife, Lynn, when he was in his 40s and dedicated the rest of his life to equine breeding and racing.
One of his first broodmares was Gradille, whose bloodline went on to produce notable winners including Soldier Of Fortune, Sholokhov, Subjectivist, and Intense Focus.
He successfully bred and raced several winners of his own including Dashing Colours, winner of the Listed Knockaire Stakes, and Shesasmartlady, dam of winner Captain Marvelous.
McGregor also had notable success with Danega which he bought for €16,000 in 2022. Her offspring, Marhaba Ya Sanafi, went on to win the Poule d’Essai des Poulains at Longchamp, which McGregor described as his greatest day in racing.
Corporate lawyer and chairman of Enable Ireland Stephen Haughey left an estate valued at €2.04 million when he died in April 2026.
Haughey, of Skibbereen and formerly of Belfast and Wicklow, also served as a senior figure at KPMG.
He used his legal and strategic expertise to serve as the national chairman of Enable Ireland, the country’s largest non-HSE organisation supporting people with disabilities.
Under his guidance, Enable Ireland campaigned aggressively to improve diagnostic wait lists and direct resources to family support networks.

title: Cork’s Séamus Harnedy retires from intercounty hurling
description: A three-time All-Star, the St Ita’s forward won four Munster titles
content:
Séamus Harnedy has retired after 15 years on the Cork senior hurling panel. The St Ita’s forward struggled with injury in the past couple of seasons and didn’t start any of Cork’s games in this year’s championship.
Harnedy never played minor for Cork but he made his breakthrough as a senior under Jimmy Barry-Murphy in 2013, having made a huge impression as a Fitzgibbon Cup player with UCC. Cork lost the All-Ireland to Clare that year after a replay but Harnedy finished the season with the first of his three All-Stars.
He won his fourth Munster medal in 2025 but a hamstring injury reduced him to a role as a second-half sub in the All-Ireland final. When Cork were beaten by Galway in this year’s All-Ireland semi-final he didn’t see any game time off the bench.
Harnedy turned 36 in July and didn’t play for his divisional team Imokilly in this year’s Cork senior hurling championship.
“And that’s a wrap. It’s hard to put into words what the last 15 years in the Cork jersey have meant to me,” Harnedy said in a statement on social media.
“I’ve had the honour of playing with and against some of the greatest hurlers of all time. On top of that I’ve had the privilege of working under outstanding management teams and mentors but the time has come to step away.
“Incredibly grateful for the support from my family, my friends, my club, St. Ita’s and the people of Cork. Rebels abú go deo.”

title: Public sector strike may be difficult to avert at this stage, Minister admits
description: Preparations are under way for the strike, which will see more than 300,000 public sector workers undertake a work stoppage
content:
The one-day national strike by 400,000 public sector employees planned for Wednesday will “probably go ahead at this stage”, a Government Minister has said.
Minister for Further and Higher Education James Lawless said €1.2 billion has been set aside by Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers for the pay demands.
He also argued the average rate for a public sector worker was “far higher” than that for a private sector worker.
Lawless indicated it might be difficult to avert the action. “I think the strike will probably go ahead at this stage,” he said.
He added he had spoken to public service employees, and believed they did not want to picket on Wednesday.
“What I’d say to the union leadership is, come in and talk. Come to the table,” he said on RTÉ ’s The Week in Politics. “It can still be avoided.”
Sinn Féin TD Rose Conway Walsh told the same programme the Government could sort it out by Wednesday but that a resolution would only be reached if focused firstly on the question of pay increases.
“There is no point in the Minister standing back arrogantly and saying, ‘Well, you know the table is open,’” she said.
Labour’s finance spokesman Ged Nash said it was no surprise trade union groups would want to prioritise pay in pay talks when there was a cost-of-living crisis.
[ Budget 2027 falls short of preventing public sector industrial action, say unions Opens in new window ]
“It is not only about pay but is about respect as well,” he said.
Lawless said he respected the rights of unions to take industrial action. But he said talks needed to take place.
“Come in with a blank sheet of paper and let’s engage. And of course it’s going to involve pay. How could it not?”
Preparations are under way for the strike, which will see more than 300,000 public sector workers undertake a 24-hour work stoppage in pursuit of a new public sector pay deal, though essential services will be maintained.
Another strike is scheduled for the following Wednesday, while senior union figures are privately warning of escalation of their action in November if negotiations do not get under way in the coming weeks.

title: AIL: Old order rise to the challenge in fiercely competitive Division 1A
description: Lansdowne fight back against Old Belvedere for first win of the season
content:
The old order rose to the challenge in the Energia All-Ireland League at the weekend as Lansdowne, Clontarf and Cork Constitution all won at home against the previously unbeaten trio of Old Belvedere, UCD and St Mary’s respectively.
The latest result mean that after three rounds in what looks the most competitive Division 1A in many years, no team remains unbeaten.
On a landmark day for Lansdowne, they hosted Old Belvedere in their first game on the main pitch at the Aviva Stadium in three seasons. When Belvo raced to a 19-0 lead inside 30 minutes through tries from Ed Byrne, scrumhalf Chris O’Connor and Patrick Dowling, they looked set for a third bonus-point win to inflict a third defeat on Lansdowne.
But Leinster academy fullback Todd Lawlor, virtually uncontainable, took a superb line just before half-time and thereafter Lansdowne were transformed. After a try by flanker Paul Wilson, centre Dylan O’Keeffe scored a brace, the second from a crosskick by Lawlor whose break then instigated a blur of offloads and support lines culminating in lock Juan Beukes scoring. A late Fionn McWey try salvaged a bonus point for Belvo.
“I knew we’d be in a good place mentally coming into the game,” said Lansdowne head coach Rhys Ruddock after his first win in charge. “I was just disappointed that we conceded so many points early on. I think the lads were very frustrated as well on the field, you could kind of feel it, but I don’t think the belief had gone, which was the main thing.
“We just tried to be a bit more accurate in what we were doing around the set-piece, discipline and playing in the right areas. I thought we did that really well in the second half and scored some good tries as well, so it was very pleasing.”
Cork Con were also staring a third successive defeat in the face when Mick O’Gara’s 74th-minute penalty pushed St Mary’s into a 24-22 lead after the sides had shared six tries in what had always been a one-score game. But Dylan Hicks’ 48-metre penalty in stoppage time avenged last season’s record 57-19 defeat to the champions.
A stacked Clontarf side went top with a nine-try 61-15 victory over UCD at Castle Avenue, securing the bonus point before the break.
At Lakelands Park, Terenure roared into a 27-7 interval lead by the half-hour mark against Old Wesley through tries from Jordan Coghlan, Ben Blaney and Max Russell, and the accurate kicking of Aran Egan. But the visitors hit back through Stephen Smyth, Paidi Farrell and David Maher, bringing Wesley within a point before Kiwi scrumhalf Griffin Culver secured maximum points for Terenure.
Having led 10-7 at half-time, Young Munster pulled clear at Tom Clifford Park through second-half ties from Luke Murphy, Oisin Minogue, Paul Allen and Benjamin Whatley to beat Ballynahinch, now the only winless side in 1A.
And in the Division 1A of the women’s league, Railway Union made a statement on the opening weekend, defeating defending champions UL Bohemian 19-15 in Park Avenue.

title: Cork drifting trio one heat away from bringing trophies home
description: Over 10,000 people turn out in Cork City to celebrate Conor Shanahan as he closes in on Formula Drift title
content:
Ten years ago, Jack Shanahan was one of the lads driving into Cork city for pizza, looping down Patrick Street and on to the South Mall. On Saturday night he was back on the same street, sideways this time, in front of more than 10,000 people.
“It’s kind of mad,” the 27-year-old said. “Almost 10 years later after getting my licence ... to come back and be able to perform basically on the street and not get arrested.”
Red Bull’s Homerun brought Formula One and drifting to South Mall to celebrate Jack’s younger brother, Conor, the two-time Drift Masters champion who could claim the biggest prize in American drifting, Formula Drift, within a fortnight.
When Formula Drift reaches its final round on the streets of Long Beach, California, on October 23rd – 24th, Conor Shanahan needs to win just one heat to be crowned 2026 champion. He leads the standings on 212 points, 47 clear of his nearest challenger: James Deane, the five-time champion who grew up a kilometre down the road.
In August, these pages told the story of three drivers raised six minutes apart between Mallow and Fermoy who had become the sport’s dominant force. Since then the picture has sharpened. Conor finished second in Europe’s Drift Masters and won Formula Drift rounds in Seattle and Las Vegas, where an engine failure, Deane’s first since joining his team, swung the American title race his way.
Yet there is little sign of the rivalry souring anything. Asked how it felt that his crown might pass to the driver from around the corner, Deane looked past the result entirely.
“It’s unreal, to be honest,” he said. “The three of us here right now are top four in the championship standings ... If we bring the three championship trophies back home, like we live a kilometre from each other, I think it’s something that you can’t even write.”
That is now the shared ambition. Jack, fourth in the standings, needs to finish at least one battle ahead of American Branden Sorensen to complete an all-Irish top three.
“I’m kind of happy that he’s [Conor] so far ahead,” Jack said grinning. “It’s kind of up to him really to make his destiny.”
Once the helmets go on, he added, they’re back to being normal competitors.
“If I have to finish third and finish behind the two lads, I’m finishing behind two of the best in the world. So it’s still a win for me.”
Deane is already picturing the end-of-season banquet. “We might be the only people at the prize-giving if the three of us were standing up there at the end.”
For Conor, now 23, the night acted as a reminder of where it all starts. “We had James to look up to when we were kids, and we were trying our best to follow the dream,” he said.
At a meet-and-greet in Glanmire in the days before, he said, children kept telling him they would be there on Saturday night. “That’s what this event is about: giving an opportunity to the fans of motorsport in Ireland.”
The next generation was on the bill too. Conor Falvey, an 18-year-old from Cork, took his first Drift Masters podium at Mondello Park in June, beating Deane on his way to the final.
When asked what his favourite car to drive has been, Deane, marking his 20th year in the sport, brought back memories of the S15 that carried him to success in America. The first time he drove it again, around his own yard in Cork, the memories came flooding back. “It was a very special moment,” he said, “and one that I hadn’t planned for.”
In two weeks’ time, three neighbours from North Cork will line up, head-to-head, on the other side of the world with the chance to make another.

title: Eight men charged with violent disorder at horse fair in Ballinasloe
description: Large Garda presence as the men – aged 18 to 30 – appeared before a special sitting of Loughrea District Court
content:
Eight men have appeared in court in Co Galway charged with violent disorder in Ballinasloe during the International Horse Fair in the town.
There was a large Garda presence as the men – aged 18 to 30 – appeared before a special sitting of Loughrea District Court on Sunday.
Seven of the men were charged with violent disorder at St Michael’s Square, Townparks, Ballinasloe, on Saturday.
They were: Bernard Cawley (24) of Canal Drive, Ballinasloe; John Ward (29) of Esker Park, Athlone, Co Westmeath; Patrick Ward (29) of Dunlo Street, Ballinasloe; John Ward (20) and Bernard Ward (25), both of Hymany Park, Ballinasloe; Bernard McDonagh of Blackberry Lane, Athlone; and Joe Joyce (24) of Moate, Co Westmeath.
Two of the men were charged with violent disorder at the Marina car park in Ballinasloe. They were Joyce – who faces two violent disorder charges – and Gerry Ward (18) of Hymany Park, Ballinasloe.
Garda Pádraig Connolly and Garda Rudy Kelly of Tuam Garda station, Garda Michelle Hallinan of Ballinasloe Garda station and Insp Declan Rock gave evidence of arrest, charge and caution.
Joyce appeared in court with a white bandage wrapped around his head. Gerry Ward was hobbling and defence barrister Martin Durack said his client had an ankle injury that needed medical attention in Portiuncula University Hospital Ballinasloe.
Judge Olivia Traynor remanded seven of the men on bail to appear before the November 26th sitting of Ballinasloe District Court for directions from the Director of Public Prosecutions.
Joyce was remanded on bail to appear before the December 3rd sitting of Ballinasloe District Court.
All eight men made cash lodgements of €500 as part of their bail conditions.
They agreed to be of good behaviour, attend all court appearances, and not contact witnesses or other parties involved in the alleged violent disorder incident, either directly or indirectly or by social media.
McDonagh and the older John Ward must stay out of Ballinasloe as part of their bail conditions.
Patrick Ward, Gerry Ward, Bernard Ward and the younger John Ward, as well as Cawley, must stay out of Athlone as part of their bail conditions.
Joyce must stay out of Ballinasloe and Athlone, apart from attending medical or legal appointments, as part of his bail conditions.
The court heard that two of the men – Cawley and the older John Ward – were unemployed and one, Patrick Ward, was working part-time.
Rock indicated there may be further charges brought against the accused, and Hallinan said further charges may be brought against other individuals arising from the same incidents.

title: Resurgent Max Verstappen holds off Charles Leclerc to seal dominant Singapore GP win
description: Red Bull driver claims second victory in a row
content:
Max Verstappen won the Singapore Grand Prix with a commanding run from pole to flag to take his first victory at the Marina Bay circuit in his 250th race.
He comfortably beat Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc into second place with championship leader Kimi Antonelli third. Defending world champion Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri were fourth and fifth for McLaren, while Lewis Hamilton was sixth for Ferrari. Antonelli’s Mercedes team-mate George Russell came through to take ninth, having started 19th on the grid.
Antonelli now leads Russell by 102 points, meaning he can mathematically win the title at the next round in Austin if he takes victory and Russell finishes lower than eighth.
In what was something of a pedestrian affair under the floodlights of Singapore, Verstappen was dominant from pole, in complete control despite his radio communications with his team failing. Behind him, Antonelli kept his cool to claim a podium place while Hamilton conceded his strategy call was instrumental in him slipping back to sixth.
Verstappen’s first win in Singapore and Red Bull’s first here since 2022 was another demonstration of how well the car is now performing, with the Dutchman untouchable all weekend. He took pole and the win in the sprint race and then pole and the win in the grand prix, the 73rd of his career.
Recent upgrades from Red Bull have transformed what was a difficult ride to manage, even for Verstappen, into an entirely different car, comfortably on top of Mercedes, Ferrari and McLaren at the last two meetings. The championship is surely beyond Verstappen after their early season travails, but he and the team will be hugely buoyed up by bringing performance to the car that they can feed into next year’s model.
The four-time champion held his lead from a charging Leclerc through the opening corners, with Hamilton and Antonelli maintaining their places in third and fourth. The Ferrari looked pacy, with Leclerc climbing all over Verstappen on the opening laps.
Hamilton was not quick on the medium rubber so pitted for soft tyres on lap 18 with more than 40 laps still to go. Going with a counter strategy to the rest of the field, Hamilton was immediately quick with the changed tyres, setting a series of fastest laps.
Antonelli pitted on lap 23, emerging behind Hamilton, whose quick laps had paid off. Leclerc pitted a lap later, also taking the medium rubber. Hamilton was right on him as he exited the pit lane but could not pass, with the British driver pointedly telling the team he had lost two-seconds over a lap behind Leclerc after Ferrari opted not to switch their drivers.
Verstappen and Norris both took stops on lap 32, with the Dutchman retaining his lead, now with fresh tyres and in complete control out front, while Norris gained a place on Antonelli.
A virtual safety car was called on lap 39 when Lance Stroll came to a halt on track and Ferrari took the chance to pit Leclerc but Hamilton opted not to come in, a decision which did not pay off.
Hamilton tried to eke out his tyres to make it to the flag, but with his pace dropping, he was set to be caught by Norris and Antonelli. Norris went at him, but in trying to pass was left vulnerable to Antonelli, who dived past to take the place and then passed Hamilton for third.
Norris followed him through a lap later as Hamilton’s tyres fell away, Piastri too completing a pass to move up to fifth. It at least provided an entertaining finale, but one long in Verstappen’s wake as proceeded to take the flag with ease. – Guardian

title: More ‘cockroach’ movement activists detained in protests over India’s elections
description: Court orders youth movement’s leaders to be released, as group challenges Narendra Modi’s grip on power
content:
Police detained hundreds of ​protesters in Delhi for a second day on Sunday as sporadic protests broke out demanding the resignation of India ’s election chief, and a court ordered the release of “cockroach” movement founder Abhijeet Dipke and two other senior leaders.
Dipke and ​the other Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders were detained when their plane landed in Delhi on Saturday as ⁠the movement planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in Central Delhi.
The court ‌ordered ‌their ​release with an undertaking to “maintain public peace”, the CJP said in a statement.
“Cockroaches never die,” the group posted on its ⁠X account shortly after Dipke’s ​release.
Youth protesters, many of them from students’ ​organisations affiliated with India’s communist parties, launched sporadic protests around the city on Sunday afternoon before ‌police detained them and hauled them away ​in vehicles.
The All India Students’ Association alleged in a post on X that ⁠those detained were assaulted by police ⁠inside the vehicles.
A video ​posted on X by the Communist Party of India (Marxist) showed one of its lawmakers, John Brittas, being helped from a bus to an auto-rickshaw as he appeared to be in distress.
Reuters could not verify claims about detainees being assaulted by police. A Delhi Police spokesperson did not respond to calls made by Reuters to seek comment.
[ The unlikely rise of India’s Gen Z rebels Opens in new window ]
The youth movement is one of the biggest political challenges ‌to prime minister Narendra ⁠Modi in his 12 years in power, during which his Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has repeatedly swept the polls and eliminated any serious challenge by opponents, including ‌the Congress party.
The protesters are calling for the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a ​revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Modi.

title: DUP accuses Bryant of ‘disgraceful appeasement’ on Garvaghy Road march
description: Party’s Upper Bann MP Carla Lockhart says party must ensure Sinn Féin’s Michelle O’Neill is ‘dealt with in the appropriate way’
content:
Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant has been accused of “disgraceful appeasement” after he stepped in to stop the Orange Order parading down the Garvaghy Road .
DUP leader Gavin Robinson called for more information about the decision to be made public, questioning whether there had been a “bending of the knee of the rule of law in the threat of terror and violence”.
DUP Upper Bann MP Carla Lockhart said it “cannot be business as usual” politically after First Minister and Sinn Féin vice-president Michelle O’Neill received a letter from police asking her to attend a voluntary interview about protests on the Garvaghy Road against the parade.
She said her party “should use whatever is in our armoury to ensure that Michelle O’Neill is dealt with in the appropriate way”, adding it has “within its gift to remove” her as First Minister.
However, Robinson indicated he is not minded to bring down Stormont, questioning whether it would make anything better and adding he would not want to hand the reins to Bryant.
A legal challenge will be heard on Monday to Bryant’s decision to act following a decision by the Parades Commission to allow the Drumcree parade to go along the Garvaghy Road for the first time in almost 30 years.
It sparked a reawakening of the former flashpoint with large crowds opposed to the parade gathering on the Garvaghy Road which effectively prevented the parade from taking place.
Police are undertaking a large-scale criminal investigation into potential breaches of the law during the 12-day stand-off.
O’Neill is one of a number of Sinn Féin members, as well as People Before Profit MLA Gerry Carroll, who have received a letter from police inviting them to attend a voluntary interview as part of that probe.
Monday will also see the issuing of a judgment in the Court of Appeal in Belfast following a legal challenge of the Parades Commission decision. Bryant has described his intervention as being in the best interests of peace, and said he had received advice from the PSNI chief constable Jon Boutcher that allowing the parade to go ahead could lead to serious injury, disorder and wider unrest.
Robinson claimed Bryant used powers extraordinarily which were never used during some of the worst days of the Troubles.
“What we saw on Friday disgracefully was the appeasement to threats of violence and disorder, appeasement in the face of threats of terror,” he told BBC Northern Ireland’s Sunday Politics programme.
“There are profound consequences for society. I think the chief constable needs to be very open with the people of Northern Ireland, what was the threat of terror? What was the threat that he perceived and that he indicated to the Secretary of State?
“An extraordinary set of circumstances, powers used that have never been used before, and that will be opened in the courts, but were dissident republicans threatening violence?
“Did he have intelligence that firearms had been brought to that area? Are we seeing a bending of the knee of the rule of law in the threat of terror and violence?
“Those are serious and significant questions.”
[ ‘Let them live in peace’: Protestants and Catholics alike express relief in Drumcree Opens in new window ]
Robinson also said he believes Sinn Féin has “given up on devolution” and is “goading unionists into taking action” over collapsing powersharing government at Stormont.
But he said the question is whether that would make the situation better. “Leadership isn’t about taking the easy choice; it’s about taking the right choice,” he said.
“Does collapsing Stormont bring the Orange men home, what happens the next day ... if we are seriously and rightly angry about the decision the Secretary of State has taken, who in their right mind would ask him to govern Northern Ireland? I certainly wouldn’t.”
Sinn Féin MLA John O’Dowd said the Garvaghy Road residents responded in a peaceful way to the prospect of the parade.
“The residents have faced an awful four weeks since this application was lodged on attempts by people who are opposed to the Good Friday Agreement, who are opposed to reconciliation, who are opposed to moving forward, attempting to drive an unwanted march down the road, and the community responded in a peaceful, democratic way to that decision,” he said.
“I don’t think that continued demonisation and attempt to criminalise the community of the Garvaghy Road is an appropriate way forward. What we need in Portadown is reconciliation.”
O’Dowd also said he had received a letter from police over their investigation after being in the Garvaghy Road area himself.
He stood by his actions, saying: “I think it was the right thing to do.
“I got into politics to stand against the intimidation of communities such as the Garvaghy Road, who went through hell and high water over many, many years.
“I stood with the people of the Garvaghy Road. I will continue to stand with the people of Garvaghy Road because it was the right thing to do, and it was in defence of the Good Friday Agreement and the institutions of the Good Friday Agreement.”
O’Dowd also contended there are “many within the unionist community who were opposed to what was going on at Drumcree Hill”.
“There were over 1,000 members of the Protestant community signed a letter urging the Orange men not to march down the road,” he said.
“There was deep concern within elements of the unionist community about what was going on, and the Orange Order does not represent the unionist community. They are an important part of the unionist community, but they are not the unionist community.” – PA

title: Meath’s Nichola Sheridan finishes third in Melbourne Marathon
description: Bohermeen AC athlete sets fastest time of an Irish woman this year
content:
Nichola Sheridan produced another breakthrough run to finish third in the women’s race at the Melbourne Marathon in 2:29:13, the fastest time run by an Irish woman this year, moving her to sixth on the Irish all-time list.
Finishing inside the famed Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG), the 29-year-old from Meath, who moved to Australia last year, improved her previous best by just over four minutes.
Though a relative latecomer to the marathon distance, having made her debut in Dublin in 2024, Sheridan ran a perfectly paced race, passing the halfway point in 1:14:33.
Her breakthrough came in winning the Dublin City Half Marathon in March 2025, representing Bohermeen AC. She then was the third Irish woman home in last year’s Dublin Marathon, running 2:39:56 for her first sub-2:40 finish.
Sheridan improved on that in July’s Gold Coast Marathon in Brisbane, clocking 2:33:26 to finish eighth, establishing herself as the top Irish women’s marathon runner this year. Her results in Melbourne now puts her just behind Sonia O’Sullivan’s best of 2:29:01 (set in London 21 years ago) on the Irish all-time list.
The women’s race in Melbourne was won by Camille French from New Zealand, who clocked 2:28:25 to finish 24 seconds ahead of Mayo-born Sinead Diver (49), who has been represented Australia since 2015. In 2022, Diver ran 2:21:34 at the Valencia Marathon in what was then an Australian record and which remains the fastest time run by an Irish-born woman.
At this rate of improvement, Sheridan is now on course for possible qualification for next year’s World Championships in Beijing and, beyond that, the 2028 Olympic Games in LA.
Kenya’s Eliud Kipchoge won the men’s race in Melbourne, running a course record of 2:09:10 for his first marathon victory since 2023. The 41-year-old former world record holder and two-time Olympic champion led a three-man group through halfway in 64:18 before making his winning move shortly before 27km.

title: Pope Leo says he will undergo surgery for small growth on lung
description: The 71-year-old pontiff said the growth was detected at an early stage and was well-contained, with recovery expected to take about a week
content:
Pope Leo XIV said on Sunday doctors had detected ‌a small growth on his lung during a recent health check and ​he would be undergoing surgery this week to remove it, in the first health scare of the 71-year-old pontiff’s tenure.
Leo told ​pilgrims in St Peter’s Square for his weekly Sunday prayer that ⁠the growth was “well-contained” and caught at an early stage.
“Recently, ‌during ‌some ​medical examinations, doctors found a localised nodule in my lung,” said the pontiff. “It ⁠was detected at a ​very early stage and ​is well contained.”
“The doctors believe it is advisable ‌to intervene, so, following their advice, ​I have decided to undergo surgery to remove it,” ⁠he said. “The operation ⁠is already ​scheduled for the next few days.”
Leo, elected pope by the world’s cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to previously have had health issues.
The late Pope Francis , ‌Leo’s predecessor, died ⁠at age 88 and was increasingly frail in his later years.
The Vatican press office said ‌Leo’s recovery from surgery was expected to take about a week. ​It did not immediately provide further ​details about the pope’s health.
He is expected to be treated at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital, which has a special apartment for the pope.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than three centimetres that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society.
Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.
[ ‘Leomania’: How secular France fell for the Pope Opens in new window ]
Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni wished the pope well.
“I would like to express to the holy father my personal support, and that of the Italian government, as he faces this challenge in the coming days,” she said in a statement.
“The serenity and composure with which he spoke about it during today’s Angelus are reassuring,” Meloni added.
Leo keeps a busy schedule and is due to make ‌an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6-17.
Before mentioning his health issue in ​his address on Sunday, the pope referred to the trip, ​thanking Catholics for their prayers “for the pastoral visit I will undertake”. – Reuters

title: Leo Cullen relieved to see Leinster ‘up and running’ with returning frontliners
description: Nine Leinster players made their first appearance of the season against Cardiff in the province’s triumphant RDS return
content:
Such are the typically gradual return-to-play protocols of the season, with Ireland frontliners drip fed back (to Leinster especially), that only in the second weekend of October did it finally feel like Leo Cullen ’s side were fully back in action.
That was exactly how Cullen put it after his side’s 29-5 win over Cardiff that was at times snazzy and other times clunky. Hardly surprising given nine of his starting XV were playing their first game in months.
“Yeah, up and running,” was the head coach’s immediate verdict, said with relief as much as elation. “It was a great build-up to the game. The players were really excited to be back now, and it’s great to see the turnout of fans that we had there today.”
While Cullen said there was “lots of good stuff in the first half”, Leinster having opened up a 22-5 lead by the break, he added: “Unfortunately, at the start of the second half, we don’t put on much of a show, it gets a bit disjointed.
[ Leinster live up to the occasion of long-awaited homecoming to blow Cardiff away Opens in new window ]
“The big challenge is when you have so many players coming back in for the first game of the season, it just looks like lads haven’t played in a while. But we stuck at it, defended well, scrambled well on lots of different stages and got over towards the end.”
Taking comfort in their use of 40 players across the opening three rounds, Cullen said it was a “really positive start”, “but we just need to work at getting better across the board”.
His enthusiasm over Leinster’s return to the RDS, now the rebranded and refurbished Laya Arena, was undimmed.
“It’s such a great venue. It’s amazing we’ve sold out today, but we would love that to be just the norm now.”
On how his team can help that endeavour, he added: “We can do better in terms of our performance. I think there’s lots of great effort and intent, but it’s just making sure we gel and get more cohesive as a group.
“We don’t have another game in the RDS during this first block of the season, so it’s into the next block of the season, but you’d love for us to have this place as a really special venue to be part of – as in, players and supporters. We all need to work at that.”
Asked about Sam Prendergast’s starring role, Cullen said: “He’s just building all the time. That’s what we’ve been saying for the last few years.
“He has a really positive mindset, wants to keep getting better at all aspects of his game. Once you have young players that are like that, they will get better. That’s the main thing. We all have to be patient.
“As young players, particularly in a critical position like that, playing at 10, there are so many moving parts to manage. He’s getting better all the time, and we want to continue the growth of all our young players.”
Prendergast certainly lived up to the occasion of Leinster’s competitive return to the RDS, the young outhalf describing the atmosphere as “unreal”.
“There’s been a serious buzz for the last number of months about getting back, and everyone was looking forward to playing in front of that crowd,” said Prendergast. “We kind of knew it was going to be a sell-out and then, as soon as we walked in off the bus, you could feel the buzz.
“Before kick-off was pretty special as well. You could see within the whole organisation, it wasn’t just the players who were excited to be home, it was all the backroom staff too, and I think that’s pretty special.”
The team came through with a winning result to cap off the celebrations, with Prendergast admitting their effort was “good in parts” and “scrappy” in others.
Of his own man-of-the-match performance, in which he took on more of a ball-carrier and running role, he added: “It’s probably something that I’m trying to work on personally, being a bit more of a running threat, so it was nice.
“There’s still a few opportunities where I probably ran when I should have passed, and I probably could have done better when I was running. There’s probably a lot of improvement on it, but it was promising.”

title: ‘Can we cancel our Help to Buy application and apply for the updated amount?’
description: Increase in amount available to first-time buyers of new homes creates confusion for those who have already applied
content:
With regards to the increase in the Help to Buy, we have signed contracts in recent weeks and are availing of the Help to Buy to make up part of our deposit.
We have not yet drawn it down as we are awaiting signed contracts from the builders’ solicitors. Can we cancel our current help to buy application and apply for the updated amount? What is the risk in doing so?
Our solicitors don’t know the answer and we are awaiting a response from Revenue also.
We are very conscious this matter is time sensitive, as payment of our deposit is required in the coming weeks.
You are just one of several first-time buyers who was in touch with us after the Minister announced an expansion of the relief available under Help-to-Buy . Purchasing a first home is always a mix of the exciting and the terrifying and the process is complex enough without last minute changes to the rules.
In a budget where pretty much everything was leaked in advance, the decision to increase the amount of tax relief available for Help to Buy applicants was not something people saw coming.
In fact, if there was to be reform of the system, it was expected it would address the reality for many looking to buy in or close to Dublin and other big urban centres – that the €500,000 cap on the value of property purchases under the scheme locks out many aspiring first-time buyers.
As one reader put it: “The scheme remains redundant to majority of buyers in Dublin, commuter towns and other cities across the country. The extra €5k does not unlock any new homes or help affordability .” Of course, that was what it was intended to do in the first place.
There is certainly a broader policy debate on whether housing incentive schemes, such as Help to Buy, which were always designed to help developers as much or more than buyers, are an effective use of government funds to ease a housing crisis but we’ll not get into that here.
Your concerns are much more practical. You are in the process and, clearly, this extra €5,000 would be beneficial to you if you are able to claim it.
So what happens to applications that are “in the system”? Do they get assessed under the new rules? Can they be withdrawn and a new application made? And what effect, if any, might that have on your home purchase?
You are not alone. Aideen was also in touch with our Q&A, wanting to know whether she would need to reapply given they have not closed on their home.
And Michelle, who is using the relief, to build her own home and has been approved for the “old” €30,000 relief but has not yet claimed the money has much the same query.
Mairéad is further along in the process, having already received €30,000 under the scheme. Is she now entitled to this additional €5,000 in relief, she wonders.
For Mairéad, the answer, unsurprisingly, is “no”. If you have already got your money, as with any other tax and relief headings, your application was assessed under rules in place at the time and you cannot benefit (or suffer) from changes in the rules subsequent to receiving your benefit.
Revenue confirmed for me that the new rules kick in on October 7th, the day after the budget. That follows the passing of financial resolution on the budget change to the scheme in the Oireachtas.
Who is eligible? Anyone who has either not signed a contract to buy their home before October 7th or, in the case of those building their own homes, has not yet drawn down the first tranche of their approved mortgage loan.
Revenue notes that some taxpayers may have submitted an application to see if they are eligible or to find out the amount they are eligible to claim under Help to Buy.
“The test to be applied, however, is whether they have signed a contract to purchase a qualifying property or made the first draw down of a mortgage (in the case of a self-build qualifying property),” they tell me.
[ Minister rules out raising cap on Help-to-Buy scheme for homes worth over €500k Opens in new window ]
So if you signed the contract with the developer to buy your home before last Wednesday (October 7th) or, for self-build projects, had drawn down any of your mortgage before that date, you will not benefit from the new, higher tax relief threshold.
In your case, although you have not yet drawn down any funds under the relief, you say you have signed the contracts – albeit you are waiting for them to come back from the builder’s side, so it appears you will not benefit from the budget measure and will be able to draw down a maximum of €30,000 in tax relief, not €35,000.
Aideen, who says she has not closed on her home, may be eligible as long as she has not signed the purchase contract. Similarly, Michelle, who is building her own place – or having it built for her – may be eligible if she has not drawn down any of her mortgage.
In her case, it does not matter whether she has actually taken ownership of the Help to Buy relief but whether she has tapped her mortgage on the property.
In those cases, where approval had been granted but not activated by any contract or draw down, I expect you will certainly have to reapply as Revenue will have completed the application paperwork.
What is not so clear is what happens for people who have applied to the scheme but have yet to receive Revenue confirmation that they have been accepted. It would make sense that Revenue would apply the new limits to cases in the system but they have not yet confirmed that for me.
You do raise an interesting related point which, though it appears is not relevant for you at this point, might be for others earlier in the process who are considering reapplying for the scheme to benefit under new rules – what is the risk in doing so?
With demand still exceeding supply, there is always a danger that any delay in the process could see the other side move on to another buyer.
If contracts are in place, everyone is bound by them – and you lose out on the €5,000 – but if there are no contracts yet in place, there is nothing to stop the developer moving on to another buyer rather than waiting for someone to reapply for Help to Buy under new rules – or raise the price of the property.
That’s not to say they will but there is certainly a risk that they might.
For those looking to apply now for Help to Buy, what do the changes mean.
Essentially, Help to Buy allows you to claim back income tax and deposit interest retention tax (Dirt) you have paid over the four tax years before the one in which you are making the application to help pull together the deposit you need to buy your first home.
All parties to the purchase must be first time buyers and the property must be newly-build, not second-hand. The property cannot be valued at anything above €500,000 and you must also be taking out a mortgage that covers at least 70 per cent of the price of the property.
The maximum you can claim under the new rules is €35,000 or 10 per cent of the property price, whichever is the lower. Before the budget, the figure was €30,000; all other Ts & Cs were the same.
That €35,000 is the relief that applies to the property, not to the individual, so if two of you are buying, you cannot double up the relief to secure €70,000.
The contractor or developer selling you the property must also be on an approved Revenue list which you can find here . That means they have registered under the scheme and, more important from the Revenue perspective, are compliant with taxes.
To be fair, it would be exceptionally unusual for a developer building new homes not to be on the list but it is always worth checking.
Finally, if you do not live in the property for at least five years, you will face a clawback from Revenue of some of the relief granted.
The scheme has been extended – both in scope and deadline – several times since it was first introduced in 2016. As of now, it is scheduled to run until December 31st, 2029.
