title: A good night’s sleep is a class issue
description: There is still a  divide when it comes to work that tramples over your body clock
content:
In the 1920s, a pair of sociologists set out to study “the interwoven trends that are the life of a small American city” at a time of rapid change.
In their subsequent book about Muncie, Indiana (which they anonymised as “Middletown”), they wrote that the community was divided by time as well as class.
At 6am, the lights were going on in working-class households because their jobs generally began between 6.15 and 7.30am (when they weren’t on night shifts), while the “business class” households remained slumbering until later.
These different working rhythms became political in 1925 when a deadlock emerged over whether the city should adopt “daylight saving time”, which would mean longer light on summer evenings.
The working-class early risers argued they would lose sleep, while the businessmen urged the change “because of golf” and the need to deal with businesses on the east coast.
The competing demands for leisure and business on the one hand, and of our body clocks on the other, have not gone away over the ensuing century. But scientists have learned a lot more about what happens to our health when we prioritise the former over the latter.
In short: nothing good. Many researchers now agree that daylight saving time can interfere with our circadian rhythms. But there are much more dangerous ways to meddle with our biological clocks, the worst of which is to work at night.
It is a myth that night-shift workers can become nocturnal over time. According to the book Life Time by professor of circadian neuroscience Russell Foster, studies suggest that 97 per cent of night shift workers remain synchronised to daytime, which means they have to sleep when their bodies are primed to be awake, and vice versa.
There are consequences for blood pressure and the immune system. The correlations with cancer are so clear that night work has been classed as “probably carcinogenic to humans” by the World Health Organisation’s International Agency for Research on Cancer.
[ Maynooth-led sleep research will examine links with mental health Opens in new window ]
Even if you don’t work overnight, evidence suggests that just working against your “chronotype” can be bad for your health. One recent study from Finland looked at what happened to people who gave information about whether they were morning people or “night owls” in 2012 when they were in their mid-40s.
Over the following 12 years, those with evening chronotypes were more likely to end up on disability pensions, even after adjusting for socio-economic factors. One possibility, according to the researchers, is that “traditional working times interfere significantly with the sleeping preferences of late chronotypes, leading to social jet lag”.
But while the prevalence of night work has declined gradually in the US since Middletown was written, there is still a class divide when it comes to work that tramples over your body clock. According to research published this year, most US night workers have no more than a high-school education.
More broadly, the pandemic-induced shift towards remote work has been a bigger boon for white-collar workers (who already had more flexibility over their hours) than anyone else.
[ What ‘smart’ watches get wrong and right when tracking the quality of your sleep Opens in new window ]
In Europe, for example, managers have the highest levels of autonomy according to 2024’s vast European Working Conditions Survey, with 40 per cent able to adapt their working hours within certain limits, and 19 per cent having full control over their schedules. In contrast, workers at the bottom end of the pay scale continue to have little control: nearly 80 per cent have schedules set entirely by their employers.
It is possible that advances in automation will eventually do away with the need for humans to work against their body clocks. Already, some logistics companies are beginning to experiment with “lights-out night shifts” in which robots work overnight alone, setting aside those orders that require human assistance until the morning shift arrives.
Self-driving trucks, meanwhile, could cover long highway stretches overnight, saving the “final mile deliveries” for human drivers to do in daytime.
Such a transition would be economically challenging for workers – not least since night-shift work usually pays a premium – but could have huge benefits for human health. It would require careful navigation by policymakers with an eye on science, inequality and the future.
Yet US president Donald Trump sounds much more like a voice from the past. His latest intervention into the “politics of time” is to push for daylight saving time to be made permanent, arguing that it would be good for people who would “like to play golf a little bit without having to run home after 14 holes”. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Taiwan fears for US support as Trump and Xi prepare for fresh talks
description: Taipei awaits approval of a $14bn arms package as uncertainty over Washington’s commitment to the island grows
content:
I n brilliant sunshine and scorching heat, Taiwan on Saturday celebrated its annual October 10 holiday with an event outside the presidential palace in Taipei featuring lion dances and other traditional arts as well as a military parade. Every branch of the armed services was on parade, with tanks and armoured vehicles rolling behind them and flyovers above by fighter jets and army helicopters.
It was a display of confidence in the self-governing island of 23 million people where per capita income has almost doubled in a decade and the economy is expected to grow 11 per cent this year. But the celebrations come amid mounting concern on the island over the strength of the American commitment to its defence following two meetings this year between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping .
In his speech on Saturday, president Lai Ching-te described Taiwan as “a city upon a hill”, an image from the Sermon on the Mount used by politicians to describe the United States and its moral mission. Lai said in Taiwan’s case, it was “built atop a chain of guardian mountains” and was the outcome of 30 years of democratic accountability.
Lai has proposed a record $35 billion defence budget for next year, which would include a $14 billion package of arms sales approved by the US Congress. But Trump has not yet signed off on the sale of the weapons and he said earlier this year that they could be a useful bargaining chip in his negotiations with Xi.
After cordial meetings in Beijing in May and Washington last month, the two leaders are due to meet again at an Asian-Pacific leaders’ summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen next month and in Miami for the G20 in December. Their talks are focused on trade and the extension of a tariff truce agreed when they met last year in South Korea but both sides have made clear that they see an opportunity for a broader reset of the relationship between the two most powerful countries in the world.
Xi has identified the future of Taiwan and its reunification with the mainland as an issue at “the core of China’s core interests” and he has warned Trump that further big arms sales to the island will have consequences for relations between Beijing and Washington. Xi also wants Trump to shift official US policy from one of not supporting independence for Taiwan to explicitly opposing it.
“The most difficult part is that we don’t have a choice. We have to rely on the US,” said Chen Fang-Yu, a political scientist at Taiwan’s Soochow University.
“There’s no replacement and because China’s international blockade is so successful, no other country can directly help Taiwan. That’s why we have to link with the US, even though the US sometimes has a problematic foreign policy.”
Chen added while Taiwan is as anxious about Trump’s unpredictability as any other US ally, Taipei has been derisking from Washington insofar as that is possible by deepening its relationships with Japan and the Philippines. And he believes because of its history, Taiwan has always prepared for the worst scenario, which is currently the prospect of chaos under Trump.
[ Europe’s China shock is hollowing out industry and shifting politics to the right Opens in new window ]
Known as the Double Tenth, the October 10 holiday on Saturday marked the 115 th anniversary of the Wuchang uprising against China’s Qing empire in 1911 which led to the foundation of the Republic of China (ROC) the following year. The Nationalists who led the ROC fought against an insurgency by Mao Zedong’s Communists, joining forces for a while to fight the Japanese during the second World War before returning to civil war.
That struggle ended in victory for the Communists and the foundation of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) in 1949. The Nationalists under Chiang Kai-Shek fled to Taiwan, which they established as the headquarters of the ROC, continuing to claim that they were the legitimate government of the whole of China.
The ROC continued to occupy China’s seat at the United Nations and was recognised by many states as the legitimate Chinese government until Richard Nixon flipped US policy in the 1970s. Washington established diplomatic relations with Beijing and the UN voted to recognise the PRC as the sole legitimate representative of China.
The US continued to support Taiwan despite the end of formal diplomatic relations and in 1982 Washington gave the island the so-called Six Assurances. The US would not set an end date for arms sales to Taiwan; it would not consult with Beijing about such sales; it would not attempt to mediate between Taipei and Beijing; it would not revise the Taiwan Relations Act; it had not changed its position on Taiwan’s sovereignty; and it would not put pressure on Taipei to enter into negotiations with Beijing.
Any conversation Trump may have had with Xi about the weapons sale to Taiwan that is awaiting his approval could be in breach of one of the Six Assurances. And a shift in US rhetoric on Taiwan’s constitutional status would be seen by some in Taipei as contravening another of them.
“The US attitude towards Taiwan has always been US does not support Taiwan independence and China wanted to push for the US to oppose Taiwan’s independence. I think probably for Donald Trump, there’s no big difference but in the diplomatic world, there’s a huge difference,” said Jasmine Lee, editor at US-Taiwan Watch, which promotes closer relations between Taipei and Washington.
“Does not support means I don’t actively or proactively support you. If you want to do that, I wouldn’t support you, but I respect you.
But if I say I oppose it, I don’t allow you. I don’t want you to do that. So there is a difference.”
The US has long been deliberately ambiguous about what it would do if Beijing sought to take Taiwan by force, although Joe Biden said a number of times that Washington would come to the island’s defence. During his visit to Beijing last May, Trump said he had no interest in fighting such a war.
“I’m not looking to have somebody go independent. And, you know, we’re supposed to travel 9,500 miles to fight a war. I’m not looking for that. I want them to cool down. I want China to cool down,” he told Fox News.
Jyun-Yi Lee, an expert in hybrid threats and grey-zone conflicts at the Institute for National Defence and Security Research in Taipei, points out that Taiwan’s defence planning has always been based on a plan to fight alone. But he said the truth is that Taiwan needs American help and that Trump’s remarks and the uncertainty surrounding the $14 billion arms sale are creating anxiety in Taipei.
“I think US arms sales always carries two senses for us. One is symbolically. It is a symbol of whether the US supports Taiwan or especially Taiwan’s defence. So I think no matter the amount of the sales, we really want the US to continue to sell arms to Taiwan,” he said.
“Taiwan relies very heavily on the US for historical, political and for practical reasons. We cannot afford to have weapon systems from different countries because they will cost a lot in terms of maintenance, repairing, and human training. So if there’s disruption when it comes to US arms sales to Taiwan, then this will affect our military capability.”
Lai won Taiwan’s presidential election in 2024 with 40 per cent of the vote against a split opposition and his Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) lost its parliamentary majority. The main opposition Kuomintang Party (KMT) favours more dialogue and engagement with Beijing and a less confrontational approach to cross-strait relations.
The KMT complains that Taiwan’s government is spending too much on defence and that some of the funds earmarked for arms purchases should go to education, health and social programmes. The DPP and the KMT will face off in local elections next month and although the constitutional question will not figure in the campaign, the election’s outcome could have implications for the next general election in 2028.
“If the KMT does well in these elections, that will be momentum for their 2028 presidential ticket. And that will probably also determine who will be on the ticket,” Lee said.
“If that person is a more moderate KMT candidate, and I’d say the DPP’s situation will be very, very intense. Even though the GDP is pretty good, the economy is going well, relations with the US are good, and with China even though it’s pretty bumpy right now still we’re doing okay. But it’s a democratic country and the DPP has been there for 12 years. For a democratic country, for democratic citizens, we want to see something different.”
[ US president Donald Trump says it is time for Ukraine to get rid of Zelenskiy Opens in new window ]
Support for early moves to Taiwanese independence or towards reunification with mainland China are in single digits, with more than 80 per cent telling pollsters they want to maintain the status quo. The DPP government claims that a strong defence to deter an attack from Beijing is the most effective way to keep Taiwan’s position unchanged.
But Yen Chen-Shen, a research fellow at National Chengchi University’s Institute of International Affairs, warns Trump’s dismissive and sometimes hostile remarks about Taiwan mean that Taipei needs to think again about how to maintain the status quo.
“We always talk about Taiwan being a value ally of the US: democracy, freedom, human rights – about which Donald Trump doesn’t give a s**t,” he said.
“And we in Taiwan talk about alternative lifestyles, we are the freest – and Donald Trump doesn’t care about this. We talk about environmental protection. Donald Trump doesn’t care, right?”
Yen believes that Taiwan’s leaders are in danger of giving people false hope by emphasising Taiwanese identity and not acknowledging that the international environment means that official independence is effectively off the table. He suggests Taiwan should return to the position of accepting the principle of One China but with a different interpretation to Beijing’s.
“We have to offer a unification formula which sounds really nice, but Beijing cannot accept,” he said.
Yen proposes that Taiwan should demand that the entirety of a unified China should enjoy freedom of expression, freedom of association, freedom of religion, a free press and the rule of law, none of which would be acceptable to Beijing. Talking about reunification is a political taboo in Taiwan today but Yen believes Taipei can better maintain its position by taking the initiative with Beijing.
“I think in Taiwan, we have to come up with something to avoid a military confrontation. And then somehow saving some money for defence, that would benefit us, right?” he said.
“I personally think we spend too much money on defence. And then you look at the young people who don’t want to be in the military, who don’t want to have this conflict. So this is the most difficult part for young people. They like to have their independence, but they don’t want to fight for it.”

title: Message from the Editor: Galway’s homeless millionaire
description: IT Sunday: The life and death of a 65-year-old Italian man raised questions that even his close family struggled to answer
content:
Two years ago, in May 2024, a homeless man named Victor Spaggiari died in Galway aged 65. Spaggiari had been a familiar face in Galway city. Day after day, year after year, he would sit on a long wooden bench in a corner of the city’s covered Cornstore Mall. He wouldn’t say much, but he was a learned man; often he would take books – archaeology and folklore were particular interests of his – from the shelves outside Charlie Byrne’s bookshop to read during the day, returning them before he left.
When his parents died more than 10 years ago, Spaggiari became the principal heir to their combined fortune. It would have made him a millionaire. But he never claimed it; instead he spent his final decade living in a homeless hostel in Galway.
Intrigued by that bare outline of the Italian man’s unusual life story, Rosita Boland and Naomi O’Leary spent some time with those who knew him in Galway and tracked down his closest living relative – a cousin in Italy. In the resulting account of his life , our reporters pore over essays he wrote as a child (“I never considered money to be an important thing, and I don’t think any intelligent person should,” he wrote as a 14-year-old in Milan in 1975), his relationship with his parents and the journey that brought him to Ireland. It’s a moving reflection on material life and Spaggiari’s rejection of it. “There was nothing conventional about Victor,” says Paudie Cunningham of Cope Galway. “He was an enigma; a very private man… He wasn’t in touch with society at all. He was living in his own head.”
The domestic story of the week was the publication of the Government’s budget for next year – an €8.5 billion package that has been denounced for being miserly and profligate, depending on the critic’s perspective. In this behind-the-scenes retelling of the negotiations leading to Tuesday’s announcement , drawing on 20 interviews with people involved, Pat Leahy and Jack Horgan-Jones give a great sense of the personal dynamics behind the process. Among its cast are the combustible Patrick O’Donovan, the ideological Jack Chambers, the tired Simon Harris and a line-up of insiders who have much more flair for language when speaking anonymously than they ever do in their public pronouncements. “Paschal [Donohoe] killed you with kindness. Jack just kills you,” says one. And another: “Politicians looking for credit should always remember that it’s a very short distance between a clap on the back and a kick up the hole.”
Leahy’s column argues that the hawkish Chambers has emerged from the week with his standing enhanced . Our editorial says this annual budget ritual is a bad way to run a country , citing the debacle over an effective cut to RTÉ’s funding – apparently the result of political gamesmanship more than any point of principle – as an example of its flaws.
In our World section, Rachel Lavin and Hannah McCarthy draw on satellite imagery and interviews with people on the ground to find out what became of Gaza’s football pitches , most of which are now in ruins.
In Opinion, Mark O’Connell reflects on former minister for housing Simon Coveney’s role as a lobbyist for the developer Johnny Ronan and what it tells us about the business and politics of housing in Ireland. Siobhán Fenton, a former Sinn Féin press officer, suggests that party might have an ulterior motive for its actions at Drumcree , while Ed Abrahamson writes that October 7 th was a piercing, shrieking alarm call for all Jews .
One of my favourite running jokes in Jonathan Franzen’s The Corrections is about the son, Caleb Lambert’s hobby – surveillance – and how it complicates family life. That novel was published 25 years ago, when the idea of using technology to watch your loved ones’ every move could in itself be a joke. Not today. As Patrick Freyne explains , the ubiquity of location-sharing tech has made it acceptable and normal for everyone from anxious parents to suspicious partners to follow the every move of those closest to them. But what, Freyne asks, does that mean for our privacy, our trust and our relationships?
The site is full of strong interviews this weekend, including conversations with David Clifford , Simon Zebo , Fontaines DC and Jordan Joy Hewson , who talks about her move into music and growing up as Bono’s daughter.
We like to hear from you. Feel free to send comments, feedback or suggestions for topics you would like to see covered to feedback@irishtimes.com .

title: Jennifer O'Connell: A playground for the living built over the bones of dead
description: We know now how badly we failed children in the past. We don’t want to know about the children we are failing today
content:
T here’s a scene in The Lost Children of Tuam , Frank Berry’s enraging, devastating film, in which Catherine Corless , played by Monica Dolan, goes back to the housing estate built on the former site of the mother and baby home in the Galway town where 796 children died without a burial record.
She stands in the playground erected shortly after the housing estate was finished in the 1970s and wonders aloud about it. Isn’t it, she asks, a very big playground for the size of the housing estate?
Because of Corless’s tireless and painstaking work, we now know the dark secrets that lay somewhere underground, beneath its smooth tarmac surface. A playground for the living built beside the bones of the dead. A supersized playground to cover a colossal stain on our consciences. Something special for the living children to atone for what this society allowed to happen to 796 dead ones.
Several times in the film someone expresses incredulity that the Bon Secours nuns, in whose care babies died at a rate of one every 16 days, despite it being a nursing order, would not have marked those babies’ graves. It seemed inconceivable that a religious order would allow children to be buried in chambers constructed in a disused sewage tank and not put up so much as a plaque or a tiny cross in their memory.
But these were not just any children. They were the children of unmarried mothers and unknown fathers. And as such, they didn’t count. They were literally referred to as “illegitimate” – a word whose ordinary meaning is “not valid” or “improper”. Better not to acknowledge their brief lives and shocking, unnecessary, often painful deaths.
Some of us may decide not to watch Berry’s film because we think we already know everything there is to know about those miserable decades in Ireland’s past. We suffer not so much from compassion fatigue as shame fatigue. We would prefer to tarmac over the past, stick a shiny new swing set and a climbing frame on top of it and – as some of the people of Tuam urged Corless – never speak of it again.
While Tuam has rightly made international headlines, not much attention is being paid to the continuing talks in Cork over plans to build an apartment block on the site of the former mother and baby home at Bessborough. As Caelainn Hogan wrote here recently , the remains of 858 babies who died there have not been located. Planning for apartments on the site was refused in 2021 on the grounds that there are “reasonable concerns” there may be “a children’s burial ground” on the site. But this summer, permission for 106 apartments was upheld. It is, as Catherine Corless said, “another Tuam”, only there is no global outcry.
In this country, to borrow from William Faulkner, the past is never dead; it’s not even past.
[ Like Nikita Hand, Cornell case’s Jane Doe is either uncommonly brave or a sadomasochist Opens in new window ]
There was another reminder this week of a time in our not-so-ancient history we’d rather forget; a time when Ireland operated its own kind of unspoken, unofficial caste system.
A family in Cork finally got an answer to the private pain they’ve carried since their beloved son and brother disappeared without trace in 1992. The family of Patrick, or Patsy, O’Sullivan knew he was gay, but in Ireland at the time it “wasn’t condoned or even spoken about”, his brother Jerry said. Patsy left home that Easter Monday and never got in touch again. In August this year, the family got a call from gardaí who told them that Patsy had gone on to have a life “full of joy” in the UK, marrying a loving husband and retraining as an auxiliary nurse. He died two years ago. “I was afraid something had happened to him back then because of his sexuality. Because I remember what happened to me for being a brother of him,” Jerry said.
[ A very touching thing happened on Capel Street last Thursday evening Opens in new window ]
That was how Ireland worked. There was “us” – the decent, ordinary, hardworking people of Ireland, as we saw ourselves – and “them”. “They” were girls considered wayward or fallen. Gay men and women. Children who were suspected of being gay. “Illegitimate” children and the women who gave birth to them.
We congratulate ourselves now on being a liberal, accepting society, with a stack of referendums to prove it. But it’s hardly credible that Ireland has completely left behind the society that allowed those babies to die unseen and forced those men and women to flee in order to be themselves. Are there, even now, people whose lives we are collectively deciding don’t count?
You don’t need an excavation team like the one at Tuam to answer that. Just open a newspaper. Read about the vulnerable children left to the mercy, or otherwise, of the profitable private residential care system because the State doesn’t have enough places for them. Some, mostly underage asylum seekers, are not even that fortunate. “On any given evening last October there were up to 20 children in Tusla’s care with no place in a group care home or even a bed in unregulated emergency accommodation run by private companies,” as Jack Power wrote recently in The Irish Times.
Or consider the 5,830 homeless children currently living in emergency accommodation because the State can’t provide them with a real home. The more than 9,000 children in Ipas centres. The 95,000 children living in consistent poverty in a country with a GDP so huge we needed to invent another index.
We know now how badly we failed children in the past. We don’t seem to want to know about the children we are failing today. A country that can afford to splash €58 million of taxpayers’ money to host the Ryder Cup – the latest tranche of €22 million, to be shared with Euro 2028, announced in the budget – can’t afford a safe place for vulnerable children to sleep. There is no merry-go-round in the world big enough to distract from the shame of that.

title: AI bubble? Nvidia is now bigger than Japan, but valuation looks modest
description: A casual observer might think its valuation screams AI bubble, but Nvidia is not an obviously expensive stock
content:
It has been a long four months for Nvidia shareholders. The world’s most valuable company has finally set a new record high, ending a 96-trading-day drought.
Of course, a 96-day wait would be unremarkable by the standards of most companies, but Nvidia is another matter, with Bespoke Investment noting this was shareholders’ third-longest wait since ChatGPT’s November 2022 launch.
The four-month lull is easier to put in perspective when the numbers – Nvidia was worth $5.8 trillion at its recent peak – are considered. Comparisons between Nvidia and entire national stock markets have become routine, but Japan was the one big exception.
No longer – Nvidia now accounts for 5.2 per cent of the MSCI All Country World Index, slightly more than Japan and more than every country except the US.
Taiwan (3.5 per cent), the UK and Canada (2.9 per cent each) trail well behind, while Nvidia’s weighting is almost three times that of Germany’s.
A casual observer might think this screams AI bubble, but Nvidia is not an obviously expensive stock. It trades on about 15 times estimated earnings, according to market data from Finviz, making it cheaper than 295 of the S&P 500’s component stocks.
The company, too, is acting as if shares are reasonably priced. A fortnight ago, Nvidia authorised an additional $150 billion share buyback, the largest such authorisation in history.
The record-breaking numbers make for an odd combination, with Nvidia simultaneously looking enormous enough to distort global equity indices, whilst remaining relatively inexpensive against the earnings it is producing.

title: TV guide: the best new shows to watch
description: October 11th-16th highlights: including Toxic Threads with Brian Dowling Gourounlian, The Zoo and new drama series Adultery
content:
In 2001, Kildare man Brian Dowling (now Dowling Gourounlian, after his marriage to dancer Arthur Gourounlian in 2015) became a household name after a successful stint on the reality TV show Big Brother. Since then he has lived in the glare of the public eye, and in the past number of years that has meant being visible on social media too. Once he and Arthur’s first child, Blake, was born in 2022, with his sister Aoife as surrogate, Dowling Gourounlian and his family became the target of vile online commentary and trolling. In this new documentary, the Six O’Clock Show presenter looks at the realities of online bullying and harassment, not just through his own experience but by speaking to others who have gone through similar. Plus, he talks to a private investigator to find out if anonymous commenters are really anonymous. It’s a “vulnerable, uncomfortable” watch, he tells us, and is likely to shed light on the gaps in how equipped the legal world is to deal with this behaviour.
The popular series is back, giving us a look at life behind the scenes at Dublin Zoo. The first episode on Monday night features the remarkable story of Imani, an 18-year-old hippo who undergoes the world’s first cataract surgery on a hippopotamus. Meanwhile, the zoo’s South American house, which was originally built in the 1860s, is undergoing a full revamp in order to host new animals including a lowland paca. Other stories include the zoo vets being called in to examine a dolphin stranded on a Dublin beach, plus newcomers to the zoo include a giant anteater, a tamandua, and a six-banded armadillo, alongside a new gang of meerkats.
While on holiday in Cork with his wife, Anita, musician Frankie Lane collapsed from a sudden cardiac arrest. This short documentary looks firstly at how paramedic Pat McCarthy – against all odds – was able to resuscitate him using CPR and a defibrillator. Then we learn about Frankie and Anita’s journey with Cúram, Ireland’s leading medical research centre, and in particular the work of cardiovascular surgeon Dr Niamh Hynes. The film brings us news of cutting-edge innovations, from 3D-printed heart tissue to AI-designed stents. It’s a look at a personal story as well as at how science and technology could potentially transform how cardiovascular disease is treated globally.
Have you heard about Cill Stuifín, which legend has it lies off the coast of west Co Clare? It’s a village that it’s believed was swallowed by the sea, perhaps due to a freak wave … or maybe because of an ancient curse. In this beautifully shot documentary, the folklorist Aindrias de Staic follows in his late father, folklorist Eddie Stack’s footsteps to examine the truth behind the legend. De Staic speaks to geologist Martina McCarthy, folklorist Dr Ailbhe Nic Giolla Chomhaill, senior weather-buoy technician Donal Kennedy, Infomar marine mapping specialist Felim O’Toole and marine biologist Jack O’Donovan Trá, as well as big wave surfers Ollie O’Flaherty and Callum Curtin and artist Marie Connole about their thoughts on Cill Stuifín and the inspiration the Atlantic holds for them. One for those who love the beauty of Ireland’s coastline as well as Irish folklore.
If you missed it first time around, now’s your chance to catch this gorgeous American series on the small screen. Jonathan Bailey and Matt Bomer – two actors you can always depend on to do the most with their roles – play two men who meet while working in Washington DC in the 1950s. Hawkins Fuller (Bomer) is a military hero who sets out to work his way up the ladder at the State Department, but is also closeted and intent on hiding his private life due to societal prejudice. But then he meets Tim Laughlin (Bailey) and the pair – though different in some ways – fall in love despite the dangers. We follow their relationship through several decades and big moments in US history, from the Vietnam war to the Aids crisis.
In 2010 two Irish nationals were arrested for trafficking rhino horn after being caught in a sting run by US Fish and Wildlife outside Denver, Colorado. The evidence all pointed back to Rathkeale, Co Limerick, and soon Irish authorities and Europol began to join the dots regarding other rhino horn thefts in Europe, believing that there was an organised crime group behind them all. In this episode of The Case I Can’t Forget, we meet John Reid, former head of the Europol Irish desk, and hear how he launched a co-ordinated effort across 19 countries to dismantle the gang targeting rhino horn in Europe’s museums. We also meet Cyril Claffey from Ireland’s Criminal Assets Bureau, who helped to discover more about those involved in the trafficking and where the valuable rhino horns were being sold to. The gang also began targeting jade and antiquities collections in museums, leading to Adrian Greene and Rebecca Tipping of the Metropolitan Police becoming involved. This is the real life story of how teams across Europe were tasked with catching thieves who saw themselves as untouchable.
If you’re looking for a juicy new series, give this one from writer Danny Brocklehurst (who was also behind the Netflix hit Fool Me Once) a go. This is for fans of shows such as War (now on Sky) and the series The Affair, and stars Dominic Cooper and Romola Garai as two married people who start a passionate affair. This naturally throws their lives into turmoil. But adding even more drama into the mix is that their own teenage children also start their own relationship.
On the couch and ready to chat to Graham Norton this week is the Oscar-winning Pulp Fiction and Reservoir Dogs director Quentin Tarantino , who’s there to talk about his new West End farce The Popinjay Cavalier, starring Sacha Baron Cohen. He’ll be joined by our own Colin Farrell, there to chat about the documentary The Slightest Touch about EB campaigner Emma Fogarty, with whom he has a long friendship. Comedian and chatshow host Ellen DeGeneres will also be there, as will Gemma Chan to talk about the new thriller Josephine. An A-list line-up as usual.
Robert Louis Stevenson’s maritime romp has stirred the imaginations of many film-makers, and this new six-part reimagining hopes to and strike streaming TV gold, with help from its stars, Hayley Atwell, David Oyelowo and Tom Sweet. Atwell is Bess Hawkins, a tiger mom who has found the legendary map, and sets off with her son, Jim Hawkins (Sweet), on the Hispaniola to find the treasure. But there’s mutiny in the air as the charismatic and ambitious Long John Silver (Oyelowo) puts Jim’s loyalties to the test. KEVIN COURTNEY
Its name sounds like some corporate motivational programme from the 1980s, but VisionQuest is the third and final series in the trilogy that began with WandaVision and continued with Agatha All Along. Paul Bettany returns as Vision, the former superhero who is now in hiding, living a quiet life mostly inside his own head, where he communes with a group of AI personas embedded in his brain, one of whom happens to be the notorious Ultron (James Spader), the dude who tried to destroy all human life on Earth. But it’s not long before a bounty is put on Vision, and he has to go on the run, accompanied by a boy named Thomas Shepard, who might actually be Vision’s son. VisionQuest promises more mind-bending Marvel fun, but it will have to be a real brain-fryer to match the wacky and wonderfully inventive WandaVision. KC
It’s hard enough to keep a marriage together when your husband is having an affair or gambling away the family’s fortune. What happens when you discover he has helped to steal an apocalypse weapon from Russia, threatening to plunge the US into all-out war? Keri Russell returns as Ambassador Kate Wyler, with Rufus Sewell as her husband, US vice-president Hal Wyler, in series four of the political thriller that double-jobs as a relationship drama in the rarefied atmosphere of Capitol Hill. Alison Janney is the reckless and capricious US president Grace Penn, whose marriage to first gentleman Todd Penn (Bradley Whitford) is also on shaky ground. The Diplomat is an awkward blend of high-stakes political intrigue and marital strife: you can’t tell which is more urgent, preventing nuclear Armageddon or serving the divorce papers on time. KC

title: Breda O'Brien: Ireland may not have the death penalty, but we have no reason for complacency
description: Christa Pike has already spent 30 years on Death Row, and 28 in what amounted to solitary confinement
content:
One of Christa Pike’s swollen and blistered arms and both her feet were shackled as she lay in hospital after two doses of lethal injection in Tennessee that failed to have their intended effect. She is now walking with assistance and eating normally . The state may still follow through with the execution.
In The Irish Times, Keith Duggan has outlined her unrelentingly grim childhood . Born to an alcoholic mother, Pike has foetal alcohol syndrome, was neglected and brutally beaten in childhood, sexually abused from the age of two and subjected separately to at least three rapes by the age of 17. She attempted suicide aged 12 after the death of her grandmother, the only person Pike believed really loved her.
Nothing excuses the prolonged torture and death that Pike and Tadaryl Shipp, her abusive gang-member boyfriend at the time, inflicted on 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. But because Shipp was 17, just a year younger than Pike, he avoided the death penalty, and is now eligible for parole. Shadolla Peterson, who acted as lookout for Shipp and Pike, was given probation because she testified against them.
Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison. Since being medicated, she has had no further history of perpetrating violence. She expressed remorse for the murder and became a Buddhist. According to her spiritual adviser, Rev Mikey Noechel, Pike went to her supposed execution practising metta, the Buddhist loving-kindness meditation. Other prisoners record her many small acts of kindness to them.
Pike has already spent 30 years on death row, and 28 years in what has amounted to solitary confinement. It was not until 2024 that her legal counsel secured her the right to mix with other women in the general prison population. Men always had that right, but as the only woman on death row, she was kept confined for 22-23 hours a day in a 7ft by 12ft cell.
The US may not be Iran , where by July this year, 980 people, including 37 political prisoners, 18 women, and one juvenile offender, had been executed – or China , where figures are a State secret, but suspected to be in the thousands. Nonetheless, the continued use of capital punishment, including firing squads, means the US is far outside the global trend towards universal abolition of the death penalty.
On Friday, the US announced plans to livestream the execution by firing squad , which is planned for December, of a gunman who killed 13 people in 2009 . Nidal Hasan is set to become the first person ​to be executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945.
Irish people have never been great enthusiasts for capital punishment. Before his violent death in 1922, even Michael Collins supported a move to abolish it. The Civil War put paid to abolition. Nonetheless, hangmen such as the notorious Pierrepoints had to be imported from Britain because no Irish person, despite attempts to train one , would do it . We abolished the death penalty for murder in 1964 and passed a referendum in 2001 to prevent its reintroduction.
Achieving a balance between retribution and reintegration of those who have served their time is never easy
Wrongful convictions are one powerful argument against capital punishment. Harry Gleeson was reinterred in Holycross, Tipperary, two years ago – 83 years after he was wrongfully convicted and hanged for a murder . The large and sombre crowd which gathered reflected how strongly people felt about the injustice.
While we may no longer have State-sanctioned killing of prisoners, we still have few reasons for complacency. Life sentences are considered a humane alternative to the death penalty. Yet life sentences have been creeping up in length for decades, from an admittedly low average of 7.5 years in the 1970s and 1980s, to 24 years in 2023. For prisoners granted parole in the Republic between 2022 and 2025, t ime served in custody ranged from 16 to 43.6 years .
The number of prisoners serving life has also risen. This may reflect increasingly brutal crimes, but it also stems from significant understaffing of the Parole Board, only established in 2019. Processing an application takes 18 months. The slow turnaround on mandatory reports from State agencies, such as An Garda Síochána, the Probation Service and the Irish Prison Service ’s Psychology Service, is one major bottleneck.
This slow pace contributes to chronic prison overcrowding, although short sentences for much more minor offences contribute far more to the problem.
Conditions for the general prison population are dire. Chief Inspector of Prisons, Mark Kelly, branded it a “national disgrace” that 599 prisoners were forced to sleep on mattresses on the floor. The Irish Penal Reform Trust reports that 65 per cent of prisoners were unable to use the toilet in private due to cell sharing.
Prisons are not only devoid of privacy and dignity, but they also rely on restricted regimes, which often amount to solitary confinement. Part of that is driven by requests from prisoners themselves, especially gang members, but the Council of Europe Committee for the Prevention of Torture found that the 22-23 hours a day spent in lock-up without meaningful activities “may amount to inhuman and degrading treatment”.
Families of victims often understandably resent so much focus on prisoners’ rights. Prisoners convicted of murder can apply for parole after 12 years and every two years after.
Although victims’ families have statutory rights to be heard since 2019, they still often find the process frightening, draining and retraumatising.
Achieving a balance between retribution and reintegration of those who have served their time is never easy. But even in the absence of the death penalty, we are still far from a penal system that respects the rights of everyone.

title: ‘Let them live in peace’: Protestants and Catholics alike express relief in Drumcree
description: On Garvaghy Road the last of the tents that filled the road during the standoff are being dismantled
content:
In a loyalist enclave of Portadown a group of young men cheer as they watch a Premier League football match on their friend’s phone.
It is lunchtime on Saturday and a high court challenge against a decision to ban an Orange Order march down the nationalist Garvaghy Road is due to begin 30 miles away in Belfast .
One of the men is from a Protestant background and says he is “relieved” that the two-week standoff has ended.
“Let them live in peace. Give it up. There was no need for a march,” says the man, who does not wish to be named.
They are standing on a street in the Brownstown area of the Co Armagh town, a short distance from the loyalist Corcrain and Edgarstown housing estates.
Murals of the Portadown True Blues flute band and Mid Ulster UVF are painted on gable ends in Edgarstown.
Pointing to his six friends, the man says three of them are Catholic.
Leeds United have just scored a goal against Arsenal and they are celebrating on the street.
There is no talk of Northern Secretary Chris Bryant ’s intervention the previous evening that led to the Orange Order march from Drumcree Church being halted “in the best interests of peace”.
Instead, the group is looking forward to travelling to Belfast for the evening to celebrate a friend’s birthday (a Leeds fan).
They work together in a large manufacturing company in Co Armagh.
Bosses banned the Drumcree dispute being discussed in the workplace from “day one”, says the man.
“A lot of people from my background aren’t happy and have a different opinion to me,” he adds.
“But we’re all friends. We all think the same thing, there was no need for it.
Another friend from the Garvaghy Road joins him.
“As soon as the parade got the go-ahead, everyone was talking about it. There have been a few heated conversations in work.
“We speak it among ourselves but it’s only banter.
“We’re all in our late 20s and knew there was no point in going back to dark days, especially when there’s been peace.”
Orangemen gathered at Drumcree Church on Saturday ahead of the legal challenge, which has been adjourned until Monday.
One man manning a tea station outside the church refuses to discuss the fallout following Bryant’s ruling.
[ Orange Order legal challenge to Garvaghy Road parade ban adjourned to Monday Opens in new window ]
Only two police cars are parked on the road leading to the church; officers chat in the sunshine.
Overnight the order issued a statement expressing its “profound disappointment” and said it was seeking urgent meetings with the Northern Secretary and PSNI chief constable Jon Boutcher .
Blue and Orange flags in support of the Orangemen – emblazoned with “Here we stand and we can do no other” – fly outside some homes in the loyalist housing estates.
A resident, who has one of the flags hanging from an upstairs window, is unwilling to give his reaction to developments over the past 24 hours.
“I don’t trust Irish newspapers,” he says.
A woman in her 20s who grew up in the loyalist stronghold says she was “happy” when she heard the news on Friday night.
She adds she is too frightened to speak publicly.
“My family wanted the parade at the start but then they got sick of the circus around it. They felt it was dragging on for too long and causing too much tension,” says the woman.
On the Garvaghy Road the last of the tents which filled the road during the standoff are being dismantled.
Just one gazebo remains standing by midafternoon.
A week ago, this road was filled with 15,000 people at a ‘No Going Back’ rally in support of the residents.
Much like Brownstown and Edgarstown, nationalist residents living on the Garvaghy Road are reluctant to go on record.
“We work with people from the other side and we don’t want any tension,” says a man packing away crates of bottled water.
A concert was due to be held on the Garvaghy Road on Sunday but has been cancelled.
“It’s over. We’re relieved someone saw sense – but there’s to be no triumphalism,” says the man.
He admits he is worried about the impact of the standoff on his three children.
A Facebook post has appeared overnight warning parents from a Protestant background not to let their children “mix with those from Catholic schools”.
“My wee lad’s school is beside a Protestant school. There’s probably only one person that owns that unionist [Facebook] page but that’s the level of hatred,” he says.
“You would be wary about going into town. If you went into a bar, you’d be on edge now.”
Some older residents are more optimistic for the next generation.
There has been no violence throughout the dispute, one pensioner remarks.
Sectarian tensions during the Drumcree standoff in the 1990s were linked to 21 murders.
The loyalist community “has been told to obey the law, which it’s done the whole way through,” says the pensioner, who lives on the Brownstown Road.
“In this town now, the amount of hardline loyalists is basically nil. All the old hands are gone,” he adds.
“I honestly don’t think the younger generation is interested.
“I’m a Protestant in my late 60s living in a loyalist area and I don’t believe there’ll ever be the trouble that we saw about here 30 years ago.

title: Sing for joy: ‘One of the best things you can do for your mental health is join a choir’
description: Group singing is proving more than just an enjoyable pastime or  tradition. It’s becoming an antidote to loneliness and diffidence
content:
Choirs may be synonymous with the magic of Christmas and festive carolling, but the uplifting power of group singing has no seasonal sell-by date. On any given evening in local venues around the country, people are gathering together to sing. Some are seeking connection in an increasingly fragmented world, others an escape from the pressures of everyday life or a boost in self-confidence – but whatever draws them through the door, they all leave feeling lighter than when they arrived. Group singing is proving to be more than just an enjoyable pastime or Yuletide tradition. It’s becoming an antidote to loneliness and diffidence.
“When we sing, we release oxytocin, the human love hormone,” says Rachel Dempsey, founder of Singing for Change, an initiative within her Full Circle Change project, which aims to foster connection, wisdom and resilience for the benefit of people and the planet. Dempsey holds an MA in ethnomusicology from Queen’s University Belfast , a discipline she describes as “the anthropology of music and how it intersects with society and culture”. While the physical and mental health benefits of singing are now well-established, she says it’s the effect on human connection that fascinates her most of all.
“The science of how singing creates and strengthens bonds between individuals is especially interesting,” she says. A 2015 University of Oxford study followed adults taking part in weekly singing, creative writing and craft classes. After just one month, those in the singing group reported significantly greater feelings of closeness and social connection than participants in the other classes.
The mother-of-two describes singing as “a bio-psycho-social technology for connection and a pathway to wellbeing”, and hosts regular singing circles in a cosy cabin in the back garden of her home in Newtownmountkennedy, as well as workshops in Dublin 2. They are all guided by the same philosophy: singing is for “wellbeing and connection, not perfection or performance”.
For Dempsey, the greatest barrier for people isn’t ability, but belief. “People are so inhibited about their voices these days,” she says. “They’re so full of shame because someone once told them they can’t sing. But really, it’s denying people their human right – to sing with others.” She argues that singing has become unnecessarily exclusive. “It’s this niche activity that you either qualify for or you don’t. Very few of us feel like we do.”
Tara Heffernan, founder of Waterford-based Sing for Joy, shares this view. The organisation was established to make singing accessible to everyone, regardless of experience or ability. “We take on outside beliefs so easily,” says the music teacher and vocal coach. “If someone has told you you’re not a good singer, then it becomes something you’re simply not used to doing.”
Her choir actively challenges this mindset. “We’re not in competition and we choose all of our soloists from within the group. Some other choirs bring in professional singers, but we pull from the people sitting in the chairs in front of us.” Heffernan says that watching somebody step up to the microphone, who may never have sung solo before, is one of the most beautiful experiences. “When you hear them sing, it’s so perfect and everybody is clapping – it’s just such an incredible confidence-booster.”
Over the summer, Heffernan posted a solo performance of Wild Mountain on Instagram. Within days, it had attracted more than 30,000 views. The former secondary schoolteacher explains that the soloist had recently been diagnosed with autism and had always found it difficult to communicate and to have friends. “She says the singing group has helped so much with her confidence, and really supported her through her diagnosis.”
[ Choir gives Beijing’s retirees a reason to get up Opens in new window ]
For Dempsey, this is exactly what group singing is about. “Singing out is learning to speak out ... It’s a wider interpretation of voice,” she adds. The benefits of group singing extend beyond community and connection. “Members of the group have reported becoming more assertive – in the workplace, for example. In the past, they may have found it difficult to speak up, but working on their voice has helped them to advocate for themselves.”
Heffernan is currently completing a master’s in mental health practices for young adults. One of her lecturers is Colman Noctor, the child and adolescent psychotherapist, author and Ted Talk speaker. “He often says research shows that two of the best things you can do for your mental health is join a choir and volunteer.” Sing for Joy embraces both. “We recently held a concert for the Solas Cancer Support Centre in Waterford, and I think it really helps to be part of something bigger than yourself. It helps you to feel positive about yourself and who you are as a person.”
For Dubliner Karen O’Shea, singing has been a constant outlet since her school days. The lifelong choir enthusiast believes its benefits go far beyond music. “Singing gets you out of your own head,” she says. “It’s a bit like yoga. When you’re practising yoga, you’re learning to inhabit your body. When you’re singing, you’re accessing a different part of your brain.”
These days, O’Shea is a regular at Casual Choir, the drop-in singing group founded in 2018 by musical director Róisín Savage. Its appeal is captured in its playful tagline: “One song, one session. No audition, no sheet music, no commitment”. Participants arrive with nothing more than a willingness to sing – learning, rehearsing and recording a complete song in a single evening, which is then uploaded to social media.
“I love being able to turn up unprepared,” says O’Shea. “By the end of the session you’ve had a great time, because Róisín is great fun, but also you’ve created something tangible. The performance is recorded, so you have something to look back on afterwards.” When the 51-year-old first became a primary schoolteacher, she took ownership of her school’s choir. “Our principal had been kicked out of her school choir as a child for ‘not being good enough’, so she had a very strong belief that everybody should get involved.”
Savage believes auditions and the fear of not being good enough are a barrier to entry for many. “I wanted to set something up where people didn’t have to audition, didn’t need to know how to read sheet music and weren’t under pressure to commit to a weekly choir. They could just come along for the evening and sing.” After floating the idea on social media, the response was immediate. “Within a couple of weeks, I’d sold out the first event, with 150 people turning up.”
[ Facing the music: St Patrick’s Cathedral Choir School struggles to attract boy singers Opens in new window ]
Since then, Casual Choir has outgrown the lecture halls where it began, moving into larger – and livelier – venues, including The Sugar Club, The Button Factory, Whelan’s and Vicar Street. Savage describes the evenings as closer to a traditional sing-song than a formal choir. “As Irish people, we’re comfortable with sing-songs, but not necessarily with the idea of a choir,” she says. “Everybody has been part of a sing-song at one time or another.”
This informality, combined with the energy of singing in a crowd, is central to the experience. “There’s huge comfort in being part of a big group,” says Savage. “I’m not going to single anybody out for singing flat. It’s the power of the group – and the bigger the group, the better.” At the most recent gathering at The Button Factory, the Casual Choir did a rendition of Young Hearts Run Free by Kym Mazelle.
This collective spirit is what keeps people coming back. Savage says the camaraderie at every event is remarkable, while Heffernan sees a similar sense of belonging at Sing for Joy, which currently has a waiting list of 250. “Members anchor their week around Tuesday evenings,” she explains. “They tell me that no matter what they have going on in their lives, they can come here and leave it at the door. At the end of the session, people are slow to leave. Everyone is chatting and helping to clean up. There’s a lovely sense of community. It’s joyful.”
[ In pictures: Guinness Choir celebrates 75th anniversary Opens in new window ]
Dempsey describes her community of singers as “a tribe”. “A lot of women in the group rely on one another; they’ve become a source of support for each other.” For anyone feeling intimidated by the idea of turning up alone, Dempsey has a simple message: everyone was a newcomer once. “Everybody who’s now a regular, or considers themselves part of the group, walked into the room for the first time feeling nervous and worried that they couldn’t sing,” she says. “Showing up anywhere on your own can be difficult, especially if you’re going through a tough time, but it doesn’t take long to realise that everybody is incredibly laid-back and friendly.”
O’Shea likens group singing to a team sport, “but for people who are not into sports”. It has the same sense of shared purpose, the same collective creativity and, above all, the deep feeling of belonging associated with being a team player.

title: Will rent-a-room scheme increase encourage more landlords to participate?
description: Numbers availing of tax-free income have increased steadily in recent years, with student tenants a target
content:
Caroline Gleeson has been renting a room in her three-bedroom home in Whitehall, Co Dublin , for 25 years. The rent-a-room scheme allows her to earn up to €14,000 tax-free while not affecting her pension entitlements.
While providing her with an extra income, it also provides her with company. She has had the same tenant, a Sri Lankan chef named Nalaka, for a few years.
In the budget, the Government raised the tax-free threshold for the rent-a-room scheme from €14,000 to €16,000 for people like her and those thinking of availing of the scheme.
Gleeson says she remains well within the threshold, but it would be a help if she decided to rent out a second room in her home on a permanent basis. She is renting out a second room at present, but only on a short-term basis, and will still be under the tax threshold.
“If you are renting out two rooms, €16,000 is not enough,” she said. “I wish more people would do it. It makes a lot of sense. I live on my own. Also, as a senior, I’m not very techy. It helps to have somebody around who knows what they are doing.”
The number of taxpayers availing of the rent-a-room scheme has almost doubled since 2020, according to the latest figures provided by the Department of Finance.
The rise from €14,000 to €16,000 is the first increase since 2017. Taxpayers will now be able to earn up to €16,000 from the scheme without having to pay tax on their earnings. Rent-a-room relief can only be claimed by individual taxpayers. It is not available to corporate entities.
If rental income goes above €16,000, the landlord becomes liable for taxation on all the rental income, not just the figure above €16,000.
[ What are the key takeaways from Budget 2027? From income tax cuts to surprising omissions Opens in new window ]
According to figures provided by the Department of Finance, the number of taxpayer units (single or couples) claiming the tax relief increased from 9,310 in 2020 to 18,180 in 2024, the latest year for which figures are available. It rose to 10,730 in 2021, 14,180 in 2022, the first post-Covid year, and then to 16,580 in 2023.
Those availing of the scheme in 2025 have until next month to file their tax returns.
[ How Budget 2027 will impact families: From renters to stay-at-home parents Opens in new window ]
The Government has been promoting the rent-a-room scheme especially as a means of solving the accommodation crisis for students.
The push seems to have had some success, with higher education institutions showing “digs accommodation” rising from approximately 2,000 units in 2022 to more than 5,000 by September 2026.
The Minister for Higher Education James Lawless lobbied before the budget to have the threshold increased to €20,000.
It did not emerge at that scale, but the Minister nevertheless welcomed the increase, describing it as a “positive and practical step towards unlocking much-needed student accommodation”.
“This measure is about increasing the availability of accommodation, not increasing rents. Importantly, these are beds that can be made available immediately, without the need for planning permission or new construction,” he said.
[ Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work Opens in new window ]
The rent-a-room scheme has also been extended to so-called garden homes, or detached cabins on homeowners’ properties. Owners will be able to avail of the tax retrospectively from July 27th.
The Minister of State at the Department of Housing John Cummins delivered a robust defence of the measure which has been heavily criticised by the Opposition.
“I would encourage anyone to go and see the factories that are producing top-quality product,” he said at the budget press conference.
“We have a fledging industry in this country that’s producing good quality homes, and the future of housing is in modern methods of construction. It is just an option for people, nobody is forcing people to avail of this extension, but it is a sensible measure.”

title: Mark O'Connell: There is nothing more Irish than a former housing minister lobbying on behalf of a developer
description: The Irish Glass Bottle site was once a symbol of the Celtic Tiger era. Now it’s a symbol of our intractably absurd housing situation
content:
L ast week I had dinner with a writer who was visiting Dublin for a story he was working on for an American magazine. He was attempting to get to grips with Ireland’s political culture, and with the country’s strange sclerotic incapacity, despite the great windfalls of corporation tax continually gusting into a supposedly overflowing treasury, to deal with the problems affecting public life. Not least among these is an increasingly grave housing situation .
At points during the conversation, I found myself struggling to articulate what exactly I felt was going on with Ireland, with the continuous failure of the Coalition parties to – as the popular saying goes – “tackle the housing crisis”. And with the electorate’s apparently unshakeable insistence on voting them back in regardless. The best I could offer was a somewhat lame diagnosis of a national malaise, characterised by a toxic admixture of complacency and fatalism. We seem, if not quite incapable of imagining a politics that might deliver better results for the country, then disinclined to pursue it for fear that it might make things worse. (The exception to this, of course, is the great national tradition of periodic referendums, which does wonders for our esprit de corps. It allows us to believe that ours is a culture of vital democratic energies and political dynamism.)
All that, as I say, was last week. If the conversation had happened a week later, I’d simply have pointed him towards a report by Olivia Kelly in Wednesday’s The Irish Times headlined “Council urges Johnny Ronan lobbyist Coveney to honour Glass Bottle site affordable housing plan” as a kind of scale miniature of this country’s systemic dysfunction.
[ Simon Coveney: Former minister once lobbied by developer Johnny Ronan, now lobbies for him Opens in new window ]
At the former Irish Glass Bottle site in the Dublin neighbourhood of Ringsend, a consortium led by the property developer Johnny Ronan is building up to 3,800 apartments. In 2017, when the development was being planned, a deal was struck between Dublin City Council, Nama and the Department of Housing – then led by Simon Coveney, in which the council agreed to fast-track the development. The deal stipulated that 25 per cent of the homes, amounting to some 900 apartments, would be allocated for social and affordable housing. At the time, councillors and locals understood that, after the 10 per cent requirement for social housing, the remaining 15 per cent of the development would be used for an affordable purchase scheme, offering homes for sale at a State-subsidised discount.
Four years later, in 2021, a cost-rental scheme was introduced by a subsequent government. The council has now obtained legal advice that such cost-rental units could satisfy the “affordable” requirement, despite the fact that such a category didn’t exist at the time of the initial agreement. Councillors and residents argue that this is not in keeping with the original understanding.
Here’s how Dermot Lacey, Labour councillor for Dublin Bay South, put it: “The affordable element was always understood to be affordable purchase. The concept of cost-rental didn’t exist at the time. We always saw the affordable housing as being housing local people could afford to buy. Genuinely, I had no doubt about that.”
Patsy Doolin, the chairwoman of the Irish Glass Bottle Housing Action Group, pointed out that cost-rental was not what was promised to the community at the time of the deal. “People,” she said, “want to be able to buy them and own them.” Of Coveney – who, to repeat, was minister for housing at the time the deal was made – and his new private-sector proximity to the site of actual power, she said this: “I’d love to just talk to him, have a cup of coffee with him and ask him to help us.”
[ Postponing parenthood: How Ireland’s housing crisis is forcing people to delay having children Opens in new window ]
The attempt by the councillors and other local representatives to prevail on Coveney to appeal to the decency of his new property-developer client, Johnny Ronan , is the most absurd and dispiriting aspect of the whole situation. It is also its most irreducibly Irish aspect. Coveney retired from politics in 2024; a 12-month “cooling-off” period, during which he was not allowed to lobby for clients, elapsed last November. After that, he began working as a lobbyist for Ronan.
The former tánaiste is, of course, perfectly entitled to do whatever he wishes with his career now that he has left politics (and accountability to the public) behind. Within the logic of the system we have, with its revolving doors between government and the private sector, it makes perfect sense that he would pivot to this new role. Who better to lobby the government for the interests of a property developer, after all, than a man who was not so long ago minister for housing?
[ Housing the Nation by Lorcan Sirr and Brittle by Ronan Lyons: indictments of an untenable system Opens in new window ]
The site itself, 37-odd acres of prime Dublin 4 real estate between Ringsend and South Wall, is charged with a certain historical symbolism. As the name suggests, it was originally the Irish Glass Bottle plant; when that factory closed in 2002, it lay vacant for years, some of the most valuable land in Europe. The site was purchased in 2006 for €412 million by a consortium of developers that included the Dublin Docklands Development Authority, which, as a State body, had the authority to fast-track the planning.
Anglo-Irish Bank backed the deal with a loan for €288 million. The docklands authority’s chairman, Lar Bradshaw, was at the time on the board of Anglo, and the bank’s chairman Sean Fitzpatrick was on the authority’s board. Before any building actually got done, however, the global economy crashed, bringing down with it the Jenga tower of Ireland’s property market. The whole enterprise wound up in Nama, and the site remained derelict until Ronan’s group came along in 2020 and bought a controlling interest in it for some €200 million.
And so it has progressed from being a symbol of the Celtic Tiger era to a symbol of our intractably absurd housing crisis.
Property prices in the State have more than doubled since 2015. Dublin is tied with Stockholm as the most expensive capital city in the EU, with the average monthly rent for a two-bed flat now just under €2,700. And yet here is how the business and politics of housing is conducted: public representative and community groups reduced to pleading with a housing minister-turned-lobbyist to intercede with his property-developer client, in the hope that a deal made while he was minister might be delivered on, and in the hope that the property developer might see fit to deliver affordable housing for the public. It’s the sort of thing that makes you wonder what a government is even for. Though this is not, presumably, a question Johnny Ronan or Simon Coveney need to waste much time considering.

title: Bad news for Dublin’s coolest neighbourhoods – there’s a plan to bring them tourists
description: Plus: the magical disappearing youth culture card, church vs popular music, and An Post goes electric
content:
The six million or so tourists visiting Dublin every year can make the streets busy. The situation is a challenge for locals, who find prices high, paths congested and hotels growing out of cracks in the pavement.
Until now, you could just stay out of town and things would be all right. But Fáilte Ireland has had an idea. If some of those tourists – or excess future tourists – can be lured out of their traditional Christ Church-to-Trinity heartland in the city centre, then more of their spending can be absorbed into the city’s wider economy.
Enter the neighbourhood plan. On offer is a contract for any clever agency that can bring footfall to different areas of Dublin. Fáilte Ireland wants things worked out for up to eight neighbourhoods, followed by a pilot running in three that can point the way for expansion in the future, once stakeholders are placated.
“Place-based and neighbourhood-focused tourism development can help disperse visitors and visitor spend, spread the economic benefits of tourism more widely, strengthen local identity, support community participation and contribute to sustainable tourism growth,” says the tender document.
This is concerning news for Dublin sophisticates, coming so soon after the cost of a flat white was left unaddressed in Budget 2027. Some of the vibes-ier inner suburbs so beloved of Time Out’s Coolest Neighbourhoods In The World could be at risk – Phibsborough, the Liberties, Stoneybatter, Smithfield and Inchicore among them.
There’s not an enormous amount to see in some of these areas – no castles or vellum manuscripts – but they do have pints of Guinness, which is often enough for tourists these days.
Is there a youth culture card or is there not a youth culture card? That is the question facing artistic directors considering whether they need to develop a rap version of Hamlet for next year.
Jack Chambers , Minister in charge of shooting down kites, seems to think not.
“It wasn’t possible to fund and deliver the cultural card for next year,” he told reporters after delivering his culture-card-free budget on Tuesday.
This stood in stark contrast to the confidence of headlines mere weeks before. Taking advantage of a strategy favoured by Overheard when it comes to housework, the Fine Gael side appears to be maintaining that just because no progress has been made toward doing it, it doesn’t necessarily mean it’s not being done.
[ Why did an Irish Army plane go on a dream family holiday? Opens in new window ]
Was the culture card ever real? Sort of. Overheard understands that the dynamic officials of the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport were at one point tasked with getting things moving for delivery early in 2027, researching continental versions, although the pressure may now be off.
And the Arts Council , more familiar with surrealist long-durational performance art than most, kept the faith, and still welcomed the card in its post-budget response despite the lack of an announcement.
“The Arts Council is supportive of this project and the ongoing development work as part of the Programme for Government,” it told Overheard when asked why, before obliquely adding: “The Arts Council continues to support our colleagues in the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport and wider Government as an adviser on many arts and culture initiatives.”
This is little consolation to the 17-year-olds of today, who will be grown and gone long before they get their free sample of the cultural life.
It was in Connacht that the war on jazz was fought most fiercely in the 1920s and 1930s. Not one of the major meccas of swing, Mohill, Co Leitrim, nonetheless perceived itself to be in an existential battle for the bodies and souls of its young people as Fr Peter Conefrey, various TDs, newspapers and the Gaelic League tried to beat back the bands.
The nation moved past the threat in the end, with jazz declared “not evil” in the Dáil in the 1960 during a debate about whether television was evil. But echoes of the war were heard half an hour down the road this week in Boyle, Co Roscommon.
Nathan Carter , who is more country-n-Irish than Count Basie in his musical sensibility, was forced to cancel a Christmas concert in the town over clerical opposition. The hierarchy had the upper hand on this occasion: the gig was scheduled to take place literally inside St Joseph’s church in the town, until it wasn’t.
What happened? Fr Gerry Hanly PP retired on August 14 th . Fr John Gannon, his successor, is apparently more of a traditionalist. Carter’s management said it was “extremely disappointed to get a phone call from Fr John in Boyle” cancelling the concert.
But Kevin Doran, Bishop of Elphin, defended the principle of keeping the profane out of the sacred space. “I’ve nothing against concerts, I love music. One of the things I lost out on a little bit by coming west is that I used to love going to the National Concert Hall , but that’s neither here nor there,” he told the symphony-starved listeners of Shannonside FM.
But there’s a difference between “hymns and songs that reflect the Christmas story” and “deck the halls”, he said – and the church is for worship.
With 2,000 electric vehicles in its fleet, it’s fair to say An Post has a high demand for electricity. More vans are reliant now on the charger than the diesel pump after several years of investment – and just in time, given the problems in the Middle East.
It also manages more than 200 properties, which fact undoubtedly lit up an efficient modern LED light bulb at headquarters: why not install loads of solar panels? So it is that the mail carrier has moved to harness the power of the sun at “approximately 53” of its locations nationwide.
This follows a prior wave that took in 30 buildings, beginning in 2020. The roll-out seems promising. An installation at Athlone last year showed “strong generation potential” for both on-site consumption and future export to the grid, An Post’s most recent sustainability report said. As long as the weather holds.

title: It’s not just the Berlin Marathon. Cheating runners everywhere are now being closely watched
description: Social media’s bad influencers looking for shortcuts at marathons
content:
D id you hear the one about the social media influencer who hopped on the back carrier of a bike shortly before finishing last month’s Berlin Marathon? At the time it seemed like a bit of a joke, but some people are mad as hell, and they aren’t going to take it any more.
Indeed, it’s fast turned into something of a marathon running scandal, after Yuanyuan Sun, a 30-year-old Chinese fitness influencer with over half a million social media followers, this week publicly apologised when several images emerged of her sitting on the back of a bike in the final 5km in Berlin.
Sun managed to finish in 4:53:46 – presumably hopping off the back of the bike by then – and thus breaking the five-hour barrier which appears to be some sort of running benchmark for social media acceptance. Her original post under the name Abeeeer claimed this was a personal best time, also showing her posing afterwards for photos with her Berlin finisher’s medal.
Suspicions were initially raised by the Official Marathon Time Integrity Unit (OMTIU), a sort of Instagram watchdog page set up in Australia last year for the purpose of “protecting the integrity of the marathon, upholding chip times, and exposing Strava inflation” – Strava being the fitness tracking app based entirely on the good faith of the runner.
After this revelation was picked up on by several international news outlets, including the BBC and The New York Times, it became clear it was no longer a simple laughing matter. On Wednesday, the Berlin Marathon organisers announced that Sun was officially disqualified, with her finishing time and place struck off the results list. Though no word yet on whether she’s handed back her finisher’s medal.
Compared to some other sporting scandals doing the rounds right now, namely Manchester City being found guilty of “sham payments” of more than £900 million between 2009 and 2018, this may appear a very minor misdemeanour. Especially given the only person Sun was really cheating here was herself.
Still, all this running outrage is a reminder that for all the different scales of cheating in sport, they almost all come back down to simple honesty being the best policy. Few people outside of the so-called Marathon Majors such as London, Berlin or this Sunday’s Chicago Marathon will be losing any sleep over the fear that some runners aren’t being entirely honest about their finishing times, although that isn’t making this any more acceptable.
[ Managers react to Manchester City’s guilty verdict: ‘Uncertainty is not good for anyone’ Opens in new window ]
For some runners, it’s partly about the growing “influence” of social media influencers when it comes to their participation in any sporting event. Particularly in marathon running, where starting places in events including the Dublin Marathon are now at such a premium. Sun’s little sojourn on the back of the bike has added to the impression they’re only in it to promote themselves.
She might well have got away with it too. She’d dropped her fastest 5km split of the marathon between 35km and 40km, covering that six minutes quicker than the previous segment, before “running” the last 2km, which only later caught the suspicion of OMTIU.
All this comes with a further cost beyond her disqualification. Sun has since posted an apology on the Chinese social media platform Rednote, which was shared by OMTIU, saying: “I won’t make any excuses for this behaviour. I was feeling physically unwell on the course, [but] that is absolutely not an excuse for breaking the rules. My attempt to take a shortcut was disrespectful to the fairness of the competition and the spirit of the marathon.”
Brooks Running, one of her main sponsors, also called this “an oversight on our part”, and added it has “immediately terminated its relationship with the influencer and publicly reaffirmed the brand’s commitment to integrity, fairness, and the spirit of running”.
