As The New York Times also noted this week, there’s a long history of athletes who have attempted to use shortcuts or other illegal aids to improve their finishing times or position, including at the very front of the race. The most notorious of those was Rosie Ruiz, who faked her way to come 11th in the 1979 New York Marathon and to “win” the 1980 Boston Marathons; taking the subway to the finish at the former when passing herself off as an injured athlete, and by only running the final half mile at the latter.
Four years ago, the Dublin Marathon organisers also announced that a male runner had been disqualified and his finisher’s medal returned, after it emerged that he had likely travelled a significant portion of the 26-mile course on the Luas.
Suspicions were aroused there after the runner’s average 5km times had dramatically improved, at the beginning and at the end of the race, coinciding with Luas stops also along the route. If he’d run the entire race at that pace, he should have finished in just over two-and-a-half hours, which would have ranked him among the leading runners.
This week the Berlin organisers also announced that 94 runners have now been disqualified for cutting short last month’s marathon, saying: “In cases of proven fraud, we contact the individuals concerned directly and disqualify them. Any such disqualification can be seen in the official results lists. Following a thorough review of each individual case, we decide on appropriate measures and, where necessary, impose further sanctions.”
[ Mary McAleese questioned the GAA’s attitude towards women – now they’ve replaced her with a man Opens in new window ]
In their event summary, OMTIU also said Berlin had “more infringements than any other major marathon in recent history”, including, “early watch pauses, creative cycling commutes, false sub-three claims and the ongoing Strava PR sticker cover-up ...”
OMTIU added that “our work to crack down on time fabrication is just getting started ... more work is required”.
All of which should come as a clear warning to anyone who might somehow be contemplating taking a shortcut in the Dublin Marathon later this month, or in any big city marathon for that matter, because you are now being closely watched.

title: ‘Nobody wants to work’: Why doesn’t Ireland grow more veg?
description: About 83% of fruit and veg consumed in the Republic is imported from overseas, report finds
content:
“N obody wants to work,” Jenny McNally laughs when asked what might turn someone away from a career in vegetable growing.
“It’s hard labour; your bones ache. There’s nothing easy about horticultural farming.”
Since 1997, she and her husband Patrick have operated an organic, family farm in north Co Dublin , selling their produce directly at markets and from a shop on-site. On the couple’s 99 acres, they cultivate a wide variety of vegetables, salad and some fruit.
At one point during the 1990s, there were more than 600 commercial vegetable growers in Ireland. Today, there are fewer than 70.
A recent report by the Climate Change Advisory Council noted that an estimated 83 per cent of fruit and vegetables consumed in the Republic are imported from overseas.
“When you hear about another veg producer going out of business, sometimes it’s because there’s nobody there following behind,” McNally says.
“There are no children, or the farmer’s children are not interested. They’ve seen mum and dad work so hard all their life and why should they do it?”
Fortunately, three of the five McNally children are part of the family business. If it weren’t for their involvement, “Pat and myself would be growing a tunnel of salads or something and that would be it,” McNally says.
Before 1997, they had been conventional farmers, raising livestock and growing barley and oats as well as vegetables.
People like us, we had moved into growing courgettes and beans and mangetout
From a commercial point of view, McNally says that there was no security around veg in the open market. You were “always on a wing and a prayer”, and never guaranteed a sale.
That culture made life difficult for smaller farms, and it was compounded by a growing need for expensive equipment and machinery.
McNally says that over time, a lot of sellers were pushed out. It suited supermarkets to work with larger, specialised operations focusing on large-scale production of individual vegetables.
“People like us, we had moved into growing courgettes and beans and mangetout,” McNally says.
“We were told if you don’t have a refrigerated van and a cold store, you’re not up to our expectations and our levels, so that was that. At the time, we had five small children and there was no way we could afford to even think of anything like that.”
The solution was a stall at Temple Bar Food Market where they could sell “wonky courgettes”, beans that weren’t topped and tailed, and “cabbages that weren’t all exactly the same size”. It turned out a market for this sort of food existed.
McNally Family Farm veg can be bought at three markets today. Queues often form before they have had a chance to lay out their produce. They have built up relationships with their customers over three decades, many of whom have grown to appreciate the journey from farm to fork, are understanding of seasonal setbacks that impact the size or volume of what’s being sold.
This summer of 2026 – Ireland’s hottest on record – was difficult for vegetable producers.
A recent report carried out by Teagasc, the national agriculture and food development authority, found that in 2026, there were yield and quality losses of 25 to 40 per cent on unirrigated vegetable crops.
Irrigated fields were protected, albeit at a price. For some crops, growers spent more than €2,700 per hectare on water alone, before equipment and infrastructure costs.
Only 30 to 35 per cent of the Irish vegetable production area carries sufficient irrigation capacity.
“Ultimately, it’s an increased cost of production,” says Dermot Callaghan, head of horticulture at Teagasc.
“Irrigation costs money to do, between ‘cap-ex’ and ‘op-ex’ – so, capital expenditure on the equipment and infrastructure, including reservoirs which may be needed in the future, and operational costs, the ‘op-ex’, which is the cost of actually moving irrigation systems, pumping stations, running diesel pumps to extract water and so on.”
The positive, he explains, is that Ireland has something of an advantage on its European neighbours when it comes to accessing water.
Though investment will be needed for farmers to adapt to the effects of the climate crisis over the coming years, it should be cheaper to irrigate here than in hotter countries.
Over the last few years, Teagasc has carried out a series of cost studies on horticulture farms, documenting a trend of rising costs that has not been matched by the farm gate price – in other words, the value of the farmer’s produce as it leaves the farm.
According to the agriculture and food authority’s most recent report, labour accounts for 43.4 per cent of costs on horticulture farms.
It is a figure that echoes Jenny McNally’s concerns around the availability of labour in horticulture. Callaghan says the answer, where possible, is to adopt technology, automation and even robotics.
Ireland could be growing huge quantities of fruit and vegetables
“Still, there are crops which have to be touched by the human hand,”says Callaghan, “and those are the crops which will obviously have a higher labour cost associated [with them], and will probably be the last to get automated. Having labour to do that job will be paramount.”
Six supermarkets signed up to a “horticulture grower-retail charter” this year, establishing five ‘key principles’ intended to support a stronger and more sustainable sector.
The charter commits to improved communication and promotion around Irish produce, as well as a sustainable approach to cost inputs and reduced food waste.
“They’re prepared now to work on a longer, three- to five-year arrangement with growers, which is a big change because that will allow growers to invest in their businesses,” Callaghan says.
“They have a line of sight on having a market for their product.”
Efforts are being made to encourage more domestic growers. Over the last couple of years, the Department of Agriculture’s Organic Farming Scheme (OFS) was opened up to horticultural producers.
Recently, the scheme helped fund the digging of a new well on the McNally family farm.
More than 250 commercial growers across fruit, vegetable and potato sectors are operating under Bord Bia’s Sustainable Horticulture Assurance Scheme (SHAS), generating a farm gate value of about €652 million in 2025.
Emer Gallahar Hall, the senior manager for horticulture at Bord Bia, says the drop in the number of individual vegetable growers in Ireland since the 1990s “should not be interpreted as a proportional decline in output”, but rather a reflection of the reality that vegetable production is “increasingly concentrated among fewer, larger, highly specialised businesses”.
Ireland is a “net importer of fresh produce,” Gallahar Hall says, though a substantial portion of imported fruit and vegetables, such as citrus fruits, bananas and Mediterranean crops, cannot be commercially produced in Ireland due to the Irish climate.
Bord Bia recently launched HortLink, a community network for growers and professionals in horticulture to come together and share their experiences.
It ties into another concern Jenny McNally raises: that sometimes the most important thing “is to be able to chat to other farmers”.
Despite the various ongoing initiatives, Gallahar Hall notes that economic viability remains a key challenge in horticulture, with growers facing an increase of 51 per cent in production costs since 2021.
The Vegan Society of Ireland suggests looking abroad. In October 2023, Denmark launched a world-first, plant-based action plan designed to increase the number of vegetarian foods in the national diet and reduce the climate footprint of its agricultural industry.
Backed by a €170 million government fund, it targets a full suite of improvements to the Danish domestic food chain, from farms and food processors to retail and restaurants. In advance of Budget 2027, the vegan society called on the Irish Government to introduce a similar programme.
“[Ireland and Denmark are] super similar,” says the society’s chairperson James O’Donovan on the potential for the agricultural sector.
“Ireland could be growing huge quantities of fruit and vegetables.”
O’Donovan suggests that less food could be imported across the board. Sugar and bread, he says, have potential to become stronger domestic products.
The vegan society advocates for a move towards organic foods – a transition that is also prioritised by Denmark’s action plan.
In May, the society commissioned a survey to gauge the Irish public’s attitude to plant-based foods. Four in five respondents said they wanted to eat more fruit, vegetables and legumes, while 62 per cent said Ireland should make healthy, sustainable diets a national political priority. O’Donovan sees this as a “clear mandate” for politicians to act.
“The quantity of fruits and vegetables that we’re importing is huge,” he says.
“The quantity of legumes and grains and tillage crops that we’re importing is also huge. That’s why we’re calling for a holistic approach – just increasing Ireland’s food security.”

title: Tolkien: the original Greta Thunberg-style eco‑warrior or a proto‑Elon Musk?
description: Those who love what the writer really stood for despair at the misuse and misunderstanding of his works
content:
I f not quite the greatest story ever told, then JRR Tolkien ’s The Lord of the Rings (LOTR) is certainly the greatest story ever to feature wizards and warriors, cursed rings and hairy-footed hobbits.
Since its publication in the mid‑1950s as a trilogy of doorstoppers, Tolkien’s masterpiece has become one of the world’s favourite books – the sort that changes lives, rewires brains and soothes the soul.
Its fans run from Led Zeppelin – who based a fair chunk of their repertoire on it – to Barack Obama , who said that encountering LOTR in his youth revealed to him some dark truths about human nature (“how some people are kind and some are cruel”).
But just as Tolkien’s novel chronicles a vast war for control of Middle‑earth, so LOTR has now itself become a battlefield – where individuals with radically different mindsets fight to claim his words as an articulation of their worldview.
Depending on who you listen to, Tolkien was either the original of the Greta Thunberg -style eco‑warriors or a proto‑ Elon Musk , with a fetish for strong men waving big swords. Hero, villain, saviour, dangerous codger. Everyone has a take on LOTR and Tolkien in 2026.
What is beyond question is the blockbuster appeal of his writing. This weekend, thousands will descend on 3Arena in Dublin to witness an orchestra provide live musical accompaniment to the first of Peter Jackson’s LOTR adaptations, The Fellowship of the Ring. Meanwhile, Hollywood is barrelling ahead with a prequel to the Jackson films, The Hunt for Gollum , while season three of Prime Video’s wretched Tolkien spin‑off The Rings of Power arrives in November. Everywhere, people are talking Tolkien.
But whose voice should carry the most weight when assessing Tolkien and the LOTR legacy? As is often the case with contested art, the loudest have tended to come from the right. Perhaps the most famous LOTR fan today is trillionaire Musk, who encountered it as a nerdy nine‑year‑old in South Africa and, by his telling, was never the same again.
Musk has carried that love with him into adulthood. He has described LOTR as “probably his favourite book” and says he was inspired by how its heroes “always felt a duty to save the world”. When he met his future partner Grimes and she mentioned her devotion to Tolkien, he immediately quizzed her on Middle‑earth trivia. Their relationship was sealed when she aced his quiz and, for bonus points, compared Musk to the wise wizard Gandalf.
[ Elon Musk’s view of pre-immigration Ireland: Lovely small towns full of ‘hobbits, frankly’ Opens in new window ]
Yet Musk’s passion for Tolkien has metastasised into something more sinister as he has gone from techie boy genius – which is remarkably how the world saw him as recently as a decade ago – to bête noire of progressives. That much became clear when the social media mogul went on the Joe Rogan podcast in 2025 and attacked immigration into Ireland and the UK through the lens of his Tolkien fandom.
“These lovely small towns in England, Scotland and Ireland, they’ve been living their lives quietly. They’re like Hobbits,” he said. “They’re lovely people who liked to, you know, smoke their pipe. And have nice meals. And everything is pleasant. The Hobbits in the Shire ... And so one day, 1,000 people show up in your village of 500.”
Musk isn’t the only one on the American right to herald Tolkien as a lodestar. His former business partner Peter Thiel named his AI data analytics company Palantir after Tolkien’s mystical seeing stones. Then there is Anduril, the military tech company named after the hereditary sword that the ranger Aragorn brandishes when he travels across Tolkien’s vast patchwork of kingdoms to reclaim his rightful place as king of Middle‑earth.
But it isn’t just the tech bros who have Tolkien on the brain. Italy’s right‑wing prime minister Giorgia Meloni grew up on Tolkien, attending “Camp Hobbit” youth meetings as a teenager, while US vice-president JD Vance says his books helped shape his conservative worldview. Last October, the US department of homeland security canvassed for recruits to Ice by quoting noted law‑and‑order expert Meriadoc Brandybuck – Merry to friends – and his warnings that, unless right‑thinking people stand up to evil, then “there won’t be a Shire”.
What would Tolkien have thought of all of this? While we obviously can’t say with 100 per cent certainty, he would surely be aghast at how some of the world’s most unpleasant people have taken so much from his trilogy.
He might also have wondered if they were paying attention to his story about underdogs standing up to bullies, of everyday people working together to battle far mightier foes. Above all, he would have questions about their humanity and their commitment to justice – qualities that run, like spools of golden thread, through all of LOTR.
‘He is misunderstood. Often by people who haven’t read him or engaged with the original work’
“The Hobbits are the ones who surprise everybody. The little people who spring the surprises and save mankind basically. It was mankind who would be saved by the Hobbits, rather than the heroic races such as the humans. It was definitely a defence of the little people,” says Phil Hughes, the Wexford‑based fantasy author who has just published his latest novel, The Rebel and the Seeress.
“Those of us who love what Tolkien really stood for despair at the misuse and misunderstanding of his works by folks who only seem to have given them a surface reading,” agrees Janet Croft, editor of fantasy journal Mythlore, in a 2025 interview with Wired. “They become blind to the deeper moral issues and implications of his life‑long project.”
[ Jamie Dornan to play Aragorn in new Lord of The Rings movie, The Hunt for Gollum Opens in new window ]
Tolkien’s conservative fans also seem not to have noticed the environmental message at the heart of LOTR. Among the most vividly drawn characters in the novels are the Ents – ancient sentient trees whose forests have been ravaged by the evil wizard Saruman.
Here Tolkien is blatantly taking sides. The Ents are wise and gentle and believe civilisation and nature can live in respectful harmony. Saruman, by contrast, is a tech bro in multicoloured robes. He loves clever machines and is big on the sort of territorial land grabs that have been a hobby horse of Vance’s boss, Donald Trump .
Tolkien’s writings on nature provide some of the most beautiful and profound passages in LOTR. They are the expression of a worldview forged in early childhood in the bucolic English West Midlands village of Sarehole, which ended when he was accepted into a prestigious school in Birmingham and his family relocated to the city’s suburbs, with their smoke‑stacks and industrial darkness. It is a loss he never quite got over – an ache discernible throughout LOTR.
“Obviously he was a man of his time. You couldn’t write a book that was so overwhelmingly male now and not have it commented on as an odd choice,” the award‑winning fantasy author Emily Tesh told me in 2020.
“[But] he is misunderstood. Often by people who haven’t read him or engaged with the original work. The themes of nature and the natural world and beauty and destruction of that world stand up. There are moments in The Lord of the Rings that are impossibly sad.”
Tolkien is undeniably old‑fashioned in many ways and has been rightly condemned for his crude depiction in LOTR of “The Easterlings”, a “swarthy” horde that rocks up in Middle-earth from the Asiatic east.
He also seemed to share the low regard many English people of his generation held for Irish culture, despite making extensive visits to the West of Ireland during his time as external examiner at what is today the University of Galway . He disparaged the Irish language (“mushy”), while the Celtic races are the inspiration in LOTR for Saruman’s uncivilised allies, the Dunlendings – primitive tribes thrown off their land by the Germanic Riders of Rohan and who have lusted for revenge ever since.
But he was in other ways a progressive figure. The most powerful character we meet in LOTR is the elf‑queen Galadriel, while the greatest victory chronicled by Tolkien is that of the Lady Éowyn, who defies the patriarchal culture of Rohan to ride into battle in disguise – and slay the ultimate Big Bad, the Witch‑king of Angmar. So while Tolkien was a fuddy‑duddy, he was no head‑banging reactionary, and was vocal about his detestation of racism, reacting with horror when his German publishers inquired whether the Hobbits were “Aryan”.
Of course, regardless of its author’s views, a book as popular as LOTR will always be open to multiple interpretations. But it would be a disservice to Tolkien to allow his life’s work to be hijacked by tech bros and right‑wing politicians. They see LOTR as a tale of might making right – when in fact it is the very opposite.
The climactic heart of the story comes when Frodo and Sam scale the flanks of Mount Doom with Sauron’s accursed, all-corrupting ring. Frodo is half‑starved and almost wholly broken; Sam is sustained by nothing but a stout heart. All of the odds are against them, yet they do not give up. The lesson is that, when you have nothing else, courage can keep you going – and in today’s troubled world it is a message that resonates more powerfully than ever.
The Fellowship Of The Ring will be screened with a live orchestra and choir at the 3Arena in Dublin on Sunday at 12 and 6pm

title: Who is affected by the public sector strike and can it be averted?
description: Public sector industrial action presents a big challenge for parents and patients amid escalation of dispute
content:
A remarkable era of industrial peace seems to be at an end.
Within days, almost every school in the State may be shut as a result of industrial action , while thousands of patients could find their appointments cancelled and disrupted.
Hundreds of thousands of public sector workers are still without a new pay deal and there appears little sign of a rapprochement between the unions and the Government.
Even through the very worst years of austerity that followed the economic crash, major days of industrial action were largely avoided through dialogue.
The Croke Park deal, for example, was struck in the summer of 2010 after two punishing budgets and just in advance of the international bailout.
Unions agreed to efficiencies in return for the protection of jobs. Further deals followed. Each ensured that major strikes were avoided.
Years on, the situation has changed. On Wednesday, public sector workers are due to strike.
The industrial action began at the end of last month as more than 100,000 public sector workers began a work-to-rule in a dispute over pay.
The escalation of the dispute and the closure of schools, due to the actions of striking teachers and support staff, will on Wednesday present many working parents with a difficult choice.
[ Budget 2027 falls short of preventing public sector industrial action, say unions Opens in new window ]
Members of the Irish National Teachers’ Organisation and the Association of Secondary Teachers Ireland are expected to picket at their school gates.
With schools doubling as childcare for many families during the day, the prospect of having to take time off work arises.
One Family, a charity that supports single parents, says the planned work stoppages on October 14th and 21st will present a big challenge to many of the families they assist.
“Unexpected school closures will affect all working parents, but even more so for people parenting alone who do not have backup and are already struggling with school drop-offs and trying to find after-school care,” says the charity’s chief executive Karen Kiernan.
“We know of some parents who are having to use precious annual leave, or make themselves unavailable for shifts meaning their incomes will be lower at an expensive time of year.”
Health workers are also due to join the industrial action on Wednesday. Thousands belonging to Siptu, Fórsa and the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation are taking part. So too is the Irish Medical Organisation.
[ Public sector pay dispute ‘unwarranted given our willingness to talk’, Taoiseach says Opens in new window ]
Charities working with older people are concerned by the potential effect on health services, but are reluctant to comment on the standoff between the unions and the Government.
They point out that the elderly should not be too concerned about the impact on the emergency services, but that there will be a significant amount of disruption to elective procedures, clinics and appointments.
“Previously, ambulance and emergency services have largely been unaffected by strike action,” says one person in the sector. “The last thing the unions will not want is to have a situation where someone suffers a health catastrophe due to industrial action.”
The strike action has moved into new areas.
For the first time ever, dentists working in the Health Service Executive belonging to the Irish Dental Association will be taking part in such action.
The standoff is framed around the rising cost of living.
The unions maintain that their members’ wages have not kept pace with inflation and accuse the Government of putting preconditions in the way of constructive negotiations.
Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers has said a deal could have been struck by now that would have replaced the last public service agreement that expired in June. He said unions walked away from talks after two meetings.
However, he has said there must be discussion about “reform of our public services and value for money”.
On Tuesday, as part of the budget’s publication, he announced that there was €1.2 billion being set aside for a new deal. The figure has been dismissed by the unions as being far from enough.
Paul Sweeney was the main number cruncher for the unions during the golden years of social partnership. As economic adviser and chief economist to the Irish Congress of Trade Unions, he would frequently present the unions’ case in public.
They won’t be looking for an insane amount of money
“The worry when I was there was always about a wages-prices [inflation] spiral. In the old days the prices were leading the way and the wages were catching up – much like it is now.
“Just because the country is awash with money doesn’t mean the unions aren’t cognisant that a huge pay deal would just boost inflation. They won’t be looking for an insane amount of money.”
Sweeney believes there is a lack of overall direction from the current Coalition Government and the tabling of the €1.2 billion figure before negotiations had begun to have been “naive”.
“It seems to me the whole country has broken down,” he says. “It’s awash with money and nobody is happy.
“This is a government that has no direction whatsoever and that disappoints me. I have a lot of respect for Micheál Martin – he is a Fianna Fáiler and they know how to negotiate.
“He brought in the smoking ban with the help of the unions – what’s wrong with them now? Where is the direction?”
There is similar dismay from the other side of the old partnership. Turlough O’Sullivan was director general of the employers’ group Ibec, a powerful lobby group for businesses, during the 2000s.
“It is awful that a partnership of some kind is not in effect,” he says. “It just strikes me that what is happening is putting the cart before the horse.
“It was unheard of, when I was operating in the field, that unions would be talking about industrial action before exhausting negotiations. Something is basically wrong in the set-up.”
O’Sullivan says it appears the two sides are now on a “collision course”, but there are plenty of people around with the ability to find some sort of resolution.
“There are still some very experienced people around in the unions and you’d be looking at them to do the right thing,” he says. “They have been around this mulberry bush before and I’m surprised at them. You would hope sense would prevail.”
Standing between the unions and Government in the past was the likes of Kieran Mulvey, the former head of the Labour Relations Commission. He was regarded as the go-to industrial strife troubleshooter – and was centrally involved in striking the Croke Park deal of 2010 and the implementation of the Haddington Road agreement, the 2013 deal between the government and the unions that achieved pay and pensions savings to the public purse of €1 billion.
“I’m surprised that we are at the level of a war-of-words on this,” says Mulvey, who believes the “arithmetic” on a deal shouldn’t be difficult.
“I would have expected that very discreet tick-tacking would have gone on between the Ministers’ departments and Ictu [Irish Congress of Trade Unions]. They have a good history of resolving these issues over the years.
“I’m a bit surprised that this tick-tacking, if it has taken place, hasn’t led to a more fruitful outcome at this stage.”
[ Are the unions right? Did the Government’s budget abandon workers? If they lost, who won? Opens in new window ]
Mulvey says he has detected that the Government has “moved away” from the social partnership model over recent years and this has manifested itself in the last two budgets.
“I would be concerned that there would be any drift on this,” he says.
“Stability is very important to the economic outlook of the country. We also have the European presidency. Strikes are not normal in this country and it is not necessarily the message we want to be giving to the world.”
He also worries that strike action could be seized upon by fuel protesters, who last April managed to exert the sort of impact trade unions had been unable to achieve “since the 1960s”.
“At the time of fuel protests, the congress was very audible and forthright that it undermined those who took the representative route to negotiation,” says Mulvey.
“Suddenly out of the blue comes this unrepresentative body that was not on the landscape and brings the country to a standstill.”
Mulvey is still hopeful that some coming together is possible, but that urgent steps will need to be taken by the end of next week at the latest.
“If the one-day strike goes ahead, it cannot be allowed to escalate. What we don’t want is other groups using the opportunity to add further fuel to the fire,” he says.
“In some ways, unions may have needed to ventilate the anger of members. The work to rule has a nuisance value – it is the one-day strike that makes the difference.

title: Meet the former garda who found a new role in the Church of Ireland after retirement and divorce
description: Meet Mike Buchanan ... ex-garda and Catholic, a pilot, divorcee and now Church of Ireland rector in south Dublin
content:
How women are treated in the Catholic Church drove Rev Mike Buchanan (58) from the tradition into which he was born to the Church of Ireland priesthood.
It cost him his marriage, but, unexpectedly, it has also brought him a fiancee.
There are interesting lives, and then there is Buchanan’s varied and most unusual preparation for Anglican ministry.
Next Tuesday, he will be installed as Rector of Tullow parish in south Co Dublin, which includes Carrickmines and Foxrock.
“I’ve been around the block a little,” he says.
Mike Buchanan grew up in Old Bawn, Tallaght, with a brother and sister.
His late father was a wages supervisor at Roadstone, formerly Clondalkin Concrete, while his mother, now in her 80s, remains Catholic, but also proud of him, her rector son.
He attended the Christian Brothers in Dolphin’s Barn, which he described as “a great education”.
“I loved the Brothers and I was actually asked to become a Brother after my Inter Cert,” he says, but he “politely declined, because I had in mind the priesthood”.
[ Clare councillor quits politics to enter Catholic priesthood Opens in new window ]
“I was talking to the Jesuits at the time – I was always drawn to the Ignatian form of spirituality,” he says.
A teacher he found to be particularly impressive there was Br John O’Reilly, who had spent years in South America, including Uruguay.
O’Reilly was a teacher at the order’s Stella Maris College in Montevideo, and “of the guys who were involved in that plane crash”.
Buchanan is referring to the rugby team from Stella Maris, who with their family and friends were among 45 people involved in the Andes plane crash of October 1972 in which all were killed except 16. The survivors were not found for 72 days.
O’Reilly “was very ecumenical for the ’80s and had a great outlook on life, a very measured man, and I talked to him about the priesthood”, says Buchanan.
But the Dubliner had a problem with the Catholic Church.
“I didn’t like the way women couldn’t be involved. One of my earliest influences, my paternal grandmother; she was fantastic, and I used to go to Knock with the ladies on pilgrimage when I was small,” he says.
He recalls those women being “so focused on the Church” and yet they “couldn’t really actively participate in a meaningful way”.
“In conscience, I couldn’t make the final step,” he says, abandoning a path towards the Catholic priesthood.
Instead, he joined the Garda , which he says “seemed the next attractive proposition – I was drawn to public service”.
Over the following 31 years he served across Dublin, including in stations in Kevin Street, Kilmainham, Ballyfermot, Ronanstown and Blanchardstown, as well as in specialist appointments, among them Garda communications.
“The guards were always a community-oriented police force, building on relationships, getting to know people,” he adds.
Buchanan was promoted to the rank of sergeant in 1999 and spent two years at Garda headquarters in internal affairs, which meant investigating colleagues.
He also survived a plane crash. A member of the Garda Flying Club, in 1999 he and an instructor colleague at Weston in Dublin were flying on a blustery summer afternoon when their engine cut out.
“It took a couple of seconds for it to sink in,” he says.
They landed upside down in a cornfield and, smelling fuel, unstrapped themselves fast and ran. The plane did not go on fire.
On arrival back at Weston , a man who ran a flying school there “threw a set of keys at Tom [the instructor] and said: `Take my plane and go and do a circuit – back on the horse.’ So we did. And then we went to the Deadman’s Inn,” he says drily, referring to the well-known west Dublin pub.
Buchanan also spent a year serving with the United Nations in Cyprus.
Through all the decades – and his adventures – he says he “never lost my faith; I always had a strong faith”, even if he did not “attend church as often as I should”.
A significant influence on that faith has been his friendship with Rev Mark Hayden, now Archdeacon of Ossory and Leighlin.
‘We had originally planned to go to Spain, buy a house there and looked into schools and all the rest of it, but something was drawing me back towards the Church’
“Mark and I go back a long way,” he says; both share an interest in military memorabilia.
Rev Hayden had been rector in Gorey, Co Wexford, where Buchanan had a house.
“I started going to Mark’s services, so when I went to Cyprus – where there’s a lot of British Army presence – services there were Church of England. I got to know the chaplains and attended the services,” he says.
He discovered “that Anglicanism was more where I belonged. It was more in line with my theology.” There were also women priests, another factor which helped him realise “that’s where I really belong”, he says.
In 2019 he began studying for a BA in Theology at Dublin City University. Around 2020-21, he was also coming up to 30 years of service in the Garda, at which point he could retire.
“We had originally planned to go to Spain, buy a house there and looked into schools and all the rest of it, but something was drawing me back towards the Church,” he says.
[ ‘My proposal was to stop Confirmation’: Ireland’s ageing priests under pressure as numbers drop Opens in new window ]
He was “thinking about possible ordination”.
Buchanan retired from the Garda on September 6th, 2021 – a Tuesday; the following Friday he began studying for the priesthood at the Church of Ireland Theological Institute in Dublin.
He and Marti had been married 20 years.*
“Marti decided she didn’t want to be part of a Church. That was fine. So we made a decision to go our separate ways, which is unfortunate, but it just wasn’t for her,” he says, saying that the split was not expected.
“It was a blow. It was quite sudden. I knew there was a reticence on Marti’s part. She was kind of agnostic, and I respected that. There was no pressure on her to do anything or to be involved, but she just decided it wasn’t her path,” he says.
There was “no animosity. It was very amicable”.
And the Church had no difficulty with his divorce? “Not at all, no.”
As unexpected as the break-up of his marriage had been, so too was what happened some years later: he met his new partner Jill – “quite by accident; literally by accident”, he says.
“I was in for coffee one day in Ranelagh, one of the Butlers coffee shops – it’s on a corner. I was about to walk in the door when Jill walked around the corner and, basically, into me.”
They “just got chatting in the queue and now are engaged”.
From Kildare, Jill works in tourism. Buchanan says she is “Church of Ireland born and bred, as it happens”.
“Her family are very involved in the Church,” he says.
She has been “incredibly supportive, which is wonderful, because I didn’t realise how much support you really need in ministry”.
In Tullow, Buchanan will be a first-time rector.
“From the very beginning, I’ve had a strong sense that’s where I should be. It wasn’t where I envisaged ministry in the beginning because I was very much on the liberation theology, social side of things, and thought, I might be veered more towards city-centre ministry,” he says.
“But actually, as it happens, Tullow is an incredible fit. There’s a lot of community work going on there with a lot of potential,” he adds.
“There’s a good social ethos in Anglicanism; there always has been.”

title: ‘They poked a bear’: The pro-Palestine Columbia University graduate still fighting deportation from the US
description: The Columbia University graduate, a green card holder, who still faces the threat of deportation, has written a book about his arrest by Ice and subsequent detention
content:
‘I’m still struggling with the fact that some people consider me a symbol for resisting this administration,” Mahmoud Khalil tells me from his home in Brooklyn.
Khalil, who is speaking with me from his one-year-old son’s bedroom, is soft-spoken and gracious – somewhat sheepish, even. So much so that it’s easy to forget that he has become one of the most recognisable faces of the organised resistance to the Trump administration. It is also easy to forget that he is mired in a series of immensely high-risk legal cases against both the administration and his alma mater, Columbia University.
Khalil speaks calmly throughout our conversation about his legal troubles and his uncertain future in the US. He was arrested last year and detained for more than three months. He was not charged with a crime but it was alleged by the administration that his pro-Palestinian organising constituted a national security threat. These events are detailed in his new memoir, No Land to Stand On: Notes from Detention. The memoir – which jumps back and forth between his time in an Ice detention centre in Louisiana, to his adolescence in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria, his decade spent living in Beirut, and, eventually, to New York – is destined to become a staple of dissident literature and an important record for future historians of the second Trump administration. No Land to Stand On, which was born out of the diary entries and observations Khalil recorded during those nightmarish 104 days, is his first book.
[ US immigration judge rules Palestinian Columbia student Khalil can be deported Opens in new window ]
[ Mahmoud Khalil released after US judge says standards for detention ‘clearly not met’ Opens in new window ]
“There is so much in my life that could have been included,” Khalil says of his decision to withhold much of his life story and instead focus on the events surrounding his arrest. “I lived in Beirut 10 years and I only mentioned it in a few pages.” Also only mentioned are his family’s expulsion from Tiberias (now part of Israel) during what Palestinians call the Nakba – the mass displacement and dispossession of Palestinians during the 1948 war surrounding the creation of Israel – and the multigenerational story of loss and displacement that followed as they moved across Syria , Algeria and Germany (where his parents now live) – itself worthy of a book. He devotes more time to his adolescence in Syria, where he and his friends became politically engaged during the 2011 Arab Revolutions and began taking part in pro-democracy protests against dictator Bashar al-Assad . That same year, when he was 16, Khalil was shot in the leg by Israeli security forces, when he, along with hundreds of others, marched towards the border Syria shares with the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights to commemorate the Nakba.
The violent reality of political dissent is never far from Khalil. In 2013, as Syria was engulfed in civil war, he learned that two of his friends had been disappeared by Assad’s security forces. That same day, fearing for his own life, he packed a bag and crossed the border into Lebanon. He had the equivalent of less than €1 in his pocket when he began his new life. More than a decade later, a few months after Assad was eventually deposed, Khalil learned that his two friends had been killed under torture. “They were in the wrong place at the wrong moment, and I had been in the right moment,” he writes in No Land to Stand On. “That was the only difference between us. I made it to Beirut. I made it to New York. They never made it home.”
He then spent much of his twenties living in Beirut working in various jobs, including at the British consulate, picking up French and English along the way. In August 2020 the Beirut port explosion levelled parts of the city. It blew out all of the windows and glass in his apartment. “I was this close to being killed,” he says. Years earlier Khalil met Noor Abdalla, the woman who would become his wife – a Syrian-American who had grown up in Michigan, who was studying to become a dentist – while she was volunteering at an educational programme in Lebanon for Syrian refugees that was being managed by Khalil. They maintained a long-distance relationship for several years, crossing the Atlantic once or twice a year to see each other. In 2022 Khalil received a place at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs and he moved to New York, he says, seeking “stability and permanence”. The couple married a year later, making Khalil a green card holder.
When protests and counterprotests began at Columbia following the bombing campaign Israel launched in response to the October 7th attacks, Khalil – already affiliated with the campus’s Palestinian organisations – unwittingly found himself both a spokesperson for the students and a go-between with the university. As tensions rose on the campus, and Columbia permitted the New York Police Department to enter and remove pro-Palestinian encampments, he (along with several others) was targeted by pro-Israeli groups. While many students chose to wear face coverings to minimise their chances of having identifying information published online or being expelled, Khalil chose not to.
The pro- Palestine campus movement of which Khalil found himself in the centre was composed of several different groups with a wide variety of opinions. Because of his close relationship with the movement, Khalil was, by association, accused of extremist views that he has never supported or endorsed. “I know I have views that would differ from a lot of the people in the movement itself, given just so many experiences through life that shaped me in so many different, very nuanced ways,” he says. “ I don’t want to let people down when they discover, for example, I’m not a supporter of Hizbullah or of Iran for their role in Syria, where I was subject to their atrocities.” What mattered most to him was raising awareness of Israel’s war on Gaza and its occupation of the West Bank. Months later, in March 2025, he and his wife were returning to their apartment one morning when Ice agents arrested him and he was detained.
Beyond seeking to deport Khalil – who had no criminal record – he believes the administration wanted to chill speech and remind people that it could marshal the levers of government against anyone who dared criticise its policies: “The king wanted to send a message,” Khalil writes, “and I was the messenger.”
But, Khalil says: “This government is incompetent. The fact that they did not know I had a green card before coming to arrest me ... ” Noor was eight months pregnant when agents came to take Khalil away, and says he was refused supervised day release to witness the birth of his son. “They’ve already ruined my life, and the moments I lost in detention I would never get back.”
In response to this and ongoing efforts to deport him, Khalil has brought several legal cases against the US government, challenging the legality of his deportation order, which has been variously dropped and upheld by different courts. As part of his legal strategy, Khalil is using the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871, which banned law enforcement agencies from partnering with private groups to conspire and deprive citizens of their constitutional rights. Khalil alleges that the “government acted upon a conspiracy with right-wing groups” to target and attempt to deport pro-Palestine activists. Most recently he launched another lawsuit against Columbia University, alleging that it failed to protect students who supported Palestine from harassment and doxxing (publishing identifying information about an individual on the internet), campaigns. Khalil has stated that any proceeds from these lawsuits would support others who have been targeted.
Is he worried that suing the administration will invite retribution? Of course, he says – but he’s more worried about what happens if he doesn’t stand up for himself and others like him who choose to speak out. “To me, they poked a bear,” he says. “I want to make an example out of them . But of course I’m afraid. Courage to me is not about not being afraid. It’s about doing the right thing despite the fear.”
“This administration,” he adds, “act like bullies, and our parents teach us with a bully you have to fight back because they won’t stop.”
[ How Donald Trump is using fear, obscure laws and immigration agents to crack down on dissent Opens in new window ]
While he has been overwhelmed by the support he has received since his detention, he is not totally surprised by it. “I’ve been part of this movement for so long and I know that there’s so much care in this movement. People actually care about each other. I’ve seen the jail support, the encampments, how people showed up for students when they were arrested.” He writes in the book of how a wide network of people came together to support Noor and their son while he was in detention. That network has grown bigger since, with some of the US’s most prestigious civil rights organisations and specialised advocacy groups, such as the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), the Center for Constitutional Rights and others taking his cases on. A lot of his time, he says, is now taken up with legal proceedings along with their attendant meetings and preparations.
While he will be promoting his book, he keeps a relatively low profile these days. Despite how drastically his life has changed, he appears positive and determined about what lies ahead. He is keenly aware that he is, in his own words, one of the luckier Palestinians. “I’m still one of the privileged ones, actually, who’s now in the United States. I have a roof above my head.”
When I ask what’s next, he says he’s not sure – he is taking things day by day. I tell him it sounds like he has enough stories to fill several books. “We’ll see,” he says, laughing. Years of compartmentalising his emotions – a result of growing up in a refugee camp, being shot by Israeli security forces, witnessing friends being disappeared by the Syrian security forces, being thrown in prison and, most recently, learning that his future in the country in which his wife and son are citizens is contingent on the outcome of very lengthy, very costly legal battles – has made accessing his emotions and the act of writing difficult, he says.
There will be no straightforward route back to a life in diplomacy after what he has endured, that much seems sure. Though, by seeking to suppress and deport Khalil, the administration may have strengthened his resolve to find a different, perhaps more impactful, way to continue with what he sees as his calling. “Whether it’s through [being a] diplomat, whether it’s through writing, whether through leading protests, whether through a grassroots movement – it all serves the same purpose,” Khalil says. “Which is advocating for the rights of the Palestinian people, for Palestinian liberation, for the end of the occupation.”
No Land to Stand On: Notes from Detention is published by Picador

title: ‘I’ve fallen for a man at work, but he might still be married’
description: Ask Roe: One of my friends thinks we are already an ‘item’ just by the way we interact
content:
I have a dilemma that has been gnawing at me for some time. I met a man through work that I have strong feelings for. I sense he feels the same. We communicate regularly and like all the same things in terms of music, hobbies and interests. He is extremely emotionally supportive, and I think I am to him also. I really want to tell him how I feel, but I am also scared it will ruin the friendship.
One of my friends thinks we are already an “item” just by the way we interact, but there has been no physical contact yet. She said we are emotionally closer than some married couples. I really like him, and he has been dropping hints about us going to places together, weekends away, conferences, etc. I know he was married but has stopped wearing his wedding ring for a good while (before I got to know him). He seems to spend a lot of time away from his wife and never mentions her. He is very cautious about talking about his home life, and he does go off on holidays and on lads’ trips on his own – more so than is normal for a married guy.
He does not seem to have a regular couple’s life with her, but they seem to live in the same house. I know many people cannot afford to move out nowadays when they separate. Will I just let him know how I feel and take the risk? I sense sexual chemistry between us and would be afraid of what might happen if I went somewhere with him without knowing the full story. He is very gregarious but also extremely shy underneath and sometimes I feel like he is waiting for me to say something first. He is very emotionally aware, just not good at communicating things openly. Should I ask him his marital status to see what happens?
Yes, you should ask this man who you’re incredibly close with, who is suggesting you go on weekends away with, who you are getting increasingly emotionally attached to, whether he is, in fact, married. And you should do this before declaring any feelings for him.
Your question is about risk – the risk of the awkwardness of asking him outright what his marital status is, and the risk of losing the friendship if you declare feelings for him that are not reciprocated. But you’re already undertaking an even greater risk, one I need you to pay attention to: the risk of becoming increasingly intimate with and emotionally attached to someone when you don’t know if they are available.
Ironically, if this were genuinely just a platonic friendship that wasn’t imbued with romantic and sexual undertones, you probably would have felt comfortable casually asking him aeons ago. Instead, you have spent a huge amount of time and energy acting like a freelance Nancy Drew trying to interpret clues and guess his marital status without actually knowing anything concrete.
And you do need some concrete answers. You need to know whether the man you are interested in and who also seems to be pursuing you is married before you go any further, for your sake and (frankly, more importantly) the sake of the woman who may still be his wife.
And she may still be. He has described himself as married; they still live together and he hasn’t said anything publicly to indicate a split. All evidence right now points to Not Single.
People take off their wedding rings for all kinds of reasons, and him going on holidays a lot and not mentioning her does not mean he’s single. He could be a private but still very married person; they could be non-monogamous; they could be monogamous and madly in love but just enjoy some separate holidays; he could be a practised serial philanderer who takes off his ring every day before work specifically because he fancies you and is hoping to start an affair.
You don’t know. And you need to, because the ambiguity is not serving you. It’s keeping you unclear, increasingly emotionally invested, and – if he is married – keeping you emotionally unavailable to anyone else who is actually available to date.
You can actually ask this casually. If you are indeed speaking all the time about all manners of topics, and he’s mentioning the possibility of you spending weekends together, you can literally just drop the question into conversation. Say, “Can I ask you something slightly personal? I know you were married, but I’ve realised I actually don’t know what your situation is now. Are you still together?” Ask – and then pay attention to the specifics of his answer.
If he says, “We’ve been separated for two years and are in the process of divorcing. Figuring out the house has been tricky, so we’re still technically living together. We’re cordial, but I spend a few nights a week at a friend’s place. We’re Sale Agreed, and I’m moving into my own place in January,” then that’s pretty clear, and you have a timeline for when you could possibly pursue something. If he says something more general, obfuscating and non-specific like “It’s complicated” or “We’re not happy”, then this man is not available for a romantic connection, and you should redirect your energies accordingly. Do not go on weekends away, do not engage in emotionally intimate conversations, do not spend all your time talking to him, do not Pass Go, do not collect £200, do not be That Girl.
If he is genuinely single, out of the house he and his ex once shared and not in a position of authority over you at work, then sure, go to a concert or a movie. Do this before a weekend away, which is too much pressure, and don’t let him use a work conference in a hotel as a way to hook up casually. You have to see this man every day. It’s already not casual. If you want to date, do it deliberately and consciously and thoughtfully. Openly discuss what happens at work if it doesn’t work out, and move carefully.
But no matter his situation or what happens, I want you to think about something. You have emotionally invested in this man very deeply, without knowing or feeling comfortable even asking whether he is single. That choice is worth thinking about. Because just as he may be unavailable, investing in a man who might not be available for a relationship may have been keeping you emotionally unavailable for something open, honest and real with somebody else. Ambiguity can be intoxicating, because nobody has been rejected, nobody has had to make a choice and every glance and conversation and brush against each other can feel charged and full of fantasy and possibility. And unavailable people can actually feel strangely safe, because you can experience longing, connection, excitement and enormous emotional closeness while avoiding all the practical vulnerabilities of a real relationship.
I don’t know if that is what is happening here. But I would ask yourself the question. Because sometimes we say we don’t want to “ruin the friendship” when what we actually don’t want to ruin is the intoxicating, agonising, fantasy-driven period in which every possibility remains possible – because if that period ended, we would have to decide to make ourselves available to something else; something that demanded real vulnerability and real risk.
Ask him. Listen to his answer. Take it from there. Whether it’s with him or someone else, make sure you’re investing in something real. You deserve it.

title: Michael Walker: Liverpool v Manchester City is no longer simply a football match
description: Now that sham has entered the Premier League lexicon, City as a collective and as a series of individuals will feel the full force of criticism
content:
Or it will do. Judging by the amount of red preparations mentioned in Liverpool over the past 48 hours, Manchester City will, well before arriving at Anfield on Sunday, encounter irrefutable evidence of what all of the past days, seasons and years have accumulated. And it isn’t just trophies.
Along their silver way, City have also gathered scepticism, anger and hostility, a lot of it. This club with two league titles – 1937 and 1968 – in their 104 years before being acquired by Abu Dhabi, won eight more between 2012 and 2024. Eight league titles in 13 seasons – the statistic alone provokes disbelief.
Today that sentiment stands shoulder to shoulder with belief in City’s guilt. It is the size of England. It will be heard loud and shrill at Anfield.
Sunday is no longer simply a football match. The decision announced during this extra-long international break that City had used “ sham payments ” to artificially enhance their income by £900 million (about €1 billion) between 2009 and 2018 has been met with a mix of fury and frustration. Outside the City fan base, there has been no understanding of context, or a desire to unearth any. The drawn-out nature of the Premier League’s investigation has led to a great impatience.
In the court of public opinion, City’s case has been lost. While it is no court of law, opinion matters. Sunday’s kick-off has been transformed into an event and Anfield will be seething. That is no guarantee Liverpool will perform efficiently; it is the reaction within City’s starting XI that will be instructive. Pep Guardiola once said Anfield’s reputation is “not marketing”, that when Liverpool score, suddenly it seems they have “players everywhere” and visitors “look small”.
[ Malachy Clerkin: Pep Guardiola said Manchester City destroyed football – he didn’t know how right he was Opens in new window ]
Now that sham has entered the Premier League lexicon, City as a collective and as a series of individuals will feel the full force of criticism. The physical dimensions of Anfield, internally and externally, leave little room for escape. The only way City can neutralise the atmosphere is to put on a masterclass of clinical football, and that won’t be easy in a whirlwind.
How City’s players cope with the noise and Liverpool players’ energy will shape not just Sunday, but City’s season – on the pitch – and potentially the future make-up of the squad. There is a notion Erling Haaland or Rayan Cherki could deal with anything insouciantly – “stick together, enjoy the ride and smile” was Haaland’s message on Thursday . Within money-defined professional football plenty think the millions continuing to wash into City players’ bank accounts will determine their attitude more than riled opposition supporters. But we will not know for certain until kick-off.
Plus, individuals differ. How will, for example, Iliman Ndiaye respond on his first return to Merseyside?
Ndiaye left Everton on September 1st as the transfer window closed. Terms had been agreed with Tottenham on a move south, with Everton gaining Richarlison as well as cash. But then City walked in and dropped a reported £65 million on the table. Tottenham no more, off popped Ndiaye to City. So easy.
Something niggled about the deal, the manner of it. Maybe it’s because Ndiaye was Everton’s best player. From a perspective of sporting democracy, it would be healthy to see him thrive there. Maybe it is because Everton were being denuded, just as Bournemouth were in January when Antoine Semenyo was snipped away by City, just as Crystal Palace were when Marc Guéhi was extracted the same month.
Or maybe it was the reported fee. Because one of the consequences of City’s inflated wealth and inflated spending is they have made £60-£65 million seem routine. It’s not. Everton, Bournemouth and Palace - the previous clubs of Ndiaye, Semenyo and Gueéhi - have never spent that amount on a player.
On accepted figures in the public domain, nor have Brentford, Brighton, Coventry, Fulham, Hull, Ipswich, Leeds, Nottingham Forest or Sunderland. Aston Villa may do, should Nicolas Jackson reach certain targets.
Those are 12 or 13 of Man City’s Premier League contemporaries who have not reached the £60 million figure. Some are nowhere near it.
Yet City – again on accepted figures – have spent £60 million or more 11 times in the past eight years. Three times they have spent more than £100 million.
It could be argued this is football’s food chain and always has been, but it is the inflation of City’s income that enabled it to make such signings – repeatedly. There was also an acceleration in wages.
Sometimes the brutal power City’s finances gave them in squad-building appeared almost casual. It began with Robinho joining for £32.5 million in September 2008 as a show of what Abu Dhabi could do. It was day one of the takeover. People now smirk about Robinho and City, but it was a British record transfer fee.
Only Manchester United and Chelsea had ever spent more than £20 million on a player – Juan Veron and Rio Ferdinand for United and Andriy Shevchenko for Chelsea. By the end of summer 2009 City had done it four times – Robinho, Carlos Tevez, Emmanuel Adebayor and Joleon Lescott.
Forward to 2015, Chelsea tried three times to peel John Stones away from Everton. Everton were able to resist a £30 million top offer. Their fans raided The Beatles and sang “money can’t buy you Stones”.
[ Liverpool’s Cody Gakpo reflects on ‘tough summer’ after collapse of Manchester City move Opens in new window ]
One year on, when City turned up at Goodison Park with £50 million, money did buy Stones. When the music stopped Stones had helped City to six league titles, a Champions League and much else. Everton have not been champions since 1987.
Stones had a sustained impact. Semenyo has started well, scoring the winner in the FA Cup final – you may have forgotten. Ndiaye is impressing.
Other transfers have been less successful. But City’s stockpiling of talent – and Chelsea have done the same – has meant ill-judged recruitment can be absorbed. At other clubs it leads to exposure. There is no airline sponsorship bailout.
Arsène Wenger, in his pre-Fifa period, called it out. In the Lance Armstrong era he named it “financial doping”. Kolo Touré, Adebayor, Bacary Sagna, Gaël Clichy and, most painfully of all, Samir Nasri, all left frugal Arsenal for lavish City. Half a team.
It was not just about City strengthening, it was about opposition weakening. From there lies dominance.
[ Kylian Mbappé reveals he was ‘close’ to Liverpool move after Jürgen Klopp talks Opens in new window ]
For neutrals there were some sublime moments from Guardiola’s teams, but their trophies brought shrugs. It felt hollow, the culmination of economic supremacy, an entitled attitude and questionable paperwork.
“Sportsmanship” sounds like a weak word, but in sport it is the bottom line. Sunderland were the most recent team to play City and on Thursday their manager Régis Le Bris said “we want fair competition”. What a good idea.

title: Mother rearing addict son’s children alleges threat to ‘burn us out’
description: Family Court Sunday
content:
A woman who took on rearing her adult son’s young children because of their parents’ drug addiction got a protection order against her son after he allegedly threatened to “burn us out”.
Her son and his partner are drug addicts who are “on everything”, and she and her husband have been rearing their children for more than two years now, she told the emergency domestic violence court at Dolphin House in Dublin.
The children are doing much better, the school reports are “great”, and Tusla has told her it has closed the children’s file and is very happy with their progress since they moved in with her, she said.
Her son and his partner live nearby and are constantly coming to her home demanding money for drugs, she said.
Her son is “very abusive”, threatening to do things “like burn us out”, if money is not forthcoming, she said.
In recent days, he smashed a window in her home while she was inside, she said.
His drug abuse has been going on for years, she said.
She has obtained guardianship of the children, but their children’s allowance payments continue to be collected by their mother, she said, adding she is seeking to change that.
Judge Gerard Furlong said he would, “without hesitation”, grant the protection order.
The application was one of several made ex parte (with one side only represented) under the Domestic Violence Act before the judge on Friday. Due to industrial action by public sector workers, two of the five courts in the Dolphin House complex were unable to sit, leading to multiple case adjournments.
Other applications included separate ones by a mother against her adult son and daughter.
The woman said she asked her son, aged in his 30s, to leave her home about two years ago due to conflict between him and her partner. After her partner was assaulted in her home by several people, some of whom were masked, she became ill, she said.
While she was in hospital, her son moved back in without her permission and she asked him to move out because she was returning home and wanted her partner with her, she said.
Her son verbally and physically abused her, including slapping her in the mouth, threatening to cut her throat and “make our lives a living hell”, she said. He called her “horrendous” names and grabbed her house keys and jewellery “while choking me”, and she had soiled herself while this was happening, she said.
Gardaí were called and had advised her to seek protection from the courts, she said.
“I don’t feel safe, I fear for my life and for my partner’s.”
The judge granted an interim barring order against the son.
The woman also got a protection order against her adult daughter, aged in her 40s, over alleged verbal threats made by her after she arrived at her mother’s home to collect her brother’s belongings.
Another woman who recently left her husband got a protection order against him over alleged threatening behaviour.
He drinks alcohol every night and uses cocaine every two days, and his drug use led to him being hospitalised during a previous family holiday abroad, she said.
She was subjected to coercive control for some two years, including him monitoring a home doorbell camera daily and threatening to hit her if she visited her mother and sister, she said.
She left him recently and is living at a confidential address with their young children, but he is threatening to take the children and telling her she will never see them again, she said.
He had threatened to smash the house up and she was obliged to block him “on everything”, she said.
In another application, a woman said she was in a relationship for a time with a man whom she first met a few months ago. She tried to break up with him a few times over the past month, “but he did not let me do it”.
He wanted to come over to her apartment in recent days, but she told him she was not feeling well and not to come. He had arrived anyway and started trying to break in, she said.
She eventually opened the door, and he started fighting with her, and she has bruises as a result, she said.
She wanted “to run away” and took up her laptop and headphones, but he smashed them, she said. Her neighbours called gardaí and, before they arrived, she compelled the man to leave her home.
The man is now blaming her for that and is still calling and texting her, she said.

title: Ireland vs Europe apartment living: ‘When family come over... this is not what they envisioned’
description: Irish people happily living in apartments on the Continent highlight a chasm in building standards, attitudes to communal living and sense of stability
content:
“Y ou can’t raise kids in apartments .” Donal Quinn recalls someone in Ireland telling him this, unaware that his son, along with most of Barcelona’s children, was growing up in such a dwelling.
“I looked at her and said, ‘Actually you can’,” recalls the Co Galway man, whose son is now 12. “World Cup winners: they all probably grew up in apartments,” he adds.
Spain and Ireland are at opposite end of the housing-type spectrums: Spain has the highest proportion of apartment-dwellers in the EU (65.3 per cent), Ireland has the lowest (9.7 per cent), Eurostat Data shows . Across the EU it’s the reality for almost half (48 per cent) of households.
So why are Irish people so out of sync with many of their European counterparts? This question was recently considered in an opinion piece by housing policy analyst Lorcan Sirr, who pointed to how the size, facilities, location and design of Irish apartments are among reasons many prefer houses.
But what’s the experience of Irish people living in apartments in continental Europe? Is resistance simply down to Ireland’s mix of housing stock and poorer-quality apartments, or is there something ingrained deep within us that makes the appeal of our own front door so immovable?
Quinn concedes that a back garden would have been nice for his son to run around when he was about five. But close to their apartment there are enough playgrounds, parks and tree-lined street for any child.
This density of living gives his son increasing freedom, he says: “It’s a short distance to his school, to his grandparents.” It also makes daily life easier, not just regarding Quinn’s short commute. “There’s eight-storey apartments all around here. The density of people brings the density of everything else. So there’s always life ... When you go to the dentist or the doctor, it’s just 100m away.” As the teenage years approach, Quinn believes his son will be much better off here than in one-off housing in rural Ireland where he would have to be driven everywhere.
Like most of his neighbours, Quinn is there for the long term, having lived in the same apartment in Barcelona since moving 17 years ago. Property ownership levels in Spain are broadly similar to Ireland (73 versus 69 per cent).
“There’s much less of a sense that you are on the property ladder. That you’ll move on. So this means you’ve a longer-term relationship with your neighbours,” he says. This helps when dealing with problems like noise, a concern raised by Irish apartment dwellers in studies .
“Barcelona apartments are designed so the sittingrooms are on the street and the bedrooms face each other [in an inner courtyard] at the back,” he says. If a party occasionally gets a bit loud “the cops are quick to turn up if it goes past midnight”.
[ Irish people don’t want to live in ‘mostly awful’ apartments. Here are five ways to fix them Opens in new window ]
Having rented an “extremely dark” apartment in Smithfield, Dublin, before moving to the Catalan capital, having good light is a big factor for Quinn. Most apartments in his area are dual aspect, and his is south facing, getting light all day – though hot in summer, he concedes.
Julie-Ann Wall lived in apartments in Dublin city centre for 10 years before moving to Nice in France for work two decades ago.
“I never knew any of my neighbours [in Dublin] ... They don’t have a lot of communal areas ... In France it’s very different.”
Wall’s experience is that apartment residents are “invested” and building management meetings “can be quite emotional”. In her previous Dublin apartment, “nobody went to the management meetings”.
[ Irish people who live where we holiday abroad: ‘My only regret, I didn’t move sooner’ Opens in new window ]
Wall lives in a large one-bed apartment in a 1960s building with plenty of storage. But the mix of apartment types is key to this sense of community, with three- and four-bedroom apartments accommodating different types of people and families.
“The age groups go from people in their 20s to someone who is almost 100.” The different generations of neighbours in her apartment building all interact. “This gives it a nicer atmosphere.”
“It feels like people are here for the long term rather than seeing it as a temporary home,” she says.
For Wall, the two concierges, who have worked at the block for more than 30 years, are key to this atmosphere. “They just see everything, and know everything that’s going on. So they do a bit of cleaning, co-ordinating plumbers, and so on, and that really makes a big difference.” The concierges in her building also help to “bring everyone together” by organising social events.
When she returns to Co Offaly, Wall encounters people who struggle with the concept of not having “their own front door”. But for her the apartment firmly feels like home.
“Standards are a factor in Irish attitudes,” says Orla Hegarty, assistant professor at UCD’s School of Architecture, Planning and Environmental Policy.
She notes how Ireland has “had this steady deterioration of standards”. Space is one of the key declines in the latest apartment planning guidelines, introduced last year. Allowing a 32sq m studio is the equivalent of “two parking spaces with a bathroom and a wardrobe ... so small you need air conditioning to ventilate it”, says Hegarty.
The guidelines’ provision for fewer balconies and outdoor spaces will have an impact on “ mental health ” and where people actually want to live, says Hegarty. She bemoans the “continuous picking away” at Irish apartment standards.
The change in guidelines also allows for one lift on long corridors with many apartments, Hegarty says. While hotels with long corridors are monitored, in such blocks you won’t know your neighbours and it can feel unsafe if there’s no security, she says.
[ ‘I grew up in an apartment in another country. I bought an apartment in Dublin and had to get out after a year’ Opens in new window ]
She notes how concierges are commonplace in apartments in other countries. They “keep the peace and security” and help to “build community and give people a reason to behave well”. A strong mix of socio-demographics is also important to building community, she says.
Unlike countries such as France, Ireland was slow to purpose-build apartment blocks. Historically in Ireland flats were converted buildings of a poor standard and were seen as a short-term measure, says Hegarty. “We only got going [building apartments] in the 1990s, and apartments in Dublin were generally built to a poor standard – with long corridors, no soundproofing or storage.”
Dublin City Council worked hard to improve standards in the 1990s, with decent balconies and proper storage, she says. After the recession it emerged just how poor many of the Celtic Tiger apartment standards were, she says. The changes in apartment building standards that followed the recession were “really detrimental” and “ill-conceived”, she says.
Damien Lynch lives in a suburb of Frankfurt, Germany where he has raised two (now young adult) children in a three-bedroom apartment.
But returning to visit the semidetached house in Swords, Co Dublin, where he was raised, it’s the noise there that often strikes him. “The amount of noise that travels between the houses is actually unbelievable.” In his apartment block with 250 units, he has “never had a complaint about noise”. “Sometimes my son will have a little party here and the neighbours won’t know because they are so well insulated.”
“It amazes me how well-designed and thought-out it was, though built in 1972.” He notes that his apartment, at 110sq m, is the same size as his parent’s semidetached house. Alongside that it has good-size balcony, a private locked cellar, communal laundry rooms, bike storage and a full time live-in caretaker.
And this density of living means Lynch is just a three-minute walk from the train station, where he can be in the centre of Frankfurt in 20 minutes. He doesn’t mind the lack of a back garden: “We have a green space and playground attached to the complex, and within a few minutes there are three other playgrounds.”
When he bought the apartment first, some in Ireland assumed it was a “starter home”. “There’s definitely a bit of a snobbish attitude in Ireland towards apartment living ... but when family come over and see the size of our apartment, our balcony, the cleanliness of the common areas ... this is not what they envisioned.”
[ What has happened to the cowboys who built defective apartments? Absolutely nothing Opens in new window ]
In Germany almost 60 per cent of people live in apartments and, with strong tenant protections, long-term rental is the norm. More than half of households (53 per cent) are rental (compared with 30 per cent in Ireland).
And this long-term nature of tenancy improves the experience of living there (“we leave keys with our neighbours”) and it means there is no stigma attached to not being in a house, he says.
For Lynch the lower quality of apartments in Ireland reinforces the idea that they are intermediary rather than long-term housing solutions.
Ann McKiernan and her husband got their first taste of apartment living during the Celtic Tiger, albeit in Canada, where they had moved from Ireland. “We looked at each other and said, ‘Oh my God, an apartment, what are we going to do about this?’ But we moved in and we took to it, like a duck to water.”
A quarter of a century later and now retired, McKiernan is a firm convert to the benefits of apartment living. The couple split their time between their apartments near Murcia on Spain’s Costa Cálida and Meath.
In her experience “there is no comparison” between standards in Ireland and Spain. “They have taken a more realistic approach to real long-term living requirements for all types of family sizes. They recognise that apartment dwellers have the same requirements as house dwellers.”
McKiernan’s three-bedroom apartment in the Spanish block, which is full of retirees, has a utility room, a generous livingroom and a large kitchen. It’s close to the sea and amenities, with parks nearby and a roof terrace.
Her biggest concern – noise – turned out to not be an issue. “There seems to be a recognition that this is communal living and we all respect each other.”
Although the couple encountered scepticism when buying an apartment in Meath, having sold a house in Ireland, it made sense for McKiernan: “We didn’t want a garden, or to be locking up a house.”
Her Irish apartment experience is positive, but she puts this down to buying a high-end place in a very small development. “It’s a good way to live if you can get the right management company and the right co-operation between people who live in apartments.”
However, she believes Ireland needs to change in the culture of communal living. Issues such as shared bins: “Things get dumped in all three [organic, recycling, waste] willy-nilly.” Parking can be a source of tension, with drivers “taking anybody’s space”, something she has never encountered in Spain. “We have a lot to learn about the realities of apartment living in Ireland,” she says.

title: Tesco dines out on customers staying in to cook its Finest range
description: Amid cost-of-living pressures, sales of the chain’s premium range are growing fast
content:
The finals of the World Steak Challenge in Amsterdam didn’t escape the eye of Cantillon in recent weeks.
