Two Irish entries made it into the winners’ enclosure, with cuts from the country taking home the prizes for world’s best grass-fed ribeye and sirloin.
The winners were Lidl Ireland and Tesco Ireland. Tesco followed up the steak win by going on to claim 86 prizes at the Blas na hÉireann Irish Food Awards.
The UK supermarket chain, led by Irish man Ken Murphy, has sought out these industry awards as seals of approval for its Finest range as it bids to push premium.
Consumer sentiment and spending data would imply it’s a curious time for the supermarket to be pushing its premium own-label range.
Irish shoppers are well aware they have been forced to suck up sustained increases to their weekly shop in recent years, with their annual bill up about €3,000 since 2021.
Last month, when polling showed cost-of-living pressures dominated voters’ priorities ahead of Budget 2027, the latest figures from Worldpanel by Numerator showed grocery inflation was up 4.3 per cent. If a household was spending €200 a week on groceries, that would add close to €450 to their annual bill.
More recent data this week from the Central Statistics Office showed Irish consumer prices were up 4.1 per cent year on year in September, which was the fastest annual rate of increase since January 2024.
Amid these cost pressures, Tesco has focused on upselling premium. Or downselling dining out, depending on how you look at it.
The company’s recent annual report said the rising cost of dining out has “resulted in a shift towards eating in and a higher demand for restaurant-quality food at home”.
If would-be diners are thinking twice about going out for their steak, they will want something to fill that void. Tesco thinks, why not our steak?
Results by the company this week suggest its bet on premium is paying off. After launching 750 new Finest products in the past year, sales of its premium range were up 12.8 per cent in Ireland.
Tesco chief financial officer Imran Nawaz was buoyed by the Irish numbers. In a call with investors, he singled out the growth in Ireland as an “exceptional performance”. A result to dine out on.

title: Patrick Smyth: France is looking for another de Gaulle. The far-right thinks it could be Jordan Bardella
description: Worldview: The French far-right was not built on admiration for de Gaulle, but on persistent hostility. Now it wants to rewrite history
content:
General Charles de Gaulle , France ’s second World War leader, complained prophetically of his American allies that “One day, the United States will try to be the moral authority of the entire world.”
He had every reason to be fearful. President Franklin D Roosevelt looked down on him as an arrogant fantasist, and barely tolerated his place in the anti-Hitler alliance. He demanded that postwar France be divided up, and effectively become hardly more than a glorified US dependency.
It was not to be, but de Gaulle’s distrust of all things American ran deep, a powerful anti-Atlanticism that divided Nato and drives France’s foreign policy to this day. His legacy still sets the agenda – questioning American reliability, debating strategic autonomy and wondering anew what sovereignty means in an age of military dependence and technological vulnerability.
In French cinemas over the summer, Homer’s epic tale of flawed Greek hero Odysseus vied with the two-part biopic of France’s own Homeric hero, de Gaulle. Based on British historian Julian Jackson’s biography, it had a poor early start but within weeks, 5 million people had flocked to see the film. To those weaned on Hollywood, it appealed as a 1960s-like classic war movie, with a dash of Casablanca’s stirring evocation of heroic subjugated French patriots standing up to the Nazis. Roosevelt does not come out well.
There is a paradox embodied by the hero of Free France. Although omnipresent in public life, plastered on street names, inspirer of the constitution and a role model for the centre and right, de Gaulle rarely featured in films or TV.
As Agnes Poirier writes in the Financial Times, “Like all successful historical films, La Bataille de Gaulle tells us less about the past than about the needs of the present.” Six months out from the presidential election, a deeply divided France is disillusioned by the political mainstream and desperately looking around for another de Gaulle. His uprightness and unflinching man-for-all seasons persona would seem to accommodate all pretenders to his crown. His “ni droite, ni gauche, mais la France” (“neither right nor left, but France”) remains a perfect, meaningless rallying cry.
Step up far-right Rassemblement National (RN). Formerly the Front National (FN), with origins in the collaborationist Vichy regime and nationalist successors that de Gaulle fought so tenaciously, it has tried to co-opt his legacy. The French far-right was not built on admiration for de Gaulle – and for many years displayed persistent hostility to him.
Former leader of the FN, Jean-Marie Le Pen , persuaded a grandson of de Gaulle to run for the party in 1999.
But when in 2012, the party’s number two Florian Philippot laid a wreath at de Gaulle’s grave, its diehards turned on him.
When former president Jacques Chirac – a long-standing Gaullist – controversially went as far in 1995 as admitting a degree of French complicity in the Nazi rounding-up and deportation of Jews, he was confronting a long-standing de Gaulle myth
Le Pen’s daughter Marine , who is leader of the RN group in the National Assembly and topping polls as presidential candidate, has made reclaiming de Gaulle’s legacy the central element of her “de-demonisation” or normalisation campaign.
A poll for La Tribune Dimanche asked voters which political figure best embodies the de Gaulle legacy. Le Pen’s deputy, Jordan Bardella (14 per cent) and Le Pen herself (13 per cent) topped the list.
[ Who is Jordan Bardella, Marine Le Pen’s loyal lieutenant? Opens in new window ]
Le Pen’s strategy has been to invert the accusation. The usurpers of de Gaulle’s legacy are not those who suddenly declare themselves Gaullists, but those who, they claim, have betrayed the legacy they pretend to hold.
When former president Jacques Chirac – a long-standing Gaullist – controversially went as far in 1995 as admitting a degree of French complicity in the Nazi rounding-up and deportation of Jews, he was confronting a long-standing de Gaulle myth. In the interests of preserving postwar unity, de Gaulle denied French guilt on the basis that the Vichy government was illegitimate and could not represent France. France, the general suggested, was in essence a nation of resisters, with few Nazi collaborators.
Chirac’s attempt honestly to face up to deliberate historical forgetfulness was opportunistically attacked by Le Pen and the far-right as an insult to France’s honour. Far-right essayist and presidential candidate Eric Zemmour denounced it as the “death warrant of Gaullism”. Vichy’s inheritors shamelessly demanded the right to his mantle.
[ Marine Le Pen denies French guilt over Holocaust Opens in new window ]
To draw attention to the grotesque rewriting of history that is the hijack of de Gaulle is not entirely to equate RN with its antecedents in the brutal Vichy collaborationist regime. But the party’s determination to whitewash its past speaks volumes about its real nature. The French say “qui s’excuse, s’accuse”: excuses are self-incrimination.
True to form, the party is also currently involved in another shameless whitewashing exercise, implausibly denying allegations that a young Bardella circulated poisonous anti-Semitic Facebook messages. Few will believe him, but will cynical young voters care?

title: How much are we being watched in our everyday lives without realising?
description: How much are we being watched in our everyday lives without realising?
content:
Last week I took a bold step. I disabled my personal location sharing on my iPhone . It hadn’t been available to many people, but switching it off felt like a monumental decision as a tech journalist. I could go where I pleased without anyone knowing my precise location. It was liberating.
That lasted about five minutes. I forgot the car keys have a Bluetooth tag that is used at least three times a week to hunt them down; it is a shared device, though, so even if my own phone is in stealth mode, the network will ping the tag’s location to anyone with access.
That is the trade-off we face every day: we give up elements of our privacy for convenience. I could see my husband’s iPhone location in real time – somewhere over the North Atlantic Ocean on a transatlantic flight – and its battery status (plugged in and charging according to the app). I resisted the urge to remotely send an alert to his phone to amuse myself.
[ Is location tracking the new norm? ‘I can easily see where 80% of the people I know are’ Opens in new window ]
Tracking each other’s precise location isn’t a regular occurrence in our household. We occasionally use it to see if it is a good time to start on dinner if a message goes unanswered, or to remind the other to pick up milk if we see they are on the way home.
But that is only one example. How much are we being watched in our everyday lives without realising? It depends on how many smart devices you use and encounter. Every night, my smart home alarm arms itself automatically. The system is remotely monitored by both the security company and the adults in the house. If a window or door opens after a certain time, a notification pops up. Ditto when the alarm is armed or disarmed. The days of wandering home at 5am and swearing that you crossed the threshold at 2am are gone. If the alarm doesn’t tell on you, the cameras watching you will.
Walk down any Irish street, and you will notice a relatively new addition: the video doorbell. Intended to beef up home security and deter the rise of the “porch pirate”, as they are known in the US , these smart doorbells have become almost expected. The high-tech bell is more often used here to check if a child came home wearing a school jumper or not, and to keep an eye out for the cat. Occasionally, it catches me at 3am on bin day, bleary-eyed and cramming things into an over-stuffed recycling bin. Or plugging in the car to charge because inevitably I’ve forgotten to do it and I am deep in (justified) range anxiety territory. Either way, it is a dead giveaway that I haven’t managed to make it to bed yet.
It is one of the perils of having a smart home. While it offers a certain level of convenience, you can’t do anything without your devices ratting you out. Once, while away at a conference in the US, I texted my husband who was at home in Dublin . “What did you burn for dinner?” The smart smoke alarm had alerted me that there was smoke detected in the hallway, a feature that was intended to give homeowners a heads-up before the alarms start blaring, but was also a handy eye on the house. “Feck off with your smart smoke alarm,” was his entirely appropriate response.
Speaking of the car, even that has its own data connection and app, which allows anyone logged in to see the car’s current location and details of my recent journeys, such as the time and distance, plus the average speed. The maps app I use in the car for sat nav saves my most recent journeys, and whether I got directions or just viewed the location.
[ Humans must always be responsible for AI Opens in new window ]
On my way to the office, I pass a growing number of houses installing security cameras, relatively inexpensive systems made by Amazon , Google , Tapo, Ezviz and others to watch out for our property. When something happens, the footage can be shared with gardaí – or in a local WhatsApp group to help keep the neighbours informed. But it can also be monitored by anyone with access to the account, and our every move is being increasingly documented and, in most cases, uploaded to the cloud.
There are occasionally good reasons to share location data. Among friend groups, we frequently use the live location feature in WhatsApp on nights out to either track each other down to meet or make sure we all get home safely at the end of the night, setting sharing for an hour.
It occasionally backfires, though, causing more anxiety than reassurance. Once, when I made a detour on the way home, one spotted the changed route and immediately thought something catastrophic had happened. It was much less interesting: I was getting milk rather than hitting an ATM to pay a ransom demand.
The taxis I get into often have a dashcam installed too, viewing both inside and outside the car. On those occasions, I immediately become more aware of any conversations happening in the car. More personal cars on the road are also installing the devices, usually for insurance purposes. It has become so commonplace that when a road crash happens, gardaí put out a call for any dashcam footage that may have been captured by passersby.
Not even the family pets are immune. GPS-enabled pet trackers are constantly finding their way into my social media feeds, offering us an easy way to watch where our pets go and how active they are. Our cat has not one, but two trackers – a GPS one made for pets and a Bluetooth AirTag on her collar. She recently went missing for two weeks, and while I’d like to be able to tell you that the trackers played a key role in locating her, she had managed to lose the collar off one – we were waiting on a replacement – and she had slipped the AirTag collar off a few days before she went missing. I could, however, tell you where she lost the AirTag: 3.5 metres behind a high garden wall. I couldn’t hear the alert, but the location tracking on the app led me straight to it.
[ ‘Duo is the most pricey iPhone to date’: reactions to Apple’s foldable phone Opens in new window ]
Apple intended the tags to track items rather than pets or people. But the tags started turning up in the most unlikely of places: in cars, hidden by ex-partners, slipped into the pockets of women in bars or on the street. The company had to introduce more safety features, including a regular chirp if the tag is not connected to the owner’s phone for a few hours. That would alert you to an unknown tracker and allow you to dispose of it, along with a pop-up on your phone. The cat’s collar and tag eventually turned up, much faster than the cat herself.
All that data can add up to a frighteningly accurate picture of your daily life. And in the wrong hands, it can be weaponised.
Things are about to get even more difficult. The rise in popularity of devices such as smart glasses means we are liable to be recorded without our knowledge in places where you previously could have expected privacy. Meta has seen significant backlash for its expensive AI-enabled glasses that can record video, with the only indication they are active being a small LED on the frame. That has led to a growing number of videos where someone wearing the glasses has covertly recorded interactions – usually with women – and posted them online for likes and shares. While Meta has taken action to stop the indicator light from being disabled or otherwise tampered with, and removed some of the videos, that does not mean the problem has gone away.

title: Laura Slattery: Bookshops are lovely places, but they do create this one hazard
description: These repositories of joy, knowledge, respite and armchairs need to be cherished
content:
B ookshops make people happy. I’ve heard books can do this too, but bookshops are a mood improver in their own right, and this may or may not be connected to reading.
A YouGov poll commissioned by the Booksellers Association of the UK and Ireland and reported by The Bookseller attempts to quantify the effect. Nine in 10 people who visited a bookshop in the last six months say it improved their mood in the moment, while almost as many (84 per cent) say it had a positive impact on their overall wellbeing.
That’s all lovely, but it does make me wonder what happened to the one in 10 people whose mood either deteriorated or was resolutely unchanged by the experience. Things can go very wrong in bookshops, and we shouldn’t gloss over the trauma.
You can, for instance, bump into someone you know but whose name you can’t instantaneously remember, obliging you to swerve that particular establishment in perpetuity. You can indulge in a complacent browse of the nonfiction new releases only for a golf umbrella to come flying down the adjacent stairwell, its pointy end missing you by millimetres and giving you a fright you frankly weren’t expecting as you read the blurb on the latest Tom Holland.
You can lumber up one set of steps only to remember that the lone wall guide is down on the ground floor and you have no idea if there’s another flight of cruel steps to climb before you locate the music section. Or you can be delighted that the bookshop has the Mick Herron back-catalogue title you want, only to find its one copy has this tiny dealbreaker of a crease running across the top corner and that’s your day ruined.
I’m not saying these things have happened to me, but I’m not saying they haven’t either. Are bookshops really hellish places in disguise? I think it’s notable that the poll didn’t cover the Christmas-shopping frenzy, when you get the casuals exuding last-minute desperation as they enlist half the available sales assistants in a self-important quest for that book with a blue cover by that woman off that TV show – or was it a green cover?
But the answer is that, no, bookshops are not secret hellmouths masquerading as the home of the latest Barbara Kingsolver or William Boyd. They are places of joy, knowledge, respite and, ideally, armchairs.
The survey found that almost eight in 10 people said they helped them switch off from social media and screen time, while 72 per cent said visiting a bookshop or attending a bookshop event helped them feel better during difficult times.
[ Berlin bookshop’s Kafkaesque trial raises questions over German government Opens in new window ]
I’m fully on board with all of this. Bookshops, by design, are places of possibility, curiosity and vibrant colour, and that’s not down to the array of enticing tote bags. Some books are portals to other worlds, helping us escape our own. Others contain the answers to questions we didn’t even know we had. It should go without saying, but probably doesn’t, that if the Government’s mooted culture card for teenagers ever goes ahead, it should include an element reserved for spending in physical bookshops.
We might even read the books we buy. A previous survey commissioned by the trade body indicates that 93 per cent of people believe bookshops encourage reading. This sounds like too self-evident a truth to be polled, but I think there’s no harm checking.
One crime bookshops have been getting away with for years is their blatant role in incentivising the creation of “TBR” (to-be-read) piles. These hazards start off innocuously enough with just a few books on the bedside table, bookmarks protruding here and there, good intentions hovering in their vicinity.
[ Books about bookshops? That’s escapism to the power of infinity! Opens in new window ]
Soon they mutate into unwieldy towers of failure, becoming the literal manifestation of the gulf between how much of a reader we like to think we are and how much we actually are. They mushroom, taking over entire tables, sofas and rooms, destroying our equilibrium and destabilising our self-identities.
Over time the books in these piles yellow and fade, becoming less appealing as objects and reducing the chances that they will ever be anything other than stubbornly unread.
It’s a dichotomy that has attracted attention in recent years as we increasingly seek explanations for the many ways in which it is possible to disappoint ourselves. The act of reading is about concentration, commitment and empathy. The act of buying books is about acquisition, thrill-seeking and idealism. They are two completely different forms of entrancement.
Still, a little prune, a spot of lending or some strategic blindness to existing TBR piles should do the trick. Because I’m with the Booksellers Association: few pleasures are more potent than simply being in the company of new books. So, once more, with hope and loyalty cards. It’s the weekend, after all.

title: Donald Clarke: Mark E Smith’s bongos rule faces its first serious challenge
description: Grumbling has arisen around a new posthumous album of vocal gurglings from the foreman of The Fall with music added after his death. Which is fairly on-brand
content:
‘If it’s me and your granny on bongos, it’s The Fall,” Mark E Smith once remarked.
To this point nobody has much argued with this classification. Since their formation in 1976, the abrasive postpunk band have gone through something like 66 members, but Smith, foghorn prophet of Greater Manchester, was always to the front, always growling in blank verse. It seems even death could not silence him.
The first serious challenge to the bongos rule comes with the recent release of a new album, titled Post Script, from an artist called The Fall. Mark E Smith, despite dying in 2018, is certainly on it. The gurgling vocalisations, yelled as if from the other side of a wide street, are characteristic of the singer in the last decade of his life. So this is actually The Fall. Right?
It transpires that the album was salvaged from vocals recorded by Smith from 2001 to 2014. Ed Blaney, former band member and tour manager, and Simon “Ding” Archer, sometime bassist for the band, then added musical arrangements to create nine suitably cacophonous new tracks. The two men have experience engineering and producing late Fall records.
“Mark’s life was complicated and Mark was very disorganised when it came to any sort of protection for his legacy,” Pamela Vander, who was in a relationship with Smith for the last three years of his life, is quoted in the Guardian as saying. “I was the manager and I’m not even sure who owns the name ‘The Fall’. It’s a cash grab; just a collection of some shit from the cutting room floor.”
“Is it The Fall?” Archer pondered on Facebook. “Well, I know that when Mark was delivering his vocal takes and directing me in what he wanted, he was being Mark, from The Fall. He was in charge and being The Fall in his demands and expectations.”
[ Mark E Smith: bingo masters, witch trials and totally wired, his genius remembered Opens in new window ]
Never mind the semantics. Was this project worth attempting under any name?
Speaking as a Fall fan of some decades, I would say we are better having it than not having it. Blaney, on guitar and vocals, and Archer, on bass, guitar and keyboards, deliver a cleaner, more conventional rock sound than we encounter in most earlier Fall records. (There are more than 30 of them. So such generalisations are tricky.)
Smith’s diction was never confused with the crisp delivery of Neil Tennant of Pet Shop Boys, but here it is rougher and more swampy than ever. The first single, 30 Degrees, lollops along at the speed of a wonky shopping trolley. Retro Song finds Smith pursued by a wall of sludge metal.
Unsurprisingly, this writer was most drawn to a track titled Irish Northern Man. Beginning as a sinister sludge, it eventually gives into a sort of call and response, the latter part of which has Smith bawling the title to the unlucky heavens. It is utterly mystifying and borderline magnificent.
The record now joins a longish list of recordings released after their creator died and before the work was properly honed. Fully six albums by Tupac Shakur emerged following the rapper’s death. Sketches for My Sweetheart the Drunk by Jeff Buckley, as the title suggests, was fashioned from unfinished work for the singer’s second LP.
Buckley planned to scrap the recordings, made with Tom Verlaine, and, when he drowned in 1997, was contemplating starting again from scratch. Mary Guibert, the singer’s mother, initially objected to Sony’s plans, but she and the record company came to a compromise whereby a double album was released featuring both the Verlaine recordings and later demos. It remains an interesting curio.
Less contentious was the release of what one might generously refer to as The Doors’ final album. Released as late as 1978, while the Sex Pistols were disbanding and Siouxsie and the Banshees were forming, An American Prayer found the living band members playing beneath the late Jim Morrison’s notorious spoken-word recordings.
It received decent reviews at the time, but it now seems like a grand folly: the sort of thing that might have started a punk revolution if one hadn’t just ended.
[ Mark E Smith: passionate, occasionally psychotic high priest of post-punk Opens in new window ]
Some artists care deeply about their legacy. Anderson .Paak, the California rapper, has a tattoo reading “Please don’t release any posthumous albums or songs with my name attached.” Agatha Christie, eerily, wrote the last Poirot and Miss Marple novels – Curtains and Sleeping Murder, respectively – in the early 1940s, with instructions for them to be published after her death (which didn’t arrive for another three decades).
That would never have been Mark E Smith’s way. It seems appropriate that the coda to an extraordinary career would be shrouded in some creative disharmony. Would he have wanted it any other way? Would we? Awkward is an energy.

title: Bono’s daughter Jordan Joy Hewson on music and growing up in Dublin: ‘No one was expecting a record from me’
description: Bono’s eldest child has decided to go into the family business
content:
F or most of her life, Jordan Joy Hewson has navigated the arts world from a side-angle. Photographed at launches and parties with her famous family – she’s the eldest child of U2 singer Bono and his wife Ali , and the sister of actor Eve – Hewson has long been viewed as the business-minded member of the clan, known for her entrepreneurship in the area of social enterprise rather than for her ambitions in the arts.
That’s changing now. In April, Hewson (37), announced on her Instagram page that she was releasing a single under the moniker Jordan Joy: her full name is Jordan Joy Stillwater Iris Hewson. The song Don’t Kill the Vibe – a winsome slice of indie electronica – isn’t a one-off. Earlier this week, Hewson dropped her first EP, LED Moon, a five-track alt-pop affair that is as sleekly made and quietly persuasive as the first single. Praise has come from friends Jessica Alba and Laura Whitmore , with Michael Stipe of REM calling Don’t Kill the Vibe the song of the summer.
Hewson is on a video call from Los Angeles, where she spends a lot of time writing and recording. It’s the week after U2’s 50th birthday bash playing on Dublin’s Grafton Street from the balcony of Bewley’s Cafe (she didn’t make it to Dublin, but says “I FaceTimed in, I was really excited to see them playing together”), and she’s also excited, if tentative, about having a big moment in her own life to mark.
“No one was expecting a record from me,” she says. “I’ve obviously grown up with music around me. But it took going through a rupture in my life and the life I was building to be open to songwriting.”
This time 10 years ago, Hewson was a tech entrepreneur living in New York. She founded a company, Speakable, in 2016, which had a product, Action Button, designed to promote civic engagement by helping people to get involved in movements or causes. She became a name to watch, making it on to Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list for European Social Entrepreneurs in 2019. Then, in 2021, Speakable was acquired in an off-market deal. “My life did a 180,” she says.
When NationBuilder bought the company, Hewson left New York – her home for 11 years – to fly to Dublin, not realising she would have trouble getting back in again because of the pandemic. From living a big city life, she was back in her childhood home in Killiney in south county Dublin, with her parents, Eve and her two younger brothers, Elijah, frontman of the indie band Inhaler, and actor brother John. She had also recently gone through a relationship break-up.
“It was a lot of change,” she says. “Music helped me get through things I was going through personally. Music came and found me.”
Music has saved Hewson’s life before. When Ali and Bono were in hospital waiting to have their first baby in May 1989, Bono – who had brought a portable tape-recorder – decided to try to record his daughter’s heartbeat when still in the womb.
He noticed that her heartbeat was starting to slow, so he told the doctor, who recognised he was right. “I understand tempo,” Bono told the Huffington Post podcast . Hewson was born in a rush, weighing just five pounds, and spent a lot of the first two weeks on her father’s chest as she was nursed to full health.
As a little girl, she and her sister Eve spent long days on tour with U2 with their teddy bears squeezed into backpacks, and a tutor on the road; the pair shared a bedroom until they were 12 and are extremely close.
[ Bono on U2’s first days, 50 years ago: ‘Edge and Larry could play. Adam and myself were bluffing’ Opens in new window ]
Hewson grimaces resignedly – the way any sister might – when I say Eve has called her sibling the A+ student in interviews.
While Eve was prank-calling Justin Timberlake, having spirited the number from her father’s phone book, Jordan was the one carefully crafting English essays and inhaling reading lists. “Yeah, I was nerdy,” she says. “I liked school. I liked reading books and I was good at it. And I really did want to take that seriously.”
At 19, Hewson went to Columbia University in New York to study political science, influenced by her early experiences touring the world. “Growing up with my parents being activists, I was exposed to really serious issues at a very young age. Even in school, we took a trip as a class to Uganda and visited schools over there. I felt inspired by people I’d met. I wanted to figure out if I could be useful.”
There was another draw in her life, however. At Columbia, she was allowed to take classes outside her direct degree. “I took an introduction to poetry class with an insanely good poet called Josh Bell. He became a mentor to me. He was like, ‘What are you doing when you graduate?’ And I was like, ‘Oh I’m going to go and work in communications.’ He was like, ‘Why? We have an MFA programme here and I’d be happy to write you a letter of recommendation.’ I was like, ‘No, it’s cool, I’m going to get a job.’
A year spent working in the non-profit and communications sector changed her mind.
‘I hope that I can put an album together soon. That would be the goal. I’m happiest making music’
“A year in, I was on the phone to him, being like, ‘Can I please get a letter of recommendation? I would love to study this.’ Studying under Tim Donnelly and the late Lucie Brock-Broido, she graduated with a master of fine arts in poetry, publishing work in Boston Review and A Public Space.
It may seem odd to some that Hewson didn’t pick up a pen in those early years to write songs as well as poetry. Did the family business have an inhibiting effect?
“I didn’t think it was possible for me to be an artist,” she says. “The industry looked intimidating. I think you have to really know who you are to be an artist. I was too young ... And it wasn’t a part of myself I was open to.”
Hewson had played piano from a young age, studying with the well-known composer and musician Dawn Kenny. “She was very inspiring to me,” she says. “She taught me a lot by ear and made sure I kept my love of piano going. We still text all the time.”
Hewson also had the virtues that come with a life less ordinary – at a joint birthday celebration for George Clooney at Cafe Habana in Malibu in 2014, Bono and Jordan (father and daughter share a May 10th birthday) sang karaoke, performing the duet Something Stupid. The best-known version had been recorded by Frank Sinatra and his daughter Nancy.
In 2023, with an early, musical project called Tenderhooks, she was trying to find both her sound and her nerve: “With Tenderhooks it was about getting comfortable with the vulnerability of being an artist.”
Her siblings all helped around the recording. “Eve has a lot of experience with putting herself out there. She’s very focused,” she says. “John is very wise and he’ll tell me if something is good or crap. He’s got a great musical sensibility. In the early days, when I was just starting to write songs, Eli [Inhaler’s Elijah] was showing me the ropes. And my cousin Duncan is the person who would help me demo my first songs to send to producers. So there’s a lot of support and interest in the family.”
The gorgeously woozy closing song on the EP came about when Eli accidentally slowed down the title track while attempting to record backing vocals, and Jordan sang over her own pitched-down vocals, with harmonies from her frequent collaborator Jackson Phillips.
Recently, Hewson went back to New York for a photo-shoot. “I had tears in my eyes,” she says. “I realised I was writing about my life in New York, and processing leaving it. But now I live in London and I love it too. A lot of my Irish friends are in London.”
The EP is independently released, suggestive of an artist keen to do things her own way.
Right now, she says, she’s “creativity dating”, finding new collaborators, and doing writing sessions in LA, Norway and London. “When you’re a solo artist you’re constantly meeting collaborators and figuring out whether you work well together. We have live shows coming up as well, so that’s exciting and also,” she laughs, “very scary. I’ve done open-mics and stuff, but no official shows for this project. The first official project will be in the UK in November.”
[ Bono interview: ‘I have spent my life looking for the blessing of father figures’ Opens in new window ]
London may be her home, but she credits growing up in Dublin as being the reason she and her siblings stayed grounded. “It’s been the best blessing for our family that we stayed there. Irish people respected our privacy and let us be kids and make mistakes.”
She admires the new crop of artists coming out of Ireland – Galway band NewDad are on her playlist, she says, and she’s also enjoying LA band Warpaint. She’s currently reading the book I Dream of Joni by Henry Alford, an exploration of the songwriter Joni Mitchell ’s life.
“I hope that I can put an album together soon,” she says. “That would be the goal.” So there’ll be no turning back to tech? “I’m happiest making music,” she says. “This is not a side-project.”

title: A Dún Laoghaire barbershop transformed into a modern home: ‘I used to get my hair cut here as a kid’
description: Securing a vacant home grant was key to this complex renovation of a 19th century commercial premises. Now, after years of work, the owner enjoys a bright, warm and stylish home
content:
F orget about living above the shop. Chartered surveyor Nick Taaffe is living in the shop, having brought a former barbershop in the heart of Dún Laoghaire back to life, through a combination of knowledge, grit and sheer determination.
Where once stood a row of barber chairs, and a line of customers waiting for a short back and sides, now lies a bright and stylish three-bedroom home, with colourful terrazzo tiles on the floor, Crittall-style doors, an oak-crafted staircase and a carefully designed lighting scheme.
But the renovation of Champs was neither quick nor easy.
A construction professional, Taaffe is of a generation that graduated into the financial crisis and resulting recession around 2009.
“It was brutal,” he recalls. He headed to New Zealand around 2015 to work on the post-earthquake rebuild in Christchurch, but it was never a long-term move.
“I left to come back,” he says, remarking upon his return around 2017. He had saved up while away, with a plan to buy a home, and started looking at all different types of buildings around the Dún Laoghaire area, where he is from.
“I always had an ambition to live in the area,” he says.
Then an old barbershop, Champs, came up for sale. “I used to get my hair cut here as a kid,” he recalls.
The property, which dates from the mid-19th century, had residential space above, but was in need of a significant revamp.
“I knew this was going to be the one,” he says. It was late 2019, and a vigorous bidding process ensued, but he came out sale agreed, subject to planning permission, which subsequently came through.
However, that same week the pandemic was called in Ireland. And then the world turned upside down.
The bank decided to pull finance –“this was a risky project even before the pandemic” – and Taaffe was stuck. Should he pull out or look for another source of funds?
“I spent my lockdown walking around a town looking at a ‘sale agreed’ sign that I had no finance for,” he says.
But he was determined to see it through. He eventually got finance once more, and by 2021, he had finally closed the sale and got the keys.
“I was then in ownership of a vacant barbershop in the middle of a pandemic. It was a bit better, but still difficult,” he says. But he was still determined.
“I took the risk that the pandemic would end sooner than I’d run out of cash.”
He focused on undertaking enabling works on the structure, and continued planning the project, getting four planning permissions through, while the pandemic rolled on.
But, as the Covid years drew to a close, another challenge reared its head: inflation. Costs were becoming “intolerable”, putting the viability of the project in doubt.
“I didn’t know how I could get the finance needed to execute it.”
Then, the Society of Chartered Surveyors in Ireland (SCSI) rang him, having heard about his project. They were looking at getting grants for vacant buildings, and asked if he would be involved in the campaign.
While the Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant was subsequently introduced, in July 2022, it was only available up to €50,000. That November it was expanded nationwide, but following the SCSI report published in March 2023, which recommended boosting the grant to address ongoing viability issues, it was increased: to €50,000 to renovate a vacant property, or €70,000 if the property is derelict. Latest figures show that the grant has been used to restore more than 6,300 vacant and derelict homes across Ireland.
“That was my way out of my situation,” says Taaffe, who secured grant approval in September 2023. “The grant saved this project and got me to the finish line. What it allowed was it gave me comfort to understand my own financial risk, and borrow at appropriate level and ultimately execute the project.”
The grant also meant he received input from the vacant homes team at Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown council .
“It’s not just about the grant funding, it’s about the assistance that comes with the fund from the vacant homes grant,” says Taaffe.
Once you get the grant, you then have 13 months to finish it out. But of course the grant is paid at the end of this period, so Taaffe had to finance this part himself, through a mixture of cash and personal loans, before claiming it at the end. But it provided a welcome impetus to the project.
“The site was full of lads, the boot was down and we were flying. The grant allowed me to complete with speed and confidence.”
As chair of the SCSI committee for vacancy and dereliction, Taaffe would like to see the grant extended to developers converting vacant properties into multi-unit developments. The society is due to publish further research on this in the coming weeks.
Then, just as the project was back on track, Taaffe’s father, Tom, died. The loss hit hard, and the project stalled again.
“He was a good guide in my life in general,” says Taaffe. “Grief knocked me, it took my focus and energy from me.”
He eventually got the project back on track to complete it, but it remains a sadness that his dad never got to see the finished project.
But he’s still a part of it. Taaffe took a table from his dad’s old business premises, and got the legs sprayed yellow. And as fate would have it, the charity shop across the road had two chairs in the exact same colour. Now it’s a brightly coloured desk at the front of the house, positioned in front of the oak staircase.
It has been a long process, going from sale agreed in 2019 to completion today, but as well as the impact of Covid, inflation and his father’s death, the project was also undoubtedly complex.
[ Five decision-making strategies to make your renovation less daunting Opens in new window ]
If you could rank vacant properties on a scale of 1-10 in complexity, Taaffe gives his a 10; it’s an infill site; the building dates from the 1850s; it needed a full structural upgrade; and it had no rear access, which meant everything had to come in and out the front door, which opened on to a main street.
To take something like this on, he says you need “knowledge, drive and money”.
“You have to have the drive, and if you don’t have the knowledge you have to buy it. These three ingredients are needed.”
If there is a “secret sauce” to the barbershop project, it’s undoubtedly Taaffe’s professional expertise.
“Finance will only be provided if the bank believes the project is viable and that the purchaser can successfully execute the project,” he says.
But complex or not, Taaffe has achieved a lot with his barbershop renovation, which includes a structural steel and timber frame three-storey extension – a spider crane had to be used to bring in the steel through the front door – and it now has a B2 energy rating.
“I didn’t want it to look too modern, I wanted it to look warm,” he says.
Indeed, despite how narrow it is – at only 3.2m wide – it is very bright, which Taaffe achieved by carefully positioned rooflights – such as those at the top of the stairs and above the living area – as well as a floor-to-ceiling door opening on to the courtyard.
Travelling up through the central core of the building, the staircase “was extremely challenging” says Taaffe – and made more so by his desire to fit three bathrooms within this core.
Storage is considered throughout; the washing machine is hidden behind a sliding door in the downstairs bathroom, while the sink sits on top of the toilet.
His skills as a chartered surveyor are evident everywhere. At the front of the house, for example, he didn’t want to get rid of the original windows, but it was very expensive to replace the glass. So instead, he added new windows to the deeply set window sills, giving an extra layer of insulation, as well as keeping the noise from the street out.
[ Managing your own home renovation? Here’s what you need to know Opens in new window ]
“It’s a really good solution in line with the look of the building and my budget,” Taaffe says.
When quoted a couple of thousand for a black Crittall-style door in between the entrance room and kitchen, he instead opted for some “value engineering” and made the door frame specifically to fit an off-the-shelf door.
Air conditioning is another feature he wanted. “Buildings need to be able to live and breathe at different times of the year,” Taaffe says.
And the tradesmen made a difference to the project. “One of my very good friends was a plumber on the project – I wouldn’t have achieved what I wanted without his expertise,” he says.
As well as the joy of a new home, there’s an added bonus in renovating such properties of being part of the local history of the area. When the barbershop previously featured in Open House, before it was renovated, Taaffe got a request from an elderly lady to visit. It turned out that she had been born in the property, living with her family upstairs, while her father ran the barbershop downstairs.
Now the barbershop sign is back up outside – it came from a vacant building in Athy, as the existing one was broken – and Dún Laoghaire has one more formerly empty unit that has been brought back to life.

title: Author Bonnie Garmus: ‘I’ve gotten so many death threats. The Andrew Tate crowd is alive and well’
description: The best-selling author on surviving a near-death experience, her new novel, and what it’s like to be a ‘global phenomenon’
content:
Eleven years ago, Bonnie Garmus almost drowned in a lake in Switzerland . She was swimming across Lake Zurich, near where she and her family were living, before they moved to London in 2017. She was a strong swimmer, but it was dark, 5.30am, before the ferries had started, and it was foggy, far foggier than she had realised when she set off.
Usually it took her 25 minutes to swim across the lake. But when Garmus glanced at her watch, she realised she had been swimming for 45 minutes. She started to panic. She couldn’t feel her feet, her hands or her face. “The fog was getting much worse. My goggles were fogging up. I kept getting turned around. I kept thinking, ‘any minute I’ll see the lights of the bridge, or I’ll see the lights of something’, and I never did. I began to think I was going to die.”
Then, all of a sudden, she looked up and saw this huge swan, wings flapping, bearing down on the water, “like an enormous duvet cover” or – she feared, thinking death – “an angel”. The swan hustled her in the water, harrying her like a sheep dog, until it was positioned behind her. “It started hurting me and I started to swim, and then it went out in front of me. I decided that maybe it was going to lead me to shore where its babies were. I wasn’t sure – swans don’t like people. But every time I took a stroke, it let me touch its back. About 25 minutes later, I saw the schwimmbad come into view. There was the ladder. The swan had stuck with me the whole way.”
Comfortably ensconced in her London home, wearing a red and white floral top, glasses perched atop her head, Garmus says over a video call that “it was the stupidest mistake I’ve made with my life ever”.
As a story retold, however, it’s the kind of unnerving, fairy-dust-laden anecdote you could only imagine coming from the author of Lessons in Chemistry, a global bestseller that features a dog, Six-Thirty, who has learned nearly 1,000 words and helps Elizabeth Zott, the novel’s brilliant chemist turned TV chef, to the point where he even teaches words to her unborn child.
Surprising, endearing, joyful, heartbreaking and strongly feminist, Lessons in Chemistry took everyone by surprise when it was published in 2022, not least Garmus herself.
Until that point, Garmus was a copywriter coming up to retirement age. Lessons in Chemistry changed everything. Garmus wrote the first chapter after a meeting in which her voice went unheard by her male counterparts. Elizabeth, her lead character, was a woman in 1950s California who triumphed against the patriarchy; against convention and against that chorus of put-down voices.
The book was adapted into a successful Apple+ series starring Brie Larson . It inspired women around the world. And it made Garmus into a kind of flash point – a hero to some, a target to others.
“A lot of people assume it must be fun to have a bestseller, but I can’t tell you, I’ve gotten so many death threats over Lessons in Chemistry,” she says. “It was really hard to take. It’s ongoing.” Why? “A woman chemist? The Andrew Tate crowd is alive and well. They contact me through my website or send DMs. And I’m not the only one. Women novelists especially go through this.
[ Lessons in Chemistry: An alchemy of dry wit, sharp satire and original premise Opens in new window ]
“When I get attacked like that for being female, I just think, they clearly don’t know their chemistry, because if they did know their chemistry, they would understand what women are made of,” she says.
For every horrible message Garmus has received, she has received another from a woman who tells her how much the book has helped them. She is a firm believer in helping people believe in themselves. “I don’t think anyone with a dream is ridiculous,” she says. “Everything that you do, if you don’t take action on it, then it won’t get done. But all it really requires is a thick skin and perseverance.”
“What I love about that book is how it’s inspired people to say, ‘It’s not over for me yet’. Since Lessons in Chemistry came out, I have seen a whole mass of women who decided in their 40s and 50s to go to med school, and they did, and they’re doctors. To get [those] emails and DMs from people, I didn’t see that coming.”
The youngest of four girls, Garmus didn’t come from a wealthy background. Raised in California (she has also lived in Seattle and Geneva), her mother was a nurse in the 1980s, during the Aids crisis, and her father was an entomologist. She grew up wanting to write, but understanding she needed to make a living. “Fiction is terrible in terms of making a living.”
She did a three-month writing course at Curtis Brown, but it was her career in copywriting, she says, that turned her into a successful novelist. “We are always pretending we know and we have to do enormous research to come up to speed, like I did with chemistry,” she says. “You get to learn and it’s this gift that you get on the job. I didn’t always love what I learned, but it keeps you curious, it keeps you alive.”
Garmus’s new novel, Peck & Peck, takes her into uncharted waters once more. Set around the offices of Peck & Peck, a prestigious poetry quarterly in New York in the 1980s, it’s a whimsical, lovingly crafted and frequently very funny story of Batter, a college graduate named after a dog (a heroic dog naturally), whose dream is to become an editor at the poetry house.
Batter has an ear – he naturally knows that “an anapaest is a metrical foot consisting of two unstressed syllables followed by one stressed syllable, which, when written as a tetrameter, makes the sound of galloping hooves”. But that doesn’t make him savvy in all areas of his life. As he bumbles into unfolding chaos in the senior ranks at Peck & Peck, he must try to score a promotion, appease his parents and improve his romantic prospects.
For the new novel, Garmus realised she needed to investigate the world of poetry. “I am not a huge poetry person. I went into it kicking and screaming, thinking, ‘I’m not sure this should be my centre point, but when I started researching it – it took six or eight months of intensive study – I realised, first of all, how little I knew of this art form. Second of all, how stunning it is. It’s like buried treasure. For one of the most overlooked, underloved art forms, it packs one of the strongest punches you can find in the art world.”
[ The best new books to look out for in autumn 2026 Opens in new window ]
Surprisingly, for a novel that is so consumed with poetry, there is very little poetry in the book. “I had a poem from Seamus Heaney in the book and I had trouble getting permission for it, so I had to take it out,” she says ruefully. “I didn’t realise this about poetry, but if you use one line you have to get permission for it. I’m a huge fan of his. It really hurt to take his [poem] out. I also had to take out Carl Sandburg and [Charles] Bukowski, it was a nightmare.”
Instead, the novel is peppered with references to poems, from Adrienne Rich’s Diving into the Wreck to TS Eliot’s The Love Song of J Alfred Prufock. There are also contemplations about the life of a poet (“The words, ‘I made a killing in poetry’, have never been uttered,” reflects Batter), and literary jokes: the slightly woo-woo WB Yeats is on a list of poets who must always receive an automatic rejection letter from Peck & Peck.
Garmus keeps the tone uplifting and warm. “I want the books to be perceived as serious but fun,” she says. “In Lessons in Chemistry, I’m talking about misogyny. In Peck & Peck, I’m talking about conformity. I want to talk about serious topics but put some fun around it. I think it’s imperative that we keep our sense of humour. It’s sometimes the only way people will connect.”
She’s talking about fiction, but she might as well be referring to the vogue for carefully skirting the fraught subject of US politics. Garmus has amassed considerable wealth since the publication of Lessons in Chemistry (to the extent that her two adult daughters changed her name in their phones from “Mum” to “global phenomenon”). She gives much of it to charities that kick against the Trump regime – Pen in the US (against book banning), Planned Parenthood (for safe and available abortions ) and “anything to preserve and help children’s lives around the world”.
[ Benjamin Alire Sáenz: '‘As a former Catholic priest, I understood what it meant to have a calling to poetry’ Opens in new window ]
Money hasn’t changed her, except to give her more latitude to be exactly as she is: low-key and low-maintenance. She gleefully recounts the story of a time on stage during a US book tour when she put her hand into her jacket pocket, the pocket ripped and her keys fell out on to the stage. “The moderator said: ‘Can’t we afford a new jacket?’,” she recalls with a laugh. “I wore my [male] publicist’s jacket after that. We didn’t have time to go shopping.”
Generous with her time, Garmus is surprisingly candid for a global phenomenon. Of the Lessons in Chemistry adaptation, she doesn’t mince her words. “I got advice after I’d sold the book from some very famous authors. They reached out and said, ‘Okay, so now Hollywood has your book. So here’s what you do: you run the other way, you never turn around, you never look back.’ And of course I did turn around and I did look back, and that causes problems.’”
What did she struggle with? “Oh like, they’re missing Six-Thirty or the rowing is completely wrong – that’s not how you erg. The tone was a little different. But I’m lucky to have it made. I’m grateful.”
When it came time for her to write her second book, she says, there were publishing types who had a rinse-and-repeat version of Lessons in Chemistry on their vision board. She didn’t care. “With age, you already know what you’ve survived,” she says. “The fact that people want this win or that win, they want a very certain kind of story. That has no impact on me at all. I’m sure some of these people wish it did. I think they wanted me to write the sequel to Lessons in Chemistry and I said, ‘No, I’m writing something new’.”
She smiles, and you can hear the spirit of Elizabeth Zott in her words. “I’m a copywriter. We never write the same thing twice.”
[ Poem of the Week: Towards Rapture by Charlotte Buckley Opens in new window ]
Peck & Peck is published by Manilla Press on October 13th

title: ‘I love the evening primrose in my garden. But will it become invasive?’
description: ‘I assume must have self-seeded as I never planted it’
content:
The plant growing in your garden is most likely the large-flowered evening primrose, or Oenothera glazioviana, a striking, non-native, sun-loving, hardy biennial hybrid species that has a habit of popping up in newly established gardens unannounced, especially in coastal parts of the country where the soil is sandy/stony and free-draining. It flowers in its second year, producing 1.5m-2m tall, long-lasting spikes of acid yellow flowers from July to October that are loved by pollinating insects, especially moths and butterflies. Garden birds, especially finches, like to feed on the seeds in late summer and autumn. Evening primrose oil, which is extracted from the seeds, also has a long history of traditional use in the treatment of a variety of ailments from multiple sclerosis to PMT.
While its origins remain cloudy, it seems likely that the large-flowered evening primrose originally arose in Europe in the 1800s and was then cultivated as a decorative garden plant. Its common name comes from the fact that the yellow flowers open quite late in the day.
Despite your husband’s fears that it will become invasive, I think this is unlikely. Instead, evening primrose typically behaves in Irish gardens as what’s known as a pioneering, nonpersistent colonising species that can often appear in large numbers in the early years of a garden but then gradually disappears as other plants take over. As such, it’s included in Invasive Species Ireland’s Amber List ( invasivespeciesireland.com ) and is considered relatively low risk in terms of its potential negative impact on native biodiversity .
The large-flowered evening primrose spreads mainly by seed, which it produces in great profusion, so if you do decide to minimise its presence in your garden, make sure to deadhead the faded flowers quickly before the seed pods have a chance to properly ripen and spill. Look out also for its overwintering low rosettes of foliage, which form in the first year prior to the plant flowering in its second year, and use a sharp trowel or garden spade to dig up any that you don’t want, making sure to remove the deep tap roots to prevent them from reshooting from the base.

title: Bordeaux basics: four red wines that epitomise this classic region
description: I had expected to find a huge range of inexpensive Bordeaux when I looked in Irish supermarkets, but no
content:
In the 1980s, 75 per cent of the wine we consumed was French. Much of the remainder was sweet German Liebfraumilch and Rioja from Spain. And sherry. White wines were almost exclusively from the Loire (Muscadet and Sancerre) and Burgundy (Chablis and Mâcon). The favoured red wines were Beaujolais, Burgundy and – the most popular of all – Bordeaux.
Many of the supermarkets didn’t sell wine at this stage and there were few wine shops, so most wine was sold through off-licences. Their shelves were generally lined with inexpensive red Bordeaux. Some had the grand title of Château, technically a castle or great house although the reality was usually a modest farmhouse.
I have always retained an affection for inexpensive Bordeaux. They are light- to medium-bodied with just-ripe dark fruits and a gently tannic kick on the dry finish. On their own they can seem a little austere, but with food they come into their own. Roast lamb would be one of the local favourites, but any red or white meat, game or firm cheese will do nicely.
Bordeaux is going through something of a crisis. Production increased in the 1990s and the first decade of this century, saturating the market. This left producers unable to sell their wine. Since then the French government has been paying vignerons to pull up their vines. I had expected to find a huge range of inexpensive Bordeaux in all our big retailers when I looked recently but didn’t. I did, however, come across four wines that epitomise red Bordeaux at very good prices.
This is the fourth vintage of this wine I have covered. It offers great value; light, fresh clean redcurrant and plum fruits with dried herbs.
This was quite delicious; classic Bordeaux flavours of blackcurrants and plums with light tannins. Very Bordeaux, very drinkable and fantastic value.
From Whelehans, Loughlinstown, Dublin 18, Whelehans.ie
Medium-bodied with fine raspberry and red cherry fruits, a touch of spice and gentle tannins.
From Wines Direct, Mullingar and Athlone, Co Westmeath, Winesdirect.ie
Another lovely classic Bordeaux. Medium-bodied with sleek ripe dark fruits, a touch of oak and a smooth finish.

title: Fiction in translation: from inner conflict in Ukraine to a Norwegian descent into madness
description: Books by Valerian Pidmohylnyi, Sevgi Soysal, Olga Tokarczuk, Hernán Ronsino, Glenn Bech and Thure Erik Lund
content:
We have no choice about the elements that constitute our past. The family we are born into and the place of our birth embed an inescapable aspect of our identity. If we are born in a small village, will the city promise possibilities to a hidden self? Or will the city’s indifference blend with self-doubt to reinstate the reassurance of home?
Such questions play out in a wholly convincing way in The City (Harvard Library of Ukrainian Literature) by Valerian Pidmohylnyi, translated by Maxim Tarnawsky from the Ukrainian, a novel first published in 1928.
When Stepan Radchenko, the central character, travelled by boat from his birthplace to Kyiv, “he felt an indistinct agitation and dizziness, as if in his own village and in all those he had seen he had left not only the past, but his faith in the future as well”. Wavering indecisiveness will characterise much of what we see of Stepan, in his self-evaluation and in his fraught relationships with women, beginning with Nadika, a woman from his home village, to whom he declares his sincere love but ultimately treats appallingly.
His ambition to be a writer is another source of inner conflict, and it adds to an absorbing portrayal of a flawed, diffident individual. The writing is clear-cut and linear, but allows for the contrast between high-minded reflections and base actions. The epoch in which Pidmohylnyi lived, dominated by Stalin’s paranoia, led to his premature death when he was executed in 1937 for counter-revolutionary activity, at the age of 36.
Although considered a modernist novel, The City lacks the metropolitan disorientation of Andrei Bely’s Petersburg, which represents urban experience so effectively, as does Walking (Archipelago Books) by Sevgi Soysal, translated from the Turkish by Maureen Freely.
A scattered, impressionistic opening gives us glimpses of lives and atmospheric recognitions of the past, without centring any particular characters. We meet schoolchildren, experiencing the mixture of fun, cruelty and discovery that characterises childhood, and we continue to encounter some of these characters as they progress through the caprices of adult life.
But Soysal’s style is deliberately disruptive, with no setting up of characters or contexts, little sense of continuity and, most surprisingly, paragraphs about animals. But once the reader acclimatises to the jump-cuts and time-shifts, this becomes an exhilarating portrayal of human lives in a Turkish city, encompassing their wishes, desires, secrets, envies and emptiness. Soysal trusts the reader, and we trust her.
Those who wish to escape the elbowing bustle of cities might welcome time spent in the village that is pivotal to Primeval and Other Times (Fitzcarraldo Editions) by Olga Tokarczuk, translated from the Polish by Antonia Lloyd-Jones, a novel originally published in 1996.
But as the narrator states at the start of the novel, “Primeval is the place at the centre of the universe”, bringing to mind John Burroughs’s great observation in Studies in Nature and Literature: “Do not despise your own place and hour. Every place is under the stars, every place is the centre of the world.”
While the novel begins about 100 years ago, there is a medieval feeling to the way Primeval life is lived through resolute nature in those early timeless “times” (each chapter being titled “The Time of…”); finite lives lived through eternal rhythms. But as we become familiar with the traits of several bewitchingly realised characters, we recognise how much must change as we follow them through the unforgiving 20th century.
Elements of Tokarczuk’s writing that recur in her later work are present here: the spiritual dimension of an affinity with nature, particularly as experienced by women, and the formalisation of that pagan spirituality through religion. The universality of history presses against the village of Primeval, and its people, and Tokarczuk illuminates both in the 60 episodes that comprise this powerful early novel.
There is a less successful attempt to achieve a resonant significance in Hudson (Charco Press, 214pp, £11.99) by the Argentinian writer Hernán Ronsino, translated from the Spanish by Mallory Craig-Kuhn. The novel opens strongly with a pianist, Juán Sebastián Lebonté, about to go on stage, told that his father has died. He decides to play: “I want to carry on ... so the keys become a precise point of pain”.
The musical term “fugue” brings to mind his father’s obsession with a pianist called Bill Turner. Instead of returning for the funeral, he wanders around Ostende, Belgium, meets a woman called Anne and tells her a story that will recur throughout the novel about the time he visited Ostende in Argentina with his father.
That Anne’s presence serves little purpose presages a problem that will become acute later. Bill Turner’s rare and elusive record, Hudson, together with Turner’s reclusive nature, impelled Lebonté’s father to firmly persuade his young son to take up the piano. When his property developer father passed away, he left his son a property that he discovers is occupied by a community of drifters and political radicals.
Much is thrown into the novel at this stage, but an accumulation of secondary characters pushes the novel further from the revelatory transformation this material needs. In a book so concerned with music, this novel is a chord that is never resolved.
By contrast, The Fathership (Prototype, 544pp, £14.99) by Glenn Bech, translated from the Danish by Hazel Evans, takes many risks with style, format and narrative perspective and makes every one of them reverberate.
One device used throughout the novel is to isolate a short, single sentence alone on a page. Thus, the opening page, containing only these words, could hardly be starker: “With your suicide you killed the child I’d just been.” This is addressed to the author’s father, who “had told Mum he was off for a round of billiards that evening, but instead went to the woods, where he killed himself.”
As suits the desperately sad subject matter, the narrative is fractured, self-inquisitive and discombobulated (though not for the reader). The narrator’s mother and brother fulfil roles as foils and targets for frustration, though neither brings forth the anger induced by the violent drunkard stepfather he is subsequently forced to live with.
The details are grim, but the way the author conveys the intensity of his emotions and the irresolvable questions makes this one of the most impressive novels of recent years. There are white pages and black pages; capital letters and italics; a play-script used to recount a holiday; pages with a single dot to represent the inexpressible; a testimony from his mother in which, knowing that the author is writing about her, she is allowed to give her perspective; there is pathos and the darkest of humour.
This is also a remarkable work of translation by Evans, given the demands of the text’s many shifts of tonal register, narrative delivery and linguistic invention. By the conclusion, the author’s searingly poignant seven last words have been earned.
Another convincing narrative voice commands The Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch (And Other Stories, 302pp, £14.99) by Thure Erik Lund, translated from the Norwegian by David M Smith. However, after 300 unbroken pages of monomaniacal rambling, one might be forgiven for finding the voice of this contradictory, bifurcated man too convincing and relishing the blessed silence that finally descends.
Yet, it’s a book with many distinctive qualities. The lone narrator, Thomas Olsen Myrbråten, begins by defining and defending his status as a “life-of-the-mind-individual”, one of those who “never do anything superfluous”. To begin he is an ascetic, railing against a materialistic Norwegian society in a Thomas Bernhard-like screed that is by turns convincing and alarming.
Proclaiming these reproachful opinions in a “thought piece” for the Norwegian Ministry of Culture precipitates an immediate change of circumstance. His move from Oslo to the countryside with “ol’ Helena”, a fellow alcoholic, hastens a rapid decline that will see him move through stages of degradation while indulging his peculiar and disturbing sexual proclivity, but also initiates a further fracture, caught as he is between embodying the natural world and his awareness of the inescapability of the technological, ever-watching world.
As he descends into madness and the earth, he remains, inescapably, at the centre of the world.

title: Do you get Botox or fillers? Share your experience
description: Have you noticed a societal shift in attitudes towards ‘anti-ageing’ tweakments like Botox?
content:
The Irish Times is working on a feature about the rise in Botox and filler injections in Ireland, and we would like to hear from readers about their views and experiences, whether they have had such aesthetic treatments or not.
If you get Botox or filler regularly, what motivates you? How much do you spend? What are the benefits, and are there any drawbacks? If you’ve had these treatments in the past but stopped, why? Have you strong views against them? Have you noticed a general societal shift in attitudes towards ageing and “anti-ageing” tweakments like Botox?
We’d also be interested in hearing from professionals who administer the injections (or who have decided not to).

If you would prefer to remain anonymous in any published articles, please indicate this in your submission. We will not publish your story without first contacting you.

title: Role of women, married priests and sexuality featured early in the synodal pathway
description: Rite & Reason: Not everything we heard in those early conversations has travelled through the process in the same way
content:
F ive years ago, the Irish Synodal Pathway began with a question: “What does God want from the church in Ireland at this time?” Since then, thousands of people have participated in conversations in parishes, dioceses, movements and communities across the island. Some spoke with hope, others from experiences of hurt, distance or frustration. All of these voices belong within the story of the pathway.
Next Saturday, October 17th, delegates will gather in Gormanston, Co Meath , for the National Synodal Assembly, bringing the pathway to a close.
While the recommendations that emerge matter enormously, these five years have given us something that reaches beyond the outcomes of any single gathering. We have learned that, as the people of God, we can discern together. We listened, brought contributions into synthesis, experienced the circularity of dialogue between the local and universal Church, and through conversation in the Spirit learned to listen for what the Holy Spirit might be saying in and through one another.
The National Synthesis of 2022 was part of this development within the Universal Synod and Towards October 2024 helped us to receive what was emerging from that process. Further discernment found expression in Baptised and Sent, with seven priorities entrusted to working groups for deeper reflection. Their work was then received by the national synodal team as part of the continuing process that shaped the five pathways and 35 proposals presented in the document: “Is not this what God asks of you?”
Read together, all the documents – available on www.synod.ie – trace a five-year process since 2021 of listening. What emerged was received, tested, deepened and returned to the people of God. These documents show that we have been learning how to become a discerning, synodal Church. Discernment does not promise that everything expressed at the beginning will emerge as a recommendation at the end. Not everything we heard in those early conversations has travelled through the process in the same way.
Questions concerning the role and ministry of women, including priestly ordination, healing, married clergy, sexuality, governance and belonging featured strongly in the early listening. Some remain, while others are not among the proposals before the assembly.
That is part of the nature of discernment – it is not like a parliamentary process in which the largest number or loudest voice carries the day. We are learning how to remain in communion while taking seriously questions which provoke pain, disagreement and sometimes impatience with the pace of change.
What we have heard remains part of this journey and will continue to shape the questions we carry forward. This way of proceeding is rooted in Baptism. We often say: “I was baptised.” But Baptism is a living reality. From this flows our equal dignity and shared responsibility for the Church’s life and mission. Synodality gives practical expression to that baptismal identity by asking us to recognise one another’s gifts and to share responsibility for mission.
[ Should I start a message with ‘I hope you’re well’? If not well, should I say so? Opens in new window ]
This is why the five pathways in the working document are more than a framework for the proposals attached to them. Their value does not depend on the fate of individual proposals. Together they express a vision of a Church that proclaims the Gospel, is a community of belonging, is a place of healing, accompanies people and empowers for ministry and co-responsibility.
At the National Synodal Assembly on October 17th, individual proposals may be recommended, require further discernment, or not be recommended, but the pathways can continue to generate new possibilities for how this vision might be lived.
[ Paternity leave shouldn’t be a privilege only the likes of Simon Harris can afford Opens in new window ]
In that sense, the assembly is not only about what we decide, but about our growing capacity to discern how this vision can be lived. To gather as the pobal Dé, discern, pray, listen and deliberate together, and then make recommendations for the Church in Ireland tells us something important. We can do this and because we have learned how, we can do it again.
Here the greater challenge begins. It is one thing to talk and learn about synodality through a five-year national process. It is another to make it ordinary.
Can this way of listening and discerning shape parish pastoral councils and diocesan decisions? Can those who have been wounded not simply be spoken about, but genuinely help shape our conversation? Can we implement what we discern, evaluate it, listen again and change course when necessary?
Structural reform and spiritual renewal must accompany one another.
While the Irish Synodal Pathway will come to an end on October 17th, the journey of becoming a synodal Church will continue for everyone.
Julieann Moran is the General Secretary of the Irish Synodal Pathway

title: Leinster live up to the occasion of long-awaited homecoming to blow Cardiff away
description: Sam Prendergast in fine form with man-of-the-match display at redeveloped Laya Arena
content:
The Laya Arena looked resplendent and there was enough in a satisfactory bonus-point win at their refurbished home to send the 20,035 crowd into the night content.
But there was also enough rustiness and clunkiness in the performance, not least in a near 40-minute spell without a score, to leave head coach Leo Cullen with plenty to work on.
Perhaps the slight sense of an anticlimax was unfairly heightened by Leinster having set the bar so high in the first quarter, by far their best period in the game. There was purpose aplenty in their carries and recycling, with Sam Prendergast looking fit and strong as he glided over the turf, producing some typically sublime touches in a man-of-the-match performance.
Yet there were also times when Leinster’s attack became narrow and pedestrian, and it was a mite discomfiting that Cardiff were able to outflank the defence so readily with bridge passes, albeit Leinster restricted their lively attack to one off-the-cuff try from a quick penalty.
Mindful of facing Clermont, who will have played six games when they meet at the Stade Marcel Michelin next Saturday, Cullen gave his returning frontliners long shifts, with Jack Conan going for over an hour and Dan Sheehan for more than 70 minutes. Joe McCarthy finished at blindside flanker, while James Ryan lasted the full 80 on his return.
Leinster’s grand and overdue homecoming was blessed with a still autumnal night in D4. With its spacious surrounds, there was almost a carnival-like atmosphere surrounding the ground in the build-up.
The sense of anticipation must have been acute among the home team, and despite nine of their starters making their seasonal bows, the hosts were razor-sharp out of the blocks.
Prendergast’s every involvement seemed to attract additional approval and, in tandem with Joe McCarthy and Jack Conan, they executed a choke tackle on Harri Millard. Deft work up the blindside from inside halfway thanks to Conan’s quick hands released Jimmy O’Brien, who exchanged passes with Prendergast before Oliver Coffey arrived in support, but his offload inside was just too low for his outhalf to gather.
There was an inevitability about the opening try. Tadhg Furlong passed out the back for Prendergast, and Dan Sheehan provided the link for Hugo Keenan to chip, left-footed, over the last defender perfectly and gather just short of the tryline.
A scrum penalty to the corner led to Aled Davies being binned for playing the ball as the second man, and Leinster utilised their numerical advantage with a simple blindside move for O’Brien to score in the corner.
Leinster’s ambition to work turnover ball into the edge – something they had sought to harness last season – was a striking feature of the game, and when McCarthy popped a Cardiff knock-on up to Furlong, the tighthead looped a long pass to Prendergast.
The outhalf eyed up a frontrower and sped around before releasing O’Brien. Though he was tackled short, Conan took a sharp out-in line to score from Max Deegan’s transfer off the recycle.
The one blemish of Prendergast’s game was over the kicking tee, missing his opening three conversion attempts.
Hunting for a bonus-point try, Leinster lost their way for a spell and were caught unaware when Callum Sheedy quick-wittedly crosskicked a penalty for Mason Grady to gather and score.
Taine Basham, a late call-up in place of Taulupe Faletau, beat Scott Penny off the base of a scrum and Le Roux Malan would have outflanked the Leinster defence to release Jacob Beetham but his pass was forward.
From there, Leinster rediscovered their mojo to secure the bonus point before half-time. A phased attack wore down the Cardiff defence, Coffey and Garry Ringrose combining to hit Prendergast, who was again the instigator-in-chief, beating Beetham on his inside and dummying Matty Young to give O’Brien another clear run-in to the corner. This time, the 23-year-old landed the conversion for a 22-5 interval lead.
A low-key third quarter becalmed the home crowd, save for some defensive sets, as Cardiff’s replacement halves, Johan Mulder and Jarrod Evans, injected some tempo. After Coffey’s covering tackle on Mulder denied one try, Malan hit Beetham on the edge with a bridge pass, but Keenan’s tackle and Prendergast’s counter-ruck kept Cardiff out.
But the occasion and crowd demanded a late flourish from Leinster. And they provided when Robbie Henshaw injected some urgency into another phased attack and Ringrose dummied to make big inroads.
A few phases later, Prendergast took Ringrose’s pullback to dummy a defender and deftly hung a popped pass into space for Jamie Osborne to gather and spin out of a tackle to score adroitly over his right shoulder while landing on his back, leaving Prendergast to slot the conversion for the full-time score.
