title: ‘We’re playing matches like they’re training sessions’: Richie Murphy frustrated by Ulster’s lack of intensity
description: Head coach urges consistency after Ulster fight back for second week running
content:
Ulster head coach Richie Murphy didn’t seek refuge or solace in his side’s recovery against Munster , rejecting the notion of having mixed emotions after the 26-26 draw in Belfast.
“Bitterly disappointed to tell you the truth, not mixed emotions,” he said after the game.
Trailing 26-5 at the interval, the draw was a decent riposte under the circumstances, but Murphy wasn’t looking for consolation.
[ Ulster overcome slow start to claw back draw against Munster Opens in new window ]
“We’re disappointed with our start, we’re disappointed with how we’ve gone about our business. A 17-5 penalty count is astronomical. It didn’t feel like that, I didn’t feel like it should have been that. That’s on us.
“The biggest part of our game that we need to improve on, there’s obviously things in defence that we need to get better on. We want to be the team that plays, and people think that we’re entertaining, but everyone talks about how inconsistent we are. We need to find some consistency in our performances. If we do that, we’ll be a really good team.”
On his side’s slow start, he added: “We allowed Munster to set the tempo. We were inaccurate with our first launch and on the back of that penalty, you’re back in your corner, fighting for your life.
“You can see that once you’re five metres out and the opposition have a lineout, it’s very hard to stop, so that gave them control of that first half.”
While the hosts reacted well after some half-time changes, Murphy said they were still inaccurate after the break and “didn’t look after the ball well enough”.
“We didn’t control field position at all in the game. But ultimately we got ourselves into a situation where, in the last play of the game, we were running at them, and we gave them the ball back again. So, our turnover rate needs to come down.”
The Ulster pack also came under significant pressure, with Murphy acknowledging that while their scrum had been going well, “[it] took a backward step tonight”.
“I feel like we just didn’t really attack the game like we needed to,” he added. “At the moment, we’re playing matches like they’re training sessions.
“We need to start applying some more pressure to the opposition, and that’s going to be a key part that we need to learn from this week.”
For Munster head coach Clayton McMillan , it was a victory that they let slip away.
“[We] talked about it at half-time that Ulster are a quality side that won’t go away,” he said. “We needed to continue to be accurate and just apply pressure in the right parts of the field. But we didn’t quite get the same quality of possession in the second half, and Ulster were good enough to find a way back into the game.”
He pointed to the late changes, losing Shane Daly, Tom Ahern and Diarmuid Barron, but added: “We had a lot of young guys out there at the back end of the game, and they would have learned a huge amount from the last 10 or 15 minutes, which will put us in good stead later on.
“But we don’t have any excuses. We just weren’t as tidy, and we didn’t apply the same amount of pressure in the right areas that we did in the first half and paid a price.
“But take nothing away from [Ulster]. They found a way, and that’s the way it rolls.”

title: Solanke strikes late as 10-man Spurs salvage point at Manchester United
description: Rodrigo Bentancur sent off for Luke Shaw challenge
content:
After 72 laboured minutes, this match was lit up by a moment of quality. Matheus Cunha was fed by Luke Shaw down the left and the Brazilian crossed to Bryan Mbeumo, who spun and finished for Manchester United .
It drew delirious chants of “you’re going down with the City” with Spurs , at that stage, rock bottom of the Premier League and Manchester City’s long-term future in the division in question.
Uglier scenes followed for Spurs when Shaw chased Bruno Fernandes ball, leading Rodrigo Bentancur to launch a scissor challenge that, if it had connected with the left-back, might have caused serious injury.
An incensed Shaw, surely reminded of his horrific double-leg break sustained 11 years ago at PSV, hared after Bentancur and shoved him over. Up came the midfielder to push his head into Shaw’s, who went down as a melee ensued.
Stuart Attwell sent Bentancur off, and the referee issued yellow cards to Shaw – lucky to escape a red, too, for the push – and Jan Paul van Hecke.
All of this followed what had been a near snoozefest in which Spurs could not finish and United were disjointed: the tale, in microcosm, of their seasons.
There was more, though, as Tottenham registered an added-time equaliser and only their third league goal this season. Senne Lammens and Lisandro Martínez were United’s culprits as Sandro Tonali’s floated cross from the left should have been cleared by the Argentinian but, instead, Dominic Solanke outfought him and headed past Lammens, who watched it go in.
While averting a fourth defeat, Spurs still remain winless after their opening six league games for only a fourth time. This draw means there is no clear answer to the pregame question of which manager is under more pressure, as both Roberto De Zerbi and Michael Carrick remain in need of a victory.
When the Italian scans the table, he will see his beleaguered side off the bottom but still in the relegation zone, while Carrick’s United remain in 12th and with a solitary victory.
De Zerbi now takes his squad to Marbella for warm-weather training, while Carrick’s men are at Atlético Madrid on Tuesday in the Champions League. They both need to conjure something.
After volleys of “you cheating b*****ds, you know what you are” rang out from both sets of fans, Lammens struggled with a nightmare start. A loose pass was intercepted by Lucas Bergvall and the ball rolled into Solanke. Yet, as has been Spurs’ problem, the centre-forward failed to finish, his shot saved by a relieved Lammens, who was jittery again when Martínez passed to him on his goalline, where he dawdled before hoofing clear.
The reports had stated how De Zerbi’s men have played well, at times this season, but cannot finish: a hindrance in this sport. No boon, too, for any team is hesitation, as when Youri Tielemans waited for the ball to bounce, Tottenham pounced, and suddenly Sávio was heading forward, the sliding challenge of Leny Yoro, fielded today at right back, saving a scattered rearguard.
This pointed to a Spurs ascendancy that was a headscratcher for Carrick and yet more Spurs profligacy saved United when Mohammed Kudus’s cross found Archie Gray and the young right-back beat Lammens but not his right post.
Carrick wants his team to control contests, but there was close to zero control throughout. On the hour, Carlos Baleba entered for his debut and immediately spun and flicked deftly into Fernandes’ path in a reminder of what skill can do.
Now came the breathless denouement – a point, at the close, feeling about fair. – Guardian

title: Ulster overcome slow start to claw back draw against Munster
description: Jacob Stockdale with a brace of tries on his 150th appearance for Ulster
content:
A game of two halves. Munster utterly dominant in the first 40 minutes, racking up a bonus point and a 26-5 lead that looked unassailable. But Ulster re-emerged after the interval and, despite it being a slow burn initially, recalibrated all the misfiring parts to hold their visitors scoreless while crossing for three tries of their own to grab a draw.
Relief and regret may well have been the feelings shared by both sides after the final whistle.
Munster will reflect on a 17-5 penalty count in their favour, a dominant scrum and maul that provided the leverage to score three of their four tries, weighed against how little bits of their patterns unravelled, principally some costly lineout turnovers, but not everything can be laid at that door.
Ulster awoke from a torpor, one that has afflicted them in each of their URC outings so far this season, but for the second week in succession clawed back a draw. It arrived off the back of an impactful bench and quality moments from Jacob Stockdale and Stuart McCloskey, but Richie Murphy’s side will have much to ponder, having failed to manage the game and showing a carelessness in possession.
Munster made several late changes to the matchday 23, Shay McCarthy replacing Shane Daly on the right wing while Max Clein and Michael Foy were added to the bench in place of Diarmuid Barron and Tom Ahern respectively. They didn’t miss a beat though, and produced 40 minutes of hard-nosed rugby.
Alex Kendellen had one of those matches. Omnipresent, a scourge at the breakdown, bagging tries and playing the role of villain; he was brilliant for his 53 minutes on the pitch.
While the start was blighted by knocks-on due to the wet surface and cold hands, Munster quickly warmed to their task. The Ulster scrum was eviscerated on their put-in and forced to concede a penalty shortly after on the Munster feed.
The visitors kicked to the corner and Ulster continued to rack up the offences, four in total. Munster scrumhalf Craig Casey was tackled short, but the respite was brief, another penalty tapped to the corner and, from the lineout maul, Kendellen dotted down.
Jacob Stockdale, on his 150th appearance for his province, marked the occasion with a try as he beat both Ben O’Connor and JJ Hanrahan with slick footwork. It survived a TMO intervention, a ludicrous review to put it politely.
But the home side’s ill-discipline resurfaced from the restart, penalised in their 22. Munster produced a carbon copy of their first try, this time hooker Marnus van der Merwe the one to finish off the move. Hanrahan kicked the conversion and things got immediately worse for Ulster as they lost Eli Snyman to injury and the scrum suffered another shellacking.
The home side were a liability in possession, their passing unsympathetic or wild, while their rising penalty count through the first quarter was a spiralling concern.
Munster in contrast, ran hard and straight, took better care of the ball, and were patient in building phases until they could squeeze a transgression. They found their hosts obliging.
At the half-hour mark, Cormac Izuchukwu received a yellow card for a shoulder to the head of Gavin Coombes at a ruck. Munster built pressure again from the penalty, Dan Kelly’s intelligent line took him through a gaping hole in the defence and over for a try. Hanrahan converted.
The visitors were soon back inside the Ulster 22 but conceded their first penalty of the match on 36 minutes. But not long after, Munster had the bonus point try. Ulster transgressed, Hanrahan kicked to the corner and they worked the fringes until Kendellen found the space to power over for a second try.
Ulster had conceded 14-points while a player down and changed both props at half-time. The first scrum of the half came after 90 seconds. Ulster survived, but that’s all it was, and when Munster had a put-in soon after, another penalty came.
Ulster’s occasional line-breaks hinted at what was possible if they could get continuity and they underlined the assertion with Stockdale’s second try.
It galvanised the home side, and suddenly it was Munster who looked a little fragile. It was especially noticeable in the lineout, where a turnover five metres from their own line gave Ulster a scrum. From there, the hosts pounded away until Dave McCann barrelled over. Murphy converted to put them just seven behind, 26-19.
Munster conceded two penalties in quick succession and were forced to back-pedal into their own 22. Ulster powered their way from a lineout launch to a try for centre Stuart McCloskey and a beauty of a conversion from Murphy drew the sides level.
But there was still time for a slightly bonkers finish. Ulster were pinged at a scrum and replacement outhalf Charlie O’Shea nudged it to touch rather than take on the long-range chance. McCann stole the lineout and the ball was moved to Rob Baloucoune, who raced 50 metres before his inside pass was picked off and hoofed into touch in the Munster 22.

title: Man dies after entering tiger enclosure at Yorkshire wildlife park
description: Animal was uninjured and remained in enclosure following incident and there is no wider risk to the public
content:
A man has died after entering an enclosure and being attacked by a tiger at Yorkshire wildlife park in Britain, police said.
Emergency services were contacted after the man entered the enclosure and was attacked by the tiger shortly after 1.30pm on Saturday.
Despite the efforts of medical personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene, and his family have since been informed, South Yorkshire Police said.
Videos circulating online appear to show a man being pawed at and grappled by a tiger in an enclosure at the park.
The tiger was uninjured and has remained in the enclosure since the incident, while the wildlife park was subsequently evacuated, the force said.
A police spokesperson said: “At 1.35pm on Saturday we received reports of a man entering a tiger enclosure at Yorkshire wildlife park.
“The tiger subsequently attacked the man, resulting in serious injury.
“Emergency services attended and sadly, despite the best efforts of medical personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene.
“The man’s family is aware and is being supported by specialist officers. Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time.
“Regarding rumours surrounding the condition of the tiger, the animal was uninjured and remained in the enclosure following the incident and there is no wider risk to the public.”
A Yorkshire ambulance service spokesperson also confirmed that two land ambulances, Yorkshire air ambulance and a doctor attended the scene.
A statement posted on the wildlife park’s social media channels read: “We can confirm that a serious incident has occurred today at the tiger enclosure.
“Our emergency response procedures were immediately activated and emergency services are currently attending the scene.
“We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened.
“The safety and wellbeing of our visitors, staff and animals remain our highest priority. The park is now closed and will remain closed tomorrow.”
Yorkshire wildlife park opened in 2009, with the Land of the Tigers attraction opening in 2011.
The attraction is on a purpose-built two-acre reserve for endangered Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with about 500 left in the wild.
Photos of the enclosure on the park’s website shows a high walkway for visitors and fencing above the section where the tigers can roam.
The police said they were aware of the footage online and asked people not to share it. – PA

title: Nine people, including children, dead after mass shooting in Pennsylvania
description: Suspect among dead in house after standoff with police in Erie and there is no ongoing threat, authorities say
content:
Nine people, including children, died in a mass murder on Friday in Erie, Pennsylvania, in the United States , after a gun-wielding attacker opened fire outside a home and then entered the property, according to authorities.
The suspected attacker was also found dead as police responded to the deadly violence, which triggered a standoff involving Erie police officers and tactical teams.
Police discovered the killings at about 5pm when officers were called to a residence following reports of gunfire. Witnesses told authorities they had seen an attacker with a gun outside the property before making his way inside.
Responding officers discovered two women lying dead in the street, both having suffered fatal gunshot wounds.
The situation quickly developed into a standoff as police officers and tactical personnel surrounded the residence. More gunshots were heard coming from inside the home, and officers entered the place.
Inside, police said they made a devastating discovery, finding seven additional victims, including children, along with the suspected attacker. Investigators believe the attacker died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
Erie’s police chief, Rick Lorah, spoke about the scale of the mass murder, describing the scene as among the most distressing and heartbreaking he had witnessed.
“The loss of life is devastating and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing,” Lorah said. “At this time, we can confirm that the suspect is deceased. Based on the information currently available to us, there is no ongoing threat to the public.”
He added: “Our hearts are with the victims, their families and everyone affected by this tragedy. There are no words that can adequately express the magnitude of the loss of life here.”
Authorities on Saturday said they were still investigating the circumstances surrounding the killings, with authorities attempting to determine a motive for the violence.
The city of Erie also issued a statement on social media confirming that the suspected shooter had died and that the immediate danger had passed.
The statement described the case as a “terrible tragedy”, although the city’s statement did not provide further information about the events leading up to the shooting.
“We understand that the news brings deep shock and sorrow to our residents, and we want to assure the public that the situation has been contained,” the city said.
[ Christa Pike, who survived US execution attempt, is discharged from hospital Opens in new window ]
Figures from the Gun Violence Archive indicate that the killings in Erie marked at least the 19th mass murder of the year. Such cases are defined as ones in which four or more victims are murdered.
Many of those mass murders have been what are considered family annihilations, in which an attacker kills multiple close family members.
The non-partisan archive also indicated that the killings in Erie were among more than 500 mass shootings across the US since the beginning of January. Mass shootings are defined as cases in which four or more victims are shot whether fatally or non-fatally.
Mass shootings for years have remained a persistent problem in the US, often intensifying public demands for stronger gun control measures at the federal level.
Despite those calls, Congress has not enacted such restrictions sought over the years. – Guardian

title: US president Donald Trump says it is time for Ukraine to get rid of Zelenskiy
description: Extraordinary intervention came after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region
content:
US president Donald Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Volodymyr Zelenskiy has not done enough to end his country’s war with Russia .
Speaking at the White House on Saturday, Trump said: “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal″, adding that “for some reason [Zelenskiy] never does”.
He has also sought to blame record US diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the US-led war in Iran , which has elevated world energy prices.
“He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel,” Trump said, before departing for Tennessee where he was set to rally Republican voters.
Trump also suggested that if he had been US president in 2022, “that war would have never started. There was no reason that that war with Ukraine and Russia started. It started due to incompetence.”
He said Zelenskiy had “lost 30 per cent of your country and you’ve had over a million people go between the two of them, over two million people killed”.
“That’s a war that should have never started. And I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump said.
[ Trump agrees diesel supply deal with Russia Opens in new window ]
The extraordinary intervention came after Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian officials said on Saturday.
Three children were among those killed when Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine’s state emergency service said. At least 18 people were wounded.
The attacks came a day after Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel that Kyiv warned would help bankroll Moscow’s war.
Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4½ years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed more than 55 people over the past four days.
Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian president Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he had been expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia.
Instead, Trump announced that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and a million tons “immediately thereafter”.
Russia will deliver an additional three million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
Trump’s shock announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed to clamp down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia’s war against Ukraine.
In a lengthy post online reacting to the deal, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Russia would repay it “with further terror and perfidy”. He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged.
“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.
According to a statement released by the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, Zelenskiy called it “a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners”.
Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to end the war.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” Zelenskiy said. – AP

title: Shane Lowry eight shots off leaders at Open de Espana
description: Early eagle helps Offalyman to four-under third round
content:
Shane Lowry rallied to a four-under third round at the Open de Espana on Saturday, fighting his way up the leaderboard for a share of 17th heading into the final round.
The Irish Open champion started the day at Real Club de Campo Villa de Madrid with a bogey on the par-four first, recovering with an eagle on the fourth to go one-under for the day. He managed two birdies either side of the turn, with a bogey on par-five 14th to sign for a round of 67.
It left him eight shots off the joint leaders, Scotland’s Grant Forrest and England’s Joe Dean, who sit one shot ahead of the trio tied for third on 12-under – Victor Perez, Jacob Skov Olesen and Joel Girrbach.
Forrest began the day with a one-shot advantage but slipped down the leaderboard after bogeying the fifth hole. But birdies at the 11th, 14th and 16th gave the Scot a four-under round of 67.
“I’m happy with how I handled today,” said Forrest after his round. “I didn’t have my best stuff but I’m really proud of how I dug in and made some nice putts, a couple of good recovery shots, and all in all a decent score again.
“This is one of my favourite tournaments, it’s been good to me in the past, and I’d love nothing more than to go home with a trophy tomorrow.”
Dean, meanwhile, will feel he could have produced an even better outcome than his round of 65.
He followed five birdies on the front nine with three more on the 12th, 14th and 15th to open up a three-shot lead, but the 32-year-old then double-bogeyed the 16th and dropped another shot on the 17th before finishing on a high with a 31-foot putt for birdie on the last.
“It gave a little bit of hope after those previous two holes,” said Dean. “We’ll go again and see what happens.”

title: About 10,000 people march through Dublin in support of Palestine
description: Taoiseach Micheál Martin has failed Gaza, Ireland-Palestine Solidarity Campaign chairwoman Zoe Lawlor says
content:
Taoiseach Micheál Martin told the United Nations the world has failed the people of Gaza , “but he has also failed Gaza”, a crowd estimated at 10,000 attending a march for Palestine in Dublin on Saturday was told.
Addressing a rally outside Leinster House at the end of the March from Parnell Square, Zoe Lawlor, chairwoman of the Ireland-Palestine Solidarity Campaign, called on the Government to impose sanctions on Israel .
To roars of “shame, shame” from the crowd, with many people waving Palestinian flags, Lawlor said Ireland continued to trade with Israel and send exports to the Israeli weapons industry.
She said the Government “took years to even enact the Occupied Territories Bill , but they refuse to include services”.
Lawlor said the Government continued to allow the US military to use Shannon Airport and had allowed “the Central Bank fund genocide until we stopped it”.
“So this shame is also on the Irish Government , and no amount of grandstanding at the UN will ever take that away,” she said.
Lawlor also took issue with the Government on the question of issuing visas for Palestinian students to study in Ireland.
According to Department of Justice figures, more than 100 Palestinian student visas were refused earlier this year. The visa approval rate dropped from about 84 per cent in 2025 to 27.5 per cent this year.
“They told the students to send their appeals by post when they know there is no postal system in Gaza,” Lawlor said. “This is one of our Government’s most shameful acts on Palestine.
“We will never forget the record number of students, healthcare workers, children, journalists, medics, UN employees, sports people, and aid workers murdered by Israel .
“We will never forget that they shot children in the head, that they shot people that were starving as they queued for food, that they made thousands of children amputees,” she said.
“There is malnutrition and hunger, disease and rats, and all of these crimes are presided over by the sham board of peace and enabled by the international community, including Ireland.”
Lawlor also criticised the Football Association of Ireland , which she said was “enabled by the Government” to cross a Palestinian picket line and play Israel.
She said the Government “missed a huge opportunity to be on the right side of history, but the broad civil society Stop the Game campaign was a success, with immense support from sports people, from trade unions, from all Opposition parties and the public”.
The rally was also addressed by Palestinian human rights activist Talha Al Ali, who described life in Palestine under an occupying “apartheid state”. He accused Israel of stealing land and ethnically cleansing the West Bank .
He said in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian communities were being violently expelled from their land and homes.
The Ireland-Palestine Solidarity Campaign is supported by more than 160 Irish civil-society groups, many of whom were represented at Saturday’s march and rally, which was called to mark three years since the beginning of “Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza”.
The full march took more than an hour to travel through the city centre. It was the 21st such national mobilisation since October 2023.

title: Christa Pike, who survived US execution attempt, is discharged from hospital
description: Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital in botched Tennessee execution attempt
content:
Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection, has been moved back to prison, according to a statement released by her lawyers.
Pike (50) was discharged from the hospital and is back at the Deborah K Johnson Rehabilitation Centre, the women’s prison where she was housed for 30 years, her lawyers said in a statement.
“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances.
“She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery,” her lawyers said in a statement.
Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state attempted to execute her by lethal injection on September 30th for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer.
Pike had been in a hospital since the failed execution.
The recovery marks a dramatic turnaround after Pike was declared brain-dead on Monday, before waking up and beginning to speak on Tuesday. Her ordeal has shocked many in the United States and overseas and galvanised critics of the death penalty.
Stephen Ferrell, a lawyer on Pike’s legal team, told the BBC that she was able to walk but remained mentally foggy. “What’s been described to me is that physically there’s quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she’s not able to use them very much,” Ferrell said.
“She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far,” he added.
[ The Irish Times view on US executions: a barbaric practice Opens in new window ]
Pike, was taken to hospital unconscious but alive from Tennessee’s execution chamber on September 30th, after receiving two doses of the barbiturate pentobarbital.
After the botched execution attempt, one of her lawyers called the process “cruel and torturous”, adding that he had counted seven needles in Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”.
Pike had lifted her head from the execution gurney to say her arms were burning as the drug was administered.
Pike’s team is seeking psychological support for her, given that “clearly is necessary now”, Ferrell said. On Wednesday, Pike was described as “angry and confused” after regaining consciousness.
Ferrell said of Pike’s mental state: “I think it’s kind of good and bad. Good that she is fairly with it, but she’s also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she’s going.”
He said it remains to be seen whether Pike makes a full recovery.
“I assume [Pike’s condition] will keep improving, but there could be some permanent damage. We don’t know that yet.” – AP

title: Michael Duffy brace sends Derry City to FAI Cup finale
description: Candystripes to meet Waterford in Aviva decider on November 8th
content:
Michael Duffy was the hero yet again for Derry City as his two first-half goals sent the Candystripes into an FAI Cup final against Waterford.
The City captain was at the heart of a dominant performance in both halves, the first attacking, the second defensive, as Derry set up a clash with the Blues at the Aviva Stadium on November 8th.
It is now 10 goals in nine games for Duffy since the departure of Tiernan Lynch in August. As a result, City’s season – which had previously been plummeting towards disappointment – now has the chance of a very different ending.
Derry opened the scoring on 26 minutes, and there could have been little argument that it wasn’t deserved after a growing period of pressure on the Galway goal.
Adam O’Reilly found Darragh Burns completely unmarked deep in the Galway half, and the midfielder raced at goal before shooting towards the bottom corner. Pires Da Cunha did well to stop the initial shot, and got some luck when Wasiri Williams halted James Clarke’s rebound on the line, but there were too many red and white shirts lining up. Duffy was there to ultimately put Derry in front, heading home the second rebound for his 15th goal of the season and his ninth in nine games under Mark Connolly.
Galway attempted a quick response and Jimmy Keohane brought a brilliant flying save from Tom Norcott at the other end, the first time in the opening half-hour that the hosts looked a real threat.
But it didn’t signal any change in momentum from John Caulfield’s side, as Derry continued to dominate for the remainder of the first half.
They deservedly doubled their lead in added time before the break. A disaster from a Galway point of view, the hosts wasted a free kick in a dangerous area, and with the Derry area packed with players awaiting a delivery, City broke in devastating fashion.
James Clarke hooked the ball clear to halfway, where Duffy brought the ball down before finding Ellis Chapman on the left wing. Chapman picked out the perfect return pass as Duffy raced in behind, and the captain made no mistake as he slid the ball past Da Cunha to make it 2-0 with the final kick of the half.
In response, Caulfield made two changes at the break. Francely Lomboto almost made an immediate impact on his introduction as he used his pace to latch on to Keohane’s lobbed pass to go through on goal. But he was unable to beat Norcott, who did enough to turn it behind for a corner.
Caulfield added Frantz Pierrot to his attack midway through the second half, and the striker had an opportunity to seize a lifeline when a free kick into the area was spilt by goalkeeper Norcott, but the ball bounced as Pierrot aimed it at the open goal, sending it high over the crossbar.
Galway huffed and puffed, but with Patrick McClean and Jamie Stott at the heart of a strong defensive display, there was no sign of even a consolation, and the final whistle drew huge celebrations among the hundreds of travelling fans.
GALWAY: Da Cunha, O’Connor (Wolfe 73), Barrett (McCarthy HT), Keohane (Connolly 89), Walsh (Pierrot 65), Bolger, Hurley, Twardek (Lomboto HT), Facchineri, Williams, Devitt.
DERRY CITY: Norcott, Fleming, McClean, Stott, Dummigan, O’Reilly, Twisk, Chapman, Burns (Olayinka 78, Smith 90), Duffy, Clarke (Barr 89).

title: Bruno Guimarães completes Arsenal comeback to end Leeds’ unbeaten run
description: Dara O’Shea sends Ipswich to victory, Brentford fight back to draw at Villa
content:
Arsenal came back from a goal down to defeat strong opponents and reset their form after a lengthy international break. The Gunners were not great against Leeds , and the defence continues to look more vulnerable than last season, but the impact from their bench and the belief that roared through the team after they forced an equaliser suggested they have acquired the resilience of champions. Or as the home support put it: “We know who we are.”
Some had predicted a goal-fest, others another upset for the champions. There was a real sense of uncertainty as to the outcome as the game began.
The first half was a tight affair, but one that allowed both sides to hope for more. Leeds were typically resilient, but able to get up the pitch in two touches. Arsenal were too intricate and, at times, alarmingly vulnerable, but also close to unpicking the visiting defence.
Leeds had the best chances, with deliveries from either side of the field appearing to unsettle Arsenal’s redoubtable back line. In the 25th minute, a Gabriel Gudmundsson delivery was well met by Jayden Bogle but blocked, inadvertently, by Anton Stach. Two minutes later, Bogle was denied again, this time picking up the loose ball from an Ao Tanaka cross and firing at Raya from a tight angle. With just a minute remaining of the half, the Arsenal goalkeeper produced a carbon-copy save to deny Gudmundsson himself.
Arsenal could not have complained had they gone in a goal down at the break. There was some frustration in the ground too, where it appeared that flashbacks of stodgy performances of old were occupying the minds of the crowd. There were things that were working, such as the selection of Noni Madueke – one of four changes – who was having the better of James Justin on the left-hand side. Madueke’s deliveries deserved better from his forwards, Kai Havertz especially, who directed a header straight at James Trafford from eight yards out with the goal at his mercy in the 21st minute.
With no changes at half-time, the second period offered an opportunity for one side to impose themselves and Leeds duly accepted the invite. For the first 15 minutes they dominated play, overpowering Arsenal in midfield and running beyond their full-backs. Justin and Tanaka had both seen long-range efforts go narrowly wide before the visitors got the opener at last, Justin firing home after Gudmundsson had run off Ben White and delivered a low cross from the left that Raya could not cut out.
That was the 55th minute, and Noah Okafor nearly doubled the lead three minutes later but could not get the final touch to a Bogle cross. Little did the visitors know that it would ultimately prove to be their last opportunity. Within three minutes, the game had snapped into a new direction.
Arsenal grabbed an equaliser in the manner Leeds had been threatening for so long. A deep cross from Madueke was met at the back post by White, whose header eluded Trafford and was bundled home by Riccardo Calafiori for his second Premier League goal of the season.
Then, before play restarted, Mikel Arteta made a triple substitution and unleashed Bruno Guimarães. If Arsenal had had a familiar look to this point, if there had been echoes of familiar weaknesses, then the Brazilian put paid to all that. Not only snapping into tackles, not only moving the ball at pace, he was desperate for everything to go faster, more aggressively, with sharper intention. Nine minutes after coming on, he had scored the winner.
It was a goal that deserved to decide the contest and reflected the best of what the Gunners had been trying to achieve. Again, play developed down the left, but here it was Saka swapping in for Madueke and playing a one-two with Odegaard. The captain then poked a short pass to Declan Rice who – with Bruno now covering him – had ventured into the opposition area. Rice back-heeled the ball first time to the edge of the area and there was Bruno waiting, poised, to steer the ball unerringly into the corner of Trafford’s goal.
Further chances fell to the Gunners, including Odegaard from just two yards out and Saka, who failed to execute a one-on-one with Trafford, but the misses did not ultimately matter, such was the transformation in this game. Leeds, for their part, left the field looking shocked.
In the 3pm kick-offs, Jordan Henderson and João Pedro found braces for Chelsea as they beat Bournemouth 5-1 at Stamford Bridge, while Keith Andrews ’ Brentford salvaged a 2-2 draw away to Aston Villa.
Dara O’Shea netted the winner for Ipswich against Fulham at Portman Road, and a 10-man Brighton took a 2-0 away win over Sunderland. – Guardian

title: Max Verstappen takes Singapore GP pole after sprint win
description: Charles Leclerc pushed into second, Lewis Hamilton to start from third
content:
Max Verstappen took pole position for the Singapore Grand Prix , beating the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc into second in a close fight on the streets of the Marina Bay circuit.
Drivers championship leader Kimi Antonelli was fourth for Mercedes, a decent return after he has struggled with the car over the weekend and given his team-mate and title rival, George Russell, will start from the back of the grid on Sunday.
Verstappen was in fine form to take pole having already scored a victory in the sprint race earlier in the day, with the Red Bull looking hugely impressive. Lewis Hamilton was third for Ferrari, with Lando Norris in fifth for McLaren.
Despite Russell taking sixth place on track he will be opening at the back of the field because of the penalties applied for taking a new engine, one more than the permitted allocation. He had no control over the reliability issues that led to his engine failing at the last round in Malaysia but his weekend was compromised hugely after he made an error in the sprint race.
He had taken to the front, passing Verstappen into the first corner, but put his wheels on to the white lines at the final corner at the end of the opening lap. In the wet conditions he lost the rear, spun and went into the barriers, out of the race and the team had to work fast to repair the car before qualifying.
Russell held his hands up for the mistake that played into Antonelli’s hands. “Miscalculation,” he said. “Came through the corner had more battery deployment than I thought, pushed me a little bit wider than I hoped and went on to the white line. Silly mistake. Big consequences.”
After Russell’s engine failure in Malaysia, Antonelli’s lead over his team-mate was 84 points, a gap the Italian extended to 89 after the sprint.
In qualifying on the opening quick laps in Q3, Verstappen set the pace with 1:31.373. An impressive benchmark at his first attempt, throwing himself into the lap, on the absolute edge of the tight street circuit where he found the limit with precision. Hamilton chased him hard to the line, a tenth back, setting up a showdown.
For the final runs, however, Hamilton could not improve, while Leclerc went quicker and edged into second place. No one could challenge Verstappen and he retained the top spot for pole by five-hundredths from Leclerc.
It is another demonstration of how the tranche of recent upgrades have improved the Red Bull. Verstappen took his first pole and win of the season in Malaysia and has followed it with pole for the sprint, the win and a further pole for the GP, with a control that proves how much more comfortable he is with the car and able to exploit it.
His 50th career pole is his first in Singapore, a track where he has yet to win a GP, one of only two, alongside the Madring, on the current calendar where he has yet to take victory.
Earlier in the day, Verstappen won the sprint, which had been delayed because of heavy rain, with complete control from the front once he had inherited the lead after Russell’s crash. He had enough pace to comfortably see off Hamilton in second who had made a superb start to move from sixth to third off the line. It was very much a processional affair, with overtaking all but impossible as drivers managed their tyres to the flag.
The short form dash was enlivened by late drama when Norris made a move on his team-mate, Oscar Piastri, on the final lap. The pair clashed, taking the Australian out and dropping Norris to eighth, to the consternation of his McLaren team.
That moved Antonelli up from sixth to fourth, another indication that everything is going the Italian’s way, even when he is just keeping his head down and grinding out a result.
The street circuit track was holding a sprint for the first time as F1 seeks to enliven some of the more processional circuits, including having Monaco host a sprint next season. However, it was not welcomed with any enthusiasm by the drivers.
“If it was dry that would probably have been the most boring race to have watched,” said Hamilton. An opinion echoed by Leclerc. “I don’t think it makes sense to have any sprint races on city tracks in general. Here or Monaco, I don’t think it adds anything to the weekend.” – Guardian

title: Mona McSharry adds to World Cup medal haul
description: Sligo swimmer secures silver in Uzbekistan ahead of final stop in three-meet series
content:
Mona McSharry added another medal to her growing World Cup haul, finishing second in the 50m breaststroke in Uzebkistan on Saturday.
The Olympic bronze medallist finished in 29.85 to take silver, one tenth of a second behind Russia’s Ralina Giliazova.
McSharry won gold in the 100m breaststroke on Friday and bronze in the 200m breaststroke on Thursday.
The meet in Tashkent is the second stop of the World Aquatics World Cup. The series kicked off in Baku, Azerbaijan last week and will conclude in Astana, Kazakhstan next week.
Having won the 100m breaststroke in both Baku and Tashkent, a third win for McSharry in the event in Astana will see her claim the triple crown title and a $10,000 bonus.
Ellen Walshe also reached the finals of both the 100m butterfly and 200m individual medley on Saturday.
The Templeogue swimmer finished just outside the medals in the 200m IM, taking fourth in 2:07.74, and touched the wall in 58.22 for eighth in the 100m butterfly.

title: Cristiano Ronaldo provisionally suspended after Portugal walkout
description: Striker subsequently apologised for his actions
content:
Cristiano Ronaldo has been provisionally suspended by Portugal after walking out on the national team.
Ronaldo left the Portugal squad after he was an unused substitute for a 2-1 win away to Norway in the Nations League on September 27th.
The 41-year-old, who has scored a record-breaking 146 goals in 234 appearances for his country, subsequently issued a near 2,000-word statement saying he withdrew from the squad after a “breach of trust” between him and head coach Jorge Jesus.
The Portuguese Football Federation has now stepped in, confirming in a statement reported by Lisbon-based newspaper A Bola: “Disciplinary proceedings were initiated against Cristiano Ronaldo, by decision of the non-professional section, on October 9, 2026, with the objective of ascertaining the potential disciplinary relevance of the facts reported on October 7, 2026.
“Without prejudice to the automatic preventive suspension to which he was subject until the date of initiation, a non-automatic preventive suspension of the player was determined, and the proceedings were given urgent status.
“The proceedings were sent, on October 10, 2026, to the disciplinary instruction committee of the FPF (Portuguese Football Federation), with publicity excluded until the end of the investigation.”
Ronaldo missed Portugal’s following two fixtures, wins over Denmark and Norway, which left them top of Group A4 with four straight victories, fuelling speculation his international career could be over.
Jesus left the door open to the veteran forward in a press conference after Sunday’s win against Norway, saying: “If he wants to, he’ll return to the national team.”
Ronaldo argued Jesus had reneged on an agreement about how many minutes he would play, but apologised for his actions and accepted he deserved to be sanctioned.

title: Michael Flatley pays tribute to his wife Niamh O’Brien at funeral Mass
description: ‘I’m looking forward to our next dance in heaven together,’ Flatley says in eulogy in Dublin on Saturday
content:
An emotional Michael Flatley said the pain caused by his late wife Niamh O’Brien’s long illness and death was the worst he had ever experienced.
Flatley hesitated many times, his voice breaking during the funeral eulogy for a woman he described as the “love of his life” and “my dream girl”.
The funeral Mass for O’Brien (52) took place at the Church of St Thérèse in Mount Merrion in Dublin on Saturday.
O’Brien, originally from Kilbride, Co Meath , danced with Flatley for many years before the couple got together in 2006. They married 20 years ago this month.
[ Michael Flatley thanks people for ‘beautiful gestures of sympathy’ after wife’s death Opens in new window ]
“How did we get here?” Flatley asked the congregation at the start of his tribute to his wife. “They say God gives the heaviest burdens to those with the broadest shoulders, but I don’t feel like that right now.
“As I woke up in the middle of the night and Niamhy wasn’t next to me, I couldn’t sleep thinking about what I was going to say. You can appreciate and understand that I can’t remember a word of what I was about to say.”
Flatley told a packed congregation that he had experienced much physical pain as a boxer and as a dancer, but the emotional pain that he experienced in losing his wife “was like something I thought I would never feel in my life”.
His wife had been diagnosed 12 years ago with scleroderma, an autoimmune disease, and given two years to live at the time.
“Every day of her life she fought it, the last two years were very difficult. I told her: ‘Focus not on the storm, but focus on the hand of the Lord’,” said Flatley.
The last year was “particularly difficult” and the last three weeks “were torturous and unbearable for her because she could not breathe,” he recalled.
He thanked the O’Briens for welcoming him into the family and for their “remarkable devotion” to his wife right until the end of her life.
“I can’t believe how lucky I was that she said yes to me. She wasn’t just a lady, she was my dream girl, she was my everything,” he said.
“She was the lady of the dance, she was the mother of my son. She was the most beautiful girl in the world.”
[ Niamh O’Brien, Irish dancer and wife of Michael Flatley, dies aged 52 Opens in new window ]
Flatley recalled how he and O’Brien had danced around the world together before becoming romantically involved with each other.
She had told him before he went on stage at Madison Square Garden in New York that he had worked for it and was fulfilling his dreams. “That was before we became involved romantically.”
His life changed for the better after they married. “She was the calming force in my life in every day,” he said.
“Everything went better because of Niamh. She was the voice of calm always. I was so lucky and so blessed to marry her.
“I believe Niamh is standing right beside me at this moment. I love you Niamhy, dream girl, and I’m looking forward to our next dance in heaven together.”
Flatley finished his eulogy with a tribute to his wife which he played on his flute.
The couple’s son, Michael St James, recalled the “deep love” that his parents had for each other. “They fought so hard until the end. My mam would not complain in any capacity. My dad fought so hard to make sure that my mam had the best care she could get,” he said.
“She was the most wonderful person. She was the best mother anyone could ask for. She put everyone else first.
“I will always miss her but I know she is with us in spirit. She is always with me in the person that she raised me to be.”
The chief mourners, along with her husband and son, were Niamh O’Brien’s parents Monica and Tommy, her sisters Derval and Aoibheann, her niece Dempsey Rose and nephews Dillon, Lochlann and Lennon.
Comdt Joe Lennon represented Taoiseach Micheál Martin . The funeral Mass was followed by a private family burial.

title: The unlikely rise of India’s Gen Z rebels
description: Abhijeet Dipke started the Cockroach movement as a joke. But after ousting a minister over dysfunctional college entrance exams, younger people say they want to save democracy
content:
H e uncorked a generation’s anger at a broken college entrance exam system. Now the Gen Z movement that Abhijeet Dipke birthed five months ago and called the Cockroach Janta Party has become a formidable finger in the eye of the Indian government.
The cockroaches’ latest aim is the resignation of the country’s chief election commissioner, over what they say is a politically motivated purge of 130 million voters from the election rolls.
On Saturday, in perhaps their biggest challenge to prime minister Narendra Modi ’s administration, supporters defied a police ban and staged a mass protest in New Delhi over they they said was a politically motivated revision of the nation’s voter roll.
Thousands of demonstrators met walls of security forces as they tried to protest. Leaders of the Cockroach party were detained when their flight landed in Delhi shortly before 11 am local time on Saturday.
“This is dictatorship,” said Abhijeet Dipke (31), as police officers approached him and the two other leaders before they could disembark, according to a video he shared on social media. Police officers were heard telling him that their protest had been refused permission.
In central Delhi, protesters were rounded up by the dozens starting early on Saturday morning and led, sometimes forcefully, into detention buses.
They were defying extraordinary measures taken by the authorities to prevent them from reaching the protest site, called Jantar Mantar.
The demonstration comes after a week of nationwide protests demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the head of India’s election commission, a body that has recently come under intense public criticism because of the voter roll revision.
In fact, India ’s youth have many more grievances: failing schools, insufficient jobs, violence against women, a lack of government accountability. Their frustrations have been boiling for years. There are so many of them – 367 million people between ages 15 and 29, the world’s largest Gen Z cohort.
Dipke said in advance of Saturday’s demonstrations that he felt intense pressure.
“It’s like someone has dropped a baby at my doorstep,” he said on a recent road trip to highlight the problem with state schools in the countryside. “It actually scares me, to be very honest.
“People have too many expectations, too many hopes,” he went on. “It’s like people are expecting me to resolve everything at once.”
Modi has not commented on the cockroach protests, though criticism has come from senior politicians of his Bharatiya Janata Party, including the chief minister of Maharashtra state, Devendra Fadnavis, who said their “fake narrative” over the voter roll revision would not succeed.
For Dipke – and the cockroaches – the risks are enormously high.
In a country where space for dissent has shrunk, they could be crushed as quickly as they appeared. Delhi police have detained hundreds of people who defied the ban and protested in Delhi this week.
The cockroaches’ four leaders are all younger than 32, with no political experience. Signs of friction have appeared with the main opposition party, the Indian National Congress. Its leader, Rahul Gandhi, is holding another rally across the country, in Chennai, on Saturday.
The cockroaches already have one win under their belt: the rare ouster of a government minister in connection to the entrance exams. They seem to have emboldened many more Indians to speak out against the government. Over the last week, a range of groups, from left-wing student activists to conservative regional politicians, have rallied in several cities.
“We are just frustrated by everything. Everything,” said Aayushi Gaikwad (18), who travelled three hours by train to attend a cockroach protest in Mumbai last Friday.
It was her first time at a protest. Around her, thousands of people waved Indian flags. As evening fell, Dipke led the crowd in singing the national anthem.
Ram Guha, a historian and outspoken critic of Modi, credited the cockroach leaders for puncturing the “invincibility of the Modi government”.
“They clearly have a raw courage,” he said.
Not long after they forced the resignation of the education minister in July, the cockroaches turned to India’s rural schools. A range of Instagram-worthy horrors awaited them. Clogged toilets. Broken water taps. Overheated tin sheds for classrooms. Rotten onions in a school kitchen. Children wading through floodwaters to reach school.
Dipke visited a remote district in western Maharashtra state, called Nandurbar, where he had spent the first five years of his childhood before his family moved to a city.
[ How India’s young ‘cockroach’ movement has posed the biggest challenge to Modi in years Opens in new window ]
He was born to a Dalit family, seen as low on the Hindu caste ladder, in Nandurbar, a remote district in western Maharashtra.
He attended private schools. But his cousins, whose parents were not as educated as his, attended rural government schools, and the contrast was obvious to him, even as a child. He sat at a desk; they sat on the floor. He drank filtered water; they sometimes had no water. He went on to Boston University for a master’s degree; they repaired cars or worked in construction.
“That has been one of the most neglected things since independence. Government schools have never been given the attention they need,” he said.
At a residential girls’ school in a village called Sari, he learned there was no running water in the fourth-floor bathrooms. The girls hauled buckets of water up four flights of stairs.
At a primary school, he met the one teacher who taught a class of first through fourth graders. There was no electricity, and the girls had to fetch water for their bathroom from across a field. The boys had no toilet at all.
Vishwas Thakarey, the teacher, said he, like many teachers, had been diverted from the classroom because he had been told to work on the voter roll revision. (Teachers are often pulled away on other government duties.)
Education experts say they hope the cockroaches will continue their campaign on schools to shine a light on an issue politicians had long ignored.
[ India protests ‘could become lightning rod’ for disillusionment with Modi’s leadership Opens in new window ]
“The kind of attention they’ve been able to bring to schools, no one I can think of has been able to do that for 20 years,” said Reetika Khera, an economist at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi who has researched rural schools for decades.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

title: Ireland in line for a kicking from all sides after publishing EU budget
description: Irish diplomats privately remarked that if everyone ended up unhappy, they had done their job
content:
T he Government was well aware it would be in line to get a kicking from its European counterparts, and from all directions.
While the ink was still drying on the speeches Simon Harris and Jack Chambers were due to deliver in the Dáil on Tuesday, another set of officials were finalising a very different budget document.
Ireland, in its role holding the EU presidency, was preparing to propose a compromise on the size of the union’s next seven-year budget. The proposal, published on Saturday, suggested chopping €141 billion off the €1.7 trillion draft on the table.
The reduction falls short of the belt-tightening a group of fiscally conservative governments had sought. The “frugal” camp, led by Germany , wants the proposed budget to be several hundred billion euros smaller.
“The numbers that have been put on the table still present a widely unaffordable increase and we are therefore nowhere near an agreement,” said Jessica Rosencrantz, Sweden ’s minister for European affairs.
For others, the compromise drafted by Irish diplomats and politicians went too far and undercut big ambitions for the EU to become a serious geopolitical player.
The bread and butter of the EU’s shared pot – Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) subsidies and “cohesion” money for infrastructure projects in poorer regions – were protected from further cuts.
Instead, Ireland suggested cutbacks to EU international development aid and to scale back a new “competitiveness fund”.
The Irish proposal, known in Brussels bureaucrat-speak as a negotiating box, is the Government’s best stab at nudging the other 26 member states towards a final, messy deal.
[ Increasing levels of debt carried by EU institutions a concern, says top auditor Opens in new window ]
There’s a rush to conclude the budget talks before the French presidential election next spring, on the (very possible) chance the Eurosceptic far-right leader Marine Le Pen is swept to power.
Leaders have set themselves a deadline to strike an agreement by the end of this year.
The budget, which will run from 2028 to 2034, is put together by the European Commission . The EU’s executive body always aims high, in the knowledge its plans will be pared back by national governments.
The EU pot is predominantly financed through national contributions. The net contributors, who chip more in than they get out, are naturally keen to keep a check on spending.
The Irish proposal expectedly reduced the amount budgeted for overseas development aid and the running costs of the EU’s institutions.
The Government also suggested trimming back the size of a bumper “competitiveness fund”. The fund will throw money behind European industry to help efforts to go green, keep pace in the tech race, channel cash into the defence sector, and fund research.
[ Europe is changing, but Ireland has yet to notice Opens in new window ]
Ironically, it is one of the few areas where the Nordic frugals, Germany and the Netherlands , do not want to slash back.
A larger group, led by Italy, Spain and Poland, which includes most southern and eastern member states, made it clear they would fiercely resist reductions in CAP money or “cohesion” funds.
“We protected to the extent the member states wished, the traditional policies of the union, which are very, very important,” Minister for European Affairs Thomas Byrne told a press conference on Saturday.
The seven-year budget needs the support of all 27 EU member states to be approved.
MEPs are unhappy at the proposed cuts, and their concerns shouldn’t be ignored. The European Parliament has to sign off on the final deal as well.
Siegfried Mureșan, one of the parliament’s budget co-negotiators, said the Irish proposal would amount to a smaller package than the existing one, which runs out in 2027, when inflation and other factors were counted in.
“We firmly reject the Irish presidency’s negotiating box ... It cuts defence as threats multiply, reduces investment in competitiveness as Europe loses ground, and leaves farmers and regions underfunded,” the centre-right Romanian politician said.
Senior Irish diplomats have privately remarked that if everyone was unhappy, their negotiating box had done its job: teeing-up the big fight to come between the 27 leaders.

title: Orange Order legal challenge to Garvaghy Road parade ban adjourned to Monday
description: Chris Bryant uses power to intervene and quash Parades Commission decision
content:
A legal challenge to a decision by Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant to halt an Orange Order parade route along the Garvaghy Road in Portadown has been adjourned until Monday.
Lawyers for the Orange Order are applying for the judicial review of the decision announced by Bryant on Friday evening.
Judge Denise McBride said she recognised there was urgency in the case but said it was not an emergency, adding significant material was still to be obtained.
Bryant revoked permission for the Drumcree parade, which had led to a stand-off between Orangemen and nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road in Portadown lasting almost two weeks.
It came after Northern Ireland’s chief constable Jon Boutcher asked Bryant to review the Parades Commission determination which ruled the controversial Orange Order march at Drumcree could go ahead.
The Orange Order is also seeking urgent meetings following the banning of the parade.
Overnight the Orange Order issued a statement to say it is seeking urgent meetings with Bryant and Boutcher in the coming days.
It expressed “profound disappointment” at the decision of the Secretary of State to “overrule the legally established rights of Portadown District Orange Lodge No 1”.
It also claimed a “capitulation to the threat of mob rule and violence”.
“This unprecedented action, and the abdication of responsibility by the Chief Constable, can be seen as nothing more than a capitulation to the threat of mob rule and violence,” it said.
“In stark contrast, the Brethren of Portadown have complied with the rule of law, exercised restraint and maintained a dignified and resolute stand in the face of intimidation and intolerance.
“It is evident that those who, in defiance of the law, have been content to stand alongside the representatives of those who murdered 345 of our members, have no interest in extending any degree of tolerance or respect towards those who share an Orange heritage.
“Furthermore, it is evident that the statutory authorities have neither the will or ability to uphold the law in this instance.
“We commend the Brethren of Portadown for their resolute stand and reinforce their message that this is a time for responsibility and lawfulness.
“We cannot undermine our cause by adopting the illegal and offensive actions of our opponents.
“Urgent meetings with both the Secretary of State and Chief Constable will be sought in the coming days where their decision making and actions in this matter will be robustly challenged.”
In a statement confirming he was now banning the parade, Bryant said he had not taken the decision lightly.
He thanked the Portadown Orangemen “for their peaceful and law-abiding approach and their co-operation at all points with the PSNI”.
He added: “Respect for the rule of law is fundamental to our society and I am grateful to those who have behaved peacefully and legally and sought to ease tensions in their respective communities. Those who have acted unlawfully should face the consequences of their actions.
“I am also grateful to all those who took part in good faith in the negotiations at Hillsborough. I heard the concerns of people on all sides and I only regret that we could not reach a compromise on a way forward and that many residents across Portadown have felt anxious and worried.
“With this in mind, I call for all protests, rallies and demonstrations to be stood down. There is no excuse for a continued ratcheting up of tensions.”
In a statement on behalf of Sinn Féin, the party’s president and Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill welcomed the decision.
“Today belongs to the residents of the Garvaghy Road, who have shown remarkable strength and dignity in the face of provocation and intimidation. There will be an enormous sense of relief within the community this evening,” they said.
But DUP leader Gavin Robinson said: “These decisions are a mistake, and send profound signals that the country should be run on force of numbers and who shouts the loudest.
“The framework for both parading and protests now lies in tatters and the rule of law has been fundamentally undermined ... The PSNI must now pursue the evidence of lawbreaking without fear or favour.”
The parade, on September 27th, was blocked by protesters on the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road and did not go ahead, and a stand-off between the two sides developed.
In his statement, Bryant said: “The chief constable has advised me that it would not be possible to enable the procession to happen without a major intervention which would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect across Northern Ireland.”
He said the Parades Commission had also advised him that, “while ultimately a matter for the courts to determine, the Commission is of the view that, in light of this current assessment by the chief constable, the original determination does not now have enduring legal effect“.
The PNSI’s chief constable welcomed Bryant’s decision, saying he had asked him to review the matter under section 9 of the Public Processions (Northern Ireland) Act 1998.
“I outlined in my letter to the Secretary of State that my current assessment was that all available, lawful and proportionate options to facilitate completion of the procession had been exhausted.
“Any remaining options would have required a substantial public order intervention that was not assessed to be proportionate, and which would have carried an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion affect across Northern Ireland. Further to this, such an operation would in my view have had not only catastrophic long term consequences for trust and confidence in policing, but for the Northern Ireland Executive and the peace process.
“I also outlined in the letter that mediation and political engagement had not produced a sustainable agreement, and the position of the respective parties had become more entrenched.
“Finally, I highlighted that the current and continuing costs and impact upon the Police Service of Northern Ireland were significant and in the context of our existing funding challenges could not be sustained indefinitely.”
Boutcher added: “This past two weeks has had a marked impact on relationships within and between communities and the police. It is in everyone’s interest that time and space is now created for conversations about finding long term solutions to this complex and sensitive issue.”
A judgment in the latest court challenge to the Parades Commission’s original determination is due to be delivered at the Court of Appeal in Belfast on Monday.
Prior to Bryant’s decision, the Orange Order had warned of “serious consequences” if the Northern Secretary stopped the march.
DUP MP Carla Lockhart said on Friday she expected Bryant would “most likely allow for the court hearing” and reiterated her concerns that “the lawful people ... seem to be cast to the side, and the lawbreakers are being rewarded”.
Earlier on Friday it emerged that Northern Ireland’s First Minister, Michelle O’Neill, is to be interviewed by police in relation to her participation in a protest which blocked an Orange march in Portadown.
In a statement on Friday afternoon, O’Neill – who is also the Sinn Féin vice-president – confirmed she had “ received a letter inviting me for a police interview in relation to a peaceful protest on the Garvaghy Road.
“I will co-operate with the investigation.”
She said that “for the last two weeks, I have stood in solidarity with the Garvaghy Road residents as attempts were made to force an unwanted Orange march through their community.
“I will continue to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents who should be allowed to live in peace and free from sectarian intimidation” because “it is always right to stand up for what is right and there can be no going back”.
[ Who is Chris Bryant, Secretary of State for Northern Ireland? Opens in new window ]
Earlier, Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald had told reporters at a press conference on the nationalist Garvaghy Road that she had not received a letter, but expected to.
On Thursday, a senior PSNI officer confirmed the service was issuing letters to those “reasonably suspected” of having committed a criminal offence in relation to the ongoing stand-off in Portadown .
The Irish Times has seen a copy of one of the letters, which informs the recipient that “it is reasonably suspected that you may have committed offences” linked to the protest against the Orange parade in Portadown, and invites the recipient to a “voluntary interview under caution”.
Sinn Féin Senator Conor Murphy , and MLAs John O’Dowd (Minister for Finance in the Northern Assembly), Gerry Kelly and Deirdre Hargey have received them.
“There will be processes now, legal processes, investigative processes that will be under way, and of course, just like every citizen, of course we are subject to the law, and we will co-operate with it,” McDonald said.
She reiterated her party’s call on Northern Secretary to step in to resolve the dispute, saying she had spoken to him on Friday morning “urging him again to act”.
People Before Profit MLA Gerry Carroll said on Thursday he had been invited by police to attend a voluntary interview under caution in connection with the protest.
It is understood that, as of Friday afternoon, no SDLP members had received letters.
SDLP leader Claire Hanna told The Irish Times she recognises that she may receive such a letter in the coming days.
A statement said she would “always be accountable for her actions and will engage fully with any policing or judicial process”, but “when faced with a choice between standing with the Garvaghy Road community or doing nothing, she is clear that she made the correct decision”.
[ Sinn Féin and the DUP are happier arguing over a parade than agreeing a budget Opens in new window ]
This year was the first time in 28 years that the march, which in the 1990s sparked serious violence which led to more than 20 deaths, was given permission to proceed by the Parades Commission , the body which rules on applications for marches in Northern Ireland.
The decision has been the subject of multiple legal challenges, and the latest judgment is expected in the Court of Appeal next week.
The Garvaghy Road protest was not notified to the Parades Commission, and as an “unnotified” parade is therefore deemed illegal.

title: Palestine president Mahmoud Abbas postpones legislative elections
description: New date in September 2027 set for elections, as well as a vote on the presidency
content:
Palestine’s president Mahmoud ‌Abbas on Saturday cancelled legislative elections scheduled for November due to worsening conditions within the Palestinian ‌territories.
Abbas set a date of September 11th, 2027, for both presidential and legislative elections, ​the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.
Abbas’s decree cited “obstacles posed by Israeli measures” to holding elections in November and the need to establish suitable political, security and on-the-ground conditions ​for “free, fair and inclusive elections”.
It called on Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank and ⁠ Gaza to participate in the polls.
There had been serious doubts that ‌the ‌ Palestinian ​Authority vote would go ahead in late November.
[ Game over: Inside the ruins of Gaza’s football stadiums Opens in new window ]
The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since ⁠2005-2006, after which Abbas’s rival, the Islamist group Hamas, ​seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists.
The decree said Israeli military ‌attacks, settlement expansion, settler violence and ​movement restrictions in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, along with Israel’s continued ⁠withholding of Palestinian tax ⁠revenues, created challenges ​to preparing for and holding elections on the previous date.
In Gaza, the decree pointed to “exceptional security and humanitarian conditions”, the incomplete withdrawal of Israeli forces, the lack of progress in reconstruction and the failure to implement arrangements for deploying international stabilisation forces and police.
[ In pictures: Three years of war in Gaza Opens in new window ]
Israeli restrictions on access for election commission staff and international observers to ‌Gaza and East ⁠Jerusalem also complicated preparations, the decree said.
The decision to postpone followed a resolution by the Palestine Liberation Organisation ’s executive committee and consultations ‌with Palestinian factions and political forces.
It also aimed to allow time for a comprehensive ​Palestinian national dialogue to strengthen unity and address ​challenges facing the electoral process. – Reuters

title: Wallabies blown away by All Blacks blitz to retain Bledisloe Cup
description: Les Kiss’s side given second-half reality check in Auckland
content:
New Zealand preserved rugby’s established hierarchy with a 50-19 blowout victory over Australia that secures the Bledisloe Cup for a 24th year and pushes the All Blacks’ unbeaten run over the Wallabies at Eden Park into a fifth decade.
The Wallabies lost touch with their hosts in the second half despite a valiant but futile defensive performance led by the captain Harry Wilson, who had scored a try just before half-time to keep his side in the contest.
Les Kiss’s side will return home bruised and disappointed, with their unbeaten run extinguished at six matches. Most of all, however, they will rue a missed opportunity early in the second half that marked the match’s decisive point.
An attacking lineout five metres from the All Blacks’ tryline was comfortably brought to ground, but the Wallabies’ forwards were over-eager in forming the maul. The ensuing obstruction penalty and the All Blacks’ patience in possession flipped the field, and beginning with a try for their scrumhalf Cam Roigard, the hosts were soon out of reach.
Wilson said the result was disappointing. “We came in tonight with real belief that we’d get the result and we didn’t,” he told Stan Sport. “We’ve been on a good trajectory, we’ve gotten some good results, six games in a row [unbeaten], and this was probably a setback for us because we didn’t win those big moments and as a team we try to pride ourselves on that.
“[At the] start of the second half, we had an opportunity to get some points and really put some pressure on them and we missed out there and, gee whiz, when you give the All Blacks the ball it’s hard to get it back.”
The imperious New Zealanders scored five tries in the second half and kept the Wallabies scoreless until a late consolation try from Josh Nasser. The All Blacks reached 50 points at the final whistle with a runaway try for Will Jordan.
Though the defeat will sting, and continues the All Blacks’ long dominance in their trans-Tasman series and at Eden Park, the Wallabies will find positives in pushing the world’s No 2-ranked side at their site of historic dominance for the first 50 minutes.
The second period, however, shows how much work Kiss and his players need to do if they hope to contend for the World Cup on home soil next year. Indeed, another heavy loss to the All Blacks in Sydney next week will undo much of the momentum cultivated under their first-year head coach.
The Wallabies dominated the early proceedings, and had the home side pinned inside their half for the first 10 minutes of the match. Their confidence was obvious when Wilson declined the opportunity to kick for goal.
Although a Len Ikitau knock-on prevented a try following that promising position, the visitors were soon over anyway. A lovely backline move from around the halfway line, featuring a delicate tip on from five-eighth Ben Donaldson that sent a streaking Tom Wright over for the first try.
The Wallabies looked immaculate, and very much the side that had knocked off the world champion Springboks. It proved a mirage.
Donaldson kicked out on the full when the Wallabies were looking to consolidate their advantage, and the contest turned. Within five minutes, they found themselves down by two tries to one. Both could be put down to defensive lapses in the midfield, where the All Blacks carved up the gold jerseys like they were butter in the afternoon sun.
Apart from that initial 10 minutes, the All Blacks spent most of the first half in control. After 29 minutes, they turned down the chance for a penalty goal. Though an error prevented a score in that forward foray, they were soon up by 10 thanks to another penalty.
The Wallabies produced their best series of phases just before half-time, however, to haul themselves back into the contest. Strong running from Joseph Aukuso-Suaalii helped them march into the New Zealand half, then interplay between Wilson and Donaldson cracked open the home side just outside the 22.
All Blacks’ No 8 Wallace Sititi was committed to the straight run of Wallabies’ flanker Rob Valetini, creating space on the outside for Donaldson who slipped through the gap. Wilson remained alive for the inside ball, crossing for a try that left the contest evenly poised at 17-14 at half-time.
Though the Wallabies’ tries book-ended the first 40, it was largely controlled by the All Blacks. Australia remained in the contest thanks to their lineout, which secured possession twice against the throw via the stretched left arm of Jeremy Williams, who also forced a turnover at the ruck. The Australia defence shored up after their early leaks, but their effort was not enough.
Roigard’s 48th minute try became the first in a procession, added to by captain Codie Taylor, substitute Josh Moorby, Jordan, and winger Leroy Carter. The latter was unfortunately forced off injured when scoring due to an apparent hip drop tackle by Valetini. – Guardian

title: The most interesting assessment of the budget is the one you haven’t yet heard
description: Despite the corporate tax boom, Irish budgets are not boosting real spending power. There’s one good reason for that
content:
Y ou’d be best to ignore most of the debate on the budget . The performative nature of it all would wear you out. The Minister for Finance riding to the rescue of people who are “getting up early or staying in work late”. Sinn Féin’s Pearse Doherty dismissing it as “an insult to workers”.
