The trade unions calling it as a “halfhearted apology” for last October’s decision not to have an income tax package and not enough to get them to call off industrial action. You could have written it all beforehand.
What is the reality? Perhaps the most interesting assessment came from the researchers at the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) . The headline is that the budget tax and welfare changes more or less made up for expected inflation next year, with slightly bigger gains for some less well-off sections of the community. In other words, Budget 2027 was neither a triumph nor a disaster for living standards.
The basis for this falls into the basket of a bit wonky but nonetheless important. The ESRI looks at inflation and expected wage increases next year and asks what the budget will mean to a sample section of the population. Its conclusion is that spending power will more or less mark time for most groups. In other words, if you get a 4 per cent pay rise, then the budget does enough to ensure tax does not take a bit more of your income. And people on welfare have been broadly insulated from higher inflation – some of the basic increases were on the low side, while some specifics like the extra disability allowance helped.
Nor is this unusual. The ESRI’s assessment is that this has generally been the case over the last seven budgets. Tax and welfare changes have more or less adjusted for inflation, with the less well-off doing a bit better. In other words, there has been no great change in living standards since before the pandemic due to budget policy, bar a bit of extra support for the least well-off.
[ Budget 2027: Big business pays the bills as Coalition rolls the dice Opens in new window ]
It took a fair bit of cash to achieve this. Ireland’s budget this year is way ahead of others published so far across the EU, many still in draft form. According to figures from Ibec, the business lobby, the discretionary budget measures – the extra tax and spending – per head of population for 2027 will be €1,500 in Ireland, compared with under €100 in Finland and the Netherlands and minus €600 in France. The Coalition has room to put inflation protections in the welfare and tax systems; France is facing into a period of austerity.
You would have to reflect that, despite the corporate tax boom, Irish budgets are not boosting real spending power. One missing piece to the puzzle here is the rising Irish population, up by 600,000 people or 14 per cent since before the pandemic. Total employment has risen by more than 19 per cent over the same period. It costs more for the Government to provide services and give any tax relief. Irish budgets have, in part, been running to try to keep up. Spending growth of 9 to 10 per cent annually has been too high, but part of the story is providing healthcare, education and so on for a bigger population.
This standstill in spending power probably explains an element of public grumpiness. So do fears that official inflation forecasts undershoot the likely trend over the winter. Voters are told that the economy is booming – and it is. More jobs are being created. The number of better-off households has grown sharply. But there are also many who don’t have more cash at the end of the month and could be hit hard by higher fuel costs over the winter. And a middle ground not feeling better off. Spending power has not soared alongside GDP.
There are, of course, options for reform. An Irish government could, for example, plan to raise tax elsewhere to cut the burden on low and middle earners. Sinn Féin and the other Opposition parties generally favour higher tax on the €100,000-plus earners to fund some relief elsewhere. But the more economically sensible routes to move tax away from incomes – like taxing property more heavily, for example, are off the table. Sinn Féin even wants to abolish the local property tax. Nobody argues for significantly lower spending growth.
So don’t expect any big reforming budgets in the near future. In the short term, tax bands and credits and welfare rates will be nudged along, at least for as long as corporate taxes keep flowing in. Budgets will continue to be “bigged up” by the minister of the day and damned by the angry opposition – and the sugar rush will continue to be quick. In a sensible world, the tax and welfare systems would be adjusted automatically for expected inflation. But Irish politics doesn’t do sensible very well.
[ What are the key takeaways from Budget 2027? From income tax cuts to surprising omissions Opens in new window ]
Without any real boost to living standards from budgets, the more fundamental public concerns remain about delivery. They focus on areas like the availability and price of houses – up more than 50 per cent since 2019; social services, which are struggling to cope with a larger population and creaking infrastructure. Crowded and inadequate public transport, lack of social housing, waste, water and power infrastructure are all struggling to keep up. There are too few childcare places – the budget impact here remains to be fully fleshed out. And so on. These have a real impact on people’s lives – and often knock-on costs in time and money. But from Government they require relentless focus and a lot of grinding work to deliver.
This is where the budget still sent some unsettling messages. The chaotic negotiations that led up to it do not suggest a coherent Coalition with a clear focus. The post-budget debate focused on things that were not planned at all by the wider Cabinet – notably threatened cuts to the RTÉ budget .
Budgets can only skate over the surface in a lot of areas, at most setting a direction. There was good, bad and average in this one. The welcome increase in State investment goes on. But the chaotic run-in does not inspire confidence – there really must be a better way to do it than a multilateral, complex, negotiating process that ends up as a zero-sum game for Ministers and leaves a lot of last-minute decisions. It is no way to run a railroad.

title: Dáil sitting next Wednesday cancelled due public sector workers’ strike
description: Government had provisionally scheduled a full day of Dáil business but this was contingent on staff at Leinster House being available
content:
The Dáil sitting scheduled for next Wednesday has been cancelled because of a planned one-day national strike by public sector workers.
A majority of the employees in Leinster House are members of public sector unions that have signalled a daylong strike on Wednesday, followed by further industrial action the following week.
The Government had provisionally scheduled a full day of Dáil business for Wednesday. However, this was contingent on staff at Leinster House being available to facilitate the sitting.
An emergency meeting of the Dáil business committee is scheduled for Saturday afternoon to discuss the situation.
A spokesman for Government chief whip Mary Butler said the committee would discuss parliamentary business for Tuesday and Thursday only, meaning there would be no sitting on Wednesday.
Social Democrats deputy leader Cian O’Callaghan welcomed the decision to suspend the sitting. “I am pleased that the Government has seen sense and has climbed down,” he said.
He added that the Social Democrats and other Opposition TDs had made clear they would not cross a picket line during Wednesday’s strike action. O’Callaghan also criticised Taoiseach Micheál Martin ’s initial response to the dispute.
[ Public sector strike ‘inevitable’ and will see up to 150,000 medical appointments cancelled Opens in new window ]
Martin had said Dáil business should go ahead next Wednesday, though Labour and Sinn Féin said they would not pass pickets at Leinster House.
Butler, who is responsible for proposing the business of the Dáil, told a meeting of the Dáil’s business committee on Thursday that the Dáil should sit as normal for three days next week.
Labour whip Duncan Smith welcomed the move after Labour called for TDs not to cross the picket line, and called on the Government to now “engage properly” on future pay for public sector workers.
“Labour made it clear we would not be passing a picket line outside the Dáil next Wednesday, and called on the Government not to go through a Dáil sitting that would force their own backbenchers to break a picket,” he said.
“This action would also have been at the expense of our own Private Members’ time debate. The revised Dáil schedule circulated today recognises that principled position but does not change the underlying issue that has led to this strike.”
[ Public sector pay dispute ‘unwarranted given our willingness to talk’, Taoiseach says Opens in new window ]
Preparations are under way for the strike, which will see more than 300,000 public sector workers undertake a 24-hour work stoppage in pursuit of a new public sector pay deal, though essential services will be maintained.
Another strike is scheduled for the following Wednesday, while senior union figures are privately warning of escalation of their action in November if negotiations do not get under way in the coming weeks.
Widespread disruption is inevitable as schools and other public services also close. There is little expectation in trade-union or Government circles that the strike can be averted at this stage, with senior union figures stressing the frustration felt among their members.
The Taoiseach has said there was no need for the strikes and that the €1.2 billion provision in the budget this week was a basis for negotiations, but unions dismissed the figure as insufficient.

title: Income from ‘broken’ television licence fee down €5.7m in first nine months
description: Projected 715,401 television licences to be sold for the year likely to generate about €114.46m, down €8.5m on last year
content:
Income from the television licence fee continues to decline, with €5.7 million less collected to date this year compared with the same period last year.
New figures provided by Minister for Media Patrick O’Donovan show 536,551 licences have been sold for the first nine months of this year, which represents TV licence income of €85.86 million.
In figures provided to Social Democrats TD Aidan Farrelly in response to a written Dáil question, O’Donovan said the number of licences sold to the end of September was down 35,748, or 6 per cent.
The income generated was €91.56 million, down €5.7 million year on year.
Based on the data for the first nine months, the income generated from the projected 715,401 television licences to be sold for the 12 months of 2026 is likely to be about €114.46 million.
That would represent a €37.2 million hit on the €151.66 million in TV licence revenue generated by the 792,000 licences sold in 2022, which predated the RTÉ payments controversy of 2023.
The projected €114.46 million for this year will be €8.5 million down on the €122.98 million generated from the sale of 768,657 licences in 2025.
In response to the figures, Farrelly, who is member of the Public Accounts Committee , said: “The TV licence system is not just fundamentally broken, it has collapsed.”
Farrelly said the figures provided demonstrated a prevailing theme. “There is no doubt that the TV licence system needs an overhaul and full reform. It is not fit for purpose,” he said.
[ RTÉ funding snub not a good look for Patrick O’Donovan Opens in new window ]
“It is an area I intend to explore with RTÉ and the department when they are before the Public Accounts Committee.”
The €160 TV licence is collected by An Post and the revenues go to the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport , which provides about 85 per cent to RTÉ to carry out its public service media commitments.
A further 7 per cent is paid to Coimisiún na Meán and An Post is paid approximately 6 per cent of the licence fee in respect of television licence collection activities.
In his reply, O’Donovan told Farrelly: “In July 2024, the Government agreed to retain the TV licence system, underpinned by new measures designed to improve collection and compliance in order to maximise revenue generation.
“To this end, the interdepartmental technical working group on the reform and enhancement of the television licence was reconvened by Government in order to examine potential administrative, technical and legislative measures.”
He said the group submitted its report to him before the summer recess.
[ RTÉ likely to get back €20m lost in Budget 2027 ‘if it proves reforms are on track’ Opens in new window ]
“I intend to bring the report to Government shortly to decide on the next steps,” O’Donovan said. “The timing of the publication of the report will be contingent on when this decision is made.
“It would not be appropriate for me to disclose the contents of the report prior to it being considered by Government.”
Asked to comment on the television licence model, a spokesman for RTÉ said: “While we believe clarification regarding funding of public service media is vital, questions regarding the funding mechanism are for Government.”
Along with the RTÉ payments controversy, the number of TV licences sold has also been hit by the increase in households without a TV set.
Another issue the system faces is an ageing population, which means the number of households that qualify for a free licence increases every year by between 13,000 and 20,000.

title: FAI reveals ‘inconsistencies’ in Garda vetting process for coaches and match officials
description: Up to 60 coaches in the League of the Ireland have yet to be approved by the vetting system, a source informed The Irish Times
content:
The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) has written to its registered clubs and coaches to inform them of “inconsistencies” in the “recording and validation” of Garda vetting information.
Up to 60 coaches in the League of Ireland have yet to be approved by the vetting system, a source informed The Irish Times.
The FAI also issued instructions to clubs this week to not play under-18 players on teams with coaches that have not been Garda vetted.
The association said in a statement on Friday night that it was “undertaking a comprehensive review of safeguarding compliance records”.
“Following a review by the FAI safeguarding department, inconsistencies were identified in the recording and validation of Garda vetting information on FAI Connect,” the statement said.
“The association is now undertaking a comprehensive verification and reconciliation of its compliance records.
“What does this mean for you [as coaches]? All registrations of coaches, staff and officials of children’s teams or vulnerable persons require Garda vetting, where current compliance cannot be verified.”
The FAI also said that clubs and individuals remain responsible for ensuring Garda vetting requirements are satisfied “before undertaking relevant roles”.
FAI chief executive David Courell, speaking during an appearance before the Oireachtas sports committee, said the Girls in Green documentary by Mark Tighe and Marie Crowe, had “shone a light on an evolving situation across all aspects of Irish society in terms of adult safeguarding”.
[ FAI tells Uefa gathering about Ireland team’s experiences during Israel games Opens in new window ]
“That is something to which the association has taken a huge amount of energy and focus,” Courell said. “We have introduced that new role of head of safeguarding.
“We are pivoting the organisation from a child welfare and safeguarding focus to an expanded adult and child welfare safeguarding focus.”
When Fianna Fáil TD Pádraig O’Sullivan asked the FAI delegation last month if all the registered referees and coaches in the country had been Garda vetted, the association’s director of football John Martin said there were 1,400 referees “licensed and Garda vetted”.
“The list of all the referees was communicated to the relevant leagues around the country,” he said.
“All the referee records on FAI Connect are updated on an ongoing, continual basis, whereas their licences are renewed annually.”

title: Ireland’s EU presidency proposes budget cut of €141bn for the bloc
description: Compromise package follows months of behind-the-scenes negotiations
content:
The European Union’s next seven-year budget should avoid any further cuts to agriculture subsidies, but scale back ambitions for overseas aid spending and an economic “competitiveness” fund, the Government has proposed.
Ireland, in its dealmaking role holding the Council of the EU presidency, has tabled a revision to the bloc’s draft common budget, which member states will spend the coming months fighting over.
The Government, in a proposal published on Saturday, pitched cutting €141 billion from an existing draft budget package of €1.76 trillion.
This would result ⁠in ​a budget ​of €1.6 trillion, ‌subject to contentious negotiations ​among EU countries ⁠in ⁠the ​coming months. The EU budget is the main source ‌of financing ⁠for all of the 27-country bloc’s ‌main policies.
EU leaders will discuss a scaled back budget when they meet in Brussels next week after negotiators slashed the initial proposal in response to pressure from some member states .
Ireland, which holds the bloc’s rotating presidency, presented a compromise plan on the EU’s next seven-year budget on Saturday.
The proposal “is the product of intensive exchanges undertaken by the Irish presidency with member states and EU institutions over the last three months”, Europe Minister Thomas Byrne said in advance of a press conference in Brussels on Saturday.
The compromise package follows months of behind-the-scenes negotiations on the budget, known as the multiannual financial framework. European Council president Antonio Costa, who chairs meetings of EU leaders, is pushing for a deal by December.
The size and scope of the EU’s seven-year budget has long been a subject of contention, with countries like Germany, Austria and the Netherlands advocating a smaller package while other member states including Italy and Spain are opposed to cuts.
There have been growing calls for the EU to direct spending away from areas like agriculture and funding for poorer countries – which have traditionally represented more than half of EU spending – to new priorities such as research and innovation as well as defence.
Under Ireland’s proposal, money for the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and cohesion funds – those earmarked for less affluent EU members – will be protected. Instead, the reduction from the earlier €2 trillion proposed price tag will be offset by cuts to development funding, administration, and the bloc’s competitiveness fund, relative to the initial proposal.
[ Increasing levels of debt carried by EU institutions a concern, says top auditor Opens in new window ]
The bulk of the EU’s budget is financed by contributions from member states, with so-called “net contributors” coughing up most of the money. Germany has been one of the most critical voices, dismissing the commission’s initial price tag hours after it was presented last year as “unacceptable”.
The proposed cut is unlikely to be enough to appease the so-called “frugal” member states. Speaking alongside Costa on Friday evening in advance of the announcement, Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten said a budget increase compared with the previous seven-year budget was “simply not viable at a time when national budgets are already under pressure”.
Jetten said the budget must reflect concerns such as security, economic resilience and competitiveness. “We cannot just saddle our citizens with high costs unless we offer solutions to today’s challenges,” he said.
Irish Farmers’ Association president Francie Gorman described the budget, including the allocation for CAP, as “a huge let down” for Irish farmers.
“In the original commission proposal, the EU CAP budget was cut by 22 per cent which would result in a 24 per cent cut to Irish payments,” he said. “The Irish presidency proposal today has not improved this at all. It is huge let down for Irish and EU farmers.
“Farmers will feel that EU is turning their back on farming and that the Irish Government is not delivering for them.
“The proposal today is to allocate €293 billion to the EU CAP budget. EU farmers need €500 billion to build on-farm resilience, to encourage young people into our sector, to ensure food security and to enhance the sustainability of a very fragile sector,” he added.
Irish MEP Barry Andrews, who is chairman of the development committee at the European Parliament, described cuts to development co-operation as a “serious error”.
“The Irish presidency’s negotiating box for the next EU budget proposes to cut Global Europe, the EU global development co-operation funding, by around 17 per cent,” he said. “This would be a serious error, and one Europe will pay for with its own security and standing in the world.
“Our neighbourhood is more unstable than at any point in a generation. Conflict, democratic backsliding and climate shocks are driving displacement and fragility on our borders and beyond.
“At the same time, the withdrawal of US development funding has opened a gap that partners, and our competitors, are already moving to fill.
“Reducing our own external action now would mean retreating at the moment our partners most need reliability and our own interests and long-term security are most exposed.”
Andrews said development co-operation “is not charity” but how Europe “prevents crises rather than paying far more to manage them”.
“It underpins stability in our neighbourhood, supports partners who share our interests and values, and gives Europe a credible alternative to the offers of other powers. A smaller Global Europe means less influence, less leverage and less security.
“The European Parliament has consistently called for an external action budget that matches the EU’s ambitions and responsibilities. A cut of this size is incompatible with those ambitions, and with the commitments Member States have made on development, humanitarian response and global partnerships.” – Additional reporting: Bloomberg/Reuters

title: Offaly man (30) pleads guilty to sexual assault and rape of younger sister
description: ‘Watching my parents continue to support my abuser while I try to rebuild my life is one of the most painful experiences,’ victim says
content:
A woman who was sexually abused by her older brother throughout her childhood has described the pain of losing her family when she disclosed the years of trauma he put her through.
The now 30-year-old Offaly man pleaded guilty to eight counts of sexual assault and one count of raping his younger sister in their family home on dates between 2010 and 2017. The pleas were entered on a full facts basis, prosecuting counsel Philipp Rahn told the Central Criminal Court .
The abuse started when the girl was aged eight years old, but the charges on the indictment are from when she was 10 and he was 14 years old, the court heard. The abuse ended when she left the family home at the age of 18.
A local detective garda told the court that the abuse occurred when the girl was asleep in bed and initially took the form of inappropriate touching and grinding against her. She pretended to be asleep throughout, the court heard. If she moved, he would leave the room and return when he thought she was sleeping again.
It occurred on a near nightly basis, the court heard.
The rape occurred when she fell asleep on the sitting room couch one night, the court heard, and awoke to find her brother raping her. On another occasion, he tried to anally rape her.
The abuse stopped for a year when the then teenage girl became pregnant with her first child with her boyfriend, but resumed after her baby was born. At the age of 18, with her mental health deteriorating, she moved out to live with a relative.
When she returned to live in the family home about a year later, she awoke to find him in her bed with his hand on her neck. She screamed at him to get off her, threatening to stab him. He never went near her again, the court heard.
The woman disclosed the abuse to a counsellor and made a statement to gardaí in 2023. The man was arrested and interviewed, but denied abusing his sister. He entered the guilty pleas on the first day of his trial last May.
In her victim impact statement, which she read herself to the court, the woman described how the abuse robbed her of her childhood and also of her family – as she said her parents have chosen to stand by her brother.
“Watching my parents continue to support my abuser while I try to rebuild my life is one of the most painful experiences,” she said.
The woman said she spent years living in “fear and silence”. “I lost my sense of safety, my trust in people, the support of my parents, when I needed them the most.”
She said one of the hardest things was having to accept that it was her brother who caused her so much pain. “He was someone I should have been able to trust. Instead, he took away my sense of safety.”
She said the trauma has followed her throughout her life and she suffers with anxiety, intrusive thoughts, nightmares and night terrors. She dreads going to sleep at night.
She said she has found her voice and is glad she told her truth. “I did not choose what happened to me – the years of fear, trauma and the loss of my family,” she said. She continues to rebuild her life with the support of her children, she said.
Defending counsel Diarmuid Collins read out a letter of apology from the man, in which he said: “I am genuinely sorry for the hell I put you through.”
“As the oldest sibling, I should have had your back,” he said. “There is a special place in hell for someone like me ... I won’t ask for forgiveness as what I did was unforgivable.”
A letter from the siblings’ mother was also read out in court, in which she said she loved both her children and regretted not knowing what was happening.
“As parents we failed,” she said. “We didn’t protect [our daughter] nor get [our son] help before it got to a stage of no return. All we can try to do is be there for both of them.”
In his plea of mitigation, Collins said the man lives at home with his parents, works for a local company and lives an “isolated” existence. He has not had any meaningful romantic relationships.
A psychological report found the man has low intellectual functioning. His mother reported he would struggle to live on his own.
Judge Karen O’Connor set a sentence date of November 6th and remanded the man in custody. She commended the woman for her bravery in coming forward about the abuse.

title: One child has been killed in Gaza every day since the so-called ceasefire
description: The killing and deprivation cannot be normalised
content:
Sir, – As we mark one year of the so-called Gaza ceasefire, the world must ask what it actually means for the almost two million people who are still displaced and living in dire conditions.
The ceasefire exists only in name and has not delivered protection or recovery. There must also be accountability for what happened to civilians in Israel on October 7th, 2023 .
What does the ceasefire mean for the mother whose desperately sick child cannot get urgently needed medication? Or the family who are hungry because they can’t get enough food?
Since the so-called ceasefire, one child has been killed a day in Gaza , and more than 1,400 Palestinians in total.
The reality is that not one of Gaza’s 36 hospitals is fully operational. More than 18,500 patients, including at least 4,000 children, need medical evacuation. More than 1,000 patients have died waiting.
There are 1.4 million people facing hunger and disease with food supplies scarce, and bombed sanitation systems continuing to drive the spread of preventable disease.
Women and girls are suffering most. Nearly one in four households is headed by a woman.
Devastated health services mean pregnant women with potentially fatal complications go without care. There is a significant increase in women seeking obstetric and gynaecological care due to miscarriage, threatened miscarriage, pregnancy-related bleeding, hypertension, severe anaemia and other conditions closely linked to extremely challenging conditions.
Another harsh winter is around the corner and families living in shelters and tents will freeze and be washed out with floods. The closure of crucial border points and the Israeli restrictions on life-saving aid and construction materials are threatening lives and hampering recovery.
More than 100 humanitarian, human rights and other civil society organisations, including ActionAid, have signed a statement saying that the killing and deprivation in Gaza cannot be normalised under the cover of a ceasefire agreement. They say the ceasefire exists in name only and has not delivered protection or recovery.
Ireland must use every diplomatic channel, including its presidency of the council of the European Union, to demand an end to attacks on civilians, unhindered humanitarian access and materials needed to rebuild.
It must also press for accountability under international law.
The test of a ceasefire is whether people can live safely. This test has miserably failed for the people of Gaza. – Yours, etc,

title: Cyclist killed following collision with a van in Co Clare
description: The driver of the van, a man aged in his 30s, was uninjured, while road remains closed with local diversions in place
content:
A cyclist has died following a collision with a van in Co Clare on Friday.
Gardaí have appealing for witnesses following a fatal two-vehicle road traffic crash on the N67 at Baunmore, Kilrush, that occurred at about 8pm.
The incident involved a van and a bicycle. The male cyclist was pronounced dead at the scene.
His body was taken to the mortuary at University Hospital Limerick where a postmortem examination will take place in due course.
The coroner has been notified. The driver of the van, a man aged in his 30s, was uninjured.
The road remains closed with local diversions in place.
Anyone who may have been travelling in the area of Baunmore, Kilrush, Co Clare, on Friday between 7.15pm and 8.15pm, and who may have camera footage or mobile phone recordings, are asked to make this footage available to investigating gardaí.

title: Hurricane Isaias weakens to post-tropical cyclone after making landfall in Florida Panhandle
description: Emergency services urge residents to shelter in place and watch for hurricane conditions
author_name: David Ovalle, Rick Rojas, Soumya Karlamangla, Laura Chung
content:
Hurricane Isaias made landfall late Friday on the Florida Panhandle, lashing the Gulf Coast with heavy rains and howling winds that toppled trees, flooded coastal highways and left hundreds of thousands of people without power.
The storm’s eye came ashore about 8.30pm Central time near Destin, Florida , on a stretch of barrier islands with evacuated beach towns. Isaias landed as a category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105mph, and quickly dropped over the next half-hour to a category 1 storm with winds of 85mph.
By 1am Central time, Isaias degraded to a post-tropical cyclone, with winds of 65mph, the National Weather Service said.
Forecasters warned residents near the storm’s centre to expect powerful wind gusts, and to take shelter as though a tornado were approaching. Some 4 to 7 inches of rain had fallen across parts of the Florida Panhandle even before landfall, with downpours continuing to soak the area.
The US National Hurricane Center warned against a life-threatening storm surge affecting the Gulf Coast as dangerous hurricane conditions and flash floods spread ​inland.
The hurricane is expected to cross Alabama and ​into the Tennessee Valley on the weekend, the agency added.
Nearly ‌380,000 ⁠people in Florida and more than 210,000 in Alabama were left without power as the storm hit shore, the website Poweroutage.us showed.
Isaias is the first Atlantic hurricane of the year, arriving late in a relatively quiet season. It had been two years since a hurricane, Milton, made landfall in the mainland United States, striking the west coast of Florida near Sarasota in 2024.
Heavy flooding is expected to follow landfall. The western half of the Panhandle is likely to see the most dangerous conditions, with forecasters predicting that the water could rise 6 to 9 feet along the coast.
In some beach towns, visitors and tourists appeared to heed local officials’ warnings to evacuate or stay away, leaving hotels and restaurants empty during a typically busy season.
Flight disruptions have been mostly limited to smaller airports in the Panhandle through landfall, though airlines warned that could change as the storm moves inland.
This article originally appeared in The New York Times . Additional reporting: Reuters

title: How can runaway spending in the health service be reined in?
description: The budget overrun in the health service could reach €1bn by the end of year, despite spending curbs being put in place
content:
T he health service’s warning sign came early, like the smell of smoke before the flames.
It took only the first three months of the year – a period that sent the Health Service Executive ’s (HSE) 2026 financial deficit to €250 million – for senior health officials to become concerned.
The first quarter is always a difficult time financially. Winter illnesses lead to increased numbers of people attending hospital emergency departments and higher than typical rates of sickness among healthcare staff. This, in turn, leads to the health service needing more agency staff to provide cover, which, in turn, leads to higher costs.
This year marked the first time funding was devolved into the newly established six health regions, which would be responsible for managing their own individual budgets.
HSE chief executive Anne O’Connor put three of the six HSE regions – HSE Dublin and Midlands, HSE Dublin and South East, and HSE South West – into what is known as “tier three escalation”, which triggered employment controls and greater scrutiny on spending.
It wasn’t enough. The figures deteriorated further over the summer, resulting in what appeared to be a loss of patience within Government and a dramatic U-turn in policy by September.
Four of the six regions were stripped of their powers to oversee day-to-day spending, with Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers indicating this would continue into next year.
These regions are the West and North West, the South West, Dublin and South East, and Dublin and Midlands regions
The deficit has continued to climb, reaching €781 million by the end of September – 8.6 per cent higher than the same period last year, despite the sector only receiving a 5 per cent budget uplift during that time.
The Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO), which provides independent analysis and advice to the Oireachtas, warns the trajectory risks an estimated overrun in health of €1 billion by the end of year.
The Government maintains that steps are being taken to prevent the deficit from reaching this level, but concerns abound nevertheless.
According to the PBO, health is a “consistent source of current expenditure overruns, accounting for a large share of the total overrun expenditure in recent years”.
But if the health system is no stranger to financial overruns, what is causing them and what can be done to prevent them?
[ Hospital waiting lists climb above one million people Opens in new window ]
Each October, when the Government unveils its annual budget for the following year, the headlines announce that a record health budget has been allocated.
Next year it will receive €29.1 billion, rising from the €27.4 billion budget this year, but Opposition parties fear this uplift in funding will largely be swallowed by the gaping hole in this year’s accounts.
Killian Carroll, senior economist at fiscal watchdog the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (Ifac), says health overruns are often discussed as a failure to control spending during the year.
“But some of the problems start earlier, when budgets are set. In health, and especially in hospitals, budgets have repeatedly been set as if the previous year’s actual level of spending did not happen,” he said in analysis published before the budget in September on the council’s website.
“This means they have implicitly assumed large savings from efficiency or better care models, even though similar savings failed to materialise in previous years.”
Carroll says a “realistic” budget must be set for health in order to avoid overruns, with Ifac advocating for multiannual funding.
[ It takes a giveaway budget of €8.5bn to not annoy anyone – except Patrick O’Donovan Opens in new window ]
This is an argument many of the voluntary hospitals – HSE-funded organisations that are run by their own boards of management – also make.
A recent survey of voluntary hospitals, which includes Beaumont Hospital, the Mater and St Vincent’s in Dublin, found almost two thirds (63 per cent) reported carrying deficits accumulated over previous years.
Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill said this year’s deficit has been largely driven by two elements: the pay bill and the increasing cost of drugs and medicines.
Medicines was a success story, but an expensive one, she said, adding that the pay bill is something that “we can control”.
“There was provision for 3,300 people on average salaries to be recruited in the second half of 2026 – contingent on reducing overtime and agency spend,” she told The Irish Times earlier this week at a post-budget press conference.
“Unfortunately, 3,600 people were recruited in the first half of the year without the commensurate and necessary reduction in agency and overtime.”
Last month she singled out Cork University Hospital as a hospital that exceeded its pay budget, after it hired 233 people this year.
“That is more than any other Model 4 hospital in the country, and that includes Beaumont, the Mater, St James and UHL [University Hospital Limerick] and by some distance,” she said.
Agency spend and overtime are consistently pointed to as a reason behind breaching budgets.
The HSE is setting up staff banks – established within the HSE with the aim of replicating the flexibility of agency staff at a better value cost.
But senior sources have suggested expenditure on agency has actually increased in recent months as tighter employment controls take effect.
Two regions – Dublin and North East, and the Mid West – have stayed within budget.
The Minister said the West and North West, which covers Donegal, Sligo, Leitrim, Roscommon, Mayo, and Galway, has improved its position, and may come in less than 2 per cent over budget by end of year.
But the other three areas have “over-recruited” this year, she said, and “very clearly have eaten into next year’s [budget] provision”.
[ Budget day has lost all excitement. It is now an attritional struggle between ministers Opens in new window ]
Ronan Mahon, lecturer in health economics at the University of Galway, said this could serve as an “incentive” for regions to stay within their budget, rather than being “rewarded” with additional funding when they exceed it.
“If you look to the UK, the care trust have a statutory break-even requirement. They just have to do it. There are equivalents in other countries as well,” he says.
Carroll MacNeill has consistently criticised the productivity of the health service, saying there has not been a commensurate increase in activity to match the investment into the system.
Government focus has been on increasing evening and weekend working shifts, primarily driven by the public-only consultant contract (POCC) which seeks to remove private care from public hospitals.
Though a majority of consultants are now on the new contract, recent figures showed one in seven were rostered to work Saturdays, while 38 per cent were working extended days.
The move to the POCC is having a financial impact too, with the HSE stating the shift to the new contract is likely to result in a 2026 shortfall in private patient income of about €145 million.
Mahon says productivity is not just about return for investment, but also whether or not the State is funding the right mix of healthcare.
“In the Irish context, that means trying to move activity out of the acute hospital setting into primary care and the community,” he says.
[ How Budget 2027 will impact families: From renters to stay-at-home parents Opens in new window ]
Hospital care is considerably more expensive to the taxpayer than community care, and Budget 2027 points explicitly to a focus on increasing primary resources.
In addition to this, Mahon believes further work could be done when making funding decisions.
The cost-effectiveness threshold when deciding on whether or not to reimburse a drug in the public system is “too high”, he says.
“Meaning when we price drugs to that threshold we are probably paying too much and the opportunity costs are too high,” he says.
“We use health technology assessment and cost effectiveness when trying to decide what brand of drug to use and for what price. That same methodology could be applied across the health system.”
Some elements of increased expenditure are unavoidable; an ageing population results in increased demand and complexity of care on health services.
Add this population change to inflation, and representative unions claim the additional funding will only enable the system to stand still rather than expand – unless a systemic change to the way it operates takes place.

title: Never mind the ‘risk to humanity’, Anthropic’s IPO raises more prosaic concerns
description: Anthropic has plans to raise up to $100bn, part of a trend that could result in too much stock coming to market
content:
Anthropic ’s IPO (initial public offering) prospectus warns its AI model could cause a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity”.
Some investors may have more prosaic concerns, not least the amount of new stock coming to market.
Anthropic is expected to make its market debut next month, and it’s already clear that building a $2 trillion AI giant requires a very large cheque.
Revenue rose twelvefold last year to almost $4.6 billion but the company still recorded operating losses of more than $8 billion.
More strikingly, it envisages spending $518 billion on cloud computing and infrastructure in coming years. Extraordinary amounts of capital are therefore needed. Saudi Aramco’s $29 billion flotation in 2019 was the previous record, but SpaceX tripled it in June when it raised $86 billion at a $1.77 trillion valuation.
Now Anthropic will probably blow past even that, with plans to raise up to $100 billion at a valuation of about $2 trillion. And there’s more, with OpenAI expected to follow Anthropic with a trillion-dollar listing in early 2027.
The implications extend beyond the companies themselves. In a recent note, investment manager GMO warned that the sheer amount of new equity coming to market could become a catalyst for an AI bubble break.
For almost all of the past 20 years, US companies have bought back more shares than they issued. That is now going into reverse, with hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Oracle issuing shares to fund AI spending, a wave of giant IPOs adding new stock, and roughly $2 trillion of SpaceX shares becoming freely tradeable by June 2027.
GMO estimates that, if history is any guide, the resulting increase in equity supply could leave the market about 20 per cent below where it otherwise would have been over the following 18 months.
Today’s AI-driven market may therefore face a more prosaic threat than disappointing or even dangerous technology: simply having too much stock coming to market.

description: Now we await the reaction of Donald Trump
content:

title: Leinster look to restore their home fortress against Cardiff
description: Province return to competitive action at the redeveloped Laya Arena
content:
It’s entirely fitting that Cardiff are the visitors to the refurbished, rebranded Laya Arena, given the Blues provided the opposition when Leinster took their first tentative steps into their new home at the RDS over two decades ago.
Almost 21 years ago to the day – October 15th, 2005 – Leinster hosted Cardiff in a televised Celtic League match in the showjumping arena. The then Leinster CEO Mick Dawson and head of commercial and marketing Conor Hanratty had realised that the province had simply outgrown Donnybrook, with its 7,000 capacity, and a pitch churned up by hosting Bective Rangers, Old Wesley and Leinster schools matches.
With the West Stand being demolished and rebuilt, the old Lansdowne Road wasn’t a viable option, while the RDS CEO, Michael Duffy, was enthusiastic to the idea of Leinster becoming tenants. But the move wasn’t without its hiccups or opposition.
“We brought the floodlights over from the UK,” recalls Dawson. “The van stopped behind the Anglesey stand. The next thing, a big arm stretched up and the floodlights went over the roof of the Anglesey stand.
“John D O’Brien of RTÉ was standing in the middle of the pitch holding some light measure or something. And he came to me and said: “I don’t think we’d be able to do this. I don’t think they’re bright enough’. I thought I was going to start crying.
“But anyway, it all worked out, although we had to bring in two sets of floodlights for the next match just to make sure everything was okay,” Dawson adds, referring to Leinster’s Heineken Cup game against Bath a week later.
“We brought them in from the UK again, but they were delayed en route. ‘Where are the effin’ floodlights?’ I said to Conor. He said: ‘They’re in Enniscorthy now. They should be here shortly’. It was high-risk stuff at the time.”
Leinster hosted four games there in that 2005-06 season, but none the next as the RDS installed floodlights, relaid the pitch and upgraded facilities before the province signed a 20-year lease and made the switch at the start of the 2007-08 season.
There was opposition to the move at committee level, with some believing that Donnybrook was Leinster’s spiritual home. But the relocation has been more than vindicated, with the recently completed Anglesea Road stand completing the arena’s refurbishment.
When Leinster signed a new 25-year lease with the RDS in October 2022, extending their stay to 2047, Dawson described it as one of the best decisions in Leinster’s history. A statement he stands by. “You’ll see that in Saturday’s full house,” he says.
And absence has made Leinster hearts grow fonder. In the just over two years since their last competitive game at the venue, ‘Aviva fatigue’ has long since set in. As a home, a full RDS is more intimate and more atmospheric than a half-full Aviva. It will also restore a sense of occasion to Leinster’s trips to Lansdowne Road.
But the overdue return also heightens the importance of this game, for as Leo Cullen acknowledges, the onus is now on his team to immediately rebuild that connection with their fans by delivering a statement performance and win.
This game also comes a week before Leinster’s difficult first Champions Cup pool game at home to Clermont, all of which further explains the rationale behind bringing 15 of Ireland’s summer tourists on Leinster’s initial two-week trek to South Africa.
Although nine of the cohort did not feature in the defeats to the Lions and the Sharks, instead returning to Ireland before the latter game, they should be better primed to hit the ground running on their seasonal reappearances on Saturday.
The trip to South Africa last season yielded zero points, part of Leinster’s three defeats from their opening four fixtures. By contrast, this time around, late tries in both games earned them three bonus points, suggested fitness and conditioning levels are better than last season.
There will for sure be rustiness against Cardiff given nine players are lining out in their first game in almost three months, while six of the matchday 23 are playing here for the first time in Leinster colours. All in, their enthusiasm and energy should be through the roof. Surrounded by so much quality and experience, it looks like a good game to give 22-year-old academy scrumhalf Oliver Coffey his debut. The bench is also a little callow, but all played in South Africa.
In these grim times domestically, there’s a buzz around Cardiff. They are the leading Welsh side, having finished sixth last season, and sit second after wins away to the Scarlets and at home to Zebre.
“We lost to them twice last season – in preseason in Tallaght and then we lost a classic 8-7 in the pissing rain [in Cardiff] during the Six Nations,” said Cullen, although admitting this team is “completely different”.
He added Cardiff had “good fundamentals”, including a strong kicking game, having retained 11 of their own kicks over the opening two weekends.
Defence coach Gethin Jenkins will have them fired up, and they retain the attacking legacy of their departed head coach Matt Sherratt. “They’re a good team, well coached,” Cullen added.
Corniel van Zyl has made seven changes, including the return of Taulupe Faletau for his first game since January. But Cardiff have not won outside of Wales since defeating Zebre last November, while Leinster have lost just one of their last 18 matches at the Laya Arena.
A statement win here would be the first step towards making the venue a fortress again.
LEINSTER: H Keenan; J Kenny, G Ringrose, J Osborne, J O’Brien; S Prendergast, O Coffey; A Usanov, D Sheehan (capt), T Furlong; J McCarthy, J Ryan; M Deegan, S Penny, J Conan. Replacements: R Kelleher, P Dooley, T Clarkson, A Spicer, J Ericson, F Gunne, C Gabriel, R Henshaw.
CARDIFF: M Young; J Beetham, H Millard, L Malan, M Grady; C Sheedy, A Davies; D Southworth, L Belcher (capt), J Sebastian; J Mcally, T Williams; A Mann, D Thomas, T Faletau. Replacements: E Lloyd, R Barratt, S Wainwright, G Nott, S Paea, J Mulder, J Evans, S Emanuel.
Forecast: Leinster to win with a bonus point.

title: Superstar medical team deserves recognition
