title: Pat Leahy: The remaking of Jack Chambers
description: Not yet restored as a leadership contender perhaps, but the Minister for Public Expenditure’s stock is higher than it has been for a long time
content:
T his week’s budget has already been analysed to within an inch of its life on these pages and elsewhere, but one aspect that has received little attention is how it has revived the political fortunes of Jack Chambers , the Minister for Public Expenditure.
Almost terminally damaged by the Jim Gavin omnishambles last year which had Fianna Fáil TDs baying for his head on a spike, Chambers – according to soundings with several knowledgeable figures at various levels of the party – has resuscitated his standing and authority within both Fianna Fáil and the Government as a result of his management of the budget process.
While he has not been restored as a leadership contender (not yet, anyway) his stock is higher this weekend than it has been for a long time. Even some Fianna Fáil TDs who would have liked a more generous budget that they could sell in the constituencies tended to begin their assessment of Chambers with: “In fairness to him ...” One backbencher said there was “huge praise” for him in the parliamentary party.
The appreciation of Chambers does not extend to some of his colleagues in the Cabinet with whom he was – they think – unnecessarily brutal during the weeks of budget negotiations. There are complaints of personal brusqueness and high-handedness in meetings. Veterans wistfully recalled Paschal Donohoe ’s bedside manner and made favourable comparisons with Dr Chambers. The walkout after eight minutes by Patrick O’Donovan during a hot-tempered bilateral was well documented, but there were others who felt like doing the same thing. Chambers made no friends – well, no new ones anyway – during the process and he might have lost a few.
But it is not his job to make friends with ministers looking for money. It is to safeguard the public finances by keeping a lid on public expenditure increases – the spending increases that his colleagues endlessly demand. He had moderate success on that front this week. It is noteworthy precisely because the constituency for caution and restraint is so rare in Irish politics.
Let’s not overstate it, though: as the Fiscal Council has pointed out, the budget continued the trend of spending most of the corporation tax revenues rather than saving them for the less abundant times that are surely ahead at some stage. We may well repent having a politics that needs a €10 billion budget to stand still. It would be better if our entire political culture was not wedded to the McCreevy doctrine of when-we-have-it-by-jaysus-we-spend-it. But it is, and it seems unlikely to change in the immediate future.
So Chambers’ achievement of sticking to the 6 per cent limit deserves to be recognised. Would a 5 per cent increase, or a 4 per cent increase, have been better in the long term, notwithstanding the political problems it might cause? Yes. But that doesn’t mean we shouldn’t recognise that expenditure growth in recent years was habitually higher than this year, even under St Paschal the Prudent. One Department of Finance mandarin, a veteran of many budgets, was full of admiration: “He has played it extremely well.” Another insider spoke of him “holding the line” on spending over the weekend when there was pressure on all sides (including some from party leaders) to let the 6 per cent limit slide a bit.
The immediate challenge for him now will be to minimise the supplementary estimates for overspending departments at the end of this year and eliminate them next year. That’s a long shot, but he has established a lot of credibility in recent months, and that has built his political capital.
Does this make him a leadership contender for whenever Micheál Martin departs? Ah no. Not at this point anyway. But it probably means that whoever is Fianna Fáil leader when the Taoiseach’s office switches to Fine Gael in November of next year will appoint Chambers as Minister for Finance then. At a very basic level, you need to be able display competence in government. Setting his 6 per cent target in July and achieving it in October has done that.
[ There’s a good chance Ireland will come to regret this boomtime period as a missed opportunity Opens in new window ]
Despite O’Donovan’s best efforts, Chambers delivered a budget that did not cause political problems. But it all takes place against a slightly peculiar political background. While anaemic poll ratings and public sourness about the cost of living worry Ministers, the Government retains a sense of grip and continues to make the political weather. Opposition budget proposals all involved taxing and spending vastly greater sums and the critiques of the budget this week were all built around complaints that the Government didn’t spend enough in various areas. I am not sure this will convince middle-ground voters – hammered by the cost of living but nervous of fiscal profligacy – that there is a viable alternative government in waiting.
Sinn Féin is strangely becalmed, retreating to the comfortable redoubts of economic populism and united Irelandism. Finishing her budget speech, Mary Lou McDonald struck a slightly peculiar tone, acknowledging that right now a different government “could seem really far away”. She urged people: “Do not give up. Do not lose hope.” It sounded like she was talking to herself.
Labour and the Greens are treading water. Independent Ireland and Aontú are having a bit of a moment in polls, and so are the Social Democrats on the other side of the spectrum. But the Independents seem to regard the Government as a sort of conspiracy against the plain people of Ireland.
The Social Democrats show little sign of being prepared for the hard compromises of power when difficult choices are required. How many TDs would they lose at their first budget?
So this is where we are: the Government is unpopular but getting on with things. A standstill budget costs nearly €10 billion. The Opposition is fractured and directionless. But if politics seems stagnant, don’t be fooled: it’s always moving. A year ago, Chambers was dead. Now he rises. Politics is never static. Stay on your toes, everyone.

title: Lots of Ministers floated budget ideas that failed to materialise, Simon Harris says
description: No desire in Government to ‘rerun’ drama over RTÉ governance, Simon Harris says
content:
There were “lots of Ministers” who floated ideas and proposals in the media that ultimately never materialised in the budget announced by the Government this week, Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris has said.
Defending his Fine Gael colleague Minister for Culture Patrick O’Donovan , Harris said a €100 culture card for 16-year-olds would be delivered at some point in the lifetime of the Coalition, to get teenagers “away from the smartphones”.
There was nothing unusual about Ministers pitching policies and schemes during budget negotiations, Harris said.
“I’m not saying this to be provocative but there were lots of Ministers who put forward the case for lots of things,” he said. “Some of the things were in the budget, some of the things were in the papers and not in the budget.”
O’Donovan had pushed for a €100 voucher for 16-year-olds to participate in cultural activities, and a spokeswoman for the Minister suggested at one point money to fund the scheme had been secured.
Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers intervened to clarify funding had not been set aside for the culture card.
[ Chambers and O’Donovan at odds over ‘culture card’ idea Opens in new window ]
Separately, the Government had no desire to “rerun” the drama and controversy around RTÉ’s governance, and a dispute over State funding for the public service broadcaster would hopefully be resolved soon, Harris said.
The €20 million that RTÉ had been left short of what it expected to receive in Budget 2027 was not an “insignificant sum”, but it was fiscally “manageable” in the context of the total budget package, he said.
“It’s right and proper, though, that the Government just satisfies itself that all the reforms are in place ... I think there’s good leadership in RTÉ, there’s a robust board in RTÉ, they’re on a journey of reform. It’s not easy and Government wants to support that,” he said.
[ RTÉ likely to get back €20m lost in Budget 2027 ‘if it proves reforms are on track’ Opens in new window ]
Harris was speaking to The Irish Times in Luxembourg after a meeting of EU finance ministers.
There could come a day when changes to corporation tax, intellectual property regimes and multinational group planning meant the State’s budgetary situation looked quite different, the Minister said.
“It would be imprudent and foolish to operate and run your economy on the assumption that this will all continue forever,” he said.
However, Harris said politicians should not be “fatalistic” about such a scenario coming to pass. “You’d rather have this set of economic challenges that Ireland has [than] many others,” he said.
The healthy surplus, buoyed by bumper corporation tax receipts, had allowed the Government to take significant steps to buffer people from the impacts of the global energy shock.
“We’ve brought in – I’m confident – the largest level of intervention of any EU member state per head of capita,” Harris said.
The Government had begun to hit the “outer limit” of what it could do to help with the rising cost of fuel and energy. “These aren’t consequence-free decisions – it’s real money,” Harris said.
There was no easy or simple way to address rising costs as long as the US war in Iran kept the Strait of Hormuz closed, he said.
The global economy had held up better than initially predicted in the face of the vital shipping route for oil and gas being choked off, but ordinary people were still “acutely” feeling the pinch, Harris said.
The Tánaiste said there was no reluctance to criticise US president Donald Trump, but doing so would not make a “meaningful difference” to the situation the world was facing.
“There’s absolutely no doubt the Strait of Hormuz, its closure, the situation in Iran, the failure to de-escalate between the US and Iran, is having a real, painful economic impact on the world,” he said.

title: Frank McNally solves the mystery of columns
description: Jostlestones prevented damage to the wheels of carriages and traps in days gone by
content:
Sir, – Frank McNally is to be congratulated on providing an answer to a question for many of your readers of a certain age ( Irishman’s Diary , October 8th).
By identifying those pillar or column-like stones that lie on either side of the entrances to our older estates and houses as jostlestones, he has allowed many of us to finally stop wondering what they were called.
Now we can dement our walking and travelling companions by pointing out these jostlestones and describing how they prevented damage to the wheels of carriages and traps as they turned to enter older properties. – Yours, etc,

title: The river Slaney needs to be protected, not dredged
description: We dredge gutters but it is no way to treat a river or its inhabitants
content:
Sir, – The river Slaney is a stunning natural wonder. It is also a special area of conservation, supporting abundant wildlife. Unfortunately, it is a river on the brink, and in a generation we could lose salmon and it may already be too late for the freshwater pearl mussel.
We need to move away from the shortsighted messaging that to dredge, straighten and engineer our rivers will solve all our problems. We must let our rivers be exactly what they should be – natural wild places.
Dredging 200m of a special area of conservation would be utterly pointless – it will simply refill with materials and water during the next significant flood.
As the old saying goes: “No river reaches the sea without first making peace with the rocks in its path.” Don’t dredge it, protect it. – Yours, etc,
A chara, – David Doran advocates for dredging as a solution to flooding ( Letters , October 7th). While dredging rivers may provide short-term relief locally, it ignores river behaviour and is a simplistic solution to a complex issue.
Rivers are dynamic systems that naturally transport sediment and will actively fill sediment deficits when material is removed. Dredged channels frequently silt back up – sometimes within weeks or months – making for a costly, repetitive and unsustainable maintenance cycle. Moreover, by deepening the channel and clearing “blockages”, dredging speeds up the velocity of water flow. This reduces lag time and can significantly worsen flood peaks further downstream by dumping larger volumes of water into communities faster.
Islands, gravel bars, vegetation or other features found in rivers are natural manifestations. These features also provide habitat for river species that are constantly under pressure from human activities, not least from dredging. We dredge or “clean” gutters but it is no way to treat a river or its inhabitants.
While I have every sympathy for those who suffer from the impacts of flooding, people do not live “above a river”. Rather they are living on the river floodplain. Floodplains naturally hold vastly more water than the river channel itself, rendering dredging ineffective during heavy flooding.
With ever worsening flooding caused by climate change, a longer-term approach is to allow fields to flood rather than towns downstream and consider a strategic retreat where we cannot. – Is mise,

title: True meaning of Irish unity
description: Work, not tiresome rhetoric, required by all to achieve desired objective of united Ireland
content:
Sir, – Eoghan Mac Cormaic, appears to view Irish unity as “ a case of reversing the wrong done to those who were against their wishes shut out ” 100 years ago (Letters, October 9th). Where that leaves those members of the majority tradition in Northern Ireland who support partition is not clear.
Article 3 of Bunreacht na hÉireann envisages Irish unity as an outcome which, in the first instance, involves uniting all the people of this island in “harmony and friendship”, including those of the tradition which supports membership of the United Kingdom.
That essential precondition for a peaceful and successful united Ireland needs to be borne in mind by those of us from the majority tradition on the island, if we are serious about the issue. I fear, however, that we are more comfortable with rhetoric about a Border poll, rather than undertaking the necessary work, and perhaps painful sacrifices, towards that desired objective.

title: James McClean standoff with Derry City looms over FAI Cup trip to Galway
description: Candystripes travel to Eamonn Deacy Park for FAI Cup semi-final against John Caulfield’s side
content:
One of the more uncomfortable aspects of James McClean’s public falling out with Derry City is the regular presence of his brother Patrick McClean in the Candystripes ’ line-up.
The younger McClean has been a mainstay in a Derry defence that leaked 42 goals in 32 Premier Division outings so far. He also scored in the quarter-final win over Dundalk to leave Mark Connolly’s side one win away from a 13th FAI Cup final appearance at the Aviva Stadium on November 8th.
“I’ve gone to the Aviva for years watching James in an Ireland jersey, and I would love to share the pitch with him at the Aviva in the cup final and see him lift a trophy with Derry City, because I’ve watched how his love for Derry City has shown over the years,” McClean told The Derry Journal ahead of Saturday’s semi-final at Eamonn Deacy Park.
“He’s never shied away from being a Derry lad, and it’s obviously sad how things have turned out.”
Patrick McClean, surprisingly, spoke this week about the standoff between his brother and his employer, even as the situation threatens to spoil Derry’s season.
“I don’t find it difficult, not at all. I grew up with it,” he joked when asked about this week’s PFAI statement supporting his brother, and the club’s response. “I’m used to it. I just come in and do my job every day, and that’s all I can do.
“I spoke to James once it all came to a head a while ago. I spoke to James personally. I sat down with him and his wife [Erin] and we had that conversation then.
“I’m my own man and have to get on with my own job. Obviously I support my brother as much as I can. James is who he is, he’s always been that way and I’ll back him to the hilt. Again, I have my own career here at Derry City and it’s about making the most of that for me as well.”
James McClean has not featured for Derry since July. In April, the 37-year-old took to social media to reveal that a hip injury is close to forcing him to retire from football. In June, while appearing as a World Cup pundit on RTÉ, he took aim at how the club was being managed.
The chance of the brothers playing together at the Aviva seems farther away than ever, especially since Connolly sparked an upsurge in results following Tiernan Lynch’s departure in August.
Captain Michael Duffy remains the star turn, with 14 goals and eight assists, while Ellis Chapman has found form in midfield and former Ireland under-21 winger Darragh Burns is bringing quality down the right since signing from Grimsby Town.
All this attacking ability is charged with unpicking Galway United’s back five, marshalled by Canadian Gianfranco Facchineri and the wily tactical brain of manager John Caulfield.
“The team that goes out on Saturday will run through the wall for Galway United, there be no problem for that,” said Caulfield.
“If you’re Derry City and if you’re Philip O’Doherty investing millions and publicly saying you’re building a team to win the league, then your intentions are to win a league or a cup.
“Unfortunately, Galway aren’t in that position at the moment. We’re not in that financial position.
“Of course, I’d love to get to the Aviva for the supporters. Yes the players [too], but the supporters, because they’ve had no success. The club had been in a bad way for a long, long time.”

title: LDA does not ‘pay ransom money’, chief executive says after €2m bungalow deal
description: Move was ‘pragmatic’ one so former Central Mental Hospital site could be turned into homes
content:
The Land Development Agency (LDA) “does not pay ransom money” or buy properties “willy-nilly” to eliminate legal challenges to the State’s housing programme, LDA chief executive John Coleman has said.
Coleman was speaking after The Irish Times reported on Friday how the agency had paid more than €2 million this year to buy a dormer bungalow to settle a High Court case against the development of almost 1,000 homes at the former Central Mental Hospital in Dundrum , Co Dublin .
Mark Leonard, who owned the house at 36 Friarsland Road, Goatstown , initiated judicial review proceedings in February against planning permission for the State’s flagship affordable housing development.
He withdrew the case a fortnight later. It was the second legal challenge Leonard had taken to the LDA’s plans for the site.
The previous month Coleman had said the LDA intended to press ahead with construction on the old hospital site “even if we do get a judicial review” taken against the development.
When it had published its master plan for the site in April 2021, the LDA had hoped the first homes would be available in 2024. “We can’t wait any longer,” he said. “We’re moving on regardless.”
Speaking to The Irish Times on Friday, following a sodturning event at the Dundrum site, now called Dún Brí, Coleman said there was “no deal” to buy the house in place when he had made his comments in January.
Leonard’s house was one of more than 20 on Friarsland Road that backed directly on to the hospital site. Coleman confirmed the LDA has not bought any of the other houses on the road, nor has it bought any other houses surrounding Dún Brí.
Time has expired for any challenge to be taken against the planning permission for the development.
The LDA has not previously bought any other properties to stop or deter legal challenges, Coleman said.
However, he was not concerned the purchase of Leonard’s bungalow for €2.15 million would expose the State to spurious litigation from property owners seeking “go away” money.
“We don’t see any risk there. What’s very important to note is that the LDA does not pay any ransom money,” he said.
“But I think it’s important to set our stall out in terms of how determined we are to move on with our developments.
“We will always look to try and cut time out of processes and head off legal challenges where possible.”
Dún Brí was “a landmark development, very important for the area, very important for Dublin, very important for the LDA”, Coleman said.
“We don’t do transactions willy-nilly. We don’t pay any ransom money and we deal just purely on independent valuations when we acquire properties.”
The LDA had taken a pragmatic approach, he said.
“I would have a very hard time explaining to the future 2,500 people that need to live here in affordable homes, and the €30-€40 million additional cost that we’d incur, just to avoid a particular situation where we acquire someone’s house at an open market value,” Coleman said.
“You have to be pragmatic and balanced in these situations and our job is to deliver homes, not to embed ourselves in legal processes for years.”
Although the LDA has not previously bought out objectors, another State agency, Transport Infrastructure Ireland , last December agreed to buy a row of houses last December at Dartmouth Square in Ranelagh, Dublin, for a combined total of more than €30 million to end a legal challenge to the MetroLink railway line.
The board of the National Transport Authority in August last year approved an undisclosed settlement to halt legal action taken against its planned BusConnects corridor from Swords to Dublin city centre.
In June last year Irish Rail said it reached a “confidential settlement” with two parties that had taken judicial review proceedings over the €1 billion Dart+ West project.

title: Trump blind to irony or just a sneering bully?
description: Keith Duggan’s portrayal of the president’s indifference to division and strife inflicted on the midwest hits the mark
content:
Sir, - I would like to commend Keith Duggan on his superb depiction of the American heartland (“ Sublime evenings and empty downtowns: Democrats threaten comeback in America’s heartland ”, US, October 9th).
Towards the end of the article, I found his portrayal of Donald Trump’s indifference to the division and strife he has inflicted on the midwest to be among the finest I have read.
Trump’s recital of The Snake is reflective of his odious character and the poem is almost chillingly reminiscent of the relationship between the president and the midwestern working class.
Is he oblivious to this, his sense of irony worn by years of decline? Or did he know exactly what he was doing and mocking us all? - Yours, etc,

title: Public sector strike ‘inevitable’ and will see up to 150,000 medical appointments cancelled
description: First of two scheduled walkouts will bring widespread disruption, with further escalation possible in November
content:
Up to 150,000 medical appointments will be cancelled for next Wednesday due to the strike by public sector unions, according to briefings circulated in Government.
Preparations are under way for the strike, which will see more than 300,000 public sector workers undertake a 24-hour work stoppage in pursuit of a new public sector pay deal, though essential services will be maintained.
Another strike is scheduled for the following Wednesday, while senior union figures are privately warning of escalation of their action in November if negotiations do not get under way in the coming weeks.
A spokesman for the HSE could not confirm the 150,000 figure, but nor did he dispute it. He said that the cancellations would be among non-urgent outpatient appointments, elective surgery, community appointments and primary care clinics (though not GPs).
Widespread disruption is inevitable as schools and other public services also close. There is little expectation in trade union or Government circles that the strike can be averted at this stage, with senior union figures stressing the frustration felt among their members.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin said that there was no need for the strikes and said that the €1.2 billion provision in the budget this week was a basis for negotiations.
But unions dismissed the figure as insufficient. Fórsa general secretary and chair of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions ’ public service committee Kevin Callinan reiterated that the unions would be seeking a pay settlement that covers the period in 2026 not covered by the previous agreement, that protects the living standards of workers in the future and that reflects the ground public sector workers had lost to inflation in recent years.
He said that “a lot of resentment” had built up among public sector workers, something that has been echoed by several unions in recent days.
Another senior trade union figure said that “Wednesday is inevitable and kind of has to happen now”.
Unions are having discussions about potential escalation of the industrial action if no resolution comes in sight in the coming weeks.
One union leader said: “Unless there is a mindset shift from [the Department of Public Expenditure] in their attitude to pay and the talks at large then all unions are currently planning for what their escalations will be in November.”
Another senior union figure said that he hoped for meaningful engagement with Government after this month’s strikes. “If that doesn’t work an escalation will be inevitable,” the source said.
The Taoiseach said Dáil business should go ahead next Wednesday, though Labour and Sinn Féin have said that they will not pass pickets at Leinster House. Government chief whip Mary Butler, who is responsible for proposing the business of the Dáil, told a meeting of the Dáil’s business committee on Thursday that the Dáil should sit as normal for three days next week.
Last night a spokesman for Butler said the business committee would reconvene on Monday, adding: “The Government chief whip may propose that votable business takes place on Tuesday and it remains to be determined what other two days next week the Dáil will sit.”
Asked about preparations in schools for the strike, the Minister for Education, Hildegarde Naughton, said that her officials had been in contact with schools about “communicating to parents”.
“But if we want to see a resolution here, we really do need people to sit around the table to get a resolution,” she said.
A spokesman for the Department of Public Expenditure said that the Government has “repeatedly made clear that officials are available to engage constructively to discuss the issues raised, without preconditions”.
The department said that “extensive contingency planning is under way across the civil and public service to minimise disruption and maintain continuity of services. However, there is no doubt that this industrial action will have an impact on the delivery of public services, particularly in the health sector, where disruption will affect patients and other vulnerable service users.”

title: Shaky start for AIL standard bearers has challengers eyeing away wins
description: Lansdowne, Clontarf and Cork Constitution host Old Belvedere, UCD and St Mary’s respectively in round three
content:
The old order hasn’t seemed so endangered for years. Lansdowne, Clontarf and Cork Con – standard bearers and annual playoff contenders – have only one win between them so far this season. In this weekend’s third round of the Energia All-Ireland league, they host Old Belvedere, UCD and St Mary’s respectively, each with two opening wins to set the early pace.
Old Belvedere have backed up a strong summer of recruitment with eye-catching results in beating Young Munster and Ballynahinch, scoring 15 tries in the process.
Lansdowne have been given permission to play their first game on the Aviva main pitch in three years. Fittingly, it’s this fierce local derby. Recognising the threat posed by Belvo and seeking to avoid a third defeat in three games, Lansdowne have picked the Lawlor brothers, fullback Todd and number eight Donough, to start.
The former started both of Leinster’s recent URC games in South Africa, while his older sibling is back from a year in the USA, promoted having started on the bench last week. The same is true for Leinster scrumhalf Cormac Foley, with centre Dylan O’Keefe, loosehead Seán Dunne and openside Paul Wilson making up the other changes.
Belvo have recall Ed Byrne and the tough and industrious number Will McDonald.
Siting second after wins over Ballynahinch and Lansdowne, Emmet McMahon’s high-flying students travel to Clontarf, who have bolstered their tight five with the Leinster duo of tighthead Niall Smyth and lock Brian Deeny, as well as flanker Luke Brady.
McMahon recalls Ireland under-20s tighthead Sam Bishti, as well as lock Dylan McNeice and centre Andrew Osborne, both of whom featured for Leinster in South Africa, the latter scoring the bonus-point try against the Sharks.
Like Lansdowne, Cork Con are seeking to avoid a third successive defeat at home to St Mary’s, who plundered a record-shredding 57-19 win at Temple Hill in February. Without prop Mark Donnelly and flanker Michael Foy, both covering for Munster, Con make five changes up front, including a new frontrow of Mike Cogan, Billy Scannell and Luke Masters, while Dylan Hicks starts at fullback.
Mark McHugh has also named a new Mary’s frontrow in Thomas O’Reilly, Richie Bergin and Andrew Sparrow, and gives a debut to 29-year-old former Australia Sevens openside Michael Icely.
Terenure, still smarting from losing at home to Young Munster, select former Leinster academy back Henry McErlean for the visit of Old Wesley in a first AIL meeting of the sides since 2013, and welcome back hooker Max Russell and talismanic lock Harrison Brewer from injury.
Stephen Smyth, who scored Leinster’s bonus-point try against the Lions, makes his first appearance of the season for Old Wesley, who recall tighthead Adam Watchorn and Ireland under-19s number eight Cian Butler.
Buoyed by their latest win over Terenure, the Cookies are at home to Ballynahinch and recall Tony Butler, whose six-week contract with Munster meant he has been covering for his province for the last two weeks. Ger Slattery also gives a first start to Ireland under-20s centre Rob Carney among his four changes, while Aaron Sexton has been added to the visitors’ injury list and Joe Hopes is covering for Ulster.
Division 1B leaders Nenagh Ormond host winless Instonians, and MU Barnhall travel to Dooradoyle for a first ever AIL meeting with Garryowen. Division 2A leaders Cashel host winless Galwegians, and second-placed Galway Corinthians host unbeaten Dungannon.
The Women’s Division 1A season begins with Railway Union and UL Bohemian – finalists in 2023 and 2024 – renewing their rivalry at Park Avenue, while Old Belvedere and Galwegians, who both reached the knock-out stages last season, meet at Ollie Campbell Park.

title: Government to propose EU budget compromise as conservative states push for more cuts
description: Republic’s revision to €1.7tn EU common pot intended to narrow gap between opposing camps
content:
The European Union’s next long-term budget should be trimmed back below €1.7 trillion to accommodate concerns about increased spending, the Irish Government is expected to propose.
Several fiscally conservative European governments are preparing to criticise a compromise tabled by the Republic, in anticipation that it will not go far enough to reel in the proposed size of the union’s common budget, which will run from 2028 to 2034.
The Government will on Saturday lay out a revised headline figure for the joint EU budget, the product of months of behind-the-scenes diplomatic back-channelling, to help nudge all 27 member states towards a deal before the end of this year.
It is understood the State will likely propose cutting the total size of the draft budget by somewhere in the region of between €100 billion and €200 billion.
The State, in its dealmaker role holding the rotating Council of the EU presidency, has taken soundings from all national capitals and the union’s institutions to propose a fresh draft of the European budget package.
Some EU member states want a larger budget and are seeking to protect traditional funding for Common Agricultural Policy (Cap) subsidies and money for “cohesion” infrastructure projects in poorer regions.
Other capitals want to scale back the proposed EU package by cutting the Cap and cohesion schemes, and instead pushing additional funding towards new priorities such as defence, border control, and a fund to boost Europe’s economy.
While the exact figures have been kept under tight wraps, the Irish revision will propose to scale back the €1.7 trillion draft package currently on the table.
The Government will pitch its compromise as a credible step towards a final budget deal, narrowing the distance between the previous draft and the “frugal” demands.
Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and other “frugal” Nordic countries have called for cutbacks in the region of several hundred billion euros as the price of their sign-off.
One Brussels-based diplomat from that camp said they expected the Irish compromise would shave about €150 billion off the top of the draft budget.
A larger group led by Italy, Spain and Poland, which includes most southern and eastern member states, are fighting to protect EU spending ambitions from being chopped back too aggressively.
Proposed cuts will be made to development aid funding and the administrative costs of staffing the union’s institutions, one source said.
The European Commission, the EU’s powerful executive body in Brussels, had initially sought to increase the bloc’s common budget to €1.9 trillion.
That was viewed as the starting point in what is always a long and often bitter political arm wrestle between the commission and national governments.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin has discussed the Republic’s budget compromise with French president Emmanuel Macron and German chancellor Friedrich Merz, among other EU leaders, in the past 10 days. Martin also spoke to commission president Ursula von der Leyen.
The seven-year budget needs the support of all 27 member states to be approved.
The Irish presidency proposal will also include an “ambitious” package assessing several ways extra revenues could be raised to plug part of the funding shortfall, one senior source said.
Once the Republic sets out its budget compromise, known as a “negotiating box”, the contentious debate will shift up to the 27 national leaders.
European leaders are hoping to trash out a final deal over a series of crunch summits between next week and the end of the year.
Minister of State for European affairs Thomas Byrne said the Government’s revision would provide a “realistic basis” for leaders to carry the debate to a final deal.

title: Lionel Messi’s World Cup behaviour tarnishes his legacy
description: Cristiano Ronaldo does not have a monopoly on unsportsmanlike conduct
content:
Sir, – Gavin Cooney says the debate between Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo on who is the greatest has been settled in favour of the former (“ Ronaldo v Messi debate has surely been settled – there is only one winner ”, Sport, October 9th).
I’m no real fan of the Portuguese national who began his career as a winger, but Messi’s form after Argentina lost to Spain 1-0 in the 2026 World Cup final, where he and his team-mates turned their backs on the podium during Spain’s trophy presentation, was very unsportsmanlike.
Ronaldo may be soccer’s biggest crybaby, but Messi’s bad form at the World Cup has tarnished an otherwise exemplary sporting lifework. – Is mise,

title: Coimisiún na Meán has no business taking sides in RTÉ funding row
description: The regulator should not be acting as an advocacy organisation for the entities it regulates
content:
Sir, – The most surprising aspect of the latest RTÉ funding row is the extraordinary decision of Coimisiún na Meán to wade into the controversy by criticising the Minister’s decision as “disappointing” (“ RTÉ DG says he has confidence in Minister after ‘constructive’ meeting on funding ”, News, October 8th).
Coimisiún na Meán regulates the broadcasting sector on behalf of the Oireachtas. While it is an independent body, it has no role or function to provide a running commentary on day-to-day government decisions, or to act as an advocacy organisation or press office for the entities it regulates.
As an unelected body, it should most not have any role in commenting on a decision made by the Government, which can hardly have come as much of a surprise to it or anyone else. – Yours, etc,

title: Coolmore and Godolphin superpowers pursue racing’s next big star in Dewhurst clash
description: Darkness Falls leads Aidan O’Brien’s hopes for a record ninth success in Europe’s top two-year-old prize
content:
Racing’s remorseless pursuit of the next big star will be key to Saturday’s Newmarket action and the prospect of a superpower clash in the 151st Darley Dewhurst Stakes.
Having flexed their financial muscles over dizzily priced yearlings at the nearby Tattersalls sales ring during the week, Godolphin and Coolmore now fight it out on the track in what is traditionally Europe’s most coveted two-year-old prize.
Just a handful line up but Aidan O’Brien and Charlie Appleby saddle two runners apiece with Andrew Balding the sole interloper.
O’Brien is chasing a record ninth success in a race he first won 25 years ago through Rock Of Gibraltar. Now he sets his number one hope Darkness Falls quite the task against Appleby’s unbeaten Champagne Stakes winner Desert Castle.
Moving from the Champagne to the Dewhurst is a tried and trusted route. For Darkness Falls, the challenge is dropping back a full quarter mile from the nine-furlong test he passed with flying colours at last month’s Irish Champions Festival.
It reverses Ballydoyle’s usual modus operandi of climbing in distance and reflects perhaps the pressing need for a proper top-flight juvenile colt to step up and establish himself as a classic favourite for 2027.
O’Brien’s outstanding triple-Group One winning filly Sun Goddess has been the juvenile standout so far this campaign. But, in a business where Sheikh Mohammed splashed out 26,910,000 GNS (about €33 million) on just 25 yearlings this week, mostly in the hope of finding the next big stallion, a filly’s commercial heft is limited by simple biology.
Darkness Falls has been the sole two-year-old colt to contribute to O’Brien’s tally of 20 Group One victories this season and it ensures the sport’s two major operations are competing for big stakes.
Appleby has had the better of the Dewhurst argument in recent times and is chasing a fourth win in eight years.
Desert Castle has plenty to prove too, having hung alarmingly left in the closing stages of his win at Doncaster. He beat O’Brien’s Sergei Diaghilev on that occasion, and there will be plenty of Godolphin interest in how that colt fares in the preceding Autumn Stakes.
O’Brien also runs Drumbeat in the 10-furlong Zetland Stakes although there’s a sense they are two colts in Ballydoyle’s second division. Even the Coventry winner Great Barrier Reef who accompanies Darkness Falls in the Dewhurst, might fall into that category.
Balding, who’s got a fighting chance of denying O’Brien a ninth British trainers’ championship this season, upset calculations with the ill-dated Gewan a year ago although it’s hard to see a repeat through Gentle Hurricane.
But just six days after Daryz established much of 2026’s pecking order with Arc glory – and his retirement to stud was confirmed on Friday – there quickly follows the potential for a glimpse of some of 2027’s classic scenario.
Where Daryz stands as a stallion remains to be decided. The Aga Khan Stud’s team has the option of bringing him to stand alongside his sire, Sea The Stars, at Gilltown Stud in Co. Kildare, or he could remain in France.
[ Racing’s true greats are obvious and dual Arc winner Daryz isn’t one of them Opens in new window ]
The first colt since Alleged in 1977-78 to win the Arc back-to-back retires on a rating of 128 in the latest global racehorse rankings. It puts him third on the current table behind the outstanding Hong Kong sprinter Ka Ying Rising (135) and Ombudsman (131), who beat Daryz in Royal Ascot’s Prince of Wales’s Stakes during the summer.
The Aga Khan team also confirmed that their star gelding Calandagan will bid to retain his Champion Stakes crown at Ascot next weekend. Their French 2000 Guineas and Marois winner Rayif will also take his chance in the Queen Elizabeth II Stakes.
With regular jockey Mickael Barzalona serving a suspension, Christophe Soumillon steps in to ride both horses.
There are six Irish challengers for this weekend’s big cross-channel handicap, the Cesarewitch, which has been significantly profitable for horses from this country in recent years.
The quartet of Willie and Emmet Mullins, Tony Martin and Charles Byrnes have all been successful and are back for more, joined by Joseph O’Brien, who has engaged Ryan Moore for the JP McManus-owned Dawn Rising.
Moore’s 17-year-old son Toby will ride Manxman, who was beaten a nose by old rival Alphonse le Grande in 2024, got the race days afterwards due to a breach of the whip rules, only to lose it again weeks later on appeal.
Last year’s winner Beylerbeyi will bid to become the first horse in the Cesarewitch’s long history to win the race back-to-back. Champion jockey elect Billy Loughnane again takes the ride on the Ian Williams runner.
Only one horse, Aaim To Prosper, has ever won the Cesarewitch twice, in 2010 and 2012.
[ Mary McAleese questioned the GAA’s attitude towards women – now they’ve replaced her with a man Opens in new window ]
Ryan Moore will be on duty for Sunday’s leg of weekend action at Naas with four Ballydoyle rides. They include Drop Dead Gorgeous and Moments Of Joy who are among a large group of fillies pursuing winning black type in a pair of Listed contests.
The big Irish handicap this weekend is a €100,000 two-mile contest where the Curragh Cesarewitch fifth Shoda could relish the soft ground conditions.
Sunday’s Naas fixture also has the €120,000 EBF Series Final for juveniles where course and distance winner Diamonds And Dames may go close.
In other news, the David Marnane trained Sonic Sabiha was able to line up in Friday evening’s Dundalk opener after a successful appeal that morning by connections against “Non-Trier” penalties imposed at the Listowel festival.
Sonic Sabiha, under apprentice jockey Rebecca Parsons, finished fifth in a Listowel maiden after which Parsons was banned for 14 days and the horse suspended from racing for 60 days. Marnane was fined €3,000.
Friday morning’s appeal was successful across the board on the basis that the Listowel stewards erred in their judgment.
Sonic Sabiba, who started a 3/1 shot, was beaten a neck by the 50/1 outsider Donner Dancer in the Dundalk race.

title: Excellent Junior Cycle results did not receive the media recognition they deserved
description: A significantly high number achieved grades in the top three bands
content:
Sir, – Sometimes success slips under the radar. The issuing of outstanding results in the Junior Cycle exam last Wednesday (“ Junior Cycle: Record numbers receive their results ”, Education, October 7th) to more than 73,000 young people was overshadowed by other events – the Ireland-Israel soccer match controversy, the Garvaghy Road stand-off and the interminable budget postmortems that dominated the news.
A significantly high number achieved grades in the top three bands, with 8.6 per cent awarded a distinction, 30.2 per cent a higher merit and 34.7 per cent a merit. That means that a whopping 73.5 per cent of all grades were in the top three grade bands.
The Junior Cycle exam is important because it is the first opportunity for second-level students to engage with a public exam. With few students now leaving school after junior cycle, it is a significant safeguard against early dropout of at-risk students and a significant force in the reduction of inequality in Irish education.
Congratulations to all the exam candidates and their dedicated teachers for achieving superb results. Mol an óige agus tiocfaidh sí! – Yours, etc,

title: Barbarous botched execution and livestreaming a firing squad
description: Washington has lost its moral compass at home and its respect abroad
content:
Sir, – As your editorial states, capital punishment is a “barbarous practice” (October 8th).
There have been two botched attempts by the United States to execute someone, with the world’s press now wondering what their next move is.
The US defence secretary, in a separate case, is demanding a public execution by firing squad of a serviceman.
One is acutely aware the US has lost all sense of proportion, all sense of compassion and is much the weaker for it. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – The US is being dragged back into the middle ages and into barbarity. Why isn’t there uproar in the US about this regime? Why aren’t people out on the streets?
There have been threats to invade Greenland , open hostility to their long-time ally and trading partner, Canada , and Donald Trump’s armed militia has been running riot in America’s cities, kidnapping and killing people.
But who in the US is resisting this? As with many fascist regimes, this leader was elected to office. Americans must now resist in every lawful way possible. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – You report that the US government intends to livestream an execution by firing squad (“ US says firing-squad execution of Fort Hood gunman will be livestreamed ”, World News, October 9th).
This represents a rare opportunity for social media companies to prove their claims that they have controls to protect children from harmful content. Unlike, say, footage of joyriding on motorways or violence, they will know the date and time of this incident being broadcast live online.
Whatever about children seeing this grotesque spectacle, any defence under freedom of speech or non-liability for sharing third-party material on the basis that this is not illegal material will expose the rotten core of social media. – Yours, etc,

title: Improving Ulster can claim home win against revitalised Munster
description: But visitors hope return of captain Tadhg Beirne could tilt game in Clayton McMillan’s side’s favour
content:
Interprovincials have a unique charm, one that’s predicated on the number of layers with which it’s possible to examine a contest.
First, there is the collective performance of the respective teams, before drilling down to individual tussles, and finally the result, all wrapped in an 80-minute bow.
Then there is the broader context. What will Ireland head coach Andy Farrell glean? No one talks directly or publicly about that in the build-up to the match, but it hovers in the background. The Irish squad for the Nations Championship games in November will be announced on Wednesday week.
Tadhg Beirne returns to captain Munster in this United Rugby Championship (URC) fixture, his first outing of the season, and he is joined in the secondrow by the promising Evan O’Connell.
Two of the summer signings, hooker Marnus van der Merwe and tighthead prop Kieran Brookes, have already made a positive impression, namechecked by head coach Clayton McMillan .
The New Zealander has pointed to the manner in which his team excelled against the Bulls in the scrum, an area that he conceded was “problematic” last season, before saying: “We feel like we have recruited really well, even though we were criticised for some of those recruitments over the summer.”
McMillan singled out another summer recruit, tighthead prop Jack Aungier, as his team’s player of the match against the Bulls. He starts on the bench.
Ulster, too, had their scrum issues last season and it’s interesting that a Munster old boy, South African-born, Irish-qualified Keynan Knox, starts alongside captain and hooker Tom Stewart and Eric O’Sullivan.
Irish international Tom O’Toole is on the bench, ostensibly covering loosehead, with 21-year-old Tom McAllister, a former age-grade international with eight Ulster appearances and two starts, slated to cover the other side – although head coach Richie Murphy might be less linear in choosing how he refreshes the frontrow resources.
The lineout will also inform who gets to play off a decent platform. Ulster’s Cormac Izuchukwu, playing in the backrow, and Munster’s Jack O’Donoghue are standout exponents, irrespective of the throw. The backrows are built along similar lines, a power carrier at eight and good athletes at six and seven.
The two benches contain a selection of the best backrow prospects in Irish rugby: James McNabney and David McCann for the home side and Brian Gleeson in the red of Munster. Then there is John Hodnett, who rarely disappoints in unearthing game-changing moments. McMillan’s 6-2 split is a gamble, but he’ll argue that it’s shrewdly calculated in anticipation of where the wear and tear will be keenest.
Jimmy Duffy, Ulster’s forwards coach last season, and now Munster’s, will bring a certain “intel”, while another visiting assistant coach, Jared Payne, was once revered as a player in Belfast.
The respective scrumhalves Nathan Doak and Craig Casey are Ireland squadmates and contest the backup role to Jamison Gibson-Park. It will be instructive to note who has the bigger influence on proceedings, but it will come down to the platform provided by the respective packs.
Indeed the performances of four number nines, including replacements Ben O’Donovan (Munster) and Matthew Devine (Ulster), will be of short- to medium-term interest to Farrell.
McMillan took time during the week to explain how well JJ Hanrahan played against Glasgow as he has returned to the 10 jersey in place of last week’s player-of-the-match Charlie O’Shea. The 20-year-old O’Shea took his chance and will no doubt be looking for a standout cameo when summoned.
When Ulster are humming, Jack Murphy is intrinsically involved in decision-making and distribution. The returning Ireland international Stuart McCloskey will offer a benchmarking process for Dan Kelly and Alex Nankivell, who are fluid in a positional sense.
Irish-qualified Jamie Benson gets a chance to show his versatility by moving one position to outside centre, while there are few more potent wings in the URC than Robert Baloucoune and Jacob Stockdale. Ethan McIlroy has the pace and footwork to break open a game.
Munster’s edge out wide is different, but in Shane Daly and Seán O’Brien they possess players who bring a consistent quality. Fullback Ben O’Connor has the talent to be a factor if given some decent ball. The visitors’ bench has an edge in experience in the forwards, but Ulster have the jet-heeled Chay Mullins in reserve.
Both teams appreciably stepped up the quality last weekend from week one, Munster in beating the Bulls, Ulster in earning a draw in Glasgow .
The key for Munster is to squeeze in the set piece and get their hosts to overplay off slow ball. For Ulster it’s about front-foot, high-tempo possession and getting to width. The team that gets closer to those goals will prevail. The odds suggest that Ulster are favourites to do so.
ULSTER : E McIlroy; R Baloucoune, J Benson, S McCloskey, J Stockdale; J Murphy, N Doak; E O’Sullivan, T Stewart (capt), K Knox; B Donnell, E Snyman; C Izuchukwu, N Timoney, J Augustus. Replacements : H Walker, T O’Toole, T McAllister, J McNabney, D McCann, M Devine, J Flannery, C Mullins.
MUNSTER : B O’Connor; S Daly, A Nankivell, D Kelly, S O’Brien; JJ Hanrahan, C Casey; J Loughman, M van der Merwe, K Brookes; E O’Connell, T Beirne (capt); J O’Donoghue, A Kendellen, G Coombes. Replacements : D Barron, J Wycherley, J Aungier, T Ahern, B Gleeson, B O’Donovan, C O’Shea, J Hodnett.

title: Carmel Heaney obituary: Diplomat who took on dissident Irish republicans and sympathisers in US
description: Republicans would ring her home at all hours of the day to abuse her and play rebel songs down the line
content:
Carmel Heaney was Ireland’s Consul General in Boston, covering the US ’s New England states of Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont from 1969 to 1983, during the earlier years of the Northern Ireland Troubles.
It was a fraught period in Irish America.
Her brief from the Department of Foreign Affairs was to dissuade Irish Americans in the New England states, sympathetic to those suffering injustices in Northern Ireland, from sending money to support paramilitary causes there, then estimated at $3,000-$4,000 a month.
This had immediate effects where she personally was concerned. In January 1973, republican sympathisers besieged the Irish Consulate General offices in Boston and took control of it for a day in protest at then taoiseach Jack Lynch’s government’s proscribing membership of republican and loyalist paramilitary organisations.
Heaney and her team were trapped inside, their communications blocked. However, they succeeded in phoning local TV and radio stations and the newspapers before police arrived to arrest the occupying protesters.
Republicans and other sympathisers then began ringing her home at all hours of the day and night to abuse her and play rebel songs down the line. Such was the level of harassment that she and her husband had to move out temporarily.
She continued to be proactive in preventing dissident Irish republicans from being honoured in Boston parades. Then came 1981 and the IRA hunger strikes in Northern Ireland.
In April of that year, 10 members of the Irish Prisoners of War Committee, Noraid, and the Irish National Caucus burst into the Irish consulate in Boston with a signed letter given to Heaney, which demanded that the Irish government intervene to prevent further hunger striker deaths. They refused to leave the Consulate unless she met them. She did so, for two hours of what was described as robust discussion, the content of which was not revealed by her.
As the hunger strikers died, protests by Irish republican sympathisers grew ever more intense in Boston, with some picketing Heaney’s home, carrying placards and throwing stones at her door, while others picketed the Consulate building.
In subsequent correspondence with foreign affairs, Heaney made a point of noting that the great majority of Irish organisations in Boston had not been involved in any of this.
The eldest of eight children, Carmel O’Leary, as she was then, grew up in Dublin’s Fairview . She entered the Civil Service and then began studying at UCD in the evenings for a BA in history and French, followed by an MA in history, becoming a tutor in history there. In 1965, she became a third secretary at the then department of external affairs.
As the US was perceived then to be more accepting of women diplomats, she was posted to San Francisco as Vice-Consul that year and was later transferred to Boston in the same capacity, soon becoming Consul General. While there, she met and married US citizenHenry Heaney.
Her marriage meant she was required, under Irish law, to retire, but she resisted this. A local arrangement was agreed whereby, on retirement, she was brought back to the Consulate as a local employee, there being no marriage bar on women working in the US since 1964.
She continued acting as Consul General on the understanding that she would be removed as soon as the department could find a man, or a single woman, to fill the role.
When the marriage bar was finally removed in 1973, following Ireland’s entry to the then EEC, then minister for the now Department of Foreign Affairs, Garret FitzGerald, reinstated her as a civil servant, and she continued as Consul General in Boston.
Such was her work for Irish culture during her time at the Consulate that she was awarded an honorary doctorate by Stonehill College, Massachusetts, for her services to Irish studies.
Concurrent with her role in Boston, Heaney was also the only woman on the Irish delegation to the UN between 1966 and 1971, where she vigorously presented the Irish government’s opposition to Britain’s policy of internment without trial in Northern Ireland. In 1979, she rejoined the Irish delegation at the UN and was appointed to the Special Political Committee as Ireland’s Middle East and Cyprus expert, the second woman to do so for Ireland.
Before leaving the US in 1983, Heaney was awarded the title Dean of the Boston Consular Corps in recognition of her services while in Boston. On return to Dublin, she was soon appointed to join Ireland’s representation at the UN in Geneva.
Not long after she retired in 1989, her husband Henry died, but she continued to remain active in Dublin. She was an adviser to the US Embassy on its Fulbright scholarship programme for a time, as well as on the board of the National Library and at the RDS library in Ballsbridge.
With a particular interest in Young Irelander William Smith O’Brien, believing he was something of a forgotten figure in Irish history, she prepared a lengthy study on his life.
She began to write for Irish and Irish-US newspapers on international affairs, as well as travel pieces and book reviews. It included regular contributions to the Rite and Reason column in The Irish Times.
She was a participant in the weekly philosophical discussion group, the Colloquy, and also took up hiking. To mark her 80th birthday, she climbed Carrauntoohil, Ireland’s highest mountain.
At 100, Heaney wrote concerning the afterlife in one of her Rite and Reason columns, saying that: “The essential nature of heaven, whether referred to in the prayers of medieval mystics or used metaphorically in a secular, contemporary context, is that it is a state of happiness and that it lasts forever.”
She died last August, aged 102, in Dublin’s Blackrock hospice. Her remains were donated to medical science.

title: Location tracking: ‘I can easily see where 80% of the people I know currently are’
description: We live in a world of surveillance. Our phones, our apps, security cameras and doorbells can track us. Does this enable or inhibit people’s development?
content:
When Orla Leahy, who is in her 70s, collects her husband from his appointments at the Beacon Hospital in Dublin she puts their dog’s collar, which has a location tracker, on to her wing mirror. “It’s a terrible place to park, so rather than have him waiting in the rain, he can see where I am [on his phone]. It’s a bit stalkerish but it’s a good use of the technology.”
A teenager I know was recently snared having a surreptitious party thanks to the family home’s doorbell camera. Sitting with his parents at the time, we watched all the youngsters coming to their door on his father’s phone before the event was shut down. I couldn’t help feeling it was a bit of a shame.
Someone else describes a friend whose girlfriend kept track of his every movement via location sharing – constantly ringing to ask questions about why he was where he was and who he was with.
We live in a world of surveillance. Our phones track us. Our apps track us. Security cameras on houses and businesses track us. Our data is circulated and shared and sold and hacked and leaked. Increasingly, assisting this process for the corporations who profit from it, we also voluntarily track each other.
Some people consensually track older relatives living alone. Very many parents track their teenage children’s movements. A surprising number of parents also track their adult children and, sometimes, their spouses via family connection apps such as Life 360 or the Apple Family Sharing facility. Meanwhile, most young people can constantly see the locations of their peers via the location-tracking software on messaging apps such as Snapchat .
There has been a huge change in social norms, says child and adolescent psychotherapist Colman Noctor . “Technology changes culture ... What was deviant is now acceptable and what once was acceptable is now deviant. I always use the example of calling to someone’s house unannounced. It used to be something everyone did and now you’d never do it. You have to text first and give warnings. We can’t underestimate how quickly these things seep into the societal narrative ... I didn’t see problems with it until an 18-year-old girl was in therapy with me, and she said her boyfriend tracks her. [I said] ‘That’s not good.’ But she didn’t see it. ‘My parents have tracked me since I was 15 years old. Doesn’t everyone just track everyone?’… Tracking an intimate partner, which would have seemed dreadfully inappropriate five years ago, has seeped into culture as something almost acceptable.”
The Irish Times put a call out to readers asking how people were using tracking technology and got an array of responses, which we followed up with more in-depth interviews over the phone. A number of people said they shared location-tracking details with older relatives who lived alone and they and their relatives derived a lot of comfort from it. Eoin Licken, an Irish engineer living in France, works with a Belgian company called Zembro that provides location-tracking services designed for people with dementia . “We have some nursing-home customers where you might want to monitor somebody and just know that they’re okay,” he says. “You can draw what we call a ‘safety zone’ on the map, and if [they] go outside that safety zone, it then starts sending its location every minute. “My [93-year-old] mother lives on her own in Dublin, so I would typically have a safety zone around her house, the park, the shops ... She walks that daily. But if she went outside that, I click on it ... She doesn’t have dementia, so she doesn’t need that. She’s only doing that because she knows I want to test this.”
His mother is a fan of her location-tracking emergency pendant, however. “She knew somebody who was putting the washing on the line and fell on a cold day and died. She’s very comforted by the fact she knows she can press a button and, in this case, actually talk to one of her children.”
She resisted being tracked in a more detailed fashion inside her home. “When I put that to my mum, she said: ‘Nobody’s tracking me in my house.’”
Many people track their teenage children. Ten years ago, Stephen (who didn’t want his full name published) disturbed his teenage son while his son was trying to take his own life. The family, school and the families of his friends rolled in to provide support. Later, Stephen adopted family tracking. “I was working overseas, still am a lot of the time. We were conscious he still needs to live a life. [There was] a little bit of comfort knowing that if he was half an hour late home that he’s in his mate’s house.”
Since then all of his family are on the Apple family-tracking app except for his oldest son, who lives abroad; and his wife, because she has a work phone with a different network provider.
Nowadays his son is healthy and well, but they still use location tracking. “My wife and family would be having dinner [when I’m out of the country] and she’d go ‘I wonder what dad’s doing?’ and my daughter would look at her phone and say: ‘Oh he’s in his apartment.’” He says with a laugh. “Sometimes the kids would be ignoring my wife’s calls and I have the capacity to set the alarm off in their phone. When they go, ‘What?’, I say: ‘Just answer your mother, will you?’”
There were other stories like Stephen’s from parents worrying about vulnerable children. Niamh, a mother of teenage girls, says she has location tracking on the phone of the 14-year-old, who often goes missing, but not the phone of the 15-year-old, who is always where she says she will be. “With my husband,” she quips. “I’d be more inclined to say: ‘Please don’t tell me where you are.’”
Noctor understands why a parent would feel a need to monitor a vulnerable child or why an adult child might monitor an elderly parent. But he worries that more widespread use of this technology will change our sense of privacy. “From a psychological point of view, we all need our private thoughts,” he says. “We need our own space. We need our own existence, our true self. But the more we display that, perform that, or broadcast that, the less is the likelihood we will ever gain the advantages of it. Our privacy and even our true self is being basically concealed because we’re performing as these avatars of ourselves.”
It is increasingly common to keep family tracking functioning for college-aged children. Pearl is a 19-year-old college student from Donegal in her second year of university in Dublin. Her parents have tracked her phone since she was a young teenager and continue to do so. “As a teenager I despised the idea of my parents knowing where I was [but] I just grew to like the idea ... When I’m walking back from college to my apartment, because I live in town, and it’s not the best of areas. I just know, well, my parents have my location. It really is like two guardian angels ... If I was without my phone, I probably would be a bit like, ‘okay, I’m definitely by myself here. If anything goes wrong, it’s just me.’”
‘I can’t really imagine being 30 years old and having my parents have my location’
Does she ever worry about her parents judging her activities? “If I was out too late, I wouldn’t think, ‘oh God, I better get home because my mum or dad’s going to see my location’ ... It’s more Dad [might say] I should probably go to the library early tomorrow morning and it’s 11 o’clock and I’m still in my apartment. I’ll wonder if he’s [looking] at my location and thinking to himself, ‘she didn’t get up and do that.’”
Most of Pearl’s friends are also on family-tracking systems and they share their location with each other. She sometimes wonders about this, asking. “Should I know what my friends are doing?” She says it can occasionally make her anxious, as she finds herself thinking “‘oh my friends are here and no one told me about that’ ... But I’ve almost become desensitised to it. I enjoy the thought of people knowing where I am ... Some people are quite into stalking Snap Maps [the map mode on Snapchat]. You can see where all your friends who have turned on their location on Snapchat are. I don’t have my location on on Snapchat. I only have it on for eight or 10 of my closest friends.”
[ Poetry for a surveillance society Opens in new window ]
As she gets older, does she think she might opt out of tracking? “I can’t really imagine being 30 years old and having my parents have my location,” she says. But then she thinks about it: “I’m fine with them having it now, even though I’m an adult and I’m away from home. So why not at 30? ”
Noctor thinks tracking young people too closely could affect their development. A space for private mistakes “is absolutely developmentally essential”, he says. “Not getting back on time and missing the bus encourages you to learn about responsibility ... Lots of these things can’t be taught, they have to be lived.”
Twenty-one-year-old Charlie Beaudelot from Offaly studies human nutrition and dietetics at Trinity College and TU Dublin and has a more cautious take on location trackers. “When I’m on my way home, I’ll share a location with one of my friends or share a location with one of my family members. And then there’s a few people who I let track my location all the time, but that’s mainly because they are people that are very close to me.”
Beaudelot has been “burned” by more extensive location tracking in the past. When they first came to college, sharing locations was the norm in their new friend group. But people often ended up getting angry with each other due to feeling left out if they saw other people hanging out together. “There is that feeling of underlying stress of being watched all the time, which is one of the reasons why I don’t share my location with many people now. The norm now is actually just sharing your location constantly ... I have definitely been questioned on it a few times by less close friends ... [and sometimes] felt pressured to share my location”.
Part of the reason they think they might be uncomfortable with more widespread tracking is that Beaudelot’s parents never tracked them in their teens. “I know some friends who have their location constantly tracked by their parents even now in college,” they say. “They come from stricter households ... Tracking has really affected not only their relationship with their parents, but their social lives as well because they feel they are being watched.”
[ The Irish Times view on CCTV in Dublin: Light camera action Opens in new window ]
They have also seen the ways location tracking can be weaponised in problematic romantic relationships. “I’ve seen it with friends who have got into more controlling relationships where people feel that they need to be able to watch their partner doing everything,” they say.
“There’s a difference between privacy and secrecy. I volunteer with Too Into You, part of Women’s Aid, [a programme for young people experiencing abuse in intimate relationships] so I keep an eye out for red flags in behaviour. I know some people who have been in situations where their locations are tracked and they’ve been accused, when turning off their location, of cheating ... I think sharing location is too normalised.”
Dola Twomey from the Stalking in Ireland Project, which is part of the Sexual Violence Centre in Cork, agrees that location tracking can be very problematic in the context of toxic relationships. “Every case [of stalking] will have a technological aspect to it. We carry the tech in our pockets all the time, and what that tech can actually do is just phenomenal compared to even 10 years ago,” Twomey says.
Often people are tracked without their knowledge, but she is also keen to stress that if someone feels coerced into accepting being tracked, that doesn’t constitute real consent. A controlling partner demanding someone’s location at all times, she says, is like “putting a leash on someone ... It’s typically hard for somebody stuck in that scenario to see it clearly, because making sure somebody doesn’t see things clearly is part and parcel of the abuse”.
[ Teenage boys in Ireland: ‘Now that everyone has a phone, the bullying never stops’ Opens in new window ]
Jason Broe, a 22-year-old business and management student at TU Dublin, has also seen it become an issue in relationships. “I’ve seen people get texts, ‘Where are you? Why are you with this person?’,” he says. And if someone who normally has location tracking on turns it off for a period, everyone assumes they’re “up to something”, he says.
As we speak, he looks at the Snap Map on Snapchat on his phone. “Looking at it now, I can easily see where 70 per cent or 80 per cent of the people I know currently are. It’s still a bit mad to me ... There is an option to keep it off, it’s called ‘ghost mode’.”
Even the name “ghost mode” indicates it’s the weird option, he notes. Broe worries about young people advertising their location to bullies and others who mean them harm. He also thinks location tracking adds to anxiety. “When you see on the map that there’s four of your friends in the same cafe it can hurt a little bit,” he says. “It could be because of something simple, that they were just in the same area and it worked out for them to meet up ... Some people are constantly looking at this [map].”
[ Mark O'Connell: A mother stalking her 19-year-old online is demented – but not in the way you think Opens in new window ]
Sometimes when travelling abroad, Broe will choose to be tracked for convenience and safety. But most of the time he chooses “ghost mode”. “I’ve been asked many times, why don’t you have your location on? They add me on Snapchat, and I follow them back, and they’re like, ‘oh, I can’t see where you are’. But that would feel like a weird thing to me. I like to keep it private.” He adds with a laugh: “Not that I’m up to anything.”
Michael Murphy, a 23-year-old final-year computing and software development student at TU Dublin, has also largely opted out of tracking software. “It would weird me out having everyone see my location live at all times.”
But many people in his generation are comfortable with it, he says. He thinks this might be because people grew up with their families tracking them. “A lot of people have their location [on Snapchat] on at all times. This one’s in Dún Laoghaire and this one is in Wicklow ... Oh, this one’s in Rathmines having a ramen. They just have a lower threshold for what they care about people seeing, or their privacy.”
For others, such as Murphy, their caution around the issue is part of a wider political awareness. He has some tech-savvy friends who go to extraordinary lengths to protect their data and location. “I do not like the thought that I’d be driving down the road, and there’s about 17 photos being taken of me in real time that are now stored somewhere,” he says. “It’s an odd feeling.”
He can’t understand why people would choose to be tracked at all times. “When I know I’m being tracked, it feels like there’s an eye in the sky watching where I’m going. Big Brother is watching.” He adds, laughing: “Big Brother being my friends.”

title: Rhasidat Adeleke on burnout; Kate O’Connor on her ‘turning point’
description: Athletes explain what they learned from Paris and how they hope to navigate the next 21 months to the LA Games
content:
When Rhasidat Adeleke and Kate O’Connor visited the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum last Monday morning, they were entering an arena that has already staged glorious moments in Irish athletics history. They hope to enjoy a couple more if they get to return there less than two years from now.
During their trip, Adeleke and O’Connor scouted out several venues that will provide backdrops to the 2028 Olympics, including the Coliseum.
It was there, in 1932, where Bob Tisdall won Olympic gold in the 400m hurdles, followed by Pat O’Callaghan winning his second gold in the hammer. Fifty-two years later, John Treacy arrived to the Coliseum after running 26 miles around the streets of LA to take silver in the marathon, the last event of the 1984 Games.
Adeleke and O’Connor’s promotional visit came after a summer in which, for the first time, both won medals at the same championships; Adeleke taking European silver in the 200m in Birmingham before O’Connor struck heptathlon gold. Their trajectories are neatly aligned as they approach LA, two years on from their contrasting experiences in Paris.
Their time in LA – they travelling as ambassadors of Allianz, title sponsor of the Olympic Federation of Ireland (OFI) and Paralympics Ireland – gave them the chance to bounce ideas off each other and reflect on how they’ve got to where they are, and what they need to do to be at their best if they return to LA in 21 months.
“Just being at the Coliseum, it really puts it into perspective,” says Adeleke. “We were just speaking about how huge it is, and envisioning the track being laid out here, and the fans screaming up. It just makes it all feel a lot more real.
“But staying mentally fresh, I think that’s something that, for me, we’re going to definitely try implement a bit more. Especially after the [Paris] Olympics, and 2025 and 2026, with the injuries, and the constant need to make sure that I’m at the top of my game.
[ Dr Pat O’Callaghan ‘the greatest all-round athlete in the world’ Opens in new window ]
“I’ve realised how important it was to get that downtime, get that family time, get that time to get away, and have that mental break. But also working smarter, not necessarily working harder. Because we’ve done the working hard part, the really difficult sessions and the gruelling work. And that essentially caused me a lot of injuries.
“So now we’re going to take things back to basics, focus on what works, and the quality of the work. And also making sure I’m living a full life, that I can enjoy, have fun, and time to breathe. And when I do come back to the track, when I do go to train, I’m in the best position to give 100-per-cent effort, and just not experience any burnouts again.”
Paris for me was that turning point ... Just the switch in mindset over the last two years is crazy
From here, Adeleke returns to her training base in Texas, continuing to work under coach Edrick Floréal, with no plans to change that before LA. Her 200m silver medal at the European Championships, where she improved her Irish record to 22.28 seconds, has given the Dublin sprinter another option for next year, and possibly 2028. But at her peak fitness and potential, she still considers the 400m her strongest event.
“At the moment, the 400m is still my main goal. But the 200m this year has shown that there is a possibility. But it’s all about timing, we’ll see how it plays out. The season can be unpredictable sometimes. You can set out to do one thing, and one event, then things can change.”
For O’Connor, the LA trip is a first excursion to the west coast, making the visit to Venice Beach, Santa Monica Pier or Old Route 66 almost as exciting as the Coliseum. She’s approaching the Olympics with a completely different frame of mind compared to Paris. At the 2024 Games, O’Connor finished 14th in the heptathlon on the same day Adeleke finished fourth in the 400m her heptathlon competition in 14th place – a mere footnote to the Irish performances over the entire 16 days.
“Paris for me was that turning point,” says O’Connor. “Those Games opened my eyes to the athlete I wanted to be. And from there I kicked on, so that going into LA, my goal is to be on the top of the podium. Just the switch in mindset over the last two years is crazy.
“And 2024 was such a tough year for me. I had a really bad injury, in December of 2023, where I ruptured two ligaments in my ankle and had a flaring of my tibia and fibula. It was a terrible injury, I couldn’t walk for months, and I thought that my season was over.
“I’d this lifelong dream of qualifying for the Games, and I managed to make that happen. And while I was there, I enjoyed every single second of competing. I absolutely loved it, and that buzz of the village, the buzz of the crowd in the stadium, it’s indescribable.
“But I definitely left feeling unsatisfied, and trying to figure out probably at the time whose fault was it. I was pointing the finger at my dad [Michael], at my other coaches, and everybody that was working with me. I was saying to them, ‘Maybe I need to try something different, something new?’
“Then, maybe after a week, I was doing some self-reflection, and I came to the decision to try to change everything that I’m able to – whether that was sleep, nutrition, recovery, turning up to training and giving 100 per cent.”
Seven months after Paris, O’Connor won bronze in the pentathlon at the European Indoors. With that, the Dundalk athlete kick-started her extraordinary run of seven medals in seven successive championships, the latest of which was gold in Birmingham.
“This year, I probably had a lot more improvement in my locker that I didn’t end up showing,” she says. “So I just plan on chipping away on all seven events. The top girls are scoring 7,000 points, I’m still sitting at 6,750 and need to get closer to that 7,000-mark if I want to stand a chance for what could happen. I don’t feel like I’ve reached my ceiling at all, but with multi-events, it’s also about staying healthy.”
[ John Treacy on running his last-ever marathon in 1993: ‘I was fulfilled, simple as that’ Opens in new window ]
