O’Connor will be 27 by the time the LA Olympics roll around, Adeleke, just 25. Both very much coming into their sporting prime.
“We’ve been speaking a lot over the last couple of days, and Rhasidat had so much success as an underage athlete and right into the senior ranks. And then 2025 and 2026, she faced her first bit of adversity. Whether that was injury or just different things going on in her camp, and she’s managed to come out of it.
“For me, it was almost the opposite. [When] I was a kid, growing up and coming into the senior ranks, I was injured quite often, and really trying to figure out what works for me.
“Now, the two of us are very much of the same mindset, that we want to be the best possible athletes that we both can be by the time LA comes around.”

title: Ninety-four people from US sought asylum in Ireland last year, none were successful
description: Ninety-four people from United States sought protection here last year, up from 22 the year before
content:
Transgender rights, persecution by a religious sect and school shootings are among the reasons a growing number of United States citizens have sought asylum in Ireland in recent years.
A review of asylum appeal judgments shows a broad range of claims for international protection by Americans, Canadians and British people.
However, none to date has been successful.
Applications for international protection from US citizens were previously few and far between. However, as of 2022 there has been a gradual increase, followed by a sharp rise in 2025 when Donald Trump assumed the US presidency for the second time.
Ninety-four US citizens sought asylum in Ireland in 2025, up from 22 the year before.
So far this year, 43 have applied for asylum, according to the Department of Justice .
Despite the rise, US citizens still form a tiny fraction of the 13,160 total who sought asylum in Ireland last year.
Asylum applications are initially heard by a civil servant from the International Protection Office .
If an application is rejected, asylum seekers can appeal to the Tribunal for Asylum and Returns Appeals (Tara), which took over from the International Protection Appeals Tribunal (Ipat) last June. Ipat continues to hear appeals lodged before June.
In 2022, a woman claimed asylum citing increasing violence in the US, including the rising number of school shootings. She cited an incident where her son’s day care was locked down due to a nearby shooting, and said she had been forced to buy a gun to protect her restaurant from looters during riots.
Refusing the application, the tribunal found that while gun violence was an issue in the US, it was not enough of a specific threat to the woman to grant her asylum.
Another case lodged by a US citizen in 2023 concerned alleged abuse of her by members of a religious sect. The woman said she was abused and tortured by members of the group and forced into marriage.
She said she underwent abuse by church members at various locations in the US and that she feared persecution if she returned due to the influence of a powerful member of the group.
The tribunal found the woman’s account of abuse was credible, but declined to grant refugee status or other international protection on the basis that there “is not a state of indiscriminate violence in America”.
The finding that the US was a democratic country based on the rule of law featured in most refusals of asylum by Ipat members.
In a case heard in 2025, Ipat refused asylum to a transgender woman who said she was a victim of transphobic abuse and domestic violence in the US and that her parents had murdered her sister.
The tribunal rejected the woman’s claims due to a lack of evidence and ruled that she was unlikely to be subject to state persecution in the US on her return.
However, it did note that the Trump administration had little sympathy or understanding of trans people.
“This attitude trickles down, and many of the majority who voted for president Trump can be assumed to share his views on LGBTI people.”
Another case dating to 2023 dealt with a black transgender woman who said she was kidnapped and tortured by the FBI .
[ State wins appeal over €21,877 damages award to international protection applicant Opens in new window ]
Denying her claim, the tribunal said that while black people are treated unequally in the US in many respects, there is not enough evidence to show state persecution.
In 2024, an American woman lodged an appeal against a decision to refuse her asylum based on allegations of domestic violence and continuing threats from her ex-husband and his family.
She said her former partner was sexually abusive, had tried to run her over in his truck and had fired a gun in the house. The Ipat member said there were issues with the credibility and consistency of the woman’s account and ruled that she would not face persecution if returned to the US.
Ipat also refused asylum claims from two Canadian citizens in the last five years, including in one 2026 case where the applicant claimed he was at risk of murder due to being a Catholic.
Last year, it refused asylum applications from two United Kingdom nationals, including one claiming a risk of persecution by people linked to the IRA.
[ Ireland’s asylum system is flawed, but a factory for fast decisions is not the answer Opens in new window ]
The tribunal noted the man was entitled to Irish citizenship due to having been born in Northern Ireland, but had not applied.

title: The Government won’t raise carbon tax again but promises to decarbonise the economy – how?
description: Climate change and energy experts have their say on the reasons for the budget U-turn – and whether they will work
content:
T he carbon tax cuts and freezes announced in this week’s budget may help appease hard-pressed consumers but the consequences for the Government’s decarbonisation strategy is not clear.
Is the strategy sufficiently firmly established to withstand the repositioning of one of its key pillars?
Or is carbon tax so foundational that without its full-strength support, the plans to wean households off dependency on fossil fuels will wobble?
Opinions are mixed even among those who stand fully behind the carbon tax as a principle and a practical measure.
“Carbon tax is the right policy, but now is the wrong time for a high carbon tax,” says Paul Deane, senior lecturer in clean energy futures at University College Cork.
“Climate policies must be seen as progressing us towards a better future rather than punishing those who cannot afford it.
“You need to take into account the circumstances of the time. It’s important that we don’t end up being tone deaf to those who are really struggling.”
Kelly de Bruin, co-ordinator of climate research at independent think tank, the Economic and Social Research Institute, however, fears the rollback risks reinforcing the perception of carbon tax as a punitive measure.
“Carbon tax is not there to punish people. It’s often perceived as that but it’s not and we need to push back on that,” she says.
“You introduce a carbon tax so that people switch to low-carbon alternatives and you support them in that transition.”
[ Carbon tax U-turn calls Government’s climate commitments into question Opens in new window ]
Carbon tax was meant to do just that with most of its revenues providing free and grant-aided retrofits, boosting the fuel allowance and other welfare payments to offset the extra cost of fuels, and funding farmers’ environmental schemes.
But by cutting the rate on home heating oil and gas back to 2023 levels for the remaining lifetime of the Government and pausing increases on petrol and diesel, revenue will be down €177 million annually.
This amounts to about 17 per cent of the €1.1 billion raised from the carbon tax every year. Coincidentally, the Department of Agriculture receives €173 million from carbon tax revenues so the loss is significant.
Ministers said there would be no drop in spending on supports but Michelle Murphy, policy analyst with the think-tank Social Justice Ireland , questions how the gap will be made up.
“There is no clarity around how they are going to fund that,” she says.
She also criticises the untargeted nature of the cuts that means the wealthy also benefit.
“We have Susi [the third-level education grants system] and the national childcare scheme that are means-tested,” she says.
“It should not be beyond Government to come up with a scheme that can verify what sort of heating system you have and then assess your income for support.”
Murphy also worries the rollback exposes carbon tax to more severe action.
“There is a narrative around abolishing the tax completely and it feeds into that,” she says.
Independent TDs Mattie McGrath and Danny Healy-Rae were certainly quick to revive that narrative this week.
McGrath recalled how he fought against “this codology” when the system of annual increases was introduced in 2020. “I opposed it fundamentally as I do today,” he said.
Healy-Rae said abolition should be the next step. “It should be well gone by now with the torture people are going through,” he said.
While there is no suggestion the Government will completely unwind the tax, Kelly de Bruin of the ESRI says tampering with it is harmful enough.
“We had committed to this carbon tax. It’s in writing, it’s in law, it’s in the [programme for government], it’s submitted to the EU and now suddenly there’s backtracking on it,” she says.
“If we want people on board the transition to a low-carbon economy, we need to show that we are committed to that and let them make decisions based on policies we won’t backtrack on.
“If we’re asking people to buy EVs [electric vehicles] because we’re taxing carbon and then we suddenly stop taxing carbon, then people have bought an EV that doesn’t give them the same economic benefit as was promised.
“How can we take the Government seriously?”
Paul Deane at UCC does not believe there will be any general backsliding on decarbonisation, saying the momentum is unstoppable.
“We are seeing a huge increase in retrofitting. We’re seeing extraordinary take-up of solar and the number of EVs is growing fast now,” he says.
Besides, he says: “Fossil fuel prices are doing the job that carbon tax was meant to do, turning people off fossil fuels and making them want alternatives.”
But he is not saying decarbonisation should be left entirely to market forces.
“I just think we need to be more flexible. We need carbon tax to be high when fossil fuel prices are low and carbon tax to be low when fossil fuel prices are high but not both at the same time.
“And if there are shortfalls in funding, we need to pull in more general taxation. Carbon tax is currently contributing to that general taxation.”
He’s referring to the arrangement by which only the annual increases in the tax since 2020 are ring-fenced for climate measures while the baseline intake goes to general spending.
[ Scrapping carbon tax means handing ‘billions of euro to Ursula von der Leyen’ Opens in new window ]
Diarmuid Torney, director of Dublin City University’s Institute for Climate and Society, fears that the funding gap could widen, especially if the Government runs scared of reinstating the carbon tax hikes for petrol and diesel next year as pledged.
“I am not convinced that will definitely happen,” he says.
“But the bigger point is that the Government should be doing much more. There was only a small increase in funding for SEAI [Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland, which administers the national retrofit scheme]. The current level of support is insufficient.”
He questions then why the Government broke the rigid agreement to have annual increases in carbon tax only to replace it with a rigid pledge to have no annual increases – for home heating fuels at least.
“It’s a one-way intervention in that the Government is prepared to intervene when prices are very high by reducing the carbon tax but would the opposite happen if prices start to fall?”
It is perhaps a sign of the sensitivity around carbon tax that the scathing criticism of the budget by the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council, the fiscal watchdog, did not reference it.
Eddie Casey, the council’s chief economist, treads carefully on the issue.
“I don’t think anybody would argue people should be forced to choose between heating their home and paying their bills this winter,” he says.
“But the bigger risk is that short-term relief becomes a substitute for action. Ireland is far behind on its EU climate targets, and missing them could cost the State billions.
[ Ireland will not hit 2030 carbon targets and could face billions in fines, says Darragh O’Brien Opens in new window ]
“The real gains for households will come from progress on the energy system, electric vehicles and retrofitting homes.”
Michelle Murphy agrees but, like Torney, fears the increases on petrol and diesel due to resume next year will not materialise.
“It’s always hard when you put something like this off to try and reintroduce it again.
“That’s not going to help change things. The carbon tax was supposed to discourage fossil fuel use and support people to make the switch away from them.
“If you don’t use that tool properly, you’re leaving people in the same position with the same problems for the next fuel crisis.”

title: ‘It is labour intensive but vital work’: An island-hopping GP on the west coast
description: Dr Noreen Curtis takes a curragh out to remote islands off the Co Mayo coast in her role as a medicine-dispensing GP
content:
S mooth sailing when she heads out for appointments with her island patients isn’t the only priority for Achill islander Dr Noreen Curtis.
Among a litany of issues facing remote rural medical practices is an urgent problem: the dramatic fall of dispensing GPs.
This issue will be a priority when she is scheduled to meet Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill later this month.
Curtis is a passionate advocate on behalf the Rural Island and Dispensing Doctors of Ireland, a group set up in 1984 to protect local medical care for people living in rural, isolated and offshore locations.
She is acutely aware of the fact that since 2016 there has been a 64 per cent drop in general medical practitioners who also dispense medicines – in the absence of nearby pharmacies – throughout the most remote areas of the country.
“There were 108 dispensing GPs a decade ago, but this number has now dropped dramatically to 30,” she says.
“It is no surprise when the fees they are being paid are about 10 per cent of what pharmacists receive, that is about €4 per patient per month, and you can well imagine the workload.”
Among the other challenges facing remote rural GPs is the perennial problem of finding locum cover.
Curtis, who, like her father, worked with one of the two group practices on the Co Mayo island of Achill for many years left in 2020 to become a GP for three nearby islands: Clare, Inishbiggle and Achillbeg.
On Thursday The Irish Times joined with Curtis on her five-minute curragh journey across to Inishbiggle in driving rain. She is ferried across to the island by a local man who brings her when she has to visit her patients.
Curtis uses an old schoolhouse on the tiny island for her GP clinic but she also makes house calls to patients, which included island resident Jeremy Holt on Thursday.
[ GP shortages: Where are the most acute problems across the country? Opens in new window ]
Notwithstanding the unique challenges she faces – not least stormy weather – her smaller number of patients facilitates her work with the University of Limerick’s School of Medicine: supervising and “exposing” medical students in the northwest “to the joy and challenge of rural practice”.
“I bring them all to Achill and out to the islands, and they absolutely love it. Rural practice is not for everyone, but I know for a fact that several of these students will go on to become rural practitioners after their experiences here,” she says.
Curtis believes there needs to be extra supports put in place to attract young GPs to more remote areas.
“Dispensing is a vital component of rural practice. In a remote community without a pharmacy close at hand, GPs perform this vital service, but at a fraction of the cost it entails,” she says.
“It is labour intensive but vital work to ensure elderly patients, sometimes living alone, are supported.”
Curtis outlines the fact that the General Medical Services (GMS) contract makes a GP responsible for patients on a 24-7 basis, but for the many single-handed GPs there is “no equitable access to cover when they need leave, whether maternity, illness or annual.”
She says this is “the single biggest obstacle to newly qualified GPs taking on a rural post”.
The Mayo GP points to a 2024 survey of rural GPs, cited by the Irish College of General Practitioners, that found 72 per cent were unable to access locum support in the previous 12 months, while 47 per cent could not avail of locums due to cost.
[ ‘I decided to take a leap of faith’: Largest ever number of GPs graduate Opens in new window ]
Rural areas typically have 60 GPs per 100,000 people, compared with 90-100 in urban areas, even though rural GPs account for 11 per cent of the GP workforce but care for 20 per cent of the population.
She adds that 30 per cent of these rural GPs are aged over 65.
It is those patients living on the rosary of islands along the west coast who are the beneficiaries of groundbreaking medical practice using new technology.
Piloted on Clare Island, the Healthy Islands initiative is a telemedicine project designed to improve healthcare and reduce social isolation. The initiative is being led by the University of Galway’s Hive Lab (Health Innovation via Engineering) in association with the HSE.
[ The modern Irish GP: How a new kind of doctor is reinventing general practice Opens in new window ]
The highlight of the launch event in 2023 was the delivery by a drone, called Madra, of an epi-pen from the mainland to the island.
The project is working on services with 12 offshore islands and aims to expand the technology to other isolated communities to improve access to care “without travelling”, she says.
Caring for her island patients still involves rainwear and life-jackets, curraghs and currents, shimmying down ladders at the harbour in Cloch Mór on Achill, the pier from where she departs weekly on the ferry for Clare Island and her patients there.
When acute emergencies arise, her work escalates to calling for the Irish Coastguard helicopter Rescue 118 to evacuate the patient.
“This is often supported by our RNLI Lifeboat, which luckily, if it is during the night, just involves me nudging my husband, Dave, in the bed, as he is the coxswain of the lifeboat,” she says.

title: Land Development Agency staff share €2m in bonuses
description: State’s affordable homes builder says rewards help it compete with private-sector firms for workers
content:
The Land Development Agency (LDA) paid close to €2 million in bonuses to staff last year, its latest annual report showed.
The State body’s headcount has risen rapidly in recent years as it brought in experienced private-sector staff from firms such as private landlord Ires Reit and homebuilder Evara . Last year, it recruited almost 80 people.
Its annual report said it has put in place a short-term incentive programme (STIP) for staff, which was listed under the organisation’s staff costs. It paid out €1.98 million last year.
The report did not confirm how many LDA staff received a bonus. The LDA employed 250 staff at the end of last year. If the €1.98 million bonus payment were evenly distributed among them, then staff would have received €7,900 each.
Chief executive John Coleman, who was paid a base salary of €200,000, was not paid a bonus in the year. No STIP bonuses were paid to any staff in 2024.
The Irish Times asked the LDA to confirm how many staff were paid a bonus under the incentive programme.
An LDA spokesman said the organisation “competes with private-sector construction industry firms for the experienced staff needed to deliver its large-scale housing programme comprising in excess of 40 projects.
“In order to secure the recruitment and retention of these skills, performance-related awards form part of the agency’s remuneration arrangements, with the exception of the CEO. They are in line with those of other commercial State bodies.”
The LDA was established in 2018 to develop affordable housing on State lands. It has since expanded its remit to partner with developers to help activate private projects to deliver affordable homes.
Coleman, who has led the LDA since it was set up, renewed his contract this year and received a €50,000 increase to his base salary to bring it up to €250,000.
In the past eight years, the LDA has grown to become one of the biggest developers in the State with a total capitalisation potential of €8.75 billion.
It has more than 6,500 homes under construction on about 20 sites. A progress report published in July said the agency would complete 1,800 new homes this year, nearly 3,000 next year and more than 3,500 in 2028.
The annual report showed the LDA’s turnover rose from €78.2 million to €115.9 million last year, with €30.8 million linked to the sale of affordable homes while €23.5 million came from cost-rental revenues.
The agency’s earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) were €6.5 million compared to a loss of €17.5 million the previous year.
In 2025, the LDA made an after-tax loss of €17.2 million, less than the €33 million loss the previous year.
At the end of last year, the LDA controlled €2.5 billion worth of assets, up from €1.4 billion a year earlier, due to the acquisition of new development sites and the completion of many new residential projects it owns and leases to tenants.
The LDA paid €19.3 million in wages to its staff last year, with €2.6 million of this amount paid to the 10-person executive management team and board of directors combined. In 2025, a severance payment was made to one employee, totalling €46,691.

title: ‘Pablo doesn’t patronise’: The Irish animated show with an autistic star
description: Eleven-year-old Alexander Myles, from Co Antrim, takes over the main role for Pablo: Next Level, as the protagonist wrestles with the move to secondary school
content:
P ablo is an animated children’s television series, made in Belfast, featuring a preschool-age autistic boy who uses magic crayons to navigate life’s challenges.
A new spin-off series, Pablo: Next Level, aims to show the importance of inclusivity for neurodivergent children at mainstream schools.
The voice of the older Pablo is provided by 11-year-old Alexander Myles. His newfound stardom doesn’t stop Alexander from feeling a little nervous about doing an interview. Just like Pablo, Alexander is autistic, and he can overthink things at times, he says.
He has his “beautiful mum”, who responded to an advertisement for voice actors for the show, to thank for his new career, he says. “[The studio] called me over and we just did a couple of wee auditions and then I found out I’d gotten the role.”
Alexander lives in Ballycastle, Co Antrim . Like other children his age in Northern Ireland, he has just started secondary school and is adjusting to the huge change. “Being in school can be very overwhelming sometimes – rules changing, loud noises – but I feel when the right adjustments are in place, it makes it a lot easier”.
While secondary is a big leap from primary, Alexander has found he enjoys many of the differences: “The movement breaks definitely help, getting to go to different classes. I enjoy having different teachers in different classes as well.”
He loves lots of the subjects he’s studying, but is reluctant to point out his favourites for fear of upsetting anyone: “That’s another thing with autism. I feel like if I say one thing, the other person will get offended. And then I feel bad.”
“Facial expressions and tones can be hard too. That’s probably one of the biggest problems for me,” he says, explaining that it can create issues with his friends sometimes. “Sometimes if my friends tell me I’ve annoyed them, I’ll dramatise it and think: is that us done?” It’s something he hopes the show will help other people to understand.
“I hope it [the show] will let other people see that they’re not alone. I hope it shows ... if you have the right measurements in place, that can make a big difference: ear defenders, for everyone whenever they need them; written instructions, because maybe sometimes verbal instructions can be hard; age-appropriate fidget toys,” he says by way of example. “Divided plates as well. That’s what I have. I don’t like foods touching. I feel they should also be available to everyone.
“And, I think, choices for uniform. So if you’re a boy, for example, you have to wear a tie. And maybe you don’t like the texture of the tie so you have to be uncomfortable for six hours straight. They should maybe take that away.”
[ ‘I don’t have words to describe this stress’: No school places for twin sisters with autism Opens in new window ]
Feeling and being included is “very, very, very important”, Alexander says.
Alexander’s mother, Therese McCurdy, knows how difficult things can sometimes be for her son. While all can appear well on the surface, for Alexander, “on the inside things can be really tough. The anxiety about things. The worrying about food or certain textures annoying [him] during class.”
Having to mask – work hard to adapt his behaviour to neurotypical norms in order to fit in – at school all day means Alexander can feel totally exhausted in the evenings. I’ve “been overwhelmed”, he says. “When he comes home he needs that time to decompress,” McCurdy says.
In the programme, she adds, “Pablo has got really good friends. He’s got a really good teacher who takes the time to listen. Who stops and gives him one-to-one. Who tries to understand what he’s going through in that moment. And simple things like that are so important for including kids and making them feel seen.”
Alexander is similar in some ways to Pablo, the character he plays. But he’s quite different in others. Two similarities are “not liking food touching and being annoyed when you’re told to do something”. However, “I’m not as shy as Pablo”. The differences show that autistic people are all different, his mother says.
McCurdy is also neurodivergent, which gives her some insights into the challenges her son faces. Checklists are key to making things run a little smoother at home, she says. And she’s conscious of how beneficial a cartoon such as Pablo: Next Level might have been for her had it existed when she was a child.
“Something like that would have made a massive difference to me when I was younger: seeing myself represented. I was diagnosed [with ADHD ] quite late on, so to raise that awareness, and get that out to people so they can understand they are not on their own. And that there is a reason why they feel the way they feel, and maybe do the things they do, without feeling totally strange,” she says.
The cartoon is also helpful for teaching neurotypical children how differently their neurodivergent classmates experience the world, McCurdy says: “Small things can make a huge difference to somebody who is neurodivergent.”
One of the show’s writers, Carol Walsh, became involved with the production when Paper Owl Films and Crayola Studios were looking for autistic writers with a comedy background. Her seven-year-old son is also autistic, and some of her writing and storylines were inspired by her own childhood experiences and those of her son.
“It’s always really joyful to be able to write kids’ TV. It doesn’t patronise. There’s a huge gap of shows that shows an autistic perspective from a really joyful perspective, and a funny perspective,” she says.
[ Most neurodivergent children have a neurodivergent parent – diagnosed or not Opens in new window ]
“A lot of the time they come from a really good place but they do focus on the limitations of living with a neurodivergent brain, and Pablo gets to look at things from a really holistic, child-centred, point of view.”
The show is for all children. “You can sit any kids in front of Pablo and they’ll enjoy it,” Walsh says. And they’ll see things in it, whether they’re neurodivergent or not, that are going to resonate for them”.
Pablo: Next Level is broadcast on RTÉ Kids and the RTÉ Player, CBBC and BBC iPlayer

title: Woojer Vest 4 review: This vibrating vest might be the weirdest gadget I’ve ever reviewed
description: It can all be a bit much after a while instead of making you feel more immersed in the content
content:
I have tried out some unusual tech in my time. Bands that tap into nerves to help you lose weight or tackle insomnia. Sensors that encourage you to drink more water. Headphones that also act as a personal air purifier.
But a vibrating vest? That could be the weirdest yet.
The Woojer Vest 4 pitches itself as a “powerful and accurate 360-degree immersive experience”, a similar proposal to the acoustic therapy mat the company makes, but with a different target market. Instead of targeting wellness warriors, the vest is aimed at gamers, movie fans and music lovers who want to feel the audio, although you can use it for meditation too.
The Woojer Vest 4 takes audio and turns it into physical vibration, through six haptic transducers you strap to your body.
It doesn’t matter what the audio is – a movie, a game, Sabrina Carpenter on Spotify – as long as there is a bit of rumble to it. Low-frequency audio rumbles become vibrations and, in theory, you become fully immersed.
Sounds odd? Yes. Did it live up to the promise? Not really.
The device itself looks more like a life jacket than a wellness device or a gaming accessory, but I’ll keep an open mind.
Handily, it comes with instructions printed on the inside. Waist straps get tightened first, then the chest straps, and finally the shoulder straps.
[ Can a €1,100 high-tech vibrating mat help you sleep? Opens in new window ]
That was where the first issue became obvious. I’m shorter than average, so the distance between my shoulders and my waist is not quite what it would be for everyone. There isn’t much adjusting I can do on the shoulder straps to get that ideal “snug fit” the vest mentions.
That has knock-on effects. There are two pads on the chest, two on the back and two at the waist. Because of my lack of height, the chest vibration plates are, shall we say, interestingly placed, and the back vibration plates may as well not be there.
To get things working, you need to connect the vest to the Woojer app on your phone.
The unit sent for review needed a firmware update before I could get going, which requires the vest to be plugged in. That led to the second issue: there are two USB ports on the vest, one is on the back and the other on the front left side. Guess which one is for charging? The one I can’t reach without unstrapping the entire vest.
I unhook everything, plug the vest in and get going on the firmware update. Time for problem number three: it fails the first time and takes its time with the second attempt, so I shut it down, reboot the vest and try again. That requires a hard reset (there’s a small pinhole for that).
Ten minutes later we are updated and ready to go. Back on with the straps.
Now you can choose your audio source. The vest will work with everything from iPhone or Android device to PCs, consoles, smart TVs and VR headsets. If it is a phone, tablet or laptop, you can connect via Bluetooth and use either wireless or wired headphones for audio.
Other devices can be hooked up with cables, which effectively tethers you to your seat.
Music is the easiest to test. A wireless connection to the vest, wireless headphones, plus some bass-heavy audio makes for vibration overload. You can dial down the effect either through the app or the physical control panel on the vest. I made the mistake of cranking it up to the highest level on a particularly bass-heavy track and it felt like being hit in the chest. Would I buy a haptic vest for this experience? Unlikely.
Gaming seems like the natural use for the vest. Being able to feel the action instead of just seeing and hearing it would ratchet up the realism.
It didn’t quite work out like that. The haptics are based on audio rather than the game experience. The loudest sound triggers the biggest reaction. If that is the sound effects of the action, great; on some games it was the less crucial background noise, such as the rumble of vehicles and background music.
The problem is that it can all be a bit much after a while. Instead of making you feel more immersed in the content, it can get a bit muddy.
If I am running around a battlefield being shot at, I want the vibration pattern to reflect that. Shot in the chest? The chest plates should vibrate to reflect that. Instead everything blends together, and you can forget the vibration is even there. It is the same for movies and TV shows; sound effects and soundtracks are almost indistinguishable.
Some games have lag when connected to the vest via Bluetooth, even using the dedicated gaming modes. That makes the vibrating sensation distracting rather than immersive because it is coming too late. The settings don’t allow you compensate for it enough, focusing more on audio lag, so your best bet is to use a cable.
The most effective use for the vest is hooking it up to Calm or other meditation apps. But would you spend almost €500 to haul yourself into a vest and vibrate your way to inner calm?
Connects to a range of audio sources, so you have choices about what you want to immerse yourself in. Works well for guided meditation and bass-heavy music, or stealth games that don’t overlay a soundtrack.
It just doesn’t seem too effective. It works on low-frequency audio – so anywhere there is a rumble, it translates to the vest and the end result isn’t targeted; it just becomes background noise.
The lag on some games devices makes the vest’s effects more of a distractions
There are different modes in the app that can help tailor the experience. You can change modes, choosing between broad, focused, gaming and low latency – each has its own strengths. If you are using the vest for gaming, either low latency or gaming mode will be your best bet.
The vest makes for an interesting accessory, but it isn’t as effective as I hoped.

title: Simon Zebo: Joe Schmidt’s double standards drove me mental, made me dislike the Irish camp
description: Ireland’s head coach nailed the build-up to the clash with the All Blacks in 2016; if he’d always been like that, I’d never have gone to France
content:
Axel’s spirit was with us in Chicago in November 2016 . I’ve often described it as my favourite week ever in an Irish jersey and it wasn’t just purely because of the result. It was the whole week.
I think Joe was brilliant that week and if you could bottle that Joe from Chicago for my whole career, I’d never have left for France. Well, not as soon as I did anyway. There was a huge novelty around travelling to the USA and playing our first fixture of the November series in Chicago against the All Blacks , in Soldier Field, the home stadium of the Chicago Bears, which was insane when you put it all together. At the time, there hadn’t been a fixture remotely like this in the history of Irish rugby. There were eight Munster players in the squad. Pete, John Ryan and Donnacha Ryan, Earlsy, Billy Holland, Conor, CJ Stander and myself.
That whole week was quite relaxed because the long-haul flight was on the Monday, so Tuesday was just a recovery day, and then when we were on the pitch it was very light on the feet. We enjoyed each other’s company and while training was still important, it was that little bit lighter and less stressful than most Test weeks. There was less detail around our attacking plays and how we were going to approach the game. I thought Joe balanced the workload very well, taking the pressure off the team while treating the match as the huge opportunity that it was for us.
We had plenty of time to explore Chicago, to eat in nice restaurants and do fun things. We had the deep-base pizza that Chicago is famous for and went to cafes while walking up and down the Golden Mile. On a day off, some of the lads went to the Chicago Bulls training facility. We stayed in Trump Tower and whatever you think about him, that hotel is spectacular. The match itself almost snuck up on us. Not that we didn’t think about it. There were constant reminders. Pockets of us ran into pockets of the All Blacks several times, either walking around Chicago or after ending up in the same cafes. I bumped into Tawera Kerr-Barlow and we saw Malakai Fekitoa, TJ Perenara, Julian Savea and a few others. We were crossing paths or saluting them walking down the street or seeing them in the Nike shop. The excitement was building all week and on the Wednesday night thousands of fans spilled on to the streets after the Cubs beat the Cleveland Indians in a dramatic and deciding seventh game to win the World Series for the first time in 103 years. When an estimated five million people took part in the victory parade on the Friday, we were able to watch it from the roof of the Trump Tower, which is a hundred storeys high. Probably the best view in Chicago. The following day, we had our chance to make history by beating the All Blacks for the first time in 111 years.
I think it was Joe who suggested we face the haka by forming a figure of eight. That was incredibly powerful. We rehearsed it once and Joe made a point of having the Munster boys at the front, to underline our links with Axel. When the crowd realised what we were doing, their response sent a tingle up the spine. It was one of the best atmospheres I ever played in and forming that figure of eight had a huge impact on Irish sport as a whole. It created an iconic image and was a brilliant way of paying tribute to Axel. I would say that Joe has a lot of class and he is a brilliant coach and he nailed that week. It was a touching moment and it fired us up. TJ Perenara led their alternative haka, the Kapa o Pango, which was incredible, but I think we were more inspired by their haka than they were.
We really went after that game with an attacking mindset from the first minute to last. We built a lead and even when they came back at us with three tries in the second-half, we weren’t afraid to throw the ball to the wider channels. I thought we played with more freedom, and that reflected the week we’d had. Joe didn’t have his paws on us as much – I mean that in the nicest possible way! He had a brilliant game plan and it was a little less restricted, a little looser. We were set up to be ambitious off set-pieces and, of course, he had detected kinks in the All Blacks’ armour that we could exploit, such as channels farther out or space in the back field.
From the pack’s lineout maul, Conor and Johnny gave me a run-in on the blindside to put us 30-8 ahead with our fourth try, but six minutes from the end our lead was down to 33-29. Joey Carbery had turned 21 on the Monday and he replaced Johnny before the hour on his debut. From a scrum in our own half, he passed to Jared Payne. He ripped a pass to me on the edge and I kicked deep into their 22. There was a lot of space for Julian Savea to cover because we knew he was slow off the blocks to get across and cover kicks. He didn’t have a great appetite for it and if I was able to hit grass and keep the ball in play, it would be trouble for them.
So, when Fekitoa picked up and passed to him, Savea was smashed into touch-in-goal by Mur and Andrew Trimble. From the 5m scrum, Jamie Heaslip picked quickly when they might have been expecting us to hold the ball at the base. He worked a switch with Robbie Henshaw, who scored with an in-out line. Joey converted and that was it. It felt incredible to be part of the first Irish men’s team to beat the All Blacks. But it was only when we did the lap of honour and saw all the Irish supporters, and saw Paulie alongside Doug Howlett in the stands, that it actually hit home.
There were loads of massive moments in that game, but it started with Joe giving us the ambition and license to go after them with that type of riskier play. Everybody was buzzing for the game, which wasn’t always the case because of the amount of stress and nerves that sometimes you could potentially be under. I loved being in Irish camp that week and I clearly wouldn’t say that about all my time with Ireland.
I can go through all my caps and pick out plays and moments in games where a team-mate missed a horrendous tackle, one-on-one, and just dived at the floor to pretend he had made an attempt, to make it look like an ankle tap or whatever. But really, he was just diving on the floor. However, if I stayed on my feet and tried to make a tackle, which I have done to every player in my career, and I lost to better offence, I would invariably be singled out in front of the squad at a review. But if it was anyone else? Rob or Felix or Earlsy or whoever, in the review Joe would say: “Oh mate, I know you can do better than that.” And then he’d quickly move on, almost as if it did not happen. That double standard drove me mental, and drove me to dislike Irish camp.
I know Johnny and Paulie would swear by him, but those lads never got a bollocking. Paulie was never called out in front of the squad and God forbid he’d call out Johnny because he could do no wrong. Rob Kearney and Seán O’Brien were the same. Yet myself and others might get slaughtered. And it hurt, because I never thought I’d want to avoid wearing a green jersey. I loved to represent my country. I’m a proud son of Blackrock in Cork. I will happily show off my hometown to anyone. I was so proud to play for my country, and especially singing Amhrán na bhFiann.
All of this was on my mind when I met with Joe and David Nucifora, the IRFU’s director of performance. I watched and listened as they made the worst attempt to retain a player you could ever imagine.
It felt to me like a token gesture. It was a pathetic conversation.
Joe and Nucifora didn’t say anything along the lines of “Please, we really need you to stay” or “You’re so important to Munster and look what you’re going to sacrifice”. Nothing like that. It was as cold as ice.
In my view, they were just carrying out a box-ticking exercise for the benefit of the media, so that when my departure was announced they could claim they tried to make me stay. I wish I’d had the balls to say that to them there and then. Nothing about that conversation made me remotely inclined to stay. And it wasn’t meant to do so.
So, while it was difficult to leave Munster and Ireland, Joe being head coach of Ireland made it very easy to decide that 2018 would be the time in my career when I would maximise my contract value by joining Racing. There, I’d have the chance to play my best rugby with some of the best players in the world and also have the best chance of winning a Champions Cup. I had a good relationship with Andy Farrell , both before and after my three years with Racing. He coached me on the Lions tour and later brought me back into camp when he was Ireland head coach, but different injuries meant a recall could never happen. If he had been head coach all along, however, it could all have been so different. I don’t think I would have left a green jersey, or at least not as early in my career as I did.
I was the number-one left winger at the time and I was the likely starting 11 for Ireland in the Six Nations and in the World Cup. Jacob Stockdale was emerging, but he had zero caps and he was the only other Irish left-winger on the horizon. Of course, Earlsy could play on the left wing, but it would be over a year before James Lowe became eligible to play for Ireland.
I had started every game in the 2017 Six Nations, so I decided to leave as a starter, not as a squad member or a player in the wider extremities. But it was that bad, I felt I had to go. I would have stayed longer had Andy or someone else been the Ireland head coach and then have gone to Racing or somewhere in France at the age of 29/30/31. I would have gone eventually, but it would have been later. I wouldn’t have left at the age of 28. I missed the 2019 World Cup when I was in my pomp and ripping up trees. I scored 16 tries in my first season with Racing, was nominated for European Player of the Year and was named in the Midi Olympique Team of the Season.
I was ready to be called up for that World Cup and if I had been, I would have said yes in a heartbeat. But of course, the call never came. So, I effectively sacrificed playing in the World Cup because I no longer enjoyed Irish camp. That was a sad state of affairs.

title: Siobhán Fenton: Sinn Féin might have an ulterior motive for its actions at Drumcree
description: Michelle O’Neill’s confident and defiant responses appeared almost to goad the DUP into walking out of Stormont
content:
The recent scenes on Garvaghy Road carried grim echoes of the darkest days of the conflict to a community for whom the acute and lasting trauma never really went away.
Older generations thought this was a past that belonged only in their own harrowing memories and grainy archival television footage.
Now they are forced to hear it, see it play out again on the smartphones of their children and grandchildren as they followed updates about the dispute on TikTok.
The reaction to the prospect of the Orange Order’s march was visceral distress and genuine sense of panic not just locally, but in communities across Northern society. This was reflected in the unusual united front formed by a broad spectrum of nationalist politicians, including Sinn Féin , the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), People Before Profit and Aontú .
The ins and outs of the legal status of the Garvaghy Road parade will play out in court in the coming days and weeks, while the police are now investigating “unlawful protests” that blocked the marchers. And in parallel, a distinctly political dimension is now beginning to play out at Stormont .
[ Back on the Garvaghy Road, people are wary and rather worried ]
Unionist politicians have seized on the opportunity to make political capital from the dispute. They have cited the presence of Sinn Féin ministers, including First Minister Michelle O’Neill , as evidence that senior party figures broke the law by taking part in an unlawful protest.
Yesterday, O’Neill confirmed she has been called for police interview in relation to the protest. She has defended her presence, explaining she was “proud to stand with the residents” on the basis that “when the law is wrong, I will stand firmly against it.”
Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson warned: “We have lawmakers acting as law breakers and they need to face the consequences for their actions.”
“The stakes are high” and they could “get even higher” for Stormont, he said, seeming to float the prospect of the DUP walking away from powersharing at Stormont.
In the Stormont chamber this week, the DUP demanded that O’Neill commit to resigning as First Minister if she is found to have breached the ministerial code or the law. The more hardline Traditional Unionist Voice tabled no confidence motions in O’Neill and other Sinn Féin ministers. These are likely to be debated next week.
Unionist politicians’ decision to pursue O’Neill in this way share all the same hallmarks of their decision to back Brexit. It is a knee-jerk response devoid of long-term strategy and it plays straight into Sinn Féin’s hands.
The DUP has been in a strategic tailspin since the Brexit vote. The 2022 Assembly election saw the party lose its prized place as the largest party at Stormont to Sinn Féin.
Recent months have seen it incur further reputational damage. Former leader Jeffrey Donaldson has been convicted of sexual offences against children. A serving DUP MP was charged with an alleged assault of a woman – he denies it and is contesting the charge. Another DUP MP is being investigated by a Westminster watchdog in relation to an alleged spending breach . He denies this, and the party has dismissed it as a “politicised complaint”.
The DUP has slumped repeatedly in recent polls. The May 2027 Assembly election now looms large on the horizon. The party faces the prospect of losing seats if these trends continue. In this context, the DUP’s attempts to capitalise politically on Drumcree are an attempt to reverse this decline by riling up their grassroots.
However, in doing so, it is handing a gift to Sinn Féin. Sinn Féin’s response to Drumcree was not opportunistic – it reflected a principled stance and genuine desire to show leadership within, and solidarity for, the local community.
However, it is also true that events there suit the party very well.
Sinn Féin has also been struggling in opinion polls. The most recent poll for the Belfast Telegraph showed the party at a five-year slump. It ran a highly emotive campaign about the historic significance of electing a nationalist First Minister in 2022, but struggled to deliver meaningful change during the ensuing Assembly term. It has become painfully clear that the First Minister position is symbolic.
The party has also suffered the consequences of choosing its ministerial departments unwisely. It selected finance and economy at a time when it still expected getting into government in Dublin and was keen to show its competency on economic matters to impress southern voters. Instead, these departments have struggled to be relevant to voters’ day-to-day lives – and least not to the degree that might have been possible had Sinn Féin selected health, education or communities instead.
The SDLP leader of the opposition, Matthew O’Toole, has carved out a reputation in this Assembly term for doggedly holding ministers of all parties in the executive to account for their failure to deliver. Sinn Féin ministers often seem to struggle when confronted with this level of systematic scrutiny.
The behaviour of unionist parties recently means Sinn Féin can now fight next year’s Assembly election on the basis that a vote for the party is a vote to stand with O’Neill against political unionism.
The DUP’s veiled threats to bring down Stormont are working in Sinn Féin’s favour. Many Sinn Féin members continue to be, at best, ambivalent about the party’s presence at the executive table.
A senior figure in the party once explained his misgivings to me about the Stormont strategy – amounting to Sinn Féin telling voters “look at how good we are at administering British rule in our own country”. Some feel Sinn Féin’s presence at the Stormont executive legitimises partition and the “ Northern Ireland ” state. The end of Stormont would add to the wider argument that Northern Ireland is unworkable and a united Ireland is the only way forward.
However, Sinn Féin strategists are also aware that pulling down Stormont would be seen as opportunistic by some voters. If the DUP triggers a collapse, Sinn Féin would be quite content for them to take the flak for the decision instead.
Similarly, if O’Neill or any other Sinn Féin leadership figures are found to have behaved unlawfully in relation to Drumcree, this would be seen as a badge of honour by many nationalist voters, who would consider it as being part of Northern nationalism’s proud civil rights tradition.
This is why O’Neill appeared so unruffled in the face of unionist attacks in the Stormont chamber this week. If anything, her defiant responses appeared almost to goad the DUP into walking out of Stormont. She will be aware that unionists have much to lose from their political attacks, while she has much to gain. She is much more comfortable facing criticism about her attendance at Drumcree than being grilled about Sinn Féin’s track record of delivery.
The fault lines on which the 2027 Stormont election will be fought have been drawn. In the eight months left until that election, expect fractious scenes to continue at Stormont. A parliament that already struggles with delivery will likely drag to a halt and see squabbling prioritised over policy.
The people who suffer the effects of such performative antics are those who languish on hospital waiting lists, struggle to afford the cost of living or to access disability services while sectarian charades at Stormont continue.
Siobhán Fenton is the author of Ourselves Alone: Sinn Féin Behind Closed Doors

title: ‘They were all sick of each other by then’: Inside the Government rooms where the budget was made
description: Fraught last-minute haggling in back rooms dominated the final days of negotiations as spending Minister Jack Chambers dug in
content:
Four days on from Budget 2027 , the dust has largely settled on the €8.5 billion package of spending increases and tax cuts.
Voters are neither blown away nor blowing up after the budget; the proving ground is likely to be in the cold weeks and months ahead rather than the immediate aftermath.
But, like every budget, it tells us something about how the Government is trying to balance the politics of the day – and how it is succeeding, or failing.
The Irish Times spoke to more than 20 people, including Government Ministers and senior officials across the two Coalition parties who worked on the budget, to understand how it was put together.
The budget choreography is a well-worn one, but this year had some important differences.
Towards the end of summer, officials from each department begin to engage with counterparts in the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform (DPER, described more casually as “D-per” in Government speak). The tax side is no less important, but most budgets are focused on spending on new measures.
Long and technical engagements on pay, the cost of maintaining the existing level of services (“ELS”) and technical allocations proceed while the political system begins to find its feet again after the summer recess.
As budget day looms closer, Ministers start talking to Minister for Public Expenditure, Fianna Fáil’s Jack Chambers , who makes an initial offer. This has a sort of ritual role-playing. “I pretend it’s an insult; he acts like he is Santa Claus,” confides one Cabinet source.
This offer is again narrowed down and in the week before the budget, Ministers sit down, flanked by advisers and officials, at one big table in the TK Whitaker room in the Department of Public Expenditure. Chambers and his cohort sit on the other side.
Even Chambers’ closest allies would admit he was taking a much harder line this year than ever before. It was signalled early and often, and several participants in the fabled budget bilateral meetings complained afterwards.
Nowhere was this more the case than with Minister for Culture Patrick O’Donovan , who met Chambers on the Wednesday before the budget.
Chambers’ meeting with O’Donovan was short and non-conclusive. Nobody rejects the suggestion it ended after around eight minutes, saying it was “fractious”, “brusque” and ended in a way that was “not pleasant”.
Fine Gael’s O’Donovan – not one to shy away from conflict – seemed unbothered by the perception that there had been a showdown between the men, saying afterwards that if he had to “step on toes” to stand up for his department, then “that is my job”.
The Limerick County TD had sought €899 million, later shaving that down to €858 million, but by the Friday before the budget, Chambers was standing firm with an offer of €828 million.
O’Donovan and his junior Minister, Fianna Fáil’s Charlie McConalogue, went up through the gears, penning a letter to Chambers and the Coalition leaders warning that the “proposed offer is a disproportional cut and an undermining of clear Government objectives” while listing a range of consequences for agencies under the department – most notably RTÉ, where he said the Government was at risk of reneging on a 2024 bailout agreement with the broadcaster.
[ Last-minute €20m funding cut for RTÉ could have messy consequences Opens in new window ]
Ultimately, O’Donovan was successful in prising another €21 million from DPER over the last weekend after his gambit – though, for reasons still unclear, he decided not to use that money to increase RTÉ’s allocation as agreed. It sparked a big post-budget row.
Cabinet colleagues are puzzled by his approach. “He did not need to pick that fight,” says one, describing it as “pretty petulant and badly thought out”.
O’Donovan would later claim with some justification that RTÉ had delivered neither the reforms nor the promised redundancies, but he had made the mistake of not informing either the Taoiseach or the Tánaiste of his decision over the weekend; the first they knew about it, multiple sources attest, was on the day of the budget.
By the day after the budget, O’Donovan’s bosses were looking to de-escalate the row with the national broadcaster, which – needless to say – was leading its own news bulletins with the story. It was not what they wanted to be talking about in the days after the budget.
Cabinet colleagues will watch closely what happens, especially if more money flows towards RTÉ.
“The department can’t be seen to get extra money because he threw the toys out of the pram,” says one. “If this is the way to get extra money we’ll all be doing it next year.”
O’Donovan wasn’t the only Minister to successfully persuade Chambers and the Coalition leaders to loosen the purse strings in the final days.
Despite a universal cut to student contribution fees being firmly ruled out on Monday after a few days of back-and-forth, €18 million was found for Minister for Further and Higher Education James Lawless to proceed with the measure in the hours before the budget was signed off.
Minister for Finance Simon Harris was also said to be manoeuvring in support of the extra cash, anxious to up the universal supports for middle income earners. University chiefs, who prefer increased funding for them than cuts to student fees, are said to be less impressed.
This year health, so often a budget battleground, was comparatively quiet – Chambers and Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill are said to have carried over work on the yawning HSE overspend into the budget.
“Jenny played it very well,” says one person involved in the process. “She has convinced them all that the overspend is not her fault, it’s all the HSE’s fault. She gets on with Chambers and is working with him on all the cost control stuff.”
Despite the emphasis on prudence and Chambers’ hawkishness, there is no budget tradition as time-honoured as the few euro being found down the back of the couch at the 11th hour.
And yet, two people who have participated in many budgets and were in the room this year reported a changed approach. Both identified an ideological devotion to spending discipline and rooting out what Chambers believes to be inefficiencies that was even harder than suggested by his public statements.
“[Chambers] is running an ‘all public employment is waste’ agenda,” claimed one; another described the DPER side as having “ideological confidence” that they “know better than everyone else”.
Both contrasted Chambers with his predecessor Paschal Donohoe’s firm but conciliatory approach. “[Donohoe would] feel your pain ... this guy is just saying: ‘You’re full of shit; fix it.’”
“Paschal killed you with kindness. Jack just kills you,” says the second person, describing Chambers as “one of the most arrogant people I’ve ever met in my entire life”.
This person says they have been in budget talks with officials “shouting with rage and spittle flying” and this has been replaced with less hostility from DPER, but no less intransigence.
“They’re not trying to bully you, they just think they’re better than you.” One of the budgetary process veterans wonders whether the Taoiseach “has any control” over Chambers.
Allies of Chambers, and at least one other Cabinet Minister, reject the idea he is arrogant.
“He can be direct and blunt in engagements. This isn’t helped by colleagues who come in looking for allocations many multiples of what Government has agreed and is able to give them ... But I don’t believe there’s any arrogance,” says one source close to Chambers.
Colleagues and officials are also nervously eyeing Chambers’ plan for a public spending efficiency taskforce – mischievously dubbed “Pest” by political wags – that will insert itself into departments and ask difficult questions about spending and efficiency outside the formal budget process.
Chambers is said to be insistent that the body is needed to rifle through departments in pursuit of cultural change – which could get messy, if it gets off the ground.
The final pre-budget jousting took up a long and draining weekend at Government Buildings. The two leaders were due to meet on Sunday at 11am to agree the final details of the spending package, but the meetings were repeatedly postponed, and in the end didn’t start until about 6.30pm, says one person involved.
Harris’s wife had just had a baby and he was obviously drained; officials wondered how he was managing to get on with business at all.
There was also a discernible edge between him and the Taoiseach, according to two senior sources. Their respective chiefs of staff, Deirdre Gillane for Martin and Sarah Bardon for Harris, were trying to put out fires and solve problems for their bosses – a measure, according to some of the civil servants who were watching, of how relations between the principals had deteriorated.
[ ‘A KitKat budget from a TikTok Tánaiste’: Ivana Bacik takes a bite out of the Coalition Opens in new window ]
Monday’s final sessions to agree the tax package were equally scratchy, sources say.
“There was a lot of hassle over the tax package,” says one official.
But they got there, as they do with all budgets. Sometimes the talking and the tweaking goes on until later the night before.
This time, with Ministers and officials exhausted and irritated after hours and hours of wrangling over the weekend, everything significant was agreed relatively early, by about 4.30pm, reckons one participant.
“They were all sick of each other by then.”
There is one thing that the budget will not change: this will be a winter stalked by the possibility of further strife. Even setting public sector strikes aside, some backbenchers are already worried about the prospect of intense bad weather coupled with higher grocery costs and further unrest in energy markets.
The budget is the budget, but, as has been seen so far this year, the surplus is also there – and the Government seems unable to stop itself from reaching into it. A Cabinet source says that if something “catastrophic” happens, “we do have the resources to respond”.
In the aftermath of this year’s budget, one veteran says that Ministers hoping for congratulations might be a long time waiting – and should be careful what they wish for.
“Politicians looking for credit,” this person counsels, “should always remember that it’s a very short distance between a clap on the back and a kick up the hole.”

title: Kenmare better off holding out in Irish takeover sweep – for now
description: Miner part-owned by Oman sovereign wealth fund is coveted by firm controlled by Abu Dhabi ruling dynasty
content:
The United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Oman , which lie on either side of the Strait of Hormuz , have drawn closer since the Iran war began despite reports that some Gulf states privately accuse Muscat of being soft on Tehran as it casts itself as mediator-in-chief.
Most recently, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, UAE’s deputy ruler and overseer of the business interests of Abu Dhabi’s ruling Al Nahyan family, paid a visit to Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said in Oman last week.
The official readout was diplomatically anodyne, citing “strong fraternal ties” and pledging to expand co-operation in the mutual interests of both countries.
While it was unlikely to have featured during the tete-a-tete, a Dublin-listed company has suddenly become an area of common interest: part-owned by Oman’s sovereign wealth fund and, as we learned this week, coveted by a company ultimately controlled by Abu Dhabi’s ruling dynasty.
The Irish Times reported on Tuesday how Kenmare Resources , whose Moma mine in Mozambique produces about 6 per cent of global titanium minerals, had attracted bid interest from Abu Dhabi-based International Resources Holding (IRH).
[ Kenmare shares soar on confirmation of Abu Dhabi bid approach ]
IRH, a unit of International Holding Company (IHC), which is chaired by Sheikh Tahnoon, previously ran the rule over Kenmare two years ago, but it came to nothing.
The investment arm of the sultanate of Oman, meanwhile, acquired a 29 per cent stake in Kenmare a decade ago by committing between $100 million (€89 million) and $275 million rescue fundraising, mainly to pay down debt.
While the Oman Investment Authority has been the biggest seller into share buy-backs by Kenmare over the past five years, it retains a stake of more than 17 per cent (held through a vehicle called Africa Acquisitions) and a seat on the board.
That puts the Omanis in a pivotal position should IRH, a mining and trading group, come up with a bid by the November 17th deadline imposed by the Irish Takeover Panel.
It’s hard, however, to see Abu Dhabi coming up with anything near an acceptable price even if Kenmare has become increasingly uninvestable for long-term institutional investors in recent times.
Shares in the company closed on Monday, before news of the non-binding proposal from IRH, at £1.81 apiece. That was 69 per cent below a £5.30-a-share offer made in March last year by Kenmare’s former long-time managing director Michael Carvill and another Abu Dhabi firm, private equity house Oryx Global Partners.
Kenmare rejected that consortium’s proposal as undervaluing the company, but continued talks for more than three months before walking away when Carvill and Oryx indicated they planned to lower their original pitch.
Tom Hickey , who had succeeded Carvill as managing director in August 2024, told The Irish Times in September last year that the exercise was far from futile and had “shone a light” on the fundamental value of Moma – estimated to have a lifespan of another 100 years – even if the price of titanium minerals such as ilmenite, its main product, has fallen sharply in recent years.
But it also served as a reminder that Kenmare is, as Hickey put it, “ a small-cap, single-country, single-commodity ” company.
Only months after walking away from the Carvill talks, Hickey was forced to take a $301.3 million impairment charge against its Moma assets as Kenmare lowered its long-term revenue assumptions amid uncertainty over pricing.
Ilmenite is now well into its fourth year of decline – driven by Chinese producers, operating at home and in Africa, continuing to oversupply the market. And there’s no sign, as yet, of cyclical recovery. Berenberg analysts recently cut their ilmenite forecasts again and they now reckon it will be 2028 before a recovery occurs.
It’s of minor comfort that the price of zircon, which accounts for about a quarter of Kenmare revenues and is used to make ceramic tiles, has stabilised and is starting to increase again.
The biggest reason stock market investors have been sticking to the sidelines is Kenmare having been in talks for about four years with Mozambican authorities on a key royalties agreement covering Moma. The previous 20-year accord expired just before the end of 2024, though the terms were to remain in place until a new one was reached.
Kenmare, which committed $341 million in recent years on a project to upgrade and relocated its main mining plant in Moma, said in mid-August, as it announced interim results, that it was continuing to “engage constructively” with the Mozambique government and that “significant progress” had been made over summer.
But the longer this drags out, the greater the chances that it ends up in international arbitration.
IRH’s parent, IHC, has a market value of more than €200 billion. The company moved into mining in late 2023 by acquiring Zambia’s Mopani copper operations in a transaction valued at $1.1 billion.
Its mining portfolio grew further last year when it paid $367 million for a 56 per cent controlling stake in Mauritius-based Alphamin Resources, giving it exposure to one of the globe’s largest tin-producing mines in the Democratic Republic of the Congo .
IRH’s limited dependence on external debt gives it greater flexibility in financing acquisitions. Its Mopani transaction, for instance, was mainly funded through equity and shareholder loans.
This could allow it to submit a more aggressive offer than a listed mining company or private equity firm could make for Kenmare, both of which might need to secure bank financing to complete a deal.
But would it make a bid before the deadline that’s anywhere near the level that Carvill and Oryx pitched? Unlikely.
Having held out so far, Kenmare may be better served holding its nerve until the ilmenite market at least stabilises and the royalty issue is resolved.
That would offer the best chance of Abu Dhabi putting forward a proposal that its Omani friends – and other big shareholders – would be willing to entertain.
The fifth Irish plc to be subject to a takeover approach this year, Kenmare may be the only one of the quintet to hold on to its independence. For now, at least.

title: Pepper rate hike to heap more misery on distressed borrowers
description: Someone with a €200,000 outstanding loan at Pepper worse off by around €300 every month
content:
T he news that Pepper Advantage is increasing its standard variable interest rates by up to half a percentage point next month will come as a bitter blow to around 13,000 borrowers who have their loans managed by the company.
In a news release confirming the hike, Pepper did not say what the new rates would be because, as a spokeswoman subsequently explained to this newspaper, “these loans sit across multiple portfolios that originated with different lenders and at different points in time. As a result, there is no single Pepper variable rate”.
What we do know is they will be substantially higher than those available from more traditional lenders. A person with a Pepper-managed loan is likely to be paying at least two percentage points above what is on offer elsewhere. And that makes a huge difference to affordability.
Someone moving from a Pepper variable rate to a fixed rate with one of the more traditional lenders could see their rate fall by 2½ percentage points or more.
Many Pepper customers – those who saw their loans moved from other banks after they got into financial difficulties during the crash and subsequent years – have been unable to refinance elsewhere because of poor repayment records.
[ Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: What you need to know Opens in new window ]
Being unable to switch and avail of cheaper rates available elsewhere will see someone with a €200,000 outstanding loan at Pepper worse off by around €300 every single month.
That is, by any measure, grossly unfair.
Pepper says it “derives no commercial benefit from changes in interest rates on the portfolios it services on behalf of beneficial owners”. And we have no reason to doubt that but someone, somewhere, is making money out of the misery of a significant number of Irish people, many of whom are still paying a heavy price for the property crash almost 20 years on.

title: Is wine really going out of fashion?
description: How to Drink Better: There is a slump, particularly in red wine, but not necessarily in this market
content:
T rade magazines and social media are full of stories predicting the demise of wine . They point to figures showing production at its lowest level since 1961. Vineyards in Bordeaux and Rioja are being grubbed up as producers are unable to sell their wine. The process is hastened by a globa drop in consumption.
Red wine seems to be hardest hit by the slump. This is partly down to changes in the way we drink wine. Traditionally, red wine was seen as something to enjoy sitting down with a plate of food. But many consumers today prefer to enjoy wine by itself in a pub, a wine bar or at home. So, while white wine sales are doing okay, and sparkling wine is increasing, the figures for red wine are falling. Even with dinner, many now prefer to drink cocktails before and during meals, and a large group of younger consumers don’t drink alcohol of any kind.
For a long period, the wine trade here and abroad assumed wine consumption would increase every year – with new markets opening up in China, India and the former Soviet bloc. In Ireland, wine consumption showed double-digit increases almost every year throughout the late 1980s and 1990s. We were really only catching up with most of the rest of the world, and we still drink far less than most of our European neighbours. Many assumed the boom would go on forever, and the latest Irish figures do in fact show a very small increase in wine sales at the expense of beer.
The biggest drop in sales has been elsewhere around the world. Whereas wine is seen as a sophisticated drink in Ireland, the opposite is the case in producer countries such as Spain and France . Younger consumers there see wine as something their parents drank and therefore boring rather than aspirational. Wine sales have been plummeting for years in these markets.
The wine trade hasn’t really helped itself. Wine has always been complicated, with a nomenclature that is difficult for new consumers to master. All of those different regions, grape varieties, the impenetrable language of terroirs, vintages, those long wine lists in restaurants and all those ridiculous tasting notes; just to buy a drink! Little wonder that consumers moved elsewhere.
So, should producers be concerned? All is not lost. Consumers are buying less wine but switching from entry-level to more expensive premium wines. There are vast swathes of vineyards that may have been planted in unsuitable areas where the vines need irrigation or where it may become too hot to grow grapes due to climate change . The future for these producers looks grim. But other cooler regions will thrive.
It seems likely that there will always be room for quality wine; it isn’t disappearing, it is just being redefined by a new generation of drinkers.

title: The late photographer Colin Keegan’s best work
description: Keegan won awards through the Press Photographers’ Association of Ireland for work capturing news, politics and entertainment
content:
Award-winning press photographer Colin Keegan died following a crash in Co Meath last weekend .
Keegan had worked for Collins photo agency for three decades, and won a number of awards through Press Photographers Ireland for his work capturing news, politics and entertainment across Ireland.
Here we show a selection of Keegan’s finest work, including his 2005 photograph of then-minister for defence Willie O’Dea holding a gun – an image that sparked significant controversy at the time.
Mary Dunne, office manager at Collins photo agency, set up by Charlie Collins, recalls the origin of that famous photograph, taken during an Army exercise at the Curragh camp in Co Kildare: “It was him that asked Willie O’Dea to pick up the gun, and he picked it up and pointed it at him. Colin said he nearly dropped the camera!”
Recalling Keegan fondly, Dunne continued: “He was never big-headed he was always modest about his talent. He was a very talented photographer who won a lot of awards.
“Colin was always a perfectionist. I never had to worry about Colin. He’d always come back with the goods. He’d sit there for hours on end.
“He was just a very diligent worker and great fun to be with.”
She remembered Keegan starting work with the agency: “It was the same year Veronica Guerin died. Thirty years ago.”
Dunne said she had spoken to Keegan on the Friday before he died: “I had a chat with Colin on Friday, it was nice that we did have that. I was just asking him about how he was. He was so young.”
Laura Hutton, deputy head of visual media at The Irish Times, described Keegan as a “gentleman”. “His loss is devastating, my thoughts are with his family, his two children especially,” she said.

title: Irish showjumping Olympian Bertram Allen found guilty over Florida drink-driving
description: He is put on probation for a year, must pay restitution to other driver and do 75 hours’ community service
content:
Irish Olympic showjumper Bertram Allen has been found guilty of drink-driving causing damage by a court in Florida.
Allen had changed his plea to guilty after failing to strike out incriminating statements he made to police following his arrest last January on grounds he was too drunk to consent to an interview.
Allen was in Florida competing in the 12-week-long Winter Spectacular Show Series in Ocala when he was arrested at the scene of a crash in West Palm Beach.
He is the son of Bert Allen, the multimillionaire whose family formerly owned Slaney Foods. Allen is ranked 55th in the world in the latest Fédération Équestre Internationale (FEI) rankings.
This year he was part of the Irish showjumping team that qualified for the LA Olympics in 2028 . Allen previously represented Ireland at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021 .
According to an arrest report, officer Lester Escaran said he saw a four-door white Florida-registered vehicle with front-end damage in the inside centre lane of Southern Boulevard. Samuel Bertram Allen was in the driver’s seat.
Escaran said he “observed Mr Allen to have glassy watery eyes and there to be an odour of an unknown alcoholic beverage coming from the interior of the vehicle”.
He said when Allen exited the car he had “an orbital sway while standing”.
­Allen is alleged to have said he was driving and attempted to stop, but was unable to do so and collided with the vehicle in front of him. Allen said he was coming from Okeechobee Steakhouse and had landed in Florida earlier that day from Amsterdam.
Allen is said to have failed a number of field sobriety tests before he was arrested and taken back for breathalyser tests, which showed he was over three times the legal limit.
Allen testified via Zoom at a hearing after the court was told he would not be able to return to the United States until the immigration issues raised by the case were resolved. He said he split his time between Germany and Ireland and did not understand the US criminal justice system.
Judge August Bonavita put him on probation for 12 months and fined him $1,526 (€1,362), including court costs. He ordered Allen to pay $2,149.75 in restitution to the person whose car he crashed into.
The judge ordered the revocation of Allen’s driving licence for 12 months and required him to attend DUI (driving under the influence) School and do 75 hours of community service.
Allen’s attorney, Julian Kessel, was approached for comment. He previously described him to The Irish Times as “a good, skilled and fair young man” and “an accomplished equestrian player”.

title: Leitrim housing body linked to FF council chair under investigation
description: Inquiry into Cluainín Voluntary Housing Association by regulatory authority under way
content:
A housing body with Leitrim County Council (LCC) mortgage debts – whose board includes the Fianna Fáil chairwoman of the council - has been placed under formal investigation by regulators.
The inquiry into Cluainín Voluntary Housing Association (VHA) was started three months ago by the Approved Housing Bodies Regulatory Authority when it sent in inspectors with sweeping powers to examine its books and officers.
