The AHBRA is the supervisor of not-for-profit approved housing bodies (AHBs) such as Cluainín that receive public funds to provide affordable housing to tenants.
This is only the second statutory investigation by the AHBRA since it was established in 2021, but the regulator did not notify media when appointing the inspectors. In July the regulator published a statement about the investigation on its website, but not on its homepage.
Cluainín has since filed financial statements in which it said the inspectors are examining its “accounting records and governance”.
The Cluainín directors include Mary Bohan, a Fianna Fáil councillor since the 1970s who became cathaoirleach of LCC in June.
“I have no comment to make,” Bohan said in reply to questions on the AHBRA investigation.
Bohan declined to discuss Cluainín dealings with the council, saying she was “relatively new” to the housing body’s board, which she joined in 2019.
“They’re in existence for the guts of 20 years and they do fantastic work,” she said.
“There’s an investigation. We await the result of that and we’ll be talking legal advice.
“As far as I’m concerned, and the other board members, everything is in order. I’m happy that everything is 100 per cent above board with Cluainín VHA.”
A founding director of Cluainín former Fianna Fáil councillor Aodh Flynn, did not return a phone call to his home or reply to emailed questions.
LCC said it issued a communication in February to Cluainín outlining the remaining balances on its four 30-year mortgages with the local authority, as had been requested. Such loans supported the provision of 66 housing units in the county.
“Since the [capital assistance scheme] CAS mortgages in question have not yet reached maturity, Cluainín Voluntary Housing Association is required to continue full compliance until the end of the 30‑year term,” the council said, noting Cluainín was “not at any stage” deemed non-compliant.
“Should the AHB fail to comply at any stage, non‑compliance may trigger repayment, as the loan would no longer qualify as non‑repayable once the CAS scheme conditions are breached.”
[ Hundreds of homes transferred from Circle to housing bodies after regulator intervention Opens in new window ]
Replying to questions, the AHBRA declined to set out the terms of reference for the Cluainín investigation.
In July, the regulator said the appointment of inspectors followed “an extended period of regulatory engagement” with Cluainín.
“Having considered information obtained through these engagements, together with information arising from its ongoing regulatory oversight, AHBRA determined that a statutory investigation was warranted,” it said then.
Cluainín, which also is a registered charity, previously came to the attention of the Charities Regulator over a property deal in the 2010s. Cluainín acquired a Co Sligo property from a company, Blackmud Developments, which is owned by two long-time Cluainín directors, Flynn and Padraic McGowan.
The Cluainín financial statement for the year to October 2015 said Cluainín contributed €320,850 to Blackmud for the purchase of a site at Calry and a contributed a further €122,400 to Blackmud to buy a bond.
“Two housing units and a portion of the site at Farrancarday, Calry, Co Sligo, were subsequently transferred to Cluainín.”
Asked about Cluainín transactions with Blackmud, the Charities Regulator said: “While the Charities Regulator does not usually comment on matters regarding individual charities, we confirm that we have engaged with the trustees of this organisation in relation to a number of different charity governance issues over a period of time.”
The Blackmud deal in the 2010s took place apparently earlier than the unspecified issues under AHBRA investigation.
In financial statements signed off in August and filed with the Companies Office in September, Cluainín said the AHBRA inspection covered the period from mid-February 2022 onward.

title: Omagh bombing witness says suspected bomb car passenger ‘made eye contact and grinned’
description: Another eyewitness says suspected driver let her and her daugther cross road and thought at the time it ‘was decent of him’
content:
A t 3.05pm on August 15th, 1998, Lance Corporal Errol Thompson made a note in the logbook at Lisanelly army barracks in Omagh .
“A large bomb exploded,” he wrote. “Location unknown.”
It is the first written record of the explosion that, only a minute before, had devastated the centre of the Co Tyrone town and that, it was immediately evident, had caused multiple deaths.
The death toll was one of the worst in the history of Northern Ireland’s three-decade Troubles. The bombing killed 29 people, including a woman pregnant with twins, and injured hundreds of others in the Real IRA atrocity.
How it happened – and how it could have been prevented – is being pieced together in evidence at the Omagh bombing inquiry at a Belfast court.
Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) constable Alan Palmer previously described the moment of the bombing to the inquiry as “a flash of light, a great suction and a great, piercing pain in my back” as he was hit by shards of glass from shop windows.
He remembered “seeing all the people who were in front of me lying dead, and those who remained alive had sustained serious injuries”.
Another former soldier, former captain Michael Peebles, recalled hearing “screams and cries” as they listened in to the RUC radio in the barracks ops room.
“It was pandemonium, understandably,” he said.
The inquiry heard the British army was not notified about the bomb warnings by the RUC, Northern Ireland’s police force at the time, but learned of them from listening to that same radio, as was the custom at the time.
It also heard soldiers were not deployed to Omagh until after the bomb exploded because they were not requested by the RUC, again in line with procedure.
“Had the RUC immediately requested your support ... at 14.30 could you, in theory, have had 15 extra bodies and 15 extra sets of eyes on the streets of Omagh?” barrister Stephen Toal, representing some of the bereaved families, asked Peebles.
The barrister replied: “And we will never know if the outcome could have been different.”
This is an independent public inquiry, which opened in 2024 and is charged with examining whether the atrocity could reasonably have been prevented by British state authorities.
This week it passed the halfway stage of its current evidence session, which is looking at how the bombing was carried out, and by whom.
The inquiry’s working hypothesis is that, while the Real IRA “was responsible”, at an “organisational level, both the Real IRA and Continuity IRA planned and carried out the Omagh bombing”.
[ Omagh inquiry names 27 ‘key individuals’ related to 1998 bomb attack Opens in new window ]
It has identified 27 “key individuals” – 14 of whom have convictions for terrorist offences – including Michael McKevitt, Colm Murphy, Seamus Daly and Liam Campbell – who were found liable in a civil case for the Omagh bombing – and Seamus McKenna, who was found not liable but who, according to that hypothesis, “played a key role”.
The inquiry considers there are “sound reasons” to believe Seamus McKenna was in the bomb car and Seamus Daly in the scout car, and its “working hypothesis” is that Liam Campbell “either made, or was responsible for causing to be made, the warning calls”, said lead counsel to the inquiry Paul Greaney.
“Sat like a spider at the centre of the web of the plan to detonate a bomb in Omagh” was Colm Murphy, the barrister said.
The inquiry has viewed a detailed timeline compiled by inquiry analyst Mark Safranauskas, which used available data, including from the Police Service of Northern Ireland , An Garda Síochána and the British army, to name those they believe to be responsible, and the links between them.
The presentation tracked the progress of the bomb car and scout car on the basis of data from mobile phone cell sites.
It showed handsets connected to McKenna and Daly moving over the Border to Omagh on the day of the bombing and reappearing on the southern side of the Border after the explosion.
But, as the inquiry has highlighted, much remains unknown, not least their precise route, as there is “no conclusive eyewitness testimony” nor CCTV footage.
Testifying before the inquiry, Det Supt Emmet Casserly of the Garda agreed that the force’s investigation was not able to “establish definitively” where the so-called bomb car was taken after the theft, where it was kept or where the bomb was loaded.
[ Omagh bombing lawyers question whether fingerprints were ever sent to Scotland Yard Opens in new window ]
He also agreed with Greaney that “although it is thought that the bomb car was accompanied by a scout car”, there is no evidence “conclusively to confirm there was another vehicle”.
It is not known where precisely the bomb run began, nor where the cars crossed the border, though it is believed to have been at Aughnacloy, Co Tyrone – 32km southeast of Omagh.
The inquiry was told the bomb car was not on the footage from the permanent British army checkpoint at Aughnacloy, but that it was not recording for about 25 per cent of the time and did not always capture every vehicle.
The bomb and scout cars are believed to have crossed the Border between 1.13pm and 1.29pm on August 15th.
The inquiry heard an eyewitness later told police he noticed two cars parked on the side of the road outside Omagh at about 2pm.
He said “two males ... were reading a map on the roof of the Corsa” and another man was in the passenger seat of a “dark red or maroon Vauxhall Cavalier” that matched the description of the bomb car.
Det Chief Insp Peter Billingsley, who gave evidence to the inquiry as a corporate witness on behalf of the PSNI, confirmed there was no investigative follow-up of this sighting and the second car – potentially the scout car – was never identified.
“The sighting was effectively set aside,” a barrister said.
Other eyewitnesses reported seeing what they believed was the bomb car in Omagh from about 2pm. That included one woman who believed the driver of the car allowed her and her young daughter to cross the road, and thought “it was decent of the driver”.
Another eyewitness, Ruth Buchanan, thought she saw the car parked in front of her on Market Street, and the driver and passenger get out and walk away from the town centre.
She had the impression they were in a hurry, but the passenger “caught eye contact with her and grinned with her”.
“The driver was standing staring down Market Street ... He appeared to have a serious expression on his face.”
The first of three warning calls was made to UTV from a public call box in the Newry area at 2.29pm.
The member of staff who answered the phone told police a man said: “Bomb, courthouse, Omagh Main Street, 500-pound explosion, 30 minutes”, and giving a recognised code word used by dissident republicans.
The police deployment began at 2.32pm and a “clearance operation” commenced outside the courthouse, the inquiry heard.
Billingsley told the inquiry the inaccuracy of the locations given in the warnings was a big contributor to the loss of life.
“It caused the evacuation to ultimately direct people towards the bomb,” he said.
When asked about the timer on the bomb, he said: “More time could have been given had the timer knob been turned fully.”
At 2.58pm, the RUC confirmed the streets near the courthouse “had been cleared and sealed off”.
The inquiry was shown a photograph, taken in those final six minutes, of a man with a child on his shoulders, both smiling, and in the background, the car containing the bomb.

title: Katie Taylor named Sportswoman of the Month for September
description: Peerless boxer signs off storied career with a magical night in Croke Park
content:
It was back in early 2005 that an email came in from a man we’ll call only Mick, lest he find himself admonished. “Have you done anything on this Katie Taylor girl yet, Ireland’s first female boxer? She’s a full Irish soccer international too, great looking moth.” Mick signed off by forecasting that we’d hear plenty about her in the future.
He wasn’t wrong, of course. Although he didn’t get it quite right when he said Taylor was Ireland’s “first female boxer”; the likes of Deirdre Gogarty would be entitled to say “hello?” And, if you don’t mind, we’ll stay out of the “great looking moth” discussion.
But back then – hands up – we knew Taylor more for her football, her name first popping up when she won the Wicklow Schoolboy Player of the Year award. That they had no category to accommodate schoolgirls couldn’t but make you smile. Then again, there were few categories into which Taylor fit for much of the early part of her sporting career(s), so she just went about creating them.
It was a couple of months later that our Sportswoman of the Year judges selected her for the May 2005 award, the first of 20 – 20! – she has won down the years.
That month, she became the first Irish woman to win a gold medal at the European Boxing Championships in Norway when, at the age of 18, she beat Finland’s Eva Wahlström in the 60kg lightweight final.
To be honest, some of us still didn’t see any future in women’s boxing, so hoped that she’d focus on her football. She was, after all, looking decidedly promising on that front, being named the 2005 FAI Under-19 Player of the Year. A couple of years later she was offered a trial by Arsenal, then the behemoths of the women’s game in England. She turned the offer down, she had other plans. And you know how that went.
We’d love to think that there’s nothing she values more than the record five Irish Times Sportswoman of the Year awards she received, but we’ll concede that she might rank that Olympic gold medal and multiple world titles marginally above them.
And perhaps above them all she’d rank that magical night in Croke Park.
September was yet another month when our sportswomen excelled on the international stage, among them Katie-George Dunlevy and Linda Kelly, who won their fourth consecutive time-trial at the World Para Cycling Championships; sisters Lisa and Aoife O’Rourke, who both took gold at the European Boxing Championships; and Róisín Ní Ríain, who collected three medals at the European Para Swimming Championships.
As we always say in these circumstances, at any other time those names would have been certainties for the roll of honour, but how do you overlook a night when 80,000 people filled the stadium of Taylor’s dreams to see her wrap up her remarkable career?
[ Ronaldo v Messi debate has surely been settled – there is only one winner Opens in new window ]
It was the largest attendance ever recorded for a sporting event headlined by an individual sportswoman, the occasion drawing an audience of 1.6 million on RTÉ – bigger even than the 2026 World Cup final.
“Croke Park has never seen a night like it,” our Malachy Clerkin wrote . “The love for Katie Taylor bounced off the stadium roof in a way that would be hard to fathom for any other Irish sportsperson. The crowd came to see her finish her career as the greatest to ever do it. She didn’t disappoint.”
For the 20th and last time, then, Katie Taylor is our Sportswoman of the Month.
Previous monthly winners – December : Lauren Walsh (Golf); January : Michelle Clarke (Basketball); February : Sarah Lavin (Athletics); March : Kate O’Connor (Athletics); April : Eve McMahon (Sailing); May : Siobhán Rutledge (Horse racing); June : Caitlin Hayes (Soccer); July : Beth Coulter (Golf); August : Ellen Walshe (swimming) and Margaret Cremen (rowing).

title: ‘An intelligent, nonconformist man’: Galway’s homeless millionaire
description: ‘An intelligent, interesting, nonconformist man’ – we speak to the people he interacted with in the city
content:
H e inherited an estate worth €1.29 million, yet he never accessed the money. Instead, he chose to remain living in a homeless hostel in Galway city centre, where he stayed for more than 10 years. His name was Victor Spaggiari . He was an Italian citizen, and a long-term resident of Galway . He died aged 65 on May 22nd, 2024.
Why did a man with access to significant means spend the last 10 years of his life in a homeless hostel?
Who was Victor Spaggiari and what led him to make these choices?
“I’ve never considered money to be an important thing, and I don’t think any intelligent person should,” Victor Spaggiari wrote as a 14-year-old schoolboy in Milan in 1975.
People spend “empty lives in the continual search for it”, his cursive handwriting reads in an essay kept by his family. “You could say that it was one of the worst inventions in the history of humanity.
“Unfortunately in this society a man is only judged for the basis of the amount of money he can produce and accumulate, and not for his moral and intellectual qualities,” he wrote.
Victor Spaggiari was drawn to Galway for a very specific reason.
“He wanted to learn Irish,” says his cousin Alberto Tota, his closest living relative and the head of a family-owned chemical manufacturing company outside Milan.
“That’s why he ended up in Galway, because as you know, in that area it’s widely spoken.”
An only child, Spaggiari grew up in a spacious top-floor apartment in central Milan. His father was a successful architect who had designed the building the family lived in; his mother loved high society.
It was a comfortable background, but not a happy one.
“The relationship with his parents was not the best,” Tota says. “It was a very conflictual relationship with his mother.”
When Spaggiari turned 18 he moved into a smaller Milan flat owned by their grandmother, “to be as independent as possible”.
“He was very intelligent. He read a lot,” Tota says. “He was probably shy.”
He began travelling, primarily to Ireland, drawn by a fascination with all things Celtic.
“He went through a very wide range of religions when he was younger, from Hare Krishna to Scientology,” Tota says.
[ Polish chocolatier in Clare: ‘There’s something very special about Irish people’ Opens in new window ]
One day in the 2000s, he left Italy never to return. His Milan flat was “abandoned”, only opened up again many years later, coated in dust.
“His parents never knew where exactly he was living,” Tota says. “But they were always ready to help him when he phoned and asked for money. After all, he was their son.”
The first news about Spaggiari’s difficult circumstances came with a telephone call to his mother in 2007.
“The police phoned my aunt, saying that he had been taken to the hospital because they found him sleeping on the street,” says Tota, who flew to Ireland to see his cousin in hospital in Tralee, Co Kerry. “At that time, he was drinking heavily, and the doctors were afraid he could die.
“Ireland was a good choice, I have to say. When I went to Tralee to meet him, even if he was in the hospital and not very present, I told him: ‘Victor, you chose a really nice place to stay,’” Tota says. “It was wonderful there in Tralee, and all around there was the Ring of Kerry. The landscape was really marvellous. That was my first contact with Ireland. Not for nice reasons, but I said: ‘Wow, beautiful. I have to come back.’ And I did.”
Spaggiari recovered and moved in to a bed-and-breakfast in Tralee. The owners kept in touch with Tota, trying to encourage a family reconciliation as they grew concerned about their guest’s declining hygiene and the condition of his room.
In 2012, Tota called Spaggiari’s lodgings from a Milan hospital and asked to be put on to Victor. He informed his cousin that his father had died.
“He told me: that’s impossible,” Tota says.
Spaggiari’s mother died a year later. Once again, “he didn’t want to believe me”, Tota says.
With the deaths of his parents, Spaggiari became the principal heir of his parents’ combined fortune, mostly accumulated through his father’s work as an architect. Under Italian law, a sole surviving child must inherit at least 50 per cent.
He never had a real house because he didn’t want any responsibilities
Whether Spaggiari was aware of the inheritance but rejected it, was in denial about it, or was incapable of dealing with it is unclear.
“Even if he lived as a homeless person, he was probably happy like that. He never had a real house because he didn’t want any responsibilities,” Tota says.
Spaggiari seemed to live out the credo he had expressed as a teenager, when he wrote in his essay that wealth and fine clothes held no appeal for him.
“To find oneself in solitude and peace, read good books and listen to good music,” he wrote.
From Tralee, Spaggiari moved on to Galway. There, he could be found most days sitting on a long wooden bench in the corner of the covered Cornstore Mall.
“I’d say hello to Victor every morning like I’d say hello to my colleagues,” says Vinny Browne, manager of the nearby Charlie Byrne’s Bookshop.
“He would be here in the morning from about nine o’clock, usually until six o’clock when the mall gets locked up.”
“Victor usually had a plastic bag. He would often have the paper with him; Le Figaro and The Irish Times. I don’t think you can buy an Italian newspaper in Galway. A bottle of water, maybe vodka sometimes. You would sometimes see him drinking but I don’t think drinking was his problem. He wasn’t a wino. That wasn’t his thing. He was more controlled than that.”
He recalls Spaggiari as routinely wearing jeans, variations of a plaid shirt, and rotating a black jacket and a blue denim jacket. “He didn’t encourage contact with people. He didn’t seek it. I think he had opted out. Initially he used to smoke. In recent years he didn’t smoke any more, and I think I had some kind of interaction with him one day when someone offered him a cigarette and he said ‘I quit’.
“There was something very likeable about him, I respected him. I thought he was an intelligent, interesting, nonconformist man.”
Charlie Byrne’s Bookshop has an exterior wall in the mall, lined with shelves of books that are usually cheaper or more worn than the books inside the shop. Spaggiari often took books from these shelves to read during the day, returning them before he left. He occasionally went inside the bookshop too and bought books “at neighbourhood rates”, as owner Charlie Byrne puts it.
“Archaeology and folklore. That was his special interest. Irish fairy tales. Mythology,” Browne says. “There was always an air of mystery about him.”
“I sometimes got him a small naggin of vodka,” Byrne says. “He’d be tipping away at the vodka very discreetly. You’d never know that he had drink on him. He never begged for money. I gave it to him a few times – he always took it when I gave it to him, but he never asked for it.”
“He used to stand down by O’Brien’s Bridge and people would give him money but he never asked for it,” Browne adds.
The Café Temple in the Cornstore Mall is gone now, but back when Spaggiari frequented the bench, he visited it once a week or so. Steve Taylor, now retired, ran the cafe as a non-profit.
“He used to come in and just sit down. Once we saw him, one of our staff would say, ‘Victor’s here,’” he says. The first time Spaggiari asked for a sandwich, he specified chicken and cheese. Ever afterwards, he simply requested “that sandwich”. He drank only sparkling water. The cafe always gave him the items for free.
At the start of his time in Galway, he was sleeping rough at a bus shelter near Spanish Arch. He would occasionally avail of the cold-weather response initiative of Cope Galway, a long-standing social services and homeless charity that provides additional emergency beds during winter months.
Over a decade ago, the Galway 2020 organisation, then based in the Cornstore Mall, noted Spaggiari’s frequent presence by their office, and brought him to the attention of Cope, which runs the 26-bed Fairgreen Hostel for homeless men not far from Ceannt railway station.
Spaggiari would end up spending the last 10 years of his life in the hostel.
“First you try and understand what their situation and circumstance was, and that took time, to build up a relationship and build up trust with him,” says Cope Galway assistant chief executive and team leader Martin O’Connor. “If that outreach bit hadn’t happened, he would have carried on sleeping rough.”
“He never told us why he came to Galway,” says Paudie Cunningham, who also works at Cope. “He had a real connection with the land ... He was real spiritual.”
[ Ardmore receives Ireland’s Greenest Places award from Eamon Ryan Opens in new window ]
The Fairgreen Hostel does not generally provide long-term accommodation. Each man has his own single room, and is provided with three meals a day. They do not have to vacate the premises during the day if they don’t wish to. The reasons men come to the Fairgreen Hostel vary, but the most common two are mental health challenges and addiction issues.
Each resident also has a key worker who spends time with them to build a trusted connection, and try to figure out what particular support that person needs, whether it’s access to things such as medical care or help with the paperwork that can lead to a way out of homelessness. The residents pay rent of €10 a night for the hostel.
“The ultimate goal is for them to move on from services to a better place,” says Cunningham.
“Victor was atypical of people you would see who use our homeless service,” says O’Connor. Referring to the unusual length of his stay, he says: “That would have been exceptional. But it was based on vulnerability. There wasn’t another option for him.”
“There was nothing conventional about Victor,” Cunningham says. “He was an enigma; a very private man. He very rarely spoke to anyone. He was very much into his books. He had his own personal library down there in Charlie Byrne’s. He was into Celtic history, shamans, he was very alternative. He told us he had been a yoga master. He never had a phone. He was not connected to that side of the world at all. He wasn’t in touch with society at all. He was living in his own head. That’s the way I would describe Victor. He didn’t communicate with anyone, and if you’re not communicating with anyone, you’re going to go internal.”
“He liked his Perrier water,” O’Connor says.
“He wouldn’t drink anything else,” Cunningham says.
[ Travel ‘I’m swooning as I come in the door’: A trip to Milan to buy cottons, linens and silks Opens in new window ]
The Cope team deduced over time that there had been some unspecified trauma in Spaggiari’s life that had led him to leave Italy and become homeless in Galway.
“Whatever had happened to him was still going on for him,” O’Connor says. “And the fact that he was accommodated in a shelter was an improvement in his circumstances.”
Everyone who comes through the Fairgreen Hostel is asked to provide some basic information about themselves. “We would sit with them and do paperwork: name, surname, date of birth, place of origin, next of kin, mobile number, why are you presenting to the service, your GP, medication you may be on, addictions, mental health,” says O’Connor.
Over time, in the course of assessing Spaggiari’s housing needs and using information he had provided them with, Cope did their usual research into his background. “That gave rise to it becoming known he had access to funds,” O’Connor says.
So Spaggiari knew he had considerable means?
“He knew,” O’Connor says. “I know some people out there would look at this case and say, here you had somebody who had what most people can only dream about, in terms of the kind of wealth he had, and there he was occupying a space in a homeless service that someone else could have benefited from.
“Standing back and looking at his access to all that money, you’d think he should be on his way, get his own housing sorted, because he had the means to do that. The reality was that he would most likely have simply returned to the street in that situation. He wasn’t able. He had this inheritance but it didn’t change anything.”
“He would have died on the streets if we didn’t keep him,” Cunningham says. “That’s the reality of it. He didn’t have the skill set to survive. He was an old young man.”
Spaggiari was buried at Rahoon Cemetery in Galway, in Section W, Row 25, Plot 10. The graveyard’s caretaker, Michael Davoren points out a fresh pink rose that someone left on the grave recently. Davoren was one of a handful of people who attended the funeral.
The others included his cousin Tota, staff from Cope Galway, the undertakers conducting the funeral, and a couple of members of the public who had heard on the Galway grapevine that the familiar figure with the Italian accent and bushy white beard had died.
Vinny Browne and Charlie Byrne, who attended the reposal at Conneely’s on Flood Street, helped carry Spaggiari’s coffin. He died intestate; probate was granted to Tota.
Tota has wondered whether Spaggiari had autism. He is not aware that his cousin had any diagnosis for any condition. To his knowledge Spaggiari never had a job, or any romantic partner.
He thinks back to the 1990s, when the two cousins bonded as young men in conversations about Spaggiari’s Celtic interests.
“For sure, he passed to me some of his love for the Celtic culture, history, and Ireland,” Tota says. On Spaggiari’s recommendation, he visited a shop in Milan, Ceilt Siopa, and bought a triple-spiral necklace.
Information about Cope Galway can be found at copegalway.ie

title: Founder of Peploe’s in Dublin leaves more than €2.8m in will
description: Former UCD professor and philanthropist Tony Hourihan left €2.1m, Probate Office records show
content:
Dublin restaurateur Barry Canny , founder of Peploe’s restaurant, left an estate valued at €2.86 million, papers published by the Probate Office have shown.
Canny, of Dalkey, Co Dublin, established Peploe’s – named after the Scottish post-impressionist painter Samuel John Peploe – in the style of an upmarket New York brasserie, located at 16 St Stephen’s Green, in 2003.
The restaurant became quickly notable, hosting such celebrities as former US president Bill Clinton , Luciano Pavarotti, Julia Roberts and Bono .
Canny famously got into a spat with then CEO of Intel , Craig Barrett, when the latter publicly complained of the price of eating in Peploe’s.
Barrett had referred to the cost of the meal for two as an example of the high costs of doing business in Ireland. Canny reportedly replied: “He can’t come in here with his big cigar and tell us how to run our country.”
Among Canny’s other hospitality ventures was Brownes Townhouse on St Stephen’s Green, which opened in 1998. This was one of Dublin’s first boutique hotels and featured 12 luxury bedrooms above a brasserie grill. He ran it with his wife Dee for five years before selling to a Spanish group. The building later became The Cliff Town House, then Floritz.
Another venture was The Olive restaurant in Sandycove, Co Dublin. He was also involved in a clothing boutique, Browns Boutique, which he operated before fully committing to the restaurant industry.
Other records at the Probate Office show Tony Hourihan, University College Dublin professor, finance expert and philanthropist, left €2.093 million when he died in October last year.
Hourihan, of Crosswaite Park, Dún Laoghaire, Co Dublin, specialised in banking and finance. Beyond his work in Irish academia, he championed charitable causes and was a primary supporter of Casa Nano Nagle – a foundation aiding vulnerable families and children in Alto Hospicio, Chile .
He died suddenly in Chile, where a formal funeral mass was held in Santiago.
The figures quoted in this article include all assets, typically including a family home, investments and land

title: This man had found one of the scarcest craneflies around in Ireland
description: Most of us have encountered a daddy-long-legs, but that is just one of 211 known cranefly species in Ireland
content:
O ne day in May last year, Sligo-based entomologist Ryan Mitchell surveyed Union Wood in the county, an old oak woodland on the eastern bank of the river Ballysadare. It’s legally protected for its mature sessile oak habitat. Mitchell was researching flies for the National Parks & Wildlife Service . Finding species as small as flies and identifying them accurately isn’t an easy job. Mitchell used a standard technique that, by his own admission, can make researchers like him look “a bit mad” – he swished a large white “sweep net” through the vegetation and then put his head into the net and put any captured flies into a pooter, a small jar fitted with two tubes.
By chance, he swept a fern that was hanging off an old oak tree and stuck his head into the net to see what he had got. He spotted a bright yellow rostrum, or beak, on a cranefly. He had found one of the scarcest craneflies around. According to Mitchell, there are only 20 records in Britain and, until that May afternoon, it had never been found in Ireland before.
It’s called Tipula luridorostris, and it was first described and named in 1833 – rostris, from the Latin for a beak; luridus meaning pale yellow. In 1840 a Danish entomologist found and named the same fly but called it Tipula flavirostris, using the Latin for yellow, flavus. The yellow snout that caught Mitchell’s eye is the fly’s defining feature.
Many of us have encountered one common cranefly: the daddy-long-legs, Tipula paludosa, blundering about the bathroom light in late summer and autumn. Its larvae, the leatherjackets, spend autumn, winter and spring underground eating grass roots (they’re the bane of golf course managers). The fly we encounter at the window or scrabbling around a light is only the briefest final chapter.
[ The ‘Daddy Long-Legs’ may appear meek and mild, but it can devour larger spiders Opens in new window ]
It’s one of 211 known cranefly species in Ireland. Mitchell believes another 20 could be waiting to be found. Most of them will never come near a house, school or apartment – their needs are much more specific than that: stream beds, in sodden moss, in bog, in ground that floods every winter or in ground that never does. Take Lipsothrix remota. It spends its early life inside waterlogged dead branches submerged in woodland streams – a fallen branch, in water and nowhere else. If the deadwood is taken away or the stream goes dry, the cranefly is gone.
For Mitchell it makes craneflies especially useful. They can tell you something plants can’t. Two woods can share the same oaks yet still be very different underneath. One is damp, old and full of deadwood, the other drier and tidier. While the plants look the same, the craneflies that live their minuscule lives can be very different.
For other species, craneflies are food. On bogs they emerge in vast numbers in spring at the same time when wading birds are raising chicks. Research in England’s Peak District found that golden plover numbers rose and fell with August temperatures two years earlier. A hot, dry summer kills cranefly larvae in the drying peat, fewer adults emerge the following spring and fewer golden plover chicks survive. Wetter bogs, the researchers found, held up better.
In Ireland golden plover breeds in just a handful of places in the uplands of the northwest. In 2019 a resurvey of their Mayo stronghold, the Owenduff/Nephin bogs, found only five breeding territories in the same 27 one-kilometre squares that, in 2005, held more than 60 pairs. Its food supply depends on wetness, and wet peat is what we’ve spent nearly a hundred years draining and removing.
For Mitchell the pressures on craneflies are familiar: drainage, peat cutting that continues even on protected habitats, coniferous forestry planted on bog, climate change, pesticide use, agricultural intensification, and the clearing of scrub. Craneflies love damp, dark, humid places. We’ve spent decades making the landscape tidier, drier and brighter. “We don’t know how much we are losing,” says Mitchell.
[ Department’s €130k ‘turf agent’ a masterclass in loose oversight Opens in new window ]
We still don’t know enough about them. As recently as the early 1980s, Ireland’s list was so thin that a single visitor to the country, Hans Mendl, a schoolteacher from Bavaria, boosted it. Over three separate trips, he spent weeks driving around western Ireland with a net, stopping wherever he saw potential. His wife, he noted, put up with hours of roadside stops, while he collected 3,400 specimens of 85 species of one family of cranefly. One cranefly particularly obsessed Mendl: a tiny, pale species called Molophilus pusillus that had, apparently, only ever been found as females. He caught four near Oughterard and came back the following year to look for a male. He found 41 more flies in Kerry, every one of them female. Mendl wondered whether it needed males at all, but added that it would take someone who lived in Ireland to find out.
In Union Wood, Mitchell’s yellow-snouted cranefly is now a dried specimen glued to card for preservation and held in the Natural History Museum in Dublin. Twenty species remain undiscovered. “We can still discover species on our doorstep,” Mitchell says. The question is whether we’ll keep the bogs and woods they need long enough to find them.

title: Conor O’Clery: I forced myself to attend an execution in the US and came away sickened
description: The condemned man was truly evil but I found myself shaking after the experience
content:
L ike half the population of Newry, Co Down , I saw the murderer, Robert McGladdery , as he walked freely around the Border town in February 1961 in the days after he stabbed and killed his girlfriend, Pearl Gamble.
Everyone knew he had done it, and townspeople turned out to witness the spectacle of an RUC constable following a few paces behind McGladdery, as police searched for evidence to arrest him. He taunted his escort, once, according to legend, swimming across the Newry canal with the policeman a few breast-strokes behind.
The evidence was eventually found – his bloodstained suit hidden in a septic tank – and McGladdery was tried and sentenced to death. He was hanged at Crumlin Road goal in Belfast five days before Christmas that year, by the English executioner Harry Allen, who wore his customary white bow tie.
The Newry man was the last person to be executed in Northern Ireland. Capital punishment was abandoned in the Republic seven years earlier, after the hanging of Limerick man Michael Manning, for raping and killing 65-year-old nurse Catherine Cooper. Throughout Europe, state executions declined in the last half of the 20th century and were formally ended throughout the EU with the Treaty of Lisbon in 2009, on the grounds that they were an irreversible violation of human dignity and the right to life and ineffective as a deterrent.
I have always believed that capital punishment should be abolished because of the number of innocent people executed on the basis of ineffective defence, forced confessions and false testimonies, and most of all because it makes the state a killer. In 1993, when based in the United States, where cruel and inhuman punishment is prohibited by the US constitution, I forced myself to attend an execution so I could report precisely what this meant in practice.
The condemned man was truly evil. His name was Michael Durocher, and he had gone on a killing spree in Florida, murdering his girlfriend, their infant son, her five-year-old daughter, a shopkeeper, and his flatmate. Before dawn on August 25th, 1993, at Florida State Prison near Jacksonville, I was relieved of belt and tape recorder, given a pencil and a sheet of paper, and escorted with a few other witnesses to a glass-fronted observation room. Durocher, who had consumed a breakfast of jumbo shrimp, chocolate ice cream and Coke, was strapped by his arms, chest and waist by two prison officers on to a three-legged electric chair, known to the guards there as “Old Sparkie”. They clamped a leather chin strap over his mouth and tied a black hood over his head. One rolled up Durocher’s right trouser leg and bound an electrode and sponge below the knee.
At 7.06am a hidden executioner, who would receive a fee of $150, pulled a switch. A large puff of smoke rose from Durocher’s knee. At that moment his clenched right fist snapped inward, the thumb sticking out. Two doctors in white coats fussed around Durocher with stethoscopes. I learned afterwards that a person literally fries in the electric chair, and that in post-electrocution autopsies, the liver can be too hot to touch. It was six more minutes before they were able to pronounce him dead.
[ ‘It’s very complicated’: The psychic impact of living in a town famous for executing prisoners Opens in new window ]
Outside the prison I took a cigarette from one of the local reporters, though I didn’t then smoke. I found myself shaking. We talked about Durocher. “He’s a sweetheart,” spat out my colleague, who fully approved of what we had just seen. Another wisecracked that executions were “a way of life” in Florida. They still are. I came away from the experience sickened by what I had seen and convinced that capital punishment brutalises the state itself and everyone associated with it.
This was never more evident than the botched attempt on September 30th in Tennessee to execute Christa Pike, who murdered her teenage friend Colleen Slemmer in 1995. Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has worked to preserve her daughter’s memory and described her, in an interview with the New York Times, as a vibrant, generous presence, who volunteered at the Special Olympics and loved bowling and computer games.
What happened to Pike last month was a particular gruesome example of the many attempted executions by lethal injection in the US that were messed up because of the use of inferior killer drugs and fumbled attempts to find veins.
In his famous nonfiction novel In Cold Blood, Truman Capote wrote about two home intruders, who killed a Kansas farmer and his wife and two children, and were hanged. He found the process of their execution morally troubling, drawing attention to the mental state of the two perpetrators, and questioning whether capital punishment offered justice or deterrence. As with the killers in Capote’s novel, Pike was a vulnerable person, just 18 at the time of the murder, who had a traumatic childhood and was dehumanised by her environment. We know little about the troubled lives of Durocher and McGladdery.
In a supreme irony, state officials, having failed to kill Pike with two botched injections, rushed her to hospital and shackled her to a bed while she received life-saving care. On October 6th she regained consciousness and spoke to her lawyers. Now 50, she was on death row for 31 years and faces an uncertain future. The extraordinary long delay for prisoners on America’s death row is yet another form of cruel and unusual punishment, both for inmates and their relatives.
The good news is that executions in the US have steadily declined this century. Of the 50 states, 23 have abolished the death penalty and five more have a moratorium on executions. The not-so-good news is that US president Donald Trump is urging more death sentences. Just this week he authorised the execution by firing squad of Nidal Malik Hassan, who killed 13 unarmed soldiers in Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. In the past half-century, only six people have been executed by firing squad* in the US, three of them in South Carolina last year.
[ Christa Pike is ‘angry and confused’ after failed execution, say lawyers Opens in new window ]
Perhaps the publicity surrounding the attempt to kill Christa Pike, with its inherent cruelty, will fuel campaigns to end not just execution by lethal injection, firing squad, electric chair or hanging, but to the eventual abolition of capital punishment in all US states. At least for now, executions have been suspended in Tennessee.
Conor O’Clery is a former Washington correspondent of The Irish Times
This article was amended on October 20th to make clear that six people were executed by firing squad in the US in the past half-century, rather than by hanging.

title: David McWilliams: We have just seen a perfect example of Ireland’s fiscal incontinence
description: The Irish State has become a monstrously bloated organisation that has lost all sense of value for money
content:
N othing focuses the mind like a hanging,” noted Samuel Johnson , according to his biographer James Boswell. The condemned man, realising that he has only a few weeks to live, focuses on what is truly important. The economic equivalent of this expression is: “Nothing focuses the mind like a hard budget.” Hard budgets make countries and organisations efficient, innovative, thoughtful and, by injecting financial discipline, ensure that decision-makers work through their options to get value for money. The hard budget in itself leads to better management, getting more from less, which requires more effort.
In contrast, a sloppy, bloated budget where money is not a problem will lead to waste, cynicism, cutting corners and the abandonment of accounting discipline. When money is wasted, the essential connection between the cost of something and the delivery of quality breaks down.
Without a hard budget, management becomes almost impossible and the corporation, organisation or country drifts, becoming gradually unable to deal with any shocks to the system that might lie ahead. Like someone who allows themselves to get out of shape, their muscles to weaken, and their weight to soar, the person becomes more susceptible to physical and potential emotional or psychological fragility.
Countries and corporations operate in a similar fashion. If they become addicted to easy money, particularly if that money is someone else’s, a gap opens up between reality and fantasy. The managers begin to feel that the money is theirs and they are entitled to it, creating a dependency. Successful management no longer revolves around the best use of the resources to achieve a specific outcome, but rather it becomes a smash-and-grab exercise centred on how much of the “easy” money the managers can get their hands on.
Without a budget constraint, the objective of management becomes size, not efficiency. The organisation becomes an extractive machine, extracting money from the central budget and, as that part of the organisation gets bigger, the fact of its expanding size means that it gobbles up more and more money, needing more every year just to stay still.
This is what has happened to the Irish State . It is a monstrously bloated organisation that has lost all sense of value for money and exists to gorge on cheap, endless cash that is cascading into the coffers from the US multinationals.
In development economics this process, whereby the State becomes hollowed out by too much rather than too little money, is termed the ”resource curse”. When an underdeveloped country without proper institutions finds a resource like oil, money flows in and it is often wasted, ending up in the pockets of the rulers, driving up costs for everyone else. The country ends up unbalanced – rich in parts but without the public infrastructure that the financial windfall could have paid for. Think Nigeria, Angola or Venezuela, where huge oil finds have not elevated the position of the citizens who own the natural resources of the country.
If these countries are synonymous with bad management, the exemplar of good behaviour is Norway , where the oil windfall has been invested judiciously and democratically for future generations , rather than blown on goodies for today.
Now look at Ireland’s equivalent of an oil find – the gusher that is the US multinational money, a spigot of cashflow, the product of clever tax arbitrage, which is flowing into the system to be pilfered by public sector management in a country that can’t even build a proper national rail system.
This week’s budget is a perfect example of the fiscal incontinence that a soft budget generates. First the Government flatters to deceive by announcing an overall surplus of about €9 billion next year. This looks great, but when you consider that the Department of Finance regards about €23 billion of the €34 billion in projected corporation taxes received this year as being transient, then we are in a different world. If we were to strip that out, our underlying surplus becomes a significant deficit of €13 billion to €14 billion for 2027; and, given commitments outlined in this budget, that deficit will widen to about €20 billion by 2029.
Even from a cyclical perspective, a country at full employment does not need any more money thrown at it – the economy is already bursting at the seams – and yet this week’s Budget 2027 is throwing a net €7.4 billion extra into an already bloated system.
[ New public spending efficiency taskforce to be established within three months Opens in new window ]
The Government presents it as cost-of-living relief. But the cost of living has risen because prices have risen. Throwing extra money at this problem will not cause prices to fall, but will cause them to rise, while the extra handout to soften the blow will simply increase dependency on handouts rather than cut prices and permanently. So you get the worst of all worlds: handouts which drive prices higher that are mistakenly put forward as a solution to high prices.
The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council’s analysis says spending is growing at double the pace of the Government’s own 5 per cent sustainable limit. Basically, our windfall is being spent rather than saved.
The lack of a hard budget also means that tough decisions are not taken, not just in the area of financial management but in organisational management too. Take, for example, this rotating taoiseach codology. With two bosses – one on the way out, the other on the way in – the lad on the way in is more important for tomorrow, undermining the lad in situ today.
Such management structure means that the incentive for all senior public servants and politicians is to curry favour with the next guy, not the guy in charge, thus undermining the guy in charge.
And by splitting the Department of Finance in two, with the Department of Finance and the Department of Public Expenditure , what’s the aim? Rather than have one department looking after the money, we now have two departments – and, critically, the Department of the Taoiseach , which used to be the nerve centre of final decision making, is now neutered because no one knows which taoiseach is more important: the incumbent or the next guy.
All the while global financial markets, the font of the windfall money that finances the large US tech companies, are becoming more and more nervous about the future.

title: If you’ve a foot fetish or an appetite for real talk, this column is for you
description: Three years after wondering if I’d still be around to do anything much at all, I’m grateful to be preoccupied with something so mundane
content:
T he contents of this column will mostly, but not exclusively, concern the exciting, ongoing issues with my dodgy big toes. I mention this as a sort of trigger warning. The last time I wrote about my toenails looking like a crime scene, a disgruntled reader wrote in to object.
On that note, I’ve also since received correspondence from a woman who thinks I talk too much about the fact that I am living with cancer . So before I get on to my big toe adventures, I’d first like to address that.
I do have some sympathy for her position. Reading about my cancer causes this woman pain because she lost a person close to her from the disease. Many of us have. It’s a year since my friend Manchán died of neuroendocrine cancer and I’ve been thinking about him a lot. His final book Seeing What’s Hidden has just been published. I haven’t read it yet but I know it will be like having an esoteric, uplifting, mind-expanding conversation with him. More than anybody I ever knew, he understood that line from Hamlet: ‘There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy.’ He saw beyond the rational and logical. He knew there was much more to know hiding in plain sight. He knew about connectedness. He lived and breathed it every day.
Manchán and I talked a great deal about our experience with cancer. We laughed about it. We were sometimes sad. We talked about death. We had conversations where neither of us held back and we challenged each other to be honest about how we really felt. We told each other truths we might have been afraid to say out loud to others. And I suppose, more than anything else, that’s where I am coming from when I write about living with cancer.
Back when I was diagnosed, I had serious doubts that three years later I’d still be here to tell anyone about anything.
At first, I thought I would write back to the woman and apologise – but when I thought about it more deeply, I realised that an apology would be hollow and disingenuous. I write about my cancer because I can. I write because it’s a big part of me. I write because there are people living with stage 4 cancer and many other medical challenges who might like to see another person also living their life as fully as they can. Laughing when funny things happen. Being emotional when it all feels overwhelming. I write about it because it’s always there and it always will be. Realistically, I’m probably not going to stop writing about it. Not until I am forced to.
So if you don’t like knowing about the minutiae of ingrown toenails or hearing existential musings on life’s challenges, I’m going to respectfully suggest you go elsewhere. The rest of you, foot fetishists and those with an appetite for real talk, please stay around and enjoy.
You might be aware that chemotherapy can play havoc with the nails on your fingers and toes. I’m not complaining about this, just stating it as a fact. My big toe issues began after several months of the treatment. My fingernails grew frail and the ones on my big toes began to grow in unhelpful directions.
For months I went to a podiatrist called Orla, a soothing-voiced woman in Dublin city centre who clipped away at my toes and didn’t mind my nosy questions about her life. I learned about her boyfriend and their new flat and her close-knit family in Cork. I grew very fond of Orla, who did her best with my toenails but always warned, in her kind, reassuring voice, that they may continue to grow in the wrong directions and that surgery may be required.
[ My inner Grumpy Old Woman is intent on making her presence felt lately. She’s mad as hell Opens in new window ]
I did everything she suggested. I wore flip-flops even when the weather was freezing, honouring my late Uncle Christy who wore flip-flops all year round. When my ingrowing big toenails got infected, I took antibiotics. Things cleared up for a while but soon got gross again. I talked to my medical professionals in the Mater and they got me a referral to a surgeon. Months passed, and then the other day the lovely foot surgeon took one look at my disgusting big toes and said that the nails would have to be surgically removed under local anaesthetic. I will get an appointment within a month.
I can’t believe I am saying this, but I am looking forward to it. Not having big toenails is the only solution to what has been a painful problem for coming up on 2½ years. The toenails might grow back, the surgeon says; on the other hand (or foot), they might not. The big dramas (cancer) fade sometimes to be replaced by the urgency of life’s small stuff (big toes).
We’ve had our differences, me and my big toenails. They grew wild, rendering most closed-toe shoes uncomfortable. They have cost me a small fortune in podiatry. I can’t say I’ll miss them, but three years after wondering if I’d still be around to do anything much at all, I’m grateful to be preoccupied with something as mundane as toenails. I’m chuffed to still be here, still complaining about them. And I’m not apologising for that.

title: How to reimagine your garden with fresh eyes
description: A ‘might do’ list for your garden doesn’t necessarily involve radical change
content:
T here are times when a gardening to-do list can feel downright discouraging, especially when you’re looking down the barrel of an Irish winter. So instead this week I’d like to propose the idea of a “might do” list. By its nature hypothetical, all it asks of us is that we try to reimagine our gardens with a fresh eye.
This doesn’t necessarily mean radical change. It could be something as seemingly small as skirt-lifting a maturing tree to let light flood in and to give it a more sculptural silhouette. Or deciding to dig up that very old and ailing rose bush to replace it with something more vigorous and with a longer season of interest. It might be considering the possibility of reducing the size of a lawn to give more space for ornamental or productive beds, or to cultivate a native wild-flower meadow. Or simply hard-pruning an old hedge that has slowly stolen precious light and space to the point where it feels constrictive.
Which is not to say that we should neglect the opportunity to contemplate more dramatic change, because this, after all, is what our gardens sometimes need. Given full licence to freely roam, for example, your imagination might find itself pondering the possibilities of creating a garden pond or a natural swimming pool. Or introducing theatrical changes of level to provide interest by creating a series of sculptural landforms.
You could discover yourself considering substantially reorienting an important entrance way so that it provides far more privacy and a sunny, secluded place to sit outdoors. Or wondering about building a dry-stone wall to provide shelter as well as a sense of enclosure.
Whatever the specifics, at its heart is the possibility of change as something both exciting and transformative, a process that starts with gardeners asking ourselves the leading question: “What if?”
Blinded by familiarity, this process is often much harder than it sounds. But a simple way to begin is by writing a list of the things about your garden that you love, and a list of the things you don’t. Take plenty of photos too for reference, including some views of the garden from key vantage points inside your home. These interior views are crucial, both in terms of visually and stylistically linking the house and garden as well as for your overall enjoyment of the latter.
Take some key measurements of the site too so that you can roughly draw it out to scale on paper, marking out key elements such as doors/gateways, windows, paths, steps, important changes of level, any paved areas or garden sheds and important trees and shrubs. If using a measuring tape feels like too much of a faff, you can pace it, though this won’t be as accurate. Just count your steps, allowing for the fact that the average length of a human step is between 66cm and 76cm, depending on your height.
[ ‘I would like to transfer my late mother’s beloved rose bushes to my own home. But how?’ Opens in new window ]
Take careful note of your garden’s aspect too (use your mobile phone’s compass app if you’re not sure) as well as of any nearby tall buildings or very mature plants creating shade for at least part of the day. Bear in mind that south- and west-facing parts of any garden are typically classed as its sunniest and warmest areas in terms of selecting suitable plants, while east- and north-facing areas are classed as cooler and shady. Note also that flower or vegetable beds positioned beneath a north-facing wall or garden fence are especially challenging as these are typically very dry.
Tech can help too, although while there are a ton of garden design apps available, not all of them live up to their promises. Rather than seeing them as equivalent to the services of a talented garden designer, which they most certainly aren’t, instead treat them as just another potentially useful tool to provide inspiration. A list of the better ones includes SpaceLift, which will also map your garden for you, ( spaceliftapp.com ); SmartDraw ( smartdraw.com ); MyGarden ( gardena.com ) and iScape (download from apple.com ).
[ How to set your garden ablaze with autumn colour Opens in new window ]
Although not intended specifically for gardens, Canva ( canva.com ) is another excellent design app that allows you to remove individual unwanted elements from images, as well as to extract individual elements from one image and then add them to another. If you’ve ever struggled to imagine, for example, how your garden might look with the addition of a new flower bed or with its walls a different colour (use the AI option), this will do a lot of the hard work for you. Finally, if you’re unsure of the names of any existing plants in your garden that you’d like to note for the purposes of your design, then PictureThis is one of the most reliable apps available.
[ What climbers grow well in a shady city courtyard garden? Opens in new window ]
Apps aside, take inspiration online from the Instagram and Facebook feed of great gardeners and garden designers such as Paul Martin @pailmartindesigns ; June Blake @juneblakegarden ; Des Doyle @des.doyle; Liat and Oliver Schurmann @mountvenusnursery ; Jimi Blake @huntingbrookgardens ; Hester Forde @hesterforde ; TJ Maher @patthana_garden ; Seamus O’Donnell @cluainnadtor ; Carl Wright of @Caher Bridge Garden (Facebook only); Robert Miller @altamont_plants ; John Little @grassroofco ; Adam Hunt @urquhartandhunt; Dan Pearson @coyotewillow ; Sarah Price @sarahpricelandscapes ; Fergus Garrett @fergusmustafasabrigarrett ; Mary Keen @keenkeengardener ; Jack Aldridge @jackjaldridge ; and Joe McKerr @jo_pratensisgardens
Last but not least, don’t forget gardening books as an endlessly rich seam of inspiration, from classics such The Education of a Gardener by Russell Page; Sylvia Crowe’s Garden Design ; Beth Chatto’s The Gravel Garden ; Christopher Lloyd’s The Education of a Gardener ; Derek Jarman’s Garden by Derek Jarman ; and John Brooke’s Room Outside: A New Approach to Garden Design ; to more contemporary texts such as Planting: A New Perspective by Piet Oudolf and Noel Kingsbury; The Contemporary Garden , edited by Annie Guilfoyle; The RHS Encyclopedia of Garden Design: Be Inspired to Plan, Build and Plant Your Perfect Outdoor Space, edited by Chris Young; Gardening in a Changing World: Plants, People and the Climate Crisis by Darryl Moore; and Wild: the Naturalistic Garden by Noel Kingsbury. Encouraged to roam freely, we never know where our minds, and eventually our gardens, will take us.
· Heavy rain and high temperatures have resulted in explosive weed growth that can be hard to manage using traditional methods of hand-weeding and hoeing. But even a temporary mulch of cardboard or plastic will kill off unwanted seedlings and suppress germination until temperatures cool and growth rates decline.
· Very lush grass growth has been another consequence of the mild, wet weather of recent weeks, so try to keep on top of mowing any lawn areas to prevent them from getting so overgrown that they’ll create problems for your lawnmower.
RHSI Bellefield Open Weekend. Bellefield House and Gardens, Shinrone, Co Offaly ; this Saturday and Sunday, October 10th and 11th. With plant sales, refreshments, tours of the garden, and a talk by Carl Wright of Caher Bridge Garden (Saturday at 2pm, booking essential, see rhsi.ie ).

title: Fontaines DC: ‘We just hang out with ourselves and don’t really interact as much with other people’
description: Conor Deegan and Tom Coll on Dopamine Chamber, which the band’s lead singer, Grian Chatten, says needed to be a ‘catastrophic warning’
content:
F ontaines DC have no issue declaring their insularity as a band. Their capacity to create, they say, is down to the fact that their main artistic connections are between one another, as well as to a work ethic they’ve had ever since they formed in Dublin more than a decade ago.
But insularity doesn’t mean they’re closed to the existential questions of our time. The scope of Dopamine Chamber, their new album, tells us so.
Its predecessor, Romance , won the Choice Music Prize and was nominated for the Mercury Prize and two Grammys. It brought an aesthetic shift and a demanding touring schedule. One might think Fontaines DC were due a break. But that’s not how they operate.
The new album, their fifth in seven years, is arguably their finest. Previously bathed in the neon of Romance, the band return filtered through the cold blue tones of an LP that articulates the oppressive nature of our age – its anxieties, uncertainties and sense of tipping points – through smashing guitars, sweeping strings, wonderfully coloured synths and songs that speak to a band dropping a pin in a glitching map, with new territory loading in real time.
Thematically, it touches on artificial-intelligence scepticism, the residue of crumbling European grandeur, hedonism, climate anxiety and despondency. The band’s lead singer, Grian Chatten , says Dopamine Chamber needed to be a “catastrophic warning”.
Impeccably sung and played, it is also, in its scale and ambition, made for enormous crowds. With production from James Ford and engineering led by Marta Salogni, Fontaines DC have made an album on which avant-garde textures sit happily alongside stadium-sized gestures.
Conor Deegan III , the band’s bassist, and Tom Coll , their drummer, are in New York when we talk. They’re in the city to prepare for a US festival with some of the biggest rock bands around: The Strokes , Turnstile, Geese .
Fontaines DC are a rock band too, of course, but much will likely be made of the way this album, inky with synths, stretches the limits of such categorisation.
“It’s trying to mix a lot of different things together that seem like they don’t make sense together on paper, or that they’re conflicting,” Deegan says.
“But in actual fact, they really well describe what it feels like to be in this moment in time. You can doomscroll while sitting at the Parthenon. Do you know what I mean?”
Before Romance, Deegan says, their development process was “very much of The Rolling Stones’ world: if you can’t play it with your hands and sing it with your voices all at once, you’re not doing it”.
Fontaines now have a different approach. Having come off tour in the early autumn of 2025, the band spent a month apart. “When you’re so institutionalised with seeing each other every day, a month felt like a f**king year,” Coll says.
When they reconvened, they spent three months together in a studio in London, developing the album’s sound and recording demos, Deegan says, like “a group of mad scientists in the lab, with all the equipment and tools at our disposal, trying to find sounds”.
“Everyone was really firing,” Coll says. “It’s always interesting trying to break new sonic palettes. Sometimes you want to go too far, and then rein it back a bit. I found that process amazing.”
As they set about “trying to figure out how we were all feeling about the world, about our environment”, as Deegan puts it, they were also attempting to discover what “the spark for this new collection of work” would be.
It turned out to be Six Shot Morning, the album’s opening track. Its pulsating machine heartbeat underpins a sense of teetering on a precipice. Two songs later, on Mimesis – potentially the best pop song the band have made – Chatten captures the album’s duality, sunnily singing, “Well, everybody’s depressed / We’re running on a wheel.”
“There’s a lot of anxiety as well that we’re experiencing and people are experiencing,” Deegan says of the album’s themes. “A lack of hope. Disconnection. Everyone is looking for something to escape into and make themselves feel better.”
The work of the French sociologist Bruno Latour was a touchstone.
“There’s this great book. It’s called Où Suis-Je? – Where Am I?,” Deegan says. “Our friend Nikolaj Schultz was working underneath [Latour]. He has this great line in it: ‘The moon is the only thing in nature I can look upon without guilt.’
“That’s a very powerful and haunting line, and it’s very true. We look at rivers, we look at trees, and we feel guilty for what we’ve been doing to the natural world.
“The moon is this kind of thing, a celestial body, we could look at and feel okay.”
Yet when the band were recording the album in the English countryside and looking at stars in a night sky free from the light pollution of London, “we were realising a lot of them were satellites”.
[ Joy Division: Eternal review – A buttoned-down band unbowed, unravelled and gloriously unleashed Opens in new window ]
“It was this reminder that we can’t even look into the night sky and look at these celestial bodies any more without feeling some kind of guilt – how much we have disturbed even space.”
The closing lyrics of Mimesis come to mind: “If you’re a star, show me / If you’re not, let me be.”
The “innate claustrophobia to the modern world”, as Deegan puts it – “ironically because of the amount of connection we have to everyone else, and the amount of information we have” – is fundamental to the album.
“This big window we have to the outer world in our pocket, everywhere we go, somehow makes everywhere much more claustrophobic.”
Chatten travelled around Europe to write his lyrics, stopping in Vienna to visit the Sigmund Freud Museum, viewing work by Egon Schiele and Gustav Klimt at the Leopold Museum and reading Arthur Schnitzler ’s Dream Story, the novella from which Stanley Kubrick made his film Eyes Wide Shut.
But Venice , the band say, is the album’s defining metaphor. Chatten wrote lyrics there before recording them in Palermo, in Sicily . He was also obsessively listening to the mid-20th-century Italian singer Mina.
A pair of remarkable songs anchor the album. The first, One Man, contains the album’s title in a track bookended by the sounds of children playing football outside Palermo cathedral: “Dopamine chamber, just tryna kill the pain / you can’t escape the feeling once you’ve given it a name.”
The second, Where Is Gone?, is a sweeping ballad featuring the Spanish star Rosalía . “That’s my favourite song on the record,” Deegan says. “I think that’s something really special Grian came up with.
“He was having this bit of a thing where he was uncontactable for a week, and we were just kind of hearing snippets from the friends he was with that he was in Europe.”
When a voice note arrived from Chatten about Where Is Gone?, Deegan thought it was “crazy good”.
The band is effusive about Rosalía. “We’ve respected her music for years,” Deegan says. Coll and Carlos O’Connell , the band’s guitar and synth player, went to one of the Catalan singer’s concerts last year.
“It was a dance piece, a theatre piece, an orchestra pit in the middle. The visual work, the camerawork – amazing,” Coll says.
Where Is Gone? makes Deegan think of the Ingmar Bergman film Wild Strawberries and of Proust’s madeleine – “or, if you want to be less pretentious about it, the ratatouille in Ratatouille”.
The song poses an existential question, he says.
“We are spinning out so much now, we don’t even know where we’re going to end up, and not just where we’re going to end up but what that’s going to look like.”
Fontaines DC have always been committed artists. “We started with a really high work ethic,” Deegan says. “We really did spend five days a week in that rehearsal room when we were starting off.”
Then, as their profile grew, they took on twice as many summer bookings as before. “That set a standard of busyness,” Deegan says. “So when we were releasing an album or two – recording two albums in a year, like we did with Dogrel and Hero’s Death – we didn’t notice. Also, we didn’t know any different straight into the music industry.”
Since then, he says, their insularity has been their strength. “We’ve just been ticking along, not watching what anyone else has been doing too much, not doing too much comparison, just doing our own thing. We have our goals of what we want to achieve, and we know what we have to do to do them.”
Later, Coll says, “We’re really awkward to be in social settings as a band, so we just hang out with ourselves and don’t really interact as much with other people. Trev always kept us on the ground, you know? So trying to continue in his spirit, for sure, is a very important thing.”
Trev is Trevor Dietz , the band’s manager and, they say, sixth member. His death , in June, devastated the band. It remains too sad and sensitive a topic to broach.
[ Trevor Dietz and Fontaines DC emerged in a Dublin that seems to be slipping away Opens in new window ]
Dietz’s early belief in the band set Fontaines DC on their remarkable trajectory. They paid tribute to him in their headline set on the final night of Electric Picnic , in August, during which Chatten brought his fist up to the lens of one of the cameras relaying their performance to the arena’s big screens: each of his knuckles was inked with a letter to spell out Trev.
As the set ended, the screens flashed the news that Fontaines will play Slane Castle next year. Was Slane on a vision board at some stage?
“To be honest, no. It’s crazy. I’ve actually never been to Slane ... I think Curley” – his bandmate Conor Curley – “was at a Kings of Leon show there. In fairness, this wasn’t on the cards when we were starting at all. We were stupidly ambitious, but Slane is a different f**king thing. It’s kind of just mad.”
[ Fontaines DC to play two nights at Slane Castle in June 2027 Opens in new window ]
Next summer they will also be playing stadiums in Britain.
“It’s all just a bit overwhelming, but in a great way, you know?” Coll says.
At Electric Picnic this summer, he thought back to his first time at a music festival, watching Arctic Monkeys play the same Sunday night slot, just before the English band released their fifth album, AM. Now he’s in the same position.
“I just feel a bit blown away sometimes that the lads who met each other in Dublin in Bimm” – the music college they went to – “and were in that tiny rehearsal room for years, trying to tune their guitars, ended up rising to it all, and that there wasn’t a moment where any of us went ‘I can’t do this’.”
According to Deegan, part of Dopamine Chamber’s creative process was exploring the kind of band they want to become. What is that band?
“What really excites me still is the philosophy of The Velvet Underground ,” he says, “where they were simultaneously pushing boundaries of pop music but, also, it was still pop music.”
He characterises the blend of John Cale and Lou Reed ’s artistry as finding “some really interesting Zen balance”.
“I want us to be able to keep pushing the boundaries more and more, and be more experimental, but never compromise on the fact that it should be a functioning song – that it should be an enjoyable song – even if we do crazy things within it.”
More and more, he believes, Fontaines are capable of being increasingly innovative, making songs that have evolved significantly since those on their debut album “but still feel like Fontaines. We could end up doing things that are very, very diverse and it still feels like us. That’s such an amazing place to be in as an artist.”
Dopamine Chamber is released via XL Recordings on Friday, October 16th

title: Rising fuel costs arising from Middle East conflict hits Eason’s online business
description: Eason’s revenues rose last year helped by new store openings but profits fell, in part due to a ‘disappointing’ Christmas books market
content:
Irish retailer Eason ’s online operations have been affected this year by increased fuel costs as a result of the US-Iran war.
In a letter to shareholders on its annual results, chairman David Dilger said that while the business was trading well overall, its “online net contribution has been impacted by significant increases in distribution costs arising from the Iran conflict and the associated increase in fuel costs”.
He said book sales were in advance of budget year-to-date and Eason had enjoyed a strong back-to-school season.
“Our underlying online revenues have continued to grow. We have also seen a modest uplift in revenues following the introduction of the new €3 EU customs charge on certain deliveries from overseas.
“However, our online net contribution has been impacted by significant increases in distribution costs arising from the Iran conflict and the associated increase in fuel costs,” he said.
In the year to January 25th, 2026, Eason Retail plc posted a 1.7 per cent increase in revenue to just over €128 million. This was due mostly to the addition of three stores to its network.
Pretax profit fell by a quarter to €3.3 million. This reduction was put down to a “disappointing Christmas book market”, with an absence of “significant bestselling titles, together with a general lack of depth in new releases”.
A combined €4.8 million was returned to shareholders in dividends and share buy-backs, and Eason closed the financial period with a cash balance of €15 million.
Another €2 million in dividends is due to be paid to shareholders in December.
“This financial performance was achieved despite several external pressures, most notably pay inflation, a disappointing book market and an uneven competitive environment,” Dilger said.
The company cited a 25 per cent increase in the national minimum wage since 2023, which would have added €4.2 million to its costs by 2026.
The chairman said cost pressures imposed by the State were largely offset by efficiency programmes in its retail and warehousing activities.
“Nevertheless, Government policy in this area continues to create a significant risk to the competitiveness of bricks-and-mortar retail businesses generally,” he said.
The company employed 563 staff during the year, with its total payroll costs flat at €24.8 million. Directors’ remuneration rose marginally to €1.08 million, with the company taking a provision of €318,000 during the year relating to share awards that are part of an executive incentive plan.
The plan runs from 2023 to 2028, with the cumulative provision to date of €551,000.
Dilger said Eason was working on a new three-year strategic plan with external advisers.
[ French fund seeks €19.7m for fully-let trio of investments in Dublin and Galway Opens in new window ]
“Although still at an early stage, the new plan is likely to involve selective increases in capital investment. This is expected to include the next iteration of the Eason store experience and a programme of estate refurbishments, with many of our stores now more than 10 years old. A warehouse relocation project is also anticipated.”
An independent share valuation by Mazars has valued the group at €65.2 million. Since the year-end, a valuation by estate agent Bannon of its two remaining company-owned properties – its flagship store on O’Connell Street in Dublin and its outlet in Blanchardstown – put a value of €27.1 million on a vacant possession basis and €29.2 million if subject to a sale and leaseback arrangement.
Eason operates three divisions – its store estate (42 company units and eight franchisees), Eason online and Dubray, which has 15 outlets. The company will hold its annual general meeting on November 5th.

title: ‘The driver talked all the time for the three-hour journey. I understood maybe 20%’
description: Rosetta Cucchi, Wexford Festival Opera’s artistic director, on discovering Irish hospitality, revisiting past works for the event’s 75th anniversary and letting the public choose what to perform
content:
Rosetta Cucchi ’s first memories of Wexford Festival Opera are of the driver who picked her up at Dublin Airport back in 1995.
“I didn’t really understand one word of what he was saying, because the Irish accent was really strange for me.
