But I felt his welcome, his passion about having me in the car – a pianist repetiteur; nothing special. He was so happy. He talked all the time for the three-hour journey. About everything. I understood maybe 20 per cent.”
What Cucchi, who is now the festival’s artistic director, picked up was that it was “a welcoming place for artists”. Like so many before her, she had difficulty believing the directions she’d been given. High Street seemed just too narrow for a theatre. “Ah, wrong place,” she thought. “There’s no theatre here.”
Now, of course, the National Opera House , on the same site, does have the signage that the Theatre Royal lacked. When she eventually made it through the stage door she entered what she calls “a new world, a new reality” for musical performers. “Parties. People that get to know each other in these parties. People dancing together. And so I fell in love with it.”
For the festival’s 75th anniversary she has, unusually, chosen to revisit three works from past repertoire. The first, which she is directing herself, is also the first opera she worked on in Wexford: Pietro Mascagni’s Iris (1898), with its exotic Japanese setting, which predates Puccini’s Madama Butterfly by six years.
Mascagni is best known for Cavalleria Rusticana, his 1890 hit. But Cucchi is fascinated by the stylistic shift away from realism in Iris.
“Mascagni had a wide range of ideas. Cavalleria is verismo. Beautiful music but also a way of shouting about the everyday. Iris is pure symbolism. At some moments it’s as if you can hear Ravel, Debussy. But in other passages you can hear Kurt Weill [who was only born in 1900].
“For a stage director it’s not easy to approach the libretto, because there’s no deep dramaturgy. There is a story, yes, but suspended in a kind of watery world where they talk about purity, about feelings, about ... nothing. But even if they talk about nothing, there is a rare depth underneath the music.”
Back in 1995, Cucchi was moving from playing piano in orchestras to opera, and Iris was a turning point in her career.
“I fell in love with the music. My big goal was to play it properly. To accompany the singers, to be there for them. Now I realise that there is so much more in the piece.”
[ Jason Moran: ‘I have a lot of gratitude for Cork Jazz Festival. And I still have that wonderful crystal vase’ Opens in new window ]
Prokofiev ’s The Gambler, based on the 1866 story by Fyodor Dostoevsky, which premiered in 1929, was first staged at Wexford in 1973 – “in French”, she says, “probably because it was too difficult to do it in Russian”.
It marked a leap into a new area of 20th-century music for the festival.
“The Gambler is a difficult opera, and not an easy listen for the audience. It’s so deeply into the idea of addiction, and it’s a psychological drama.”
In the world of Russian opera, Cucchi says, it’s “easy to do Tchaikovsky. More difficult to do Prokofiev. When I was a solo pianist I worked on Prokofiev’s First Sonata. It’s not the most difficult, but for me it was a kind of mountain to climb. I got to the top, and I won one competition with it.”
She’s also attracted by the “modern vocabulary”, the “tight dramaturgy” and the fact that the work reflects the years when her predecessors Elaine Padmore and Luigi Ferrari looked a lot to Russian, Polish and Czech music.
Rossini , this year’s third main composer, was born in Cucchi’s hometown, Pesaro. But she didn’t choose his L’Equivoco Stravagante (The Bizarre Misunderstanding) directly. It was put to public vote, in competition with works by Donizetti (which she expected to win) and Paisiello.
[ ‘It was like Moses coming down from the mountain’: John Coltrane and the creation of A Love Supreme Opens in new window ]
“The older generation of Wexford’s public has been so linked to Donizetti. But, surprisingly, they chose Rossini. I’m happy. Rossini is my bread and butter, and L’Equivoco Stravagante is still rarely done.”
The opera was banned from the stage three days after its premiere, in 1811.
“It’s an opera that’s about a woman who masquerades as a man pretending to be a castrato. The sexual misunderstandings were considered a little bit too bold. But the en travesti of Rossini is all over his work. He liked the humour of talking about those kinds of things. He liked to play with sex.”
The composer, she says, “is a genius of disguise”. She elaborates.
“The iconography of Rossini is a funny man, a fat man. But he was depressed for a long time. He arrived to romanticism before anyone else, in my opinion. If you look at his Semiramide [from 1823], or Ermione [from 1819], you can feel the early Verdi already.
“And he decided to stop writing opera very young. For another 37 years he didn’t do anything but little pieces like his Péchés de Vieillesse [Sins of Old Age], and then suddenly he composed the Petite Messe Solennelle. A masterpiece.”
Reflecting on Rossini’s exit from opera, she says: “Sometimes when you’re forced to stop, you learn things. You sometimes learn: ‘This is awful. I must get back to where I was.’ Sometimes it’s okay. ‘I can stay like this. I don’t miss having all that pressure.’
“It’s good. This would apply to lots of artistic directors who get wedded to the idea that their event couldn’t possibly happen without them. Of course, all they have to do is disappear and it’ll be sorted.”
I ask for a personal highlight from each of the operas.
“For The Gambler the special moment is the casino scene. It’s a mess. A real mess. You have 21 small characters with one phrase each, all together in one room, where the obsession is beyond them, over them, casting a big shadow.
“All the addiction, all the rage comes out through little things. Like the croupier who keeps saying, in French, ‘Les jeux sont faits. Les jeux sont faits. Rien ne va plus. Les jeux sont faits.’ [‘The bets are placed. The bets are placed. No more bets. The bets are placed.’] After that climax the end is like an octopus that goes inside the black hole.”
[ ‘We can all see you’: Gillian Anderson addresses ‘distracting’ fans in front row Opens in new window ]
The two comic characters in L’Equivoco Stravagante, Gamberotto and Buralicchio, “are always balancing stupidity and cleverness. For me Equivoco doesn’t have a proper climax. It’s all about understanding where we are and how to save yourself from being a dummy. In all of this Ernestina [the fake castrato] is the clever one. The core idea is the eternal fight between cleverness and stupidity.”
In Iris the climax is tragic. “It’s at the end of the second act,” Cucchi says, “where the naive and innocent Iris will be presented to the world. Up to that point you can believe in the possibility of hope. After that there’s no hope for humankind. The battle is a war between purity and fango – mud.” Literally, as it turns out.
Cucchi, whose early years as artistic director were blighted by social distancing and lockdowns, is optimistic about the future, even though she feels Wexford is “established as an international festival” but not quite “perceived as a national festival”. She would, of course, still like both to grow the number of international visitors from other continents and to take productions on tour abroad.
Her pride and joy is the Wexford Factory , which she initiated in 2020. It’s a professional-development academy with Irish and international partners, originally for young singers in the early stage of their careers but now facilitating pianists and stage managers, too.
As a director herself, she believes she has brought about “a tighter relationship with the stage” in Wexford. She is full of praise for the festival’s new executive director, Suzanne Nance, a trained singer with a starry career in public radio in her native United States. “She has a clear idea of where to go,” Cucchi says.
And both seem to grasp that “little things sometimes are more effective than the big gesture”.
Cucchi already has her (near) disaster story to keep the tradition of operatic misfortunes alive.
“In my time we had a tenor who was going to do a lunchtime recital. I was the pianist. And suddenly he looked at me and said: ‘Who am I?’ I replied: ‘What? Sorry? In 10 minutes we have to give the concert.’ ‘Yeah. But who are you?’
“We were so scared we brought him to the emergency department. I remember the doctor saying: ‘Who is the president of the America?’ ‘No idea.’ After 24 hours he was perfectly normal. So we did the concert a day later. We never found out what had happened.”
Wexford Festival Opera runs from Thursday, October 15th, to Saturday, October 31st. Michael Dervan has given presentations at the Wexford Factory. His next play, an Impossible Interview with Rossini (played by Peter McCamley), is at the festival on Wednesday, October 21st

title: Irish cosy gaming: Where the stakes are low and the stress is lower
description: Forget about high-octane car chases. Sushi on Wheels and Éalú are about relaxation, creativity and mindfulness
content:
B ack in 2000, a new phenomenon was about to break. Playing digital puppet master to families of virtual characters, The Sims gave you god-like control over every aspect of their lives. There was no finish line to cross or goal to achieve; you just had to tend to their needs – or not, should the mood take you – and occasionally try to stop them from burning down the house or getting trapped in the pool.
It spawned a host of follow-ups and expansion packs, from parties and holidays to magical new abilities and career paths. And it’s still going: The Sims and its follow-ups have sold more than 200 million copies.
More than a quarter of a century later, the low-stakes gaming genre has exploded in popularity, particularly since Covid lockdowns turned unlikely people into gamers.
Perhaps you’ve taken up tending digital crops, found yourself power-washing a digitally rendered fire engine until it gleams or raising a small family of colourful cartoon creatures. If so, congratulations: you are officially part of the cosy-gaming movement.
Forget about high-octane battles, car chases and climbing the leader boards via fast reflexes; cosy gaming is all about relaxation, creativity and mindfulness. You can make coffee, decorate homes, grow plants, organise fridges and lunch boxes, oversee an island and solve puzzles.
“Your mind is always trying to be busy,” says Brendan Rooney, director of the media and entertainment psychology lab in University College Dublin’s school of psychology.
“The right busy is when it’s not overly stimulating, not overly challenging but can give your mind something to do, almost like a treadmill or chewing gum, something like a rocking chair for the mind. It keeps us busy, but in a low-effort way.
“Those patterns can be fashionable or marketed, but they can also be about what people need as well.”
The growth of the cosy genre has also expanded what it means to be a gamer. Forget about the (misleading) stereotype of gamers as largely teenage boys. “I think the average age of a gamer is much higher than people expect,” Rooney says. “There’s a huge number of female gamers compared to people’s estimations of how many women are playing games. And that’s because games are now so broad.”
A quick look at the numbers shows exactly how popular it has become. Nintendo’s Animal Crossing: New Horizons set digital sales records when it launched in 2020, selling between 44 and 50 million copies. The farm-simulation game Stardew Valley has sold more than 50 million copies across console, PC and mobile platforms.
[ Virtual holidays: Eight video-game destinations offering a break from the real world Opens in new window ]
In 2020 the games platform Steam had just 19 titles tagged as cosy games; a search for the cosy tag today will turn up thousands.
It’s a market that Neil O’Sullivan Greene, an Irish games developer, is hoping to tap into. Greene Rapture , his Cork-based development company, is preparing to launch Sushi on Wheels, a cosy management game that sees players inherit their grandmother’s sushi truck on Japan’s Izu Peninsula.
Players must build the business, serving customers and upgrading the truck as they go, with the ultimate goal of opening a permanent restaurant – something the recently deceased grandmother never got to achieve.
Greene was inspired to create the game after spending six months living in Tokyo and travelling around the Izu Peninsula. “I thought it had a huge character that I hadn’t seen in a place before, and I thought it would be a really interesting setting for the game.”
He had originally been considering a horror game based on Celtic mythology. “I was going to be looking at this every single day for a while, and how enjoyable is it to make something with loads of gross monsters versus making the funnest, cutest animations?
“Also, I thought, do I want to make something that also brings fear and anxiety into the community of people that play games in a time when there’s so much of that around anyway, or do I want to make something that’s comforting and provide some escapism?
“I went for that at the end, because I just felt it was better for me and maybe for the people I was making it for.”
Sushi on Wheels can be as stressful or as stress-free as the player chooses. “For the most part it’s just ‘I’m going to be a nice cute cat, travelling around, trying to grow a little food-truck business at a nice pace and meet nice characters. Which sounds to me like a more comfortable experience that you want to play for a while longer.”
Greene Rapture isn’t the only Irish developer that has recognised the potential for the growing genre. Beyond the Bark , which is based in Limerick, found a cult online following with Éalú, its handcrafted stop-motion game starring a wooden mouse.
The idea came about following Ivan Fisher-Owen’s work with the musician Will Wood on the Tomcat Disposables video. Fisher-Owen wanted to give the mouse a better ending than falling through darkness. He considered creating a stop-motion short film for TikTok, encouraging audience participation in a sort of choose-your-own-adventure, but decided against it.
“I’m not really on social media much other than for business purposes,” he says. “I was taking a look at TikTok as an application, and it really disturbed me – not so much the content but the way in which content was presented and the algorithm was driving it,” he says. “I realised I had no idea how any of this works and I felt like I’m also in a maze.”
Fisher-Owen approached a friend who knew about coding with the idea to use stop motion as the medium. “We could tell this story, create something that is centred around the themes of algorithmic loops and the potential for them to be self-destructive, but also for there to be a way to avoid and escape them, and have a lovely time and turn that into a silent narrative.”
About 18,000 photographs and 1,200 hours of work later, Fisher-Owen – along with Wood, the programmer Benjamin Orr and the illustrator JT Paton – had Éalú. He wanted it to be photorealistic, with all the lighting, shadows and surface reflections recreated perfectly. Relying on high-tech shortcuts wasn’t an option.
“We didn’t have access to that nor the skills required to do that kind of 3D design. The only way to do it was to literally animate everything with the mouse in situ,” he says.
Part of what Fisher-Owen was trying to create was the childhood experience of playing Myst, a game published in 1993.
“It is a piece of art,” he says. “I have these memories of sitting with my sister; we’d have a notebook and a pencil, and as we tried to figure out and solve that game together, we would be taking notes and writing things down and talking to each other. I wanted to recreate that kind of experience in a modern context.”
The reactions from players suggests the team has managed to achieve that. “There were some people that would sit down and play it together and chat with each other about how to solve the puzzles,” Fisher-Owen says.
“The game responds to the way that you play it, essentially. What we’re hoping is that for a lot of people it would create a feeling of cosiness and relaxation but also just the slightest bit of mystery.”
[ Struggling to get your children off Fortnite? There’s a reason for that Opens in new window ]
Research into cosy gaming conducted by Sago across the US, UK, France, Spain and Germany last year found that more than half of players were looking for stress relief, using the games as a way to switch off from anxiety.
Rooney says using gaming as a coping mechanism isn’t negative in itself; it’s about doing it healthily.
“If we continue to do it from a place of ‘I can’t cope’, ‘I don’t want to think; things are too much,’ ‘I’m going to get lost in this game’ or this music or this TV show, then we’re training ourselves to not regulate our own emotions or look after ourselves,” he says.
“What we need is a diverse range of strategies, coping mechanisms, activities that we can engage in for pleasure so that if we need to calm down we can do some cosy gaming – or if we need to motivate ourselves, maybe we’ll use upbeat music. It’s about diversity and choice. If we’ve no diversity, then our agency is gone as well.”

title: Who needs takeaway? Fake it with two of Mark Moriarty’s easiest and tastiest dishes
description: You might not realise it, but even the half an hour you spend in the kitchen putting together these meals will help with winding down
content:
T his week I’m taking on the takeaway while using some high-quality Irish ingredients. On long weeks in our home, I’m one of the first to reach for the takeaway menu. Every now and then, however, it’s nice to grab the apron and throw together an alternative. Even the 30 or so minutes in the kitchen, with the phone set aside and some music filling the air, can bring an energy that a scroll on the couch while awaiting a doorbell just cannot replicate. This week’s recipes focus on simplicity, speedy flavour and great Irish food that won’t break the bank.
First up, we have cumin and chilli lamb skewers, inspired by the beautiful Xi’an Famous Foods in New York, which showcases western Chinese flavours at accessible prices (even for Manhattan). The key is in the seasoning paste, which involves toasting simple spices and blending them in oil before massaging the mix into some fat-laden, diced lamb chops. Note the addition of onion powder, a natural flavour enhancer that is a vital component of any serious store cupboard. The skewers are charred and rested before being crowned with lime, dill and mint. These can be served with everything from a simple salad to baked potatoes or some dressed couscous. Regardless of the garnish, they deliver on flavour, particularly with that beautiful late-season Irish lamb.
The second recipe looks and feels a little closer to something you would see coming in the brown paper bag. It has the classic look of crispy chicken and vegetables glazed in a translucent sauce thickened with cornflour. The difference here is the use of free-range Irish chicken breast and local honey, which gives the sauce its signature sheen and sweetness. Balanced with chilli, rice wine vinegar and soy, this is a match for any takeaway titan. These dishes prove that simplicity is key when it comes to home cooking, so simple in fact that it may convince you to put away the phone. You’d be surprised at how half an hourt can do wonders for your mind and body. It’s takeaway minus the guilt and with the added bonus of taste.
Tip of the week: Make sure you add onion powder to your store cupboard; it’s a natural flavour enchancer you’ll use again and again.

title: Victorian silver tea service from the Maud Gonne collection for auction
description: Meissen porcelain, landscape paintings and a stunning marble chimney piece are some of the finds at country house sales this month
content:
A uctions of the contents of country houses can throw up an extraordinary variety of antiques and collectables from around the world. When previewed in the country house itself, they also give viewers an insight into the lifestyle of the owners and their personal tastes and preferences.
Such is the case with the forthcoming Fonsie Mealy auction of the contents of Newport House, Co Mayo. Purchased by the late Kieran and Thelma Thompson in 1985, the 18th-century Georgian house was run as a Blue Book country house hotel for a number of years.
“Kieran was an amazing character who loved to talk about good food and good wine. He spent a lot of time in the Middle East as an oil executive and relied on his brother, Anthony Thompson, for a lot of decisions on what he bought,” says George Fonsie Mealy. Anthony Thompson was a Bond Street art dealer and founding member of the Irish Antique Dealers Association. This is the first house contents auction to preview in Newport House.
Newport House was originally built in 1785 for Sir Neale O’Donel, who purchased the lands from the Medlycott Estate. It remained in the O’Donel family until the widow of George Frederick Thomas-O’Donel (who was killed in the first World War) sold it in the 1940s. It was briefly owned by returned Irish emigrant, Michael McShane, before being purchased by English businessman and avid angler Henry Mumford-Smith, who transformed the house into a luxury fishing lodge. The Thompsons bought it from Mumford-Smith and established Newport House as a popular destination for good food and fly-fishing. The house is for sale with Sherry Fitzgerald for €1.3 million.
Items in the auction – an executor’s sale – will include some pieces original to the house, as well as a large collection of items Kieran Thompson purchased on his travels, and from other auctions in the UK and Ireland. African tribal face masks and ceremonial spears, a native American totem pole with an eagle, bear and human carved into it (€700-€1,000) and a taxidermy salmon caught in the Newport river in 1990 are among the items for sale.
A porcelain blue and white plate from the Chinese Qing dynasty (1644-1911), with an estimate of €1,500-€2,000, is an example of some of the more exotic items. An elaborate pair of 19th-century Meissen Schneeballen vases (€4,000-€6,000) are from the first European manufacturers of hard-paste porcelain near Dresden in Germany. Bracelets, necklaces, rings and pocket watches are also for sale, including a 19th-century 18-carat-gold cased gentleman’s pocket watch (€1,500-€1,800). The Victorian bijou ebonised gilt and floral painted side cabinets (€800-€1,000) are among the more intriguing items of furniture included in the sale.
The auction also includes a wide range of antique flatware (cutlery) and hollowware (cups and tankards) silver made in Ireland. The silver drinks labels for port, Madeira, sherry, whiskey and wine are more unusual items in the silver lots. A group of three solid engraved drink bottle rings, for claret, hock (a German white wine) and moselle (a light white wine), stamped Elkington & Co, are particularly rare (€120-€140).
And, there are several landscape paintings by 19th-century and early-20th-century artists, including Letitia Marion Hamilton, William Conor, and Mabel Young. A coastal scene from Nathaniel Hone the younger possibly depicts the coastline near Kilkee, Co Clare, where rain clouds gather on the horizon above a slate green sea (€6,000-€8,000).
The preview of the Fonsie Mealy auction of 900 lots in the Grace Hotel in Westport Demesne on October 20th and 21st will be in Newport House on Saturday-Monday, October 17th-19th.
Meanwhile, the Adam’s Country House collections of period furniture, decorative arts and rare objects, Old Masters paintings and sculpture, is previewing on Saturday, Sunday and Monday (October 10th-12th) in Townley Hall, Drogheda, Co Louth. The auction itself will take place live at Adam’s salesrooms, 26 St Stephen’s Green, Dublin 2, on Tuesday, October 13th.
The auction has a wide variety of garden furniture and ornaments, as well as lots of silverware. That last category includes a Victorian silver tea service (€8,000-€10,000), owned by the descendants of Maud Gonne McBride, the prominent Irish revolutionary. Made in London in 1865, the year before Maud Gonne’s birth, the set is engraved with the Gonne family crest and motto.
The neoclassical George IV white marble chimney piece (€50,000-€80,000) is a rare item at auctions these days, while the Adam’s auction also includes a George III giltwood mirror (€40,000-€60,000) from Hamwood House near Dunboyne, Co Meath. The house is one of the last Georgian houses occupied by the same family since it was built for Charles Hamilton in 1777. It was also the childhood home of Irish painters Letitia Marion Hamilton and her sister, Eva Hamilton.
Finally, staying with the country house theme, the Irish Antique Dealers Association will host an Irish Antique and Decorative fair in Russborough House, Blessington, Co Wicklow on Saturday and Sunday, October 10th and 11th, 11am-5pm. Admission is free to the fair, which will include items from dealers across Ireland selling rugs, furniture, paintings, jewellery, ceramics, glass and porcelain. Car parking costs €4 for the day.

title: Corinna Hardgrave obituary: A widely respected food writer and restaurant critic
description: The Irish Times restaurant critic was known for her astute palate, elegant writing style and attention to detail
content:
Corinna Hardgrave, restaurant critic at The Irish Times since 2020, has died at the age of 64 . Known for her astute palate, elegant writing style and attention to detail, she was hugely respected, if perhaps sometimes feared, by chefs and restaurant owners. She also wrote informative and lively travel pieces for the paper.
She won the Irish Food Writing Awards Restaurant Writing prize a record three times, in 2021, 2024 and 2025. While never shy to voice her opinion on a poorly cooked piece of fish or (heaven forbid) the use of truffle oil, she cared deeply about the hospitality industry and how it treated its workers.
She championed Irish produce relentlessly, and her last column for this paper revealed that Sole Restaurant on Drury Street, Dublin, was serving non-free-range Polish and Dutch chicken . This was an embarrassing revelation for the restaurant’s co-owner Larry Murrin, Chairman of Bord Bia , an organisation dedicated to the promotion of Irish produce.
Hardgrave’s first published piece in The Irish Times was an account of a meal in Ferran Adria’s restaurant El Bulli in 2006 , the second year of a record five times that it was voted best restaurant in the world.
More than one million people had applied for just a few thousand dining spaces, so after an initial rejection, she convinced her husband Steve to write to the restaurant in Spanish expressing their deep sadness and disappointment and requesting a copy of the El Bulli cookbook at a cost of several hundred euro. A few weeks later, they were offered a cancellation slot.
Family holidays were always planned around restaurants, both fine dining and more humble spots serving local food. Hardgrave adored restaurants and eating out, but these meals were also seen as important training for her palate and for developing her culinary knowledge.
Despite her love of fine dining, however, her favourite meal was sitting outdoors at a picnic table having the twin lobster and steamed clams dinner served at the Muscongus Bay Lobster shack in coastal Maine, not far from where her husband spent his childhood summers – a meal that costs about $25 and to which you bring your own wine.
Corinna Hardgrave was born in Bagenalstown (Muine Beag), Co Carlow, in August 1962, to Carmel (née Kelly) and Peter Dunne. The family moved to Templeogue in Dublin, where she attended national school and for secondary school attended Presentation College Terenure.
Her love of food and cooking can be traced to time spent in the kitchen with her mother and Aunt Jo, who was a passionate cook and gave Hardgrave a lifelong love of baking. In her early teenage years she took to collecting menus from every restaurant she visited, however humble.
Following her Leaving Cert, Hardgrave worked at Guinness for some years before moving to Bahrain to work as a flight attendant for Gulf Air. Serving first-class passengers with the airline led to a lifelong love of caviar and champagne, whenever she could afford them.
Once her contract with Gulf Air ended, she remained in Bahrain working for a promotions and marketing agency while also selling her paintings of flowers through a local gallery.
Arriving back in Dublin in 1990, she attended NCAD for a year before returning to work in PR and marketing agencies. In 1997 in the Horseshoe Bar of the Shelbourne, she met her husband-to-be Steve Hardgrave, a former US Navy pilot. She was about to leave Ireland to work for Nestlé in the UK, but eventually Steve moved there too, and they married in 1999, moving back to Ireland the following year. She gave birth to Katherine in 2000 and to Isabelle a year and a half later.
In 2005, Corinna Hardgrave began contributing to eGullet, the internet’s most influential food discussion forum at that time. Contributors included Anthony Bourdain and many other well-known names. In 2007 she was appointed as moderator of the “cooking” and “UK & Ireland” forums, where she regularly had to put manners on some of these islands’ best known food writers.
In 2008 she was diagnosed with breast cancer and underwent extensive chemotherapy, eventually returning to full health.
[ Corinna Hardgrave’s favourite takeaways in Ireland: From pizza in Dublin to crab rolls in Galway Opens in new window ]
By this time she was an established food writer, writing on food and wine for Irish Tatler magazine. In 2011 she began writing food features for The Sunday Times at the invitation of Ernie Whalley, who became a close friend and mentor, and who also died earlier this year. In 2012, she was invited to join the Irish Food Writers’ Guild.
Hardgrave had occasionally written about wine, but decided to take the subject more seriously, enrolling for and quickly passing a Wine and Spirit Education Trust (WSET) diploma. Soon she became The Irish Independent wine columnist in 2017, giving her opportunities to travel around Europe and to New Zealand, Australia, California and South Africa.
In 2020 she moved to The Irish Times as restaurant critic. It was a dream job but the timing couldn’t have been worse, with all restaurants having to close due to the pandemic. Those early columns focused on food boxes and occasionally on outdoor dining spots.
Her deep knowledge of the restaurant world, finely honed palate and sheer love of dining out made her columns authoritative and rigorous, but above all joyful to read. She never forgot her duty to her readers and was unafraid to call out bad value, service or food.
She had a knack for remaining undercover during her reviews, only occasionally being spotted. Her technique was to book under a pseudonym and dress a little less glamorously than she might ordinarily.
Her detailed questions to chefs and owners about sourcing were not always welcome, but she persisted, digging into evasive answers with follow-up questions. It could take several phone calls and emails to get the information she needed, always insisting on replies in writing.
[ Corinna Hardgrave’s 2025 food awards, including her restaurant of the year Opens in new window ]
Following Hardgrave’s death, many younger food writers whom she advised have paid tribute. She also gave advice and reassurance to many people with cancer, as acknowledged by many survivors. .
Though her illness returned recently, she never missed a column and her taste buds were unaffected.
While she was a highly successful writer, her family was always her top priority. On September 12th, she attended the marriage of her daughter Katherine to David Nugent. Photos from the day show her beaming with pride and happiness.
Despite the illness, her death was sudden and unexpected. She will be deeply missed by the Irish food world and by her thousands of readers.
Corinna Hardgrave is survived by her husband Steve, daughters Katherine and Isabelle, her mother Carmel, sister Olive, brothers Liam and Pat, son-in-law David and nieces and nephews.

title: John McGahern, A Writing Life: Biography of literary giant who understood the human condition
description: Frank Shovlin provides an authoritative insight into a reclusive figure who was dedicated to his craft
content:
Prof Frank Shovlin edited John McGahern’s letters in 2021, a task that involved serious background research into the writer’s friends, literary acquaintances, family and people involved in the publishing business. This would have undoubtedly assisted him in writing this long-awaited authorised biography.
The book’s title reveals that this is not a straightforward description of what was an interesting, though not overly exciting life, spanning the years 1934 to 2006. Rather, the emphasis is placed on the “writing life”, the composition and publication of his various books, the literary figures who influenced him, and his views on his own and other writers’ art.
What emerges is a fine tapestry of a man committed to his craft, who wrote in a room in his house in Foxfield, Co Leitrim , at a table facing a blank wall, so as not to be distracted by the view of the beautiful lake that could be seen from the window in that room.
From the start, Shovlin makes us aware of the difficult task he faced: “How can one map the life of any other individual? Never mind try to construct an accurate biography of a quiet, private man who spent so much of his writing life avoiding the literary world”.
McGahern shunned the limelight, believing that a quiet, uneventful personal existence suited his artistic output best. While he definitely drew on episodes from his own life to inspire his fiction, he always sought to follow Flaubert’s advice that an author should be like God in nature: present everywhere, but nowhere visible.
That said, the landscape and characters in his fiction are a reflection of what he knew most intimately, the area and inhabitants of Leitrim, Roscommon and Sligo , where the vast majority of his work is set. In response to a request from his German translator in 1975 to provide a context to the settings in his books, he replied: “It is a landscape of the heart and the imagination, as different and as similar to the world it grew out of as we are to our parents.”
The writer’s appreciation of that landscape was influenced by his mother Susan, who died when McGahern was just 9½ years old. Shovlin observes: “She (Susan) had a deep love of the natural world, sincerely believing that its splendour was evidence of divine creation, a belief that informed her life from first to last”.
In later life, the decision to return to live in Leitrim with his second wife Madeline was undoubtedly prompted by a desire to be close to his mother, who was buried in the beautiful graveyard of Aughawillan. Sometimes, while walking along the same lanes that she and he threaded on their way to school, John was transported back in time, an experience that produced what he describes in Memoir as “an extraordinary sense of security, a deep peace, in which I feel I can live for ever”.
The relationship with his widowed father was very different. The garda sergeant and former Old IRA commandant Frank McGahern, at least in the portrayal of him in Memoir , was prone to outbursts of violence, self-absorbed and unpredictable. He could not tolerate any opposition to his authority and used religion as a weapon to control his wife and children.
Memoir was an attempt to work through the difficult father-son relationship, but it doesn’t seem to have succeeded: the bitterness is still palpable, almost 30 years after Frank’s death. Shovlin argues that the writer was affected a lot more by his father’s passing than he let on, pointing to a copy of the short story collection Getting Through, signed by John in memory of the sergeant, that can be found among many other artefacts in the Garda Museum in Dublin.
The biography skips through McGahern’s youth quite quickly, before moving to Dublin where he would attend St Pat’s for his training as a primary school teacher. The Dublin years are used to trace the stirrings of a literary vocation. His first published book, The Barracks, was showered with praise when it came out in 1963. The poet John Montague compared it to Flaubert’s Madame Bovary and welcomed the arrival of a genuine literary talent: “Irish provincial life had never been transcribed with such exactness before”.
Many marvelled at how such a young writer could capture the death from cancer of the heroine, Elizabeth Reegan, the second wife of a widowed garda sergeant and step-mother to the children from his first marriage.
Interestingly, Faber had not originally contracted McGahern for this particular novel, but for another, The End or the Beginning of Love, extracts of which had appeared in the literary and art quarterly, X , thanks in large part to the influence of McGahern’s friend, Patrick Swift, a co-founder of this journal.
The positive response of the critics to The Barracks did not blind John to the feathers it ruffled in conservative official Ireland, with the scene of Elizabeth Reegan and her husband making love on Christmas Eve causing a certain amount of unease – one priest went so far as to demand the removal of the book from local libraries.
Hence, when The Dark was published in 1965, just as its author was returning from a sabbatical made possible by the Macauley Fellowship, the Censorship Board was highly unlikely to ignore the novel’s descriptions of an adolescent’s masturbatory habits, the “grooming” he is subjected to by a priest-cousin and his father’s abuse.
Shovlin argues that McGahern had to write this second novel “if he was going to progress and mature as an artist”. Writing to Charles Monteith, his editor at Faber, about the problems the novel had caused him, McGahern said: “I feel pretty lousy. I had almost to fight for my life in it.” The Dark was duly banned and the young author, disenchanted by his dismissal from his position as a primary school teacher, due in no small part to the intervention of the Archbishop of Dublin, John Charles McQuaid, decided to live abroad for a few years.
Shovlin is adroit at describing the writing life and what it entailed. He also gives an insight into McGahern’s various romantic interludes; his affair and subsequent marriage in a registry office to a Finnish theatre director and writer, Annikki Laaksi, which was a contributory factor in his dismissal; another with Joan Kelly, that resulted in the birth of a son, Joseph, in England, an episode that is rarely discussed in the literature on McGahern; and a brief but intense dalliance with Nuala O’Faolain , to mention but a few. Shovlin doesn’t shy away from the controversial aspects of McGahern’s life, but neither does he feel it is his role to judge his subject’s behaviour.
Money, or the scarcity of it, can be seen in the wrangling with journals about fees for short stories and articles, the negotiations with Faber in relation to advances, and the teaching stints he took on in Reading, Newcastle and Colgate Universities, which paid well, but did not help the creative process. Up until 1990, McGahern clearly had very little money.
The huge success of Amongst Women ensured his position as a canonical writer. The novel was nominated for the Booker Prize and won several awards, which brought with it financial security. It sold more than 30,000 hardback copies before the end of 1990, followed by more than 175,000 paperbacks in 1991. It was also made into a four-part television drama in a joint production between BBC Northern Ireland and RTÉ in 1998 with Tony Doyle superb in the role of Moran.
McGahern’s adaptation of a Tolstoy play, The Power of Darkness, directed by Garry Hynes and with a stellar cast, was staged in the Abbey as part of the Dublin Theatre Festival in October 1991 and was a spectacular flop. McGahern was not a playwright and the decision to adapt someone else’s work rather than write his own material most likely contributed to the poor reception the play received.
Better things were to come, however, as the late works That They May Face the Rising Sun (2002) and Memoir (2005) cemented McGahern’s position as the greatest Irish prose writer in English of the latter half of the 20th century. I had the privilege of attending readings by McGahern of both texts and you could tell how much it meant to him to be a revered and much-loved figure. When one experiences the opprobrium and alienation that McGahern did in the wake of the banning of The Dark, it is only natural that success and popularity would be relished.
A Writing Life provides wonderful insights into many aspects of McGahern the man and writer. He may have lived a simple life, but he accumulated much wisdom about the human condition and the joys and sorrows that accompany all of us on our journey towards whatever awaits us after our earthly existence.
It would be difficult to disagree with this comment from Fr Liam Kelly’s homily at the funeral Mass: “John was a gifted writer and his work, like all good art, is essentially spiritual.” Colm Tóibín , on the other hand, admits to having been blown away by The Pornographer when it was published in 1979, saying that it could have been written by a French existentialist writer.
All of which goes to show that McGahern’s work can be read on many levels, as can his life. Frank Shovlin has melded both key aspects to produce a biography worthy of its subject.
Eamon Maher is co-editor, with Kate Costello-Sullivan, Derek Hand and Barry Houlihan, of The John McGahern Companion (Peter Lang).
Young John McGahern: Becoming a Novelist by Denis Sampson (Oxford University Press, 2012)
Sampson was perhaps the most influential McGahern critic, with his Outstaring Nature’s Eye (1993) the first book-length study of the author’s work. Young McGahern covers the hours McGahern spent as a child in the library of the Moroneys, eccentric Protestant brothers living close to the barracks in Cootehall; his education with the Presentation Brothers in Carrick-on-Shannon; the training at St Pat’s, which was less than enjoyable; his embrace of the cultural life of Dublin. Discussion of The End or the Beginning of Love is one of the most interesting aspects of the study.
John McGahern: Authority and Vision by Željka Doljanin and Máire Doyle (eds) (Manchester University Press, 2017)
A very interesting collection containing essays by people not usually associated with McGahern, most notably Roy Foster, Frank McGuinness, and Melvyn Bragg, along with well-known McGahern critics. The interview by Stanley van der Ziel of McGahern is extremely revealing, as is the afterword by McGahern’s former pupil, Declan Kiberd. Máire Doyle’s premature death deprived us of a most perceptive reader of McGahern’s work.
Essays on John McGahern: Assessing a Literary Legacy, edited by Derek Hand and Eamon Maher (Cork University Press, 2019)
Based on the papers delivered at a conference in McGahern’s alma mater St Pat’s 10 years after his death, this multidisciplinary collection situates McGahern in his literary context and explains what made him unique. Themes include violence, love and desire, ecology, memory, friendship, photography, rage and sin, a span that shows how McGahern scholarship had evolved since his death.

title: The Boy by Mark Gyves: Promising underworld premise diluted by attention to detail
description: Cork-based story at its strongest when focusing on The boy and a villainous land baron with eyes on the gangland throne
content:
The Boy by Mark Gyves has a promising setup. It’s a debut about a precocious young Cork boy, a washed-up genius of a father who married into a family with IRA connections, and a mother’s death that is not surprising but nonetheless staggering. It makes for a grief-driven gangland tragedy that slowly lets the gas leak from its emotional engine.
Soon after his mother’s funeral, the titular Boy gets caught up in a tensely-rendered assassination that opens a power vacuum in the Cork underworld and sets the plot in motion. On a line level, Gyves is a clear talent, and the novel’s dialogue works wonderfully when not labouring to explain the machinations of the drug-dealing world and its various players. But the narrative strains under an explanatory impulse that distracts from the journey of its protagonist, who enters the criminal underworld in the wake of his mother’s death and brother’s murder in a bid to make things right.
The Boy is a compelling character, given what we learn of his family. His story threatens to intertwine with that of a well-drawn villain in paedophile land baron Gordon Cromby, who has his sights on the underworld throne.
The people in this book feel alive and memorable, but the plot struggles to accommodate the perspective of what feels like every passing character, and Gyves can’t quite seem to siphon out the details that matter. Some scenes baffle with their inclusion, like a flashback in which a side character purchases a house years previous, just to explain its existence, or the life story of someone that exists only to offer backstory that would have been more convincingly absorbed through a tighter perspective.
Where the novel shines are the chapters that stay with The Boy, and the villain Cromby. Here the writing is at its funniest, its most dangerous and its most emotionally salient. It just risks getting lost in the noise.
Gyves’ attempt at weaving a tapestry of lives interconnected by drug deals and gun violence puts a considerable distance between reader and the titular character in a novel that spends more energy on the logistics of his circumstances than on the emotional weight of them.
Djamel White is a novelist from Dublin. His debut novel All Them Dogs, was longlisted for the Booker Prize 2026.

title: John McPhee: Encounters in Wild America; Hemingway Knows Nothing; Ninety-Two: A Life in Football Grounds
description: Showcasing the natural world; Ukraine from the front line; football, ground by ground
content:
John McPhee: Encounters in Wild America (Library of America, €44.99)
A collection of a masterful writer on the natural world who crafts his non-fiction subjects with a novelist’s hand. McPhee created four quiet masterpieces of reportage with translucent prose and an objective eye: from wandering with wonder through a near wilderness situated incongruously beside a city’s main arterial highway; sympathetically comprehending canoe builders using the methods of American Indians; courageously roaming through parts of Alaska where you’re as likely to meet a bear as its gold miners and fur trappers. Brilliant in seeking out his trails of curiosity, McPhee then unlocks the places and lives intertwined: 1971’s Encounters with the Archdruid feels more relevant now than ever in its framing of best utilisation of our resources. For fans of Rachel Carson, Roger Deakin and Thoreau.
Hemingway Knows Nothing by Artur Dron’, translated by Hanna Laliv (Jantar Publishing, £14.99)
The title is a clue on the subject: war, from the close-up perspective of the author who volunteered for the Ukrainian army following the invasion by Russia in 2022. (Dron’ was invalided out of service last year). There’s no glorious war writing, or notions of heroism here though, as Dron’ relates life on the front line in a range of vignettes (rather than stories) in a stripped-back style that’s indebted as much to Raymond Carver as Big Ernie. There’s humanity and heart in the writing, and no shortage of fatalistic, dark humour too, as Dron’ describes his soldiering and the stranglehold on Ukrainian citizens by a war that might feel like it’s being forgotten about sometimes. A promising new voice, excellently translated by Hanna Laliv.
Ninety-Two: A Life in Football Grounds by Oliver Holt (Quercus, £22)
The title might make you think this is a formatted, box-ticking football journey. Instead it’s an earnest, unadorned memoir of a life following and working in the sport: part paean to the joy of attending matches at varying grounds, and an elegiac reckoning on how the game has changed; some things for the better, some for the worse. Not many football books reference a favourite poet, Edward Thomas, but journalist Oliver Holt has always been different gravy as one of his generation’s finest sportswriters. Holt looks affectionately at his trade, too; how journalism has had to reinvent itself with coverage of the beautiful game that has no final whistle any more. A Mancunian, he provides a lovely narrative thread on his mum, too: Corrie’s Emily Bishop.

title: What Should My Children Do? by Daniel Susskind: An optimistic book about AI
description: Susskind leans heavily on the analogy of the calculator as a disruptor to maths education
content:
What Should My Children Do? is the most common question put to Daniel Susskind when he speaks about artificial intelligence ( AI ) and the future of work . He answers this question with a thought-provoking book addressing AI and how it will impact education and work. Susskind discusses how society can prepare to harness the opportunity and mitigate the disruption AI brings. It’s a positive book, optimistic about the potential and excited about the future.
Covering family life, traditional education, adult education, the workplace, the economy and how AI will interact with all of these domains, Susskind imbues the pages with genuinely helpful suggestions and themes that can assist us in navigating this transformational period in our journey as a species.
He leans heavily on the analogy of the calculator as a disrupter to maths education. The principle of “teach both, test both” was the brainchild of Wilfred Cockcroft, a maths expert who was recruited in the late 1970s to address slumping maths performance in UK schools. It also happened to be a time when the calculator was coming into mainstream use. “What Cockcroft understood, almost half a century ago, was the true nature of the challenge that his society faced – not a choice whether to adopt a new technology or to ignore it, but how to do both at the same time.”
This approach works well for AI: we should teach both children and adults how to use AI, and how to retain critical skills that could deteriorate if we hand them completely over to the machine. Another interesting point is that, counter-intuitively, it is the less advanced skills that AI is proving worst at replicating, given full credence to your grandad’s advice to “learn a trade”.
Unfortunately, all of Susskind’s insights and suggestions are undermined by his lack of attention to who controls AI. We can’t transform our education system to facilitate a safer introduction of AI as long as Big Tech hold the reins. In fairness, he alludes to this issue in the final pages, and mentions that he’s written about it elsewhere. But this book would have been strengthened by greater treatment of this critical facet of AI and society.
Sinéad Gibney is a Social Democrat TD for Dublin-Rathdown.

title: Eoin McNamee: ‘I’m from Kilkeel so I know exactly what an Orange march is’
description: The author on new short story collection The Comets, the plight of refugees, and his admiration for Gavin Bazunu
content:
Two short novels and 15 short stories. A seam of work started in my early 20s that when put together felt as if this had been the real life’s work all along.
I don’t know if rereading is the correct term. Being repossessed by them is more appropriate.
I think the refugee and those who arrive among us from other worlds are both a burning political issue and an allegory of spiritual displacement. They are the ghosts among us. They bring their own realm.
I couldn’t see the point of arranging the stories chronologically. When they were written doesn’t matter. The correspondences are internal, not temporal.
There is an affinity of form between the short story and the radio play. There’s no room for redundancy or the inauthentic. Some of the stories in The Comets became plays. I had the privilege of working with Heather Larmour and the late John Simpson. And great actors: 12-year-old Amybeth McNulty incandescent in North of Riga; Gerard McSorley haunting in The Road Wife.
[ Eoin McNamee: ‘The ghosts of airmen have always been with me’ Opens in new window ]
Sorrow, empathy, longing, money, voices in the night, memory, beauty, fear of death, mystery, envy, how light works in the world, justice, anger, distrust, regret, love I hope.
It is a great privilege to be admitted into the writing consciousness of people learning their craft. Doing that in the house where Oscar Wilde was born is an added privilege.
I think it would be more difficult to avoid them.
I’m from Kilkeel, as you say, so I know exactly what an Orange march is. I’ll let Pat Boran’s Garvaghy Road sonnet speak for me: “But if beliefs of mine had somehow led/To the murder of three innocent wee boys/In a fire whose flames were fanned by what I’d said/Would I be out there calling for my toys/my fancy clobber, my sash, my fife and drum?”
[ The North Road: A short story by Eoin McNamee Opens in new window ]
You begin by haunting them. Then they start to haunt you.
Annie Dillard said: “I had been my whole life a bell and never knew it until at that moment I was lifted and struck.”
You have to make a bell of yourself and allow the world to ring it. (Although being lifted and struck might well be what I deserve.)
There’s a follow-up to the last novel, The Bureau, called The Roxboro. Some film work.
God no. Although I did go to South Dakota recently to see the place where Crazy Horse was murdered, as part of a film recce.
[ The Bureau by Eoin McNamee: If you’re interested in what the Border truly means, read this exceptional novel Opens in new window ]
I would require Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan to abolish the utterly shameful use of petty regulation by the Department of Justice to deny visas to Gazan students with full scholarships to Irish colleges.
Film: Marc Evans’s remarkable Effi O Blaenau; Book: Adania Shibli’s Minor Detail ; Podcast: My daughter Kathleen’s women’s football podcast, COYGIG.
Events take you in different ways and rise up out of the past with new meanings so there isn’t a most.
Every time you open the front door you step into a remarkable place, but recently Wounded Knee. All of history at a lonely prairie crossroads with a rusted tin sign and a Lakota girl at a folding table selling bracelets made of porcupine quill.
A Damask rose taken as a cutting from my mother’s garden.
[ ‘I would like to transfer my late mother’s beloved rose bushes to my own home. But how?’ Opens in new window ]
Recently a friend of my aunt Phil McNamee gave me a box of her possessions including an autograph book belonging to my grandmother Nora O’Neill when she was 12. Her friends had written short poems, jokes, messages, full of the longings of the young. I can hardly bear to open it. You can be a refugee in time as well.

title: Protocols by Andrew Huberman: A book about the brain that could change lives
description: This is science made accessible in the golden age of neuroscience
content:
Before the launch of this health guide, the publisher promised a fanfare of publicity that would have outdone memoirs from presidents and Nobel Prize winners. This was muted in Europe, which is a pity because it is a remarkable work that explains the brilliant structures of our brains.
Andrew Huberman, a neuroscience professor at Stanford University, draws on five years of interviews he carried out in his podcast series. Many recent findings are covered: why walking improves memory; how physical books beat ebooks at bedtime; why sea swimming cuts stress; and how the day’s emotions are processed in the nightly “therapy” of REM sleep.
Neuroscience, assisted by scanning technology, is experiencing a golden age, revealing that we have far more options to control our physicality and mentality than we previously realised. Neuroplasticity – which creates all “sustained behavioural and cognitive change” – is the process of laying down new cognitive pathways between our trillions of neurons.
Huberman’s research focused on the optic systems that occupy a third of the outer shell of our brain – a signalling network of such versatility that the blind convert it into auditory and other sensory infrastructure. All of us have similar reusable regions.
Seven main areas are covered: sleep, exercise, stress control, nutrition, light, focus (including motivation and learning) and personal growth. While these might sound like the usual self-help headings, they come from about 200 podcast interviews – some as long as three hours – with leading experts in subjects as diverse as dopamine and addiction, the analytics of wellbeing and the science of efficient learning.
On the last of these, for example, he explains how two neuromodulators (adrenaline and norepinephrine) create “all the necessary conditions for plasticity to occur”. He then describes how to summon them in order to enter the best learning state by being “alert but calm. Not stressed ... It’s in that state of mild agitation that learning is sparked.”
Huberman, an academic counterpart of our own professor of psychiatry Anthony Clare, should be congratulated for making science so accessible. This is a book that has the power to change lives.
Neasa MacErlean is a journalist and author

title: Ply by Hernan Diaz: Sci-fi thriller and philosophical treatise a marvel of breadth and concept
description: Multiple threads converge into a research-crammed, physics-dense exploration of consciousness and human essence
content:
Following his Pulitzer-winning novel Trust in 2022, this much-anticipated new book from Hernan Diaz will not disappoint in its brilliance, breadth and concept. Hugely ambitious, it explores the big themes that haunt us all, including climate change , AI , the breakdown of world power structures and more traditional philosophical thought about identity, time and our role in the universe.
Ply is set several centuries hence, in the remains of a decrepit city where the state is dead and random communes struggle for fresh water and electricity, both controlled by private corporations.
A rebel known as “the Pincher” survives by leeching energy illicitly from the grid into home-made batteries with which she trades and provides power for bands in a thriving downtown music scene. When she invents a new device that holds a massive charge, she takes up with a wealthy scientist who covets its potential to unleash a new reality.
The writing, while on occasion rambling, is more frequently immersive and beautiful. Yet just when you’re settling into a Neuromancer meets Gravity’s Rainbow sci-fi thriller, the second part of the book kicks in and the narrative morphs at speed into what could either be an end-of-days philosophical treatise or a PhD thesis in quantum physics.
Among other ideas, the author postulates that civilisation, which began letting go of God at the end of the Middle Ages in favour of the Renaissance and the glory of man, has, by the end of the “modern age” (21st century), began to let go of man too. “Our devices redefined what both ‘intellect’ and ‘consciousness’ meant,” we read. “The very notion of experience, which is how we meet reality, was challenged; people’s lives and their humanity, once precious, became cheap ...”
[ AK Blakemore: ‘The best historical fiction is comfortable living with the sheer weirdness of the past’ Opens in new window ]
As momentum builds with experimental complexity, its multiple threads converge into a research-crammed, physics-dense exploration of consciousness and human essence, where pronouns and points of view slice quickly across each other in a thunderous, fragmented denouement. In the book’s acknowledgments, Diaz thanks, among other intellectual hubs, the CERN nuclear research facility and a Mind Brain Behaviour Institute in Columbia University; perhaps indicative of the level of science that informs this work of fiction.
It will undoubtedly challenge and perplex the reader to a degree that neither of his previous works have done.
Helena Mulkerns is a writer and publisher.

title: Sleepers in the Snow by Joanne Harris: Novel is a mix of ghost story and personal tragedy
description: Author’s elegant prose captures the anguish of dementia
content:
Ghost story? Family tragedy? Distressing account of a mind unravelling in a series of painful, stuttered jumps? Sleepers in the Snow is all these – and often all at once.
Kirkhill is an isolated house on a moor. A man, newly divorced and looking for a fresh start, buys the house sight unseen. Only then does he discover why the house was inexplicably cheap: it sits in the shadow of a huge electricity pylon.
The previous owners, Arthur and Caroline, left their possessions behind. Though initially disconcerted by this, the narrator finds that Arthur’s shoes and clothes fit him, the smell of Caroline’s perfume is familiar. When he finds Arthur and Caroline’s diaries, he becomes drawn into their different narratives, trying on their memories and thoughts for size.
But the diaries reveal a terrible tragedy in Kirkhill’s recent past, and as winter draws in, the house appears to turn on its inhabitant. Objects disappear and reappear. Foxes shriek incessantly, birds fall from the sky. The pylon becomes a “sleeping monster”.
Or has he just moved in? The reader soon understands there is another reason why Arthur’s slippers fit, why the house is both new and familiar. Sleepers in the Snow runs from autumn 2024 to the winter of 2025, the same span of time in which Joanne Harris wrote the first draft. Her father had died the previous summer after years of ill-health and dementia. After his death, her mother, who had cared for him at home, “quickly and efficiently swept the house of all trace of him”. Harris recovered the notebooks in which he kept names and words he wanted to remember. This recording of detail becomes central to Sleepers in the Snow , for the narrator also begins to record his daily life.
[ The Strangers by Naomi Alderman: A wonderful blurring of lines between sci-fi and memoir Opens in new window ]
The narrator’s thoughts circle and misfire. As an interpretation of dementia, this feels authentic and empathetic. The flipside is that, as a narrative, it creates repetition; layers peel back, revealing shadows of themselves. Harris’s prose is elegant as always; pheasants rattle “their rusty-can cries”, the pylon stands “poised like a mantis” over the nearby trees. She captures the anguish of dementia particularly vividly with the line: “Of all the ghosts we encounter here, the ghosts of ourselves are the cruellest.”
Henrietta McKervey’s latest novel is The Woman in the Water

title: X + Y = K by Ciaran Carson: Excellent examination of reality in the context of art and war
description: Novel about modern Spiritualism mixes investigative journalism, ekphrastic essay and swampy detective fiction
content:
Pushed to say what X + Y = K is about, I’d maybe say it begins, at least, with an investigation into modern Spiritualism, beginning in new York in 1848 with the Fox family and their famous “rappings”, and continuing on to the Goligher Circle in Belfast around the first World War.
All of this is brought to our attention by a man named Kilpatrick, who is in London to speak to his editor about an idea he has for a fictional account of the Golighers’ story. What you might expect from that is a fairly straightforward story about adaptation, ghosts, deception, maybe about belief. Though this novel has all of that, it approaches it in a much more interesting way and delves a lot deeper.
Anyone familiar with Carson’s work will expect this. Carson has always been known for his ability (perhaps need ) to contextualise everything. With him, nothing is left alone. It’s all investigated and connected, whether through etymology, history or sheer coincidence. It’s like he’s trying to contextualise the whole world and it makes everything you’re reading feel huge and important.
There are parts of this novel that read like investigative journalism, parts that feel like ekphrastic essay, parts that feel like swampy detective fiction. Often times you may be left wondering where exactly is he going with this? But he always brings it back.
Carson’s characters pick up books and think of all the hands who’ve held them. They stand before a Turner and know that their presence is changing the painting. They quote William Denton when he said: “You cannot enter a room by night or day, but you leave on your going out a portrait behind you.”
[ Letters to Our Sons by Stephen Graham and Orly Klein: On men living out a crisis Opens in new window ]
Concerned with permanence, and often straying into the speculative, X + Y = K examines all aspects of reality: the physical, the mental, the spiritual, all in the context of art and war. Reading this excellent book, I couldn’t help but wonder whether some part of Carson himself remains – a molecule of his breath, an atom of his skin. Is he in the soil or the trees? Perhaps he is in the fibres of the pages of this book, or indeed the newspaper you hold in your hand.

title: Trump agrees diesel supply deal with Russia
description: ‘Gifts to Putin will not bring peace ‌or ‌any ​benefit to the civilised world,’ says Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy
content:
US president Donald Trump said on ‌Friday that Russia had agreed ​to immediately supply more than 300,000 tons (272,000 tonnes) of diesel fuel ​to the American and ⁠global marketplace after what Trump ‌described ‌as ​a “highly successful” discussion with Russian president ⁠Vladimir ​Putin .
Trump added ​that Russia would ‌then deliver three ​million tons of diesel fuel ⁠within ⁠a ​short period of time, based on the condition of its diesel refineries, and would immediately ‌supply another 500,000 ⁠tons in November and one million ‌tons immediately thereafter.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy criticised the accord, calling it “an ​investment in a war that must be ended”.
The deal was announced while a Ukrainian delegation was in the US to discuss how ​to seek a resolution of the war with Russia.
“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace ‌or ‌any ​benefit to the civilised world,” Zelenskiy wrote on the X social media platform.
“Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with ⁠further terror and perfidy. Allowing ​Russia to sell petroleum products ​is an investment in a war that must be ended, not ‌prolonged. What is needed is real ​de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis,” Zelenskiy said.
Trump said in ⁠a post on social ⁠media that ​he had agreed in a call with Putin that Russia would immediately supply diesel to the US and global marketplace. Trump said lower prices for Americans “is my Greatest Priority”.
Zelenskiy, speaking to reporters later on WhatsApp, said the accord would provide Moscow with additional funds to wage ‌war and undermine any ⁠attempts to work towards a settlement.
[ Russian bomb attack kills dozens at Ukraine bus stop Opens in new window ]
“I believe our team is simply being used as a front. And that is ‌certainly not fair, nor is it how partners should treat each other,” he ​said. “In my view, it is a weak ​decision on the part of strong partners.”
Confirming the deal with Trump, Putin said in a statement on Friday ‌that his country was ready ​to supply oil and oil products to the US and ​global markets, and that this would ⁠help the global economy ‌as ‌a ​whole.
Putin’s statement, published by the ‌Kremlin, said ⁠the two leaders also discussed resolving the Ukraine ‌conflict and the situation in ​Iran.
Russian deputy prime minister Alexander ‌Novak said Russia was ready to start supplying ​additional volumes of diesel ⁠to the US ‌and other ​countries in October.
He ⁠also ⁠said Russia’s ​exports are set to increase further in November and December as ‌refineries return ⁠to operation following maintenance.

title: Waterford stun Bohemians at Dalymount to reach FAI Cup final
description: Noah Mawene and Tommy Lonergan on target for Graham Coughlan’s side
content:
Waterford bridged a 22-year gap to reach the FAI Cup final after belatedly sparking to life with a devastating seven-minute spell in the second-half that left Bohemians wondering what on earth had just happened.
For 51 minutes, the Gypsies were in control of this semi-final, wracking up chance after chance, leaving supporters to question when, not if, they would score.
But Waterford – who haven’t won this trophy since 1980 – had other ideas and showed them how, scoring from their first two opportunities of the game.
Noah Mawene set the Blues on their way and Tommy Lonergan continued his own fine form to secure their ticket to the Aviva Stadium showpiece for the first time since 2004. Lonergan is certainly the man of the moment, having scored four goals for Ireland’s under-21s in the recent international window.
But he also mucked in to clear a Bohemians effort off the line in the first-half, a sliding doors moment for the visitors as the game could have easily unravelled at that point, such was the pressure they were under.
Bohs still have a league title to play for and must park this frustration heading for leaders Shamrock Rovers on Monday night. But starved of silverware since 2010, the manner in which they let this opportunity slip through their grasp will sting. So be it, Waterford will argue, as Bohs were wasteful when it mattered.
They showed great intensity throughout the first-half and dominated all aspects of play, leaving Waterford scrambling at the back and without chances of their own at the opposite end. And yet for all Bohemians’ endeavour, Waterford had them where they wanted – going in scoreless at the break.
How it remained so is a wonder, as the Gypsies – benefiting from a strong breeze – attacked early and often with clever, intricate moves posing all sorts of questions for the visitors in the final third, while Dawson Devoy and Jordan Flores orchestrated attack after attack from midfield.
Waterford goalkeeper Stephen McMullan did well to parry a ferocious Flores drive from 40-yards before denying Devoy from closer range, after Bohs saw a penalty appeal waved away when Mawene clipped Connor Parsons in the build-up.
Bohemians’ high-octane approach was serving them well at this point and they continued to pepper Waterford all the way to the break. McMullan’s save with his chest to thwart Douglas Jame-Taylor from six yards kept Waterford in the hunt, but James-Taylor should have scored, and team-mates were not shy in telling him.
Still, the pressure kept coming and Patrick Hickey must have thought his header off a corner was going in before Lonergan stuck out a boot to clear the ball off the line with McMullan beaten. After his brace in Ireland’s famous win over England on Tuesday, Lonergan wasn’t afraid to roll the sleeves up.
Bohs were playing with a swagger and they were puncturing Waterford’s defence with repeated raids down both flanks, low balls into the box causing all sorts of issues for Graham Coughlan’s big defenders. Home fans were preparing to celebrate when McMullan dropped a Ross Tierney header near his line, only to recover in a scramble.
The Gypsies faithful cheered their team off at half-time, energised by what they had seen and believing it was only a matter of time before one of their many punches would land. But Waterford had other ideas and silenced Dalymount Park with the opening goal after 51 minutes.
Benny Couto hurled a big throw into the box that James-Taylor headed clear, but only as far as Mawene. He met the ball at full stride and unleashed a powerful shot from 20 yards that smashed into the ground and beat outstretched goalkeeper Paul Walters as it started to climb again at pace.
From nowhere, Waterford were suddenly alive and had more punishment to dish on Bohemians for failing to make hay during that first-half show of strength.
Seven minutes after their opening goal, the Blues doubled their lead with Lonergan slotting home after Padraig Amond expertly dealt with a long punt down the pitch, turning Hickey before teeing up the in-form striker to leave Bohs shell-shocked.
Bohemians piled more pressure on for the remainder, but in keeping with their night they got nowhere with it and could have lost by more late on only Conan Noonan hit the post after rounding Walters.

WATERFORD: McMullan; Houston, Cann, Mahon, Long, Couto (Ashton 90); Mawene, Heeney (McMenamy 82), Noonan (Faria 88); Amond, Lonergan (Voilas 82).

title: Poor discipline costly for Connacht in Glasgow defeat
description: High penalty count and two yellow cards spell destruction for Connacht at Scotstoun
content:
Connacht were the victims of some very inconsistent and at times downright poor officiating, but it doesn’t fully excuse the lack of discipline, which led to yellow cards for both Sam Illo and Josh Murphy, and the concession of four tries from lineout mauls.
There were flashes of good rugby from the visitors and some fine individual displays, but Connacht just couldn’t get out of their own way for long enough. A brace of tries from Josh Ioane and one for Sean Jansen won’t offer much consolation.
The province conceded 14 penalties against Benetton last week and within half an hour at Scotstoun had coughed up eight.
Hooker Gregor Hiddleston and flanker Rory Darge were the beneficiaries of the maul dominance, grabbing a try apiece for the hosts, while scrumhalf George Horne added a conversion.
Connacht started superbly, winning the collisions and setting up camp in the Glasgow 22, but an inability to protect breakdown ball cost them penalty turnovers.
Undaunted, the visitors continued to dominate. With Cian Prendergast, Bundee Aki, Illo and Shayne Bolton all breaking the gain-line, prompted by Ciarán Frawley, they eventually got the try they deserved through Jansen, converted by Frawley.
From 7-0 up, discipline was an insurmountable obstacle to the province’s ambition, Illo receiving the first yellow card of the game after Connacht’s 12th penalty. While Glasgow’s maul set-up from the lineout was illegal, blocking off a contest, referee Ben Breakspear let it slide and Hiddleston drove over for a second try to give his side a 19-7 interval lead.
Josh McKay grabbed the bonus point try two minutes after the restart with Connacht still a man down. Ioane scored a try to keep the visitor’s in contention, but Breakspear then ignored a head-on-face collision that saw Bolton depart with a jaw injury, before the fullback grabbed a second try after a superb team effort.
At 26-19, Connacht dared to dream, but Murphy’s yellow, for a shoulder charge arguably less serious than the Bolton incident, proved costly.
Replacement hooker Seb Stephen was driven over for his side’s fourth maul try, converted by Horne, and Lancaster then added a late penalty for 36-19.
