title: Three Palestinian students granted visas after Minister reverses refusal
description: A fourth student lost their appeal to the visa refusal
content:
The Minister of Justice has reversed a decision to refuse three Palestinian students visas allowing them to pursue Irish university scholarships.
The granting of the visas comes after the students challenged Jim O’Callaghan’s refusal of visas in the High Court.
The court had been due to hear the students’ judicial review challenges this week. However, Judge Anthony Barr was told on Wednesday the cases had settled following an offer by the Minister to determine the students’ appeal of the refusals by close of business on Friday.
Susan Doyle of SMD Solicitors and Phoenix Law’s Sineád Marmion, solicitors for the three students, confirmed on Friday that the visas had been granted.
A fourth student who had also challenged the Minister’s refusal in the High Court lost an appeal.
The High Court is expected to hear further challenges by prospective Palestinian students to visa refusals next week.
The initial visa refusals were for reasons including that the Gazan students had not provided original documents with their application.
On their behalf, it was argued that the civilian infrastructure for them to go to a bank or post office to get such documents no longer exists in Gaza and the Minister’s stance was irrational, unreasonable, disproportionate, discriminatory and failed to react to the necessary urgency of the situation.
In the wake of Israel’s war in Gaza, more than two million displaced people are living in tents and temporary shelters in the enclave, where an estimated 80 per cent of structures – roughly 200,000 buildings – have been damaged, with about two-thirds of those destroyed, according to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, Unrwa.
The Minister had opposed the challenges.

title: The Irish Times view on the budget process: flawed and short-termist
description: The system’s shortcomings have been laid bare by the absurd contortions over funding for RTÉ
content:
Critics of Ireland’s approach to annual budgets argue that it is a crude and reductive way to manage the public finances, rewarding political short-termism at the expense of strategic vision.
They have a point. The leaks, the “something for everyone” giveaways, the once-off measures, the pro-cyclical spending and the chronic overruns flagged by the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (Ifac) are all at their worst in the autumn ritual in which final numbers are hashed out.
It need not be this way. Better-managed countries such as Sweden settle these questions years in advance through a multi-annual process, a more sensible approach for a complex modern economy.
The system’s shortcomings have been laid bare by the absurd contortions over next year’s funding for RTÉ. The previous government agreed a three-year arrangement, contingent on restructuring at the broadcaster. Three hours before Tuesday’s budget speeches, RTÉ learned it would receive €20 million less than agreed.
Against total spending of €125 billion, the sum is tiny. But how it was reached is telling. Internal correspondence reveals a gulf between the departments of Media and Public Expenditure, with Minister for Media Patrick O’Donovan warning of reputational damage to the Government if cultural and sporting bodies lost out. This suggests a dispute over departmental funding produced the RTÉ shortfall. Yet O’Donovan blamed slow reform at the broadcaster, before appearing to row back.
None of this reflects well on O’Donovan. It also shows how easily a multi-year commitment can unravel in the annual scramble for money.
The RTÉ arrangement was itself a fudge. The last government rejected its own Future of Media Commission’s recommendation to replace the licence fee with direct State funding, opting for an interim hybrid that runs until the end of 2027. A lasting solution remains to be found.
Budget reform seems even more remote. But what Budget Day does offer is a measure of the government of the day, its priorities and its divisions. This Government knows Ifac is right about its reliance on windfall revenues from a handful of multinationals, yet finds it politically impossible to act. The strains in Cabinet over J ack Chambers’s attempt to slow spending growth prove that. It is, however, well attuned to pressure from sectoral interests. Last year hospitality won a VAT cut. This year it was the turn of the hauliers and farmers whose fuel protests caused such disruption in April.
Simon Harris framed his speech around Ireland’s economic health relative to its European neighbours. But what is lacking is any plan for the day the corporate tax windfall dries up, or any sense of where the country is heading.

title: Ryder Cup at Adare Manor set for fireworks on the first with drivable Par 4
description: Decision influenced by need to accommodate a giant horseshoe grandstand
content:
The box office drama will be evident from the very first tee shots of next year’s centenary Ryder Cup at Adare Manor , with the decision by the European Tour – in consultation with Europe captain Luke Donald – to make the first hole a drivable Par 4 of 294 yards.
Although the Tom Fazio redesigned course has a back tee of 433 yards on the first hole, the move to play it as a short Par 4 has been influenced by the need to accommodate a giant horseshoe grandstand around and along the first tee box which will seat 6,500 spectators at the sold-out match between Europe and the United States.
The sheer scale of the proposed horseshoe grandstand for Adare Manor has led to the decision to use the most forward tee at 294 yards rather than the back tee or the other tees at 376 yards and 341 yards. However, it won’t be simply a case of players standing up to grip-it-and-rip-it as accuracy will also be required, with the green guarded by a stream in front of it.
Traditionally, a drivable Par 4 would have been considered an advantage for the Americans, who through the years statistically have longer average driving distances on the PGA Tour . However, the gap has closed in more recent years, to the extent that Europe’s players can often outdrive their US counterparts.
The grandstand on the first tee at Adare Manor will be one of the largest constructed for the opening hole experience at any Ryder Cup, comparable to the one used at Le Golf National in Paris in 2018, while a smaller grandstand by the first green will accommodate another 900 fans for what should be a drama-filled opening hole.
The first hole experience has become an integral part of the Ryder Cup down the years, including the 2023 match at Marco Simone in Rome – where the grandstand, based on a gladiatorial theme around the Colosseum, had 5,000 seats – which also started with a drivable Par 4.
When the 2025 Ryder Cup was held at Bethpage, the grandstand at the first tee combined with the 18th for a dual seated structure which catered for 5,000 spectators.
The first use of an opening tee grandstand was at The K Club in 2006 when it was a rather more modest and compact affair with seats for a couple of hundred people.
Over the years, that first tee experience has seen grandstands grow bigger, There was seating of 2,148 for the one at Gleneagles for the 2014 match and 1,668 at Hazeltine in 2016. The 2018 match in Paris was the game-changer with a multi-tier stand accommodating 6,5000 – which will be matched at Adare Manor next year.
[ ‘It’s us against the world’: Jim Furyk says USA need to have chip on shoulder to win Ryder Cup Opens in new window ]
In all, the grandstand capacity at Adare Manor for next year’s event will be able to accommodate 20,000 seats with a daily attendance for the match on September 13th-19th, 2027, of 50,000 spectators.

title: Order sought against former Clare TD and her six children to vacate rented property
description: Violet-Anne Wynne and John Montaine owe alleged rent arrears of more than €18,000, court heard
content:
A landlord is seeking a court order directing former Independent Clare TD Violet-Anne Wynne and her six children to vacate a rented property in Clarecastle, Co Clare concerning alleged rent arrears of more than €18,000.
At Ennis District Court on Friday the owner of the property, Patricia Warshell, of Parliament Street, Ennistymon, was seeking an order from the court under Section 124 of the Residential Tenancies Act for Wynne, John Montaine and their six children to immediately vacate their rented home at Main Street, Clarecastle, Co Clare.
Warshell’s solicitor John Halpin told Judge Adrian Harris that there was an urgency to the matter and his client was seeking an order on Friday but was happy for a stay to be put on the order for one month.
Representing herself in court, Wynne told the judge she was a single mother and on Wednesday of this week had obtained alternative accommodation for herself and her six children.
Montaine was also in court and applied for an adjournment in the case to allow him to get a solicitor to represent him in the case.
Wynne and Montaine stood on opposite sides of the court when addressing the judge individually.
In the application, Warshell is seeking a judgment against the respondents, Wynne and Montaine, of €18,000 for rent arrears up to January 31st, 2026 together with further arrears which may have accrued up to the hearing of the application.
Warhsell is also seeking an order directing the property be vacated.
The judge said he would adjourn the case to November 25th.
The rent arrears case was one of two cases concerning Wynne on the court’s civil list on Friday.
The second case concerned Wynne owing a residual debt to an ex-employee, Fiona Smyth, from an €11,500 Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) award, and it was before the court for monitoring of payments being made.
Smyth’s solicitor Daragh Hassett said payments were ongoing and Wynne told the judge she wanted to reassure the court that the payments would continue to be made until the money is paid off in full. Judge Harris adjourned the case to next year to allow further monitoring.
Wynne – who received a TD’s annual salary of €113,679 – lost her seat in the November 2024 general election in Clare. Standing as an Independent, she received only 310 first preference votes having topped the poll in the 2020 general election as a Sinn Féin candidate.

title: Hospital waiting lists climb above one million people
description: Irish Patients’ Association chief calls on Coalition to advance ‘credible recovery plan’
content:
Pressure on hospital waiting lists continues to intensify as the number of patients climbs further above one million.
The latest figures issued by the National Treatment Purchase Fund (NTPF) on Friday showed that 1,040,698 patients were on a waiting list of some kind at the end of September.
Of these, 114,722 patients were waiting for an appointment for their inpatient or day case treatment, 43,285 patients were waiting to receive an appointment for a GI (gastrointestinal) endoscopy, and 692,524 patients were waiting for a first hospital outpatient consultation.
[ Child waits 11 years for psychology assessment, another waits nine for occupational therapy Opens in new window ]
Furthermore, 35,273 patients have been given a date for their inpatient, day case or endoscopy procedure, while 114,422 patients are recorded in the planned procedure category.
These are patients who have already had treatment, require further treatment and have been assigned indicative dates for treatment.
A total of 40,472 patients are classified as suspended, which includes patients who are temporarily unfit or unable to attend due to clinical, personal or social reasons.
The figure topped one million for the first time in June.
A statement by the Department of Health acknowledged some “positive signs”, including a continued reduction in the inpatient or day cases list since the end of July.
“However, recent waiting lists have been impacted by the ongoing trend of higher demand and increased referrals, which has offset the significantly increased levels of activity that are being delivered in acute hospitals,” ran the statement.
“Demand for scheduled, or planned, care has increased significantly in recent years, exceeding both pre-pandemic levels and demographic expectations.”
The department said while it aims to prevent waiting lists from growing, “higher levels of referrals can also indicate better access to necessary care, increased awareness of available services, and expanded service provision”.
[ Letters: Reports on radiotherapy and neurology services and children’s hospital a cause for worry Opens in new window ]
Irish Patients’ Association chairman Stephen McMahon acknowledged the improvement in day cases, but said there has been “substantial increases in prolonged waits”.
September’s figures show that 64,718 patients were waiting 18 months or longer, while 86,482 were waiting between 12 and 18 months.
“The NTPF has confirmed that it does not collect the activity data needed to show how many waiting-list patients were actually treated or seen,” said McMahon.
“Without that information, the public cannot reconcile who joined the lists, who received care and who was removed without treatment.”
McMahon called on the Government to publish a “credible recovery plan”, stating patients need “clear evidence of sustained reductions across the waiting-list system”.

title: The Irish Times view on the living wage: firmly on the back burner
description: The Government needs to outline what happens next
content:
The Government has to all intents and purposes reneged on its commitment to introduce a living wage by 2029. Defined as 60 per cent of the median or mid-point of hourly earnings, the statutory living wage was to replace the legal minimum wage, which has been in place since 2000.
Unlike the minimum wage, which must be set each year by a Low Pay Commission comprised of employers, employees and independent experts, the living wage would be directly pegged to wage growth in the economy.
In the end, bridging the gap between the current minimum wage and the predicted living wage by 2029 proved a step too far and the Government has abandoned the target date. There is some debate about whether the failure to set a new date amounts to it being abandoned, but the effect is the same. Hiding the move in a departmental document was a poor way to communicate it.
Syncing the two measures amounted to chasing a moving target as wages grew strongly in recent years. Employer groups have welcomed the development, which brings some certainty to the issue from their point of view. Trade unions have criticised the move and the issue may well feature in talks about a new public sector pay deal which have yet to commence. Few public sector workers are on the minimum wage, but its increase does tend to feed through to pay levels at the lower end.
The case for a “living wage” is socially persuasive and politically attractive but the economic realities of introducing one have led to difficulties.
Most of our European peers adopt a social partnership model like that used here until 2010 to deal with these kind of issues, or a hybrid approach combining a statutory minimum wage with targets similar to the 60 per cent of median earnings benchmark envisioned by the living wage. The latter may prove a more viable alternative for Ireland. But some clarity is needed and a pathway towards progression for those at the lowest earnings level needs to be set out.

title: Minister’s appointee to Inland Fisheries said he was not briefed on blackmail allegation
description: Former chief executive alleges he was blackmailed by sitting senator
content:
One of two ministerial appointees who took over from a former board of Inland Fisheries Ireland (IFI) has said he was not briefed on an accusation by its ex-chief executive that he being blackmailed by a sitting senator.
Tom Barry was giving evidence under cross-examination on Friday at the Workplace Relations Commission as the agency defends complaints of whistleblower penalisation and unfair dismissal brought by its former chief executive, Francis O’Donnell.
Barry and another appointee, Seamus Neely, took the place of a former IFI board in February 2023 following the resignations of a number of directors, the WRC has heard.
O’Donnell’s case is that he suspended a senior employee pending an investigation into allegations of theft and fraud in the organisation raised in anonymous correspondence.
O’Donnell has said he reported to gardaí that he was being pressured to reinstate the senior employee.
This included “being blackmailed” by a sitting senator with an alleged threat to make public “very damaging” allegations about him, O’Donnell said.
A separate external investigation process commenced when O’Donnell himself was subject to a complaint, the tribunal heard.
His case is that the board’s decision to commence disciplinary action was an act of whistleblower penalisation – an allegation denied by IFI.
Cross-examining Barry today, O’Donnell read a part of a transcript of proceedings in the Seanad into the record in which the IFI chief executive was stated to be “targeting” an employee.
“The whole saga is not just disgusting, it’s rotten, corrupt,” the transcript read.
“Is it fair to say he [the speaker in the Seanad] was in possession of a significant amount of confidential information he shouldn’t have?” O’Donnell asked.
“Ideally from a governance perspective, of course not,” Barry replied.
O’Donnell then asked whether Barry had seen correspondence O’Donnell’s solicitor had sent in December 2022 setting out “issues with the same senator”.
O’Donnell said his solicitors had written “quite a detailed letter” to then-IFI chair, Prof Frances Lucy, on December 14th, 2022.
“That was never brought to your attention to do any handover at all?” O’Donnell said.
O’Donnell asked Barry whether he thought it “unusual” that nobody brought matters of “significant magnitude” which were on record in IFI to the attention of the ministerial appointees.
“The only comment I can make was if I was in the situation myself as CEO and I felt something needed to be brought to the attention of a new board, I presume I’d bring it to their attention,” Barry said.
IFI’s barrister Tiernan Lowey told a hearing on Friday that Barry and Neely were “completely unaware” of disclosures made by O’Donnell the year before to the Department of the Environment .
The same went for the new board chaired by Prof Tom Collins, to which Barry and Neely ceded responsibility in January 2024, Lowey submitted.
O’Donnell is pursuing complaints under the Protected Disclosures Act 2014, the Payment of Wages Act 1997, and the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977 against the State agency, where he was employed as chief executive from September 2020 to July 2025.

title: Irish children forced into criminality inappropriately punished, major report finds
description: The US State Department says gaps in victim identification mean Irish children are rarely recognised as trafficking victims
content:
Irish children forced into criminality are being inappropriately punished, as authorities fail to identify them as victims of trafficking, a major report from the US State Department finds.
The 2025 Trafficking in Persons (TIP) report on Ireland , published on Friday, is one of hundreds on individual countries from the US government’s TIP office which monitors international human trafficking trends.
It says while Gardaí are identifying more trafficking victims – 114 last year compared with 67 in 2024 – current regulations do not allow for the identification of Irish victims “and officials rarely identified child victims”.
People trafficking does not have to mean the victim is brought into Ireland. Trafficking can happen within Ireland.
In the case of children, travel does not have to be involved. Children forced into criminality, begging, labour or sexual exploitation are defined by the UN as having been trafficked.
Overall, says the report: “The Government of Ireland does not fully meet the minimum standards for the elimination of trafficking but is making significant efforts to do so.”
It designates Ireland as a ‘tier 2’ country, where designations are from tier 1 – countries that fully meet standards to eliminate trafficking, to tier 3 where they do not and are not making efforts to.
The report finds “increasing investigations, prosecutions, and convictions” are taking place, and notes two convictions for forced labour trafficking last year, and one for forced criminality.
However, there are “continued systemic deficiencies and gaps in victim referral, assistance, and identification”.
Plans for a beefed-up process to identify victims, which would empower agencies other than Gardaí – eg Tusla, HSE – to determine a person has been trafficked, have not progressed. The revised national referral mechanism (NRM) would also provide for the identification of Irish nationals as trafficking victims.
The new NRM, provided for in 2024 legislation, would allow victims to access supports without having to give a statement to Gardaí or act as a witness in any prosecution. It has yet to be fully implemented.
“As in 2024, all identified victims in 2025 were foreign nationals and the majority were female sex trafficking victims,” says the report.
“Due to limitations in the current NRM, the Government did not report identifying any Irish nationals, and observers reported proactive identification of children remained infrequent.”
[ Drug barons ‘a cancer’ on State, says judge, as two boys sentenced for drug-debt intimidation Opens in new window ]
The report comes days after the president of the Circuit Court said drug barons using children as foot soldiers were “like a cancer”.
Judge Keenan Johnson, in the case of two boys involved in a drug-debt intimidation shooting at a house in Mullingar, Co Westmeath, said “all State resources should be used to catch and lock [gang leaders who traffic children] up”.
He said these criminals “prey on children like the accused, plying them with drugs, building debts, to manipulate them to act as their foot soldiers in completion of their nefarious activities”.
The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission (Ihrec) said the TIP report showed progress in combating human trafficking had stalled.
“The Government must not step back from commitments already made but not yet implemented,” said chief commissioner Liam Herrick.
“Ireland has made progress, and we welcome it. But the test now is whether that progress is sustained and built upon in critical areas such as victim identification, specialist accommodation and child trafficking.”
He called on Government to “reaffirm its commitment to the statutory national referral mechanism and provide a clear pathway to its implementation.
“At a time when the evidence shows that victims – particularly children – are still being missed, strengthening our identification and protection systems must be an urgent priority.”
The US TIP report said provision of accommodation to trafficking victims remained inadequate, and there was a lack of trafficking-specific training for the judiciary.
Last month, an Ihrec report found the level of “victim blaming” of children caught up in crime was “horrific”, and of “a high risk” children were being misidentified as suspects and offenders rather than as child trafficking victims.
[ Children trafficked into criminality face ‘horrific’ level of victim blaming, report says Opens in new window ]

title: Deadline closes for further legal challenges to 1,000 affordable Dundrum homes
description: As Central Mental Hospital site build begins, Taoiseach plays down Land Development Agency ‘go away’ payment
content:
Construction has started on almost 1,000 homes at the former Central Mental Hospital in Dundrum , south Dublin, which has been beset by planning and legal challenges since it was first planned five years ago.
The Irish Times reported on Friday that the Land Development Agency paid more than €2 million earlier this year to buy a dormer bungalow from a local developer who had taken a High Court challenge against the State’s flagship housing scheme.
Mark Leonard, who owned 36 Friarsland Road, Goatstown initiated judicial review proceedings in February. He withdrew the case a fortnight later. It was the second legal challenge Leonard had taken to the agency’s plans for the site.
The house is one of more than 20 on Friarsland Road that back directly on to the site. The agency has not bought any of the other houses. Time has since run out for any further legal challenges to the planning permission for the scheme.
Speaking at a sod turning event at the site on Friday, Taoiseach Micheál Martin , while not addressing the specific case, said the State had incurred “excessive costs in the courts for years on a lot of projects” as well as significant delays in the ability to provide homes due to planning and court challenges.
“Government wants development at pace, and one of the key areas that we’ve been focusing on in the last 18 months has been the speed of delivery, accelerating infrastructure, not to end up in the courts on a prolonged basis,” he said.
As to whether the State was setting a dangerous precedent by paying “go-away” money to end challenges to the development of sites, Martin said the agency had been in a position where it made a “judgment call” in balancing the need to provide homes for “thousands of people” against any issued related to the purchase of a single property.
“I don’t know is that go-away money,” he said. “Every specific issue is a judgment call by those involved at the coal face in respect of any particular development.
“I think what’s important here is we have a site with 1,000 homes about to be built. For years we’ve been going on in this country about the delay, delay, delay. You know, we’ve got to get moving, get things done.”
A total of 934 homes, almost all of which will be apartments in blocks of up to eight storeys tall, will be built in the estate, which is now called Dún Brí. Most (753) will be cost-rental or affordable purchase homes aimed at low and middle-income workers, as well as 181 social homes.
The first are expected to be available in the second half of 2028, with the full estate completed in late 2029 or early 2030. The State-subsidised cost-rents and sale prices for affordable purchase homes will not be set until closer to completion dates. However, Land Development Agency chief executive John Coleman said the average rent across its 3,000 cost-rental homes completed to date was €1,450 a month.
The split between the number of cost rental and affordable purchase homes had yet to be determined, Coleman said, but most would be cost-rental.
When it published its master plan for the site in April 2021, the agency had hoped the first homes would be available in 2024 and that the scheme would be completed by 2028.
Coleman told an Oireachtas committee last year that the first court challenge delayed the plans by two years and added “at least €30 million” to the €400 million project cost. This was the equivalent of putting at least €30,000 on to the cost of each home.

title: Darkness into light: Frank McNally on a history-themed quiz in Joyce’s Nighttown
description: The pub quiz was just around the corner from World’s End, and one of the more famous corners in world literature
content:
D own around World’s End Lane on Wednesday, for the Dublin Festival of History table quiz, I was struck by a sudden gloom. It was cast not just by the onset of October but also by the Loop Line Bridge, which was over my head at the time.
“The what lane?” you ask. Oh yes. Well, “World’s End” is an old name for what is now Foley Street. It featured on John Roque’s 1756 map of the city and others of that era. The lane was then renamed Montgomery Street, and as the main drag of Dublin’s red light district, became notorious as “Monto”.
To be honest, I didn’t know the bit about World’s End until it came up in the quiz. But I’m an expert now. It turns out that “World’s End” was once widespread in these islands as a name for the edge of town. There is still one in London, among many other places.
The pub quiz was just around the corner from World’s End, in fact, in Cleary’s of Amiens Street. And nondescript as it looks, that’s one of the more famous corners in world literature, thanks to James Joyce .
His protagonists in Ulysses, Leopold Bloom and Stephen Dedalus, turn not just a new leaf there but also a new chapter. At the start of it, Dedalus is recovering from being punched to the ground by a drunken British soldier in the previous scene, set in “Nighttown”.
Now they pass the “Signal House” (Cleary’s in a former guise) and Amiens Street railway terminus en route to the Cabman’s Shelter and a restorative coffee.
Cleary’s was an apt venue for a history quiz. It’s a pub-cum-museum, displaying one of the most impressive collections of material relating to Ireland’s Home Rule and Revolutionary periods, with a strong emphasis on Michael Collins (and no De Valera anywhere as far as I could see).
But what was I saying when you interrupted me about the street name? Oh right – the Loop Line bridge, which crosses the street here and only narrowly misses the pub.
[ ‘By 1925 Catholic Ireland was coming and the madams saw the writing on the wall’: Centenary of the Monto red light district’s end Opens in new window ]
So close are they, according to Cleary’s website, that the railway company “was forced to pay the electricity bills on the proprietor’s behalf due to the lack of natural light coming through the façade”.
My quiz team could have done with a bit of added enlightenment too. Still, we fumbled our way through the Nighttown darkness and emerged with a fighting second place.
Long-time correspondent Terry Moylan takes me mildly to task for committing an Americanism earlier in the week by referring to a “square dance” ( Diary, October 6th ).
Guilty as charged. I should have known that when the characters in Joyce’s The Dead take the floor for a thing called “Lancers”, they are performing a quadrille – or a set of quadrilles, to be more exact.
Hence set dances, a latter-day, hibernicised form of the steps, which includes the Clare (aka Crusheen) Lancers, now widely performed not just in Ireland but throughout the Irish dancing empire.
Still, everyone makes mistakes, even Joyce. And Terry suspects the author of The Dead erred in having Molly Ivors – a feisty Gaelic Leaguer prone to calling opponents “West Britons” – join Gabriel Conroy for Lancers.
“At the time, the Gaelic League banned the practice of quadrilles from their social occasions, condemning them as ‘foreign dances’,” he writes. “A committed member of the League such as Miss Ivors would have refused to participate.”
While I’m correcting myself, Jim Doherty – the great piano man – tells me that The Siege Of Sidney Street (1960), which was shot in Dublin and which he first watched when 21, is not exactly a “thriller”.
[ ‘The holy men thought it was vulgar and obscene’: Irish jazz pianist Jim Doherty on 70 years in music Opens in new window ]
It’s more a historical drama, depicting real-life events involving Latvian revolutionaries in London’s east-end circa 1911.
But it was shot in Dublin in more ways than one. According to an online fan account, it set a British record for the quantity of ammunition used. And at one inner-city Dublin film location, this evoked nostalgia. Between many takes of a shoot-out, a local woman in a shawl was heard to comment: “It’s just like old times.”
Anyway, Jim’s main point was to recall a story about a scene filmed among the redbrick terraces near (he thinks) Westland Row.
It was supposed to be a scene-setter, of an empty street. But every time the director said “Action!”, a certain resident with too much time on his hands would come out his front door and ruin the shot, just for badness.
Soon, others started doing the same and take after take was sabotaged. Eventually a man named Charlie Roberts, who worked with RTÉ but was with the film crew as a fixer, hit on a solution. He went to the ringleader’s door with a job offer.
The film’s “CCO” – crowd control officer – was temporarily indisposed, he explained. They needed an emergency stand-in, for the going rate of £20. The man was duly hired and went on to perform his duties zealously, threatening violence against any neighbour who broke the curfew.

title: Global stocks rise despite US bonds ticking higher
description: Dublin market ends week on a negative note
content:
Global stocks rose on Friday despite US government bond yields ticking higher and oil prices holding above $100 ‌(€89.35) a barrel after US president Donald Trump said the US would not attack Iran before next month’s midterm elections.
Brent crude futures added about 0.2 per cent to $104.48 per barrel after surging more than 4 per cent in the previous session.
The Dublin market ended the week on a negative note, with the Euronext Dublin down almost 1.1 per cent on Friday.
Banking stocks dipped, with AIB down 1.9 per cent and Bank of Ireland falling 1.7 per cent. Permanent TSB was up 1.35 per cent, following news that long-term dissident shareholder, Scotchstone Capital, has become the latest party to say it is considering making an offer for the bank. Shares in the bank notched up a weekly loss of 1 per cent.
Insurer FBD fell 1 per cent by the close of the session.
Airline Ryanair saw its shares decline 2.6 per cent over the day, bringing it to a weekly loss of almost 3.6 per cent.
At the other end of the market, insulation specialist Kingspan was up 0.5 per cent, while food group Kerry rose 0.75 per cent to finish the week on a positive note.
London’s FTSE 100 rose on ‌Friday and capped a volatile week with modest gains as a retreat in gilt yields helped ‌sentiment, while telecom stocks fell after SpaceX’s acquisition of low-band spectrum rattled the sector.
The blue-chip FTSE 100 ​index rose 1 per cent to 10,552.05, while the midcap FTSE 250 climbed 1.1 per cent.
For ⁠the week, the FTSE 100 ​and FTSE 250 posted 0.9 per cent and 0.1 per cent ​rises, respectively, recovering from volatile trading driven by higher oil prices and renewed ‌concerns over inflation, borrowing costs and ​the outlook for interest rates
Shares in Airtel Money fell 5.6 per cent, below ⁠their offer price on Friday, in ⁠a muted ​start to trading for the African mobile money service after a heavily oversubscribed initial public offering
Telecom stocks were among the biggest decliners after SpaceX’s deal to acquire a nationwide portfolio of low-band spectrum licences, paving the way for Starlink Mobile to become a big US telecom operator
Vodafone, Airtel Africa and BT Group fell between 2.4 per cent and 6.3 per cent, ‌making them the FTSE ⁠100’s weakest performers.
The pan-European STOXX 600 closed 1 per cent higher on Friday, wiping out its weekly fall. The index closed at ​a nearly four-month low on Thursday as a surge in oil prices and bond yields pushed investors ​away from risky assets.
Deutsche Telekom fell 7.9 per cent, marking its steepest one-day fall in more than three years. Deutsche Telekom holds a 54 per cent stake in T-Mobile US, which slid 12 per cent in US afternoon trading.
Britain’s Vodafone and Spain’s Telefonica dipped over 4.5 per cent each, while France’s Orange fell 2.5 per cent.
US stock indexes advanced broadly on Friday ‌and were on pace to clock weekly gains, as investors looked forward to the earnings season next week.
Big banks, including JPMorgan Chase, will kick off the reporting season for ​the July-September period on Tuesday, as Wall Street remains optimistic about robust earnings that could keep the rally going despite the shaky geopolitical landscape and towering government bond yields.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq was set for a fourth straight weekly advance after hitting record highs earlier this ⁠week. Both the S&P 500 and the Dow were also on pace for a positive weekly finish.
By late morning the Dow ‌Jones ‌Industrial ​Average rose 323.25 points, or 0.63 per cent, to 51,554.89, the S&P 500 gained 37.28 points, or 0.48 per cent, to 7,802.64 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 145.76 points, or 0.54 per cent, to 27,339.70.
Megacap growth stocks were broadly higher, with ⁠Amazon.com climbing 2.8 per cent, Microsoft up 2.2 per cent and Tesla rising 2.1 per cent. – Additional reporting: Reuters

title: US sanctions International Criminal Court, hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize
description: Move against court came just hours after South African jurist Navi Pillay was honoured for her work on international justice and human rights
content:
US president Donald Trump’s administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court on Friday, hours after ‌one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies.
The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay, a South African human rights lawyer and jurist, in an endorsement of the importance of international law as it comes under “tremendous pressure”.
The Nobel committee said on Friday that Pillay (85), who has served on International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court , was a “lawyer and legal pioneer”.
It added the 2026 award came as “the system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack”.
The prize is likely to be seen as a shot across the bows of many autocrats and even democratically elected leaders such as US president Donald Trump and Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu .
Within hours of the announcement, the US issued sanctions against the entire International Criminal Court in an attempt to hobble its ability to function, stepping up Trump’s campaign to dismantle what he says is an “anti-American tribunal”.
Under the sanctions order published on Friday, companies have 180 days to stop trading with The Hague-based war tribunal. US secretary of state Marco Rubio said that the US was still hoping for “a diplomatic solution” that addresses US “concerns”, without specifying what that would involve.
Amazing moment. Navi Pillay has received the Nobel Peace Prize ! https://t.co/HL3r1PJzLO We are at the Nuremberg Court; I cannot think of a stronger symbol for her Nobel prize. We are all so thrilled! This is her first reactions upon hearing the news: pic.twitter.com/Crbj6XdiyQ
Last year, Pillay chaired a UN commission that determined that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, an accusation Israel has vehemently denied.
The Nobel committee said that from her early work as a lawyer, including defending Nelson Mandela , Pillay has become “one of the most respected international jurists of our time”.
“Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law,” it added.
In a video shared on social media shortly after the announcement, a visibly surprised Pillay quipped: “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”
Speaking later in Nuremberg, where she was attending a gathering of international lawyers, she described the news as “so totally unexpected that I’m still reeling with surprise”.
She said that while she had received many honours in her life, “this is the highest and best”. She dedicated the award to “survivors of international crimes”.
Pillay was born in 1941 in Durban, South Africa, to a family of Indian Tamil origin. Her father was a bus driver, while her mother was denied education under apartheid.
“I was treated like dirt just because of my skin colour,” she told South Africa’s The Citizen newspaper in 2023, recalling how even her later legal qualifications could not shield her from discrimination. But she said that she “learned not to succumb to that”.
Pillay opened her own legal practice in 1967 because no white law firm in South Africa would hire a woman of Indian descent, and went on to defend anti-apartheid activists on Robben Island.
But it was her subsequent work in Rwanda that would reshape international criminal law. As president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, Pillay co-authored a groundbreaking 1998 judgment that established that mass rape and sexual violence constitute acts of genocide.
The Nobel committee said Pillay’s work confronted “deep structural discrimination, segregation and exclusion”.
It said that in “historic” international court cases, Pillay has shown that “legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence” and contributed to strengthening the institutions of international law.
Israel reacted angrily to the choice of Pillay. Its foreign ministry called her prize “the grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice”.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell,” it added.
The award signalled the Nobel committee’s intent to underscore the importance of the rule of law in an increasingly volatile geopolitical environment.
“The institutions that uphold the international law are under tremendous pressure, sanctions and attack,” said Jorgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
“In the world we are living in, with more conflicts [than] in a long time, supporting, strengthening and also expanding the work of these institutions are key to a more peaceful world,” he added.

title: Managers react to Manchester City’s guilty verdict: ‘Uncertainty is not good for anyone’
description: Fallout continues after City found guilty of breaking financial rules over a nine-year-period
content:
Manchester United manager Michael Carrick has said retrospectively receiving a winner’s medal would not make up for being robbed of emotional moments of glory by Manchester City ’s breaches of the Premier League ’s financial rules.
Carrick was part of the squad that lost out on the Premier League title to City on the final day of the 2011-12 season when Sergio Agüero scored a last-minute winner to secure top spot on goal difference. Carrick and his United team-mates were left solemn on the touchline at Sunderland while City, found guilty of breaking financial rules during a nine-year-period between 2009 and 2018, celebrated.
“The emotion, the feeling about winning, a lot of it is in the moment,” Carrick said. “Whether you’re successful, whether you lose, whether it goes against you, That initial [feeling], the beauty of sport and the beauty of football and the beauty of trying to win trophies here, is a little bit on the journey towards it and then the finale, and does it go for you, does it go against you.
“Once that’s done, there’s no getting that back in any direction. The feeling we all crave is coming out on top – that kind of sums it up. Whatever’s done in the past tense is in the past, but in that moment is how you feel in that moment. Certainly as a participant, as a performer, and I’m sure the supporters feel the same, that’s why we love it so much because of the emotion in the moment.”
Carrick was also part of United’s staff under Ole Gunnar Solskjær when they finished second, 22 points behind City, in 2021. City continue to plead their innocence and have appealed against the verdict. If they fail to overturn the independent commission’s ruling, they will probably face a serious punishment.
“It’s affected me personally in different ways,” said Carrick. “But as the case is ongoing now I don’t know where that stands and how it’s going to end up, so we’ll just have to wait and see. What I will say, the sooner it gets sorted I think for everyone’s benefit is essential.”
Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola has called for the Manchester City case to be dealt with swiftly. “I think uncertainty is not good for anyone involved, but there is the process ongoing and we have to be patient like everyone else and see what happens at the end,” he said.
“No one knows what’s going to happen. We have to focus on Liverpool and being the best club we can be, the best team we can be. That’s my challenge. My opinion is not valid because I haven’t spent that time and I haven’t read as much as they’ve [the commission] done.
“The challenge of the game is so high that I don’t think players think too much outside of this. They are thinking: ‘I have to mark this player’ or ‘I have to go and deal with this one’ or ‘I have be at this level because the level of the game is so high’. They will be focused on those things.
“Obviously they will have their own opinions, but I think they will be fully focused on what happens on the pitch.”
Former Manchester City captain Vincent Kompany insists he is still “really proud” of his success with the club after it was found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules. The Bayern Munich manager won four Premier League titles and multiple domestic cups during his spell at City from 2008 to 2019.
An independent commission last week ruled that City broke more than 100 Premier League financial regulations, but the club has appealed.
The former Belgium international was a key figure in City’s dominant era under their Abu Dhabi-based owners and is honoured with a statue outside the Etihad Stadium.
“I played 11 years for the club. I’ve loved all of the years I played for the club and everything we achieved and (did) on the pitch – that’s something I’m really proud of,” Kompany told reporters on Friday.
Kompany signed for City from Hamburg just weeks before Sheikh Mansour completed a takeover that turned the club from also-rans to serial winners. Asked about the off-pitch issues at his former club, he said: “Everything else, as a player you’re not a part of that and right now as a coach of Bayern Munich I’m not too much occupied with that topic. I’m preparing the game next week and preparing the game we have tomorrow and everything I have as a coach.”
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta has insisted the Premier League “100%” remains the best in the world despite the ongoing uncertainty surrounding Manchester City’s guilty verdict.
Arteta, who was an assistant to Pep Guardiola at City for more than three years before taking over at the Emirates in December 2019, was unsurprisingly bombarded with questions about his former club on Friday before Saturday’s lunchtime fixture against Leeds and responded “100 per cent” when asked whether he thought the Premier League remains the best.
“It’s very important that we respect the process,” he said. “I think the timelines and it’s still an ongoing process that is not resolved because it’s been appealed. And my position, I think the club’s position, is not to make any further comments.”
Asked whether he thought the Premier League’s reputation has been damaged, Arteta added: “There is a process there again that is not resolved. It’s ongoing and we can have a much clearer opinion when it’s been resolved. I’m not prepared to make any comments.”
Arteta confirmed Christos Tzolis is out for a few weeks with a hamstring issue but said he will make a decision on whether Kai Havertz and Ezri Konsa will feature gainst Leeds.
Tottenham manager Roberto De Zerbi insists he has no time to dwell on Manchester City’s guilty verdict with Tottenham bottom of the table. De Zerbi was a Napoli player when they faced Juventus in the 2006-07 season after Juve were found guilty of match-fixing and relegated to Serie B.
Juventus had an initial 30-point deduction reduced to nine and still won promotion straight back to Serie A. Asked what the experience was like, De Zerbi replied: “I was crazy as a player, I don’t remember my thoughts, just think on the ball, just think on our job.
“When you are a player, you don’t think too much. When you are a coach, the same because the focus is on your players, especially now because we are on the bottom of the table. I have no time to think of the other problems than my team, my club.”
De Zerbi said the scandal did not change Italian football, adding: “There are the people who have to decide to take the decision, with responsibility, with courage, and honesty, always. It’s not my job. My job is to be a coach. But I love respecting the rules, like all people in our club.” – Guardian

title: English language school owner gave materially misleading statements to court
description: Mostly South American non-EEA students paid school fees in advance pending approval of visas
content:
A High Court judge said the owner of an English language school, which announced its closure last month, gave sworn statements which proved “materially and inexcusably misleading”.
Judge Cian Ferriter said questions had been raised over the statements of Limerick Language Centre (LLC) sole shareholder and director Sharif Ahmed Sarker after the court was told on behalf of a Pakistani agency that €50,000 paid for 29 prospective overseas language students had not been repaid despite claims that all refunds had been made.
There was also a complaint from that agency about an alleged practice by the LLC of deducting “accommodation fees” from refunds even where the relevant students never travelled to Ireland and never occupied any accommodation, the judge said.
The judge made his comments in a ruling in which he refused a stay on a decision of the Department of Justice to remove LLC and another school from an eligibility scheme whereby people from the non-European Economic Area (EEA) could apply for student visas to study English in Ireland.
The scheme was called the Interim List of Eligible Programmes (ILEP) for student immigration permissions for English language programmes.
Non-EEA students, who the court heard were mostly South Americans, paid the school fees in advance pending approval of their visas, and if they did not get the visas, the money was to be refunded. Significant numbers of students paid through agents.
On July 24th last, following complaints about refund difficulties and an investigation by the Department of Justice, LLC and Erin College, which operates English teaching outlets in Dublin and Cork, were dropped from the ILEP scheme.
The schools brought separate High Court proceedings challenging those decisions against the Ministers of Justice and of Further and Higher Education, who opposed the challenge.
In his judgment, given last month and published this week, dealing with both challenges, Ferriter refused a stay on the decisions.
He said it seemed to him, from the evidence, that both schools had displayed “a fundamental disregard” for the core requirement of the ILEP that fees paid by all student applicants which ended up with colleges were required to be ring-fenced pending visa decisions.
Their approach to agency-sourced student application fees “created obvious risks for the security of such fees in the event the businesses ran into difficulties”, the judge said.
This may explain why both schools struggled significantly to meet refund applications for visa-refused students within the stipulated 20-day periods and where significant numbers of their students were sourced via agents, he said.
In relation to claims of reputational damage to the schools if a stay on the decisions was not granted, the judge said he could not overlook the reality that both had inflicted such damage on themselves by being in admitted breach of the requirements of the ILEP.
The evidence before the court, including that from the Pakistani agency about deductions by LLC for accommodation for students who never came here, demonstrated that LLC’s “current reputation in this sector is far from unblemished, and it only has itself to blame for that state of affairs”, he said.
The court would not grant the relief being sought by LLC on the basis of averments (from Sarker) “that have proved materially and inexcusably misleading”, he said.

title: Fianna Fáil Minister of State Robert Troy ordered to pay €500 in damages after tenant left without working oven
description: Troy’s Co Westmeath tenant Priscilla Ryan alleges she was hospitalised after receiving notice of termination over rent arrears
content:
Minister of State Robert Troy has been ordered to pay €500 in damages to a tenant of his after a Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) tribunal heard she was without a functioning oven for at least three months.
The Fianna Fáil TD for Longford-Westmeath, who previously resigned as a minister of State in 2022 after he failed to fully declare the extent of his property holdings in the Dáil register of interests, did not attend the tribunal hearing in July.
His tenant, Priscilla Ryan, who had been renting an apartment from Troy on Mary Street in Mullingar, Co Westmeath, since 2021, claimed she had been without a functioning oven for two years.
She also alleged a range of other issues with the apartment, including that there was no fire extinguisher or fire exit, and that the kitchen floor covering was “stuck down with duct tape”.
However, the tribunal accepted Troy’s agents had not been made aware of some issues and that works were carried out in a “timely manner” on others, with the exception of the oven.
Troy lists three “studio apartments” as being rented out at the property at Mary Street in his most recent register of interests, covering last year, published by the Oireachtas.
Ryan told the tribunal the oven was ultimately replaced a month before the hearing, according to a tribunal report published on Friday.
She claimed she had been told not to use the cooker, which she described as having “melted”, and that she had bought a microwave in its place.
Ryan, whose rent was set at €730 per month, also told the tribunal she received a notice of termination in July 2025, which was due to rent arrears, and claimed she was “hospitalised due to stress”.
Adam Dunne of Egan Auctioneers, a representative of the Minister, said the rent arrears matter had been resolved.
He told the tribunal the apartment had been fully renovated in 2020, and his firm attempted to resolve any issues as they arose, though delays were sometimes caused by difficulty in sourcing parts.
Dunne denied Ryan was left without a cooker for two years, but accepted it may have been three or four months at a “maximum”.
He said no issues had ever been raised relating to some problems alleged by Ryan, including the kitchen floor covering, which he said was laminate, installed in 2020.
Asked by the tribunal whether he was denying there had been a breach of landlord obligations, Dunne said the number of issues raised by Ryan “greatly exceeded” the norm and that “far more” problems were raised by her than tenants in other apartments in the building.
He said Egan Auctioneers was a professional company and that the majority of issues had been rectified.
Dunne said they were “happy to apologise” if Ryan deemed that appropriate, adding that his firm would do “whatever was needed, within reason, on an ongoing basis”.
The tribunal said it was satisfied that Troy – “through his managing agents” – was aware the apartment lacked a functioning oven for at least three months.
Noting a “clear breach” of regulations, it ordered him to pay €500 in damages within 28 days.
Ryan had also claimed she suffered a stroke and had to quit her job as a result of stress associated with the sale of the apartment building after photos of her family and “personal information” appeared in a sale listing on Daft.ie.
She said this was a breach of her privacy and that it caused “tensions”, resulting in her being unable to see her grandchildren and losing contact with her family.
The tribunal said these issues related to privacy and data protection, and it had no jurisdiction to make findings on such complaints.
In a statement to The Irish Times, Troy said he accepted and respected the RTB’s determination and confirmed he had paid €500 in damages.
“I firmly believe that tenants should be able to expect a high standard of service, with any concerns or maintenance issues responded to and dealt with appropriately,” he said.
“That is the reason I employed a letting agent to manage the property, to ensure that any issues would be dealt with appropriately. That is the standard I expect to be upheld in the management of a property.”
Troy said any maintenance requests were approved and facilitated through Egan Auctioneers, which the Minister said was “responsible for its [the property’s] day-to-day management, maintenance and engagement with the tenant”.
He said a repair technician was sent to inspect the cooker within days of the issue being reported, and when repair proved unsuccessful, arrangements were made for a replacement.
The replacement oven was installed on June 29th, 2026, before the tribunal hearing.
Troy said the RTB plays a “vital role in our housing system” and that its work is “essential to protecting the rights of all parties and maintaining confidence in the rental sector”.
Following Troy’s resignation as minister for state in 2022, an investigation by the Standards in Public Office Commission (Sipo) found the Longford-Westmeath TD had contravened part of the Ethics Act by his failure to declare fully some properties he owned and other interests, but concluded that he “acted in good faith”.

title: ‘One fall without a helmet changed my life forever’: Cyclist fronts new road safety campaign
description: Niall Connor was left with a permanent brain injury after coming off his bike aged 14
content:
A fall from his bike aged 14 has changed the trajectory of Niall Connor’s life, leaving him with a permanent brain injury. Now, the Dundalk man is the face of a new road safety campaign encouraging cyclists to wear a helmet.
Connor (45) was cycling home, lost control on a downhill stretch and collided with a wall, he told The Irish Times . He was not wearing a helmet that day, falling into a 10-day coma and suffering a significant brain injury.
“I had my whole life in front of me up until that day,” he said. “One fall from a bike without a helmet changed my life forever.”
“I have lived with this brain injury for 30 years. If I could turn back time, I’d wear a helmet.”
The fall which “changed everything” for Niall Connor has impeded his speech and left him with lifelong physical impairments in his arms and along his left side.
“Big time,” he said, when asked if cyclists and young people lack an understanding of the consequences they face from failing to wear a helmet.
“We can’t stop kids being fearless, but we can protect them. We only get one life, protect it.”
He said it is crucial that people wear their helmets: “Everybody has only one life. Be safe on the road, wear a helmet if you’re cycling, including you.”
Under Irish law, although wearing one is strongly recommended, adult cyclists are not legally required to wear a helmet. Connor believes that should be changed.
“It should be a law now that you must wear a helmet, especially on e-scooters and e-bikes,” he said.
In recent years, Connor has become a campaigner for safer cycling, bringing his advocacy to Leinster House and meeting the Minister of State for Road Safety, Seán Canney .
[ Former Kerry footballer says ‘10 seconds of recklessness’ by driver changed his life forever Opens in new window ]
Canney said the story is a “powerful reminder that the decisions we make on the road can have lifelong consequences” and that he was “very moved by [Connor’s] story and his willingness to take part in this very important campaign”.
Nuala Carey, RSA director for external affairs, said Connor’s experience is a “powerful reminder that a split-second moment can change a life forever, even when the moment that causes it lasts only seconds.”
She said personal stories “can reach people in a way statistics never will”.
In 2026 to date, 12 of the 143 people who died on Irish roads were cyclists with a further four being e-scooter or e-bike riders.
With three months left in the year, this figure is ahead of the five-year average from 2020. During that period, an average of 9 cyclists were killed and an average of 256 cyclists were seriously injured each year.
Men made up 87 per cent of deaths during those five years, and 78 per cent of those seriously injured.
Connor’s experience is also included in a report by Rehab Group, an Irish voluntary organisation supporting disabled people, which has identified serious issues with the accessibility and affordability of public transport.
While fleets have been made affordable, the infrastructure is lagging behind, the report found, with many stops in regional areas not enabling wheelchairs to board buses.
The impact, Rehab Group said, is that people with disabilities are prevented from working, accessing education and taking part in community life because of the inaccessibility and unreliability of the transport network.
[ Under-18s banned from using e-scooters Opens in new window ]

title: Manchester United’s early wobble makes Tottenham visit a must-win for Carrick
description: After a scratchy start in the league, injuries and an underwhelming Rashford, Spurs’ visit to Old Trafford is already crucial for the hosts
content:
The noise in the Premier League was focused elsewhere for the last two weeks of the international break, allowing a glorious silence to drift across Manchester United . Without Manchester City’s woes, Michael Carrick may have faced a more difficult time, with plenty to review in regards to the first five games of the season.
United sit solemnly in 12th with only one league win, and misery needs company. The hosts will find just that at Old Trafford on Saturday evening. Tottenham, bottom of the Premier League, visit, with both sides hoping to kickstart their season. Spurs have secured a measly two points after a summer where £300m was spent on Roberto De Zerbi’s rebuild but the architect’s drawings are already at risk of being set alight. For Carrick and United, beating the worst team in the league is close to a necessity as they enter a very difficult run of fixtures.
October is theoretically and practically problematic for United, who have six fixtures this month, with away games against Leeds, Atlético Madrid, Como and Chelsea, who play a variety of styles that need preparing for, making a home game against Spurs a must-win. On paper, the second easiest game of the month is Bournemouth at home.
Carrick has plenty of credit in the bank from his work in the second half of last season, and will be afforded as much time as possible to get things right because no one is eager for another mid-season change of manager. United need to be in a better position by the end of October than they started it, which will require significant improvement on the pitch.
For Carrick there are plenty of small margins he can point to. The opening-day defeat at Hull was a grisly performance and worthy of criticism; Ipswich were eventually dispatched, while the derby was a tight and controversial loss, coming between two draws.
The truth of the matter is United know they need to be better in both boxes. United have conceded fewer opposition touches in their box than any other team in the league but, on the other hand, they are the only side yet to keep a clean sheet. They can also boast the most touches in opposition boxes but are largely incapable of killing matches off.
United, like Tottenham, are very good at dominating possession, averaging 60% per match, but cannot translate that to goals and points. Even in the victory against Ipswich, United were unable to put a full 90 minutes of composure together, relying on Bruno Fernandes to drag them through against a promoted side. The forwards are yet to synchronise, with Matheus Cunha, the man tasked with leading the line, having only one goal to his name, and even that took a heavy deflection.
No one has more than one assist so far, while only Fernandes and Bryan Mbeumo have scored twice or more, the Portuguese getting a hat-trick against Ipswich. Marcus Rashford has shown glimpses of promise on the left but has no goal involvements, giving the impression of a man who requires a confidence boost after returning to the club where he was not wanted for 18 months.
Nor is there the option of Benjamin Sesko playing as a more traditional central striker given he is sidelined with injury, while Joshua Zirkzee cannot even class himself as a plan B. But United are prolific compared with Tottenham, whose only league goals came in a 3-2 defeat by Aston Villa just before the international break.
Losing to 10-man Manchester City was the most worrying of United’s defeats, showing how far off they look against a Champions League side. Phil Foden’s red card gave United plenty of space but they were unable to take advantage, instead plodding around, short of ideas, barely threatening. United are expert at dominating possession but not games, traits that create hope and frustration in equal measure.
The summer signings of a goalkeeper who cost nothing and three central midfielders is coming under as much scrutiny as Carrick’s tactics. At least Carlos Baleba is poised to finally make his debut after joining from Brighton for £65m in August and Carrick desperately needs him to provide the energy lacking in central areas thus far. Having recovered from an ankle injury, the Cameroonian has what it takes to snuff out the danger that has been leading to the concession of goals.
Sesko is not the sole injury concern; Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford were ruled out of playing for England, while Patrick Dorgu and Noussair Mazraoui’s international breaks ended prematurely. Meanwhile, Matthijs de Ligt has not played competitively for 10 months and Amad Diallo is yet to feature this season.
The run of 12 wins in 17 games after Carrick took interim charge in January showed plenty of individual and collective improvements, but whether certain players can crash through their current ceiling requires clear evidence sooner rather than later. With finances tight, it is imperative that United improve from within. More academy players have spent time with the squad in recent weeks, with Noah Ajayi impressing the coaches Steve Holland and Jonathan Woodgate. It is thought a number of youngsters could make first-team debuts before the season concludes, which would be a display of Carrick’s long-term vision. Results, however, will decide if he gets a chance to implement it in the first place.
United are desperate for a catalyst and if it does not come against Tottenham at the weekend, Carrick will become fearful of Halloween. — Guardian

title: Recall notice issued over three Marks & Spencer ready-to-eat meal products
description: FSAI notice issued on behalf of food firm Greencore amid concerns over possible presence of Salmonella in pistachios
content:
Three ready-to-eat Marks & Spencer products have been recalled amid concerns about the possible presence of Salmonella in pistachios.
A recall notice issued by the Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI) on behalf of convenience food company Greencore requested retailers to remove the affected products from sale and display.
According to the notice, the 200g container of M&S Food Super Nutty Wholefood with a Soy & Ginger Dressing has been recalled. The notice applies to all use-by dates up to and including November 10th.
The M&S Food Nutrient Dense Nutty Super Wholefood has also been recalled, applying to all dates up to and including November 11th.
The final recall applies to the M&S Collection Pistachio and Parmigiano Reggiano Cheese Pesto, affecting all expiration dates up to and including November 13th.
The FSAI said consumers are advised not to eat the implicated batches of the recalled products.
People infected with Salmonella typically develop symptoms between 12 and 36 hours after infection, but this can range to between six and 72 hours.
The most common symptom is diarrhoea, which can sometimes be bloody. Other symptoms may include fever, headache and abdominal cramps. The illness usually lasts four to seven days.
Diarrhoea can occasionally be severe enough to require hospital admission. The elderly, infants, and those with impaired immune systems are more likely to have a severe illness.

title: Trump administration condemned for plans to livestream execution
description: ‘People need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,’ says Hegseth
content:
The Trump administration has been condemned for planning to livestream a firing squad execution of a gunman who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in Texas in 2009.
The Pentagon announced earlier this week it would execute former US Army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan in the first military execution in more than 60 years.
The UN human rights office said livestreaming the execution would be “tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture”.
US defence secretary Pete Hegseth said the firing squad will carry out the sentence at Fort Hood, Texas, at 1pm on Thursday, December 3rd. This would be the first US military execution in more than 60 years.
“It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said.
Jack Reed, the Senate armed services committee ranking member, condemned the Pentagon’s decision to broadcast the shooting.
Reed, a Democrat, called the decision “a barbaric spectacle”, adding: “This is yet another stunt by secretary Hegseth to distract from his tenure’s repeated failings which have only weakened our national security and standing in the world.”
[ The Irish Times view on US executions: a barbaric practice Opens in new window ]
Reed called on US president Donald Trump to “reconsider this abhorrent move” and said that a livestream would be a “gift to anti-American terrorist recruiters”.
At the White House on Friday, Trump said he “absolutely” ​approved ⁠of the ‌execution ‌of Hasan ​but ​said ‌he had ​not ⁠made ⁠a ​determination on showing the death ‌via ⁠livestream.
Trump said that Hasan deserves the death penalty ​by firing squad, calling him “a maniac”, but has not said whether he thinks the event should be shown on a livestream.
A senior White House official familiar with the matter said that Trump “doesn’t oppose the idea” of a livestream of the execution, but that his position is not yet final and he could change his ⁠mind.
US vice-president JD Vance said on Friday he does not know whether the Pentagon will proceed ‌with a livestream of the execution.
“I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” Vance told reporters in Cincinnati, referring to the livestream. He added that if a livestream does go ahead, “I’m not going to be watching it”.
Hasan opened fire at a medical processing centre on the Texas base on November 5th, 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. A military jury sentenced him to death in 2013, and he has been held at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas ever since. He exhausted his appeals last year, which cleared the way for Trump to approve the sentence this week on a recommendation from Hegseth.
Investigators had found that Hasan had exchanged 18 emails with Anwar al-Awlaki, a radical cleric who was subsequently killed in a US drone strike, in the months before the attack. At his court martial, Hasan said he had acted to stop American soldiers from deploying to Afghanistan to kill fellow Muslims, before his own impending deployment.
A review led by William Webster, a former FBI director, concluded that the bureau should have investigated his correspondence more thoroughly.
In his interview, Hegseth said Barack Obama had called the attack “workplace violence”. The Pentagon initially treated the shooting as a workplace-violence incident rather than a terrorist attack, a classification that affected the victims’ eligibility for Purple Hearts and other combat-related benefits.
But there is no record of Obama himself using the phrase. At a memorial days after the attack, he instead described the victims as Americans who had been unable to escape “the horror of war”, while calling the shooting a tragedy and saying the killer would face justice.
The last known case of a military firing squad in the US was in November 1945, but the Trump administration has sought to bring it back in Trump’s second term to expedite capital punishment cases. Five US states allow for firing squads: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah.
Amnesty International’s most recent annual review lists Afghanistan, China, North Korea, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Taiwan, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen among the countries that still use firing squads.
Asked whether Hasan had made a final request or reached out to Trump, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3rd.”
– Guardian; additional reporting: Reuters

title: EU and China strike deal to curb car exports and avert trade war
description: Brussels claims Beijing will more than halve hybrid vehicle exports as bloc secures concessions on rare earths and market access
content:
China and the European Union have reached a deal on hybrid cars that could mean Chinese exports to Europe cut by more than half, according to EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič .
The agreement came after two days of talks in Beijing between the commissioner and Chinese commerce minister Wang Wentao aimed at averting a trade war.
“We have reached a shared understanding to moderate China’s exports of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the EU,” Šefčovič told reporters in Beijing after the talks ended on Friday.
“This opens the prospect of cutting China’s exports by more than a half.”
In the days leading up to the talks, EU leaders threatened to introduce measures that could shut Chinese goods out of the single market overnight if Beijing did not agree to take action to address the trade imbalance.
[ ‘We’re at a tipping point’: EU prepares its toughest weapon yet against China Opens in new window ]
The EU imports €1 billion more in Chinese goods every day than China’s imports of European goods, and some sectors, including the car industry, are especially vulnerable to the surge in imports.
Šefčovič said that China had agreed to lower tariffs on a number of European products ranging from car parts to olive oil and footwear, worth almost €4 billion.
He said the duty saved was the equivalent of a quarter of the savings secured under some of the EU’s most ambitious trade agreements with countries such as Japan and Australia.
China agreed to ease the export of rare earths and permanent magnets that are essential to advanced manufacturing and which Beijing has used as leverage in its trade negotiations with a number of partners, including the United States.
Šefčovič said the outcome of his negotiations in Beijing was a first step towards rebalancing the trade relationship, but it was far from the end.
“It’s a crucial first step, but only a first step in the process of rebalancing. As [European Commission] president [Ursula] von der Leyen has said, dialogue needs results. And where the dialogue cannot deliver, the EU will use its tools to ensure a rebalancing. Naturally, the president will now assess the outcomes and discuss next steps with the leaders at the upcoming European Council in Brussels. That is where the final decision lies,” he said.
Before Šefčovič spoke to reporters, China’s commerce ministry released a joint statement from the two sides, describing the talks as “pragmatic and productive”.
They agreed to meet next March again and to maintain close communication in the meantime, including in a video call in January.
“Both sides reaffirmed their commitment, as key trading partners, to properly managing their differences within the framework of World Trade Organisation (WTO) rules, and to continuing to stabilise bilateral economic and trade relations while making them more balanced,” noted a statement.
Before the formal talks began on Thursday, Šefčovič met representatives of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China, who briefed him on the reality faced by European businesses operating in China. The chamber’s president, Jens Eskelund, said Chinese market access and regulatory barriers handicapped European companies not only in the Chinese market but throughout the world.
“What happens in China does not just stay in China. The lack of a level playing field, present in many industries in the country, has facilitated Chinese firms to build the scale and technological capabilities required to offer lower prices in third markets that European suppliers competing on market terms cannot match. The result is global competition on unequal terms,” he said.
[ Europe wants to get tough on China. The risks could be enormous Opens in new window ]

title: Men who planned Galway mosque attack claim they have distanced from radicalising groups
description: Garrett Pollock (36) and Darren Gorman (34) made pleas in mitigation after pleading guilty
content:
Two men who planned to attack a Galway mosque using improvised explosive devices (IEDs) have claimed they were radicalised by anti-immigrant groups but have since distanced themselves from those influences.
The three-judge Special Criminal Court heard pleas in mitigation on Friday for two of the three would-be mosque bombers, Garrett Pollock (36) and Darren Gorman (34). Karolis Peckauskas (39) offered an apology earlier this week, saying he had also been radicalised by online groups.
Peckauskas, with an address at Newfoundwell Road, Drogheda, Co Louth, previously pleaded guilty to a charge of attempting to engage in a terrorist activity or a terrorist-linked activity.
Between November 4th and 5th, 2025, the defendants attempted to engage in terrorist activity or terrorist-linked activity by attempting to set fire to the Maryam Mosque at Old Cottages, Monivea Road, Galway, an offence that was aggravated by hatred.
Gorman, of O’Moore Place, Portlaoise, Co Laois, and Pollock, of Kilhorne Greene, Annalong, Co Down, both pleaded guilty to the same offence.
The three-judge court previously heard that the plot was foiled when gardaí carrying out a routine drug stop became suspicious and searched the car that Pollack and Peckauskas were travelling in. In the boot, gardaí discovered bomb-making equipment along with a manifesto for a group calling itself the Irish Defence Army, complete with crests and logos.
They also discovered a statement written in the past tense claiming responsibility for bombing the Galway mosque.
Solicitor Kevin White, for Pollack, said his client is deeply ashamed of his behaviour, apologises “unreservedly” to everyone impacted and accepts that what he did was wrong, criminal and offensive.
White said he had sought a report from a psychiatrist to try to understand why Pollack, who has no history of violence or political activism, would find himself before a court for this offence. The report states that Pollack worked as a gym instructor, but in 2024 he started abusing alcohol and cocaine and lost his job following a relationship breakdown.
[ Would-be Galway mosque bombers made video warning they would carry out further attacks, court hears Opens in new window ]
He began spending hours online consuming radical content, including material about immigrants committing sexual assaults or posing a threat to the Irish community. Much of the content, White said, appeared to be AI-generated and was emotive and ill-informed.
Pollack began communicating with people associated with the Irish Citizens Army, a radical anti-immigrant group. He was invited into smaller, more radicalised groups where he discovered a sense of belonging.
