The doctor further stated that Pollack was not committed due to a robust ideological principle, but acted in the context of poor mental health, substance abuse and low self-esteem.
Solicitor Marc Thompson, for Gorman, said a psychologist had found his client to be vulnerable and diagnosed him with “extreme submissiveness”. Gorman has no history of violence, aggression or hatred and “certainly no history of terrorism,” Thompson said.
Thompson reminded the court that Gorman was not in the car with Peckauskas and Pollack and was only implicated by further investigations showing his participation in the Shadows of Eire chat group where the members discussed their plans. He also drove a vehicle associated with the group’s activities, sourced an accelerant that was to be used in the explosives, purchased clothing for the group and said he would contribute money.
Thompson said Gorman is a drug addict with mental health difficulties but he is trying to deal with his issues and has been drug-free throughout his period on bail in advance of the sentencing hearing. Thompson said Gorman has not made contact with any radical influences and asked the court to structure his sentence “to allow light at the end of the tunnel”.
Judge Caroline Biggs, sitting with Judge Sarah Berkeley and Judge Kevin Staunton, adjourned sentencing until October 13th. The court remanded all three men in custody to that date.

title: Woman (49) who sublet room as ‘weed’ store to help pay her rent is jailed for four years
description: Oana Onofrei told gardaí she found it hard to pay rent on her Lucan house and was offered €1,000 a month for the room
content:
A 49-year-old woman with no criminal record has been jailed for four years for storing more than €1.5 million worth of cannabis in her Dublin home.
Oana Onofrei, who will turn 50 next week, was finding it hard to pay the rent on her Lucan house when she agreed to sublet a room to men “for weed”.
Onofrei, with an address at St Edmunds Grove in Lucan, who was before Dublin Circuit Criminal Court on Friday, pleaded guilty to possession of the drugs for sale or supply at her home there on November 13th, 2025.
The court heard gardaí searched her home after receiving information and observing a delivery there. A total of €1,556,000 worth of cannabis was found.
Onofrei told detectives she had lost a tenant the previous Christmas and she had struggled to pay her rent. She then met a number of men in a local park who offered her €1,000 a month for the room.
She said she “knew it was for weed” and that they just needed a room to store and sort the drugs, and she provided them with a key.
As well as getting €1,000 a month for the room, sometimes the men would leave money on bags and text her, asking her to deliver them. She had been asked to download the Signal App, and this was used to give her instructions.
She said the first deliveries were small, and referred to one that was larger. There was €50 left on top of that bag.
The defendant, who had no previous convictions, said she was very sorry about it and would rather kill herself than get involved again. She said it was to help her family to live.
Diana Stuart, defending counsel, noted her client was not on the Garda radar before this and did not fit the profile of the person they expected to meet that day. She had always worked full-time and came from a good family, who had now effectively disowned her.
Counsel said her client had been working at Tesco Home Deliveries and renting a home in Lucan, a very affluent part of Dublin, but that her rent was extremely high.
She had been finding life very difficult and ended up smoking cannabis, which was when she agreed to keep “this enormous amount of cannabis in the house”. She had no understanding of how grave her offence was, she added.
“She now realises she can’t afford to live in this property,” she said.
Judge Martin Nolan accepted that she had made little or no profit, having heard that she never had the money to take up her €5,000 bail. However, he said she was a reasonably vital cog in the gang’s operations.
“I’ve come to the view that she’s unlikely to reoffend,” he said.
Nolan said the headline sentence for this offence would ordinarily be eight years but, given mitigation, he would cut it in two.
He sentenced her to four years in prison, and backdated it to November when she went into custody.

title: Men benefit more from budget tax reforms, National Women’s Council says
description: Feminist analysis criticises lack of investment in hormone replacement therapy and fertility treatment
content:
A “huge” number of parents will see no reduction in their childcare costs after the budget , a woman-centred analysis of Tuesday’s announcements finds.
The National Women’s Council of Ireland , in its feminist analysis of Budget 2027 published on Friday, said tax reforms announced on Tuesday would benefit far more men than women, while the allocation for domestic violence services was “disappointing”.
“In summary: is this a worker’s budget? It’s not for women workers,” the council said.
It welcomed the extension in eligibility for free contraception to women aged up to 36, but criticised the lack of further investment in hormone replacement therapy and in publicly funded fertility treatment.
Deficits in the affordability and availability of childcare “remain the single biggest barrier to women’s equal participation in Irish society”, the analysis found. “And many early years educators continue to be underpaid and undervalued.”
The budget contained a commitment that childcare fees would be capped at €550 a month for children in care for 45 hours a week, up to senior infants level, and in providers under the Department of Children ’s core funding scheme.
“Children in early years education beyond these hours (such as those in childcare from approx 8am-6pm) avail of more than this 45-hour week, and thus, may still pay far above €550,” the analysis said.
The bulk of savings will be to parents of babies, toddlers and preschool age.
“Junior and senior infants typically have their own after-school care, which is significantly less than 45 hours. Access, capacity, regional availability gaps, as well as staff recruitment and retention issues, remain unaddressed by Budget 2027.”
[ Childcare providers face squeeze with fees due to drop further despite funding increase Opens in new window ]
The council reiterated its call for “a detailed plan of action for transitioning to a public system of childcare, including timelines, funding allocations, planning reforms, and governance structures”.
Social protection increases of €10 a week “are not in keeping with inflation rates ... people in Ireland living on lower incomes, who are reliant on social transfers to maintain income adequacy, will see little impact from these reforms”.
Lone parents, the vast majority of whom are mothers, “are also the demographic at the most acute risk of poverty and deprivation in Ireland”.
Echoing others in calling for welfare rates to be benchmarked against inflation, the council said: “Without a commitment to benchmarking and indexation, social protection payments will continue to fall behind, leaving women, including disabled women, without an adequate and secure income.”
Women, particularly those on low incomes, are especially dependent on access to quality public services – including childcare, transport, healthcare and housing.
More than half of homeless families are headed by lone parents.
“All housing policy and investment should be gender-sensitive, to ensure that they are tackling gender and social inequalities rather than exacerbating or maintaining them,” the council said.

title: Government nominates Síofra O’Leary for appointment as judge of European Court of Justice
description: O’Leary was previously first female president of European Court of Human Rights
content:
The Government has nominated Síofra O’Leary for appointment as a judge of the Court of Justice of the European Union .
Dublin-born O’Leary (58) previously served as president of the European Court of Human Rights from November 2022 to July 2024. She was the first female president of that court .
Before joining the ECHR in 2015, O’Leary worked for almost two decades at the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) in both judicial and administrative capacities.
Judges of the CJEU are appointed by common accord of the governments of EU member states for a six-year term.
Each member state adopts their own domestic process for the nomination of judges and the Irish nomination was made in accordance with the process set out in the Judicial Appointments Commission Act 2024.
O’Leary, whose nomination was recommended to Government by the Minister for Justice, Jim O’Callaghan , will now be presented to a panel established under the EU treaty. The panel gives an opinion on a candidate’s suitability to perform the duties of judge of the CJEU before representatives of the member states deciding on the appointment.
O’Leary is expected to take up her new role when the second term of office of Judge Eugene Regan, Ireland’s current appointee to the CJEU, ends in October 2027.
[ Are the unions right? Did the Government’s budget abandon workers? If they lost, who won? Opens in new window ]

title: Nobody wants to see teachers go on strike but preparations are being made, Minister says
description: Almost all schools likely to close next Wednesday and again a week later as public service dispute escalates
content:
Nobody wants to see teachers going out on strike next week, Minister for Education Hildegarde Naughton has said, but preparations are being made in the event schools close as scheduled on Wednesday.
Almost all schools across the country are likely to close on Wednesday October 14th and again on Wednesday October 21st, as teaching unions join the escalation of a public service-wide dispute over pay.
An additional €1.2 billion was included in the budget on Tuesday for public service pay increases, but unions say this is not enough to move the dial and displays a lack of seriousness on the Government’s behalf to go into negotiations.
The school closures will have a significant impact on both parents and students over the coming weeks, as well as school management.
There is no guarantee that closures will end after this, or that negotiations will begin.
“We wrote to schools just yesterday about preparing and communicating with parents in the event of strike action. We’re also in contact with school transport services as well,” Naughton said on Friday.
“But I have to say, none of us want to be in a position where people are going on strike and our teachers are striking. We really need people to sit around the table to resolve this.”
Asked whether the record funding her department received in the budget this week was enough to ensure every child had access to an appropriate school place next year and that school building projects could be progressed, the Minister said they were now able to forward plan better.
“But there will be children who will come forward throughout the year, and even after 2027, who will need additional supports. We have factored that in, but it is a demand-led department,” Naughton said.
In relation to school building projects, where many schools in various states of disrepair across the country remain stuck on waiting lists for upgrade works, the Minister said they are “working through the next list of schools to go to tender and construction”.
“Those who are on the list [to go to construction] are happy, but there’s also those who want to get on, and I’m absolutely acutely aware of that. So we are moving at pace through that,” Naughton said.
The Minister was speaking at the final day of the National Association of Principals and Deputy Principals (NAPD) annual conference in Galway city.
The conference heard of the increasing administrative burden being placed on school principals and their deputies in the handling of State interventions such as the free schoolbooks scheme.
“School leaders are smothered by an avalanche of paperwork,” NAPD president Brian Doran told delegates. He said the organisation was seeking an administrative officer in every school to alleviate this.
Responding to those concerns, Naughton said the department is currently running a pilot programme where a select number of schools are receiving an administrative support role, and this will inform decisions made around what extra supports are needed.
School principals also raised the issue of the CAO points system for college entry and the impact this is having on secondary school teaching and the children trying to navigate it.
The race for points and a college place has created an “education economy” where students feel they need to pay for grinds and online platforms in order to get an advantage, Doran said.
“The CAO tail continues to wag the dog of senior cycle. Too many students now think: if it doesn’t count for CAO points, it doesn’t count at all,” he told delegates.
“Education becomes a competition where paying for additional supports and tuition is the price of keeping pace,” Doran said.
A significant change in how the system works is needed in order to ensure CAO points do not become the overriding purpose of young people’s education, he said.

title: Budget 2027 continues extraordinary rise in State spending
description: Inside Politics: Hard to know who’ll blink first in standoff between Government and public sector unions
content:
It was Simon Harris’ s first budget this week. He and his wife, Caoimhe, also welcomed their third child the previous weekend. The joke around Leinster House was that the poor child didn’t get much sleep, as it was kept up all night with the Minister for Finance.
The budget was delivered on Tuesday. As Patrick Freyne wrote in his colour piece , all the references to millions and billions of euro make it all sound like Monopoly money.
The acceleration in State spending is extraordinary. Some €125 billion will be spent in 2027. We’re quickly moving towards a situation in which the State will be spending twice as much at the end of the decade as it was at the beginning, before Covid came along.
Of course, Covid can be blamed for the increase in State spending, along with the huge lump of debt that most European countries have accumulated. France , in particular, has a huge debt burden at the moment. Recent studies there show that the purchasing power of families has decreased by as much as €1,200 over the past two years alone.
Most European countries, of course, don’t have the levers to deal with the huge changes that have occurred, including inflation, the spike in energy prices and the increase in the cost of living .
Ireland does. It has been handed the golden beans that allow the magic beanstalk to grow. But, of course, anybody who has read the fairy tale will know that there is a price to pay.
Corporation tax receipts allow Ireland’s national debt to remain low compared with that of other European countries, and they have given the Government the latitude in its budgets that other states do not have.
That’s why diesel is 20 cent cheaper in Ireland than in most other European countries. It’s also why the Minister for Finance was able to publish a generous income tax package that will benefit lower- and middle-income households to the tune of €1,500.
It’s difficult to be in Opposition because you have to criticise the macroeconomic aspects of the budget while also calling for more spending. Politicians on both sides of the Dáil will tell you that a budget is about choices and priorities, but it seems that the choice they make is to spend even more.
The responsibility on the Opposition is less onerous, as it does not have to balance the books.
Nevertheless, as you would expect, the two institutions on the State side that critique the Government’s economic and fiscal policy were not impressed by the budget.
The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council and its straight-talking chair, Seamus Coffey, said the budget had put the economy on a worse trajectory. He spoke about the Government’s failure to adhere to its own spending limits, which is true, and again referred to the over-reliance on corporation tax.
You sometimes wonder whether, instead of being a blessing, corporation tax is a curse. If there is a precipitous fall in receipts any time soon, it will have very worrying consequences for the Irish economy.
In relation to spending, the signs for 2026 and 2027 are not encouraging.
Overall, spending is projected to increase by 6 per cent in 2027, provided the State stays within its own self-imposed limits. If recent years are anything to go by, however, that is unlikely to happen.
State spending was meant to be limited to either 5 per cent or 6 per cent each year from 2020 onwards, but in most years the increase was in double digits.
At a press conference after the budget, Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill said four of the six HSE regions were already eating into their 2027 budgets.
She also referred to the fact that the maximum number of new staff recruitments had been exceeded. The figure was supposed to be 3,300 but it had already reached 3,600. She argued that the requisite savings in agency staffing costs and improvements in productivity, which were expected in return, had not been achieved.
Jack Chambers has set out his stall, however, as a public expenditure hawk. His negotiations with line ministers was described as tough and one, Patrick O’Donovan , ended a meeting with Chambers after eight minutes.
He has set up a new public spending efficiency taskforce with a focus on cutting costs and seems determined to make sure that State spending, for once, stays within limits.
The non-appearance of the culture cards for teenagers in the budget was an own-goal for O’Donovan. He had flagged it in the run-up to the budget and when it didn’t materialise the unavoidable optics whereas that he had lost out in his battle with Chambers.
[ Chambers and O’Donovan at odds over ‘culture card’ idea Opens in new window ]
To compound matters, he found himself on the back foot again over another bit of budget news that seemed to catch everybody by surprise, including Government leaders.
O’Donovan announced he was withdrawing €20 million from the €260 million committed to RTÉ for 2027 because of what he set out as a suboptimal performance by the broadcaster in fulfilling its part of the deal, particularly its voluntary redundancy programme.
It sparked an immediate row with RTÉ, with its director general Kevin Bakhurst responding immediately and forcibly.
Our own reporting this week showed O’Donovan had written to leaders on Saturday saying that among other things that would have to be “reneged” on, if extra money was not forthcoming for his department, would be the funding agreement with RTÉ.
Other Ministers were of the impression that that issue was resolved in the run-up to the budget. Obviously not. Was it connected with the row Chambers had with O’Donovan over the culture card? Possibly? In any event, a clear-the-air meeting between Bakhurst and O’Donovan gave the first indication that the funding may be restored .
It’s hard to know who’s going to blink first, the Government or the public sector unions. One is saying that everything is being discussed. The others (the unions) are saying that pay has to be dealt with first, and then other things can be agreed.
The rationale from the union side is that it could take months before the talks come to an end. That at a time when its members are really feeling the pressure of cost-of-living increases.
From the Government perspective, if it concedes and confines negotiations to pay, the unions, having got what they want, will not have any incentive to negotiate on the other aspects of the talks – efficiencies, reforms and working hours – and will string them along.
Chambers in his budget speech said he had set aside €1.2 billion as a contingency for pay awards for public servants. Problem is, the unions say that is not enough, that at least €2 billion will be required.
Meanwhile, there is a one-day strike on Wednesday that will affect nearly everything everywhere. Besides schools, universities, public offices, it also looks like the Dáil will not be sitting, as the civil servants who work in Leinster House will be on strike and it will not be possible for any proceedings to happen in the chamber.
Pat Leahy and Jack Horgan-Jones have done a big read on the background to the budget and the various horse-trading and rows (and there were some) that took place before Harris and Chambers rose to their feet in the Dáil on Tuesday. See The Irish Times this weekend.
And don’t forget our Inside Politics Wrap of the Week podcast which you can find here .

title: Irish nun is first woman appointed to lead Vatican’s network of missionaries
description: Donegal native has worked as missionary in Nigeria and Tanzania, helping to improve status of women
content:
A Donegal nun has become the first woman appointed to a senior Vatican position as head of the Catholic Church’s global network of missionary societies.
From January next, Sr Mary Teresa Barron (57) will be adjunct secretary of the Dicastery for Evangelisation and president of the Pontifical Mission Societies, the Vatican has announced.
Since 2018, she has been superior general of her own congregation, the Missionary Sisters of Our Lady of Apostles, set up to establish missions in Africa, and also head of the International Union of Superiors General, which represents the leaders of women’s religious congregations worldwide.
She had worked as a missionary in Nigeria and Tanzania, helping to improve the status of women, in pastoral work and in HIV/Aids-related projects.
Bishop of Raphoe Niall Coll “warmly” welcomed the Vatican announcement as “in many ways, a tribute to the countless Irish missionaries, past and present, who have given so generously in service to God’s mission throughout the world”.
Barron’s appointment was “a source of immense pride not only for the missionary community but also for the people of her native parish of Drumoghill, near Manorcunningham, in Co Donegal”, he said.
The Co Donegal bishop offered “special congratulations to her mother, Mena, who will undoubtedly take great pride in this achievement, and I remember with gratitude her late father, Jim”.
A past pupil of Loreto secondary school in Letterkenny, Barron joined the Sisters of Our Lady of Apostles in 1992 and was professed in 2001 at her home parish in Donegal.
Archbishop of Cashel and Emly Kieran O’Reilly, chairman of Missio Ireland and the Irish Bishops’ National Mission Council, said her appointment was “a great honour for the Irish Missionary Church, the Sisters of Our Lady of Apostles, Sr Mary’s family and for Sr Mary herself”.

title: Profits at Denis O’Brien’s Algarve golf resort rise marginally
description: Quinta do Lago has three golf courses, hotels, a sports campus and residential units
content:
Profits at the company that manages businessman Denis O’Brien ’s Quinta do Lago golf resort in the Algarve rose marginally last year to £6.38 million (€7.53 million).
Accounts for UK-registered Algarve Golf Courses Ltd show that a subsidiary that manages the complex in Portugal – Sociedade do Golfe da Quinta do Lago SA – made the £6.38 million post-tax profit for 2025.
The £6.38 million profits for 2025 are marginally ahead of the £6.28 million profits for 2024.
The accounts show that Quinta do Lago finished the financial period with capital and reserves of £35.6 million.
In a note with the accounts the directors for Algarve Golf Courses said that they were satisfied with the performance of Quinta do Lago in 2025.
O’Brien acquired the Quinta do Lago resort in 1998, and has expanded it substantially in the years since. It comprises three golf courses, hotels, a sports campus and residential units.
The bumper year for the business followed O’Brien extending his business footprint in Portugal in 2024 where he completed the purchase of Conrad Algarve resort in Quinta do Lago for about €200 million.
It has 134 rooms and 20 suites with a luxury spa, a techno gym and various restaurants.
At the end of 2025, Algarve Golf Courses had net assets of £7.27 million – unchanged from the end of the previous year. The directors noted that it did not make a profit in 2025 as it did not trade.
Separately, accounts for another Denis O’Brien-owned entity, Catalunya Golf Ltd, show that it recorded a pretax profit of £1.8 million last year.
The directors said that the gain arose from the foreign exchange conversion of the underlying investment and not from trading.
This followed the firm recording a loss for 2024 of £1.5 million.
The firm is a holding company for companies engaged in the ownership and management of golf courses and the directors state both the level of business and the year-end financial position were satisfactory.
O’Brien’s five-star Camiral resort in Girona in Spain has been awarded the 2031 Ryder Cup and has yet to file accounts for 2025.
The group that operates the resort, Murryhill Holdings Ltd, recorded pretax losses of £2.56 million in 2024 as revenues decreased by 17 per cent from £59.42 million to £38.8 million.

title: Mona McSharry wins second 100m breaststroke title of World Cup series
description: Sligo swimmer on track for $10,000 ‘triple crown’ bonus next week in Kazakhstan
content:
Mona McSharry won her second 100m breaststroke title on Friday as part of the three-stop World Aquatics World Cup, setting herself up for a go at the $10,000 ‘triple crown’ bonus at the final meet next week.
The Sligo swimmer, who also won the event at the first stop of the series in Baku, Azerbaijan last week, clocked 1:04.25 to win Friday’s final in Tashkent, Uzebkistan ahead of Russia’s Evgeniia Chikunova.
If McSharry wins the 100m breaststroke next week in Astana, Kazakhstan, she will claim the triple crown title for the event and pocket the $10,000 bonus.
Ellen Walshe was also in action in Tashkent on Friday, finishing fourth in the 400m individual medley in 4:32.71, improving on her fifth-place finish from Baku.
Later in the session, the Templeogue swimmer was back on the blocks for the final of the 50m butterfly, finishing marginally outside her 25.94 from the morning’s heats to touch the wall in 26.00 for eighth.
McSharry will be back in the pool on Saturday for the 50m breaststroke, while Walshe will race in the 200m IM.

title: Childcare providers face squeeze with fees due to drop further despite funding increase
description: Minister announces record €650m-plus funding for next year for sector
content:
Childcare providers who have signed up to the Government’s “core funding” programme will be obliged to cut their fees by almost 11 per cent next year.
Parents will also benefit from a near 17 per cent increase in National Childcare Scheme subsidies, which will cut the cost of care by up to €209 a week – or €2,509 over a year – for those relying on long creche hours.
The changes are due to come into force in September next year.
[ ‘This budget is not for families’: Childcare and new savings scheme the Budget 2027 measures you most want to know about Opens in new window ]
But the Department of Children says it will not be making funding available to childcare providers to fully offset the fall in their revenues.
A spokesman for Minister for Children Norma Foley said that childcare operators would be only “partially compensated” for the net reduction in fees.
The cuts to existing rates that only came into force last month will come as the minimum national wage climbs by close to 6 per cent to €14.94 in 2027. Creche owners rely largely on staff earning around the minimum wage.
The department said that making early learning and childcare more affordable for families was a key priority of the budget.
Foley said core funding for more than 4,600 providers of early learning and childcare will increase by more than €170 million, to a record €650 million-plus in the next programme year from September 2027.
The department spokesman said many providers countrywide were not charging the maximum fees permitted and that only 23 per cent would have to reduce fees next year.
Childcare operators say the current funding model is not viable and will mean more providers, especially smaller-scale operations, walking away from core funding in a move that would allow them to set their own fees.
While welcoming the increased support for parents, Childhood Services Ireland, the Ibec group representing early learning and care providers, warned that providers still lack sufficient clarity on how the Government’s new fee reductions will be funded at service level.
“You cannot tighten fee controls and restrict provider income while wages, energy, food and insurance continue to rise and simply assume the numbers will work,” said Stephanie Roy, director of Childhood Services Ireland.
“Parents understandably want lower bills, but they also need childcare places to remain available and high quality.
“Until we see the detailed core funding allocations and how they translate at provider level, we simply cannot know how much of the shortfall on fees providers are expected to absorb themselves.”
[ Budget 2027’s childcare package has triggered storm of protest from parents. Here’s why Opens in new window ]
Calling on the Minister to step back from unilateral decisions and engage in meaningful co-creation with providers, Roy said: “Right now, what we are hearing from our members is deep anxiety over whether they can keep their doors open. The capacity to absorb further cost increases is exhausted.”
Elaine Dunne of the Federation of Early Childhood Providers said the Government’s core funding model was not working for the independent operators her organisation represents.
“The department needs to wake up and come into the real world. Services are closing because they are financially strapped.”
She added that “you cannot just give on one end and not the other end” in relation to Government demands that providers facing higher costs must lower fees and bear much of the cost themselves.
The department says that 92 per cent of childcare providers across the State are signed up to the core funding model. And it is confident even more providers will sign up to core funding over the coming months.
“We are not seeing these threatened mass withdrawals,” said its spokesman. “The more money you put into core funding, the more reluctant people will be to leave.”
The Department has meanwhile moved to clarify confusion surrounding a statement issued on Budget Day that was received as suggesting that the current maximum costs were €735 per child per month when some families were spending considerably more than that.
In a statement on Friday, figures were set out for five different scenarios for families with young children receiving childcare, with a maximum of €959 per month under current structures.
For example, children with a place for 25 hours per week will see the price cap fall from €458 a month to €350 a month from September 2027.
The capped cost for parents for a child with a full-time place of up to 50 hours a week will fall from €959 to €750 per month. For children availing of a place for up to 45 hours a week, the cap will fall from €735 per month to €550.
Government sources said negotiations between Foley and Jack Chambers were the last to be completed on the eve of the Budget and did not allow sufficient time to prepare more than one case study.
Sinn Féin spokeswoman Claire Kerrane has said she received numerous calls from parents telling her that they paid well in excess of €735 per month.
She said that there were no figures available on how many parents were in that category. It is understood the Department is in the process of setting up a system to collate those figures.
“It is unclear. My simple question is how many families will pay €550 a month from next September. That has not been answered.”
She also expressed doubt that the aim of delivering a service at €200 per month per child was possible under current trajectories.

title: Germany’s political centre is not holding. It is tearing itself apart
description: As the Christian Democratic Union and the Social Democratic Party lose support, each accuses the other of flirting with political extremists
content:
J ust 18 months in, few in political Berlin expect the luckless coalition of chancellor Friedrich Merz to last its full four-year term. And this week a likely cause of his government’s premature demise was pencilled into the death certificate: mutual recrimination.
In May 2025 the coalition of centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and centre-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) took office facing three inherited problems: a moribund economy, a two-decade reform backlog and an increasingly aggressive Russia.
As they struggle with all three, and haemmorage political support, both have turned instead to finger-pointing, in particular claims the other is flirting with political extremists.
Amplified by social media discourse, the two foundation stones of Germany’s political centre openly accuse each other of undermining the political centre and digging the grave of modern German democracy.
The CDU, backed by the right-wing Springer media group, has denounced the SPD for beginning exploratory talks for a new city-state government in Berlin led by the hard-left Linke.
“A day of disgrace” was the shrill verdict of the Bild tabloid, which sees Linke as a hotbed of woke radicals and proto-Islamists, united by hatred of Jews.
Meanwhile the SPD rounded on the CDU for, in its eyes, stepping up its flirtation with far-right extremism.
In Saxony-Anhalt, 90 minutes southwest of Berlin, CDU MPs were instructed to abstain in a vote to choose a state parliamentary president. Though it was a secret ballot, it is likely four CDU MPs backed the candidate from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) candidate Tobias Rausch.
His was a taboo-shattering victory: for the first time since 1945 a far-right politician holds a parliamentary office in Germany.
SPD and other parties fear a repeat vote – or worse – when Saxon-Anhalt MPs choose a new prime minister in December – and most likely elect local AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund.
Furious at Tuesday’s outcome, SPD federal politicians in the federal capital called a spontaneous protest march to Bebelplatz, the Berlin square where, in May 1933, books of authors deemed “un-German” by the new Nazi authorities were burned in a pyre.
SPD defence minister Boris Pistorius, who initiated the march to this sensitive spot, called Tuesday’s gathering a “singular event that demanded a singular answer”.
SPD co-leader and vice-chancellor Lars Klingbeil agreed: “The CDU has to explain urgently how this could happen.”
Fighting words from one coalition partner to another. A few streets away, CDU chairman Merz told a public event that “playing with extremists is not compatible with the values of my party”.
A day later, leading CDU politicians chose attack as the best form of defence. They came out en masse to denounce SPD and Green leaders in Berlin state politics for opening preliminary coalition talks with the hard-left Linke.
It stormed to victory in last month’s state election with 25.7 per cent support. The likely next governing mayor of Berlin, Linke leader Elif Eralp, says voters backed her party’s “make Berlin affordable” promise, echoing rent control and cost-of-living interventions of New York mayor Zohran Mamdani .
[ ‘Berlin’s Mamdani’ could carry Left party to power in Berlin Opens in new window ]
As in New York, Linke succeeded in activating first-time voters and a previously neglected demographic: second- and third-generation Germans of Turkish and Arabic descent.
Similarly to the UK Greens and New York Democrats however, Linke faces claims of structural anti-Semitism, in particular in the post-October 7th discourse. Berlin’s Jewish community, in particular, has sounded the alarm at an election that, alongside the Linke surge, saw 16 per cent of voters for the AfD and 4 per cent for the BSW, a Linke-breakaway grouping.
“The vote share for neo-fascists and neo-Stalinists in Berlin combined is 46.7 per cent,” said Max Feldhake, a Berlin-based rabbi. “This is truly alarming and very disconcerting for the city’s Jews.”
Even before formal Berlin coalition talks, the city’s SPD and Greens face stiff headwind from even within their own ranks.
Former Green foreign minister Joschka Fischer and ex-SPD parliamentary speaker Wolfgang Thierse have signed a public letter of alarm over Linke’s failure to distance itself from “anti-Semitic, Islamist, terrorist and criminal structures”.
That letter was a response to a previous letter, signed by 150 Jewish leftist academics and writers in Germany, arguing the repeated allegations against the Linke amounted to “cynical political instrumentalisation which equates almost any criticism of Israeli policy with anti-Semitism”.
Among the criticisms of Linke: an election event with a Berlin rapper who sang a song with lyrics that include “stop the genocide”, “Yalla Yalla Intifada” and “death to the IDF”. Another focus is a Berlin Linke politician with alleged ties to extremist Kurdish and Palestinian groups, as well as an organised crime family.
Predictably, the CDU and SPD have taken umbrage at the other’s accusations – but give no signs of backing down.
Signs of economic recovery may provide a respite from the bickering, but analyst Klaus Schubert fears persistent weak political leadership will prolong this period of what he calls German “Punch-and-Judy-show politics”.
“The population of this conservative country is unsettled,” said Schubert, political scientist at the University of Münster. “Instead of seeking the centre ground, voters are testing the political fringes.”
[ AfD passes milestone with first parliamentary speaker post in Saxony-Anhalt Opens in new window ]
[ The astonishing fall of a German spymaster Opens in new window ]

title: McEvaddys clear Bain debt on Dublin Airport lands after sale of Omega Air
description: Confirmation of the repayment has come soon after Ulick and Desmond McEvaddy sold Omega Air to defence industry investor Augustus Global
content:
Ulick and Desmond McEvaddy, who sold aviation business Omega Air in recent weeks, have repaid debts linked to a large site they own between Dublin Airport’s two runways.
Defence industry investor Augustus Global last month confirmed its acquisition of the McEvaddy brothers’ Omega Air, which has supplied mid-air refuelling services to the US military for more than 25 years.
Based on comparable deals in the sector recently, mergers and acquisition transaction database Dealert estimated the company was sold by the Irish businessmen for between €19.7 million and €26.7 million.
Following the sale, a McEvaddy-controlled business that co-owns a large parcel of land beside Dublin Airport has now published new financial accounts that show it has cleared its debts with Bain Capital Credit.
At the end of 2024, D.A. Terminal 3 Limited owed €56.1 million to the US group, compared to €46.3 million at the end of the previous year.
The debts were linked to the businessmen’s share in a 105-hectare development site , which they co-own with three other farmers.
The company accounts added that €31.6 million of interest had built up on the McEvaddys’ debt linked to the land bank by the end of 2024.
A note in the directors report said the McEvaddy brothers “reached a settlement in September 2026 with the external funding providers and that funding plus all accrued interest and charges has now been repaid in full”.
The accounts did not disclose the final settlement payment.
It added they are now funding the company directly and are “committed to providing continued funding as is required for the foreseeable future”.
In 2023, the McEvaddy brothers and three other landowners put their combined sites, spanning 105 hectares, on the market. A reported €75 million bid by Dublin Airport operator DAA for the lands was rejected.
Ulick McEvaddy told RTÉ in September 2023 that the Dublin Airport operator’s bid for the land, which he said was worth more than €205 million, was “derisory”.
A spokesman for Desmond and Ulick McEvaddy told The Irish Times that following the repayment of the debt, they remain focused on exploring future development opportunities for the lands.
He added the lands remain suitable to form a key part of Dublin Airport’s expansion plans. In December 2023, Dublin Aiport asked Fingal County Council for permission to develop 11 infrastructure projects and increase its passenger capacity from 32 million to 40 million passengers per annum.
“It makes little sense to spend an estimated €5.7 billion increasing the capacity of Terminals 1 and 2 to approximately 45 million passengers per annum when a Terminal 3 development on the lands could increase Dublin Airport’s overall capacity to approximately 70 million passengers for an estimated €3.5 billion,” he said.

title: Former US soldier charged with murdering Mike Gaine wants new barristers, court told
description: Michael Kelley, a native of Maine in the US but of no fixed abode in Tralee, Co Kerry, charged with single count of murder
content:
A former US soldier charged with murdering Co Kerry sheep farmer Mike Gaine wants new barristers in advance of his nine-week trial next January, the Central Criminal Court has heard.
Michael Kelley, a native of Maine in the US but of no fixed abode in Tralee, Co Kerry, was sent forward for trial in Dublin last May after being served with the book of evidence.
Kelley (54) is charged with a single count of murdering Mike Gaine (56) at Carrig, Kenmare, Co Kerry, on a date unknown between March 20th and 21st, 2025.
Kelley is expected to go on trial at the Central Criminal Court on January 11th, 2027.
The court was previously told by counsel for the Director of Public Prosecutions that there are 191 witnesses in the book of evidence and it is estimated the case will last up to nine weeks.
In a brief hearing before the Central Criminal Court on Friday, defence counsel Brendan Grehan told Judge Paul McDermott that he had been instructed by solicitor Frank Buttimer on behalf of Kelley, alongside Richard Liston BL.
Grehan told the judge that his legal team had met Kelley “a few times”, but he understood that the accused man now wished for alternative counsel in the case.
Defence counsel said Kelley wishes to retain Buttimer as his solicitor and he [Grehan] understood “alternative arrangements” are being put in place to instruct other counsel in the case.
Grehan said he was making an application to the court under the Legal Services Regulation Act on behalf of himself and Liston for permission to withdraw from the case.
Addressing Kelley, who appeared via video-link, the judge said: “You have heard that – and that is an appropriate application for counsel to make as outlined to me.”
Grehan went on to say that Buttimer would remain in the case and he understood Kelley was happy with that arrangement.
Kelley told the judge that he was agreeable to this.
Fiona McGowan, for the Director of Public Prosecutions, said disclosure was at a very advanced stage in the case and is “ongoing”.
The lawyer asked for another case management date in two weeks’ time.
The judge said that, as there had been a changeover of counsel, he would list the matter for a case management review on October 23rd.
“That will enable new counsel to read themselves into the case and read the papers,” he said.
McDermott said the trial date remained “as is” but “with a change of counsel in the case”.
Gaine was first reported missing from his home on March 21st, 2025, prompting an extensive search of his farm and surrounding areas.
On April 29th, almost six weeks after he went missing, the case was upgraded to homicide.
The sheep farmer had been missing for more than eight weeks when remains found on his farm at Carrig in May 2025 were identified as those of Mike Gaine.

title: Tributes paid to former Irish Times journalist Dick Hogan, who has died  aged 76
description: ‘His career in journalism reflected his strong values and his many talents,’ says former editor Conor Brady
content:
Tributes have been paid to former Irish Times southern correspondent Dick Hogan, who died on Wednesday in the Mercy University Hospital in his native Cork at the age of 76.
Former editors of The Irish Times Conor Brady and Paul O’Neill were among those to praise Hogan for the quality of his journalism. He started his career in The Cork Examiner and then moved to Dublin to work for RTÉ before returning to Cork as Irish Times southern correspondent.
Brady said: “Dick Hogan’s career in journalism reflected his strong values and his many talents. I first worked with him when he was recruited from the then Cork Examiner by the legendary Mike Burns to the newly formed RTÉ news features unit in the 1970s. He was a colleague of immense charm, good humour, energy and conviviality – qualities that can carry one a long way in journalism.
“But his heart was in Cork – and in print rather than broadcasting – and when he was given the opportunity to return there as southern correspondent for The Irish Times , he jumped at it. His deep local knowledge of Cork, its people, its places and its culture was to prove immensely valuable to the paper and its readers over the many years of his tenure.”
O’Neill echoed Brady, noting how Hogan had a deserved reputation for quality journalism that greatly enhanced The Irish Times’s standing on Leeside, where he reported for the paper for some two decades until his departure in 2002, when he went to assist University College Cork with its communications.
“Over a long career, Dick was the definitive voice of Cork and beyond, who, whether reporting on events of local, national or international significance, applied the same standards of accuracy, thoroughness and fairness,” said O’Neill.
“He was a champion of the region rather than a cheerleader for it, reflecting what he saw as good or bad with the same honesty and candour, which were integral to both his journalism and his character.”
Hogan is survived by his partner Aileen, his sons Cian, Shane and Richard and their mother Helen as well as his siblings Alex, John, Mary and Niamh, and he was predeceased by his brother Eddie.
Requiem Mass takes place at 1pm on Friday at St Michael’s Church, Upper Glanmire, Cork

title: Mary McAleese questioned the GAA’s attitude towards women – now they’ve replaced her with a man
description: John Horan is well qualified to chair the Integration Steering Committee, but were there really no women who could have done it?
content:
The first thing to say about John Horan is that he’s likely to do a good job as the new chair of the Integration Steering Committee . Nothing is guaranteed, of course – if it were, Mary McAleese would have stayed, and the whole process wouldn’t be snarled up like the M50 at breakfast time. But Horan is capable, willing, experienced and battle-hardened. On the basic fundamentals, he is an obvious fit for the role.
Still. Doesn’t look great, does it? The former chair of the steering committee storms out the door, complaining about a GAA management committee in which she suspects “there are people who are not entirely happy about the idea of including women in decision-making”. And their response is ... to replace her with a man.
Not just any man, either – a former president of the GAA. The whole concept of the steering committee was that three organisations were being brought together as one, hence the idea of the wrangler in the centre of it all being someone independent. Now, maybe that was the wrong framing. Maybe this was always, in reality, a GAA project requiring a GAA project manager. Whither or which, that’s what we have now.
Horan isn’t just a past president of the GAA, he is somebody who is still deeply enmeshed in various GAA projects around the country. He’s chairman of the board of Páirc Uí Chaoimh. He is on the committee in charge of building the new Louth GAA stadium in Dundalk, as well as being a director of Páirc Tailteann in Navan as it undergoes its rebuild. He has a reputation within the GAA as someone who can work with people, a wise head who is good at taking the long view and getting things done.
But none of that is really the point. The point is that integration is always going to be as much of a selling job as a doing job. It’s not just about the association making things right – it’s about them being seen to make things right. That’s a more difficult thing to achieve when you choose as a figurehead someone who looks like a GAA man, who sounds like a GAA man, who literally is the quintessential GAA man.
They do themselves no favours sometimes. How often during the skorts wars of 2025 did you find yourself correcting ordinary members of the public, informing them that this actually has nothing to do with the GAA and that it was, in fact, a camogie problem, created by a separate organisation called the Camogie Association? That drove people within the GAA to distraction – and rightly so.
The same will happen here, you can be sure of it. Appointing John Horan was a choice made by all three organisations, but that’s not how it looks. Instead, it looks like the GAA deciding that they’re done with outsiders coming in and making a hames of the thing so they’ve put one of their own in charge of it. Try convincing people otherwise, see how long they listen.
Optics matter. The optics here say one of three things. Either (a) they couldn’t get a woman to do the job; (b) they couldn’t think of a woman to do the job; or (c) it didn’t occur to them to get a woman to do the job. None of those are good.
They are particularly not good in the context of McAleese’s departure. Even if some of her comments as she left the stage were unfair and overblown, there’s no getting around the fact that they set the agenda for what happens next. One of the most high-profile female leaders in the history of the State, someone who has always been well-disposed towards the GAA, called them out in the most public way possible. And their response is to ask an ex-GAA president to do her job.
Again, this is nothing against John Horan personally. There’s a good argument to be made that he would have been the right person to get in from the start. McAleese seemed like an inspired appointment, but instead maybe they should have recruited Horan, or someone like him – a native speaker when it comes to navigating the spaghetti junction of Gaelic games admin.
But that’s not what happened. And the reason it didn’t happen was because they made the determination, not unreasonably, that a good way of signalling their intentions around integration was to put a strong female face and voice front and centre. It was a decent idea then, and it hasn’t stopped being a decent idea just because the last woman criticised them in a radio interview.
This isn’t about tokenism. Or at least it shouldn’t be. What it should be about is the GAA acknowledging its original sin. If you were designing it from scratch now, of course you’d make the association fully integrated from the get-go. Times were different in 1884 and for a long time after. But we are in 2026 now, and the idea that all the distaff options were exhausted before turning to an old-hand GAA man just feels unlikely.
This will blow over. It always does. The steering committee will get on with its work and somewhere down the line, integration will get done. None of that was ever in doubt. The questions were only ever around the way and the how and the who.
The GAA decided to play it safe on the last question. If they wish to prove Mary McAleese wrong in her accusations, this wasn’t the way to go about it.

title: Saudi Arabia confirms that Houthi strikes on Riyadh airport killed three
description: Yemen’s civil war now the fiercest front in regional fighting triggered by the US and Israeli ⁠attack on Iran
content:
Thursday’s attacks on Riyadh airport killed three ‌people, Saudi authorities said on Friday, as Yemen ’s Houthi group stepped up missile strikes on the kingdom and tried to shut down its airspace in an escalating war triggered by the US-Iran conflict .
The strikes, which also injured several people, damaged a Saudia Airlines ​plane and sent smoke billowing over the airport, led many airlines to cancel flights to the Saudi capital days before it is due to host a major meeting of global oil officials, minsters and executives.
Saudi air strikes hit Houthi targets in the Yemeni capital Sana’a overnight, Houthi officials and affiliated media said, part of an intensifying air war against the Iran-allied group aimed at reversing its recent territorial gains, threats to international shipping, and attacks on the kingdom.
A Saudi-led coalition backing government forces in Yemen said it ​had destroyed three missile-launch platforms used by the Houthis and warned it would respond firmly to attacks on civilians.
The Houthis, who have encircled Yemeni government forces in Yemen’s third-largest city of Taiz and are trying to defend positions on the Red Sea coast ⁠against a Saudi-backed offensive, had already killed three people with strikes on airports in the kingdom earlier this week.
The Saudi civil aviation authority said air traffic at Riyadh airport had returned ‌to ‌normal ​and flight-tracking site Flightradar24 showed a gradual resumption of flights, including from some Middle Eastern airlines.
Saudia Airlines said one of those killed on Thursday was an employee.
Yemen’s civil war has rapidly emerged as the fiercest front in a wider regional conflagration triggered by the US and Israeli ⁠attack on Iran that started on February 28th.
The conflict is critical for global ​energy markets, with the Houthis firing on shipping in the Red Sea and its southern gateway the ​Bab el-Mandeb Strait, further squeezing Gulf oil supplies with Iran partly blocking the Strait of Hormuz .
Last month the Houthis staged a lightning advance down Yemen’s Red Sea coast to take full control over the coastline around ‌the strait, prompting Saudi Arabia to re-enter the long-dormant conflict and back ​a government counteroffensive.
On Monday government forces took back territory around the Bab el-Mandeb coastline after intense Saudi air strikes and fighting continues there.
Saudi Arabia’s ambassador to Yemen, who has managed the kingdom’s engagement in ⁠Yemen for more than a decade, said in a social media post on Friday that ⁠Bab el-Mandeb had been cleared of Houthis.
Reuters was not ​able to verify that and Houthi forces remain in Mocha, a little way up the coast, with government forces focused on a battle in nearby hills that overlook the region.
The Houthis have also managed to cut off a key road connecting Taiz, a city of more than half a million people with a garrison of thousands of pro-government fighters, with advances in mountain districts.
The group has announced repeated rounds of ballistic missile fire at Saudi Arabia, proclaiming it would shut down Saudi airspace and warning workers at oil facilities that it would strike those too.
Saudi Arabia is seeking assistance from Pakistan and Turkey, its partners in a mutual defence pact, to help ward off Houthi attacks, and has pushed for wider help from allies to aid it in reversing the group’s gains inside Yemen.
The Houthis on Friday repeated their threats against aircraft flying over Saudi Arabia, except above the holy Muslim cities ‌of Mecca and Medina, describing Saudi airspace ⁠as a theatre of operations for its missile forces.
While some regional airlines were still operating flights through Riyadh, many others were still suspended and Flightradar24 showed many cancellations and delays.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency said it was extending the area in which it advised airlines not to fly, citing the recent attacks on Riyadh airport and risks to ‌civil aviation. Aviation risk-monitoring advisory body Opsgroup advised against flying over the kingdom.
The US embassy in the United Arab Emirates warned Americans to exercise increased vigilance, citing Houthi attacks on civilian targets in Saudi Arabia and saying the hostilities could ​rapidly escalate.
Riyadh is due to host the WPC Energy Congress, a major meeting of oil ministers, other government officials and oil company executives, from ​Sunday and it was still advertising the event on Friday.
Italian energy minister Gilberto Pichetto Fratin said he would not attend in person, but take part via video, without mentioning the reason for his decision. – Reuters

title: Boy injured while playing hurling settles action over hospital care for €165,000
description: Fionn Barrett sustained corkscrew fracture to thigh and alleged failure to treat it appropriately
content:
A Co Cork boy who was injured while hurling and brought to a Kerry hospital has settled a High Court action over his care there for €165,000.
Fionn Barrett was six years old when he sustained a corkscrew fracture to his thigh bone during the incident in August 2020. He was brought to University Hospital Kerry in Tralee.
He was in hospital for two weeks and later had to have three surgeries, the court heard.
Richard Kean, counsel for Fionn, told the court the boy suffered a significant break. At the hospital he was taken to theatre where a splint was placed, counsel said.
Counsel said an X-ray taken five days after the incident showed non-alignment of the fracture, and further scans by September 2020 showed there was further fracture displacement.
Kean said the boy had to undergo three surgeries and was left with one leg longer than the other, which has now improved, counsel said.
The boy’s side contended that Fionn had to have one or two additional surgeries as a result of alleged substandard care.
Aileen O’Connor, the boy’s mother, told the court that the family were unhappy with an offer of €145,000 to settle the case. She said her son has not fully returned to sport.
O’Connor said the situation had been highly traumatic for all the family and she said she was talking about accountability for what her son had been through.
At that stage, Judge Leonie Reynolds adjourned the hearing for a short time. When the parties returned to court, the judge was told that the amount offered to settle the case had been increased to €165,000.
The judge said it would be remiss of her to do other than to approve the settlement.
Fionn, now aged 13, of Enniskeane, Co Cork, had, through his mother, sued the Health Service Executive.
In the proceedings, it was claimed there was an alleged failure to manage or treat the boy’s spiral femur fracture appropriately and an alleged failure to recognise that splintage was not working, and that the fracture had displaced within three days of application.
There was also an alleged failure to recognise that the splint had slipped and was no longer functioning as a treatment device, and an alleged failure to correct the worsening deformity, it was claimed
The boy, it was contended, was subjected to months of physical and mental suffering and he had to endure further intervention.
The HSE admitted a breach of duty in failing to act on the radiographs of the left femur taken on September 2nd and September 11th, 2020.
The management of the fracture initially was satisfactory and the option of using traction was reasonable and appropriate, the HSE contended.
However, the HSE admitted that alternative treatment should have been considered when the deformity was identified on radiographs on the two occasions in 2020.
It also said that the boy’s thigh will likely continue to heal and any length discrepancy will improve as he reaches skeletal maturity.

title: Kazakhstan 0 Ireland 8: Ireland stroll to World Cup playoff win – as it happened
description: Tuesday’s second leg at Páirc Uí Chaoimh now a formality for Carla Ward’s side
content:
“The Republic of Ireland scored eight goals – five from headers – at the Astana Arena to remain on course to face the winners of Belgium v Poland in a playoff final next month to qualify for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil,” Gavin Cummiskey writes in his report.
“Carla Ward’s team make the long journey home for Tuesday’s second leg at Páirc Uí Chaoimh in Cork following a comprehensive dismissal of a Kazakhstan side that looked out of their depth from kick-off.”
[ Eight-goal Ireland move closer to World Cup spot as they outclass Kazakhstan in Astana Opens in new window ]
That’s all for today, thanks for your company.
Gavin Cummiskey’s match report will be up shortly. We’ll be back on Tuesday for what is unlikely to be a nerve-shredding second leg at Páirc Uí Chaoimh.
Here’s player of the match Chloe Mustaki after a game to remember for the defender. “I was a bit nervous stepping into Katie McCabe’s shoes tonight,” she said. She needn’t have worried.
“I was a bit nervous stepping into Katie McCabe’s shoes.” Chloe Mustaki reacts to a player of the match performance – and a first senior goal – as the Republic of Ireland took Kazakhstan apart in Astana. pic.twitter.com/yTThdAOF1H
A stroll for Ireland in Astana, goals from Kyra Carusa (two), Chloe Mustaki, Emily Murphy, Abbie Larkin, Jamie Finn, debutant Shanade Hopcroft and Jessie Stapleton (all but) settling this play-off with the second leg still to come on Tuesday at Páirc Uí Chaoimh.
It was a heck of a day for player of the match Mustaki - she scored her first senior international goal and provided just the three assists. Even Katie McCabe (suspended for this game), whose usual left-wing-back role Mustaki filled, would have been happy enough with that haul.
Carla Ward can, you’d imagine, already start planning for the play-off final which will be played over two legs in November and December against Belgium or Poland - who meet this evening in Leuven in the first leg of their semi-final.
A looping header from the defender who scores her third international goal from Abbie Larkin’s right wing cross. That’s Ireland’s fifth headed goal of the game
Kazakhstan 0-7 Republic of Ireland A debut to remember for Shanade Hopcroft as she diverts home Ireland’s seventh in Astana. 📺 RTÉ2 💻 https://t.co/b2OI4OoWVJ 🖥️ https://t.co/0S1yQiYSEh pic.twitter.com/X3NhPvfJLX
She’s hardly been on the pitch for her debut and Shanade Hopcroft marks it with a goal, smartly turning home Aoife Mannion’s cross from the right. There won’t be a cow milked in Tubbercurry for a month.
70 mins : Shanade Hopcroft comes on for her Irish debut, the Crystal Palace midfielder replacing Caitlin Hayes - a proud day for Tubbercurry, where her granny Nora was born. Hopcroft’s Palace team-mate Hayley Nolan also comes on for Anna Patten
Jamie Finn marks her belated return to the Ireland starting line-up with the away side's sixth goal - and it's yet another header. 📺RTÉ2 💻 https://t.co/b2OI4OoWVJ 🖥️ https://t.co/0S1yQiYSEh pic.twitter.com/wdHAii74lp
You know the way we were just saying that Kazakhstan looked a bit more solid at the back? Well, it’s 6-0 now. Jamie Finn marks her 23rd appearance for Ireland with her first goal, the Burnley midfielder heading home Aoife Mannion’s cross from the right.
56 mins : Ireland continue pressing, Kazakhstan barely getting a touch of the ball, but the hosts are looking a teeny bit more solid at the back in the early stages of the second half, helped by often having 10 bodies in their own box.
45 mins : We’re off again. Carla Ward has made three changes at the break, Amber Barrett, Leanne Kiernan and Tyler Toland on for Kyra Carusa, Emily Murphy and Megan Connolly.
By the by, Ireland’s record win came five years ago in Tallaght when they beat Georgia 11-0. Even if they don’t match that tally, let’s just say, the return leg in Páirc Uí Chaoimh next Tuesday is likely to be, well, a bit of a formality.
Half-time: Kazakhstan 0-5 Republic of Ireland Abbie Larkin heads home just before the break and Carla Ward's side are completely outclassing their hosts. 📺RTÉ2 💻 https://t.co/b2OI4OoWVJ 🖥️ https://t.co/0S1yQiYSEh pic.twitter.com/PwnQty6CjS
A walk in the park. Two goals from Kyra Carusa and one each from Chloe Mustaki, Emily Murphy and Abbie Larkin have sent Ireland on their way to what could yet become a scoreline of cricket-ish proportions. Kazakhstan are down to 10 players too after their captain Yulia Myasnikova was (very harshly) sent off, and they’ve also had to replace their goalkeeper. Apart from that, it’s all gone well for them.
Oh Lord, it’s carnage. Chloe Mustaki - again! - provides the assist, tapping Aoife Mannion’s cross from the right in to the path of Abbie Larkin who heads home.
Yes, things have got worse for Kazakhstan. Abbie Larkin weaved her way past three defenders, her shot was saved by Angelina Portnova but the ball fell straight to Emily Murphy who tapped home for her third international goal.
37 mins : Nazym Ismailova has gone off and has been replaced by Angelina Portnova. We will no longer say “things couldn’t get any worse” for Kazakhstan because they appear to be doing just that.
35 mins : And now Kazakhstan’s goalkeeper Nazym Ismailova has gone down injured with what looks like a shoulder injury after she crashed in to Anna Patten while attempting to collect a corner. They’ll be relieved when this day is over.
32 mins : As if things couldn’t get any worse for Kazakhstan, Norwegian referee Karoline Jensen has sent off their captain Yulia Myasnikova for hauling down Abbie Larkin outside the box. It looked like an extremely harsh decision, marginally mad, it was a yellow at most.
And once again Chloe Mustaki is the creator - that’s a goal and two assists for the left wing-back. Her cross floats over goalkeeper Nazym Ismailova and an unmarked Carusa heads home. This is a stroll. (So far).
Chloe Mustaki has her first senior Republic of Ireland goal and Carla Ward's side are in cruise control in Astana. 📺 RTÉ2 💻 https://t.co/b2OI4OoWVJ 🖥️ https://t.co/0S1yQiYSEh pic.twitter.com/USANjiuoyS
The Nottingham Forest defender’s first goal for Ireland on her 20th appearance. Emily Murphy hit the post when the goalkeeper failed to hold Abbie Larkin’s shot, the rebound falling to Mustaki on the left who rifled the ball in to the roof of the net.
11 mins : It’s still all Ireland, Emily Murphy just failing to get on the end of another fine cross from Anna Patten. Wing-backs Aoife Mannion and Chloe Mustaki are playing so far up the pitch Ireland’s formation is beginning to look like 0-0-10.
The perfect start for the Republic of Ireland as Kyra Carusa’s looping header has them ahead in their World Cup Euro play-off in Kazakhstan. 📺RTÉ2 💻 https://t.co/b2OI4OoWVJ 🖥️ https://t.co/0S1yQiYSEh pic.twitter.com/VU310cG1WN
A terrific header from Carusa from a Chloe Mustaki cross, her 14th international goal. The Kazakhstan goalkeeper Nazym Ismailova looked decidedly ropey in the build-up, it could be a long afternoon for her.
5 mins : Ireland playing keep-ball in the opening stages, Kazakhstan struggling to get out of their own half. The first chance of the game fell to Abbie Larkin who headed Anna Patten’s cross over the bar - should have done better.
We’re up and running , a very sparse crowd in their seats at the 30,000 capacity stadium. A few hardy Irish folk have made the trip, though. It’ll be January before they get over the jet lag.
Carla Ward has been waving away questions this week about her contract situation with the FAI. Her current deal is due to expire at the end of this qualifying campaign - December, at the latest - but she has refused to confirm or deny whether she is in talks with the FAI over an extension. The fact that Aston Villa, who she managed before taking the Irish job, are currently looking for a new manager after sacking Natalia Arroyo 10 days ago has added to speculation about Ward’s position. She insists, though, that her sole focus is on getting Ireland to Brazil next summer.
Stretching the legs in Astana ☘️ pic.twitter.com/x5pR4E5tAo
Astroturf alert : This game will be played on an artificial surface, a factor Ward said played a part in her team selection. “Let me tell you, players don’t like playing on 3G,” she said earlier in the week, so anyone carrying joint niggles and the like will be used sparingly, if at all.
The temperatures were close to zero when the squad arrived in Astana on Monday, after an 11-hour trip, but it’s warmed up a bit since - it’ll be around the 10 degrees mark at kick-off time, Astana being four hours ahead of us. The roof will be closed in the Astana Arena, so that should help keep any chill out.
One new name among the subs today is Shanade Hopcroft, the Crystal Palace midfielder a surprise inclusion in the squad Ward named last week. The 29-year-old qualifies for Ireland through her Sligo grandmother.
Good morning - or if you’re in Astana, a highly pleasant afternoon to you. That’s where the Republic of Ireland’s women kick-start their efforts to get through four World Cup qualifying play-off games, the prize, if they prevail, a place at next summer’s finals in Brazil.
They start, then, away to Kazakhstan (kick-off: noon, live on RTÉ 2), the return leg in Páirc Uí Chaoimh next Tuesday. And if they can come out on top of that play-off, the final hurdle will be Belgium or Poland over two legs in November and December.
All week, the Irish camp has been stressing that they won’t take Kazakhstan for granted, but seeing as they are ranked 77 places below Ireland in the Fifa list, it would be - not to be dramatic or anything - a calamitous catastrophe if they failed to get the better of them.
STARTING XI | Kazakhstan v Ireland Kick off at 12:00pm (Irish time) 🙌 #COYGIG pic.twitter.com/KYvrXmrqFy
We’ll take you through the line-up shortly, meanwhile you can have a read of Gavin Cummiskey’s preview of the game.
[ Ireland without four key players as they face Kazakhstan in World Cup playoff semi-final Opens in new window ]
Republic of Ireland head coach Carla Ward is without four of her most trusted players for this game - captain Katie McCabe and Marissa Sheva (both suspended), Denise O’Sullivan (spared the long trip to Kazakhstan due to recent injury problems) and Ruesha Littlejohn (the 36-year-old still without a club having been released by Crystal Palace in May).
To add to Ward’s woes, Jess Ziu, a likely replacement for O’Sullivan, was ruled out yesterday with a shin problem.
Opportunity has knocked, then, for a few other players, notably midfielder Jamie Finn, who starts her first game for Ireland in three injury-interrupted years, and defender Jessie Stapleton, who hasn’t made the starting line-up since last October.
It looks like Stapleton will make up a back three with Anna Patten and Caitlin Hayes, with Aoife Mannion and Chloe Mustaki the wing-backs. Finn is likely to partner Megan Connolly in midfield behind a front three of Kyra Carusa, Emily Murphy and Abbie Larkin.
In the absence of McCabe and O’Sullivan, goalkeeper Courtney Brosnan captains the side.

title: Eight-goal Ireland move closer to World Cup spot as they outclass Kazakhstan in Astana
description: Abbie Larkin and Chloe Mustaki put in fine performances as Carla Ward’s side show ruthless streak
content:
The concern for this Republic of Ireland group has always centred around how they would cope without Katie McCabe and Denise O’Sullivan.
Especially in a World Cup playoff over 5,000 kilometres from their adopted home patch of Páirc Uí Chaoimh in Cork.
Turns out, Abbie Larkin and others like Chloe Mustaki were ready to carry the load in the absence of the nation’s two world class players.
Larkin, the 21-year-old Crystal Palace winger, who hails from Ringsend, was outstanding as Carla Ward’s side scored eight goals – five from headers – at the Astana Arena in Kazakhstan.
An 8-0 victory in the first leg of a World Cup semi-final playoff keeps Ireland on course to face the winners of Belgium and Poland in a decider next month to qualify for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil.
Belgium beat Poland 1-0 in Leuven on Friday night ahead of the return fixture in Gdansk on Tuesday.
“We want to be front-footed and play with personality in the final third,” said Ward. “We are showing we are a good side, and good teams can win in different ways.”
Larkin and Mustaki, in particular, ensured that Ward’s understrength starting XI did not miss the rested O’Sullivan, injured Jess Ziu or the suspended McCabe and Marissa Sheva.
Kyra Carusa brought her international tally to 15 goals, up alongside Troy Parrott, with two headed finishes from Mustaki deliveries into the box.
Mustaki, now 31, and finally living up to the potential she showed as a younger player before she had to step away from the game to receive treatment for Hodgkin lymphoma. She scored her first international goal after Nazym Ismailova fumbled Larkin’s shot before Emily Murphy hit the rebound off the post for the Nottingham Forest defender to finish from an acute angle.
“I was a bit nervous stepping into Katie McCabe’s shoes tonight,” Mustaki, the player of the match, told RTÉ. “The girls made it easy for me. We had actually practised early deliveries from out wide throughout the week.
“We want to qualify for Brazil,” she added. “If we make it through Tuesday we got a big opponent in Belgium or Poland in November. We need to turn the screw again. Three cup finals to get through”
Any chance of the home team keeping in touch with Ireland was ended by the sending off of Yulia Myasnikova for a foul on Larkin in the 30th minute. Controversially, VAR intervened before Norwegian referee Karoline Marie Jensen showed the Kazakhstan captain a straight red card.
Ismailova, who was at fault for Ireland’s opening three goals, was replaced with an injury after an innocuous fall 10 minutes before half-time. Kazyna Norbayeva was not much better; she was unable to deny Murphy scoring after Larkin took on four defenders before stinging the reserve goalkeeper’s hands with a shot, that her strike partner followed up.
Larkin made it 5-0 in first-half injury time.
The game lacked intensity in the second half as an attack versus defence, training ground feel developed between the Irish professionals and local part-timers. Ward took the opportunity to replace Carusa, Lazio’s Megan Connolly and Murphy with Amber Barrett, Leanne Kiernan and Tyler Toland.
It made little difference. Kazakhstan crowded the middle, which invited Aoife Mannion and Mustaki to raid down the flanks and cross at will.
Mannion assisted two second-half goals; her clever crossing invited Jamie Finn to make it 6-0 before Shanade Hopcroft, on debut, made it 7-0 with a nice touch at the front post. Jess Stapleton claimed an eighth in the 90th minute.
Ward can run her squad for the second leg next Tuesday in Cork when O’Sullivan, McCabe and Sheva are expected to return.
KAZAKHSTAN: Ismailova (Portnova, 39); Burova, Myasnikova (capt), Nurusheva, Vlassova; Babshuk, Nizamutdinova (Norbayeva, 62), Zhumabaikyzy (Popova, 75); Gaistenova, Bibossynova (Osipova, 75), Turlybekova (Sadykova, 75).
REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Brosnan; Patten (Hopcroft, 70), Hayes (Nolan, 70), Stapleton; Mannion, Connolly (Toland, 46), Finn, Mustaki; Murphy (Kiernan, 46), Larkin; Carusa (Barrett, 46).
Referee: Karoline Marie Jensen (Norway).

title: Will El Niño and the polar vortex bring snow to Ireland this winter?
description: UK Met Office prediction has led some commentators to fear a very cold winter across Northern Europe
content:
Why is the polar vortex in the news this week?
The UK Met Office has predicted a combination of changes to the polar vortex and El Niño could bring severe weather to northern Europe this winter.
El Niño is a naturally-occurring phenomenon in the southern hemisphere. It happens when the trade winds that blow east to west in the south Pacific weaken and warm water flows, which usually follows the same east to west pattern, reverse. An El Niño happens every two to seven years. The last one was in 2023-2024.
It usually leads to higher temperatures globally and extreme events. Though it is naturally-occurring, global warming has exacerbated this year’s El Niño with some forecasters calling it a super-El Niño .
Sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific Ocean have already surpassed the highest recorded during any previous El Niño events.
The polar vortex is a current of air 50 kilometres above the North Pole. It keeps the jet stream in place which drives the relatively mild winters that Ireland and Britain experience as it funnels in mild, wet weather from the Atlantic.
When it weakens, it can lead to a sudden stratospheric warming event.
This causes the jet stream to divert southwards, dragging cold easterly winds across northern Europe. If it hits an Atlantic depression, it can bring significant snow events like the Beast from the East in 2018 .
In northern Europe it could lead to a wetter and milder winter, but following the peak of El Niño, the polar vortex can become weaker.
This increases the likelihood of a Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) event. An SSW can lead to a prolonged period of very cold, dry weather from the east. Alternatively, if low pressure lurks on the boundary of the weather system, the combination could trigger significant snow storms.
[ Is Ireland ready for a monster El Nino? Expect ugly potatoes, transport chaos and widespread disruption Opens in new window ]
The UK Met Office has cautioned against assuming the worst-case scenario.
In response to some doomsday reporting, it clarified: “These are shifts in probability rather than guarantees. El Niño does not determine individual weather events, and the current forecast does not support the suggestion that the UK is about to be ‘smashed’ by widespread snow associated with changes to the polar vortex.”
Met Éireann has been even more cautious, saying: “The global mean temperature tends to be higher than average under El Niño conditions, usually with a time lag of several months.
“While El Niño has clear impacts on many regions worldwide through teleconnections (for example affecting monsoon systems), its influence on Ireland and Europe is comparatively weak, highly variable, and not robust in the present-day climate.”

title: Orange Order legal challenge to Garvaghy Road parade ban adjourned to Monday
description: Chris Bryant uses power to intervene and quash Parades Commission decision
content:
A legal challenge to a decision by Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant to halt an Orange Order parade route along the Garvaghy Road in Portadown has been adjourned until Monday.
Lawyers for the Orange Order are applying for the judicial review of the decision announced by Bryant on Friday evening.
Judge Denise McBride said she recognised there was urgency in the case but said it was not an emergency, adding significant material was still to be obtained.
Bryant revoked permission for the Drumcree parade, which had led to a stand-off between Orangemen and nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road in Portadown lasting almost two weeks.
It came after Northern Ireland’s chief constable Jon Boutcher asked Bryant to review the Parades Commission determination which ruled the controversial Orange Order march at Drumcree could go ahead.
The Orange Order is also seeking urgent meetings following the banning of the parade.
Overnight the Orange Order issued a statement to say it is seeking urgent meetings with Bryant and Boutcher in the coming days.
It expressed “profound disappointment” at the decision of the Secretary of State to “overrule the legally established rights of Portadown District Orange Lodge No 1”.
It also claimed a “capitulation to the threat of mob rule and violence”.
