“This unprecedented action, and the abdication of responsibility by the Chief Constable, can be seen as nothing more than a capitulation to the threat of mob rule and violence,” it said.
“In stark contrast, the Brethren of Portadown have complied with the rule of law, exercised restraint and maintained a dignified and resolute stand in the face of intimidation and intolerance.
“It is evident that those who, in defiance of the law, have been content to stand alongside the representatives of those who murdered 345 of our members, have no interest in extending any degree of tolerance or respect towards those who share an Orange heritage.
“Furthermore, it is evident that the statutory authorities have neither the will or ability to uphold the law in this instance.
“We commend the Brethren of Portadown for their resolute stand and reinforce their message that this is a time for responsibility and lawfulness.
“We cannot undermine our cause by adopting the illegal and offensive actions of our opponents.
“Urgent meetings with both the Secretary of State and Chief Constable will be sought in the coming days where their decision making and actions in this matter will be robustly challenged.”
In a statement confirming he was now banning the parade, Bryant said he had not taken the decision lightly.
He thanked the Portadown Orangemen “for their peaceful and law-abiding approach and their co-operation at all points with the PSNI”.
He added: “Respect for the rule of law is fundamental to our society and I am grateful to those who have behaved peacefully and legally and sought to ease tensions in their respective communities. Those who have acted unlawfully should face the consequences of their actions.
“I am also grateful to all those who took part in good faith in the negotiations at Hillsborough. I heard the concerns of people on all sides and I only regret that we could not reach a compromise on a way forward and that many residents across Portadown have felt anxious and worried.
“With this in mind, I call for all protests, rallies and demonstrations to be stood down. There is no excuse for a continued ratcheting up of tensions.”
In a statement on behalf of Sinn Féin, the party’s president and Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill welcomed the decision.
“Today belongs to the residents of the Garvaghy Road, who have shown remarkable strength and dignity in the face of provocation and intimidation. There will be an enormous sense of relief within the community this evening,” they said.
But DUP leader Gavin Robinson said: “These decisions are a mistake, and send profound signals that the country should be run on force of numbers and who shouts the loudest.
“The framework for both parading and protests now lies in tatters and the rule of law has been fundamentally undermined ... The PSNI must now pursue the evidence of lawbreaking without fear or favour.”
The parade, on September 27th, was blocked by protesters on the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road and did not go ahead, and a stand-off between the two sides developed.
In his statement, Bryant said: “The chief constable has advised me that it would not be possible to enable the procession to happen without a major intervention which would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect across Northern Ireland.”
He said the Parades Commission had also advised him that, “while ultimately a matter for the courts to determine, the Commission is of the view that, in light of this current assessment by the chief constable, the original determination does not now have enduring legal effect“.
The PNSI’s chief constable welcomed Bryant’s decision, saying he had asked him to review the matter under section 9 of the Public Processions (Northern Ireland) Act 1998.
“I outlined in my letter to the Secretary of State that my current assessment was that all available, lawful and proportionate options to facilitate completion of the procession had been exhausted.
“Any remaining options would have required a substantial public order intervention that was not assessed to be proportionate, and which would have carried an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion affect across Northern Ireland. Further to this, such an operation would in my view have had not only catastrophic long term consequences for trust and confidence in policing, but for the Northern Ireland Executive and the peace process.
“I also outlined in the letter that mediation and political engagement had not produced a sustainable agreement, and the position of the respective parties had become more entrenched.
“Finally, I highlighted that the current and continuing costs and impact upon the Police Service of Northern Ireland were significant and in the context of our existing funding challenges could not be sustained indefinitely.”
Boutcher added: “This past two weeks has had a marked impact on relationships within and between communities and the police. It is in everyone’s interest that time and space is now created for conversations about finding long term solutions to this complex and sensitive issue.”
A judgment in the latest court challenge to the Parades Commission’s original determination is due to be delivered at the Court of Appeal in Belfast on Monday.
Prior to Bryant’s decision, the Orange Order had warned of “serious consequences” if the Northern Secretary stopped the march.
DUP MP Carla Lockhart said on Friday she expected Bryant would “most likely allow for the court hearing” and reiterated her concerns that “the lawful people ... seem to be cast to the side, and the lawbreakers are being rewarded”.
Earlier on Friday it emerged that Northern Ireland’s First Minister, Michelle O’Neill, is to be interviewed by police in relation to her participation in a protest which blocked an Orange march in Portadown.
In a statement on Friday afternoon, O’Neill – who is also the Sinn Féin vice-president – confirmed she had “ received a letter inviting me for a police interview in relation to a peaceful protest on the Garvaghy Road.
“I will co-operate with the investigation.”
She said that “for the last two weeks, I have stood in solidarity with the Garvaghy Road residents as attempts were made to force an unwanted Orange march through their community.
“I will continue to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents who should be allowed to live in peace and free from sectarian intimidation” because “it is always right to stand up for what is right and there can be no going back”.
[ Who is Chris Bryant, Secretary of State for Northern Ireland? Opens in new window ]
Earlier, Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald had told reporters at a press conference on the nationalist Garvaghy Road that she had not received a letter, but expected to.
On Thursday, a senior PSNI officer confirmed the service was issuing letters to those “reasonably suspected” of having committed a criminal offence in relation to the ongoing stand-off in Portadown .
The Irish Times has seen a copy of one of the letters, which informs the recipient that “it is reasonably suspected that you may have committed offences” linked to the protest against the Orange parade in Portadown, and invites the recipient to a “voluntary interview under caution”.
Sinn Féin Senator Conor Murphy , and MLAs John O’Dowd (Minister for Finance in the Northern Assembly), Gerry Kelly and Deirdre Hargey have received them.
“There will be processes now, legal processes, investigative processes that will be under way, and of course, just like every citizen, of course we are subject to the law, and we will co-operate with it,” McDonald said.
She reiterated her party’s call on Northern Secretary to step in to resolve the dispute, saying she had spoken to him on Friday morning “urging him again to act”.
People Before Profit MLA Gerry Carroll said on Thursday he had been invited by police to attend a voluntary interview under caution in connection with the protest.
It is understood that, as of Friday afternoon, no SDLP members had received letters.
SDLP leader Claire Hanna told The Irish Times she recognises that she may receive such a letter in the coming days.
A statement said she would “always be accountable for her actions and will engage fully with any policing or judicial process”, but “when faced with a choice between standing with the Garvaghy Road community or doing nothing, she is clear that she made the correct decision”.
[ Sinn Féin and the DUP are happier arguing over a parade than agreeing a budget Opens in new window ]
This year was the first time in 28 years that the march, which in the 1990s sparked serious violence which led to more than 20 deaths, was given permission to proceed by the Parades Commission , the body which rules on applications for marches in Northern Ireland.
The decision has been the subject of multiple legal challenges, and the latest judgment is expected in the Court of Appeal next week.
The Garvaghy Road protest was not notified to the Parades Commission, and as an “unnotified” parade is therefore deemed illegal.

title: Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: How does it work if I have €1 or €12,000 to put in?
description: On The Money: How will this new savings scheme work and is it right for you?
content:
Budget 2027 was, in keeping with the personality of the Minister for Finance Simon Harris , an exercise in soundbites – a little across a wide range of areas for everyone . The one exception was the personal investment account.
First flagged back in February, Harris finally provided some of the key details that will govern how people can use these accounts.
With the Central Statistics Office reporting strong savings by households and more than €170 billion sitting in bank deposits – most earning little or nothing in interest – he hopes the new accounts will encourage people to take a little risk with their money in the hope of better returns while providing funding that can help Irish businesses grow.
It’s a move that harks back to the great (and ultimately disastrous) exercise in widespread public engagement with the stock markets that was the flotation of Telecom Éireann.
The Government will hope fervently for a different outcome this time around. The last thing it needs come the next general election is disgruntled investors in a government-sponsored scheme who have lost some of their money.
The personal investment account allows individuals above a certain age to put some money into tax efficient investments rather than keeping it in cash on deposit at their local bank or with An Post or a credit union.
Harris said in the budget that people will be allowed to invest up to €12,000 a year in an account that can be invested in a range of assets. No tax will be charged on these accounts at all until your account balance tops €50,000 and, even then, tax will be levied only on any amount above that tax-free threshold.
The tax rate will be 1 per cent. There will be no capital gains tax, no income tax on any dividends or exit tax as applies on similar investment funds.
You can invest €1 or €12,000 in any year and you can invest it all at once or spread it out weekly or monthly across the year. If you do not use the full limit one year, you lose it. You cannot just carry over some of it to increase contributions the following year above €12,000.
There are no restrictions on taking your money out of these accounts either. You can withdraw some or all of your money when it suits you – subject to the limits of the actual investment product you choose.
These is not like the SSIA scheme where the State actually made contributions alongside you to the accounts. Here, the perk is really the fact that the first €50,000 in the account will be tax free.
Although the details were announced in the budget, they will not be available until July of next year, according to the Minister. This is to allow the Government pass the necessary legislation to set the scheme up and also time for the various investment houses to sort out what options they will offer consumers under the programme.
Anyone over the age of 18 with a personal public service (PPS) number will be entitled to invest. While it has not yet been made expressly clear, the assumption is that they will have to be tax resident in Ireland.
There has been some interest from parents in opening these accounts for their children but, for now, no account can be opened in the name of anyone younger than 18. The Minister did hold out the possibility of the scheme being widened down the line to include children but not for now.
Tell me more about how the tax will work
The headline tax rate is very low – just 1 per cent – which certainly makes it sound attractive. However, you are not just taxed on the gains you make in any year but on the total amount in the account above that €50,000 threshold.
Let’s say you have €50,000 in your account at the start of the year and a strong investment return means your account balance rises to €56,000 by the end of the year. The 1 per cent tax is levied on the €6,000 above the €50,000 threshold – a tax bill of €60.
The following year, the investment return is not so good; in fact, your account loses value and by year end is worth €53,000. Even though you have made no money in that year, the 1 per cent tax charge will still apply to the €3,000 in excess of the tax-free threshold, so you will have to pay €30 in tax on an account that lost money.
That will take a bit of getting your head around.
If I’m going to have to worry about Revenue returns and paperwork, I’m not sure I’m interested
Good news, there will be no paperwork and no tax returns – at least not for you. It will be down to whichever fund manager you invest with to make the returns and ensure Revenue gets what it is owed.
The Government is concerned about the amount of “dead money” sitting in bank deposits earning little or nothing. Inflation means this money is actually losing real value every year. The only “winners” are the banks who deposit it with the Central Bank at European Central Bank rates far in excess of what they offer their customers and then use it as a source of “cheap money” to fund their mortgage lending for which they charge you again, boosting their profits every step along the way.
It is also under pressure along with other states across the EU to do more to encourage investment.
If they are so keen to encourage us to invest, why the €12,000 annual limit? Other countries offer far more scope
True, other countries have significantly higher caps on the amount you can invest in such tax-efficient schemes. Why not here? In part, it’s probably a case of taking a fairly cautious approach to a very new type of investment. The Government really isn’t sure how popular this new account will prove to be and they are also wary of people who understand little about investment throwing money at high-risk products only to suffer losses.
And then there are the banks. They are doing very well off this €170 billion on deposit and will no doubt have let the Government know that an exodus of such funds would only lead to higher mortgage costs as banks had to turn to the market to raise funds for lending.
So what interest rate will the new scheme offer?
Now, see, this is the reason everyone is a bit nervous about this scheme.
This is actually one of the questions that was put to our team in the post-budget Q&A . But this is not a scenario where the State is setting an interest rate on your savings. And, in fact, Harris’s team has previously noted that they are not looking at offering the option to invest in cash funds – which are very low risk and operate a bit like a deposit account.
How well a person does under the personal investment account scheme depends on the return on their investment which will be determined by a host of factors – including your choice of investments.
Even with bonds, for instance, which do offer a set interest rate, your return is also determined by the underlying performance of the bond, which can itself rise or fall. You’ll definitely get your interest – unless the bond issuer defaults – but whether you get your original investment in the bond back depends on the market.
We will get more detail when the legislation is published but what the Minister and his team have said so far is that you will be able to invest in publicly listed company shares, in bonds and in investment funds, including exchange-traded funds – funds that contain a basket of assets that can either mimic a wider index or encourage diversification. These investment funds include those offering exposure to commodities – things like gold or oil.
What will not be permitted is investment in areas of particularly high risk. This includes cryptocurrencies and leveraged investments like derivatives. Areas like private equity and investment in the shares of private companies also seem set to be ruled out.
I know little or nothing about such things. Who will advise me on where to put my money?
You are far from alone. Irish people in general are fairly risk averse when it comes to money, in part because they simply do not understand how markets work. The Government is promising a major financial literacy campaign and the consumer watchdog – the CCPC – has already set up a page to help people understand the concepts around investment. You can find that here . It has also put together a quick online self-assessment quiz with 8 multiple-choice questions to see how ready you might be to consider making investments.
Then, of course, there will be some information provided by the companies that will be selling these investments to you.
You can expect that they will. Fund managers are going to be keen to keep fees low on the products they sell to people under these personal investment accounts but the lower the charge, the less hand-holding you can expect.
The cheapest (and not necessarily the best) products will offer execution only. That means no guidance or personal interaction with the fund manager. It is up to you to do the homework; they simply sell the product if you decide you want it. The hope is that fees here will be around 0.5 per cent or even less.
If you want a more personal service, you can expect the fee will be higher – closer to 1.5 per cent per annum or more.
Only you can determine if this is right for you. The focus on the Government side is to make these accounts as simple as possible to use. They will certainly offer you the chance to make more than you ever will on deposit but, yes, there is an element of risk involved.
It is not all or nothing; different products will have very different levels of risk. And, over time, such investments have outperformed the return on cash deposits.
As it stands, you are losing money on anything you have on deposit in the bank as inflation is now running at 4.1 per cent, way ahead of any interest you are being offered, even before Dirt is deducted.
You can contact us at OnTheMoney@irishtimes.com with personal finance questions you would like to see us address. If you missed last week’s newsletter, you can read it here .

title: Labour holds on to Starmer’s seat as Polanski and Greens lose sheen
description: Greens have been on the slide in polls since Polanski became the target of intense media scrutiny
content:
F urther evidence that some of the political sheen was coming off the briefly once-indomitable Green Party leader Zack Polanski came last month during a gathering of the London Assembly, of which he is a member.
London’s Labour mayor Sadiq Khan faced questions before assembly members. Polanski asked him about data centres and climate change . Khan, who is of Pakistani origin, answered him in fluent Urdu, leaving Polanski flummoxed and embarrassed.
Salford-born Polanski, who was soundly defeated by Labour overnight in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, has a habit of recording campaign videos in pidgin Urdu as part of the Greens’ unabashed and hitherto-successful appeal to Muslim voters.
He didn’t have a clue what Khan was saying. It was a clinical skewering by the London mayor and peer of the Greens’ former it-boy of British politics.
Polanski had once mocked Labour as a party en route to irrelevancy: “We are here to replace you.” Now somewhat revitalised under Andy Burnham , Labour had the last laugh overnight against its main challenger on the left, left clinging to political survival.
The Holborn and St Pancras byelection in inner north London was called after former prime minister Keir Starmer , ousted in July by Burnham, also quit as an MP. The seat was won by the local leader of Camden Council, Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali .
Her victory cements a narrative for Burnham. Having already shown he can beat Nigel Farage ’s right-wingers in Reform UK , which he vanquished during his own Makerfield byelection victory, the Labour leader can now also creditably argue he has a recipe for protecting Labour’s left flank, which under Starmer was menaced by Polanski’s Greens.
It was always going to be a tall order for Polanski to win the Holborn and St Pancras seat. Firstly, it was outside his core political heartland. Although a northern Englander, Polanski’s stronghold is in and around the Hackney area of east London, with its mix of left-leaning, socially conscious hipsters and ethnically diverse communities – for whom the Greens’ mix of anti-Israel rhetoric and left-wing politics is catnip.
Holborn and St Pancras is a much different area, comprising some of London’s legal district, tourist areas around Bloomsbury and settled communities further north in Kentish Town and Camden. Despite Polanski’s widely mocked Urdu exploits, there were never going to be enough anti-Labour Muslims here to get the Greens over the line.
[ Labour retains Keir Starmer’s seat in London byelection Opens in new window ]
He may have been trying to change the narrative for a party that has been on a rollercoaster for more than a year since he became leader. In the spring, the Greens threatened to overtake Starmer’s Labour as second biggest party on more than 20 per cent: the main left-wing challenger to then-leaders Reform.
But the Greens have been on the slide in polls since the summer, when Polanski became the target of intense media scrutiny . Burnham’s elevation compounded matters, and now the Greens, according to the latest YouGov poll, are 16 points behind newly reinvigorated leaders Labour on just 11 per cent.
As well as, potentially, heading back to the fringes, Polanski’s party is now also bitterly divided after its members passed a motion last week declaring that “Zionism is racism” and calling for the abolition of the state of Israel .
The party’s old guard, including former leader Caroline Lucas, have lambasted the divisive motion, which was backed by activist new entrants to the party, akin to the Corbynites who swarmed Labour and hauled it to the left from 2015.
Lucas also criticised Polanski for a lack of leadership on the matter; he is Jewish, but he prevaricated over the motion for fear of upsetting its new activists.
[ British Green Party votes to equate Zionism with racism Opens in new window ]
Polanski still managed to triple the Greens’ vote share in Holborn and St Pancras, so it wasn’t a completely wasted endeavour for the Green leader.
Abdi-Wali’s 45 per cent share for Labour was also ahead of her party’s vote share there in May’s local elections, underlining the existence of the “Burnham bounce”. But her majority is still less than a paltry 3,500, a third of Starmer’s.
Polanski is down, but not yet out. Given the dramatically mercurial nature of recent British politics, who knows what will be the next chapter of the Greens versus Labour.
[ Labour retains Keir Starmer's seat in London byelection Opens in new window ]

title: Garda watchdog Fiosrú logs breaches including laptop left in Dublin taxi
description: Sensitive personal information sent to wrong recipient and correspondence delivered to the Garda Commissioner in error
content:
Garda watchdog Fiosrú logged 38 data breaches in the space of a year and a half, including sensitive information shared with the wrong people and a laptop left in a taxi.
One of the most serious breaches involved an email sent to the wrong person with two attachments containing personal information including a name, address, age, gender and details of allegations.
The incident was categorised as high risk, reported to the Data Protection Commission (DPC) and the individuals involved were notified of what happened.
In another case, a Fiosrú staff member left a laptop in a bag in a Dublin taxi along with a notebook and a document.
The incident was reported to the DPC although the bag was recovered later that day and Fiosrú said the laptop had not been accessed.
The other missing items were also recovered, according to a log of breaches.
Records released under FOI also detail how a letter meant for a complainant was accidentally sent to the Garda Commissioner.
A note of the incident said: “Sixteen update letters were to be sent to the Garda Commissioner and the complainant.
“The [official] tasked with completing the task, inadvertently forwarded the complainant’s letter to the Garda Commissioner.”
Another email intended for Fiosrú’s own data protection unit was instead sent to the data protection office at Dublin Bus .
“Staff members’ emails only personal data disclosed,” said a log.
“Dublin Bus has confirmed double deletion of emails and that they haven’t been shared with third parties.”
Four of the incidents reached the threshold for mandatory reporting to the DPC, according to a statement provided by the watchdog.
The records covered incidents during 2025 and the first six months of this year, spanning the period in which the Garda Síochána Ombudsman Commission was replaced by Fiosrú.
[ Gardaí ‘acted appropriately’ before fatal M9 crash, Fiosrú says Opens in new window ]
The database also lists repeated cases of emails, attachments and correspondence being sent to incorrect recipients, including material relating to complainants and garda members. One case saw a staff member leave a mobile phone in a shop while another involved a copy of an online complaint submission getting issued to an “unintended recipient”.
However, most cases were classified as having a “low” level of risk and did not require notification to the DPC. Asked about the records, a Fiosrú spokesperson said: “In all the recorded incidents, appropriate steps were promptly taken to mitigate the largely low-level breaches, most of which involved email correspondence.”
“Fiosrú has security software on all of its laptops, including two-factor authentication systems and passcode technology for network access. Each laptop hard drive is encrypted.”
The Garda watchdog also said it had introduced data-loss prevention software to ensure that all staff members verify the correct identity of external email recipients and sensitive content attachments before sending messages.
“The software integrates directly into Outlook and prompts users to review and verify external recipients and sensitive content before sending,” the spokesperson added.
[ Donald Trump’s visit forecast to cost Garda up to €30m Opens in new window ]

title: Enzo Maresca refuses to confirm he will stay at Manchester City if club lose appeal
description: Appeal is expected to be heard before Christmas, with a verdict due in the new year
content:
Enzo Maresca refused to confirm he will remain as Manchester City manager should the club lose their appeal against being found guilty of the vast majority of more than a hundred charges related to breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules.
Maresca was speaking publicly for the first time since a verdict that has thrown English football into turmoil was published. City continue to strenuously deny any wrongdoing and their appeal is expected to be heard before Christmas, with a verdict due in the new year.
In May 2022, Pep Guardiola said he would leave the club if he discovered the executive had not told him the truth about their financial dealings. “I said to them: ‘If you lie to me, the day after I am not here. I will be out and I will not be your friend any more.”
Maresca was asked if he shared the same position as his predecessor. “Listen, I would like to speak about this situation when we’re going to win the appeal,” the 46-year-old said. “It’s no sense to speak about anything because I don’t have many pieces of information. I trust the club because I trust the people and this is also the reason why I joined the club. There is not another club in the world where I would like to be. I’m very happy to be [here] I’m very proud.”
Maresca was asked if his trust may change should the appeal be lost. “But it’s the same. I don’t know. We are predicting the future. Again, I’m worried about tomorrow, in two days, in three days,” he said. “I don’t know what’s happening in the future. The only thing I can say is that I think it’s fair, from my point of view, from all of us, to respect the process. The process, verdict. There is an appeal ongoing. We see what’s happening.”
One sanction that might be levied against City is expulsion from the Premier League. Guardiola joked that he would manage City in League One or, even, the National League. Maresca refused to be drawn on that scenario. “I won the Championship with Leicester [in 2023-24]. So in case we [are in] League One, we’re going to see. We are thinking about something that we don’t know,” he said.
Maresca also denied that the many honours City have won under the current ownership are now tainted. “Absolutely not,” he said. “The last time I was here was in the treble [winning] season [2022-3, as assistant manager] and I know the effort from the players, the club, the manager. I know the effort that the club put to achieve that kind of target so I don’t have any doubt about that.”
City lead the Premier League having taken maximum points from their opening five games and travel to Liverpool on Sunday. Maresca has no concern that the uncertainty regarding the club’s future will affect them at Anfield.
“We understand the seriousness of the situation. I’m not saying that we don’t understand that,” he said. “The players understand. But it’s our duty, our job, to try to control the noise. Also, the manager and the players are focused on winning games, not on something different.
“It is nice – at this moment, we are top of the league. So the players have all the reasons to be happy and excited. It will be a tough game for sure. But the most important thing is that we continue to do the right things. We are on the same page with the players, the owner, the CEO, the sport director, and the fans.”
Maresca was asked if referring to the guilty verdict as “noise” was dismissive of the anger felt towards City from sections of the wider football community. “I understand the reason why most of you are here,” he said. “But the only thing I can say is that is something that I already said, that there is a process ongoing.”
Maresca said Erling Haaland was fit after the striker asked to come off last weekend with Norway. – Guardian

title: Pepper hikes rates by up to half a point
description: Increase will add around €30 to the monthly repayments on a €100,000 loan
content:
About 13,000 people with mortgages managed by Pepper Advantage will be hit with interest rate hikes of up to half a percentage point from next month, the mortgage service provider has announced.
The rate increase will mean many of those who have loans with the provider will see the cost of their annual repayments climb by hundreds of euro.
Pepper Advantage blamed the rate increases – which will range from 0.35 to 0.5 of a percentage point – on two distinct interest rate hikes totalling half a point that have been announced by the European Central Bank (ECB) since June.
A 0.5 percentage point increase in lending rates will add about €30 to the monthly repayments on a €100,000 loan.
If a person still has €200,000 outstanding on their mortgage, they will have to pay close to €60 more each month from the end of the year.
The hike will be unwelcome news for thousands of borrowers, not least because Pepper already has variable rates that can be considerably higher than fixed rates offered by traditional lenders.
Many of its customers already struggle to switch to more traditional lenders in search of better value as a result of historic issues with repayments.
When asked the variable rates, a Pepper spokeswoman said the company managed about 130,000 loans, of which about 14,000 were on variable rates.
“These loans sit across multiple portfolios that originated with different lenders and at different points in time. As a result, there is no single ‘Pepper variable rate’ and we don’t have a standard variable rate schedule that applies across all customers.”
She said there were “hundreds of different variable rates across the portfolios we manage. The rate applicable to an individual loan depends on a range of factors including the original lender, when the loan was originated and the type of loan involved.”
Across these portfolios, the current average variable rate on principal dwelling home mortgages managed by Pepper Advantage is approximately 5.2 per cent, she said.
She added that some higher rates still existed within legacy portfolios but “they are very rare, applying to fewer than 100 accounts managed by Pepper Advantage Ireland. Most accounts are around the average rate, with some lower.”
She said it was also worth noting that Pepper Advantage Ireland derived no commercial benefit from changes in interest rates on the portfolios it serviced on behalf of beneficial owners.
The rate hike will inevitably put some borrowers whose loans are owned by Pepper under significant financial pressure.
“Since the ECB started modifying interest rates in July 2022, Pepper has continued to make decisions on interest rates on a delayed and incremental basis, in line with its variable interest rates policy,” the company said in a statement.
“Subject to the criteria and any further announcements by the ECB, Pepper Advantage Ireland continues to review the situation for customers, including any customers not affected by the current announcement.
Pepper Advantage is owned by a US private equity firm JC Flowers. It entered the Irish market in 2012 and is best known for servicing mortgages secured by collateral.
It is used by a number of investment funds for Irish loans acquired after the financial crash.

title: Are the unions right? Did the Government’s budget abandon workers? If they lost, who won?
description: For most people the value of tax cuts looks likely to be more than cancelled out by inflation
content:
S ince details of what was billed as a “workers’ budget ” were confirmed last Tuesday, the various Ministers sent out to meet the press have been at pains to point to all the money the Government is putting back in taxpayers’ pockets.
But although an income tax package of €1.3 billion might sound impressive and a €10-per-week hike in pensions and social welfare payments is more than might have been expected (though lower than Fianna Fáil’s pre-election promise of €12 ), the day-to-day numbers affecting people’s lives don’t lie.
Virtually all the numbers suggest almost everyone will still be poorer next year than in 2026, emboldening public sector workers as they head into two 24-hour strikes on Wednesday and October 21st in an attempt to extract from the Government a new pay deal that would assist with these cost-of-living increases.
Central Statistics Office figures published on Thursday highlight the difficulties many are facing, with prices climbing by 4.1 per cent over the last 12 months, the fastest rate in nearly three years.
“The fact that all spending categories have now recorded annual price increases for three consecutive months highlights the breadth of the cost pressures facing Irish households and businesses,” says Dermot Daly of consultants EY.
He added, however, that the budget “should provide welcome support for households and businesses and help offset some of the cost pressures many continue to face”.
But just how much will it help with those cost pressures?
“This budget was about helping workers stand still,” says Daragh Cassidy of price comparison and switching website bonkers.ie.
“But I don’t view it as some sort of big tax giveaway or boon for workers.”
The big problem, he argues, “is that households are being faced with numerous new cost pressures that will erode most, if not all, of the gains from the budget.
“While workers might be slightly better off next year if they can get a 4 or 5 per cent pay hike, the tax changes alone are unlikely to leave people much better off.”
The cost pressures are easy to identify.
All the domestic electricity and gas providers have imposed hikes in recent weeks, with most households set to be worse off by about €300 over the next 12 months as a result.
The cost of a litre of motor fuel has been on an upward trajectory for weeks and is about 40 cent more than it was in February, even with temporary cuts in excise duty factored in.
A typical Irish motorist uses about 1,100 litres of fuel annually the price spike means it will cost €450 more to keep their car moving in 2027 than in 2025. And, as industry sources have been repeatedly pointing out in recent weeks, the situation might get even worse in the run-up to Christmas.
In January, 500 litres of home-heating oil cost just under €500. Today it’s closer to €800. Most of the 700,000 homes that rely on it will use about 1,500 litres between now and next May and many will probably pay close to €1,000 more for it than they did last winter.
The most recent figures from retail analysts Worldpanel put grocery inflation at 4.3 per cent and if that level is maintained – although it is likely to get worse – a household that spends €200 a week on groceries will be €450 poorer in 2027.
The cost of health insurance has also climbed, with hundreds of thousands of households getting renewal letters in the months ahead likely to pay at least €300 more for the same level of cover.
[ ‘Tipping point’: Why are people giving up their health insurance? Opens in new window ]
People with tracker mortgages are also facing higher repayments as a result of two interest rate hikes from the European Central Bank since June. A person with €150,000 remaining on their mortgage over 10 years will be paying just over €30 extra a month or about €350 annually in 2027 – or even more if rates climb again in December.
A quick tot-up makes it clear that most – if not all – households will be worse off by more than €2,000 next year, a sum that more than cancels out all the tax cuts for even the biggest winners in the budget
The marquee move by Minister for Finance Simon Harris was the raising of the entry point for the higher rate of income tax from €44,000 to €46,500, which will see the annual tax bill of the “winners” on the top rate falling by €500 a year.
Also, increases of €125 in both the personal and PAYE tax credits will be worth another €250 to an individual.
A couple in a double income house where both are earning in excess of €50,000 will probably pay about €1,300 less in tax in 2027 than in 2026.
It sounds impressive but, as Cassidy notes, the increase in the rate at which people start paying the top rate of tax was only 5.7 per cent and there was no increase last year.
“Over the past two years inflation has gone up by around 6 or 7 per cent. So the entry point hasn’t increased in ‘real’ or inflation-adjusted terms,” he says.
“And back in 2010, the cut-off rate was €36,400. Had the rate simply increased in line with inflation and wage growth over the past 15 years or so, it would be over €50,000 today. And of course there was no USC [universal social charge] back then either.”
If those who have fared well out of the budget are still worse off, those who missed out are likely to feel the financial sting even more.
For those on the margins – the half a million people that earn between €32,000 and €44,000 who won’t benefit from the key tax breaks in Tuesday’s budget – the pain will be worse still.
Labour leader Ivana Bacik described the budget as “pathetic” and “underwhelming” and said the money the Government stressed “will go back into people’s pockets could barely buy a chocolate bar a week”.
It was a “sort of KitKat budget from a TikTok Tánaiste”, she said in the Dáil.
“In seeking to please everybody, you’ve ended up pleasing nobody,” she said.
[ There’s a good chance Ireland will come to regret this boomtime period as a missed opportunity Opens in new window ]
Although the Government parties will no doubt bristle at such a suggestion, it has certainly been hard to find anyone outside those circles who was happier after the budget speech than they were before it.
The discontent is only likely to grow as the dark winter evenings set in and the cost-of-living crisis drags on.

title: Eoin Murphy went from being a reluctant goalkeeper to a peerless source of miraculous saves
description: Murphy’s retirement means that only TJ Reid remains from the last Kilkenny team to win the All-Ireland title in 2015
content:
Eoin Murphy, one of the greatest goalkeepers of the modern age, has announced his retirement after 16 years on the Kilkenny panel. “Dreamt it - Lived it - Loved it!” Murphy wrote in a statement released by Kilkenny GAA on Friday morning.
“For more than half my life, I have had the honour of playing with Kilkenny through minor, under-21 and then senior,” wrote Murphy. “I’ve been lucky to be part of some incredible teams and to play alongside some of the greatest players in the game.”
Murphy emerged in time to win four All-Irelands under Brian Cody in the early years of the last decade, but his retirement means that only TJ Reid remains now from the last Kilkenny team to win the title in 2015.
In a golden age for hurling goalkeepers Murphy and Nickie Quaid separated themselves from the herd over the last decade. Quaid established himself as the pre-eminent commander general while Murphy was a boundless source of miraculous saves.
Murphy’s point-blank stop from Peter Duggan in the 2023 All-Ireland semi-final was described by Brendan Cummins on The Sunday Game as the greatest save he had ever seen. Five years earlier, when The Sunday Game panel discussed the Save of the Year, every save on the shortlist was made by Murphy.
David Herity, who has joined Henry Shefflin’s management team for the coming season, was the player Murphy unseated as the Kilkenny goalie in 2013. He said years later that he felt like the Barcelona player who had played in Lionel Messi’s position before Messi arrived.
At some point in the 2012 season, Cody asked Herity for his opinion of Murphy. “Whenever that lad gets in goal,” he said, “no one will take the position off him.”
Just like Quaid, though, Murphy was an outfield player for his club and at the beginning of his intercounty career he was unconvinced about being a goalie. Richie Mulrooney, the former Kilkenny minor manager, tells a story about inviting Murphy to goalkeeping trials for the Kilkenny minors.
In a blizzard of drills he eclipsed the competition but at the end of the session he asked Mulrooney if he could have a trial as an outfield player too, as if he wanted to undo what he had just done. Mulrooney processed the request with the speed of an algorithm: he told Murphy he could have the trial, but it would make no difference.
In Murphy’s mind, that conflict continued for a while. When Waterford IT won the Fitzgibbon Cup in 2014 Murphy captained them from centre back, and when Glenmore won the junior club All-Ireland two years later, he lined out in attack.
Brian Cody fleetingly entertained the possibility of playing Murphy outfield. During the 2011 season Murphy was the third goalie on the panel but they sometimes needed numbers for training matches and in the week before the All-Ireland final Murphy scored 3-3 in an A versus B game, blowing a fuse on someone’s circuit board.
It was too late to make any material difference to his status. On All-Ireland final day his name appeared in the small print on page 45 of the match programme, alongside the other members of the extended panel. But six months later Cody gave him a chance at corner forward in a National League match against Cork. Seven minutes into the second half, that experiment was abandoned.
It wasn’t all plain sailing in the early years. In 2014 Kilkenny conceded five goals in the drawn Leinster semi-final against Galway and Murphy was dropped. After the All-Ireland semi-final against Limerick, though, Murphy was recalled and he didn’t lose his place again until the first round of this year’s championship.
In the second half of Murphy’s career Kilkenny struggled with modern puckout strategies. Going long to self-sufficient forwards was Cody’s preference, which naturally simplified the demands on the Kilkenny goalie. In recent years, and against local convention, Kilkenny tried to manage their restarts more efficiently. Just like all the other intercounty goalies in their peer group, though, Murphy never reached Quaid’s levels as a distributor.
He was extremely comfortable on the ball in open play, though, and wasn’t afraid to use his feet and to take the ball around an incoming tackler. His capacity to keep the ball out of the net, though, was extraordinary in an era when forwards were encouraged to shoot from as close to the goal as possible.
Even in Kilkenny’s fallow years, he stood out: in 2018 and 2021 he was the only All-Star.
“There’s no point in telling lies, you do want to be the difference maker,” Murphy told Christy O’Connor a couple of years ago. “I get a great buzz out of that. In terms of training for that scenario [the save from Peter Duggan], you’d never put yourself in that position. But you still have visions of yourself doing it. It’s exciting. Anyone who says they want to just blend into the background is only talking bullshit.”

title: Paddy McKillen jnr consents to judgment over €2.3m owed to lender
description: Entrepreneur now in personal insolvency process, High Court hears
content:
Businessman Paddy McKillen jnr has consented to a judgment against him over a debt of €2.3 million owed to a lender.
McKillen jnr’s concession arises in circumstances where he is seeking a personal insolvency arrangement.
He recently obtained a protection certificate after a court heard he had debts of €27.7 million. The certificate, obtained late last month, protects him from his creditors for 70 days.
At the High Court on Friday, Martin Hayden, for McKillen jnr, told Judge Eileen Roberts his client was conceding Herbert Street Finance’s (HSF) claim for €2.3 million. He said his side was not in a position to advance its claims, given the personal insolvency process now embarked upon.
The concession comes in proceedings brought by McKillen jnr, in which he claimed HSF was not authorised under Central Bank regulations to grant the loan.
[ Paddy McKillen jnr built a hospitality empire – now the man with €270 in the bank owes €27.7m Opens in new window ]
Bernard Dunleavy, for HSF, asked the judge to grant judgment in favour of the lender for €2,313,970. He asked for McKillen jnr’s claim against HSF to be struck out.
Last month, in an application seeking court protection from creditors, lawyers for McKillen jnr said he was “firmly insolvent” and had just €270 in his bank account.
McKillen jnr, of Torquay Road, Foxrock, Co Dublin, owes €2.9 million to his wife Edel McKillen and €1.8 million to his mother Maura McKillen, the court heard.
In August, McKillen jnr’s bid to strike down HSF’s bankruptcy summons over the lender’s claim was rejected by Judge Liam Kennedy.
The judge found McKillen jnr had not established that the summons was an abuse of process and brought for “an ulterior motive”.
Kennedy also said he was not satisfied McKillen jnr had raised a real and substantial issue to be tried in plenary proceedings. Establishing such an issue is grounds to set aside a summons, the judge said.
McKillen jnr was the co-founder of the hospitality group Press-Up .

title: Ed Abrahamson: October 7th was a piercing, shrieking alarm call for all Jews
description: To some people it makes no difference whether we are Zionist or not, distressed by images of Gaza or not. We are Jews
content:
No one said being Jewish was supposed to be easy; and as the fictional Tevye implored to the Boss in Fiddler on the Roof, in the face of impending pogroms, “I know we are the chosen people, but for once could we just be a little less chosen?”. That sentiment feels truly relevant to our collective experience over the past three years.
Jews have endured thousands of years of tragedy, hardship and attempted eradication. In Ireland, the majority of Jews arrived following pogroms in the late 1800s. They came with nothing, but prospered and became a vibrant, well-liked part of Irish society.
Sadly, the pogroms they escaped heralded a far greater danger to Jews in Europe. At least in Ireland they were safe. Given the current hostility we are experiencing in some quarters, it is ironic Ireland was one of the safest places in Europe for Jews during the Nazi era. This does not mean the wartime government was sympathetic to the plight of the surviving Jewish refugees. The door was firmly dúnta.
The apotheosis of the historical scourge of anti-Semitism, with the elimination of 60 per cent of Europe’s Jewish population, led to the fervent hope it would render this most ancient of hatreds obsolete.
However, although they did not manage to eradicate us, anti-Semitism did not go away. Like the herpes group of viruses, it sat largely dormant, waiting for the right moment, the right vulnerability, to re-emerge.
Never could we have imagined the indescribable horror that once again would afflict the Jewish people on October 7th, 2023 – and as in the Holocaust, it was not only Jews who were slaughtered. This act of war by Hamas and its proxies led to the widely-accepted legitimate right and necessity for Israel to respond to ensure this could never happen again. For years before that, Israel had been accustomed to constant rocket attacks and other terror atrocities against innocent civilians, a fact that receives little attention.
The testimony and images of October 7th are so horrific that Israel decided not to share them widely initially (although there is an argument that perhaps it should have done to show the world the absolute depravity that had occurred). Postwar, and all that has followed, it has been difficult to ventilate witness testimony. A play by two Irish writers, Phelim McAleer and Ann McElhinney, titled October 7: In Their Own Words – which simply repeats the victims’ words through actors’ voices – cannot get a host theatre in Ireland to stage it. This is shameful.
Even before the Israeli military response, the anti-Israel voices were loud. Before a single bullet had been fired, marches were planned, protesters mobilised. Even as Hamas was still rampaging and livestreaming this butchery, the anti-Zionist core, including in Ireland, was printing “Ceasefire now”, “Free Palestine” and “From the river to the sea” posters that became ubiquitous. That last slogan demands the erasure of Israel: how is this not a clear call to genocide by the accepted definition - not the new-moulded and informal one in widespread use?
War is ugly and brutal, and this one has been no exception. Some features of this conflict, including an enemy embedded within the civilian population and a deep subterranean, multibillion-dollar network, have made it highly challenging for the Israel Defense Forces (IDF).
Nevertheless, the scale of destruction in Gaza is immense, and many civilians including children have tragically been killed. There has been undoubted extreme suffering at times, even if there have been widely differing accounts of access to shelter and aid throughout the war.
No child should ever die from hunger, but - according to data supplied by the Gaza ministry of health and published by Unicef and the UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs - the number of children who had died of malnutrition during the war up to August 2025 was thankfully low, at 119, much lower than some people would have you believe and a surrogate indicator of food-delivery efficacy.
Jews have been left in an invidious position, increasingly isolated and explicitly threatened – for being Jewish. A clear example of collective punishment. And it makes no difference when we explain how distressing we find the images from Gaza. We are Jews. That is good enough for those who hate us.
[ Fear of ‘physical harm’ prevents public October 7th events, says Ireland’s chief rabbi Opens in new window ]
There have also always been some Jews who do not support the Zionist construct (I doubt they would be spared), but for most Jews it is a core belief. The word Zionist might seem anachronistic and redundant, as Israel now exists; however, it is just as relevant today, as Israel has lived under constant threat of extinction since its creation.
Many, like me, while passionate about Israel, see no contradiction in feeling able to criticise and deplore the words and actions of the few bad actors in the Israeli government, individuals as detestable as they are racist. They are a minority despite the external perception.
I also call out the small number of execrable far-right Jewish terrorists operating in the Palestinians heartlands within Judea and Samaria, not sited within established Israeli communities. I do not make these statements to enjoy favour among the anti-Semites. Indeed, very many voices in Israel, including the admirable and extraordinary part-Irish president Isaac Herzog , are critical of these extremists.
Extending far beyond criticism of Israeli government or of military actions, we have seen obsessive, cult-like anti-Israel fervour in Ireland and increasingly in the UK, particularly in parts of the sporting, media, academic, trade-union and of course political spheres. The frenzy over the Nations League matches crystallised this. There was an opportunity for sharing perspectives in a civilised, constructive way. Sadly, the oppressive campaign against the players put them in an unenviable position, leading to disrespecting the opponent’s national anthem, Hatikvah, which literally means hope.
[ Chief Rabbi: All the good that might have come from Ireland v Israel has been lost Opens in new window ]
There must be hope; hope for a better future for Israelis and Palestinians. The forthcoming election may bring a reset. I also find hope in Ireland, despite the loud noise amplified and exaggerated via social media. I have come across so many who are neither anti-Semitic nor against the Israeli people, while of course sympathetic to the plight of innocent Palestinian civilians caught up in this war, as anyone with compassion and empathy must surely be.
[ Denis Staunton: How Israel lost the world’s support after October 7th Opens in new window ]
October 7th was a piercing, shrieking alarm call for all Jews regardless of religious observance or attitude towards Zionism. The prevailing global narrative against Israel’s response to October 7th is confirmation of the need for Israel to exist.
For all Jews, our very existence and survival are inextricably linked to Israel. As the great Elie Wiesel wrote: “It is clear to me that one can’t be Jewish without Israel; Religious or non-religious, Zionist or non-Zionist ... all these will not exist without Israel.”
Dr Ed Abrahamson is a consultant paediatrician who writes about Israel and anti-Semitism

title: EU governments agree on long-stalled capital markets reform
description: Deal shifting more financial oversight to European regulator ‘biggest move in decades’, Simon Harris says
content:
Governments have agreed a deal to centralise more oversight of financial markets at European rather than national level, ending years of deadlock that had stalled the key reforms.
Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris said the agreement would represent the biggest overhaul of the EU’s market for capital in “decades”, making it easier for funds and investment to move across national borders.
The proposed changes will shift responsibility for regulating the architecture underpinning financial markets from national central banks and authorities to a European body.
The reforms will expand the remit of the Paris-based European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), a step seen as necessary to align the union’s 27 national markets closer together. Politicians hope the changes will allow more businesses to expand on a European scale.
Officials from the 27 member states have spent months fighting over the scope of the changes.
[ Harris wants deal on contentious EU capital market reforms by October Opens in new window ]
Ireland and Luxembourg have traditionally opposed attempts to centralise oversight of financial markets at European level.
However, because Ireland holds the rotating Council of the EU presidency, a deal-making role in the Brussels political system, the Irish Government has been responsible for negotiating a compromise a majority of member states will back.
“We’ve been talking about this for a hell of a long time. We’ve been talking about deepening capital markets union, completing the single market for decades,” Harris said on Friday.
A large majority of the union’s finance ministers gave the thumbs-up to the complex financial reforms at a meeting in Luxembourg.
Harris, who chaired the discussion, said the agreement represented “the biggest move in decades”, creating a bigger pool of finance businesses could tap into.
“When Europe deepens its capital markets, everybody benefits. When you grow the size of the pie, there is more pie to go around,” the Fine Gael leader said.
The European Commission, the EU’s executive arm that proposed the reforms, sharply criticised how the draft legislation had been watered down by national governments.
“We deeply regret that the compromise now on the table falls significantly short of the level of ambition needed,” Maria Luís Albuquerque, European commissioner for financial services told ministers on Friday.
The most contentious changes, negotiated by the Irish presidency, exclude key financial players from the scope of EU-level oversight. This decision to accommodate “narrow national considerations” undercut the thrust of the reforms, the commissioner said.
The compromise will mean Deutsche Börse Group, who run the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, and three other large trading venues, will remain regulated at national rather than EU level.
The German government argued a carveout was justified on the basis Deutsche Börse only operated in Germany, rather than across EU borders.
Belgium and several other member states, and the commission, were unhappy at the perceived special treatment shown to the German trading exchange.
Speaking to reporters before the meeting, Harris defended the outcome of the negotiations. “It is a compromise proposal. It is the [Irish] presidency’s best assessment of what can bring people with us,” he said.
“If any one of us was sitting down and writing this deal on our own, you’d have a different deal but that’s not how the European Union works, we’re 27 member states,” he said.
At the start of Ireland’s six-month EU presidency in July, Harris said he wanted to secure a capital markets deal by early October, a timeline many politicians and industry figures viewed as overly ambitious.
The Government will now represent the compromise agreed by member states in negotiations with the European Parliament, where MEPs are expected to push for their own revisions and changes before the reforms become law.

title: Visions review: Eoghan Quinn’s play has a lot to say. But rarely has so much been asked of a lamp
description: Dublin Theatre Festival 2026: Derbhle Crotty and Ghaliah Conroy give especially strong performances, but Visions is weighed down by its symbolism
content:
Early on in Visions, the narrator tells us that the play is set in the basement of an old Georgian building in Dublin. Yet the stage is a sparsely furnished rehearsal room. And an enormous chandelier hangs above it. So where are we, exactly, and at what point does it all become a play? These questions hang over Eoghan Quinn’s play like a big, symbolically loaded lighting fixture.
Visions is presented as a rehearsal, with actors reading from a script. Denise (Derbhle Crotty) is project-managing the renovation of what was once a dance hall in the north inner city. She’s part of the sandwich generation, caught between caring for a parent and her embarrassing relationship with a younger man.
To do the job, she has charitably enlisted a friend of her late father, the gruff yet sentimental Tadhg (Mark Lambert), who is less interested in conservation than in preservation – he has too many memories of halls like these to actually finish the work. To make matters worse, the room is being renovated for a gormless thirtysomething tech bro (Oliver Flitcroft). A millennial activist named Aimee (Lauren Larkin) would rather see it become a space for creatives.
The faded dance hall becomes a stage for competing visions of Dublin, while the real city outside is convulsed by far-right rallies, water-charge protests, terror attacks and, perhaps most menacing of all, Leinster rugby fans.
After Denise leads a particularly effective mindfulness session for the group, Visions starts to shift formally. The rehearsal room becomes a liminal space where dreams of the past and visions of the future unfurl and collide.
The narrator (Ghaliah Conroy) tries to maintain some structure, through words and movement, before the boundaries between character, text and set dissolve. It’s less a play within a play than a play without a play.
As director, Claire O’Reilly deftly guides us through this metamorphosis, helped by Katie Davenport’s lithe set and John Gunning’s deceptive lighting design.
Visions has a lot to say, and in O’Reilly’s hands it makes its points well. Perhaps too well. No moment or prop is safe from being loaded with meaning about life in Dublin or the mechanics of theatre. Rarely has so much been asked of a lamp.
If the set is mostly sparse, the script is crammed. Quinn’s text asks big questions about what we preserve and what we reinvent, in our city and in ourselves.
It also includes so many observations about life in contemporary Dublin that it feels more like hot-button bingo than a play. Vulture funds; no spaces for creatives; Irish men can’t express their feelings: it’s all there. The observations on generational divides, which are of the older-people-have-trouble-using-smartphones variety, are also familiar.
Visions has strong performances, particularly from Crotty and Conroy, and is occasionally funny. But with everything in service of theme and idea, the play becomes schematic. Its characters seem to exist only to make a point, never developing beyond what they’re supposed to represent.
For all its formal inventiveness, the result is a play that ends up being exactly the sum of its parts. Visions is all dramaturgy, no drama.
Visions, staged as part of Dublin Theatre Festival , is at the Abbey until Saturday, November 14th

title: Driver (20s) seriously injured in single-car crash in Co Cork
description: Another man has been discharged from hospital following N71 incident near Clonakilty
content:
Two men were brought to hospital following a single-vehicle crash in Co Cork on Thursday night.
The men, both in their 20s, were in a car that crashed on the N71 at Ahalisky near Clonakilty shortly before 11pm on Thursday. They were driving from Bandon towards Ballinascarthy.
The driver of the car suffered serious injuries and was brought to Cork University Hospital, gardaí said.
The other man suffered minor injuries and has been discharged from the same hospital.
Witnesses to the incident, and those who may have dashcam footage in the area between 10.30pm and 11pm on Thursday, have been asked to contact Clonakilty Garda station.

title: ‘It was a tough year’: David Clifford on Kerry, red cards and the demands of being David Clifford
description: Kerry forward reflects on All-Ireland final loss in exclusive interview
content:
With less than six minutes left in the All-Ireland final Kerry were wriggling in quicksand, making one last lunge for an overhanging vine. Every team has a dance to create a two-point shot and in Kerry the music stops when David Clifford sets himself in the launch position.
There were five points between the teams when the ball reached him at a remote northwesterly point on the arc, in front the Cusack Stand. The chance, though, promoted a right-footed attempt. Clifford made a smooth pass at the ball, like Ernie Els or Roger Federer, generating speed in the shot without any sudden movement. It climbed above the tip of the uprights and sailed over the bar.
On the RTÉ commentary, Éamonn Fitzmaurice immediately understood the significance of the shot. “It’s an incredible kick, Marty,” he said. “It’s probably the first two-pointer he has kicked off his right leg this year and what a moment to do it.”
More than that: it was the first right-footed two-pointer he had ever kicked for Kerry. With their season on the line, he trusted that shot.
A couple of months later, Fossa were leading by a point in the Kerry intermediate county final with less than six minutes remaining. In the last three years they had lost two finals and one semi-final, and, in their history, they had never reached the senior grade. All of that was loaded on the scales.
Clifford gathered the ball around centrefield and slalomed into Kilcummin territory and then he performed the most daring pivot: he moved inside the two-point arc and intentionally dropped outside again, as if he had stepped on to a washed kitchen floor and suddenly realised it was still wet.
The referee had his arm raised for an advantage, but Clifford carried on: the chance to shoot was on his right side. “Clifford off the right boot,” said the Clubber commentator in a tone of subtle scepticism. “Surely not. Can he kick it with the right? I think he can. It’s an unbelievable score.”
In an interview four years ago, by which time he had won three All Stars and was about to be named Footballer of the Year for the first time, Clifford said that there was still room for improvement on his right side. So, he chased it. Thomas Edison coined the equation for genius: only one per cent inspiration.
How good was he this year? Clifford lives on the equator between winning and losing, where the climate is always tropical: the sun scorches down, the rain falls hard. Whatever he does, his performances are never divorced from the outcome. In the county final he scored 15 points for Fossa; in the semi-final he scored 16; for East Kerry last week he kicked a two-pointer on the hooter to turn a loss into a win.
His performances are chained to numbers too and when the language of praise and adoration is clapped out, they sometimes shoulder the load. In the All-Ireland final he scored 1-6, which was more than anybody else on the field. Over the span of the championship, he was the overall top scorer, the top scorer from play and scored the most goals. With Clifford, all of it is blended into the sauce until you can’t distinguish the basil from the oregano.
Nobody notices until the numbers drop suddenly, like a bad day on the Iseq index. He says there are “always other fellas I can throw the ball off to if I’m getting extra attention or whatever and there’s been loads of days where I might hardly score at all and other fellas will step up”.
But he never has permission to be just a provider or a cog in the wheel. The auditors only want to see the numbers. “I probably don’t look at the personal numbers on it,” he says. “Like, I suppose my job with Fossa is to get the scores, do you know what I mean? That’s the way our game plan is set up.”
That is also true, though, of Kerry and East Kerry and every team he has played for since he was a boy. Finishers are yoked to the bottom line.
“I suppose, look, that’s what I enjoy doing.”
In a superb piece of analysis in the Irish News last month, Cahair O’Kane drilled into the three nominees for Footballer of the Year and produced a comparative panel of their statistics from the championship. Across more than a dozen metrics, Clifford had the best numbers in two-thirds of the categories, but among the exceptions one stood out: Ryan O’Donoghue had been involved in 17 turnovers for Mayo and Clifford had been involved in none for Kerry.
“I suppose, it’s not as if you shouldn’t be tackling either,” he says. “Like, I suppose, the manager wouldn’t be too happy with that.”
[ Cillian O’Connor gets the ending he deserved to one of the greatest careers in GAA history Opens in new window ]
Some species of sharks can lay motionless at the bottom of the sea for long periods and there are times in Kerry games, when the ball is elsewhere, that Clifford is a study in stillness. It always seems like it is by design.
“Well, sometimes it is anyway,” he says, smiling.
In Kerry, every season has a binary quality. Without an All-Ireland, it is a failure. Clifford suggests that it must be like that in other counties too, but only from time to time and in very few other places. In Kerry, the commandments are handed down from the Old Testament.
“Obviously, there’s major disappointment that you didn’t get over the line [against Mayo]. You kind of watch it back and see snippets of it and stuff and you try to come up with your own ideas about why it didn’t go well. We started relatively well and got a big lead in the game [with Clifford’s first-half goal] and then Mayo thundered back into the game. We missed three or four shots in the next few attacks.
“We kind of couldn’t find the answers for a while and they took over in the second half. Everyone knows momentum can be hard to wrestle back. We rallied late in the game, but we came up short ultimately.”
After his right-footed two-pointer Clifford had another chance to draw the game from outside the arc. In those situations, he was never going to shovel it off to somebody else: the shooter shoots. “I struck it well, but it seemed it was kind of always just offline. It started probably at the right post, and I needed to start it at the left post. I’d love to have it back and take it again, but sure, we can’t.”
It had been a topsy-turvy year. When Kerry won the All-Ireland in 2025 there were long stretches of the season when the exhaust was hanging down and it was sparking against the tarmac as they went; this year, they slid into the ditch a couple of times, but until the final, it never looked like they wouldn’t reach their destination.
“It was definitely a tough year. I suppose we had a couple of kind of peaks and troughs. We were kind of flying in the league and then got rocked back in the league final [against Donegal]. Then you’re having to come again. We did well in Munster, but Donegal beat us again in the first round of the group so you’re having to come again. We were poor [that day]. We missed a lot of chances in the first half and then they were clinical. They were a good bit better than us on the day. It was a gun to the head situation then that we had to improve.”
That game went rogue. Jim McGuinness escaped censure for pushing a Kerry player during a melee at the end of the first half; earlier Clifford had evaded punishment for leading with his elbow into the neck area of Caolan McGonagle. Both incidents were lightning rods for uproar and the usual rounds of whataboutery for the next couple of days, but no retrospective action was taken by the GAA. Did Clifford think he was lucky?
“I was happy to stay on the pitch, definitely,” he says, without entering a plea.
Did he think it would come back to bite him?
“I don’t know really. I suppose in the middle of a game you don’t think about it. Then the fact that we had got beaten so well you’re kind of saying, ‘we got to sort this out’.”
For all of his playing life he has been a marked man. Before the new rules came in, it wasn’t unusual for Clifford to be double-teamed; that is harder now. Was he blackguarded along the way? The answer must be yes, although he deflects the question. At other times in his career his response to provocation wasn’t always as controlled as it is now. He came to a reckoning with that.
“Did I get upset with someone marking me? Not in a good few years anyway. I was sent off a couple of times when I was younger. One time with Kerry and I got sent off a couple of times with East Kerry [and in the final minute of the All-Ireland junior final with Fossa]. It was just stupid stuff. It’s a shitty feeling when you do get sent off.”
After the All-Ireland he went on holiday with his partner and son to a part of Spain where “it wasn’t a big Irish spot”. At home it is impossible to take cover. Every GAA star lives in the mainstream of local life. The people who talk about him want to talk to him. In his job as a teacher in Killarney, his public are looking up at him from behind their desks.
[ For the average GAA player, this time of the year brings a mix of regret and relief Opens in new window ]
But the attention is omnipresent: it has no filters or boundaries. In an interview with Michael Foley after he retired, Brian Fenton spoke about a night he spent in Clifford’s company in Killarney.
“He was a Beatle. People were genuinely coming up and just touching him. Like they were touching Jesus Christ,” he said.
You wonder if he tires of it: the micro intrusions on his time from strangers and people he might know a little; the endless rounds of questions about football, as if he had thoughts on nothing else.
“It’s an interesting one. Like everyone says that I probably get sick at times of talking about Kerry and the intercounty game, but I would never get sick of talking about underage football or club football, because it’s not concerning me, do you know what I mean?
“All of my friends are playing with different clubs, so I never get sick of it in that sense. But there are times I suppose with the whole intercounty thing, when the seasons are long and stuff, there are times when you are tired.”
On Tuesday night, a proposal to create a four-to-six week break in the off-season for Kerry’s intercounty players was defeated after what was described as a “fiery” debate at the county board. Clifford has experienced those seasons where the horizon keeps moving. In 2022 he lined out in nine different competitions for five different teams and ended up winning eight of them. Winning shortens the road.
In January 2023 that season ended with Fossa in Croke Park. For the Cliffords, Croke Park had always been a place of pilgrimage. His parents had been stalwarts of the Kerry Supporters Club and David, Paudie and their sister Shelly joined them on the bus trips to wherever Kerry would lead them.
“We basically went to every championship match and a good shot of league games and stuff like that. I remember being at games in Croke Park and being jealous of the people living in Dublin because you’d be mad to go for a kick after watching the game. But then you’d have to travel home four or five hours or whatever so it would be too late by the time you got home.
“It’s one of the days that stands out, being there with Fossa, and seeing players [that you grew up with] getting to play there and the supporters being up there. And even the idea of having a function in Dublin and it not being with Kerry, but being with Fossa.”
[ Halfway there? Gaelic games integration timeline is no clearer after Dáil committee Opens in new window ]
News of Éamonn Fitzmaurice’s appointment as the new Galway manager broke on the day before we met. Fitzmaurice gave Clifford his senior debut with Kerry, eight years ago now, and after he finished with Kerry he was involved with Fossa for four years. You can imagine what Clifford thought: “They’re lucky to have him. Definitely.”
Before this year’s All-Ireland final Fitzmaurice wrote a beautiful portrait of Clifford in the Irish Examiner and, in that piece, he told a story about the one-on-one meetings that management used to have with each player before the season began. As a rookie, Clifford wasn’t spared friendly fire.
“Liam Hassett [Kerry selector] was the dog that went after fellas with hard questions. He thrived in the role. He threw a few scuds in David’s direction, to assess him. He didn’t even blink and handled everything with aplomb. I struggled not to laugh. Liam was doing his level best to ruffle David’s feathers but try as he might he couldn’t.”

title: Ireland under-21s to face Finland in Euro 2027 playoffs
description: Evan Ferguson is still eligible to play if he can return from ankle surgery in time
content:
The Republic of Ireland under-21s will face Finland in a playoff to reach the 2027 European Championships in Serbia and Albania.
Jim Crawford’s side must travel to Finland for the first-leg on November 11 th before the second-leg potentially returns to Turners’ Cross in Cork on November 17 th .
Ireland finished runners-up in Group D behind England following a 3-1 defeat of Lee Carsley’s defending Euros champions last Monday in Cork thanks to a brace from Waterford striker Tommy Lonergan and Gillingham midfielder Conor McManus.
Crawford has a strong pool of players, with Rory Finneran and Adam Brennan capped by senior Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrímsson last summer, but Evan Ferguson is still eligible to play for the under-21s if he can return from ankle surgery ahead of the playoffs.
Ireland complete their Nations League campaign away to Austria on November 14 th and at home to Kosovo the same night the under-21s host Finland in the second-leg.

title: PTSB dissident shareholder Scotchstone latest to signal possible bid
description: PTSB agreed in April to be taken over by Austria’s Bawag in €1.62 billion deal
content:
A long-term dissident shareholder in PTSB , Scotchstone Capital, has become the latest party to say it is considering making an offer for the bank, weeks before the High Court is due to hold a sanctioning hearing on its takeover by Austria’s Bawag .
Scotchstone is led by Piotr Skoczylas and had pursued a series of cases in the Irish courts stemming from PTSB’s taxpayer bailout and effective nationalisation in 2011.
“There can be no certainty that any offer will be made or as to the terms on which any offer might be made,” the company said in a statement on Friday.
Skoczylas declined to comment when asked by The Irish Times about investment banking advisers and funding for a potential deal.
The announcement comes seven days after a corporate finance firm cofounded by former Bank of Scotland (Ireland) chief executive Mark Duffy said it is considering a bid for PTSB , almost six months after the bank agreed to sell itself to Austria’s Bawag for €2.97 a share, or €1.62 billion in total.
[ Has Mark Duffy left it too late to spoil the PTSB party? Opens in new window ]
Axis Capital, which was set up in Dublin three years ago, said any possible offer would be in cash at a price of €3.20 per share – 7.7 per cent above the agreed price with Bawag.
However, the firm said that it has yet to line up funding for such an offer.
Both Skoczylas and Duffy were open critics of the Bawag deal.
Scotchstone launched proceedings in May in the High Court – which is ultimately overseeing the sale process, structured as a so-called scheme of arrangement – seeking a second vote on the deal by minority shareholders, excluding the Government.
