The State owns 57.5 per cent of PTSB and voted in favour of the Bawag transaction at an extraordinary general meeting (EGM) in July.
Judge Mark Sanfey said in the May court proceedings that the usual practice is for shareholder voting class composition to be decided at a High Court deal sanctioning hearing. That is due to take place on October 27 th .
PTSB secured backing from 91.3 per cent of shareholders – led by the Government – for the Bawag takeover at the July EGM. However, some 36 per cent of minority investors voted against the transaction at the meeting.
PTSB has repeatedly said that it has “very strong” legal advice that only one vote is necessary.

title: How to talk to your children about school strikes
description: While it might be tempting to air your frustrations, a better approach might be a clear, open discussion
content:
This week, more than 70,000 members of the Irish National Teachers Organisation (INTO) and Association of Secondary Teachers Ireland (ASTI) joined a work-to-rule that started in other sectors last week as part of a public service-wide dispute over pay.
This means teachers are only working their core hours, not before or after class times. Parent-teacher meetings are not taking place outside of school hours, nor are staff meetings.
There is also no supervision before or after the school day officially starts, meaning parents have been limited in terms of when they can drop off or pick their children up from school.
The first thing is that the Teachers Union of Ireland (TUI) is due to join the industrial action on Monday, October 12th.
Then, in what is a serious escalation, almost all schools across the country are likely to close for two 24-hour periods.
The first will be Wednesday, October 14th, and the second on Wednesday, October 21st.
Pickets will be placed at school gates and children across the country will not be able to attend.
The industrial action centres around a dispute over pay.
The latest public service pay agreement expired in June, and initial talks between the unions and the Government to initiate a new deal did not end positively, which has led to the industrial action.
ASTI said the unions were seeking a “meaningful public service pay deal” that “addresses the cost of living crisis for teachers”.
Meanwhile, senior Government figures have been out this week saying they are willing to sit down and talk.
[ Public sector pay dispute ‘unwarranted given our willingness to talk’, Taoiseach says Opens in new window ]
The budget does not appear to have eased tensions. Chairman of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions (ICTU) Kevin Callinan, who will lead the union side in any negotiation, said on Wednesday it failed to “move the dial”.
It is worth preparing them (and yourself) for the very real prospect that schools could be closed on Wednesday.
Depending on their age, you could try to explain that their teachers are looking to be paid more for their work in an increasingly expensive world.
The strikes, the picket lines, the megaphones and chants are how workers sometimes try to get the attention of the Government to secure better conditions at work.
While it might be tempting to air your frustrations about the disruption these closures will cause in your own life, a better approach might be a clear, open discussion about what is about to happen and why.

title: DCC investors to receive a lower extra payment as tech unit sells below target price
description: DCC said its shareholders are set to receive 42 pence per share from that Nexora deal
content:
DCC Energy shareholders are only set to receive a third of the additional maximum £1.25 (€1.47) payment on offer as part of the group’s takeover deal, contingent on a follow-on sale of it is technology unit.
The Dublin-based group agreed in late July to sell itself to US private equity firms KKR and Energy Capital Partners (ECP) for a £65.25-a-share upfront payment and the prospect of £1.25 extra per share if the Irish company’s tech division achieves at least $800 million (€712.7 million) in a sale.
However, DCC said on Friday that it is set to only receive net proceeds of $701 million for the tech unit, which it has agreed to sell to New York private equity firm One Equity Partners.
DCC said its shareholders are set to receive 42 pence per share from that deal. The technology unit, called Nexora, was already on the market before the consortium make their bid approach in April.
“Under the terms of the transaction agreement [with KKR and ECP], if the technology disposal net proceeds are between $650 million and $800 million, the technology disposal additional consideration will be between zero and 125 pence per DCC Energy share calculated on a linear basis,” DCC said.
That reduces the total value of DCC’s imminent takeover from £5.73 billion to £5.66 billion.
The High Court in Dublin is due to hold a sanctioning meeting on the takeover, which was approved by shareholders last month.
“Nexora has been an important part of the DCC Group for many years and has built a strong market position through the expertise and commitment of its people,” said DCC chief executive Donal Murphy .
“This transaction recognises the quality of the business that the Nexora team has built and, subject to completion, will deliver additional value for DCC Energy shareholders. We believe One Equity Partners is well placed to support Nexora’s continued growth, investment and long-term development, benefiting employees and customers alike.”
DCC, whose businesses once spanned Robert Roberts tea and coffee and waste management, decided in late 2024 to abandon the remaining elements of its conglomerate roots to focus on energy. It subsequently sold its healthcare division and part of its tech business last year, before putting the larger part of the tech unit Nexora on the market.
Murphy signalled in a phone interview with The Irish Times after the shareholder meeting last month that he would like to remain on board to see out DCC’s goal to double the operating profit of the remaining energy division to £830 million between 2022 and 2030.

title: Up to 700,000 people estimated to have died due to USAid cuts, Minister to say
description: Neale Richmond to tell EU ministers that cuts to international development cost lives
content:
Up to 700,000 people around the world are estimated to have died as a result of cuts to international aid put in place by the Trump administration, the Government will tell a meeting of EU development ministers on Friday.
Minister of State at the Department of Foreign Affairs Neale Richmond will say that “cuts to development and humanitarianism cost lives”.
He will tell a meeting of EU development ministers and other key figures in international humanitarian assistance and global crisis response at Dublin Castle that “people across the world have and will die from political decisions”.
“It has been calculated that the cuts to USAid alone has cost the lives of between 500,000 and 700,000 people globally.”
The US Agency for International Development (USAid) was closed down by the Trump administration in July last year. In the preceding months more than 80 per cent of its programmes had been cancelled with the remainder absorbed into the US State Department.
Richmond will tell EU ministers in his speech on Friday that HIV and malaria rates are “going back up”. He will say that this is “something that we have not seen for decades”.
“It is estimated that up to 10.8 million additional new HIV infections and up to 2.9 million HIV-related deaths in children and adults could occur up to 2030. This is as a direct impact of cuts to global development, but the impacts of these and similar crises will not be contained by higher walls.”
Richmond will also say that instability is on the rise across the world and global food security is “on the edge”.
[ Lone star Trump believes he can bend Texas and midterm elections to his will Opens in new window ]
“Experts are warning that the coming months will see increasing inflation in global food costs as a consequence of conflict, economic disruption and climate impacts. The consequences will have particularly severe implications for vulnerable countries and communities,” he will say in the speech.
“It is a sad fact that in 2026, we are witnessing two man-made famines – in Sudan and in Gaza, and significant food insecurity in Mali, Haiti and South Sudan, among many other places. This is an intolerable situation which we must seek to address with the highest level of urgency. Indeed, the World Food Programme has warned that we could soon see four active famines.”
[ Christa Pike ‘up and walking’ after botched execution, lawyer says Opens in new window ]
Richmond will say that ministers and others gathered at Dublin Castle on Friday have a power with “the potential to drive change and save the lives of millions of people around the world”.
“This is particularly vital as we face a world with more autocracy, in which democracy and our other deeply held values are under threat, and in which conflict and humanitarian suffering is on the rise.
“We cannot allow the political decisions of others and the financial pressures that we all face to contain our commitment to our values. To put it even more starkly, the question that we must answer is: how do we secure the future of the development and humanitarian system?”

title: A Man from the Future review: What took Pet Shop Boys so long to release this wonderful album?
description: The tragedy of Alan Turing’s life is at the heart of Neil Tennant and Chris Lowe’s synth-pop rock opera about the gay computer pioneer
content:
The most pressing question raised by this wonderful new Pet Shop Boys album is not why Neil Tennant and Chris Lowe have chosen to release a synth-pop rock opera about the gay computer pioneer Alan Turing but why they didn’t get around to it sooner.
Turing was one of the fathers of modern computing – a title he of course must share with the 19th-century University College Cork mathematics professor George Boole – but his career was severely damaged when he was prosecuted for gross indecency in 1952.
That tragic story carries obvious resonances for Pet Shop Boys, who were still very much in the closet in the 1980s, when gay celebrities lived in mortal terror of being outed by the tabloids.
There are other, more modern resonances to the story of Turing’s ground-breaking work in computer science and his subsequent downfall. We live in the age of the thinking algorithm, with AI promising, or perhaps threatening, to remake our lives in radical and not necessarily pleasant ways.
Nobody can predict how this story ends, but we know that it begins with Turing, who devised the “Turing test”, a process to judge whether a machine can exhibit human-level intelligence. Left to his own devices, who knows what other contributions he could have made to AI or how he might have impacted on the future.
He was instead arrested for gross indecency and subjected to chemical castration.
Had any of this happened in Ireland it would still be rolled out as a signifier of how priest-ridden the country was in the mid-20th century. But because it was Britain, Turing has instead ascended to pop immortality as the subject of one of the better Pet Shop Boys albums of the past decade, a significant improvement on the undercooked Nonetheless, from 2024.
That record was a halfhearted tilt at capturing the dance-floor glories of the mid-1980s, when Tennant and Lowe ruled the charts as a two-headed Noël Coward of disco hedonism. But there has always been another, more melancholic Pet Shop Boys, and that’s the register they adopt throughout A Man from the Future, which unfolds under a deep hum of sadness.
The tone is set with an opening narration by the actor Juliet Stevenson , who imperiously frames Turing’s life as a tug of war between the flesh and the intellect.
Tennant takes up that message on He Dreamed of Machines, a synth odyssey where his vocals tremble and Lowe’s synths stab with woozy majesty. It’s like encountering Wagner in a funeral home.
The ache is even more pronounced on The Enigma, a quietly pounding floor-filler, and on the ballad Other Ranks, which lurches into a sinister jazz refrain. Here Turing is a man on the town, enjoying whatever the night has in store, not yet understanding how his private pursuits will lead to his public undoing.
The sense that something awful is hurtling down the electronic ley lines is intensified on The Memory and the Control, a stringed piece underpinned by a rising claustrophobia.
Down and down we go into Turing’s personal hell on The Trial, where violins sigh and an electronic beat twitters as Tennant reads out the charges of “gross indecency” brought against him under British law.
The album, which Pet Shop Boys recorded with Manchester Camerata Octet – the orchestrations are by Sven Helbig – finishes with the elegiac title track. “Can you feel what I feel?” Tennant sighs, capturing what it must have felt like to Turing as the country he had given so much to turned on him so viciously.
A Man from the Future was originally performed at the Royal Albert Hall, in London, in 2014, as part of the BBC Proms, when critics were puzzled by its restraint. Fair enough: a lament for a tragically misunderstood postwar boffin is not everyone’s idea of a cracking night out. On record, however, that moderation proves highly effective, bringing Turing to life as a genius whose thoughts and emotions were too big for postwar Britain to comprehend. (The album is credited as a collaboration with Andrew Hodges, one of Turing’s biographers.)
What Pet Shop Boys don’t do is wrestle at any great length with the darker aspects of Turing’s legacy, particularly his role as a founding figure in AI. That would be a very different album. Instead, A Man from the Future positions Turing as a visionary ripped apart by the British establishment. He had so much left to say – and, on this understated LP, he is allowed to roar.

title: Ireland ready for midday meeting with Kazakhstan
description: Carla Ward’s team face into first leg of World Cup playoff in Astana
content:
On the rare occasion over the last decade and a bit that Ireland went in to a game without the services of both Katie McCabe and Denise O’Sullivan it would have been framed, writes Gavin Cummiskey, “as an impending disaster”. Not so much this time, Kazakhstan, their opponents this afternoon in the first leg their World Cup qualifying play-off , ranked a whole 77 places below them in the Fifa list. Gavin previews the game in Astana, the return leg taking place in Páirc Uí Chaoimh next Tuesday.
Mercifully, Republic of Ireland head coach Carla Ward doesn’t have to cope with egos quite as humongous as the one Cristiano Ronaldo possesses, his carry-on with Portugal recently, including issuing a bizarre 1,800 word statement, persuading Gavin Cooney that the Ronaldo v Messi debate has been settled . And there is only one winner.
On the home front, Paul Buttner reports on Shamrock Rovers going top of the table after their 3-1 win over Drogheda United on Thursday night, John McGovern helping himself to a double.
In Gaelic games, Malachy Clerkin doffs his cap to Cillian O’Connor, the Mayo man who announced his retirement from intercounty football earlier this week. He was “one of the all-time greats of the game” , who produced “one of the greatest careers in the history of the GAA”.
Gordon Manning has news on John Horan being confirmed as the new chair of the Steering Group on Integration , the former GAA president taking over from Mary McAleese in the role. And Gordon also talks to Dublin goalkeeper Evan Comerford who, after a decade as Stephen Cluxton’s understudy, has set his sights on a long stint as number one.
In rugby, it’ll be a poignant occasion at Pairc Ui Chaoimh tomorrow week when Munster will mark the 10th anniversary of Anthony Foley’s death before their Champions Cup game against Racing 92. And as Gerry Thornley reminds us, it was on the eve of a game against the same opponents in Paris in 2016 that the Munster legend died.
Gerry has all the team news ahead of this weekend’s URC games , Bundee Aki set to make his first start of the season for Connacht away to Glasgow Warriors this evening. Leo Cullen has named a completely changed Leinster starting XV for tomorrow’s meeting with Cardiff at the RDS , their first competitive game at the venue in over two years. And there are changes aplenty too in the Ulster and Munster line-ups ahead of their tussle in Belfast tomorrow afternoon.
And in racing, after Daryz won back-to-back Prix de l’Arc de Triomphes , where does he sit among the pantheon of greats? Look away now, Daryz: “It’s an easy starter for 10, since the answer is that he’s hardly on it at all,” writes Brian O’Connor.
TV Watch : The Republic of Ireland’s World Cup qualifying play-off away to Kazakhstan kicks off at noon (RTÉ 2), and an hour later Sky Sports Golf starts its coverage of the second round of the Spanish Open - Shane Lowry had a solid opening round of 70 , leaving him four shots off the lead. Connacht are away to Glasgow in the URC (TG4 and Premier Sports 1, 7.45pm), and at the same time Bohemians and Waterford square up in the FAI Cup semi-finals (RTÉ 2).

title: Alleged victims of paedophile priest may seek winding up of school if damages not paid
description: Lawyers threaten petition against St Colman’s College in Newry over alleged abuse by paedophile priest Malachy Finegan
content:
Five men who claim a paedophile priest groomed and abused them may seek the winding up of a Co Down school if agreed damages of £1.2 million (€1.4 million) are not paid out.
Lawyers for the group have threatened to lodge a high court petition against St Colman’s College in Newry unless their demand over the settlements is met.
The development came amid continuing uncertainty over the Catholic Diocese of Dromore’s financial capability to fund historical clerical abuse compensation cases.
A number of actions have already been temporarily suspended under a moratorium on outstanding lawsuits. The diocese is seeking legal clarification on whether parish property can be sold to help meet any liabilities to victims.
It has been sued in a series of cases, many of them centred on the activities of paedophile priest Malachy Finegan.
Finegan, who died in 2002, allegedly groomed and sexually abused boys while he taught and worked at St Colman’s College in Newry, Co Down.
Millions of pounds in damages have already been paid out in lawsuits mounted over failures to prevent him from targeting pupils.
Church authorities set up a redress scheme in 2021 for survivors of sexual abuse perpetrated by clergy within the diocese, with payments capped at £80,000.
Other steps have been taken to liquidate or realise assets to help compensate claimants. Last year the sale of the bishop’s house in Newry was completed, while the sale of associated land remains pending.
Proceedings before the chancery division of the high court in Belfast are examining what other assets are available to trustees for any settlements in compensation claims.
In October 2025, however, five former pupils at St Colman’s agreed combined total settlements of £1.2 million.
The group sued the diocese and the school’s board of governors over alleged failures to protect them from Finegan.
Their actions, based on claims of historical sexual and physical assaults, were settled without any admission of liability.
But, according to the men’s legal team, legal counsel William Gowdy and solicitor Claire McKeegan of Phoenix Law, the settlements remain outstanding.
McKeegan said that a statutory demand for payment has now been lodged as a potential first step towards seeking a winding up petition against St Colman’s.
“The victims and survivors are now more than a year on and despite agreeing settlements ... not one penny has been paid to them,” she said.
“They are further traumatised by the delay and uncertainty which unfortunately has characterised the approach of the diocese and the college to this series of serious and grave cases.”
Further information during a review hearing about the school’s insurance has provided no comfort, the solicitor claimed.
“Our clients have served statutory demands, and if they are not satisfied they are left with no option than to [seek to] wind up the college,” McKeegan said.

title: Ireland weather update: Met Éireann forecasts rain showers and sun for weekend
description: Unsettled weather will continue into next week, Met Éireann says
content:
More unsettled weather is on the way this weekend with a mix of sun and showers, according to Met Éireann .
Friday has started off dull and rather wet in many parts of the country, with a band of rain moving southwards across Leinster and Munster, the national forecaster said.
Brighter conditions will follow later with a mix of sunshine and scattered showers. It will be a breezy day in some areas, though much of the east and south of the country will remain dry.
Highest temperatures will range from 11 to 14 degrees during the day, dropping to 8 to 11 degrees tonight.
Saturday will be another breezy day with northwesterly winds. Overall, tomorrow will be a mix of sunshine and isolated showers. It will be dry in many areas by Saturday evening with highest temperatures of 11 to 15 degrees.
Saturday night will be cloudy and cool across much of the country with just some light rain in Connacht and Ulster, Met Éireann said.
It is expected to be mostly dry elsewhere, but rain will push in across southern counties overnight. Lowest temperatures will range from 3 to 7 degrees.
Sunday is due to be a rather unsettled day with overcast skies and some rain moving in across Munster and south Leinster. Temperatures will reach 12 to 16 degrees.
More cloud will build later in the day with rain becoming widespread throughout the evening.

title: Sentencing of Polish man who imported cocaine valued at €8.4m delayed again
description: Michal Luczak flew Cessna plane that transported drugs to Abbeyshrule aerodrome in Co Longford
content:
A Polish pilot found guilty of importing cocaine valued at more than €8 million on a four-seater plane into a midlands airport has appeared before the Circuit Court again.
Michal Luczak (45), formerly of Primrose Avenue, Jigginstown, Naas , Co Kildare , was produced from custody on Thursday to Mullingar Circuit Court and appeared before Judge Deirdre Browne.
His trial last year heard he wanted to become a commercial pilot and often brought his friend, Timothy Gilchrist, who was interested in flying and travelled as a passenger.
Evidence was given that a Cessna 182 aircraft, owned by eight shareholders, including Luczak, left Abbeyshrule aerodrome bound for le Touquet Airport, France, on August 3rd, 2022.
Luczak was accompanied by Gilchrist and the pair stayed overnight before flying to Dieppe airport the next day.
Jurors heard the aircraft returned with 120kg of cocaine worth €8.4 million. A Garda surveillance operation had been put in place at Abbeyshrule aerodrome, where the Cessna was unloaded.
All six bags were put in Gilchrist’s Alfa Romeo car and driven away before Gilchrist was stopped by gardaí at Lough Owel outside Mullingar , Co Westmeath . He was jailed for 11 years for his role.
Luczak had left the aerodrome in a black Mercedes car. He was stopped and arrested at Collinstown, Co Westmeath.
Luczak was described by the prosecution during his trial as a vital asset, irreplaceable and “key to the success” of the smuggling plot.
Browne heard that since the guilty verdict in Luczak’s case in October 2025 his sentencing had been adjourned on five occasions.
On two of these occasions Judge Roderick Maguire, who tried the case, was unavailable while the remaining three adjournments were granted to Luczak.
Browne heard Luczak changed his legal team in March from that which represented him during his trial, and that they needed time to familiarise themselves with his case.
Browne also heard Luczak’s case was adjourned in July to Thursday to allow for the preparation of a psychological report.
Cathal Ó Braonáin, barrister for the Director of Public Prosecutions , said it was his understanding the report would be ready for the sentence hearing fixed by Maguire for November 9th.
Luczak, who wore a double-breasted suit and tie on Thursday, also handed a handwritten letter to the court.
Ó Braonáin said the one-year anniversary since the guilty verdict in Luczak’s case was approaching and the State was anxious to finalise matters.
Andrea Callan, barrister for Luczak, and who was standing in for Ciaran Mulholland, Luczak’s solicitor, said Luczak was not trying to be difficult but wished to put his “best foot forward” for the sentence hearing.
Callan also inquired as to the bail bond previously supplied by Luczak, who during his trial was granted bail on his own bond of €17,000 and an independent surety of €3,000.
While it appears that this will be retained as Luczak’s case is ongoing, further clarification on this point may be forthcoming in the future.
Browne listed Luczak’s case for mention to October 22nd to Mullingar Circuit Court, to allow for Mulholland’s attendance and for any other matters to be added.
Browne also reiterated the direction of Maguire that the sentence hearing is fixed for November 9th, followed by his judgment as to sentence on November 16th.

title: OpenAI tells investors revenue run rate is $20bn below earlier indication
description: The AI firm previously indicated its annualised revenue for September was $70 billion (€62.36 billion)
content:
OpenAI has told investors its annualised revenue for September was almost $50 billion (€44.54 billion), a drop from what ‌it signalled earlier.
The company previously ​indicated to investors at a separate event that its revenue run rate for last month was approaching $70 billion, Reuters and other media reported.
The discrepancy mainly arose from ​an attempt to produce a direct comparison with figures from rival Anthropic , a source told Reuters on condition of anonymity.
OpenAI did not respond to a request for ‌comment.
The ‌latest ​revenue figure was first reported by the Financial Times.
OpenAI, unlike Anthropic, does not include, for instance, revenue from ⁠sales via cloud partners ​such as Amazon’s AWS and Alphabet’s Google ​Cloud.
Anthropic pays cloud partners about 16 per cent of every dollar earned through them, ‌which last year accounted for ​half of revenue, a Reuters analysis showed.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic are preparing ⁠to go public, a process ⁠through which ​Wall Street is likely to gain a clearer view of finances, including the sustainability of rapid revenue growth brought about by a boom in demand for AI applications.
OpenAI started this year with $20 billion in annualised revenue versus $6 billion in 2024. Its quarterly revenue was eclipsed by Anthropic for the first time in the ‌second quarter, with OpenAI ⁠reporting $6.7 billion compared with Anthropic’s $11.5 billion.
Anthropic’s annualised revenue crossed $65 billion in July, and is set to reach $100 billion by year-end, sources ‌previously told Reuters.
Analysts consider annualised revenue run rate a sometimes misleading sales metric, which often involves ​multiplying one month’s revenue by 12. It has ​nonetheless become a popular metric among fast-growing Silicon Valley startups.
Further reporting by The Financial Times on Friday said SoftBank Group chief executive Masayoshi Son was ‌seeking to raise up to $100 billion from Gulf investors to ​fund a new wave of AI investments.
Citing people familiar ​with the matter, The Financial Times reported Son had held discussions in recent ⁠weeks with senior figures, including in the United ‌Arab ‌Emirates, ​about the potential fundraising, the report said.
The move comes as ‌Son ramps up AI ​bets, with the company announcing last week⁠it completed its $30 ⁠billion investment ​in OpenAI as part of its commitment to the ChatGPT maker’s last fundraising round.
SoftBank also raised $11.1 billion last month in the largest high-yield corporate bond sale globally to fund its ‌mammoth bet on OpenAI.
The ⁠Japanese investment conglomerate would use the proceeds to establish a fund that ‌would acquire companies and improve their operations using AI ​and other advanced technologies, according to ​the report. - Reuters

title: Labour retains Keir Starmer’s seat in London byelection
description: Sagal Abdi-Wali defeats Green Party’s Zack Polanski
author_name: David Sheppard and Jim Pickard in London
content:
Labour has held on to Keir Starmer’s old seat in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, seeing off a challenge from Green Party leader Zack Polanski and thwarting his attempt to become an MP.
Labour’s candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali won 12,292 votes in the north London seat, beating Polanski who received 8,928. Turnout was 39 per cent, well below the 54 per cent of constituents who voted at the 2024 general election.
Abdi-Wali, a Somalia-born refugee and leader of Camden council, will enter Westminster when parliament returns from recess on Monday.
The result will be hailed by Labour as a boost for prime minister Andy Burnham and evidence that the party can win back voters on the left who have been drifting to the Greens.
Polanski had said “we know we can win here” when putting himself forward for the Holborn and St Pancras seat, one of Labour’s safest. It became vacant after Starmer stepped down as an MP following his resignation as prime minister.
Green activists had flooded into the area, and Polanski even encouraged members to cancel tickets to the party conference in Brighton last weekend to join him in campaigning.
But he failed to recreate the Greens’ shock victory over Labour at the Gorton and Denton by-election in February.
The Green vote in Holborn tripled from 10.4 per cent to 32.8 per cent compared with that received in the general election. Andrew Feinstein, an independent left-winger who received 19 per cent in 2024, did not stand in Thursday’s by-election.
A Green spokesperson admitted the party was “disappointed” but described the result as a “huge swing” in one of Labour’s safest seats.
“The voters have delivered a message to the Labour government today. They want real change, they want rent controls, they want to see an end to the privatised water rip-off and they want to see justice for Palestinians,” the person said. “On the climate crisis, Labour will not have an easy political ride if they bring in new North Sea drilling.”
Burnham’s government had delayed contentious decisions on two North Sea fossil fuel projects until after the by-election.
Yet Polanski’s failure to win is likely to increase questions over his leadership and whether he can turn the Greens around.
The Green Party’s standing in opinion polls has slumped since Burnham took power in July, while Labour’s has risen. Labour is now on 27 per cent versus 11 per cent for the Greens.
He was already under pressure after party members backed a controversial “Zionism is Racism” motion at the conference, which has been heavily criticised by UK Jewish groups for stoking anti-Semitism.
Two Green councillors have quit the party, while senior Greens have described it as “divisive”.
Polanski avoided voting on the motion, which calls for a single Palestinian state to replace Israel, and senior figures in the party have privately criticised his inability to control the Greens’ more radical activists.
Former party leader Caroline Lucas declined to back Polanski when asked if he should stand down on Thursday, telling BBC Newsnight she was “sure” he would face additional criticism once the by-election was over.
“Let’s just see what happens in the coming days and weeks,” Lucas said. “I think it was a mistake not to show leadership on this and I think it was a mistake not to be there to vote.”
Under Polanski, Green Party membership has more than tripled to above 200,000, with many new members motivated by the party’s critical stance on Israel’s conduct in the war in Gaza .
Long-standing Green members are concerned, however, that the party’s traditional environmental message risks being crowded out by activists’ focus on Gaza, with new members now holding significant sway within the party.
Co-deputy leader Mothin Ali, a councillor in Leeds, voted in favour of the “Zionism is Racism” motion even as four of the party’s five MPs opposed it.
Abdi-Wali said it was an “extraordinary honour” to become the first female MP for the constituency. “People need to believe that politics can make their lives better,” she said.
She said she wanted to “tackle rough sleeping while addressing the wider housing crisis” and hoped to see Thames Water “brought into public ownership”. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: ‘Liam will be forever missed’: Teen who died following ‘tragic accident’ in Tuam named
description: Gardaí treating death of youth in Tuam on Wednesday as a ‘tragic accident’
content:
A teenager who died following a “tragic accident” involving a vehicle at a private property in Co Galway on Wednesday has been named as Liam Mannion.
The 18-year-old was from Lavally, near Tuam.
His death notice said he was the “cherished and deeply loved son of Tommy and Jackie, and adored brother of Lisa, Tomas, Emma, Ciara, Shane and his nephew Eric”.
“Liam will be forever missed and lovingly remembered by his heartbroken parents, brothers, sisters, nephew, aunts, uncles, cousins, extended family, neighbours and his many wonderful friends,” the notice said.
His funeral Mass will take place at the Church of Our Lady and St Jarlath in Lavally at noon on Monday with burial afterwards in Cortoon cemetery.
Gardaí said they are treating the death as a “tragic accident”.
A Garda spokesperson said the teenager was pronounced dead at the scene.
His body was removed to University Hospital Galway for a postmortem.

title: Sublime evenings and empty  downtowns: Democrats threaten comeback in America’s heartland
description: I drove across Ohio on Route 40, one of the many states in which Republican strategists are responding to distant sirens
content:
E arly October days at Ohio State University in Columbus are arcadia days: warm sunshine, new-term optimism and the green in front of the Thompson library filled with people sitting out reading, having lunch, making the most of a golden afternoon.
Across the pavilion is “The Shoe”, the century-old football stadium designed in the Romanesque tradition. For Ohioans, it’s not so much a sports stadium as a cathedral.
On this afternoon, the gates are closed, waiting for the bitterness and snow of winter and the true heart of the season. But from the interiors comes the sound of a lone brass instrument, as if a band player had been left behind from the previous weekend game.
Near the statue of Archie Griffin, Ohio’s fabled 1970s-era running back, the Piatt family are taking photos. Evie Piatt, a junior from Millersburg, is hoping to attend on Ohio State and her family are on an arranged visit. She has yet to attend a full Ohio game. “But we watch ’em every Saturday. I’ve been to the spring games – defence versus offence,” she says.
“It’s really cool. It just gives you a sneak peek of how they play.”
Craig, her father, inherited his passion for the Buckeyes from his own father. We chat for a bit in the sunshine about their mortal enemy, three hours north, the University of Michigan.
In a state the size of Ohio, a patchwork of 88 heavily agrarian and industrial counties, the performances of the Buckeyes have, for over a century, offered a source of conversation and pastime through Novembers and Decembers.
The Piatt family has two older boys in college in Capital University, east of Columbus. For Craig Piatt, that has meant five significant intrastate drives within the past few weeks. “That’s a lot of money for gas,” he acknowledges.
Piatt says he is a registered Republican but doesn’t always vote that way and, right now, is weighing up the various candidates on their own merits.
Although Ohio voted for Donald Trump by 11 percentage points in the 2024 election, it’s one of the many states in which Republican strategists are responding to distant sirens.
In the Senate election for the seat JD Vance vacated after the 2024 election, Sherrod Brown, the veteran Democrat, is leading Jon Husted by anything from three to eight points in a succession of polls.
In the gubernatorial election, Amy Acton, the Democrat hoping to beat Republican Vivek Ramaswamy (one of the presidential fantasists steamrolled by Trump early in 2024), has built a 54 to 48 per cent lead over her opponent. More alarmingly for Republicans, Ramaswamy trails his opponent by 57-32 per cent among Independent voters.
“I’m still looking at each of the candidates,” Craig Piatt says.
“I try not to follow through the TV because it so biased.”
It seems a sensible policy. In Ohio, the advertisements are both relentless and relentlessly grim.
[ Lone star Trump believes he can bend Texas and midterm elections to his will Opens in new window ]
“For 50 years, Sherrod Brown voted how he was told. Higher taxes. Open borders. Sex changes for kids,” opens an attack advert on Brown.
“He’s been called the face of data centres in Ohio,” begins a counter advert prosecuting Husted.
But the Republican is lagging behind. As a response, the Trump administration sent out a message that the president himself would visit the Buckeye state on Saturday, October 3rd, to rally with Husted. It would be part of Trump’s hastily announced barnstorming tour of Republican strongholds, in defiance of plummeting personal approval numbers.
The messy conflict with Iran is the obvious reason for the high fuel prices that have dismayed Midwesterners and the Piatt family are among the thousands acutely conscious of its cost.
“I don’t,” Craig Piatt says, when asked if he feels the punitive fuel prices are worth it.
“I feel like it is going to be like any other war in the Middle East. It is going to go on, and on, and on. And I’ll be honest with you, as patriotic as most folks are in this country, we are just tired of war. We are tired of being in other people’s business. We have issues here we need to fix.
The last couple of months have given me pause for thought
“I don’t follow politics that closely, but I would say we are pretty blessed where we live. Housing is high but we are blessed to own our house. Groceries are kind of going up more and more. All in all, it’s been a pretty good place for our family to raise our kids. But I know we’ve got friends all over the state and country that are hurting.
“I will say this: I think that if he [Trump] could stop spending time on his social media account and making enemies and making dirt and just worry about our country, I think it would be a lot better. And the last couple of months have given me pause for thought – just concerns over his actions and things he said. I think a lot of us are looking forward to the next presidential election.”
Over the course of a few days, I drove across Ohio on Route 40, the fabled “national road”, a narrow, thin ribbon running through quiet villages and corn and soybean fields which, in the October light, looks cinematic.
This is the land that generations of presidential aspirants have dutifully referred to as “the heartland”. Ohio has delivered a staggering seven presidents born in the state, all Republican, while an eighth, William Henry Harrison, a Whig, forged his political career there.
Route 40, the first federally-funded road in the United States, is a moseying, peaceful saunter through bucolic countryside, silent towns, churches, car junkyards, antiques shops, well-tended gardens and posters on the telegraph poles honouring local military members from the Civil War through to Iraq. It’s a world of many ice-cream parlours and few bars.
Springfield, Ohio, is about an hour’s drive west of Columbus. After decades in national obscurity, it created a firestorm of controversy during the 2024 election after, first, Vance – who was raised in Ohio – and then Trump made the notorious claim that a local Haitian community were eating cats and dogs.
When Trump repeated the bizarre idea during his lone televised debate against Kamala Harris in Philadelphia, Springfield officials immediately phoned the broadcasting network to stress that it wasn’t true. But the damage was done. The stigma stuck.
In its industrial glory years, when it marketed itself as Champion City, Springfield’s population swelled to 80,000. It had fallen to just over 30,000 when Haitians, attracted by job opportunities and the affordable living costs began to arrive in the city. There was a swell of new arrivals in 2021 and 2023, bringing the total number to around 15,000. Almost all arrived through legal pathways.
The ending of the Temporary Protected Status privilege has led to an intensification of summer Ice arrests and deportations, terrifying the community.
“It has not been huge activity compared to Minnesota, but they seemed to absorb the lessons of that and moved stealthily,” explains Michael McGovern, who works for Innovate Ohio, a Columbus-based non-profit.
“A lot of folks did the right things here and so provided the federal government with all their details. So, it was easy for Ice to arrive in homes and scoop them up. That’s what’s been happening in the late summer period. And one really draconian aspect was that a number of Haitians were forced to wear ankle monitors and there’s a lot of stigma to that.”
Trump’s visit to Vandalia, about an hour west, coincided with the funeral service held in Springfield for Pierre Damas Bel.
The 20-year-old had excelled since arriving in Ohio from Haiti; a soccer star who had won a full scholarship to study neuroscience at Wright University. He had been forced to wear an ankle bracelet by immigration, even while playing football.
He detailed his distress in a July post that read: “I came here to this country to pursue my education. I didn’t come here to commit a crime or hurt anyone. Yet now I’m walking through the streets of the United States with a GPS monitor on my leg, carrying a feeling of shame and humiliation I never imagined I would experience.”
On the morning of August 31st, Pierre Damas Bel pulled his 2006 Toyota Avalon on to the hard shoulder of the 1-70. In a harrowing account in The Atlantic, the driver of a tractor trailer explained how he was unable to avoid the pedestrian as he walked out into oncoming traffic in an apparent suicide.
They are hearing stories of these deportations back to Haiti
Mike DeWine, the Republican governor of Ohio, was among those in the funeral congregation on Saturday. DeWine has repeatedly defended Ohio’s Haitians, arguing that they had revivified Springfield’s local economy – and pointing out that as of 2030, Ohioan death rates would exceed birth rates. In other words, the Buckeye state is going to need new people.
A Creole restaurant I visited on lunchtime was empty. The host was smiling and welcoming but said that his boss warned him not to speak and pointed me towards the houses behind the Speedway station. He said that’s where everyone was, at home. Haitians are hiding out.
“They are hearing stories of these deportations back to Haiti – stories of people kidnapped off the plane or hassled for bribes because they know these planes are coming from the US so there are resources,” says Michael McGovern.
“And a lot of people feel in mortal danger if they are deported back to Haiti. It’s under-recognised and it’s a shameful thing for our country.”
Downtown Springfield was, at least on the evening I visited, disconcertingly empty. Like so many Midwestern towns, it expanded quickly with the optimistic certainty that the manufacturing boom would last forever. On a sublime evening – striated sky, warm breeze – its downtown was deserted apart from a tour guide in costume and lantern escorting a small group on a ghost tour and, at the hotel, two guys from Las Vegas who were contracted to work on a nearby data centre. They’d been living in the hotel for months.
One of the contractors, Valen, compared his turbulent youth in Sin City against the quietness of Springfield. He said he liked to unwind by sitting outside, smoking a blunt and watching the world not go by, which is what he was at when I encountered him.
“I like it,” he said of Springfield. “People here are ... very ... cordial.”
A short drive north of Springfield is Urbana, one of those dream-factory American towns with a succession of craft shops and coffee shops and candy-striped awnings and a retro-film theatre. I call in unannounced to the branch of the Champaign County Democratic headquarters.
A group of volunteers has just finished meeting and are immediately welcoming. We talk for an hour about what it feels like to experience life as an American here, in this pleasant, obscure Ohioan town.
As it turns out, Urbana is like a crossroads for the issues that are driving the national sentiment in 2026. The farmers are stressed by months of spiralling fuel costs. Locals are petitioning against a data centre contract signed without public knowledge by city officials. The voting patterns here have been distorted by redistricting, or gerrymandering, over the past 20 years. Champaign County voted for Donald Trump by 74 per cent two years ago (15,344 votes to 4,944 for Kamala Harris) but the group has sensed a dissatisfaction that transcends old allegiances.
“My father is a long-term judge here who was elected twice as a Republican,” Clay Newlin says.
“He is disaffected and he knows a lot of Republicans who are motivated to get out and vote Democrat because they are p****d off. Sorry! Farmers and rural people are very ticked off with what is going on. Tariffs are hitting all the people around us. So, it’s not just Democrats.”
They want cheap water and cheap land, so we are a perfect site
Fears over the energy price hikes, the potential impact of the nearby Cedar Bog conservation area and noise and air pollution concerns for students in the elementary middle school and a senior citizen home are the driving factors in local opposition to a data centre. The issue is subject to a lawsuit that both parties are trying to resolve. A settlement proposal would see Thor Equities waive its $115 million (€102.5 million) damages lawsuit, future tax abatements and agree to pay the city of Urbana some $50 million in several project phases. It’s a lot of money for a small rural community. But a recent meeting drew more than 100 people holding placards that read “No Deal”.
“They want cheap water and cheap land, so we are a perfect site,” explains Kay Nutter.
“They say in their site plan [there will be] one building. But they bought 500 acres, so we fear they are going to build a campus, with eight or nine units and then the generators: it is going to be loud, and bright, 24-7.”
We talk for a while about life in Buckeye state. “I love Ohio,” Suzanne McCoy says and the others chip in. Colvin Bear was raised in New Jersey but gravitated towards the Midwest for college and never left.
“I like the open spaces, but I can still be at an airport in an hour. My house is in the country a mile from my neighbour, but we can get in the car and get to the shops in 10 minutes. While we may wish that many of the residents were more sensitive to others and a willingness to be open to those who are different, most of them still have a good heart. Even though they may have their blind spots.”
On Saturday last, Carl Ruby, a pastor in Springfield, spoke at Pierre Damas Bel’s funeral. He assured the congregation that they were “a blessing and not a burden” to the town and they had many allies among the traditional Springfield community, some of whom were in attendance.
“You have brought life, energy, love and a renewed sense of hope to Springfield and we not only welcome you, we also want to thank you.”
On the same day, across in Vandalia, president Trump also had Springfield on his mind. Over the course of a 90-minute speech, he called out John Gruden, the former Superbowl winning coach, who was in attendance. “This is rougher than a football game,” he joked about the energy of the crowd. “They have more spirit,” he said, before returning to the theme of enemies vanquished.
“They’ve tried to smear us, slander us, persecute us, demoralise us, they’ve attacked me, they’ve impeached me, they’ve arrested me and they’ve even tried to kill me, I guess. But with you by my side we have always prevailed.”
Then he asked the crowd if they’d ever heard the parable of “The Snake”.
“This is in honour of Springfield, Ohio,” he told them.
“A quaint little town of 32,000 people where they took in 35,000 people and put ’em into Springfield and it didn’t work out too well and they are being removed. It was an idyllic place – that’s a word they use in high scripture. It was an ‘idyllic’ place. ‘Was’ is the better word. Not any more, but it soon will be and they are being brought back to their country.”
So, while the Haitians mourned in Springfield, Trump read a rendition of The Snake with its strange refrain featuring a “tender-hearted woman” who voluntarily takes in a “poor, half-frozen snake”. She feeds him milk and honey before she is inevitably bitten and before dying, asks the snake why, after all her compassion, he had done this.
“Shut up, silly woman, said the reptile with a grin,” the president quoted, deepening his voice for dramatic effect as the crowd in Ohio listened in silence.
“You knew damn well I was a snake before you took me in.”

title: Michael Flatley thanks people for ‘beautiful gestures of sympathy’ after wife’s death
description: Funeral Mass for Niamh O’Brien will take place on Saturday at the Church of St Thérèse, Mount Merrion, Dublin
content:
Michael Flatley has thanked the people of Fermoy in Co Cork for their “beautiful gestures of sympathy and support” following the death of his wife Niamh O’Brien earlier this week.
The Chicago-born Irish dancer has had a long-standing association with the town. He bought Castlehyde House, which sits on the River Blackwater in Fermoy, in 1999.
In a post on social media the creator of Riverdance and Lord of the Dance said the flag was flying at half mast at Castlehyde in memory of their “beloved Niamh”.
Flatley (68) said he was “touched by the kindness and compassion shown by the people of Fermoy” in the wake of the death of Niamh O’Brien (52) last Monday.
“To those who have taken the time to leave flowers at the gates of Castlehyde, thank you from the bottom of our hearts. Your beautiful gestures of sympathy and support mean more to our family than words can express.”
Niamh O’Brien will lie in repose at Ryan’s Funeral Home, Ashbourne, Co Meath, on Friday from 4pm to 7pm.
Her funeral Mass will take place on Saturday at 11am at the Church of St Thérèse, Mount Merrion, in Dublin. A private burial will follow.
The mother of one – son Michael St James – died at the Beacon Hospital in Dublin on Monday following an illness.
The native of Kilbride, Co Meath, is also survived by her parents Monica and Tommy; sisters Derval and Aoibheann; her nieces and nephews; and extended family and friends from school, college and the dancing world.
Niamh O’Brien performed in the troupe for the original production of Riverdance in 1993. She took the lead role in Lord of the Dance and also danced in Feet of Flames and Celtic Tiger.
She came fourth in the Irish Dancing World Championships when she was just 17 years old.

title: Ice agent shoots and wounds man in New York City with five-year-old reportedly in car
description: Mayor Zohran Mamdani says child unharmed as he condemns ‘unconscionable’ situation amid angry protests in Bronx neighbourhood
author_name: Sam Levin in Los Angeles, Lex McMenamin in New York
content:
A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (Ice) agent shot and injured a man in New York City on Thursday afternoon during an enforcement operation, federal officials said.
The man was conscious and hospitalised, authorities said, and the shooting quickly sparked angry protests from local residents and elected officials in the neighbourhood.
Early reports indicated that agents had surrounded the man and a five-year-old child in his car in a residential area before firing multiple rounds, the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, said in a statement on Thursday evening. The child was unharmed, he said.
The shooting took place at roughly 4pm in the Marble Hill neighbourhood of the Bronx, according to the New York police department.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement on social media that Ice officers were conducting an operation targeting an undocumented man from the Dominican Republic. The statement did not explain what led to the shooting, saying: “During the incident, an Ice officer discharged his weapon and the criminal illegal alien was injured.”
The extent of the man’s injuries was unknown. The department’s statement alleged that the man had “associations” with a gang and prior criminal convictions, but DHS did not name the man or provide evidence of his background.
The department has previously faced backlash for falsely accusing immigrants of being gang members after they were shot by agents.
DHS spokespeople did not immediately respond to questions about what led to the shooting, the extent of the man’s injuries, or the reports that a five-year-old was in the car during the shooting.
“This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation,” Mamdani wrote in an X post. “I have called the President; when we speak, I will demand that he ends all Ice enforcement actions in our city.”
Cellphone video published by the New York Times appeared to show the immediate aftermath of the shooting, with an agent in a yellow vest holding what appeared to be an assault rifle while talking on the phone. The newspaper said other witness video appeared to show several agents in the middle of the street in the aftermath, with one armed and another restraining a man on the ground.
One witness told the City Reporter, a local news outlet, that she saw a man bleeding on the ground in front of a car and observed an agent holding a small child. Videos also showed bullet holes in the windshield of an SUV, NY1 reported.
Mamdani expressed outrage in his post, saying: “I will not stand by while Ice agents terrorize our communities. Our thoughts are with the injured New Yorker and his family tonight. We are praying for his recovery. Get Ice out of our neighborhoods. Get Ice out of our hospitals. Get Ice off our streets. Get Ice away from our children.”
The mayor ended his statement with: “Abolish Ice.”
Protesters began to gather in the area soon after the shooting, with some demonstrators holding signs saying: Jail all killer Ice agents and Leave our neighbors alone.
Hands Off NYC and the New York Immigration Coalition, two local groups, held an emergency press conference in the area where elected officials and organisers expressed outrage and decried Ice’s ongoing presence in the neighbourhood.
“Ice, get the f**k out of our neighbourhood,” shouted Vanessa Gibson, Bronx borough president. “I’m angry that we have to be here ... We are a working-class community. We don’t deserve this type of treatment from the White House.”
She encouraged the crowd to get involved in opposing Ice, saying: “There are more of us than there are of them. I want this to be a moment that we turn into a movement.”
New Yorkers of all ages flowed into the streets from the nearby 1 train, and protesters soon also gathered at a local hospital where the man shot by Ice was reported to be receiving treatment. Outside the hospital, NYPD set up barricades and protesters quickly clashed with police officers in a chaotic scene.
Demonstrators banged drums and shouted: “Shut it down,” and “Ice out!” as cars driving by honked in support.
DHS has faced growing backlash over immigration officers’ use of deadly force in the field over the last year. Last month, an immigration officer shot Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez (28) while he was in his car during a traffic stop in Texas.
Federal prosecutors then charged the man with assault, alleging he had struck an officer with his side mirror while trying to drive away.
The Trump administration has repeatedly accused immigrants and protesters of “weaponising” their vehicles, alleging that agents fired their weapons in response to “vehicular attacks”, but a Guardian analysis in July found most of those claims touted by federal officials have fallen apart under scrutiny.
Since Trump returned to office last year, US immigration officers have shot at least two dozen people, according to one analysis, including three US citizens who were killed.
The shooting comes as Ice arrests have hit record levels, with the agency pivoting from the high-profile raids it carried out last year and instead more quietly dispatching agents into communities across the country. – Guardian

title: Tips from Australia for public transport
description: The horse has bolted for most of our motorway network in Ireland, unless retrofit is considered
content:
Sir, – I agree with Eileen Bannan, particularly in relation to the installation of train lines, or at least the setting aside of space for them when acquiring land for motorways (“ A5 upgrade is welcome, but why not a train service too? ”, Letters, October 8th).
I witnessed this “combination” approach on a visit to Western Australia some years ago. Among a number of examples is the Mitchell Freeway/Joondalup line that runs north from Perth with passenger tracks built down the centre median of the motorway.
Whether done by retrofit or planned from day one, this approach provides a considerable saving on land acquisition costs and the inordinate amount of time taken to agree a route and then to compulsorily acquire the land.
Unfortunately, the horse has bolted for most of our motorway network in Ireland, unless retrofit is considered. But for the improved A5, and indeed for any future motorway development, whether in the Republic or cross-Border projects, there is an argument for a policy shift whereby consideration be given to adding a rail line, or at least the space for it, in the land acquisition process. Anything to improve public transport links should be embraced wholeheartedly. – Yours, etc,

title: Declining overseas aid illustrates worrying pattern
description: The suspension of foreign aid by the US administration has set the trend, but Ireland must not follow it
content:
Sir, – While the increase in overseas aid of €14 million announced in the budget is welcome, it has to be seen in context. Our overseas aid budget rose by €30 million in 2026, by €45 million in 2025, by €60 million in 2024 and by €177 million in 2023.
So, to use Government speak, the direction of travel is downwards and if this trend continues the budget will, at best, stay static next year.
The other factor that needs to be considered is that Ireland remains, in theory at least, committed to reaching the UN target of 0.7 per cent of GDP for overseas aid. We are going backwards with respect to this target, however.
While there is no question that there are numerous competing demands for public funding at home, where poverty is relative, there are even more demands from developing countries, where poverty is absolute.
The suspension of USAID by the US administration has set the trend, with many larger funding nations following suit and drastically reducing their aid budgets in favour of spending on arms.
This is a trend Ireland should not, and must not, follow. We should instead continue to demonstrate Ireland’s values of co-operation and sharing by increasing our aid budget by a specific percentage of GDP year on year and until we reach, and pass, the UN target we are committed to. – Yours, etc,

title: Getting up later to avoid extra childcare costs
description: We were told this budget was intended to reward those who ‘get up early’
content:
Sir, – Dominic Coyle provides welcome clarity on the budget (“ Budget 2027’s childcare package has triggered storm of protest from parents. Here’s why ”, Budget 2027, October 8th).
We were told that this budget was, among other things, intended to reward those who “get up early every morning and go to work”. However, the Minister did not make clear that the cited reduction in childcare fees applies to Band E, covering 40–50 hours of childcare a week. As the article notes, most parents in and around Dublin fall into Band F, which covers 50 hours or more a week. Even with the increased subsidies, their monthly childcare costs will remain between €750 and €810 – well above the Minister’s proposed net figure of €550 per month. Should we get up later to avoid the extra costs? – Yours, etc,

title: HSE deducted €100,000 from autism charity after governance concerns raised
description: Autism a Chara, which previously traded as Autism Initiatives Ireland, provides specialist care and support for adults with autism
content:
The Health Service Executive (HSE) deducted €100,000 from an autism charity in 2019 as a “value improvement payment” after concerns were raised about its financial governance.
Autism a Chara, which until this year traded as Autism Initiatives Ireland, provides specialist care and support for adults with autism in the Republic.
In 2019, concerns were raised by a former Irish charity official about the alleged transfer of €1,522,778 from the HSE-funded organisation’s cash reserves to its UK parent company over a four-year period.
The HSE announced earlier this year that it was reviewing the governance and funding of the organisation in light of the allegations.
In a briefing note to the Oireachtas Public Accounts Committee (PAC), dated September 24th, the HSE said from 2018 it had “ongoing engagement with Autism Initiatives Ireland regarding financial governance, use of reserves, cross-charges/management fees and funding for business supports”.
“In April 2018, Autism Initiatives Ireland formally set out its position to the HSE regarding the use of reserves for central business costs,” the note said.
“From early 2019, concerns were raised by the HSE regarding the scale and use of reserves, specifically the apportionment of central/management charges from the UK parent organisation, and transparency in financial reporting.”
The HSE said the matters were “discussed extensively” at meetings during 2019 and an independent external review was commissioned by Autism a Chara.
“It concluded that the board and senior management had acted appropriately, that the central cost recharge arrangements represented value for money and that there was no evidence that any funder, including the HSE, had been adversely affected,” the note said.
“The review found the shared services model to be cost-effective, equitable and beneficial to operational charities, with the allocation methodology considered fair and reasonable.”
“Notwithstanding” the assurances, the HSE continued to engage with the organisation regarding the HSE’s “authority to seek a contribution from reserves” in the context of wider governance.
“In 2019, the HSE sought a once-off value improvement contribution of €100,000, which was subsequently deducted from Autism Initiatives Ireland’s funding allocation,” the note said.
“In 2020 Autism Initiatives Ireland absorbed service cost pressures within their funding allocation including invoices relating to the changing needs of two individuals.”
[ Autism charity under review told HSE it was ‘transitioning away’ from UK parent Opens in new window ]
An earlier letter to the committee showed the HSE provided €46.415 million in total to the organisation in the years between 2022 and 2025.
In internal correspondence within the charity, the official had alleged the €1.5 million was transferred in three ways, claiming €973,400 was transferred on one occasion after the charity’s Northern Ireland branch issued a “recharge for services rendered”.
Alongside an alleged €200,000 charge from the UK parent group on the proceeds from the sale of a property owned by the Irish charity, the official alleged there was a “current annual recharge” from the UK arm for services rendered, further claiming that no services were requested or approved.
The charity said concerns were raised in 2019 “in relation to the recharge to a UK company”, but that an independent auditor found “no substance” to them and that the processes regarding recharging were “robust and represent value for money”.
[ Alleged transfer of €1.5m by autism body to UK parent charity ‘possibly criminal’ Opens in new window ]
Autism a Chara confirmed it received a “formal request” in July 2019 to make a “formal cost savings contribution” to the HSE.
Following this, the organisation “subsequently absorbed service cost pressures within their funding allocation”.
In a statement earlier this year, the Irish charity said it had transitioned away from its UK parent in March due to “divergence between the Irish and UK governance and regulatory environments for disability services”.
Noting it had received funding from the HSE for more than 17 years, the charity said it had “fully complied” with the health service’s monitoring and reporting requirements, which are “constantly checked and scrutinised by the HSE”.

title: Cut costs and abolish Ifac
description: Watchdog is consistently ignored with a gentle pat on the head
content:
Sir, – If the Government needs to look at some cost-cutting measures, they could consider abolishing the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (“ Budget puts public finances on worse trajectory, watchdog warns ”, Budget, October 6th).
It is clear that this watchdog body , which was established to provide some common-sense advice against misspending by Government, has no role whatsoever other than to consistently warn against how the Government is handling the public finances and to be ignored just as consistently with a gentle pat on the head and some plámás about how important their advice is. – Yours, etc,
