title: Justine McCarthy: Paternity leave shouldn’t be a privilege that only the likes of Simon Harris can afford
description: Fatherhood is not so visible in the workplace where patriarchal conventions persist
content:
S imon Harris has left the stage. After a brief trip to Luxembourg to chair a meeting of finance ministers, he will return home to Greystones to spend time with his new baby daughter, born this day last week.* The lights have not guttered and died in the Department of Finance , nor have the screaming and shrieking abated in Leinster House. It’s business as usual in Merrion Street. The world has not – so far – slammed to a standstill without the three-hatted Tánaiste , Minister and Fine Gael leader.
Never has so senior a Government member upped and left the ship of state to go on paternity leave. Harris delivered his budget speech on Tuesday and did his morning-after media appearance on Wednesday. Then he went home to help mind the children. More power to his ambitious elbow.
This is his third fatherhood break. The first two times, he was lower down the Cabinet pecking order, holding briefs in health and higher education respectively. This time, he has gone awl (absent with leave) smack in the middle of Ireland’s EU presidency and just as he is poised to take over from Micheál Martin as taoiseach next year.
Everyone is dispensable. The world is beset with wars, plagues, floods, droughts and a litre of diesel costing more than €2, but Harris’s furlough has been reported in the media as meriting little more than an aside. As incidental as Michael Healy-Rae ’s cap or Mary Lou McDonald ’s new fringe. What a contrast with the extensive coverage not so long ago, when Helen McEntee , then the minister for justice, and Social Democrats leader Holly Cairns first took maternity leave. As Fine Gael’s deputy leader, McEntee becomes her party’s de facto leader now, a move which, like Cairns’ current maternity leave, has proved unremarkable. Hip-hip-hooray for that too.
Seeing is normalising. When high-vis fathers avail of the €299-a-week statutory leave they are entitled to, going up to €309 from January, their children are not the only beneficiaries. Mothers gain too, along with the rest of society. Fathers are active parents these days. You see them on the school run, in the playground, at the supermarket checkout and on the playing field; rugby and soccer stars scooping up their offspring to share their triumphs in the Aviva Stadium. Unfortunately, fatherhood is not so visible in the workplace where patriarchal conventions persist. A man dashing from the office to be with his sick child still risks being noted by some bosses as lacking ambition and commitment to the job.
In a time when the dingbat twin doctrines of Stepford wives and macho misogyny have taken hold, the example Harris is giving is to be applauded. It certainly beats JD Vance’s suggestion to give parents extra voting rights and his draft proposal to reward married couples by paying them if one spouse stays at home to rear the children. In most cases, that would be the mother, seeing as women are paid roughly 15 per cent less than men in the US .
Research shows that, in Ireland as elsewhere, the gender pay gap often starts when women have babies. In crude productivity terms, creating a workplace that is family-friendly for fathers makes economic sense. An acceptance that co-parents’ child-rearing concerns need to be better balanced has a potential spin-off effect as an antidote to declining birth rates.
[ Séamas O’Reilly: Am I a soft, overprotective dad bringing his own childhood traumas to bear? Opens in new window ]
Harris went off home this week without including in the budget any extension to the State’s miserly two-week paternity leave. By that calculation, he is due back at his desk by October 21st. Hardly enough time to get through a pack of Pampers. In Japan, fathers are entitled to a year off with two-thirds fully paid. Iceland allows six months’ leave. It’s 19 weeks in Spain.
Harris, of course, could avail of parental leave, which allows 26 weeks off for each child up to their 12th birthday but, as that is entirely unpaid, the optics would be fireworks for a politician on a €236,427 basic salary – more than quadruple the average Irish pay.
Paternity leave payments are based on a flat rate rather than on a percentage of salary and, it seems, many fathers cannot afford to take a cut in pay. A study last year by the Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission in conjunction with the Economic and Social Research Institute found that only about half of fathers avail of paternity leave. Compared to two-thirds of mothers, just a quarter of fathers take parental leave, the nine-week paid entitlement. The report said that higher-paid fathers were more likely to take paternity leave because their employers were disposed to topping up the State payment.
[ Don’t be a ‘permissive parent’, warns an expert with decades of experience helping families Opens in new window ]
Setting an example, therefore, is not enough without making it viable for other parents. Fine Gael seemed to accept this when Garret Ahearn, one of its senators, said last year that the party wanted “to see the amount of benefit received linked to earnings, so families don’t feel financial pressure when parents’ leave is needed”.
Oddly, nobody is substituting for Harris as minister for finance in his absence. Nor is McEntee expected to officially assume the temporary role of tánaiste. This is especially odd as, when she took maternity leave for the birth of her second child in December 2022, Harris was the one who stood in for her as acting minister for justice. With no stand-in arrangement in place, are we to assume the Tánaiste remains available to work if needed? If that is so, is he on leave? Or is he on call?
Imagine what might have happened if Jacinda Ardern had not been substituted by her deputy, Winston Peters, when she was on six-weeks’ maternity leave from running New Zealand as its prime minister in 2018. “Hold on two ticks,” she might have told the midwife in the throes of giving birth. “I have to take this call – my country needs me.”
Leading by example is all well and good, but the Tánaiste’s absence from the office for a fortnight is not going to trigger a rush to the door by new fathers throughout the land. Paternity leave needs to be viable for fathers. Perhaps Harris could get to work on that for next year’s budget.
*This column was amended on September 9th 2026 to include a reference to Simon Harris’s meeting in Luxembourg

title: FAI Cup semi-final preview: In-form Bohemians can overcome revitalised Waterford
description: Gypsies unbeaten in seven since 3-1 away defeat to Blues in August
content:
Chasing a league and cup double for the first time since 2008, Bohemians are unbeaten in seven domestic games, dating back to the trip to Waterford on August 9th where they came unstuck against the most lethal strike force in the country.
Waterford led 3-0 at half-time, and it finished 3-1, after a soaring header by Republic of Ireland under-21 Tommy Lonergan and a scrappy brace from the evergreen Pádraig Amond.
Graham Coughlan’s side are fighting a four-way battle with Drogheda , Galway and Shelbourne to avoid a relegation playoff despite a 13-match unbeaten streak that was only ended by Shamrock Rovers before the international break.
Waterford have looked like title contenders since Coughlan replaced Jon Daly as the manager in May. There are plenty of examples. Like when Norwegian winger Jorgen Voilas benefited from assist-machine Benny Couto to cut through St Patrick’s Athletic at Richmond Park on August 28th .
Couto, a Portuguese left back, has 13 assists in all competitions, which goes a long way to explaining how Lonergan and Amond have amassed 28 goals between them.
Bohs were uncharacteristically silent this week, before what should be their last FAI Cup semi-final at Dalymount Park before the old ground is bulldozed and rebuilt, citing what they believe is unfair fixture rescheduling by the Football Association of Ireland .
The media shutout stems from Shamrock Rovers’ game against Drogheda on Thursday night giving Stephen Bradley’s side a 24-hour advantage to recover before welcoming Bohs to Tallaght on Monday.
The Premier Division title race is a three-way affair between Rovers, Bohs and St Pat’s, so the advantage afforded to Rovers, with Alan Reynolds’s men facing a tricky three-day turnaround, does seem unfair.
Bradley described the silent protest before two matches being broadcast live on RTÉ and Virgin Media as “daft”.
“I understand they’re trying to create a siege mentality and all that, but we’ve done [a quick turnaround] time and time again,” he said.
Markuss Strods, the Dublin-born winger, returns to the Bohs squad having made his debut for Latvia and featured in all four Nations League ties over the past fortnight. Strods scored in the 2-1 loss to Montenegro.
Bohs should have just enough to reach the final at the Aviva Stadium on November 8th, where either Galway United or Derry City will join them after Saturday’s second semi-final at Eamonn Deacy Park.

title: ‘Cool, quirky, lots of character’: Leo Cullen wants Laya Arena to be special place to play
description: After absence of more than two years, Leinster host Cardiff on return to redeveloped home ground
content:
It’s a quirky ground, as Leo Cullen puts it, and strictly speaking a showjumping arena amid a thicket of Dublin 4 rugby clubs for more than a century and which has only become Leinster’s home since 2007. Yet Leinster are home again.
The former CEO Mick Dawson described the move to the RDS as “one of the best decisions Leinster Rugby ever made” on foot of signing a new 25-year lease with the Royal Dublin Society in 2022 ahead of redeveloping the new, three-floored Anglesea Stand as part of a €52 million refurbishment.
Now, after an absence of two years and four months, Leinster will host their first competitive game at what is now called the Laya Arena when facing Cardiff on Saturday (kick-off 7.45pm) in the United Rugby Championship (URC).
Fans, players and coaches alike have missed the place.
“It’s a very unique ground. There’s lots of rugby clubs in and around the RDS, and that sort of stands on its own as not a rugby club, traditionally, if you wind back the clock when all the rugby clubs were being formed 100 years ago,” Cullen said.
“It’s an insane amount of rugby clubs in a very small area. And then we’re in the showjumping arena, playing rugby. It’s an amazing thing, because obviously my mum breeds horses and ponies, as some of you may well be aware of. I’ve been going there since I was literally a baby.
“It is a cool venue. It’s quirky, but it’s got lots of character. It’s just different to every other rugby ground that’s out there.”
[ ‘It’s a proper club ground’: Captain Dan Sheehan relishing Leinster’s return home ]
His first memory as a player were the “prefab dressingrooms” that were “beyond basic” before being moved to the back of the old Anglesea Road stand, which “for a long time [had] a feeling it was about to fall down on top of you.”
The dressingrooms have now been moved across to the grandstand.
“It’s always like you’re pushing things into different spaces around the place. It’s not like your natural pristine stadium, is it. It’s multipurpose. I would be very nostalgic towards the place. I think it still has lots of character,” Cullen said.
“We haven’t been there for two years, so we need to work on making it quite a special place to play the game.
“What we can control as a team, as a group of coaches, is trying to get a performance right that fans ultimately want to come and see and support.”
Only “a few” of the 20,500 tickets had still to be sold for Saturday evening’s game.
Nine of the matchday squad were involved in the last competitive game here, a 33-7 win over Connacht on May 31st, 2024. Six of the 23 on duty for this homecoming have never played at the ground.
More pertinently, Cullen has named nine of Leinster’s 16-strong contingent in Ireland’s southern hemisphere expedition for the Blues’ seasonal reappearance in a completely changed starting XV, as well as Sam Prendergast, a replacement in last week’s 26-20 loss to the Sharks.
Dan Sheehan captains a side also featuring Tadhg Furlong, Joe McCarthy, James Ryan and Jack Conan up front, as well as Jamie Osborne, Garry Ringrose, Hugo Keenan and Jimmy O’Brien, who scored his second and Leinster’s fifth try in that aforementioned last game here.
Leinster will thus have used 40 players in their opening three games and the only summer tourist yet to feature this season is Jamison Gibson-Park, who should return “next week or the week after”, Cullen said. “He’s not far, but this week is too soon. He just hasn’t done enough training with us.”
In his absence, Cullen has given 22-year-old academy scrumhalf Oliver Coffey a full debut after four appearances in total off the bench.
“He has very good basics. He’s a good communicator, he’s a good leader in his academy group. He’s into year three now in the academy, but we would have worked quite closely with him from a leadership point of view as well over the course of last season,” Cullen said.
“It’s just trying to get time into some of these guys. They need to start somewhere and we just thought it would be worthwhile him starting.
“All these things come with a little bit of risk, but there’s plenty of experience around him, so the players need to make sure they look after him, particularly the fellas in front of him, and he is able to deliver proper service, so he can deliver on his basics, which he’s very, very strong at.”
Harry Byrne as well as Hugo McLoughlin were ruled out with head knocks, meaning backup outhalf Caspar Gabriel will be one of the six RDS newcomers, as Joey Carbery’s prodigal second debut had been delayed by “a minor setback”.
Cullen said their two-week, two-game trek to South Africa in the URC was “overall, hugely positive” after taking three points rather than one from their comparative safari at the start of last season. The players looked fitter and better conditioned, he said, this time, although it was “frustrating” not to win one of two matches that he felt were winnable.
“Lots of territory, lots of possession, more entries into the opposition 22 than the opposition, but we’re not clinical enough,” the Leinster head coach said.
“This week, Cardiff, a totally different challenge. They’re two from two. We’ve made a lot of changes to our team. Some of those coming in for the first game of the season. Obviously, it’s gearing up because we’ve got the Champions Cup next week [away to Clermont] and then Munster the week after.”
LEINSTER (v Cardiff) : Hugo Keenan; Joshua Kenny, Garry Ringrose, Jamie Osborne, Jimmy O’Brien; Sam Prendergast, Oliver Coffey; Alex Usanov, Dan Sheehan (capt), Tadgh Furlong; Joe McCarthy, James Ryan; Max Deegan, Scott Penny, Jack Conan.
Replacements : Rónan Kelleher, Peter Dooley, Thomas Clarkson, Alan Spicer, Josh Ericson, Fintan Gunne, Caspar Gabriel, Robbie Henshaw.

title: ‘Massive challenge’ for Connacht as they look to upset the odds against Glasgow
description: Bundee Aki will start as all Irish internationals return to starting lineup for URC clash
content:
It doesn’t get any easier for Connacht . After rolling with the punches and springing off the ropes with a late knockout blow in Treviso when playing the core of the Italian team, a week on they face the bulk suppliers to the Scotland side. And Saracens come calling next week.
“Yeah, Italy away, followed by Scotland away,” noted captain Cian Prendergast in the wake of last week’s win. “We’ll take a lot of confidence and a lot of belief from that game [against Benetton]. It’s always good to learn when you’re winning. We’ll learn and we’ll try to produce a better performance.”
To that end, Stuart Lancaster gives a seasonal debut to the last of their seven-strong Irish contingent on the summer tour in the talismanic Bundee Aki as one of eight changes to the starting XV. This includes the five forwards who made such a telling impact in the Stadio di Monigo, the frontrow of Billy Bohan, Eoin de Buitléar and Sam Illo, as well as Niall Murray and Paul Boyle.
The fit-again Shayne Bolton also makes his seasonal reappearance, while Josh Ioane, another influential replacement last week, starts at fullback. To a degree, Lancaster’s hand has been forced by injuries, but this gives Connacht a third playmaker along with Ciarán Frawley, after his two-try debut last week, and Mack Hansen, who has hit the ground running in his two games to date after being restricted to one outing for his province last season. They also have Sean Naughton and Sam Gilbert on the bench, which significantly means Frawley will assume place-kicking.
“I was very proud of the way the lads dug out the five points in Italy last week against a strong Benetton side,” said Lancaster after his team overcame a 14-3 penalty count in favour of the home side. “It’s great to have all seven Irish players now available so there’s plenty of competition for places, which is what we need in the squad.
“We’re expecting a massive challenge from Glasgow who have quality across the field and are always tough to beat in Scotstoun. That said, we know them well after recent meetings with them, so [we] have to be at our very best.”
Glasgow winger Fergus Watson is one of five changes to the side which drew 33-all with Ulster, along with loosehead Nathan McBeth, lock Scott Cummings and number eight Macenzzie Duncan, with centre Ollie Smith replacing Stafford McDowall. After scoring three tries in their opening two games, Jamie Dobie shifts from wing to scrumhalf.
“Connacht will pose a strong challenge tomorrow night,” said coach Franco Smith. “We know from our meetings with them last season that they will test us both with and without the ball and have a squad that can cause problems for any team in the league.”
The Warriors will have had mixed feelings about last week’s draw, having seen out the last eight minutes with 13 players, although George Horne hit the upright with a penalty to win the game.
Connacht are returning to the ground where their campaign ended last season in a 33-21 defeat in the quarter-finals. They went toe to toe with Glasgow for much of that game and were within a score of their hosts inside the last 10 minutes before a decisive 75 th -minute try by Kyle Steyn.
Having begun the season with a win away to Munster and draw at home to Ulster, Glasgow are nine-point favourites and have not been beaten by an Irish side at Scotstoun since Munster won their quarter-final clash in May 2023 by 13-5. Connacht’s last victory over Glasgow in Scotland was by 19-17 at Firhill Stadium back in September 2010.

title: Racing’s true greats are obvious and dual Arc winner Daryz isn’t one of them
description: There have been just two indisputably great racehorses in our expert’s time scribbling on the game
content:
F ollowing his back-to-back successes in Sunday’s Qatar Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe , the Racing Post queried: “Two Arcs is no mean feat – but where does Daryz sit among the pantheon of greats?” It’s an easy starter for 10, since the answer is that he’s hardly on it at all.
Even if the rather lily-livered qualification “modern” is applied to the greatness stakes for Daryz, the answer’s the same. He’s a top-class, magnificent looking middle-distance star who pulled off a fantastic double in an Arc that was well up to par. But no way is he one of the greats.
Splitting the “G” word into some specific measurement is obviously impossible, but it still must mean something. Even at a time when so much public discourse is about volume rather than accuracy, such distinctions matter even in the trivial matter of sporting legacy.
It doesn’t have to be the sort of linguistic gymnastics that a certain vintage of TV audience got used to when RTÉ’s former football panel twisted itself into knots about Ronaldo or Beckham being good players, but very definitely not great. But it can’t be some irrelevance either.
There have been just two indisputably great racehorses in this corner’s time scribbling on the game.
Sea The Stars was so good during his epochal 2009 campaign that Mick Kinane remains convinced we only ever saw about 80 per cent of what was under the bonnet. The next year along came Frankel. Each has their fan base as to who was better, but no one can seriously dispute their status as great champions.
Prior to them, it’s necessary to go back to 1986. Dancing Brave lost a Derby he should have won and a Breeders’ Cup he should never have run in. However, his performance in perhaps the finest Arc field ever sealed a superb CV.
Before him it’s back to a vintage era in the early 1970s when Brigadier Gerard, Mill Reef and Nijinsky strutted their stuff. Real old-timers insist France’s 1965 Derby and Arc winning paragon Sea Bird was nonpareil.
Other horses through the decades have exhibited superb brilliance. Montjeu couldn’t pull off an Arc double, but he was at another level to Daryz in terms of overall accomplishment, although without quite getting there as a true great.
[ Ronaldo and Messi’s final playing days show a clear difference between the modern game’s two greats Opens in new window ]
It’s the same with Enable and Treve, who did win the Arc back-to-back. Timeform rate Harbinger the equal of Sea The Stars, Dancing Brave and Shergar on the back of a single spectacular success in the 2010 King George. But no way is he a defining talent and, whisper it, maybe neither was Shergar, who beat up a poor year and wouldn’t have been sighted in a Guineas.
All of it is subjective but as in all sports there are greats, and then there are greats.
Roy Keane was a top player but Messi’s greatness is at a very different level. Cruyff was great, and Maradona too, but Best, kind of like Harbinger, flickered too briefly to really figure. David Clifford is already a great of Gaelic football in a way that none of the Dublin six-in-a-row team ever was.
And yes, all of it is barstool stuff that can never come to some universally acceptable and decisive verdict. None of it pays the bills and as reasons for dispute go it’s all a relatively harmless exercise in futility.
Maybe there’s a recency bias when it comes to judging it, rooted in a desire to believe that one’s witnessing a performance that will resonate over time. Racing fans can be quite wistful in wanting to believe there’s ultimately more to their passion than horses running round a fancy field.
From a commercial point of view there’s certainly more to it than that. In a week of ostentatious spending at the Tattersalls sales in Newmarket, it pays to remember that there’s a lot of money in bigging up the next big stallion prospect.
Aidan O’Brien’s near annual exercise in acclaiming his best three-year-old colt as the best he’s ever had has almost reached parody. But it still looks good on a shiny new stallion brochure, and one of those is all but sure to be run off soon once confirmation comes of Daryz going to stud.
[ New Munster CEO Avan Lee says ‘it would be a real shame’ if there wasn’t a role for Peter O’Mahony Opens in new window ]
From an accompanying media point of view too, rushing to acclaim new stars can be a profitable piece of content creation. It’s a boring clip that has perspective or context in a headline. But it can lead to premature elevation, which in this case it does Daryz a disservice.
He should be acclaimed for what he is, which is an outstanding dual Arc winner who is a major talent around a mile and a half at Longchamp. That’s more than enough without trying to bill him as what he isn’t, which is an all-time great. When you see the real thing, everyone knows it.
That only eight runners line up for the historic Birdcatcher Nursery at Naas on Saturday will be parsed for meaning, although it could help PINK VENOM (2.50pm) complete a handicap hat-trick. Johnny Murtagh’s filly won on quick ground at Fairyhouse before following up on soft at Cork. She’s got a 10lb hike in the ratings for that but is clearly in form and that going versatility can prove a big plus.
Six of the last 10 Cesarewitch winners have been Irish trained and six travel from Ireland for Newmarket’s big marathon handicap prize on Saturday. Four of the five trainers involved have won the race before, including Charles Byrnes who scored with Run For Oscar in 2022. He sends REVEREND HUBERT (3.40pm) this time. Fancied for the Galway Plate, he never figured at Ballybrit but he brings course and distance winning from to this task. A stamina test on quick ground appears to be what he likes and gets here.

title: Diarmaid Ferriter: France is caught in the politics of emergency, oscillating between nostalgia and extremism
description: Emmanuel Macron did much to upend the traditional two-party system in France but has fallen between stools
content:
G eneral Charles de Gaulle was in Ireland in June 1969, seeking peace on a Kerry beach a few months after his resignation as French president. French voters had rejected his proposed regionalisation and senate reforms.
Well might de Gaulle have sought solace on the edge of Europe; the previous year had produced remarkable scenes of defiance in Paris and other French cities, as students and workers protested, occupied and defied. De Gaulle struggled to make sense of it all.
As the historian Tony Judt , author of the 2005 book Postwar: A History of Europe Since 1945, saw it, in France “the Fifth Republic had accentuated the long-standing French habit of concentrating power in one place and a handful of institutions. France was run, and was seen to be run, by a tiny Parisian elite; socially exclusive, culturally privileged, haughty, hierarchical and unapproachable”.
Yet de Gaulle was able to rally the Gaullist political movement, stressing the danger of a communist, revolutionary coup; it was a choice, he insisted, between anarchy and legitimate government. The Gaullists won the ensuing national assembly election handsomely, but the sting came the following year.
Because of 1968, but also the older French tradition of barricades on French streets, and the reach of French cries of liberty, the current protests carry much historic weight and symbolism.
But they also come as France has embraced the de Gaulle legacy and mythology, reflected in the success of La Bataille de Gaulle, Antonin Baudry’s two-part epic film based on British historian Julian Jackson’s biography of de Gaulle. It is estimated five million people have seen it in France, and for all its artistic licence, it raises intriguing questions about the state of France and its identity now.
De Gaulle recorded in his memoirs: “All my life, I have had a certain idea of France.”
This was about recovery from humiliation during the second World War, the renewal of French grandeur and removing the stain of the Vichy collaboration with the Nazis. But it was also about authoritarianism, by creating an exceptionally powerful office of president, and de Gaulle was sustained, writes Judt, “by his institutions, his record, his personality and French memories of the alternative”.
The contemporary question of the alternative is also of great significance amid a frayed social contract and fractured politics. Emmanuel Macron , on his last lap of power, has at various stages attempted to channel the haughty de Gaulle gravitas. He has also been vocal about French international influence and leadership and the tensions about the Atlantic versus European alliances, faultlines magnified in the recent films as de Gaulle grappled with exile, a disdainful US president Roosevelt and a more sympathetic Winston Churchill .
[ French students at forefront of global stirring of disaffected youth Opens in new window ]
In May 2018, Macron told a French literary journal, “What makes me optimistic is that the history we are living through in Europe is becoming tragic again.” But this now reads as delusional and he has lost the domestic battle.
In June 2024, he made a television address to capture the gravity of his centrist coalition losing elections to the European Parliament; it secured just 15 per cent of the vote, less than half of far-right National Rally’s 31 per cent. He announced he was dissolving the French National Assembly and finished with a rhetorical flourish: “To be French is always to rise to the times when they demand it ... It is choosing to write history rather than be subjected to it.” But what France now faces, two years on, is the strong possibility of a far-right presidency.
Macron did much to upend the traditional two-party system in France but has fallen between stools. According to the Sorbonne sociologist Nathan Sperber, “Macron branded himself as a figure transcending the supposedly obsolete divide between right and left, blending technocratic expertise, disruptive entrepreneurialism and youthful optimism. To the more discerning public, what he appeared to offer was a deepening of neoliberal reforms under a sheen of cultural liberalism.”
The gilets jaunes protests of late 2018 and early 2019 were one measure of the anger, as were massive protests against pension reform; now we are witnessing the latest phase, ensuring, in Sperber’s phrase, that much of Macron’s time in office has been about “the politics of emergency”. Those emergencies can facilitate nostalgia and extremism, a potent cocktail. Appeals to “The Republic” become increasingly desperate, and a strategy of voting tactically to block far left or far right is hardly sustainable, given that it requires sufficient numbers not to embrace a movement they identify with but to voter en se bouchant le nez (“vote pinching their nose”).
According to French journalist Agnès Poirier, the interest in the de Gaulle film piques interest because it raises this fundamental question: “What kind of people do we believe ourselves to be?” In answering that, the number of nose pinchers could reduce dramatically.

title: Land Development Agency buys Dundrum objector’s house for €2.15m
description: Land Development Agency pays more than €2m to buy dormer bungalow to settle High Court case
content:
The Land Development Agency (LDA) paid more than €2 million to buy a dormer bungalow in south Dublin to settle a High Court case by the owner that threatened to further delay almost 1,000 new homes at the former Central Mental Hospital in Dundrum .
The public body charged with building homes on State land bought the extended property at Friarsland Road, Goatstown , in the spring.
The deal was completed weeks before Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII) bought four Dartmouth Square houses near the city centre for more than €9 million to settle MetroLink litigation – the first in a series of TII transactions that could lead to the purchase of 15 homes on the square.
Taoiseach Micheál Martin is scheduled to visit the former Central Mental Hospital site on Friday for an event marking the start of building work to develop 934 homes for the LDA and Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council . The project has suffered years of planning and legal delays.
[ LDA closes in on €21m deal for UCC’s IMI campus in Sandyford Opens in new window ]
Official data on property prices and ownership shows the LDA acquired the Friarsland Road house for €2.15 million on April 30th. The house backs on to the grounds of the former hospital.
Residential property price register data suggests the last home to be sold on Friarsland Road changed hands for €1.085 million in 2023. The market has been rising in the three years since.
Mark Leonard, himself a developer, initiated judicial review proceedings in February against An Coimisiún Pleanála and Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council to challenge planning permission in December for the LDA project.
Leonard withdrew the case a fortnight later, before receiving High Court permission to pursue the action.
[ LDA agrees to buy what will be Ireland’s tallest building Opens in new window ]
A note with the 2025 LDA annual report, lodged in the Dáil on Thursday, said the agency “acquired a residential house in Goatstown, Dublin 14” last April. No further information was provided.
Replying to questions, the LDA did not provide the Goatstown address but said it acquired a house “at market value as part of a legal settlement”.
Data from Táilte Éireann , which maintains the official land register, shows the unique folio for the Friarsland Road house was updated in June to show the LDA taking over ownership from Leonard.
Cork solicitors O’Donovan Baker, who acted for Leonard in the High Court, were asked whether they or their client had any comment on the deal. They had no comment.
LDA chief executive John Coleman told an Oireachtas committee in 2025 that delays from an earlier High Court case against the scheme added “at least €30 million to the estimated delivery cost”.
That previous case, in which Leonard was plaintiff, was conceded in 2024 by An Coimisiún Pleanála predecessor, An Bord Pleanála.

title: RTÉ likely to get back €20m lost in Budget 2027 ‘if it proves reforms are on track’
description: Taoiseach and Tánaiste’s offices intervene with Patrick O’Donovan ahead of crunch meeting with broadcaster’s leadership
author_name: Pat Leahy, Cormac McQuinn, Marie O’Halloran, Ian Curran
content:
RTÉ is likely to get the €20 million it lost in the budget if the broadcaster satisfies Government that its reform and redundancy programme is on track, senior Coalition figures believe.
There were interventions from both the Taoiseach’s and the Tánaiste’s offices yesterday after the revelation that RTÉ had been left €20 million short of the funding it expected for next year.
Following these contacts with Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan from Government’s leadership, there was a hastily arranged meeting between the Minister and RTÉ’s director general Kevin Bakhurst and chairman Terence O’Rourke.
Both sides were tight-lipped on the contents of the discussions afterwards but they sought to de-escalate tensions, with both Bakhurst and the Department of Communications describing the meeting as “positive”.
However, senior Government figures, granted anonymity to discuss a sensitive issue, are clear that they expect the RTÉ funding row to be defused by restoring the expected funding to the station on condition that it satisfies O’Donovan that its reform programme is on track.
[ Analysis: Last-minute €20m funding cut for RTÉ could have messy consequences Opens in new window ]
It is understood that O’Donovan is due to bring a memo to Government within weeks on funding at the station which may include proposals for licence fee reform which could increase revenues at RTÉ.
After yesterday’s meeting, Bakhurst said: “We’ve agreed that we’re going to carry on working with his [O’Donovan’s] officials to try to find a resolution to this.”
On whether RTÉ will get the money it expected, Bakhurst said he did not know but asked if he has confidence in the Minister, Bakhurst said: “Absolutely, yes.”
A department statement said O’Donovan listened to the RTÉ concerns and that “the chair and director general provided assurances on the delivery of reforms and their timing”. It added: “The department and RTÉ will continue to engage constructively on all the issues discussed over the next few weeks.”
[ RTÉ DG says he has confidence in Minister after ‘constructive’ meeting on funding Opens in new window ]
Earlier on Thursday, Coimisiún na Meán expressed disappointment that the budget has “not allowed for the delivery of the level of funding to RTÉ that was previously outlined in the Government’s plans”.
It said that “both RTÉ and TG4 require funding that is adequate, sustainable and predictable” and said it had set out recommendations for the funding of both organisations in its Annual Review of Performance and Public Funding for the broadcasters.
Meanwhile, the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), of which RTÉ is a member, said it was “deeply concerned” by the funding decision.
The Department of Communications saidnow that Budget 2027 has been published O’Donovan “intends to issue a formal response to the 2025 Annual Review of Performance and Public Funding and funding recommendations for 2027 submitted by Coimisiún na Meán”. All of this will be published in the coming weeks.
The commission and an external consultancy firm told the Government last year that RTÉ’s 2026 budget allocation of €240 million was not adequate to support the broadcaster’s five-year strategy and deliver the reforms the Coalition expected.
[ Irish Government was warned last year that RTÉ funding was too low Opens in new window ]
The Government was also told the national broadcaster would face “particularly acute” cash flow issues in 2027, even if it received the €260 million earmarked for next year under the funding deal agreed with the previous government.
In the Dáil, Social Democrats TD Sinéad Gibney accused O’Donovan of “blowing up RTÉ’s budget” and she asked Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke how many redundancies the Government wants at the broadcaster.
Burke called for “cool heads”, and insisted that the Government did not expect compulsory redundancies at RTÉ.
Meanwhile, TG4 has also requested a meeting with O’Donovan to discuss its budget allocation for 2027 after it was confirmed that it would remain static despite the Irish-language broadcaster requesting an additional €11 million.

title: There is no dignity in not being able to heat your home
description: Older people deserve the right to live without fear of poverty or loneliness
content:
Sir, – I refer to the letter of Brian O’Brien, and his being “ surprised at older people and pensioners’ expressions of annoyance and dissatisfaction with the latest budget ” (Letters, October 8th).
This contribution to the residual, if subtle, ageism pervading Irish society does us all a disservice.
The Government reneged on their commitment made under the 2018 Roadmap for Pensions to raise the State pension to 34 per cent of the average wage to ensure that the fixed income of elders keeps some pace with the cost of living . The maximum State pension, currently at €299.30, would be €355.93, based on the average industrial wage of €1,046.88 published by the Central Statistics Office .
The number of people aged 65 and over now stands at 891,000, accounting for 16.1 per cent of the population. The recent Survey on Income and Living Conditions indicates that more than 122,400 elders were living in poverty in 2025, an increase of 15 per cent compared with 2024.
After a life of work, contributing to the building of the present wealthy Ireland, older people, or elders – to use a more positively perceived label for this age – have merited the right to live in older age with dignity.
Not least, our elders have contributed to raising and educating their children to adulthood, thereby creating generations of fantastic young Irish people that have been a cornerstone of the betterment of the Irish nation, even if somewhat regrettably, also of countries abroad through the Irish diaspora, many of whom today are again being forced into economic emigration.
Where is the dignity in not being able to heat one’s home? Or having to choose between paying utility bills and affording sufficient groceries, or whether or not to access healthcare, to socialise with friends or, dare I mention, taking a holiday, all of which are now becoming luxuries? Where is the dignity in loneliness? – Yours, etc,

title: Dublin City Council proposes tree preservation order at Kenilworth Square
description: Owner of south Dublin square, St Mary’s College in Rathmines, plans expansion of sports grounds
content:
A tree preservation order prohibiting the felling of more than 50 mature trees at the site of contentious redevelopment plans at Kenilworth Square, Rathgar , has been proposed by Dublin City Council .
The council is launching a public consultation on the matter from Friday and, if implemented, it would be its first tree preservation order since 2008.
Just six such orders have been made by the council to date, four of which concern trees at Dartmouth Square Park near Ranelagh in Dublin 6 .
The proposal could affect controversial plans from the owner of the Victorian square, St Mary’s College in Rathmines, to develop the site currently used as sports grounds.
Residents surrounding the square, which has been owned by the school since the 1940s, have opposed the plans, citing concerns over ecology and heritage.
The proposed redevelopment involves reconfiguring three pitches to two, one of which would have an all-weather surface.
St Mary’s planned to remove eight “lower-value trees” for the all-weather pitch at the north end of the square, saying it would plant 74 new trees.
However, the proposed tree preservation order would prohibit the felling, topping or “wilful destruction” of 54 trees surrounding the square, a large portion of which are situated at the north end, according to a report by the council’s tree officer.
[ Kenilworth Square residents get leave to appeal over school’s rugby pitch redevelopment Opens in new window ]
It was first proposed by Green Party councillor Carolyn Moore, who argued the trees are “absolutely intrinsic” to the square’s character and integrity.
“For me, it just seemed that the tree preservation order was there as a mechanism within the planning system to sort of safeguard against the kinds of exemptions that may ultimately end up chipping away at the biodiversity and heritage value of Kenilworth Square,” she said.
Moore said she was not against St Mary’s plans to develop the square and improve sports facilities, though such works “must take into consideration the ecological and heritage value of the square”.
She said she was hopeful the order would be implemented and that “any future development of the square will be constrained by the need to protect these trees”.
Earlier this year, a High Court judge urged residents to “ calm down” their response to plans to fell trees after a protest resulted in a match being cancelled.
Judge David Nolan granted campaign group Protect Kenilworth Square and resident Martin Joyce an injunction preventing St Mary’s from felling while they sought to appeal his prior ruling.
Nolan had ruled St Mary’s did not require planning permission for some works at the square after Dublin City Council decided they were exempted development.
The group subsequently received leave to appeal in May.
On Thursday, Joyce said residents were “very pleased that Dublin City Council has recognised the importance of the 19th century trees in the park, not just for the locals in Rathgar but for the city of Dublin.”
[ ‘It is money talking’: Rathgar has mixed views on Kenilworth Square plan Opens in new window ]
Mary Daly, a spokeswoman for the Kenilworth for the Kids group, which supports St Mary’s plans, said “common sense” was needed and approved of a “balanced approach that recognises the importance of both our natural environment and the needs of children”.
“Across Dublin, we are seeing much-needed sporting improvements delayed by increasingly contentious planning disputes. Protecting nature and giving children the space to play, develop and thrive should not be an either-or choice. There is a better way forward, and our children deserve it,” she said.
Daly argued the “loudest voices in this debate” have “overshadowed the needs of children and families across the wider community”.
“We encourage parents, local sports clubs and the wider community to make their views known through Dublin City Council’s consultation. A vocal minority should not be mistaken for the voice of an entire community.”

title: Donore Avenue on the big screen
description: TV had yet to reach us in 1950
content:
Sir, – Frank McNally refers to the suitability of the houses on Donore Avenue for the filming of The Siege of Sidney Street (“Another sighting of the lesser-spotted Dublin fanlight horse”, An Irishman’s Diary , October 8th).
As a local kid who hung around the film crew at the time, my understanding of the suitability of the area was that the film was meant to depict 1912 London, and the houses in the East End in 1950, at the time of filming, all had TV aerials attached to their chimneys.
In Donore Avenue, however, TV had yet to reach us, thus our chimneys were, for the most part, free of TV aerials. Admittedly, Dublin was not entirely TV aerial-free, as a weak signal could be obtained from the North of Ireland BBC, and some posh people had early TV sets, which required huge aerials attached to their chimneys. – Yours, etc,

title: Border poll is about reunification of the island
description: We must reverse wrong done to those who were shut out 100 years ago
content:
A chara, – Paul Nash writes about a Border poll, using the retort: “You can’t choose your neighbours, but you can choose who you wish to invite into your house” (“ Garvaghy standoff and ‘the worn out dreams of yesterday’ ”, Letters, October 8th).
It’s an inappropriate metaphor: no one is looking to come in anywhere, the poll would be about reunification, not incorporation.
Rather than an invitation to “come in”, it is more a case of reversing the wrong done to those who were – against their wishes – shut out of the metaphorical house 100 years ago. – Le meas,

title: Proper river management, not dredging, will help prevent flooding
description: Removing silt from riverbeds just sends floodwater downstream to somewhere else quicker
content:
Sir, – David Doran suggests dredging the river Slaney in Enniscorthy , Co Wexford , to prevent flooding (“ Enniscorthy river blockages contributing to flooding ”, Letters, October 7th).
Experience in Britain and Ireland has shown that this seemingly simple solution may not be the best way to proceed.
Upstream management with restoration of woodland, re-meandering and removal of flood banks to allow reconnection to flood plains has worked in the Tweed Catchment Management Plan on the Scottish-English border.
Similar work has been done in Dartmoor/Holnicote, southwest England, with compensation paid to farmers for interventions.
Trinity College Dublin has published nature-based solutions, modelling and field intervention studies showing successful intervention is possible in Ireland.
Simple dredging would send the flood water downstream to Wexford more rapidly and do nothing to address the real causes: a man-made combination of overgrazed hills and canal-like riverbanks. – Yours, etc,

title: Government should apply transparency standards to themselves and their bike sheds
description: Or is accountability something best demanded of others, like RTÉ?
content:
Sir, – Is there an element of political pettiness in the continued scrutiny of RTÉ and its funding? One wonders whether a national broadcaster that holds politicians to account is being held to a different standard.
Twenty million is, unquestionably, a significant amount, but pales beside the extraordinary cost overruns at the national children’s hospital, running into hundreds of millions .
Where is the equivalent political outrage, accountability or consequence? Surely politicians demanding financial discipline and transparency from RTÉ should be equally enthusiastic about applying those standards to themselves and their bike sheds.
Or is accountability something best demanded of others? – Yours, etc,
[ Media Commission ‘disappointed’ budget allocation for RTÉ falls short of expected sum Opens in new window ]

title: Three-day abortion wait must be removed
description: No health-related reasons have been shown for the imposition of the mandatory waiting period
content:
Sir, – A private member’s Bill to remove the mandatory three-day waiting period from the 2018 abortion act is before the Oireachtas health committee. The task is straightforward: consider the evidence and decide whether there are any health-related reasons for retaining the provision.
The committee has a wealth of expertise at its disposal. It has heard evidence from reproductive healthcare experts, including representatives of the Irish College of GPs , the HSE and the National Women and Infants Programme. At the request of the committee, the Irish Family Planning Association ( IFPA ) and other abortion care providers also provided written observations.
All concurred that a mandatory waiting period in law must not be confused with informed consent. The former is a coercive legal barrier, with no health benefits; the latter is an intrinsic element of healthcare and professional ethics.
The independent review of the Termination of Pregnancy Act recommended removing the mandatory waiting period. The health committee endorsed the review report in December 2023.
The IFPA has published a five-year analysis of clients who were required by law to undergo the mandatory waiting period. This data shows that, of the 2,749 clients who attended an initial abortion consultation with the IFPA from 2021 to 2025, and for whom we know the outcome, 98 per cent proceeded to access abortion care with our service or in hospital-based settings.
In each year, some clients made no further contact with the IFPA after their first appointment. The law respects women’s right to privacy and does not require them to give reasons for their decisions. We do not intrude on our clients’ privacy or speculate about outcomes. Indeed, we only contact clients or former clients for reasons related to their health.
However, we know from our services that this legal barrier causes pregnant people to experience anxiety, distress, additional expense and unnecessary travel. Combined with the rigid 12-week gestational limit, this can cause patients to become ineligible for care in Ireland and force them to travel abroad to access services. Rural, low-income and marginalised patients are particularly affected.
Moreover, we can categorically state that everyone who accesses our service receives expert medical advice in a non-judgmental healthcare environment, supplemented by specialist pregnancy counselling, if requested. It is the availability of quality healthcare at no cost that supports informed consent, not the enforced three-day delay.
[ As a religious teen, I was against abortion. But even I could see the flaws in the logic Opens in new window ]
Everyone who accesses the healthcare system has the right to do so with dignity and respect for their bodily autonomy, free from coercion. Policy should support access to healthcare, not obstruct it.
No health-related reasons have been shown for the imposition of the mandatory waiting period; the World Health Organisation recommends the removal of such barriers from abortion laws. If the health committee is serious about making good healthcare policy, it must do the same. – Yours, etc,
Director of advocacy and communications,

title: ‘We knew we weren’t being rescued’: Irish survivor of Mozambique massacre gives evidence at inquest
description: Philip Mawer was killed during a 2021 jihadist attack on the TotalEnergies gas project
content:
An Irish project manager led the evacuation of 192 colleagues from a jihadist attack in Palma, Mozambique , in 2021, after a day waiting for TotalEnergies to send help, a British coroner’s court heard.
Gordon James Rhattigan gave evidence at an inquest into the death of his friend and colleague Philip Mawer (58) from Shaftesbury, England, who was killed by a rocket-propelled grenade which struck his vehicle as he tried to escape.
The coroner, Jason Peggs, ruled that Mawer died of “unlawful killing”. Rhattigan was rescued by helicopter and survived the attack.
Both worked for Dubai-based contractor RA International Group plc, which was contracted by TotalEnergies to help build its $20 billion liquefied natural gas project.
Mawer was a senior leader responsible for overseeing the company’s operations, and Rhattigan oversaw the construction of an employee accommodation camp, approximately 12km from the gas compound.
TotalEnergies maintains the project was operated by its Mozambique subsidiary, TEMPA1.
Detective chief inspector Patrick Allen, giving evidence on behalf of the British Metropolitan Police’s counterterrorism command, confirmed it was “right” to view the attack as the biggest terror attack since 9/11. A total of 1,354 people were killed.
The first day of the attack “was just a normal day”, Rhattigan told the court.
Mawer collected him from the airport on March 24th, 2021, and drove him to the Amarula Hotel to drop off his bags. They then made their way to the camp construction site, the court heard. Rhattigan recalled that in their last exchange, Mawer had invited him back to the hotel for lunch, but he declined and stayed at the camp to work, while Mawer returned to the hotel.
Within hours of their conversation, insurgents linked to Islamic State, locally known as Al-Shabaab, attacked the town.
In testimony, Rhattigan said he received a message from Lars Narfeldt, chief operating officer of RA International, telling him to “get all the staff together” and “go back to the hotel”, before then instructing them to stay put and lock themselves at the camp.
About half an hour after the attack began, all communication was cut.
That night, Rhattigan said he sheltered in the accommodation camp with the rest of the workforce. He cut holes in the perimeter in case they needed to flee into the jungle, the court heard.
“We knew we weren’t being rescued” after the first day, he said. “The gunfire, the explosions were so intense.”
Rhattigan’s statements during the hearing on September 24th, attended by reporters from environmental investigations outlet Land and Climate Review, described how he and his colleagues left the site on the second day. The Mozambican military guided a convoy of 192 people out along “old roads and dirt tracks” to the Afungi peninsula, the main base for Total’s LNG compound.
There, Rhattigan said he approached security while the rest of the convoy waited and told them that they were expected and would be given sanctuary.
“He knew I was talking rubbish,” Rhattigan said of the security guard.
When TotalEnergies’ security asked, “Do you trust all of those people in those buses?” Rhattigan replied, “Of course I do; I’ve been working with those guys for a year”, he told the coroner’s court at Winchester.
On that basis, security let all 192 people into the site after an hour, Rhattigan said. He claimed security later sent away local residents but allowed contractors to stay.
Rhattigan and the remaining contractors were collected by helicopters from the LNG compound three days later.
After his evacuation, Rhattigan told the court that he regained phone signal and found two messages from Mawer, both from the day the attack had begun. The first instructed him not to leave camp. The second said Mawer had been in contact with TotalEnergies, and the company had promised to send an armed convoy to collect them the next morning.
Rhattigan said help from TotalEnergies never arrived. TotalEnergies denies this.
Evidence presented to the court by the Mawer family’s legal team claimed the scale of the threat had been building for months.
A report by the British counterterrorism command detailed how ISIS-linked insurgents had seized the island of Vamizi, some 25km from Palma, six months before the attack. Roughly 50 people were beheaded in the province in April 2020.
TotalEnergies signed a memorandum of understanding with the Mozambican government in August 2020, establishing a joint task force to provide security for the LNG project in Cabo Delgado.
The company has come under scrutiny over whether it did enough in response to the attack.
The inquest heard that TotalEnergies allegedly refused to provide aviation fuel to rescue helicopters, which the Mawer family believe could have saved Philip Mawer. Adam Payter, the representative for TotalEnergies’ Mozambican subsidiary, disputed this evidence.
Total’s representative also told the court that there was “no duty on or for TEMPA1 to cover persons that were not employed by it and remain outside [their area]”.
In a statement after the inquest, TotalEnergies said it took note of the coroner’s conclusions, “which made no finding against TEPMA1 or TotalEnergies”.
Total’s Mozambique LNG project was suspended after the 2021 attack. Construction resumed earlier this year, and production is expected to begin in 2029.
When asked in court to describe his late friend, Rhattigan said Philip Mawer was “very kind, funny, down-to-earth”, and “honest”.
Rhattigan now works for a fuel, aviation services and logistics firm in Somalia.

title: Jennifer Walshe: AI music has become ‘the Ozempic of the industry’. Everyone is on it
description: One platform, Suno, outputs the equivalent of Spotify’s entire catalogue once a fortnight, but it’s impossible to know who’s using it
content:
S weet treats in a child’s lunch box. Good idea? Bad idea? Is it possible to be neutral about such a thing? A woman’s Instagram account, @ashleighjamz , went viral at the start of the new school year for posting text messages the creator claimed were from the “mom’s group chat” at her daughter’s school. The messages revolved around a request from “Michelle” for the other mothers not to pack Oreos in their children’s lunch boxes. Over a series of 40+ videos, the “moms” castigate one another over their parenting choices and plot against “Michelle.” The posts have been viewed millions of times, reposted, stitched, commented on by everyone from parents to dietitians to the official Oreos account (“Oreo-gate was NOT on my 2026 bingo card”). So far, so clickbait.
It didn’t seem to matter if the messages were entirely fictional – it’s fair to say their authenticity is, at best, uncertain. Doesn’t really matter as long as they go viral, right? The storm became known as #oreogate, and media outlets from Good Morning America to Business Insider reported on it. Generally the reporting focused on parents’ opinions around allowing kids to have treats in their lunch boxes, coupled with a strong helping of disdain for the fictional women involved in the chat, a disdain that effortlessly spilled on to real women.
Posting ludicrous texts or group chats to social media is nothing new. What struck me about it was that @ashleighjamz’s posts were set to music using the generative AI platform Suno, and presented in video form. She explicitly acknowledges this, describing herself as “a mom turning her hectic life into songs using @sunomusic” and “Suno Partner”. The music is funny and absorbing enough. The text is delivered in the high-camp mode of a Broadway musical comedy, full of drama and flair. In contrast, the images in the videos are fairly boring, featuring screenshots of the texts overlaid on an extreme close-up of Ashleigh’s emotionless face.
Watching it unfold, I thought of the French film theorist Michel Chion, who developed the concept of “added value” to describe how sound functions in cinema. In his 1993 book, Audio Vision: Sound on Screen, Chion outlines how when we watch a clip soundtracked with sad music (for example), it’s the music that induces the emotion, making us feel the images are inherently sad, rather than the images themselves. In the case of #oreogate, it’s clear that the music is doing the heavy lifting; without the ability to rapidly turn the texts into comedic music using Suno, I doubt the posts would have gone viral.
There are plenty of generative AI platforms for music – including Eleven Labs, Udio and Riffusion – but Suno is considered the most powerful globally. The company is valued at $5.4 billion. In a recent pitch deck, Suno claimed that users were creating more than seven million songs per day on the platform. To put this in perspective: the platform outputs the equivalent of Spotify’s entire catalogue once a fortnight.
The first of the #oreogate videos has had more than 12.7 million plays on Instagram at time of writing. It appears to be the most viral piece of verified AI content since 2024’s “BBL Drizzy”, a Drake diss track featuring a Udio-generated sample, released by producer Metro Boomin at the height of the Kendrick Lamar-Drake feud.
Tracking the success of Suno-generated material is difficult.
It’s impossible to tell who is using the platform, because users who pay for subscriptions automatically gain commercial rights, can download their tracks and post them outside of Suno.com with no obligation to disclose that Suno was used in the process.
There are plenty of musical slop merchants releasing an album every week by fictional artists such as Masters of Prophecy (36.2 million subscribers on YouTube). But it is impossible to know how many real musicians have signed up for the higher-tier subscriptions and quietly integrated Suno into their practice. The company is very much aware of this. Earlier this year Mikey Shulman, the company’s chief executive, described to The Guardian how Suno was “the Ozempic of the music industry – everybody is on it and nobody wants to talk about it”.
However, @ashleighjamz didn’t just use Suno to create the music for her videos: she was paid to generate the videos. This detail is lost in much of the reporting, but as a musician I find it critical. Mikey Shulman describes Suno’s mission as facilitating a future “where music is a bigger, more valuable, and more meaningful part of people’s lives than it even is today”. But Suno’s latest viral success is not with a musician, it’s with a paid influencer using their tech to make short-form video – the dominant medium of our time – more compelling. The Oreogate influencer is not looking to sell albums or concert tickets: she’s selling T-shirts and mugs with quotes from #oreogate printed on them.
Is this what music is for now? Is this the inevitable use the logic of generative AI impels us to put music to: music not just as a way to “add value” to short-form video, but as the grease that keeps the wheels of content creation turning?
Jennifer Walshe is professor of composition at Oxford University

title: ‘With great privilege comes great responsibility’: Evan Comerford on Dublin keeper role
description: Ballymun player sets his sights on a long stint between the posts after injury woes
content:
Evan Comerford has already put down one of the most unique intercounty careers in the history of Gaelic football .
Still, maybe it was just coincidence that the Ballymun goalkeeper was one of the players on hand to launch Dublin ’s new alternative jersey at Parnell Park on Thursday.
Comerford has been on the Dublin squad for a decade, during which time he has accumulated five All-Ireland medals, eight Leinster titles and three National Leagues. But most of those limelight years were spent in the shadows as understudy to the greatest goalkeeper in the game, Stephen Cluxton.
So, at 28, it feels now like Comerford’s days between the posts for Dublin might only be in their infancy.
With Cluxton putting away his gloves to focus on a coaching role with the Dubs in 2026, Comerford and Hugh O’Sullivan battled it out for the No 1 jersey.
O’Sullivan started four league games to Comerford’s three. However, Comerford lined out in seven of Dublin’s eight championship matches, including the All-Ireland quarter-final and semi-final.
If his body and form allow, he hopes to be the capital’s custodian for a little while yet.
“We’re blessed in Dublin, our facilities are pretty close,” says Comerford. “From that standpoint, I think it is set up for longevity. I can see 10 more years in the legs, provided the body allows me to do it.”
[ Cillian O’Connor gets the ending he deserved to one of the greatest careers in GAA history Opens in new window ]
He was first called up to the senior panel in 2017 and Comerford has since made 18 championship appearances. He had to wait for his opportunity. In doing so, he chose patience rather than frustration.
“Early in my career, it was easy, I kind of call it my apprenticeship phase,” he says. “You’re learning from the best. You have icons like Stephen [Cluxton], Jonny Cooper, James McCarthy around the dressingroom. You’re just in awe of these guys.
“When Stephen stepped away in 2021, that was a real justification of, ‘okay, I’ve plied my trade, my chance is here now’. So there was massive motivation to go out in 2021 and prove that I wasn’t just here as a coaster hanging off the coattails of Stephen.
“I really wanted to prove that I could add value, bring my own identity to things. Then the injuries hit. That was probably the most challenging phase. I’d just got my chance, then you feel like the tide is washing against you with the injuries.
“So, you can either pack it in, you can give up on it or you can fight and work your way against it. Thankfully, it did work out from the injury standpoint and I feel like I’m nearly back to 2021 again, where the chance is here again to put the best foot forward.”
The injuries: two groin surgeries, a broken collarbone and a torn cruciate. Comerford is a qualified physio so that helped with perspective and recovery, but the second groin injury in 2022 was the most worrying, because there was no certainty he’d ever get back between the sticks.
[ Halfway there? Gaelic games integration timeline is no clearer after Dáil committee Opens in new window ]
He had been Dublin’s first-choice goalkeeper in the 2021 and 2022 championships.
“I tore the groin off the bone,” he says. “The physios were great with it but there was a kind of not knowing will you kick again, not knowing will you play again.
“It was on my kicking leg and being a goalkeeper you didn’t know if you were going to kick properly again, but thankfully it worked out in the end.”
He was just returning from injury when Cluxton made a shock Dublin comeback in the middle of the 2023 season.
Comerford didn’t make any championship appearances between 2023-2025. Another test of patience. But when Cluxton moved to the role of coach for the 2026 campaign, it opened the way for a battle between his understudies for the jersey.
The mythology that surrounds the position of goalkeeper in Dublin is not something Comerford has chosen to ignore either. From 1967 until 2021 the number one jersey more or less belonged to only four players – Paddy Cullen, John O’Leary, Davy Byrne and Cluxton.
“I kind of sum that up with one sentence: with great privilege comes great responsibility,” he says.
“The privilege of pulling on that jersey, being the closest man to Hill 16 for half a game, is massive. It’s a real honour to break out from the huddle, jog down to the goal and just see the colour and hear the noise.
“But I know that there’s a massive responsibility with that too and that you’re holding up a lot of hopes, a lot of dreams for a lot of those supporters.
“That’s something I probably didn’t appreciate when I first started out, but certainly in the last couple of years I’ve really grown to know that it is a massive privilege. It is a dream to be in there and I want to make sure the body goes for as long as it possibly can.
“But the reality is each year there’s two or three other fellas who have that dream too. Like at the minute we’ve Hugh O’Sullivan and Gavin Sheridan, both excellent goalkeepers.
“All of us probably could sit here and say we want 10-15 more years as number one, but if I’m not performing the best on kick-outs or on shot-stopping, someone else is going to get it.
“I do romanticise that idea and I do dream of that, but I’m acutely aware that there is consistent work to be done.”
– Comerford was speaking at the launch of Dublin’s new alternative jersey for the 2027 season.

title: US-backed social housing landlord returned €15m to investors ahead of sale
description: First Step Homes was sold to Home For Life for close to €70m in April
content:
First Step Homes, a company that leased homes to local authorities for social housing , distributed €15 million to investors before it was sold for €70 million in April.
The low-profile private housing investor was set up in 2015 by UK-based Trinity Investment Management and backed by US real estate investment firm TPG Angelo Gordon. In April, it was acquired by Irish mortgage-to-rent scheme provider Home For Life for €69.7 million.
New filings by First Step Homes Ltd show the company distributed €15.1 million to its immediate Netherlands-based parent firm last year prior to the sale to Home For Life.
The company entered the Irish market in 2015. It acquired homes in Dublin and other cities including Cork, Limerick and Galway, renovated the units and then leased them to the State for social housing.
At its peak, First Step Homes had a portfolio of around 800 mostly second-hand homes in Ireland, which were then leased to councils for more than 10 years at slightly discounted market rates.
This practice of leasing homes for social housing has faced heavy criticism from Opposition parties, including Sinn Féin and the Social Democrats, which have criticised the deals as a poor use of taxpayers’ money.
Based on Department of Housing data, the State has agreed deals to lease around 10,000 homes on a long-term basis for €3 billion over their 25-year lifetime. Many of the homes are being leased for more than €2,500 a month.
Last year, First Step Homes director Richard O’Boyle told The Irish Times the firm reduced its portfolio here to about 300 homes in recent years.
[ Fall in number of units added to social housing stock Opens in new window ]
The company began to divest from Ireland following a commitment by the previous government in 2021 to phase out long-term social housing leasing deals with private companies and funds by the end of 2025.
Last year, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said the Government backtracked on its plan to phase out leasing homes for social housing.
He said the Government needed to “pivot more strongly to getting private sector investment in the market” and take “very difficult political decisions” as it targets the building of 300,000 homes by 2030 – equating to an average of 60,000 a year.
Following the comments from the Taoiseach, O’Boyle said First Step Homes was exploring the potential to expand again in Ireland. In April, it was confirmed the company was acquired by Home for Life, a company led by Paul Cunningham, Charlie O’Reilly Hyland and Max O’Reilly Hyland.

title: Who’s hiring and who’s firing in Ireland’s technology sector?
description: Some firms see AI as ‘an easy way to reduce headcount’, but what is really behind recent layoffs?
content:
The announcement by Stripe last week that it would create 200 jobs at its Dublin headquarters was a welcome piece of good news for the tech sector in Ireland.
The company has grown its workforce by 35 per cent since the start of the year, with plans to further expand its engineering operation here. But it also underscored the wildly changing fortunes of a crucial sector of the economy.
Ireland’s tech sector has been a driving force for the economy in recent years, but as companies try to cut costs globally and keep shareholders onside, the threat of job losses has returned. Across the Irish industry, cuts have been implemented across a number of different areas. Social media, payments technology, productivity and workflow – all have been hit by lay-offs since the start of the year.
Just this week, it emerged that Oracle is looking to cut another 70 Irish jobs this year as it continues to trim costs to fund its expensive push into artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and data centres .
That has caused understandable nerves in the sector. The memory of the “tech wreck” of 2022 and 2023 is still fresh, when the cuts came fast, and they came with big numbers. Could we be heading for another?
For those who take a glass half-full approach, the work the economy has done to attract new investment has clawed back some of the ground we lost in the dark days. Employment in tech and related sectors hovered around 121,000 in September 2022 according to payroll data, or 159,500 according to the quarterly labour force survey compiled by the Central Statistics Office . At the end of 2025, those figures were 120,700 and 170,500 respectively.
With AI being touted as a game-changer for companies already seeking to cut costs, the State agencies’ moves to capture at least some of the opportunity offered by the growth of the technology might also offset the inevitable losses.
Meta was the first big name to announce a serious cull in 2026, and provided a warning of what was to come. The social media giant, which owns Instagram , Facebook and WhatsApp , said in May it would reduce its Irish staff numbers by up to 350 jobs – a 20 per cent reduction and well in excess of the 10 per cent that had been expected.
When you tot it all up, the number of jobs lost at Meta over the past few years leaves the company at around half the size it was before the post-Covid reductions started. The plans to occupy a large campus in Dublin were scaled back some time ago, with Meta announcing it would sublet part of the development on the former AIB Bankcentre grounds.
There are repercussions, too, for companies that rely on multinationals for business. While the name Covalen may not have meant a lot to people working outside the tech sector, it is intertwined with some of the biggest names in the business. Part of the CPL Group, the contractor provides content moderation and AI training services for Meta. But the outsourced nature of the business means it – and its staff – are in the most precarious position when it comes to job security,
In April, the company notified workers that more than 700 jobs were at risk. That followed Meta’s announcement in March that it would rely more on AI systems in the future for content moderation, reducing the need for contractors. Again, the implication was that AI was being blamed for the reduction in numbers.
Meta isn’t the only social media company making cuts. Video-sharing platform TikTok has also been culling roles across the company in the name of efficiency.
The most recent round of cuts were a handful of roles in its ecommerce team – around a dozen, according to sources. But that came on the back of the loss of 670 roles concentrated on the company’s trust and safety division – which was loudly trumpeted when it located here – along with jobs in the company’s AI data service and operations team responsible for annotation and search operations services. Once again, AI played a role in the reasoning; the plan was to take the work currently being done by those staff and redistribute it among other TikTok offices, outsource it, or hand it over to AI.
The blow was softened somewhat by the creation of about 320 roles in the Dublin office, which were open to affected employees. That brought the total down to 350 jobs, but it was a significant reduction for a company that had, at its peak, employed about 3,000 people in Ireland.
Oracle told staff this week it would cut up to 70 roles, with the cuts concentrated in engineering and development. Some sales and finance positions are also expected to go. That follows the loss of 150 jobs earlier this year.
The move is part of a global restructuring of the business that has seen it cut its workforce by 13 per cent, or about 21,000 employees, as the company focuses on trimming areas where AI is expected to make roles redundant.
While Stripe is hiring, rival and one-time acquisition target PayPal is cutting back. The payments company, which has come under serious pressure from competitors in recent years, told staff in August that it would cut jobs at its Irish business. While initial numbers estimated the losses to be about 30, with the business support department primarily affected, it later emerged that a further 130 jobs across a range of departments were also at risk. That added up to almost 12 per cent of its Irish workforce.
The redundancies were not a surprise, although the figures might have been. PayPal had signalled plans to cut jobs globally in April, as part of strategy to trim costs, simplify operations, remove duplication and clarify reporting lines.
It is hard to pin the cuts down to a single business area or role. The type of work being hit across the tech sector is mixed, although high-tech roles are more likely to be spared, while people management – human resources, team leaders – and support services are being reduced as companies try to flatten their management structures.
When it comes to hiring though, the picture is a little clearer. Highly skilled tech roles are in demand, with AI, cybersecurity and data skills topping the list of new hires for companies.
Morgan McKinley’s quarterly employment monitor backs that up. It notes the shift in the third quarter from traditional development skills towards AI-enabled roles.
[ Ireland’s great AI job displacement: ‘Every employer, every worker should be talking about this’ Opens in new window ]
It notes software and data engineers are still in demand, albeit ones with practical AI capabilities.
“US companies establishing AI engineering hubs and centres of excellence in Ireland are adding further demand for AI, machine learning operations, data engineering, cloud, DevOps and security skills, as traditional contract demand for full-stack, Java and React/Node roles softens,” said Trayc Keevans, global FDI director, Morgan McKinley Ireland.
One of those companies establishing an AI centre of excellence in Ireland is Workday. Almost a year ago, the business software company announced it would create 200 jobs over three years at an AI centre at its new Dublin headquarters.
But Irish-based staff at the US-founded business were told last month that the company was cutting jobs, with as many as 80 at risk as part of a global move to trim numbers. About 80 per cent of the company’s 2,000 Irish employees are involved in research, product development and software engineering – the type of high-value roles that you would expect the company would hang on to.
This time, people management roles are in the firing line, although they are spread across the product and technology teams. At the same time, Workday is continuing to recruit for high-tech positions such as AI software and machine-learning engineers, with open roles on its website.
AI company Anthropic is also expanding, adding 200 jobs across engineering, sales and finance by 2027 as part of the expansion of its Dublin hub. Rival OpenAI is doing similar, creating 250 jobs over the next two years in engineering, finance, HR and other support roles.
[ Rise of AI threatens about 110,000 Irish jobs, study finds Opens in new window ]
Cloud company Version 1 is recruiting for 250 new jobs, driven by the opening of its new AI studio in Dublin. That is in addition to 400 roles it previously announced for Northern Ireland.
US database company MongoDB, meanwhile, is investing €74 million, opening a new office in Cork and adding 200 jobs in engineering, product development, and customer-facing teams. The company is preparing to tap into demand for its data platform that could be supercharged by the increased adoption of agentic AI – systems that can carry out tasks without human intervention.
AI is becoming increasingly important in the labour market. But it can also be used as a handy smokescreen for companies. There is a level of scepticism around the claims by companies laying off employees that the layoffs are solely down to targeted investments in AI paying off.
