“There’s no doubt in my mind that AI is an easy way to reduce headcount, but also claim it in a really positive, forward-thinking way,” says Christopher Paye, country director for The StepStone Group for Ireland. “Forty-six per cent of employers are increasing hiring; for the IT and the tech sector, 28 per cent of firms in Ireland are hiring for highly specialised roles such as AI and machine learning.”
Others note that there are broader market pressures that are coming into play, forcing companies to re-evaluate their workforce.
“While recent headlines have focused on job cuts, the reality is more nuanced. We have seen a number of high-profile reductions, particularly across parts of the technology sector, but AI is not the sole driver of these decisions,” said Laoise Mullane, director of Workforce Consulting and AI enablement at PwC Ireland.
“Organisations are also responding to broader pressures such as cost reduction, restructuring, and changing market conditions. While many of the headlines have come from the technology sector, the underlying forces shaping these decisions are extending far beyond technology roles alone.”
Looking at hiring trends though, there are jobs to be had in tech, as long as you have the right skills. As AI threats increase, so too does the need for AI-augmented cybersecurity. Mullane said many of the organisations were continuing to recruit for skills in areas such as AI, cybersecurity, data, cloud and technology engineering. There is also demand for candidates who can combine technical expertise with judgment, leadership and business understanding.
“Rather than a simple story of jobs being replaced by AI, we’re seeing a broader reshaping of work, with some roles declining, others emerging, and many more evolving as organisations rethink how work gets done,” Mullane said.
The shift in the labour market has also brought an important element to the fore: lifelong learning and keeping skills up to date.
[ AI job losses in Ireland likely to hit women and ‘younger workers’ hardest, says report Opens in new window ]
“One of the things that we’re seeing is that there is a realisation that lifelong learning has become more important. Seventy-six per cent of people who responded to our last hiring trends update said that they believed that their skills were still relevant, but that they would need to upskill to remain relevant in the next five years. I don’t think that’s just across the tech sector,” says Paye.
“Everyone is realising we need to upskill.”
But concern remains around entry-level roles, long flagged as a target market for AI. A reduction there means graduates and those early on in their career have fewer opportunities to get on the career ladder. The latest hiring trends data from IrishJobs.ie found almost half of employers have reduced the number of entry and graduate level roles available in their organisation.
Paye says that could prove to be a short-sighted strategy for companies seeking to keep their shareholders happy.
“If you are no longer hiring graduates or bringing people in straight out of college, you are creating a skills gap for three, four or five years down the line. I’ll be interested to see how this reverses over the next few years, because I think you will see a lot of businesses, whether in the tech sector or not, who realise graduate recruitment wasn’t just about bringing people in to do entry-level tasks – it was about building for the future. The next middle management, the next senior management – a lot of them come through graduate schemes. In three or four years’ time, when your middle managers decide to move on, that pool of candidates is now going to be quite low,” he says.
“It is much harder to hire externally. It’s normally more costly, it takes longer, and salaries are higher when you’re when you’re hiring from outside your organisation. I think you will see businesses realising that it is short term Ebitda [earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation] help, and long-term it might take a little bit more of a chunk out of their bottom line.”

title: French riots a wake-up call for us to heed the grievances of our young people, too
description: Students here and elsewhere need proper structure to express their concerns
content:
Sir, – On reading Naomi O’Leary about the student protests in France (“ France’s school protests: What lies behind the anger ”, World News, October 8th), I remembered the student unrest in Paris in May 1968 and how it inspired so many of us who are now in our mid to late 70s.
I echo William Wordsworth’s words as he looked back on the early days of the French Revolution: “Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive / But to be young was very heaven!”. – Yours, etc,
Sir, –Sean Keavney makes a good point: Ireland is not immune and should pay heed to what is happening here in France (“ French protests a timely warning for Irish schools ”, Letters, October 8th).
Some of the dysfunction in the system here only applies to France and goes back decades. There are desperately low teacher salaries and absurdly long school days, often from 8am to 6pm.
But what is achievable, and where French mismanagement serves as a wake-up call, would be to give students a proper structure to express their grievances and not leave it to political groups to organise them and bring them on to the streets.
Is aoibhinn beatha an scoláire? Only if the grown-ups get their act together. – Yours, etc,

title: Séamas O'Reilly: I routinely have intrusive thoughts about all the horrible things that could happen my children
description: I imagine the GP asking ‘When did you first realise your daughter had grown antlers?’, ready to call social services
content:
M y daughter stares plaintively at me in the doctor’s office. She’s been sick for three days now, dawdling in a state of pure pathos with runny eyes and a cough like a barking seal. Actually, no, let’s get that right. It sounds, without a doubt, much more like the call-and-response yelps of the velociraptors in Jurassic Park.
Her breathing, too, is alarmingly audible. Through her mouth, it sounds like shovelled gravel. Through her nose, slowly ripping Velcro. We’ve had her out of school for three days, and since she hasn’t been improving as fast as we expected, I’ve taken her to our GP to make sure it isn’t anything more serious.
Soon, we’re in the waiting room at our local surgery, entertaining ourselves with the orgy of text on its info-packed walls. Some posters offer cheerily broad advice – “Stay hydrated!”, “Eat 5 fruits and vegetables a day!” – while others, such as those advising recent visitors to Bermuda what to do if they show signs of scombroid fish poisoning, are too specific for me to explain to a still preliterate four-year-old. The most numerous signs are those highlighting that abuse against staff will not be tolerated, spread across the room in sufficient number that one must imagine they’re depressingly necessary.
[ I met my son crying at the school gates and felt like a war criminal Opens in new window ]
A screen hanging over the far corner runs a silent carousel of images and short videos on everything from flu preparedness to the tell-tale signs of scarlet fever. Here, too, text is in great supply, with huge essays displayed much too quickly to be consumed at once. One particularly prolix fact-sheet about spotting the signs of an abdominal aortic aneurysm, challenges the reader to digest roughly 4,000 words of text in 15 seconds before it flashes off again, replaced with a video of a smiling doctor and a nurse – both, it seems, AI generated – reminding people, once again, that abuse against staff will not be tolerated.
My favourite is the unwieldy mnemonic they advertise for sepsis, in which the letters of that condition are helpfully acronymised with warning signs for the condition. Unfortunately, the person charged with creating said acronym appears to have been a small child who wandered into the building by mistake, resulting in a bafflingly vague word salad that is almost impossible to remember. While I can forgive the clumsy wording of “E – extreme shivering or muscle pain” or “P – passing no urine all day”, I am rendered wide-eyed with glee on reading “I – it feels like you are going to die”.
My shameful mirth is cut short as we are called up to be seen. My daughter is greeted by the lovely doctor, who calls her a “beauty” and compliments her glasses. This does a great job of soothing her nerves, and my own.
I always feel slightly nervous taking my kids to the doctor. True, the prospect of them being seriously ill is never far from my thoughts. Like most dads, I spent much of my children’s early lives believing them to be in imminent mortal danger, and routinely experienced intrusive thoughts about all the horrible things that could happen to them; a rare exotic disease; a button lodging in their throat; a slip of my hand sending their pram directly beneath a passing bus.
But there’s also a less noble trepidation within me any time a trip to the doctor is needed; a sense that I’ll be immediately sussed as a bad parent for not spotting something obvious. “So tell me, Mr O’Reilly,” I imagine the GP asking, one hand on her phone ready to call social services, “when did you first realise your daughter had grown antlers?”
[ Séamas O’Reilly: ‘Would you rather have no stomach or no bum?’ my son asks Opens in new window ]
Thankfully, this visit proves uneventful. My daughter’s ears and throat are checked with those futuristic light-probe things doctors use, while her chest and back are examined with a stethoscope – I am happy to report kids are still alarmed by how cold those are – and my poorly little poppet does a great job of coughing on command. After this, she is judged to be still a little unwell, but very much on the mend. She gets a unicorn sticker, and there are no calls to social services made in my presence, so I consider it a win-win.
On the walk home, perhaps overestimating my medical knowledge, she asks me how to avoid getting sick in the first place. “Well,” I say, faltering slightly, “umm, drink plenty of water and eat lots of fruits and vegetables!” She seems content with this. And I can teach her the tell-tale signs of sepsis another day.

title: Victorian home with vibrant garden overlooking a leafy Dún Laoghaire square
description: Number 23 Royal Terrace West is a spacious four-bedroom home laid out over three levels
content:
Royal Terrace West is a row of large Victorian houses built in the 1860s that overlook a leafy four-acre square in Dún Laoghaire , Co Dublin . They were among the first and largest houses to be built on this square, and still exude a certain grandeur more than 150 years later. Wealthy merchants in the prosperous port town lived here, and there are still a few of the original hay sheds on the laneway running along the rear of the terrace, where horses were fed and stabled.
The owners of Fortrose, at number 23, bought it six years ago and their timing couldn’t have been better, as it had been renovated and refurbished by its previous owner, who engaged conservation architect Róisín Hanley to oversee the design. They therefore acquired a pristine period home that had been reconfigured for modern life while maintaining the elegance of a bygone age. Extending to 310sq m (3,337sq ft) and Ber exempt, 23 Royal Terrace West is now for sale through Sherry FitzGerald, seeking €2.695 million.
The only work the owners had to do was put their own stamp on the front and back gardens; as keen horticulturalists, they put skill and imagination into the design. The railed front garden features raised beds filled with reeds, hydrangea, lavender and tree ferns, while the superb west-facing back garden has a large Indian sandstone patio with steps up to a lawn surrounded by raised beds, and featuring giant echium, colourful Peruvian lilies and Victoria plum trees. Outdoor lighting beautifully illuminates the garden at night.
Inside, the scale of this fine home is clear to see, with high ceilings, wide hallways, spacious reception rooms and expansive living areas spread out over three floors and two returns. From the glazed front door, the sightline runs down the hallway, through a large livingroom and out to the lush plantings of the back garden.
The scope of the refurbishment is also clear to see, from the intricate cornicing and centre roses, to the wide-plank oak floors, to the contrasting light and dark grey paint on the walls. Most striking, though, is the way the rooms have been configured and connected to allow its residents to get the full benefit of every part of the house, with nowhere shut away or left unused.
The architect moved the kitchen from its traditional basement location up to the ground floor, turning the two main reception rooms on this level into an inviting open-plan kitchen/breakfast/diningroom, with a dual aspect looking out to the front and back gardens.
At the end of the hall is a large livingroom with recessed wood-burning stove and full-height glass doors leading out to the back garden and patio.
Upstairs on the first floor return, the architect blended a bedroom and the original bathroom into one big family bathroom, with a feature fireplace, bay window overlooking the back garden, and a cast-iron rolltop claw-on-ball bath.
Then we come to the formal drawingroom on the first floor, spanning the width of the house, with two big windows – one sash and one bay – giving a commanding view over Royal Terrace Square. The lofty 14ft ceiling, with intricate cornicing and centre rose, makes the room feel even bigger, and it’s no surprise that many convivial soirées have been hosted here over the years. It has a feature fireplace with wood-burning stove and an antique-style radiator.
The principal bedroom is next to the drawingroom, and has sliding sash windows with working shutters overlooking the back garden, a feature fireplace, and large fitted wardrobes by Newcastle Design on each side of the fireplace. These run all the way up to the high ceiling, but there’s no need for a stepladder as the upper reaches are fitted with pull-down hanging rails.
The top-floor return has a landing with Velux window; adjoining that is a shower room. Bedroom two is also on this level, a good-sized double bedroom overlooking the back garden.
Downstairs at garden level are two more large double bedrooms. Also at this level is a versatile family/games room to the back and a modern shower room tucked under the granite front steps of the house. There’s a handy front entrance here for kids trooping in from the square, and a side door out to a lower patio with steps leading up to the back garden. This entire floor has been tiled throughout and has underfloor heating.
While there are no upgrading works required at this beautifully refurbished home, there is scope to do something with the garage at the end of the garden. It is a versatile space with a bathroom and access to the rear laneway that could become an artist’s studio, workshop, home office or gym.
There is a vibrant community in the area, the owners say, and the square plays host to neighbourhood celebrations throughout the year. It’s just a short walk from the shops, restaurants and seaside strolls of Dún Laoghaire, and within easy reach of public transport and schools .

title: I’ve tried many red lipsticks over the years – these are my favourites, old and new
description: From classic favourites to head-turning new launches, these are the best red lipsticks across a range of price points and finishes
content:
We’re entering red lip season, spoiled for choice with new launches and old favourite formulations.
I’ve always been partial to a swipe of red lipstick , particularly those with a blue undertone – beautiful, clear, punchy reds that look classic on every complexion and pull more cool in tone than warm. You won’t find many orange reds in my make-up bag.
Red lipstick is incredible for lifting the mood, elevating a look and making you feel like the most put together version of yourself. That said, there’s no point opting for a higher maintenance lipstick shade if it’s not going to stay put. So, with that in mind, here are six excellent red lipstick options across a range of price points and finishes that are sure to turn heads, and to last.
Victoria Beckham has taken her first foray into true red lipstick with not just one but six shades designed to suit every complexion. Victoria Beckham Beauty Rouge Victoria (€83 each from Brown Thomas) is a bold, pigmented, exceptionally luxurious red lipstick with a demi-matt finish, each with its own one-of-a-kind packaging.
“Every lipstick is hand-treated with an alabaster finish, so no two are the same,” Beckham says. The range includes a rich burgundy red, a classic crimson and a burnished, almost mahogany red, so there’s a shade to suit every complexion.
Nars Powermatte High Intensity Lip Pencil (€33 from Space NK) is a delicious, intensely pigmented, head-turning range of do-it-all lip pencils that deliver a no-budge finish that will last for as long as you decide to wear it.
A cream-to-matt formula, it gives you just enough playtime to apply as you like, before it sets in place. My go-to shade has always been Cruella, a deeply moody, crimson-red.
When I don’t know what to reach for, MAC Cosmetics MACximal Silky Matte Lipstick in Ruby Woo (€30 from Brown Thomas) is often the solution – a red that has reached hall-of-fame levels over the years for its vibrancy, impact, matt finish and exceptionally long wear time. The brand launched a matching Ruby Woo lip liner (€25 from Brown Thomas) several years ago to help carve out the perfect, colour-cohesive shape.
Excellent formulation meets affordability in the form of Max Factor 2000 Calorie Mellow Blur Lipstick (€10.99 from Boots), specifically in the shade cashmere cherry.
Pleasingly pigmented with a comfortable, balm-like feel, this matt-finish lipstick is comfortable to wear and delivers an impressive pop of colour with a soft, slightly blurred finish, which I’m very partial to – it’s the type of lip that looks lived-in and wears well throughout the day and night.
One of my favourite red lipsticks for several years now, Sculpted by Aimee Lip Duo in Ruby Rouge (€21 from Sculpted by Aimee) is a juicy, bright red with a conveniently attached matching lip liner for the perfect pout at any time.
The formula also contains nourishing ingredients, including shea butter and rosehip oil, to keep the lips feeling soft and comfortable, with a glossy finish that feels worlds away from some of the drier, more traditional red lipstick formulas.
It was only a matter of time before Dyson entered the hot brush category. Airsmooth (€249 from dyson.ie) is the brand’s first dedicated hot brush that dries, styles, smooths and, once you get the knack of it, adds volume too.
[ Haircare products I always buy again, from dry shampoo to the perfect brush Opens in new window ]
It’s lightweight and easy to use, and I particularly like how the bristles bend and adjust so there’s no pulling or snagging on the hair. It also has universal voltage, which is handy for travel.

title: Actor Tadhg McMahon: ‘Going to Ireland always feels like going home. My accent is gone’
description: McMahon appears in The Westies, a drama series about Irish gangsters in New York City in the early 1980s
content:
I started auditioning like a madman here in Toronto . It was nine auditions a week. I was just in the grind. I got a show here. I got a show there. I was just getting by. And then The Westies came along last year ... and boom!
The Westies is set in the 1980s in New York. There were all these union rackets and no-show jobs. All this classic gentleman-gangster stuff. JK Simmons’s character and Cliffie, my character, and all the older Westies – that’s our thing. We’re like: okay, we finally hit the jackpot. Then the young guys come in, and it’s all coke.
We had the premiere in Chelsea. Over the next couple of days I hung around in New York . I went for a walk around the old Hell’s Kitchen neighbourhood. It didn’t look anything like it. It’s completely changed. You’re not actually shooting in New York. Where could you shoot that would look like that?
But I don’t feel like there’s any paddywhackery going on there. The plastic Paddy thing doesn’t feel like it’s happening to me with this.
Tony McMahon, the accordion player, was my dad’s brother. My dad grew up in Ennis and then moved to Dublin. He met my mum in Dublin . Her family is from Kilkenny . I grew up in Inchicore , back in the day when Inchicore was just that little cul-de-sac with kids running around. I went to Gaelscoil Inchicore when it was just being founded.
My dad was a social worker, and it was just a tough living. So my mum was like: “Let’s go try out Canada.” So we ended up in Winnipeg. That was a bit of a culture shock. Winnipeg’s got some really rough parts. Going from somewhere so insular like Inchicore into a big spread-out place was interesting.
I had auditioned for a play that they were doing at the Olympia Theatre just before I left Ireland. I got down to the callbacks. I went all the way to the end of it, and they said I lied about my age. They said: “You’re too young. We can’t put you in a show.” I was 11.
I lost interest in it a little bit from 16 to maybe 18 or 19. And then, when I finished high school, I started to go to these Irish amateur groups around Winnipeg, and we would tour plays. We did The Field and O’Casey plays. I really got into it. And then, when I was touring out in the US, somebody saw me there who was involved with the Gaiety School of Acting. They were like: “You’re probably good enough. You could get in. You should try and get in.” And then it took me two years to figure out how to do that. But I moved to Dublin, and then I went to the Gaiety. I worked as a roofer when I wasn’t doing that.
I got a scholarship to go over to Oxford right after the Gaiety School got done. I worked with the Royal Shakespeare Company. I actually got trained by John Barton. So then a couple of years of working, doing Shakespeare, touring Shakespeare plays – and writing comedy shows and stuff.
And then to Toronto, and I kind of started from scratch, but I really started to focus on TV and film. It was tough. I really wasn’t getting anywhere. So, in 2012, I made my own short film, Shooting Oliver. It was a comedy on the set of an action movie. And when that came out, I had a demo reel. The people who were making Brooklyn [with Saoirse Ronan] saw that, and I auditioned for that. I got a small role.
[ Author Ellen Ryan: ‘Ireland is my muse. That’s where my conviction for writing comes from’ Opens in new window ]
The Irish scene is definitely bigger in Toronto. It was pretty small in Winnipeg, but I was really involved in it. There’s an Irish club that’s in downtown Winnipeg. It was a two-storey building. In the basement, they had a bingo hall, which would get money coming in all the time. And I would work in this bingo hall too.
I would do the cooking in the kitchen. Upstairs there was a pub where we would do dinner theatre. We had a 100-seat theatre. You come in. You buy your ticket. You’d sit down. You go to the little pub and have your pints of Guinness.
Here in Toronto, I’m not as connected to it. There’s a trad session every Sunday; I go down and see. But there are so many young people in these pubs around this neighbourhood, and I hang out with them. I have got an Irish writer buddy that I hang out with here.
Going to Ireland always feels like going home for me. My accent is gone. I flip my accent on and off depending on what show I’m working on. People ask the question: “What? Are you American?” And then I have to explain the whole thing. Some people say things like: “Oh, you have a confused accent. It sounds kind of strange.” But Ireland is always going home for me. I just walk in and I’m right back. I feel like we’re the luckiest Irish generation in some ways. My cousins are traditional musicians. I chat to them on WhatsApp all the time. It’s not like you go and you’re just gone any more.
The Westies is on RTÉ One on Tuesday nights and on the RTÉ Player

title: Game over: Inside the ruins of Gaza’s football stadiums
description: Sports stadium, bomb site, detainment yard, refugee camp – the three-year evolution of Gaza’s football stadiums
content:
“I am Omar al-Jamasi. I owe one shekel (€0.29) to a boy named Abdul Karim al-Nirab [who] lives on Abu Nafez Street. And I, my loved ones, love you...”
This was a note, scribbled on a scrunched-up piece of paper, of a young football player who carried it with him until March 2025, six months before the current ceasefire was agreed, when he was killed.
Omar was one of 10 boys killed in the last three years at a single club, Al Helal Football Academy, that, 10 years ago, had sent their under-16 team to Ireland – a trip commemorated by hanging the Irish flag outside their new astroturf pitch on the beachfront in Gaza City .
Today, the pitch, like many in Gaza, has been reduced to a pile of sand and rubble.
“The war brought sports activities in Palestine to a halt,” said Mustafa Siam, who serves as secretary general of the Palestinian Sports Media Federation, speaking to The Irish Times via WhatsApp from Gaza. “Sports infrastructure has been a direct target of the Israeli military machine.”
In a statement, the Israeli military said it does not deliberately target sports facilities and that any such site struck would have been targeted because of what it described as military activity or infrastructure in or around it.
Since October 2023, Israel’s bombardment and ground operations in Gaza ​have killed more than 1,000 people from Gaza’s sporting community, according to the Palestine Olympic Committee in Ramallah, destroying 70 per cent of sports facilities, and damaging the remaining 30 per cent. Football clubs on the ground report that Israel continues to block the deliveries of footballs to the Strip.
Here, The Irish Times analyses the fate of Gaza’s largest football stadiums with satellite imagery, and what they reflect about the evolution of Israel’s military assault on Gaza since October 2023.
Beit Hanoun Municipal Stadium in May 2022 compared with November 2023
Before October 2023, the Ittihad Beit Hanoun Sports Club trained at one of the few stadiums in Gaza with artificial grass, allowing them to play in varying weather. Situated around 2km from Israel in northern Gaza, Beit Hanoun Stadium was among the first stadiums to be destroyed, after Israeli forces launched their first ground invasion in Gaza weeks after the October 7th attack.
Large vehicles destroyed the centre of the pitch in particular, with the artificial grass dug up and piled in mounds of earth either side of the centre line, making it impossible to be played upon.
The pitch was progressively destroyed with vehicle tracks since then and lies in ruins today within territory the IDF continues to occupy one year on from the October 2025 ceasefire.
Al-Yarmouk Stadium in May 2022 compared with April 2024
Built in the 1930s, Al-Yarmouk Stadium featured a football pitch surrounded by a running track used by aspiring Palestinian Olympians since Palestine joined the International Olympic Committee in 1995.
By Christmas Eve in December 2023, the stadium had been converted into a detainment yard, according to a video uploaded to YouTube by an Israeli soldier.
The footage showed images of men of all ages, including what appears to be at least two young boys , stripped to their underwear, with some forced by IDF soldiers to kneel in the middle of the pitch, according to CNN.
Palestinian women were pictured blindfolded kneeling by one of the stadium’s goals under an Israeli flag, with their hands bound behind their backs.
Thousands of Gazans were detained throughout the past three years and moved to Israeli prisons or makeshift IDF detention camps, including Sde Teiman detention camp in the Negev desert.
At the end of June 2026, the Israel Prison Service was holding 9,187 Palestinians in detention or in prison on what it defined as “security” grounds, including 1,554 from the Gaza Strip, according to BT’Selem, an Israeli human rights organisation.
Al Helal Football Academy and Gaza Sports Club in October 2023 compared with November 2024
For nearly a century, Palestinians have played football on the Gaza Sports Club’s pitches. The beachfront sports complex in Gaza City received over $500,000 from the now defunct United States Agency for International Development (USAid) in 2022 to develop facilities for boys and girls to learn sports like tennis, basketball and martial arts.
Not far from the club in Gaza City is Al Helal Academy, which before October 2023 trained some of Gaza’s young football talent. In 2016 and 2017, a team of under-16 boys from the Al Helal Club travelled to Ireland with the assistance of Gaza Action Ireland, an Irish pro-Palestinian solidarity group.
The Palestinian teenagers played local teams in Ballybrack in Dublin, Nenagh in Tipperary, Kinvarra in Galway and the People’s Park in Limerick.
Ahmed Jahjouh (24), a professional Palestinian footballer, was one of those children.
“Those were some of the most beautiful days of my life,” Jahjouh said, speaking to The Irish Times via WhatsApp from Gaza. “The first team to come out of Gaza to represent Palestine was Al Helal Club. We received the warmest welcome from the Irish people.”
After Israel launched an all-out military assault on Gaza after the October 7th attack, the sports clubs suffered bomb damage.
Satellite footage from October 2023 shows three bomb blasts encircled by craters in the vicinity of the clubs, including: one 6m crater on the southeastern pitch of the Gaza Sports Club; while one crater filled the road outside the main Al Helal club building, causing damage to the pitch.
By November after over a year of conflict, every pitch had been completely destroyed and rendered unrecognisable from before.
The next satellite footage available is from December 2024. By then, almost every building in the block appeared to have been destroyed, either by bulldozers or by the impact of bombing, including the roof over the Al Helal indoor astroturf pitch.
“There are no stadiums or buildings left for Al Helal Club,” Jahjouh said. “All the stadiums have been bulldozed and demolished.”
Jahjouh said 10 children who played for Al Helal Club had been killed since October 2023, and six adult professional players on the club’s first team, including 20-year-old Muhammad Khalifa , a young footballer who had visited Ireland with him and played football in 2016 . He was killed with seven other members of his family when Israel bombed their home in Nuseirat refugee camp.
“Khalifa was one of my closest friends,” Jahjouh said. “He was killed in the war. The missile tore his body apart because of the force of the explosion.”
Khalifa was one of more than 1,000 athletes killed in Gaza since October 2023, and one of over 73,000 deaths officially recorded by Gaza’s health ministry. A further 10,000 deaths are unconfirmed due to bodies believed to be under rubble.
The Israeli government had long denied the death toll as “exaggerated tolls” from Gaza’s health ministry as it was officially run by the Hamas-led government. But in January 2026, a senior Israeli military official confirmed to The Times of Israel that the IDF believed the figure of roughly 70,000 killed to be accurate.
This would account for at least 3 per cent of Gaza’s population - or roughly one in 33 people who were alive in September 2023.
Before October, Palestine Stadium had capacity for 10,000 football fans to support their teams, while the football grounds in one of Gaza City’s most affluent neighbourhoods, Al Rimal, became a regular training venue for the Palestine national team.
After October 2023, the pitch became arid as north Gaza’s population was forcibly evacuated south and then besieged for months starting in October 2024.
Today Palestine Stadium sits just within the limits of the so-called “yellow line”, which marks the boundary line between territory in Gaza controlled by the Israeli military and territory where Palestinians can live.
Gaza’s population of more than two million people now live on land roughly half the size of what was available to them before October 2023. With space at a premium, the Palestine Stadium’s famous pitch is now crowded with tents housing displaced Palestinians.
Most of the boys playing for Al Helal Football Club, who once travelled to Ireland are now displaced in tents across Gaza, with little access to play football, said Zoe Lawlor, chairperson of the Ireland-Palestine Solidarity Campaign and co-ordinator of Gaza Action Ireland.
“Sport is so important as an outlet to any young people but especially to those living under siege and occupation and now surviving genocide,” said Lawlor, who had visited Al Helal Club in Gaza as part of an Irish sports outreach programme in 2013.
“Gaza was so beautiful even under siege. To see every aspect of civil society destroyed by Israel is horrendous,” she said. “It is a crime … what has been done.
“There must be accountability for the international community.”
“To see every aspect of civil society destroyed by Israel is horrendous”
In December 2023, South Africa initiated proceedings against Israel before the International Court of Justice (ICJ) alleging that Israel’s military actions in Gaza constituted genocide against the Palestinian people. In January 2024, the ICJ issued a provisional measures order. An ICJ ruling on the substantive genocide claim against Israel is not expected for years.
As part of parallel criminal proceedings at the International Criminal Court (ICC), arrest warrants were issued in November 2024 for Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu and former Israeli defence minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity, in addition to Hamas military leader Mohammed Deif who was later confirmed to have been killed in an Israeli strike in July 2024.
In issuing the arrest warrants, the ICC chamber stated that it “found reasonable grounds to believe that Mr Netanyahu and Mr Gallant each bear criminal responsibility as civilian superiors for the war crime of intentionally directing an attack against the civilian population”.
“Sports facilities are by definition civilian objects,” said Heidi Matthews, assistant professor at Osgoode Law school in Canada and expert in international criminal law. “When they are intentionally and directly attacked, that constitutes the war crime of attacking civilian objects.”
Under international law, Matthews said, civilian objects can only be targeted if there is evidence that militants were using them to “make an effective contribution to military activity” and even then, only if the destruction “offered a clear and concrete military advantage to Israel”.
In response to a request for comment from The Irish Times, a spokesperson for the Israeli military stated “the IDF does not deliberately target sports facilities”.
The spokesperson said: “If a sports facility was struck, this was due to its military use or the presence of military infrastructure or military activity in or around the site, and not because it was a civilian sports facility.”
The statement continued: “The IDF does not seek to cause excessive damage to civilian infrastructure, and its strikes are carried out solely on the basis of military necessity and in accordance with international law. It must be emphasised, however, that Hamas unlawfully embeds its military assets in, beneath, and in proximity to densely populated civilian areas, and cynically exploits civilian infrastructure for terror purposes.” The IDF did not respond to a further request for evidence supporting the allegation that Hamas used sporting grounds in Gaza.
Matthews said: “There are separate crimes of causing disproportionate damage and extensive and wanton destruction to civilian objects. The level of destruction of sports facilities raises the question whether there is a justification based in military necessity or is this unjustified destruction? All of the evidence points in the direction of the latter.”
“Football is a part of our lives. We don’t want to give up on it.”
For now, Gaza’s footballers are without pitches to play on, and according to Mustafa Siam, secretary general of the Palestinian Sports Media Federation, even footballs are denied entry to the Strip.
“The destruction of sports facilities has undoubtedly had a profound impact on players, clubs, and local communities … leaving players without an income, depriving children, and the local community of the opportunity to play football and engage in other sports, as large and small stadiums – as well as schools – have been demolished.
“Israel continues to impose a total blockade on Gaza, banning the entry of sports equipment – specifically footballs – which further exacerbates the suffering of players. Many are now living in tents under dire humanitarian conditions after the destruction of both their homes and their clubs.”
Jahjouh, a former professional footballer, said: “ Before the war, we actually received a salary from playing football. Now, we have to pay out of our own pockets just to be able to play. Renting a football pitch costs around $50 for just one hour.
“The balls we have are very few and of poor quality. Footballs are not allowed,” he said. “Before the war, they cost $30. Now they cost $300 and are in terrible condition.”
Cogat, the unit within the IDF that is responsible for facilitating the delivery of aid to occupied Palestinian territories, declined to comment and then did not answer further requests regarding whether football equipment and building material to repair sports facilities were allowed to enter the war-torn Palestinian enclave.
In February of this year, following the tentative ceasefire, Fifa announced a “landmark partnership agreement” with the Board of Peace – Donald Trump’s alternative to the United Nations that he has tasked to rebuild Gaza’s infrastructure.
Fifa’s president Gianni Infantino appeared alongside the leaders of the Board of Peace to announce that Fifa would implement a five-phase recovery plan for Gaza’s football facilities.
The plan promised that in the first three to six months, Fifa would install 50 arena mini-pitches and the rollout of a Fifa Football for Schools programme, which would see the distribution of equipment and structured grassroots activities.
By phase five, it promised to build a 20,000-seat national stadium in Gaza within three years of initiation.
[ Ireland v Israel was no ordinary match assignment. Irish journalists were watched and filmed Opens in new window ]
“Together with the support of the Board of Peace, Fifa will drive this partnership which is built to deliver impact at every stage,” a post to Infantino’s Instagram page read.
However, when approached by The Irish Times, a spokesperson for Fifa said that, while the organisation was still committed to the plan, phase one was yet to begin as it was tentative on the stated condition that “implementation will proceed in line with ongoing monitoring of safety and security conditions”.
Fifa declined to comment on requests for further information on a planned timeline and budget.
For now in Gaza, despite few footballs being delivered and most pitches destroyed, last week a group of former professional football players found a way to play.
In the same week Ireland was playing Israel in the Uefa Nations League, two teams in green and blue jerseys took to one of Gaza’s few remaining green pitches in their first club game in three years for a new tournament – the Thousand Martyrs Cup.
Surrounded by destruction and the grey dust of Gaza’s rubble, spectators watching players from atop dilapidated buildings.
“It is very difficult, but we still play,” said Jahjouh, who lost his mother, brother and his brother’s family as well as his best friend Khalifa in the past three years.
“Football is a part of our lives and we don’t want to give up on it.”
All satellite imagery sourced through Google Earth

title: AIB chief Colin Hunt eyes shares worth 100% of salary as bank expected to raise targets
description: Bank set up new share awards plan to get around continuing limit on bonuses
content:
AIB may nudge its 2026 net interest income forecast higher again in an upcoming trading update, with the expected boost from rising interest rates over the next 12 months lifting its shares, as chief executive Colin Hunt is on track to receive stock this year worth 100 per cent of salary.
The consensus call among analysts is that AIB will post €3.83 billion of net interest income this year, with Denis McGoldrick, an analyst with AIB’s Goodbody unit, estimating it will top €3.85 billion.
AIB projected in July that its net interest income would exceed €3.8 billion this year, up from last year’s €3.75 billion.
On Thursday, McGoldrick also raised his AIB net interest income estimates by 2 per cent for the next two years, which would see it reach €4.21 billion in 2028.
AIB’s shares have risen as much as 23 per cent since it started issuing stock to Hunt and other senior executives in May under a new share awards plan – with no performance conditions attached – to get around a continuing ban on bonuses above €20,000 across Irish banks.
AIB revealed in two filings with the stock exchange, in May and August, that it had issued a total of 75,010 shares to Hunt under the so-called fixed share allowance scheme. The filings were previously unreported by news organisations.
They were valued at a total of €1.02 million when issued, equivalent to 75 per cent of his €1.35 million base salary this year. Hunt sold about 35 per cent of the shares to cover income tax and social security due on the delivery of the shares.
AIB had said in March, as it unveiled plans to introduce a share awards plan, that it would be set at a maximum of 100 per cent of salary, but declined at the time to give details on the trajectory to that level.
With another quarterly release expected after AIB issues its next trading update in early November, Hunt is on track to hit the 100 per cent level in the first year of the programme.
[ Regulator warned Government last year that RTÉ funding was too low Opens in new window ]
Hunt’s annual salary was €500,000 before the Government lifted crisis-era salary restrictions at AIB in June 2025 as it sold its remaining shares in the bank.
Bank of Ireland opted for a more gradual approach to fixed share awards when salary caps were removed at that lender as it returned to full private ownership four years ago. Chief executive Myles O’Grady’s allowance has increased in increments from 25 per cent of salary in 2024 to reach a maximum 100 per cent this year. That will bring his fixed pay package to almost €2 million in 2026.
The AIB filing in August showed that Hunt was among 10 senior executives to benefit from the share awards, including Geraldine Casey, managing director of retail banking; group chief operating officer Graham Fagan; managing director of capital markets Cathy Bryce; and Mike Frawley, group chief risk officer. Former chief financial officer Donal Galvin received shares in the first issue in May, before handing his notice.
Shares in AIB have jumped as much as 29 per cent so far this year to a post-financial-crisis high of €11.85 in late September, leaving it briefly as the most valuable company on the Iseq 20, with a peak market value of €24.4 billion.
The shares have since given up a fifth of their gains as central bankers on both sides of the Atlantic pushed back on market expectations of an aggressive series of rate hikes – and as France’s rising debt costs have stoked memories of the euro zone debt crisis.
[ Lower-than-expected annual €12,000 investment account limits may curb take-up Opens in new window ]
“AIB has introduced a range of benefits over a number of years for all colleagues, including variable remuneration, healthcare benefits and employee share schemes such as the Save As You Earn and Approved Profit Sharing Schemes and the Share Incentive Plan, reflecting our broader approach to attracting, retaining and rewarding employees,” a spokesman for the bank said.
“This year, we also introduced a fixed share allowance for our leadership team. AIB remains focused on our customers, delivering our three-year strategy and keeping the bank on a strong and sustainable footing.”

title: Emergency electricity plants to cost customers €1.4bn
description: Last resort power stations to remain on grid for next two winters as energy pressures grow
content:
Homes and businesses face a €1.4 billion bill to cover the cost of emergency power plants to bolster stretched electricity supplies after regulators declared they will be needed for the next two winters.
National electricity grid operator EirGrid had four temporary fossil-fuel power plants built in Dublin , Offaly and Kerry in 2023 in a scheme to allow it provide last-resort emergency electricity supplies.
Delays in building new-generation capacity and power lines prompted the energy industry overseer, the Commission for the Regulation of Utilities (CRU), to order recently that the emergency plants remain in place up to February 2029 at a cost of €229 million.
Extending the emergency electricity supply scheme into the next two winters will drive its total cost to €1.44 billion, details published by the commission confirm. Figures from last year showed that its cost had, by then, topped €1 billion.
Homes and businesses ultimately shoulder the cost of maintaining the emergency power plants through network charges on their electricity bills.
Those customers have already paid for their installation, the most expensive element of the scheme, and continue to pay to keep them available.
A CRU note estimates that households could pay between 79 cent and €14.96 a year towards maintaining the backup generators on the system over the next two winters.
How that cost is spread over the years up to 2030 will determine the annual share of the bill paid by residential customers, one industry source familiar with the scheme explained on Wednesday.
EirGrid initially installed the backup plants for three-year terms with optional extensions.
The extensions run to February 2029 in the case of one plant at Huntstown, Co Dublin, and December 2028 for another on North Wall in the capital’s docks. Generators at Shannonbridge, Co Offaly, and Tarbert, Co Kerry, will remain until March 31st, 2028.
[ Surge in demand for power forces EirGrid to switch on emergency power plant twice Opens in new window ]
Minister for Climate, Environment and Energy Darragh O’Brien had to approve the extensions given to the facilities before the CRU published its order.
The commission cited delays in building new power stations and in the construction of the Celtic interconnector linking Ireland with France among the reasons for keeping the emergency facilities on the system.
EirGrid has called on the last resort plants only twice since they were built, both occasions this year.
Most recently the grid operator deployed the Tarbert plant for more than an hour after August’s eclipse shut down solar power plants that were then supplying much of the State’s electricity.
EirGrid subsequently confirmed that it used the North Wall facility in June to “manage generation adequacy”.
The grid company always stresses that the emergency power plants are a last resort. EirGrid commissioned them under a plan agreed with the CRU in 2021 to offset the threat of shortages in the Republic’s electricity supplies.

title: A police raid on a gay bar, in Asia’s most liberal jurisdiction
description: Mayor’s apology did little to cushion the shock that such an action could take place in Taiwan, the most liberal jurisdiction in Asia for LGBTQ+ rights
content:
D own a flight of steps from the street in Taipei ’s Ximen neighbourhood, a heavy door opens into a small, dark basement bar called Commander D. The walls are painted black and steel grids and metal bars give the place the atmosphere of a high-security prison, slightly offset by a few bordello-style chandeliers clamped to the ceiling.
A handful of customers are gathered at the bar and seven young men are chatting sedately around a small table laden with trays of vodka shots. Two of them are wearing leather dog masks.
Last Saturday, police barged into Commander D, arrested the owner and detained more than 50 people, holding some of them for a number of hours. During the raid, police forced the bar’s patrons to squat on the floor and made derogatory remarks to one customer who was disabled.
Commander D is a gay cruising bar and it was crowded and hot. So many of the customers were shirtless, something the police viewed as evidence that they may have been violating Taiwan’s Social Order Maintenance Act, which bans “wantonly exposing one’s naked body or presenting a lascivious posture in a public place or publicly accessible place”.
Taipei police said later that four officers, the on-site supervising officer, and the local precinct chief received disciplinary penalties for their part in the conduct of the raid.
The city’s mayor Chiang Wan-an apologised to those affected but his statement did little to cushion the shock that such an action could take place in Taiwan, the most liberal jurisdiction in Asia for LGBTQ+ rights. The island legalised same-sex marriage in 2019, it has banned conversion therapy and allows people to change their gender identification and Taipei’s annual Pride parade at the end of October attracts queer people from all over Asia.
[ Europe wants to get tough on China. The risks could be enormous Opens in new window ]
“The LGBTQ+ community should never face heightened state surveillance or humiliation simply for gathering, socialising, expressing gender, practising intimacy, or exploring sexual cultures. The Taipei city government must demonstrate through concrete policy and verifiable action that, in a self-proclaimed diverse and progressive city, the dignity, freedom, and safety of LGBTQ+ individuals will not be arbitrarily sacrificed,” 10 Taiwanese LGBTQ+ rights groups said in a joint statement.
Police raids and mass detentions in gay bars are almost unknown in democratic societies, although they have become more common in Russia in recent years. More importantly for Taiwan, such incidents have not been reported in mainland China for many years, despite a recent crackdown on LGBTQ+ activism.
There are no longer any public Pride marches or parties in cities such as Beijing or Shanghai and when western embassies host such events, police routinely question Chinese citizens who attend. But the authorities generally leave LGBTQ+ people to pursue their private lives in peace and gay clubs, bars and dating sites continue to flourish.
The Chinese authorities take a 1950s Legion of Mary approach to obscenity so lewd behaviour is risky. But transgressions are usually dealt with discreetly and if venues close down because of excessive enthusiasm among the patrons, they often reopen a few weeks later.
In recent years, the Communist Party has been waging a covert war on Halloween, chiefly because the costumes offer an ungovernable opportunity for free expression. Last year, one big gay venue in Beijing closed on the night of the festival, ostensibly because of fire safety concerns due to the possibility of overcrowding, but it reopened the following day.
[ Bangkok Letter: Pink tiger roars as Thailand’s marriage equality law takes effect Opens in new window ]
Taiwanese LGBTQ+ groups are challenging the legal basis of the police raid on Commander D, arguing that “gay men dancing naked, BDSM performances, or other forms of bodily and erotic expression that differ from mainstream culture cannot be summarily classified as ‘violating public morals’ simply because law enforcement officers are unfamiliar with or disapprove of them”. A coalition of 10 rights groups called for an independent investigation into the raid and said it awakened memories of the oppression endured by LGBTQ+ people as late as the 1990s, as Taiwan was moving from a military dictatorship into democracy.
“Today, when a venue providing space for specific sexual cultures experiences another large-scale search, mass inspection of patrons, and police discrimination, humiliation, and intimidation, the community feels far more than a routine law enforcement action – it reawakens the collective memory of state intrusion and oppression,” they said.
“Taiwan has progressed through gender equity education, same-sex marriage legalization, and increasing LGBTQ+ visibility. However, institutional progress must not remain confined to laws and slogans. If law enforcement officers continue to view LGBTQ+ venues, sexual cultures, intimacy, and sexual autonomy through heteronormative, binary, and moral-panic frameworks, it demonstrates that equality has yet to reach the front lines of policing.”
[ Marriage equality a decade on: ‘Things have gone backwards’ Opens in new window ]

title: What will €975,000 buy in France, Italy, Spain, Portugal and Cork?
description: One price, home and away: from a traditional Alpine villa to a home overlooking Blackrock Castle
content:
The Lodge is located directly across the road from Blackrock Castle and 800 metres from the Cork village. Built in 1984 on a 0.2-acre elevated site to make the most of the views over the river Lee, the 211sq m (2,271sq ft) property is surrounded by a beautifully landscaped garden. Inside there is a kitchen, utility room, open-plan living/diningroom, conservatory, four bedrooms and two bathrooms. It was upgraded in 2023 and now has a C2 energy rating.
This 19th-century Savoyard farmhouse in Les Landoz, Seytroux, is like something from a fairy tale. Originally built in 1834, it was renovated in 1999 but has retained every bit of its quirky character. Inside it is set out over 145sq m (1,563sq ft) with accommodation including a sittingroom, diningroom, kitchen and four large bedrooms. Outside is an original barn with 104sq m (1,119sq ft) of space for potential conversion, bordered by woodlands.
In the Tuscan hills near the village of Montecatini Val di Cecina is this restored country house that is 65km from Pisa airport and 22km to Volterra. There are electric gates into the 2.5-acre estate that comes with a pool, outdoor shower and eating area, pizza oven and olive trees. The beautifully styled house, which has a floor area of 200sq m (2,153sq ft), comes with a kitchen, diningroom, four bedrooms and four bathrooms.
This modern villa in Cala Llonga has been built on a private, elevated site with views over Mahon harbour. There are three bedrooms on the ground floor, including the principal suite, and on the first floor there is a kitchen, diningroom, and lounge. The lounge opens out to a rooftop terrace with an infinity pool. It has a floor area of 150sq m (1,615sq ft) and is in showhouse condition.
Coimbra is a university city located a couple of hours north of Lisbon. This villa is 20 minutes away from the city and five minutes from the town of Penela. It sits on a large plot of land that includes a working vineyard. The house has four bedrooms, three bathrooms, livingroom, converted attic, a fully fitted kitchen and utility room that doubles as a fermentation room for wine.

title: Aaron Sorkin: ‘I only ever heard Jeremy speak in Mark Zuckerberg’s voice until his last day of shooting’
description: Aaron Sorkin’s new film, The Social Reckoning, dramatises Frances Haugen’s whistle-blowing on Facebook and Meta’s approach to business
content:
A aron Sorkin, creator of The West Wing and ace screenwriter behind A Few Good Men, shakes his head and smiles. “I keep saying Facebook ,” he says apologetically. “But it’s Meta now.”
Sorkin , who won an Academy Award for his screenplay for The Social Network, the 2010 film about how Mark Zuckerberg devised Facebook (as it then was), really ought to know.
For more than a decade, every time the social media billionaire made headlines – his MMA training, his kill-what-you-eat dinner with Jack Dorsey, his science-dinner brush with Elon Musk , his purchase of an Irish castle – fans have asked Sorkin to write a follow-up to that origin story.
“There have been so many times in the last 16 years, really anytime Facebook would be in the news – Cambridge Analytica, that kind of thing – when I’d get a phone call saying, ‘You should really return to Facebook. Write a sequel.’”
And on an unusually bright, autumnal morning in London, Sorkin has landed with just that. Sort of.
The Social Reckoning, he says, is not a follow-up in the strictest sense.
“But I’ve realised that there is going to be no convincing anyone that this isn’t a sequel to The Social Network, even though what it is really is another movie about Facebook, written by the same writer who wrote The Social Network, wherein one of the characters from The Social Network is also a character in this. It’s as if Henry Hill from Goodfellas showed up in Casino.”
Sorkin finally found his hook for a second Zuckerberg-centred feature in the 2021 Facebook leak by the whistle-blower Frances Haugen. A data engineer and former company loyalist, Haugen was nothing like the disgruntled or wronged workers one might expect to find testifying against a former employer before the United States Senate.
“I’m introduced to her,” Sorkin says. “She has a book proposal, and she seems very interesting to me, but I don’t understand a word that she’s saying. She has an IQ of 3,000 or something.
“And I meet Jeff Horwitz, the Wall Street Journal reporter who broke her story, and the same thing is happening there. Until I asked Jeff Horwitz – this is now about a year into banging my head against the wall and trying to figure out if there’s a movie there – a dramatist’s question, which was: ‘What was the inciting action for Frances?’ One day she wasn’t a whistle-blower, and the next day she was. What happened?”
The Social Reckoning dramatises the inciting action in a punchy overture about Meta’s algorithms and the purposeful radicalisation of the platform’s users.
“I imagined a prologue and wrote it,” Sorkin says. “I knew I had to write another 100 scenes if anyone was going to watch this movie. But once I had that scene I had to write the rest.”
The peculiar polarisation of US politics that has slowly swamped the rest of the planet, courtesy of Facebook and other social media platforms, also sneaked up on Sorkin. In particular, he was shocked by some of the Maga demographics.
“You assume it’s a certain kind of person,” he says. “The stereotype is a poorly educated, southern, redneckish kind of person. I live in Los Angeles, and I was frightened by the fact that some were people who live and work in Beverly Hills. Who are women! Who live and work in Beverly Hills! I don’t know what the source of anger or ignorance is.”
The Social Reckoning stars Mikey Madison as Haugen, who was originally a Facebook engineer in the company’s “civic integrity” division. Alarmed by the platform’s wilful spreading of misinformation and threats to electoral security, she reluctantly turns to Horwitz (played by Jeremy Allen White ).
Their cagey, chatty encounters often resemble a screwball comedy more than the Deep Throat sequences in All the President’s Men. But a masterly turn by Jeremy Strong as Zuckerberg flags an obsession with power and the bottom line.
“I don’t, or didn’t, with Social Reckoning, try to really get inside Mark’s head for a motivation,” Sorkin says. “I was inside his head, or tried to be inside his head, for other things. But motivation? It’s tough for me to figure.
“The money can’t possibly be motivational. I think, right now, he is worth $120 billion. There’s nothing you can buy for $120 billion that you can’t buy for $119 billion. So it can’t be money.
“Why this need for growth at all costs? Once you are twice as big as the biggest country on Earth, wow, what’s getting you up in the morning to go to work? And why are you making these terrible decisions?”
The ethics of Zuckerberg’s actions, as depicted in The Social Reckoning, are queasy. Sadly, he’s not wrong about the business model. Ragebait sells.
“What Frances Haugen and Jeff Horwitz uncovered is that, not only is Facebook pumping misinformation out into the water supply, the air supply – alarming misinformation – but the distribution is industrial-strength.
“In an effort to get you to stay on the platform a little bit longer, they want to give you things that you’re going to reshare. That’s what keeps you on the platform the longest.
“And they know the things you’re most likely to share are anything that makes you angry. Facebook is trying to make you angry. That’s the business they’re in, and business is booming.”
Sorkin has never met Zuckerberg. But he is familiar with Zuckerberg’s legal representatives.
“When Meta got wind of this movie, I know that Sony got some strong letters from their lawyers. They wanted to see the script. Of course, we don’t show the script to people who aren’t making the movie, but they let us know that they’re there.”
The Social Network, Sorkin acknowledges, was a tough act to follow. The film, widely regarded as David Fincher’s best, received eight Oscar nominations and won three: best adapted screenplay for Sorkin, best original score and best film editing.
[ Mark Zuckerberg’s few coins thrown to the GAA should not fool us Opens in new window ]
Sharp dialogue, memorable characters, Fincher’s stylish direction and the groundbreaking soundtrack by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross continue to win it new fans.
Diehards still approach Jesse Eisenberg, who played Zuckerberg so memorably, to ask him to sign autographs with his line “I’m CEO, bitch.” That’s part of the reason the actor didn’t want to revisit the role.
“Jesse has a lot of fun memories of The Social Network, and he understands that it did a lot for him,” Sorkin says. “But he doesn’t like being conflated with Mark Zuckerberg. He doesn’t like the guy. And Jesse is also a very well-respected writer and director now.”
It has all worked out. The best scenes in The Social Reckoning concern Zuckerberg preparing to face US authorities, aided by a small squadron of media advisers fussing over every phrase and tie.
The film is another chance for Jeremy Strong to shine. The actor told GQ last month that he contacted Zuckerberg after being cast.
“I wrote to him – I’m probably going to give Sony an aneurysm – I sent him an email,” he explained. “Just to say that I take this responsibility very seriously, and the veracity of it seriously, and I’m approaching it with respect.”
We don’t yet know what Zuckerberg said in response, but Strong channels just the right amount of weird to convey the inscrutable billionaire.
[ Try! review: In this charming Irish documentary, everyone’s a winner Opens in new window ]
“There’s no disrespect to Jesse – and I did go to Jesse first – but Jeremy had said to me, if for some reason Jesse doesn’t want to do it, that he wanted to do it,” Sorkin says.
“And he gives a thunderous performance. He is, as you know, a very immersive actor. So he showed up on his first day of shooting. And I only ever heard him speak in Mark’s voice.
“He never used his own voice until his last day of shooting. After I called, ‘Cut – check the gate,’ he walked up to me and was using his own voice. And I would bet you anything that, off the set, when he went back to his hotel, when he was talking to his wife and kids, that he was also using Mark’s voice.”
Sorkin seems bemused by the idea that The Social Reckoning is his fourth film as a director. He still thinks of himself as a playwright.
“I’m most comfortable doing that,” he says. “With film, with television, I kind of try to fake my way.”
In 2017 he turned in Molly’s Game , a biopic based on the Olympic-class skier turned poker mogul Molly Bloom, to his producer. “They told me, ‘You’re not done,’” he says.
So began a directorial run that has also taken in The Trial of the Chicago 7 from 2020, and Being the Ricardos from 2021.
“I was my second choice to direct The Social Reckoning,” Sorkin says, laughing. “David Fincher was my first choice. But David has some exclusive deal at Netflix. He just wasn’t able to do this. He was also kind of busy directing Quentin’s movie.”
Fincher has wrapped on The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, a spin-off from Once Upon a Time ... in Hollywood, written by Tarantino, and heading to cinemas in November before landing on Netflix in early December.
Sorkin’s accidental directing career is typical of his haphazard path into the arts. An aspiring actor, he graduated with a degree in musical theatre from Syracuse University, in New York state, before heading to New York City, where he worked odd jobs, including as a singing-telegram performer.
He had scored some early off-off-Broadway successes when his sister’s experiences as a lawyer with the United States Navy’s legal branch, the Judge Advocate General’s Corps, inspired the stage version of A Few Good Men. Sorkin is reviving that play-turned-Oscar-winner on Broadway.
“I love that I’m able to do both,” he says. “My last two films both opened during Covid. A lot of people saw them, but they never played in front of an audience.
“There’s nothing that replicates that experience of sitting with a group of strangers in a dark room. Laughing at the same thing. Crying at the same thing. Gasping at the same thing. When it works, there’s nothing like it.
“And, as it happens, A Few Good Men previews on Broadway the day before The Social Reckoning opens. October is a big month for me.”
Sorkin’s mother was a teacher. His father was a copyright lawyer and second World War veteran who went to college courtesy of the GI Bill. The younger Sorkin was, he notes, the first person in his family to get into show business. But not the last.
“I don’t know where the gene came from, but my daughter, Roxy, has just finished her first feature,” he says, laughing. “It’s a material breach of the deal I made with God on the day she was born. But here we are.”
The Social Reckoning is in cinemas from Friday, October 9th

title: Lethal Katie Hannon dismantles the budget and dismisses Jack Chambers
description: Radio: RTÉ host’s precision-guided dismantling of Government’s thinly spread profligacy is arguably more lethal than the brickbats of Opposition TDs
content:
I t’s the day after the budget , and Morning Ireland (RTÉ Radio 1, weekdays) carries the verdict of people in Kinnegad, Co Westmeath. “Spoiler alert,” its presenter Gavin Jennings warns. “They’re not happy.”
Well, colour me stunned. The day when a vox pop yields a glowing evaluation of Government expenditure policy will surely be the harbinger of the apocalypse, the rapture or the singularity, depending on your belief system of choice.
That said, the sample of views that the reporter Cian McCormack hears is revealing. All his respondents voice concern about the spiralling cost of living , even those who stand to benefit from budget tax cuts . Others offer blunter views. One man calls the budget a disgrace, complaining about his €300-a-week expenditure on diesel in authentically angry, if faintly farcical, terms.
“I just hope the demonstrations start again, the blockades,” he says. “And this time I’ll be going. The last time I didn’t because I was working.” Start the revolution without me, as Gene Wilder’s 1970 comedy film counselled.
McCormack cautions that his report is “only a snapshot of opinions” – he’s broadcasting from a service-station plaza, which may account for the priorities of some respondents – but the dissatisfied mood chimes with the wider restiveness conveyed by other items on Morning Ireland.
Speaking to Jennings’s fellow host Justin McCarthy, Owen Reidy of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions characterises the Government’s package as “anything but a worker’s budget”, rejecting the call by Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers to stand down planned industrial action in the public service: “Public sector workers are very angry.”
But while Reidy disdains the budget for being aimed at farmers, hauliers and investors, the mood music from those sectors is hardly encouraging. Peter Brown of Baggot Investment Partners doubts the wisdom of the tax-free personal investment accounts announced in the budget, suggesting the Government has fashioned a rod for its own back by encouraging inexperienced savers to sink their money into the volatile world of stocks and bonds.
[ Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work Opens in new window ]
The underwhelming mood even extends to the presenters, as Jennings apologises for getting the date wrong at the start of Wednesday’s programme. “It’s the seventh of October, not the ninth,” he says ruefully. “The budget didn’t cut the year by two days.”
Maybe not, but one suspects some Cabinet members may wish that was the case. Chambers, for one, endures a long week on the airwaves. No sooner has the Minister delivered his budget address to the Dáil than he’s being grilled by Katie Hannon on Drivetime (RTÉ Radio 1, weekdays), where the host’s precision-guided dismantling of the Government’s thinly spread profligacy is arguably more lethal than the brickbats of Opposition TDs.
Hannon initially focuses on the fuel allowance, suggesting that the €5 increase will be offset by a curtailment of the payout period, while curtly dismissing Chambers’s assertions to the contrary. “It will be less next year than this year, that’s the truth of it,” she says, with the firm manner of someone scolding an errant child.
In contrast, when it comes to the €3 increase in the weekly living alone allowance, the host’s tone is one of scornful puzzlement: “Was it worth your while putting it in at all?”
Faced with such assessments, Chambers doggedly lays out the reasons for each measure while pointing to the wider context: “We’re managing significant geopolitical conflict.” True, but as the old saw has it, if you’re explaining, you’re losing. This may explain why the Minister eventually lays out the limits of his budgetary ambitions in tetchy terms: “The Government can’t insulate every price increase.”
It’s not all gloom for the Coalition. True, Sinn Féin’s finance spokesman Pearse Doherty excoriates budget tax cuts as inadequate when interviewed by Claire Brock, repeating his snappy judgment – “Gone before you get it” – with the relentlessness of a salesman parroting an ad slogan.
But qualified support comes in the shape of the Kerry Independent TD Michael Healy-Rae, who welcomes the reduction in fuel tax, and even makes a stab at defending the minuscule living alone allowance rise.
“You have to do something, and you have to try to help,” he says. That said, the deputy’s can-do positivity speaks more of a politician seeking to rebuild bridges with the Government he reluctantly exited rather than someone truly pleased with the budget.
(As for the news that RTÉ’s funding is to be cut by €20 million next year , the show’s coverage is studiedly neutral, though its reporter Barry Lenihan describes the reaction of the Montrose hierarchy in exquisitely understated style: “This has come as something of a surprise.”)
Having been dragged over the coals on both Drivetime and its Newstalk rival, The Hard Shoulder, on Tuesday evening, Chambers is back on air the following morning, joining Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris on Today with David McCullagh (RTÉ Radio 1, weekdays).
The Cabinet colleagues are there for the programme’s traditional postbudget phone-in, a once-lively ritual that has grown stale in recent years, to the point that the main point of interest is how McCullagh performs in his debut turn as host of the annual special.
Proceedings start promisingly enough, with Noel, an octogenarian widower, describing how his household income was halved when the State cut off his late wife’s pension, a practice he describes as unfair and cruel.
Chambers, whose on-air persona hovers between the unruffled and the rote, makes emollient noises before highlighting the already much-derided increase in the living alone allowance. “That in itself is a joke,” Noel acidly comments. “I’d love to meet the genius who decided that.”
Mostly, however, the phone-in is dominated by questions about specific budgetary measures, from the lack of grants for second-time buyers – “It might push prices higher,” Harris says – to the persistence of the universal social charge, which the Ministers candidly admit is integral to running the country’s finances.
[ A hushed Brendan O’Connor amplifies Nikita Hand’s traumatic testimony Opens in new window ]
This detail-oriented approach is of course welcome in our fake-news age. But with most people gaining something, however puny, from the budget, the narrow remit tamps down the potential for drama that ran through similar phone-ins in harder times. (And social media allows disgruntled voters to vent their fury on Ministers more directly than during the crash.)
Even the dependably droll and laconic host occasionally sounds flustered by the format, hurriedly wrapping up exchanges with individual callers as he keeps an anxious eye on the clock. Much like the ostensibly bonanza budget McCullagh covers, the programme leaves few people happy.
Given he’s also an impressionist, it’s no surprise that Oliver Callan (RTÉ Radio 1, weekdays) should be fascinated by the vagaries of speech, as shown by his chat with the author Kunak McGann about her new book on regional slang, Around Ireland in 80 Words.
McGann gives an entertaining tour of Ireland’s linguistic quirks, from “brusk” – Cork shorthand for boiled-sweet shrapnel, from the Gaeilge word for rubbish, bruscar – or “foundered”, the Ulster-Scots term for freezing.
Callan enthusiastically joins in; when his guest notes that runners are called “tackies” in Limerick, the Monaghan-born host cites the equivalent northern term, “gutties”.
Amid the lively vocabulary, however, Callan spots one problem: “Imagine trying to learn English in this country.”
It’s certainly an illuminating lesson for this listener.

title: ‘Hi Leo, from the Piglet!’: Dublin wine bar at the centre of a 2021 political scandal prepares to close
description: Ahead of Piglet’s final service, owners Enrico Fantasia and Thibaut Harang reflect on ‘Piglet-gate’
content:
“It was great to be the centre of attention in the media for a few days,” says Piglet co-owner Enrico Fantasia, recalling how the Temple Bar wine bar became the backdrop to a political scandal five years ago.
It was summer 2021 when former minister for children Katherine Zappone messaged then taoiseach Leo Varadkar via text: “Hi Leo, from the Piglet! I was expecting to hear from Simon C [Coveney] about my appointment as special envoy for human rights and LGBTQ+ issues. Have you heard anything? If you are around next Wed, hope to see you and Matt.”
The text became central to a saga over the controversy of Zappone’s appointment to the newly created position of special envoy to the UN for freedom of opinion and expression, which she subsequently did not take up.
“Everyone was asking, ‘What is The Piglet? Was it secret code for something?’,” says Fantasia, head of wine at the wine bar in Dublin 2 .
“I remember I wasn’t in Dublin that day, I was in Connemara meeting some friends and one arrived and said, ‘Everyone is talking about Piglet on the radio, in the news, in the media.’ The first thing I thought was a fire or something because the last thing that you expect in this place is to be in a political scandal.”
Co-owner Thibaut Harang says Varadkar was a regular at the time, but did not return “for a while” after the story broke.
Piglet offers an extensive wine list, with bottles ranging from €33 to above €1,000, as well as a small food menu featuring dishes such as côte de boeuf, halibut and cacio e pepe.
Harang and Fantasia opened the wine bar in late 2015 and will host its final service on October 12th.
[ Hidden in plain sight in Temple Bar Opens in new window ]
Harang says that while he enjoyed hosting famous politicians over the years, he most looked forward to welcoming people from the food and drinks industry.
“We also had a couple of famous chefs and wine makers within the industry. That’s our celebrities – the ones that we have on the shelves.”
Fantasia agrees: “And we were very popular with the trade – we were offering what everyone in the trade wanted”.
He says Piglet was born because he, an Italian, and Harang, a Frenchman – friends for almost 20 years – wanted to open the kind of place they would go to themselves.
“I don’t think there was something like that in Dublin at the time,” says Fantasia
“The idea was simple food, really tasty, loads of wines – way too many wines. Our list got out of control pretty quickly and still is.”
The closure comes as a result of increased financial pressure.
“The first decision is financial,” says Harang. “This is what dictates if you can make it or not.”
Piglet could have spent another year with the duo “seeing how we could change it or seeing if the market is changing”, says Harang, but they decided this was not a good idea. They will now focus on separate ventures.
“I am involved in a new place now with my partner, Enrico has more and more things to do also in his wine business. It’s just a bad time. Everything came together at this one point,” says Harang.

title: Solar panel mounting firm’s former CEO set up rival business, court hears
description: Judge grants orders at ex-parte hearing for preservation of company’s property and documents
content:
The former chief executive of a company that supplies roof mounting racks for solar panels has set up a rival firm, it has been claimed in the High Court .
Solrmount Ltd is seeking orders against its former CEO, Christian Jensen, his wife Cathrine Elisabeth Feerup and a new business they set up called Roof Professor Ltd.
On Thursday, Judge Brian Cregan granted orders to Marcus Dowling, for Solrmount, compelling the defendants to preserve any Solrmount physical property in their possession as well as all computer files and information of the company.
The application was made with only the Solrmount side represented at the hearing and was adjourned to next week when the application for declarations and orders in relation to profits or money received by the defendants and alleged breaches of fiduciary duty are to be heard.
Dowling said the founder of Ireland’s largest supplier of solar panels, Failte Energy Solutions, trading as Failte Solar, had discussions with Jensen in 2024 about the sourcing of mounting racks. As things stood, these came from Germany but were sourced in China which it was decided they could do themselves.
Abhilash Borana Abhilash, founder of Failte Solar, said in an affidavit that as a result of discussions, they set up Solrmount, which is based in the Shannon Free Zone at Shannon, Co Clare .
Abhilash held 80 per cent of the shares through a holding company. Jensen and his wife, through a corporate vehicle, held 20 per cent. Jensen was also CEO of the company and his wife was employed by the business.
Jensen was not required to provide any capital but to supply his knowledge of mounting systems and work as an employee of the company, Abhilash said.
With the commercial, operational and market support provided by Failte Solar, Solrmount was a success, Abhilash said.
In the context of that success, he said Jensen began seeking more advantageous terms for him, his wife and their corporate vehicle.
