Last July, Jensen resigned as CEO of Solrmount although issues had already arisen in relation to the business and his conduct, Abhilash said.
Earlier, in March, Abhilash said he was told by a Chinese supplier that Jensen had travelled to China in January when Jensen said he intended to set up a competing business.
Abhilash said he asked Jensen if he had any problems with Solrmount, but Jensen denied he was setting up a separate business.
Abhilash said the defendants attempted to solicit Solrmount’s customers and have also obtained orders from them.
He said CCTV footage showed that the day after Jensen resigned he attended Solrmount’s warehouse and loaded a van with goods. Jensen had no permission for this or to be in the building, Abhilash said.
He also said the “deceitful and fraudulent nature” of wrongdoing by Jensen, which, he alleged, included receiving “backhand personal benefits” and the clandestine establishment of a competing business while working as CEO of Solrmount, showed there was a real risk Jensen would destroy or delete evidence unless orders were made.

title: Affordable wines: A red and white from Bordeaux, both discounted
description: Wines for the Weekend: This bone-dry white and easy-drinking red come from the same producer
content:
We feature two wines from the same producer this week. Marc Lurton is part of a wine dynasty based in Bordeaux that now produces wine in Spain, Portugal, Argentina, Chile, and Australia, as well as France. His brother Pierre runs some of the most prestigious châteaux in Bordeaux. Marc is the fourth generation to run Château Lurton, a property based in the less fashionable (and therefore less expensive) Entre-Deux-Mers sub-region of Bordeaux.
The white wine is made from a blend of sauvignon blanc, sémillon and muscadelle. Don’t be concerned by the vintage; older sémillon ages beautifully. The red wine is made from a classic Bordeaux blend of 50 per cent cabernet sauvignon and 50 per cent merlot.
A very attractive light, crisp, bone-dry white with a lively acidity and waxy, slightly honeyed fruit. With oysters or grilled plaice.
A very pleasant, easy-drinking red Bordeaux with soft, ripe plums and a dry finish. Try it with a steak, roast beef, or firm cheeses.

title: There’s a good chance Ireland will come to regret this boomtime period as a missed opportunity
description: Country acts like it’s poor when it’s actually rich and should be thinking more strategically about its wealth
content:
The difference between Ireland and Norway is not just that Norway saves more of its tax windfall, it knows when it will run out.
Geologists can estimate accurately when Norway’s oil and gas reserves will expire.
According to the Norwegian Offshore Directorate, oil and gas production will stay steady until 2030 after which point there will be a steep “tapering off” unless there are new finds.
In Ireland, we have no line of sight. We’re completely in the dark. The tax windfall could go on for another decade or could fall off a cliff tomorrow. Even the chief financial officers of Apple , Microsoft and Eli Lilly , the State’s three biggest taxpayers, don’t know.
And yet we’re funnelling a huge amount of this windfall (€6 out of every €7) into everyday spending, into income tax breaks, into rent supports, stuff that won’t easily be resiled from.
We’re probably the only State in the world that bases its budgetary arithmetic on a handful of multinationals and the revenues they generate outside Ireland.
“The budgetary arithmetic is constructed on the crucial assumption that corporate profitability continues to expand; any decline in profitability could put a (potentially large) dent in corporate tax revenues,” the Department of Finance said in a report released with Budget 2027 on Tuesday.
If we had saved the windfall element of corporation tax since 2015 – approximately 50 per cent of annual receipts – the State would now have a war chest of €130 billion, capable of generating about €10 billion annually in interest (a typical stock market return).
[ Government ‘will need to borrow’ for new wealth funds as spending rises at fastest rate in EU, says watchdog Opens in new window ]
This would be enough to do away with the Universal Social Charge (USC) in one fell swoop, without having to raise tax elsewhere.
So much of Ireland’s tax system is still on an emergency setting from the financial crash, USC being the most obvious example.
The tax-free inheritance threshold of €420,000 and the 33 per cent capital acquisitions tax (CAT) that applies thereafter compares with a pre-crash threshold of €542,000 and CAT of 20 per cent.
Of course Ministers will point to the political straitjackets they find themselves in, the realpolitik of a modern democracy.
If Minister for Finance Simon Harris announced this week that he was planning to save €17 billion of the expected €34 billion in corporate tax this year in the midst of a cost-of-living crisis , he would, like Michael Collins, have been signing his own political death warrant and that of Fine Gael.
Big change requires a break from the sort of electoral budgeting, the winners and losers narrative, that we’ve had to date. A break from the firefighting, from the sticking plaster measures.
[ We’re apparently rolling in money, but everyone feels poorer and nobody is happy Opens in new window ]
We’ve had four years of energy credits and we still have the most expensive electricity prices in the European Union (EU). The credits are not a solution so much as a stop-gap. It’s the same with housing . The more money we spend on the housing assistance payment and other rent supports, the more there is a general erosion in affordability.
One senior figure said that Ireland acts like a poor country, spending money as it gets it, gambling on the back of future revenues, when it is actually a rich country that should be thinking more strategically about its wealth.
“Why don’t we feel the budget day numbers? One reason is that it’s going on hiring more staff across the public sector,” he said.
General government spending jumped by 54 per cent between 2019 and 2025, from €86.9 billion to €133.8 billion, facilitated by record corporate tax receipts.
At the same time, employment in the public sector rose by almost 80,000, from 339,000 to 417,000.
“If the Government thinks this (the additional employment) is warranted, it should be paying for it with money it can depend on,” the senior figure said.
[ Public spending hits record level as watchdog sharply criticises Budget 2027 Opens in new window ]
The Government seems to have shelved any semblance of a plan to widen the tax base and seems content to play the game with the chips it gets from Corporate America.
Experts disagree on whether Ireland has what’s known in economics as “Dutch Disease” – where a sharp increase in wealth in one sector (usually from the discovery of oil or gas) bids up prices, creating cost challenges and a gradual loss of competitiveness.
The National Competitiveness and Productivity Council says Ireland is now “firmly part of the high-cost cluster in Europe”, with labour costs rising faster than the EU average since 2021. In the three years after the pandemic, labour costs rose faster than in the 13 years previous.
After playing a stellar role in financial crisis, Ireland now sits in an ivory tower at one remove from the financial zeitgeist: debt and fiscal constraint.
Tax receipts more than cover spending, resulting in healthy budget surpluses, while Government debt as a percentage of gross domestic product is now under 35 per cent. In the UK (in 2025) the equivalent was 101 per cent. In France, it was 115 per cent. In the US, 121 per cent.
There’s a good chance we’ll come to regret this period as a missed opportunity.

title: ‘Retirement is the start of the next stage of my life’: Rachael Blackmore on life after the racecourse
description: The first woman to win the Grand National features on Detours with Craig Doyle, a podcast by Irish Times Content Studio created in association with Volvo
content:
Rachael Blackmore doesn’t remember the first time she sat on a pony. Growing up on a dairy farm in Killenaule, Co Tipperary, animals were simply part of everyday life. “I had a brilliant childhood,” she says. “I had pet lambs, who I fed before school every morning, and I loved ponies and riding from the youngest age.”
Freshly retired from life as a national hunt jockey, Rachel now contends with morning routines of a different complexion. The woman who made history as the first ever winner of the Grand National is a new parent, as she and her husband, jockey Brian Hayes, welcomed baby Bowie to the world earlier this year.
“Bowie is brilliant,” she smiles, “he’s a great sleeper. Being a parent really amazing.”
Blackmore is in the passenger seat for Detours, the podcast from The Irish Times Content Studio created in association with Volvo Cars. Hosted by Craig Doyle, Detours explores the twists, turns and unexpected moments that shape life’s journey, and for Rachael Blackmore, becoming an internationally-renowned jockey was one such unexpected outcome.
Her parents gave her every opportunity to develop her riding as she grew up, but despite her love of horses, a career as a jockey was never part of her plan. Her mother, a retired teacher, had hoped Blackmore might follow in her footsteps and pursue a career in education. “She was always dropping subtle hints that teaching was a great job, but I didn’t want to stay in school my whole life, I suppose.”
Riding horses and being outdoors made her happiest. “I thought I’d become a vet because that was a more realistic dream than having a career as a jockey. I never even allowed myself to imagine that; it was so far removed from what I thought could be possible.”
Blackmore’s route to the racecourse was indirect. She studied science at University College Dublin for two years before moving to the University of Limerick to study equine science. She later enrolled at Griffith College, where she earned a diploma in business studies. By the time she finished college at 25, a pivotal decision presented itself. “I was at a major crossroads in my life,” she recalls. “I had been riding as an amateur for years, but now I had to decide whether to knuckle down and get a real job.”
Then came an unexpected turn of events. John Hanlon, the trainer whose horses Blackmore had been riding as an amateur, and more commonly known as “Shark”, suggested that she turn professional. This was mooted as a practical move that would give her more rides and more opportunities to practice. It was to change the course of her life. “That decision allowed me to live a dream I never thought possible,” she says.
The work ethic required to carry her to the top of her profession was forged long before she ever entered a weighing room, having learned by her parents’ example. “Seeing my parents work so hard had a massive influence on me. For my dad, being a farmer is a way of life. When things had to be done, they were done. Animals had to be fed on Christmas Day; if an animal was sick at 3am, he was out looking after it. I grew up around two parents who both worked very hard but never made anything about that.”
Hard work, determination and a healthy dose of ambition have propelled Blackmore to the pinnacle of her sport, delivering an unrivalled level of achievement. From becoming the first woman to win the Grand National, earning her the BBC world sport star of the year 2021 award, to amassing 575 wins across her decade-long career as a professional jockey, Rachael Blackmore has never been anything less than extraordinary.
Pragmatism has however underpinned her success. “When it comes to racing and heading into a week at Cheltenham, you get all your thinking done beforehand, so that when you get legged-up in the parade ring, you’re fully confident that you’ve done your homework. The minute the race starts, you ride on instinct. That’s the only way you can ride because in a race, anything can happen. You have to be able to ride completely on feel,” explains Blackmore. “And a horse will give you a feeling in a race. It’s important that you can park all of your thinking and just ride that particular horse at that particular moment.”
This ability to trust her gut and adapt quickly has served her well through what she describes as “the many twists and turns” on her journey from rural schoolgirl to pioneering sportswoman. It has also made the transition into retirement a relatively smooth one. “Of course I miss competing,” she says. “The feeling you get when you ride a big winner is indescribable, but as a jockey you’re privileged to be able to decide for yourself when to retire. I look back on so many incredible moments in my career happily and now I’ve started a new chapter.”
Safety and risk management have been constant considerations throughout her professional life. “Being a jockey is an extremely dangerous sport,” she says. “Safety is something that is constantly talked about; the safety of horses, riders and jockeys.” The precarious nature of the sport carries its challenges, but it has also forged a strong sense of camaraderie within the horse racing world. “The weight room is a fantastic place. Everyone there is a competitor, but because we are all so aware of the dangers of the sport, there’s a great sense of community. Jockeys are mutually supportive and will often give each other advice; it’s that kind of an environment.”
The 37-year-old understands more than most that risk can never be completely eliminated. “But you can do everything possible to make a situation as safe as possible.” This mindset applies beyond competitive racing; Blackmore drives a Volvo, a brand synonymous with putting safety at the heart of its designs. “Driving is similar to riding, I think. You can never completely eliminate danger or risk, but you can put yourself in the safest circumstances possible.”
She has a car seat in the back for baby Bowie and relishes the freedom that driving affords her. Perhaps unsurprisingly for a former jockey, freedom for Blackmore is, quite simply, the ability to move, whether driving or riding. It’s also having the power to make her own decisions. Her path to the sporting hall of fame may have involved a few detours, but every turn was hers to choose.
Craig Doyle and Rachael Blackmore drove the Volvo EX60, the fully-electric SUV that marks a new beginning. Learn more at volvocars.ie , watch the full episode on YouTube and listen to Detours on Spotify

title: Planning a new kitchen? Here’s how to choose appliances that make life easier
description: Once you understand how you use your kitchen, it becomes easier to identify the features that will make a genuine difference
content:
Planning a new kitchen is exciting, but it can also feel overwhelming. There are layouts to consider, finishes to compare and decisions to make about everything from flooring, cupboard doors and handles to tiles and splashbacks.
With so much attention naturally given to how the room will look, it is easy to spend less time considering the appliances at its heart. Yet these are the elements you will rely on every day, long after the worktops have been fitted and the final paint colour chosen.
Ben Murphy, country manager Ireland and director with Miele, shares his advice on choosing appliances that will work intuitively, efficiently and beautifully for years to come: “The best starting point is not a list of appliance features, but to think carefully about how you live and use your kitchen. Do you cook from scratch, batch-cook or entertain regularly? Do you rely heavily on your oven or tend to prepare quicker meals on the hob? Is the dishwasher constantly running? Do you buy plenty of fresh food, or need generous freezer storage?”
Once you understand how you use your kitchen, it becomes easier to identify the features that will make a genuine difference. Miele develops appliances across cooking, refrigeration, dishwashing and laundry, with technology designed to make everyday life easier, more intuitive and more efficient.
Your oven and hob are likely to be among the most-used appliances in the kitchen, so consider what you regularly cook rather than what you imagine making on special occasions.
Selected Miele ovens include automatic programmes to make everyday cooking simpler, alongside more distinctive features such as TasteControl, which prevents food from continuing to cook once a programme has finished. For keen bakers and cooks, Moisture Plus adds moisture during baking and roasting, helping to produce light dough, browned crusts and succulent roasts.
Think about positioning too. Installing an oven at a higher, more comfortable height makes it easier to check and remove food. A Miele Gourmet drawer can preheat crockery, keep dishes ready to serve and be used for low-temperature cooking.
Induction hobs provide fast, responsive heat and transfer energy directly to the pan, giving you precise control while minimising wasted energy. A Miele TwoInOne induction hob with integrated vapour extraction removes the need for a conventional hood overhead, helping to create a clearer view across the room – ideal for an island.
Shopping habits should also inform your choice of refrigeration. A household buying plenty of fruit, vegetables, meat and fish will have different requirements from one that relies more heavily on frozen or pre-prepared food.
Selected Miele refrigeration appliances include PerfectFresh Pro compartments, designed to provide suitable temperature and humidity conditions to keep food fresher for longer. Clear, well-organised storage also makes it easier to see what you have, helping to prevent food from being forgotten and wasted.
‘The most useful technology is not necessarily the most conspicuous. It should remove effort from the things you do regularly’
Refrigerators operate continuously, so compare the energy label, annual energy consumption and usable capacity rather than looking at the rating alone. Choose a size that works for your household.
The dishwasher can be an afterthought, but it is often one of the hardest-working appliances in a busy kitchen. Look for flexible baskets that can accommodate everyday crockery alongside pans, delicate glasses and larger serving dishes. Noise levels matter in an open-plan space, particularly if the machine will run while the family is eating, working or relaxing nearby.
Selected Miele dishwashers offer AutoDos, which automatically dispenses detergent from the integrated PowerDisk. QuickPowerWash delivers cleaning results for normally soiled crockery in just 58 minutes, while AutoOpen drying opens the dishwasher door automatically at the end of the programme.
For everyday use, look for a dishwasher with an Eco programme. It may take longer, but it is designed to reduce energy and water consumption. Waiting until the dishwasher is full before running it will also help you use resources more efficiently.
A home improvement project can be a useful opportunity to reconsider the utility room too. When choosing a washing machine, look for a capacity that reflects the loads you regularly wash. On selected Miele models, TwinDos automatically dispenses detergent, while the honeycomb drum is designed to care for fabrics as they move through the wash, helping them to last longer.
When choosing a tumble dryer, heat-pump technology offers an energy-efficient alternative to conventional condenser drying. Miele heat-pump dryers provide economical, gentle drying.
“The most useful technology is not necessarily the most conspicuous,” says Murphy. “It should remove effort from the things you do regularly, whether that means helping you select a cooking programme, dispensing detergent automatically or providing a useful notification through an app.”
Energy considerations should extend beyond the letter on the label. Compare appliances of a similar size and type, check their stated annual or per-cycle consumption and consider whether the capacity is appropriate for your household. Using Eco programmes, running full loads and avoiding unnecessarily high washing temperatures can all reduce energy and water consumption over time.
To help make your final choices, visit the Miele Experience Centre at Liffey Valley to explore the appliances first-hand and receive expert advice. Miele Ireland also offers cooking events and product demonstrations, providing an opportunity to see how different features could work in your own home.
“Major appliances are a significant investment, so it is important to look beyond their initial appearance and purchase price,” says Murphy. “Consider energy and water consumption, the care provided for food, cookware and clothing, and whether the appliance has been designed for lasting use.”
Miele tests its household appliances for up to 20 years’ use. During product development, appliances undergo rigorous durability tests designed to simulate average household use over that period.
Design matters too, especially when several appliances are grouped together. Miele’s built-in range is designed to sit neatly within kitchen cabinetry, while co-ordinated design lines, including PureLine, VitroLine and handleless ArtLine, offer different visual treatments. With finishes such as Stainless steel, Obsidian black, Graphite grey and Pearl beige available on selected models, the collection can complement kitchens ranging from traditional and transitional to ultra-contemporary.
For anyone planning a kitchen or wider home upgrade, Miele is offering up to €1,200 cashback on selected major domestic appliances purchased in Ireland between September 1st and December 31st 2026
Customers can claim from €75 cashback on one appliance, and up to €1,200 cashback on six or more appliances. Terms and conditions apply. To explore eligible appliances and find full details of how to claim, visit miele.ie .

title: ‘AI Minister’ Niamh Smyth: ‘I’d have a very different view than President Trump’
description: Minister says she is ‘cautiously optimistic’ and excited by AI - but also has concerns over its impact on Irish labour market
content:
A fter a month in which the people driving AI ’s technological revolution suggested even they have only minimal control over where it might all lead us, it’s not surprising that Ireland’s Minister for Digital Transformation is concerned by the worst-case scenarios.
Niamh Smyth , Minister of State at the Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, says she is “cautiously optimistic” about the balance of pros and cons AI has in store for us during the years ahead, but admits she still worries about the potential for a hugely negative impact on the labour market.
“I’d have concerns around displacement and I would never shy away from that,” she tells The Irish Times in the run up to the Government’s International AI Summit at the RDS next week. The event boasts an impressive line-up of speakers including Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis and a long list of political, tech sector and business heavyweights.
“I do believe there will be new jobs created. I do think the human oversight of any technology will have to remain in place. And AI jobs have certainly been on the rise in Ireland,” she says, referring to the substantial growth in numbers since 2023.
“But obviously, there will be displacement. There will be people impacted by the capability of the technology, because [in various areas] it won’t take as many humans.
“So I am optimistic and I am excited by the technology, but I have concerns. I don’t want to see mass displacement, because that innately causes civil unrest. It causes anarchy. And I’m very conscious that things can be whipped up very quickly on platforms and with the use of AI too.”
Just this week, it emerged that Oracle is looking to cut another 70 Irish jobs this year as it continues to trim costs to fund its expensive push into AI infrastructure and data centres.
AI is the perfect tool with which to make the damage AI itself might do worse.
Smyth, the first person to serve as Minister of State with responsibility for the area – her particular responsibilities are for Trade Promotion, AI and Digital Transformation – says the technology, and the speed at which it is evolving, present huge challenges, for business, the Government and the EU but believes Europe, and Ireland, are in a better place to navigate the landscape than many other jurisdictions.
‘I’d have a very different view, obviously, than President Trump. I don’t think self-regulation is any regulation’
Many Americans, she says, envy the legal framework established on this side of the Atlantic to deal with the tech giants and the way they are changing the business, social and human environments.
“In my view, the legislation is there,” she says, referencing the EU AI Act, the Digital Services Act and others. The companies know what’s acceptable and what’s not acceptable; the prohibitive practices piece, the ban on high-risk systems, the requirement that companies ensure that due diligence is taken with any of the AI tools they have developed, or more importantly, released.
“Then obviously we have our own domestic legislation around that, and the establishment of the National AI Office. Obviously, [European] Commission president [Ursula] von der Leyen has also talked about an EU Kids Act, to address the protection of young people online, too. So there’s so much going on,” she says.
In the US, meanwhile, Donald Trump has come out against legal regulation even in the face of the most prominent owners’ appeals for it, and has recently corralled them into a system of self-regulation that even he described as only “morally binding”.
“I’d have a very different view, obviously, than President Trump,” Smyth says. “I don’t think self-regulation is any regulation.”
It is one of the reasons, she believes, why many legislators at state level in the US are envious of the framework established within the EU.
“I was in the [United] States on a trade mission before the summer, meeting with political colleagues, at a state level, and they actually look to Europe,” Smyth says.
“You’ll never hear this in the geopolitical debate. In that, people are always hammering Europe for being stifled by red tape and stifled by legislation, preventing innovation. But the truth is, when you’re out there and you’re speaking to legislators in the [individual] states, they’re looking to Europe to see what we’ve done because they feel we have done more than they’ve been able to do. Because at a federal level there, the attitude is different, but they’re really craving more guardrails and oversight on the development of these technologies.
“What we’re attempting to do is to get the balance right to ensure that innovation is encouraged, that we’re allowed to be creative in terms of the designs of technology, but, more importantly, to look at how businesses who maybe aren’t technology-based can adopt it to put more efficiencies in place.”
That, she admits, is not quite where she would like to see it, particularly in the SME sector, where she feels take-up has been hindered by practical or financial considerations.
“We’re trying to address that,” she says. “I know we have done a roadshow where we’ve been to a number of counties working with the Local Enterprise Offices [LEOs]. Some of the LEOs have been working on digital transformation and the impact of AI long before it became a ministerial role. They have become a good source of feedback for us on where the supports are needed, or where we need to go and tell businesses about the supports that are already there.
“Because sometimes people are so busy when they’re running SMEs and they don’t have a HR section or a finance section to know what is even available to them. So we have a job of working to ensure the SME sector is completely aware of what supports are there.”
The Government itself, she acknowledges, meanwhile, has been getting to grips with how seemingly all-pervasive the issue of AI is. She lists off some of the Ministers whose departments are involved in some aspect or other – training, health, protection of children, employment, cyber security – the list goes on. Smyth says a growing amount of collaboration on both pursuing the opportunities and tackling challenges is happening.
The Government’s own AI advisory council, chaired by Patricia Scanlon and including academics, entrepreneurs and others with expertise in the area, had done some work on this and suggested much more, but it was disbanded as the AI Office of Ireland was established – which might be regarded as somewhat premature given the need for informed opinion on what are very big issues for the country, economy and civil society.
Smyth says the working papers the council completed are still regarded as important documents feeding into current work programmes, and that she still calls on members of the council to hear their views and consider their advice on a wide range of issues.
Scanlon, she says, was with her the day before this interview, and encouraged her and the Government to do more to promote the innovation sector, to nurture and champion the sorts of start-ups that can become significant players in the sector over the coming years.
[ Ireland’s great AI job displacement: ‘Every employer, every worker should be talking about this’ Opens in new window ]
The previous evening, she says, she took that suggestion to the Taoiseach, and argued it was something that might be addressed in the budget . Quite how much the conversation fed into the measures unveiled on Tuesday is impossible to gauge, but there were moves to assist start-ups and to help companies to scale up, as well as increases to research and development credits to encourage investment.
More widely, she believes Government and the EU has to find a way of using AI to remain competitive during what is set to be a dramatic shift in the way workplaces operate, while keeping the safeguards and ensuring their presence does not hand a competitive advantage to rivals.
‘The technology is developing at breakneck speed and the impacts of it are throwing up different problems, different challenges, every day of the week’
“Citizens right across Europe have demanded that safeguards be put in place. And I think the European Commission is very aware of where our citizens are at around this. They want to know they can use the technology but they want it to be safe, and I suppose that’s the balancing act for us.”
It remains to be seen whether this can really be done when the biggest players are US firms with little regard, it often seems, for European-style regulation which enjoy the backing of a president who sometimes seems to see such controls as a personal and political affront.
The past few weeks, however, have highlighted the need for tighter controls, with Smyth, like many others, openly taken aback by some of the stories of AI agents gone slightly rogue.
“It’s such a fluid situation,” she says. “The technology is developing at breakneck speed and the impacts of it are throwing up different problems, different challenges, every day of the week. We’ve gone from the Hugging Face intervention, with OpenAI ’s bots, you know, making their way out of the systems they were supposed to stay in, and also how the bots themselves seemed to be aware of the fact they weren’t supposed to be doing what they were doing, and so they tried to disguise it ... it’s really remarkable. Incredible.”
Since then there has been the Australian healthcare hack and others in the US, with companies coming in for criticism over delays in realising what their own technology was up to – and an apparently relaxed approach to impacts upon the authorities.
[ Message from the Editor: prophets of AI catastrophe Opens in new window ]
The episodes raise obvious questions about what might be possible if bad actors were actually directing things and how vulnerable the Government, agencies such as the HSE , or financial institutions might be to cyberattack, when the budgets for security measures are being dwarfed by the amounts being spent on advancing these very systems, most obviously in the US and China.
Ireland’s National Cyber Security Centre chief Richard Browne acknowledged the seriousness of this issue again this week.
“Of course, I would be worried,” says Smyth. “It’s the one piece of technology that needs all arms of the State. You’ve got the cybersecurity aspect, which falls under the Department of Justice. You take the social media platforms, which fall under the Department of Culture. There is the AI piece, which is part of my own remit. So it takes a collective approach, from the Irish State, from the European Union, to ensure people are protected and kept safe; ensure that you know European values are adhered to. That people are protected and safe.”
When it comes to the arts, for instance, or newspapers, their views on “fair use” seem firmly rooted in the US legal definition, something that has allowed AI’s scraping of words, sounds and images on a colossal scale without, most of those being scraped would say, anything like commensurate compensation.
Smyth has, she says, strong feelings on the issue. Having studied arts-related areas at the National College of Art and Design, the University of Limerick and the Institute of Arts Design and Technology and chaired the Oireachtas committee on the arts before taking up her current role, she is conscious of the challenges facing those working in the sector while retaining a belief that human creativity will retain a valued edge over that of machines.
“I was out recently in Brussels at a copyright committee, and obviously, as we hold the presidency, we’re very mindful of how we address it. I can’t say I have all the answers on that yet. But I completely understand their desire to protect their original work. It is awful that it would be scraped, copied, plagiarised. What we need to make sure is that they are remunerated correctly for that work.”
The potential impact on the arts touches on the wider potential impact on human engagement and all that entails. The previous day, she says, she was at an event in Maynooth where some big questions were asked, including where this all leaves us as humans.
Smyth readily acknowledges “I don’t have all the answers.”

title: Forget the tech stack. Digital transformation is all about the customer
description: Good digitalisation puts the ‘you’ into UX, Dentsu’s Dave Winterlich hears from tech guru Garvan Callan
content:
Digital transformation is not just all the rage, it’s EU policy. But what exactly does it mean?
If anyone knows, it’s Garvan Callan, founder of OneZero1, a business transformation consultancy. He not alone helps leaders to develop and execute their business strategies but when it comes digital transformation, he wrote the book.
Digital Business Strategy: How to Design, Build and Future-Proof a Business in the Digital Age, came out in 2023.
Yet even now, three years on, there remains confusion about what digital transformation entails, and indeed, the difference between digitisation and digitalisation.
It’s a code worth cracking because, given the pace of technological acceleration and the exponential growth in AI capabilities, strategy is no longer a static play, he points out, but an increasingly dynamic one.
What is urgently required is an adaptive strategy, or, as he calls it, ‘stradaptability’.
That goes from the very front of the business – its consumer facing brand - right through to the back-end office processes on which every organisation is built.
Having worked in financial services, helping legacy banks take on upstart neobanks, as well as lecturing on the topic and sitting on boards of enterprises getting to grips with it, successful digital transformation is something he has enormous experience in.
He defines digitisation as the taking of a task, and, instead of doing it in a traditional manual or physical way, reinventing its execution, through the use of code, as a virtual or computer-based service.
Digitalisation refers to the digitisation of a series of such events. It goes beyond just one task, to getting an entire job done via software.
In financial services, for example, it is what allows you to complete an entire loan application digitally, from seeing an ad online, to clicking through to a website, to uploading forms, undergoing credit scoring, securing approval and receiving funds into your bank account electronically.
Digital transformation runs even deeper.
It is where an organisation looks at itself and says, ‘We should digitise, and digitalise the things we do in order to make it better for our clients, easier for us to deliver, able to reach more people by doing things smartly, more cheaply, and maybe taking risk out of the system as well,’ he explains.
As such it represents a systemic overhaul, not just of products and services but of processes.
It’s not unlike the journey the marketing industry has been on wherein, initially, ‘digital’ simply meant a new channel to market. Today by contrast, in areas such as programmatic marketing, software and algorithms have automated the entire process of buying and selling of digital ad space.
Yet the technology underpinning all this transformation actually sits at the bottom of the totem pole, not the top. That’s because, despite its central importance, the kit you are running on doesn’t stand still.
“Technology is changing perpetually. Therefore, the successful, thriving organisations are taking an adaptable approach by trying to build and layer and continuously accelerate the adoption and the application of the latest, the newest, the prowess and power of digital technologies,” he says.
They do this “to get disproportionate market share, to get ahead, to create that best brand, whatever their strategic objectives are,” he explains.
A business can approach digital transformation by a variety of routes. Some will digitalise existing practices, others will set up entirely new digital native enterprises instead. Others still will achieve it on the acquisition trail.
He points to the success of Polish digital bank, mBank, created as an offshoot of legacy firm BRE Bank, as one example.
“They created an entirely new digital organisation that thinks and acts differently,” he says. “Within a couple of years, they had done a leapfrog.” The BRE brand no longer exists, “and the new bank is flourishing,” he adds, “because the experience is better, the efficiency is better, the risk profile is better.”
But all digital transformations are different, he says: “There is no one journey.”
It’s never just about digital either. Increasingly what is required is what he calls a “phygital” approach, one that blends both real life and online services.
That’s because, for basic transactions, consumers want the quickest route, which is typically online. But for high value purchases such as mortgages, cars, or health services, consumers “want to look a human in the eye”, he tells Winterlich.
For brands, it’s about “appreciating the moments when humans need humans,” he adds.
Moreover, “we need to be more human in a more technologically driven world. We can digitise away all the micro moments ... It’s in those emotional moments, those more complex moments, that we really rely on, need and value the human interaction,” he says.
Understanding that fact revolutionises how brands interact with the market. He points to an Audi showroom he visited in London as a case in point. Surprisingly, it had no cars.
Rather than the traditional approach of trying to shift whatever vehicles were in the lot, the process focused entirely on Callan’s lifestyle, needs and budget. “They said, let’s take out all the cars and start with the customer,” he explains.
“So it started with a conversation about me. What was happening behind that profiling was a picture of an A6 estate, with a pet grille for the dog at weekends and a darker leather interior that would suit my young kids. The ‘Audi of Garvan’ was being constructed and it was a very compelling experience.”
The technology involved has since moved on to include virtual reality, augmented reality and now AI. In the meantime Callan, by then home in Ireland, bought an Audi.

title: Doom Painting by AK Blakemore: A dense, finely crafted narrative  of the Peasants’ Revolt
description: Author’s full-on, pitch-perfect retelling blends visceral brutality with pure poetry
content:
1381 was a long time ago, but a few pages into Doom Painting, the reader can almost hear the grinding gears of a literary Tardis at work, catapulting them back 645 years to a savage, disgruntled England. The peasantry has been reduced to near starvation and is ruled by injustice and cruelty. When King Richard II implements a new poll tax, an already starving serfdom are ready to detonate.
Enter Wat Tyler, a Kent farmer back from the war in France, whose charisma turns to leadership as he and a band of rebels go medievally viral and a furious people’s army is born. Over 16 days in the summer of 1381, we sink into a dense, addictive and finely crafted narrative that follows the rise of “the Commons” in Essex and Kent as they take Rochester, Canterbury and the Tower of London. For a brief, but ground-breaking episode, they partially achieved their goal and changed England’s history.
Reliable accounts of “the Peasants’ Revolt” are scarce, but Blakemore has taken available research, run it through her extraordinary imagination, and here delivers a full-on, pitch-perfect retelling. It’s her most ambitious and successful work yet. You can practically smell the blood and the muck of the rebels’ victories; the luxury of the royal court’s silk and ermine is almost tangible. In between, the ambitions of a nascent English burgher class are ruthless and conniving.
The scope of the novel is at once broad and intensely focused on its vividly drawn characters, their dialogue uproarious and vulgar. Retaining historical purity overall, Blakemore’s skill at splicing medieval with contemporary parlance is daring and effective. On occasion, quirky references to present-day culture such as the flight of a drone or lyrics by the Sex Pistols serve to enrich the text.
There are even weird, post-Covid parallels in terms of theme. Brother John Ball, the rising’s philosopher, notes: “I did what I could, but it was not enough. England’s still f**ked.”
[ Mary and Padraic Colum - Lives and the Dream: Bringing a singular literary duo back to life Opens in new window ]
One of the book’s most rewarding aspects is the author’s exceptional ability to blend visceral brutality with pure poetry. At times the prose is mesmerising in its beauty. If the book’s 664 pages are initially daunting, it’s these narrative sparks and shimmers that keep you reading. A remarkable achievement.
Helena Mulkerns is a writer and publisher

title: Venezuelan ousted leader Maduro charged with conspiracy to commit torture
description: Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, accused of torturing American citizens and others held in Venezuela to repress opposition
content:
The US justice department of justice on Thursday announced new charges against ousted Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, accusing them of torturing American citizens and others held in Venezuela to repress opposition and preserve their power.
The charges, which were unsealed in federal court in Manhattan, adding to accusations already levied by the government against Maduro (63), and Flores (69).
They already face charges of conspiring to commit narco-terrorism and import cocaine, along with other crimes, which they have pleaded not guilty to. Both are scheduled to go on trial in June.
The 30-page indictment released Thursday includes a new count charging Maduro and Flores of conspiracy to commit torture. It says that from at least 1999 through 2025, the couple and high-level Venezuelan officials inflicted severe physical and mental pain to punish members of the political opposition, silence dissent and protect their authority.
One official ordered the murder of opponents of the Maduro regime, oversaw torture and personally threatened the murder of a prisoner’s child, the indictment said. - The New York Times
Another senior Venezuelan officer who reported directly to Maduro developed torture methods that he presented for Maduro’s approval and led an agency responsible for torturing scores of victims, according to the indictment. A third official personally ordered and participated in the torture of civilians and military members, including U. citizens, who were believed to pose a threat to Maduros’s rule, the document said.
Maduro’s and Flores’ lawyers have argued that they should not be prosecuted in a US court, on the grounds of sovereign immunity. The judge overseeing the case, Alvin K Hellerstein, has yet to rule on their motions to dismiss on those grounds.

title: The Lion, the Witch and the Ulsterman on RTÉ: Andrew Trimble takes on the thorny issue of CS Lewis’s Irishness
description: Television: Lewis is a beloved but polarising figure, which may explain his exclusion from the pantheon of significant Irish literary figures
content:
CS Lewis was an author born in Ireland – but can he be considered an Irish author? That is the question posed by ex-rugby international Andrew Trimble in The Lion, the Witch and the Ulsterman (RTÉ One, Thursday, 10.15pm), an engaging documentary in which Trimble, a former Christian theology student from Coleraine, considers Lewis’s complex connection to the island of his birth through the prism of his own multifaceted relationship with Irishness.
Lewis’s Narnia novels have sold in the hundreds of millions and are a key fantasy text, alongside Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings. Yet despite his stature, he is rarely thought of as an Irish writer, despite growing up in Belfast to a family from Cork .
One reason, Trimble discovers, is that Lewis did not sound Irish. He learns this in Oxford, where Lewis worked as a “fellow” and tutor for 29 years, and where Trimble listens to a recording of the writer from the 1950s. His Britishness is striking. He pronounces “prayer” as “pray-ah” and “idea” as “idea-r” – betraying a thorny relationship with the letter “r” that many Irish people would regard as bordering on the obscene.
“That’s a caricature of an Oxford accent,” Trimble observes to Prof Suzannah Lipscomb. She suspects that Lewis’s Irish accent would have been the first thing to go when he was packed off to an English boarding school aged nine, following the death of his mother. “He went to schools that were brutal to him,” she says. “The Irish accent was probably beaten out of him.”
Yet if he sounded thoroughly British, he retained an abiding fondness for Belfast and its rolling hinterlands, as the amiable Trimble discovers. In a Lewis-themed coffee shop in East Belfast, Prof Margaret O’Callaghan says Lewis would have known growing up that the city was rived with divisions between unionists and nationalists, and suggests he may have taken refuge in flights of fantasy. She says the “escapism into ideal rurality” is a “reaction to a polarised city”.
Lewis is a beloved but controversial figure due to his Christian beliefs – and his enthusiastic use of his fiction as an ideological Trojan horse (in the Narnia books, the wise lion Aslan is a stand-in for Jesus). British fantasy author Philip Pullman was so annoyed by Lewis that he wrote an entire trilogy, His Dark Materials, simply to scold Lewis over his cruel and chilling final Narnia novel, The Last Battle – in which Susan Pevensie is condemned for growing up and developing an interest in lipstick and nylon.
Trimble doesn’t get into the weeds of Lewis’s divisiveness. And he does not quite identify the reason why Lewis is excluded from the pantheon of significant Irish literary figures – which surely has more to do with the lack of any tradition in Ireland of celebrating “regional” authors. It could be argued Frank O’Connor, the Cork Chekhov, receives short shrift for similar reasons – he doesn’t fit in the Dublin bubble and is thus snubbed.
But Trimble never pretends to have the answer and, across a documentary that is as shaggy as a lion’s mane, he proves agreeable company. The best thing that can be said about The Lion, the Witch and the Ulsterman is that – and apologies in advance to Philip Pullman – it makes you want to reach for one of your faded Narnia paperbacks and read it end to end.

title: McGovern scores twice as Shamrock Rovers ease to important victory over Drogheda
description: Burke scores fastest goal in Tallaght Stadium as Rovers go back on top of the Premier Division table
content:
Having scored a double when beating Waterford before the international break, John McGovern did so once again as champions Shamrock Rovers eased back to the top of the Premier Division table.
The Down striker had also hit a brace when Rovers beat Drogheda 4-1 at Tallaght Stadium back in May as they stretched their unbeaten run against the Louth side here to 15 games.
Despite the trying weather, the comfortable win was just what Rovers’ head coach Stephen Bradley would have wanted, putting them three points clear at the summit ahead of Monday’s big derby against Bohemians back in Dublin 24.
A second successive defeat means Drogheda remain second bottom in the relegation playoff place with three games to play.
With their head coach Kevin Doherty having to watch from the stand as he served a suspension, Daire Doyle took charge of Drogheda who gave a full senior debut to 20-year-old striker Ryan Markey in three changes from their loss to Bohemians before the break.
McGovern, one of three switches Rovers also made from their last outing, played his part as Rovers took the lead after just 34 seconds to record the fastest goal scored by the club at Tallaght Stadium.
The former Northern Ireland under-21 international flicked on Dan Cleary’s long ball out from the back. A slip by defender Andy Quinn then gifted Graham Burke a clear run on goal which he duly accepted with aplomb when sweeping home off his left foot for his ninth league goal of the season.
Clearly rattled, Drogheda survived falling further behind in the following minutes thanks to goalkeeper Fynn Talley who made fine stops to deny McGovern and then Matt Healy’s drive from distance.
Rovers maintained their onslaught on the Drogheda goal, frantic defending coughing up four corners over the next 10 minutes or so.
Drogheda then survived a reasonable penalty shout when skipper Conor Keeley appeared to push over McGovern inside the area before, almost inevitably, conceding again on 20 minutes.
Another sublime long ball, this time from captain Roberto ‘Pico’ Lopes, sent Burke through on goal down the middle. And though Tally raced out to get there before the Hoops’ number 10, he merely batted the ball into the path of McGovern who side-footed to the corner of the net from the edge of the area.
McGovern struck again to further extend the lead three minutes before the interval. Once more the striker was in the right place, when teed up by Tunmise Sobowale from Jake Mulraney’s cross, to almost nonchalantly shoot home from close range to also bring his league tally for the season to nine goals.
The width of a post prevented Drogheda getting a goal back three minutes into the second half, Markey’s hooked volley coming back off a post and bundled out for a corner by Ed McGinty.
The Rovers goalkeeper was twice worked in the following minutes by Markey and his own defender Cleary’s misplaced header as Drogheda maintained their admirable press for a way back into the game.
McGinty touched a Brandon Kavanagh free-kick round a post before the Drogheda midfielder scored their consolation goal on 88 minutes, rifling Shane Farrell’s corner to the net with the help of a deflection.
Substitute Aaron Greene had earlier missed the proverbial sitter for Rovers, their first-half dominance proving more than sufficient for victory.
Shamrock Rovers: McGinty; Cleary, Lopes, Grace (C O’Sullivan, h-t); Sobowale, Watts (Razi 60), Healy, Byrne (J O’Sullivan, 67), Mulraney; Burke (Greene, 60); McGovern (Afolabi, 60).
Drogheda United: Talley; Quinn, Keeley, Burney (Bolger, h-t); Agbaje, O’Brien (Godden, 62), Farrell, Kane; Kavanagh; Markey (Oluwa, 72), Davis (Doyle, 62).

title: Courts facing further disruption as judicial review of new legal aid model delayed
description: Minister for Justice said talks not appropriate when the regulations establishing the new scheme are subject of a High Court challenge
content:
The courts could be facing further disruption after the judge dealing with a High Court challenge to the new legal aid payment model told lawyers she would not be ready to make a decision next week.
The model, introduced on July 1st, provides for a flat €520 fee for solicitors irrespective of the number of clients or appearances.
It led to a widespread withdrawal of services by criminal defence solicitors, leading to thousands of case adjournments and serious disruption to the work of the criminal courts.
John Quinn, a lawyer at John M Quinn & Co Solicitors, brought an action in July seeking to quash the statutory instrument underpinning the new model.
He is suing the office of the Minister for Justice, with the Law Society of Ireland a notice party to the action.
Last Saturday, Law Society president Rosemarie Loftus invited O’Callaghan to enter last minute mediation on the dispute before the new legal year opened on Monday.
In a reply on Wednesday, O’Callaghan said mediation was not appropriate when the regulations establishing the new scheme are the subject of a High Court challenge.
Judgment on that challenge was due next Tuesday but, on Thursday, Judge Mary Rose Gearty informed lawyers a judgment in the case will not be ready.
The Chief Justice, Donal O’Donnell, said this week the judiciary was very concerned about the dispute and hoped it would be resolved soon.
Solicitors say the new system means they will not be paid for the work they do in more complex cases, including involving children and people with addiction and mental health issues.
O’Callaghan has repeatedly said the new scheme is aimed at improving efficiencies and is in the public interest.
[ Over 200 solicitors and barristers protest outside Criminal Courts of Justice in Dublin Opens in new window ]
O’Callaghan, in his Wednesday letter, disputed Loftus’ suggestion the new scheme was based on a “fundamental misunderstanding” of the operation of the District Court.
He said it was informed by a “detailed understanding” of District Court processes and “extensive analysis” of previous legal aid arrangements.
Addressing the society’s complaints about his continuing failure to provide the data on which his department’s review of criminal legal aid payments was based, O’Callaghan said the data could not be released because it related to “thousands” of individual cases and personal privacy concerns were involved.
He said data relating to criminal legal aid cases under the new scheme showed most were disposed of in one hearing and almost all were dealt with within five appearances, the average under the previous legal aid system.
Separately, in replies on Wednesday to parliamentary questions from Social Democrats TD Gary Gannon, the Minister said 2,400 new legal aid certificates have issued under the scheme and about 36 solicitors who had resigned from the legal aid panel had been reinstated.
In response to the Minister’s claims the old system was being “abused”, with people “getting 50/60 certificates for one accused before the court”, Gannon said that had happened in three instances. The Minister replied there were “much more than three instances”.
What is happening in courts around the country is “a shambles” and the Minister “can fix it”, said Gannon.

title: Nationalist politicians receive PSNI letters over protest blocking Garvaghy Road
description: Unionist politicians have led calls for arrest of Sinn Féin First Minister Michelle O’Neill
content:
Nationalist politicians are among those who have received letters from the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) over their participation in a protest blocking an Orange Order march on Portadown’s Garvaghy Road.
On Thursday, a senior PSNI officer confirmed the service was issuing letters to those “reasonably suspected” of having committed a criminal offence in relation to the dispute in the Co Armagh town.
First Minister Michelle O’Neill was among several Sinn Féin representatives who stood on the Garvaghy Road with more than 1,000 protesters to prevent Orangemen walking along the nationalist road from Drumcree church on the morning of Sunday, September 27th.
Unionist politicians have led calls for O’Neill’s arrest.
Sinn Féin issued a statement on Thursday evening, confirming that “a number” of elected representatives and party members have received letters from police.
It declined to comment on which individuals had received the correspondence.
“Sinn Féin have stood with the residents of the Garvaghy Road for the last two weeks in the face of provocation and the threat of an unwanted Orange march through their community,” it said.
“Standing up for what is right is always the right thing to do.”
[ From local row to peace-process shambles: How the Drumcree standoff developed Opens in new window ]
Police refused to comment on how many letters were being sent or the names of suspects. People Before Profit MLA Gerry Carroll confirmed in a statement that he had received one.
The standoff entered its twelfth day on Thursday.
PSNI Assistant Chief Constable Davy Beck said a team had been “methodically working” through evidence collected so far in the “large scale” investigation.
“This work will now proceed to the next phase where individuals will receive letters regarding the interview process,” he added.
SDLP Assembly member Justin McNulty, who has not received a letter but is expecting one, is among those who took part in the protest on September 27th.
He stood linking arms on the front row of protesters to stop Orangemen walking the road for the first time in 28 years.
[ Fintan O'Toole: Drumcree is theatre of the absurd, straight from Monty Python’s Ministry of Silly Walks Opens in new window ]
The MLA for Newry and Armagh – who was last week deselected by his party to run in next year’s Assembly election – said a “police letter is not going to hurt me”.
“Fundamentally, I feel I did the right thing by the residents of the Garvaghy Road who were fearful and who believed their rights were being trampled on,” he told The Irish Times.
“When the sirens started going off that Sunday morning, all of us at the front were very scared. We thought they (the police) were coming through with the shields and the batons.
“Thankfully there was no violence. Our greatest right is to protest for what is right.”
O’Neill is due to face a no-confidence motion in the Assembly next week.
She has defended her actions and told the Assembly Chamber on Monday, “when the law is wrong, I will stand firmly against it.”
DUP leader Gavin Robinson has called on police to act “without fear or favour” in its investigation.
“A political title is not a shield, and no one is above the law,” he said.
“For anyone found to have broken the law, the consequences must be the same, whether that is for a First Minister or anyone else.”
People Before Profit MLA Carroll said he had been invited by police to attend a voluntary interview under caution in connection with protests during the stand-off.
“I make no apology for standing with the residents of the Garvaghy Road,” he said.
“For almost three decades, this community has said no to a sectarian march being forced past their homes.
“When ordinary people peacefully stand together to defend their community, that is not criminality.
“It is the same civil disobedience that won every gain working-class people have ever made, from the suffragettes to the civil rights movement to the right to strike.”
Carroll said he will seek the advice of his solicitor.

title: Former GAA president John Horan named as new chair of Steering Group on Integration
description: Horan takes over role after Mary McAleese vacated position early last month
content:
Former GAA president John Horan has been confirmed as the new chair of the Steering Group on Integration.
Horan, who was president of the GAA from 2018-21, takes over the role after Mary McAleese vacated the position early last month .
The Na Fianna clubman was ratified by the management committees of all three organisations – the GAA, LGFA and Camogie Association – on Thursday night.
Horan said: “I come from a club that has achieved success on and off the field by valuing all of our members and harnessing our full potential across the GAA, camogie and LGFA.
“Being elected uachtarán was an enormous honour, and to be asked to chair the Steering Group on Integration and work with everyone who is committed to having a new dawn for Gaelic games is a responsibility and a privilege that I am excited to take on.”
There had been a feeling the SGI committee might look to bring in a completely independent chairperson with no strong links to any of the organisations. However, they have instead opted for a former president of one.
Horan is a retired secondary school principal. He was at the helm of the association when the Covid pandemic struck. Since his tenure ended, the former Leinster chairman has headed up the Páirc Uí Chaoimh stadium board. He is also currently chair of the stadium development committee in Louth, as well as serving on the committee overseeing the construction of the new Páirc Tailteann in Navan.
President of the LGFA, Trina Murray said: “John Horan is an outstanding appointment. He knows Gaelic games inside out, and his experience will be a huge asset as we drive integration forward. We’re delighted to have him on board, and we look forward to working with him.”
Those sentiments were echoed by Brian Molloy, president of the Camogie Association: “The Camogie Association welcomes John Horan’s appointment, at what is a crucial time for integration.
“There is a significant body of work already complete on the project. John’s deep knowledge and understanding of Gaelic games, and particularly the GAA landscape, ideally position him to help us achieve buy-in and deliver integration in the shortest timeframe possible.”
GAA president Jarlath Burns believes Horan is the right person to bring integration to reality.
Burns said: “John Horan was at the helm as we navigated our way through the worst of times that was the pandemic. His proven leadership, experience, integrity and ability to meet challenges head on make him an outstanding choice as our new chair, and to lead us to what will be the best of times as an integrated Gaelic games community.
“He brought representatives of Camogie and LGFA on to GAA Management during his tenure, and he has the respect of all three associations to make this work. I look forward to working with him in creating a GAA for all and a GAA Where We All Belong.”

title: Number of mother and baby home redress applications triples after awareness campaign
description: Some 6,200 payments have been made to successful applicants since the scheme launched in March 2024
content:
Applications to a scheme providing redress to those who spent time in a mother and baby institution have more than tripled since a nationwide campaign was launched to raise awareness.
Weekly applications for the Mother and Baby Institutions Payment Scheme rose to an average of about 51, up from an average of 14 before the awareness campaign launched in August.
Overall, a further 308 people applied since August, bringing the total number of applications to more than 7,600, according to new figures from the Department of Children .
Some 6,200 payments have been made to successful applicants since the scheme launched in March 2024. However, about 34,000 survivors are estimated to be eligible to apply.
Patricia Carey, who was born in Bessborough mother and baby institution in Cork and who advocates on behalf of survivors, previously voiced “grave concern” that less than 7,400 had applied to the scheme by August.
About €78 million had been paid out at that point out of a budget of €800 million. Payments averaged at €15,500 but ranged from €5,000 to €94,000.
The “marked increases” in applications following the latest campaign coincided with a rise in calls, requests for paper application forms and online enquiries, the department said.
Minister for Children Norma Foley welcomed the increase in applications and enquiries.
“I want people to know that they can contact the scheme in confidence, with information, guidance and support available throughout the process,” she said.
“The scheme will remain open until March 2029, giving potential applicants time to find out more, consider their options and, if they wish, make an application.
“I encourage anyone who thinks they may be eligible, or who is supporting them, to visit paymentscheme.ie or contact the Freephone service.”
Applications are confidential and applicants do not need to provide institutional records, “exact dates” or detailed accounts of their experiences, the department said.

title: Eddie Dunbar returns to competition weeks after collarbone fracture
description: Irish cyclist lined out in Gran Piemonte race, less than a month after injuring himself at Vuelta a España
content:
Vuelta a España stage winner Eddie Dunbar made a return to racing on Thursday, less than a month after fracturing his collarbone in that event.
He lined out in the Gran Piemonte race, riding in support of his Pinarello Q36.5 Pro Cycling team. He confirmed to the Irish Times Thursday evening that he had no problems with his shoulder in the race and that he will ride the Il Lombardia classic on Saturday. He will be supporting designated team leader Tom Pidcock there.
Dunbar raced to a superb victory on stage 19 of the Vuelta, taking his first win in two years. That appeared to bring to an end a long period affected by injuries, but he crashed close to the finish of stage 20 and withdrew from the race.
While fractures can often take six weeks to heal, he received prompt medical care at the Santry Sports Clinic and underwent surgery.
He started on the indoor trainer just over a week after his crash, and was recently pictured out training in Monaco with Tadej Pogačar. The Slovenian was injured earlier in the Vuelta and since declared he would end his season early.
Being able to race so soon is a boost for Dunbar and while his own form will have dropped since the Vuelta because of the time off the bike, getting some racing in before the end of the season should help him build well towards 2027.
His contract with the team runs until the end of next year. His Vuelta mountain victory was a breakthrough for his squad, marking its first Grand Tour stage win.

title: The Irish Times view on third-level funding: the shortfall remains
description: In 2022, Simon Harris accepted that there was an annual gap of €307m
content:
Linda Doyle, the provost of Trinity College Dublin, took the unusual step for someone in her position of rebuking the Government, via a social media post a few days before the budget for the parlous financial state of Irish universities amid buoyant exchequer returns.
It is important to note that the Government was besieged with funding requests from every sector in advance of the budget and it is not possible to placate every interest group. But the hallmark of any good budget process is that it invests in the productive capacity of the economy in order to create a solid platform for future growth. In this regard, Budget 2027 leaves questions hanging in a few key areas. Third-level education is one of them.
The Government’s approach to funding the third level sector is contradictory and short-sighted. Its ambition is to make Ireland a high-tech knowledge economy that not only produces the talent needed for the multinational sector but also provides a foundation for a healthy domestic sector. Well-funded universities and other third-level institutions are a crucial component of this ecosystem.
Third-level fees were scrapped in 1996 as part of sweeping reforms. The Irish economy was taking off so sufficient tax revenues were available to invest in the third-level sector. But when the economy crashed in 2008, funding fell precipitously.
In the intervening years, successive governments have commissioned reports on how to solve the funding gap. Among the recommendations have been the reintroduction of fees along with a student loan system. Since each option carries political risks, governments have repeatedly deferred much-needed reforms in favour of fee relief for students and parents.
In 2022, Simon Harris, the then minister for Higher Education, accepted that there was an annual funding gap of €307m and pledged to close it by the end of this decade.
The Irish University Association estimate that the gap at the start of this week was €250m on the back of unfunded growth in student numbers and unfunded pay awards and that Budget 2027 delivered only €10m in core new funding. This has left some institutions looking for cutbacks.
Ireland is close to the bottom among EU member states in investment in third-level education.
Doyle concluded her social media post last week with a pithy observation: “We have such ambition but ambition without investment is just a daydream.” Universities have a responsibility, too, to manage their resources more effectively. But the Government would be well advised to take heed of the increasingly desperate calls from the sector and to focus both on affordability and on the provision of the highest level of education possible.

title: The Irish Times view on US executions: a barbaric practice
description: Last year 23 individuals were sentenced to death, joining some 2,000 on death row
content:
Could the state of Tennessee, having twice botched the execution of Christa Pike, then assiduously revived her, handcuffed to her hospital bed, now try once more to put her to death? Quite possibly. Although the governor has put a temporary halt on state executions, he has refused to be drawn on Pike’s fate, hoping perhaps that her parlous medical condition will make his decision for him.
Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for governor in next month’s election, says simply they should abandon drug injections and bring back the electric chair.
Yet, despite near universal abhorrence at the botched attempts to kill Pike with two lethal doses of pentobarbital, the US death penalty machine rolls on. On Wednesday Texas executed Jamaal Howard (46), the 30th US death row inmate to die this year. And on Monday, Donald Trump approved the execution by firing squad of soldier Nidal Hasan, who in 2009 killed 13 of his colleagues at Fort Hood, Texas.
The US is among the 17 countries still carrying out the death penalty. Twenty-seven US states retain it on their books, although only 16, plus the federal government, have carried out an execution in the past decade. Last year 23 individuals were sentenced to death, joining some 2,000 on death row, many of them, like Pike, there for as long as 30 years.
The number of Americans who find the death penalty morally acceptable has declined to 52 per cent. For the last several decades, abolitionists have made progress in changing the national conversation by moving from arguments about morality to focus on frequent miscarriages of justice, false convictions, racial discrimination in sentencing, and the cruelty inherent in the process itself as well as that inflicted in botched executions. One study estimated that 276, or 3.15 per cent, of the 8,776 executions carried out from 1890 to 2010 were botched. And since 1973, at least 203 people wrongly convicted and sentenced to death have been exonerated.

title: Jim O’Callaghan dismisses claims of Garda ‘resignation crisis’
description: Jim O’Callaghan and Garda Representative Association clash over recruitment and retention of Garda members
content:
The strength of the Garda force is about to reach record levels, despite claims for years from the Garda Representative Association (GRA) that resignations and retirements are at crisis levels, Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan has said.
He has also dismissed suggestions the expected all-time peak in Garda numbers, from 14,500 at present to 15,000 in the coming months, will prove very brief and will be almost immediately followed by a surge in age-related retirements that could continue for about a decade.
During that period, according to the Garda’s own projections, the number of gardaí who will reach compulsory retirement age in any one year is set to increase 10-fold.
The GRA, which represents more than 11,000 rank and file gardaí, said while there was provision made in the budget for recruiting up to 1,000 additional gardaí next year, in the first nine months of this year some 400 members had retired or resigned. But O’Callaghan has insisted recruitment is far ahead of retirements or resignations.
“The number of resignations from An Garda Síochána is extraordinarily low, if you look at the PSNI, or any of the police forces in the UK,” O’Callaghan said in a budget event in Dublin on Thursday, insisting that, despite claims to the contrary, the Garda force does not have a resignations problem.
“(Garda resignations) are at about 1 per cent, 140 resignations a year. And, talking to the Garda Commissioner, he tells me that many people who resign come back, and they can be fast-tracked back in.”
He added Garda recruitment was “going well”, with classes of 200 or more now passing out regularly at the Garda College, Templemore, Co Tipperary, and he hoped there could be five such passing out ceremonies per year.
“It’s a great job and a lot of people now realise they want to do a job that doesn’t involve sending and receiving emails all day. And if you become a garda, you’re not doing that,” he said.
[ Garda retirements set to surge in ‘ticking time-bomb’, projections show Opens in new window ]
O’Callaghan added retirements from the Garda were “inevitable”. However, he regularly approved extensions of service for members who had reached 62 years, the compulsory age of retirement, but had applied for special permission to continue working for an extra one or two years.
GRA general secretary Ronan Slevin said successive governments had made the same budget promises to increase the Garda by 1,000 members the following year, with minimal impact.
“We presented the Government with a six-point plan suggesting how we could solve a recruitment and retention crisis but have been ignored,” he said.
“We are now on the eve of national pay talks and we still haven’t been told if we will even be in the room when our financial futures are being shaped.
“As of this week, almost 400 gardaí have left the job in 2026 through resignations and retirements, and this number will only get higher by the end of the year.
“The sheer lack of direct engagement by Minister Chambers and his department with the elected members of the GRA has been, for us, disappointing, disingenuous and almost disrespectful.”
The retirement age for Garda members was last year increased from 60 to 62. This had the effect of postponing the start of a projected decade-long retirement spike.
[ Some gardaí working until age 64 for the first time in history of force Opens in new window ]
For example, the latest projections by Garda Headquarters show that next year and the year after, the number of Garda members who will reach compulsory retirement age is 37 and 49. However, that is then set to increase every year, for the next decade and will reach 373 by 2035, a ten-fold increase.
Furthermore, the retirement spike will probably start sooner, and worsen more quickly than Garda Headquarters’ projections. This is because the projections are based on all Garda members continuing to work until they are aged 62 years.
In reality, many serving members have a full pension once they reach 30 years service and can retire at any point after they reach the age of 50 years.

title: Cillian O’Connor gets the ending he deserved to one of the greatest careers in GAA history
description: The championship’s all-time leading scorer wasn’t content to pile up the numbers – his belligerence typified Mayo’s refusal to bend the knee
content:
Y ou have to hand it to the lads on Reservoir Dubs – they were never going to let Cillian O’Connor sail off into the sunset without launching some cannon fire over his head. His retirement was always going to be a triggering event to one or two denizens of the Dublin GAA supporters’ online forum. In fairness, they were pretty balanced in their tributes. They made sure to send a few scuds in Aidan O’Shea’s direction too.
“Must have saw the writing on the wall…” “Got his medal as a panellist…” “Elbows O’Connor…” “Never had the guts to take the hits to get the crucial scores…” “Big Aido will probably keep going... Will play the odd league game and then phased out again…”
Now, some will say that’s small and petty. Not just of them but of us too. That an appreciation of Gaelic football ’s all-time leading scorer deserves better than to be giving airtime to fellas still fighting the last decade’s wars deep into 2026. But to ignore them would be to ignore a fundamental truth about one of the all-time greats of the game.
Namely, that in the years that Jim Gavin’s Dubs rolled across the championship plains like Panzer tanks, nobody was a bigger pain in their ass than Cillian O’Connor. This was very important – and not just for Mayo . At a time when other teams all but laid their coats down over puddles so Jack and Con and Mannion wouldn’t get their feet wet, O’Connor typified Mayo’s refusal to play nice and usher them up the Hogan Stand steps.
He did so in two distinct and crucial ways. One, by putting more goals and points on the scoreboard than anybody else, ever. As Rob Carroll, of the brilliant Gaelic Stats website has pointed out, O’Connor is by a distance the highest scorer in championship matches against Dublin this century. He has scored more against Dublin (2-65 in 11 matches) than David Clifford and Colm Cooper combined (3-48 in 12 matches).
And two, by being the sort of cranky, belligerent antagonist that the Dubs just didn’t come across most of the time. For all his forensic coolness when tasked with putting the ball between the posts, O’Connor was chippy as hell and never shied away from the darker alleys of the game. He could have spent his time diligently accumulating scores and leaving the rough stuff to the bigger horses out the pitch. That was never him.
He retires 98 points clear of Michael Murphy at the top of the all-time scoring charts, having run up a monumental 32-364 (460 points). All things being equal, David Clifford (29-272, or 359) will likely pass him in the next couple of seasons and you’d back Seán O’Shea (7-261, or 282) to make his way up towards O’Connor’s total around the turn of the decade. But everyone else is a mile back the road and even in a world of two-pointers (and potentially four-point goals), the wider peloton has a lot of climbing to do before they can see him on the horizon.
The gas thing is it could have been more. O’Connor kicked precisely one two-pointer in intercounty football and it came in this year’s league when he was brought on as a sub against Roscommon. More to the point, the vast majority of his championship scoring was done long before he finally called it a day.
