He has scored just 2-27 since the 2020 All-Ireland final. Incredibly, his last championship score from a free came in the 2022 All-Ireland quarter-final against Kerry. If you want to really break it down, around 93 per cent of his total scores for Mayo came before his 29th birthday. Imagine where his numbers would be had he stayed healthy.
[ For the average GAA player, this time of the year brings a mix of regret and relief Opens in new window ]
But your story can only be what it can only be. Had O’Connor been fit and firing through the back end of his career, what would have happened to Ryan O’Donoghue’s development? A couple of days after O’Connor did his Achilles against Clare in the league in 2021, O’Donoghue went to James Horan and touted for the role of team free-taker. He was only in his second season on the panel and the likes of Conor Loftus had deputised for O’Connor in the past. But O’Donoghue grabbed the job and made it his.
Five years later, look what happened. O’Donoghue, himself a fairly spiky and bellicose individual, driven by his own All-Ireland final heartache, led Mayo to the All-Ireland O’Connor and his generation had lived and died for. Anyone who met O’Connor that day in Croke Park or in the weeks and months since were left in no doubt that missing out on being on the pitch didn’t lessen his enjoyment one jot. He earned his All-Ireland medal.
Aidan O’Shea made an acute observation in the hotel the day after Mayo won, something to the effect that anytime RTÉ showed an end-of-season montage, there was always a shot of himself or O’Connor, down on their knees or in tears. That’s all gone now. Six weeks later, O’Connor got married in Mount Juliet and had to find room in the table plan for Sam Maguire.
A fitting grace note to one of the greatest careers in the history of the GAA.

title: Plane billows smoke at Riyadh airport as Houthis escalate attacks on Saudi Arabia
description: Lufthansa and Air India to suspend flights to Riyadh after ​Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
content:
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis escalated their campaign of strikes against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, trying to shut down the kingdom’s airspace and oil facilities with missile fire that has killed three people this week.
The group said it had ‌struck Riyadh airport, where witnesses saw smoke billowing from a plane, and it warned workers to stay away from energy plants. Saudi officials said debris from an intercepted missile had hit a kindergarten and medical complex.
Lufthansa and Air India said they were suspending flights to Riyadh after ​Houthi attacks.
The Houthis say they are targeting the kingdom over its support for government forces in Yemen’s reignited civil war. Saudi Arabia says it is backing an offensive by Yemen’s UN-recognised government to take back territory from the Houthis.
The conflict, now an overspill of the US-Iran war , has added new chaos to a region already aflame, and threatens to draw other states into gruelling mountain fighting – with Syria now considering deploying troops to assist Saudi Arabia.
The kingdom has pushed for support from allied nations, including Turkey and Pakistan, even if only in a ​logistical or defensive capacity, as it tries to reverse Houthi gains in southwest Yemen, by the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
Those requests have taken on more urgency since Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people had been killed this week in strikes on Riyadh airport and ⁠Abha airport in the southwest.
The Houthis have made Saudi airports a focus of their strikes, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said it had destroyed two ballistic ‌missiles ‌launched ​by the group towards Riyadh and another towards Khamis Mushayt, home to a major airbase.
[ How Iran has adapted its missile war and given the US a strategic dilemma Opens in new window ]
A thick black column of smoke and flames were shown rising from Riyadh airport in video verified by Reuters. A witness and three people briefed on the matter said a commercial plane had caught fire and was the cause of the smoke.
There was no immediate confirmation ​from Saudi authorities on the Houthi claims of ballistic missile attacks on Riyadh airport and the cause of the smoke billowing from the plane was not immediately clear, though people briefed on the matter said the fire had been put ‌out.
However, the flight tracker Flightradar24 indicated numerous delayed arrivals and departures at Riyadh’s King ​Khalid International Airport on Thursday. The airport advised travellers to contact airlines to check the status of flights before trying to travel.
Saudi authorities said debris from an intercepted Houthi missile had landed in Riyadh, causing damage to ⁠a kindergarten and a medical clinic complex, state media reported.
Riyadh is due to host a ⁠major meeting of energy policymakers, the WPC Energy Congress, ​this week.
Several multinational firms based in Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) told staff to work from home after loud booms were heard on Thursday morning, five people familiar with the matter said, including some affected staff.
The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment, and KAFD was not immediately available for comment.
[ Three killed and more than 30 injured in attacks on two Saudi airports, aviation authorities say Opens in new window ]
Some diplomats said they had received warnings, and some schools in Riyadh told parents there were orders to shelter in place, though authorities did not issue a public alert. Reuters could not identify the source of the booms.
The Houthis also warned workers to stay away from oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, saying they would be targeted.
Yemen’s long-running civil war, which paused with a ceasefire in 2022, has erupted again in recent weeks with the Houthis seizing stretches of the Red Sea coast last month, including along the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthis have said they were responding to attacks from the Saudi-backed government, which the government denies.
Their threats to shipping and attacks on Saudi cities and infrastructure have drawn ‌the kingdom back in. This week, Saudi-backed forces launched ⁠a counterattack, taking back areas around the strait.
However, in a war with several front lines, the Houthis have made gains of their own, surrounding Yemen’s third-largest city, Taiz, by taking territory along its main mountain road to Aden.
The fighting, which pits the Houthis against a coalition of Saudi-backed forces under the internationally recognised government, has led to a humanitarian crisis in the poorest Arab state, ‌displacing 200,000 people since the conflict resumed.
One US and one Syrian defence official said Syria was carefully considering options for military support, including defensive aid to protect Saudi Arabia from attacks, or an offensive deployment to help take the fight ​to the Houthis.
In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia but that ​its focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from its own civil war.
Nato-member Turkey said on Wednesday it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom to help in the fight against the Houthis. A Turkish official said this was expected to take the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems. – Reuters

title: Russian bomb attack kills dozens at Ukraine bus stop
description: At least 30 die after aerial strike hits two passenger buses in frontline city of Kramatorsk
content:
A Russian glide bomb killed dozens of Ukrainians at a bus stop in the eastern city of Kramatorsk on Thursday, in one of the deadliest attacks on civilians in recent months.
Two buses were hit by the bomb during rush hour, killing at least 30 people and injuring 18, according to Ukraine’s state emergency service. A separate attack nearby killed another three people, authorities said.
“Some of those killed have still not been identified because of the severity of their injuries,” Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskiy said. Many of those injured in the attack were fighting for their lives, he said, warning that the death toll may rise.
The strike came after Zelenskiy told the Financial Times last week that Vladimir Putin had instructed his generals to abandon all rules of war in Ukraine . Deliberately targeting civilians is considered a war crime under international law.
Russia has used aerial bombs since its full-scale invasion in 2022, launching them from behind the front line to destroy entire buildings.
“Russia is systematically destroying Kramatorsk and terrorising civilians,” Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian parliament’s commissioner for human rights, wrote on X.
Regional governor Vadym Filashkin said in a post on Telegram that the victims “are not ‘the consequences of war’, nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army.”
He said public transport in Kramatorsk and the neighbouring city of Slovyansk had been suspended because of the threat of Russian attacks.
The bus-stop bombing came a day after a wave of Russian missiles and drones killed at least 28 people across Ukraine, including 22 in an attack on an apartment building in Pryluky, about 150km east of Kyiv.
The building suffered a direct hit from a Russian missile, burying residents beneath debris. Dozens of injured people were pulled out by rescuers – as were the lifeless bodies of four children. In Kyiv, three people were killed in Wednesday’s strikes, the capital’s mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The combined death toll from Russian strikes over the past day and a half has risen to at least 64 people.
[ Zelenskiy says ‘despicable’ Russian bombing was birthday gift for Putin Opens in new window ]
On Thursday, sirens howled throughout Kyiv as explosions from Russian drone strikes and Ukrainian air defence interceptions shook the city’s buildings. A blanket of dense black smoke was visible over the capital around midday.
DTEK, Ukraine’s largest energy operator, said it had imposed power cuts in Kyiv and the surrounding region after Russian strikes hit its energy facilities for a second straight day.
Zelenskiy said Putin was also increasing his attacks on civilians because the Russian army had failed to achieve its military goals on the battlefield.
Ukrainian forces have made gains along the eastern frontline in the Donbas in recent weeks, thwarting Russian efforts to encircle Kramatorsk and nearby cities that make up Ukraine’s “fortress belt”, according to military analysts who track the war.
“Over the month of September, the Russian net gains were negative 190sq km,” the Finland-based Black Bird Group, which tracks the war, reported last week. “This marks the greatest monthly net territorial loss for Russia in our data set since the June of 2023.”
Zelenskiy said last week the counteroffensive, dubbed Operation Vivaldi, had liberated some 125-140sq km of territory.
Putin has demanded that Ukraine give up the remaining 25 per cent of the Donbas region still under its control to even begin peace talks. US president Donald Trump and his special envoy Steve Witkoff have also pushed Kyiv to hand over the land in order to bring Putin back to the negotiating table.
But Zelenskiy has insisted that territorial concessions are a red line for Kyiv and said giving the Donbas to Russia would only aid Putin’s army in its broader goal of launching attacks deeper inside Ukraine to bring it to heel. Ukrainian polling throughout the war has supported his stance.
On Thursday, while visiting Pryluky with UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband, Zelenskiy said his negotiating team would travel this week to the US to meet Trump’s team to discuss strategy around peace negotiations. The Ukrainian leader also called on the US to increase pressure on Putin to end his war. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Top o’ the mornin’ to ya: Frank McNally on a piece of Route 66 that is forever Irish
description: Details of how the town of Shamrock acquired its name are somewhat obscured
content:
N ear the halfway point of Route 66 – the US “Mother Road”, which will be a century old next month, at least in name – is a town called Shamrock.
It’s not mentioned in the eponymous song, unlike Amarillo, Flagstaff, Winona and many other places where it’s said you can get your “kicks” on the journey from Chicago to Los Angeles.
But it does have one of the route’s classic buildings, constructed in the art deco style that became visually synonymous with the route’s glory days.
The U-Drop Inn was built in 1936 as a cafe and filling station servicing motorists on the increasingly busy road. Closed in the 1990s, it was then restored as a museum and visitor centre.
And when Pixar eulogised Route 66 in its 2006 animated movie Cars, set in the fictional Radiator Springs, the town’s garage bore the U-Drop Inn’s unmistakable outline.
Details of how Shamrock acquired its name are now somewhat obscured by the mists of history, American style.
It was so christened in the 1890s by a man named variously as George Nickle or Nichol(s) who, in some accounts, was an Irish emigrant and, in others, just had a mother from here.
Either way, according to the Texas State Historical Association, he won permission to open a post-office in his home (described by the TSHA as a “dug-out”). And since the postal system required a place name, he chose Shamrock “for good luck and courage”.
However, that post office never opened because, with the luck of the Irish, George’s home burned down. Then another man opened a post office and called it “Exum”, his own surname. But when the Rock Island Railroad came through here, circa 1903, it overruled that and called the stop Shamrock.
[ Strong words: America’s ‘greatest diarist’ whose many dislikes included the Irish Opens in new window ]
Thus, before the famous road, the town owed its existence to a famous railway: the “Rock Island Line”, also celebrated in song.
Other hamlets in the area included one called Story. That, aptly, was home to the local newspaper, the Wheeler County Texan. But the paper relocated in 1928 to become the Shamrock Texan (Story seems to have been buried in the process) and further secure the town’s place on the map.
Tenuous as its links with Ireland may be, Shamrock claims to have a piece of the Blarney Stone set into a column in a local park. The plaque says it was “imported & erected in 1959” and officially dedicated on St Patrick’s Day of that year.
The town is not unique in the US, or even in Texas, for purporting to have such a relic. Texas Tech University, in Lubbock, claims to have a bit of the stone too. And such is the hold the Blarney myth has on American imaginations; there have been attempts elsewhere in the US down the decades to buy the whole thing.
Anyway, inspired by its own supposed share, Shamrock greets visitors with a sign saying: “Top o’ the mornin’ to ya!” It also has a local college football team that, like a more famous one in South Bend, Indiana, calls itself the “Fighting Irish”.
Mind you, by one recent count, there are 52 US college football teams that style themselves “Fighting Irish”, “Fightin’ Irish”, or just “Irish”. Maybe Ireland should seek Unesco intangible heritage list protection for its reputation in this sphere. Or maybe not.
[ Dance to the Music of Time – Frank McNally on a forgotten Irish-American revolutionary Opens in new window ]
The exact midway point of Route 66 is in a township called Adrian, about 140 miles west of Shamrock, on the other side of Amarillo. There, a sign points to the opposite destinations of Chicago and LA and informs you that both are 1,139 miles away. The official midpoint is also marked with a white line across the road, much photographed by passers-by.
Adrian’s slogan recognises the town’s essential transience: “When you’re here, you’re halfway there”. Not many people are “here” permanently. At the last census, the population was 128.
Route 66 was itself always a transient phenomenon, continually changing. The imminent centenary is of the adoption on November 11th, 1926, of a uniform highway numbering system, replacing the former patchwork of unconnected roads and trails.
That became a promotional opportunity for places along the route and, at first, even numbers were considered most prestigious. The “Mother Road”, as John Steinbeck would immortalise it in The Grapes of Wrath, would have been Route 60 if an early promoter had had his way.
Route 62 was then briefly considered. But even after the road acquired its now celebrated number, it was another 12 years before it became fully connected and paved from end to end.
That was just in time for Steinbeck’s Dust Bowl epic, set on the section between Oklahoma and California. The “kicks” song, recorded by Nat King Cole and many others after him, came a decade later.
But by the 1950s, Route 66 was already being bypassed by bigger, faster highways. It was officially decommissioned in 1985, before undergoing revival as a heritage attraction. On many surviving stretches, identifying markers must now be painted on the road itself, thanks to the popularity of detachable signs as souvenirs.

title: Opposition parties ‘will not’ cross picket lines if Leinster House staff strike next week
description: Government Chief Whip says Dáil ‘must’ sit on Wednesday, the day earmarked for public sector strike
content:
Opposition parties have said they will not cross any picket line at Leinster House next week if staff go on strike along with other public sector workers on Wednesday.
A row over the form talks on a new public sector pay deal should take has seen unions start industrial action, with more than 100,000 members involved in work-to-rule measures. Wednesday, October 14th, has been earmarked for strike action by teachers and other public sector workers.
Oireachtas authorities are not expected to learn whether the unions will grant a derogation from potential strike action by Leinster House staff so that Dáil proceedings can proceed until Friday evening.
The prospect of such industrial action impacting on business in the Oireachtas next week was discussed at a meeting of the Dáil’s Business Committee on Thursday.
Government Chief Whip, Minister of State Mary Butler, set out the Coalition’s position that the Dáil should sit on the usual three days next week.
[ The Irish Times view on public sector pay: time to sit down and talk Opens in new window ]
However, Opposition parties warned they will not cross a picket line at Leinster House next Wednesday.
The committee is due to meet again on Monday to consider the matter once the Oireachtas hears back from the unions involved.
Sinn Féin chief whip Pádraig Mac Lochlainn told The Irish Times that he has made it clear to the Government that “Sinn Féin TDs and staff will not be walking past our fellow workers in Leinster House who are picketing, if that’s what goes ahead that day.”
Social Democrats TD Cian O’Callaghan also said his party is “supporting the public sector worker’s industrial action and we will not be crossing the picket line if Oireachtas staff are on strike next Wednesday”.
Labour Party whip Duncan Smith said: “We’re expecting a picket outside Leinster House on Wednesday morning and we in the Labour Party won’t be crossing it.”
Richard Boyd Barrett of People Before Profit also said his party would not pass any picket at Leinster House but said it would be “a different matter” if striking workers want the politicians to go in “if they felt it was to their benefit”.
Boyd Barrett added: “I would only do that if I heard that directly from workers.”
[ Budget 2027 falls short of preventing public sector industrial action, say unions Opens in new window ]
The Green Party also confirmed its politicians and staff would not cross a picket line at Leinster House next week.
A spokesman for Butler said: “The issue is under discussion between the whips and the Houses of the Oireachtas service and they have been dealing with it at the Business Committee today and will continue engagement over the coming days.
“The Government Chief Whip, Minister Mary Butler, made it clear at the business committee today that Dáil Éireann must sit Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday next week.”

title: Shane Lowry makes solid start to Spanish Open in Madrid
description: On the Ladies European Tour, Lauren Walsh is the best of the Irish in Korea
content:
Shane Lowry has made a solid start to the Spanish Open after a one-under-par opening round of 70 at Real Club de Campo Villa de Madrid.
The Irishman, who is fourth in the European Ryder Cup standings after victory at the Irish Open last month, took advantage of the par 5s with three birdies and another birdie from eight feet at the 16th after a fine approach.
Lowry dropped shots at the third, eighth and 13th holes, but is four shots off the leaders on five under, a trio of Spain’s Eugenio Chacarra and Scots Connor Syme and Grant Forrest. Tom McKibbin shot a one-over-par 72 on day one of the DP World Tour event.
Lowry had enjoyed two weeks off which he said he celebrated the win in Doonbeg with his family, and is now playing in four of the final five events of the DP World Tour season, heading to India next week, as he targets significant points to consolidate his place on the team for Adare Manor next September.
Chacarra, a two-time winner on Tour this season, is playing through the pain barrier having fractured his toe and said after his round he had not decided if he would tee it up for the second round.
“It’s not good,” Chacarra said. “I suffered a lot from the 16th hole and it’s been tough. It’s a struggle.
“It doesn’t hurt when I swing, that’s the only good thing. It’s why I can still make a score, but it’s been really tough to walk.
“The pain I had on the last 12 holes, I don’t know if it is worth it as I have a lot to play the next couple of weeks. I’ve got 24 hours to rest and see how it feels in the morning.”
One shot off the lead is Sergio Garcia, who said he has not ruled out future involvement with LIV but his focus is on qualifying for the Ryder Cup.
The record points scorer in the event, the 46-year-old has not represented Europe since 2021, but has told captain Luke Donald that he would like to be involved in Limerick.
“I told [Donald] that I’m going to do everything ⁠possible to see if I can get into that ⁠team and I also told ​him that if I don’t get into that team, I’ll help in any way I can.”
On the HotelPlanner Tour, Liam Nolan shot a five-under-par 67 to lie tied-seventh after the opening round of the Hainan Open, five shots behind leader Joseba Torres as he chases one of 15 available DP World Tour cards for next season. Nolan is currently 12th after winning in Abu Dhabi last week.
On the Ladies European Tour, Lauren Walsh is the best of the Irish after the opening round at the Aramco Korea Championship on two under, five shots behind leader Patricie Mackova. Sara Byrne and Anna Foster are on even par, while Áine Donegan had a day to forget, shooting an eight-over-par 80.

title: Triple murder accused told gardaí he only meant to kill father and brother, not mother, court hears
description: Robert O’Connor (32) told gardaí he was ‘not sorry’ for two killings, including special needs brother
content:
A man (32) accused of murdering three members of his family at their Co Louth home last year told gardaí that he only meant to kill his father and brother, but not his mother.
Roisin Lacey, barrister for the Director of Public Prosecutions, said in her opening speech on Thursday that the accused told gardaí he had a row over drugs and lost his head, killing his parents and his brother with special needs.
When re-arraigned before the Central Criminal Court on Thursday afternoon, Robert O’Connor, of Drumgowna, Louth Village, Dundalk, Co Louth, pleaded not guilty of murder by reason of insanity or guilty of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility to the triple murder of his mother Louise O’Connor, his father Mark O’Connor and his younger brother Evan O’Connor at their home in Drumgowna between September 28th and 29th, 2025, both dates inclusive.
Opening the prosecution’s case, Lacey said the accused, Robert O’Connor, accepted he caused the death of the three victims in the case.
Referring to the accused man’s younger brother, Evan O’Connor, Lacey said he had very significant special needs, was severely autistic and had learning difficulties.
Counsel said a carer had arrived at Drumgowna on the morning of September 29th when she saw the heavily bloodstained body of Mark O’Connor inside the front gate of the house. When the carer looked across at the house, she saw Evan’s body lying across the step of the patio door with blood on the bottom of his legs.
The jury will hear that the carer got back into the car and drove to a neighbour’s house, where she called 999 at 9.38am that morning. Gardaí and members of the Armed Support Unit arrived at Drumgowna later that morning.
Lacey said the evidence would be that beside Mark O’Connor’s body was a beer bottle, an orange kitchen knife and a butter knife. The lawyer told the jurors that when gardaí entered the house sometime later, they saw Louise O’Connor’s body “equally heavily bloodstained” on the kitchen floor.
Counsel said the jury would hear evidence from a neighbour who would say he recognised the accused man’s voice coming from the O’Connor household on the night of September 28th saying: “I’ll end you, I’ll f**king end you.”
Lacey said that when the accused was arrested on suspicion of killing his parents and brother he told gardaí: “I killed them; I killed my mother, father and my brother.” The accused man also told detectives: “I slashed my mother, she gave me a look and I could see a reflection of my dad in her face”.
When asked why he had killed the three members of his family, counsel said Robert O’Connor told gardaí he had a row over drugs, only meant to kill his father and brother, but not his mother and had “lost my head”.
The accused man also told gardaí he had stabbed his brother Evan like a “blood bag”.
Lacey said when the accused was in the back of a Garda car, he said he was “not sorry for his father or brother” but was sorry for stabbing his mother to death.
Counsel said the jury would hear that the accused told gardaí he had been using cocaine lately and had bought some “Wildcat”, which counsel said was a slang word for mephedrone and was an amphetamine. Lacey said the evidence would be that the accused told gardaí his parents had wanted to speak to him about his drug consumption but Robert O’Connor had told them he did not want to stop taking cocaine.
There will be evidence that gardaí had seen the accused on foot walking in the direction of Tallanstown that morning. When they stopped the accused, he was highly aggressive and agitated and shouted at them: “I’m looking for ye.”
When gardai asked the accused to show them his hands, he refused and shouted: “Shoot me, shoot me.” The accused’s hands were blood-stained at the time, the court heard.
Counsel said the jury would hear that Mark O’Connor had 44 stab wounds, with nine of those to his head; that Louise O’Connor suffered 20 stab wounds, with eight to her trunk, while Evan O’Connor had 75 stab wounds, with 25 of those to his head and neck.
Lacey will continue her opening speech on Friday before Judge Mícheál P O’Higgins and a jury of six men and six women. The trial is expected to last until October 30th.

title: ‘It’s ruined, tens of thousands in damage’: Outcry after Limerick house trashed amid student party
description: Walls and ceilings were knocked through, fixtures and fittings torn down, while shelving unit thrown through window
content:
The interim provost of the University of Limerick (UL) has written to students lamenting the reputational damage to the college after a break-in and serious criminal damage to a house was linked to a student party.
Gardaí are investigating the incident at a refurbished vacant house in College Court in the heartland of the university’s off-campus accommodation in the early hours of Wednesday.
Videos showing young people running amok in the house were shared on social media . Walls and ceilings were knocked through and fixtures and fittings were torn down.
One video showed young people throwing a shelving unit through a window. The video showed a group screaming and laughing as more damage was caused to the property.
A spokeswoman at UL said on Thursday the identities of those involved in the incident had not been established.
However, Ann Ledwith, who is deputy president and interim provost, wrote to students on Thursday and said she was “deeply concerned” at the incident.
She said “antisocial behaviour not only damages property, but it also damages our reputation and our valued community relationships”.
“University of Limerick treats all complaints concerning individuals with the utmost seriousness,” she said.
“While the identity of those involved in the incident has yet to be ascertained, let me be very clear – this sort of behaviour is simply unacceptable from any member of our community.
“Acts of antisocial behaviour, including property damage, public disorder and other actions that impact negatively upon local residents and landlords are a matter of very serious concern.”
Ledwith urged students to remember they were expected to “act as an ambassador for UL, both on and off campus, and ensure that your actions reflect positively on our community”.
Walls and ceilings were torn down in the property. At one point during the video footage, the camera is pointed up at a ceiling on the first floor, revealing no ceiling but a gaping void into the attic and roofing joists.
The first floor of the six-bedroom property was also littered with what appeared to be attic and wall insulation, and fixtures and fittings in an upstairs bathroom were also destroyed.
Videos also showed mattresses thrown on to the garden and used as landing mats by students who also filmed themselves jumping off the roof.
Ledwith reminded students of the Garda’s appeal for information, and included the Garda contact details in her email.
[ Walls, windows and ceilings of Limerick house destroyed during ‘student party’ Opens in new window ]
Eric Nelligan, a secondary school assistant principal, who lives nearby, posted on X: “My kitchen window looks on the entrance of this estate, it’s carnage in there, most traditional residents have moved out ... College Court is notorious.
“What would possess college students to do this? The house is ruined, tens of thousands in damage.”
The two-storey house was recently sold after it was advertised as a vacant possession with a guide price of almost €445,000, and according to local sources, it had been in “turnkey” condition before last Wednesday.
The property was advertised online by Rooney Auctioneers, Limerick, as having an “easily accessible pedestrian entrance to the nearby University campus, and a much sought-after location for student accommodation”.
“Investors will be drawn to a lucrative investment opportunity with proximity to the University of Limerick, with superb rental potential,” added the property pitch.
It’s understood investigating gardaí are following a definite line of inquiry, as several of the perpetrators of last Wednesday’s break-in and damage were clearly identifiable in video footage circulated on social media.

title: Elon Musk’s ‘X’ loses High Court challenge over Irish regulator’s handling of complaints
description: X argued that Coimisiún na Meán was acting beyond its powers
content:
Elon Musk ’s X , formerly known as Twitter, has failed in a High Court bid challenging how the Irish media regulator, Comisiún na Meán , deals with user complaints against social media platforms.
On Thursday, Judge Cian Ferriter ruled that the commission is entitled under law to refer information from complaints made under the Digital Services Act to a “supervisory” unit, which also has the power to retain those complaints to identify possible future compliance issues.
X had submitted that the commission could not legally refer information garnered from complaints to the supervision team if those complaints were already concluded or undetermined. They also submitted that information contained within those complaints could not be used for broader, future systemic investigations and that the regulator had therefore acted outside of the law.
X further submitted that it regularly takes “unilateral” removal action, such as in cases of child exploitation, which it is obligated to do by its own regulatory policies. The company submitted that the commission was acting in an “extra statutory” manner.
X had argued that complainants were entitled to an outcome instead of the commission “kicking the can down the road without notification” on any possible future purported breaches.
David Fennelly, senior counsel for the regulator, had said that X was attempting to undermine the watchdog’s important role in cases that had implications across the EU.
The judge said in his judgment that the commission has discretion as to who investigates complaints, adding: “In the circumstances, I do not believe it can be said that the commission improperly disabled itself from exercising its statutory discretion by reference to any of the matters available to it.”
The judge said there was no “improper fettering of discretion involved and no legally impermissible steps on the part of the Commission or its delegates”.

title: Man (68) suspected of raping woman twice in her south Dublin home in 2003 is charged
description: Accused suspected of rape, false imprisonment and burglary after posing as a TV technician
content:
A man suspected of raping a woman twice in her own home while posing as a TV technician investigating faults in the area more than 20 years ago has been charged and has appeared before court.
The accused, a 68-year-old Irishman based in Dublin, was arrested in Dublin on Wednesday and was detained for questioning before being charged and being brought before Dublin District Court on Thursday evening.
He is charged with two counts of rape, one court of false imprisonment and one count of aggravated burglary, all arising from an attack on a woman, then in her 30s, in her own home in a housing estate in south Dublin in March 2003.
Dressed in a blue sweatshirt and grey tracksuit bottoms, the accused, who cannot be named under court rules covering sexual crime cases, spoke only to say “thank you, judge” at the end of the brief appearance.
The accused man was led away by prison officers after being remanded in custody to Cloverhill Prison, Dublin, pending his next court appearance next Monday.
His arrest followed a Garda investigation into the attack on the morning of March 31st, 2003, during which the victim was allegedly sexually attacked in an ordeal that lasted a long time.
The State now alleges the man arrested for questioning on Wednesday, and who has now appeared before the courts, was the attacker on the day, though no findings have been reached. The accused would have been aged about 45 years at the time.
Gardaí said an extensive investigation took place in 2003, with “hundreds of investigative jobs undertaken and over 100 statements taken”.
The investigation had remained open despite the passage of more than 23 years. In 2023, a Garda peer review of the inquiry was initiated by a new investigation team attached to the Garda’s Dublin Metropolitan Region East Serious Crime Unit under a senior investigating officer.
The work carried out on the case since then resulted in the suspect’s arrest and court appearance on Thursday before Judge Michelle Finan.
Det Insp Trevor Scanlon of the Protective Services Unit based at Dundrum Garda Station in south Dublin told the court sitting when the accused man was charged and caution at 3.50pm, he had replied “not guilty” as each of the four charges was put to him.
Solicitor Andrew Vallely, representing the accused man, said his client was reserving his right to apply for bail, with an application expected to be made as early as Monday. A statement of means was also requested linked to the accused’s application for free legal aid.
Vallely told the court his client had no specific medical needs that required attention in the prison setting. The accused man was remanded in custody to appear before the courts, in Dún Laoghaire, south Dublin, next Monday, October 12th.

title: Kingspan faces €40m fine for misleading EU regulators over abandoned deal for Slovenian rival
description: European Commission says Irish group provided misleading and incorrect information to mergers investigation
content:
Insulation maker Kingspan faces a €40 million fine for misleading European Commission competition regulators during their investigation of its bid for Slovenian rival, Trimo.
Kingspan ultimately dropped plans to buy the roofing and insulation materials manufacturer in 2022. The planned transaction had triggered a commission investigation into the deal’s potential impact on competition in several insulation panel markets.
The Commission has now fined Kingspan €40 million for providing “incorrect and misleading information” to its review of the Irish group’s bid for Trimo in 2021, a statement said on Thursday.
The Co Cavan-based multinational said it would appeal the ruling.
Kingspan misled the commission on how it tracks the use of mineral fibre sandwich boards, the insulation product made by both companies, against other insulation materials, the statement noted.
The Irish group provided incorrect or misleading information about the availability of bidding data, generally used to assess the competitiveness of a given industry, the Commission said.
It also provided incorrect or misleading information on research and development carried out by Kingspan into mineral fibre sandwich panels.
“This kind of information, which usually only the company itself can provide, is key to understanding a company’s position in the relevant market,” said the commission.
In addition, Kingspan gave incorrect or misleading information about its board members’ involvement in the planned acquisition of Trimo, other deals considered by Kingspan and industry trends and strategy, the commission added.
Kingspan gave the incorrect or misleading information to the commission in either its notification of the proposed acquisition of Trimo or in replies to requests for information under EU merger rules, according to the statement.
The commission has fined Kingspan €10 million for each of the four breaches of merger regulations that it identified.
The EU executive body said it considered Kingspan’s infringements serious as they obstructed the mergers investigation, making it difficult for the commission to properly review the transaction.
“It also considers that Kingspan could not have been unaware of its obligations under the EU merger regulation, meaning that the breach was at least negligent,” the commission said.
“In particular, the commission found that Kingspan asserted the non-existence of key documents, misrepresented facts, or claimed the impossibility to provide key information that only Kingspan was in a position to provide,” it added.
Kingspan responded that it noted the commission’s decision regarding a deal that it ultimately decided not to pursue.
“We look forward to appealing the decision in full,” the Irish group said.
Kingspan did not comment beyond that. But when the commission first questioned the information the company provided to the mergers investigation in March 2024, the group said that it had fully co-operated with the European authorities throughout the Trimo bid.
“This Trimo application was unusual and uniquely onerous given both the level of information sought and the fact that the process occurred during Covid,” Kingspan noted at the time.
“It is in no way representative of the long and productive relationship that Kingspan has with the European Commission.”
Kingspan pointed out that, by March 2024, the Commission had approved four other acquisitions completed by the Irish group since 2020 when it first bid for Trimo.
The European Commission routinely investigates mergers across member states to assess their potential impact on goods and services.

title: Man abused by ex-Terenure College teacher John McClean settles action
description: Case arose from historical sexual abuse ‘of the most significant and substantial type’, court heard
content:
A man who was abused by recidivist paedophile and ex-Terenure College teacher John McClean has settled a High Court action for an undisclosed sum.
Lawyers for Niall Walsh – who sued McClean, the school’s board and the Carmelites, the religious order that runs the school – told Judge Tony O’Connor on Thursday the case had been settled.
McClean (81) has previously been convicted at Dublin Circuit Criminal Court of abusing 49 boys at Terenure College. He is currently incarcerated, having formerly resided at Casimir Avenue, Harold’s Cross.
Siún Leonowicz, appearing for Walsh instructed by Coleman Legal, asked the judge to strike out the proceedings, with an order for her client’s legal costs against the school’s board and the Carmelites.
The court heard earlier this week that a case taken by another of McClean’s victims, Paul Kennedy, had settled following mediation for an undisclosed amount. It is understood to be a substantial six-figure sum.
Kennedy’s case arose from historical sexual abuse “of the most significant and substantial type”, occurring over a sustained period from the 1970s to the 1980s, the court was told previously.
Other High Court actions against McClean remain live.
McClean taught at Terenure College between 1966 and 1996, becoming first-year form master in 1980. He was also a rugby coach.
During the criminal prosecutions, the Circuit Court heard that McClean perpetrated the abuse mainly in his office, a windowless physiotherapy room, or in a room under the concert hall known as the smoking room, to which only he had a key.
Victims described how McClean, nicknamed Doc, would call boys into the physio room under the pretext of treating sports injuries, before sexually assaulting them.

title: Dublin 4 residents oppose new embassy in Ballsbridge due to fear of ‘protests’
description: Plans to convert 80 Northumberland Road, Ballsbridge into an embassy have stalled due to appeal
content:
A Dublin 4 residents association has opposed plans for a new embassy on Northumberland Road in Ballsbridge due, in part, to concerns that the new embassy may attract protests.
Last month, Dublin City Council granted planning permission to the Co Waterford-based Causeway Group to convert 80 Northumberland Road into an embassy.
The Causeway Group lodged the change of use planning application from “residential” to “embassy/office” after purchasing the red-bricked property built in the late 1800s for €2.25 million from charity MS Ireland in February of this year.
In granting planning for the change of use, the city council’s planner’s report stated that the embassy use “would be in keeping with the zoning objective of the site and would not detract from the residential amenities of the area”.
However, plans to convert the property into an embassy are now stalled after the Pembroke Road Association lodged an appeal against the grant for “this speculative planning application” with An Coimisíun Pleanala (ACP).
While the embassy at the centre of the plans is not named in the documents, it is understood to be Algeria’s embassy in Ireland.
In the appeal, chair of the residents association, Susan McCarrick told ACP “embassies do not, necessarily, make good neighbours, as they attract protests”.
She said the association refers specifically to the Israeli embassy which was at 122 Pembroke Road “and to the American embassy further down the road which is subject to daily protests”.
She said: “At times, very large protests have been held over weekends which affect/ed both embassies.”
Under the heading of “protests” as grounds for opposing the proposal, McCarrick said protests were “becoming more of a feature of everyday life, and embassies can be flash points”.
[ Dublin 4 residents fail to stop plans for Indian embassy Opens in new window ]
She said foreign missions frequently require specialised security upgrades for example external bollards, continuous CCTV monitoring, blast-proof barriers and private security guards.
She said that “this aggressive, highly visible security apparatus is entirely incompatible with the peaceful, open visual amenities of an historic residential neighbourhood”.
She also pointed to “consular footfall” as a reason to refuse planning permission, writing: “Visitors are transient, and unpredictable, leading to crowds waiting outside, localised congestion, all of which has an impact on neighbourhood privacy.”
McCarrick added: “When we have a severe ‘housing crisis’ the applicant should provide robust justification for the loss of a viable home.”
A spokesman for MS Ireland, which provides services for people with multiple sclerosis, said it sold its former premises “as part of its plans to consolidate its operations and further develop the MS Respite Centre in Rathgar, Dublin”.
He said: “The proceeds from the sale were used to repay the mortgage on the property, with the remaining funds supporting the organisation’s long-term sustainability and delivery of services.”

title: Last-minute €20m funding cut for RTÉ could have messy consequences
description: Broadcaster is unlikely to touch its big tent poles, but the breadth of its offering could suffer and some shows could be delayed
content:
T he Government’s abrupt and extraordinary withdrawal of €20 million in funding promised to RTÉ for 2027 is a fresh punch on the nose for the public service broadcaster.
If no political resolution can be found, RTÉ will be forced to scramble to slash its services, programming and headcount.
It has little room to manoeuvre, however, with its options constrained by fixed costs, existing spending commitments, legislative requirements, and the usual lead times involved in the making of television.
RTÉ will have budgeted for public funding of €260 million in 2027. Taking €20 million out of that total at the eleventh hour will be a messy and fractious process – one that would be impossible to complete without damaging both RTÉ and the broader Irish screen industry.
RTÉ director general Kevin Bakhurst described an emergency meeting with Minister for Media Patrick O’Donovan as “extremely constructive”, having earlier said that if nothing changed, the organisation would be left with “some pretty difficult choices to make”.
The most obvious place it would turn to in the “difficult choices” scenario is its commissions from independent production companies.
RTÉ was, before the Minister’s intervention, aiming to allocate about €60 million to independent commissions in 2027. This is about €10 million above the sum that it must spend under statutory minimum spending rules.
[ RTÉ DG says he has confidence in Minister after ‘constructive’ meeting on funding Opens in new window ]
That €10 million could now be vulnerable. If RTÉ was to retreat on this spending – it is expected to spend about €58 million on independent commissions in 2026 – it would undermine the breadth and quality of its programming in 2027.
The big tentpoles in its schedule are unlikely to be affected. RTÉ has deals in place for independently produced shows such as The Traitors Ireland and Dancing with the Stars. Axing these shows would make little sense in any case, as they are popular and bring in much-needed commercial revenue.
During previous crises, RTÉ responded by delaying the transmission of dramas and comedies, even when those same shows were broadcast internationally as planned.
To do this again in 2027 – for instance, by postponing the third season of the drama Kin – would mark a major setback in its ongoing bid to attract audiences in a competitive industry.
Instead, it is the long tail of lower-budget programming – the six-part factual series, the one-off documentary – made by smaller independent producers that could be placed in doubt.
This would not only substantially diminish the richness of its offering, it would also cause hardship and loss of work in the independent sector.
In-house production – already being whittled back – would likely have to bear some of the brunt too. The problem here is that RTÉ doesn’t make very much programming itself any more beyond news and current affairs, which sits at the heart of its remit.
Two notable exceptions are Fair City, which has seen its episode frequency temporarily reduced in the past , and The Late Late Show, which already runs for a shorter season than it did before the crisis year of 2023.
[ At 65 years old, isn’t it time for RTÉ to retire The Late Late Show? Opens in new window ]
Sports rights are expensive, meaning any bids currently in train could need to be rethought as a result of the Government’s move. But less sport also means less of that vital advertising money, while politicians tend to notice and vociferously object whenever RTÉ tries to skimp on the genre.
Elsewhere, there is a risk that the necessary continual investment in the RTÉ Player and its new Listen app could suffer, while a plan to move out of its obsolete Cork studios on Fr Mathew Street into new premises in the city next year could also be in jeopardy.
Voluntary redundancies, meanwhile, remain a key element of Bakhurst’s five-year strategy to shrink RTÉ, with the official expectation still being that 400 people will leave the organisation by 2029.
About 100 people departed RTÉ last year, with 67 people leaving under a voluntary exit scheme – the launch of which was delayed by the Government. But even if RTÉ was to shortly receive fresh approval for a second scheme, this would not represent a path to quick savings.
Industry insiders are dazed by how Budget 2027 has left the sector – not just RTÉ – in disarray.
They point to the irony of €20 million being pulled from RTÉ at a time when the Minister is pushing through the Broadcasting (Amendment) Bill 2026, which is designed to implement the EU principle of “adequate, sustainable and predictable” funding for public service media in Irish law.
The Department of Media said it would “continue to engage constructively” with RTÉ on the issues discussed at Thursday’s meeting.
But anything less than the restoration of the €20 million pledged to RTÉ could prove a lasting blow to the relationship between its current management and this Government.

title: Global shares fall as oil tops $105 amid fresh tanker attacks by Iran
description: Ryanair falls as Michael O’Leary warns that ‘insanely higher’ jet fuel prices could last until 2028
content:
Global shares fell on Thursday as oil topped $105 amid fresh tanker attacks by Iran, which threaten to curtail a recent uptick in flows from the Middle East and adding to worries over rising inflation globally.
Risk assets took a hit, while a sell-off in bank stocks that started in Asia fed into other markets. Meanwhile, the bond market rout showed no sign of abating as US and French yields continued to rise.
The Iseq index underperformed its peers, falling by more than 2 per cent. Ireland’s pillar banks were caught up in a global sell-off of lenders, with AIB, down by 3.6 per cent to €10.90, the worst performer on the index.
Bank of Ireland shed 2.5 per cent to close at €18.43. The Irish Times reported on Thursday that the lender has managed to contain losses in its US leveraged acquisition loan book through insurance deals with specialist investors.
Ryanair fell by 2.5 per cent to €23.37 per share after Michael O’Leary warned that “insanely higher” jet fuel prices could last until 2028.
All of the big names on the index finished in red, including Kerry Group, down by 0.4 per cent, and Kingspan, which slid by 0.7 per cent.
British shares dipped, with the benchmark FTSE 100 falling by 0.2 per cent and the mid-cap FTSE 250 shedding almost 0.5 per cent.
The big names in British banking faltered. Lloyds gave back almost 1.7 per cent amid renewed attacks on tankers in the Gulf. HSBC shed almost 2 per cent after the FT reported that the bank plans deep job cuts in its ‌UK wealth business ⁠as part of a broader, AI-driven efficiency push.
Among individual stocks, Tesco surged by more than 5 per cent after the food retailer raised its profit forecast.
Asset management company ‌Aberdeen rose 1.4 per cent after selling 52 million ​shares in Standard Life for about £436 million.
Europe’s main equity indices were dragged lower by falling bank stocks. The blue-chip Stoxx 50 was down by almost 1 per cent and the pan-European Stoxx 600 dipped by 0.7 per cent ata nearly four-month low.
European lenders have this week suffered their worst two-day slump since March amid concerns over France’s fiscal deficit and political gridlock.
Italy’s Intesa Sanpaolo shed almost 3 per cent as Spain’s BBVA and Santander fell by 1.8 per cent and 2.9 per cent, respectively.
France’s BNP Paribas fell by 2.4 per cent, while its compatriot, Société Générale, dipped 2.3 per cent.
Among individual stocks, Argenx tumbled by almost 16 per cent, making it the worst performer on the Stoxx 600, after the Netherlands-based biopharmaceutical ​company discontinued a trial.
Most sectors on the STOXX traded lower. Energy shares were a bright spot as oil prices climbed more than 3 per cent on persistent concerns about supply from the ‌key Middle East producing region.
US stocks fell as a surge in oil prices and treasury yields ‌near multiyear highs stoked inflation worries before a crucial earnings season that is expected to test recent market gains.
Megacap growth stocks were broadly lower, ​with Amazon falling by around 1 per cent and Tesla down 1.4 per cent.
Chip-related companies also dropped after forecasts of record quarterly profit from memory-chip giant Samsung Electronics failed to lift sentiment, with its shares closing ⁠lower in South Korea.
Rival Micron Technology was down 1.8 per cent.
Meanwhile, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Broadcom is lining up $50 ‌billion ‌in ​financing for OpenAI, with Oracle also seeking an unspecified sum, spurring fears that large debt issuance by technology companies could intensify the competition for capital.
Broadcom and Oracle were down 1.4 per cent and 2.1 per cent, respectively, amid wider weakness in ⁠tech stocks. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg, Reuters

title: FAI tells Uefa gathering about Ireland team’s experiences during Israel games
description: Chief executive David Courell and president Paul Cooke spoke at annual gathering of Uefa leaders in Berlin
content:
The FAI chief executive David Courell and president Paul Cooke have both relayed to Uefa members the “challenging experiences” of Ireland players and staff during the recent Nations League games against Israel .
Courell and Cooke both spoke during the annual gathering of Uefa executive leaders from all 55 member associations in Berlin on Thursday.
The FAI had previously asked European football’s governing body to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future Nations League, European Championship and World Cup qualification campaigns.
This position was reiterated after the recent fixtures in Hungary and Serbia have led to the possibility of three separate investigations.
Uefa appointed an ethics and disciplinary inspector this week to gather evidence following a claim by Damien Doyle, the FAI head of athletic performance, that he was spat on by an Israeli player at half-time last Sunday during the second meeting between the countries in Backa Topola, Serbia.
A spokesperson for the Israel Football Association denied the allegation, saying “no one had spat towards the [Irish] coach.”
Both associations are considering separate reports to Uefa about allegations of racist behaviour during the first game in Hungary on September 27th.
Ireland midfielder Jayson Molumby said he heard racist chants from Israeli fans directed at one of his team-mates, Adam Idah, during the game at the Nagyerdei stadium in Debrecen.
The Israeli media reported that a source within their national squad claimed to hear a racist comment by an Irish player, also in the Hungary game. The Israel FA have yet to report this to Uefa.
Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrímsson stated that Uefa should consider keeping the nations apart ahead of the Euro 2028 draw on December 6th.
“They can’t have this happening again, just for the players’ welfare,” he said.
Any Uefa decision to separate Ireland and Israel will need to be agreed by the national teams competitions committee, that will next meet in November, before it sends a recommendation to the executive committee.
Currently, Armenia and Azerbaijan; Bosnia & Herzegovina and Kosovo; Serbia and Kosovo; Spain and Gibraltar; and Ukraine and Belarus cannot been drawn together in Nations League or qualification groups.
Meanwhile, the Uefa president Aleksander Čeferin has backtracked on his previous decision not to stand for re-election, until 2031, at Congress in Kazakhstan next April.
Čeferin has held the position since he replaced Michel Platini in 2016.
“There is still important work ahead, and I have therefore accepted the [national associations] request [to continue],” Čeferin said. “My ambition remains the same: to keep European football united, make our game stronger and leave Uefa ready for the next generation.”
Uefa continue to call on Fifa president Gianni Infantino to resign. They are also demanding a reform of the global body’s institutional governance following Infantino’s attempt to sell a commercial stake in the World Cup to a private equity firm.

title: Two Latvian men arrested near RAF base in England
description: Men were rearrested on suspicion ⁠of an offence under the UK National Security Act ‌2023
content:
British counter-terrorism police are ‌investigating two Latvian men who were arrested near a Royal Air Force ​base in Cambridgeshire in the early hours of Thursday, police said in a statement.
The men were initially arrested on suspicion of ​trespass on a prohibited site and criminal damage, then rearrested on suspicion ⁠of an offence under the National Security Act ‌2023 – namely “entering ‌a ​prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK ”.
“We’re very aware of the recent ⁠heightened interest and concern ​around military sites, but ​at this stage there is nothing to suggest this ‌incident is connected to the ​events at RAF Fairford last week,” Helen Flanagan, head ⁠of counter-terrorism policing London, ⁠said ​in a statement.
She was referring to a separate incident at the Fairford airbase, which had been used by US bombers to strike Iran , in which several men were arrested over a suspected plot which the government has linked to Iran.
In ‌relation to Thursday’s ⁠arrests, police said they were also carrying out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area ‌in connection with the investigation.
An abandoned vehicle was recovered by ​police and later checked by bomb disposal ​officers, however nothing of concern was found. – Reuters

title: Erling Haaland calls for unity amid turmoil at Manchester City: ‘We have to stick together’
description: City travel to Liverpool for first game since guilty verdict; Pep Guardiola to attend Champions League game against PSG
content:
Erling Haaland has called for unity amid the uncertainty at Manchester City after the club were found guilty of serious financial breaches of Premier League rules.
City maintain their innocence and have appealed the decision but if that fails, a hefty sanction is expected. Players have sought reassurances over the past fortnight since the news was announced but most only returned to the club on Thursday after international duty.
On Sunday City play at Liverpool in their first game since the verdict was announced. It is expected to be a fiery occasion, with the animosity between the clubs heightened after the judgment.
“We have to stick together,” the striker told Sky Sports News. “We have to stay with each other, and we have to stay positive.
“No matter what happens in life, we always have to have a smile. So we have to stay positive, look ahead, and try to win football games and try to enjoy the situation and win the game. We have to stick together; we have to spread the love to each other. So yeah: stick together, and enjoy the ride and smile.”
The striker is following his father Alf-Inge, who played for City in a less successful era, so has witnessed the changes that have come since the takeover in 2008. “I care a lot about City, I have to say,” he added. “I care a lot about the fans because I’m a fan myself, and I feel with them as well.”
Pep Guardiola is expected to attend City’s first home match since they were found guilty of serious breaches of Premier League financial rules when they face Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday.
It would be the former head coach’s first return since leaving in the summer after 10 years. Guardiola’s attendance is regarded as a show of support for City’s hierarchy after the guilty verdicts that have rocked the club.
Guardiola wrote on social media last week: “I want every single fan to know I am here; more than ever. I am, always have been, always will, be behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran [Soriano, the CEO], the players, staff, Enzo [Maresca, the head coach] and you, our unique supporters. Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all.”
The Catalan took on a role as a City Football Group ambassador when he departed as head coach. Guardiola was a close ally of Soriano, who brought him to Manchester, the pair having worked together at Barcelona.
Guardiola faced regular questions during his tenure over City’s financial conduct after they were charged by the Premier League in 2023 and always reiterated his belief in what he was told by those above him. City deny wrongdoing and have appealed against the verdict of an independent commission.
Meanwhile, his former Real Madrid rival José Mourinho joked that he may not live to see ⁠the end of City’s legal battle. Mourinho managed Manchester United from 2016 and led them to a second-placed Premier League finish behind Guardiola’s City in 2018.
“I would rather ‌laugh about it,” Mourinho said, when asked about the case in an interview with Italy’s Corriere dello Sport. “I ​think we will eventually get an ending, but we are both in our 60s and we’ll need to be lucky enough to still be around when the final verdict arrives. There will be a verdict, ⁠then appeals, then more appeals.”

title: Manchester United offer JJ Gabriel new deal but risk losing prodigy for £350,000
description: Teenager almost certain to leave despite fresh offer, with compensation for move to European rival to be low
content:
Manchester United have made JJ Gabriel an official scholarship contract offer, but remain at risk of losing the teenage forward for as little as £350,000 (€414,000).
The prodigy, who turned 16 this week, stunned the club when he asked for his registration to be cancelled last month, setting in motion a scramble among Europe’s elite clubs for his signature.
Under Premier League youth rules, Gabriel would have been able to leave for a rival for nothing in January if the club had not offered him a formal scholarship for next season. The Guardian can reveal that the offer has now been lodged with the player.
Whether he accepts it or not – and it appears unlikely he will stay at Old Trafford – any Premier League club must now negotiate a fee directly with United for the player. If one is not reached, compensation will be set by a Professional Football Compensation Committee tribunal.
[ Joe O’Cearuill: The ex-Ireland international who says his son JJ Gabriel is the next Messi Opens in new window ]
At a tribunal, United would expect to receive in excess of £3 million, plus a clause in the deal granting them 20 per cent of his next transfer fee. In a previous tribunal for a high-profile academy player, Liverpool were required to pay Chelsea £2.8m up front – with an additional £1.2m in performance-related add-ons – for Rio Ngumoha, and a 20 per cent sell-on clause was inserted in the deal.
A United team photograph released earlier this week featuring Gabriel briefly raised fan hopes of a reconciliation. But a breakdown between his representatives and the club means the forward – who has been at United since he was 11 – is now almost certain to leave.
He was permitted under Premier League rules to sign a pre-agreement after his 16th birthday, but his camp were not prepared to enter discussions after a disagreement over first-team minutes.
His next move is yet to be decided, though it is believed he favours a move to Europe, where compensation would be significantly lower. Real Madrid are favourites to sign him, with Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain all monitoring developments.
According to official Fifa compensation figures for a Category I academy, United would receive about £350,000 if he moves abroad. He would ordinarily have been prevented from transferring before his 18th birthday, but is eligible for an EU passport through his parents. His father Joe O’Cearuill made two appearances for the Republic of Ireland in 2007.
The club will consider taking legal action if they believe recruitment rules have been breached.
Gabriel has not appeared at training for more than three weeks and, according to sources, the club has made multiple attempts to check on his wellbeing. To fast-track his progression into the first team, Gabriel had worked with specialist staff usually reserved for senior players. – Guardian

title: Ireland without four key players as they face Kazakhstan in World Cup playoff semi-final
description: Opponents’ lowly world ranking suggests it will be Carla Ward’s team facing either Poland or Belgium in final
content:
At any other time in the life cycle of this Republic of Ireland squad, taking the field without Denise O’Sullivan and Katie McCabe for the away leg of a World Cup playoff would be framed as an impending disaster.
The emergence of Emily Murphy and Abbie Larkin, in particular, significantly reduces the concern around Ireland’s two world-class players being unavailable for Friday afternoon’s first-leg away to Kazakhstan in Astana.
O’Sullivan, with her problematic knee, is rested until the second leg at Páirc Uí Chaoimh in her native Cork on Tuesday night.
Ireland manager Carla Ward is adamant her team will not take Kazakhstan for granted in this playoff semi-final to reach Brazil 2027 next summer.
“Why would we [give anything away], it’s a World Cup qualifier?” Ward told RTÉ when pressed on how she plans to replace O’Sullivan, the suspended pair of McCabe and Marissa Sheva, or the injured Jess Ziu.
“It does not matter who we are playing, Kazakhstan, France, Brazil, Netherlands – this is the business end of it, so we will prepare like we would prepare for anyone.”
However, the benefit of facing a country ranked 98th by Fifa – Ireland are 21st – does make it easier to spare O’Sullivan from a 22-hour round trip to Astana.
There is also the bigger picture to consider. At least one member of Ward’s staff will be tuned into Poland versus Belgium in the other playoff semi-final as Ireland expect to face the winner from that tie, home and away, between late November and early December.
Still, if Ward’s counterpart, Begaim Kirgizbaeva, could choose four Irish players to be missing from the first leg in the chilly Kazakh capital, then O’Sullivan, McCabe, Sheva and Ziu would make a lot of sense.
Alongside Ireland’s Super League centre halves, Caitlin Hayes and Anna Patten, the missing foursome make this team tick.
Without McCabe and O’Sullivan, the emphasis shifts to other players, such as Crystal Palace midfielder Shanade Hopcroft, who is set for an international debut at 29-years-old, having qualified for Ireland via a Sligo grandmother.
Ward said: “We’ve got to get the job done professionally. If you look at the balance of the squad there are going to be players out of position, but these girls step up whenever they are asked. They are hungry to play for their country, they want to learn.
“Shanade has only had a few sessions, but she has looked good, tidy, and is somebody who will add value to the squad. She has been knocking on the door for a few years. Vera [Pauw] looked at her. She wants to get on the ball. She can link the units and she can play forward.”
Heather Payne and Tyler Toland must be keen to regain starting roles after such bright starts to their international careers, but Ward is more likely to lean into a more reliable performer, such as Lucy Quinn.
Megan Connolly will probably sit in midfield, where she is expected to maintain the high standards of dead-ball delivery until McCabe returns.
Arguably, the loss of the all-action Sheva and Ziu’s natural instinct to run at the opposition will be felt just as much as an Ireland team without McCabe and O’Sullivan.
Patten, Hayes and Aoife Mannion are expected to keep the defence watertight, particularly from crosses, while the attacking focus switches to Murphy and the in-form Larkin, who could feature up front, at left wing back or in midfield.
“Abbie has been in form for a while now and she doesn’t get the praise she deserves,” Ward said. “Any time she puts on the Ireland shirt she performs.”
Larkin is growing into a top player for Palace and Ireland with her consistency edging her away from super-sub status.
The playoff final will take place from November 26th to December 5th when Ireland could play the second leg at the Aviva Stadium. Ward’s side were marginally better than Poland and Belgium when they beat both countries last season.
IRELAND (possible) : Brosnan; Patten, Hayes, Stapleton; Mannion, Hopcroft, Connolly, Mustaki; Murphy, Larkin; Carusa.
Referee : Karoline Marie Jensen (Norway).

title: Galway bar manager dismissed just 11 days after miscarriage awarded €25,000
description: HR manager allegedly said miscarriage meant worker would ‘only want a baby more’
content:
A Galway hospitality firm which dismissed a manager just 11 days after she suffered a miscarriage , before trying to claim that maternity protection law didn’t apply since she wasn’t pregnant any longer, has been ordered to pay her €25,000.
Fadeside Ltd, a subsidiary of the Connacht Hospitality Group, has been ordered by the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) to compensate a former manager at its Residence Hotel and 1520 Bar in Galway City for terminating her employment in October 2023 on the stated basis of underperformance.
It is said to be the first time a worker has sought to have the minimum service requirements of the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977 set aside under maternity protection law in the circumstances of a miscarriage.
Normally, an employee requires 12 months’ service before they can pursue a complaint for unfair dismissal – a limitation disapplied in relation to pregnant workers, who are shielded from day one.
The complainant fell ill and was admitted to A&E in September 2023. She found out then that she had been pregnant and was having a miscarriage, she said in evidence to the tribunal.
At the time, she was just under 11 months into a new €60,000-a-year job as general manager at the hotel and bar in Galway’s Latin Quarter.
She said that, after phoning in sick, group HR manager Jackie O’Dowd reached her by phone and said the miscarriage “would make [the complainant] want to have a baby even more”.
At the WRC, O’Dowd denied making the remark.
The complainant said she told O’Dowd in reply that getting pregnant was not something she had planned.
Having returned to work in the first week of October 2023, the worker met her line manager, Wayne Neilon, later telling the WRC she wanted to discuss her working hours and other business maters, she said.
The complainant said Neilon told her she “did not have the core competencies” for the job.
O’Dowd then arrived and asked whether the complainant wanted to resign, remarking that perhaps she “needed a break” because of the miscarriage, the complainant said.
She was told at the meeting that her probation would not be extended and received a letter of dismissal citing “work performance” the following day, the tribunal was told.
The complainant said Neilon had told her months earlier, in May 2023, that she had passed her probation, and that she said so at the October meeting.
In any case, the WRC noted the complainant’s contract capped the maximum probation period at 11 months; by the time of the October meeting, she had 11 months and two days’ service.
The firm’s solicitor, Pat Mullins of O’Flynn Exhams LLP, failed in March of last year in an attempt to have the case thrown out, arguing that enhanced workplace protections under the Maternity Protection Act did not extend to the complainant.
“At the time of the dismissal, the complainant was not, in fact, pregnant, and I say it is a substantial stretch of the interpretation of that part of the Act to state that it includes a previous miscarriage,” Mullins said.
Counsel for the worker, Ian FitzHarris, with Orlaith J Byrne & Co solicitors, said the sacking was just 11 days after the pregnancy loss, his client having worked just five more days after her absence, he said.
“Five days and then they sacked her. The phrase in the legislation is ‘pregnancy-related matters’,” counsel said.
Adjudicator Louise Boyle rejected the respondent’s stance on maternity rights. “It is not in dispute that a miscarriage arises from pregnancy,” she wrote.
“I find that in all the circumstances it lacks credibility that the complainant’s employment was terminated for poor performance,” she wrote.
She concluded the respondent had failed to demonstrate there were the “exceptional circumstances” required to dismiss a worker entitled to maternity protections and awarded €25,000 for unfair dismissal.

title: ‘Doing the work of two nurses and not getting the pay of one’: Nurses stage midday protest
description: Protesters demand Government address nurses’ cost-of-living concerns as strike looms
content:
“I just feel like I can’t work here any more,” says Juliana Daly, a 23-year-old nurse at St Vincent’s University Hospital who is nearing her first year as a fully qualified medical professional.
“I can’t work in Ireland any more. It devastates me as well that I’m going to have to leave my family to go over, but I just don’t see how I can even do another year here, to be honest.”
The Co Galway native has lived in Dublin for the past five years, but that will soon change. Come January, she will move to Sydney in Australia , following other two nurses around her age who recently emigrated.
The three young women all worked on the same ward, but one by one they have left Ireland for Australia shortly after qualifying as nurses.
Daly feels as though there’s little choice in the matter. “The working conditions in the hospital aren’t acceptable,” she says. “We’re doing the work of, essentially, two nurses – and we’re not even getting enough pay for one”.
Alongside her stands Elise Ryan, also 23 years old and from Co Kilkenny . The pair studied nursing together at University College Dublin .
“We weren’t naive,” Ryan says. “We knew we weren’t going to make millions: everybody knows that when you’re going into nursing. You’re doing it because it’s a profession that you feel you want to do – but I still don’t think that’s a reason for us not to be paid enough money.
“We love our jobs and we put a lot of effort into caring for our patients – it is an honour to care for our patients, to help through hard times in their lives and the end of their lives.”
“But, at the end of the day, when you go home and you get your pay cheque: it’s a lot of tax, it’s not much to cover your rent and bills.” She says you ask yourself: “Why am I pouring myself out for this?
“Every ounce of energy I have is going into this job and I’m not getting a lot back. I think that’s really important, that’s why we’re out here today,” she says, as dozens of her nursing colleagues chant: “What do we want? Fair pay. When do we want it? Now.”
St Vincent’s University Hospital, in Ballsbridge, Dublin 4, is one of nine hospitals nationwide that witnessed lunchtime protests on Thursday to call attention to the impact of cost-of-living pressures on nurses and midwives.
Dozens of staff at the hospital, and hundreds across the State, picketed for one hour, with a strike planned next Wednesday by their union, the Irish Nurses and Midwives Association , alongside other public-sector unions.
At St Vincent’s they protested through rain, with beeps of support from passing cars, trucks and public buses.
Emma Morake, a 66-year-old originally from South Africa who has worked at the hospital since 2007, is at ease in leading the demonstration’s chants.
“We just want to say to the Government : come see us – because the patients see us, their relatives see us. Can the Government at least see us?”
“A little bit of compassion” is what she wants to see, “because nursing salaries haven’t really kept up with the cost of living.
“When you’re working under a lot of pressure, it’s unsafe, it’s unhealthy ... Nurses are psychologically, mentally and physically exhausted” during work hours. “Even the patients recognise it: they always say: ‘You work so hard.’ So why can’t the Government recognise that?”

title: Mona McSharry picks up bronze medal in 200m breaststroke at World Aquatics World Cup
description: Competing in Uzbekistan in second of three World Cup stops, McSharry finished third behind Russia’s Evgeniia Chikunova
content:
Mona McSharry got her World Aquatics World Cup stop two campaign off to a strong start in Tashkent, Uzbekistan on Thursday, claiming bronze in the 200m breaststroke, while Ellen Walshe finished fifth in the 200m butterfly.
McSharry, who won gold, silver and bronze at the opening World Cup stop in Baku, Azerbaijan last week, added another medal to her tally with a third-place finish in the 200m breaststroke in 2:20.41. The time was just outside the 2:18.45 she produced to secure silver in Baku.
Russia’s Evgeniia Chikunova once again claimed gold in the event in 2:17.23, with the Netherlands’ Tes Schouten taking silver in 2:20.07, narrowly ahead of McSharry.
Walshe, who won silver in the 200m butterfly in Baku, opened her Tashkent campaign with a fifth-place finish in 2:08.69.
China secured two places on the podium, with Yiting Yu taking gold in 2:02.75 and Mohan Chang winning bronze in 2:05.61. Finland’s Laura Lahtinen claimed silver in 2:05.20.
The Irish pair return to action on Friday, with McSharry set to contest the 100m breaststroke, an event she won in Baku, while Walshe competes in the 400m individual medley.
McSharry and Ellen Walshe will compete in Astana, Kazakhstan next week in the final stop of the World Cup.

title: Clare man (61) avoids e-scooter driving ban as ‘the penalty is not available’ to courts
description: Clare man Peter Morrissey, of Rathkeane, Ennis, fined €500 for drink-driving an e-scooter
content:
A Co Clare man (61) has been convicted of drink-driving an e-scooter after being found to be three times over the limit applied to motorists.
At Ennis District Court, Judge Adrian Harris imposed a €500 fine on Peter Morrissey after he was detected driving under the influence of an intoxicant on his e-scooter on Ennis’s Gort Road on July 26th after exiting an off-licence.
Garda Sgt John Burke said this is the first such case he has come across and he told the judge that an e-scooter driving ban is not a penalty that is available to the court for “drink-driving” an e-scooter.
