In the prosecution brought by Garda Kieran Doody, Morrissey pleaded guilty to driving or attempting to drive a powered personal transporter while under the influence of an intoxicant to such an extent as to be incapable of having proper control of the transporter at Gort Road, Ennis, on July 26th.
The charge is contrary to section 6 of the Road Traffic Act 2010 amended by the section 35 of the Road Traffic Act 2023.
Solicitor for Morrissey, John Casey said his client was using the e-scooter because he received a three-year driving ban in May 2023 for drink-driving.
Outlining the facts against Morrissey of Rathkeane, Ruan, Ennis, Co Clare, Burke said that a garda on mobile patrol observed Morrissey stumble off his e-scooter after coming out of an off-licence.
The garda saw Morrissey was “weaving” on the road on the e-scooter and when stopped by gardaí, he stumbled off the e-scooter and his speech was slurred.
Burke said that Morrissey was arrested at the scene and brought to Ennis Garda station where he was tested for drink-driving. The breath test returned a result of 76mg of alcohol per 100ml breath.
The legal limit for drivers of cars is 22mg of alcohol per 100ml of breath.
However, in court, Morrissey disputed the Garda account that he stumbled off the e-scooter or was weaving on the road.
Morrissey told the court: “I wasn’t staggering like he said. The Garda car came from behind me and put on the sirens and that frightened the life out of me and that is when I was wobbling.”
The judge said there was a lot of coverage currently of new laws concerning e-scooter users and Morrissey said that this was “for young people”.
In reply, the judge said: “It also applies to mature people and you need to get the message that you can’t drive an e-scooter intoxicated.”
He said: “If you were driving a car, this would have been a serious level of intoxication – maybe if you were that intoxicated you should be walking to places and not on an e-scooter at all.”
The judge said that Morrissey’s 39 previous convictions include one for drink-driving.
Casey said that Morrissey “is very embarrassed” over what occurred and he was just making his way home.
He said: “An e-scooter is the only form of transport he uses.”
The judge imposed the fine of €500 and gave Morrissey nine months to pay.

title: ‘Measurable rise in hate’ prompts calls from Irish human rights group for new national plan
description: Calls for a national action plan to combat hate are ‘fully supported’ by the Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission
content:
Calls for a national action plan to combat hate are “fully supported” by the Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission (IHREC), its chief commissioner Liam Herrick said on Thursday.
Herrick was speaking at a press conference hosted by LGBT Ireland and Outhouse as part of the ILGA-Europe Conference, which is the largest annual gathering of LGBTI activists, organisations and allies in Europe and Central Asia.
A national action plan to combat hate was proposed to address the root causes of hate, through prevention, education, community investment and measures that strengthen social cohesion.
The IHREC said the “measurable rise in hate” in communities across Ireland was “one of the greatest human rights and equality challenges facing our society”.
Representatives of communities affected by hate across Ireland called on the Government to develop and implement a “comprehensive, fully resourced” national plan to combat the matter.
“We understand hate as something that’s manifested in different degrees of severity, ranging from microaggressions up to hate speech and hate crime, with devastating consequences for individuals and communities,” Herrick said.
“The impacts of hate are not new, but the rise of technology has changed the nature of how hate can be spread.
“The growing problem of hate in Ireland, including homophobic and transphobic hate, requires a co-ordinated, whole-of-society response.”
[ Children trafficked into criminality face ‘horrific’ level of victim blaming, report says Opens in new window ]
Herrick said the answer “cannot be limited to criminal justice measures”. Instead, a “sustained response that tackles the conditions in which hate can flourish and supports the communities experiencing it” is needed.
Kieran O’Donovan, chief executive of Belong To said he sees “the real human impact of this rising hate” most clearly in young people, every day.
He said 72 per cent of members of the LGBTI+ community have experienced online and verbal abuse with one in four having experienced physical abuse.
“When a young person sees this hostility in the world, of course it does real, long-lasting damage ... to their mental health.”
He said members of the LGBTI+ are three times more likely to self-harm and are five times more likely to attempt suicide than their peers. He too called for the national action plan to combat hate.
Speaking on the national panel on hate and extremism in Ireland, Tim Hanley, advocacy and research manager at LGBT Ireland, spoke of the impact that rising hate is having on LGBTI+ people.
He said some people were afraid to hold hands in public, afraid to show affection to their partners in public, change the way they dress, and don’t go to certain places.
[ Reports of hate crimes up 15% in 2025, with racism and xenophobia most common motives Opens in new window ]
He said when the marriage equality referendum passed in Ireland in 2015, LGBTI+ people “won the right to walk down the aisle”.
However, now in 2026, too many LGBTI+ people “have to look over our shoulders when we walk down the street”, he said.
Kate O’Connell, equality and intercultural programme officer with the National Youth Council of Ireland, said some youth workers say changes happen “really quickly” regarding the normalisation of hate and hostility.
Though “on the flip side” she said there have never been more Pride parades in rural areas and more Pride flags on display.

title: Circling the Square returns
description: Books newsletter: a wrap of the latest news and preview of tomorrow’s pages
content:
Founded to honour the memory of poet Dennis O’Driscoll, Circling The Square is now in its fifth year and has established itself as one of the country’s best poetry festivals. Thomas McCarthy said: “A festival in the Tipperary heartland, inspired by the memory of the great Dennis O’Driscoll, Circling the Square is the one place poets want to turn to year after year.”
Moya Cannon said: “In addition to being a wonderful poet and discerning critic, Dennis O’Driscoll was famous for his affirmation of poets and poetry and his commitment to excellence. With warm Tipperary hospitality, the Circling the Square festival celebrates and perpetuates his gracious and generous spirit.’
This year’s Circling The Square will take place from October 16 th to 18 th in Thurles, Co Tipperary – the town in which Dennis grew up – and will open with a free event in Bookworm Bookshop, at which Rita Ann Higgins and Molly Twomey will read. On the afternoon of Saturday 17th, at The Source Arts Centre, Fintan O’Toole and Mick Heaney will speak to Declan O’Driscoll at an event called Fieldwork: The Public Life of Seamus Heaney.
This will be followed by readings from Maija Mäkelä, Adam Wyeth, Katie Donovan, Stephen Sexton and Catriona O’Reilly, plus music by classical flautist Emma Roche and cellist Richard Angell. That evening, also at The Source, poets Vona Groarke, Dean Browne, Leontia Flynn, John Kelly, Martina Evans and Nidhi Zak/Aria Eipe will read their work. Ed Dwan Quartet, Daniel Byrne Ensemble and Emma Roche will play music interludes.
On Sunday a free event in O’Gorman’s pub, Thurles will include readings by poets Róisín Leggett Bohan, Emily Cullen, Anne Donnellan, Paddy Moran, Jaki McCarrick, John D. Kelly, Eithne Lannon, Noelle Lynskey, Eoin Devereux and Karen J. McDonnell.
Tickets can be booked at thesourceartscentre.ie
In The Irish Times tomorrow, Bonnie Garmus tells Nadine O’Regan about her new novel, Peck & Peck, and the misogynistic reaction to her bestselling debut Lessons in Chemistry. Mahmoud Khalili talks to Tadhg Hoey about his memoir, No Land to Stand On: Notes from Detention . There is also a Q&A with Eoin McNamee about his new book of collected short fiction, The Comets.
Reviews are Eamon Maher on John McGahern by Frank Shovlin; Ruby Eastwood on The Glass Cage by John Healy; Sinéad Gibney on Daniel Susskind’s What Should my Children Do?; on the best new translations; Breándan Mac Suibhne on Brian Cowen: Anatomy of a Taoiseach by Gary Murphy; Neasa MacErlean on Protocols: An Operating Manual for the Human Body by Andrew Huberman; Andrew Lynch on Hawking: His Life and Work by Graham Farmelo; Greg Londe on O Now! By Niall Williams; Djamel White on The Boy by Mark Gyves; Henrietta McKervey on Sleepers in the Snow by Joanne Harris; Helena Mulkerns on Ply by Hernan Diaz; Dean Fee on X&Y=K by Ciaran Carson; and Declan Burke on the best new scifi.
Hannah Kent, author of Always Home, Always Homesick, is the winner of the 2026 Ilse Schwepcke Prize for women’s travel writing. The winner of the sister prize, Der Ilse Schwepcke Preis, for a travel book written by a woman in German, is Marianne Jungmaier for Kontinentaldrift (Continental Drift).
Irish Book Week 2026, the annual celebration of the vital contribution bookshops makes to Irish culture, the economy and communities, runs from Saturday, October 17th to Saturday, October 24th.
Almost 200 Irish bookshops have registered to take part in this year’s campaign, run in partnership by Bookselling Ireland as part of their Books Are My Bag campaign and Publishing Ireland.
Events include: Irish Book Week Ambassador, Carina McNally, visiting Kerr’s Bookshop, Clonakilty, on Friday, October 23rd, at 3pm to sign copies of her historical novel, Mithim. info@kerrsbookshop.ie
Award winning author and illustrator Oisín McGann will visit Chapters Bookshop, Dublin on Saturday, October 17th, at 11am for a hands-on workshop for readers aged 10+ exploring how writers and illustrators bring creepy characters to life.
The Maynooth Bookshop will host a free illustrated historical talk with Titanic historian Alan Cleary on Thursday, October 22nd, at 6.30pm, exploring Ireland’s fascinating maritime connections from the passengers and crew to the tragic sinkings, loss of life and communities across Ireland touched by the ships.
Halfway Up the Stairs, Greystones, will host an interactive family print workshop on Saturday, October 17th, at 11am with Anne Atkins based around her new book Cackle Crackle: Letters from the Witch. This event is suitable for children aged 6+.
For further information on Irish Book Week 2026, follow Bookselling Ireland’s on Facebook and Instagram: @booksellingireland.
Belfast writer Wendy Erskine has been shortlisted for her debut novel The Benefactors in the Literature category in this year’s Sky Arts Awards, which will be broadcast live on Sky on Tuesday, October 13th, live from The Roundhouse, London, hosted by hosted by Grayson Perry and Rebecca Lucy Taylor (aka Self Esteem). Also nominated are Oyinkan Braithwaite for Cursed Daughters and Robert Macfarlane for Is a River Alive?
A new evening series features some of the many stories of the Irish Jewish experience. Hosted by Trinity’s Centre for Jewish Studies, the Trinity Long Room Hub and in co-operation with the Irish Jewish Museum, the series includes lectures, music and film offering new perspectives on the Jews of Ireland and their experiences.
The first session, From the Venice Ghetto to Dublin’s ‘Little Jerusalem’ and beyond by Bryan Cheyette, takes place on Tuesday, October 13th, at 6.15pm and tickets can be booked here .
On November 17th, Prof Eugenio Biagini will speak about his new book, The Minority Mind: Jews and Protestants in Catholic Ireland, 1912-1968 (Cambridge University Press, 2026). On December 15th, Katrina Goldstone presents The Aliens File: A Story of Us and Them. Jewish migration in post-independence Ireland. On Tuesday, January 26th, there is a screening and panel discussion of Der Veg Abhaile (2024), a documentary film, directed by Hannah Bloom and produced by Saul Woolfson, exploring Irish Jewish identity from the perspectives of culture and migration. On February 13th, Natalie Wynn discusses Isaac Herzog and the Irish Chief Rabbinate. On March 9th, Seán Gannon explores Christian Mission and Irish Jews. On April 13th, Trisha Oakley Kessler discusses Nationalism and the economy: Jews, Identity and Belonging in Twentieth-Century Ireland. Finally, on May 18th, Zuleika Rodgers’ subject is Jacob Weingreen: A Jewish Journey and a Trinity Story.
Paul McVeigh and Sarah Maria Griffin are among 12 writers longlisted for the Polari Book Prize 2026. Founded in 2019 and previously awarded to Andrew McMillan, Kate Davies, Diana Souhami, Joelle Taylor, Julia Armfield and Jon Ransom, the £2,000 prize is sponsored by DHH Literary Agency.
The Polari Prize 2026 longlist is: The Decadence by Leon Craig; Pride and Prejudices: Queer Lives and the Law by Keio Yoshida; This Is How I Fight by Rosie Garland; Green Ink by Stephen May; I Hear You by Paul McVeigh; On the Boardwalk by Martin Sherman; The Light of Day by Christopher Stephens & Louise Radnofsky; Maryville by Joelle Taylor; Our Better Natures by Sophie Ward; Well Done, You Didn’t Die by Max Wallis; Eat the Ones You Love by Sarah Maria Griffin; and Six Conversations We’re Scared to Have by Deborah Frances-White.
The judges are literary critic Suzi Feay, Dr Gurmit Singh of Lancaster Literature Festival, Katy Jon Went of The Human Library, and Garry Wilson, CEO of sponsor EasyJet Holidays.
Sam Furlong is one of 12 writers on the Polari First Book Prize 2026 longlist.
The longlist is: The Ayatollah’s Gaze by Majid Parsa; What A Girl Wants by Roxy Bourdillon; Where You Go, I Will Go by Christina Fonthes; Altar by Desree; Summer Hours by Alessandra Thom; Pig by Matilde Pratesi; Prairie Oyster by Sophie Robinson; Crowd Work by Sam Furlong; Smoke and Silk by Fiona Keating; A Family Matter by Claire Lynch; I’m Fine by Richard Hall; Miss Veal and Miss Ham by Vikki Heywood.
This year’s shortlist will be announced on November 3rd. The winners will be announced on November 30th at the Polari Prize ceremony at Heaven nightclub, London.
Seven Stories Press has acquired world rights to Jennifer Bartlett’s The Mechanics of Reality, the authorised biography of Paul Auster, who died on April 30th, 2024. The book will include considerable archival material from Auster’s personal papers and photographs not yet made public.
The forthcoming book, currently scheduled for Autumn 2029, has the full support of Auster’s widow and literary executor, the internationally recognised novelist and scholar Siri Hustvedt, whose memoir of her life with Auster, Ghost Stories , topped bestseller lists all over Europe in the spring.
Longford County Library and Archives Services will host the annual Padraic Colum Gathering in Granard Community Library this Saturday, October 10th, from 11am to 4pm. The event celebrates the lasting contribution of Padraic Colum, one of Longford’s most important literary figures, and his wife Mary Colum, a respected writer and critic.
The programme opens with writer and film producer John Connell, who will discuss Colum’s place in Longford’s literary tradition. A highlight will be the launch of the inaugural Clíona Ní Shúilleabháin Letter-Writing Competitions, established in memory of Padraic Colum’s grandniece and long-time supporter of the Gathering.
In the afternoon, Prof Margaret Kelleher will launch her new book, Mary and Padraic Colum: Lives and the Dream, introduced by Vona Groarke, Ireland Professor of Poetry. The day concludes with music from Aoife Mulligan and visitors can also view a special exhibition of letters exchanged between Padraic and Mary Colum, recently donated to Longford County Archives.
This Saturday, October 10th, UCD Village Auditorium will be the venue for a day of celebration of the life and work of Pádraig Ó Snodaigh (1935-2025), publisher, historian and language activist. The event will feature poetry and prose readings, music, a keynote talk by Alan Titley and discussions of Ó Snodaigh’s contribution to publishing.
Ó Snodaigh set up the publishing house Coiscéim in 1980 and over 45 years published nearly 2,000 books in Irish. A Carlow native, he spent his working life in Dublin where he married the artist Clíodhna Cussen. In the National Museum he was responsible for 1916 holdings. His early retirement allowed him to found Coiscéim. He was Uachtarán of Conradh na Gaeilge (1974-79) and was awarded an honorary Doctorate of Celtic Studies by UCD in 2019.
The discussion and celebration of his unique contribution to Irish life and letters will take place in UCD from 1pm until 9pm. SNOD 26 is free to the public but it is advisable to book through Eventbrite.
Little Island is publishing He Loves Me (Not) by Máire Zepf, originally published in Irish as Nóinín by Irish indie Cois Life, when it won the main Book of the Year prize at the KPMG–Children’s Books Ireland Awards 2020, the first and still the only Irish-language book to do so. Now translated into English by the author, Little Island is proud to bring this terrific YA verse novel to to a new audience for the first time. For the launch event on October 8th, at 6pm, in the Seamus Heaney Centre, Queen’s University Belfast, Máire will be in conversation with fellow former Children’s Writing Fellow for Northern Ireland, Shirley-Anne McMillan (author of Little Island’s 2023 YA title Grapefruit Moon).
Emma Dabiri presents a programme on Jamaican poet Ferdinand Levy this Sunday, October 11th, at 6pm on RTÉ lyric fm and RTÉ Listen. Levy enrolled as a medical student at Trinity College Dublin in 1933, and in 1941 published his only collection of poetry, Flashes from the Dark, believed to be the first collection by a black poet published in Ireland. His poems range in theme from life in Ireland to racism, colonialism, the beauty of the Caribbean and the vitality of Harlem, and they brought to the grey streets of 1940s Ireland the rhythms and language of the Harlem Renaissance.
HarperCollins Children’s Books, celebrates the 50th overall translation deal for Oliver Jeffers’ iconic collection of award-winning picture books.
The 50th language signed was Indonesian rights for three books: Here We Are, I’m Very Busy and Where to Hide A Star. His global sales now exceed 22 million copies worldwide.
He will be appearing at the Dublin Book Festival on Saturday, November 7th and will be signing books in Eason Dundrum on Friday, November 6th and Kennys Galway on Sunday 8th. He will be signing in No Alibis Belfast on December 20th.
Judges Leontia Flynn (chair), Ishion Hutchinson and Daisy Lafarge have chosen the T.S. Eliot Prize 2026 shortlist from 174 poetry collections submitted by 65 British and Irish publishers. The adventurous list comprises poets both well-known and less familiar, including writers of multiple collections, one previously shortlisted poet, two second collections and one debut. Poets hail from Canada, Ireland, Jamaica and the US.
Ireland is represented by Cork poet Billy Ramsell for Render, published by Banshee Press. Also shortlisted were: Killing Spree by Jorie Graham; Hide Me Under the Blood by Keith Jarrett; and I Shall Be Satisfied by Imani Mason Jordan; Sleep Gate by Sylvia Legris; Behold by Shara McCallum; The House of Broken Things by Kim Moore; Gravity Archives by Andrew Motion; Cafés by Holly Pester; and The Channel by Jana Prikryl.
Flynn said: “Though very different in voice, style and preoccupation, these ten collections share a determination to meet the challenges faced in difficult times with closer attention to language. Linguistic disruption, personal reflection, humorous lyricism – or indeed all these things at once – can be found in this work. Each of these books reminds us why, when nothing else makes much sense, it’s to poetry we turn to reorient ourselves.”
The winner of the £25,000 prize will be announced at the Wallace Collection, London, on January 18th. The shortlisted poets will each receive £1,500. Last year’s winner was Karen Solie for her collection Wellwater (Picador Poetry).

title: Top Goldman Sachs executives to get $500m in one of largest such payouts in Wall Street history
description: Wall Street bank preparing to hand out equity awards from five-year scheme to senior leaders
content:
Goldman Sachs ’ most senior executives are in line to receive more than $500 million (€446.2 million) in special bonuses from a five-year incentive plan, one of the biggest payouts of its kind in the Wall Street bank’s history.
The lender is preparing to hand out equity awards to a group of its most senior leaders that would exceed $500 million at Goldman’s current share price, according to a person familiar with the matter.
The payout is part of a long-term incentive scheme the bank disclosed in 2021, with the final value of the bonus pool determined by the bank’s stock market performance relative to peers at the end of October, meaning it could still change, another person said.
The bumper package, first reported by Bloomberg, comes after Goldman’s share price outperformed most of its Wall Street rivals over the past five years.
The special incentive scheme was agreed at a time when Wall Street banks were benefiting from record dealmaking and a boom in “blank cheque” companies as the industry rebounded from the Covid pandemic.
[ Goldman Sachs reports best quarter in five years even as fixed-income traders disappoint Opens in new window ]
Goldman chief executive David Solomon is expected to receive the largest chunk of the bonus pool, taking home about $100 million in share-based awards.
John Waldron, Goldman’s second-in-command who is widely seen as the heir apparent to Solomon, is also among the beneficiaries of the scheme, as well as other members of Goldman’s management committee from 2021 who are still with the bank.
The performance-based stock for Solomon was worth about $30 million when Goldman announced the plan in 2021, while Waldron’s was worth about $20 million.
Solomon and Waldron, who is Goldman’s president and chief operating officer, have led the investment bank since 2018. The pair were also both granted five-year retention bonuses, worth $80 million apiece, at the start of 2025.
Goldman paid Solomon $47 million last year, an increase of more than one-fifth from the previous year and his highest remuneration since he took the helm at the Wall Street bank.
The first half of his tenure was marred by a lossmaking expansion into retail banking, which was at odds with the investment bank’s Wall Street pedigree and prompted fierce criticism of Solomon’s leadership.
After billions of dollars in losses, Goldman largely exited the consumer push and has since doubled down on investment banking, trading and money management. The bank’s shares are up about 180 per cent over the past three years.
Goldman said: “The board created these awards to achieve three principal objectives: align compensation with rigorous performance thresholds, ensure leadership continuity and enhance retention of our top talent in an increasingly competitive market.” - Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: EasyJet to cut 700,000 seats from winter flight schedule amid rising fuel costs
description: Budget airline to scale back capacity by a further 700,000 seats to save on expensive fuel
content:
EasyJet will cut another 700,000 seats from its winter flight schedule to save on fuel as the low-cost airline steps up efforts to curb costs during the industry’s lean season.
Chief executive Kenton Jarvis said the company was scaling back capacity over the quieter months to prevent it paying higher sums for fuel, which has rocketed in price since the Iran conflict in February.
Earlier in the summer, Easyjet cut about 700,000 seats from its winter flights. Jarvis said the airline would now remove between 600,000 and 700,000 more – the equivalent of about two days’ worth of flying.
The budget carrier, one of Europe’s biggest airlines, typically offers about 50 million seats on flights over the winter season, which runs from October to end of March.
“People are taking capacity out, we see that across all competitors,” he told the FT, adding that was “no surprise” given fuel costs. “I honestly think it’s been quite a surprise for the industry that fuel has stayed as high as it is. ”
Jet fuel costs roughly doubled after the start of the Iran conflict, which led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Though prices have started to fall, they remain far higher than airlines expected when the conflict began, Jarvis added.
European airlines hedge some of their fuel exposure, but have been left paying higher prices for the remainder, Jarvis said. By cutting capacity, Easyjet could reduce its use of more expensive fuel, he added.
His comments come after Ryanair last week said it was cancelling some flights on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and quieter weekend services to save money over winter.
Boss Michael O’Leary said on Thursday that he expected higher fuel costs to continue for another 18 months, due to elevated prices but also lower hedging rates for the coming year. “We are all facing an enormous cost challenge next year,” he said.
Global industry group Iata has already warned that rising fuel costs will cost the sector an extra $100 billion this year. Several carriers have fallen into bankruptcy since the conflict started, including Spirit in the US and AirBaltic in Europe.
O’Leary, Jarvis and other bosses have warned that higher costs come as airlines face an additional burden from environmental rules, particularly a proposed extension of the EU’s emissions trading system and a rise in the need for airlines to buy more expensive “sustainable aviation fuel”.
“There’s real pain for passengers next year because of higher oil prices and, at the same time, Europe is extending ETS [the Emissions Trading System],” O’Leary said.
Ourania Georgoutsakou, who leads lobby group Airlines for Europe, said: “Let’s be honest, that’s not a sustainable situation if the cost of fuel continues to remain at these levels and looking ahead at all the business and regulatory costs that Europe is placing on European airlines.”
The European Commission has said that the extension of the system is required because international agreements have failed to deliver effective means of reducing emissions. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Former prince Andrew wins legal challenge over lawfulness of search warrants
description: Police accept unlawfulness of warrants obtained to search properties but say investigation continues
author_name: Alistair Gray and Robert Wright in London
content:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor , the former British prince, has won a legal challenge over the lawfulness of warrants that police officers obtained to search two of his properties before his arrest in connection with the Epstein files .
A judge at the high court in London on Thursday said “a significant error was made in the application for and grant of” warrants obtained by Thames Valley Police ahead of his arrest on his 66th birthday earlier this year on suspicion of misconduct in public office.
Mr Justice Hilliard said in a ruling that the police and Mountbatten-Windsor had agreed that the search warrants were unlawful.
However, it remains unclear how significantly the ruling will change the former prince’s legal position. The court heard that a criminal investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor was ongoing.
Thames Valley Police insisted the ruling was about the narrow point of the legislation used to obtain the warrants and said it was continuing legal action over the status of the material seized during the searches.
“The agreement that led to the quashing of the warrants relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgment on our ongoing investigation,” the force said.
It said it retained the evidence and expects to be able to examine and use it in its investigation if it succeeds in the continuing legal action.
“Legal proceedings are currently ongoing to decide how material seized during the searches will be managed and whether we can lawfully retain it in support of our ongoing investigation,” the force said.
The Old Bailey issued warrants to allow Thames Valley Police to search Mountbatten-Windsor’s home on the Sandringham Estate in Norfolk and his former home at Royal Lodge in Windsor Great Park before his arrest on February 19th.
His arrest was the first of a member of the royal family on a criminal warrant since King Charles I at the end of the English civil war.
“Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office by a man in his 60s from Norfolk remains ongoing, and we continue to pursue all reasonable lines of enquiry to effectively and fairly progress this investigation,” Thames Valley Police said.
Police launched an investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor’s conduct after revelations in the US department of justice’s Epstein files about his conduct while an unpaid special representative for UK Trade and Investment between 2001 and 2011.
Communications in the files between Mountbatten-Windsor and Jeffrey Epstein, a convicted sex offender, show that the then-prince advocated for Epstein on a state visit to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) with the late queen Elizabeth in 2010.
They also showed he sought to broker an $8 billion loan between China and the UAE before the start of an official visit to China later the same year. They showed that he had shared information acquired as a result of his trade role with Epstein and his associates.
Mountbatten-Windsor denies wrongdoing. Thames Valley said on Thursday that it was continuing with its inquiries. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: RTÉ DG says he has confidence in Minister after ‘constructive’ meeting on funding
description: Broadcaster’s managing director and chairman Terence O’Rourke met Patrick O’Donovan for just over an hour
author_name: Martin Wall, Ian Curran, Cormac McQuinn, Marie O’Halloran, Vivienne Clarke
content:
RTÉ director general Kevin Bakhurst has described a meeting with Minister for Media Patrick O’Donovan as “extremely constructive” after a row broke out over funding for the State broadcaster.
The meeting came after RTÉ was allocated €240 million in the budget, €20 million less than was expected under the terms of a deal with the last government.
Bakhurst and RTÉ board chairman Terence O’Rourke met O’Donovan for just over an hour on Thursday afternoon.
“We’ve agreed that we’re going to carry on working with his [O’Donovan’s] officials to try and find a resolution to this,” Bakhurst said afterwards.
He described the meeting as “very positive” and said RTÉ welcomed this, but insisted he would not be answering questions as the situation is “delicate enough”, adding: “We want this process to be properly carried out”.
On whether RTÉ will get its money, Bakhurst said he did not know. Asked if he has confidence in the Minister, Bakhurst said: “Absolutely, yes.”
In a statement, the Department of Media described the meeting as “positive”.
“The Minister listened to the concerns of the RTÉ chair and director general in relation to Government funding and the support for the implementation of the strategy,” it said.
“The chair and director general provided assurances on the delivery of reforms and their timing. The department and RTÉ will continue to engage constructively on all the issues discussed over the next few weeks.”
Meanwhile, TG4 said it had requested its own meeting with the Minister and is awaiting a response.
“Reliance on annual budget decisions limits TG4’s long-term planning and investment and creates uncertainty for the Irish independent production sector, much of which is made up of SMEs,” the Irish-language broadcaster said in a statement.
“The budget outcome is particularly disappointing given TG4’s very strong performance in 2025,” it went on, highlighting audience growth and increasing audience share.
Earlier, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) said it will ask RTÉ and the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport to appear before it in the coming weeks regarding RTÉ funding and staffing numbers.
The move came after it emerged that RTÉ is to be funded to the tune of €240 million next year, €20 million less than it had been expecting under a multiyear bailout deal between the last government and the broadcaster.
On Wednesday, O’Donovan denied the move was a “cut” to RTÉ’s funding, despite the previous Government promising to increase the amount to €260 million next year.
He said the deal made with RTÉ amounted to “almost three-quarters of a billion euros ... an enormous amount of money from the taxpayers”.
O’Donovan also said he was not happy with the pace of change at the broadcaster and its transition to being a “more agile, smaller” organisation.
Bakhurst has rejected O’Donovan’s assertion that the pace of reform at Montrose has been inadequate.
The PAC chairman, John Brady of Sinn Féin, said on Thursday that there had been a comprehensive discussion among members at a private session and it had been agreed to schedule an engagement with the parties after the October break.
He said there had been “considerable concerns” expressed by members of the committee.
James Geoghegan of Fine Gael said the State had provided RTÉ with €50 million as part of the broadcaster’s reform strategy to fund a voluntary exit programme of 400 people. He said RTÉ had maintained that 100 people had left the organisation.
He said actually 67 people had departed under the exit scheme and the balance to the 100 figure was made up of posts that had been suppressed – following the retirement or resignation of staff members.
“We need to hear from the secretary general of the department about what control mechanisms are being put in place so we don’t arrive at the situation we are currently in where one side is saying the strategy is not being delivered and the other side is saying the strategy is being delivered and we don’t know where the truth lies,” he said.
On Thursday morning, The Irish Times reported that O’Donovan warned Coalition leaders in a letter last Friday that the Government would “renege” on its funding deal with RTÉ if more cash wasn’t found for his department.
It is understood that Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers , Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris and Taoiseach Micheál Martin believed that extra funding made available to the Department of Communications during tense negotiations over the weekend would solve any difficulties with the RTÉ allocation, but were only made aware of this issue on the day the budget was announced.
[ TG4 and Screen Ireland budget funding amounts to ‘cut’ in real terms, industry warns Opens in new window ]
Separately, it was confirmed that TG4 ’s funding would remain static next year. The Irish-language broadcaster had requested an additional €11 million in funding in Budget 2027, bringing its total allocation to €76.4 million. TG4 ard-stiúrthóir Deirdre Ní Choistín said the broadcaster would now have to “assess the impact” on its plans and strategic priorities for next year.
Ireland’s media watchdog, Coimisiún na Meán , has expressed disappointment that Budget 2027 has “not allowed for the delivery of the level of funding to RTÉ that was previously outlined in the Government’s plans”.
[ Most skirmishes before and after the budget featured Patrick O’Donovan Opens in new window ]
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) meanwhile said it is “deeply concerned” by the Government’s decision to cut RTÉ’s funding.
The EBU is an alliance of public service media organisations of which RTÉ and TG4 are members.
In a statement it said RTÉ “entered into agreements with independent producers and other partners, invested in Irish drama, live sport and digital services, and continued to deliver trusted, independent news and analysis”.
“Withdrawing €20 million in the final year, with those commitments already in place, breaks the agreement and leaves RTÉ to fund commitments it made in good faith.”
In Leaders’ Questions in the Dáil, Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke said the two sides would “try to work this out”.
But Social Democrats media spokeswoman Sinéad Gibney criticised O’Donovan, questioning the sequence of events that led to the cut.
“He lashes out, be it the Arts Council, be it An Post and now RTÉ,” she said. “So what is the truth? Because if RTÉ wasn’t fulfilling its commitment, why wasn’t it raised until three hours before the budget, and why wasn’t the reason given to RTÉ or to anybody indeed until the press conference a day later?”
The co-chair of the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) group in RTÉ, Trevor Keegan, told Morning Ireland he was shocked to hear of the €20 million reduction in funding for the State broadcaster next year.
[ RTÉ ‘caught off-guard’ by €20m cut in funding in Budget 2027 Opens in new window ]
The announcement had come as a “bolt from the blue” and would have an impact on his members and colleagues and fellow unions across the organisation, he said.
Keegan said the NUJ did not “necessarily support” the voluntary exit package and other elements of the five-year strategy.
“What we do support is correct funding for this organisation. If the Minister really was brave, instead of just simply going for the easy option of docking money from the organisation, he and his colleagues would actually grasp the nettle that is the funding for this organisation that was mooted in the Future Media Commission Report 2022, a joint committee from the Oireachtas in 2024 saying that it should be exchequer funding that funds this organisation properly. None of them are willing to do that.
“Instead, it’s the easy option: cut more money from RTÉ and expect us to do its remit for less.”

title: ‘Astonishing and bizarre’ elm in Co Down crowned tree of the year
description: Tree originally planted in the mid-19th century as part of a row on town’s promenade to shelter the main street from sea winds
content:
An “astonishing and bizarre” tree in Northern Ireland has been crowned the winner of this year’s tree of the year competition in the UK.
The wych elm tree, located in Newcastle, Co Down , owes its name to its near horizontal trunk, which has grown sideways owing to the strong seaside winds coming off the Irish Sea.
The 150-year-old tree has resisted Dutch elm disease, a fungus that has destroyed most of the UK’s 30m (98ft) elms, making it a worthy winner of the competition’s “against the odds” theme.
The tree was originally planted in the mid-19th century as part of a row of wych elms along the town’s promenade to shelter the main street from sea winds.
Many of those trees were felled during redevelopments of the town, with the so-called “bendy tree” now the last one standing.
“When you look at this astonishing and bizarre tree, there’s no doubt about what it has endured,” said May Chemais, ancient tree inventory lead for the Woodland Trust, the charity that runs the annual competition.
“We’ve all been through changes and hardships that have shaped who we are: I think that’s why the bendy tree has struck a chord with people,” she said.
For John Martin, director of the Woodland Trust NI, it is the whimsical nature of the tree that makes it a worthy winner.
[ The drive to plant trees on Ireland’s farmland: ‘In the future a field without trees will be worthless’ Opens in new window ]
Having grown up visiting Newcastle as a child, Martin recalls seeing the tree out of the corner of his eye and being surprised to see a tree growing this way.
“You expect nature to behave in a certain way and we would expect a tree, most of the time, to grow upwards, whereas this one has grown sideways,” he said. “I guess it gives people a bit of a smile on their day.”
The tree’s unusual shape has also provided welcome shade to residents and visitors resting on the bench located beneath its branches.
“Older trees like this one are providing our communities with so much – from shade, wellbeing and health benefits, to stories, culture and pride of place,” said Chemais.
Other trees nominated in this year’s competition included the Crowhurst yew in Crowhurst, Surrey, England.
Villagers hollowed out the trunk in 1820 to create a parish meeting room within the tree. The roof of this room collapsed during a storm in 1845, but the tree lived on, with the wooden door to the secret room remaining to this day.
Also in the top 10 shortlist was the Culmstock yew in Culmstock, Devon, England. This tree is perched on top a 20m high church tower, with its existence predating residents’ living memories.
Last year’s honour went to a 75ft ash tree that shades homes on one of Glasgow’s busiest roads. – Guardian

title: Christa Pike ‘up and walking’ after botched execution, lawyer says
description: Pike, whose ordeal has galvanised critics of the death penalty, remains in hospital
content:
Christa Pike is “up and walking” in hospital, her lawyer said, eight days after she survived two lethal injections during a botched execution in Tennessee.
The recovery marks a dramatic turnaround after Pike was declared brain dead on Monday, before waking up and beginning to speak on Tuesday. Her ordeal has shocked many in the US and overseas and galvanised critics of the death penalty.
Stephen Ferrell, a lawyer on Pike’s legal team, told the BBC that she was able to walk, but remained mentally foggy. “What’s been described to me is that physically there’s quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she’s not able to use them very much,” Ferrell said.
“She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far,” he added.
Pike (50), was taken to hospital unconscious but alive from Tennessee’s execution chamber on September 30th, after receiving two doses of the barbiturate pentobarbital.
After the botched execution attempt, one of her lawyers called the process “cruel and torturous”, adding that he had counted seven needles in Pike’s left arm, “one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her”. Pike had lifted her head from the execution gurney to say her arms were burning as the drug was administered.
Pike’s team is seeking psychological support for her, given that “clearly is necessary now”, Ferrell said. On Wednesday, Pike was described as “angry and confused” after regaining consciousness.
Ferrell said of Pike’s mental state: “I think it’s kind of good and bad. Good that she is fairly with it, but she’s also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she’s going.”
He said it remains to be seen whether Pike makes a full recovery.
“I assume [Pike’s condition] will keep improving, but there could be some permanent damage. We don’t know that yet.”
On Wednesday Randy Spivey, another attorney for Pike, said she was unable to move her arms and has pneumonia and a blood clot. Despite her condition, Pike was still being restrained, her team said, shackled to her hospital bed by her feet and right arm.
Pike’s lawyers had warned before the execution that officials might struggle to locate veins and cause her suffering in the process, but the state had pushed to proceed and the US supreme court allowed the prison to move forward.
There is speculation from medical experts that perhaps some or a lot of the drug missed her vein and went into tissue, that one of her veins, which were problematic and this fact flagged by her lawyers months earlier – blew, or that the drug was faulty, or a combination.
Pike was 18 and her then boyfriend 17 at the time when they killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps, in Tennessee in 1995.
According to prosecutors, Pike was worried Slemmer was trying to take the boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, away from her. Together, they lured Slemmer into a wooded area, tortured and killed her.
Shipp was convicted of first-degree murder in 1997 and was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Pike has never denied her involvement in Slemmer’s killing. She was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder but, because she was 18, she was sentenced to death and has been on death row, isolated, for 30 years.
Pike’s attorneys have argued that her original legal team failed to present evidence about the sexual and physical abuse she suffered during childhood. Tennessee’s governor, Bill Lee, blocked Pike’s request for clemency. He has since halted the state’s remaining executions for the rest of the year and has ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred”. – Guardian
[ Keith Duggan: Life, death and a botched execution in Tennessee Opens in new window ]

title: ‘I said I had a headache every day’: Hospital apologises for Mayo woman’s brain tumour diagnosis delays
description: Mary Keane (49) had two MRI scans after suffering severe headaches, but these were misreported, it was claimed
content:
A hospital has apologised in court for “the deficiencies in care” to a woman on two occasions, which led to a delay in the diagnosis of her brain tumour.
Mary Keane (49), who was suffering from severe headaches, had two brain MRI scans at University Hospital Galway in 2013 and 2016, but it was claimed these were misreported, the High Court heard on Thursday. The woman was not diagnosed with a brain tumour until she had another MRI scan in 2023.
Jonathan Kilfeather, counsel for Keane, instructed by solicitor Damien Tansey, told the court Keane could have had surgery had the brain tumour been spotted in 2013 and 2016. He said she would still have a terminal cancer diagnosis, but her life would have been extended by five years.
The apology was read to the court as Keane, from Westport, Co Mayo , settled a High Court action against the HSE .
In a letter of apology, hospital general manager Chris Kane apologised on behalf of the Galway hospital “for the deficiencies in care in 2013 and in 2016 which led to the delay in the diagnosis of your brain tumour”.
The letter added: “We wish to acknowledge the upset and distress that this caused you. We deeply regret this and offer you our sincere apologies.”
Outside court, Keane, who uses a wheelchair, said she was distraught and devastated.
“I don’t know how many years I have left to live. I can’t work, I can’t stay in the house on my own. I was let down, I was up and down to the hospital in Galway, I said I had a headache every single day,” she said.
[ Boy (8) settles action over circumstances of birth at Cork hospital for €7.5m Opens in new window ]
She described the apology as “disgusting” but said, “at least I got something”. She said it was “a little too late”.
Keane had sued the HSE over her care at University Hospital Galway.
She had, in 2005, suffered a head injury when she hit her head off the pavement during an assault. She was seen at Mayo University Hospital and diagnosed with a mild traumatic brain injury, and a scalp laceration was treated.
From October 2005 to November 2006, Keane complained of headaches and was referred to neurology in University Hospital Galway.
A number of investigations were carried out, with an MRI brain scan in January 2013. It was claimed that this scan was misreported, which suggested that the lesion was established and probably related to trauma.
It was claimed this would have misled the treating neurologists into believing that Keane’s only issue related to features arising from her head injury in 2005. The scan, it is claimed, should have been reported as showing an incidental but very significant new brain lesion.
It was contended that, had the January 2013 scan been correctly reported, Keane would have been referred to neurosurgeons and had a surgical resection in March 2013.
A repeat MRI was planned but not performed until January 2016. It was claimed that the reporting of this 2016 scan fell below the standard of a competent general radiologist and an immediate referral for a neurological opinion should have been recommended.
[ Man who suffered stroke in Cork hospital settles action for €1.2m Opens in new window ]
Had the January 2016 scan been correctly reported, Keane, it is claimed, would have been referred to neurosurgeons in January 2016 and seen the following month, which would have led to surgery in March of that year.
In 2020, Keane reported an episode of blurred vision, and she had up to 12 headache episodes a month. She continued to have periodic headaches, but in 2023 she began to have more significant headaches
An MRI scan in 2023 showed the lesion, which had spread. Keane was transferred to Beaumont Hospital Dublin, where a brain biopsy was carried out and she was told that the tumour was not suitable for surgical resection and instead she had radiotherapy.
Noting the settlement, Judge Leonie Reynolds said Keane had been through a very difficult time.

title: Dan Sheehan to lead Leinster as Leo Cullen names completely changed side to play Cardiff
description: Key Irish internationals return for all four provinces for URC weekend
content:
Leo Cullen has named a completely changed Leinster starting XV for Saturday’s homecoming URC game at the Laya Arena against Cardiff (kick-off 7.45pm, live on TG4 and Premier Sports 1). Among them are 10 of Leinster’s 16 summer tourists with Ireland, all but one of whom will be making their seasonal reappearance.
The returning Dan Sheehan will lead the side, having also captained Ireland in the Nations Championship games last July against Australia and New Zealand in the absence of Caelan Doris. He will be joined by Tadhg Furlong, Joe McCarthy, James Ryan and Jack Conan up front.
Hugo Keenan, Garry Ringrose, Jamie Osborne and Jimmy O’Brien also return with Sam Prendergast starting at outhalf after his eye-catching cameo in last week’s 22-20 defeat away to the Sharks.
He is partnered by academy scrumhalf Oliver Coffey, who was also a replacement last week, and winger Josh Kenny, who was not part of Leinster’ South African trip. Alex Usanov, Max Deegan and Scott Penny, who started in the opening 27-26 loss to the Lions in Johannesburg, complete the starting team.
Aside from Peter Dooley, who was a replacement in that game, the bench is comprised of players who started last week in Durban, namely Rónan Kelleher, Thomas Clarkson, Alan Spicer, Josh Ericson, Fintan Gunne, Caspar Gabriel and Robbie Henshaw.
Leinster: Hugo Keenan; Joshua Kenny, Garry Ringrose, Jamie Osborne, Jimmy O’Brien; Sam Prendergast, Oliver Coffey; Alex Usanov, Dan Sheehan (capt), Tadgh Furlong; Joe McCarthy, James Ryan; Max Deegan, Scott Penny, Jack Conan. Replacements: Rónan Kelleher, Peter Dooley, Thomas Clarkson, Alan Spicer, Josh Ericson, Fintan Gunne, Caspar Gabriel, Robbie Henshaw.
Bundee Aki will make his first start of the season as Connacht head coach Stuart Lancaster has named his team to play Glasgow Warriors at Scotstoun Stadium (kick-off 7.45pm, live on TG4 and Premier Sports).
A strong line-up includes all seven players who were named in the Irish summer tour.
Props Billy Bohan and Sam Illo start after impressive cameos off the bench last week, while Darragh Murray, captain Cian Prendergast, Sean Jansen and Ciarán Frawley are all retained.
There are five other changes from the team that started against Benetton, with hooker Eoin de Buitléar, lock Niall Murray, backrower Paul Boyle, and backs Shayne Bolton and Josh Ioane all coming in.
Ioane starts at fullback and is named an exciting back three alongside Bolton and Mack Hansen, while Cathal Forde continues at with Aki. Scrumhalf Caolin Blade completes the team.
The bench includes the returning Shamus Hurley-Langton who missed last week’s game due to injury.

Replacements: Matthew Victory, Francois van Wyk, Finlay Bealham, Josh Murphy, Shamus Hurley-Langton, Colm Reilly, Sean Naughton, Sam Gilbert.
Captain Tadhg Beirne starts as Munster make nine changes to their team to play Ulster at Affidea Stadium (5.30pm, live on Premier Sports).
It is Beirne’s first appearance for Munster since the home win over Ulster in April as he missed the end of last season through injury.
Beirne, Ben O’Connor, Alex Nankivell, JJ Hanrahan, Jeremy Loughman, Kieran Brookes, Jack O’Donoghue, Alex Kendellen and Gavin Coombes have all been chosen in the starting line-up by head coach Clayton McMillan.
O’Connor, Shane Daly and Seán O’Brien start in the back three with Dan Kelly and Nankivell forming the midfield partnership. Craig Casey and Hanrahan start together in the halfbacks.
Jeremy Loughman and new signings Marnus van der Merwe and Kieran Brookes pack down in the frontrow. Evan O’Connell and Beirne are named in the engine room. O’Donoghue, Kendellen and Coombes form an all-new backrow.
Diarmuid Barron, Josh Wycherley and new signing Jack Aungier provide the frontrow backup as Tom Ahern, Brian Gleeson and John Hodnett complete the forward cover. The 21-year-old scrumhalf Ben O’Donovan and 20-year-old outhalf Charlie O’Shea are the backline replacements.

The frontrow remains unchanged as loosehead prop, Eric O’Sullivan, hooker Tom Stewart and tighthead prop Keynan Knox all keep their places.
In a new look secondrow, Ben Donnell starts alongside Eli Snyman.
There are wholesale changes to the backrow, with Ireland internationals Cormac Izuchukwu and Nick Timoney starting at blindside flanker and openside flanker respectively. South African number eight Juarno Augustus makes his first start of the season after a try-scoring cameo from the bench against Glasgow Warriors.
Irish international scrumhalf Nathan Doak makes his first start of the season, joining outhalf Jack Murphy in the half-back partnership.
Ireland centre Stuart McCloskey makes his return at 12, partnering Jamie Benson at outside centre.
McCloskey is in line for his 218th appearance in an Ulster jersey, equalling that of former captain Rory Best and moving him to joint-third in the most senior appearances in Ulster Rugby history.
