title: Man charged over 2003 sexual assault of young mother during south Dublin burglary
description: Assailant posing as a repairman forced his way into woman’s home in Kilmacud and bound her with plastic ties
content:
A man in his 60s has been charged in connection with a serious sexual assault on a young mother at her home in Kilmacud, south Dublin , 23 years ago.
He is due to appear at the Criminal Courts of Justice this afternoon.
The woman was assaulted during an aggravated burglary on March 31st, 2003.
The man, aged about 40 at the time, came to the woman’s home pretending to be a cable television technician .
He forced his way into the house and bound the woman with plastic ties before sexually assaulting her while threatening her with a knife.
The woman’s young baby was in the house at the time of the attack.
An extensive Garda investigation took place with over 100 statements taken, but the suspect was not caught.
Gardaí reviewed the case three years ago, ultimately leading to a breakthrough.
A man was arrested by investigating gardaí on Wednesday. He was detained under section four of the Criminal Justice Act 1984 in a Garda station in Dublin.

title: Former Kerry footballer says ‘10 seconds of recklessness’ by driver changed his life forever
description: Seán O’Leary sustained multiple fractures and developed PTSD after collision in 2021
content:
A former Kerry footballer has said “10 seconds of recklessness” by a young driver changed his life forever.
Seán O’Leary (27) was seriously injured in a crash on July 10th, 2021, while travelling home from a match with his girlfriend Emma O’Connor.
Their car was struck near Abbeyfeale, close to the Limerick - Kerry border, when another driver overtook traffic on a bend on the wrong side of the road.
O’Leary said the actions of Michael Harty had “severe consequences for myself and Emma, and for all our loved ones”.
The All-Ireland minor football winner sustained life-changing injuries and developed post-traumatic stress disorder after the “horrific” crash.
He was unconscious for about 15 minutes after the crash, and O’Connor thought he was dead. He woke up in “excruciating” pain and saw “my right femur bone hanging out through my leg”.
O’Leary was rushed to University Hospital Kerry in Tralee, where he was resuscitated.
He recalled the crash while speaking at the Road Safety Authority’s ( RSA ) annual conference in Dublin on Thursday. The theme of the event was young driver risk.
Seán Canney , Minister of State with responsibility for road safety, also addressed the conference. He said the fatal M9 motorway crash in August “showed the terrible harm that reckless behaviour can cause”.
“ Wrong-way driving is extraordinarily dangerous, and no moment of attention, online or otherwise, is worth putting a life at risk,” Canney said.
[ A5 ruling a ‘relief’ for bereaved families, All-Ireland winner who lost two siblings says Opens in new window ]
Five teenagers, who were in a car driving the wrong way down the motorway, died in the collision on August 16th. Three women and a child, who were in a vehicle struck by the teenagers’ car, were seriously injured .
The crash highlighted a trend of young people filming themselves driving the wrong way down roads and posting the footage on social media.
Canney said the crash brought the reality of reckless driving “home in the starkest possible way”.
O’Leary said, following the crash in 2021, he “had to endure an absolute rollercoaster of a journey, both physically and psychologically, in order to get myself and my life back on track”.
He sustained several injuries, including fractures to both femurs, a fracture to his right tibia and fibula, a fractured sternum and a significant concussion.
He spent four months in a wheelchair and underwent multiple surgeries, including the insertion of titanium rods into both legs. His recovery involved a lengthy period of physical and psychological rehabilitation.
[ Calls for ban on rickshaws in Dublin following death of young mother Opens in new window ]
The crash brought his inter-county football career to an end.
“In the years since the crash, Emma and I have had to travel the length and breadth of this country, working with physical and rehabilitation specialists and psychological professionals trying to rebuild our lives.”
O’Leary said he and O’Connor are aware they are very lucky to have survived the crash, but added: “I don’t think lucky describes what people have to deal with after a serious car crash, especially the ones that they do not cause themselves.”
Harty, who had a previous conviction for speeding, pleaded not guilty to dangerous driving causing serious bodily harm, but was found guilty by a jury and jailed for four years with the final year suspended in 2024.
O’Leary said the fact Harty received a jail sentence and a driving ban “really mattered to us, because people convicted of dangerous driving must be held accountable ... but nothing that happened in court that day can undo the damage”.
[ What one Kerry road tells us about speed limits and road safety Opens in new window ]
O’Leary said he speaks publicly about his story to “prevent it from becoming someone else’s”. He received a standing ovation after his speech.
The crash O’Leary was injured in happened at about 11pm, while the M9 crash occurred at around 3am. Research published by the RSA on Thursday showed that late night and early morning are particularly high-risk periods for young drivers involved in fatal crashes.
Between 2021 and 2025, 189 drivers aged between 17 and 25 were involved in 178 fatal crashes in the Republic. These young drivers accounted for 19 per cent of all drivers involved in fatal crashes during this period.
Nearly one-third of fatal crashes involving a young driver occurred between 8pm and midnight. A further 21 per cent occurred between midnight and 4am. Of the 189 young drivers, 156 (83 per cent) were male.
Sam Waide, RSA chief executive, said the research “shows that while young drivers account for a relatively small proportion of the driving population, they are over-represented in fatal collisions”.
“The concentration of fatal collisions during late-night and early-morning hours, alongside the strong representation of young men, highlights particular areas for continued focus in road safety policy, education, enforcement and intervention.”
[ Seven years after asking, gardaí cannot access driving licence photos Opens in new window ]
Canney said the Government is committed to reducing the number of deaths on Irish roads, which have increased in recent years after “decades of reducing road deaths”.
“Reversing that trend is a central priority for me, for my department and for this Government.”
He said he hoped new learner permit rules, stricter regulations on e-bikes and scramblers and education campaigns targeting young drivers would help reduce collisions and fatalities.

title: Ronaldo v Messi debate has surely been settled – there is only one winner
description: Final playing days show a clear difference between the modern game’s two greats
content:
R emember when we used to argue about Messi and Ronaldo ?
Theirs has been the defining individual rivalry in the history of professional football, and, in fairness, it used to be a reasonably fair fight. But the final few years of their respective international careers have seen Messi decisively settle the debate as to who has been the greatest of them all.
Just look at the contrast of this week. Where Ronaldo flounced out of the Portugal squad amid a storm of recrimination and bad feeling, Messi said farewell to Argentina at a specially arranged game in Buenos Aires that was less a farewell match than a last sacrament of consecration.
Benin provided the necessary cast of extras known as the opposition for a game that stopped in the 10th minute to celebrate Messi with a fireworks display and one last theatre of supplication from the Argentina fans in the stands. Messi would score, obviously, from the penalty spot in a 3-0 win, and afterwards everyone craned their necks to watch a drone light show in the sky. This was the first time Messi joined everyone in looking upwards in wonder – he was usually the subject of these slack-jawed gazes.
Messi took the microphone and delivered a farewell address to the stadium in that quiet, reticent tone of his while some of his team-mates sobbed uncontrollably. That Messi has inspired this level of devotion among team-mates is a reminder that not all leaders need to be stentorian speechmakers.
While Messi was saying goodbye, Ronaldo had taken a brief vow of silence. Having apparently fallen out with head coach Jorge Jesus over his decision not to use him as a substitute against Norway, Ronaldo exiled himself from the Portugal squad, saying little beyond issuing a gnomic promise to one day tell the truth as to what happened.
That day arrived on Wednesday, when Ronaldo published a statement of almost 1,800 words giving his version of events. In being so critical of the head coach, Ronaldo revealed he has a different kind of Jesus complex.
Across the long statement, Ronaldo claimed Jesus had denied him three times. First the coach told Ronaldo to stay at home for the Nations League games away to Norway and Denmark, only to relent. Secondly, Jesus agreed to put him on the bench against Norway and promised to play him for 30 minutes, only to have him warm up without playing at all. Finally, Ronaldo claims the coach promised to clarify the whole situation by reading a statement approved by Ronaldo at the prematch press conference, only for Jesus to allegedly renege on the deal.
[ Malachy Clerkin: Pep Guardiola said Manchester City destroyed football – he didn’t know how right he was Opens in new window ]
The most absurd element of the whole story is the fact Ronaldo published the eight points that had been given to Jesus to read at the press conference. They read as an abject coda to Ronaldo’s career. They include Jesus taking full responsibility for what had happened against Norway and are heavily seasoned with gratuitous tribute to Ronaldo.
Jesus was supposed to describe Ronaldo as “exemplary, loyal, and professional”, herald the “the weight he has in the world”, and then castigate himself for his short-sightedness for “putting someone of the stature of Pelé or Maradona on to warm up and then not putting him in the game”. (That Messi isn’t listed here may mark a brief outbreak of self-awareness on Ronaldo’s part.)
Ronaldo’s briefing document did not acknowledge that Jesus may have chosen to leave him on the bench because he is 41 years of age.
Ronaldo’s career end is now the familiar tale of the great player who has gone on too long. In Ronaldo’s case, he has played for much too long and is perhaps the only player in the history of the game who has gone on two World Cups too far. He did once stand in haughty defiance of his advancing age, but that was five years ago, when he broke the international scoring record with two late goals against Ireland. He has since been routed by Father Time at the top level; his tap-ins and penalties against low-ranking opposition a poor compensation for his inhibiting a hugely talented Portugal team at three straight major tournaments.
And yet Ronaldo has been unable to step away from the main stage, and has instead tried to pretend that everything is still as it ever was. He has tried to do with Jorge Jesus as he has done with so many others, continuing to try to arrange supplicants around him like a child arranging a teddy-bear picnic. It must be galling for Ronaldo that the deference that once came automatically from those around him must now be consciously demanded.
[ The fight was dubbed ‘a fascinating experiment’: would boxing fans show decency and taste? Opens in new window ]
But this is the consequence of going on for too long. Messi’s career winter has been far more graceful because he is simply a better footballer. Unlike Ronaldo, his game is not rooted in belligerent physicality, but in an astounding ability to compute time and space. Messi’s gifts have a longer lifespan, and they have allowed him to retire an icon among Argentinians who embraced him more coolly in the early part of his career.
Ronaldo will ultimately be remembered in similar terms in Portugal, and he will surely be given a similarly grand farewell game at some stage. But his pretensions to be the greatest player of all time are over: he has lost the argument with Messi, and he has lost it partly because he has been unable to stop fighting it.

title: Bank of Ireland contains losses on US leveraged finance loans with insurance deals
description: Specialist institutional investors took on credit risk for millions of euro of potential losses on loans
content:
Bank of Ireland has contained losses in its US leveraged acquisition loan book through insurance deals that shared the risk with specialist investors.
The leveraged acquisition loan portfolios were typically issued as part of a club of banks to companies internationally going through a buyout or capital reorganisation.
The bank decided last February to wind down its US leveraged acquisition finance unit, which had a portfolio of €2.5 billion a few years ago. That had fallen to €1.2 billion by the end of June. It will be wound down over three years.
Bank of Ireland entered into transactions in December 2021 and May 2024 that saw specialist institutional investors take on credit risk for millions of euro of potential losses on the portfolios of loans. These deals, carried out by issuing bonds , are known as significant risk transfer (SRT) deals.
Bloomberg reported on Thursday that ArrowMark Financial, a long-standing investor in SRTs, now values the remaining bonds from Bank of Ireland’s 2021 transaction at around 34 US cents on the dollar. This reflects the losses being borne by the bondholders from a surge on problem loans in the US leveraged finance market in recent times, driven by a spike in interest rates following an extended period of cheap finance.
Meanwhile, First Trust Alternative Opportunities Fund marked down its outstanding position in a similar SRT issued in 2024 to 91 cents, Bloomberg said.
A spokesman for Bank of Ireland, which is led by chief executive Myles O’Grady , declined to comment.
Under SRT transactions, the original bank lenders typically face initial losses on a problem loans, with SRT investors assuming an agreed amount of potential losses thereafter. These insurance deals allow banks to free up some expensive capital that they would otherwise have to hold against the loan portfolios.
Bonds relating to both the affected transactions paid coupons – or interest – of more than 13 per cent a year, reflecting the perceived risk involved at the outset.
Bank of Ireland said in its 2024 annual report that specific corporate defaults in the US acquisition finance portfolio drove a €127 million group loan loss charge that year. Defaults in this business made up a portion of €110 million of impairment losses booked in its non-property small and medium enterprise (SME) and corporate loan portfolio in 2025, according to its latest annual report.
The opacity of the structures and private nature of the market means it’s often difficult to establish the magnitude and frequency of these writedowns.
Still, SRT issuance has boomed in recent years, enabling mostly European and North American lenders to offload risk tied to $1 trillion (€890 billion) in loans and to release capital for new lending or shareholder payouts. – Additional reporting, Reuters

title: Price of Porsche’s top models to rise by 20% to more than €330,000 by 2030
description: German sports-car maker echoes Ferrari with bet on exclusivity to boost profits
content:
Porsche will raise the average price of its most expensive models by about a fifth by 2030, as the German sports-car maker aims to echo Ferrari’s strategy of using exclusivity to boost profits.
Chief executive Michael Leiters outlined a years-long plan at an investor day on Wednesday to revive Porsche’s fortunes by selling fewer but more upmarket cars following a costly unwinding of its electric vehicle ambitions last year.
“We want to further elevate our positioning, protect the exclusivity of Porsche and gain pricing power,” said Leiters, the former McLaren boss who took over in January. “This brand has a lot of power.”
The average price of Porsche’s top models will increase to more than €330,000 by the end of the decade from about €270,000 this year, while the proportion of its portfolio made up of top-end models is expected to rise to 45 per cent from a third currently.
Porsche’s shift towards higher-margin sports cars and limited editions of exclusive models echoes a signature Ferrari strategy that has helped the Italian carmaker achieve an industry-beating operating profit margin of 30 per cent.
Porsche historically contributed outsize profits to the Volkswagen Group thanks to explosive growth in China . But its fortunes have reversed dramatically as sales plummeted in the world’s largest car market and it was hit by higher US tariffs . The company has also taken huge writedowns to reinvest in petrol models it abandoned during a big pivot to electric cars.
Leiters’ strategy will result in a much smaller Porsche, with the company reducing the number of vehicles it needs to sell to turn a profit to fewer than 200,000 units. The group delivered about 320,000 cars in 2023, when it had an operating profit margin of 18 per cent, but last year its margin plunged to 1.1 per cent on deliveries of roughly 280,000 cars.
The group on Wednesday maintained its target to achieve an operating profit margin of 10 to 15 per cent and an automotive net cash flow margin of up to 12 per cent by 2030. It will target a profit margin of 15 per cent by 2035.
Porsche is betting on a new combustion-engine version of its bestselling Macan, due in 2028, to revive its profits and offset falling sales in China.
It also plans to unveil a new SUV, which will come in petrol and plug-in hybrid versions, in the same year and develop a new super-sports car to be priced higher than its signature 911 model.
“We are becoming more selective about where we can compete and more ambitious in the segments where we see the strongest fit with our brand,” Leiters said.
Leiters, who previously served as Ferrari’s chief technology officer, said its plan to shift sales towards more expensive, higher-margin products would be accompanied by 20 per cent cuts in product development costs and the number of model variants it makes.
The company has already reached a deal with unions to cut 9,000 jobs – or roughly 20 per cent of its workforce – by 2035.
UBS analyst Patrick Hummel said Porsche should “comfortably” return to double-digit profit margins by the end of the decade if Leiters was successful in executing his strategy.
“It’s replicating what Ferrari has been successful at. Porsche also has the potential to [sell] more at the upper end and offer more exclusivity with the right models,” he said.
Leiters told the FT last week that “there won’t be a 911 electric”, although the company is going ahead with the electric version of its 718 sports car next year.
On Wednesday, Porsche said it would aim for a two-to-one split between petrol and plug-in hybrids versus EVs.
Scott Sherwood, an independent analyst of luxury car brands, said Ferrari had been able to build its strategy around “scarcity” because it only sold about 14,000 models a year. Even with the right sizing, Porsche’s scale would be much bigger, he said.
“They have a big brand challenge. Porsche is a sports car brand, and sports cars at supercar pricing only works with a small group of brands with the most hard-core loyalists,” Sherwood said. “It’s a bit like Rolex deciding they want to go after Patek Philippe buyers.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: UK royal navy member appears in London court charged with spying for Russia
description: Teddy Young (24) was accused of obtaining protected information that could benefit unnamed foreign power
content:
A serving member of the UK royal navy has appeared in court charged with spying for Russia .
Teddy Young (24) was accused of obtaining protected information that could benefit an unnamed foreign power. He was arrested at his home in Bedfordshire on Tuesday after an investigation by Counter-Terrorism Policing London (CTPL).
He was charged with offences under the national security Act, the Metropolitan police said on Thursday.
Young, a naval intelligence rating, is alleged to have abused high-level security clearance to access secret defence and intelligence data after being deployed on a navy vessel.
He is accused of drafting a message in Russian containing classified information and had allegedly taken steps to make direct contact with the Russian authorities.
Young was first arrested in May last year. At that point he was suspended and relieved of his duties, and he was on gardening leave until his latest arrest.
Young appeared at Westminster magistrates’ court wearing a grey navy tracksuit, and he spoke only to confirm his name.
While there was no application for bail, the district judge Annabelle Pilling told Young: “On the basis of the information I have already read, there are substantial grounds to believe that if granted bail you would not come back to court and that you would make efforts to avoid further court appearances and would commit further offences.”
Young was remanded in custody to appear before a specialist judge at the Old Bailey on October 16th.
The crown prosecution service authorised the charges on Wednesday. They allege that between November 26th, 2024, and May 21st, 2025, Young engaged in conduct in preparation for committing an offence of disclosing protected information.
It is also alleged that in the same period he obtained, copied, recorded or retained protected information, intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power.
Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of CTPL, said in a statement issued before the court appearance: “These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces. We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the ministry of defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter.”
The arrest and charges are not connected to the recent investigation into an incident at RAF Fairford .
A royal navy spokesperson said: “A member of the royal navy has been charged with national security Act offences following an investigation by Counter-Terrorism Policing London. As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage.” – Guardian

title: Irish Government was warned last year that RTÉ funding was too low
description: Coimisiún na Meán said broadcaster would face ‘particularly acute’ cash flow issues in 2027
content:
Ireland’s media regulator and an external consultancy firm both told the Government last year that RTÉ ’s 2026 budget allocation of €240 million was not adequate to support the broadcaster’s five-year strategy and deliver the reforms the Coalition expected.
The Government was also told the national broadcaster would face “particularly acute” cash flow issues in 2027, even if it received the €260 million earmarked for next year under a 2024 agreement with the previous government.
Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan confirmed on Wednesday that the publicly owned broadcaster will receive €240 million again in 2027, €20 million less than the previous government had guaranteed in 2024.
The decision has ignited a row between Montrose and the Government.
In a report submitted to the minister in July 2025, consultancy firm Oliver & Ohlbaum Associates said that even the €240 million allocated for 2026 “is insufficient to fully support RTÉ’s sustainability, strategy and delivery of public service objectives”.
The report was commissioned by Coimisiún na Meán as part of its annual review of public funding for RTÉ and TG4 .
In its letter to the minister accompanying the report, the regulator said it shared the consultants’ view that “the €240 million allocated to RTÉ for 2026 is not fully adequate to support RTÉ’s sustainability, Statement of Strategy and delivery of the [public service media] objects over time”.
The commission said this view aligns with findings of a separate five-year review of funding adequacy for the Republic’s two publicly owned broadcasters, RTÉ and TG4. That review “raised significant concerns regarding RTÉ’s projected cash balance – particularly in 2027″.
Under the terms of the multiyear framework agreed in 2024, most of the broadcaster’s funding is to come from licence fees. RTÉ required a €41.3 million top-up from the exchequer last year and director general Kevin Bakhurst said it would require €54.8 million this year.
On Wednesday, O’Donovan suggested the decision to cut RTÉ’s funding next year relative to the 2024 agreement was due to the slow pace of reform in Montrose.
However, in a letter to Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers, seen by The Irish Times, O’Donovan warned last week that the putative €827 million that was set to be allocated to his department in Budget 2027 was insufficient.
O’Donovan and his junior minister, Charlie McConalogue, said that, among other things, it would mean his department would have to “renege” on the final year of the three-year funding deal for RTÉ.
“In fact, we now envisage a cut to RTÉ funding next year in the order of €11 million,” the ministers told Chambers.
The department received a further €21 million after tense budget negotiations over the weekend, which avoided the €11 million cut. Yet, funding for the broadcaster next year was reduced to €240 million from an expected €260 million.

title: Aleksander Ceferin to stand for a fourth term as Uefa president
description: Ceferin had already ruled himself out of standing for the Fifa presidency against Gianni Infantino
content:
Aleksander Ceferin will stand for a fourth term as Uefa president.
The Slovenian, who was first elected in 2016, told national association bosses he intended to seek re-election at a meeting in Berlin on Thursday morning.
Ceferin had already ruled himself out of standing for the Fifa presidency against Gianni Infantino, but a further four years of Ceferin arguably brings certainty and unity to Uefa at a time when it is focused on robustly challenging the Fifa presidency of Infantino.
Ceferin is only able to stand again after controversial changes were made to presidential term limits in Uefa’s statutes at its 2024 Congress in Paris.
The Football Association opposed those changes, but after the alterations were voted through Ceferin said he would not be standing again in any case, saying he had made up his mind six months previously to step away when his third term ends in 2027.
However, he has now told delegates he will seek re-election through to 2031 at next year’s Uefa Congress in Astana, Kazakhstan.
Ceferin has been vocal in his opposition to Infantino after it emerged in July the Swiss was working on a plan to seek private investment in a company to manage the commercial interests of Fifa’s tournaments, including the men’s and women’s World Cups.
Uefa said it had lost confidence in Infantino over his handling of that plan and announced in August it would seek to identify a credible alternative to stand against him.
There had been speculation in September that Thursday’s meeting in Berlin could be the point at which Uefa coalesced around a candidate, but that has not materialised. The deadline for candidates to be submitted for the Fifa presidency is November 18th, and Uefa sources have indicated a confidence that a candidate will be identified by then.
On Wednesday, former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega became the first person to officially announce their intention to challenge Infantino.
Infantino, who has also been in post since 2016, still appears to be a formidable opponent, with a strong power base particularly in Africa and South America but also among many Middle East nations, including Qatar and Saudi Arabia.
The president of the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, also appears to have softened his stance towards Infantino in a letter seen by the Press Association.
Sheikh Salman has previously joined Ceferin and Victor Montagliani, the president of Concacaf, in calling on Infantino to step down. However, his new letter suggests the creation of an internal working group to examine potential Fifa governance reforms.

title: Toy retailer Smyths sees revenues top £1bn for first time at UK business
description: Mayo group operates 127 stores in England, Scotland and Wales
content:
Revenues at the UK arm of the family-owned toy retailer, Smyths last year topped £1 billion for the first time.
New accounts filed by Smyths Toys UK Ltd show that revenues increased by 7 per cent to a record £1.01 billion (€1.19 billion) in 2025 due to increased footfall to stores and new store openings.
Sale of goods accounted for £957.85 million of turnover with the balance attributed to services to group companies.
Pretax profits were 10 per cent stronger at £20.5 million (€24.1 million).
Separate accounts for the NI operation show that pretax profits there fell by 7.5 per cent to £1.42 million last year, despite a 7 per cent increase in sales to £61.07 million.
The Smyths Toys retail business stretches across Ireland, Britain, Germany, France, Austria, the Netherlands and Switzerland. The Mayo group operates 127 stores in England, Scotland and Wales.
The directors for the UK unit said the £64 million increase in the company’s turnover was “primarily due to an increase in footfall in the stores and the addition of five new stores during the year”.
They said gross margins increased from 18.6 per cent to 19.1 per cent “due to the increase in sales and continued focus on cost reduction”.
The directors were pleased with the results “particularly given the current economic climate and the competitive marketplace”.
The five new stores opened last year came on top of seven new openings in 2024.
The firm’s buoyant performance saw the business paying out a dividend of £15 million.
Numbers employed by Smyths Toys UK Ltd increased by 60 from 3,563 to 3,623 as staff costs rose from £75.34 million to £78.27 million.
On future developments, directors expect further expansion in the UK market in the coming years through the opening of new stores. The company’s lease costs last year totalled £37.12 million.
The business is operated by the Smyth family from Co Mayo. The profits take account of non-cash depreciation costs of £18.32 million.
Shareholder funds at the end of December totalled £9.7 million, including accumulated profits of £6.7 million. Cash funds increased 21 per cent to £10.38 million.

title: Donald Trump’s visit forecast to cost Garda up to €30m
description: Operation for US president’s visit in September was entirely publicly funded, Garda chief tells PAC
content:
The visit of US president Donald Trump to Ireland at the start of September is forecast to cost An Garda Síochána up to €30 million.
The policing operation was entirely publicly funded, Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly confirmed to the Public Accounts Committee on Thursday.
The final figures for the cost are not yet available and actual expenditure may be lower.
“We think we’re going to come in under what we forecast, but obviously we’re still waiting on some of the claims, particularly for overtime and subsistence,” he said.
There were “a number of elements to the visit”, with Trump visiting President Catherine Connolly in Dublin, travelling to Doonbeg, and at the Irish Open golf tournament.
[ Was Catherine Connolly ‘trolling’ Trump by giving him an obscure medieval book? Opens in new window ]
[ ‘He’s keeping our village alive’: Doonbeg residents prepare to host Donald Trump Opens in new window ]
“We weren’t down there to police the golfing event, we were down to protect the president of the United States,” Kelly said.
The Oireachtas committee also heard that gardaí have made 17 protected disclosures so far in 2026, with a total of 113 made since the start of 2021.
The Garda has examined the functioning of its protected disclosure unit following allegations of targeting of staff members who identified potential wrongdoing in the organisation, Kelly said.
The commissioner said he was “very content” with its policies and structure but “it would be remiss of me really not to relook at that and to make sure everything we have in place is absolutely rock solid”.
[ In pictures: Donald Trump’s visit to Ireland Opens in new window ]
Garda management was questioned about revelations in the recent RTÉ documentary that alleged maltreatment of whistleblowers and protected disclosures.
Garda Assistant Commissioner Catharina Gunne stated that 20 protected disclosures were made in 2021, 15 in 2022, 26 in 2023, a further 12 in 2024 and 23 in 2025. So far in 2026, some 17 disclosures have been made.
Following on from the RTÉ programme, Kelly said he had met the senior leadership team of the Garda and “looked at what we are doing in this area”. He also “interacted extensively” with Transparency International Ireland, he said.
Kelly said the force has done “considerable work in strengthening” its protected disclosure unit and now has a full-time manager of the unit.
The commissioner said the Garda “certainly want people to come forward” should they be aware of wrongdoing in the force, in response to questions from Fine Gael TD James Geoghegan.
Kelly said he has not reviewed any protected disclosure files from before or during his time as commissioner and only has a “very limited role” in that area, but noted he has “absolutely no concern around any decision” made by former Garda commissioner Drew Harris.
Separately, the committee reviewed the force’s €590,000 spend on hotel accommodation over three nights for members policing the 2024 Uefa Europa League final, which was held at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.
The committee heard that a Comptroller and Auditor General report said 40 per cent of those costs, or €248,500, was on accommodation that was never used. The full €7.8 million spent on policing the event was borne by the State.
[ New Garda spending rules to follow booking of nearly €250k worth of unused hotel rooms Opens in new window ]
The committee heard that the use of a manual spreadsheet left a number of gardaí booked into multiple rooms in the same and different hotels. Some 13 gardaí were assigned two rooms in the same hotel, and 11 were assigned two hotel rooms in two different hotels.
Weaknesses in planning by the force were identified, with no public procurement process being carried out. The rooms, the committee heard, were booked in bulk before the Garda knew the staffing requirements of the event.

title: What is the row over the UK’s nearly 200-year-old consulate in Jerusalem?
description: UK’s diplomatic mission will operate on a smaller scale after Israel ordered it shut over a sanctions row
content:
The UK said on Thursday its nearly 200-year-old consulate in Jerusalem would continue operating on a smaller scale ‌and be renamed as the UK Mission in the city, after Israel ordered it shut in a dispute over sanctions on settlements.
Here’s what to know about the dispute ‌and diplomatic missions in the Holy City.
The dispute is over sanctions. Israel’s order for the consulate to shut was retaliation for ​the UK government saying it would impose a ban on the trade of goods made in Israeli settlements.
On September 8th, Israel ordered the UK to close the East Jerusalem consulate within 30 days and remove its diplomats from the city. The deadline expired on Thursday, with the UK and Israel announcing a compromise that would keep the facility open.
The consulate is located in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East Jerusalem and handles the UK’s relations with Palestinians ⁠in the city as well as in the occupied West Bank and in the Gaza Strip. It also provides consular ‌services ‌to Palestinians.
The ​consulate has been in Jerusalem since about 1839, according to the National Library of Israel, when the area was part of the Ottoman Empire and long before Israel’s establishment in 1948.
East Jerusalem is ⁠considered occupied territory under international law.
The UK’s embassy in Israel, ​like most countries’, is in Tel Aviv, which is also home to ​some government departments. The Israeli prime minister’s office, presidency and parliament are in Jerusalem.
Jerusalem has long had a ‌bitterly contested status.
It was under British control under ​the Mandate for Palestine. That ended around the time of Israel’s creation in 1948.
Under a United Nations resolution, Jerusalem was meant ⁠to come under international governance due to its special status ⁠in Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
In ​the event, Arab countries attacked Israel after its establishment, and the 1948 Arab-Israeli war resulted in Israeli control of West Jerusalem and Jordanian control of East Jerusalem, including most of the city’s holy sites.
Israel captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Six-Day War and annexed it in 1980, coming to control the entire city.
Israel considers the whole of Jerusalem as its capital, but most countries do not recognise that claim and consider East Jerusalem occupied by Israel.
Palestinians want East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state. Decades of negotiations have failed to determine a final status.
Turkey and several western ⁠countries including France, Belgium, Greece, Italy, Spain and Sweden.
No. France joined the UK in announcing sanctions, along with Canada, which does not have a consulate in Jerusalem. Israel has not taken action against ‌Paris.
The United States moved its embassy from Tel Aviv and merged it with its consulate in Jerusalem during US president ​Donald Trump’s first term in 2018, the first US administration to make the move.
The US ​was meant to have moved it by 1999 under a Congressional law, but successive presidents postponed the move on national security grounds, in efforts to avoid scuttling chances for peace between Israel and the Palestinians. – Reuters
