title: Does Patrick O’Donovan’s explanation for €20m RTÉ funding cut add up?
description: Row between Minister and State broadcaster raises questions about who knew what in Government about decision
content:
A row between RTÉ and Minister for Media Patrick O’Donovan over a €20 million cut in funding for the State broadcaster is casting a long shadow over Budget 2027. But what exactly is going on? And does O’Donovan’s explanation for the cut add up?
Back in 2024 the then-government sought to draw a line under the scandal unleashed at Montrose triggered by secret payments to its former star presenter Ryan Tubridy. Damage to public confidence in the broadcaster led to a fall in licence fee payments, further damaging RTÉ’s finances.
The government agreed to guarantee a certain level of funding to RTÉ every year, coming to €725 million, saying the funding was conditional on delivery of reforms at the broadcaster.
While the money for RTÉ was supposedly guaranteed, talks between O’Donovan’s department and the Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers were particularly fraught this year.
O’Donovan initially asked for a package of €899 million to fund current spending (that is non-capital spending on things like building or renovation works).
His department is not high-spending, but it does have a lot of agencies under it. In addition to RTÉ, it has the likes of the Arts Council, Sport Ireland, TG4, and funding for sporting bodies like the FAI and GAA.
O’Donovan also wanted money for policy measures like a culture card: a pre-loaded €100 voucher for 16-year-olds to participate in cultural activities.
This was whittled down to an ask of €879 million – then €858 million – over the course of last week. But, as of late last week, Chambers was only willing to approve €827 million.
Last Friday, O’Donovan and the junior minister in his department Charlie McConalogue put pen to paper, sending Chambers a letter stuffed with stark warnings about the consequences of not increasing funding for the department.
The letter, seen by The Irish Times, warned that with €827 million on the table, there was an extensive list of things which O’Donovan said his department wouldn’t be able to do if it didn’t get more money. These included:
O’Donovan warned Chambers of “significant reputational damage to the wider Government” if these things came to pass.
O’Donovan warned that based on the money on offer, the Government – not just the department – “will renege on the three-year funding deal agreed with RTÉ in July 2024”, going on to add that “in fact, we now envisage a cut to RTÉ funding next year in the order of €11 million”.
This suggests that RTÉ would have got €229 million for next year, down from the €240 million it received for 2026.
Amid tense budget negotiations over the weekend, another €21 million was found for O’Donovan’s department.
The extra money appears to have addressed the risk of an €11 million cut for RTÉ, with some presumably being spread over other agencies.
As for RTÉ, it was allocated just €240 million – not the €260 million that was agreed in 2024. RTÉ said it was only informed of this three hours in advance. O’Donovan suggested this was down to the slow pace of reform, which RTÉ director general Kevin Bakhurst rejected.
The Minister said it would be a “fair extrapolation” of his remarks at a long post-budget press conference that the funding situation played a role as well but, confusingly, added: “That’s not actually what I said at all.”
The controversy throws up a number of questions.
First, there is the question of reneging on the agreement. O’Donovan denies the decision amounts to a “cut” in funding. But will RTÉ argue that failing to deliver the extra €20 million constitutes reneging – and what are the implications of this?
Also, the justification for the cut is still unclear. Is the decision down to a lack of funds, as suggested by the department’s letter, or a failure to speedily reform as claimed by O’Donovan?
After talks on Thursday, it seems all sides are eager for an off-ramp. But a clean settlement may be harder to achieve.

title: Munster to mark 10th anniversary of Anthony Foley’s death at Champions Cup meeting with Racing 92
description: Foley died in Paris in 2016 on the morning that Munster were due to face Racing in that year’s Champions Cup
content:
Munster Rugby will mark the 10th anniversary of Anthony Foley’s passing with a series of special tributes and commemorative activities around their Champions Cup clash against Racing 92 at SuperValu Páirc Uí Chaoimh next Saturday week, October 17th.
That will be one day after the anniversary of Foley’s sudden passing in Paris in 2016 on the morning of the scheduled first round match between Racing 92 and Munster at the Stade Yves du Manoir, which was postponed and played the following January.
A statement by the province said: “A much-loved former player, captain and Head Coach, Anthony remains one of the most important figures in Munster Rugby’s history, and the fixture will provide an opportunity for the Munster family to come together in remembrance of his extraordinary contribution to the province.
“A number of tributes will take place before and during the game, with supporters encouraged to play their part in commemorating Anthony’s legacy and the special place he continues to hold within Munster Rugby.
“Before kick-off, Jean Wallace and members of Shannon RFC will perform ‘There Is An Isle’ in tribute to Anthony.
“A photo display showcasing Anthony’s incredible career will be present in the ‘Red Shed’ area of Marina Park, immediately outside the stadium.
“The Munster players will wear special commemorative presentation jackets featuring the Munster crest and the number eight.
“A pre-match presentation involving the captains of Munster and Racing 92 will also take place, with both captains exchanging jerseys featuring the number eight.
“During the match, the Munster Rugby Supporters Club will lead a round of applause in the eighth minute to honour Axel. At half-time, Minis matches will take place on the pitch involving boys’ and girls’ teams from Ballina-Killaloe RFC and Shannon RFC, two clubs which are synonymous with Axel.
“Further matchday details will be confirmed closer to the fixture.”

title: Energy prices drive Irish consumer price inflation to highest level since January 2024
description: Energy product prices increased by 13.7% in 12 months to September, CSO says
content:
A surge in home energy bills last month drove consumer price inflation in the Irish economy to its highest level in more than two years, the Central Statistics Office (CSO) said on Thursday.
A basket of Irish consumer goods cost 4.1 per cent more in September than the same month last year, with the annual rate of increase rising from a level of 3.7 per cent in August.
That was the fastest annual rate of increase since January 2024, the CSO said.
It means that prices in the Irish economy increased at a faster pace in September than the previous month. The statistics agency’s consumer price index (CPI) increased by 0.2 per cent between August and September.
The headline increase was driven by a surge in the price of energy products, including electricity, gas and other household fuels, which were up by 13.7 per cent in the year to September.
[ Home heating oil prices rise almost 60% Opens in new window ]
Petrol prices, meanwhile, increased by 14 per cent in the 12 months to the end of September, with diesel up by 22 per cent.
Energy prices have soared this year in the aftermath of the US-Israeli war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Dermot Daly, EY Ireland consumer products and retail lead, said the jump in energy prices in the latest CSO data is “particularly noteworthy”.
“Consumers have shown resilience – household spending is likely to grow 2.5 per cent after inflation this year – but many will have to prioritise essential purchases while taking a more considered approach to discretionary spending,” he said.
“As we move closer to the important Christmas trading period, retailers will be hoping that consumer spending remains resilient despite ongoing cost pressures.
The Central Bank is now forecasting headline inflation to average 3.4 per cent in 2026, moderating to 3.1 per cent in 2027 and 2 per cent in 2028.
However, in its most recent quarterly economic bulletin, the bank warned that there were significant upside risks to these inflation projections given the uncertainty over the path of the conflict in the Middle East.
Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM Ireland and RSM UK said last week that the higher energy prices will likely feed into other areas.
“Utility bills will continue to reset higher, keeping energy inflation sticky throughout 2027,” he said. “At the same time, the sustained rise in energy prices this year means it’s increasingly likely that food, manufactured goods and other energy-intensive services such as airfares inflation will pick up pace in the coming months.”

title: The Irish experience of making England home
description: Mammy’s House is a play that tells the untold story of Irish in London during the 1980s Aids crisis
content:
Having taken a visit to the East Midlands region of England last weekend, I was struck by how easily I forgot that I wasn’t in Ireland. The signs were there, but hard to grasp, like a shift in the breeze: drivers diligently stuck to speed limits, front gardens I passed were suspiciously well groomed and the toaster queues at my hotel breakfast were remarkably orderly and lacking in elbows.
This unusual feeling of being Irish in England is something Hugo Harvey touches on in his column. “The particular anxiety of being Irish in London is the proximity of British identity. London is an international city, a melting pot, but the British capital is still the British capital. For Irish people, there might be a nagging fear that if you are not paying attention, you might be assimilated; mistaken for British, or worse, not minding whether you are.”
Making England home is not always straightforward for Irish people. It has often been a place of safety, including for many LGBTQ+ emigrants. But the Aids crisis brought complexities to this refuge, which are examined in an Irish play that premiered in London last month.
It was created by two Cork natives, playwright Amy Clarke and actor Derek Murphy , with assistance from the Emigrant Support Programme. It tells the untold true stories of the Irish during the 1980s Aids crisis in London.
We spoke to Murphy and Clarke earlier this year. “We are all familiar with the stories, but you never hear about it from an Irish point of view,” Murphy said.
The Irish have been coming and going from England for generations, but Birmingham resident Robert Murphy writes of something that took him by surprise: “Despite the strong historic links, many people here seem to know little about Ireland. They often seem to be less interested in us than we are in them. I am not sure why this is. It may be a quirk of the relationship between a small country and a large one.”
It’s something that made him lean in to his Irishness: “I have a newfound enjoyment of Irish traditional music, I read Irish news every day and stay connected with literature,” he writes.
The relationship with the Irish language as a child and as an emigrant is something that London-based Laura Kennedy reflects on in her column . Irish “was entangled in a thick mesh of obligation, Catholicism and citizenship. It was a rote-learned procession of refrains written and recited for exam practice; less a window into a culture and history and more a series of noises you made with your face to pass an oral exam and get out of dodge”.
Now she has begun to learn it again: “It is pleasant, though, to uncover the secret knowledge I had presumed lost, buried so deep in my mind that it had been abandoned with the muscle memory entailed in how to use a hula hoop. It’s nice to recall that you can recall a fox is called a ‘sionnach’, and to find the shape of lost words forming in your mouth. It’s nice to be able to lift the weight of a grudge off the shoulders of that angry younger self, and to simply say ‘itheann an madra mo geansaí’,” she writes.
Thank you for reading this newsletter. If you’d like to contribute to Abroad email, abroad@irishtimes.com , follow us on Instagram and sign up for this newsletter to your inbox.

title: Man accused of ‘totally unprovoked’ attack on Michael Healy-Rae granted bail
description: Anthony Foley (51), of Rosary Road, Dublin 8, must abide by bail conditions, including a curfew and a complete exclusion from Dublin 2
content:
A man accused of carrying out a “totally unprovoked” attack on Kerry TD Michael Healy-Rae as he sat in traffic in Dublin has been granted High Court bail.
Anthony Foley (51), of Rosary Road, Maryland, Dublin 8, is charged with assault causing harm to the politician on September 16th, 2026, at Cork Street, and was denied bail two days later in the District Court.
However, he appealed that decision before Judge Cathleen Noctor, who heard evidence and legal submissions at the High Court in Cloverhill, Dublin, on Wednesday.
She reserved judgment until Thursday. Noctor emphasised that the accused was entitled to the presumption of innocence and to bail.
Addressing objections that Foley would fail to appear in court and Garda concerns over potential witness interference via social media or at the TD’s workplace, she held that there was no evidential basis for those fears.
The judge noted the seriousness of the broad daylight attack and was satisfied that a conviction would likely result in a custodial sentence.
However, she rejected Garda apprehensions that granting bail would lead to another serious offence targeting a politician specifically. The judge said she was “not convinced it was clearly politically motivated”, but rather an alleged general attack on a person who happened to be an elected representative.
[ Assault on Michael Healy-Rae increases fears over TD safety Opens in new window ]
Bail was granted subject to stringent conditions. The judge required an independent surety of €500 to be approved – though the surety does not have to pay any cash – while the accused must lodge his own bond of €1,400.
Upon taking up bail, he must reside at an address approved by gardaí before his release. He must sign on twice daily at his nearest Garda station.
Additional terms include an 8pm-to-8am curfew and a complete exclusion from the Dublin 2 area.
Objecting to bail, Garda Sgt Dave Griffin alleged the accused approached Healy-Rae’s car outside the Coombe Hospital just after 4pm and that the politician was the victim of an unprovoked assault.
He said the Independent TD had been in his car stuck in traffic when the assailant, who was walking a dog, began shouting obscenities before punching him in the face.
The former minister of state was not required to attend the bail hearing.
Foley vehemently denies being the person in the video evidence.
Healy-Rae received treatment from an ambulance crew. He was later taken to hospital for a laceration to his lip.
The court heard that the investigation file was in its latter stages of preparation.
The court heard Foley was on disability benefit, receiving €254 a week.
Foley is due back in the District Court later this month for the DPP’s directions to be outlined.

title: Is the State’s new investment account going to be a good deal?
description: Investors need to realise they are going to be largely on their own when it comes to assessing risk
content:
I s the State’s new investment account going to be a good deal? The announcement of key details in the budget has certainly attracted renewed public interest. But it is essential to understand the fundamentals of the scheme to judge how it might fit in to your personal financial plan. And in assessing this, investors need to realise that they are going to be largely on their own.
Most of those providing the plans – the big banks and insurance companies initially – are likely to follow a low-charge model, meaning they will not offer personalised advice. Instead people will get some online essentials about the various plans on offer and choose – via a bank app, for example – what level of risk they wish to take.
It will, of course, be open to potential investors to seek personalised guidance from an adviser, or sign up for a more bespoke scheme, but this will cost more. All kinds of funds offered by brokers will be “wrapped” in the new scheme, in other words constructed to take advantage of it.
But charges here will be higher. As the offers develop, options are likely to grow. But cheap and cheerful will be the hallmark of the initial approach when the big players kick it off next July.
The tax -free nature of the scheme on holdings up to €50,000 is attractive. But still, there are some steps to assessing whether taking part works for you.
The first key point is that the return has to be greater than that available on a risk-free asset such as a bank account. Many people have cash currently in demand accounts with the main banks offering very low returns. But they could get 2 to 3 per cent – or even a bit more – if prepared to move into a savings account which might require notice on withdrawals.
[ Lower-than-expected annual €12,000 investment account limits may curb take-up Opens in new window ]
Returns are subject to deposit interest retention tax (Dirt) at 33 per cent, so that needs to be deducted – a third of your interest goes to the taxman.
Traditionally, stock markets have offered significantly higher returns than this. The Stoxx Europe 600 index, for example – the kind of index which an investment under the scheme might be based on – has had an average return of 8 per cent over the past 20 years. Most European indices has returned at least 6 per cent over that period.
But the Stoxx index lost 12 per cent in 2022, as inflation surged following Russia’s full scale invasion of Ukraine. So the first thing for new investors to understand is that you have to be able to ride out the bad years and let the averages – the fact that equities tend to go up more years than they go down – lead to gains over time.
Of course we cannot be sure that stock markets will behave in future like they did in the past. And we don’t know what markets will look like next July when the funds are launched, but this will need to be taken into account.
A bursting of the artificial intelligence (AI) bubble or the wider knock on to bond markets from rising interest rates present risks.
Investors will have a broader exposure than those who put cash into Eircom when it floated in 1999, but its initial rise and then fall as tech shares were hit as the dot.com bubble burst is worth noting, nonetheless.
If investors are happy to lock in their money for a period, then history suggests that equity market will beat deposits. Their next key call will be how much risk to take. At least initially, funds are likely to be marketed as high, medium and low risk. The latter will put some cash in traditionally less volatile areas such as bonds (though these have been on a volatile run of late).
This is where the lack of advice on basic products could be difficult for new investors in choosing where to put their money. We will have to see how the offers line up, but the funds will make more sense for those willing to take a somewhat higher level of risk and thus get a higher return over time. You need to beat the bank account return and also take into account the costs of the scheme.
The key cost most investors will need to factor in is whatever the provider is charging to offer the service. The indications are that there will be an effort to keep costs on basic offers down below 0.5 per cent – but remember this is a charge on the total value of the fund. There are also likely to be products offer bespoke advice but with higher charges, likely more than 1 per cent.
A charge of 0.5 per cent would be €100 on a €20,000 pot, while 1 per cent would be €200. This may not sound like a big difference. But over time charges matter as more money is taken out of the pot and there is a cumulative hit. Over 10 years the difference between a 0.5 per cent fee and a 1 per cent one on a €50,000 pot would be well in the thousands of euro.
The best hope for investors is that the big banks and their investment arms will keep the charges low to try to hold on to money which people are moving from deposits with the same group. But charging structures will be vital to assess. And these low-cost products leave investors making their own decisions.
The next bar to jump is the State tax. A big attraction of the scheme is that normal taxes on investment – capital gains tax and the taxes paid on exchange-traded funds – will not apply. It is only on pots of more than €50,000 where the new 1 per cent charge on the balance above this figure applies. So a couple could have two accounts summing to €100,000 and pay no tax.
Like charges from the provider, the 1 per cent will be significant for bigger investors. If an investor has saved, say, €100,000 then the annual charge will be €500 (1 per cent of €50,000).
As with charges, this eats away at the pot over time. And – crucially – this will be charged in good years and in bad – in other words in years when the value of your investment falls you will still pay the 1 per cent charge on balances of more than €100,000.
In Sweden this type of levy was initially charged on the whole sum saved and this led some experts to conclude that the tax advantage offered by the products – which like Ireland spared investors from capital gains tax – was limited.
The key attraction, they said, was simplicity, the fact that the provider does all the administration and also avoiding having to pay a big capital-gains bill all at once when the investment was sold.
More recently Sweden also introduced a tax-free scheme this year, which means a pot of up to €27,000 will not face a levy. The tax on amounts above this is 1.065 per cent.
For Ireland, investors will need to realise that the sums change significantly when savings become subject to the 1 per cent charge. There will probably still be tax advantages, but they will be narrower on the part of the fund exceeding €50,000 – and having to pay no matter how the fund performs is significant in bad years.
The bottom line is that the new investment vehicle is better suited to slightly riskier investments which offer a higher potential return. It also requires the investor to understand the risks and the need to be able to leave money where it is – if necessary – to recover from bad years. And to understand the impact of the 1 per cent charge on larger sums and the fees on all investments.
For many it may still offer an attractive part of a wider savings plan, which might also include a pension plan, some highly tax-incentivised additional voluntary contributions and some money in the bank for the “rainy day” when funds might be needed quickly.
But understanding what is and what is not on offer is vital. Just because this is a “State” scheme does not mean any kind of guarantee is on offer. It is not a special savings incentive account Mark 2. As the radio ads say. investments can fall as well as rise.

title: Recording supports claim employee pressured to omit Deloitte partner name from HR complaint, WRC told
description: Complaint of constructive dismissal against the Big Four accountancy firm is being heard at the WRC
content:
A recording exists supporting an allegation that a Deloitte employee was pressured to remove references to a partner in the firm from a formal HR complaint, the worker’s barrister has told an employment tribunal.
Lawyers acting for Viviana Jakomin, who is pursuing a complaint of constructive dismissal against the Big Four accountancy firm at the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC), are seeking to introduce a transcript of the tape as evidence in the case.
Brian Jackson, the Deloitte partner said to have been identified in the grievance, told the WRC on Wednesday he had “absolutely not” interfered in the investigation.
He said Deloitte had “robust non-retaliation policies”. “As far as I’m aware, under no circumstances would anyone in the organisation break those,” he added.
Jakomin quit the firm in November 2023, five years after starting as temporary maternity cover in its pool of personal assistants.
The parties dispute the nature and seniority of Jakomin’s role in the business after she secured a permanent contract as an administrator.
Jakomin’s legal team have said she was subject to “gaslighting” about her prospects for advancement to a management grade in the context of work as a project manager on audit work because of her past expertise in that field.
The evidence presented on behalf of the company has been that Jakomin’s job description made project management-type tasks “stretch” goals, but that in reality her work was administrative.
Jakomin would later tell the company during an internal grievance process that she believed she was “mis-sold a role” when she took the job, the tribunal was told.
In a submission, counsel for the worker Eoin Morris BL, instructed by Crushell & Co Solicitors, said his client “was put under pressure to amend her grievance and remove references to Brian Jackson”.
Counsel said he wished to introduce a transcript of the recording, which he said had been taken during a conversation between Jakomin and a person involved in investigating a workplace grievance she had raised.
Jackson, Deloitte’s head of audit for financial services, was appointed chief operating officer in Ireland in January 2020, the WRC heard.
Jackson’s evidence earlier this year was that Jakomin approached him in February 2020, asked him into a room and “just shouted at me” about being promoted to a management grade.
“Viviana kept shouting over me: ‘No, no, no, no, promote me now’,” the partner said.
“I said: ‘Viviana, if you are unwilling to listen to a single word I am going to say, you will never be promoted’,” Jackson told the tribunal earlier this year.
The WRC heard that Jakomin complained about the interaction to Jackson’s boss, Michael Hartwell, who referred the matter to Deloitte’s HR department, the tribunal heard.
Jackson said he was made aware by HR that there was a complaint against him.
“Did HR ever make you aware that complaint was removed, that you were no longer a subject of the investigation?” Morris said.
“Not that I can recall,” Jackson said. He said he struggled to see how Jakomin “could possibly have had a complaint” against him.
He said he knew a remark had been attributed to him telling Jakomin: “If you come up against me, you will never be promoted.”
“That’s not something I’d said,” he told the WRC.
Morris said it arose in Jakomin’s direct evidence that she was “put under pressure to discount that part of her complaint” when she later pursued a workplace grievance.
Harry Wall of IBEC, for the company, said that process was in 2023 and Jackson had “zero input”.
“Did you ever interfere in the process?” Morris asked the witness.
“Do you accept Ms Jakomin’s position that somebody intervened and put pressure on her?” Morris said.
“You understand there was a recording of a conversation where she was put under pressure,” Morris said.
“He can’t know that,” said adjudication officer Penelope McGrath.
“There is a recording of a conversation between Ms Jakomin and Deloitte where that is borne out, I’m putting it to you,” Morris told the witness.
Jackson replied: “I’m not sure what you’re putting to me. We have the most robust non-retaliation policies and as far as I’m aware under no circumstances would anyone in the organisation break those, in any circumstances.”

title: Italy’s Giorgia Meloni secures final approval for controversial electoral reform
description: Opponents accuse government of self-serving reform in advance of vote, with one lawmaker on hunger strike
content:
The Italian parliament passed a contentious electoral reform on Thursday that prime minister Giorgia Meloni says will increase political stability but opponents criticise as self-serving in advance of an election due by the end of next year.
The new law awards parties that win more than 42 per cent of votes with extra seats in both houses of parliament, cementing their majority while toughening requirements for new parties to contest elections.
Meloni said the law was “giving citizens back the power to directly choose who represents them” as it introduces an element of preferential choice among candidates.
It will also incentivise the formation of large coalitions of parties to contest elections, which will have to set out a programme and a prime ministerial candidate in advance of the vote rather than leaving these for post-vote government formation talks.
But opposition parties have accused the prime minister of changing the rules to favour her own party and have promised to challenge the Bill in Italy’s constitutional court.
[ Meloni electoral plan ‘authoritarian’ Italy’s opposition says Opens in new window ]
“Meloni, just months before the election, is changing the rules of the game,” said centre-left leader Elly Schlein, accusing Meloni of fearing the electorate.
Lawmaker with the More Europe party Riccardo Magi has been on hunger strike for a week in protest against a large increase in the number of signatures that parties would need to collect under the law in order to stand in any multiseat constituency, from 1,500 to 6,000.
“We will continue to fight, including outside of parliament, because this isn’t about us but about democracy, which can’t be locked away with a key by those who are temporarily in power,” Magi said.
He estimated that parties would have to collect 450,000 signatures, all in person, in order to run nationwide, calling this “blatantly unconstitutional”.
The Meloni government is reportedly already preparing potential tweaks to the law in case the court rules against it, including adjustments to the seat bonus that would be awarded in the Senate to reflect a constitutional requirement that Italy’s upper house is elected regionally.
Successive Italian governments have sought to change the country’s electoral system, promising to increase stability and move away from a tendency for short-lived governments that defined much of its postwar history.
Each law is given a mock-Latin nickname with the suffix “ellum”.
The “Matarellum” in 1993 ended a proportional electoral system that had been in place since 1946, introducing a mix of proportional and first-past-the-post elements.
This was replaced by the 2005 Porcellum, a derogatory nickname that stuck after the law’s author publicly described it as a “porcata”, a piece of crap.
The Porcellum was found to be unconstitutional and was replaced in 2013 by the Italicum, which was also found to be unconstitutional, and was repealed before it was ever used.
The current Rosatellum system was introduced in 2017. Meloni’s government was elected under it and won a significant majority in parliament, helping it to become Italy’s longest-ruling administration since the second World War.
However, Meloni and her party have long sought a reform that would make Italian parliamentary elections more “presidential”, with a prime ministerial candidate named on the ballot.
This idea has troubling associations for some due to the cult of personality that surrounded its former fascist leader Benito Mussolini, who is part of the political heritage of Meloni’s party.
Due to internal opposition within their governing coalition, this idea did not make it into the current proposed law, though parties will have to name a prime ministerial candidate during their election campaign.
The Meloni government has given its law the flattering name “Stabilicum”, but opponents refuse to use it and call it the “Melonellum” after Meloni herself, which sounds like “melon-law”.

title: Judge who said ‘it kills me’ to fly Ryanair urged not to deal with any of airline’s cases
description: Ryanair claims District Judge’s comments suggest ‘hostility’ towards the airline
content:
Ryanair has asked a judge not to hear any further cases involving it due to comments made by her in some earlier cases, including saying “it kills me stone dead” to fly with the airline.
Ryanair claims that other comments made by District Court Judge Stephanie Coggans in different cases suggest a “hostility” towards, and “dislike” of, the airline such that an objective observer would think there was a risk it would not get a fair hearing before her.
On that basis, senior counsel Martin Hayden applied to Coggans at Balbriggan District Court on Thursday to recuse herself (withdraw) from hearing any cases involving Ryanair.
It is “trendy” to complain about Ryanair; the airline “has to face that day in and day out” but it “should not have to deal with it from the bench”, counsel said during submissions.
After the application concluded, Coggans said she needed time to consider the evidence and the case law submitted and would give her decision on December 2nd.
In an affidavit put before the judge, Thomas McNamara, Ryanair’s director of legal, referred to a number of cases dealt with by her, including one by a man who sued Ryanair over missing his flight despite claiming to be at the gate at the time of it closing.
The man had claimed he had not received “a last call” and Ryanair’s solicitor said last calls are not done by the airline, said McNamara.
He said Coggans then “inexplicably commented that she believed they should”, went on to say she knew Ryanair did not do last calls “because I travel with them myself, although it kills me” and later said: “It kills me stone dead.”
Coggans also remarked to a witness there “is frequently what I can only describe as a forceful method of dealing with people and that is what drives them mad, and that is what drives me mad, and I think sometimes people are treated very badly when very, very, very, very, very considerable amounts of money are made in profit”. She had added: “It wouldn’t kill you to be halfways polite to people.”
[ Ryanair’s plan for €50m hangar at Shannon Airport stalls Opens in new window ]
In another case, where it became apparent an individual’s claim before the small claims court must fail as a matter of law, Coggans “again became antagonistic” towards Ryanair, describing what had happened in relation to its booking process as “an absolute disgrace” and saying the airline had “got lucky”, said McNamara.
In that case, involving a claim for €950 from Ryanair, the claimant said she believed she had booked a flight for her family to Italy and was unaware her payment had been denied and, as such, her booking was not complete. It was only when she went to check her booking the day before the flight that she saw a message from Ryanair stating there was a problem with the booking.
McNamara said, in another case, Ryanair had complained to the judge about comments she had made, including about a quote attributed in a newspaper article to the judge about a “complete imbalance of power” between Ryanair and the particular claimant.
He said Coggans had responded that she had not used those words and had said: “I said that the issue of Ryanair appearing with solicitor and counsel at all times when people are here as claimants with nobody lacked balance.” She also said she stood by a previous comment that “it wouldn’t kill Ryanair to be halfway polite to people”, said McNamara.
She had further said: “I have said plenty about how Ryanair conducts its business; I am not denying that. I am not taking it back either.”
In submissions, Hayden, with barrister Roland Rowan, said the application was based on repeated comments going beyond the adjudication of particular issues and capable of being understood as disclosing an adverse personal view of Ryanair as an airline, commercial operator and litigant.
[ Why did it take Michael O’Leary 10 days to cop on that his comments on rape were wrong? Opens in new window ]
The comments were such that a reasonable, objective and informed observer, in possession of all the facts, would have a reasonable apprehension that Ryanair may not receive a fair and impartial hearing before the judge, he submitted.
Hayden referred to a 2010 case in which then High Court judge Peter Kelly initially refused an application by Ryanair to recuse himself arising from a previous comment by him, in another case, that, having regard to “untruths” by Ryanair to the court, about the court and about the minister for transport, “the truth and Ryanair are uncomfortable bedfellows”. Kelly rejected Ryanair’s arguments that the comment amounted to objective bias.
In 2011, after Ryanair had indicated it would appeal his refusal to recuse to the Supreme Court, Kelly said that, only because of the delays of up to three years such an appeal would mean, in relation to the particular case, he would recuse himself from hearing that case.

title: Nurses stage lunchtime protests at number of hospitals nationwide
description: Protests are planned in advance of work stoppages that will begin in public health service next week
content:
Members of the Irish Nurses and Midwives Organisation (INMO) are holding lunchtime protest at a number of hospitals across the country on Thursday.
The staff, who are engaged in a work-to-rule, are protesting over cost-of-living measures and the impact they are having on staffing levels.
Protests were being held held at Cork University Hospital, University Hospital Limerick, St Vincent’s University Hospital, The Mater, Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital Drogheda, Letterkenny University Hospital, Galway University Hospital, Naas General Hospital and Midlands Regional Hospital, Mullingar.
The protests are planned in advance of work stoppages that will begin in the public health service next week.
Members of Fórsa , Siptu and INMO began a work-to-rule across large portions of the civil and public service on September 30th.
These unions, along with Unite and a number of others, are scheduled to stage a one-day stoppage on October 14th.
INMO general secretary Phil Ní Sheaghdha rejected a comment by Taoiseach Micheál Martin that public sector workers wanted industrial action “irrespective of what happens”.
In a post-budget interview with Claire Byrne on Newstalk on Wednesday, Martin said: “I just get the sense that people want industrial action almost now, irrespective of what happens. And that’s a problem. I think that’s wrong.”
[ Budget 2027 falls short of preventing public sector industrial action, say unions Opens in new window ]
The Taoiseach was not right, said Ní Sheaghdha. “I think everybody in the country understands the job that public servants do. They respect it. They value it. And right now, public servants are very clearly saying that they don’t believe enough was done in this budget. They don’t believe it was a worker-facing budget,” she told RTÉ’s Morning Ireland on Thursday.
Ní Sheaghdha said the last public service agreement expired on June 30th.
“Me and my colleagues in the trade union movement have been involved in many negotiations of public service agreements. But what we hadn’t faced previously was that just two weeks prior to that, the minister with responsibility went to Cabinet seeking approval to engage.
“There hasn’t been a commitment from Government to really focus on what it means to have a strong industrial relations system which provides for a collective agreement, which provides for industrial peace. And in the absence of that, clearly, you have the opposite, which is exactly what we’re facing next week.”
Ní Sheaghdha said industrial action could be avoided, but workers had a right to have their say.
“And when workers in thousands across the public service have voted in very large numbers to say we’re not happy with the approach the Government is taking to our dispute, to our pay, to our cost-of-living crisis, which there is, there’s serious, significant cost-of-living issues for all of our members, well, then the Government must listen to that.
[ Public sector pay dispute ‘unwarranted given our willingness to talk’, Taoiseach says Opens in new window ]
“To say that public servants are just taking strike action for the fun of it, I think is a little bit glib. And I would think that if we’re serious about trying to find a resolution, I would avoid that type of commentary because it’s absolutely inflammatory,” she told RTÉ.
When asked what impact the INMO’s work-to-rule was having on patients, Ní Sheaghdha said her members had been asked not to engage in taking up the work of posts that had not been filled.
“The majority of the requests we have from the employer to date is that we would give additional hours and that people would be asked to work and fill vacant posts that haven’t been filled,” she said.
“So we know that there’s been a huge embargo in the health service on filling posts, and people are actually doing the job of two people most times when they go to work. And that has been really exposed by the work-to-rule. And that means services have been slower, services have been curtailed and next week, when we have a work stoppage, we understand that the health service will be announcing to the public today that services will be closing.”

title: Avan Lee returns to Ireland with a vision for Munster
description: Meanwhile, Dan Sheehan is a big fan of the new RDS while the build-up continues to Ireland’s playoff against Kazakhstan
content:
Avan Lee had two spells living in Ireland before, the New Zealander playing rugby and cricket for Clontarf in the 1990s before returning to Dublin in 2012 when he worked with World Rugby. His third shift here, which begins in a fortnight, is likely to prove the most challenging of all after his appointment as interim chief executive at Munster Rugby . John O’Sullivan heard from him on Wednesday, Lee acknowledging that “there have been issues” with how the province has been run , ones that need to be addressed - and fixed. And he’s more than willing to sit down with former players like Peter O’Mahony who has been vocal with his criticism of late.
Ahead of Leinster’s URC meeting with Cardiff at the RDS on Saturday, Michael Scully talks to Dan Sheehan who is chuffed to be back at the venue. “It’s a proper club ground, edgy and not perfect, which is what a home ground should feel like.”
In football, we hear from Republic of Ireland defender Jessie Stapleton in the build-up to tomorrow’s World Cup qualifying playoff against Kazakhstan in Astana, tomorrow also a big day for Ireland’s under-21 side - they’ll find out who they will play in the European Championship playoffs. Stephen Barry talks to left-back Conor McManus about that superb 3-1 win over England at Turners Cross . “Honestly, I can’t describe it,” he said. “It’s the closest thing to what I imagine drugs would be like.”
In Gaelic games, Mayo’s Cillian O’Connor announced his retirement from intercounty football on Wednesday. Some career it was too - he is the leading scorer in the history of the senior championship with just the 32-364.
Gordon Manning, meanwhile, listened in on the Dáil committee exchanges when the leadership of the GAA, LGFA and Camogie Association fielded questions on the rocky road to integration . After two hours and 14 minutes, all concerned were none the wiser about a timeline for when it might happen. Bon Jovi, incidentally, featured quite heavily in the proceedings.
Paul Keane brings us the latest on the new format for the Leinster hurling championship . “There is still the hurdle of Congress to be navigated, but a green light there would see the existing six-team round-robin format binned in favour of two new groups of four.”
And Ciarán Murphy ponders the woes of clubs making early exits from their county championships , among them Kilcoo who, after 14 titles in the last 15 years, didn’t even make it to October in Down. An early bath.
TV Watch : Shane Lowry and Tom McKibbin are in the field for the Spanish Open which gets under way today (Sky Sports Golf, 1pm), and at 8pm, Virgin Media Two has live coverage of the league game between Shamrock Rovers and Drogheda United - even a draw would see Rovers go top of the table.

title: Anger, misogyny and radicalisation: the online trail of the Flydubai attacker
description: Co-pilot of flight 1073 gravitated towards the ‘manosphere’ and expressed misogynistic views
content:
T he Flydubai co-pilot who tried to hijack a flight to Tel Aviv is a former cryptocurrency speculator who, four years ago, was living with his parents and calling women “rotten meat” on a now disabled social media account.
Public information about Omani-Syrian aviator Hamam al-Hammami is scarce . Emirati investigators are keeping a tight hold on information gleaned from their interrogation of the would-be hijacker, diplomats say, and his online presence has been mysteriously scrubbed.
However, his prodigious online output between November 2021 and October 2022 includes more than 3,000 posts on Twitter . Although his account has been deleted, the posts are still available on an internet archive.
Often sending dozens of tweets in Arabic a day, the then 25-year-old Hammami bickered with other users, dispensed advice, opined about nutrition and fitness and enthused about flying – which he called the “safest means of transportation”.
His frequently furious online presence fused highly conservative interpretations of Islam with the sexist language of the “ manosphere ”, a misogynist online movement that derides feminism and promotes sexist gender roles. There are also hints of conservative religious beliefs, with Hammami saying he did not listen to music.
How and when Hammami was radicalised remains unknown.
Emirati interrogators are also investigating whether or not Hammami acted alone when he used an emergency axe to attack his pilot and attempt to take control of the plane on September 30th. The United Arab Emirates ( UAE ) has said this was a terrorist act. Israeli investigators are convinced that Hammami was a lone wolf, people briefed on the matter said.
[ ‘No one is passing through this door’: Inside the Flydubai cockpit fight Opens in new window ]
But this insistence has failed to assuage anger in Israel over what critics are calling systemic security failures, with media reports that Hammami was flagged as having radical views by his previous employer, Oman Air, and relegated to a desk job.
The co-pilot spent time in multiple countries in the Middle East. According to Hammami’s tweets, his Omani father wed his mother, a member of the Shamar tribe from southern Syria, in 1993. She “raised us on religion, morals, and virtue”, Hammami tweeted.
He grew up partly in the UAE, according to media reports, but moved to Syria in 2011, the year the Arab Spring inflamed the region, a person familiar with the matter said. The teenager then lived for four years in the country as it was engulfed in civil war, a conflict which spawned and sustained a plethora of Islamist militant groups.
Hammami undertook aviation studies in Australia from 2015 to 2017, where he said he had lodged with two local families, but did not graduate. From 2018 to 2019, he spent six months studying in New Zealand, at one of the world’s two major pilot training centres, with a flying school that was subsequently taken over by a British company, according to New Zealand officials.
Hammami did an online course with a British university, although he never entered the UK, according to people with knowledge of the situation. One of Hammami’s tweets mentions that his brother studied in the UK.
His five years in the West, he tweeted, were the “golden years of my religious commitment”, although he said his observance lapsed upon his return to the Middle East.
The details mentioned in his Twitter account match with his biographical details and with his profile on LinkedIn, also now deleted.
Investigators looking in to Hammami’s private online search history have found that he accessed extremist Islamist content while he was living in Australia, according to two people familiar with the investigation.
Rather than completing his flying qualifications abroad, Hammami returned to Oman and got a job at the state-owned airline, a move that he tweeted was the “best decision I ever made”. Oman Air did not respond to a request for comment on his employment there.
[ Flydubai flight: Indian pilot praised after disaster averted Opens in new window ]
Around 2019, Hammami got into spot trading and cryptocurrency speculation, a mistake he later blamed on being tempted by “the devil”. His attempted investments ended in failure, and he said he lost “120,000”. While he did not specify the currency, if it were Omani rials, that would be a loss of more than $300,000.
Aged 25 by 2022, Hammami lived with his lawyer father and homemaker mother in a classy neighbourhood in the Omani capital Muscat. “I wouldn’t dare think about moving out of my family’s house as long as I’m not married,” he tweeted.
Hammami joined Twitter – now rebranded as X – in late 2021, and was desperate to secure an arranged marriage. “I’m 25 and I want to get married today, before tomorrow!” he tweeted in January 2022.
He stipulated that the lady should be an 18- to 23-year-old religious Saudi from a tribal background, wear a face-covering niqab, agree not to work outside the home and be willing to live abroad. He had no success using an online matchmaking platform for Muslims, he said, but had become convinced that most women “care primarily about money” and were “skilled at pretence”.
His posts regularly evoked violence against women and used derogatory sexual slurs.
“Her only obligation is to lift her legs,” he wrote. Discussing a woman seeking a divorce over a dispute about posting pictures online, he said: “She needs a good thrashing.”
[ Passenger recounts taking control of Flydubai plane Opens in new window ]
Hammami peppered his diatribes with the language of the manosphere, repeatedly using terms like “simp”, which refers to an affectionate man, or the approving moniker “Alpha” for a strong man, and interacting with accounts that promote sexist ideology.
Despite his vitriol against women, Hammami boasted about the approaches he received. “I have never touched a girl in my life,” he wrote in January 2022, “even though I swear I have many opportunities ... God has protected us from temptations”, he added, saying he would not “chase after cheap, rotten flesh”.
