title: Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in Literature 2026
description: There have been 122 literature laureates to date, of whom only 18 have been women
content:
Canadian writer Anne Carson has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature .
According to the Swedish Academy in Stockholm, which awards the prize, Carson won “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”.
Carson, who was born in Toronto in 1950, has, throughout her career, combined poetry writing with translation work and teaching classics at various universities in North America.
The 76-year-old writer revealed in a London Review of Books essay in 2024 that she has Parkinson’s disease. “A symptom particularly mortifying to me was that my handwriting disintegrated,” she wrote. “I scrub out whole paragraphs in shame.”
Carson is married to the artist Robert Currie. The couple were granted Icelandic citizenship in 2022.
Former Irish Times poetry critic John McAuliffe, choosing Carson’s Float as his book of the year in 2016, wrote: “Float is the best new ‘book’ I’ve read this year, funny, bleak and urgent, as might be gathered from Carson’s definition of her art: ‘If prose is a house, poetry is a man on fire running quite fast through it.’
“Float collects 22 pamphlets in a clear slipcase, including poems about the death of her older brother, which she so memorably wrote about in Nox (2010), brilliant litanies which draw on ancient Greek poets and 20th-century visual art (and, in one case, the instruction manual for her microwave), funny, theatrical poems for Laurie Anderson and Lou Reed, and cross-genre essays, including the reflection on Francis Bacon, Variations on the Right to Remain Silent, which was initially commissioned by Belinda McKeon and first performed at the Poetry Now festival in Dún Laoghaire.”
A highly-regarded translator of classical writers such as Sappho and Euripides, including her triptych rendering of An Oresteia (2009), Carson has published poems, essays, libretti, prose criticism, and verse novels. Her subjects include love, desire, sexual longing and despair.
Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning, Anders Olsson, chair of the Nobel committee, said, “She has identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work.” Her translations from classical Greek include her interpretation of Sappho’s poem fragments, If Not, Winter (2002), along with tragedies such as Sophocles’s Electra (2001) and Antigone (2015) and Euripides’s Bakkhai (2015).
In her long essay Eros the Bittersweet (1986), Carson laid the foundation for her work, Olsson said. She speaks of a “stereoscopic vision” that allows her to “hold in equipoise two perspectives at once”. Her method of writing leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and artforms.
In the 1990s, Carson published a series of notable works such as The Glass Essay in Glass, Irony, and God (1995), which demonstrates the potential of the long poem where genre boundaries are seen to blur. While the work is written in verse form, it is also a long story about grief and unrequited love, in which the first-person narrator, a woman who has been left by her husband, visits her lonely mother in the desolate moorlands. On the journey there, she takes with her the works of her favourite author Emily Brontë, whose own moorlands and inner world are intricately woven into the text. Constructed around three lonely women sitting at a kitchen table, the long poem, which is also a reading of Brontë, is thus transformed into an essay about abandonment.
The same decade saw the publication of another work, often heralded as Carson’s greatest, Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse (1998). This demonstrates her eminent ability to actualise the classical literary tradition with a precise feel for contemporary idioms and experiences.
“Carson once described boredom as her arch-enemy, and it is a state she confronts with drastic humour and wit,” Olsson said. The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos, published in 2001, tells of a cutting and sardonic row with a deceitful husband, its 29 episodes each opening with lines of verse by the romantic poet John Keats.
“Carson often crosses over into various artistic and academic fields. Her collaborations with visual artists and choreographers and with opera and theatre directors demonstrate the freedom with which she relates to literary expectations and rule systems. It is this that lies behind the outstanding importance her work since the 1990s has had for the international art and literature scene.”
The Nobel Prize in Literature is worth 12 million Swedish crowns (€1.07 million). The prize was won last year by Hungarian author László Krasznahorkai. There have been 123 literature laureates to date. Carson is only the 19th woman to be awarded the prize.

title: Home heating oil surges 58% as energy bill hikes wipe out budget gains
description: The cost of filling a 1,000 litre domestic oil tank has gone up €400 since June and July
content:
Families face bills of €1,600 to heat their homes this winter as soaring energy prices threaten to wipe out workers’ budget tax gains.
Home heating oil prices rose by 58.6 per cent in September when compared with the same month last year, new figures from the Central Statistics Office (CSO) released on Thursday show.
Sharp rises in energy prices sparked by the US-Iran war helped drive up the cost of living by 4.1 per in the 12 months to September, the highest increase in two years, according to the CSO.
The cost of filling a 1,000 litre domestic oil tank now varies between €1,500 and €1,600, according to Daragh Cassidy, head of communications at price comparison website, Bonkers.ie.
“It’s gone up €250 since the start of August and €400 since June and July,” he added.
Around 700,000 homes across the Republic use this oil as their primary source of heating their homes.
News of the increase comes as householders prepare for the winter, when the need for home heating is at its greatest.
Home heating oil prices rose by 7.2 per cent from August to September alone, the CSO noted.
Rises in heating oil, natural gas and motor fuel costs could wipe out most of what workers will gain through tax cuts and other benefits announced this week in Budget 2026.
Those gains will simply “help people to stand still”, the consumer advocate remarked of the measures announced by Minister for Finance, Simon Harris, on Tuesday.
The US-Iran war, a resulting squeeze on global refining capacity and a weakening in the value of the euro against the dollar, are combining to drive up the price of the kerosene used by Irish people to heat their homes, Cassidy explained.
Motorists also continued to deal with sharp price increases on forecourts, according to CSO.
[ Fuel excise cuts extended to February as carbon tax is slashed to ease home heating costs Opens in new window ]
Petrol prices were 14 per cent higher in September than a year earlier, while diesel rose by 22 per cent. This was against a backdrop of a renewal in air strikes by the US on Iran and the absence of a deal that would fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and ease trade blockages.
Diesel cost €2.06 a litre on average in the Republic last month while petrol cost €1.96 a litre.
The CSO does not publish national average prices for home heating oil.
“In the month of September we saw significant price movements for fuel and home heating oil,” Anthony Dawson, a statistician in the CSO’s prices division acknowledged.
The CSO’s Consumer Price Index, which measures the cost of living in the Republic, rose 4.1 per cent year-on-year in September, the office confirmed on Thursday.
The most significant increases in the 12 months to September were in housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels, Dawson noted.
Dermot Daly, EY Ireland consumer products and retail lead, said the jump in energy prices in the latest CSO data is “particularly noteworthy”.
“Consumers have shown resilience – household spending is likely to grow 2.5 per cent after inflation this year – but many will have to prioritise essential purchases while taking a more considered approach to discretionary spending,” he said.
“As we move closer to the important Christmas trading period, retailers will be hoping that consumer spending remains resilient despite ongoing cost pressures.
The CSO’s Dawson confirmed that the 4.1 per cent rise in the cost of living was the highest since September 2024, when the increase was also 4.1 per cent.
The Government this week increased the social welfare fuel allowance by €5 to €43 a week in Budget 2026.
It also cut carbon taxes levied on home heating oil to €48.50 a tonne for the current Government’s remaining term in office.

title: 4.48 Psychosis review: Marty Rea gives a riveting performance in Sarah Kane’s final play
description: Dublin Theatre Festival 2026: In a staging directed by Tom Creed, the actor makes someone depressingly isolated seem intimately real
content:
“The doctor gave me eight minutes to live,” someone says, in a set-up to a typically arch joke, in 4.48 Psychosis. “I’d been sitting in the f**king waiting room half an hour!”
It’s a neat jab, a reminder of how funny the playwright Sarah Kane could be, in a work lashing out at medical mistreatment – although, since the play’s premiere, in 2000, the breezy feel of such zingers has been easily swallowed by its wildly abstract form, which is itself an attempt to put a shape on something as amorphous as clinical depression.
Perhaps the best that can be hoped for when it comes to Kane’s final work – a jungle of scenes depicting psychiatric consultations, drug sedations and doomsday prophecies – is, quite simply, a lucid production.
Tom Creed , the director of this staging at Dublin Theatre Festival , resists the temptation of other revivals to divvy the text between multiple performers (a literal interpretation of a fragmented mind) and instead allows all the pieces to be held by one person: Marty Rea .
From the opening moments of this riveting production, the figure we meet onstage is an acute observer. He calmly leans forward in impersonation of an inquiring psychiatrist; he gallops breathlessly through a nocturnal epiphany (“I had a night in which everything was revealed to me!”).
Despite existing within a void, and resembling a soul on the edge of oblivion, he is as personal as he is remote, as humiliated as he is removed, as if finding the meeting point between Lena Dunham and Samuel Beckett . Addressing a lover enviously asleep beside him, he says, seething, “You’ve touched me somewhere so f**king deep I can’t believe and I can’t be that for you!”
This resembles, in the sublime detail of Rea’s performance, a touching achievement in making someone depressingly isolated seem intimately real. Watch as, while describing a life sapped by mental illness, his voice weakens, releasing a slow drip of tears with a gentle blink: “I cannot write… I cannot love…”
Rea shows every thought process and emotional state: rageful after feeling betrayed by doctors; adrift with numbness and drugs; frightened of losing their mind; in free fall during a breakdown; and cracking fatalist jokes warning of destruction.
[ Sarah Kane’s 4.48 Psychosis: ‘It’s not for everyone. But I feel very alive when I watch it’ Opens in new window ]
It’s a journey assisted by the design of this Once Off production, a once-familiar world now shadowy and unrecognisable in Stephen Dodd’s lighting; a psychiatrist’s opinion becoming artificial feedback in Ivan Birthistle’s sound design.
Kane’s play may be indirect in parts – see the staccato sequences resembling flashing incomplete moments (“flicker, punch, slash…”), or a cognitive exam involving counting down from 100 – but there’s no questioning its final admiration for human connection, achingly yearned for from a distance.
Ultimately, 4.48 Psychosis is to theatre what The Bell Jar is to fiction: easily dismissed as morose, discussed more as biography than as art, when, in truth, it’s the work of a ferocious mind resurfacing from depression, sculpting hidden, numbed oblivion into something tangible and observable.
This is probably its most distilled production, arriving like clarity. Devastatingly, I can see them, before they vanish again.
4.48 Psychosis is at Project Arts Centre, as part of Dublin Theatre Festival , until Sunday, October 11th, then at the Mick Lally Theatre , in Galway, from Wednesday, November 4th, until Saturday, November 7th

title: The fight was dubbed ‘a fascinating experiment’: would boxing fans show decency and taste?
description: Proposal to stage bout between Oliver McCall and Ike Ibeabuchi offers yet more evidence of boxing’s bid to win race to the bottom
content:
Thirty-two years have passed since Oliver McCall flew to London to fight Lennox Lewis for the WBC heavyweight title. The one-time sparring partner of Mike Tyson was meant to give the undefeated champion a decent workout and another straightforward win to enhance his credibility. Somehow living up to his rather exaggerated billing as “The Atomic Bull”, 29-year-old McCall dropped Lewis in the second round, stunning Wembley Arena, and, judging by the frenzied way he gambolled around the ring celebrating, maybe even himself too.
By the time of their rematch at the Las Vegas Hilton in February 1997, a gap of less than 2½ years, McCall had lost the belt to Frank Bruno, spent time in rehab and incurred multiple arrests for possession of crack. An all too familiar boxer’s tale of that era. Just weeks before the second bout, he went berserk in a Tennessee hotel, hurling a Christmas tree across the lobby and spitting at a police officer. Then, he found God conveniently located on the road from his cell to Nevada. The portrait was of a woebegone character exhibiting the troubling behaviour of somebody who belonged anywhere but in a boxing ring. So it proved.
In the fourth round of an otherwise dull encounter, McCall effectively downed tools, no longer bothering to protect himself or to fight back. “I thought he was playing possum,” said referee Mills Lane, “then I saw his lip quiver”. After the bell spared him further punishment, Lane followed him back to his stool and asked whether he wanted to continue. His corner said he did. Fifty-five seconds into the fifth, Lane stopped the contest because McCall, hands by his side, now mostly walking away from the bemused Lewis, was sobbing, obviously suffering some sort of breakdown.
The crowd jeered lustily at the most bizarre denouement to a heavyweight title fight, his purse of $3 million was withheld, and within weeks he was committed to a psychiatric hospital as “an imminent danger to himself and others”. Even by boxing’s historically parlous standards, the entire episode shamed everybody with skin in the game.
Inevitably, depressingly, McCall returned to the ring within eight months of that debacle and stayed there more or less ever since. Never formally hanging up his gloves, any gaps in his resume were enforced absences due to stints in rehab or recurring brushes with the law. Twice he fought on the same card as his son Elijah. Once an up-and-comer, the kid is long retired and nearing 40 himself. A sentence making the recent announcement that his father, now 61, would fight Ike Ibeabuchi, a stripling of just 53, on Thanksgiving Day this November even more startling.
An outfit called PrizeFighting.tv put together this very special, meaning utterly reprehensible, show to be staged in Ibeabuchi’s native Nigeria . Definitely a bout with a difference. In order for it to take place, they required 12,500 fans of slow-motion car crashes from around the globe to stump up $9.95 (€8.90) for pay-per-view before October 31st. The unique selling strategy and senescent combatants offered yet more proof boxing would always and forever try to win modern sport’s race to the very bottom.
[ Newry’s Conor Wallace comes up short in world title eliminator against Ben Whittaker Opens in new window ]
“The promoter is putting the fight’s fate in the hands of the fans,” wrote Eric Raskin on Boxingscene.com. “Here is this absolute horror show between two men both about double their prime ages, two boxers with documented mental health problems ... They are daring boxing fans to be discerning and to show a little taste and a sense of decency. It’s a fascinating experiment, as ‘discerning,’ ‘taste’ and ‘decency’ aren’t the first three words that come to mind when one thinks of us bloodthirsty savages. But even if we’re tasteless, indecent and undiscerning ... there’s still no audience for this creak show, right?”
While McCall was having his very public breakdown in 1997, Ibeabuchi was gatecrashing the heavyweight division top 10, causing a stir of his own. He was born in Nigeria, where watching Buster Douglas dethrone Tyson fired his fistic imagination, and, following a move to Dallas, his defeat of the highly rated David Tua turned him into an instant contender. Just weeks after that victory, he drove his car (in which his ex-girlfriend’s teen son was a severely injured passenger) straight into a concrete pillar in an apparent suicide attempt. Diagnosed as bipolar, he once called his promoter at 3am claiming he was being visited by demons.
[ Weird fishes: Alison Healy on obscure competitions and the contestants they attract Opens in new window ]
By 26, his best days were already behind him, the next decade, prime fighting years, were squandered as he filled a lengthy, disturbing police blotter with sexual assault cases that earned him prison time. Befitting a sport where what-ifs have always been prized currency, a legend grew up around him, some wondering whether Ibeabuchi was surely the great lost heavyweight of that generation. Never mind the heinous nature of the crimes he committed against a slew of women, or that he didn’t fight between 1999 and 2025, boxing gyms remain fecund spaces for coulda, woulda, shoulda.
[ Dave Hannigan: Cus D’Amato, famed coach of Mike Tyson, was portrayed as a saint. He was far from it Opens in new window ]
With one loss and one win to his name since returning to the ring last year, somebody reckoned there was an appetite out there for Ibeabuchi against McCall, the soon to be pensioner boasting two wins from three outings since turning 60. Turns out there isn’t. Last Monday, four weeks before their self-imposed deadline, the promoters shockingly announced advance sales were so slow this farce was cancelled. Good taste or sanity or perhaps financial reality prevailed.
Maybe there’s hope for boxing yet. As if.

title: ‘We’re at a tipping point’: EU prepares its toughest weapon yet against China
description: As lay-offs spread across parts of Europe’s industrial heartland, Brussels believes Beijing’s export surplus can no longer be absorbed by the single market
content:
E uropean Union trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic arrives in Beijing on Thursday for two days of talks with China’s commerce minister, Wang Wentao, aimed at averting a mutually destructive trade war.
The EU is considering an arsenal of measures if the negotiations fail to trace a path towards a more balanced trade relationship, including one that could shut Chinese companies out of the European market within 24 hours.
In advance of the talks in Beijing, China’s foreign ministry said dialogue and consultation were the best way to resolve differences, reminding the EU of how much its industry relies on Chinese components for its supply chain.
“Between China and the EU, the industrial and supply chains are highly integrated and mutually dependent, and our economic and trade relations are mutually beneficial in nature,” foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said in a written statement.
“It is hoped that the EU will work with China in the same direction and resolve each other’s concerns through dialogue and consultation, so that the two parties can jointly keep the global industrial and supply chains stable and unimpeded and promote the sound and steady development of China-EU economic and trade relations.”
Guo’s statement contained the implied threat that Beijing could use its near-monopoly on rare earths and permanent magnets that are essential to advanced manufacturing as leverage if the EU follows through on its most serious threats. China last year demonstrated its willingness to use critical minerals as a coercive instrument when it introduced export controls in response to Donald Trump’s tariffs.
The Europeans are looking for a commitment from China that it will moderate its huge flow of exports into the EU market, at least initially in specific sectors most at risk of being hollowed out by a flood of hyper-competitively priced goods coming from the east.
China’s economy grew in the first half of this year by 4.7 per cent on an annualised basis but much of that growth was driven by exports and investment in high-tech sectors, while domestic growth was sluggish.
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen has argued for a tougher stance towards China, something the German and Spanish governments have long resisted. Spain’s left-wing prime minister, Pedro Sánchez , has pursued closer ties with Beijing, and Berlin has traditionally been keen to avoid a destabilising trade war.
However, German chancellor Friedrich Merz this week backed a more assertive posture, a politically significant shift. Urgent action was needed to protect Europe’s position as a “sovereign” industrial power, he said in a joint letter to von der Leyen written with French president Emmanuel Macron .
The European Commission , which is the EU’s executive arm that leads on trade, has been warning national capitals about a second “China shock” hitting Europe’s economy for some time. Intense competition from China has been blamed as one reason factory jobs are being shed across Europe’s industrial base, from the automobile to the chemicals sectors.
China’s economic model relies heavily on exports, in part because it produces more goods than its domestic market can consume.
Commission officials have complained that this “overcapacity” has increasingly resulted in the excess being directed towards the EU’s open market, often at low prices that undercut home grown European businesses.
A trade dispute over electric vehicles (EVs) has become emblematic of this friction between Brussels and Beijing. More affordable Chinese-made EVs have been taking over a larger share of the European market, as people make the switch from diesel and petrol engines.
A 2024 investigation by the commission’s trade department established that BYD, SAIC and Geely had benefited from generous state subsidies, giving the Chinese EV-makers an edge over European competitors struggling to compete on price. In response the EU announced hefty tariffs on future imports of Chinese-made electric vehicles, to protect the fledgling European industry from being snuffed out over the next decade.
At the time Spain and Germany opposed placing tariffs on Chinese EVs. Beijing pushed back hard against the measures as well.
It is understood Germany’s then-chancellor Olaf Scholz hit the phones and called around to warn fellow EU leaders against the tariffs, according to one senior source with knowledge of the high-level lobbying efforts. Scholz feared the German car industry would be locked out of China’s massive market in retaliation.
The German chancellor’s efforts came up short. EU member states backed the EV tariffs, over the objections of Berlin and Madrid. Relations between Brussels and Beijing have been prickly since.
Senior commission officials want to make it easier for the EU to quickly run through a subsidy inquiry and levy defensive tariffs on Chinese products believed to be flooding the European market.
There is an acceptance in Brussels that existing anti-subsidy inquiries take too long.
It was a full year between the commission beginning an investigation into Chinese-made EVs and the approval of trade tariffs to try to redress the situation. The broader strategy pursued by von der Leyen has been to get European leaders to first recognise that the growing imbalance in the EU-China trading relationship is unsustainable and then settle on what they should do about the problem.
Earlier this year the trade deficit between the two economic blocs crossed a symbolic threshold of €1 billion a day, which helped the commission president’s case. Still, nobody around the table wants to kick off a damaging trade war.
Top figures in the commission’s Berlaymont headquarters have detected a shift in Berlin’s thinking over the last number of months, in response to worrying trade data.
The recent letter from Merz and Macron sets out the extent of the German leader’s pivot.
“We need a credible instrument in the hands of the Commission to allow for decisive and systemic reaction,” they wrote.
This proposed new instrument could limit access to the EU’s single market and be triggered quickly, to hit back hard in the event Brussels is locked in a trade war.
The two leaders, who did not mention China by name in their letter, suggested the commission needed to launch more investigations into “persistent market distortions” caused by trading partners. At the same time Europe had to reduce the areas where its economy was overly dependent on Beijing, or others, to guard against crucial supply chains being squeezed. The EU’s 27 leaders will pick up the discussion at a European Council summit next week.
The timing of the Franco-German intervention is intended to strengthen Sefcovic’s hand in talks in Beijing. The commission is hoping for some commitment China will tamp down excessive exports, to avoid things escalating into a full-blown trade war.
While Paris will always be more gung-ho about tariffs and protectionist measures, this is new territory for Berlin.
“Since 2024 there has been a dramatic increase in the number of lay-offs in the German car industry due to Chinese overcapacity,” said Esther Goreichy, visiting fellow at the Mercator Institute for China Studies think tank in Berlin.
It is striking that France and Germany, the EU’s two largest economies, were now lined up together behind the commission, a dynamic that gave the Brussels-based executive a mandate to be more assertive.
“We are now at the tipping point,” Goreichy said.

title: Motorcyclist (50s) seriously injured after crash with car in Donegal
description: Part of the N13 remained closed on Thursday morning to allow investigators to examine the road
content:
A motorcyclist in his 50s has been hospitalised after a crash with a car near Letterkenny, Co Donegal , on Wednesday.
The crash occurred on the N13 at Correnagh, near Letterkenny, shortly after 5pm.
The motorcyclist suffered what gardaí described as “serious injuries” and was brought to Letterkenny University Hospital , where he remained on Thursday.
The driver of the car, a woman in her 60s, was brought to the same hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, gardaí said.
Part of the N13 remained closed on Thursday morning to allow investigators to examine the road.
Gardaí asked any witnesses to the crash to contact them, and requested that anyone with relevant video or dashcam footage from the N13 near Correnagh, Letterkenny, in the lead-up to the crash contact Letterkenny Garda station.
So far in 2026, 143 have lost their lives on Irish roads, including 22 motorcyclists.

title: Man stole nearly €2,000 in ATM distraction thefts where victims included an elderly nun
description: Levers Zinca (31) claimed he was carrying out the thefts in order to send money to his sick grandmother in Romania
content:
A man who stole almost €2,000 in a series of ATM distraction thefts targeting elderly and vulnerable victims has been jailed for four and a half years.
Levers Zinca (31) claimed he was carrying out the thefts in order to send money to his sick grandmother in Romania. He used leaflets to cover the cash dispensing area as he distracted victims using the ATMs including an elderly nun, a man with poor sight and a wheelchair user.
Gda Oisin Burke told the court he was of the opinion Zinca was loitering around ATMs to target vulnerable victims. Zinca was identified from CCTV.
Zinca, of no fixed abode, but formerly with addresses in Dublin 8 and Co Kildare, pleaded guilty to seven counts of theft at ATMs totalling €1,940 on dates between July and December 2025.
Dublin Circuit Criminal Court heard that Zinca has similar previous convictions here and in Belgium, Denmark and Germany.
Judge Cephas Power said the aggravating factors included the fact these thefts were planned and part of an organised strategy by the accused to take the property of the victim.
He noted Zinca was desperate at the time with a sick grandmother and financing a drug addiction.
He said it was also aggravating that many of the victims were elderly or incapacitated in some way and that Zinca has prior convictions for similar offences.
In mitigation, he considered his co-operation and admissions, as well as his guilty pleas and his prior work history. He noted Zinca had fallen into financial hardship on losing his job.
The judge imposed a five-year sentence with the final six months suspended for two years. He backdated the sentence to January 2026, when Zinca went into custody.
Burke told Eimear Delargy BL, prosecuting, that Zinca’s modus operandi involved distracting the victims while they were trying to take money out of an ATM.
The court heard Zinca would cover the ATM screen or cash dispensing area with a leaflet or map and distract the victims, some of whom were vulnerable due to age or disability, while he pressed buttons and took the cash dispensed.
The first victim was an 80-year-old woman using an ATM at the AIB branch in Dundrum Town Centre, followed a week later by an 80-year-old nun checking her bank balance at an ATM on O’Connell Street.
In both these cases, he approached the women at the ATM, spoke to them as they used it while obscuring their view of the ATM with leaflets. Both women subsequently discovered €200 missing from their accounts and reported it to gardaí. There were seven victims in total over six months.
CCTV was reviewed in all the cases and Zinca was identified. He was arrested in January 2026.
Keith Spencer BL, defending, said Zinca has made a full apology and his family had brought €2,000 to court to reimburse the victims.
He said his client had been working in a recycling company but lost his job and was “down on his luck” around this time.
Zinca, a father of three, has now linked in with the drug counsellor while in custody.

title: Sardinian village where high number of women reach 100 could be new centenarian ‘blue zone’
description: Longevity of the women in Bolotana is three times higher than that of most western women, scientist says
content:
The secret to longevity is being a woman – specifically, a woman in one part of Sardinia. At least, that is the conclusion of a study on centenarians in a tiny mountain village on the Italian island.
Sardinia became known as a haven for longevity, especially for long-lived men, in 1999 when a cluster of remote villages nestled in the slopes of its central and eastern provinces were classified among the world’s five “blue zones” – geographic areas with high concentrations of centenarians.
Now Bolotana, located in the Margine area of central Sardinia about 110km from the island’s original blue zone, has emerged as a new potential candidate, researchers say, generating centenarians every year in a trend driven by women.
A study by professors at Sardinia’s University of Sassari and the University of Alabama at Birmingham in the US, published in the scientific journal Frontiers in Aging, found that 13.8 per cent of women in the village who reach the age of 70 will live to 100 – placing it second in the world for female longevity after Hong Kong.
In Italy, where the number of centenarians has more than doubled since 2009, 3.5 per cent of women who make it to 70 will achieve the milestone.
The researchers analysed records of people born in Bolotana between 1900-1925 and found that 38 had lived beyond 100, putting their longevity rate at 57 per cent higher than the Italian national average.
The study began in 2024 and as of last year there were 12 centenarians among a population of 2,266 in Bolotana – roughly 12 times the Sardinian average.
Six have since died and the six who are left are all women, the two eldest being 102. More residents are expected to reach the milestone age by the end of this year and during 2027.
The findings also showed that, compared with the world’s other four blue zones – Okinawa in Japan, the Nicoya peninsula in Costa Rica, Ikaria in Greece and Loma Linda in California in the US – Sardinia’s zone was expanding.
“The important thing is that, for the first time in more than 25 years, we have found a place for longevity outside of the conventional blue zone [in Sardinia],” Giovanni Mario Pes, the study’s lead scientist and a co-creator of the blue zone concept, told the Guardian.
“But while Bolotana shares the same characteristics, it is even more exceptional. Whereas the original zone had an unusual balance between the two sexes, here female longevity prevails.”
Pes said that while it was already well established that women lived longer for biological reasons, “the extraordinary thing is that the longevity of the women in Bolotana is three times higher than that of most western women”.
Pes, a Sardinian whose great-grandfather lived to 110 and whose mother is 101, declined to be drawn into hypothesising over the secrets to the village’s longevity, saying the study was “limited to pointing out the existence of the phenomenon”.
However, after spending time with sprightly centenarian women there, he said what struck him most were the “very intense and very real social relations” maintained throughout their lives.
He gave the example of Giovanna Marras, 101, who lives with her sister. “They live together, they cook together, they talk to each other easily,” said Pes. “There was absolutely no sign of cognitive decline.”
Francesco Manconi, the mayor of Bolotana, offered some theories. “I’m not a scientist but it’s probably a mix of things,” he told Corriere della Sera, citing a clean, fresh diet, although he said nobody renounced seada, a traditional local pastry filled with cheese, or mustazzolus, a spiced biscuit often eaten at breakfast.
The “uncontaminated nature” surrounding the village could also play a role, Manconi added, as well as physical activity, despite Bolotana not having a gym. “Elderly people have always walked a lot … as much as 20km [a] day. And I would say they were mostly women.”
As of November 2025, official statistics showed there were 23,548 residents in Italy who were aged 100 or over, up 2,000 from the previous year. Of those eclipsing a century last year, 82.6 per cent were women.
Women also take the lead among Italy’s 724 semi-supercentenarians, people aged 105 and over – and among the 19 supercentenarians, those in the 110-plus age bracket. – Guardian

title: Two men freed on bail after being charged with €500,000 cannabis seizure in Cork city
description: Judge David Waters remanded both men on bail on their own bonds of €200 each
content:
Two men have been freed on bail after they were charged in connection with the seizure of cannabis valued at €500,000 in Cork city earlier this week.
Lee Crinnion (21) from Blackwater Grove, Togher, Cork, and Aaron Austin (24) of Araglen Court, Togher, Cork, were brought before Cork District Court on Wednesday afternoon in connection with the seizure of 25kg of cannabis on Monday.
Both men were charged with possession of cannabis contrary to Section 3 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1997, and possession of cannabis for sale or supply contrary to Section 15 of the Misuse of Drugs Act at Togher Road, Cork on October 5th.
Det Garda Darren Twomey of the Cork City Divisional Drugs Squad gave evidence of arrest, charge and caution in relation to Crinnion and told the court that he made no reply to the charges when they were put to him after caution.
Det Garda Ruairi McGovern, also of the Cork City Divisional Drugs Squad, gave evidence of arrest, charge and caution in relation to Austin and told the court that he made no reply to the charges after caution.
Sgt David Fleming said gardaí were not objecting to bail with conditions, and defence solicitors Joe Cuddigan and Eddie Burke confirmed that their clients were consenting to the bail terms.
Under the terms, Crinnion would reside at Blackwater Grove, Togher, and Austin would reside at Araglen Court, Togher, and they would abide by a 11pm to 7am curfew and sign on three times a week at Togher Garda station.
The two accused also agreed to surrender their passports and not apply for any other travel documents, provide gardaí with mobile phone numbers on which they could be contacted 24/7, and have no contact with each other directly or indirectly.
Judge David Waters remanded both men on bail on their own bonds of €200 each to appear again at Cork District Court on November 3rd for the DPP’s directions on the matter.

title: Another sighting of the lesser-spotted Dublin fanlight horse
description: A second surviving specimen stands in the window of a Hendrick Street house in Smithfield
content:
I am delighted to report the sighting, thanks to another eagle-eyed reader, of a second surviving Dublin fanlight horse. As Brian Galvin emailed to let me know, this one is on Hendrick Street, near Smithfield. And it looks in even better shape than the specimen previously identified, at Erne Street .
Whereas that seemed a bit downcast, this one has its head up, and is in full prancing mode. In any case, although the once-prolific species must still be considered endangered, the fact that there are at least two horses still out there may open the possibility that they could breed again.
The location of the latest discovery is unquestionably apt. It was a talk by city historian Cathy Scuffil on how horses have left their mark on Dublin that first alerted me to the subject of these formerly ubiquitous fanlight figurines.
But the stamp of equine history is obvious even on a map of the Smithfield area. Just opposite Hendrick Street, for example, is a place still called Haymarket. Nearby also is a Stable Lane. And then of course there is Smithfield itself, long synonymous with the horse fair.
Other vestiges of the animal’s former dominance are “cobblestones and jostlestones”, to quote part of the title of Scuffil’s talk, also still prevalent around there.
Cobblestones were first used as a hard-wearing, drainage-friendly street surface for horses pulling heavy loads.
Jostlestones, now devoid of context but still standing in many places, were short, stumpy stone pillars designed to protect gate piers and other vulnerable building parts from cartwheels cutting corners.
Hendrick Street itself is somewhat nondescript these days, although it merits a sizeable entry in an excellent blog I found called historyeye.ie . Even that begins by acknowledging the street’s limitations, including its failure to be mentioned in Ulysses, a stigma hard to live down.
“It was never a fashionable place,” says the blog: “a short street slotted between the city’s hay, corn and cattle markets to the east and the enormous Royal Barracks to the west. A street that might be used on the way to or from somewhere else: so overlooked that it never made it once into the huge canon of Joyce’s Dublin.”
Back in the 1700s, apparently, it was dominated by “Dutch Billies”, the gable-to-the-road style of architecture that was the city’s defining look before the Georgian era.
But today, says the blog, the last remnant of the 18th century is an old house, now two-storey but once taller and perhaps gabled, occupied by Bourke’s Funeral Directors, on the corner with Queen Street.
That, as it happens, is where the fanlight horse resides. So perhaps in keeping with one of the theories about how the statuettes originated, this one is itself is a relic of a time when King Billy’s memory was still revered.
Short as Hendrick Street is, it has had its share of well-known residents, none more famous than Willie the “Toucher” Doyle (1880-1933).
He too was associated with horses: by some accounts he was a professional gambler. But he can’t have been that good because what he was more noted for, and earned his nickname from, was asking people for loans.
He was painted by Harry Kernoff (from whom he sought “ten bob” while posing) as one of a pair of drinkers in a picture called A Bird Never Flew on One Wing, which hung for years in a Dublin Pub, O’Brien’s of Leeson Street.
And as previously mentioned here , this may have had far-reaching consequences.
The story goes that a Hollywood designer visited the pub once and was struck by Doyle’s pointy noise and almost alien ears. The designer later worked on Star Trek and so, according to legend, the Toucher lent his features to Mr Spock.
Whether that’s truth or imaginative fiction, Hendrick Street’s claims to cinematic history do not end there.
Just as Smithfield posed as postwar Berlin in the 1965 film version of The Spy Who Came in From the Cold, it seems the old house on Hendrick Street’s corner featured in a 1960 thriller, set in London half a century earlier, called The Siege of Sidney Street.
I can’t find it mentioned in Irish newspaper archive reports of the film scenes shot here. But describing another of the locations, Donore Avenue, the Cork Examiner’s Dublin correspondent noted (a little defensively): “Take it whichever way you will ... one of the reasons for making this film in Dublin is that we still have streets here which are like those of London’s East End fifty years ago.”
Today there is at least one conspicuously modern building on Hendrick Street: the eponymous Hendrick, a hotel billing itself as the first in Ireland devoted to “street art”.
It also, however, trades on the area’s past, including “the city’s darker side”. Thus, the hotel website boasts that Hendrick Street “has long carried whispers of hauntings” and “tales of restless spirits”. These are not specified, but perhaps the horse in the fanlight nearby can now be added to the list.

title: Ireland weather: Yellow rain warning issued for counties Donegal, Galway, Leitrim, Mayo and Sligo
description: Met Éireann forecasts wet and breezy weather for the country over the coming days
content:
Status yellow weather warnings have been issued for counties Donegal , Galway , Leitrim , Mayo and Sligo , as Ireland experiences wet and breezy conditions, according to Met Éireann .
The warning for those counties is valid from 9am Thursday to 4am Friday, with potentially difficult travelling conditions and possible localised flooding.
The weather in Ireland will be mainly dry at first on Thursday with some sunshine in the east. Outbreaks of rain and drizzle will develop in the west and gradually spread eastward in the morning, becoming widespread in the afternoon.
Rain will be heaviest and most persistent in the west and north. It will also be breezy with the arrival of rain.
Highest temperatures will be 10 to 13 degrees.
Met Éireann says it will become milder from the west on Thursday evening.
On Thursday night it will be mostly cloudy, breezy and mild, with patches of rain and drizzle, turning heavy at times in the west and northwest.
Lowest temperatures of 12 to 15 degrees for most, but dropping to between nine to 11 degrees towards morning in the northwest.
The national forecaster says Friday will have a dull and damp start in the east and south with rain and drizzle gradually clearing southeastward through the morning.
The west and northwest will see brighter, fresher conditions with sunny spells and scattered blustery showers, which will extend to all parts by the afternoon.
Highest temperatures will range from 11 to 14 degrees.
There will be clear spells and scattered showers, some possibly heavy in the north on Friday night with lowest temperatures of six to 10 degrees.
Saturday will be another breezy day with a mix of cloud, sunshine and scattered showers, says Met Éireann. The showers will become increasingly isolated from the south in the evening, with highest temperatures of 11 to 14 degrees.
Showers will become isolated on Saturday night as lowest temperatures range from four to eight degrees.
Sunday will be mainly dry with bright or sunny spells to begin.
However, it will turn cloudier from the southwest as the day goes on. Patchy rain and drizzle is possible in Atlantic coastal fringes towards the evening. Highest temperatures will reach 11 to 15 degrees.

title: Most skirmishes before and after the budget featured Patrick O’Donovan
description: Inside Politics: Minister has central role in row over the ‘culture card’ and his decision to cut State subvention to RTÉ by €20 million
content:
At a lively press conference in his department on Wednesday, Patrick O’Donovan said he did not have an abrasive style as a Minister.
But all eyes are on the Minister as he has played a central role in the two fracas that have occurred pre- and post- budget : namely a row over the “culture card”, and his decision to reduce the State’s subvention to RTÉ by €20 million for 2027 because of his view that it had a suboptimal performance.
The lead story for The Irish Times shows both of the issues are related to pre-budget discussions with Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers on the funding allocated to O’Donovan’s department for 2027.
We report that in a letter last week, O’Donovan told Chambers that, based on what was being offered, “the Government (not the department) will renege on the three-year funding deal agreed with RTÉ in July 2024”.
At the heel of the hunt, an additional €21 million was allocated to O’Donovan’s department after the letter. And that seemed to be that.
But in a move that caught most people unawares, O’Donovan confirmed yesterday that RTÉ’s allocation for 2027 remained the same as 2026 at €240 million . It had been expecting €260 million under its three-year deal with the Government.
O’Donovan said he was not happy with the pace of change at the broadcaster and its transition to being a “more agile, smaller” organisation.
That led to a swift and very assertive response from RTÉ. In an email to staff, RTÉ director general Kevin Bakhurst said he “completely rejects” O’Donovan’s assertion that the pace of reform at Montrose has been too slow.
[ What are the key takeaways from Budget 2027? From income tax cuts to surprising omissions ]
Bakhurst said the station now had “some important decisions to make” if the previous agreement made with the Government “will no longer be honoured”.
RTÉ’s chair, Terence O’Rourke, is now seeking a meeting with the Minister over the decision to effectively cut promised funding and its impact on the broadcaster.
One of the contested issues is the voluntary exit programme. Almost 100 people have left the organisation. O’Donovan’s view is that only abut 30 were part of the voluntary exit programme. RTÉ has countered by saying it has managed that programme well despite the fact that it was agreed and started at a late stage.
O’Donovan, at the conference, was also asked to respond to Irish broadcaster Doireann Ní Ghlacáin’s description of him as a “f**king eejit” after he said that media regulator Coimisiún na Meán would have been better off with an English title.
On the budget in general, the latest Inside Politics Podcast – Budget 2027: buying the peace by pouring fuel on the fire – is here .
There are “afters” too with the unions because of the unfinished business of a public sector pay deal and the prospect of increasing industrial action over the winter months.
Ictu general secretary Owen Reidy said the measures did not go far enough to prevent a nationwide strike by public servants planned for next Wednesday. Already some unions in the public sector have told their members to operate on a work-to-rule basis.
Reidy said the budget announced on Tuesday was a “halfhearted apology for last year’s” and did not do enough to address the income tax bands, which were untouched in the previous year’s budget.
“The changes to income tax are a step in the right direction, and these changes were something trade unions have pushed for. However, they do not go far enough to make up for last year’s budget, when bands were left untouched,” he said.
In his speech on Tuesday, Chambers said that €1.2bn in additional resources set aside for public sector pay increases showed the “seriousness” of the Government in wanting to reach a new agreement. He added: “I would now call on Ictu and other associations to match this intent by re-engaging as a matter of urgency and standing down the ongoing industrial action.”
As Marie O’Halloran reports, Taoiseach Micheál Martin weighed into the row in the Dáil yesterday . He defended the Government ’s approach to public sector pay negotiations and said a dispute “would be unwarranted given our willingness to talk”.
He pointed to an increase in the number of public service positions and willingness to implement “substantial pay agreements”.
“What no one can expect us to do is to accept unilateral preconditions before discussions, or to give up our right to table proposals,” he told the Dáil.
“Any dispute on this basis serves no positive purpose and simply delays negotiations which we have shown time and again that we always approach in good faith.”
In her column, Sinéad O’Sullivan points to the EU undergoing substantial change , with discussions ongoing between it and Ukraine and Canada. That might prompt a new era of industrialisation where Ireland, with its almost-total emphasis on a service economy, may get left behind.
Newton Emerson argues that Sinn Féin and the DUP are happier going to their default positions of arguing over the ‘national question’, in this instance parades, than debating the everyday political issues such as securing a budget.
Dublin’s primary synagogue chose not to organise a public memorial to commemorate the October 7th attacks on Israel due to concern over “the possibility of somebody seeking to cause actual physical harm” to the Jewish community, Chief Rabbi of Ireland Yoni Wieder has said. Stephen Conneely reports.

title: Grafton to seek new board chair
description: Company owns Woodies and Chadwicks
content:
Builders merchant and DIY retailer Grafton is on the hunt for a new chair for its board.
The group said current chair Ian Tyler has informed the board he will step down, citing other commitments.
Tyler, who was previously chief executive of Balfour Beatty, joined Grafton’s board as a non-executive director in March 2024, and became chair following the 2024 annual general meeting.
He is also chair of BP and design and technical consulting firm BMT Group, and is senior independent director of Anglo American.
The London-listed group, which owns Woodies and Chadwicks, will now start the process to recruit a new chair.
It will be led by senior independent director Dr Rosheen McGuckian, with the assistance of an external search firm.
The company did not specify a timescale for the completion of the process.

title: Tesco to open four new Irish stores as expansion continues
description: Retailer raises group profit outlook floor after first-half rise
content:
Tesco plans to open four new Irish stores, including large supermarkets and further Express outlets, in the coming months.
Interim results published on Wednesday by the British grocer showed it has plans to add a further 60,000 sq ft of Irish retail space before February next year.
A spokeswoman for Tesco, which opened nine new Irish stores in the past 12 in months, told The Irish Times that the expansion would include two new superstores in Donegal Town and Clongriffin in Dublin.
She added that new Express stores will also be opened in Montpelier in Dublin and Ballincollig in Cork.
The company’s latest results showed sales at Tesco’s Irish business rose in the first half of the year, driven by growth in its fresh and packaged food offering.
Tesco, which claims a 24.1 per cent share of the Irish grocery market, said strong like-for-like sales growth of 4.1 per cent was driven by volume increases. Total sales growth of 6.7 per cent was driven by a contribution from new space.
Like-for-like sales in its food business grew 4.4 per cent compared with the same period in 2025, with the company’s Tesco Finest sales rising almost 13 per cent year on year.
The company’s online business also surged, growing by close to 12 per cent, lifted by the wider roll-out of its Whoosh same-day delivery service to more stores in the second half of 2025.
Non-food sales were up 1.5 per cent on a like-for-like basis.
The wider Tesco group lifted the bottom end of ‌its full-year profit outlook on Thursday after reporting a 6.5 per cent increase for its ​first half, even as a very hot summer weighed on sales volumes across the industry.
The group said it made an adjusted operating profit ⁠of £1.78 billion for the 26 weeks to August ‌29th, ‌on ​sales, excluding VAT sales tax and fuel, up 2 per cent to £33.8 billion.
UK like-for-like sales ⁠for the half ​rose 1.5 per cent, having been up ​1.8 per cent in the first quarter.
Monthly industry data has ‌shown Tesco lost a little ​market share in the second quarter. However, it was ⁠up against a tough comparative ⁠performance ​in the same quarter last year when UK like-for-like sales rose 4.6 per cent, helped by disruption at competitors Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Asda.
The conflict in the Middle East, and its impact on energy prices, also created uncertainty for many ‌households during the first ⁠half.
Tesco, whose shares have risen 8 per cent so far this year, is now forecasting adjusted operating ‌profit of £3.15 billion to £3.3 billion for its year to end-February ​2027, versus previous guidance of £3 billion to £3.3 ​billion and the £3.152 billion made in 2025/26. – Additional reporting: Reuters

title: Margaret Hamilton, trailblazer whose software powered Apollo 11 moon landing, dies at 90
description: MIT computer scientist led development of software for moon mission
content:
Margaret Hamilton, the computer pioneer whose software powered the first moon landing , has died, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) said. She was 90.
In an era before titles such as software engineer and computer scientist became mainstream, Hamilton, who died on 30 September, learned to program under the tutelage of a renowned MIT meteorologist.
She continued to perfect the craft in an MIT laboratory, writing software that could detect enemy aircraft. When the institute received a Nasa contract to develop the Apollo on-board flight software, she jumped at the opportunity.
“I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired,” she told the Guardian in 2019.
In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was set to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an on-board computer’s alarm rang, indicating an emergency.
Faced with a decision of whether to abort the mission, the spacecraft continued on. The software was working just as Hamilton and her team intended.
“It quickly became clear the software was not only informing everyone that there was a hardware-related problem but was compensating for it – restarting and re-establishing the highest priority tasks. The error detection and recovery mechanisms had come to the rescue,” Hamilton said.
Barack Obama referenced the incident when he presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016.
“Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said.
Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great grandchildren, according to MIT.
Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.” – Guardian

title: Lone star Trump believes he can bend Texas and midterm elections to his will
description: US president’s essential message to Maga voters on campaign tour has been ‘pretend I am on the ballot’
content:
Not so long ago, the snub would have been unimaginable. On Wednesday afternoon, president Donald Trump boarded Air Force One and headed to San Antonio to rally for beleaguered senatorial candidate Ken Paxton. Conspicuous by his absence in the Freeman Coliseum was veteran Texas governor and Trump booster Greg Abbott.
After 11 years in office, Abbott is, sensationally, trailing Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa in the Texas gubernatorial race by four points, according to a New York Times/Siena poll released this week. Media inquiries as to why governor Abbott would not be in the Houston arena to receive the president were met with a terse response from his campaign team.
“The governor is running a re-election campaign and has other previously scheduled events with Texas voters.”
Or, like an increasing number of Republican politicians up for election, Abbott is seeking to place a subtle distance between himself and the president. Trump’s national disapproval rating is reflected even in Texas, with a Civiqs poll finding a 57 per cent disapproval of his job performance.
Polling of Latino voters, a demographic that swayed decisively towards Trump’s message of affordability two years ago, show they are deserting in droves, disenchanted by the brutal Ice approach to deportation of immigrants, and the national dismay at ongoing inflation.
Democratic strategists popping up on the television networks are visibly giddy at the deluge of data showing resurgent numbers in deep red states like Kansas, Iowa, Oklahoma and even Mississippi, places that were for decades, as veteran Louisiana senator John Kennedy put it, “fat guy lay-ups” for the Republican Party.
Thom Tillis, the veteran Republican senator for North Carolina who decided to retire after repeated disputes with Trump, has predicted that the Republicans’ worst fears will materialise in the November midterms. The GOP has all but conceded that Democratic candidate and former governor Roy Cooper will take that seat.
“We have chosen the proverbial chainsaw shed time and time again, kowtowing to the White House’s every demand even when we know the end result is going to be a bloodbath,” Tillis wrote in one much-quoted section.
“As of this writing, it seems almost certain that this is what’s going to happen come November 2026.”
One of the speculations is that midway through his second term, Trump has been largely shielded from negative or, rather, realistic appraisals of his public standing by a White House staff eager to assuage his ego and moods. But it would be impossible for Trump to remain unaware of the siege mentality that has taken hold of the GOP as the midterm date of November 3 rd approaches.
They are throwing millions of dollars into Paxton’s attempt to keep pace with the formidable fundraising campaign of James Talarico, and at least five million to shore up the seat formerly held by the late Lindsey Graham in South Carolina. Graham’s sister Darline, running with little to no political experience, is holding a narrow lead over Democrat Annie Andrews. Talarico leads Paxton by 51 per cent to 45 per cent; in June, the candidates were neck and neck.
The political publication Axios released an audio recording of Paxton privately grumbling about the repercussions of the Iran war on his campaign.
“It’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel. People are feeling the pinch. I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the, like, the campaign, and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming from DC. I don’t have the ability to change anything so I have to live with what I got.”
The conventional wisdom was that Trump has, through the months of the Iran war, become a disadvantage to Republican politicians on the campaign stump. But who was going to tell the president that? It would be like trying to convince Mick Jagger that Rolling Stones fans would rather see the concert without him.
No, having expressed indifference and even disinterest in the midterms throughout the year, Trump suddenly announced a barnstorming tour through late September and October. Visits to Alabama and Ohio preceded this, his third trip to Texas, within a month. His essential message to Maga voters has been the same: pretend I am on the ballot.
Abbott’s decision to skip last night’s event was a discourtesy that would have been unimaginable at the beginning of the year.
At the other end of the country, Susan Collins, the three-decade Republican senator facing a stiff battle to hold her Maine senate seat, equivocated when asked in a Tuesday night debate whether she would welcome Trump to her state.
“I have heard nothing from his office and I’m not exactly his favourite senator, I would say he is not coming to Maine.”
Don’t bet on it. Facing into the autumn storm, Trump is either embarking on a mad gamble or returning to his favourite theme of grievance and defiance – and his enduring belief in the limitless appeal of Donald J. Trump.
So in Ohio at the weekend, he promised supporters that “we are going to win” and “stuff it up their ass”.
“We are gonna have a great success and, John, [Husted, the Ohio candidate] nobody counted on the fact that Trump was going to go out and campaign for all these people. When I do, we win. When I don’t for some reason, we draw 44 per cent less people. So, what I’m gonna do is ask you to just pretend I am running. Everybody here tonight is part of the greatest political movement. This is, by the way, Maga, this is the greatest political movement in the history of our country.”
That has been his message that he is banking will reach the Maga masses. Ignore the stiffs that are on the ballot. Just pretend you are voting for me. Husted earned Trump’s passing admiration by virtue of being a college jock of distinction but here was what Trump had to say about Ken Paxton on a recent visit to Texas.
“You might not like the way he looks. He may not dress right, he may not talk exactly perfectly and he may not be the best lookin’ guy I’ve ever seen,” he said, before lauding the candidate as a Maga-disrupter who, as he repeated on Wednesday night, is “the greatest attorney general in the history of the state of Texas. He is tough and he is going to be with us all the way”.
But that’s what it’s like to have Trump bigging you up.
His message to Texans on Wednesday night was a reprise of the explicit warnings which propelled him to the presidency in 2024. Not only would a failure to prevent James Talarico winning the seat represent a betrayal of Texan traditions, he said, it would usher in a new era of lawlessness.
“If Talafreako and the Democrats get their way, all of that squalor and misery and homelessness ... you know, I said it the other day: when the Blues get in everything becomes dirty. The streets are dirty. The doorknobs going into stores are dirty. The sidewalks are dirty. Everything becomes dirty and has a bad smell. But we’re going to escape all that lawlessness and dysfunction that is coming to your beloved state if this guy ever gets in.”
Can this messaging cut through to an electorate dismayed by the shocking fuel prices and the inflation crisis that ultimately sunk the Biden/Harris campaign? Will the thought of sullied doorknobs at the grocery store rouse the masses? Notably, none of the conservative television networks carried Trump’s speech on Wednesday night. He was interrupted repeatedly over the first half-hour by hecklers and protesters sitting in the audience in San Antonio, another new departure for a Trump rally.
Trump’s rationale for the flatlining poll numbers is an acute failure of public relations by key members of administration, and by the lawmakers seeking votes in the upcoming election: a dismal inability to sell the message that in less than two years of the Trump administration, the border crisis has been ended, crime and murder rates are at their lowest in a century. The stock market – and therefore pensions – are at an all-time high. He has delivered tax cuts through the Big, Beautiful Bill. The soaring prices are a hangover from the Biden administration and if the war with Iran has forced higher fuel prices, well, it saved the world from nuclear annihilation.
He reminded them of other triumphs, like the raid on Venezuela. “It was a violent, incredible, beautiful raid. Not like past administrations where they had helicopters bumping into each other ... and just as I promised, Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. And we’ll be out of there soon and you watch those oil prices come down like a rock.”
This is the message he will deliver for the next month. There is, as ever, a singular cunning logic to Trump’s gamble on himself. His appraisal of the GOP candidates seems shrewdly made. They are, in the main, underwhelming. And despite the startling momentum the Democrats have gained, the balance of power for Senate control remains precarious and may come down to a few thousand votes in a handful of toss-up states, including Texas, Michigan, Maine, Alaska and, as of late, Kansas.
Trump has repeatedly defied polling predictions. He is relying on animal instinct that his performances, familiar and routine as they frequently are, will still register more deeply with the disillusioned fan base than candidates for whom it didn’t much care about in the first place.
If the Republicans lose heavily in November, Trump can easily lay the blame on the sorry cast of candidates. If they hold on to the Senate, then the story becomes that Trump beat the Democrats – and the ‘fake news’ media machine – by himself. And if that happens, then watch the dangerous clamour for Trump 2028 take off again.
All indicators are that the administration is facing into a hard reality check from US voters early next month.
But in Texas, Trump is banking that he can bend reality to his will. The state has not elected a Democrat senator since 1988, and Ann Richards was the last Democratic governor, before losing out to George W. Bush in 1994. If Texas holds yet again, Trump will be back to take a victory lap – and nobody will be surprised if he singles out Gregg Abbott for a choice mention.
Remember the Alamo? Trump forgets nothing.

title: Teacher who kissed student in special school removed from register for decade
description: Fitness-to-teach committee found teacher guilty of professional misconduct for physical contact and inappropriate messages sent to then 18-year-old
content:
A male teacher in a special school who hugged and kissed a female student on the lips has been removed from the register for 10 years by a fitness-to-teach committee .
Committee chairman Fergal McCarthy said the teacher would not be eligible to apply to be admitted to the register for 10 years from the date of any High Court judgment confirming the ruling.
The teacher was found guilty last month of professional misconduct and breaches of the code of professional conduct for teachers.
The committee found that on May 13th, 2025, the teacher hugged the student, put his arms around her waist and lifted her.
It was claimed that three days later the teacher hugged the student, who was 18 at the time, kissed her on the cheek and on the lips, and stroked her on the cheek,
He also told her, “Don’t tell anyone”, the committee heard.
The incidents were found to have taken place in a cupboard located to the side of the PE hall in the school.
The teacher was found to have sent the student inappropriate private messages on Instagram.
The committee heard that he told her in messages: “Well it looks like you will have to miss me a little bit longer” and “it’s not like you can say ‘no’ to me”.
The committee previously ruled that the identity of the student and the identity of all witnesses, along with the name and location of the school, be anonymised.
McCarthy said the teacher’s conduct was “undoubtedly serious”.
The teacher had been trusted “not to abuse the position of power and trust” that he had in the school and the subject he taught was one that students enjoyed, said the chairman.
He said the teacher was aware the student was “vulnerable”, that she had “a desire for connection” and had, as a consequence, “a willingness to disclose [to others] personal details” about herself.
He found the teacher’s conduct to be “deliberate and intended”.
McCarthy said that the sanction arrived at was “not disproportionate” in light of the type of school involved, the “known vulnerability” of the student and “the need to protect the public into the future”.
McCarthy said that there were two incidents of physical conduct, involving hugging and kissing, and that the teacher’s conduct was not an isolated incident and involved “a specific pattern”.
Kate Egan, counsel for the director of the Teaching Council, said the teacher’s behaviour was “especially serious” as he was teaching in a school for students with general mild learning disabilities.
After the student’s mother told the school of the teacher’s alleged conduct towards her daughter, an investigation took place in the school.
The teacher, who is no longer working at the school, did not attend the sanction hearing and was not legally represented in front of the committee.
Egan said that following the inappropriate physical behaviour there was “a full weekend” of “private and inappropriate communication via Instagram” between the teacher and the student.
This added to the seriousness of the behaviour and was further evidence of a “sustained pattern”, said Egan.
She said the teacher’s behaviour undermined the trust of parents and students at the school, who were “particularly vulnerable” and required an increased level of trust from those taking care of them.
Egan said that although the teacher was apologetic, he tried to explain “to an extent” what happened and did not make full admissions.
The committee had heard in September that the teacher claimed that it was the student who initiated the physical interactions in May 2025.
