title: Oil rises as supply concerns persist amid shipping attacks
description: US cuts output as hurricane threatens offshore production
content:
Oil prices rose on Thursday on persistent worries about supply from the key Middle East producing region amid an increase in attacks on shipping in the Gulf ​and the Strait of Hormuz, while the US cut output as a hurricane menaced offshore production.
Brent crude futures rose $2.28, or 2.28 per cent, to $102.28 a barrel by 0427 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures gained $1.66, or 1.88 per cent, to $89.94.
Prices settled lower on Wednesday after the International Energy Agency agreed to accelerate the release of oil stocks and to prioritise diesel supplies under ​a plan launched in March, as governments seek to tackle record fuel prices and supply disruptions caused by the Iran war.
However, threats to oil shipping in the Gulf and the ⁠Strait of Hormuz, which carried shipments equal to about 20 per cent of global oil and fuel before the war, have increased in October ‌as ‌the US-Israeli ​conflict with Iran enters its eighth month.
Attacks on tankers sailing through the Strait of Hormuz hit their highest last week of any week since the Iran war began as Gulf producers increased exports. The expansion of ⁠attacks is occurring as more crude is flowing out of ​the Gulf but at higher costs and risk to cargoes and crew.
In ​the latest attack, a tanker north of Qatar was struck by multiple projectiles, causing casualties, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Wednesday.
“The frequency ‌of Iranian attacks on ships is now at ​the highest point since the war began, and likely to intensify further,” said Saul Kavonic, MST Marquee head of energy.
He noted that “constrained product flows, ⁠extreme logistics costs and high likelihood of Iranian escalation are ⁠keeping prices elevated”.
ANZ analyst Daniel Hynes said ​in a note on Thursday the IEA’s oil release would likely consist of barrels that were already part of the group’s original 400-million-barrel release plan at the start of the Middle East conflict, meaning it does not appear to represent an additional draw on strategic inventories.
“Ultimately, strategic stock releases can augment supply flows temporarily but do not create new production capacity,” Hynes said.
Prices are also gaining on supply curtailments as a hurricane moves toward offshore production areas in the US, the world’s biggest oil producer, causing companies to shut their platforms.
Shell and Chevron said on Wednesday they were curtailing offshore operations in the Gulf as Hurricane Isaias approached.
Overall, US Gulf of Mexico ‌oil and gas producers had ⁠shut in about 25.08 per cent of current oil production and 16.37 per cent of current natural gas production as of Wednesday because of the storm, according to the Marine Minerals Administration.
Inventory data from the US, also the world’s biggest oil consumer, were supportive for prices as ‌crude stockpiles fell by a higher-than-expected amount, while diesel inventories declined slightly.
Crude inventories fell by 3.2 million barrels to 424.1 million barrels in the week ended October 2, the Energy Information ​Administration said on Wednesday, compared with analysts’ expectations in a Reuters poll for a 1.7 million-barrel decline.
Distillate ​fuel inventories, including diesel fuel and jet fuel, dropped by 42,000 barrels to 105.14 million barrels, well below their levels reported for this time of year in the past five years. - Reuters

title: Solicitor behind Forest Fest music event suspended from legal practice by High Court
description: Philip Meagher is founder of the annual music and arts festival held in Emo, Co Laois
content:
A solicitor known for establishing a Co Laois music festival has been suspended from legal practice by the High Court and ordered to disclose all information about his bank accounts.
The suspension of Philip Meagher of Midland Legal Solicitors in Portlaoise, Co Laois, comes amid a Law Society case which has led to severe measures against him.
He has been directed to set out proposals within a fortnight for the orderly wind-down of his practice and hand over all his client ledgers, computers, hard drives and passwords.
In addition to his legal work, Meagher is founder of the annual Forest Fest music and arts festival in Emo at which Echo & the Bunnymen and Madness performed in July.
The interim suspension order forbids Meagher from disposing of any of his assets or directing the disposal of any assets without permission from the High Court. He must lodge any client money he has received to the appropriate client accounts.
Asked about his suspension, Meagher said: “Further to the recent order my office is now positively engaged in a process with the Law Society.”
In a statement issued by text message, he added: “This process will incorporate a number of actions to include various positive proposals to move on from this point, details of which are being actively worked on.
“The primary issue giving rise to the order had been addressed prior to the order being made. As this is an active process no further comment would be appropriate at this point.”
Asked whether the music festival will continue, Meagher said: “Plans for Forest Fest 27 are ploughing ahead and the team are hoping to build on the amazing weekend that people so enjoyed last July.”
[ Forest Fest 2026: Madness top off a nostalgia-filled weekend featuring The Boomtown Rats, James and more Opens in new window ]
The ruling from Judge Oisín Quinn orders banks holding client or office accounts for Meagher’s firm to pay the contents of the accounts to the Law Society for reimbursement to clients as part of the wind-down.
The Law Society, which regulates the solicitors’ profession, has been considering an interim investigation report from an accountant who carried out an inspection of Meagher’s practice.
In an order issued on October 1st, the High Court directed Meagher to swear an affidavit within 14 days disclosing all information about any bank accounts in his own name. The order covers any accounts held in the name of his firm, any joint accounts or accounts held by third parties in which he has a beneficial interest.
In addition, banks in which Meagher’s legal firm holds client or office accounts were directed to hand over to the Law Society all bank statements from such accounts for the last six years.
Meagher must also swear an affidavit within 14 days disclosing all information on his assets and any assets no longer in his control. In relation to any assets no longer in his possession, he must set out his belief as to where those assets are and provide expert written evaluations in relation to same.
He must also set out proposals for the disposal of client files from his practice to another firm or firms of solicitors and the distribution of client files, documents, title deeds and wills to the clients or newly appointed solicitors.

title: Fear of ‘physical harm’ prevents public October 7th events, says Ireland’s chief rabbi
description: Jewish community ‘taking the necessary precautions’ after attacks in United States, Britain and Australia
content:
Dublin’s primary synagogue chose not to organise a public memorial to commemorate the October 7th attacks on Israel due to concern over “the possibility of somebody seeking to cause actual physical harm” to the Jewish community, Chief Rabbi of Ireland Yoni Wieder has said.
Wieder said the community was taking additional precautions as there had been increasing attacks on Jewish institutions worldwide after the Hamas-led attacks when, according to Israel, 1,200 people were killed and 250 taken hostage and abducted to Gaza .
“I believe that Jewish people in Ireland should be able to remember relatives, friends and fellow Jews who were murdered or taken hostage without being confronted while doing so,” said Wieder.
[ Israelis gather to remember victims of October 7th attack Opens in new window ]
“Of course there is a right to protest, but I do think there should be a basic human boundary around people who are simply coming to mourn their dead.
“Over the past three years, we’ve seen fatal attacks on synagogues and Jewish community events in Britain, America and Australia, as well as repeated attacks and attempted attacks on synagogues and Jewish institutions around the world,” he added.
“Against that background, Jewish communities globally have increased their security, and here in Dublin we’re taking the necessary precautions,” he said.
Wieder said “a short commemoration” was held in its Terenure synagogue, south Dublin, on Saturday, to coincide with the third anniversary of the attacks per the Hebrew calendar.
About 150 people attended the Shabbat service, he said, including regular synagogue-goers and “those who wouldn’t usually attend synagogue, but who made the effort to be there for the anniversary. The service included the traditional memorial prayer and a powerful reflection on the lives and legacies of those brutally murdered on October 7th.”
The congregation is equally concerned with protests surrounding any publicised commemoration, especially as they are attended by people who lost family members on October 7th or since, or whose relatives were taken hostage, he continued.
“I don’t think that a grieving daughter who has come to mourn her father, who was murdered by terrorists, should have to walk past somebody shouting at her that she’s a ‘baby killer’. But that’s precisely the kind of thing that’s happened at vigils and commemorations in Dublin in the past.
[ In pictures: Three years of war in Gaza Opens in new window ]
“So while the community commemorates the atrocities of October 7th and will certainly not be deterred from doing so, there is greater caution about publicising these events openly,” he added.
Just under 2,200 people in the Republic wrote “Jewish” as their religious identity on the 2022 census, about 1,500 of whom are believed to live in Dublin. The population number often fluctuates due to temporary migration of people from Israel.
While it is understood that no big commemoration has been organised to mark three years to the day since the attacks, one has been planned at an unspecified time under the direction of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland.
Details, however, are yet to be shared even with those registered to attend the event, who will learn of its location 24 hours in advance of its start time – again, due to what prominent voices in the Irish Jewish community have called security concerns.
A protest march from the Garden of Remembrance to the front gates of Leinster House in Dublin city centre, named “The National Demonstration for Palestine: Three Years of Gaza Genocide”, is also scheduled to take place this weekend.

title: French students at forefront of global stirring of disaffected youth
description: Global Briefing: While education budgets are squeezed, EU governments are borrowing billions of euros to spend on defence
content:
The French school students whose demonstrations have been making headlines are part of a global stirring among young people tired of getting a raw deal from older generations who are often indifferent or contemptuous towards their concerns.
The school protests that have been roiling France spread to Belgium this week when hundreds of students demonstrated in the eastern city of Liège in protest against rising costs, overcrowded classrooms and a shortage of study materials. Police detained more than 100 people but responded to the protests with less brutality than their French counterparts and the city’s mayor has called for dialogue with the students.
The protests in France and Belgium are part of a wave of unrest among students around the world in recent months and the European Students’ Union monitored 54 protest actions across the continent between March and May this year. Fourteen of them involved multiple cities and campuses, including demonstrations in 50 Italian cities in May, and some protests have been going on for months or even years.
The triggers behind the protests are various but most are driven by frustration linked to the material conditions of education and extra burdens imposed on students. They are acts of resistance by a generation that is tired of being either hectored and bullied or ignored and dismissed by a governing class that is often indifferent to the concerns of young people as it squanders their future.
In Romania last month, students across the country went to school dressed in black in protest against a bill that would introduce mandatory school uniforms. The students argue that instead of policing their clothing, the government in Bucharest, which spends less on education than most European Union member-states, should address structural problems in the school system and get serious about tackling child poverty.
India’s Cockroach movement launched one of the most successful student protests in recent history when it forced the resignation of Narendra Modi’s education minister over leaked exam papers that saw more than two million people forced to re-sit a medical school entrance exam. The movement initiated fresh protests last week over changes to India’s electoral roll that have seen millions of people stripped of the franchise.
Governments around the world have responded to student protests with violence which has in some cases led to the deaths of demonstrators. Abdoulaye Ba, a second-year dental student at Cheikh Anta Diop University in the Senegalese capital of Dakar, died last February of multiple internal haemorrhages after police entered a dormitory and attacked students with batons.
The students had been demonstrating against the failure to pay the government stipends that are the only source of income for many, leaving them unable to afford food or rent. The university authorities suspended student associations and closed student housing and the cafeteria when students were unable to pay for meals and accommodation.
In the EU, education’s share of government spending has been flat or falling in recent years despite the fact that more students are being encouraged to enter third-level institutions.
The EU has a target for the proportion of 25-34 year-olds to reach 45 per cent by 2030 but the funding per student has been falling, something which might be contributing to weaker European performance in the PISA study of educational attainment.
While education budgets are squeezed, European governments are borrowing hundreds of billions of euros to spend on defence and some EU member-states have reinstated national military service while others are considering it. This means that if their governments’ diplomatic incompetence leads to war, the generation that stayed at home during the pandemic to protect their elders will be better trained to go away and die for them.

title: A Greek peninsula that bars women and holiday homes in Denmark: unusual exemptions to EU law
description: A Greek peninsula that bars women and a VAT-free Italian town also feature among the list of odd exemptions
content:
Would you rather keep your sommerhus or your snus? Spend enough time looking, and you’ll come across some interesting exemptions countries have secured from European Union law to account for a national quirk.
There’s a peninsula in Greece on which women are barred from setting foot and an Italian town in the Alps that doesn’t charge VAT. Denmark has a law preventing outsiders from buying holiday homes, known as a sommerhus, in the countryside.
When Sweden joined in 1995, it secured an exemption from an EU ban on the sale of oral tobacco to protect its culturally cherished snus , a tobacco pouch placed between the gum and upper lip or cheek.
Sweden is the only member state in the EU where snus can still be produced and sold, though one of the main producers, Swedish Match, which is owned by tobacco giant Philip Morris , has fought to overturn the export ban.
Perhaps the most unusual carve-out was secured by the Greeks in the early 1980s. They insisted on preserving the special status of Mount Athos, a self-governing community of about 2,000 Orthodox monks in the north of the country.
For more than 1,000 years, women have not been allowed to enter the Athos peninsula. The religious ban, called the ávaton, extends to pets, except cats.
At first glance, this type of arrangement should run up against EU rules protecting the free movement of people or legislation preventing gender-based discrimination.
But the treaty covering Greece’s accession into what was then the European Economic Community was accompanied by a declaration recognising the “special status” of Mount Athos, as laid out in the Greek constitution.
[ Europe rearms: files reveal extent of plans for a new ‘defence union’ Opens in new window ]
In another quirky historical holdover, Italy does not charge VAT on purchases in Livigno, a town in the Alps near the Swiss border. The peculiar duty-free status has its roots in efforts by authorities centuries ago to encourage people to live in the isolated mountain region. Today, it’s one reason why Livigno has become a holiday spot popular for skiing and shopping.
Denmark leads the field when it comes to opt-outs and exemptions.
Copenhagen has historically been sceptical about deeper EU integration. It kept its own currency, the Danish krone, rather than adopting the euro. It negotiated what became an “opt-out” from common policy covering justice and defence, which meant laws and regulations agreed in Brussels in those areas would not apply to Denmark.
However, it is part of the Schengen zone that removed border checks across much of Europe and must follow changes decided by other EU states on that front without being able to vote.
Public attitudes on EU defence co-operation shifted when Russia invaded Ukraine. The Danish people decided to stop opting out of the common security policy by a two-thirds majority in a 2022 referendum.
It is also very difficult for residents of other EU countries to buy a holiday home in Denmark, if not impossible, thanks to a special exemption.
A lot of Danes have a second home in the countryside, a “sommerhus”.
[ ‘Made in Europe’ rules should not ‘undermine’ UK relations, Britain’s new envoy tells EU Opens in new window ]
Fearful of neighbouring Germans or other wealthy outsiders buying up property, Denmark has a law that dates to the postwar years restricting the purchase of second homes to Danish residents, or people who can prove a close connection to the country.
Denmark negotiated for a line to be tagged on to the Maastricht Treaty in 1992, allowing Copenhagen to maintain its existing legislation on the acquisition of second homes, firming up the status of the sommerhus exemption in European law.
EU officials hate anything that undercuts the union’s single market and its free movement of people, goods, services and capital. There are unlikely to be any national exceptions made for new members who join the 27-state bloc in the coming years.
Ireland has a unique “opt-in” when it comes to legislation covering justice and migration. The Government can decide on a case-by-case basis whether it wants to sign up to new reforms coming from Brussels. For example, Ireland chose to join the EU migration pact overhauling asylum procedures.
[ Why is the tobacco industry celebrating Sweden’s anti-smoking success? Opens in new window ]
The UK had the same opt-in on justice matters when it was a member state, along with opt-outs such as protections for the pound.
Andy Burnham’s kite-flying about being open to going “all the way” and someday taking the UK back into the EU caused surprisingly little chatter in Brussels. In fact, Brexit is hardly mentioned at all over here any more.
A future British government beginning negotiations about rejoining might find the terms on offer to be less advantageous to the set-up the UK enjoyed before it left.

title: Budget makes me worry whether my grandchildren will benefit from today’s prosperity
description: How transformative would it be if the entire resources of the State were directed towards solving one problem?
content:
Sir, – As a pensioner, I am not primarily concerned with how this budget impacts me. I am far more concerned about the problems it may create for my grandchildren’s generation.
Over the decades I have witnessed how economic circumstances can change with startling speed because of poor fiscal management at home and international instability outside our control. Invariably, the fallout hits ordinary people.
The 2008 crash dictates that the buffer must be built before the crisis, thus demanding that the Government build resilience, distinguish temporary windfalls from sustainable income and preserve sufficient financial manoeuvring space for inevitable oncoming “unknown unknowns”.
The Fiscal Advisory Council has not merely raised a concern about this budget, it has been warning about the same pattern that underpins it for several years.
It is troubling that the council’s warnings, yet again, do not appear to have been given the weight that prudence would suggest, thus leaving my key concern unresolved, as to whether my grandchildren will inherit the benefit of today’s prosperity or the consequences of us having foolhardily spent it. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Pat Leahy’s assessment of Budget 2027 is apt: “When you try to please everyone, sometimes you can end up pleasing nobody” (“ It takes a giveaway budget of €8.5bn to not annoy anyone – except Patrick O’Donovan ”, Opinion, October 7th).
Is an alternative possible? How transformative would it be if the Government decided to direct the entire resources of the State towards solving one problem only. Rather than tinkering on the edges of tax or social welfare, ignore these and just fix housing, for instance. This is not an abstract idea. We saw during the Covid pandemic that such an approach can deliver results. Alas, in today’s world of risk averse politics it’s unlikely that any politician would take this idea on board. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – I’m surprised at older people and pensioners’ expressions of annoyance and dissatisfaction with the latest budget. It has broadly sought to alleviate hardship at a time of serious global volatility.
Although I’m 10 or more years away from retirement, I can recall times when our annual budgets seemed to make life more difficult, raising taxes and prices simultaneously. It seems remarkable how we’ve moved from watching them with a sense of dread to one of entitlement or optimism. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – Ireland ranks third in the EU in per capita spending on gambling. In Budget 2027 the funding to horse and greyhound racing was increased to a whopping €102 million. Perhaps with such a huge injection of taxpayers money we will rise to the top of the gambling rankings? Irony aside, it is not just families and individuals who are harmed as a consequence of gambling addiction. At the core of these industries is animal suffering. In the past 11 years, 1,396 greyhounds were killed on the track and a further 3,696 were injured. The worst year on record for track deaths was 2024. – Yours, etc,
Sir, – In the many reports about yesterday’s budget, there is frequent reference to increases in welfare payments . These stories include references to the State Contributory Pension. It’s about time we ceased referring to this as a welfare payment – it is not.
As the name illustrates, it is based on contributions, from employer and employee, over our working lives. One might argue that it is more akin to a defined contribution scheme as fewer contributions will result in a smaller pension.
This pension has been earned and is directly related to what we have contributed. No one would suggest that the payment of a private pension or occupational pension is a welfare payment and the fact that the State Contributory Pension is paid by the State doesn’t make it different.
Why does it matter? Because every year, at budget time in particular, there are voices suggesting this is giving something to the retired community that is based on some form of altruism on the part of the Government. It isn’t. – Yours, etc,
Sir – The cost of a packet of cigarettes has now gone up by €1. The average price for a packet of 20 cigarettes in Ireland is €16.70-€20.85 depending on the brand. One could argue that this price increase will push more people who smoke into buying illegal cigarettes.
I wish the money raised in taxes from cigarettes were specifically targeted towards the healthcare of people who vape and smoke. – Yours, etc,

title: From syrups, teas, poultices and culinary uses, our gardens can offer so much
description: Learning about the health benefits of herbs and plants on my doorstep has been a revelation
content:
I have spent this year faffing about with a number of vegetable patches in the garden . This is after a few seasons of poor but somewhat acceptable attempts at growing a few staples for the veggie basket.
This year has been a bumper crop, with the success rate better compared to previous years. Courgettes, potatoes, scallions, lettuce, spinach, red and white onions and broad beans have been my favourite to not only eat but to watch grow. Rich red strawberries filled our summer and the blackberries are ready to pick. Nature is a pretty amazing thing for giving back to us mere mortals who don’t always appreciate its force.
I’ve made plenty of mistakes. Forgetting (or not concerning myself with) the importance of soil health, avoiding a midnight wander to collect slugs and snails, and not harvesting quick enough or watching the growth patterns of certain plants (I’m looking at you, my lovely courgettes). Butterflies have enjoyed quite a few of the crop and I’m happy to share with these pollinators. But I’m sure avid growers would effectively protect from leaf damage. What netting I have used is not as secure as it should be.
And, of course, let’s not forget the hosepipe ban and dribbling water butts. But with these mistakes has come great learning. The vegetables are still growing, producing, and I’m still sowing, learning and cultivating a healthy habit over conscious food choices from my very own back garden. The kids are learning too and my hope is, as my skills grow and the earth continues to turn, that their generation may see this as normal.
As much as I love the stir fry and sauces these foods produce for our family, I have leant more towards the herb table outside our back door – a reclaimed, heat-treated pallet raised with four industrial-style metal legs nailed together by my own trusty hands. Pots line the table with various herbs used for cooking and medicinal uses.
Now, I’m no expert, and I’m learning my way through the various uses for specific herbs that I can source from our local garden centre – and the welcomed snips from family – but it’s safe to say that the herb table has become my new “project”. Yes, I have had herbs bolt, curl inward and disappear to nothing. But I have also had enough rosemary, coriander, sage, thyme and chamomile that I didn’t know what to do with. Until I did.
I’m not a herbalist, and you have probably already determined that I am a somewhat lazy gardener. This herb table of mine sits by the back door, so I’m not traipsing down to the vegetable garden in our large and sprawling space (which I am eternally grateful for). I choose plants purely on the sun or shade aspect and nine times out of 10 forget to “feed” these beautiful plants and vegetables that, in spite of me, are roaring with growth because, once more, nature is pretty amazing like that. My efforts are minimal, but again, I’m learning. And willing to do so.
I am learning that there are side effects to certain herbs, that identifying the right herb is paramount as there could be toxic varieties, and choosing the right method to infuse or decoct will see better results. And so, I have chosen certain herbs for their benefits.
[ How psychoeducation can help with depression, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia Opens in new window ]
I grow chamomile for its obvious soothing and calming tea. Lavender for the pollinators but also as a natural air freshener. Peppermint for stomach aches and rosemary for focus. I was drawn to sage and later learned this super herb contains over 160 antioxidants and oestrogen-like properties. Quite beneficial for a woman of my age in perimenopause. And there are so many more cluttering my herb table.
And, all summer long, a five-litre jug of electrolyte water has rotated with varying fruits and herbs for soothing, healing and thirst-quenching drinks. Every drop offering significant benefits.
[ How to set your garden ablaze with autumn colour Opens in new window ]
Plants I thought were a nuisance, like the mountains of horsetail in our garden, suddenly had a purpose. It always had a purpose, a prehistoric one at that. We are told some things are weeds, a problem, and to get rid of them (if you can; horsetail is notoriously difficult to remove), but what if we looked at why it is there, what it can be used for. Luckily for me, others have already asked this question and the answer was right there. Sustainably foraging in our back garden means taking enough for our comfort while leaving more for the earth to continue growing.
For instance, the hawthorn nestled within our hedging is more than a hardy tree. Harvesting and drying the young leaves, drying the berries and crushing both in a tea have cardiovascular health benefits. The aforementioned horsetail is said to have an effect on skin, hair and bone health while promoting wound healing. Using a method called decoction, boiling the stems can derive the benefits.
From syrups, teas, poultices and culinary uses, our gardens offer so much. I am hoping for a few fruit trees when the season is right, to understand more about herbs and how to use them throughout the year and to mark out a bigger vegetable plot.
I will choose to grow what we eat and use, learn what each plant needs from its soil and how to nurture the health of every plant and, in turn, our family.
This is partly about reminding ourselves that our grandparents knew how to do all of this and we can again.

title: French protests a timely warning for Irish schools
description: If the system continues to be broken, it may be students on the picket line next
content:
Sir, – The crisis unfolding in the French education system is a timely warning to those who take the quality of our own schools for granted (“ Police fire tear gas and charge at demonstrators as French school protests escalate ”, Europe, October 6th). A severe teacher shortage, bloated class sizes and crumbling infrastructure have brought the French education system to breaking point – and we should not assume Ireland is immune.
In Ireland a teacher recruitment and retention crisis has been allowed to fester for years. Class sizes remain among the highest in Europe, while many schools operate in ageing, inadequate facilities.
Teachers in Ireland are about to embark on a campaign of industrial action (“ Teachers’ Union of Ireland latest group to overwhelmingly back industrial action ”, Education, October 2nd).
If the system continues to be broken, it may not be teachers standing on the picket line next – it could be students.
As the French government and society are now finding out, student demands and anger are not easily contained and can quickly escalate into severe, widespread disruption. – Yours, etc,

title: Live Nation moves €76m to UK parent firm following bumper profits at 3Arena
description: Ireland’s largest indoor venue built up €69m in profits after earning about €14m to €18m annually in recent years
content:
Live Nation’s Irish company that owns the 3Arena has made a €76 million payout to its UK parent firm in recent months, according to new accounts.
The payout, which was more than seven times larger than the amount paid in 2025, has come following large profits of up to €18 million being recorded by the 3Arena.
New accounts for Live Nation Ireland Holdings Ltd, which owns the firm behind the 3Arena, show it paid a €10 million dividend last year and €5.7 million in 2024.
The company’s directors in Ireland, Michael Adamson, Sean Duffy and Stuart Douglas, noted in the latest accounts for Live Nation Ireland Holdings Ltd that it received an €82 million dividend from 3Arena operator Amphitheatre Ireland Ltd in 2026.
The accounts also disclosed a €76 million dividend paid to its UK parent, Apollo Leisure Group Ltd, which has brought total dividends paid in the past three yearsto €91.7 million. Live Nation did not respond to a request for comment.
3Arena, Ireland’s largest indoor entertainment venue which has hosted acts including Lily Allen and Westlife this year, has been highly lucrative for Live Nation in recent times.
Accounts that cover the 2025 financial year for 3Arena have not yet been released, but filings for each year between 2022 and 2024 show it has consistently made after-tax profits of between €14 million and €18 million.
The eight-figure profits booked by the venue led to accumulated profits rising to more than €69.3 million at Amphitheatre Ireland Ltd by the end of 2024.
[ Live Nation plans new music and sports venue bigger than 3Arena in Dublin’s docklands Opens in new window ]
Last year, Live Nation’s directors indicated there would be a further boost to reserves as they expected after-tax profits for 2025 “to be in line with 2024”.
Live Nation, one of the biggest entertainment groups in the world, also runs many of the country’s big venues on behalf of their owners, including the Bord Gáis Energy Theatre, the Gaiety and Olympia theatres.
The entertainment group is also the owner of Ticketmaster in Ireland and majority owns promoter MCD. It also has a controlling interest in the Electric Picnic festival.
In June, The Irish Times revealed Live Nation has plans to expand its Irish operation through the development of a new 20,000-seater facility in Dublin.
The US group’s Irish entity has joined a consortium with US entertainment giant Oak View Group and the Desmond family’s Gaiety Investments that has plans to invest €500 million to create a new music and sports venue in Dublin’s docklands.
The group struck a deal to acquire a site in Dublin’s docklands called Brick Yards for close to €90 million on which it will develop the venue that is expected to be larger than the 3Arena.
Live Nation’s stake in this project is also held in Live Nation Ireland Holdings Ltd. The latest accounts showed it has committed €15.9 million to the project this year.
In June, a spokeswoman for Live Nation said the consortium was “in the early stages of plans to develop” the 20,000-seater venue on the site located close to the 3Arena and beside Dublin Port.

title: Those fighting for greater protection of natural world need support, not scorn
description: High Court judge’s comments on fighting lost battles were unhelpful
content:
Sir, – A judge’s comparison of people who challenged a wind farm in court to a soldier still fighting a war that ended long ago deserves more than a passing wince (“ Judge compares wind farm objectors to ‘dogged Japanese soldier’ still fighting second World War ”, News, October 4th).
The objectors were not fighting an obsolete war. The judge upheld their challenge on the freshwater pearl mussel and the kingfisher, but accepted that the planning commission’s errors made no difference and refused to overturn the planning permission.
Even so, these one-shot litigants merit support, not scorn. Nature cannot go to court. It depends on ordinary people willing to ask difficult questions before irreversible damage is done. This voluntary effort is not done lightly.
Ireland spends less of its economy on environmental protection than any other EU country. Ninety per cent of its protected habitats are in unfavourable condition. And this year the European Commission opened infringement proceedings over its marine nature sites.
With the State’s duty of care for nature so poorly met, community groups have every reason to be a stone in the shoe of the planning commission and the Minister for the Environment.
Ridicule by a judge, in this climate, risks a chilling effect on community groups prepared to uphold environmental law and on public confidence that the courts are open to all.
We must soldier on regardless. – Yours, etc,

title: Climate change idiom with the wrong bird
description: When disaster struck the bird did not squawk
content:
Sir, – I have just finished reading Denis McClean’s interesting article about the loss of glacier volume in the Swiss Alps (“ I saw Switzerland’s Alpine treasures melting away. It was a sobering experience ”, An Irish Diary, October 2nd).
He describes the Swiss glaciers as “the squawking chicken in the coal mine of climate change”, indicating the impending disaster. I cannot dispute this but I think he has got the wrong bird.
My understanding is that it was a canary that was brought into a mine to indicate possible disaster and when disaster struck the bird did not squawk but succumbed to the effects of the mine gas. – Yours, etc,

title: Avan Lee: With an Irish wife and past playing days in Clontarf, new Munster CEO is on familiar ground
description: Experienced Kiwi rugby executive arrives two days before Leinster clash to take over from Ian Flanagan
content:
Avan Lee will return to live in Ireland for a third time when he takes up his new role as interim chief executive at Munster Rugby succeeding Ian Flanagan, who held the position since October 2019 and will step away at the end of the month .
Lee arrives on October 22nd, two days before Munster take on Leinster in a United Rugby Championship clash at the Aviva Stadium, Dublin. The New Zealander is house-hunting in Cork , but will spend a day or two a week in Limerick .
The appointment is for 12 months, but Lee was unequivocal about his desire to win the role on a full-time basis.
“It’s 12 months, is the interim, which is whatever you take from that. But ... from my perspective, my attitude is that it’s permanent,” he said.
“And, you know, once I do a good job, I’m sure that will happen. But I’m not coming over to look at a 12-month job. I feel like I’m leaving New Zealand for this opportunity.”
[ ‘Opportunity knocks’: Ian Flanagan’s departure will intensify calls for a Munster reboot ]
On the two previous occasions he was based in Dublin , playing rugby and cricket for Clontarf during a seven-year spell in the 1990s in which he met his wife, a Dubliner, and then later he returned for a further three years while working at World Rugby as a commercial manager (2012-2013) initially, then general manager of Sevens (2013-2015).
Born in Dargaville, he grew up in Whangarei on New Zealand’s North Island where his dream was to play for the All Blacks , but, as he said in an interview, “that’s akin to saying I wanted to be a superhero, to be honest, because not many people become All Blacks”.
He did management studies and marketing at Waikato before travelling to Dublin where he played for Clontarf in a team that contained Bernard Jackman and with Brent Pope as a player-coach.
“After university I went straight to Ireland to play rugby. I went straight to Clontarf. I had two phone numbers in my wallet: one was for Old Crescent, one was for Clontarf. It wasn’t anything formal or much money involved, I can assure you, but I went to Clontarf first and stayed. It’s sort of been a second home for me, to be perfectly honest,” Lee said.
“I didn’t play AIL because, as a foreign player, I wasn’t allowed to play [in accordance with the rules at the time]. I played Leinster League and Floodlit Cup and all those nice things. Then I retired at 23 [due to a] shoulder reconstruction. That was the end of it.
“I got there. I flew in on a Tuesday [to Ireland]. Didn’t know anybody and I played at Lansdowne Road on the Saturday. I thought that was pretty good.”
His contemporaries in team-mate terms included some well-known names.
“Yeah, Bernard Jackman was a bit of a star. Dave Moore, Colin Power, Mark Woods; Brent Pope was sort of a player-coach. Matt Smith ... so it was a good team, a good solid team. They were in the second division then and they got promoted, but I loved it, genuinely loved it. It’s an awesome place, like any rugby club, really, it’s a lovely place [with] awesome people,” he said.
“I’ve had two different stints. First one was nearly seven years, and the next one was three when I came back over to work at World Rugby after I finished with New Zealand Rugby.
“So, yeah, I’ve always felt like I would go back and now with 10 years of Super Rugby experience under my belt I feel like I’ve got something to contribute to a place like Munster. So it’s all aligned, which is great.”
[ Munster’s problems cannot be laid at the door of one person ]
Lee spent five years at the New Zealand Rugby Union, three of these as broadcasting and commercial operations manager from 2007-2012, returned to Ireland for a stint with World Rugby and was then appointed CEO at the Wellington-based Super Rugby franchise the Hurricanes in June 2015. He led the club through a significant period of their history, which included a first Super Rugby title in 2016.
He stepped down last November after 10-and-a-half years. A tribute paid to Lee from the club read: “Under his guidance, the Hurricanes have developed a diverse commercial network both in New Zealand and abroad, a robust culture, and high-quality playing and coaching rosters, that provide a strong platform for the next chapter of success.”
Lee worked as a consultant for World Rugby and was a member of the board of trustees at Special Olympics New Zealand in a part-time capacity. Last year his name was linked in speculative terms with the CEO position at Cricket Ireland.
Speaking to those who know him reasonably well, there is a confidence that Munster have got an excellent and very capable administrator.

title: For the average GAA player, this time of the year brings a mix of regret and relief
description: County finals and the privilege of training on dark, cold autumn nights
content:
There’s a moment every September as you head out training, when the evening is still dry and warm, and you struggle to imagine going out of the championship this early in the year. It seems to have gone by in a flash, and one finds oneself desperate for one more win, just to make the year feel like it hasn’t been woefully, drastically cut short.
Two weeks later, you could be at the same pitch, at the same time of the week, asking yourself how much longer a season can possibly go on for. These are liminal times. It’s suddenly dark at 7pm, and now being finished for the year seems, if not preferable, then maybe just about right.
And plenty of teams are finished. At the start of any season, everyone has the right to think a championship quarter-final is an achievable aim, with a fair wind and a bit of luck. But the rubber has to meet the road eventually, and it has happened up and down the country over the last 14 or 21 days.
There will have been teams that departed their championship with regrets, but also with an underlying sense of relief that their last game of the season wasn’t a relegation playoff. For teams in that bracket, the disappointment of a defeat is leavened by the relief that senior status (or intermediate, or junior) has been secured for another year.
Other teams have no such consolation. After 14 titles in the last 15 years Kilcoo didn’t even make it to October in Down, and two of last year’s provincial champions – Ballyboden St Enda’s and Dingle – said goodbye last weekend. Ballyboden exited the Dublin championship at the semi-final stage, and All-Ireland champions Dingle fell at the first hurdle of the Kerry county championship.
That All-Ireland semi-final between Dingle and Boden in Páirc Uí Chaoimh in January was seismic, but the fact that they were whaling away at each other in an absolute thriller three days into the new year must surely have been a factor in their inability to keep winning nine months later.
So who’s left? A lot of seasoned champions, such as the other two provincial winners, Scotstown in Monaghan and Roscommon’s St Brigid’s. There’s romance in Mayo, with Garrymore beating Belmullet on Sunday, and in Tyrone, where Edendork are in their first-ever senior final.
TG4 is showing two county finals this weekend – the Westmeath football final and the Tipperary hurling final – and it’s usually around this time that we as a public can start to cohere and coalesce around what the big GAA stories are again. Before now, we had 40 or more county championships with big interest inside their own county boundaries (and some hurling championships that no one was too bothered with, alas), each competing for some elusive, unnecessary illusion of national relevance.
If the story at times over the last six weeks proved too diffuse, if there was a feeling that interest in the games nationally was a mile wide and an inch deep, that doesn’t alter what August and September meant to hundreds of thousands of GAA fans around the country. It will be easier to follow the club championships over the next two months than it was over the last two months, but for a huge percentage of the club population the really important stuff is already behind us. Watching as a spectator is fine, but being an active participant is rather different.
There are still people making the argument that county championships are finishing at around the same time they always did, before the split season ever came in. And the Mayo county final will be played in mid-October, which is in and around the time it might often have finished in the 2010s.
But instead of a headlong race to get it run off with six games in seven weeks before the Connacht club championship begins, it’s been a festival of football, played in summertime conditions, with correct breaks between games, and now a romantic final pairing. Castlebar Mitchels and Garrymore are still alive, but everyone else felt like they had a real competition.
The club season isn’t a guarantee of anything. I would love to be able to tell you that the double-header of Galway senior hurling quarter-finals I saw in Kenny Park last Sunday afternoon was a wonderful advertisement for it ... but it was bloody awful. The two games were bad, neither losing team really raised much of a gallop, and the rain that threatened throughout the first game arrived with aplomb during the second.
Tom Monaghan hitting nine points from play for Craughwell against Sarsfields and continuing discussion of Éamonn Fitzmaurice’s appointment as Galway football manager were about the only two things that lifted the mood all afternoon. Them’s the breaks.
Monaghan marches on with his club, but first he had to watch his Galway captain Darren Morrissey go off with what looked like a serious shoulder injury. The injury happened in a Sarsfields jersey, but Morrissey’s recovery will be with Galway in mind – a reminder that the club and intercounty season is not split at all. Morrissey will have the first round of the national league circled in his diary now as a target, but most of us can forget about the boots entirely for a month or two. It’s the privileged few who get to keep training in the winter murk, with glory on their mind.

title: ‘Closest thing to what I imagine drugs would be like’: Ireland’s Conor McManus revels in win over England
description: Left-back scored goal against England in 3-1 win at Turners Cross to secure spot in Friday’s draw
content:
Conor McManus was high on life after the Ireland Under-21s overturned Lee Carsley’s treble-chasing England to reach the European Championship playoffs on Tuesday night in Cork.
The Gillingham left-back scored the goal to give Ireland a 2-1 lead, with Tommy Lonergan bagging the other pair, sparking scenes of ecstasy around a sold-out Turners Cross.
“Honestly, I can’t describe it. It’s the closest thing to what I imagine drugs would be like,” McManus beamed. “Everything just happened so quickly. I get a bit of a nosebleed up the other end, so not having time to think helped me, just based off instinct, and luckily it went in, so I can’t complain.
“The fans were unbelievable. They helped us through the whole game. That’s just an Irish crowd through and through. It’s an honour to play for your country and especially on a night where you can make history. And we did make history. It’s always going to be special.”
The setting was completely unlike McManus’s previous international goals. He netted a friendly double on his debut against Hungary in Spain 18 months ago.
“Whether you’re scoring in front of 10 people and your mum or 10,000 people, it all matters,” smiled the Cabinteely native.
McManus captained Ireland during the March window, but didn’t get the nod from Jim Crawford against either Kazakhstan or Slovakia.
“It was difficult. I was frustrated when I was not playing. I spoke to Jim and he assured me that I was going to get my chances,” he said.
“Listen, it’s football. Football is a mental game. You don’t know which way it’s going to go. You’ve got to keep the head, you’ve got to keep working hard, and you’re going to get your opportunities. That’s the main thing. Once you get your opportunity, you have to take it.”
They needed all that belief against an England squad valued at €400 million, which included Fulham’s Arsenal-linked wonderkid Josh King, Ethan Nwaneri, on loan at Borussia Dortmund from the Gunners, and Spurs’ Archie Gray.
“It was just all about faith. The lads had faith. We’d proven over the last two or three games the trajectory we were on,” said McManus. “Our main message was that we’re just as good as them on our day and we proved that.
“It’s a tough place to come for them. We knew that if we put together a performance, we were going to get the better of them, and that’s the confidence you have to have in yourselves.
“No matter what the outside noise is saying, you have to have that belief in yourself, because in football it’s a horrible game. Nobody else is going to have that belief for you.
“Like my mum always says, if you don’t have the confidence in yourself, nobody else will.”
On the home support, McManus added: “The energy that the crowd gave us was unbelievable.
“We’re an emotional team, but I like to think we’re emotional in a smart way where you can rein it in when you need to and not get overly emotional and make sure we’re sticking to the game plan.”
Beating the Young Lions capped a remarkable Irish fightback following a 4-0 defeat to Andorra and 1-1 draw with Moldova. That left them eight points adrift of second-placed Slovakia with just four games to turn it all around.
“The quality is abundant and we just needed to find a way to best put that on the pitch,” said McManus. “We knew ourselves, let alone what the media were saying. We knew ourselves that the performances weren’t up to our own standards, let alone the country’s standards.
“We had confidence in ourselves that once that clicked, we’d start getting performances. Tonight shows that we can compete against the best, and I look forward to November and hopefully next summer.”
Friday’s draw will reveal Ireland’s playoff rivals as the Boys in Green bid to make the Under-21 Euros for the first time.
The potential opponents are the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, Greece, Iceland, Netherlands and Turkey.
“Hopefully we get a good team,” said McManus. “No matter who we get, we’ve proven that we can compete against any team that’s put in front of us on our day. That’s the main thing.”

title: Man charged with murder of father of three in stabbing incident in Cork
description: Kieran Long (56) remanded in custody after being charged with murder of Mark O’Connell (36) in November 2025
content:
A 56-year-old man has been remanded in custody after he was charged with the murder of a father of three, who was stabbed outside a house in Cork City .
Kieran Long, of Ardcullen, Hollyhill, Cork, was brought before Cork District Court where he was charged with the murder of Mark O’Connell (36) at Hollyville, Hollyhill, on November 16th, 2025.
Det Garda Mick Dolan of Gurranabraher Garda station gave evidence of arrest, charge and caution and said that Long made no reply to the charge when it was put to him after caution.
Sgt David Fleming said that the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) had directed trial by indictment on the charge, and he said the DPP was also consenting to Long going forward on a signed plea of guilty.
Defence solicitor Shane Collins Daly said that his client understood that bail was not available to him at the District Court and he would be applying to the High Court for bail on the charge.
“He is disappointed at not being able to apply for bail today because he has co-operated with the investigation from the outset and has made himself available to the gardaí at all times,” said Collins Daly.
“He will be pleading not guilty to the charge – he has maintained his innocence at all times so a book of evidence will be required in the case.”
Judge David Waters noted the solicitor’s submissions on the matter and he remanded Long in custody to appear again at Cork District Court by video-link on October 14th .
Earlier this year, an inquest at Cork City Coroner’s Court heard that a postmortem revealed O’Connell had died from haemorrhage and shock due to a stab wound to the upper thorax.
Assistant State Pathologist Dr Margot Bolster said the stab wound led to bleeding into the cavity between the lung and the chest wall and into the pericardial sac surrounding the heart.

title: ‘There’s help out there’: Adults struggling with literacy get new start with tailored supports
description: Looking back, Brian O’Donnell says ‘now they’d have found I was dyslexic but there was no such thing back then’
content:
With the help of his wife Siobhán, Brian O’Donnell had ducked and dived his way to about the halfway point in his working life without anyone ever realising he had trouble reading and writing.
When, aged 45, he finally had no option but to confide in a manager, he was startled when they sat him down and said: “Don’t worry, there’s help out there.”
That help, which came in the form of classes at the Carlow Education and Training Board (ETB), to which he was referred by the National Adult Literacy Agenc y (Nala), dramatically changed his life, he says enthusiastically a decade later.
At the age of seven, O’Donnell spent a year in hospital with a hip problem and then had a couple of years struggling to get about. Though probably well intentioned, the decision not to keep him back a year in school meant he suddenly found himself trailing his schoolmates in class.
“I think now they’d have found I was dyslexic but there was no such thing back then. I’d be trying to take something down and then suddenly the board would be wiped clean,” he remembers.
“I just fell farther behind and the problems carried on into secondary and in the end I just sort of became the class clown because I didn’t want to be disturbing things all the time with my hand up to ask questions.”
When the Inter Cert (now the Junior Cycle) came around, he recalls, “I walked into the first exam, put an X on the answer book and walked out”. He was 14 and that was his last day in school.
O’Donnell got work in a local Teagasc store, where being unable to read well was not an issue until his manager died suddenly and he was thrust into a front-of-house role. He managed by laying the catalogue out in front of customers and then walking away so they would have to call out their orders. Stints followed in manufacturing and contract cleaning and he worked away for spells, too, in the United States and Australia.
When he returned and looked for something more permanent, Siobhán filled out the application for a porter’s job in the UPMC Aut Even Hospital in Kilkenny. When he went for the interview, one of the nurses who had cared for him as a seven-year-old was in charge of hiring. “She gave me the job on the spot.”
Things generally went well and, apart from having to make excuses to get out of meetings when it was his turn to take minutes for a health and safety committee, his secret remained safe. That was until an opportunity for 10 of the hospital’s staff to attend a course at University of Limerick came up a decade ago and a manager put his name forward.
“I was selected and thought: ‘Oh my God, I have to do it.’ I had to go back to the stores manager and tell him: ‘Look, I’m struggling with reading here.’ He was the first person outside of my wife and family to know. He sat me down and said: ‘Look there’s help out there, you’re a good candidate for this.’”
A few months later, with the support of his employer, he walked anxiously into an adult literacy class at Carlow ETB. “Within 10 minutes it was like being wrapped in a warm blanket. It changed my life ... the sleepless nights, the sweats, the panic attacks ... they were all put to bed.”
On the home front, he says, he was able to help his three sons with their homework for the first time, something that had always previously fallen to Siobhán.
Linda Waldron from Dublin, and now living in Mountmellick, Co Laois, with her partner Brendan, echoes many of O’Donnell’s experiences. Her issues first arose in school where she did not seek help and none was really offered, and she carried on into adulthood and her working life.
Like O’Donnell, she worked from a young age and felt more at home in that environment than in education. When she got a job in a nursing home after a spell on work experience during her Leaving Cert Applied, she survived because she had a good head for the names of conditions and medications and got on well with people. “It all came kind of naturally and if I was stuck with a form or something, I’d always get help at home from my parents or family,” she says.
What pushed her to return to learning was her niece’s surprise that she did not know what a word was on a leaflet when the pair were in a GP’s surgery one day. “She asked me what it meant and I told her I didn’t know and she was saying, ‘you should know, you’re an adult’. She was only five or six. But that really haunted me.”
Her relationship with her 12 nieces and two nephews was affected by the problem, she recalls. “If they were playing board games, I’d distance myself and I couldn’t help them with homework,” she says. That spurred her on, “and I wanted to do it for myself”.
Of getting help, she says: “It was amazing, it changed so many things for me. It was during the pandemic so they [Nala] sent me out workbooks and a tutor would ring me every day and she would go through the spellings, the reading of sentences and all that. It was brilliant.” Later she attended classes at Laois and Offaly ETB.
She continues: “I went back to college for two years to do a course in healthcare and there were people there to help you but I didn’t need it. The support from the people in your class was brilliant, though.”
It has, she says, changed every aspect of her life.
Nala chief executive Colleen Dube says the organisation gets about 500 calls a year from people who, like Waldron or O’Donnell, have decided to tackle long-standing literacy issues. They are offered help with finding classes, often run in local ETBs, while the Learn with Nala programme also includes online or tutor-assisted courses currently supporting more than 3,500 people, all provided for free.
[ Prisoner literacy: ‘When you pick up a book you’re not thinking of being locked in the cell’ Opens in new window ]
Much of the funding is provided by Solas although its public funding has not increased since 2022 and it has been, like so many other organisations, making the case for more in recent weeks.
About one in five Irish adults lacks basic literacy skills with one in four having similar issues with numeracy. Those figures include many people who are holding down jobs, particularly older workers. With full employment that is more manageable, but few are available to take courses while working full-time and Dube says Nala wants to see more employers supporting their staff through available initiatives.
“For many people, the courses are a gateway to work, further education, apprenticeship programmes, but for many others it is about building confidence,” she says.
Those taking the courses come from all walks of life, she suggests, but numbers have been driven in recent years by remote working during and since Covid with its greater emphasis on written communication and the increases prevalence of online training and certification required in many workplaces.
[ Finn McRedmond: The cause of the great reading crisis is unknown. But the solution is obvious Opens in new window ]
“You have people working on construction sites and they’d be told to do an online safety course but they can’t read. It’s all sorts of people: civil servants, office workers ... But a lot of our focus would be on the farthest behind first, providing level-one to -three courses, meeting people where they are and seeking to maximise the opportunities available to them.”

title: A5 upgrade is welcome, but why not a train service too?
description: Donegal is the ‘forgotten county’ when it comes to rail system
content:
Sir, – I have just heard the good news that the A5 is at last getting an upgrade (“ A5 ruling a ‘relief’ for bereaved families ”, Ireland, October 6th).
Living in Co Donegal since the early 1980s, this road to Dublin has always been the worst part of our journey.
Do you think any of the enlightened planners would now consider running a rail link alongside it to Monaghan and hopefully onwards to Dublin, stopping at Castleblayney, Carrickmacross, Ardee, etc? Why not do all the work at once rather than, in a few years’ time, deciding to build a rail link at a much higher expense?
Just think of the daily commuter traffic this could take off the roads and alleviate stress and time-wasting.
The last train left Donegal in 1959. We are truly “the forgotten county” when it comes to a rail service. – Yours, etc,

title: EU must not cut support for communities facing poverty, crisis and exclusion
description: Ireland has unique opportunity to send clear message on value of humanitarian assistance
content:
Sir, – When European Union ministers responsible for development meet in Dublin on October 8th and 9th, Ireland has an opportunity to send a clear message: slashing humanitarian assistance has immediate and dangerous consequences.
Aid must remain focused on people and communities facing poverty, crisis and exclusion – and development co-operation should not be sacrificed or misdirected to serve EU interests.
Reports that cuts of up to 40 per cent to the EU’s Global Europe instrument are being considered should ring alarm bells. The negotiations on the next Multiannual Financial Framework will determine not only how much money is available for development assistance, but also what that money will be used for.
Such cuts could wipe out much of the recent increase in resources available to tackle poverty, conflict, humanitarian emergencies and climate shocks , leaving little capacity to respond to future crises.
We do not need to speculate about the consequences of drastic aid reductions. The fallout from recent USAID cuts has been devastating.
In the Democratic Republic of Congo , the loss of support for clean water services contributed to a surge in cholera deaths. HIV treatment programmes have been disrupted, and clinics have closed in Malawi . Life-saving health services have been suspended in Uganda and Mozambique . Demining work has been halted in countries from Afghanistan to Ukraine . Behind every budget cut are real people whose lives will be affected.
At a time of escalating conflicts, climate disasters, shrinking civic space and rising debt burdens, development assistance remains one of the most important tools for building global stability and creating opportunities for those who need it most.
Cutting aid will not make the challenges disappear. It will make them worse and more expensive to address later. Every euro invested in disaster prevention can save many times that amount in recovery costs. And every investment in stability and development reduces the risk of future conflict.
Europe faces difficult budget choices, but there are other ways to raise the necessary resources while supporting Europe’s climate ambitions and efforts to reduce inequality. Fair taxation of extreme wealth and high-emitting sectors such as fossil fuels and aviation could generate significant revenue while supporting Europe’s climate ambitions.
Equally important is ensuring that aid remains focused on its core purpose: reducing poverty and supporting sustainable development for those battling crises outside of their control.
Development budgets should not be cut to make room for increased defence spending. Nor should development assistance be repurposed primarily to control migration, secure access to critical raw materials or create commercial opportunities for European companies.
Aid that serves geopolitical interests rather than community needs is less effective and risks undermining achievable objectives.
Instead, the EU should invest in humanitarian action, gender justice, local civil society and community-led development.
Communities most affected by poverty, conflict and the climate crisis should have a meaningful role in deciding how aid is designed and delivered.
Ireland has rightly earned international respect for its commitment to development co-operation. As holder of the presidency of the Council of the EU, it should use this moment to champion an ambitious Global Europe budget and ensure Europe’s aid remains focused on those who need it most.
Development aid is an investment in people and our shared future. – Yours, etc,

title: Increasing levels of debt carried by EU institutions a concern, says top auditor
description: The union’s borrowing is projected to hit €1 trillion by 2027
content:
There is a worrying tendency to view funds collectively borrowed by the European Union as “virtual money”, rather than a debt national governments would eventually have to cover, the union’s top auditor has said.
Tony Murphy, president of the European Court of Auditors ( ECA ), the bloc’s spending watchdog, said the increasing levels of debt carried by EU institutions were a concern. The union’s borrowing is projected to hit €1 trillion by 2027.
“In terms of common debt, this concept that it’s sort of virtual money and it’s not real, I mean it’s real debts, which have to be paid back,” Murphy said.
Governments are heading into bitter negotiations about the size and focus of the EU’s next seven-year budget. Capitals are divided over how much money should be put towards defence, Common Agricultural Policy subsidies for farmers, “cohesion” funding for infrastructure projects in poorer regions and a competitiveness fund to boost Europe’s lagging economy.
A draft €2 trillion budget proposal has been criticised as too expansive by a coalition of frugal governments , who want to scale its size back substantially. A larger group of 17 states are resisting attempts to slash funding set aside for agriculture subsidies and development projects.
The Irish Government holds the rotating EU presidency and, on Saturday, will table a compromise budget to bridge some of the gaps between the opposing camps. European leaders want to land a deal by the end of this year.
Speaking on Wednesday, Murphy said repayments to cover past borrowing would take up 8 per cent of the proposed €2 trillion budget.
[ Ireland criticised for not doing enough to tackle tax avoidance in report by EU auditor Opens in new window ]
“We’re not policymakers or legislators ... What we’re doing is trying to inform people that this, you know, just that they’re aware of the level of debt. What we’re trying to point out is that this is real money and it’s a real debt and it has to be paid back,” he said.
Murphy, who is originally from Cabra, north Dublin , has led the ECA since 2022. He was re-elected for a second three-year term late last year.
The Luxembourg-based watchdog audits how EU funds are spent and the quality of controls in place to make sure money is put to proper use.
Rolling over the bloc’s debts would only kick “the can down the road” and the money had to be repaid at some point, Murphy said.
Governments previously borrowed money as an EU bloc to finance a massive package of grants and loans to help their economies bounce back during the Covid-19 pandemic. Germany, the Netherlands and other fiscally conservative states have traditionally opposed taking on debt at EU-level, often referred to as common borrowing.
More recently, the EU borrowed €90 billion last December to finance a loan to Ukraine, to plug a hole in its stretched wartime budget.
[ How the EU’s €90bn loan to Ukraine will work Opens in new window ]
The loan was approved on the basis that Kyiv would repay the money when Russia made reparations for the destruction caused by its invasion, or from Russian financial assets frozen inside the EU by economic sanctions.
Murphy said the European Commission was already making accounting provisions to cover an eventuality where the €90 billion wasn’t repaid.
Ireland’s contribution to the joint EU budget, calculated on the basis of gross national income, was likely to face a “quite significant increase”, he said.
“I’m sure the Irish have their own figures calculated as to what this will actually mean for them in terms of their contribution.”

title: How much longer can the world absorb the Iran war shock?
description: Disruption to oil supply, oil prices and the world economy has been surprisingly manageable so far
content:
The war that was intended to deliver a swift overthrow of the Iranian regime is now in its eighth month, with no end in sight. So, what might happen next? My preliminary conclusion is that one should never underestimate human stupidity or human ingenuity. So far it is a rough draw between the two. How long will this last? That is the question.
In a devastating analysis, John Mearsheimer of the University of Chicago describes the war on Iran as “the mother of all strategic blunders”.
Among other things, he says, the United States went into the war on the false claim that Iran was on the verge of acquiring a nuclear weapon; Washington thought air power alone would produce regime change, which has never worked; it had no contingency plan for dealing with Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz .
It has also failed to achieve any of its four principal objectives: regime change; ending Iran’s nuclear enrichment capability; ending its long-range missile capability and ending its support for Hamas, Hizbullah and the Houthis.
The closure of the strategic waterway has done significant damage to the international economy and may do much more; and the US alliance structure (in the Gulf and elsewhere) has been damaged. All this, moreover, is only about half of the full charge sheet.
The stupidity is indeed impressive. Even now we cannot guess how it ends. Yet there is a counterargument. The war may indeed be a strategic blunder. But the economic damage has been surprisingly modest.
As Johannes Urpelainen of the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies said in August, “Many experts initially thought that this supply disruption would send oil prices to USD 200 per barrel, causing massive inflation and a global recession. Instead, oil prices peaked at USD 126 per barrel in April 2026.” Today, the real price of crude oil is still near its long-run average since 1972.
[ World’s oil stockpiles are ‘scarily thin’, says Saudi Aramco boss Opens in new window ]
How can this be, given that Fatih Birol, head of the International Energy Agency , said in March this was “the greatest global energy security threat in history”? The ingenuity is the answer.
Urpelainen says that: “First, the energy transition has reduced the global economy’s dependence on oil. Second, supply chains have proven resilient and adaptive. Third, producers outside the Middle East have acted fast to produce more oil and natural gas. Finally, drawdowns of global oil inventories have filled the remaining gap.”
Flexibility is notably true of the Gulf. As former diplomat Mohammed Elsoukkary writes: “By the end of September preliminary estimates placed regional crude exports at approximately 16.3 million barrels per day, compared with 19.5 million in February, including roughly 9.7 million moving through Hormuz.”
This is an impressive achievement. Yet do not forget that we consume products, not crude oil. There has been substantial damage to refineries in the Gulf. Moreover, refineries are set up to process specific crude oils, so shortages of products have emerged.
One notable example is diesel. This even led Donald Trump to consider a plan (now abandoned) to halt the US exports. But other products have also had bigger price rises than crude, notably natural gas and sulphur.
Nevertheless, the disruption to oil supply, oil prices and the world economy more broadly has, in truth, been quite surprisingly manageable. In terms of the overall economy, this is, as Nouriel Roubini says in Project Syndicate, in large part due to the investment boom triggered by artificial intelligence (AI).
But, for the future health of the world economy, it is not the level of investment, but its rate of growth, that matters, as does the ultimate economic contribution of AI itself. Surely at some point investment will slow. As to the economic contribution of AI (or indeed its doomsday properties), who knows with confidence?
There exist other sources of fragility. One, which I discussed previously, is the manageability of global debt at a time of rising interest rates. France, the United Kingdom and US are in the crosshairs. There is a particular risk for countries whose public debt is overwhelmingly short-term since, as a result, they enjoy little insurance against the impact of higher inflation on interest rates.
One of the biggest questions, then, is whether the stand-off between stupidity and ingenuity will continue. If it does, the energy shock at least should remain contained. But that cannot be taken for granted: the present situation, not least the drawdown in stocks, cannot continue forever. China’s noteworthy suppression of domestic demand might not last either. If these come to a halt, crude prices might jump to more disruptive levels.
A still bigger question is where the war itself will go. Might the US president greet the passing of the midterm elections as a chance to release his bellicosity? Then a lame duck, he might think it would be the right time to sort out those pesky Iranians.
If so, how far might Iran be able (and willing) to go in damaging the oil infrastructure of its neighbours? What is remarkable, after all, is how much Gulf oil is still flowing. Might that again be disrupted?
Alternatively, could (or would) a post-midterm Congress halt such efforts? Or might Trump get bored with the whole thing and let hostilities peter out into an ill-tempered (and probably informal) ceasefire?
An advantage of arbitrary despots is that they can so easily get bored. I cannot imagine that Trump finds the war with Iran much fun any longer. Even he must also find it really difficult to believe that it has been a great triumph.
After all, as Mearsheimer says, he has achieved none of his objectives. Iran is battered, but its ghastly regime and influence in the Gulf look rather secure. Trump will surely be tempted to declare victory and move on. The US people would be delighted. So might it all end “not with a bang but a whimper”? – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Dublin 1’s disproportionate concentration of social services
description: Responsibility should be shared more evenly across the city
content:
Sir, – In the debate following Robert Watt ’s comments on the overconcentration of social services in Dublin 1 (“ Dublin 1 unfairly burdened with ‘huge overconcentration’ of social services ”, October 2nd), a recurring argument has been that while Dublin 1 may carry a disproportionate share of such services, efforts to redistribute them more evenly across the city are unrealistic because land and property values are higher in more affluent areas such as Dublin 4.
While concern for the prudent use of public funds is understandable, we do not apply this logic when considering amenities and services that are widely regarded as desirable, such as parks, libraries, sports facilities, schools and other public amenities.
Why, then, should homelessness , addiction and support services for vulnerable people be treated differently?
It is high time this argument was challenged whenever it is advanced, because it is increasingly used to defend the status quo rather than address the imbalance itself.
Property values are rarely allowed to stand in the way of public amenities. It is curious that they become decisive only when the responsibilities concerned are those that affluent communities would rather not host.
I support Watt’s assertion that Dublin 1 carries a disproportionate concentration of such services and welcome efforts to ensure that responsibility is shared more evenly across Dublin and across the country. – Yours, etc,

title: Sinéad O'Sullivan: Europe is changing. Ireland has yet to notice
description: Obvious hazard is not that we make bad decisions in this brave new era, but that we fail to realise there are changes to decide upon at all
content:
To be-EU or not to be-EU? I wrote here recently about the changing nature of the European Union: that it was once a peace project built on trade, which has turned its economic gaze to military-industrial development. More specifically, that it is drawing in outside powers on a scale never seen before, by way of Canada and Ukraine .
Ukraine is an official European Union candidate, while Canada is deepening its trade, security and defence relationship with the bloc. The last two weeks, however, have shown that Europe is not only changing in size and structure, but in how much power it wishes existing member states to retain.
This new economy is not one in which the Republic is likely to thrive. Reindustrialisation will reward countries that had, at some recent time, a deep expertise in manufacturing and high-value physical output. In other words, the benefits accrue to the factories that France, Italy, Germany and even the United Kingdom can presumably dust off and reopen. Even better if they can be repurposed for defence, one of Europe’s fastest-growing areas of industrial investment. Ukraine and Canada are obviously winners in this new Europe, as they are enormous agricultural and industrial economies with an eye on a permanent defence footing.
This State, on the other hand, has very intentionally – rightly or wrongly – decided to become the opposite: a services economy with no industrial defence base and a cultural tradition of never building one.
Discussions here of a new defence-oriented Europe are frequently met with disbelief. “Maybe, but it will never happen; accession takes years, so why the panic? And in any case, it will never be voted through.”
That was true of Europe – but of the old Europe, when accession took years. Many member states would have been happy to say no to Ukraine’s agricultural sector and to the corruption that lives deep inside its institutions. But the Europe in which those objections were decisive has changed beyond recognition. In the Republic we do not seem to have noticed this yet.
