Unless you look at Europe through its new lens of geopolitical power, you might miss the fact that integration has effectively already happened. The questions people here think need to be answered are now mostly irrelevant: should Canada be voted the European Union’s first-ever associate member? Should Ukraine be voted a full one? Functional integration is already under way, and by the time any procedural integration is needed by way of a vote, it will be little more than a technicality. Granting Ukraine or Canada their new titles will simply be naming something that already exists.
Defence integration is already in train, too.
The EU’s new defence-industrial strategy isn’t just a one-way deal to supply weapons for Ukraine; Ukrainian defence manufacturing is being integrated into the European economy. In addition, Ukraine is already inside Europe’s energy market, its customs co-operation and the European Union’s €90 billion loan architecture. Meanwhile, Canadian foreign minister Anita Anand came to the Republic last month to discuss joining the broad defence financing frameworks Ukraine is already part of.
Now look at EU market access – the precise thing accession used to be for. The European Commission recently announced it will attempt to allow candidates access – albeit conditional and reversible – before being voted in. In the words of commission president Ursula von der Leyen ’s top adviser: “Earlier integration would open opportunities for union businesses, strengthen European value chains and reduce strategic dependencies” before any votes are needed.
[ Aughinish Alumina steps up lobbying as European Commission considers sanctions Opens in new window ]
These benefits once typically arrived at the end of the process. But today, they are beginning to be transferred beforehand, which changes the meaning of a “no”. In the old Europe, saying no meant preventing integration from happening. In the new model, after integration has already happened, saying no would mean deciding how much of it to unwind.
All of this assumes there will be a vote at all. Commission documents show Von der Leyen will imminently put forward a vote to move from unanimity to majority voting on certain issues involving accession – as vetoes “can delay or prevent timely decisions”.
The commission is also proposing to drop the principle that every EU country has a commissioner, which it believes will be unworkable in a union of 30 or more members. The last time this was mooted in 2013, the Republic was unsurprisingly one of the most vocal opponents of the move.
As always, the trade-offs between speed and proportional democracy are about to come face to face.
However, and ironically, the commission needs states to vote unanimously to abolish the need to vote. This means that we, along with the other states, must agree to this; a matter which will either be voted on via referendum in the Republic or, less democratically, be passed with only both Houses of the Oireachtas approving it.
[ Increasing number of foreign-born recruits joining Defence Forces Opens in new window ]
So instead of debating whether Ukraine and Canada will join the European Union in their proposed capacities, we need a conversation in the Republic about what it means to be part of this new, larger EU. Giving single market access to countries with comparatively few obligations, and doing so with limited vetoes, surely cheapens the benefits of “full” membership. Needless to say, nobody wants to pay the annual fees for a golf course when non-members can pay as you go. So what does this mean for Irish politics?
The stakes for this State are high as we try to figure out our place in this new Europe. It will require rebuilding the relationship between politicians unable to deliver urgently needed reform and a public whose trust is not guaranteed, for whom right-wing populist politics look ever more appealing. All of this is happening under the spotlight of the State’s EU presidency, at a moment when Brussels most needs us to enlarge its economic and military union – an impetus that is in conflict with the desire at home for the public to have a say in the decisions that will affect the State.
But the danger for this Republic isn’t that we make bad decisions in the coming era – it’s that we don’t realise there are changes to decide on at all.

title: European stocks fall as Wall Street retreats from record highs
description: Shares in Kenmare Resources continued to rise on Wednesday following confirmation of a bid approach
content:
Stock markets hit a wall on Wednesday following a record-breaking run as oil price increases caused a lift in bond yields, which stoked concerns the Federal Reserve may be triggered to hike rates in reaction to inflationary pressures.
These worries led to the S&P 500 falling from an all-time high and halted the Nasdaq 100’s six-day gain.
On Wednesday, brent crude also hit $102 (€91.13) a barrel due to a pickup in Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz .
The Iseq All-Share Index fell by 0.83 per cent to close at 14,344.11 on Wednesday afternoon.
Rare earths miner Kenmare Resources again recorded the most notable gain in the day, with its shares up 2.99 per cent to €2.76.
Shares in the firm have surged in recent days following confirmation by the company that Abu Dhabi’s International Resources Holdings has made a bid approach for the Dublin-based minerals miner.
Engineering company Mincon was the only other Iseq-listed firm to record a rise in share price of more than 2 per cent on Wednesday. Energy firm Greencoat Renewables was the next-best performer, with a marginal 0.9 per cent gain.
On Wednesday, shares in insulation group Kingspan slid again as its price fell 1.87 per cent to €99.60, while shares at Bank of Ireland and pharma services firm Uniphar both fell 1.84 per cent.
In London, the FTSE 100 index ended down 83.19 points, 0.8 per cent, at 10,458.50.
Lenders bore the brunt of the falls, with Standard Chartered , HSBC , NatWest and Barclays down between 2.8 per cent and 4.5 per cent, while insurer Prudential slid 4.7 per cent.
HSBC said consultations were under way, after the Financial Times reported that hundreds of jobs were at risk from the bank’s adoption of artificial intelligence.
“We are currently in a consultation period,” a spokesperson said after it was reported the firm has plans for sweeping job cuts in its UK wealth management business.
JD Sports Fashion was among the biggest risers, up 3.93 per cent, while health and nutrition products firm Reckitt Benckiser saw its share price rise 2.6 per cent after positive comments from broker Goldman Sachs.
Water company Pennon plunged 20 per cent after it said it was cutting its dividend to support increased investment plans. The company’s chief executive Keith Haslett said it’s clear that Pennon has “real strengths, but there are areas where we need to improve and deliver better outcomes”.
European stocks traded close to their lowest level in around ‌four months on Wednesday as the ‌pan-European Stoxx 600 index was down 1 per cent.
In European equity markets on Wednesday, the Cac 40 in Paris ended down 1.4 per cent, as did the Dax 40 in Frankfurt.
The sense of global unease in the stock markets has been compounded by France’s fiscal woes, which are threatening to drag the European Central Bank into the kind of face-off with markets it hasn’t seen since the euro area’s debt crisis more than a decade ago.
The French yield spread against safe-haven German Bunds – a market gauge ⁠of the risk premium investors demand to hold French debt – was ​about 11 basis points (bps) wider after narrowing for two days. It was last ​at 140 bps, and reached almost 160 bps last week.
French bonds have been under pressure as expectations of higher European Central Bank rates and political uncertainty before the ‌2027 election raise doubts over France’s ability to fix its finances.
On Wednesday, the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 eased from record highs as Treasury yields and oil prices rebounded, keeping investors cautious as they awaited the minutes of the Federal Reserve’s September meeting.
In early afternoon trading, the Dow Jones was down 0.92 per cent, the S&P 500 fell 0.56 per cent and the Nasdaq was 0.85 per cent lower.
Sentiment turned more cautious as investors reassessed the outlook ​for interest rates and energy costs. Brent crude was back above the psychologically important $100-a-barrel level as Middle East supply concerns persisted.
“We’re seeing a little bit of profit-taking today. The market is very focused on the Fed minutes, but ultimately it’s where oil prices and yields move that will determine the market’s direction today,” said Peter Cardillo, chief ​market economist at Spartan Capital Securities.
Chip stocks were among the top decliners. Memory chip firm Micron Technology dropped 2.3 per cent, chip giant Nvidia eased 0.7 per cent and the broader Philadelphia chip index fell ⁠2.3 per cent.
Elon Musk’s SpaceX lost 1.7 per cent after a Financial Times report that the rockets-to-AI firm was seeking $40 billion in financing to fund purchases ‌of ‌Nvidia ​chips.
– Additional reporting by Reuters, Press Association and Bloomberg

title: Sinn Féin and the DUP are happier arguing over a parade than agreeing a budget
description: The normalisation of ultra-short-termism has entrenched financial irresponsibility
content:
S tormont was about to have an emergency budget imposed on it by London before the Drumcree dispute suddenly changed the subject. The financial crisis continues to fester and will have to be addressed within weeks.
Although Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionist Party ( DUP ) did not deliberately engineer a Drumcree distraction, they are clearly happier arguing over a parade than confronting their failure to agree a budget.
The other two Executive parties, Alliance and the Ulster Unionist Party , share the blame. Sinn Féin’s Minister for Finance in Northern Ireland, John O’Dowd, is responsible for preparing a budget. DUP ministers have been most vocal in rejecting it. However, all four parties agree that the problem is underfunding, and London simply needs to give them more.
Their agreement on this has only grown as they have fallen out over everything else. All hands to the begging bowl is their final point of unanimity.
Yet Stormont has plenty of money, more than ever before and enough to meet its needs according to its own financial experts. What it lacks is the ability to say no to anyone – a historic irony.
Budgets are meant to span the assembly’s five-year mandate, but since 2016 there have only been one-year budgets due to collapses and disruptions to devolution. Five were agreed by the Executive; another five were imposed via the Northern Ireland Office.
This has kept the lights on, but made it impossible to plan investment and reform. In the health service, which accounts for half the budget, managers blame this for failure despite spending 52 per cent more a head than in England. Other services are similar.
The normalisation of ultra-short-termism has entrenched financial irresponsibility. What began as finger-crossing and can-kicking has descended over the past two years into wilful overspending, mainly on public sector pay increases, while hoping something turns up. London has a track record of bailing Stormont out of a crisis. Although conditions are always attached to use the money wisely, this has incentivised Stormont to spend its way into a crisis.
[ Susan Sarandon and Noel Gallagher among artists calling for independent Drumcree mediator Opens in new window ]
When O’Dowd began planning a multiyear budget last year, he was forced to consider an unorthodox time frame due to the most recent collapse of devolution.
He proposed a three-year budget, covering the final year of this mandate and the first two years of the next.
Powersharing means parties might as well plan for the next Government as they are all almost certain to be in it. But only if they can make any plan stick.
The budget should have been in place by April, the start of this Assembly’s last financial year. It has still not been agreed. The Executive parties have only agreed to transform a standoff among themselves into a standoff with the British government. They argued that Scotland and Wales are funded above their official level of need due to legacy problems with budget formulas, so Stormont should be overfunded as well.
London is understandably unmoved by this line of reasoning, as are Edinburgh and Cardiff.
Hilary Benn, the Northern secretary until July, asked the Executive to “meet the Government halfway” on cuts and revenue-raising.
If Stormont was capable of cuts and revenue-raising, it would not be in this position.
[ O’Neill accused of choosing politics over ministerial responsibilities in Drumcree standoff Opens in new window ]
Chris Bryant , the new Northern Secretary, made a “final offer” last month of £1.5 billion spread over three years, adding about 3 per cent to Stormont’s basic grant.
But the Executive has already committed itself to £1.6 billion of overspending this year alone. Closing the gap would involve more political pain than most of its parties and their fragile relationships could bear – although Alliance has called this week to admit defeat and accept Bryant’s offer.
When Stormont fails to agree a budget, the law allows each department to authorise up to 95 per cent of last year’s spending. This keeps the lights on for the first half or so of the financial year, but taking current inflation into account it means an 8 per cent real terms cut that is beginning to cause serious difficulties.
Before Drumcree intervened, Bryant had set a strict deadline of October 1st to agree a budget or have one imposed. If he does still have to impose a budget, it will be another one-year wonder – a simple set of departmental spending limits with a lecture attached to do better next time, the most London feels it can do to intrude on devolution. That can only further entrench the Executive’s short-termism and fiscal delinquency. It should be clear by now to everyone that bailing out Stormont is sinking it.
[ Drumcree is theatre of the absurd, straight from Monty Python’s Ministry of Silly Walks Opens in new window ]
The British and Irish governments have reportedly discussed reforms of powersharing in advance of next May’s elections, including removing certain unionist and nationalist vetoes and equalising the titles of the first and deputy first ministers.
That will all be beside the point without a fundamental review of Stormont’s attitude to money.

title: New Munster CEO Avan Lee: ‘a real shame’ if there wasn’t a role for Peter O’Mahony
description: We ask the new man in charge about the big-ticket items on his agenda, getting input from past players and his impression of the system he is going into
content:
Munster ’s new interim chief executive Avan Lee gave a media briefing on Wednesday morning about his background, his rugby bona fides, priorities and aspirations for the province when he starts on October 21st, and why he’s returned to Ireland.
“As a rugby fan, growing up in New Zealand, you know about Munster. You know about the history, you know they beat the All Blacks , so there’s always been a bit of a mystique around it. There’s obviously been some change, some challenges. But there’s a big opportunity here to make a difference and make Munster better; produce teams that the fans and the community love.
“They do now, but can it be in more numbers? That’s really the motivation, to be honest. I’ve worked in rugby for 20 years, [have] a strong connection with Ireland. Ten and a half years as a CEO at Super Rugby. It just feels like the right time to take those skills to Europe and, ideally, Ireland, which has worked.”
“Given my background in Ireland, family, etc, I’ve always thought about heading back to that part of the world and working in rugby again. It goes back probably five or six years with [the late] Philip Browne and then Kevin Potts, just staying in touch.
“I finished with the Hurricanes at Christmas and then just let Kevin know that I was looking. I did some consultancy for World Rugby, a few other things. I’ve been in a lot of ways, ready to go. [I’m] very passionate about Ireland and Irish rugby. The right opportunity came up and we’re just sort of making it happen as a family.”
“It needs a non-financial audit, to sit down and go through the whole organisation, the systems, the structure. Is it high performing? Is the whole organisation high performing? Is it aligned? I’ve read a lot of commentary in the media, which is fine. But obviously, with the IRFU and with Munster Rugby board, I need to work through that stuff myself.
“Clearly, there are some challenges, and there have been some issues [that I am aware of] through the media. And obviously, you don’t want that going forward. You want to draw a line under some of that stuff and focus on the positives and how you make the organisation better.
“Certainly, from the review, I’ve not seen a word, so it’s not fair for me to comment on what I think might be in it. I genuinely don’t know.”
“For me, it’s about galvanising the community of Munster and Munster rugby fans behind the organisation and the teams. I haven’t started, so I’m not going to be too specific yet, because I don’t necessarily know the answer. But it’s obvious there’s been some controversy, some stories through the media, and people being critical of Munster rugby.
“So, clearly going forward, that’s not acceptable. You know, the organisation needs to be performing. And you want your fans to love the teams. For me it’s about alignment of vision, values, culture, whatever words you want to use, because if you’re not really effective in all those areas, it’s difficult to be successful.”
“I’ve met Clayton a couple of times in New Zealand, obviously, been in his company several times at various meetings. I spoke to him earlier, so we had a conversation. I’ve spoken to Ian Costello and Tadhg Beirne in the last one and a half, or two hours. I’m getting a good feel for the people of Munster and what they’re looking for.”
“Irish rugby has been very strong for the last decade on the field. The people I’ve met from the IRFU and Munster have been extremely impressive across the board, and very supportive of what I’m going to do and what I need to do. So, I couldn’t be more impressed with the people that have given me this opportunity and that have supported me already.”
“Yes, absolutely. I’ve already reached out. I’ve connected with Peter O’Mahony and Donncha O’Callaghan. I would have done so even if Peter hadn’t said the sort of comments he said in the last week.
[ Avan Lee appointed interim chief executive of Munster Opens in new window ]
“Having a connection with past players is critical. You’re never going to please everybody all the time, but I think it’s important to have those kinds of people inside the camp. Peter obviously had a fantastic career. He’s got a lot to offer. He loves Munster.
“He’s a natural person for me to sit down and talk to and, I guess, understand what it means for him to be part of Munster and what he wants Munster to look like. I think ultimately, is there some sort of a role for a guy like Peter? I think it would be a real shame if there wasn’t in some capacity [a role]; that would be difficult to understand, if he wanted to.”
“Yeah, I think so. My perception of Munster is there’s a bit of a disconnect between high-performance rugby and business and that was exactly the same when I joined the Hurricanes. I come from a commercial business background, but I have obviously worked in high performance for 20 years, so I do understand both and it’s critical to have alignment between the two.
“That would be the most obvious one. Second to that, and not less important, is the importance of recruitment, pathway development, and bringing players through for four, five, six years together. The Hurricanes have just won Super Rugby, and that’s a major reason why we did.
“We had, I think, five All Blacks when I started. When I left, we had 12. So, I think having international players in your squad is very important. Recruiting well if they’re [the talent gaps] not locals, and keeping a team together, developing over time. There’s a big opportunity [to do that] with Munster.
“You look at the under-20 players who’ve come through [here] and the Irish set-up. I was watching Gordon Wood and Charlie O’Shea and guys like that at the weekend, who are young men, but if they’re together for four, five years, that could be an awesome team. That’s the other part of it.
“But also the importance of commercial, having the revenue to drive high performance and be successful and create an environment where people can succeed. Again, I don’t know a massive amount about the revenue profile, but the demand on that is never diminishing. So, it’s a key part of it too.”

title: Jessie Stapleton hoping fresh start at club level will give her Ireland boost
description: The Leicester City player is settled and enjoying her football after being sent out on loan three times by West Ham
content:
It was a summer of upheaval for over half of the Republic of Ireland squad currently limbering up in Astana for the first leg of their World Cup qualifying playoff against Kazakhstan on Friday.
Thirteen of the 25 players Carla Ward selected for this international window moved clubs since the end of last season, most in search of more regular playing time – which, in turn, they hope will boost their prospects with the national team.
Among them are Jessie Stapleton and Jess Ziu, the former Shelbourne team-mates who both left West Ham for Leicester City in August. “I can’t get away from her,” says Stapleton.
It’s a fresh start for both players who’ve had their ups and downs the last few seasons, Ziu having to overcome two anterior cruciate ligament injuries in the space of two years.
Stapleton, meanwhile, endured the frustration of being sent out on loan three times by West Ham – to Reading, Sunderland and Nottingham Forest – despite them extending her contract and predicting a bright future at the club for the Ballyfermot native.
“A big thing for me was finally finding a club that I could call home, rather than being out on loan spells,” she says. “It’s been absolutely brilliant. I’m getting a lot of game time, I’m able to show some different qualities that you can’t really showcase when you’re on loan because you don’t really feel part of the club.”
Mind you, choosing Leicester was a gamble seeing as they had just suffered a woeful season in the WSL, finishing bottom of the table and, after losing on penalties to Charlton in a playoff, relegated to the WSL2.
But Stapleton, who signed a three-year contract with the club, was reassured by their determination to rebuild. An added bonus was the presence of two familiar faces at the club, fellow senior international Heather Payne and young goalkeeper Katie Keane.
“And it’s so good when you go into a new team and you have friendly faces. They made it so much easier for me and Jess to settle in, they helped us around the area and to make new friends on the team. And I think Leicester need a few characters with that fighting Irish mentality, that’s helping the club get back to a good place. It’s a work in process, but we definitely have the squad to go on and do good things.”
It’s hard to credit that Stapleton is only 21 seeing as she had her first involvement in the senior Irish set-up a whole eight years ago. So impressed was then manager Colin Bell, he called the 13-year-old up for a home-based training camp. She had, though, to wait until the rusty old age of 17 before Vera Pauw gave her a senior debut against the Philippines.
She initially prospered under Ward, starting eight successive games, but she’s fallen down the pecking order in the last year. While she can also play in midfield, Ward sees Stapleton primarily as a central defender, with the competition for those slots fierce.
But opportunity could knock for both Stapleton and Ziu in the absence of captain Katie McCabe, Denise O’Sullivan, Marissa Sheva and Ruesha Littlejohn for this first leg.
She’s more eager to talk up Ziu, though, than herself. “She’s a brilliant girl. She’s had a tough run with injuries, but you can see in training every day how her ability and confidence is coming back. She’s been so good for Leicester, on and off the pitch. She’s great at dribbling, great at attacking, great at linking play. I always say to her that’s she’s brilliant. I hope that she stays injury-free. She’s in a good place now.”
As for Kazakhstan, Stapleton maintains the themes of the week: don’t take them for granted. “When we’re the underdogs, we go into games with that fighting Irish spirit. But that doesn’t go away just because we’re favourites. We have so much respect for Kazakhstan, they’re not going to give us an easy game. But yeah, I think we have everything in our team to get through to these two games.”

title: AI deepfakes: Let’s remove ‘we didn’t mean it’ from tech companies’ book of excuses
description: Companies that have enabled this, intentionally or not, need to take a long, hard look in the mirror
content:
V irgin Media’s Deepfake Ireland was never going to be an easy watch. The subject matter was skin-crawling: the growing problem of deepfake and nudification images that are primarily being used as a weapon against women and girls.
Seeing it laid out in such a stark manner was sobering.
The programme initially focuses on presenter Gráinne Seoige ’s own experience of having a deepfake image created of her while she was campaigning in the general election in 2024. Two years on, the distress it caused was evident.
But things got worse. With the help of Ceartas, a tech company that started as a free service to tackle so-called revenge porn, she found out the real extent of the problem. A visibly upset Seoige was told that they had uncovered more content, images she hadn’t known about.
There were stories from others who had been similarly affected – model and presenter Maria McGuigan, poet Noel Fleming and an unnamed 15-year-old girl – each one horrifying in its own way.
The message was clear: this isn’t an isolated issue, and it isn’t going away any time soon.
By the end of the year, nudification apps are expected to be banned in the EU . But it has taken far too long to get to this point.
Nudification apps were thrust into the spotlight in January, when images of mainly women and sometimes underage subjects that had been digitally undressed by xAI’s Grok chatbot were published on social media platform X .
If you needed any other reason to remove yourself from the platform, the company’s response – first ignore it, then make access to the image-editing feature available only to paying subscribers – might have pushed you over the edge. Eventually, X cut off Grok’s ability to alter images of real people in places where it breached the law, but only after heavy pressure from authorities. The move came too late for women – and children – who had been affected by the incident, and is not a watertight solution to the problem.
[ Data Protection Commission investigates X over ‘nudification’ of images via Grok Opens in new window ]
While the Grok incident may have highlighted just how easy it is to fake such images, it wasn’t the first to do it, nor was it the worst offender. It was just the most visible. I used an AI image editor to change an innocuous photo of me, fully clothed at a sports event, into one where I was posing in a skimpy bikini. The software refused to do anything more extreme than that, but it is enough. The image editor was a free tool that surfaced in a quick Google search; imagine what you could find if you were willing to spend time to hunt down the most lax software out there. Another few clicks brought me to an AI girlfriend creator and a NSFW (not safe for work) image generator.
This is just scratching the surface of the issue. As the analogy goes, if you see two ants in your home, you don’t have a two-ant problem. Somewhere there is a nest, and until you deal with that, you will continue to have problems.
The difficulty here is that it is almost impossible to root out the nest. While the EU may ban nudification apps and Irish law can take action against those who share nonconsensual explicit images, it cannot stamp out the technology behind it. Apps can be – and are – removed from app stores to make them less visible. But as we already know, things can live on in the quieter corners of the internet, just out of sight but still accessible. As AI skills grow, AI models can and are being modified by users to fit their needs.
Unless there is a concerted global effort to deal with the issue, the apps and those behind them will simply move out of the law’s reach.
That is assuming the ban is passed without being watered down or challenged in some way. In Minnesota, where similar action on such software has been almost unanimously backed by politicians, the proposed law is currently on hold after xAI brought a legal action against it, claiming it imposes an “overbroad, content-based ban on free speech and the tools of visual expression”.
Let that one sink in for a minute. An AI company, owned by a billionaire, claims that a law that bans apps and websites using AI to create nonconsensual sexualised images and videos of people infringed free-speech rights. Even where the political will is there to do it, there are challenges to overcome.
[ Female-looking AI agents were paid less than male ones in virtual office, study finds Opens in new window ]
Who asked for this? Why do we need it? The AI companies that have enabled this, intentionally or not, need to take a long, hard look at themselves in the mirror. I once asked an executive in a tech company why, given the obvious potential for abuse, the company was developing tools to generate increasingly realistic images.
The answer? Because the company’s competitors would do it.
The one weapon we have to fight back is education. The idea that the image is fake so it doesn’t have an impact or any legal repercussions is being eradicated by programmes aimed at educating children. Perhaps we should focus on adults, too. Make “I didn’t know” an invalid defence against creating the images.
And while we are at it, erase “we didn’t mean it” from the tech companies’ book of excuses.

title: Finn McRedmond: University education has become meaningless - and now it doesn’t even promise a job
description: We have made education transactional and have forgotten that learning is a good in and of itself
content:
“U n parfum de guerre civile” – or “whiff of civil war” – is how the centre-right French newspaper Le Figaro described the atmosphere in Britain in August 2024. The streets of the north east of England and beyond had been consumed by angry and destructive rioters in the wake of the Southport killings .
Rich, I thought, coming from the French. Burning upturned bins and firing missiles at law enforcement is just as Gallic as burgundy, rillettes and smoking. A nation built on enlightenment values and the rationality of Montesquieu sometimes succumbs to a destructive and often bloodthirsty id.
I recommend The Rest is History’s recent series on the French Revolution for anyone in search of a refresher.
But even given France’s state of semi-perma rioting , the recent civil disobedience stands out. Partially because – not being a rural French working class business owner – I found it hard to relate to the gilets jaunes, to properly parse their politics. But mainly because the source complaint of the protesters now is something universally understood; something central not just to the social health of the French republic but to the values of the West. That is the state of education.
It started with teenagers angry about the conditions of their schools: buildings that are inadequately designed for the extremes of French weather; decrepit and decaying classrooms; classes that have too many pupils; bathrooms with no soap. Then university students joined in, teachers too.
As is always the case, the root problem has somewhat been lost and what was a narrow complaint has spiralled into an omnivore movement: police brutality, vague and directionless frustration with government.
But never mind that for now. The kids have a point. Even though France spends a comparatively higher amount of GDP on the education system – 0.3 percentage points higher than the European average, and 2.4 percentage points above Ireland (although the usual caveats to any data point as a percentage of Ireland’s GDP apply) – students complain about a lack of resources, shoddy buildings and a shortage of teachers. And so who is surprised? First, they are French: protesting is what they do. But second – everyone has to go to school, everyone has time to develop strong feelings about how it should work and what fairness looks like, how high the ceiling and the floor should be set. Given the decrepitude described, this episode seems inevitable. Or to make a long point short, if I were a French teenager I would be rioting too.
And maybe if I was still an Irish teenager, I would be as well. Because aside from the peculiarities of the French system, the riots speak to a bigger existential moment for education systems everywhere.
[ French prime minister to address nation as school protests escalate Opens in new window ]
I worry that somewhere in recent decades, maybe even years, we have forgotten what school – and university – is for. No matter the quality of the facilities: the small class sizes, the state of the art interactive whiteboards, the AstroTurf hockey pitches in the school colours, the sleek labs and Home Ec kitchens – or any other accoutrement of the Dublin private school in 2026. This is not France. But what is the point of any of that without properly articulating the philosophical goals of an education?
Friends who are teachers report on a cohort of students who can’t or won’t read anything beyond summaries of books. I speak to academics from my alma mater university who regularly tell me – head in hand – about whole classes who refuse to sit handwritten exams, who believe the function of an education is not to acquire knowledge but to learn how to effectively extract information from ChatGPT.
In England, when Rishi Sunak suggested making mathematics compulsory for all students until the age of 18, it was though he had announced conscription. The children can’t possibly handle something so challenging, the detractors responded, blinded by the bigotry of their low expectations.
And so, in place of literature and standards, we have opted for something far more transactional – an “education” in exchange for the promise of a job. We hand out meaningless degrees to students who don’t really want them because – in Ireland especially – we have functionally made third level qualifications a necessary condition for office employment. School and university are spiritually transforming into training grounds for the workplace – just at the same time that AI looks set to eradicate a huge number of entry level corporate jobs.
It is the worst of both worlds – to forget that learning is a good, in and of itself, while not even being able to follow through on the promise that it will at least lead to work. I think about the French classrooms falling apart, a tragedy in a nation that really is the historical epitome of Western civilisation. They are right to protest. And then I look beyond France and wonder, huh – why does no one else seem so angry?

title: ‘It’s a proper club ground’: Captain Dan Sheehan relishing Leinster’s return home
description: Blues’ opener at revamped Laya Arena against Cardiff is getting players and fans excited
content:
When he dreamt of being Ireland captain, Dan Sheehan didn’t know that deciding when lunch should be would be part of the remit. Now he does.
Such decisions were among the less glamorous duties of leading Andy Farrell’s squad on the summer tour of Australia and New Zealand.
The Leinster hooker had captained Ireland before, but taking the armband for an extended period brought new responsibilities, some far removed from what happens on the pitch.
“You almost become the logistics manager of the team in some ways,” Sheehan said. “A lot of people, whether it be players or staff, asking you what time meetings are on and what you think of putting a meeting in here or lunch at this time.”
It was a different perspective for the 28-year-old and one he enjoyed. “I’d be of the mindset to be keeping things more simple rather than over-complicating things, so it was nice to be able to even take things out of the schedule and just simplify things,” he said.
That time away confirmed to Sheehan that leadership brings an increased internal expectation that helps to sharpen his own performance. He believes his team-mates are more inclined to follow what he does than by any grand speechmaking.
“It excites me that I have that position to lead and put my own spin on things. It makes me get the best out of myself, which is probably the most important thing,” he said.
“I’m not a guy that’s going to shout the changing room down with this emotional speech. The best way I can go about leading is how I show up to training, the intent I bring. If I’m expecting lads to get off the line and hit people, I need to do it first.”
With Caelan Doris not expected to return until the new year, it is likely Farrell will name Sheehan in the role again for the resumption of the Nations Championship next month.
Like Ireland, Leinster have similarly retained a leadership group that Sheehan says has been strong for several years, with responsibility rotating depending on the game, while Doris remains a central presence despite his injury.
“He’s definitely the club captain that everyone looks up to,” Sheehan said. “He’s very diligent at making sure that he stays connected while out injured. We’ve got a lot of good leaders. It gets the most out of a number of other people, rather than just relying on Caelan or myself or whoever is captain.”
Leinster’s move back to the redeveloped Laya Arena has generated excitement in advance of Saturday’s game against Cardiff in the United Rugby Championship . Sheehan’s childhood memories of the RDS have centred on the occasion rather than an interest in watching the rugby itself.
“But then I remember distinctly being in the grandstand and watching Brian O’Driscoll going down that right wing, I think it was against Wasps, and that double kick. That’s the one that stands out to me,” he said.
Brian O'Driscoll for Leinster against Wasps in 2008. pic.twitter.com/SpQ1UPMiIN
“If you got to go to a game you’d be telling everyone in class, so we need to make sure we get that sense of occasion back because it’s a nice, intimate ground with good access to players. You feel like you’re on the pitch.”
His senior debut there stands out as a playing highlight, although it was in front of an empty ground during Covid against Zebre.
“I remember the interview after, I was effing and blinding because I was very untrained,” Sheehan said.
“A lot of early memories for players and their careers are in the Laya Arena.
“Then you think of the European games. We’ve played Gloucester and Sale. There was a frozen pitch – I remember Leo [Cullen] leaving these lights around the pitch for the full day before.
“It’s a proper club ground, edgy and not perfect, which is what a home ground should feel like. Sometimes you go to these big stadiums, it’s all too manicured, but this is a club ground. We want to make sure that it feels a bit special and there’s a bit of history there, which you can feed off.
“It’s definitely been a theme to make sure that we hit the ground running. We should have a full house there on Saturday. Everyone’s looking forward to it.”
The players are equally enthusiastic about having their Champions Cup pool games there. “It’s a closer, more intimate feel,” Sheehan said. “We all look back on nice European days in the Laya Arena and hopefully we can replicate the same.”

title: Heads or tails, 3D printing can make fish waste appetising
description: Beril Bayrak is a PhD student at Munster Technological University, Cork
content:
My research is mainly about developing a way to turn marine byproducts into something more usable. The marine industry generates a significant amount of waste, but even though we call it waste, it contains valuable proteins and bioactive compounds. We are looking at how to recover and transform these compounds using environmentally friendly technologies.
We obtain proteins from marine waste and investigate their properties and potential for bioactivity. Then we harness these properties to develop 3D-printed food products. Pure fish products can sometimes look unappetising, but with 3D printing you can make them more colourful and well-designed, and you can even personalise it to what someone wants to eat. Finally, we analyse the final product for texture, sensory, and microbiological properties.
3D printing is a layer-by-layer process, and in our case we also include bioactives and proteins obtained from byproducts like fish skin and heads into the layers of the marine paste. That creates 3D food products that we can design to help people who have difficulty eating or swallowing, and we can create appealing shapes and designs, which really helps with consumer satisfaction.
My interest goes back to childhood. I was always curious about food. I used to ask questions like, does popcorn weigh more after popping? Why does a cake become more delicious when baked? Why do jelly sweets have such a nice texture? That curiosity naturally developed into an interest in food science and engineering.
I completed my bachelor’s degree in food engineering in Izmir (Turkey) and then my master’s degree in food engineering at Çukurova University in Adana. From there, I came to Cork to pursue my PhD at Munster Technological University.
I have been very grateful for the support of the MTU TU Rise scholarship, which is co-financed by the Government of Ireland and the European Union through the ERDF Southern, Eastern and Midland Regional Programme 2021–2027, and for the guidance of my supervisor, Saravana Periaswamy Sivagnanam.
The most important thing I have learned is to see unexpected results not as failures, but as information that helps you decide on the next step. Research is never a straight line. I can design everything carefully in an experiment and then something doesn’t work. That is frustrating, but it is also where you learn the most. You have to rethink your approach and keep going.
I love exploring Ireland, especially the nature, the seafood and the traditional music and dance. I am also very passionate about chess. I have been playing since I was young, and last year I was lucky enough to win a championship at a chess tournament and finish third in the women’s category at an intervarsity tournament representing the MTU chess team.
For me, chess and research have a lot in common, because in both you have to think ahead and adapt when things don’t go according to plan.

title: ‘A KitKat budget from a TikTok Tánaiste’: Ivana Bacik takes a bite out of the Coalition
description: The day after Budget 2027, Sinn Féin seemed to have forgotten about it, but no amnesia among Labour and Soc Dems
content:
W as Budget 2027 among the most unmemorable budgets of recent years? It certainly appeared so in the Dáil on Wednesday.
The day after the Government unveiled an €8.5 billion budget package bringing public spending to a record level, Sinn Féin , the main Opposition party, seemed to have forgotten about it already.
As Leaders’ Questions, the chamber’s traditional showpiece of the day, began at noon, it seemed inevitable that Mary Lou McDonald would relish hammering Taoiseach Micheál Martin and his Government over their budgetary shortcomings.
Yet the Sinn Féin leader instead turned her attention to the situation on the Garvaghy Road and the standoff between Catholic residents of the Portadown estate and the Co Armagh Orangemen looking to march down their road.
In fairness to McDonald there were more than seven hours allocated for budget statements later in the day, while her colleagues had been vocal with their criticism across the airwaves.
The Coalition needn’t have worried that their efforts had gone unnoticed; the Social Democrats and Labour Party took up the mantle and adopted a sort of one-two combo approach.
First up was the Social Democrats’ deputy leader Cian O’Callaghan , who accused the Taoiseach of breaking Fianna Fáil’s general election manifesto promise to give pensioners a €12 increase.
Holding up a printed copy of said manifesto, O’Callaghan said there was a time when Fianna Fáil had “the backs of older people” and stood up for “the men and women who worked so hard to build this country”.
“But those days are gone, because pensioners have been bitterly betrayed by you in your budget,” he said.
Referencing the €3 increase in the living alone allowance, the Dublin Bay North TD said the amount would “not even buy a cup of tea in a cafe”.
“It would just about cover the cost of a pound of butter in the supermarket.”
In his response, Martin insisted his party does “have the back of pensioners and always do and our Coalition colleagues likewise”. The Taoiseach told the Social Democrats TD that his attitude was “spend, spend, spend”.
“You don’t care about the economy,” he said. “You don’t care what creates the resources that we need to allocate to social protection. An increase in the social protection budget of €2 billion is quite substantial. The €10 pension increase is above the rate of inflation.”
Next up was Labour leader Ivana Bacik , who provided the most lively soundbite of the afternoon.
“You might call it a pathetic fallacy that it was pouring rain as your plans were revealed,” she began. “Indeed, the word ‘pathetic’ is appropriate in many ways because the money you say will go back into people’s pockets could barely buy a chocolate bar a week in reality. It’s a sort of KitKat budget from a TikTok Tánaiste.”
The Labour TDs alongside her enjoyed that one, prompting the Minister of State at the Department of Justice Colm Brophy to ask: “Did you work that one up yourself?”
[ It takes a giveaway budget of €8.5bn to not annoy anyone – except Patrick O’Donovan Opens in new window ]
Bacik continued: “In seeking to please everybody, you’ve ended up pleasing nobody, especially not the Minister for Missing Culture Cards Patrick O’Donovan. In seriousness, this underwhelming budget has failed so many.”
The Taoiseach said he disagreed fundamentally with the Dublin Bay South TD’s analysis of the budget and, with a grin on his face, added: “You’re hardly blaming us for the rain, are you?”
Martin reiterated the budget was “quite substantial”, that it could not be looked at in isolation and there had been a “sea change” in the Government getting back into building social housing since 2020.
“We will deliver five budgets, not just one, and you can’t look at any one in isolation.”
Perhaps next year’s will be a little more memorable.

title: Regulator says ‘forever chemical’ found in Irish cereals should be classified as toxic
description: Department of Health disputes validity of tests but waits for directions from European Union
content:
The European chemicals regulator has said a so-called “forever chemical” found in high levels in Irish cereals in a test last year should be classified as toxic to people and water supplies.
The European Chemicals Agency made the recommendation to the European Commission in relation to trifluoroacetic acid (TFA).
It said TFA should be classified as “persistent, mobile and toxic” due to its spread, longevity and adverse effects.
Specifically, it should be classified as “toxic to reproduction” through its effects on sexual function, fertility and development.
For the environment, the concern is particularly long-term, said the agency’s risk assessment committee.
“TFA is extremely persistent and highly mobile, meaning that it does not easily break down and can travel through soil and water. This can lead to widespread and very long-lasting contamination of groundwater and other water resources.”
TFA is a synthetic chemical widely used in manufacturing foams, plastics, disinfectants and pesticides for plants.
Research by environmental group Pesticide Action Network Europe last year found particularly high levels of it in Irish cereals.
The study analysed 66 popular cereal-based products in 16 European countries, including breakfast cereals, pasta, bread and pastries.
Irish breakfast cereals had the highest levels of TFA followed by Belgian wholemeal bread, German wheat flour and a French baguette.
The European Commission, along with member states, will now consider the agency’s recommendation and what labelling or regulations might be required.
The Department of Health said Pesticide Action Network Europe’s study was a “non-peer-reviewed” report.
“This was based on a small number of products purchased in Ireland, most of which were of unknown origin, and it does not establish the prevalence of TFA in Irish-produced grain-based foods,” it said.
However, it said it was aware of the agency’s recommendation on trifluoroacetic acid.
“TFA can arise from the breakdown of certain refrigerant gases, active substances used in plant protection products and other sources, so the issue spans the remit of several Government departments,” it said.
“The Department of Health ’s role relates principally to food safety and public health, in conjunction with the Food Safety Authority of Ireland .
“The Department of Health and the Food Safety Authority of Ireland will continue to monitor developments at EU level and will consider any implications for food safety and consumer protection in Ireland.”
The Department of Agriculture and Department of Environment have also been contacted for comment.
Forever chemicals, or perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), are a collection of thousands of man-made chemicals so-called because they do not break down in the environment or human body and build up over time to potentially toxic levels.
They are widely used, often to coat everyday products to make them non-stick, waterproof, stainproof or fireproof.

title: Funerals are the only aspect of Catholic life I engage with any more
description: Every time I’m in a church and listening with adult ears, I’m struck by the reality that religion is a response to fear
content:
I was Down Home last week for a removal and a funeral. Funerals are the only aspect of Catholic life I engage with any more, so my visits to the church are sporadic and usually coloured with heightened emotion. I go to pay my respects and support the family and will honour whatever ways the deceased and their loved ones choose to mark the end of their life.
On this occasion, the Mass was set for a weekday morning, with prayers at the funeral home the preceding evening.
We were expecting a priest to lead the evening prayers, so were surprised when two women – lay people – took on the task. Afterwards in the pub (naturally) there was much chat about the role the women had played at the removal, not least because the decade of the rosary had tipped along at a great pace and we all agreed they had done a lovely job. This, coupled with news from my mother about the loss of the local priest from my own small childhood parish, led to one logical conversation topic: They’re going to have to start letting women be priests and allowing priests to get married and, ideally, give up the vow of celibacy.
Listen, I’m in no hurry to restore the Catholic Church to its former glory in numbers, but I can appreciate the solace that religion brings. Every time I’m in a church and listening to the prayers and sermons with adult ears (as opposed to the indoctrinated ignorance of a child), I’m struck by the reality that religion is a response to fear; a way to make sense of our fleeting time on Earth and to temper the terror of what lies beyond death or, worst of all, that nothing lies there at all. If believing in heaven and eternal life assuages that fear, then who am I to deny that?
At the same time, the level at which the church in Ireland has been such a poor steward of its influence and power and the harm it has caused leaves me largely unmoved by its demise in community presence.
I’ve always assumed that the church’s refusal to allow the ordination of women was based in misogyny, and it would be difficult to convince me that this isn’t the case.
The official line, simplified, is that while women are and always have been hugely important in the church, Jesus decided not to call any women to be apostles and therefore the church does not have the authority to ordain women.
In December 2025 the Vatican reaffirmed that even the possibility of women as deacons – a deacon can do everything a priest does except celebrate the Eucharist and hear confessions – remained firmly off the table, something former president Mary McAleese said was indicative of “an institution on its way to self-inflicted oblivion”.
The Vatican commission report said: “The masculinity of Christ, and therefore the masculinity of those who receive Holy Orders, is not accidental but is an integral part of sacramental identity, preserving the divine order of salvation in Christ.”
[ Krispy Kreme rage, Teresa Mannion, HomeToVote: The moments that made the Irish Internet truly great Opens in new window ]
At this stage, after 2,000 years of the masculinity of Christ, would a women even want to be a member of the clergy given the church’s long-held dedication to a leadership of men? You can appoint as many women as you want to important and lofty positions, but if they’re never allowed to break through the glass steeple then what loyalty do they owe?
It’s a grim reality that the lifting of the vow of celibacy and ban on marriage for priests is more likely than women ever being ordained. Celibacy is a rule rather than a doctrine, and therefore open to change by the church. It dates back many centuries and has its roots in avoiding nepotism as well as a belief that single, celibate men can better devote themselves to their ministry. With such a vocational crisis in the church, how much longer can it hold? It’s mind boggling how much influence over issues of sexuality and reproduction a (supposedly) celibate and single workforce of clergy had over Ireland for so long.
One thing that struck me during my time at the funeral and associated rituals was the age of all of those involved, in the prayers, the Mass, the communion. They were elderly, or close to it. It may be that the ship has already sailed on any hope of bringing young blood to leadership positions in the church, even if they ripped up the rule book in the morning.

title: The last thing Macron needs is a letter from an Irish mother, but I have my two cents to offer
description: The long French school day gives the state a sizeable presence in my son’s childhood
content:
T he last thing French president Emmanuel Macron needs right now is a letter from me. With lycées (upper secondary schools) blockaded and students and teachers out on the streets from Paris to Marseilles, I reckon he’s occupied enough without my two cents.
I do have two cents to offer though, and until the eruption of these protests, I had assumed that it was only under our roof that the national education system was debated.
In 2019, the same year I emigrated to France , a law was passed which made school compulsory for all children from the age of three. The idea is to place everyone in the same starting blocks, thereby levelling the playing field when it comes to primary school and beyond.
A quick investigation of the complaints from the current school protesters would make you question whether that has had any effect. Dilapidated buildings, absent teachers, diminished resources in places with the greatest need, large classes in urban areas, and long hours don’t sound much like a level playing field to me – much less a fair one.
When I dug a bit deeper, I learned that my own son could stay in school next September from 8.30am until 4.30pm, admittedly with a lunch break and nap included in those hours. And while the very youngest children in the petite section, as it’s called, can leave after the morning session, from age four the length of the school day is cemented. I feel this gives the state a sizeable presence in my toddler’s childhood.
That’s where I become unstuck. France is my family’s home. We go to the local market on Sundays; my son asks for a baguette in the village boulangerie, his French is without an accent. Although I have adopted France and feel adopted in turn, my uncertainty about enrolling my son raises a different question: do I consent to what feels like a co-parenting relationship with the state?
I am a product of the Irish system. The Leaving Certificate , some 17 years ago, still morphs into the occasional nightmare. I find myself asking how far the shadow of those anxious hours of memorisation, ingrained competition for points and university places has stretched across my own life.
In freezing winter temperatures, my classmates and I wore our Regatta coats over our uniforms for the majority of our lessons, but it would have been a considerable leap to imagine coming together to protest attending those lessons in the first place.
[ Inside the school protests in France that have spiralled into arson and street violence Opens in new window ]
And while I disagree with the violence of the protests, I’ve always admired a certain force in French society: that change is a very tangible thing, not merely an intellectual pursuit held behind closed doors, and that it can be effected by anyone who considers themselves a citizen.
It’s one of the reasons I probably felt I could write to the president about my concerns.
When education begins at three years old, is this one of its shadows?
I am not without options for next year. Montessori, forest schools, private and international schools remain alternative, if expensive, avenues. But I’m not convinced.
If I put my son into the public system, I am consenting for the state to play a significant role in what his education means. If I choose a different route, am I creating a chasm that will make him, though a French national, a citizen without the codes that collective experience provides, school being one of them?
I have until enrolment begins in March to make a decision. For now, the letter on the dresser remains stamped but unsent.

title: Belt holes or BMI? Experts must weigh up best way to talk about obesity
description: ‘Displaying nutritional information and communicating it effectively are not quite the same thing’
content:
Amid the myriad of deeply unimpressive characters in prominent positions across politics, business, and society, it’s easy to forget that many leaders are actually quite good at what they do.
Take James Timpson, chief executive of services company Timpson, for instance. It has successfully carved out a niche (almost literally, since it specialises in pop-up units within larger retailers) providing unspectacular but useful services including dry cleaning, key cutting, reheeling shoes, and phone repairs.
It has also pioneered efforts to rehabilitate offenders by employing ex-prisoners. Recognising that, Timpson was appointed UK prisons minister under Keir Starmer, a role he held for two years.
Last month, Timpson demonstrated another string to his bow when he posted on X about weight loss . “You can tell Ozempic and Mounjaro are popular ,” he wrote. “We have seen a 680 per cent increase in the number of free holes in customers’ belts we’ve been doing this year.” This was expert-level communication; belt notches are more immediate than an amount of weight lost. This is a specific insight that you wouldn’t get elsewhere, and now we know Timpson offers this free service.
Of course, an increase in belt alterations isn’t concrete evidence about the efficacy of weight management drugs, much less about their social consequences. But it did get me thinking about how we communicate about weight, particularly as a new report commissioned by the European pharmaceutical trade body EFPIA suggests that high BMIs (body mass index) could cost the Republic €3.2 billion annually. Obesity is a significant public health issue here; the Department of Health estimates that 56 per cent of us are living with overweight or obesity.
The department is developing a successor to the national obesity policy and action plan. The previous plan’s most obvious achievement was the sugar-sweetened drinks tax, especially because it drew attention to how much sugar many of us were actually drinking rather than eating.
Some of its other measures, such as mandatory labelling, were more difficult to implement, not least because their planned implementation coincided with the pandemic. Yet behavioural science shows us that the same principle that made the sugar tax effective – the surprise when food labelling shows how many calories could be hiding in a particular product – can be a powerful tool in reducing obesity.
This approach is most useful when applied to ostensibly healthy options that contain large amounts of saturated fat, sugar, or both; prepared salads slathered in dressing, granola, and smoothies are some of the worst offenders. It’s less useful at dissuading us from eating things that we don’t expect to be healthy. In those cases, it seems that we have already made our peace with its nutritional value and so are not surprised to learn that it is high in calories.
[ Science: What you should know Opens in new window ]
Other countries have struggled with how to inform people while at the same time encouraging healthier choices. In the Netherlands this summer I was struck by the Nutri-Score labelling on many products, including paprika crisps that were rated C on a scale from A to E. Needless to say, I wanted to eat crisps and no amount of nutritional information was likely to affect that decision. But I couldn’t help but wonder what if sliced potatoes deep-fried in oil and then doused in salt and flavourings could be a mid-ranking option a food would have to do to end up in the two lower tiers. Deep-frying in lard, perhaps.
I was even more bemused when I saw that frozen chips were rated an A. This, it turns out, was because foods are rated as sold; uncooked chips are essentially sticks of peeled potato. Foods are also generally rated per 100g or 100ml, so before a recent revision to the rating algorithm this meant that olive oil, which packs close to 1,000 calories in 100g, tended to be rated D.
The revised algorithm – which gives most olive oils a B rating – is being rolled out on a voluntary basis in France, Belgium, Germany, Spain, Luxembourg, and the Netherlands. It has received fierce opposition in Italy and Greece, where it is seen as penalising the traditional Mediterranean diet, particularly olives and cheese, which are generally rated C or D. This shows the difficulty in using an algorithm to grade individual foods, rather than a diet, as healthy.
And of course it’s possible to lose weight while eating unhealthily, as professor of nutrition Mark Haub demonstrated in 2010 by shedding 12kg in two months while eating a calorie-controlled diet based on Twinkies.
Displaying nutritional information and communicating it effectively are not quite the same thing. But if the new obesity policy needs any tips, James Timpson might be able to offer some.

title: School principals under ‘unmanageable burden’ with free books scheme
description: Over half of surveyed school leaders said scheme was a positive step in assisting families with costs
content:
School principals are being put under an “unmanageable administrative burden” with the free schoolbooks scheme, according to a new survey.
The scheme was first introduced to primary schools in 2023 and expanded into secondary schools in 2024.
It provides a grant to schools to buy textbooks, workbooks, copybooks and other essential resources, but does not include digital devices.
Individual schools buy the books themselves from suppliers and decide what their students need. Children are expected to return the books at the end of the school year.
However, a new survey by the National Association of Principals and Deputy Principals ( NAPD ), which received 300 responses from members, found 90 per cent of school leaders felt the administration of the scheme was creating a major burden on principals and deputies.
While every school receives an administrative grant to support them in organising the scheme, some 78 per cent of respondents said this was not enough support to implement it.
Despite this, over half (51.4 per cent) of school leaders said the scheme was a positive step in assisting families with back-to-school costs.
These principals and deputies believe the scheme should continue, but the majority (62.8 per cent) said it should be managed off-site.
President of the NAPD, Brian Doran, said: “This survey shows that school leaders recognise that reducing costs to parents is an important and worthwhile objective. However, we are losing sight of what is important in our schools when we continue to ask our educational leaders to prioritise admin.
“Principals and their staff are being asked to manage procurement, budgets, deliveries, stock, storage, book returns, recycling and distribution. This is in addition to their core responsibility of leading teaching and learning within their schools.”
Director of the NAPD, Paul Crone, said: “Without meaningful changes, there is a real risk that schools will struggle to find people willing to take responsibility for administering the scheme in future years and our students will continue to be disadvantaged while school leaders are distracted by admin work.”

title: Distinctive coastal home sits pretty amid dramatic landscape for €695,000
description: Culleenamore home has bay views and a backdrop of the Knocknarea mountain
content:
Rockview House has a distinctive setting in Co Sligo . Just south of Strandhill, it faces Ballysadare Bay, with Knocknarea rising behind it. The heat-retaining mountain cliffs create a microclimate around the house, while the absence of light pollution means the beauty of the night sky flourishes.
The area is home to one of the most famous and extensive midden sites – an ancient refuse heap comprised mainly of shells – in western Europe, dating from the Bronze Age to the Middle Ages. The ancient oyster beds here are considered some of the oldest in the country, with the molluscs in demand across the world since as long ago as the 18th century.
The owner of Rockview House bought the property just over 25 years ago. It was in need of renovation, and he and his wife brought it back to bare bones before taking their time to sensitively restore it.
The house was originally built in the late 1700s or early 1800s and is thought to have been a staff cottage belonging to the old Culleenamore estate. A second floor was added in the early 20th century, and the current owners added a livingroom during their time here. Now extending to 194sq m (2,088sq ft), it is on the market guiding €695,000 through Sherry FitzGerald Draper.
“Doing the house was a challenge, to say the least. It would have been very easy to disturb the integrity, and we really didn’t want to do that. We pulled it back to bare walls and, I’ll be honest, there were times that we wondered ‘what have we done?’, but we got it back to a cosy, warm home and kept its character.
“The only thing we really added was the livingroom to open out to the sea, but we made sure to make it look like it’s original.”
A stone wall with riveted double gates on the coast road marks the entrance to the property, with a gravelled driveway leading to the house. The old-style porch has space for mucky boots or sandy shoes, while inside, the hallway has an antique tiled floor and panelled walls.
Although renovated, the house retains the feel of an old country cottage, with interiors in keeping with its origins and earthy tones throughout.
There is a compact kitchen with fitted units, and a larger diningroom with timber beams, the original cottage fireplace surround and a solid-fuel stove. The drawingroom also has a stove in the original fireplace, with French doors opening on to the front lawn. The newer livingroom has a solid wooden floor and leads out to the gardens.
One of the nicest rooms in the house, and the owner’s favourite, is the study with fully panelled walls and rows of bookshelves with a recessed window looking out to the garden. There is also a utility room and guest bathroom on the ground floor.
Upstairs the landing has been opened up and provides a second office space or a reading room that could very easily be converted back into a bedroom. There is a bathroom beside this with a cast-iron bath, followed by the main bedroom with views out over the bay.
A second staircase at the back of the house leads to another bedroom with access to a balcony at the back of the house that looks out to Knocknarea mountain.
The gardens are mature, with fig, olive, magnolia, bay, apple and plum trees, as well as eucalyptus and beech. There is a fishpond, glasshouse, two garages and a timber animal shelter. Between the trees, views of the bay open out, with the lawn wrapping around the house.
It was the location that initially drew the owners to Rockview House, although it took time to fully appreciate the particular conditions of the setting. The mountain acts as a large curtain or wall to keep out light, while the cliffs create the microclimate that provides a longer flowering seasons in the garden.
“The lawn is elevated and looks out at the sea which is one of the largest sea colonies in Ireland. I am very biased, but I think it’s one of the best locations in Sligo. It’s hard to get this privacy so close to the sea,” says the owner.
“On the other side of the mountain is Sligo town and all its lights but we just have pitch-dark sky here. We are also sheltered in the bay, so we don’t have the winds like Strandhill. The changing light is amazing from the low and high tide, which I find extraordinary.”
The D2-rated house has history and heart that is not as easy to find, and is a home the owner will find difficult to leave behind.
“It’s a gem of a place. I’m extremely attached to the house. I’ve been enjoying it for 25 years but now it’s time for someone else to enjoy it. I hope they will take good care of it.”

title: Minister signalled Government was set to ‘renege’ on RTÉ deal in budget talks
description: Minister told Jack Chambers broadcaster’s €260m allocation could not be maintained without more funding for his department
author_name: Jack Horgan-Jones, Pat Leahy, Ian Curran, Cormac McQuinn
content:
Minister for Media Patrick O’Donovan warned before the budget that the Government would “renege” on its funding deal with RTÉ if more cash wasn’t found for his department.
In a letter last week, O’Donovan told Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers that, based on what was being offered, “the Government (not the Department) will renege on the three-year funding deal agreed with RTÉ in July 2024”.
In the final reckoning, an additional €21 million was allocated to O’Donovan’s department after the letter.
However, RTÉ’s allocation remained the same as 2026 at €240 million, €20 million less than it was expecting under a multi-year bailout deal between the then-government and the broadcaster.
The RTÉ funding allocation has sparked a major row between Montrose and the Government.
O’Donovan warned in his letter last Friday that based on the offer then on the table for his department, which stood at €827 million, RTÉ’s funding would in fact be cut by €11 million.
He also warned of funding consequences for a raft of other agencies including Sport Ireland and the Arts Council if no more money was forthcoming.
The final allocation to his department, which is responsible for culture and sport as well as media, was €848 million.
[ RTÉ says €20m cut in funding will impact on strategy as Minister criticises pace of reforms Opens in new window ]
It is understood that the budget ministers Chambers and Tánaiste Simon Harris, and Taoiseach Micheál Martin, believed that extra funding made available to the Department of Communications during tense budget negotiations over the weekend would solve any difficulties with the RTÉ allocation, but were only made aware of this issue on the day the budget was announced.
A Government source said “this only came to our attention yesterday [on budget day].”
On Wednesday O’Donovan denied that the move was a “cut” to RTÉ’s funding, despite the previous government promising to increase the broadcaster’s funding to €260 million next year.
“Over the lifetime of the three-year package of the bailout, it amounts to almost three-quarters of a billion euros,” he said. “That is an enormous amount of money from the taxpayers.”
He said he was not happy with the pace of change at the broadcaster and its transition to being a “more agile, smaller” organisation.
[ Minister calls for ‘cool heads’ in RTÉ funding dispute Opens in new window ]
In an email to staff, RTÉ director-general Kevin Bakhurst said he “completely rejects” O’Donovan’s assertion that the pace of reform at Montrose has been too slow.
Bakhurst said the station now had “some important decisions to make” if the previous agreement made with the government “will no longer be honoured”.
RTÉ reached a multi-year funding deal with the previous government in 2024. Under the agreement, the broadcaster would receive €725 million over three years: €225 million in 2025, €240 million in 2026, and €260 million in 2027.
Bakhurst told staff the decision to cut the funding for 2027 “is one we had not anticipated and will inevitably impact our ability to deliver our five-year strategy.”
The station’s chairman, Terence O’Rourke, is seeking an urgent meeting with O’Donovan, RTÉ said.
It is understood O’Donovan is due to bring a memo to Cabinet in the coming weeks on future funding options for RTÉ.
Elsewhere, public sector unions said Budget 2027 was a missed opportunity for Chambers to signal his seriousness about preventing next week’s one day national strike.
Kevin Callinan, who chairs the Irish Congress of Trade Unions - and will lead the union side in negotiations to replace the expired public pay deal - said in the summer the unions would take account of whatever measures were in the budget when it came to framing their pay claim in talks. Callinan said on Wednesday the Minister had failed to “move the dial”.
[ TG4 and Screen Ireland budget funding amounts to ‘cut’ in real terms, industry warns Opens in new window ]
In the Dáil, the Taoiseach said a dispute “would be unwarranted given our willingness to talk”.
Some €1.2 billion has been set aside in the budget for a public pay deal. Martin said “there is no basis for industrial action or for disrupting people in education, health or anything else when this platform is there as a basis for negotiation on a new pay agreement”.

title: Lower-than-expected annual €12,000 investment account limits may curb take-up
description: Industry taskforce expects fees ‘similar to other jurisdictions, to be competitive’
content:
The lower-than-expected annual tax-free investment limit and 1 per cent tax on assets above €50,000 in the Government’s new personal investment accounts could limit participation in the scheme, according to investment industry sources.
However, the latest details of the plan in Budget 2027 have been broadly welcomed as a strong first step to move Irish households from having one of the highest savings ratios in Europe to investing to meet financial goals.
People will be able to put €12,000 a year tax-free into the new accounts, which will be available from next July, Minister for Finance Simon Harris said in his budget speech on Tuesday.
Brokers Ireland chief executive Rachel McGovern said she had expected the cap to be about €20,000, close to the UK regime – echoing a widespread view from accountancy to stockbroking firms.
“But the most egregious element is the 1 per cent tax that will apply to anything over €50,000 built up in an account. It’s a stealth wealth tax. And it applies whether an account has made gains or losses in a given year,” said Michael Healy, chief executive of IG Consumer at UK investing and trading platform IG Group, which launched commission-free investing in stock and exchange-traded funds in the Republic last year.
Healy said that these will limit uptake by households in the scheme and possibly put off some overseas investment service providers that have been looking at participating in the initiative. This, he said, would result in lower competitive pressure on fees and charges.
[ Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work Opens in new window ]
However, an industry taskforce organised by Financial Services Ireland said in a report published earlier this year that it expects fees “similar to other jurisdictions, to be competitive”.
Industry sources say that all-in annual fees, including charges by service providers, underlying investments, and trading costs, could range from 0.5 of a percentage point, for accounts where no advice is offered, to 1.5 per cent, with advice. However, they said that pricing structures will not be finalised until closer to the planned July 1 st launch date.
James Costello, head of Davy’s portfolio management group, also said that the lower-than-expected annual tax-free investment allowance will lead to a lower participation rate than if it were set at €20,000.
“This is meant to be for people who are trying to address financial resilience of their household outside of retirement provision, such as saving for things like their kids’ education, a deposit for a house, or elderly care for parents,” he said. “But I’d have an expectation, and very significant hope, that the €12,000 would increase over time.”
McGovern, of Brokers Ireland, agreed that the plan “is a good start” and will likely evolve over time. But while the tax treatment of investments in personal accounts has been designed to be simple for individuals to understand, she noted the wider regime for retail investors remains complicated, with an ongoing “deemed disposal” or exit tax regime (both reduced in Budget 2027 to 35 per cent from 38 per cent), and 1 per cent life insurance levy.
[ Fewer than one in four interested in investment accounts, survey shows Opens in new window ]
Any tax due on the new investment accounts will be calculated and paid at source by the companies providing the investment funds available under the scheme.
Teresa Kelly Oroz, head of public policy at Irish Life, welcomed the fact that there is no minimum investment for the new accounts. “This allows people to grow more comfortable with investing and developing that behaviour,” she said.
Revenue said on Wednesday it plans to set up a forum between it, prospective investment account providers and their third‑party software providers to focus on the technical aspects of the project. This will include account opening, eligibility validation, account life cycle processes, and pay‑and‑file obligations.
