While not clarified in Tuesday’s announcement, there is an expectation that the 1 per cent stamp duty on purchase of shares in Irish public companies with a market value of more than €1 billion will not apply to trades in the new accounts.
A Department of Finance spokesman declined to comment, saying more details will be in the upcoming finance act.
It is also expected that the initial €12,000 maximum investment will cover the first six months of the scheme, in the second half of 2027, and be aligned with the calendar year thereafter.

title: A Pacific island ‘will be swallowed’ by the sea within decades. Is Ireland paying attention?
description: Ireland and Tuvalu are joining forces in an attempt to hold back the tide of apathy as sea levels rise
content:
T he term “digital nation” means very different things to Ireland and Tuvalu.
For Ireland it means having a large IT sector, embracing AI and pursuing a deliberate policy of digitising everyday transactions in the home, school, business and public services in the name of progress.
For Tuvalu, it’s a desperate attempt to keep itself in existence via the online virtual world when all traces of the physical country disappear beneath the rising sea.
These two countries, with such different experiences of modern life, are partnering up to cohost the second International Conference on the Just Transition away from Fossil Fuels next July.
The handover from Colombia and the Netherlands, who shared the task of hosting the inaugural conference last April, took place on the fringes of the United Nations General Assembly in New York at the end of September.
Details of next year’s event are scant, with the complex logistics, official agenda, side events programme and assignment of duties yet to be worked out.
But the UN gathering in New York provided abundant context for the challenges the conference aims to address, namely getting countries to stop using climate-destroying fossil fuels fast and forever.
During a high-level session, world leaders or their representatives delivered statements on sea level rise and its consequences, ending by formally approving the UN Declaration on Sea Level Rise.
The document was two years in negotiation and begins with a solemn shared message.
“We are deeply concerned about sea level rise,” it states. “Sea level rise is not a distant scenario but a real and lived experience for many.
“Rising sea levels are primarily driven by ocean warming and melting ice sheets and glaciers, and we note with concern this phenomenon is accelerating.”
To put the phenomenon in figures, the background report for the declaration says the seas globally rose by an average of 4.75mm per year from 2012-2025 – more than six centimetres in just over a decade.
But it was 5mm in 2023 and 5.9mm in 2024 so the rate is increasing as climate change intensifies.
In 2023 the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, comprising the world’s top scientists, warned levels could rise by 20-29cm by 2050, and by 50cm to a metre by the end of the century.
But, it says, since then, further studies have warned of much more dramatic increases, particularly if tipping points are reached such as the collapse of the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets.
Either way, the backgrounder concludes, almost 770 million coastal dwellers – a tenth of the world’s population – are directly at risk.
These are a diverse group of people – beachside billionaires in California, small farmers in Co Wexford, fishing communities in Bangladesh, bankers in Manhattan, rice-growers in Vietnam and the citizens of some of the smallest, low-lying Pacific islands.
Tuvaluans are among them, fighting a fierce battle against the encroaching seas in a tiny archipelago where the highest point rises no more than 4.6m.
[ Ireland and Tuvalu to cohost international climate conference next July Opens in new window ]
The four-page declaration agreed by world leaders last month commits in quite a vague way to doing whatever is possible “to safeguard long-term habitability, livelihoods and critical infrastructure” in such places.
“We emphasise the need for strengthened partnerships and co-operation to mobilise and provide financial, technical and policy support to address sea level rise for developing countries, particularly Sids (small island developing states) and LDCs (least developed countries),” it says.
“We call for scaled-up finance to localise action on sea-level rise.”
That is a call they are making to themselves so it would be of greater significance if they actually pledged to scale up finance.
The declaration gets a bit more specific when addressing the issue of “nature-based solutions and ecosystem-based approaches”.
“Restoration and protection of mangroves, coral reefs, coastal wetlands, kelp forests and seagrass meadows can strengthen resilience while providing ecosystem services and co-benefits,” it says.
It also makes some sensible points about planning and development in coastal areas.
There is something for Ireland to learn from this, the tendency of developers being to trumpet the virtues of coastal living as all sea views and no storms while too often public representatives make zoning decisions based on what has not happened to date rather that what is projected to occur.
“We recognise the need to integrate sea-level-rise projections into the planning, design, implementation and maintenance of critical coastal infrastructure to ensure their resilience,” the declaration states.
It includes as critical coastal infrastructure, “ports, energy, transport, water systems, healthcare facilities, telecommunications, digital infrastructure, and coastal protection measures including land reclamation and elevation”.
[ Ireland’s coastline – erosion in Wexford: ‘There’s nobody protecting my land for me’ Opens in new window ]
But not everything that will be stolen by the sea is visible or tangible.
For the past two years, negotiators grappled with the existential question of whether a country can exist as a legal entity if it doesn’t have physical form and its people have had to leave.
They concluded, and the declaration backs this, that it can and, in most cases, should.
“Once a State is established, the disappearance of one of its constituent elements would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood,” it says.
“We affirm the presumption in favour of continued statehood and in this respect we underscore the continuity of statehood in the face of sea level rise, as well as sovereignty, sovereign rights and responsibilities, and membership of the United Nations of such states, consistent with international law.
“We call for international support for states facing land territory changes due to sea level rise to continue to maintain institutional functions.”
Marine territories will also be respected even if the country they once surrounded, or part of it, is gone.
“Once established in accordance with UNCLOS (the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Seas), we affirm that states can accordingly maintain their maritime zones in the face of physical changes resulting from sea level rise,” the declaration says.
“We encourage the provision of relevant technical support to assist states to finalise their baselines under UNCLOS.”
[ ‘Powerful storms are more common’: Threat of rising sea levels and coast erosion in Galway Opens in new window ]
Beyond territory, infrastructure and legal status are the characteristics that make a country unique and the declaration addresses these too.
“Sea level rise impacts culture and cultural heritage, including the loss of access to physical sites, living heritage, traditional lands, burial grounds, underwater cultural heritage, archaeological and sacred sites, and culturally significant coastal landscapes,” it says.
“Protection, preservation and documentation of cultural heritage is a priority, including through digitisation.”
This is a project Tuvalu has already embarked upon, with the aim of capturing, preserving and recreating the essence of island life, past and present, for when it has no physical future.
The project is only in its infancy and needs international help – finance and expertise.
Ireland may be able to assist. We certainly have a big enough, brash enough IT sector to pitch in on both fronts.
We will know more when the formalities of the Transition Away Conference are finalised how prominently the quest features on the agenda.
Tuvalu may end up assisting Ireland too over the course of the partnership between the two countries, by prompting some reassessment of attitudes.
The Climate Change Advisory Council warned last week, for the umpteenth time, that Ireland is not taking sufficiently seriously the coastal change we are seeing with climate change – and will see much more of.
[ Flood map: See the Irish coastline areas at ‘very high’ risk from flooding, erosion or sea level rise Opens in new window ]
Low-lying areas will be lost to sea level rise, higher coastal lands will crumble to worsening erosion and large, often densely populated, areas will be subject to more severe, more frequent storm surges and flooding.
Ireland still has time to prepare for much of this. By contrast, Tuvalu’s Digital Nation website opens with the statement: “Rising sea levels will swallow Tuvalu in a matter of decades.”
It’s a startling forecast that puts the UN declaration and the Transition Away Conference pledges in context. At the moment, they are just words on digital paper but making their commitments real might just allow Tuvalu to exist as more than a digital memory.

title: Five homes on view this week in Dublin from €275,000
description: New to the market in Foxrock, Dundrum, Sandymount, Howth and Dublin city centre
content:
Located in the much sought-after south Dublin suburb of Foxrock , this well-maintained detached three-bedroom house of 94sq m (1,012sq ft) features an open-plan kitchen/ breakfastroom, diningroom and a large livingroom. The house has a private rear garden, landscaped front garden with off-street parking, and is convenient to a number of schools including Loreto College Foxrock, Clonkeen College CBS, Blackrock College, and Hollypark and St Brigid’s primary schools. The N11 and M50 motorway are easily accessible. Ber C2.
Set on the ground floor of a small and well-established development just off Stoney Road in Dundrum , this two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment of 79sq m (850sq ft) comes for sale in turnkey condition and features wooden floors, a stone fireplace with coal-effect fire, built-in wardrobes and en suite bathroom in the main bedroom, and a fully equipped kitchen. The apartment has a designated underground car-parking space with remote-control access. Ber C.
On view: By appointment at Hunters Estate Agent
Situated within a quiet courtyard setting to the rear of the Park Court scheme just off Park Avenue in Sandymount , this two-bedroom townhouse (75sq m/807sq ft) comprises a large livingroom, kitchen, lounge/diningroom and two large double bedrooms. There is ample car parking within the development and a communal, south-facing rear garden. Park Court is located within a short walk of Sandymount village and Sandymount Strand and 3.5km from Dublin city centre. Ber C3.

The property, which has been extended, renovated and modernised, extends to 110sq m (1,184sq ft) and comes with gas-fired central heating and double-glazed windows. There is an open-plan kitchen and diningroom, bedroom and livingroom on the ground floor, and two bedrooms, a study and family shower room upstairs. On view: By appointment at Kelly Bradshaw

title: Modernised Stoneybatter Edwardian with south-facing garden
description: Aughrim Street four-bed walking distance from amenities and close to the city
content:
There’s a lot to be said for a recently renovated home, especially when the cost of building materials and labour is on the rise. The fact that 48 Aughrim Street in Stoneybatter had already been modernised was what appealed to the current owners when they bought it three years ago.
In fact, the owner and her husband, who have two children, acquired the keys on the day they had their first child in September 2023.
Built in 1901, the three-bedroom Edwardian terraced house had formerly been the parochial house for the Church of the Holy Family on Aughrim Street and was renovated in 2015. “It had a B Ber rating, double-glazed windows and had been rewired, but it still had many of the classical elements, too, which we liked,” says one of the owners.
The window shutters are original, there’s cornicing on the ceilings of the two downstairs reception rooms and the upstairs floorboards are original.
A long narrow hallway with an elegant archway has a door leading to a comfortable sittingroom, which has white walls that act as backdrop for their art collection. It connects to another equally comfortable reception room. Both have high ceilings and wood-burning stoves.
The kitchen at the back has modern units in light grey and features a section of the original wall with exposed brickwork. It gives an earthy quality to the pale grey walls.
They’ve made only made minor changes to the interior, such as to their daughter’s bedroom. Here they painted the floorboards a pretty pillarbox red and applied the same paint halfway up the wall, finishing the other half in red and blue Mickey Mouse patterned wallpaper.
They also created an outdoor utility area with a roof that houses their appliances.
The south-facing garden at the back has a patio, a lawn and a small shed. It’s flanked by the original walls on both sides, and backs on to an apartment complex, which is mostly hidden by a long wall on one side.
The house is set back from Aughrim Street and has on-street parking. Stoneybatter is well served for amenities and has a strong sense of community.
The couple are selling the house and moving to Co Meath due to family commitments, but they’re doing so reluctantly. “We love Stoneybatter and we love the house. We wish we could stay.” Number 48 Aughrim Street, extending to 140sq m (1,507sq ft) with a B Ber, is now for sale through Sherry FitzGerald seeking €920,000.

title: Fine four-bed with a high-end finish in Blackrock
description: Large detached house has been fully refurbished and upgraded by current owners
content:
Number 65 Avoca Park is in a quiet residential area just off Avoca Avenue in Blackrock in south Dublin . It’s a four-bedroom detached house that has been totally transformed by its owners into a bright, efficient home with superb contemporary features, high-end finishes and an eye for comfort and luxury.
There is evidence everywhere of high-quality design, from the Kube kitchen with floor-to-ceiling cabinetry, heat-resistant Dekton worktops and splashback and top-end appliances to the family bathroom with porcelain tiling, underfloor heating and premium sanitary ware. The house is fitted with contemporary triple-glazed Carlson windows and NorDan doors, and the kitchen and bathrooms have underfloor heating.
Number 65 Avoca Park measures 179sq m (1,927sq ft), with a B Ber rating, and is on sale through DNG asking €1.725 million.
The owners removed some inner doorways and walls to open out the downstairs, but also closed up one doorway to create a cosy family area beside the kitchen/diningroom. Where there used to be a porch there is now a tiled entrance area leading to a hallway laid in a combination of herringbone and plank laminate flooring. Off the hall is a guest toilet with decorative tiling and Villeroy & Boch sanitary ware with Grohe fittings, and there’s storage underneath the contemporary solid oak and black metal staircase.
A large double opening leads into a large livingroom with bay window looking out to the front, a feature integrated LED fireplace and a bespoke media wall. Opposite the livingroom, also looking out to the front, is a second reception room with floor-to-ceiling wardrobes. It’s in use as a home office but can also be a kids’ playroom, study or fifth bedroom.
The open-plan kitchen/dining/familyroom looks out to the back garden, with triple-glazed rooflights and a sliding garden door in the dining area. What the owners did here was remove an old-fashioned conservatory jutting out from the back and incorporate the area as part of the open-plan room, adding an insulated roof. Now it’s a wide, light-filled dining area that beautifully complements the Kube kitchen next to it, and links smoothly to the cosy familyroom, which has a large triple-glazed window looking out the back garden.
The kitchen is designed to cater to the owners’ passion for cooking, with no shortage of Dekton work surfaces made by Cosentino, premium appliances by Bosch and Siemens, and a Falmec extractor fan that runs quietly and efficiently, allowing the chef to chat with their guests while cooking up a storm. Adjoining the kitchen is a very well-equipped utility room, with washing machine and overflow fridge and a hidden treasure: a bespoke larder with floor-to-ceiling storage and shelving.
Also here is the central distribution hub for the Cat 6 Ethernet cabling that the forward-thinking owners installed throughout the house. There is access to a wide side passage via a triple-glazed composite door.
Upstairs, the landing has engineered oak flooring, and the four bedrooms – two doubles and two singles – have bespoke floor-to-ceiling fitted wardrobes. The main bedroom, looking out though a bay window to the front, has automatic internal lighting and remote-controlled blinds. It has a beautifully tiled en suite with a vanity unit by Falper and an illuminated mirror by Villeroy & Boch.
The family bathroom has luxurious porcelain tiling, underfloor heating below and a skylight above.
Above the landing is an extra-large attic hatch with a solid-wood integrated ladder. The attic is floored and fitted with shelving, offering even more storage in a house where you’ll never have to worry about where to put away your stuff.
The low-maintenance back garden is west-facing and is laid with granite paving and an artificial lawn, and surrounded by solid timber fencing and raised plant beds. Atmospheric lighting turns the garden into a great space for outdoor entertaining, and there’s a large bespoke shed for storing all your garden furniture for the winter. To the front is parking for two cars on a granite-paved driveway. A secure pin-controlled iron and composite side gate opens into a wide side passage to the back, with storage for bikes and bins.
Avoca Park is directly behind the scenic Carysfort Park, a popular place for Blackrock locals to stroll. Blackrock village and the busy Frascati and Blackrock shopping centres are close by, while Dart and bus services are within easy reach. Nearby schools include Carysfort National School, Willow Park, Blackrock College, Booterstown National School, All Saints’ National School and Sion Hill.

title: Will AI kill our rosy jobs growth forecasts?
description: Department of Finance draws attention ‘to risks to employment prospects from AI over the medium-term’
content:
Among the avalanche of figures in his Budget 2027 speech, Minister for Finance Simon Harris held out the prospect of 53,000 jobs being created next year, practically 1,000 every week.
“There are now over 2.8 million people working in Ireland, the highest level since records began. We have had four and a half years of full employment, the longest stretch ever,” Harris noted.
To emphasise the intensity of growth this year and next, the Department of Finance budget documents suggest the number of jobs might well increase by 74,000 to the end of 2027 from the second quarter of this year.
Take note. The longer the forecast the more fallible. But the department figure suggests the number of jobs might yet come close to three million by 2030 (2.98 million). This assumes the employment rate averages around 68.5 per cent in the next few years. The 2026 estimate is 68.2 per cent.
Of course, there are always risks to these forecasts. After all, there is no avoiding glaring risks from heavy multinational investment and supersized corporation tax revenues. The department draws attention “to risks to employment prospects from AI over the medium-term”.
Even the current picture is cloudy, with budget documents saying “mixed signals” from data point to a degree of uncertainty in the underlying pace of job growth.
For one thing, administrative payroll figures suggest “solid” job growth: the number of payrolled workers rose by 2.5 per cent in the first half of 2026. For another, labour force survey data suggest a more “subdued” growth rate, with employment rising only by 0.4 per cent in the same period.
Which is it? The department finds income tax receipts and strong consumer spending are “more closely aligned with the [stronger] payroll data”.
Still, the “decoupling” of data complicates the calibration of employment forecasts. Yes, the current figures are good. But uncertainty remains elevated.

title: Elegant Belgrave Square home in Rathmines
description: Four-bed home filled with interesting architectural features and beautifully proportioned rooms
content:
Filled with interesting architectural features and beautifully proportioned rooms, 15 Belgrave Square presents to the market with Sherry Fitzgerald with an asking price of €2.595 million.
Overlooking the square from its eastern side, the 247sq m (2658sq ft) two-storey-over-basement property is in great condition, having been previously renovated when the current owner, who is downsizing, bought it in 2013. She then proceeded to renovate further, particularly on the garden level, where she added a new kitchen.
Its layout and proportions should prove ideal for a family seeking a turnkey home in the area, with four bedrooms and three bathrooms. The entrance hall is magnificent, with elaborate original cornicing, a dramatic feature light, a carved lion on the lower stair banister and an archway leading into the reception rooms.
The drawingroom lies to the front of the house and has two separate doors into it; like the doors throughout this level, they are rosewood, heavy and elegant. Elaborately carved pediments top the doors; one of the reasons the owner fell for the house was the recurring carved plasterwork. A pair of 12-pane sash windows overlook the square. A marble fireplace is original and has a brass inset and a simple slate hearth.
Beyond the drawingroom lies a diningroom, also with a fireplace, and it serves as another sittingroom, with a window overlooking the garden. Back in the hall is a family bathroom on the return and a doorway with iron steps below it that leads to the garden.
On another return on the way to the first floor is a generous bedroom that overlooks the garden. On the first floor are two bedrooms and a small bathroom at the rear. The main bedroom has two large windows, and both bedrooms at this level have pretty cast-iron fireplaces.
On the basement level, the kitchen, by Neptune, has a vast centre island with a Corian worktop that the owner loved working at. The rest of the kitchen features a five-ring gas hob, a pantry unit and a quirky and chic combination of stainless steel counters and French-style country wall units.
The utility is equally well fitted out, with more stainless steel shelves. There’s a guest loo at this level off the hallway, and a small bedroom that could make a great home office. Finally, leading off the kitchen and opening on to the back garden via French doors is a living area with a very fine and intricate cast-iron fireplace.
The back garden of this property is bound to be one of its key selling points and is quite something. It is long, bounded by granite walls and studded with mature sycamore trees that add character and shade. At the back of the house are two patio areas, one of which is perfectly positioned to capture the morning sun for outdoor breakfasts.
Extending to more than 170ft, there is an old stone shed, vegetable beds, and at its end a fully self-contained garden room that is plumbed and electrified, so ready to be used as a home office or garden studio.
The owner has loved living here and enjoyed walking her dog in Belgrave Park and having the amenities of both Rathmines and Ranelagh so close at hand. Nearby sporting facilities include Fitzwilliam Lawn Tennis Club, David Lloyd and Dartry fitness clubs and Milltown Golf Club. There are nearby Luas stops at Beechwood and Ranelagh and a number of schools nearby.

title: Russell T Davies: ‘I keep a kitchen knife by the front door’
description: Queer as Folk writer and Doctor Who showrunner has written a memoir about his career. It’s ‘a nice moment to take stock’, he says
content:
Russell T Davies keeps a kitchen knife by his front door at his home in Swansea. The Welsh screenwriter and television showrunner doesn’t want to go into detail, but there have been “a couple of instances” where people have worked out his address, and though in one case it was someone who wanted to give him a Doctor Who script, other things have happened to alarm him as a gay man in the public eye.
“I laugh at myself for having a knife by the front door. I would probably just stab myself and drop it and be a complete idiot. But it just psychologically made me think, right, I could be ready for trouble at my front door. The point is I don’t think trouble at my front door is impossible now.”
Davies reveals these fears in The Queerest of Folk, a memoir of his five-decade television career written with Boyd Hilton, a journalist who voiced support for Queer as Folk at the Channel 4 drama’s feverish press launch in 1999. With his second stint overseeing Doctor Who now over and his searing state-of-the-nation drama Tip Toe arriving earlier this year, it seemed “a nice moment to take stock” of his time in the industry he loves.
Davies is speaking from his other home, in Manchester, where a small Dalek is visible on the bookshelves behind him. He didn’t want to give the memoir a “Doctor Who-ey” title because he thought it was “quite important to make it more adult in feel”, so he opted for a spin on the “fine old northern phrase” he employed for his career breakthrough. “I’ve got to say, it was Manchester Pride this weekend, and I went out on those streets for three days running, and I am not the queerest of folk!”
Davies is funny, but he didn’t always know how to be funny in drama. He got his start in television as an assistant producer on the BBC children’s magazine show Why Don’t You? before moving into children’s dramas and soap operas. When Granada, the Manchester-based ITV franchise holder, recruited him to write a 1920s period drama called The Grand, he devised a string of dark storylines about postwar trauma, domestic abuse and revenge murders.
His “entire writing life” changed course when his friend Sally Watson said, “over a cheese sandwich or something”, that he was a laugh, so why didn’t he write a laugh? “I believed that drama equalled tragedy. That was my mistake. They’re two very different things,” he says.
Queer as Folk, which aired when I was a student, was a laugh, but it was, of course, more than that. As “the first gay drama” on television – a stark sentence to read now – it was a daring statement. Davies says he was lucky to be on “the crest of a wave”. Gay characters had been added to Coronation Street, EastEnders, Byker Grove and Grange Hill, while the BBC sitcom Gimme Gimme Gimme was just starting and ITV’s Bad Girls, “with its fantastic lesbian stories”, was on its way.
Cynical insiders expected Queer as Folk would be “boring and worthy”, but the series, set in the gay clubs of Manchester’s Canal Street, was confident and new. It featured a controversial age gap – one character, Nathan, was 15, reflecting what Davies was seeing on Canal Street at the time – and sex scenes that were rendered more explosively abrupt in the edit by a Channel 4 higher-up’s request for “less of that”.
Davies remains proud of it all, and says his heart was lifted when Jacob Tierney, who adapted Rachel Reid’s novels into last year’s smash-hit gay ice-hockey romance Heated Rivalry, wrote to him to say he was inspired by Queer as Folk. The Canadian series is “a lovely, sexy, successful show”, while his own work remains “shocking to this day”, he thinks. “The radicalness of it and the explicitness of it still stands up. Actually, everything’s calmed down slightly now, and no one goes as far as we did.”
He recalls the volatile atmosphere at the launch. “The straight journalists were appalled by what they’d seen, and the gay journalists were appalled by what they’d seen, because we didn’t do enough to represent HIV or Aids or safe sex, and we had people taking drugs and having sex promiscuously. They were furious.”
But Davies understands that people will always have their own ideas of what a show should be. “I’m not just a writer, I’m a viewer as well. I need to be capable of sitting down and watching a drama and going, ‘Oh, I don’t like that gay man,’ ‘I don’t like that lesbian,’ or ‘I don’t like that version of trans representation: I think that’s wrong.’”
It was Nicola Shindler, his long-term collaborator and the founder of the production companies Red and Quay Street Productions, who encouraged him to become a showrunner before that term was in common usage in the UK. From Queer as Folk onwards he tended to be part of the casting, the shoot, the edit, the music, “everything”, though he has “a slight regret” that he never directed, and thinks, at 63, that he’s too old to do it now.
Davies’ list of writing credits includes some of the best and cleverest television of the past 30 years, from Bob & Rose (2001) and The Second Coming (2003) to Years and Years (2019) and It’s a Sin (2021). A Davies script is, by turn, emotional, thrilling, hilarious, unnerving, joyful and incendiary, and it will often showcase his penchant for a big speech – Helena Bonham Carter has a brilliant monologue in Nolly (2023), his drama about the Crossroads star Noele Gordon being sacked by angry male executives, while Paul Rhys delivers a spellbinding one in Tip Toe.
“Yes, I love my speeches. Nicola always says, ‘Oh, you’re writing speeches again.’ It’s probably how I talk. I probably don’t let anyone else get a word in edgeways,” he says. “But also I like being on the nose about things. People get very timid in drama.”
No one queries big speeches in theatre, he points out. “It’s, like, why is television not allowed that art form? I love it.”
Davies has done “an awful lot of shows” that didn’t work, but he doesn’t dwell on the disappointments too much. “Every show that didn’t work I wish had worked, but then you love all your children. You don’t love the ones that fail their exams less.”
He tends to move on from shows but not from people. Being hired by lofty Old Etonians to write A Very English Scandal (2018), his entertaining account of a bizarre 1970s scandal involving the former Liberal Party leader Jeremy Thorpe, wasn’t an entirely comfortable process, but when he works with trusted friends, they share a shorthand. He would “rather die than deliver a bad script” to Shindler.
“The day will come when she phones up and says, ‘Sorry, I really don’t think this works.’ Oh my God, I’ll die. I’ll die. Whereas if it was a complete stranger, or if it was those Old Etonians, who I didn’t like at all, I would just think, ‘Oh, you’re idiots.’”
A Very English Scandal coincided with a period when Davies was caring for his husband, Andrew Smith, who was diagnosed with an aggressive brain tumour in 2011. Working on “this mad old tale from 1979” did him good, but as Smith’s health worsened, Davies increasingly stayed at home.
A low career ebb came in 2017 when he was writing both Years and Years – a dystopian thriller pitched to the BBC the morning after Donald Trump was elected – and the devastating 1980s Aids drama It’s a Sin. He had wanted to do both shows for ages, but it seemed no broadcaster was in the market.
“It was the same time that my husband was very ill with brain cancer, and it was an odd moment. I remember standing in my kitchen at Christmas, wondering if that was it. I’m a constant storyteller, so maybe I’ve exaggerated, maybe it was October.
“But in my mind it was Christmas and the wind was whistling, and the snowflakes were falling, and I was like the Little Match Girl. To have two big ideas like that turned down, it made me think, ‘Oh, maybe you’ve had your time.’”
He rallied. The BBC greenlit Years and Years after a rewrite, and the final episode is dedicated to Smith, who died in 2018. It’s a Sin eventually found a home on Channel 4, but Davies thinks the BBC should have commissioned this piece of history – instead, one of its executives asked if he knew Elton John and pondered whether it would be better as a musical. “At that moment, you very clearly think, ‘I don’t want to work with you.’”
The chapter in Davies’ memoir on Disney’s short-lived backing of Doctor Who contains illuminating nuggets about how little it understood the show. A whole season’s worth of scripts remain unmade following the streamer’s exit from the series, which the BBC has now put out to tender.
I declare my lifelong Doctor Who fandom and say I try not to get involved in the online discourse. “It’s a pit you might never get out of,” Davies says, laughing. “If I was to go into that discourse, I’d just vanish!”
Episodes such as Turn Left, Midnight and 73 Yards rank among his finest hours of television, but is it simply being the person to spearhead the revival of Doctor Who in 2005 that he’s most proud of when it comes to the BBC’s science-fiction flagship?
“I think it’s probably the Daleks, actually. Everyone lined up to say the Daleks won’t work,” Davies says. He was under pressure to “completely reinvent” the villains and turn them into “modern-day CGI droids”, but he insisted on using the original 1960s mouldings, paying private collectors to obtain them. It felt “like such a victory” when their “little darling” Daleks became the top-selling toy in Britain soon after.
The BBC-Disney era of Doctor Who was “expensive”, but most of his shows have had “very ordinary budgets”, and Channel 4’s Tip Toe was cheap, he says. This was by design. Tip Toe “was so opinionated about Trump, the rise of the radical right and populism” that they were sure they wouldn’t get any American money for it anyway.
The same fractious political climate that prompted Davies to install a kitchen knife by his front door is explored in this five-parter, which deals with how “the porous wall between our online lives and our real lives is becoming more and more breakable”.
It begins by showing the strung-up body of Leo, a gay man played by Alan Cumming , in a flash-forward.
“It’s a tough piece of work,” he says. He has friends who have never watched the final episode, which depicts the lead-up to Leo’s horrific murder with sickening tension and escalating brutality. But he felt he had to write it. “I was looking at the world and thinking, ‘This is where we’re heading.’”
Davies is delighted that Tip Toe had a “nice and noisy” reception. As for his public profile, there are upsides. It means he can have “a go on that big spinning thing” on the BBC gameshow The Wheel, which he loves. And when writers “pop up everywhere”, it tells children that it’s not a job done by “remote, impossible people” but something they can do too.
In the book, he writes that Oliver Cole, his boyfriend of a year, recently persuaded him to go on his first holiday in 14 years. Indeed, British tabloids now report on Davies’ holidays with the 27-year-old – that’s “very, very strange” – but he takes the view that it will be forgotten about tomorrow. “I said to Oliver, there might be 500 comments underneath, but that’s all, out of a population of 60 million. It’s nothing.”
He’s not ill, and he’s not retiring, Davies says. Writing is the kind of job he can’t stop. Stories, characters, lines of dialogue follow him around the house, and his imagination is populated by people from dramas that don’t yet exist. “I think I’ll die without getting to write them all,” he says. “Which is fine. I’m glad to have that big storehouse of ideas burning away.”
The Queerest of Folk: A Life in Television, by Russell T Davies, is published by Transworld

title: Patrick Freyne: In The Real Rooneys on Disney+, everything is white. The rich do not fear stains
description: Wayne’s role is to sit near Coleen, looking confused. Her role is to sit near Wayne, looking disappointed
content:
T here’s trouble down at the Instagram meme factory. It’s a new age of John Osborne-style kitchen-sink dramas, but now they’re TV documentaries, starring the richest people who ever lived, who want to show us the bleakly luxurious mundanity of their day-to-day lives.
These new gilded-age tycoons bicker before the cameras. They roll their eyes when their children “interrupt” a shot. (Their domestic staff do not appear on-screen, but I imagine they are bustling about nearby.) They have intimate moments together, just casual instances of connection between them and their camera crews and the people of Britain, Ireland and the world. Sometimes they cry. But their tears are exclusive and expensive, like frankincense or myrrh.
A new rich-person documentary just dropped on Disney+ : The Real Rooneys. The Beckhams were the patients zero of the celebumentary. Now the infection has broken containment, and the Rooneys have come spluttering and coughing across the inside of our tellies, like a latter-day Pob.
The message is always the same: “We’re just regular folks like the rest of you pigs. Do we not also struggle to get our children to school on time? Do we not also fail to work the coffee machine? Does our husband Wayne Rooney not also test our last nerve? Do we not also drive dune buggies around the grounds of our mansion? Do we not also negotiate brand deals with Primark? Do we not also film advertisements for the rapacious gambling industry that has destroyed the lives of so many? Buy our stuff. When the revolution comes, remember we entertained you.”
Who are the Rooneys? Wayne once made his living hoofing an inflated orb into a suspended mesh while a field of large millionaires tried to stop him. This arcane and odd behaviour is a big industry. It’s the type of phenomenon that occurs when a species evolves beyond reason, has no natural predators and must manufacture scarcity to make things interesting.
In keeping with the tropes of great northern drama, Wayne has lost his job as a sportsfolk herdsman (coach?) and now his wife, Coleen , must seek work in the rag trade (she does a Primark deal) in order to fund the data-centre-sized house in which they live.
So tragic is their situation that they must also put their children to work in the nepo-baby industrial complex, goofing and girning for Disney’s hungry cameras. Observe these tot tycoons and consider that they are already much richer than you.
Oh, yes, how we all delight in the antics of other people’s children. Take my nephews, for example. Seriously, take my nephews.
Nonetheless, Coleen aims to become an avatar of the Everywoman. Her name means, literally, Girl, which indicates that this is a work of symbolism akin to The Pilgrim’s Progress or Peppa Pig or this week’s budget speeches.
Thanks to expensive skincare, Coleen’s face is a blank page on to which the viewers get to write their own story. She was once the Wag – wife and girlfriend – of Wayne, but she has, in recent years, eclipsed his fame, thanks to her high-profile defence against another Wag who unsuccessfully sued her for libel.
To be honest, I’m not sure I’ll be telling generations unborn about Wagatha Christie . It felt important at the time, but since then there have been fires all over Europe, as well as several wars, and we’ve learned how to make robots that want to kill us.
Anyway, Wayne’s role now is to sit near Coleen, looking confused. Her role is to sit near Wayne, looking disappointed. At times Coleen is quite angry with Wayne. She is a Waging bull, if you will.
But Wayne isn’t merely a bestubbled Cocomelon character, an unravelled Mr Bump or a deregulated Mitchell brother. He is also an out-to-pasture footballist who will sleep until death on a pile of gold and glory. And he has a persistent podcast, but I think there’s a cream you can get for that.
The reality is that Coleen is disappointed, I think, not with Wayne but with the emptiness of material success and the inevitability of the grave. It’s etched in the gleaming white halls of her echoing mansion, and it was definitely in the pitch deck for this show.
“This is ultimately a show about death,” I imagine one TV executive saying to another before flicking to a slide of burning European forests and a photograph of Victoria Beckham at a tasteful kitchen island.
Between each segment, the Rooneys sit in colour-co-ordinated clothing in vast livingrooms that look very like hotel lobbies and speak directly to camera in a slightly stilted fashion, as if they’re preparing a deposition in the wake of a devastating product failure.
[ Deepfake Ireland on Virgin Media One: Gráinne Seoige’s distress in this grim film is palpable Opens in new window ]
Everything is white. The rich do not fear stains like the rest of us. There is also an upsetting number of cushions on their huge couch, and they appear to be multiplying. Each time we come back, there are more cushions.
Does nobody else see all the cushions? Perhaps they are multiplying according to the principles of compound interest. Or is it possible this is an “elevated” horror movie and, by the end of it all, the Rooneys will have suffocated in grotesque, overcushioned luxury?
That’s a metaphor, by the way. Those of you with arts degrees will have noticed. Those of you without arts degrees are too busy having jobs, probably.
I was concerned watching the new series of Slow Horses on Apple TV to discover that the dysfunctional MI5 unit at the core of the series is not only being targeted by unknown forces, but has also been deleted from the personnel files of their employer.
As a member of The Irish Times’ equivalent of Slow Horses (the features department), one who has expensive tastes in corduroy trousers and fancy notebooks, this is terrifying.
In the new series, scented spy master Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman), sullen sourpuss River Cartwright (Jack Lowden) and the rest must evade their would-be assassins and figure out what’s going on.
One of the things I really like about Slow Horses, apart from all the things I have written about several times before (the acting, writing, pacing and humour), is the way everything in it takes place in the grey liminal spaces of urban England.
In the same way that the scenery of Cornwall was another “character” in Poldark, the drab social-democratic brutalism of the postwar consensus is a character in Slow Horses.
These are, in fact, the urban vistas the Rooneys escaped in order to live in gilded rural isolation. In fact, if you watch both shows at the same time, you gain a shattering insight into the British mind. Is that a thing you’d like to have?
[ Small Prophets on Apple TV: A new genre that is funny, fantastical and heartbreakingly tender Opens in new window ]

title: The Uprising review: Paul Greengrass’s touch seems to have left him
description: There are several clumsy moments in this puzzling take on the Peasants’ Revolt
content:
This maggoty medieval drama has, to this point, gained most notoriety for a bizarre (and, to be fair, brief) attempt by US distributors to tie its story in with that of Robin Hood.
To clarify, there is no mention whatsoever of that durable hero in Paul Greengrass ’s puzzling take on the Peasants’ Revolt. (The UK distributors noted that marketing materials “referencing Robin Hood are not issued or approved by us”.)
If you scrunch up your eyes in later stages you get some sense of what the American PR folk were getting at. But this is a grumpy, mud-encrusted affair with fewer merrie men – or women, for that matter – than you would expect to encounter at a pet’s cremation.
It is 1381 and, as the Black Death retreats, the council of Richard II, still a boy king, elects to increase taxes on a denuded population. You get a sense of where Greengrass is going here when the tax collectors manually and publicly check the genitals of female citizens to determine if they are of adult age. It feels like the sort of detail nobody would make up. One still wonders if it belongs in such a gung-ho entertainment.
A lone farmer named only Ploughman (Andrew Garfield), who has lost his wife and children to the plague, gets caught up in an affray with the tax collectors that triggers wider rebellions throughout the land.
Enter Cosmo Jarvis, well cast as the storied rebel leader Wat Tyler, and Jamie Bell, equally solid as the dissident cleric John Ball. It is eventually decided the rebels will march to London and petition the king for reforms. It goes well. Then it goes badly.
Greengrass, famously kinetic director of United 93 and the Bourne films, also takes on sole writing duties, with mixed results. The film makes a point of clarifying that Tyler, who fought for England in the Hundred Years War, was no sort of republican. “The traitors have stolen our king!” the rebels (perhaps naively) chant. “Free the king!”
Some odd contemporary parallels are run up the flagpole. One can sense murmurs of Occupy Wall Street in the angry protests.
More puzzling is an establishment figure’s brief description of the peasants – echoing a perceived faux pas by Hillary Clinton in 2016 – as “these deplorables”. Wait? Is the film really comparing a formative moment of English radicalism with the disturbances in Washington on January 6th, 2021?
Probably not. This feels more like one of several careless moments in a film that lacks discipline throughout. There is no denying the picture is largely pro-peasant. Though the revolt’s leaders may occasionally seem misguided, the king and his court cackle and hiss as if auditioning for baddies in a reboot of Blackadder. Flavours of that show are stronger still among the dissenters, many of whom are just a few turnips short of a Baldrick.
The tip-top cast works hard throughout. Garfield is characteristically squash-faced as an Everyman – his mononym references the contemporaneous narrative poem Piers Plowman – who carries the suffering of a nation on two shoulders.
Jarvis and Bell have voices that can be heard over any din. Thomasin McKenzie adds a female perspective. The indestructibly charismatic Irish actor Stanley Townsend adds growling menace as the king’s chief justice.
None, however, can overcome a script that generates neither human drama nor political nuance. Worse still, Greengrass’s famous touch for clattering, propulsive violence seems to have temporarily left him.
Giving in occasionally to lazy slow motion before reverting to juddering Grasserama, the battle sequences feel as perfunctory as re-enactments from mid-budget history programmes on the telly.
One more thing. The least said about the idiotic epilogue the soonest mended and the smallest amount spoiled.

title: Demon Hunter: Time 2 Kill review – This scrappy film’s Irish director is as plucky as her heroine
description: Zoe Kavanagh has fashioned an imaginative supernatural franchise from a microbudget
content:
Zoe Kavanagh’s scrappy indie sequel to Taryn Barker: Demon Hunter veers away from the vengeful gothica of the 2017 original. The go-for-broke camp is more than a sequel: this relentless transatlantic follow-up pitches the titular Nimrod against a satanic chief executive with a temporal jump that leaves Taryn stranded in a 1980s slasher movie.
The resulting old-school corpse pile-up couldn’t look less than the winking, academic concerns of Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma .
The Irish director, who has been exploring the nexus between horror tropes and first-person gaming long before Backrooms went mainstream, somehow gets away with the clutter.
Niamh Hogan, a former stunt performer on Vikings and a fifth dan in Shotokan karate, returns with a formidable back kick as Taryn Barker, a demon hunter unspooling a vast demonic conspiracy. The chief executive standing in her way is Elysia Cronika (Nightmare of Elm Street’s Lisa Wilcox), who has a sideline in satanic rituals, vampires and lizard people.
When Taryn acquires a piece of the Necrox, a powerful ancient relic, Elysia magically deposits her in Camp Beaver, a mid-1980s summer resort where a masked killer is already making merry with the nubile young visitors.
Hogan’s experience as an (unbeaten) international martial artist, coupled with old-school gore, gives Demon Hunter: Time 2 Kill a pleasingly physical presence. Kavanagh, who often uses claustrophobic walk-and-slash close-ups, pulls back to allow Hogan’s choreography to shine.
The computer-generated demons and an interdimensional interlude recall the retro villains and screensaver backdrops of Mighty Morphin Power Rangers.
Eschewing the gloom of The Crow for the giddiness of Buffy the Vampire Slayer, this gleefully gory film recalls the Evil Dead sequence before that franchise lost its sense of humour and its mojo.
The 1980s material settles into a scuffed slasher groove, while Taryn’s contemporary cohort, including Kevin O’Malley’s tech support and Angel Nichole Bradford’s Nancy Drew-like investigator, throw welcome Scooby-Doo shapes.
For all the high kicks, genre pleasures and scrappy FX, the film-maker is the real star for her determination to make an imaginative supernatural franchise from a microbudget.
Working alongside her equally dogged producer, Leeona Duff, Kavanagh – who has scraped together funds by making music videos for The Birthday Massacre and Clan of Xymox, soft-drink commercials and pet-training videos in Sweden – is every bit as plucky as her slayeress heroine.

title: We want to give our nephew €10,000 – will he have to pay tax?
description: The level of capital acquisitions tax depends on the relationship between the beneficiary and the person making the gift
content:
Q: My husband and his three siblings would like to give a gift of up to €10,000 in total to a nephew whose dad, their brother, died shortly after the boy’s birth.
What would be the tax situation for their nephew if they do this?
A: These four siblings want to do a lovely thing. Their brother died some years ago, shortly after his son was born. The aunts and uncles subsequently lost touch with their nephew, but happily they have now reconnected with him.
Having come into a legacy sum, the siblings would like to share some of it with their nephew. But what is the situation with such gifts – will their nephew face a tax bill?
Capital acquisitions tax (CAT), sometimes referred to as gift or inheritance tax, is a beneficiary tax. It’s payable whenever a beneficiary receives a gift or inheritance that exceeds their tax-free threshold amount.
What determines the level of CAT is the relationship between the beneficiary and the person making the gift or inheritance, says solicitor Matthew Johnston, managing partner at Nooney & Dowdall Solicitors in Mullingar.
When a beneficiary receives a gift or inheritance, they can fall into one of three different tax-free threshold groups, depending on their relationship to the person giving the gift, says Johnston.
A child falls into the Group A threshold and can now inherit up to €420,000 tax free from a parent, a €20,000 increase announced as part of Budget 2027 .
A nephew or niece falls into the Group B threshold of close blood relatives, which also includes siblings, a grandparent, aunt and uncle. They can now receive a maximum gift or inheritance of €44,000 tax free from each other due to a change in this week’s budget.
[ Do I still owe tax if my mother’s house sold for less than expected? Opens in new window ]
Cousins, close friends, neighbours, carers or others all fall into a Group C threshold. The most they can receive tax free is now €22,000.
There is also the small gift exemption to consider. Anyone is entitled to give €3,000 per calendar year tax free to someone else. If a gift is more than €3,000, the first €3,000 is tax-exempt and the balance is deducted from the lifetime tax-free threshold they have in relation to the person giving the money.
With all of this in mind, it would be wise for the aunts and uncles here to give their nephew the €10,000 by way of four gifts of €2,500 each, says Johnston.
This way, the individual gifts fall below the allowable €3,000 small gift exemption.
“There will be absolutely no tax consequences for the nephew if they do that,” says Johnston.
It also means that, should any of his individual aunts or uncles want to give him a more substantial sum in future, their nephew’s €44,000 Group B tax-free threshold remains intact and can be availed of.
[ Still paying bank fees? It may be time to switch Opens in new window ]
“You are preserving the entirety of the nephew’s lifetime tax-free threshold from his aunts and uncles,” says Johnston.
Be sure to give the €10,000 as four individual gifts, he advises.
“If the aunts and uncles give it to one sibling and he transfers it to the nephew, it might look like that uncle gave the entire sum, rather than €2,500 coming from each individual,” says Johnston. “Get the nephew’s Iban and do four separate transfers.”
It would be wise to keep a record of the gift too, says Johnston.
This could be a simple email to their nephew from each aunt and uncle, explaining that the money is a gift, he says.
This record will be useful for the nephew too, showing that the money is indeed a gift and not potentially taxable income.
