title: EirGrid seeks feedback on offshore wind farm infrastructure
description: Public consultation focuses on new electricity infrastructure needed to connect Tonn Nua, located off the Waterford coast, with national grid
content:
EirGrid is engaged in the latest phase of public consultation for the Powering Up Offshore – South Coast programme, seeking feedback on emerging best performing options for the construction of the new transmission grid infrastructure required to bring electricity generated by offshore wind farms into Ireland’s national grid.
The consultation focuses on the new electricity infrastructure needed to connect Tonn Nua, the first maritime area detailed in Government’s South Coast Designated Maritime Area Plan for Offshore Renewable Energy.
Located off the Waterford coast, it is envisaged that wind farms in the Tonn Nua area, also known as Maritime Area A, will deliver approximately 900 megawatts of offshore renewable energy, enough to power almost one million homes and support Ireland’s longer-term climate and renewable energy ambitions.
“While EirGrid is not responsible for generating electricity or building wind farms, we are responsible for connecting electricity generation infrastructure, such as offshore and onshore wind farms, into our national electricity grid,” says EirGrid head of public engagement Sinéad Dooley.
The Powering Up Offshore – South Coast project will involve the construction of two offshore substation platforms located within Maritime Area A; offshore transmission cables connecting the offshore substations to landfall locations; new onshore substations; connections between landfalls and new onshore substations by underground cables; and loop-in connections to the existing electricity transmission network from the new substations by either underground cables or overhead lines.
The 12-week consultation, running until December 8th, presents potential landfall zones, offshore transmission cable corridors, offshore substation zones, grid connection subzones and onshore transmission cable route corridors in counties Cork and Wexford.
According to Dooley, the consultation is the fourth step in the organisation’s six-step approach to grid development, where options are brought forward for public consultation and stakeholder consideration. Feedback received through this consultation, alongside ongoing technical and environmental assessments, will help shape the next stage of project development.
“This consultation is an important milestone in the development of the Powering Up Offshore – South Coast programme,” she says. “The emerging best performing options we are presenting have been informed by extensive technical and environmental studies and engagement with key stakeholders including local communities and landowners. We have looked at all the constraints that need to be considered and put each of the options through a rigorous analysis. We now want to hear directly from communities and interested parties on these proposals.”
That community input is critically important, she emphasises. “You can’t underestimate the value of local intel. We have a team of liaison officers talking to stakeholders, explaining the project and the options, getting feedback and bringing it back into the process. The results of that engagement are every bit as important as the technical analysis. It is all put into the mix and plays a vital role in helping us make informed decisions and develop the best possible project.”
That local knowledge and input will assist at a practical level, she adds. “We have to deal with a lot of constraints in terms of narrow roads, special areas of conservation in the area and so on. We have built a very good reputation for working well with communities and listening to them. EirGrid is a State body and we are going to do things correctly. We are committed to looking after communities and the environment.”
That commitment has already been demonstrated in the region through the Celtic Interconnector project. “We are fortunate to have that example on the south coast. Communities have been kept informed throughout and have seen how we restore roads following cable installation and so on.”
A series of information events are being held in Cork, Waterford and Wexford over the coming weeks. “We encourage everyone with an interest in the project to attend these events and share their views. We want people to come along, see what we are proposing and make their voices heard to inform the progress of the project. If people can’t make it along to one of our open days or mobile information units, they can attend one of our online meetings on Zoom.”
The next step for the project following the consultation phase will see planning applications submitted to the Marine Area Regulatory Authority (Mara) and An Coimisiún Pleanála. “We have a bit of work to do before we get to that stage,” says Dooley. “There is a huge amount of work involved in getting a planning application ready for Mara. Hopefully we will get there next year. We have been very lucky this year in the progress we made on marine surveys with a lot of site investigation works done in collaboration with fishers in the area. From our perspective, protection of the environment on the land and at sea is very important.”
That extends to the Government’s climate action targets. “A key pillar of the Government’s strategy is to have 5GW of power coming from offshore wind in the coming years and we are working to keep this project moving forward to deliver the economic and sustainability benefits of offshore wind.”

title: Legal risks pile up for Altman as OpenAI uncovers dozens of hacks
description: Cybersecurity incidents involving company’s AI tools leave ChatGPT maker vulnerable to wave of lawsuits
content:
A spiralling legal crisis threatens to engulf OpenAI after its AI agents hacked dozens of companies and governments worldwide, with the prospect of a barrage of lawsuits marking the latest test of Sam Altman ’s leadership.
Staff at OpenAI, alongside senior legal, tech and policy figures, say the company has been left open to legal damages and government actions after cybersecurity breaches involving its AI agents were revealed around the world.
Last week saw new legal actions and regulatory probes launched against OpenAI almost daily, from California to Australia, with more expected to follow as details of other incidents come to light.
As the creator of the hit app ChatGPT, OpenAI and its chief Altman have become emblematic of the AI boom sweeping Silicon Valley and Wall Street.
But new questions over legal liability from these hacking incidents present the latest in a rolling series of crises facing Altman since the chatbot launched in 2022, including employee revolts, legal tangles with shareholders including Elon Musk , copyright disputes and political clashes.
Altman is fending off accusations that he is sidelining security concerns and deprioritising “alignment” training – which ensures models do not take actions harmful to humans – to regain ground against rival lab Anthropic.
On Saturday, David Robinson, a safety leader at OpenAI, announced his resignation from the company in an essay for the Atlantic, citing concerns over its “trial and error” approach to developing models.
Masayoshi Son, the SoftBank founder who has been a prominent evangelist for AI and funnelled almost $65 billion (€58 billion) into OpenAI and other huge bets on the technology, expressed concern on Sunday about the dangers of ever more powerful models in the wrong hands.
If AI were used by “bad” humans, he said at an event in Kyoto, “this can become super dangerous”.
In the wake of the dramatic attack on AI site Hugging Face by hundreds of OpenAI agents, Altman has acknowledged the risks presented by AI’s advances and joined calls by his arch-rival, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, to “pace the frontier” of AI development.
Any investor who was not previously put off by [Altman’s] recklessness will not be put off by a few agents
However, several OpenAI investors and others close to the company rejected the idea there would be any meaningful slowdown.
“If you’re Sam Altman and you want to beat your competitor ... there’s no way you’re going to pump the brakes,” said a former senior OpenAI employee. “Knowing the psyche of the people there, there’s no way they’re slowing down.”
Still, citing safety concerns, Altman has already postponed OpenAI’s planned stock market listing and scrapped the release of its most advanced model, Astra 6.1.
Uncertainty over the extent of its legal liabilities now hangs over his latest efforts to raise tens of billions in a private financing that could value the company at as much as $1.4 trillion. Prospective investors are weighing whether the company can outrun its latest crisis and continue a recent upturn in commercial fortunes.
On Monday, Florida’s attorney-general asked a court to halt OpenAI’s development of new models without additional safeguards.
Then on Tuesday, OpenAI was sued by a public interest group that alleges it broke a California law introduced last year to ensure “humans are on the hook for harms they cause”.
The next day, the US Federal Trade Commission broadened a probe into whether OpenAI and its peers misled customers over the potential harms of its technology. US officials have also said that AI companies should not expect protection from the government and that executives will remain liable for their products’ actions.
[ AI agents are hacking government agencies. It’s ‘really scary’ for cybersecurity Opens in new window ]
Meanwhile, Australia has launched a taskforce to investigate OpenAI agents’ unauthorised access to government systems.
The Greens, who hold the balance of power in the Australian senate, accused the San Francisco-based company of hiding the severity of the incidents in recent meetings, including one between Altman and deputy prime minister Richard Marles in September.
“It’s an insult not just to him, it’s an insult to Australia,” said Greens senator David Shoebridge, adding that Marles had been treated “like a mushroom”.
OpenAI has apologised for the incident. Jason Kwon, its chief strategy officer, is set to appear before a parliamentary committee in Sydney on Tuesday.
“The ‘my AI did it, don’t blame me’ defence is legally weak. It’s already failed for chatbot suicide cases,” said Max Tegmark, an AI safety campaigner and researcher at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
One Silicon Valley lawyer who has worked with several Big Tech companies said that while there were “definitely legal risks” from OpenAI’s agent attacks, so far they were “not material” due to the limited damage suffered by victims. But that could change fast, the lawyer added.
“The real exposure is when the agents are released to users, and then go rogue or are used to commit crimes,” they said. “The key issue, which will go on for years, is to whom should liability be assigned: the creator of the agent, or the person sending it on its mission?”
[ If AI has a ‘10% chance’ of killing us all by 2030, should I invest in a pension? Opens in new window ]
The lawyer doubted that the legal risks would impact OpenAI’s initial public offering. “Any investor who was not previously put off by [Altman’s] recklessness will not be put off by a few agents,” they said.
OpenAI’s internal investigation found “dozens” more such incidents. Asymmetric Security, a digital forensics company, found evidenceOpenAI’s agents pulled data from 55 websites, including the US Securities and Exchange Commission and the International Energy Agency, the Financial Times reported last week.
OpenAI said it was reviewing potential breaches and notifying those affected.
[ Meet the philosopher who thinks AI ought to have the same moral rights as humans Opens in new window ]
A spokesperson for the European Commission said the Brussels AI Act was designed to address such risks, warning that “frontier labs must take responsibility and be fully transparent, including about unintended incidents”.
“I suspect [OpenAI is] very aware of the legal risks of what their agents are doing,” said Vivian Dong, programmes director at Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology, the public interest group suing OpenAI. “It’s one thing to say ‘sorry’ in your blog post, and another to say outright: ‘We just engaged in illegal behaviour.’”
At the company’s annual developer conference last Tuesday, the upbeat mood on the stage was overshadowed by protesters on the fringes urging OpenAI to “put people over profits”.
One attendee described the contrast as like “something out of Black Mirror”, the satirical dystopian technology TV show.
The hacks have also revived tension inside the company between staff seeking to prioritise safety and those pushing to commercialise the technology. On Thursday, a trio of safety researchers were fired after allegedly handing confidential information to an external AI safety organisation, which OpenAI said violated their contracts.
“This is a concerning development, a callback to OpenAI trying to suppress workers with their illegal 2024 non-disparagement agreements, and a familiar playbook massive tech companies have been using against employees to cover up harms for a long time,” said Karl Koch, founder of non-profit The AI Whistleblower Initiative.
“The actions against well-intentioned researchers is an object example of why the AI industry cannot regulate itself,” he added.
OpenAI declined to comment. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: ‘AI should give us more room for the human’: What can we learn from the office superusers?
description: Leaders who have gone all-in on new tech tools describe how they are reimagining their working lives
content:
C alls to slow the pace of development on artificial intelligence for fear of its claimed potential to destroy humanity are unlikely to resonate with many office workers, most of whom are still primarily using the technology for basic tasks.
Only a quarter of UK adults use AI tools every day for their jobs, according to a Deloitte survey of 25,000 employees published this month. It found the most popular uses were searching for information, writing emails, fact-checking and creating summaries.
But a smaller group of AI “superusers” have restructured their working lives around intensive use of new tools. Microsoft’s 2026 Work Trend Index report says 16 per cent of AI users fall into this category and identifies three things that define them:
But what does it mean to class yourself as an AI superuser in the office? Senior corporate executives share their experience.
For some bosses, an AI agent acts like a chief of staff. Pamela Maynard, chief AI transformation officer for Microsoft customer and partner solutions, describes hers as holding “institutional context – my priorities, my calendar, what I care about, even my boundaries”.
She says the agent uses this “to set me up: shaping my week, surfacing what needs my attention and making sure I walk in prepared”. It also pushes back: “It has actually asked me why I was working on a Sunday afternoon when I should have been with friends or family.”
[ Rules of AI etiquette: be upfront, check accuracy, and don’t burden people with ‘workslop’ Opens in new window ]
Angela Tangas, head of the UK marketing agency Oliver, part of AI and digital advertising group Brandtech, has an “Ask Ange” agent, not yet an avatar, but a useful first line of support for her direct reports when she is not available.
“It started with some of the most common questions I am asked when speaking to customers, and how I would typically respond to those questions, and where I go for sources of information.” It is a work in progress: ask it something too complex and it “cuts off” and refers questioners to the real chief executive.
At law firm Lewis Silkin, senior associate Jordan Quartey uses specialist legal AI tool Harvey to gather client-specific files containing the firm’s previous advice and decisions, as well as current email chains. This means he no longer has to ask senior colleagues for advice at an early stage, getting further along in the process on his own by learning what has been done before, and using that context to develop his judgment.
“It’s more efficient, and it’s a better way of learning for myself,” he says.
Ivan Zhao, cofounder and chief executive at Notion, a collaboration and productivity platform, likens the shift in working patterns to the difference between a marching band and a jazz ensemble. “The marching band is like the old way of working – everyone in lockstep formation, following the same old sheet music, spending a lot of energy just to stay in lockstep.”
[ Will AI really kill most desk jobs ‘within the next 12 to 18 months’? Opens in new window ]
A jazz band, meanwhile, “has talented people improvising around a shared sense of where the music is headed”.
In his workplace this means agents handle the “boring and repetitive stuff” so staff can “spend their time on the improvisation and fine-tuning”. There are “more long conversations with colleagues, riffing on what we are building, why we’re building it that way, and what we should do next”.
Maynard at Microsoft says “AI should give us more room for the human, not less”. Time saved through efficiency gains should be used for “relationships, the mentoring, the messy human conversations no agent can have for me”, she says.
“The real risk ... is that we let the recovered time quietly refill with more tasks.”
While some leaders are keen to cut meetings, Maynard makes them “count for more”. An agent does the pre-briefing so teams can use the time for “actual conversation”. “The recap and follow-ups write themselves, so the time in the room goes to people, not process.”
Zhao says Notion staff have eliminated “boring meetings”, because “an agent can summarise what products shipped this week or what sales were made”. That means “there’s more time for spontaneous meetings, where you realise something over lunch or drop by someone’s desk and chat about what’s on their screen. This is often where the best ideas come from.”
[ If AI has a ‘10% chance’ of killing us all by 2030, should I invest in a pension? Opens in new window ]
Tangas says she does not measure the benefits from her team of AI agents in “time I’m saving” but how it makes her “more effective as a leader”.
She starts the day with an AI-generated news round-up, prompted and refined to give her news about relevant sectors. “For example, if [a client] has a profit warning, would I have seen that if I didn’t have my prompt? Probably not. It’s enabling me to be much more proactive.”
She then works with agents within the company’s own AI platform to stimulate ideas and prepare for client meetings.
“Let’s say before I am going to see an executive, I would say, ‘My profile of the customer looks like this’ and ‘this is what I hope to achieve from the conversation. Can we role play how that conversation might play out?’”
Leanne Taylor, chief executive of Syspro, a software maker, says how many hours she saves “is the wrong question”. Her company’s AI tool is trained on corporate routines and discussions but also learns how she personally thinks and makes decisions, and what her priorities are.
It understands the “language I use when I’m thinking something through, versus when I am landing [at] a conclusion”, she says. This means the technology can help her make better decisions that “reflect how I lead and not a generic version of leadership”.
Berry Diepeveen, a senior partner at BCG and leader of the consultancy’s tech and digital practice for the UK, the Netherlands and Belgium, says he has “virtual teams working for me day in and day out”.
But he stresses that proper oversight is vital: “If I create a lot of AI-enabled content, but I pass it over the fence, and a human needs to suddenly deal with five, 10, 15 times the volume of work, then, of course, that bottleneck has shifted.”
“The most surprising thing about AI? How much fun it is,” says Taylor at Syspro. “I expected useful and I expected efficient. I wasn’t expecting to really enjoy the way I work more than I did before. But there’s something that happens when the friction drops – you start playing.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: Lessons in governance from a career spanning public and private sectors
description: Former secretary general Jim Breslin on bringing his broad experience to the faculty of the Institute of Directors Ireland chartered director programme
content:
If anything, Jim Breslin has been busier than ever since stepping down from the secretary general role at the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science (DFHERIS). He has advised Ukraine’s health ministry on EU accession talks, chaired the Local Democracy Task Force, holds a range of directorships and advisory roles across the private, not-for-profit and public sectors including chair of Renewable Energy Ireland and a board member of St Vincent’s Healthcare Group.
Alongside that work he is now bringing his experience to bear as a faculty member of the Institute of Directors (IoD) Ireland’s chartered director programme , the institute’s flagship professional qualification for directors, leading to the certificate and diploma in company direction and, for eligible candidates, the internationally recognised chartered director (CDir) designation.
It is little surprise that he is in such high demand given his vast experience in the public sector at times of extreme challenge and disruption. “I always seem to be somewhere where the clampdown was happening,” he says.
That includes establishing the Department of Children in the middle of the last recession as its first secretary general. “We were starting a new department in the financial crash, working within diminishing resources, but trying to do something quite distinct and new and developmental,” he recalls. “I remember in those days there was a three-year spending review, and we were cutting 15 per cent out here, 30 per cent out there. The idea was to fundamentally try to protect things in order to rebuild programmes that were going to be effective over the medium term.”
He subsequently moved on to lead the Department of Health, where budgetary challenges are a perennial feature, and later to being the first secretary general of DFHERIS.
Governance has been a recurring theme. “I happened across departments that were redoing governance on a number of occasions,” he says. Setting up Tusla required “first principles thinking” about the governance design of an organisation. “It became a template for what I did with some other organisations and my approach to state bodies.”
Subsequently, he played a key role in the reform of HSE governance at the Department of Health, which at that time had no independent oversight. “We changed that and brought in a non-executive board led by a chair.”
Lessons learned from these experiences were reinforced when he completed the IoD Ireland chartered director programme himself, which focuses on four key areas of strategy, leadership, company finance, and corporate governance. The insights he gleaned proved invaluable on the last big governance reform he worked on, reshaping university governance from stakeholder-based “mini-parliaments” towards more focused boards with a majority of independent members “all selected on the basis of competency.”
He doesn’t see governance in the public, private and not-for-profit sectors as completely separate things. “I think there are principles that cut across all of those sectors,” he says. “It is often about the nature of the decision or the nature of the project rather than which sector the organisation is in. If you’re managing a very significant, irreversible decision where once you commit you can’t pull back, or if you do pull back, there is a huge cost, you will see a very deliberate approach to governance in the private sector. In the energy sector for example, where the upfront costs are really, really significant at the start and the payback is over 25 or 30 years there’s a very thoughtful and deliberate process before making that decision.”
In regulated sectors organisations are not only deliberate in their decisions but also deliberate in documenting the decisions, he notes. “In much the same way as the public sector, because they are exposed to scrutiny, they have to take that approach. And then of course, there are other occasions where it’s a much more agile decision-making process. I like the approach they use in Amazon. They have a saying about two-way doors and one-way doors. A one-way door is once you do it, there’s no coming back from it. They are really slow in making those decisions.”
It is the context of the decision or the project that should inform the type of governance overlay put on it, he explains. “There is something to learn from everybody’s experience in that. And I’m certainly learning now in the private sector, in the not-for-profit sector, and that is great. I am a very curious person; getting into a sector and trying to understand it from start to finish is something that motivates me.”
Part of what he does is to take that learning and use it to translate different sectors for each other, he explains. “People look at government and see it as very hard to understand and very complex and I can help them with that. But equally now that I have a perspective on commerciality and the private sector and what is needed – how you structure opportunity that the private sector will be willing to take on – I can have that conversation in a government context.”
He is keen to emphasise the value of a blend of experience. “When I engage with people on behalf of the IoD Ireland, I’m not trying to sell them my experience in the public sector as the answer,” he says. “I am trying to interpret with them what their situations are. Sometimes my experience is relevant, and I can give an insight into that, but I am not trying to dictate to them because I want to learn from their experience as well.”
That peer-to-peer learning is a very important part of the IoD Ireland chartered director programme ; the classes provide a forum for it while allowing participants to expand their director network. “What is really good in the IoD Ireland classroom is the diversity of experience. Part of my job is to facilitate that. It is a class that is learning from each other as much as from me, as the content includes real work case studies, while also having regard for the theory and the core set of principles that are firmly embedded in everything the IoD Ireland does. I have immersed myself in those codes of governance to ensure that when people ask questions we’re not improvising, that we are going back to first principles all the time.”
Breslin advises others to consider the opportunities presented by non-executive directorships and advisory roles. “I would highly recommend it. But do it with intentionality and due diligence. Don’t just find yourself doing something because somebody asked you. You need to have thought about it well ahead of time.”
He also recommends serving on State boards. “People might criticise the public sector, but it is a fantastic place to make an impact for the public and for your community. And I think it is still a respected thing to do. If you are playing that role, you’re doing the State some service and you are doing your fellow citizens some service.”
A sense of civic responsibility and an acknowledgment of the value of learning from different perspectives are threads that run through Breslin’s career and his approach to governance, threads he now weaves into his contribution to the IoD Ireland chartered director programme, where participants learn alongside other experienced directors and senior leaders from across the private, public and not-for-profit sectors.
Enrolment for the next intake of the Institute of Directors Ireland chartered director programme is now open for January 2027. Learn more about the programme on the IoD Ireland website

title: Minister misses the target with increase in Help to Buy tax break
description: Little point in offering first-time buyers greater tax relief unless there are properties they can buy
content:
Budgets are always a balancing act, a bit like ensuring appropriate geographical and gender spread in a ministerial Cabinet. When announcing the budget goodies, Minister for Finance Simon Harris and his advisers will have been conscious of the need to accommodate different constituencies.
It may have been the “budget for those who work”, with the lion’s share of the package going in income tax measures, but there was also a need to reassure the elderly and the young that they too were cherished.
Enhancement of the Help to Buy property scheme appears to have been the target of choice at the younger end of the demographic scale. But it might not prove to be the winner the Government hopes.
Harris announced a €5,000 increase in the amount of tax relief aspiring first-time homeowners can get under the scheme, which allows purchasers to claim back income tax and deposit interest retention tax they have paid over the previous four years.
Before the budget, the maximum available was €30,000 or 10 per cent of the purchase price, whichever was the lower. That limit has now risen to €35,000.
The issue for the Minister is twofold. First, there was no great clamour outside Government to increase the threshold. First-time buyers seem to be far more concerned with the limited supply of properties available to them.
That brings us to the second issue: if there is a concern about Help to Buy and other similar schemes, such as the First Home shared equity incentive, it is that the price of properties eligible is capped at €500,000.
In large parts of the State’s urban centres, especially in and around Dublin, that means first-time buyers are effectively priced out of the market regarding the relief.
In 2023, in a report on the Real Cost of New Housing, the Society of Chartered Surveyors Ireland noted the average cost of a new build three-bed semi in the Greater Dublin Area was €461,000. Property price inflation has certainly exceeded 10 per cent since then, taking those homes out of reach of Help to Buy.
More recent figures show that apartments are firmly over the €500,000 threshold.
As one reader of The Irish Times noted: “The scheme remains redundant to majority of buyers in Dublin, commuter towns and other cities across the country. The extra €5k does not unlock any new homes or help affordability.”
If anything, the Minister’s move has simply highlighted how increasingly unfit the scheme is for its stated purpose – allowing first-time buyers access to housing.
Or could he just be allowing it wither on the vine while seeming to promote it?

title: For a comfier home this winter cosy up to SEAI’s hottest ever energy grants
description: SEAI studies show that living in a warmer home provides a greater sense of wellbeing and comfort
content:
With colder weather approaching, now is a good time to think about making your home warmer and more comfortable.
With increased Home Energy Upgrade grants available from the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI), there is significant support available to help make your home warmer, more comfortable, and more energy efficient.
You do not have to upgrade your whole home at once. SEAI’s individual grants allow you to start with one or more measures and take further steps when you are ready.
For many homes, attic and wall insulation is a good first step. It’s quick and easy, and you’ll see immediate benefits in terms of increased comfort and reduced heating bills.
“If you want to get a grant just for attic insulation on its own, or for wall insulation, you can do that. Or you can bundle them together. They are all individual grants,” explains SEAI’s Brian McIntyre, programme manager for high-performance building technologies.
Unlike a complete home energy upgrade through a One Stop Shop, individual grants do not require the home to achieve a minimum BER rating. Each individual grant does however have its own requirements, and the SEAI website goes into this in more detail.
Euro for euro, attic insulation will give you the biggest bang for your buck in terms of heat retention. That’s because a house loses around 30 per cent of its heat through the roof.
SEAI increased its attic insulation grants earlier this year which significantly reduces the cost for homeowners.
For a detached home, attic insulation grants are now worth up to €2,000, a sizeable chunk of change compared with the current median cost of works coming in at approximately €2,700.
Roughly another third of our valuable heat goes out through poorly insulated walls. Depending on the type of home, the available grant options are for cavity, internal and external wall insulation. Significant individual grants are available for all three measures. Homeowners who previously received a grant for either cavity or internal wall insulation can now apply for a grant to undertake a second wall insulation measure.
For a detached house, grants range from €1,800 for cavity wall insulation and €4,500 for internal wall insulation, to €8,000 for external wall insulation. Actual costs will vary and we encourage homeowners to obtain at least three quotes for their own property – shopping around is recommended.
“Attic and cavity walls are the most straightforward and easy things you can do. While nothing is cheap, and everyone is a bit squeezed right now, they are relatively inexpensive and the impact they can have, for the level of work that’s being done, is enormous,” says McIntyre.
The Warmer Homes Scheme provides free home energy upgrades to eligible low-income households. As of this year, to guard against fuel poverty, homeowners in receipt of certain welfare payments can apply for even higher individual grants to help pay for attic and wall insulation while keeping their position on the Warmer Homes scheme.
Many Irish homes don’t have enough attic insulation, particularly those built before 2011, before better building regulations were introduced.
“Around 30 per cent of homes, about 280,000, were built before 2011 and do not have good levels of insulation,” says McIntyre.
“They typically have four inches of yellow insulation, instead of 12 inches now, which means they are losing about three times the amount of heat through their attic than they would do if they just got their attic insulated properly.”
If a home has poorly performing windows and doors, replacing them may be worth considering once you’ve achieved the right levels of insulation.
New individual grants for energy-efficient windows and doors were introduced by SEAI in March.
For a typical Irish detached home, the current median cost for replacement windows is around €10,453, and there is an SEAI grant of up to €4,000 to help with these costs. The median cost for replacing doors is around €4,300, with an SEAI grant of €800 available per door (up to a maximum of two doors).
If you’re unsure where to begin, “getting a BER assessment will give you a clearer picture of your home’s current energy performance and what areas need improvement,” he adds.
Now that your home is well insulated, the next step is to move from fossil-fuel heating to a more energy efficient heat pump system to keep your home at a constantly comfortable temperature. The typical price for our sample detached householder to switch to install a heat pump is €17,000. For comparison’s sake, the grant available, at up to €14,500 makes the net cost comparable to an oil or gas boiler.
However, if your current oil or gas boiler is working well and you are not yet ready to replace it, there is an interim step you can take which will also save you money and reduce your carbon footprint – smart heating controls.
These help you to match your heating and hot water schedules to the way you live, for example, ensuring the radiators upstairs aren’t belting out heat when everyone is downstairs.
By eliminating inefficiencies these smart controls will save you money. They currently cost around €3,700 for our sample house but there is a grant worth €700 for them.
Once you have invested in your insulation and improved the energy efficiency of your heating system, the next step is to consider solar PV. This is where rooftop panels capture light from the sun and convert it into electricity to power your home.
For a typical detached house, SEAI estimates the median cost of installing solar PV is €11,100, for which there is a grant of up to €1,800.
The benefits of a home energy upgrade are about far more than saving money.
“In a well-insulated house, the temperature is much more stable and comfortable,” says McIntyre.
SEAI studies, undertaken with the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, also show that living in a warmer home provides a greater sense of wellbeing and comfort and, especially for people with more acute respiratory illnesses, fewer doctors’ visits and prescriptions. “People are also more likely to want others to visit,” he adds.
Of course, if you are keen to complete a full home energy upgrade in one go, an SEAI registered One Stop Shop can manage the entire project for you and deduct all grants from the cost of the work upfront.
“It often occurs when people’s options are to move house or stay where they are and to extend and renovate at the same time instead, turning the house they have into their forever home,” he explains.
For everyone else, the Home Energy Upgrade grants mean “you can essentially do a lot of the same work through the individual grants as you can do with the One Stop Shop,” says McIntyre.
“Not everybody has the money to do the full job in one go. So now you can say ‘Right, I’m doing the attic insulation now and maybe in a year’s time, I’ll get the walls done and look at getting the heating systems done after that’, as your finances allow.”
SEAI’s individual grants will support you at every step. “It’s a longer journey, but it gives you greater flexibility to suit your needs, and ultimately you will still get to the same destination in the end,” he says.
Whether you start with one or more upgrades or plan a complete home energy upgrade in one go, SEAI has significant grants to support you with your home energy upgrades. Saving energy, saves money. Search SEAI Home Energy Upgrades now .

title: Event guide: Angine de Poitrine, Gilbert O’Sullivan and the other best things to see in Ireland in the week ahead
description: October 10th-16th highlights: Our pick of music, art, theatre and more coming your way
content:
Fair play to the anonymous Canadian duo Angine de Poitrine, who perform dressed head to toe in light-up black-and-white polka-dotted costumes, and who describe their increasingly popular music as “mantra-rock dada Pythago-cubist”. If you have a ticket for their debut gig in Ireland, which has been upgraded from the smaller Opium venue, don’t expect the Quebecois pair to say much. Klek de Poitrine (on drums) and Khn de Poitrine (on guitars), whose music went viral earlier this year, prefer to communicate, if that’s the right word, via triangular hand signals that their fans emulate. In The New York Times’ opinion, the band fully understand “the power of rhythm, repetition, dissonance, surprise and noise”, and while their costumes and anonymity “have clearly helped draw attention, Angine de Poitrine’s music is no gimmick; it’s a feat of live unity and dexterity, hand played with zero margin for error”.
At 75 years of age – it began in October 1951 as the Festival of Music and Arts – Wexford Festival Opera has long been regarded as one of the world’s leading celebrations of the form. Highlights of this year’s event include Pietro Mascagni’s Iris (O’Reilly Theatre, National Opera House, October 15th, 20th, 23rd, 28th and 31st), Gioachino Rossini’s L’Equivoco (O’Reilly Theatre, National Opera House, October 16th, 21st, 25th and 29th) and the world premiere of Colm Tóibín and Conor Linehan’s The Next 75 (Green Acres Gallery, October 20th, 21st, 22nd, 28th, 29th and 30th). The festival’s admired Impossible Interview features Michael Dervan “interviewing” Rossini (depicted by Peter Camley).
Gilbert O’Sullivan has been a pop singer since 1967. His profile has ebbed and flowed, but he has never lost his observational, witty and highly melodic style of songwriting, which has earned justifiable comparisons with those of Randy Newman and Paul McCartney. The Waterford-born singer may use this opportunity to preview some of the tracks from his album On the Record, which come out in early November, but you can safely bet that fans will give O’Sullivan’s best-loved songs, including Nothing Rhymed, We Will, Clair, No Matter How I Try and Alone Again (Naturally) the loudest and longest cheers.
It’s rare for such a key figure in contemporary rock to tour Ireland so extensively, but the Throwing Muses and 50 Foot Wave frontwoman is no ordinary singer-songwriter, as you’ll hear if you come along to one of these gigs. Hersh is promoting her new album, Sugar on Blackstone, the 13th solo LP she has released since Hips and Makers, in 1994, but she’ll also be performing songs from the catalogues of her groundbreaking bands.
The German composer Heiner Goebbels is regarded as one of the most important innovators in the world of theatre, performance art and multimedia. This performance of his 2007 work Songs of War I Have Seen blends live music by Crash Ensemble and the Irish Baroque Orchestra with spoken extracts from wartime diary entries by the American writer Gertrude Stein. Expect a thought-provoking depiction of turmoil and conflict.
Annmarie Cullen, former member of the band Saucy Monkey, has been developing her one-woman musical for a couple of years, winning an Edinburgh Fringe Theatre Award, among other gongs, for her work. Through original songs, narration and multimedia (including on-screen appearances by the singer-songwriter Naimee Coleman and the comedian Gearóid Farrelly as outlying but encouraging friends), the Dubliner relates an autobiographical story of emigration, celebration, despair, loss of identity and staying power.
“What have the Romans ever done for us?” is a question that the eminent classicist Mary Beard will be answering most eloquently in her thought-provoking one-woman event. Noted for her rewriting of popular narratives, Beard is adept at drawing parallels between the politics of ancient Rome and contemporary political landscapes. Members of the audience will also have an opportunity to ask questions, but don’t expect too serious an evening. Beard is, after all, also the author of the book Laughter in Ancient Rome: On Joking, Tickling, and Cracking Up.
The fifth year of the poetry and music festival celebrating the life and work of the Thurles-born poet Dennis O’Driscoll includes readings from more than 20 poets, plus a discussion about the public life of Seamus Heaney. The latter will feature Fintan O’Toole and Mick Heaney in conversation with O’Driscoll’s son, Declan. Poets reading their work, as well as O’Driscoll’s, include Rita Ann Higgins, Vona Groarke, John Kelly, Emily Cullen, Martina Evans and Katie Donovan.
All things thrilling, plot-twisting, deceitful, manipulative and, yes, lethal feature at this annual festival’s conspiracy of crime writers, which features panel discussions, public interviews, masterclasses and workshops. Authors include Jane Casey, Ardal O’Hanlon, Cecelia Ahern, Sam Blake, Jen Bray, Dr Marie Cassidy, Robert Craven, Edel Coffey, TM Logan and Andrea Mara.

title: A nuanced and frankly terrifying guide to averting global annihilation
description: A nuanced and frankly terrifying guide to averting a third World War
content:
Tobias Ellwood, a former Conservative MP, chair of the UK select committee on defence and retired British army captain, has written a frankly terrifying step-by-step guide to averting an imminent global war that would lead to planetary annihilation.
At a time of proliferating conflict and a rise in authoritarianism, Ellwood charts the manner in which regional conflict could “metastasise” into an Armageddon fuelled by AI “kill webs” and “kill chains” activated by non-rational actors such as Vladimir Putin and others.
Simply put, Ellwood states we are at an inflection point in human history where “The age of the unthinkable is creeping closer to thinkable”. To prevent humanity from “sleepwalking” into a nuclear apocalypse, the central argument of the book is that the “world order” as envisaged in the 1944 Bretton Woods Conference ought to be reformed and restored, not abandoned.
Ellwood’s work is nuanced and informed by his lived experience as a professional soldier, politician and a man who understands, on a very personal level, the human cost of conflict. The book is dedicated to his brother Jonathan, who was killed in the Bali bombings of October 2002.
He critiques the West’s oft-quoted “rules-based” world order with its central pillars such as the United Nations and the rules and conventions of international warfare, observing that many emerging powers are distrustful of western hegemony. Underlining the need for major reform and a to what he terms “Bretton Woods 2.0″, he states “Western power claims universality, but practices exception”.
Essentially, the book is a call for dialogue and to “reassert statecraft”, with world leaders moving away from AI-enhanced hard power to old-fashioned, much underrated soft power and in particular what he refers to as “smart power”.
Ellwood argues that the investment we put into air strikes and drone warfare should be matched by negotiation, “accommodation” or pragmatic compromises between global powers and “managed rivalry”. The alternative is mutually assured destruction by way of weapons of mass destruction and uncontrolled climate change .
What is most sobering and alarming to me in reviewing this book – and others on contemporary conflict for The Irish Times – is the manner in which Ireland is highly exposed in all domains of 21st-century warfare. Our Government, which often appears functionally illiterate on defence and security matters, needs to invest in all-of-society resilience. As Ellwood concludes: “In the modern era, resilience is deterrence. And society itself is the front line.”
Tom Clonan is an Independent Senator and a retired captain in the Irish Army

title: Limerick start-up uses AI to take the pain out of compliance
description: Envaira is targeting multinationals struggling to keep track of hundreds of environmental, health and safety requirements across multiple sites
content:
Environmental, Health and Safety (EHS) regulations are there to protect workers, customers, the public and the environment from harm.
Companies covered by the regulations must be able to produce hard evidence that they’re abiding by the rules. But for companies operating in highly regulated industries, proving they comply with those rules involves keeping track of hundreds – and sometimes more than 1,000 – pieces of legislation.
Despite that complexity, much of the work is still being carried out using Excel spreadsheets, legacy software and information periodically updated by consultants.
It was this shortcoming that led to the formation of EHS start-up Envaira, which has developed an AI-powered platform that streamlines the compliance process to make it faster and easier to manage, especially where multiple manufacturing sites are involved.
“The three main issues currently facing those handling compliance in an organisation are too much manual work, information quickly going out of date and significant time spent preparing for audits,” explains Michael O’Shea, who cofounded Envaira with Eugene Cush and Katie Vellner in July last year.
“At the moment the compliance process is lagging behind when it comes to technology, with a lot of the work being done manually with registers maintained in Excel or older software and only updated periodically by consultants.
“As a result, information can quickly become static and outdated. Envaira was built to address these problems rather than simply digitising the traditional legal register and instead of just providing organisations with large volumes of legislation to interpret and manage themselves, we identify the requirements relevant to their specific business and translate them into clear, actionable obligations on a site-specific basis.
“We continuously monitor and highlight any regulatory changes affecting our customers and the system. It also collects relevant codes of practice, guidance, licences and permits together in one place.
“EHS teams can then assess their compliance against these obligations, attach evidence and track action as gaps are identified. This provides an ongoing view of compliance without the need for a big scramble to pull information and evidence together before an audit,” says O’Shea, who is participating in the AI Ecosystem Accelerator run by NovaUCD in partnership with CeADAR, Ireland’s Centre for Applied AI.
EHS regulations are governed by both Irish law and European directives, and if a business fails to demonstrate compliance when asked, it could face penalties and fines. For an SME in a sector with light-touch regulation, this is relatively straightforward, as only a small number of directives will apply. In large companies in sensitive industries, however, it’s a different ballgame.
For example, a single manufacturing site making medical devices or pharmaceutical products could have to comply with 150-200 pieces of Irish legislation alone, and this could rise to more than 1,000 depending on what the site is producing. On top of this, most multinationals will have several sites that may have different compliance requirements. And regulations don’t stand still. They are constantly being revised and added to on a weekly basis.
Envaira is using AI to power its system, which basically ingests all the relevant legislation for a jurisdiction as well as flagging any other site requirements, such as permits and licences. But while the AI does the heavy lifting on the basic data, the overall process is overseen by an EHS professional.
“We want to deliver speed but not at the expense of accuracy, so we specifically wanted to have expert human curation given the highly regulated environment we’re operating in,” O’Shea says. “We also consolidate any relevant changes into focused weekly updates, so teams know what matters and we’re not just adding to the noise.”
The idea for Envaira took shape in an unlikely location – on a bus after an Enterprise Ireland-IDA co-hosted event in Waterford. “I was talking to Eugene [Cush] on the short drive to the car park, and he was describing the huge frustrations faced by organisations keeping on top of an ever-growing EHS legislative burden,” O’Shea says.
“My background is in building and scaling software businesses, particularly within highly regulated financial services and fintech markets, where platforms are built on transparency, traceability and auditability. I began questioning why those same principles weren’t being applied to EHS compliance, as it seemed like a good fit to me.
“Both Eugene and Katie have deep EHS domain expertise and previously ran the Pegasus EHS legal register. Katie had also been reflecting on their experience in the sector and felt there was an opportunity to rethink the traditional approach.”
Envaira is aimed at EHS directors or managers responsible for managing compliance and implementing standards such as ISO 14001 and ISO 45001. The company’s main market will be large, multisite and multinational organisations operating across multiple jurisdictions in industries such as construction, energy and food and beverage manufacturing. The platform has been built to handle the different regulatory requirements in each country, again with local human oversight.
Envaira was launched in February, and the company has paying customers in Ireland, the UK, the Netherlands, Germany, Malaysia and Norway. Envaira is Limerick-based and employs four full-time and four part-time staff.
[ Can AI give small businesses the marketing muscle of big companies? Opens in new window ]
To date, the company has raised approximately €500,000 from angel investors and support from the Limerick Local Enterprise Office and Enterprise Ireland. The next step is a funding round of €600,000, which will go towards business development and expanding the team as the company scales across Ireland, the UK and the EU.
Envaira is O’Shea’s third start-up, and he says a lot has changed for the better since he founded Delta Index back in 2002, which was subsequently sold. “My sense is that there’s a maturity around the ecosystem that wasn’t there before, and there are definitely more varied supports available now, not all of which are financial. For example, we benefited from Prep4Seed run by AxisBIC in Munster,” he says.
“In my experience, the key thing when starting a business is product-market fit. We could have started by building the technology. Instead, we started with the problem and built the technology around it. It’s all too easy to spend time building something you think the market wants, but unless it meets a real need, people are not going to buy it.”

title: Evicted Spanish pensioner María del Carmen Abascal dies before she could return home
description: Maricarmen’s eviction from Madrid apartment after over seven decades set off wave of protests against housing crisis
author_name: Ashifa Kassam, Sam Jones in Madrid
content:
María del Carmen Abascal , the 87-year-old whose eviction set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain ’s housing crisis, has died.
News of her death came two weeks after Maricarmen, as she had come to be known across Spain, was evicted from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for more than seven decades.
The pensioner, whose apartment had been purchased by an investment firm who sought to hike her rent by 230 per cent, swiftly became a symbol of the many left behind by Spain’s surging housing market.
Scenes of the eviction, which saw police use rounds of tear gas as they carried out the order, made headlines across Spain. The shocking images – showing Abascal being forcibly removed from her home on a stretcher, flanked by protesters and police – swiftly crystallised into anger.
About 10,000 people took to the streets of Madrid hours later, wielding signs such as “Shame” and “We’re all Maricarmen”. From Spain’s north to the south, people poured into plazas to protest the suffering wrought by rents that had soared 80 per cent in the span of a decade while house prices had climbed 63 per cent.
From the hospital where she was being treated for severe exhaustion, Abascal cheered on the fledgling movement. “I would like to be there with you all,” she said in a video shot from her hospital bed. “But I’m not that lucky. So from here, I ask you all for courage and to fight and defend what is yours.”
As encampments began springing up across the country, the investment firm that bought Abascal’s home said she could return. The deal did little to quell the anger that had boiled over in the wake of the eviction.
This week the wave of outrage led the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez , to call a snap general election after rightwing and far-right parties voted down two emergency decrees his government had proposed to address the housing crisis.
[ Evicted Spanish pensioner at heart of Spain’s housing protests dies Opens in new window ]
The Madrid tenants’ union said the solution had come too late for the octogenarian. “This was a completely preventable situation following an agonising ordeal,” it said in a statement announcing that Abascal had died in hospital, reportedly hours before she was due to sign a new lease with the investment firm that had evicted her.
“The events triggered by the injustice of her eviction undoubtedly mark a turning point in the history of this country: large demonstrations, encampments in the squares, an early election, and the call for a general strike,” it added. “The housing debate is at the centre of it all, but the cost of getting to this point has been too high.”
Sánchez offered his condolences to Abascal’s family and friends. “A hug also to everyone who’s feeling this loss today as their own,” he wrote on social media. “Rest in peace.”
Spain’s health minister, Mónica García, said Abascal’s plight had “served to awaken awareness across all of Spain, lighting a fuse that cannot be put out”, and adding that her “dignity and courage” had shown the way.
The Podemos MEP and former equalities minister Irene Montero was more blunt. “This isn’t a death; it’s a murder,” she wrote on social media. “Such bloody anger. Thank you for fighting, Maricarmen.”
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP) – which voted against last week’s emergency housing measures – also offered his condolences.
“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he wrote on social media. “When a person dies there should be nothing but respect.”
Her death came a day after Sánchez’s cabinet approved two new housing decrees intended to “maintain the spirit” of the two previous decrees that were voted down in parliament last week by the PP, the far-right Vox party and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence Junts party.
The 21 measures include facilitating renting or buying a new home; extending eviction protections for vulnerable residents; regulating room rentals; imposing a new tax on seasonal rentals; prohibiting speculative real estate purchases; and granting tax breaks to property owners and tenants who pay on time.
With the lower and upper houses of parliament dissolved following the calling of the snap election, the decrees will be voted on by the permanent council of congress, a special council that operates when parliament is not in session.
The body’s 69 members are distributed proportionally among the various parliamentary groups to reflect the composition of the lower chamber, meaning Sánchez will probably have enough support to get at least one of the decrees passed.
In the heart of Madrid, where campaigners have set up a giant protest camp, news of Abascal’s death was met with a moment of silence. Soon after, hundreds marched from the camp to the country’s parliament chanting: “Maricarmen lives on, the fight continues.” – Guardian
[ Spain’s prime minister calls snap election after protests over housing crisis Opens in new window ]

title: Three killed and more than 30 injured in attacks on two Saudi airports, aviation authorities say
description: Irish airport operator DAA has contract to operate terminal at one of the Saudi airports attacked
content:
One ‌person was killed and ‌eight injured in an attack ​on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi ​capital Riyadh, and ⁠two were killed ‌and ‌28 ​injured in an attack on ⁠facilities ​at Abha ​airport, Saudi civil ‌aviation authorities said in ​a statement issued ⁠on ⁠Wednesday.
One ​of the attacks was on Wednesday and the other on Tuesday, it ‌said, without ⁠saying which attack had occurred ‌on which day.
Irish airport operator DAA has an airport management contract to operate one of the terminals at King Khalid International Airport.
Kevin Cullinane, DAA deputy director of communications, said: “We are aware of today’s incident at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and are in close contact with our teams in the region.”
The Saudi airport attacks were among a series of strikes targeting aviation infrastructure on Wednesday.
Yemen’s Houthis attacked Aden’s international airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones earlier on Wednesday, the country’s transport ministry said.
One missile landed near the runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, the ministry said. The ​airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control.
Battles in Yemen have focused in recent days on areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the conflict between the US and Iran restricted ⁠trade through the Strait of Hormuz .
The fighting, a spillover from the wider US-Iran conflict, has revived a complex 12-year war in Yemen that led to one of the worst humanitarian crises globally and fragmented the Arab world’s most impoverished country. The number of people displaced since the latest round of ⁠fighting began has risen to more than 200,000, the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) said on ​Wednesday.
[ World’s oil stockpiles are ‘scarily thin’, says Saudi Aramco boss Opens in new window ]
“People are running for their lives and finding nowhere safe to go,” said IOM director general Amy ​Pope, who called for more funding amid rising needs for food and shelter. Both sides allege that hundreds of people have been killed in fighting, without providing details. The UN says three in four families are going hungry in parts ‌of Yemen.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted infrastructure including airports, oil refineries and pipelines ​in Saudi Arabia, a US ally.
Houthi military spokesperson ⁠Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group ​had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones. – Additional reporting Reuters

title: Louth man accused of murdering parents and brother pleads not guilty by reason of insanity
description: Robert O’Connor is accused of killing his mother, father and younger brother at their home in September 2025
content:
A 32-year-old man has pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity to murdering three members of his family at their home in Co Louth last year.
A Central Criminal Court judge warned jurors empanelled for the trial that some of the evidence they will hear may be “difficult or distressing”.
Robert O’Connor, of Drumgowna, Louth Village, Dundalk , Co Louth, is charged with the triple murder of his mother Louise O’Connor, his father Mark O’Connor and his younger brother Evan O’Connor at their home in Drumgowna between September 28th and 29th 2025, both dates inclusive.
O’Connor was arraigned before the Central Criminal Court on Wednesday on three counts of murder.
When the registrar read the indictments to the accused and asked him how he was pleading, O’Connor replied: “Not guilty by reason of insanity” to each of the three counts that were put to him. Judge Siobhan Lankford told the jury panel that this case involved members of the accused man’s family.
The judge warned the jurors that some of the pathology evidence may be “difficult or distressing” and if they felt they could not maintain impartiality then to let her know.
The judge also informed the potential jurors that acting on a panel is a difficult but an important task. “Any judge when hearing a case like this will make accommodations for those on the jury. If you think you will have difficulty dealing with this properly you should bring it to my attention,” she added.
The judge told the panel that they must be in a position to put their sympathies aside and direct their minds in “an objective fashion” to the hearing of the evidence.
The judge further informed the jurors that she anticipated the evidence would not take more than three weeks and that they needed to be available to sit until October 30th next.
The prosecution case is being led by senior counsel Roisin Lacey, while Michael Bowman is heading up the defence team. A jury of six men and six women was sworn in to hear the trial, which is due to begin on Thursday afternoon before Judge Mícheál P O’Higgins.

title: Mayo’s Cillian O’Connor retires from intercounty football
description: Two-time All Star is top scorer in senior football championship history and leaves as an All-Ireland champion
content:
Mayo forward Cillian O’Connor has announced his intercounty retirement.
O’Connor, the leading scorer in the history of the senior championship with 32-364, made his Mayo debut in 2011 and retires with 129 appearances for the county, including 75 in championship.
A two-time Young Footballer of the Year, the 34-year-old said: “I have decided to retire from intercounty football. Representing Mayo GAA has been the greatest honour of my life.
“To my wife, Hannah, my parents, Tony and Mary, my family and close friends, thank you for your patience, understanding and constant support throughout my football career.
“I will always be grateful to my club, Ballintubber, and to the coaches, team-mates, volunteers and club members who helped me develop and supported me throughout every season.
“In the dressingroom, I feel fortunate to have seen my childhood heroes become team-mates and, later, to have watched the youngsters become stars.
“Thank you all for your commitment and perseverance, and for the friendship, memories and laughs. I also want to thank all the Mayo coaches, managers, back room teams and medical staff who believed in me and who I learned so much from over the years.
“To the supporters, at home and abroad, who always stood by the team, thank you for your unwavering support. You were a constant reminder of what a privilege it is to represent this county. I want to thank the Mayo County Board, our late chairman, Seamus Tuohy, who will be sorely missed, and our loyal sponsors.
“To the players and supporters across the country, I will always cherish the competition, passion and respect shared throughout the years. Thank you.”
[ Ciarán Murphy: Cillian O’Connor is one of football’s greats, the numbers don’t lie Opens in new window ]
The two-time All Star concluded: “To Andy and the 2027 Mayo team, the best of luck for the season ahead. Make every moment count.
“Thank you to everyone who has played a part in the journey since October 2010. Straightforward, no. Exhilarating, yes. To leave with Mayo as All-Ireland champions is more satisfying than words can say.”
It remains to be seen if other players will follow over the coming weeks and months, but Mayo manager Andy Moran praised O’Connor for his contribution to the green-and-red cause.
Moran stated: “It has been a privilege for me to have experienced Cillian’s Mayo career from two very different perspectives. First as a team-mate and, in recent years, as his manager.
“Cillian leaves the intercounty game having made an extraordinary contribution to Mayo football. His scoring record speaks for itself, but those of us who shared a dressingroom with him know that his influence went far beyond the points and goals he scored.
“His preparation, standards and commitment to the Mayo jersey were exceptional. For well over a decade, he carried enormous responsibility for this team and consistently delivered on the biggest days.
“I am particularly grateful for the role Cillian played in 2026. His opportunities on the field were more limited than he had been accustomed to throughout his career, but his importance to the group never diminished.
“He led quietly, advised younger players and supported the management and his team-mates throughout the year. He put the needs of the team ahead of his own. I am delighted that after everything Cillian gave to Mayo football, he leaves the intercounty game as an All-Ireland champion.
“On behalf of the management team and the entire playing group, I want to thank Cillian for everything he has given to Mayo.”

title: Walls, windows and ceilings of Limerick house destroyed during ‘student party’
description: Gardaí investigate damage caused to property in the city in the early hours of Wednesday
content:
Gardaí are investigating a break-in and criminal damage at a house in Limerick linked to a student party in the early hours of Wednesday.
Investigating gardaí are seeking the “public’s assistance” as part of their investigation into “burglary and criminal damage at a domestic residence”.
Videos showing young people running amok in the house was shared on social media .
Walls and ceilings were knocked through and fixtures and fittings were torn down in the overnight vandalism.
One video showed young people throwing a shelving unit through a window.
“Shortly before 1am, gardaí were alerted to a large public gathering in a domestic residence. Gardaí attended the scene and no persons were present inside the domestic residence which had undergone significant criminal damage,” gardaí said.
A technical examination of the scene was carried out and Garda investigations were “ongoing”.
Other homes in the same estate and surrounding areas have been badly damaged in similar incidents over the years.
The video showed a group of suspected students screaming and laughing as more damage was caused to the property.
A male voice is heard shouting, “Oh my god”, as a wheelie bin is thrown at glass doors.
Walls and ceilings were also torn down in the property.
At one point during the video footage, the camera is pointed up at a ceiling on the first floor, revealing no ceiling but a gaping void into the attic and roofing joists.
The first floor of the property was also littered with what appeared to be attic and wall insulation, and fixtures and fittings in an upstairs bathroom were also destroyed.
“This is f*cked,” said another male in the video, while a female voice is heard saying: “No lads, every f*cking room, welcome to our house tour.”
A local person at the scene said: “All the windows have been knocked out of it. A couple of students said there was a party there; they must have all gone berserk.”.
A Garda spokeswoman said: “Gardaí received a report of an incident of criminal damage that occurred in College Court, Castletroy, Co Limerick, in the early hours of Wednesday morning 7th October 2026.”
The spokeswoman said gardaí conducted a “technical examination of the scene” and “investigations are ongoing”.
It was unclear if the youths filmed inside the property have any affiliation with University of Limerick ( UL ), which is located close to College Court.
However, in a statement, UL said it was “aware of an incident that took place off campus and that an investigation by An Garda Síochána is underway”.
“UL strongly promotes responsible behaviour and positive engagement with the community. While the vast majority of students are respectful and valued members of the community, the university recognises that instances of antisocial behaviour, including property damage, public disorder and other actions that negatively impact residents, are a matter of serious concern,” it said.
“There are mechanisms within the university student code of conduct for breaches of the code to be dealt with and complaints made to the University about individuals are taken very seriously.”

title: Halfway there? Gaelic games integration timeline is no clearer after Dáil committee
description: Mechanics of how the three organisations get there and when they’ll get there didn’t become any clearer on Wednesday
content:
Nobody, it seems, is quite sure where Gaelic games currently is along its rocky road to integration. And in the Houses of the Oireachtas on Wednesday, the journey veered down an unexpected off-ramp where Jon Bon Jovi was deemed as reliable a weathervane on the matter as anybody else right now.
For two hours and 14 minutes, the leadership of the GAA, LGFA and Camogie Association fielded questions on integration.
At times, the discourse meandered off point, from the Garvaghy Road to the GAA’s ongoing sponsorship arrangement with Allianz, from Man City’s overspending to 80s big-hair rockers Bon Jovi.
But within the jumble of it all, it was evidently clear that more than anything else the one morsel of information the 12 members asking the questions wanted to know was if there was a new target date for integration.
Some called it a timeline, others a timeframe. A timetable. A deadline. Call it what you will. “Just tell us, when will it be done?”
But if that was the general thrust of the questions, those in the dock didn’t come with answers.
In that regard, while the GAA, LGFA and Camogie Association arrived to the Oireachtas with good intentions, they also arrived with very little detail.
About 40 minutes in, on questioning about the letter that prompted Mary McAleese to step away from the process , GAA director general Tom Ryan namechecked the day Bon Jovi played Croke Park at the end of August (as he couldn’t recall the precise date) as the afternoon the association essentially resolved to step back from the 2027 commitment.
Senator Rónán Mullen later suggested it seemed the GAA had for a period been Livin’ on a Prayer in hoping the mess would somehow untangle itself.
GAA president Jarlath Burns grabbed his opportunity: “The line before Livin’ on a Prayer is, ‘We’re halfway there’.”
Laughter spread across Committee Room One. Mullen – who had handpassed the ball across the small parallelogram to Burns – congratulated the GAA president for taking full advantage of that open goal. Everybody was delighted with themselves.
Somewhere in New Jersey, one can only presume Jon Bon Jovi was busy laying out cones for under-14 camogie training when he received a text from the club chairperson to tell him he’d just been namechecked in Government Buildings in Ireland. “Oh, and by the way Jon, you’ll have to move to the back field tonight because the senior men’s footballers need the main pitch. Good lad.”
Integration. Everybody wants to make it happen. Everybody has committed to making it happen. But the mechanics of how the three organisations get there and when they’ll get there didn’t become any clearer on Wednesday.
It was a source of frustration in the room for the duration of the meeting.
All six power brokers arrived together – Ryan and Burns from the GAA, CEO Lyn Savage and president Trina Murray from the LGFA, and Camogie Association CEO Karen Dessain-Gelinet and president Brian Molloy.
They sat with each other in the upstairs lobby beforehand and they descended the stairs in lockstep. The optics were clear. Nothing like a show of unity to reassure the doubters. We’re all in this together, lads.
But of course it was a lack of unity that had brought them back to Leinster House. When they had appeared last in June, chairperson of the Steering Group on Integration (SGI), McAleese, had reaffirmed the group’s commitment to achieving integration by 2027.
A couple of months later the SGI was back in front of an Oireachtas Committee, McAleese had resigned, and the aspiration of 2027 had proven to be nothing but a fanciful fairytale.
And so Labour’s Alan Kelly, chair of the meeting, threw the ball in by pulling hard across the ankles of those seated to his left.
“I’m quite conscious of the fact, having read the transcripts of the last two meetings with this group, of the narratives and statements that were made previously and in some cases only a few months ago, so I’m going to ask members and witnesses to bear that in mind, the content of what was stated to this committee only three months ago, I think it’s important, I rarely ever have had to say that before.”
It was an early scolding. But not an unexpected one.
[ GAA integration will take ‘years’ to come together, says director Opens in new window ]
Senator Alison Comyn was the first to ask questions. And the first to seek a new timeline. She was not to be the last.
Over the course of the meeting, mostly Burns and Ryan offered various “personal” aspirations but they stopped short of committing to any date. They had been too badly burnt with the 2027 target to go stoking the cinders of that firestorm.
“I think that is a process that will take a number of years,” said Ryan.
Over the course of the conversation, vague possibilities about progress in 2028 were put forward, while Burns offered that it could take three meetings of Congress – for each association – to get it over the line incrementally.
They did, however, provide more clarity on the appointment of a new SGI chair, with an announcement expected in the next 48 hours.
“We met as a group on Monday and we agreed unanimously on a nominee for that position and that person has agreed to take up that role,” confirmed Ryan.
“Each organisation over the course of the next, I want to say 24 hours, will be meeting to formally ratify that person.”
Fianna Fáil’s Peter Cleere went for a straightforward approach, asking each organisation if they were completely committed to integration.
“Absolutely 100 per cent, that’s the easiest question I’ve been asked today,” replied Burns.
“Yes Deputy, we’re fully behind integration,” added Murray.
Cleere raised his arms out wide and smiled: “Jeez lads, we’re halfway there.”
But if the meeting starting with a scolding from Kelly, it ended with one too. Perhaps the GAA had hoped the loose promise of having something tangible to show at their Congress next February had sated the Oireachtas members, but they were mistaken.
[ GAA, LGFA and Camogie Association to present united front at Oireachtas hearing on integration Opens in new window ]
Because Kelly informed them he was scheduling another meeting for December.
“We look forward to a very positive meeting come December where we should have a lot more information,” he said.
Across the way, some folk started to scribble in their notebooks. A meeting that provided no timelines had ended with one. December, best to put that in the diary.

title: Christa Pike is ‘angry and confused’ after failed execution, say lawyers
description: Judge says she will order Tennessee officials to preserve ‌all evidence from attempt to execute Pike
content:
Christa Pike is “angry and confused” after regaining consciousness almost six days after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her, one of her lawyers has said.
Randy Spivey was speaking on Wednesday after a judge told the state to preserve evidence related to the case.
Pike (50) survived after executioners tried to give her two lethal doses of pentobarbital on September 30th. She was sentenced to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer.
“She is angry and confused about everything right now. She is very aware of what they did to her up to a point,” Spivey said during a news conference.
“I do not have an explanation for what happened between Monday night and Tuesday morning but I do know she has a long road to recovery,” he added.
“On Monday night, it was our understanding that Christa was brain-dead and that life support would be removed the next day. But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone ... Christa woke up and began talking.”
Spivey, who was not with Pike when she woke up, said he was told her first words were, “Where am I?” and “Who are you?”
The Death Penalty Information Centre says Pike is the only person to survive after receiving lethal injection drugs during an execution.
At a hearing on Wednesday in Nashville, Pike’s lawyers asked the court to order the Tennessee Department of Correction to save evidence in the case and provide more information about what went wrong.
[ Christa Pike conscious and speaking after failed execution in Tennessee, say lawyers Opens in new window ]
A judge ordered the state to preserve “anything that was in the actual room”.
“Part of the issue that we are facing is up until yesterday, our client was unconscious, unable to communicate with counsel, unable to communicate with medical providers, and without her consent,” a new lawsuit cannot be filed, Luke Ihnen, a federal public defender, told the court.
Her legal team said on Tuesday Pike’s prognosis remains unclear and, at a minimum, she faces a lengthy recovery. Her arms were burned and blistered after the attempted lethal injection and she is handcuffed to the hospital bed, they said.
