Costing at least €3,000 each, the department says the integrated modular body armour system (Imbas) combines the latest technology and is modified in the wake of lessons learned from conflicts in Afghanistan and Ukraine.
All 8,100 members of the Defence Forces will receive the armour and it will cost the exchequer €25 million.
The new system will replace the General Service Body Armour (GSBA), which has been in service since 2006.
The Defence Forces are also working on a modified helmet that will cost at least €1,000 each.
The armour comes in different sizes and 1,500 members of the Defence Forces were fitted last year to ensure all sizes could be accommodated.
The first deployment of the equipment in the field will be next month with the 69th Infantry Group, which, as it stands, will be the last United Nations interim force deployed to Lebanon.
It is also being designed for the needs of women who have previously struggled with body armour made exclusively for men.
Col George O’Connell said the armour, which weighs 12kg (26½ lbs) when complete kit is worn, contains components from Romania, Italy, Austria, France, Germany and Turkey.
The most important part of the equipment is the ceramic plate, which is intended to be a shot stopper.
Contrary to the name, the word “bulletproof” is a misnomer, he says, as no vest is fully bulletproof. He did, however, produce a plate which stopped rounds from a Russian-made Dragunov sniper rifle.
“We’ve taken what we consider to be the most common armour-piercing version of that, and we’ve tested our body armour against it,” he said.
“I don’t want our soldiers to know what this protects them against, because I don’t want them thinking, ‘Sure, I’ll be okay’.”
However, it did show indentations from the round, which would cause significant trauma to internal organs, though the soldier would be likely to survive.
The Imbas system is designed with ergonomics in mind and will provide a significant improvement on the GSBA regarding protection, size, fit and comfort.

title: Protests across Israel call for October 7th inquiry on third anniversary of attack
description: Thousands observed a moment of silence as Netanyahu promised to ‘complete the mission’
content:
Israelis gathered on Wednesday at some 400 protests across the country to mark the third anniversary of the October 7th, 2023, Hamas -led attack on southern Israel.
They renewed calls for a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that preceded the worst day in the country’s history, when 1,200 people were killed and 250 taken hostage to Gaza .
Israeli president Yitzhak Herzog launched the commemorations by lighting a memorial candle at the president’s residence at 6.29am, the time the Hamas attack started.
Herzog then travelled to Netiv HaAsara, a farming community on the Gaza border, where militants on hang gliders landed on October 7th at the start of the invasion.
Memorial services took place at kibbutzim and other communities along the Gaza border that bore the brunt of the Hamas onslaught after the border fence was breached at more than 100 separate locations in the first hour of the attack.
At noon on Wednesday, hundreds of thousands of people observed a moment of silence across the country.
Protesters brought the burnt-out shells of cars belonging to victims of the Nova music festival massacre to the demonstration outside the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, in Jerusalem.
Some 378 people were killed at the Nova site, the vast majority of them young revellers who were still dancing when the first rockets landed in the area. The rockets were followed minutes later by gunmen on motorcycles who opened fire indiscriminately.
Provocative art installations were also a feature of Wednesday’s events. At Tel Aviv’s Dizengoff Square, protesters dyed the fountain water red. Rows of cut-out human figures were laid along a Tel Aviv beach, alongside a message reading: “October 7th – the price of the failure.”
Nine-month-old Kfir Bibas was the youngest victim of the Hamas attack. He died in captivity in Gaza along with his mother and elder brother, Ariel (4). His father Yarden, who was kidnapped separately and returned to Israel, issued a heartfelt message at the ceremony in kibbutz Nir Oz. “Shiri, Ariel and Kfir. Sorry. Sorry that you are up there and I am here.”
Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu lit a memorial candle honouring the October 7th victims, saying: “We will complete the mission. We came to settle the score with all the murderers, and we will.”
Netanyahu has rejected blame for the security breach and resisted calls for an independent investigation.
A survey released on Wednesday found that most Israelis believe the goals set out by Netanyahu at the beginning of the war, described as “total victory”, have not been achieved.
Fewer than 20 per cent believe these goals have been achieved to a large extent or in full. Fewer than half of respondents believe Israel is safer today than it was before October 7th, while nearly a third believe the country is not as safe.
Israel’s bombardment and ground operations in Gaza ​since the October 7th attack have killed more than 74,000 people, including at least 1,400 killed in the past year since a US-brokered ceasefire, which halted major fighting but has failed to stop Israeli attacks or ​secure the disarmament of Hamas.

[ How Israel lost the world's support after October 7th Opens in new window ]

title: Jon Rahm’s LIV exit set to trigger mass exodus of players from stricken tour
description: Northern Ireland golfer Tom McKibbin is among the players who may follow Rahm’s lead
content:
Confirmation that Jon Rahm will play no part in LIV Golf in its post-Saudi Arabian form is likely to be only the start of a mass exodus from the breakaway circuit.
A bankruptcy hearing on Wednesday heard Rahm’s lawyer say “unacceptable” terms proposed by LIV 2.0 mean the Spaniard will shortly walk away from a tour which has lingering hopes of continuing as a going concern. Rahm’s departure from LIV, which he joined in 2023, was inevitable, but still a significant blow and moment in time given his status in his sport.
“Mr Rahm has independently reviewed the proposed terms of LIV 2.0 and has determined that those terms are unacceptable to him and he will not be participating going forward in LIV 2.0,” the two-time Major winner’s attorney, John Beck, said.
The expectation from those with knowledge of the LIV situation is that a batch of other players including Northern Ireland golfer Tom McKibbin, Tyrrell Hatton, Cameron Smith, Joaquin Niemann and Adrian Meronk will also flee the scene when legalities permit. The initial habitat for those players, from the start of next season, is likely to be the DP World Tour. LIV faces a race against time to earn commitment from players of even average quality in its mission to continue with 75-man events into 2027.
Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) abruptly confirmed in April it will end funding of LIV at the end of 2026. It is estimated the PIF spent more than $5 billion (€4.46 billion) on the project, which was intended to challenge golf’s established tours. LIV entered Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in the US last month, which was always likely to facilitate the departure of big names such as Rahm. They had signed for LIV on multiyear, multimillion dollar contracts which had become unaffordable.
Rahm’s representatives are “in advanced discussions for a consensual separation agreement” with LIV. Documents listing creditors had previously shown that Rahm had an unsecured claim of $7.5 million (€6.7 million).
The status of Bryson DeChambeau, LIV’s remaining marquee name, is unclear. DeChambeau is known to have little appetite to return to the PGA Tour in the US, with that sentiment thought to be mutual. DeChambeau’s preference has always been an elongated version of LIV but that competitive model remains open to much question.
LIV Golf, along with BC Partners Credit, has been outwardly bullish about its future. “Our goal is to facilitate LIV Golf’s emergence from the restructuring process on sound financial footing and with renewed momentum heading into the 2027 season,” said Ted Goldthorpe, partner and head of BC Partners Credit, in a statement.
An immediate winner from this mess is likely to be the DP World Tour. Golfers are expected to gravitate towards that circuit for 2027 as a means to potentially play their way back on to the PGA Tour. LIV has already cut ties with all but a skeleton staff.
LIV entered into a formal restructuring support agreement with BC Partners Credit on Tuesday. Full detail of that, including potentially $300 million (€268 million) financing, remains unclear.
Scott O’Neil, LIV’s chief executive, said: “We believe deeply in the future of this league and in the opportunity to build something distinctive alongside our players. We’re delivering on our major milestones and while there is still work ahead, today marks meaningful progress toward a player-owned, team-focused, truly global league that complements the wider game and creates new opportunities for players, fans, partners, and the next generation of golfers.”
Rahm withdrew from this week’s Spanish Open in Madrid in order to remain at home as his wife, Kelley, is expecting their fourth child. He previously settled a dispute with the DP World, formerly European, Tour which could have impacted his future Ryder Cup involvement. – Guardian

title: In pictures: Three years of war in Gaza
description: October 7th marks three years since a Hamas-led attack in Israel
content:
Israelis have marked the October 7th anniversary of the Hamas-led attack which saw 1,200 people killed and 251 taken hostage.
In the days after the attack, Israel launched a campaign of war in Gaza which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured more than 175,000, according to Gaza’s health ministry.
Last year’s US -brokered ceasefire calls for eventual reconstruction of Gaza. But little progress has been made as negotiators have failed to agree terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.

title: France’s school protests: What lies behind the anger
description: French government acknowledges country faces a ‘serious moment’
content:
E veryone in France was expecting protests, which are practically a seasonal tradition alongside autumn budget talks.
People were braced for a particularly challenging protest season too, given the ominous combination of a looming presidential election, soaring energy prices, and a government simultaneously facing spending demands from the public and the scrutiny of markets concerned about French debt.
But no one foresaw a revolt among teenagers, starting with one high school in a Paris suburb on September 17th before spreading across the capital and the country.
Governments are well versed in dealing with protests by unions. There are leadership structures, representatives to call, and a transactional aspect, with a shared understanding of what form a win could take.
But a grassroots wildcat protest movement by high schoolers is very different. Who are the leaders? What are their demands? Can the movement be directed or contained?
Casting around for student representatives to question, some journalists have focused in on an impressively articulate and telegenic student of the well-regarded lycée Jacques-Decour called Elwan, whose discourses from the barricades have repeatedly gone viral on social media.
Elwan brushed away questions as he marched this week, urging journalists to look for answers in the more deprived suburbs of Paris rather than among the comfortable.
“Go speak to the people in the banlieue, who need your support and need to be heard by the media,” he said. “They’re the ones with things to say.”
The protesters’ school-related complaints are quite concrete: no more gaps in teaching because substitute teachers can’t be found; improvements to school buildings that struggle with extremes of heat and cold; days that don’t run from 8am to 6pm.
They want a broader reorientation of attitudes around students’ needs, rather than treating pupils as silent recipients of choices made from above.
But protesters are also expressing far larger dissatisfactions. Many Palestinian flags and keffiyehs could be seen among the protest crowds. There is anger at “those in charge” for not preventing the destruction of Gaza .
Students also express existential questions: what kind of job can they expect to get in an age of artificial intelligence ?
Concern about the climate crisis factors in too. What future can they look forward to?
It could all be summed up as a sense of being failed by older generations, which is being expressed in a traditionally French way.
How can the government meet such wide-ranging concerns?
[ Inside the school protests in France that have spiralled into arson and street violence Opens in new window ]
So far, the response of the government has been to set up an online platform to receive students’ complaints and to bounce the issue back to schools, introducing half-days indefinitely to allow for “internal democracy” to resolve problems.
But it’s unclear this will be enough, and the pressure is on. Senior international figures have begun issuing dark warnings to France about the gravity of its situation.
“My message is, get your house in order,” IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva said on Wednesday.
Fears centre on the risk of a downward spiral of debt if the government cannot control spending, with markets forcing its cost of borrowing higher and higher. There are murmurs of another Eurozone crisis.
Eleonore Caroit, who is French development minister and due to visit Ireland on Thursday for an EU presidency meeting, says the government’s priority is “de-escalation”.
The minister has two children in school herself. Theirs is unaffected, as are the majority of schools in France, she is keen to stress: about 459 high schools are shut out of France’s 3,700.
The issues in schools aren’t so much a result of a lack of funding, she says – France spends more than average in the OECD – but a need for better allocation of funds.
Some schools need to be rebuilt. Those with the most problems already get additional money, but need more: they are in difficult neighbourhoods, are starting with less, and often struggle to hire teachers.
Nevertheless, “it is a serious moment,” she acknowledges.
“We have a serious budget that is not an austerity budget,” she says – you can almost hear the French government trying to thread the needle – “but that provides for the good trajectory to reassure, hopefully, the markets.”
But there are many parties who may not have an interest in the protests ending soon.
There is a long road ahead in budget talks, and some will want to continue momentum to place maximum pressure on the government.
The leading candidates for the presidential campaign, the hard-left Jean-Luc Mélenchon and hard-right Marine Le Pen , represent two poles of the political response to the protests and the bond markets restrain neither.
Mélenchon marches with the crowds, suggesting French debt can simply be cancelled and vowing to prosecute the governor of the central bank for “treason” for warning about the country’s finances.
Le Pen meanwhile condemns the chaos and promises to restore law and order, and somehow to cut the deficit while also lowering taxes and lowering the retirement age to 62.
It may suit both of them to continue like this, their differences starkly highlighted, and positioned as each other’s ideal political foils.

title: ‘I still miss my wee girl every day’: Families remember Creeslough victims on fourth anniversary
description: Áine Flanagan, who lost her partner Robert and daughter Shauna in the blast, said families ‘deserve answers’
content:
Hundreds of people, including the families of those who died in the Creeslough explosion of October 7th, 2022, gathered at the site of the tragedy on Wednesday to remember their loved ones four years on.
Ten people, ranging in age from five to 59, died in the blast. Robert Garwe and his daughter Shauna Flanagan-Garwe (5), Catherine O’Donnell and her son James Monaghan (13), Jessica Gallagher, Martin McGill, James O’Flaherty, Martina Martin, Hugh Kelly and Leona Harper (14) were all killed in the explosion.
Heavy rain gave way to bright sunshine at the scene of the tragedy, as prayers were said for lost loved ones.
At the stroke of 3.17pm, at the exact moment of the explosion, an eerie silence fell over the village.
Some family members who lost loved ones in the tragedy spoke after the short service.
Áine Flanagan, who lost her partner Robert and daughter Shauna in the blast, said that the families were now entering a fifth year without their loved ones.
She said it was “heartbreaking”, and all they wanted was the truth of what happened on that Friday afternoon in October 2022.
“We, the families, we deserve answers,” she said.
When asked what life was like without her partner and daughter, she replied, “It’s painful. I’m missing them every day.”
Donna Harper, whose daughter Leona was just 14 when she was killed in the explosion after entering the garage for an ice-cream, said the pain simply never gets any easier.
She said: “We’re standing here four years on, and it never gets any easier. I still miss my wee girl every single day, every moment of every day.”
“I stood here for almost 24 hours, across the road, waiting for my wee girl to be found, hoping and praying for a miracle that she would be brought out. That didn’t happen, and my wee girl never came home.”
She added that unless the families get the truth of what caused the explosion, they will never be able to move on.
“We need answers, we need to know what happened, why it happened, how it happened. We need to know the truth to be able to move on,” she said.
Her husband, Hugh, said he still recalls waiting at “this very spot” for his daughter’s remains to be taken out from the scene of the carnage.
However, he says it’s wrong to say that his only daughter is not with her family still.
Choking back tears, he said: “She is here. She’s with me. She’s there in the morning, she’s there at night ... first and last thoughts.
“But life is not the same. It’s changed.
“It’s just hard to put it into words, it really is, but the loss, it can’t be measured. It just can’t be measured,” he added.
He said he had one simple request for the Government – to never allow something like this to happen again to any other family.
“I just wish that the Government would come on board, that they would establish a public inquiry for the simple reason as to examine every possible avenue of how this was allowed to happen, and not let it happen again.”
Fr John Joe Duffy read out the names of the victims in the order that they were pronounced dead at the time of the tragedy at the service.
The families were joined in solidarity by members of the Stardust Victims’ Committee as well as members of the Bloody Sunday Trust.
Fr Duffy appealed to everyone gathered to support each other on their journey of healing.
He said: “As we gather here today, as we stand here in this place today, grief does not end, and everyone, while on a collective journey, is at a different stage on the road towards healing.
“Some may have started that journey, while others have found that they have not yet been able to even begin on that journey to healing.”
Members of the emergency services who attended the scene on the day were also present, as well as senior gardaí and a number of elected members of Donegal County Council.

title: TG4 and Screen Ireland budget funding amounts to ‘cut’ in real terms, industry warns
description: Concern for independent production sector after €20m reduction in State funding for RTÉ
content:
Budget 2027 will create a “very challenging environment” for the Irish film and television industry, screen producers have warned, after the Government cut RTÉ’s funding and decided against increasing TG4’s and Screen Ireland’s allocations.
The Coalition also opted against reintroducing an enhanced tax incentive for regional film and TV production companies, which Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport Patrick O’Donovan said he would like to revisit after last year’s budget.
Meanwhile, RTÉ was allocated €240 million in public funding for next year, €20 million less than it was promised after reaching a multiyear funding agreement with the previous government in 2024.
The minister also confirmed at a press conference on Wednesday that TG4’s funding would remain static next year. The Irish language broadcaster had requested an additional €11 million in funding in Budget 2027, bringing its total allocation to €76.4 million.
TG4 ard-stiúrthóir Deirdre Ní Choistín said the broadcaster would now have to “assess the impact” on its plans and strategic priorities for next year, “at a time when interest in the Irish language is at a record high and demand for Irish-language content is stronger than ever”.
RTÉ and TG4 are two of the biggest revenue engines for the Irish screen industry, commissioning millions of euros in programming each year.
RTÉ spent €51.8 million through its Independent Production Unit (IPU) last year, while TG4 spent €36.4 million to commission 910 hours of programming from outside production companies.
Susan Kirby, chief executive of industry group Screen Producers Ireland , said that the sector was “significantly concerned” about the decisions made in the budget.
She said the lack of an uplift to TG4’s and to Screen Ireland’s funding amounted, in effect, to “reductions” when expected inflation is taken into account.
[ RTÉ says €20m cut in funding will impact on strategy as Minister criticises pace of reforms ]
“We would be extremely concerned that the reduction in funding would be most acutely felt by the independent production sector,” Kirby said of the decision to reduce RTÉ’s funding relative to what was promised in the 2024 agreement.
“This is the creative sector that RTÉ has identified as key to its reform plans under the New Direction Strategy, but the IPU budget is the easiest non-fixed element of the budget to reduce.”
The screen industry had also pushed for the reintroduction of an enhancement to the section 481 tax credit, for productions outside the Dublin and Wicklow corridor, which was phased out after three years in 2023.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, O’Donovan said the enhanced rate for regional productions was “something that we would keep under discussion with the Department of Finance”.
However, he did increase TG4’s allocation and roll out an enhancement to the relief for the film industry in last year’s budget, specifically aimed at the State’s growing visual effects industry.

title: ‘Irish Government is clearly not listening’: Nature groups criticise lack of budget funding for restoration
description: Budget allocates just €6m extra to NPWS despite experts saying €700m needed annually for nature restoration
content:
A dedicated Government fund to save Ireland’s nature will be announced soon, Minister of State Christopher O’Sullivan has said.
Confirmation of plans for the new Nature Restoration Fund came as it emerged that nature received hardly any additional funding in this week’s budget .
That is despite experts saying nature restoration needed new, dedicated funding of up to €700 million annually.
The budget allocated just €6 million extra to the National Parks and Wildlife Service ( NPWS ), the main agency tasked with overseeing nature restoration, bringing its overall budget to €113 million.
The Environmental Pillar, a network of 32 environmental NGOs, said that extra allocation equated to a “standstill” when inflation was taken into account.
“Government is clearly not listening to the needs of the country when it comes to investing in our critical nature infrastructure, which is buckling under a multitude of pressures,” said Oonagh Duggan of pillar member BirdWatch Ireland .
“At a time of most need to restore nature, Government has no message, no funding”.
Oliver Moore of Cultivate and Talamh Beo said the lack of additional funding in the budget was very disappointing.
“Ireland is legally bound to restore degraded ecosystems following the adoption of the EU Nature Restoration Regulation, and yet there is still no clear funding mechanism,” he said.
[ What are the key takeaways from Budget 2027? From income tax cuts to surprising omissions Opens in new window ]
O’Sullivan acknowledged the concerns, saying: “There’s no doubt that we need significant investment to restore nature across our island.”
However, he said money was already being invested in nature not only by NPWS, but by other agencies responsible for water quality, native woodland planting, river flow restoration, urban green spaces and agri-environment schemes.
“I want to add to this with an additional, multiannual Nature Restoration Fund that will sit on top of existing schemes,” he said.
“I’ve been working on this for a number of months with colleagues across Government, and I hope to have news to share on this soon.”
The Minister did not indicate the level of finance sought.
In April, the independent advisory committee formed to make recommendations on the State’s Nature Restoration Plan said it would need ring-fenced funding of €700 million a year to implement.
EU member states must prepare nature restoration plans to bring 30 per cent of degraded habitats back to health by 2030, 60 per cent by 2040 and all by 2050.
[ Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work Opens in new window ]
Ireland has some of the most degraded habitats in the EU, with 90 per cent of protected sites in bad or unsatisfactory condition.
Ireland was among the first countries to complete its draft nature restoration plan, submitting it to the EU last month, an indication, O’Sullivan said, of how serious the Government was about tackling the problem.
“We remain committed to ensuring that Ireland has the necessary resources in place to deliver on our ambitious nature restoration goals,” he said.

title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded to two scientists who solved century-old mystery
description: French and Japanese scientist win 2026 prize for discoveries that have been important in manufacturing of pharmaceuticals
content:
A French and a Japanese scientist won the 2026 Nobel Prize in chemistry for discoveries that have been important in the manufacturing of pharmaceuticals .
Henri B Kagan and Kenso Soai will share a 12 million-krona ($1.2 million) award, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm said in a statement on Wednesday.
Their work helped lay the scientific foundations for asymmetric synthesis, a central technique in modern pharmaceutical chemistry. It allows drugmakers to selectively produce the desired mirror-image form of a molecule with a therapeutic effect instead of making the other one that can cause unnecessary and sometimes harmful side effects.
An example of where the active substance’s mirror image caused harm was the thalidomide scandal in the early 1960s. Thousands of children were affected by birth defects caused by the drug, used as a sedative and morning-sickness remedy.
Kagan (95), is affiliated with what used to be called Université Paris-Sud in Orsay, France. Soai, who was born in 1950, is professor emeritus at Tokyo University of Science.
“Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously,” Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in the statement. “The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular.”
Outside medicine, the optimised reaction can help companies that manufacture “substances that are intended to interact with living beings, such as pharmaceuticals, flavours, scents and agricultural chemicals,” the committee said, adding that it can also be used to produce new materials.
The Nobels are annual prizes for achievements in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace and have arguably become the world’s most prestigious science awards.
[ Trio awarded Nobel Prize in medicine for research on mysteries of brain Opens in new window ]
The five prizes were established in the will of Alfred Nobel, the Swedish inventor of dynamite, who died in 1896. A prize in economic sciences was added by Sweden’s central bank in 1968.
The prize money this year was increased by 1 million kronor per category in connection with the 125th anniversary of the awards.
The laureates are announced until October 12th in Stockholm, with the exception of the Nobel Peace Prize, whose recipients are unveiled on Friday by the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo. – Bloomberg

title: RTÉ ‘caught off-guard’ by €20m cut in funding in Budget 2027
description: Patrick O’Donovan said he was not happy with progress to date on broadcaster’s transition ‘more agile, smaller’ organisation
content:
RTÉ director general Kevin Bakhurst has rejected Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan ’s assertion that the pace of reform at Montrose has been inadequate after the Government cut the national broadcaster’s funding in Budget 2027 .
RTÉ reached a landmark multiyear funding deal with the previous government in 2024. Under the agreement, the broadcaster would receive €725 million over three years: €225 million in 2025, €240 million in 2026, and €260 million in 2027.
However, O’Donovan announced on Wednesday RTÉ would receive €240 million next year, saying that he was not happy with the pace of change at the broadcaster and its transition to being a “more agile, smaller” organisation.
The decision appears to have been made at the last minute and, according to Bakhurst, it caught the broadcaster off guard. He told staff in an email on Wednesday that he “completely rejects the assertion that the pace of reform has been too slow.”
Bakhurst said the decision “is one we had not anticipated and will inevitably impact our ability to deliver our five-year strategy”.
Over the past two years, RTÉ has axed its in-house documentary unit, outsourced its religious affairs programming, and cancelled Upfront with Katie Hannon. It has also set out plans to outsource Fair City and The Late Late Show.
However, the Government has reportedly been disappointed by the pace of a job-shedding programme, through which RTÉ aimed to cut 400 jobs.
“I think it is well documented that you know that there were issues with regard to the voluntary redundancy that could be achieved in the last round, and obviously we would hope that that would be able to be advanced,” O’Donovan said on Wednesday.
[ RTÉ set to run up four-year €960,000 Dublin hotels bill for contributors and celebrity guests Opens in new window ]
Speaking at a press conference, the minister also said his department had “very little scope, in relation to what resources we had available”.
Most of the State funding to RTÉ is to come from licence fees. However, RTÉ required a €41.3 million top-up from the exchequer last year. Bakhurst told the Oireachtas Public Accounts Committee in July that the organisation will also need €54.8 million in direct funding this year from the Government, due to an ongoing decline in licence fee revenues.
In a statement earlier, Bakhurst said RTÉ had “some important decisions to make” if the funding agreement it had with the Government “will no longer be honoured”.
On job cuts, he said the broadcaster had “already managed to exit almost 100 people from the organisation, despite the late approval of the voluntary exit programme and a short window to enable people to leave.
“The Government’s decision to reduce this public funding agreement by €20 million at this late stage, when we have already made important commitments to our audiences, to the independent sector, to other important stakeholders and to RTÉ staff, is one we had not anticipated and will inevitably impact on our ability to deliver our five-year strategy.
“If the three-year multiannual agreement will no longer be honoured – we now have some important decisions to make.”
[ RTÉ’s new Listen app tells us some things about its future direction but keeps others hidden Opens in new window ]

title: ‘Very disturbing behaviour’: Teen jailed for two years for ‘appalling’ abuse of half-sisters
description: The boy was between 14 and 15 when he abused his half-sisters in the family home
content:
A teenager jailed for two years for the “appalling” abuse of his two young half-sisters will also be subject to an eight-year post-release supervision order, a court has ruled.
The Central Criminal Court heard that the abuse came to light in March 2023 after the children’s mother walked into the boy’s room and saw him abusing his five-year-old half-sister while recording it on his phone. His then two-year-old half-sister was also in the room.
The now 18-year-old pleaded guilty to multiple counts, including three of sexually assaulting the older half-sister and one of orally raping her, and two of sexually assaulting the younger half-sister.
The investigation found a video of the boy masturbating on a bus, the court heard. In September 2023, after the abuse of his half-sisters was discovered, he was found viewing child sexual abuse material on a school laptop during a class.
On Wednesday, the boy was handed a four-year sentence with the final two years suspended on very strict conditions for four years.
He will also be subject to the Sex Offender’s Act for five years and an eight-year post-release supervision order.
The boy was between 14 and 15 when he abused his half-sisters in the family home on various dates between 2022 and 2023.
He cannot be named as all parties have a legal right to anonymity.
When the boy’s phone was analysed, 408 images and 11 videos were found, including some of him sexually abusing both girls.
Thousands of videos and images of adult pornography were also found.
[ Boy (8) settles action over circumstances of birth at Cork hospital for €7.5m Opens in new window ]
The boy was sent to stay with his father the next day, but returned to sit his Junior Certificate. He then went back to his father’s home for the summer before going back to school.
While there was a safety plan, it later became clear that the boy couldn’t remain in the family home. He went into specialised foster care, as he could not live with others under 18. More recently, he has been living in an aftercare placement and completed his Leaving Certificate online.
After hearing the facts earlier this year, Judge Paul McDermott agreed to a defence application to allow the boy to complete his Leaving Certificate and a therapeutic programme.
However, there had been concerns in recent months that the boy was not fully complying with his strict bail conditions.
The court heard earlier this week that the boy was seen by a case worker with a mobile phone in August.
[ Woman’s High Court case against adult websites adjourned over $120m US settlement Opens in new window ]
Michael Bowman, defending, said his client is aware he can’t have a phone.
The judge finalised sentence on Wednesday.
The judge noted this case was about “very disturbing behaviour” by a young teenager who had repeatedly abused his “very young” sisters over a protracted period.
He said that the footage was “appalling”.
The judge said the mother had been placed in the “most difficult position imaginable” and had “done her very best by each of her three children”.
The boy is assessed as being at high risk of reoffending by the Probation Service.
A multidisciplinary structure is considered necessary by adult services.
Last month, the boy admitted to buying and selling 10 smartphones since his 18th birthday, downloading certain apps, viewing pornography and having a “deviant sexual interest in young girls”.
McDermott indicated that a “different approach is now required” and that a custodial sentence would be imposed.
The judge noted both girls have received counselling and the family decided not to make a victim impact statement. He said the court respected this decision, and considered that “terrible damage” had been done to the girls and to the family unit.
The judge outlined the headline sentences which would apply on each count for an adult, including 12 years for the oral rape.
[ Man charged with murder of Tadhg Farrell (4) and Mary Holt (60) in Edenderry house fire Opens in new window ]
He reduced each headline sentence to reflect that the boy was a child in the eyes of the law at the time of the offending.
The judge also noted the mitigation, including the boy’s early guilty pleas, admissions, his social isolation and exploitation by others.
McDermott suspended the final two years to incentivise his engagement with services and to supervise his return to the community.
The conditions for the part-suspended sentence include that the boy engage with any programmes to address his sexual offending.
A full Tusla investigation also took place.
The court heard his mother is willing to allow him to remain in her life, so long as he addresses his offending behaviour.

title: Mark Zuckerberg paid more than €50m for Strancally Castle in Co Waterford, register shows
description: Sale figure published on Wednesday includes the amount paid for the principal residence and up to an acre of land
content:
Mark Zuckerberg , the billionaire chief executive behind social media giant Meta , and his wife, Priscilla Chan, paid more than €50 million for Strancally Castle in Co Waterford, according to the Property Price Register.
The sale figure of €51,171,155, which was published on Wednesday, is close to double the estimated price tag put on the property at the time of sale by property market sources.
It includes the amount paid for the principal residence and up to an acre of land. Therefore, the couple’s total spend would greatly exceed what appears on the register when the entirety of the 440-acre estate is considered.
The date of sale was recorded as August 17th, 2026.
When the sale was first reported by The Irish Times three days later, on August 20th, it was believed to have achieved in the region of €20 million to €30 million based on the quality of the residence, which has undergone a full restoration over the past 20 years.
Zuckerberg and his wife completed the purchase of the Gothic-revival style house and estate on the banks of the river Blackwater from owners Michael and Giancarla Alen-Buckley.
“Mark and his family are excited to continue caring for this historic home and look forward to spending time in Ireland, where Meta maintains its international headquarters,” a spokesman for Zuckerberg said.
Built originally around 1830 for John Keily, a former Tory MP, Strancally Castle was, according to its description in Brian De Breffny and Rosemary Ffolliott’s book The Houses of Ireland, “designed by the Pain brothers on a lavish scale; it took a brisk walk of 4½ minutes to reach the diningroom from the kitchen”.
Architects James and George Richard Pain designed the main house and a nearby folly tower house and an inlet quay on the banks of the river Blackwater.
Alen-Buckley, a cofounder of London-headquartered private investment firm RAB Capital, and his wife, who is a daughter of the late Charles Forte and sister of Rocco Forte of the Rocco Forte Hotels group, acquired Strancally Castle 25 years ago.
[ Original home of Mark Zuckerberg’s Irish castle is immortalised in verse as the site of gruesome deeds Opens in new window ]
The three-storey building extends to 16,000sq ft. In a statement issued to The Irish Times, the Alen-Buckleys said: “We leave our home of 25 years fondly and are grateful for the opportunity we have been given to save and restore Strancally Castle ... We are delighted that Mark and his family intend to build on our stewardship by continuing to invest in maintaining and enhancing the property and grounds as their home in a sustainable manner ... We wish them and their family much happiness in this unique and blessed place.”
It is understood Zuckerberg and his wife will continue to live in the United States and intend to use Strancally Castle when in Ireland, where Meta, owner of social media platforms Facebook and Instagram, has had its European headquarters since 2009. The company employs about 1,500 people in Ireland.
Zuckerberg’s interest in acquiring a home here emerged last summer when Liberty Media billionaire owner John Malone told the Wall Street Journal that the Meta chief had offered to buy his Castlemartin House and Estate in Kildare from him.

title: Oracle to cut another 70 jobs in Ireland in AI cost-cutting push
description: Cloud computing giant has already shed around 150 Irish roles this year
content:
Oracle is looking to cut another 70 Irish jobs this year as it continues to trim costs to fund its expensive push into artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure and data centres.
The US cloud computing giant, which has already shed around 150 jobs in Ireland this year, started a collective redundancy process today after informing staff of its plans on Tuesday.
The Irish Times understands that staff were told Oracle is planning to cut 70 jobs, mostly concentrated in engineering and development roles, with some sales and finance positions also expected to be eliminated.
It is understood that Oracle, which has not responded to requests for comment, employs around 650 people in the Republic after its most recent round of redundancies.
Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke has been notified about the collective redundancy process.
Speaking at a press conference in Dublin on Wednesday, Burke said the Government wants to offset the impact of AI and its displacement of jobs in the Republic by training and retraining workers.
“I am aware of [the Oracle cuts],” he said. “You’re always going to have challenges with companies. Every single week, I get in a series of redundancy [notices].
“It’s one of the areas that took a while to get used to when I got this job, because when you have an economy with over 2.8 million people employed, you’re always going to have transition in that economy, and particularly right now, when you see some roles which are changing.
“You can see that happening through AI and other measures taking hold, but new opportunities are arising just as fast.”
[ Profits jump 80% at Oracle as it starts global redundancy programme Opens in new window ]
Oracle, which has offices in Dublin and Galway, has embarked on a large-scale programme of data centre building as it looks to bulk up its cloud computing unit with a focus on AI.
Citing people familiar with the situation, Bloomberg reported in March that the Larry Ellison-founded group was planning to shed jobs in areas of the business that it expects AI to make redundant.
Against this backdrop, Oracle said in June that it had slashed its global headcount by around 13 per cent, or about 21,000 employees, as it dramatically restructured the business. Oracle spent $1.84 billion (€1.64 billion) on severance payments and other exit costs related to the restructuring activities in the 12 months to the end of May.
Oracle’s share price, which has fallen by more than 25 per cent so far this year, has been under pressure as investors queried its enormous capital expenditure on data centres and AI infrastructure.
However, the S&P 500-listed company’s shares advanced during Tuesday’s session as rumours about more US job cuts spread online.
Separately, Ellison’s son, David Ellison, is at the centre of the $111 billion merger that will bring his Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros Discovery together into a new Hollywood titan. The deal was completed on Tuesday.
[ Female-looking AI agents were paid less than male ones in virtual office, study finds Opens in new window ]

title: Boy (8) settles action over circumstances of birth at Cork hospital for €7.5m
description: Senior counsel for the boy said his first breath was four minutes after his birth
content:
An eight-year-old boy who sued over the circumstances of his birth at Cork University Maternity Hospital ( CUMH ) has settled a High Court action for €7.5 million.
The settlement to Alex Marcio Hunka Riberio, who now lives in the Czech Republic , is against the HSE . The settlement is without an admission of liability.
Liam Reidy, senior counsel for the boy instructed by Cantillons Solicitors, told the court it was their case that from the very moment Alex’s mother went into the Cork hospital to the moment she left, she did not meet a consultant obstetrician. The boy was born in August 2018.
Counsel said at a very early stage it was realised the baby’s mother had gestational diabetes, and her pregnancy was regarded as high risk due to a high BMI and other matters.
The CUMH protocol in a high-risk case lays out certain things that should be put in place, including a clear delivery plan, counsel said. Counsel said it was their case that “all were broken in this case”.
Counsel said there was no consultant obstetrician and no birth plan. Alex was a large baby, he said.
He said during the birth, the baby’s shoulder became lodged and it was claimed that the baby suffered a fracture to the right shoulder area during a forceps delivery.
It is claimed the baby suffered an acute hypoxic ischemic episode during the delivery and was in a very poor condition when born and he required urgent resuscitation.
Reidy said that the boy’s first breath was four minutes after his birth.
Counsel said experts on the boy’s side would say the boy’s neurodevelopmental issues were caused by an alleged brain injury.
Alex had, through his mother Magdalena Hunkova, sued the HSE.
It was claimed that the baby was caused to have an allegedly extremely traumatic labour lasting almost eight hours before instrumental delivery, where he suffered a shoulder dystocia.
It was claimed the baby suffered neonatal encephalopathy, which his side contended occurred over a short period of time immediately before delivery.
His side also contended that the boy’s neurodevelopmental, neurobehavioral and neurocognitive difficulties were allegedly as a result of perinatal hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy.
In the proceedings, it was claimed there was an alleged failure to put in place an agreed management plan for delivery of the baby, which should and would have included the option of delivery by Caesarean section.
It was also claimed there was an alleged failure to consider or recommend delivery by Caesarean section to the mother who had poorly controlled diabetes, an increased BMI and a recognised large baby.
It was also contended there was an alleged failure to provide the mother with adequate informed advice to enable informed maternal choice in the method of delivery of her baby.
All claims were denied, and the HSE contended that the care provided to the mother during the antenatal period was of a reasonable standard.
Judge Denise Brett said she had no hesitation in approving the settlement. The judge noted it as quite a complex case, and she now hoped the settlement would bring Alex a better quality of life.

title: Andy Burnham faces first ballot box test in Holborn and St Pancras byelection
description: Holborn and St Pancras byelection will offer the first indication of whether Labour can retain disillusioned progressive voters under its new leader
content:
T he nascent leadership of Britain’s prime minister and Labour leader Andy Burnham faces its first electoral test on Thursday in a byelection in the Holborn and St Pancras seat vacated by the man he ousted from Downing Street , Keir Starmer .
Labour’s candidate, Camden council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali, is seen as being in a two-horse race for the inner north London seat with the high-profile leader of the Green Party, Zack Polanski .
Labour sources are cautiously optimistic about winning the seat but a shock victory for Polanski, whose political base is seen as stronger further east in London towards Hackney, is not being ruled out.
The slate of 15 candidates also includes veteran byelection candidate, George Galloway, of the Workers Party of Britain, although he is not expected to figure in the shake-up for the constituency, which includes well-known London landmarks such as King’s Cross and Euston stations and the British Museum in Bloomsbury.
The southern end of the constituency, closer to the centre of London, includes large numbers of students and young professional flat-sharers, as well as a larger-than-average contingent of foreign-born residents.
Further to the north, the constituency profile changes to include more settled communities around areas such as Kentish Town, where Starmer lives, and also Camden Town, which was traditionally an area with high numbers of Irish and Caribbean immigrants.
Polanski has energised the Green Party since he became its leader in September 2025, although it has also fallen sharply in the polls over the past five months and has been leaking support back to Labour since Burnham ousted Starmer in July.
A YouGov poll this week gave Labour a 16 point national lead over the Greens, although its lead in Holborn and St Pancras would be seen as far tighter.
The Green leader’s byelection bid is taking place against the backdrop of a tumultuous period for his party, which held its annual conference in Brighton last weekend; Polanski missed most of the gathering to campaign in London.
The Greens were roiled by an anti-Israel motion passed by members at its conference stating that “Zionism is racism”. Yet four of the party’s five sitting MPs were opposed to the motion, while Polanski, who was banned from Israel after it was passed, also did not back it. He has since suggested the party needs to “move on” from the divisive debate.
Labour, meanwhile, is on a high after Burnham’s successful first conference as leader. Abdi-Wali, a Muslim woman who arrived in Britain with her family aged six as a refugee from Somalia, has largely avoided wading too deeply into the Israel-Gaza debate during the campaign.
Instead, her campaign has focused more on local issues in the constituency. Polanski has also tilted his campaign more towards water services and rent controls in the latter stages of the campaign.
Labour’s campaign is being run by an MP based in south London, Liam Conlon, whose father is from Fermanagh and whose mother is Sue Gray, Starmer’s former chief of staff.

title: ‘We were chasing inflation’: DCU grilled over almost €4.4m loss on student accommodation plan
description: Oireachtas committee hears about university’s ‘viability gap’ in plan to house more than 1,200 beds
content:
Dublin City University (DCU) has planning permission until March 2029 to build accommodation housing 1,235 beds, but a “viability gap” is preventing the construction from proceeding, an Oireachtas committee has heard.
The university faced questions on Wednesday on its writing off expenditure amounting to €4.38 million (including VAT) incurred on professional fees for the proposed project, as reported in its financial statement for 2024/2025.
Dr Declan Raftery , DCU’s chief operations officer, said in 2017, the university commenced a capital project to construct 1,235 new student beds on its Glasnevin campus. The project was due to go to tender in September 2020 but “the Covid-19 pandemic changed everything for all of us”.
He noted that by March 2020, the DCU student accommodation project had incurred 69 per cent of the €4.38 million, as the project was “proceeding according to plan”.
He said another €700,000 was spent in 2020.
“We re-scoped the original project from 1,235 beds into a first phase consisting of 405 beds and completed two procurement competitions to try and seek best value for money.
“However, we have not been able to bridge the viability gap between the cost of construction, capital grant support from Government and the resulting rental levels that we believe by any reasonable measure students could afford to pay.”
[ Units for thousands of campus student beds unbuilt despite having planning permission Opens in new window ]
He told the committee that DCU is “disappointed and frustrated”.
After coming out of Covid, “we hit unprecedented inflation and supply chain issues that none of us expected or could understand”, he said. “We were chasing inflation.”
Raftery was addressing the Joint Committee on Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science. On Wednesday, it heard from representatives from DCU, University of Limerick, University of Galway, Munster Technological University and Technological University Dublin on the National Student Accommodation Strategy.
People Before Profit-Solidarity TD Richard Boyd Barrett asked Raftery if there was a viable financial model that would allow DCU to progress the 1,235 beds, but it could not be done unless the Government stepped in to help the university bridge the viability gap and deliver genuinely affordable accommodation.
Raftery responded: “Exactly ... can’t put it any better myself.”
When asked if the €4.38 million that DCU had written off could be salvaged to deliver the student accommodation, Raftery said “a large portion of it” could be.
He said the €4.38 million included costs such as integrated design team fees, a project manager, some surveys and “a tiny amount” of legal fees.
[ Most third-level colleges increase on-campus accommodation costs for coming year Opens in new window ]
“The capital grant aid available from the department, as far as they thought they could go at that time and the gap between what we thought we needed was €6.7 million. That was the gap we couldn’t bridge.
“What can students afford to pay versus the cost? The gap then is either tax incentives, capital grants ... there is still a viability gap.”
He added that the “pressures are everywhere in terms of cost of living”, citing students who choose to commute as they can’t get accommodation and have part-time jobs “to try and make ends meet”.

title: New Leinster SHC format to bring eight teams into expanded championship from 2028
description: Former GAA president Nickey Brennan says new structure would give tier two counties greater opportunities to establish themselves
content:
A little like the budget, the proposal for a new Leinster SHC structure appears to offer something for everybody.
Former GAA president Nickey Brennan is chair of the work group that devised the model and the Kilkenny man cut a genuinely excited figure at the launch of the proposal. Players, officials, supporters and, in particular, improving tier two counties; Brennan’s belief is that they will all see significant merit in the recommendation which gained Leinster Council approval on Tuesday evening.
There is still the hurdle of Congress to be navigated, but a green light there would see the existing six-team round-robin format binned in favour of two new groups of four.
Group A would comprise the top four teams from the previous season, while Group B would be made up of the fifth and sixth teams from the previous season, along with the two Joe McDonagh Cup finalists.
The new format wouldn’t kick in until 2028, although the 2027 championships would be used to determine starting positions, lending extra importance to next season’s results.
With Leinster quarter-finals and semi-finals included, as well as a playoff – between the two beaten semi-finalists – for an All-Ireland quarter-final place, the eastern championship could suddenly be loaded with fresh possibility and intrigue.
“I am excited, absolutely, I think it’s a new development for Leinster,” enthused Brennan, a former manager of the Kilkenny senior hurlers.
For supporters, his feeling is that it would be an enhanced product and he used the word jeopardy on several occasions.
“We have one knock-out game in Leinster at the moment – we’re now adding two Leinster quarter-finals, two semi-finals, a final and a third place playoff,” said Brennan. “So we’re now adding six what you could call knock-out games where there’s only one at the moment.”
Not all of those teams would be entirely eliminated, of course, but the feeling of the eight-man work group is that it would add a layer of unpredictability to proceedings.
“That’s real jeopardy,” said Brennan. “And we feel that in terms of supporters, they’ll be excited about that. Because there’s nothing certain, in terms of results.
“We also don’t know who the pairings might be in the semi-finals until we finish the quarter-finals. So there’ll be a draw there. There are all sorts of possibilities here.
“We do feel this will excite patrons, the amount of knock-out games. Because look, if you make it to a quarter-final and you lose it, that’s your year gone. And that has the potential to be what we might call a strong county at the moment.”
[ GAA integration will take ‘years’ to come together, says director Opens in new window ]
For the existing tier one counties, they will be part of an attractive Group A that stacks up well against the blockbuster five-team Munster round-robin.
Brennan was quick to state that Leinster’s Group B teams would be afforded the same respect as their Group A counterparts and, where possible, equal billing.
“I’d like to think they’d get decent coverage and decent respect,” he said, pointing to the possibility of Group A and Group B double-headers. “We know that some of these games may not equate to some of the big games in Munster, but I think that’s a narrow focus to be looking at it just like that.”
Further down hurling’s food chain, the threat of immediate relegation for teams promoted from the Joe McDonagh Cup, such as Kildare, who were highly competitive last summer before ultimately dropping back down to tier two, will be removed.
“I know Brian Dowling is particularly delighted about this,” said Brennan of the Kildare manager.
For county and provincial officials, the new format carries a similar overall fixture footprint and guarantees a number of revenue-spinning games. Brennan is also confident that the format would prepare teams well for the All-Ireland series.
“That’s the hope anyway, because I totally accept that based on the 2026 All-Ireland quarter-finals, it was a no-show by Leinster teams, there’s no point in us saying otherwise,” said Brennan.
“Dublin and Offaly just didn’t fire on those particular days. Hopefully the extra bit of competition that’s built in here around the knock-out stages will put teams in a better shape going forward to take on their Munster counterparts.”
Brennan acknowledged potential issues further down the line should New York reach the Joe McDonagh Cup competition. After winning the Lory Meagher and Nickey Rackard Cup competitions, the Exiles will play in the Christy Ring Cup in 2027. He also said Kerry potentially reaching a McDonagh Cup final – the two finalists would be included in the following season’s Leinster SHC – would be problematic.
“There’s ways around this, but it would be remiss of me not to mention it,” said Brennan of the New York and Kerry situations.
National head of hurling Willie Maher described it as a “very, very clear and simple championship” format.
“It allows for sustainable competition over time, that we don’t have that yo-yoing effect of, for example, Kildare going down after a gallant effort this year,” said Maher.
