title: ‘This budget is not for families’: Childcare and new savings scheme the Budget 2027 measures you most want to know about
description: Hundreds contact our post-budget Q&A seeking clarity on some of the initiatives announced
content:
Key details of Minister for Finance Simon Harris’s new personal investment account were the centrepiece of his budget speech. But childcare was the issue that really animated readers in the Budget Q&A run by The Irish Times on Wednesday.
Talk of the weekly cost of care falling to €550 a month per child from a current “maximum” of €735 read like fantasy to parents currently paying monthly bills of close to €1,000.
“Why is there not more scrutiny on the fact that the childcare reductions only apply to a very specific set of terms for childcare of under 50 hours a week. Next to no creches in my area, north Dublin, offer anything less that 50,” one reader, Dermot, wrote.
“I feel the sneaky underhanded nature of this announcement should be called out and it’s despicable that the Government say the budget is for families when it could not be further from the truth.”
Crunching the numbers, it looks like those parents will be paying closer to €750 or even €800 when the budget measures come into play in September next year, not €550.
That’s still a significant benefit, but the Minister’s choice of words left a bad taste among readers.
The new investment scheme was not forgotten, with plenty of readers questioning our panel of Beryl Power and Ruth Gilligan from PwC and Dominic Coyle on how they could make the best use of it. Others, however, highlighted the need for an associated financial literacy campaign.
“What is the interest rate in the new investment scheme,” Maria asked, not quite grasping the minister’s determination to tap some of the €170 billion in bank coffers into what he sees as more productive and certainly higher-risk investments.
Quite a few readers had one eye on the new scheme as a way of putting money away for their children. That’s not on the cards at the outset – you will have to be 18 to open an account – though Harris held out the possibility of extending the scheme to children in the longer term.
Other issues that were engaging readers were the old reliables of when welfare increases would kick in and how much people would get, and issues around access to grants for people looking to make their homes more energy efficient.

title: Naughton makes ‘no apologies’ for extra €646m in education funding after budget overrun
description: Department of Education is allocated €14.4 billion for Budget 2027, an increase of €712 million on last year
content:
Minister for Education Hildegarde Naughton has said she makes “absolutely no apologies” for the additional €646 million funding her department required last year, as she announced details of the record education budget for 2027 .
The Department of Education was allocated €14.4 billion in total for 2027, an increase of €712 million on last year when the supplement is included.
At a post-budget press briefing on Wednesday, Naughton was asked if she would apologise to her ministerial colleagues for the levy imposed on other departments to cover this supplementary funding.
“I make absolutely no apologies for fighting for €646 million earlier this year,” Naughton said, adding her department was “underfunded” last year and that her “priority was to reset the base”.
“I am confident that the base has been reset, but I’m also conscious that we are a demand-led department,” she said, meaning they did not have control over school numbers.
One issue the Department of Education would be seeking cost savings on was the school transport scheme, examining whether existing local bus services could be used for school transport places, Naughton said.
On the issue of pending school closures due to teacher strikes, the Minister urged teachers’ unions to go into negotiations with the Government on a new public sector pay deal.
“Nobody wants to see disruption. Teachers, parents, nobody wants to see closures, so I’d encourage everyone to sit around the table to try and come to some deal as soon as possible,” Naughton said.
[ Ireland spends less on education than OECD average, new data shows Opens in new window ]
Almost all primary and secondary schools are due to close on October 14th and 21st as unions escalate their dispute over a new national pay deal.
Details of how the €14.4 billion would be spent were outlined by the department on Wednesday.
Among the key measures was an extra €17 million for capitation funding in schools, which covers utility bills, maintenance and insurance costs.
That equates to an increase of €68 per pupil at primary level, and an increase of €40 per pupil at post-primary level.
Some €21 million has been set aside for curriculum development across senior cycle, primary and Gaeltacht education.
An additional €6 million will go into the DEIS Plus programme, allowing for the expansion of the funding scheme for the most disadvantaged schools in the country.
A further €9 million will go towards more Home School Community Liason teaching posts.
[ How Budget 2027 will impact families: From renters to stay-at-home parents Opens in new window ]
In terms of special educational needs, there is funding in this budget for 1,353 more special education teachers and 2,339 additional special needs assistants.
There will also be €6 million allocated to the expansion of special education training for teachers, including the roll-out of a new inclusive education accredited course, which will be paid for by the State.
This course will cover numeracy, literacy and other elements of special education teaching, including dyslexia.
There will also be an €11 million allocation to fund school leadership support, increasing the numbers of deputy principals in primary and post-primary schools.

title: New papal nuncio likely to continue radical downsizing of Catholic dioceses in Ireland
description: Polish nuncio succeeds Archbishop Montemayor, who oversaw some of most radical changes in 900 years
content:
A new papal nuncio to Ireland has been appointed by the Vatican from Poland. Archbishop Jan Romeo Pawlowski (65) is currently papal nuncio in Greece.
He was born in 1960 in Biskupiec, northern Poland, and was ordained in 1985 before studying for a doctorate in canon law at the Gregorian University in Rome.
Pawlowski then entered the Vatican’s diplomatic service and was made archbishop in 2009 when appointed papal nuncio to the Republic of the Congo and Gabon.
In 2015 he returned to the Vatican , serving as its secretariat of state becoming head of its section for diplomatic staff in 2017. In 2022 he was appointed papal nuncio to Greece.
He speaks Italian, French, Russian, English, German and Portuguese.
A papal nuncio is effectively the Vatican’s ambassador to Ireland. He will also automatically become dean of the diplomatic corps in the State.
In church terms his primary role is in the appointment of bishops, making recommendations to Rome. More recently in Ireland the nuncio has also played a key role in the reduction of Irish Catholic dioceses.
[ Called to the church: ‘I broke her heart but I felt I could do more for people by being a priest’ Opens in new window ]
The new nuncio succeeds Archbishop Luis Mariano Montemayor (70), who served in Ireland from February 2023 until July this year, when he retired.
In his three years, Archbishop Montemayor, originally from Argentina and another Vatican career diplomat, oversaw some of the most radical changes in the structure of the Irish Catholic Church in 900 years, with a significant reduction in the number of dioceses.
In 1111, at the Synod of Ráth Breasail, Ireland’s current diocesan structure was set up.
Some “downsizing” had taken place before Archbishop Montemayor’s arrival in 2023. In 2021 Clonfert was joined with Galway. But on his watch this process was sped up, with Achonry joining Elphin in 2025 and, earlier this year, Killala with Tuam. It meant six west of Ireland Catholic dioceses were reduced to three.
Last July, Ossory diocese – mainly Kilkenny – was similarly joined under one bishop, with Ferns diocese, mainly Wexford.
[ ‘My proposal was to stop Confirmation’: Ireland’s ageing priests under pressure as numbers drop Opens in new window ]
When it came to the appointment and transfer of bishops, Archbishop Montemayor was similarly active. He appointed Fr Paul Connell Bishop of Ardagh and Clonmacnoise in 2023 and Fr Donal Roche as auxiliary bishop of Dublin in 2024.
In 2024 he oversaw the transfer of then Bishop of Raphoe (Donegal) Alan McGuckian SJ to Down and Connor diocese, mainly Belfast and Antrim. Also that year, then bishop of Achonry Paul Dempsey became an auxiliary bishop of Dublin.
In 2025 Bishop of Elphin Kevin Doran was named also Bishop of Achonry, while last February, Archbishop of Tuam Francis Duffy was named Bishop of Killala.
Last year too Bishop of Ossory Niall Coll was transferred to Raphoe diocese. Last February, Archbishop of Tuam Francis Duffy was also named Bishop of Killala while last July Auxiliary Bishop of Armagh Michael Router, was appointed Bishop of Derry and Bishop of Ferns Ger Nash was also named Bishop of Ossory.
It is likely such downsizing will continue under Archbishop Pawlowski.
More immediately, both Bishop of Clogher (mainly Monaghan) Larry Duffy and Bishop of Cloyne (mainly east Cork) William Crean are due to retire later this year, and there has been speculation for some time that Clogher may be joined with its neighbour Kilmore (mainly Cavan) and Cloyne with Cork and Ross diocese.
Further, since 2018 the Catholic Primate and Archbishop of Armagh Eamon Martin has been administrator of the small Co Down diocese of Dromore. It followed the resignation of then Bishop of Dromore John McAreavey in a controversy over his handling of child abuse allegations against the late Fr Malachy Finnegan. That arrangement is expected to be formalised.

title: Pretax losses at Clerys Quarter firm more than halve to €6.8m
description: Company envisages selling asset by end of year
content:
Pretax losses at the firm that has developed Clerys Quarter on Dublin’s O’Connell Street last year more than halved to €6.85 million.
Accounts filed by OCES Property Holdings Ltd show that the 2025 loss arose chiefly from interest payments of €7.1 million.
The company last year recorded an operating profit of €261,135 compared to an operating loss of €7.9 million in 2024.
Pretax losses at the company reduced as the group recorded a €353,505 gain in the value of an investment property compared to a €5.5 million impairment in 2024 – a positive swing of €5.86 million.
The pretax loss of €6.85 million last year is 55 per cent down on the pretax loss of €15.27 million in 2024.
At the end of 2025, the group’s investment property had a book value of €55.44 million that comprises assets currently undergoing redevelopment.
In a note with the accounts, the directors said that the company’s business plan was to increase occupancy levels within the property and subsequently sell the asset, which is not envisaged until the end of 2027.
The note said that the main property development is completed with the lease-up ongoing.
Some of the brands operating from Clerys Quarter include Decathlon, H&M, Pret A Manger and on-the-go sushi brand, ROLLED.
A third of the office space was also sold to the HSE on behalf of the Rotunda Hospital, for a new maternity outpatient hospital catering for over 100,000 outpatients annually.
[ Clerys Quarter developer does not expect full occupancy until 2027 Opens in new window ]
Last year, revenues at OCES Property dipped marginally from €1.45 million to €1.41 million due to an increase in lease incentives offered to tenants in the current year.
The accounts showed that rental income last year increased by 7 per cent from €1.57 million to €1.68 million but lease incentives more than doubled from €124,181 to €266,603 resulting in the slight net revenue increase.
Paddy McKillen jnr is a director of the company and has a very small shareholding in the business through his Isle of Man registered Keillan Ltd.
Recently, the High Court granted McKillen jnr a protection certificate that will protect him from his creditors for 70 days as part of personal insolvency proceedings.
The court was told that McKillen jnr has liabilities of €27.7 million and has just €270 in his bank account.
In the new accounts for OCES Property Holdings, the directors state that they consider the result for the financial year and the financial year end position to be satisfactory.
The directors said that cash flow remained positive bolstered by an additional equity injection by the parent company, and the repayment of the debt facility during the year reduced finance costs incurred.

title: Tory party conference might have revealed British right’s new Brexit
description: Kemi Badenoch uses conference to sketch a low-tax, anti-migration vision while ruling out pact with Reform UK
content:
C onservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch promised to abolish inheritance tax on UK family homes, while also claiming Britain is heading for a “battle for the soul of the nation” with a Labour government she painted as fiscally profligate.
“We are running out of money,” she said, promising to focus on economic growth during her Tory conference speech at the International Convention Centre (ICC) in Birmingham.
Badenoch promised to restore her party’s trusted values on the economy and defence.
“It’s like the old days,” said one visibly delighted delegate to a volunteer usher, as party members filled the ICC’s Symphony Hall before Badenoch’s big speech. She was over-egging it. A YouGov poll has the Tories still seven points behind an accelerating Labour.
Still, there was an apparent outbreak of optimism among the party’s faithful, two years after its historic battering in 2024’s election. Ever since her barnstorming conference speech in Manchester a year ago, Badenoch’s Tories have found their feet.
“This party has two modes, panic and complacency. They’re not panicking,” said one seasoned observer, on his 11th Tory conference. “They say the mood is up, but that’s because they’re not at work and drinking here all day. Why wouldn’t the mood be up?”
Before Tories could find their way back from historic defeat, first the party’s delegates had to find the entrance into the Birmingham city centre venue.
This year’s “CPC 26” Conservative Party Conference emblem included an arrow pointing up and, naturally, to the right. This arrow emblem was on fences all around the venue’s meandering perimeter. Scores of confused delegates trying to find their way inside appeared to take the arrows literally, blindly following them down side streets.
Badenoch spent much of the conference pushing back against suggestions that, despite the sense of optimism, the numbers at the event were down.
[ The affluent English village that declared independence to stop an asylum centre Opens in new window ]
Broadcaster Jeremy Clarkson was hauled in on Monday to add stardust. Even he couldn’t resist remarking upon the visibly thin crowds. As he surveyed the hall from the stage, he quipped that some Tory delegates had come “dressed as empty seats”.
The party did not say how many were in attendance, but it was a fraction of the estimated 20,000 in Liverpool last week for the Labour conference.
There also seemed to be a decline in the number of business lobbyists attending compared to some previous years, a judgment on the Tories’ proximity to power.
No British political party conference is complete without hot-button cultural references among the exhibits. The Tories delighted in hitting a double.
Britain is currently enraptured with the Bayeux Tapestry on display in London, the first time the historical masterpiece has been in the country for almost 1,000 years. Separately, Westminster is also obsessed with AI.
Conference Tories lined up to view the “Birmingham Tapestry”, a full-sized 88 metre mock-up of the real thing, created using AI.
Instead of depicting Norman battles on horseback, it showed the first two years of UK politics under a Labour government, complete with a crying former chancellor Rachel Reeves. It also included scenes of Nicola Sturgeon unable to see her husband’s fraudulently paid-for motorhome, and Reform UK’s Nigel Farage arguing with a bin.
Over the past decade, Brexit has been a big issue at Tory conferences. This year, party members and Tory MPs seemed unsure how to react to Labour prime minister Andy Burnham’s recent attempt to reopen debate on rejoining the European Union.
One way to get Tories interested in Europe is to – literally – feed them. The EU delegation laid on a lavish spread on Tuesday afternoon, which drew a crush of Tories to hear shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugenhadt speak.
He vaguely referenced Brexit by urging Britain and the EU not to focus on reviving “the structures of the past”. Then, when mentioning Britain’s modern ties with India, he seemed to barely stop himself referring to it as a former colony.
[ Is Brexit back on the agenda for Britain? Opens in new window ]
One EU official watching Tugendhat speak told The Irish Times he was more worried about the party’s calls, led by Badenoch, for it to leave the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) so it could tighten up migration law.
Every mention by Badenoch of leaving the ECHR was loudly cheered in the main hall. Perhaps leaving the convention, which would have profound effects on Britain’s relationships with other countries, including Ireland, is the British right’s new Brexit.
Robert Jenrick, the former Tory front bencher who defected to become a senior member of Reform, was the conference’s pantomime villain. The crowd roared when Badenoch humorously hinted at his apparent treachery by alluding to a Tory “export boom” to its rivals – including Jenrick and also Suella Braverman.
The irony is that the Tory crowd in previous years cheered almost every public utterance by Jenrick and Braverman when they were senior Tory members seen as then-better representing grassroots views than the party leadership.
In her speech, Badenoch reiterated a promise from earlier in the conference to spend £10 billion (€11.8 billion) on a “Britannia Shield” missile defence system. She also rebuffed calls from some party’s supporters to “unite the right” by teaming up with Reform to defeat Labour.
Listing some of Reform’s supposed failings around financial probity and, she suggested, its problematic attitude to race, Badenoch said: “I’m not uniting with that.”

title: Minister rules out raising cap on Help-to-Buy scheme for homes worth over €500k
description: Budget increases in tax refunds do little to help those searching in Dublin market
content:
There will be no increase in the €500,000 cap on the Help-to-Buy scheme for first-time buyers, despite data indicating many new builds in Dublin are selling well above that price.
The amount first-time buyers can avail of to purchase their first home was increased in this year’s budget by €5,000, meaning they can now avail of a refund on taxes paid over the previous four years up to €35,000.
The scheme is only available for new-builds up to a limit of €500,000.
Speaking at a budget briefing, Minister for Housing James Browne ruled out increasing the €500,000 threshold on the basis it could add to house price inflation.
However, the Daft.ie quarter three report this year revealed the median price of a newly-built home in all parts of Dublin was either at or above the €500,000 threshold.
The median price ranged from €500,000 in north Dublin to €650,000 in south Dublin. Outside Dublin, the median price ranged from €337,548 in Co Monaghan to €453,744 in Cork city. The national median figure for new builds, according to Daft.ie, was €448,000.
“We didn’t touch the €500,000 limit because that is having to control over the overall costs of new builds,” Browne said.
“I think it is also driving productivity too, as it is making builders focus their mind in terms of how they want purchasers to be able to benefit from the Help-to-Buy scheme by keeping that house price below €500,000.”
He said the construction industry across Europe was not the most efficient or productive sector, “so we have to drive on that side of it as well”.
Browne said he did not believe that the Help-to-Buy scheme is driving inflation.
“House prices have been increasing, but we are satisfied that [the Help-to-Buy] scheme is not a key driver of house price increases and it is helping people get on the housing ladder who otherwise would not be able to do so.”
Minister of State at the Department of Housing John Cummins said the Help-to-Buy scheme, which was introduced in 2020, had helped 60,000 people to get on the housing ladder to date.
Figures released in August showed 48,878 applications for the Help-to-Buy scheme were approved since 2020. However, 88,532 people applied for the scheme.
Speaking on the Today with David McCullagh programme on RTÉ, Minister for Finance Simon Harris ruled out extending the Help-to-Buy scheme beyond first-time buyers or to the purchase of second-hand homes.
“To give you the honest answer, even if it is not the most popular answer, the idea of extending the Help-to-Buy has been toyed with whether it is a second-time buyer or somebody buying a second-hand home,” he said.
“The reason we haven’t done it is a fear that it will actually push up house prices more. While the first-time buyers grant is, of course, about giving people back some of their own money for a deposit, it is actually being brought in as a demand measure to get people to build more first-time homes.”
He said those who are thinking of buying a second-hand property can avail of the vacant property refurbishment grant.

title: ‘This is only the beginning,’ vows Mikel Arteta after signing £80m-plus Arsenal deal
description: Four-year contract secures Spaniard’s future and makes him the Premier League’s best paid manager
content:
Mikel Arteta has promised “this is only the beginning” of what he can achieve as Arsenal manager after signing a new long-term contract that would take his reign at the club beyond a decade if he sees it out.
The Spaniard is understood to have signed a four-year deal worth more £20m (€24m) a season, making him the best-paid Premier League manager. That is a hefty pay rise in recognition of his success last season as Arsenal ended their 22-year wait to be crowned champions after three successive runners-up finishes.
Arteta, who took over from Unai Emery in December 2019, is the Premier League’s longest-serving manager after the departure of Pep Guardiola from Manchester City. After losing the Champions League final last season to Paris Saint-Germain in a penalty shootout, the 44-year-old is targeting more success as he seeks to build a winning dynasty at Arsenal, where he previously served as captain under Arsène Wenger.
“It’s a privilege to commit my future to the club and to continue to work with exceptional people who want the best for Arsenal,” said Arteta. “This club is unique, its character and the way it makes you feel, and I have a great sense of privilege that our journey together will continue. We have already built a special bond and created memories that will last a lifetime, and what is so exciting is that this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together.
“This is such a proud moment for me and my family. I feel the love and respect from our fantastic supporters, and they have mine – and ours – in return.”
Arteta’s previous contract, which was due to expire at the end of this season, was believed to be worth about £10m a season plus a £5m bonus for reaching the Champions League. The new deal, to June 2030, cements his status as one of the best-paid managers in the world. His coaching staff have also signed extended deals.
“It has been an incredible journey so far and we are excited for what lies ahead in this special relationship,” said Arsenal’s co-chairs, Stan and Josh Kroenke. “Last season was an incredible moment in Arsenal’s history, a moment in which we created memories that will last a lifetime. We’re determined to create many more in the years ahead.
“We share a special bond with Mikel. We are so proud of everything we have achieved since he returned to the club in 2019. He has a deep understanding of Arsenal’s values and carries them in his heart. He knows what this club means to everyone connected to it and is committed to building on everything we have achieved together.”
Arsenal confirmed this week that they have shelved plans for a major expansion of the Emirates Stadium after Arteta is believed to have expressed concern over the disruption that would have been caused by any temporary move. His side face Leeds on Saturday as they attempt to bounce back from a surprise 3-0 defeat at Brighton before the international break that ended the champions’ 100 per cent start to the new campaign.

title: ‘He never lost his accent’: How missing Cork native built a happy life as a gay man in England
description: Patsy O’Sullivan disappeared without trace on Easter Monday from Lombardstown, Co Cork in 1992
content:
W hen Patrick O’Sullivan disappeared without a trace in 1992 , his family feared what might have happened to him.
The man from Lombardstown, Co Cork , was much loved by his late parents and six siblings, but unfortunately it was a very different time in Ireland and he went missing 34 years ago, his family believes, because of his sexuality.
They knew he was gay, but it “wasn’t condoned or even spoken about”, his brother Jerry said.
Patrick “Patsy” O’Sullivan disappeared without a trace just after he visited his family home on Easter Monday in 1992.
They received a call from gardaí in August this year, who told them that Patsy went on to have a life “full of joy” in the UK, marrying his partner and retraining as an auxiliary nurse.
The chef, who was 35 years old at the time, was due to return from his job in Kerry for a christening.
His older brother Jerry said it wasn’t easy for Patsy to grow up gay in the Ireland of the 1970s and 1980s.
“I was afraid something had happened to him back then [when he went missing] because of his sexuality. Because I remember what happened to me for being a brother of him. I can’t imagine what he went through himself.
“In the 80s and early 1990s that [being gay] wasn’t condoned or even spoken about. It was different times. The church was different. The older people were a very different generation than what they are now.”
Jerry said Patsy was much loved but circumstances were very difficult.
“I came up with the old generation. My father would have been very strict. They [his parents] knew [Patsy was gay] but it was never spoken about. My mother didn’t have an issue with it but my father would have. But him being gay was never spoken about.”
[ ‘A closure for us’: Cork family learns brother missing since 1992 died in UK two years ago Opens in new window ]
Patsy went to the UK in 1992 with “nothing” and experienced hard times, before receiving help from a nun called Sr Bridget Anne.
Life improved for him and in 1994 he met his lifelong partner. Jerry had a heartening hour-long phone call with a niece of Patsy’s partner in the UK on Tuesday.
“It gave me so much solace to what kind of life he had and the enjoyment he had in his life. He had been with his partner since 1994 and he changed his name [to Aldridge] in 1995.”
He and his partner were married by a priest who knew them very well and Patsy changed his surname in 1995 to take the name of his partner.
“I can’t think as to what he had to go through as he had to start a life all over again and leave six siblings and his parents behind him. And to never turn back and speak to anyone again. That must have been horrendous for him.
“I can only imagine what he went through. I can take a lot of comfort from what I am after being told today.”
Jerry was told that Patsy never forgot his Irish roots.
“He never lost his Cork accent and always carried a green, white and gold flag. He always drank from an Irish mug. He drank about 15 cups of tea a day which we do to this present moment. It is a big thing in our family. He was a very proud Irishman and never lost any part of that.”
He went on to train as an auxiliary nurse and Jerry said he was always “on the caring side as a person”.
His partner died in 2022 and his niece calls Patsy her uncle.
The O’Sullivan family never gave up looking for Patsy. Jerry and his brother Eugene made an appeal for information as recently as two years ago on RTÉ’s Crimecall.
Heartbreakingly, it has emerged that Patsy was living just over an hour away from a brother who died in the UK last year.
“I used to go over to my brother in the UK eight or ten times a year. I was very close to my eldest brother. And Patsy was only an hour up the road. That is a killer.”
Patsy died of sepsis two years ago and his ashes were spread alongside the ashes of his late partner in a place that meant a lot to them in London.
Jerry plans to put a memory box together for Patsy. He also intends to put his name on a headstone in order to give him the closure that he deserves in his native country.
The case was investigated by gardaí when Patsy went missing. Jerry says that in recent years Garda PJ Roche and his team left no stone unturned in order to find out what happened to him.
“Since 2015 checks were done with DNA, Interpol, Canada, Australia, America, New Zealand, England, Scotland and Wales. Everything came back a blank even down to the John Does who were dead and buried and had no name. It was looking bleak.”
He was astonished when he found out what had happened to him. He plans to travel there next month to speak to people who knew him.
“I am going to meet as many people and get as many stories as I can. I believe Patsy started looking very like our brother Eugene [as he got older].”
He cherishes his memories of his wonderful brother and adds he hopes that people who go missing realise that they can always go home.

title: GAA integration will take ‘years’ to come together, says director
description: Meeting heard from GAA, LGFA, the Camogie Association and Sport Ireland
content:
That’s all from me for now, Gordon Manning will have a report on proceedings later.
Ladies Gaelic Football Association CEO Lyn Savage and Camogie Association president Brian Molloy discuss how, when integration is achieved, it’s important that women’s football and camogie are properly represented and that it has to be seen as a “new GAA”.
GAA president Jarlath Burns says he will not be president for when it will happen but would love for it to be achieved by 2028. He says they need to move from aspiration to action.
He says it would be difficult to achieve the three congresses and have it ratified by 2028 but he thinks it’s better to do it incrementally, unlike Molloy, who believes the focus should be on structures first and then the rest.
Brennan says that some of the people in the room will no longer be here next year and the next president has said it could take eight years, that leaves a feeling of disconnect, he asks for reassurance? He says it would go down like a lead balloon if they have to wait another eight years.
Burns says he can’t speak for Derek and needs to be cool and calm, they’ve missed one deadline, they haven’t abandoned integration. He said at all those congresses next year, they should have more concrete deadlines.
Alan Kelly brings up the plan Burns mentioned earlier about three different congresses, in three organisations – one on membership, one on structures and one on the lightbulb moment.
Molloy says that was a suggestion by the GAA, not by the Camogie Association. He says it hasn’t been ratified and not the opinion of all organisations. He said that it was their opinion that all could be agreed within a 12-month period, with the two congresses next year so that it was all done by 2028.
Savage says they haven’t set a position on their timeline on congresses.
Alan Kelly speaks for the case of Mary McAleese that as a former president she would have felt like she was promising things to the people and when timelines weren’t met she was letting people down.
He asks the Department of Sport what the timeline is, but Cian Ó Lionáin, assistant secretary general with responsibility for sport, says he is waiting on the three organisations but it has been agreed it is important that there is action at congresses in 2027.
Ahearn asks Sport Ireland what can it do to ensure timelines are hit?
Nora Stapleton of Sport Ireland says it has a lot of experience to guide and it’s important there are key milestones inserted where they can track, follow and see transparency in what is happening.
Garret Ahearn of Fine Gael says there is an undercurrent of messaging from certain people in the GAA regarding it being difficult to work with Mary McAleese.
Burns says strongly that he wouldn’t say that and that didn’t come from himself or GAA director general Tom Ryan Ryan. He says he is not responsible for what other people might say.
He says that McAleese is a woman of the utmost integrity, erudition and academic ability, and they worked well with her on the process.
GAA president Jarlath Burns speaks about the federation model concept that the GAA has with handball and rounders, and how it was explored as a concept.
The Camogie Association was against the model and want full integration, whereas LGFA was more open to it. He says whatever definition you want to give integration is up to the people.
Some clever wordplay on the Bon Jovi reference by Senator Rónán Mullen as he says they were “living on a prayer” from August 30th thinking everything would be fine. He says why didn’t they tell us some of their fears in a previous meeting with the Oireachtas?
Burns keeps the Bon Jovi references going by saying the line “we’re halfway there”, which gets plentiful laughs. He says McAleese said there were “pockets of resistance” and he said there were some “anxieties”.
Peter “Chap” Cleere from Fianna Fáil asks how would life be different for an 11-year-old girl for example after integration.
GAA president Jarlath Burns says it depends whether she is in a one-club model. If she is in a one-club model with fairness and equality already then it won’t change, he says.
But those who experience unfairness with facilities will see a change when they bring in infrastructure under the new organisation, he says.
Aengus Ó Snodaigh of Sinn Féin asks what is the timetable, similar to earlier questions.
GAA director general Tom Ryan says it will take years for it all to come together. He says it is a huge undertaking, the biggest thing the organisation has ever done. He says it cannot be done quickly and simply and needs to be done right.
Burns is asked what are the “insurmountable challenges” that are delaying things.
He says what the exact structures would be at the highest level. He says they had plans where there would be a GAA president and two vice-presidents from the other two organisations to make sure all the power was not resting solely with the GAA.
That was seen by some as the GAA getting the president and that was a long-term set structure, which would not have helped people in the LGFA and Camogie to agree. Burns and Savage say they are looking to improve their communication.
Ennis asks what supports are given to county boards regarding alleviating fears.
Ryan says supporting the intercounty game is a challenge financially, but it brings a big benefit. He says he has a new licensing programme next year, to seek to codify the level of backroom staff that goes into a team and to help counties to manage costs.
He says it would be remiss not to deal with those issues first before transporting them on to a new organisation.
Daniel Ennis of the Social Democrats asks what the deadline is for integration?
Burns says there will never be a deadline because they are a constantly evolving movement. That whenever they think they have enough facilities there will always be something else.
Ennis talks about a female charter for minimum standards for Gaelic sports players, there was talk of a €1 million funding three years ago, which expires this year, and it wasn’t to be negotiated as integration was supposed to be done by 2027.
Savage says the charter is up to the end of this year and they asked for it to roll over. She says they have added to it – €1.6 million, over 10 per cent of their income for the charter. Support for all the workings of the organisation.
Ní Chuilinn says false narratives and some GAA figures that went out to the public were damaging to the process. She asks were they discussed in the Steering Group on Integration to Molloy.
Molloy says the €90 million figure (double the €45 million currently) mentioned by Burns was a factual statement. He said they received feedback from the GAA into the steering group that there was significant concern. The primary perspective was the cost of elite intercounty teams and how that was going to be dealt with post-integration.
Evanne Ní Chuilinn of Fine Gael, speaking about the GAA, says that a previous motion was too vague. Tom Ryan says motions have to be forensic in detail. She asks about the day the position paper was written up. Ryan says he is not sure of the date but it was about the time of the Bon Jovi concert.
She says the GAA has done a body of work on integration so how is the GAA not prepared in its words?
He says there is the staff part, but there is also the voluntary part.
GAA director general Tom Ryan says they have agreed to nominate someone to lead the process and that person will be formally ratified in the next 24 hours and will be announced in the next few days.
Joanna Byrne TD from Sinn Féin talks about equality for pitches, fixtures and other things for men and women. She asks how they go forward in that regard and about timelines?
Burns says the February 2027 congresses will have much more specific motions. On equality, he says there was a lot of comment and misunderstood comment. Equality, he says, is that all 32 counties can go into the Liam MacCarthy Cup. He says equity is putting the strongest counties in the Liam MacCarthy Cup and using money to fund the other counties in other competitions so that there is full participation.
He says he has two daughters who play Gaelic football and two granddaughters who will play camogie. He says he wants to get to the situation where they have a rightful place within the GAA but says they have to do it in a way that is right.
Malcolm Byrne of Fianna Fáil says he heard that the timeline being rushed could have scuppered the project and the worst thing would be to bring proposals that were defeated. He asks why there is a fear that the proposals were being defeated.
Tom Ryan, GAA director general, says people were fearful and it is a tricky process. He said he listened to people and you have a responsibility to hear the feedback. He said he would have been approaching something that they wouldn’t have been comfortable with, based off feedback from the roadshows.
Lyn Savage, CEO of LGFA, said it was a brave decision to halt things as they knew there was going to be a backlash but they had to make sure things were right. They needed more time to make sure the structures were there. Brian Molloy, president of the Camogie Association, says for them there was no point in having a special congress if the GAA wasn’t having one. He says they got to a point, where the three organisations realised they weren’t ready.
Brennan asks what the timeline is again. He says if it was up to Tom Ryan and him, it would have been in 2016 when it was first proposed. Brennan says they don’t know how much it costs?
Burns says if they want to address everything properly, it is going to cost a lot of money for infrastructure. He says he is not going to give exact costs but he met the Minister for Sport.
He says if they give out costs today, it will be used against them as the GAA is throwing out costs to be prohibitive and not supportive of the process.
He says he has proposed a plan to get that money in. He said he doesn’t want to get all the Government’s money.
Brian Brennan of Fine Gael talks about the importance of the GAA in small towns and villages. He asks Burns why McAleese left. Brennan said she made a strong statement that the GAA had no vision for the future.
He talks about 22 infrastructure projects and says the GAA gives the Camogie Association a €500,000 grant every year and it has committed €2 million for accommodation for integration on the Croke Park campus. He says they do various things together like broadcasting, advertising, commercial and ticketing. He says they put out a statement to get people to come to the camogie final and that there are many double-headers with the two organisations.
He says what McAleese said is not characterised by reality or on the ground.
He says she resigned because she was adamant they were going to reach every deadline that they had. And once she realised they were going to miss the first deadline, she decided she was going to walk away from the process, which was disappointing, he says.
Comyn says there have been concerns about resistance to women having a meaningful role in senior decision making, is that a myth?
Burns says it is regrettable that it is seen by some as a gender issue, he says some of the best females are working in the GAA and some of the best males are working in the other two organisations. He says women have genuine influence.
Cian Ó Lionáin, assistant secretary general with responsibility for sport says the department is satisfied that women have influence in the GAA.
He says there will be three congresses each for it to happen and if there are any doubts, then they have to go back and revise. He says a nightmare scenario would be if they were getting messages that one county wasn’t ready.
He says not to get caught up on timelines, but he says camogie are keen by 2028. He says he hopes by 2027 Congress, they would have motions going to the floor that are very specific where you can take an implementation committee to start working on what is agreed. He hopes they would lead out a very navigable path where everyone knows where they stand.
Alison Comyn of Fianna Fáil says McAleese is not prone to hyperbole, and that she said the situation was “devastating” and “heartbreaking”. She asks why did McAleese say that?
Burns says he thought the last meeting before McAleese stepped down was positive and they were surprised. He says there were differing perspectives when they spoke to people on the road. He says they were not ready to have a special congress on structures.
He says the Camogie Association and LGFA were voting themselves into extinction and had to have structures in place for what they were going into. He says they are back on the wagon and they want it happen.
Chaired by Labour TD Alan Kelly, who is explaining parliamentary privileges.
The leadership of all three Gaelic games associations are braced for an interrogation on integration when they sit before an Oireachtas committee on this afternoon, writes Gordon Manning .
The foremost officials from the GAA (director general Tom Ryan and president Jarlath Burns ), LGFA (CEO Lyn Savage and president Trina Murray) and Camogie Association (CEO Karen Dessain-Gelinet and president Brian Molloy) will attend the 12.30pm meeting
Rather than submitting separate opening statements, the three organisations – in a clear desire to demonstrate solidarity – will deliver joint opening remarks.
The Committee on Arts, Media, Communications, Culture and Sport will meet to examine the ongoing process to integrate the GAA, LGFA and Camogie Association.
The meeting takes place between 12.30pm and 2.30pm at Leinster House.
It will examine where the process stands, the reasons for the revised timetable and hear how the organisations intend to address the outstanding issues.
The committee will also discuss the reasons behind Mary McAleese’s decision to step down as chair of the Steering Group on Integration.
The former president of Ireland launched a stinging criticism of the GAA’s leadership last month after stepping down.
She criticised the GAA’s management committee as being “less than impressive” and “lacking in vision”, adding that the decision to resign had left her “devastated”.

title: Budget 2027’s childcare package has triggered storm of protest from parents. Here’s why
description: Not for the first time, there appears to be a substantial ‘reality gap’
content:
Childcare is among the big bills for any young family, so it was not surprising that the budget announcement that the cost of care would fall next year to €550 a month per child from €735 attracted a lot of attention. Not all, it appears, is as it might seem.
Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers said he was reducing the “maximum childcare fees paid by parents from €735 to €550 per month” for children up to senior infants from September of next year.
The Government is increasing the universal subsidy payable under the National Childcare Scheme to €2.50 an hour from €2.14. That subsidy is payable for care of up to 45 hours per week.
He also said he was reducing the maximum weekly fee cap that childcare facilities operating under the State’s core funding system can charge to €250 from €280.
The Minister said the measure would save parents €2,220 annually per child, a significant saving from after-tax income.
There are several, not least surprised parents hearing that the maximum monthly bill should be €735 per child at the moment when they are paying well above that figure.
Angry parents were getting in touch with our Budget Q&A on Wednesday, wondering why they are paying anything from €959 to €1,400, well above the Minister’s figure.
[ How Budget 2027 will impact families: From renters to stay-at-home parents Opens in new window ]
Not for the first time, there appears to be a substantial “reality gap” between the Government’s understanding of the “maximum” cost of care and the real maximum under its own core funding rules.
The amount childcare providers can charge is divided into bands based on the hours of care provided. The Minister’s figures are based on Band E, covering children in care for between 40 and 50 hours a week.
The issue is that most parents – certainly in and around Dublin – are paying under Band F, for children in care for 50 or more hours, which is significantly more expensive.
The issue is not so much how long they are in care as how many hours the providers have to stay open. In urban areas and the commuter belt, childcare facilities are open before 8am to allow parents to drop children off on the way to work. And they are still open at 6pm or later to accommodate parents getting back from their jobs.
The childcare providers need to staff up for those hours regardless of how long your child is actually there, so increasingly, the only package they are offering is the Band F package, providing for care of 50 hours or more.
The €1,400 figure is the full gross cost before you deduct the subsidy parents are entitled to under the National Childcare Scheme. Once you apply the subsidy, the figure falls to €959. Some parents may just be looking at the top line of their childcare bill.
[ What are the key takeaways from Budget 2027? From income tax cuts to surprising omissions Opens in new window ]
[ Budget 2027 Q&A: Your questions answered Opens in new window ]
Far from it. The Minister said Band E charges would fall from €280 a week to €250 a week before the subsidy next year. We don’t have any certainty what the charge for Band F would be but if it fell pro-rata, parents could expect to pay around €300 a week before subsidies – or between €750 and €810 a month.
That’s a separate issue. Childcare providers say they are really struggling to survive under the current charging structure, with one provider we spoke to on Wednesday saying there was a need for the department to “get real” on the cost of running a business. With energy, staff and other costs still rising, providers say they are unlikely to be able to cut the amount they charge parents, even if they get greater funding from Government.
[ Budget Calculator 2027: Here’s how this year’s budget will affect your income Opens in new window ]
The Government seems to have taken “good news” – the 36-cent-an-hour increase in the subsidy – and taken the good out of it by overpromising what it would mean for childcare fees next year and by being poorly briefed on what parents are actually paying at the moment.

title: Zelenskiy says ‘despicable’ Russian bombing was birthday gift for Putin
description: Russian officials said a Liberian-flagged tanker was attacked and a crew of 23 Indian nationals rescued
content:
Volodymyr Zelenskiy has accused Russia ’s military of deliberately killing civilians and bombing residential buildings as a macabre gift for Vladimir Putin , who celebrates his 74th birthday on Wednesday.
Ukraine ’s president described Russia’s overnight drone and missiles strikes, which killed at least 24 people, as “despicable”. “The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” he said.
Video showed a ballistic missile slamming into a five-storey apartment block in the town of Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The concrete building collapsed, entombing those inside. Eighteen people died, including three children, officials said.
Rescuers picked through the rubble in an attempt to find survivors. “Today, on Putin’s birthday, the Russian army ‘presented’ him with the destruction of a residential block in Pryluky. It was an ordinary five-storey block of flats,” Zelenskiy wrote on social media.
He acknowledged that Ukraine was struggling to shoot down enemy ballistic missiles, and appealed to allies to provide US-manufactured Patriot interceptors. “Air defence packages for us right now are a vital necessity,” he said.
The bombardment featured 70 ballistic missiles, as well as 46 jet-powered drones, which in recent weeks have been terrorising Ukrainians on a daily basis. Ukraine’s air force said it managed to down just over 80 per cent of the fast-moving drones – an improvement on the previous average of 50 per cent to 60 per cent.
Eleven regions were hit. Two people were killed in Kyiv, with other deadly strikes in the central cities of Kremenchuk and Oleksandriia, where four civilians died. There was also extensive damage in Dnipro.
Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said Russian generals had given Putin his favourite birthday present: “war crimes”. Moscow’s grim strategy of bombarding the country’s population so it capitulated would not work, he said.
“The Ukrainian people are not going to give up, because it’s about Ukraine’s survival as a nation and as a state,” he said. The “ultimate” present would be a dock in The Hague, home to the International Criminal Court, where the Russian president would stand trial, Sybiha said.
One resident in Kremenchuk said the attack happened early on Wednesday. The woman told Ukrainian media: “We were making tea in the morning. My husband was getting ready for work. And that was it. I found myself on the floor. What can I say? It was very scary.”
Local people in Dnipro said a blast wave affected 16 buildings, blowing out doors and windows. One woman, Iryna, said her auto parts workshop had been hit for the sixth time. The ceiling collapsed in Wednesday’s strike, she said, with toilets, sinks and equipment damaged.
“The explosion happened around three in the morning. We were sleeping at home. Everyone was scared, probably the whole city heard it. We will restore the shop and continue to work,” she told the Suspline channel.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine had carried out its own long-range strikes on economic and military sites inside Russia. He said they included two oil complexes and a training ground in the ⁠Perm, ​Samara ‌and Astrakhan ‌regions. “These are ‌justified Ukrainian responses to ​all Russian attacks on ⁠our people,” ​he said.
The president posted dramatic video of a burning oil tanker close to the southern resort city of Sochi. Russian officials said naval drones had hit the Liberian-flagged ship, adding that “crude oil was burning openly on the Black Sea”. Its Indian crew of 23 was rescued, they said.
Both sides have heavily targeted commercial shipping around the Black Sea since Putin’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In recent weeks Russia has picked off vessels carrying Ukrainian grain, paralysing maritime traffic from Ukraine’s southern ports including Odesa.
Earlier this week, a civilian cargo ship sank after a suspected attack by Russian drones in the Black Sea. Its crew is still missing.
A second vessel carrying grain was also hit while sailing in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, said the Bulgarian prime minister, Rumen Radev. The search for survivors was called off on Wednesday, according to vice-admiral Rumen Nikolov of the Maritime Administration Executive ⁠Agency. “There are no ​traces of the sailors from the ‌first ship, and there will ‌be none,” he said. – Guardian

title: Woman claims videos of her abuse appeared on adult sites linked to Pornhub, court hears
description: ‘Jane Doe’ says recordings of her being abused as a minor were published on video-sharing sites
content:
A High Court case in which a woman claims recordings of her being sexually abused as a child appeared on adult websites associated with Pornhub has been adjourned for six months after a judge was told that approval is awaited of a $120 million (€107 million) settlement of an associated class action in the United States .
The woman, who lives in the US and has been given the name “Jane Doe” to protect her identity, claims she was drugged and raped by a man when she was a minor.
She claims her abuser recorded what happened and posted the images online.
It is alleged that videos of her abuse were published and distributed on adult video-sharing websites owned by the group of companies that own, control and manage internet pornography websites including Pornhub.
As a result, a class action on behalf of the woman and others has been brought in the US courts against various parties within the MindGeek (now renamed AYLO) group of companies. MindGeek, before its name change, is Pornhub’s parent.
The woman’s allegations of wrongdoing by the group have been denied.
In a damages claim before the US courts, the woman alleges she has been victimised and has been exploited by the defendants for profit.
Due to the international structure of the defendant group, the woman sought to bring parallel proceedings before the Irish courts. It is also alleged that the Irish entities have substantial assets.
The defendants in the Irish action include the limited companies AYLO Billing, Mirmay, Nutaku Publishing, Appatomic and Liquidum, which all have a registered address at The Black Church, St Mary’s Place, Dublin.
Other defendants in her proceedings include MG Freesites Ltd, MG Freesites II Ltd, AYLO Premium Ltd, MG Social Ltd, MindGeek USA Incorporated and MindGeek SARL, which is registered in Luxembourg.
In her Irish proceedings the woman seeks orders including aggravated and exemplary damages for what she claims is the defendants’ breach of duty and for breaches of GDPR, conspiracy and her right to privacy.
She also wants an order directing the defendants to identify and remove images of child sexual abuse from the websites and the identities of users who have uploaded the images.
The woman also wants an order directing the defendants to preserve all assets and cash reserves in Ireland below an amount of $630 million pending the outcome of the actions in Ireland and the US.
In the US, the defendants recently agreed to settle a class action, on behalf of the woman and others depicted in the material, and pay $120 million.
MindGeek also agreed to injunctive relief, which will see it make substantial changes to its sites in order to protect children. The settlement is subject to court approval in the US.
The Irish case was back before the High Court on Wednesday when barrister Robert O’Reilly, for the woman, sought an adjournment to allow for the approval of a $120 million settlement of the US proceedings in Alabama.
Judge Brian Cregan adjourned the case to March.

title: Minister backs Bord Bia chair after business found using non-Irish meat for second time this year
description: The food promotion board got €60.7m in this week’s budget
content:
The chairman of Irish food promotion agency Bord Bia continues to have the Minister for Agriculture’s support despite one of his businesses being found using non-Irish meat for the second time this year.
“My views on the chairman of Bord Bia have been well aired. They haven’t changed,” Minister Martin Heydon said.
Heydon backed Larry Murrin early this year when controversy flared over the use of Brazilian beef in his Dawn Farm Foods company when one of Bord Bia’s jobs is to promote Irish beef.
Murrin has faced criticism again in recent weeks after Sole restaurant in Dublin, which he part-owns, was found serving chicken from the Netherlands .
The issue was highlighted by the late restaurant critic, Corinna Hardgrave , in her final restaurant review for The Irish Times last month.
Members of the Irish Farmers’ Association staged a sit-in at Bord Bia’s offices in January and also protested outside Sole restaurant last weekend.
The restaurant has said it occasionally used imported chicken as it had difficulty getting a secure supplier of Irish produce because demand outstrips supply.
In the wake of the initial controversy, Heydon, who repeatedly backed Murrin, initiated a review of Bord Bia which was published during the summer.
It recommended revising policies on conflict of interest, declarations by board members and crisis management.
[ Budget 2027 Q&A: Your questions answered Opens in new window ]
Heydon said work on implementing the review was continuing. “We had an extensive process, the Government’s review process, that came up with a number of recommendations,” he said
“I’m committed to the implementation of all of those recommendations. We continue to work with all stakeholders in that regard.”
The Minister spoke on the issue while taking questions about budget measures announced by his department, which included €60.7 million for Bord Bia – a small increase on last year.
He defended providing emergency funding of €100 million for fuel subsidies for farming in the wake of the fuel price protests last April, when fewer than one in four farmers claimed it and €62 million ended up unspent.
He said the €100 million was an estimate of the need at a time when he was trying to respond to a crisis in real time.
The underspend was being diverted to a fertiliser subsidy scheme instead, details of which he would be announcing shortly.
Leaders of April’s protests, which blockaded Dublin city centre, regional towns and ports, have said there will be further demonstrations in the near future as the carbon tax and excise freezes on fuel did not go far enough.
Heydon said people in a democracy had a right to protest.
However, he said: “I do believe that farmers do recognise that Government has supported them this year and will continue to support them into this winter.”

title: Ryanair’s plan for €50m hangar at Shannon Airport stalls
description: Clare council has ‘serious concerns’ over berm for storage of contaminated oils
content:
Ryanair’s plans for a new €50 million four-bay aircraft maintenance hangar at Shannon Airport have beenki stalled by the company’s plan to erect a 2m-high berm for the storage of contaminated soils.
In placing the hangar application on hold, Clare County Council has written to the Ryanair applicant firm, Wonderlight Ltd, to say that it has “serious concerns” over the berm planned for a site southeast of the hangar.
The council has told the Ryanair firm that its concerns arise from the proposed berm’s proximity to sensitive environmental receptors including – indirectly – the Shannon estuary and the potential environmental effects arising from the construction and operational phases.
The council also cites the potential impact on human health and the long-term effects of the berm, which may sterilise development lands within the airport.
In the letter, the council said that the proposed development of the aircraft hangar represents an appropriate form of development at this location in the context of the continued growth and development of Shannon Airport.
However, the council has asked the Ryanair firm to submit a comprehensive justification for the proposed berm, including an assessment of alternative soil management options and to demonstrate why the proposed approach represents the most appropriate solution.
A planning report lodged on behalf of Wonderlight Ltd by Enviroplan Consulting said that, when undergoing site investigations, it was discovered that part of the site, which was used as a fire training ground, contained contaminated soil primarily from firefighting foam.
Enviroplan Consulting said that it was proposed to remove the contaminated soil and use it to construct a berm in a designated area to the southeast of the proposed hangar.
The material, according to the planning report, would “be deposited in this area and capped with an engineered barrier system to ensure that it stays in place”.
The report said, “the berm would be fenced off and secured and it is estimated that the maximum height of the berm will be two metres”.
The proposed new four-bay aircraft would be Ryanair’s largest aircraft maintenance facility in Ireland.
Ryanair operates a three-bay aircraft maintenance hangar at Shannon Airport, which has a workforce of more than 200.

title: ‘Unforgivable’: Arrest of US marine reopens old wounds  in Japan’s Okinawa
description: The suspected murder of an Okinawan woman by a US soldier has reignited anger about the heavy presence of US forces on the tiny island
content:
A speck in the Pacific about 1,500km from Tokyo, the Japanese island of Okinawa bears the weight of Japan’s military alliance with the United States .
The islanders live uneasily with about 30,000 US troops and dozens of military installations, including the US Marine Corps’ only jungle warfare training unit.
Okinawans have long resented the burden of hosting 70 per cent of all US military facilities in Japan. The facilities include the Futenma airbase, which occupies about 4.8sq km of crowded Ginowan city, bringing noise, pollution and crime.
So locals have reacted with predictable fury to the weekend murder of a local woman. Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal, has been arrested on suspicion of strangling local woman, Anna Yagi (39) in a hotel room. Ballard, who denies the charges, also allegedly stole his dead victim’s wallet.
Security camera footage showed Ballard entering the hotel with Yagi and fleeing alone, according to the Japanese media .
The behaviour of the US guests on Okinawa is closely watched, and politically sensitive. Last year, local police recorded more than 100 crimes by US military personnel and their families.
In 2024, the Tokyo government admitted that it had concealed a string of sex crime cases involving US servicemen in Okinawa, presumably because of their political sensitivity.
Anger at the US presence climaxed in 1995 with mass protests following the kidnapping and rape of a 12-year-old schoolgirl by three US servicemen.
Under pressure, Tokyo and Washington agreed the following year to close Futenma and build a replacement in Okinawa’s north.
But the plan to replace the base with a 1,800m runway off the coast of a quiet fishing village is bitterly controversial: 72 per cent of Okinawans opposed it in a 2019 prefecture-wide referendum.
The proposed new base, rising on reclaimed land out of Oura bay, is supposed to check China’s maritime expansion and maintain US military primacy in Asia.
The marines waded ashore in 1945. The battle to take the island left up to 100,000 civilians dead along with 100,000 Japanese soldiers and more than 12,000 Americans. Many Okinawans have grown up believing they were sacrificed as a buffer between the invading Americans and the Japanese mainland. Okinawa was under US occupation until 1972 when it reverted to Japan.
Yagi’s murder is the first big political test for Okinawa’s new governor Genta Koja, who is backed by prime minister Sanae Takaichi. Koja ejected his anti-base predecessor, Danny Tamaki, in an election last month and is under pressure to dampen down public anger about the murder amid protests on Okinawa.
“The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to US bases,” Koja said after news of the murder broke. “It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged,” he said, adding that US military discipline was “not working”. On Wednesday US forces imposed a month-long curfew on soldiers based in Okinawa. They were banned from drinking alcohol while they undergo disciplinary training.
Prime minister Sanae Takaichi has condemned what she called a “brutal” crime, which raises the stakes for the drive to make Okinawa a linchpin in Japan’s strategy to contain China.
A succession of Japanese governments has passed record military budgets and is beefing up defences across roughly 200 islands in the Ryukyu chain that includes Okinawa, which is close to China, Taiwan and the Korean Peninsula.
Japan is training an amphibious assault force , modelled on the US marines, all part of a strategic shift to the south and southwest.
This strategy would crumble if Okinawa were to eject the US military guests, which is why Tokyo and Washington will be carefully monitoring the reactions of Okinawans over the coming days and weeks.

title: Budget 2027 Q&A: Your questions answered
description: Advice on the latest budget measures, from tax and pensions, to inheritance, childcare and more
author_name: Dominic Coyle, Beryl Power, Ruth Gilligan
content:
We are ending our live Q&A now. Anyone with further queries can contact Dominic Coyle at dominic.coyle@irishtimes.com and he will endeavor to provide answers in his weekly Q&A column.
Q: Will I get the benefit of the inheritance tax threshold increases for a bequest from a will where the disponer’s death was in early 2026 and the grant of probate was in September 2026?
A: Inheritance tax-free threshold are assessed against date of death, not probate or when the inheritance is received. So, in this case, where the person died earlier this year, it is the pre-budget thresholds that will apply. – DC
Q: Will it be possible to invest the full €12,000 per annum in one go rather than in monthly amounts?
A: We’re waiting for the enabling legislation for the fine detail on this but, given that Minister Simon Harris announced an annual contribution limit rather than, say, a monthly limit of €1,000, which would have had the same effect, it seems that you will be able to invest the full €12,000 annual limit in one go rather than drip-fed across the year.
That would also help keep costs down, though whether that is recognised by providers has yet to be determined. – DC
Q: For the reduction in crèche fees, the given example seems to be for a crèche in Band D. Will it apply proportionally to all bands?
A: The illustration provided by Government, somewhat misleadingly, is based on Band E – for people using childcare for between 40 and 50 hours a week.
The reality in many cases is that operators who are open for 10 or more hours a day and have to staff up accordingly offer only Band F coverage.
Not only is this currently €56 a week more expensive under core funding before subsidies, but those subsidies run out after 45 hours.
So while people will benefit from the rise in subsidy from €2.14 to €2.50, regardless of band, if they are in Band F, some of their hours are not covered by the subsidy and so the reduction is fees will not be strictly pro rata. – DC
Q: Can I transfer funds from a current investment account into the new scheme, and, if I can, will I have to pay tax on any increase in value of the current fund?
A: Some of the detail will only emerge with the legislation establishing these new investment funds.
I don’t see why people would not be able to move savings from an existing investment fund (subject to any lock-in conditions on that investment) to a new personal investment account – up to the €12,000 annual limit.
However, such a transfer will effectively be an exit from your current investment and I can say with confidence that any exit will be treated under the rules applying to that class of investment, so yes, you will have to pay tax on any profit on your investment up to the point of any transfer. – DC
Q: Does the reduction in capital gains tax apply to individuals as well as business?
A: Capital gains tax was one of the surprises in the budget as, while there has been a long-standing view in the business and investment communities that Ireland’s rates are out of kilter with international comparison, there was no specific clamour for change ahead of the budget.
And in a budget that followed recent practice of leaking essentially every detail before Ministers got to their feet, there had been no suggestion that a cut in capital gains tax was coming.
The good news for you, however, assuming you have capital gains on your investments, is that the two percentage point cut in the capital gains tax rate – to 31 per cent from 33 per cent – applies equally to individuals and business. – DC
Q: What income is allowed for a couple over 66 [before tax]?
A: Marginal relief is available where your total income is not in excess of double the €18,000 (ie €32,000).
Where marginal relief applies, you will only be subject to income tax on difference between your total income and the exemption limit of €18,000 for single persons (subject to increase depending on whether you have dependent children). – BP
Q: If your portfolio is above €50,000 and you decide to sell them, are you subject to capital gains tax on the capital gain?
A: It is not anticipated there will be any capital gains tax on the disposal of your investment in the new Irish investment account. The proposal suggests that there will be an annual tax charge of 1 per cent on the value in excess of €50,000.
This 1 per cent tax charge will arise on an annual basis and it will be the fund administrators’ responsibility to collect this tax from your fund – this should hopefully ease the administrative burden on the investor.
There should be no further tax arising on a disposal or cash withdrawal. Further guidance on this should be available when the Finance Bill is published next week. – RG
Q: Was there an inflationary increase added for the child benefit (€140 per child)? If not, why not?
A: Nope, there was no change in the €140 monthly payment under child benefit.
Why? well, you’d need to ask the Ministers, but I suspect they may have decided to concentrate their financial firepower in this area on childcare costs rather than child benefit. – DC
Q: Do you get to choose where your money is invested or does the Government supply guidance via a reliable broker?
A: The detail on how the investment accounts will operate has yet to be issued. We are expecting more detail on these accounts in the Finance Bill, which is due to issue on October 15th.
That said, the Minister did say that only eligible products, such as shares, bonds, investment funds and insurance based investment products, can be held in these accounts. – BP
Q: I submitted a claim for the Help to Buy scheme earlier this year and received the maximum €30,000. Am I entitled to the additional €5,000 announced yesterday?
A: Unfortunately, the increased amount is effective from today and will not be backdated. – RG
Q: From what date do the changes in capital gains tax come into effect?
A: The 31 per cent capital gains tax rate will come into effect from today. The 31 per cent rate of capital gains tax applies to the disposal of assets with the exception of development land.
Gains made on the disposal of development will continue to be subject to a rate of 33 per cent. – RG
Q: From what date does the new Minimum Wage of €14.94 apply?
A: The new minimum wage will take effect from January 1st, 2027.
Q: When is the increase in fuel allowance coming in?
A: The fuel allowance has increased by €5 per week and we understand that this change will come into effect from January 2027. – BP
Q: Has the budget got anything for single people? I feel like we’re a growing cohort the Government never even considers!!
A: Well, you will benefit from the €2,500 increase in the standard rate income tax band as long as your earnings are above €44,000.
You will also be €250 a year better off due to the increase in the personal tax credit and either the PAYE/employee or earned income tax credit, whichever applies to you. If you are renting, there is also the €150 increase in the rent tax credit. – DC
Q: I have two children in afterschool care. Twenty-five hours per week. One in junior infants and one first class.
Current National Childcare Scheme is €2.14. Will this remain unchanged next September? Or will my son who will be senior infants next sept get €2.50 subsidy?
A: The subsidy under the National Childcare Scheme is rising, as you say, from €2.14 an hour to €2.50 although that will not happen until September next year.
The good news is that your child continue to be eligible in afterschool care next year when he is in senior infants. – DC
Q: Any help for graduate medicine fees?? Will the €150 capitation fee cover grad med fees?
The Government was talking about paying for fees in return for a service commitment to HSE. I can’t find any further talk about it.
Fees are €16,000 per year and accommodation is on top of that. It is crippling. There are no loans available for graduate medicine so we are trying as a family but very costly. Would appreciate any help.
I get the rental credit and 20 per cent off tuition fees which is about €800 per year. Was hoping for some news.
A: There was no specific mention of graduate medicine fees. You are correct that there has been speculation the Government might look at covering/subsidising fees in return for a commitment to work in the HSE for a certain period as part of efforts to stem to drain of new and recently qualified doctors abroad.
However, there was absolutely no mention of it in the Ministers’ speeches, and I cannot find a single mention of any such measure in the associated budget documentation.
I’m kind of surprised that there is no access to loans for graduate medical students but so be it. You should get the benefit of the €150 reduction in fees. – DC
Q: What is happening with disability allowance?
A: The disability allowance should increase by €10 per week with effect from January 1st. There is also an increase of €10 per week in the employment earnings disregarded for disability allowance from July 1st.
This means a single person on disability allowance can earn over €9,000 a year without impacting their allowance. The Minister also announced a new €500 cost of disability payment for people receiving long-term disability payments. This payment is expected to be made as a lump sum in 2027. – RG
Q: Was there any increase in the fuel allowance means test limit currently set at €534 per week?
A: From January 2027, the income limit for a single person aged 66 or over goes from 50 per cent of the couple limit to 60 per cent of the couple limit. In money terms, the single limit rises from €534 to €641 a week. – BP
Q: We currently have a claim for Help to Buy in for the €30,000 amount. We have signed contracts but have not yet drawn down. Can we avail of the €35,000?
A: The new, higher relief under Help to Buy kicks in from today but, as of now, it appears Revenue, which operates the relief, is unsure exactly what that means.
Certainly, going forward, any first-time buyer applying to the scheme will be able to claim relief of up to €35,000 towards the cost of purchasing a newly-built home, up from €30,000 previously.
However, Revenue cannot tell me at this point whether applications already made but not yet approved will be assessed under the new rules or whether those applicants will be required to make a new application.
They are also not yet able to clarify whether applications that have been approved but not yet drawn down can be amended to avail of the extra €5,000 in relief or not.
It is a subject we will return to when Revenue has had time to determine how the new relief plays out on applications made before budget day.
Q: We are in a crèche in south Dublin and already pay well above the €735 cap. It’s five days a week which equates to 55 hours landing it in Band F.
The budget didn’t mention if banding impacts the cap, so will we be entitled to the €550?
A: No, you will not. The €550 monthly cost relates to people availing of Band E care (creche care for up to 50 hours a week).
This year, Band E providers can charge €280 before the National Childcare Scheme subsidies of €2.14 per hour up to 45 hours. That subsidy brings the charge down to €183.70 a week, or €735 a month.
Band F providers can charge €336 a week under core funding. Even with the National Childcare Scheme subsidy, that still amounts to €239.70 a week, or €958.80 per month.
You will benefit from the increase in National Childcare Scheme subsidy to €2.50 an hour for a maximum of 45 hours from September of next year but it will not get your cost anywhere near €550 a month. – DC
Q: Why do you keep referring to it as the tax-free investment scheme? Is there deduction on contributions? It appears not so we have already paid tax on any money we pay into it.
A: Unfortunately, there is no income tax deduction on contributions. The reference to tax-free investment is in referring to the income and gains arising on your investment in the scheme.
Minister for Finance Simon Harris announced there will be a tax-free threshold of €50,000. As such, where the value of your investment does not increase above €50,000, no tax should be payable.
Where you investment increased above €50,000, there is a 1 per cent tax on the value in excess of the €50,000. The 1 per cent tax will apply on an annual basis to the value in excess of €50,000 in that year.
There will be no requirement for you as the investor to engage with Revenue to make this tax payment should it arise, as this responsibility is expected to fall on the investment provider.
The maximum contribution limit is expected to be €12,000 per annum. We expect to see further details on this in the Finance Bill which is due to be released next Thursday. – RG
Q: Is there any change to the €3,000 tax free gift amount per year?
A: Unfortunately, the Government has not announced any changes to the €3,000 small gift exemption. – RG
Q: Please explain more about €2,000 grant for replacing old central heating boilers. Can it be replaced by a new and more efficient kerosene fuelled boiler?
A: The grant is targeted to remove old fossil fuel or electric heating systems when switching to renewable alternatives. It is not expected to apply for the replacement of new oil, gas or Kerosene boilers. – RG
Q: On mortgage tax relief, will this scheme be offered again in 2027?
A: Unfortunately, there was no extension of mortgage tax relief in the budget. As such, it is not intended that this will extend to 2027, but there may be provisions relating to this that have yet to be seen in the Finance Bill which is expected to be published next Thursday. – RG
Q: Any changes to benefit-in-kind, especially in relation to electric vehicles?
