A: Yes, there has been a further reduction in the relief available where electric vehicles have been made available by employers.
From 2019 to 2022. where you made an electric car available to your employee for private use, the value of the vehicle was not subject to benefit-in-kind. In more recent years, the Government has begun tapering the relief available.
In 2026, where electric vehicles were provided to an employee, the value of the electric vehicle subject to benefit-in-kind was reduced by €30,000 and the excess value was subject to benefit-in-kind.
For 2027, the deduction available will be €15,000 with excess value being subject to benefit-in-kind. – RG
Q: Is the level at which a couple pay the 40 per cent tax rate increased in the budget? I notice there is an increase for a single person.
A: It is. A single person will not pay 40 per cent income tax until their income exceeds €46,500 next year (up from €44,000 this year).
The outer limit of the standard rate tax band for a married couple where two people are working will be twice that – €93,000 – up from €88,000 this year.
For a married couple where only one spouse is working, the band threshold will rise from €53,000 this year to €55,000 next year. – DC
Q: I am 75 years old and married for 46 years. I have a small pension and a contribututory one, and my husband has a pension and contribututory pension. What did we actually gain from this budget?
A: You should benefit from the increase in the State pension which has increased by €10 per week.
There are also tax changes which may benefit you such as the increase to the standard rate band of €2,500, the increase to the personal tax credit of €125 and the USC changes.
I have attached a link to the Pwc calculator which will give you a more detailed calculation of your tax savings from Budget 2027 based on your circumstances.
Q: For childcare providers who opted out of core funding, what changes will apply to those fees?
Currently paying €320 per child per week (some months charged as five-week months) for two children. After National Childcare Scheme deduction it is €2000+ per month – absolutely crippling.
A: If your childcare provider has opted out of core funding, it is up to them and you what they charge and what you are prepared to pay.
Speaking to providers in the sector, there certainly seems to be growing concern about the sustainability of the current core funding model.
As you say, you will benefit from the increased National Childhood Scheme subsidy, but that increase will amount to €16.20 per child per week, assuming they are in care for 45 hours. And, of course, it does not kick in until September of next year. – DC
Q: What are the details of the oil boiler replacement scheme?
A: The grant is available to remove old fossil-fuel or electric heating systems when switching to renewable alternatives. It is not expected to apply for the replacement of new oil, gas or Kerosene boilers.
The Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland has already updated its website to reflect the budget announcement. Further information can be found here . – RG
Q: Regarding childless couples/individuals and inheritance. As no significant change occurred to the category B and C inheritance/capital acquisition tax groups – is it possible there might be an increase in the small gift exemption threshold contained in the Finance Bill that wasn’t announced in the budget speech?
A: The Group B threshold has increased from €40,000 to €44,000 and the Group C threshold has increased from €20,000 to €22,000. These changes will apply to gifts or inheritances taken on or after October 7th 2026.
While these changes are welcome, they do little in terms of reducing the tax burden for beneficiaries who fall within these categories.
It is possible that the small gift exemption of €3,000 per annum could be increased in the Finance Bill, which is due to issue on October 15th. That said, I would think the likelihood of any change is probably quite low. – BP
Q: I’m a pensioner. My annual total pension is about €22,6450 per annum. Will I be paying less tax next year?
A: You should benefit from some of the tax changes. The exact amount will depend on your personal circumstances.
I have attached a link to the PwC calculator which will give you a better understanding of the tax savings based on your personal circumstances. – BP
Q: Once investments accumulate to above €50,000, it is not clear whether the imposition of a flat rate 1 per cent tax on the value in excess of this is by implication the only tax liability on this value; or if capital gains tax and income tax on dividends is also applied to any gains.
A: Based on the documentation issued from the Department of Finance, it would appear that a 1 per cent flat rate of tax will apply to the value of the account above €50,000, but we will need to see the detail in the Finance Bill to understand exactly how the new Investment Accounts will operate. We understand that no other Irish tax should apply to the Investment Accounts. – BP
Q: My income is circa €100,000 per annum. My wife and I are pensioners. My wife does not have any income of her own. She doesn’t qualify for the State pension as she gave up her nursing career to be a stay-at-home mother.
Will we benefit to the same extent as a married couple whose €100,000 income is split more evenly between the two of them?
A: As a single income married couple, the applicable standard rate threshold should increase from €53,000 to €55,000. – RG
A: Maternity benefit is expected to increase in line with increases to social welfare. As such, the weekly rate should increase from €299 per week in 2026 to €309 per week in 2027. – RG
Q: Has a pensioner’s tax free allowance of €18,000 increased?
A: Unfortunately, the Government did not announce any changes to the tax-free allowance which currently applies to individuals over the age of 65. – RG
Q: What’s the benefit for single income household for married person?
A: The standard rate band (being the band that you pay tax at a rate of 20 per cent) has increased for married couples or civil partners with one income from €53,000 to €55,000.
In addition to this, the personal tax credit which is available to both, you and your spouse increased by €125 per individual.
Where your spouse is caring for a dependent person (such as a child for whom child benefit is payable, a person over 65-years-old, a person who is permanently incapacitated) you should benefit from the increase in the home carer tax credit.
As everyone’s personal circumstances are different, I would encourage to use the income tax calculator which has been updated to reflect the changes announced in Budget 2027. This will allow you to compare your take home pay in 2026 to 2027. – RG
Q: When does the grant of €600 for solar battery commence?
A: The Battery Energy Storage Grant opened yesterday for applications. Please refer to the SEAI website for more details. I have attached a link . – BP
Q: If the profit on your investment brings you over the €50,000 tax-free threshold, is the 1 per cent applied just to the profit?
A: It would appear that any value over €50,000 (as opposed to profit) will be subject to the 1 per cent flat rate tax annually. That said, we will need to see the detail in the Finance Bill to confirm exactly how the new investment accounts will operate. – BP
Q: I am living in Japan for the past 20 years. My mother recently died. I understand I get more bang for my buck with the increased inheritance threshold.
Does it matter on the timing probate is paid? Can I avail of the increased €420,000 threshold if probate is passed next year? All advice appreciated.
A: You will not benefit from the increase in the Category A inheritance tax free threshold to €420,000 from €400,000 previously.
When it comes to assessing liability to inheritance tax – or capital acquisitions tax as it is more formally called – the key date is the date of death, not probate. Whatever limit was in place when your mother died is the one that applies to you.
In this case, given her recent passing, you will be able to receive up to €400,000 free of tax. This threshold also covers anything you might have received from your father in inheritance if he has died previously. – DC
Q: I understand it has been confirmed that from September next year the maximum childcare cost per month is €550, reduced from the current €730 maximum payment monthly.
I am in reciept of full National Childcare Scheme grant, 45 hours and my son (one year and a half) attends a participating creche in Dublin City.
However, I pay €920 monthly. Can anyone explain to me why this is? I am in a WhatsApp group of mums with children in various creches in Dublin and only one mum is currently paying €730, all the others are €800-900+.
Thank you for keeping my name anonymous. I don’t want to be seen as a trouble maker as I was on a waitlist for over two years for a spot in this creche.
A: Getting your head around childcare costs seems to be an absolute head-wrecker. My understanding is that someone in your position – with a child in creche care for between 40 and 50 hours a week – falls into Band E under core funding.
Core funding is the scheme operated by Government to subsidise creche costs as long as those creches commit to conditions – including how much they charge parents.
For the current year, which runs from September 2026 to August 2027, the maximum charge to parents under Band E is €280 a week before the National Childcare Scheme subsidy of €2.14 per hour up to 45 hours per week.
That subsidy maxes out at €96.30, bringing the weekly charge to parents down to €183.70. Multiplying this by four takes your monthly payment to €735.
Under Budget 2027, the Government says this figure will drop to €550 from September 2027 (partly on the basis of an increase in the National Childcare Scheme subsidy to €2.50 an hour).
So, in the absence of services being offered outside the parameters of core funding, or the creche offering care over longer hours, you should not be paying more than €735 a month as I understand it.
I have put your query directly to the Department of Children and we will update readers on this as soon as we have any further clarity.
I understand why parents would be nervous of putting their head above the parapet when it is so difficult to source childcare in the first place in so many parts of the State, but there seems to be no reason within the rules why you and others would be facing fees on the scale you outline. – DC
Q: Is there a reduction in college fees or just in disregard amount?
A: A €150 “permanent” reduction in college fees was announced by Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers. That would bring them down to €2,850 from the current €3,000. This will not kick in until the next academic year.
The disregard measure was simply working in tandem with this cut to ensure you can claim relief at 20 per cent on fees for a second or more children attending third level. – DC
A: There has been no change to the maximum annual income cap (currently €115,000) which is used to calculate relief on pension contributions.
However, a change to the standard fund threshold was announced in the budget, but we will need to see the detail in the Finance Bill to understand the effect of this change. – BP
Q: Has their been an increase in the National Childcare Scheme core universal subsidy to parents?
A: The National Childcare Scheme subsidy will increase from €2.14 to €2.50 per hour for children in early years, junior infants and senior infants for up to 45 hours per week. However, this will not take effect until September 2027. – RG
Q: My husband and I got married last year and we are still assessed individually for income tax purposes. My question remains the same irrespective of the increase in the standard rate of tax threshold from €44,000 to €46,500 and is as follows.
I earn €93,000 gross salary, with a performance bonus this year of €23,500, pension contributions of 5 per cent on my gross income, health insurance as a benefit in kind to the value of €1,785.72 and a Christmas bonus of approximately €1,615.
My total package is €124,288.60. My husband’s gross salary is approximately €67,000 and contributes 8 per cent of the gross to his pension.
Based on the amount we are earning (both individually and when aggregated), I don’t think there is any use in us being jointly assessed for income tax purposes but I would be very grateful if this could be confirmed – just in case we are paying some extra tax when being individually assessed.
A: Based on the information provided, there would not be a tax saving if you were jointly assessed for income tax purposes.
You will both benefit from the increase in the standard rate band of €2,500, the personal tax credit increase of €125 and the USC changes.
I have attached a link to the PwC calculator which will give you a more accurate calculation of your tax savings based on your circumstances. – BP
Q: When will the reduction in capital gains tax come into effect?
A: The capital gains tax rate change comes into effect today. Therefore, any gains made on disposals from today will be subject to capital gains tax at 31 per cent. Please note the reduced rate does not apply to gains made on the disposal of development land. – BP
Q: How much has defence spending increased by?
A: Funding to the Department of Defence has been increased by 9 per cent to address its recruitment deficit and to fund the delivery of four new helicopters and a new long-range military radar system.
The record €1.6 billion package will support the recruitment of 850 permanent members of the Defence Forces, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers said in the Dáil, as well as help with the purchase of new equipment. – RG
Q: Why can’t Ireland have the 27-year-old UK individual savings account that UK Labour introduced in 1999: £20,000/year investment limit and all gains tax-free. Simple. Low fees.
Harris complicates it and average Irish investors lose tens of thousands of euros over a lifetime to 1 per cent tax drag and 1-2 per cent high provider fees since providers are forced to administer this tax.
Why can’t FF/FG get rid of deemed disposal despite the 2024 Funds Sector Report and rhetoric from Harris. Dragging their heels.
A: Certainly the Government has adopted a fairly cautious approach to the investment limits allowed under this new personal investment account scheme.
Minister for Finance Simon Harris did make the point in his post-budget press conference that, in reality, not many people will have more than €12,000 a year to put into such schemes – or €24,000 for a family.
This presumably refers to the “squeezed middle” the Government loves to say it is looking to help out.
They did look at the UK individual savings account scheme but clearly decided to go for a variation of that but more in line with the Swedish scheme, without buying into the unlimited contributions which are a feature of the Swedish scheme – cautious, as I said.
As for deemed disposal, it was always likely to be at least a year too soon for fundamental action there.
Deemed disposal was initially put in place as a measure to stop the “gross roll-up” investment tax regime being used for tax avoidance purposes following Revenue pressure. Action is promised but I would expect a lot of study and reports before that happens. – DC
Q: What is a married couple’s cut off rate for higher earners? For 2026 it was €53,000?
A: The married couples (one income) standard rate band has increased by €2,500 from €53,000 to €55,500. The personal tax credit has also increased by €125 and there is a small change to USC which is favourable.
I have attached a link to the PwC calculator which will give you a more accurate calculation of your tax savings based on your circumstances. – BP
Q: [What is happening with the] living alone allowance?
A: The State pension has increased by €10 per week and the Living Alone Allowance has increased by €3 per week. The Fuel Allowance has also increased by €5 per week. – BP
Q: As a pensioner who has recently received an increase in my UK state pension, has the tax-free allowance of €18,000 increased for pensioners in receipt of state pensions, Irish contributory and UK?
A: That income exemption limit has been unchanged over many years. The focus of successive governments seems to have been on keeping people out of the higher 40 per cent tax rate rather than raising the income exemption limit.
The only real change for you is the €125 increase in both your personal tax credit and the earned income or PAYE tax credits, a total of €250. – DC
Q: What does tax free mean in relation to the investment account? Does it mean there is no capital acquisitions tax on capital gains?
Can you continue investing €1,000 after five years and not be liable for capital acquisitions tax but you pay 1 per cent tax on the balance of the investment over €50,000?
A: Budget 2027 introduces a new investment account which will be launched by providers on or after July 1st, 2027. The account will be available to Irish resident individuals aged 18 or over who hold a PPS number.
The account will include a flat rate 1 per cent tax applied annually to the value of the account above €50,000. No other Irish taxes should apply to the account. The maximum contribution to the account in a particular year will be €12,000.
All tax reporting and the payment of any tax due will be managed by the providers. We will have to wait for the Finance Bill to see more detail on the investment account. – BP
Q: Nothing about the Apartment And Duplex Defects Remediation Scheme? Seems like we have all been forgotten again.
A: It did not get specific mention in the Ministers’ speeches but there is provision in the budget arithmetic for remediation of building defects, which I presume will at least in part be directed at the scheme you mention.
These include “over €750 million to address specific housing needs, including adaptation grants for homes, retrofitting of additional social homes, remediation of homes affected by defects and expanded State-owned temporary accommodation capacity”.
The Department of Housing budget also includes provision for €948 million to be spent under the “Other Housing Capital Programme”.
This is to “support the continued expansion of housing remediation programmes, funding an expected higher volume of defective concrete block remediations, the completion of remaining pyrite cases, and the anticipated commencement of the statutory apartment defects remediation measures nationwide” among other things. – DC
Q: On the personal investment accounts, are they open to children too?
A: For now, no. As it stands, the accounts can be opened only by someone who is 18 or older with an Irish PPS number.
However, Minister for Finance Simon Harris did hold out the prospect last night at his post-budget press conference that these accounts might be available to children at some later point. – DC
Q: The old age credit appears still stuck on the odd amount of €490 for two people. Why do they not raise this to €500? Why does this credit not get more attention?
A: I can only assume the Government decided to focus their firepower on the increase in State pension weekly payments this time around.
As you say, while the main tax credits – the personal credit, the PAYE credit and the earned income credit for those filing as self-employed – all went up by €125, which is more than had originally been expected.
There was no move on the age tax credit which applies to people who are 65 or older. – DC
Q: Has there been any extra funding provided to expand rail or bus services?
A: The Government announced there would be capital funding of €4.2 billion to invest in roads and public transport in 2027.
This includes progression of the DART+ and BusConnests programmes, including continued construction of Core Bus Corridors. – RG
Q: Just wondering if there’s a Christmas bonus? Haven’t heard anything about it.
A: The Department of Social Protection has confirmed the Christmas bonus will be paid to 1.4 million long-term social welfare recipients. – DC
Q: What is the interest rate in the new investment scheme?
A: We’re a long way from that yet – the accounts will not even be available until July of next year. But your question also highlights one of the things people are going to have to familiarise themselves with under this new scheme.
This is not like a bank account or An Post savings cert that offers a set rate of interest; these will be investments in things like shares and bonds.
And the investment gain will be determined by what investments or fund you pick and how they perform. You could do very well or, if unlucky with market volatility, you could lose money. So the concept of “interest rate” does not really apply. – DC
Q: Has there been any meaningful changes in the situation for people renting? Not the Rent a Room scheme, but the cost of renting and availability of rental properties itself?
A: The only real change in Budget 2027 is the €150 increase in the rent tax credit from €1,000 to €1,150 for a single person and by €300 to €2,300 for a couple from January.
Other than that, no measures were announced to affect the cost of renting or the availability of property apart from the Rent a Room scheme you mentioned.
This has been extended to include standalone buildings in people’s gardens so, in that sense, it might make more properties available, but that is it. – DC
Q: As a public servant retiree on a low to moderate pension with no other benefits or pensions, are there any advantages in this budget that will benefit and raise my income?
A: The State pension has been increased by €10 per week. There have been tax changes that you might benefit from such as the increase in the standard rate band by €2,500, and also the personal tax credit has been increased by €125.
I have attached a link to the PwC calculator which will be able to give you a more accurate calculation of the tax savings based on your circumstances. – BP
Q: For the childcare increase for up to senior infants, is there a National Childcare Scheme increase from €2.14?
Yes, the National Childcare Scheme subsidy will increase from €2.14 to €2.50 per child for up to 45 hours per week. However, this will not come into effect until September 2027. – RG
Q: Why raise the Help to Buy rebate by €5,000 while not adjusting the €500,000 property price cap?
The scheme remains redundant to majority of buyers in Dublin, commuter towns and other cities across the country. The extra €5,000 does not unlock any new homes or help affordability?
A: It is a little puzzling alright. There was no massive pressure to increase the value of the Help to Buy relief.
Where there was some concern was this €500,000 cap, given that properties in many parts of Dublin and surrounding counties are no longer available to first-time buyers using Help to Buy as they are priced above that level.
Yet the Minister has raised the value of the relief but left the cap in place. As you say, with the cap on property values in place, the extra €5,000 relief does not “unlock any new homes” for first-time buyers.
It remains to be seen whether this will be amended come the Finance Act but, as it stands, the Minister’s choice serves only to draw attention to the limitations of the scheme rather than its generosity, which seems an odd choice. – DC
Q: Can I open an investment account in my child’s name and use it as a future investment fund for them and invest the maximum annual exempt inheritance?
Given any current savings scheme for them would be subject to deemed disposal etc.
A: No, that will not be allowed. Access to these new personal investment accounts will be limited to people over the age of 18. – DC
Q: I am retired and have a pension of €56,000. My husband earns €70,000. How will will we benefit from budget tax wise?
A: The budget announced an increase in the standard rate cut off point, meaning you will pay less at the higher income tax rate of 40 per cent.
In addition to this, they have increased the personal tax credits, employee tax credit and earned income tax credits by €125.
As everyone’s circumstances are different, you may input your personal details to the income tax calculator to find out how the budget changes directly impact you.
This will compare your 2026 take home pay to the 2027 take home pay which is a useful tool. – RG
Q: I have three children in university, and I’m paying rent and fees for them. No SUSI grants due to us having saved hard for this time. Anything in this budget for us?
There are a couple of things here... and a few unknowns. Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers did announce a “permanent reduction to the student contribution fee of €150”, which brings the fee down to €2,850 from €3,000.
The disregard of the first €3,000 in fees before tax relief can be claimed will be adjusted to match this. So you will, as now, be able to claim tax relief against the fees of your second and third children at 20 per cent.
Also, as now, you will be entitled to a rent tax credit if you’re paying their rent – at least on one property.
Chambers in his speech also said: “I will also provide for enhanced and new student contribution fee grants for families with more than one child attending higher education.”
What that means we will have to wait to find out. SUSI maintenance grants will increase by 4.5 per cent. The Minister said the grant changes will benefit over 150,000 students and their families.
The SUSI grant increases and rent tax credit changes – it rises by €150 for a single person to €1,150 and by €300 for a couple to €2,300 – kick in from January. – DC
Q: Is the rent tax credit increase applicable to 2026?
The rent tax credit is increasing by €150 to €1,150 for a single person and by €300 to €2,300 for a couple.
Those increases will apply only for the 2027 and 2028 tax years – not this year – so you will be able to claim only at the existing level – €1,000 for a single person or €2,000 for a couple – for 2026. – DC
Q: Will the increased Help to Buy not just result in increased house prices? Has the Government determined the pros of doing this will outweigh the cons?
A: There is an ongoing debate as to whether the Help to Buy scheme is of genuine assistance to aspiring first-time homebuyers or simply something that only further inflates property prices.
From a Government perspective, it is certainly seen as giving the impression of positive action to support homebuyers.
One issue with the latest increase in the amount available under the scheme is that the €500,000 cap on properties that it applies to remains in place, effectively locking swathes of homebuyers in Dublin out of the market. – DC
You can submit any questions you have on the form below.
Q: Now that the Government has brought out this investment scheme, do you believe it is likely the momentum to do away with the deemed disposal rule for exchange traded funds will stall, or do you still see progress towards eventually scrapping that rule?
A: The Government has committed even in this budget to “continue the work on the wider [investment] regime, including the rate of taxation, deemed disposal and the administrative burden facing investors” with Minister for Finance Simon Harris also saying: “I intend to make further progression removing barriers to investment.” – DC
Good morning and welcome to our live Budget 2027 Q&A.
Here we are going to dig down into the detail of what it all means for you with Dominic Coyle, Deputy Business Editor at The Irish Times; Beryl Power, tax director at PwC Private Clients; and Ruth Gilligan, manager at PwC Private Client Services.
Q: Was there any indication the Mortgage Interest Tax Credit would be extended?
A: The mortgage interest tax credit was conspicuous by its absence from the budget speeches. The credit is due to expire at the end of this year and, despite the fact that mortgage rates are now rising again, it appears that it may be allowed to expire. – DC
Q: What does this budget mean for homeowners with solar panels? Many people have installed solar panels at considerable cost, banking on selling a certain amount of electricity back to the grid, to help cover the cost.
A: The exemption from income tax, USC and PRSI for the microgeneration of electricity is being increased from €400 to €600 for profits arising to an individual who generates energy from renewable resources for their own consumption.
The exempted profits are those arising from the domestic generation of electricity which is supplied to the grid. – BP
Q: Was there any movement in the €115,000 relevant earnings cap when applying the age-based percentage limits for tax-free pension contributions? Did the percentage movements change?
A: There was no change in relation to tax relief on contributions to private pension schemes – either in the percentage of income you can put into a pension in a year for tax relief purposes or the €115,000 cap on earnings against which those percentages apply. – DC
Q: The income tax band has been raised to €46,500. Is this double indexed to make up for no indexation in last year’s budget?
A: The Government is not likely to admit that the scale of the increase this year has been influenced by their failure to do anything on the standard rate band in the last budget.
However, Minister for Finance Simon Harris did say: “I want people at home to know that we’ve heard loud and clear the importance of a personal income tax package.”
The €2,500 increase is slightly more than had been expected, but only slightly. Anything below a €2,000 increase would have been seen as a letdown. – DC
Q: How much control do individuals have into the investments made under the scheme?
A: We don’t yet know how products under the scheme will be designed. They will not become available until July of next year.
However, you would expect that there will be a fair degree of choice among providers in the range of investments and investment approach.
And it also appears there will be nothing to prevent people moving investments from one product to another. – DC

title: UK wealth manager Rathbones secures Irish licence to operate across European Union
description: Permit enables firm, via Dublin-based entity, to serve new and existing clients across bloc
content:
UK wealth manager Rathbones has secured an Irish licence to set up an EU hub to target clients in the Republic and across the bloc.
The firm is known to be particularly keen to use the Irish Markets in Financial Instruments Directive licence to tap UK expatriate networks.
It highlighted in a press release on Wednesday that its research has shown nearly 6,000 “high-growth entrepreneurs” had left the UK between 2024 and 2026.
[ UK wealth manager Rathbones advances plan for EU hub in Dublin Opens in new window ]
The licence enables Rathbones, through its Dublin-based European entity, Rathbones Ireland, to serve new and existing clients here and across the EU. It marks an important step in strengthening the group’s international capabilities, supporting its long-term growth ambitions, it said.
“People’s lives no longer fit neatly within national borders. Careers, families, businesses and investments increasingly span several countries – and wealth management has to move with them,” said Camilla Stowell, chief executive of wealth at Rathbones.
“Securing our Irish licence is therefore central to what we do. It gives Rathbones a firm base from which to support clients in Ireland and across the EU, combining local presence with the investment expertise, financial planning and personal relationships of the wider group.”
Rathbones Ireland is led by managing director Dolores Geaney, a financial sector compliance veteran.
Geaney has 30 years of experience in global financial services, including leadership roles at Davy, Investec and more recently with Wells Fargo International.
The Central Bank of Ireland authorisation comes less than four months after Rathbones’s UK operation paused taking on certain higher-risk clients in the wake of a review prompted by engagement with the UK financial conduct watchdog.
The London-based firm said that it was pausing taking on new clients that require “enhanced due diligence” – or potentially higher-risk clients – as it focuses on implementing changes in procedures and controls. In the 12 months before the pause, the firm received £370 million (€437 million) from such clients to manage.
[ Household wealth in Ireland hits record €1.4tn Opens in new window ]
Rathbones had £115.6 billion of funds under management and advice at the end of last year. It started as a family-run timber merchant in 1742, and by 1912, it focused entirely on managing clients’ wealth.
Ireland’s wealth management industry has gained significant momentum in recent years. AIB and Bank of Ireland expanded their offerings through the purchases of Davy and Goodbody between 2021 and 2022, while several UK-based firms are launching operations in Ireland to support UK clients residing across the EU.
The Irish units of the likes of RBC Brewin Dolphin , Gresham House and Quilter Cheviot have also invested heavily in developing their businesses.

title: Half of HSE regions have ‘eaten into’ next year’s budget due to overruns, Minister says
description: Jennifer Carroll MacNeill said steps are being taken to prevent the overruns from reaching the billion figure
content:
Half of the Health Service Executive ( HSE ) regions have already “eaten into” next year’s budget allocation due to over-recruitment and financial overruns, the Minister for Health has said.
Budget 2027 announced a record €29.1 billion in funding for next year, of which €1.72 billion is for capital investment.
This year marked the first year that funding has been devolved into six regions, a key pillar of Sláintecare , the health service reform plan.
However, the health service has been under significant financial pressure in recent months, with the financial deficit being forecast to hit €1 billion by the end of the year.
Consequently, in September, four of the regionswere stripped of their powers over day-to-day spending.
Speaking at a press conference on Wednesday about her department’s budget allocation, Jennifer Carroll MacNeill said steps are being taken to prevent the overruns from reaching the billion figure.
The deficit for the end of September was €781 million, the Minister said, adding that there are two contributing factors, namely pay and medicines.
“There are two breakdowns on it. There is an area that we should be in control of, which is the pay budget. We have had a very significant uplift in resources,” she said.
[ Free contraception for women under 37 and homecare hours boost: Inside Budget 2027’s health package Opens in new window ]
“There was provision for 3,300 people on average salaries to be recruited in the second half of 2026 – contingent on reducing overtime and agency spend. Unfortunately, 3,600 people were recruited in the first half of the year without the commensurate and necessary reduction in agency and overtime.”
Carroll MacNeill said four of the six regions breached their pay budget by more than two per cent, though she acknowledged the West-North West region has made improvements and could bring it under this level by the end of the year.
“That’s not acceptable. That has to be reined in. If you’ve overrecruited this year, you’ve eaten into next year. This is about workforce planning. This is a test for management of the different regions that if you are given a budget by the taxpayers and patients of Ireland to recruit in strategic ways, you cannot do everything every single year,” she said.
“Within the first year of this regionally-funded structure, we have two regions that have performed very well, one that could come to below two per cent and three others that very clearly have eaten into next year’s provision.”
The Minister said the rising cost of drugs is an “expensive success story” and one which is “not part of the budget we can control”.
“There are no circumstances in which I would see the supplementary [additional budget] for a pay budget that hasn’t been managed, but we agree the cost of funding medicines is so very important and we will look at that as the year goes on.”
[ ‘I was shocked by it because of the spin beforehand’: How a healthcare worker, engineer and student view Budget 2027 Opens in new window ]
Meanwhile, Carroll MacNeill said a shingles vaccination programme is expected to start next June on a phased basis, starting with older people who are immunocompromised before gradually expanding to all over 65s.
There will also be a focus on recruiting into community services, rather than acute hospitals, and the State’s drugs budget will increase by €324 million to more than €4 billion next year
In mental health, Minister of State Mary Butler announced four new Jigsaw youth mental health services, two additional crisis resolution teams, six crisis cafes and 40 additional clinicians for a new ADHD pathway and enhanced intellectual disability capacity in the Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (Camhs).

title: Cruz Beckham to play Dublin date while on tour with band
description: Beckham and his band, The Breakers, will support The Reytons at Dublin’s 3Olympia
content:
Cruz Beckham has announced he is going back on tour with his band, The Breakers.
The 21-year-old musician, who is the son of David and Victoria Beckham , will serve as the opening act for rock band The Reytons.
The tour will begin in Dublin’s 3Olympia on October 9th, followed by dates in Belfast, Hull, Edinburgh, Cardiff, London and Manchester.
Cruz shared the tour dates on his Instagram and wrote: “Going back on tour this Friday, gonna be opening for @thereytons, seee yaaaa there xxx.”
The singer released his debut EP, Wear & Tear in August and made his UK festival debut that month when he performed with his band at the Reading Festival.
He also toured the US with gigs in Chicago, Seattle, Portland, San Francisco and Los Angeles.
Cruz has followed in the footsteps of his mother Victoria, who rose to fame as a member of the Spice Girls where she became known as Posh Spice.
He shared a photo of the pair together in a recording studio last month and wrote: “Yeah we got posh back in the studio.” – PA

title: The Social Reckoning review: Jeremy Strong is unblinking as Mark Zuckerberg
description: More stylish TV special than Academy Award prospect, the film lacks the toxic bang of its predecessor
content:
David Fincher ’s The Social Network is a tough act to follow. Anchored by Jesse Eisenberg ’s chilly, potent portrayal of the emotionally aloof Facebook creator Mark Zuckerberg , a pioneering score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, and Fincher’s Wellesian deep-focus framing, the 2010 biopic left an indelible footprint in popular culture.
This slanted sequel is similarly powered along by Aaron Sorkin ’s machine-gun dialogue. There are moments when the exchanges between Jeremy Allen White ’s intrepid tech reporter and Mikey Madison ’s whistleblower sound more like a screwball comedy than Deep Throat.
Sorkin, who leans into the tried-and-tested tropes of All the President’s Men, is the only principal to return for The Social Reckoning: Fincher is busy directing Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood spin-off for Netflix, and Eisenberg declined to reprise the main role, citing a dislike of Zuckerberg.
The screenwriter and West Wing creator also assumes directing duties. He finds a dramatic locus in Frances Haugen (Madison), the Facebook data engineer and whistleblower who leaked thousands of the company’s internal documents proving that Facebook’s algorithms intentionally rewarded inflammatory, divisive ragebait and misinformation to boost engagement.
Haugen, a Facebook loyalist, is carefully coaxed by Jeff Horwitz (White), a Wall Street Journal reporter.
The best scenes in the movie feature an unblinking Jeremy Strong as Zuckerberg. Strong simultaneously channels ruthlessness and oddness. The sequences in which Strong’s Zuckerberg attempts to model humility and human responses for an upcoming United States Senate hearing are what we came here for. Behind closed doors, he describes his empire as “post-government”.
Betty Gilpin is characteristically impactful as Horwitz’s no-nonsense commissioning editor, and Portia Doubleday is equally impressive as a privileged drunk driver. But the new film lacks the toxic bang of its predecessor: there’s no one as memorable as Justin Timberlake ’s sleazy Sean Parker or Armie Hammer ’s entitled Winklevoss twins in the margins.
[ Aaron Sorkin: ‘I only ever heard Jeremy speak in Mark Zuckerberg’s voice until his last day of shooting’ Opens in new window ]
Sorkin’s script is lively, even if its dramatisation of the events of January 6th, 2021, is overblown. Would that unruly display give the Meta chief executive pause? Seems like a reach. No matter.
The dark motivations underpinning the platform’s algorithms remain as unsettling as they were when Haugen first leaked the documents. And Madison and White are engaging, even if the film often feels more like a classy TV special than an Oscar contender.
The Social Reckoning is in cinemas from Friday, October 9th

title: Man charged with murder of Tadhg Farrell (4) and Mary Holt (60) in Edenderry house fire
description: Michael Dunne (22), with an address in Co Kildare, was charged with the murder of Tadhg Farrell (4) and Mary Holt (60) on December 6th
content:
A man has been charged with murder in relation to the house fire in Co Offaly last year that claimed the lives of a four-year-old boy and his grand-aunt.
At Tullamore District Court, Michael Dunne (22), with an address in Co Kildare, was charged with the murder of Tadhg Farrell (4) and Mary Holt (60) at Castleview Park, Edenderry, on December 6th.
Dunne was also charged with assault, causing serious harm to Pauline Holt.
Detective Tom Dunne gave evidence of charging Dunne on Wednesday and said he made no reply after caution.
The accused, who is in custody and whose full address cannot be published by order of the court, had previously been accused of arson at Castleview Park, Edenderry.
That charge remains before the court as does another of endangerment on the same date.
However, the endangerment charge has been amended.
Judge Andrew Cody permitted the amendment, which results in the charge now alleging that Dunne broke the front window of the house and intentionally caused a fire that created a substantial risk of death or serious harm to four named males.
Sergeant Richard Thornton said the DPP had directed trial by indictment on the new charges.
There was no application for bail and Dunne was remanded in custody to appear in court again by video-link in advance of another court appearance on October 28th when a book of evidence will be served.
Tadgh Farrell, and Mary Holt died following the fire at Castleview Park on December 6th, 2025.

title: When budget changes kick in and how to claim them
description: Dates that consumer changes - such as income tax, fuel allowances, childcare and rent relief - come into effect
content:
In Budget 2027 , Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris and Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers announced a number of consumer changes such as to income tax, fuel allowances, childcare and rent relief.
But when will these changes kick in and what do I need to do to claim them?
Harris said the changes to income tax will come into effect from January 2027.
The changes to income tax will be automatically applied.
This increase will take effect from January 1st.
This will also come into effect in January.
This will be paid to all adult long-term recipients of disability benefits, including the disability allowance, full incapacity pension and the blind pension, accessible to some 240,000 people.
The first payment will happen early next year, in the first quarter.
Both will be available from January 2027.
[ Budget 2027 main points: everything you need to know Opens in new window ]
The carer’s allowance is a payment for people on low incomes who are caring for a person who needs full-time care and attention because of age, disability or illness.
However, Minister for Social Protection Dara Calleary said the Government will “get rid of” the means test for the carer’s allowance during the lifetime of this Government, but it has to be done on a “sustainable basis”.
[ Q&A: How will social welfare changes affect you? Opens in new window ]
To avail of the Help-to-Buy scheme, first time buyers must apply through Revenue Online Service and go through application, claim and verification stages.
The increase comes into effect on October 7th.
Both of these will come into effect from January.
The rent tax credit and the rent-a-room relief can be claimed through your Income Tax Return with Revenue Online Service.
However, the rent tax credit increases will apply only for the 2027 and 2028 tax years – not this year – so you will be able to claim only at the existing level – €1,000 for a single person or €2,000 for a couple – for 2026.
[ Budget 2027 Q&A: Your questions answered Opens in new window ]
The three inheritance tax thresholds have been increased.
The changes will apply to gifts and inheritances taken from October 7th.
Gift and Inheritance tax can be paid and filed through Revenue Online Service.
Yes, the fuel allowance was increased by €5 per week to €43 per week from this season with a higher income threshold for single people over 66 of €641. This change will happen in January.

Yes, excise duty on a box of cigarettes rises by €1 from October 7th.
A 20 cent tax per ml of vape e-liquid, exclusive of VAT, was also introduced. However, it does not come into effect until January 1st.

title: Refusal of Irish visas for Palestinian students is ‘trapping’ people in Gaza, court hears
description: Refusal of Irish visas is ‘trapping’ people in Gaza, says counsel for students
content:
Appeals by four Palestinian students against the refusal of visas allowing them to pursue Irish university scholarships will be decided by the end of the week, following an agreement between their lawyers and the Minister for Justice.
The High Court was due to hear the students’ judicial review challenges against the refusals this week.
However, Judge Anthony Barr was told on Wednesday the cases had settled following an offer by Minister Jim O’Callaghan to determine the students’ appeals by close of business on Friday.
Three of the students are in Gaza, while the fourth is in Spain after being evacuated there with the assistance of the Spanish government. He is pursuing a second-choice course in Spain, but his preference is to take up his first choice of an engineering course in Dublin’s Trinity College .
Among the orders sought by the students was one requiring the Minister to prioritise the hearing of their appeals, because otherwise the courses could not be pursued this academic year. Normally, such appeals can take more than a year to resolve.
Blinne Ní Ghrálaigh, senior counsel for the students, asked the judge for the cases to be adjourned generally, and asked for permission to re-mention the cases if required.
Ní Ghrálaigh indicated the possibility of further judicial review challenges if the appeals are unsuccessful.
Ní Ghrálaigh, who is acting in further cases brought by Palestinian students in similar circumstances, said two of her clients had been refused British visas off the back of the refusal of Irish visas. She submitted that the Irish refusal was “trapping” people in Gaza.
Eoin Carolan, senior counsel for the Minister, said there was agreement to the appeals being determined by Friday. He said his side disagreed with certain characterisations of the negotiations between the parties.
The judge made orders noting the Minister’s agreement to determine the appeals.
The visa refusals were for reasons including that the Gazan students had not provided original documents with their application.
On their behalf, it was argued the civilian infrastructure for them to go to a bank or post office to get such documents no longer exists in Gaza and the Minister’s stance was irrational, unreasonable, disproportionate, discriminatory and fails to react to the necessary urgency of the situation.
[ ‘It’s off the charts’: Satellite images show how three years of war have devastated Gaza Opens in new window ]
More than two million displaced people are living in tents and temporary shelters in Gaza, where an estimated 80 per cent of structures – roughly 200,000 buildings – have been damaged, with about two-thirds of those destroyed, according to the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, Unrwa.

title: France pauses use of stun grenades in school protest operations after boy’s hand blown off
description: French prime minister Sébastien Lecornu to address nation as school protests escalate
content:
The French government said on Wednesday it was pausing the use ‌of stun grenades in its policing of student protests after a 15-year-old boy’s hand was blown off during a clash with riot police .
Rights groups, students and some political opponents have accused the French police ​of using disproportionate force during a more than two-week-old wave of student protests that has exposed deep-seated public anger in advance of elections next year.
French prime minister Sébastien Lecornu is to address the nation on Wednesday evening after hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets on Tuesday.
Emmanuel Macron, the French president, held emergency talks with Lecornu and the education and interior ministers at the Élysée Palace on Tuesday night. Few details have emerged, but Lecornu has promised discussions on increased school funding and possible changes to the university admissions system.
[ Inside the school protests in France that have spiralled into arson and street violence Opens in new window ]
Lecornu has acknowledged the “legitimate” demands of France’s students but also described the unrest as the most violent ⁠student demonstrations in decades.
Interior minister Laurent Nunez, meanwhile, said he had ordered the stun grenade suspension until there was more clarity around the events that took place in the northern city of Lens on Monday. Nunez said there was a “strong possibility” the firing of a non-lethal stun ​grenade had caused the teenager to lose his hand.
“I am suspending their use for the high school students’ movement until light has been shed on what happened in this case,” said the minister, who ⁠added that 18 investigations in total had been referred to the police inspectorate.
The high school students are ‌angered ‌over ​dilapidated infrastructure, teacher shortages, overloaded schedules and a lack of funding in education.
They blame the poor learning conditions for France’s worsening scores in the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa), which have fallen faster than the OECD average since 2015, according to ⁠the rankings.
In reading, French 15-year-olds, the age when high school begins, ​scored 43 points lower in 2025 than a decade earlier, the biggest drop ​in the OECD. Their math scores also dropped the most.
Protests showed no sign of easing on Wednesday, with more than 500 schools closed a day after demonstrations swept ‌across the country. Unions called for another day of street ​marches later in the week.
Far-right and hard-left parties are front-runners in the presidential ⁠race to replace Emmanuel Macron six ​months in advance of the election.
Under pressure to tame public debt amid weak growth, the government has little spare cash to address the students’ complaints of understaffing, a lack of investment in ageing school buildings and inequality between regions.
The left-wing CGT trade union, France’s second-largest, said it would rally behind the student union’s call for further street protests on Thursday.
“The CGT will continue to shoulder its responsibilities in supporting the young people who have mobilised and protecting them from violence and police repression,” a CGT statement said.
In a sign the protests in France might spur unrest elsewhere in Europe, where budgets have been under pressure as governments respond to successive cost-of-living and energy crises, students in parts of Belgium have launched copycat ‌actions.
In the Belgian city of Liege in ⁠the southern French-speaking Wallonia region, at least 107 people have been arrested in connection with student protests this month, the Belga news agency reported.
In Portugal, the main teachers’ union launched an indefinite strike in mid-September against overtime, with teachers refusing to do ‌any unpaid work beyond 35 hours a week mandated by law.
“The underlying causes of the (French) protests reflect problems familiar to teachers and students in other countries: deteriorating school conditions, teacher shortages, excessive workloads, and ​widening inequalities in access to education,” the union said in a statement.
And in Spain, teachers’ unions have been ​protesting conditions in state schools. Teachers in Madrid plan a strike on October 14 to press demands including a reduction in hours, smaller class sizes and higher salaries. – Reuters

title: Michael Lynn associate refused to provide passwords for phones seized during Garda search in Dublin
description: Yavor Poptoshev pleaded guilty to not handing over passwords for phones seized by the Garda National Economic Crime Bureau
content:
A friend and business associate of convicted solicitor Michael Lynn has been fined €500 over his refusal to provide passwords to two mobile phones seized during a Garda search of his Dublin apartment.
Yavor Poptoshev (50) failed to disclose the passwords when armed members of the Garda National Economic Crime Bureau , acting on warrants, arrived at the apartment at St Raphaela’s Road, Stillorgan, Dublin, just after 7am on January 9th, 2024, and seized the devices.
The raid on the apartment was one of many carried out by gardaí investigating possible money laundering associated with the massive frauds carried out by Lynn, the High Court was subsequently told. Poptoshev was a director of some of the Irish property companies under investigation.
The Bulgarian national told gardaí he would provide the passwords if he was advised by his solicitor that he was obliged to do so. He was taken to Dundrum Garda station where, after speaking with a solicitor, he said he was refusing to provide the passwords based on legal advice.
The failure to disclose the passwords led to Poptoshev being charged. Progress in the case was delayed by an unsuccessful challenge to the High Court and the Supreme Court, where he argued that the 2001 Criminal Justice (Theft and Fraud Offences) Act did not give the authorities the power to compel him to disclose his passwords.
Following the Supreme Court ruling, the data was extracted from the devices by the Garda National Cyber Crime Bureau, without the assistance of Poptoshev, the District Court in Dún Laoghaire was told on Wednesday.
Poptoshev pleaded guilty to the two charges, the court heard.
When Judge Conor Fottrell sought confirmation that no other charges had been brought arising from the search of Poptoshev’s apartment, Brian Coveney, for the Director of Public Prosecutions , said there was an ongoing Garda investigation but “as things stand, there is nothing arising”.
The judge then imposed a fine of €250 in respect of each of the two charges, with six months to pay. Poptoshev, he said, had been given two opportunities to provide the passwords on foot of warrants issued by the court.
Earlier, Det Garda Anthony Woods said Poptoshev, his wife and their children were in the Dublin apartment at the time of the 2024 search, which was part of a wider “extensive” investigation.
Barrister Aoife McCann, for Poptoshev, said her client’s life had been “extremely impacted” by the search, which “changed everything” for him.
Popstoshev, who had come to Ireland in July 2022 in pursuit of his career in property development, was now living back in Bulgaria where he worked as the manager of a sports goods shop and had “left his career in property”, she said.
She asked that the Probation Act be applied. Her client had no previous convictions, she told the court.
In 2023, Michael Lynn was convicted on 10 counts of theft in 2006 and 2007 from various financial institutions of amounts totalling €17.9 million. He was sentenced to 5½ years in jail.
In his civil challenge to the legality of the charges brought against him, Poptoshev said he had known Lynn for 14 or 15 years and had worked with him on projects in several countries, including Portugal, Hungary and Slovakia.
Poptoshev said he assisted him with “forensic analysis” of Lynn’s affairs during the solicitor’s 2023 criminal trial.
The Bulgarian is a former director of the Irish company that bought the house in Co Wicklow where Lynn’s family has been living in recent years. Lynn was released from prison earlier this year under the community return scheme and is understood to be living in the house.

title: The astonishing fall of a German spymaster
description: Espionage, state secrets and foreign agents: the case engulfing former head of Germany’s intelligence reads like a spy thriller
content:
N ot even John le Carré could have dreamt up a story like the one swirling around his former friend August Hanning. The spy novelist met Hanning regularly during his tenure, from 1998-2005, as head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND).
In his memoir, Le Carré described the gaunt BND head as “courtesy itself”, yet their friendship fell apart after modern Germany’s greatest-ever intelligence failure: the 9/11 plot hatched in Hamburg under the clueless noses of German spy chiefs.
Hanning’s subsequent passivity during Washington’s so-called “war on terror”, including the detention and torture of an innocent Turkish man living in Germany, was, Le Carré later told him, a “moral failure of the highest order”.
Had he not died in 2020, the novelist might have revised that view over the charges Hanning faces now.
After a dawn raid on his home on Tuesday, the 80-year-old Hanning was detained overnight and brought before a remand judge on Wednesday. He faces charges of treason, illegal spying of state secrets and espionage for a foreign power.
Prosecutors say the ex-spy chief himself turned spy in retirement, buying classified information from his former BND office manager – identified only as Manfred D and reported assistant to many BND heads after Hanning – and selling the information to foreign intelligence services.
His lawyer acknowledged Hanning had indeed had unauthorised possession of classified documents but described as “incorrect” the claim “that he passed on information contained therein to the detriment of the Federal Republic of Germany - let alone for payment”.
Azerbaijan is reportedly top of Hanning’s client list but other buyers are likely, potentially making this Germany’s greatest espionage disaster since 1974, when a senior aide to former West German chancellor Willy Brandt was exposed as an East German spy. Just as damaging as the alleged espionage is how it emerged only by chance.
[ John le Carré ‘died an Irishman’ after gaining citizenship, son says Opens in new window ]
In retirement Hanning set himself up as a security consultant and built up an eclectic client list, from Baltic banks to Russian oligarchs, that raised eyebrows – and protest – in Berlin.
Hanning’s most unusual client emerged in a high-profile custody court case, running since July 2025 in Hamburg, involving Christina Block, heiress to the Block House steak restaurant fortune.
Block is accused of hiring Israeli ex-secret service agents to kidnap two of her children, living with her estranged husband in Denmark, to return them to Germany. Hanning’s name was mentioned in court as the man who allegedly helped her find the agents.
In light of that claim, Hamburg criminal police raided Hanning’s home a year ago. As part of their search, they reportedly found a hard drive containing 2,000 classified documents, including eyes-only BND reports for the chancellor.
Alarmed at what they saw, and determined to outfox the ex-spy chief, a Hamburg security services officer posed as a disgruntled former police man and applied for a job with Hanning’s consultancy. Once inside, the spy reportedly gained full access to Hanning’s information trove, client list and more. It was on the basis of this information that police raided Hanning’s home on Tuesday.
For Germany, though, the worst may be yet to come. For decades, Hanning’s civil servant career was clouded by speculation about his loyalties, with persistent whispers of too-close-for-comfort ties to Israel and Russia. The latter date back to his days in West Germany’s permanent representation in East Berlin, where he was responsible for the political prisoner release programme.
As BND head during the 9/11 attacks, his ties to the US brought him considerable blowback. As part of the aftermath, US special forces abducted Murat Kurnaz, a Turkish citizen and German resident. They accused him of ties to the 9/11 plot and he was tortured during a year in the Guantánamo Bay detention camp. In 2002, when US authorities concluded Kurnaz was innocent, they offered to return him to Germany. Hanning protested and Kurnaz was kept at Guantánamo Bay for another five years.
Hanning’s notoriety grew in 2002 after he passed on to the CIA what he called “plausible and convincing” evidence, from an Iraqi asylum seeker in Germany, that he had worked on mobile plants in his homeland producing chemical and biological weapons. Weeks later the claims, which Hanning told the CIA “couldn’t be confirmed”, made it into US president George W Bush’s state of the union address.
Curveball was later revealed to be a fantasist who, in the opinion of spy thriller writer Frederick Forsyth, was responsible for the “biggest fiasco in the history of secret intelligence”.
[ How the sexual problems of a KGB double agent may have stopped the cold war from going nuclear Opens in new window ]
Unless, that is, Hanning proves to be an even greater fiasco. The latest BND scandal is just the most recent test of its partner agencies’ patience in recent years. The last scandal from 2022, the subject of an ongoing trial, involves claims a senior BND agent passed high-level security secrets to the Kremlin. Furious BND partner agencies demanded to know then whether any information they had provided the Germans – on trust that it would be safe – was part of those alleged leaks to Russia. It is likely that BND chief Martin Jäger is fielding similar calls today.
Hours before Hanning’s arrest, in a public parliamentary hearing, Jäger warned of the growing threat from Russia and demanded an upgrade to his agency’s finances and competences to match those other western intelligence services.
“We are serious,” he said, “about being Germany’s first line of defence.”
A day later, Germany’s supposed first line of defence was revealed to have been breached – allegedly from the inside.

title: Small Prophets on Apple TV: A new genre that is funny, fantastical and heartbreakingly tender
description: Television: The magical realism is unexpected - it’s like turning on Alan Partridge only for someone to ride in on a dragon
content:
Back when he played David Brent’s hapless lackey, Gareth, in The Office , it would have been surreal to imagine Mackenzie Crook one day eclipsing Ricky Gervais to become the doyen of bittersweet British comedy.
Yet that is precisely what has happened. As Gervais burns up all the goodwill he acquired playing Brent with his tragic live shows and dire Netflix comedies, Crook has quietly created a new genre where wry laughter and heartbreaking whimsy live together in uneasy coexistence.
That was the formula he unlocked on Detectorists, with its droll profile of male friendships, and his funny/spooky revival of Worzel Gummidge . He now ascends to a Pokémon-style final evolutionary stage with the wonderful magical realist chuckle-fest Small Prophets, which comes to Apple TV eight months after it debuted on the BBC .
In theory, the story of depressed middle-aged DIY store worker Michael (Pearce Quigley) and his quest to grow Biblical homunculi in his shed (the eponymous small prophets) really should not work at all. But Crook, who writes and directs all six episodes, invests such humanity in his portrait of a man quietly drowning in his maudlin existence that it is irresistible.
Crook himself plays Michael’s David Brent-esque boss, while Lauren Patel shines as a sarcastic coworker roped into the homunculi plot. But their thunder is thoroughly stolen by Michael Palin as Michael’s ageing dad Brian, who has been bunged off to a care home and is in the early stages of dementia.
It is during one of his increasingly rare moments of clarity that he beseeches Michael to cultivate the homunculi – Brian picked up the know-how in Egypt – so that they can solve the mystery around the whereabouts of Michael’s girlfriend, who vanished without a trace seven years previously, condemning Michael to a state of permanent stasis.
The magical realism of Small Prophets places it firmly in the firmament of urbane British fantasy and figures such as Terry Pratchett – but this isn’t what all viewers will have signed up for, and to some it is going to be a deal-breaker. It’s like turning on Alan Partridge only for someone to ride in on the back of a dragon.
They would do well to persevere however as these elements only serve to accentuate the sad plod of Michael’s daily life and to raise the dramatic stakes of his quietly affectionate exchanges with his ailing dad. Mashing together the bizarre and the banal, Small Prophets is funny, fantastical and, above all, heartbreakingly tender.

title: Avan Lee appointed interim chief executive of Munster
description: Former Hurricanes chief executive will replace Ian Flanagan at the province
content:
Avan Lee will take over as interim chief executive of Munster when Ian Flanagan steps down at the end of the month. The initial appointment is for 12 months but, by his admission, Lee is looking at locking down the position on a full-time basis.
He said: “It’s 12 months, is the interim, which is whatever you take from that. But ... from my perspective, my attitude is that it’s permanent. And, you know, once I do a good job, I’m sure that will happen. But I’m not coming over to look at a 12-month job. I feel like I’m leaving New Zealand for this opportunity.”
The New Zealander served as chief executive of the Hurricanes rugby franchise for more than 10 years (2015-2025) and since then has been a consultant for World Rugby and a member of the board of trustees for Special Olympics New Zealand in a part-time capacity.
Lee brings more than a decade of leadership at the highest level in a career spanning rugby administration, governance, commercial development and high-performance sport where he built a strong reputation for strategic leadership, organisational growth and stakeholder engagement.
Born in Dargaville, he grew up in Whangarei on New Zealand’s north island. His dream was to play for the All Blacks, but, as he said in an interview with the Business Desk media outlet, “that’s akin to saying I wanted to be a superhero, to be honest, because not many people become All Blacks”.
He did management studies and marketing at Waikato before travelling to Dublin, where he played for Clontarf in a team that contained Bernard Jackman and with Brent Pope as a player-coach.
“After university I went straight to Ireland to play rugby. I played premier rugby, the top division. My first job there was for a marketing company doing event marketing and management; it was very much an entry-level role. I was pretty happy living in Dublin.”
He took up his role with the Hurricanes in June 2015 and led the club through a significant period of their history, which included a first ever Super Rugby title in 2016. In a tribute paid to Lee when he stepped down, a statement from the club read: “Under his guidance, the Hurricanes have developed a diverse commercial network both in New Zealand and abroad, a robust culture, and high-quality playing and coaching rosters, that provide a strong platform for the next chapter of success.”
Lee said of his appointment: “I am honoured to be appointed interim CEO of Munster Rugby. This is a province with a proud history, passionate supporters and a strong reputation within the game. While my professional career has taken me around the world, Ireland has been an important part of my own rugby journey.
“I spent nearly a decade living here, including playing club rugby, and I developed a deep appreciation for the game’s place in Irish communities and the unique connection between rugby clubs and their supporters.
“There are important challenges ahead but I firmly believe there is also tremendous opportunity. I am excited to work alongside our players, coaches, staff, volunteers, partners and supporters as we build on Munster Rugby’s strengths and shape a successful future.
“My message to everyone connected with the province is simple: we are stronger when we stand together. If we unite behind a shared ambition and a commitment to excellence, I am confident Munster Rugby can achieve great things in the years ahead.”
Munster Rugby chair Ger Malone welcomed the appointment, having indicated that Lee interviewed well: “We are delighted to appoint Avan as interim CEO of Munster Rugby. Throughout the interview process, Avan impressed the board with both the breadth of his rugby experience and his clear understanding of the opportunities and challenges facing professional sports organisations today.
[ Munster’s problems cannot be laid at the door of one person Opens in new window ]
“He brings strong leadership credentials, significant rugby expertise and a collaborative approach that we believe will be hugely valuable to Munster Rugby. The board has every confidence he will provide strong stewardship of the province, and we look forward to working closely with him in the months ahead.”
Lee will take up the role towards the end of this month – he arrives in Ireland on October 21st, the same week Munster travel to take on Leinster at the Aviva Stadium.

title: Is your bus or train always overcrowded? Share your story
description: Pressure on State’s transport services is greater than ever
content:
Demand for public transport is at a record level. Almost 22 million rail journeys, excluding the Luas, were taken between January 1 st and May 24 th 2026, which was up 13 per cent on the same period in 2025, according to the Central Statistics Office .
The strain on the State’s transport services is seen in overcrowded train carriages and buses. Commuters can find themselves being left behind on platforms or at bus stops at peak times because services are full.
With schools back after the summer and some employers starting to cut back on remote working, the pressure on transport links is greater than ever.
