title: In search of Llandudno’s Kashmiri goats and their rebel spirit
description: Llandudno Letter: Wild herd on the Great Orme became famous for taking over the deserted town during Covid lockdown
content:
Covid lockdowns are best erased from our memories, but who could forget Llandudno’s renegade Kashmiri goats?
They went viral worldwide in March 2020 during Britain’s first lockdown when the wild herd on the Great Orme descended from the headland, taking over the deserted streets of the Welsh seaside town below.
As the world reeled from the onset of Covid, it seemed like a dystopian animal uprising might be under way. People also needed a laugh. The goats gobbled up all of Llandudno’s flowers and wouldn’t do social distancing. Rebels. I had to meet them.
My chance came last weekend while in town for a Plaid Cymru political conference.
Llandudno’s wild Kashmiri goats are descended from a herd kept by the British queen Victoria, who got them as a gift from the Persian Shah. He thought she might like her own cashmere – the goats’ shaggy coats are prized.
Lord Mostyn, a Welsh nobleman, was granted a few from the royal herd. They ate all his flowers too, so he released them at the end of the 1800s on to the limestone headland of Great Orme, the great big slab of grey overlooking Llandudno’s pier.
The distinctive white goats with their shaggy coats, beards and dramatically curved horns have roamed the headland ever since, with the herd now up to about 180. I once read that the Welsh authorities used contraception to keep the numbers down. For clarity, they used injections.
As soon as I could wriggle free of the Plaid conference on Friday, I headed for the Great Orme in the little hire car I had driven over from other engagements in England’s northwest. It was spitting rain and windy. There was no way I would roam the hills. I’d have to find my shaggy rebel heroes from the road instead.
[ At Plaid Cymru’s annual party conference, it wasn’t always clear who the protesters were Opens in new window ]
I drove past Llandudno’s pier – voted “Pier of the Year 2025” – and up the hill to the spectacular road that hugs the underside of the crags. Soon I hit a fork in the road. Which way? Up is surely a good bet when looking for goats.
Soon I stumbled upon a wonderfully picturesque and, in the inclement weather, eerie old cemetery. Its gnarly trees had been bent into unnatural shapes by decades of wind. It was the cemetery of St Tudno, a sixth century hermit monk who founded the town. I found ancient graves and lots of sheep. No goats.
It was getting dark and there was nobody else stupid enough to be still out on Great Orme, but I kept going. Always up. I passed the deserted cable car station, the 4,000-year-old copper mines and an old tramway before, eventually, I reached the summit.
The car rocked in the stiff breeze. I parked overlooking the village of Dwygyfylchi across an inlet below. Ten consonants before a lone vowel – how very Welsh, I thought. I watched seabirds being buffeted in the big wind. Boats skipped across the water. Still I saw no goats. As the light declined, I had to abandon my search.
Next morning I was speaking to Liz Saville-Roberts, who leads Plaid Cymru’s group of MPs in Westminster. We were on the promenade, a mile from the headland. She claimed she could see goats from there: “Look at the white blobs moving on the cliff.”
God bless her eyesight. I raced up the promenade. Sure enough, as I reached the pier, people were taking pictures of two goats precariously perched a hundred metres away on a cliff edge above the Elm Tree hotel – the goats still regularly pop down to town.
I wanted to get closer, but first I had to work. As I made my way back to the Plaid conference, I was assailed over loudspeaker on the promenade by Dave, a busking ventriloquist from Chester, and his sarcastic puppet, Archie.
For some reason that I now cannot fathom, I gave Dave £3. Archie sang me a witless song over the loudspeaker. A crowd gathered, so I discreetly backed away. As I left, a homeless man in a hoodie said to me, deadpan: “I bet that cheered you up.”
I didn’t know why it was now so important to me, but I had to find those goats.
It was a glorious sunny day. I headed back up the Great Orme in the afternoon. I parked beneath a cliff. I climbed halfway up but abandoned it when it got too steep: I was wearing a pair of centrist-Dad black Vans and a blazer, not hiking gear. I had goat fever.
I found another route up a shoulder to access the open headlands. Eventually, I spotted a lone Kashmiri goat, a female identifiable by her shorter, less curved horns. Her beard, however, was worthy of ZZ Top.
It was rutting season, so I followed her from a distance, lest a bigger-horned suitor was nearby and feeling frisky. She led me to the other side of the headland, looking out towards the Isle of Man. Dozens of the goats were fanned out, lying on the hill in the sun.
I watched them for half an hour as they stared out at the blue waters below. A few munched from the heather as the grass all around them quivered in the slight breeze.
One goat, a big male with looping horns, kept bullying the others, butting them for no apparent reason. Finally, one of the smaller goats butted him back.
Good on these rugged Kashmiri goats of Wales. They never do what they’re told.

title: Man in ‘critical’ condition after attempted e-scooter robbery in Co Louth
description: One suspect has been arrested, another is being sought by gardaí
content:
A man (40s) has been hospitalised with “serious injuries” following an attempt to steal his e-scooter by two men in Co Louth on Tuesday night.
One man has been arrested in connection with the incident. Gardaí are searching for the second suspect.
The victim of the attempted robbery, in his 40s, was brought to Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital in Drogheda and remains in “critical condition” after being approached in Muirhevnamor at about 8.30pm by two men who tried to steal his e-scooter.
Gardaí arrested a man in his 30s in connection with the attempted robbery.
He is being held in a nearby Garda station under Section 4 of the Criminal Justice Act 1984.
Garda have appealed for any witnesses to the incident, or anyone who may have video footage from the Muirhevnamor area between 7pm and 9pm on Tuesday to contact investigators.

title: Three challenges to Galway City Ring Road permission settled
description: A fourth action against the permission remains live
content:
Several Galway residents have settled their High Court challenges to permission granted for the long-delayed Galway ring road.
The touted N6 Galway City Ring Road is an 18km project intended to provide an orbital route around Galway city, linking the N56 Moycullen Road to the N6 Dublin Road corridor.
On Wednesday, barrister Damien Keaney told Judge Richard Humphreys that three challenges to the permission, granted by An Coimisiún Pleanála to Galway County Council , had been settled.
A fourth challenge, brought by software engineer Shane Foran, remains live, and is due to be heard next month.
Foran, a cyclists’ advocate from Rahoon, Galway, claims An Coimisiún Pleanála breached its duties under the Climate Action and Low Carbon Development Act 2021 by granting the permission. Foran is representing himself in the proceedings.
The commission approved the ring road project in April after several decades of false starts.
Galway city has had severe traffic problems for more than 30 years, and various proposals for a ring road have been advanced in that time.
High Court challenges to a previous grant of permission for the project led to An Coimisiún Pleanála’s predecessor conceding its decision contained legal flaws, so the planning application was considered afresh.

title: Two men (20s) to appear in court charged over suspected €350,000 cannabis seizure
description: Gardaí searched Cork city home in effort to stop sale of drugs
content:
Two men have been arrested after suspected cannabis thought to be worth €350,000 was found during a raid of a home in Cork city.
The men, who are in their 20s, were arrested and charged. They are both due to appear before Cork District Court on Wednesday morning.
The seizure came as part of a Garda search operation in Togher conducted by the Cork City Drugs Unit targeting the sale and supply of drugs.
A series of small-scale drug seizures have been made by the unit in the area in the past year, it is understood.
On Monday night, gardaí searched a home in the southwest of the city on foot of a search warrant and discovered a large amount of what is suspected to be cannabis.
The identification of the suspected cannabis will be confirmed upon analysis by Forensic Science Ireland. It is believed to have a street value of €350,000.
The investigation into the drug dealing operation remains “ongoing”, the force said.

title: Cristiano Ronaldo says he approved eight points for Portugal coach Jorge Jesus to make about him
description: The 41-year-old says Jesus ‘broke his word’ when he did not read out the agreed document at press conference
content:
Cristiano Ronaldo said in a lengthy statement on Tuesday that the Portugal head coach, Jorge Jesus, had agreed to make eight points relating to him in a press conference before the team’s game in Denmark last week.
Ronaldo left Portugal’s training camp last week after he was an unused substitute in their 2-1 Nations League win against Norway on September 27th.
Ronaldo said he had approved a document listing the points after a video meeting involving him, Jesus, his adviser Tiago Craveiro and his club Al-Nassr’s sporting director, Simão Coutinho.
The meeting, according to Ronaldo, was at “the coach’s request” and he said the document was then “delivered to the coach, as he had requested”.
Ronaldo said Jesus’s failure to make the points in the press conference constituted “the second time he had broken his word to me” and that he then “decided to leave the camp without waiting for any further breach of word”.
Ronaldo’s statement included reference to his failure to salute Portugal’s fans after the game in Norway during which he warmed up extensively but was not brought on.
He said: “The notes I validated were the following: ‘I think it is important, also because it is the truth, to clarify a few things before talking about Denmark:
Ronaldo’s statement then said: “That was all. None of these notes, therefore, said that the coach should even apologise to me.”
Reflecting on Jesus’s conduct in the press conference Ronaldo said: “I heard expressions and an aggressiveness that I do not believe I deserved, an attitude of ‘I want, I can and I command’ that he never showed me, not even remotely, in private the day before.”
Ronaldo apologised in his statement to his Portugal team-mates and to the Portuguese people and said he would be available to play for his country in future.
“The consequence of this act of mine must be assessed and punished by the Portuguese Football Federation,” Ronaldo said on Instagram.
“I believe the punishment should have no mitigating factors. I am not just any player. I am a team captain and that is an aggravating factor.
“I have already apologised but I know that actions must have consequences.”
Jesus revealed he had read Ronaldo’s explanation but opted not to comment further on the matter.
Jesus told reporters when leaving his home on Wednesday: “I read the statement and now I do [like I do] every day. I’m going to the federation to work, think about the team.”
Jesus left the door open to Ronaldo in a press conference after Sunday’s win against Norway, saying: “If he wants to, he’ll return to the national team.”

title: Court clears way for hearing following row sparked by complaint about child alone in car
description: It was claimed father left two-year-old son asleep in his car while he went shopping
content:
The High Court has cleared the way for the hearing of a prosecution against a father for public order offences allegedly arising out of an incident following a complaint to gardaí about his two-year-old child being left alone sleeping in his car while he went shopping.
The man was arrested in the Liffey Valley Shopping Centre, Dublin, following an altercation between him and gardaí, who had been informed about the child in the car on August 25th, 2019.
It was claimed that he left one of his sons, who was asleep at the time, in the parked car for a brief period while he made a purchase at a shopping centre.
He was charged with threatening, abusive or insulting behaviour in a public place, failure to comply with a garda direction and refusal to give his name and address.
He denied those charges and sought to bring his own private prosecution against the gardaí over what he said were three wrongful prosecutions from the incident.
The private prosecution application was refused by the District Court and ultimately the Court of Appeal dismissed a challenge to that refusal.
Before the public order case went ahead in Blanchardstown District Court, the man brought separate High Court proceedings over a refusal by the district judge to give him a separate preliminary hearing to address his request for further disclosure by the prosecuting authorities.
He wanted video and audio recordings from the shopping centre and Garda station, together with any recording from a garda recording device. The DPP said disclosure obligations had been complied with.
In a judgment, the High Court’s Judge Garrett Simons refused his application for a separate preliminary hearing before his criminal trial.
[ Dublin teen sent video of himself inhaling aerosols a year before he died from fumes, inquest hears Opens in new window ]
There was no fixed rule which dictated that there must always be a separate preliminary hearing in advance of a criminal trial in the District Court, still less that such a hearing must take place at least four weeks before trial, the judge said.
The decision on disclosure, and the identification of any procedural measures necessary to secure a fair trial, were matters for the District Court in the first instance, Simons said.
The judge said the man remains at liberty to seek additional disclosure when the proceedings next come before the District Court.
A reporting restriction on naming the man to protect his children will remain in force unless and until varied by further order, the judge said.
However, a party to the proceedings, or any bona fide member of the media, may apply to vary the order on seven days’ notice to the man, Simons said.

title: Hostelworld shares slide as earnings to miss estimates amid Middle East conflict
description: Irish company said drag on bookings to last into 2027
content:
Hostelworld , the Irish hostel-booking group targeting millennial and Gen Z backpackers, saw its shares slide to a four-year low on Wednesday after warning that its full-year earnings will miss market expectations as the Middle East conflict weighs on bookings.
The Dublin-based group added that it expects the drag on volumes to last into 2027.
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) is now forecast to come between €20 million and €21 million this year, below the €22.9 million consensus expectation of analysts. It reported earnings of €19.9 million in 2025.
Hostelworld shares slumped as much as 16.5 per cent to 85.2 pence in early trading in London, where they are more frequently traded than in Dublin. It had recovered some ground by early afternoon to be down by 8.5 per cent at just more than 93 cent.
“With Asia and Oceania entering their seasonal peak in the fourth quarter, we now expect the Middle East conflict, together with the softer long haul demand between Europe and the Americas, to continue to weigh on volumes for the remainder of the year and into 2027,” Hostelworld said.
Net revenue growth eased to an annual rate of 7 per cent in the third quarter of the year, from a rate of 12 per cent reported for the first half of the year.
Net bookings fell 2 per cent in the third quarter to 1.6 million transactions.
“The conflict reduced our volume growth by approximately four percentage points, up from about three in the first half, concentrated on routes between Europe and Asia or Oceania,” said chief executive Gary Morrison.
[ Hostelworld says Iran war shaved 3% off growth in first half Opens in new window ]
“The balance arose in roughly equal measure from softer long-haul demand on routes between Europe and the Americas and from lower organic web traffic, across the industry, as AI answers more searches. Demand within Europe and from North America was broadly flat.”
Meanwhile, Hostelworld said it does not plan to bring another resolution at its annual general meeting (AGM) next year to make political donations, after 20 per cent of shareholders voted against a motion at this year’s meeting to allow it to make donations up to an aggregate amount of €100,000.
Hostelworld told shareholders before this year’s AGM that while it did not plan to make donations to political organisations or election candidates, the definition in legislation of “political donations” and “political expenditure” can extend to bodies such as those concerned with policy review, law reform, the representation of the business community and special interest groups that the group may wish to support.
“Following the AGM, the group engaged with shareholders who did not support the resolution in order to understand their views. Based on that engagement, the board understands that the votes against the resolution principally reflected certain shareholders’ general voting policies on political donations authorities, rather than concerns specific to the company,” it said.
“Although the board is satisfied that seeking the authority was an appropriate precautionary measure, it remains committed to maintaining an open and transparent dialogue with shareholders and, after carefully considering the feedback received, does not intend to propose a similar resolution at the 2027 annual general meeting.”

title: ‘Securing a place on the Lidl Graduate Development Programme set me on course for an ambitious career in retail’
description: From early responsibility to senior mentorship and a clear path for progression, Lidl Ireland’s graduate development programme is designed to turn a first step into a rewarding career
content:
“If you’re good enough, you’re old enough,” is a phrase echoed by many of those who have completed Lidl Ireland’s graduate development programme. It also explains why the 18-month programme can kickstart a truly exciting career in retail.
This rings true for Ornaith Mahon and Emma Ryan.
Ornaith joined the programme in 2021 and is now a senior project manager working across store layouts, in-store experience and technology, while Emma ​​started the programme after finishing college in 2025 and now occupies a permanent project manager role with Lidl.
Four years may separate their experiences, but each describes being given responsibility from day one, having a clear view of where a career at Lidl could take them and deriving a genuine sense of satisfaction in their role.
Emma became aware of the Lidl graduate development programme long before she applied, thanks to a Lidl ad at a Dublin bus stop featuring a former graduate sitting on an unbelievably large croissant.
“It definitely caught my eye,” she says.
Graduates taking up the programme for 2027 can expect to earn a salary of €45,500 and while Emma confirms that the overall remuneration package is attractive, what sets the Lidl graduate development programme apart is that graduates get real responsibility from the start.
The breadth of the graduate development programme added to the appeal. “What made it stand out was how much of the business I’d have access to. Graduates are either on the shop floor, at one of our regional distribution centres or in head office learning how the business operates.”
That exposure starts the same way for all graduates irrespective of academic background, with a three-month placement in store learning the operational side of the business. This gave Emma an understanding of how every part of a store works, from the tills and shop floor, to store KPIs and rostering, before she moved into the store layouts, in-store experience and technology team.
“What interested me compared to other programmes is how much of the business you get to see,” she says. “You’re not left to the side; you’re out on the shop floor and learning the frontline operations. The three months of operational training at the start really show you what the business is​,​ and how it actually works. You get to understand how the business really works from the inside-out, which gives you incredible well-rounded experience."
Ornaith Mahon relished the opportunity to make an impact. “I got stuck in from the start,” she says. “Retail requires that commitment. If you show up with willingness Lidl will give you the work and the opportunities.
“Today I get great job satisfaction from seeing the direct impact on the shop floor,” she says. “It’s very rewarding when we launch a new system that takes the friction out of a customer’s visit or makes a store colleague’s job on the floor easier​,​ or when you see customers enjoying a clear, well-organised middle aisle layout. Lidl has more customers come through its doors than any other retailer across the island of Ireland and knowing that projects I work on make a genuine difference to thousands of people every day is a great feeling.”
Emma, working as a project manager within the store layouts, in-store experience and technology team, feels a similar connection to the customer. Unlike work where the outcome can feel removed from the person doing it, retail offers an almost immediate opportunity to see how something has landed, she says. She can finish work, walk into a Lidl store and see customers engaging with something her team may have rolled out a short time ago.
That visibility extends to career progression, too. For Emma, seeing former graduates move through the business has made it much easier to envisage her own career. “If you can see it, you can be it,” she says.
Mentorship plays an important role in that. Emma was paired with Lidl chief commercial officer Kevin Duffy as her mentor, alongside having a business partner and graduate buddy, giving her support at different levels of the organisation.
“Mentorship is a massive part of the culture in Lidl,” she says.
​​Ornaith Mahon’s mentor, Lidl’s chief customer officer Ivan Ryan, had a lasting influence on how she works. Ivan introduced Ornaith to​​ the ‘five whys’ approach to problem-solving, something she still uses today.
Five years after joining Lidl as a graduate, she has now become a mentor herself. She says that good mentorship includes creating an environment where people can learn when things do not go to plan. “As managers we can set the tone for the day, so even when a day doesn’t go to plan, it’s an opportunity for us to learn and grow together.” ​
Her career has already taken her well beyond early expectations. She recently spent just under a year working at Lidl’s international headquarters in Germany, an opportunity that came with one fairly obvious challenge.
“I was thrown in at the deep end with my lack of understanding of the German language,” she says. “But Lidl never throws you into a pool you can’t swim in.”
Applications for the 2027 Lidl graduate development programme intake are open until the end of October. Ornaith Mahon has advice for potential candidates. “Be curious,” she says. “Back yourself, and don’t be afraid to put yourself out there. Lidl is a place where if you work hard, show initiative​,​ and have drive, people take notice and you will be rewarded for it. Trust the process and trust the leaders around you, they’ll push you out of your comfort zone because they see potential in you. Just bring high energy, be genuine​,​ and be ready to hit the ground running.”
Emma has finished the programme and secured a permanent role; Ornaith has progressed from graduate to senior project manager, worked internationally and is now helping mentor the graduates coming behind her. Each remains ambitious about what comes next​,​ and each sees those next steps at Lidl.
To find out more and apply see jobs.lidl.ie

title: James McClean’s unhappy alliance with Derry City
description: Meanwhile, the Ireland under-21s pulled of a brilliant victory over England to secure a Euro 2027 playoff spot
content:
There’s rarely a dull moment with James McClean. And there have been fewer still since he rejoined his hometown club, Derry City. On Monday, he had his say on their attempts to terminate his contract, and no, he isn’t best pleased about it all. McClean has had an “habitual inclination to pour online petrol onto any available fire” , but Malachy Clerkin questions the wisdom of him picking this particular fight.
Uefa, meanwhile, has launched an investigation in to claims that an Israeli player spat at a member of Ireland’s coaching staff at half-time in Sunday’s Nations League game, match officials including the allegation in their post-match reports.
In substantially happier news, our under-21 team produced an outstanding result in Turner’s Cross on Monday evening, beating back-to-back European champions England to secure their berth in next month’s play-offs for the 2027 European Championships.
The Republic of Ireland’s women’s team are about to embark on their final push for qualification for next summer’s World Cup in Brazil, test one the first leg of their play-off away to Kazakhstan on Friday. We hear from head coach Carla Ward and defender Chloe Mustaki who is wary of this potential “banana skin” .
In rugby, Nathan Johns talks to Mike Prendergast about life as Bath’s backs and attack coach , his decision to move on from Munster, he says, having nothing to do with Clayton McMillan beating him to the head coach role.
Speaking of whom - John O’Sullivan hears from McMillan ahead of his team’s URC meeting with Ulster on Saturday , while Michael Scully talks to Joe McCarthy (with his new hair-do) in the build-up to Leinster’s game against Cardiff.
Cool Hand Luke and John McEnroe, meanwhile, both get a mention in Owen Doyle’s column, communication issues the topic. “Non-stop chatter” from referees? There’s only so much more Owen can take.
In Gaelic games, Gordon Manning previews the appearance of the GAA, LGFA and Camogie Association before an Oireachtas Committee this afternoon where they will be questioned about the unravelling of the integration roadmap.
Tuesday, you might have noted, was budget day, and Ian O’Riordan has news on how sport fared in it all. The 2027 Ryder Cup at Adare Manor will receive a further €22m in support - that’s not a typo - having already being granted €9 million last year.
And Philip Reid was at that very venue on Monday where he heard from both Ryder Cup captains, Jim Furyk and Luke Donald , at the ‘Year to Go’ event, there being, yes, a year to go before the 46th playing of the competition. “It’s us against the world,” said Furyk , which isn’t technically true, but it might feel that way when it all gets under way.
How do you know the seasons are changing? Yes, darker mornings offer a clue, but as Brian O’Connor tells us, so does the return of jumps action at Cheltenham .
TV Watch : There’s not a great deal of live sport on your screens today, but if you’ve a soft spot for cycling then you can tune in to the European Championships on TNT Sports 1 from 1.15pm, the elite men’s time trial the star attraction.

title: Eva Marie Saint, one of the immortals, radiated old-school Hollywood glamour
description: Saint’s death at the mighty age of 102 marks the loss of another beacon of Hollywood’s postwar golden age
content:
Another beacon of Hollywood’s postwar golden age goes out with the death of Eva Marie Saint at the mighty age of 102. She was, at the time of her death, the earliest surviving Oscar winner. Awarded the best supporting actress prize in 1954 for her breakthrough turn in Elia Kazan’s On the Waterfront, she exhibited a seriousness of purpose that proved vital opposite Marlon Brando in that famously gritty dockside drama. But she also radiated old-school glamour, never more so than when she gleamed beside Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock’s indestructible North by Northwest from 1959.
That director was a famously tough taskmaster, but leading women from three successive Hitch films in that period have proved resilient. Kim Novak, star of Vertigo from 1958, is still with us at 93. Vera Miles, who dominates the second half of Psycho from 1960, is still aloft at 96.
Saint was strong opposite Paul Newman in the smash adaptation of Leon Uris’s Exodus, the story of the birth of Israel, in the same year as Psycho. She had a role in the loud motor racing epic Grand Prix from 1966. But Saint couldn’t quite sustain the pace set by those early classics. She was, nonetheless, a welcome presence on television from the 1970s onwards and glossed up many features with undimmed charisma in smaller roles. Recall her as the Man of Steel’s adoptive mum in 2006. Her last big-screen performance saw her, in 2014, share space with a rising Colin Farrell in Akiva Goldsman’s weird, magical realist A New York Winter’s Tale.
[ Eva Marie Saint, star of movies North by Northwest and On the Waterfront, dies at 102 Opens in new window ]
Saint was born in 1924 in New Jersey to Quaker parents. She studied acting at university in Ohio before moving on to television roles in the immediate post war years. She was nominated for an Emmy for work on The Philco Television Playhouse in 1955. That captivating performance in On the Waterfront, as the grieving sister of a murdered whistleblower, was her first ever in a theatrical feature. It must have been a daunting experience. The crisp monochrome film, bolstered by method actors such as Brando and Rod Steiger, brought a new school of naturalism to American cinema. It won eight academy awards and changed the whole industry.
Hitchcock liked employing the star of the moment and was, accordingly, happy to accommodate the Oscar winner in one of his most propulsive pictures. Not every one of his “Hitchcock blondes” relished the experience, but Saint seemed to have got on well enough with the old rogue.
“Hitchcock was a gentleman, he was funny, he was so attentive to me, with the character, and he cared about everything my character, Eve Kendall, wore,” Saint later told Turner Classic Movies. “Everybody had a different experience with him. There were six of us Hitchcock blondes, and it’s like we all were married to the man at one time or another and we all have a different take on him.”
It remains a startlingly cool performance. It required a certain class of resolve to remain human opposite the glamorous enigma that was Cary Grant, and Saint was more than up to that task.
“I tipped the steward $5 to seat you here if you should come in,” her character says in the train dining car.
“I never discuss love on an empty stomach,” she quips back.
North by Northwest now seems as if it was marking the end of an era. The imperial thug that was James Bond was about to usher in a rougher school of thriller. The rebel angels of the later 1960s were set to drag Hollywood down still grubbier corners. Those beautiful gowns and elegant hairstyles seen in Hitchcock’s great 1950s pictures were soon period pieces.
Saint continued to work, winning an Emmy for the television series People Like Us as late as 1990. She was married to Jeffrey Hayden, the busy producer and director, from 1951 until his death in 2016. Film fans were deeply moved by her last appearance at the Oscars in 2018 to present the award for costume design.
One more memory will stick in the minds of anyone awake to indie music (as it wasn’t yet called) in 1984. The chorus to Rattlesnakes, the thumping title track of Lloyd Cole and the Commotions’ debut album, kept returning to a version of her name. “She looks like Eva Marie Saint in On the Waterfront,” Cole sang. “As she reads Simone de Beauvoir in her American circumstance.” He actually seems to say “Eve” rather than “Eva”. And he pronounces her surname as might the French. But we knew who he meant. One of the immortals.

title: Barrister disagrees with defence that death on stag night was ‘a single punch’ case
description: Ruling on sentence following manslaughter verdict in Athlone death due later in month at Mullingar Circuit Court
content:
CCTV footage was played at a Mullingar Circuit Court hearing on Tuesday of a Co Offaly man being punched before he died on a stag night in Athlone.
Paul “Babs” Connolly (48), of Edenderry, Co Offaly died in the early hours of August 13th, 2022, on Church Street, Athlone after falling at least twice during a number of physical altercations, involving punches and kicks, with two other men, namely David Higgins of St Paul’s Terrace, Athlone, and Seán Munnelly (39), of Irishtown, Athlone.
Munnelly was produced from Limerick Prison to Mullingar Circuit Court on Tuesday to appear before Judge Deirdre Browne for sentencing regarding the manslaughter of Connolly.
Higgins was previously jailed by Judge Keenan Johnson for one year for assault causing harm to Connolly and engaging in violent disorder.
On the CCTV footage played on Tuesday, a man, who contacted emergency services, is seen performing chest compressions on Connolly, who was immobile and lying on the ground on Church Street outside the Prince of Wales Hotel.
A female nurse, who was out socialising at the time, can also be seen trying to give assistance to Connolly.
Barrister Cathal Ó Braonáin, for the Director of Public Prosecutions, said the nurse also witnessed the final punch, which was delivered to Connolly’s temple by Munnelly.
Munnelly is seen in the footage to hold a cigarette in his other hand and remonstrating with Connolly before delivering the punch.
Members of Connolly’s family were emotional during the hearing, and some left the court while the footage was shown.
On the footage, prior to the final punch, three other members of the stag party are seen returning to the Prince of Wales Hotel, one of whom is seen running after Munnelly.
Munnelly is also seen to shake hands with members of this group.
Det Sgt Kevin Craig agreed with John Shortt, counsel for Munnelly, that no one in the stag party had appeared to understand or be aware of what had taken place between Connolly and Munnelly.
Craig agreed with Ó Braonáin that a witness said he heard Connolly ask a woman, who was sitting on benches close to the Prince of Wales hotel earlier that night, a question that appeared to trigger Munnelly, who was also sitting there at the time.
Craig said that Munnelly, who had his head bowed for much of Tuesday’s hearing, had been drinking.
Craig agreed that a garda recognised Munnelly later that day, and after a foot race, apprehended him and conveyed him to Athlone Garda station.
Ó Braonáin submitted that a headline sentence within the range of four to 10 years should be imposed. He disagreed with Shortt that this was “a single punch” case and referenced the CCTV footage.
Shortt submitted that the headline sentence should be within the zero to four years range.
Citing the pathologist’s report, Shortt said this was a “complex case” regarding the cause of death, and involved over 130 witnesses, and he submitted that it also involved provocation.
Two victim impact statements were read to the court, including one from Deirdre Lynch, sister of Connolly.
Lynch said Connolly had the “Babs” nickname as he was the youngest in the family and as a result was particularly close to his nephews and nieces, who would not now be able to share life milestones with him.
Browne conveyed her condolences to the Connolly family and said that she would deliver her ruling as to sentence on October 16th at Mullingar Circuit Court.

title: Man (30s) charged after drone smuggling contraband into Midlands Prison crashes
description: The drone crashed into the nearby Prison Officers Training College on Tuesday afternoon
content:
A man is due in court after a drone attempting to smuggle contraband into Midlands Prison in Portlaoise crashed into the nearby Prison Officers’ Training College on Tuesday afternoon.
The man (30s) will appear before Tullamore District Court on Wednesday morning.
Another man (40s) has been released without charge while a file is prepared for the Director of Public Prosecutions.
The two men were arrested by gardaí after the drone crashed into the roof of the training college.
It was subsequently recovered by the Laois Fire and Rescue Service alongside a package containing mobile phones and suspected cannabis and tablets.
The contraband will undergo a forensic examination to confirm its contents.
Gardaí began a search of the area after officers at Midlands Prison were notified of drone activity. It is understood the two men were found in the grounds of the nearby Midland Regional Hospital.
“Gardaí responded to a report of drone activity in the vicinity of the Portlaoise Prison Campus, Co Laois, this afternoon,” a statement said.
A spokesman confirmed the Irish Prison Service ( IPS ) is working with An Garda Síochána in relation to the incident.
“As the matter is subject to Garda investigation, it would not be appropriate to comment further,” a statement said.
Separately, nine inmates overdosed and three required hospital treatment following an incident at Midlands Prison last month .
At the time, a representative for the IPS said the suggestion that the drugs involved arrived in the prison via drone was a “good assumption”.

title: Emotional Lionel Messi ends Argentina career in perfectly scripted finale against Benin
description: Playing in his 208th international, the 39-year-old signed off with a goal at the Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires
content:
Lionel Messi brought the curtain down on his 21-year international career on Tuesday, bidding farewell to adoring Argentina fans in an emotional final appearance for the former world champions in Buenos Aires.
In a perfectly scripted finale, the 39-year-old widely regarded as the greatest football player in history signed off with his 126th international goal in front of 85,000 supporters as Argentina cruised to a 3-0 victory over Benin.
Messi, playing in his record-extending 208th international, also provided the assist for the opening goal scored by veteran Nicolás Otamendi, with Nico Paz also scoring.
But the match was a footnote to the occasion itself, which saw Messi savoring the adulation of the Monumental Stadium crowd one last time for an event which had been billed as The Last Tango.
Beforehand, Messi wiped away tears as the bus carrying him and his Argentina teammates made its way through crowds of well-wishers en route to the stadium.
Messi took the field alongside his three children and received affectionate waves from his wife, Antonela Roccuzzo, and his mother, Celia Cuccittini, who were watching from a VIP box.
Shortly before kick-off, a giant Argentina jersey bearing the word “Gracias” (Thank You) above the football superstar’s No 10 was laid out on the pitch as the crowd roared their approval.
Messi welled up again as Falklands War veteran Fabio Santana sang the national anthem beside a banner which read – “The Malvinas are Argentine” – the same banner held aloft by players after their 2-1 World Cup semi-final win over England.
The match was halted in the 10th minute – in tribute to Messi’s famous shirt number – for a minute-long ovation to the former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain star.
He crowned the occasion with a goal from the penalty spot in the 71st minute.
At the final whistle a drone show lit up the night sky above the stadium, showing Messi’s image and thanking the eight-time Ballon d’Or-winner for his career.
Messi’s farewell came two and a half months after Argentina’s World Cup final defeat to Spain in New Jersey, where Messi exited in tears after making little impression in an ill-tempered 1-0 loss. “I gave it my all; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance,” Messi wrote at the time.
Before Tuesday’s game, the University of Buenos Aires awarded Messi an honorary doctorate in a ceremony at the Argentine Football Association (AFA) headquarters. Messi, who has in the past spoken of his regret at not studying more, expressed pride at the distinction. “To be able to say that I am an honorary doctor!,” he joked.
Outside the Argentina Football Association headquarters, fans unfurled a huge Argentine flag with his image inscribed “The joy of my life”.
Former Barcelona teammate Neymar paid tribute to the departing champion on X. “It’s not just Argentina that thanks you, the world thanks you for everything you did for football. Thank you for making me love football even more,” he said.
Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami until 2028, although following the death of his father, Jorge, two months ago, he revealed he may hang up his boots for good sooner than anticipated.
Messi’s departure comes four years after his greatest triumph in international football, leading Argentina to victory at the 2022 World Cup to end the country’s 36-year wait for a third title, cementing his status as Diego Maradona’s heir.
“I believe Messi gave everything, absolutely everything, so it doesn’t bother me at all that he’s leaving. He has more than earned it, let him enjoy himself, let him rest,” Cecilia Adriano, 52, told AFP.
During his time with the Albiceleste, Argentina won one World Cup, were runners-up twice (Brazil 2014 and North America 2026) and were also crowned Copa America champions in 2021 and 2024. – Reuters

title: CRH to buy aggregates operations in Denmark and Finland
description: Value of deal was not disclosed
content:
CRH , the Irish building materials and services giant, has agreed to buy Swedish construction group NCC Industry’s operations in Denmark and Finland for an undisclosed sum.
NCC’s Danish network of asphalt plants, land- and marine-based aggregates sites, together with its substantial high-quality reserves, will significantly expand CRH’s presence in the market and its exposure to demand from big road, infrastructure and industrial projects, said CRH.
The group’s reserve-backed hard-rock quarries, backfilling and recycling operations in Finland will complement CRH’s existing operations in that market.
“This acquisition is strongly aligned with CRH’s strategy to build an aggregates-led, connected portfolio aligned with growing infrastructure megatrends,” said Peter Buckley, president of CRH International, the group’s operations outside of the Americas.
“NCC Industry’s extensive operating footprint and strong customer relationships in Denmark and Finland will strengthen our business in the Nordics, enhancing our ability to support customers across key high-growth urban markets and infrastructure end-segments.”
The transaction remains subject to applicable approvals and customary closing conditions. Completion is expected during 2027.
CRH’s shares have fallen by a third so far this year in New York, leaving it with a market value of $55.1 billion (€49.1 billion), amid concerns about the global economy and the extent to which central banks will need to raise interest rates to rein in inflation that’s been fuelled by the Middle East conflict.
In June, CRH agreed to buy US peer Arcosa in a deal worth $8.5 billion (€7.4 billion), which would make it the Irish group’s largest purchase to date.
Arcosa is a leading aggregates company and maker of critical infrastructure products, which, CRH says, would be “highly complementary” to CRH’s existing business. The value of the deal includes both Dallas-based Arcosa’s equity and debt.
CRH chief executive Jim Mintern set out a strategy 13 months ago for CRH to spend $40 billion on investment and cash returns to shareholders over five years as it continues to grow revenues and earnings apace. Some $28 billion was earmarked for investment.

title: A flat tyre that’s also about to blow out from over-inflation – welcome to Budget 2027
description: Inside Politics: A notable absence from the budget leaves Patrick O’Donovan feeling rebuffed
content:
Budgets are classic “eye of the beholder” events in Irish politics. The Government sees a tyre that been primed perfectly for the uncertain road ahead. The Opposition sees a flat tyre that has not been pumped up sufficiently. The economists see a tyre overinflated so much that a dangerous blowout is inevitable at some point along the journey.
What was unveiled by Minister for Finance Simon Harris and Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers was an expansionary budget that followed a well established pattern in recent years of giving an election budget in a nonelection year.
As our main lead reports , it’s an €8.5-billion package that has drawn sharp criticism from the State’s budgetary watchdog for increasing the reliance on “high-risk corporation tax”.
“The package will bring public spending to €125.6 billion next year despite tensions in Government over the insistence of Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers to limit spending growth to 6 per cent next year,” write Pat Leahy, Jack Horgan-Jones, Cormac McQuinn and Marie O’Halloran.
The changes will particularly favour middle-class and lower-middle-class voters, with a raising of the higher-income tax-entry bracket benefiting a family with two earners, each with salaries of more than €50,000, to the tune of €1,500.
Chambers is adamant that in 2027, unlike every previous Government since Covid, this Government will not break its self-imposed rule of keeping spending growth to 6 per cent. As Martin Wall reports, he is channelling the Troika and has set up a new public spending efficiency taskforce to monitor spending and to make recommendations on where cuts can be made.
One Minister, Patrick O’Donovan , suffered a very public rebuff when his widely touted plan for a €100 “culture card” voucher for 16-year-olds to attend cultural events was entirely absent from the budget.
“There won’t be a culture card in 2027 and it’s not funded in the allocation that’s set out,” Chambers said. O’Donovan and Chambers were said to have had tense exchanges during budget negotiations.
But given that State spending in 2026 is already running at 9 per cent more than 2025, 3 per cent more than the limit, there are plenty of voices who doubt the Government will stick to its rule.
As Leahy points out in his analysis, the extra spending in the budget will mean an extra €10 billion will need to be spent every year just to keep things on an even keel.
“To fund that, tax receipts need to keep growing by that much every year. If they grew only by half that much – never mind actually declining – then the budgetary implications would be severe. A budget that only increased spending by, say, €5 billion would feel to many people, inside and outside Government, like an austerity budget. And this Government would almost certainly not survive an austerity budget.”
For even more sobering analysis, the budgetary watchdog, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council , warned that Budget 2027 put the public finances on a worse trajectory.
It gave two reasons: the Government keeps breaking established spending limits, and it relies more and more on high-risk corporation tax.
Sinn Féin’s Pearse Doherty said the extra money would be “gone before you get it”. His colleague Mairéad Farrell called it a “budget for Scrooges”.
Cian O’Callaghan of the Social Democrats said the budget was “tinkering around the edges”, with energy bills the central issue. He accused Harris of spinning on social protection payments.
Labour’s Ged Nash baptised both Ministers as “Soundbite Simon and JackGPT”.
Ruth Coppinger claimed Chambers had gone “full-on Musk” to announce a US Doge-style [Department of Government Efficiency] operation in the public sector.
Leahy’s excellent analysis piece riffs a little on the Coppinger quote saying that Chambers has emerged as a form of “hard man” in Government. It also has a great headline: It takes a giveaway budget of €8.5bn to not annoy anyone – except Patrick O’Donovan.
Patrick Freyne’s colour piece on the proceedings observes that there is only “so much talk of millions and billions that a person can take before their eyes glaze over and it begins to feel like Monopoly money”. Except, of course, it is not.
Jack-Horgan Jones has more details of the tension between Chambers and O’Donovan over the non-existent culture card
Elsewhere, Martin Wall has details on An Garda Síochána spending €250,000 on rooms that were not used for the 2024 Europa League final in Dublin.

title: Donald Trump says he will speak with Vladimir Putin about pneumonic plague
description: Washington increases pressure on Moscow to share more about the incident in which one person has died
content:
US president Donald Trump said he was scheduled to speak with Russian president Vladimir Putin about the suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia “very soon”, as Washington has urged Moscow to share more about the incident.
The US president on Tuesday night said he would speak with his Russian counterpart after US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the White House has received “limited information” on the situation.
Trump on Tuesday declined to provide more information on when the call would take place, but added the US’s intelligence agencies are “in very deep discussions” about the suspected case of the plague. “We’ll be able to report about it probably tomorrow,” he added.
Russia has imposed sweeping quarantine measures in the Siberian region after an employee at Siberia’s Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute was admitted to hospital outside the city a week ago.
[ What do we know about death of anti-plague researcher in Siberia and is there a wider risk? Opens in new window ]
Daria Shipilova (28) died two days later from what public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor described as “pneumonia of unknown” origin. Local media reported pneumonic plague may have been the cause of death.
Rubio earlier on Tuesday called on Moscow for increased transparency.
“I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” he said. “That’s what they should do, that’s what we hope they will do. And the more we can learn about what happened, the better all of us can be in a position of responding.”
“Maybe there’s nothing there, maybe it’s bigger than we thought, we don’t know,” Rubio added. “Suffice it to say we’re watching it very closely.”
The US secretary of state on Monday said it appeared a worker at the Siberian lab was infected, though he added he did not believe the apparent case was “cause for alarm”.
If confirmed, it would be the first case of plague in a decade in Russia, which has insisted there has been no outbreak.
China’s foreign ministry, in response to a question about the suspected case, said it maintained close communication with Russia on disease prevention and control. “China and Russia maintain close exchanges and co-operation on the prevention and control of infectious diseases, including plague,” ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov urged reporters on Monday “not to listen to rumours about a plague outbreak” and to “rely on Rospotrebnadzor’s statement”.
Trump had said Washington would be willing to help Moscow with the situation.
“We’ll help. Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we’re always willing to help,” he said on Monday.

title: Bid to cut smoking ‘abject failure’, Dáil told, as budget pushes cigarette prices higher
description: TDs vote by 110 to 48 to increase 20-pack by €1 to €21.02
content:
A packet of 20 cigarettes will cost €20.15 following a €1 increase in the budget , bringing the tax take to €16.03 or almost 80 per cent of the retail price.
Ireland continues to have the most expensive cigarettes in Europe and now has the second highest cigarette prices in the world behind Australia, where a 20-pack costs €21.02.
The €1 increase was accepted in the Dáil on Tuesday night by 110 votes to 48.
The pro-rata increase in the price of a typical pouch of roll-your-own tobacco is €1.39, bringing the retail cost to €29.72.
Introducing the tax, Minister for Further and Higher Education James Lawless said the increase on tobacco products would yield approximately €63.1 million in a full year, and €5.1 million for the remainder of 2026.
He claimed the State’s policy to cut smoking rates “is working, according to the evidence”. In 2007, 29 per cent of people were daily smokers. “By contrast, in 2025 that figure is reduced to 17 per cent,” he said.
But Labour TD Duncan Smith described the Government’s policy as an “abject failure” as he called on the Government “to be honest”.
The Tobacco-Free Ireland strategy launched in 2013, when smoking rates were at 22 per cent, set a target of a 5 per cent smoking rate by 2025 but “they’re at 17 per cent”, Smith said.
Smith added the price increase had “become a substitute for what should be a robust public health policy, because there are 100 deaths a week, a thousand hospitalisations a week due to smoking”.
The Dublin Fingal East TD added that cigarettes are now €1 each but the figure might as well be €10. “If you’re not backing up the taxation side with a robust public health approach, you’re going to continue to fail.
“This Government has to be honest about their failure” and acknowledge that “we’re miles away from where we need to be”, Smith said.
He said successive governments “abandoned the robust approach in favour of this old reliable” of tax increase, which is not making a difference.
It is “regressive, not to mention the fact that almost a billion euro in revenue is being lost to the black market”.
Independent TD Danny Healy-Rae said if people smoked five packs a week, it would cost them more than €100.
He said he smoked a cigarette once. “I didn’t like it and I never smoked after that” but he said people tell him “it’s the only comfort we have”.
[ From 20 cigarettes a day for 55 years to finally quitting: ‘I took it up thinking I was the big man’ Opens in new window ]
The Kerry TD did not think it would affect smoker behaviour but it would mean “they’ll endure more hardship” to keep smoking, particularly those on low incomes.
Sinn Féin Cork North-Central TD Thomas Gould said there was a time when a price increase “had an impact” but, calling on the Government “to be honest on where we are now”, he said “this strategy has diminishing returns”.
Just pushing prices up as a strategy “is not enough” and education was needed. He pointed to reports that almost €1.1 billion of unregulated illicit cigarettes were consumed in Ireland last year at a cost of more than €800 million to the Revenue Commissioners.
Independent Paul Gogarty said the campaign to reduce tobacco usage had not worked as people hoped it would. Now there is also vaping and “synthetic chemicals out there” causing psychosis. This “new stuff needs to be stopped.”
He said “the revenue from excise duty on cigarettes is half of the cost to our healthcare system from people who have fallen ill because of tobacco products”.
Gogarty said “even allowing for the black-market risk”, there was scope “for it to be increased further”.
The Dublin Mid-West TD said “cigarette-butt tossers get away with murder. It’s a €250 fine but trying to actually get that fine out of them is quite difficult because of the burden of proof”. He said trying to get them to court was equally difficult because “you’re not allowed to use DNA evidence”.

title: Oil gains as US storm and Houthi air strikes threaten supply
description: Storm forming in the Gulf of Mexico will likely hit oil and gas producing facilities
content:
Oil prices climbed on Wednesday as the market weighed supply constraints from a storm heading for US oil-producing regions and attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis on ​Saudi Arabia against increased supplies of Middle East crude.
Brent futures rose $1.05, or 1.04 per cent, to $101.63 a barrel by 0400 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures rose 80 cents, or 0.89 per cent, to $90.24 a barrel.
US forecasters said on Tuesday a storm forming in the Gulf of Mexico would become the first Atlantic ​hurricane of 2026 within two days and would likely hit oil and gas producing facilities.
The offshore areas in the Gulf in the storm’s path produce 15 per cent of ⁠US crude oil and 5 per cent of the country’s natural gas.
KCM Trade chief analyst Tim Waterer said the ‌storm ‌was ​an “unwelcome complication for crude, raising the prospect of production and refining disruptions at a time when the market already has enough supply-side headaches”.
The storm could affect six refineries. Refineries in ⁠US Gulf states account for about 50 per cent of ​the national capacity of 18.2 million barrels per day (bpd).
US crude oil ​inventories fell last week, market sources said on Tuesday, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Crude stocks fell by 2.09 ‌million barrels in the week ended October 2nd.
“For now, ​the market is likely to remain nervous to any potential supply disruptions,” said ING commodity strategists, adding that supply risks ⁠from the Middle East are still very real amid ⁠continued attacks on ships.
Supply ​has been recovering. Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline hit 5.8 million barrels a day, the kingdom’s energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, said on Tuesday.
Around 12 million barrels per day of crude oil and 2 million bpd of refined products have left the Middle East on tankers in the last seven to 10 days, the head of Vitol said.
However, Saudi Arabia’s airports in Jazan and Najran were targeted in two attacks on Monday evening, the Saudi aviation authority said, as hostilities between the kingdom and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis escalated.
The attacks occurred as Saudi-backed ‌Yemeni government forces pressed a major ⁠offensive to retake territory from the Houthis, after weeks of rebel advances, with Riyadh stepping up airstrikes in support of the campaign.
Attacks and refinery outages are “likely to keep the cracks elevated and scarcity will transmit to ‌crude,” said Mukesh Sahdev, chief oil analyst at X Analysts in Sydney, referring to the premiums for refined products over crude.
Crude prices would hold ​near $100 “without any material de-escalation emerging,” he added.
US-Iran relations are no closer to repair with ​US president Donald Trump saying on Tuesday that nobody knew who was running Iran during the eight-month US-Israeli war with Iran. - Reuters

title: Three unionist parties back motion of no confidence in Michelle O’Neill
description: Motions also listed against John O’Dowd, Caoimhe Archibald and Liz Kimmins
content:
The three main unionist parties in Northern Ireland have backed a motion of no confidence in First Minister Michelle O’Neill .
No-confidence motions have also been listed against Finance Minister John O’Dowd, Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald and Infrastructure Minister Liz Kimmins over their alleged backing of a protest on the Garvaghy Road against the Drumcree Orange Order parade.
They are set to be debated in the Assembly next Monday.
The move comes amid a 10-day impasse in Portadown, which developed after the Parades Commission gave the green light for the first time in almost 30 years for the parade to complete its traditional route along the Garvaghy Road.
The parade has been protested against with large-scale gatherings on the road in Portadown, leading police to say they cannot safely facilitate the parade.
The Police Service of Northern Ireland is investigating the prevention of the parade, and potential offences of unnotified protest, obstructing a lawful parade and breaching the Parades Commission determination.
The motions against O’Neill and the Sinn Féin ministers were proposed by TUV MLA Timothy Gaston and have since been backed by DUP MLAs Jonathan Buckley and Diane Dodds, as well as UUP leader Jon Burrows.
They claim that those ministers no longer enjoy the confidence of the Assembly, alleging they took part in an “unlawful protest” on the Garvaghy Road on September 27, 2026, which “prevented a permitted parade from proceeding”.
They go on to say that by doing so they “failed to observe the pledge of office, requiring them to uphold the rule of law and support it unequivocally in word and deed”.
The motions propose that the ministers be excluded from holding office as ministers or junior ministers for a period of 12 months.
Speaking in the Assembly on Monday, O’Neill stood by her actions, and said “when the law is wrong, I will stand firmly against it”.
She told MLAs she was “fully committed to the Good Friday Agreement, including the ministerial code and pledge of office”.
“I stand resolutely with the residents of the Garvaghy Road … they have suffered generations of sectarianism and generations of domination, of intimidation and of violence … as a result of a reckless demand for an unwanted sectarian march through this peaceful community,” she said.
No-confidence motions must be backed by a majority of both unionist and nationalist members of the Stormont Assembly to succeed. - PA
