title: As the class of 2026 begins college, a masked shadow lingers
description: We should not forget that the chaos caused by Covid can still be impacting on young adults as they begin the next chapter
content:
For the Leaving Cert class of 2026, an exciting new chapter has just begun, with many moving on to college campuses or apprenticeships. These institutions of further study have become filled with their enthusiastic and hopeful faces.
These are the same faces that were hidden behind masks for a considerable period, as this cohort of young people navigated the transition into secondary school amid the pandemic . And not only did many in this group start secondary school behind masks, they also had to keep their distance from classmates, and navigate these early years of adolescence through lockdowns and social restrictions.
According to developmental psychologist Erik Erikson, the central task of adolescence is identity-formation. This involves discovering who you are through friendships, feedback from peers and social participation. For the class of 2026, the opportunity to socialise and start the “job” of identity-formation was interrupted just as they entered one of the most formative periods of their lives. We should not forget this, and neither should we forget that this interruption can still, in subtle ways, be impacting on them now as they begin the next chapter and the early stages of adulthood.
For this group, the transition into adolescence happened at the exact moment that the world shut down. One day they were attending sixth class at primary school, and the next, that abruptly ended. They did not get the gradual ending to their primary school years that previous cohorts got, despite the great efforts of school staff in remote learning. They then started secondary school in September 2020, with masks, social distancing and all the rest.
There were no corridors filled with potential friends – instead, there was fear if people came too close. Masks made it impossible to read facial expressions; many students weren’t identifiable by their teachers for a long time – never mind being known by potential new friends. Interruptions to activities such as sport was also part of the deal during Covid, and while people often speak of that era in terms of the learning loss or educational disruption, it is also vital to look at the potential impact this all had on psychological development.
The central question being grappled with by teenagers on an unconscious level is “Who am I?” – and this question is largely worked out over time by having social encounters, taking a few risks socially, joining clubs or teams, making mistakes, reading facial expressions, and learning, bit by bit, how they fit in with different types of people. Because of the Covid restrictions, opportunities to work on the task of identity-formation were hampered for a significant time and, as a result, many young people retreated from social interaction or turned to their phones for social connection.
As a systemic psychotherapist, I meet young adults at the beginning stage of adulthood who describe a lingering sense of uncertainty about who they are and what their place in the world is. Some struggle with social anxiety and feel they should be able to manage situations better than they can. Some describe a wish to feel more confident than they do, particularly in social situations with people who are new.
All of this struggle makes sense when you take a wider view of what this resilient group of young people had to deal with in the context of their developmental journey. If part of their adolescence at the beginning stage was spent avoiding close contact with peers, communicating through screens or trying to manage heightened anxiety by themselves, it is completely normal that the result is that it takes longer for their confidence in social situations to develop.
If a person reaches 18 without a clear sense of who they are, it matters that they are reminded of the fact that Covid stole some of the time they ideally would have had for that. A shift from self-criticism if they find social situations hard to self-understanding is part of what many young people need when it comes to their internal self-talk.
This next chapter isn’t just about qualifications; it is about young adults reclaiming the opportunity to continue the job of getting to know themselves
If any of this group feel they are “behind” in terms of their confidence in themselves or their social skills, or if they feel that they don’t yet have a clear sense of self, they can be reminded that Covid took away some of the ordinary day-to-day experiences that normally help young people settle into that steady sense of self-identity. Knowing who you are will come – but it might just take a bit more time.
[ Why did you choose Ireland? Graduates from around the world give their views Opens in new window ]
Erikson believed that each stage of a person’s psychological development ended with them reaching a conclusion that then becomes stored as truth in the unconscious mind. This truth then becomes part of what influences behaviour. If the conclusion or truth reached is “I am not good socially”, that is going to have an impact on how a young person approaches the next social encounter – whether they join societies in college, or approach new social groups. If any of the class of 2026 are feeling a little unsure of themselves at this new stage, remember that doing the “job” of identity-formation was interrupted, and therefore may not be complete.
This next chapter therefore isn’t just about qualifications; it is about young adults reclaiming the opportunity to continue the job of getting to know themselves. Self-knowledge, for everyone, is power, and becoming aware of what is happening unconsciously for themselves in terms of normal psychological development. It means young people getting to take some power back into their lives. That process helps their mental health .
A lot of learning opportunity was effectively taken from the class of 2026 during those harsh Covid years. Let’s hope that where these young people are now landing in life can nurture more than just academic success.
[ The power of confidence: ‘Chronic high levels of success create high levels of influence... it can go to people’s heads’ Opens in new window ]
Let’s hope that there can be space too for psychological nourishment and growth. It is what they all deserve.

title: ‘I panicked during an interview and said I have a qualification I don’t have. I got the job’
description: Tell Me About It: ‘There is a woman in my team I would really like to ask out but what if she finds out that I am a fraud?’
content:
My issue is work-related. I did a job interview recently for a position I really wanted, but I panicked during the interview. I am well qualified for the role, but very stupidly said that I have an additional certificate (in a sensitive area) that I don’t have.
Now I got the job and am in fear of this being discovered and I think it is only a matter of time. This job is sensitive so honesty is held in high regard and I’m not sure what to do. The worst thing is that I am finally working for a company that I have dreamed of and I would love to spend the rest of my working life here.
It is all having a big effect on me, I am not sleeping well and am agitated, edgy and jumpy, as I keep expecting the axe to fall. I am early for work every day, but I know I am not settling in like I should. I keep jumping when someone asks me a question or comes up behind me. I have always been bad at lying and my confidence is at an all-time low now. There is a year’s probationary period, and I will have two meetings before passing it. The first one is in a month’s time and I’m wondering if I should come clean.
I spoke to my dad, who says that I should ride it out and that I have all the knowledge that the certificate would require. But what if I’m found out? There is a woman who works in my team, and I would really like to ask her out but what if she finds out that I am a fraud or is it even worth it if I am leaving the company anyway.
I feel like I have put my whole life in jeopardy.
The immediate effect of this deception on you is that you cannot be yourself, cannot relax or allow yourself to enjoy the job. Being on alert all the time will drain your energy and make you secretive and unapproachable, so others will find you difficult to be around and this will have a detrimental effect on your assimilation into the workplace. So, something needs to be done.
It seems that the lie told at the interview goes against your principles (otherwise you would not be suffering so much) so facing up to this will get you back in alignment with yourself. However, there may be a way of doing this that can demonstrate your capacity for taking responsibility and your determination to stay in the job.
[ ‘It was my dream job – and now I feel like an utter failure’ Opens in new window ]
Your dad says that you already have the knowledge that the certificate would provide so it should be possible for you to upskill without too much effort. Can you enrol on a course immediately – try for an evening course and pay for it yourself, so that it does not impact your work hours. If you can have this in situ, it might show that you are determined to fulfil your commitment from the interview.
You need to set up a meeting with your manager, pick a time when you won’t be disturbed and when there is time for discussion. Start by saying that you are privileged to find a job in a business that excites and challenges you and that you are committed to it for the long term. Then, when you are sure that the manager is listening, tell them simply and honestly that you overstated your certificate at the interview and that, in fact, you are still in the process of achieving it. It will help to acknowledge the sensitivity of the business and the importance of trust and honesty in its delivery and of your commitment to these principles. Then allow the manager to absorb the disclosure and ask if it is possible to reflect on this and have another conversation in the coming days.
Whatever the outcome – and it may lead to dismissal – be gracious in accepting it and don’t overthink it. This is a tough lesson, but it also requires some self-compassion.
At interviews we want to show ourselves in the best possible light and in the effort to impress, we can overstate our competencies, and this can (as you know) backfire and instead of impressing, we end up disappointing those who have invested in us. True confidence is having faith in ourselves as we are and being open to development. This is a development opportunity for you and see it as such, rather than a failure to hide.
[ ‘I am back in the workplace full-time and it is unbearable. Managers have become mistrustful’ Opens in new window ]
Shame is toxic emotion that can eat away at your wellbeing and the way out of it is usually to own it, apologise and move on. This is what you will do with your manager and once it is done, you have learned the lesson and there is no need to keep poring over it. Trust that this won’t happen again and do not pile guilt or regret on yourself. You say you are attracted to someone at work and this shows that your desire and aliveness continues to work, in spite of the stress that you are under, and this is a good thing.
You are having negative thoughts about the job that are blocking you from making a connection, but it might be good to trust your instinct that this is a possible relationship option for you and open yourself up to taking the risk.
As you are already feeling vulnerable about the job, you might understand that adding this possible rejection might be a bit much for you, but it would add to your self-worth if you put yourself forward and trust that you will handle the pushback if it comes.

title: Has Mark Duffy left it too late to spoil the PTSB party?
description: Former Bank of Scotland Ireland chief executive has his work cut out to gatecrash Bawag bid for PTSB
content:
The first problem facing Mark Duffy in his efforts to gatecrash the €1.62 billion takeover of PTSB by Austrian banking group Bawag would appear to be money.
Axis Capital, the company he has said is considering a late €1.74 billion counter bid for the State-owned bank, has €100 to its name, according to its most-recently filed accounts.
The second problem facing the former chief executive of Bank of Scotland Ireland (BOSI) – once dubbed a “suitcase banker” by a rival – is the credibility of the offer. Duffy has been busy since leaving BOSI in 2009 and has tried his hand at everything from buying distressed assets to online non-bank finance, data analytics and hybrid home finance. According to the Axis website, Africa has been a particular focus. He has not bought a bank.
This is not to say that Duffy and his fellow director the German corporate lawyer Lutz Hartmann will not be able to raise the finance. They already had a bit part in the PTSB saga, brokering talks between New York private equity firm Centerbridge, the Department of Finance and PTSB last year.
“Axis will now engage with a number of potential funding and investment partners with a view to raising the necessary financing that would support the announcement of a firm intention to make an offer for PTSB,” it said last week.
Getting the bidding process reopened is his third problem. Under the terms of the deal agreed with Bawag, the board of PTSB has the right to accept a “superior proposal” which must be at more than €3.1377 per share. Bawag, which has bid €2.97, can increase its offer and if not, it will be able to recoup its costs.
Duffy has pitched his bid at €3.20, well above this threshold, but he has his work cut out to turn it into a “superior proposal” as in theory this provision of the PTSB agreement with Bawag expired after shareholders voted on the offer on July 30th and the sale was approved by whopping 91.28 per cent. In reality the board of PTSB would find it hard to consider a fully funded offer given their wider obligations to shareholders.
Given the mountain he must thus climb, Duffy’s bid is best seen in the context of an expected challenge to the sale, which must be approved by the High Court on October 27th.
Court approval is required because the takeover is being done via a scheme of arrangement, often used in friendly takeovers where the majority shareholder is on board. One of the attractions of a scheme of arrangement is that it makes it hard for awkward small shareholders to hold out for more money.
[ The Irish Times view on the PTSB sale: stick with the plan Opens in new window ]
A scheme of arrangement requires 75 per cent of the votes cast at the meeting to approve the transaction to be in favour of the deal, as happened in July.
The challenge will most likely argue that the shareholders should have been split into two classes: the Government, which owns 57 per cent, and the rest. If there are more than one class of shareholders then 75 per cent approval by every class is required.
The scheme could well have failed if the vote had been done on this basis. The small – or non-Government shareholders – own almost 43 per cent of the bank and were split 64 per cent to 36 per cent in favour, but crucially they did not pass the deal by the required 75 per cent.
The most likely candidate to challenge the scheme is Piotr Skoczylas’s Scotchstone Capital, which opposed the scheme of arrangement from the get-go. He has already challenged the class structure and was basically told by the court to come back and argue his case if the deal went through.
The challenge – if it materialises – is not without merit. Among the usual grounds for splitting the shareholders into classes is that the classes do not share the same interest and objectives.
That is a reasonable assertion in the case of PTSB. The small shareholders just want as much money as possible but the State has other fish to fry.
It wants out of the banking sector, in which it has been embroiled since the crash, and faces a conflict of interest given its role – via the Central Bank – as regulator of the banking sector and also ultimately the lender of last resort.
It also wants to make sure – as far as possible – that the buyer of PTSB is both capable and committed to promoting competition in Irish banking. And finally, there is an industrial relations headache and other negative fallout should the buyer take a chainsaw to staff numbers.
All that said, the courts tend to want to see some sort of legal or technical difference between shareholders in order to approve voting by class.
It is an open question as to what impact the existence of a higher offer from Duffy might have on the process. But one way or another the former suitcase banker has a dog in the fight.

title: Enniscorthy river blockages contributing to flooding
description: Dredge it
content:
Sir, – Yesterday I drove through Enniscorthy ( “‘We’re in limbo’: Enniscorthy businesses feel defenceless after latest flood,” October 2nd).
Between the two bridges now exists a large island, which has grown over recent years, covered in vegetation.
The entire riverbed between and below the bridges is full of gravel washed down from upstream, raising the riverbed level and consequently the river itself.
Blockages in the riverbed, like the island, block the flow of floodwater and add to the risk of the lower town flooding.
Dredging out the riverbed between and to a distance above and below and especially under the bridges, would seem to be the quickest, cheapest and most common sense way to help reduce flooding events (at least smaller ones) in Enniscorthy.
It won’t protect against all flooding events, but it would certainly help floodwaters get away more quickly, when the tide falls.
I cannot believe that it is not being done on a regular basis along this short stretch of river.
I’m all for supporting our flora and fauna in the riverbed, but what about the fauna (people) who live above the river? Are they and their businesses not worthy of some consideration along this short stretch of the river? Dredge it. – Yours, etc,

title: Divorcing couple’s €1.4m properties distributed between them after marriage ‘full of strife’
description: ‘Incomprehensible’ that funds were depleted by €150,000 due to children attending boarding school abroad, says judge
content:
A judge has made orders for distribution of assets including three properties valued at about €1.4 million in proceedings involving a couple whose marriage was “full of strife”.
Under the orders, the wife gets the family home, while the husband will receive two other properties. Most of a €587,000 cash sum will be divided equally between them.
The core dispute was over the €587,000 that the man argued should go entirely to him.
He appealed to the High Court over Circuit Court orders concerning proper provision in divorce proceedings involving the couple whose children are aged over 18. Two continue to receive financial support from their mother, and one from their father.
In her recently published judgment, Judge Nuala Jackson said the history of the long marriage appeared “somewhat joyless, chaotic, angst-ridden and full of strife”.
Both parties have professional qualifications, but while the woman worked outside the home throughout the marriage, the man only occasionally did so and had a recent diagnosis of a neurodivergent condition.
He argued he was the primary carer for the children over the years and contributed to the family income through rental of two properties owned by him before he married, plus management of investments. The woman said his care role was no more than hers, and she was exclusively responsible for many household and family tasks, while also working.
Both sides made allegations about the behaviour of the other, which both denied, and the woman’s lawyer said it was not a case where claims of gross and obvious misconduct were being pursued.
The marriage ended after the woman got an interim barring order, leading to the man suffering a “very distressing psychiatric episode” and later moving into one of his properties.
The assets of the parties are clear, including three mortgage-free properties, all requiring significant repair, plus cash investments, said Jackson. The liabilities were “modest”, except for legal and accountancy costs incurred in the proceedings.
Having held the provenance of the assets was “of considerable significance”, the judge ruled the woman is entitled to the €640,000 family home, having bought that before the marriage.
The man is entitled to the two investment properties, to which there will be tax liabilities attached. she held. One, where he now lives, was acquired by him before marriage and is now valued about €510,000. He acquired the second, valued about €240,000, via inheritance during the marriage.
The judge rejected the man’s claim he was entitled to all the €587,000 frozen cash. He argued that this reflected his own pre-marriage funds and an inheritance sum, but the judge said it would not be proper provision to ignore certain expenditures.
Prior to the separation about four years ago, sums amounting to just over €1 million were held in joint accounts, Jackson said. It was alleged the man withdrew more than €875,000, of which he spent about €136,000, including about €30,000 on legal fees, €33,000 for a car and monies on “very expensive” furniture.
The man, who does not have a pension, continues to receive, under court order, €750 in weekly income paid out of the joint accounts.
The woman appeared to have spent about €128,000 on family outlays, including about €58,000 in school fees and €6,000 for a car.
It was “incomprehensible” that the family’s resources were depleted by €150,000 due to the children attending boarding school abroad, a move apparently instigated by their father, Jackson said.
Another “vast waste” of money involved a forensic trawl of finances over the duration of the marriage aimed at “enhancing” the man’s position, while “demeaning” that of his wife.
Both parties brought property to the marriage; the woman used hers to house the family, and the man used his to some degree in terms of rental, “but in a manifestly sub-optimal manner”. The woman contributed to family resources from her work outside the home and the man did so to a more limited degree.
The judge found the man’s evidence “unimpressive”, saying he appeared “more focused on being right, as he perceives it, than being sensible, pragmatic or advancing the overall betterment of the family”.
Among orders concerning the monies in the joint accounts, the judge directed that the woman be paid €20,000 child support and the man a lump sum based on €750 weekly up to November 1 st , 2026, to allow time for his other investment property to generate income.
Apart from a €27,000 inheritance for the children, the remainder must be divided equally between the parties, and the man must pay the forensic accountants’ fees and witness expenses regarding those.

title: Sinn Féin and Drumcree stand-off
description: No need for Michelle O’Neill or Mary Lou McDonald to be there in person
content:
Sir, – Following the reports and articles about the stand-off on Garvaghy Road, two of your commentators struck me as particularly accurate.
Justine McCarthy concluded that Ireland should have been united years ago; and that getting bogged down in the past can prevent one seeing a better future.
While Pat Leahy suggested that Mary Lou McDonald and Michelle O’Neill’s presence on Garvaghy Road is not going to further Irish unity.
Surely the residents of Garvaghy and the nationalist population of the North can take Sinn Féin leadership support as given?
With Gerry Adams on hand, there is no need for O’Neill or McDonald to be there in person. Wouldn’t they be better employed – and serving their constituents – by talking to Emma Little-Pengelly and other unionists about how to persuade the Portadown Orange Order to look for a better way forward? Rather than thinking about the next election? – Yours, etc,

title: Junior Cycle: Record numbers receive their results
description: Percentage of Distinctions aggregated across all subjects stays unchanged at 8.6% this year
content:
Almost 74,000 students will receive their Junior Cycle results on Wednesday, a record number to sit the State exam.
Results will be issued to individual schools through the State Examinations Commission’s (SEC’s) School Portal from 10am, and it will then be up to principals to distribute the scores.
Students can also access their results on examinations.ie.
Some 73,879 candidates sat the exam this year, up by less than 1 per cent on the 73,336 who sat it in 2025. Some 651,123 grades across 21 individual subjects will be issued by the SEC on Wednesday.
This is the fifth year of the revised Junior Cycle curriculum, which combines classroom-based assessments with a final exam.
The grading scale no longer features As, Bs and Cs, but instead is marked in Distinction, Higher Merit, Merit, etc. These grading bands were tweaked further in 2025, with the top four grade descriptors now evenly distributed in bands of 15 percentage points.
This is the first year the revised grade bands were incorporated directly into the normal marking process - in 2025, they were implemented by the SEC through a technical intervention following the marking.
[ Junior Cycle French: Question on Down Syndrome causes controversy Opens in new window ]
All subjects in Junior Cycle are examined at Common level, except Irish, English and Mathematics, which are examined at Higher and Ordinary level.
The percentage of Distinctions, aggregated across all subjects, was 8.6 per cent this year, the same as last year.
The percentage of Higher Merits was 30.2 per cent this year, compared to 30.4 per cent last year.
One exam that students found difficult this year was French, with one teacher, Elizabeth Lyne, describing it as “an absolute horror show” .
Students sitting the Common level paper do not have any element of choice, and Lyne said many were thrown by a question about pocket money.
“A lot of teachers want to see the reintroduction of higher and ordinary level French at Junior Cycle. The current Common level paper discriminates against the weaker student. At a time when language learning should be to the forefront, it is making it harder for younger people,” Lyne told The Irish Times after the exam in June.
Results show some 9.8 per cent achieved a distinction in French, up from 8 per cent last year.
However, more of the lowest grades were issued, with some 1.4 per cent not graded, compared to 0.9 per cent last year, 11.5 per cent Partially Achieved compared to 10.5 per cent last year, and 25.1 per cent Achieved compared to 23.6 per cent last year.

title: Childcare scheme leaves part-time working mother worse off
description: Once the subsidy is applied, I am paying more for fewer hours
content:
Sir, – As a working mother of four who has paid for childcare for 12 years, I have watched the National Childcare Scheme from the paying end. The fee cuts now being discussed will not affect me – my youngest is in senior infants and will have aged out by the time they take effect. Nor will they fix the rules underneath them.
Providers carry a heavy monthly administrative burden of claiming and passing on subsidies, on top of a fee freeze that has already pushed many of them to drop flexible and part-time places. Parents are only subsidised for the hours a child attends, not for the place they have paid for.
I work part-time so I can spend more time with my children, yet I pay a full-time fee. Because I use fewer hours, I receive less back than a parent whose child is in all day, every day. Once the subsidy is applied, I am paying more for fewer hours.
Surely a system meant to support working parents should not leave the part-time mother worse off. – Yours, etc,

title: Here’s a lasting solution to society’s throwaway thinking
description: Isn’t this something our education experts should consider?
content:
Sir, – Sadly, our society is learning we are a throwaway lot, not fixing things, nor even maintaining what works. Retailers constantly recommending the latest, greatest model pushes us to replace perfectly good and still useful stuff.
Increasingly we’re realising this is not a good route to the kind of world that will sustain us into the uncertain future.
In the past, even in my time, we learned practical skills from our parents. But this can’t be relied on now when so many parents both work, or don’t have the necessary skills themselves.
A good solution can be learned from China, where in mandatory weekly classes students learn essential domestic and practical skills, including cooking, cleaning, using basic tools, farming and community volunteering.
In addition to academic studies, they learn what are considered essential life skills.
Isn’t this something our education experts should consider? – Yours, etc,

title: GAA, LGFA and Camogie Association to present united front at Oireachtas hearing on integration
description: Leaders of the three organisations will be questioned on Wednesday after Mary McAleese’s resignation
content:
The leadership of all three Gaelic games associations are braced for an interrogation on integration when they sit before an Oireachtas Committee on Wednesday afternoon.
Representatives from the Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA), Ladies Gaelic Football Association (LGFA) and Camogie Association (CA) have been invited to a sitting of the Joint Committee on Arts, Media, Communications, Culture and Sport at Leinster House to discuss the unravelling of the integration roadmap.
The foremost officials from the GAA (director general Tom Ryan and president Jarlath Burns ), LGFA (CEO Lyn Savage and president Trina Murray) and Camogie Association (CEO Karen Dessain-Gelinet and president Brian Molloy) will attend the 12.30pm meeting.
And rather than submitting separate opening statements, the three organisations – in a clear desire to demonstrate solidarity – will deliver joint opening remarks.
The six attendees are also members of the Steering Group on Integration (SGI). Mary McAleese ’s resignation as chair of the SGI in early September sparked a national debate on the integration process.
In that joint opening statement, the message will be that the three bodies remain “totally and unequivocally” committed to integration.
They will double down on that message by adding that Gaelic games “are for everyone” and insist their commitment to making integration “happen is as firm as ever and we say that with one voice”.
[ Malachy Clerkin: If you’re coaching kids with your county in mind, you’re just as transactional as Aussie Rules Opens in new window ]
And while paying tribute to McAleese, they will strongly outline their view that her “work has not been lost”.
They will tell the Oireachtas that over the “past month there have been some who have equated Dr McAleese’s departure to the end of integration” but insist her efforts have “brought us a huge way down the road and we are closer to that goal because of her work – not further away.”
They will concede that the deadline was missed, saying the organisations simply weren’t ready to proceed. And they will admit that some have questioned the commitment of the associations, “specifically the GAA”, towards integration.
But the overriding message will be that they are united in achieving integration.
Members of all three associations have held private meetings with ministers since McAleese’s resignation but Wednesday’s summit will be their first formal public questioning since the controversy erupted.
Government ministers had asked that a new chairperson of the group be appointed at an SGI meeting on October 5 th .
And while sources say that matter will be addressed on Wednesday, no appointment has yet been announced, with the process said to be “progressing but not yet finalised”.
Speaking on RTÉ’s Prime Time in the immediate aftermath of McAleese’s resignation, Minister of State for Sport Charlie McConalogue had stated: “It is really important a new chairperson is appointed on the October 5 th and we would expect coming out of the October 5 th [meeting] that clear outlines are provided from the three organisations in relation to how this can proceed.”
The three associations can expect some difficult questions in Leinster House on Wednesday.
McAleese was appointed independent chairperson of the SGI in September 2022. In February 2024, a timeline for full integration by April 2027 was announced at a press conference in Croke Park.
But while McAleese had remained steadfast in her belief the timeline would be met, there had been reservations expressed by some of the other members of the SGI.
Indeed, at a meeting of GAA’s Management Committee last December, it was concluded that 2027 was no longer a realistic target for full integration.
The Management Committee’s view came just days after McAleese, while sitting next to Burns and Ryan, had told a December 17 th Oireachtas committee meeting that 2027 was still a realistic and achievable goal.
“It is our target date for integration, for one organisation representing all codes in 2027,” she said.
“If we were starting today, yes of course it would be ambitious, but in 2023 it was not ambitious and it is not ambitious, it is a realisable target. That is the plan we’ve been working towards, that’s what we’ve been scheduling everything towards and we believe firmly that it is achievable.”
[ The five main stumbling blocks on the road to Gaelic games integration Opens in new window ]
But within days of that Oireachtas meeting, the Management Committee of the GAA were questioning the likelihood of McAleese’s ambition coming to fruition. The failure of either side to budge on their opposing viewpoint in the months that followed ultimately led to her resigning in September.
And on the way out the door, the former president of Ireland launched a stinging criticism of the GAA’s top brass.
“I did meet the Management Committee, and a body, quite frankly, that was less than impressive and very disappointing to me as a long-term GAA supporter to meet a body so lacking in vision for the future of the GAA,” said McAleese last month.
“But it boils down to, in their view, finances, which incidentally we had taken great trouble to meet their concerns [about] and to have answers for their concerns that were more than credible and more than workable.”
“But I also suspect, and I hate to say this, but I suspect that there are people who are not entirely happy about the idea of including women in decision making at the top level of Gaelic sports.”
GAA president Jarlath Burns and director general Tom Ryan both rebutted the claims.
The power brokers, minus McAleese, will now be back in front of an Oireachtas committee on Wednesday. The meeting will be chaired by Labour’s Alan Kelly.
And after a tumultuous September the three organisations will put forward a united front in Leinster House.
But words alone might not placate the gallery because members of the Oireachtas will expect evidence that some manner of a fresh, achievable roadmap forward has been agreed.

title: Homeowner, business owner and farmer react
description: ‘We’ll get a few bob off,’ says Co Galway homeowner who delayed buying her winter heating oil to await help in Budget 2027
author_name: Dara Bradley in Galway, Stephen Conneely, Barry Roche in Cork
content:
“I t’s better than nothing, I suppose,” said homeowner Ailish Scully, responding to reductions in carbon tax rates on home heating oil announced in Budget 2027 .
The rate of carbon tax on kerosene and natural gas was due to increase to €78.50 per tonne by next May. But Minister for Finance Simon Harris told the Dáil the tax would reduce to €48.50 and remain at that level for the lifetime of this Government.
Ailish had delayed ordering heating oil this winter for her four-bedroom detached home in Moycullen, Co Galway until after the budget.
That delaying tactic paid off; Fine Gael estimated the new rate of carbon tax will save people about €86 on a 1,000-litre fill of heating oil this winter.
“We’ll get a few bob off, and hopefully it won’t go up any more. They make out that they’re giving you loads of money back but at the end of the day you pay one way or another,” said the 62-year-old.
“We have to wait and see what happens with the [Iran] war as well because the price increases are to do with that. If things calm down there, prices might go down further.”
The Government has included more than €650 million for residential and community energy upgrade schemes in the budget.
Ailish said this would encourage her and her husband Declan to explore what grants are available to retrofit their 24-year-old home to improve its energy rating, including wall and attic insulation and solar panels.
[ How Budget 2027 will impact families: From renters to stay-at-home parents Opens in new window ]
“We talked about it before but haven’t done anything about it,” she said.
“I’d strongly consider getting it done because it would be better for the environment and we’d be saving electricity or selling electricity back to the grid.”
Despite the flurry of budget announcements on tax cuts and spending increases, bike shop owner Ruairí Parsons felt, as a small business owner, there “really wasn’t much that got me excited”.
Parsons, general manager of Donnybrook Bikes in Dublin 4, had been keeping an eye on the budget coverage from the Dáil but there “wasn’t anything that jumped out at me that I could say would benefit the shop”.
“It is probably a disappointment,” he said.
But he added that there “were a couple of small things” that caught his eye.
The bike shop employs eight people, four full-time and four part-time.
[ Budget Calculator 2027: Here’s how this year’s budget will affect your income Opens in new window ]
“For anyone on minimum wage, they would be coming out with a few extra bob,” Parsons said, noting the 79 cent increase to €14.94 per hour.
There was also a “slight” reduction in the PRSI paid by an employer with the increase in the PRSI threshold rising from €552 to €600 per week.
This would save small businesses “between €650 and €700 per employee” over a year, he said.
Harris said the Government would review the Cycle to Work Scheme in 2027 “to determine ways to boost take up among all workers”, though Parsons was not convinced that “take up” was an issue”.
The scheme is a tax incentive programme that allows people to repay the cost of a bike directly from their annual salary through an agreement with their employer.
“Sometimes when we hear the words ‘bike to work scheme’, we’re almost dreading it if [the customer] comes in with a voucher,” he said.
[ What are the key takeaways from Budget 2027? From income tax cuts to surprising omissions Opens in new window ]
He explains that often large organisations will issue vouchers to their employees for the scheme that come from third-party companies, which can charge commission to the shop on sales paid for with its vouchers.
“The customer loves the bike to work scheme because, for them, it’s pretty much a half-price bike.
“But bike shops aren’t the biggest fan of it ... sometimes it’s more hassle than it’s worth.”
“A standstill budget at best,” said North Cork farmer Noel Hurley (58), summing up measures announced in the budget.
While Minister for Finance Simon Harris delivered some decent measures to assist farmers, they won’t put farming back to where it was a year ago, he says.
Hurley points out that in the 10 days since he last spoke to The Irish Times about the budget the price of green diesel has increased by 20 cent a litre.
“It was €1.50 a litre back then; today I’m paying €1.70 a litre so that’s what you’re up against – Energy prices that are threatening to spiral out of control and it affects everything,” he said.
Hurley, who is milking 200 cows on a 300-acre holding in Kildorrery with his son Sean (26), welcomes the extension of the Fuel Income Support Scheme which, if it follows the last scheme, will give farmers a rebate of 20 cents on every litre and should hold the price at €1.50 a litre – for now.
“That’s welcome because it is ring-fenced for farmers and contractors so it will bring the price of diesel back down to €1.50 a litre but that’s still an 80 per cent rise on this time last year when I was paying 90 cent a litre,” he said.
“It’s a stop gap measure because the cost of doing business is going through the roof.”
He noted that the carbon tax was being reduced on home heating oil and gas but there was “no mention of it being reduced on green diesel”.
“That’s disappointing because while I might like to use an electric tractor, that day is a long way off and I’m paying a carbon tax on something I can’t change,” he said.
[ All inheritance tax-free thresholds rise in the budget but no wider reforms Opens in new window ]
Hurley welcomed the continuation of the Fertiliser Rebate Scheme where the Government will again add 200 per cent to the €15 million given by the EU.
This should again lead to a rebate of €34 euro per tonne but with fertiliser averaging about €700 a tonne, it’s of modest help at most, says Hurley.
He had hoped that the Government would cut VAT on animal vaccines across the board and in full, but the Government has instead cut it from 23 per cent to 9 per cent on respiratory vaccines only.
“It’s something but it’s only a start,” he said.
“Overall, it’s a standstill budget at best and it would be a big stretch to say you’d be holding your own.”

title: It takes a giveaway budget of €8.5bn to not annoy anyone – except Patrick O’Donovan
description: The emergence of Chambers as a hard man fiscal hawk is a significant development in the internal dynamics of the Coalition
content:
T he first budget of the Simon Harris - Jack Chambers combination, and the second of this Coalition, was presented on Tuesday to a somewhat muted reaction from all sides. Virtually all its main features had been flagged in advance and there were no last-minute surprises to excite supporters or inflame opponents; surprises, after all, can be risky and this Government is highly risk-averse.
The budget speeches were mostly received in polite silence. Government supporters were appreciative, but hardly ecstatic; Opposition TDs were critical but not exactly brimming with righteous fury. The responses flooding into the inboxes of TDs and journalists from the army of interest groups were mostly of the “we welcome ... but not enough was done” variety.
If a budget is an opportunity for a government to provide a statement of what it is about, then this Government is about keeping things going as they are, making incremental improvements, and above all, not annoying anyone.
“Ireland has been an island of economic and political stability,” insisted Harris at the start of his speech, hailing the country’s performance as “phenomenal”.
In a country where the political mood is grumpy and the public desire for change is strong, the stability argument is not without risk. Especially when the cost of keeping things steady and stable is escalating so significantly.
[ Are Budget 2027’s tax and social welfare measures enough? Conor Pope delivers his verdict Opens in new window ]
This is, in itself, a statement of where our politics and political economy now sit: it takes a giveaway budget of €8.5 billion just to more or less stand still. Actually, it’s more than €8.5 billion: by the end of next year, overspending by the usual suspects will have brought that figure up to €10 billion, you can be sure.
Think about that another way: the Government needs to increase spending by nearly €10 billion every year just to keep things on an even keel. To fund that, tax receipts need to keep growing by that much every year. If they grew only by half that much – never mind actually declining – then the budgetary implications would be severe. A budget that only increased spending by, say, €5 billion would feel to many people, inside and outside Government, like an austerity budget. And this Government would almost certainly not survive an austerity budget.
For those who take any account of the economic critiques of Government policy from any of the official sources (the Fiscal Council, the ESRI, the Central Bank), Chambers deserves credit for his efforts to limit spending increases and therefore build the resilience of the economy.
It is a thankless task – there have been squeals from Ministers for weeks that he had been unyielding in the face of the usual barrage of requests for more spending. The humiliation of Minister for Culture Patrick O’Donovan, who had touted a €100 culture card for 16-year-olds in (not so inspired) media leaks in recent weeks only to see not a whisper of it in the budget, was brutal.
The emergence of Chambers as a hard man fiscal hawk is a significant development in the internal dynamics of the Coalition. He announced the formation of a “Public Spending Efficiency Taskforce”, which if it does its job, will become one of the most unpopular bodies in public life.
But bear in mind – again – that Chambers is not cutting spending, or anything like it; he is just reducing the rate at which it has been increasing. And while it was apparent on Tuesday when the figures were published that he had got his way – spending will increase by 6 per cent – this is still objectively a substantial rise.
Chambers and Harris will point to ongoing surpluses and to the savings funds – into which an extra billion euro was bunged yesterday – as evidence of their commitment to prudence. And, in fairness, they have a point. They have built up a buffer. But they – or any other government – won’t be long burning through that cash if the growth in corporation tax receipts doesn’t last.
Still, such apocalyptic thoughts were not on the minds of most Government TDs on Tuesday afternoon. A bigger than expected income tax package for middle-income voters eased their anxieties, and there were plenty of giveaways – for parents, those with disabilities, college students, renters and the inevitable tenner on social welfare payments and pensions – in the budget talking points for Coalition TDs.
There was progress towards some key goals. Harris finally unveiled his savings accounts, with relatively generous tax concessions. There was real progress towards the goal of €200-a-month childcare. There are investments in MetroLink and in housing.
[ Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work Opens in new window ]
None of that guarantees the budget a warm reception. As costs rise across the economy, and with a winter of higher fuel and food prices around the corner, many voters will agree with the cries from Opposition parties and special interest groups that the Government has not done enough to help them.
The tax cuts will do little more than keep pace with inflation. The people who get up early in the morning will still wonder where all their money is gone by the end of the month. Those who depend substantially, or entirely, on the State must deal with costs rising more quickly than their fixed incomes.
It is a feature of our politics that the only criticism of the Government’s budgetary policy from the Opposition – that it should spend more – is the exact opposite of most economic critiques. But that does not make that criticism any less politically pungent.
In government, as in life, when you try to please everyone, sometimes you can end up pleasing nobody.
[ What are the key takeaways from Budget 2027? From income tax cuts to surprising omissions Opens in new window ]

title: Bank of Ireland invests €10m in ‘tech-for-good’ fund
description: Bank says investment is aligned with its wider sustainability ambitions
content:
Bank of Ireland is to invest €10 million in the Impact Ireland USA Fund, an investment vehicle run by Dublin-headquartered Venturewave Capital and backed by U2 members The Edge and Adam Clayton.
The fund invests in what Venturewave Captial describes as “mission driven” tech start-ups that have the potential to deliver social and environmental benefits while ensuring financial returns for stakeholders.
The Impact Ireland USA Fund is the third fund operated by Venturewave Capital and the target for the fund is €100 million.
“It invests commercially in high-growth, mission-driven technology companies across health, education, food and agriculture, climate and sustainable finance,” it said.
“Its investments are focused on businesses aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals,” it said, noting the approach was designed to demonstrate that commercial performance and positive impact can be “complementary objectives”.
Bank of Ireland’s investment is the first by a pillar bank here and follows a similar investment from Bank of America .
“Bank of Ireland becoming our first Irish pillar investor is particularly significant,” Kieran McLoughlin, co-founder and managing partner of Venturewave Capital, said.
“Impact Ireland was created in Ireland with a global ambition, and having an Irish financial institution with such reach and reputation invest alongside our international partners strengthens both the fund and the businesses we support,” he said.
[ ‘I’m trying to build the next Stripe’: Two Irish start-ups accepted into top Silicon Valley programme Opens in new window ]
Myles O’Grady, group chief executive of Bank of Ireland, said: “At the core of Bank of Ireland’s strategy is our strong support for Irish businesses at home and on the global stage.
“We pair this with a firm commitment to sustainability and to playing our part in helping tackle some of the challenges society faces today,” he said.
The bank said the investment was aligned with its wider sustainability ambitions.
Bank of Ireland’s strategy to 2028 includes support for green transition, housing and social infrastructure, and social inclusion, “with the objective of supporting a resilient economy.”
Sustainability-related lending at Bank of Ireland reached €17.7 billion by the end of 2025, exceeding its €15 billion target, with the bank aiming to get it to €30 billion by 2030.
The bank also aims to reduce carbon emissions by 49 per cent by 2030 in line with its Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) carbon reduction target.
[ Big tech firms lead Top 1,000 companies for 2026 Opens in new window ]
Alan Foy and his business partner Brian Martin, who previously led Irish tech company Blueface, became managing partners of Venturewave in 2020 along with Kieran McLoughlin, who stepped down as the New York-based chief executive of The Ireland Funds in 2018.
Venturewave led a $40 million (€35.5 million) investment in angel investing and trading platform Funderbeam, taking a majority stake, in 2023.

title: ‘We swim with our faces out of the water’: how Lough Derg’s algal bloom affects locals
description: Swimmers, anglers and campaigners raise concerns over recurring algae, pollution and water abstraction
content:
F iona Ward and Orna Cooke have been cold water swimming in Lough Derg at Twomilegate, just north of Killaloe in Co Clare for the past eight years.
Rain, wind or snow, they never miss an early morning dip.
The only time they are forced to stay out of the water is at the warmest time of the year when a blue-green algae on the surface makes swimming dangerous.
Over the past five to seven years the presence of the algae has become a regular summer time occurrence on Lough Derg, the third largest lake on the island of Ireland that borders Clare, Galway and Tipperary.
This year’s bloom, which appeared after one of the driest and warmest summers on record, is the largest ever seen on the lake, and has prompted swimming restrictions from both Tipperary and Clare county councils.
“During recent summers there has always been some bit of bloom there, particularly when the temperatures are high, but over the years we have noticed more of it and it is lasting a little longer each year,” says Ward.
“We tend to swim with our faces out of the water when there is any algae. Or maybe just have a very quick dip or sometimes we make the decision as a group not to get in at all.”
A number of swimmers in the Twomilegate group have reported skin irritation and sinus issues after swimming when there is an algal bloom.
“Sometimes we get algae in our togs and we can get an allergic reaction, that does happen sometimes and it is a bit alarming. There can be a sinus reaction, a respiratory reaction. It is very real,” says Cooke.
“I think [besides the impact on swimmers] we are really concerned with the quality of the water for everybody. It is a really big, urgent concern.
“As swimmers, yes, this affects us, but we still swim. We are concerned, but we feel that this is something that can be tackled. We can make this better.”
Tony O’Brien’s relationship with Lough Derg and the river Shannon began almost 50 years ago when as a teenager he spent his summer holidays working as a crew member for a boat hire company.
Raised within sight of the water in Killaloe, he believes one thing very strongly: the lake is changing and not for the better.
“I have a long association with the river and I can see that it has changed. The blooms have been going for a number of years, particularly during times of low levels of water,” says O’Brien, who is a Fianna Fáil councillor on Clare County Council.
“When it comes, we don’t go swimming in it because it may be unsafe. It is a huge concern. We need to establish what is the cause of it, why it is happening.
“We have local authorities on both sides of the lake issuing precautionary notices not to swim in the water, not to use this great natural resource because of this blue algal bloom.
“If we don’t address this problem it will have a huge impact on the development of our local area.”
[ Polish chocolatier in Clare: ‘There’s something very special about Irish people’ Opens in new window ]
Algal blooms are usually triggered by a combination of high phosphorus and nitrogen levels in water and high temperatures.
There are a number of ways in which excess phosphorus and nitrogen can enter Irish rivers including run off from farm fertilisers, nutrients being flushed from soil during clear-felling of forestry as well as from sewage treatment plants and septic tanks.
Drought conditions also contribute to the severity of the blooms as lower water levels result in a higher concentration of nutrients and higher water temperature.
O’Brien says when the weather is hot, the condition of the water deteriorates with the amount of nitrates and phosphates ending up in there.
“There are a lot of factors that we know about. But low water levels, lack of flow and a bit of heat, that is the perfect storm for it,” he says.
“This is forecast to get even more extreme as we go along because of climate change.”
Mike Quinlivan has been fishing on Lough Derg for more than 30 years.
Originally from Clare, he now lives across the bridge in Ballina, Co Tipperary and believes that a number of fish species have become extinct from the lake in recent years.
“Over my lifetime I have seen a major deterioration in the water quality. It’s very sad. The whole environment is being degraded,” he says.
“I think the people making decisions [which impact on water quality] don’t seem to see the results of their decision on the ground.
“I still go out and try to do a bit of fishing. In the past this was mainly a trout fishery and 100 years ago this was the prime salmon fishery in the world but that has all changed.
“There is still fishing going on, there is still some trout but a couple of species of fish have gone. We had a population of arctic char here once, for example, but we haven’t seen them for 25 years.
“The blue-green algae can be harmful. The algae uses up all the oxygen and the fish need the oxygen, so if there is a lot of bloom and high temperature the fish will die.”
Ballina woman Kay Mullane help establish the river Shannon Environmental Protection Alliance in 2013 in response to the multibillion euro plans to pump water from the Shannon to be used as drinking water in Dublin.
She believes that taking water from the Shannon at the Parteen Basin will make the annual algal blooms on Lough Derg even worse.
“The algal bloom is all over Lough Derg and it does have effects for health, tourism and the recreational industry,” she says.
“When the levels drop, the water quality will drop even more. If you are going to be abstracting 330 million litres a day, obviously that is going to be an issue.
“Uisce Éireann says it’s just going to be 2 per cent, which I think has been a really clever marketing ploy for them.
“It doesn’t seem like a lot, but it is 2 per cent of the yearly average. So when there is a drought situation, and there isn’t enough water, we have done calculation which suggest it will be about 35 per cent to 50 per cent of the available water.”
There are so many issues with the water in the Shannon that locals wonder, “why the people of Dublin would want it?”
“There is then the cost of treating it and bringing it a hundred miles to Dublin where much of it will be lost to leaks,” she says.
A spokesperson from Uisce Éireann says it is “inaccurate and misleading” to suggest that discharges from waste water treatment plants are a “significant contributing factor” to the recent algal bloom on Lough Derg.
“According to EPA [Environmental Protection Agency] research on algal blooms in Irish lakes, agriculture is the most significant pressure, impacting 60 per cent of the 35 at-risk water bodies within the Lower Shannon and Mulkear catchment, followed by 26 per cent being impacted by hydromorphological pressures and 11 per cent by forestry,” said a spokesperson.
Hydromorphological relates to the physical structure of the river and how human interference affects habitats and water flows.
The spokesperson says that in the abstraction of water for public drinking supplies, a range of raw water quality conditions, including algal blooms, can affect water supplies.
“These are managed effectively through monitoring, risk assessment and advanced water treatment to ensure strict EU drinking water standards are met and there is no impact on the safety of drinking water supplies,” the spokesperson says.
“This would similarly be the case with any abstraction from the Parteen Basin for drinking water supplies.”
