title: Michael McDowell: Where’s the feelgood factor? Budget has become an attritional struggle between ministers
description: Increase in basic income tax credits of €125 is small beer by any standard, with inflation soaring
content:
B earing in mind the political reality that the Government is facing the prospect of a national wage agreement which is expected to increase nominal wages by 5 per cent at least, the structure of our income tax system means that tax bands and credits would have had to increase proportionally just to leave people where they are in terms of take-home pay. It is difficult to predict an annual rate of inflation at this point for the short to medium term. But an inflation rate of between 3.5 per cent and 4.5 per cent seems realistic, especially in the context of rising grocery and energy costs .
So an increase in the basic income tax credits, the personal and PAYE credits, of €125 each is small beer by any standard.
For a self-employed person, an increase in the personal tax credit of €125 is equivalent to just over €2 per week. Likewise, increasing the standard rate income tax band by €2,500 a year makes much less difference in the context of general wage increases in the order of 5 per cent plus.
Social partners are exerting pressure on the Government through industrial action in the form of working to rule to bring about a nominal national wage agreement for the public sector of at least 5 per cent. Government, for its part, is hoping to peg a public sector wage deal at 5 per cent by sweetening it with adjustments to tax credits and tax band widening.
All this may avoid a public sector winter of discontent, if the Government is lucky. But with inflationary pressures and the cost of home heating, public and private transport costs, growing grocery bills and health insurance costs, there is little room for any feel-good factor going into the autumn and next spring.
The budget cut the carbon tax rate applying to home heating oil and gas to €48 instead of a planned rise.
The logic of carbon tax increases in the present circumstances would have been difficult to articulate. Ring-fencing carbon taxes to finance or subsidise sustainable energy grants and incentives may be a sacred cow for the green lobby. However, explaining any further increases in carbon taxes to households facing bills of €1,200-€1,500 for a refill of their oil tank was politically impossible.
In the context of a general acceptance that house prices are overvalued when compared to earning capacity, there has been increased pressure on the Government to adjust inheritance taxes. Raising the children’s inheritance threshold from €400,000 to €420,000 is required to prevent the State from taking an ever-increasing share of the capital value of family homes.
Experts are sharply divided as to whether increasing the Help To Buy assistance by €5,000, as the budget did, will have any significant impact on home ownership, much less homelessness .
It seems that a major relaxation on one-off housing development in rural areas could still boost homebuilding at little cost to the exchequer.
Taxation of capital gains is a battleground between theory and practice. Capital gains tax ( CGT ) was increased from 20 per cent to 33 per cent between 2008 and 2011 as a response to the financial crash. Many people have forgotten that when Charlie McCreevy reduced CGT from 40 per cent to 20 per cent in 1997, its exchequer yield rose from €450 million in 1999 to €3.1 billion by 2006. The real question in relation to CGT is its systemic effect rather than theoretical concerns with taxation equity. Put simply, the 33 per cent rate has acted as a major brake on capital transactions, which is not justified by doctrinal tax equity theory.
The 2 percentage point cut in CGT from 33 per cent to 31 per cent will not have any game-changing stimulus effect. On the contrary, nibbling CGT at the margin is politically and economically almost worthless.
Many families will have been watching carefully to see what the budget would do for their childcare costs. The Government should have adopted a pragmatic approach by increasing the amount that home-based childminders can earn tax-free and by addressing the cap on monthly childcare costs.
Right across Ireland, there are derelict and unused homes. In urban areas, unused building land and derelict sites still proliferate. Although there are relatively generous grants towards refurbishing derelict and unoccupied houses, uptake is still low. What is needed is a “carrot and stick” policy. Every local authority (every one of which is a housing authority) needs to carry out an emergency survey of its entire functional area to identify unused and derelict homes for reoccupation. We badly need an effective “use it or lose it” compulsory purchase regime that would put such properties on the market, if necessary, with the local authority as vendor. I would add that while we all get a warm glow watching a derelict cottage being refurbished on a TV programme like Cheap Irish Homes, the logic of grant-aiding such activity while prohibiting one-off rural housing is difficult to justify. Does it really matter whether the structure of a newly occupied rural home has been semi-ruinous, newly built or built by modular techniques?
Budget day, for all the hype, has lost all sense of excitement and has degenerated into an attritional struggle between ministers. To raise hope, we needed more than marginal tweaking of an underperforming State sector.

title: Minister should see Cork University Hospital staffing levels
description: Talk to staff and patients - and listen
content:
Sir, – The Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill makes the classic mistake of thinking only what can be measured is what matters, stating “by every metric that it is possible for us to have, Cork has been safe all year”, (“ Minister for Health stands over Cork University Hospital safety and staffing levels ”, Health, September 30th).
Or, perhaps, it is the mistake of picking and choosing what to measure.
In any case, my suggestion to McNeill is to visit Cork University Hospital unannounced and observe. Talk to staff and patients – and listen. I hazard a guess this might be a more useful approach for learning what is actually going on than looking at numbers on a page.
I’m not sure about your readers but I know myself if someone on the ground, in this case the CEO of the hospital, says things are unsafe I’d be inclined to take their word for it over a Minister in an office far removed from the realities on the floor. – Yours, etc,

title: State spending must reflect responsibility to children in care
description: A system under pressure has real consequences for young people in care
content:
Sir, – Appearing before the Committee for Public Accounts last week (September 30th), Tusla once again put on record its concerns about the impact further cost saving measures would have on frontline services and care placements.
At EPIC, Empowering People in Care, we see the consequences of gaps in the systems through our work with children in care and young care leavers.
We work with children held in special care because suitable onward placements are not available, and children living in emergency arrangements who don’t know where they will go next.
A system under pressure has real consequences for children and young people in care. Too often experienced as traumatic disruption to their relationships, education and wellbeing.
Where the State assumes the role of a parent, that responsibility carries a fundamental duty to protect, support and nurture. EPIC called for an additional investment in Tusla in the budget.
However, sustained investment in Tusla must be matched by a cross-governmental commitment to meeting the needs of care-experienced youth.
Children in care and young care leavers need safe, stable places to live and timely access to health services – including mental health and trauma informed therapeutic interventions – and adequate aftercare and educational supports as they transition from care at 18.
The Government asking departments and agencies to find savings and savings may be necessary but children and young people who rely on the State for their care cannot carry the cost of these decisions. Government spending must reflect the State’s responsibility to them and provide the investment needed to meet it. – Yours, etc,

title: James McClean isn’t one to back down, but he has little to gain in row with hometown club
description: Latest spike in ongoing fallout drew a measured response from Derry City, but their sense of irritation was also clear
content:
For the moment at least, Derry City are adopting a fairly sanguine approach to the latest chapter in the James McClean saga. Their statement late on Tuesday afternoon was measured, although the pointed reference to McClean’s intervention coming “four days before the biggest match of the Club’s season” left no doubt as to how annoyed they are by the timing. Saturday’s FAI Cup semi-final against Galway United represents far bigger fish to fry.
Equally, though, they surely can’t imagine it will all just die down eventually. McClean isn’t in the habit of stepping back from conflict, particularly when he feels sinned against. In any public spat, it can be difficult sometimes to discern things like timelines and facts and truths. But the one thing you can take as read with McClean is that he’ll fight until there’s no more fighting to be done.
In all truth, the particulars of this row with his boyhood club are relatively humdrum and probably not all that interesting to many people beyond the parties involved. McClean isn’t the first pro footballer to get into a barney with his club as his career winds down and he won’t be the last. It feels unlikely that any other player in the League of Ireland would hoover up such attention in similar circumstances.
Essentially, this feels like a collective failure of foresight, with plenty of blame to go around. If Derry had buyer’s remorse in the months after bringing McClean home, the onus was on them to find a way to make a clean break. They had to know that unless they were comma perfect in the process of moving him on, they would get drawn into a legal conkers match with someone who has no problem hoarding chestnuts.
Did Derry really think McClean was just going to shrug and say, “Fair enough lads, no hard feelings”? If they did, they were sorely mistaken – and found out as much back in August when they ended up having to withdraw their attempt to end his contract. The fact that they signed McClean without conducting a medical, as claimed in the PFAI statement, does not speak well of the club’s ability to see around corners.
As for McClean, the very fact that he went as far as apologising for going public with his criticisms of the club back in the summer is telling in and of itself. “I accept that some of my actions over the past few months were misjudged, and my frustrations should have remained in-house,” he said. “I take responsibility for that – and I apologise.”
It’s one thing being a truth-teller and holding the club higher-ups to account. As a seasoned professional, with experience of every level of the game, McClean could reasonably have assumed that was expected of him, part of the package Derry were signing up to when they got him.
But whatever his grievances, it was neither wise nor helpful to be going on RTÉ during the World Cup and bad-mouthing the set-up at his new club. And certainly not when, by his own admission, he is only intermittently fit enough to actually play. People aren’t generally inclined to listen to you pronounce from your high horse when they think you have to be helped up into the saddle.
McClean’s endless lust for battle has, on balance, been an admirable thread running through his career. People forget that he looked for a long time like he wouldn’t make it out of Derry in the first place. He was 22 by the time Sunderland brought him to England, in an era when most talented players in Irish football were going over in their mid-teens.
He forced his way into the Republic of Ireland squad for Euro 2012, only to find himself having to apologise to Giovanni Trapattoni for complaining about playing time in an ill-advised tweet a couple of months later. Whatever future anyone had in mind for him then, not many were predicting he would end up with 103 Ireland caps, behind only four men in history.
Of course, he has got into interminable scrapes along the way, which would have long since worn on most people’s patience if it wasn’t for the fact he sometimes had right on his side. Taking on the broad swathe of English football in the poppy wars of the mid-2010s must go down as one of the most admirable stances ever taken by a pro footballer, especially considering the endless abuse he took for it. Most public figures would have quailed in the face of the hate he engendered; McClean ran face-first into it.
The poppy fight bought him plenty of store credit when it came to his other misdemeanours. Putting on a balaclava during Covid while apparently giving his kids a “history lesson”, and posting a picture of it, was idiotic. His habitual inclination to pour online petrol onto any available fire has done him no favours either. By now, most people have a rounded enough view of James McClean – a full-hearted footballer, commendably solid in his convictions, probably a bit of a pain in the arse at the same time.
Ultimately, he is within his rights to take the fight to Derry City if he feels he has standing. Just as they are within their rights to fight back. But the feeling persists that he might have misjudged this one. Derry were there long before him and they’ll be around long after him. Even if he scraps his way to a legal victory – whatever that might look like – what will he really have won?
He’ll be a wealthy footballer who finished his career going to war with his hometown club. For someone who made such a brilliant career out of humble beginnings, that’s no sort of legacy to leave.

title: Carbon tax U-turn calls Government’s climate commitments into question
description: Environmental groups despair as Budget 2027 sees polluter-pays principle reversed
content:
It was hard to agree at its inception and tough to defend since, but in the end the efforts this Government and the previous one put into holding firm on the carbon tax were easily abandoned.
Minister for Finance Simon Harris walked back years of embedding the polluter-pays principle into public policy by reversing some of the most recent carbon tax increases and freezing others.
“[Carbon tax on home heating fuels] will not increase again in the lifetime of this Government,” he said.
“The changes do not in any way signal a weakening of our resolve to decarbonise the economy,” he also said.
He did not see a contradiction in those two statements, unlike environmental and climate non-governmental organisations (NGOs), who saw nothing but conflict in them.
While the Government justified the move as providing much-needed relief to households struggling with rising energy prices, Friends of the Earth said it was designed primarily to provide “political relief” for a Government struggling with falling public support.
[ Are Budget 2027’s tax and social welfare measures enough? Conor Pope delivers his verdict Opens in new window ]
“Fuel-tax cuts do nothing to insulate families from global fuel shocks in the long term, while simultaneously draining the exchequer of the funds needed to get off fossil fuels for good,” said Clare O’Connor, the group’s programme coordinator.
Oisín Coghlan, policy adviser to the Irish Environmental Network, had a similar reaction.
“We need to accelerate supports to get people off fossil-fuel home-heating. And the Government will now have to use more non-carbon tax revenue to do that.”
Green Party leader Roderic O’Gorman said Harris had written off four years of carbon tax revenue without giving any indication how the hole would be filled.
He said the funding announced for the national retrofit scheme was just €14.5 million more than last year, an increase so small it was “laughable”.
The Department of Climate, Energy and Environment didn’t find that funny, insisting the increase was closer to €100 million, but it seems there are different ways of counting – and announcing – allocations.
[ Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work Opens in new window ]
O’Gorman linked the “tinkering around the edges” climate budget directly to the fall-off in carbon tax revenues the Government had now walked itself into.
This “does not show a Government serious about transitioning away from fossil fuels and making renewable energy easily available for all households”, he said.
The fall-off is serious, however: €25 million this year and €177 million in each full year to follow. Even for a tax that was due to bring in over €1 billion in revenue this year, that’s a considerable loss.
The U-turn on carbon tax also presents wider difficulties for Government policy.
[ What are the key takeaways from Budget 2027? From income tax cuts to surprising omissions Opens in new window ]
The Tax Strategy Group, an interdepartmental group of senior civil servants and advisers, examined the tax in their pre-budget analysis.
“The carbon tax trajectory is an important part of Ireland’s overall commitment to tackling climate change and has provided a clear long-term signal to industry and society of the need to decouple from our reliance on fossil fuels,” they said.
“It has been positively referenced in international forums as a clear, unambiguous and, when combined with the ring-fencing, progressive transition measure.”
[ Budget Calculator 2027: Here’s how this year’s budget will affect your income Opens in new window ]
Veering off that trajectory suggests a dent in Government commitment, a fuzzying of the signals and a reversion to regressive measures.
Minister for Climate Darragh O’Brien insisted the decision was “not taken lightly” and did not indicate any lack of commitment to the energy transition.
But while the treatment of home-heating fuels has gone back in time, the deferral of the increases on petrol and diesel are only until next year, when two hikes will be due.
Having walked back on the tax this budget, the pressure will be on to remain in reverse gear next year.

title: Drivers should not have to guess whether their car is visible from behind
description: A trick of the light jeopardises road safety
content:
Sir, – A common sight on roads across the country is a car using the automatic light setting, with only the front lights illuminated and no rear lights. Drivers often assume their full lighting system is active.
The Road Safety Authority says daytime running lights do not illuminate the rear. Gardaí advise using dipped headlights in darkness and poor weather to ensure tail lights are on.
The Department of Transport should examine this issue and require manufacturers to ensure rear lights operate automatically with the front lights.
Dipped beams and rear lights should also activate in poor visibility. Drivers should not have to guess whether their car is visible from behind. – Yours, etc,

title: Medical Council complaints
description: Guiding people to more appropriate complaint routes would benefit patients, doctors and the regulator
content:
Sir, – Shauna Bowers’s article “ Complaints about doctors to the Medical Council were up 12% in 2025 ” (October 2nd) highlights that, of the 387 complaints investigated by the Medical Council’s Preliminary Proceedings Committee last year, almost 80 per cent (301) resulted in no further action. Furthermore, 156 concerns were closed by the Medical Council earlier on, with complainants redirected to a more appropriate route.
It is positive that the Medical Council is closing complaints earlier if they do not meet the criteria for an investigation into a doctor. The Medical Protection Society (MPS) has for some time called for the implementation of powers that enable the regulator to better triage complaints, so those not requiring further action can be closed swiftly.
We also welcome the recognition from the Medical Council that many concerns about doctors – including those related to communication – could be best dealt with locally so patient safety concerns remain the focus of its fitness-to-practise process, in line with its remit.
These statistics do, however, raise serious questions about the types of complaints the Medical Council is processing.
We believe more could be done by the Medical Council and HSE to educate the public on the range of complaints processes available, and the high bar that is set for a regulatory investigation.
Signposting patients earlier to more appropriate complaint routes would also benefit patients, as their concerns could be dealt with locally, leading to more relevant action and earlier resolution.
However, this is about more than just ensuring the Medical Council is not devoting significant resources to complaints that do not require regulatory intervention. A Medical Council complaint can be long and incredibly stressful for the doctor involved, with many facing significant mental wellbeing issues and some even leaving clinical practice.
It is vital that they do not go through these investigations unnecessarily. Improving awareness of the different routes available for raising concerns will ultimately benefit patients, doctors and the regulator. – Yours, etc,

title: Power station shutdown cost ESB almost €11m
description: Turbine repairs put Coolkeeragh plant out of action for six months
content:
Shutting down a power plant for six months for repairs cost State energy company ESB almost €11 million last year, new figures show.
The group, which sells electricity and gas through Electric Ireland, operates the Coolkeeragh gas-fired power plant in Northern Ireland, among other subsidiaries.
Coolkeeragh ESB Ltd lost £9.16 million (€10.8 million) before tax last year after it was forced to close the power plant from June to December, according to recently filed accounts.
Last year’s loss compares with a £26 million profit earned by the business in 2024, the filings with the UK companies registrar show.
The shutdown, which affected operations at Coolkeeragh power station from the end of June to December 2025, was in relation to turbine maintenance and repair works, said the ESB on Tuesday.
The company fully resolved the problem with no impact on the power plant this year, it added.
The ESB gave no indication of the plant’s financial performance so far this year.
A surge in natural gas prices since the US-Iran war shut the Strait of Hormuz in February has put electricity companies under pressure.
About half the electricity used in Ireland is generated by burning natural gas.
Most companies hedge their risk. That usually means they buy supplies well in advance to cut risks posed by volatile price movements, but they have been unable to avoid increased costs as the conflict has dragged on.
Coolkeeragh ESB Ltd’s accounts show revenues slumped to £196 million last year from £317 million in 2024 as a result of the shutdown.
Its balance sheet also suffered as a consequence.
Net assets slipped to £23.7 million on December 31st from £31.6 million 12 months earlier as cash due from customers tumbled to £35 million from £111 million.
Coolkeeragh primarily sells electricity to other subsidiaries within the ESB Group, the accounts note.
Falls in liabilities eased the impact of the slide in sums due from debtors.
Built on the site of an older oil-fired power plant close to Derry , Coolkeeragh can generate up to 455 megawatts of electricity and supply up to one third of total demand in the North, according to the ESB.
The newer gas turbine plant began operating in 2005.
The ESB is one of the biggest players in the Irish market. The group earned profits of €377 million after tax in the first half of this year, according to accounts published last month.
Along with most other suppliers, it increased household electricity charges by 8 per cent in July to counter rising natural gas bills.
The Republic’s and Northern Ireland’s electricity markets were joined to create a single entity in 2007.
However, the failure to build the proposed North-South interconnector, a 138km high-capacity electricity line between counties Meath and Tyrone, has left the market with bottlenecks that prevent power from flowing freely between both sides of the country.

title: Chloe Mustaki: Ireland defender enjoying best spell of career ahead of Kazakhstan playoff
description: Nottingham Forest defender has overcome serious injury and illness to become a key part of Carla Ward’s Ireland side
content:
It’s a whole 17 years since the Republic of Ireland’s women played in Kazakhstan, the game proving to be the last in the senior international career of one of their midfielders who had decided to focus on another sport. She did all right at it too, did Katie Taylor .
Ireland had to come from behind to win their World Cup qualifier 2-1 that day in Taldykorgan, a repeat of the result between the sides the previous month in Turner’s Cross. They were narrow shaves against a team that went on to suffer its record defeat – 17-0 at the hands of Germany – just two years later.
Considering they’re at 98 in the world list, with Ireland up to their highest ever ranking of 21, there might be some who expect Kazakhstan to cause as little trouble to Carla Ward’s crew as they did to the Germans back then.
“People will just expect us to win pretty comfortably, but I’m sure that won’t be the case,” says Chloe Mustaki. “As Carla said, this could be a banana skin for us.”
It would, though, be the mother of all slips if Ireland failed to win over these two legs – the first in Astana on Friday, the second in Cork next Tuesday – to set up a final World Cup qualifying playoff against Belgium or Poland.
It was back in June that the draw paired Ireland with Kazakhstan. Mustaki greeted the news with glee – at first. “I remember listening to it in the summer, I was on holidays at the time, and I was absolutely buzzing when we got Kazakhstan, just based off their ranking. But then looking into the journey there and having looked at how they play and the type of opposition that they are, it’s more of a challenge than I initially expected.”
“So we just can’t underestimate them at all. On the journey on Monday, we had a look at some of the ways they play in and out of possession, and based on that we know it’ll be a tough game. It’ll require different things from what we’ve come up against before, every team at this level will cause different problems. But we’ll be well prepared and we have to be at it. It’s a cup final, so we just need to be ready for that.”
[ Ireland v Kazakhstan World Cup playoff: Team news, kick-off time, where to watch Opens in new window ]
After so many injury-interrupted years, and a battle with Hodgkin lymphoma when she was 19, Mustaki, now 31, is enjoying her best ever spell in football. She was rewarded with a new two-year contract by Nottingham Forest during the summer, after being named in the WSL2 team of the season, and Ward has started her in defence in the last six games.
“I’m extremely grateful to have played the amount of games that I have for both club and country over the past 12 to 18 months. The main thing is just staying fit and I have been lucky to do that. The older you get, the more professional you are and the more you learn about your body and keeping it right. It was a bit tough initially, but I am in a good place now. Long may it continue.”
[ Carla Ward urges Ireland to thrive as favourites in World Cup playoff against Kazakhstan Opens in new window ]

title: Housing crisis perpetuating child poverty crisis
description: Cross-departmental ownership, action and attention needed
content:
Sir, – The Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage latest monthly figures for those living in emergency accommodation revealed that 5,830 children are now in such accommodation.
The number has risen by more than 1,200 since the Government was formed in January 2025.
In just one month, that number increased by 171. We cannot continue to watch these numbers rise and not do everything in our power to prevent this from happening.
The ripple effect of living in such circumstances seeps into every aspect of a child’s life. Research shows that homelessness can affect a child’s relationship with their parent(s), their ability to engage in education and their physical and mental health. Children have to say goodbye to their family pet and dinners at the table.
Charities working directly with children and families experiencing homelessness have been highlighting the need to address the harm caused by homelessness for too long. Yet despite the continuous increase in the number of children being exposed to homelessness, to date we await a co-ordinated approach to address the impact this is having on them.
Last year, the Government published Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025-2030, which includes a commitment to develop a cross-departmental and agency-led Child and Family Homelessness Action Plan guided by the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. The plan promises to include enhanced supports for children and measures to speed up exits and reduce the time spent in homeless emergency accommodation and address issues around education and nutrition.
While we welcome this in principle, the plan has yet to be published. If it is the budget that has stopped this then the next step is clear.
What is needed is significant investment for child support workers and family support services, and significant investment in services that provide the scaffolding for vulnerable families the State has failed to deliver – the domestic violence refuges, the mental health services, the community organisations who work day in, day out to support children and families experiencing homelessness to live as normal a life as possible.
This housing crisis is perpetuating a child poverty crisis. If we do not see cross-departmental ownership, action and attention, we will be condemning this generation to a future hampered by the cycle of inequality. – Yours, etc,

title: ‘I’m a young buck still’: Joe McCarthy on becoming a senior figure at Leinster
description: Second row taking on more leadership as part of his continuing development in dressingroom
content:
Whisper it, but former young tyro Joe McCarthy is beginning to sound, and behave, like one of Leinster ’s senior men.
The 25-year-old was asked to step beyond his usual role during the province’s recent trip to South Africa. Part of a group of Ireland internationals who travelled knowing they would not play, McCarthy was among those given responsibility for analysing the Lions and Sharks and presenting his findings to coaches and players.
“We were kind of in a player-coach role,” McCarthy said. “So it was a bit of a different thing, putting together a few clips of the opposition and deciding what points do we really hammer home. It was useful. You hear a lot from the coaches, but I think the players enjoyed hearing from the players on things like that.”
He was among the group that left Durban on Friday before the 26-20 loss to the Sharks , and returned to UCD on Monday, training with Leinster’s sub-academy players, many of whom are only 18 or 19.
“I’m a young buck still,” McCarthy said. “But it’s so weird because they probably look at me like I’m quite an old player. They’re all 18, 19, so I’m like, ‘jeez, it feels like it was yesterday when I was coming out of school’.”
The second row is normally happy to leave the talking to more established voices in the pack, such as Tadhg Furlong, Dan Sheehan and James Ryan, but he acknowledges that his duties on the South Africa trip were part of his continuing development as a more senior dressingroom figure.
“I definitely wouldn’t be the most talkative out of the group,” he said. “I don’t want to overcomplicate things, but I would try to take a bit more leadership. Sometimes I might be running the line of defence plan during a week, so there’s a bit of leading in that.”
McCarthy believes that, while the trip failed to yield a victory for the second year running, it did provide an ideal foundation after the fragmented nature of last season’s start, when the involvement of so many players with the British and Irish Lions delayed their return.
Naturally, he can’t wait to get up and running against Cardiff Blues on Saturday. “The lads are really buzzed to get back into the Laya Arena,” he said.
“You want to put on a proper show that fans are happy and proud to show up to and watch. There are no guarantees, but it definitely felt like we were a lot more on the same page on how we were trying to evolve our attack and get better at defence. It definitely feels like we’ve bedded in and we’re going to have a fresh attack and feel.”
Leinster’s RDS return marks the beginning of another marathon season for McCarthy that will eventually lead into the World Cup year.
“We have a lot of big games coming up,” he said. “We’ve got Cardiff, Clermont and Munster and then we’re into the internationals, so it is in the back of your mind.”
And, amid all the talk of personal evolution, there is a visible sign of change. The renowned McCarthy mullet is no more. He is happy enough to compare Sam Prendergast’s “furry” haircut to a badger or a beaver, but accepts that his own record does not leave him in much of a position to judge.
[ Rugby referees need to cut out the first name chummy approach to players Opens in new window ]
“Maybe I’ll go for a shaved head this weekend,” he said, smiling. “I’ve had some dodgy ones. It was just looking a bit raggedy, wasn’t it? It had maybe run its course a bit, but once you cut it then you kind of miss it a bit. I miss the feeling of it whipping around.
“I just cut it to change it and maybe tidy up my appearance, make me look more serious. I’m getting older. I have to leave that behind me. But I think Sammy’s hair actually looks all right.”

title: New Garda spending rules to follow booking of nearly €250k worth of unused hotel rooms
description: Garda chief Justin Kelly to tell Committee of Public Accounts about lessons learned regarding big events
content:
New spending controls and oversight for policing of large-scale events are being introduced following controversy over unused accommodation booked for officers working at the 2024 Uefa Europa League final, Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly is expected to tell an Oireachtas committee this week.
In an opening statement to the Oireachtas Committee of Public Accounts , it is anticipated that Kelly will outline how the policing operation for the May 2024 football final in Dublin 4 provided “important organisational learning”. He will say that reviews carried out subsequently “resulted in a number of changes to how major events are managed”.
Kelly is likely to be questioned at Thursday’s hearing about findings by the Comptroller and Auditor General that An Garda Síochána spent €590,000 on hotel accommodation over three nights for members policing the match. The report maintained that the bill included €248,500 on accommodation that was never used.
[ Gardaí booked €248,500 worth of unused hotel beds for 2024 Uefa Europa League soccer clash Opens in new window ]
The comptroller’s report said that a month before the match the force had 727 rooms booked, with a potential occupancy of 1,454 members, but the Garda Representative Association had complained that shared rooms were unsatisfactory.
The report also found 13 Garda members were assigned two rooms in the same hotel, and 11 were assigned two hotel rooms in two different hotels.
Kelly is expected to say that reviews subsequently carried out showed the force had “strengthened the organisational framework governing their planning and command and introduced improved technology to support resource and duty planning”.
“Now ... where organisational booking of accommodation is required, this will operate on an exceptional basis and subject to senior-level approval, documented justification, oversight and controls,” he will say.
“We have also developed an event-costing template to strengthen financial planning for big events, while work continues to further strengthen our approach to debriefing and organisational learning.”
Kelly is also likely to tell the committee that Garda strength is approaching its highest level ever. Its fleet of vehicles is already the largest it has ever had.
“We have continued to increase Garda numbers during 2026 and I am looking forward to the next group of approximately 200 Garda trainees passing out later this month, which should see us have the highest number of gardaí in the history of the State. We are highly ambitious in this regard and want to meet (and exceed) the Government target of recruiting 5,000 gardaí by 2030,” he is to say.
The committee will be told that during 2025, 407 vehicles were allocated, bringing the Garda fleet to 3,650, including approximately 300 electric vehicles.
[ Rank and file gardaí ‘delighted’ with introduction of Tasers Opens in new window ]
There has been investment in new aeroplanes, helicopters, an armoured vehicle for emergency and armed response units, equipment for public order units and rigid hull inflatable boats for the water unit.
Separately, a briefing document submitted by the force to the committee maintains there was a 167 per cent increase in spending on the witness security programme last year to €1.2 million. The report says this is a demand-led programme and there was a rise in the number of requests for such services.
Receipts from fixed charges issued on foot of evidence from safety cameras increased by 30 per cent to €23.425 million last year. That was due to an increase in contracted hours of the service providers, together with additional cameras, the briefing document states.

title: Kathy Sheridan: Like Nikita Hand, the Cornell case Jane Doe is either uncommonly brave or a sado-masochist
description: Toxic masculinity is real and we should not be afraid to say so. What needs refreshing is how the term is used
content:
E ven on the most liberal reading, the circumstances in which seven Cornell University fraternity boys are alleged to have raped a woman student add up to a repugnant, contradictory nightmare of modern sexual mores. A 20-year-old woman’s date at a frat house with abundant supplies of ketamine allegedly quickly turned into a threesome with a second male student and ended with several more young men in the room.
It was when the embarrassed young woman – known as Jane Doe – was browsing an online college forum some weeks later that she first encountered posts describing that night’s events as gang rape.
The resulting social media firestorm is fuelled by a point of New York law, which states that voluntary intoxication is no bar to consent.
Somewhere in there is a central truth contained in a Snapchat message sent that night signalling an accused man’s view of the drugged-up woman still in their fraternity house: “free pussy upstairs”. A vulnerable, intoxicated woman’s body seen as a thing to grab, use, boast about and trade.
Like Nikita Hand at the beginning of her reckoning with Conor McGregor , this Jane Doe is either uncommonly brave or a stone-cold sadomasochist. A deluge of threatening, hate-filled misogyny is too mild a description of the response to the news that she had filed a lawsuit against the university, the frat house, seven current and former students and others.
Reports of the subsequent opening of a criminal investigation hit the headlines last week. The Dublin Rape Crisis Centre ( DRCC ) was at the same time in the process of releasing a survey showing that nearly half of our 18 to 24-year-old men believe that “a lot” of rape allegations are false. Nearly four in 10 of them believe a victim under the influence of alcohol or drugs is partially responsible for being raped – ie is capable of fully consenting to sex. And three in 10 of them wouldn’t believe a claim of rape if it hadn’t been reported to the gardaí.
The figures are staggering. It seems doubtful that any of these sceptical young men have even scanned the headlines in the court pages or been encouraged to absorb and discuss the details of a rape case or spoken to a woman relative who was assaulted.
How would they respond to the case of an Irish 14-year-old, already drunk and vulnerable, when she was given more alcohol by a 19-year-old man at a house party before he raped her – and then told her if she revealed what happened, he would “ruin her life”. Does she, too, bear partial responsibility for her own rape? The desperately familiar charges included two counts of non-fatal strangulation, as well as two counts of oral rape and two of sexual assault. Just as predictable was the rapist’s use of pornography, which, according to his defence counsel, had skewed and warped his view of what is normal and acceptable in a healthy sexual relationship.
[ Trial by everyone: Cornell case shows why Ireland’s strict court reporting rules matter Opens in new window ]
Imposing a six-year sentence, Judge Tony Hunt noted how young men were acting out what they were seeing in online pornography as well as being exposed to “a kind of toxic masculinity shown by influencers ...”
It was notable to hear an experienced judge feel bound to use that term “toxic masculinity”. It comes at a time when the preference is to avoid it at all costs for fear of driving young men into deeper radicalisation and rage through Andrew Tate and ilk.
In an RTÉ interview last week, Rachel Morrogh, chief executive of the DRCC, suggested there is a job for us all “to do much better in bringing these men along with us ... simply criticising them isn’t going to work”. We need to help them, she said, to understand the reality of sexual assault without making them feel blamed or abused.
[ How Cornell University punished seven men accused of sexual assault Opens in new window ]
But to some women, that sounds like a newly-minted version of the age-old understanding between the sexes: that women and girls must modify their behaviour and manage their feelings and language so they “bring men along” rather than merely criticising them. Morrogh didn’t say so, but the suggestion in many of these conversations is that we must avoid further enraging men – because it is girls and women inevitably who bear the brunt of that rage. But it’s not women’s fault that boys are bombarded with toxic influencers or violent pornography, or that some are afflicted with what masculinity scholar Michael Kimmel called “aggrieved entitlement”.
Toxic masculinity is real and, like the judge, we should not be slow to say so. What needs refreshing is how the term is used. It’s plainly ridiculous to say that masculinity is bad. What makes it toxic is the unhealthy societal expectations of it, the kind that require “real” men to suppress emotion, be dominant, to devalue the feminine and prove status through physical threats and sexual conquest. For prominent examples, see the US president or the spotty career of the so-called US secretary of war, Pete Hegseth, for whom testosterone screening for “warfighters” is a priority. Or get those boys to check out the numerous posts from a ridiculously whiny Andrew Tate, currently in a US federal jail awaiting extradition on dozens of charges for crimes against women.
Above all, tell them the revelations of this DRCC survey have real-life consequences for the girls and women they love. Tell them that recorded sexual offences have fallen sharply in the past year and discuss why that might be. The answer might surprise them.

title: Clayton McMillan not interested in a revenge motif ahead of Ulster clash
description: Munster head coach said last fixture in Belfast was ‘one of those games you remember in detail, but not for the right reasons’
content:
A positive result, a fine performance visible to the naked eye and a set of statistics that endorsed the hard work from the training ground to the match environment. What’s not to like about Munster’s victory over the Bulls last weekend? The result is a tonic to take to Belfast for Saturday’s first interprovincial of the URC season.
There’s generally an addendum that dilutes good news a little. On this occasion it comes in the form of injuries. Munster head coach Clayton McMillan touched on the legacy of a bruising encounter in the direct aftermath of the game. He updated the medical bulletin.
Wing Diarmuid Kilgallen (hamstring), prop Michael Milne (ankle) and secondrow Fineen Wycherley (shoulder) are all unavailable this weekend. The prognosis for Kilgallen is two to three weeks; Milne may be back next week, the same time frame that applies to Wycherley. Hooker Lee Barron has an ankle issue.
Number eight Brian Gleeson and flanker John Hodnett both passed head injury assessments on Saturday and are available for selection. Hooker Diarmuid Barron, flanker Jack O’Donoghue and centre Alex Nankivell are completing the return-to-play protocols. Academy hooker Max Clein (neck) is increasing his training exposure.
How that washes out in terms of the team for the weekend will be known on Thursday afternoon but, until then, there’s time to reflect on a job well done in beating the Bulls. Munster’s set piece was first class: scrum (100 per cent against their opponents’ 80), 94 per cent win-rate at lineout, which also eclipsed the South African visitors, and they conceded just five penalties over the 80 minutes.
That last metric is seriously impressive against physically big, abrasive opposition. Munster benefited from a good attitude and application, but also some excellent individual performances to supplement an accomplished team dynamic.
McMillan was asked about academy outhalf Charlie O’Shea and understandably pleaded for context and breathing room to allow the 20-year-old to grow into the role without having unreasonable expectations foisted on him.
The New Zealander explained: “I think what gives people confidence, what gives him confidence, what gives the coaches confidence, what gives the players around him confidence is what you do on a daily basis, your ability to prepare.
“And he’s a real student of the game for a young guy, and all preseason he’s probably made an impression through the way that he’s presented. He’s an impressive young man. We saw evidence of that on Saturday.
“But like everyone, like a team and individuals, you’re going to have good days and not so good ones, and it’s just important that we just temper our excitement around him and just allow him to just continue to be Charlie O’Shea.”
McMillan also paid tribute to the work of forwards coach Jimmy Duffy, who joined from Ulster during the summer. The scrum, which he acknowledged had been troublesome last season, went superbly and he singled out two tighthead props Kieran Brookes and Jack Aungier in that regard.
“The Bulls, you probably don’t come across too many bigger provincial sides in world rugby, and we accept that.
“They had a number of quality players that weren’t there, and so we probably got them at a good time, but that’s not to undermine the huge effort our forward pack put in, particularly at scrum time which is an area that has been problematic at times, certainly last year, and it’s an area Jimmy Duffy has put a huge amount of time into.
“There’s some of the obvious areas that we did well in. Our set piece functioned pretty well; [we had] some nice strike [plays]. I thought our defensive effort, the ability to really dig in, especially when we’d made a lot of changes and we’d lost a little bit of structure, both in attack and defence, was admirable. We want to just keep going on with those things.”
McMillan wasn’t interested in a revenge motif in advance of Saturday’s game. Munster lost 28-3 on their last trip to Belfast before exacting revenge a few months later with a 41-14 victory at Thomond Park. He hasn’t forgotten the sense of acute disappointment, but he isn’t clinging to it.
“It’s one of those games that you remember in detail, but not for the right reasons. We think we’ve put in decent performances [to date in this campaign] against teams that we believe will be there at the business end of the season.
[ Munster have been digging this hole for years as they slide into tortured mediocrity Opens in new window ]
“We have acquitted ourselves well. We’re a long way short of where we need to be. The challenge gets even greater, I believe, when you go up to Ulster and play a quality team.
“If we consume ourselves with what happened 12 months ago, then we might do ourselves a disservice. We’ve got that awareness, but we’ve got to put our attention into what we think we need to do, from a mindset point of view, from playing our game, and how we go about executing.”

title: ‘We don’t talk about it much’: Three years after October 7th attacks, Emily Hand is rebuilding her childhood
description: Three years on from the October 7th attacks, Dún Laoghaire-born Thomas Hand says his daughter Emily (11) has rebuilt a normal childhood after 50 days in captivity in Gaza
content:
On October 7th, 2023, Thomas Hand’s daughter was abducted from Kibbutz Be’eri, close to the Gaza border, where 102 people were killed. She was held in Gaza for 50 days before being released as part of a truce deal.
She’s doing amazing to be honest. Unbelievable. Just like a normal, everyday kid. Just like all her friends.
No, we don’t really talk about it. We put it in the past and left it there. It’s all around us all the time anyway so we don’t dwell on it.
No. I don’t have it on the television. She doesn’t need to be submersed in that. She’s 11 years old. She’s just doing girlie things.
No, there’s no more triggers. The only thing I might say is that she has nightmares, but that’s normal for a kid that age. She sleeps in her own bed now pretty much every night.
I’m okay. I’m obviously not the same person I was before October 7th. I’m more introverted. I don’t go out much. I don’t meet many of my old friends. It’s pretty sad really but I’m comfortable with it. I’m not depressed or anything, it’s just a different way of living now.
Yes. After October 7th everything else is not so important. I find it very hard to do small talk and I don’t particularly want to talk about October 7th forever.
Most of the kibbutz is still here on Kibbutz Hatzerim. They’ve been very good to us. We’ve been waiting until the demolition of the neighbourhoods destroyed in Be’eri is completed and the new neighbourhoods are built. We are waiting for all-clear and by the middle of next year we will hopefully be going back.
Yeah, she can’t wait. This is her bat mitzvah year and her biggest dream is to celebrate her bat mitzvah in Be’eri. It’s a very, very special occasion.
Absolutely, it will be back to normality instead of living like refugees. But it will always be in the back our heads that it could happen again one day.
[ Uefa to investigate alleged spitting incident at half-time in Ireland v Israel Opens in new window ]
It’s a shame but politics should not enter into sports, music and the arts. It’s separate.
Not in this climate, no. A big problem is that politicians are vying for the Muslim vote, in Britain and New York.
Not yet, but it will be, though. Believe me.
Not in the near future, but I’m sure we will. I’ve got family over there and it’s always nice to visit.
[ ‘It’s off the charts’: Satellite images show how three years of war have devastated Gaza Opens in new window ]
In the 2014 Gaza war (between Israel and Hamas), the eight-, nine- and 10-year-old kids then became the Hamas fighters, the Nukhba force, and they are the ones who attacked us. In another five or 10 years the kids who feel the retaliation of Israel now will be the next wave.
Of course. If anyone can give me a solution, I will be very happy. But it will only ever be managed, there will never be peace. If we, God forbid, ever gave them a state of their own we’re finished. It won’t be very long after that. They had their chance with Gaza. I was for it – land for peace. It worked with Egypt and it could have worked with these people ... In Jordan they tried to overthrow the royal family. Why do you think the Arab countries don’t accept any Palestinian refugees any more? They’re not stupid. They’ve learned their lesson. But apparently the West hasn’t.

title: Inward migration is actually good for Ireland
description: We could not function without economic migrants
content:
Sir, – In light of the recent, and occasionally less than positive, reaction of some in Ireland to the topic of inward migration , it might be useful to look at the opposite side of the coin.
Inward migration is actually a positive good for Ireland, greatly expanding our employed workforce, improving the ratio of employed people to dependent people and enabling the provision of vital services, especially in the areas of care, health and technology, which we could not otherwise sustain.
Ireland’s “new economy” simply could not adequately function without ongoing inward economic migration.
Very many of us have had the pleasant experience of interacting with nursing home care staff, hospitality workers, medical clinical staff, social care workers, therapists, taxi drivers, bus drivers, retail workers, library staff, catering staff and university staff, each from abroad, and all now part of our modern and diverse Ireland. Our experience of that interaction has been invariably helpful and advantageous.
Economists and others are able to make a strongly supportive economic and social case for inward economic migration into Ireland, and even to quantify the material advantages that accrue to all of us from the positive phenomenon of controlled inward migration. There are also non-quantifiable benefits, possibly even more valuable. – Yours, etc,
We could not function without economic migrants

title: Look inside: Extended Sandymount home a riot of colour and whimsy
description: Tritonville Road period terrace with garden studio features spacious kitchen and main bedroom suite
content:
Renovating number 103 Tritonville Road in Sandymount was not the first such project for its custodians, who modernised their Victorian apartment in London before moving to the south Dublin seaside suburb.
They bought the four-bedroom redbrick terrace in 2020 – attracted by its period features, generous proportions and the flow of light through the home – and set about extending it to create a spacious open-plan kitchen-diningroom on the ground floor and a larger principal bedroom above it. As part of the works, they installed underfloor heating, so there is not a radiator in sight, and added built-in storage and cabinetry throughout.
Every room in this welcoming home is a riot of colour, pattern and texture. “I just love colour,” the owner says. “The winter nights are long, and I just want our home to feel cosy with pattern and warmth.”
It’s impossible not to get a dopamine hit from being surrounded by the considered colour palette of greens and blues, with pops of pinks and oranges, in this home. I can only imagine how delighted friends of the owners’ daughter must be when they’re invited to play at the house of whimsy.
The interior design of the home was spearheaded by one of the owners, who says her husband gave her free rein, asking only that the front door be painted green. The front door also has a stained-glass fanlight and surrounds, and opens to an airy hallway with high ceilings.
[ Strikingly modern Sandymount four-bed Opens in new window ]
Two linked reception rooms lie to the front of the ground floor. The livingroom, painted Oval Room Blue (by Farrow & Ball whose hues are used throughout the home), was designed around the blue and white bespoke blinds that the owners brought from their London home. They added built-in shelving, lined with fan-print wallpaper, and cupboards on either side of the tile-framed cast-iron fireplace.
Passing a flat arch of blue and white stripes, the room flows into “the pink room” that the family use as a playroom. Here the fireplace has been tiled in large blue and white patterned tiles, and a TV cover has been fashioned out of wood with framed prints covering the screen.
A step leads down to the spacious kitchen-diningroom with units painted in rich Studio Green. The kitchen is configured in an L-shape to allow you to face the garden and dining area while cooking; its also has a breakfast bar. Everything is accommodated for within the extensive built-in joinery, including a desk, a pantry for small appliances and a wine rack.
A round dining table for six is placed in the middle of the remaining space, with a fully glazed rear wall centred by French doors leading out to the patio. A comfy sofa and armchair provide further seating on either side of the dining table.
In the garden, steps from the patio lead up to a lawn framed by a variety of potted plants, and a garden room to the rear that is used as a guest bedroom with a bathroom. The bedroom is wallpapered in a trailing wisteria design.
[ How to create a garden room of your own: ‘It’s somewhere to go without going anywhere’ Opens in new window ]
Back in the house, a lovely bathroom with blue floral wallpaper completes the ground floor. It was designed with their then young children in mind, and it was handy to be able to go straight from dinner to bath time when they were small, the owner says.
Upstairs the extended main bedroom sits on the first-floor return, where large windows, mirroring the patio doors downstairs, open completely to allow the outside in. The room features wall panelling and a walk-in wardrobe of built-in storage, including drawers and hanging space, all drenched in restful Breakfastroom Green. It connects to a luxurious en suite shower room.
Two further double bedrooms and a single room with built-in wardrobes occupy the first floor, along with a loo.
The owners have loved how friendly the neighbourhood is, and being so close to the village and the sea. Now moving for more space as their children get older, they are placing this B-rated 175sq m (1,884sq ft) home on the market with Sherry Fitzgerald, seeking €1.85 million.

title: London is a city where Irishness gets shouted out, rather than smoothed over
description: The nagging fear of Irish in London: If you don’t pay attention, you might end up being assimilated
content:
I keep thinking about one gig I went to where you would have had no clue you were in England once the doors shut. An Irish rapper was performing at a venue decked out in Irish tricolours and Palestinian flags. Half the accents around me were Irish.
At one point, the rapper asked the crowd for a Union Jack flag on which to urinate, to raucous applause. I found myself wondering how comfortable an English person would have felt in that room, and then amazed I could be asking myself such a question in the middle of England’s capital city.
I left thinking how much what it means to be Irish in London right now has changed.
It’s not long since being Irish in Britain was unfashionable; we were dismissed as provincial or backward, or far worse. In some parts, we still are.
I felt a version of that studying at Oxford, where being Irish was the nail that stuck out and risked getting hammered down – if you were ever to divulge your true feelings about, say, Margaret Thatcher.
London has turned out to be the opposite: a city where Irishness gets shouted out, rather than smoothed over.
No single image captures the shift better than a certain product does – Guinness. The drink spent decades as shorthand for a certain kind of Irish cliche: the flat-capped labourer, the rugger crowd, the pensioner at the end of the bar.
[ Seán Burke, Irish comedian in London: ‘My accent goes a long way when I’m on stage’ Opens in new window ]
I used to make non-Irish people taste it when I was a teenager, and they would screw up their faces, asking how anyone could drink that. But things have changed. Northern Irish designer Jonathan Anderson put Guinness in pearls on a sweatshirt in 2024, and Instagram influencers have made a trend out of “splitting the G”.
Now those same people swallow Guinness with a smile and tell me how smooth stout is. It is the in-drink for anyone in London chasing a trend.
Guinness is a small example of a larger inversion, however. Irish culture is genuinely in fashion. In part, the reputation of the Irish has been earned through their solidarity with Palestinians and other oppressed peoples.
As a culture journalist in London, I have heard this shift in almost every interview I have done with Irish acts, from Sprints to Gurriers to Maverick Sabre and Curtisy. The conversation always finds its way back to Irishness, and their confidence in their own identity.
But in London, this confidence has an edge. I am not sure it is purely about pride. Joy Crookes, who is south London-born to an Irish father and a Bangladeshi mother, told me how her father had given her no choice but to learn trad music and Irish dancing. Irish music and culture was there to counteract erasure, she said.
That word, erasure, is key. The particular anxiety of being Irish in London is the proximity of British identity. London is an international city, a melting pot, but the British capital is still the British capital.
For Irish people, there might be a nagging fear that if you are not paying attention, you might be assimilated; mistaken for British, or worse, not minding whether you are. In London, Irish people become unlikely friends with other Irish, partly because they need each other to remember who they are.
People are reaching for Irish when they live in a city where nobody speaks it. This suggests something else: that the act of learning it is what matters
At that same rapper’s gig, the crowd seemed to sing his bars back to him a little louder than was strictly necessary, just to show they were in the know.
And then there is the Irish language, with waiting lists and sell-outs of courses in Irish in London. I attended a beginners’ session run by the Irish language collective Croí na Gaeilge, which filled the basement of a pub with people in their 20s. Many were prompted to learn by Kneecap and the renewed coolness of the tongue.
You might think that movement shows how much Irish people value their own language. But people are reaching for Irish when they live in a city where nobody speaks it. This suggests something else: that the act of learning it is what matters. It is a way to set yourself apart in a city that would not otherwise notice you blending in.
Some of what looks like Irish pride is, if you look at it carefully, an attempt to drown out insecurity. Shouting out how proud you are is a loud insistence on not being at home in a city that is very good at making everyone, eventually, feel at home.
Hugo Harvey is a writer and presenter from Cork who has lived across France and the UK.

title: A pedestrian sees red
description: Why do we have to keep stopping, pressing buttons and waiting while motor traffic just keeps moving?
content:
Sir, – At some junctions, pedestrians must ask twice to cross once.
Press the button, wait for the green man, cross to a traffic island – then press another button and wait again, sometimes through a full light cycle, to cross the rest of the way. Meanwhile, cars, trucks and bicycles cross the entire junction on a single green light.
One journey becomes two permissions, with pedestrians repeatedly stopping, asking and waiting while motor traffic keeps moving.
Are pedestrians an afterthought – or second-class road users?
If we genuinely want people to walk rather than drive, we should stop putting obstacles in their way. – Yours, etc,

title: Zimbabwean workers awarded €30k each after arriving in Ireland to find they had no jobs
description: Workplace Relations Commission awarded maximum amount available citing ‘particularly egregious’ treatment
content:
Awards of more than €30,000 each to two Zimbabwean healthcare workers who travelled to Ireland believing they would have jobs, only to find the work did not materialise, have been upheld by the Labour Court .
Tatenda Ncube and Brenda Mubaiwa had both been offered work by Unity Healthcare, which had a contract with Tusla to provide emergency care to vulnerable children, and were told they would be working at a centre in Virginia, Co Cavan .
The pair were among nine Zimbabwean workers to take cases to the Workplace Relations Commission ( WRC ), saying they were left without work or money to pay basic bills by the company. They said it only told them almost a year after they arrived that its contract had been cancelled and there would be no work.
The workers said they had been unable to take up alternative employment because of delays by Unity in issuing them with the letters they required under permit regulations to allow them to work for another employer.
The WRC awarded the nine workers a total of €273,780 (€30,420 each), twice the wages they said they were owed for the six-month period they were permitted to claim for. It was the maximum amount it was entitled to order Unity to pay, having described the treatment of the workers as “particularly egregious”.
In decisions just published relating to the first three appeals taken by the company, one of the awards, made to Silibaziso Nondo, was overturned as she had managed to take up a role with another company a month before the period covered by her case. The court found this severed the employment relationship with Unity and meant it had no jurisdiction to consider her claim.
In the cases of Ncube and Mubaiwa, however, it found the company’s appeals had been filed one day after the 42-day limit, and so they were out of time.
One of the company’s directors, Bruce Magama, told the court he had believed a firm of solicitors was dealing with the lodgement of the appeals but had been informed two days before the deadline it would not be doing so.
He then struggled, and ultimately failed, to complete the process himself in the two days remaining. He argued that these circumstances met the criteria of “exceptional circumstances” required by the court to grant an extension.
In its decision, signed by Labour Court deputy chair Niamh McGowan, the court said “no valid explanation to properly account for the delay has been furnished that offers an excuse or explains the delay in lodging an appeal to the Labour Court outside the statutory time limit”.
“Insofar as excuses or reasons have been proffered, they do not, on any definition, amount to exceptional circumstances. In all the circumstances, the Court is of the view that a justifiable basis upon which an extension of time could be granted has not been put forward in this case.”
During the original cases, the company had argued it tried to stop the workers travelling when it realised there would be no work for them.
The workers denied this and told the court they had been required to contribute towards the cost of permits and accommodation in advance and then left without any income, causing them considerable hardship. One worker said there had been periods when she had been left “wondering where you’re going to get your next meal”.
Decisions in the other six cases, which were heard on later dates, have yet to be published. At the time of the WRC decisions, Pretty Ndawo of the Migrant Rights Centre Ireland, which represented the workers along with DJM Legal, called for better protections for workers coming to Ireland under the permit system.

title: DAA made €1.73m per week from car parks in 2025
description: Airport operator has more than 27,000 car park spaces in Dublin and Cork
content:
Airport operator DAA made €90 million in revenues last year from its car parks in Dublin and Cork , according to new disclosures in a document for its debt investors.
It marked a 3.4 per cent increase on 2024 and equated to an average of €1.73 million a week. It meant that its 27,049 short- and long-term public car parks in the two airports generated an average of close to €3,330 in 2025.
The car parking revenues equated to almost 8 per cent of the group’s total turnover of €1.18 billion, according to the new investor document, known as a prospectus, which gives some additional disclosures to its 2025 annual report published earlier this year.
The prospectus also said that DAA last year recorded €164 million of revenues from “non-retail” concessions such as the provision of car hire and foreign exchange facilities, as well as airport lounge activities, security fast track, advertising activities and airport-campus property rental activities at Dublin and Cork airports. That was up 7.8 per cent on the year.
DAA’s travel-retail business ARI, which has direct and indirect interests in airport retailing concessions, businesses, joint ventures and management contracts in Europe, the Middle East, Canada, US and Barbados, posted consolidated turnover of €235 million last year, up 8.2 per cent year-on-year.
ARI includes a 20 per cent shareholding in Düsseldorf Airport in Germany and 11 per cent of Larnaca and Paphos airports in Cyprus. The majority of ARI’s retail activities are subject to arrangements that are fixed period contracts that include guaranteed minimum concession fees or concession arrangements payable by subsidiary undertakings, joint ventures and other entities within ARI.
DAA International, which manages and operates King Abdulaziz International Airport and the Red Sea International Airport in Saudi Arabia and also provides consultancy and training services to airports in countries such as the Philippines, Vietnam, Australia and Canada, reported €47 million of revenues last year.
The Irish Aviation Authority (IAA) proposed in July cutting charges levied by Dublin Airport on airlines to €8.58 per passenger next year, from €10.39 currently, despite a request from State company DAA to be allowed to increase charges to fund expanded facilities.
[ Air travel in Ireland is ‘growing faster than expected’ Opens in new window ]
Airlines have cut flights at Dublin Airport in response to surging fuel prices sparked by the US-Iran conflict, an escalation of the Ukraine war and economic uncertainty, DAA told the aviation authority in a formal response to the proposed cut in charges.
DAA wants to increase charges to a maximum of €13 a head up to 2031 to pay for a €5.6 billion expansion that will allow it to handle 10 million more passengers a year.
However, the IAA, which sets the airport’s charges, argued that as Dublin could grow to 44.5 million annual passengers from about 36 million, there will be more people to share the cost of the expansion, allowing DAA to reduce what it charges airlines for each individual.

title: How Israel lost the world’s support after October 7th
description: Global Briefing: Three years after Hamas’s attack, the war in Gaza and mounting international outrage have made Israel more isolated and possibly less secure
content:
The Hamas attacks three years ago today left 1,200 people dead and shook Israelis ’ sense of security within their borders. But its government’s actions since then have made Israel more isolated and possibly less secure.
When Binyamin Netanyahu spoke at a ceremony in Jerusalem’s Mount Herzl military cemetery this week to mark the third anniversary of the October 7th, 2023 attacks, he was interrupted by the father of one of those who died.
“It’s a disgrace that you didn’t protect those murdered on October 7th,” shouted Yaakov Godo, whose son Tom died in the attacks. “The blood of my son and of another 1,200 people murdered in a single day is on his hands and on his head.”
The official event at Mount Herzl on Monday was the first of a succession of commemorations this week of the attacks led by Hamas that saw the greatest number of Jews killed in a single day since the Holocaust: 251 people, among them women, children and old people, were abducted that day and taken into Gaza, where many were subjected to abuse and 83 died.
Victims’ families have long called for an official commission of inquiry into how the attacks were possible, the failure of intelligence and what warnings the government received. Netanyahu has refused to open such an inquiry, prompting a number of former hostages to stand as candidates in this month’s general election.
Israel laments that the world has forgotten the atrocities committed at the Nova music festival, in kibbutzim and other communities near the Gaza border. A United Nations Independent international commission of inquiry found reasonable evidence to conclude that Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups involved in the attacks committed war crimes, including attacks against civilians, murder, torture and cruel treatment, and hostage-taking.
But the victims of October 7th may not have been forgotten so much as they have been submerged beneath the images from Gaza afterwards, when Israel killed more than 70,000 people, including 20,000 children. The Israeli campaign displaced almost all of Gaza’s 2.1 million people from their homes, laid waste to much of the territory including its hospitals, leaving the Strip with the highest proportion of child amputees in the world.
In the days after October 7th, Israel came under missile attack from Hizbullah in Lebanon, from militias based in Iraq and Syria and backed by Iran, and from the Houthi rebels in Yemen. But Israel soon went on the offensive, not just in Gaza but in Lebanon, Syria and Iran, assassinating many of the leading figures in Hamas and Hizbullah.
By 2025, Israel had killed Hamas’s political leader Ismail Haniyeh and prominent military leader Yahya Sinwar along with other senior figures including Saleh al-Arouri and Mohammed Deif. Hassan Nasrallah, who had led Hizbullah for more than 30 years, was assassinated in September 2024 after Israel had already killed eight senior military figures in the organisation.
Israeli forces also struck Houthi targets in Yemen and succeeded in degrading the three main elements in the so-called axis of resistance. Three years on, Hamas and Hizbullah are much diminished but they survive, while the Houthis are making advances in their war against Yemen’s official government.
The October 7th attacks undermined Israelis’ sense of security within their own borders and the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran were meant to strengthen the country’s security. But after the slaughter of the Palestinians and two wars against Iran, Israel remains vulnerable to attack, as last week attempted hijacking of a Flydubai aircraft demonstrated.
Perhaps the most important long-term threat to Israel’s security is its increasing isolation and the almost universal revulsion against its actions in Gaza, even among its traditional allies. Public opinion in the United States has moved sharply against Israel and condemnation of its war in Gaza has become a litmus test for Democratic candidates throughout the US.
Donald Trump remains supportive of Israel but his vice-president, JD Vance, is more sceptical, as is much of the conservative base, which tends towards foreign policy isolationism. Three years after much of the world shared Israel’s shock and sorrow at the October 7th attacks, Netanyahu’s actions have drained the well of global sympathy, even though the victims deserve it as much as ever.
