title: Council urges Johnny Ronan lobbyist Coveney to honour Glass Bottle site affordable housing plan
description: No affordable purchase homes secured with council negotiating for alternative cost-rental scheme
content:
Rental apartments, instead of homes for sale, can be used to fulfil a 2017 commitment to provide “affordable housing” on the former Irish Glass Bottle site in Ringsend, according to legal advice obtained by Dublin City Council .
A consortium fronted by developer Johnny Ronan is building up to 3,800 apartments on the site, once a totem of the property crash. Affordable housing is required as part of the site’s zoning.
However, the council has been unable to reach agreement with the developer for the provision of any affordable-purchase housing and is negotiating to secure some homes for a cost-rental scheme.
Councillors and residents are urging former tánaiste and housing minister Simon Coveney to appeal to Ronan to provide affordable homes for sale, after it emerged he now lobbies for the developer .
A 2017 affordable-housing deal between the Department of Housing – led at the time by Coveney – the council and the National Asset Management Agency (Nama) was instrumental in securing the consent of city councillors to designate the site a “fast-track” strategic development zone (SDZ). The deal was contingent on 25 per cent – more than 900 apartments – being used for social and affordable housing.
Planning laws at the time required 10 per cent of the homes be used for social housing. Councillors, and locals, understood the remaining 15 per cent would be used for an affordable-purchase scheme, where homes would be offered for sale at a State-subsidised discount.
Cost-rental schemes, where the State subsidises below market rents, had yet to be established.
Although 176 social apartments have recently been completed, the council has not secured agreement with Ronan, who has controlled the site for almost six years, on the provision of any affordable-purchase homes.
It is understood the potential costs have stymied talks. Two years ago, in advance of construction, it was indicated apartments could cost €495,000 for a one-bed unit and €675,000 for a two-bed.
The council executive has secured legal advice that cost-rental housing could be used to fulfil the “affordable” element, as an alternative to the delivery of housing for sale.
Labour councillor Dermot Lacey said this was not what the councillors and community understood they were signing up to.
“The affordable element was always understood to be affordable purchase, the concept of cost-rental didn’t exist at the time. We always saw the affordable housing as being housing local people could afford to buy. Genuinely, I had no doubt about that,” Lacey said.
The legal advice, seen by The Irish Times, states: “The composition of the 15% social/affordable could be met by providing cost rental units as defined in the Affordable Housing Act 2021”.
The council was “not precluded from considering cost rental as an option for delivery of affordable housing under the SDZ by virtue of the fact that the cost rental statutory provisions were not in place at the time”.
This interpretation does not reflect what councillors agreed to, Lacey said. “Morally, politically and policy-wise, we entered into an agreement, and I would like to think Mr Coveney would say to Johnny Ronan and company, ‘this is what I agreed to, and I think we should honour it’.”
Green Party councillor Hazel Chu agrees. “I get what the council is trying for on this one, but this is retrospectively rewriting what we had previously agreed. I would urge Mr Coveney to remember the commitments he made.”
Independent councillor Mannix Flynn said a price should have been fixed for the affordable apartments, with an agreed adjustment for inflation, when the Ronan consortium was selected as the preferred bidder for the site in 2020.
“All we did was negotiate a certain percentage of housing, we didn’t see the deal between the department, the council and Johnny Ronan. Can the state afford to buy those affordable units at the cost that Johnny Ronan wants to sell them?”
Patsy Doolin, chairwoman of the Irish Glass Bottle Housing Action Group, said cost-rental is not what the community was promised. “People want to be able to buy them and own them,” Doolin said.
She was excited to hear the former minister was working with the developers. “I’d love to just talk to him, have a cup of coffee with him and ask him to help us,” she said.
Lobbying returns show Coveney and Ronan met Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris in August for talks “concerning the development of Bremore Port and related ports/infrastructure policy”.
Coveney did not respond to queries in relation to the Ringsend site over the last week. The Glass Bottle consortium, which includes the Ronan Group, Lioncor and Oaktree Capital, declined to comment.
The council is negotiating with the developers to use a block of 273 apartments for cost-rental housing. “Affordable purchase may be examined in future phases,” it said.
The Irish Glass Bottle Company closed in 2002. The site was bought in 2006 for €412 million by a consortium involving developer Bernard McNamara and the Dublin docklands Development Authority. Nama bought the debt associated with the site from the now defunct Anglo Irish Bank after the property crash.
The council in 2019 entered into negotiations with Nama for affordable homes and said it would be willing to buy plots of land from the State agency. However, Nama instead offered the site to the market, with the Ronan-led consortium confirmed as the preferred bidder in December 2020.

title: Private-sector workers could see ‘small’ benefit from public sector wage increase
description: Work Q&A: Minimum wage rises can also have ‘modest’ effect on low-income workers
content:
With thousands of public and civil servants taking part in industrial action seeking higher pay to address inflation, some private sector workers could benefit if a favourable deal is reached.
The last public sector pay deal expired at the end of June, and unions say a new arrangement should address what they claim is a drop in real earnings of “at least” 5 per cent since 2020.
But what effect, if any, could a pay increase have on those working in the private sector?
Ireland’s private sector is the “leader” over the long term when it comes to setting wages. This means the public sector often adjusts to match them, according to Paul Redmond, an associate research professor with the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI).
However, this does not mean “you can’t have spillovers in the other direction”, he says.
“What we think is that over the longer run, it’s the private sector really that leads the way and dictates what the wage level is generally, but in a near-term or short-term basis, if something happens to public sector wages, there can still be adjustments to the private sector.”
Redmond, who has a particular interest in labour economics, says the private sector can adjust when public sector wages increase to remain competitive. Without adjusting or matching public wages, it can be difficult to attract or retain staff in certain occupations or industries, he says.
However, the effect is not seen across the entire private sector, with Redmond saying international research shows roles more likely to be affected are those that “directly compete” with the public sector, such as health.
Adjustments in the private sector can “happen quite quickly”, he says, though the spillover effects are “quite small”.
“For example, if you have a 1 per cent increase in public sector wages, the potential spillovers to the private sector are only a fraction of that. It’s not a one-to-one, it’s much, much lower,” he says.
Similarly, Redmond says research shows increases to the minimum wage can lead to spillovers.
However, the overall effect is “quite modest” and limited to those typically earning just above the minimum wage.
“If someone is earning just above the minimum wage, you can see spillovers that kind of trickle out to low-paid workers,” he says.
Although there can be concerns that increases to the minimum wage can lead to general price inflation, a study published by the ERSI last month found no impact on prices following seven of the eight increases implemented from 2016 to 2025.
The study found the overall effect on inflation by minimum wage increases has been “pretty much negligible”, Redmond says.
“There was one minimum wage increase in 2024 that was the largest minimum wage increase to date. It was 12.4 per cent, so it was a big one,” Redmond says.
“What we found for that is that there was some effect on a small category of goods that are produced using a large number of minimum-wage employees, so things like takeaway coffee, takeaway sandwiches and meals, and meals in restaurants.”

title: Seán Moncrieff: This season is not for thinking, it’s just one continuous, mindless Go
description: Working to survive leaves little or no room to do or think about anything else
content:
T here are certain periods of the year when it feels as if there is a bit more space in our lives and in our brains. You can have a bit of a think: consider where you are in life and what, if any, changes you might want to make, minor or drastic. You may conclude that things are pretty much where you want them to be, and because you have this extra head space, you have the time to appreciate it. It’s like a seasonal form of mindfulness, but without having to do a course or buy a self-help book.
But it’s not this season. Thinking is more a summer pastime. Now it’s just one continuous, mindless “Go”.
Some people contend that autumn is more like the new year. A new start. Back to work and school and college. But it can also be a shocking reminder of how much activity you were stuffing into each minute before the holidays started.
For instance: Daughter Number Four has a few extracurriculars. She has swimming, which is supposed to be on a Friday, but because her usual swimming pool is broken, we have to schlep out to the National Aquatic Centre on Saturdays and Sundays. After the Saturday session, she has to get dried, changed and eat lunch in the car to arrive just in time for the two-hour Jazz Hands classes. (We’re not forcing her to do any of this. She loves it.)
You’re right: I’ve little to be complaining about. It’s relatively easy to get back into the old/new routine. But because it is this time of the year, there’s also an inordinate amount of planning. Halloween is just over a fortnight away, and for some weeks now there’s been negotiations over, and preparations for, what we are doing for Christmas .
Similar talks about talks are going on in relation to next year’s summer holidays, and after that there will be a big family wedding. This is on top of all the usual work and life stuff, so this time of the year can feel like a blur: what’s next, what’s next. (And yes: most of the mental burden for these kinds of things tends to fall on women.)
It’s still the case that people will ask, as a conversation opener: “Are you busy?” The expectation is that the other person will confirm this is the case, and then list all the things they are up to as if busyness is an intrinsically good thing. The same applies to: “Any plans for the weekend?” You have to be organising a parachute jump or applying the finishing touches to the opera you’re composing. To answer truthfully, to admit that you’ll do the big shop, ferry the kids around to all their activities, tackle a mountain of laundry and then watch some crap on Netflix seems to be regarded as an unacceptable reply; even a form of rudeness.
[ Our daughter has barely started fifth class and the secondary school chat has intensified Opens in new window ]
Ireland – on paper, anyway – has never been so prosperous. Yet so few of us seem to experience that prosperity. Some 12.6 per cent of our population live with the constant risk of poverty – many of them the working poor. But outside of that is a huge swathe in the middle – that archetypal Garda married to a teacher – who notice when the cost of groceries tick upwards; who are perhaps one or two wage slips away from disaster.
And with that comes time poverty. Working to survive leaves little or no room to do anything else, to think about anything else. It’s not totally grim, of course. There’s the odd night out or meet-up with friends – events that can be posted on Instagram. But Instagram accounts rarely depict the long periods of trudge in between: the sitting in traffic jams while minutes of our existence tick away; the unsettling suspicion that our lives are not entirely our own.

title: French fund seeks €19.7m for fully-let trio of investments in Dublin and Galway
description: Three-point portfolio generates €1.34m in annual rental income from range of tenants, including Eason, Fresh and Brown Bag Films
content:
Having paid about €17.5 million across separate transactions in 2019 to secure ownership of three mixed-use investment properties in Galway city centre, Churchtown, Dublin 14 , and Smithfield, Dublin 7 , French fund MNK Partners has instructed agent Colliers to find a buyer for the portfolio in one or more lots. The assets, which are fully let and generating annual rental income of approximately €1.34 million, are being offered to the market at a combined guide price of €19.7 million.
The details of the three-point portfolio are as follows:
Located on Galway’s main pedestrianised retail street, 33 Shop Street comprises a landmark three-storey retail building extending to 1,043sq m (11,226sq ft). The property is fully let to Eason Ireland and is producing a passing rent of €551,250 a year.
The investment offers a weighted average unexpired lease term (WAULT) of approximately 8.4 years to break and 18.4 years to expiry, with open-market rent reviews every five years. The property is guiding €7.5 million, reflecting a net initial yield of 6.68 per cent.
Located on the site of the former Braemor Rooms and McGowan’s pub in Churchtown, this mixed-use investment extends to 1,139sq m (12,260sq ft) and is occupied by Centric Health, Glorious Flowers and a restaurant unit which is scheduled to open shortly. The property is generating €376,087 in annual rental income and has a WAULT of 9.8 years to break and 13.65 years to expiry. The income profile combines CPI-linked and open-market rent review provisions across the tenancy mix. The guide price is €6 million, reflecting a net initial yield of 5.7 per cent.
Block F at Smithfield Square comprises 1,504sq m (16,191sq ft) of retail and office accommodation within the established Smithfield Market development. The property is fully let to Fresh and Brown Bag Films and is producing passing rental income of €417,243 a year. The investment benefits from a WAULT of 12.4 years and incorporates both CPI-linked and open market rent review provisions. The property is guiding €6.2 million, which equates to a net initial yield of 6.12 per cent.
Michele McGarry, who is handling the sale of the portfolio on behalf of Colliers, says: “This offering brings three well-located investment opportunities to the market across Galway and Dublin, underpinned by established occupiers and long-term income profiles. The assets provide exposure to a diverse range of sectors including retail, healthcare and office.
“The choice of acquiring the properties individually or as a portfolio should appeal to a broad range of domestic and international investors.”

title: Middle Eastern investor seeks €15.4m for Kerry retail park
description: Current owner acquired Killarney scheme for about €10.5m in 2024
content:
Having paid about €10.5 million in 2024 for Killarney’s Deerpark Retail Park as part of a wider €40 million deal in which it also secured ownership of Donegal’s Letterkenny Retail Park, Bahrain-headquartered Investcorp has instructed agent Cushman & Wakefield to offer the Kerry scheme to the market. The retail park is guiding at a price of €15.4 million (exclusive of VAT), reflecting a net initial yield of 7.83 per cent assuming standard purchaser’s costs of 9.96 per cent.
Developed in 2006, Deerpark Retail Park occupies a high-profile location 1.3km west of Killarney town centre. The scheme extends to a total area of 10,482sq m (112,835sq ft) and is distributed across 13 units with a mix of part-open/ part bulky-use planning permission. The units range in size from 94.6sq m (1,018sq ft) to 1,994.9sq m (21,473sq ft), and comprise a mix of retail warehouse stores along with a complementary neighbourhood centre and 248 car-parking spaces.
The retail warehouse portion of the scheme is occupied by a mix of Irish and international retailers, including Marks & Spencer, Boots, DID Electrical, Maxi Zoo and Mountain Warehouse, while the neighbourhood centre is home to well-known names such as Costa Coffee, Boots, Card Factory and Salon B.
[ ESRI seeks €10.5m for Dublin HQ and begins search for office to suit hybrid-working policy Opens in new window ]
The first floor of the neighbourhood centre is fully let to Peak Performance Academy, providing additional rental income. The retail park also has a lease agreement with Tesla, which is set to operate eight electric-vehicle charging bays within the car park. Deerpark Retail Park is generating overall rental income of €1,326,458 a year and has a weighted average unexpired lease term of 4.45 years to break options and 6.46 years to expiry. The park is 100 per cent occupied.
Quite apart from its own retail offering, the retail park also provides its customers with direct road access to the adjacent Tesco Extra, Tesco petrol filling station, JYSK and Aldi, all of which are held in separate ownership and not included in this sale.
Peter Love of Cushman & Wakefield says: “Deerpark Retail Park offers investors the opportunity to acquire a fully occupied retail park in one of Ireland’s most resilient and sought-after sectors [retail warehousing] ... the scheme is firmly established as one of Killarney’s premier retail destinations. The asset also offers investors an attractive income profile, supported by opportunities for future rental growth and additional income generation.”

title: Aviva seeks operator for new luxury hotel on Dublin’s Clarendon Street
description: Proposed 184-bedroom hotel will have frontage on to Clarendon Street and South William Street
content:
Aviva Life & Pensions Ireland is seeking an experienced hotel operator to lease a new, luxury hotel it intends to develop near Grafton Street in Dublin’s south city centre. The hotel, which will have frontage on to Clarendon Street (number 38-44) and South William Street (number 52-55) will comprise a seven-storey-over-basement 184-bedroom along with a restaurant, bar and commercial space, subject to planning permission. The proposed scheme will involve the refurbishment of four Georgian buildings on South William Street which will comprise commercial use at ground floor and basement level (364sq m) and 10 apartment suites on the upper floors, extending to a total area of 864sq m.
The subject site was acquired in 2016 by Aviva’s predecessor, Friends First, as part of its wider €30 million purchase of nine retail and office properties within the Madrid Portfolio, which was assembled by developer Bernard McNamara at the tail end of the Celtic Tiger era to facilitate the development of an upmarket shopping enclave between Clarendon Street and South William Street.
Aviva’s proposed hotel will occupy a prime location within a short walk of Grafton Street and St Stephen’s Green, and numerous of the capital’s visitor attractions including Trinity College, Christ Church Cathedral, The Guinness Storehouse, The National Gallery of Ireland and the National Museum.
The area is well connected by public transport and is near the Luas green line stop at St Stephen’s Green and numerous Dublin Bus routes. The planned MetroLink will improve the proposed hotel’s accessibility in years to come, with the planned St Stephen’s Green station increasing connectivity to Dublin Airport particularly.
Alexandra Sheeran of CBRE’s hotels division says: “This hotel development is a fantastic opportunity for operators to secure a prime, turnkey development in Dublin’s most sought-after location. The project offers hoteliers the chance to collaborate with the developer to create a wonderful hotel in one of Dublin city’s most exclusive areas.”

title: Netanyahu faces fresh scrutiny over pre-October 7th warnings
description: New reports on warnings received before the Hamas attack threaten the Israeli prime minister’s general election campaign
content:
Israeli prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu is under growing pressure over what he knew before Hamas’s October 7th, 2023 attack, with new reports casting fresh light on warnings received by Israeli authorities in the months leading up to the assault.
For the last three years Netanyahu has argued that his military and security chiefs were taken by surprise and failed to warn him. He said if they had only woken him earlier before the dawn attack, he could have ordered an appropriate military intervention.
The entire military and security echelon has since resigned, with most of the key figures accepting their own failures that led to the biggest disaster in Israel’s history.
About 1,200 people, mostly civilians, were killed on October 7th, with 250 taken hostage into Gaza . The ensuing Israeli war in Gaza has to date resulted in the deaths of more than 77,000 residents, according to local authorities.
Despite the magnitude of the catastrophe, Netanyahu has refused to appoint a state commission of inquiry to investigate what went wrong and, critically, to make sure the same mistakes are not repeated in the future.
Last month the anti-government Haaretz newspaper published an excerpt from a book by two Israeli journalists which claimed that an encrypted call was made by the Emirati president Mohamed bin Zayed less than two weeks before October 7th, warning Netanyahu that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a large-scale attack that could destabilise the Middle East.
Netanyahu did not pass on the warnings to his security aides, according to the authors, Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval.
Following the Haaretz exposé, both the Atlantic and the Wall Street Journal published reports that then-Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel also warned Netanyahu before October 7th that Hamas was planning to attack.
[ ‘They want to kill all of us’: Life on Israel’s anxious frontier Opens in new window ]
Yoav Gallant, Israel’s defence minister at the time, said Netanyahu never informed him or the army chief of staff of these warnings, and that they learned of them only recently from the media.
According to media reports, Netanyahu was reluctant to initiate action against Hamas because he feared a conflict could derail efforts to normalise diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia .
[ ‘It’s off the charts’: Satellite images show how three years of war have devastated Gaza Opens in new window ]
Netanyahu denied all the reports, accusing the opposition, the “left-wing media” and former intelligence chiefs of generating fake news in an attempt to discredit him in advance of the October 27th election.
After he implied a conspiracy by intelligence chiefs to deliberately misinform him, Ronen Bar, the former director of Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic intelligence agency, sued Netanyahu for defamation, accusing him of “trying to deflect fire from himself by hurling accusations at the person who warned him in real time”.
A recent survey by the Institute for National Security Studies found that an overwhelming 75 per cent of Israelis – including a majority of coalition voters – support a state commission of inquiry into October 7th. All the main opposition parties have pledged to set up such an inquiry as a top priority for an incoming government.
Israel’s president Yitzhak Herzog and Eyal Zamir, the army’s chief of staff, called for accountability and a thorough investigation into the security failures that led to October 7th, in their addresses at memorial ceremonies this week.
“We must investigate with determination and courage, and without bias, and to understand: How did this happen to us?” said Herzog.
A bereaved father heckled Netanyahu during his speech, shouting: “You didn’t protect my son on October 7th. You didn’t protect 1,200 murdered on one day, on October 7th – disgrace!”

title: Rathgar four-bed with 1930s features bursting with potential
description: Thorncliffe Park semidetached home with 1930s features
content:
Thorncliffe Park, on Orwell Road in Rathgar , is a mature estate of semidetached and detached houses located beside Milltown Golf Club. Number 7, dating from 1941, has arrived on the market with DNG Terenure, seeking €1.4 million.
It’s a fine four-bed semidetached home extending to 177sq m (1,905sq ft). On a quiet side road, it is set well back from the busier stretch on Orwell Road, with a bank of mature trees shading this small enclave.
A front garden has off-street parking and the double-fronted property has bay windows and a balcony terrace to the front. Original stained glass decorates the front door on either side and above and the entrance hallway has a guest loo under the stairs.
Many of the house’s 1930s features such as the staircase, doors, the fireplace in the main reception room and coving are still in place. An interconnecting pair of reception rooms are on the right side of the hallway, and they are both light-filled and generous. The front of the house faces south, so the drawingroom is sunny and warm. The diningroom to the rear has direct access to the rear garden, through French doors.
At the end of the hall is a family room, which is very comfortable, dual aspect, has built in shelving and a most unusual and attractive Dutch-style cast-iron stove. Behind it the kitchen, which like the drawingroom, sits at the front of the house and benefits from a sunny aspect.
The configuration reflects the original layout of the house, and new owners may want to improve the access to the kitchen, by opening through to the side of the house, which has a side passage, or looking at incorporating the family room at the rear into the kitchen. Another option would be to further extend, subject to planning permission, into the garden, as some of the neighbours have already done.
It’s a versatile house, bursting with potential and possibility. The Ber rating is C and heating is gas. Upstairs are four bedrooms. The main bedroom has a deep bay window, on the far side of the landing it is a smaller bedroom with a large teak door that swings open on to a small balcony.
Reflecting the age of the house, all the bedrooms have sink units, but the family bathroom has been renovated and is in good shape. The house has a large attic, which offers further potential to extend upwards.
The garden, the jewel in this property, extends to 60ft, has been meticulously tended and planted over the decades and is in perfect condition. Mature beds are filled with hydrangeas, roses and turning acers; vibrant clouds of jasmine cloak the walls, there is a garden shed and a bower in the furthest corner.
Thorncliffe Park as a location is sought-after, being close to both Rathgar and Terenure villages, the Dodder Park is only a few hundred metres away, as are the fairways and greens of Milltown Golf Club. The Luas stop at Windy Arbour is a 10-minute walk away and it is within easy reach of schools.

title: Cherrywood town centre site with scope for hundreds of new homes guiding at €10m
description: Site extending to 4.79 acres currently in use as car park and generating €492,000 in annual income
content:
Having paid about €145 million in 2018 to secure ownership of a portfolio of eight office blocks at Cherrywood Business Park in south Dublin , San Francisco-headquartered real-estate investor Spear Street Capital has instructed agent JLL to find a buyer for a nearby site with residential development potential which it acquired as part of that transaction. The 4.79-acre (1.94-hectare) holding is being offered for sale at a guide price of €10 million.
Located within close proximity to both junction 16 of the M50 motorway and the junction of the N11 and Wyattville Road (R118), and within a short walk of the Luas green-line terminus at Bride’s Glen, the subject site is zoned “town centre environs” under the Cherrywood strategic development zone (SDZ). This zoning allows for a range of uses including residential and strategic urban employment.
In a recent amendment (number 11) to the Cherrywood SDZ, Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council increased the share of residential space to 55 per cent along with a commensurate reduction in employment space to 45 per cent. The variation in the plan also provides for buildings ranging in height from three to six storeys with a maximum gross floor space of 38,800sq m (417,600sq ft). Under the SDZ developers will also be able to submit fast-track planning applications, with the local authority required to issue a decision within eight weeks. The selling agent believes the site has the potential to accommodate about 250 apartments subject to planning permission .
[ South Dublin apartment portfolio primed for €130m sale Opens in new window ]
The arrival to the market of the Spear Street site land comes just four months after DLR Properties (DLRP), a subsidiary of Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council, sought expressions of interest from developers for the adjoining 5.4-hectare (13.3-acre) Town Centre 3 site, which has full planning permission in place for 418 apartments. The site’s capacity could, however, potentially be increased to up to 1,150 residential units along with 52,000sq m (559,723sq ft) of other town-centre-type uses (retail, office and civic) following the council’s aforementioned amendment to the Cherrywood SDZ.
In June, Hines and King Street Capital put another nearby site of 8.65 acres up for sale through agent CBRE at a guide price of €40 million. A feasibility study, prepared by architects Henry J Lyons and Allford Hall Monaghan Morris, indicated that site’s potential to accommodate up to 600 apartments, alongside about 30,000sq m (322,917sq ft) of retail, leisure and complementary uses, subject to planning permission.
Commenting on the sale of Spear Street Capital’s site, Ollie Lyons of JLL said: “We expect a high level of engagement from prospective buyers given the attractive lot size and the site’s potential to deliver a high-density residential-led scheme in an acutely undersupplied market, subject to planning permission.”

title: Fully let Dublin city centre residential investment guiding €3.85m
description: Portfolio comprises 14 apartments and is generating annual rental income of €258,672
content:
Private investors and family offices looking for immediate income from an established and well-located residential investment may be interested in the sale of Mabbot Lane, a portfolio of fully let apartments in the heart of Dublin city centre.
Located just off Talbot Street and within walking distance of O’Connell Street, the IFSC, north and south docklands, and the wider city centre, the investment, which comprises 14 apartments, is guiding at a price of €3.85 million. There are three one-bedroom apartments and 11 two-bedroom units and these are generating an average rent of €1,540 a month, giving an overall annual rental income of €258,672.
All the apartments are occupied under standard residential tenancy agreements, providing investors with an established and proven residential income stream. Existing tenants will not be affected by the sale.
The subject property also includes vacant ground-floor commercial accommodation, offering investors an asset-management opportunity with potential for alternative uses, subject to planning permission.
Conor Steen of Hooke and MacDonald says: “Mabbot Lane offers investors the opportunity to acquire an income-producing residential asset in a strong Dublin city-centre location.”

title: Prime residential site next to Pat Kenny’s Dalkey home for €3.9m
description: Richard Barrett’s Bartra seeks buyer for 1.56-acre holding after rejection of nursing home plan
content:
The sale of a prime residential site next to Bullock Harbour in Dalkey is likely to attract strong interest from developers and investors.
Located on Ulverton Road and Harbour Road, the subject site, which extends to 1.56 acres, had until recently been the subject of an ambitious plan by developer Richard Barrett’s Bartra Property for the development of a five-storey, 104-unit nursing home. The proposal was ultimately rejected by An Coimisiún Pleanála in February of this year following a successful High Court challenge brought by broadcaster Pat Kenny, his wife Kathy, and their neighbours against a grant of planning permission given by An Bord Pleanála in July 2023.
With Bartra’s bid to build a nursing home on the site now ruled out, the land is being offered for sale by agent Knight Frank at a guide price of €3.9 million on the basis of its potential to accommodate residential accommodation aimed towards the traditional owner-occupier market or private rented sector.
Positioned about 250m from Bullock Harbour, 750 metres from Dalkey village and 1km from Dalkey Dart station, the lower section of the site, known as Yonder, is accessed from Harbour Road while the upper section is accessed from Ulverton Road. The lower portion of the site is occupied by Maple Tree House, a detached seven-bedroom house.
The entire site falls under the Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Development Plan 2022–2028 and is zoned Objective A Residential. The aim of this objective is “to provide residential development and improve residential amenity while protecting the existing residential amenities”.
[ Commercial property in The Irish Times Opens in new window ]
Parties with an interest in developing residential accommodation will note the site had, in relative terms, a more positive planning history before the current owner’s bid to develop a nursing home there. In 2019, planning permission was granted for the construction of 24 residential units comprising a mix of 18 apartments and six houses. This planning permission has since expired.
A feasibility study has now been prepared for the site with two options for its development. Option one provides for the construction of 14 houses consisting of two four-bed detached units, four three-bed terraced units, six three-bed plus-study terraced units, and two two-bed semidetached units.
Option two replaces four of the terraced houses in option one with six apartments/duplexes, allowing for a total of 16 units. The mix would comprise three two-bed apartments, three three-bed duplexes, two four-bed detached houses, six three-bed plus-study terraced houses, and two two-bed semidetached houses.
Finín O’Driscoll of Knight Frank says: “This site offers an attractive lot size in a highly sought-after coastal residential location ... we expect to see high demand for this opportunity.”

title: Technologies of Peace: Give Imma’s sprawling exhibition the time and attention it deserves
description: The Irish Museum of Modern Art show incorporates work by artists from 17 countries, including Frances Hegarty and the Slavs and Tatars collective
content:
How do you picture peace? War is easy, on so many levels. Conflict has given rise to some of art’s great masterpieces. Francisco Goya’s The Third of May 1808 (painted in 1814) and Pablo Picasso’s Guernica , from 1937, haunt the mind. And what of peace? Doves and rainbows just don’t seem capable of the same sucker punch, even if Picasso’s Dove, a visual essay on peace from 1949, has been reproduced at peace congresses around the world.
Despite the weight of war, the emphasis at the Irish Museum of Modern Art is on paths to peace, but don’t expect to be washed with waves of optimism, or of answers, when you get there.
Kicking off in 1989, the year the Berlin Wall fell, its exhibition Technologies of Peace: Art and Transition in Contemporary Europe (1989-2026) explores art from countries in Europe in which peace processes have paralleled our own.
It is another instalment in Imma’s series of ambitious exhibitions tackling big themes, such as its excellent Self-Determination: A Global Perspective , from 2023, which looked at nation building after the first World War.
Things open with a nicely undermining paradox: Ursula Burke’s brilliant Peach Caryatid stands imperiously at the entrance to Imma’s long corridor gallery. A caryatid is one of those sculpted robed female figures that support the roofs of Greek temples, and here it is a nod to ancient Greece ’s role in the development of democracy – the word itself translates as “people power”.
But Burke’s Caryatid is wearing knitted robes, reminding us that support takes many forms, including female labour and the domestic, which are not generally elevated in society’s eyes. Democracy can include exclusion, and a closer look reveals tears running down the figure’s painted face, flecking the peach wool clothes.
This aspect is later taken up in Sanja Ivekovic’s Invisible Women of Solidarity (2009-10), in which the Croatian artist includes the names of the many women who contributed to the Solidarity movement in Poland but whose names were not celebrated.
Threads connect throughout the galleries, but despite being deeply researched, and organised across a series of themes – and perhaps like peace itself – the exhibition feels a little diffuse and hard to pin down.
Just beyond Caryatid, the Cypriot artist Christodoulos Panayiotou shows seven large “pulp paintings”, the colours of which may be vaguely familiar. They are made from mashed-up euro banknotes, with one frame for each denomination.
The notes were obtained from the European Central Bank after they were taken out of circulation – literally demonetised. Again, there is a paradox: while the shared currency is a symbol of the hard-won and harder-maintained unity within the eurozone countries, the whole money-and-the-root-of-all-evil thing is going on.
The calming colours are at odds with the lurid ills that money inspires into the world. War, exploitation, envy, treachery: who knows where these notes went or what their temporary owners did? And here they are now: just faded colour, and art.
If Panayiotou’s work shows the transmutation of paper and ink to money as a matter of collective agreement, or imposition, what, then, about the borders drawn on maps?
Driton Selmani, while on a residency in the UK, had discovered that his native Kosovo was hard to find on online maps. At the time it couldn’t be selected as a destination or as a point of origin. He responded by asking compatriots to draw Kosovo from memory, creating a shifting set of outlines from which he made an embroidered map. In Tell Me Where I Am From (2012), southeast Europe dissolves into unfamiliar and imagined lands.
But borders, once made, must be held. The Slovenian artist Nika Autor’s Red Forests (2022) is a video showing the extent of razor wire at EU borders since 2015. Rita Duffy’s Watchtower 2 (2005-06) imaginatively transforms surveillance towers from the Northern Ireland border lands, post-peace process, as nature reclaims them.
Photographs by another Northern Ireland-born artist, Anthony Haughey, from his Disputed Territory series, take in border regions in Ireland, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Kosovo. Shotgun Cartridges, Armagh-Louth Border (2006) shows how the legacies of violence remain in the land.
Another take on mapping comes from Lana Cmajcanin with 551.35 Geometry of Time (2014), a large illuminated wall piece in which the Sarajevo-born artist traces the outlines of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s borders over 551 years. War, negotiation and the shifts of power and political ideologies demonstrate how borders are both fluid and endlessly contested.
That idea of “endless” is interesting. As a species, humanity appears to live with the myth that we are getting to a fixed destination, and that once the right boundaries, the right governments, the right people and politics bed in, there will be no more war.
But a problem with peace is that we never quite get there, at least not in a way that is everlasting.
Despite the exhibition dates of 1989 to 2026, the timeline that flows across two of the smaller side galleries at Imma begins in 1968, sketching in the global events that informed the politics of our contemporary period.
From the assassinations of Martin Luther King jnr, in Tennessee, and Robert F Kennedy, in Los Angeles, on, it makes for bloody reading. Even in that first decade there was the Battle of the Bogside, in Derry; Idi Amin set up his brutal dictatorship in Uganda; the CIA-backed coup in Chile overthrew the elected socialist president, Salvador Allende; and more than two million people were massacred in Cambodia. The eye slides from injustice to atrocity, and on it goes.
In art this is reflected in works such as Cathy Wilkes’ Untitled (2021), a small installation that lingers on the aftermath of aspects of the conflict in Northern Ireland, such as the Abercorn restaurant bombing of 1972.
Wilkes, who also has an excellent solo exhibition at the Model in Sligo until January 2027, catches subtly at the quieter legacies of violence: fragility, absence and grief.
But look again at that timeline and you see brighter spots. There is the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, Greenpeace is founded, the Paris Peace Accords close US involvement in Vietnam, dictatorships end in Portugal and Greece. Hypocrisies are outed, hurts emerge, healings begin. Exhibitions take place and civil-rights movements are born. Is it just that we are more attuned to grim news? Our survival, or so the theory goes, prioritises looking out for danger.
Then there is the matter of context: it’s hard to experience Technologies of Peace without its more positive messages being subdued by the apocalyptic nature of the news these days.
And, going back to that timeline, what is an exhibition, the establishment of a gallery, a cross-border picnic or a song contest in the face of a massacre, a new conflict, a famine? The answer is that, just as people make war, so they make peace. Sometimes they are figureheads and sometimes they simply, but profoundly, sow the seeds of a new idea.
The Polish artist Malgorzata Mirga-Tas works in collaboration with the Romani activist Edis Galushi and members of the Prizren Romani community. The resulting large textile collages draw portraits of Romani luminaries including the social-justice activist, writer and performer Alina Serban and the activist and multimedia artist Luna De Rosa.
People make peace. Ideas can also come through noticing: Aleksandar Battista Ilic, Ivana Keser and Tomislav Gotovac show a series of works, Weekend Art: Hallelujah the Hill, 1996-2000. As Croatia emerged from communist rule, the trio of artists explored the idea of leisure time by turning their weekend walks into performance-art experiences. There is freedom in these scenes, and joy.
Another element of noticing comes in spotting embedded inequalities. Mladen Stilinovic’s silk banner is painted with “An artist who cannot speak English is no artist”. Made in 1992, it underlines the stranglehold the English language has over the arts globally, consequently inflecting what can be expressed.
Language is there too in Sejla Kameric’s rotating EU/Others (2022), a riff on the signs that appeared at European Union border crossings during the early years of EU integration, in a literal demonstration of “us and them”.
The Bosnia and Herzegovina artist also shows a flashing neon sign that, at a distance, seems to flicker from “Refugees will come” to “Refugees welcome”. Just like the malfunctioning sign, the artist said in 2022, “the society in which we have to discuss whether someone in need (refugees/migrants) should be welcome or not is ill”.
Words matter. Locky Morris’s Comm (1992) takes the small messages written on toilet paper and wrapped in clingfilm before being bodily smuggled by prisoners during the Troubles and makes them monumental.
Whatever your political affiliation, there can be no peace without communication. Just beware of anyone who claims to know the “truth”. Alán Carrasco’s History Loves Paradoxes (2023) is a grid of 20 newspaper mastheads, each a translation of the word “truth”. Including La Vérité, LaVerità, Pravda and De Waarheid, the piece nicely balances our desire to know and believe with the dangers of media partisanship, reductive simplicities and absolutism.
The mastheads also underline the diversity of voices within the exhibition, which includes artists from 17 countries, with noteworthy pieces by Frances Hegarty, the Slavs and Tatars collective, and Goshka Macuga.
Marina Abramovic’s The Hero (2021) is a little glib – the artist is holding a white banner atop a white horse – yet nonetheless beautiful. More beautiful still is William McKeown’s glowing Open Drawing – Primrose #2 (2003), a reminder that there is still the possibility of renewal, growth, healing and love.
Despite its sprawling nature and occasionally tangled threads, give this exhibition the time and attention it requires. Hope is not naive, and sometimes seemingly small gestures are the results of phenomenal bravery.
As dictatorships and censorship wane and wax, the achievements of peace go beyond bringing these artists together. Instead, they are embodied in the fact that some of these works could have been made at all, and that we are free to see them.
Technologies of Peace, curated by Mary Cremin and Johanne Mullan, is at the Irish Museum of Modern Art , Dublin, until May 9th, 2027

title: Lesbian Lines review: Cara Holmes’ fine film is much at home to retrospective joy
description: Holmes takes us back to the establishment of the titular helpline towards the close of the nation’s damp, grey 1970s
content:
Here is a fine documentary that manages to be funny and inspiring despite rooting itself in an often unhappy corner of Ireland’s past.
Cara Holmes , long resident in Cork , takes us back to the establishment of the titular helpline towards the close of the nation’s damp, grey 1970s. Not just a helpline. The volunteers were certainly there to pass on useful information to often isolated lesbians. But they were also there to chat, divert and bolster. Calling together a fair swathe of the original listeners, this is a film much at home to retrospective joy.
The contributors speak of their virtual invisibility in the decades before the Celtic Tiger boom. “The lines were like beacons of hope,” one says. “Sending out a signal and a beam. We’re here.”
It hardly needs to be said that The Late Late Show plays a part. Joni Crone, now a playwright, appeared on the programme in 1980 to talk about her experiences. Nothing communicates the existing situation more clearly than the news that Gay Byrne – perfectly polite, to be fair – explained he was going to tell us only her first name.
Why? She was not a bank robber or a KGB whistleblower. At this remove, all that seems as absurd as Monty Python’s The Mouse Problem sketch, a satire, aired a decade earlier, of similar attitudes on the BBC.
The zippy Lesbian Lines could hardly have less in common with the worthy hand-wringing that Python so gleefully parodied.
Holmes’ film will stand as a useful record of grim times and of how lively minds managed to shoulder the nation towards invigorating daylight.
But it is no mere compendium of talking heads. The combination of archive footage and sly re-creations conjures up the era beautifully: cigarette smoke, rotary telephones, Anglepoise lamps and lots and lots of orangey brown.
The image of a young woman alone in a weather-blasted phone box reminds us that the callers often struggled to secure sufficient privacy to reveal their problems. Some would phone and offer only nervous silence.
The director also has the bright idea of, towards the close, bringing the younger cast members together with the women who answered the phones all those years ago.
What strikes one most is the continuity of spirit. “It felt like we were changing the world,” one of the veterans says. Maybe they were.

title: Patrick Freyne: Budget day in the Dáil would turn you to cigarettes if they hadn’t gone up
description: Simon Harris looked miserable as he ran through the numbers, but that’s probably because he’s been up all weekend with a new baby
content:
A man goes to the doctor and says: “Doctor, I am depressed. The world is in a terrible state. Everything is burning (including the budget surplus burning a hole in my pocket).”
The doctor says: “Go see the Tánaiste and Finance Minister Simon Harris orating in the Dáil. The country is flaithiúlach because of the Yanks. He’s throwing money around. Great celebrations will be had. It will surely cheer you up.”
The man bursts into tears: “But doctor, I am Tánaiste and Finance Minister Simon Harris.”
It’s budget day in Dáil Éireann, the day when the Government makes us all do sums. We’re rolling in money these days (apparently) but everyone also feels poorer (evidently) and nobody is happy (clearly).
Harris looks miserable. Though that’s probably because he’s been up all weekend with a new baby, not the budget! His wife Caoimhe gave birth to their third child over the weekend.
Barbara and Frank Chambers are in the distinguished visitors’ gallery observing the work of their own baby, Jack Chambers , the Minister for Public Expenditure. I believe they were up all night with him too.
Anyway, at 12 o’clock, out come the best boys from behind the bike shed of Government Buildings, professional budget models Chambers and Harris, holding up their big colourdy budget books, opening them up to reveal mysterious charts and doing some synchronised waving at the behest of the snappers. (“Finally!” they say, “a photo of men in suits.”)
Ah, we love the symbolic theatre of it all. Chambers wears a salmon pink tie. Harris a blue one. Once upon a time, people took bets on the Minister for Finance’s tie colour on budget day. It’s clear to conspiratorial types that the colour choices are signalling coded messages to their masters in the bond markets.
An hour later, Harris takes to his feet in the Dáil. He recently brought back an old Fine Gael greatest hit favouring people who “get up early” and this budget, he tells us, is for hard-working people. He presents his budget as an attempt to manage the cost-of-living crisis. He talks for some time.
Then he figuratively high fives Jack Chambers into the fray to name-drop Seán Lemass twice and champion the cause for fiscal responsibility (the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council keen audibly from somewhere beyond the chamber). He talks for some time.
The gist of budget day is that the Government lists all of the things that are right with the country (unemployment rates, budget surpluses, tax cuts) with the numbers that support that.
And then the opposition spokespeople list all of the things that are wrong with the country, using the numbers that support that (housing issues, homelessness, child poverty, poor disability services).
The short version is that the Government are focused on future global volatility. The opposition are more focused on the failures of the present.
Sinn Féin’s Pearse Doherty kicks off the Hour of Hate. He quickly segues from the shortcomings of the budget (he dubs it the “Gone Before You Get It” budget) into a more general assessment of the missteps of Government when it comes to the number of children in poverty and the number of people who are homeless.
He targets a lot of his ire at Taoiseach Micheál Martin, which is a little insulting to Harris and Chambers on their big day. The Taoiseach rolls his eyes and shakes his head and looks appalled with the impertinence of it all. Harris mutters and Chambers stares into the middle distance, thinking no doubt of his days budget-modelling in the forecourt.
It’s enough to make a man start smoking, really. Sadly, they have added a euro to the cost of a packet of fags.
The other spokespeople follow the same theme.
There are lists of shortages and service failures. The gist of the opposition critique is that this is not a progressive budget targeted at those who are suffering. Instead, they say, it is one that largely benefits wealthier voters, tinkering with the higher rate of income tax which a majority of Irish workers do not pay and offering untargeted measures to alleviate cost-of-living pressures. It has enough references to risk-takers to trigger those with collectivist tendencies.
People Before Profit-Solidarity TD Richard Boyd Barrett angrily tells the people of Ireland to “get their placards ready”.
Socialist Party TD Ruth Coppinger accuses Chambers of going “full Musk”, setting up “Doge” with his newly announced public spending efficiency taskforce – a reference to the Tesla boss’s Department of Government Efficiency that took an axe to US government spending.
Labour’s Ged Nash says it’s not a budget for “those who get up in the morning” but one “for those who can afford a bloody good lie-in”. (I think people in the entertainment industry call this “a callback”).
On both sides of the house, there’s a sense that it’s very important to make the most of our current budget surpluses, given the state of the world. There is, after all, no way of knowing what the exchequer receipts will look like in the future.
But TDs differ significantly on what it means to make the most of it. There is also only so much talk of millions and billions that a person can take before their eyes glaze over and it begins to feel like Monopoly money.
But it’s real money. And everyone is very aware that the Monopoly board might someday be yanked off the table.

title: How solar is making light work of energy costs at K&K Produce
description: ‘Solar panels will help insulate us from the unpredictability of what happens around the world,’ says Thomas Kennedy, the company’s financial controller
content:
As a business with products depending on sunlight to grow, there’s something very satisfying about the way K&K Produce has incorporated solar energy into its day-to-day operations. For an energy-intensive business, the investment also offers a practical way to reduce operating costs and gain greater control over a key business expense.
The family-owned business produces and sources fresh potatoes, fruit and vegetables in north Co Dublin. It was founded in 1984 by Tommy and Deirdre Kennedy and has grown into one of Ireland’s leading suppliers. Now supported by the second generation of their family, it supplies supermarkets, independent retailers, the food service industry and export markets.
The company combines its own growing operations with a trusted network of Irish farmers and growers, helping to bring home-grown produce to consumers throughout the year.
The business also operates packing and distribution facilities and maintains a fleet of temperature-controlled vehicles, making energy a critical resource across its operations. Investing in solar is now helping this growing company reduce its exposure to energy price volatility and plan its longer-term energy costs with greater confidence.
The business’s success story is one of continuous innovation, says Thomas Kennedy, the company’s financial controller. He remembers how his parents started their business driving into the fruit markets of Smithfield in Dublin, buying potatoes and delivering them to stores directly, because there were no chilled distribution centres back then.
His parents first built a small warehouse beside the family home and were one of the first to offer washed potatoes, an innovation many of us still give thanks for today.
By the 1990s they had built up a customer base that included many of the country’s best-known stores, such as Spar and SuperValu, and expanded their range, buying a wider range of home-grown vegetables direct from farmers and importing fruit from overseas.
“They were very enterprising and innovative, they focused on quality and they offered a reliable service,” says Thomas. By the late 1990s, with the introduction of chilled depots in Ireland, they were able to deliver nationwide.
As the business grew, in the early 2000s his parents moved it to new premises, just up the road in The Ward. New accounts included the discounter supermarkets and the next generation of the business was confirmed when Thomas’s brother, Michael, joined at the age of 18.
A few years later Thomas, who trained as a chartered accountant, joined too, about a decade ago. “I brought some of that experience of other industries with me,” he says.
Today the business has a 30,000 sq ft facility that combines a mix of chilled and ambient produce, both with Kennedy-branded potatoes and supermarkets’ own brands. It supplies three of Ireland’s top five supermarkets, independent retailers and employs 65 people.
Constant innovation has been central to its success, from the introduction of microwaveable packaging to the sourcing of vegetables suited for air fryers, helping to save time and energy to cook.
‘It’s all about trying to look at different technologies to see how you can improve efficiency, boost quality and save on costs’
“It means that for potatoes you’re looking at 10 or 12 minutes’ cooking time, versus the 35 minutes it might take to boil or steam them,” he says.
Today K&K Produce has a pipeline of new products in development focused on delivering convenience to consumers with busy lives “who still want a healthy meal”, he says.
It’s a focus on innovation and sustainability that has helped the family business ride out a variety of challenges, from recession and inflation to the rising cost of doing business.
“Managing costs is a key part of that, into which sustainability falls,” says Thomas. “For us sustainability is becoming a much bigger part of the planning side of the business, looking at things like long-term energy costs; water usage and product waste; and what we can do to innovate on that side too.”
The business has cut its water usage by 95 per cent, for example, by introducing better water recycling systems. “It’s all about trying to look at different technologies to see how you can improve efficiency, boost quality and save on costs, not just energy but insurance, labour, packaging and transport costs too,” says Thomas, adding that the company has a fleet of 14 trucks.
“We operate seven days a week here, and use a lot of energy for washing, grading and packing produce, as well as running cold storage for 12 months of the year. We’re always trying to get that balance as much as possible, reducing packaging and offering reusable crates rather than outer bags where we can, while also ensuring we reduce food waste as much as possible.”
As part of the company’s drive to introduce more sustainable practices, it began looking at installing solar panels on its premises in 2025.
“We were at a customer conference where a number of guest speakers from the food and beverage industry were highlighting the changes they were making, which included solar,” says Thomas. That prompted him to call Electric Ireland, his energy provider, to understand what a solar installation could deliver for the business.
Electric Ireland assessed K&K Produce’s energy requirements, including the number of panels needed, the expected output and the proposed cost.
He also called in two other suppliers for quotes, before opting to go with Electric Ireland, valuing the reassurance of working with an established provider for such a significant, long-term investment.
Electric Ireland guided him through the SEAI grant process, managed the application and installed his solar panels in March of this year. It was a significant, “six-figure” investment by the business, he explains, paid for via a low-cost green bank loan.
Thomas expects the investment to pay for itself within three years, after which the panels will generate annual savings. For a business with substantial year-round energy requirements, the benefits are not limited to lower costs: generating more of its own electricity also reduces exposure to future energy price volatility.
“A lot of that is to do with the cost of energy being so high, but also because the technology has improved so much. When I first looked into it six or seven years ago, the payback time was nearly six years,” he points out.
“We believe it will produce 20 per cent of our energy a year, and we’re hoping for 25 per cent. That’s for our first phase. A second phase, which we hope to install in 2028, will save us another 15 per cent off our energy costs,” he says.
Given that climate change is one of the biggest challenges facing farmers and the food production sector generally, it feels good to be doing what he can to reduce his carbon impact too, he says.
“Three years ago we had awful rain from September to December, and people couldn’t harvest crops. This summer we’ve had drought throughout Ireland and Europe.”
But Thomas also sees genuine opportunity for the industry here. “People are more focused on healthy eating than ever, and in Ireland we produce some of the best food in the world,” he says.
That sense of control is particularly important against a backdrop of geopolitical uncertainty and the potential for further energy price increases. “Our solar panels will help insulate us a little bit from the unpredictability of what happens around the world, the things we can’t control,” he says.
“The way we looked at it was as a long-term investment, rather than focus on the upfront cost. But we are seeing the benefits of it already.”
