title: Shaping the future of farming, with financial support that counts
description: At just 22 years old, Aisling Neville took on a dairy farm in Co Westmeath. Eight years on, it’s a thriving enterprise and Aisling is helping to drive Irish farming forward
content:
Growing up on her family’s dairy farm outside Tullamore in Co Offaly, Aisling Neville knew she’d end up with a career in agriculture, one way or another. “I’m the youngest of five children, and we all got roped into helping out on the farm at a young age,” she says. “We were all doing it together, as a family. You take it for granted now, the amount of time we spent together.”
Her love of farming led her to study agricultural science in university, and the course provided the opportunity to travel to Australia. “Shane, my now-husband, and I went to Australia and did our work placement out there for six months,” she says. “We worked with really good people on two different farms, and it sparked a belief that we’d be able to go farming ourselves.”
The couple had returned to Ireland when fate intervened. “A farm came up for lease about a half an hour from my home place, and I felt it was an opportunity,” Aisling says. “We chased that down and were lucky enough to take it on a lease. We’ve been there ever since, and it’s been going well since then too.”
Aisling was just 22 years old when she took on the farm in Moate, Co Westmeath along with responsibility for a 150-cow dairy herd. A bold move for a young woman but Aisling says she’s always been fearless. “Because I was the youngest in the family, I’ve always had the attitude of ‘I can do just as good as the rest of them’,” she explains.
When it came to financing the project, Aisling expected a challenge and so it proved, at first. “The biggest barrier to young people getting into farming is access to finance.
“Initially when I took on the farm, we needed to buy stock, cows for milking, so I reached out to a few banks. I wasn’t entertained by too many because I had no security. I was a bit of a risk, and I had nothing behind me, but AIB was willing to help.”
AIB, with 170 branches in communities across the country, has a dedicated team of regional agri advisors, all from farming backgrounds themselves, who combine financial expertise with an understanding of the sector’s unique opportunities and challenges. The aim? To support the next generation of young farmers like Aisling to invest, innovate, and build resilient, sustainable farm businesses that ultimately lead to more vibrant rural communities.
The bank’s practical approach made all the difference, Aisling explains. “Some people get very fearful of banks, but in my experience AIB are easy to work with,” she says. “They are very people-oriented and they’re not afraid to give you advice on how to go about something in order to get the necessary finance.
“Once I got set up and established, other banks wanted to work with me, but the AIB agri team were willing to put themselves out there from the very beginning. They could see where we wanted to go and they backed us.”
That initial support marked the start of a long-term relationship. As Aisling’s business and personal goals have developed, the AIB agri team has worked with her changing needs. When Aisling and Shane decided to buy a house close to the farm, it made sense to return to AIB to obtain their mortgage, and the bank has also helped the couple buy more land since they first took on the farm.
By pursuing her own path, Aisling is also inspiring a new generation of young female farmers. In all areas of life, visibility is a key factor in helping people realise what’s possible and the opportunities for women in agriculture are increasing all the time, Aisling says. “With technology nowadays, the real hard labour has gone out of farming, so women aren’t at a physical disadvantage anymore,” she explains.
“Farming as a sector is probably ahead of most other sectors in adopting new technology and the work is only going to become easier as time goes on. So, if parents see that there’s a daughter in the house that has an interest in farming, they shouldn’t look past them. That’s the main thing.”
If any daughter, or parent, needs inspiration they need only look to Aisling. Along with running her successful dairy farm, she is the first woman to sit on the board of Lakeland Dairies and is three years into a five-year term. “It was a good opportunity, so I stuck myself in the race and got elected by the people in the area,” she says.
“It can be challenging at times but it’s brilliant, and it’s a different aspect to the business that you wouldn’t see on your own farm. It’s the scale of it and you see where your milk goes, what’s making money and what’s not, and what we have to do for sustainability and all those other parts that are involved.”
Back on her own dairy farm, Aisling says that things are going well. “I’m happy with where we are at the moment,” she says. “It’s nice to be able to run the business we have today with myself, my husband, and some part-time labour. We milk 180 cows and I think if we can keep doing a better job tomorrow than what we’re doing today, that will be progress. Down the line, it would be nice to be able to purchase a farm of our own and grow that end of it. But we won’t put a noose around our necks either.”
She says that she would return to AIB when the time comes to progress the business further. And for those looking to get into the farming industry, or to take their business to the next level, Aisling has a few words of guidance. “My advice would be, don’t be afraid to reach out to the AIB agri team,” she says. “It doesn’t matter what you’re thinking about doing, it’s always worth having the conversation, so just pick up the phone.”
For more information on AIB’s agriculture and farming supports, see aib.ie

title: How to make it as a digital creator? Find something unique
description: Easy access and high rewards draw millions to careers in social media but agents say the challenges are underestimated
content:
H ew Moran was a teenager playing computer games for fun at home in Long Island, New York , when he started filming himself acting out scenes from the games and uploading them to YouTube .
He would play after school then make the comedy clips before grabbing a few hours’ sleep and heading back into lessons.
By 2023, he was gaining one million subscribers every month and his videos now regularly get more than 100 million monthly views.
“It just kind of worked, which was kind of crazy,” he says, thinking back to a period of juggling college, then a part-time job and his fledgling YouTube channel. “It was pretty exciting but it was overwhelming.”
Moran eventually quit his job, then dropped out of college to focus on content creation. “My parents were like, what the heck is this?”
Closer to home, fashion blogger and influencer Lisa McGowan only started her online promotional work after she won the best-dressed ladies competition at the Galway Races in 2016.
Before then, McGowan, an insurance broker by profession, had just set up Lisa’s Lust List, a fashion blog which was, in her own words, “only ever meant to be a hobby”.
Lisa’s Lust List site specialises in promoting products including fashion items, beauty, health, travel and homeware, mainly produced by Irish-based SMEs.
[ ‘I love my job, but the loneliness is hard’: Reality of life as a travel influencer Opens in new window ]
Her Facebook page has 214,000 followers while on Instagram it has increased to 197,000. Figures published this week show she enjoyed a remuneration package last year of €1.9 million.
Similar questions to those of Moran’s parents are now being asked by millions of young people trying to make it as digital content creators and social media influencers, as viewers flood to YouTube, TikTok and Instagram as their main source of news and entertainment.
There is money to be made, with advertising spending backing the US creator economy expected to reach almost $44 billion (€39 billion) in 2026, according to the trade body IAB, as the industry ditches institutional media to get closer to popular individual voices.
The UK’s creator economy on YouTube alone was worth £2.8 billion (€3.3 billion) and supported 60,000 jobs in 2025, according to research by Oxford Economics, while estimates of the numbers it employs around the world stretch into hundreds of millions. Last year, a UK parliamentary group was launched to recognise the importance of the rapidly growing sector.
How do the top creators monetise content, which businesses are benefiting from the boom and the multibillion dollar infrastructure behind it and how are traditional companies racing to catch up?
Smartphones mean almost anyone, anywhere, can create content. AI tools and data analytics are making it easier to produce and monetise their output at professional levels.
[ Age of influencers: how content creation has become the toughest of dream jobs Opens in new window ]
Such low entry costs and the potential for high rewards have prompted a gold rush for fickle digital audiences.
Professions have been created that did not exist a decade ago. Many of the industry’s most successful figures are newly minted millionaires. And companies and traditional media networks and agencies are rethinking how they do business, keen to tap into influencers’ ability to command audiences, change cultural norms, sway elections and sell products.
Talking to The Financial Times at a Disney event in Los Angeles this year, Jimmy Donaldson, better known as MrBeast, explained that increasingly he felt like a data scientist – spotting and riding the different trends of popular content on the internet – rather than a simple creator of digital content.
He now sits at the head of Beast Industries, an empire that spans TV shows to soft drinks and snacks, with the sorts of high production values that are far removed from his early days posting gaming and humorous videos on a YouTube channel a decade ago.
But behind the billions of dollars being made by the superstars such as MrBeast, lies a long tail of content creators and influencers scratching out a living with little support and uncertain prospects in the fast-changing algorithmically-led world of social media.
Many complain about long hours and futile attempts to build audiences, leaving them stranded without the attention of the brands whose payments they need to turn a channel into a career. Women creators say they are often subject to online abuse.
You have to be the thing that people want to watch
Creators also face the increasing creep of AI influencers – digital avatars that compete for their audience and income.
To attract engaged followers, creators often find a niche or hobby that can be turned into content for specific audiences. “We’re in an attention economy, there has to be something unique about you,” says GothamChess, aka Levy Rozman, who has two million Instagram followers and a YouTube audience of eight million for his analysis of and tips about the game.
“You have to be the thing that people want to watch rather than watching their limited series, rather than a movie, a documentary, listening to music, listening to podcasts,” he says. His earnings can fluctuate by 20 to 50 per cent from year to year, due largely to shifts in algorithms, he adds.
When scouting for new talent, Molly McDonald, founder of Blue Door Productions, a London-based production company built for the creator economy, looks for individuals with “a sharp, distinguishable point of view ... If people can’t explain who you are succinctly, the algorithm won’t pick up on it.”
She identifies the essential skills as “story structure, business literacy and burnout management ... The algorithm only favours your platform more if you distribute more content but there also has to be quality. If they stop posting, users drop.”
During lockdown, and out of work as a journalist, Lucy Edwards, who is blind, started posting videos on TikTok. “I got to about 27,000 subscribers then TikTok blew up for me. I suddenly had a million followers,” she says.
Everything I do, I think, can I make content out of it?
“The video that did it really was ‘blind girl does her own make-up’, which got 20 million views.”
She feels she has a bond with her audience that goes beyond any gimmick. “People know me. They want to know more about my life, what I do, my IVF journey, pregnancy journey. But if you don’t diversify ... you’re not going to do very well.”
Rozman says he “dabbles with different spaces other than chess”. “Everything I do, I think, can I make content out of it? Cooking, building a house, doing your taxes, immigration law, like anything to educate people.”
Many creators seek to ride more short-lived waves of internet popularity. Shira Jeczmien, founder of viral marketing agency Screenshot Media, points to a brief trend of people eating whole cucumbers that led to shortages of the vegetable in supermarkets.
“With social listening, you can see what conversations are starting to pick up in real time. What we look out for is content that might have a disproportionately high view count relative to the volume of videos being created on that topic.”
Mum Bum, a parenting influencer, started to post videos as a frazzled young mother and says she is now earning similar to a graduate job. “I essentially have no skills and qualifications ... I hadn’t even really used social media before. It is crazy that you can just jump in ... and make a success out of it.”
We have to be nimble. It’s long days. It’s uploading on the weekends
The lines have blurred between different sorts of creators and the different sorts of routes to the audience, says Oren Rosenbaum, co-head of the creators division at talent agency UTA. “The podcasters are making content for YouTube. YouTubers are making podcasts. Everyone has TikTok, everyone has Instagram.”
Such demands – along with the fact that most people starting out are doing all the idea creation, shooting and editing themselves – mean the difficulties of forging a sustainable creator career are often underestimated. “I think too many people are like, well, it’s so easy, anybody can do it ... it’s a very challenging job,” adds Rosenbaum.
Working hours can be more uncertain than a traditional media job. “You don’t really switch off,” says Edwards. “We have to be nimble. It’s long days. It’s uploading on the weekends, it’s changing things really quickly ... If a brand wants ... something, they pay a premium for you to prioritise them.”
Romany Henry, who shares cooking content drawing on her Asian heritage with her 460,000 Instagram followers, says the pressure of “creating the recipe, to shooting it, to speaking” can cause “constant exhaustion”. She took time out of content creation to work in kitchens to spark her passion for cooking again.
Newer challenges are arising as the industry becomes oversaturated. “[The] attention creators can access is waning as the proliferation of creators and brands [has grown],” says Dom Smales, who started and sold creator agency Gleam Futures.
Entrepreneur and reality TV star Jamie Laing, who has 1.7 million followers on Instagram, agrees there is pressure to “constantly be creative and different from someone else. You can’t be boring”. Burnout, he says, is “rife”.
[ Raising Chelsea: Conception, birth and first brand partnership of an aristocratic nepo baby Opens in new window ]
Moran now films from 11am to 5pm most days, making on average about five minutes’ worth of content, but then can spend until the early hours writing and editing multiple clips for YouTube, even with his own team of a cameraperson and editor.
Edwards sets out to make four or five pieces a week. “You have to feed the beast.”
The trade-off is worth it for many creators, who have found the freedom to make a career on platforms designed to connect them with audiences like never before.
But whether it is a secure long-term career can feel unclear.
“It feels like somebody has just handed me a golden ticket sometimes,” says Mum Bum. “But as time goes on, I can feel this is not sustainable. I need to be present for my children, and I don’t want them to see mummy with a phone in her hand all the time.” – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

title: This Cursed Beautiful Land review: Evan Gershkovich tells his story of imprisonment in Russia
description: The Wall Street Journal reporter recounts his arrest, trial and 16 months in Moscow’s Lefortovo prison
content:
Many of us first saw Evan Gershkovich standing inside a glass cage, facing charges of espionage in Vladimir Putin ’s Russia . We might have wondered what he was thinking at that moment. His detention, from March 2023, marked the first time since the Cold War that an American journalist had been arrested on charges of spying inside the country.
Now, free at last, he is finally telling his side of the story, at length and on his own terms. Of the glass cage images, Gershkovich writes of the “performative opening ceremonies” before his legal hearings began where he would try “to present a stoic figure as I always did… knowing this was a chance for my loved ones to see me holding strong.”
His new book is the story of this arrest and sham trial, but also an account of his impressive reporting efforts in the years before his detention; and his upbringing as the child of Jewish Soviet émigrés, torn between two cultures whose people often so deeply misunderstand each other. This memoir is immensely readable, with Gershkovich’s personality, humour and journalistic instinct shining throughout it.
His plan to treat prison like a reporting assignment must have helped. Gershkovich details his efforts to dedicate hours a day to reading and writing, protecting his notebooks and mailing his work out regularly; several of the individuals he encounters in the prison apparatus reference the book he is likely to produce from the experience.
Each encounter offers him new opportunities to speak to individuals - FSB agents; prison guards; political prisoners; judges; Russians willing to fight in Ukraine in exchange for their freedom - who had been off-limits before, and these recounted exchanges are illuminating. Yet none of this is to belittle the suffering that Gershkovich went through and witnessed, which he details calmly - keen to highlight small victories and joys as well as the myriad absurdities and travails.
Gershkovich was born in New Jersey in 1991, two months before the collapse of the Soviet Union. His family history is caught up with present-day Russia’s, for better and worse. His great-grandfather vanished after being arrested in 1937, at the height of Stalin’s purges; thousands of kilometres away and decades later, his mother still sang Gershkovich a Soviet patriotic song as a lullaby. In 2017, he reverse-migrated, leaving the US and a desirable job with the New York Times to relocate to Russia. Gershkovich worked for the Moscow Times and then AFP, before landing at the Wall Street Journal.
[ Russian foreign minister vows to see Ukraine war ‘through to the end’ Opens in new window ]
In Russia, he details his growing awareness of invisible boundaries and his efforts to push back at them, despite the constant uncertainty around what could be reported and who was safe. He details being tailed; never knowing if his accreditation would be renewed; wondering when to ignore odd threats circulating, directed at himself, and when to heed them.
“We were constantly alerting ourselves to potential dangers while also trying to make sure we weren’t overreacting. Otherwise we wouldn’t be able to do our jobs. And with each new rise in temperature, we were getting more used to it,” he writes. He remains inside Russia as a growing number of friends depart the country for safer places.
Early on in his reporting career, he learns of the risk of being set up: he is specifically warned not to accept documents from overly eager sources.
Yet this is effectively how his prison time comes about. He is arrested by the FSB in Yekaterinburg, during a second meeting with a source, just over a year after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Like all good journalists, his first concern is for his source’s safety - though he soon realises the source, Pavel, is fully complicit in what transpires. Doigralsya - a Russian word which means “you’ve played your way into trouble” - is what Gershkovich thinks as he ends up in prison.
Most of Gershkovich’s incarceration is spent in Lefortovo, on the outskirts of Moscow - a place that is “something of a contradiction: It was Russia’s most notorious prison, reserved for the highest-profile inmates - both Russian and foreign - but it also had the best conditions among Russian detention centres.”
His close relationship with his cellmate there, Seryoga, is emotionally affecting, though this was the one stated part of the book where he blurred reality, given the potential risks (in the author’s note, Gershkovich clarifies that Seryoga is a single composite character, when he actually lived with more than one cellmate). His other close relationships are with his lawyers, who tell him early on that while being cleared of crime is almost impossible, “our real goal is to help you go through this ordeal with dignity”.
At one point, Gershkovich remembers Gulag historian Yury Dmitriyev telling the journalist about his own year in prison: “I don’t make a great tragedy out of that year. I just think of it as a work trip. I’ve gained a better understanding of what my subjects - the people I dig up and write about - were thinking.” He invoked a common Russian saying: “if you’re afraid of wolves, you shouldn’t go into the forest.” Dmitriyev has since been arrested again, and for a much longer term.
Thankfully released, Gershkovich lived to tell the tale - both his own and that of so many others. His resulting book is a gripping, courageous and important one.
Sally Hayden is the author of My Fourth Time, We Drowned and This is Also a Love Story and an Irish Times journalist.

title: Peugeot’s electric E-208 GTi proves that fun still lives. This is a real 1980s throwback
description: Electric cars don’t have to be dull and Peugeot’s hot hatch proves it
content:
We don’t buy cars the same way we buy other consumer durables. Our fridges are, generally, not extensions of our personalities. We are generally unworried about how well or ill our choice of washing machine reflects upon our lifestyle choices. But a car? A car speaks volumes. Even those who think themselves uncaring of cars buy with one eye on image, on perception.
Which is why it’s important that we have more enjoyable, engaging and downright fun electric cars . It’s the fun cars that allow us to tell more entertaining stories and to build legends, and which therefore make electric vehicles more desirable. Until now, with rare exceptions for the likes of Alpine, Cupra and Porsche , buying an electric car has been all about rationality at its most extreme, even downright penny-pinching.
Peugeot is about to change that. It’s not that the new E-208 GTi is the first electric hot hatch (the Alpine A290 and the Cupra Born and Raval VZ got there first), but it’s the first that you don’t have to explain.
Thrown down a set of Alpine or Cupra keys on the table at the cafe and you’re in an aeon of explaining what the brand is and why you bought it.
Throw down, instead, a Peugeot GTi keyring and, since 1984, everyone knows what you’re about. If explaining is losing, then a GTi is definitely winning, and Peugeot is bringing the celebrated badge to electric motoring just before VW with its one-two punch of the new ID. Polo GTI (which will be this E-208 GTi’s sternest competition) and the ID.3 GTI.
The E-208 GTi is also a fond farewell to a car that’s been around since 2019 and which will shortly be replaced by an all-new 208 with far more avant-garde styling, both inside and out. In the grand tradition of such things, a hot hatch version seems an appropriate way to wave goodbye to a car that, more than once, took Peugeot to the top of the European sales charts.
To turn it into a GTi, visually, Peugeot has dipped into the Eighties back catalogue and brought forth memories of the original 205 GTi. Arguably the best hot hatch ever (although Renault and Volkswagen would dispute that), the 205 GTi set the template for a succession of gorgeous, fast, nimble Peugeots to follow. In invoking that memory, the E-208 is setting a bear trap for itself – fail to live up to the legacy and it will be roundly pilloried.
It gets off to a good start. The 205 GTi’s red pinstripes are brought up to date for 2026, and there’s a wealth of gloss black exterior trim and 208 GTi badges on the rear roof pillars, just as per the original.
More importantly, both aesthetically and in an engineering sense, the suspension is 25mm lower and as much as 58mm wider, which gives the E-208 an aggressive, but not outré, stance. Combined with some gorgeous 18-inch alloy wheels, it looks great.
It looks good inside too, with the 208’s ageing cabin titivated with fabulous high-back bucket seats which are among the best chairs in the game, lots of black leather and red stitching and bright red carpets. These are utter dirt magnets, but they couldn’t be more Eighties.
Space in the back is more usable than it is generous and the 309-litre boot is only just about able to keep the E-208 GTi on the right side of practical, but so far it’s fulfilling the hot hatch mantra – everyday use, happy day thrills.
Power comes from a 281hp electric motor driving the front wheels through a grip-sniffing limited slip differential, and energy comes from the same 51kWh battery which powers the regular E-208. Range is claimed at 375km on the no-cost option efficiency tyres, or 352km on the grippier, sportier Michelins which are a standard fit.
To make the E-208 GTi work properly, Peugeot turned to the boffins at Peugeot Sport, the company’s in-house racing team, which designs and runs its Le Mans racing efforts. That Le Mans 9X8 – only fitfully successful – is a hybrid, and that means Peugeot Sport has much expertise in batteries and motors working under the toughest conditions imaginable. So, the Sport guys didn’t just work on the suspension, steering and brakes, but also on the battery cooling and motor tech.
This is possibly why the E-208 GTi doesn’t suffer too badly from an underfed range. On our brisk test drive around the lowlands of Scotland – where you’ll find some of the best and most GTi-friendly roads in the world – we were on course to squeeze around 330km out of a full charge. It’s not intercontinental range, but it’s decent.
[ Range Rover Sport goes electric without losing its appetite for performance Opens in new window ]
Better by far than decent is the way the E-208 GTi drives. The steering, controlled by that small, hexagonal wheel, is sharp and talkative, and the wider, lower suspension plants the Peugeot firmly to the ground. That front differential – much less aggressive in its actions than in the related Opel Mokka GSE – finds grip and traction where others wouldn’t, and so the E-208’s nose sticks to the inside of a corner like honey to the bottom of a bowl of porridge.
The suspension is firm – it gets a bit rough around town – but the E-208 GTi feels wonderfully fluid on the open road, inducing grins and giggles in roughly equal measure. It is an utter delight to drive and wears its celebrated GTi badge with insouciance.
[ Volkswagen ID.Polo first drive: The Germans remember how to make a VW Opens in new window ]
It will be a car of limited appeal nonetheless. Only 40 are allocated to Ireland, arriving next February with a price tag orbiting around the €40,000 mark, which makes the Peugeot pricier than rival VW, Alpine and Cupra products, but also more powerful.
Crucially, it’s also the car that might – just maybe – convince petrolheads that being an electron-head is actually a good idea. A little more range would be welcome, of course, but this E-208 GTi is such good fun that you’ll forgive that literal shortcoming. It’s a fitting electric debut for an acclaimed badge and, hopefully, a car that inspires enthusiasm well into the coming all-electric era.

title: First look at Jaguar Type 01: Can this 1,030hp electric car save the brand?
description: It has taken five years to design and two years to hype, but will Jag’s electric reinvention take root?
content:
Some cars wow you with their design, to the point where you take a step back, trying to establish a baseline of understanding. The Jaguar Type 01 isn’t like that. Perhaps because we all saw the Type 00 concept and made up our minds about how this production four-door coupe (a GT in Jaguar-speak) would look.
Perhaps because the Type 01’s styling is in some ways less dramatic than you’d think. Perhaps because the photos simply can’t fully capture how this car actually looks. The surfacing is incredibly clean and free of needless flourishes. To appreciate this, you need to see light play across its surfaces.
Instead of stepping back, the Jaguar Type 01 draws you in. You start to notice the fine detailing, such as the incredibly slim four lines of LED lights (some 120 individual bulbs) that make up the headlamps. The way the rear “grille” looks far more dramatic, and enticing, than that of the concept car, which looked like an air conditioning unit had got lost on the way to the recycling centre.
Then your eyes make their way – via the sheer sides and the long, flat bonnet – to the rear three quarters. Here the sweeping rear pillar – which looks like a combination of a 1960s E-Type’s rear haunches and a 1970s XJS’ “flying buttress” pillars – meets the top of the rear wings; there’s a triangular indentation, almost as if someone pressed the nib of a fountain pen into the soft clay of a styling model.
That whole rear panel, which extends from the rear wheelarch to the roof to the edge of the windscreen, is one pressing, which was genuinely thought to be impossible to make until Jaguar’s engineers spent 1,500 hours developing new pressing tools, which are four storeys high and press the aluminium panel with up to 2,500 tonnes of force. It’s indicative of how much effort Jaguar has put into this new car and, indeed, into the wholesale reinvention of the brand.
To recap: Jaguar was shedding customers and cash at an unsustainable rate. A line-up of handsome, sharp-driving cars wasn’t enough to take on the might of BMW, Mercedes, and Audi, and an early lead in EV tech – with the I-Pace – was squandered as that model was only fitfully updated.
At the last moment, a ready-to-go all-electric new XJ saloon was canned, as Jaguar management realised that only a full and total reinvention of the brand and its cars would suffice.
Cue a two-year production shutdown, the creation of a new line-up of all-electric models, a concept car that drew admiration and ire in equal amounts, and a marketing campaign that had the anti-woke brigade reaching for their predictable poison pens. Phew.
Rawdon Glover is Jaguar’s managing director and has been at the centre of this storm to recreate one of the most storied brands in motoring and move it into a new era of selling fewer cars, albeit more profitable with prices closer to Bentley than BMW. A more boutique brand, then, leaving more mass-market premium sales to its sister brand Land Rover. How, then, will we know whether this has all worked?
“I think the challenge for any new car isn’t necessarily year one sales, but how it sells in year four,” Glover tells The Irish Times. “There will be other models, so it’s all about the success of the product cycle. So we’ll get a good idea now whether we’ve been successful or not, but it’s about the longer term. Does someone buy one of these and then move on to another model in the line-up?”
Jaguar is, of course, owned by the vast Indian-based conglomerate Tata who bought JLR (Jaguar Land Rover) from Ford in 2008. The Indian owners apparently make Glover’s life a little easier.
“We need to get a return on the investment in this platform, and the key thing for me is that Jaguar has not been additive financially to the organisation for some time. It needs to be,” Glover says.
“I’ve not seen anything from our shareholders thus far that isn’t totally supportive of the direction that we’re going in. Jaguar in India means something quite different to what it does in many other markets. It’s really held in very, very high esteem, and it was one of the big reasons that Tata bought up JLR. That was the emotional draw for them, but as a company, Tata is not a short-term company.”
The business case might seem tricky to make from the outside. A luxury car with electric power is, it seems, not really what many luxury car buyers want just yet. But Jaguar says its research shows that 78 per cent of the potential customers it polled were far more interested in style, branding and performance than on the power source. Crucially, an equal 78 per cent of those buyers would be new to the Jaguar brand, and conquest sales will be crucial.
Certainly, the Type 01 will have a more than adequate technical specification. Three electric motors (two at the rear, in a single compact unit) developing 1,030hp, with 0-100km/h acceleration in just 3.2 seconds (although Jaguar says that the “in-gear” acceleration times were far more important during development).
A large 120kWh battery with a potential range of 700km. Air suspension that drops the car 15mm on its springs for better efficiency at speed, and ultra-fast charging that adds 300km of extra range in 13 minutes of charging if you can find a rapid enough charger. The “sustained highway driving” range (motorways, in other words) is reckoned to be around 520km.
Inside, the cabin is calm, uncluttered and light. There’s no rear window, so you get a rear-facing camera instead, whose display screen is mounted low on the dash, in a position familiar to driver of 1960s cars.
There’s a single 24-inch sweep of digital screen behind the wheel and a small seven-inch screen on the console between the seats for major controls. Brass (actually anodised aluminium because brass is heavy) trim runs along a dramatic central spine that divides the cabin into four individual seats, and there’s soft carpeting that extends to the lower parts of the doors so that you feel as if you’re enveloped in a soft bathtub.
There’s not a lot of space. This is a large, long, low car (just 1,400mm tall) and headroom front and rear is only just about adequate. Getting into the back seats involves heaving yourself over a broad sill and then in through a small door, but it’s comfy once you’re in there.
Jaguar does admit that it’s focused on the comfort and layout for front seat passengers, but it has separated out the battery pack, leaving a deep well into which rear-seat feet can fit and allowing both front and rear seats to be mounted lower to keep that plunging roofline. This is a selfish car, in that respect. The boot is small and shallow – although there’s some deeper underfloor storage – and there’s a shallow “frunk” under that endless nose for stashing your charging cables.
[ Range Rover Sport goes electric without losing its appetite for performance Opens in new window ]
At the rear, the aerodynamics have been so finely honed that there’s actually 4kg of overpressure – a gentle push from the air – to aid efficiency. The distance between the top of the front wheel arch (which houses 23-inch alloys as standard) and the beginning of the bonnet is actually even more shallow than that of the F-Type sports car, yet there’s far more suspension movement.
While the earlier messaging was all about how the Type O1 was breaking with Jaguar’s tradition, it couldn’t be further from the truth. The E-Type and the XJS shocked and stunned when they made their debuts, and the Type 01’s handling and ride have been inspired by that of the gorgeous mid-1970s XJ12-C Coupe.
[ Best used electric estates: what should replace my diesel Mazda6? Opens in new window ]
This is a car that allows some body roll to keep its occupants comfy, rather than trying to knock their fillings out in search of sportier handling. It seems to be a car with soul, rather than the faceless hordes of stamped-out-by-the-hundred Chinese competitors.
Will it work? Can Jaguar pull off its all-electric moonshot? We can’t wait to find out. Now we know what the new Jag finally looks like in the showroom-ready metal, we have but a few more months to wait until we, and customers, get behind the wheel of the actual production car. The effort, the hype, and the hope will be answered.

title: Kenmare shares soar on confirmation of Abu Dhabi bid approach
description: International Resources Holding given until November 17th to make a formal bid for Kenmare Resources
content:
Kenmare Resources shares soared by as much as 41 per cent in London on Tuesday as the titanium minerals miner confirmed it has received a bid approach from a company controlled by the de facto business head of Abu Dhabi’s ruling family.
It follows a report in The Irish Times that International Resources Holding (IRH), a unit of International Holding Company (IHC), which is chaired by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, has been running a fresh round over Kenmare two years after it previously looked at pursuing a bid.
Sheikh Tahnoon is a brother of the president of the United Arab Emirates and a key figure overseeing the business interests of the Al Nahyan family, Abu Dhabi’s ruling royal family. IHC has a market value of the equivalent of more than €190 billion.
“The board of Kenmare Resources plc notes recent press speculation and confirms that it has received a non-binding proposal from International Resources Holdings RSC Ltd regarding a possible cash offer for the entire issued and to be issued share capital of Kenmare,” Kenmare said in a statement.
Kenmare, led by chief executive Tom Hickey , added that discussions are ongoing and that IRH has been given a deadline of 5pm on November 17th to at least declare a firm intention to make a formal offer or walk away.
Shares in Kenmare jumped as much as 41 per cent to £2.555 on Tuesday in London , where they are more frequently traded than in Dublin . That gave the company a market value of £228 million (€268.6 million).
Kenmare’s shares were trading more than 50 per cent below their 2024 highs before the news – their lowest level in more than seven years – amid ongoing falling prices for titanium minerals and uncertainty and protracted talks over a new royalties agreement regarding its key Moma mine in Mozambique.
The mine produces about 6 per cent of global titanium stocks. Its main products, ilmenite and rutile, are used in everything from paints, plastics and paper to aircraft, medical equipment and golf clubs.
News of the fresh interest from IRH comes 16 months after Kenmare Resources walked away from takeover talks with its former managing director, Michael Carvill , and another Abu Dhabi company, private equity firm Oryx Global Partners, after the consortium made it clear it would only be willing to proceed with a bid that was below an initial £473 million proposal previously made in March 2025.
The proposal is another example of Abu Dhabi’s willingness to continue doing outbound deals amid the upheaval in the region due to the Iran war.
Sheikh Tahnoon oversees vast swathes of the city’s oil wealth as chairman of its biggest wealth fund, its top lender and its main artificial intelligence investor. These institutions have become some of the main vehicles for deploying the emirate’s substantial capital around the world.
IHC is Abu Dhabi’s largest listed firm and counts IRH as one of its units. Like other IHC units, the mining group has been prolific in recent years. It entered the mining industry in late 2023, when it struck a $1.1 billion deal for Zambia’s Mopani copper complex.
Last year, it agreed to acquire a majority stake in Alphamin Resources Corporation, gaining access to one of the world’s biggest tin mines.
Kenmare said its statement on Tuesday, in response to The Irish Times report, was made without IRH’s approval. IRH declined to comment.

title: Eva Marie Saint, star of movies North by Northwest and On the Waterfront, dies at 102
description: One of the last survivors of Hollywood’s golden age of the 1940s and ’50s dies of natural causes at her home
content:
Eva Marie Saint, one of the last survivors of Hollywood’s golden age of the 1940s and ’50s, has died aged 102.
Saint’s screen work spanned six decades. She made her screen debut opposite Marlon Brando in On the Waterfront, starred in Alfred Hitchcock ’s celebrated thriller North by Northwest, and in one of her last screen appearances, played Superman’s adoptive mother Martha Kent in the 2006 superhero film Superman Returns.
A family spokesman said on Tuesday that Saint had died of natural causes at her home in Los Angeles.
[ Eva Marie Saint, one of the immortals, radiated old-school Hollywood glamour Opens in new window ]
Born in 1924 in New Jersey to a Quaker family, Saint had an early career as a jobbing radio and TV performer that was chronicled in a 1949 feature in Life magazine which started with the prophetic words – “The name of Eva Marie Saint may someday be a household word” – then documented her struggles to gain a foothold in the entertainment industry. By the early ’50s she was making some headway, appearing in 1953 in both the original telecast and the premiere Broadway production of the Horton Foote play The Trip to Bountiful.
Saint told the Santa Barbara Independent that On the Waterfront director Elia Kazan spotted her in The Trip to Bountiful and invited her to audition by improvising a scene with Marlon Brando. Saint said she found the experience difficult, but was offered the role of Edie Doyle, Brando’s love interest, in the hardhitting drama about mob union activities; she would go on to win the Oscar for best supporting actress in 1955.
After this meteoric success, Saint quickly began securing a wide variety of leading roles. She starred opposite Bob Hope in That Certain Feeling, played a woman married to a secret drug addict in the Fred Zinnemann-directed issue picture A Hatful of Rain, and co-starred with Elizabeth Taylor in the period western Raintree County.
Saint then achieved a highly coveted role opposite Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock’s 1959 spy classic North by Northwest: secret agent Eve Kendall, “a blond who has all the answers”. She said in a TCM interview that she in part secured her career-defining role by wearing beige and white gloves to a lunch appointment with Hitchcock.
[ Happy birthday, Mel Brooks: 100 gloriously tasteless years. Long may you remain above ground Opens in new window ]
Saint kicked off the 1960s by playing American nurse Kitty Fremont in Exodus, the hit adaptation of Leon Uris’s novel about the creation of the state of Israel, but subsequently eased up on her workload to prioritise her young family. In 1962 she appeared opposite Warren Beatty in All Fall Down as a woman infatuated with Beatty’s drifter; starred as Richard Burton ’s wife in The Sandpiper in 1965 alongside Elizabeth Taylor, and played a journalist who has an affair with Yves Montand’s race driver in Grand Prix in 1966.
Despite critical acclaim for her role in the 1970 infidelity drama Loving alongside George Segal, Saint’s film parts largely dried up in the ’70s and ’80s, with the actor instead turning to TV movies and guest appearances.
Sporadic film appearances ensued after a “comeback” in the 1986 Tom Hanks /Jackie Gleason comedy Nothing in Common; later appearances included as Sam Shepard ’s mother in the Wim Wenders -directed western Don’t Come Knocking in 2005, and a year later she was cast in Superman Returns – where she was “reunited” with On the Waterfront star Brando, whose estate gave permission for 1978 footage to be used in the film after his death in 2004.
Saint worked more consistently in TV, winning a best supporting actress Emmy award for the 1990 mini-series People Like Us, adapted from Dominick Dunne’s novel. Her final onscreen role was in Winter’s Tale as the sister of the seemingly immortal Colin Farrell .
Saint married Jeffrey Hayden in 1951 and had two children; they remained together until his death in 2016. – Guardian

title: Christa Pike conscious and speaking after  failed execution in Tennessee, say lawyers
description: Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as authorities  attempted to end her life over stabbing death of classmate
content:
Christa Pike, the inmate who survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her , is awake and speaking as she receives treatment in hospital, her lawyers have said.
“Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care. Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” lawyers for Pike said in a statement.
Her lawyers said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital “who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her”.
The statement was the first indication that Pike has improved since an ambulance took her from a Nashville prison last Wednesday.
A spokeswoman for the Tennessee Department of Correction said she could provide no information other than that Pike remained in hospital on Tuesday.
Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as the authorities attempted to put her to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The lethal injection drug did not kill her, but her lawyers said her arms were left burned and blistered.
Dr Joel Zivot, a professor of anaesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike’s legal team, said the development “bodes well for a good recovery”.
But, he added, it could be weeks or months before anyone knows exactly what Pike’s recovery might look like, and whether her competency could be restored to a level that might enable the state to try again to execute her.
“She’s still in the ICU,” he said. “She has recovered to a certain degree that she’s able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk.”
Pike’s lawyers are set to go to court on Wednesday as they seek to learn more about what happened in the failed lethal injection.
They are seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, records and other information from the attempted execution on September 30th.
Chancery Court Judge I’Ashea Myles scheduled a Wednesday morning status conference in the case. – AP

title: Budget 2027: Budget puts public finances on worse trajectory, watchdog warns
description: Help-to-buy scheme increases; free contraception age rises; fuel allowance to increase by €5
author_name: Sarah Burns, Katie Mellett, Laura Coates
content:
Thank you for following our live budget coverage today. We’ll be back tomorrow with all the latest budget news, reaction and analysis. If you have a query for our expert budget panel, please submit it here as they will begin answering your questions from 7am Wednesday morning.
The planned new personal investment accounts are “not a get rich scheme”, Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris has said, as he also raised the prospect of a future phase of the scheme allowing people to set up accounts for their children.
Harris was speaking at a post-budget press conference where he was asked about the possibility of increasing the €12,000-a-year contribution limit and what would be included in the second phase of the scheme, writes Political Correspondent Cormac McQuinn .
He noted that phase one “only started today”, and on the level of contributions allowed, added: “What’s the aim here? So this is not a SSIA scheme. It’s not a get-rich-quick scheme”.
“This is a scheme to build up financial resilience in the years ahead.”
Harris said: “I was always very clear that this was not about wealthy people getting wealthy and I don’t know or represent that many people who are in a position to save in an investment account, after their bills, in a cost-of-living crisis, 12 grand a year.
“So I think that limit is significant. I think it’s helpful to have a 12 grand limit that somebody might come into a once-off thing. You could come upon as a gift or inheritance.
“You know, different things can arise and give people that flexibility.”
He also said: “There’s a duty to care when we’re in a country where participation rates in retail investments have been very very low.”
On phase two of the scheme, Harris said: “let’s not jump over phase one” but added: “different things are being suggested by different people”.
“The idea of an account for your children, some countries have done that. That’s certainly something that could be considered in due course.”
He said there is also the idea of specific accounts to target specific social issues or parts of the economy and he has “an open mind on all of that”.
The “sole motivation” in setting up a new Public Spending Efficiency Taskforce“ is to try and deliver better services for people and build a better State”, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers has said.
He made the remarks at a post-budget press conference as he responded to Solidarity TD Ruth Coppinger’s claim that he had gone “full-on Musk” to announce a US Doge-style [Department of Government Efficiency] operation in the public sector, writes Political Correspondent Cormac McQuinn .
Chambers noted that he and Coppinger share the Dublin West constituency and said “both of us see the challenges that face many families around public service delivery, where we’ve seen an exponential increase in spending in the last five to six years, but not necessarily a level of delivery that people expect”.
He added “we shouldn’t just have a conversation about efficiency, reform, and delivery, at a time of economic contraction where we have a big fiscal deficit and it’s a very negative cycle.
“How can we use a period of growth of a general Government surplus to drive better efficiency of spend for every area of public expenditure.
“I think it’s smart budgeting. It’s better management of our public finances.”
He continued: “ultimately, my sole motivation here is to try and deliver better services for people and build a better State that works better in communities across the country”.
“And we know that in different areas of spending, that’s absolutely possible, where it’s scrutinised in a more extensive way, and ultimately that creates space to do more in a budgetary cycle where we’re moderating day-to-day spending.”
Speaking earlier in the Dáil Coppinger also said the efficiency taskforce would be news to public sector workers “taking to the streets” next week, and she accused Chambers of arrogance in his approach to the threat of industrial action amid the row over talks on a new public pay deal.
Chambers denied public sector workers should be concerned about the efficiency taskforce, saying “public servants want to work in organisations that are organised to deliver better”.
Government proposals to increase the inheritance allowance from €400,000 to €420,000 for sons or daughters, before capital acquisition tax is applied, will benefit just three per cent of the population, Sinn Féin’s David Cullinane has said.
He said the measure showed Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael “represent a cosseted, privileged class”.
Minister for Agriculture Martin Heydon introduced the financial resolution on the inheritance tax allowance in the Dáil, which he said would come into effect from midnight on Tuesday, writes Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
A second bracket includes siblings inheriting from a brother or sister, where the allowance increases from €40,000 to €44,000 before tax is applied, with an increase from €20,000 to €22,000 for anyone else. The measure was accepted by 96 to 65 votes.
Cullinane said it was a tax break for the wealthy and privileged, which was vehemently disputed by Independent Ireland TD Ken O’Flynn who called for equality for those leaving their estate to nieces and nephews.
He said there are 300,000 childless couples in this country and “there is something seriously wrong when you have bought your home, paid your tax, you can leave the property to a niece or nephew but the house will be sold to pay the tax”.
The Cork North-Central TD said: “I don’t believe there is any difference between a son or daughter, or niece or nephew or someone who has loved you all your life.”
The measure also penalises single people, he said. He added Sinn Féin talked about millionaires and the wealthy but he said “this affects a lot of people in this country” and he described Cullinane’s remarks as “disingenuous”.
His party colleague Michael Fitzmaurice said TDs had been approached over the last number of years by people who never got married or had no family, or by same sex couples “and there is a frustration out there that they are not being treated equally”.
He added: “We need to listen because there were a considerable 300,000 people who “don’t have a next generation” and want to help a niece or nephew who may not have a house to get on the property ladder.
People Before Profit TD Paul Murphy said, however, the main inequality relates to a small number of people who are passing on a major inheritance.
He said the €400,000 increase to €420,000 will benefit just three per cent “at a time when 40 per cent of parents” say they have to cut back on food for their families.
Murphy added that if people are passing on a farm or a business, that tax is written down by 90 per cent with an allowance before tax of €4.2 million.
But Independent TD Michael Healy-Rae criticised his argument, saying people were not going to sell off the farm and go “heading off to the Bahamas”.
“On paper the land may look like it is worth a lot but unless you are disposing of an asset it is only a way for you to make a living,” he added.
At a post-budget press conference Tánaiste Simon Harris responded to criticism from the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (Ifac) of the Government’s spending plans, writes Political Correspondent Cormac McQuinn .
Ifac responded to the budget saying it “puts the public finances on a worsening trajectory by repeatedly breaking established spending limits and increasingly relying on high-risk corporation tax”.
In response, Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris said Ifac had an important role to play, and added it is a reminder to avoid “group think or the herd mentality”.
However, he also said he does not believe that “all types of spending are the same” adding: “when you make a decision to invest in capital, that is in many ways a saving because it is investing in public infrastructure. It is an asset that the State has”,
He also pointed out that the Government is putting an extra €1 billion into the Future Ireland Fund and said the the Coalition continues to run a general general Government surplus.
Harris said the tax package does go beyond what was announced in the Summer Economic Statement, but said: “That is our right as a democratically elected Government, and we’ve done that on the basis of the energy proposals that we brought forward” to respond to the energy crisis.
“I think the citizens in this country quite rightly expect us and indeed require us to take measures on both the tax and expenditure sides to try and help with that.”
Harris said the reliance on corporation tax is “a real concern, and I think they’re [Ifac] right to say that”.
“That’s one of the reasons why we are trying to actually build up the funds.
“It’s one of the reasons why we’re investing now in infrastructure.”
He said it is one of the reasons why the Government has to “prepare for a time when our public finances won’t look like they do today.”
Harris also said there are efforts to build up indigenous industry citing the announcement of an extra €1 billion to be invested by the Ireland Strategic Investment Fund to help “scale up the next generation of Irish companies”.
Some 41 per cent of approved claims for the Help to Buy housing scheme “are for people who do not need it”, Labour housing spokesman Conor Sheehan has claimed.
He was speaking during a Dáil debate on the financial resolution introduced by Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke to increase the level of support to first time buyers by €5,000 to €35,000, writes Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
The increased grant was accepted by 92 to 68 in the first financial resolution vote.
In the debate, the Minister said 69,000 Help to Buy claims had been approved from 125,702 applications, with a total value of €1.6 billion.
He said the level of support was worth €35,000 or 10 per cent of the cost of the home, or the amount of income tax or Dirt paid in the four years before the application for the relief in the scheme.
Burke stressed “it ensures taxpayers get more of their money back while buying a house”.
But the Labour spokesman asked why the Government was “ignoring all of the available evidence” from the Parliamentary Budget office, the ESRI and the Central Bank, who warned it would result in increased house prices.
Sheehan said it was a “direct wealth transfer” to private developers.
“We know that 41 per cent of approved claims are for people who do not need it.”
Sinn Féin’s David Cullinane said Help to Buy “is a demand side subsidy” which “clearly doesn’t work”, and he told the Minister “you’re putting in place a scheme that “drives up prices”.
He said house prices increased by €25,000 last year and the same the previous year.
Social Democrats housing spokesman Rory Hearne highlighted his “serious concerns this will inflate house prices further”.
He pointed out that in 2020 the median house price was €250,000 and is now €396,000. “Fianna Fail and Fine Gael in Government have added €146,000 to the cost of a house”, he said, but it seemed the Government had reduced the investment in affordable housing by €200 million.
People Before Profit TD Paul Murphy said it was not a help to buy scheme, but a “help to profit” scheme for developers. He said the funding “temporarily passes through the hands of buyers but ends up in the hands of developers”.
Sinn Féin housing spokesman Eoin Ó Broin claimed the €5,000 increase was to save the Minister for Housing from embarrassment after he had called for a €20,000 increase in the scheme.
He said Minister for Finance Simon Harris had said he did not want to do anything that would increase the price of houses. “What changed?” the Dublin Mid-West TD asked.
Ó Broin believed it was to give the Minister for Housing “cover to say he got something”.
Independent TD Carol Nolan said the Irish Aid budget should be cut in light of the crisis affecting Irish families, writes Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
She said the Government had opted for a series of incremental measures to deal with the cost pressures facing carers and ordinary families while the budget allocation to the Department of Foreign Affairs was €1.3 billion.
“Of that, $85 million euro is allocated to overseas development and international cooperation programmes, and some of the countries that are included in that aid have a record of human rights abuses.”
The Offaly TD was “very concerned about that” and said the Irish Aid budget should be cut when she had pensioners in her office “every day of the week are telling me how difficult it is to make ends meet. And these are people that worked all their lives”.
Independent Ireland leader Michael Collins said people are being stretched “to the extreme limit” by the cost-of-living crisis, writes Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
He said the Government does not appreciate the depth of the “crisis situation” for people.
Citing one consumer’s experience, he said a woman saw her weekly shopping bill go up “at least 17 or 18 quid in one week and she got the same list and the same shop as she did the week before”.
Criticising the €10 increase in the weekly State pension, he said it was “nowhere near” what is required, adding that pensioners are afraid to turn on the lights because they are “experiencing savage expense every week”.
People Before Profit TD Richard Boyd Barrett said there is “no good reason” in the budget for workers to stop their plans to go on strike on October 14th and 21st, over public sector pay, writes Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
He said: “This Government has given them less than nothing in this budget when you look at how the tax changes relate to the actual increase in the cost of living.
“Even by the Government’s own budget book, nobody is getting more than about 1.5 per cent and many are getting less than one per cent.”
The Dún Laoghaire TD said more than two million workers “will not benefit at all from the changes in the higher tax band. They will not get anything from that. They will get something from the USC change but you are talking at best about 1.5 per cent and in some cases, only 0.5 per cent when inflation is currently running at 3.9 per cent and projected to be about 3.5 per cent.”
Boyd Barrett said workers needed a pay increase of about 10 per cent “just to keep pace with inflation and they have got nowhere near it. ‘Get your placards ready’ is what I am saying to workers. ‘Get out on those pickets’.”
He added: “It should not just be the public sector workers who are going on strike, it should be the private sector workers as well.”
The State’s budgetary watchdog has strongly criticised the Government’s budget, warning it puts the public finances on “a worse trajectory”, while increasing the State’s reliance on “high-risk corporation tax”.
The criticism from the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council comes as the Department of Finance projected corporate tax revenue will rise to nearly €45 billion by the end of the decade.
That projection is on the basis Ireland will benefit from the new minimum global rate for multinationals and as companies exhaust allowances for domiciling assets here.
In its critique of Budget 2027, Ifac said spending increases net of tax measures have been running “at a blistering pace in recent years”.
It noted that a “sustainable speed limit” of 5 per cent for both was set in 2021. “But governments have since budgeted for around 6 per cent growth, before actually delivering about 10 per cent a year on average, double the speed limit,” the council said.
If overruns continue on their current trajectory, net spending will increase by 9 per cent this year, it warned.
Solidarity TD Ruth Coppinger claimed Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers had come into the Dáil and gone “full-on Musk” to announce a Doge-style [Department of Government Efficiency] operation in the public sector, writes Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
She said: “He’s setting up this Public Spending Efficiency Taskforce that will monitor on a daily basis, scrutinise day-to-day spending, making greater efficiencies.
“That will be news now to the tens of thousands of public sector workers who are going to be taking to the streets next Wednesday. And let’s face it, there is nothing in that budget.
“It was so high-handed and arrogant of Minister Chambers to call on them not to go ahead with the industrial action when he never once mentioned how he’s going to deal with pay for public sector workers.”
In his budget speech, the Minister said, over the past year “I have introduced stronger expenditure controls, greater scrutiny of how staff resources are deployed and a renewed emphasis on accelerating infrastructure delivery”.
He stressed: “Reform can never be an occasional exercise or a response to emerging pressures. It must sit at the heart of everything we do.
“And through the Accelerating Infrastructure Taskforce, we have made great strides on infrastructure reform this year. And I believe we can emulate this when it comes to day-to-day spending.
“Therefore, it is my intention to establish a new Public Spending Efficiency Taskforce whose mandate will be to extensively scrutinise day to day public spending.”
He said it would “identify areas across public spending where there is scope to drive greater efficiencies and it will recommend specific actions that can deliver better services and greater value for money”.
“I have asked my officials to establish this taskforce, with terms of reference to be finalised and work to commence within three months.”
A central talking point in the lead-up to Budget 2027 was whether the Government’s promised tax cuts for middle-income earners would be meaningful or just a partial hedge against inflation, writes Economics Correspondent Eoin Burke-Kennedy .
If the tax bands and credits, which determine how much individual workers pay in tax, are not adjusted for wage inflation each year, then workers end up paying proportionately more in tax to the exchequer.
In the end, workers got a higher-than-expected tax break than initially signalled. The point at which people pay the higher 40 per cent rate of income tax is to be increased by €2,500 to €46,500 while personal, employee and earned income tax credits will increase by €125 to €2,125, reducing the liability for all earners.
Aontú leader Peadar Tóibín described the Government’s policy on the cost of fuel as “absolutely bonkers”, writes Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
He said if a worker pulled into a petrol station and puts €100 in his or her tank, €45 in excise duty “will still go to the Government”.
The Meath West TD added: “Given the fact that petrol is around €1.97 for petrol and €2.20 for diesel (a litre) at the pump, it is this Government’s expressed plan to increase diesel by 32 cents and petrol by 27 cents a litre from next February.
“That is absolutely bonkers. The Government also intend to hike carbon taxes on petrol and diesel, not once, but twice next year. It is absolutely unbelievable.”
He asked: “Are the Government living in a parallel universe?”
The Government and its money Ministers, Simon Harris and Jack Chambers, will go to great lengths to highlight how people will benefit from the raft of measures announced in the budget, writes Consumer Affairs Correspondent Conor Pope .
But, despite all the money spent, it’s clear almost nobody will be better off in 2027.
Geopolitical unrest and the spike in the price of pretty much everything will more than cancel out the welfare and allowance increases, as well as the tax changes central to what could be termed Schrödinger’s budget – one which is simultaneously generous and mean.
The big winners – if that’s not too strong a word – will be couples in a household where both people earn more than €50,000 a year.
Independent Kerry TD Michael Healy-Rae made his first speech in the Dáil since he was assaulted in Dublin while sitting in his car in traffic in Dublin on September 16th, writes Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
The former minister of state for agriculture who resigned over the national fuel protest crisis defended much of the Government’s budget and hit out at the Opposition’s alternative budgets.
He said if they were relying on the Opposition’s proposals “we’d be in a very dire place”.
He said: “For 15 or 16 years we’ve had the same thing being thrown out all the time. It’s a case that this is wrong and that is wrong.”
Healy-Rae compared the Opposition’s complaints to the weather. He said “if it was a fine day they’d say there was something wrong, that we might get sunburn”.
He welcomed the commitment to no further carbon tax increase for the duration of this Government but said the reduction on home-heating oil and extension of the fuel subvention “would be so quickly evaporated by the high cost of living”.
The cost of fuel “really has to be looked at”, he said.
“It is a problem, it is contributing to the cost of living.”
On agriculture, he also welcomed the extension of the fuel subvention scheme but said there were people who did not qualify for the scheme and he believed “there is tweaking that could be done there” to allow farmers and contractors currently excluded to allow them to apply for the subvention.
Healy-Rae, who served for just over a year as a minister of state, pointed to his area of responsibility and said investment in forestry “seems to have stalled and not been increased”, when it should have and “that is of concern to me”.
Ibec, the group representing Irish business, welcomed Budget 2027’s “strong emphasis on workforce transition and praised the decision to unlock €150 million from the National Training Fund".
The group was “disappointed by the Government’s decision to accept the Low Pay Commission’s recommendation for an increase which is almost double what most businesses were forecasting for 2027.”
Ibec also welcomed the introduction of the Savings and Investment Scheme, which “creates opportunities for savers to see a better return on their money and has the potential to generate capital investment.”
Fergal O’Brien, executive director of policy, lobbying, and global affairs said: “while much of this budget commentary will focus on household supports, the decisions around AI and innovation are vital to future-proofing our economy and workforce opportunities.
Budget 2027 points to a Government “that doesn’t see and doesn’t understand the impact that the cost of energy crisis has for large parts of our society”, Green Party leader Roderic O’Gorman told the Dáil, writes Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
He criticised the Government’s failure to make provision for targeted energy credits “the most effective way of providing immediate support to those who are desperately struggling, as well as to those in the squeezed middle”.
The Dublin West TD said: “I’ve no doubt that the Government will be forced to do a U-turn and bring in energy credits at some point this winter.”
He also hit out at the “significant rhetoric around energy transition” that provided nothing “to help households reduce their use of expensive oil and gas”.
Focus Ireland said: “Budget 2027 fails to prioritise homelessness or even discuss the crisis despite a record of nearly 18,000 in emergency accommodation.”
The organisation said that while it is welcome that homelessness was acknowledged in this year’s budget, the measures announced “fall far short of what is needed to address the crisis”.
It noted that over the period since homelessness was last referenced in a budget speech, the number of children experiencing homelessness has risen by 46 per cent, from 3,991 in October 2023 to 5,830 on Tuesday.
Mike Allen, director of advocacy at Focus Ireland, said: “In such a massive giveaway budget there are some things to welcome, but the overall conclusion is that the Government has decided that homelessness is something it has no answers for.
“This budget shows that groups that make the biggest noise receive the greatest attention, but families experiencing homelessness are focused on finding stability and caring for their children.”
Labour finance spokesman Ged Nash described Minister for Finance Simon Harris and Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers as “soundbite Harris and Jack GPT”, writes Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
He described the budget as one for those who already have “a few bob in the bank” and said the Tánaiste had “some hard neck” to describe it as a “workers’ budget”, especially “after leaving them out last year”.
He said the cliched phrase “‘the people who get up early in the morning’ was brought off the bench ahead of this budget for the pre-match warm-up. But those waking up this evening for the night shift will be sorely disappointed with what they’ve heard from Government this afternoon.
“Far from being a budget for those who get up early in the morning, this is a budget for those who can afford the bloody good lie-in. A budget for those who are already have a few bob in the bank, who can afford to save thousands of euro and where their money is burning a hole in their pockets.”
He said it was a budget that “does the business for the lucky few who inherit a bit of cash”.
The Louth TD said Ireland in 2026 is a rich country but it is a country “that’s full of contradictions, unprecedented numbers of people at work alongside growing, shameful child poverty, and deprivation, climbing inequality, set against overflowing tax revenues, embarrassing public service gaps after a decade”.
His party colleague Marie Sherlock said “there’s a serious whiff of a parallel universe” that the Government is inhabiting “when we look at the terms of the detail of this budget”.
Pointing to the sports budget she said “it sits uneasily with me” that at a time when there is “enormous need across in clubs” and when so many “cannot access sports capital grant, they’re allocating €14 million to bring rich yanks” to Adare Manor next year for the Ryder Cup.
She loved sport and loved watching golf “but I believe that that amount of money is a seriously scandalous amount of State support to that event”.
Family Carers Ireland said Budget 2027 “falls short of what is needed to support family carers and fails to respond to the growing care challenge facing Ireland”.
While welcoming measures that will provide some additional support to carers, Family Carers Ireland said the overall package “falls short of what is needed to address the financial pressures, cost-of-living, lack of respite and growing demand for care facing families across the country”.
It said the failure to abolish the carer’s allowance means test represents “a missed opportunity”.
Sharon Foley, chief executive of Family Carers Ireland, said: “While there are some welcome measures in today’s package, many family carers will struggle to see how this budget changes the reality of their everyday lives.
“For too many families, the pressures remain the same. Rising costs, inadequate services and little or no access to respite.
“This budget asks family carers to continue carrying huge responsibility while offering too little in return.”

People will be able to put €12,000 a year tax-free into the Government new personal investment accounts, Minister for Finance Simon Harris announced in his Budget 2027 speech, writes Deputy Business Editor Dominic Coyle .
The accounts will feature a low tax rate of just 1 per cent. However, this tax will be levied on any amount in the account over a tax-free threshold of €50,000, not just the profit the account made over that year.
This holds out the prospect of people paying tax on their savings in years when they lost money simply because the balance of their account was above the €50,000 tax-free threshold.
Harris said the new accounts will be available from July 1st next year. About €170 billion is currently on deposit in Irish bank accounts, with the Minister having previously described that money as “sitting idle”.
The Government was accused of having “no idea” of the impact its decisions make “by the simple stroke of a pen”, writes Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
Social Democrats TD Aidan Farrelly said “there’s something deeply unethical about Government Ministers, consistently briefing journalists every time you’ve had a nice idea”.
The Kildare North TD said in the budget process over the last number of months Government parties are “all too busy fighting with each other over who gets to announce sports capital grants”.
“You’re fighting with each other over culture cards for young people, about pensions, excise cuts, childcare costs, all the time knowing that you’re not just playing a game between yourselves, but you’re playing a game with people’s realities.”
The party’s education spokeswoman Jen Cummins said the Government promised to reduce student contribution fees. “This year, we see there’ll be a reduction for those with siblings and whose families earn less than €120,000.
“You are not sticking to your promise of reducing this. Last year you reduced the fees by €500, but the previous year it was €1,000. And now this year it’s going to be €150.”
She said what the Government is giving students is “materially nothing” and “what this Government is doing is playing with words, because the maths is not mathing”.
This budget “represents a failure to protect the most vulnerable”, according to Social Democrats social protection spokesman Eoin Hayes.
He said it should be the “most important and urgent work of Government to alleviate poverty levels” and to help the 200,000 children living in consistent poverty, but “it is this Government that falls short in that work”.
Budget 2027 fired money around in various directions to try to address the cost-of-living crisis and react to the demand of a whole range of sectors, but you would search hard to find a central theme, writes Managing Editor Cliff Taylor .
Perhaps it is responding to events and that is in part understandable, given the big increases in energy prices and their impact on inflation.
But budgets are about priorities and when the package emerges from fractious last-minute negotiations between the two big parties of Government, some of these can be fudged or lost. Tactics get priority over strategy.
And the ante is inevitably upped when it comes to how much money is dispersed as both sides argue for “their” policy.
The public’s cry for support with energy costs “has fallen on deaf ears”, according to Social Democrats energy spokeswoman Jennifer Whitmore, writes Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran .
Their hopes to finally get help from the “suffocating” cost-of-living and from the “extortionate energy costs they are being crushed by” were ignored.
The Social Democrats’ proposed €400 targeted energy credit has “never been more necessary” with more than half a million people in arrears on their energy bills.
The Wicklow TD pointed to the ESRI’s calculation that families would need €480 to escape energy poverty, very similar to her party’s energy credit.
Energy companies are “upping the price” of electricity and gas “again and again” and “families simply cannot catch a break”.
She did however welcome “one area” where the Government had made progress extending the solar supports through the warmer homes scheme.
“I genuinely welcome that decision. For too long the conversation about home energy upgrades has focused solely on efficiency, while neglecting energy poverty and solar panels help both.”
