Arsenal prospect Tommy Setford made an early stop from Jamie Mullins before disaster struck in the seventh minute.
Divin Mubama’s deflected shot fell for Everton’s Tyler Dibling to tap in at the back post. Noah Jauny’s offside appeal fell on deaf ears as Turners Cross was silenced.
Ireland stuck to their plan of pressing England high. In the 22nd minute, they were level.
Jacob Devaney provided the spark, pushing up to steal possession. Rory Finneran quickly laid the ball into Lonergan’s path and he rifled beyond Setford into the far corner.
Turners Cross went up a decibel in the 38th minute as McManus demonstrated Ireland’s best attributes, hard tackling and instinctive finishing, to grab the lead.
First, the Gillingham left-back won the ball from Josh King, who was toppled over, and released Trent Kone-Doherty. McManus continued his run and when picked out by the Molde winger, he squeezed a first-time shot between Setford and his near post.
The hosts fought the urge to drop back and they had their insurance goal in the 63rd minute.
Seán Grehan’s long throw fell perfectly for Lonergan, who had previously won the ball back, to swing a boot and rattle the roof of the net.
It felt like Ireland’s night when Divine Mukasa dragged a glorious opportunity wide. It was just the start of an English siege.
Will Lankshear struck the post and Harrison Armstrong poked the follow-up wide. Jauny made a series of saves, with the best coming to deny Tyrique George.
Republic of Ireland: Jauny; Gallagher, Grehan, Murphy; McCarthy, Finneran, Devaney, McManus (Lipsiuc 64); Mullins (Noonan 82), Kone-Doherty (Akachukwu 75); Lonergan (McDonnell 82).
England: Setford; Gray, Alleyne, Simpson-Pusey, Mfuni; Peck (Lankshear 68), King (Armstrong 61); Dibling (Amo-Ameyaw 82), Nwaneri (Mukasa 46), Cozier-Duberry (George 61); Mubama.

title: Muted welcome for childcare cost reduction measures including €550 cap on fees
description: Sligo mother of three wants to see ‘more strategic thinking’ in Minister’s long-term plan for childcare
content:
One of the most anticipated measures in Budget 2027 – a significant decrease in childcare costs – has received a muted welcome.
Caroline De Bank, a Co Sligo mother of three, including one child in creche, said the cap on fees of €550 a month “sounds great ... [but] I’m not sure about it,” she said.
“They’re talking about capping childcare fees but that’s not going to happen until September of next year.”
In addition, while her four-year-old daughter will be eligible for it, the fees cap applies only to children aged up to senior infants class [about six years old] and will apply only to childcare facilities within the core funding scheme.
Core funding is the funding stream provided by the Department of Children to providers who sign up to it.
Minister for Children Norma Foley , at a budget briefing on Tuesday, said the goal was, within the lifetime of the Government, to bring fees down to €200 a month for all children, irrespective of their age, in core funding care.
Currently fees for a child up to six, in 45 hours of care a week, are capped at €735 a month. From September next year these families look set to save about €2,000 a year.
Providers expressed concern the €550 cap on what they may charge would not be adequately compensated by the core funding scheme, which could force some providers out of core funding.
Childhood Services Ireland (CSI), an Ibec group representing early learning and care providers, said: “Any measure that puts money back into parents’ pockets is good news.”
“However, what we find very concerning is that providers are being told they will have to reduce fees without yet knowing how much additional core funding, if any, will be available to compensate for that reduction in income,” said CSI director Stephanie Roy.
Foley said, however, the overall increase in the core funding budget was 35 per cent, which she believed would offset the reduction in fees they could charge.
Improving childcare availability and affordability is a key measure in addressing child poverty – a policy priority for the Government – by enabling more parents take up employment.
Barnardos, the charity working with the most vulnerable children and their families, welcomed the promised reduction in fees.
“The increased subsidy will significantly reduce costs for many families paying high fees,” it said.
“However, we need to see more detail to determine whether the measures will better support those community providers providing places for children experiencing the highest levels of disadvantage, who most benefit from early years care.”
[ The Irish Times view on childcare: a crunch issue for Budget 2027 Opens in new window ]
Echoing the charity, De Bank said she too had hoped to see measures to support staff at family resources centre crèches, such as the one her daughter attends.
“There is a mention of an increase in [childcare worker] wages ... There’s nothing tangible there in regards to how much are you going to increase salaries [or] what are you going to do to retain staff? How are you going to help owners to run their businesses and stay in the green?”
De Bank wants to see “more strategic thinking” in a “five- or 10-year plan for childcare”.
A feared reduction in Tusla’s budget to help pay the department’s contribution towards overruns in the Department of Education did not materialise. Tusla will see its budget increase next year to €1.4 billion – up from €1.2 billion this year.
Included in the budget uplift for the agency will be funds to fully open all 26 special care beds. Currently just 15 of the most secure care beds, for the most at-risk children, are open due to severe challenges recruiting and retaining staff.
Foley said the “target” was to have the remaining 11 beds open by the end of 2027.
Funding had been secured for 33.5 new posts at Oberstown Children’s Detention Centre, she said. The 46-bed campus in north Co Dublin has been at the centre of bitter industrial actions in recent months over pay and conditions.
A further priority for this Government is improving the position of disabled people, with the publication of a National Human Rights Strategy for Disabled People this year, and a looming first examination by the United Nations on compliance with the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, early in 2027.
The Minister of State with responsibility for disability, Emer Higgins, detailed an additional €62 million secured for disability residential services, plans for 212 new residential placements for disabled people, and 150 new posts secured in children’s disability network teams.

title: Rent tax credit increased to €1,150 for single people
description: Minister for Housing James Browne said there was no need for an increase in the €500,000 ceiling despite construction inflation
content:
The rent tax credit was increased by €150 for single people in Budget 2027 , but there was no increase to the €500,000 ceiling in the Help to Buy scheme , which rules many first-time buyers in Dublin out of it.
The budget will mean the value of the rent tax credit for single people rises from €1,000 to €1,150, while for couples renting it will increase from €2,000 to €2,300.
The programme for government committed to a gradual increase in the renters tax credit over the lifetime of the Government, but did not specify an annual amount. A rise of €200 in the renters’ tax credit was mooted before the budget. When asked if he felt the increase of €150 per person in the tax credit was enough, Minister for Housing James Browne admitted it was a “small help and not everything that people need”.
[ Social welfare, Help to Buy, tax changes and childcare costs: Everything we know about Budget 2027 so far Opens in new window ]
He said the Government “is never going to be able to” alleviate all rent pressures. “Rents are too high,” he said. “The way to address rents being too high is to increase supply and get more properties on to the market.”
He said the increase had to be seen in the context of other supports announced in the budget, including an increase in the 40 per cent income tax standard rate cut-off from €44,000 to €46,500.
He also stated that a lot of tenants who are eligible for the renters’ tax credit have not availed of it, and that they should come forward.
Browne announced that the Government is providing an additional €3.1 million to the Residential Tenancies Board to ensure it has the resources to monitor the private rental sector. That represents a 13.1 per cent increase in funding.
[ Chambers and O’Donovan at odds over ‘culture card’ idea Opens in new window ]
The Help to Buy scheme has been increased from €30,000 to €35,000. The money is available for first-time buyers for properties up to a value of €500,000.
Under Help to Buy, a first-time buyer who is buying a new home worth less than €500,000 can get a tax refund of up to €35,000 or 10 per cent of the purchase price of their house, or the total income tax and deposit interest retention tax they have paid over the last four years, whichever is lowest.
However, very few new-build homes in Dublin fall beneath the €500,000 cap used by the scheme, meaning it is effectively inaccessible to first-time buyers in the capital.
Browne said there was no need for an increase in the €500,000 ceiling despite construction inflation. “We never look for guarantees from developers, but we have done an awful lot to help their viability,” he said.
“We expect them to step up and deliver the homes that are needed across the country. Despite the recent inflationary pressures, there should be no excuse for developers not to be building.”

title: ‘A closure for us’: Cork family learns brother missing since 1992 died in UK two years ago
description: Jerry O’Sullivan believes brother Patsy may have started new life because being gay wasn’t as accepted in the Ireland of the ‘90s as it would be now
content:
The family of a man who went missing in 1992 aged 35 after an Easter visit home recently learned that he took on a new name and died in the UK two years ago.
Patrick (Patsy) O’Sullivan’s last-known contact with his family was in his native Lombardstown, Co Cork , in April 1992.
He had been working in Killarney, Co Kerry, and visited the family home on the Easter Bank Holiday weekend that year.
Patsy was due to return home for a christening a few weeks later, but his family never saw him again.
Patsy often went away to work for several weeks at a time, in different locations. The talented chef maintained contact with his family and returned home every few months.
He was “full of life”, a much-loved middle child in a family of seven who loved dancing and cooking.
His family never gave up looking for him. As recently as two years ago, his siblings Eugene and Jerry O’Sullivan issued a fresh appeal for information about their missing brother on RTÉ’s Crimecall.
They said it was “heartbreaking” not to know what had become of their beloved brother, who they described as having a “heart of gold”.
The mystery of what became of him was recently solved when the surviving siblings were told he had been located deceased in the UK.
His brother Jerry told the Opinion Line with PJ Coogan on Cork’s 96FM that Patsy died of sepsis on July 5th, 2024.
Poignantly, at the time of his death, he was living an hour’s drive away from another of their brothers who also lived in the UK. That brother also died, last year.
Jerry said that the family still has “a lot of unanswered questions” relating to Patsy.
“We waited so long for this [news]. It is a closure for us, that we were looking [for] for so long. He died of natural causes. He had underlying health conditions and died from sepsis.
“What we have found is that he changed his name in 1995 to Patrick Aldridge, which was the [surname] of his partner. His partner died in 2022.
“The solace we can take is that he lived his life – and it was a good life as far as we can gather. Starting off a new life by himself and leaving everything behind him. That must not have been easy.
“We always hoped that one day he would turn up at an event we were having, or whatever the case may be. Or get a phone call. But it never happened, unfortunately for us.”
Jerry believes Patsy may have started a new life in the UK because being gay wasn’t as accepted in the Ireland of the early 1990s as it would be now. Homosexuality was only decriminalised in Ireland the year after Patsy disappeared.
The O’Sullivan family say they had no issue with Patsy being gay.
Jerry said he could not thank gardaí enough for all of their efforts relating to the case over the years.
“They are an incredible team. Garda PJ Roche in Mallow took over the case in 2015. He has been a breath of fresh air because he went above and beyond.
“The team who came in with him left no stone unturned until he [Patsy] was found. This was incredible for us as a family. I never thought we would see the day that we would get closure.”
Investigating gardaí thanked the media and the public for their assistance with the case over the years.

title: Germany arrests former spy chief over alleged spying
description: August Hanning served as president of federal intelligence service from 1998 to 2005
content:
Germany is facing its greatest-ever espionage scandal amid claims that a former foreign intelligence head sold secrets to other countries for more than 12 years after his retirement.
August Hanning, head of the BND foreign intelligence agency for seven years until 2005, faces charges of treasonous espionage after the 80-year-old was arrested during a dawn raid on his home on Tuesday.
Hanning is accused of paying his former BND office manager to pass on classified information, which prosecutors allege he used in dealings with unspecified foreign intelligence agencies.
From early 2010 to June 2022, Hanning is believed to have secured – and allegedly sold on – thousands of documents, including highly sensitive briefing documents.
According to reports, the documents included intelligence on Iran ’s nuclear programme and on the Russian military.
Hanning’s inside contact at the BND, identified only as “Manfred D”, also faces charges of treason.
While Manfred D appeared before a remand judge on Tuesday, Hanning was held overnight and goes before a remand court in Karlsruhe on Wednesday.
[ History casts shadow over plans to overhaul German intelligence services Opens in new window ]
The raid comes a day after current BND chief Martin Jäger, warned of a “new, more dangerous dimension” in Germany’s growing standoff with Russia.
Hanning was modern Germany’s most visible intelligence head, giving regular briefings and rubbing shoulders in public with politicians and even espionage writers such as John le Carré.
In 2010, five years after retiring as BND chief, Hanning set up his own business consultancy – the same year he is accused of buying and using classified information.
Some of his post-BND jobs brought him into contact with German authorities. In recent years, they paused Hanning’s state pension in protest at his consulting work for a Baltic bank reportedly controlled by a Russian oligarch.
The far-reaching revelations are likely to damage still further Germany’s already modest prestige in the intelligence world, in particular given Hanning’s alleged espionage was exposed by chance.
In recent years he worked for the heiress to a steakhouse fortune, on trial in Hamburg accused of hiring Israeli ex-spies to snatch her children from her ex-husband in Denmark.
Documents supplied to the Hamburg court indicated that Hanning was the go-between with the Israelis. According to media reports, these Hamburg court documents contained clues to his other business activity with classified BND information.
In a 2021 interview with the Jerusalem Post, Hanning said he had “very close working relationships, even friendship” with many Israeli spies, including former Mossad head Danny Yatom.
While government and BND officials remained tight-lipped on Tuesday, German opposition politicians called it the “scandal of the century”.
“This is a shocking and deeply disturbing affair,” said Konstantin von Notz, a Green MP and member of the Bundestag intelligence oversight committee. “We expect a swift and complete clarification of these outrageous allegations.”
Meanwhile, Clara Bünger, domestic policy spokesperson for the opposition Left Party, said: “The investigations into former BND chief Hanning show once again that the intelligence agencies themselves are a security risk.”
[ Russian attacks continue during German chancellor’s solidarity visit to Kyiv Opens in new window ]

title: The Irish Times view on French school protests: an autumn of discontent
description: The students point to teacher shortages and decaying buildings as evidence of the failure to invest in their education
content:
Traditionally, the rentrée, when France returns to school and to work after the summer break, is a time to focus on the tasks ahead. Not this year.
Public sector strikes, bond market turmoil and political paralysis have darkened the national mood. The most dramatic expression of the unease is protests by school students, which began in suburban Paris in mid-September and spread nationwide, reaching a crescendo with Tuesday’s day of action. Police have clashed with demonstrators in cities from Paris to Bordeaux. Two dozen schools have been torched or wrecked, a teacher has been seriously assaulted and a 15-year-old in Lens lost his hand.
The students point to teacher shortages and decaying buildings as evidence of the failure to invest in their education. They may be correct, but these are symptoms of a broader malaise, as France struggles to reconcile public demand for social services with insufficient revenues.
Public debt is about 119 per cent of national output, with interest payments rising. To contain the deficit, the budget now before the hung parliament proposes freezing teachers’ salaries. Unsurprisingly, teachers’ unions endorsed the students’ grievances and joined them on the streets.
Outsiders may see the current disturbances as simply the latest manifestation of France’s long tradition of vigorous street protest. The images of tear-gas-filled streets, baton charges and masked demonstrators hurling flares are certainly familiar from previous outbreaks of discontent.
But a political clock is ticking. After nine years in the Élysée, Emmanuel Macron is in the final months of his presidency. As yet, no ideological successor has emerged and polls consistently show Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally beating all potential opponents in next April’s election. That might change if centrists coalesce around a single candidate. Alternatively, the energy and anger unleashed by the protests could propel hard-left standard-bearer Jean-Luc Mélenchon into the second round of the election, where pollsters suggest he would lose to Le Pen.

title: ‘There’s no favouritism’: Luke Donald says every player will ‘earn their way’ to Ryder Cup
description: Englishman will attempt to become first European captain to win three straight matches at next year’s tournament
content:
A man who, as captain, can seemingly do no wrong. Luke Donald did the merry-go-round of media duties in the grand ballroom of Adare Manor – the magnificent Murano crystal chandeliers overhead casting him in a glowing light wherever he went – as part of the Ryder Cup’s year-to-go countdown, impressively delivering the kind of calm, authoritative messaging that has formed part of his successful captaincies in Rome in 2023 and Bethpage in 2025.
Next year’s Ryder Cup, in the splendid setting of Adare Manor alongside the river Maigue, will be special for the fact it is the centenary edition – 100 years since the first match in Massachusetts in 1927 – but also for Donald’s attempt to become the first European captain to win three straight matches.
And while the Englishman played the Irish card in terms of how the crowd can act as an extra man for whatever 12 players actually make up the team for the defence of the famous trophy against the US side on September 13th-19th, 2027, Donald insisted there would be no “favouritism” shown should it be needed when it comes time to dispense his six wild cards.
Clearly, Rory McIlroy , the Masters champion and world number two, and Shane Lowry , who showed nerves of steel in ensuring Europe retained the trophy in New York before Tyrrell Hatton guaranteed victory, are primed to continue their great association with the match that each holds dear to their hearts.
But Donald said: “Every person’s going to have to earn their way; there’s no favouritism from me. They’re going to have to perform at a high level. I think one of the big advantages of playing at home is the support [of] the home crowd and using that energy in a positive way. I think, we saw, the US tried to use it to try and put us off [in New York] but we asked our fans to get behind us and use that energy to push us, and that can be very strong and very beneficial.”
Lowry’s runaway win in last month’s Amgen Irish Open at Doonbeg got him off to a flying start in the Europe team qualifying, which finishes at next year’s British Masters on August 22nd, 2027, when the leading six players on those standings will earn their places.
Of that win feeding Lowry’s confidence, especially following tough finishes with the winning posts in sight in Dubai and the Cognizant in Florida earlier in the season, Donald remarked: “I think it was so important for him. He certainly had a few doubts [during the season]; you could see even just in his language that he used to the media, and he knew he’d let some go and probably held on to those [losses] a little bit too long. But this [Irish Open win] was important and, to play well and just to gallop away from the field, it was so impressive.”
Lowry – who is currently fourth in the rankings, which are led by Matt Fitzpatrick at this early stage – has played in three Ryder Cups so far, including those wins in Rome and Bethpage, with Donald observing how he has matured in the environment.
“I just think he’s gotten more comfortable. His love for team sports has always been there, but it just grows every time. The Ryder Cup means everything to him; it means so much. And in terms of being someone with a great vibe, a great energy, he brings that to the team. He’s upbeat. He’s up for the challenge. He puts his arm around team-mates, and he’s just very engaged. I think obviously with the Ryder Cup being here in Ireland, he’s very motivated to try and make the team.”
As for McIlroy? Well, his name can be put on the team now, unquestionably.
And Donald has witnessed first-hand the evolution of McIlroy and the Ryder Cup, from being a team-mate at Celtic Manor in 2012 to being his captain for the past two victories in 2023 and 2025.
[ ‘Being the centenary makes it extra special’: Luke Donald wants Ryder Cup hat-trick at Adare Manor Opens in new window ]
“Rory’s role has evolved from saying it was an exhibition to understanding quite quickly that this was more than an exhibition; it was something very worthwhile ... he’s certainly gone from someone that would be listening in the team room to now feeling the responsibility to speak up and say things when he feels that he needs to say things.
“What makes Rory good is that he understands that, you know, what makes a great player isn’t necessarily just putting three or four points, or five points, on the board; it’s making your team-mates a little bit better, and he is good at that. He’s a very nice asset to have on your team.”

title: Chambers and O’Donovan at odds over ‘culture card’ idea
description: No funding to enable prepaid €100 voucher for concerts and cultural events, says Minister for Public Expenditure
content:
There won’t be a “culture card” in 2027 , and there is no budget funding for it, said Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers, despite Cabinet colleague Minister for Culture Patrick O’Donovan pushing the idea.
The potential for a prepaid €100 voucher for 16-year-olds to attend concerts and other cultural events was floated in the run-in to the budget , but no announcement was made on Tuesday .
“There won’t be a culture card in 2027, and it’s not funded in the allocation that’s set out,” said Chambers following the budget announcement.
“Lots of ideas or suggestions would have been made by different Government colleagues, but we have been tightening fiscal parameters,” he said.
He added that in the area of culture, priority had been given to the basic income for the arts scheme, funding for the Arts Council and additional cash for national cultural institutions.
This is despite O’Donovan suggesting on the eve of the budget that funding had been secured to progress the idea and that he hoped it would begin being rolled out towards the end of next year.
[ Budget 2027: Teenagers set to receive €100 voucher for cultural events Opens in new window ]
In a statement on Monday, O’Donovan’s spokeswoman said that funding to progress the card had been secured, adding: “All going well, we anticipate being able to roll it out by the end of next year.”
Following the budget, his spokeswoman said the Limerick County TD was focused on developing the concept of the card and would continue to engage with EU counterparts on it, while broadening engagement to include wider stakeholders countrywide and across Government.
A source close to O’Donovan said he has discretion within his allocation to develop policies such as the culture card, arguing that final decisions on the programme for government – which contains a commitment to examine the introduction of such a measure – were a matter for Taoiseach Micheál Martin and Tánaiste Simon Harris.
Harris said on Tuesday that the idea was “still being worked on”. He also defended the income tax package in the budget, which the Opposition said favours higher earners.
“Rightly, if you’re on lower incomes in this country you actually are also entitled to a lot of other things that people on middle incomes aren’t‚” he said, while arguing that about one-third of workers don’t pay income tax but are eligible for other payments not available to the so-called squeezed middle.
“This is why the squeezed middle have been left squeezed for so long, and they’re so frustrated in this country,” he said, adding that a working couple with a combined income of €100,000 were not wealthy people.
Harris also stood over the Government’s decision to bring in higher childcare subsidies later in the year during 2027, despite suggesting at an earlier point in the budget preamble that they could kick in from January.
“We made a conscious decision to do more and bring it in later,” he said. “People in this country want to know how we’re going to get to €200 per month per child in the lifetime of this Government and what we’ve done today is show a roadmap”
This was about not spreading things too thinly and being able to do more by bringing it in in September. These are judgment calls, but I think the balance is right,” he said.
Harris also defended the decision to increase the amount available under the Help to Buy scheme by €5,000, despite saying before the budget that he didn’t intend to bring in any property-related tax measures.
“On balance I think this was the right measure to do and I’m happy enough to do it,” he said, adding that the benefit would “far outweigh” any inflationary impact.

title: Student contribution fees permanently cut by €150 in Budget 2027
description: Budget 2027 also includes a €56m increase in special educational needs support, including 2,339 more special needs assistants
content:
Student fees have been permanently reduced by €150 in a budget that also saw the Department of Education secure record base funding following the top-ups required in previous years.
The €150 reduction in Budget 2027 , announced on Tuesday, will bring the maximum student contribution fee per third-level student down to €2,350.
The move follows some confusion over recent days, with a €250 cut first mooted before doubt was cast over whether any reduction would be included at all.
However, the €150 cut falls far short of the €500 reduction sought by student unions in advance of the announcement.
Other measures targeted at students and their families include a new student contribution fee grant for families with more than one child in higher education, and an increase in Student Universal Support Ireland (Susi) maintenance grant rates by 4.5 per cent from January.
Another measure that could help third-level students is the increase in tax relief available to those who let out rooms in their homes under the rent-a-room scheme.
This tax relief will increase from €14,000 a year to €16,000 a year in the hope this will in turn encourage more people to open their homes up for students seeking accommodation.
Some €5.3 billion was allocated to the Department of Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to fund a new three-year national training fund skills package with a total investment of €360 million.
Out of that, funding of €150 million has been set aside to upskill people across the economy in artificial intelligence (AI).
“The development and diffusion of AI is not just a new trend,” said Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers . “It is a paradigm shift that will have profound implications for our economy and society.
“As a country, we are well placed to take advantage of the opportunities that AI offers, but only if we equip our people with the skills of the future.”
Elsewhere, the number of apprenticeships will be expanded, while college places in health and social care professions will also be increased.
In primary and secondary level education, the Department of Education was allocated €14.4 billion in total for 2027. That is up from €13.5 billion in 2026, though the department required an additional €646 million in additional funding in April, bringing its final budget to €14.1 billion. A levy was imposed on other departments to cover this supplementary funding required by education.
The budget provided an extra €17 million for capitation funding in schools, which covers utility bills, maintenance and insurance costs. That equates to an increase of €68 per pupil at primary level, and an increase of €40 per pupil at post-primary level.
There will be an additional €2 million for the Deis Plus programme, a funding scheme for more than 100 of the most disadvantaged schools in the country that was launched this year.
Alongside that, there will be funding for an extra 100 home school community liaison co-ordinators – teachers who work within the community to improve outcomes for children at most risk of educational disadvantage.
The budget also includes a €56 million increase in special educational needs support, including 2,339 more special needs assistants, and 1,353 more special education teachers.
The school transport scheme, which brings 180,000 children to school every day, will get €1.6 billion of the education budget.

title: Budget puts public finances on worse trajectory, watchdog warns
description: If overruns continue on current trajectory, net spending will increase by 9% this year, Irish Fiscal Advisory Council says
content:
The State’s budgetary watchdog has strongly criticised the Government’s budget , warning it puts the public finances on “a worse trajectory”, while increasing the State’s reliance on “high-risk corporation tax”.
The criticism from the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council comes as the Department of Finance projected corporate tax revenue will rise to nearly €45 billion by the end of the decade.
That projection is on the basis Ireland will benefit from the new minimum global rate for multinationals and as companies exhaust allowances for domiciling assets here.
In its critique of Budget 2027, Ifac said spending increases net of tax measures have been running “at a blistering pace in recent years”.
It noted that a “sustainable speed limit” of 5 per cent for both was set in 2021. “But governments have since budgeted for around 6 per cent growth, before actually delivering about 10 per cent a year on average, double the speed limit,” the council said.
If overruns continue on their current trajectory, net spending will increase by 9 per cent this year, it warned.
The watchdog also warned that the Government was continuing to use “high-risk receipts” to paper over cracks in its budgeting, and to fund permanent tax and spending measures.
[ Budget 2027 main points: income tax rate changes; €10 increase in pension and welfare rates Opens in new window ]
In his budget speech, Minister for Finance Simon Harris said the Government was running budgetary surpluses “so that we do not spend tax revenues that cannot be relied upon in the future”.
But Ifac claimed the Government planned to spend about €6 out of every €7 it collects in corporation tax – most of it on current spending.
When excess corporation tax is stripped out, it said, the Government plans to run larger deficits, rising from €12 billion in 2026 to €20 billion in 2030.
It warned that the Government will effectively have to borrow to put money into its long-term savings funds for ageing costs from next year.
In its annual economic and fiscal outlook, published alongside the budget, the department said it expected receipts from the business tax to generate €34 billion this year before rising to €39 billion in 2027.
It projected receipts would grow to €44.7 billion by 2030 as Ireland benefits from the new minimum global rate for big multinationals and as tax allowances here run out.
The new projections came with a spate of warnings about the fragility of the public finances.
“The budgetary arithmetic is constructed on the crucial assumption that corporate profitability continues to expand; any decline in profitability could put a (potentially large) dent in corporate tax revenues,” the department said.
“Overall, the geopolitical situation remains fragile, and the probability of a long-lasting conflict in the Middle East – and, hence, a more prolonged energy outage – remains non-negligible,” it said.
In its annual economic and fiscal outlook, published alongside the budget, the Department of Finance upgraded its growth forecast for the economy.
It said it expected modified domestic demand, a measure of domestic economic activity, to expand by 3.7 per cent this year, which represents an upgrade of 1.5 per cent on its spring projections.
It said the upgrade comes on the back of “solid” consumer spending and AI -related investment. Growth for next year is expected to be 3 per cent.
“These projections are calibrated on the assumption that the energy price shock begins to recede over the course of next year,” it said.
“On this basis, headline inflation is expected to stabilise at around 2 per cent over the medium-term,” it added.

title: Omagh bombing lawyers question whether fingerprints were ever sent to Scotland Yard
description: Senior garda says limited CCTV of 1998 meant there was ‘very little or none’ of use to inquiry
content:
The Omagh Bombing Inquiry ’s legal team has said it understood that no fingerprint material relating to the atrocity was sent by police to the UK’s main antiterrorist hub for analysis.
Lead counsel to the inquiry, Paul Greaney, told the inquiry on Monday that “my understanding is that no fingerprint material was sent relating to the Omagh bombing to New Scotland Yard”.
Fingerprint expert Kevin Kershaw, responding to questions from Greaney, said he would have expected any fingerprints found to have been sent to London “because of the type of offence, this was a terrorist offence and ... New Scotland Yard was the hub of the UK terrorist fingerprint team”.
He agreed there was nothing in the materials he had seen to indicate it did in fact occur.
A total of 31 people, including unborn twins, died and hundreds were injured when a car bomb planted by dissident republican group the Real IRA exploded in the centre of Omagh on August 15 th , 1998.
The inquiry into the atrocity, which opened in 2024 under Lord Alan Turnbull, is examining whether the atrocity could reasonably have been prevented by British state authorities.
Its third chapter, which opened in Belfast last month, is examining how the bombing was carried out, and who was responsible.
On Tuesday, Greaney told the Inquiry the position of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) was that it was “usual” at the time for such fingerprints to be sent to New Scotland Yard for analysis, but the body acknowledged it has been “unable to locate any written policy or other document” which established that this had taken place.
“There is no document that PSNI can point to that establishes that fingerprints relating to the Omagh bombing were sent to New Scotland Yard,” he said.
However, he added “no documentation ... doesn’t determine the question of whether, in fact, it was sent, because it is obviously a possibility it was sent without it being documented”.
Asked by Greaney for his view “of the likelihood as to whether fingerprint material was submitted” without generating documentation, Kershaw replied: “I would have expected a considerable amount of documentation available to me to review.”
The expert witness also said that, at New Scotland Yard, “I wouldn’t expect anything less than very clear documentation relating to any submission made by any police force to the fingerprint hub.”
The inquiry also heard on Tuesday from Garda Det Supt Emmet Casserly, who gave evidence on the investigation in the Republic which was launched following the explosion, including house-to-house inquiries and a vehicle checkpoint near the address in Carrickmacross, Co Monaghan, where the car used to transport the bomb was stolen.
He said the “decades”-long investigation generated “1,077 separate lines of inquiry”, statements were taken from “over 480 people”, 99 arrests were made and there were 92 recorded searches, and, he said, information exchange between An Garda Síochána and the RUC was “seamless”.
Asked by Greaney about CCTV evidence, Casserly noted the limitations of CCTV coverage and quality in 1998 compared to the present day, and said this meant “there was very, very little or none; no CCTV produced which was of any use to the inquiry or investigation”.
“So .. there was no CCTV footage harvested by the Garda investigation team,” Greaney asked.
“That’s correct,” the senior garda said.
Asked whether this had limited the investigation team in identifying suspects, capturing the sequence of events, and corroborating the statements of eyewitnesses, he replied, “it did”.

title: ‘It’s us against the world’: Jim Furyk says USA need to have chip on shoulder to win Ryder Cup
description: Captain says side are underdogs for Adare Manor and will make reconnaissance visit with possible players next July
content:
Jim Furyk ’s poker face doesn’t flinch when he delivers the “underdogs” tag which he has attached to his own team for next year’s centenary Ryder Cup at Adare Manor .
His eyes don’t dance. His lips don’t form a grin. If Neuro Linguistic Programming detection were at play, you’d believe him.
Even with a USA team that will have world number one Scottie Scheffler as its talisman?
But Furyk – in his second stint at USA captain, having previously lost to Europe in the 2018 match in Paris – has the weight of history on his side of the assertion. Remarkably, the USA’s last time to win the Ryder Cup in Europe was at the Belfry in 1993 and, for next year’s encounter in Co Limerick, Furyk is of the opinion that a change in mindset and planning will be required to end that losing sequence.
“We’re not really happy with the last two results, so, yes, change will be made,” said. “We’re going to evolve. We’re going to get better, [we have] a new points system and a new analytics team. But [we have] a number of different changes coming and stuff that we’re very excited about,” said Furyk of leading that move for change.
The new points system will be based off points earned during the year leading up to the 2027 matches in Ireland, rewarding form players on the US side. Previously, major winners from the year before the Ryder Cup, along with the Players Championship winner, would get points.
Furyk’s narrative continued to be one of pitching Europe as strong favourites. “It’s us against the world at this point, or us against Europe. There’s going to be 50,000 people [each day] making a lot of noise.
“The Ryder Cup is such a great atmosphere, such a great arena. But we know what we’re up against. We also know that it’s been 34 years since we won in Europe. There’s no secret. I’m going to hear it over and over again, so I’m going to embrace it.
“We’re the underdogs. We understand that. We’ve got a lot of work ahead of us. And I’m excited about that process. I’m a process guy and [like to have my] ducks in a row. We will put these guys in a good position and let our guys go out and show their talent.
“It’s going to be difficult. The Irish sports fans are amazing but folks are going to come in droves from all over Europe to support their favourite countrymen. I need 12 guys that love that atmosphere and love walking into that type of arena because it takes a certain mentality. We have to have that chip on our shoulder, that mentality that it’s us against the world.”
As part of that process, Furyk intends to get as many of his possible team to attend a reconnaissance visit to Adare Manor ahead of next year’s Scottish Open and The Open at St Andrews. A similar exercise ahead of the 2018 match in Paris proved less than inspiring when only eight possibles attended that get-together whereas Furyk would expect to see as many as 16 attend in Adare Manor.
Of his own development as a captain since his first stint in Paris in 2018, Furyk elaborated:
“I understand the leadership role a little bit better, and I’ve been in these team rooms for a number of years now and been a little bit of a support for captains the last few years as an assistant or a vice captain. But I’m still trying to learn. I’m still reaching out, trying to better myself from other coaches, from other captains, from you name it, CEOs, businessmen alike.
“Leadership’s a unique trait. I love to say we grow up in golf, mostly an individual sport. We put a team around us. You’ve got a physio, you’ve got a coach, you’ve got a putting coach, your family, and they’re all focused on you and how we’re going to make you play better.
“And [then] they give you a role as a captain, and you become a CEO and a leader. And some folks have that skill. Some don’t. Some it doesn’t come naturally. I love the process of learning that role along the way, and I’m going to enjoy the process the next 12 months.”

title: Man settles action over abuse by former Terenure College teacher John McClean
description: Court hears ‘of the most significant and substantial type’ of sexual abuse between the 1970s and 1980s
content:
A man who was sexually abused by recidivist paedophile and ex-Terenure College teacher John McClean has settled a High Court action.
Paul Kennedy – who sued McClean, the school’s board and the Carmelites, the religious order that runs the school – settled his action following mediation for an undisclosed amount. It is understood to be a substantial six-figure sum.
The court heard previously that Kennedy’s case arose from historical sexual abuse “of the most significant and substantial type”, occurring over a sustained period from the 1970s to the 1980s.
McClean (81) has previously been convicted at Dublin Circuit Criminal Court of abusing 49 boys at Terenure College. He is currently incarcerated, having formerly resided at Casimir Avenue, Harold’s Cross.
On Tuesday, barrister Andrew Nugent, appearing for Kennedy and instructed by Coleman Legal, told Judge Tony O’Connor the case had been settled.
Counsel asked that it be struck out against McClean, with no order for legal costs.
He asked that the case be struck out against Terenure College’s board of management and a representative of the Carmelites. Counsel asked for an order for Kennedy’s legal costs to be made against the board and the representative. The judge made the orders as sought.
Other High Court actions against McClean remain live.
McClean taught at Terenure College between 1966 and 1996, becoming first-year form master in 1980. He was also a rugby coach.
During the criminal prosecutions, the Circuit Court heard that McClean perpetrated the abuse mainly in his office, a windowless physiotherapy room, or in a room under the concert hall known as the smoking room, to which only McClean had a key.
Victims described how McClean, nicknamed Doc, would call boys into the physio room under the pretext of treating sports injuries, before sexually assaulting them.

title: After inflating expectations, Coalition faces budget hangover
description: Business Today: Budget 2027 looks a lot like  ‘Schrödinger’s budget – simultaneously generous and mean’
content:
Forgive our automated morning greeting, we are coming to you this evening as the leaks, kites, promises and haggling end.
Budget 2027 was published this afternoon to a decidedly muted response.
For all the money committed in various areas, and the income tax packed swelled considerably in the final hours, Conor Pope describes this as “Schrödinger’s budget – simultaneously generous and mean”.
As Conor writes, for all the money spent, pretty much no one will be better off in 2027, once the relentless rate of inflation is factored in.
If there are winners, they are likely to be working couples in a household where both earn more than €50,000 a year. The combined benefits for such a double-income household will be €1,500 annually.
The budget fired money around in various directions to try to address the cost of living crisis and react to the demand of a whole range of sectors, but you would search hard to find a central theme, writes Cliff Taylor . Perhaps it is responding to events and that is in part understandable, given the big increases in energy prices and their impact on inflation. But budgets are about priorities and when the package emerges from fractious last-minute negotiations between the two big parties of Government, some of these can be fudged or lost.
The Government’s decision to reduce the standard rate of capital gains tax (CGT) – a central plank of the business measures outlined in the budget – will cost the exchequer an estimated €186 million in a full year, making it the single most expensive measure announced outside the personal income tax package, writes Ian Curran.
[ Budget 2027 main points Opens in new window ]
So what of the measures? Fiona Reddan, in her examination of what the measures mean for different demographics , reports that the big change is the standard rate band shifting by €2,500 to €46,500 from January.
This it means that someone earning at least €46,500 will now save €500 a year, thanks to paying more of their income at the lower rate of 20 per cent.
Workers will also save thanks to the €125 increase to personal, employee and earned income credits, which will go up to €2,125.
No change was made to tax rates, which means our top marginal rate is now 52.35 per cent for PAYE workers.
We (finally) got more details on the oft flagged personal investment accounts with savers able to invest €12,000 a year tax-free into the Governments’ new personal investment accounts.
People will be able to receive greater amounts in gifts or inheritance without paying tax under changes announced in the budget but there has been no wider reform.
Smokers face another price hike (€1 for a packet of 20), while a 20 cent per ml increase was applied to in vaping products, but excise duties on alcohol are untouched.
The decision to increase most Vehicle Registration Tax (VRT) rates by 1 per cent will affect prices for nine of the 10 bestselling models in the Irish new car market. Cars with CO2 emissions over 80g/km will see a 1 per cent increase in VRT from January 1st next year, impacting tax bands three to 20.

title: ‘Confidence’ that Horse Sport Ireland can survive in face of €3m liabilities
description: High Court judge says examiner’s report on equestrian body shows ‘reasonable prospect’ it can continue
content:
A High Court judge has said there is “confidence” that Horse Sport Ireland (HSI) will survive after a financial examiner asked for added time to design a scheme of payments to creditors for the company, which supports the multimillion euro Irish equestrian industry.
At the High Court on Tuesday, barrister Ross Gorman, for the court-appointed examiner, applied for the extension, which was granted by Judge Cian Ferriter.
Gorman, instructed by Kane Tuohy LLP solicitors, told Ferriter that the examiner, chartered accountant Joe Walsh, had undertaken “a lot of productive work” to secure funding for the indebted HSI.
Walsh’s report, he said, “expressed optimism” for a resolution of HSI’s liabilities, which amounted to approximately €3 million.
Gorman said there had been constructive engagement with key stakeholders and notice parties in the matter.
The judge said he had read Walsh’s report and commented that the examiner believed there was a “reasonable prospect” of the survival of the company.
The judge said Walsh’s report also expressed “confidence for a scheme of arrangements” of payments.
Last Month, Walsh told the High Court that HSI performed a “very important function within the equestrian industry in Ireland”. He said he was aware that sporting horses were worth in excess of €1 billion annually to the Irish economy and supported upwards of 20,000 jobs.
“Horse breeding in Ireland is world renowned and is a significant export business, with the majority of breeders selling horses outside the country,” Walsh said.
[ Minister for Justice offers to prioritise Gaza students’ appeals over visa refusal Opens in new window ]
HSI employs 47 people from its headquarters in Naas, Co Kildare. It was granted a petition for its examinership last August.
It receives about €5 million a year from the Department of Agriculture in addition to another €3 million annually from Sport Ireland . It further generates €2 million a year through sports fees and equine passports.
The matter returns before the High Court on October 30th.

title: ‘I was shocked by it because of the spin beforehand’: How a healthcare worker, engineer and student view Budget 2027
description: Student says budget lacks any ‘meaningful’ action to resolve accommodation crisis and fails to protect students from fare increases
author_name: Emmet Malone, Niamh Towey, Jack White
content:
HSE healthcare assistant Dermott Foy had wanted to see substantial movement on fuel prices in the budget to help him with the cost of running his car, but he said he has come away disappointed.
The first thing he mentioned when asked what he thought of the package was the changes to income tax , from which he will only benefit to the tune of a couple of hundred euro a year.
“I’m one of these hard workers that gets up and every morning goes out to work, but I’m still under the €44,000 bracket and so, to be truthful about it, the uplift in my payslip is going to be very poor,” he said.
“When you break it down to a weekly figure, it’s not going to go anywhere close to the increase in the price of petrol we’ve seen over the last six months, which is costing me more than €50 a week on top of what it used to, so it’s no help really to me as a worker going out to do my job.”
He said he was “really shocked about it” because of the “spin” that was put out about it beforehand. “There was all that talk about the working person and the middle earner and this budget being about them because last year’s was absolutely shocking,” he said.
“But I’m someone who has worked my way up from being a lower earner for a long time ... I left school with a very poor education and so I drove buses and trucks for a long time.
“No disrespect to the people doing it now because it’s tough work and long hours, and, as I got older, that was one of the reasons I looked at a way to get out.”
Foy reskilled and became a healthcare worker because there was “so much talk” about how many were needed.
“I was lucky enough to get a job with the HSE, in the public sector, that came with what people would describe as a middle income,” he said. “But it certainly doesn’t feel as though this budget was about me.
“The cuts to the carbon tax, they’re not going to make a big difference to the people I’m dealing with – pensioners who are sick or vulnerable on low incomes who can’t pay their heating bills.
[ Budget 2027: ‘Gone before you get it’ - Opposition criticises cost-of-living measures Opens in new window ]
“They’ve kicked the can down the road, but there just seems to be a lack of imagination down there. They’re completely disconnected from working people.
“But the supports for new cars have been extended ... There isn’t the infrastructure in Donegal. An electric car just wouldn’t cut it up here.”
“What’s the famous phrase – ‘the curate’s egg’? It’s good in spots,” says Damien Owens, laughing after hearing what was in the budget on Tuesday afternoon.
Nearing retirement after more than 40 years working as an engineer, Owens, who lives in Clontarf, Dublin, says there was little in Budget 2027 for him.
The 64-year-old, who has been director general of the representative body Engineers Ireland for the last four years, did not sound surprised.
Regardless, he was primarily concerned about what the budget would do for young professionals like his daughter.
Aged in her late 20s, she moved home in recent years to save a house deposit.
Housing measures in the budget aimed at young workers like her appear to have left much to be desired.
The maximum relief available under the Help to Buy scheme has been increased by €5,000, though Owens believes it will not help, arguing there is “nothing to buy”.
“A lot of the new developments are rent-only,” he says.
The decision not to increase the value of eligible properties from €500,000 “won’t move the dial much”, particularly in Dublin.
[ Budget 2027: Big business pays the bills as Coalition rolls the dice Opens in new window ]
Elsewhere, while tax bands have “only widened a bit”, he says the income tax package will help if it coincides with pay rises to offset inflation next year.
Regardless, the changes “send a positive message”, Owens says, though he believes it was a missed opportunity not to set out plans to gradually increase tax bands over the coming years.
This would have given greater certainty to young professionals, he says.
He welcomed measures around cutting childcare costs, alongside details of capital spending, which he says will give professionals confidence to “stay put”, arguing that many are being pulled abroad.
“Those sorts of things really lift the spirits of an economy,” he says, adding that such “tangible symbols” like MetroLink, the long-awaited rail line connection the city centre and north Dublin, give confidence to young professionals that they have a future in Ireland.
Nothing jumps out for him personally from Tuesday’s budget, aside from the increase to the amount of electricity he will be able to sell back to the grid without paying tax.
[ Budget 2027 families: a ‘keep more of what you earn’ result - but are the savings enough? Opens in new window ]
That rate will rise from €400 to €600. Owens installed solar panels last year, saying they have made an “enormous difference” to his bills.
Having previously paid about €200 every two months, he has been receiving money after selling excess electricity back to the grid over the summer months.
Aside from that, he mentions the inheritance tax, saying it “didn’t move much”.
Budget 2027 lacks any “meaningful” action to resolve the student accommodation crisis and fails to protect students from public transport fare increases.
This is the view of student Daniel Walsh, who is president of Aontas na Mac Léinn in Éirinn (AMLÉ), the student advocacy group.
“This year’s budget does very little to support the thousands of students around the country who are getting up at 5am every morning to begin their hours-long commute to college, a journey that they’re forced to make as a result of the student accommodation crisis,” Walsh said.
The student union had campaigned to protect students from the scheduled 15 per cent fare increase across bus and rail services from January.
[ Are Budget 2027’s tax and social welfare measures enough? Conor Pope delivers his verdict Opens in new window ]
This was not included in Tuesday’s budget, meaning “students who are already being forced to commute long distances due to the shortage of student accommodation on our campuses are effectively going to be doubly penalised by fare hikes”, Walsh said.
Walsh did welcome the reduction of the student contribution fee by €150, bringing the maximum fee per third level student down to €2,350.
“This move signals a positive commitment to promises that there would be a continual reduction to the fee over the lifetime of this Government,” he said.
He said he was “quite disappointed” to see such a small reduction in the student contribution charge at a time when the cost to college has risen by €500 this year, Walsh said.
The budget failed to provide funding to support purpose-built student accommodation “on the kind of scale which could meaningfully reduce the cost of student accommodation for families up and down the country”, Walsh said.
While there has been an increase in the tax relief available to homeowners who let out a room in their house under the rent-a-room scheme, which has risen from €14,000 to €16,000 a year, there continues to be a lack of protections for students who may avail of this type of accommodation, he said.
“We’re yet to see any progress on the expansion of renters’ protection to students living in that dig-style accommodation – it’s really the wild west,” he said.
“There’s no protection available to students at all. They can be turfed out overnight, and the only recourse available to them then is effectively just small claims court.”

title: How Budget 2027 will impact families: From renters to stay-at-home parents
description: How much will each family be better off by?
content:
I t’s the year of playing catch-up. In last year’s budget, changes on the income tax front were minimal. Even though there have been some sizeable changes on the income tax front this year, they’re unlikely to be enough to help families brush off the burden of ever-rising prices and diminishing purchasing power.
As Katie O’Neill, a tax director with PwC , says of the impact for Irish families, it’s about “easing pressure, rather than transforming their finances”.
“This is a budget built around the idea that if people are earning more, they should feel it in their pockets rather than lose it through the tax system,” says O’Neill, who has compiled the figures below. She describes it as a “keep more of what you earn” budget.
But just how much are families getting to keep?
Tax changes announced at lunchtime mean that from next January, Irish families with one earner will save about €58 a month on tax, or €700 a year, based on an income of €50,000 – or double that for two earners, on €100,000.
The big changes came on the personal tax front, specifically to the standard rate band.
This is going to increase by €2,500 to €46,500 from January, and it means that someone earning at least €46,500 will now save €500 a year, thanks to paying more of their income at the lower rate of 20 per cent.
Workers will also save thanks to the €125 increase to personal, employee and earned income credits, which will go up to €2,125.
[ Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day Opens in new window ]
Our single worker Tom, for example, just short of the standard rate band ceiling on earnings of €45,907, will save €400 a year on income tax come 2027, while our dual-income family, on earnings of €175,000, will save €1,000 a year, although their net income will only increase by €753 due to an increase in PRSI earlier this month.
Indeed no change was made to tax rates, which means, as O’Neill notes, that this PRSI increase means our top marginal rate is now 52.35 per cent for PAYE workers, and 55.35 per cent for the self-employed earning in excess of €100,000.
This continues to put Ireland at the higher end of the burden for middle-income earners; figures from EY show that in France, for example, the top rate of tax is 45 per cent – but you don’t start paying this until you earn income of €180,294. The rate is the same in the UK, and applies on income from €145,000.
[ Budget 2027: Big business pays the bills as Coalition rolls the dice Opens in new window ]
It’s not just middle- and higher-income earners who will benefit from Tuesday’s pronouncements – albeit the easing will again be modest enough.
Rebecca will see her income rise come January, up to €30,298 a year, given the decision to increase the minimum wage by 79 cent to €14.94. This will add about €1,300 a year to her pretax income, and she will be helped by the accompanying increase in the entry threshold for the 3 per cent USC band. This will increase by €1,600, from €28,700 to €30,300.
[ Budget 2027 main points: €10 increase in pension and welfare rates; 20 cent per ml tax on vapes Opens in new window ]
The cumulative increase means her overall effective tax rate will fall from 8.4 per cent to 8 per cent, and her net monthly income will increase by €110.
She, like Tom, and other renters across the country, will also benefit from the rent credit, which has been increased by €150 to €1,150 for single claimants and €2,300 for couples.
A welcome increase perhaps, but unlikely to offer much relief, given continued increases in rents – figures from the Residential Tenancies Board show that average rents for new tenancies now stand at €1,839 per month, and €2,232 in Dublin, while the increase in the relief works out at just €12.50 a month.
“The additional rent credit will not transform anyone’s finances, but it is another acknowledgment of the pressure renters continue to face,” says O’Neill.
Putative home buyers like Tom might also benefit from changes to the Help to Buy scheme, which come into play immediately. This has just been increased by €5,000 to €35,000, and means that someone buying a house for €350,000, will now be able to get 10 per cent of this back, provided they meet the tax requirements. Of course the challenge is finding a home; the price ceiling remains at €500,000, and a cursory glance at myhome.ie shows a paucity of homes in the capital under this price level. The increase is expected to cost €16 million on a full-year basis.
There are other tweaks that can benefit families around the country. Jian and Sean, for example, currently earn €10,000 a year from the Rent-a-Room scheme. But this limit is going to increase to €16,000 from January, which means they can earn another €6,000 – tax-free. To reach this new target, they will consider installing a new modular unit in their garden, given the Minister gave the go-ahead for this.
[ Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work Opens in new window ]
As a stay-at-home parent, Sean might also benefit from the €100 increase in the home carer credit, which has increased to €2,050.
Pensioners Leslie and Kitty will also see an increase in their incomes, thanks to an increase in the State pension, which means they will earn an additional €1,040 a year. As they are exempt from PRSI, this increase won’t impact them, and due to the tax cuts, they will see their net income increase by €1,332 a year, or €111 a month.
The couple are also pleased that the threshold for inheritance tax has increased somewhat, up by 5 per cent to €420,000. The change means that they will be able to pass on an additional €60,000 to their three children without any extra tax.
Rebecca is 33 years old. She rents a one-bedroom apartment. She works as a customer service representative for a online retailer, remotely, from home. Her annual earnings are €29,000, which will rise to €30,298 thanks to the increase in the minimum wage.
Tom is 30 years old and a single parent. He lives and works in north County Dublin, as a nurse. Tom earns €45,907 annually.
He is paying €2,000 rent for a two-bed apartment.
However, he would like to get on the property ladder soon and is hoping to use the Help To Buy scheme to assist in getting his deposit together.
Ekene is married, in his 50s, and lives in Louth with his wife Alison. Ekene is a self-employed hotelier. Alison has a part-time job as a beautician and earns a salary of €23,000.
They have four children, two of whom now live at home. Ekene’s annual income over the last number of years was €152,000.
Leslie and Kitty are married and living in Cork. They own their family home, having paid off their mortgage. Leslie and Kitty are in their late 70s.
Leslie receives an occupational pension of €22,000 along with the State contributory pension. Kitty also receives the State contributory pension. Their combined income is €54,167, up from €53,127.
Jian and Sean are in their late 30s. They live in Kilkenny in a four-bed semidetached house. They have two children aged 13 and 7. Jian is a pilot.
He gave up his job over 10 years ago when their son was born, and has now returned to work. Sean, who used to work full-time in a tech company, now stays at home with their children. Their annual income is €47,500.
They receive rent from renting out a room in their home and have boosted their income by €10,000 a year thanks to the rent-a-room scheme.
This is within the current tax-free limits of €14,000, so they receive this amount, tax-free, on top of Jian’s salary.
Mark and Linda are in their early 40s with two children. They live in a €1.5 million four-bed detached house they own in Dún Laoghaire. Both Mark and Linda are accountants and earn a combined annual salary of €300,000.
They own a rental property that has an annual rental income of €25,000.

title: Dead Ringer – Frank McNally on a tragic real-life counterpart of a fictional Joycean character
description: Eveleen Nicolls drowned while trying to save a girl on the Great Blasket in 1909
content:
Among autumn’s events at the James Joyce Centre in Dublin, I see, is the unveiling next week of Na Mairbh, a new Irish language version of The Dead. This is a development that would greatly have cheered at least of one the characters in Joyce’s great short story: Molly Ivors.
Readers may recall that “Miss Ivors” is the spirited, outspoken young nationalist with whom Gabriel Conroy (the author’s alter ego) is paired for a square dance called “Lancers”.
Their quasi-military manoeuvres become a verbal skirmish during which she questions his commitment to Irish culture, berates his journalism for the Daily Express, and calls him a “West Briton”.
Then she refuses to stay for supper, having a political meeting to attend. “Well, you’re the comical girl,” remarks Conroy’s wife, Gretta. To which Miss Ivors replies laughingly, “Beannacht libh,” and runs downstairs, out of the story.
The character of Ivors was inspired by one of the daughters of David Sheehy MP, a Joyce family friend. The name for Gretta, meanwhile, was borrowed from the woman half of a couple the author of Dubliners also knew well.
James and Gretta Cousins had a home in Dublin ’s Sandymount, where Joyce stayed for a time during his pivotal summer of 1904 before falling ill from what he claimed was a “typhoid turnip” (the Cousinses were committed vegetarians) and fleeing.
As mentioned here previously (Diary September 7th, 2023 ), the Belfast-born James was a prominent figure in Irish literary life for a time, befriended by WB Yeats who shared his interest in eastern religion.
But Yeats went off him eventually, while the nonconformist couple felt increasingly at odds with life in Ireland. They moved to India in 1915, embraced Hinduism, and merged their personalities to the extent of writing a joint autobiography, the 800-page We Two Together (1950), in alternating chapters.
Which brings us back to Molly Ivors, sort of, because in one of the early chapters of that sprawling memoir, James Cousins describes a real-life equivalent of the fictional character, who came to a tragically heroic end.
He and Eveleen Nicolls had already met somewhere before, he recalls, “at one or other of the meetings within the Irish movement”.
[ Frank McNally: Ulysses updated, with apologies to James Joyce Opens in new window ]
But their paths crossed again on the Dingle Peninsula in July 1909, where Nicolls – a Gaelic League lecturer – was adding Kerry Irish to her battery of dialects.
Cousins (whose wife was campaigning in Kerry as a suffragist) had secured a room in Dunquin – the same bed previously occupied by JM Synge. Nicolls, alas, could be accommodated only on the Great Blasket Island, across the sound.
Before going there, she first scandalised locals by sitting in the men’s aisle at Sunday Mass. Then, having secured from Cousins a promise to visit her soon, she left for the island, unconsciously echoing Miss Ivors with the parting phrase “Beannacht leat”.
Cousins described her at the time: “She was twenty-five, tall, stately; an embodiment of sweetness and gentleness, but a sweetness that had no mawkishness in it, and a gentleness resting on fixity and fearlessness.”
A month later, he and his wife took a boat to the Blaskets, landing amid great commotion. Another currach had rushed to get in before them: clearly an emergency.
They soon learned it contained the body of Nicolls, who had got into difficulties while trying to save the life of a local girl. The girl – one of the Crohan family later immortalised by her father Tomás Ó Criomhthain in An t-Oileánach – survived. Her teenage brother Domhnall died alongside Nicolls in the rescue.
It’s not known (to me anyway) whether Joyce ever heard of Eveleen Nicolls, dead or alive. He had already written, although not yet published, The Dead by then. But the real-life tragedy in Kerry has other echoes of his famous story.
There, his alter ego is haunted by his wife’s memory of a former lover: “I think he died for me”. Of Nicolls’s actual demise, Cousins records visiting her parents in Dublin afterwards and hearing about a gathering of her woman friends before the holidays at which each was asked what sort of death she would prefer. “To be drowned saving another” was their daughter’s prophetic choice.
Still with the James Joyce Centre, but back among the living, my indefatigable long-time correspondent Owen Morton tells me the venue will also play host this coming weekend to a conference on “Social Cohesion and a New Inclusive Humanism”.
New humanism, I gather, is a humanism “stripped of its sometimes-aggressive atheism”. It harks back to, among other places, the Belfast Enlightenment of the 1790s. And I’m told its bridge-building spirit was very much alive in that recent visit by Protestant women to Garvaghy Road, as reported in this newspaper .
We could do with more of it, clearly. In the meantime, the two-day symposium at the Joyce Centre opens on Friday at 4.30pm. You can register online , but I’m told they will also take cash (€35 for Friday only, €70 for the weekend) at the door.
[ For Irish women writers, James Joyce was never a shadow but a light Opens in new window ]

title: What do we know about death of anti-plague researcher in Siberia and is there a wider risk?
description: Russia tells World Health Organisation there are no plague cases in Siberian city
content:
A fter a 28-year-old lab technician died last week reportedly after an accident at an anti-plague research laboratory in Russia , we take a look at what we know about the incident.
The exact details remain unclear but reports from Russia have suggested Darya Shipilova, an employee at the anti-plague institute in the city of Irkutsk, died on October 2nd, two days after becoming unwell at work.
According to Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, Shipilova died from “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”.
However, there are other accounts: Alexey Tsydenov, the head of the neighbouring Buryatia region, initially said Shipilova had died of plague, before editing his social media post to say she had “possibly” died of the disease.
Russian authorities have denied this to the World Health Organisation (WHO), stating: “No case of this dangerous disease has been recorded in the city of Irkutsk, ​Russian Federation.”
If it is the plague, what are we talking about?
We are talking about a disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, typically found in small mammals and the fleas that feed on them. It is the same organism that was behind the bubonic plague or “black death” that swept Europe in the 14th century.
However, the bubonic form is different from the pneumonic plague that some have suggested caused Shipilova’s death.
The former is more common, results in swellings called buboes and is spread by the bite of infected fleas, whereas the latter is lung-based. Pneumonic plague has a higher mortality rate and can be spread between people.
[ US ‘monitoring’ suspected case of plague in Russia after lab worker dies Opens in new window ]
How might Shipilova have ended up with pneumonic plague?
One report in the media is that Shipilova was admitted with the disease after returning from Thailand, while another is that she became infected after breaking a test tube in the laboratory. Rospotrebnadzor has denied any such accidents have occurred at the institute.
It is worth noting that the plague is not a disease of the past.
“There are a few hundred cases of plague reported each year globally usually in geographically restricted areas, particularly in Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of the Congo – although there are a small number of cases in the western United States, central Asia, Mongolia, etc,” said Dr Malick Gibani at Imperial College London.
That might not seem reassuring, but we no longer have to rely on medieval medicine.
Dr Simon Clarke at the University of Reading said: “Unlike many viral respiratory diseases, plague is caused by bacteria, and antibiotics such as fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides work well against this pathogen if administered early enough and are often given prophylactically, post-exposure.”
However, Prof Brendan Wren at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine said there were multi-antibiotic-resistant strains emerging, “and if the laboratory is working on such a strain, then treatment options may be limited”.
There have also been reports that almost 200 people with whom Shipilova may have had contact are now under medical observation, and that quarantines have been imposed in a number of hospitals.
“Isolation and monitoring are sensible strategies,” Wren said.
The UN health agency’s spokesperson Christian Lindmeier has said the risk to others is low. “The WHO initial risk assessment from the information available estimates the risk to be moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole, and very low for the WHO European region,” he said.
Dr Zania Stamataki, an associate professor of viral immunology and academic lead for containment level 3 laboratories at the University of Birmingham, said the control systems used in the UK for hazardous organisms work, meaning laboratory-acquired infections are rare.
But, she added: “They are not impossible, and this is why an incident warrants a full account of what happened. That account matters beyond Russia.” - Guardian
[ Russia tells WHO there are no plague cases in Siberian city Opens in new window ]

title: Mike Prendergast: ‘Munster were going in a different direction to where I wanted to go as a coach’
description: The Irish rugby coach moved to Bath last year to be attack coach
content:
Two games into his new role at Bath, Mike Prendergast has the air of a man enjoying his work.
Now working under another former Munster figure in Johann van Graan , Prendergast swapped Thomond Park for The Rec last summer, leading the backs and attack at the west country club.
A fortnight into the new campaign, Bath have two wins, 73 points on the scoreboard and 10 league points that has them joint top of the table. Early days and all that, but with the likes of Finn Russell and Santi Carreras running in scores, it’s easy to see why an attack coach would enjoy such surroundings.
This Santi Carreras interception deserves your full attention 🤯 📺 Stream TNT Sports on HBO Max https://t.co/WyCGBZpKvZ pic.twitter.com/5ZUaS8o4oy
All of which explains the pull of a side like Bath, but not the push factors that opened up the opportunity. When Prendergast left Munster, he still had a year left on his contract. He was on the coaching ticket when Munster won the 2023 URC.
While overlooked for his home province’s head coach role, Clayton McMillan instead proving the final choice, Prendergast was held in sufficient regard to be asked by the IRFU to coach Ireland A back in 2025.
Clearly, there was a reason for the former scrumhalf to decide to leave Irish rugby. One theory was that in any walk of life it can be difficult to work with someone appointed to a role for which you unsuccessfully applied, but Prendergast quickly pushes back on any such notions.
“It was nothing to do with that in terms of Clayton getting the job and me not,” he says. “It’s like anything in professional sport, if you sit around and feel sorry for yourself, that will be picked up very quickly. I’m a professional coach, I’ve got to do what’s best for myself and the team and that’s what I did last season.
“I had four years back in Munster, I played there, it was my home club. I’d brilliant memories, good success as a player. I went off to France for 10 years, came back to Munster and really enjoyed the first couple of years. The last season or so was less enjoyable and I probably felt I needed a change personally.
“I knew Johann [van Graan] through coaching against him, I knew Finn [Russell, the two previously worked together in France with Racing] and had that connection. I had conversations and felt that at this stage of my career it was the right move for me.”
Prendergast was subsequently asked why the last year was not as enjoyable as what went before. Was it a problem with the style of play or something away from the coaching ticket? Munster have dealt with a number of off-field matters in recent times, not least an independent review into their governance and the recent resignation of chief executive Ian Flanagan.
“I’ll be honest with you, certain people in the club wanted to go one direction and that wasn’t the direction I wanted to go in,” says Prendergast, without naming individuals.
“I had no muddied waters with anyone at all. I went in and spoke to the club, spoke to Clayton and I said I think it’s time for a change. He said ‘Look, I know you’ll work to the end of the season and move on’ and that’s the way it was. There was a direction certain people were going in and that’s not the direction that I wanted to go in as a coach.”
Once the decision was made to leave, the link to Van Graan and Bath came into view, even if Prendergast never actually overlapped with the former Munster boss in Limerick. Russell also proved a useful sounding board, given the strong relationship between an attack coach and outhalf who have previously worked together.
“I’ve known him [Van Graan] for a couple of years, we had a chat about it,” explains Prendergast. “He outlined exactly what was here in the club, the set-up etc, the squad. It appealed to me quite a lot.
