“With an attack coach, the 10 is always someone you’ll have a close link with. I still keep in contact with number 10s that I coached back in Grenoble 10, 12 years ago. I’m sure most attack coaches will tell you the same, they’re nearly like your little son as such. You always keep those relationships and I’ve a very strong relationship with Finn.
“He spoke highly of the club and I see that now I’ve been over here in the last couple of months.”

title: Relatives of shooting victim spotted his tracksuit under freshly dug grass, court to hear
description: Kurt Ryan (33) is charged with murder of Lee Slattery at Delmege Estate in Limerick in 2010
content:
Relatives of a man shot twice at close range called gardaí after they came upon freshly dug grass, poked around in it with a stick and spotted the fabric of a blue tracksuit similar to the one worn by their missing loved one, a murder trial has heard.
Kurt Ryan (33), from Moylish Crescent in Limerick , is charged with the murder of Lee Slattery at Delmege Estate, Knockalisheen Road in Limerick on a date unknown between May 27th to May 31 st 2010.
Michael O’Higgins, for the prosecution, gave the jury a “roadmap” of the anticipated evidence in the case on Tuesday at a sitting of the Central Criminal Court in Cork .
He said that Delmege Estate was the site of a grand old house from the 19th century that stood on 80 acres. By 2010 it was in a state of dereliction.
“It is not too difficult to imagine what it must have looked like in its heyday, or what it would have looked like in the small hours of the morning on the night of the murder.”
Relatives of Slattery had gone out looking for him at Delmege Estate on May 31st, 2010. The 25-year-old had failed to return home four days earlier. They had become increasingly concerned for his safety as it was unusual for him not to come home.
They raised the alarm when they spotted the tracksuit fabric in the ground.
O’Higgins said that Slattery was shot twice at close range in a very overgrown area close to Delmege House. The cause of death was a gunshot wound to his trunk and injuries to his heart and lungs.
O’Higgins said Slattery had also sustained blunt force trauma to his face, a fracture to his facial bones and teeth and injuries to his skull.
“Mercifully, it would appear those blows may well have been administered after he was shot.”
O’Higgins said gardaí carried out a search of the area and the outhouses on the derelict Delmege Estate.
They found a pistol in a sock which had been concealed under a brick in one of the old outhouses. He stated that this was the weapon used to kill Slattery.
Meanwhile, the jurors were told that Slattery lived “a stone’s throw” away from the accused in the case.
O’Higgins said that the late Lee Slattery was “well liked” and “a bit of a character”. The native of Moyross sold drugs to support his drug habit while Ryan, who was then 17, was also dealing drugs in the area.
O’Higgins said that when Ryan was interviewed by gardaí he denied having any involvement in the murder.
The case will continue on Wednesday in front of the jury and Judge Eileen Creedon. It is expected to last in the region of a month.

title: New public spending efficiency taskforce to be established within three months
description: Jack Chambers says new body will scrutinise day-to-day public spending and see where greater value for money can be delivered
content:
The Government is to establish a new public spending efficiency taskforce to “extensively scrutinise” day-to-day expenditure across departments and agencies.
Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers said he wanted to see the new body established within three months.
He said the work of the new taskforce would inform the approach to subsequent budgets aimed at delivering efficiency and delivery in all day-to-day spending.
He said it would identify areas across public spending where there was scope to drive greater efficiencies and would recommend “specific actions that can deliver better services and greater value for money”.
The Government’s expenditure report published on Tuesday said the new taskforce would “examine current expenditure with the objective of identifying a small number of key areas where there is scope for improvement and recommending specific actions to improve economy, effectiveness and efficiency”.
Chambers had told Ministers in the run-up to the budget that the introduction of efficiencies and reforms would be crucial, and examples of measures put forward by departments to be implemented over the next year are published in the expenditure report.
Plans for the taskforce came in for criticism from the opposition in the Dáil.
Solidarity TD Ruth Coppinger claimed Chambers had gone “full-on Musk” by announce a “Doge”-style operation in the public sector, a reference to the Department of Government Efficiency set up by Tesla boss Elon Musk to slash US government spending under President Donald Trump
“He’s setting up this public spending efficiency taskforce that will monitor on a daily basis, scrutinise day-to-day spending, making greater efficiencies,” she told the Dáil.
“That will be news now to the tens of thousands of public sector workers who are going to be taking to the streets next Wednesday,” she added, referring to next week’s industrial action by public sector workers.
“It was so high-handed and arrogant of Minister Chambers to call on them not to go ahead with the industrial action when he never once mentioned how he’s going to deal with pay for public sector workers,” she said.
The Department of Foreign Affairs said in the Government spending report it envisaged that an anticipated 25 per cent increase in applications for passports – covering about 200,000 people – next year would be delivered with existing staff resources.
The Department of Culture and Communications said it would commence a periodic critical review of Sport Ireland later this year. This review will include the external environment, organisational capacity and organisational performance.
The Department of Health said it envisaged an increased utilisation of theatres, outpatient clinics and diagnostic equipment through improved scheduling, reduced downtime and stronger performance management to maximise activity from existing capacity. It also said there would be more evening and weekend care.
The Department of Housing highlighted planning reforms under which 10-year statutory development plans would be implemented, “providing greater certainty for communities, developers and infrastructure providers through a longer-term and more strategic approach to land-use planning”.
The Department of Education will review the English as an Additional Language policy “to ensure resources are allocated effectively and efficiently in line with changing demand”.
Revenue said it would continue to work with the Department of Finance in preparing for the introduction of legislation confirming that all tax appeal hearings must be held in public, with the exception of applicable special circumstances.
The Department of Justice said it planned to boost the Garda recruitment pipeline. Capacity at the Garda College will be increased to accommodate up to 250 trainees per intake.
The Department of Public Expenditure said savings would be delivered from an organisational restructuring following the integration of the Office of Government Procurement and the Office of the Government Chief Information Officer spending votes. It said a review of staffing structures identified opportunities to streamline management and support functions, resulting in the suppression of a number of posts and recurring annual pay savings.
Savings are also envisaged on the costs involved in running recruitment interviews. It is envisaged that a pool of serving Civil Service personnel would be established to serve as interview board members.

Solidarity TD Ruth Coppinger claimed Chambers had gone “full-on Musk” by announce a “Doge”-style operation in the public sector, a reference to the Department of Government Efficiency set up by Tesla boss Elon Musk to slash US government spending under President Donald Trump
“He’s setting up this public spending efficiency taskforce that will monitor on a daily basis, scrutinise day-to-day spending, making greater efficiencies,” she told the Dáil.
“That will be news now to the tens of thousands of public sector workers who are going to be taking to the streets next Wednesday,” she added, referring to next week’s industrial action by public sector workers.
“It was so high-handed and arrogant of Minister Chambers to call on them not to go ahead with the industrial action when he never once mentioned how he’s going to deal with pay for public sector workers,” she said.

title: Shares climb amid relative calm on oil markets
description: European healthcare stocks perform strongly as US AI rush continues
content:
Falling oil prices spurred further advances across stock markets on Tuesday, while early reaction to the Budget 2027 announcement in the Republic boosted Irish builders and banks.
Benchmarks Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude fell on Tuesday, helping to somewhat ease inflation fears.
Rare earths miner Kenmare Resources surged 25.2 per cent to €2.68 after the company confirmed an Irish Times report that Abu Dhabi’s International Resources Holdings had approached it.
Kenmare has given the prospective buyer until November 17th to declare a firm intention to make an offer for the Irish-based company.
Ryanair climbed 2.28 per cent to €24.21 as the slide in oil prices was seen to boost airlines.
Traders noted that Budget 2027 aided house builders. Cairn Homes gained 2.28 per cent to close at €2.69 while rival Glenveagh Properties added 2.36 per cent to reach €2.385.
Banks also benefited. AIB advanced 0.75 per cent to €11.38. Its peer Bank of Ireland rose 1.53 per cent to €19.25.
“It’s generally positive across the board,” said one dealer. “Oil prices are down, so there’s a bit of relief out there.”
Insulation and building materials group Kingspan was one of the few fallers in Dublin on Tuesday.
Shares in the Co Cavan-based multinational slid 1.17 per cent to €101.50.
The London market climbed on the back of falling oil, but defence stocks suffered as the British government appeared to waver on spending pledges.
Business information and events group Informa rose 3 per cent to 887.2p. The company plans to raise £940 million (€1.1 billion) to fund the £2.24 billion acquisition of Clarion Events, and hive off its academic operation, Taylor & Francis.
Online fashion retailer Asos plunged almost 10 per cent to 454p after confirming a cyberattack.
Reports that the British government may defer defence spending pledges for a year in the hope that growth recovers hit the industry’s stock.
BAE Systems fell 4.1 per cent to 1,855p and Babcock International slipped 2.1 per cent to 906.6p.
Aircraft engine maker Rolls-Royce shed 2.7 per cent to 1,438.2p.
It was a similar picture on the Continent. The Stoxx 600 Index rose 0.4 per cent while Germany’s Dax Index rose 0.8 per cent. In Paris, the CAC40 Index added 0.4 per cent.
Danish biotech Genmab climbed ‌7.6 per cent in early trade after a late-stage study showed that the blood cancer drug combination it is developing with US drugmaker ⁠AbbVie’s cut risk of progression ​or death. The shares were up 4.4 per cent at 2,482 Danish kroner in the late afternoon.
Healthcare stocks fared well in Europe on Tuesday. Italian pharmaceutical manufacturer Recordati ’s shares advanced as much as 1.8 per cent to €53.15 in Milan.
Private equity player CVC Capital Partners raised its take-private offer for the pharma business to €10.5 billion after minority shareholders complained that it undervalued the company.
The cash offer of €53 per share compares with an earlier bid of €51.29. CVC says the new bid is final.
Dutch chipmaker BE Semiconductor Industries shares were down almost 6 per cent at €191.35 shortly before 5pm Irish time.
BE faces competition in pioneering new processes for bonding microchips from another Netherlands player, ASML, whose stock had slipped 0.8 per cent in late afternoon.
Among other stocks, ​Italy’s Technoprobe gained 2.8 per cent to €36.84 after analysts at merchant bank JP Morgan initiated ​coverage of the microchip testing specialist with an “overweight” rating, which is an effective recommendation to buy the stock.
US stocks advanced for a fourth straight day, driving the S&P 500 toward its first record close since August. AI chip giant Nvidia’s market value approached $6 trillion (€5.3 trillion). Advanced Micro Devices’ Lisa Su predicted “very high” chip demand over the next few years.
Paramount Skydance closed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, completing one of the biggest media mergers of all time after engaging in a bruising battle for control with Netflix and fending off antitrust lawsuits. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg/Reuters

title: Smokers to see price of cigarette pack rise to more than €20 for first time amid €1 hike
description: Alcohol Action Ireland expressed disappointment that excise duties on alcohol had not been increased
content:
The smokers of Ireland will be fuming following a €1 hike in the price of a packet of 20 cigarettes, a tax increase that will take the cost of many well known brands to more than €20 a pack for the first time.
Cigarettes – and related tobacco products – are once again the only one of the so-called old reliables that have been singled out for a tax increase, with alcohol and motor fuel spared a similar fate.
However, a 20 cent per ml increase in vaping products was also announced, which will add around 40 cent to the price of a disposable vape.
Smoking lobby groups and campaigners have criticised as “outrageous” and “unfair” the price increase, with warnings the hike will drive more people into the arms of tobacco smugglers.
Retailers Against Smuggling (Ras) said the Government had “blatantly ignored warnings that further tobacco tax increases will push more consumers away from Irish retailers towards cheaper tobacco sourced abroad, duty-free and through the black market”.
It pointed to a poll it commissioned in the run up to the budget which suggested 43 per cent would look outside the State for tobacco if prices increased again, compared with just 19 per cent who said they would continue buying from Irish retailers.
Simon Clark, of the smokers’ rights group Forest, said the €1 increase was “an outrageous and unfair attack on law-abiding consumers, especially the low paid who can ill afford such a significant increase in the cost of cigarettes purchased legally”.
He added: “The only winners will be criminal gangs who will be delighted that many more smokers will be driven to the black market.”
[ What are main points from Budget 2027? Opens in new window ]
Alcohol Action Ireland (AAI), the national independent advocate for reducing alcohol harm, expressed disappointment that excise duties on alcohol had not been increased.
The group said that decision was “compounded by the misguided decision” to give €15 million to publicans.
“With excise duties on tobacco rising by a substantial €1 on a pack of cigarettes, it is clear the Government understands the value of price controls as a policy option to change consumer behaviour and promote public health,” said its chief executive Shelia Golheany.
“AAI therefore finds it disappointing that Government refuses to increase alcohol excise duties, which would have the dual benefit of helping reduce population-level consumption and its associated harms, while at the same time raising much needed revenue to help cover the cost of cleaning up the mess alcohol causes.”

title: Dublin teen sent video of himself inhaling aerosols a year before he died from fumes, inquest hears
description: Daniel Maguire (14) died from ‘cardiac toxicity due to inhalation of butane and propane’
content:
The parents of a Dublin teenager who collapsed and died within two hours of inhaling the contents of an aerosol deodorant last year have called for greater awareness among young people of the dangers of such products.
Daniel Maguire (14) from Ashfield Grove, Huntstown, Dublin 15 , suffered fatal injuries to his heart after being discovered unresponsive in the bedroom of his home at around 11pm on September 27th, 2025.
He was formally pronounced dead at Children’s Health Ireland in Temple Street , Dublin, at 12.40am the following morning.
Speaking after an inquest into his death at Dublin District Coroner’s Court on Tuesday, Daniel’s parents Yvonne and Dermot Maguire welcomed information they received this week that raising awareness about the dangers of solvents and “fast gas” is going to become part of the Junior Certificate curriculum.
“We just want teenagers talking about this to each other because they don’t listen to their parents,” said Dermot Maguire.
The couple, who have been campaigning on the issue since their son’s death, have also called for more warning labels on aerosol containers.
The inquest heard Daniel had gone to the gym and played soccer earlier that day after having a half-day at Hartstown Community College, where he was a third year student.
Dermot Maguire gave evidence that his son had been “in great spirits” and was “laughing and joking around” after he had got home.
He said the last time he spoke to his son was when Daniel went upstairs to his room, saying goodnight after the family had eaten a takeaway dinner together.
At around 11pm, he shouted up to see if his son had the keys for the front door when he was locking up the house.
Maguire said his son replied “yes, Dad”, but then there was silence when he asked for the keys to be thrown down. The inquest heard he went to Daniel’s bedroom and found him collapsed between a desk and chair.
In reply to questions from coroner Cróna Gallagher, Dermot Maguire said: “I knew straight away what was happening”, as he had discovered an aerosol can and a sock in his son’s bedroom.
The inquest heard Daniel had previously sent a video of himself inhaling aerosols in his bedroom to a friend on Snapchat in June 2024.
On learning of the video, Dermot Maguire said his wife had immediately brought their son to their GP, where the seriousness of inhaling aerosols was explained to him.
Yvonne Maguire said Daniel was very upset, teary and regretful about the incident and remembered her son claimed it had been the first time he had inhaled an aerosol.
She agreed with the coroner that he would have been aware that he was under parental surveillance after what had happened, but she was satisfied that there was no evidence of any long-term use of aerosols by her son.
In reply to further questions, Dermot Maguire said his son was happy in school, was “very fit and healthy”, regularly participated in football and MMA and went to the gym.
He said they did not know why Daniel had inhaled aerosol deodorant on the night of the fatal incident.
“Everything was normal. There was nothing out of the ordinary,” he said. He surmised it might have been a TikTok challenge, a dare or just being curious.
However, Maguire said they had spoken openly to Daniel’s friends following his death and inhaling aerosols was not something they did.
They had checked his son’s mobile phone following his death, but it had also contained “nothing unusual”.
The inquest heard that an examination of Daniel’s medical records showed no evidence of any underlying physical or mental health issues.
Dr Gallagher said the results of a postmortem showed the presence of butane and propane in the teenager’s blood. The coroner said they are volatile substances which are commonly found in aerosol containers as propellants.
She noted that they can result in sudden death “even in small doses” either by asphyxia or by causing irregular cardiac rhythms.
Dr Gallagher confirmed no alcohol or other drugs were detected in the teenager’s body and attributed the cause of death to “cardiac toxicity due to inhalation of butane and propane”.
Recording a verdict of death by misadventure, the coroner observed that the circumstances of the case should act as a warning about inhaling the contents of aerosol containers, which she noted is “an inherently dangerous thing to do”.
Offering her condolences to the deceased’s family, Dr Gallagher said: “I’m very sorry that you have lost your precious son, brother and friend in this very tragic manner.”

title: Budget 2027 sees some €22m set aside for Ryder Cup in Adare and Euro 2028
description: Gaelic Players Association and League of Ireland academies welcome increased funding in budget
content:
There was a €22 million allocation in the budget to further support Ireland’s hosting of the Ryder Cup in Adare in 2027 , and preparations for the co-hosting of the 2028 European Football Championship (along with England, Scotland and Wales).
Last year, the Government set aside €9 million for Ryder Cup preparations.
In total, Sport Ireland will receive €121 million in funding next year. Although not yet specified, this is to include an increase in the 2026 high-performance allocation of €28.5 million, ensuring the four-year Olympic cycle investment towards Los Angeles 2028 will exceed €100 million.
The previous high was €89 million across the Paris Olympic cycle (2021-2024), which was an increase on the €59 million for the Tokyo Olympic cycle (2017-2020).
The Department of Culture, Communications and Sport has yet to comment on the submission from the Olympic Federation of Ireland (OFI) Athlete’s Commission, which was seeking a new tax break for all Irish athletes that would allow for a €50,000 annual tax credit, and expand the Sportspersons Relief, currently limited to 13 sports, so that all Olympic sports would qualify.
According to a spokesperson for the department, “Ministers O’Donovan and McConalogue will outline the department’s budget allocation at the press conference at 3pm tomorrow [Wednesday]. The Department will not comment until that point.”
The €1 million increases in Government funding for both the Gaelic Players Association (GPA) intercounty grants scheme and the League of Ireland (LOI) academies were among other sporting measures announced.
Although short of the additional annual investment of €2.8 million originally sought by the GPA, the €1 million increase was welcomed as marking “further progress in the players’ campaign for enhanced investment”.
It brings to €8.2 million the total annual funding towards the near 4,000 players in intercounty football, hurling and camogie. The increase is worth on average an additional €250 for each player, bringing their annual grant from €1,800 to €2,050.
In a statement, the GPA said it builds on last year’s €1.6 million increase and was “another important step towards our target of €10 million in annual player funding”.
The GPA added: “We look forward to continued positive and constructive engagement throughout the lifetime of this Government, with our focus firmly on achieving fair recognition and sustainable support for every intercounty player.”
In his budget speech, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers referenced Mayo’s All-Ireland football final win over Kerry last July as a backdrop to these sporting increases, saying: “We’re a country that understands the immeasurable contribution sport makes to our shared sense of belonging.”
There was also an additional €1 million ring-fenced for the hurling and camogie academy initiative, which is aimed at growing hurling and camogie in non-traditional and urban areas. Last year’s allocation was under €750,000.
On that allocation, the GPA said: “We also welcome the additional investment in hurling and Gaelic games announced today, reinforcing the Government’s tangible commitment to strengthening our national games and sporting heritage.”
The extra €1 million in funding for the League of Ireland academies brings that allocation for 2027 to €4 million, representing a 33 per cent increase on last year’s allocation of €3 million, the first of a multiannual commitment to help build a professional soccer academy system.
Although short of the FAI’s original submission for a €2 million increase, it means the FAI is now set to introduce a new performance lead at each League of Ireland club. Last year’s initial funding ensured two full-time academy positions at each club.
Horse racing’s finances were boosted with its share of the Horse & Greyhound Fund increased to €81.6 million for 2027. That’s a close on 3 per cent increase on the 2026 figure of €79.3 million, which was the same as in 2025.
Horse Racing Ireland’s last five-year strategic plan, released in 2024, targeted a figure of over €92 million in State support for the sector by 2028. In 2020, racing’s ruling body said it was aiming for a figure of €98 million in State funding by 2024.
The Horse & Greyhound Fund is split 80-20 between horses and dogs and is increased to €102 million next year. The equivalent figure in 2021 was €96 million.
A HRI statement on Tuesday said it noted the increase and added: “The continued support of the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine is essential for the Irish horse racing sector.
“HRI’s budgeting process for 2027 is under way and will be focused on prioritising spends on key strategic deliverables in line with the HRI Strategic Plan 2024-2028.”

title: Campaigners to make case for re-establishing stem cell laboratory in Cork
description: Lab would increase national capacity to treat cancers and save patients and families long journeys to Dublin or Galway
content:
The HSE has been urged to re-establish a stem cell laboratory in Cork , which would not only save cancer patients from Munster having to travel to Dublin or Galway for treatment but also increase national capacity to treat cancers such as leukaemia, lymphoma and multiple myeloma.
Campaigner Mags McCarthy of the Irish Blood Cancer Patients advocacy group is due to meet members of the Oireachtas in Leinster House on Wednesday to make the case for re-establishing a stem cell laboratory at Cork University Hospital (CUH).
McCarthy told The Irish Times how the lack of stem cell treatment at CUH has meant patients from Munster must now either attend St James’s Hospital in Dublin or Galway University Hospital if they are to receive the treatment – which in some cases can be life extending, and, in others, life-saving.
“My own father Michael had to go to St James’s Hospital for treatment in June 2022,” said McCarthy. “He was an in-patient for six weeks and, after his discharge, he had to stay close to the hospital in an apartment provided by the Leukaemia Trust for another six weeks because he had to be monitored closely.
“That was just in case he got an infection, because patients undergoing stem cell transplantation can have severely compromised immune systems, so he had to be nearby in case he had to be brought back into St James’s quickly because infections can be serious and, in some cases, life-threatening.”
The stem cell treatment worked for McCarthy’s father, and he is now in good health, but the experience made McCarthy aware of the challenges facing not just patients from Munster diagnosed with cancers but also their families as they face long and arduous journeys for treatment.
“These are people who are already seriously ill, but to access the specialist treatment that they need they have to travel to either Dublin or Galway and then spend weeks or even months away from their homes and families, so it takes a huge toll on both them and their families,” she said.
McCarthy, together with the president of European Society for Blood and Marrow Transplantation, Dr Ibrahim Yakoub Agha, will make the case at Leinster House for reopening a stem cell transplant unit at CUH – a move backed by clinicians at the Cork hospital.
CUH consultant haematologist Dr Vitaliy Mykytiv said that until 2006 CUH had been carrying out stem cell transplantation therapy at a laminar flow cabinet in the hospital, but new regulations required the therapy to be carried out in a full laboratory, so CUH was forced to stop.
[ Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international study finds Opens in new window ]
Mykytiv said there were three types of stem cell therapy: autologous transplants where a patient receives their own cells; Car-T therapy where a patient’s own white blood cells are re-engineered to destroy cancer cells; and allogeneic transplants where a patient receives cells from a donor.
He said St James’s had 28 beds in its unit in Dublin and catered for patients receiving autologous, Car -T and allogeneic transplants, while Galway had five beds to cater for stem cell transplant patients but offered only autologous transplants and Car-T therapy.
“The main problem in Ireland is the lack of national capacity for allogeneic transplants and Car-T therapy,” he said. “If we were to open in Cork, what we would be looking to do would be autologous transplants – but that would free up allogeneic and Car-T capacity at both St James’s and Galway.”
Mykytiv said 89 patients of CUH, the Mercy University Hospital and the Bons Secours Hospital in Cork were attending either St James’s or Galway for treatment, which was a huge imposition on both the patients and their families.
He said it was a sad reality that some people waiting for transplant would die before they had the opportunity to receive the treatment because there was insufficient capacity nationally to meet demand.
“We need to increase capacity, and one way would be to re-establish stem cell therapy in Cork. At the moment Ireland is doing around 50 transplants per one million population, whereas Germany is doing around 95 transplants per million, so our transplant rate is very poor, it needs to improve.”

title: First payments under new derelict property tax not due until June 2028
description: Dereliction an ‘unacceptable spectacle’ in depths of housing crisis, says Minister for Finance Simon Harris
content:
The first payments under a new tax to tackle dereliction in towns and cities, announced by the Government in last year’s budget, will not be made due until June 2028.
Last year, as part of the previous budget, the Government said it would replace the current derelict sites levy, under which local authorities could impose a 7 per cent tariff on owners of properties listed on their derelict site registers.
Minister for Finance Simon Harris said on Tuesday the old levy system would be replaced with a new derelict property tax, which will be administered by local authorities and Revenue .
He added dereliction has been “a scourge in many of our towns and cities, and quite simply an unacceptable spectacle in the depths of a housing crisis”.
The tax will apply to residential and non-residential properties, and the rate of the tax will be “7 per cent of the self-assessed value of the property”.
The reformed approach to tackling dereliction in towns and cities will involve local authorities being responsible for identification of derelict properties, with Revenue in charge of collecting any taxes due.
Preliminary registers of derelict properties will be published by councils in September 2027, and property owners will have until the end of November to appeal the inclusion of their property on a register.
[ Budget 2027: big business pays the bills as Coalition rolls the dice Opens in new window ]
Local authorities are required to adjudicate on appeals by the end of February 2028. Final registers of derelict properties will be published in March, and owners of properties on the register will be required to pay the 7 per cent tax by June 23rd, 2028.
During the first year, the derelict property tax will apply to towns and cities with a population of 4,000 or more, and be expanded to towns with populations of 2,000 or more in the second year. A total of 107 towns will be in scope in the first year, and that will rise to 171 in the second year.
[ All inheritance tax free thresholds rise in the budget but no other reforms Opens in new window ]
In June, Harris said local authorities have “not done enough” to tackle dereliction and “failed” in their job to administer the current derelict sites levy.
The Irish Times previously reported that Dublin City Council is owed more than €10 million in outstanding dereliction levies in relation to more than 300 properties.
Grant Thornton Ireland tax partner Robert Fitzgerald said the reformed dereliction measures “can influence behaviour, but their success depends on design”.
“Clear definitions of what constitutes a derelict property, straightforward compliance processes and appropriate exemptions for genuine redevelopment activity will be essential for its success,” Fitzgerald said.
[ Budget 2027 main points: €10 increase in pension and welfare rates; 20 cent per ml tax on vapes Opens in new window ]
During his budget speech, Harris also confirmed some changes to existing housing supply measures, including the Help to Buy scheme.
Under the Help to Buy scheme, set up in 2017, first-time buyers can get up to €30,000 from the State for a home deposit through a grant paid as a refund of income tax.
Harris said the maximum refund a first-time buyer can claim under the scheme would rise by €5,000 to €35,000, with immediate effect.
Sherry FitzGerald Group chief executive Marian Finnegan said the increase would be welcomed by prospective first-time buyers, but that it would not tackle the root cause of the housing crisis.
“This was a missed opportunity to broaden the focus from first-time buyers through targeted, time-bound measures to other households seeking accommodation,” Finnegan said.
The rent tax credit, first introduced in Budget 2023, has also been increased by €150 to €1,150 for single claimants and €2,300 for couples. The credit is typically claimed by about 400,000 people annually.
Harris added the tax-free threshold a homeowner can earn under the Rent-a-Room scheme would also rise from €14,000 to €16,000 in a bid to incentivise more people to rent out more rooms within their homes.
The tax relief incentive has also been extended to apply to detached cabins of between 32 and 45sq m installed since July of this year.

title: Fuel excise cuts extended to February as carbon tax is slashed to ease home heating costs
description: Budget 2027 energy measures: Cuts in excise duty on petrol and diesel, due to end this month, are now being extended until the end of February
content:
The carbon tax has been slashed for home heating and frozen for motorists in a big reversal of Government policy.
The price of home-heating oil will fall by about €40 for a 900-litre tank as the tax is reversed to its 2023 level. Gas will fall in price by about €34 on an average annual bill under the same measure.
The savings will benefit about 1.5 million households whose homes are heated primarily by gas or oil in the form of kerosene.
A planned carbon tax increase on these fuels, postponed since May and due to take effect this month, will not go ahead. A further increase due to be announced this month and take effect next May is also being abandoned.
In a surprise move that went further than expected, Minister for Finance Simon Harris said it would “not increase again” in the lifetime of the Government.
If the Government lasts its full term, that means it will not increase before 2030, which would spare households having to pay annual increases that would hit roughly between €85 and €100 by the end of the decade.
Annual increases in the tax, adding €6.50-€7.50 per tonne of carbon per year, were set down in law.
They meant that, by 2030, the tax was to be imposed on fossil fuels at a rate of €100 per tonne of carbon emitted. The budget announcement scraps that plan and also strips back the increases of the past two years to return the rate to €48.50 per tonne for gas and home-heating oil.
Last year’s increase did proceed for petrol and diesel, so the tax is currently levied on those fuels at €71 per tonne of carbon.
It will remain at that level but the increase due to take effect this month that would have seen it rise to €78.50 per tonne will not now go ahead.
That will spare motorists from having to pay what would have been around €1.30 extra for a full tank of petrol and almost €1.50 for a tank of diesel.
[ Budget Calculator 2027: Here’s how this year’s budget will affect your income Opens in new window ]
Cuts in excise duty on petrol and diesel, introduced in April but due to end this month, are now being extended until the end of February.
That amounts to continued savings of 27 cent per litre of petrol and 32 cent per litre of diesel.
“I want to be very clear there will be no increase in any form of tax either at the pump or in your home during this winter period,” Harris said.
He said from the end of next February there would be a “gradual and responsible restoration” of excise in four phases, with a full restoration not occurring until June 30th, 2027.
[ Scrapping carbon tax means handing ‘billions of euro to Ursula von der Leyen’ Opens in new window ]
Harris said the changes were necessary to help people cope with the rising cost of living where energy was “the most acute area of pressure”.
“While no government can fully absorb the impact of the Middle East conflict, we must act,” he said.
Revenues from the carbon tax are used primarily for climate action measures and the revenue from it will now be less than anticipated.
However, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers announced a record allocation of €654.5 million for the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) to spend on grant-aiding residential and community retrofit schemes.
The aim was to ensure more households had access to “secure, sustainable and affordable sources of energy”, he said.
In another move that will assist up to 140,000 households, they will be allowed earn up to €600 from supplying surplus solar electricity to the grid before having to pay tax on the income – up from the previous limit of €400.

title: Minister for Justice offers to prioritise Gaza students’ appeals over visa refusal
description: Proposal would see cases of four scholarship students heard and decided by Friday
content:
The Minister for Justice has offered to prioritise the hearing of appeals by four Palestinian students against his refusal of visas to allow them to pursue fully-funded Irish university scholarships, the High Court heard.
The offer by Minister Jim O’Callaghan would see the appeals, which could otherwise take a year or more to decide, heard and decided by 5pm Friday.
Lawyers for the students from Gaza and the Minister were in continuing talks on Tuesday evening to see if the offer would be sufficient to achieve a settlement of the students’ judicial review challenges over the refusals.
Judge Anthony Barr was told of the offer as he was set to begin a hearing of the challenges on Tuesday.
Among the orders sought by the students are ones requiring the Minister to prioritise the hearing of their appeals because otherwise the courses could not be pursued this academic year.
The hearing of the cases was fast-tracked by the High Court for reasons including the fact that October 15th is the last date by which Israeli authorities must be given notification for evacuation of the students in time for the November 2nd deadline for them to take up their courses.
Three of the students are in Gaza, while the fourth is in Spain after being evacuated there with the assistance of the Spanish government. He is pursuing a second-choice course in Spain, but his preference is to take up his first choice of an engineering course in Dublin’s Trinity College .
On Tuesday, Barr was told the Minister’s offer was received by the applicants on Monday afternoon and led to correspondence.
[ The one thing Israel hasn’t managed to take from us in three years is hope Opens in new window ]
Senior counsel Blinne Ní Ghrálaigh, instructed by Phoenix Law, initially indicated her side would be unable to accept the offer if the Minister intended to decide the appeals applying the stricter criteria that led to the July refusals, rather than a less strict policy that applied last year.
Her side just wants the Minister to act fairly, in a non-discriminatory manner and not to unlawfully fetter his discretion, she said.
Eoin Carolan, with barrister Sarah Cooney, for the Minister, said they had understood the offer to fast-track the appeals had been accepted and he was “astonished” at the applicants’ stance. His side had not complied with directions concerning filing the legal papers necessary for the full hearing to proceed on Tuesday because it understood the offer was accepted, he said.
After further exchanges, Ní Ghrálaigh said there “may be room for negotiation”.
The judge said he would give the sides time to discuss matters outside court. He said if the hearing was to proceed this week, he had “to warn” about a very recent decision by the Supreme Court concerning general non-availability of judicial review where there is an adequate alternative remedy. There is an offer of a full appeal in this case, he noted.
At 3.45pm, Ní Ghrálaigh said the sides were “close to resolution” but “not quite there yet”.
They wished to exchange correspondence by 6pm on Tuesday, and her side still had to get hold of one client in Gaza to take instructions, counsel said.
Carolan said he fully appreciated the difficulties in getting instructions from Gaza.
[ ‘They want to kill all of us’: Life on Israel’s anxious frontier Opens in new window ]
The judge adjourned the matter to Wednesday and made directions for exchange overnight of the necessary legal papers for the cases to proceed on Wednesday if no settlement is reached.
The court previously heard that the visa refusals were for reasons including that the students had not provided original documents with their application.
On their behalf, it was argued that the civilian infrastructure for them to go to a bank or post office to get such documents no longer exists in Gaza and the Minister’s stance was irrational.
In the correspondence this week, the Minister indicated the appeals would be determined on various documents the students had produced.

title: Woman who helped commission 2017 gangland murder rang victim on night of shooting, court hears
description: Murder of 24-year-old Jamie Tighe-Ennis nine years ago, remains unsolved
content:
A woman who helped to commission the 2017 murder of a Dublin man rang him a number of times and met him on the night he was shot dead, a court has heard.
Ciara Mahony knew Jamie Tighe-Ennis “from around the area”, her sentencing hearing at Dublin Circuit Criminal Court was told on Tuesday.
Mahony (46) with an address in Edmondstown Road, Ballyboden, Dublin 16, but originally from Artane, was extradited from Birmingham in the UK last year in connection with the murder of the 24-year-old man nine years ago, which remains unsolved.
She pleaded guilty to the sole count on the indictment of facilitating a criminal organisation in the commission of the murder of Tighe-Ennis between October 27th and 28th, 2017.
Tighe-Ennis died instantaneously after he was shot in the head as he walked along Moatview Avenue, Coolock, in the early hours of October 28th, 2017. A black Audi getaway car was found burnt out in Finglas a short time later.
Mahony’s involvement included purchasing the petrol that was used to burn out the Audi, the court heard. She was seen on CCTV footage filling a red jerry can in a Topaz petrol station that was later found in the burnt-out vehicle, Det Sgt Domhnall O’Connell told Conor McKenna, prosecuting.
Gardaí also discovered her involvement from a phone that was found in the car and a limited edition bottle of wine, which was only sold in about 12 places in the country and which they tracked down to Priorswood Inn in Clonshaugh.
Tighe-Ennis was socialising in Priorswood Inn on the night of his murder and Mahony met him there briefly, the court heard. The pair went outside and spoke briefly before Tighe-Ennis went back inside and Mahony left.
Gardaí also used phone mast data to track Mahony’s movements that night. She phoned Tighe-Ennis a number of times that night and again the following morning after he was dead, the court heard.
When asked by Judge Martin Nolan what their relationship was, O’Connell said they would have known each other from “around the area”.
Mahony, who has no previous convictions except for road traffic matters, was arrested in October 2018 and released, with a file sent to the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP).
The DPP decided to prosecute in November 2024, at which point Mahony was living in the UK and extradition proceedings began. Her guilty plea is an early one, the court heard.
Tighe-Ennis’s parents and family members were in court for the sentence hearing, which was marked by emotional scenes.
In a victim impact statement read out by the detective sergeant, Tighe-Ennis’s father, Kevin Ennis, recalled arriving on the scene shortly after his son had been shot and seeing the pool of blood around his body.
“My son was dead,” he said. “It’s with me every day and will be for the rest of my life.” He said he was sickened when he heard Mahony was herself a mother.
“How would you feel if it was your child?” he said. “You can rot in hell.”
Tighe-Ennis’s mother, June Tighe, said her son’s death was “violent, sudden and devastating”.
“The night I got the knock on the door and was told my son was dead was the worst moment of my life,” she said. She said the memory of her son’s father standing over his son’s body, unable to hug him, will stay with her for the rest of her life.
“He was loved,” she said. “He mattered. He had a life, a future. We will never make the memories that should have been made with him.”
Cross-examining the detective sergeant, Jack Ryan, defending, put it to him that while Mahony knew “a very serious offence” was planned that night, she did not necessarily know Tighe-Ennis would be killed.
“She was aware something serious was going to happen to (him),” O’Connell replied.
The detective agreed with defence counsel that Mahony had a severe addiction to crack cocaine at the time and was under the influence of people involved in organised crime, including two of her previous partners.
There was “an element of coercive control”, defence counsel said.
Nolan adjourned the case to October 19th, when a full plea of mitigation will be heard on Mahony’s behalf.

title: Former RTÉ finance chief Mari Hurley in line for Ires Reit shares worth €325,000
description: Hurley moved to Ireland’s biggest landlord earlier this year following a stint with national broadcaster
content:
Former RTÉ finance chief Mari Hurley has been awarded shares valued at close to €325,000 in her new role with landlord Ires Reit, subject to performance targets, some of which could be released early if a takeover of the company is completed.
A stock exchange filing from Ireland’s largest residential landlord has also confirmed chief executive Eddie Byrne, who earned a basic salary of €475,000 last year, has also been granted a conditional award of a further €73,384 in shares.
Ires Reit said in January Hurley would join the company to replace the outgoing chief financial officer Brian Fagan. She agreed to join the landlord after fewer than 18 months in the chief financial officer role at RTÉ.
A new filing by Ires Reit shows Hurley has been granted a conditional award of 299,260 ordinary shares valued at €1.086 in accordance with the company’s long-term incentive plan.
The filing indicates Hurley’s annual base salary is approximately €325,000, as the conditional award of shares has been described as equivalent to 100 per cent of her salary.
The decision to make these conditional share awards was made in February by Ires Reit’s remuneration committee, but the details have only been announced this week.
In July, the national broadcaster’s latest top -earners list showed Hurley was the sixth-highest paid person at RTÉ prior to her exit, earning €276,344 in 2025, including a basic salary of €240,910.
The filing said vesting of the near €325,000 of shares by Hurley is subject to “satisfactory attainment of stretching performance metrics over the three-year performance period to year-end 2028”.
Ires Reit last week disclosed Barings International has proposed a possible cash offer of €1.386 a share for the company, which would value it at approximately €726.9 million.
Ires said its board “would be minded to recommend” a deal if a formal offer were to emerge by a deadline of November 9th set by the Irish Takeover Panel . Following the announcement of the possible takeover offer from Barings International, shares in Ireland’s largest private-sector residential landlord have risen to around €1.30 a share.
Completion of a takeover could trigger a partial payout of the conditional shares awarded to Hurley and Byrne. In 2024, Ires Reit said in the event of a change of control of the company, “unvested awards will vest as determined by the board”.
It added any awards would take into account performance, and rewards could be reduced to reflect the proportion of the performance period completed, unless the board decides otherwise.
Further details in the stock market announcement by Ires Reit also confirmed Byrne has been granted a conditional award of 67,573 ordinary shares valued at €1.086 each.
The filing said these shares represented an additional award of 15 per cent of his base salary, which has brought the total for 2026 up to 150 per cent of base. Vesting of these shares is also subject to performance milestones over a three-year period to the end of 2028.

title: Free contraception for women under 37 and homecare hours boost: Inside Budget 2027’s health package
description: Next year’s budget provided an additional €1.8 billion for the health service
content:
Free contraception will be made available to women aged up to 37, homecare hours will be increased and improved access to out-of-hours general practitioner (GP) services will be funded as part of a suite of health measures announced in Budget 2027 .
Next year’s budget provided an additional €1.8 billion for the health service, of which €160 million is for capital investment – bringing the total health budget to a record €29.1 billion in 2027.
The health service’s finances have been under increasing pressure in recent months, with overruns forecast to reach €1 billion by the end of the year.
Senior health officials have largely attributed the deficit to pay and agency spend.
According to the Government’s budget expenditure report, there is a €12.471 billion pay bill ceiling for 2027, equating to 139,744 whole-time equivalent staff.
In his budget speech, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers said the additional funding would support frontline and community workforce growth “within agreed pay budgets”.
However, the budget documents place a specific focus on the workforce being “organised around patients”.
“Better care for patients will be provided by making sure the health workforce is organised to provide services for patients at evenings and weekends,” the expenditure report said.
“A continuing expansion of services will be achieved through reducing agency dependence and better deploying the workforce.”
[ Conor Pope: This is Schrödinger’s budget – simultaneously generous and mean Opens in new window ]
This move will be largely disappointing for health unions that have repeatedly called for increased staffing and capacity to improve working conditions and patient outcomes.
In light of the growing and ageing population, the State has sought to move away from its overreliance on the acute hospital system and provide more care in the community.
[ Budget Calculator 2027: Here’s how this year’s budget will affect your income Opens in new window ]
As part of this initiative, Budget 2027 announced there would be a new programme to expand the range of cancer care delivered in clinically appropriate community settings, 1.8 million additional home support hours and an additional €2 million in funding for Meals on Wheels services.
The surgical hub network will be expanded in 2027 through the opening of additional theatres and six-day operations at hubs in Cork, Galway, Waterford, Limerick and Dublin.
Two more surgical hubs – in Letterkenny and Sligo – are in the planning stages.
A total of €7 million has been allocated to the reform of GP services, “with a focus on improving equality of access to GP out-of-hours services”, while €18 million was set aside for dental and orthodontic services for children.
[ All inheritance tax free thresholds rise in the budget but no other reforms Opens in new window ]
Additionally, €108 million has been allocated for mental health services, which will be used to expand crisis support services, early intervention youth services and new ADHD pathways in the Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (Camhs), among others.
The relocation of the National Maternity Hospital would also be progressed next year, Chambers added.

title: Defence gets record €1.6bn in funding amid plans for four new helicopters and long-range radar system
description: An Garda Síochána has got more funding in Budget 2027 to allow intake of 1,000 new recruits next year
content:
Funding to the Department of Defence has been increased by 9 per cent to address its recruitment deficit and to fund the delivery of four new helicopters and a new long-range military radar system.
The record €1.6 billion package will support the recruitment of 850 permanent members of the Defence Forces , Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers said in the Dáil, as well as help with the purchase of new equipment.
Separate funding from the National Development Plan of €340 million has been earmarked to help acquire a military radar programme and allow investment in maritime surveillance and cybersecurity.
The Department of Defence signed a contract in September with a French procurement agency for five deployable Thales radar systems, which include long-range capabilities.
The system will provide a complete recognised air picture of Irish airspace. It will close off a historic gap where aircraft with turned-off transponders could not be tracked.
Delivery of the system is expected in 2027, with full operational capability expected by the end of 2028.
[ Budget 2027 main points: €10 increase in pension and welfare rates; 20 cent per ml tax on vapes Opens in new window ]
Under the five-year strategy for the Defence Forces, there is a commitment to procure four Airbus H145M helicopters during 2027 and 2028. Chambers said the allotted funding would allow those acquisitions to be made.
In the longer term, the Defence Forces has plans to acquire eight super medium helicopters but they have not yet committed to a date for delivery.
Meanwhile, part of the €5.9 billion allocation for the Department of Justice will be used to recruit 1,000 trainee gardaí . The additional numbers would bring the total strength of the force to more than 15,000 next year.
A number of ministers of justice have vowed to bring Garda numbers to 15,000 more than the past 20 years, but successive governments have faced challenges in maintaining the numbers.
[ Budget Calculator 2027: Here’s how this year’s budget will affect your income Opens in new window ]
Garda Representative Association general secretary Ronan Slevin said the announcement “does very little to inspire” members of the force.
“We are under-resourced, under pressure and under huge strain and are not immune to the cost-of-living crisis that other workers are feeling,” he said.
“Successive governments have rolled out promises of 1,000 extra gardaí and yet here we are, at the end of 2026, and the dial has hardly moved on the number of gardaí on our streets in over a decade.
“So while we give a very guarded welcome to this announcement, we must again question how exactly they plan on making the job more attractive to recruits to hit these targets.”
Extra funding has also been allocated to dealing with domestic, sexual and gender-based violence, including an increase in budget for Cuan, the specialist Government agency.
More money has also been made available to increase the capacity of prisons. A total of €11.5 million in additional funding has been made to youth justice initiatives, with the National Cyber Security Centre also getting an extra €7.5 million in funding.

title: What are the key takeaways from Budget 2027? From income tax cuts to surprising omissions
description: After months of leaks and kite-flying, what are the key takeaways of Budget 2027?
content:
A central talking point in the lead-up to Budget 2027 was whether the Government’s promised tax cuts for middle-income earners would be meaningful or just a partial hedge against inflation.
If the tax bands and credits, which determine how much individual workers pay in tax, are not adjusted for wage inflation each year, then workers end up paying proportionately more in tax to the exchequer.
In the end, workers got a higher-than-expected tax break. The point at which people pay the higher 40 per cent rate of income tax is to be increased by €2,500 to €46,500 while personal, employee and earned income tax credits will increase by €125 to €2,125, reducing the liability for all earners.
Michael Rooney, tax partner at EY Ireland, calculates that a single person earning €50,000 annually will be €691 better off as a result of widened tax bands and higher tax credits (marginally offset by an increase in PRSI).
A couple with a combined salary of €100,000 will be better off by €1,382. Additional supports via rent credits, childcare and energy will also boost income.
[ Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day Opens in new window ]
So the Government is doing more than merely inflation-proofing the budget against wage growth. But it can’t shield households from inflation in the wider economy. Utility and grocery bills are set to accelerate in the coming months while fuel (petrol, diesel, home heating oil) has already spiked.
The Government can’t chase this cost-of-living squeeze as much of it stems from wider geopolitical events. And to chase it, in an economy already running up against capacity constraints such as full employment, will only result in more inflation.
Since being appointed Minister for Finance last year, Simon Harris has championed the idea of a State savings scheme to unlock the €170 billion sitting in deposit accounts here.
[ Budget 2027 main points: €10 increase in pension and welfare rates; 20 cent per ml tax on vapes Opens in new window ]
The new Savings and Investment Account, announced as part of Budget 2027, incentivises ordinary people to invest by offering them an investment scheme with a tax-free threshold of €50,000 and a flat tax of 1 per cent on the value of the account thereafter.
There is a maximum contribution limit of €12,000 annually.
The Government appears to have gone for a more restricted version of the schemes seen in other countries, perhaps under pressure from banks which are making a tidy profit from holding the €170 billion on deposit with the European Central Bank (ECB) while paying minimal rates of interest here.
The UK’s counterpart scheme is tax-free with an annual contribution cap of £20,000 (€23,600), while the Swedish equivalent has a flat tax above a certain threshold but no annual contribution cap.
The Government, which examined both those schemes, seems to have adopted a cautious approach, one that is unlikely to change the retail investment culture here. “For a lot of taxpayers, in the long term, it will probably be more tax efficient to maximise tax relief arising on pension contributions before contributing to an investment account set up after July 2027,” said Robert Dever, head of tax at Eversheds Sutherland.
The Government has agreed to a recommendation by the Low Pay Commission for a further 79 cent increase in the minimum wage, which will bring the current rate from €14.15 per hour to €14.94. But there is speculation that it may have deferred the introduction of a living wage, which was due to replace the minimum statutory rate in 2029, with businesses complaining of cost pressures.
Last year, Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke announced a three-year delay to the introduction of the living wage (a higher rate of pay that covers basic living costs), pushing the target date out from 2026 to 2029. This may have been moved again as the Government tries to placate the business lobby. The Department of Public Enterprise are due to release details on Wednesday
[ Budget 2027: big business pays the bills as Coalition rolls the dice Opens in new window ]
The minimum wage has become a big flashpoint, with worker advocates demanding relief from the high cost of living and business groups warning of severe labour cost pressures.
Being cash rich in a world characterised by excessive Government debt comes with moral hazard. The State’s record corporate tax receipts have run in parallel with a worrying build-up in spending. General government spending has jumped by 54 per cent since 2019, from €86.9 billion to €133.8 billion last year.
According to the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council , net spending, which includes tax changes, has increased by an average of 10 per cent over the last four years, which is double the rate of increase that the Department of Finance deems sustainable.
[ Budget Calculator 2027: Here’s how this year’s budget will affect your income Opens in new window ]
Judging from the fractious negotiations in the lead-up to Budget 2027, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers appears to be trying to halt this expenditure creep. In current spending terms, this budget allows for an annual increase of 6 per cent, but spending overruns have become routine and what’s announced on budget day has a habit of being revised up.
One of the novelty kites flown in recent weeks was the idea of a culture card for 16-year-olds. Minister for Culture Patrick O’Donovan floated the idea of giving teenagers a one-off voucher to spend on arts, cultural and music venues, an idea that seemed to have the support of Harris.
However, the move appears to have been slapped down by Chambers amid reports of a testy encounter between the two Ministers. One version has it that O’Donovan walked out of the meeting after being told his department’s budget allocation was already too high. The €100 voucher would have cost €8 million.

title: There is no such thing as ‘resetting’ the nervous system – and we shouldn’t want to
description: Ways to ‘reset’ your nervous system are saturating the internet, but experts say there is no such thing - flexibility should be the focus
content:
W hether it’s tapping the side of your hand or standing on a vibrating plate, suggestions on how to “reset” your nervous system are saturating the internet. Cold water plunges, humming, gargling, yawning and spiky acupressure mats are all being touted as ways to help us “regulate” and return to calm. If you’re still talking about feeling “stressed”, you’re behind the times; now, says the internet, you are “dysregulated”.
The nervous system is an integral part of being human. “It’s essentially the body’s communication and control network,” says Dr Serena Lai, consultant psychiatrist and associate medical director at London Psychiatry Clinic. “Made up of the brain and spinal cord, it communicates with the entire body through nerves, helping us to sense what is happening around and inside us. When we have that information, we can process it and coordinate a response.”
The autonomic nervous system is one part of this network, regulating things the body does automatically, including heart rate, blood pressure and digestion. It has two main branches. “The sympathetic system creates our fight or flight response, helping us mobilise resources when we need to respond to a challenge,” says Lai. “The parasympathetic nervous system – or rest and digest mode – conserves energy, slows the heart and supports recovery.”
Sympathetic activity increases during stress, whether that’s an urgent email or a family bereavement. The heart beats faster, muscles tense, digestion can change and we become more alert. These evolutionary responses help us respond to threats – but while once that might have been a predator, now it’s as everyday as seeing a celebrity death on Instagram. Perhaps it’s no surprise, then, that the idea of a nervous system reset is so appealing to so many of us – we’re overstimulated and in desperate need of ways to feel more level.
Except, as every expert I spoke to agreed, there is no such thing as “resetting” the nervous system – and we should not want to. We need sympathetic activation to exercise, concentrate, meet deadlines and respond to demanding situations. The problem is when we struggle to recover once that demand has passed, leaving us feeling wired and tired, and potentially contributing to increased inflammation and cardiovascular and metabolic problems. A healthy autonomic nervous system is not permanently calm; it’s able to adapt to changing circumstances.
Much of the conversation about nervous system regulation revolves around the vagus nerve – which is actually a pair of nerves, made up of about 80,000 fibres apiece – that starts in the brain and travels down through the neck into the chest and abdomen. Because it helps slow heart rate and plays a role in the body’s rest-and-recovery processes, it is associated with stress relief and relaxation – you might see people referring to increased “vagal tone” as a sign of enhanced vagus nerve activity.
One of the most common ways vagal and parasympathetic activity is assessed is through heart rate variability (HRV), says neurosurgeon Dr Kevin Tracey, author of The Great Nerve. “This is the time in between individual heartbeats – generally, greater variability is associated with greater vagal influence,” he explains. The higher the vagal influence, the more likely our parasympathetic system is to be dominant – cue feeling of calm. “Sympathetic activity tends to shorten the time between heartbeats.”
Learning how to work with your nervous system could make it more flexible, meaning you rise to challenges when you need to, then recover when they have passed. These simple, science-backed habits can help.
Breathing slowly has been shown to increase HRV and promote parasympathetic dominance. “One study showed that slow-paced breathing of around six diaphragmatic breaths [breathing deeply into the belly rather than just into the chest] a minute is one of the most effective ways of producing an acute change in heart rate variability,” says Lai. She recommends inhaling for about five seconds, exhaling for five, and repeating for five to 10 minutes.
Cyclic sighing is another option. It involves taking one deep inhale, followed by a second, shorter “sip” of air to fully inflate the lungs, before a long, slow, lung-emptying exhale through the mouth. In one study, practising for five minutes a day improved mood and reduced respiratory rate – an effect that became more pronounced over the course of the month-long trial.
“Meditation – where you practise bringing your attention to the present moment – is a great way to help slow down the heart rate,” says Tracey. “It’s especially good when done in tandem with paced breathing, as you can really measure your heart rate decreasing.” Apps including Headspace, Insight Timer and Calm, he adds, can make it easier to build the practice into everyday life.
Other contemplative practices, from body scanning (where you relax, close your eyes and contemplate physical sensations) to yoga, may also support parasympathetic activity. One 2018 paper proposed that many of these practices naturally slow the breath, which in turn influences vagal activity.
“Sensory quiet” in general may be important for autonomic recovery, explains Dr Vishnuraj Prakash, head of Ayurveda and functional medicine at Tulåh Clinical Wellness in Kerala, India, so practise doing nothing – no podcasts, phones or other stimuli.
“Movement is incredibly useful because it changes your state,” says somatic practitioner Nahid de Belgeonne. “For example, if you sit at a desk for a long time, your muscles are contracted and fixed and your breathing shallow. As soon as you get up and move, you interrupt that fixed state.” She advises embracing being “fidgety” throughout the day and taking regular walks.
There is plenty of evidence that regular aerobic exercise – whether walking, cycling or swimming – can improve autonomic regulation and HRV over time. Tai chi is particularly interesting because it combines movement, breathwork and meditation and it produces more parasympathetic activation than conventional exercise of the same intensity.
Crucially, more exercise isn’t necessarily better. Research has found reduced HRV in athletes who overtrain, so recovery matters too. “Simple exercises are really all that’s needed,” says Dr Karen Chung, consultant neurologist at Welbeck. “I often tell patients who are overwhelmed to get off the bus a stop early and walk a little further. ”
Moderate-pressure massage has been associated with reduced heart rate, anxiety and cortisol, as well as increased parasympathetic activity – and as little as 20 to 30 minutes seems to be enough. Pressure does matter: a very light, feathery touch could actually be more stressful than calming. Even a 10-minute head massage can increase HRV – by as much as 66 per cent, according to one small study.
Stimulating acupressure points, whether through touch or acupuncture needles, may also help, although, as Lai points out, the evidence is less consistent. Auricular acupuncture is one obvious route in – a branch of the vagus nerve supplies parts of the outer ear. Other commonly used acupuncture points to promote parasympathetic activity are found around the wrists, outer shins, top of the head and sternum – although which are used, and why, is best left to a qualified practitioner.
Some research suggests acupuncture can influence autonomic activity, including increasing parasympathetic action. The evidence is thinner when it comes to acupressure mats. Anecdotally, they may help some people relax, but there are cheaper and better evidenced ways to achieve the same end.
Our nervous systems respond well to regularity – consistent sleep and wake times, eating at similar times each day and resting. “For many of my patients, life is incredibly fast-paced, so mostly it’s as simple as going to bed a little earlier or taking an hour away from our phones,” says Chung. “Repeating the same behaviours daily helps the body’s ability to move from activation back into recovery,” adds Lai.
Building breaks into the working day can help too. For those spending hours on screens, de Belgeonne recommends working in focused 90-minute blocks, followed by a 20-minute break. Evenings should signal a change of pace where possible. “Reduce evening stimulation during stressful periods,” advises Prakash.
Does cold exposure work as well as social media influencers would have us believe? As Tracey explains, the body’s initial response to cold water immersion is actually a sympathetic one, triggering the release of stress hormones and increasing the heart rate. It is only afterwards, research suggests, that there is a parasympathetic rebound, which could help explain why some people report feeling calmer after a cold plunge.
You don’t necessarily need to submerge yourself. Dunking your face in cold water can trigger the diving reflex, which slows the heart rate through increased parasympathetic activity – even a couple of splashes may be enough to elicit a response. However, Tracey points out that there still isn’t enough credible evidence to conclude that cold water immersion has meaningful benefits for nervous system regulation. But if you enjoy it and find you feel calmer afterwards, great – that’s really all the evidence you need.
Surgically implanted vagus nerve stimulation is an established medical treatment for conditions including epilepsy and treatment-resistant depression. But that doesn’t mean the consumer device showcased on your Instagram feed is backed by the same evidence.
Noninvasive devices typically use electrical stimulation through the skin – often at the ear or neck – in an attempt to stimulate branches of the vagus nerve. While the US Food and Drug Administration has cleared some for specific medical conditions, such as migraines, that is very different from being approved to reduce stress, says Tracey. For the majority of wellness devices, independent clinical evidence is limited. That’s not to say they definitely don’t work, but the less exciting basics – sleep, movement, slow breathing and rest – might be a better first port of call.
One study found that just 15 minutes of walking in a forest reduced sympathetic and increased parasympathetic activity, while others have linked time in nature with lower cortisol levels. So get outside – ideally without your phone.
“Eat a balanced diet, get regular exercise, spend time in nature and with people you love, and get some hobbies,” says Tracey. “And have a plan for dealing with stress. Beyond all the elaborate reset practices, these are the things that are actually worth doing.” - Guardian

title: Irish Investment Account: Here’s how the scheme will work
description: Consumers can save up to €50,000 tax-free in new personal investment accounts
content:
P eople will be able to put €12,000 a year tax-free into the Government new personal investment accounts , Minister for Finance Simon Harris announced in his Budget 2027 speech.
The accounts will feature a low tax rate of just 1 per cent. However, this tax will be levied on any amount in the account over a tax-free threshold of €50,000, not just the profit the account made over that year.
This holds out the prospect of people paying tax on their savings in years when they lost money simply because the balance of their account was above the €50,000 tax-free threshold.
Harris said the new accounts will be available from July 1st next year. About €170 billion is currently on deposit in Irish bank accounts, with the Minister having previously described that money as “sitting idle”.
Alongside the new accounts, the Minister announced a financial literacy campaign. The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) has set up a webpage that will allow people to read up about issues around investing, and the choices available.
It also offers a quick multiple choice self-assessment quiz that allows consumers to assess their investment readiness.
Irish households hold just 2.3 per cent of their financial assets in direct investments such as listed shares and debt securities, compared with an EU average of approximately 7.5 per cent.
[ Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day Opens in new window ]
The new scheme has been designed to encourage people to move their savings into market investments.
“The long-mooted investment account is an important step towards making long-term investment more accessible,” said Cróna Clohisey, director of members and advocacy at Chartered Accountants Ireland. “Now that the broad design has been announced, Government should move quickly to finalise the legislation, systems and guidance so that financial service providers can establish these accounts and people can begin using them.
“It is critical that there is no delay to the introduction timeline of mid-2027,” she said.
Michael Healy, chief executive of IG Consumer, said the Government had missed the chance to get Irish people investing.
“While the decision to set the tax-free threshold at €50,000 is better than we expected, it is a small victory within a fundamentally flawed model. The €12,000 annual contribution limit is far too low if the ambition is to get people investing seriously and building meaningful long-term wealth.
“But the bigger problem is the proposed 1 per cent annual tax on investments above the threshold,” said Healy. “Taxing the value of an investment rather than the return it generates means someone could face a tax bill even when their investments have fallen in value – effectively paying tax on losses. That is the wrong principle for an account designed to encourage people to invest.”
[ Budget Calculator 2027: Here’s how this year’s budget will affect your income Opens in new window ]
Robert Dever, head of tax at Eversheds Sutherland, agreed. The Government he said had adopted a cautious approach to the new scheme. “For a lot of taxpayers, in the long term, it will probably be more tax efficient to maximise tax relief arising on pension contributions before contributing to an investment account.”
However, Rory O’Brien, head of wealth management, Dublin, at Baker Tilly Ireland Wealth was more upbeat.
“On the whole, the new Irish Investment Account looks like a fantastic opportunity for those looking for better returns from the investment markets over the medium to long term to do so without being harshly punished when their investments do well. The opportunity for younger investors to start small and build up to the 50k without CGT is very positive and l would expect those looking to build deposits, to consider this as a viable option.”
The Government also announced a lowering of the rate of tax under the “deemed disposal” or exit tax regime that applies to investors in products currently available in the market.
[ Budget 2027 main points: Minimum wage to rise 79 cent; €12,000 per year limit for investment scheme Opens in new window ]
Last year, as part of Budget 2026, the deemed disposal tax rate was reduced from 41 per cent to 38 per cent. In 2024, a report by the Department of Finance into the funds sector advised the deemed disposal rule should be ended for exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and investment funds.
Exit tax is levied on profits when an investment is cashed in. Deemed disposal sees that tax levied every eight years after an investment is taken out, even if the investment is not cashed in.
Chartered Accountants Ireland’s Cróna Clohisey said it was “extremely disheartening that the eight-year deemed disposal rule remains. It has no place in a modern Irish investment landscape.
“Requiring people to pay tax on gains they have not realised undermines the benefits of long-term investment, adds unnecessary complexity for individual investors, and contradicts the wider Government drive to foster retail investment and encourage greater financial literacy.”
Irish Funds chairwoman, Andrea Kelly welcome dthe three point cut in the rate of tax but said the lack of any clear path to phasing out deemed disposal was “deeply disappointing”.
“The Government should now use the Finance Bill to provide the certainty that was missing from the Budget,” she said.
Anyone over the age of 18 who is resident in the State and holds a PPS number can invest in the new personal investment scheme, but they can only have one account.
Eligible investments will include listed shares, listed bonds, financial instruments traded on a regulated market and a range of investment funds suitable for retail investors, including ETFs.
Investors will not be permitted to invest in what are deemed highly complex and risky products, including derivatives and crypto assets.
[ Catch up with all your Budget 2027 news here Opens in new window ]
There will be no minimum holding or lock-in period, and moving investment accounts between providers will be allowed, where possible, on a tax-neutral basis.
Any tax due will be calculated and paid at source by the companies providing the investment funds available under the scheme.
