What is not yet clear is how much providers will charge for the products they offer.
Harris first announced his intention to introduce a new form of consumer-friendly investment account back in February.
He has returned to the theme regularly since then but, until Tuesday, had declined to confirm the amount that could be put into such accounts each month or year, the threshold above which the funds will be taxed, or the rate of taxation.
Harris’s department had examined similar types of accounts operating in other countries. Ultimately, it opted largely for the Swedish model despite strong industry lobbying in favour of the rival UK individual savings account (ISA) model.

title: Paramount closes $110bn Warner merger in historic Hollywood deal
description: Deal makes David Ellison one of the most important power brokers in entertainment industry globally
content:
Paramount Skydance closed its $110 billion (€98 billion) acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery on Tuesday, completing one of the biggest media mergers of all time after engaging in a bruising battle for control with Netflix and fending off antitrust lawsuits.
The new company, which will be called Skydance, combines two of the five largest Hollywood film studios, uniting major franchises such as Harry Potter and Mission Impossible. It will now be home to dozens of TV networks, from CBS to TNT, and two major subscription streaming services, Paramount+ and HBO Max.
David Ellison, who only completed the merger of his Skydance Media film production company with Paramount in August 2025, has continued to consolidate power in the media industry and has become one of Hollywood’s biggest moguls. Still, he brought in Ynon Kreiz from Mattel to share oversight of Skydance as co-chief executive officer. Kreiz will manage day-to-day operations while Ellison maintains the creative, big-picture vision and handles relationships with talent.
“Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” Ellison said in a statement.
After pulling off two mega-mergers of century-old Hollywood companies in just over a year, Ellison now faces the significant challenge of making it all work. That means eliminating overlapping businesses and jobs without fanning the ire of Hollywood, which is already suffering through a downturn and has opposed the consolidation from the start. Skydance also will need to manage nearly $80 billion in debt while adhering to a strict calendar of theatrical releases as stipulated by the lawsuit settlement.
[ Hugh Linehan: Paramount’s takeover of Warner Bros more than just another Hollywood power play Opens in new window ]
The path to closing the merger was often a rocky one and at times seemed likely to derail. But Ellison was determined to succeed and saw the deal as essential to be able to compete with the likes of Netflix, Disney, Amazon and Apple.
“They’re starting off at a great place,” Michael J Wolf, CEO of Activate Strategy, said. “The logic makes sense. Scale puts them in the right position. Now they have to deliver against scale.”
Paramount agreed to acquire Warner Bros in February following a months-long bidding war against Netflix, which had previously committed to purchasing Warner Bros’ studios and streaming business, but not the cable channels. Ellison clinched the deal by sweetening the offer price and bringing his father Larry Ellison in to personally guarantee funding. Paramount paid a $2.8 billion break-up fee to Netflix on behalf of Warner Bros and argued it would be able to clinch a speedy closing of its own deal, promising to pay fees to Warner Bros shareholders $7 million a day if the deal wasn’t finalised by September 30th.
Though Paramount did manage to get quick antitrust approval from the US department of justice, the European Union and other key jurisdictions, it was delayed by a pair of lawsuits brought by 12 states and the Writers Guild of America, who were concerned about the threat of higher prices for consumers and fewer jobs. Thousands of actors, directors, writers and producers signed a letter protesting the deal.
Much of the fear stems from Paramount’s pledge to extract more than $6 billion in annual synergies within three years of closing the merger. Gerry Cardinale, founder and managing partner of RedBird Capital Partners, a Paramount investor, said there are other ways to cut costs and operate more efficiently than simply reducing headcount. A company wouldn’t spend billions of dollars a year making movies, “and figure your entire premise of your business plan is to fire everybody in Hollywood”, Cardinale said last week. “It’s just the opposite.”
In the statement, Skydance said savings would come primarily from combining technology and other operations, such as negotiating deals with suppliers and reducing overlapping marketing expenses as well as consolidating real estate. That will make the company “leaner and more nimble”, and allow it to reduce its debt load to three times annual adjusted earnings by the end of 2029. The new company expects to generate more than $10 billion in free cash flow by 2030. – Bloomberg

title: Are Budget 2027’s tax and social welfare measures enough? Conor Pope delivers his verdict
description: Smokers and people who earn between €35,000-€44,000 could reasonably feel like they’ve been forgotten about
content:
T he Government and its money Ministers, Simon Harris and Jack Chambers , will go to great lengths to highlight how people will benefit from the raft of measures announced in the budget .
But, despite all the money spent, it’s clear almost nobody will be better off in 2027.
Geopolitical unrest and the spike in the price of pretty much everything will more than cancel out the welfare and allowance increases, as well as the tax changes central to what could be termed Schrödinger’s budget – one which is simultaneously generous and mean.
The big winners – if that’s not too strong a word – will be couples in a household where both people earn more than €50,000 a year.
As had been widely flagged, the entry point for the higher rate of income tax has climbed from €44,000 to €46,500. It means the annual tax bill of people at the top rate will fall by €500 a year.
On top of that, an increase of €125 in both the personal and PAYE tax credits will be worth another €250 to an individual.
According to Harris, the combined benefits for a double-income household earning more than €100,000 will be €1,500 annually.
[ Budget Calculator 2027: Here’s how this year’s budget will affect your income Opens in new window ]
There has also been a tweak to the ceiling on the second band of the universal social charge (USC), which is worth around €20 a year. However, to get a more accurate measure, the PRSI increase that kicked in this month has to be added to the mix.
Over the course of next year then, the tax bill of a double-income household on the average industrial wage of just under €55,000 each will fall by just over €1,300.
The other headline changes include a €10 hike in the State pension and broader welfare rates, while an annual cost-of-disability payment will be worth about €500 to 240,000 qualifying people.
The income disregard for carer’s allowance is rising by €150 to €1,150 for a single person and by €300 to €2,300 for a couple. The child support payment will rise by €6 with the living alone allowance climbing by €3 per week.
The Government has also given the green light to a 79 cent increase in the minimum wage, which will take the rate to €14.94 from its current rate of €14.15.
[ Budget 2027 main points: €10 increase in pension and welfare rates; 20 cent per ml tax on vapes Opens in new window ]
That was always going to be a hot topic in the budget and while there was no room for the universal energy credits of times past, there will be some modest relief for some people.
Reductions in the carbon tax on home-heating oil for the lifetime of this Government will save about 700,000 households between €50 and €100 a year. The fuel allowance is to climb by €5 per week to €43 per week, with a higher income threshold for single people over 66 of €641, up from €534.
The temporary reduced fuel excise rates have been extended until February 28th, with a “gradual and responsible restoration” in four phases leading to a complete restoration by June 30th.
The vehicle registration tax relief for electric vehicles is also being extended until the end of 2028, but the flip side of that will see the tax for “more pollutant cars” – or nine of the top 10 sellers in Ireland – going up by 1 per cent to “incentivise purchase of low-emissions cars”.
It seems inevitable that the tax cuts will make many of the headlines in the hours and days ahead.
The €10-per-week increase in welfare and pension payments, along with the money spent on supporting those on lower incomes to heat and light their homes over the winter months, will also occupy minds.
But one cohort will see many of the tax benefits and welfare supports pass them by.
Up to 400,000 people earn between €35,000 and €44,000. Many of them will probably be taking home too much in pay to benefit from the increase in allowances and too little to benefit from the widening of the lower rate tax band from €44,000 to €46,500.
They will see their annual tax burden fall by €250 thanks to the increase in their tax credits and will make marginal gains from the changes to the ceiling on the second USC band, but that will be pretty much that.
The news is indisputably worse for Irish smokers and vapers, with an increase of €1 on a box of 20 cigarettes and a 20 cent-per-ml tax on vapes, adding about 40 cent to a small, single-use disposable vape.
Context is key when discussing the budget.
Grocery inflation is likely to add about €500 on to household bills in 2027, while the higher cost of heating and lighting our homes as well as keeping our cars on the road will cost about €800 more. Then there are insurance products and other everyday costs that have to be added to the bottom line.
As he came to the end of his budget speech, Harris stressed that the State “cannot do it all but must do what it can to help people in the here and now, and plan for the future”.
The question many will be asking now is: has he done enough?

title: Ardmore receives Ireland’s Greenest Places award from Eamon Ryan
description: Other category winners include Treasure the Tolka, Cloughjordan Community Development Association, Rosewood Estate and Jacinta Barrins
content:
Ardmore, Co Waterford , was honoured as the overall winner of Ireland’s Greenest Places at a ceremony in Dublin on Tuesday.
In the second year of the competition, run by The Irish Times in association with Electric Ireland, the seaside fishing village beat competition from about 90 other entries. With a population of just 500, its collaborative ethos was key.
“We’re a small community,” said Henry Murphy, who accepted the award on behalf of Ardmore. “There’s relationships there. The Tidy Towns, the GAA club, the schools – we’re all interlinked.”
Education is central to Ardmore’s operations – building a succession plan for their environmental work by teaching local children what they do. They offer a blueprint for any town or village around the country looking to improve its climate action.
“It’s making that initial start really,” Murphy said. “There’s one or two of us in the village are probably guilty of being addicted to applying for grants at this stage.”
Ireland’s Greenest Places judge and former Irish Times environment editor Kevin O’Sullivan said the victory was well deserved and “the clear verdict of all the judges”.
“It’s that long-term perspective,” added his fellow judge Eamon Ryan , the former minister for the environment. “It takes time to change things, but if you don’t start, [it doesn’t happen].”
[ Ireland’s Greenest Place 2027: the winners in all categories Opens in new window ]
The title of Ireland’s Greenest Community went to Treasure the Tolka, a project devoted to cleaning and depolluting its titular river.
Cloughjordan Community Development Association (CCDA) was crowned Ireland’s Greenest Town.
Rosewood Estate in Ballincollig, Co Cork, won Ireland’s Greenest Suburb.
Paul Johnston accepted the award of Ireland’s Net Zero Hero on behalf of his wife, Jacinta Barrins.
Treasure the Tolka, a group founded eight years ago by GP Toby O’Mahony Adams, meets regularly on Saturdays, often in packs of 20.
“I think a lot of people appreciate the river and how important it is, but don’t feel that they can do anything about it because it’s behind a barrier,” O’Mahony Adams said. “Treasure the Tolka has overcome some of those barriers with ladders and with gumption.”
Amid a wide range of green initiatives, Cloughjordan Community Development Association (CCDA) managed to convince 52 landowners to assist in its flagship project, the rewetting of Scohaboy Bog.
“It’s really [about] getting people on board,” said Gearóid Ó Foighil, accepting the prize for the CCDA. “What’s brilliant about this award is this is for all of wider Cloughjordan.”
Rosewood Estate is “an older estate” with a “great sense of community”, according to Dan O’Riordan.
Five years ago, the Rosewood residents’ association set about tackling a two-acre field that had been “unloved, overgrown, ignored” for years. It began by planting a variety of trees, developing the site over time into the thriving wildflower meadow and amenity it is today.
Paul Johnston said his wife Jacinta Barrins’s environmental work revolved around empowering older adults to take meaningful climate action. It was that project – her climate course for over-55s – that kept Barrins from attending the event herself.
“Quite often, the older cohort is a group that really argues. Why should I bother with climate change?” Johnston said. “What motivates her is to try and explain to them why they should be bothered.”
Jillian Saunders, group sponsorship and PR manager at the ESB, said the energy provider was pleased to be involved with Ireland’s Greenest Places for a second year, and thanked the winners for attending the ceremony and sharing their stories.

title: Cheltenham action returns after extensive work on new drainage system
description: More than 1,000 metres of drainage has been replaced ahead of Cheltenham’s return to jumps racing
content:
There’s Group One flat action this week but a sure sign of the changing of the seasons is the return of jumps action at Cheltenham later this month, where the home of National Hunt racing ’s upgraded drainage system will be put to the test.
Cheltenham’s two-day ‘Showcase’ fixture on October 23rd and 24th will be the first action at Prestbury Park since major drainage work at the track finished in August.
A trio of fixtures in April and May had to be abandoned to facilitate the project, which was needed after a hole appeared on the track at January’s Trials Day programme.
Remedial work allowed the four-day festival in March to go ahead but Cheltenham officials are happy the fundamental problems are solved. An upgrade of the 600-metre main drain began in April, and more than 1,000 metres of drainage has been replaced overall.
Cheltenham’s clerk of the course, Jon Pullin, said: “We’re very happy with how the drainage upgrade and recovery has gone. We worked closely with specialists in turf management and drainage throughout the project to make the right decisions for the long-term management of the track.
“Starting the work in April was critical because it gave us the time to investigate the drainage system properly and take the opportunity to replace other areas that would benefit from an upgrade. For the first five weeks, our in-house team worked with our agronomists to understand exactly what was happening within the system.
“There are five main drains running down the track, with a network of other drains feeding into them before reaching the outlet at the bottom of the straight. We had to open up various stretches of the home straight as part of the investigation process and this gave us a much better understanding of what was happening beneath the surface.”
When the work finished, watering began immediately on the back of a dry summer that saw regular summer temperatures of 30 degrees.
“While there is more dry weather forecast over the next two weeks, we will continue watering to ensure we are able to provide safe ground for jump racing,” Pullin added.
[ Two-time Cheltenham Champion Hurdle winner Hurricane Fly dies, aged 22 Opens in new window ]
If that’s good news for jumps enthusiasts, attention on the flat is turning more to establishing a pecking order in the juvenile ranks ahead of the 2027 Classics.
Saturday’s Darley Dewhurst Stakes has a peerless pedigree for identifying Europe’s two-year-old champion and a heavyweight clash between Aidan O’Brien’s Darkness Falls and Godolphin’s unbeaten Desert Castle is on the cards.
“The Dewhurst has been on the agenda for him for some time. At the moment the plan is to go to Newmarket with him,” a Ballydoyle spokesman commented on Darkness Falls.
“What he did in his maiden win, he backed up in a Group One afterwards so he is in the ‘could be anything’ category. The Dewhurst is the logical step to see if he can then start off in the Guineas route next year,” he added.
Andrew Balding won last year’s Dewhurst with Gewan and has the sole non-Godolphin or Coolmore owned runner in Saturday’s race with Gentle Hurricane. Balding also has Forbidden Fire for Friday’s bet365 Fillies’ Mile, another Group One that could be important in his attempt to dethrone Aidan O’Brien as Britain’s champion trainer. O’Brien has topped the cross-channel table eight times.
Balding currently has a marginal lead over his Irish rival with over £8.2 million (€9.7 million) in prize money compared to O’Brien’s £8.1 million (€9.6 million).
“The Dewhurst, for as long as I’ve been alive, has been the number one two-year-old race in Europe. It really defines which is the best colt of each generation, and it’s historically always a very strong race,” Balding said.
Forbidden Fire is unbeaten in her two starts, including when scoring over seven furlongs in a Doncaster Listed race. She takes on the unbeaten Godolphin favourite Musical Times on Friday.
“The question mark is probably stepping up to a mile. Her siblings have deceived me in staying further than we ever thought they would. It’s probably worth a go, and she’s got the class. I’d hope to be very competitive,” Balding commented.
Wednesday’s Navan action could provide Darkness Falls fans with a form boost as Jesus Green bids to make it third time lucky in a mile maiden.
Joseph O’Brien’s runner was second on his debut but still got jumped straight into Group One company at the Irish Champions Festival and got closest to Darkness Falls in the Golden Fleece Stakes.
The Ballydoyle team run three against him, including a Sea The Stars newcomer in Choctaw Nation, who appears to be the stable number one. However, Jesus Green holds a Futurity entry later this month and should be up to scoring here.
Verified relished easier ground conditions when scoring at Cork last week and may be up to going in again under a 7lb penalty in a sprint handicap.

title: AfD passes milestone with first parliamentary speaker post in Saxony-Anhalt
description: Far-right party’s election manager Tobias Rausch elected to key role on 48 votes, with 29 opposing and five abstentions
content:
Germany ’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) passed another political milestone on Tuesday when it secured its first parliamentary speaker post in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
A month after the AfD state victory there, with 44 per cent support, party election manager Tobias Rausch was elected to the influential political role on 48 votes, with 29 opposing and five abstentions.
In a secret ballot with 42 votes for a majority, the 35-year-old property manager was backed by 39 AfD members and most likely five MPs from the BSW grouping – meaning he attracted four votes of MPs from other parties.
That sets a precedent for December, when the AfD will propose its leader Ulrich Siegmund as state prime minister. He would be Germany’s first far-right leader since 1945.
“This is a step in the right direction, setting a clear signal for the political future of this country,” said Siegmund of Tuesday’s vote on national radio. “For many years all kinds of state roles were blocked to us, but now the tide has turned .”
Rausch made similar observations in his first speech as parliamentary speaker while insisting that, while in office, he would “not settle any scores from the past”.
“I will discharge the duties of this office as speaker of the entire state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt,” he added.
In Germany’s constitutional hierarchy, a state parliamentary speaker ranks higher than a prime minister. As well as overseeing parliamentary procedure, the speaker receives high-ranking visitors and represents the state at key events – including memorials of Nazi-era crimes.
On Tuesday, opposition leaders promised to push back against any AfD revisionism towards Germany’s fascist past – or incitement against minorities in the present, such as a so-called “remigration” party policy to forcibly deport non-ethnic Germans.
Green Party parliamentary leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz, said her party would “speak out when people are disparaged because of their origin, their faith, or their way of life ... and if minority rights and the opposition are curtailed”.
About 500 protesters gathered outside the state parliament building on Tuesday, many carrying signs referencing the local AfD’s “confirmed extremist” classification from the state intelligence service. Others carried placards reading “never again is now”, a reference to a postwar German motto.
AfD advances in Saxony-Anhalt are likely to have a wider knock-on effect on German politics, in particular on the so-called “firewall” that proscribes mainstream political parties co-operating with the far-right.
One key exception is the BSW. Its founder Sahra Wagenknecht praised her state MPs for “ending the firewall idiocy” of German politics.
[ Anti-immigration and pro-Russia – why did Germans vote for the AfD? Opens in new window ]
She denounced Nazi-AfD parallels made by other parties as a “trivialisation” of Germany’s fascist past.
Ahead of the vote, the leader of the Left Party compared Rausch to Hermann Göring, the first Nazi Reichstag parliamentary speaker. “It’s not a [Hermann] Göring 2.0 being elected here,” Wagenknecht added.
Rausch, an AfD MP in the state parliament in Magdeburg for the last decade, masterminded the party’s TikTok-driven election surge to its highest-ever election result.
He attracted critical attention last year when it emerged that he had placed relatives – and members of his local football team – in well-paid parliamentary jobs in Magdeburg and Berlin.
[ Voters in eastern German state have blown up post-unification politics Opens in new window ]
As power looms in Magdeburg, AfD leaders in Berlin and Brussels are planning a major pivot away from the party’s founding political promise of 2013 to take Germany out of the euro.
Instead, a new paper proposes holding a referendum on continuing Germany’s EU membership unless the bloc is transformed into a looser ‌alliance ​of sovereign nations, with national opt-outs on sensitive issues such as migration and jointly-issued EU debt.

title: Man who suffered stroke in Cork hospital settles action for €1.2m
description: Mercy hospital offers ‘sincere and heartfelt’ apology for failings in care
content:
A Cork hospital has offered a “sincere and heartfelt” apology for the “failings in care” to an elderly man who suffered a stroke while a patient there.
The man, who is in his 70s, suffered a stroke after the blood-thinning medication he was on was stopped for three days while he was a patient at Mercy University Hospital , Cork, the High Court heard.
The letter of apology was read to the court as the pensioner settled his action against the hospital for €1.2 million.
His counsel, Dr John O’Mahony, with Cian O’Mahony instructed by solicitor Brigid O’Donnell, told the court the elderly man had previously been diagnosed with heart failure and had a heart monitor device implanted.
He was admitted to Mercy University Hospital in November 2025 with worsening heart failure symptoms after a monitor battery change the month before. Counsel said unfortunately while in hospital, the pensioner was not given usual blood thinners for three days and he suffered a stroke.
Counsel said the elderly man required an emergency thrombolysis and thrombectomy at another hospital. O’Mahony said the man suffered facial droop and had problems with his mobility and with speech, but is now in better shape, being cared for by a very dedicated family.
A letter of apology from Mercy University Hospital chief executive Margaret McKiernan, which was read to the court, stated: “I would like to offer a sincere and unequivocal apology to you and your family for the failure to administer your oral anticoagulant between November 14th and 17th, 2025, which was a significant causal factor in the development of the stroke you suffered.
“The hospital fully accepts and acknowledges that this should not have happened.
“I wish to state and assure you that this occurrence has been taken very seriously by the hospital, and there has been considerable organisational learning as a result of the review of your case, which has provided valuable learning outcomes for hospital staff.
“Again, on behalf of all at Mercy hospital, I wish to offer a sincere and heartfelt apology to you and your family for the failings in care and the implications it has had for your wellbeing, ongoing treatment and clinical management,” the letter stated.
In the proceedings, it was claimed the hospital had failed to arrange for the pensioner to take his usual anticoagulant blood-thinning medication in appropriate dosage at appropriate time intervals while he was a patient at the hospital.
It was further claimed there was a failure to respond appropriately or at all in an appropriately timely manner to a pharmacy note on November 14th, 2025, alerting the clinical and nursing team that the blood thinner had been omitted.
The hospital admitted that the stopping and “non-restarting of the anticoagulant” between November 14th and 17th, 2025, constituted substandard care. It also accepted the admitted failure regarding the man’s oral blood thinner as a significant causal factor in the development of thrombosis and subsequent embolism causing stroke.
Approving the settlement, Judge Leonie Reynolds said it was a very unfortunate sequence of events which clearly had a significant impact on the elderly man. She said it was a very good settlement and said the parties who had resolved the matter after mediation were to be commended.

title: ‘I won’t be having any plush holidays’: A Dublin pensioner reacts to Budget 2027
description: Robert Walker, who lives alone in north Dublin, struggles with energy bills, and especially running electric storage heaters
content:
Tuesday’s budget will not deliver any “plush holidays” for pensioner Robert Walker, but he said he was “happy enough” with other measures, including an increase to his pension .
Walker (75) lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment he bought in north Co Dublin after the end of his marriage. He has neither rent nor mortgage, but property maintenance fees of €1,800 a year.
He said he was relieved at the €10 increase in the State pension to €309.30 a week, along with a €3 increase in the living alone allowance to €25 a week.
The fuel allowance, which he – along with more than 470,000 – gets for 28 weeks a year is going up by €5 to €43.
“I heard a few days ago in the headlines the pension was going up only €7.50 a week, which would not have been nice at all,” he said. “They got some backlash on that so I’m happy they listened.
“It’s not too bad, the increases. I’d say it is average on what they have been doing the last few years. If I count the Christmas double payment, it’s €530 extra a year for the pension and €106 extra for the living alone allowance.
“It is just going to help me stand still. I see the prices in the shops going up all the time.
“I remember when I was child if there was an extra tuppence on the loaf of bread, it would be headlines. Now you go into the supermarket every week and the prices are up.”
[ Budget 2027 main points: €10 increase in pension and welfare rates; 20 cent per ml tax on vapes Opens in new window ]
Walker struggles with energy bills, especially running electric storage heaters. While the fuel allowance increase is welcome, he will not benefit from the reduction in VAT on home-heating oil and natural gas.
“That is a bit disappointing, but I know other people are struggling too,” he said. “I see people who are working very hard, paying taxes every week and not qualifying for anything. So, I am happy enough.”
He said he was pleased to hear of increased funding for the Department of Health and the particular reference to increased funding for home-support packages for older and disabled people to stay in their own homes.
He added he was saving “a few bob every week” to go to Lourdes, France, next year. “I won’t be having any plush holidays after the budget, but I’d like to go to Lourdes.”

title: Graeme McDowell company pays out €13m dividend
description: Golfer set up company up in 2002 to manage his commercial interests
content:
Golfer Graeme McDowell received $15 million (€13.33 million) in dividends from his golf promotions firm last year.
New accounts for the former US Open champion and Northern Ireland native’s Boyport Services Ltd show the firm also disposed of its investments properties with a book value of $20 million.
The $15 million dividend payout by Boyport Services to McDowell for 2025 followed the firm making a dividend payout of $6.9 million in 2024.
The dividend last year, along with the $20 million disposal, resulted in a hit to the firm’s balance sheet with accumulated profits dropping from $16.26 million to $991,198.
The company’s principal place of business is at an address on Sorrento Road in Dalkey, south Co Dublin, while its registered office is based at a London address.
Cash funds at the company increased from $71,150 to $1.05 million.
Overall, the company recorded a loss of $275,885 for the year. At the end of 2025, the firm’s shareholder funds totalled $991,392.
The 47-year-old golfer enjoyed a career high when he won the US Open at Pebble Beach in 2010, becoming the first European since Tony Jacklin in 1970 to triumph at that major.
McDowell has also played twice for the European Ryder Cup team and has been a joint captain twice.
McDowell was one of a number of high-profile golfers who signed up for the controversial LIV golf tour in 2022 but confirmed earlier this year that he has paid off the applicable fines to the DP World Tour that would allow him to compete again on the European Tour.
Speaking about his move to LIV in an interview with Sports Illustrated earlier this year, McDowell said: “I regret a few things I said in the beginning, stuff like ‘growing the game’.
“I should have just said it for what it was: this is good for my bank account , and I’m getting a runway to play the game of golf for as long as I can.”
McDowell turned pro in 2002 and established Boyport Services that same year to manage his commercial interests.

title: ‘Infectiously good craic’: Ireland tops Condé Nast poll for friendliest country in Europe
description: Travel publisher says Ireland is full of ‘soulful musicians and pioneering writers’
content:
Ireland has topped the 2026 Condé Nast Traveller reader’s poll for friendliest countries in Europe.
The poll, which had 300,000 voters, saw Ireland score 98.39, while runner-up Portugal scored 96.67.
Other countries featured on the list include Italy, Greece and Spain.
“Consistency seems to be key for Ireland, as this is their third year within the top three. After two years in second place, Ireland claims the title of the friendliest country in Europe for 2026,″ Condé Nast Traveller said.
The travel publisher went on to say that Ireland is filled with “soulful musicians and pioneering writers, and they warm the hearts of all they touch with their infectiously good craic”.
“Wander into a traditional pub and, within seconds, find yourself striking up conversation with jolly strangers, proving these cosy bolt-holes are so much more than simply a place to drink, or to visit during St Patrick’s Festival to witness communities turn green in a hearty celebration of their beloved home,” the publisher said.
Also topping the list for Ireland in the readers’ choice awards was Ballyheigue Strand in Co Kerry, which was crowned a winner of one of the best beaches in the world along with Sperlonga in Italy, Llanddwyn Beach in Wales, Arugam Bay Beach in Sri Lanka and Hanauma Bay in Hawaii.
Ballyheigue received a score of 95.39. Other Irish beaches named were Barleycove, Co Cork, with a score of 93.33 and Sherkin Island, Co Cork, scoring 90.67.
Another acknowledgment of Irish tourism in the readers’ choice awards went to Ballyfin Demesne in Co Laois, which was named among readers’ favourite hotels in Europe with a score of 98.77.
Condé Nast Traveller’s Ballyfin review, published in April 2026, described the luxury hotel where rooms start at €710 per night as “the most considered grand house stay in Ireland”.
The 2026 awards survey was conducted between April 1st and June 30th. The questionnaire contained lists of candidates in various categories and must receive a required minimum number of responses and a minimum overall rating to be eligible for a readers’ choice award.
The readers’ awards come a few months after the publisher revealed its seven wonders of Ireland , featuring “less instantly recognisable places to visit”.
Among the spots highlighted in April’s list were Waterford’s greenway and Copper Coast, Fermanagh’s Lakelands, northwest Donegal and Tory Island.

title: ‘I will decide when I retire’ - James McClean says he is ‘ready to play’ for Derry City
description: Ireland international has not played for his home town team since July 3rd
content:
James McClean says he “will decide when I retire” and that he is “ready to play when called upon” for Derry City .
The 37-year-old Ireland international has not played for his hometown club since July 3rd and has been receiving ongoing treatment for a hip injury. He is currently “fit and well” according to a statement released by the Professional Footballers Association of Ireland (PFAI), who are representing McClean in his dispute with Derry City.
In the statement, McClean admits that some of his public comments were “misjudged” and apologises, while adding: “Derry City is my club, and I respect everyone who cares about it as much as I do.”
His full statement reads: “This has been one of the most difficult periods of my life, both personally and professionally. When I agreed to come home from Wrexham, I did so in good faith, based on commitments made to me both playing wise and regarding my future after football. I uprooted my family midway through the school year because I believed in the vision presented to me, both for the short term and the long term.
“I accept that some of my actions over the past few months were misjudged, and my frustrations should have remained in-house. I take responsibility for that – and I apologise. Derry City is my club, and I respect everyone who cares about it as much as I do.
“I was asked to help drive standards, to speak up, and to use my experience to further professionalise my hometown club. From the start of the season, I tried to do this to the best of my ability, but I felt when I did my opinions were not well received.
“While I’m happy to hold myself accountable when I am wrong and when my performances have not been to the levels I expect of myself, I cannot understand or accept that I have been treated this way over the past few months.
“For any club to feel it is ok to attempt to terminate a player’s contract without any due process or just cause is incomprehensible, and it sets a dangerous precedent for every player in this league.
“I was approaching 37 years old when I signed for Derry City. It is well accepted that any player of that age will have occasional injury issues. I have been open about what my body now faces, and that has not been easy to come to terms with.
“But I am not permanently incapacitated, or anything even remotely close to that. I am capable of contributing and doing well in the League of Ireland. I train as hard and give as much as anyone.
“I will decide when I retire. Nobody else will make that decision for me. When that time comes, my body will tell me. This is my life and my career. I deserve the same duty of care and fairness given to the majority of other players at Derry City FC.
The PFAI statement reads: “As has been widely reported, we are representing James McClean in a dispute with Derry City FC over the terms of his contract.
“There has been a lot of conjecture and misinformation about the situation pertaining to James’ medical status and we would like to take this opportunity to clarify matters.
“In short, James has had a hip injury which had been causing intermittent issues for him. This has caused him to miss some games and occasional training sessions. He has sought medical treatment for this and is currently fit and well.
“He has trained fully for the last nine weeks and has made himself available for selection. He recently played in an internal match arranged by the club. He believes he can help the team and has not been provided with a satisfactory reason for being left out of the squad.
“He believes that the reason for this is a dispute which first arose in early August when the chairman of the club stated that his contract had been terminated. As a result of this, he contacted this association and has been provided with legal advice from PFA Ireland’s solicitor, Stuart Gilhooly SC.
“The upshot of this advice has been protracted correspondence between Mr Gilhooly and the club. Instead of terminating the contract as alleged, it transpires that they had in fact set about invoking Section 18 of the Standard Players Contract which states that if a player is deemed to have a permanent incapacity as determined by an agreed and independent physician, then the club is entitled to terminate the contract with six months notice.
“To date, no physician, either independent or agreed, has reached such a conclusion. Indeed, an Orthopaedic Surgeon, Mr Desmond Gibson, who saw him at the request of the club as recently as 21 September said he believes he can continue to play football as long as he is not in severe pain. He is not in severe pain and is willing, able and anxious to return to playing for Derry City.
“The club has a duty of care to James, who they signed without conducting a medical. He is much loved native of Derry and highly regarded Irish international centurion. We would hope that this matter can be resolved in an amicable and sensible manner and in such a way that would allow James to play again for the club he loves.”
Derry City have released a statement in response, which they say was “made without prior notice to the club, just four days before the biggest match of the club’s season”.
“The club welcomes James’ acknowledgment that some of his recent actions were misjudged and that his frustrations should have remained in-house.
“At all times, the club has sought to resolve this internal matter privately. Out of respect for confidentiality and the fact that this dispute involves sensitive medical details regarding James’ hip condition, the club have previously refrained from making any public statement on the matter.
“While the PFAI and James have chosen to publicise selective elements of the medical advice received, the club does not propose to comment further on James’ current medical condition.
“The club is fully aware of the obligations it owes to all contracted players. All squad members who are deemed fully fit remain available for selection. Ultimately, matchday selection remains the sole prerogative of the management team, acting in conjunction with guidance from our medical staff.
“The club’s absolute focus is on Saturday’s FAI Cup semi-final against Galway United, and the club will make no further comment on this matter at this time.”

title: Garda arrest driver found to be disqualified  after he came to pick up uninsured friend
description: Two cars seized after gardaí stopped BMW without insurance and friend with disqualification came to get him in Audi
content:
A man has been arrested and two cars were confiscated after a driver arriving to collect the owner of an uninsured vehicle was found to be disqualified from driving.
Gardaí stopped a BMW on the M50 after it was flagged by automated number plate registration technology (ANPR).
The car was flagged as having no active insurance. It also has not been taxed for 274 days. Gardaí seized the car under section 41 of the Road Traffic Act.
The driver then asked a friend to collect him after his vehicle was seized. When the friend arrived in an Audi, he was arrested.
“Turns out the Audi driver had an active court disqualification, and an active bench warrant was also in existence,” the Garda said.
“The only place this pair will be road-tripping to is the District Court,” the Garda said on social media.
Motor insurance is compulsory in Ireland for any vehicle being driven on public roads. They must also pass vehicle safety testing and annual tax must be paid.
Driving an untaxed vehicle is penalised with a fixed charge notice of €60.
Uninsured driving can lead to a fine of up to €5,000 and five penalty points, and repeat offenders may face a prison sentence of up to six months.
In 2025, 19,673 vehicles were seized for driving without insurance. A further 25,009 charges and summonses were issued for that offence over the same period.
About one in every 15 vehicles in Ireland is uninsured, according to estimates from motor insurance body the Motor Insurers’ Bureau of Ireland (Mibi).
At the end of 2025, Mibi said there were 211,371 uninsured or unregistered vehicles being used – about 6.5 per cent of the overall number on the roads.

title: Budget 2027: Big business pays the bills as Coalition rolls the dice
description: Money has been sprayed everywhere but hard to find a central theme
content:
B udget 2027 fired money around in various directions to try to address the cost-of-living crisis and react to the demand of a whole range of sectors, but you would search hard to find a central theme.
Perhaps it is responding to events and that is in part understandable, given the big increases in energy prices and their impact on inflation.
But budgets are about priorities and when the package emerges from fractious last-minute negotiations between the two big parties of Government, some of these can be fudged or lost. Tactics get priority over strategy. And the ante is inevitably upped when it comes to how much money is dispersed as both sides argue for “their” policy.
The questions about Budget 2027 rest on two things. The first relates to the overall extent of the money allocated and whether the budget numbers will be held to. The second is whether the resources were well spent – and what the political reaction will be.
Like any other budget of recent years, the Irish health warning applies. Due to the influx of corporation tax, the Government has leeway not afforded to most other EU countries.
It can spend more, tax less, announce an extra €1 billion next year for one of the two funds saving cash for the future – and still target a budget surplus of €9.5 billion. Take the windfall element of the corporate tax money away, the Department of Finance calculates, and this surplus becomes a big deficit.
[ Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day Opens in new window ]
In response to cost-of-living pressures, the Government decided to roll the dice again and spend the vast bulk of the corporate revenues. And perhaps Ireland will get lucky again. The real exposure is impossible to calculate, but Ireland’s reliance on a few very big companies – four or five – is obvious.
In reaction to this, the Government has committed to reduce spending growth to 6 per cent – in many recent years it has been 9 to 10 per cent. Jack Chambers , the Minister for Public Expenditure, incurred the wrath of Cabinet colleagues by ensuring the budget increase stuck to this figure.
He has also put in place a public spending efficiency taskforce to oversee current spending and try to increase efficiency.
But the big question is whether the new targets can be stuck to or will spending, as has happened in recent years, again run way over target.
A lot hangs on this. The full cost of overruns this year may again not have been counted into the base for 2027. There is, crucially, a public sector pay deal to be done. The pressure to increase spending further will be intense. To reduce future risk, a way must be found to stop the runaway spending train.
This was the framework. What about the details?
Having made a big political error last year by having no income tax package in favour of cutting the VAT rate on hospitality, the Coalition tried to make amends. Its tax package aimed firmly at middle earners, who will see less income taxed at the higher 40 per cent tax rate. A single middle earner will gain some €700, when account is also taken of higher PRSI next year. The changes are more than would be required to index the band for next year’s wage inflation - ensuring tax does not take a higher chunk of income - and to make up a bit of ground from the non-indexation this year.
The cash gains for lower earners are a lot less – they do not earn enough to benefit from the extension of the tax band. This is a political point of exposure for the Government, immediately tackled by Sinn Féin finance spokesman Pearse Doherty .
[ Budget 2027 main points: Minimum wage to rise 79 cent; €12,000 per year limit for investment scheme Opens in new window ]
And the risk for the Coalition is that with general cost increases elsewhere many people will still feel worse off next year. Selling the budget in the context of this will be difficult enough.
The Government is trying to do what it can to hold down energy costs , but is entirely reliant on international events. This is a key exposure heading into 2027 – and could yet lead to adjustments in tax and spending plans next year.
What happens to excises on tax and petrol, for example, if come next March when they are due to increase, prices are still at or above current levels? Or if inflation heads back towards 5 per cent?
As has been the case for many years now, this is a “spending” budget, with a lot more allocated here than to cutting tax. There is a hike in investment and cash for current spending spread across a whole range of areas, meaning incremental changes in many.
The Government will feel it has made a step forward on childcare by cutting costs to parents even if places remain an issue in many parts of the country. In other areas progress was slower. Promises of a cost-of-living payment for disabled people turned into a once-off €500 payment.
[ Ireland’s new personal investment accounts: Here’s how the scheme will work Opens in new window ]
The much-discussed second rate of child benefit to tackle poverty remains undelivered. The €10 welfare increases will only go so far to meet rising prices. Having raised expectations across the board, the Coalition will still face flak.
At a wider level, a Government strategy for how to manage the public finances as the population ages remains absent. As does a strategy to meet Ireland’s vital climate goals and avoid paying large fines.
The cash being put aside and the promise to slow spending growth are welcome. But Budget 2027 was one for the now, rather than the future. With capital and income taxes both being cut, there is no medium-term strategy for paying the costs of ageing and climate change – beyond hoping for the best on the multinationals.
Perhaps it is politically difficult to address this when the topline budget figures are still in huge surplus. But it will surely be even harder when the public finances tighten.

title: How ketamine emerged as key factor in alleged Cornell University sex assault
description: Use of the drug could complicate the revived criminal investigation, legal experts say
content:
The woman who would come to be known as Jane Doe walked into her sorority house in a daze, feeling bruises starting to ache on her body. When her sorority sisters asked what had happened, she remembered responding with one word: “Ketamine.”
The recollection, detailed among the more than 1,000 pages of Cornell University files obtained by The New York Times, underscores the central role played by the powerful anaesthetic in an alleged gang rape that has spurred outrage and debate about sexual assault and consent on college campuses across the US.
The drug, which has surged in popularity in recent years, appeared time and again on the night in question, at a Chi Phi fraternity party in October 2024, according to the documents and a lawsuit filed last month by the former Cornell student who identified herself as Jane Doe.
She said in her lawsuit that during the party, she felt pressured by some members of the fraternity to take ketamine with them – her first time doing the drug – before seven of them sexually assaulted her.
Before the night was over, she said in her lawsuit, all seven of the men would also snort lines of ketamine off her body.
All of the men have denied any wrongdoing, saying any sexual contact that night was consensual. None has been charged with a crime.
In her initial interview with campus investigators in November 2024, Jane Doe said a combination of drugs and alcohol – she had been drinking heavily before arriving at the fraternity and continued drinking once there – made it impossible for her to consent to sexual activity that night.
She said she did not remember taking the first hit of ketamine, only realising she had done so later in the night when a Chi Phi brother asked whether she wanted “more” ketamine.
“Whenever the ketamine went down, I would say, is when things really start becoming a problem,” she told investigators.
In the investigative files obtained by The New York Times, the word ketamine appears hundreds of times, and the witness statements allude to a drug culture on campus where ketamine was easily accessible in certain social circles.
In August alone, the Cornell University police responded to two reports of ketamine potentially being stolen from the university’s veterinary medical centre, according to agency’s crime log.
In interviews with 11 current and recently graduated Cornell students, many of them told The New York Times that cocaine and marijuana were common at regular campus parties, while ketamine was more typically found within the heavy partying crowd, including in certain fraternities.
“It was not hard to get your hands on it if you wanted it,” said Hasham Khan (22), a former fraternity member who was not in Chi Phi and graduated from the university this year.
Jane Doe told campus investigators the first time she had ever seen ketamine was about two weeks before the night of her alleged assault.
She was hanging out with some of the Chi Phi members she would later accuse of rape, she said, when one of them took out a plastic bag filled with white powder.
She said she turned down an offer to try it then.
At one point on the night of the alleged assault, Jane Doe said she was upstairs in a room at the Chi Phi fraternity, surrounded by men. She told one of the Chi Phi members she felt uncomfortable.
She said he laughed and poured a line of ketamine on to his erect penis, and she said she felt coerced into snorting it, according to her interview in November 2024 with campus police. (He later told investigators he had “no recollection” of this.)
“I had become extremely uncomfortable with how this night was turning out, so my thought was, if I do ketamine again, maybe I will pass out,” she told investigators, according to the files. “My thought was that if I passed out and these men had sex with me, then they could be charged with rape.”
Another fraternity member then asked whether all the men in the room could do drugs off her body, and she replied “Sure”, she told investigators.
As she snorted more ketamine throughout the night, “it made my eyes feel like they were spinning in opposite directions”, she said.
She said she felt coerced into having sex with the men – and that they should have known how intoxicated she was based on how she was slurring her words.
The investigative records suggest the men in the room were also feeling the effects of the ketamine.
One fraternity brother wrote in a statement to investigators that within 10 minutes of taking ketamine, he was gasping for breath, lost consciousness for several seconds and told Jane Doe he thought he was about to die. Another said the mix of ketamine, alcohol and marijuana made him vomit violently for about 15 minutes.
The accused male students gave conflicting accounts to investigators of the ketamine use that night. One of the fraternity members said he never took ketamine that night, nor did he see anyone taking it – directly contradicting another member who recalled seeing this person inhale ketamine off Jane Doe’s body.
A third fraternity brother acknowledged inhaling ketamine off Jane Doe’s body but said he did so only after she gave him verbal permission.
At about 6am, as Jane Doe was drifting in and out of sleep inside a fraternity member’s bedroom, she heard a group of men knock at the door, she told investigators. They wanted to snort cocaine off her body, but one of the men who had assaulted her earlier told them to leave, she alleged.
[ How Cornell University punished seven men accused of sexual assault Opens in new window ]
In Jane Doe’s lawsuit last month, she said Cornell should have known that the fraternity had a history of ketamine use, citing a response from police officers to a drug-related incident at the fraternity house a week before the alleged assault.
The Tompkins County district attorney who reviewed Jane Doe’s initial statement and declined to bring criminal charges, Matthew Van Houten, said he was unaware of that police visit.
Cornell’s crime log shows the campus police made a drug-related arrest at the Chi Phi fraternity less than 24 hours before Jane Doe’s alleged assault, an arrest first reported by The Cornell Sun.
The timing of the arrest matched a reference in court records to a ketamine overdose that took place at the house “on or about” October 18th, 2024.
The investigative files also show that on the night of the alleged assault, Jane Doe ran into a fraternity member she knew. Later on, she said another student told her that the fraternity member had overdosed on ketamine and other substances the night before, the records show.
“I feel like OD’ing is a pretty big deal,” she told investigators. “But to be back at it again the next day? It’s crazy.”
Cornell is far from the only place where ketamine has recently gained a foothold, both as legitimate treatment and as a party drug.
Legal with a prescription and often used to anaesthetise both humans and animals, ketamine has become an alternative treatment for depression and anxiety. That has made it more widely available – but has also created more opportunities for abuse.
Joseph Palamar, a professor at the New York University Grossman School of Medicine who has researched ketamine for decades, found that from 2017 to 2024, the percentage of New York City nightclub attendees who reported having used ketamine has nearly doubled.
He warned that the dissociating and numbing effects of the drug can be especially dangerous if mixed with alcohol, as alleged in the lawsuit by Jane Doe.
“Even on relatively small doses, you’re very detached from things,” Palamar said. “You’re not as in touch with your emotions. It’s very hard to communicate, especially as you hit larger doses.”
Although Jane Doe said ketamine played a role in making her vulnerable to assault – it can have hallucinogenic effects and impair memory – its use is also likely to complicate the revived criminal investigation into her accusations, legal experts have said. New York state’s rape law makes it difficult for a person who knowingly became intoxicated to prove they did not consent to a sexual encounter.
That investigation will now be led by state attorney general Letitia James, whom governor Kathy Hochul appointed as special prosecutor after saying she had lost faith in Van Houten. – This article originally appeared in The New York Times .
